Several possible examples are as follows.\\n\\nIf the co-owned land was originally bare land and the Defendant unlawfully installs above-ground objects such as buildings, fences, or trees on it, the Plaintiff may first seek against the Defendant an order to cease the installation of above-ground objects, and if the above-ground objects have been installed as a result of the violating act, may seek removal or collection of the installed above-ground objects. Once the installation of above-ground objects ceases and the above-ground objects are removed, the land becomes bare land, and the Plaintiff can enter and use the land without any active action by the Defendant. In most cases, removal of only the above-ground objects is sufficient to dissolve the Defendant’s exclusive possession, and if, even after the above-ground objects are removed, the Defendant acts in the same or another way to interfere with the Plaintiff’s joint possession, or is expected to do so, the Plaintiff may seek against the Defendant prohibition of such acts (prohibition of installing above-ground objects, prohibition of interference with entry onto the land).\\n\\nIf there were originally a fence and gate installed on the co-owned land and the Defendant exclusively possesses the land by locking the gate, then if the fence or gate is co-owned property, the Plaintiff cannot seek their removal. However, because the Defendant must also give the Plaintiff a key to the locking device of the co-owned gate (an ancillary affirmative obligation) and must not interfere with the Plaintiff’s entry onto the co-owned land (a negative obligation), the Plaintiff may seek against the Defendant performance of such affirmative and negative obligations.\\n\\nIf the Plaintiff and the Defendant, as co-owners, jointly live in a house co-owned in equal 1/2 shares, there may be cases where they agreed to use separate rooms separately, but there was no particular agreement as to common spaces such as the living room and kitchen, and the Defendant exclusively possesses and uses those spaces while excluding the Plaintiff. In that case, the Plaintiff may seek prohibition of the Defendant’s acts interfering with joint possession and use of the living room and kitchen, for example, physical obstruction by the Defendant of the Plaintiff’s use of the living room and kitchen, or the Defendant’s act of piling up the Defendant’s furniture, etc.\\n\\nIf the Defendant uses a co-owned parking lot for business and thereby interferes with the Plaintiff’s use of the parking lot itself, the Plaintiff may seek against the Defendant prohibition of acts interfering with the use of the parking lot.\\n\\n(3) Even if, in the absence of a decision concerning management of the co-owned property, the co-owners’ methods of use are limited to non-exclusive forms, such methods of use cannot be said to be highly exceptional or abnormal. There may also be cases where the co-owned property is regarded as jointly possessed and used without a decision concerning management among the co-owners. If the co-owners tolerate another co-owner’s possession and use, there may be room to recognize an implied agreement, but one cannot always infer an agreement from such a state. If the state of joint use is formed by each co-owner’s possession and use without any particular consultation among them and the co-owners use it as is without disputing it for a time, then it would be unreasonable always to deem that an implied agreement concerning management of the co-owned property has been reached, because in that case the use state could not be overturned without a management method determined by majority shares.\\n\\nNor is it the case that a co-owner’s temporary sole use of the relevant thing automatically amounts to exclusive possession and use. Whether co-owned property is jointly possessed and used must be determined in accordance with social common sense, comprehensively considering various circumstances.\\n\\nIn the example of the co-owned house above, according to Dissent 2, the Plaintiff cannot exclude the Defendant’s exclusive possession and use of the common spaces, namely the living room and kitchen, and must either receive only monetary compensation while being unable to use them at all, or abandon the purpose of residence and seek partition of the co-owned property. According to Dissent 1, the Plaintiff may completely exclude the Defendant’s possession through a claim for delivery and execution regarding the living room and kitchen occupied by the Defendant. These two views are at the extremes of either denying the Plaintiff’s original right altogether or recognizing a claim beyond the Plaintiff’s right, and their impropriety requires no further explanation. The Plaintiff can achieve the purpose, to the extent of the Plaintiff’s lawful rights, by seeking prohibition against the Defendant’s acts interfering with joint possession and use of the living room and kitchen in order to exercise the right of joint possession and use over them.\\n\\n(4) Dissent 1 says that it is not valid for the majority opinion to change precedent without sufficiently discussing the specific content of the claim for injunction against interference that would replace a delivery claim or the limits of the right to clarify. The reason the majority opinion did not discuss the specific content of the claim was that the Plaintiff did not bring such a claim, so it was not an issue in the appeal. After remand, the court below need only determine the propriety of the claim if the parties specify the content of the claim; if the claim is unclear or not sufficiently specified, and the duty to clarify is recognized, the court may exercise the right to clarify and give an opportunity to amend. Before the Plaintiff changes the claim in the court below after remand, the court cannot pre-judge the propriety of a claim by assuming what claim the Plaintiff will make.\\n\\nE. May a claim for delivery be made against a third party who leased from a minority share-right holder?\\nDissent 1 says that where a minority share-right holder leases the co-owned property to a third party and the third party possesses the co-owned property, the other co-owners may seek delivery of the co-owned property against the lessee, and that the majority opinion would presumably be the same; it then argues that the majority opinion improperly treats the case where the minority share-right holder possesses the property him- or herself differently from the case where the minority share-right holder leases it out (Dissent 1 cites Supreme Court Decision 2010DA569 rendered on May 27, 2010, among others, but the case there involved the Plaintiff seeking damages or return of unjust enrichment corresponding to the Plaintiff’s share ratio against a lessee who leased the co-owned property from the Defendant, a minority share-right holder, not a case seeking delivery, and the legal principle of that judgment also presupposes the legal principle of the existing Supreme Court decisions affirming the minority share-right holder’s claim for delivery).\\n\\nHowever, this issue is not the issue in this case, and because there are separate considerations, the majority opinion did not make an explicit determination on it. While a lease by a minority share-right holder does not have effect as an act of management of the co-owned property vis-à-vis the co-owners, it does not necessarily follow that the other co-owners may seek delivery of the co-owned property against a third party who leased it from a minority share-right holder.\\n\\nA lease made by one who lacks authority to lease is valid as between the lessor and the lessee. Also, if A has the right to possess a thing and therefore the owner cannot seek return of the thing from A, then the owner cannot seek return of the thing from B, who acquired the right to possess from A through sale, lease, etc. (see Supreme Court Decision 87DAKA1682 rendered on April 25, 1988; Supreme Court Decision 2001DA45355 rendered on December 11, 2001, among others). Supreme Court Decision 87DAKA1682 held that, where the purchaser of land receives delivery of the land in performance of the sales contract, the purchaser has the right to possess and use the land, and a person who acquires a building erected by the purchaser on that land also acquires the purchaser’s right to possess and use the land, so the vendor cannot seek against the building owner removal of the building and delivery of the land. Supreme Court Decision 2001DA45355 held likewise that even a person who has leased real property from one who is to receive transfer of ownership under a contract for substitute performance cannot be subject to a claim for delivery or return of unjust enrichment.\\n\\nA minority share-right holder has the right to possess the co-owned property jointly, and since the lessee acquires the right to possess from that minority share-right holder through the lease agreement, if the other co-owner cannot seek delivery of the co-owned property against the co-owner lessor, it may be understood that the other co-owner likewise cannot seek delivery against the lessee.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, we seek to supplement the reasoning of the majority opinion.\\n\\n8. Supplementary opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek to the majority opinion concerning the claim for delivery of co-owned property\\nDissent 1 says that the Plaintiff, a minority share-right holder, may seek delivery of the co-owned property as an act of preservation of co-owned property against the Defendant, a minority share-right holder who exclusively possesses the co-owned property, and that if the Plaintiff, after receiving delivery of the co-owned property, exclusively possesses and uses it without consulting the other co-owner(s), the other co-owners, including the Defendant, may again seek delivery of the co-owned property against the Plaintiff. However, in such a case, the Defendant’s renewed claim for delivery against the Plaintiff cannot be permitted, from a procedural-law perspective, because it would contravene the res judicata of the prior delivery judgment, and I wish to supplement the majority opinion with the argument that such an unjust result arises from the original affirmation of the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery and therefore the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery should not be allowed in the first place. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\nA. A later claim seeking to reverse the result of compulsory execution pursuant to a final judgment in a prior suit is not permitted because it is in a contradictory relationship with the final judgment in the prior suit and thus contravenes its res judicata effect. Precedents have held that, where registration of transfer of ownership has been completed pursuant to a final judgment ordering the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership, a claim seeking performance of the procedure for registration of cancellation on the ground that such registration is null and void ab initio denies the right to claim registration of transfer established in the prior suit and therefore contravenes res judicata (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA61649 rendered on February 9, 1996; Supreme Court Decision 2002DA44014 rendered on December 6, 2002, among others), and that where a creditor files a suit for a loan and obtains a final judgment in the creditor’s favor and execution is completed, the debtor’s claim against the creditor for return as unjust enrichment of the money corresponding to the amount repaid, on the ground that partial repayment was made before that judgment, contravenes the res judicata of the prior judgment (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA41430 rendered on June 29, 1995).\\n\\nB. If the Plaintiff obtains a final judgment ordering delivery of the co-owned property against the Defendant, substantive finality arises with respect to the fact that the Plaintiff has the right to claim delivery of the co-owned property, and between the Plaintiff and the Defendant, who are parties to that judgment, making assertions contradictory thereto by way of suit is prohibited. If the Plaintiff receives delivery of the co-owned property from the Defendant pursuant to the delivery judgment and possesses it, then if the Defendant, who was a party to the prior suit, again seeks delivery of the co-owned property against the Plaintiff, this cannot be permitted because it would contravene the res judicata of the prior delivery judgment. This is because the Plaintiff’s possession results from execution of the prior delivery judgment, and for the Defendant to again receive delivery would mean denying the Plaintiff’s right to claim delivery established in the prior suit and reversing the result of compulsory execution pursuant to the prior judgment.\\n\\nC. Dissent 1 says that, because the prior delivery judgment does not justify the Plaintiff’s exclusive possession and use of the co-owned property, if the Plaintiff, who received the co-owned property as an act of preservation, exclusively possesses and uses it contrary to the purpose of the act of preservation, the Defendant in the prior suit may again seek delivery against the Plaintiff, and this would not contravene the res judicata of the prior delivery judgment.\\n\\nThe res judicata effect of a judgment arises only with respect to matters included in the operative part of the judgment (Article 216(1) of the Civil Procedure Act). The operative part of the delivery judgment is that “the Defendant shall deliver the co-owned property to the Plaintiff,” and the res judicata effect arising therefrom concerns the fact that the Plaintiff has the right to claim delivery of the co-owned property against the Defendant. This is the same whether the legal basis for seeking delivery is an act of preservation of the co-owned property, exclusive ownership, or a contractual claim such as sale. The legal meaning of “delivery” commanded in the operative part of the judgment is the same in all cases: the Defendant bears the obligation to transfer possession of the co-owned property to the Plaintiff. That the legal basis is an act of preservation cannot be used to shrink the meaning of “delivery” to mean merely transferring possession of the co-owned property to the Plaintiff for the purpose of later joint possession again. The Plaintiff is in possession of the co-owned property after receiving it from the Defendant as a result of the exercise of the right to claim delivery, which has been definitively established with res judicata effect. If, notwithstanding the unchanged legal relationship and continuing state, the Defendant were able again to seek return of the co-owned property against the Plaintiff as an act of preservation based on ownership, merely because no new fact has occurred such as the Plaintiff voluntarily making the delivered co-owned property available for all co-owners, this would be in a contradictory relationship with the fact established in the prior suit that “the Plaintiff has a right to claim delivery against the Defendant,” and cannot be permitted.\\n\\nThe res judicata system is essentially intended to prevent the same parties from repeatedly contesting matters established by a judgment. Repeated delivery litigation between the same parties, such as that contemplated by Dissent 1, is contrary to the essence of the res judicata system and cannot be permitted.\\n\\nD. In the end, even if the Plaintiff, after excluding the Defendant pursuant to the delivery judgment and exclusively possessing the co-owned property, continues to possess it, the Defendant cannot bring a suit to correct such state. Such unjust result arises, as the majority opinion points out, because the Plaintiff was originally only a minority share-right holder and had no legal basis to exclude the co-owner Defendant and exclusively possess the co-owned property, yet the Plaintiff’s claim for delivery was granted. Dissent 1 is not valid because it conflicts not only with the grounds presented by the majority opinion but also with the theory of the res judicata of the delivery judgment as above.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, we seek to supplement the reasoning of the majority opinion."}

{"[2021DA276256]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower-court judgment and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. On 2003. 7. 28., the Defendant constructed and originally acquired ○○○○○ Apartment (hereinafter referred to as “the instant apartment”), a seven-story aggregate building, on land of 1,646.6㎡ in (address 1 omitted), Seocho-gu, Seoul (hereinafter referred to as “the instant land”), and on a road of 73.7㎡ at (address 2 omitted). The Plaintiff acquired ownership by winning the auction of the instant land on 2013. 3. 21.\\n\\nb. On 2014. 12. 11., the Plaintiff filed this action against the Defendant, seeking removal of the portion of the instant apartment located on the instant land and delivery of the instant land, and obtained a judgment in his favor at first instance. In the appellate instance, the Defendant transferred part of the co-ownership shares in certain exclusive sections of the instant apartment to Nonparties, etc. and effected registration of transfer of shares, and the Nonparties, etc. participated in the lawsuit as succeeding intervenors. On 2017. 4. 6., the appellate court rendered a judgment (hereinafter referred to as “the prior judgment in this case”) stating that “the Defendant and the Nonparties, etc. shall, in accordance with their respective ownership share ratios, remove each exclusive section and common area of the building in this case and deliver the instant land to the Plaintiff.” The prior judgment in this case excluded from the demolition the portion of the instant apartment located on the road. The Defendant filed an appeal against the prior judgment in this case, but on 2017. 8. 23., the appeal was dismissed, and the above prior judgment became final and binding as it stood.\\n\\nc. After the prior judgment became final and binding, the Defendant continued to possess the instant multi-purpose room, which is a common area of the instant apartment, and the Plaintiff filed this action against the Defendant seeking an order that he vacate the instant multi-purpose room.\\n\\n2. Lower Court's Judgment\\nThe lower court held as follows. The final and binding prior judgment in this case ordered the Defendant to remove the instant multi-purpose room with respect to his ownership share, and ordered the other owners, not the Defendant, to remove it with respect to the remaining shares. The Defendant is in possession of the instant multi-purpose room while not being in a position to bear the duty to remove the instant multi-purpose room with respect to the remaining shares other than his ownership share, and thereby can be seen as obstructing the Plaintiff's exercise of ownership rights over the land.\\nAccordingly, the Defendant bears the duty to vacate the instant multi-purpose room vis-à-vis the Plaintiff.\\n\\n3. Supreme Court's Judgment\\na. Even where the owner of a building is in possession of land owned by another by virtue of ownership of the building, the landowner may only seek removal of the building and delivery of the site portion, and may not demand that the person in possession of the building vacate the building (see Supreme Court Decision 98DA57457, 57464, rendered 1999. 7. 9., etc.). This legal principle likewise applies to co-owners of a building where the building is in co-ownership. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Every co-owner may use and derive profits from the whole common property in proportion to his or her share (Article 263 of the Civil Act). Although a co-ownership share right held by a co-owner in the common property is a quantitative part of ownership, it has the nature of an independent ownership right; therefore, a co-owner has the right to use and derive profits, which falls within the powers of ownership. Even if one of the co-owners exclusively possesses, uses, and derives profits from the common property, it is different from a third party who is not a co-owner unlawfully possessing the common property (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2018DA287522, rendered 2020. 5. 21.). Accordingly, possession of a building by a co-owner must be regarded as possession of his or her own building regardless of the ownership share, and the portion exceeding the ownership share cannot be conceptually separated so as to regard that portion as the possession of another.\\n\\n(2) A landowner may, through the exercise of the right to claim removal of interference based on land ownership, seek only demolition of the building standing on the land and delivery of the corresponding land, and has no authority to recover possession of the building itself or to determine the use relationship among the co-owners regarding the building. If the landowner were allowed to bring a claim for vacatur against the co-owner of the building standing on the land, it would result in the landowner recovering possession of the building itself or arbitrarily determining the use relationship among the co-owners regarding the building.\\n\\n(3) A co-owner who has received a final and binding judgment ordering demolition within the scope of his or her ownership share and continues to possess the building is nothing more than a reflex effect arising from the situation in which the landowner failed to obtain a final and binding judgment ordering demolition of the entire building and thus enforcement of demolition is impossible. The landowner may obtain relief by securing an enforceable title regarding demolition of the entire building and proceeding directly to enforcement, or by seeking return of unjust enrichment concerning possession of the land until demolition enforcement is carried out.\\n\\nb. In light of the legal principles above, considering the factual relations set forth in 1. above, since the Defendant, as one of the co-owners of the instant multi-purpose room, is in possession and use thereof, it is proper to view that the Plaintiff, as the landowner, has no legal basis to demand against the Defendant that he vacate the instant multi-purpose room.\\nNevertheless, the lower court accepted the Plaintiff's claim for vacatur against the Defendant on the grounds set forth in 2. above. The lower-court judgment contains error that affected the judgment by misapprehending legal principles concerning the existence of a landowner's right to demand vacatur from a co-owner of the building standing on the land. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well taken.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nSince the Defendant's appeal is well taken, the lower-court judgment is reversed and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination, and the judgment is rendered unanimously by the Justices as stated in the order."}

{"[80DA756]": "The Defendants’ grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nThe court below determined that the building in this case was erected without title on land owned by the Plaintiff, and that the deceased, Non-Party 1, had owned it until his death on 1973.9.21., whereby the Defendants and Non-Party 2 jointly inherited it. The court further held that, in such a case, the co-heirs’ obligation to remove the building is, by its nature, an indivisible obligation, and therefore each co-heir must bear the obligation to remove the entire building in dispute; accordingly, it cannot be said to be erroneous for the Plaintiff, as the landowner, to seek removal of the entire building only against the Defendants, who are the remaining heirs, excluding the above co-heir, Non-Party 2.\\n\\nIt is legally correct to determine, as the court below did in this case, that the Defendants’ obligation to the Plaintiff to remove the building constitutes, by its nature, an indivisible obligation. Further, the court below’s determination that, in such a case, each Defendant bears the obligation to remove the entire building means that each Defendant bears the obligation to remove the entire building only within the limit of his or her respective share (see this Court’s Decisions 68DA1102, rendered on 1968.7.31., 69DA609, rendered on 1969.7.22., etc.), and does not mean that the Defendants are being made liable for the removal obligation even with respect to the separate share of Non-Party 2, another co-heir. Therefore, the ground of appeal asserting that the court below erred in its interpretation of the law concerning indivisible obligations, on the premise that the court below made the Defendants bear the obligation to remove even with respect to Non-Party 2’s share, cannot be accepted.\\n\\nAccordingly, this appeal is without merit and is dismissed. The costs of the appeal are to be borne by the losing Defendants. It is so adjudged, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: A entered into a sales contract on 2020. 2. 10. with B concerning X real estate owned by B, and on 2020. 3. 10., while paying B the entire purchase price, simultaneously had the registration of transfer of ownership made directly from B to C in C's name pursuant to a title trust agreement between A and his friend C. Which of the following statements based on these facts is incorrect? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law governs)
A: The agreement between A and C and the registration of transfer of ownership in C's name resulting therefrom are void, but A cannot seek registration of transfer of ownership of X real estate against C on the ground of restitution of unjust enrichment.
B: Where A entered into a sales contract with A concerning X real estate and, based thereon, had the registration of transfer of ownership made directly from C to A, such registration, absent special circumstances, is a registration conforming to the substantive legal relationship and is valid.
C: Where creditor B with a monetary claim against C applied for a provisional seizure against X real estate with his monetary claim as the preserved right and the provisional seizure registration was completed, B's provisional seizure is valid.
D: If C, on his own, entered into a sales contract concerning X real estate with C, who knew the agreement between A and C, and, simultaneously with receiving the purchase price, completed the registration of transfer of ownership to C, C may bear liability to A for damages under Article 750 of the Civil Act.
E: If C, on his own, established in favor of his creditor D a mortgage by way of security in D's name concerning X real estate, C obtained a benefit equivalent to the amount of the secured obligation under the mortgage by way of security, and thereby B suffered a loss from infringement of ownership, C bears a duty to return unjust enrichment to B.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2008DA36022]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. As to Ground 1 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nThe Plaintiff (selected party; hereinafter referred to simply as the “Plaintiff”) argues, as a ground for appeal, that after the Gyeongju Branch of the Daegu District Court rendered and the judgment became final on April 20, 2001 in Case No. 2001GAHAP123 (hereinafter referred to as the “First Prior Suit”), which ordered the Defendant to pay to the Defendant the amount of unjust enrichment equivalent to rent from April 1, 1997 until the termination of possession on the ground that the building at issue in this case was owned by Non-party 1, the building at issue in this case was inherited by Non-party 1, the Plaintiff, and the selected parties (hereinafter, when collectively referring to the Plaintiff and the selected parties, they are referred to as “the Plaintiff et al.”) at each respective inheritance share ratio, and thereafter the Daegu High Court rendered and the judgment became final on July 10, 2003 in Case No. 2003NA1039 (hereinafter referred to as the “Second Prior Suit”), which ordered the Plaintiff et al. to pay to the Defendant, in accordance with their respective inheritance shares, the amount of unjust enrichment equivalent to rent for the period from April 1, 1997 to February 7, 2001, and the Plaintiff et al. fully repaid the amounts accordingly to the Defendant, so that the portion of the judgment in the First Prior Suit that was repaid by the Plaintiff et al. pursuant to the judgment in the Second Prior Suit lost its effect, execution by force based on the judgment in the First Prior Suit should not be permitted against the Plaintiff et al.’s inherited shares in the building at issue in this case.\\n\\nHowever, such circumstance that part of the amount of the obligation finalized under the judgment in the First Prior Suit was repaid is a ground to be asserted by Non-party 1, who is the debtor under that judgment, by an action of objection to a claim under Article 44 of the Civil Execution Act, and is not a ground to be asserted by the Plaintiff et al. by a third-party objection action; therefore, the argument in the grounds for appeal is not accepted.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 2 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below determined, with respect to the Plaintiff’s argument that the Defendant, through the Second Prior Suit brought against the Plaintiff et al., had already known that the building at issue in this case was in fact co-owned by Non-party 1 and the Plaintiff et al., although it had been registered for preservation of ownership in the sole name of Non-party 1, and that, despite the fact that the Defendant, as the owner of the land, had received from the Plaintiff et al. the rent pursuant to the judgment in the Second Prior Suit, the Defendant’s filing of an application for compulsory auction against the said building in this case in the present action while asserting that the building was owned by Non-party 1 and based on the judgment in the First Prior Suit constitutes an act contrary to social order, and that therefore the said application for compulsory auction is void, that such fact alone does not permit a conclusion that the Defendant’s application for compulsory auction constitutes an act contrary to social order; and such determination by the court below is proper and acceptable in light of the record, and there is no error of law or inadequacy of review as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nIn addition, the Plaintiff argues that the Defendant’s act of applying for compulsory auction against the building at issue in this case by using the judgment in the First Prior Suit against Non-party 1 as a title of execution constitutes a violation of the principle of good faith or an abuse of rights; however, this is an argument raised for the first time at the final appellate stage and cannot constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n3. As to Ground 3 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nUnder the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholders’ Names (hereinafter referred to as the “Real Estate Real Name Act”), where a person who entrusted a real right in real estate by title trust before the enforcement of the Act does not make registration in the real name within a period of one year from the enforcement date of the Act (hereinafter referred to as the “grace period”), or where, before enforcement of the Act or during the grace period, a lawsuit concerning a real right in real estate is brought before a court and, if the real-name registration is not made within one year from the date on which a final judgment regarding such lawsuit (including cases having the same effect) is rendered, except where the matter falls under the exception provisions prescribed by the Act, the change in real rights in real estate by virtue of the title trust agreement and the registration made pursuant thereto becomes void from the day after the expiration of the grace period or the one-year period from the date of the final judgment (Articles 4(1), 4(2) main text, 11(1) main text, 11(4), and 12(1) of the Act), but such voidness cannot be asserted against third parties (Article 4(3) of the Act). A “third party” in this context means a person who, on the premise that the trustee is the owner, establishes a new legal relationship with that person, and includes not only a person who has acquired a real right such as ownership or a mortgage, but also an attachment creditor or a creditor who has made a provisional attachment; the good faith or bad faith of the third party is immaterial (see Supreme Court Decision 99DA56529 rendered on March 28, 2000, among others).\\n\\nAccording to the record, Non-party 2, the father of the Plaintiff et al. and Non-party 1, built the building at issue in this case and the building not at issue in this case (one factory building appraised on the same land lot) on the land at issue in this case, and title-trusted the land at issue in this case and the building at issue in this case and the building not at issue in this case to Non-party 1; Non-party 1 completed registration of preservation of ownership for the building at issue in this case on May 29, 1992; however, the land at issue in this case and the building not at issue in this case were purchased at auction by the Defendant on or about March 31, 1997, managed by the Defendant, and the ownership was transferred to another person on March 26, 2001; meanwhile, after the death of Non-party 2 and his wife, the Plaintiff et al. filed an action against Non-party 1 before the Gyeongju Branch of the Daegu District Court in Case No. 95GAHAP4056 seeking registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of termination of title trust, and on July 11, 1996, that court rendered a judgment ordering that “Non-party 1 shall, with respect to the shares listed in Attached Table 3 of the judgment of the court below among the building at issue in this case and the building not at issue in this case, complete the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of termination of title trust as of September 12, 1995 in favor of the Plaintiff et al.”; the said judgment became final on August 4, 1996; however, the Plaintiff et al. did not make real-name registration within one year from the date on which the said final judgment was rendered; thereafter, the Defendant, using the judgment in the First Prior Suit against Non-party 1 as the title of execution, filed an application for compulsory auction regarding the building at issue in this case in Case No. 2001TAGYEONG9096 before the Gyeongju Branch of the Daegu District Court, and it is ascertainable that the said court rendered a decision to commence compulsory auction on September 11, 2001 with respect to the above real estate.\\n\\nThe title trust agreement and registration between the Plaintiff et al. and Non-party 1 became void under the Real Estate Real Name Act; given these circumstances, even if the Defendant knew of such title trust facts (that is, even if the Defendant was a third party in bad faith), the Defendant falls under a third party under Article 4(3) of the Real Estate Real Name Act as an attachment creditor who obtained a decision to commence compulsory auction concerning the building at issue in this case, which is registered in the name of Non-party 1 on the premise that the title trustee, Non-party 1, is the owner; therefore, as against the Defendant, the Plaintiff et al. cannot assert that the title trust agreement and registration at issue in this case are void.\\n\\nThe determination of the court below to the same effect is proper, and there is no error such as a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning “third party” under Article 4(3) of the Real Estate Real Name Act or an inadequacy of review as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n4. As to Ground 4 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nEven if the subject matter of litigation in the earlier-filed action (hereinafter referred to as the “prior suit”) and the later-filed action (hereinafter referred to as the “subsequent suit”) is not identical, if the determination regarding the subject matter of litigation in the prior suit becomes a prerequisite issue in the subsequent suit, or if the subject matter of litigation in the subsequent suit is in a contradictory relationship with the legal relationship established in the prior suit, the res judicata effect of the judgment in the prior suit extends to the subsequent suit, thereby operating to preclude the subsequent suit from asserting arguments different from the determination in the prior suit; however, since the res judicata effect of a final judgment extends only to the conclusion of the determination regarding the existence or nonexistence of the legal relationship asserted as the subject matter of litigation, and does not extend to the existence or nonexistence of the underlying legal relationship serving as its premise, the legal relationship established in the prior suit means the legal relationship to which the res judicata effect of the final judgment extends, and does not mean the underlying legal relationship itself (see Supreme Court Decisions 2000DA47361 rendered on December 27, 2002, and 2004DA55698 rendered on December 23, 2005, among others).\\n\\nExamining the matter in light of the record, the existence or nonexistence of the claim for return of unjust enrichment, which is the subject matter of litigation in the First Prior Suit and the Second Prior Suit, is not only different from the existence or nonexistence of the right to object to execution, which is the subject matter of litigation in the third-party objection action in this case, but also the legal relationship to which the res judicata effect of the aforesaid prior suit judgments extends, namely the legal relationship asserted as the subject matter of litigation, is the existence or nonexistence of the Defendant’s claim for return of unjust enrichment against Non-party 1 or the Plaintiff et al., and the existence or nonexistence of the ownership of the building at issue in this case is merely the underlying legal relationship; thus, the res judicata effect of the aforesaid prior suit judgments does not extend thereto. Therefore, it cannot be said that the determination regarding the existence or nonexistence of the claim for return of unjust enrichment, which is the subject matter of litigation in the prior suits, becomes a prerequisite issue in the third-party objection action in this case, or that the existence or nonexistence of the right to object to execution, which is the subject matter of litigation in the third-party objection action in this case, is in a contradictory relationship with the existence or nonexistence of the claim for return of unjust enrichment, which is the subject matter of litigation in the prior suits; accordingly, it cannot be said that the res judicata effect of the prior suit judgments extends to the third-party objection action in this case, and thus it also cannot be said that the Defendant’s continuation of compulsory execution while asserting that the building at issue in this case is solely owned by Non-party 1 conflicts with the res judicata effect of the prior suit judgments.\\n\\nThe determination of the court below to the same effect is proper, and there is no error such as a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the objective scope of res judicata as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the appellate costs shall be borne by the losing party; it is so adjudged in accordance with the order by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2018DA284233]": "The grounds of appeal (the statements in each supplemental brief on the grounds of appeal filed after the period for submission of the statement of grounds of appeal has elapsed shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal) are examined.\\n\\n1. Outline of the case\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts may be found.\\na. On 2010. 3. 31., the Plaintiff entered into a sales contract with the Non-party, who was the owner, concerning the real estate at issue, and paid the full purchase price of KRW 1 billion to the Non-party by 2010. 5. 13. Pursuant to the title trust agreement between the Plaintiff and the Defendant, the Non-party completed the registration of transfer of ownership concerning the real estate at issue in the Defendant’s name on 2010. 5. 17.\\nb. On 2014. 12. 11., the Defendant obtained a loan of KRW 500 million from Standard Chartered Bank Korea Limited (hereinafter referred to as “SC Bank”) and established on the real estate at issue the mortgage at issue with a maximum claim amount of KRW 600 million.\\nc. The registration of establishment of the mortgage at issue had not been cancelled by the time oral argument was concluded in the court below.\\n\\n2. The determination of the court below and the issue\\na. The Plaintiff asserted that the title trustee, the Defendant, established the mortgage at issue and obtained the loan, thereby obtaining benefits equivalent to the amount of the secured debt and thereby causing the Plaintiff damage in the same amount, and sought restitution of unjust enrichment against the Defendant.\\nThe court below did not accept the Plaintiff’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment on the ground that, in the case of a three-party registered title trust, both the title trust agreement and the transfer registration of ownership made pursuant thereto are void, and ownership of the real estate remains with the seller, so the person who suffered damage from the establishment of the mortgage at issue is the Non-party, who is the seller and owner, and not the Plaintiff.\\nb. The issue in this case is whether, in a three-party registered title trust, where the title trustee disposes of the real estate by selling it to a third party or by establishing a mortgage over the real estate, and the third party acquires rights concerning the real estate pursuant to Article 4(3) of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name (hereinafter referred to as the “Real Name Registration Act”), the title trustor may directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee with respect to the benefits obtained by the title trustee in the process.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s determination\\na. Whether, in a three-party registered title trust, the title trustor may directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee when the title trustee has transferred the ownership title of the real estate to a third party\\nIn a three-party registered title trust, where the title trustee’s voluntary disposition, or compulsory expropriation, or acquisition by consultation for public land, etc. serves as the cause and the transfer registration of ownership is completed in the name of a third party, the third party, absent special circumstances, validly acquires ownership (Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act). As a result, the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership to the title trustor becomes impossible to perform, and the title trustor becomes unable to receive a transfer of ownership of the real estate, while the title trustee acquires the proceeds from the disposition of the real estate or compensation, etc. The precedents hold that the title trustee bears an obligation to return such proceeds from the disposition or compensation, etc. to the title trustor as unjust enrichment (see Supreme Court Decisions of 2011. 9. 8., 2009DA49193, 49209; 2015. 9. 10., 2015DA207235; 2019. 7. 25., 2019DA203811, 203828, etc.). These precedents are proper and should be maintained. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) A three-party registered title trust is a transaction in which, while the title trustor acquires the real estate from the owner, the title trustor enters into a title trust agreement with the title trustee and causes the transfer registration of ownership of the relevant real estate to be made directly in the title trustee’s name from the owner.\\nIn such a case, since the title trust agreement is void pursuant to Article 4(1) of the Real Name Registration Act, no direct legal relationship exists between the title trustor and the title trustee with respect to the real estate. However, the title trustor still has a claim for transfer registration of ownership against the seller based on the sales contract, and the seller bears toward the title trustor an obligation to register transfer of ownership under the sales contract, while at the same time, against the title trustee, the seller may seek performance of a transfer registration of ownership, as a claim for removal of interference based on ownership, by requesting cancellation of the transfer registration of ownership or restoration of the true title registration. The title trustee is in the position of bearing toward the seller an obligation to cancel the transfer registration of ownership or an obligation to register transfer of ownership based on restoration of the true title registration. As such, the title trustor, title trustee, and seller in a three-party registered title trust relationship each have contractual or legal rights with respect to the real estate and bear corresponding obligations. This is consistent with the purpose and intent of the Real Name Registration Act, which is to have ownership and other real rights in real estate registered in the name of the actual right holder so as to conform to the substantive rights relationship.\\n\\nHowever, where the title trustee’s voluntary disposition, compulsory expropriation, or acquisition by consultation for public land, etc. (collectively referred to below as “the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.”) serves as the cause and transfer registration of ownership is completed in the name of a third party with respect to the real estate, under Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act the third party validly acquires ownership, thereby causing changes in the rights and obligations of the title trustor, title trustee, and seller as described above. In such a situation, the purpose of the Real Name Registration Act, namely to have registration made in the name of the actual right holder so as to conform to the substantive rights relationship, can no longer be achieved.\\n\\nWhere, due to the application of the third-party protection provision, changes occur in the contractual or legal rights and corresponding obligations concerning the real estate held by the title trustor, title trustee, and seller, in adjusting the resulting interests through restitution of unjust enrichment it is necessary to consider, together with the purpose and intent of the Real Name Registration Act to realize registration in the name of the actual right holder, the purpose of the unjust enrichment restitution system, namely to impose an obligation of return on the person who obtained a property benefit without legal cause, vis-à-vis the person who suffered loss by reason of that benefit, based on the ideals of fairness and justice.\\n\\n2) The title trustee is neither a party to the real estate sales contract nor a person who validly acquired ownership of the real estate, and thus has no rights in relation to the real estate. However, when the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., and Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act result in the valid transfer of ownership of the real estate to a third party, the title trustee, though not the owner of the real estate, obtains the proceeds from the disposition or compensation, etc. in relation to the third party by reason of having held the title of ownership. However, such benefit was obtained by the title trustee as the exchange value of the real estate despite not being its owner, and therefore constitutes a benefit without legal cause that must be returned to the rightful holder.\\n\\n3) The title trustor has already performed the obligation under the sales contract by paying the purchase price, yet remained unable to acquire ownership; therefore, the title trustor is in the position of being able to, by using as the preserved right the claim for transfer registration of ownership against the seller, subrogate the seller’s claim for cancellation registration of the transfer registration of ownership against the title trustee or the claim for transfer registration of ownership based on restoration of the true title registration, and after restoring the title to the seller, demand the seller to perform the transfer registration of ownership to the title trustor. However, when ownership of the real estate is validly transferred to a third party pursuant to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act, the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership to the title trustor becomes impossible to perform, and the title trustor suffers loss in that, despite paying the purchase price to the seller, the title trustor loses the right to receive the ownership of the real estate, which is the counter-performance.\\n\\n4) Even though the seller, at the title trustor’s request, effected the transfer registration of ownership in the title trustee’s name, the title trust agreement and the transfer registration of ownership in the title trustee’s name become void, and the seller is in the position of having to regain the title to the real estate from the title trustee and complete the transfer registration of ownership to the title trustor based on the sales contract. However, when there is a title trustee’s disposition act, etc., as noted above, the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership to the title trustor becomes impossible to perform. Before the Real Name Registration Act came into force, the Supreme Court held, in a case where the seller, at the title trustor’s request, transferred the registration title to the title trustee, that if there is a title trustee’s disposition act, etc., it is difficult to find the seller at fault for the conclusion or performance of the sales contract, and therefore it is not permissible in good faith to require the seller to return the purchase price or to complete the transfer registration of ownership again in the title trustor’s name by reason of the title trustor’s failure to register under his/her real name (see Supreme Court Decision of 2002. 3. 15., 2001DA61654). Likewise, even after the Real Name Registration Act came into force, if a three-party registered title trust is created, it is still difficult to find the seller at fault for the conclusion or performance of the sales contract, and even if the seller is at fault, it is still not permissible in good faith for the title trustor, who caused the violation of the Real Name Registration Act, to seek return of the purchase price from the seller or to seek damages arising from the impossibility of performance of the duty to register transfer of ownership. By reason of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the seller loses ownership of the real estate under Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act and is no longer liable to the title trustor for the duty to register transfer of ownership or for damages arising from impossibility of performance thereof, while retaining the purchase price received from the title trustor; thus, it cannot be said that the seller suffers economic loss due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.\\n\\n5) The benefit obtained by the title trustee as consideration for the disposition act, etc. concerning the real estate is the benefit obtained through the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and the valid acquisition of ownership by a third party pursuant to Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act; the title trustor originally had the right to acquire ownership of the real estate through the seller but, due to such valid acquisition by the third party, suffered loss in that, even through the seller, the title trustor can no longer acquire ownership of the real estate; whereas the seller cannot be said to have suffered an economic loss to his/her property despite the valid acquisition of ownership by the third party as above. Considering these circumstances, the benefit unjustly obtained by the title trustee through the disposition act, etc. concerning the real estate without legal cause should, in social common sense, be regarded as caused by the loss suffered by the title trustor and therefore be returned to the title trustor.\\n\\n6) In this way, even if in a three-party registered title trust the title trustee, through the disposition act, etc., causes a third party to acquire ownership of the real estate, and the title trustee thereby bears a direct obligation to return unjust enrichment to the title trustor, this does not deprive the seller, one of the parties to the three-party registered title trust relationship, of rights or impose additional obligations on the seller; nor does it deprive the title trustee of rights or impose additional obligations on the title trustee, because the title trustee originally had no independent right of defense, etc. against the title trustor or the seller; nor does it grant the title trustor any unjust benefit or right.\\n\\nRather, if, in a three-party registered title trust, the legal relationships of rescission or damages arising from the impossibility of performance of the duty to register transfer of ownership under the sales contract between the title trustor and the seller, and the legal relationships of restitution of unjust enrichment or damages arising from tort between the seller and the title trustee due to the title trustee’s infringement of the seller’s ownership, are separately identified and their interests individually adjusted, then depending on the concrete circumstances there may be cases where no claim for restitution of unjust enrichment or damages is recognized, and cases where such claims are recognized only in a limited manner due to contributory negligence, etc., resulting in insufficient compensation for loss and, at the same time, an unexpected gain. Tolerating such a result is contrary to the purpose of the unjust enrichment restitution system grounded in the ideals of fairness.\\n\\n7) In a three-party registered title trust, the title trustor, title trustee, and seller understand that the sales contract has been fully performed and the legal relationship has ended, because the seller receives the purchase price from the title trustor and transfers the registration title to the title trustee pursuant to a tripartite agreement, namely the title trust agreement between the title trustor and the title trustee and the agreement that the seller will transfer the registration title to the title trustee at the title trustor’s request. Even if, thereafter, the title trustor cannot acquire ownership of the real estate due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., so long as the seller is found to bear no fault therefor, the seller retains the purchase price received from the title trustor and does not suffer economic loss. Although a legal relationship requiring adjustment of interests among the three persons, namely the title trustor, title trustee, and seller, may arise due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., there is no need to draw the seller, who is in the above-mentioned position, into the adjustment of interests arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. The changes in rights and obligations among the title trustor, title trustee, and seller due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. stem from the invalidity of the title trust agreement entered into between the title trustor and the title trustee, and therefore the problem of adjusting interests accordingly should be resolved between the title trustor and the title trustee, who are the parties to the title trust agreement; there is no logically necessary reason why the seller must necessarily intervene in this process. Even if the seller is included in the adjustment of interests, the benefit such as the proceeds from disposition or compensation obtained by the title trustee through the disposition act, etc. is, in substance, the same as being attributed to the title trustor through the seller. Therefore, rather than unnecessarily drawing in the seller, it is reasonable to allow the title trustor to directly exercise a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee as a simple way to resolve the legal relationship.\\n\\nb. Whether, in a three-party registered title trust, the title trustor may directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee when the title trustee has established a mortgage over the real estate\\nEven where the title trustee has established a mortgage over the real estate in favor of a third party, it should be treated in the same manner as where ownership of the real estate is transferred to a third party.\\nWhere the title trustee establishes a mortgage over the real estate in favor of a third party, the third party validly acquires the mortgage pursuant to Article 4(3) of the Real Name Registration Act. In such case, the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership concerning the real estate is not impossible to perform; thus, the title trustor may still, by subrogating the seller, receive transfer of ownership from the seller through transfer registration of ownership based on restoration of the true title in the title trustee’s name concerning the real estate, but such ownership is ownership with the mortgage established by the title trustee still validly remaining. By establishing the mortgage in favor of the third party, the title trustee obtains a benefit equivalent to the amount of the secured debt; the title trustor suffers loss in that, even through the seller, the title trustor can acquire only ownership with exchange value limited by the amount of the secured debt; while the seller, having received the purchase price from the title trustor and thereby achieved the object of the sales contract, does not suffer a substantial loss because he/she bears no liability for damages with respect to transferring ownership in the mortgaged state.\\nAccordingly, where in a three-party registered title trust the title trustee establishes a mortgage over the real estate in favor of a third party, the title trustee obtains a benefit equivalent to the amount of the secured debt of the mortgage and thereby causes corresponding loss to the title trustor; therefore, the title trustee bears an obligation to return that benefit to the title trustor as unjust enrichment.\\n\\nc. Determination in this case\\n1) With respect to the portion of the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal concerning the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment (grounds of appeal, points 4 and 5)\\nReviewing the factual circumstances set forth in paragraph 1 above in light of the legal principles stated above, the Defendant, as the title trustee, completed the registration of establishment of the mortgage at issue in favor of SC Bank, whereby SC Bank validly acquired the mortgage; the Defendant, as the title trustee, obtained, using the real estate at issue not owned by the Defendant, a benefit equivalent to the amount of the secured debt of the mortgage; and the Plaintiff, as the title trustor, suffered loss in that the Plaintiff could only acquire ownership with exchange value limited by the amount of the secured debt. Therefore, the Defendant must return to the Plaintiff the benefit as unjust enrichment.\\nUnlike the above, the court below’s determination, which did not accept the Plaintiff’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment, erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment in a three-party registered title trust, thereby affecting the judgment. The Plaintiff’s argument in this part of the grounds of appeal is well-founded.\\n\\n2) With respect to the portion of the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal concerning the claim for delivery of shares (grounds of appeal, points 1, 2, and 3)\\nThe court below, citing the judgment of the first instance, held that there was no evidence of a title trust concerning the shares listed in Attached Table 2 to the judgment of the court below (hereinafter referred to as the “shares at issue”) between the Plaintiff and the Defendant, and that, in light of circumstances such as the Defendant having also acted as a shareholder of Yeongcheon Seal Tech Co., Ltd., it was insufficient to find that the Plaintiff had title-trusted the shares at issue to the Defendant and that the Defendant was merely a nominal shareholder. On this basis, the court below dismissed the Plaintiff’s appeal on this point.\\nReviewing the reasons of the judgment below in light of the record, the court below’s determination contains no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, of exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience without fully examining the necessary matters, or of affecting the judgment by misapprehending the law on the allocation of the burden of proof, violating the adversarial principle, or rendering contradictory reasons.\\n\\n3) With respect to the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\nThe court below recognized a three-party registered title trust concerning the real estate at issue among the Plaintiff, the Defendant, and the Non-party, and then granted the Plaintiff’s claim, by which the title trustor, the Plaintiff, subrogated the seller, the Non-party, and sought performance from the title trustee, the Defendant, of the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership to restore the true title in favor of the Non-party.\\nReviewing the reasons of the judgment below in light of the record, the court below’s determination contains no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, of exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience without fully examining the necessary matters, or of rendering contradictory reasons, etc., thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nAccordingly, the part of the judgment below dismissing the Plaintiff’s claim concerning restitution of unjust enrichment is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; the remainder of the Plaintiff’s appeal and the Defendant’s appeal are each dismissed. It is so adjudged as stated in the disposition. This judgment includes a dissenting opinion by Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Park Jeong-hwa, Kim Seon-soo, No Tae-ak, and Lee Heung-gu on whether the Plaintiff may directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the Defendant. Otherwise, the opinions of the participating Justices are unanimous, and there is a supplementary opinion by Justice Jo Jae-yeon to the majority opinion, and supplementary opinions by Justices Park Jeong-hwa and No Tae-ak to the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n5. Dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Park Jeong-hwa, Kim Seon-soo, No Tae-ak, and Lee Heung-gu on the issue\\nThe majority opinion states that if, in a three-party registered title trust, ownership of the real estate is transferred from the title trustee to a third party or a mortgage is established in favor of a third party, thereby enabling the title trustee to obtain a benefit, the title trustor may directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee.\\nHowever, even if ownership is transferred to a third party due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., and the title trustee obtains a benefit such as the proceeds from disposition or compensation of the real estate in a three-party registered title trust, the title trustor cannot directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee. Unlike the majority opinion, Supreme Court Decisions of 2011. 9. 8., 2009DA49193, 49209, etc., cited by the majority opinion as precedents recognizing the title trustor’s direct claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee, can no longer be maintained after the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act and therefore should be changed. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\na. The case where ownership of the real estate is transferred to a third party due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.\\n1) After the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act, there is no direct legal relationship between the title trustor and the title trustee.\\nA) According to Article 4(1) and (2) of the Real Name Registration Act, in a three-party registered title trust the title trust agreement is void, and the transfer registration of ownership made pursuant thereto in the title trustee’s name is also void. However, because the sales contract between the title trustor and the seller is valid, the title trustor merely acquires from the seller a claim for transfer registration of ownership under the sales contract and does not form any legal relationship with the title trustee. Therefore, for the title trustor to exercise rights against the title trustee, the title trustor must subrogate the seller. In other words, in order to preserve the claim for transfer registration of ownership against the seller, the title trustor may only, by subrogating the seller, request cancellation registration of the void transfer registration of ownership made in the title trustee’s name or request transfer registration of ownership in favor of the seller based on restoration of the true title registration. This legal principle does not change merely because there is a title trustee’s disposition act, etc. Even if the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. occurs while the title trustor is suing the title trustee by subrogating the seller, it cannot be said that from that point the title trustor may exercise rights directly against the title trustee without subrogating the seller.\\n\\nB) According to the majority opinion, until the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. occurs, the title trustor could exercise rights against the title trustee only by subrogating the seller in order to preserve the claim for transfer registration of ownership against the seller; however, because of the accidental circumstance that the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. occurred, a claim against the title trustee that did not previously exist arises, making direct exercise of rights possible. This leads to the effect of affirming a direct legal relationship between the title trustor and the title trustee if the trust real estate is transformed into the object of disposition proceeds or compensation, etc., thereby producing an effect equivalent to validating the title trust.\\n2) The person who suffered loss directly causally connected to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. is the owner, namely the seller, and not the title trustor. Therefore, the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment concerning the benefit obtained by the title trustee through the disposition act, etc. vests in the seller.\\nA) Before the Real Name Registration Act came into force, the title trust agreement was valid, and the registration in the title trustee’s name made pursuant thereto was recognized as ownership externally; therefore, if the seller, at the title trustor’s request, transferred ownership to the title trustee, the seller thereby lost ownership and his/her obligations as seller were terminated, and the title trustor had only the legal relationship arising from the title trust agreement with the title trustee.\\nHowever, after the Real Name Registration Act came into force, as noted above, in a three-party registered title trust the title trust agreement and the transfer registration of ownership in the title trustee’s name made pursuant thereto are both void, so ownership of the real estate still remains with the seller, and the title trustor is in the position of holding a claim for transfer registration of ownership against the seller. Therefore, when a third party validly acquires ownership through the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the seller loses ownership of the real estate. At this time, the title trustee’s acquisition of the benefit such as the proceeds from disposition or compensation, etc. on the ground that the title trustee held the title of ownership over the real estate constitutes so-called unjust enrichment through infringement, because the title trustee unlawfully infringes another’s right, thereby causing its loss and gaining a benefit from the infringement. Therefore, the title trustee must return the benefit obtained through the disposition act, etc. to the rightful owner, namely the seller.\\nB) The precedents also clearly stated that where a person without title disposes of another’s right to a third party, and the original right holder loses the right due to the protection provision for a good-faith third party, the right holder may demand return from the person without title, treating what the person without title received from the third party as consideration for the disposition as so-called unjust enrichment through infringement (see Supreme Court Decisions of 2011. 6. 10., 2010DA40239; 2020. 5. 21., 2017DA220744, en banc, etc.). This legal principle should likewise apply where the title trustee disposes of the trust real estate to a third party.\\n3) Between the title trustor and the title trustee, there is no legal relationship such as performance without legal cause, expenditure of costs, or exclusive infringement of rights that would justify directly recognizing a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment.\\nA) The title trustor merely entrusted the title trustee with registration title pursuant to the title trust agreement; the title trustor did not directly make any performance or incur any costs to the title trustee, and the provision of such performance does not itself constitute the content of the title trust agreement. The title trustor is merely a creditor of the seller, having purchased the real estate from the seller and paid the purchase price to the seller, and thereby holding against the seller a claim for transfer registration of ownership concerning the real estate; such a claim is not a right that can be asserted against a third party other than the seller. Therefore, even if the title trustee, who is a third party and not a contractual party, carries out a disposition act, etc., it infringes only the seller’s ownership and cannot be regarded as infringing any exclusive right belonging to the title trustor.\\nFurther, even if, due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the title trustor’s claim for transfer registration of ownership against the seller becomes impossible to perform, this does not mean that the title trustor’s claim against the seller is extinguished, and the title trustor still retains the right to claim damages or to rescind the contract against the seller.\\nThus, even if ownership of the trust real estate is transferred to a third party, such transfer does not give rise, as against the title trustor and title trustee, to a direct settlement relationship of performance or a compensatory relationship arising from infringement of rights. Therefore, even if the seller loses ownership due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., thereby causing the title trustor’s claim for transfer registration of ownership to become impossible to perform, there can be no direct formation of a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title trustor and the title trustee excluding the seller.\\nB) Precedents have held, in a case where a three-party registered title trust was created before the Real Name Registration Act came into force, that even when the title trust agreement and the registration made pursuant thereto became void upon the lapse of the grace period under the Real Name Registration Act, the title trustor could not, once ownership of the real estate had reverted to the seller, seek transfer registration against the title trustee, the nominal title holder of the void registration (see Supreme Court Decisions of 2008. 11. 27., 2008DA55290, 55306, etc.); and, in a three-party registered title trust, because the title trustor is neither the owner of the real estate nor in a relation of trust and confidence with the title trustee, the title trustee cannot be said to be a person in custody of the title trustor’s property, so even if the title trustee disposes of the real estate without authorization, embezzlement does not arise in relation to the title trustor (see Supreme Court Decision of 2016. 5. 19., 2014DO6992, en banc, etc.). These precedents may be understood as having been based primarily on the premise that no direct legal relationship exists between the title trustor and the title trustee in a three-party registered title trust.\\n\\n4) It cannot be concluded that, due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the seller can definitively retain the purchase price received from the title trustor or that the seller suffers no loss.\\nA) The majority opinion cites Supreme Court Decision of 2002. 3. 15., 2001DA61654, to the effect that if the seller, at the title trustor’s request, transferred the registration title to the title trustee, it is not permissible in good faith to require the seller to return the purchase price or to complete the transfer registration of ownership in the title trustor’s name again on account of the title trustor’s failure to register under his/her real name, and states that even after the Real Name Registration Act came into force, it is still not permissible in good faith for the title trustor to seek return of the purchase price from the seller or to claim damages arising from impossibility of performance of the duty to register transfer of ownership. However, this is not proper. Supreme Court Decision 2001DA61654 held, on the premise that before the Real Name Registration Act came into force the title trust was valid, that it is not possible to find fault on the part of the seller who complied with the title trustor’s request, and therefore it is not permissible in good faith for the title trustor to seek return of the purchase price or transfer registration of ownership from the seller. However, where, after the implementation of the Real Name Registration Act, a three-party registered title trust is created in a situation where it is clear that the title trust agreement and the resulting changes in real rights are void, it is difficult to apply the legal principle of Supreme Court Decision 2001DA61654 as is. The majority opinion says that because the title trustor caused the state of violation of the Real Name Registration Act, even after the Real Name Registration Act came into force the title trustor cannot seek return of the purchase price or damages from the seller; however, this is not correct. A three-party registered title trust relationship violating the Real Name Registration Act is formed only because the seller consents thereto, and cannot be created by the title trustor alone. This is clearly different from the case under the latter sentence of Article 4(2) of the Real Name Registration Act, where the title trustee becomes a party to one side and the counterparty is unaware of the existence of the title trust agreement, so the title trust agreement and changes in real rights are not treated as void. In addition, unlike before the Real Name Registration Act came into force, the title trustor has not formed any reliance on the seller. Before the Real Name Registration Act came into force, since the title trust agreement was valid, there was a need to protect the seller who believed that the sales contract would validly come to an end. However, after the Real Name Registration Act came into force, since the title trust agreement is clearly void, there is no room for any reliance on the seller that the sales contract would validly come to an end, nor is there any need to protect such reliance. The issue between the title trustor and the seller should be governed by the general law of contracts, such as Article 390 of the Civil Act, and there is no room for the application of the principle of good faith.\\nB) It is also not correct for the majority opinion to assume that because the seller need not return the purchase price or transfer ownership to the title trustor until the seller regains title from the title trustee, the seller suffers no loss. In unjust enrichment through infringement, the loss suffered by the right holder means the fact itself that the possibility of enjoying the benefits exclusively allocated to the right holder has been fundamentally blocked by the infringing act; it does not require that the right holder suffer concrete, actual loss. Furthermore, it cannot be said that the seller, having lost ownership, suffers no loss. This is because the seller’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee is a statutory claim arising from the title trustee’s infringement of the seller’s ownership of the trust real estate.\\nC) The restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the seller and the title trustee and the sales contract relationship between the title trustor and the seller are separate legal relationships. To say that, in the restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the seller and the title trustee, one must consider whether the seller and the title trustor have retained the purchase price or suffered loss is premised on the existence of a valid title trust agreement between the title trustor and the title trustee, and therefore does not conform to the purpose of the Real Name Registration Act, which treats title trust agreements as void.\\n5) The title trustor may exercise contractual rights against the seller.\\nWhen, due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the title trustor is unable to acquire the real estate, the title trustor may obtain relief against the seller by exercising the right of rescission against the seller and claiming restitution so as to recover the purchase price, or by claiming damages arising from breach of contract. Owing to the nature of a three-party registered title trust, in which the seller receives the full purchase price from the title trustor and transfers the title of ownership to the title trustee, unlike an ordinary sales contract, even after the seller has received the full purchase price and performed the transfer registration procedure to the title trustee at the title trustor’s request, the transfer registration of ownership is void; therefore, the seller still bears toward the title trustor the obligation to register transfer of ownership concerning the trust real estate, and has not completed performance as seller. Accordingly, if the seller knowingly neglects this obligation and the obligation to register transfer of ownership becomes impossible to perform, the seller must bear responsibility to the title trustor for such impossibility of performance. The seller bears liability to the title trustor for damages arising from breach of contract under Article 390 of the Civil Act, and the title trustor may rescind the sales contract and claim restitution from the seller under Article 546 of the Civil Act.
