Criminal liability for unlawful acts, in that it imposes liability for acts that violate the legal order of society and has as its content criminal punishment, which is a public sanction against the actor, whereas civil liability, in that it imposes the actor’s personal liability for infringing another’s legal interest and has as its content compensation for the loss incurred by the victim, and the damages system is guided by the principle of fair and equitable allocation of losses. Accordingly, even if an act of infringement does not constitute a criminal offense, whether it constitutes a tort under civil law must be examined from a perspective separate from criminal liability (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2016DA34007 rendered on June 3, 2021).\\n\\n(3) In a three-party registered title trust, where registration of transfer of ownership is made in favor of a third party due to the title trustee’s arbitrary disposition, etc., such third party acquires ownership validly, unless special circumstances exist (Article 4(3) of the Real Estate Real-Name Act). As a result, the seller’s duty to register transfer of ownership to the title trustor becomes impossible to perform, and the title trustor can no longer receive transfer of ownership of the real property. If the title trustee, knowing that the title trustor’s claim right to demand registration of transfer of ownership is being infringed, arbitrarily disposes of the real property held in title trust, this constitutes an unlawful act that violates social order or economic order according to social norms, and, unless special circumstances exist, tort liability arising from infringement of a third party’s claim is established.\\n\\n(4) The above en banc Decision 2014DO6992 held only that the essence of embezzlement lies in the unlawful appropriation of another person’s property entrusted on the basis of a fiduciary relationship, and that the relationship between the title trustor and the title trustee is not a fiduciary relationship worthy of protection under criminal law, and thus embezzlement cannot be recognized with respect to the title trustee’s arbitrary disposition; it did not mean that the title trustor’s claim right to registration of transfer of ownership cannot be protected in a title trust relationship. Therefore, insofar as the title trustor’s claim is infringed by the title trustee’s arbitrary disposition, it is reasonable to regard the title trustee as bearing civil tort liability toward the title trustor regardless of whether embezzlement is constituted under criminal law.\\n\\nb. Examining the facts set forth in 1. above in light of these legal principles, there is room to view the Defendant’s act of disposing of each of the parcels of land at issue, which the Defendant held pursuant to the title trust agreement concluded with the Plaintiff, to D without the Plaintiff’s consent, as a tort infringing the Plaintiff’s claim right to demand registration of transfer of ownership.\\n\\nHowever, the lower court determined that even if the Defendant disposed of each of the parcels of land at issue without the Plaintiff’s consent, no tort was established. The lower judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning whether a tort is established by the title trustee’s arbitrary disposition in a three-party registered title trust. The ground for appeal pointing this out is well founded.\\n\\n3. Claim for Restitution of Unjust Enrichment (Grounds for Appeal 1 and 2)\\n\\nThe ground for appeal on this point contends that the lower judgment erred in holding that it cannot be concluded that the Defendant actually obtained any benefit through the disposition of each of the parcels of land at issue; however, this merely disputes the selection of evidence and fact-finding, which fall within the exclusive province of the lower fact-finding court, and therefore does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal. Furthermore, even upon review of the record, there is no error in the lower judgment, such as exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or incomplete deliberation, or violation of the duty of explanation, as alleged in the grounds for appeal. The Supreme Court Decision cited by the Plaintiff, rendered on May 27, 2010 in 2009DA12580, concerns a specific matter different from this case and is not appropriate for application to this case.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nSince the Plaintiff’s appeal is well founded, the lower judgment shall be reversed and the case remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. The judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices."}
{"[2022DA228933]": "The lower court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the Seoul High Court."}

question: Among the explanations concerning inheritance, which is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: If a predeceased person received a house as a gift from the decedent before the occurrence of the cause for representation, that benefit may be regarded as the special benefit of the heir by representation.
B: If a person disqualified from inheritance received a gift from the decedent after grounds for disqualification from inheritance arose, then, absent special circumstances, that benefit does not constitute the special benefit of the heir by representation arising from inheritance disqualification.
C: A coheir who received a special benefit exceeding the value of the statutory share of inheritance must return the excess when the inherited estate is divided.
D: If no agreement is reached among the coheirs, unless there are special circumstances under which the status of the person presiding over ancestral rites cannot be recognized, the eldest among the decedent's lineal descendants, regardless of sex or whether legitimate or illegitimate, who is nearest in degree, becomes the person presiding over ancestral rites.
E: If the decedent, by an act inter vivos or by will, disposed of his or her body and remains or designated a burial place, the person presiding over ancestral rites cannot be said to bear even a legal duty to be unconditionally bound by such intent of the decedent.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2007DA27670]": "The grounds of appeal are considered.\\n\\n1. On Ground 1 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. Method of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites\\n\\n(1) Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act provides that “the ownership of the forest land reserved for ancestral rites within 1 jeongbo belonging to a grave, the agricultural land serving as burial ground within 600 pyeong, the family genealogy, and the ritual implements shall be succeeded by the person who presides over the ancestral rites.” Originally, the former Civil Act enacted by Act No. 471 on 1958. 2. 22. had no general provisions on inheritance of ancestral rites, thereby leaving inheritance of ancestral rites to the category of morals and customs; however, Article 996 provided that the ownership of the forest land reserved for ancestral rites within 1 jeongbo belonging to a grave, the agricultural land serving as burial ground within 600 pyeong, the family genealogy, and the ritual implements (hereinafter referred to as “property for ancestral rites”) should be succeeded by the family head heir. Then, the former Civil Act amended by Act No. 4199 on 1990. 1. 13. abolished the family head heir system and adopted the family head succession system, and accordingly provided in Article 1008-3 that the succession of the above property for ancestral rites would be one of the effects of property inheritance, not of family head succession, and changed the person entitled to succeed from “family head heir” to “the person who presides over the ancestral rites.” Further, the current Civil Act amended by Act No. 7427 on 2005. 3. 31. even abolished the family head succession system, while leaving Article 1008-3 intact.\\n\\n(2) However, as above, neither the former Civil Act amended by Act No. 4199 on 1990. 1. 13. nor the current Civil Act contains any provision that merely states that “the person who presides over the ancestral rites” succeeds to the property for ancestral rites, and there is no provision as to who that person is or how that person is to be determined.\\n\\nWith respect to this, the Supreme Court has consistently held that, if among the co-heirs there is the eldest descendant of the main line, he or she ordinarily becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites, except where there are special circumstances such that the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites cannot be maintained by that person (see Supreme Court Decision 97NU7820 dated 1997. 11. 25., Supreme Court Decision 96NU18069 dated 1997. 11. 28., Supreme Court Decision 2001DA79037 dated 2004. 1. 16., etc.).\\n\\nGenerally, the term “eldest descendant of the main line” refers to the “legitimate eldest son as the male descendant of the eldest son line,” and the traditional custom in our society was that, irrespective of consultation among heirs, the legitimate eldest son first became the heir to ancestral rites, and if there was no legitimate eldest son, then the heir to ancestral rites would be determined in the order of legitimate descendant, younger son, illegitimate son, younger descendant, and illegitimate descendant. Thus, the above Supreme Court decisions may be said to have been grounded on such traditional custom.\\n\\n(3) However, even custom or customary law as a social norm generated by repeated social practice cannot be accorded effect as a legal norm or recognized as having judicial effect where, contrary to the entire legal order with the Constitution as the highest norm, it lacks legitimacy and rationality (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2001DA48781 dated 2003. 7. 24., etc.).\\n\\nAs seen above, the system of inheritance of ancestral rites that prioritizes the status of legitimate eldest son was based on the past patriarchal lineage ideology, intended to maintain and continue the family centered on the patrilineal bloodline through ancestor worship, and rested on a patriarchal extended family system and an agrarian society premised on self-sufficiency. However, since the 1970s, our society has, through rapid economic growth, become a highly industrialized and urbanized society; the extended family system has changed into a nuclear family system; within the family, the will of each individual family member has been respected; discrimination between legitimate and illegitimate status has disappeared; and together with the decline of son preference, the proportion of families with only daughters has increased. Accordingly, Article 34(1) of the Constitution, fully amended by Constitutional Amendment No. 9 on 1980. 10. 27., proclaimed that “marriage and family life shall be formed and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and gender equality,” and this has been maintained as Article 36(1) of the current Constitution. Thereafter, institutions were improved in the direction of realizing equality among family members in all areas of society; through several amendments to the Civil Act, the inheritance shares of siblings became equal; the family head system was abolished and the family system centered on the individual and spouse was reorganized into a new family system; and even the family register system was eventually replaced by the new family relationship registration system on 2008. 1. 1.\\n\\nAs the lifestyle of members of our society and various laws and institutions changed as above, the traditional custom that the legitimate eldest son must, irrespective of consultation among heirs, succeed first to ancestral rites ignored the autonomous will of the heirs as family members and discriminated between legitimate and illegitimate status, and thus no longer conformed in principle to the changed family system based on individual dignity and equality. The legal conviction of members of our society with respect thereto has also been substantially weakened; accordingly, it can no longer maintain its force as custom or customary law, and it is reasonable to conclude that the prior Supreme Court decisions grounded on such custom likewise can no longer maintain their force as case law.\\n\\n(4) Meanwhile, Article 1 of the Civil Act provides that in civil matters, if there is no provision in law, customary law shall apply, and if there is no customary law, reason shall apply. As to who becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites, there is no statutory provision at all. In the present situation where the traditional custom or case law concerning the person who presides over the ancestral rites can no longer maintain its force, the method of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites should be determined by reason, taking into comprehensive consideration the general principles of the Civil Act, the nature of property for ancestral rites, the legislative purpose of Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act concerning succession to property for ancestral rites, and the historical and social meaning of ancestral rites.\\n\\n(a) Our Civil Act is based on the principle of private autonomy as its basic principle, and the Civil Act has been amended in the direction of pursuing equality among heirs. Moreover, ordinarily, where the views of multiple interested parties conflict in a legal relationship, resolving the matter first through consultation may be deemed most consistent with reason. Thus, where there are co-heirs, it is reasonable to regard the person who presides over the ancestral rites as being determined by consultation among the co-heirs.\\n\\n(b) However, where consultation among the co-heirs is not reached, it is reasonable to regard the eldest son of the deceased (or, if the eldest son has already died, the eldest son’s son, namely the eldest grandson) as the person who presides over the ancestral rites, unless there are special circumstances such that he cannot maintain the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites; and where none of the co-heirs is a son, it is reasonable to regard the deceased’s eldest daughter as the person who presides over the ancestral rites.\\n\\nOriginally, property for ancestral rites accompanies the traditional inheritance of ancestral rites and is not only necessary to secure continuity of ancestral rites for one’s ancestors, but also has spiritual and cultural value symbolizing the family lineage and features as family pride and a medium for tribal unity. Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act concerning succession to property for ancestral rites aims to preserve our tradition of ancestor worship and performance of ancestral rites by maintaining and preserving property for ancestral rites that bears such special meaning. Although succession to property for ancestral rites is essentially part of inheritance (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DA45452 dated 2006. 7. 4.), distributing property for ancestral rites among co-heirs in the same manner as general inherited property is not in accord with the sentiment of members of our society; moreover, if done so, property for ancestral rites for the performance of ancestral rites would become dispersed and diluted as inheritance is repeated, and would ultimately cease to function as property for ancestral rites. Therefore, property for ancestral rites should be regarded as special property different from general inherited property, to which the legal principle of equal division among co-heirs applicable to general inherited property does not apply. The reason why Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act specifies the person who succeeds to property for ancestral rites not as a property heir but as “the person who presides over the ancestral rites” is to reflect the special nature of succession to property for ancestral rites and to simply process the legal relationship concerning such succession.\\n\\nTherefore, in order to maintain and preserve such property for ancestral rites and to simplify the legal relationship concerning succession thereto, it is appropriate to determine a specific single person, rather than jointly determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and it would be desirable to determine that specific person as someone whose status is to some extent foreseeable and who can be recognized by social common sense as having legitimacy as the person who presides over the ancestral rites.\\n\\nHowever, the system of ancestral rites and the succession of property for ancestral rites are based on the past patriarchal lineage-centered family succession through ancestor worship. Although the character of ancestral rites has changed significantly today, it cannot yet be said to have completely escaped the above traditional character of family succession. In addition, among the members of our society today, while there may be variations depending on individual values and regional traditions or culture, it appears that the perception that, where consultation is not reached, the eldest son or eldest grandson becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and if there is no son, the daughter becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites, is widely accepted; and among persons of equal conditions and status, giving priority to the elder is our traditional good custom and general social common sense. It is also difficult to say that such perceptions or traditions of our society are contrary to the present entire legal order.\\n\\nTaking all of the above circumstances together, where consultation among the co-heirs of the deceased is not reached, it is more relatively legitimate in social common sense, and predictability is secured to some extent, to regard the eldest son or eldest grandson, regardless of legitimate or illegitimate status, or, where there is no son among the co-heirs, the eldest daughter, as the person who presides over the ancestral rites, rather than regarding another heir as the person who presides over the ancestral rites; thus, this is most consistent with reason.\\n\\nMeanwhile, even if, where consultation is not reached, the eldest son or eldest grandson becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites and independently succeeds to property for ancestral rites, thereby resulting in discrimination between heirs in that status and other heirs, such result is caused not only by the non-formation of consultation among the co-heirs, but also, such discrimination should be regarded as having a rational basis because it is for the preservation of the tradition of ancestor worship and performance of ancestral rites and for simplifying the legal relationship concerning succession to property for ancestral rites (see Constitutional Court Full Bench Decision 2005HEONBA7 dated 2008. 2. 28.).\\n\\n(c) In the end, the person who presides over the ancestral rites should first be determined by consultation among the co-heirs of the deceased; if consultation is not reached, then, unless there are special circumstances such that he or she cannot maintain the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites, the eldest son of the deceased (or, if the eldest son has already died, the eldest son’s son, namely the eldest grandson) shall be the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and where none of the co-heirs is a son, the deceased’s eldest daughter shall be the person who presides over the ancestral rites.\\n\\nHowever, the Supreme Court’s new declaration of legal principle regarding the method of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites changes the foundation of the custom concerning the system of inheritance of ancestral rites. The Supreme Court reached the declaration of new legal principle in this judgment because, as noted above, members of our society’s perception of the ancestral rite system and the entire legal order have changed. If the above new legal principle were applied retroactively, the effect of numerous successions to property for ancestral rites formed in reliance on prior Supreme Court precedents would be determined all at once, contrary to legal stability and protection of the parties’ reliance based on the principle of good faith and fair dealing. Thus, it is reasonable to regard the above new legal principle as applicable only where succession to property for ancestral rites occurs after the rendition of this judgment.\\n\\nHowever, because the Supreme Court’s declaration of a new legal principle in this case is intended to make it the adjudicative norm for this case, the new legal principle should be applied retroactively in this case (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2002DA1178 dated 2005. 7. 21.).\\n\\n(5) The court below, after preconditioning that, where there is the eldest descendant of the main line by custom, such person is recognized as having the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites unless there are special circumstances such that that person cannot maintain that status, held to the effect that the Plaintiff, the eldest son of the deceased non-party, is in the status of the person who presides over the ancestral rites for him as the eldest descendant of the main line.\\n\\nAlthough the legal principle preconditioned by the court below differs from the legal principle on the method of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites as seen above and is therefore erroneous, according to the facts lawfully found by the court below, it can be seen that no consultation was reached among the Plaintiff, who is the eldest son of the deceased, and the other co-heirs including the Defendants as to who should be the person who presides over the ancestral rites of the deceased. Therefore, under the above legal principle, the Plaintiff, who is the eldest son of the deceased, should be regarded as having become the person who presides over the ancestral rites of the deceased. Accordingly, the conclusion of the judgment below is proper, and the above error of the court below did not affect the result of the judgment, so the grounds of appeal on this point are not accepted.\\n\\nB. Effect of the method of disposal of the remains and bones or designation of the burial place\\n\\n(1) Human remains and bones are corporeal things that may be the subject of burial, management, ancestral rites, and offerings. The remains and bones of ancestors enshrined in a grave succeed, together with the grave, which is property for ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, to the person who presides over the ancestral rites; and the deceased’s own remains and bones likewise succeed, analogously to such property for ancestral rites, to that person who presides over the ancestral rites.\\n\\nA grave means a place where a deceased person is interred by burying the body, bones, remains, hair, etc. inside it, and if it merely has the external form of a grave but no body is interred inside, it cannot be called a grave (see Supreme Court Decisions 76DA1359, 1360 dated 1976. 10. 26., 91DA18040 dated 1991. 10. 25.). Thus, the remains and bones are the very body of the grave; without them, a legally valid grave cannot be established. In addition, the Civil Act regards a grave as the object of succession in ancestral rites, and the right of protection and management over a grave belongs to the person who presides over the ancestral rites regardless of who established the grave, unless there are special circumstances (see Supreme Court Decision 95DA51182 dated 1997. 9. 5.). This is premised on the understanding that the remains and bones belong to the person who presides over the ancestral rites as the object of succession in ancestral rites.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the deceased’s own intent or emotion concerning the method of disposal of the remains and bones or the designation of the burial place should duly be respected. However, burial, management, ancestral rites, offerings, etc. with respect to the remains and bones left after the deceased’s soul has departed are carried out by the family members, including the person who presides over the ancestral rites, out of personal feelings such as respect and remembrance for the deceased, and since the deceased’s remains and bones succeed to the person who presides over the ancestral rites, management and disposal thereof should ultimately be carried out according to that person’s intent. Furthermore, the method of disposal of the remains and bones or the designation of the burial place does not constitute a statutory testamentary matter, and there is no other basis on which legal binding force can be recognized.\\n\\nTaking the above circumstances together, where a decedent, during life, by act or by will, disposed of his or her own remains and bones or designated the burial place, that intent should be respected so long as it does not violate good morals and other social order, and this would be the same for the person who presides over the ancestral rites; but the duty to respect the decedent’s intent is merely moral, and it cannot be said that the person who presides over the ancestral rites bears a legal duty by which he or she is absolutely bound.\\n\\n(2) Examining in light of the above legal principle, even if the court below found that some co-heirs buried the deceased’s remains in the grave in this case in accordance with the deceased non-party’s intent during life, it is proper to conclude that the deceased’s act of disposing of his own remains during life is not legally binding upon the Plaintiff, who acquired rights to the remains after the deceased’s death, and thus there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principle concerning the rights of the person who presides over the ancestral rites, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. On Grounds 2 and 3 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. As to in what circumstances there are special circumstances such that the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites cannot be maintained, because the ancestral rite system is based on custom, custom should be considered; however, the custom here does not mean past custom, but the present custom newly formed and continuing in accordance with social changes. Therefore, the basic ideas or social order dominating our society and the changes in the customs newly formed accordingly must be considered. Accordingly, it is reasonable to regard cases involving serious illness, severe wasteful and dissolute living, long-term residence abroad, serious economic deprivation to the extent that livelihood is difficult, habitual abuse of parents or severe insults or harms, failure to protect or manage an ancestor’s grave, refusal to perform ancestral rites, or conduct that, without reasonable grounds, significantly contravenes the deceased’s wishes or last instructions as cases in which there is no intention or ability to preside over ancestral rites normally.\\n\\nB. Examining in light of the above legal principle, the court below found that, since around 1961 the deceased non-party, of his own volition, had lived separately from the Plaintiff’s mother and cohabited with the Defendants’ mother, there had been no intercourse between him and the Plaintiff or support by the Plaintiff, and that there was no evidence showing that the Plaintiff, during the deceased’s lifetime, expressed an intent to refuse to support the deceased or to refuse ancestral rites after death; on that basis, the court below held that no special circumstance existed such that the Plaintiff could not maintain the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites. That determination is acceptable, and contrary to the grounds of appeal, it cannot be said that the Plaintiff’s claim in this case constitutes “conduct that, without reasonable grounds, significantly contravenes the deceased’s wishes or last instructions” to the extent of causing loss of the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites.\\n\\nAccordingly, the judgment below is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principle on special circumstances such that the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites cannot be maintained, or violation of the law concerning the rules of evidence evaluation, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal are borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged as stated in the Disposition. In this judgment, the opinions of Justices Park Si-hwan, Jeon Soo-an, Ahn Dae-hee, and Yang Chang-soo dissenting as to Ground 1 of the grounds of appeal, and the dissenting opinions of Justices Kim Young-ran and Kim Ji-hyung as to the method of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites among Ground 1 of the grounds of appeal, aside from those dissenting opinions, the opinions of the participating Justices are unanimous. There are also the concurring opinions of Justices Lee Hong-hoon and Kim Neung-hwan as to the majority opinion, the concurring opinion of Justice Ahn Dae-hee as to the dissenting opinions of Justices Ahn Dae-hee and Yang Chang-soo, and the concurring opinion of Justice Kim Young-ran as to the dissenting opinions of Justices Kim Young-ran and Kim Ji-hyung.\\n\\n4. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Park Si-hwan and Jeon Soo-an on Ground 1 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. As to the method of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites\\n\\n(1) I agree with the majority opinion that the successor to the remains and bones is the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and that the person who presides over the ancestral rites should first be determined by consultation among the co-heirs. However, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that, where consultation is not reached, the eldest son, eldest grandson, or, depending on the case, the eldest daughter (hereinafter collectively referred to as “the eldest son, etc.”) becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites unless there are special circumstances such that the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites cannot be maintained, for the reasons below.\\n\\n(a) A dispute as to who becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites would usually arise because no consultation has been reached among the co-heirs. In such a case, to say that the eldest son, etc. naturally becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites makes virtually no difference from the position of the prior Supreme Court precedents that the eldest descendant of the main line becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites from the outset. This is because, from the standpoint of the eldest son, etc. who is in a position to become the person who presides over the ancestral rites, he or she can simply refrain from participating in the consultation altogether or take a passive attitude so that consultation is not reached.\\n\\nGiven that former Civil Act (before amendment by Act No. 4199 on 1990. 1. 13.) prescribed the eldest son as the first-ranking family head heir, the majority opinion ultimately only changed, in form, the person who enjoys the privilege regarding property for ancestral rites from “family head heir” to “eldest son, etc.”, while in substance bringing about the same result as before, thereby nullifying the purpose of the 1990 amendment to the Civil Act, which sought to separate property for ancestral rites from the privilege of the family head heir. Furthermore, since succession to property for ancestral rites under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act is essentially part of inheritance (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DA45452 dated 2006. 7. 4.) and may include assets having a considerable level of economic value, it also contradicts the purpose of the repeated amendments to the Civil Act equalizing the inheritance shares among siblings.\\n\\n(b) Considering the legislative purpose of Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act and the nature of property for ancestral rites, I agree that it is necessary to preserve and maintain property for ancestral rites and to simplify the legal relationship concerning succession thereto, and that for this purpose it is appropriate to determine a specific single person rather than the person who presides over the ancestral rites jointly. However, I find it difficult to agree with the majority opinion that having the eldest son, etc. as the person who presides over the ancestral rites better serves this purpose than having another heir do so, and is relatively more legitimate in social common sense and thus most consistent with reason.\\n\\nAs the most important grounds, the majority opinion cites the patriarchal lineage-centered family succession character of the ancestral rite system, and the fact that, among members of our society today, the perception that, where consultation is not reached, the eldest son or eldest grandson becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and if there is no son, the daughter becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites, is widely accepted, and that such perception does not contradict the present entire legal order.\\n\\nHowever, as the majority opinion itself points out, the family succession character of the ancestral rite system and the traditional custom by which the legitimate eldest son became the heir to ancestral rites were originally based on a patriarchal extended family system and an agrarian society premised on self-sufficiency; they do not accord with the nuclear family system in which individual will and value are respected, nor with our present society that has achieved high industrialization and urbanization. In fact, ancestral rites today may be said to have a stronger character of remembrance for the deceased than of family succession.\\n\\nMoreover, in the course of the above nuclear-family, urbanization, and industrialization process, our society has become marked by a tendency for conversations between spouses and the will of each individual family member to be respected rather than the unilateral will of the family head, and for brothers and sisters to be treated equally regardless of age or sex; with the decline in the birth rate and the decline of son preference, the proportion of families with only daughters has increased; it has become common to list sons and daughters together in family genealogy books; many clan associations have emerged that grant clan-member status to women; and it is no longer unusual for women to serve as chief mourners or attend ancestral rites. Thus, there have been many changes in the consciousness and lifestyle of members of society.\\n\\nThese changes are reflected in our Constitution and laws: the Constitution amended on 1980. 10. 27. newly provided in Article 36(1) that “marriage and family life shall be established and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and gender equality, and the State shall guarantee this,” expressing the constitutional decision that family relations should be established and maintained on the basis of human dignity and gender equality, away from patriarchal family relations. The Civil Act has also been amended in many respects, such as equalizing inheritance shares among siblings, eliminating discrimination between patrilineal and matrilineal blood relatives, and between collateral relatives by blood and collateral relatives by marriage, abolishing the family head system entirely and implementing the family relationship registration system centered on the nuclear family. In addition, by marriage registration, children may take the surname and family origin of the mother by consultation between spouses. In line with such changes in the basic ideology and legal order of our society grounded in gender equality, the Supreme Court, through en banc Decision 2002DA1178 dated 2005. 7. 21., held that the traditional customary law limiting the qualification of clan members to adult males no longer had legal effect and recognized women as having clan-member status.\\n\\nThrough the above process of change, not only has the legal conviction of members of our society concerning the traditional custom favoring the eldest son already substantially disappeared, but it is also questionable whether such custom conforms to the present entire legal order of our society, and this phenomenon will intensify further in the future.\\n\\nMeanwhile, it is needless to say that merely by reason of being in the position of eldest son, etc. among the co-heirs, a person is not necessarily in the best position to preserve and maintain property for ancestral rites. Furthermore, even according to the majority opinion, since consultation takes precedence over the status of eldest son, etc., the purported objective of simplifying the legal relationship concerning succession to property for ancestral rites has already been largely abandoned and thus cannot carry much significance.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that, where consultation is not reached, the eldest son, etc. becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites, because that better accords with the legislative purpose of Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act and is relatively more legitimate in social common sense and thus most consistent with reason.\\n\\n(c) The majority opinion states that even if, where consultation is not reached, the eldest son, etc. becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites and succeeds to property for ancestral rites, thereby creating a result of discriminating between the eldest son, etc. and other heirs, this is caused by the non-formation of consultation among the heirs and that such discrimination is rationally justified as being for the “preservation of tradition” of ancestor worship and performance of ancestral rites and for simplifying the legal relationship concerning succession to property for ancestral rites. I cannot agree with that view either.\\n\\nAs noted above, if consultation is not reached and the eldest son, etc. is made the person who presides over the ancestral rites from the outset, the eldest son, etc. can induce the non-formation of consultation in any number of ways. Accordingly, such discrimination is not caused by the objective circumstance of non-formation of consultation among the heirs, but rather depends on whether consultation is formed, which is subject to the subjective intent of the eldest son, etc., and therefore cannot be deemed a rationally justified discrimination.\\n\\nIn addition, the term “tradition” and “traditional culture” in the Preamble to the Constitution and Article 9 of the Constitution are concepts with historicity and temporality, and must be understood in the sense of the present age, taking into account the constitutional order of values, universal human values, and the spirit of justice and humanity. Since the tradition/traditional culture concerning the family system has a limitation in that it must not run counter to the constitutional ideals of the family system, namely “individual dignity” and “gender equality,” if any part of the inherited family system contradicts the individual dignity and gender equality required by Article 36(1) of the Constitution, one cannot invoke Article 9 of the Constitution to assert its constitutional justification (see Constitutional Court Full Bench Decision 2001HEONGA9, etc. dated 2005. 2. 3.).\\n\\nFrom this perspective, to say that, where consultation is not reached, the eldest son, etc. naturally becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites is, in effect, no different from saying that the eldest son, etc. becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites from the outset. This is substantially the same result as the former Civil Act (before amendment by Act No. 4199 on 1990. 1. 13.), which provided property for ancestral rites as a privilege of the family head heir. Therefore, even considering the legislative purpose of preserving the tradition of ancestor worship and performance of ancestral rites, it is difficult to recognize its legitimacy, and one cannot help but question why such tradition must be preserved only through the eldest son, etc.\\n\\nFurthermore, even if such discrimination has some unavoidable aspect from a legislative purpose standpoint, if in reality it brings about discrimination based on sex and age among heirs, it would be desirable not merely to accept it as unavoidable, but to seek a rational solution through a new interpretation consistent with the changed consciousness of the members of our society and the entire legal order.\\n\\n(2) As seen above, where consultation among the co-heirs is not reached, the eldest son, etc. cannot be said to become the person who presides over the ancestral rites; and if so, I think that determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites by majority vote is the most appropriate.\\n\\nAncestral rites are an event within the family, and who succeeds to property for ancestral rites is likewise a family matter. Therefore, it is desirable to leave the question of who will be the person who presides over the ancestral rites and who will succeed to property for ancestral rites to be autonomously determined according to the will of the family members themselves. I think that the purpose of Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, which only designates the successor to property for ancestral rites as “the person who presides over the ancestral rites” and does not provide any rule as to who should become that person, lies there as well. Even in light of the basic principle of a democratic society that, among methods of decision-making between persons in equal positions, the method that follows the will of the majority is the most reasonable and democratic, in the present age where the traditional custom recognizing priority for the eldest son is losing its legitimacy, it would be most consistent with reason to determine the person who presides over the ancestral rites among heirs in equal positions by majority vote.\\n\\nEven if the majority vote method itself is not perfect and, depending on the case, cannot exclude the risk that a decision by majority vote may arrive at a conclusion lacking validity in a specific case, such exceptional irrational result must be endured, at least in view of the fact that it is the most rational method among the decision-making methods devised so far. As to such irrational results arising from formal majority voting, it may be possible to handle them by treating them as special circumstances that preclude maintenance of the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites, or, while not reaching the level of denying the status itself, to appropriately control the individual irrationalities that may result from a majority-vote-selected person who presides over the ancestral rites exercising all powers granted to that status without restriction, through the application of general clauses such as abuse of rights or violation of the principle of good faith and fair dealing.\\n\\nIn addition, in exceptional cases where even majority voting, such as an equal number of votes for and against, cannot determine the matter, it would inevitably be necessary to supplement the process by having the court determine the matter according to reason after comprehensively considering the various circumstances. However, as proposed in the dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran and Kim Ji-hyung, the method of having the court directly determine the person who presides over the ancestral rites where consultation is not reached would not only amount to excessive judicial intervention in a family matter that should be autonomously decided among heirs, but also, without presenting even minimal objective and uniform standards, having the court always determine the person who presides over the ancestral rites case by case after comprehensively considering various circumstances would unduly destabilize legal relations concerning property for ancestral rites, and thus is inappropriate.\\n\\nMeanwhile, taking into account the possible negative effects arising from specifying the person who presides over the ancestral rites as a single person, one may also consider the method of having heirs jointly preside over ancestral rites. However, this would produce the same result as distributing property for ancestral rites among co-heirs as in the case of general inherited property, and would therefore not only fail to accord with the legislative purpose of Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, which provides for separate succession to property for ancestral rites, and the general sentiment of members of our society, but also make it ultimately difficult for property for ancestral rites for the performance of ancestral rites to survive. Thus, it is likewise inappropriate.\\n\\n(3) In conclusion, the person who presides over the ancestral rites should first be determined by consultation among the co-heirs, and where consultation is not reached, it is proper to determine that person by majority vote; however, such new legal principle, for the same reasons as the majority opinion, should be applied only to cases in which succession to property for ancestral rites occurs after the rendition of this judgment, except for this case.\\n\\nAccordingly, although the Plaintiff was not designated as the person who presides over the ancestral rites by majority vote among the co-heirs of the deceased non-party, the court below, by recognizing the Plaintiff’s status as person who presides over the ancestral rites solely because he is the eldest son of the deceased, and thereby holding that the Plaintiff had rights to the deceased’s remains and bones as the person who presides over the ancestral rites and granting the Plaintiff’s claim, committed an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principle concerning the method of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites.\\n\\nB. As to the effect of the method of disposal of the remains and bones or designation of the burial place\\n\\nThe majority opinion holds that when a decedent, during life, by act or by will, designates the method of disposal of his or her own remains and bones or the burial place, that intent should be respected unless it violates good morals or other social order, but the duty to respect the decedent’s intent is merely moral and cannot be said to be a legal duty by which the person who presides over the ancestral rites is absolutely bound.\\n\\nFirst, I agree with the majority opinion that the deceased’s remains and bones, together with the grave, which is property for ancestral rites, succeed to the person who presides over the ancestral rites. However, I cannot agree with the majority opinion insofar as it can be understood to allow, merely because the person who presides over the ancestral rites has the right to manage and dispose of the decedent’s remains and bones, the disposal of the remains and bones or the change of the burial place against the decedent’s intent without just cause.\\n\\nThe right over one’s own body is at the core of personality rights, and the right of self-determination over one’s body must be respected to the fullest during the person’s lifetime and even after death. Although the general principle under current law is that, after a person dies, he or she can no longer be the subject of rights and duties, it is not necessary to deny recognition of legal binding force even where, before losing legal capacity, the person expressed by act during life or by will an intent regarding the disposal of his or her body, funeral method, burial place, etc., thereby causing the effect of that expression of intent to continue even after death.\\n\\nIn light of the fact that the purpose of vesting rights over the deceased’s remains and bones in the person who presides over the ancestral rites lies in respect and remembrance for the deceased, this should be understood as a limitation inherent in the rights of the person who presides over the ancestral rites concerning property for ancestral rites, including remains and bones. Although the traditional custom and current law provide that rights over property for ancestral rites are succeeded solely by the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and this may be viewed as the result of taking various considerations into account, if one considers that in substance the succession is effected in the status of representing the bereaved family, then the person who presides over the ancestral rites cannot be allowed to disregard the deceased’s lifetime intent and dispose of the remains at will or conduct the funeral in another manner. Such conduct should be seen as harming the respect and remembrance for the deceased held by other bereaved family members, and as exceeding the authority granted to the person who presides over the ancestral rites.\\n\\nAs properly pointed out in the dissenting opinion of Justices Ahn Dae-hee and Yang Chang-soo, the argument has been made today that even for the deceased, general or limited personality rights should be recognized, and considering that criminal law contains the offense of defamation of the deceased, the Copyright Act contains provisions protecting moral rights after the author’s death, and individual statutes such as the Press Arbitration and Remedies Act contain provisions protecting the personality rights of the deceased, it cannot be said that recognizing legal binding force for a decedent’s lifetime expression of intent concerning the disposal of remains and bones or funeral method runs counter to the entire system of current law. Moreover, considering that the Organ Transplant Act recognizes primary binding force in the deceased’s intent, the person who presides over the ancestral rites should be deemed unable, absent special just cause, to dispose of the remains and bones or to change the funeral method or burial place against the decedent’s lifetime intent.\\n\\nIn light of the above legal principles and the record, the court below held that the deceased non-party’s lifetime act of designating the burial place of his own remains has no legal binding force upon the Plaintiff, who is the person who presides over the ancestral rites and acquired rights over the remains after the deceased’s death, and therefore concluded that the deceased’s remains must be delivered to the Plaintiff without inquiring whether the deceased actually designated the burial place. In doing so, the court below committed an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principle concerning the rights of the person who presides over the ancestral rites and by failing to fully examine the matter.\\n\\nC. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment below should be reversed and the case remanded to the court below for further trial and determination.\\n\\n5. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Ahn Dae-hee and Yang Chang-soo on Ground 1 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. The Plaintiff, premising that he is the person who presides over the ancestral rites, seeks delivery to himself of the remains interred in the grave in this case on the basis of ownership over the remains in this case. In response, the Defendants have consistently argued since the first instance that because the remains in this case were interred in the grave in this case in accordance with the deceased’s intent, the Plaintiff cannot seek delivery of the remains in this case in the status of person who presides over the ancestral rites. Ground 1 of the grounds of appeal likewise argues that, where a funeral is conducted in accordance with the deceased’s lifetime intent concerning the disposal of his own remains, such as the funeral arrangement he determined during life, then, unless there are other special circumstances, delivery of the remains cannot be sought by relying on the rights of the person who presides over the ancestral rites.\\n\\nViewed in this way, for the resolution of this case, the legal question of who is the person who presides over the ancestral rites may also arise, but separately therefrom, it may be more significant to consider what effect the deceased’s intent concerning funeral and other posthumous handling of the body has, regardless of who the person who presides over the ancestral rites is, on the attribution or exercise of ownership over the remains. I will discuss only to the extent necessary for the resolution of this case.\\n\\n(1) The majority opinion treats the issue of attribution of the remains analogously to Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, and states that the remains belong to the “person who presides over the ancestral rites” as defined therein, and discusses who that person is. It further states that the person thus determined as the person who presides over the ancestral rites may claim delivery of the remains even where the funeral was conducted according to the deceased’s intent. In this regard, the majority opinion says that, because the disposition of one’s own remains is not a statutory testamentary matter and there is otherwise no basis for recognizing legal binding force in such intent, where a decedent, during life, by act or by will, disposes of his or her own remains or designates the burial place, the duty to respect such intent is merely moral, not a legal duty that heirs, including the person who presides over the ancestral rites, or other third parties must follow.\\n\\n(2) First of all, I can no longer accept the prior precedents and the majority opinion in this case that the attribution of the remains should likewise be treated analogously to Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, which designates the person to whom a grave, etc. belongs as the “person who presides over the ancestral rites” {in particular, the grave in this case was established in January 2006 after obtaining a burial site use right from the first-instance co-defendant Yangpyeong Park Foundation, and, as a “private graveyard” under Article 14 of the Act on Funeral Services, etc., it is subject to that Act. Therefore, the grave in this case has nothing to do with the forest land reserved for ancestral rites or the “agricultural land serving as a graveyard” as defined in Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, and the parties to this case also appear to have no interest in the family genealogy or ritual implements. To that extent, the grave in this case is in fact far removed from the grave, etc. premised by Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act}.\\n\\nFurthermore, where a decedent expressly manifested during life a final intent concerning the handling of the remains according to their inherent nature, such as the manner and place of burial, it is proper to regard that intent as legally deserving respect and as having corresponding legal effect. Also, even if the decedent’s intent concerning the handling of the remains had no particular legal effect, once funeral rites or establishment of a grave, etc., or other posthumous handling of the remains has been carried out pursuant to that intent, then regardless of to whom ownership of the remains belongs, such ownership is limited to that extent and, unless there are other special circumstances, no one can dig up the grave and demand delivery of the remains to himself or herself.\\n\\nB. Under prior precedents, not only remains and bones buried in a grave (hereinafter simply referred to as “remains”) but also the attribution of remains generally had been treated analogously to Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, which provides for succession of graves, etc. The majority opinion and the court below likewise proceed on that premise.\\n\\nThis starts from the idea that resolving the legal question of to whom a grave containing the remains belongs also determines to whom the remains buried therein belong. However, that mode of thinking may have been appropriate in an era when there was no doubt that, upon a person’s death, the remains should be buried in the ground to establish a grave, and ancestral rites should be performed for the deceased buried inside the grave, and such were rules that had to be enforced. But now that funeral methods have diversified, funerals without graves have become common, and there is no basis to compel burial or grave establishment, the attribution of the remains should be treated separately from the attribution of the grave.\\n\\n(1) It no longer requires discussion that establishing a grave by burying the remains and making a burial mound is not the only method of “funeral and interment” as one process of handling the remains. Today, funerals other than grave establishment are not only something we always experience, but also are clearly reflected in the Act on Funeral Services, etc., which provides as methods of funeral and interment not only “burial” of a corpse or ashes in the ground (and “grave” is defined as a facility that buries remains, etc. in such manner; Article 2(6) of that Act), but also “cremation,” which burns the remains in fire for funeral, and “natural burial,” which buries the bone powder of cremated ashes under or around trees, flowers, etc. (Article 2(2) and (3) of that Act).\\n\\nAs cremation or natural burial has now become common so that no grave is established, it is obvious that the logic that the attribution of the remains is determined by Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, which provides for the attribution of a grave, can no longer be valid. A person is inevitably destined to die, and the remains always remain after death, so the need to determine their attribution always arises upon death, whereas burial or the establishment of a grave is merely one method of funeral.\\n\\n(2) The content and history of Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, which bears the title “Succession of graves, etc.,” are as stated by the majority opinion at the very beginning of its reasoning. That provision states that the grave and other items listed therein belong to the “person who presides over the ancestral rites.”\\n\\nHowever, that provision contains no rule as to what happens to the legal fate of graves, etc. when the bereaved family does not perform ancestral rites. The “ancestral rites” referred to therein need not necessarily be confined to the traditional Confucian rites of our country, and there may be no reason to wholly exclude the interpretation that, for example, a simple memorial gathering in which the bereaved family merely gathers on the memorial date also constitutes “ancestral rites” here. But if “ancestral rites” includes rites in the broader sense mentioned above, one cannot help wondering again what justification there would be for attributing the grave, and further the forest land reserved for ancestral rites or ritual implements, etc., to the person who presides over such rites. And there may well be cases in which there are no ancestral rites even in the broad sense.\\n\\nMeanwhile, our law is based on general freedom of action and, more specifically, recognizes freedom of religion and, unlike in the Joseon Dynasty, does not recognize a state religion (Article 20 of the Constitution). Therefore, the State cannot compel a person to conduct a funeral in the manner of burying the deceased’s remains and establishing a grave, and further cannot compel the performance of “ancestral rites” by law. This should also extend to the point that the State cannot compel even consideration of whether “ancestral rites” should be performed. Nevertheless, under prior precedents, the descendants of a person buried in a grave must perform ancestral rites if they wish to determine to whom the grave, certain property, or even the person’s remains belong.\\n\\nMoreover, even where there is no person performing ancestral rites, and even particularly where parents or other ancestors are not buried in a grave, in order to determine the attribution of parents’ remains, prior precedents require “the person who presides over the ancestral rites” or “the person who should preside over the ancestral rites” to be “created” in the name of customary law or reason.\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, even where the remains are buried and a grave is established, the establishment and maintenance thereof are governed by the above-mentioned Act on Funeral Services, etc. (“Act on Funeral Services, etc.”; originally the “Act on Burial and Graves, etc.,” whose title was changed when it was fully amended by Act No. 6158 on 2000. 1. 12. After several amendments, it was again fully amended by Act No. 8489 on 2007. 5. 25., but its content has been maintained without major change). Under that Act, burial (and thus establishment of a grave) may not be carried out unless the site is a public cemetery under Article 13 of that Act or a private cemetery under Article 14 thereof (Article 7(1)). The installation period of a grave established in that manner is, in principle, 15 years, though extension is possible (Article 19(1) and (2)). Upon expiry of the installation period, the bereaved family member or the cemetery installer must remove the facilities installed at the grave and either cremate or “entomb” the buried ashes (Article 20(1) and (2)).\\n\\nThus, under current law, a grave may be maintained only within a limited period such as 15 years, even if once established. However, because rights over the remains buried in a grave must be determined so long as they remain in the form of bones, etc., there is no reason to inseparably tie that issue to the attribution of a grave that can be maintained only for such a limited period.\\n\\n(4) The majority opinion says that burial, management, ancestral rites, offerings, etc. with respect to the remains left after the deceased’s soul has departed are carried out by the family members, including the person who presides over the ancestral rites, based on personal feelings of respect and remembrance for the deceased, and that because the deceased’s remains succeed to the person who presides over the ancestral rites, management and disposal thereof should ultimately be carried out according to that person’s intent. However, as noted above, I cannot agree with the premise that the deceased’s remains should succeed to the person who presides over the ancestral rites, etc. Also, ancestral rites or offerings, etc. are carried out by the bereaved family out of personal feelings and are left to their freedom, but that does not mean that the deceased cannot decide during life how the body left after death is to be handled. Generally, ancestral rites or offerings, etc. can be performed even in the state in which the deceased was buried according to his or her own intent, so it is questionable whether merely holding ancestral rites can justify requiring the already buried remains to be placed under one’s own management and disposal.\\n\\nFurther, the majority opinion says that a grave means a place where the deceased’s bones or other corpse is buried inside it; if it merely has the external form of a grave but no corpse is buried inside, it is not a grave, and because the remains are the very body of the grave, no legally valid grave can be established without them; moreover, the right of management and disposal over a grave belongs to the person who presides over the ancestral rites regardless of who established the grave.\\n\\nHowever, the issue central to this case is the remains, not the grave. From that standpoint, to say that, because the remains are the body of the grave, the attribution of the remains must coincide with the attribution of the grave is a reversal of logic. That may be so with respect to remains buried in a grave, but it is self-evident that remains not so buried have no relation to a grave, much less can one speak of the “body” of a grave as to such remains.\\n\\n(5) I here wish to raise a methodological objection to the majority opinion’s position that who becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites should be determined by reason.\\n\\n(a) The majority opinion cites as grounds: ① “there is no statutory provision whatsoever as to who becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites,” and ② the “present situation where the traditional custom or case law concerning the person who presides over the ancestral rites can no longer maintain its force.” However, ② is logic to justify legal discovery based on reason under Article 1 of the Civil Act, premised on ①; thus, in the end, ① is the key issue.\\n\\nAs to ①, it would suffice for the court, in cases where succession of graves, etc. is at issue, to interpret and clarify what “ancestral rites,” “preside,” or “the person who presides” mean in Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act so as to apply their meaning to concrete cases. Therefore, to say that there is no statutory provision as to who becomes the person who presides over the ancestral rites is as meaningless a proposition as saying, under the immediately preceding Article 1008-2(1) of the Civil Act, that there is no statutory provision as to who becomes “a person who has specially contributed to the maintenance or increase of the decedent’s property” and therefore that matter must be determined by reason pursuant to Article 1 of the Civil Act.\\n\\n(b) The majority opinion’s introduction of reason as the basis for legal judgment and its conclusion that the eldest son, etc. thereby becomes the “person who presides over the ancestral rites” under Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act actually functions as follows. That is, even where, whether in a broad or narrow sense, ancestral rites are not actually performed at all, it seeks to determine the grave, and further the person to whom the remains belong, by that standard. This could be justified only when the statutory text is interpreted not in its ordinary meaning but as “the person who should preside over the ancestral rites” or “the person who ought to preside over the ancestral rites.”\\n\\nIf so, there is no denying that this raises substantial problems. That is because it indirectly suggests that the eldest son, etc. should preside over ancestral rites and, further, that ancestral rites should generally be performed for one’s ancestors.\\n\\n(6) As seen above, Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act can no longer serve as a general standard for determining the person to whom the remains belong because of its partial systematic character (there is no need here to discuss specifically what the conditions for application of that provision are, what its legal effect is, or how its application affects the attribution of the remains). Therefore, we need to seek a general legal principle regarding the handling and attribution of the remains outside the framework of Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act.\\n\\nC. As for funeral rites and other posthumous handling of the remains, the deceased’s final intent becomes the primary standard, without needing to look to numerous foreign examples (the heirs would be in a status analogous to that of the deceased’s testamentary executor to that extent).\\n\\n(1) The human body is an essential attribute of the person. And the body, as the most conspicuous “mine,” belongs to me more clearly than any object I own and is governed by my will. Upon a person’s death, however, the “person” to whom the body belonged during life disappears, and the handling of the remains becomes a matter for the living. Even if the remains now become “things” and ownership arises in them, they are necessarily special objects subject to posthumous handling such as burial rites, as well as the power to perform ancestral rites and offerings, and concomitantly the corresponding duties.\\n\\n(2) The right a person has over his or her own body is of a personality-right nature and, regardless of whether it is a statutory testamentary matter, should have legal effect as part of so-called “posthumous personality protection” with respect to funeral rites, organ donation, grave establishment, and other posthumous handling of one’s own remains.\\n\\nThis is a separate issue from whether personality rights should be generally recognized for the deceased in the same content and scope as for living persons or in a similar manner. Here I only wish to point out that the legal concept of personality rights itself was gradually formed as individual interests of a personality nature were increasingly accorded legal protection in individual contexts.\\n\\n(a) Human dignity does not return to complete nothingness upon death, and the necessity of protecting the personality of living persons does not completely disappear upon death. Our law also makes this point clear through Criminal Act Article 308, which protects the honor of the deceased; Copyright Act Article 14(2), concerning postmortem protection of moral rights of the author; and particularly Article 5(3) through (5) of the Press Arbitration and Remedies Act, which directly and in detail provides for cases where there is infringement, or a risk of infringement, of the personality rights of a deceased person.\\n\\n(b) It is natural for a person to express interest in how his or her body will be handled after death and to wish that his or her final intent be determined and carried out as such. Our law gives legal effect, in the name of a will or testamentary gift, to the decedent’s final juristic act regarding property held during life. If so, then, regarding the body that belonged to the decedent more conspicuously than any object he or she owned and was governed by his or her will, this should be even more so by its nature. However, the final intent need not comply with formalities such as a will, but it must be clearly expressed (see also Organ Transplant Act Article 11(1)1).\\n\\n(c) Also, one may wonder whether making the deceased’s intent the primary standard results in a conflict with the personality interests of the bereaved family in remembrance and respect for the deceased. However, that can be adequately addressed by appropriately defining the content and limits of legal protection of the deceased’s intent, and this does not mean that the primacy of that standard should be denied altogether.\\n\\n(3) Furthermore, respecting the deceased’s intent in relation to the handling of the remains may secondarily serve as one way to prevent, in advance to some extent, the undesirable situation in which the bereaved family becomes embroiled in disputes over “serving” the deceased’s remains after death.\\n\\nMeanwhile, we know the notion of “peace of the deceased.” No one can know the world after death. But just imagining that after one’s death, one’s beloved bereaved family splits into camps and fights over the remains is horrifying. Even to avoid such a situation, it is necessary during life to give legal effect to the decision on how to handle the remains left after death, and leaving the realization of that intent to morality alone cannot properly prevent such a situation. That is precisely how, for living persons, one secures to the extent possible present peace concerning death, which will befall everyone, after death.\\n\\n(4) Our positive law is also based on the premise that the deceased’s will governs the remains. Above all, this is so under the Organ Transplant Act.\\n\\nLooking at Article 18(3) of that Act, which sets the basic requirements for removing organs from the remains of a deceased person, if the person himself or herself has expressed a final intent concerning organ removal, that intent is the primary standard and the intent of the bereaved family is considered only secondarily. In other words, on the one hand, if the deceased opposed organ removal during life, then in no case, even if the bereaved family actively consents to the organ removal, can organs be removed from the remains. On the other hand, if the deceased consented to organ removal, then, in principle, that intent is followed. However, if there is an express objection from the bereaved family, the organs may not be removed (proviso to the same paragraph, subparagraph 1). Considering this exceptional express objection of the bereaved family is comparable to the system of reserved portion in inheritance law, which was established taking into account the family’s pecuniary interests in a testament concerning property. In particular, because organ removal is without exception a conscious dismemberment of the remains, special consideration is given, to that extent, to the feelings and other personality interests of the bereaved family. Therefore, caution should be exercised against understanding this proviso as a legal basis supporting the superiority or primary character of the bereaved family’s intent over the handling of funeral rites and other handling of the remains generally.\\n\\nThat the person’s intent should be primarily respected with regard to organ removal is also supported by Article 2 of the same Act, which sets out the “basic ideology” of the Act and provides in paragraph (2) that the voluntary intent expressed by a person who wishes to donate organs must be respected.\\n\\nD. Furthermore, even if legal effect cannot be recognized for the deceased’s final intent concerning the handling of the remains, if funeral rites or other posthumous handling of the remains, such as grave establishment, has already been carried out in accordance with the deceased’s intent (or, where there is none, in accordance with the intent of a majority of the heirs, as noted above), then, unless there are other special circumstances, the bereaved family’s ownership over the remains must now be limited according to its nature regardless of who among them owns it, and no one may rely on that ownership to dig up the grave and demand delivery of the remains to himself or herself.\\n\\n(1) As noted above, ownership over the remains, unlike ordinary ownership of things, entails certain powers and duties in accordance with the special nature of the remains as a “residual personality,” such as burial, ancestral rites, and offerings. However, in the legal issue discussed here, burial rites have already been performed, so there is no room for question. The remaining content of rights such as ancestral rites or offerings gains meaning only as acts expressing remembrance, respect, and reverence for the deceased.\\n\\nYet, if the funeral rites were conducted and a grave established in accordance with the deceased’s intent, to dig it up and claim delivery of the remains to oneself runs counter to the deceased’s own final intent concerning the posthumous handling of the remains, and does not conform to the original purpose of ancestral rites, etc., namely expressing remembrance, respect, and reverence for the deceased. And such ancestral rites or offerings can be performed without necessarily digging up the grave and receiving delivery of the remains. If the bereaved family is hindered in visiting the grave for ancestral rites, legal remedies such as an injunction may suffice. Legal disputes over remains should not become, as in this case, a means to resolve a battle over “legitimacy” among the bereaved family or to relieve each person’s resentment.\\n\\n(2) The majority opinion states that the bereaved family bears a moral duty, but not a legal duty, to follow the deceased’s intent concerning funeral rites and other posthumous handling of the remains. If so, to grant the Plaintiff’s claim for digging up the grave established according to the deceased’s intent, which the Plaintiff has a moral duty to respect, and to deliver the remains, is for the law to overturn what has already been realized in accordance with the content of the moral duty. However, that ultimately encourages immorality, and the law should not assist that.\\n\\nOur law also stands on such an attitude. Above all, Civil Act Article 744 provides that even if performance was made without any debt, if that performance was “conformable to the idea of morality,” its return may not be claimed. This provision eloquently states that the law should not participate in harming the ethical consciousness of the people, and that where a morally proper state has already been formed, it is impermissible to restore it to its original state by legal means.\\n\\n(3) If one adopts the view, as in the majority opinion, that the deceased’s intent concerning the posthumous handling of the remains cannot be given legal effect, it may be said that treating differently, in law, a case where the posthumous handling of the remains has not yet been performed and a case where the remains have been handled in accordance with that intent may not be permitted.\\n\\nHowever, even when the law makes the same legal requirement at issue, it is not uncommon to treat differently cases related to legal effects that newly form a state in the future and cases related to legal effects that rectify an already formed state. In addition to the aforementioned Civil Act Article 744, for example, in the case of a contract invalid for being contrary to good morals or other social order, not only is no claim for performance allowed based thereon, but once performance has been made thereunder, it is deemed illegal cause performance, and the recipient may not claim return of the performance (Civil Act Article 746). With respect to illegal cause performance, I also wish to note that, in the context of this case, the fact that the recipient of the performance acquires ownership and the transferor’s ownership is lost altogether when performance is received for an illegal cause (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 79DA483 dated 1979. 11. 13.) is not without suggestiveness.\\n\\nE. As seen above, where a decedent, during life, clearly expresses a final intent concerning the handling of his or her funeral and other remains according to their inherent nature, that intent should also be legally respected and should be deemed to have certain legal effect. Furthermore, particularly in this case, as the Defendants assert, where funeral rites, grave establishment, or other handling of the remains has already been carried out according to the deceased’s intent, then, unless there are other special circumstances, even the owner of the remains cannot rely on ownership to dig up the grave and demand delivery of the remains to himself or herself.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, premised on the view that ownership over the remains belongs to the person who presides over the ancestral rites analogously to Article 1008-3 of the Civil Act, held that in this case the Plaintiff, who is the eldest son of the deceased, acquired ownership over the remains in this case as the person who presides over the ancestral rites, and that the deceased’s lifetime intent did not affect the legal handling of the remains in this case based on that ownership; accordingly, it rejected as plainly without merit the Defendants’ argument that, if the deceased selected his own burial place during life and was buried there, then, absent serious circumstances preventing preservation of that situation, even the person who presides over the ancestral rites may not arbitrarily change that state.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment below should be reversed and the case remanded to the court below so that it may further examine whether the funeral rites and grave in this case were conducted and established according to the deceased’s intent.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran and Kim Ji-hyung on the method of determining the person who presides over the ancestral rites among Ground 1 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nA.
