In light of the purpose of the mortgage system as security for claims, unless there are special circumstances, the disposition of the secured claim is naturally understood to include the disposition of the mortgage; however, it cannot be said that whenever there is a disposition of the secured claim, the mortgage is always disposed of together (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 97DA33997, rendered on February 5, 1999, and 2003DA61542, rendered on April 28, 2004).\\n\\nTherefore, where a pledge is created over a claim secured by a mortgage, as a rule it is reasonable to view that the mortgage also becomes the object of the pledge together with the secured claim. However, it is also possible for the pledgee and the pledgor to make only the secured claim the object of the pledge and not the mortgage, and this does not run counter to the accessory nature of the mortgage. This is distinguishable from the case where only the secured claim is transferred separately from the mortgage, in which case the transferor loses the claim and the mortgage in the transferor's name is extinguished.\\n\\nLikewise, where a pledge is created over an unsecured claim and thereafter a mortgage is created to secure that claim, as a rule the mortgage also becomes the object of the pledge. However, if there are special circumstances, such as where the pledgee and the pledgor made only the secured claim the object of the pledge and thereafter the pledgor received the mortgage without the intention of providing it to the pledgee, the mortgage does not become the object of the pledge. In such a case, the mortgage exists for the pledgor who is the mortgagor, and if the pledge is extinguished for reasons such as satisfaction of the pledgee's claim or termination of the pledge agreement, the mortgagee may enforce the mortgage in order to be repaid its own claim.\\n\\nB. Meanwhile, Civil Act Article 348 provides that when a claim secured by a mortgage is made the object of a pledge, the effect thereof shall extend to the mortgage only if an additional entry of the pledge is made in the registration of the creation of the mortgage. If, when a pledge is created over a claim secured by a mortgage, it were said that the pledge right, which is established without registration due to the accessory nature of the mortgage, naturally extends to the mortgage as well, this would run counter to the principle of public notice and could impose an unforeseeable burden of pledge on a person who acquires or seizes the claim secured by that mortgage, or on a third party who acquires the mortgaged real property, thereby harming transactional security. Accordingly, Civil Act Article 348 provides that the effect of the pledge extends to the mortgage only when an additional entry of the pledge is made in the registration of the creation of the mortgage. This constitutes a change in a real right under Civil Act Article 186. In light of the legislative purpose of Civil Act Article 348, there is no reason to treat differently the case of “a pledge created over an unsecured claim followed by the creation of a mortgage to secure that claim” and the case of “a pledge created over a claim secured by a mortgage.”\\n\\nIn addition, as noted above, where a pledge is created over an unsecured claim and a mortgage is then created to secure that claim, if there are special circumstances such as an agreement between the parties, the mortgage may not become the object of the pledge. Therefore, in order for the effect of the pledge to extend to the mortgage, it is necessary to make this public by means of an additional entry of the pledge.\\n\\nAccordingly, even if a mortgage was created after a pledge had been created over an unsecured claim in order to secure that claim, absent an additional entry of the pledge in the registration of the creation of the mortgage by analogical application of Civil Act Article 348, it cannot be deemed that the effect of the pledge extends to the mortgage.\\n\\nC. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below and the evidence duly admitted and examined by the court below, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n(1) Topia Dobong Language Academy Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Topia Dobong Language Academy”) leased the building at issue from the Non-Party on April 27, 2009, by setting the lease deposit at KRW 1,800,000,000 and the lease term at 2 years from April 27, 2009 to April 26, 2011, and paid the Non-Party the lease deposit of KRW 1,800,000,000 (hereinafter referred to as “the lease deposit at issue”).\\n\\n(2) On October 29, 2009, Topia Dobong Language Academy provided the claim for return of the lease deposit at issue as security in order to secure a debt of KRW 3,000,000,000 for the return of debenture funds owed by its parent company, Eduance Co., Ltd., to the Plaintiff, and entered into an agreement with the Plaintiff establishing a maximum pledge right over the above claim for return of the lease deposit, with a secured limit amount of KRW 3,600,000,000.\\n\\n(3) On March 21, 2012, Topia Dobong Language Academy received the creation of a maximum mortgage over the building and the site at issue owned by the Non-Party in order to secure the claim for return of the lease deposit at issue, with the maximum claim amount at KRW 2,450,000,000, the debtor being the Non-Party, and the mortgagee being Topia Dobong Language Academy (hereinafter referred to as “the mortgage at issue”).\\n\\n(4) After an agreed divorce with the Defendant, the Non-Party transferred ownership of the building at issue to the Defendant on July 6, 2012, on the ground of property division.\\n\\n(5) On December 27, 2012, Topia Dobong Language Academy and the Defendant cancelled the registration of the creation of the mortgage at issue on the ground of termination.\\n\\n(6) The lease agreement between Topia Dobong Language Academy and the Non-Party contained no provisions regarding the creation of a mortgage. Although, at the time of the agreement establishing the maximum pledge right between the Plaintiff and Topia Dobong Language Academy, the parties expressly and in detail provided for the pledgee's obligations, the conditions and methods for the enforcement of the pledge, including the obligation to ensure notice bearing a fixed date to the Non-Party or consent thereto, the prohibition on assignment or provision as security of all rights under the lease agreement, and the prohibition on renewal of the lease agreement or conclusion of a new lease agreement, there was no provision whatsoever regarding a mortgage. The Non-Party, who was the de facto manager of Topia Dobong Language Academy and the debtor with respect to the obligation to return the lease deposit, testified to the effect that “the mortgage at issue was not created for the Plaintiff, but was created for purposes such as accounting audits, and after I transferred property to the Defendant by way of property division, the existing prior-ranking mortgage was in danger of being enforced, so the mortgage at issue was cancelled in order for the Defendant to obtain a new loan using the building at issue as security.”\\n\\nD. Examining these factual circumstances in light of the legal principles discussed above, there is room to find that the Plaintiff, as pledgee, and Topia Dobong Language Academy, as pledgor, fall within the case where only the claim for return of the lease deposit at issue was made the object of the pledge and the mortgage at issue was received without the intention of providing it to the pledgee, that is, where there are special circumstances in which the mortgage does not become the object of the pledge. In addition, because the Plaintiff did not complete an additional entry of the pledge with respect to the registration of the creation of the mortgage at issue, it cannot be said on this point as well that the effect of the Plaintiff's pledge extended to the mortgage at issue.\\n\\nE. Nevertheless, the court below, on the premise that where a mortgage is created after a pledge has been created over a claim in order to secure that claim, the effect of the pledge naturally extends to the mortgage under the principle of the accessory nature of the mortgage, rather than by agreement between the parties to establish a pledge over the mortgage, held that in such a case Civil Act Article 348 is not applied by analogy and that, even though the Plaintiff did not make an additional entry of the pledge, the effect of the Plaintiff's maximum pledge right naturally extended to the mortgage at issue. Accordingly, the court below determined that Topia Dobong Language Academy and the Defendant's cancellation of the registration of the creation of the mortgage at issue without the consent of the Plaintiff, who was the holder of the maximum pledge right, infringed the Plaintiff's maximum pledge right, and that the Plaintiff could demand, as a claim for removal of interference, the performance of the procedure for restoring the registration of the creation of the mortgage at issue that had been unlawfully cancelled.\\n\\nThis determination by the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the requirements for the effect of a pledge to extend to a mortgage where a mortgage is created to secure a claim over which a pledge has been created, and by failing to conduct the necessary examination. The Defendant's ground for appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\nF. Since the portion of the judgment below regarding the principal claim, namely the claim for restoration of the cancelled registration of the creation of the mortgage, must be reversed, the alternative claim inseparably combined therewith must also be reversed.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the portion of the judgment below concerning the claim for restoration of the cancelled registration of the creation of the mortgage and the portion concerning the alternative claim relating thereto are reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. The Plaintiff's appeal is dismissed. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[2016DA265689]": "I determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Where, pursuant to Article 3(1) of the former Housing Lease Protection Act (the version before amendment by Act No. 12043 on 13 August 2013, hereinafter the same), there is a lessee who has acquired opposability, the transferee of the leased house shall be deemed to have succeeded to the status of the lessor pursuant to paragraph (3) of the same Article. As a result, the transferee of the leased house shall assume, with discharge effect, the obligation to return the lease deposit, and the transferor shall withdraw from the lease relationship and be relieved of the obligation to return the lease deposit to the lessee. However, even a leaseholder who may assert rights against the transferee of the leased house should be regarded as able to be released from the binding force of the lease relationship to be succeeded if he or she does not wish to succeed to the lease relationship on his or her own accord (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA37646, decided 12 July 1996, and others), and thus may terminate the lease agreement by agreement with the lessor before the expiration of the lease term and receive the lease deposit returned from the lessor; in such a case, the transferee of the leased house does not succeed to the status of the lessor.\\n\\nMeanwhile, where a pledge over a claim against a third-party obligor is created as security for another person’s obligation, the pledgor may not, without the pledgee’s consent, extinguish the pledged right or make any change detrimental to the pledgee (Civil Act Article 352). This is to protect the pledgee’s exclusive control over the exchange value of the claim that is the object of the pledge (see Supreme Court Decision 97DA35375, decided 11 November 1997, and others). Accordingly, where the pledgor notifies the third-party obligor of the creation of the pledge, or the third-party obligor consents thereto, even if the third-party obligor, without the pledgee’s consent, performs the debt that is the object of the pledge, this cannot be asserted against the pledgee, and the pledgee may still directly demand performance of the debt from the third-party obligor pursuant to Civil Act Article 353(2) (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO5665, decided 29 April 2016). The same applies where the third-party obligor, without the pledgee’s consent, extinguishes the debt that is the object of the pledge by entering into a set-off agreement with the pledgor; in such a case as well, it should be deemed that this cannot be asserted against the pledgee, and the pledgee may still directly demand performance of the debt from the third-party obligor.\\n\\n2. a. According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n1) The non-party leased Apartment ○○○, Building △△△, in Siheung-si (address omitted) from the Defendant on 6 March 2012 for a lease deposit of KRW 110,000,000, and completed a change of address registration around that time.\\n\\n2) On 13 March 2012, while borrowing KRW 82,000,000 from the Plaintiff, the non-party created in favor of the Plaintiff a pledge over KRW 98,400,000 out of the claim for return of the lease deposit relating to the above apartment. On 6 April 2012, the Defendant consented to the creation of the above pledge vis-à-vis the Plaintiff, and agreed that, in the event of returning the lease deposit due to the expiration of the lease term, etc., it would directly return to the Plaintiff, within the amount subject to the pledge, the lease deposit corresponding to the above loan principal and interest, etc.\\n\\n3) On 30 June 2012, the Defendant entered into a sales contract to sell the apartment at issue to the non-party for KRW 155,000,000, and agreed to receive from the non-party the balance remaining after deducting the lease deposit of KRW 110,000,000 and the amount of the obligation borrowed by using the apartment at issue as security, etc., from the sales price of KRW 155,000,000; after completing the settlement under the above sales contract, it completed the ownership transfer registration procedure concerning the apartment at issue in favor of the non-party on 2 July 2012.\\n\\nb. In light of the foregoing facts and the legal principles stated above, the non-party, who was a lessee with opposability, purchased the apartment at issue from the Defendant, the lessor, and at the same time agreed to terminate the lease agreement and set off the claim for the purchase price against the claim for return of the deposit; therefore, the non-party does not succeed to the status of the lessor. Furthermore, since the Defendant consented to the creation of the pledge as the third-party obligor for the pledge, even if the Defendant, without the Plaintiff’s consent as pledgee, extinguished the obligation to return the lease deposit concerning the apartment at issue, which is the object of the pledge, by entering into a set-off agreement with the non-party, who created the pledge, this cannot be asserted against the Plaintiff, and the Plaintiff should be deemed to remain entitled to directly demand return of the lease deposit from the Defendant.\\n\\n3. Nevertheless, the court below, to the contrary, premised that the non-party succeeded unchanged to the status of the lessor from the Defendant by acquiring ownership of the apartment at issue, and then held that, in cases where ownership of real property and lease rights vest in the same person, the lease right is in principle extinguished by merger, but if that lease right satisfies the requirements for opposability, the proviso to Civil Act Article 191(1), which is an exception to the principle of extinguishment of real rights by merger, applies, and thus the sale of the apartment at issue cannot be deemed to have extinguished the non-party’s claim for return of the lease deposit or to have brought about any change detrimental to the Plaintiff, who is the pledgee. The court below’s determination contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning a transferee’s succession to the lessor’s status and the restriction on disposition of rights by the pledgor under the former Housing Lease Protection Act. The ground of appeal asserting this point is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2018DA21326]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Where the pledgor notifies the third debtor of the fact that a pledge has been created, or the third debtor gives consent thereto, pursuant to Article 349(1) of the Civil Act, if the third debtor satisfies the debt that is the object of the pledge without the pledgee’s consent, the third debtor may not assert such payment against the pledgee, and the pledgee may still directly demand payment of the debt from the third debtor (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DA265689, rendered on December 27, 2018). Even where, with respect to the claim that is the object of the pledge, a seizure and assignment order is issued upon the application of the pledgor’s general creditor, if the pledgee had satisfied the requirements for opposability prescribed in Article 349(1) of the Civil Act by means of a document bearing a certified date prior to the date on which such order was served, the assignee creditor merely acquires the claim subject to the pledge, and the third debtor may not assert against the pledgee that it has paid the assignee creditor.\\n\\n2. The court below, on the ground that, because the Plaintiff had obtained a document bearing a certified date from the lessor, who was the third debtor, at the time it established a security pledge over the claim for return of the lease deposit, even if the Defendant, who received the seizure and assignment order later, had received the lease deposit, the Plaintiff could still demand payment of the lease deposit from the lessor, rejected the Plaintiff’s assertion that the Defendant had obtained unjust enrichment by infringing the security pledge. In light of the legal principle seen above, such determination by the court below is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misapprehending the law concerning the priority of a pledge over a claim. The Supreme Court Decision 2009DA43621, rendered on October 15, 2009, invoked by the Plaintiff in the grounds of appeal, concerns a different matter and is not appropriate for application to this case.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

{"[2020DA296840]": "We decide the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the case\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts can be found.\\na. Korea Citibank Inc. received and completed registration of a mortgage with a maximum secured amount of KRW 520,000,000 on 2007. 12. 17., and a mortgage with a maximum secured amount of KRW 195,000,000 on 2008. 2. 27., from the debtor, the non-party, with respect to the real properties A, B, and C listed in Schedule 1 attached to the first-instance judgment (hereinafter referred to as \"the real properties at issue\"). On 2015. 4. 15., Onion Asset Management Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as \"Onion Asset Management\") acquired each of the mortgages at issue by reason of assignment of claims and completed the registration of transfer of those mortgages.\\nb. On 2015. 4. 15., Onion Asset Management entered into a general loan agreement (hereinafter referred to as \"the First Loan Agreement\") with JB Woori Capital Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as \"JB Woori Capital\"), under which it borrowed KRW 470,000,000 at a contracted interest rate of 7% per annum, a delay damages rate of 16.5% per annum, and a repayment term of 1 year. Onion Asset Management established in favor of JB Woori Capital a pledge over a mortgage-secured claim with a claim amount of KRW 520,000,000 and a pledge over a mortgage-secured claim with a claim amount of KRW 195,000,000 (hereinafter collectively referred to as \"the pledges over the mortgage-secured claims at issue\") and completed the supplementary registration thereof; at that time, only the contracted interest of 7% per annum was entered in the register, and default damages were not entered. Onion Asset Management sent the notice of establishment of pledge with such content to the non-party on 2015. 4. 20., and around that time the notice reached the non-party.\\nc. On 2016. 5. 30., the Defendant entered into a contract (hereinafter referred to as \"the Second Loan Agreement\") providing for a loan of KRW 300,000,000 to Onion Asset Management, etc., at an interest rate of 25.2% per annum, a delinquency interest rate of 27.9% per annum, and a loan maturity date of 2016. 10. 30. On 2016. 5. 31., the Defendant, in lieu of Onion Asset Management, repaid to JB Woori Capital the remaining balance of KRW 300,000,000 of the debt under the First Loan Agreement, and then received transfer of the pledges over the mortgage-secured claims at issue from JB Woori Capital by reason of assignment of claims dated 2016. 5. 31., after which the supplementary registration thereof was completed. JB Woori Capital prepared for the Defendant a certificate stating, \"I confirm that, by subrogated payment, the pledges over the mortgage-secured claims at issue and all related rights are transferred.\" On 2016. 7. 8., JB Woori Capital sent the non-party a notice of pledge and assignment of claims with the above content, and around that time the notice reached the non-party.\\nd. The real properties at issue were sold on 2018. 10. 1. in the non-judicial foreclosure sale proceedings for real estate. On 2019. 3. 8., the Defendant submitted in the non-judicial foreclosure proceedings a statement of claim describing \"Claim amount: KRW 533,442,739 [principal KRW 300,000,000 + interest KRW 233,442,739 (27.9% per annum on the principal from 2016. 5. 30. to 2019. 3. 13.)],\" and in the distribution proceedings received KRW 520,000,000 as the pledgee over the mortgage claim of the first-ranked mortgage and KRW 13,442,739 as the pledgee over the mortgage claim of the second-ranked mortgage.\\ne. The Plaintiffs, who were subordinate pledgees over mortgage-secured claims on the real properties at issue, appeared on the distribution date and objected to the amount to be distributed to the Defendant, and thereafter filed the present action objecting to distribution.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 1 of the reasons for final appeal\\nThe court below did not accept the Plaintiffs' assertion that \"because only the contracted interest rate of 7% is entered in the register with respect to the pledges over the mortgage-secured claims at issue, the Defendant, who received the pledge by transfer, has a preferential right of repayment only within the scope of the contracted interest rate and cannot receive preferential repayment for default damages exceeding that.\"\\nArticle 334, main sentence, of the Civil Act, which is applied mutatis mutandis to a pledge of rights pursuant to Article 335 of the Civil Act, provides that \"a pledge secures the principal, interest, penalty, expenses for enforcement of the pledge, expenses for preservation of the object of the pledge, and claims for damages arising from non-performance of obligations or defects in the object of the pledge.\" Article 76(1) of the Real Estate Registration Act provides that, when a registrar registers a pledge over a claim secured by a mortgage pursuant to Article 348 of the Civil Act, the registrar shall record, in addition to the matters prescribed in Article 48 of the Real Estate Registration Act, \"the amount of the claim or the maximum secured amount of the claim, the name or title and address or business office location of the debtor, and, where there is an agreement on the due date and interest, the details thereof,\" and does not prescribe default damages on the claim as a matter of registration. In light of such circumstances, even if the default damages on the claim were not separately entered in the register, it cannot be deemed that the scope of the secured claim for the pledge over the mortgage-secured claim is limited to the contracted interest entered in the register.\\nExamining the reasons for the judgment of the court below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the scope of the secured claim for the pledge over the mortgage-secured claim, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n3. As to Ground 2 of the reasons for final appeal\\na. The court below determined as follows.\\nBecause the Defendant entered into the Second Loan Agreement with Onion Asset Management, etc., it may exercise not only the right of subrogation as a person who performed the debt by subrogated payment of the debt under the First Loan Agreement, but also the claim under the Second Loan Agreement. In light of the contents of the statement of claim submitted by the Defendant in the distribution proceedings at issue, the Defendant may be deemed to have exercised the claim under the Second Loan Agreement in the distribution proceedings at issue. Therefore, up to the total amount of the pledges established, KRW 715,000,000 (= KRW 520,000,000 + KRW 195,000,000), the Defendant may receive preferential repayment of the principal claim under the Second Loan Agreement of KRW 300,000,000 and the interest and default damages thereon at the contracted interest rate.\\nb. However, the foregoing determination of the court below cannot be accepted as it stands for the following reasons.\\n(1) A person who performed for the debtor may, at the time of performance, with the creditor's consent, be subrogated to the creditor (Civil Act Article 480(1)). Where a third party performs the debt for the debtor and thereby acquires a right of reimbursement against the debtor, the creditor's former claim and the rights concerning its security transfer by operation of law to the person who performed, while maintaining their identity, to the extent of the right of reimbursement (see Supreme Court Decision 95DA11009, rendered on 1997. 11. 14., etc.).\\n(2) By subrogated payment to JB Woori Capital of the remaining balance of KRW 300,000,000 of the debt under the First Loan Agreement for Onion Asset Management, the Defendant acquired a right of reimbursement against the debtor Onion Asset Management, and to that extent the former rights of JB Woori Capital concerning the claim under the First Agreement and its security transfer by operation of law to the Defendant while maintaining their identity. The pledges over the mortgage-secured claims at issue received by the Defendant are valid within the scope of securing the above claim for reimbursement, and the secured claim is the original claim, that is, the claim under the First Loan Agreement extinguished by the performance of the subrogated payer.\\n(3) There is no basis for deeming that, beyond the Defendant's claim for reimbursement, the pledges over the mortgage-secured claims at issue secure the claim under the Second Loan Agreement, which is Onion Asset Management's debt to the Defendant. However, if there was a concurrence of intent between the Defendant and Onion Asset Management that the pledges over the mortgage-secured claims at issue would secure the claim under the Second Loan Agreement, there may be room to view this as an agreement to use the registration; but even upon examination of the record, no assertion or proof was made as to the existence or effect, etc. of such agreement.\\n(4) The court below should have exercised its power to explain by urging assertions and proof as to the basis on which the pledges over the mortgage-secured claims at issue secure the claim under the Second Loan Agreement in excess of the claim for reimbursement, and then, on that basis, examined and determined the scope of the secured claim for the pledges over the mortgage-secured claims at issue.\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below concluded, without any particular basis, that the claim under the Second Loan Agreement became the secured claim for the pledges over the mortgage-secured claims at issue, and determined that the Defendant should be distributed the full amount of the claim under the Second Loan Agreement.\\nThe judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending, inter alia, the legal principles concerning the secured obligation of a security right acquired by subrogation and by failing to conduct the necessary examination. The grounds for final appeal by the Plaintiffs pointing this out are well founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nThe portion of the judgment of the court below that went against the Plaintiffs is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged, with the concurrence of all participating Justices."}

question: Which of the following is the correct combination of the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (×) regarding statutory superficies in X land? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law applies.) (a) After A established a mortgage in B’s name with respect to X land owned by A, A constructed a Y building on X land with B’s consent. If the mortgage is enforced and C acquires ownership of X land, A acquires a statutory superficies under Article 366 of the Civil Act. (b) After C, A’s creditor, provisionally attached the Y building owned by A on X land owned by B, B acquired ownership of the Y building. If principal seizure and compulsory auction proceedings based on the above provisional attachment proceed and D acquires ownership of the Y building, D acquires a customary superficies. (c) A, after making a provisional registration in B’s name in order to secure a claim against B with respect to X land owned by A, thereafter constructed a Y building on X land. If B later completes the principal registration based on the above provisional registration, A does not acquire a customary superficies. (d) Where A and B co-owned X land and Y building in equal 1/2 shares, and A donated his co-ownership share in the Y building to C, C acquires a customary superficies.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2003DA26051]": "1. As to Ground 1 of the reasons for appeal\\n\\nThe statutory superficies under Article 366 of the Civil Act is recognized only where a building exists on the land that is the object of the mortgage from the time the mortgage is created, and where, after a mortgage is created on land on which no building exists, the creator of the mortgage by way of security builds a building thereon and, by reason of auction, the land and the building thereon come to have different owners, not only is the statutory superficies provided for in the above Article not recognized, but customary statutory superficies is also not recognized (see Supreme Court Decisions 87DAKA869 rendered on 1987. 12. 8., 92DA20330 rendered on 1993. 6. 25., 95DA24524 rendered on 1995. 12. 26., etc.). However, if, at the time a mortgage is created with respect to land, a building thereon was under construction by the landowner, and even if it had not yet reached the extent that it could be regarded, as a matter of social convention, as an independent building, where construction had progressed to the extent that the size and type of the building could be externally anticipated, it is appropriate to recognize the establishment of statutory superficies, because the mortgagee can foresee the completed building and therefore does not suffer unexpected loss by recognizing statutory superficies, and because there is also a social and economic need to preserve the building (see Supreme Court Decision 92DA7221 rendered on 1992. 6. 12.).\\n\\nIf, at the time a mortgage is created with respect to land, construction of a building by the landowner had not yet commenced on the land, even if the mortgagee, at the time a mortgage is created with respect to land on which no building exists, consented to the landowner’s construction of a building, such circumstance is a subjective matter and cannot be publicized, so it is unknown to a third party who purchases the land at auction; therefore, if statutory superficies were recognized on the basis of such circumstance, the legal relations would become highly unclear, including harm to the legal stability of third parties seeking to acquire ownership of the land, and accordingly statutory superficies should be deemed not to arise.\\n\\nAs duly determined by the court below, the land at issue was in a vacant lot state at the time the mortgage by way of security dated 1996. 8. 30. and the mortgage by way of security dated 1996. 8. 31. were created, and the building at issue had not even commenced construction; thus, with respect to the land at issue, ownership of which passed to Non-Party 1 by reason of a successful bid in the compulsory auction proceedings based on the mortgage by way of security dated 1996. 8. 30., there is no room to recognize statutory superficies for the ownership of the building at issue or customary statutory superficies, and even if, as the Defendant contends, Non-Party 2, who was the owner of the land at issue, had obtained the mortgagee’s consent to the construction of the building at issue at the time the mortgage by way of security dated 1996. 8. 30. was created with respect to the land at issue, statutory superficies would not arise. The court below’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no error of law concerning the formation of statutory superficies or customary statutory superficies, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 2 of the reasons for appeal\\n\\nThe court below determined that, even if Non-Party 1 bid for the land at issue for an amount less than one-half of the appraised value in anticipation of statutory superficies, and even if the Plaintiff purchased the land at issue cheaply from Non-Party 1, such circumstances alone do not mean that the claim for removal of the building at issue is contrary to the principle of good faith or constitutes an abuse of rights.\\n\\nUpon examination of the record, the court below’s above determination is proper, and there is no error of law as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are to be borne by the losing party, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2009DA62059]": "We examine the grounds of appeal, and the contents of the supplemental statement of grounds for appeal submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal has elapsed are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding Ground 1 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe lower court, upon comprehensively considering the evidence admitted, found that Non-Party 1, using his own labor and materials, constructed on the land described in Item 1 of the attached list to the lower court judgment (hereinafter referred to as “the Land at Issue”) the buildings described in Items 10 through 13 of the same list and the portion of the building described in Item 14 of the same list (hereinafter referred to as “the Buildings in Items 10 through 13 at Issue and the Portion of the Building in Item 14 at Issue”), and then held that Non-Party 1, who newly constructed the above buildings, originally acquired ownership thereof. In light of the record, the lower court’s above fact-finding and determination are justifiable and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in that it did not violate logic or the rules of experience and did not exceed the limits of free evaluation of evidence, nor did it err in its understanding of the legal doctrine concerning the original acquisition of a building.\\n\\n2. Regarding Grounds 2, 3, and 4 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nA. As to the portion concerning Defendants 1, 2, 3, 6, 5, and 7\\n\\nWhen land and a building thereon, which had belonged to the ownership of the same person, come to have different owners as a result of sale, gift, compulsory auction, public auction under the National Tax Collection Act, or the like, the owner of the building acquires a customary statutory superficies right for the ownership of the building against the owner of the land, unless there is a special agreement to demolish the building. And for a customary statutory superficies right to arise, it is sufficient that, at the time when ownership of the land or the building thereon validly changed, the same person owned both the land and the building thereon.\\n\\nMeanwhile, where ownership of land or a building thereon is transferred to the purchaser in the compulsory auction procedure, the existence of a customary statutory superficies right must be determined not based on the time when the purchaser acquires ownership upon full payment of the purchase price, but based on whether the land and the building thereon belonged to the same person at the time when the effect of seizure arises by the order commencing compulsory auction; and where a provisional seizure had been made on the land or building thereon that became the object of compulsory auction before the order commencing compulsory auction, and such provisional seizure was transformed into principal seizure by the order commencing compulsory auction and the auction procedure proceeded, the existence of a customary statutory superficies right must be determined based on whether the land and the building thereon belonged to the same person at the time when the effect of the initial provisional seizure arose (see Supreme Court en banc Decision dated October 18, 2012, 2010DA52140, etc.).\\n\\nFurthermore, where a mortgage had been created on land or a building thereon that became the object of compulsory auction before seizure for compulsory auction or provisional seizure preceding such seizure, and the mortgage is extinguished later by reason of the compulsory auction, if the existence of a customary statutory superficies right were to be determined based on whether the land and the building thereon belonged to the same owner at some specific time after the establishment of the mortgage, then the mortgagee, despite having evaluated the collateral value of the land or building thereon at the time the mortgage was established, would, due to external and accidental circumstances that the owner of the land or building thereon changed after the creation of the mortgage, obtain an unexpected benefit or suffer a loss by acquiring collateral whose value had become unjustly higher or lower than what it had originally ascertained. Accordingly, the existence of a customary statutory superficies right should be determined based on whether the land and the building thereon belonged to the same person at the time the mortgage was established.\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the lower court judgment and the evidence duly admitted and examined by the lower court, ① Non-Party 2, around June 2003, entrusted to Non-Party 1 the construction of a four-unit multifamily house on the Land at Issue owned by Non-Party 2 and obtained a building permit, and Non-Party 1 began the construction of the above multifamily house around that time; ② thereafter, Non-Party 2 transferred the Land at Issue to Non-Party 1, and registration was transferred in the name of Non-Party 1 on September 8, 2003; ③ accordingly, on September 8, 2003, Non-Party 1, while taking out a loan from Chohung Bank by using the Land at Issue, which had become his own property, and the like as joint collateral, established the No. 1 mortgage over the Land at Issue; at that time, construction on the Land at Issue had already progressed to the stage of the structural work of the third floor of a building consisting of one basement floor and four above-ground floors; ④ thereafter, one multifamily house divided into the Buildings in Items 10 through 13 at Issue and the Portion of the Building in Item 14 at Issue was constructed on the Land at Issue; and by around October to December 2004, when some persons had completed the resident registration transfer and began residing there, the form of the building was almost complete; ⑤ with respect to the Land at Issue and the like, real estate compulsory auction proceeded under Seoul Northern District Court Case No. 2004TAGYEONG41262, 2005TAGYEONG4932, and 2005TAGYEONG38461, and the Plaintiff purchased the Land at Issue and the like in the above auction procedure and fully paid the purchase price on April 25, 2007; ⑥ with respect to the Buildings in Items 10 through 13 at Issue among the multifamily house constructed on the Land at Issue, as of May 11, 2005, each registration of preservation of ownership was completed in the name of Non-Party 2, the nominal permit holder, at the request of creditors’ applications for provisional seizure and the like by court commission; thereafter, in Seoul Central District Court Case No. 2005GAHAP84230, brought by Defendants 1, 2, 6, 5, and 7, Non-Party 3, and Non-Party 4, on April 11, 2006, a decision in lieu of conciliation was rendered ordering Non-Party 2 to implement, in favor of Non-Party 1, the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership of the above buildings on the ground of restoration of true title; ⑦ pursuant to the contents of the above decision, with respect to the Buildings in Items 10, 12, and 13 at Issue, registration of transfer of ownership was completed in the name of Non-Party 1 on August 6, 2007, and on the same day registration was transferred in the names of seven persons, including Defendants 1, etc., with respect to each 1/7 share of the above buildings; among them, with respect to Non-Party 4’s share, registration was transferred again on August 14, 2007, to Non-Party 5, the father of Defendant 4; and with respect to Building No. 11 at Issue, in Seoul Northern District Court Case No. 2005GADAN38628, brought by Defendant 3, who was to receive it in satisfaction by way of performance in kind from Non-Party 1, against Non-Party 2 by subrogating Non-Party 1, registration of transfer of ownership was completed in the name of Defendant 3 on December 28, 2006 pursuant to a decision in lieu of conciliation; ⑧ the Portion of the Building in Item 14 at Issue is a common area of the multifamily house on the Land at Issue, and is jointly owned by the owners of the exclusive sections; and Defendants 4 and Non-Party 5 are in possession of Building No. 10 at Issue, while Defendant 3 is in possession of Building No. 11 at Issue.\\n\\nIn light of the above legal doctrine and the above factual relations, the mortgage right in favor of Chohung Bank had originally been established on the Land at Issue before the order commencing the compulsory auction at issue regarding the Land at Issue; at the time the above mortgage right was established with respect to the Land at Issue, construction of a building on the land by Non-Party 1, the owner of the Land at Issue, had progressed to the extent that its scale and type could outwardly be anticipated; and thereafter, insofar as, in around October 2004, before the purchaser, the Plaintiff, fully paid the purchase price in the auction procedure, the building had already satisfied the requirements for a building as an independent real property, it is reasonable to view that both the Land at Issue and the building thereon belonged to the ownership of Non-Party 1 from the time the mortgage right was established; accordingly, with respect to the Land at Issue, a customary statutory superficies right arose for the Buildings in Items 10 through 13 at Issue that were constructed as a result of completion of the new construction work then in progress at the time the mortgage right was established, and thus, with respect to the Buildings in Items 10, 12, and 13 at Issue, Non-Party 1, the owner of the above buildings at the time of full payment of the purchase price, acquired the customary statutory superficies right, while with respect to Building No. 11 at Issue, it is reasonable to view that Defendant 3, who had completed a valid registration of transfer of ownership conforming to the substantive legal relationship regarding the above building at the time of full payment of the purchase price, acquired the customary statutory superficies right.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Plaintiff’s claim for demolition of the buildings on the Land at Issue owned by Defendants 1, 2, 6, 5, 7, etc., who purchased the Buildings in Items 10, 12, and 13 at Issue from Non-Party 1, who acquired a customary statutory superficies right over the Land at Issue, and are in a position to seek implementation of the registration procedure for creation of a customary statutory superficies right in favor of the Plaintiff, or against Defendant 3, the holder of the customary statutory superficies right, cannot be permitted under the principle of good faith and fair dealing.\\n\\nB. As to the portion concerning Defendant 4\\n\\nDefendant 4’s argument is to the effect that, since he acquired Building No. 10 at Issue from Non-Party 1 on March 21, 2004, he thereby acquired from Non-Party 1 the statutory superficies right under Civil Act Article 366 or a customary statutory superficies right, and therefore the Plaintiff’s claim is contrary to the principle of good faith and fair dealing. However, in light of the factual relations seen above, Non-Party 1 could not have acquired the above statutory superficies right for the ownership of Building No. 10 at Issue on March 21, 2004, before the building on the Land at Issue satisfied the requirements for a building as an independent real property; accordingly, it cannot be said that Defendant 4 acquired from Non-Party 1 the statutory superficies right as alleged. Nevertheless, as seen above, Defendants 6, 1, 2, 5, and 7 and Non-Party 5, the father of Defendant 4, own each 1/7 share of Building No. 10 at Issue; and, as noted above, insofar as the Plaintiff cannot seek demolition of the above building and delivery of the Land at Issue, which is the site thereof, against the shareholders, including Defendant 6, who hold the customary statutory superficies right, even if Defendant 4, who is not the owner of the building, is in possession of the above building, the Plaintiff, as the owner of the Land at Issue, cannot seek against Defendant 4, the possessor of the above building, that he vacate the above building as the removal of interference based on his ownership, because the ownership of the Land at Issue is not being obstructed in its smooth realization by such possession.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, although there are some improper or insufficient points in the lower court’s statement of reasons, the conclusion of the lower court, which dismissed the Plaintiff’s claim, is proper, and there is no illegality that affected the judgment result, such as an error in understanding the legal doctrine concerning customary statutory superficies, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court involved."}

{"[2018DA218601]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\nA. On 1991. 12. 31., the Plaintiff and the Plaintiff’s grandfather, the late Non-Party 1 (hereinafter referred to as “the deceased”), completed registration of transfer of ownership in one-half shares each with respect to a site in Jongno-gu, Seoul (address omitted) (hereinafter referred to as “the land at issue”) and a house, etc. thereon (hereinafter referred to as “the building at issue”).\\n\\nB. Among the building at issue, the Plaintiff’s share was transferred on 1994. 7. 15. to Non-Party 2, then again through the Plaintiff on 2002. 12. 10., and then on 2005. 6. 22. to Defendant 1, the Plaintiff’s paternal uncle, while the deceased’s share was transferred on 2006. 11. 14. to Defendant 2 incorporated foundation (hereinafter referred to as “the Defendant Foundation”), and currently the Defendants co-own one-half shares each in the building at issue.\\n\\nC. After the deceased died on 2006. 11. 26., as to the deceased’s share in the land at issue, Defendant 1 completed registration of transfer of ownership on 2012. 10. 26. on the ground of inheritance by judgment, and then completed registration of transfer of ownership in favor of the Defendant Foundation on 2013. 4. 8. on the ground of gift, and currently the Plaintiff and the Defendant Foundation co-own the land at issue in one-half shares each.\\n\\n2. The lower court recognized that, as the Plaintiff and the deceased co-owned the land at issue and the building, and then the Plaintiff’s building share was transferred to Defendant 1 and the deceased’s building share was transferred to the Defendant Foundation, a customary legal superficies with respect to the land at issue was established in favor of the Defendants, who are the co-owners of the building at issue, and determined that they are obligated to pay ground rent to the Plaintiff, the share owner of the said land.\\n\\n3. However, the lower court’s determination is difficult to uphold for the following reasons.\\n\\nA. If, where both the land and the building thereon are each subject to co-ownership, one of the co-owners of the land and the building gifts only his or her building share to another so that the owner of the land and the building becomes different, and this is deemed to have established a customary legal superficies for the ownership of the building with respect to the entire land, this would amount to allowing one co-owner of the land to engage in a dispositive act of setting a superficies even over the shares of the other co-owners other than his or her own share, without relying on the will of the other co-owners, which is improper (see Supreme Court Decision dated 1993. 4. 13., 92DA55756; Supreme Court Decision dated 2014. 9. 4., 2011DA73038, 73045, etc.). Therefore, it cannot be acknowledged that a customary legal superficies with respect to the land at issue was established in favor of the said Defendant merely because Plaintiff, who is one of the co-owners of the land and building at issue, transferred the co-owned share of the said building to Defendant 1, thereby making the owner of the land and the building different.\\n\\nB. Furthermore, a customary legal superficies is acknowledged on the premise that land and the building thereon, which were owned by the same person, have become owned by different persons due to sale, gift, or any other lawful cause (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2021. 7. 8., 2017DA204247; Supreme Court en banc Decision dated 2022. 7. 21., 2017DA236749, etc.). However, when the Defendant Foundation received the one-half share of the building at issue, the land at issue was being co-owned by the Plaintiff and the deceased in one-half shares each, and the building at issue was being co-owned by Defendant 1 and the deceased in one-half shares each, so it cannot even be said that the land and the building themselves were owned by the same person; thus, a customary legal superficies cannot be acknowledged to have been established also against the Defendant Foundation.\\n\\n4. Nevertheless, the lower court, contrary to the foregoing, ordered payment of ground rent on the premise that a customary legal superficies with respect to the land at issue had been established in favor of the Defendants, and in so doing erred by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning customary legal superficies, thereby affecting the judgment. The Defendants’ argument in the grounds of appeal pointing out this error has merit.\\n\\n5. Therefore, without deciding the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the lower court judgment and remand the case to the lower court for further proceedings and determination, and so decide as follows by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[94DA5458]": "We examine Ground 1 of the reasons for appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below found as facts that each parcel of land described in the attached list to the judgment below (hereinafter referred to as “the respective parcels of land at issue”) is owned by the Plaintiff, and that the Defendant owns the building described in the attached list to the judgment below on the respective parcels of land at issue (hereinafter referred to as “the building at issue”) and is occupying and using the respective parcels of land at issue; that the respective parcels of land at issue were originally owned by Non-party 1, and were provided as collateral by said Non-party 1, whereby provisional registrations for the preservation of the right to claim transfer of ownership had been completed in the name of Non-party 2 on 1982.5.21. with respect to the first parcel of land at issue, and in the name of Non-party 3 on 1981.4.24. with respect to the second parcel of land at issue; thereafter, ownership transfer registrations with respect to the respective parcels of land at issue were completed in the names of Non-party 4 on 1984.5.12. and Non-party 5 on 1985.3.26., respectively, but as principal registrations were completed based on the above provisional registrations on 1985.4.27. with respect to the first parcel of land at issue and on 1985.10.11. with respect to the second parcel of land at issue, the respective ownership transfer registrations completed in the names of said Non-party 4 and Non-party 5 were all cancelled ex officio; that thereafter, on 1988.5.27., ownership transfer registration with respect to the respective parcels of land at issue was completed in the Plaintiff’s name; that, on the other hand, the building at issue was completed by said Non-party 4 on 1984.10.2., and after ownership preservation registration was completed in his name on 1984.10.29., it was transferred to said Non-party 5 on 1985.3.26.; thereafter, in the forced auction proceedings applied for by Non-party 6 on 1985.8.10., the Defendant successfully bid for it on 1986.4.25.; and on the basis that there was no evidence to support that the above provisional registrations in the names of Non-party 2 and Non-party 3 with respect to the respective parcels of land at issue were provisional registrations for collateral and thus invalid because the secured obligations had all been extinguished, nor was there any evidence to support a finding that the building at issue owned by Non-party 1 already existed on the respective parcels of land at issue before the above provisional registrations, and that there was no evidence whatsoever to support a finding that the respective parcels of land at issue and the building at issue belonged to the same person at the time the Defendant purchased the building at issue in the above forced auction proceedings or at the time of the above provisional registrations, rejected all of the Defendant’s argument that either the Defendant or Non-party 1, Non-party 5, etc. had acquired a customary statutory superficies for the building at issue with respect to the respective parcels of land at issue.\\n\\nWhere a provisional registration was completed on vacant land in order to secure a claim, and thereafter the landowner constructed a building thereon, if principal registration based on that provisional registration is later completed and the owner of the land and the building becomes different, recognizing a customary statutory superficies would greatly harm the interests of the person who originally completed the provisional registration for the purpose of securing the claim against the land, and therefore, absent special circumstances, it cannot be said that a customary statutory superficies for the above building arises. Accordingly, Non-party 5, who was the owner of the respective parcels of land and the building at the time principal registration was completed based on the above provisional registration, cannot be deemed to have acquired a customary statutory superficies.\\n\\nIn addition, since compulsory auction was initiated against the building at issue and a registration of seizure was completed, and during the course of the compulsory auction proceedings the principal registration was completed based on the above provisional registration for collateral established earlier with respect to the respective parcels of land at issue, it cannot be said that the Defendant, the successful bidder for the building at issue, acquired a customary statutory superficies for the building at issue with respect to the respective parcels of land at issue.\\n\\nThe lower court’s determination, which rejected all of the Defendant’s argument concerning customary statutory superficies on the same purport, is just and acceptable, and there is no illegality therein in misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning customary statutory superficies. The argument on this point is without merit.\\n\\nWe examine Ground 2 of the reasons for appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below found that on 1984.9.6. the Defendant leased the respective parcels of land at issue and the building at issue from Non-party 4, who was then the owner thereof, with a lease deposit of KRW 50,000,000 and a lease term of 5 years; that the Defendant, on 1986.4.25., purchased the building at issue in the above-noted forced auction proceedings and obtained ownership transfer registration therefor on 1987.7.3., and completed ownership transfer registration in the Defendant’s name with respect to the building at issue without registering the above leasehold right with respect to the respective parcels of land at issue; and held that, although the above leasehold right with respect to the respective parcels of land at issue has opposability under Article 622 of the Civil Act, since the above provisional registrations or the principal registrations based thereon with respect to the respective parcels of land at issue were all completed prior to the above ownership transfer registration in the Defendant’s name, who is the lessee with respect to the building at issue, the Defendant cannot, by virtue of the above leasehold right, oppose the holder of the above principal registration or the Plaintiff, who obtained ownership transfer registration with respect to the respective parcels of land at issue from such holder, and accordingly rejected the Defendant’s above argument.\\n\\nHowever, even according to the reasons stated in the judgment below, it is clear that the lease agreement concerning the respective parcels of land at issue concluded between the Defendant and said Non-party 4 was not a land lease agreement for the purpose of owning a building, and therefore the Defendant’s leasehold right with respect to the respective parcels of land at issue did not satisfy the opposability under Article 622 of the Civil Act. Although the reasons are different, the result of the lower court’s determination rejecting the Defendant’s above argument must be regarded as correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality in misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the opposability of a leasehold right with building registration under Article 622 of the Civil Act. Ultimately, the argument is without merit.\\n\\nWe examine Ground 3 of the reasons for appeal.\\n\\nIn order for a landowner’s exercise of ownership over the land to be deemed an abuse of rights, subjectively the purpose of exercising the right must be solely to inflict pain and cause damage on the other party, with no benefit whatsoever to the person exercising the right, and objectively the exercise of the right must be such that it can be seen as violating social order; unless such a case exists, even if the loss suffered by the other party as a result of the exercise of the right is markedly greater than the benefit obtained by the person exercising the right, such circumstance alone cannot constitute an abuse of rights.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below rejected the Defendant’s defense of abuse of rights on the ground that the Plaintiff’s claim in this case does not constitute an abuse of rights contrary to the principle of good faith; upon examination of the record, the above finding and determination of the court below are just and acceptable, and there is no illegality therein that affected the judgment by violating the rules of evidence or by misapprehending the legal doctrine on abuse of rights. The argument is also without merit.\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. The judgment is rendered as stated in the Disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following explanations concerning the creditor's avoidance action is incorrect? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, precedents shall apply)
A: Where, after ownership of real property has been transferred by a fraudulent act, a third party acquires rights such as a mortgage or superficies over the real property, the creditor may claim against the beneficiary avoidance of the fraudulent act and performance of the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership to the debtor.
B: Where A, around July 2023, title-trusted X real property, which was A's only asset, to his spouse B; and A, on the premise of terminating the said title-trust agreement, sold X real property to C, and by agreement among A, B, and C, completed registration of transfer of ownership from B directly to C, the sale between A and C may constitute a fraudulent act harming A's general creditors.
C: An act by which a debtor, with respect to real property that is his only asset, newly enters into a sale reservation in order to extend the peremptory period when the expiration of the peremptory period for the right to complete the reservation under the sale reservation is imminent may constitute a fraudulent act subject to the creditor's avoidance action.
D: Where, after a fraudulent act has occurred, a creditor, knowing that there is a ground for avoidance, assigns the claim to be preserved, and the assignee exercises the creditor's avoidance action to preserve that claim, whether the peremptory period has elapsed should be determined based on the day on which the assignor of that claim became aware of the ground for avoidance.
E: Where B, pursuant to a title-trust agreement concluded around July 2023 with his friend A, concluded a sales contract for X real property with C, the owner of X real property who did not know of the title trust, and after registration of transfer of ownership was effected in B's name, A, who was in a state of insolvency, became the de facto party and sold X real property to a third party, then A's act of sale becomes a fraudulent act against A's general creditors.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2007DA74874]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. The lower court, after citing the first-instance judgment and finding the facts as stated therein, determined that Non-party 1, because he was unable to enter into the sales contract directly due to lack of association member qualifications and other reasons, obtained the consent of his son-in-law, Non-party 2, entered into a sales contract with the Suji 2nd Hyundai Joint Housing Association (hereinafter referred to as “the Association in this case”) in the name of Non-party 2 for an apartment in Dongcheon Village, Dongcheon-dong, Yongin City, Hyundai 2nd Hometown (building and unit numbers omitted) (hereinafter referred to as “the Apartment in this case”), completed payment of the sales price, and then completed registration of preservation of ownership in the name of Non-party 2, the contract holder; accordingly, it inferred that a so-called contract title trust agreement (hereinafter referred to as “the title trust agreement in this case”) had been concluded between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2 in connection with the above sales contract, and it found it reasonable to regard the Association in this case, the other party to the sales contract, as having entered into the contract while unaware of the existence of the title trust agreement in this case and believing Non-party 2 to be the true purchaser.\\n\\nExamining the submitted evidence in light of the record, the above factual findings and determination by the lower court are justifiable, and there is no illegality such as a violation of the rules governing the assessment of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. With respect to real estate, where the main clause of Article 4(2) of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name applies and a registration of transfer of ownership in the name of the title trustee, who is the Debtor, is void, the real estate is not owned by the Debtor, and therefore it cannot be deemed property subject to liability that is made available for the joint security of the Debtor’s general creditors; even if the Debtor entered into a sales contract with a third party concerning such real estate and completed registration of transfer of ownership in that party’s favor, it cannot be said thereby to have caused a reduction in the Debtor’s property subject to liability, and thus it cannot be regarded as a fraudulent act harming the Debtor’s general creditors, nor can it be said that the Debtor had an intent to defraud (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2000. 3. 10., 99DA55069; Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2007. 12. 27., 2005DA54104). However, where the title trustor and the title trustee have entered into a so-called contract title trust agreement and the title trustee, as a party, has entered into a sales contract for real estate with an owner who is unaware of the existence of the title trust agreement, and thereafter completed registration of transfer of ownership of the real estate in the name of the title trustee pursuant to that sales contract, then notwithstanding the invalidity of the title trust agreement between the title trustor and the title trustee, the title trustee acquires full ownership of the relevant real estate pursuant to the proviso of Article 4(2) of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name, and merely bears an obligation toward the title trustor to return unjust enrichment in an amount equivalent to the purchase funds received from the title trustor (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2005. 1. 28., 2002DA66922). In such a case, the real estate acquired by the title trustee becomes property subject to liability that is made available for the joint security of the general creditors of the title trustee, who is the Debtor, and since the title trustor is nothing more than one of the monetary creditors in relation to the title trustee, where the title trustee’s property is insufficient to satisfy the entire debt, the act of the title trustee transferring the above real estate to the title trustor or a person designated by the title trustor constitutes, absent special circumstances, an act harming the interests of the other creditors and thus amounts to a fraudulent act in relation to the other creditors.\\n\\nThe argument in this part of the grounds of appeal is to the effect that Non-party 2 did not acquire ownership of the Apartment in this case and had an obligation to return it to the Association in this case or to Non-party 1, who subrogated to the Association; therefore, the transfer of the Apartment in this case to the Defendant designated by Non-party 1 as performance of that return obligation does not constitute a fraudulent act. However, as noted above, since the Association in this case entered into the contract while unaware of the existence of the title trust agreement in this case and believing Non-party 2 to be the true purchaser, notwithstanding that the title trust agreement in this case is void under Article 4(1) of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name, Non-party 2, as the title trustee, acquires full ownership of the Apartment in this case pursuant to the proviso of Article 4(2) of the same Act, and since the Apartment in this case becomes property subject to liability of Non-party 2 in relation to the general creditors, the act by which Non-party 2 sold and disposed of the Apartment in this case, his only property, to the Defendant, his brother-in-law, constitutes a fraudulent act against the Plaintiff, who is a creditor.\\n\\nThe lower court’s determination to the same effect is correct, and there is no illegality in the lower court judgment, such as an error in the legal principles concerning revocation of a fraudulent act, restitution of unjust enrichment, and Article 4 of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court decisions cited in the grounds of appeal concern different factual circumstances from this case and are not appropriate for application by analogy here.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing Defendant. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as set forth in the order."}

{"[2015DA56086]": "The grounds of appeal are determined (the statements in the supplemental brief of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. With respect to Ground 1 of the Grounds of Appeal\\n\\nA. (1) The appellate court, based on the evidence it admitted, found the facts as stated in its opinion and then held that it was reasonable to conclude that Nonparty 1, as the actual owner of the land and building at issue, had, by an implied title trust agreement with his wife, Nonparty 2, completed registration of transfer of ownership of the land at issue in the name of Nonparty 2, obtained a building permit for the building at issue in the name of Nonparty 2, and then completed registration of preservation of ownership in the name of Nonparty 2.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the above determination by the appellate court is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning the presumption of separate property acquired in the sole name of one spouse during marriage and the proof of a title trust agreement, or failure to conduct the necessary deliberation, or exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience.\\n\\n(2) Among the grounds of appeal concerning this part, the argument to the effect that the appellate court should also have examined whether the title trust agreement between Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 was for the purpose of tax evasion, evasion of compulsory execution, or avoidance of statutory restrictions is not a proper ground of appeal because it is being raised for the first time at the appellate stage.\\n\\nB. (1) A title trust agreement between spouses is valid absent special circumstances (see Article 8 of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name), and in such case the title truster may terminate the trust vis-à-vis the title trustee and, on the sole ground that the trust relationship has ended, demand performance of the registration procedure for transfer of title; moreover, on the ground of such termination and also based on ownership, the title truster may make such a demand (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2000DA55171 rendered on May 10, 2002). Furthermore, where the title trust relationship has ended in this manner, the title truster’s claim for registration of transfer of ownership against the title trustee becomes responsible property that is provided as common security to the general creditors of the title truster.\\n\\nHowever, where the title truster, on the premise of terminating such valid title trust agreement, directly disposes of the entrusted real estate to a third party and, by agreement with the title trustee and the third party, omits the intermediate registration and has registration of transfer of ownership completed directly from the title trustee to the third party, the title truster’s claim for registration of transfer of ownership against the title trustee, which constitutes responsible property, is extinguished as a result; if this causes the title truster’s liabilities to exceed his assets or worsens the state of insolvency, and the title truster was aware of such facts, then such juridical act of the title truster constitutes a fraudulent act that harms the general creditors of the title truster.\\n\\n(2) Examining the factual relationship found by the appellate court in light of the legal principles set forth above, it is to be deemed that the title trust relationship between Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 was terminated when Nonparty 1 directly sold the land and building at issue, which he had title-trusted to his wife, Nonparty 2, to the Defendant with the consent of Nonparty 2; as a result, the claim for registration of transfer of ownership that Nonparty 1 acquires thereby becomes responsible property provided as common security to the general creditors of the trustor, Nonparty 1; but because Nonparty 1, by agreement with Nonparty 2 and the Defendant, had registration of transfer of ownership completed directly from Nonparty 2 to the Defendant, the claim for registration of transfer of ownership, which is responsible property, was extinguished, and this caused Nonparty 1’s liabilities to exceed his assets or worsened the state of insolvency. Therefore, the above real estate sales contract constitutes a fraudulent act that harms the general creditors of Nonparty 1.\\n\\nThe portion of the appellate judgment that, contrary to the above, stated that the land and building at issue themselves were responsible property provided as common security to the general creditors of Nonparty 1 is not appropriate; however, the appellate court’s cancellation of the sales contract at issue as a fraudulent act and its order of monetary compensation as restitution is proper in conclusion, and there is no error that affected the judgment.\\n\\n2. With respect to Ground 2 of the Grounds of Appeal\\n\\nA. In determining at what point there was a juridical act constituting a fraudulent act, it should be carefully determined in view of the serious impact on the interests between the parties, and the time when the juridical act constituting the fraudulent act occurred should be determined based on the day on which such fraudulent act actually took place (see Supreme Court Decisions 2001DA73138, 73145 rendered on July 26, 2002); unless there are other special circumstances, one has no choice but to determine whether such fraudulent act actually took place by focusing on the date of cause of registration in the register, which appears to be based on a dispositive document (see Supreme Court Decision 2002DA41589 rendered on November 8, 2002).\\n\\nB. In light of the record, it is proper that the appellate court, by comprehensively considering the circumstances as found in its opinion based on the evidence it admitted, held that the sales contract at issue was concluded on July 6, 2012, the date of cause of registration in the register; and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or failing to conduct the necessary deliberation.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and the judgment is rendered as follows by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2016DA272311]": "Grounds for Final Appeal (the statements in the supplemental brief filed after the period for filing the statement of grounds for final appeal shall be considered to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal) are examined.\\n\\n1. With respect to the part of the lower judgment concerning revocation of the fraudulent act (contract establishing a mortgage)\\n(1) In the exercise of the creditor’s right of revocation, “the day on which the creditor became aware of the cause for revocation,” which is the starting point of the exclusion period, means the day on which the creditor became aware of the requirements for the creditor’s right of revocation, that is, the day on which the creditor became aware of the fact that the debtor had committed the fraudulent act while knowing that it would harm the creditor. In this context, in order to find that the creditor was aware of the cause for revocation, it is insufficient merely to know the fact that the debtor engaged in an act of disposing of property; rather, the creditor must know of the existence of the specific fraudulent act and furthermore know that the debtor had the intent to prejudice creditors. It cannot be presumed that the creditor was aware of the cause for revocation merely because the creditor knew the objective facts of the fraudulent act, and the burden of proof regarding the lapse of the exclusion period rests on the opposing party in the action to revoke the fraudulent act (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DA79320 rendered on March 27, 2014). Further, where, after a fraudulent act, the creditor transfers the preserved claim while being aware of the cause for revocation and the transferee exercises the creditor’s right of revocation in order to preserve that claim, the question whether the exclusion period has elapsed must be determined based on the day on which the transferor of that claim became aware of the cause for revocation.\\n\\nThe lower court, after presuming that whether the action to revoke the fraudulent act in this case, which was filed by the Plaintiff who acquired the loan claim after the fraudulent act for the purpose of preserving that claim, had been brought after the lapse of the exclusion period should be determined based on the Plaintiff, who is the transferee of that claim, held that the action in this case was lawful because the Plaintiff filed the action within 1 year from the day on which the Plaintiff became aware of the cause for revocation.
