Furthermore, as an alternative ground, the lower court held that even if the lapse of the exclusion period were to be determined based on the transferors of that claim, the action in this case is lawful because, since there is insufficient proof that the transferors knew of the cause for revocation before they sequentially transferred that claim, the action in this case was brought before the lapse of the exclusion period in any event.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles set forth above, the lower court should have first determined whether the transferors of the loan claim knew of the cause for revocation before the transfer of the claim, and if they did, should have determined whether the exclusion period had elapsed based on the transferors. Nevertheless, in the lower judgment, the court immediately determined whether the exclusion period had elapsed based on the Plaintiff, who is the transferee, before determining whether the transferors knew of the cause for revocation before the transfer of the claim. This was erroneous as it misapprehended the legal principles concerning the starting point of the exclusion period upon transfer of the preserved claim, as stated above.\\n\\nHowever, upon reviewing the record, the lower court’s alternative determination that there is insufficient proof that the transferors of the loan claim knew of the cause for revocation before the transfer of the claim is proper, and there is no error in that determination such as a violation of the rules of logic and experience, thereby exceeding the limits of the free evaluation of evidence, or a misapprehension of legal principles. Although the lower judgment contains the above-mentioned error in the statement of reasons, the lower court’s conclusion that the exclusion period had not elapsed is proper; accordingly, the above error in the lower court did not affect the judgment.\\n\\n(2) In an action to revoke a fraudulent act, the beneficiary’s bad faith is presumed, and thus the beneficiary must prove that, at the time of the relevant juristic act, the beneficiary did not know that it would harm creditors. In such case, whether the beneficiary knew that it would harm creditors must be reasonably determined in accordance with the rules of logic and experience, by comprehensively considering various circumstances such as the relationship between the debtor and the beneficiary, the content of the act of disposal between the debtor and the beneficiary, and the circumstances or motive leading thereto (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DA37001 rendered on April 26, 2013).\\n\\nThe lower court, after determining that the contract establishing a mortgage concluded by the Defendant with the nonparty, who was a joint guarantor of the loan claim at issue, constituted a fraudulent act, rejected the Defendant’s defense of good faith on the ground that there was insufficient proof that the Defendant, as beneficiary, did not know at the time of concluding the contract that it would harm creditors.\\n\\nUpon reviewing the record in light of the legal principles set forth above, the lower court’s above determination is proper. There is no error therein in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the beneficiary’s good faith in an action to revoke a fraudulent act.\\n\\n2. With respect to the part of the lower judgment concerning restitution to the original state (payment of money)\\n(1) Where a contract establishing a mortgage is revoked as a fraudulent act, if an auction proceeding has been conducted, a third party has acquired ownership, and the registration of the mortgage has been cancelled, restoration in kind is impossible, and thus restitution to the original state is ordered by way of compensation in value. In such case, if the distribution has already been completed and the beneficiary has received the distribution funds, the beneficiary is ordered to return the distribution funds; and if the distribution schedule has become final but the beneficiary has not actually received the distribution funds due to an injunction prohibiting payment of distribution funds obtained by the creditor, the assignment of the claim to payment of the distribution funds and notice of the assignment of that claim are ordered. If the creditor attended the distribution date and objected to the beneficiary’s distributive share, that creditor may file an action to revoke the fraudulent act as well as an action to object to distribution as a means of restitution to the original state (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DA90708 rendered on February 10, 2011).\\n\\n(2) The lower court found that in the case of the involuntary auction of real property 2015TAGYEONG9225 at the Busan District Court concerning the real property at issue, the registration of the Defendant’s mortgage was cancelled and the Defendant received 130,000,000 won as a mortgagee in distribution, and held that, as restitution to the original state following the revocation of the mortgage contract at issue, the Defendant is obligated to pay the above amount to the Plaintiff.\\n\\n(3) However, the lower court’s above determination is difficult to accept.\\n\\nAccording to the record, it can be seen that the distribution schedule for the above involuntary auction case, prepared to distribute the above money to the Defendant, was submitted as evidence in this case; however, the distribution schedule alone does not show whether the Defendant actually received the above money as distribution funds. Accordingly, the lower court should have examined whether the Defendant actually received the distribution funds and, based thereon, determined the method of restitution to the original state. Nevertheless, the lower court immediately held that the Defendant was obligated to pay the above money to the Plaintiff without properly examining such circumstances. In this lower judgment, there is an error of misapprehending the legal principles concerning the method of restitution to the original state following revocation of a fraudulent act and failing to conduct the necessary examination.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the part of the lower judgment concerning restitution to the original state (payment of money) is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination; the remainder of the final appeal is dismissed. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2017DA247190]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Article 564 of the Civil Act provides that, in a sale reservation, the right of the other party to the reservation to make a declaration of intent to complete the reservation and thereby cause the sale to take effect, that is, the right to complete the sale reservation, is a kind of right of formation, and where a period for exercise has been agreed between the parties, it must be exercised within that period, and where no agreement has been made, it must be exercised within 10 years from the time the reservation was formed; after the lapse of that period, the right to complete the reservation is extinguished by the lapse of the preclusive period (see Supreme Court Decision 91DA44766, 44773, decided July 28, 1992, Supreme Court Decision 2016DA42077, decided January 25, 2017, etc.).\\nWhere, in a state in which the right to complete the reservation under a sale reservation concerning real property owned by a debtor, which is the debtor’s only asset, is likely to be extinguished as the lapse of the preclusive period is imminent, the debtor newly enters into a sale reservation in order to extend the preclusive period, such act results in the debtor newly assuming a debt that the debtor would not have had to bear, and thus may constitute a fraudulent act subject to a creditor’s right of revocation.\\n\\n2. According to the judgment of the court below, the following facts can be found.\\n\\nA. The Plaintiff applied against the non-party to the Seoul Central District Court for a payment order in Case No. 2004CHA23149 concerning 3,475,528 won of payment made by subrogation, and on October 26, 2004, the above payment order became final and conclusive. Thereafter, in order to extend the statute of limitations, the Plaintiff filed a lawsuit against the same court in Case No. 2014GASO551128 seeking reimbursement, and on July 30, 2014, received a performance recommendation decision ordering payment of 3,475,528 won and delay damages thereon, and on August 21, 2014, this decision became final and conclusive.\\n\\nB. On September 5, 2005, the non-party entered into a sale reservation with the Defendant, his younger sister, concerning each real property listed in the attached list of the first-instance judgment (hereinafter referred to as “the real properties at issue”) (hereinafter referred to as “the first sale reservation at issue”), setting the sale price at 42,000,000 won and the exercise period for the right to complete the reservation at December 30, 2005, and providing that it could thereafter be exercised so long as the sale reservation remained validly in force. Thereafter, on September 20, 2005, the non-party completed, in the Defendant’s name, a provisional registration of the right to demand ownership transfer based on the first sale reservation at issue concerning the real properties at issue (hereinafter referred to as “the first provisional registration”).\\n\\nC. On April 6, 2015, the non-party entered into a sale reservation with the Defendant concerning the real properties at issue, setting the sale price at 42,000,000 won and the exercise period for the right to complete the reservation at June 30, 2015, and providing that it could thereafter be exercised so long as the sale reservation remained validly in force (hereinafter referred to as “the second sale reservation at issue”). On the same day, the non-party completed, in the Defendant’s name, a provisional registration of the right to demand ownership transfer based on the second sale reservation at issue (hereinafter referred to as “the second provisional registration”).\\n\\n3. A. The court below determined that the Defendant had the duty to implement the procedure for cancellation registration, on the ground of the lapse of the preclusive period, for the first provisional registration in favor of the non-party as of September 5, 2015. As the basis for this determination, the court below stated that the first sale reservation at issue did not specify the period by setting the exercise period for the right to complete the reservation as December 30, 2005 while providing that it could thereafter be exercised so long as the sale reservation remained validly in force, and therefore the right to complete the reservation was extinguished by the lapse of the preclusive period on September 5, 2015, 10 years after the date of the first sale reservation at issue.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the relevant legal principles, the court below’s determination contains no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the lapse of the preclusive period or the extinguishment of the subrogated right in the creditor’s subrogation right.\\n\\nB. The court below determined that the second sale reservation at issue between the Defendant and the non-party should be revoked, and that the Defendant had the duty to implement the procedure for cancellation registration of the second provisional registration in favor of the non-party. As the basis for this determination, the court below stated that, in a state in which the right to complete the reservation under the first sale reservation at issue concerning the real properties at issue, the non-party’s only asset, was likely to be extinguished as the lapse of the preclusive period was imminent, the non-party’s making the second sale reservation again with the Defendant concerning the real properties at issue constituted a fraudulent act.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the relevant legal principles, the court below’s determination is proper as being in accordance with the above legal principles. The court below’s determination contains no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in departing from the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of a fraudulent act and the starting point for calculating the preclusive period of the creditor’s right of revocation.\\n\\n4. Since the Defendant’s appeal is without merit, it is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices, as stated in the order."}

{"[2017DA265815]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Circumstances of the Case\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. On 2010. 2. 1., Non-party 1 entered into a sales contract with the Defendant concerning each of the real properties listed in the attached list to the first-instance judgment, which were the only assets registered in Non-party 1’s name (hereinafter referred to as “the real properties at issue”), and on the 4th of the same month completed each ownership transfer registration in favor of the Defendant, under receipt No. 2892 at the Gimje Registry Office of the Jeonju District Court (hereinafter referred to as “the ownership transfer registrations at issue”).\\n\\nb. (1) The Plaintiff is a creditor who, on 2011. 7. 25., filed an action against Non-party 1 seeking return of unjust enrichment, on the grounds, inter alia, that Non-party 1 had used the Plaintiff’s funds to acquire the real properties at issue, and who, on 2013. 5. 2., obtained a judgment in his favor ordering payment of 289,058,600 won and delay damages thereon in the appellate case, Gwangju High Court (Jeonju) case (Jeonju)2012NA1042.\\n\\n(2) On 2011. 7. 25., the Plaintiff filed an action against the Defendant with the Jeonju District Court, case No. 2011GAHAP4345, seeking revocation of a fraudulent act, etc.; and on 2014. 1. 16., in the appellate case, Gwangju High Court (Jeonju) case (Jeonju)2013NA1544 (oral argument concluded on 2013. 12. 19.), a judgment was rendered stating, “The first-instance judgment is reversed; the sales contract at issue is revoked; and the Defendant shall implement the procedures for cancellation registration of the ownership transfer registrations at issue in favor of Non-party 1.” That judgment became final and binding as rendered (hereinafter referred to as the “prior judgment”).\\n\\nc. However, on 2013. 12. 4., the Defendant completed a registration of creation of a mortgage, based on the mortgage creation agreement dated that day, in favor of Donggimje Agricultural Cooperative, and on 2014. 1. 17., completed a registration of creation of a mortgage, based on the mortgage creation agreement dated that day, in favor of Non-party 2, with respect to the real properties at issue.\\n\\nd. (1) Accordingly, on 2014. 3. 24., the Plaintiff filed the present action with the Jeonju District Court, case No. 2014GAHAP1804, seeking, as follows: ① as against Donggimje Agricultural Cooperative, Non-party 2, etc., an expression of intention to consent to the procedures for cancellation registration of the ownership transfer registrations at issue and implementation of the procedures for cancellation registration of the mortgage creation agreement concluded between the Defendant and Non-party 2 and the mortgage registration based thereon; and ② as against the Defendant, in the alternative, compensatory damages on the grounds of impossibility of performance of the obligations ordered in the prior judgment or impossibility of execution of the prior judgment, etc.\\n\\n(2) In the appellate instance, the Plaintiff withdrew the action against Donggimje Agricultural Cooperative and Non-party 2, and as against the Defendant amended the prayer for relief and the cause of action to seek: ① principally, value compensation on the ground that the sales contract at issue had been revoked as a fraudulent act; ② as the first alternative, compensatory damages on the ground that the Defendant’s obligation to cancel the ownership transfer registrations was impossible to perform or impossible to execute; ③ as the second alternative, damages on the ground that the Defendant’s act of creating the mortgage constituted an unlawful act; and ④ as the third alternative, return of unjust enrichment.\\n\\nOn 2015. 11. 12., the appellate court rendered a judgment [Gwangju High Court (Jeonju) case (Jeonju)2015NA231], in which it: ① dismissed the principal claim and the first alternative claim on the ground that, although the Plaintiff had filed an action seeking revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration to the original condition and the prior judgment ordering return of the original property had become final and binding, seeking value compensation or compensatory damages, which in substance are no different from value compensation, again lacked a legal interest in protection of rights; and ② dismissed the second and third alternative claims on the ground that the existence of a tort or unjust enrichment could not be recognized. The Plaintiff’s appeal therefrom was also dismissed (Supreme Court Decision 2015DA72262, decided 2016. 3. 24.).\\n\\ne. On 2016. 6. 8., the Plaintiff filed the present action against the Defendant, seeking, on the ground that the sales contract at issue had been revoked as a fraudulent act, that, as restoration to the original condition thereunder, the Defendant implement the procedures for ownership transfer registration of the real properties at issue in favor of Non-party 1.\\n\\n2. The Supreme Court’s Determination\\na. Where a creditor’s claim for revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration to the original condition is sustained, the beneficiary bears the obligation to return the subject matter of the fraudulent act to the debtor as restoration to the original condition. If return of the original property is impossible or substantially difficult, then as performance of the duty of restoration to the original condition, compensation equivalent to the value of the subject matter of the fraudulent act must be made. Here, the cases in which return of the original property is impossible or substantially difficult do not refer merely to cases where return of the original property is absolutely and physically impossible, but rather to cases where, in light of the law of experience in social life or transaction conceptions, the creditor cannot expect performance to be realized from the beneficiary or a transferee. Accordingly, where, after ownership of real property has been transferred through a fraudulent act, a third party acquires rights such as a mortgage or superficies over such real property, unless there are special circumstances such that the beneficiary can restore the real property free from encumbrances such as a mortgage and transfer it to the debtor, the creditor may seek compensation equivalent to the value of the real property from the beneficiary in lieu of return of the original property; however, this does not mean that the creditor is not permitted to seek return of the original property while bearing the risk or disadvantage himself. The creditor may, as a method of restoration to the original condition, seek cancellation of the registration in the beneficiary’s name instead of value compensation, or may seek against the beneficiary implementation of the procedures for direct ownership transfer registration in favor of the debtor. In such a case, the right to claim restoration to the original condition is fixed as either return of the original property or value compensation according to the creditor’s choice at the time the factual hearing is closed. Once the creditor has obtained a final and binding judgment after first seeking, as revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration to the original condition, cancellation of the registration in the beneficiary’s name, even if for any reason it has become impossible to cancel the registration in the beneficiary’s name, the creditor may not again exercise the right to claim restoration to the original condition against the beneficiary and seek value compensation, nor may the creditor seek, as return of the original property, implementation of the procedures for direct ownership transfer registration in favor of the debtor; therefore, such a claim is impermissible for lack of legal interest in protection of rights (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DA54978, decided 2006. 12. 7.).\\n\\nb. In light of this legal principle, we examine the determination of the court below. The Plaintiff filed an action against the Defendant seeking revocation of the sales contract at issue as a fraudulent act and obtained a judgment in his favor, which became final and binding, revoking the sales contract at issue as a fraudulent act and ordering the Defendant to cancel the ownership transfer registrations at issue. If so, the present action, by which the Plaintiff again exercises the right to claim restoration to the original condition following revocation of a fraudulent act and seeks against the Defendant implementation of the procedures for direct ownership transfer registration in favor of the debtor, must be deemed inadmissible for lack of legal interest in protection of rights. Nevertheless, the court below, solely for the reasons stated in its holding, rejected the Defendant’s preliminary defense that the present action is inadmissible for lack of legal interest in protection of rights; in this regard, the court below erred by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the res judicata effect of a final judgment and legal interest in protection of rights, thereby affecting the outcome of the judgment. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nAccordingly, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Supreme Court Justices participating therein."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding parent-child relationships is incorrect? (In the event of a dispute, based on precedents)
A: Even if a conciliation or judicial settlement containing a statement confirming that there is no natural parent-child relationship between the parties is concluded, it has no effect.
B: Even a relative prescribed in Article 777 of the Civil Act is recognized as having standing as a plaintiff in an action to confirm the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship only when that person qualifies as an interested party prescribed in Article 865 of the Civil Act.
C: Where, after co-heirs B and C of the decedent A (female) have already divided or disposed of the inherited property, it is clearly revealed by a final and conclusive judgment confirming the existence of a natural parent-child relationship that D is A’s child, the proviso to Article 860 of the Civil Act concerning the limitation on the retroactive effect of acknowledgment does not apply, and therefore D cannot deny the validity of the division or disposition made by B and C.
D: Where a child born through artificial insemination is born between a husband and wife who are living a normal marital life, the child born through artificial insemination is presumed to be the husband’s child, and if the husband later retracts his consent to the artificial insemination and files an action to disavow paternity, such action is not permitted.
E: A gender correction must not be denied merely on the ground that a transgender person has a minor child, without making a substantive determination by considering various circumstances for balancing legal interests so as to harmonize the protection of the transgender person’s fundamental rights with the protection and welfare of the minor child.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2015MEU0000]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Summary of the case and issues\\na. Summary of the case\\nNon-party 1 (deceased on August 10, 1909) was designated on August 15, 2010 as a recipient candidate for the Patriotic Medal, Grade 4, of the Order of Merit for National Foundation. After Non-party 3, a child of Non-party 1’s eldest daughter, Non-party 2 (deceased), was recognized through administrative litigation as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under the former Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence (the version before amendment by Act No. 11332 on February 17, 2012; hereinafter the “former Independence Merit Treatment Act”), the Plaintiff, who is the grandson of Non-party 1’s eldest son, Non-party 4 (deceased), filed this action against the Prosecutor seeking, among other things, a confirmation that no natural parent-child relationship exists between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2.\\nThe lower court dismissed this action as inadmissible on the ground that even if the Plaintiff were to obtain a judgment confirming the nonexistence of the natural parent-child relationship as described above, he could not be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under the standards prescribed by the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, and that there was no other legal interest in seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of the natural parent-child relationship. In response, the Plaintiff appealed, arguing that because he is in a kinship relationship with Non-party 1 within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777, he necessarily has an interest in filing an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, in accordance with prior Supreme Court precedents.\\n\\nb. Issue in this case\\nThe issue in this case is whether the Plaintiff, merely by virtue of the fact that he is in a kinship relationship with Non-party 1, may necessarily file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. In order to determine the issue, we shall first examine the scope of standing as Plaintiff in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under Civil Act Article 865, and then consider whether to maintain the prior Supreme Court precedents holding that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may necessarily file such an action merely on the basis of being in such a status relationship.\\n\\n2. Standing as Plaintiff in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under Civil Act Article 865\\na. Persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship\\nA parent-child relationship, which is a parent-child relationship, is divided into a natural parent-child relationship based on blood ties and an adoptive parent-child relationship based on the parties’ intent. As to the natural parent-child relationship, the Civil Act provides several provisions for determining the existence or dissolution of the relationship, unlike the mother-child relationship, which is clearly determined by the natural facts of conception and birth. These include the provision on the presumption of legitimacy that a child conceived during marriage is presumed to be the child of the husband (Article 844, paragraph (1)); the provisions concerning an action for disavowal of paternity, which is the method for rebutting that presumption (Articles 846 through 851); the provisions concerning the determination by the court of paternity where a remarried woman gives birth (Article 845); the provisions concerning acknowledgment of a child born out of wedlock (Article 855, paragraph (1), and Article 863); and the provisions concerning revocation of acknowledgment and an action to object to acknowledgment (Articles 861 and 862). Accordingly, in litigation seeking the establishment or dissolution of a legal natural parent-child relationship, it is in principle the person entitled to file the action as expressly specified in each of the above provisions who may file suit upon satisfying the requirements prescribed by those provisions.\\nCivil Act Article 865, paragraph (1) (hereinafter the “provision at issue”) provides: “A person who may institute an action pursuant to the provisions of Article 845, Article 846, Article 848, Article 850, Article 851, Article 862, or Article 863 may institute an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on another ground.” This is intended to permit filing of an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship so as to correct a mismatch between the legal parent-child relationship and the parent-child relationship indicated in the family relations register.\\nConsidering that the provision at issue does not directly specify and regulate in concrete terms who may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, but instead cites provisions concerning other litigation procedures with similar objectives and grants standing as Plaintiff to the person entitled to file each such action while only changing the grounds, the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under the provision at issue is supplementary to other litigation procedures concerning the establishment or dissolution of a legal natural parent-child relationship.\\nIn light of the form, wording, and structure of the provision at issue, the characteristics of the litigation procedures prescribed by the above provisions, and the supplementary nature of the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, it is appropriate to view the persons who may file such an action as limited to the persons entitled to sue under the provision at issue.\\n\\nb. Specific scope of standing as Plaintiff\\n(1) Father, mother, and child as parties to a natural parent-child relationship\\nThe father, mother, and child, who are parties to a natural parent-child relationship, are persons who may file an action pursuant to Civil Act Articles 845, 846, 862, and 863, which are listed in the provision at issue, and may therefore file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship where the cause is another ground.\\n\\n(2) Lineal descendants of the child and their legal representatives\\nThe lineal descendants of the child, who is a party to a natural parent-child relationship, and their legal representatives are persons who may file an action pursuant to Civil Act Article 863, which is listed in the provision at issue, and may therefore file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship where the cause is another ground.\\n\\n(3) Adult guardians, testamentary executors, and lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife\\nCivil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851, which are listed in the provision at issue, are all provisions that supplementarily expand standing as Plaintiff on the premise of Civil Act Article 846, which is the basic provision regarding standing as Plaintiff in an action for disavowal of paternity. Accordingly, adult guardians, testamentary executors, and the lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife, who are persons entitled to sue under Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851, should be regarded as having standing only when they satisfy the requirements for filing suit under those provisions. In other words, an adult guardian may newly file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship where the husband or wife has come under adult guardianship (Article 848); a testamentary executor may newly file such an action where the husband or wife has indicated by will an intent to deny the natural parent-child relationship (Article 850); and the lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife may newly file such an action where the husband dies before the child’s birth or the husband or wife dies within the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity (Article 851). If they do not satisfy the above requirements, it cannot be said that they necessarily have standing as Plaintiff to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under those provisions.\\n\\n(4) Interested persons\\nAn interested person may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on another ground pursuant to Civil Act Article 862, which is listed in the provision at issue. Here, an interested person means a third party who has a legal interest, such as obtaining certain rights or being relieved from obligations, by a final judgment stating that a natural parent-child relationship exists or does not exist between other persons. Accordingly, only where the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship between other persons will, by judicial determination, have a concrete impact on the interested person’s own rights or obligations concerning inheritance, support, or the like, or on his or her legal status, may such person file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as an interested person.\\nA person who files an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship while asserting that he or she is the natural father or natural mother of a child, even though no kinship relationship is indicated in the family relations register, is included among interested persons because, depending on the result of the judgment, that person will be directly affected with respect to the very existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship with the party.\\nIn the end, unless the Plaintiff who filed the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is a person whose standing as Plaintiff is necessarily recognized as described in (1), (2), and (3) above, standing exists only where the Plaintiff falls within the category of interested persons referred to here. Whether a person falls within such an interested person category must be determined by individually examining, on the basis of the allegations made by the Plaintiff and the circumstances revealed in the pleadings, what concrete impact exists on the Plaintiff’s rights or obligations concerning inheritance, support, or the like, or on the Plaintiff’s legal status.\\n\\n3. Whether kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may necessarily file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship\\na. Prior Supreme Court precedents\\nIn Supreme Court en banc Decision 80MEU60, rendered on October 13, 1981, the Court held that Article 35 of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation (enacted by Act No. 803 on December 6, 1961, effective as of January 1, 1962, and repealed by Act No. 4300 on December 31, 1990; hereinafter the same) applied mutatis mutandis Article 26, which provides that “the party, the legal representative, or the kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may file an action for nullity of marriage at any time,” to the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship prescribed in Civil Act Article 865, and thus held that standing as Plaintiff was necessarily recognized merely by the fact that one is in a kinship relationship prescribed in Civil Act Article 777.\\nThereafter, the Supreme Court reached the same conclusion not only in cases governed by the former Act on Personal Status Litigation (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 81MEU77 rendered on March 8, 1983, and Supreme Court Decision 90MEU347 rendered on May 28, 1991), but also in cases governed by the Family Litigation Act newly enacted upon the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation (enacted by Act No. 4300 on December 31, 1990 and effective as of January 1, 1991; hereinafter the same) (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 97MEU1585 rendered on October 20, 1998, and Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503 rendered on February 12, 2004).\\n\\nb. Necessity of changing the precedent\\nHowever, in light of the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and other statutes, the enactment and implementation of the Family Litigation Act, changes in the family system such as the abolition of the head-of-family system, the special characteristics of status litigation, the diversification of family composition and the respect for the parties’ intent in that regard, and balance with other litigation procedures aimed at the establishment or dissolution of a legal natural parent-child relationship, it must be concluded that the prior Supreme Court precedents holding that an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship may necessarily be filed merely on the ground that one is kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 can no longer be maintained. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n(1) The former Act on Personal Status Litigation, which set special provisions regarding litigation procedures concerning personal status in relation to the Civil Procedure Act, the basic Act governing ordinary civil litigation procedures, contained an express provision (Articles 35 and 26) stating that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may necessarily file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. In fact, this became the core basis of the prior Supreme Court precedents. However, unlike the former Act on Personal Status Litigation, the Family Litigation Act, which integrated the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the former Family Affairs Adjudication Act (enacted by Act No. 1375 on July 31, 1963, effective as of October 1, 1963, and repealed by Act No. 4300 on December 31, 1990), contains no provision at all concerning who may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. The Family Litigation Act merely applies mutatis mutandis the provisions concerning the opposing party in an action for nullity of marriage, etc. (Article 24) to an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, while not applying the provision concerning the person entitled to file suit (Article 23). Accordingly, with the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the implementation of the Family Litigation Act, the legal basis of the prior Supreme Court precedents disappeared.\\n(2) As legal norms surrounding family relations and social circumstances changed, social perceptions regarding natural parent-child relationships, which together with marital relations form the foundation of family relations, also changed.\\nAt the time of the enactment of the Civil Act and even after the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the enactment of the Family Litigation Act, for a considerable period of time Korean civil law maintained the household head system, under which family relations were publicly recorded in the family register organized by household unit based on the head of family. At that time, most persons in a kinship relationship, such as the lineal ascendants and lineal descendants of the head of family, collateral relatives, and their spouses, were entered in the family register as members of the household centered on the head of family. However, with the 2005 amendment to the Civil Act, the household head system was completely abolished and reorganized into a family system centered on spouses and children, and as of January 1, 2008, when the Act on the Registration, etc. of Family Relations (enacted by Act No. 8435 on May 17, 2007; hereinafter the “Family Relations Registration Act”) came into force, the family relations registration register replacing the family register has recorded, centered on the individual, the occurrence and changes of family relations through marriage, birth, and the like. In addition, in our society, the nuclear family consisting of parents and unmarried children has already become the norm, rather than the traditional extended family, and with the progress of urbanization and industrialization, individualism and liberalism have become widely prevalent in family life as well.\\nIn light of these legal and social changes concerning the family system and the like, unlike the period when the household head system was maintained, the legal and social basis for viewing kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 as having a close status-related legal interest has weakened today.\\n(3) The action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is a litigation procedure designed to correct entries in the family relations registration register that do not correspond to the true blood relationship (Family Relations Registration Act Article 107). However, today family relations are formed not only on the basis of blood relations but also diversely on the basis of the parties’ intent. The Supreme Court has held that the presumption of legitimacy also applies to a child born through artificial insemination during marriage, and that even if it is revealed that a child conceived and born by a wife during marriage has no blood relationship with the husband, it cannot be said that the presumption of legitimacy does not apply (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016MEU2510 rendered on October 23, 2019). The Supreme Court has also held that where a party registers a child as born of the party’s own biological child with the intent to create an adoptive parent-child relationship, the effect of adoption is recognized if the requirements for adoption are satisfied (however, the Civil Act amended by Act No. 11300 on February 10, 2012 and effective as of July 1, 2013 requires approval from the Family Court as a requirement for adoption of a minor), and that a claim for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not permitted in relation thereto (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2000MEU1493 rendered on May 24, 2001). This is because legal protection is needed not only where the presumption of legitimacy applies to a parent-child relationship formed without a blood relationship, but also where, even if the presumption of legitimacy does not apply, that parent-child relationship has been substantially formed on the basis of the parties’ intent. Accordingly, while respecting the free intent of the parties regarding the formation of the legal parent-child relationship that underlies marriage and family relations, it is necessary to impose certain limitations so that third parties do not improperly intervene in that regard.\\n(4) An action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship falls under a “Category A family litigation case” under the Family Litigation Act (Article 2, paragraph (1), subparagraph 1(a) of the Family Litigation Act). The effect of a judgment granting such an action extends to third parties as well (Article 21 of the same Act), and the court must investigate facts and take necessary evidence ex officio and may examine the parties at any time (Article 17 of the same Act). In particular, considering the reality that blood relationship can now be proved relatively easily through DNA testing and the like, broadly viewing the scope of third parties who may contest the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship in the name of finding the truth of blood ties and allowing the case to proceed to the merits is highly likely to inevitably undermine the stability of status order and infringe the parties’ autonomous decision-making regarding marriage and family life. Accordingly, it is not desirable to expand arbitrarily, by interpretation and without an express statutory basis, the scope of third parties who may bring an action contesting the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship.\\nAlthough the Family Litigation Act provides in Article 24, paragraph (2), and Article 28 for cases in which a third party files an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, these are provisions concerning the opposing party (defendant capacity), not the person entitled to sue, and therefore cannot serve as a basis for expanding the scope of persons entitled to file suit.\\n(5) Since an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is supplementary to other litigation procedures aimed at the establishment or dissolution of a legal natural parent-child relationship, it is clear that where such an action may be filed under another litigation procedure, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not permitted.\\nMeanwhile, where there is a dispute concerning a legal natural parent-child relationship, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is often used in place of other litigation procedures whose filing requirements are relatively strict, and current practice also shows such a tendency. The Supreme Court has extended the legal principles concerning an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship to adoptive parent-child relationships as well (see Supreme Court Decision 92MEU372 rendered on July 16, 1993), and moreover, the filing period for an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not prescribed except where one or both parties to the natural parent-child relationship have died (Civil Act Article 865, paragraph (2)).\\nIn this way, the filing requirements for an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship have already been relaxed in several respects, and further expanding the scope of standing as Plaintiff to kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 is not balanced even when compared with the other litigation procedures described above. This is even more so because of the risk that the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship may be distorted into a means of circumventing the requirements or restrictions established by statutory provisions concerning other litigation procedures.\\n(6) The natural parent-child relationship, which forms the basis of status relationships, does not end merely as a matter between the parties, but may affect inheritance issues among relatives and various other legal relationships based on kinship, such as parental authority and support (see Supreme Court Decision 2004MEU405 rendered on June 24, 2004). It is therefore of course necessary that certain third parties also be given the opportunity to contest the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship through a proper judicial procedure. Since the Civil Act, in the provision at issue, allows a third party who is not a party to the natural parent-child relationship to contest its existence or nonexistence if that third party qualifies as an interested person, a third party who is kin also has standing if that person qualifies as an interested person. Accordingly, even if not all kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 are uniformly granted standing as Plaintiff, it cannot be said that the rights or right to a judicial remedy of third parties who have a legal interest in the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship are unjustly restricted.\\n\\nc. Change in precedent\\nAccordingly, Supreme Court Decision 97MEU1585 rendered on October 20, 1998, which held in relation to cases governed by the Family Litigation Act that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777, absent special circumstances, have a litigation interest in filing an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship merely by reason of being in such a status relationship, and Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503 rendered on February 12, 2004, and other judgments to the same effect, are changed to the extent they are inconsistent with the view of this judgment.\\n\\n4. Determination in this case\\na. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the following facts may be found.\\n(1) Non-party 1 was designated on August 15, 2010 as a recipient candidate for the Patriotic Medal, Grade 4, of the Order of Merit for National Foundation, and Non-party 1’s children were the eldest son, Non-party 4, the eldest daughter, Non-party 2, and the second daughter, Non-party 5. Non-party 4 and his spouse and children, as well as Non-party 5 and her spouse, all died before the date on which the recipient candidate was designated, and the only surviving child of Non-party 5 was Non-party 6 (date of birth omitted, male). The Plaintiff is the grandson of Non-party 4.\\n(2) On August 30, 2010, Non-party 6 applied to the Gwangju Regional Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs for registration as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under Article 6 of the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, on the ground that he is a grandson of Non-party 1, and was registered on November 24, 2011 as the first-priority bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence.\\n(3) Meanwhile, Non-party 3 (date of birth omitted, female) applied on November 25, 2011 to the Gwangju Regional Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs for registration as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence, asserting that she is a child of Non-party 1’s eldest daughter, Non-party 2, and thus the first in priority among Non-party 1’s grandchildren, but the head of the Gwangju Regional Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs rejected the application on November 30, 2011. Thereafter, Non-party 3 filed an action for cancellation of the refusal to register her as a person of distinguished service to independence against the head of the Gwangju Regional Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs (Gwangju District Court Case No. 2011GUHAP4510), obtained a judgment in her favor on all claims, and that judgment later became final and conclusive after appeal and further appeal.\\n\\nb. Examining the above factual relations in light of the legal principles discussed above leads to the following conclusion.\\n(1) The Plaintiff is in a kinship relationship with Non-party 1 as Non-party 1’s lineal descendant (great-grandchild), but does not fall within the category of persons whose standing as Plaintiff is necessarily recognized under the provision at issue.\\n(2) According to Article 5, paragraph (1), and Article 12, paragraph (2), paragraph (4), subparagraph 1 of the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, compensation is paid only to one first-priority bereaved family member among the person of distinguished service to independence and his or her bereaved family members, and the scope of bereaved family members entitled to receive compensation is limited in the order of spouse, child, grandchild, and daughter-in-law of the person of distinguished service to independence, with the older person receiving priority if there are two or more persons of the same rank. Therefore, under the standards prescribed by the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, the Plaintiff, who is merely the great-grandchild of Non-party 1, cannot be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence, and since Non-party 6 in addition to Non-party 3 (child of the eldest daughter, Non-party 2) appears to be alive as a grandchild of Non-party 1, the Plaintiff cannot be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence even if he obtains a judgment confirming the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2. Nor does the question whether the Plaintiff may be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence depend on whether Non-party 2 is the child of Non-party 7, the wife of Non-party 1.\\n(3) Even if a judgment confirming that no natural parent-child relationship exists between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2, and between Non-party 7 and Non-party 2, respectively, becomes final and conclusive, the Plaintiff cannot be said to have a legal interest therein. Accordingly, this action must be regarded as unlawful because it was filed by a person lacking standing as Plaintiff.\\n\\nc. The lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper as it follows the legal principles discussed above. The lower court did not err, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, by misapprehending the law on standing as Plaintiff in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, by failing to conduct the necessary examination, or by exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the principles of logic and experience.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nThe Plaintiff’s appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; accordingly, judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition. Except for the separate opinion of Justice Ahn Cheol-sang and Justice Min Yoo-sook, the views of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there are supplementary opinions by Justice Park Jeong-hwa, Justice Kim Seon-su, and Justice Roh Jeong-hee regarding the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Separate opinion of Justice Ahn Cheol-sang and Justice Min Yoo-sook\\nWe agree with the majority opinion regarding the change in Supreme Court precedent. However, we differ from the majority opinion as to the scope of persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship and whether the Plaintiff in this case falls within that category.\\n\\na. First, our view regarding the change in precedent.\\n(1) The provision at issue states, “A person who may institute an action pursuant to the provisions of Article 845, Article 846, Article 848, Article 850, Article 851, Article 862, or Article 863 may institute an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on another ground.” Accordingly, it is clear from the wording of the provision at issue that the person entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is limited to the persons specified therein.\\nHowever, the former Act on Personal Status Litigation provided that “kin under Civil Act Article 777” may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship (Articles 26 and 35). Yet, since the provision at issue in the Civil Act had already expressly specified the person entitled to sue with respect to an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, the former Act on Personal Status Litigation’s inclusion of a separate provision concerning the person entitled to sue created systemic confusion. On December 31, 1990, the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the former Family Affairs Adjudication Act were both repealed and the integrated Family Litigation Act came into force, and the Family Litigation Act deleted the provision from the former Act on Personal Status Litigation concerning the person entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. With the implementation of the Family Litigation Act, the overlapping provisions were eliminated, and the persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship became governed solely by the provision at issue in the Civil Act.\\n(2) Supreme Court Decision 97MEU1585 rendered on October 20, 1998, which the majority opinion cites as a precedent to be changed, held that if a person is kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777, that person may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship merely by reason of being in such a status relationship, and thus failed properly to reflect the changes brought about by the repeal of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation and the implementation of the Family Litigation Act. However, Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503 rendered on February 12, 2004, also cited as a precedent to be changed, unlike Supreme Court Decision 97MEU1585, held that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as an “interested person” who is a person entitled to sue under the provision at issue. Accordingly, if one takes the later Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503 as the benchmark, the current Supreme Court precedent is not that kin under Civil Act Article 777 “become persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship even though there is no longer any legal basis” (the premise of the majority opinion), but rather that they “become persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as interested persons under the provision at issue.”\\n(3) Although the Civil Act as amended by Act No. 4199 on January 13, 1990 reduced the scope of kin, Supreme Court Decision 2003MEU2503, which held that kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 necessarily fall within the category of “interested persons,” may still be evaluated as merely following the repealed provisions of the former Act on Personal Status Litigation, and it is therefore appropriate to change it. Accordingly, the change in precedent should target the holding that “kin within the meaning of Civil Act Article 777 fall within the category of interested persons under the provision at issue merely by virtue of their status relationship,” and we agree with the majority opinion as to such change in precedent.\\n\\nb. In this case, the issue is whether the Plaintiff, as the great-grandchild of Non-party 1, falls within the persons entitled to sue under the provision at issue, namely “lineal descendants of the husband or wife” or “interested persons.” Since we differ from the majority opinion on this point, we set forth our view in detail below.\\n(1) Before addressing the issue, we first consider the majority opinion concerning the necessity of changing precedent.\\n(a) According to the majority opinion, because family relations today are formed diversely not only on the basis of blood relations but also on the basis of the parties’ intent, the free intent of the parties should also be respected as to the existence or nonexistence of a legal natural parent-child relationship. However, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is a judicial procedure for confirming the existence or nonexistence of a true blood relationship, and the existence or nonexistence of the legal natural parent-child relationship that is the subject matter of the litigation is not of a nature that can be determined by the free intent of the parties.\\nUnder the Civil Act, the chapter on kin (Part IV) is broadly structured around Chapter 3, “Marriage,” and Chapter 4, “Parents and Child,” and Chapter 4, “Parents and Child,” is again divided into provisions concerning Section 1, “Natural Child,” and Section 2, “Adopted Child.” This shows that the relationship between parents and children is formed on the basis of blood ties and the parties’ intent, but that among them the natural parent-child relationship is based on blood ties (the Supreme Court en banc Decision 2000MEU1493 rendered on May 24, 2001, cited by the majority opinion, concerns the legal doctrine of adoption, under which the parent-child relationship is formed by the parties’ intent).\\nIn addition, in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, admission of the claim and confession are not permitted (Article 12 of the Family Litigation Act), and the prior mediation principle also does not apply (Article 50, paragraph (1) of the same Act), so it is impossible in such proceedings to determine the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship by the parties’ intent. Disposition by the parties’ free will concerning the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not permitted.\\n(b) The majority opinion takes the view that the scope of persons entitled to sue should be limited so that third parties do not improperly intervene in family relations. We fully agree that private life and domestic peace should be protected against threats by third parties. Indeed, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016MEU2510 rendered on October 23, 2019, held, in substance, that in a natural parent-child relationship to which the presumption of legitimacy applies, third parties must be prevented from intervening indirectly in another person’s family matters by allowing only an action for disavowal of paternity, which strictly limits the persons entitled to sue and the filing period.\\nHowever, the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship in this case is fundamentally different from an action for disavowal of paternity in this respect. Because a natural parent-child relationship to which the presumption of legitimacy applies can be denied only by a judgment in an action for disavowal of paternity, there is practical benefit in limiting the persons entitled to sue in order to achieve that purpose. By contrast, a natural parent-child relationship to which the presumption of legitimacy does not apply may not only be contested through an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, but when it becomes a preliminary issue in other litigation procedures such as civil litigation, anyone may allege and prove its nonexistence in that litigation procedure (see Supreme Court Decision 78DA71 rendered on April 11, 1978). Therefore, even if the scope of third parties who may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is limited, such limitation cannot prevent them from contesting the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship through civil litigation, etc. Limiting the scope of persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, as in the majority opinion, has little practical effect in preventing third parties from intervening in another person’s family matters and cannot be said to be an appropriate method. Rather, permitting certain third parties to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship makes it possible to finally resolve disputes surrounding status relationships and thereby also ensure the accuracy and authenticity of the family relations registration register. This is because only when the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is determined in the “disposition” of a judgment by filing an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship can the family relations registration register be corrected, the effect of a judgment granting the claim extends to third parties as well, and special provisions such as orders to undergo testing are more helpful in ascertaining the true blood relationship.\\nEven in this case, Non-party 3, a relative whose interests are opposed to those of the Plaintiff, had already, through administrative litigation, asserted that there is a natural parent-child relationship between her mother and Non-party 1, obtained a final and conclusive judgment in her favor, and the reasons for that judgment include a determination regarding blood relationship. It does not appear easy to preserve the peace of these families merely by blocking the Plaintiff’s filing of this subsequent action.\\n(c) Looking at the statistics on “litigation relating to parent-child relationships” in the Judicial Yearbook published annually by the courts over the past five years, actions for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship account for 75 to 80 percent of all litigation relating to parent-child relationships, occupying an overwhelming share. In actions for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, the rate at which the Plaintiff’s claim is granted at first instance exceeds 75 percent, and the appeal rate is only around 1 percent. Unlike the fact that an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is prescribed under the Civil Act as a supplementary form of litigation, in practice it has become the principal form of litigation relating to parent-child relationships, and although the Family Litigation Act is structured to have an adversarial-party framework, in practice there are mostly not serious disputes between the relevant parties concerning the very “existence or nonexistence of blood relationship.”\\nEven today, as in the past when public registers, etc. for publicizing status relationships were not adequately established, birth registrations and the like are often made contrary to the actual blood relationship due to legal restrictions or personal circumstances. Under the Supreme Court precedents that a family relations registration register cannot be corrected absent a final and conclusive judgment concerning matters that have a significant impact under the law of kinship or inheritance, as prescribed in Article 2, paragraphs (1) and (2) of the Family Litigation Act (see the Supreme Court en banc Decision on correction of family registers, 93SEU14, 15, 16 rendered on May 22, 1993), even if there is no substantive dispute between the parties regarding the “existence or nonexistence of blood relationship,” an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, which is a family litigation with an adversarial structure, must nonetheless be filed in order to correct the family relations registration register (see the above statistics on the rate at which claims are granted and the appeal rate).\\nFurthermore, whether a person falls within the category of persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is a matter of standing as Plaintiff, which is a litigation requirement, and thus a matter to be examined ex officio. The more strictly the scope of standing as Plaintiff is limited or the more complex the criteria for judgment are set, the more likely it is, as noted above, that even where there is no substantive dispute between the parties regarding the existence or nonexistence of blood relationship, the court will ex officio examine standing as Plaintiff and dismiss the action, resulting in an increased number of such cases.\\n(d) The majority opinion is concerned that if the scope of persons entitled to sue is broadened, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship may be distorted into a means of evading legal restrictions. However, that is a matter for the family court handling the case to faithfully examine the relevant issues and distinguish the genuine from the spurious; it is not a matter to be resolved by limiting standing as Plaintiff and thereby blocking the filing of the action itself.\\n(2) We now consider the first issue, namely the part of the majority opinion that limited the filing requirements for “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife.”\\n(a) The majority opinion states that “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife” may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship only where the husband dies before the child’s birth or the husband or wife dies within the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity.\\nHowever, because an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is a litigation procedure entirely different from an action for disavowal of paternity in terms of litigation structure and legal nature, it is not appropriate to require separate conditions, as in an action for disavowal of paternity, even when lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship.\\n(b) An action for disavowal of paternity may be filed only by one of the spouses, and therefore it is necessary to make provision for the case where the person entitled to file it has died. Civil Act Article 851 provides that in such a case, the “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants” of the husband or wife may file the action. However, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship expressly contemplates, from the outset, filing not only by the parties to the natural parent-child relationship but also by third parties (Article 24, paragraph (2), and Article 28 of the Family Litigation Act). Therefore, the structure in which, if the party entitled to file an action for disavowal of paternity dies, his or her lineal ascendants or lineal descendants become supplementary persons entitled to sue does not fit an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship.\\nAn example will clarify this. Since the mother-child relationship arises from the natural facts of conception and birth, the wife (hereinafter “A”) may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship against a person recorded in the family relations register as her biological child (hereinafter “B”), alleging the nonexistence of a blood relationship without any time limit, and if A dies, A’s lineal descendants may file such an action against B. In such a case, the majority opinion says that A’s lineal descendants may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship only if A died within the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity (two years from the date on which the cause for disavowal was known). However, since there is no room for the presumption of legitimacy itself to arise between A and B, it is impossible to assume a date on which the cause for disavowal became known, and the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity cannot run either. According to the majority opinion, it is difficult to tell how one is to determine whether the requirement of the filing-period limitation has been met. Moreover, while A could have filed the action at any time during her lifetime, once A dies, one arrives at the strange conclusion that, retroactively to some specific point in the past, the filing period had already expired.\\n(c) The parties to a natural parent-child relationship are the parent and the child. The lineal descendants of the child may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship pursuant to the provision at issue and Civil Act Article 863 without satisfying any other filing requirements, and the majority opinion does not differ on this point.\\nIf the lineal descendants of the child are allowed to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship without any further restriction, it is balanced and natural in terms of textual interpretation to regard the lineal descendants of the parent as likewise being able to file such an action without any time limit. In practice, there is much greater possibility or necessity for the lineal descendants of the parent to file an action contesting the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship after the parent’s death than there is for the lineal descendants of the child to do so after the child’s death.\\n(d) In addition, where the parent, who is a party to the natural parent-child relationship, dies without filing an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, and only a testamentary executor is appointed, or where adult guardianship has commenced while the parent had not filed such an action, the adult guardian and testamentary executor, as persons entitled to sue, will have the question of whether filing is permitted separately determined under the Civil Act provisions concerning the scope of their duties even if standing as Plaintiff is recognized under the provision at issue, and thus the issue differs from the present case.\\n(e) The reasons why descendants file an action after the parent has not, during the parent’s lifetime, resolved the family relations registration register so that it matches the blood relationship vary depending on individual circumstances and family relations. There may be cases in which a child files an action against the parent’s wishes during the parent’s lifetime, but as in the Judicial Yearbook statistics mentioned above, in most cases the first-instance judgment in favor of the Plaintiff is accepted by both sides and becomes final and conclusive as rendered. There are even cases where a person who, because there was no blood relationship and thus no substantive status as a child during the parent’s lifetime, claims inheritance rights on the basis of the family relations registration register after the parent’s death, causing other heirs to bring litigation.\\n(3) We now consider the second issue, namely the part of the majority opinion that explained the requirements for an “interested person.”\\n(a) The majority opinion states that an “interested person,” as a person entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, is a third party having a legal interest, such as obtaining certain rights or being relieved from obligations, by a final judgment confirming the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship between other persons. The majority opinion’s view on this point is almost identical to the holdings in Supreme Court Decision 4293MINSANG314 rendered on September 29, 1960, and Supreme Court Decision 90MEU88 rendered on July 13, 1990, so it is in effect understood as relying on those decisions. However, because all of those Supreme Court decisions were holdings in cases governed by the already repealed former Act on Personal Status Litigation, it is not appropriate for the majority opinion to continue to rely on them.\\n(b) The primary criterion for determining the scope of an interested person should be whether the person suffers detriment in his or her legal status based on a status relationship due to the registration of a natural parent-child relationship different from the true blood relationship in the current family relations registration register, and whether there exists a legally protectable interest worth correcting through a judgment confirming the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. The criterion presented by the majority opinion, namely whether the person “obtains certain rights or is relieved from obligations,” is not an appropriate criterion because it may be extended to cases where there is no effect on status relationships but only a property interest (for example, an insurance beneficiary or a creditor of an heir).\\n(c) If whether a person qualifies as an interested person is to be determined case by case on the basis of the circumstances shown in the Plaintiff’s allegations or pleadings, there is a risk of a side effect whereby the focus of the family court’s examination and determination shifts from the “existence or nonexistence of blood relationship,” which is the subject matter of the litigation, to the “impact on rights, obligations, or legal status.” This is because, in litigation procedures in which the court must determine the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, the Plaintiff’s order of succession or order of support must first be alleged and examined in order to determine standing as Plaintiff.\\nSuch side effects are more pronounced where the legal interest is related to public law status. The “impact on the rights and obligations of third parties” may appear, as in this case, in the form of public-law legal relationships where special statutes, including the former Independence Merit Treatment Act, provide for payment of compensation or benefits to a certain range of “bereaved family members,” etc. In such cases, if the above principle is applied in determining whether a person qualifies as an interested person, the family court will bear the burden of ex officio examining and determining the compensation standards, the beneficiaries of benefits, and the scope of bereaved family members prescribed by various administrative statutes. It cannot be said to be appropriate to compel interpretation and determination of administrative statutes, which are not within the family court’s area of expertise, in a family litigation case.\\nIn fact, before determining the “existence or nonexistence of blood relationship,” which was the cause of action, the lower court in this case examined in detail the standards prescribed by the former Independence Merit Treatment Act and whether the Plaintiff could be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence. It is not desirable for such examination and determination of administrative statutes to become the center of an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, which is a family litigation case.\\nc. In conclusion, we consider this case.\\n(1) Since the Plaintiff is a lineal descendant of Non-party 1 and Non-party 7, namely a great-grandchild, he falls under “lineal descendants of the husband or wife,” which is a person entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under the provision at issue and Civil Act Article 851.
