Moreover, whether the Plaintiff may be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under the former Independence Merit Treatment Act is not something to be strictly examined and determined ex officio, and once it is shown that the result of this case is likely to affect whether he may be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence, he should be included among the persons entitled to sue as an interested person. Nevertheless, the lower court erred in its legal interpretation concerning standing as Plaintiff in an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship by failing to determine at all whether the Plaintiff, as a lineal descendant of Non-party 1, falls within the category of persons entitled to sue, and by holding that he lacked standing because he could not be registered as a bereaved family member of a person of distinguished service to independence under the former Independence Merit Treatment Act.\\n(2) However, the lower court, as an alternative determination, found that the evidence was insufficient to conclude that no natural parent-child relationship exists between Non-party 1 and Non-party 2 and between Non-party 7 and Non-party 2, and instead recognized that such natural parent-child relationships exist in light of the various circumstances. This falls within the exclusive province of the lower court as the trier of fact, and it does not appear to contain any error exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence. If so, even if this action is deemed lawful, the Plaintiff’s claim cannot be granted. Moreover, in this case, where only the Plaintiff appealed, setting aside the lower court judgment and dismissing the claim would result in a disadvantage to the Plaintiff; therefore, under the principle prohibiting reformatio in peius, the appeal has no choice but to be dismissed.\\nAs stated above, although we agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion of the case, because the reasons differ, we state this in a separate opinion.\\n\\n7. Supplementary opinion of Justice Park Jeong-hwa, Justice Kim Seon-su, and Justice Roh Jeong-hee regarding the majority opinion\\nWe offer supplementary reasoning to the majority opinion on several points.\\n\\na. The majority opinion stated that among the “adult guardian, testamentary executor, or lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife” listed in Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851, which are cited in the provision at issue, only those who satisfy the requirements for filing suit under those provisions have standing as Plaintiff, and that standing as Plaintiff is not necessarily recognized where those requirements are not met. This is reasonable for the following reasons.\\n(1) The provision at issue does not directly regulate who the persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship are. The provision at issue merely states that “a person who may institute an action pursuant to the provisions” listed therein may institute an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on another ground. Accordingly, in light of the form, wording, and structure of the provision at issue, it is natural to interpret the persons who may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as “persons who may file suit by satisfying the requirements under each provision” listed in the provision at issue.\\n(2) The requirements set forth in Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851 all pertain not to the grounds of an action for disavowal of paternity but to the “person entitled to sue.” Accordingly, the requirements concerning the “person entitled to sue” under those provisions should also apply to the persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship.\\n(3) Since Civil Act Articles 848, 850, and 851, which are cited in the provision at issue, are all supplementary provisions concerning the person entitled to file an action for disavowal of paternity, the interpretive standard for determining “persons who may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship pursuant to those provisions” must be consistent. In other words, in the case of a testamentary executor under Civil Act Article 850, it should be interpreted that the executor may file an action for disavowal of paternity only when the husband or wife expresses by will an intent of denial, and that, pursuant to the provision at issue and Civil Act Article 850, the testamentary executor may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship only when the husband or wife has indicated by will an intent to deny the natural parent-child relationship. There is neither need nor reason to recognize standing as Plaintiff for a testamentary executor where there was no such will by the husband or wife.\\n(4) The separate opinion states that “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife” under the provision at issue and Civil Act Article 851 may, without needing to satisfy the requirements set forth in those provisions, file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship without restriction. Civil Act Article 851 does not automatically allow the lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife to file an action for disavowal of paternity merely because the husband or wife has died; rather, it limits the filing period to cases where the husband dies before the child’s birth or where the husband or wife dies within the period for exercising the right of disavowal of paternity. This reflects the purpose of respecting the lifetime intent of the parties regarding the natural parent-child relationship and promoting stability in status order by permitting, exceptionally, persons other than the party entitled to disavow paternity (lineal ascendants or lineal descendants) to file an action for disavowal of paternity where the husband or wife had no opportunity during life even to file such an action or died before the period for exercising the right of disavowal expired and thus could not realize that intent.\\nHowever, if, as in the separate opinion, “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife” may file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship without any restriction under the provision at issue, the result may be to undermine the purpose of Civil Act Article 851, which exceptionally allows persons who are not entitled to disavow paternity to file an action for disavowal of paternity only in limited cases. As the majority opinion explains, a natural parent-child relationship can be formed diversely not only on the basis of blood relations but also on the basis of the parties’ intent, and the presumption of legitimacy may also apply to a parent-child relationship formed without a blood relationship. However, where the parties to such a parent-child relationship formed without blood relation (especially the parent) die and a considerable amount of time passes, it may become difficult to objectively determine whether the person recorded as a child in the family relations registration register is a person to whom the presumption of legitimacy applies. In such cases, “lineal ascendants or lineal descendants of the husband or wife,” who originally could not file an action for disavowal of paternity due to the restrictions in Civil Act Article 851, may nonetheless contest the existence or nonexistence of the blood relationship against the intent of the parties by filing an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. Furthermore, where a parent-child relationship formed without blood relation is substantially formed on the basis of the parties’ intent, as in cases where a child born through artificial insemination is registered as a biological child even though the presumption of legitimacy does not apply, or where a child born out of wedlock of a spouse is registered as a biological child while satisfying the requirements and intent to adopt (the Civil Act as amended in 2012 and effective as of July 1, 2013 requires approval from the Family Court when adopting a minor, but the supplementary provisions limit retroactive effect), legal protection should not be excluded merely because the presumption of legitimacy does not apply. Even where the parent did not raise any issue during his or her lifetime regarding the existence or nonexistence of blood relation with the child, allowing the parent’s lineal ascendants or other lineal descendants to seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship against the child on the ground that there was no blood relation after the parent’s death may infringe the personality rights or right to pursue happiness of the parties concerning the formation of family relations. Accordingly, the separate opinion’s view that an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship may be filed without restriction merely because one is a lineal ascendant or lineal descendant of the husband or wife is not appropriate.\\n(5) The majority opinion’s interpretation, which narrows as much as possible the scope of persons whose standing as Plaintiff is necessarily recognized under the provision at issue, is not unrelated to the fact that the provision at issue designates interested persons as persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. Even if standing as Plaintiff is not necessarily recognized under the provision at issue, an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship may still be filed where the person qualifies as an interested person; therefore, it is appropriate to interpret the scope of automatic persons entitled to sue under the provision at issue as above.\\n\\nb. We now consider the standard for determining the scope of an interested person.\\n(1) The persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under the provision at issue include interested persons. Because an interested person is a broad concept meaning a third party with a legal interest in the existence or nonexistence of another person’s natural parent-child relationship, it is important in practice to determine its specific scope. The majority opinion limits interested persons to those whose rights, obligations, or legal status concerning inheritance, support, or the like are concretely affected by the final and conclusive judgment on the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. By contrast, the separate opinion states that in order to have standing as Plaintiff as an interested person, the person must have an interest worthy of legal protection to correct the record in the family relations registration register, and that this should be based on whether the person suffers detriment in legal status grounded in a status relationship due to a record in the family relations registration register contrary to the true blood relationship. However, the respective standards proposed by the majority opinion and the separate opinion do not in practice create a significant difference in determining whether a person is an interested person. This is because, even under the majority opinion, one examines what concrete effect exists on the person’s rights, obligations, or legal status concerning inheritance, support, or the like, and therefore, contrary to the concern expressed in the separate opinion, a third party who has no effect on status relationships and only a property interest will not be included among interested persons. In fact, it is difficult to find cases in prior Supreme Court precedents or lower court practice in which such a person was recognized as an interested person.\\n(2) The separate opinion points out that if the issue of whether a person qualifies as an interested person is to be determined individually in each case, there is a side effect whereby the focus of the family court’s examination and determination shifts from the subject matter of the litigation, namely the “existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship,” to the Plaintiff’s “rights, obligations, or impact on legal status,” or that the family court will bear the burden of having to interpret and determine administrative statutes.\\nHowever, since the provision at issue expressly designates interested persons as persons entitled to file an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, where the Plaintiff asserts that he or she filed such an action as an interested person, a stage must be gone through to determine whether the Plaintiff actually qualifies as such. Such review of party capacity also has practical value in harmoniously realizing the two ideas governing parent-child relationships, namely securing the legal stability of parent-child relationships and the principle of blood truth. Moreover, the need to reasonably adjust the scope of party capacity and establish criteria for such determination before proceeding to the merits is not a problem unique to family litigation cases. Today, family litigation cases often raise legal issues from other areas, including public law relations, but this is an unavoidable result of the very diverse and complex manner in which legal interests surrounding status relationships are manifested. Accordingly, the side effects pointed out by the separate opinion are not matters that must essentially be considered in determining the scope of interested persons and the principles for examining and deciding that issue.\\n\\nAs stated above, we present this supplementary opinion regarding the majority opinion."}

{"[2016MEU2510]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Judgment on the grounds for appeal as to Defendant 1\\n\\nA. Parent-child relationship of a child conceived and born through artificial insemination during marriage by the wife\\n\\n(1) Whether the presumption of paternity provision applies to a child conceived through artificial insemination\\n\\nThe Civil Act classifies the parent-child relationship between parents and children into a natural parent-child relationship based on blood ties (the Civil Act has provisions on natural children in Article 844 et seq.) and an adoptive relationship based on the parties’ intent (the Civil Act has provisions on adoption in Article 866 et seq.). Among these, the natural parent-child relationship is a parent-child relationship arising by birth; since it presupposes the case where parents give birth to a child conceived through natural sexual intercourse, in principle there exists a biological blood relationship between the parents and the born child.\\n\\nEven in a natural parent-child relationship, the mother-child relationship and the father-child relationship appear differently. Unlike the mother-child relationship, which is clearly determined by the natural fact of conception and birth, the father-child relationship requires separate requisites for establishing the relationship. The Civil Act has a presumption of paternity provision that presumes a child conceived by the wife during marriage to be the husband’s child (Article 844(1); hereinafter referred to as the “presumption of paternity provision”). In the case of a child born out of wedlock, legal parent-child relationship may be created by having the biological father acknowledge the child (Article 855(1)) or by the child filing an action for acknowledgment against the father (Article 863) and thereby establishing the existence of a natural parent-child relationship; here, whether there exists a blood relationship between the father and the child constitutes the principal fact to be proved (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on June 14, 2002, 2001MEU1537; Supreme Court Decision rendered on June 11, 2015, 2014MEU8217).\\n\\nThe issue in the present case against Defendant 1 is by what standard the parent-child relationship of a born child should be recognized where the wife, during marriage, receives sperm from a third party other than her husband and becomes pregnant by artificial insemination rather than natural means and gives birth to a child (hereinafter referred to as an “artificial insemination child”). (There are various forms of artificial insemination. Here, matters other than the above-mentioned “third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination” are not addressed.) Under the current Civil Act, there is no express provision regarding the establishment of the parent-child relationship of an artificial insemination child. At the time of the enactment of the Civil Act on February 22, 1958, the possibility that a wife could conceive a child through artificial insemination was not contemplated, and therefore no provision on this matter could be made.\\n\\nHowever, in light of the text and structure of the Civil Act provisions relating to natural children, particularly the presumption of paternity provision; the basic legislative purpose and history of the Civil Act in providing the presumption of paternity provision with respect to the legal status of children born during marriage; and the marriage and family system guaranteed by the Constitution, it is reasonable to regard the presumption of paternity provision as applying even where the wife, during marriage, receives sperm from a third party other than her husband and gives birth through artificial insemination, and to understand that a child born through artificial insemination is presumed to be the husband’s child. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(a) First, the meaning of the presumption of paternity provision shall be considered.\\n\\nThe mother-child relationship is the so-called natural parent-child relationship, in which the parent-child relationship is established by the fact of birth, whereas the father-child relationship is a legal parent-child relationship in the sense that it is established only when recognized by law because the existence of a natural fact cannot be ascertained. The presumption of paternity provision provides that, where the wife gives birth to a child conceived during marriage, the child shall be presumed to be the husband’s natural child. Furthermore, considering that direct proof of conception during marriage is not easy, the Civil Act provides that a child born within 200 days from the day marriage is formed or within 300 days from the day the marital relationship ends shall be presumed to have been conceived during marriage (Article 844(2), (3)), thereby enabling the determination of whether conception occurred during marriage according to uniform criteria. Such a presumption of paternity provision is premised on the fact that scientific verification of parent-child relationships is practically impossible and that, based on the social and legal background that a wife in a legal marital relationship will conceive a child of her husband, there is a high probability that a child born during marriage has a blood relationship with the husband.\\n\\nThe presumption of paternity provision by itself contains the possibility of creating a legal parent-child relationship that does not correspond to a true blood relationship. Since it may be regarded as a principle of the marriage and family system guaranteed by the Constitution that the legal parent-child relationship should conform to the true blood relationship (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on March 27, 1997, 95HEONGA14, 96HEONGA7, etc.), the Civil Act, for this purpose, recognizes in the husband and wife a right to deny paternity as a means to remove the father-child relationship formed pursuant to the presumption of paternity provision (Article 847; hereinafter referred to as the “provision on the action for disavowal of paternity”). However, if the period during which the right to disavow paternity may be exercised is recognized as too long or is not limited, the need to promptly determine a child’s status and the stability of legal relations surrounding status may be impaired; therefore, the Civil Act sets a filing period by providing that an action for disavowal of paternity must be filed within 2 years from the day the husband or wife became aware of the cause for disavowal of paternity (Article 847(1)). Thus, under the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity, which limits standing and the filing period, the effect of the presumption of paternity has stronger force than other presumptions recognized by law. Unless paternity is disavowed and the child remains presumed to be a natural child, the biological father cannot acknowledge the child as a child born out of wedlock, nor can the child file an action for acknowledgment against the biological father; and after the filing period has expired, the presumption cannot be overturned even if it is later revealed to be contrary to the truth.\\n\\nThe Civil Act strictly provides for the presumption of paternity provision and the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity as the method of rebutting it, and where paternity cannot be disavowed, the child’s legal status is finally determined. Accordingly, the father-child relationship of a child born during marriage is uniformly determined pursuant to the Civil Act provisions, and is not determined by individually and specifically examining the blood relationship. In other words, the Civil Act normatively forms a family relationship called parent-child relationship based on the fact that the child was born in a marital relationship and affords strong legal protection to the family relationship so formed. While protecting the child’s welfare in such general and institutional respects, the basic attitude of the Civil Act is to coordinate the conflicting interests surrounding the establishment of parent-child relationships by allowing those who seek to deny the status relationship formed under the presumption of paternity provision to escape that status relationship through reasonable methods and within a reasonable period.\\n\\nThe question of how to set the standard for the presumption of paternity regarding a child born during marriage concerns the legal status and relationship of spouses and children, and is a matter of how to harmonize, in accordance with social reality or traditional conceptions, the “interests of spouses and children in aligning the legal parent-child relationship with the truth” and the “child’s interest in securing legal stability through prompt determination of the parent-child relationship.” This is a matter to be decided in consideration of the basic rights of the interested parties and the constitutional decisions regarding marriage and family life, and in principle is left to the legislature’s discretion (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on April 30, 2015, 2013HEONMA623). It can be said that the Civil Act has made a legislative decision regarding the standard for establishing a parent-child relationship for children conceived and born during marriage through the presumption of paternity provision and the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\n(b) Next, the reason why the presumption of paternity provision should be applied equally to artificial insemination children shall be considered.\\n\\nThe objective of interpretation of law is to seek concrete appropriateness within the bounds that do not impair legal stability. For this purpose, while it is a principle to interpret the law as faithfully as possible to the ordinary meaning of the words used in the statute, within the limits of not departing from the ordinary meaning of the text, a reasonable interpretation in accordance with the goal of legal interpretation may be achieved by additionally employing systematic and logical methods of interpretation that take into account the legislative purpose and object of the law, the history of enactment and amendment, harmony with the legal order as a whole, and relations with other laws and regulations (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on April 23, 2009, 2006DA81035; Supreme Court Decision rendered on December 11, 2014, 2013MEU4591; Supreme Court Decision rendered on November 25, 2016, 2015DU37815). Moreover, even phenomena not contemplated at the time of legislation must, if not resolved legislatively, be incorporated into the structure of the existing legal system so as to seek a more reasonable solution.\\n\\nThe presumption of paternity provision merely provides that a child conceived by the wife during marriage is presumed to be the husband’s child. As a matter of text, the presumption of paternity provision does not limit the application of the presumption based on the specific circumstances by which conception occurred, nor exclude from its application a child conceived through artificial insemination rather than natural means. Such a form of the presumption of paternity provision was maintained unchanged even when amended by Act No. 14965 on October 31, 2017. Nor do other provisions of the Civil Act exclude or limit the application of the presumption of paternity provision to artificial insemination children. Accordingly, applying the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child falls within the scope of interpretation permitted by the statutory text.\\n\\nArticle 36(1) of the Constitution provides, “Marriage and family life shall be established and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and equality of the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this.” Thus, it protects marriage based on individuals’ autonomous intent and equality of the sexes, and family life formed on that basis. On the basis of these constitutional principles, the presumption of paternity provision contributes to maintaining domestic peace by affording a stable legal status to family relationships formed on the basis of the spouses’ normal married life. The marital relationship that forms the background for the birth of an artificial insemination child, and the family relationships such as the parent-child relationship that arise as a result of the artificial insemination child’s birth during marriage, are likewise formed on the basis of the individual and family autonomy that should be respected, and therefore should not be treated differently from other children born during marriage. The need to protect family life formed on the basis of marriage does not change merely because a child born during marriage is an artificial insemination child. There is no legal basis for concluding that the legal status of a child born during marriage differs depending on the specific circumstances of conception. Nor is there any reasonable basis to exclude the application of the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child born while the marital relationship remains normal, merely because the child was not born through sexual intercourse.\\n\\nThe presumption of paternity provision was intended to eliminate the legal protection gap by affording children born during marriage a stable legal status from the moment of birth. The same applies to children born through artificial insemination during marriage.\\n\\nTaking sexual intercourse or biological blood relationship alone as the basis for the establishment of a parent-child relationship, or regarding the artificial insemination child as incapable of being presumed to be the husband’s child on that basis, would result in a situation where paternity cannot be determined for an artificial insemination child born during marriage. This would destabilize the legal status of the artificial insemination child and directly run counter to the purpose of the system that led the Civil Act to adopt the presumption of paternity provision, and is therefore unjust. If the presumption of paternity provision is not applied to an artificial insemination child and biological blood relationship alone is prioritized, even more unjust results would follow. If the sperm donor is anonymous, it is difficult to identify the donor. The sperm donor cannot reasonably expect to act as a father because he cannot anticipate that he must bear paternal responsibility for a child born from his sperm, and apart from anonymously donating sperm, he plays no other role that would warrant attributing to him the status of father with respect to conception and birth of the child. Therefore, it is not reasonable to immediately treat the sperm donor as the legal father or to hold him responsible as such merely because of the blood relationship. If the father-child relationship of an artificial insemination child is not determined pursuant to the presumption of paternity provision, absurd results will follow, such as making it impossible in practice to determine paternity or causing a father-child relationship not contemplated by the Civil Act to come into existence.\\n\\nIn short, the presumption of paternity provision applies to children born during marriage; and in light of the text and legislative purpose of the presumption of paternity provision, as well as the constitutional guarantee of marriage and family life, it must be understood that artificial insemination children born during marriage are included among children born during marriage.\\n\\n(c) Since the child’s welfare is the foremost factor to be considered in the establishment and maintenance of the parent-child relationship, even when considering whether the presumption of paternity provision applies to an artificial insemination child, emphasis must be placed on the child’s welfare. The child’s welfare is not limited merely to providing the substance of a parent-child relationship in the form of protection and upbringing for the child; rather, it must enable the child to function in a parental role by forming a corresponding legal parent-child relationship, and accordingly the system must ensure that parents can sufficiently support the child’s development. It is beneficial to the child’s welfare to attribute the status relationship with the child to the parent who continuously bears responsibility for the child’s welfare. Concluding that no natural parent-child relationship arises with respect to an artificial insemination child would be a significant shock not only to the married couple who have been raising the artificial insemination child but also an irreparable risk to the child who has formed family relationships on that basis.\\n\\n(d) Even in light of the birth process of an artificial insemination child and the actual form of the family relationship surrounding it, social appropriateness may be recognized in applying the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child.\\n\\nIn the case of artificial insemination, instead of the element of natural sexual intercourse, there exists the auxiliary act of artificial insemination or embryo transfer. Where the husband consents to the wife conceiving a child by artificial insemination using a third party’s sperm, the spouses would have anticipated that they would jointly bear responsibility for the child even if the child has no blood relationship with the husband, and it should be understood that a parent-child relationship with the child born pursuant to that consent is formed. The husband participates by consenting to the wife’s process of conception and childbirth through artificial insemination, and the child born in that process may be regarded, like a child conceived and born through the spouses’ natural sexual intercourse, as a child born during marriage between the spouses. Based on such a parent-child relationship, the artificial insemination child forms and maintains a substantive parent-child relationship with the spouses as their child. Socially as well, such a formed parent-child relationship is accepted as the spouses’ child, just as in the case of a child born through natural sexual intercourse.\\n\\nNevertheless, if the application of the presumption of paternity provision were excluded or if it were said that no legal parent-child relationship is established between the spouses and the artificial insemination child, it would destroy legal stability and peace and place the artificial insemination child in a vacuum with no legal protection, which is difficult to accept in our society.\\n\\n(2) Whether disavowal of paternity should be permitted as to an artificial insemination child\\n\\n(a) As seen above, the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity was established for the benefit of aligning legal parent-child relationships with the truth. However, where it becomes clear that a child not having a blood relationship was born, the premise for applying the presumption of paternity provision may be regarded as having disappeared. In such a case, the Civil Act allows the husband and wife to file an action for disavowal of paternity within a reasonable period in order to protect their personality rights, rights to pursue happiness, and fundamental rights concerning marriage and family life based on individual dignity and equality of the sexes, which they should enjoy in family life and status relations (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on March 27, 1997, 95HEONGA14, 96HEONGA7).\\n\\nThe reason the presumption of paternity provision presumes an artificial insemination child to be the husband’s child is that applying the presumption of paternity provision to a child born between spouses who participated in the conception and childbirth process by giving “consent” is justified in light of the entire family law system, including the Constitution and the Civil Act. Applying the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child is intended to guarantee the family life and status relationship of spouses in marriage, and to legally secure, in accordance with their free will, family relationships and the substance of family relationships socially recognized.\\n\\nIn light of the process of conceiving and giving birth to an artificial insemination child, the fact that the child was not conceived through sexual intercourse between husband and wife and, accordingly, has no blood relationship with the husband are all matters already taken into account when applying the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child, and are not different from the facts known to the husband at the time the artificial insemination child is born. Presuming an artificial insemination child to be the husband’s child through the presumption of paternity provision, based on such premise facts, is intended to guarantee and realize the husband’s personality rights, rights to pursue happiness, and fundamental rights concerning marriage and family life based on individual dignity and equality of the sexes, which he should enjoy in family life and status relations. Conversely, it cannot be said that allowing the husband to file an action for disavowal of paternity is a fundamental right of the husband.\\n\\nAn action for disavowal of paternity may be filed on the ground that, as to a child conceived and born through natural sexual intercourse, there was no sexual intercourse process and, accordingly, there is no biological blood relationship. If an action for disavowal of paternity may also be filed as to an artificial insemination child on the same grounds, this presupposes that the natural parent-child relationship is determined by biological blood ties, resulting in the denial of the formation of parent-child relationships through artificial insemination. This does not accord with the purpose or object of the Civil Act, which, by providing the presumption of paternity provision and the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity, sought to determine natural parent-child relationships while also considering factors other than blood ties.\\n\\n(b) Where an artificial insemination child is born between spouses who are normally maintaining their married life, the husband participates in the child’s conception and birth by way of consent, and this may be said to be the basis on which the presumption of paternity provision applies. A husband who consented to artificial insemination cannot later reverse that consent and file an action for disavowal of paternity. Furthermore, in light of the current legal system’s deficiencies regarding consent to artificial insemination, the medical realities of artificial insemination, and the purpose of Article 852 of the Civil Act, which restricts disavowal of paternity by a person who has acknowledged paternity, it should not immediately be concluded that the parent-child relationship is denied or that an action for disavowal of paternity may be filed merely because circumstances exist in which such consent was not clearly established.\\n\\nThe current law does not have an adequately developed system regarding consent to artificial insemination and therefore lacks express provisions on the preparation of consent forms or their retention period. The Bioethics and Safety Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Bioethics Act”) requires medical institutions to provide necessary explanations and obtain written consent from the person undergoing in vitro fertilization and his or her spouse (Article 24(1)); however, because the explanation and consent content primarily concerns matters related to the procedure, such as the purpose of embryo creation, if a dispute arises over whether consent regarding the establishment of a parent-child relationship existed, it may be difficult to clearly prove the presence or absence of consent. In addition, even if a consent form under the Bioethics Act or medical records clearly confirming whether the husband consented in relation to the determination of legal parentage were prepared, there is also concern that such materials may disappear because the retention period is limited to about 10 years (according to Article 20(4) of the Enforcement Rule of the Bioethics and Safety Act, the retention period for consent forms is also set at 10 years). In such a situation, to regard the existence of a parent-child relationship as differing depending on whether a consent form was prepared or retained is not an appropriate solution in light of the nature of status relations, which require clarity and stability. Therefore, as to whether disavowal of paternity is possible for an artificial insemination child, it should be interpreted according to the following standards, while in any case carefully determining the matter so as not to contravene the child’s welfare or to nullify the legislative purpose for which the Civil Act established the presumption of paternity provision.\\n\\nWhere spouses are normally maintaining their married life, there is a high probability that the husband consented as to an artificial insemination child born during marriage. Therefore, with respect to an artificial insemination child born during marriage, the husband’s consent should be deemed to have existed unless other clear circumstances are proven.\\n\\nAccording to the Ethical Guidelines for Assisted Reproductive Technology of the Korean Society of Obstetrics and Gynecology (hereinafter referred to as the “Ethical Guidelines”), sperm donation procedures using a third party’s sperm are in principle to be conducted only for legally married couples, and, in order to receive another person’s sperm, it must be confirmed that the husband cannot otherwise conceive naturally, such as where he is determined to have irreversible azoospermia. The Ethical Guidelines further provide that the couple subject to the procedure must be fully informed of the Ethical Guidelines and relevant laws and regulations, and that the procedure must be carried out after both spouses accept and consent thereto; they also provide that the couple subject to the procedure must be able to normally raise the child born through sperm donation and that the child born shall, in all cases, be regarded as identical to a child by blood. In light of this medical reality of sperm donation procedures, it is practically very difficult for a married wife to conceive and give birth to an artificial insemination child without the husband’s consent.\\n\\nEven if the preparation of a consent form or its retention is not clearly established, where, after the birth of the artificial insemination child, the husband performs an act that publicly represents the artificial insemination child as his own child, such as filing a birth registration while knowing that the child is an artificial insemination child, or where, after the birth of the artificial insemination child, he has maintained a substantive parent-child relationship for a considerable period and has informed society that the artificial insemination child is his own child, it should be treated the same as where consent existed.\\n\\nArticle 852 of the Civil Act limits the opportunity to disavow paternity by providing that a person who, after a child’s birth, acknowledges the child as his or her natural child may not thereafter file an action for disavowal of paternity. In this way, if the person who may file an action for disavowal of paternity acknowledges the child as his or her natural child, the parent-child relationship is thereafter fixed, thereby promptly stabilizing the status relationship of parent and child and producing results consistent with the child’s welfare. Where the husband performs acts that publicly represent or accept the parent-child relationship, such as filing a birth registration for the artificial insemination child or maintaining a substantive parent-child relationship for a considerable period after the child’s birth, this may be evaluated as an act by which the husband, who can be deemed to know the entire birth process of the artificial insemination child, acknowledges the child as his own child on the premise of such facts. Thereafter, the husband’s assertion of disavowal of paternity must be regarded as contrary not only to the purpose of Article 852 of the Civil Act, but also as conduct inconsistent with prior acts and thus impermissible in light of the principle of good faith.\\n\\nB. Factual background\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the lower court and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n(1) The Plaintiff and the non-party were a married couple who completed their marriage registration on August 2, 1985. After marrying the non-party, the Plaintiff was diagnosed with azoospermia at ○○○ Hospital around 1992. Accordingly, with the Plaintiff’s consent, the non-party received sperm from a third party and conceived a child through artificial insemination by in vitro fertilization, and then gave birth to Defendant 1 at the above hospital on (date 1 omitted).\\n\\n(2) In the portion indicating personal details among the photographs taken immediately after the birth of Defendant 1 that are attached to Defendant 1’s birth record, the acronym “IVF” for in vitro fertilization is written in the upper right corner.\\n\\n(3) On March 29, 1993, the Plaintiff completed the birth registration of Defendant 1 as his and the non-party’s child without raising any issue regarding Defendant 1’s birth.\\n\\n(4) Due to marital discord, the Plaintiff and the non-party filed an application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement with the Seoul Eastern District Court on June 28, 2013. Defendant 1, having lived without knowing that there was no blood relationship with the Plaintiff, learned of this when, around the time of the above application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement, he heard the Plaintiff say during an argument with the non-party that Defendant 1 was not his own biological child.\\n\\n(5) The Plaintiff and the non-party lived together with Defendant 1 from after their marriage until around the time of filing the present action. Until then, there are no circumstances suggesting that the Plaintiff raised any particular objection to the parent-child relationship with Defendant 1.\\n\\n(6) The court of first instance and the lower court in this case made a factual inquiry to the above hospital in order to confirm whether Defendant 1 was born at ○○○ Hospital through in vitro fertilization using a third party’s sperm donation and whether the Plaintiff consented at that time; however, the hospital replied that no medical records existed because the retention period for medical records had expired.\\n\\n(7) According to the transcript of the conversation recorded on July 28, 2013, after the Plaintiff filed the application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement (Exhibit 4), it can be seen that, at the time of the artificial insemination of Defendant 1, the Plaintiff knew that he was azoospermic and had consented to giving birth to Defendant 1 at the above hospital, and accordingly he had stated an intention to treat Defendant 1 as his daughter and to take responsibility until Defendant 1’s marriage.\\n\\nC. Existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as to Defendant 1\\n\\n(1) Examining the above factual circumstances in light of the legal principles discussed above, Defendant 1, the child born through artificial insemination during the Plaintiff’s marriage to the non-party, should be presumed, pursuant to the presumption of paternity provision, to be the Plaintiff’s natural child. Moreover, since the Plaintiff acknowledged Defendant 1 as his own child, it should be understood that the Plaintiff cannot seek to disavow paternity as to Defendant 1. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(a) After marrying the non-party, the Plaintiff underwent hospital testing and was diagnosed with azoospermia, and, recognizing that he could not have a child through natural sexual intercourse, consented to the non-party conceiving and giving birth to Defendant 1 using a third party’s sperm. Although the medical record retention period has expired and it is not possible to specifically verify in what form the Plaintiff gave consent, the Plaintiff consented to the non-party conceiving and giving birth to Defendant 1 using a third party’s sperm not long after receiving the diagnosis of azoospermia after having been unable to have a child for a long period after marriage. The Plaintiff’s consent may be viewed not merely as consent to a medical procedure, but as consent given with the intent to establish a parent-child relationship with Defendant 1.\\n\\n(b) The Plaintiff completed the birth registration of Defendant 1 as the child of the Plaintiff and the non-party without raising any issue regarding Defendant 1’s birth on (omitted date) which was 9 days after (date 1 omitted) when Defendant 1 was born. The Plaintiff filed the birth registration regarding Defendant 1 while clearly recognizing that he could not have a child due to azoospermia and that, with his consent, the non-party had conceived and given birth to Defendant 1 using a third party’s sperm. Through this, it may be seen not only that the Plaintiff consented with the intent to form a parent-child relationship with Defendant 1, but also that the Plaintiff acknowledged Defendant 1 as his own child and publicly represented this through the birth registration.\\n\\n(c) After Defendant 1 was born, the Plaintiff lived together with Defendant 1 for more than 20 years until he and the non-party applied for divorce by agreement around 2013, forming a substantive parent-child relationship, and he had never acted inconsistently with that relationship. Even until shortly after the application for divorce by agreement, he expressed an intention to fulfill the role of a father to Defendant 1. Thus, by protecting and educating Defendant 1 for a long period while Defendant 1 was registered as his own child and by forming a substantive parent-child relationship, the Plaintiff may be evaluated as having acknowledged Defendant 1 as his own natural child.\\n\\n(2) In the same vein, the lower court’s determination that the Plaintiff’s action seeking, against Defendant 1, who is presumed to be the Plaintiff’s natural child under the presumption of paternity provision, a confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship by an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship provided in Article 865 of the Civil Act is unlawful, is proper as it is based on the legal principles discussed above. The lower court made no error affecting the judgment, such as misunderstanding the legal principles on presumption of paternity as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. Judgment on the grounds for appeal as to Defendant 2\\n\\nA. Whether the fact that there is no blood relationship may be a reason for the presumption of paternity not to apply\\n\\nIn order to rebut the presumption of paternity under Article 844(1) of the Civil Act, one spouse must file an action for disavowal of paternity as provided in Articles 846 and 847 of the Civil Act and obtain a final judgment. It is unlawful for one spouse to seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship through an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under Article 865 of the Civil Act rather than an action for disavowal of paternity (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 25, 1984, 84MEU84; Supreme Court Decision rendered on August 22, 2000, 2000MEU292).\\n\\nTaking together the text and structure of the presumption of paternity provision discussed above, the basic legislative purpose and history of the Civil Act in providing the presumption of paternity provision regarding the legal status of children born during marriage, the marriage and family system guaranteed by the Constitution, the secrecy and freedom of private life, and the concrete balancing of interests related to the legal status of spouses and children, even if it is revealed that a child conceived and born by the wife during marriage has no blood relationship with the husband, it cannot be said that the presumption of paternity does not apply. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Determining the scope to which the presumption of paternity provision applies based on the existence or nonexistence of a blood relationship is not only contrary to the text of the Civil Act provisions, but would in effect render the presumption of paternity provision dead letter, thereby contravening the purpose and structure of the Civil Act, which treats the presumption of paternity provision as a basic rule concerning the establishment of parent-child relationships.\\n\\n(a) The presumption of paternity provision does not distinguish the scope of its application based on the existence or nonexistence of a blood relationship. To regard the presumption of paternity as not applying where it is later revealed that the child has no blood relationship with the husband is not consistent with the text of the Civil Act provisions.\\n\\n(b) As seen in 1.A.(1)(b) above, the presumption of paternity provision is intended to recognize a parent-child relationship based on the fact that the child was born during marriage so as to afford the child a stable legal status from birth and eliminate the legal protection gap at the time of the child’s birth. It also recognizes an action for disavowal of paternity so that a legal parent-child relationship that does not correspond to the true blood relationship can be aligned with the true blood relationship, while setting a filing period to promptly determine the child’s status and seek stability in legal relations.\\n\\nIn light of such legislative purpose and the form of the provisions, it should not be concluded that the presumption of paternity does not apply or falls under an exception merely because it is confirmed that a child conceived and born by the wife during marriage has no blood relationship with the husband, or that anyone may at any time dispute the father-child relationship presumed to be a natural parent-child relationship under the presumption of paternity provision. This is because it is contrary to the original legislative purpose of the presumption of paternity provision, which is to maintain family peace on the premise that the spouses are living a normal married life and to promptly stabilize the child’s legal status to prevent a vacuum in legal status. Where the legal relationship formed through the presumption of paternity provision has persisted for a long time and become solid, there is also a social need to ensure the child’s status is stably guaranteed by making it difficult for anyone to easily infringe upon the status so formed.\\n\\nExcluding the application of the presumption of paternity provision on the ground that there is no blood relationship destabilizes at once the parent-child relationship formed over a long period on the basis of the presumption of paternity provision, as well as the family relationships underlying social life, including the marital relationship closely connected thereto. Leaving the parent-child relationship in a state of long-term instability cannot be said to conform to the form of parent-child relationship that the Civil Act sought to establish by providing the presumption of paternity provision, and it is inconsistent with the inherent nature of a status order that requires stability.\\n\\n(c) How to determine the standard for the presumption of paternity regarding a child born during marriage is a matter concerning the fundamental rights of interested parties such as spouses and children and the constitutional decision concerning marriage and family life, and in principle is left to the legislature’s discretion (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on April 30, 2015, 2013HEONMA623). Ultimately, the parent-child relationship should be understood as something the legislature may specifically determine within the bounds of the Constitution, taking into account social reality and traditional conceptions.\\n\\nWith the recent development of genetic testing technology, scientific paternity testing has become possible. Social perceptions regarding divorce and remarriage have changed, and there is a greater possibility that, when the marital relationship has broken down, the wife may conceive and give birth to a child of another man rather than her husband. Thus, the social and legal circumstances have changed from the time when the presumption of paternity provision was introduced in the enacted Civil Act. However, such changes do not render the presumption of paternity provision itself, which is the fundamental rule regarding the presumption of paternity between father and child, meaningless, nor can it be said that the presumption of paternity provision has become unconstitutional.\\n\\nFamily relationships, including status relations, basically begin from the biological relationship of blood ties, but they are not necessarily composed only of blood relationships. Just as there are family relationships formed through social relations such as marriage, even when limited to parent-child relationships, in modern society not only blood ties but also parent-child relationships substantially formed while living as a family together have important value, so the need to protect them has increased. This does not change merely because scientific testing techniques have developed so that blood relationships can be easily confirmed.\\n\\nToday, in most countries, the principle of presuming natural children pursuant to the presumption of paternity provision is universally accepted, and the presumption of paternity provision continues to be maintained even in the course of amending laws relating to parent-child relationships. There are countries that allow the right to disavow paternity without limitation where there is no blood relationship, but even in such cases the persons entitled to exercise the right to disavow paternity in litigation are limited to the spouses, the child, and the biological father who have direct legal interests in the parent-child relationship. It is difficult to find a comparable example in comparative law where anyone may, without restriction, dispute the existence or nonexistence of a parent-child relationship merely because the absence of a blood relationship between father and child has been revealed.\\n\\n(d) Presuming, under the presumption of paternity provision, that the wife’s conceived child is the husband’s child is premised not only on the high probability that a child born during marriage is the husband’s child, but also on the high probability that a substantive family relationship will actually be formed on that basis. However, family relationships formed without blood ties also constitute family relationships that the Constitution and the Civil Act seek to protect. If such a family relationship has matured socially and become solid over a long period, for example by continuing until the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity has expired, the need to protect such family relationship and the trust placed in it becomes even greater, and it should not be allowed for anyone to easily overturn it (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on March 26, 2015, 2012HEONBA357).\\n\\n(2) If the scope of the effect of the presumption of paternity provision is determined based on the existence or nonexistence of blood ties, it is unavoidable that a third party who is not a party to the family relationship will become deeply involved in the private sphere inside the home, such as the marital relationship and family relationship. In order to make the presumption of paternity not apply to a child who is presumed to be a natural child, or to obtain a public confirmation thereof, a judicial determination must ultimately be obtained, and in such a case state agencies, including the courts, become deeply involved in the parent-child relationship. Marriage and the family relationship based thereon are guaranteed by the Constitution against state interference, and if such involvement is broadly permitted, it may instead result in the State or a third party infringing on the marriage and family relationship that the State should guarantee, which also runs counter to the constitutional purpose.\\n\\nDetermining a natural parent-child relationship based on the existence or nonexistence of blood ties requires, for a child born between spouses who were living a normal married life, proof individually that the child was conceived by the husband during marriage, or otherwise prevents the parent-child relationship from being finally established until such proof is made. In such a state, anyone may recklessly dispute the child’s legal status, and family peace is also destabilized. If the natural parent-child relationship is determined based on the existence or nonexistence of blood ties, then in a case where a suit related to the parent-child relationship is filed, it would be necessary to conduct a paternity test or investigate even the confidential aspects between spouses in order to objectively and scientifically prove that the parent-child relationship does not exist, and the spouses’ intimate private life may be infringed in the process. If a third party were allowed to intrude into another person’s family and, claiming to be the parent of a child born to another person’s wife, demand paternity testing and the like, family peace would be difficult to maintain. Broadly allowing third-party involvement in matters belonging to the spouses’ and family’s private life in the name of blood truth is contrary to the purpose of the presumption of paternity provision, which takes the maintenance of family peace as one of its important legislative objectives.\\n\\nThe harm caused by such invasion of privacy is not limited to the relationship between spouses alone. Privacy formed in the parent-child relationship under the presumption of paternity provision is also infringed. All of these persons have the right to privacy, and the child’s privacy in particular is directly related to the child’s welfare and requires greater protection. Such privacy deserving protection does not change in the extent of its protection merely because it is a matter of the past or because the marital relationship currently has been dissolved. In other words, such invasion of privacy cannot be justified on the ground that the spouses are no longer forming a family, for example because they have divorced.\\n\\nEven if the spouses’ marital relationship ends and the family is dissolved, it cannot be said that the need to maintain the legal stability of the child’s status relationship naturally disappears. The presumption of paternity provision does not merely protect the married couple or the child individually, but also functions to protect the parent-child relationship itself. Even after the dissolution of the family, the former family members have a legal interest in continuing to conduct their social life fully and stably based on the existing legal relationships.\\n\\nArticle 36(1) of the Constitution clearly states that marriage and family life must be formed and maintained while respecting individual dignity. Marriage and family life are the most fundamental and private spheres of human life. In marriage and family life, the individual must be respected as an independent person, and the individual and family’s autonomous decision-making regarding how to organize marriage and family life must be respected. It is desirable for the State to respect family life formed on the basis of individual dignity and equality of the sexes and not to intervene in family relations based on personal and affectionate human relationships (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on April 27, 2000, 98HEONGA16, 98HEONMA429; Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on February 3, 2005, 2001HEONGA9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 2004HEONGA5, etc.). Unless marriage and family relations infringe upon another person’s fundamental rights or the public interest, state interference in marriage and family life should be restrained.\\n\\n(3) Even as a matter of legal theory, the existence or nonexistence of a blood relationship may constitute a ground for rebutting the presumption of paternity, but it cannot be a ground for determining the scope within which the presumption of paternity does not apply.\\n\\nWhile providing for the presumption of paternity, the Civil Act also allows the husband to file an action for disavowal of paternity within 2 years from the day he became aware of the cause for disavowal of paternity; thus, unless the husband knows of the cause for disavowal of paternity, the filing period for the action for disavowal of paternity does not run. This gives the husband, who seeks to align the legal parent-child relationship with the truth based on awareness of the true blood relationship, a practical opportunity to deny the presumption of paternity. Once an action for disavowal of paternity is lawfully filed, whether there exists a biological blood relationship between the parents and the born child becomes the principal fact to be proved. Ultimately, when one learns that there is no blood relationship, the filing period for bringing an action for disavowal of paternity begins to run, and the actual absence of a biological blood relationship is a ground on which the presumption of paternity may be rebutted by action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nThus, the existence or nonexistence of a blood relationship, or awareness thereof, is a ground that allows the presumption of paternity to be rebutted through an action for disavowal of paternity, serving as the basis for whether such action is well-founded or as the starting point for the filing period. It cannot, however, be a factor that causes the presumption of paternity not to apply at the outset so as to eliminate even the need to file an action for disavowal of paternity. Treating the absence of a blood relationship as a premise fact causing the presumption of paternity not to apply would make the existence of the action for disavowal of paternity, which imposes limitations on standing and filing period, meaningless, and is difficult to accept as a matter of interpreting the current Civil Act. Even if a practical opportunity to exercise the right to disavow paternity has been afforded, if it is not exercised within the filing period and can no longer be contested, such a state cannot be regarded as infringing the husband’s personality rights, rights to pursue happiness, and fundamental rights concerning marriage and family life based on individual dignity and equality of the sexes (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on March 26, 2015, 2012HEONBA357). It is also difficult to recognize any special necessity that would warrant granting the husband a renewed opportunity to disavow paternity by resorting to an interpretation contrary to the Civil Act provisions.\\n\\nB. Factual background\\n\\nThe factual circumstances found by the lower court are as follows.\\n\\n(1) The non-party conceived Defendant 2 through an extramarital relationship and gave birth to Defendant 2 on (date 2 omitted). On August 6, 1997, the Plaintiff completed the birth registration of Defendant 2 as the child of the Plaintiff and the non-party.\\n\\n(2) By no later than around 2008, when Defendant 2 was in fifth grade of elementary school, the Plaintiff appears to have already known through a hospital examination that Defendant 2 was not his biological child.\\n\\n(3) Nevertheless, for a long period until around the time of filing this action, the Plaintiff lived together with Defendant 2 without raising any issue regarding the fact that Defendant 2 had been registered as a natural child at birth, and protected and educated Defendant 2 as a father.\\n\\n(4) During the process of divorcing by agreement with the non-party around 2013, the Plaintiff notarized a memorandum stating that he “waives parental authority and custody over the minor Defendant 2, and will pay 500,000 won per month as child support for Defendant 2 until high school graduation.”\\n\\n(5) Defendant 2 grew up not knowing that there was no blood relationship with the Plaintiff, and learned of this when, around the time of the above application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement, he heard the Plaintiff say during an argument with the non-party that Defendant 2 was not his own biological child.\\n\\n(6) The Plaintiff and the non-party eventually reached a mediation in the divorce action, and on October 30, 2015, a mediation was established to the effect that they would divorce.\\n\\nC. Existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as to Defendant 2\\n\\n(1) The lower court determined that the Plaintiff’s action as to Defendant 2 was unlawful for the following reasons.\\n\\nEven in the case of genotype incompatibility, the effect of the presumption of paternity should be regarded as not applying, and it is clear that no natural parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2. However, at least before the application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement, all substantive requisites for adoption were satisfied, and an adoptive parent-child relationship was validly established between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2. There are no special circumstances such as the need to terminate the adoptive relationship between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2 by dissolution of adoption. Accordingly, the present action by the Plaintiff seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as to Defendant 2 lacks a legal interest in confirmation.\\n\\n(2) However, according to the legal principles discussed above, since the non-party conceived and gave birth to Defendant 2 during marriage to the Plaintiff, Defendant 2 is presumed, pursuant to Article 844(1) of the Civil Act, to be the Plaintiff’s natural child, and even where the fact of genotype incompatibility is revealed afterward, the presumption of paternity still applies. Accordingly, unless the Plaintiff filed an action for disavowal of paternity within 2 years from the day he became aware of the cause for disavowal of paternity as to Defendant 2, who is subject to the presumption of paternity, and obtained a judgment denying paternity, it is unlawful to seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship by an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship.\\n\\nAlthough there are inappropriate aspects in the lower court’s determination, its conclusion, which dismissed the Plaintiff’s appeal and upheld the first-instance judgment dismissing the Plaintiff’s action as to Defendant 2, is proper. The lower court committed no error affecting the judgment, such as misunderstanding the relevant legal principles as alleged in the grounds for appeal or exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence in violation of logic and experience.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAs the Plaintiff’s appeal is without merit, all of it is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged. Except for the separate opinions of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Noh Jeong-hee, and Kim Sang-hwan, and the separate opinion (as to Defendant 1) and dissenting opinion (as to Defendant 2) of Justice Min Yoo-sook, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, and Justice Kim Jae-hyeong filed a concurring opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n4. Separate Opinion of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Noh Jeong-hee, and Kim Sang-hwan\\n\\nA. As to the grounds for appeal concerning Defendant 1\\n\\n(1) The majority opinion states that where the wife, during marriage, receives sperm from a third party other than her husband and gives birth to a child conceived through artificial insemination, it is reasonable, when determining the parent-child relationship of the born child, to apply the presumption of paternity provision under the current Civil Act and regard the child born through artificial insemination as presumed to be the husband’s child, in the absence of a provision on this matter in the current Civil Act. However, although we agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion that a child born through artificial insemination during marriage should be regarded as the husband’s child, we differ as to the reasons therefor, and therefore clarify this point.\\n\\nThe Civil Act presupposes that the natural parent-child relationship between parents and children is based on the existence of a biological blood relationship between the parents and the born child. Thus, since the mother-child relationship can be clearly ascertained externally by the natural facts of conception and birth regardless of whether the woman is married, there is no need for the Civil Act to have a provision on this. By contrast, because it was practically nearly impossible to verify blood ties in the father-child relationship, the Civil Act established the presumption of paternity provision that a child conceived by the wife during marriage is presumed to be the husband’s child. This presumption of paternity provision is based above all on the high probability that a child born during marriage will have blood ties with the husband under the social background that it is naturally expected that a wife in a marital relationship will conceive the husband’s child.\\n\\nHowever, with the recent rapid development of medical technology concerning assisted reproduction, including artificial insemination, the social and cultural background underlying the Civil Act provisions on natural children has itself changed in the area of family law, and ethical issues and legal tasks that cannot be resolved by the existing Civil Act provisions and the traditional legal doctrine have newly arisen. Representative examples include the fact that persons who previously could not have children due to infertility or sterility are now able to become parents with the help of assisted reproductive technology, and how to regulate the parent-child relationship of a child born through such technology. What was once a so-called “problem of fate” has today become a “problem of choice,” and public discussion of the accompanying ethical and social responsibility is urgently needed. Due to the development of genetic testing technology, the uncertainty of blood ties in the father-child relationship, which is the premise for applying the presumption of paternity provision, can no longer exist. As the majority opinion does, it should not be said that a separate legal requirement such as presumption of paternity or acknowledgment is necessary for determining the father-child relationship, unlike in the mother-child relationship. It is now time to seriously discuss the legal evaluation of the “intent” of the husband and wife who wished to have a child through artificial insemination and the limits of their responsibility.\\n\\n(2) As a principle, legal regulation of newly arising social phenomena should be made through legislation, that is, enactment or amendment of statutes. However, even though legal disputes arising from a new social phenomenon are actually occurring, if legislation of the law to be applied in adjudication has not yet been enacted, the courts vested with judicial power by the Constitution cannot refuse to adjudicate. Therefore, courts must discover and declare the legal principles that a reasonable legislator would naturally have taken as a standard norm in such situations. Such judge-made law must be understood as properly included in judicial power as an effort to bridge the gap between social reality and the legal order when a “vacuum in law” arises due to the legislature’s failure to exercise its legislative power despite changing social reality. This judicial process of identifying the law is distinct from analogical application or analogical interpretation of statutes. Analogical application of statutes means applying legal norms concerning a similar matter, to the extent deemed justified in light of the legal system, legislative intent and purpose, etc., to matters for which there is a gap in regulation that the legislature did not intend despite the legislation (see the concurring opinion of Justice Kim Jae-hyeong to the majority opinion in the en banc judgment rendered on March 22, 2018, 2012DA74236). Even only for the case of the birth of an artificial insemination child through assisted reproduction technology, there are various types, including not only cases such as this one where sperm donation procedures using a third party’s sperm other than the husband are performed, but also cases where an egg from a third party other than the wife is provided or a child is born through a surrogate mother agreement. Whether such matters should be permitted from the standpoint of the legal order as a whole, and if so, how the establishment of their parent-child relationship should be regulated from the standpoint of family law, are matters to be resolved by legislation, not matters to be solved by applying existing presumption of paternity provisions, as the majority opinion argues. The courts must exercise judicial power by going through the process of forming the most appropriate dispute-resolution standard for resolving the matter at hand, that is, a “concrete and historical law,” by comprehensively considering the constitutional provisions relating thereto and their relationship with other statutes, the fundamental values pursued by the law, and the generally shared legal consciousness of society.\\n\\nComparatively speaking, many legal systems have resolved this issue by separately enacting legislation. In Korea as well, although legislative efforts have been made several times, they have not borne fruit. As the majority opinion also points out, at the time of the enactment of the Civil Act in 1958, it could not be envisaged that a wife could conceive and give birth to a child through artificial insemination, and therefore there was of course no need to have a provision on this matter.\\n\\n(3) The parent-child relationship between parents and children, together with the marital relationship, belongs to the most fundamental and private sphere of human life and at the same time becomes the basis of family relations under the Civil Act as the foundation for forming our community. The Constitution declares in Article 10 that “All citizens shall be assured of human dignity and worth and have the right to pursue happiness,” in Article 17 that “All citizens shall not be infringed upon in their privacy,” and in Article 36(1) that “Marriage and family life shall be established and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and equality of the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this.” Therefore, parents’ efforts to have children constitute an exercise of the right to pursue happiness and of the autonomous decision-making right concerning the formation of family relations, and must be respected to the fullest extent unless they infringe upon another person’s fundamental rights or the public interest; their secrecy must also be guaranteed.\\n\\nThe Civil Act provides procedures such as an action for disavowal of paternity or an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship so that the parent-child relationship and the true blood relationship may be aligned on the premise that natural parent-child relationships between parents and children require a blood relationship between parents and the born child. Nevertheless, on the other hand, where the legal interest of the child’s welfare and prompt determination of the parent-child relationship is deemed to take precedence, it prevents the arbitrary denial of an already formed parent-child relationship from a social perspective. The imposition of limitations such as standing and filing periods on the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity is an example. In this way, the Civil Act normatively first forms a family relationship called parent-child relationship on the basis of the fact that the child was born in a marital relationship and grants strong legal protection to the family relationship so formed; as the majority opinion aptly points out, this is a legislative decision left to the legislature’s discretion and should be understood as reflecting the basic values pursued by the law and the generally shared legal consciousness of society.
