Such values pursued by the Civil Act regulating family relations, and the social sentiment or legal consciousness generally discernible therefrom, should also be respected in setting the standard for the establishment of the parent-child relationship of an artificial insemination child born through assisted reproductive procedures.\\n\\nIf the husband and wife, in the course of the artificial insemination child’s birth, consented to the implementation of assisted reproductive procedures through a true concurrence of intent, this carries the meaning that, both privately and socially, they assume parental responsibility for the child with the intent of becoming the child’s parents. At this point, the husband is not merely consenting to the wife’s artificial insemination procedure. It is more consistent with reality to understand that the husband participates in the artificial insemination procedure from an equal position with the wife, by the unified intent of the spouses, and thereby actualizes the intent to establish a parent-child relationship with the child born therefrom.\\n\\nAs discussed above, where a husband and wife who are in a marriage have a concurrence of intent regarding the birth of an artificial insemination child and, on that basis, consent to the assisted reproductive procedure of artificial insemination using a third party’s sperm, the child should be regarded as the spouses’ natural child. This best accords with the Constitution’s principles of the people’s right to pursue happiness, the secrecy and freedom of private life, and the guarantee of family life; harmonizes with the Civil Act provisions concerning family relations; and accords with the basic values pursued by law as well as society’s generally shared legal sentiment and consciousness. Furthermore, the husband and wife’s concurrence of intent and consent to the procedure cannot be reversed retroactively. This is because doing so would contravene the constitutional decision on human dignity and value, the basic order of the Civil Act concerning parent-child relationships, and good morals and social order.\\n\\n(4) The lower court did not accept the Plaintiff’s appeal against the first-instance judgment dismissing this part of the Plaintiff’s action, and gave the following circumstances as reasons. The non-party, with the consent of the Plaintiff, who was the spouse, received sperm from a third party and conceived and gave birth to Defendant 1 through artificial insemination, and therefore Defendant 1 is presumed to be the Plaintiff’s natural child pursuant to Article 844(1) of the Civil Act. It is unlawful for the Plaintiff to seek, against Defendant 1, who is subject to the presumption of paternity, confirmation of the nonexistence of the natural parent-child relationship by an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as provided in Article 865 of the Civil Act.\\n\\nAs described in detail by the majority opinion, according to the factual circumstances discernible from the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, it can be seen that the Plaintiff agreed with the non-party, his then wife, with the intent to establish a parent-child relationship with Defendant 1, that is, with the intent to become Defendant 1’s parent, and that Defendant 1 was born through artificial insemination on that basis. Therefore, Defendant 1 constitutes the Plaintiff’s natural child, and the action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship filed by the Plaintiff against Defendant 1 should be dismissed as without merit. However, in this case, where only the Plaintiff has appealed, under the principle prohibiting reformatio in peius, the Court cannot render a judgment more unfavorable to the Plaintiff than the lower court’s judgment deeming this part of the action unlawful and accordingly dismissing it. Ultimately, the Plaintiff’s appeal as to Defendant 1 is dismissed.\\n\\nB. As to the grounds for appeal concerning Defendant 2\\n\\n(1) Under the existing Supreme Court precedents, as to the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision, the Supreme Court in the en banc judgment rendered on July 12, 1983, 82MEU59, stated: “Article 844 applies where the spouses are cohabiting and in a state where the wife can conceive a child of the husband, and where there are outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive a child of the husband due to lack of cohabitation, such as where one spouse has been abroad for a long period or the spouses are separated due to de facto divorce, the presumption does not apply.” Since then, through a number of decisions, the Court has consistently maintained the position of recognizing “exceptions to the presumption of paternity” under certain requirements (hereinafter referred to as the “limitation theory regarding the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision”) (see Supreme Court Decisions rendered on April 25, 1988, 87MEU73; May 10, 1988, 88MEU85; July 24, 1992, 91MEU566; January 28, 2000, 99MEU1817; August 22, 2000, 2000MEU292, etc.).\\n\\nIn the present case, however, the majority opinion states, “Even if it is revealed that a child conceived and born by the wife during marriage has no blood relationship with the husband, the presumption of paternity still applies,” and gives the “detailed reasons” therefor. Examining these reasons, first, determining the scope to which the presumption of paternity provision applies based on the existence or nonexistence of blood relationship is not only contrary to the text of the Civil Act provisions but also effectively renders the presumption of paternity provision dead letter; second, if the scope of the effect of the presumption of paternity provision is determined based on the existence or nonexistence of blood relationship, it is unavoidable that a third party who is not a party to the family relationship will become deeply involved in private areas inside the home such as the marital relationship and family relationship; and third, even as a matter of legal theory, the existence or nonexistence of blood relationship may constitute a ground for rebutting the presumption of paternity, but cannot be a ground for determining the scope within which the presumption of paternity does not apply.\\n\\nConsidering the majority opinion in light of its reasons, it may appear to suggest changing the existing “limitation theory regarding the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision” that the precedents have taken, by holding that no exception to the presumption of paternity may be recognized even where the absence of blood relationship is confirmed. On the other hand, it may also be read as maintaining the precedents by not expressing a view on this issue on the ground that this case is, in any event, not one to which the existing precedents concerning exceptions to the presumption of paternity apply. Although it is necessary to avoid unnecessary legal confusion on this point, the majority opinion is not clear as to its position. Accordingly, while we agree with the majority opinion that it cannot be said that the presumption of paternity does not apply merely because it has been revealed that the child conceived and born by the wife during marriage has no blood relationship with the husband, we wish to state our own separate opinion regarding whether there should be limits on the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision and the standards for such determination.\\n\\n(2) The above en banc judgment in 82MEU59 changed the prior unlimited theory regarding the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision to the limitation theory, and stated the reason as follows: “Article 844, together with the provisions on the action for disavowal of paternity in Article 846 et seq., was established for the peace of the family on the premise that the spouses are carrying on normal married life; therefore, applying it even where the factual premise is not satisfied and causing the matter to be resolved by the action for disavowal of paternity, whose requirements are strict, would rather run counter to the purpose of the system and may produce unjust results, such as promoting the establishment of father-child relationships contrary to true blood relations.” This was an effort, under the historical background of a time when it was practically difficult to scientifically prove blood ties and when the old Civil Act (before amendment by Act No. 7427 on March 31, 2005) limited the standing of the plaintiff in the action for disavowal of paternity to the “husband” and the filing period to “within 1 year from the day the child’s birth became known,” to harmoniously interpret the legal interest of domestic peace protected by family law and the principle of truth in blood relationships. The Constitutional Court also understands the issue of the scope of application of the presumption of paternity provision as a matter of how to harmonize, according to social realities and traditional conceptions, the “interests of the mother, child, biological father, and father in aligning the legal parent-child relationship with the truth” and the “interest of the party in seeking legal stability through prompt determination of the parent-child relationship.” Thus, the matter is in principle left to the legislature’s discretion; however, if the standard for the presumption of paternity is excessively unreasonable or the means of escaping from it are excessively limited so that it compels a parent-child relationship contrary to the true blood relationship, then it exceeds the limits of legislative formation and is unconstitutional (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on April 30, 2015, 2013HEONMA623).\\n\\nHowever, compared with the time of the above en banc judgment in 82MEU59, which first recognized an exception to the presumption of paternity in 1983, today’s circumstances have greatly changed in social, technological, and legal respects; therefore, the existing precedents that adopt the outward appearance theory as the criterion for recognizing exceptions to the presumption of paternity need to be comprehensively reconsidered.\\n\\nFirst, divorce and remarriage have increased sharply, and social perceptions of divorce and remarriage have also changed significantly. Accordingly, relevant laws and institutions have also changed, and the Civil Act provision that prohibited remarriage of women for a certain period was abolished, while the period from the breakdown of the marital relationship to the effectuation of divorce has become longer, increasing the possibility that a woman may conceive and give birth to a child of a man other than her husband. There are also many cases in which one spouse resides for a long period in a remote place or abroad, or both spouses reside in different foreign countries while maintaining married life. Above all, with the development of genetic testing technology, scientific paternity testing is no longer difficult. In today’s circumstances, where the absence of blood ties can be directly proven through scientific paternity testing, it is not an exaggeration to say that the need to restrict the application of the presumption of paternity provision by indirectly proving the absence of blood ties through the outward appearance or formality of “lack of cohabitation” has almost disappeared.\\n\\nFurthermore, through the 2005 amendment to the Civil Act, the person entitled to file an action for disavowal of paternity was changed from the “husband” to the “spouses,” and the filing period was changed from “within 1 year from the day the child’s birth became known” to “within 2 years from the day the cause for disavowal of paternity became known.” A sufficient period was thereby granted for the spouses to carefully deliberate, based on awareness of the existence or nonexistence of blood relationship, whether to maintain a parent-child relationship with no blood ties. Nevertheless, if the spouses raise no objection during that period, it may be regarded as an implied intent to accept the already presumed parent-child relationship as the legal parent-child relationship or not to exercise their right to disavow paternity. In such a case, there is a need to limit the spouses’ interest in being able to disprove the presumption of paternity in order to align the legal parent-child relationship with the blood relationship (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on March 26, 2015, 2012HEONBA357). Therefore, it should be understood that a parent-child relationship cannot be denied by an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship simply because the spouses and child lack a blood relationship, and moreover by proving outward appearance or formality such as “lack of cohabitation,” which is only an indirect means of proving blood relationship.\\n\\n(3) On the other hand, as already noted above, under Articles 10, 17, and 36(1) of the Constitution, all citizens have the right to pursue happiness and the autonomous decision-making right concerning the formation of family relations, and these rights should be respected to the fullest extent unless they infringe upon another person’s fundamental rights or the public interest. Further, although legal parent-child relationships or family relationships in our society are generally based on blood ties, legal parent-child relationships or family relationships are not composed solely of blood ties or necessarily coincide with them. Under our Civil Act, the adoption system, although distinguished from the natural child system, was early on transformed from an adoption system for the household head or adoptive parents to an adoption system for the child, and an adopted child without blood ties to the adoptive parents has the same status as the adoptive parents’ natural child from the time of adoption (Article 882-2(1)). A special adopted child under the special adoption system introduced by the 2005 amendment to the Civil Act is regarded as born during the married life of the spouses (Article 908-3(1)), is also indicated in the family relation register as the adoptive parents’ natural child, and takes the surname and family origin of the adoptive parents. Since a parent-child relationship subject to the presumption of paternity provision may be dissolved only by an action for disavowal of paternity, this necessarily presupposes the formation and maintenance of a legal parent-child relationship without blood ties. As seen above, even in cases where a child is born after receiving sperm from a third party through assisted reproduction technology, a social parent-child relationship different from biological blood ties is formed. Thus, while legal parent-child relationships or family relationships may still be said to start from biological blood ties, social parent-child relationships or family relationships unrelated to biological blood ties already exist in our society’s traditions and are accepted and recognized in more diverse ways within today’s social system.\\n\\nFurthermore, in light of today’s heightened consciousness of rights among the people, the concept of equality between the sexes, and the highly diversified forms of family in social reality, status-law regulation of children should above all be aimed at improving the child’s welfare, and the constitutional demand that the autonomous decisions of the parties to a parent-child relationship should be respected as much as possible must also be heeded (see Supreme Court Order rendered on January 31, 2019, 2018SEU566; Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on February 3, 2005, 2001HEONGA9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 2004HEONGA5; Constitutional Court en banc decision in 2012HEONBA357, etc.). In light of the ideals of family law and the purpose of the presumption of paternity and disavowal provisions—namely, prompt determination of the child’s status and legal stability—the need to recognize exceptions to the presumption of paternity should be examined from the standpoint of the child’s welfare. As discussed above, since the parent-child relationship has important value not only in blood ties themselves but also in the substance of social life as parents and children, if a social parent-child relationship has been formed and matured between legally recognized parent and child, it cannot be denied that there is a need to limit the trust in that social parent-child relationship so that it cannot be arbitrarily destroyed by one party or a third party (see the above Constitutional Court en banc decision in 2012HEONBA357). On the other hand, there are also cases where, beyond scientific proof that there is no blood relationship between the husband and child, no social parent-child relationship has been formed between them, or such social parent-child relationship has broken down irretrievably so that no interest exists to be protected by the presumption of paternity system. Moreover, the Civil Act does not provide a provision recognizing the right of disavowal of paternity for the child or biological father, who are the direct parties in interest to the legal parent-child relationship formed by the presumption of paternity provision. Although the mother’s right to disavow paternity is recognized, it cannot be said to necessarily coincide with the child’s interests. Where the mother and the legal father do not raise the child and, due to indifference toward the child, do not file an action for disavowal of paternity or let the filing period lapse, while the biological father has in fact formed a parent-child relationship by raising the child or there is a high probability that such a relationship could be formed, it is difficult to find a justifiable reason to restrict the personality rights and rights to pursue happiness of the interested party seeking the truth of the blood relationship, absent special circumstances. In such cases, limiting the application of the presumption of paternity provision may better accord with the child’s welfare that the presumption of paternity system seeks to protect.\\n\\nAccordingly, the traditional limitation theory that has recognized exceptions to the presumption of paternity only on the criterion of whether there are “outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive a child of the husband” can no longer be maintained as is. Considering the aforementioned constitutional demands, where scientific proof establishes that there is no blood relationship between the husband and child and no social parent-child relationship has been formed or it has broken down, it should be understood that the parent-child relationship may be denied without an action for disavowal of paternity as an exception to the presumption of paternity; however, even if the absence of blood relationship is scientifically proven, it is reasonable to understand that the parent-child relationship may not be casually denied by the law of exception to the presumption of paternity where a social parent-child relationship exists. Here, a social parent-child relationship may be understood to mean a state in which an emotional bond as father and child has been formed between father and child and the actual circumstances of life have been formed, such as the father’s intent to play the role of a father and to protect and educate the child. In determining this, various circumstances surrounding the family relationship should be comprehensively considered, such as whether the spouses’ marriage continues, whether and for how long there has been a living arrangement that may be regarded as a former family community, whether an emotional bond has been formed between father and child, the cause of the breakdown of the parent-child relationship and the parties’ responsibility therefor, the child’s age, the possibility of restoring the social parent-child relationship, and the effect that recognizing the breakdown of the parent-child relationship has on the child’s personality formation and emotions.\\n\\n(4) Examining the factual circumstances discernible from the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record in light of the legal principles discussed above, as the majority opinion states. In this case, the Plaintiff has maintained the parent-child relationship for a long period after Defendant 2’s birth while knowing that he had no biological blood relationship with Defendant 2. Defendant 2, knowing that there was no blood relationship with the Plaintiff, has the intent to maintain a parent-child relationship with the Plaintiff and does not yet know who his biological father is. Although Defendant 2 learned of this when, while the Plaintiff and the non-party were divorcing, he heard the Plaintiff say that Defendant 2 was not his biological child, having lived without knowing that there was no blood relationship with the Plaintiff, he still regards the Plaintiff as his father and is litigating the present claim while hoping that the Plaintiff will remain his father.\\n\\nIf such are the circumstances, it cannot be said that the social parent-child relationship between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2 has been extinguished, nor can it be said that there is no interest to be protected through the presumption of paternity provision. Therefore, Defendant 2 is still presumed to be the Plaintiff’s natural child pursuant to Article 844(1) of the Civil Act, and it is not permissible for the Plaintiff to seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship by an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship against Defendant 2, who is subject to the presumption of paternity.\\n\\nAlthough there are inappropriate aspects in the lower court’s determination, its conclusion, which dismissed the Plaintiff’s appeal and upheld the first-instance judgment dismissing this part of the Plaintiff’s action, is proper. The lower court made no error affecting the judgment, such as misunderstanding the relevant legal principles as alleged in the grounds for appeal or exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence in violation of logic and experience.\\n\\nC. Conclusion\\n\\nAs stated above, although we agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion of the case, we differ as to the reasons, and therefore state this in our separate opinion.\\n\\n5. Separate opinion of Justice Min Yoo-sook (as to Defendant 1) and dissenting opinion (as to Defendant 2)\\n\\nA. Premise for discussion\\n\\nThe parts concerning Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 share many issues. Both Defendants were born while the lawful marriage relationship between the Plaintiff and the non-party remained in force and while they were cohabiting as spouses, but genetic testing revealed that there was no blood relationship with the Plaintiff. However, Defendant 1 was born through artificial insemination using sperm from a third party with the Plaintiff’s consent, while Defendant 2 was born from the non-party’s extramarital relationship. The Plaintiff filed this action seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as to the Defendants, and argued that the presumption of paternity under the Civil Act did not apply because there was no blood relationship and because the Plaintiff had azoospermia, among other circumstances.\\n\\nThe lower court, as to Defendant 2, held that the effect of the presumption of paternity does not apply where the genotype is incompatible, but as to Defendant 1, it took a somewhat inconsistent stance by holding that, even though the genotype incompatibility was apparent in the third-party-sperm artificial insemination, the child is presumed to be the husband’s natural child if the husband consented.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Supreme Court is now in a situation where it must make a clear determination as to the scope of the effect of the presumption of paternity and the permissibility and, if permitted, the scope of any exception thereto.\\n\\nThe majority opinion, in its determination as to Defendant 2, states that even if it is revealed that there is no blood relationship between the child and the father, the child is still presumed to be a natural child, and it devotes the entire majority opinion to explaining the basis therefor, pointing out, inter alia, that because the presumption of paternity provision under the Civil Act is strictly framed, the father-child relationship of a child is uniformly determined according to the Civil Act provisions and cannot be determined through individual and concrete examination. The majority opinion then concludes that since Defendant 2 was born during the marriage of the Plaintiff and the non-party, the effect of the presumption of paternity applies even though genotype incompatibility was revealed, and therefore the lower court’s contrary determination is improper.\\n\\nIn other words, the majority opinion takes the position that even where there is no blood relationship, no exception to the presumption of paternity is allowed, and then immediately concludes that the presumption of paternity applies without further examining whether there are any other exceptions to the presumption of paternity.\\n\\nHowever, Supreme Court precedents have adopted the so-called outward appearance theory and have allowed exceptions to the presumption of paternity in certain cases. Because the lower court held, as to Defendant 2, that “the effect of the presumption of paternity does not apply,” if the majority opinion had held that “the absence of blood relationship does not fall under an exception to the presumption of paternity,” it would then have had to determine, as the next step, whether there are cases in which an exception to the presumption of paternity is recognized by Supreme Court precedent or interpretation, and whether this case falls within that scope, before reaching the conclusion as to whether the presumption of paternity applies to Defendant 2.\\n\\nConsidering the logical stages of such determination, the majority opinion appears to mean not only that the absence of blood relationship does not fall under an exception to the presumption of paternity, but also that no exception grounds to the presumption of paternity are allowed at all as a matter of interpretation. This is not only contrary to the position of prior Supreme Court precedents, but this opinion rather takes the position that the Supreme Court precedents should be expansively interpreted; therefore, we dissent from the majority opinion.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the concurring opinion to the majority opinion states that “the majority opinion did not address whether exceptions to the presumption of paternity may be recognized as a matter of interpretation because it did not mention prior Supreme Court precedents.” Although we find this difficult to accept, if the majority opinion’s intention is indeed not to express a view on the “interpretation and application of the Supreme Court precedents concerning exceptions to the presumption of paternity,” we wish to state our opinion in the sense that, in future cases where this issue arises, the matter should be interpreted as set out below.\\n\\nFor convenience of discussion below, we shall first address the part concerning Defendant 2, to which the general legal doctrine of presumption of paternity applies, and then address the part concerning Defendant 1, where the unique legal doctrine of artificial insemination is at issue.\\n\\nB. Dissenting opinion as to Defendant 2\\n\\n(1) Summary of the dissenting opinion\\n\\nThe lower court held that the presumption of paternity under Article 844(1) of the Civil Act does not apply to Defendant 2, but that all substantive requisites for adoption were satisfied between the Plaintiff and the above Defendant, and therefore a valid adoptive parent-child relationship was established. The majority opinion and the separate opinion of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Noh Jeong-hee, and Kim Sang-hwan (hereinafter referred to as the “First Separate Opinion”) both conclude that the presumption of paternity applies to Defendant 2 without even proceeding to a determination on the effect of adoption.\\n\\nHowever, Defendant 2 should be regarded as not subject to the presumption of paternity, and the lower court’s determination as to whether the effect of adoption is recognized is erroneous in that it misunderstood the legal principles concerning the effect of adoption and implied ratification and failed to conduct the necessary examination.\\n\\nFirst, the majority opinion, on the premise that the presumption of paternity under the Civil Act is to be strictly applied and that no exception is allowed in any case except for the action for disavowal of paternity provided in the Civil Act, denies even the area where existing Supreme Court precedents had allowed exceptions to the presumption of paternity in certain cases.\\n\\nAlthough the majority opinion may present a legally superior interpretation, it cannot derive a reasonable conclusion in many cases where “there is no parent-child relationship, but the family relation register has erroneously registered such relationship and the parties seek to correct it.” It is for this reason that, together with two successive improvement legislations easing the requirements for disavowal of paternity, existing Supreme Court precedents recognized exceptions to the presumption of paternity under the so-called “outward appearance theory.”\\n\\nWe agree with the First Separate Opinion to the extent that it pointed out the problems in the majority opinion regarding the permissibility of exceptions to the presumption of paternity and concluded that exceptions to the presumption of paternity should be allowed within a certain scope as a matter of interpretation. However, we differ as to the First Separate Opinion’s presentation of the so-called “social parent-child relationship theory,” which the Supreme Court had not previously adopted, and as to its view that the presumption of paternity applies to Defendant 2.\\n\\n(2) Whether the presumption of paternity applies\\n\\n(a) The majority opinion says that the presumption of paternity still applies even though the absence of blood relationship has been revealed. However, the nonexistence of blood relationship is a basic element in allowing exceptions to the presumption of paternity. Rather, the issue here concerns whether the existing “exception where the presumption of paternity does not apply,” which Supreme Court precedents have formed over time, should be maintained and, if so, to what extent; in other words, whether the legal doctrine that, by departing from the rigidity of the action for disavowal of paternity provided in the Civil Act, recognizes cases in which the presumption of paternity does not apply under certain requirements, should be maintained and what its scope should be.\\n\\n(b) Supreme Court precedents and their application in practice\\n\\nThe established Supreme Court precedents have held that where there are outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive a child of the husband, due to “lack of cohabitation,” such as where one spouse has been abroad for a long period or the spouses are separated due to de facto divorce, the presumption of paternity does not apply (see Supreme Court en banc judgment rendered on July 12, 1983, 82MEU59; Supreme Court Decision rendered on August 22, 2000, 2000MEU292, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the Supreme Court precedents, even in cases where the child is born during marriage and the presumption of paternity under the Civil Act should apply, if the absence of blood relationship is proven by showing outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child due to “lack of cohabitation” during the period in which the wife could have conceived the child, one may exceptionally escape the presumption of paternity and correct the status relationship in the family relation register to conform to the truth through an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship. The reason Supreme Court precedents have allowed exceptions to the presumption of paternity is, needless to say, that in the reality of our society there are diverse circumstances and reasons by which persons lacking true blood ties are registered as parent and child in the family relation register, and there is a need to correct the registration afterward to conform to the facts, while the interests surrounding this are diverse and complex, and the rigidity of the presumption of paternity provision in the Civil Act and the strict filing requirements for the action for disavowal of paternity cannot resolve this.\\n\\nThe presumption of paternity provision, combined with the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity, bars a person subject to the presumption of paternity from disputing the child’s status relationship if the person with standing under the action for disavowal of paternity does not file suit within the filing period, and thereby causes unreasonable results by requiring that even where the substance of marital and family cohabitation has already disappeared and the parties also seek to escape the legal regulation of the parent-child relationship, and there is little legal interest that the presumption of paternity provision was intended to protect, the matter can be rebutted only by the strict action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nThe previous Supreme Court decisions held that it is not in all cases where it is outwardly apparent that the wife cannot conceive the husband’s child, but rather where there are outwardly apparent circumstances due to “lack of cohabitation,” that the exception to the presumption of paternity is to be recognized.\\n\\nAccordingly, through the interpretation and application of the standard of the “outward appearance theory,” it was intended to harmonize, in concrete cases, the legislative purpose of protecting privacy and domestic peace and ensuring the child’s stable status, with the fundamental rights of the parties seeking to align the legal parent-child relationship with the truth.\\n\\nHowever, because using only “lack of cohabitation” as the criterion for recognizing an exception to the presumption of paternity poses the following problems, it is necessary to expansively interpret, in line with current circumstances, the meaning of “outwardly apparent circumstances” that the previous Supreme Court precedents use as the standard for determination.\\n\\n(3) Exception to the presumption of paternity\\n\\n(a) Reflection of social change\\n\\nLimiting “outwardly apparent reasons making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child” solely to lack of cohabitation would make it impossible to reflect changes in the surrounding conditions of adjudication in concrete cases.\\n\\nThe presumption of paternity and the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity have existed since the enacted Civil Act, and the first Supreme Court precedent recognizing an exception to the presumption of paternity was rendered in 1983. At that time, it was normal for spouses to cohabit in one place after marriage, so “lack of cohabitation” became an outwardly apparent circumstance showing that the wife could not conceive the husband’s child, as a means of clearly proving the absence of blood relationship without infringing on the secrecy and freedom of private life, which is the intimate sphere between spouses.\\n\\nHowever, at present, together with the rise in divorce rates and a general shift in social perceptions regarding gender relations, several circumstances have changed from the time when the presumption of paternity provision was introduced, including stricter regulation of divorce (introduction of the property division system upon divorce and reinforcement of the noncustodial parent’s duty to pay child support after divorce), which has lengthened the period from breakdown of the marital relationship to divorce. Forms of marriage in which women work while residing in different regions or countries from their spouses have also increased. With the development of genetic testing technology, scientific paternity testing has become possible at low cost and with remarkable accuracy without infringing privacy. In such circumstances, using only “lack of cohabitation” as an indicator of whether normal married life is maintained or whether the wife had the possibility of conceiving the husband’s child does not fit the current form of married life or the dispute situations arising therefrom. Thus, under the changed current circumstances, the “lack of cohabitation” formerly emphasized by the Supreme Court has become difficult to function as a reasonable criterion for recognizing an exception to the presumption of paternity.\\n\\nWhile recognizing the presumption of paternity principle, the courts must, through legal interpretation of the presumption of paternity provision, determine who may, until when, and on what grounds assert an exception where the presumption of paternity does not apply, and by what standards such a claim will be accepted, in order to decide whether to permit the parties to escape the situation where the presumption of paternity applies. This does not negate the significance of the existence of the presumption of paternity provision; rather, it is to determine through interpretation the permissible scope of escape from the unjust results that may arise from the uniform application of the presumption of paternity provision, which was already contemplated when the provision was created.\\n\\n(b) Amendment to the Civil Act and its limits\\n\\nAmendments to the Civil Act regarding the presumption of paternity have proceeded in the direction of easing the requirements for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nThe enacted Civil Act set the filing period for an action for disavowal of paternity as a short period of “1 year from the day the child’s birth became known” and limited the person entitled to file the action to the husband, but this was held to be unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court in its decision of March 27, 1997, 95HEONGA14, 96HEONGA7, on the ground that it infringed the husband’s fundamental rights to deny the parent-child relationship according to free will. As an improvement legislation, Article 847(1) of the Civil Act, amended by Act No. 7427 on March 31, 2005, set the filing period for the action for disavowal of paternity as “within 2 years from the day the cause for disavowal of paternity became known” and added the wife to the persons entitled to file. What is notable is that the above improvement legislation not only eased the requirements beyond the amendment recommendation then presented by the Constitutional Court, thereby recognizing a longer filing period, but also did not provide a rule limiting the filing period to within a certain period after the child’s birth.\\n\\nSubsequently, the Constitutional Court also rendered an unconstitutional decision in Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on April 30, 2015, 2013HEONMA623, holding that the portion of Article 844(2) of the enacted Civil Act that presumes a child born within 300 days after the termination of marriage to be the natural child of the former husband infringed the mother’s fundamental rights. As an improvement legislation in response, the Civil Act amended by Act No. 14965 on October 31, 2017 maintained the principle of presumption of paternity while newly introducing a system for a permission request for disavowal of paternity and a permission request for acknowledgment, so that, for a child born within 300 days from the date the marital relationship ended, the presumption of paternity could be excluded by a simpler method than an action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nIn particular, Articles 854-2 and 855-2 of the Civil Act provide that, for a child born within 300 days from the date the marital relationship ended, the presumption of paternity in principle applies, but if the family court grants a permission request for disavowal of paternity filed by the mother or the mother’s former husband, or a permission request for acknowledgment filed by the biological father, taking into account the results of examinations by scientific methods such as blood typing tests by blood sampling and genetic testing, or other circumstances such as long-term separation, the presumption of paternity shall not apply. Although limited to a specific period, this may be assessed as reflecting the legal doctrine that the scope of non-application of the presumption of paternity can be reasonably set through judicial determination by a court taking into account the surrounding circumstances.\\n\\nThe two rounds of improvement legislation demonstrate that, in response to social change, the need to allow exceptions to the presumption of paternity has become increasingly high. In areas not resolved by the improvement legislation, the need to expand the existing Supreme Court precedents is raised.\\n\\nAlthough the scope of relief has been broadened by the improvement legislation, in light of the reality of disputes surrounding the family system and the changed system, the filing period of “2 years from the day the cause for disavowal of paternity became known” is still not sufficient for the person entitled to file in some cases.\\n\\nIn actual family relationships, a party seeking to file an action for disavowal of paternity inevitably must prepare for the termination of the marriage. Accordingly, an action for disavowal of paternity is filed on the premise of a divorce suit or a divorce by agreement procedure. Where a husband learns that a child has no blood relationship with him and decides to divorce, and then chooses between divorce by agreement and judicial divorce procedures, the period of 2 years may be insufficient before filing an action for disavowal of paternity. The reason is that the family court’s protective role in divorce procedures has been strengthened.\\n\\nIn the case of divorce by agreement, the divorce cooling-off period system was introduced on December 21, 2007 (Civil Act Article 836-2), so where there is a child to be raised, the time required to obtain confirmation of the intent to divorce is extended by 3 more months. Whether by divorce by agreement or judicial divorce, matters concerning the upbringing of minor children, including the custodian and child support costs, must be determined pursuant to Civil Act Articles 843 and 837.\\n\\nFurthermore, even after divorce procedures have commenced, there are cases where the spouses seek to maintain the family again. If the 2-year filing period is uniformly applied, the person entitled to file is forced into a dilemma of either, instead of attempting to maintain the family, filing an action for disavowal of paternity within a short period and thereby extinguishing not only the parent-child relationship but also the family relationship, or forever losing the opportunity to disavow paternity by renouncing the right to do so. Such a result is undesirable because it runs counter to the purpose for which the Civil Act established the marriage and family system by legally regulating the child’s status through the presumption of paternity provision and the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nThe more efforts are made to improve divorce procedures and prevent indiscriminate divorces and family dissolution, the greater the need becomes to allow exceptions to the presumption of paternity proportionately.\\n\\nThe child and the biological father, who are the direct interested parties, are still denied standing (the concurring opinion to the majority opinion argues that the child may file an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship even if there are grounds for disavowal of paternity, but this directly contradicts the established Supreme Court precedents, which held that as long as the presumption of paternity applies, “no one” may deny the parent-child relationship and an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship is not allowed). In a large number of lower-court cases in which the presumption of paternity provision appears to apply, it is not difficult to find cases where judgments granting claims for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship filed by a child or biological father have become final without objection. The Korea Legal Aid Center for Family Relations, which provides legal consultation and litigation support regarding legal issues arising in family relations, submitted an opinion in this case (Civil Procedure Rules Article 134-2), stating that the presumption of paternity provision is excessively strict in light of social changes, and that in counseling practice it sees many people who suffer because they cannot register births, and that for this reason the scope of recognizing exceptions to the presumption of paternity should be expanded so that parent-child relationships based on true blood ties may be formed, while giving priority to the child’s welfare. This shows that, depending on the concrete case, applying the presumption of paternity provision may instead produce results contrary to the original legislative purpose for which the presumption of paternity provision was established.\\n\\n(c) Intermediate conclusion\\n\\nThe existing Supreme Court precedents recognizing exceptions to the presumption of paternity under certain requirements should be maintained, and indeed need to be interpreted expansively. The “outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child,” which the existing Supreme Court precedents used as the criterion for recognizing exceptions to the presumption of paternity, should be interpreted as including not only “lack of cohabitation” but also, in light of the various changes in the circumstances surrounding the presumption of paternity provision and the purpose of the amended Civil Act discussed above, “other circumstances that may be outwardly apparent as making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child.” Which cases fall under “outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child” cannot be stated uniformly. The family court hearing each case will reasonably determine the matter so as to seek concrete appropriateness by considering various circumstances. In the process, it may comprehensively consider not only the results of tests by scientific methods such as blood typing tests and genetic testing, but also the existence and duration of separation, whether one spouse had a separate residence or frequently traveled to distant places or abroad, and other surrounding circumstances. Furthermore, the court will be able to determine “outwardly apparent circumstances” by hearing and evaluating various circumstances, such as whether the spouses’ marital relationship has ended or broken down to such an extent that the former cohabitation surrounding the child cannot be maintained, the circumstances and process thereof, the attitudes and intent of the persons concerned, whether the person asserting the nonexistence of the natural parent-child relationship is a direct interested party in that relationship such as the parent or child, whether the biological father has the intent to acknowledge and raise the child if he is the claimant, and whether, in the case of a third-party claimant, there are signs of intentions other than the original purpose of establishing true status relationships, such as property interests.\\n\\n(d) Propriety of the lower court’s determination\\n\\nThe part of the lower court’s determination that, if a child conceived and born by the wife has a genotype incompatible with that of the husband, the presumption of paternity does not apply, is not appropriate. However, the lower court’s determination as a whole appears not to have recognized an exception to the presumption of paternity merely on the basis of the absence of blood relationship, but rather to have judged that the presumption of paternity did not apply by comprehensively considering all the surrounding circumstances revealed in the proceedings, including the substance of the marital relationship, the circumstances by which Defendant 1, who is four years older than Defendant 2, was obtained through artificial insemination, the fact that the Plaintiff learned that Defendant 2 was not his natural child, and the circumstances leading to the divorce from the non-party, who is the mother of the Defendants. Accordingly, the lower court’s determination denying the presumption of paternity as to Defendant 2 is proper.\\n\\n(4) Effect of adoption by birth registration\\n\\n(a) The lower court held that all substantive requisites for adoption were satisfied between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2, and that an adoptive parent-child relationship had been established.\\n\\n(b) Even where a false birth registration of a natural child is filed, the legal doctrine that gives effect to adoption where the substantive requisites for adoption are satisfied has been established and maintained since the Supreme Court en banc judgment rendered on July 26, 1977, 77DA492.\\n\\nDespite criticism that the above precedent lacks a theoretical basis or does not fit the adoption-registration system, it has remained firmly in place to date. This is because adoption had substituted for the system of raising a blood-unrelated child as if he or she were a natural child under legal constraints that made it impossible for an adopted child to take the adoptive father’s surname in a reality that negatively viewed adoption. This not only produced results consistent with the welfare of minor children, but also played an important role in stabilizing status relations by preventing third parties from disputing the effect of adoption. The fact that the existing Supreme Court precedents sought to ensure the welfare of children, especially minor children, by protecting the substance of parent-child relationships such as upbringing and support and by seeking stability in the child’s status relationship continues to have value today.\\n\\n(c) However, even if one respects the value of the Supreme Court precedents, if the adoption system and legal regulations have changed, one must follow accordingly. The 2005 amendment to the Civil Act introduced the special adoption system, reflecting the adoptive parents’ intent to raise the adopted child as their own natural child while requiring strict requisites and procedures. Furthermore, under the Civil Act amended by Act No. 11300 on February 10, 2012, it was provided as a requisite for adopting a minor that permission from the family court must be obtained, and adoption of a minor without permission from the family court was made a ground of invalidity (Articles 867 and 883(2)). The existing precedents also require as a requisite that there be no ground for invalidity of adoption between the parties; therefore, in cases to which the amended Civil Act applies, even if a false birth registration was made with intent to adopt, it would, absent permission from the family court, fail to satisfy the requisites for adoption and fall within the case of a ground for invalidity of adoption. Accordingly, where the amended Civil Act applies, the existing Supreme Court decisions granting effect of adoption to birth registration as to minors will no longer be sustainable. However, the amended Civil Act provisions have been in force since July 1, 2013, and in order to ensure stability in status relationships formed previously, they provide that they do not affect the effects arising under the prior provisions even after the amended Civil Act enters into force (Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions to the above amended Civil Act). Therefore, if all substantive requisites for adoption were already satisfied before the amended Civil Act took effect in a concrete case, the above legal doctrine would not apply.\\n\\n(d) Even where the amended Civil Act does not apply, the fact that the adoption system and legal regulations have changed as above is a factor to be considered when applying the purpose of the existing Supreme Court precedents to a concrete case.\\n\\nFor adoption to be effected, the adoptive father, adoptive mother, and adoptee must each express an intention to adopt. Supreme Court precedents have eased the requirements by recognizing adoption retrospectively where, even absent the consent of a statutory agent to substitute for the adoptee in giving consent to adoption, the adoptee can be regarded as having implicitly ratified the adoption after acquiring capacity to be adopted (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on March 9, 1990, 89MEU389). Meanwhile, where the effect of adoption by birth registration is at issue concerning a child born out of wedlock by one spouse, the consent of the blood-related spouse is not an issue and the biological father is excluded from the person entitled to consent (see, e.g., Supreme Court Order rendered on April 25, 2011, 2011SEU62; Supreme Court Decision rendered on May 24, 2012, 2011MEU3389). Ultimately, the “intent to adopt by the remaining spouse,” who has no blood relationship, becomes the sole factor determining the agreement to adopt. In such cases, when the spouse himself denies the intent to adopt and asserts the nonexistence of the natural parent-child relationship, careful attention must be paid in determining the existence of an intent to adopt, particularly an implied intent to adopt by ratification, after thorough examination.\\n\\nEven in the area of property law, in order to recognize implied ratification, there must be circumstances from which it can be seen that the person fully understood the legal status arising from the act and, based on true intent, acknowledged that the consequences of the act would be attributable to him or her (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on March 27, 2014, 2012DA106607), and merely allowing matters to stand without objection for a long period while knowing of the defect is insufficient to recognize implied ratification (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on January 11, 2007, 2006DA50055). Even without invoking the above legal principles, it is necessary to exercise caution in recognizing implied ratification solely on the basis that the person knew of the invalid adoption and “did not object.”\\n\\n(e) Propriety of the lower court’s determination\\n\\nThe lower court held that the Plaintiff appears to have already known through a hospital examination by no later than around 2008, when Defendant 2 was in fifth grade of elementary school, that Defendant 2 was not his natural child, and that, for a considerably long period until around the time of filing the present action, the Plaintiff had lived together with Defendant 2 without raising any issue regarding the fact that Defendant 2 had been registered as a natural child at birth, while protecting and educating Defendant 2 as a father and continuously maintaining an adoptive parent-child relationship, and on that basis determined that at least until before the application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement, all requisites for adoption were satisfied and a valid adoptive parent-child relationship had been established.\\n\\nAccording to the lower court’s findings of fact and determination, the application for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement was made before the amended Civil Act took effect, so the amended Civil Act does not appear to apply.\\n\\nHowever, the lower court’s determination is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nAccording to the facts found by the lower court, the Plaintiff clearly learned in 2008 that Defendant 2 was not his natural child, so it is difficult to see that the Plaintiff had an intent to adopt from the time of the birth registration concerning Defendant 2 until that time. The lower court only found that the Plaintiff did not object to the fact that Defendant 2 had been registered as a natural child until around 2013 when the present action was filed, or that the Plaintiff lived together with Defendant 2; it cannot readily be concluded that the Plaintiff thereby implicitly ratified an invalid adoption.\\n\\nFurthermore, according to the record, during that period the Plaintiff appears to have repeatedly pressed his wife as to who Defendant 2’s biological father was, and conflict appears to have continued until the present action was filed. The Plaintiff applied for confirmation of intent to divorce by agreement on June 28, 2013, and after the application was withdrawn, he filed an application for mediation seeking divorce on October 8, 2013, and a mediation was established on October 30, 2015, resulting in divorce. In the process, he alleges that the fact that Defendant 2 was a child born of an extramarital relationship became known to those around them, including the wife’s family, and to the Defendants, and that conflict with the spouses as well as with the children intensified, so that normal family life could not be maintained.\\n\\nIf so, the Plaintiff’s argument is that, at the time of Defendant 2’s birth registration, he was not certain that Defendant 2 was not his own natural child, and thus registered him as a natural child because he thought so, but by 2008 he clearly knew he was not, and yet spent about 5 years in a situation where he had to choose whether to end the marital relationship—which would also affect his relationship with Defendant 2, his spouse, and the other children—or to maintain the marital relationship as is. The lower court should have carefully examined the circumstances at the time and all surrounding circumstances, including the Plaintiff’s attitude, in addition to the fact that he did not object, and then determined the existence of an intent to adopt and whether there was ratification. The ground of appeal alleging that the lower court misunderstood the legal principles concerning the effect of adoption and implied ratification and failed to conduct the necessary examination is well-founded.\\n\\nC. Separate opinion as to Defendant 1\\n\\n(1) Summary of the separate opinion\\n\\nAlthough we agree with the majority opinion and the First Separate Opinion as to the conclusion that the Plaintiff cannot deny the parent-child relationship with Defendant 1, we differ as to the reasons. First, we agree with the majority opinion that, in the absence of legislation concerning the parent-child relationship of children born through artificial insemination, the presumption of paternity under the Civil Act applies. However, we differ from the majority opinion regarding the scope to which this legal doctrine applies, whether disavowal of paternity is permitted, and its requirements. Next, the First Separate Opinion is an entirely different view in that it does not find the basis for recognizing the parent-child relationship in the Civil Act.\\n\\n(2) Application of the presumption of paternity provision\\n\\n(a) In Korea, there is no legislation governing artificial insemination and parent-child relationships. In countries that have legislation on this matter, they generally recognize the establishment of the parent-child relationship between the husband and the child born through artificial insemination on the basis that the husband of the mother consented to the artificial insemination. However, because there are differences regarding whether an action for disavowal of paternity is allowed, and regarding the requirements and manner of consent, it is difficult to find a uniform standard.\\n\\n(b) In the absence of legislation, there is an aspect in which it is difficult to apply as is the presumption of paternity provision that was established on the premise of a child conceived through sexual intercourse.\\n\\nHowever, the legislative purpose of eliminating the legal protection gap at birth is also valid in the case of artificial insemination, and taking into account that the presumption of paternity system for determining the father-child relationship has a structure similar to this case, where the husband and the sperm donor are separate, and further that if the sperm donor is anonymous it is not only difficult to identify the donor but also impossible to expect an acknowledgment procedure, it is appropriate, in third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination, to apply the presumption of paternity provision in Article 844 of the Civil Act between the husband and the born child.\\n\\nMeanwhile, third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination presupposes from the outset, prior to conception, that the child born to the spouses will have no biological blood relationship with the husband. In artificial insemination conducted with the husband’s consent, this is a circumstance already known to and accepted by the spouses, and the auxiliary acts of “the husband’s consent” and “artificial insemination or embryo transfer” substitute for sexual intercourse. Therefore, in such cases, it is difficult to find the necessity or justification for applying the outward appearance theory as an exception to the presumption of paternity.\\n\\n(c) However, this legal doctrine applies only where the wife, during marriage, gives birth to a child through artificial insemination using “third-party-donated sperm” with the “husband’s consent.” In this point, we differ from the majority opinion.\\n\\nAlthough the majority opinion expressly stated at the outset that it was dealing only with the case of “third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination,” in its actual reasoning it concludes otherwise that “the presumption of paternity applies to a child born through artificial insemination during marriage,” and thus says that the Civil Act presumption of paternity provision applies uniformly to all artificial inseminations.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states, “The legal status of the child does not differ depending on the specific circumstances by which conception occurred. Nor is there any reasonable basis to exclude the application of the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child on the ground that the child was not born through sexual intercourse.” Whether the conception occurred through sexual intercourse or artificial insemination is a factor entirely unrelated to the recognition of a natural parent-child relationship. There is no doubt that the presumption of paternity provision under the Civil Act applies where the wife, for medical reasons or other circumstances, receives the husband’s sperm during marriage and gives birth through artificial insemination; such a case is entirely different from “third-party sperm donation type artificial insemination.” The reason the presumption of paternity issue arises in this case is also not that “Defendant 1 was not born through sexual intercourse,” but that “Defendant 1 has no blood relationship with the Plaintiff.”\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that “it is unjust to take biological blood relationship alone as the basis for establishing a parent-child relationship.” However, it is questionable whether the core of the parent-child relationship can be divorced from biological blood relationship. Cases where the existence of a blood relationship is clear and cases where the nonexistence of a blood relationship is clear cannot be regulated in the same way.\\n\\nNext, this discussion does not apply even to cases in which assisted reproductive methods are used on the “wife” side. Generally, the mother-child relationship is interpreted as a natural parent-child relationship established by childbirth, but with medical advances, if all or some of the following differ: the “woman who provided the egg,” the “woman who actually gave birth by implanting the in vitro fertilized embryo into her uterus,” and the “woman who requested childbirth through surrogacy with the intent to become a parent,” then the scope of “wife” in “a child conceived by the wife during marriage” under Article 844(1) of the Civil Act and the scope of “husband” in “presumed to be the husband’s child” must be interpreted and determined under separate legal principles.\\n\\n(3) Whether disavowal of paternity should be permitted as to an artificial insemination child\\n\\n(a) Since the application of the presumption of paternity provision is affirmed regarding the establishment of the parent-child relationship of an artificial insemination child, the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity must also apply, and accordingly an action for disavowal of paternity may be filed.\\n\\nHowever, where the husband has consented to artificial insemination, it is interpreted that the natural parent-child relationship cannot be denied by analogical application of Article 852 of the Civil Act. This is because the husband’s consent is given to the medical act of artificial insemination, but since artificial insemination is carried out pursuant to that consent and is inevitably connected to conceiving, giving birth to, and raising the child, the consent should, absent other special circumstances, be regarded as intended to recognize the parent-child relationship of the child to be born in the future.\\n\\n(b) However, the majority opinion goes further and says that “in the absence of other proof, consent should be deemed to have existed,” and in that part regarding the requirements for recognizing consent, we differ from the majority opinion.\\n\\nSince consent has an important legal significance, whether consent was given must of course be recognized by evidence, and neither where the fact of consent is not recognized nor where the existence of consent is unclear and thus the fact of consent is difficult to recognize can consent be presumed or deemed. Also, unless the husband knew of the fact of artificial insemination birth, even if he registered the child’s birth and raised the child believing him or her to be his own child, this cannot be taken as consent. As long as there remains the probability that artificial insemination was carried out on the basis of a consent form prepared without consent or against the spouse’s will, the requirements for recognizing consent must be strengthened, not relaxed.\\n\\n(4) The First Separate Opinion says that if a husband and wife who are in a marriage had a concurrence of intent regarding the birth of an artificial insemination child and, on that basis, consented to an artificial insemination procedure using a third party’s sperm, the child should be regarded as the spouses’ natural child. It also excludes an action for disavowal of paternity in such a case by saying that the husband and wife’s concurrence of intent and consent to the procedure cannot be reversed after the fact. The legal doctrine proposed by the First Separate Opinion creates, by interpretation, a parent-child relationship so firm that it cannot be reversed after the fact where there is “concurrence of intent between spouses” and “the act of giving birth pursuant to artificial insemination procedures.”\\n\\nThe Civil Act does not provide that the effect of establishing a natural parent-child relationship arises solely on the basis of the “intent” to become a parent. Parent-child relationships form the basis of family relationships and have important status-law effects that serve as the basis for various related legal effects. It is difficult to agree with the First Separate Opinion, which excludes the related provisions of the Civil Act that can be applied in the absence of legislation and, through interpretation, seeks to achieve greater legal effects than the Civil Act anticipates.\\n\\nD. For the above reasons, although we agree with the majority opinion and the First Separate Opinion as to the conclusion concerning Defendant 1, we differ as to the reasons, and state this in our separate opinion; as to Defendant 2, we cannot agree with the majority opinion or the First Separate Opinion.\\n\\n6. Concurring Opinion of Justice Kim Jae-hyeong to the Majority Opinion\\n\\nI would like to present an opinion supplementing the majority opinion concerning several questions raised about the majority opinion.\\n\\nA. Can the presumption of paternity provision be applied to an artificial insemination child?\\n\\n(1) When new circumstances not anticipated by the legislature arise due to changes in society, how the law should be interpreted or applied often raises difficult problems.\\n\\nDue to the limits of human cognitive and predictive ability, the legislature cannot enact laws while anticipating all concrete cases to which the laws will apply. Nor can it preliminarily determine the contents of laws to fit a wide variety of cases in response to ever-changing social reality and various problem situations. Therefore, the law must continue to maintain vitality as a norm regulating real life not only for cases specifically contemplated by the legislature at the time of enactment, but also for cases not so contemplated. If the law were applied only to the specific cases anticipated by the legislature, then as society changes and science and technology develop, the law would easily lose vitality and require constant new legislation.\\n\\nEven where a case arises that the legislature had not anticipated at all at the time of enactment, the courts cannot refuse to adjudicate. Where neither written law nor custom serving as the standard for adjudication in a civil case exists, the judge must adjudicate according to reason and logic (Civil Act Article 1). The courts, in order to determine whether existing laws can be applied to new cases not anticipated by the legislature, must utilize various methods of legal interpretation to ascertain the meaning of the law and carefully examine whether it can be applied to the new case.\\n\\nGenerally speaking, unless contrary to the ordinary meaning of the statutory text, the courts must respond to changes and developments in the times by interpreting and determining the meaning of the law as concretely applicable through systematic and logical interpretive methods that consider the legislative purpose and object, the history of enactment and amendment, harmony with the legal order as a whole, and relations with other laws and regulations. It is not desirable to simply conclude that a case requires judge-made law and attempt to solve it by new legal doctrine merely because it is a case the legislature had not anticipated at all at the time of enactment, without carefully examining whether existing law can be applied or applied by analogy.\\n\\n(2) As the majority opinion notes, at the time the Civil Act was enacted, it was not conceivable that a child could be born through artificial insemination, and therefore no express provision could be established concerning the attribution of the parent-child relationship of a child conceived through artificial insemination. Even after the phenomenon of children being born through artificial insemination emerged, no legislation was enacted to determine the attribution of the parent-child relationship of such children. Thus, it may be said that there is a legal vacuum with respect to the issue of attribution of the parent-child relationship of children conceived through artificial insemination.\\n\\nHowever, to resolve this issue, one must begin from the Civil Act’s provisions determining parent-child relationships. The Civil Act does not have an express provision excluding the application of the presumption of paternity to an artificial insemination child. The presumption of paternity provision in the Civil Act is framed very broadly, providing that a child conceived by the wife during marriage is presumed to be the husband’s child. Therefore, interpreting this provision as generally applying to the father-child relationship of a child conceived by the wife during marriage is consistent with textual interpretation.\\n\\nThe Civil Act legislator anticipated that a child conceived by the wife during marriage might not have blood ties with the husband, and contemplated the application of the presumption of paternity provision even in such a case. Even if a child born through artificial insemination by receiving a third party’s sperm has no blood relationship with the husband, applying the presumption of paternity provision to such a child cannot be regarded as contrary not only to the statutory text but also to the legislature’s intent and purpose. Accordingly, the fact that the Civil Act legislator did not anticipate conception and birth of an artificial insemination child when establishing the presumption of paternity provision cannot, by itself, exclude the application of the presumption of paternity provision.\\n\\nThe meaning of statutory text is not fixed. It may change according to socioeconomic changes and the development of science and technology. Objects that were not previously expected to fall within the scope of the statutory text may, with the passage of time and social change, be included within the subject matter regulated by the law. Even where the wife conceives through a new method such as artificial insemination by receiving a third party’s sperm, it is reasonable, from today’s perspective, to regard this as included in the concept of “conception,” which is a requirement for the application of the presumption of paternity provision. Because the presumption of paternity provision does not specify a particular regulated subject such as natural conception, but instead sets forth the rule in a broad manner, it can be seen as flexibly responding to the new phenomenon of artificial insemination.\\n\\nIf the presumption of paternity provision does not apply to artificial insemination, at minimum analogical application should be affirmed. This is because there are similarities between the case contemplated by the legislature when establishing the presumption of paternity provision and the case of an artificial insemination child, and in light of the system of legal norms and the legislative intent and purpose, applying the presumption of paternity provision by analogy can be assessed as justified. However, the legal effect does not differ depending on whether the presumption of paternity provision is applied or applied by analogy to an artificial insemination child. It is not the case that analogical application must always be considered merely because a case was not anticipated by the legislature; as noted above, in light of the textual form of the presumption of paternity provision, applying the presumption of paternity provision to an artificial insemination child is a reasonable method of interpretation and application of law.\\n\\nB. Can parent-child relationships be determined according to social parent-child relationships?\\n\\n(1) The separate opinion states that where no social parent-child relationship has been formed between legally recognized parent and child, or where a social parent-child relationship has broken down and there is no interest to be protected by the presumption of paternity system, and where scientific proof establishes that there is no blood relationship between the mother’s husband and the child due to genotype incompatibility, an exception to the presumption of paternity should be recognized. Through this, the separate opinion takes the existence or nonexistence of the so-called “social parent-child relationship” as the standard for determining parent-child relationships. However, this standard lacks legal basis and cannot serve as a standard for determining parent-child relationships.\\n\\n(2) Legal interpretation should, as a principle, faithfully follow the ordinary meaning of the text, and furthermore should aim to produce the most reasonable interpretation for the concrete case by additionally employing systematic and logical methods of interpretation that consider the legislative purpose and object of the law, the history of enactment and amendment, harmony with the legal order as a whole, and relations with other laws and regulations. However, if the statutory text itself is composed of relatively clear concepts, other methods of interpretation are in principle unnecessary or may be used only in limited fashion (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on April 23, 2009, 2006DA81035, etc.).\\n\\nAs the majority opinion notes, the presumption of paternity provision determines whether the presumption of paternity applies solely by reference to conception during marriage, and does not distinguish application on other grounds. The factors determining whether the presumption of paternity provision applies are marriage, conception, and birth. Since all of these are determined at the time of birth, it cannot be said that whether the presumption of paternity applies changes according to circumstances arising after birth. Treating the existence or nonexistence of a “social parent-child relationship,” which is a circumstance after birth, as a ground for exception to the presumption of paternity is not consistent with the Civil Act’s approach of determining the application of the presumption of paternity provision based on the time of birth.\\n\\n(3) Circumstances that a social parent-child relationship was not formed or has broken down after birth are not only difficult to function as a consistent standard, but interpreting them as grounds on which the presumption of paternity does not apply also runs counter to the purpose and object of the presumption of paternity provision.\\n\\nThe “social parent-child relationship” proposed by the separate opinion as a standard of determination contains many evaluative elements and is difficult to operate as a consistent standard. Also, the breakdown of a social parent-child relationship may be intentionally created by the parties and is mutable. Even if the relationship appears broken down at the time of trial, it may be restored. The separate opinion views that where a child has formed a social parent-child relationship with the biological father, an exception to the presumption of paternity should be recognized so that a legal parent-child relationship with the biological father can be secured; however, it should not be overlooked that the social parent-child relationship between child and biological father may also be mutable.\\n\\nFurthermore, it is not reasonable to treat such criteria as grounds for exception to the presumption of paternity so as to deny the legally presumed parent-child relationship. The presumption of paternity provision has the legislative purpose of maintaining family peace and promptly stabilizing the child’s legal status. Moreover, the fact that the Civil Act limits standing and the filing period in the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity, thereby giving the presumption of paternity stronger force than other presumptions recognized by law, was also intended to protect the legal interests of the persons concerned through the stability of status relations.
