Since there is no express exception provision in the statute and interpretation contrary to the statutory text in a direction opposed to legislative intent and purpose should be restrained.\\n\\nGermany’s recognition of the biological father’s right to disavow paternity even with respect to a child presumed to be his and its limitation of the biological father’s right to disavow paternity where there exists a “social family relationship” between the legally formed father and child can also be understood from this perspective. German Civil Code laws prescribe the procedure for disavowal of paternity by statute and limit the eligible applicants and the application period for the stability of the child’s legal status (Sections 1600 and 1600b). In particular, although it allows not only the father (where recognized by marriage or acknowledgment, etc.), the mother, and the child, but also the biological father to exercise the right to disavow paternity, it further limits the biological father’s right by providing that, unlike the other applicants, the biological father may exercise the right only on the premise that no “social family relationship” exists between the legally formed father and child. It permits the biological father’s disavowal of paternity only where no social family relationship exists between father and child. Thus, in Germany, the concept of “social family relationship” is introduced for the purpose of protecting the social family relationship formed pursuant to the presumption of paternity provision and maintaining the legal stability of status relations. This results in social family relationships being placed above blood relationships by protecting the legal relationship under the presumption of paternity provision. Conversely, allowing, regardless of who seeks to deny the natural parent-child relationship, denial of the legally presumed parent-child relationship on the basis of the “breakdown of the social parent-child relationship” may rather result in emphasizing clearly established biological parent-child relationships or blood relationships, and therefore cannot be accepted as a theory of interpretation of our Civil Act.\\n\\nC. Why the majority opinion did not change the existing precedent\\n\\nThe Civil Act presumes that a child conceived during marriage is the husband’s natural child, and recognizes an action for disavowal of paternity as a means to rebut this presumption, while strictly limiting standing and the filing period.\\n\\nThe enacted Civil Act provided that only the husband could file an action for disavowal of paternity within 1 year from the day the child’s birth became known. Since the husband often cannot know within that period whether the child is his natural child, it was necessary to ease the requirements for filing an action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court, in cases governed by the enacted Civil Act, held that where there are outwardly apparent circumstances making it impossible for the wife to conceive the husband’s child due to lack of cohabitation, such as where one spouse has been abroad for a long period or the spouses are separated due to de facto divorce, the presumption of paternity does not apply (see the above Supreme Court en banc judgment in 82MEU59; Supreme Court Decision in 2000MEU292, etc.). The reason given was that the presumption of paternity provision was established for the peace of the family on the premise that the spouses are carrying on normal married life, and that applying it even where that factual premise is not satisfied and allowing it to be denied only by the action for disavowal of paternity, whose requirements are strict, would run counter to the purpose of the system and could produce unjust results, such as causing the establishment of a father-child relationship contrary to the true blood relationship. The precedents can be understood as recognizing the above problems and developing a theory of interpretation that preserves the purpose of the presumption of paternity provision while preventing unjust results from its application.\\n\\nThere are arguments both for and against these precedents. Some argue that not only in cases of lack of cohabitation but also where genotype incompatibility is present, the presumption of paternity should not apply, while others argue that the precedents should be changed so that the presumption of paternity provision applies without limitation to children born during marriage. The majority opinion does not mention these precedents and does not address this issue.\\n\\nThe issues in this case are: ① whether the presumption of paternity provision can be applied to an artificial insemination child, and ② whether an exception to the presumption of paternity can be recognized on grounds other than the exceptions recognized by existing Supreme Court precedents.\\n\\nAs stated above, the presumption of paternity still applies even in the case of genotype incompatibility. Whether the existing exceptions to the presumption of paternity, recognized by Supreme Court precedents under the outward appearance theory, should be maintained, or whether the precedent should be changed so that the presumption of paternity provision applies without limitation to children born during marriage, are matters not directly related to the concrete resolution of this case, and such arguments are not included in the Plaintiff’s grounds for appeal seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship as to the Defendants. The majority opinion, without addressing whether to change the above precedents, limited its determination to whether the presumption of paternity applies to the Defendants under the issues discussed above.\\n\\nD. How should the problems arising from limiting standing in the action for disavowal of paternity be resolved?\\n\\nThe Civil Act has eased the strictness of the action for disavowal of paternity through the following amendment process. Article 847(1) of the Civil Act, amended by Act No. 7427 on March 31, 2005, set the filing period for the action for disavowal of paternity as “within 2 years from the day the husband or wife became aware of the cause,” so that the filing period does not run until the husband or wife becomes aware of the truth of the blood relationship with the child, and grants a practical opportunity to deny the presumption of paternity by providing a period for careful deliberation on whether to maintain the parent-child relationship based on awareness of the true blood relationship. Articles 854-2 and 855-2 of the Civil Act, newly established by the amendment Act No. 14965 on October 31, 2017, while in principle allowing the presumption of paternity to apply to a child born within 300 days from the date the marital relationship ended, allow the mother and the mother’s former husband to file a permission request for disavowal of paternity, and the biological father to file a permission request for acknowledgment, thereby allowing the presumption of paternity to be excluded by a simpler method than an action for disavowal of paternity.\\n\\nNevertheless, arguments continue to be made that the scope within which the presumption of paternity does not apply should still be expanded. The most important reason is that the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity does not contain a provision allowing the child or biological father, who are direct interested parties in the parent-child relationship (as to the child, the need for allowing the right to disavow paternity is even greater than for the biological father, and there is much controversy as to whether the biological father should be granted the right to disavow paternity and, if so, what restrictions should be imposed; therefore, below we limit our discussion to the child), to exercise the right to disavow paternity. If disavowal of paternity is not allowed for the child without exception, the child’s personality rights may be seriously infringed, or there may be a marked discrepancy between the legally presumed father-child relationship and the socially recognized father-child relationship, and yet the opportunity to correct this may be blocked from the outset.\\n\\nAs a matter of legislative policy, it is desirable to amend the Civil Act and grant the right to disavow paternity to interested parties including the child, provided certain requirements are met. Before such legislation is enacted, it is necessary to seek a solution at the level of interpretation. To solve this problem, opinions are being presented that the scope of exceptions where the presumption of paternity provision does not apply should be further expanded; however, this risks damaging the form of the parent-child relationship that the Civil Act sought to create by providing the presumption of paternity and the action for disavowal of paternity, and is also difficult to accept as a matter of legal doctrine. Here, we wish to propose a solution whereby, for husbands or wives who are recognized as having standing under the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity, the parent-child relationship is determined according to that provision, and for children and others who are not recognized as having standing under that provision, the parent-child relationship is determined by an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship through a systematic and rational interpretation of the current Civil Act.\\n\\nInterpretation and application of statutes in adjudicating concrete cases is an inherent authority and mission entrusted to the courts, and if a reasonable method of interpretation that considers both the connotation and extension of the statutory text can be achieved within that range, the courts should adopt such a constitutionally conforming interpretation.\\n\\nUnder the current Civil Act, which recognizes standing to file an action for disavowal of paternity in the husband or wife, the husband or wife may, upon learning that the child is not a natural child, file an action for disavowal of paternity within 2 years from that day and thereby remove the legal parent-child relationship with the child. However, unless paternity is disavowed, the child cannot escape the legal parent-child relationship under the presumption of paternity provision by means of an action for disavowal of paternity even if he or she learns that he or she is not a natural child. Meanwhile, the Civil Act provides, in addition to the action for disavowal of paternity, a provision on an action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship (Article 865) as a means to correct discrepancies when the substantive legal parent-child relationship and the legal parent-child relationship in the family relation register do not match. According to Article 865 of the Civil Act, a person having an interest in the natural parent-child relationship may file an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on the ground of “other reasons.”\\n\\nSince the husband or wife may file an action for disavowal of paternity pursuant to the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity where there are grounds for disavowal of paternity, seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on such grounds is not permitted as it violates Article 865 of the Civil Act. However, although the child is the direct party in interest subject to the effect of the presumption of paternity under the presumption of paternity provision, standing is not recognized for the action for disavowal of paternity. Yet, if the Civil Act is interpreted in a direction that completely excludes the opportunity for the child, the direct party in interest, to align the legally presumed parent-child relationship with biological truth merely on this ground, it would seriously restrict the child’s personality rights, right of self-determination, right to pursue happiness, and fundamental rights concerning marriage and family relations based on individual dignity and equality of the sexes. This is not the proper method of interpretation that the Supreme Court, which takes as a principle of statutory interpretation the interpretation of statutes in harmony with constitutional norms, should adopt. Accordingly, it is necessary to examine whether the unreasonable result above may be removed through the action for confirmation of the existence or nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship recognized by the Civil Act. If, even according to the ordinary meaning of the statutory text, it is possible to interpret that the child subject to the presumption of paternity may file an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, and such a result does not run counter to the legislative purpose of providing the presumption of paternity provision and the action for disavowal of paternity, then through such interpretation it may be a reasonable method to realize the child’s constitutionally guaranteed fundamental rights by allowing the child an opportunity to escape the consequences of the presumption of paternity.\\n\\nFirst, in the child’s case, although grounds for disavowal of paternity exist, the child cannot file an action for disavowal of paternity, so seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship on such grounds is not, in light of the text of Article 865 of the Civil Act, naturally prohibited. That said, it should not be understood that anyone with an interest in the parent-child relationship of a child presumed to be a natural child may seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship under Article 865 of the Civil Act in relation to the child’s status. As seen above, the legislative purpose of restricting the action for disavowal of paternity in the Civil Act can be found in the early stabilization of status relations, the child’s welfare, and prevention of third-party interference in the marital family; through this, it protects the privacy of the child and spouses subject to the presumption of paternity and the peace of the marital family. Considering the legislative purpose of the presumption of paternity provision and the purpose of strictly prescribing the procedure and period for seeking disavowal of paternity in the action for disavowal of paternity, interested parties who may dispute the status of a child born during marriage and subject to the presumption of paternity should be recognized only within the extent that does not undermine such legislative purpose. Therefore, the child subject to the effect of the presumption of paternity should be understood as able to file an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship because the child has a direct interest, but in addition, a person with a status-related or property-related interest should not, absent special circumstances, be understood as being able to seek confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship.\\n\\nEven if the child may file an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, it cannot be said to be allowed without any limitation. The provision on the action for disavowal of paternity sets a filing period, requiring the husband or wife to file the action within 2 years from the day the cause for disavowal of paternity became known. Even where a child subject to the presumption of paternity files an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, absent special circumstances, the filing period should be limited by analogically applying the provision on the action for disavowal of paternity, and the starting point should be understood as when the child became aware of the cause for disavowal of paternity (if the child learned of the cause while still a minor, the day the child reached majority).\\n\\nIn this way, if a child subject to the presumption of paternity receives a final judgment declaring the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, the res judicata effect of that judgment extends to third parties as well pursuant to Article 21 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Registration, etc. of Family Relationships, so that no one may assert, in or out of litigation, any claim contrary to the effect of such disavowal of paternity, and the effect of the presumption of paternity disappears. However, even a child who can file an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship with the effect of disavowal of paternity cannot immediately assert an exception to the presumption of paternity or deny the effect of the presumption of paternity in the absence of such a judgment. In other words, unless there is a final judgment granting such a claim for confirmation of the nonexistence of a natural parent-child relationship, a child subject to the presumption of paternity cannot file an action for acknowledgment against the biological father, nor can the biological father acknowledge such a child.\\n\\nIt is desirable to resolve the problems arising from the strict limitation of standing in the action for disavowal of paternity by allowing the effect of the presumption of paternity under the presumption of paternity provision to be rebutted within the extent that the purpose of the presumption of paternity provision or the action for disavowal of paternity is not nullified.\\n\\nI present the above supplemental opinion to the majority opinion."}

{"[2018DA1049]": "We consider the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Civil Act Article 860 provides in its main text that “acknowledgment shall have effect retroactively from the time of the child’s birth,” while its proviso states that “however, it shall not prejudice rights acquired by a third party,” thereby limiting the retroactive effect of acknowledgment; and Civil Act Article 1014 provides that “if a person who became a co-heir by acknowledgment or by a final and conclusive judgment after the opening of succession claims partition of the inherited property, and another co-heir has already partitioned or otherwise disposed of it, such person has the right to claim payment of an amount equivalent to his/her share of the inheritance.”\\nHowever, between a child born out of wedlock and the birth mother, a legal parent-child relationship arises automatically by the child’s birth without waiting for the birth mother’s acknowledgment or birth registration (see Supreme Court Judgment 67DA1791, rendered October 4, 1967), and it is not the case that such relationship may be recognized only where there is an entry in the family relation register or a judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship by a court (see Supreme Court Judgment 92NU3199, rendered July 10, 1992). Therefore, the proviso to Civil Act Article 860 concerning the limitation on the retroactive effect of acknowledgment does not apply, nor is it applied by analogy, to a mother-child relationship that does not require acknowledgment, and it cannot be said on the basis of Civil Act Article 1014, which prescribes the right of a person who became a co-heir by acknowledgment or by a final and conclusive judgment after the opening of succession to claim payment of value, that such person may not deny the effect of the division or disposition of inherited property made by the mother’s other co-heir. The same applies even if the mother-child relationship was only later made clear through the finality of a judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship, etc., after another co-heir had already partitioned or disposed of the inherited property.\\n2. a. According to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below determined as follows. Inherited property that was partitioned or disposed of by co-heirs before acknowledgment definitively vests in the co-heir who received the partition or the transferee, pursuant to the limitation on the retroactive effect of acknowledgment prescribed in the proviso to Civil Act Article 860, and this legal principle also applies where a person who was later determined to be an heir by the finality of an action for confirmation of the existence of a parent-child relationship after the opening of succession comes into existence. The judgment that a biological parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiff (selected party) and the designated parties (hereinafter referred to as “the Plaintiffs, etc.”) and Non-party 1 became final after Defendant 1 disposed of the real property listed in Attached List 1 of the judgment below (hereinafter referred to as “the Real Property”) to Defendant 2 and completed the registration of transfer of ownership. Ultimately, the Plaintiffs, etc. fall under “a person who became a co-heir by the finality of a judgment after the opening of succession” under Civil Act Article 1014, and therefore may exercise only the right to claim payment of value equivalent to the purchase price against Defendant 1, and may not deny the effect of the disposition of the Real Property, whose ownership was definitively vested in Defendant 2.\\nb. However, the above determination by the court below is difficult to accept as it stands for the following reasons.\\n1) According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\na) Non-party 1 married Non-party 2 and gave birth to Defendant 1, and thereafter divorced, while maintaining a de facto marital relationship with Non-party 3 and giving birth to the Plaintiffs, etc.\\nb) Non-party 1 owned the Real Property and died on January 27, 2015. After Defendant 1 completed the registration of transfer of ownership on the Real Property on the grounds of inheritance on June 8, 2015, Defendant 1 sold the Real Property to Defendant 2 on June 25, 2015 and completed the registration of transfer of ownership around that time.\\nc) On February 12, 2016, the Plaintiffs, etc. filed an action seeking confirmation that a biological parent-child relationship existed between Non-party 1 and the Plaintiffs, etc., and on July 1, 2016, the judgment granting that claim became final and conclusive.\\n2) In light of the foregoing legal principle, the facts above indicate that between the Plaintiffs, etc. and their birth mother, Non-party 1, a legal parent-child relationship arose automatically by the birth of the Plaintiffs, etc., and it is not the case that such relationship may be recognized only if there is a judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship by a court.\\nTherefore, the proviso to Civil Act Article 860 does not apply, nor is it applied by analogy, between the Plaintiffs, etc. and Non-party 1, and it cannot be said on the basis of Civil Act Article 1014 that the Plaintiffs, etc. may not deny the effect of Defendant 1’s disposition of the Real Property. The same applies even if the judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship between the Plaintiffs, etc. and Non-party 1 became final and conclusive only after Defendant 1 had already disposed of the Real Property, thereby making the mother-child relationship clear only then.\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below, on the grounds set forth above, dismissed the Plaintiffs, etc.’s claim seeking cancellation of the registration of transfer of co-ownership shares in the names of the Defendants with respect to the Real Property, thereby committing an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the mother-child relationship and the scope of application of the proviso to Civil Act Article 860 and Article 1014. The allegation in the grounds of final appeal pointing this out has merit.\\n3. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds for final appeal, the part of the judgment below against the Plaintiffs, etc. is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination. It is so decided by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision.\\n\\n[Attachment] List of designated parties: Omitted"}

{"[2020SEU616]": "We decide the grounds for the re-appeal.\\n\\n1. Overview of the Case and Issue\\nA. Overview of the Case\\nThe applicant and the person concerned in this case, born male (hereinafter referred to as the “Applicant”), had a sense of belonging to the female sex since childhood. Upon reaching puberty, the Applicant suffered mental anguish as the facial features, physique, and voice became increasingly masculine, but lived while concealing his or her gender identity, married, and then divorced about 5 years and 10 months after marriage because of issues concerning gender identity. Thereafter, in or about November 2018, the Applicant underwent surgery at a plastic surgery clinic in Thailand to remove the testicles and penis and to form the appearance of female external genitalia, and has since lived socially as a woman, wearing women’s clothes and hairstyle. While having 2 minor children (twins born in 2012), the Applicant filed an application for permission to correct the gender entry in the Family Relations Register (hereinafter referred to as the “permission application in this case”).\\n\\nThe court below upheld the first-instance decision dismissing the permission application in this case on the ground that, because the Applicant has minor children, permitting correction of the gender entry would have a negative effect on the welfare of the minor children.\\nB. Issue in this Case\\nThe Supreme Court’s En Banc Decision dated September 2, 2011, 2009SEU117 held that, in granting permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, if the person is presently married or has minor children, correction of the gender entry is not permitted. The issue in this case is limited to the latter, that is, whether it is appropriate to regard the existence of minor children in the case of a transsexual person who is not presently married as an independent negative requirement for correction of the gender entry.\\n2. Determination of the Sex of a Transsexual Person and Correction of the Gender Entry in the Family Relations Register\\nA. The factors determining a person’s sex include not only biological factors such as sex chromosomes and the genitalia corresponding thereto, but also mental and social factors, such as the individual’s own sense of belonging to the male or female sex and the performance of sex roles, namely, the socially approved behavior, attitude, and personality traits appropriate for a male or female.\\nIn the case of a person with transsexualism (Transsexualism, a term defined in the Guidelines for the Processing of Applications for Permission for Correction of the Gender Entry of Transsexual Persons, etc.), during the process of growth after birth, such person consistently has a sense of incongruity, discomfort, and aversion toward the biological sex at birth and feels a sense of belonging to a different sex, while continuously and firmly performing roles appropriate to the sex with which he or she feels a sense of belonging, so that mental and social adaptation has been achieved as a sex different from the sex at birth. Further, if such person can be recognized, by ordinary medical standards, as not easily being assessed as the sex at birth, and has reached the degree of recognition and acceptance as the transitioned sex in physical appearance such as genitalia, clothing, and hairstyle, as well as in personal domains such as sexual relations and friendships and social domains such as occupation, and thus can be deemed, even from a social-normative perspective, to have the transitioned sex, then such a transsexual person may be legally evaluated as having the transitioned sex, not the sex at birth.\\nB. The Supreme Court, in its En Banc Decision dated June 22, 2006, 2004SEU42, held, on the basis of the foregoing legal principles, that with respect to an application for permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, in the case of a transsexual person the sex at birth and the sex legally evaluated at present are different, and therefore the entry of sex in the family register [which can now be regarded as corresponding to the Family Relations Register under the current Act on the Registration of Family Relations, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Family Relations Registration Act”)] would fail to publicly disclose the current true status relationship, so the sex legally evaluated at present must be reflected in the family register, and accordingly permitted correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person. Furthermore, because such permission for correction of the gender entry is a decision intended to confirm the current true sex newly legally evaluated according to transsexuality, it was held that the effect of the decision granting permission for correction of the family register or the correction of the gender entry based thereon does not affect the existing status relationship and rights and obligations.\\nHowever, the Supreme Court’s En Banc Decision dated September 2, 2011, 2009SEU117 held that, if a transsexual person has minor children, the welfare of the minor children must be considered first, and that the correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children is not permitted, on the grounds that correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register may cause mental confusion and shock to the minor children, and that disclosure of the family relations certificate may expose the minor children to social discrimination and prejudice or cause difficulties in daily life.\\n3. Whether Permission for Correction of the Gender Entry of a Transsexual Person with Minor Children Should Be Granted and the Standard for Such Determination\\nEvery human being has the right to form a personality according to his or her gender identity and to live his or her life. A transsexual person also should be able to realize personality and individuality based on his or her gender identity and live together with others as an equal member of our society while pursuing happiness. In order to fully exercise such rights, a transsexual person has the right to have his or her sex according to his or her gender identity legally confirmed as the true sex. This is a fundamental right derived from human dignity and value, and forms the essence of the right to pursue happiness; therefore, it must be guaranteed to the fullest extent.\\nMeanwhile, a transsexual person with minor children also has the duty, as a parent, to protect and educate the children (Civil Act Article 913), and must prioritize the welfare of the children even when exercising parental authority (Civil Act Article 912). Therefore, when determining whether to grant permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children, the court must make a substantive determination by comprehensively considering various circumstances for the balance of legal interests so as to harmonize protection of the transsexual person’s fundamental rights with the protection and welfare of the minor children. Accordingly, one must not refuse correction of the gender entry merely on the ground that the transsexual person has minor children, without making a substantive determination in light of the above circumstances. The reasons are as follows.\\nA. Regarding Whether to Grant Permission for Correction of the Gender Entry of a Transsexual Person with Minor Children\\n1) Protection of Fundamental Rights Such as Human Dignity and Value, and the Right to Pursue Happiness of a Transsexual Person\\n(a) All citizens have dignity and value as human beings, have the right to pursue happiness, and shall be equal before the law (Constitution Article 10, Preamble; Article 11(1)). Human dignity and value imply that each individual should be respected for his or her unique personality and individuality, and should be able freely to choose and develop the content and direction of life deemed most suitable, thereby forming the self and destiny. A transsexual person, too, as an equal member of our society, has dignity and value as a human being, the right to pursue happiness, and the right to live a life worthy of a human being, and these rights must be protected. Therefore, even when determining whether to grant permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, such fundamental rights of the transsexual person as a human being must be guaranteed to the fullest extent.\\n(b) Considering the role that the distinction and recognition of sex plays in society, it is ultimately consistent with maintaining order in society as a whole and with the public welfare to ensure that an individual’s actual sex and the sex publicly disclosed do not conflict by having the individual publicly confirm and disclose his or her sex in a manner consistent with the sex currently legally evaluated. That a transsexual person publicly obtains legal sex in accordance with his or her gender identity through correction of the gender entry does not in itself have any potential to directly harm other members of society. Rather, if the true sex confirmed according to an individual’s gender identity exists, but the sex publicly disclosed through the Family Relations Register does not correspond to it, and that situation is left uncorrected, there is a high likelihood that confusion and misunderstanding will arise among other members of society as a result.\\n(c) It is correct to view the confirmation of sex in both private and public spheres as an essential condition of life for maintaining human dignity, which is determined prior to a person’s position or role within the family order. If permission for correction of the gender entry were denied merely because a transsexual person has minor children, then, contrary to the appearance and actual life formed in accordance with his or her gender identity, the person would be displayed in the official records as the sex before transition, and would be compelled to live an absurd life in which the sex as actually existing and the sex as shown in official records are inconsistent. If such an absurd situation is forced upon the person for a long period until the minor children reach adulthood, the magnitude of the suffering that the transsexual person must endure personally and socially, and the urgency of confronting absurdity in order to exist, would inevitably become immense. Such a result infringes the essential content of the constitutional demand to respect human dignity and value and to guarantee the right not to be discriminated against on the basis of gender identity, and is thus unacceptable.\\n(d) An individual’s family life forms the beginning and core of social relationships, and the State must guarantee it (Constitution Article 36(1)). A transsexual person, too, as a member who forms a family within the overall legal order, should be granted equal rights and duties, and the State must protect such rights of the transsexual person.\\nAlthough granting permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children may bring about changes in family relations, this is nothing more than a natural process in which the manner in which the rights and duties of the parent are realized changes accordingly as the fact of one parent’s transsexuality occurs. The parent-child relationship and family order thus formed must also be equally respected and protected within the overall legal order. This does not change merely because the transsexual person is divorced and not presently married, or because correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register has been made. A transsexual person with minor children must still exercise the rights and perform the duties that accompany his or her role as father or mother, and is able to do so.\\n2) Welfare of Minor Children\\n(a) It is not correct to uniformly conclude that granting permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children by itself causes a major change in the status relationship between the person exercising parental authority and the minor children, or is manifestly contrary to the welfare of the children, or leaves minor children exposed without protection to social prejudice and discrimination.\\n(b) Correction of the gender entry merely accepts the actual situation of a transsexual person who has completed transition and reflects it in the official record; it does not newly cause major changes in the status relationship between the transsexual parent and the minor children, or affect the substance of rights and obligations. This is because the personal, social, and legal parent-child relationship between a transsexual person and his or her minor children does not change regardless of whether it is before or after correction of the gender entry. Nor can the correction of the gender entry itself be regarded as impairing the essential and core content of the transsexual person’s status and role as father or mother within the family system, or the rights of the minor children.\\n(c) Even if minor children in some cases suffer mental confusion and shock due to a parent’s transsexuality, such confusion and shock arise because the parent has already undergone the transition, making it an irreversible fait accompli. Correction of the gender entry is a measure that corrects the sex entry in the official record so that a person who has already transitioned in social common sense can be legally evaluated as having the transitioned sex. Therefore, one must not hastily conclude that the permission itself for correction of the gender entry, which can be said to be the final stage of the transition process, causes mental or psychological shock to the minor children.\\nLikewise, the premise that adult children can accept a parent’s correction of the gender entry without much confusion, whereas minor children will suffer mental confusion and shock, is also incorrect. This overlooks the possibility that minor children, with their flexible minds, may naturally accept the existence of a transsexual parent.\\n(d) If an emotional and familial bond has already formed between the transsexual person and the minor children based on the transitioned sex of the father or mother, then it is desirable to grant permission for correction of the gender entry even for the sake of the minor children.\\nFurthermore, even in cases where the minor children have not yet adapted psychologically to the transitioned sex of the father or mother and are suffering psychological and emotional difficulties, if a divorced transsexual father or mother, through correction of the gender entry, provides a social and economic foundation enabling him or her to continue stably raising and supporting the minor children as a parent and an opportunity to seek understanding of transsexuality, this can ultimately serve the welfare of the minor children in that it may restore the bond between them. This is because a transsexual person whose actual sex conflicts with the sex publicly disclosed in the Family Relations Register may in some cases find it difficult in society to choose a job suited to appearance or to engage in economic and social activities corresponding to ability and aptitude, and the minor children of such a transsexual person are likely, while observing such father or mother, to become emotionally more unstable and to face the risk of being placed in a financially poorer environment.\\nTherefore, without examining the various situations existing or arising between the transitioned father or mother and the minor children, the court may, in a substantive sense, fail to act in accordance with the welfare of the minor children by barring correction of the gender entry merely on the ground that there are minor children.\\n(e) It cannot be concluded that, if permission for correction of the gender entry is granted to a transsexual person with minor children, the minor children will be left exposed without protection to social discrimination and prejudice or placed in difficulties in daily life merely because of the submission or disclosure of the corrected Family Relations Register.\\nEven if there is a concern that disclosure of the Family Relations Register may expose the minor children to social prejudice and discrimination, the State should protect the minor children by taking measures to block such disclosure for the purpose of safeguarding the fundamental rights and privacy of transsexual persons and their minor children; it is not proper to use that concern as a reason for refusing permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children.\\n(1) Our society has for quite some time now recognized transsexual persons, regardless of whether correction of the gender entry is granted, by assessing a person’s sex normatively according to individual and social recognition, and not merely the biological sex at birth. In reality, transsexual persons are a minority in our society, but as neighbors they live ordinary daily lives like everyone else, and many of them increasingly communicate actively by revealing the forms of their lives through the mass media and the like. Although the level of average understanding of transsexual persons in our society has increased, it is also true that discrimination against and exclusion of transsexual persons still exist in our society. As a result, if the fact that the sex of a transsexual father or mother has been corrected is disclosed to the outside through the Family Relations Register, de facto discrimination may arise for the minor children. However, such a problem can be solved by the State’s improving the contents and procedures of the Family Relations Register system and taking measures to prevent the fact of a transsexual person’s correction of the gender entry from being disclosed, thereby protecting the privacy of transsexual persons and their minor children.\\nAlso, in light of the spirit of our Constitution, which places human dignity as its ultimate goal, the State bears the duty to be careful that acts unlawfully exposing matters related to correction of the gender entry in an individual’s Family Relations Register to the outside do not occur, and to make legal and institutional efforts to correct prejudice and misunderstanding on the part of those who discriminate against transsexual persons or their families; yet refusing permission for correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register of a transsexual person on the above grounds is difficult to accept, because it abandons the State’s fundamental duty to prevent harm that transsexual persons and their minor children may suffer from social prejudice and to guarantee the stability of family life.\\n(2) The Personal Information Protection Act was enacted on March 29, 2011 and came into force on September 30, 2011 in order to promote the rights and interests of citizens and realize individual dignity and value, and the Family Relations Registration Act has also improved the problem that personal information was easily disclosed for the protection of individual privacy.\\nThe current Family Relations Registration Act, in principle, allows certificates containing only essential information for each type of certificate to be used, allows the applicant to obtain a certificate by selecting only the information necessary for the purpose of use, or restricts the persons entitled to request issuance of a certificate, and newly introduced certificates in the form of partial certificates showing only some recorded items. Meanwhile, a person requesting submission of a certificate must request a certificate containing only the minimum family relation registration information necessary for the purpose of use, and use of a submitted certificate for purposes other than the purpose of use is prohibited.\\nUnder the Family Relations Registration Act, only the person concerned, his or her spouse, parents, or children may inspect the Family Relations Register (Article 14(7)); only the person concerned, his or her spouse, or lineal blood relatives may obtain certificates under the Family Relations Registration Act (Article 14(1)); and in the case of obtaining a family relation certificate for a minor child, either the father or the mother may be selected, and a family relation certificate (specific certificate) certifying the parent-child relationship only between that parent and the child may be issued (Articles 15(4) and (5), Article 21-2 of the Rules on the Registration of Family Relations, etc.).\\nAlso, due to the enforcement of the Electronic Government Act, schools, administrative agencies, and public institutions, unless special circumstances exist, process matters that can prove family relations after verifying them in an information system available within the scope of the relevant duties without requiring submission or presentation by the party.\\n(3) In light of the current statutory provisions and the social reality concerning the operation of the system as described above, the possibility that, at the stages of inspection, issuance, and submission of a family relation certificate for a minor child, the fact that the minor child’s father or mother has had the gender entry corrected will be carelessly disclosed to a third party is low.\\n3) Current Status of International Norms and Global Trends Regarding Correction of the Gender Entry of a Transsexual Person\\nArticle 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides: “Everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in this Declaration, without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status.” On July 15, 2016, the United Nations Human Rights Council reaffirmed that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights and are entitled to the freedoms and rights set forth in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and adopted a resolution opposing violence and discrimination worldwide based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and our country, as a member state, voted in favor of that resolution.\\nAlso, the majority of countries in the world, including Germany, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Sweden, and the United States, permit correction of the gender entry for transsexual persons, and most countries except Japan do not treat the fact that a transsexual person has minor children as an absolute reason for denying correction of the gender entry. Therefore, refusing to permit correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person merely because the person has minor children runs counter to international human rights norms that all human beings, including transsexual persons, have dignity and rights as human beings and are entitled to enjoy them, and does not conform to the attitudes of countries around the world or the demands of the times.\\nB. Standard for Determining Whether Permission for Correction of the Gender Entry Should Be Granted\\n1) When determining whether to grant permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children, the constitutional fundamental rights of the transsexual person himself or herself, such as human dignity and value, the right to pursue happiness, and the right to equality, must be guaranteed to the fullest extent, while at the same time the welfare of the child, including the child’s right to receive protection and care, must be kept in mind. Therefore, in such cases, in addition to whether the general requirements for permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person have been satisfied, the court must examine, by considering all circumstances such as the age and physical and mental condition of the minor children, the degree of the minor children’s consent to or understanding of the father’s or mother’s correction of the gender entry, the form of protection and upbringing of the minor children, the manner in which the transsexual person performs his or her role as father or mother, the relationship and bond the transsexual person has formed and maintained with the minor children and other family members, and other family circumstances, whether granting permission for correction of the gender entry of the transsexual person affects the welfare of the minor children, and determine whether to grant such permission.\\n2) In individual and concrete cases, the court must, according to such standards, closely examine the actual emotional, economic, and social circumstances experienced by the transitioned father or mother and the minor children, and make a substantive determination as to which decision protects the transsexual person’s fundamental human rights while also conforming to the welfare of the minor children, whether the disadvantages suffered by the minor children from granting permission for correction of the gender entry are markedly greater and more serious than restricting or infringing the transsexual person’s rights based on human dignity under the Constitution, and whether, despite the existence of alternatives that could reduce the disadvantages to the minor children, refusing permission for correction of the gender entry of the father or mother until the minor children reach adulthood and thereby forcing the transsexual person’s suffering arising from the mismatch between actual sex and the sex shown in the official record is consistent with the principle of proportionality. Without doing so, to treat the transsexual person’s correction of the gender entry as contrary to the welfare of the minor children based on vague and abstract concerns and uniformly and completely deny it may, in light of the balance among legal interests, not only infringe the transsexual person’s constitutional fundamental rights but also produce a result that undermines the substantive welfare of the minor children.\\n4. Change of Precedent\\nTherefore, the Supreme Court’s En Banc Decision dated September 2, 2011, 2009SEU117, which held to the effect that correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register of a transsexual person is not permitted when the transsexual person has minor children, as well as decisions to the same effect, are all to be changed to the extent they are contrary to the view of this decision.\\n5. Determination in this Case\\nWe examine the reasoning of the court below’s decision in light of the legal principles seen above. The court below cited the Supreme Court’s En Banc Decision dated September 2, 2011, 2009SEU117, and, viewing the existence of minor children as an independent negative requirement for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, refused the permission application in this case merely on the ground that the Applicant has minor children, without specifically examining the various circumstances appearing in the record of this case and making a substantive determination. In the court below’s determination, there is a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the constitutional fundamental rights under the Constitution’s Preamble to Article 10 that all citizens have dignity and value as human beings and the right to pursue happiness, Article 11(1) that all citizens are equal before the law, and the criteria for granting permission for correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, and there is also an error affecting the judgment by failing to conduct the necessary trial. The Applicant’s assertion of the grounds for re-appeal pointing out this error is well-founded.\\n6. Conclusion\\nTherefore, we reverse the court below’s decision and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and so decide as stated in the order. Except for the dissenting opinion of Justice Lee Dong-won, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there are supplementary opinions to the majority opinion by Justice Park Jung-hwa, Justice Noh Jeong-hee, and Justice Lee Heung-gu, as well as supplementary opinions by Justice Kim Seon-su and Justice Oh Kyung-mi.\\n7. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Lee Dong-won\\nJustice Lee Dong-won’s dissenting opinion is as follows.\\nA. The previously existing Supreme Court’s En Banc Decision dated September 2, 2011, 2009SEU117 (hereinafter referred to as the “Second En Banc Decision”) held that, if a transsexual person has minor children, correction of the gender entry is not permitted. As grounds, it stated that under our Civil Act system, in legally evaluating the sex of a person exercising parental authority, the welfare of the minor children must be considered first, and that if such permission were allowed, the special status relationship between the person exercising parental authority and the minor children and the negative impact on the welfare of the minor children would be significant.\\nThe majority opinion appears to view the Supreme Court’s Second En Banc Decision as newly establishing the fact that a transsexual person has minor children as an independent negative requirement for permission to correct the gender entry. However, even before the Second En Banc Decision, the Supreme Court had already, in its En Banc Decision dated June 22, 2006, 2004SEU42 (hereinafter referred to as the “First En Banc Decision”), presented the basic principle that, in order to permit correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, “it must not cause a significant change in the status relationship with others or have a negative impact on society, and therefore must be socially acceptable.” The Second En Banc Decision merely clarified that the case of a transsexual person with minor children falls within a case contrary to such basic principle; it did not newly establish an independent negative requirement for permission to correct the gender entry.\\nBecause the Second En Banc Decision is consistent with our legal system and the welfare of minor children, and is also a rational decision conforming to the general common sense of society, it should be maintained as is. I cannot agree with the majority opinion attempting to change it. Below, I will examine the reasons in detail.\\nB. Article 36(1) of the Constitution provides: “Marriage and family life shall be founded and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and the equality of the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this.” This shows that our Constitution presupposes that the marriage and family system, the most basic unit of our society and the foundation of common life in all spheres, is founded and maintained through the union of differentiated sexes on the premise of the distinction between the sexes. In addition, the Constitution contains various provisions dividing men and women and requiring special protection of women within a certain range, and especially in the field of the marriage and family system, it requires the State to strive to protect women, that is, maternity, which is directly related to pregnancy and childbirth of children (Article 36(2)).\\nAlthough the provisions concerning kinship in our Civil Act (Part 4, Kinship) were amended several times since enactment in 1958 up to recent years, the provisions regarding the parent-child relationship in blood define the requirements for establishment and the rights and obligations on the premise that such relationship is formed by the birth of a child by a mother who conceived through sexual relations between the father and mother or through artificial insemination, and the provisions regarding legal parent-child relationships are not substantially different from those concerning the parent-child relationship in blood, except that there is no blood relation between them.\\nConsidering the text of the Constitution and the Civil Act and the history and structure of enactment and amendment thereof, it is clear that our legal system, including the Constitution and Civil Act, presupposes that a father is a male and a mother is a female. Therefore, under our Constitution, Civil Act, and other statutes, a female father or male mother cannot be permitted. Accordingly, granting permission for correction of the gender entry to a transsexual person who has children would amount to creating a parent-child relationship not permitted under our legal system. It goes without saying that such a new status relationship cannot be created without a legal basis. By contrast, because our statutes, including the Constitution and Civil Act, do not distinguish between male and female with respect to the sex of children, even if correction of the gender entry is permitted for a transsexual child, the parent-child relationship does not deviate from our legal system. The argument that, because correction of the gender entry of a transsexual child is possible, correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person who has children must also be possible is based on a failure to properly see the essence of the issue. This issue is also on a different level from the fact that correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person does not affect the existing status relationship and rights and obligations.\\nHowever, according to the Second En Banc Decision, if a transsexual person has minor children, correction of the gender entry is not permitted, whereas if a transsexual person has adult children, the conclusion is that correction of the gender entry may be permitted if, by comprehensively considering various circumstances, it is recognized that the person has the transitioned sex physically in social common sense; and it is true that this aspect is not consistent with the above legal system. Although it is not legally consistent to distinguish between cases where there are adult children and cases where there are minor children and to treat the permissibility of correction of the gender entry differently, this can be understood in that it was done by weighing the systematic conformity of our legal system and legal stability against the need for correction of the gender entry, considering that if the same legal logic were adhered to and correction of the gender entry were not permitted even when the transsexual person has adult children, the rights of the transsexual person would be excessively restricted. To claim, conversely, that because correction of the gender entry may be permitted when there are adult children, it must also be permitted when there are minor children, is to fail to properly appreciate the Supreme Court precedent that, while wrestling with legal logic and the necessity of correction of the gender entry, derived a harmonious solution.\\nC. In the First En Banc Decision, the Supreme Court took the position that correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person cannot be permitted in cases “where it causes a significant change in the status relationship with others or has a negative impact on society,” and in the Second En Banc Decision, “where a transsexual person has minor children” was given as a representative example. This stems from the fact that, from the transsexual person’s perspective, if correction of the gender entry is permitted, the person gains the benefit of full protection of constitutional fundamental rights, whereas from the perspective of the minor children in a parent-child relationship with the transsexual person, the status relationship or welfare is bound to be seriously adversely affected, and there is no legal basis sufficient to justify the disadvantages the children would suffer in such a case.\\nWhere a person with issues of sexual identity marries of his or her own choice and has children, or, even without marrying, has children, this is because the person has consented to accept the sex at birth and has decided to form family relations and carried that out; therefore, if the person changes sex at that stage, this cannot be viewed merely as a matter at the personal level. This is because a significant impact is caused to the status relationship or rights of others who formed family relations with that person. The issue of transsexuality at such a stage should be viewed as a matter of change of sex, not correction of the gender entry.\\nIt was possible in the existing First and Second En Banc Decisions to resolve the issue of a transsexual person changing sex through the legal theory of correction of the gender entry because the Court carefully examined whether the case fell within the category of “causing a significant change in the status relationship with others or having a negative impact on society,” and thereby preemptively blocked disadvantages that others would suffer. However, if the Supreme Court now adopts a completely different position and makes a decision requiring others to bear such disadvantages, this would go beyond the limitations of the legal theory of correction of the gender entry as originally contemplated by the First and Second En Banc Decisions.\\nFurthermore, such a decision by the Supreme Court will bring about significant changes to the family system, which has long been established as a core element of our society. In particular, this concerns essential issues in our society deeply related to ethical, philosophical, and religious issues, and should be approached at the level of change of sex with legal grounds prepared through legislative decision by the National Assembly, the representative organ of the people, after gathering the opinions of the general public and going through careful discussion and deliberation; it is not desirable to force an expansion of the legal theory of correction of the gender entry.\\nThe court must clearly recognize its responsibility for the performance and maintenance of family life guaranteed by the Constitution and for the maintenance and development of families, and must protect their dignity and value; it must also aim to improve the happiness and welfare of family members by assisting citizens to faithfully fulfill the legal, moral, and ethical duties they bear as members of families, and interpret and apply the law in a direction that avoids family dissolution (Framework Act on Healthy Families Articles 1, 4, and 9).\\nD. Our Civil Act provides that parents become the persons exercising parental authority over their minor children (Article 909(1)), that a person exercising parental authority has the right and duty to protect and educate the child (Article 913), and that in exercising parental authority, the welfare of the child must be considered first (Article 912). Although parental authority is provided in the form of a right in the statutory text, by its nature it has both the character of a right and the character of a duty, and in particular in modern times its aspect as a duty is more emphasized. Therefore, a person exercising parental authority must exercise it in a manner consistent with the “welfare of the child,” and in some cases must also endure restrictions on the fundamental rights of the individual person exercising parental authority for the “welfare of the child.”\\nSuch an interpretation is also consistent with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, which declares the principle of the “best interests of the child” that the interests of the child shall be a primary consideration in all actions concerning children (adopted on November 20, 1989, and ratified by our country, coming into force domestically on December 20, 1991).\\nFurthermore, in light of our society’s view of family, which particularly values bonds and consideration among family members, expecting a person exercising parental authority to refrain as much as possible from entering into the series of processes for transsexual transition and correction of the gender entry for the welfare of the child, and even if not possible, to maintain a more cautious and sincere attitude in deciding each step, is the minimum request for consideration that current our society can make of a person who, of his or her own choice, married the opposite sex, gave birth to children, and formed a family.\\nHowever, the majority opinion appears to prioritize the individual fundamental rights of the person exercising parental authority on the ground that it is difficult to conclude that the mere correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person in the Family Relations Register will harm the welfare of the minor children. If the concept of the “welfare of the child” is treated lightly on the ground that it is vague and abstract, and if claims regarding the possibility of its infringement are dismissed as empty, then not only the “welfare of the child” but ultimately also various precious values, invisible though they may be, that our society must protect are ignored.\\nMoreover, compared with the minor children of families whose parents have not undergone transsexual transition and correction of the gender entry, the mental confusion and shock suffered by minor children who have parents who have done so can be easily imagined, and irrespective of the social pros and cons regarding transsexuality or correction of the gender entry, social discrimination and prejudice against these matters are an undeniable reality. Since minor children who are not yet mature will be directly exposed to this reality and the suffering they may endure is sufficiently foreseeable, converting the circumstance that the welfare of the child is harmed into a mere issue of abstract possibility can only be seen as deliberately turning away from such a problem.\\nThe court, even when hearing and deciding on whether to permit correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, should stand in a protective position and interpret and apply the law so as to prioritize the welfare of the child and avoid negative effects thereon, which is consistent with the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the provisions and purpose of the Civil Act.\\nE. Even if, as the majority opinion states, one were to take the position that the Court must determine whether permission for correction of the gender entry of the Applicant would specifically and seriously affect the minor children and significantly contradict their welfare before deciding whether to grant permission, in this case, considering the following circumstances in combination, the Applicant’s correction of the gender entry cannot be permitted, and therefore the court below’s decision must be maintained as is.\\n1) The Applicant formed a parent-child relationship with the children by giving birth to them through sexual relations with the opposite sex by the Applicant’s own choice. In such a situation, it does not seem excessive to require the Applicant to place the welfare of the minor children first.\\n2) In this case, the Applicant has concealed from the children the fact that the Applicant is their father and is pretending to be an aunt. Such a situation cannot be regarded as a case where a natural family relationship has formed according to the transitioned sex of the parent. Nevertheless, if the Applicant’s correction of the gender entry is hastily permitted, there is ample room to regard that as contrary to the welfare of the child.\\n3) There may be an argument that, since the Applicant is concealing his or her status from the children by pretending to be an aunt, and correction of the gender entry would merely change the sex of the Applicant who had been pretending to be an aunt, there would be no additional mental confusion or shock for the minor children. Such an argument is possible only when the issue of a transsexual person’s correction of the gender entry is viewed solely as an issue after the point at which the sex is corrected and entered in the Family Relations Register. The court must not merely measure fragmentary advantages or disadvantages after a certain point, but must seriously and cautiously consider what decision is best for the welfare of the child by comprehensively examining all circumstances anticipated throughout the process before and after.\\n4) In ordinary cases, the mental shock or confusion of minor children is more likely to arise not during the correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register concerning a transsexual person, but from the actual change in the physical appearance of the father or mother that occurs beforehand. However, in this case, the minor children knew the Applicant as an aunt rather than as a father, and thus did not experience the Applicant’s physical appearance change. Rather, they are very likely to experience mental shock or confusion later in the process of inspecting or obtaining the family relation certificate and thereby becoming aware of it.\\nThere may be an argument that if minor children suffer mental shock, it can be addressed through psychological counseling or treatment. However, that is not a position that a court, which must interpret and apply the law by prioritizing the welfare of minor children whose ability to adapt has not matured and whose sensitivity is acute, should adopt.\\nF. In light of the above legal principles and factual circumstances, the court below’s action in upholding the first-instance decision dismissing the Applicant’s application for correction of the gender entry, where the Applicant has minor children, is proper, and there is no error such as that alleged as grounds for the re-appeal. Therefore, the re-appeal should be dismissed.\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state that I cannot agree with the majority opinion.\\n8. Supplementary Opinion to the Majority Opinion by Justice Park Jung-hwa, Justice Noh Jeong-hee, and Justice Lee Heung-gu\\nWhile supplementing the majority opinion, I wish to rebut, to the extent necessary, some of the arguments presented in the dissenting opinion.\\nThe dissenting opinion says that the Second En Banc Decision should be maintained because it is a rational decision consistent with our legal system, the welfare of minor children, and the general common sense of society. However, such dissenting opinion is difficult to accept because it is contrary to the purpose of the First En Banc Decision, infringes the essential content of the transsexual person’s fundamental rights, and may also run counter to the welfare of minor children. The reasons are as follows.\\nA. Gender identity refers to the internal and personal experience and deep sense of belonging that a human being feels with respect to gender, irrespective of the sex assigned at birth. Every human being, through gender identity in society, recognizes the self and completes a personal narrative by reinterpreting and reconstructing personal experiences and giving them meaning. The right concerning gender identity is one of the principal contents of the general personality right derived from the Preamble to Article 10 of the Constitution, which prescribes human dignity, value, and the right to pursue happiness, and has significant meaning in the very existence of the individual or the mode of life.\\nA transsexual person refers to a person whose manifestation of gender identity differs from the biological sex possessed at birth. Human society has divided human beings into male or female based on biological sex at birth and regarded this as an unchangeable absolute, and by recognizing transsexual persons as a third existence that is neither male nor female, or by denying the very existence of those who do clearly exist in actual society, has religiously and socially forced transsexual persons to abandon or conceal their own gender identity. However, it has long been medically, scientifically, and philosophically verified that transsexual persons are also one form of human existence. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that such a custom, which is essentially no different from denying the very existence of human beings, still persists with respect to minorities in our society. The State has a duty to uphold the rights concerning gender identity of transsexual persons guaranteed by the Preamble to Article 10 of the Constitution, which prescribes human dignity, value, and the right to pursue happiness, even in order to overcome this reality.\\nB. All citizens have the right to have the sex corresponding to their gender identity indicated consistently in the official record. This right has particular significance for transsexual persons. Because a transsexual person who has acquired a gender identity different from the biological sex at birth is publicly recorded in the Family Relations Register according to biological classification, such a person inevitably faces serious problems arising from inconsistency between reality and public record during the process of transition. If the State does not guarantee a procedural right to correct the official record so that it accords with their true gender identity, this infringes the essential content of the transsexual person’s right concerning gender identity, which is a fundamental right under the Preamble to Article 10 of the Constitution.\\nC. When fundamental rights or public interests and other legal interests conflict, the issue must be resolved according to the principle of practical concordance of legal interests (norm-harmonizing interpretation). Because restricting the right of a transsexual person to correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register constitutes an infringement of the essential content of the transsexual person’s human dignity and value and the right to pursue happiness, and the degree of restriction of fundamental rights is very large and serious, there must be serious and clear circumstances showing the necessity to protect or realize other legal interests or values through such restriction, and that there is no alternative other than such restriction. In other words, the right of a transsexual person to correction of the gender entry can secure the justification of its restriction only if it is harmoniously adjusted in a direction that recognizes the dignity of the transsexual person to the fullest extent even in relation to minor children.\\nHowever, according to the Second En Banc Decision, a court dealing with a case of correction of the gender entry by a transsexual person with minor children must refuse permission for correction of the gender entry merely because the person has minor children, without conducting a concrete hearing as to what constitutes the welfare of the minor children, what kind of infringement of welfare may occur depending on the parent’s correction of the gender entry, or whether that infringement is serious and clear. Even in cases where the relevant minor children accept the transsexual father or mother as having the transitioned sex and live stably according to that status while hoping that the father’s or mother’s gender entry in the Family Relations Register will be corrected to reflect reality, the court has no choice but to deny it. This conclusion creates a contradictory situation in which the court, which must protect the rights of transsexual persons and minor children and ensure their peaceful lives, infringes both their rights and destabilizes them. This is the result of understanding the value of the welfare of the minor children in an abstract and conceptual manner and disregarding the substantive meaning of correction of the gender entry for a transsexual person with minor children in a concrete case.\\nD. The dissenting opinion says that the First En Banc Decision presented as a basic principle that, in order to permit correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person, it must not cause a significant change in the status relationship with others or have a negative impact on society, and that the Second En Banc Decision did not newly establish the fact that a transsexual person has minor children as an independent negative requirement for permission to correct the gender entry, but merely clarified the purport of the First En Banc Decision. However, this interpretation by the dissenting opinion unjustly narrows the significance of the First En Banc Decision in order to maintain the Second En Banc Decision denying correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with minor children.\\nThe First En Banc Decision declared as a principle that, in determining sex, biological factors and mental and social factors must be comprehensively considered, and accordingly, if a person can be recognized as having the transitioned sex, then a transsexual person must be permitted correction of the gender entry in the official record because, unlike at birth, the transitioned sex is to be legally evaluated as that person’s sex. Also, contrary to the dissenting opinion’s assertion, the First En Banc Decision announced that “the effect of a decision granting permission for correction of the gender entry or the correction of the sex entry based thereon does not affect the existing status relationship and rights and obligations.” In the supplementary opinion to the majority opinion, it was also made clear that “it should be understood not as establishing a negative requirement that the transsexual person must not cause a change in the status relationship with others or a negative impact on society, but rather that if the transsexual person is confirmed to be a transsexual person in the true sense, and furthermore if correction of the gender entry is made accordingly, the effect may be permitted as long as it does not retroactively have a significant effect on existing status relationships, etc., and the effect is limited to a restricted scope.”\\nE. The dissenting opinion says that because the Constitution and our legal system, including the Civil Act, clearly presuppose that a father is male and a mother is female, granting permission for correction of the gender entry to a transsexual person who has children would create a parent-child relationship not permitted under our legal system and thus cannot be allowed.\\nHowever, it cannot be said that a transsexual parent’s correction of the gender entry creates a parent-child relationship or new status relationship not permitted under our legal system. The fact that a parent is a transsexual person does not mean that the person is no longer the child’s biological parent or that the child is not the transsexual person’s biological child. A transsexual person and his or her child retain their unique rights and duties as parent and child regardless of whether it is before or after the transition. The fact that there is no appropriate term other than father or mother to refer to a transitioned parent does not mean that the original rights and duties or status relationship they had as parent and child disappear, cease, or become void. This was already declared in the First En Banc Decision.\\nF.
