Article 36(1) of the Constitution provides: “Marriage and family life shall be founded and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and the equality of the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this.” The dissenting opinion, using the expression “equality of the sexes” in the above provision, says that our Constitution presupposes that marriage and the family system are founded and maintained on the basis of the distinction between the sexes and the union between differentiated sexes, and that the correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person who has children is not permitted by our Constitution and laws, but that the Second En Banc Decision, although not legally consistent, distinguished between cases where the transsexual person has adult children and cases where the person has minor children by weighing the systematic conformity of our legal system and legal stability against the need for correction of the gender entry, and accordingly treated the permissibility of correction of the gender entry differently.\\nFirst, it must be pointed out that the dissenting opinion unjustly interprets the meaning of the Second En Banc Decision regarding correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with children. In the Second En Banc Decision, the Supreme Court did not expressly state the view that, in the case of a transsexual person with minor children, because our Constitution presupposes the distinction between the sexes in the marriage and family system, correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with children is not permitted under our Constitution and laws, or that correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with children causes a change in the children’s status relationship or rights and obligations. Rather, the Second En Banc Decision reaffirmed and declared the legal principle of the First En Banc Decision, which held that the permission for correction of the gender entry in the Family Relations Register for a transsexual person is a decision intended to confirm the current true sex newly legally evaluated according to transsexuality, and therefore the effect of a decision granting correction or the correction of the sex entry in the Family Relations Register based thereon does not affect the existing status relationship and rights and obligations. It only held that, in the case of minor children, in light of the significant negative impact of a parent’s correction of the gender entry on the welfare of the minor children due to social discrimination and prejudice, the parental duty to protect the minor children from such negative impact, and other circumstances, “considering that it is difficult to conclude that merely because the effect of correction of the sex entry does not affect ‘existing’ parent-child relationships and other legal relationships, all of the newly arising difficulties in the living relationship of the minor children are thereby resolved,” correction of the gender entry is not permitted when the transsexual person has minor children.\\nIf Article 36(1) of the Constitution is interpreted as the dissenting opinion does, it leads to results not harmonious with the provisions of Article 10, Article 11(1), and Article 37(1) of the Constitution. With respect to the protection of the family community, together with Article 36(1), one must apply the Preamble to Article 10 of the Constitution, which guarantees human dignity and value and the right to pursue happiness, the latter sentence of Article 10 of the Constitution, which states that “the State shall have the duty to confirm and guarantee the inviolable fundamental human rights of individuals,” Article 11(1), which guarantees the right to equality, and Article 37(1), which states that “the freedoms and rights of citizens shall not be neglected on the ground that they are not enumerated in the Constitution.” Ultimately, the State must equally protect the family community of a transsexual person and his or her children without discrimination, just like any other family community. Furthermore, because Article 36(1) of the Constitution declares that the family community’s meaning and preciousness, together with the idea that they must be based on “gender equality” and individual dignity, are protected and guaranteed by the State, it cannot be used as a basis for excluding such protection according to the type of family life. Article 36(1) of the Constitution should be interpreted affirmatively so as to include the family community of a transsexual person with minor children as a protected subject.\\nThe importance of the family community cannot be overemphasized, and this is no different in the case of transsexual persons. The bond between a transsexual person and his or her family members must also be socially respected and legally protected without discrimination. If transsexual persons and their family members wish to cherish the family community they have formed and continue to live while maintaining that bond, the State and society have the duty to respect such wishes to the fullest extent and guarantee their family life. In the case of modern family communities, including those of transsexual persons, which are manifesting in diverse forms, actively accepting and protecting them within the existing family order to the extent that they do not violate social order and the public welfare strengthens the diversity and soundness of our society and reinforces the safety net surrounding society, thereby promoting the ultimate welfare of members of society.\\nG. In our society, transsexual persons still have to endure the threat of internal division and existence in an environment of discrimination and exclusion both in daily life and legally, and suffer the pain of failing to fully complete their own narrative in accordance with their actual gender identity. Transsexual persons are easily exposed to various forms of danger, including sexual violence, because of the characteristics of their appearance or their attitude, and this is even more so where the sex they personally disclose and the legal sex indicated in official certificates or documents such as identity cards and passports do not match.\\nHowever noble the light of the constitutional spirit that guarantees human dignity and value may be, its meaning will fade if that light does not reach equally the members of society, including transsexual minorities. It is necessary to lay an institutional foundation so that transsexual persons may seek their life in accordance with their true gender identity and to improve the culture of discrimination that persists in reality. Through this, the constitutional guarantees of human dignity and value and the realization of fundamental rights can become substantive, not merely slogans.\\nThe First En Banc Decision was the fruit of such efforts. The Supreme Court, sharing the hardships transsexual persons must endure as a minority, declared that they, as equal members of our society, have the right to seek correction of the gender entry in accordance with their gender identity as an extension of human dignity and value and the right to pursue happiness. Correction of the gender entry for transsexual persons does not solve all problems, but it is an important starting point for their resolution. Starting from this point, in order to truly resolve their difficulties and remedy infringements of fundamental rights, the voices of transsexual persons and their families must be institutionally reflected through legislation. Since the First En Banc Decision, for 16 years, the establishment of a legal system for transsexual persons has been delayed, and transsexual persons who must still remain in the shadow of exclusion are urgently calling for the guarantee of equal rights. There is a need to listen to the voices of transsexual persons, who break the icy silence produced by the rigid existing order and resound from within, and to sympathize with their suffering. While emphasizing once more the importance of the judiciary’s role in protecting the rights of transsexual persons, who are a minority in our society, and the urgency of legislative measures concerning correction of the gender entry, I state this supplementary opinion to the majority opinion.\\n9. Supplementary Opinion to the Majority Opinion by Justice Kim Seon-su and Justice Oh Kyung-mi\\nI fully agree with the content and thrust of the supplementary opinion of Justices Park Jung-hwa, Noh Jeong-hee, and Lee Heung-gu regarding the issue in this case, and add a few opinions thereto.\\nA. One must deeply reflect that the issue of a transsexual person’s gender identity and correction of the gender entry is a matter of human existence preceding institutions. For that reason, unlike the dissenting opinion’s remarks, this cannot be the subject of “social pros and cons.” Transsexual persons have existed throughout the history of human society, yet only in recent times has their existence been affirmed. Based on this affirmation, the term transgender was also created and established. It is not easy to imagine to what extent the suffering and frustration that transsexual persons had to bear as a minority were in order to reach this point. Because most people do not experience a mismatch between biological sex and the internal sex personally felt, they rarely face issues of gender identity, and thus it is difficult for them to know what the fundamental fear and abyss of self-denial arising from that gap of mismatch is. The same is true of the difficulties transsexual persons face in struggling, in order to find their gender identity, to overcome internal division and self-denial and form a complete self-image. This is because the majority of people who are not transsexual have many opportunities to objectify and observe them from the perspective of the majority in this society, leaning on the majority’s vested interests. These inherent difficulties transsexual persons inevitably face because of issues of gender identity are extremely intensified by the gaze of a society that discriminates against and denies them.\\nB. Modern democratic society pursues freedom, equality, and respect for human dignity as values more precious than anything else, but it also has the limitation that various institutions and cultures inevitably can be formed mainly by the values of the majority according to representative democracy and the principle of majority rule. As a result, the voices of minorities are easily buried and unheard. The situation of transsexual persons, who are a minority in our society, is likewise. The social, institutional, and cultural structures reflecting the majority’s values regard biological sex as an unchangeable absolute, restrict the exercise of the fundamental rights of transsexual persons, tacitly compel them not to reveal their existence, and cause others to regard this situation as natural. But now we must no longer turn away from their urgent cry demanding treatment as equal members of this society, and must not leave them in a state of Homo Sacer. Although correction of the gender entry is essential for transsexual persons to live a life in accordance with their gender identity, refusing it is to deny their human existence and drive them to the edge of the cliff, and further, one must deeply recognize that it undermines the core values of freedom, equality, and respect for human dignity pursued by a democratic society. This is why an institutional foundation must be created so that transsexual persons can live in this society as our ordinary neighbors, including through correction of the gender entry.\\nC. The status of a biological parent as a legal relationship transcends the concept premised on the sex of a male father or female mother. It is determined on the basis of blood relation through birth, presumption of paternity, acknowledgment, etc., and the occurrence of transsexuality does not change such status or rights and obligations. A transsexual person, like anyone else, is someone’s child and remains the biological or legal parent of the child he or she has given birth to. The fact that a parent has transitioned and become male or female does not negate the already legally arising parent-child status relationship so as to say that the parent is no longer the child’s biological parent or that the child is not the parent’s biological child.\\nThe dissenting opinion says that permitting correction of the gender entry for a transsexual person who has children would create anew, without legal basis, a parent-child relationship or a new status relationship not permitted under our legal system. If a parent with children undergoes transsexual transition, the father becomes female and the mother becomes male, and the dissenting opinion says that under the constitutional provisions and our legal system, including the Civil Act, a female father or male mother cannot be permitted.\\nHowever, human existence precedes the language that denotes it and transcends language. Language itself is also a social product and reflects the existing order of the majority and the prejudice or discrimination within it. Without considering these characteristics of language, to say that a father becoming female and a mother becoming male cannot be permitted under our legal system is nothing more than the majority absolutizing its own linguistic system and denying the existence of minorities not encompassed within it. Even if the expressions female father or male mother seem unfamiliar and contradictory in the usage of existing language, it is wrong to casually deny that the status and rights of transsexual persons and their children as parent and child are impermissible. Like the word transsexual, language can later be created in accordance with the reality of existence. As stated by the majority opinion and the supplementary opinion of Justices Park Jung-hwa, Noh Jeong-hee, and Lee Heung-gu above, correction of the gender entry of a transsexual person with children, like that of a transsexual person without children, is merely a measure to make the factual occurrence of transsexuality already arisen coincide with the official record, and cannot be regarded as creating a parent-child relationship or a new status relationship not permitted under our legal system.\\nD. {"[98MEU1698]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (a supplementary statement of grounds for appeal filed after the expiration of the period shall be considered only to the extent that it supplements the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Looking at the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the record, the court below lawfully found the following facts by comprehensively considering the evidence it adopted.\\n(1) Non-Party 1 met Non-Party 2, who was operating the ○○○ Hotel, etc. while attending Kyung Hee University, around May 1958, and began dating him; then, after holding a simple ceremony on the premise of marriage secretly from her family and continuing their conjugal relations, she gave birth to Plaintiff 1 on June 10, 1959, and to Plaintiff 2 on April 2, 1962.\\n(2) However, since Non-Party 2’s parents and others strongly opposed the marriage on the ground that Non-Party 1’s conduct was not upright, Non-Party 2 had been delaying the marriage registration, but in around 1963 he suffered a large loss from securities investment and left home around April 1963, concealing his whereabouts for several months; during that time, on September 3, 1963, Non-Party 1, using Non-Party 2’s seal without authorization, filed a marriage registration with Non-Party 2, and also filed birth registrations for the Plaintiffs as their natural children between them, so that Non-Party 1 and the Plaintiffs were each entered in Non-Party 2’s family register as his wife and children.\\n(3) Accordingly, Non-Party 3, the mother of Non-Party 2, filed a petition with the Seoul Family Court against Non-Party 1 and Non-Party 2 seeking a ruling confirming that their marriage was void; meanwhile, Non-Party 1 filed, with the Seoul Family Court Case No. 65NEO911, an application for mediation against Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3 seeking an order designating Non-Party 1 as the custodian of the Plaintiffs and requiring them to jointly and severally pay 2,500,000 won as consolation money because they had made it impossible for her to live together with Non-Party 2.\\nThereafter, when a judgment confirming the invalidity of the marriage between Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 1 was rendered, Non-Party 1 appealed, then received a judgment dismissing the appeal, and again filed an appeal, but while the case concerning the claim for confirmation of invalidity of marriage was pending before the Supreme Court, on January 17, 1966, in the above mediation case, a settlement was reached to the effect that “the relationship between Non-Party 1 and Non-Party 2 as a man and a woman shall be dissolved; it shall be confirmed that no natural parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiffs and Non-Party 2; Non-Party 1 shall bear all responsibility for the care and other matters concerning the Plaintiffs; Non-Party 1 shall hereafter be barred from making any and all judicial claims relating to the Plaintiffs; Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3 shall transfer to Non-Party 1 the land and building located in Jangchung-dong, Jung-gu, Seoul; and Non-Party 1 shall withdraw the appeal in the case concerning the claim for confirmation of invalidity of marriage.” Pursuant thereto, Non-Party 1 withdrew the appeal in the case concerning the claim for confirmation of invalidity of marriage, the judgment of invalidity of marriage became final and conclusive, and the Plaintiffs became children born out of wedlock.\\n(4) On June 1, 1967, after the judgment of invalidity of marriage had become final and conclusive, Non-Party 2 married Defendant Intervenor 1, and between them, gave birth to Defendant Intervenor 2 on March 18, 1968 and Defendant Intervenor 3 on June 26, 1970, while, against the Plaintiffs, he filed a claim for confirmation of invalidity of acknowledgment with the Seoul Family Court Case No. 67DEU877; in response, Non-Party 1, in the capacity of the Plaintiffs’ special representative, filed with the Seoul Family Court Case No. 68DEU236 a petition against Non-Party 2 seeking an order designating Non-Party 4, the Plaintiffs’ maternal grandmother, as the custodian of the Plaintiffs and requiring payment of the costs of their care.\\nAccordingly, on September 6, 1968, a ruling was rendered confirming that “the acknowledgment (birth registration) made by Non-Party 2 to the Head of Jongno-gu Office, Seoul Special Metropolitan City, as of September 3, 1963, identifying the Plaintiffs as his children is invalid.” In the case concerning the petition for designation of custodian, etc. filed by Non-Party 1 on behalf of the Plaintiffs, on September 19 of the same year, a judicial settlement was reached to the effect that “it is confirmed that the Plaintiffs are not the natural children of Non-Party 2, Non-Party 2 shall pay 3,500,000 won to the Plaintiffs, and the Plaintiffs shall make no further monetary claim.” And as the ruling confirming invalidity of acknowledgment became final and conclusive, the Plaintiffs were removed from Non-Party 2’s family register, and by the establishment of separate family registers, each was entered as the head of a family, with the father column left blank and the mother designated as Non-Party 1.\\n(5) After the above judicial settlement had been reached, Non-Party 1 married another man and cut off relations with the Plaintiffs; meanwhile, Non-Party 2, while substantially performing the role of the Plaintiffs’ father by, inter alia, giving them school expenses so that they could study abroad and attending their weddings, died on November 30, 1994, and the Plaintiffs filed the instant action for acknowledgment on January 4, 1995.\\n2. Regarding the grounds of appeal on the preliminary defense portion\\nThe court below, in response to the intervenors’ assertion that the instant claim for acknowledgment conflicts with the res judicata effect of the final and conclusive ruling confirming invalidity of acknowledgment and of the mediation and judicial settlement that included confirmation that no natural parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiffs and Non-Party 2, and that it also violates the principle of estoppel in light of the contents of that mediation and judicial settlement, and further constitutes an abuse of the right of action as the exercise of a right of action that had already ceased after de facto waiver or extinction of the right to claim acknowledgment, held that the final and conclusive ruling confirming invalidity of acknowledgment clearly had as its subject matter a confirmation that the voluntary acknowledgment by birth registration was invalid because, despite the fact that Non-Party 2 himself had never acknowledged the Plaintiffs as his natural children or filed their birth registrations, the family register was entered as if such act had been done by Non-Party 1; accordingly, its res judicata effect arises only to the extent that the voluntary acknowledgment by birth registration of Non-Party 2 is invalid, and its effect does not extend even to whether a natural parent-child relationship exists between Non-Party 2 and the Plaintiffs; therefore, the effect of that final and conclusive ruling does not extend to the instant claim seeking judicial acknowledgment on the premise that a natural parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiffs and Non-Party 2, and that a claim concerning confirmation of the existence or non-existence of a natural parent-child relationship, which corresponds to a Category A domestic relations litigation case under the current Family Litigation Act, by its nature concerns matters over which the parties cannot freely dispose, and thus even if mediation or judicial settlement is reached thereon, it cannot have legal effect (see Supreme Court Decision 65DA139, 140 rendered on April 6, 1968); therefore, the above mediation or judicial settlement has no effect with respect to confirming that no natural parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiffs and Non-Party 2, and there is no room for res judicata to arise, and moreover, the right to claim acknowledgment cannot be waived, and even if waived, no effect can arise (see Supreme Court Decision 85MEU70 rendered on January 20, 1987), so it cannot be said that the Plaintiffs waived their right to claim acknowledgment or forfeited it due to the mediation or judicial settlement, and thus the instant claim cannot be said to violate the principle of estoppel or to constitute an abuse of rights, and accordingly rejected all of the intervenors’ arguments.\\nExamining the record, the above determination by the court below is correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as misapprehension of the law concerning res judicata, issue preclusion, loss of rights through lapse, waiver of rights, or the principle of estoppel. The grounds of appeal on this point cannot be accepted.\\n3. Regarding the grounds of appeal on the merits\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below, on the basis of the commissioned genetic testing results and factual inquiry results among the evidence it adopted, found that the possibility that the deceased Non-Party 2 was the biological father of the Plaintiffs could not be ruled out, and that the probability of paternity was, in the case of Plaintiff 2, as low as 88.029% and as high as 99.9999999998%, and, in the case of Plaintiff 2, as low as 91.891% and as high as 99.99999999995%; then, comprehensively considering the factual circumstances noted above, it recognized that the Plaintiffs were the natural children of the deceased Non-Party 2 born between Non-Party 1 and the deceased Non-Party 2, and granted all of the Plaintiffs’ claims for acknowledgment in this case.\\nComparing the relevant evidence with the record, such factual findings by the court below are acceptable, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as violation of the rules of evidence, factual error due to insufficient deliberation, omission of judgment, or misapprehension of the law concerning the burden of proof. The grounds of appeal on this point are likewise not accepted.\\n4. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties. The judgment is rendered as per the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: A, who operates a furniture manufacturing business, received lumber worth 10,000,000 won from B, a raw materials supplier, and delivered to B the following promissory note. Which of the following statements is incorrect? (If there is any dispute, according to case law) <FRONT> Promissory Note To A Amount: 10,000,000 won I will pay the above amount to you or your order against this promissory note. Due date: 2023. 12. 5. Date of issue: 2023. 5. 1. Place of payment: 105, Sunae-dong, Bundang-gu, Seongnam-si Issuer: C (Jonghyeon Sofa) Place of payment: Hyochang Bank Co., Ltd., Sunae-dong Branch <BACK> Please pay the amount stated on the front to B or B's order. Protest waived. 2023. 6. 20. Address: 123, Hadan 1-dong, Saha-gu, Busan Name: A (Gyeongjin Furniture)
A: Unless there are special circumstances, A is presumed to have delivered the promissory note to B for payment to B.
B: A may, in principle, raise a defense of simultaneous performance that he will pay against the note when B demands payment of the lumber price; however, if the rights under the note have been extinguished by the expiration of the statute of limitations and A faces no risk of double payment and also cannot exercise rights against the other obligor on the note, the right to assert the defense of simultaneous performance is denied.
C: B may first exercise the claim on the note, and only when satisfaction cannot be obtained thereby may B exercise the claim for the price of the lumber against A.
D: If, because B did not take the necessary measures to interrupt the statute of limitations, the statute of limitations for the rights under the note has expired, and if A, after receiving the note back, can obtain satisfaction of his own underlying claim against C by exercising that claim, A cannot exercise a claim for damages against B.
E: If C issued the above promissory note to A for payment of the furniture price, and thereafter the furniture sale contract was rescinded, C may assert this against B's claim for payment on the note.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2009DA69692]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. As to Ground 1 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nA judgment takes effect upon its pronouncement, and such pronouncement shall be made by the presiding judge reading the operative part in accordance with the original of the judgment; meanwhile, the record shall state matters concerning the pronouncement of the judgment (Civil Procedure Act Articles 205, 206, and 154 item 6).\\n\\nAccording to the record, the record of pronouncement of judgment in the judgment of the court below in this case states, “Judgment pronounced in accordance with the original of the judgment,” and the original of the judgment filed after that record has as its operative part, “The Defendant’s appeal is dismissed.” If so, it is recognized that the presiding judge of the court below pronounced judgment on the date of pronouncement by reading, in accordance with the above original of the judgment, the operative part, “The Defendant’s appeal is dismissed.”\\n\\nMeanwhile, the argument of this part of the grounds for appeal is to the effect that, since a certified copy of the judgment stating, “The judgment of the first instance is reversed. The Plaintiff’s claim is dismissed,” was served on the parties before a certified copy of the judgment containing the same content as the above original of the judgment was served on them, the content of the certified copy of the judgment first served should be regarded as the judgment of the court below in this case. However, such circumstance alone does not allow the conclusion that, on the date of pronouncement of the judgment of the court below, the presiding judge pronounced a judgment different in content from the operative part of the above original of the judgment (the certified copy of the judgment that was served first appears to have been erroneously registered and served as one of the drafts of the judgment prepared by the court below), and thus this part of the grounds for appeal is not accepted.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 3 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe court below, taking all the evidence it cited into account, found the following facts: on June 5, 2002, the Defendant agreed with the Plaintiff that the 40,000,000 won which the Plaintiff had invested in Muhyeongjawon Research Institute Co., Ltd., operated by the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as “the company at issue”), would be returned to the Plaintiff by August 31, 2002, and, in addition, that from the above agreement date until the return date (August 31, 2002), 1,000,000 won per month would be paid to the Plaintiff under the name of installment payment of profits (hereinafter referred to as “the agreement at issue”); and that in or around July 2002, the Defendant endorsed as second endorser and delivered to the Plaintiff a promissory note in the face amount of 45,000,000 won, issued by Wanggeon Oil Co., Ltd., payable on October 17, 2002, and bearing Segi Vocational School Foundation as first endorser (hereinafter referred to as “the bill at issue”), in relation to the above agreed debt obligation (hereinafter referred to as “the debt at issue”). The court below then determined, taking the circumstances as stated in its judgment into account, that the bill at issue was delivered not in lieu of payment of the debt at issue, but for the purpose of such payment.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the foregoing determination of the court below is sustainable as correct. There is no illegality, such as erroneous understanding of the law regarding the purpose of delivery of the bill at issue, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. As to Ground 4 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe gist of this part of the grounds for appeal comes down to the assertion that the court below’s factual finding that the amount due on the bill at issue was not paid violated the rules of evidence.\\n\\nHowever, the finding of facts, and the selection and evaluation of evidence undertaken as its premise, belong to the exclusive authority of the trier of fact so long as they do not exceed the bounds of free evaluation of evidence. Even upon review of the judgment of the court below in light of the record, in this case where no reason can be found to conclude that the court below’s factual finding exceeded the above bounds, the above grounds of appeal amount merely to criticism of matters within the exclusive authority of the court below.\\n\\n4. As to Grounds 2 and 5 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe court below, after finding the facts as stated in its judgment, determined that the debt at issue, being based on an agreement by the Defendant (it is manifest that “Plaintiff” in this part of the court below’s judgment is a clerical error) in his personal capacity to return the investment funds to the Plaintiff (it is manifest that “Defendant” in the court below’s judgment is a clerical error), constitutes a civil debt and is therefore subject to the ten-year Statute of Limitations.\\n\\nIt is clear that the foregoing determination of the court below includes a rejection of the Defendant’s assertion that the debt at issue is a debt of the company at issue. In addition, in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the foregoing determination of the court below is sustainable as correct. There is no illegality, such as omission of judgment or erroneous understanding of the law on the Statute of Limitations, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n5. As to Ground 8 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nWhere the existing underlying claim and the bill claim coexist, when the creditor exercises the underlying claim, the debtor may, in principle, oppose the creditor with the defense that payment will be made in exchange for return of the bill. However, the reason a debtor may refuse to perform the underlying debt on the ground that the bill has not been returned is that it is intended to relieve the debtor from the risk of double payment arising from unconditional performance of the underlying debt, and not because there exists between the right to demand performance based on the existing underlying claim and the other party’s right to claim return of the bill a creditor-debtor relationship under a bilateral contract prescribed by Article 536 of the Civil Act, or a similar reciprocal relationship (see Supreme Court Decision 93DA11203, 93DA11210 rendered on November 9, 1993).\\n\\nAccordingly, where the rights on the bill have been extinguished by completion of the Statute of Limitations, so that there is no risk of double payment for the debtor and the debtor cannot exercise rights against the other obligor on the bill, there is no need to recognize, against the creditor’s exercise of the underlying claim, the debtor’s defense of simultaneous performance conditioned on return of the bill; ultimately, the debtor’s right to assert such defense must be denied (see also Supreme Court Decision 74DA1296 rendered on December 24, 1974).\\n\\nThe court below, on the premise of the foregoing legal principles, held that, since the rights on the bill at issue had been extinguished by completion of the Statute of Limitations and there was no risk of double payment, the Defendant could not raise the defense of simultaneous performance. This is sustainable as correct. There is no illegality, such as erroneous understanding of the law concerning the debtor’s defense of simultaneous performance conditioned on return of the bill against the exercise of the underlying claim, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n6. As to Ground 6 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nWhere a creditor has lawfully presented for payment the promissory note received from the debtor for performance of the existing debt, but thereafter the Statute of Limitations on the rights on the bill has been completed because no measures necessary to interrupt the Statute of Limitations for preservation of the rights on the bill were taken, if the debtor who received the return of the bill can obtain satisfaction of his claim by exercising either the rights on the bill against the maker, the principal obligor on the promissory note, the endorsers liable for recourse, etc., or his own underlying claim against the underlying debtor (who may be identical with the maker or endorser, or may be a third party not obligated on the bill), it cannot yet be said that damage has occurred.\\n\\nHowever, it is only when the maker, endorser, etc., who are obligors on the bill, have become insolvent after completion of the Statute of Limitations, and the underlying debtor who is not an obligor on the bill is also presently insolvent, so that even if the debtor receives return of the bill from the creditor, he can no longer obtain satisfaction from either the rights on the bill or his own underlying claim, that it can be said that he has suffered damage from failure to obtain satisfaction of his claim. Meanwhile, such damage is damage caused by the special circumstance of deterioration in the financial standing of the obligors on the bill and the underlying debtor, and only when the holder of the bill who failed to perform the duty to preserve the rights on the bill knew or could have known that the obligors on the bill and the underlying debtor would become insolvent in the future does the debtor acquire the right to claim compensation for the above damage against him, and may set off that damage-compensation claim (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 93DA12213 rendered on October 13, 1995, concerning the bill holder’s failure to perform the duty to preserve the right of recourse).\\n\\nThe court below, on the grounds stated in its judgment, after holding that there was no evidence to establish that the Plaintiff knew or could have known that the financial standing of the maker, who is the principal obligor on the bill at issue, would deteriorate, rejected the Defendant’s defense of set-off based on the damage-compensation claim arising from completion of the Statute of Limitations on the rights on the bill at issue.\\n\\nIn this case, where the record contains no materials establishing that the Plaintiff knew or could have known that the financial standing of the maker, who is the principal obligor on the bill at issue, or the first endorser, who is both a recourse obligor and the underlying debtor, would deteriorate, although there is some aspect in which the court below’s reasoning is not appropriate, its conclusion in rejecting the Defendant’s above defense of set-off is correct. There is no illegality affecting the result of the judgment, such as erroneous understanding of the law concerning the establishment of liability for damages arising from neglect of the duty to preserve rights on the bill, failure to exercise the duty to clarify, or violation of the principle of good faith, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n7. As to Ground 7 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe Defendant argued that, although the maturity of the debt at issue had been postponed from August 31, 2002 to October 17, 2002, the payment date of the bill at issue due to delivery of the bill at issue, the first instance judgment ordering payment of delay damages at 5% per annum on 40,000,000 won from September 1, 2002 to October 17, 2002 was unlawful. In response, the court below held that if the maturity of the debt at issue were recognized as postponed to October 17, 2002, then the Defendant would, under the agreement at issue, be required to pay 1,000,000 won per month from September 1, 2002 to October 17, 2002, in addition to being exempted from paying delay damages at 5% per annum on 40,000,000 won from September 1, 2002 to October 17, 2002 (equivalent to approximately 166,000 won per month), and that because such result would be more unfavorable to the Defendant than the first instance judgment, in this case appealed only by the Defendant, the argument could not be accepted under the principle prohibiting reformatio in peius.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the court below’s holding that, if the maturity of the debt at issue were postponed to October 17, 2002, then under the agreement at issue the Defendant would be obligated to pay 1,000,000 won per month from September 1, 2002 to October 17, 2002 is sustainable as correct. If so, the court below’s acceptance of the Defendant’s argument for postponement of maturity would not only be unfavorable to the Defendant, but in this case, where the Plaintiff seeks performance of the debt at issue and delay damages at the rate of 20% per annum on 40,000,000 won from September 1, 2002 until full payment, it would result in recognizing an obligation to pay profits of 1,000,000 won per month not claimed by the Plaintiff, and thus cannot be allowed.\\n\\nUltimately, the court below’s refusal to accept the Defendant’s argument for postponement of maturity is correct, and there is no illegality, such as erroneous understanding of the law concerning the principle prohibiting reformatio in peius, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n8. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed and the appellate costs shall be borne by the losing party, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the Disposition, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2009DA69692]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. With respect to the first ground of appeal\\n\\nA judgment takes effect upon pronouncement, and such pronouncement shall be made by the presiding judge reading out the operative part according to the original judgment; meanwhile, the record shall state matters concerning the pronouncement of the judgment (Articles 205, 206, and 154, subparagraph 6, of the Civil Procedure Act).\\n\\nAccording to the record, the record of pronouncement of judgment in the judgment below in this case states, “judgment pronounced according to the original judgment,” and the original judgment bound behind that record has as its operative part, “the Defendant’s appeal is dismissed.” If so, it is recognized that the presiding judge of the court below pronounced judgment on the date of pronouncement by reading out, in accordance with the above original judgment, the operative part stating, “the Defendant’s appeal is dismissed.”\\n\\nMeanwhile, the contention in this ground of appeal is to the effect that, because a certified copy of the judgment containing the same contents as the above original judgment was served on the parties after a certified copy of the judgment containing the operative part, “the first-instance judgment is revoked. The Plaintiff’s claim is dismissed,” had already been served on the parties, the contents of the certified copy of the judgment served first should be regarded as the judgment of the court below in this case. However, those circumstances alone do not permit the conclusion that the presiding judge, on the date of pronouncement of the judgment below, pronounced a judgment with contents different from the operative part of the above original judgment (the certified copy of the judgment said to have been served first appears to have been mistakenly registered and served as one of the drafts of the judgment prepared by the court below), and therefore this ground of appeal is not accepted.\\n\\n2. With respect to the third ground of appeal\\n\\nThe court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence set forth in its judgment, found the following: on 2002. 6. 5., the Defendant agreed with the Plaintiff that he would return by 2002. 8. 31. the KRW 40,000,000 that the Plaintiff had invested in Muhyeongjawon Research Institute Co., Ltd. operated by the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as “the Company in this case”), and in addition would pay the Plaintiff KRW 1,000,000 per month from the date of the above agreement until the return date thereof (2002. 8. 31.) in the name of installment payment of profits (hereinafter referred to as “the Agreement in this case”); that in or around July 2002, the Defendant, in relation to the above agreed monetary debt (hereinafter referred to as “the Debt in this case”), endorsed as second indorser a promissory note in the face amount of KRW 45,000,000, made by Wang Geon Oil Co., Ltd. as maker, due on 2002. 10. 17., and with Saegi Vocational School Foundation as first indorser (hereinafter referred to as “the Note in this case”), and delivered it to the Plaintiff. The court below then held, taking the circumstances set forth in its judgment into comprehensive consideration, that the Note in this case was not delivered in lieu of payment of the Debt in this case, but was delivered for its payment.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the above determination by the court below is justifiable. There is no illegality such as a misapprehension of law concerning the purpose of delivery of the Note in this case, as alleged in the ground of appeal.\\n\\n3. With respect to the fourth ground of appeal\\n\\nThe purport of this ground of appeal comes down to the assertion that the court below’s factual finding that the amount payable on the Note in this case was not paid violated the rules of evidence.\\n\\nHowever, the finding of facts, and the selection and evaluation of evidence made as its premise, fall within the exclusive competence of the fact-finding court so long as they do not exceed the bounds of the free evaluation of evidence. Even reviewing the judgment of the court below in light of the record, in this case where no reason can be found to say that the court below’s factual finding exceeded the above bounds, the above argument of appeal is nothing more than criticism of a matter within the exclusive competence of the court below.\\n\\n4. With respect to the second and fifth grounds of appeal\\n\\nThe court below, after finding the facts as set forth in its judgment, held that the Debt in this case arises from the agreement by which the Defendant (it is clear that the term “Plaintiff” in this part of the judgment below is a clerical error) undertook, in his personal capacity, to return the investment money to the Plaintiff (it is clear that the term “Defendant” in the judgment below is a clerical error), and therefore constitutes a civil debt to which the 10-year statute of limitations applies.\\n\\nIt is clear that the above determination by the court below includes a rejection of the Defendant’s argument that the Debt in this case is a debt of the Company in this case. In addition, in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the above determination by the court below is justifiable. There is no illegality such as omission of a determination or misapprehension of law concerning the statute of limitations, as alleged in the ground of appeal.\\n\\n5. With respect to the eighth ground of appeal\\n\\nWhere an existing underlying claim and a bill claim coexist, when the creditor enforces the underlying claim, the debtor may, in principle, oppose the creditor by asserting a defense that payment will be made concurrently with the exchange of the note. However, the reason the debtor may refuse to perform the underlying debt on the ground that the note has not been returned is to relieve the debtor from the risk of double payment arising from unconditional performance of the underlying debt; it is not because there exists, between the right to demand performance based on the existing underlying claim and the other party’s right to demand return of the note, a creditor-debtor relationship under a bilateral contract as prescribed in Article 536 of the Civil Act, or a similar quid pro quo relationship (see Supreme Court Decision dated 1993. 11. 9., 93DA11203, 11210).\\n\\nAccordingly, where the rights under the note have extinguished by completion of the statute of limitations, so that there is no risk of double payment for the debtor and the debtor cannot exercise rights against other obligors under the note, there is no need to recognize, in response to the creditor’s enforcement of the underlying claim, a defense of simultaneous performance by exchange of the note; consequently, the debtor’s right to assert such defense of simultaneous performance must be denied (see also Supreme Court Decision dated 1974. 12. 24., 74DA1296).\\n\\nThe court below, premising itself on the above legal principles, held that, since the rights under the Note in this case had extinguished by completion of the statute of limitations and there was no risk of double payment, the Defendant could not assert a defense of simultaneous performance. This is justifiable. There is no illegality such as a misapprehension of law concerning the debtor’s defense of simultaneous performance by exchange of the note in relation to enforcement of the underlying claim.\\n\\n6. With respect to the sixth ground of appeal\\n\\nWhere a creditor lawfully presented for payment a promissory note received from the debtor for the performance of an existing debt, but thereafter the statute of limitations concerning the rights under the note was completed because no measure necessary to interrupt the statute of limitations for preserving those rights under the note was taken, if the debtor, having received the note back, can obtain satisfaction of his own claim by exercising either his rights under the note against the maker, who is the principal obligor on the promissory note, or against the indorsers who are liable for recourse, or his underlying claim against the underlying debtor (who may be the same person as the maker or indorser, or may be a third party who is not an obligor under the note), it cannot yet be said that damage has occurred.\\n\\nHowever, only when, after completion of the statute of limitations, the maker or indorser or other obligor under the note has become insolvent and the underlying debtor, who is not an obligor under the note, is also presently insolvent, so that even if the note is returned by the creditor, satisfaction cannot be obtained from either the rights under the note or his own underlying claim, can it be said that the debtor has suffered damage from failure to obtain satisfaction of his claim. Meanwhile, such damage is damage caused by a special circumstance, namely the deterioration in the financial ability of the obligors under the note and the underlying debtor; therefore, only when the holder of the note who failed to perform the obligation to preserve the rights under the note knew or could have known that the obligors under the note and the underlying debtor would become insolvent in the future does the debtor acquire the right to claim compensation for the above damage, and may set off that damages claim (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision dated 1995. 10. 13., 93DA12213, concerning failure by the holder of a note to perform the obligation to preserve recourse rights).\\n\\nThe court below, on the basis of the reasons set forth in its judgment, held to the effect that there was no evidence to support a finding that the Plaintiff knew or could have known that the maker, who was the principal obligor on the Note in this case, would become insolvent, and then rejected the Defendant’s defense of set-off, which was based on a damages claim arising from completion of the statute of limitations concerning the rights under the Note in this case, as the automatic claim.\\n\\nIn this case, where no material can be found in the record to support a finding that the Plaintiff knew or could have known that the maker, who was the principal obligor on the Note in this case, or the first indorser, who was both a recourse obligor and the underlying debtor, would become insolvent, although there are aspects in which the above statement by the court below is not proper, the conclusion rejecting the Defendant’s above defense of set-off is justifiable. There is no illegality such as a misapprehension of law concerning the occurrence of liability for damages arising from neglect of the duty to preserve rights under the note, failure to exercise the right to clarification, or violation of the principle of good faith, as alleged in the ground of appeal, affecting the judgment result.\\n\\n7. With respect to the seventh ground of appeal\\n\\nThe Defendant argued that, although the due date of the Debt in this case had been postponed from 2002. 8. 31. to 2002. 10. 17., the due date of the Note in this case, by reason of the delivery of the Note in this case, the first-instance judgment’s order directing payment of delay damages at the rate of 5% per annum on KRW 40,000,000 of the Debt in this case from 2002. 9. 1. to 2002. 10. 17. was unlawful. In response, the court below held that if the due date of the Debt in this case were recognized as having been postponed to 2002. 10. 17. as the Defendant contended, then the Defendant would have to pay KRW 1,000,000 per month until 2002. 10. 17. pursuant to the profit-installment payment agreement included in the Agreement in this case, instead of being exempted from paying delay damages at the rate of 5% per annum on KRW 40,000,000 from 2002. 9. 1. to 2002. 10. 17. (equivalent to approximately KRW 166,000 per month), and that such a result would be less favorable to the Defendant than the first-instance judgment, so in this case where only the Defendant appealed, the argument could not be accepted under the principle of prohibition of reformatio in peius.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the court below’s determination that, if the due date of the Debt in this case were postponed to 2002. 10. 17., the Defendant would be obligated under the Agreement in this case to pay KRW 1,000,000 per month from 2002. 9. 1. to 2002. 10. 17. is justifiable. If so, accepting the Defendant’s argument for postponement of the due date would not only be unfavorable to the Defendant, but in this case where the Plaintiff is claiming performance of the Debt in this case and delay damages at the rate of 20% per annum on KRW 40,000,000 thereof from 2002. 9. 1. until the date of full payment, it would result in recognizing an obligation to pay profits of KRW 1,000,000 per month that the Plaintiff did not claim, and therefore cannot be permitted.\\n\\nUltimately, the court below was correct in not accepting the Defendant’s argument for postponement of the due date, and there is no illegality such as a misapprehension of law concerning the principle of prohibition of reformatio in peius, as alleged in the ground of appeal.\\n\\n8. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[93DA12213]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the first point of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe court below found that Non-party 2, the decedent of the Plaintiffs (excluding Non-party 1, the co-plaintiff in the court below; the same shall apply hereinafter) (died on 1990.11.11.), around 1990.7.20., received from the Defendant one promissory note of this case issued by the non-party Seongin Trading Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to only as “Seongin Trading”), with a face amount of KRW 10,000,000 and a maturity date of September 11 of that year, and lent KRW 10,000,000 to the Defendant; and, upon examination of the record, the above factual finding of the court below is proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in that the court erred in fact-finding by violating the rules of evidence or misunderstood the law regarding discounting of bills, as alleged, and therefore the argument is without merit.\\n\\n2. Regarding the assertion of set-off among the second point of the grounds for appeal\\n\\na. With respect to the Defendant’s assertion that, if the above Non-party 2 had lawfully presented the above promissory note for payment on its maturity date, he could have received payment of the bill amount and accordingly the Defendant’s above loan debt could also have been extinguished, but since the above Non-party 2 failed to present it for payment until the period for presentment had elapsed, and thereafter became unable to receive payment of the promissory note amount because the above issuer, Seongin Trading, effectively went bankrupt, thereby causing the Defendant to suffer damage in the amount of the face amount, the Defendant set off the above loan debt against a claim for damages against the Plaintiffs, who are the heirs to the property of the above Non-party 2, the court below held as follows: when Non-party 2 lost the above promissory note around 1990.8.30., his son-in-law, Non-party 3, filed an application for public summons with the Seoul Civil District Court on 1990.9.20., and on 1991.1.5. the said court rendered a judgment of invalidation regarding the above promissory note. Thereafter, Non-party 3 and others did not immediately exercise the rights under the above promissory note against Seongin Trading, but instead received from Seongin Trading another promissory note with a face amount of KRW 10,000,000 and a maturity date of 1991.2.25., and held it; they then presented it for payment on that date at the Ichon-dong branch of Seoul Trust Bank, the place of payment, but payment was refused for lack of transaction. Nevertheless, where a promissory note is delivered to secure performance of a loan claim, the creditor may freely choose and exercise either the loan claim or the promissory note claim at will until either claim is extinguished by the statute of limitations, and is not under an obligation necessarily to exercise the rights under the promissory note on its maturity date; moreover, there is no allegation or proof that Seongin Trading’s effective bankruptcy was attributable to the fault of Non-party 2, so even if Non-party 2 or Non-party 3 did not exercise the rights under the promissory note within the presentment period of the promissory note that had been delivered as security for the loan claim, and thus the Defendant, as the deliverer of the promissory note, suffered damage, it could not be said that Non-party 2 was under an obligation to compensate such damage; accordingly, the court below rejected the Defendant’s above assertion.\\n\\nb. In a case such as this, where the debtor delivers a bill to the creditor in relation to performance of an existing debt, and there is no special expression of intent between the parties, while, on the other hand, the principal obligor on the bill is not identical to the debtor under the underlying relationship, payment by a third party who is the principal obligor on the bill is contemplated; therefore, it shall be presumed that the bill was delivered “for payment” (see Supreme Court Decision 1993.11.9. rendered, 93DA11203, 11210).\\n\\nAnd in such a case, since it must be deemed that the parties contemplated that the creditor would first exercise the bill claim among the bill claim and the underlying claim to obtain satisfaction, the creditor should first exercise the bill claim, and only when satisfaction cannot be obtained thereby may the creditor exercise the existing underlying claim against the debtor. Furthermore, where a creditor receives an endorsed transfer of a bill for such purpose, in order to exercise the underlying claim against the debtor, the creditor must return the bill to the debtor unless there are special circumstances; therefore, it would be consistent with fairness between the two parties to regard the creditor as having a duty, as a prerequisite for exercising his underlying claim against the debtor, to duly present the bill on the maturity date and to take the procedure for preserving recourse rights. Accordingly, it would be wrong for the court below to state that the Plaintiff may freely choose and exercise either the bill claim or the loan claim at will and therefore has no duty to present the bill for payment on the maturity date of the promissory note. However, even if the creditor violates the above duty and fails to make lawful presentment for payment on the maturity date so that recourse rights are not preserved, if the principal obligor on the promissory note, namely the issuer, remains solvent, the debtor who has received return of the bill may obtain satisfaction of his own claim by exercising the bill claim or the underlying claim against the issuer, so no damage has yet occurred; only when, after the maturity date, the financial condition of the issuer of the bill deteriorates and becomes insolvent, so that even if the debtor who must perform his debt to the creditor receives return of the bill, he can no longer recover either the bill claim or the underlying claim against the issuer, does he suffer damage in that he cannot obtain satisfaction of his own claim. Such damage is damage arising from the special circumstance of the deterioration of the financial condition of the issuer, who is the principal obligor on the bill, and the holder of the bill who failed to perform the duty to preserve recourse rights may set it off only where, at the time of the default, namely on the maturity date of the bill, he knew or could have known that the issuer’s financial condition would deteriorate in the future (see Supreme Court Decision 1986.10.28. rendered, 86DAKA218).\\n\\nIn this case, however, although the Plaintiff neglected the duty to preserve recourse rights by failing to present the bill for payment on the maturity date, and thereafter Seongin Trading, as the issuer and principal obligor, became insolvent, causing the Defendant to suffer damage in that, even if he performed his underlying debt to the Plaintiff, he could not obtain satisfaction of his own bill claim and underlying claim against Seongin Trading, the record contains no materials whatsoever to support a finding that, at the time of maturity, the Plaintiff knew or could have known that Seongin Trading would become insolvent in the future. Therefore, it must be deemed that the Plaintiff does not bear liability for damages to the Defendant. Accordingly, although the court below’s reasoning is not free from inappropriateness, it is proper in its conclusion in rejecting the Defendant’s defense of set-off on the ground that the Defendant’s claim for damages against the Plaintiff is not recognized, and the error of the court below pointed out above does not affect the result of the judgment; ultimately, the argument on appeal is without merit.\\n\\n3. Regarding the assertion of concurrent performance among the second point of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nWith respect to the Defendant’s assertion that he cannot perform the obligation to return the above loan money until the above promissory note is returned, the court below lawfully determined that, as a judgment of invalidation had been rendered on 1991.1.5. regarding the above promissory note, the above promissory note had become void, and rejected the Defendant’s above assertion.\\n\\nAs generally alleged, a debtor who has delivered a promissory note and borrowed money may assert, in response to the creditor’s claim for return of the loan money, that he will perform his obligation to return it only concurrently with the return of the promissory note; however, where, as in this case, a judgment of invalidation has been rendered with respect to the promissory note and the effect of the promissory note has been extinguished, such an assertion of concurrent performance cannot be made. The court below’s judgment to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality therein. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; accordingly, the Court, by unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, renders judgment as stated in the operative part."}

{"[95DA25060]": "1. Summary of Reasons of the Judgment of the Court Below\\n\\nThe court below found, in substance, that when Defendant Kwon Jae-ho, who had stood as a joint surety, came to be in a situation where he found it difficult to pay the construction price debt owed by Defendant Deokgu Hot Spring Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the Defendant Company) to the Plaintiff Company, he, at the Plaintiff Company's suggestion, agreed to sell the shares of non-party Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd. owned by him and to pay the construction price to the Plaintiff Company with the sale proceeds; accordingly, on 1991. 10. 10., he sold the shares of Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd. owned by him to non-party Park Cheol-an. Then, on the 29th of the same month, among the Defendants, the Plaintiff Company, Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd., and non-party Sama Housing Co., Ltd., in order to pay the stock purchase price owed by Park Cheol-an to Defendant Kwon Jae-ho, Sama Housing Co., Ltd., whose representative director was Park Cheol-an, issued eight promissory notes involved in this case in an aggregate face amount equivalent to KRW 3,900,000,000, and after Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd. indorsed them as the first indorser and Defendant Kwon Jae-ho indorsed them as the second indorser, delivered them to the Plaintiff for application to the above construction price. The Plaintiff Company presented for payment the respective promissory notes described in items 1 through 4 of the list attached to the judgment below among the promissory notes in this case and had already received payment of construction price in the aggregate amount equivalent to KRW 1,600,000,000. Thereafter, however, it received from Sama Housing Co., Ltd. a request to extend the due dates before the due dates of the four promissory notes described in items 5 through 8 of the list attached to the judgment below; with respect to the respective promissory notes described in items 5 and 6, it extended the due dates to 1992. 9. 30. and received reissued promissory notes in the face amount of KRW 1,000,000,000, and with respect to the promissory note described in item 7, it extended the due date to 9. 30. of the same year, and with respect to the promissory note described in item 8, it extended the due date to 9. 8. of the same year, thereby obtaining from Sama Housing Co., Ltd. reissued promissory notes in three sheets in the aggregate face amount equivalent to KRW 2,300,000,000, each indorsed by Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd. as the first indorser and Park Cheol-an as the second indorser, and returned the respective promissory notes described in items 5 through 8 to Sama Housing Co., Ltd.; and thereafter all three of the above reissued promissory notes were dishonored on 1992. 8. 28. for the reason of no transaction (and the court below also found that, upon receiving back the respective promissory notes described in items 5 through 8 from the Plaintiff Company, Sama Housing Co., Ltd. returned them to Hanil Bank Jongno 3-ga Branch, the place of payment, and that the bank destroyed the respective promissory notes described in items 5, 7, and 8 on 1992. 4. 23. and the promissory note described in item 6 on 1. 20. of the same year), and then held that, absent special circumstances, the Defendant Company and Defendant Kwon Jae-ho, who was the joint surety for the Defendant Company's construction price debt to the Plaintiff Company, were jointly and severally liable to pay the remaining amount of the construction price, excluding the amount acknowledged by the Plaintiff Company as already having been paid, and delay damages thereon, and rejected all of the Defendants' assertions, including the argument that the Plaintiff Company's construction price claim against the Defendants in this case had been extinguished.\\n\\n2. Judgment on the Grounds of Appeal (including the supplemental grounds to the extent they supplement the same)\\n\\na. As to Point 1\\n\\nWhen a debtor delivers a promissory note to a creditor in relation to the performance of an existing debt, the parties' intent may be divided into cases where the note is delivered \"in substitution for payment\" of the existing underlying debt, that is, where they intend to extinguish the existing underlying debt and leave only the new promissory note debt in existence; cases where the existing underlying debt is left in existence and the note is merely delivered as the so-called \"for payment\" method thereof; and cases where it is delivered merely for the purpose of securing payment of the existing debt, the so-called \"for security\" delivery. Unless there is a special manifestation of intent between the parties, even if a promissory note has been delivered, it shall be presumed that the existing underlying debt remains in existence and that the note was merely delivered \"for payment\" or \"for security\"; accordingly, absent special circumstances, the existing underlying debt does not become extinguished and must be deemed to coexist with the debt on the note. In such a case, when the principal obligor on the note is not identical with the debtor under the underlying relationship, payment by a third person who is the principal obligor on the note is contemplated, and thus it shall be presumed to have been delivered \"for payment\" (see this Court's Decisions dated 1995. 10. 13. in 93DA12213, dated 1993. 11. 9. in 93DA11203, 11210).\\n\\nIn the same purport, it was correct for the court below to reject the Defendants' assertion that the eight promissory notes in this case, issued by Sama Housing Co., Ltd. and indorsed by Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd. and Defendant Kwon Jae-ho, were delivered to the Plaintiff Company in substitution for payment of the Defendants' construction price debt to the Plaintiff Company, and there is no illegality such as violation of the rules of evidence, misapprehension of facts due to incomplete deliberation, or misapprehension of legal principles concerning the nature of negotiable instruments, as alleged. The argument is without merit.\\n\\nb. As to Point 2\\n\\nThe court below rejected the Defendants' assertion that the construction price debt owed by the Defendants to the Plaintiff Company had been extinguished because Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd. had assumed, with liberating effect, the construction price debt owed by the Defendants to the Plaintiff Company, and there is no illegality such as violation of the rules of evidence, misapprehension of facts due to incomplete deliberation, or misapprehension of legal principles concerning assumption of debt, as alleged. The argument is also without merit.\\n\\nc. As to Point 3\\n\\nThe court below, based on the fact that, at the time the Plaintiff Company and the Defendants entered into the hot spring inn construction contract and the complex development construction contract in this case, it was agreed that the construction price would be paid within the scope of the revenue from the sale of the hot spring inn building and the condominium, but that thereafter, on 1991. 10. 29., the Defendants agreed to pay the construction price to the Plaintiff Company by the due dates of the promissory notes in this case irrespective of the above sales, correctly rejected the Defendants' assertion that the construction price debt in this case had not yet fallen due, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of facts due to violation of the rules of evidence or misapprehension of legal principles concerning the interpretation of juristic acts, as alleged. The argument is also without merit.\\n\\nd. As to Point 5\\n\\nThe court below, in response to the Defendants' assertion that the Plaintiff Company exchanged the respective promissory notes described in items 5 through 8 of the list attached to the judgment below for other promissory notes, and that such exchange of notes constituted a kind of novation contract, whereby the rights under the old notes were extinguished and consequently the above construction price claim under the underlying relationship was also extinguished, held that the Plaintiff Company's exchange of the respective promissory notes described in items 5 through 8, which had been issued for payment of the existing debt, for three promissory notes reissued by Sama Housing Co., Ltd. and indorsed by Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd. as the first indorser and non-party Park Cheol-an as the second indorser was for the purpose of extending the due dates, and could not be regarded as a new novation contract that changed an important part of the existing debt itself; moreover, the reissued promissory notes were also found to have been for the purpose of satisfying the Defendants' construction price debt to the Plaintiff Company as against the Plaintiff Company, and for the purpose of satisfying Park Cheol-an's debt to pay the stock purchase price to the above Defendant as against Defendant Kwon Jae-ho; accordingly, the court below held that the mere fact that the Plaintiff Company exchanged the respective promissory notes described in items 5 through 8 for the above three promissory notes could not be deemed to extinguish the Plaintiff Company's construction price claim against the Defendants under the underlying relationship, and this was correct. There is no illegality such as misapprehension of facts due to violation of the rules of evidence or misapprehension of legal principles concerning novation, as alleged. This argument is likewise without merit.\\n\\ne. As to Points 4, 6, and 7\\n\\n(1) The court below rejected all of the Defendants' following assertions: \"① Even if the respective promissory notes described in items 5 through 8 of the list attached to the judgment below were delivered to the Plaintiff Company for payment of the construction price, the Plaintiff Company failed to exercise the rights under the notes and neglected the procedures for preserving those rights, thereby causing the rights under the notes to be lost; therefore, the Plaintiff Company's construction price claim against the Defendants has been extinguished, or the Plaintiff Company's exercise of the claim under the underlying relationship constitutes an abuse of rights and cannot be permitted. ② Since the Plaintiff Company became unable to return the above respective promissory notes to the Defendants, the Plaintiff Company's construction price claim against the Defendants has been extinguished. ③ Because the Plaintiff Company failed to present the above respective promissory notes for payment on the due dates, Defendant Kwon Jae-ho lost his right of recourse and therefore acquired against the Plaintiff Company a claim for damages equivalent to their face amount; accordingly, set off, in equivalent amounts, Defendant Kwon Jae-ho's above damage claim against the Plaintiff Company and the Plaintiff Company's present construction price claim against the Defendants.\" The court below reasoned that the respective promissory notes were delivered to secure payment of or as the method of payment for the Defendants' construction price debt to the Plaintiff Company, and that in such a case, if the creditor does not exercise the rights under the promissory notes received or neglects the procedures for preserving those rights, causing damage to the debtor who delivered the notes, the creditor cannot exercise the claim under the underlying relationship. However, the respective promissory notes were delivered, as regards Defendant Kwon Jae-ho, for the purpose of securing payment of Park Cheol-an's debt to pay the stock purchase price of Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd. shares to the above Defendant or as the method of such payment; and Sama Housing Co., Ltd. and Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd. issued or indorsed the respective promissory notes for the purpose of cumulative assumption of or suretyship for Park Cheol-an's above debt to pay the stock purchase price to the above Defendant (although the court below stated as if Sama Housing Co., Ltd. also indorsed the respective promissory notes, this is manifestly a clerical error). Accordingly, even if the Plaintiff Company did not exercise the rights under the respective promissory notes and neglected the procedures for preserving those rights, such that Defendant Kwon Jae-ho could not exercise the right of recourse, etc. under the respective promissory notes, this does not mean that the above Defendant is thereby unable to exercise the claim under the underlying relationship against Park Cheol-an and against Sama Housing Co., Ltd. and Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd., who are the cumulative assumers or sureties, so that the above Defendant suffered no economic loss thereby.\\n\\n(2) However, a person who has engaged in a negotiable instrument act shall, absent special circumstances, bear only the obligation on the instrument according to the wording of the instrument (see this Court's Decisions dated 1987. 4. 28. in 86DAKA2630, dated 1994. 8. 26. in 94DA5397, etc.). Therefore, even if Sama Housing Co., Ltd. issued the promissory notes in this case in order to discharge Park Cheol-an's debt to pay the stock purchase price as its representative director, and Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd. indorsed them, absent special circumstances it cannot be deemed that Sama Housing Co., Ltd. or Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd. cumulatively assumed or guaranteed Park Cheol-an's debt to pay the stock purchase price to Defendant Kwon Jae-ho.\\n\\nNevertheless, it was wrong for the court below, without invoking any particular special circumstances, to find that Sama Housing Co., Ltd. and Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd. cumulatively assumed or guaranteed Park Cheol-an's debt to pay the stock purchase price to Defendant Kwon Jae-ho.\\n\\n(3) In addition, in a case such as this one where the notes were delivered \"for payment,\" it shall be deemed that the parties contemplated that the creditor would first exercise the note claim among the note claim and the underlying claim and obtain satisfaction; therefore, the creditor must first exercise the note claim, and only when satisfaction cannot be obtained thereby may the creditor exercise the existing underlying claim against the debtor. Furthermore, a creditor who has received an endorsement and transfer of a note for such purpose, absent special circumstances, must return the note to the debtor in order to exercise the underlying claim against the debtor. Accordingly, it may be said to accord with fairness between the two sides to regard the creditor as under a duty, as a precondition to exercising his underlying claim against the debtor, to duly present the note on the due date and take the procedures for preserving the right of recourse. However, even if, by violating the above duty, the creditor failed to duly present the note for payment on the due date and thus the right of recourse was not preserved, no damage has yet arisen so long as the maker, who is the principal obligor on the promissory note, remains solvent, because the debtor who has received the note back may still obtain satisfaction of his own claim by exercising against the maker either the note claim or the underlying claim; and only when, after the due date, the maker's solvency deteriorates and the maker becomes insolvent so that even if the creditor returns the note the debtor who must perform his own obligation can no longer obtain either the note claim or the underlying claim against the maker, does damage arise in the sense that satisfaction of his claim cannot be obtained. Such damage is damage arising from the special circumstance of deterioration in the solvency of the maker, the principal obligor on the promissory note, and may be set off against the damage claim only when the holder of the note who failed to perform the duty to preserve the right of recourse knew or could have known, at the time of the nonperformance, namely the due date of the note, that the maker's solvency would deteriorate in the future (see this Court's Decisions dated 1995. 10. 13. in 93DA12213, and dated 1986. 10. 28. in 86DAKA218).\\n\\n(4) In this case, however, the Plaintiff Company returned the respective promissory notes described in items 5 through 8 of the list attached to the judgment below to the issuer, Sama Housing Co., Ltd., and received three new promissory notes in return as a means of effectively extending the due dates of the respective promissory notes, thereby neglecting its duty to preserve the right of recourse in respect of the returned notes; and thereafter the issuer of the notes, Sama Housing Co., Ltd., became insolvent, so that Defendant Kwon Jae-ho, who was the indorser of the returned notes, would suffer damage in that even if he performed his own underlying debt to the Plaintiff Company, he could not obtain satisfaction of his note claim against Sama Housing Co., Ltd. and Deokgu Hot Spring Condo Co., Ltd.
