However, Defendant Kwon Jae-ho may not only exercise the claim under the underlying relationship, namely the claim for the stock purchase price against Park Cheol-an (there is nothing in the record to show that Park Cheol-an became insolvent), but even upon examining the record, there is no material to support a finding that, at the time the Plaintiff Company returned the respective promissory notes described in items 5 through 8 to Sama Housing Co., Ltd. and received new notes, it knew or could have known that Sama Housing Co., Ltd. would become insolvent in the future. Therefore, the Plaintiff Company did not incur liability for damages to Defendant Kwon Jae-ho.\\n\\n(5) Accordingly, although there are some inappropriate portions in the wording of the court below's reasoning, the conclusion that the Defendants' above assertions were all rejected on the ground that Defendant Kwon Jae-ho's damage claim against the Plaintiff Company was not recognized is correct, and the errors in the court below pointed out above do not affect the result of the judgment; thus, all of the arguments are without merit.\\n\\n3. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed in its entirety, and the costs of appeal are to be borne by the losing Defendants, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the judges participating in the decision."}

question: B created a joint mortgage on B-owned X land (market value KRW 120,000,000) and on Y land owned by the real guarantor C (market value KRW 80,000,000) in order to secure B’s debt of KRW 100,000,000 to A. D acquired a second mortgage right on X land (secured claim: KRW 10,000,000), and E acquired a second mortgage right on Y land (secured claim: KRW 40,000,000). Which of the following correctly combines the true statements (○) and the false statements (×) concerning this matter? (Do not consider interest, delay damages, or execution costs. Each item is independent, and where there is precedent, follow the precedents.) (a) If X land is first sold by auction and A receives payment in full from the sale proceeds (KRW 100,000,000), then when Y land is sold by auction, D can receive KRW 10,000,000 from the sale proceeds of Y land (KRW 80,000,000). (b) If Y land is first sold by auction and the entire sale proceeds (KRW 80,000,000) are distributed to A, then B may assert against E by setting off the KRW 50,000,000 matured loan claim that B holds against C against the reimbursement claim that C acquired against B. (c) If B sells X land to F and completes the registration of transfer of ownership, and thereafter B’s general creditor A (claim amount: KRW 100,000,000) has the above sale contract rescinded as a fraudulent act and must provide value compensation, then if there is no change in the market values of X land and Y land, the scope of value compensation is KRW 20,000,000.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2011DA68012]": "We render judgment on the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. On the first ground of appeal\\n\\nA mortgagee with an agreed maximum amount of secured claim may receive repayment in priority to general creditors or junior security interest holders, within the limit of the maximum amount of the secured claim, in accordance with the Civil Act, the Commercial Act, and other laws. The same applies in the case of a joint mortgage, and the right of preferential repayment of a joint mortgagee is a right to receive preferential repayment from the total conversion proceeds of the relevant property to the extent of the claims covered by such right of preferential repayment. Such right of preferential repayment may be exercised not only where the joint mortgagee itself executes the auction, but also where the auction is executed by another person, by receiving preferential repayment from the conversion proceeds according to the order of priority, instead of being able to prevent the joint mortgagee from doing so. Meanwhile, where the subject property of a joint mortgage is owned by a third-party surety, the third-party surety is naturally led to believe that the upper limit of the liability it will bear is the amount equivalent to the maximum amount of the secured claim. If, in a case where the joint mortgagee itself did not execute the auction, the joint mortgagee were able to receive dividend payments repeatedly up to the amount of the maximum secured claim from the conversion proceeds of each subject property of the joint mortgage, an unfair result would arise in which the liability of the third-party surety is determined, irrespective of its intention to provide security, depending on whether the joint mortgagee actively applied for auction or passively participated in an auction application by a third party. Therefore, regardless of whether the joint mortgagee actively applied for auction or passively participated in an auction application by a third party, where, in auction proceedings concerning some of the real property subject to the joint mortgage, the joint mortgagee exercised its right of preferential repayment and received the full amount corresponding to the maximum secured claim within the scope of that right, it is reasonable to hold that it may not later receive the same amount again through auction proceedings concerning other real property subject to the joint mortgage.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the first instance judgment cited by the judgment of the court below, as to each of the 660/2400 shares owned by Non-Party 1 among the land in Sujin-dong, Sujeong-gu, Seongnam-si (lot numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 omitted), with respect to each such share, Non-Party 2 had completed the registration of establishment of a mortgage, with Debtor Non-Party 3 and maximum secured claim of KRW 375,000,000 (hereinafter, the mortgage by such registration is referred to as “the joint mortgage at issue”), and Non-Party 4 had completed the registration of establishment of a mortgage, with Debtor Non-Party 3 and maximum secured claim of KRW 225,000,000, in the same priority; thereafter, the Plaintiff had completed the registration of transfer of ownership in the Plaintiff’s name with respect to the above land (lot number 3 omitted) (hereinafter, “the land at issue”); and, in the voluntary auction proceedings conducted, upon Non-Party 4’s application for auction, with respect to Non-Party 1’s shares among the remaining lands excluding the land at issue (hereinafter, “the first auction proceedings”), Non-Party 2 received a dividend of KRW 375,000,000, the entire maximum secured claim. In light of the legal principles stated above, it follows that the joint mortgage at issue was extinguished by Non-Party 2’s receipt of the entire maximum secured claim as a dividend.\\n\\nThe court below’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the exercise of the right of preferential repayment of a joint mortgage, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. On the second ground of appeal\\n\\nIf a mortgage has been extinguished by the extinction of the secured claim, but this is overlooked and an order to commence auction is made, and the auction proceedings proceed to become final with a decision to permit sale, then this constitutes invalid proceedings and an invalid decision made on the basis of an extinguished mortgage, and even if the purchaser has fully paid the sale price, the purchaser cannot acquire ownership of the real property (see Supreme Court Decision 98DA51855, decided February 9, 1999).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below held that, since the joint mortgage at issue had already been extinguished by Non-Party 2, who was the joint mortgagee, receiving the entire maximum secured claim as a dividend in the first auction proceedings, the voluntary auction proceedings instituted on the basis of the joint mortgage at issue with respect to the 660/2400 share of the land at issue (hereinafter, “the second auction proceedings”) were invalid, and therefore the Defendant, as the purchaser in the second auction proceedings, is obliged, unless special circumstances exist, to implement the procedure for registration of cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership concerning the 660/2400 share of the land at issue. In light of the legal principles stated above and the record, this determination by the court below is proper, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the legal principles as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. On the third and fourth grounds of appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the first instance judgment cited by the judgment of the court below, in view of the fact that the settlor of the joint mortgage at issue was Non-Party 1, the debtor was Non-Party 3, and the Plaintiff was merely a third acquirer, even if the Plaintiff received the dividend without objection in the second auction proceedings conducted on the basis of the invalid joint mortgage at issue and delivered the land at issue to the Defendant, such circumstances alone cannot be said to mean that the Plaintiff manifested to the purchaser a trust that the joint mortgage at issue was valid. On that basis, the court below rejected the Defendant’s defense that the Plaintiff’s claim at issue violated the principle of estoppel and the principle of good faith. In light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the court below’s determination is proper, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the legal principles as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe other grounds of appeal are newly asserted by the Defendant at the stage of the final appeal, and it is clear from the record that they were not asserted before the conclusion of oral argument in the court below; accordingly, they cannot constitute lawful grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. The judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court participating in the case, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2021DA258777]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. In an action to set aside a fraudulent transfer, where a mortgage is created over the subject matter transferred by the debtor to the transferee, the property subject to liability provided as common security for general creditors among such subject matter is only the remaining portion after deducting the amount of the secured claim from the maximum secured amount, and when the amount of the secured claim exceeds the value of the subject matter, it cannot be said that the transfer of that subject matter constitutes a fraudulent transfer. Where a joint mortgage is created over several parcels of real property, in calculating the property subject to liability, the amount of the secured claim borne by each parcel of real property, absent special circumstances, is appropriate to regard as the amount obtained by apportioning the amount of the secured claim within the limit of the maximum secured amount in proportion to the value of each parcel of real property that is the subject of the joint mortgage, in light of the purport of Article 368 of the Civil Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DA39989, rendered November 13, 2003). However, where among those several parcels of real property some are owned by the debtor and others are owned by a property guarantor, taking into account circumstances such as the fact that the property guarantor is in a position to exercise the mortgage right against the real property owned by the debtor by way of subrogation under Articles 481 and 482 of the Civil Act, unless there are special circumstances in which the property guarantor cannot exercise a right of reimbursement against the debtor, the amount of the secured claim concerning the real property owned by the debtor should be regarded as the full amount of the secured claim within the limit of the maximum secured amount (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DA78234, rendered April 10, 2008). This legal principle likewise applies where, among one co-owned piece of real property, some shares are owned by the debtor and other shares are owned by a property guarantor (see the Supreme Court en banc Decision 2012DA5643, rendered July 18, 2013).\\n\\n2. The court below found the following facts. D was liable to E Co., Ltd. for a loan debt in the principal amount of 30,087,181 won and to F Co., Ltd. for a mortgage debt in the principal amount of 100,487,000 won. D and the Defendant, who were husband and wife, owned the real property at issue in this case in shares of 1/2 each, and a mortgage was created over the entirety of the real property at issue in this case, with F Co., Ltd. as the mortgagee, D as the debtor, and a maximum secured amount of 118,800,000 won (hereinafter referred to as the “mortgage at issue in this case”). On June 19, 2017, D donated his entire share to the Defendant and caused the ownership transfer registration to be completed the next day (hereinafter referred to as the “donation at issue in this case”). On July 11, 2017, the Defendant paid in full the amount of the secured obligation and cancelled the mortgage at issue in this case. It may be inferred that, at the time the proceedings in the court below were concluded, the market value of the real property at issue in this case was 210,700,000 won.\\n\\nBased on these factual findings, the court below determined that D’s donation of his entire share, which was his only asset while in a state of insolvency, to the Defendant constituted a fraudulent transfer.\\n\\n3. However, the judgment of the court below cannot be upheld as it stands.\\n\\nFirst, whether a certain act of disposition constitutes a fraudulent transfer must be determined as of the time of that act of disposition, but no examination was made in the court below as to the market value of the real property at issue in this case as of the time of the donation at issue in this case. The court below appears to have relied on the market value of 210,700,000 won as of the conclusion of the proceedings in the court below, but the court below should have calculated the market value based on the time of the donation at issue in this case, rather than the time of the conclusion of the proceedings in the court below, and compared it with the amount of the secured claim under the mortgage at issue in this case.\\n\\nIn addition, in light of the legal principles discussed above, it is necessary to examine whether there are special circumstances in which the Defendant, as a property guarantor, cannot exercise a right of reimbursement against D, and to determine whether the full amount of the secured claim should be deducted or only the amount corresponding to the share ratio should be deducted in deciding whether a fraudulent transfer exists. Whether such special circumstances exist must be determined by comprehensively examining the source of funds used to purchase the real property at issue in this case, the circumstances surrounding the purchase, and the circumstances under which the Defendant came to provide property surety for D’s debt.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, without conducting any examination of these circumstances, immediately concluded that the donation at issue in this case constituted a fraudulent transfer. The judgment of the court below erred by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the formation of a fraudulent transfer and by failing to conduct the necessary examination. The ground of appeal asserting this is well-founded (the court below, on the premise that a fraudulent transfer had been established, further determined the scope of restoration to the original status following revocation of the donation at issue in this case and deducted only the amount of the secured claim corresponding to the Defendant’s share ratio; if, upon renewed proceedings after remand, the donation at issue in this case is again recognized as a fraudulent transfer, then the scope of restoration to the original status must also be determined in accordance with the legal principles of the aforementioned Supreme Court en banc Decision 2012DA5643).\\n\\n4. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for further proceedings and determination, and so, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices, render the judgment as stated in the Disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding the legal relationship between A, who operates an inn, and B, the guest of the inn, are correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents) (a) The lodging contract concluded between A and B constitutes a type of lease agreement for temporary use of a guest room. (b) In order for a bailment relationship to be established between A and B, there must be an express or implied agreement between them that A will assume an obligation to keep the object within his sphere of control. (c) Even if A has not taken the item in bailment from B, A is liable to compensate for damages when an item carried into the facility is lost or damaged due to A’s own negligence or that of his employee. (d) If A controls entry to the inn’s attached parking lot or, without confirming the fact of parking, merely provides a parking space, then even if B parked the vehicle in the parking lot and entrusted the vehicle’s custody by leaving the vehicle key at the inn, an agreement of bailment between A and B cannot be recognized. (e) If B dies due to a fire at the inn, C, B’s spouse, may claim from A damages for his or her own emotional distress on the ground of A’s breach of the lodging contract with B.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[91DA21800]": "We consider the grounds of appeal filed by counsel for Defendant (the supplemental brief on the grounds of appeal was filed after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal; therefore, we shall determine only within the extent that it supplements the grounds stated in the statement of grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below found, based on the evidence it cited, that Non-Party 1 stayed at the OOO Inn operated by Defendant from 23:40 on 1990. 2. 5. until around 08:40 on the following day, and parked his Sonata passenger car, owned by him, in a parking lot across the road (6 meters in width) in front of the inn building, whereupon it was stolen; that when staying at the inn, he did not notify any employee of the inn of the fact that he had parked the car; that said parking lot had been installed by Defendant as one of the ancillary facilities of the inn, and although its entrance was in a position visible from the inn’s cashier’s counter, it was merely constructed by erecting a sign reading OOO Parking Lot at the entrance, fencing the outer perimeter with a cloth net, and installing a roof over the place where cars were to be parked to prepare for rain and snow, without installing a door equipped with a locking device or taking any special anti-theft measures; and that there was no separate employee assigned to guard vehicles parked in said parking lot; and then, based on those findings, held that, according to the above facts found, because Non-Party 1 parked the passenger car he had driven to the parking lot of Defendant’s inn in order to stay there and then stayed at the inn, Defendant, as an operator of a public lodging business, had received the said passenger car in bailment from Non-Party 1, a guest, and therefore, in this case, where Defendant has failed to prove, pursuant to Article 152(1) of the Commercial Act, that the theft accident was due to force majeure, Defendant is liable to compensate Non-Party 1, the owner of the said passenger car, for the damage thereby caused.\\n\\n2. However, in order for a bailment under Article 152(1) of the Commercial Act to be established, there must first be an express or implied agreement between the operator of a public lodging business and the guest that the operator of the public lodging business shall assume the obligation to keep the object within its sphere of control. If a door equipped with a locking device is installed at the attached parking lot of an inn, or a caretaker controlling entry and exit is stationed there, or other measures have been taken by the inn side so that it can control or verify entry to and parking in the parking lot, then, with respect to a vehicle parked in such a parking lot by a guest staying at the inn, even in the absence of an express declaration of entrustment, it may be deemed that there was an agreement of bailment between the innkeeper and the guest. However, if no facilities or measures exist for controlling or verifying entry to the parking lot and the fact of parking, and if the inn side merely provides a place for parking and is not controlling or verifying entry to the parking lot and the fact of parking, then, apart from the question of whether there has been a breach of the duty of care as manager of the attached parking lot, it cannot be deemed that there was an agreement of bailment between the innkeeper and the guest merely because the guest parked in such a parking lot, and the establishment of bailment can be recognized only where the guest notifies the inn side of the fact of parking or entrusts the custody of the vehicle by handing over the vehicle key.\\n\\nBy the way, according to the facts finally determined by the court below, it can be seen that no door equipped with a locking device was installed at the parking lot in this case, nor was any employee assigned to guard parked vehicles; and although the entrance to the parking lot was in a position visible from the inn’s cashier’s counter, it appears that it was not to such an extent that entry and exit vehicles could be controlled or verified one by one there, so based on the facts finally determined by the court below alone, it is difficult to deem that there was an agreement of bailment between Non-Party 1, who did not notify the fact of parking at all, and Defendant with respect to the parked vehicle.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below erred in holding that a bailment concerning the parked vehicle had been established between Defendant and said Non-Party 1, thereby committing an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles on the establishment of bailment prescribed in Article 152(1) of the Commercial Act, and the argument on this point is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without addressing the other grounds of appeal, the portion of the judgment of the court below adverse to Defendant is reversed and remanded, and the judgment is rendered unanimously by the participating Justices as follows."}

{"[91DA21800]": "We examine the grounds of appeal filed by counsel for the Defendant in the litigation (the supplemental brief to the statement of grounds of appeal was submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal, and thus is considered only to the extent that it supplements the grounds stated in the statement of grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. According to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the court below found, based on the evidence it cited, that Non-party 1 stayed at the ○○○ Inn operated by the Defendant from 23:40 on 1990. 2. 5. until around 08:40 on the following day, and parked his Sonata passenger car, owned by him, in a parking lot across the street from the front of the inn building (road width: 6 meters), where it was stolen; that when he checked in, he did not inform the inn employee of the parking; that the said parking lot had been installed by the Defendant as one of the auxiliary facilities of the inn; that although its entrance was in a position visible from the inn’s cashier counter, it was made merely by erecting at the entrance a sign reading ○○○ Parking Lot, without installing a gate with a locking device or otherwise making any special anti-theft facilities, with the outer perimeter enclosed by a cloth net and a roof installed over the area where vehicles were parked in preparation for rain and snow; and that there was no separate employee assigned to guard vehicles parked in the lot. Based on the above facts, the court below held that, by parking the passenger car he had driven to the inn parking lot and then staying at the inn, Non-party 1 had entrusted the said passenger car to the Defendant, a public accommodation operator, and therefore, in this case where the Defendant has failed to prove, pursuant to Article 152(1) of the Commercial Act, that the theft occurred due to force majeure, the Defendant is liable to compensate Non-party 1, the owner of the said passenger car, for the damage thereby caused.\\n\\n2. However, for a bailment under Article 152(1) of the Commercial Act to be established, there must first be an express or implied agreement between the public accommodation operator and the guest that the public accommodation operator will assume the obligation to safeguard the object within its sphere of control. If, at the inn’s auxiliary parking lot, a gate with a locking device is installed, or a manager is stationed to control entry, or other measures are in place by which the inn side can control or verify entry to the parking lot and the fact of parking, then with respect to a vehicle parked by an inn guest in such a parking lot, even absent an express manifestation of intent to entrust, it may be regarded that there was an agreement of bailment between the innkeeper and the guest. However, if there are no facilities or measures to control or verify entry to the parking lot and the fact of parking, and the place merely provides a parking space, so that the inn side does not control or verify entry to the parking lot or the fact of parking, then, apart from whether there has been a breach of the duty of care as manager of the auxiliary parking lot, a bailment agreement between the innkeeper and the guest cannot be deemed to have been formed merely because the vehicle was parked in such a parking lot, and bailment may be recognized only when the guest notifies the inn side of the parking or entrusts the safekeeping of the vehicle by handing over the vehicle keys.\\n\\nYet, according to the facts finally determined by the court below, it can be seen that no gate with a locking device was installed at the parking lot in this case, nor was any employee stationed to guard parked vehicles, and although the parking lot entrance was in a position visible from the inn’s cashier counter, it appears that it was not to such an extent that vehicles entering or leaving the parking lot could be individually controlled or verified therefrom; therefore, based solely on the facts finally determined by the court below, it is difficult to deem that there was an agreement of bailment concerning the parked vehicle between Non-party 1, who did not notify the parking at all, and the Defendant.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below erred in holding that a bailment concerning the parked vehicle had been established between the Defendant and Non-party 1, and thereby committed an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal doctrine on the establishment of bailment under Article 152(1) of the Commercial Act; the argument on this point is well taken.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without examining the other grounds of appeal, we reverse and remand the portion of the judgment below against the Defendant, and accordingly render judgment as follows by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: Company A entered into a contract to transfer its hotel business to Company B. Although Company B did not assume Company A’s debts, it neither registered that it was not liable for Company A’s debts nor notified Company A’s creditors to that effect. After acquiring the business, Company B carried on the same hotel business and continued to use, unchanged, the business establishment name “△△Jeju” that Company A had used. Which of the following statements concerning this is incorrect? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents.)
A: If a business is transferred comprehensively, then, unless otherwise stipulated, the employment relationship between Company A and its employees is also comprehensively succeeded to by Company B as a general rule.
B: Even when the designation continued to be used by Company B is not the trade name itself but a house name or business sign, Company B shall, unless special circumstances exist, bear the debt by analogical application of Commercial Act Article 42 (Liability of a Transferee Who Continues to Use the Trade Name), paragraph 1.
C: Company B’s liability for payment with respect to the claims of third parties arising from Company A’s business is extinguished when 2 years have elapsed after the business transfer.
D: Notwithstanding the business transfer, with respect to creditors of Company A who know that there was no assumption of debts, Company B’s liability does not arise, and Company B bears the burden of allegation and proof as to the fact that the creditor acted in bad faith.
E: If a creditor of Company A did not know, around the time of the business transfer, that there was no assumption of debts, then, unless special circumstances exist, Company B’s liability for payment arises under Commercial Act Article 42, paragraph 1, and even if the creditor later comes to know that there was no assumption of debts, the already-arisen liability for payment of Company B is not extinguished.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2000DU8455]": "1. “Transfer of a business” means the transfer, as a whole, of an enterprise organized for a definite business purpose, namely, its human and material organization, while maintaining its identity; transfer of only a part of the business is also possible. Where such a business transfer has taken place, the employment relationships of the relevant workers are, in principle, comprehensively succeeded to by the acquiring company. Whether the identity of the business is maintained is a question of factual determination to be decided according to the ordinary social conception, but the question of whether the act in issue (the transfer contract relationship) is recognized as a business transfer is not to be determined merely by how much business property has been transferred or to what extent, but by whether the existing business organization has been maintained so that the organization can function as a whole or in an important part thereof; thus, even where all business assets have been transferred, if the transfer was made after dismantling the organization, it is not a business transfer, whereas even where business facilities were transferred with some assets reserved, if it is socially understood that the transferred part alone preserves the former organization, then that would be regarded as a business transfer (see Supreme Court Decision 99DU2680 rendered on July 27, 2001).\\n\\nCiting the first-instance judgment, the court below found the following facts: Donghae Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to only as “Donghae”) is a company that manufactures electric and mechanical parts such as relays, units, and car stereos for automobiles; from around 1986. 12., while entering into a technical alliance with Omron Co., Ltd. of Japan, on December 12, 1991, Donghae and Omron Co., Ltd. of Japan each contributed capital of 35% and 65%, respectively, to establish the company intervening in support of the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as the “Intervenor Company”); Donghae’s business divisions are divided into the automotive electrical equipment business division, which manufactures relays and units among automobile parts, and the electronics business division, which manufactures car stereos. Starting around 1996, Donghae began relocating the production line of the electronics business division to Namyang Company in China, and by around August 1996 assigned all production workers belonging to the electronics business division to the automotive electrical equipment business division, after which some employees of the materials department also concurrently handled work for the electronics business division to supply materials, thereby virtually suspending the production of car stereos in Korea. As Donghae faced financial difficulties due to the foreign exchange crisis that began at the end of 1997, high interest rates, and a decrease in automobile demand, and was confronted with a risk of default, on March 20, 1998, it entered into an asset sale agreement with the Intervenor Company to sell for KRW 271 hundred million all assets related to Donghae’s automotive electrical equipment business division. The main terms were as follows: as sale items, Donghae would sell to the Intervenor Company the land, buildings, machinery and equipment, tools, fixtures and furnishings, vehicles and transport equipment, inventories, leased assets, transferred technology, and goodwill listed in the attached schedule 1 of the judgment, and the Intervenor Company would purchase them from Donghae; provided, however, that items directly related to the operation of the automotive electrical equipment business would be deemed included in the sale items even if not listed in attached schedule 1; “goodwill” means the intangible asset value relating to the automotive electrical equipment business division, including customer relationships, business techniques, and consumer recognition acquired by Donghae’s automotive electrical equipment business division through long-term continuation of the business; “transferred technology” includes all intellectual property rights such as patents, utility model rights, and design rights relating to the automotive electrical equipment business, as well as technology and know-how concerning manufacturing, sales, and maintenance; rights relating to registration incidental to the sale items and licenses and permits were to be transferred together with the sale items; the Intervenor Company would not assume any debts of Donghae, whether or not incurred in relation to the automotive electrical equipment business, except that debts to financial institutions to which the sale items had been provided as security and obligations to pay lease payments to leasing companies could be assumed by the Intervenor Company as part of the sale price in accordance with the terms of this agreement after consultation with the financial institutions and leasing companies; with respect to various contracts related to product supply contracts with Hyundai Motor Co., Ltd. and SsangYong Motor Co., Ltd., the Intervenor Company would assume Donghae’s status with the consent of those companies; before obtaining the consent of those companies, the Intervenor Company would receive from Donghae the contracts to be assumed and determine the scope of the assumption; Donghae would survey the employees belonging to the automotive electrical equipment business division as to whether they wished to be employed by the Intervenor Company, notify the Intervenor Company of the results together with personnel records necessary for the recruitment screening, and the Intervenor Company would calculate the standard staffing level necessary for the operation of the sale items through job analysis and, in replenishing the required manpower, hire new employees through open recruitment procedures within the scope of the standard staffing level, while giving priority to, as far as possible, hiring the applicants for employment notified by Donghae before taking over the above sale items; Donghae would, at its own expense and responsibility, terminate the employment relationships of those who passed the Intervenor Company’s recruitment screening and settle all monetary matters such as severance pay by April 30, 1998, but the Intervenor Company would not bear any obligation to take over Donghae’s employees in connection with the takeover of the above sale items; except for Donghae’s being engaged in the automotive electrical equipment business division at the Intervenor Company’s request, Donghae would not engage, for 10 years from March 20, 1998, in any business activity of the same or similar kind as the business being transferred, unless otherwise separately agreed; the Donghae Labor Union, upon learning of the execution of the above asset sale agreement, held a labor-management council with Donghae on March 23, 1998 and demanded succession of employment relationships, succession of the union, and maintenance of the collective agreement, but, failing to reach any agreement due to differences of opinion between labor and management, the negotiations broke down. Thereupon, Donghae notified the workers belonging to the automotive electrical equipment business division through an internal notice on March 25, 1998 that “each worker must individually prepare and submit a document consisting of a letter of resignation to Donghae, an application for employment with the Intervenor Company, and a consent form for a 100% reduction of the unpaid Lunar New Year bonus (hereinafter referred to as the ‘reemployment application’)”; again, although the Donghae Labor Union on March 26, 1998 and March 27, 1998 argued that “it is improper for Donghae to have the workers individually apply for employment or to unilaterally require them to consent to resignation and bonus reduction,” and demanded comprehensive succession of employment for all union members, Donghae, despite these demands, received individual reemployment applications from a total of 176 persons by March 30, 1998 and notified the Intervenor Company thereof; the Intervenor Company received from Donghae the reemployment applications submitted by 176 workers and, without selection, hired them all as new employees effective April 1, 1998. However, nine persons, including the Plaintiffs who were members of the Donghae Labor Union, did not submit reemployment applications until April 4, 1998, after the extended deadline of March 31, 1998, having insisted on comprehensive succession of employment and opposition to bonus reductions, but Donghae rejected all applications submitted by the nine persons, including the Plaintiffs, on the ground that the submission deadline had passed, and accordingly the nine persons, including the Plaintiffs, were unable to enter the Intervenor Company; the Intervenor Company, pursuant to the above asset sale agreement, acquired all assets of Donghae’s automotive electrical equipment business division, while reemploying only Donghae’s workers in the form of new hiring and assigning them to the same departments as those in which they had worked at Donghae (though the names differed, the work content was the same) in the same positions so that they could continue their previous work, and thereafter changed the organizational structure of Donghae’s second division and tenth team to five centers, 19 groups, and one team, and introduced a small-lot multi-product production system by rearranging personnel, equipment, and offices, thereby adding 70 items to the items produced by Donghae and producing a total of 462 items. Based on these facts, the court below determined that in this case the Intervenor Company acquired from Donghae all tangible and intangible assets necessary for the automotive electrical equipment business, and also acquired the status as contractual party with respect to customers, so that if only Donghae’s human organization were combined therewith, it would immediately form the same material and human foundation as the transferred business; under the contract in this case, the Intervenor Company agreed to hire only the prescribed number of persons through recruitment screening procedures on the premise that it would not succeed to the employment relationships of Donghae’s workers, and accordingly Donghae’s workers submitted resignation letters and took the form of newly entering employment, but in reality, without going through any substantive employment procedures such as taking employment examinations, it hired all of Donghae’s workers who expressed their intention to be employed within the prescribed period; that the number of Donghae workers reemployed in the form of new hiring by the Intervenor Company reached 176 out of 199, so that most workers were rehired, and that the Intervenor Company hired only Donghae workers in the form of new hiring and did not actually hire workers other than Donghae workers in the form of open recruitment; and that Donghae workers were assigned by the Intervenor Company to positions corresponding to their positions at Donghae and were performing the same work as before. In light of these points, it was appropriate to regard the human organization of Donghae’s automotive electrical equipment business division as having been succeeded to by the Intervenor Company while maintaining its identity (even if some workers resigned voluntarily, that would not hinder recognition of the identity of the human organization). Adding to these points the fact that the Intervenor Company was carrying out the business on the basis of the material and human organization succeeded from Donghae while maintaining the basic framework of Donghae’s automotive electrical equipment business division, it concluded that the Intervenor Company had acquired the business from Donghae by comprehensively transferring, while maintaining their identity, the integrated material and human organization for the purpose of that business; and even if, when concluding the contract in this case with Donghae, the Intervenor Company expressly stated that it would take over only assets and not the human organization, or if it followed procedures of resignation and new hiring in employing workers, and did not take over all receivables and part of the liabilities, and even if some parts of the organization had changed after the business transfer, those points alone were insufficient to reach a different conclusion.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles set forth above and the record, the foregoing fact-finding and determination by the court below are proper, and there is no illegality such as violation of the rules governing the assessment of evidence or misapprehension of the legal principles concerning business transfer, as alleged in the grounds of appeal. The grounds of appeal disputing this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n2. When a business is transferred, unless there is an agreement to the contrary, the employment relationships between the transferor and the workers are, in principle, comprehensively succeeded to by the transferee; where there is an agreement between the parties to the business transfer that some employment relationships are excluded from succession, succession of the employment relationships may not occur accordingly. However, such an agreement is substantively no different from dismissal and is valid only if there is just cause under Article 30(1) of the Labor Standards Act, and dismissal of a worker solely on the ground of the business transfer itself cannot be regarded as a case in which just cause exists (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 93DA33173 rendered on June 28, 1994).\\n\\nThe court below, citing the first-instance judgment, held that although it is true that the Plaintiffs did not submit reemployment applications within the designated period, this appears to be merely because the Donghae Labor Union, of which the Plaintiffs were members, had argued that “it is improper for Donghae to have the workers individually apply for employment or to unilaterally require them to consent to resignation and bonus reduction,” and had demanded comprehensive succession of employment for all union members, but when this demand was not accepted, submitted the applications only after the deadline had passed, and not because they had no intention to be reemployed; that if the substance of the contract in this case constitutes a business transfer, it cannot be said to be improper to insist on comprehensive succession of employment, and furthermore, although there was no rational reason to link reemployment applications with bonus reductions, Donghae, taking advantage of receiving reemployment applications, attempted to obtain consent to bonus reductions as well, and the Plaintiffs’ failure to submit reemployment applications in protest thereof cannot be regarded as attributable to them; that when all persons who submitted reemployment applications were rehired, the submission of reemployment applications appears to have been merely a formal procedure; and taking these points together, it was improper to deny succession of employment to the Plaintiffs merely because they submitted the reemployment applications four days after the designated date. In light of the record, the foregoing fact-finding and determination by the court below are proper, and because the Plaintiffs did not submit reemployment applications within the designated period for the reasons stated above, it cannot be regarded as meaning that they refused succession of their employment relationships to the Intervenor Company or that they manifested an intention to terminate the employment relationship. The grounds of appeal disputing this point likewise cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. The court below, based on the evidence it cited, recognized the fact as found in the judgment that each of the Plaintiffs submitted a letter of resignation to Donghae after April 6, 1998, after having submitted reemployment applications on April 4, 1998, and still held that: (1) since the contract in this case, in substance, constitutes a business transfer, the employment contract relationships of the Plaintiffs with Donghae were transferred to the Intervenor Company on April 1, 1998, when the Intervenor Company acquired the business, as employment contract relationships with the Intervenor Company, unless there were special circumstances such as just cause for dismissal; therefore, even if the Plaintiffs, who had already acquired the status of employees of the Intervenor Company, later submitted letters of resignation to Donghae, they cannot be said to have been workers who had already resigned from Donghae before the business transfer, and thus the Plaintiffs cannot be excluded from the object of succession of employment by the Intervenor Company; and (2) moreover, there is no material showing that there were circumstances justifying the abandonment of the intention to be reemployed immediately after the Plaintiffs submitted reemployment applications to the Intervenor Company; the Plaintiffs did not submit their letters of resignation voluntarily but did so at the recommendation of the Intervenor Company side, and in particular, in the case of the younger Plaintiffs 3 and 2, due to persuasion by the Intervenor Company side involving their fathers, it appears that they drafted and submitted the letters of resignation without even properly understanding what significance the submission of the letters of resignation had; the Plaintiffs consistently insisted on automatic succession of employment while opposing bonus reductions until the submission of the letters of resignation; and in light of the fact that, not long after submitting the letters of resignation, on April 29, 1998, they filed with the Seoul Regional Labor Relations Commission an application for remedy for unfair dismissal against the Intervenor Company while insisting on succession of employment, it cannot be regarded that the letters of resignation submitted by the Plaintiffs contained an intention to abandon the application for reemployment to the Intervenor Company. Accordingly, it rejected the Intervenor’s argument that the submission of the letters of resignation constituted grounds for denial of succession of employment.\\n\\nAlthough, as a result of a business transfer, the employment relationships between the transferor and the workers are, in principle, comprehensively succeeded to by the transferee, a worker may, by expressing an intention to the contrary, either remain with the transferor company in lieu of succeeding to the acquiring company or resign from both the transferor company and the acquiring company. Even if, in the course of the business transfer, a worker has once expressed an intention to seek employment with the acquiring company, if succession employment has not yet been finalized, that worker should be regarded as being able to express the above contrary intention by withdrawing the expression of intention to seek employment.\\n\\nOn the premise of the foregoing legal principle, examination of the record shows that the court below’s holding that the Plaintiffs’ letters of resignation could not be regarded as containing an intention to abandon reemployment with the Intervenor Company is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nAccording to the evidence admitted by the court below, the Plaintiffs submitted reemployment applications on April 4, 1998, but they were rejected on the ground that the submission deadline had passed and they had not received hiring approval from the Intervenor Company. Then, when the other employees hired by the Intervenor Company reported to work on April 6 of the same month and the factory began operation, Plaintiff 1, in an interview with Nonparty 1, who was in charge of personnel affairs at the Intervenor Company, submitted a letter of resignation saying that he would seek another job for his livelihood; Plaintiff 2, while insisting on succession of employment and continuing a sit-in with another union member in the union office, submitted a letter of resignation on the same day, April 7, after Nonparty 2, a section chief in the general affairs department of the Intervenor Company, brought the Plaintiff’s father to Seoul and, through discussion with the father, urged him to take the Plaintiff back to his hometown so that the Plaintiff would not be able to participate in union activities; Plaintiff 3, while not reporting to work at either Donghae or the Intervenor Company from April 1, 1998 and stating in a telephone conversation with Nonparty 3, an employee of the Intervenor Company, that he no longer had any intention of working for either company, received from Nonparty 3, on April 8, when Nonparty 3 visited the Plaintiff’s home and delivered a resignation form to the Plaintiff’s father, and then, two weeks later, mailed to the Intervenor Company a resignation letter backdated to March 31, 1998. The employees who received the resignation letters from the Plaintiffs were persons who had worked at Donghae and then joined the Intervenor Company and were responsible for personnel affairs. The Plaintiffs, by submitting the letters of resignation, received from Donghae an additional retirement consolation payment equivalent to two months’ wages. In light of the timing of the submission of the Plaintiffs’ letters of resignation and the circumstances of their submission, it is appropriate to view the resignation letters submitted by the Plaintiffs as, although formally drafted as resigning from Donghae, in substance containing an intention to withdraw or abandon the application for reemployment with the Intervenor Company as well as to resign from Donghae, and the fact that, as the court below noted, the Plaintiffs had submitted reemployment applications while insisting on succession of employment to the Intervenor Company, or the fact that, not long after the Plaintiffs submitted their resignation letters, they filed an application for remedy for unfair dismissal against the Intervenor Company while insisting on succession of employment, does not warrant a different conclusion.\\n\\nAccordingly, the court below erred in finding that the Plaintiffs’ letters of resignation could not be regarded as containing a manifestation of intent to abandon reemployment with the Intervenor Company, by misapprehending the facts in violation of the rules governing the assessment of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning succession of employment and resignation following a business transfer, and it is clear that this affected the outcome of the judgment. The grounds of appeal pointing out this issue are well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination. The decision is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the panel of judges who participated."}

{"[2021DA305659]": "We examine the grounds of final appeal.\\n\\n1. The court below, for the reasons stated in its holding, determined that, around 2015. 1. 7., when the Defendant resumed casino operations under the name “○○ Jeju” or “○○ Jeju Casino,” the Plaintiffs knew that, through the instant contract, the Defendant had acquired △△△ Ocean’s casino-related business but had not assumed the instant chip-exchange debt, and that, in light of the temporal interval from the date of conclusion of the business transfer contract until they became aware of the non-assumption of the debt and the fact that they did not take measures such as preservative dispositions against △△△ Ocean, it is difficult to view the Plaintiffs as having lost the opportunity to pursue their claims due to the Defendant’s use of the same trade name; accordingly, it held that the Plaintiffs, as creditors in bad faith, could not hold the Defendant, as the transferee of the business, liable under Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act.\\n\\n2. However, the judgment of the court below cannot be accepted for the following reasons.\\n\\na. Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act, which provides for the liability of a transferee of a business who uses the same trade name, is a provision enacted to impose liability for payment on the transferee as well in cases where, although a creditor of the business generally has, in substance, his or her credit secured by the debtor’s business assets, if an actual business transfer is made and the assumption of debts is excluded, the creditor’s claim becomes separated from the business assets, thereby harming the creditor; that is, where a method of business transfer that causes the creditor to lose the opportunity to pursue the claim, namely, a method in which the fact of the business transfer is difficult to be externally disclosed because the same trade name is used despite the non-assumption of debts, or a method in which the fact that debts were not assumed is difficult to be externally disclosed despite the business transfer, is adopted, the transferee is also made liable for payment (see Supreme Court Decision 88DAKA10128, Dec. 26, 1989, Supreme Court Decision 96DA8826, Apr. 14, 1998, etc.). Even where the name used by the transferee is not the trade name itself but a shop name or business sign, if it is used to indicate the business entity, it is no different from the ordinary case of use of the same trade name in that the creditor cannot easily know of the change in the business operator or whether debts were assumed; therefore, unless special circumstances exist, the transferee bears liability for such debt by analogical application of Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DA35138, Sept. 30, 2010, etc.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, because the liability of a transferee of a business who uses the same trade name is intended, after all, to protect creditors who were deprived of the opportunity to pursue their claims by a business transfer without assumption of debts, no liability arises under Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act with respect to creditors in bad faith who know that, despite the business transfer, the debts were not assumed (see the above Supreme Court Decision 88DAKA10128 and Supreme Court Decision 2011DA64867, Mar. 29, 2012, etc.), and the burden of allegation and proof as to the creditor’s bad faith lies with the business transferee seeking to be relieved from such liability (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DA17123, 17130, Jan. 15, 2009, etc.). Furthermore, considering the purpose of creditor protection and the purpose of Article 42(2) of the Commercial Act, which requires registration or notice of the transferee’s non-liability to be made without delay after the business is transferred in order to be exempt from the application of Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act, if the creditor knew at the time of the business transfer, or came to know around that time, that no assumption of debts had occurred, the business transferee’s liability for payment does not arise; however, if the creditor did not know, around the time of the business transfer, that there had been no assumption of debts, then, unless special circumstances exist, the business transferee’s liability for payment under Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act arises, and even if the creditor later comes to know that there had been no assumption of debts, the business transferee’s liability for payment that has already arisen does not cease.\\n\\nb. According to the reasons stated in the judgment below and the record, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n\\n1) On 2014. 6. 2., the Defendant entered into the instant contract, a business transfer contract concerning the assets, liabilities, and rights and obligations necessary for the casino business, with △△△ Ocean. Under the instant contract, the Defendant acquired all casino business equipment, the tenant status under the lease contract concerning the business premises building and facilities, and assets such as the casino business license obtained by △△△ Ocean under the relevant statutes, but, with respect to liabilities, assumed only the obligation to pay retirement benefits to employees whose employment was succeeded from △△△ Ocean.\\n\\nThe Defendant did not register or notify the Plaintiffs, who are creditors, that it bore no responsibility for liabilities other than the above retirement-benefit payment obligation.\\n\\n2) After the instant contract, the Defendant conducted casino business, including chip exchange operations for chips previously issued by △△△ Ocean, while continuing to use the business name “△△△ Casino” that had been used by △△△ Ocean.\\n\\n3) On 2014. 10. 20., the Defendant suspended casino operations for renovation work on the business premises, and then, after completing the renovation work on 2015. 1. 7., changed the business name from “△△△ Casino” to “○○ Jeju Casino” and resumed operations.\\n\\nc. In light of the foregoing legal principles, the above factual circumstances indicate that, after acquiring the casino business through the instant contract, the Defendant conducted business using the business name “△△△ Casino” that had been used by △△△ Ocean until 2014. 10., and no registration or notice was made to indicate that there was no liability to creditors of △△△ Ocean; therefore, by analogical application of Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act, the Defendant, as the transferee of the business, bears liability to pay the instant chip-exchange debt to the Plaintiffs, who are creditors of the transferor of the business. On the basis of the circumstances cited by the court below alone, it is difficult to conclude that, around the time the Defendant acquired the casino business and used the business name, the Plaintiffs knew that, despite the business transfer, the instant chip-exchange debt had not been assumed by the Defendant; thus, it is difficult to view the Plaintiffs as creditors in bad faith.\\n\\nFurthermore, since the Defendant’s liability for payment had already arisen, it cannot be said that the Defendant’s liability for payment ceased merely because the Plaintiffs came to know around 2015. 1., approximately seven months after the instant contract was made, that the instant chip-exchange debt had not been assumed, or because they did not take measures such as preservative dispositions against △△△ Ocean, the transferor of the business.\\n\\nd. Nevertheless, the court below held that the Defendant could not be held liable under Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act on the ground that the Plaintiffs came to know around 2015. 1. of the business transfer and the non-assumption of the instant chip-exchange debt, and that, by not taking measures such as preservative dispositions against the business transferor for a considerable period after the business transfer, this case did not fall under a case in which they lost the opportunity to pursue their claims due to use of the same trade name. In such judgment of the court below, there is error that affected the judgment by violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act. The Plaintiffs’ assertion of grounds for final appeal pointing this out has merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the judgment below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for a new trial and determination, and the judgment is rendered as follows, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2021DA305659]": "We adjudicate the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. The court below, for the reasons stated in its holding, determined that, at around 2015. 1. 7., when the Plaintiff resumed casino operations under the names “○○ Jeju” or “○○ Jeju Casino,” the Plaintiffs knew that, through the contract at issue, the Defendant had acquired △△△ Ocean’s casino-related business but had not assumed the exchange debt at issue; and, considering the temporal gap between the date of conclusion of the business transfer agreement and the time when they became aware of the non-assumption of debt, as well as the fact that they did not take measures such as preservative dispositions against △△△ Ocean, it is difficult to view the Plaintiffs as having lost the opportunity to pursue their claims due to the Defendant’s use of the same trade name. However, the judgment of the court below cannot be accepted for the following reasons.\\n\\nA. Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act, which prescribes the liability of a transferee of a business who continues to use the same trade name, is a provision enacted to impose liability for performance on the transferee even where, in general, a business creditor’s confidence in the debtor is in most cases substantially secured by the debtor’s business assets, because if, in the course of an actual transfer of business, the assumption of debts is excluded, the creditor’s claim is separated from the business assets, thereby harming the creditor; thus, where a method of business transfer is adopted that causes the creditor to lose the opportunity to pursue the claim, namely, where the debts are not assumed but the same trade name is continued so that the fact of the business transfer is not easily apparent externally, or where, despite the business transfer, the fact that the debts were not assumed is not easily apparent externally, the transferee is also made liable for payment (see Supreme Court Decisions 88DAKA10128 dated 1989. 12. 26. and 96DA8826 dated 1998. 4. 14., among others). Even when the name continued to be used by the transferee is not the trade name itself but a shop name or business sign, if it is used to indicate the business operator, it is no different from the case of ordinary continuation of a trade name in that the creditor cannot easily know of the change of the business operator or whether debts were assumed; therefore, unless there are special circumstances, the transferee bears the debt by analogy to Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DA35138 dated 2010. 9. 30., among others).\\n\\nMeanwhile, because the liability of a transferee of a business who continues to use the same trade name is intended solely to protect creditors who were deprived of the opportunity to pursue their claims by a business transfer without assumption of debts, no liability arises under Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act vis-à-vis a creditor in bad faith who knows that, despite the business transfer, there was no assumption of debts (see the above Supreme Court Decision 88DAKA10128 and Supreme Court Decision 2011DA64867 dated 2012. 3. 29., among others), and the burden of assertion and proof as to the creditor’s bad faith lies with the transferee who seeks to be relieved of such liability (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DA17123, 17130 dated 2009. 1. 15., among others). Furthermore, in light of the purpose of protecting creditors and the purport of Article 42(2) of the Commercial Act, which provides that where the transferee’s non-liability is to be registered or notified in order to avoid the application of Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act, this must be done without delay after the business transfer is received, if the creditor knew, at the time of the business transfer, or came to know around that time, that there was no assumption of debts, then the transferee’s liability for performance does not arise; however, if the creditor did not know, around the time of the business transfer, that there was no assumption of debts, then, unless there are special circumstances, the transferee’s liability for performance under Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act arises, and even if the creditor later comes to know that there was no assumption of debts, the transferee’s already arisen liability for performance does not extinguish.\\n\\nB. According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n1) The Defendant, on 2014. 6. 2., concluded the contract at issue, which is a business transfer agreement concerning the assets, liabilities, and rights and obligations necessary for the casino business with △△△ Ocean. Pursuant to the contract at issue, the Defendant acquired all casino business equipment, the lessee status under the lease agreement concerning the business premises building and facilities, and the assets such as the casino business license acquired by △△△ Ocean under the relevant statutes, while, with respect to liabilities, it assumed only the obligation to pay retirement benefits for employees who succeeded to employment from △△△ Ocean.\\n\\nThe Defendant neither registered that it had no liability for liabilities other than the above retirement benefit payment obligation nor notified the creditor Plaintiffs of that effect.\\n\\n2) After the contract at issue, the Defendant conducted casino business, including the exchange of chips previously issued by △△△ Ocean, while continuing to use the business establishment name “△△△ Casino” that △△△ Ocean had used.\\n\\n3) The Defendant suspended casino operations for renovation work on the business premises on 2014. 10. 20., and after completing the renovation work, changed the business establishment name from “△△△ Casino” to “○○ Jeju Casino” and resumed operations on 2015. 1. 7.\\n\\nC. Examining these factual circumstances in light of the legal principles stated above, after acquiring the casino business through the contract at issue, the Defendant continued business operations by using until 2014. 10. the business establishment name “△△△ Casino” that △△△ Ocean had used, and no registration or notification to the creditors that the Defendant had no liability for △△△ Ocean’s creditors was made; therefore, the Defendant, as the transferee of the business, bears the duty to pay the exchange debt at issue to the Plaintiffs, who are creditors of the transferor, by analogy to Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act. On the basis of the circumstances cited by the court below alone, it is difficult to conclude that, around the time the Defendant acquired the casino business and continued to use the business establishment name, the Plaintiffs knew that, despite that business transfer, the exchange debt at issue had not been assumed by the Defendant; accordingly, it is difficult to view the Plaintiffs as creditors in bad faith.\\n\\nFurthermore, once the Defendant’s liability for performance had already arisen, it cannot be deemed that the Defendant’s liability for performance extinguished merely because the Plaintiffs came to know around 2015. 1., when about 7 months had elapsed since the contract at issue was concluded, of the fact of non-assumption of the exchange debt at issue, or because they did not take measures such as preservative dispositions against △△△ Ocean, the transferor of the business.\\n\\nD. Nevertheless, the court below held that the Defendant could not be held liable under Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act on the ground that the Plaintiffs came to know around 2015. 1. of the business transfer and the fact that the exchange debt at issue had not been assumed, and that by failing to take measures such as preservative dispositions against the transferor for a considerable period after the business transfer, this case did not fall under a case where they lost the opportunity to pursue their claim due to the continuation of the trade name. In so holding, the court below erred by violating the rules of logic and experience and thus exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles regarding Article 42(1) of the Commercial Act, thereby affecting the judgment. The Plaintiffs’ allegation of error in the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Accordingly, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination, and it is so adjudged by the concurrence of the Justices participating in the decision."}

question: Which of the following explanations concerning security by provisional registration is incorrect? (In case of dispute, according to precedents)
A: Under the Act on Security by Provisional Registration, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Provisional Registration Security Act”), where an order to commence compulsory auction has been issued with respect to real property for which a security provisional registration has been completed, if the application for auction was made before payment of the liquidation amount (or, where there is no liquidation amount, before the liquidation period has elapsed), the holder of the security provisional registration may not demand the principal registration pursuant to that provisional registration.
B: Where, in violation of the liquidation procedure under the Provisional Registration Security Act, a principal registration based on a security provisional registration has been made, if, in the auction procedure conducted with respect to the real property subject to security, the purchaser acquired ownership by purchasing the real property without knowing that the principal registration was invalid, the debtor may no longer pay the entire amount of the secured obligation to the creditor and request cancellation of that principal registration.
C: Where, after a provisional registration has been made for the purpose of securing both an obligation to repay borrowed money arising from a contract of loan for consumption and an obligation arising from another cause, the latter obligation has been extinguished by payment or other cause and only the obligation to repay borrowed money arising from the contract of loan for consumption remains, the Provisional Registration Security Act does not apply to that security by provisional registration.
D: Where a principal registration completed without going through the liquidation procedure under the Provisional Registration Security Act is void, if the debtor has concluded a lease contract with the creditor concerning the real property subject to security and has paid rent to the creditor, such rent shall, unless special circumstances exist, be deemed to have been appropriated to the satisfaction of the secured obligation.
E: In the private execution of a security right by provisional registration, execution of the security right in a manner whereby the creditor may receive the principal registration and delivery of the secured property before payment of the liquidation amount, or in a manner that does not recognize the liquidation period or the relationship of simultaneous performance, is not permitted under the Provisional Registration Security Act.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2001DA81856]": "1. According to the Act on Security by Provisional Registration, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Provisional Registration Security Act”), in order for a holder of a provisional registration security right to acquire ownership of immovable property that is the object of the security for the execution of the security right, after the due date of the claim the holder must notify the debtor, etc. of the prescribed assessed settlement amount or that there is no settlement amount (Article 3(1)); and since the debtor, etc. at that time includes not only the debtor and the in rem surety but also a third-party acquirer who has acquired ownership after the provisional registration for security (Article 2 item 2), such notice must be given to all of them, and if such notice is not given to all or some of the debtor, etc., the settlement period cannot run; accordingly, the holder of the provisional registration security right cannot thereafter, even if an appropriate settlement amount is paid or even if there is no settlement amount actually to be paid, demand principal registration based on the provisional registration, and even if principal registration was completed by an improper means, ownership cannot be acquired thereby (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA36162, decided on 1995. 4. 28.).\\n\\nAccording to the factual findings lawfully determined by the court below and the record, the Plaintiff lent money to Non-party 1 on 1998. 9. 11. and, in order to secure the same, completed a provisional registration of a right to demand transfer of ownership, naming the Plaintiff as the right holder, with respect to the house at issue owned by Non-party 2, who was a joint surety for Non-party 1; thereafter, when Non-party 1 failed to properly repay the above borrowed money, the Plaintiff filed a lawsuit seeking performance of the procedure for principal registration based on the provisional registration, with the cause of action being that the Plaintiff had exercised the right to complete the reservation for sale against Non-party 2 while concealing the fact that the above provisional registration had been completed for security purposes, and thus a judgment fully in favor of the Plaintiff became final on 2000. 1. 8.; accordingly, principal registration based on the above provisional registration was completed in the Plaintiff’s name with respect to the house at issue on the 27th of the same month; however, Non-party 2, before the Plaintiff completed the above principal registration, had already completed on 1999. 4. 12. a registration of transfer of ownership to Non-party 3, based on sale, with respect to the house at issue, and the Defendant, after purchasing the house at issue from Non-party 3 around 1999. 8. 25. and having paid only part of the purchase price, is in possession of it; on the other hand, it can be fully ascertained that, in the process of the above principal registration, the Plaintiff had never notified Non-party 1, Non-party 2, or Non-party 3, etc. of the assessed settlement amount or that there was no settlement amount. In light of the legal principles stated above, even if the Plaintiff completed the above principal registration with respect to the house at issue, since this was done without the settlement procedure prescribed by the Provisional Registration Security Act, it must be deemed that the Plaintiff could not acquire ownership of the house at issue by such principal registration.\\n\\nIn the same purport, the court below’s determination rejecting the Plaintiff’s assertion that the Plaintiff acquired ownership of the house at issue by completing the above settlement procedure is proper, and there is no error such as misapprehension of legal principles, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. The Provisional Registration Security Act, while prescribing in Articles 3 and 4 the principle of appropriation settlement as a private method of execution of a provisional registration security right, separately prescribes in Articles 12 and 13 disposition settlement, such as a request for auction and the right to demand preferential reimbursement, as a public method of execution; Article 4, in paragraphs (1) through (3), sequentially provides for the creditor’s obligation to pay the settlement amount, the expiration of the settlement period and the request for principal registration, and the concurrent performance relationship between the obligation to pay the settlement amount and the obligation to register transfer of ownership of real property and deliver the property; and then paragraph (4) provides that any special agreement contrary to paragraphs (1) through (3) and unfavorable to the debtor, etc. shall have no effect (however, excluding special agreements made after the expiration of the settlement period that do not prejudice the rights of a third party); furthermore, taking Article 11 into comprehensive consideration, which provides that the debtor, etc. may, until the settlement amount claim is repaid, pay the amount of his obligation to the creditor and demand cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership effected for the purpose of securing the claim, it must be deemed that, in the private execution of a provisional registration security right, an execution of the security right in the form of “disposition settlement,” which would allow the creditor to receive principal registration and delivery of the secured property before payment of the settlement amount, or which would deny the settlement period or the concurrent performance relationship, is not permitted under the Provisional Registration Security Act.\\n\\nIn the present case, the Plaintiff asserts, without going through any settlement procedure, that “the Plaintiff has the right to demand delivery from the Defendant, who is in possession of the house at issue for the purpose of taking delivery of the house at issue, disposing of it, and then carrying out settlement.” In light of the legal principles stated above, such conventional method of disposition settlement cannot be permitted under the Provisional Registration Security Act.\\n\\nAlthough the court below’s reasoning on this point is insufficient, the court below’s rejection of the Plaintiff’s above assertion is ultimately proper, and there is no error such as misapprehension of legal principles that affected the judgment, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and judgment is rendered as set forth in the order."}
