question: B established in favor of A, in order to secure a debt arising from continuing goods transactions with A, a security mortgage with a maximum secured amount of KRW 100,000,000 on X land owned by debtor B. B's friend C established a security mortgage with a maximum secured amount of KRW 100,000,000 on Y building owned by C in order to secure B's above debt. Thereafter, with respect to X land, D acquired a second-ranking mortgage (secured claim: KRW 80,000,000). After the goods transaction ended due to B's default, Y building was first auctioned upon A's application, and at that time A's claim for the price of goods was KRW 110,000,000 (principal KRW 100,000,000, delay damages KRW 10,000,000), and the sale proceeds of KRW 80,000,000 were distributed in full to A (applied to delay damages KRW 10,000,000 and principal KRW 70,000,000). Thereafter, X land was auctioned upon A's application, and at that time A's claim was KRW 35,000,000 (principal KRW 30,000,000, delay damages KRW 5,000,000), and the sale proceeds were KRW 75,000,000. Which of the following statements concerning this are all correct? (Execution costs are not considered. Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, precedents shall govern.)
A: (a) If the security mortgages over X land and Y building are a joint mortgage, A may receive a dividend of KRW 20,000,000 from the auction proceeds of X land.
B: (a) If the security mortgages over X land and Y building are a joint mortgage, A may receive a dividend of KRW 20,000,000 from the auction proceeds of X land.
C: (a) If the security mortgages over X land and Y building are a joint mortgage, A may receive a dividend of KRW 20,000,000 from the auction proceeds of X land.
D: (a) If the security mortgages over X land and Y building are a joint mortgage, A may receive a dividend of KRW 20,000,000 from the auction proceeds of X land.
E: (a) If the security mortgages over X land and Y building are a joint mortgage, A may receive a dividend of KRW 20,000,000 from the auction proceeds of X land.

supporting_precedents: {"[2011DA50233]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. As to Grounds 1 and 2 of the appeal\\n\\nThe court below held that, on the evidence submitted by the Plaintiffs alone, it was insufficient to find that the Defendant was the de facto debtor of the loan at issue or that the non-party repaid the loan at issue, and that the Defendant, as a real property surety, had made subrogated payment of the loan obligation of the non-party debtor at issue.\\n\\nUpon review in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, this determination of the court below is proper, and there is no illegality in that it did not exceed the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, nor did it misapprehend the legal principles concerning the right of recourse or subrogation by performance.\\n\\n2. As to Grounds 3 and 4 of the appeal\\n\\nCivil Act Article 481 provides, “A person who has a legitimate interest in making performance shall, by performance, subrogate the creditor as a matter of course.” Civil Act Article 482(1) provides, “A person who is subrogated to the creditor pursuant to the provisions of the preceding two Articles may exercise the rights concerning the claim and its security to the extent that he or she may seek recourse by virtue of his or her own rights.” Paragraph 2 of the same Article provides, “The exercise of the rights under the preceding paragraph shall be governed by the provisions of the following items,” but among them there is no clear provision concerning subrogation by performance between a real property surety and a third-party acquirer.\\n\\nHowever, with respect to subrogation by performance between a guarantor and a third-party acquirer, Civil Act Article 482(2) Item 1 provides, “Unless the guarantor has previously noted the subrogation in the registration of the leasehold right or mortgage, the guarantor may not subrogate the creditor against a third party who has acquired rights in the leased property or mortgaged property.” Item 2 of the same paragraph provides, “A third-party acquirer may not subrogate the creditor against the guarantor.” Meanwhile, according to Civil Act Article 370 and Article 341, when a real property surety has paid the obligation or lost ownership through enforcement of the security right, the real property surety has a right of recourse against the debtor pursuant to the provisions concerning “guarantee obligations,” and according to Civil Act Article 482(2) Item 5, between a real property surety and a guarantor, each is merely to subrogate the creditor in proportion to the number of persons, and no priority between them is recognized. Taking the content of these provisions together, when a real property surety has paid the obligation or lost ownership through enforcement of the security right, then, just like a guarantor who has performed a guarantee obligation, the real property surety may subrogate the creditor, within the scope of the right of recourse, for the entire amount paid out against a third party who acquired the secured real property from the debtor, whereas a third party who acquired the secured real property from the debtor should be deemed unable to subrogate the creditor against the real property surety even if that third party pays the obligation or loses ownership through enforcement of the security right. If, contrary to this, the status of a real property surety is regarded as different from that of a guarantor, so that between a real property surety and a third party who acquired the secured real property from the debtor, each may subrogate the creditor only in proportion to the value of each real property, then the real property surety, who could originally subrogate for the entire amount paid out against the debtor, would now, due to the accidental circumstance that the debtor transferred ownership of the secured real property to a third party, be able to subrogate only in proportion to the value of each real property, whereas the third party who acquired the secured real property from the debtor, having accepted the burden of the security right over the entire amount of the debt from the outset, would obtain an unexpected benefit to that extent, which is unjust.\\n\\nTo the contrary, Supreme Court Decision 74DA1419, rendered on 1974. 12. 10., which held that a third-party acquirer who purchased secured real property may subrogate the creditor against the real property surety in proportion to the value of each real property, is to be altered to the extent that it conflicts with the view of this judgment.\\n\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in its judgment, held that, as the Defendant, a real property surety, had repaid the non-party debtor’s loan obligation at issue, the Defendant could exercise subrogation rights with respect to the mortgage at issue to the extent of the full amount paid out against the Plaintiffs, who acquired from the said non-party the orchard shares at issue over which the mortgage at issue was established, and dismissed the Plaintiffs’ claim for cancellation of the registration of the mortgage creation at issue.\\n\\nUpon review in light of the legal principles stated above and the record, this determination of the court below is proper, and there is no illegality in its misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the right of recourse and subrogation by performance.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged as per the disposition, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2011DA50233]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. As to Grounds 1 and 2 of the appeal\\n\\nThe court below found that, based solely on the evidence submitted by the Plaintiffs, it was insufficient to recognize that the Defendant was the de facto debtor of the loan at issue or that the non-party had repaid the loan at issue, and further determined that the Defendant, as a real surety, had made a subrogated payment of the debtor non-party’s loan obligation at issue.\\n\\nUpon review in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the court below’s determination is proper, and there is no illegality in that it did not exceed the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, nor did it misapprehend the legal principles concerning the right of reimbursement or subrogation by a person who has performed an obligation.\\n\\n2. As to Grounds 3 and 4 of the appeal\\n\\nArticle 481 of the Civil Act provides, “A person who has a legitimate interest in making performance shall, by such performance, be subrogated to the creditor by operation of law.” Article 482(1) of the Civil Act provides, “A person who has been subrogated to the creditor pursuant to the provisions of the preceding two Articles may exercise the rights pertaining to the claim and its security within the extent that he or she may claim reimbursement by virtue of his or her own right.” Paragraph (2) of the same Article provides, “The exercise of the rights referred to in the preceding paragraph shall be governed by the provisions of the following subparagraphs,” but among them there is no clear provision concerning subrogation by a person who has performed an obligation as between a real surety and a third-party acquirer.\\n\\nMeanwhile, with respect to subrogation by a person who has performed an obligation as between a surety and a third-party acquirer, Article 482(2) subparagraph 1 of the Civil Act provides, “A surety may not, unless he or she has previously recorded the subrogation as an additional entry in the registration of a leasehold right or mortgage, subrogate to the creditor against a third person who has acquired rights in the leased property or mortgaged property.” Subparagraph 2 of the same paragraph provides, “A third-party acquirer may not subrogate to the creditor against a surety.” On the other hand, under Articles 370 and 341 of the Civil Act, when a real surety has discharged the obligation or lost ownership through enforcement of a security right, he or she has a right of reimbursement against the debtor pursuant to the provisions concerning “surety obligations,” and according to Article 482(2) subparagraph 5 of the Civil Act, as between real sureties and sureties, only subrogation to the creditor is recognized in proportion to the number of persons, and no priority between them is recognized. Considering the contents of the above provisions together, when a real surety discharges the obligation or loses ownership through enforcement of a security right, unlike a surety who has performed a surety obligation, the real surety may, against a third person who acquired the secured real property from the debtor, subrogate to the creditor with respect to the full amount paid out, within the scope of the right of reimbursement; whereas a third person who acquired the secured real property from the debtor, even if he or she repays the obligation or loses ownership through enforcement of the security right, should be deemed unable to subrogate to the creditor against the real surety. If, by distinguishing the position of a real surety from that of a surety, it were said that, as between a real surety and a third person who acquired the secured real property from the debtor, subrogation to the creditor is possible in proportion to the value of each real property, then the real surety, who originally could subrogate with respect to the full amount paid out against the debtor, would now, due to the fortuitous circumstance that the debtor transferred ownership of the secured real property to a third person, be subrogated only in proportion to the value of each real property, whereas the third person who acquired the secured real property from the debtor, having originally accepted the burden of the security right for the full amount of the debt, would undeservedly obtain a benefit to that extent, which would be unjust.\\n\\nIn contrast, Supreme Court Decision 74DA1419 rendered on December 10, 1974, which held that a third-party acquirer who purchased secured real property may subrogate to the creditor against a real surety in proportion to the value of each real property, shall be modified to the extent that it is inconsistent with the view expressed in this decision.\\n\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in its judgment, determined that, since the Defendant, a real surety, had repaid the debtor non-party’s loan obligation at issue, the Defendant may exercise subrogation of the mortgage at issue, within the extent of the full amount paid out by the Defendant, against the Plaintiffs who acquired from the said non-party the ownership interest in the orchard at issue over which the mortgage at issue had been established, and therefore dismissed the Plaintiffs’ claim for cancellation of the registration of creation of the mortgage at issue.\\n\\nUpon review in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the court below’s determination is proper, and there is no illegality in that it misapprehended the legal principles concerning the right of reimbursement and subrogation by a person who has performed an obligation.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and it is adjudged as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Judges involved."}

{"[2013DA16992]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Regarding Grounds of Appeal 1 and 4\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment, the court below found that: (1) the Defendant had, in the rehabilitation proceeding stated in the judgment of the court below against Neosteel Co., Ltd., which was both the debtor and the owner of the real property listed in Schedule 1 attached to the judgment of the court below (hereinafter referred to as “the First Real Property in this case”), with respect to the joint maximum mortgage stated in the judgment of the court below concerning the First Real Property in this case (hereinafter referred to as “the Joint Maximum Mortgage in this case”), been recognized as a rehabilitation secured claim within the appraised value of the First Real Property in this case, and on that basis had received a total of 4,109,272,480 won from the business transfer price, including the First Real Property, in accordance with the rehabilitation plan of the Rehabilitation Proceeding in this case; and then (2) this corresponds to a case in which a distribution was received in a realization proceeding over mortgaged property subject to a joint maximum mortgage by exercising the right to preferential repayment of the mortgagee, and it is difficult to regard it as having the character of a debtor’s voluntary payment.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the relevant legal principles stated by the court below and the evidence lawfully admitted, the court below’s determination is sustainable, and there is no illegality, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in that the Defendant failed to conduct the necessary examination regarding the amount distributed to it as mortgagee pursuant to the Rehabilitation Plan in this case, or that it acted in violation of the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeded the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misconstrued the legal principles regarding the exercise of the right to preferential repayment of a mortgagee.\\n\\n2. Regarding Grounds of Appeal 2 and 3\\n\\nA. (1) Where a joint maximum mortgagee, by executing the mortgage itself or through realization proceedings such as auction, public sale, expropriation proceedings, or rehabilitation proceedings, etc. (hereinafter referred to as “realization proceedings such as auction”), receives distribution or repayment in priority to other right holders with respect to part of the secured claim from the realization proceeds or compensation for expropriation, etc. concerning some of the real properties subject to the common security, the question arises whether the joint maximum mortgagee may again exercise, as a joint maximum mortgagee, the right to preferential repayment with respect to the remaining secured claim from realization proceeds, etc. in realization proceedings such as auction concerning the remaining real properties subject to the common security, again within the scope of the initial maximum claim amount.\\n\\n(2) Article 368(1) of the Civil Act provides: “Where a mortgage is established over several immovables as security for the same claim, if the auction proceeds of such immovables are distributed simultaneously, the burden of the claim shall be apportioned in proportion to the auction proceeds of each immovable.” Paragraph (2) provides: “If the auction proceeds of some of the mortgaged immovables under the preceding paragraph are distributed first, the entire claim may be satisfied from such proceeds. In such case, the junior mortgagee of the auctioned immovable may, to the extent of the amount that the senior mortgagee may receive satisfaction from the auction proceeds of other immovables pursuant to the provisions of the preceding paragraph, exercise the mortgage right by subrogating the senior mortgagee.”\\nWhen several immovables subject to a common mortgage are auctioned simultaneously, the common mortgagee need only have its right to preferential repayment satisfied by receiving distribution from the auction proceeds of any one immovable; however, the owners of each immovable, junior mortgagees, and other creditors have a significant interest in from which immovable’s auction proceeds distribution will be made to the common mortgagee. Article 368(1) of the Civil Act, in the case of so-called simultaneous distribution, in which the total realization proceeds of the real properties subject to a common mortgage are distributed simultaneously, adjusts the interests of the owners of each immovable, junior mortgagees, and other creditors by apportioning the responsibility of each immovable within the extent that does not infringe the common mortgagee’s right of choice of enforcement and right to preferential repayment; and, in addition, paragraph (2) of the same Article provides for a subrogation system so that, even in the case of so-called sequential distribution, in which the auction proceeds of some of the real properties subject to a common mortgage are distributed first, the final result of the distribution is the same as in simultaneous distribution, thereby protecting junior mortgagees who suffer disadvantages due to the common mortgagee’s exercise of the right of choice of enforcement (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DA14502 rendered on 2006. 10. 27., etc.).\\nArticle 368 of the Civil Act also applies to joint maximum mortgages, and applies not only when the joint maximum mortgagee executes the mortgage itself, but also when, in realization proceedings such as auction initiated by another person, it receives distribution in priority to other right holders with respect to part of the secured claim from the realization proceeds, etc. (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DA14502 rendered on 2006. 10. 27.; Supreme Court Decision 2013DA36040 rendered on 2014. 4. 10.; etc.).\\nWhere simultaneous distribution is made with respect to real properties subject to a joint maximum mortgage, the joint maximum mortgagee receives distribution of the secured claim, within the scope of the maximum claim amount, by apportioning it by immovable pursuant to Article 368(1) of the Civil Act and receiving amounts proportionate to the realization proceeds of each immovable; it does not receive, repeatedly for each real property subject to the joint maximum mortgage, distributions cumulatively up to the maximum claim amount.\\nAccordingly, even where sequential distribution is made with respect to real properties subject to a joint maximum mortgage, it is consistent with the purport of Article 368(1) and (2) of the Civil Act to interpret that the joint maximum mortgagee cannot receive, repeatedly up to the maximum claim amount, distribution from each realization proceeds of the real properties subject to the joint maximum mortgage, just as in the case of simultaneous distribution.\\n\\n(3) If, contrary to the foregoing, it were held that even though the joint maximum mortgagee has received distribution in priority to other right holders with respect to part of the real properties subject to a common maximum mortgage in realization proceedings such as auction initiated by another person from the realization proceeds, etc. of such property, it may later again exercise the right to preferential repayment for the entire initial maximum claim amount, unreduced, in realization proceedings such as auction concerning other real properties subject to the common maximum mortgage, the following unreasonable results would arise.\\n\\n(a) A person who seeks to acquire a junior mortgage on real property over which a senior joint maximum mortgage has been established acquires the mortgage by considering, out of the realization proceeds of all the real properties subject to the senior joint maximum mortgage, only the security value equivalent to the maximum claim amount of the joint maximum mortgage as belonging to the senior joint maximum mortgagee and understanding the remaining security value as belonging to that person. However, if the senior joint maximum mortgagee could receive repeated distributions up to the initial maximum claim amount for each real property subject to the joint maximum mortgage, it could cause unforeseen harm to the person who acquired the junior mortgage, and subrogation under Article 368(2) of the Civil Act by the junior mortgagee could become impossible or the scope of subrogation could be reduced; moreover, there is even concern that the joint maximum mortgagee may intentionally choose sequential distribution, and thus this would run counter to the purport of Article 368(2) of the Civil Act, which seeks to protect junior mortgagees who suffer disadvantages from the senior common mortgagee’s exercise of the right of choice of enforcement in the case of sequential distribution.\\n\\n(b) Where a joint maximum mortgage is established over immovable property owned by the debtor and immovable property owned by a third-party security provider, if realization proceedings such as auction are first conducted with respect to the immovable property owned by the third-party security provider and the joint maximum mortgagee receives distribution from the realization proceeds with respect to part of the secured claim, then the third-party security provider acquires, by subrogation through performance, the joint maximum mortgage over the immovable property owned by the debtor within the amount distributed; however, even in such case, the joint maximum mortgagee has the right to preferential repayment in relation to the third-party security provider who effects subrogation through partial performance as stated above (see Supreme Court Decision 93DA25417 rendered on 1994. 5. 10.; Supreme Court Decision 2001DA2426 rendered on 2004. 6. 25.; Supreme Court Decision 2011DA9013 rendered on 2011. 6. 10.; etc.). However, if, despite the foregoing partial distribution, the joint maximum mortgagee could again exercise the right to preferential repayment within the scope of the initial maximum claim amount not reduced with respect to the immovable property owned by the debtor, the third-party security provider’s subrogation through performance would become impossible or the scope of subrogation would be reduced, thereby depriving the third-party security provider, who offered its own immovable property as security in expectation of security value concerning the immovable property owned by the debtor, of its expected benefit.\\n\\n(c) In particular, where the real properties subject to a joint maximum mortgage are owned by the same third-party security provider, such third-party security provider would naturally believe that the scope of liability it would bear would not exceed the maximum claim amount of the above mortgage; however, if, merely because sequential distribution was made, the joint maximum mortgagee were allowed to receive repeated distributions up to the maximum claim amount from the realization proceeds of each real property subject to the joint maximum mortgage, this would result in an expansion of the third-party security provider’s scope of liability irrespective of its intent to provide security. Moreover, where, in the auction proceedings concerning some of the real properties subject to the mortgage, the joint maximum mortgagee passively participates and receives a distribution, and as a result the secured claim secured by the mortgage is not fixed with respect to the remaining real properties, if it becomes possible in the auction proceedings concerning the remaining real properties to receive repeated priority distributions up to the maximum claim amount for the entire secured claim, including the secured claim that has continuously accrued in the meantime, this is wholly contrary to the third-party security provider’s expectation that distribution would occur within the scope of the maximum claim amount; furthermore, irrespective of such intent to provide security, the scope of the third-party security provider’s liability may vary greatly depending on whether the joint maximum mortgagee actively filed for auction or passively participated in a third party’s auction application, thereby resulting in unfairness.\\n\\n(4) Therefore, where the joint maximum mortgagee, by executing the mortgage itself or through realization proceedings such as auction initiated by another person, has received distribution in priority to other right holders with respect to part of the secured claim from the realization proceeds, etc. of some of the real properties subject to the common security, it should be understood that, with respect to the amount so received by preferential repayment, the joint maximum mortgagee may not again exercise the right to preferential repayment in realization proceedings such as auction concerning the remaining real properties subject to the common security; and it is proper to interpret that the scope of the right to preferential repayment that may be exercised by the joint maximum mortgagee over the remaining real properties subject to the common security is limited, regardless of whether the secured claim has been fixed, to the remaining maximum claim amount obtained by deducting the amount so received by preferential repayment from the initial maximum claim amount (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DA14502 rendered on 2006. 10. 27.; Supreme Court Decision 2011DA68012 rendered on 2012. 1. 12.; Supreme Court Decision 2015DA50637 rendered on 2017. 9. 21.; etc.). This legal principle likewise applies where the secured claim exceeding the maximum claim amount consists not of principal, but of interest and delay damages.\\n\\n(5) On the other hand, Supreme Court Decision 2008DA72318 rendered on 2009. 12. 10., which held to the contrary, to the effect that where real properties subject to a joint maximum mortgage are auctioned successively in separate parts, the joint maximum mortgagee may again exercise the right to preferential repayment in realization proceedings such as auction concerning the remaining real properties, even if the sum of the principal, interest, and delay damages distributed in the prior auction proceedings exceeds the amount that is ultimately equal to the maximum claim amount, shall be modified to the extent that it is inconsistent with the view of this judgment.\\n\\nB. The court below determined, for the reasons stated, to the following effect:\\n\\n(1) The Defendant, in the prior realization proceeding, namely the Rehabilitation Proceeding in this case, with respect to the Joint Maximum Mortgage in this case, the maximum claim amount of which was 7.15 billion won, was recognized as a rehabilitation secured claim within the appraised value of the First Real Property in this case, which was part of the real properties subject thereto, and on that basis received preferential repayment of 4,109,272,480 won in accordance with the rehabilitation plan.\\n\\n(2) With respect to the amount thus received by preferential repayment, the Defendant may not, as a joint maximum mortgagee, again exercise the right to preferential repayment in the public sale proceeding conducted after the conclusion of the Rehabilitation Proceeding in this case (hereinafter referred to as “the Public Sale Proceeding in this case”) concerning the real property listed in Schedule 2 attached to the judgment of the court below (hereinafter referred to as “the Second Real Property in this case”), which is another real property subject to the Joint Maximum Mortgage in this case and owned by Blue Valley Co., Ltd.\\n\\n(3) Therefore, the above amount received by preferential repayment in the Rehabilitation Proceeding in this case pursuant to the Joint Maximum Mortgage in this case must be deducted from the maximum claim amount of the Joint Maximum Mortgage in this case by that amount, and the Defendant may receive distribution in the Public Sale Proceeding in this case only within the remaining maximum claim amount after such deduction with respect to the secured claim of the Joint Maximum Mortgage in this case.\\n\\nC. Examining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the evidence lawfully admitted, the court below’s determination appears to be based on the legal principles stated above, and there is no illegality, as alleged in Ground of Appeal 3, in that it misconstrued the legal principles concerning the scope of the maximum claim amount of a joint maximum mortgage for which preferential repayment is possible.\\n\\nAnd according to the legal principles stated above, whether the secured claim of the Joint Maximum Mortgage in this case concerning the Second Real Property in this case is fixed by the decision to commence the Rehabilitation Proceeding in this case against the debtor, Neosteel Co., Ltd., has no effect on the above conclusion of the court below; therefore, the allegation in Ground of Appeal 2 concerning the fixation of the secured claim likewise does not constitute a ground for reversal of the judgment of the court below, without the need to determine its merit.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case, as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning a possessory lien are correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) (a) The indivisibility of a possessory lien, under which the lienholder may exercise the right over the entire retained property until payment of the entire claim is received, also applies even where the subject matter is divisible or consists of several items. (b) Where a lienholder who acquired a possessory lien over several parcels of land with one claim as the secured claim violates the duty of care of a good manager with respect to some of those parcels, the claim for extinguishment of the possessory lien may, absent special circumstances, be made only with respect to the parcel on which the violation occurred. (c) Where a person whose possession of a thing has been dispossessed exercises the right to claim damages arising from the extinguishment of the possessory lien, which is the principal right, that person must exercise it within 1 year from the day possession was dispossessed. (d) In auction proceedings for real property owned by a debtor over which a maximum mortgage has been created, if no possessory lien was asserted, and the real property was sold and title was transferred to the purchaser, thereby extinguishing the maximum mortgage, and thereafter there is a person who claims that he or she had a possessory lien even before the seizure, the creditor, as the maximum mortgagee, has a legal interest in seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of the possessory lien. (e) Where there is a special agreement excluding a possessory lien, no possessory lien arises even if all other statutory requirements are satisfied; however, a person who purchased the retained property in the auction proceedings is not a party to the above agreement and therefore cannot assert the effect of the above agreement.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2016DA234043]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. As a general rule, a limited real right may be freely waived so long as it does not unjustly infringe the interests of interested persons. A lien is a statutory security right established to protect the interests of a creditor, and the parties may enter into a special agreement in advance preventing the creation of a lien; such an agreement is valid. Where there is a special agreement excluding a lien, the lien does not arise even if all other statutory requirements are satisfied, and the effect under such special agreement may be asserted not only by the counterparty to the special agreement but also by others (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of May 13, 2011, 2010MA1544).\\nMeanwhile, a condition is a collateral clause of a juristic act that makes the coming into effect or extinction of the effectiveness of the juristic act depend on whether a future uncertain fact occurs, and it may be regarded as the manifestation of intent itself forming an integral part of the intent to create legal effects in the juristic act. A condition may also be attached to a special agreement excluding a lien, and whether there was an intent to attach such a condition must be determined according to the legal principles governing manifestations of intent.\\nWhere there is a dispute between the parties over the interpretation of an agreement and the interpretation of the parties’ intent as expressed in a dispositive document is at issue, the document must be reasonably interpreted in accordance with logic and the rules of experience by comprehensively considering the contents of the text, the motive and circumstances under which the agreement was reached, the purpose sought to be achieved by the agreement, and the true intent of the parties, among other things (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of June 28, 2002, 2002DA23482, Supreme Court Decision of June 26, 2014, 2014DA14115, and others).\\n\\n2. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n\\na. Seongdu Industrial Development Co., Ltd. (whose trade name was later changed to Namhyeon Plus Co., Ltd.; hereinafter referred to as “Seongdu Industrial Development”) entered into a project agreement and an agency administration contract (hereinafter referred to as “the project agreement at issue”) on July 30, 2008, with Seonjin General Development Co., Ltd. (the contractor; hereinafter referred to as “Seonjin General Development”), Sambo Real Estate Trust Co., Ltd. (the trustee for agency administration), and Sasang Agricultural Cooperative Association (the lending institution), while carrying out a project to construct and sell the building at issue on 2 other parcels in addition to (address omitted), Buk-gu, Pohang-si.\\n\\nb. In the project agreement at issue, the contracting parties stipulated that “Seonjin General Development may not exercise a lien over the newly constructed building on the ground of nonpayment of the construction price” (Article 11, paragraph 6). Around that time, Seonjin General Development prepared and submitted to Sasang Agricultural Cooperative Association a written waiver of construction rights and lien rights, the content of which stated: “If a dishonor, bankruptcy, an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings, the occurrence of other grounds equivalent thereto, or any other circumstance in which this project cannot be carried out normally arises, I shall waive all rights, including the assertion of any lien and construction rights related to this construction.”\\n\\nc. Meanwhile, Seonjin General Development was sequentially subjected to an order commencing rehabilitation proceedings and a declaration of bankruptcy, and the bankruptcy trustee succeeded to the Plaintiff’s status of the manager, Non-Party Person, of the rehabilitation debtor Seonjin General Development Co., Ltd.\\n\\n3. On the basis of the foregoing facts, the lower court determined to the effect that Seonjin General Development, as a party to the project agreement at issue, entered into an agreement waiving the lien, and that the Defendant, as the purchaser of the building at issue in a public auction procedure, may assert the effect of the foregoing special agreement even though it was not a party thereto. Furthermore, in light of the text of the project agreement at issue and the purpose of the agreement, the lower court determined that it was difficult to view the foregoing agreement as having attached the condition that Seonjin General Development would directly receive the construction price from Sambo Real Estate Trust Co., Ltd.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above, the reasons for the lower court judgment reveal no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in that the lower court found that the Plaintiff’s lien did not arise pursuant to the special agreement excluding the lien, nor any error in exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience or misunderstanding the legal principles concerning liens. The Supreme Court Decision cited in the grounds of appeal, 2009DA77730 decided on April 29, 2010, concerns a different factual situation from the present case and is not suitable for citation. The remaining arguments in the grounds of appeal are likewise premised on the proposition that the effect of the special agreement excluding the lien does not extend to the Plaintiff, and thus cannot be accepted.\\n\\n4. Since the Plaintiff’s appeal is without merit, it is dismissed, and the costs of the appeal shall be borne by the losing party; it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2018DA301350]": "We determine the grounds for appeal, including ex officio determinations.\\n\\n1. Claim for Extinguishment of a Possessory Lien and Its Scope (Grounds 1 and 2 for appeal by CK Co., Ltd., the successor-intervenor of the Plaintiff, and the Defendant’s grounds for appeal)\\n\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\n\\n1) Since Civil Act Article 321 provides that “the lienholder may exercise his/her right over the whole of the object of lien until the whole debt is repaid,” each part of the object of lien secures the entirety of the secured claim, and such indivisibility of a possessory lien applies even where the object is divisible or consists of several things (see Supreme Court decision rendered on September 7, 2007, 2005DA16942), and it also applies to a commercial possessory lien under Commercial Act Article 58 (see Supreme Court decision rendered on December 27, 2016, 2016DA244835).\\n\\n2) Civil Act Article 324 provides that “it imposes on the lienholder the duty of care of a good manager with respect to the object of lien, and where the lienholder, in violation thereof, uses, lends, or furnishes the object of lien as security without the debtor’s consent, the debtor may demand extinguishment of the possessory lien.” Where a lienholder who has acquired a possessory lien over several parcels of land with one claim as the secured claim has violated the duty of care of a good manager with respect to some of those parcels, it is reasonable to interpret that, absent special circumstances, a claim for extinguishment of the possessory lien may be made only with respect to the parcel(s) on which the violation occurred. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\na) Where a possessory lien has arisen over several parcels of land, each parcel of land secures the entirety of the secured claim regardless of the other parcels of land by reason of the indivisibility of the possessory lien. At this time, even if possession of some parcels of land is lost, the possessory lien for securing the secured claim remains in effect over the remaining parcels of land. In the same vein, even where a claim for extinguishment of the possessory lien is made on the ground that the lienholder violated the duty of care of a good manager with respect to some parcels of land, it is reasonable to interpret that extinguishment may be claimed only with respect to the parcels on which the violation occurred.\\n\\nb) The purpose of Civil Act Article 321 in providing for the “indivisibility of the possessory lien” is to strengthen the effect of the possessory lien, which is a security right, for the benefit of the lienholder; on that basis, it is not appropriate to interpret that, to the contrary, even the possessory lien over an object of lien as to which no issue of violation of the duty of care of a good manager arises is extinguished to the detriment of the lienholder.\\n\\nc) A possessory lien is a statutory security right that secures preferential satisfaction of the lienholder’s secured claim through the thing possessed (Civil Act Article 320(1), Commercial Act Article 58). On the other hand, the claim for extinguishment of a possessory lien provided in Civil Act Article 324 is a provision intended to protect the debtor or the owner of the object of lien as a sanction for the lienholder’s violation of the duty of care of a good manager. It is a reasonable interpretation, taking into account the balance of interests between the lienholder and the debtor or owner, to recognize the effect of extinguishment of the possessory lien in proportion to the extent of the lienholder’s violation of the duty of care of a good manager.\\n\\nB. Determination in this case\\n\\n1) The court below, after finding that, following the Defendant’s acquisition of a possessory lien over the land at issue, BX was allowed or tacitly permitted to use some of the parcels as a parking lot and garage, respectively, and that BX and the site office and restroom on some land were used jointly and a warehouse was installed and allowed to be used, determined that, because the Defendant had failed to discharge the duty of care of a good manager as a lienholder, the possessory lien was extinguished by the Plaintiff side’s claim for extinguishment of the possessory lien. However, it determined that the portion of the possessory lien extinguished is limited to each parcel of land found to have failed to discharge the duty of care of a good manager, and that the possessory lien is not extinguished with respect to the remaining parcels of land.\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the court below in light of the legal principles stated above and the relevant legal principles, the above determination of the court below contains no error, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the claim for extinguishment of a possessory lien and the scope of the resulting extinguishment of the possessory lien, or the legal principles concerning abuse of rights in a claim for extinguishment of a possessory lien, or factual error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2) However, the part of the court below’s determination excluding from the land subject to extinguishment of the possessory lien the land listed as Serial No. 4 in Appendix 2 to the judgment of the court below is difficult to endorse.\\n\\nEven according to the reasoning of the court below’s judgment, BX was operating a parking lot business while possessing, among the land at issue, the remaining land within the enclosed area of 6,117㎡ formed by sequentially connecting the points 31, 89, 88, 87, 86, 85, 84, 98, 99, 100, 83, 82, 70, 71, 101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 109, 110, 94, 95, 111, 112, 113, 114, 59, 58, 61, 27, 26, and 31 indicated in Appendix Appraisal Diagram (1) attached to the judgment of the court below, excluding the portion of AY land possessed by BY; and it is found that the above 6,117㎡ forms part of the land listed as Serial Nos. 1 through 7 in Appendix 1 to the judgment of the court below and part of the land listed as Serial No. 4 in Appendix 2 thereto.\\n\\nHowever, the court below found that only the above seven parcels, excluding the land listed as Serial No. 4 in Appendix 2, are included in the above enclosed area of 6,117㎡ and accordingly determined that the possessory lien thereon had been extinguished. Thus, the judgment of the court below in this respect contains an error of contradiction in the reasons affecting the judgment. The argument advanced in the grounds for appeal by the successor-intervenor of the Plaintiff’s successor-intervenor (hereinafter referred to as the Plaintiff’s re-successor-intervenor) pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n2. Secured Claim of the Possessory Lien (Grounds 3 and 4 for appeal by the Plaintiff’s re-successor-intervenor)\\n\\nThe court below, after finding that in the lawsuit for payment of construction work costs in this case filed by the Defendant against E Co., Ltd. (hereinafter “E”), a judgment stating that “E shall pay to the Defendant construction costs of 14,432,000,000 won and delay damages calculated thereon at the rate of 20% per annum from September 21, 2012 until the day of full payment” had been rendered and become final and conclusive, held that the Defendant’s accrued construction costs as the secured claim of the possessory lien were 14,432,000,000 won, the amount of the above judgment, and ordered concurrent performance of payment of 14,432,000,000 won and the delay damages thereon with delivery of the land in which the possessory lien is recognized.\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the court below’s judgment in light of the relevant legal principles, the above determination of the court below contains no error affecting the judgment, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning liability for delay in a concurrent performance relationship or interpretation of dispositive documents, or violation of the principle of party presentation, violation of the rules of evidence, etc., as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Ex Officio Determination\\n\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nTaking into comprehensive account the provisions of the Civil Procedure Act concerning intervention by succession and the consistency with other multiple-party litigation systems under the 2002 amendment to the Civil Procedure Act, as well as the need for an integrated and non-contradictory determination of the overlapping claims of the intervenor by succession and the Plaintiff, who is the participating party, in a case where, while the litigation remains pending before the court, a third party asserts that it has succeeded to all or part of the right that is the object of the litigation and intervenes in the litigation pursuant to Civil Procedure Act Article 81, if the Plaintiff does not dispute whether the succession has occurred with respect to the intervenor by succession, and does not withdraw from the litigation or withdraw the action, etc., or if the Defendant does not consent thereto and the Plaintiff remains in the litigation, Civil Procedure Act Article 67 concerning indispensable co-litigation applies between the overlapping claims of the Plaintiff and the intervenor by succession arising from the succession (see Supreme Court en banc decision rendered on October 23, 2019, 2012DA46170).\\n\\nB. The court below’s determination\\n\\nThe court below held that the appeal by the Plaintiff’s successor-intervenor was filed in an improper manner because the petition of appeal did not state the purport of appeal and this defect was not corrected by the close of oral argument in the court below, and that, since the first instance judgment did not determine the claim of the Plaintiff’s successor-intervenor and the appeal was filed without any judgment subject to challenge, the appeal was improper, and therefore dismissed the appeal by the Plaintiff’s successor-intervenor.\\n\\nC. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\n1) According to the reasoning of the court below’s judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na) After the Plaintiff filed the present action, during the pendency of the first instance proceedings, the Plaintiff’s successor-intervenor applied for intervention by succession, asserting succession to rights on the ground that it had purchased the land at issue from the Plaintiff and completed the ownership transfer registration, and the Plaintiff withdrew from the litigation.\\n\\nb) During the pendency of the first instance proceedings, the Plaintiff’s re-successor-intervenor applied for intervention by succession, asserting succession to rights on the ground that it had received the land at issue in trust from the Plaintiff’s successor-intervenor and completed the ownership transfer registration, and the Plaintiff’s successor-intervenor, while not disputing whether the succession had occurred for the Plaintiff’s re-successor-intervenor, did not withdraw from the litigation or withdraw the action, etc.\\n\\nc) The first instance court determined the claim of the Plaintiff’s re-successor-intervenor on the premise that the Plaintiff’s re-successor-intervenor was the owner of the land at issue, and did not determine the claim of the Plaintiff’s successor-intervenor.\\n\\n2) Examining the above factual relationship in light of the legal principles stated above, since Civil Procedure Act Article 67 concerning indispensable co-litigation applies between the claims of the Plaintiff’s successor-intervenor and the Plaintiff’s re-successor-intervenor remaining in the litigation, the court below should have dismissed the claim of the Plaintiff’s successor-intervenor, who had lost ownership of the land at issue. Nevertheless, the court below’s determination dismissing the appeal by the Plaintiff’s successor-intervenor for the reasons stated in the judgment contains an error affecting the judgment due to a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the procedural relationship arising from intervention by succession.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, while accepting part of the grounds for appeal of the Plaintiff’s re-successor-intervenor, this Court reverses the judgment of the court below ex officio, and because this case is sufficiently ready for this Court to adjudicate directly, this Court renders its own judgment pursuant to Civil Procedure Act Article 437.\\n\\nThe Defendant shall, to the Plaintiff’s re-successor-intervenor, (1) demolish the office (panel) building of 174㎡ in the portion (a) and the restroom (panel) building of 22㎡ in the portion (c), each within the area enclosed by sequentially connecting the points 14, 19, 20, 17, and 14 indicated in Appendix Appraisal Diagram (2) attached to the judgment of the court below, on the land listed as Serial No. 8 in Appendix 1 to the judgment of the court below, and deliver each of the lands listed in Appendix 1 to the judgment of the court below and the land listed as Serial No. 4 in Appendix 2 thereto, and (2) simultaneously with receiving from E the amount of 14,432,000,000 won and the amount calculated thereon at the rate of 20% per annum from September 21, 2012 until the day of full payment, deliver each of the lands listed as Serial Nos. 1 through 3 and 5 through 47 in Appendix 2 to the judgment of the court below; therefore, the Plaintiff’s re-successor-intervenor’s claim shall be accepted within the above recognized scope as well-founded, and the Plaintiff’s successor-intervenor’s claim and the remainder of the Plaintiff’s re-successor-intervenor’s claim shall be dismissed as without merit. Accordingly, the first instance judgment shall be modified as above, the total costs of the litigation shall be allocated, and it is so adjudged as the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2018DA301350]": "We consider the grounds for appeal, including ex officio determination.\\n\\n1. Claim for extinguishment of the possessory lien and its scope (Grounds for Appeal Nos. 1 and 2 of CK Co., Ltd., the successive intervenor of the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor, and the Defendant’s grounds for appeal)\\n\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\n\\n1) Since Article 321 of the Civil Act provides that “The lien holder may exercise his right over the whole of the thing subject to the lien until he receives full satisfaction of his claim,” each part of the thing subject to the lien secures the whole of the secured claim, and such indivisibility of the lien also applies even where the object is divisible or consists of several things (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DA16942, Sept. 7, 2007), and likewise applies to the commercial lien under Article 58 of the Commercial Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DA244835, Dec. 27, 2016).\\n\\n2) Article 324 of the Civil Act provides that “The lien holder is under a duty of care of a good manager with respect to the thing subject to the lien, and where the lien holder, in violation thereof, uses, lends, or provides the thing subject to the lien as security without the debtor’s consent, the debtor may demand extinguishment of the lien.” If a lien holder who has acquired a lien over several parcels of land with one claim as the secured claim violates the duty of care of a good manager with respect to some of those parcels of land, it is reasonable to interpret that, absent special circumstances, the claim for extinguishment of the lien is available only with respect to the parcels of land as to which the violation occurred. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\nA) Where a lien is established over several parcels of land, owing to the indivisibility of the lien, each parcel of land secures the whole of the secured claim independently of the other parcels of land. At this time, even if possession over some parcels of land is lost, the lien for securing the secured claim continues to exist with respect to the remaining parcels of land. From the same perspective, even where a claim for extinguishment of the lien is made on the ground that the lien holder violated the duty of care of a good manager with respect to some parcels of land, it is reasonable to interpret that extinguishment may be claimed only with respect to the parcels of land where the violation occurred.\\n\\nB) The purpose of Article 321 of the Civil Act in providing for the “indivisibility of the lien” is to strengthen the effect of the lien, a security real right, for the benefit of the lien holder; on that basis, it is not appropriate to interpret that, to the detriment of the lien holder, even the lien over the thing subject to the lien with respect to which no issue arises as to violation of the duty of care of a good manager is extinguished.\\n\\nC) A lien is a statutory security real right that secures preferential satisfaction of the lien holder’s secured claim by means of the thing in his or her possession (Article 320(1) of the Civil Act, Article 58 of the Commercial Act). Meanwhile, the claim for extinguishment of the lien provided in Article 324 of the Civil Act is a provision intended to protect the debtor or the owner of the thing subject to the lien as a sanction against the lien holder’s violation of the duty of care of a good manager. It is a reasonable interpretation, taking into account the balance of interests between the lien holder and the debtor or owner, to recognize the effect of extinguishment of the lien in proportion to the extent of the lien holder’s violation of the duty of care of a good manager.\\n\\nB. Determination in this case\\n\\n1) The lower court found that after the Defendant acquired a lien over the land in this case, the Defendant permitted or acquiesced in BX’s and BY’s use of some of the parcels as a parking lot and a garage, respectively, and allowed BX to jointly use the field office and toilet on some of the land and to install and use a warehouse, and then held that, because the Defendant had not fulfilled the duty of care of a good manager as a lien holder, the lien was extinguished by the Plaintiffs’ claim for extinguishment of the lien. However, the lower court held that the part of the lien extinguished is limited to the parcels of land with respect to which it was found that the duty of care of a good manager was not fulfilled, and that the lien is not extinguished with respect to the remaining parcels of land.\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the lower court judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles and relevant legal principles, there is no error in the lower court’s determination, as alleged in each ground for appeal, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the claim for extinguishment of the lien and the scope of extinguishment of the lien therefrom, misapprehension of the legal principles concerning abuse of rights in a claim for extinguishment of the lien, or mistake in fact-finding.\\n\\n2) However, the part of the lower court’s determination excluding Item 4 of Attached Schedule 2 of the lower court judgment from the land on which the lien is extinguished cannot be upheld.\\n\\nEven according to the reasoning of the lower court judgment, BX was operating a parking lot while possessing, among the land in this case, the remaining land excluding part of AY that was possessed by BY, out of 6,117 square meters within the line connecting, in order, the points marked 31, 89, 88, 87, 86, 85, 84, 98, 99, 100, 83, 82, 70, 71, 101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 109, 110, 94, 95, 111, 112, 113, 114, 59, 58, 61, 27, 26, and 31 in Attached Appraisal Diagram (1) of the lower court judgment; and it is found that the said 6,117 square meters constitute part of the land listed in Items 1 through 7 of Attached Schedule 1 and Item 4 of Attached Schedule 2 of the lower court judgment.\\n\\nHowever, the lower court determined that only the above 7 parcels of land excluding Item 4 of Attached Schedule 2 were included in the above area within the line, and that the lien over them had been extinguished. Accordingly, this part of the lower court judgment contains an error of inconsistency in its reasoning that affected the judgment. The ground for appeal by the successive intervenor of the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor (hereinafter referred to as the Plaintiff’s further successive intervenor) pointing this out is well founded.\\n\\n2. Secured claim of the lien (Grounds for Appeal Nos. 3 and 4 of the Plaintiff’s further successive intervenor)\\n\\nThe lower court found that in the lawsuit for the claim of civil engineering construction payment brought by the Defendant against E Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “E”), a judgment had been rendered and became final and conclusive in the following terms: “E shall pay the Defendant construction payment of 14,432,000,000 won and delay damages thereon calculated at the rate of 20% per annum from Sept. 21, 2012 until the day of full payment.” The lower court then held that the Defendant’s unpaid construction payment, as the secured claim of the lien, was the above adjudged amount of 14,432,000,000 won, and ordered concurrent performance of delivery of the land on which the lien was recognized and payment of 14,432,000,000 won and delay damages thereon.\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles, there is no error in the lower court’s determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning responsibility for delay in a concurrent performance relationship, interpretation of dispositive documents, or violation of the principle of party presentation or the rules of evidence, that affected the judgment.\\n\\n3. Ex officio determination\\n\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nTaking into comprehensive consideration the provisions of the Civil Procedure Act concerning intervention by succession and the consistency with other multiple-party litigation systems introduced by the 2002 amendments to the Civil Procedure Act, as well as the need to conclusively determine, without contradiction, the overlapping claims of the successive intervenor and the plaintiff who is the intervened party, where a third party, while an action is pending before the court, claims to have succeeded to all or part of the right that is the subject matter of the litigation and has intervened in the litigation pursuant to Article 81 of the Civil Procedure Act, if the plaintiff does not dispute whether the successive intervenor has succeeded, and yet does not withdraw from the litigation or withdraw the action, or if the defendant does not consent thereto and the plaintiff remains in the litigation, Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act concerning necessary joinder applies between the overlapping claims of the plaintiff and the successive intervenor caused by the succession (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2012DA46170, Oct. 23, 2019).\\n\\nB. The lower court’s determination\\n\\nThe lower court held that the appeal by the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor was improperly filed because the statement of appeal did not specify the purport of the appeal and was not corrected until the close of oral argument in the lower court, and that the appeal was also improper because the first instance judgment did not rule on the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor’s claim, so the appeal was filed without a judgment subject to challenge. Accordingly, the lower court dismissed the appeal by the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor.\\n\\nC. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\n1) According to the reasoning of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\nA) After the Plaintiff filed the present action, during the pendency of the first instance proceedings, the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor applied to intervene by succession, asserting succession of rights on the ground that he had purchased the land in this case from the Plaintiff and completed the registration of transfer of ownership, and the Plaintiff withdrew from the litigation.\\n\\nB) During the pendency of the first instance proceedings, the Plaintiff’s further successive intervenor applied to intervene by succession, asserting succession of rights on the ground that he had received the land in this case in trust from the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor and completed the registration of transfer of ownership, and the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor did not dispute whether the Plaintiff’s further successive intervenor had succeeded, but did not withdraw from the litigation or withdraw the action.\\n\\nC) The court of first instance, on the premise that the Plaintiff’s further successive intervenor was the owner of the land in this case, ruled on the claim of the Plaintiff’s further successive intervenor, but did not rule on the claim of the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor.\\n\\n2) Examining the above factual relationship in light of the foregoing legal principles, Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act concerning necessary joinder applies between the claim of the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor, who remains in the litigation, and the claim of the Plaintiff’s further successive intervenor. Therefore, the lower court should have dismissed the claim of the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor, who had lost ownership of the land in this case. Nevertheless, the lower court’s determination dismissing the appeal of the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor for the reasons stated above contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the procedural relationship arising from intervention by succession.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, while accepting some of the grounds for appeal of the Plaintiff’s further successive intervenor, the Court sets aside the lower court judgment upon ex officio determination, and since this case is sufficiently ready for this Court to adjudicate directly, the Court renders its own judgment pursuant to Article 437 of the Civil Procedure Act.\\n\\nThe Defendant shall, to the Plaintiff’s further successive intervenor, (1) remove the office (panel) building of the 174 square meters portion within the line connecting, in order, the points 14, 19, 20, 17, and 14 in Attached Appraisal Diagram (2) of the lower court judgment, located on the land listed in Item 8 of Attached Schedule 1 of the lower court judgment, and the toilet (panel) building of the 22 square meters portion within the line connecting, in order, the points 21, 22, 23, 24, and 21, and deliver each of the lands listed in Attached Schedule 1 of the lower court judgment and the land listed in Item 4 of Attached Schedule 2, and (2) concurrently with receiving 14,432,000,000 won and the amount calculated thereon at the rate of 20% per annum from Sept. 21, 2012 until the day of full payment from E, deliver each of the lands listed in Items 1 through 3 and 5 through 47 of Attached Schedule 2 of the lower court judgment; accordingly, the Plaintiff’s further successive intervenor’s claim is well founded within the recognized scope and is granted, and the Plaintiff’s successive intervenor’s claim and the remaining claims of the Plaintiff’s further successive intervenor are without merit and are all dismissed. Accordingly, the first instance judgment is modified as above, and the total costs of litigation are allocated, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2019DA247385]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Determination on Ground 1 of the Grounds of Appeal\\n\\nA. An action for declaratory judgment is permitted only where there is a present uncertainty or danger with respect to the Plaintiff’s right or legal status, and obtaining a declaratory judgment is the most effective and appropriate means of fundamentally resolving the dispute (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision No. 2007DA69407, rendered on December 14, 2007). Also, litigation requirements such as the legal interest in seeking declaratory judgment are matters subject to ex officio examination; therefore, even if not asserted by the parties, the court must investigate and determine them ex officio, and if a litigation requirement is lacking after the close of oral argument in the fact-finding instance or if such defect has been cured, this must also be taken into account at the appellate instance (see Supreme Court Decision No. 2016DA231198, rendered on September 28, 2018).\\n\\nB. According to the record, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n\\n1) Plaintiff Wondang Heavy Industries Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Plaintiff Wondang Heavy Industries”), as the owner of the respective real properties at issue, and Plaintiff Dong-A Heavy Industries Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Plaintiff Dong-A Heavy Industries”), as the mortgagee with respect to the respective real properties at issue, sought a declaration of nonexistence of lien against the Defendant, who asserted a possessory lien with respect to the respective real properties at issue.\\n\\n2) On April 10, 2019, before the close of oral argument in the court below, non-judicial foreclosure auction proceedings (hereinafter referred to as “the auction proceedings at issue”) were commenced with respect to the respective real properties at issue on the basis of a mortgage (hereinafter referred to as “the mortgage at issue”) of which Seungjin Co., Ltd. was the debtor and Plaintiff Dong-A Heavy Industries was the creditor, and in the said non-judicial foreclosure auction proceedings, Chungwon Industrial Development LLC (hereinafter referred to as “Chungwon Industrial Development”) acquired ownership of the respective real properties at issue; on that basis, on April 11, 2019, a registration of transfer of ownership in the name of Chungwon Industrial Development was made, and at the same time the registration of establishment of Plaintiff Dong-A Heavy Industries’ mortgage was cancelled.\\n\\n3) On May 13, 2019, after the close of oral argument in the court below, Plaintiff Wondang Heavy Industries filed a motion to reopen oral argument on the ground that Chungwon Industrial Development had paid the full purchase price and acquired ownership in the auction proceedings at issue, and on the 15th of the same month, Chungwon Industrial Development filed an application for intervention by succession on the ground that it had succeeded to the rights relating to the real properties at issue.\\n\\nC. It is grounded in the risk that, if a possessory lien is asserted in an auction proceeding, bidding will occur at a low price and the amount distributed to the mortgagee will be reduced, that the mortgagee is deemed to have a legal interest in seeking a declaration of nonexistence of each possessory lien concerning the collateral object (see Supreme Court Decision No. 2013DA99409, rendered on March 10, 2016; Supreme Court Decision No. 2004DA32848, rendered on September 23, 2004, etc.), and the same applies where the owner seeks a declaration of nonexistence of a possessory lien in an auction proceeding concerning real property owned by the owner. If, as above, a possessory lien was asserted in the auction proceeding, but the owned real property or collateral object was sold and ownership was transferred, thereby causing the owner to lose ownership or the mortgage to be extinguished, then the owner and the mortgagee have no legal interest in seeking a declaration of nonexistence of a possessory lien.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 575 of the Civil Act provides that “where the object of a sale becomes the subject of a possessory lien, if the buyer did not know of this, the buyer may rescind the contract only where it is impossible thereby to achieve the purpose of the contract. In other cases, only damages may be claimed.” Article 578(1) and (2) of the same Act provide that “① In the case of an auction, the purchaser at auction may, pursuant to the provisions of the preceding Article 8, rescind the contract or claim a reduction of the price against the debtor. ② In the case under the preceding paragraph, if the debtor is insolvent, the purchaser at auction may claim against the creditor who received the distribution of the price the return of all or part of the price.” Where, as above, no possessory lien is asserted in the auction proceeding, even if the collateral object has been sold and ownership transferred, thereby extinguishing the mortgage, the creditor remains exposed to the risk of being pursued for the security liability under the above provisions by the buyer who did not know of the existence of the possessory lien, and such risk makes the creditor’s legal status unstable; accordingly, the creditor, as mortgagee, has a legal interest in seeking a declaration of nonexistence of possessory lien in order to remove that uncertainty. On the other hand, the owner, who is not the debtor, does not bear the security liability under the above provisions and therefore has no legal interest in seeking a declaration of nonexistence of a possessory lien.\\n\\nD. Accordingly, the court below, regardless of whether the parties had asserted it, should have examined ex officio whether the Defendant asserted or reported a possessory lien in the auction proceedings at issue and whether Plaintiff Wondang Heavy Industries succeeded to the secured debt of the mortgage at issue, and thereby determined whether the Plaintiffs had an interest in seeking a declaration of nonexistence of a possessory lien. Nevertheless, by overlooking this and proceeding to examine and determine the merits, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the legal interest requirement for an action for declaratory judgment and by failing to conduct the necessary examination, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n2. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without deciding the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for further proceedings and determination, and so, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices, we render the judgment as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2021DA213866]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. According to Article 204 of the Civil Act, when a possessor has been unlawfully dispossessed of possession, he may claim the return of the thing and compensation for damages (paragraph (1)), and the above right must be exercised within one year from the date on which the possession was dispossessed (paragraph (3)); the one-year period of exercise referred to here is a preclusive period, meaning the period within which an action must be brought (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on April 26, 2002, 2001DA8097, 8103). However, since Article 204(3) of the Civil Act does not apply to the exercise of a claim for damages arising from a violation of a substantive right, where a person who has been dispossessed of possession exercises a claim for damages arising from the extinguishment of the possessory lien, which is the principal right, Article 204(3) of the Civil Act does not apply, and it is not required that such claim be exercised within one year from the date on which possession was dispossessed.\\n\\n2. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, it can be seen that the Plaintiff, in filing this action, is exercising a claim for damages on the ground of extinguishment of the possessory lien, and therefore, according to the foregoing legal principle, Article 204(3) of the Civil Act does not apply to this case.\\nNevertheless, the court below, on the grounds as stated in the judgment, held that Article 204(3) of the Civil Act applies, and upheld the first-instance judgment that found this action to be improper because it had been brought after the one-year preclusive period prescribed in Article 204(3) of the Civil Act. In this determination by the court below, there is an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principle concerning the scope of application of Article 204(3) of the Civil Act. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and since this case is sufficiently ready for the Supreme Court to try and decide it directly, the Court decides the case itself, revokes the first-instance judgment, and remands the case to the court of first instance to have it retried and decided in accordance with Article 425 and the main text of Article 418 of the Civil Procedure Act, and so renders judgment as stated in the operative part by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: A entered into an insurance contract with Insurance Company A, using his father B as the insured and with B’s death as the insured event. Which of the following statements are correct? [“written form” includes the electronic documents prescribed in Commercial Act Article 731(1) (Insurance on the Life of Another), and where there is a dispute, according to case law] (a) The Commercial Act provision requiring that, in an insurance contract with another person’s death as the insured event, that person’s written consent be obtained at the time the insurance contract is concluded is a mandatory provision. (b) B’s consent must be given in writing individually with respect to the insurance contract, and comprehensive, implied, or presumed consent alone is insufficient. (c) The time by which B must express consent in writing is by the time the insurance contract is concluded. (d) A, who concluded an insurance contract with B’s death as the insured event without B’s written consent, asserting the invalidity on his own, is, absent special circumstances, an exercise of rights contrary to the principle of good faith or the principle of estoppel. (e) If B’s written consent is absent, the insurance contract is void, but if B ratifies it, the insurance contract may become valid.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2004DA56677]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the arguments concerning errors of law as to the insured’s written consent and ratification in another person’s life insurance\\nThe purpose of Article 731(1) of the Commercial Code, which provides that, in an insurance contract that treats the death of another person as the insured event, the written consent of that other person must be obtained at the time the insurance contract is concluded, is to eliminate room for disputes by clarifying the timing and method of such consent; therefore, the consent of the other person who is the insured must be given individually in writing for each insurance contract, and a blanket consent or merely implied or presumed consent is insufficient (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DA24451, decided July 22, 2003).\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the above legal principles and the record, it was proper for the court below, in the same purport, to determine that, solely on the circumstances stated in the judgment, it cannot be found that the deceased Non-Party, who was the insured, gave the written consent required by the above statutory provision at the time of concluding the insurance contract at issue, which is a life insurance contract on another person, and that there is no other evidence to recognize this point; and there is no illegality such as an error of law concerning the insured’s written consent or a misconception of facts due to a violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nIn addition, according to the above provisions of the Commercial Code, the time at which the insured must manifest consent in writing in another person’s life insurance is “by the time the insurance contract is concluded,” and since this is a mandatory provision and an insurance contract in violation thereof is void (see Supreme Court Decision 96DA37084, decided November 22, 1996; Supreme Court Decision 2003DA60259, decided April 27, 2006, etc.), if there was no written consent of the insured at the time the life insurance contract on another person was formed, that insurance contract becomes conclusively void, and even if the insured, who is not even a party to the insurance contract, ratified the insurance contract that had already become void, the insurance contract cannot thereby become valid.\\n\\nThe court below’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality such as an error of law concerning ratification of the insured’s written consent, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2.
