Regarding the argument concerning an error of law as to the principle of good faith or estoppel\\nSince the legislative purpose of Article 731(1) of the Commercial Code is construed to include not only the risk of gambling insurance and the risk of murdering the insured, but also the exclusion of the risk of infringement of public order and good morals arising from making another person’s death, without obtaining the victim’s consent, a condition under a wagering contract, if a person who, in violation of this provision, concluded an insurance contract treating the death of another person as the insured event without the insured’s written consent were denied on the ground that asserting invalidity by that very person constitutes an exercise of rights contrary to the principle of good faith or the principle of estoppel, the legislative purpose would be completely nullified; therefore, unless there are special circumstances, such an assertion cannot be deemed contrary to the principle of good faith or estoppel (see Supreme Court Decision 96DA37084, decided November 22, 1996; Supreme Court Decision 2003DA60259, decided April 27, 2006, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below determined that, even if the Defendant had received premiums for several years or had previously paid hospitalization benefits under the medical coverage rider of the insurance contract at issue, it cannot be said to be contrary to the principle of good faith or estoppel for the Defendant to refuse payment of the insurance proceeds while asserting the invalidity of the insurance contract at issue; and, in light of the legal principle stated above and the record, the court below’s determination is acceptable as proper, and there is no illegality such as an error of law concerning the principle of good faith or estoppel or an omission of judgment, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Regarding the argument concerning a violation of the rules of evidence as to whether it falls within death from a traffic accident disaster\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below determined that, even if the insurance contract at issue were valid, the death of the Non-Party cannot be said, for the reasons stated in the judgment, to have resulted from a traffic accident disaster as defined in the insurance policy terms at issue; and this part of the determination is an auxiliary and hypothetical determination, and, as stated above, insofar as the principal determination is recognized as proper, it does not affect the result of the judgment regardless of whether it is proper or not, so the argument concerning the grounds of appeal on this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are assessed against the losing party, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the operative part by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2006DA69141]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. As to Ground 1 of the grounds for final appeal\\nIn an insurance contract in which the death of another person constitutes the insured event, the consent of the other person who is the insured must be given individually in writing for each insurance contract, and blanket consent or mere implied or presumed consent is insufficient (see Supreme Court Decision of September 22, 2006, 2004DA56677). However, because the written consent of the other person who is the insured, as referred to here, does not mean only that person’s handwritten signature on the insurance application form, where the insurance contract is concluded in the presence of the other person who is the insured and the policyholder or insurance solicitor explains the contents of the insurance contract to that person and then, having expressly been authorized by that person, signs on that person’s behalf on the insurance application form, as in the case where a person who has clearly been granted, specifically and individually, authority to give written consent for a particular insurance contract by that other person gives written consent on behalf of that other person within the scope of such authority, such written consent of the other person must also be deemed to have been validly given by a duly authorized representative.\\n\\nAccording to the facts determined by the court below and the record, the following facts may be found: the Plaintiff, who was the policyholder, and Non-Party 1, who was the insurance solicitor, concluded the insurance contract at issue in the presence of Non-Party 2, who was the insured; at that time, Non-Party 2 received an explanation of the contents of the insurance contract at issue from Non-Party 1 and expressly consented thereto, and thereafter stated that he did not know how to read and write well and requested the Plaintiff, who was the policyholder, to sign on his behalf in the insured’s handwritten signature column of the insurance application form; accordingly, the Plaintiff, at that place, wrote Non-Party 2’s name in the insured’s handwritten signature column of the insurance application form on behalf of Non-Party 2. If the circumstances are as such, then, in light of the foregoing legal principles, the written consent of Non-Party 2, the insured, was validly given by the Plaintiff, who had been specifically and individually granted by Non-Party 2 the authority to act for him in giving written consent; therefore, the court below’s determination, to the same effect, that the insurance contract at issue was validly concluded upon the lawful written consent of Non-Party 2 is proper, and there is no error therein such as a misapprehension of facts due to violation of the rules of evidence assessment, inadequate deliberation, or an erroneous interpretation of the legal principles concerning written consent under Article 731 of the Commercial Act, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 2 of the grounds for final appeal\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the record, the court below, after comprehensively evaluating the evidence it admitted and recognizing the facts as stated in its decision, held that Non-Party 2 had been infected with the causative organism of sepsis due to a deep facial laceration that occurred at the time of the accident at issue, and that he died directly as a result of that sepsis; therefore, the court’s determination that this corresponds to “death resulting from a disaster,” which is the insured event stipulated in the insurance contract at issue, is proper, and there is no error therein such as a misapprehension of facts due to violation of the rules of evidence assessment, inadequate deliberation, or an erroneous interpretation of the legal principles concerning the disaster that constitutes the insured event, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, as stated in the operative part."}

question: A entered into a fire insurance contract with A Insurance Company, naming B as the insured, with respect to the bakery owned by his father B, without B's authorization. Although a fire had previously occurred at the bakery, at the time of the insurance contract A entered "No fire has occurred" in the questionnaire on the application form regarding whether a fire had occurred, and A Insurance Company was not negligent in believing this. Among the following explanations, which is incorrect? (If there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: At the time of concluding the fire insurance contract, A must notify A Insurance Company that he had not been authorized by B.
B: Whether a fire had occurred at the bakery is presumed to be an important fact subject to the duty of disclosure.
C: Even if it is not a question item stated in the questionnaire on the application form, it is not necessarily excluded from the scope of the duty of disclosure.
D: Even if a fire occurs at the bakery after the fire insurance contract is concluded, A Insurance Company may terminate the fire insurance contract on the ground of A's breach of the duty of disclosure only where there is a causal relationship between A's breach of the duty of disclosure and the fire.
E: If A, intentionally or by gross negligence, stated that no fire had occurred, A Insurance Company may terminate the contract only within 1 month from the day it learned of that fact and within 3 years from the day the fire insurance contract was concluded.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2010DA25353]": "The grounds for appeal are determined, with the contents of the supplementary brief filed after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, after recognizing the factual findings set forth in the judgment, the court below held that whether the non-party had been diagnosed with hypertension and had received medication and treatment is a significant matter serving as a standard for the insurer, the Defendant, to measure the probability of the occurrence of an insured event and the resulting burden of liability and thereby determine whether to enter into the insurance contract in this case or the contents of that contract, such as the premium or the addition of a special exclusion clause, and that, as a matter questioned by the Defendant in writing, it is subject to the duty of disclosure; and, since the Plaintiff and the non-party stated in the insurance application that there was no such fact, although, as stated above, within the most recent 5 years they had in fact been diagnosed with hypertension and had received medication, the court below found that the Plaintiff and the non-party, in entering into the insurance contract in this case, violated the duty of disclosure by failing, with intent or gross negligence, to disclose truthfully the matters to be disclosed to the Defendant. In light of the record, this determination by the court below is proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the law as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. The main text of Article 651 of the Commercial Act provides, “If, at the time of the insurance contract, the policyholder or the insured fails, with intent or gross negligence, to disclose important matters or makes false disclosures, the insurer may terminate the contract only within 1 month from the day on which the insurer learned of the fact and within 3 years from the day on which the contract was concluded,” and Article 655 provides, “Even after the insured event has occurred, if the insurer terminates the contract pursuant to the provisions of Articles 650, 651, 652, and 653, it shall not be liable to pay the insurance amount and may claim the return of the insurance amount already paid. However, this shall not apply where it is proved that the fact of violation of the duty of disclosure or the fact of a significant change in or increase of risk did not affect the occurrence of the insured event.”\\n\\nArticle 651 of the Commercial Act is a general provision concerning termination of a contract due to violation of the duty of disclosure; according to it, no causal relationship is required between the fact constituting a violation of the duty of disclosure and the occurrence of the insured event. Article 655 of the Commercial Act is a provision concerning a claim for the insurance amount when the contract has been terminated due to violation of the duty of disclosure, and therefore it is proper to construe not only the main text but also the proviso as provisions concerning the existence or non-existence of the right to claim the insurance amount. If, at the time of the insurance contract, the policyholder or the insured, with intent or gross negligence, fails to disclose or makes false disclosure of important matters, the requirements for violation of the duty of disclosure are thereby satisfied; on the other hand, because the causal relationship between the fact constituting a violation of the duty of disclosure and the occurrence of the insured event is determined only at the time of the occurrence of the insured event, it is proper to construe that, even if the insurer becomes liable to pay the insurance amount under the proviso of Article 655 of the Commercial Act because no causal relationship is recognized between the fact constituting a violation of the duty of disclosure and the occurrence of the insured event, the insurer may separately terminate the contract under Article 651 of the Commercial Act on the ground of violation of the duty of disclosure. If termination of the contract under Article 651 of the Commercial Act were not permitted merely because no causal relationship is recognized between the fact constituting a violation of the duty of disclosure and the occurrence of the insured event, an irrational result would arise: before the occurrence of the insured event, the contract could be terminated under Article 651 of the Commercial Act on the ground of violation of the duty of disclosure, whereas after the occurrence of the insured event, the contract could not be terminated even after payment of the insurance amount on the ground, retroactively, that there is no causal relationship, and, unless causation were recognized, the insurer would have to continue paying the insurance amount. Considering, in sum, that an insurance contract in violation of the duty of disclosure may be terminated by the insurer regardless of whether there is a causal relationship between the fact constituting a violation of the duty of disclosure and the occurrence of the insured event, such construction accords with the good-faith nature and collective character of insurance contracts. Accordingly, it should be construed that the insurer may terminate the contract under Article 651 of the Commercial Act on the ground of violation of the duty of disclosure regardless of whether there is a causal relationship between the fact constituting a violation of the duty of disclosure and the occurrence of the insured event. However, with respect to the right to claim the insurance amount, when the insurer terminates the insurance contract on the ground of violation of the duty of disclosure after the occurrence of the insured event, the liability to pay the insurance amount is determined according to whether there is a causal relationship between the fact constituting a violation of the duty of disclosure and the occurrence of the insured event, and within that scope the effect of termination of the contract may be limited.\\n\\nEven if no causal relationship is recognized between the Plaintiff’s and the non-party’s violation of the duty of disclosure, as set forth above, and the occurrence of the insured event, namely the non-party’s development of leukemia, the court below held that the Defendant may terminate the insurance contract in this case on the ground of the Plaintiff’s and the non-party’s violation of the duty of disclosure. This is proper as being in accordance with the foregoing legal principles, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the law as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nMoreover, the Supreme Court Decision rendered on February 25, 1994, 93DA52082, and the Supreme Court Decision rendered on January 5, 2001, 2000DA40353, which the Plaintiff cites, are cases disputing the existence or non-existence of the right to claim the insurance amount arising from the occurrence of an insured event, and differ in subject matter from this case, which disputes the effect of termination of the insurance contract, and thus are not suitable for citation here.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: A, B, and C were directors of Company A, an unlisted stock company, and D was its auditor. A had acquired shares representing 60% of the total issued shares of Company A and completed the registration of transfer, and was a major shareholder, while B was the representative director of Company A. The articles of incorporation of Company A provide that the remuneration of directors and auditors shall be determined by resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, but B, without a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, paid a special performance bonus to C in accordance with A's instructions. Which of the following statements concerning this matter are correct? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents) (a) The special performance bonus paid to C is included in a director's remuneration as consideration paid for the performance of a director's duties. (b) Even if the special performance bonus paid to C was paid pursuant to A's instructions, unless there are special circumstances, it cannot be regarded as the equivalent of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders regarding the payment of the special performance bonus. (c) Even if B, who was facing retirement due to loss of management control, etc., established a retirement allowance payment provision that was excessively excessive and markedly departed from a reasonable level in order to receive as much retirement allowance as possible and caused a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders to be adopted despite the opposition of minority shareholders through the exercise of influence by using his position, the resolution is valid, and B may exercise a claim for payment of retirement allowance on the basis of that retirement allowance payment provision. (d) If A, after acquiring all of the total issued shares of Company A and completing the registration of transfer, prepared the minutes of the general meeting of shareholders as if there had been a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders concerning the special performance bonus provision, then even if no actual general meeting of shareholders was held, unless there are special circumstances, it may be regarded as having had a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders concerning that provision. (e) The remuneration of an auditor may be determined only by a provision of the articles of incorporation and cannot be determined by resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, so Company A cannot pay remuneration to D by resolution of the general meeting of shareholders notwithstanding the provision of the articles of incorporation.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2014DA11888]": "The grounds of appeal shall be examined (with the statements in the supplemental brief of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal considered to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Grounds of appeal concerning the regulations on payment of severance pay to officers\\n\\na. The Commercial Act provides in Article 388 that the remuneration of directors of a stock company shall be determined by resolution of the general meeting of shareholders where the amount thereof is not fixed in the articles of incorporation, and such remuneration of directors includes retirement benefits or retirement consolation payments paid as compensation for the performance of the director’s duties (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 77DA1742, decided Nov. 22, 1977).\\n\\nThe reason why the Commercial Act requires the remuneration of directors to be determined by the articles of incorporation or by resolution of the general meeting of shareholders is to protect the interests of the company, its shareholders, and the company’s creditors by preventing the harm caused by the pursuit of private interests in connection with directors’ employment contracts (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DA49570, decided Nov. 23, 2006). Therefore, even if the correlation between remuneration and duties is not expressly provided for in the Commercial Act, a reasonable proportional relationship must be maintained between the duties a director provides to the company and the remuneration received therefor, and such remuneration must not be excessive beyond a reasonable level, to the extent of losing balance significantly in light of the company’s debt condition or business performance.\\n\\nAccordingly, if a director facing retirement due to loss of management control over the company, in order to receive as much remuneration as possible from the company, together with another director who concurs therewith, established a remuneration payment standard that is excessively high and far beyond a reasonable level in light of the contents of the director’s duties, the company’s financial condition, or business performance, and, by using his position, exerted influence over the general meeting of shareholders so that a resolution concerning the matter was adopted despite the opposition of minority shareholders, such conduct constitutes a breach of the duty prescribed in Article 382-3 of the Commercial Act to perform duties faithfully for the company, and thus an act of breach of trust against the company, as it causes an improper outflow of the company’s assets and thereby infringes the interests of the company and its shareholders; accordingly, even if a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders was obtained, such unlawful conduct cannot be said to be valid (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DO4915, decided Oct. 28, 2005; Supreme Court Decision 2006DO1813, decided June 1, 2007, etc.).\\n\\nIn addition, the court determines whether factual allegations are true or not, by its free evaluation of the evidence, in accordance with logic and the rules of experience, based on the idea of social justice and equity, taking into account the purport of the entire arguments and the result of the evidentiary proceedings (Article 202 of the Civil Procedure Act), and facts lawfully established by the judgment of the lower court without exceeding the limits of such free evaluation of the evidence bind the court of final appeal (Article 432 of the same Act).\\n\\nb. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below recognized the following facts and circumstances.\\n\\n(1) The Defendant is a corporation established on 1999. 8. 20. for the Haengdamdo Marine Complex Tourism Rest Facility Development Project (hereinafter referred to as “the project in this case”), Plaintiff 1 served as a director of the Defendant from 2003. 2. 17. to 2010. 9. 27., and thereafter served as the representative director of the Defendant from the next day until 2010. 11. 17., and Plaintiff 2 served as a director of the Defendant from 2008. 1. 15. to 2010. 11. 17.\\n\\n(2) Ninety percent of the issued shares of the Defendant had been held since around 2004. 6. by Econ Korea Investments B.V. (hereinafter referred to as “EKI B.V.”), and Econ Korea Investments Pte. Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “EKI Pte.”) held 100% of the shares of EKI B.V.\\n\\nAt that time, Non-Party 1, as the representative director of the Defendant and a director of EKI B.V. and EKI Pte., had control over the management rights of the Defendant. However, on 2007. 11. 23., he was indicted for fraud, etc. in connection with the project in this case, sentenced to imprisonment, and taken into custody, and thereafter, through Non-Party 2, who was his close aide and the managing director of EKI B.V. (Non-Party 2; hereinafter referred to as “Non-Party 2”), he exercised influence over decision-making by EKI B.V., the controlling shareholder of the Defendant.\\n\\nWhen Non-Party 1 was convicted by a final judgment on 2008. 4. 24. in the above criminal case, he resigned as representative director of the Defendant on 2008. 5. 15., and Non-Party 3, who had been serving as a director, assumed office as representative director of the Defendant on 2008. 4. 2. prior thereto.\\n\\n(3) Since its incorporation, the Defendant had continuously been in a difficult position in terms of business performance and financial condition, and as of 2008. 3. 31. had accumulated losses of approximately KRW 7.3 billion. Above all, the main cause of the losses was the high proportion of officers’ salaries, especially those of the representative director, relative to the scale of sales, and the Defendant had no substantial business other than leasing the rest area, while the Haengdamdo Phase 2 development project pursued by the Defendant was in fact suspended due to the detention of Non-Party 1, so that there was not much for the Plaintiffs to make managerial judgments on.\\n\\n(4) Of the Defendant’s 90% shares held by EKI B.V., a pledge right was held by Citigroup Global Markets Financial Products LLC (hereinafter referred to as “Citigroup”), the holder of the corporate bonds issued by EKI B.V. on 2005. 2. 17. (the maturity date of which is 2009. 5. 4.; hereinafter referred to as “the corporate bonds in this case”), but because EKI B.V. had almost no possibility of repaying the principal and interest on the above corporate bonds, the Plaintiffs could sufficiently foresee that the controlling shareholder of the Defendant would soon change and that they too would accordingly be replaced.\\n\\n(5) Article 19(1)(b) of the Defendant’s articles of incorporation provides: “The determination of the salaries, bonuses, and other remuneration of directors, as well as retirement benefits, shall be resolved by the affirmative votes of a majority of the voting rights of the shareholders present at the general meeting of shareholders and at least one-fourth of the total issued shares.”\\n\\n(6) On 2008. 6. 10., Non-Party 3 convened a board of directors meeting and, with the approval of the directors including the Plaintiffs, resolved to enact the regulations on payment of severance pay to officers (hereinafter referred to as “the severance pay regulations in this case”), and then, at the annual general meeting of shareholders held on 2008. 6. 26. (hereinafter referred to as “the general meeting of shareholders in this case”), despite the opposition of Korea Expressway Corporation, which held 10% of the issued shares, the proposal to enact the severance pay regulations in this case was passed with the approval of EKI B.V., which held 90% of the issued shares. Non-Party 2, who exercised voting rights on behalf of EKI B.V., approved the above proposal at the request of Plaintiff 1, a close aide of Non-Party 1.\\n\\nThe severance pay regulations in this case increased the severance pay rate, applying to the representative director a rate equivalent to five times the previous rate (5 months per year of service), and applying to directors a rate equivalent to three times the previous rate (3 months per year of service), and providing that the increased severance pay rate would apply retroactively to the period of service of the officers.\\n\\n(7) In addition, 10 executives and employees of the Defendant, including the Plaintiffs, concluded salary increase agreements with the Defendant on 2010. 9. 30. and 2010. 10. 1. (hereinafter referred to as “the salary increase agreement in this case”); in the case of Plaintiff 2, who was a director at the time, his annual salary increased from KRW 48 million to KRW 80 million, making the increase rate the highest at 66.7%; and in the case of Plaintiff 1, who was the representative director, his annual salary increased from KRW 145 million to KRW 180 million, making the increase rate the next highest at 29.7%.\\n\\n(8) Pursuant to the severance pay regulations in this case, Non-Party 3 resigned as representative director on 2010. 10. 4. and received KRW 607,638,890 as severance pay under the increased severance pay rate for the representative director. And when calculated on the basis of the severance pay regulations in this case and the increased annual salary, in the case of Plaintiff 1, who retired as representative director, merely having served as representative director for 51 days caused the increased severance pay rate for the representative director to be applied to the entire 105-month period of service since his joining on 2002. 2. 15., thereby increasing his severance pay by more than KRW 500 million; and in the case of Plaintiff 2, who retired as a director, the severance pay rate increased threefold was applied, thereby increasing his severance pay by approximately KRW 35 million.\\n\\n(9) On 2010. 10. 12., Citigroup exercised the pledge right over the corporate bonds in this case and acquired 90% of the Defendant’s shares, after which, at the general meeting of shareholders on 2010. 11. 17., new directors were appointed, and on the same day the Plaintiffs resigned from their directorships.\\n\\nc. Based on the above facts and circumstances regarding the Defendant company’s financial condition and business performance, the contents of the severance pay regulations in this case, which far exceeded the previous level of payment, the duties of directors, and the background to their enactment, the court below determined that the act by which the Defendant’s directors, including the Plaintiffs, prepared the severance pay regulations in this case through a resolution of the board of directors and induced a resolution at the general meeting of shareholders to enact the regulations as resolved by the board constituted an improper outflow of the company’s assets, and thus reduced the company’s assets liable for its obligations, thereby materially infringing the interests of Korea Expressway Corporation and other shareholders, and therefore was unlawful as a violation of the directors’ duty of faithful performance; and that such unlawful conduct could not be justified merely because resolutions had been adopted by the board of directors and the general meeting of shareholders, so that the Plaintiffs could not exercise claims for severance pay based on the severance pay regulations in this case, which were the result of such breach of trust.\\n\\nd. The grounds of appeal disputing the court below’s factual findings are, in substance, nothing more than criticism of the selection and weighing of evidence and the finding of facts based thereon, which fall within the free evaluation of the evidence by the court of fact, and thus cannot be accepted.\\n\\nMoreover, even upon examining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the evidence lawfully admitted, the court below’s above determination appears to have been based on the legal principles stated above, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality affecting the judgment, such as a misunderstanding of the legal principles concerning remuneration of directors of a stock company and acts of breach of trust, or a violation of the limits of the free evaluation of the evidence in contravention of the rules of logic and experience, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Grounds of appeal concerning the salary increase agreement\\n\\na. Grounds of appeal asserting the existence of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders\\n\\nAccording to Article 388 of the Commercial Act, the remuneration of directors of a stock company shall be determined by resolution of the general meeting of shareholders where the amount thereof is not fixed in the articles of incorporation; therefore, where the articles of incorporation provide that the remuneration or retirement benefits of directors shall be determined by resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, if there is no evidence establishing that a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders was adopted regarding the amount, timing of payment, method of payment, etc., the director cannot claim remuneration or retirement benefits (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DA25123, decided Dec. 10, 2004, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below, with respect to the Plaintiffs’ argument that a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders existed with regard to the increase in salary, because the Plaintiffs’ annual salaries increased under the salary increase agreement in this case within the limit of the total amount of directors’ remuneration (KRW 2.7 billion) determined at the Defendant’s annual general meeting of shareholders on 2010. 6. 29., determined, to the effect that because it was recognized that at the above annual general meeting of shareholders the annual remuneration of directors for 2010 had been determined to be the same as at the end of the previous year, 2009, it could not be said that there was a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders concerning the above increased annual salaries, and accordingly rejected the Plaintiffs’ claims for remuneration under the salary increase agreement in this case.\\n\\nEven when the reasons of the judgment of the court below are examined in light of the above legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, it cannot be said that the court below’s above determination contains any illegality affecting the judgment, such as a misunderstanding of the legal principles concerning the remuneration of directors of a stock company under the Commercial Act or a violation of the limits of the free evaluation of the evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nb. Grounds of appeal asserting that it does not constitute an abuse of representative authority\\n\\nThe Plaintiffs’ grounds of appeal on this point contest the court below’s determination that the salary increase agreement in this case concluded between the Plaintiffs and the Defendant constituted an act of abuse of the representative director’s authority and was therefore invalid. However, as stated above, insofar as the court below’s determination that the increased remuneration under the salary increase agreement in this case is ineffective because it cannot be said that there was a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders is without error, even if there were errors in this part of the court below’s determination as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such errors could not affect the result of the judgment. Accordingly, this ground of appeal does not, without needing further examination, constitute a basis for reversal of the court below, and is therefore rejected.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged as per the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2015DA213308]": "The grounds for appeal (supplemental written submissions to a statement of grounds for appeal filed after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds for appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal) are examined.\\n\\n1. Concerning Grounds 2 and 3 of the appeal\\na. When a person appointed as a director or auditor at a shareholders’ meeting of a stock company enters into a contract with the stock company and assumes office as a director or auditor, such person may receive remuneration in accordance with the amount, timing of payment, and method of payment prescribed by the articles of incorporation or by a resolution of the shareholders’ meeting pursuant to Articles 388 and 415 of the Commercial Act. In light of this, even if a director or auditor appointed at a shareholders’ meeting, pursuant to an express or implied agreement with the company, broadly delegates his or her duties to another director, etc., and does not actually perform substantive duties as a director or auditor, such director or auditor still bears the legal liabilities prescribed in Articles 399, 401, 414, etc. of the Commercial Act; therefore, unless there are special circumstances such as that the shareholders’ meeting resolution appointing such director or auditor or determining such remuneration is void, or that such passive performance of duties differs from the content of duties contemplated when the director or auditor was appointed at the shareholders’ meeting and thus constitutes an act in breach of trust contrary to the resolution of appointment and the resolution for payment of remuneration adopted at the shareholders’ meeting, it is difficult to deny the status of such person as director or auditor or the validity of the right to claim remuneration determined by the shareholders’ meeting resolution solely on the ground of such passive performance of duties.\\n\\nHowever, even if the right to claim remuneration is recognized in relation to the passive performance of duties by a director or auditor, remuneration for directors and auditors is paid as consideration for their performance of duties (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision dated November 22, 1977, 77DA1742), and a reasonable proportional relationship must be maintained between the counter-performance provided by such director or auditor to the company and the remuneration received by such director or auditor. Accordingly, where the remuneration is excessive beyond a reasonable level to the extent that it markedly loses balance, or where there are special circumstances such as that the person was appointed as a director or auditor solely as a means of paying company funds to an individual in the form of remuneration, exercise of the right to claim remuneration should be restricted in whole or in part, and the company may seek return of the remuneration paid in excess of the scope deemed reasonable. At this time, whether the right to claim remuneration is restricted and the scope of such restriction should be determined by comprehensively considering various circumstances revealed in the pleadings, such as the content of the benefit provided by the director or auditor performing duties passively, or the degree of duty performance, the amount of remuneration received and the company’s financial condition, the difference from the remuneration of directors, etc. who perform substantive duties, and the purpose of appointing a director or auditor who performs duties passively, as well as the necessity of such appointment and maintenance of qualification.\\n\\nb. The court below found that (1) ① Mega Golf & Leisure Consulting Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Mega Golf”) was a special purpose company established by Busan Savings Bank Co., Ltd. in order to carry out a real estate development project; ② Defendant 1 was appointed as a director of Mega Golf and received a total of KRW 25,040,638 from around April 2009 to around June 2011 as salary, etc., and Defendant 2 was appointed as an auditor of Mega Golf and received a total of KRW 69,670,000 from March 2006 to March 2011 as salary, etc., but they did not perform substantive duties as a director or auditor and merely handled ancillary tasks arising from their names as director or auditor; and then, (2) in light of such factual circumstances and the amounts of money received by the Defendants, the money received by the Defendants should be deemed not as consideration for performing duties as a director or auditor, but as consideration for lending their names, and therefore, even if the Defendants did not perform duties according to such office, it is difficult to regard the consideration received pursuant to the name-lending agreement as lacking legal cause and thus as constituting unjust enrichment, and it could not be denied as a right to claim remuneration based on Article 686(2) of the Civil Act concerning the mandatary’s right to claim remuneration in light of the contents of the entrusted affairs; and meanwhile, (3) for the reasons stated in the judgment, it determined that even if there was an agreement under which a corporate officer of a stock company would not perform substantive decision-making and business execution and would instead receive consideration for lending his or her name, such agreement could not be regarded as contrary to good morals and other social order to the extent that it would negate its private-law effect.\\n\\nc. Examining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the foregoing legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, although the Defendants did not actively perform duties according to their offices as directors and auditors, they were appointed as directors and auditors at a shareholders’ meeting, broadly delegated their duties to another director, and handled ancillary tasks arising from their names as director or auditor, and they are deemed to bear the legal liabilities prescribed in Articles 399, 401, 414, etc. of the Commercial Act. Thus, it is inappropriate for the court below to have treated the money paid to the Defendants under the name of remuneration not as consideration for such passive performance of duties but merely as consideration for lending their names, and to have based its judgment on that premise. Nevertheless, unless there are other circumstances recognizing that the shareholders’ meeting resolution appointing the Defendants as directors and auditors or the resolution for payment of remuneration was void, or that such passive performance of duties differed from the content of duties contemplated when the directors and auditors were appointed at the shareholders’ meeting and thus constituted an act in breach of trust contrary to the appointment and remuneration resolutions adopted at the shareholders’ meeting, it cannot be said that the right to claim remuneration is denied solely on the basis of such passive performance of duties by the Defendants, nor that the agreement concerning such remuneration constitutes a juristic act contrary to good morals and other social order. Therefore, the conclusion of the court below, which rejected the Plaintiff’s argument that the money paid to the Defendants under the name of remuneration constituted unjust enrichment or that the agreement concerning such remuneration was void on the basis of the duties performed by the Defendants, is persuasive; and it cannot be said that there was an error affecting the judgment due to misapprehension of the principles concerning organs of a stock company and the corporate governance of a company, a director’s right to claim remuneration, a name-lending agreement, a juristic act contrary to public order and good morals under Article 103 of the Civil Act, or the mandatary’s right to claim remuneration under Article 686 of the Civil Act, as asserted in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. Concerning Ground 1 of the appeal\\nArticle 388 of the Commercial Act provides, “If the amount of a director’s remuneration is not determined in the articles of incorporation, it shall be determined by a resolution of the shareholders’ meeting.” Article 415 of the Commercial Act applies the foregoing provision mutatis mutandis to auditors. The foregoing provisions are mandatory provisions, and where the articles of incorporation provide that the remuneration of directors and auditors shall be determined by a resolution of the shareholders’ meeting, if there is no evidence establishing that there was a shareholders’ meeting resolution concerning the amount, timing of payment, or method of payment, directors and auditors cannot claim remuneration (see Supreme Court Decision dated December 10, 2004, 2004DA25123; Supreme Court Decision dated May 29, 2014, 2012DA98720, etc.), and directors and auditors bear the burden of proving that such shareholders’ meeting resolution existed.\\n\\nNevertheless, contrary to this, the court below, on the erroneous premise that the Plaintiff must prove that there was no resolution by Mega Golf’s shareholders’ meeting concerning the amount of remuneration for the Defendants, rejected the Plaintiff’s argument that payment of remuneration to the Defendants by Mega Golf without a shareholders’ meeting resolution is void as being contrary to the mandatory provisions of the Commercial Act, on the ground that there was no evidence establishing that there was no shareholders’ meeting resolution determining the amount of remuneration.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below contains an error affecting the judgment due to misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the burden of proof regarding a shareholders’ meeting resolution determining the remuneration of directors or auditors. The grounds for appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\nHowever, in the case of a so-called one-person company, even if there was in fact no shareholders’ meeting, if minutes of the shareholders’ meeting were prepared as if a resolution had been adopted by the sole shareholder, the resolution may, absent special circumstances, be deemed to have been adopted in that content; and even if such minutes were not prepared, it may be deemed on the evidence that a shareholders’ meeting resolution was adopted. These legal principles may likewise apply to the shareholders’ meeting of a stock company that is substantially a one-person company (see the above-mentioned Supreme Court Decision 2004DA25123). Accordingly, if Mega Golf can be deemed substantially a one-person company as held in the court below’s judgment, it should be noted that, upon remand, the court below should also examine whether it may be deemed on the evidence that there was a shareholders’ meeting resolution regarding the payment of remuneration to the Defendants and the amount of such remuneration.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2018DA290436]": "The Court examines the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. As to the Defendant’s first through fourth grounds for appeal\\nA. Article 388 of the Commercial Act provides that the remuneration of directors shall be determined by a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders where the amount thereof is not fixed in the Articles of Incorporation. This is a mandatory provision intended to prevent the harm of a director seeking personal gain in relation to his or her own remuneration and to protect the interests of the company, its shareholders, and the company’s creditors. Accordingly, where the Articles of Incorporation provide that a director’s remuneration shall be determined by a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, the director may not exercise the right to claim remuneration unless there is evidence establishing that a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders was adopted concerning the amount, method of payment, timing of payment, etc. (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2012DA98720 rendered on May 29, 2014, Supreme Court Decision 2017DA17436 rendered on July 4, 2019). At this time, “a director’s remuneration” includes, regardless of designation such as salary, bonus, etc., all consideration paid as compensation for the performance of the director’s duties (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2015DA51968 rendered on May 30, 2018), and likewise includes monies paid by the company according to business performance under the name of performance-based bonus, special performance bonus, etc., or monies paid for the purpose of providing motivation to achieve performance.\\n\\nB. The court below determined as follows for the reasons stated in its opinion.\\n\\n1) The Plaintiff’s Articles of Incorporation provide that the remuneration of directors shall be determined by a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, and the monies that the Defendant, as the Plaintiff’s representative director, received from 2013 to 2014 under the name of “special performance bonus” (hereinafter referred to as the “Special Performance Bonus at Issue”) also constitute remuneration paid as compensation for the performance of duties.\\n\\n2) If, when the Defendant received the Special Performance Bonus at Issue, there was only decision-making by Nonparty, an inside director who was merely the major shareholder of the company, without a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, then such circumstance alone that a resolution would have been expected to be adopted even if a general meeting of shareholders had been convened cannot be regarded as equivalent to there having been a resolution. If the decision-making regarding payment of the Special Performance Bonus at Issue is invalid for failure to go through a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, then the circumstance that part of the Special Performance Bonus at Issue is within the limit amount of directors’ remuneration fixed by the general meeting of shareholders alone cannot mean that payment of that part is valid.\\n\\n3) Accordingly, the Special Performance Bonus at Issue paid to the Defendant constitutes unjust enrichment made without legal cause in its entirety.\\n\\nC. In light of the foregoing legal principles, the lower court’s foregoing determination does not contain any error of law, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning directors’ remuneration under Article 388 of the Commercial Act, resolutions of the general meeting of shareholders, or the limit amount of directors’ remuneration.\\n\\n2. As to the Defendant’s fifth ground for appeal and the Plaintiff’s grounds for appeal\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in its opinion, determined that, in this case where the Plaintiff deducted withholding tax amounts, including income tax, etc., and paid the Special Performance Bonus at Issue, the Defendant is obligated to return, as unjust enrichment, the amount actually paid to him excluding the withholding tax amounts. It also determined that the Defendant, as a bad-faith beneficiary, is liable to return the unjust enrichment with statutory interest accruing from the day after receiving the Special Performance Bonus at Issue.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the foregoing determination by the court below does not contain, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, any error of law such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning entitlement to claim a refund of withholding tax amounts or concerning a bad-faith beneficiary.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal are borne by the Plaintiff for the portion arising from the Plaintiff’s appeal and by the Defendant for the portion arising from the Defendant’s appeal, respectively. It is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, as per the disposition."}

{"[2018DA290436]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to Grounds 1 through 4 of the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. Article 388 of the Commercial Act provides that, if the amount of a director’s remuneration is not fixed in the articles of incorporation, it shall be determined by resolution of the shareholders’ meeting. This is a mandatory provision intended to protect the interests of the company, its shareholders, and the company’s creditors by preventing the harm of a director pursuing personal gain in relation to his or her own remuneration. Accordingly, where the articles of incorporation provide that a director’s remuneration shall be determined by resolution of the shareholders’ meeting, a director may not exercise the right to claim remuneration unless there is evidence establishing that a resolution of the shareholders’ meeting was adopted regarding the amount, method of payment, timing of payment, etc. thereof (see Supreme Court Decisions 2012DA98720, rendered on May 29, 2014, and 2017DA17436, rendered on July 4, 2019, among others). Here, “director’s remuneration” includes, irrespective of designation such as salary, bonus, etc., all consideration paid as compensation for the performance of a director’s duties (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DA51968, rendered on May 30, 2018, among others), and the same applies to monies paid by a company according to business performance under such designations as performance-based bonus or special performance bonus, or monies paid for the purpose of motivating the achievement of performance.\\n\\nb. The lower court determined as follows for the reasons stated in its opinion.\\n\\n1) The Plaintiff’s articles of incorporation provide that a director’s remuneration shall be determined by resolution of the shareholders’ meeting, and the monies that the Defendant received under the name of “special performance bonus” from 2013 to 2014 while serving as the Plaintiff’s Representative Director (hereinafter referred to as the “special performance bonus at issue”) also constitute remuneration paid as compensation for the performance of duties.\\n\\n2) If, when the Defendant received the special performance bonus at issue, there was only the decision-making of a non-party who was merely an in-house director and the controlling shareholder of the company, without a resolution of the shareholders’ meeting, such circumstances alone cannot be deemed equivalent to there having been a resolution merely because it is expected that a resolution would have been adopted even if a shareholders’ meeting had been convened. If the decision-making concerning the payment of the special performance bonus at issue is invalid because it was not subjected to a resolution of the shareholders’ meeting, the mere circumstance that part of the special performance bonus at issue falls within the limit on directors’ remuneration determined by the shareholders’ meeting cannot render the payment of that part valid either.\\n\\n3) Accordingly, the special performance bonus at issue paid to the Defendant constitutes unjust enrichment made without legal cause in its entirety.\\n\\nc. In light of the legal principles set forth above, the lower court’s above determinations do not contain any error of law, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning a director’s remuneration under Article 388 of the Commercial Act, a resolution of the shareholders’ meeting, or the limit on directors’ remuneration, as alleged.\\n\\n2. With respect to Ground 5 of the Defendant’s grounds of appeal and the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its opinion, the lower court determined that, in this case where the Plaintiff deducted withholding tax amounts, such as income tax, and paid the special performance bonus at issue, the Defendant is obligated to return as unjust enrichment the amount actually received, excluding the withholding tax amount. The lower court further determined that the Defendant, as a beneficiary in bad faith, is liable to return the unjust enrichment with statutory interest accruing from the day following the date on which he received the special performance bonus at issue.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determinations do not contain any error of law, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the attribution of the right to claim a refund of the withholding tax amount or concerning a beneficiary in bad faith, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the Plaintiff for the portion arising from the Plaintiff’s appeal and by the Defendant for the portion arising from the Defendant’s appeal, respectively. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated in the decision, as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[93DA8702]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Upon examining the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below in light of the record, the court below’s finding that the Defendant company was, in substance, a so-called one-person company in which Nonparty 1 owned all of its shares, and that the Plaintiff was merely a trustee in name only of the shareholding, is acceptable, and no illegality can be found therein for an erroneous finding of fact due to a violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged. The argument lacks merit.\\n\\n2. In the case of a stock company, where one person owns all of the total shares issued by the company, if that shareholder attends a general meeting of shareholders as the sole shareholder, the meeting is established as a meeting of all shareholders, and since it is clear that a resolution will be adopted in accordance with that shareholder’s intent, no separate convocation procedure for the general meeting is required; and even if there was in fact no general meeting held, if the minutes of the general meeting of shareholders were prepared to the effect that a resolution had been adopted by that sole shareholder, then, absent special circumstances, it may be deemed that a resolution in that content was adopted, and it cannot be contended that no resolution was adopted merely on formal grounds (see, inter alia, this Court’s Decision of 1976.4.13. rendered 74DA1755, and Decision of 1992.6.23. rendered 91DA19500, etc.).\\n\\nIn light of this purport, the court below also correctly determined that, because the Defendant company is in substance a one-person company and the intent of its sole shareholder, the above-mentioned Nonparty 1, is itself the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, even if in fact the general meeting of shareholders was not held after a lawful convocation procedure, once the minutes of the general meeting dated 1989.12.20. were prepared to the effect that a resolution was adopted, based on the intent of the above-mentioned Nonparty 1, to appoint Nonparty 2 as a director of the Defendant company, the above resolution itself cannot be said to fall within the case where it does not exist at all; and it cannot be said that there are grounds of illegality such as an error in legal principles, contradiction in reasons, or insufficiency of reasons, as alleged. This argument is also without merit.\\n\\nAnd an action for confirmation of the invalidity of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders is permitted only where the content of the resolution violates statutes or the articles of incorporation, and a resolution of the general meeting cannot be asserted to be void on the ground that the general meeting of shareholders lacked a lawful convocation procedure; accordingly, the argument criticizing the court below from the contrary view cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Also, as lawfully determined by the court below, it is as alleged that the board of directors of the Defendant company dated 1989.12.20. was not in fact held after a lawful convocation procedure; however, on the previous day, in the presence of all of the directors of the Defendant company, including the Plaintiff, and Nonparty 2, oral agreement was reached to the effect that the Plaintiff would resign as Representative Director and Director, that the above-mentioned Nonparty 2 would be appointed as the succeeding director, and that the above-mentioned Nonparty 1 would be appointed as the succeeding Representative Director; and accordingly, minutes of the above board of directors were prepared to the effect that a resolution was adopted appointing the above-mentioned Nonparty 1 as Representative Director, thereby completing the registration of a change in the corporate registration. If that is so, then even though the board of directors of the Defendant company was not held after a convocation procedure in accordance with statutes or the articles of incorporation, the matters agreed upon above should, absent any other special circumstances, properly be regarded as having validly come into existence as a resolution of the Defendant company’s board of directors. In the end, the court below’s determination to such effect is acceptable as correct, and no illegality of error in legal principles can be seen therein. This argument is likewise without merit.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are assessed against the losing party, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning companies under the Commercial Act is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Even where, in a limited company, the members’ meeting resolves to specify concretely the remuneration amount of a particular director, if the members’ meeting thereafter resolves to reduce that remuneration amount, the remuneration of the relevant director shall, unless there are special circumstances, be reduced in accordance with that resolution.
B: When a person intends to establish a limited liability company, a stock company, or a limited company, an application may be made for provisional registration of the trade name at the registry office having jurisdiction over the location of the principal office.
C: In a limited partnership, a general partner who has been adjudged to have lost the authority to execute business must newly be granted such authority under the articles of incorporation or with the consent of all partners in order to again have the authority to execute business or the authority to represent the partnership.
D: In a general partnership, whether there was intent or negligence in respect of an improper registration shall be determined on the basis of the representative partner.
E: A limited liability company may not acquire all or part of its equity interests, and where it acquires such equity interests, those equity interests shall be extinguished at the time of acquisition.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2016DA21643]": "The Court examines ex officio.\\n\\n1. In an action for declaratory judgment, the legal interest in seeking declaratory relief is recognized only when there exists an actual uncertainty or risk to the Plaintiff’s rights or legal status, and obtaining a declaratory judgment is the most effective and appropriate means of removing that uncertainty or risk (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 8, 2011, 2009DA67115).\\nMeanwhile, in a limited liability company, if the amount of remuneration of a specific director has been specifically determined by the articles of incorporation or by resolution of the members’ meeting pursuant to Articles 567 and 388 of the Commercial Act, such amount of remuneration becomes part of the appointment agreement and binds both the company and the director as parties thereto. Therefore, unless there are special circumstances warranting a finding that the director expressly consented to a change in remuneration, or at least implicitly consented to a change in remuneration resulting from a change in the content of duties, as in a case where the director took office while knowing that internal rules or practices existed concerning a remuneration system under which remuneration was paid differently according to the content of duties or was unpaid, the limited liability company may not unilaterally reduce or deprive the director of remuneration. Accordingly, even if the members’ meeting of a limited liability company passes a resolution to reduce or deprive a director of remuneration that has already been incorporated into the appointment agreement, such resolution of the members’ meeting does not affect the director’s right to claim remuneration, regardless of the effect of the resolution itself.\\n\\n2. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below and the record, it can be seen that the Plaintiffs, who are members and directors of the Defendant, a limited liability company, are seeking against the Defendant a declaration of nullity of the resolution reducing remuneration at issue, contending that the Defendant’s holding of a members’ meeting on December 30, 2014, and passing a resolution to reduce the Plaintiffs’ remuneration from KRW 2,500,000 per month to KRW 1,200,000 per month (hereinafter referred to as “the resolution to reduce remuneration at issue”) was a unilateral reduction of remuneration only as to the Plaintiffs and is manifestly unfair and an abuse of the majority rule, and therefore void.\\n\\n3. However, in light of the legal principles set forth above, the resolution to reduce remuneration at issue cannot by itself have any effect on the Plaintiffs’ right to claim remuneration, which has already been incorporated into the appointment agreement. Accordingly, the Plaintiffs, in their capacity as members, cannot be deemed to be in a legal relationship bound by the resolution to reduce remuneration at issue, which is legally meaningless, nor can it be said that there is a risk that their interests as members will be infringed in light of the objective nature of the contents of the resolution. Nor, in their capacity as directors, do they themselves bear any obligation to comply with the above resolution and pay remuneration to themselves in a reduced amount. Moreover, the uncertainty that may arise for the Plaintiffs as parties to the appointment agreement is merely a matter concerning the factual and economic interest that the Defendant may not pay the remuneration reduced pursuant to the resolution to reduce remuneration at issue, and it cannot be deemed that any risk or uncertainty has been caused to the Plaintiffs’ rights or legal status. In addition, since the Plaintiffs’ seeking payment of the reduced remuneration from the Defendant would be a direct means of resolving the dispute surrounding the Plaintiffs’ right to claim remuneration, the request for a declaration of nullity of the resolution to reduce remuneration at issue cannot be regarded as the most effective and appropriate means of removing the Plaintiffs’ uncertainty and risk.\\nNevertheless, the court below, on the erroneous premise that the resolution to reduce remuneration at issue is void absent the director’s consent or justifiable grounds and that there is a legal interest in seeking a declaration of nullity of such resolution, accepted the Plaintiffs’ claim seeking a declaration of nullity of the resolution to reduce remuneration at issue for the reasons stated in its holding; this was an erroneous determination caused by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the legal interest in seeking declaratory relief.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without addressing the grounds of appeal, the part of the judgment of the court below concerning the claim for declaration of nullity of the resolution to reduce director remuneration is reversed, and since this part is sufficient for this Court to decide directly, the Court decides to render its own judgment: the first-instance judgment concerning this part is set aside, the action concerning this part is dismissed, and the total costs of litigation shall be borne by the Plaintiffs. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2018DA225289]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. a. The purpose of the system of a judicial declaration of loss of authority to execute business in a limited partnership company (Articles 269 and 205 of the Commercial Act) is to remove impediments to the operation of the company by depriving a managing partner, who is markedly unsuitable for executing business or who has committed a serious violation of duty, of such authority. A judgment declaring the loss of authority of a managing partner is a constitutive judgment, and once that judgment becomes final and binding and the authority to execute business is lost, the authority to represent is also lost as a result (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on April 26, 1977, 75DA1341). If, in a limited partnership company, a general partner loses the authority to execute business and the authority to represent due to a judgment declaring the loss of authority to execute business, then the mere circumstance that, thereafter, for some reason, that general partner became the sole general partner of the limited partnership company does not mean that the effect of the judgment declaring the loss of authority to execute business, which is a constitutive judgment, is automatically extinguished or that the general partner’s authority to execute business and authority to represent are revived.\\n\\nb. In order for a general partner who has been declared to have lost the authority to execute business in a limited partnership company to again acquire the authority to execute business or the authority to represent, such authority must be newly granted under the articles of incorporation or with the consent of all partners (Articles 273, 269, 201(1), and 207 of the Commercial Act). A provision in the articles of incorporation of a limited partnership company that authorizes only general partners to appoint a managing partner or a representative partner is valid, and remains valid even if, due to subsequent circumstances, there is only one general partner, unless special circumstances exist. However, where a general partner who has lost the authority to execute business and the authority to represent by a judgment of a court upon the request of a limited partner is thereafter the sole general partner because another general partner has died and withdrawn from the company, it is proper to regard that the general partner who lost the authority to execute business cannot, on the basis of the above articles of incorporation, exercise voting rights alone and appoint himself or herself as a managing partner or representative partner. This interpretation accords with the purpose of the system of judicial declaration of loss of authority to execute business, with the protection of the limited partner’s right to supervise the management of the business, and with the principle of good faith. In the end, in such a case, the relevant general partner may be appointed as a managing partner or representative partner only by the consent of all partners, including the limited partners.\\n\\n2. According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. The Defendant is a limited partnership company established on June 28, 1979, for the purpose of operating taxicab passenger transportation business, etc., and as of May 29, 2009, the Defendant’s general partners were the Plaintiff and Nonparty 1.\\n\\nb. Nonparty 2 and Nonparty 3, who were limited partners of the Defendant, filed, on June 10, 2009, a claim against the Plaintiff, who was then the Defendant’s managing partner and representative partner, seeking a declaration of loss of authority to execute business, and on December 13, 2012, a judgment declaring that the Plaintiff had lost the authority to execute business became final and binding (hereinafter referred to as the “judgment in this case”).\\n\\nc. Nonparty 1 died on May 12, 2014, and as a result, the Plaintiff became the sole general partner of the Defendant.\\n\\nd. Article 18 of the Defendant’s articles of incorporation provides: “From among the general partners, one chairman and representative managing executive director, one executive director, and one managing director shall be elected as the executive officers by resolution of the meeting of the general partners.” Based on the above article of incorporation, the Plaintiff, who was the sole general partner, held a meeting of the general partners alone on June 10, 2015, and adopted a resolution appointing himself as the Defendant’s managing partner and representative partner (hereinafter referred to as the “resolution in this case”).\\n\\n3. Examining the above facts in light of the foregoing legal principles, where the Plaintiff, who was a general partner, was declared by the judgment in this case to have lost the authority to execute business, the mere circumstance that Nonparty 1, another general partner, died and withdrew from the company, thereby making the Plaintiff the sole general partner of the Defendant, does not mean that the effect of the judgment in this case is extinguished and the Plaintiff’s authority to execute business and authority to represent are revived. Nor is the resolution in this case, adopted by the Plaintiff alone based on Article 18 of the Defendant’s articles of incorporation, effective absent the consent of all partners, including the limited partners. In the end, the mere circumstance that the Plaintiff became the sole general partner of the Defendant or that the resolution in this case was adopted does not mean that the Plaintiff became the Defendant’s managing partner or representative partner.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below determined, for the reasons stated in its judgment, that the Plaintiff was in the position of the Defendant’s managing partner and representative partner. The judgment below contains an error that affected the judgment, including misapprehending the legal principles concerning the effect of the judgment in this case declaring the loss of authority to execute business. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and a new determination, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

question: A issued a promissory note to B for the purpose of facilitating B’s financing, and B endorsed and transferred the note to C in order to discharge B’s debt for the price owed to C. Which of the following statements is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: If B, having satisfied the requirements under the Bills of Exchange and Promissory Notes Act, claims payment of the note amount from A, A may raise the accommodation-note defense.
B: If C, having satisfied the requirements under the Bills of Exchange and Promissory Notes Act, claims payment of the note amount from A, A may not raise the accommodation-note defense, even if C knew that it was an accommodation note.
C: Even if C acquired the note by an endorsement after maturity, A may not raise the accommodation-note defense.
D: If B, after achieving the purpose of facilitating financing, recovered the note from C, but did not return the note to A, cancelled his own endorsement, and then used it again with D, a third party, A may assert against D the defense of re-use of the accommodation note, even if D did not know without negligence that the note was an accommodation note and that it was being used again after having already been used and having fulfilled its purpose.
E: If the maturity date of the note delivered by B to C is later than the due date for payment of the price debt, then, absent special circumstances, C should be deemed to have intended to defer payment of the antecedent debt to B.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2000DA57771]": "We consider the grounds for appeal (supplementary briefs on the grounds for appeal filed after the expiration of the period shall be considered only within the scope of supplementing the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. As to Point 2\\n\\nA material purchase guarantee, which the Defendant, pursuant to Article 8 of the former Construction Mutual Aid Association Act (repealed by Act No. 5230 on December 30, 1996), undertakes by receiving a guarantee fee from a member to guarantee the obligation to pay the price of goods borne when the member concludes a contract under which the member is to receive materials or other goods from another member or a third party, is, by its nature, a mutual insurance carried on for the mutual benefit of the members and is similar to guarantee insurance; accordingly, to that extent, the legal principles concerning insurance apply. Therefore, if the guarantee creditor has granted to a member an extension of the performance date to a date after the guarantee period, it cannot be said that the guarantee period under the Defendant’s guarantee contract is thereby naturally changed as well, and once the extended performance date falls after the guarantee period, even if the member fails to perform on the performance date under the principal contract as changed, this constitutes a guarantee event occurring after the guarantee period and thus does not fall within the grounds for payment of the guarantee amount. In addition, where a debtor delivers a bill or check to a creditor in connection with performance of an existing obligation, the parties’ intent, if there is a separate agreement, follows such agreement; if there is no agreement, it is proper to presume, depending on the specific circumstances, that it was delivered “for payment” or “for securing payment.” Where a bill delivered by a debtor to a creditor is a so-called “bank-discountable promissory note” and, between the parties, it is not merely held in safekeeping but may also be circulated to others by means such as discounting of the note, it is proper to presume that it was delivered “for payment.” And where a bill is presumed to have been delivered “for payment,” it should be deemed that the parties intended that the creditor would first exercise the bill claim, as opposed to the underlying claim, and obtain satisfaction therefrom; accordingly, the creditor may first exercise the bill claim and, only when satisfaction cannot be obtained thereby, may exercise the existing underlying claim against the debtor. Therefore, when a creditor receives a bill maturing on a date later than the due date of the existing obligation, absent special circumstances, it should be deemed that the creditor intended to defer payment of the existing obligation (see Supreme Court Decision 99DA24508, decided on Aug. 24, 1999; Supreme Court Decision 2000DA44829, decided on June 1, 2001; and others).\\n\\nThe lower court, by adopting the reasoning of the first-instance judgment, found the facts as stated in the judgment below, namely, that the contract for supply of goods in this case was concluded between the Plaintiff and Co-defendant at first instance Woorim General Construction Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Woorim Construction”), and that, in order to secure payment of the price of those goods, the Defendant issued to the Plaintiff the material purchase guarantee certificate in this case pursuant to the material purchase guarantee contract concluded between Woorim Construction and the Defendant, as well as the specific details of the supply of goods between the Plaintiff and Woorim Construction under the contract for supply of goods in this case, the records of payment of the goods price, and the records of outstanding receivables. It then held that, with respect to the total face amount of KRW 311,554,884 of the promissory notes ③ through ⑥ found in the judgment below, among the unpaid obligation to pay the price of goods in the amount of KRW 348,197,635, the due dates of which promissory notes are later than November 15 of the same year, which is the 90th day from the expiration date of the guarantee period in this case, August 17, 1997, the Plaintiff, by accepting from Woorim Construction, without any objection, promissory notes maturing after November 15, 1997, is to be regarded as having deferred the due dates of payment until the respective maturities of the promissory notes; therefore, as to this amount, the Defendant bears no guarantee liability pursuant to the proviso of Article 3 of the Standard Terms of the Material Purchase Guarantee.
