In light of the legal principles stated above and the record, this factual finding and determination by the lower court are persuasive, and there is no ground to deem it unlawful on the basis that it misapprehended the legal principles concerning the effect of rights under an existing obligation and under a bill or check where a bill or check is delivered in relation to performance of the existing obligation, or that it erred in fact by violating the rules of evidence.\\n\\nHowever, where, after the debtor has failed to pay the debt at the due date of the existing obligation and thus fallen into default, a bill is issued or endorsed for the payment of the existing obligation, absent special circumstances, it cannot be deemed that the due date of the existing obligation has been changed to the maturity date stated on the bill (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DA16367, decided on July 28, 2000; Supreme Court Decision 2000DA11560, decided on Mar. 23, 2001; and others), but it is clear that this does not apply in the present case.\\n\\nThat is, according to the record, Article 2, Item 1 of the goods supply contract (Exhibit A No. 1) provides that Woorim Construction shall pay the price of goods in cash, by current account check, or by bank-discountable promissory note, and that the method of settlement and the due date for payment may be determined from time to time by the Plaintiff in consideration of market conditions, but, in principle, payment shall be made concurrently with the order of the goods; thus, as a matter of the wording, the price is to be paid first and the time of ordering is treated as the due date for payment of the goods price. However, looking at the actual method of settlement of the goods price, there were no advance payments, and after goods were supplied on credit (sold), settlement was made, as contemplated in the goods supply contract, not only in cash but also by post-dated checks and promissory notes; and it can be seen that, when the Plaintiff received post-dated checks or promissory notes, it deducted discount charges calculated by applying a certain interest rate to the face amount, or, without calculating delay damages corresponding to the date of settlement of the check or note, treated the face amount as having been paid once such check or note was settled. Accordingly, there is room to conclude that, at the time the promissory notes in this case were delivered, Woorim Construction’s obligation to pay the price of goods to the Plaintiff was not in default.\\n\\nThe grounds for appeal disputing this point are not accepted.\\n\\n2. As to Point 1\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the first-instance judgment cited by the lower court, the lower court determined that the content of the material purchase guarantee made by the Defendant association for the Plaintiff was to guarantee performance of the obligation to pay the price of goods supplied within the guarantee period, while limiting the due date for performance of that obligation to within 90 days from the expiration date of the guarantee period, and, taking this into account, to receive a guarantee fee proportionate to the rate of such fee and the guarantee period, that is, the number of days of the risk period. In view of the fact that, if goods are merely supplied within the guarantee period, imposing guarantee liability unconditionally regardless of when the due date for performance of the obligation to pay the price of those goods falls would result in the Defendant association not being able to escape its guarantee liability until the principal debt is fully performed, thereby unreasonably increasing or expanding the Defendant association’s guarantee liability, the court held that Article 3 of the Standard Terms of the Material Purchase Guarantee in this case, which provides that “the guarantee amount to be paid by the Defendant association shall be the amount of unrecovered receivables at the due date prescribed in the principal contract, up to the limit of the guaranteed amount stated in the guarantee certificate. Provided, however, that even as to the price of materials supplied within the guarantee period, no guarantee liability shall be borne for obligations whose payment due date exceeds 90 days from the day following the expiration date of the guarantee period,” cannot be deemed void as falling under Article 6 of the Act on the Regulation of Terms and Conditions. In light of the purport of Article 6 of the Act on the Regulation of Terms and Conditions and the record, this determination by the lower court is proper (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DA11560, decided on Mar. 23, 2001; Supreme Court Decision 2000DA7820, decided on June 1, 2001; and others), and it cannot be said that there is any illegality in the form of a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the effect of standard terms.\\n\\nThe grounds for appeal disputing this point are likewise not accepted.\\n\\n3. As to Point 3\\n\\nThe lower court rejected, for the reasons stated in the judgment below, the Plaintiff’s following assertions: that, in a situation where receivable debts were increasing due to Woorim Construction’s financial difficulties, at the beginning of November 1997, before the expiration of the extension date of the guarantee period, the employee of the Defendant association in charge, Non-Party, explained to the Plaintiff’s employee and Woorim Construction’s representative director, etc., that guarantee liability would be borne on the basis of the date of the goods transaction; and therefore, an agreement was formed between the Plaintiff and the Defendant that, so long as the date of the goods transaction fell within the guarantee period, guarantee liability would be borne regardless of whether bills or checks maturing after the guarantee period had been delivered; or that, even if Non-Party had no authority to conclude such an agreement, apparent agency was established; or that the Defendant bore employer liability for such unlawful act by Non-Party. In light of the record, this measure by the lower court is proper, and there is no ground to deem it unlawful on the basis that it erred in fact by violating the rules of evidence.\\n\\nThe grounds for appeal disputing this point are also not accepted.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[79DA479]": "We examine the grounds of appeal submitted by counsel for the Plaintiff.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, based on the evidence cited in its opinion, found that the Defendant issued and delivered to the non-party two promissory notes, with both the place of payment and the place of issue being Busan City and the place of payment being the Sasang Branch of Busan Bank, namely, (1) a promissory note dated 1977.7.2 with a face value of KRW 1,000,000 and a due date of August 2 of the same year, and (2) a promissory note dated April 23 of the same year with a face value of KRW 1,000,000 and a due date of June 23 of the same year; that the said non-party, with respect to the note in item (1), arbitrarily altered the aforesaid due date to August 28, 1977, then again to October 2 of the same year, and again to November 6 of the same year, and thereafter endorsed and transferred it to the Plaintiff on September 27 of the same year; that with respect to the note in item (2), the said non-party altered the aforesaid due date to October 30 of the same year and thereafter endorsed and transferred it to the Plaintiff on October 24 of the same year; that the Plaintiff transferred the note in item (1) to the non-party Seo Deuk-gyu, and Seo Deuk-gyu presented it to the Defendant for payment on November 7, 1977, but upon refusal of payment the Plaintiff recovered it; and that with respect to the note in item (2), presentment for payment was made by service of a duplicate of the complaint in this case; and the court below further determined that the Plaintiff acquired the said notes by post-maturity endorsement, and that the Defendant had issued the said notes as so-called accommodation notes solely for the convenience of the non-party in borrowing money, without any underlying consideration relationship with the non-party. On that basis, the court below held that a post-maturity endorsement has only the effect of assignment of a designated claim, and that, in the issuance of so-called accommodation notes as in this case, the usual practice in transactions is that, where the payee has attained the purpose of finance by using the note, there exists an agreement between the issuer and the payee that funds for payment will be supplied until maturity, or that the note will be recovered and returned to the issuer; therefore, where the payee has recovered the note, unless there is a separate manifestation of intent between the parties, the payee may not use the note again for financing purposes, and accordingly, where the payee transfers the note to a third party by post-maturity endorsement, the drawer’s personal defense against the payee that payment of the note amount may be refused is not cut off, and the legal principle is that such defense may also be asserted against the said third party regardless of whether the third party acted in good faith or bad faith; thus, the court below concluded that the Defendant, who issued accommodation notes to the non-party, was under no obligation to pay the note amount to the Plaintiff, who acquired the notes by post-maturity endorsement.\\n\\nComparing this with the record, it is admitted that the Defendant issued the said notes to the non-party as so-called accommodation notes solely for the convenience of the latter’s borrowing of money, without any underlying consideration relationship, and that the said non-party, after repeatedly altering the due dates of the said notes as recognized above, endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff by post-maturity endorsement; therefore, there is no violation of the rules of evidence or insufficiency of examination as alleged, and the argument on this point is without merit.\\n\\nHowever, under the factual findings of the court below as stated above, it is not found that the said non-party, after receiving issuance of the said notes from the Defendant as accommodation notes and using them for financing purposes, recovered them and then again endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff by post-maturity endorsement; nor can the record be said to contain decisive material establishing such fact. (The court below’s established fact that the said non-party altered the due dates of the said notes several times as recognized above and then endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff does not, by itself, permit the conclusion that the said non-party used the notes for financing purposes at each original due date or altered due date, recovered them, and then again endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff; and according to the record, among the testimony of the witness Shin Jeong-ung in the first instance, there is a statement to the effect that he knew the said non-party had unlawfully circulated the note in item (1) by turning it around here and there and altering the due date on the note at maturity as recognized above, but according to the result of the first instance court’s inspection of the record, it can be seen that the said non-party received and held the said notes, and after the due dates had passed, altered the due dates as recognized above and then endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff; accordingly, the witness’s testimony, namely the meaning of “turning it around here and there,” cannot readily be regarded as meaning that there was an endorsement and transfer again after recovery upon attainment of the purpose of accommodation, and in light of the result of the inspection of the record it is difficult to believe it at first sight, and there is no other evidence to establish such fact.)\\n\\nIn my view, a person who issues a promissory note (a so-called accommodation note) for another’s financing or debt security does not bear liability on the note against the accommodated party, which is clear; however, such circumstance may be asserted only against the accommodated party, and since it was issued with the intent to assume liability on the note vis-à-vis a third party who acquired the note, it may not be asserted as a defense (personal defense) that the note was an accommodation note issued without consideration, even if the third party acquired it in good faith or bad faith or by post-maturity endorsement (see Supreme Court Decision 65DA1217, decided August 31, 1968, and Supreme Court Decision 69DA975,976, decided September 30, 1969). Where a note has been altered, the person who affixed his name and seal before the alteration shall bear liability according to the original wording before alteration (Bills of Exchange and Promissory Notes Act Articles 77 and 69). According to the lawful factual findings of the court below, the Defendant, who issued the accommodation note in this case, cannot assert against the Plaintiff, a third party who acquired the note, that it was an accommodation note or rely on reasons such as post-maturity endorsement; nevertheless, the court below, contrary thereto, held that the Defendant, as the issuer of the accommodation note, could refuse payment of the note amount to the Plaintiff, the post-maturity transferee of the note. This is ultimately not only a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning accommodation notes, but also the court below, premising its holding on facts other than the established facts that the Defendant issued the said notes to the said non-party as accommodation and that the Plaintiff acquired them by post-maturity endorsement, namely on the factual premise that the said non-party received the said notes, used them for financing purposes, recovered them, and then endorsed and transferred them again to the Plaintiff, rendered a judgment on the basis of facts not established. That is, the judgment premised on facts not established, namely whether the said non-party received the notes in this case for financing accommodation, recovered them, and then again endorsed and transferred them, constitutes insufficiency of examination and failure to state reasons, or inconsistent reasons, and since such points affected the outcome of the judgment, the grounds of appeal to the extent that they include such purport can ultimately be deemed well-founded. On this point, the judgment of the court below cannot avoid being reversed.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and in order to have this case retried and determined, it is remanded to the court below, the collegiate division of the Busan District Court. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in this case."}

{"[79DA479]": "We examine the grounds of appeal submitted by the Plaintiff’s litigation representative.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below, based on the evidence set forth in its opinion, found that the Defendant issued and delivered to the non-party two promissory notes, with both the place of payment and the place of issue as Busan City, and the place of payment as the Sasang Branch of Busan Bank, namely, (1) a promissory note dated 1977.7.2 with a face amount of KRW 1,000,000, due on 8.2 of the same year, and (2) a promissory note dated 4.23 of the same year with a face amount of KRW 1,000,000, due on 6.23 of the same year; that the said non-party, with respect to the note under item (1), altered the above due date at will first to 1977.8.28, then again to 10.2 of the same year, and then again to 11.6 of the same year, and thereafter endorsed and transferred it to the Plaintiff on 9.27 of the same year; that with respect to the note under item (2), the said due date was altered to 10.30 of the same year and then, on 10.24 of the same year, it was endorsed and transferred to the Plaintiff; that the Plaintiff transferred the note under item (1) to the non-party Seo Deuk-gyu, and Seo Deuk-gyu presented it for payment to the Defendant on 1977.11.7, but when payment was refused, the Plaintiff recovered it; and that with respect to the note under item (2), presentment for payment was made by service of a duplicate of the complaint in this case; and after determining that the Plaintiff acquired the said notes by overdue endorsement, and that the Defendant issued the said notes as so-called accommodation notes solely for the purpose of facilitating the non-party’s borrowing of money, without any consideration relationship with the non-party, the court below held that an overdue endorsement has only the effect of an assignment of a nominative claim, and that in the case of issuance of so-called accommodation notes as in this case, the general practice in transactions is that, between the issuer and the payee, there is an agreement that when the payee uses the note to achieve the purpose of financing, funds for payment will be supplied until maturity, or the note will be recovered and returned to the issuer; therefore, when the payee has recovered the note, absent any special manifestation of intent between the parties, the payee cannot again use the note for financing purposes, and accordingly, in the case where the payee transfers the note to a third party by overdue endorsement, the issuer’s personal defenses against the payee are not cut off, and such defense may be asserted against the said third party regardless of whether he acted in good faith or bad faith; thus, the court below determined that the Defendant, who issued the accommodation notes to the non-party, has no obligation to pay the amount of the said notes to the Plaintiff, who acquired them by overdue endorsement.\\n\\nComparing this with the record, the finding that the Defendant issued the said notes to the non-party as so-called accommodation notes solely for the purpose of facilitating the latter’s borrowing of money, without any consideration relationship, and the finding that the said non-party altered the due dates of the said notes several times as recognized above and then endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff, are both proper; and there is no violation of the rules of evidence or insufficiency of deliberation as argued, so the argument on this point is without merit.\\n\\nHowever, in the above facts found by the court below, it is not found that the said non-party received the said notes from the Defendant as accommodation notes, used them for financing purposes, recovered them, and then again endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff by overdue endorsement, and there is no conclusive evidence in the record to support such facts either. (From the court below’s above-determined facts, namely, that the said non-party altered the due dates of the said notes several times as recognized above and then endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff, it is not possible to conclude that the said non-party used the said notes for financing purposes at their original due date or at each altered due date, recovered them, and again endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff; and according to the record, among the testimony of the first-instance witness Shin Jeong-ung, there is a statement to the effect that the said non-party had passed around the note under item (1) and, on the maturity date, altered the payment due date on the note as recognized above and unlawfully circulated it, but according to the result of the first-instance court’s inspection of the record, it can be seen that the said non-party had received and kept the said notes, and when the due date had passed, altered the due date as recognized above and then endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff, so the witness’s testimony, namely, that he had passed it around, cannot readily be understood to mean that there had been endorsement and transfer again for the purpose of accommodation after recovery upon achieving the accommodation purpose; moreover, in light of the result of the inspection of the record, it is difficult to readily credit it, and there is no other evidence establishing that fact.)\\n\\nIt is considered that a person who issues a promissory note (so-called accommodation note) for the financing of another person or as security for another’s debt does not bear liability under the note vis-à-vis the accommodated party; however, such a cause may be asserted only against the accommodated party, and because the note is issued with the intent to assume liability under the note vis-à-vis a third party who acquires it, even if the third party is in good faith or bad faith, or if the acquisition was by overdue endorsement, the issuer cannot assert as a personal defense that it was an accommodation note issued without consideration (see Supreme Court Decision 65DA1217, decided 1968.8.31, and Supreme Court Decision 69DA975, 976, decided 1969.9.30). In cases where there has been an alteration of a note, the signer and sealer before the alteration shall be liable according to the original text before alteration (Promissory Note Act Articles 77 and 69). According to the properly found facts of the court below, the Defendant, who issued the accommodation notes in this case, should be deemed unable to assert against the Plaintiff, a third party who acquired the notes, the fact that they were accommodation notes or any ground such as overdue endorsement; nevertheless, the court below, contrary to this, determined that the Defendant, the issuer of the accommodation notes, could refuse to pay the amount of the said notes to the Plaintiff, the acquirer after maturity. This was not only a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning accommodation notes, but also a judgment premised on facts other than the facts definitively found by the court below, namely, on the assumption that the said non-party had received the said notes from the Defendant as accommodation notes, used them for financing purposes, recovered them, and again endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff; that is, a judgment premised on facts not definitively established, namely, whether the said non-party had received the notes in this case for accommodation financing, recovered them, and then again endorsed and transferred them. Such judgment constitutes incomplete deliberation and insufficiency of reasons, or contradiction in reasons, and as these points would have affected the outcome of the judgment, the grounds of appeal that include such purport are ultimately well-founded. On this point, the judgment of the court below cannot avoid being reversed.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and in order to have this case deliberated and determined anew, it is remanded to the court below, the Collegial Division of the Busan District Court, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the judges concerned."}

{"[79DA479]": "We examine the grounds for appeal by the Plaintiff’s litigation representative.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, based on the evidence set forth in its opinion, found that the Defendant issued and delivered to the third party two promissory notes, both stating Busan City as the place of payment and place of issue and Busan Bank Sasang Branch as the place of payment: (1) a note dated 1977.7.2, face value KRW 1,000,000, due date 8.2 of the same year; and (2) a note dated 4.23 of the same year, face value KRW 1,000,000, due date 6.23 of the same year; that the said third party, with respect to the note in item (1), arbitrarily altered the due date to 1977.8.28, then again to 10.2 of the same year, and then again to 11.6 of the same year, and thereafter endorsed and transferred it to the Plaintiff on 9.27 of the same year; and that with respect to the note in item (2), the due date was altered to 10.30 of the same year, and thereafter it was endorsed and transferred to the Plaintiff on 10.24 of the same year; that the Plaintiff transferred the note in item (1) to one Seo Deuk-gyu, and Seo Deuk-gyu presented it for payment to the Defendant on 1977.11.7, but when payment was refused, the Plaintiff took it back; and that with respect to the note in item (2), the Plaintiff presented it for payment by service of a duplicate of the complaint in this case; that the Plaintiff acquired the said notes by endorsement after maturity, and that the Defendant, without any consideration relationship with the third party, issued the said notes merely for the purpose of facilitating the third party’s borrowing of money, as so-called accommodation notes; and after making these findings, held that an endorsement after maturity has only the effect of assignment of a designated claim, and further, in the issuance of so-called accommodation notes as in this case, it is the general reality of transactions that there is an agreement between the issuer and the payee that, when the payee has achieved the purpose of finance by using the note, the issuer will supply funds for payment until maturity, or that the note will be recovered and returned to the issuer; therefore, when the payee has recovered the note, unless there is a separate manifestation of intent between the parties, the payee cannot use the note again for the purpose of finance, and thus, where the payee has transferred the note to a third party by endorsement after maturity, the personal defenses of the issuer against the payee are not cut off, and such a defense may be asserted also against that third party regardless of whether the third party acted in good faith or bad faith; accordingly, the court below determined that the Defendant, who issued the accommodation notes to the third party, is under no obligation to pay the bill amounts to the Plaintiff, who acquired them by endorsement after maturity.\\n\\nComparing this with the record, the factual findings that the Defendant issued the said notes to the third party as so-called accommodation notes solely for the convenience of the latter’s borrowing of money, without any consideration relationship, and that the said third party endorsed and transferred the said notes to the Plaintiff after altering the payment due dates several times as acknowledged above, are proper, and it cannot be said that there is a violation of the rules of evidence or an incomplete examination as alleged; accordingly, the argument on this point is without merit.\\n\\nHowever, the above factual findings of the court below do not recognize that the said third party received the said notes from the Defendant as accommodation notes, used them for the purpose of finance, then recovered them and again endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff after maturity; nor can there be said to be any clear basis in the record supporting such fact (the court below’s established facts, namely that the said third party altered the payment due dates of the said notes several times as acknowledged above and then endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff, alone do not justify concluding that the said third party used the said notes for the purpose of finance at their original due dates or at each altered due date, then recovered them and again endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff; and, according to the record, among the testimony of Witness Shin Jeong-woong at the first instance, there is a statement to the effect that the said third party had been passing around the note in item (1) and, by the maturity date, knew that the payment due date on the note had been altered as acknowledged above and unlawfully put it into circulation, but according to the results of the first-instance court’s examination of the record, it can be seen that the said third party received and kept the said notes, and after the payment due date had passed, altered the payment due dates as found above and then endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff; therefore, the witness’s statement, namely “passing around here and there,” cannot readily be taken to mean that, after recovery upon accomplishment of the purpose of accommodation, there was again endorsement and transfer for the purpose of accommodation, and in light of the results of the record examination it is not readily credible, and there is no other evidence proving that fact).\\n\\nIt is clear that a person who issued a promissory note for another person’s finance or for security of a debt, i.e., a so-called accommodation note, does not bear liability on the note to the accommodated party, but such a reason may be asserted only against the accommodated party; and since the note was issued with intent to bear liability on the note vis-à-vis a third party who acquired it, such third party cannot be opposed by the defense that it was an accommodation note issued without consideration, regardless of whether the third party was in good faith or bad faith or whether the acquisition was by endorsement after maturity (personal defense) (see Supreme Court Decisions 65DA1217, decided 1968.8.31, and 69DA975, 976, decided 1969.9.30); and where a bill has been altered, the signatory before alteration shall be liable according to the original wording before alteration (Articles 77 and 69 of the Bills of Exchange and Promissory Notes Act); therefore, according to the above lawful factual findings of the court below, the Defendant, the issuer of the accommodation notes in this case, should be deemed unable to oppose the Plaintiff, a third party who acquired the said notes, on the ground that they were accommodation notes or on the ground of endorsement after maturity. Nevertheless, the court below, contrary to this, determined that the Defendant, the issuer of the accommodation notes, may refuse to pay the bill amounts to the Plaintiff, the acquirer after maturity of the said notes; this is ultimately not only a misapprehension of the legal principle concerning accommodation notes, but also, since the court below based its determination on facts other than the established facts that the Defendant issued the said notes to the said third party by way of accommodation and that the Plaintiff acquired them by endorsement after maturity, namely on the premise that the said third party received the said notes, used them for the purpose of finance, then recovered them and again endorsed and transferred them to the Plaintiff, its determination was premised on facts not established, that is, it was a determination premised on facts not established as to whether the said third party received the notes as financial accommodation, recovered them, and then again endorsed and transferred them after receiving financial accommodation; such a determination is an incomplete examination and a deficiency of reasons, or a contradiction in reasons, and since these points affected the result of the judgment, the grounds of appeal to the extent that they include this purport are ultimately well-founded, and on this point the judgment of the court below cannot escape reversal.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and this case is remanded to the Busan District Court Collegiate Division, the court below, for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged as per the order by the unanimous opinion of the judges participating."}

{"[94DA50489]": "Regarding the grounds of appeal\\n\\n1. A person who issues a promissory note for the financial accommodation of another or as security for another’s debt (so-called accommodation bill) does not bear liability under the bill toward the accommodated party, but cannot oppose a third party who acquired the bill with the defense that it was an accommodation bill issued without consideration, regardless of whether that third party was in good faith or bad faith (see this Court’s Decision 93DA58721, decided on 1994.5.10., and Decision 79DA479, decided on 1979.10.30.).\\n\\nHowever, where the accommodated party, in exchange for the accommodation bill, delivered to the accommodation provider, as security, a promissory note in an amount equal to the face value of the accommodation bill, if a third party who acquired the accommodation bill knew, at the time of acquisition, that the bill had been issued as an accommodation bill and that the security note delivered in exchange therefor had been dishonored, then it should be deemed that the issuer of the accommodation bill may also oppose that third party with the defense of accommodation bill (see the above-mentioned Decision 93DA58721 and this Court’s Decision 89DAKA20740, decided on 1990.4.25.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, a person who endorsed a bill before its transfer, then canceled the endorsement, and transferred the bill again is not liable for recourse as an endorser, but there is no change in the fact that he was the person entitled under the bill who transferred the right as predecessor of the current holder of the bill; and as to the cause that could not be asserted against the person to whom the bill was transferred because that person was in good faith at the time of acquiring the bill, even if the current holder of the bill knew of that cause at the time of acquiring the bill, it cannot be asserted against the current holder on that basis (see the above-mentioned Decision 93DA58721 and the above-mentioned Decision 89DAKA20740).\\n\\n2. According to the facts lawfully determined by the court below, the non-party received the bill in this case, issued by the Defendant, from the Defendant for the purpose of raising funds, and, as security, issued and delivered to the Defendant seven bills and checks issued by the non-party Kyungmin Textile Co., Ltd., of which he was the representative director; thereafter, after sequentially endorsing the bill in this case in his own name and in the name of the above-mentioned Kyungmin Textile Co., Ltd., he endorsed and transferred the bill in this case to the non-party Shinyang Mutual Credit Association Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the non-party Association) and obtained a discount; however, as the security bills and checks he had issued were dishonored, the Defendant did not receive payment of the bills and checks issued by the above-mentioned Kyungmin Textile Co., Ltd.; meanwhile, the non-party Association, after receiving payment of the amount of the bill in this case from the Plaintiff and canceling its own endorsement, transferred the bill in this case to the Plaintiff; and the Plaintiff presented it for payment two or three days after the due date, but payment was refused. According to this, although the endorsement of the non-party Association is canceled on the bill, in this case, for which there is no material in the record showing that the non-party Association, which was the previous holder of the bill as predecessor of the Plaintiff, knew at the time of acquisition that the bill in this case was an accommodation bill and that the security bills issued in exchange therefor had been dishonored, the Defendant’s defense of accommodation bill is cut off, and the Defendant cannot oppose the non-party Association on the basis of such circumstances; accordingly, even if the Plaintiff, who acquired the bill in this case from the non-party Association, knew of such circumstances, the Defendant cannot oppose the Plaintiff on the basis of such reason.\\n\\nUltimately, the court below, by taking a different view and accepting the Defendant’s defense of accommodation bill against the Plaintiff solely on the ground that the Plaintiff knew of the above circumstances, erred by misunderstanding the legal doctrine on accommodation bills and the cut-off of personal defenses thereon, thereby affecting the conclusion of the judgment; the grounds of appeal on this point are well-founded.\\n\\n3. Accordingly, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged by the concurrence of the judges involved."}

question: A is a non-listed stock company. Its directors are A, B, and C, among whom A is the representative director, and B and C are outside directors. On the shareholder register, out of Company A’s total issued shares, D holds 0.8% of the shares, and E holds 3% of the shares. A violated statutes and regulations in the course of share cancellation for a reduction of stated capital, and as a result, Company A suffered damage. Thereafter, the board of directors of Company A prepared a merger agreement in order to merge with Company B and convened a general meeting of shareholders for approval of the agreement. Shareholder E opposes the merger and seeks to exercise the right to demand the purchase of shares. Which of the following statements is not correct? (Do not consider simplified mergers or small-scale mergers; if there is a dispute, follow case law.)
A: Company A may claim compensation for the damage against A even before a judgment invalidating the reduction of stated capital becomes final and binding, and A is liable for delay from the time the claim is received.
B: If Company A does not pursue A’s liability, D may, together with E, request Company A to file an action to pursue A’s liability.
C: If B and C, despite there being grounds to suspect that A’s share cancellation act was unlawful, negligently breached their duty of supervision and thereby left it unattended, they are liable to compensate for the damage suffered by Company A as a result.
D: In order for E to demand the purchase of shares, E must notify Company A in writing of its intention to oppose the resolution approving the merger agreement before the general meeting of shareholders for approval of the merger agreement.
E: Even if E exercises the right to demand the purchase of shares and receives payment of the share purchase price from Company A, E may exercise the right to inspect the accounting books against Company A within 2 months from the expiration of the period for demand for purchase.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2011DA57869]": "The grounds for appeal are determined as follows.\\n\\n1. Regarding Ground of Appeal No. 1\\nCommercial Act Article 403(1) provides: “A shareholder holding shares amounting to at least 1/100 of the total number of issued shares may demand that the company institute an action to pursue the liability of directors.” Article 403(2) of the same Act provides: “The demand under Paragraph (1) shall be made in writing stating the reasons therefor.” Article 403(3) of the same Act provides: “If the company does not institute an action within 30 days from the date on which it receives the demand under the preceding paragraph, the shareholder under Paragraph (1) may immediately institute an action for the company.” Article 403(5) of the same Act further provides: “Even where the shares held by a shareholder who instituted an action under Paragraphs (3) and (4) fall below 1/100 of the total number of issued shares after the filing of the action (excluding cases where the shareholder no longer holds any issued shares), this shall not affect the effectiveness of the filing of the action.” In addition, Article 191-13(1) of the former Securities and Exchange Act (repealed by Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the Act on Capital Markets and Financial Investment Business, Law No. 8635, of 2007. 8. 3.; hereinafter referred to as the “former Securities and Exchange Act”) provides: “A person who has continuously held, for six months, shares amounting to at least 1/10,000 of the total number of issued shares of a listed company on the stock market or a KOSDAQ-listed company, in the manner prescribed by Presidential Decree, may exercise the rights of a shareholder prescribed in Article 403 of the Commercial Act.”\\n\\nConsidering these provisions comprehensively, where multiple shareholders jointly institute a shareholders’ derivative suit, it is sufficient that, when they demand that the company institute an action to pursue the liability of directors and when they institute such action for the company, the number of shares they hold in aggregate satisfies the shareholding requirement prescribed by the Commercial Act or the former Securities and Exchange Act; and after the filing of the action, it is permissible even if the number of shares held falls below that requirement. However, if some of the shareholders who instituted the derivative suit, due to reasons such as disposing of their shares, come to hold no shares at all and thereby lose their status as shareholders, then, absent special circumstances, such shareholder loses standing as plaintiff, and the portion of the action instituted by that shareholder becomes unlawful; this cannot be deemed otherwise merely because the other plaintiffs who jointly instituted the derivative suit maintain their status as shareholders.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, at the time this action was filed, Plaintiff 2, Plaintiff 7, Plaintiff Tiger Asia Ltd., and Plaintiff Tiger Asia Fund LLC held issued shares of Shinsegae Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Shinsegae”), but before the conclusion of oral argument in the court below they disposed of all such shares, and at the time of the conclusion of oral argument in the court below they did not hold any issued shares of Shinsegae.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, these factual circumstances mean that the above Plaintiffs, after the derivative suit was filed, came to hold no issued shares of Shinsegae at all and thus lost standing in this case.\\n\\nThe court below’s determination that the portion of this action instituted by the above Plaintiffs is entirely unlawful is proper, and there is no error of law in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the requirements for filing a shareholders’ derivative suit, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. Regarding Ground of Appeal No. 2\\nFormer Commercial Act Article 398 (before amendment by Act No. 10600 of 2011. 4. 14.; hereinafter referred to as the “former Commercial Act”) requires approval by the board of directors for transactions between a director and the company, because the purpose is to prevent a director from using his or her position to deal directly with the company or, for the director’s own benefit, to engage in transactions between the company and a third party, thereby pursuing the director’s own interests and causing damage to the company or its shareholders (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DA71271, rendered on 2010. 3. 11.). Accordingly, for the above provision to apply, the director or the other party to the transaction with the third party must be the relevant company to which the director owes a duty of care of a prudent manager or a duty of loyalty in the performance of duties. Meanwhile, where a subsidiary has engaged in a transaction with a director of the parent company, even if the parent company owns all shares of the subsidiary, the parent company and the subsidiary are separate legal persons under the Commercial Act; and even if there is a disadvantage arising from the transaction, such disadvantage inures only to the subsidiary, while the parent company merely receives indirect effects, so the subsidiary’s transaction cannot be immediately treated as identical to the parent company’s transaction. Therefore, a transaction between a director of the parent company and the subsidiary does not constitute, in relation to the parent company, a transaction governed by former Commercial Act Article 398, and the director of the parent company is not required to obtain approval from the parent company’s board of directors with respect to that transaction.\\n\\nThe court below recognized that Defendant 1 was a director of Shinsegae at the time of the issuance of the new shares in this case, that Gwangju Shinsegae Department Store Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Gwangju Shinsegae”) and Shinsegae were independent and separate legal entities, and that the issuance and subscription of the new shares in this case took place between Defendant 1 and Gwangju Shinsegae after a resolution to waive subscription rights had been made by Shinsegae’s board of directors; and then held that the issuance and subscription of the new shares in this case is difficult to regard as self-dealing by a director in relation to Shinsegae, and that this cannot be viewed differently merely because Shinsegae was the parent company holding all shares of Gwangju Shinsegae.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above, the court below’s judgment in this regard is proper and persuasive, and there is no error of law in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the requirements for the establishment of self-dealing by a director, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Regarding Ground of Appeal No. 3\\na. The purpose of Commercial Act Article 397(1), which provides that “A director shall not, without approval of the board of directors, engage in transactions falling within the category of business of the company for his or her own account or for the account of a third party, or become a general partner with unlimited liability or a director of another company engaged in the same line of business,” is to prohibit competition that is highly likely to infringe the company’s interests by enabling a director to use his or her position to pursue personal interests, and thereby to ensure that directors fulfill their duty to operate the company effectively and appropriately with the care of a prudent manager and to perform their duties faithfully (see Supreme Court Decision 92DA53583, rendered on 1993. 4. 9.). Therefore, a director must obtain approval from the board of directors of the company to which he or she belongs not only when becoming a director or representative director of a competing company, but also when becoming the controlling shareholder of that company so as to be able to participate in that company’s decision-making and business execution. Meanwhile, if a company is engaging in transactions falling within the category of business of the company to which the director belongs, the mere fact that at that time the two companies are operating in different business regions does not by itself mean that they are not in a competitive relationship. However, if, in light of the overall circumstances of the transaction, such as the shareholding structure and control structure of the two companies, their business forms, whether they use identical or similar trade names or trademarks, and whether they are recognized as competitors in the market, the company whose status as a competitor is at issue is in substance being operated as a branch or business unit of the company to which the director belongs and is in a relationship of pursuing common interests, then there can be no room to regard there as being a conflict of interests between the two companies. In such a case, if a director acquires shares of the other company and thereby seeks to become its controlling shareholder, it is difficult to view approval by the board of directors, as prescribed by Commercial Act Article 397, as necessary.\\n\\nb. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following circumstances can be ascertained.\\n\\n(1) Gwangju Shinsegae was a subsidiary established by Shinsegae to operate department stores and the like in Gwangju Metropolitan City, and Shinsegae held all of its shares. From around 1995, it operated department stores and the like using Shinsegae’s trademark. From the time of Gwangju Shinsegae’s establishment, Shinsegae, through contract, acted as purchasing agent for goods and managed general corporate affairs, thereby effectively operating Gwangju Shinsegae as if it were a branch of Shinsegae located in Gwangju Metropolitan City, and it was also perceived externally in that manner.\\n\\n(2) After the foreign exchange crisis that occurred at the end of 1997, Gwangju Shinsegae experienced difficulties in financing and operating the company due to increased financial costs, and in order to resolve this it carried out the capital increase at issue in consultation with Shinsegae. However, Shinsegae itself was unable to participate in the capital increase due to the need for restructuring, and Defendant 1 came to acquire 83.3% of Gwangju Shinsegae’s shares through the issuance and subscription of the new shares in this case on 1998. 4. 23.\\n\\n(3) Defendant 1 was the son of Non-Party Person, the controlling shareholder of Shinsegae, and was a person in a special relationship with Shinsegae; thus there was no reason to separately manage Gwangju Shinsegae from Shinsegae or to compete with Shinsegae. In fact, although Shinsegae lost its status as controlling shareholder and became the second largest shareholder due to Defendant 1’s subscription of the new shares in this case, Gwangju Shinsegae still belonged to the same corporate group as Shinsegae.\\n\\n(4) Even after Defendant 1’s subscription of the new shares in this case, Gwangju Shinsegae continued to use the same trademark as Shinsegae, entrusted Shinsegae with the purchasing agency for goods to be sold, cooperated with Shinsegae while receiving the same management guidance as before, and Shinsegae, as before the subscription of the new shares in this case, received from Gwangju Shinsegae an annual fixed amount of management fees in return for trademark use and management guidance.\\n\\nc. In light of these circumstances and the legal principles stated above, Gwangju Shinsegae must be regarded as having been operated, even after Defendant 1’s subscription of the new shares in this case, substantially as a branch of Shinsegae just as before; and, upon examining the record as well, there is no material to support the view that Defendant 1 engaged in transactions through Gwangju Shinsegae that raised concerns of conflict of interests with Shinsegae. Therefore, even if Defendant 1 became the controlling shareholder of Gwangju Shinsegae through the subscription of the new shares in this case, it is difficult to view that approval by Shinsegae’s board of directors was required with respect thereto pursuant to Commercial Act Article 397.\\n\\nAlthough the reasoning stated in the judgment of the court below is not without some inappropriate points, the court below’s rejection of the Plaintiffs’ argument on this point is, in conclusion, proper, and there is no error affecting the outcome of the judgment, such as misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the establishment of a competitive relationship or erroneously finding facts, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n4. Regarding Ground of Appeal No. 4\\nSince a director owes a duty of care of a prudent manager to the company, the director has fulfilled his or her duty as a director only when he or she faithfully performs that duty for the company in accordance with statutes and the articles of incorporation. If there is a business opportunity that may be profitable, the director must present it to the company so that the company may take advantage of it, and must not use it for the benefit of himself or herself or a third party without the company’s approval. However, if the company’s board of directors, having collected and analyzed sufficient information and made a decision for the company’s interests through proper procedures, abandons such business opportunity or approves a director’s use of it, then, unless there is a manifest irrationality in the decision-making process, the business judgment of the directors who adopted such resolution should be respected. In such a case, even if some director comes to use such business opportunity, neither that director nor the directors who participated in the board’s approving resolution can be said to have violated their duty of care of a prudent manager or duty of loyalty as directors.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of these legal principles, the court below’s determination, on the grounds stated in its opinion, that it is difficult to view Defendant 1 as having appropriated Shinsegae’s business opportunity is not without some inappropriate points in the statement of reasons, but it is ultimately proper and persuasive; and there is no error affecting the outcome of the judgment, such as misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the requirements or procedures under which a director may acquire a business opportunity of the company or erroneously finding facts, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n5. Regarding Ground of Appeal No. 5\\nThe court below, based on the circumstances stated in its opinion, held that it was insufficient to conclude that the new shares in this case were issued at a significantly low price, and that even if the new shares in this case were issued at a somewhat low price, such circumstance alone was insufficient to conclude that Defendants’ decision not to subscribe was manifestly unreasonable and that they thereby neglected their duties as directors.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the record, the court below’s determination in this regard is proper and persuasive. Moreover, that determination is understood to include the view that, although the new shares in this case were a large-scale issuance involving the transfer of control, and despite this they were issued at a significantly low price, the Plaintiffs’ argument that the Defendants, as directors of Shinsegae, had a duty to ensure that, even if Shinsegae waived its subscription rights, Gwangju Shinsegae would not allot the shares to a third party at the same price, was rejected. Therefore, it cannot be said that the judgment of the court below contains any illegality, such as omission of a determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated in the case, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2017DA270916]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Regarding the Defendant’s grounds for appeal\\n\\na. Regarding the grounds of appeal concerning the permissibility and scope of inspection and copying\\n\\n(1) In the case of a shareholder’s request for inspection and copying of a company’s accounting books and documents, etc., as provided in Article 466(1) of the Commercial Act, the company may refuse the request by proving that it is unreasonable. Whether the shareholder’s exercise of the right of inspection and copying is unreasonable must be determined by comprehensively considering all relevant circumstances, such as the circumstances leading to the exercise, the purpose of the exercise, and the presence or absence of bad faith. In particular, where the shareholder’s exercise of such right of inspection and copying would impair the operation of the company’s business or the common interests of the shareholders, or where there is a risk that the shareholder, as a competitor of the company, will use the information obtained for competition, or where the shareholder exercises the right by choosing a time that is excessively disadvantageous to the company, it should be deemed unreasonable for lack of a proper purpose (see Supreme Court Order dated December 24, 2004, 2003MA1575; Supreme Court Order dated July 21, 2014, 2013MA657; etc.). Meanwhile, even a shareholder who has exercised the right to demand purchase of shares retains the status of a shareholder until the company pays the purchase price for such shares; therefore, absent special circumstances, where it is necessary to exercise shareholder rights, such shareholder has the above right of inspection and copying of accounting books and documents. Where a shareholder deems it necessary to exercise shareholder rights, not only for determining the purchase price of shares but also for pursuing liability through a derivative action against directors of the company, or for seeking injunctive relief or dismissal, such request, absent special circumstances, is made for the purpose of supervising the company’s management and protecting the interests of the company and its shareholders. Accordingly, the mere circumstance that the shareholder has exercised the right to demand purchase of shares does not mean that the request is unreasonable for lack of a proper purpose.\\n\\n(2) According to the reasons of the judgment below and the lawfully admitted evidence, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n(a) The Defendant is a company established around July 1999 by Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 for the purpose of manufacturing concrete admixtures and engaging in wholesale and retail sales, and the Plaintiff is a shareholder holding 100,000 of the 482,000 shares issued by the Defendant.\\n\\n(b) On February 18, 2001, the Plaintiff entered into a partnership agreement concerning the operation of the Defendant (hereinafter, “the partnership agreement at issue”) with Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2, lent a total of KRW 247,000,000 to the Defendant from February 2009 to June 2011, and served as the Defendant’s auditor from March 25, 2010 to March 31, 2013.\\n\\n(c) Around October 2013, the Plaintiff demanded that the Defendant submit minutes of shareholders’ meetings and board of directors meetings, accounting materials, and the like, alleging that the Defendant had not paid the remuneration stipulated in the partnership agreement at issue and had not provided inspection and copying of accounting books, but the Defendant did not comply.\\n\\n(d) ① On December 4, 2015, while the first-instance action in this case was pending, the Defendant notified the Plaintiff and other shareholders of the convocation of an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders with an agenda item to transfer the company site and factory facilities in order to abandon manufacturing and convert into a sales corporation, and the Plaintiff notified the Defendant on December 15, 2015, of its opposition to the transfer of the company site and factory facilities.\\n\\n② At the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders held on December 18, 2015, the Defendant approved the above agenda item, and on December 23, 2015, the Plaintiff demanded that the Defendant purchase the shares owned by the Plaintiff (hereinafter, “the shares at issue”).\\n\\n(e) On December 29, 2015, the Defendant effected registration of transfer of ownership, based on sale on the same date, in favor of the Nonparty Company with respect to 17,600 square meters of factory land at Asan-si ((Address 1 omitted)), 350 square meters of factory land at ((Address 2 omitted)), and factory buildings on each of the above parcels of land (hereinafter, the above parcels of land and buildings are collectively referred to as “the real property at issue”).\\n\\n(f) Meanwhile, when the Plaintiff and the Defendant failed to agree on the purchase price for the shares at issue on January 25, 2016, the Plaintiff filed an application for determination of the share purchase price with the Cheonan Branch of the Daejeon District Court, Case No. 2016BIHAP2000, and the case is currently pending.\\n\\n(3) The court below determined, on the grounds stated in its judgment, as follows.\\n\\n(a) Since the Plaintiff, after exercising the right to demand purchase of shares, has not yet received the purchase price for the shares at issue, the Plaintiff remains in the status of a shareholder and needs to inspect and copy the Defendant’s accounting books and documents necessary for determining the above share purchase price.\\n\\n(b) Even if the Plaintiff had previously exercised the right to request inspection and copying of accounting books before exercising the right to demand purchase of shares, the Plaintiff may newly exercise that right again according to the need arising from the subsequent exercise of the right to demand purchase of shares; and even if the Plaintiff filed an application with the court for determination of the share purchase price and brought multiple lawsuits against the Defendant, such necessity is not negated.\\n\\n(c) Accordingly, the court ordered the Defendant to permit the Plaintiff or its representative to inspect and copy the accounting books and documents listed in Appendix 3 attached to the judgment below (hereinafter, “Appendix”), and set compensation for violation at KRW 1,000,000 per day.\\n\\n(4) Examining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the legal principles stated above and the lawfully admitted evidence, the court below’s above determination does not contain any illegality, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning interest in the lawsuit, the shareholder and the scope of permissibility of inspection and copying under Article 466 of the Commercial Act, or abuse of rights. Meanwhile, the argument in the grounds of appeal to the effect that the subsidiary ledger by account is a document that is not currently prepared and does not exist is a new argument raised only at the appellate stage and cannot constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\nb. Regarding the grounds of appeal concerning the clarity of the operative part\\n\\n(1) The operative part of a judgment must be specified in its content and must be identifiable from the operative part itself (see Supreme Court Decision dated March 8, 1983, 82NU294, etc.).\\n\\n(2) According to the judgment below, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n(a) The operative part of the judgment below cites Appendix 3 as the accounting books and documents to be inspected and copied by the Defendant for the Plaintiff. Appendix 3 contains, under the heading “Accounting books and documents to be inspected and copied,” the phrase “for the purpose of preparing the Defendant’s provisional balance sheet as of November 30, 2015, during the period from January 1, 2012 to November 30, 2015,” followed by a specific enumeration of various accounting documents, and concludes with “etc. accounting documents,” and then, in parentheses, states: “Provided, however, that if each document listed in Items 2 and 3 of Appendix 2 also falls within the above accounting documents, it is included within that scope.”\\n\\n(b) Item 2 of Appendix 2 states, “Regarding transactions between the Defendant and MK Trading Co., Ltd.: (a) alternative slips and deposit/withdrawal vouchers related to the advance payments and payment commissions account titles, (b) contracts and other supporting documents and payment evidence revealing the specific details of the above advance payments and payment commissions, and (c) copies of bankbooks showing monetary transactions between the Defendant and MK Trading Co., Ltd.” Item 3 states, “copies of bankbooks showing transaction details of the account in the name of Nonparty 2, an inside director of the Defendant, at SC First Bank ((account number omitted)).”\\n\\n(c) However, among the accounting documents specifically enumerated in Appendix 3, copies of bankbooks are not listed.\\n\\n(3) In view of the above wording of the operative part, it is unclear whether the documents listed in Items 2 and 3 of Appendix 2 are included, regardless of their names, if they constitute accounting documents “for the purpose of preparing the Defendant’s provisional balance sheet as of November 30, 2015, during the period from January 1, 2012 to November 30, 2015” as stated in Appendix 3, or whether they are included only if their names correspond to one of the documents specifically enumerated as accounting documents in Appendix 3. In particular, it is unclear whether the copies of bankbooks described in Items 2 and 3 of Appendix 2 are included, and thus the scope of the accounting documents that the Defendant must allow the Plaintiff to inspect and copy cannot be specified.\\n\\nAccordingly, the above operative part lacks clarity and is therefore unlawful. The grounds of appeal pointing out this issue are well founded.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Plaintiff’s grounds for appeal\\n\\na. The court below, on the grounds stated in its judgment, determined that it was unreasonable for the Defendant to resist the Plaintiff’s request for inspection and copying of the accounting books and documents listed in Appendix 2, except for those stated in Appendix 3, on the ground that the Plaintiff, having exercised the right to demand purchase of shares, filed a shareholder derivative action against Nonparty 1 and others by challenging the transfer of the real property at issue and also filed an action to set aside a fraudulent act in order to preserve the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendant for the purchase price of the shares at issue.\\n\\nb. However, according to the reasons of the judgment below and the lawfully admitted evidence, the following circumstances may be found.\\n\\n(1) (a) On December 29, 2015, the Defendant sold the real property at issue, which had an appraised value of KRW 6,045,938,600 as of March 13, 2014, to the Nonparty Company for a sale price of KRW 3,800,000,000.\\n\\n(b) Nonparty 3, the representative director of the Nonparty Company, is the son of Nonparty 2, an inside director of the Defendant; its auditor is Nonparty 4, an inside director of the Defendant; and its head office is located at the same place as the Defendant’s head office.\\n\\n(2) According to the Defendant’s standard balance sheet, as of June 30, 2015, before the transfer of the real property at issue, the assets were KRW 9,082,069,386 and the liabilities were KRW 6,548,259,957, resulting in net assets of KRW 2,533,809,429. However, immediately after the transfer of the real property at issue, as of December 31, 2015, the assets were KRW 2,369,282,253 and the liabilities were KRW 2,466,595,421, such that the liabilities exceeded the assets by KRW 97,313,168, causing net assets to decrease by KRW 2,631,122,597.\\n\\n(3) Furthermore, the Defendant’s balance sheet prepared as of December 31, 2016 recorded assets of KRW 102,837,598 and liabilities of KRW 934,150,227, showing that liabilities exceeded assets by KRW 831,312,629.\\n\\n(4) (a) On November 29, 2016, the Plaintiff filed a shareholder derivative action against Nonparty 1, Nonparty 4, and others, who are the Defendant’s directors, with the Suwon District Court Pyeongtaek Branch, Case No. 2016GAHAP10447, seeking compensation for the damage these directors caused to the company by transferring the real property at issue (hereinafter, “the shareholder derivative action at issue”), and the lawsuit is currently pending.\\n\\n(b) The Plaintiff also filed an action to set aside a fraudulent act against the Defendant with the Seoul Central District Court, Case No. 2016GAHAP577448, on December 15, 2016, and that lawsuit is currently pending.\\n\\n(5) Meanwhile, the Plaintiff retired from public service as a tax official around July 2004 and has been engaged in tax practice ever since.\\n\\nc. Examining the above circumstances in light of the legal principles stated above, the following determination follows.\\n\\nThe Plaintiff exercised the right to demand purchase of shares but has not yet received the share purchase price and therefore still holds the status of a shareholder. The Defendant sold the real property at issue to the Nonparty Company, whose directors include persons in a special relationship with the Defendant’s directors, at a price far below market value, abandoned manufacturing, one of the Defendant’s principal purposes of establishment, and thereafter the Defendant’s financial condition deteriorated sharply.\\n\\nIn such circumstances, since the Plaintiff filed the shareholder derivative action at issue in order to pursue the liability of the directors as a shareholder, the Plaintiff has the right to request inspection and copying of the Defendant’s accounting books within the scope necessary to carry out the shareholder derivative action at issue by verifying the circumstances of the deterioration in financial condition shown in the Defendant’s financial statements through December 31, 2016.\\n\\nFurthermore, the mere facts that the Plaintiff exercised the right to demand purchase of shares and had previously brought multiple lawsuits against the Defendant before filing the shareholder derivative action at issue do not render the above request unreasonable. Nor is it easy to find that the Plaintiff, who is engaged in tax practice, would use the information obtained as a competitor of the Defendant for competition.\\n\\nd. Nevertheless, the court below, relying only on the factual circumstances contrary to the above, held that it was unreasonable for the Plaintiff to request inspection and copying of the Defendant’s accounting books for the purpose of the shareholder derivative action at issue. In so determining, the court below misapprehended the legal principles regarding a shareholder’s right to inspect and copy accounting books under Article 466 of the Commercial Act, and such error affected the judgment. The grounds of appeal pointing this out are well founded.\\n\\nHowever, the action to set aside a fraudulent act was brought by the Plaintiff in the capacity of a monetary creditor of the Defendant, not in the capacity of a shareholder. Accordingly, the court below’s determination that it was unreasonable for the Plaintiff to request inspection and copying of accounting books by relying on the filing of the action to set aside a fraudulent act is proper, and in that regard there is no illegality, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning a shareholder’s right to inspect and copy accounting books as alleged in the grounds of appeal, or any violation of the rules of logic and experience beyond the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nThe court omits determination on the remaining grounds for appeal, reverses the judgment below, and remands the case to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2018DA275888]": "The grounds of appeal are examined (the supplementary briefs for the grounds of appeal submitted after the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal are considered to the extent that they supplement them).\\n\\n1. Basic factual background\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the following facts may be found.\\nThe Defendant served as the representative director of Gyeonggi Savings Bank Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Gyeonggi Savings Bank”) from 2004. 2. 7. to 2007. 9. 10.\\nOn 2006. 8. 30., Gyeonggi Savings Bank extended a loan of 5 billion won to IHuman D&C Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “IHuman D&C”) (hereinafter referred to as “the loan in this case”), and the Defendant, as representative director, approved it. The loan in this case was a so-called project finance loan obtained by IHuman D&C for land acquisition, etc. while carrying out a new construction project for a mixed-use apartment complex in Dalseong-gun, Daegu (address omitted).\\nOn 2013. 7. 1., Gyeonggi Savings Bank was adjudged bankrupt by the Seoul Central District Court in Case No. 2013HAHAP88, and the Plaintiff was appointed as bankruptcy trustee. The Plaintiff, from 2013. 1. 21. to 2013. 4. 26., investigated whether Gyeonggi Savings Bank had made imprudent or improper loans in violation of the Mutual Savings Banks Act, the Standard Loan Regulations for Mutual Savings Banks, etc., and whether the persons concerned bore responsibility for such imprudent conduct, and determined that the loan in this case constituted an imprudent and improper loan.\\n\\n2. Whether there was a violation of the duty of care of a good manager, etc. (Grounds 1 to 4 of the grounds of appeal)\\na. An officer of a financial institution owes the duty of care of a good manager to the financial institution to which he or she belongs, and thus must faithfully perform that duty in order to fulfill his or her duties as an officer. Whether an officer of a financial institution has neglected his or her duties by violating the above duty of care of a good manager must be comprehensively determined, in light of various circumstances such as whether there was an error in the loan decision that a normal loan officer should not overlook, compliance with relevant regulations, the terms, contents, and scale of the loan, the repayment plan, the existence and content of collateral, the debtor’s property and business conditions, growth potential, etc. (see Supreme Court Decision 2001DA52407 decided on 2002. 6. 14., Supreme Court Decision 2006DA33609 decided on 2007. 7. 26.).\\nA so-called project finance loan is a financial transaction in which the feasibility of a specific real estate development project is evaluated and the future cash flow generated from the project is used as the primary source of repayment of the principal and interest of the loan; therefore, the assessment of repayment ability made at the time of the loan depends primarily on the evaluation of the project’s feasibility. In such a case, if a director of a financial institution, while reviewing the feasibility of the project as a condition for the loan, sufficiently collected, investigated, and examined the necessary information, and then, on that basis, reasonably trusted that the loan was in the best interests of the financial institution and made a business judgment in good faith, and if the content thereof was not manifestly unreasonable and fell within the range that could ordinarily be chosen by a director, then even if the company later suffered damage as a result, it cannot be said that the director bears liability for damages to the company. However, if the director of a financial institution did not perform his or her duties through such a process, but instead unilaterally performed the duties merely expecting that it would benefit the company’s business and thereby caused damage to the company, then it cannot be said that he or she made a business judgment, after sufficiently collecting, investigating, and examining the necessary information, reasonably trusting that it would be in the company’s best interests and acting in accordance with the principle of good faith; accordingly, such conduct by a director cannot be said to fall within the permissible scope of managerial judgment (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DA39935 decided on 2008. 7. 10., Supreme Court Decision 2009DA80521 decided on 2011. 10. 13.).\\nb. The lower court recognized the Defendant’s liability for damages as follows.\\n(1) Even if the loan in this case qualifies as a so-called “bridge loan,” which provides initial funds for the project, the feasibility or profitability of the project, the appropriateness of the sale price, the possibility of completion of the sales, and the expected scale of sales proceeds are important review factors in deciding whether to make the loan.\\n(2) It is difficult to say that the Defendant took all possible measures to recover the claim.\\nIHuman D&C was a corporation established around 2005. 4. with capital of 53,000,000 won and had no debt-repayment ability, as it had no sales, etc. The preferential beneficiary right established by IHuman D&C over the project site had a collateral appraised value of only about 743,000,000 won, and because the preferential beneficiary right is subject to repayment depending on the success or failure of the project, it is difficult to say that it has substantial collateral value. The Defendant formally obtained guarantees from the representative director, directors, and affiliated companies of IHuman D&C, who were joint and several guarantors, without investigating data on income or the status of assets, etc. The shares, project right transfer agreements, waivers of implementation rights, consents to change the name of the project operator, etc. provided by IHuman D&C had collateral value that depended on the success or failure of the project, so it is difficult to say that they had substantial collateral value.\\n(3) The Defendant appears to have made the loan in this case merely on the expectation that it would benefit the company’s business as a profitable loan, without establishing any specific measures for the liquidity risk of IHuman D&C, whose debt-repayment ability was uncertain, and without properly examining the feasibility of the project, etc.\\nHana Global Appraisal Co., Ltd. prepared a report reviewing the project feasibility before the loan in this case. The report stated that the project had no feasibility because the cost of acquiring the project site was excessively high, there were many unsold properties in the area of Dalseo-gu, Daegu, and the sale price proposed by IHuman D&C was excessively high, making it likely that there would be difficulties in sales.\\nThe Defendant proceeded with the loan in this case without further review or corrective measures in response. The Defendant did not properly review IHuman D&C’s project implementation record, permits and approvals, or sales possibility, and merely reviewed the project outline, etc. based on the project plan presented by IHuman D&C. The project in this case was in fact suspended after failing to obtain the necessary project permits and approvals from the competent authority less than six months after the loan in this case was made.\\nIt is difficult to conclude that the Defendant sufficiently examined the feasibility of the project merely on the basis of vague and abstract judgments that the accessibility or traffic conditions of the project site were good, or circumstances such as the fact that Samhwan Engineering & Construction Co., Ltd. was scheduled to participate as the contractor.\\nc. If the reasons of the judgment below are examined in light of the legal principles discussed above, the judgment below is proper, and there is no error that affected the judgment by, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, failing to conduct necessary examination, by going beyond the limits of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the adversarial system and trial on evidence, liability for non-performance of obligations, the duty of care of a good manager owed by officers of financial institutions, etc., or by inconsistency in the reasons.\\n\\n3. Commencement date for delay damages (Ground 5 of the grounds of appeal)\\na. Where no time for performance of an obligation is fixed, the obligor is liable for delay from the time a demand for performance is made (Civil Act Article 387(2)). An obligation to pay damages arising from non-performance of an obligation is, unless there are special circumstances, an obligation for which no time for performance is fixed; therefore, the obligor bears liability for delay from the time a demand for performance is made by the obligee (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DA22496 decided on 2017. 5. 31.).\\nUnder Article 399(1) of the Commercial Act, a director of a stock company’s liability for damages arising from neglect of duties owed to the company is liability for non-performance of obligations arising from the mandate relationship (see Supreme Court Decision 84DAKA1954 decided on 1985. 6. 25., Supreme Court Decision 2005DA51471 decided on 2008. 12. 11.).
