Accordingly, where a director of a stock company bears an obligation to compensate the company for damages pursuant to the above provision, he or she, unless there are special circumstances, bears liability for delay from the time a demand for performance is made.\\nb. According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts may be found.\\nThe Plaintiff alleged in the complaint that the Defendant bore liability for damages pursuant to Article 399(1) of the Commercial Act. In the first instance, the Plaintiff argued in response to the Defendant’s assertion of the statute of limitations that the Plaintiff’s claim for damages was based on Article 399(1) of the Commercial Act, and therefore the period of extinctive prescription was 10 years and the short statute of limitations prescribed in Civil Act Article 766(1) did not apply to the claim for damages arising from tort.\\nThe lower court, while citing the first instance judgment and recognizing the Defendant’s liability for damages, limited liability to 841,800,000 won, corresponding to 30% of the amount of damages, and determined that the Defendant was obligated to pay delay damages calculated at the rate of 5% per annum prescribed by the Civil Act from 2006. 8. 30., the date of the loan in this case, until 2016. 11. 8., when a duplicate of the complaint was served on the Defendant, and at the rate of 15% per annum prescribed by the Act on Special Cases Concerning Expedition, etc. of Legal Proceedings from the following day until the date of full payment.\\nc. Examining these factual circumstances in light of the legal principles discussed above, the following conclusion is reached.\\nIt may be said that the Plaintiff asserted against the Defendant the liability of a director of a stock company for damages to the company pursuant to Article 399(1) of the Commercial Act. This is an obligation to pay damages arising from non-performance of obligations, and, unless there are special circumstances, it is an obligation for which no time for performance is fixed; accordingly, the Defendant bears liability for delay from the time a demand for performance is made.\\nNevertheless, the lower court did not examine when the Defendant received a demand for performance and upheld the first instance judgment, which held that the Defendant was obligated to pay delay damages calculated at the rate of 5% per annum prescribed by the Civil Act on 841,800,000 won from 2006. 8. 30., the date of the loan in this case, until 2016. 11. 8., the date on which a duplicate of the complaint was served. The judgment below contains an error that affected the judgment by failing to conduct necessary examination or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the time when delay damages arise. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nAmong the judgment below, the portion adverse to the Defendant that ordered payment of the amount calculated at the rate of 5% per annum on 841,800,000 won from 2006. 8. 30. to 2016. 11. 8. is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination, and the remaining appeal is dismissed. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2021DA279347]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined (the contents of a written submission filed after the period for filing the statement of grounds for final appeal has elapsed are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\n1. Procedural History of the Case\\nAccording to the reasoning of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\nA. Status of the Parties\\n1) Daewoo Engineering & Construction Co., Ltd. (hereinafter, including this company, the designation “Co., Ltd.” is omitted from all company names) is a company engaged in civil engineering, construction, housing construction, and other business activities; as of 2011, its capital was approximately 2,078.1 billion won, sales approximately 7,031.8 billion won, operating profit approximately 364.8 billion won, net income for the period approximately 226.7 billion won, number of regular employees approximately 4,789, and its construction performance evaluation amount in civil engineering and building construction ranked 6th; the total number of issued shares was 415,622,638 shares.\\n\\n2) The Plaintiffs are shareholders who have owned shares issued by Daewoo Engineering & Construction since before 2013. 10.; the aggregate of those shares is 42,750 shares, which exceeds 1/10,000 of the total number of issued shares of Daewoo Engineering & Construction.\\n\\n3) The Defendants are persons who served as Representative Directors, inside directors, outside directors, and the like of Daewoo Engineering & Construction during all or part of the periods of each bid rigging incident to be examined below (hereinafter collectively referred to as “the bid rigging in this case”).\\n\\nB. Bid Rigging Relating to the First Turnkey Construction Works of Daewoo Engineering & Construction’s Four Major Rivers Restoration Project (hereinafter referred to as “the Four Major Rivers Project Bid Rigging”)\\n1) At the end of 2007, in order to promote the “Korean Peninsula Grand Canal Construction Project” as a private-finance project, Daewoo Engineering & Construction and four other major construction companies formed a joint venture consortium, and thereafter, after nine additional construction companies joined the consortium, an agreement was reached among the 14 construction companies that Daewoo Engineering & Construction would hold a 14.4% share in the “Korean Peninsula Grand Canal Construction Project” (Hyundai Engineering & Construction 15.4%; Samsung C&T, Daelim Industrial, and GS Engineering & Construction each 14.4%; and the remaining construction companies each 3.0%).\\n\\n2) On 2008. 6. 19., the Government declared the suspension of the “Korean Peninsula Grand Canal Construction Project” on grounds including deteriorating public opinion; on 2008. 12. 15., the National Balanced Development Committee decided to implement the suspended existing private-finance form of the “Korean Peninsula Grand Canal Construction Project” as the “Four Major Rivers Restoration Project,” a fiscal project funded by the national budget; and on 2009. 6. 8., the “Four Major Rivers Restoration Project” was finally confirmed and announced.\\n\\n3) Meanwhile, five additional construction companies joined the 14 construction companies, including Daewoo Engineering & Construction, that had formed the joint venture consortium for the “Korean Peninsula Grand Canal Construction Project,” and around 2009. 4., 19 construction companies agreed, with respect to the “Four Major Rivers Restoration Project,” that Hyundai Engineering & Construction would hold 9.0%; Samsung C&T, SK Engineering & Construction, Daelim Industrial, Daewoo Engineering & Construction, and GS Engineering & Construction would each hold 8.0%; POSCO E&C would hold 6.9%; Hyundai Development Company 6.0%; Kumho Industrial and Lotte Engineering & Construction would each hold 4.2%; and Hanwha Engineering & Construction and the remaining nine companies would each hold 3.3%.\\n\\n4) While the foregoing negotiations regarding shares were underway, the bidding for Geum River Section 1, a pilot project of the “Four Major Rivers Restoration Project,” was announced on 2009. 2. 9.; before that announcement, five construction companies, including Daewoo Engineering & Construction, who knew that Geum River Section 1 would be ordered as a fiscal project, agreed that Daewoo Engineering & Construction would be allocated Geum River Section 1; the bid was conducted on 2009. 4. 21., and around 2009. 5. Daewoo Engineering & Construction was selected as the successful bidder.\\n\\n5) Around the end of 2009. 4., when the 15 weirs to be constructed in the first turnkey construction works of the “Four Major Rivers Restoration Project” had been finalized, Daewoo Engineering & Construction and others, based on the above agreement regarding shares, reached an agreement that, among the 16 sections included in the pilot project of the “Four Major Rivers Restoration Project” (Geum River Section 1) and the first turnkey construction works, excluding the Yeongsan River sections (2 sections), for the remaining 14 sections Hyundai Engineering & Construction, Samsung C&T, SK Engineering & Construction, Daelim Industrial, Daewoo Engineering & Construction, and GS Engineering & Construction would each be allocated 2 sections, and POSCO E&C and Hyundai Development Company would each be allocated 1 section.\\n\\n6) The first turnkey construction works of the “Four Major Rivers Restoration Project” were first announced on 2009. 6. 29. and bidding was conducted around 2009. 9.; as a result, except that Doosan Engineering & Construction was selected as the successful bidder in place of Samsung C&T for Nakdong River Section 32, all eight companies including Daewoo Engineering & Construction that had participated in the section allocation were selected as successful bidders for the major sections that had been determined in advance.\\n\\n7) The Korea Fair Trade Commission, on the ground that the agreement among construction companies including Daewoo Engineering & Construction regarding shares in the “Four Major Rivers Restoration Project” as described above and the agreement regarding section allocation constituted unfair collaborative acts, etc. under Article 19(1)3 of the former Monopoly Regulation and Fair Trade Act (the version before the complete amendment by Act No. 17799 of 2020. 12. 29.; hereinafter referred to as the “former Fair Trade Act”), issued, on 2012. 8. 31., a corrective order and an order to pay a surcharge of 9.697 billion won against Daewoo Engineering & Construction.\\n\\n8) In response, Daewoo Engineering & Construction filed an action seeking revocation of the disposition; however, on 2014. 6. 13., it received a judgment dismissing the claim (Seoul High Court 2012NU29303), and although Daewoo Engineering & Construction filed a final appeal (Supreme Court 2014DU10394), it was dismissed on 2014. 10. 30.\\n\\n9) In addition, Daewoo Engineering & Construction and Defendant 1, who at the time served as Representative Director of Daewoo Engineering & Construction and oversaw management in general, were indicted on the charge that they violated Article 95(1), 95(3), and 98(2) of the Framework Act on the Construction Industry by engaging in the above agreement on section allocation and the bidding conduct thereunder; on 2014. 2. 6., Defendant 1 was sentenced to 1 year and 6 months’ imprisonment with a 2-year suspension of execution, and Daewoo Engineering & Construction was sentenced to a fine of 75 million won (Seoul Central District Court 2013GOHAP998), and that judgment became final and conclusive as entered.\\n\\nC. Bid Rigging Relating to Daewoo Engineering & Construction’s Yongju Multipurpose Dam Construction Project (hereinafter referred to as “the Yongju Dam Bid Rigging”)\\n1) The Korea Water Resources Corporation announced the order and bid notice for the Yongju Multipurpose Dam construction project on 2009. 7. 10., and the bid proceeded by the design-build turnkey method, with Daewoo Engineering & Construction and Samsung C&T each forming a joint venture consortium and participating in the bid, and both being selected as qualified bidders in the prequalification review for bid participation.\\n\\n2) Around 2009. 10. 1., Non-party 1, an assistant manager in charge of design work at Daewoo Engineering & Construction, met with Non-party 2, a department manager at Samsung C&T, and others and agreed, regarding the basic design for the above bid, that “1. The energy dissipation structure in the spillway shall be designed on the basis of a 200-year flood discharge. 2. The ecological bridge and fishway shall not be included in the design contents. 3. Only one set of sand discharge gates shall be reflected in the design. 4. The results of hydraulic model tests shall be included in the report submitted at the time of the bid.” and on 2009. 10. 8. prepared an agreement to that effect.\\n\\n3) On 2009. 11. 19., the bid opening results showed Samsung C&T selected as the qualified bidder (successful bidder) for the detailed design, and on 2009. 12. 30. it entered into a construction contract with the Korea Water Resources Corporation in the total contract amount of 221.43 billion won.\\n\\n4) The Korea Fair Trade Commission, on the ground that Daewoo Engineering & Construction, Samsung C&T, and others, in participating in the Yongju Multipurpose Dam construction bid, had in advance agreed whether to exclude or include certain processes and facilities in the basic design, etc. as unfair collaborative acts under Article 19(1)8 of the former Fair Trade Act, issued, on 2013. 3. 18., a corrective order and an order to pay a surcharge of 2.491 billion won against Daewoo Engineering & Construction.\\n\\n5) In response, Daewoo Engineering & Construction filed an action seeking revocation of the disposition (Seoul High Court 2013NU45081), and that court, on 2014. 9. 5., revoked only part of the corrective order and rendered a judgment dismissing Daewoo Engineering & Construction’s claims as to the remaining part of the corrective order and the surcharge portion; only the Korea Fair Trade Commission filed a final appeal, and thus the portion of the surcharge imposition order remained final and conclusive as entered.\\n\\nD. Bid Rigging Relating to Daewoo Engineering & Construction’s Incheon Metropolitan Subway Line No. 2 Construction Project (hereinafter referred to as “the Incheon Subway Bid Rigging”)\\n1) The Incheon Metropolitan Subway Line No. 2 construction project was divided into 16 sections from Section 201 to Section 216, and the bidding proceeded by the design-build turnkey construction method, and Daewoo Engineering & Construction participated in the bids for Section 207 and Section 209 of the Incheon Metropolitan Subway Line No. 2 construction project by forming a joint venture consortium.\\n\\n2) Around 2009. 1., Non-party 3, an assistant executive director in Daewoo Engineering & Construction’s Domestic Sales Division, contacted Non-party 4, a department manager in Hyundai Engineering & Construction’s Domestic Sales Division, and proposed that “Hyundai Engineering & Construction should participate as a dummy bidder in the bid for Section 207 that Daewoo Engineering & Construction is pursuing,” and Non-party 4, after an internal meeting, agreed.\\n\\n3) From around that time, Non-party 3 and Non-party 4 adjusted Hyundai Engineering & Construction’s design quality and bid price, and Hyundai Engineering & Construction submitted a design document prepared so as to receive a lower design score than Daewoo Engineering & Construction and bid at a price close to Daewoo Engineering & Construction’s bid price. Accordingly, in the bid for Section 207, in which Daewoo Engineering & Construction and Hyundai Engineering & Construction participated on 2009. 4. 17., Daewoo Engineering & Construction was selected as the successful bidder.\\n\\n4) Around 2009. 1., Non-party 5, the head of Daewoo Engineering & Construction’s Sales Team, received from Non-party 6, the head of SK Engineering & Construction’s Domestic Sales Team, a proposal that “Daewoo Engineering & Construction should participate as a dummy bidder in the bid for Section 209 that SK Engineering & Construction is pursuing,” and Non-party 5 agreed after an internal meeting at Daewoo Engineering & Construction. Thereafter, Non-party 5 and Non-party 6, and others, adjusted Daewoo Engineering & Construction’s design quality and bid price, and Daewoo Engineering & Construction submitted a design document prepared so as to receive a lower design score than SK Engineering & Construction and bid at a price higher than SK Engineering & Construction’s bid price. Accordingly, in the bid for Section 209, in which Daewoo Engineering & Construction and SK Engineering & Construction participated on 2009. 4. 17., SK Engineering & Construction was selected as the successful bidder.\\n\\n5) The Korea Fair Trade Commission, on the ground that Daewoo Engineering & Construction and others, in the bid for the Incheon Metropolitan Subway Line No. 2 construction project, had in advance selected the expected successful bidder and, at the same time, agreed that other business operators would formally participate in the bid so as to enable them to win the bid, and that the act of actually participating in the bid pursuant to that agreement fell under Article 19(1)8 of the former Fair Trade Act, decided on 2014. 1. 8. to file a criminal complaint against Daewoo Engineering & Construction and others, and on 2014. 2. 25. issued a corrective order and an order to pay a surcharge of 16.032 billion won against Daewoo Engineering & Construction.\\n\\n6) Daewoo Engineering & Construction was prosecuted for a violation of the Fair Trade Act on the ground that the above acts constituted unfair collaborative acts, and on 2014. 8. 20. was sentenced to a fine of 100 million won (Incheon District Court 2014GODAN2277, 2651); it appealed, but on 2015. 3. 20. received a judgment dismissing the appeal (Incheon District Court 2014NO2950), and that judgment became final and conclusive as entered.\\n\\nE. Background of the Plaintiffs’ Filing of this Action\\n1) On 2014. 4. 10., the Plaintiffs requested three audit committee members of Daewoo Engineering & Construction at the time to file an action for damages seeking to hold the directors liable pursuant to Article 403 of the Commercial Act.\\n\\n2) After receiving the request to file such action, Daewoo Engineering & Construction did not file an action for damages against the Defendants within 30 days, and the Plaintiffs filed this action on 2014. 5. 23.\\n\\n2. Relevant Legal Principles\\nWhere a director intentionally or negligently engages in an act in violation of laws, regulations, or the articles of incorporation, or neglects his duties, that director is jointly and severally liable to compensate the company for damages (Article 399(1) of the Commercial Act). Since a director of a stock company has a duty to supervise not only the duties in his own charge but also the execution of duties by the Representative Director or the director in charge of business operations, the director not only must personally comply with laws and regulations but also bears a duty to monitor and supervise the Representative Director or other directors in charge of business operations so that they perform their duties in compliance with laws and regulations. Such duty of monitoring and supervision is not to be viewed differently merely because the director is an outside director or otherwise not engaged in the ordinary business of the company. Accordingly, where a director of a stock company has grounds to suspect that the execution of duties by the Representative Director or a director in charge of business operations is unlawful, and yet, intentionally or negligently, violates the duty of supervision and leaves it unaddressed, he bears liability under Article 399(1) of the Commercial Act for the damages suffered by the company as a result.\\n\\nThe specific content of a director’s duty of supervision may vary greatly depending on the company’s size or organization, industry, legal regulations, business conditions, and financial status. In particular, even where, in a large company that is highly specialized and divided into many functions, it is unavoidable that only the Representative Director or some directors handle their respective specialized fields according to internal allocation of duties, all directors must, at minimum, perform their supervisory duty in a manner that, in light of the company’s purpose or size, the nature of its business, and legal regulations, etc., establishes and operates an internal control system capable of systematically identifying the relevant laws and regulations, managing compliance therewith, and, upon discovering a violation, immediately reporting or notifying it and taking corrective measures with respect to tasks in which a high legal risk is anticipated. (See, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2017DA222368 rendered on 2021. 11. 11.) However, for outside directors, etc. who are not responsible for the company’s business execution, where no internal control system has been established at all and they fail to make efforts such as urging the establishment of an internal control system, or where there are grounds to suspect that an internal control system, though established, is not properly functioning, and yet they turn a blind eye and leave it unaddressed, such conduct may be recognized as a breach of the duty of supervision.\\n\\n3. Determination on the Grounds for Final Appeal by the Defendants\\nA. Regarding whether Defendant 1 is liable for damages in relation to the Four Major Rivers Project bid rigging\\n1) For the reasons stated in its judgment, the court below determined that Defendant 1, as Representative Director of Daewoo Engineering & Construction, had sufficient grounds to suspect that its executives and employees were engaging in acts violating laws and regulations, including the Fair Trade Act, by colluding in the course of performing the duties of bidding for the Four Major Rivers Project, and yet negligently neglected this and thereby neglected his duties; accordingly, he is liable to compensate the damages suffered by Daewoo Engineering & Construction as a result.\\n\\n2) Defendant 1’s argument in this part of the grounds for final appeal merely criticizes the selection and weighing of evidence and the fact-finding, which fall within the exclusive province of the trier of fact, and therefore cannot be regarded as a legitimate ground for final appeal. Moreover, even upon examining the reasoning of the judgment below in light of the record, there is no error in that determination of the court below, such as exceeding the bounds of the free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, or misconstruing the legal principles concerning a director’s duty of supervision.\\n\\nB. Regarding whether liability for damages arises from the defendants’ breach of the duty of supervision in relation to the bid rigging in this case\\n1) The court below determined that, for the reasons such as those set forth below, even if the Defendants, as directors of Daewoo Engineering & Construction, had not been involved in or reported on the bidding operations for individual projects and thus did not know and could not have known about the bid rigging in this case, and even if there were no circumstances whatsoever that would have led them to suspect it, the Defendants breached their duty of supervision as directors by failing to fulfill the duty to establish and ensure that a reasonable information and reporting system and internal control system were properly operating in relation to illegal acts by executives and employees, including the bid rigging in this case.\\n\\n(a) At the time of the bid rigging in this case, Daewoo Engineering & Construction had enacted and implemented a code of ethics, ethics rules, and a code of corporate conduct, and had conducted ethics management education and Fair Trade Act education for subcontracting in the construction industry for its executives and employees. However, these were merely abstract and general guidelines or prior training concerning the performance of duties by executives and employees, and cannot be regarded as a mechanism for collecting and reporting information concerning illegal acts such as bid rigging where such acts are suspected or confirmed, much less as a device for controlling illegal acts; it appears that, at that time, no reasonable information and reporting system or internal control system whatsoever had been established internally to prevent or block attempts by executives and employees to engage in bid rigging.\\n\\n(b) According to the Defendants’ arguments, etc., all bid rigging in which Daewoo Engineering & Construction was involved, including the bid rigging in this case, was not reported to any director or the board of directors and was carried out by executives and employees belonging to individual divisions (Domestic Sales Division, Civil Engineering Division, etc.) under the responsibility of the head of the relevant division; thus, the executives and employees of Daewoo Engineering & Construction involved in the bid rigging in this case were effectively not subject to any restraint or check from the directors, including the Defendants, and Daewoo Engineering & Construction appears not to have operated any independent investigative procedure or disciplinary procedure with respect to the executives and employees involved in bid rigging; moreover, in statements made before investigative authorities, executives and employees of Daewoo Engineering & Construction stated not only that illegal acts such as bid rigging were being carried out as a matter of practice, but also that employees who led bid rigging were in fact promoted to executive positions. Such circumstances also support the conclusion that Daewoo Engineering & Construction had no internal control system at the time of the bid rigging in this case.\\n\\n(c) Daewoo Engineering & Construction had received multiple surcharge orders from the Korea Fair Trade Commission on the grounds of bid rigging occurring between 2006 and 2013, during the period in which all or some of the Defendants served as directors of Daewoo Engineering & Construction. Furthermore, with respect to the Seoul Subway Line No. 7 construction project bid rigging in which Daewoo Engineering & Construction was involved around 2004. 8., the Korea Fair Trade Commission, on 2007. 7. 25., issued a corrective order, a surcharge order, and a decision to file a criminal complaint; accordingly, Daewoo Engineering & Construction was prosecuted for violations of the Fair Trade Act, etc., and on 2008. 2. 14. a conviction and fine were imposed at first instance, and even while the Defendants were serving as directors of Daewoo Engineering & Construction, that case remained pending in the appellate or final appellate stage. Daewoo Engineering & Construction’s involvement in bid rigging, including matters that occurred before the Defendants assumed office as directors, was reported in most media outlets and became known to the public, and in the case of large-scale construction works ordered by the State, local governments, or public institutions, the construction companies capable of performing such works are limited to large construction companies ranked in the top tier of civil engineering and building construction performance evaluation amount such as Daewoo Engineering & Construction, so the possibility of unfair collaborative acts such as bid rigging among large construction companies can also be deemed to constantly exist. Nevertheless, the directors of Daewoo Engineering & Construction, including the Defendants, did not require any reports or measures to prevent or block attempts by executives and employees to engage in bid rigging, and paid no attention whatsoever to the establishment or operation of an internal control system in this regard.\\n\\n(d) Although the Supreme Court had already declared in 2008 that directors of large stock companies have a duty to establish a reasonable information and reporting system and internal control system and to manage them so that they operate properly (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DA68636 rendered on 2008. 9. 11.), the directors of Daewoo Engineering & Construction, including the Defendants, took no such measures. It was only after 2014, when all the Defendants had left office and multiple bid-rigging schemes were detected by the Korea Fair Trade Commission, that Daewoo Engineering & Construction established a compliance monitoring body known as the so-called Compliance Team.\\n\\n(e) It appears that, while serving as directors of Daewoo Engineering & Construction, the Defendants were involved only in matters placed before the board of directors and did not at all monitor or supervise the overall execution of the company’s business by exercising the authority of the board of directors under Article 393 of the Commercial Act, etc.\\n\\n2) In light of the legal principles discussed above and the record, the foregoing determination by the court below does not contain, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, any error of law regarding a director’s duty of supervision, etc.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Grounds for Final Appeal by the Plaintiffs\\nA. Where a director is liable to compensate the company for damages by intentionally or negligently engaging in an act in violation of laws, regulations, or the articles of incorporation, or by neglecting his duties, in determining the scope of damages to be compensated, the amount of compensation may be limited in light of the ideal of the damages system, namely equitable apportionment of loss, taking into account all circumstances such as the nature and characteristics of the relevant business, the circumstances of the director’s breach of duty and the manner of the breach, the objective circumstances and degree of the company’s damages and their expansion, the director’s usual contribution to the company, whether the director derived any gain from the breach, and whether there was any defect in the company’s organizational structure or whether a risk management system was established. In such a case, factual findings concerning the circumstances to be considered in limiting the amount of damages or the ratio for such limitation are within the exclusive province of the trier of fact unless they are manifestly unreasonable in light of the principle of equity (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2007DA34746 rendered on 2007. 10. 11.).\\n\\nB. The court below determined that: ① Defendants 1 and 2 served as Representative Directors at the time, and a Representative Director has authority to perform all acts, judicial and extrajudicial, concerning the company’s business and therefore bears a duty to supervise the execution of duties by all employees, so their responsibility for breach of the duty of supervision can be said to be heavier; ② in the case of Defendants 3 and 9, only part of the Four Major Rivers Project bid rigging and the Incheon Subway Bid Rigging had been implemented during their tenure; ③ in the case of Defendant 1, although he had sufficient grounds to suspect that illegal acts in violation of the Fair Trade Act, etc. were being committed in relation to the Four Major Rivers Project bid rigging and yet negligently left them unaddressed, the liability for damages borne by the Defendants, apart from this, stemmed not from an active breach of the duty of supervision but from failing to fulfill the duty to establish a reasonable information and reporting system and internal control system and to manage them so that they operated properly; ④ in the case of Defendants 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, and 10, they served as non-executive directors or outside directors and appear to have had little knowledge of Daewoo Engineering & Construction’s business or construction bidding; ⑤ the Defendants did not obtain any personal gain from breaching the duty of supervision, Defendant 1 was criminally punished for the Four Major Rivers Project bid rigging, and, taking into account all other circumstances such as the amount of salary received by the Defendants during their terms of office, it is appropriate to limit the Defendants’ liability as stated in the judgment.\\n\\nC. In light of the legal principles discussed above and the record, the fact-finding or determination by the court below concerning the grounds for limiting liability is not manifestly unreasonable in light of the principle of equity, nor can it be said that the foregoing determination by the court below contains, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, an error that affected the judgment by misconstruing the legal principles concerning the burden of proof, limitation of liability, etc.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all final appeals are dismissed, and the portion of the litigation costs arising from the Plaintiffs’ final appeal shall be borne by the Plaintiffs, and the portion arising from the Defendants’ final appeal shall be borne by the Defendants, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

question: A Company, which is a non-listed stock company, has a quorum provision in its articles of incorporation stating, “The election of directors shall be by the attendance of shareholders holding shares representing a majority of the total issued shares and by the affirmative vote of a majority of the voting rights of the shareholders present.” However, there is no separate provision regarding cumulative voting. Shareholder A, who holds shares equal to 5% of the total issued shares excluding shares without voting rights as recorded in A Company’s shareholder register, seeks to elect D as a director upon the expiration of the terms of directors B and C of A Company. Which of the following statements is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, in accordance with case law)
A: A may make a shareholder proposal to a director, in writing or by electronic document, 6 weeks before the date of the shareholders’ meeting in order to propose “the director election proposal” as an agenda item of the shareholders’ meeting and “the proposal to elect D as a director” as a resolution item of the shareholders’ meeting.
B: If A Company makes the proposed item submitted by A into an item of the shareholders’ meeting, when A makes a request, A Company must give A an opportunity to explain that item at the shareholders’ meeting.
C: Since the director who received A’s proposal must make it an item to be considered at the shareholders’ meeting unless the proposal violates statutes and regulations, it must be made an item to be considered at the shareholders’ meeting even if the proposal violates the articles of incorporation.
D: If A Company convenes a shareholders’ meeting to elect 2 persons among B, C, and D as directors, A may demand of A Company, by written document or electronic document, up to 7 days before the date of the shareholders’ meeting, that the directors be elected by the method of cumulative voting.
E: Even when 2 directors are elected by the method of cumulative voting at A Company’s shareholders’ meeting, the quorum prescribed in the articles of incorporation must still be satisfied.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2016DA217741]": "The grounds of appeal are examined (the statements in each supplemental appellate brief submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. As to the first ground of appeal\\n\\nThe lower court, on the basis that, according to the Commercial Act Article 389 and Article 386, where the term of office of the representative director has expired but no new representative director has been appointed, the rights and obligations of the former representative director continue to exist, directors, auditors, and other interested persons may petition the court to appoint a person to perform the duties of a temporary representative director, found that although the Plaintiffs, who are shareholders of the Defendant, did not take measures to appoint a new representative director after the term of office of the Defendant’s representative director, Non-party 1, expired, there was no basis to exclude the application of the above provisions of the Commercial Act to Non-party 1, and there was also no evidence to support a finding that Non-party 1 abused the above provisions of the Commercial Act to unjustly extend his term of office as representative director; accordingly, the lower court rejected the Plaintiffs’ argument that the rights and obligations of the representative director under the above provisions of the Commercial Act did not continue to exist for Non-party 1, on the ground that Commercial Act Article 389(3) and Article 386 do not protect even the case where a former representative director abuses the authority to handle urgent affairs to unjustly extend his term of office as representative director.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and upon examination of the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper, and there is no illegality, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment and scope of the authority to handle urgent affairs.\\n\\n2. As to the second ground of appeal\\n\\nA. Commercial Act Article 368(1), with respect to the requirements for an ordinary resolution of a general meeting of shareholders, provides: “Except where otherwise provided in this Act or the articles of incorporation, resolutions of a meeting shall be adopted by a majority of the voting rights of the shareholders present and by a number representing at least one-fourth of the total issued shares.” Thus, while it does not separately prescribe a quorum for the formation of a general meeting of shareholders, it permits the articles of incorporation to provide otherwise as to the requirements for an ordinary resolution; therefore, it is possible for the articles of incorporation to prescribe a quorum.\\n\\nMeanwhile, cumulative voting prescribed in Commercial Act Article 382-2 refers to a method by which, when two or more directors are to be appointed, each shareholder has voting rights equal to the number of directors to be appointed for each share, and exercises those rights by concentrating the votes on one or more candidates for director, so that those who obtain the largest number of votes are appointed as directors in sequence. This provision is, in essence, a provision relating to the exercise of shareholders’ voting rights.\\n\\nTherefore, where the articles of incorporation of a stock company provide that the appointment of directors shall be decided by the attendance of shareholders holding more than one-half of the total issued shares and by a majority of the voting rights of the shareholders present, the above provision of the Commercial Act concerning cumulative voting cannot be viewed as excluding the quorum prescribed in the articles of incorporation; accordingly, even where directors are appointed by cumulative voting, the quorum prescribed in the articles of incorporation must be satisfied.\\n\\nAccordingly, the portion of the lower court’s decision that, to the contrary, found that where directors are appointed by cumulative voting, the quorum provision in Article 22 of the Defendant’s articles of incorporation, which requires the attendance of shareholders holding more than one-half of the total issued shares, does not apply, is incorrect.\\n\\nB. However, according to the reasoning of the lower court’s judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n1) On July 10, 2014, Non-party 1, in his capacity as the Defendant’s representative director, gave notice to the shareholders convening an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders, attaching the date and place of the meeting, the agenda items, including “the appointment of 4 directors,” and the principal career histories of 7 candidates for new directors.\\n\\n2) On August 5, 2014, Non-party 1, by written request to the Defendant, demanded that directors be appointed by cumulative voting under Commercial Act Article 382-2, and on August 6, 2014, he notified the shareholders of this in his capacity as the Defendant’s representative director.\\n\\n3) On August 18, 2014, the instant general meeting of shareholders was held with all 7 shareholders, including the Plaintiffs, present in order to resolve the agenda item for the appointment of 4 directors, etc.; the chairperson, Non-party 1, placed the agenda item for the appointment of 4 directors before the meeting and notified the meeting that there had been a request for cumulative voting. The Plaintiffs proposed that only 2 directors be appointed, but Non-party 1 rejected this and proceeded with the voting procedure on the original agenda item, “the appointment of 4 directors,” and ballots were distributed to each shareholder.\\n\\n4) The Plaintiffs and 6 shareholders, including Non-party 2, remained in the meeting hall and, while indicating their intention to refuse the submission of the agenda item, did not vote; only Non-party 1 voted by the cumulative voting method. As a result, a resolution was adopted to appoint Non-party 3, Non-party 4, and Non-party 5 as directors, in sequence, starting from the person who obtained the largest number of votes.\\n\\nC. Examining these factual circumstances in light of the record, it is appropriate to view that all of the Defendant’s shareholders were present at the time the resolution to appoint directors by cumulative voting was adopted at the instant general meeting of shareholders, and therefore the quorum prescribed in Article 22 of the Defendant’s articles of incorporation was satisfied. This is not altered by the fact that 6 shareholders, including the Plaintiffs, attended the instant general meeting of shareholders but abstained without actually voting.\\n\\nD. Accordingly, although the lower court’s determination that the quorum under the Defendant’s articles of incorporation did not apply where the appointment of directors was resolved by cumulative voting is not proper, the conclusion that the resolution method cannot be viewed as violating any law or regulation or the articles of incorporation, or as being manifestly unfair, is proper; and there is no illegality, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the satisfaction of quorum at a general meeting of shareholders where the cumulative voting system is implemented.\\n\\n3. As to the third ground of appeal\\n\\nThe gist of the Plaintiffs’ argument on this part of the grounds of appeal is that when the Defendant, at the general meeting of shareholders held on March 3, 2014, decided to appoint 2 directors by cumulative voting, the Plaintiffs did not attend, and the meeting was closed without placing the agenda item before the meeting on the ground that the quorum under the articles of incorporation was not satisfied; and that the Plaintiffs made the same argument in a case involving an application for permission to convene a general meeting of shareholders against the Defendant. Thus, the Defendant’s contention that, where directors are appointed by cumulative voting at the instant general meeting of shareholders, the quorum provision in the articles of incorporation does not apply is inconsistent with prior conduct and violates the principle of good faith, and the lower court failed to determine this argument by the Plaintiffs, which constitutes an omission of judgment.\\n\\nHowever, as noted above, even where a resolution to appoint directors is adopted by cumulative voting, the quorum under the articles of incorporation must be satisfied. Therefore, this part of the grounds of appeal, which alleges an omission of judgment on a different premise, cannot be accepted.\\n\\n4. As to the fourth ground of appeal\\n\\nThe lower court determined that it was insufficient to find that the proceedings of the instant general meeting of shareholders were led by a person other than the chairperson, Non-party 1, or that, as a result, the Plaintiffs’ rights to debate and to deliberate were infringed, and therefore the method of resolution at the general meeting of shareholders could not be viewed as violating any law or regulation or the articles of incorporation, or as being manifestly unfair.\\n\\nSince the lower court’s determination includes the purport of rejecting the Plaintiffs’ argument that the proceedings of the instant general meeting of shareholders infringed shareholders’ rights to debate and to deliberate, there is no illegality, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, that affected the judgment by omission of judgment.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

question: Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are true (○) and false (×) concerning the acquisition of minority shares by a controlling shareholder under Article 360-24 of the Commercial Act (Right to Demand Sale by a Controlling Shareholder)? (In cases of dispute, according to case law) (a) A controlling shareholder may, where necessary to achieve the company’s managerial purpose, obtain prior approval of the general meeting of shareholders and demand that the minority shareholder sell the shares it holds. (b) The minority shareholder’s shares are deemed to have been transferred to the controlling shareholder when the controlling shareholder’s demand for sale is approved at the general meeting of shareholders. (c) When exercising the right to demand sale, the controlling shareholder may exercise that right with respect to only part of the shares held by the minority shareholder. (d) A minority shareholder who has received a demand for sale from the controlling shareholder shall sell the shares to the controlling shareholder within 2 months from the date of receipt of the demand for sale. (e) In determining whether a parent company falls under the controlling shareholder of a subsidiary, the subsidiary’s treasury shares are included in the total number of issued shares and are added to the shares of the subsidiary held by the parent company.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2016MA230]": "The grounds for re-appeal (the statements in the supplementary brief of grounds for re-appeal filed after the period for filing the brief of grounds for re-appeal has elapsed are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for re-appeal) shall be examined.\\n\\n1. As to the Respondent’s grounds for re-appeal\\n\\nArticle 360-24(1) of the Commercial Act provides that a shareholder (hereinafter referred to as a “controlling shareholder”) who holds 95/100 or more of the total number of issued shares of a company for his or her own account may, where necessary to achieve the company’s managerial purpose, demand that the other shareholders of the company (hereinafter referred to as the “minority shareholders”) sell the shares they hold, and the main text of paragraph (2) of the same Article provides that, in calculating the number of shares held under paragraph (1), the shares held by the parent company and the subsidiary company shall be aggregated, while Article 360-25(1) of the Commercial Act provides that a minority shareholder of a company with a controlling shareholder may at any time demand that the controlling shareholder purchase the shares he or she holds.\\n\\nIn determining whether the parent company falls under the controlling shareholder when a minority shareholder of a subsidiary company has made a share purchase demand to the parent company pursuant to Article 360-25(1) of the Commercial Act, Article 360-24(1) of the Commercial Act merely provides for the ratio of the number of shares held to be calculated on the basis of the total number of issued shares of the company, and does not place any limitation on the scope of the total number of issued shares; therefore, the treasury shares of the subsidiary company must be included in the total number of issued shares. In addition, Article 360-24(2) of the Commercial Act merely provides that, in calculating the number of shares held, the shares held by the parent company and the subsidiary company shall be aggregated, and does not provide that treasury shares held by the subsidiary company are excluded; therefore, treasury shares held by the subsidiary company must be aggregated into the shares held by the parent company.\\n\\nThe court below determined that, out of the total number of issued shares of the Company concerned, the Respondent, who is the parent company of the Company concerned, held 84.96%, and the Company concerned held 13.14% as treasury shares, and that, when these are aggregated, they amount to 98.1%, so the Respondent falls under the controlling shareholder of the Company concerned.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles seen above, upon examining the record, the foregoing determination by the court below is proper, and there is no illegality in that determination due to any misapprehension of the legal principles concerning whether the controlling shareholder status, which is a requirement for the exercise of the minority shareholder’s share purchase right, is satisfied, as alleged in the Respondent’s grounds for re-appeal.\\n\\n2. As to the grounds for re-appeal by Applicant 1\\n\\nThe court below, stating that the per-share price fixed in the sale agreement for shares of the Company concerned between the Respondent and a non-party reflected compensation for management control and therefore could not be regarded as a price that properly reflected the objective exchange value of the shares, and that “AKAMAI Technologies, INC.” could not be regarded as a comparable company of the Company concerned and thus the value of the shares of the Company concerned evaluated on that basis likewise could not be regarded as objective exchange value, determined the earnings value of the Company concerned by reflecting the net profit/loss amounts for the most recent 3 years pursuant to the Enforcement Decree of the Inheritance Tax and Gift Tax Act while assigning weight to the most recent business year, determined the net asset value of the Company concerned, took a weighted average thereof in the ratio of 3:2, and then determined the per-share sale price of the Company concerned on that basis.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no illegality in the foregoing determination by the court below due to any misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the determination of share price arising from the exercise of a minority shareholder’s share purchase right and the calculation of the purchase price of unlisted shares, as alleged in the grounds for re-appeal by Applicant 1.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all re-appeals are dismissed, and with respect to the costs of the re-appeals, the portion incurred between Applicant 2 and the Respondent shall be borne by the Respondent, and the portion incurred between Applicant 1 and the Respondent shall be borne by each party, and it is so decided in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, as ordered."}

{"[2018DA224699]": "1. Article 360-24(1) of the Commercial Act provides that a shareholder (hereinafter referred to as the “controlling shareholder”) who holds, on its own account, 95 percent or more of the total number of issued shares of the company may, where necessary to achieve the company’s managerial purpose, demand that the other shareholders of the company (hereinafter referred to as the “minority shareholders”) sell the shares they hold. This is a system intended to enhance the efficiency of corporate management by enabling, under certain requirements, all issued shares to be owned by a single controlling shareholder, if the controlling shareholder holding 95 percent or more of the shares pays a fair price to the minority shareholders. In light of such legislative intent and purpose, when the controlling shareholder exercises the right to demand sale under this provision, it must exercise the right with respect to all of the shares held by the minority shareholders.\\n\\nArticle 360-26(1) of the Commercial Act provides that a controlling shareholder acquiring shares pursuant to Article 360-24 of the Commercial Act shall be deemed to have had the shares transferred upon payment of the purchase price to the minority shareholders, and paragraph (2) of the same Article provides that where the minority shareholders to whom the purchase price under paragraph (1) is to be paid cannot be identified or the minority shareholders refuse to receive it, the controlling shareholder may deposit the amount. The “purchase price” here should be understood not as the amount unilaterally calculated and presented by the controlling shareholder, but as the amount determined by agreement with the minority shareholders or the fair value calculated by the court pursuant to Article 360-24(9) of the Commercial Act. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\na. Because the minority shareholders may be expelled from the company against their will through the controlling shareholder’s unilateral exercise of the right to demand sale, the need to protect the minority shareholders by paying a fair price is recognized. The same is true in light of the fact that the Commercial Act provides that shares are transferred not when “the controlling shareholder’s right to demand sale is approved at a general meeting of shareholders” or “the minority shareholders receive notice of the right to demand sale,” but only when “the controlling shareholder pays the purchase price,” and that, as a right corresponding to the controlling shareholder’s right to demand sale, Article 360-25 of the Commercial Act also grants the minority shareholders a right to demand purchase.\\n\\nb. Article 360-26 of the Commercial Act applies equally not only where the controlling shareholder exercises the right to demand sale pursuant to Article 360-24 of the Commercial Act, but also where the minority shareholders of a company with a controlling shareholder exercise the right to demand purchase against the controlling shareholder pursuant to Article 360-25 of the Commercial Act. However, in the latter case, it is difficult to conceive of the concept of a purchase price unilaterally calculated and presented by the controlling shareholder.\\n\\n2. a. The lower court held, for the following reasons, that because the Plaintiffs remained shareholders of the Defendant, there existed a ground for revocation in the Defendant’s shareholders’ meeting at issue for which no convocation notice was given to the Plaintiffs.\\n\\n1) Article 360-26(2) of the Commercial Act provides that where a minority shareholder refuses to receive the purchase price, a deposit may be made on the premise of a lawfully calculated purchase price. Where no agreement has been reached between the minority shareholders and the controlling shareholder and no determination of the purchase price by a court has been made, the amount arbitrarily calculated by the controlling shareholder cannot be regarded as a lawfully calculated purchase price.\\n\\n2) Since Nethor Investments B.V., the controlling shareholder of the Defendant, merely deposited the amount arbitrarily calculated without seeking a court determination of the purchase price pursuant to Article 360-24(8) of the Commercial Act when no agreement was reached with the Plaintiffs, the Plaintiffs’ shares cannot be deemed to have been transferred to the controlling shareholder of the Defendant as a result.\\n\\nb. In light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the above determination by the lower court does not contain, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, any error of law in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the purchase price of shares that the controlling shareholder must deposit in order to acquire shares from minority shareholders pursuant to Article 360-26 of the Commercial Act.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. Since there is an obvious clerical error in the dispositive part of the first-instance judgment, it is corrected. Accordingly, judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court participating in the case as set forth in the order."}

question: An unlisted stock company, A Company, has in its articles of incorporation a provision that “a contract assuming surety obligations of at least 1 billion won must undergo a board resolution.” A was elected as a director at A Company’s general meeting of shareholders, and thereafter was selected as representative director by the board of directors and completed registration. Representative director A concluded two surety contracts with D Company in the name of A Company, without a board resolution, with respect to B Company’s debt to D Company of 100 million won and C Company’s debt to D Company of 2 billion won. Thereafter, a shareholder of A Company filed a lawsuit seeking the cancellation of the shareholders’ resolution appointing A as director, prevailed, and the judgment became final and conclusive. Among the following explanations, which is incorrect? (Where there is dispute, according to case law)
A: Acts performed by A as representative director before the judgment cancelling the shareholders’ resolution appointing A as director became final and conclusive are acts performed by a person without representative authority.
B: If D Company knew at the time of concluding the surety contract, or was grossly negligent in not knowing, that A had no representative authority, then under Article 395 of the Commercial Act (Acts of ostensible representative director and company liability), A Company cannot be held liable under the surety contract for B Company’s debt.
C: If D Company, without negligence, believed that A had authority to represent A Company, then even if D Company knew at the time of concluding the surety contract that A was concluding the surety contract for the purpose of promoting B Company’s interests, regardless of A Company’s profit-making purpose, if the conclusion of the surety contract is an act within the scope of representative authority, A Company bears a surety obligation of 100 million won.
D: If, at the time A Company concluded the surety contract with D Company for C Company’s debt, D Company, through gross negligence, did not know that there had been no board resolution of A Company, then A Company does not bear a surety obligation of 2 billion won.
E: The “registration of A’s appointment as director” completed by Representative Director A, who was appointed as a director pursuant to the shareholders’ resolution to be annulled, constitutes a false registration under Article 39 of the Commercial Act.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2002DA19797]": "1. As to Ground 1 of the Grounds for Final Appeal\\n\\nWhere a judgment cancelling a shareholders’ meeting resolution for the appointment of directors becomes final and conclusive, the representative director selected by the board of directors constituted by the directors appointed pursuant to that resolution retroactively loses his or her qualification, and any act performed by the representative director before the judgment cancelling the shareholders’ meeting resolution for the appointment of directors became final and conclusive becomes void as an act performed by a person without authority to represent.\\n\\nThe court below, taking a different view and, for the reasons stated in its holding, having determined that, notwithstanding the judgment cancelling the shareholders’ meeting resolution appointing the directors in this case, its effect does not operate retroactively, erred by misunderstanding the legal doctrine regarding the retroactive effect of a judgment cancelling a shareholders’ meeting resolution.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 2 of the Grounds for Final Appeal\\n\\nHowever, even if a judgment cancelling the shareholders’ meeting resolution for the appointment of directors becomes final and conclusive so that the resolution is retroactively void, the counterparty who transacted with the representative director whose appointing resolution is cancelled may be protected by the application or analogous application of Commercial Act Article 39, and in the case of corporate registration of a stock company, the company applies for registration through its representative, but the person entitled to apply for registration is the company itself; therefore, the registration of the appointment of directors completed by the representative director appointed as a director pursuant to the shareholders’ meeting resolution that is cancelled constitutes a false registration under Commercial Act Article 39.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below duly found the following facts: Nonparty 1, who was appointed as representative director by the directors elected at the shareholders’ meeting in this case, on that same day made registration of the same content in the corporate register, and thus, as reflected in the corporate register, was listed as the Plaintiff company’s representative director from that time until the judgment cancelling the shareholders’ meeting became final and conclusive; Nonparty 2, the counterparty to the transaction, entered into a mortgage creation contract with Nonparty 1, who was listed in the corporate register at the time as the Plaintiff company’s representative director, and completed the registration of the creation of a mortgage on that basis; and the Defendants, including Nonparty 2, were entirely unaware, until the judgment cancelling the shareholders’ meeting resolution in this case became final and conclusive, that Nonparty 1 was not the lawful representative director of the Plaintiff company. On that basis, the court below held that the Plaintiff company must bear responsibility, pursuant to the legal doctrine of Commercial Act Article 39, for the mortgage creation contract entered into between the Plaintiff company and Nonparty 2, the mortgage creation registration, and all transaction acts based thereon, and therefore the Plaintiff’s claim lacks merit. In light of the legal doctrine stated above, the court below’s factual findings and determination are proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality such as misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning the requirements for false registration as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, since there is no illegality in the judgment below that affected the outcome of the judgment, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged as per the disposition by unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2002DA19797]": "1. As to Ground 1 of the Appeal\\nWhere a judgment annulling a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders appointing directors becomes final and conclusive, the representative director selected by the board of directors constituted by the directors appointed pursuant to that resolution retroactively loses his qualification, and any act performed by that representative director before the judgment annulling the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders appointing directors became final and conclusive becomes invalid as an act performed by a person without representative authority.\\nThe court below, taking a different view and holding, for the reasons stated in its decision, that notwithstanding the judgment annulling the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders appointing the directors in this case, its effect does not operate retroactively, erred by misapprehending the legal principle concerning the retroactive effect of a judgment annulling a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders.\\n2. As to Ground 2 of the Appeal\\nHowever, even if a judgment annulling the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders appointing directors becomes final and conclusive and the resolution thereby becomes retroactively void, the counterparty who dealt with the representative director whose appointment resolution is annulled may be protected by the application or analogical application of Article 39 of the Commercial Act, and in the case of the corporate registration of a stock company, although the company applies for registration through its representative, the registrant is the company itself; therefore, the registration of the appointment of a director completed by a representative director appointed pursuant to the annulled resolution of the general meeting of shareholders constitutes an inaccurate registration under Article 39 of the Commercial Act.\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the court below duly found the following facts: Non-party 1, who was appointed as representative director by the directors elected at the general meeting of shareholders in this case, had the same contents registered in the corporate register on the same day and was thereby recorded in the corporate register as the representative director of the Plaintiff Company from that time until the judgment annulling the general meeting of shareholders became final and conclusive; Non-party 2, who was the counterparty in the transaction, entered into a mortgage creation agreement with Non-party 1, who was recorded in the corporate register at that time as the representative director of the Plaintiff Company, and completed the registration of the creation of a mortgage based thereon; and the Defendants, including Non-party 2, did not know at all until the judgment annulling the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders in this case became final and conclusive that Non-party 1 was not the lawful representative director of the Plaintiff Company. Then, the court below determined that the Plaintiff Company must bear responsibility, under the legal principle of Article 39 of the Commercial Act, for the mortgage creation agreement entered into between the Plaintiff Company and Non-party 2, the registration of the creation of a mortgage, and all transactional acts based thereon, and therefore the Plaintiff's claim lacks merit. In light of the legal principle stated above, the court below's fact-finding and determination are proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality in misapprehending the legal principle concerning the requirements for inaccurate registration as alleged in the ground of appeal.\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, since there is no illegality in the determination of the court below that affected the conclusion of the judgment, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated, as stated in the operative part."}

{"[2015DA45451]": "We determine the grounds of appeal (supplementary briefs on the grounds of appeal, etc. filed after the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal has elapsed shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Whether the Plaintiff, with respect to the Defendant’s provision of the guarantee in this case without a board resolution, can be protected as a “good-faith third party” (Ground of Appeal No. 3)\\n\\na. Issue\\n\\nThe issue in this case is whether, where the representative director of a stock company is supposed to carry out a certain transaction act pursuant to a board resolution but carried out the transaction act without a board resolution, a third party who is the counterparty to the transaction is protected, and within what scope.\\n\\nb. The representative director’s authority and matters requiring a board resolution\\n\\nGenerally, the representative director of a stock company may perform all judicial and extra-judicial acts within the scope of the company’s capacity to hold rights (Commercial Act Article 389(3), Article 209(1)). However, such representative authority may be restricted by statute (hereinafter, “statutory restriction”), or may also be restricted by internal procedures such as the company’s articles of incorporation, board resolutions, and internal regulations (hereinafter, “internal restriction”).\\n\\nA representative example of a statutory restriction is Commercial Act Article 393(1). By providing that “the execution of the company’s business, such as the disposal and transfer of important assets and the borrowing of large-scale property, shall be decided by a resolution of the board of directors,” this provision expressly states that the board of directors of a stock company has the authority to make decisions regarding the execution of the company’s business. Accordingly, when a stock company carries out the execution of business such as disposing of important assets or borrowing large-scale property, it cannot leave such matter to the representative director without a direct board resolution. In other words, the execution of important business that is not part of ordinary business and that has not been generally and specifically delegated to the representative director by the board must be subject to a board resolution, regardless of whether the articles of incorporation, board regulations, or the like designate it as a matter requiring board resolution (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DA55808 decided on 2010. 1. 14., Supreme Court Decision 2019DA204463 decided on 2019. 8. 14.).\\n\\nAnd even if a matter does not fall under “the execution of business such as the disposal and transfer of important assets and the borrowing of large-scale property” prescribed in Commercial Act Article 393(1), the articles of incorporation of a stock company or board regulations may provide that the representative director must obtain a board resolution when performing a certain act; such a case is distinguished from a statutory restriction and is called an internal restriction.\\n\\nc. Internal restrictions on the representative director’s representative authority and protection of good-faith third parties\\n\\nThe representative director of a stock company has the authority to represent the company externally and to execute the company’s business internally. The representative director is not a person who acts on behalf of the company, but rather an organ of the company that itself performs the company’s acts. The company realizes its will, decided through decision-making organs such as the general meeting of shareholders or the board of directors, through the representative director, and the representative director’s act becomes the company’s act. The Commercial Act provides that restrictions on the representative director’s representative authority cannot be asserted against good-faith third parties (Commercial Act Article 389(3), Article 209(2)).\\n\\nWhere representative authority is restricted, the representative director has such authority only within that scope. However, even if the act violates such a restriction, if it is not beyond the company’s capacity to hold rights, a third party who is unaware of the restriction on representative authority would naturally believe that the act is an act of representation by the company, and such reliance must be protected (see Supreme Court Decision 97DA18059 decided on 1997. 8. 29.). Even where the representative director’s authority is restricted by requiring a board resolution for certain external transaction acts, the board resolution is merely an internal decision-making procedure of the company, and unless there are special circumstances, it accords with experience rules to view the transaction counterparty as having relied on the company’s representative having completed the internal procedures necessary for the transaction (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DA480 decided on 2005. 5. 27., Supreme Court Decision 2006DA47677 decided on 2009. 3. 26.). Therefore, even where the representative director’s representative authority is restricted by requiring a board resolution in the articles of incorporation or board regulations, a good-faith third party is protected under Commercial Act Article 209(2).\\n\\nIn order for a third party who is the counterparty to a transaction act to be protected under Commercial Act Article 209(2), gross negligence, in addition to good faith, is not required; however, if there is gross negligence, it is appropriate to construe the transaction act as invalid, on the ground that the third party’s reliance is not worthy of protection. Gross negligence means a state in which the third party, had he or she exercised only slight care, could have known that there was no board resolution, yet blindly believed that there had been a board resolution, thereby manifestly violating the duty of care required by transaction practice; it refers to a state in which the third party negligently neglected care to a degree almost equivalent to intent, such that from the standpoint of fairness there is no need to protect the third party. Whether a third party has gross negligence must be determined by comprehensively considering various circumstances such as the third party’s ability to recognize that there was no board resolution, the third party’s experience and position in transacting with the company, the prior transactional relationship between the company and the third party, and whether the transaction act performed by the representative director is extraordinary according to experience rules. However, if there is no special circumstance suggesting that the third party, while transacting with the company’s representative director, suspected that there had been no board resolution of the company, it cannot generally be said that the third party had a duty to take steps such as confirming whether there had been a board resolution (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2006DA47677).\\n\\nd. Restrictions on the representative director’s representative authority under Commercial Act Article 393(1) and protection of good-faith third parties\\n\\nCommercial Act Article 393(1), which restricts the representative director’s representative authority, applies uniformly even to persons who do not know of the existence of the provision or do not properly understand it. Since one cannot avoid its application on the ground of ignorance of the law or mistake as to legal evaluation, the restriction under this provision may be viewed differently from an internal restriction. However, even where the representative director of a stock company carries out a transaction act without a board resolution with respect to “acts such as the disposal and transfer of important assets and the borrowing of large-scale property” prescribed in this provision, the validity of the transaction act should be treated in the same manner as in the case of internal restrictions discussed in c. above.\\n\\n(1) Whether a certain transaction act falls under “the disposal and transfer of important assets and the borrowing of large-scale property, etc.” prescribed in Commercial Act Article 393(1) must be determined in light of the value of the property and its proportion in total assets, the scale of the company, the company’s business or property situation, financial condition, the purpose of holding the asset or borrowing and its use, relevance to the company’s ordinary business, and prior business handling, etc., and by determining whether it is appropriate to leave the decision to the representative director (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DA3649 decided on 2005. 7. 28., Supreme Court Decision 2007DA23807 decided on 2008. 5. 15.). However, from the standpoint of the counterparty transacting with the representative director, it is difficult to know the company’s specific circumstances, and it is neither necessary nor expected merely because one is entering into a transaction with the company to know such circumstances. Even if the counterparty knows those circumstances, it is not easy to determine whether the transaction act is one that may be left to the representative director’s decision. In a concrete case, whether a certain transaction act falls under “the disposal and transfer of important assets and the borrowing of large-scale property, etc.” prescribed in Commercial Act Article 393(1) is by no means a clear issue, as even legal experts may differ.\\n\\n(2) In light of these points, if the standard for protecting the counterparty differs depending on whether the ground for requiring a board resolution is Commercial Act Article 393(1) or an internal regulation such as the articles of incorporation, legal relations would necessarily become uncertain. The distinction between gross negligence and ordinary negligence is relative, the boundary is obscure, and in individual cases there is no choice but to determine the existence and degree of negligence by considering the concrete circumstances. The so-called dualism, which distinguishes by protecting a counterparty in good faith and without negligence when a board resolution is required under Commercial Act Article 393(1), but protecting a counterparty in good faith and without gross negligence when the requirement to obtain a board resolution is provided in the articles of incorporation, etc., creates unnecessary confusion and transaction costs in transactions surrounding the company. Under such dualism, even where the articles of incorporation or other internal company regulations require a board resolution, the company would seek to narrow the scope of the counterparty’s protection by alleging and proving that the transaction act falls under a matter prescribed in Commercial Act Article 393(1). However, since whether a transaction act falls under “the disposal and transfer of important assets and the borrowing of large-scale property, etc.” prescribed in Commercial Act Article 393(1) must be determined by considering the various concrete circumstances discussed in (1) above, there is a concern that the court’s burden of review will be increased.\\n\\nBy contrast, if Commercial Act Article 209(2) is applied to cases under Commercial Act Article 393(1) just as in the case of internal restrictions, then, for transaction acts that the company has required to go through a board resolution in its internal regulations such as the articles of incorporation, regardless of whether Commercial Act Article 393(1) applies, one need only determine whether the transaction counterparty acted in bad faith or with gross negligence with respect to the fact that there was no board resolution, thereby helping to simplify and clarify legal relations.\\n\\n(3) A counterparty who transacts with a manager or a de facto representative director is protected even if negligent, unless grossly negligent (see Supreme Court Decision 96DA36753 decided on 1997. 8. 26., Supreme Court Decision 99DA19797 decided on 1999. 11. 12.). A representative director has stronger authority than a manager or a de facto representative director. Requiring no negligence from a transaction counterparty merely because the board resolution required by Commercial Act Article 393(1) was not obtained results in less protection for a counterparty who transacted with a true representative director than for a counterparty who transacted with a manager or a de facto representative director, and is therefore difficult to accept even from the standpoint of equity.\\n\\n(4) When a representative director carries out a transaction act on behalf of the company, a board resolution is merely an internal decision-making procedure of the company. The reliance of a third party who is the transaction counterparty on the representative director’s having followed the necessary internal procedures does not differ depending on the basis for requiring a board resolution.
