Yet, if only in cases of violation of internal restrictions is a negligent counterparty protected, and the degree of care the counterparty must exercise is differentiated depending on whether the act falls under Commercial Act Article 393(1) or merely under an internal restriction, the counterparty would have to ascertain the company’s internal circumstances, which ultimately increases unnecessary transaction costs and produces an undesirable result for the company as well.\\n\\n(5) Although one can distinguish between cases in which a board resolution is required under Commercial Act Article 393(1) and cases in which a board resolution is required under internal regulations such as the articles of incorporation, prior Supreme Court precedent has not made such a distinction and has simply determined the validity of the transaction act according to whether the counterparty was in good faith and without negligence with respect to the absence of a board resolution. This is because, regardless of how the representative director’s authority was restricted, the Court considered that, as to the validity of an external transaction act performed by the representative director, it is appropriate not to treat cases under Commercial Act Article 393(1) as entirely separate from cases of internal restriction, but rather to determine the matter in each case by considering the transaction counterparty’s good faith or negligence according to the specifics of the case.\\n\\n(6) The standard by which to determine the validity or invalidity of a transaction act lacking the board resolution required by Commercial Act Article 393(1) is a matter of how to reasonably distribute the risk caused by the lack of a board resolution among the company, the transaction counterparty, and ultimately interested persons in the company’s external transactional relations. In a stock company, a board resolution is an internal procedure of the company. Unless there are special circumstances suggesting that a third party suspected that there was no board resolution of the company, it is not desirable to pass on the risk arising internally within the company to a counterparty who transacted with the representative director. The prior precedents have a reasonable basis, as noted above, in having determined the validity of transaction acts that violated internal restrictions and transaction acts that violated the statutory restriction of Commercial Act Article 393(1) by the same standard without distinguishing them. Accordingly, even where a representative director carried out a transaction act without undergoing a board resolution despite the requirement under Commercial Act Article 393(1) to do so, it is appropriate to treat it in the same manner as cases in which the representative director’s representative authority is internally restricted. Whether the representative director was required to obtain a board resolution under the statutory restriction of Commercial Act Article 393(1) or under a mere internal restriction is only one of the factors to be considered individually at the stage of determining the counterparty’s bad faith or gross negligence, and because of this distinction, the very standard for protecting a third party who relied on the representative director’s act should not be altered.\\n\\ne. Change of precedent\\n\\nAccordingly, Supreme Court Decision 78DA389 decided on 1978. 6. 27., Supreme Court Decision 94DA33903 decided on 1995. 4. 11., Supreme Court Decision 94DA42754 decided on 1996. 1. 26., Supreme Court Decision 96DA48282 decided on 1997. 6. 13., Supreme Court Decision 97DA35276 decided on 1998. 7. 24., Supreme Court Decision 98DA2488 decided on 1999. 10. 8., Supreme Court Decision 2005DA3649 decided on 2005. 7. 28., Supreme Court Decision 2006DA47677 decided on 2009. 3. 26., Supreme Court Decision 2012DA73530 decided on 2014. 6. 26., Supreme Court Decision 2014DA206563 decided on 2014. 8. 20., and other judgments to the same effect are all to be changed to the extent that they conflict with the view of this judgment.\\n\\nf. Factual relations\\n\\nThe following facts can be ascertained from the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record.\\n\\n(1) The Plaintiff is a company engaged in the manufacture and sale of electrical equipment, etc. The Defendant is a company established by succeeding to the construction business division of Daewoo Motor Sales Co., Ltd. upon the approval of the rehabilitation plan for that company while rehabilitation proceedings were pending, and the rehabilitation proceedings were terminated on 2011. 12. 30. ○○Sindosi Pilyu Co., Ltd. (hereinafter, “○○Sindosi Pilyu”) was a project implementing agent that had entered into a project implementation agency agreement with the Gwangyang ○○ District Land Readjustment Association concerning the Gwangyang ○○ District Land Readjustment Project (hereinafter, “the project at issue”).\\n\\n(2) In or around January 2012, the Defendant recruited Nonparty 1, who had served as president in charge at △△ Construction Co., Ltd., and appointed him as president on 2012. 2. 3. and as representative director on 2012. 3. 27. In around March 2012, after going through the deliberation procedure of the Order Review Committee, the Defendant decided to secure the project at issue, which Nonparty 1 had been promoting while working at △△ Construction Co., Ltd., and entered into a joint construction agreement with △△ Construction Co., Ltd. recognizing the completed work of that company at a certain share. On 2012. 3. 22., the Defendant entered into an agreement concerning the project at issue with Stock Company □□□□ and ○○Sindosi Pilyu, under which ○○Sindosi Pilyu would act as the project implementing agent for the project at issue, the Defendant would carry out the construction, and Stock Company □□□□ would arrange for the necessary initial project funds, etc.\\n\\n(3) Stock Company □□□□ failed to provide the initial project funds, and ○○Sindosi Pilyu had difficulty securing the necessary project funds, including by requesting that the Defendant lend it the initial project funds. Nonparty 1, the Defendant’s representative director, asked the Plaintiff to lend funds to ○○Sindosi Pilyu.\\n\\nWith the intention of later obtaining orders for electrical work, etc. for the project at issue, the Plaintiff decided to lend KRW 3 billion to ○○Sindosi Pilyu, and on 2012. 4. 10., in the office of Nonparty 1, the Defendant’s representative director, with the attendance of Nonparty 1, Nonparty 2, who is the de facto manager of the Plaintiff, Nonparty 3, who is the de facto manager of ○○Sindosi Pilyu, and others, the Plaintiff entered into the following loan agreement at issue with ○○Sindosi Pilyu.\\n\\n“The Plaintiff shall lend KRW 3 billion to ○○Sindosi Pilyu, and within 6 months shall receive repayment of KRW 6 billion, consisting of the principal amount of KRW 3 billion plus dividends of KRW 3 billion, in four installments. If such amount is not repaid by the due date, ○○Sindosi Pilyu shall transfer to the Plaintiff all business rights granted to it by the Gwangyang ○○ District Land Readjustment Association for KRW 3 billion.”\\n\\nIn addition, Nonparty 3, the de facto operator and director of ○○Sindosi Pilyu, and representative director Nonparty 4 jointly and severally guaranteed ○○Sindosi Pilyu’s debt.\\n\\n(4) On the same day, in the same office, the Defendant’s representative director, Nonparty 1, prepared and gave the Plaintiff a confirmation letter in the Defendant’s name (hereinafter, “the confirmation letter at issue”) containing the statement: “However, if the contents of the above loan agreement between the above two companies, concluded on 2012. 4. 10., fail to proceed, I shall make a substitute payment of the principal amount of the loan.” At the end of the confirmation letter, the Defendant’s trade name and address and the words “Representative Director” were typed, and next to the words “Representative Director,” Nonparty 1 wrote his own name by hand.\\n\\n(5) According to the Defendant’s board regulations at the time, “borrowing of large amounts of funds and guarantee acts” were designated as matters to be submitted to the board. However, when Nonparty 1 prepared the confirmation letter at issue for the Plaintiff, there had been no board resolution of the Defendant.\\n\\n(6) In 2012, the Defendant’s assets amounted to approximately KRW 170 billion and its sales amounted to approximately KRW 100 billion.\\n\\ng. Determination in this case\\n\\nExamining these factual relations in light of the legal principles discussed above, the following conclusion is reached.\\n\\n(1) Considering the Defendant’s asset scale and sales scale at the time of this case, the transactional relationship between the Plaintiff and the Defendant, and the circumstances leading to the preparation of the confirmation letter, the Defendant’s act of preparing the confirmation letter at issue and guaranteeing a debt of KRW 3 billion should be viewed as a matter requiring a board resolution under the Defendant’s board regulations.\\n\\n(2) There is no evidence showing that the Plaintiff knew that the confirmation letter at issue had been prepared without a board resolution of the Defendant.\\n\\n(3) Considering the following circumstances collectively, it cannot be said that, as a third party, the Plaintiff had gross negligence in not knowing that the confirmation letter at issue had been prepared without a board resolution of the Defendant.\\n\\nNonparty 2, the de facto manager of the Plaintiff, entered into the loan agreement at issue lending KRW 3 billion to ○○Sindosi Pilyu at the request of Nonparty 1, with whom he was on friendly terms, and had the Defendant not guaranteed ○○Sindosi Pilyu’s debt, the Plaintiff is highly likely not to have entered into the loan agreement at issue.\\n\\nIn light of the Defendant’s scale and the degree of risk that the Defendant would bear through the confirmation letter at issue, it is not externally obvious that the Defendant had to obtain a board resolution in order to prepare the confirmation letter at issue intended to guarantee a debt of KRW 3 billion. It accords with experience rules to view a counterparty dealing with a company as having relied on the company’s representative director having completed the internal procedures necessary for the transaction, and in this case it is difficult to recognize special circumstances under which the Plaintiff should have suspected that there had been no board resolution of the Defendant regarding the preparation of the confirmation letter at issue.\\n\\nh. Whether the lower court’s determination was proper\\n\\nOn the same reasoning, the lower court’s conclusion that the confirmation letter at issue is recognized not as Nonparty 1’s personal declaration of intent but as the Defendant’s declaration of intent, and that even if Nonparty 1, the Defendant’s representative director, prepared the confirmation letter at issue without a board resolution, the Defendant must perform the obligations under the confirmation letter at issue toward the Plaintiff, is correct. The lower court judgment does not contain, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, any error in misunderstanding the law regarding the interpretation of dispositive documents or the validity of a declaration of intent made without going through a board resolution.\\n\\n2. Whether the Plaintiff cannot bring a claim against the Defendant under the confirmation letter at issue because the Plaintiff’s loan claim against ○○Sindosi Pilyu was extinguished by payment in kind by way of dation in payment (Ground of Appeal No. 1)\\n\\nThe lower court held that, because ○○Sindosi Pilyu lost the right to act as the project implementing agent for the project at issue and thus became unable to transfer such project-implementation right in lieu of repayment of the loan debt under the loan agreement at issue, the loan debt could not be extinguished by dation in payment even if ○○Sindosi Pilyu later requested the Plaintiff to proceed with the transfer procedure for the project-implementation right.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the lower court judgment does not contain, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, any error in misunderstanding the law concerning the interpretation of dispositive documents, the possibility of dation in payment by a joint and several surety, or the requirements for a claim for payment by subrogation, without fully examining the necessary issues.\\n\\n3. Whether the lower court omitted a determination on the Defendant’s assertion of abuse of representative authority (Ground of Appeal No. 2)\\n\\nThe reasons of a judgment need only indicate a determination regarding the parties’ assertions and other offensive and defensive means to the extent sufficient to support that the disposition is proper, and there is no need to determine every assertion or every offensive or defensive means of the parties (Civil Procedure Act Article 208). Even if a court’s judgment does not expressly indicate a concrete and direct determination on a matter asserted by a party, it cannot be said to have omitted a determination if, in light of the overall tenor of the reasons of the judgment, it can be understood that the assertion was accepted or rejected. Even if there is in fact a part not actually determined, when it is clear that the assertion would be rejected, there is no need to reverse the judgment on the ground of omission of a determination because it does not affect the outcome of the judgment (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DA98426 decided on 2013. 10. 31., Supreme Court Decision 2017DA9657 decided on 2017. 12. 5.).\\n\\nAccording to the record, in the preparatory brief dated 2014. 4. 1., the Defendant argued that “the Plaintiff sufficiently knew or could have known that Nonparty 1 did not prepare the confirmation letter at issue for the Defendant but abused his authority for his own benefit or the benefit of a third party, so the confirmation letter at issue is invalid,” and it can be seen that at the first trial date in the lower court on 2014. 11. 12., the above preparatory brief was submitted, thereby making the argument of abuse of representative authority.\\n\\nThe lower court determined that, as guarantor under the confirmation letter at issue, the Defendant is obligated to pay the Plaintiff the principal amount of KRW 3 billion borrowed by ○○Sindosi Pilyu and the delay damages thereon, but did not expressly determine the Defendant’s assertion of abuse of representative authority.\\n\\nHowever, in light of the overall tenor of the reasons of the lower court judgment, it can be deemed that the lower court judgment includes the purport of rejecting the Defendant’s above assertion, and even upon reviewing the record, there is no sufficient evidence to recognize the facts underlying the Defendant’s above assertion. The lower court judgment does not contain any error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misunderstanding the law regarding abuse of representative authority or in omitting a determination that affected the result.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Defendant’s appeal is without merit and is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are to be borne by the losing party. The judgment is rendered as follows. In this judgment, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Park Sang-ok, Min Yu-suk, Kim Sang-hwan, and No Tae-ak, and there is a concurring opinion by Justice Kim Jae-hyung to the majority opinion.\\n\\n5. Dissenting opinion of Justices Park Sang-ok, Min Yu-suk, Kim Sang-hwan, and No Tae-ak\\n\\na. Summary of the dissenting opinion\\n\\nIn short, the majority opinion takes the view that where the representative director of a stock company carried out a transaction act without going through a board resolution, even though a board resolution was required, the transaction act is valid if the transaction counterparty acted in good faith and without gross negligence, thereby changing all of the prior established precedents that had held that the transaction act is valid only when the transaction counterparty acted in good faith and without negligence.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion opposes overruling the precedents.\\n\\nFirst, it is improper to view Commercial Act Article 209(2) as fully applicable on the premise that all cases in which the representative director of a stock company “should have obtained a board resolution” constitute restrictions on the representative director’s representative authority.\\n\\nNext, changing the standard for protecting the transaction counterparty from “good faith and without negligence” to “good faith and without gross negligence” is not only to emphasize only the protection of transaction security and disregard other values protected by company law, but also results in an “all or nothing” consequence that makes it difficult to achieve concrete and reasonable propriety in resolving individual cases. Prior precedents, under the principle of protecting transaction counterparties in good faith and without negligence, have focused on interpreting the scope of “negligence” that is protected according to the various substantive relationships of stock companies, while operating the system so that negligent transaction counterparties who are not protected may seek damages from the company, thereby promoting equitable and proper distribution of loss through comparative negligence. From this perspective, the “good faith and without negligence” used as the protection standard in prior precedents is not merely a simple expression of “good faith and without negligence.” Changing the precedents, as the majority opinion does, to the standard of “good faith and without gross negligence” for protecting transaction counterparties would, beyond substituting the term “no negligence” with “no gross negligence” in doctrinal terms, have no effect on the result of this case and does not appear likely to bring significant changes to trial practice. Rather, if the precedents are changed, a transaction act will be deemed valid even when the degree of the counterparty’s negligence is considerable, so long as it does not amount to gross negligence; this may lead, especially in the case of transaction acts such as guarantees, to the deterioration of the company’s financial soundness. In conclusion, the prior precedents are superior in terms of concrete propriety and adjustment of the interests of both parties, and there is therefore no need to change the precedents.\\n\\nBelow, it is explained that Commercial Act Article 209(2), on which the majority opinion relies, is a provision concerning the representative partners of an unlimited partnership and, when applied mutatis mutandis to the representative director of a stock company, its scope is necessarily limited, and in particular it cannot be applied as is to statutory restrictions on the representative director’s representative authority that do not exist in an unlimited partnership. Then, the arguments relied upon by the majority opinion for applying Commercial Act Article 209(2) even in cases falling under Commercial Act Article 393(1) are specifically rebutted. Furthermore, it is explained that, by excluding from protection only counterparties in bad faith or with gross negligence approaching bad faith under the purpose of protecting transaction counterparties in all cases where the representative director of a stock company carried out a transaction act without a board resolution, treating transaction counterparties with negligence uniformly as protected and validating the transaction act runs counter to the ideology and purpose of the company law system.\\n\\nb. Decision-making structure of a stock company and limits on the board’s delegation of authority to the representative director\\n\\n(1) A company is a corporation established for the purpose of commercial acts or other profit-making purposes and has independent capacity to hold rights, but as a social entity it must have organs to decide its will, execute business, and externally manifest the decided will. Among the various types of companies under the Commercial Act, in an association-type company such as an unlimited partnership, as a general rule each partner has the authority to execute business and the power of representation, and even if the business executor and representative are separately appointed, they must be appointed from among the partners, so that organ qualification and partner qualification coincide; by contrast, a stock company, as a capital-based company, is characterized in that, except for the general meeting of shareholders composed of the shareholders who are the investors and owners of the company, qualification as a shareholder is not required to become an organ of the company (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016DA251215 decided on 2017. 3. 23.).\\n\\nThe organs of a stock company can be classified by function into decision-making organs, business-execution organs, and audit organs, and among them the decision-making function can be further divided into decision-making on the company’s fundamental matters, important matters, and ordinary matters, while the business-execution function can be divided into internal business execution and external business execution. Among the organs of a stock company, the general meeting of shareholders is a necessary organ through which shareholders decide the company’s will regarding important matters concerning the company’s basic organization and management, and as to matters designated by the Commercial Act as matters requiring a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, neither another organ nor a third party may be delegated such matters by articles of incorporation or by resolution of the general meeting of shareholders (see the above Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016DA251215). However, because deciding all important matters concerning the company at the general meeting of shareholders is not efficient and is practically difficult, as it would generate enormous transaction costs, most legislative examples regarding stock companies provide that the general meeting of shareholders decides only fundamental matters, while matters concerning other important business execution are to be decided by the board of directors composed of several directors elected at the general meeting of shareholders.\\n\\n(2) Commercial Act Article 393(1) concerning stock companies provides, “The execution of business of the company, such as the disposal and transfer of important assets, the borrowing of large-scale property, the appointment or dismissal of a manager, and the establishment, relocation or abolition of a branch office, shall be decided by a resolution of the board of directors,” thereby comprehensively providing that the board of directors has decision-making authority concerning the company’s business execution. Before the amendment by Act No. 6488 on 2001. 7. 24., former Commercial Act Article 393(1) merely provided for “the execution of business of the company,” and it was not clear whether this provision merely prescribed matters within the authority of the board of directors or prescribed exclusive matters requiring a board resolution that could not be delegated to the representative director and had to be decided by the board. In reflection of the fact that this unclear provision prevented the board of directors from becoming active, the Commercial Act as amended in 2001 revised Article 393(1) to its current form. The purpose was to strengthen the board’s authority so that it would play the role of an actual decision-making organ by specifying the scope of matters requiring board resolution and by making it impossible to delegate to the representative director important matters of business execution, which the board itself must decide. Accordingly, if a matter falls under “the disposal and transfer of important assets, the borrowing of large-scale property, etc.” prescribed in Commercial Act Article 393(1), a board resolution must be obtained even if it is not designated as a matter requiring board resolution in the articles of incorporation or board regulations (see Supreme Court Decision 2014DA213684 decided on 2016. 7. 14.).\\n\\nAlso, in a stock company that in principle separates ownership and management, shareholders, through resolutions of the general meeting of shareholders, make decisions regarding the appointment and dismissal of directors who manage the company and matters that cause significant changes to the company’s basic structure or business organization as prescribed by law and the articles of incorporation, such as mergers, divisions, and transfer of business, so preventing a director from making it impossible or extremely difficult for shareholders to exercise voting rights is impermissible as it impairs the essential function of the stock company system (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DA35033 decided on 2011. 6. 24.). The legal principle that when directors or auditors are appointed at a general meeting of shareholders, the resolution of appointment and the consent of the appointee are sufficient to acquire the status of director or auditor, and that the representative director does not possess the authority to appoint directors or auditors (see the above Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016DA251215), likewise clarifies the distribution of authority between the decision-making organs of a stock company and the representative director.\\n\\nAs to matters for which the Commercial Act requires a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, delegation to another organ or a third party is not permitted (see the above Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016DA251215). In light of the nature of company law as a body of law governing organizational relations and as a mandatory law with a strong imperative character, there are limits to delegating to another organ the authority granted by the Commercial Act to a specific organ.\\n\\nc. The relationship between decision-making in a stock company and Commercial Act Article 209(2)\\n\\n(1) Commercial Act Article 209 concerning an unlimited partnership provides that a partner who represents the company has authority to perform all judicial and extra-judicial acts concerning the company’s business, and that restrictions on such authority cannot be asserted against good-faith third parties; Commercial Act Article 389(3) provides that the above provision shall apply mutatis mutandis to the representative director of a stock company. Accordingly, when the representative director of a stock company carries out a transaction act with a third party without a board resolution, the interpretation of the legal relationship and the scope of the mutatis mutandis application of Commercial Act Article 209 become issues.\\n\\n(2) As noted above, an unlimited partnership, in principle, has each partner possess authority to execute business and the power of representation, and even where the business executor and representative are separately appointed, they must be chosen from among the partners, so organ qualification and partner qualification coincide; by contrast, a stock company has a substantive difference from an unlimited partnership in the relationship between its decision-making function and its business-execution function, in that it has organs such as the general meeting of shareholders, directors, and the board of directors composed of directors, as well as auditors, according to function. In particular, Commercial Act Article 393(1) provides that the board of directors shall resolve important business execution matters of a stock company, and paragraph (2) of the same Article provides that the board of directors supervises the execution of duties by directors, thereby declaring that the decision-making function regarding important business execution is, in principle, vested in the board of directors while also requiring the board to perform the functions of monitoring and checking the representative director’s business execution.\\n\\nBecause of these circumstances, in academia there are conflicting views: ① that Commercial Act Article 209(2) is fully applied mutatis mutandis where the representative director carries out a transaction act without a board resolution under Commercial Act Article 393(1); ② that it is applied mutatis mutandis only within a limited scope; and ③ that it is not applied mutatis mutandis “where the law provides that the representative director does not have decision-making authority.” The view that ① it is fully applied mutatis mutandis follows the wording of Commercial Act Article 389(3), which states that “the provisions of Article 209 of the Commercial Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to the representative director.” The view that ② it is applied mutatis mutandis only within a limited scope interprets that if Commercial Act Article 209(2), in the case of Commercial Act Article 393(1), which is the typical case in which the representative director’s representative authority is restricted, were interpreted as not being applied mutatis mutandis at all, it would exceed the limits of the wording of Commercial Act Article 389(3); therefore, although Commercial Act Article 209(2) is applied mutatis mutandis, such “mutatis mutandis” means not mechanical application but flexible application according to context, and interpretive modification to respect legislative intent and ensure consistency in legal interpretation is possible. In particular, since in the case of an unlimited partnership the Commercial Act provides only for restrictions on a partner’s representative authority by the articles of incorporation and contains no provision, like Commercial Act Article 393(1) for stock companies, that statutorily restricts representative authority, it is a view that the scope of mutatis mutandis application may be limited by interpretation insofar as the cases of an unlimited partnership and a stock company cannot be exactly equated. The view that ③ it is not applied mutatis mutandis further argues that although Commercial Act Article 209(1), which is applied mutatis mutandis by Commercial Act Article 389(3), provides that one “has authority to perform all judicial and extra-judicial acts,” this presupposes lawful representative acts; thus, interpreting that the representative director may perform a specific representative act without going through the board resolution that is the stock company’s decision-making authority would instead deviate from the purpose of the provision. Since the representative authority of a representative director in a stock company merely constitutes the external exercise of business-execution authority granted by law and does not naturally include decision-making authority, matters that the representative director must execute after a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders or the board of directors are matters for which the representative director has no decision-making authority; therefore, if no board resolution has been obtained, there is no decision-making by the stock company, and the representative director cannot execute it.\\n\\nSuch a relationship between the board of directors and the representative director in a stock company is a universal phenomenon adopted by most legislative systems today. And it goes without saying that the above interpretive conflict fundamentally arises because, unlike an unlimited partnership, a stock company separates decision-making authority and business-execution authority in principle, yet the law merely provides that Commercial Act Article 209 concerning restrictions on representative authority in an unlimited partnership applies mutatis mutandis to the representative director of a stock company without separately considering this point. Also, if the Commercial Act requires a resolution of the board of directors or the general meeting of shareholders for matters such as issuance of new shares or merger, and provides that in the event of a defect in such resolution the matter shall be resolved by an action, then that should be followed (Commercial Act Articles 429 and 529); however, this also stems from the attempt to regulate uniformly or to treat as “restriction on representative authority” without separately considering the effects of all cases in which a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders or the board of directors is lacking, in the absence of such provisions.\\n\\nIn interpreting Commercial Act Article 209, one must approach the matter based on the major principle of the structure of stock company organs, in which decision-making organs are separated from business-execution and representative organs, and one must also bear in mind that when the representative director violates this major principle and carries out a transaction act, the validity of the act must strike a balance between conflicting values, namely “protection of transaction security” and “protection of shareholders, and ultimately corporate creditors, through securing the financial soundness of the company.”\\n\\n(3) Unlike an unlimited partnership, where legal relations are generally explained relatively simply by dividing them into internal and external relations, the legal relations of a stock company unfold not only in internal or external relations but also around capital, shares, and various organs of the company.\\n\\nAn unlimited partnership is composed of partners who bear direct and unlimited liability for the company’s debts. Unless managing partners are designated by the articles of incorporation, each partner represents the company, and a person to represent the company may be designated by the articles of incorporation or with the consent of all partners (Commercial Act Article 207), and unless otherwise provided in the articles of incorporation, each partner has the authority to execute the company’s business (Commercial Act Article 200). Accordingly, in the case of an unlimited partnership, only restrictions by the articles of incorporation are contemplated as restrictions on the representative authority of the partner executing business, and there is no provision, like Commercial Act Article 393 concerning stock companies, that statutorily restricts representative authority.\\n\\nBy contrast, in a stock company, in addition to the representative director, there exist various organs prescribed by the Commercial Act, such as the general meeting of shareholders, directors, and the board of directors, and Chapter IV, Section 3 of Part III of the Commercial Act prescribes, with respect to the organs of a stock company, the content and method of exercising each authority. As noted above, in an unlimited partnership, each partner is, in principle, vested with the authority to execute the company’s business, but in a stock company, the representative director must be selected by resolution of the board of directors (main text of Commercial Act Article 389(1)). The representative authority that the representative director of a stock company thus selected holds as the authority to make decisions regarding external business execution may be internally restricted by the articles of incorporation or board regulations, but may also be restricted by statute. In particular, Commercial Act Article 393(1) is a representative example of statutory restriction on the representative director’s authority, as it is a provision granting the board of directors the decision-making authority over important business execution of the company.\\n\\nConsidering the structural differences between a stock company, where statutory restriction of representative authority exists, and an unlimited partnership, where it does not, even if Commercial Act Article 209(2) concerning the representative partner of an unlimited partnership, which is expected to be restricted only by internal regulations such as the articles of incorporation, is applied mutatis mutandis to the representative director of a stock company pursuant to Commercial Act Article 389(3), it should not be applied as is in all cases concerning restriction on the representative director’s authority; rather, it should be applied only within the scope where mutatis mutandis application is possible in terms of its nature, and thus cannot be viewed as applying even to cases where, under Commercial Act Article 393(1), company decisions must be made by board resolution.\\n\\n(4) That Commercial Act Article 209 concerning an unlimited partnership cannot be fully applied mutatis mutandis to a stock company is conspicuously shown in the case of Commercial Act Article 374(1), which requires a special resolution of the general meeting of shareholders when a stock company transfers all or an important part of its business, etc.\\n\\nCommercial Act Article 374(1) is a mandatory provision aimed at protecting shareholders’ interests by requiring a special resolution of the general meeting of shareholders when a stock company concludes a contract that significantly affects the interests of shareholders, thereby reflecting the shareholders’ will in the decision (see Supreme Court Decision 2017DA288757 decided on 2018. 4. 26.). It is the general rule in Supreme Court precedent and the dominant academic view that if a matter for which the Commercial Act requires a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders in order for the company’s collective will to be determined is executed without such resolution, the act is void, and the counterparty to the act of execution is not protected merely because it acted in good faith (see Supreme Court Decision 91DA11148 decided on 1991. 11. 8.). This is because the act is one in which the company’s will itself is defective. It is difficult to find a doctrinal argument that Commercial Act Article 209(2) should be applied where the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders required by Commercial Act Article 374(1) is lacking.\\n\\nd. Validity of a transaction act by a representative director that lacked a board resolution even though one was required under Commercial Act Article 393(1)\\n\\nBased on the legal principles discussed above, we examine the key issue in this case: the validity of a transaction act carried out by the representative director without a board resolution even though a board resolution was required under Commercial Act Article 393(1). The majority opinion takes the view that, including such cases, all cases where the representative director acted without a board resolution should protect good-faith third parties under Commercial Act Article 209(2), and that good faith in this context should be interpreted as “good faith and without gross negligence.” However, the dissenting opinion ultimately considers that Commercial Act Article 209(2), which is applied mutatis mutandis by Commercial Act Article 389(3), cannot be applied even to cases where the law restricts the representative director’s representative authority, such as Commercial Act Article 393(1). The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) First, we examine the wording of the relevant provisions.\\n\\nThe Commercial Act does not provide for the validity of cases in which the representative director acts without going through the board resolution required by Commercial Act Article 393(1). Accordingly, whether such an act is void, or whether it is valid but the director only bears damages liability to the company, or, if void, under what conditions it is void, or who may assert invalidity, etc., are matters left to harmonious interpretation of the legal system. Commercial Act Article 209(2) also merely prescribes “good faith,” so even under that provision, whether only third parties in good faith and without negligence are protected, or whether third parties are protected so long as they are in good faith even if negligent, is a matter to be resolved by interpreting the individual provisions in their totality.\\n\\nAccordingly, although Commercial Act Article 209(2) by its wording distinguishes only between good-faith third parties and bad-faith third parties, it is also possible to take an interpretive position that, while applying the above provision mutatis mutandis and considering transaction security, limits the conditions for invalidity and the scope of protected third parties—for example, by viewing a person who “knew or could have known” as not being in good faith, or by viewing only a person who was not in good faith due to gross negligence in not knowing as not being in good faith—thus differentiating the degree of protection through a refined interpretation of the provision. Therefore, even if Commercial Act Article 209(2) is applied mutatis mutandis where the board resolution required by Commercial Act Article 393(1) is lacking, it cannot be concluded that the prior precedents, which required no negligence in addition to good faith, necessarily violated that provision.\\n\\n(2) Moreover, as examined above, in light of the system of Commercial Act provisions and the structural differences between an unlimited partnership and a stock company, to which Commercial Act Article 209(2) originally applies, it is not proper to uniformly apply that provision to all cases in which the representative director’s representative authority of a stock company is restricted.\\n\\n(3) Below, the majority opinion’s arguments are specifically rebutted.\\n\\n(a) First, the majority opinion lists the circumstances that precedents have considered as factors in determining whether an act falls under “the disposal and transfer of important assets, the borrowing of large-scale property, etc.” in Commercial Act Article 393(1), and states that “the transaction counterparty not only has difficulty knowing the company’s specific circumstances, but also has neither the need nor the obligation to know such circumstances,” or that “even if it knows such circumstances, it is not easy to determine from the standpoint of the transaction counterparty whether the transaction act is one that should be left to the representative director’s decision.” This is ultimately understood as meaning that transaction security should be protected. However, as the majority opinion itself acknowledges, Commercial Act Article 393(1) applies uniformly even to persons who do not know of the existence of the provision, so the transaction counterparty cannot avoid application of that provision on the ground of ignorance of the law. The circumstances listed by the majority opinion, namely “the value of the property and its proportion in total assets, the scale of the company, the company’s business or property situation, financial condition, the purpose of holding the asset or borrowing and its use, relevance to the company’s ordinary business, prior business handling, etc.,” are all circumstances that “the court,” not “the transaction counterparty,” considers in determining whether the matter is an important business matter under Commercial Act Article 393(1); the transaction counterparty is not required to know all of them.\\n\\nIf a certain transaction act falls under “the disposal and transfer of important assets, the borrowing of large-scale property, etc.,” which is the company’s important business to which Commercial Act Article 393(1) applies, then even from the transaction counterparty’s perspective it will be an act such as lending a large amount of funds or purchasing important assets, and it can be expected that the counterparty will make decisions and carry out the transaction with reasonable care. A counterparty that has previously transacted with the stock company would, in conducting the transaction, inevitably recognize the differences between the prior transaction and the present disputed transaction in terms of the results of performance of the prior transaction, the content and scale of the transaction, and whether the circumstances leading to the transaction were unusual. A counterparty transacting with that stock company for the first time would, when conducting ordinary transactions, rely on circumstances that can be expected by experience rules to be checked, namely the amount of the company’s capital stated in the company register of the stock company, the purpose of establishment of the company, etc., and would engage in the transaction by comparing them with the content and scale of the transaction act at issue. The standard of determination required by prior precedents is a listing of the matters that the court should consider based on such “transaction experience rules,” and the court, by comprehensively considering those circumstances, makes an objective determination as to whether the disputed transaction act falls under “the disposal and transfer of important assets, the borrowing of large-scale property, etc.” prescribed in Commercial Act Article 393(1).\\n\\nHowever, the Supreme Court decisions cited by the majority opinion, such as Supreme Court Decision 2005DA3649 decided on 2005. 7. 28., do include holdings that, shortly after the 2001 amendment to the Commercial Act, appear not to have distinguished restrictions on representative authority under Commercial Act Article 393(1) from purely internal restrictions. The case involved a situation in which the stock company side actively responded by presenting board regulations and arguing that no board resolution was required for the transaction, and this is not hard to understand if one considers that the need to protect the transaction counterparty’s reliance was clear.\\n\\nFurthermore, later precedents repeatedly held that “because Commercial Act Article 393(1) states that the board of directors of a stock company has the authority to make decisions regarding the execution of the company’s business, not only the disposal of important assets or borrowing of large-scale property by a stock company, but also important business that is not part of ordinary business and that the board has not generally and specifically delegated to the representative director, requires a board resolution” [see Supreme Court Decision 2009DA55808 decided on 2010. 1. 14., Supreme Court Decision 2009DA47791 decided on 2011. 4. 28., Supreme Court Decision 2014DA213684 decided on 2016. 7. 14., Supreme Court Decision 2012DA75352 (main action), 2012DA75369 (counterclaim) decided on 2017. 12. 22., Supreme Court Decision 2019DA204463 decided on 2019. 8. 14., etc.], thereby settling the legal doctrine by distinguishing between important decision-making requiring a board resolution under Commercial Act Article 393(1) and cases that do not.\\n\\n(b) Next, the majority opinion posits the so-called “dualism,” namely the view that “where a board resolution is required under Commercial Act Article 393(1), a transaction counterparty in good faith and without negligence should be protected, while in the case of an internal restriction requiring a board resolution by the articles of incorporation, etc., a counterparty in good faith and without gross negligence should be protected,” and criticizes that view. The dissenting opinion does not advocate the dualism so labeled by the majority; rather, as noted above, it ① points out the legal problem of the majority’s argument that transaction counterparties with negligence should be protected even as to statutory restrictions, while relying entirely on Commercial Act Article 209(2) as the basis, and ② argues that the current precedents, which in principle protect transaction counterparties in good faith and without negligence when the representative director has carried out a transaction act without a board resolution, are proper and therefore do not need to be changed; thus, the dissenting opinion differs in tenor from the dualism assumed by the majority opinion.\\n\\n(c) The majority opinion states that because a counterparty who transacted with a manager or a de facto representative director is protected unless grossly negligent even if negligent, it is inconsistent with equity to protect less only the counterparty who transacted with a representative director possessing stronger authority by requiring no negligence.\\n\\nHowever, this is not consistent with the Commercial Act’s regulation of managers or de facto representative directors.\\n\\nA de facto representative director is a system unrelated to statutory restrictions on the representative director’s representative authority, and Commercial Act Article 395 itself provides that, with respect to a person who originally has no representative authority, if that person carries out a representative act, then under certain requirements the person “shall be liable to third parties in good faith,” and the requirements and legal effects are expressly stated in that provision.\\n\\nIn addition, because it requires that the company be responsible for forming the appearance, there is a substantial difference in the requirements from the case under Commercial Act Article 393(1), where the company’s fault is not considered when the representative director carries out a transaction act without a board resolution.\\n\\nCommercial Act Article 11 concerning a manager’s agency authority likewise provides that a manager has agency authority “with respect to business” and that restrictions on a manager’s agency authority cannot be asserted against good-faith third parties; therefore, protection of a counterparty who transacted with a manager follows the interpretation of that provision, and the restriction on a manager’s authority under that provision is only whether it is included in “business,” not a provision like Commercial Act Article 393(1) that restricts the representative director’s representative authority, and no other such provision can be found.\\n\\nThus, it is not proper to speak only of whether the transaction counterparty had “gross negligence” in comparison with cases where both the form of the provision and the purpose and requirements of the system are different.\\n\\n(d) The majority opinion further views a board resolution as merely an internal decision-making procedure of the company, and, assuming that the fact that no board resolution was obtained is a risk arising within the company, develops the argument that a transaction counterparty who relied on the expectation that there had been a board resolution should in principle be protected. However, as discussed above, in a stock company the nature of the entity requires that the “decision-making subject” and the “business-execution subject” be separated, and they are so structured; this is why the issue in this case arose. The fact that a board resolution is an internal decision-making procedure is the starting point of the issue in this case, not a ground for one side or the other.\\n\\ne. Specific resolution of the issue and adjustment of the interests of both parties in a concrete and proper manner\\n\\n(1) Since the enactment of the Commercial Act in 1962, Korea has maintained the system of stock company organs centered on the general meeting of shareholders, the board of directors, and the representative director without fundamental change to the present day.\\n\\nAs time has passed since the enactment of the Commercial Act, economic conditions have changed, and in the modern era, where the scale of stock companies and the composition of shareholders are more diverse, the structure of the organs of stock companies needs to be redesigned to fit actual circumstances. Accordingly, the Commercial Act, in subsequent amendments, established provisions simplifying the procedures for convening and resolving at the general meeting of shareholders for small companies with total capital of less than KRW 1 billion (Commercial Act Article 363(4)), allowing the number of directors to be only one or two (Commercial Act Article 383(1)), and allowing no auditor to be appointed (Commercial Act Article 409(4)). As a result, in small companies with fewer than three directors, some matters that would ordinarily require a board resolution are prescribed as matters for resolution by the general meeting of shareholders, and some are prescribed as within the authority of the representative director (Commercial Act Article 383(4) through (6)). These are provisions intended to bridge the gap between law and reality and to promote convenience in the management organization of small companies, taking into account the reality that in small stock companies directors are often appointed only nominally and the board of directors is seldom convened and exists only formally. In light of the fact that companies with total capital of less than KRW 1 billion account for the majority domestically, such special provisions have substantial utility as they reflect the reality of the market.\\n\\nBy contrast, large stock companies involving diverse interested parties, especially listed companies, need to enhance the audit system for compliance while promoting decision-making efficiency, and at the same time prevent unnecessary disputes by clarifying the division of authority among company organs; in view of these points, special provisions on the governance of listed companies are established in Commercial Act Article 542-2 and following.\\n\\nThus, even among “stock companies” prescribed in Chapter IV of Part III (Companies) of the Commercial Act, there are diverse types ranging from small companies that inevitably have a strong closed-company character where ownership and management are difficult to separate in substance and scale, to the large listed companies noted above, and there is already recognition that, corresponding to this, concrete and individualized regulation is needed by comprehensively considering various circumstances for each company and each transaction.\\n\\nIdeally, the system would be designed so that future amendments to the law would provide specific and concrete express provisions regarding the composition of stock company organs and the division of authority among them; however, until such legislation is realized, such elasticity and flexibility must ultimately be implemented through processes such as determining the parties’ negligence in judicial proceedings. This is because a party’s negligence is not an a priori concept to be conclusively labeled as “exists” or “does not exist,” but rather falls within the judge’s normative judgment domain, in which a determination is made by comprehensively considering many indirect facts asserted and proved by the parties in the context of individual trials.\\n\\n(2) With this awareness, we review the trajectory of prior precedents.\\n\\nThe Commercial Act contains various provisions restricting the representative director’s representative authority, such as requiring the board of directors to decide when a stock company issues new shares (Commercial Act Article 416). The Supreme Court, while distinguishing the validity of the act according to whether the counterparty acted in bad faith or with negligence in cases where the board resolution prescribed in Commercial Act Article 393(1), the issue in this case, was lacking, nevertheless held that the issuance of new shares without the board resolution prescribed in Commercial Act Article 416 was valid [see Supreme Court Decision 2005DA77060 (main action), 2005DA77077 (counterclaim) decided on 2007. 2. 22.], and also held that, even if there was no resolution of the general meeting of shareholders required by Commercial Act Article 374(1), where “the company should be regarded as having been involved in the appearance of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders,” it is appropriate to recognize the company’s liability toward a person who relied on the company’s external act as valid in good faith (see Supreme Court Decision 91DA33926 decided on 1993. 9. 14.), thereby allowing exceptions rather than uniformly declaring invalidity regarding the validity of legal acts that should have undergone a special resolution of the general meeting of shareholders. It has thus determined the validity of acts lacking the respective requirements differently depending on the type of act in which the Commercial Act restricts the representative director’s authority and the effect on the company’s survival and its external transactional relations.\\n\\nThe prior attitude of precedents is the result of reasoning and endeavor to strike a balance between protection of the company and protection of the transaction counterparty, respecting the legislature’s intent to require a board resolution by statute, while considering that the effects on the company and the transaction counterparty differ according to the type of act, etc. At the same time, it shows that when a stock company with many interested parties such as creditors, shareholders, and employees carries out an external transaction act as a party, it is not necessarily desirable to rely only on theoretical consistency that would resolve the matter solely under the single statutory text of Commercial Act Article 209(2).\\n\\n(3) We examine the actual state of the concrete regulation by prior precedents concerning the interpretation of Commercial Act Article 393(1).\\n\\nAs already noted, prior precedents require the transaction counterparty to be in good faith and without negligence in order to regard an external transaction act carried out by the representative director without a board resolution even though one was required as valid. Furthermore, the Supreme Court has held that, unless special circumstances exist, it accords with general experience rules to view the transaction counterparty as having relied on the company’s representative having completed the internal procedures necessary for the transaction, and that the company bears the burden of proving the counterparty’s bad faith or negligence (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DA73530 decided on 2014. 6. 26., etc.), thereby broadly protecting counterparties who transacted with the representative director. In other words, the precedent doctrine in determining the issue in this case is not simply that “the counterparty is protected only if in good faith and without negligence,” but rather places the burden of proving the counterparty’s negligence on the company while also regarding the transaction counterparty’s reliance as falling within general experience rules.\\n\\nFirst, we look at the case where representative authority is internally restricted due to “board regulations,” etc., although the matter is not among important matters prescribed in Commercial Act Article 393(1) and has been delegated to the representative director’s decision-making authority. In the case of internal restrictions on representative authority, the object of the counterparty’s good faith is ① the existence of an internal regulation requiring a board resolution for the transaction in question, and ② the fact that such board resolution was not obtained. However, since ② presupposes ①, the main underlying matter is the existence of the internal restriction that a board resolution is required. Such restrictions on representative authority do not fall under the mandatory items to be stated in the articles of incorporation (Commercial Act Article 289(1)) and are not generally publicized; therefore, there is a need to protect third parties who do not know such circumstances. Accordingly, the prior attitude of precedents in this situation can be understood as freeing the counterparty from the burden of having to verify internal regulations of the stock company that the counterparty cannot know, thereby protecting the counterparty if it relied on the belief that “even if internal regulations existed, all procedures required to be followed internally had been completed.”\\n\\nBy contrast, in the case of a statutory restriction under Commercial Act Article 393(1), the counterparty cannot assert ① even if it did not know that a board resolution was required under Commercial Act Article 393(1) for the transaction in question. It can only assert ② good faith and without negligence regarding the absence of a board resolution.\\n\\nHowever, under Commercial Act Article 391-3, minutes must be prepared regarding the proceedings of the board of directors (paragraph (1)), and the minutes must state the agenda, the progress and summary of proceedings, the results, and the persons opposing and the reasons for opposition, and the attending directors and auditors must affix their names and seals or signatures (paragraph (2)). In light of the purpose of these provisions, if no board minutes were prepared regarding the disposal of important assets, etc., for which a board resolution is required under Commercial Act Article 393(1), caution is needed in recognizing that there was in fact a board resolution [see Supreme Court Decision 2012DA75352 (main action), 2012DA75369 (counterclaim) decided on 2017. 12. 22.], and if a transaction counterparty who engaged in a transaction falling under the statutory restriction requiring a board resolution under Commercial Act Article 393(1) did so without confirming the existence of board minutes, the need to protect such counterparty’s reliance is necessarily limited.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court has already repeatedly held that whether something constitutes the disposal of important assets or borrowing of large-scale property referred to in Commercial Act Article 393(1) must be determined by considering the value of the property and its proportion in total assets, the scale of the company, the company’s business or property situation, financial condition, the purpose of holding the asset or borrowing and its use, relevance to the company’s ordinary business, prior handling in that company, etc., and by determining whether it is appropriate to leave the matter to the representative director’s decision (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DA3649 decided on 2005. 7. 28., Supreme Court Decision 2007DA23807 decided on 2008. 5. 15., etc.).\\n\\nA concrete examination is as follows. ① The filing of an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings for a stock company under the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act was deemed to be important business not part of ordinary business, for which the representative director’s business authority did not extend, and thus requiring a board resolution under Commercial Act Article 393(1) (see Supreme Court Decision 2019DA204463 decided on 2019. 8. 14.). ② Even where the representative director of a stock company engaged in the housing sales business concluded a subcontract with the construction company containing terms concerning the disposition of unsold units, if the company disposed of unsold units amounting to approximately 77% of the total construction volume contrary to the subcontract terms, such disposition act was also deemed to require a board resolution under Commercial Act Article 393(1) (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DA47791 decided on 2011. 4. 28.). ③ In determining whether a share purchase agreement arising from a put option clause constituted a matter requiring board resolution under Commercial Act Article 393(1), the amount of the share purchase price, the company’s assets and liabilities, annual sales and net income, and the amount of capital at the time of the agreement were considered (see Supreme Court Decision 2014DA213684 decided on 2016. 7. 14.). ④ In a case involving an agreement to transfer shares of a stock company and management control, the Court determined whether it constituted disposal of important assets under Commercial Act Article 393(1) by comprehensively considering the value of the assets at issue, the ratio of the assets being transferred to the transferor company’s total assets, the scale of the transferor company, its business or property situation, and its financial condition [see Supreme Court Decision 2012DA75352 (main action), 2012DA75369 (counterclaim) decided on 2017. 12. 22.].\\n\\nAs such, there already exists settled precedent doctrine concerning whether a matter falls under those for which a board resolution is required under Commercial Act Article 393(1), and numerous precedents have accumulated accordingly, so contrary to the majority opinion’s concern, it cannot be said that the interpretation of Commercial Act Article 393(1) is uncertain or that the counterparty’s predictability is low.\\n\\n(4) In addition, if it is a listed company, the transaction counterparty’s duty of care is necessarily heightened, especially where a board resolution is required under Commercial Act Article 393(1).\\n\\nBecause a listed company must appoint outside directors except in cases prescribed by Presidential Decree, it must send notice of convening the board at least one week in advance as prescribed by the Commercial Act, including to the outside directors, and then hold the board meeting and adopt the resolution. In a transaction that proceeds urgently without enough time to physically comply with the procedures prescribed by law and obtain a board resolution, a transaction counterparty who did not confirm the existence of board minutes is highly likely not to have fulfilled its duty of care.\\n\\n(5) Furthermore, under prior precedents, even where a transaction with the company is void because the counterparty had ordinary negligence, the counterparty may seek damages against the company on the basis of the employer’s liability under Civil Act Article 756 or the damages-liability provision of Commercial Act Article 210 applied mutatis mutandis by Commercial Act Article 389(3), on the ground that the representative director carried out the transaction without the board resolution required under Commercial Act Article 393(1). In such a case, the court may recognize the company’s liability while taking the counterparty’s negligence into account through comparative negligence to promote equitable allocation of liability (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DA20670 decided on 2003. 1. 24., Supreme Court Decision 2003DA67007 decided on 2005. 2. 25., etc.).\\n\\nHowever, in the case of such employer’s liability or liability under Commercial Act Article 210, it is settled law that if the counterparty has gross negligence, the employer company is exonerated, and the meaning of gross negligence in this context is “a state in which, even though the counterparty could have known that the employee’s act was not lawfully performed within the scope of his or her job authority had the counterparty exercised only slight care, the counterparty blindly believed it to be an act within the scope of job authority, thereby lacking care to a degree almost equivalent to intent and manifestly violating the duty of care required of an ordinary person, and from the standpoint of fairness there is no need to protect the counterparty” (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DA41529 decided on 2011. 11. 24., etc.), which is almost identical to the content of the counterparty’s gross negligence regarding the absence of a board resolution set forth by the majority opinion.\\n\\nIn other words, the majority opinion takes the position that, so long as the transaction counterparty did not “negligently neglect care to a degree almost equivalent to intent,” such a counterparty without gross negligence should in principle be protected. Yet if, pursuant to the majority opinion, the transaction act with the company is deemed invalid only as to a counterparty with gross negligence, then it would be difficult to recognize damages liability previously acknowledged under Civil Act Article 756 or Commercial Act Article 210 for such a counterparty with gross negligence; ultimately, in most cases where a transaction with a company lacking a board resolution does not involve the counterparty’s bad faith or gross negligence, the transaction act would have to be deemed entirely valid, and in the very few cases where it does not, the transaction act would have to be deemed entirely invalid. One may question whether such an all-or-nothing conclusion is proper from the perspective of company law, and it creates the irrationality that flexible solutions according to the case would no longer be possible in lawsuits surrounding the wide variety of companies in our society.\\n\\nAs the majority opinion says, no one denies the need to reasonably adjust interests among interested parties including the company and the transaction counterparty, and this is the orientation of adjudication and the proper principle of dispute resolution. The majority opinion views it as a rational method of adjustment uniformly to “protect negligent transaction counterparties” in all stock companies, but the dissenting opinion holds that, under the principle of protecting transaction counterparties without negligence, the transaction counterparty’s absence of negligence should be recognized through the legal doctrine that, according to the substance of a stock company, “unless special circumstances exist, it accords with experience rules to view the transaction counterparty as having relied on the company’s representative having completed the internal procedures necessary for the transaction.” And where the company’s important decision-making is one that the Commercial Act requires to be resolved by the board of directors under Commercial Act Article 393(1), the validity of transactions made with a negligent counterparty should be denied; however, by examining the circumstances under which a counterparty with ordinary negligence came to rely on the representative director’s act, the counterparty’s right to claim damages should be affirmed, thereby opening a path to be compensated for part of the loss.\\n\\nThe prior precedents’ legal doctrine recognizes that there may be areas where a transaction act is deemed invalid but the counterparty may still seek damages, and under this doctrine disputes between the company and the transaction counterparty can be harmoniously resolved, especially through comparative negligence. If the precedents are changed as the majority opinion suggests to protect counterparties in good faith and without gross negligence, the flexibility of dispute resolution may be reduced in that only a dichotomous solution—deeming the transaction between the company and the transaction counterparty either valid or invalid—would be possible.\\n\\nf. Consistency with the doctrine of abuse of representative authority\\n\\nIt is established precedent concerning abuse of the representative director’s representative authority that an act performed by the representative director within the scope of that authority is initially valid as the company’s act, even if the representative director abused the authority for the purpose of benefiting himself or herself or a third party unrelated to the company’s profit-making purpose, and that only when the counterparty knew or could have known the representative director’s true intent does it become invalid vis-à-vis the company (see Supreme Court Decision 97DA18059 decided on 1997. 8. 29., Supreme Court Decision 2005DA3649 decided on 2005. 7. 28., etc.). In other words, even if the representative director acted within the scope of representative authority, if the authority was abused, the transaction counterparty is protected only if it was in good faith and without negligence. However, if the precedents concerning the representative director’s restrictions on authority are changed as the majority opinion suggests, then where the representative director acts in violation of restrictions prescribed by law such as Commercial Act Article 393(1), the transaction counterparty is protected so long as it is in good faith or without gross negligence, and the transaction act becomes valid. This would mean that, among unlawful transaction acts performed in violation of the express Commercial Act provision of Commercial Act Article 393(1), and transaction acts that comply with all requirements prescribed by the Commercial Act such as the board resolution procedure but nevertheless constitute abuse of representative authority due only to the representative director’s internal intent to pursue personal benefit, the former’s counterparty is protected more broadly than the latter’s counterparty; whether such a conclusion is proper from the standpoint of equity is also questionable. Without considering these circumstances, the majority opinion advocates changing the prior precedent doctrine concerning restrictions on representative authority, which also does not accord with the coherence of company law doctrine regarding the validity of the representative director’s acts.\\n\\ng. Review of this case\\n\\n(1) Up to the lower court, the proceedings were conducted on the premise that the act of preparing the confirmation letter at issue constituted an internal restriction under the Defendant’s board regulations. As the lower court determined, the meaning of the confirmation letter at issue can be construed as follows: “If ○○Sindosi Pilyu does not repay to the Plaintiff the loan amount of KRW 3 billion, the Defendant shall bear that debt.” Therefore it can be construed as a “guarantee” to the Plaintiff. Nevertheless, the reason the lower court did not examine whether the act of preparing the confirmation letter at issue constituted an act equivalent to “borrowing of large-scale property” under Commercial Act Article 393(1) seems to be that, once it was revealed that the Defendant’s board regulations existed requiring a board resolution for the guarantee act, it was not necessary to contest whether the act also fell under Commercial Act Article 393(1), and the focus was placed on whether the Plaintiff acted in good faith and without negligence.\\n\\n(2) There are numerous precedents that have treated the act of a company guaranteeing or jointly and severally guaranteeing another’s debt as falling under “borrowing of large-scale property” in Commercial Act Article 393(1) (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DA73530 decided on 2014. 6. 26., Supreme Court Decision 2014DA206563 decided on 2014. 8. 20., etc.). Also, whether a guarantee act is “large-scale” is not to be uniformly judged solely by the magnitude of the amount, but must be determined by considering the amount of the guarantee, the scale of the company, the company’s business or property situation, financial condition, relevance to the company’s ordinary business, and prior treatment in that company, etc., and by determining whether it is appropriate to leave the matter to the representative director’s decision.\\n\\nExamining the record in this case under these legal principles, although the Defendant needed a board resolution in order to guarantee ○○Sindosi Pilyu’s debt, there are many circumstances suggesting that Nonparty 1, the Defendant’s representative director, prepared the confirmation letter at issue without going through such resolution and that the Plaintiff knew or could have known that fact.\\n\\nIt is true that around March 2012 the Defendant decided at the Order Review Committee to secure the project at issue, but at that time there was no internal decision by the Defendant concerning guaranteeing ○○Sindosi Pilyu’s loan debt or assuming any monetary debt; rather, when the Defendant entered into the business agreement concerning the project at issue with Stock Company □□□□ and ○○Sindosi Pilyu, Stock Company □□□□ was to handle project fund procurement and other tasks, and the Defendant had no legal obligation to guarantee ○○Sindosi Pilyu’s debt. Moreover, the Defendant was a company established by succession to the construction business division upon its spin-off from Daewoo Motor Sales Co., Ltd. pursuant to that company’s rehabilitation plan, and at the time in question it was bearing debts amounting to approximately 14 times its capital, so guaranteeing another’s debt only a few months later, in around March 2012, is highly unusual.\\n\\nBoth the Plaintiff and the Defendant were companies with 2012 sales exceeding KRW 100 billion, and it accords with experience rules to view there as being a form of contract execution expected when ordinarily carrying out external transactions. Yet although the confirmation letter at issue and the loan agreement prepared by ○○Sindosi Pilyu for the Plaintiff were prepared simultaneously in the same place, namely the office of the representative director, the form of the two documents differs. Specifically, the loan agreement appears to have been completed after the parties merely affixed their seals on a document in which their names and addresses had already been typed, whereas in the confirmation letter at issue the Defendant’s indication was filled in by Nonparty 1 writing his name by hand, and it bears the personal seal of Representative Director Nonparty 1 rather than the Defendant’s corporate seal; moreover, the loan agreement received authentication of a private document through an agent on the same day, but there is no material showing that such authentication was obtained for the confirmation letter at issue.\\n\\nIt also appears that Nonparty 5, the Defendant’s vice president who was present at the time of the contract, did not then recognize particularly the proviso clause in the confirmation letter at issue referring to “payment by subrogation,” and Nonparty 1, who prepared the confirmation letter at issue, never informed the Defendant’s other officers of the preparation or reported it to the board, etc.; there is also no material sufficient to recognize that, beyond Nonparty 5, any other Defendant officer knew at that time that the Defendant could bear a monetary debt under the confirmation letter at issue.\\n\\n(3) If the circumstances are as such, the lower court should have reexamined whether the Plaintiff knew or could have known that Nonparty 1 did not go through the Defendant’s board resolution, although such resolution was necessary for the preparation of the confirmation letter at issue. Therefore, the lower court judgment contains an error affecting the outcome in that it misunderstood the law concerning the determination of a transaction counterparty’s good faith and absence of negligence where a representative director carries out a transaction act without a board resolution and failed to conduct the necessary review. Accordingly, the lower court judgment should be reversed.\\n\\n6. Concurring opinion of Justice Kim Jae-hyung to the majority opinion\\n\\nI would like to supplement the majority opinion with respect to several matters mentioned in the dissenting opinion.\\n\\na. The dissenting opinion states that the “good faith and without negligence” standard on which prior precedents relied is not merely a simple “good faith and without negligence” standard.
