However, for decades prior precedents have repeatedly held that a transaction act carried out by a representative director without a board resolution is valid unless the transaction counterparty knew or could have known that there was no board resolution, thereby determining the validity of such transaction act on the basis of “good faith and without negligence.” The Supreme Court even pointed out, with respect to a lower court judgment that held that, unless the counterparty “knew of the absence of a board resolution or was unaware of it due to gross negligence, the transaction act is valid,” that the “gross negligence” portion was erroneous in light of the prior precedent doctrine discussed above, thereby making clear that counterparties with gross negligence and counterparties with ordinary negligence are both excluded from protection without distinction (see Supreme Court Decision 93DA13391 decided on 1993. 6. 25.). Since negligence generally refers to ordinary negligence, the “without negligence” in prior precedents can only be interpreted literally as meaning “without negligence, that is, without ordinary negligence,” and the prior precedents must be understood as meaning that even if the counterparty did not have gross negligence, it would not be protected if it had ordinary negligence.\\n\\nThe law must be clear. While it is possible to use indeterminate concepts or abstract expressions in legislation, such concepts or expressions should be used only when unavoidable, and the meaning and content of the law should not vary according to a judge’s personal preferences or taste. This principle of clarity, as an expression of the rule of law, is required of all laws, and it likewise applies when interpreting laws and declaring legal doctrine. The Supreme Court, by clearly declaring legal doctrine regarding interpretation and application of the law, must guarantee predictability and legal stability for the people who are subject to the law. If, as the dissenting opinion says, “good faith and without negligence” is not a simple “good faith and without negligence,” then it becomes confusing what simple “good faith and without negligence” is and how it is to be distinguished from non-simple “good faith and without negligence.”\\n\\nb. The dissenting opinion states that, through repeated Supreme Court decisions holding that not only the disposal of important assets or borrowing of large-scale property by a stock company but also important business not belonging to ordinary business and not generally and specifically delegated by the board of directors to the representative director requires a board resolution, the legal doctrine has been organized so as to clearly distinguish between cases requiring a board resolution under Commercial Act Article 393(1) and cases not requiring one.\\n\\nHowever, if one examines the specific cases of the decisions cited by the dissenting opinion, they concern situations in which only the question whether the transaction act fell under the business of Commercial Act Article 393(1) was at issue, without any allegation or proof of the existence of internal regulations requiring a board resolution for that transaction act (see the numerous decisions including Supreme Court Decision 2014DA213684 decided on 2016. 7. 14.). In individual cases, if there is no allegation or proof of the existence of internal regulations such as the articles of incorporation, the only issue becomes whether a board resolution was required under Commercial Act Article 393(1), and it naturally results in a statutory restriction case.\\n\\nThe real issue is cases where there are internal regulations requiring a board resolution for the transaction act in question. As examined in the majority opinion, the execution of important business not belonging to ordinary business and not generally and specifically delegated to the representative director constitutes a statutory restriction requiring a board resolution regardless of whether it has been designated as a matter requiring board resolution in the articles of incorporation, board regulations, etc. Accordingly, even where internal regulations exist, there coexist cases of a purely internal restriction and cases that fall under both a statutory restriction under Commercial Act Article 393(1) and an internal restriction. However, because prior precedents did not distinguish between cases of internal restriction and cases of statutory restriction under Commercial Act Article 393(1), once it was established that internal regulations existed requiring a board resolution for the transaction act in question, it was no longer necessary to examine whether the matter constituted important business execution under Commercial Act Article 393(1), and the court determined the validity of the transaction act simply by judging whether the transaction counterparty was in good faith and without negligence (see Supreme Court Decision 2019DA259241 decided on 2019. 10. 31., etc.), and the lower court in this case likewise so determined. By contrast, it is difficult to find any example in which, despite the existence of internal regulations, the court further alleged and proved or reviewed whether the case fell under Commercial Act Article 393(1) and then determined whether the counterparty was in good faith and without negligence. It is therefore questionable whether one can say that the attitude of the prior precedents distinguished between cases requiring a board resolution under Commercial Act Article 393(1) and cases requiring a board resolution under internal regulations.\\n\\nc. It is efficient that laws be enacted and interpreted, as far as possible, in a direction that minimizes transaction costs if other conditions are equal. And it is desirable that the side that can more easily foresee the risk and avoid it at lower cost bear the risk for a given event. In particular, company law should be operated in a direction that appropriately adjusts the interests among interested parties such as shareholders, directors, and creditors, and minimizes transaction costs in the market.\\n\\nWhen a transaction occurs between the company and a third party, the party who can avoid at the lowest cost the risk that the transaction act will be invalid because there was no board resolution is the company, so it is desirable that the company bear such risk. By contrast, imposing a duty of investigation on the transaction counterparty or making it bear the risk of invalidity of the transaction act increases transaction costs for society as a whole.\\n\\nWhether a board resolution was obtained when required for the representative director to obtain one is a matter of whether the company organs, namely the board of directors and the representative director, are functioning properly. Ultimately, this is a matter of internal governance through the company’s internal organization and system of management oversight, supervision, and checks and balances. If the representative director can do some act without going through the board resolution even though it is required, this means that the company’s board of directors is not functioning properly. Ensuring that the board functions well is an internal company matter, and if the risk that the board’s function failed can be passed on to the counterparty, the company has less incentive to operate its board properly. Passing the risk arising from a defect in the board resolution to the counterparty in the name of strengthening the authority of the stock company’s board of directors is not proper from the standpoint of reasonable risk allocation and also hinders the sound operation of the company.\\n\\nTherefore, where the company’s board of directors is not properly functioning and the representative director neglected to obtain a board resolution when required, it is desirable, even from the standpoint of strengthening board authority or normalizing the board’s role, that the company bear the risk rather than protecting the company by passing the risk on to the transaction counterparty, while the company’s loss is compensated by means such as pursuing damages liability against the representative director. In that way, the company will also endeavor to ensure that the board of directors functions as the decision-making organ and as the organ supervising the representative director’s execution of business.\\n\\nd. The majority opinion first found, in light of the wording of Commercial Act Article 209(2), which provides for “good faith,” that in cases of defect in a board resolution, the standard of good faith and without gross negligence is more proper than the good faith and without negligence standard adopted by prior precedents. Further, while respecting the reason why prior precedents did not distinguish between cases requiring a board resolution under Commercial Act Article 393(1) and cases where only a pure internal restriction was at issue, it changed the precedents in a unified manner. The majority opinion’s purpose is to resolve in the future the uncertainty in transaction relations surrounding the defect in a board resolution through this means."}

{"[99DA19797]": "1. Determination on the Defendant’s Grounds for Appeal Nos. 1 and 2\\n\\nA. Facts found\\n\\nThe facts lawfully found by the lower court by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, and the record, are as follows.\\n\\n(1) On 1994. 3. 29., the Plaintiff entered into a rental contract (hereinafter referred to as “the rental contract at issue”) with the first-instance co-defendant, Dongbang Industry Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Dongbang Industry”), under which the Plaintiff would lend, in the form of a rental arrangement, KRW 2,525,342,600 for the purchase of computer testing machines and the like to be purchased by Dongbang Industry.\\n\\n(2) Beginning around 1994. 2., the Plaintiff and Dongbang Industry negotiated in order to conclude the rental contract at issue, and, in order to secure performance of the obligations under the rental contract at issue that Dongbang Industry would owe to the Plaintiff, Dongbang Industry agreed to provide the Plaintiff with, first, a mortgage over a parcel of land in Seo-gu, Gwangju, owned by Non-party 1, with a maximum secured amount of KRW 1,150,000,000, and, second, a mortgage in the first priority rank over a parcel of land in Gangnam-gu, Seoul, owned by Non-party 2, with a maximum secured amount of KRW 3,440,000,000, and to provide a joint and several surety.\\nHowever, since Non-party 2 was abroad at the time, it was difficult to establish the mortgage in time for the conclusion of the rental contract at issue; accordingly, the Plaintiff and Dongbang Industry agreed to provide, in substitution therefor until the parcel of land in OO-dong, owned by Non-party 2, was offered as collateral, a blank promissory note endorsed by the Defendant Company, a listed company, as collateral.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, Non-party 3, the representative director of Dongbang Industry, around that time prepared a promissory note payable to his own sole proprietorship, Non-party Seorin Planning Co., Ltd., on which the face amount, issue date, and due date were each left blank, and on which only the issuer was signed and sealed in the name of that entity (hereinafter referred to as “the promissory note at issue”), then indorsed it in the name of Dongbang Industry, and thereafter, after explaining to Non-party 4, who was the Executive Director of the Defendant Company and also Non-party 3’s father-in-law, the circumstances set forth in item (2) above, including the content of the rental contract at issue that Dongbang Industry was to conclude in the future and the circumstances under which the promissory note at issue had been issued, requested that Non-party 4 indorse the promissory note at issue in the name of the Defendant Company in order to provide it as collateral in place of the mortgage concerning Dongbang Industry’s obligations under the rental contract at issue until the parcel of land in OO-dong, owned by Non-party 2, was provided as collateral.\\n\\n(4) Non-party 4 rejected the request on the ground that, as his position was Head of the Housing Business Division, he could not be involved in financing-related work such as endorsement of promissory notes; however, eventually, unable to withstand Non-party 3’s entreaties, he indorsed the promissory note at issue around that time in the name of “Seokwang Industry Co., Ltd. Representative Director Non-party 6” (“Seokwang Industry Co., Ltd.” being the former trade name of the Defendant Company, and on 1994. 3. 24. the Defendant Company’s trade-name change registration was completed from “Seokwang Industry Co., Ltd.” to “Seokwang Construction Industry Co., Ltd.”).\\n\\n(5) In connection with the conclusion of the rental contract at issue, Non-party 3 and Non-party 1 jointly and severally guaranteed Dongbang Industry’s performance of its obligations under the rental contract at issue to the Plaintiff Company. On the same day, Non-party 1 completed, in favor of the Plaintiff Company, the registration of establishment of a mortgage over the parcel of land in Seo-gu, Gwangju, owned by him, in the same manner as set forth in item (2) above.\\nIn addition, Non-party 3 delivered to the Plaintiff Company, together with the promissory note at issue, a certificate granting authority to complete a blank promissory note in the name of Seorin Planning Co., Ltd.\\nNon-party 5, the manager in charge of the Plaintiff Company, received from Non-party 3 the business card of Non-party 4, on which his title as Executive Director of the Defendant Company was indicated, and was told to verify with Non-party 4 whether the endorsement of the promissory note at issue was genuine; Non-party 5 telephoned Non-party 4 and received confirmation that the endorsement by the Defendant Company was authentic (the parcel of land in OO-dong owned by Non-party 2 was ultimately not provided as collateral for the rental contract at issue).\\n\\n(6) On the same day, the Plaintiff Company delivered the rental property to Dongbang Industry pursuant to the rental contract at issue, and thereafter Dongbang Industry did not pay the rental fees under the rental contract at issue from the portion due in 1995. 4. onward, and the Plaintiff Company terminated the rental contract at issue around 1995. 5. 31.\\n\\nB. The lower court’s determination concerning the establishment and scope of the Defendant Company’s liability as an apparent representative director, etc.\\n\\nOn the basis of the above facts, the lower court further determined as follows.\\n\\n(1) Establishment of liability as an apparent representative director\\n\\nThe doctrine of an apparent representative director under the Commercial Act Article 395 applies not only where a director who uses a title that may be recognized as denoting authority to represent the company, such as president, vice president, executive director, managing director, or any other title, performs a juristic act in his own name, but also where a director using such a title acts using another representative director’s title. According to the facts found above, the Defendant Company shall be deemed liable for the obligations arising from the endorsement of the promissory note at issue, which arose from Non-party 4, an Executive Director, using the title of representative director of the Defendant Company and endorsing the promissory note at issue, thereby causing the promissory note at issue to be delivered to the Plaintiff Company.\\nIn response, the Defendant argues that, when Non-party 3 delivered the promissory note at issue to Non-party 5, Non-party 3 stated that Non-party 4 did not have authority to endorse the promissory note at issue and had informally signed and sealed it; and that when Non-party 5 telephoned Non-party 4 for confirmation, Non-party 4 also stated that the endorsement was beyond his authority. Accordingly, the Defendant contends that the Plaintiff Company knew that Non-party 4 had no authority to represent the Defendant Company with respect to the endorsement and therefore the Defendant Company bears no liability to the Plaintiff Company under the doctrine of an apparent representative director. However, even considering all of the Defendant’s evidence, it is insufficient to establish this, and the Defendant’s above argument is not accepted.\\nThe Defendant further argues that, even if the Plaintiff Company did not know that Non-party 4 had no authority to represent the Defendant Company with respect to the endorsement, the Plaintiff Company, as a financial institution, had a duty of care to verify with the Defendant Company’s representative director or finance department whether the endorsement of the promissory note at issue by the Defendant Company was proper, since the endorsement imposed a large-scale debt burden; yet the Plaintiff Company negligently failed to do so and was grossly negligent in receiving the promissory note at issue endorsed without proper authority, and therefore the Defendant Company bears no liability to the Plaintiff Company under the doctrine of an apparent representative director. However, even considering all of the Defendant’s evidence, it is insufficient to establish this, and the Defendant’s above argument is not accepted.\\nThe Defendant also argues that matters such as important debt guarantees require a resolution of the board of directors of the Defendant Company, yet Non-party 4 endorsed the promissory note at issue without going through such a resolution, and the Plaintiff Company knew or could have known of that circumstance, and therefore the Defendant Company bears no liability to the Plaintiff Company under the doctrine of an apparent representative director. However, even considering all of the Defendant’s evidence, it is insufficient to establish this, and the Defendant’s above argument is not accepted.\\n\\n(2) Content of the Defendant Company’s obligation\\n\\nAccording to the evidence, the obligation assumed by the Defendant Company toward the Plaintiff Company by virtue of Non-party 4’s act of endorsing the promissory note at issue cannot be regarded as a joint and several surety obligation for the entirety of Dongbang Industry’s obligations under the rental contract at issue, but rather should be regarded as a collateral obligation in substitution for the mortgage that was to be established over the land in OO-dong, owned by Non-party 2.\\n\\n(3) Partial exemption of the obligation\\n\\nAccording to the facts recognized on the basis of the evidence, it is appropriate to regard the Defendant Company’s collateral liability under the promissory note at issue to the Plaintiff Company as having been exempted, up to a total of KRW 1,300,000,000, by 1996. 10. 16.\\n\\n(4) Scope of Dongbang Industry’s obligations\\n\\nAs of 1995. 5. 31., the date of termination of the rental contract at issue, Dongbang Industry’s obligations under the rental contract at issue owed to the Plaintiff were KRW 2,332,494,466, comprising stipulated damages of KRW 2,301,118,000 and outstanding unpaid rental fees of KRW 31,376,466.\\n\\n(5) Scope of the Defendant’s obligations\\n\\nTherefore, on the basis of the Plaintiff’s principal claim, the Defendant has the obligation to pay to the Plaintiff KRW 1,032,494,466 (= KRW 2,332,494,466, being the obligations under the rental contract at issue owed by Dongbang Industry to the Plaintiff − KRW 1,300,000,000, which the Plaintiff exempted) and delay damages thereon from the day following the above contract termination date until the date of full payment.\\n\\nC. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\nIn order for a stock company’s liability arising from an act of an apparent representative director as provided in Commercial Act Article 395 to be established, not only good faith on the part of the third party who became the counterparty to the juristic act but also absence of negligence is not required (see Supreme Court Decision 72DA1907, rendered 1973. 2. 28.). However, the purport of the provisions concerning the liability of an apparent representative director under Commercial Act Article 395 is to promote trust and safety in commercial transactions by protecting good-faith third parties who relied upon such appearance, where a director who is not a representative director of the company conducts a transaction using a title that may apparently be recognized as having authority to represent the company, and the company is at fault for the creation of such appearance (see Supreme Court Decisions 86DAKA2936, rendered 1988. 10. 11.; 94DA50908, rendered 1995. 11. 21.; etc.). Since such reliance by a third party must be justified and worthy of protection, even if the third party believed that a director who is not the company’s representative director had authority to represent the company in conducting the transaction, if there was gross negligence in such belief, the company should be deemed not liable to that third party (see Supreme Court Decisions 91DA35816, rendered 1992. 7. 28.; 94DA7591, rendered 1994. 12. 2.; etc.).\\n\\nCommercial Act Article 395 lists titles such as president, vice president, executive director, and managing director as examples of titles of an apparent representative director. Such titles are exemplifications of titles that may serve as titles of an apparent representative director, and whether such a title falls within the title of an apparent representative director should be determined according to general transactional common sense in society.\\n\\nHowever, the Commercial Act does not recognize representative authority for the company in every director, but recognizes such authority only in a representative director selected by the board of directors or the general shareholders’ meeting (Commercial Act Article 389(1)). That system has continued unchanged for a considerable period since the Commercial Act took effect on 1963. 1. 1., and during that time the educational level of the general public has also improved and opportunities for ordinary persons to encounter the corporate system and the representative director system have markedly increased, so ordinary persons have come to understand the representative director system under the Commercial Act more fully. At least in the case of a stock company that has, in its organizational structure, positions such as president, vice president, executive director, and managing director, the Commercial Act requires that the representative director use the title “representative director” separately from titles such as president, and prohibits a director who is not a representative director under the Commercial Act from using the title “representative director.” In addition, in the case of large stock companies, while directors who hold the position of president in the organizational structure are often selected as representative directors, directors who hold the position of executive director or managing director in the organizational structure are not necessarily so selected. It is the reality of our country’s business world that directors who simultaneously hold the position of executive director or managing director and are selected as representative directors use titles such as “Representative Director Executive Director” or “Representative Director Managing Director.” Such circumstances would be the same even when viewed as of the time the rental contract at issue was concluded.\\n\\nAccordingly, even though Commercial Act Article 395 lists, in parallel, titles such as president, vice president, executive director, and managing director as titles of an apparent representative director, the degree of reliance that a third party may have with respect to each title is not uniform. Thus, as to each such title, whether a third party believed that the director using that title had authority to represent the company, whether there was gross negligence in such belief, and similar matters must be determined individually and concretely in light of transactional common sense. In particular, with respect to a director of a large stock company who uses only titles such as “Executive Director” or “Managing Director” without using a title such as “Representative Director Executive Director” or “Representative Director Managing Director,” in rejecting the company’s defense that the third party acted in bad faith or with gross negligence, a careful examination is required regarding the concrete parties to the transaction and the details of the transaction, and such defense must not be lightly rejected.\\n\\nTurning to this case, according to the facts found by the lower court and the record, the Defendant Company is a medium-sized construction company with capital of KRW 32,379,945,000 and ranking around 60th in domestic contract awards, and its articles of incorporation provide that it may appoint one chairman representative director, one vice chairman representative director, one president representative director, one vice president, one executive director, and several managing directors. It is also provided that executive directors assist the representative directors and are to allocate and execute the affairs of the Defendant Company as determined by the board of directors. In addition, under the Defendant Company’s organizational structure, there is a president representative director under the chairman representative director, and further under that there are a managing representative director in charge of administration and a vice president in charge of technology, with a Housing Business Division established under the vice president in charge of technology, and an executive officer assigned to the Housing Business Division.\\n\\nDongbang Industry is a small company with capital of KRW 300,000,000, and the item Dongbang Industry intended to use through the rental contract at issue was a computer testing machine necessary for manufacturing electrical clutches for automotive air conditioners. The Defendant Company, being a construction company, had no transactional relationship with Dongbang Industry, had no connection whatsoever with the subject matter of the rental contract at issue, and the contract amount of the rental contract at issue was a large sum of KRW 2,525,342,600.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Non-party 5, who was the person in charge at the Plaintiff Company in the conclusion of the rental contract at issue, received from Non-party 3 a business card of Non-party 4, and acquired the promissory note at issue. The business card of Non-party 4 received by Non-party 5 stated, in Chinese characters, “Executive Director / Head of Housing Business Division,” and, in English, “Dep. of Housing, Business / Managing Director.” Non-party 5 knew that there was no transactional relationship whatsoever between Dongbang Industry and the Defendant Company, and after receiving the promissory note at issue through Non-party 3, he made no inquiry whatsoever to the Defendant Company’s accounting department or the like as to whether Non-party 4 had authority to endorse the note in the name of the Defendant Company’s representative director; he merely telephoned Non-party 4 for confirmation and did not even verify who specifically had endorsed the promissory note at issue.\\n\\nIf so, for officers and employees of a financial institution such as the Plaintiff Company, which continuously and repeatedly performs business such as the rental of various items, the title itself used by Non-party 4—“Executive Director” and “Head of Housing Business Division” of the Defendant Company—cannot be regarded, as compared with ordinary persons, as a title that would be recognized as carrying general representative authority, including authority to carry out negotiable instrument acts for the company; rather, it is merely a title that would be recognized as indicating a director or employee who has been granted by the company authority to allocate and execute affairs only with respect to the company’s housing business division. Therefore, it should be deemed that they could more easily notice or suspect that Non-party 4 did not have authority to represent the Defendant Company. Nevertheless, even though Non-party 5, who was in charge of concluding the rental contract at issue, received the above business card of Non-party 4, to regard him as having believed that Non-party 4 had authority to endorse the promissory note at issue in the name of the Defendant Company for the purpose of guaranteeing, for Dongbang Industry, the performance of Dongbang Industry’s obligations under the rental contract at issue involving a large contract amount, given that Non-party 4 had no transactional relationship whatsoever with the Defendant Company and that only his son-in-law, Non-party 3, served as its representative director, and that he himself was registered as a director in the corporate registry of Dongbang Industry, is, in light of transactional common sense, difficult to accept in itself.\\n\\nEven if Non-party 5 so believed, as already examined above, there were circumstances indicating that it would be difficult to believe that Non-party 4 had authority to endorse the promissory note at issue on behalf of the Defendant Company; moreover, although Non-party 5 could have verified whether Non-party 4 had authority to endorse the promissory note at issue on behalf of the Defendant Company by easy methods such as inspecting a certified copy of the Defendant Company’s commercial register or inquiring of the Defendant Company’s accounting department, he took no such measures at all and instead merely listened to the statements of Non-party 3, who stood to benefit by obtaining funds for the rental contract at issue from the Plaintiff Company through the Defendant Company’s guarantee, and of his father-in-law Non-party 4, and thus believed that Non-party 4 had authority to endorse the promissory note at issue on behalf of the Defendant Company. Accordingly, at a minimum, it is appropriate to regard Non-party 5 as having been grossly negligent in such belief.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court, merely on the ground that, as the Defendant argued, it could not be recognized that Non-party 3 or Non-party 4 informed Non-party 5 that Non-party 4 had no representative authority, rejected the Defendant’s defense that the Plaintiff acted in bad faith, and, without any substantial examination of the circumstances noted above, also rejected the Defendant’s defense to the effect that the Plaintiff was grossly negligent. In doing so, the lower court committed illegality such as an error of law regarding Commercial Act Article 395, or factual error caused thereby through insufficient examination or violation of the rules of evidence, and such illegality affected the outcome of the judgment. The purport of the Defendant’s Grounds for Appeal Nos. 1 and 2, pointing out this point, is well-founded.\\n\\n2. With respect to the Defendant’s remaining grounds for appeal\\n\\nAll of the Defendant’s remaining grounds for appeal are premised on the recognition in this case of the Defendant Company’s guaranty liability under the doctrine of an apparent representative director. Since the Supreme Court finds that the lower court’s action recognizing the establishment of liability as an apparent representative director was unlawful for the reasons stated above, it does not proceed further to determine the Defendant’s remaining grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. With respect to the Plaintiff’s incidental appeal concerning the principal claim\\n\\nThe grounds for the Plaintiff’s incidental appeal are likewise premised on the recognition in this case of the Defendant Company’s guaranty liability under the doctrine of an apparent representative director. Since the Supreme Court finds that the lower court’s action recognizing the establishment of liability as an apparent representative director was unlawful for the reasons stated above, the Plaintiff’s grounds for incidental appeal are without merit without the need for further examination.\\n\\n4. With respect to the alternative claim\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court ordered payment of KRW 1,032,494,466 and delay damages thereon on the basis of the Plaintiff’s principal claim, and further, after examining only the remaining KRW 1,300,000,000 portion of the Plaintiff’s alternative claim, excluding the amount granted on the principal claim, dismissed it. Since the Supreme Court reverses and remands the portion adverse to the Defendant concerning the principal claim, the corresponding portion of the alternative claim that was not determined by the lower court is also remanded to the lower court together.\\n\\nMeanwhile, because the Plaintiff, by incidental appeal, seeks reversal of the portion of the lower court judgment adverse to the Plaintiff corresponding to KRW 1,055,150,000, that portion of the lower court judgment should also be regarded as being challenged. However, since no grounds for incidental appeal were submitted with respect to that portion, the Plaintiff’s incidental appeal with respect to that portion is also without merit.\\n\\n5. Therefore, the portion of the lower court judgment adverse to the Defendant concerning the principal claim is reversed, the case as to that portion is remanded to the lower court, and the Plaintiff’s incidental appeal is dismissed. It is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding dividend distribution by an unlisted stock company is incorrect? (In case of dispute, according to precedents)
A: Dividend distribution is determined by resolution of the shareholders’ meeting; however, where, pursuant to Article 449-2(1) (Special Provisions on Approval of Financial Statements, etc.) of the Commercial Act, the financial statements are approved by the board of directors, it is determined by resolution of the board of directors.
B: If the articles of incorporation impose on the company a duty to distribute dividends and specifically prescribe the conditions for payment of dividends or the method of calculating the amount of dividends, so that the amount to be distributed to each individual shareholder is uniquely determined, and there is no provision allowing the representative director or the board of directors to determine differently, according to business judgment, whether dividends are to be paid, the timing of payment, or the amount of dividends, then, exceptionally, when the payment conditions prescribed in the articles of incorporation are satisfied, a shareholder may be recognized as having a specific and definite claim right to payment of dividends.
C: The company may distribute profits by newly issued shares pursuant to a resolution of the shareholders’ meeting; however, a share dividend may not exceed an amount equivalent to one-half of the total amount of profit dividends.
D: Where a company, within the limit of distributable profits, distributes profits in violation of the principle of shareholder equality, creditors of the company may demand that the distributed profits be returned to the company.
E: A company that has established one closing period per year may provide in its articles of incorporation that, only once during the business year, by resolution of the board of directors, a certain date may be designated and profits may be distributed to the shareholders on that date.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2020DA263574]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. As the types of class shares that a company may issue were expanded by the 2011 amendment to the Commercial Act, a company became able to issue shares of different contents with respect to the distribution of profits, the distribution of residual assets, the exercise of voting rights at the general meeting of shareholders, redemption, conversion, and the like (Commercial Act Article 344, paragraph (1)). In such a case, the company must specify in its articles of incorporation the contents and number of the class shares it intends to issue, and, in particular, when issuing class shares with different contents regarding the distribution of profits, must also specify in the articles of incorporation matters concerning dividend distributions, such as the kind of dividend property to be delivered to the shareholders of such class shares, the method for determining the value of the dividend property, and the conditions for distributing profits (Commercial Act Article 344, paragraph (2); Article 344-2, paragraph (1)).\\n\\nA shareholder’s right to claim a profit dividend is merely a right in the sense that dividends may be received in the future, and until the distribution of retained earnings statement is approved at the general meeting of shareholders and the dividend is thereby fixed, no concrete and definite claim for payment of dividends is recognized in favor of the shareholder (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DA53792, rendered on October 28, 2010, etc.). However, if the articles of incorporation impose on the company a duty to distribute dividends and specifically provide for the conditions for payment of dividends or the method of calculating the amount of dividends, so that the amount to be distributed to each shareholder is unambiguously calculated accordingly, and if there is no provision allowing the representative director or the board of directors to separately determine, in accordance with management judgment, whether to pay dividends, the timing of payment, or the amount of dividends, then exceptionally, a concrete and definite claim for payment of dividends may be recognized in favor of the shareholder at the time when the payment conditions prescribed in the articles of incorporation are satisfied. And in such a case, the company may not refuse to pay the dividend amount to the shareholder on the ground that no resolution concerning profit dividends was adopted at the general meeting of shareholders or that a resolution refusing profit dividends contrary to the articles of incorporation was adopted.\\n\\n2. According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\nA. The Plaintiff held all 106,000 shares (common shares) issued by the Defendant company. Thereafter, at the general meeting of shareholders of the Defendant company, with the Plaintiff’s approval, a resolution was adopted to amend the articles of incorporation so as to permit the issuance of class shares concerning profit dividends (hereinafter referred to as “the preferred shares at issue”), and to approve the conversion of 31,800 out of the 106,000 common shares already issued into the preferred shares at issue.\\n\\nB. The articles of incorporation of the Defendant company provide as follows regarding the preferred shares at issue.\\n\\n1) The kinds of shares to be issued by the Defendant company shall be registered common shares and registered preferred shares (Article 8, paragraph (1)).\\n\\n2) The preferred shares to be issued by the Defendant company shall be registered preferred shares with preferential rights to profit dividends, and the number of preferred shares to be issued shall be 31,800 shares (Article 8-2).\\n\\n3) A shareholder of preferred shares shall have one voting right per share, the same as common shares, for each share (Article 8-3, paragraph (1)).\\n\\n4) A shareholder of preferred shares shall, while holding the preferred shares, receive preferential cash dividends equal to 1/106,000 of the net income for the current period per share, and dividends on the preferred shares shall be paid within 7 days from the date of the ordinary general meeting of shareholders (general meeting approving the settlement of accounts), and if there is net income for the relevant fiscal year, they must be paid within 7 days from that time through a resolution of the ordinary general meeting of shareholders (general meeting approving the settlement of accounts) (Article 8-4).\\n\\nC. At the respective ordinary general meetings of shareholders held in 2018 and 2019, after statements of appropriation of retained earnings containing no entry regarding profit dividends were approved even though net income had been generated in the preceding year, the Defendant company did not pay profit dividends to the Plaintiff for that reason.\\n\\n3. The above facts are examined in light of the legal principles set forth above.\\n\\nThe articles of incorporation of the Defendant company expressly provide for the obligation to distribute dividends with respect to the preferred shares at issue and specifically regulate matters related to the conditions for payment of dividends and the calculation of the amount of dividends. Therefore, once the financial statements are approved at the ordinary general meeting of shareholders of the Defendant company and the net income for the current period is thereby fixed, the amount of dividends that the Defendant company is obligated to pay in relation to the preferred shares at issue is immediately calculable.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Plaintiff, as a shareholder of the preferred shares at issue, is recognized as having a concrete and definite claim for profit dividends at the time when a resolution approving the financial statements including net income is adopted at the Defendant company’s ordinary general meeting of shareholders, and, absent any other special circumstances, may demand against the Defendant company payment of the dividends calculated in accordance with the articles of incorporation, to the extent of distributable profits under Commercial Act Article 462, paragraph (1).\\n\\nNevertheless, premised on the notion that the claim for profit dividends concerning the preferred shares at issue is merely a right whose content becomes fixed only by a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders concerning profit dividends, the lower court, without examining whether the financial statements stating that net income for fiscal year 2017 or 2018 had been generated were approved at the Defendant company’s ordinary general meeting of shareholders, or how much the distributable profits for each year were, determined that the Plaintiff could not demand payment of profit dividends related to fiscal years 2017 and 2018 from the Defendant company merely because no resolution concerning profit dividends was adopted at the respective ordinary general meetings of shareholders held in 2018 and 2019. The lower court’s determination contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the claim for profit dividends, and the Plaintiff’s assertion of grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the judgment below and remand the case to the lower court for further proceedings and determination, and it is so adjudged, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

question: A Company, a listed stock company, entered into a joint and several suretyship agreement with B for a debt borrowed by director A in A's personal capacity from B. If the relevant joint and several suretyship agreement constitutes a prohibited extension of credit under Commercial Act Article 542-9 (Transactions with Major Shareholders, etc. and Interested Parties), paragraph (1), which of the following statements is correct? (In case of a dispute, according to case law)
A: The relevant joint and several suretyship agreement is effective if, in advance, the board of directors discloses the material facts concerning the transaction and approves it.
B: The Commercial Act does not provide a criminal punishment provision concerning the person who entered into the relevant joint and several suretyship agreement.
C: If, instead of director A, A Company had entered into a joint and several suretyship agreement with B, with prior approval of the board of directors, in respect of the debt of A Company's auditor, A Company cannot assert the invalidity of the joint and several suretyship agreement against B.
D: If B did not know that the relevant joint and several suretyship agreement was a prohibited extension of credit under the Commercial Act, and there was no gross negligence in B's failure to know it, A Company cannot assert the invalidity of the relevant joint and several suretyship agreement against B.
E: Even if B was grossly negligent in failing to know that the relevant joint and several suretyship agreement was a prohibited extension of credit under the Commercial Act, if the board of directors of A Company ratifies this transaction, A Company cannot assert the invalidity of the relevant joint and several suretyship agreement against B.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2017DA261943]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Overview of the case and issues\\n\\nA. Overview of the case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the lower court and the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n1) Assignment of claim\\n\\na) Non-party 1, a private moneylender, and listed company NeoPurple Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “NeoPurple”), together with Non-party 2, a shareholder thereof, and Non-party 3, its representative director, while negotiating in or around November 2012 to the effect that Non-party 1 would lend money to NeoPurple and that Non-party 2 and Non-party 3 would provide joint and several guarantees and collateral, after being pointed out by Non-party 4, a director of NeoPurple, that if NeoPurple were to become the principal debtor without a board resolution, issues such as the crime of breach of trust could arise, entered into a loan-for-consumption contract (hereinafter referred to as the “Loan-for-Consumption Contract at Issue”) under which Non-party 1 would lend KRW 2 billion to Non-party 2 and Non-party 3, and NeoPurple would provide a joint and several guarantee and collateral.\\n\\nb) Non-party 2, based on the Loan-for-Consumption Contract at Issue, lent KRW 500 million, out of the money received from Non-party 1, to NeoPurple.\\n\\nc) On or around December 28, 2012, Non-party 1 received from NeoPurple an assignment of NeoPurple’s claim for payment of goods against Korea Yakult Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Korea Yakult”) (hereinafter referred to as the “Claim at Issue”), under the name of collateral relating to the Loan-for-Consumption Contract at Issue (hereinafter referred to as the “Assignment of Claim at Issue”).\\n\\n2) Distribution objection\\n\\na) The Plaintiff and the Defendant each obtained a preliminary attachment order with respect to the Claim at Issue, and Non-party 1 received an assignment of the Claim at Issue. The authenticated copy of the Plaintiff’s preliminary attachment order was delivered to Korea Yakult on April 17, 2013, the notice of Non-party 1’s assignment of the Claim at Issue was delivered on May 13, 2013, and the authenticated copy of the Defendant’s preliminary attachment order was delivered to Korea Yakult on May 22, 2013.\\n\\nb) Accordingly, Korea Yakult deposited the amount of the Claim at Issue on September 30, 2013, on the grounds of concurrence of seizures, etc., and thereafter, in Seoul Southern District Court Case No. 2013TAGI2293, a distribution schedule was prepared distributing KRW 102,856,383 to the Plaintiff and KRW 283,804,806 to the Defendant. Prior thereto, Non-party 1 withdrew the demand for distribution.\\n\\nc) The Plaintiff appeared on the distribution date in the above case, raised an objection, and filed this action for objection to distribution, asserting that because the Defendant attached the Claim at Issue after it had been assigned to Non-party 1, such attachment by the Defendant was unlawful and thus the Defendant should not be distributed any amount.\\n\\nB. Issues\\n\\nAt issue are whether the Assignment of Claim at Issue constitutes credit extension prohibited by Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act, and whether credit extension in violation of Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act is void.\\n\\n2. Interpretation of Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act\\n\\na) Whether a contract under private law or another juristic act, when performed in violation of a specific statutory provision that prohibits a certain act, is void, or whether a court refuses assistance in realizing the content of the juristic act or its effect is otherwise limited to another extent, is a matter relating to the legal effect of the relevant statutory provision in a broad sense, and is determined by the interpretation of that statutory provision. Accordingly, if there is an express provision on that point, it must of course be followed; if there is no such provision, then ultimately it shall be determined by examining, in light of the purpose and meaning of the prohibitory provision, whether invalidity or other restriction of effect for a juristic act contrary thereto is required (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2018DA258562, rendered on June 13, 2019).\\n\\nb) Under Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act, a listed company shall not extend credit to, or for the benefit of, a major shareholder and his or her specially related person, a director and an executive officer, or an auditor (hereinafter referred to as “major shareholders, etc.”). Here, credit extension means lending money or other property having economic value, guaranteeing the performance of obligations, the purchase of securities of a nature that provides financial support, and other direct or indirect transactions accompanied by transactional credit risk, as prescribed by Presidential Decree. Considering that major shareholders, etc. can exercise substantial influence over the management of a stock company, if a company extends credit to major shareholders, etc., there is a high risk not only that the company’s financial soundness will be undermined and the interests of general shareholders or creditors will be infringed, but also that abnormal accounting treatment may be carried out in order to conceal it. In particular, in the case of a listed company with various stakeholders, the demand for accounting and management soundness is higher than for an unlisted company; therefore, Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act aims to protect the company’s interests as well as contribute to the soundness of the stock market and investor protection by, in principle, prohibiting credit extension by listed companies to major shareholders, etc. However, from the perspective of management necessity or freedom of business of a listed company, there may be some credit extensions that need not or need only minimally be subject to prohibition; accordingly, Article 542-9 of the Commercial Act exceptionally permits certain credit extensions under paragraph (2) by considering the counterparty to the transaction, the nature or purpose of the transaction, its scale, and its impact on management soundness. Furthermore, Article 624-2 of the Commercial Act provides that a person who extends credit in violation of Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 5 years or a fine not exceeding KRW 200 million, while Article 634-3 of the Commercial Act provides a dual punishment provision applicable to the company.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above, and considering the legislative purpose and content of Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act, as well as the fact that criminal punishment is imposed for violations, the above provision constitutes a mandatory provision; therefore, credit extension made in violation thereof is impermissible and is void under private law, and anyone may assert its invalidity. Moreover, according to the wording of the above provision, credit extension made in violation of Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act is prohibited regardless of whether the board of directors approved it, unlike self-dealing by a director governed by Article 398 of the Commercial Act, and thus cannot become valid even if there is prior approval or subsequent ratification by the board of directors.\\n\\nc) However, as seen above, Article 542-9 of the Commercial Act in paragraph (1) in principle prohibits credit extension, while in paragraph (2) it permits some credit extensions. Accordingly, a third party outside the company may, in a specific case, find it difficult to know or determine whether a certain credit extension is subject to prohibition. Considering the realities of transactions, where commercial dealings with listed companies are frequent, imposing on third parties a duty to investigate and confirm, each time they deal with a listed company, whether Article 542-9 has been violated would undermine the promptness of commercial transactions and the security of transactions. Therefore, even if a credit extension violates Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act, if the third party did not know of it and was not grossly negligent in not knowing it, invalidity may not be asserted against that third party.\\n\\n3. Determination in this case\\n\\na) Whether all or part of the Assignment of Claim at Issue constituted credit extension in violation of Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act\\n\\nThe lower court determined, for the reasons stated in its judgment, that at the time of the conclusion of the Loan-for-Consumption Contract at Issue and the Assignment of Claim at Issue, Non-party 2 fell under a major shareholder of the listed company NeoPurple (Article 542-8(2)6 of the Commercial Act) or a person instructing the performance of business (Article 401-2(1)1 of the Commercial Act), and that Non-party 3 was NeoPurple’s representative director; accordingly, NeoPurple’s joint and several guarantee of Non-party 2’s and Non-party 3’s loan obligations, and its assignment of the Claim at Issue for that collateral purpose, constituted “credit extension to major shareholders, etc.” prohibited by Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act and Article 35(1)1 of the Enforcement Decree of the Commercial Act.\\n\\nIn light of the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the lower court’s determination is proper, and there is no error of inadequate examination or misapprehension of legal principles, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, regarding whether all or part of the Assignment of Claim at Issue constituted credit extension in violation of Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act.\\n\\nb) Whether the Assignment of Claim at Issue is void in violation of Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act\\n\\nThe lower court premised that credit extension made in violation of Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act is, in principle, void, but is valid in relation to the third party concerned only where the bona fide third party did not know that it constituted credit extension and was not grossly negligent in not knowing that fact. Furthermore, for the reasons stated in its judgment, the lower court found that Non-party 1 knew that the Assignment of Claim at Issue constituted credit extension prohibited by Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act, or, even if Non-party 1 did not know it, that Non-party 1 would have been able to know it with only a little care and was grossly negligent in not knowing that fact by markedly violating the duty of care required by trade usage; accordingly, the lower court determined that the Assignment of Claim at Issue was credit extension made in violation of Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act and was therefore void.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above and the record, the above determination of the lower court is proper, and there is no error of inadequate examination or misapprehension of legal principles regarding the private-law effect of credit extension made in violation of Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act, its relationship with board approval, the scope of persons who may assert invalidity, or whether there was bad faith or gross negligence.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; accordingly, the judgment is rendered as stated in the dispositive part, by unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: In Company A, an unlisted stock company, A was the Representative Director, and B and C were shareholders. On 2021. 5. 1., Company A issued only to C, who was personally acquainted with A, and irrespective of the attainment of Company A’s management objectives, a detachable bond with stock acquisition rights, in which only the stock acquisition rights were transferable. On 2023. 6. 1., A, in order to increase his influence over his own company, acquired from C all of the stock acquisition rights attached to the bond with stock acquisition rights, and by that date no action for invalidation of the issuance of the bond with stock acquisition rights had been filed. Thereafter, A exercised all of the stock acquisition rights at one time, and new shares were issued on 2023. 8. 1. Which of the following statements regarding this is correct? (If there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: The aggregate issue price of the shares to be issued by the exercise of the stock acquisition rights attached to each bond with stock acquisition rights may exceed the amount of each bond with stock acquisition rights.
B: Before 2023. 8. 1., when new shares were issued as a result of the exercise of the stock acquisition rights, B may at any time assert the invalidity of the issuance of the bond with stock acquisition rights.
C: Fearing disadvantages from the issuance of the bond with stock acquisition rights carried out under A’s initiative, B may file on 2023. 9. 1. an action to maintain the issuance of new shares.
D: B may file on 2023. 10. 1. an action for invalidation of new share issuance by asserting that the issuance of the bond with stock acquisition rights is void or by making arguments premised thereon.
E: B may file on 2023. 12. 1. an action for invalidation of new share issuance by analogy to the inherent grounds for invalidity in the exercise of the stock acquisition rights or the issuance of new shares thereunder.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2021DA201054]": "The Court examines the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Relevant legal principles\\n\\na. A bond with stock acquisition rights is a bond granted with a stock acquisition right by which a certain number of new shares may be subscribed for at a previously fixed price, and even in the case of issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights, since it affects the corporate basis of a stock company and the interests of existing shareholders, it is in substance analogous to issuing shares; accordingly, Article 429 of the Commercial Act concerning an action for invalidation of share issuance applies by analogy. The invalidity of the issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights may be asserted only by means of an action brought within 6 months from the date on which the bonds with stock acquisition rights were issued, and after the 6-month period for bringing an action has elapsed, new grounds for invalidity cannot be added and asserted (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DA202919 rendered on December 10, 2015, Supreme Court Decision 2000DA37326 rendered on June 25, 2004, etc.). Therefore, if an action for invalidation of issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights is not brought within 6 months from the date of issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights, or if an action for invalidation of issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights brought within 6 months has become final and binding with the defeat of the active party, the invalidity of the issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights can no longer be asserted thereafter.\\n\\nb. 1) However, as to the exercise of the stock acquisition right granted to the bonds with stock acquisition rights or the issuance of new shares resulting therefrom, Article 429 of the Commercial Act may be applied by analogy, and it may be challenged by an action for invalidation of share issuance. In such a case, unless there are special circumstances, only grounds for invalidity inherent in the exercise of the stock acquisition right or the subsequent issuance of new shares may be asserted, and the invalidity of the issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights or any argument premised thereon may not be raised.\\n\\n2) Meanwhile, Article 418(1) and (2) of the Commercial Act protects the stock acquisition rights of existing shareholders by providing that, when a company issues new shares, it shall in principle allocate them to existing shareholders, and may allocate new shares to a third party only when so provided in the articles of incorporation, while limiting such grounds to cases necessary to achieve a managerial purpose such as the introduction of new technology or the improvement of the financial structure. Accordingly, when a stock company issues new shares, if there is no ground prescribed by the articles of incorporation within the scope necessary to achieve the company’s managerial purpose, allocating new shares to a third party for the purpose of defending the management control or control rights of a major shareholder or management in a situation where a management-control dispute of the company has materialized violates Article 418(2) of the Commercial Act and infringes the shareholders’ stock acquisition rights, and where, as a result, a serious change is brought about in the company’s control structure and a significant consequence occurs whereby the control rights of existing shareholders over the company are substantially weakened, such issuance of new shares is invalid (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DA50776 rendered on January 30, 2009, Supreme Court Decision 2018DA289542 rendered on April 3, 2019, etc.). These principles apply equally to the case where bonds with stock acquisition rights are issued to a third party (see the latter sentence of Article 516-2(4) of the Commercial Act, the proviso to Article 418(2), Supreme Court Decision 2015DA202919 rendered on December 10, 2015).\\n\\n3) In the case of bonds with stock acquisition rights, even if they are issued to a third party for the purpose of defending the management control or control rights of a major shareholder, etc. without a managerial purpose, such issuance does not itself infringe the stock acquisition rights of existing shareholders, and only when the major shareholder, etc. later acquires the stock acquisition rights and obtains new shares by exercising them is the stock acquisition right of existing shareholders infringed and the purpose of defending the management control or control rights of the major shareholder, etc. materialized. According to this, if the company issued bonds with stock acquisition rights to a third party for the purpose of defending the management control or control rights of a major shareholder, etc., the issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights may be invalid, and such ground may be challenged by an action for invalidation of the issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights within 6 months from the date of issuance. Further, if a major shareholder, etc. acquires the bonds with stock acquisition rights issued in the foregoing manner or the stock acquisition rights granted thereto and thereafter, after 6 months from the date of issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights, exercises the stock acquisition rights and acquires new shares, this is, in substance, identical to the company issuing new shares to the major shareholder, etc. without a managerial purpose; therefore, by analogy to grounds for invalidity inherent in the exercise of the stock acquisition right or the subsequent issuance of new shares, the invalidity of the issuance of new shares may also be asserted by an action for invalidation of share issuance.\\n\\nThus, the shareholder’s right to sue challenging the unlawful issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights or the issuance of new shares based thereon can be substantially protected.\\n\\n4) In the above case, the period for bringing an action for invalidation of share issuance shall be counted from the date of issuance of the new shares, and even if the issuance of new shares results from the exercise of the stock acquisition right granted to the bonds with stock acquisition rights, it shall not be counted from the date of issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights.\\n\\n2. Judgment in this case\\n\\na. The following facts can be found from the reasoning of the judgment below and the record.\\n\\n1) The Defendant’s articles of incorporation provide that, where necessary for urgent managerial financing, the company may, by resolution of the board of directors, issue bonds with stock acquisition rights to financial institutions, etc. other than shareholders (Article 23(1)5).\\n\\n2) The Defendant issued privately placed detachable bonds with stock acquisition rights on June 30, 2016 (hereinafter referred to as “the bonds with stock acquisition rights in this case”), and Partners No. 4 Growth Investment Fund and Gudam Partners Limited Liability Company underwrote bonds with stock acquisition rights in this case in the respective amounts of KRW 2,056,000,000 and KRW 3,084,000,000. At that time, the Plaintiff held 131,449 shares of the Defendant’s stock (8.78%), and the Non-Party, who was the Defendant’s representative director, held 335,393 shares of the Defendant’s stock (22.39%).\\n\\n3) In or around September 2016, the Non-Party acquired from Partners No. 4 Growth Investment Fund and Gudam Partners Limited Liability Company a portion of the stock acquisition rights granted to the bonds with stock acquisition rights in this case (hereinafter the stock acquisition rights acquired by the Non-Party are referred to as “the stock acquisition rights in this case”).\\n\\n4) When the Non-Party exercised the stock acquisition rights in this case on October 21, 2019, the Defendant issued 100,000 common shares (par value of 500 won, hereinafter referred to as “the new shares in this case”) to the Non-Party on the same day.\\n\\n5) No action for invalidation of issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights was brought within 6 months from the date of issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights in this case.\\n\\n6) On November 19, 2019, the Plaintiff filed an action for invalidation of share issuance in this case, alleging in substance that because the Defendant issued the bonds with stock acquisition rights in this case for the purpose of strengthening the management control or control rights of the representative director, the Non-Party, without the need for urgent managerial financing, the issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights in this case and the issuance of new shares resulting from the Non-Party’s exercise of the stock acquisition rights in this case are invalid.\\n\\nb. We examine the above factual relations in light of the legal principles set forth above.\\n\\nThe period for bringing an action for invalidation of share issuance in this case shall be counted from the date of issuance of the new shares in this case, and it is not to be counted from the date of issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights in this case merely because the Plaintiff’s allegations include grounds concerning invalidity of the issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights in this case.\\n\\nHowever, since the action for invalidation of share issuance in this case was brought on November 19, 2019, within 6 months from October 21, 2019, the date of issuance of the new shares in this case, it is clear that the period for bringing the action was observed.\\n\\nTherefore, the court below should have examined whether the Defendant issued the bonds with stock acquisition rights in this case for the purpose of helping to defend the management control or control rights of the Non-Party, thereby being substantially evaluable as equivalent to issuing new shares to the Non-Party without a managerial purpose, and whether, as a result thereof, a serious change was brought about in the Defendant’s control structure and a significant consequence occurred whereby the Plaintiff, an existing shareholder, was substantially weakened in its control rights over the company, and then determined whether the issuance of the new shares in this case was invalid.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below held that the action for invalidation of share issuance in this case was unlawful on the ground that the Plaintiff asserted only grounds for invalidity of the issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights, and counted the period for bringing an action from the date of issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights in this case. The court below’s determination contains an error by misapprehending the legal principles regarding the period for bringing an action in an action for invalidation of share issuance.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is set aside, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2021DA201054]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nA. Bonds with warrants are bonds granted with subscription rights to new shares that entitle the holder to request the subscription of a certain number of new shares at a pre-determined price. Even in the case of the issuance of bonds with warrants, because they affect the company’s capital basis and the interests of existing shareholders and are thus substantially similar to the issuance of new shares, Article 429 of the Commercial Act concerning an action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares applies by analogy. The invalidity of the issuance of bonds with warrants may be asserted only by an action brought within 6 months from the date on which the bonds with warrants were issued, and after the 6-month period for bringing an action has elapsed, no new ground of invalidity may be added and asserted (see Supreme Court Decisions rendered on December 10, 2015, 2015DA202919, and on June 25, 2004, 2000DA37326, etc.). Accordingly, if no action for invalidation of the issuance of bonds with warrants is filed within 6 months from the date of issuance of the bonds with warrants, or if an action for invalidation of the issuance of bonds with warrants filed within 6 months becomes final and conclusive in the defeat of the active party, the invalidity of the issuance of the bonds with warrants may no longer be asserted thereafter.\\n\\nB. 1) However, the exercise of the subscription rights granted to bonds with warrants or the issuance of new shares resulting therefrom may be challenged by an action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares by applying Article 429 of the Commercial Act by analogy. In such a case, absent special circumstances, only grounds of invalidity inherent to the exercise of the subscription rights or the issuance of new shares therefrom may be asserted, and no assertion may be made that the issuance of the bonds with warrants is invalid or on the premise thereof.\\n\\n2) Meanwhile, Article 418(1) and (2) of the Commercial Act protects existing shareholders’ subscription rights to new shares by providing that, when a company issues new shares, they are in principle allotted to existing shareholders, and third-party allotment is permitted only where so provided in the articles of incorporation, while limiting the grounds therefor to cases necessary to achieve managerial purposes such as the introduction of new technology or the improvement of the financial structure. Accordingly, when a stock company issues new shares, if there is no ground provided in the articles of incorporation within the scope necessary to achieve the company’s managerial purpose, then, in a situation where a dispute over the company’s management control has become real, the allotment of new shares to a third party for the purpose of defending the management right or control right of a major shareholder or management, etc., violates Article 418(2) of the Commercial Act and infringes shareholders’ subscription rights to new shares, and where such issuance of new shares causes serious consequences, namely a substantial change in the company’s governance structure and a significant weakening of the existing shareholders’ control over the company, such issuance of new shares is invalid (see Supreme Court Decisions rendered on January 30, 2009, 2008DA50776, and on April 3, 2019, 2018DA289542, etc.). These legal principles apply equally to the case of issuing bonds with warrants to a third party (see the latter sentence of Article 516-2(4) of the Commercial Act, the proviso to Article 418(2), and Supreme Court Decision rendered on December 10, 2015, 2015DA202919).\\n\\n3) In the case of bonds with warrants, even if they are issued to a third party for the purpose of defending the management right or control right of a major shareholder, etc. without a managerial purpose, they do not in themselves infringe existing shareholders’ subscription rights to new shares; rather, existing shareholders’ subscription rights are infringed, and the purpose of defending the management right or control right of the major shareholder, etc. materializes, only when the major shareholder, etc. later acquires new shares by exercising the transferred subscription rights. According to this, if the company issued bonds with warrants to a third party for the purpose of defending the management right or control right of a major shareholder, etc., the issuance of the bonds with warrants may be invalid, and such a ground may be challenged by an action for invalidation of the issuance of bonds with warrants within 6 months from the date of issuance. Furthermore, if a major shareholder, etc., after acquiring the bonds with warrants issued in the foregoing manner or the subscription rights granted thereunder, exercises the subscription rights after 6 months have passed from the date of issuance of the bonds with warrants and acquires new shares, this is, in substance, the same as the company issuing new shares to the major shareholder, etc. without a managerial purpose; therefore, the invalidity of the issuance of new shares may also be asserted by an action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares, by analogy to a ground of invalidity inherent to the exercise of the subscription rights or the issuance of new shares therefrom.\\n\\nIn this way, a shareholder’s right to sue disputing an unlawful issuance of bonds with warrants or the issuance of new shares based thereon can be effectively protected.\\n\\n4) In the foregoing case, the filing period for an action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares must be calculated from the date of issuance of the new shares, and even if the issuance of new shares resulted from the exercise of the subscription rights granted to the bonds with warrants, it is not calculated from the date of issuance of the bonds with warrants.\\n\\n2. Determination in this case\\n\\nA. According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n1) The Defendant’s articles of incorporation provide that, where necessary for urgent fundraising in connection with management, the company may, by resolution of the board of directors, issue bonds with warrants to financial institutions, etc. other than shareholders (Article 23(1) item 5).\\n\\n2) On June 30, 2016, the Defendant issued privately placed detachable bonds with warrants (hereinafter referred to as “the bonds with warrants in this case”), and Partners No. 4 Growth Investment Association and Gudam Partners Co., Ltd. subscribed for bonds with warrants in this case in amounts equivalent to KRW 2,056,000,000 and KRW 3,084,000,000, respectively. At that time, the Plaintiff held 131,449 shares of the Defendant’s stock (8.78%), and the Non-Party, who was the Defendant’s Representative Director, held 335,393 shares of the Defendant’s stock (22.39%).\\n\\n3) Around September 2016, the Non-Party acquired by assignment a part of the subscription rights granted to the bonds with warrants in this case from Partners No. 4 Growth Investment Association and Gudam Partners Co., Ltd. (hereinafter the subscription rights acquired by the Non-Party are referred to as “the subscription rights in this case”).\\n\\n4) When the Non-Party exercised the subscription rights in this case on October 21, 2019, the Defendant issued 100,000 shares of common stock (par value KRW 500, hereinafter referred to as “the new shares in this case”) to the Non-Party on the same day.\\n\\n5) No action for invalidation of the issuance of bonds with warrants was filed within 6 months from the date of issuance of the bonds with warrants in this case.\\n\\n6) On November 19, 2019, the Plaintiff filed the action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares in this case, alleging in substance that the Defendant had issued the bonds with warrants in this case for the purpose of strengthening the management right or control right of the Representative Director, the Non-Party, without the need for urgent fundraising in connection with management, and that therefore both the issuance of the bonds with warrants in this case and the issuance of new shares resulting from the Non-Party’s exercise of the subscription rights in this case are invalid.\\n\\nB. The above factual relations are examined in light of the legal principles set forth above.\\n\\nThe filing period for the action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares in this case must be calculated from the date of issuance of the new shares in this case, and it is not the case that it must be calculated from the date of issuance of the bonds with warrants in this case merely because the Plaintiff’s allegations include grounds concerning the invalidity of the issuance of the bonds with warrants in this case.\\n\\nHowever, since the action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares in this case was filed on November 19, 2019, which is within 6 months from October 21, 2019, the date of issuance of the new shares in this case, it is clear that the filing period was observed.\\n\\nAccordingly, the court below should have examined whether the Defendant issued the bonds with warrants in this case for the purpose of helping to defend the management right or control right of the Non-Party, thereby making it substantially equivalent to issuing new shares to the Non-Party without a managerial purpose, whether this caused a substantial change in the Defendant’s governance structure and gave rise to serious consequences in the form of a significant weakening of the Plaintiff, the existing shareholder, in controlling the company, and then determined whether the issuance of the new shares in this case was invalid.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below held that the action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares in this case was unlawful, calculating the filing period from the date of issuance of the bonds with warrants in this case on the ground that the Plaintiff alleged only grounds for invalidity of the issuance of the bonds with warrants. In such judgment of the court below, there is an error in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the filing period for an action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares.\\n\\n3.
