As to Ground 2 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court held that on 1999. 6. 30., Asia Motors, the obligor on the reorganization claims based on the bills at issue, was merged into the reorganization company, which was the rightful creditor of the above reorganization claims, and that the surviving company, namely the reorganization company, comprehensively succeeded to the rights and obligations of Asia Motors, which ceased to exist by the merger, so that the above reorganization claims of the pre-merger reorganization company against Asia Motors were extinguished by confusion because the claim and obligation vested in the same person; therefore, the portion in which LG Comprehensive Finance received repayment, etc. pursuant to Asia Motors’ reorganization plan after the merger of the reorganization company and Asia Motors did not cause damage to the Plaintiff and thus did not constitute unjust enrichment.\\n\\nWhere a claim and an obligation come to vest in the same subject, as a rule the claim is extinguished unless there is a legitimate interest in recognizing its survival because the existence of the claim is a prerequisite to the exercise of rights against a third party by the person who has become both creditor and debtor. Accordingly, the reorganization claim of the reorganization company against Asia Motors was extinguished by confusion when Asia Motors was merged into the reorganization company, and therefore it cannot be said that any damage arose to the reorganization company merely because LG Comprehensive Finance did not attribute the reorganization claim to the reorganization company. However, if LG Comprehensive Finance should have attributed to the reorganization company the rights under the bills against Asia Motors, or the reorganization claims against Asia Motors acquired on that basis, but instead exercised the reorganization claims against the reorganization company and the Plaintiff after Asia Motors merged into the reorganization company and received repayment, etc., this should be regarded as causing damage by infringing claims that should have belonged to the reorganization company and the Plaintiff.\\n\\nIf so, the lower court’s determination that, by invoking the doctrine of confusion, even if LG Comprehensive Finance received repayment, etc. pursuant to Asia Motors’ reorganization plan from the reorganization company and the Plaintiff after the merger, no damage was caused to the Plaintiff, is erroneous in its legal understanding of damage arising from unjust enrichment. However, as noted in the determination on Ground 1 above, so long as the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendant for restitution of unjust enrichment is deemed impermissible under the principle of good faith and fair dealing even if damage to the Plaintiff is recognized, this error by the lower court cannot affect the outcome of the judgment. Accordingly, the argument in this part of the grounds of appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. As to Ground 3 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nIn civil litigation procedure, whether the court recommends settlement or issues a settlement recommendation order is a matter to be undertaken ex officio, taking into account the interests of the parties and all other circumstances. Therefore, even where the emergence of the claim itself is clear but it is rejected under the principle of good faith and fair dealing, it cannot be said to be unlawful merely because a conciliatory resolution was not attempted before judgment.\\n\\nThe lower court judgment does not accept the allegation of error of law, including violation of the Civil Procedure Act, as asserted in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as set forth in the order."}

{"[88DAKA17181]": "With respect to the grounds of appeal by the Plaintiff’s counsel,\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below held that where the supplier of goods is not a person subject to special taxation and the goods supplied do not fall under the tax-exempt items prescribed in Article 12 of the Value-Added Tax Act, the supplier of goods must issue a tax invoice at the time of supplying the goods; and, in light of the actual circumstances that suppliers often fail to issue tax invoices at the time of transaction in order to evade taxes such as income tax and are later subjected to additional collection or punishment upon subsequent discovery, the Plaintiff, whose principal business was the sale of Tosang graphite, well knowing that he was not a person subject to special taxation and that the sale of Tosang graphite in this case did not constitute a tax-exempt business, intentionally failed to issue a tax invoice and to collect value-added tax at the time of the transaction in order to evade payment of taxes such as income tax arising from this transaction.\\n\\nHowever, according to the record, it can be seen that at the time the Plaintiff sold the Tosang graphite in this case to the Defendant, he did not issue a tax invoice under the Value-Added Tax Act, but did prepare and deliver an ordinary invoice (an invoice on which the amount of value-added tax is not stated), and the Plaintiff argued that his failure to issue a tax invoice and his preparation and delivery of an ordinary invoice in this manner were because he mistakenly believed that the sale of Tosang graphite was a supply of export goods and thus subject to the zero tax rate, so that issuing a tax invoice was unnecessary, and that he therefore did not issue a tax invoice but prepared and delivered an ordinary invoice; the first-instance witness Nonparty, who had worked at a tax accountant’s office and was in charge of the tax matters of the Plaintiff’s ○○ Mining Office, also testified to the same effect. On the other hand, the Defendant’s business purposes include import-export business and mining business (see the Defendant’s certified copy of register), and it is recognized that after purchasing the Tosang graphite in this case from the Plaintiff, the Defendant exported it (see Exhibit 3-1 for the Defendant), so it is difficult to conclude that the Plaintiff’s failure to issue a tax invoice when selling it was done intentionally in order to evade taxes such as income tax, and there is no other material in the record sufficient to recognize this. Rather, there is room to view that the Plaintiff mistakenly believed that, because the sale of Tosang graphite is a supply of export goods and the zero tax rate applies, the duty to issue a tax invoice was exempted, and that he therefore, by mistake, did not issue a tax invoice but prepared and delivered only an ordinary invoice (see Article 11(1)1, Article 16(4) of the Value-Added Tax Act, and Article 57(3) of the Enforcement Decree thereof, as in force before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 12459 of June 9, 1988). Even if, as stated in the judgment of the court below, the Plaintiff knew that he was not a person subject to special taxation and that the sale of Tosang graphite in this case did not constitute a tax-exempt business, the court below did not examine at all the circumstances of the transaction in this case between the Plaintiff and the Defendant, nor the circumstances under which he did not issue a tax invoice but prepared and delivered only an ordinary invoice, and merely based on such facts and the actual circumstances of the transaction concluded that the Plaintiff’s failure to issue a tax invoice when selling the Tosang graphite was intentional in order to evade taxes such as income tax; such conclusion cannot avoid criticism for incomplete deliberation and violation of the rules of evidence.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Plaintiff sold the Tosang graphite in this case to the Defendant and, after preparing and delivering only an ordinary invoice rather than a tax invoice, omitted the above transaction in making the final return for the first half of 1986 value-added tax on July 25, 1986; however, upon indication by the competent tax office, on August 19 of the same year he again issued a tax invoice to the Defendant for the above transaction, and on September 23 of the same year, within the lawful period for filing an amended return, he made an amended value-added tax return and additionally paid KRW 3,600,000 in value-added tax for the above transaction that had initially been omitted, and it can be seen that the Defendant likewise received the above tax invoice and made the amended return within the lawful period for filing an amended return.\\n\\nWith respect to the assertion that the amount equivalent to the above value-added tax paid by the Plaintiff was unjust enrichment of the Defendant, the court below acknowledged that the Plaintiff, while well knowing that he was not a person subject to special taxation and that the sale of the Tosang graphite in this case did not constitute a tax-exempt business, intentionally failed to issue a tax invoice and to collect value-added tax at the time of the transaction in an attempt to underreport the tax base in order to evade payment of taxes such as income tax arising from this transaction; and, after explaining the function of tax invoices and the actual circumstances of transactions in which tax invoices are often not issued for the purpose of tax evasion, it held that, as the Plaintiff who attempted tax evasion and was later discovered and thereby became liable to pay value-added tax, even if the Defendant who received the goods thereby obtained a benefit equivalent to the value-added tax on that transaction, seeking restitution thereof cannot be permitted under the principle of good faith and fair dealing.\\n\\nFirst, as the Defendant did not assert, with respect to the Plaintiff’s claim in this case, that it violates the principle of good faith and fair dealing, as argued, a matter contrary to the principle of good faith and fair dealing or an abuse of rights violates mandatory provisions, so the court may determine it ex officio even if there is no party’s assertion (see Supreme Court Decision 4294MINSANG174 of December 7, 1961); thus, it cannot be said that the court below violated the principle of party presentation by making a determination on this point.\\n\\nHowever, as seen above, the court below’s determination that the Plaintiff’s act of failing to issue a tax invoice to the Defendant in the first instance was intentional in order to evade taxes such as income tax was erroneous, and even if the Plaintiff failed to issue a tax invoice by mistake, although he may be subject to sanctions therefor, it cannot be said on that basis alone that the Plaintiff’s claim in this case is contrary to the principle of good faith and fair dealing.\\n\\nThe court below must ultimately be deemed to have misunderstood the legal doctrine concerning the principle of good faith and fair dealing, and this falls under Article 12(2) of the Act on Special Cases Concerning Expedition, etc. of Legal Proceedings; accordingly, the grounds of appeal are well taken.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below, and the judgment is rendered with the unanimous opinion of the judges concurring in the order."}

{"[94DA39567]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (the supplemental grounds only to the extent that they supplement them).\\n\\n1. As to Point 1\\n\\na. The factual findings affirmed by the court below in this case are as follows.\\n\\nThat is, Plaintiff 1 (hereinafter referred to as the Plaintiff) had cervical pain, radiating pain and numbness in the right upper extremity, and weakness of the triceps brachii in the right upper extremity from around 1981; in order to treat these symptoms, on 1985.3.15. the Plaintiff was examined by Non-party 1, a neurosurgeon at ○○○○○○ Hospital operated by the Defendant corporation; as a result of examining the Plaintiff, Non-party 1 diagnosed a herniated intervertebral disc between the 6th and 7th cervical vertebrae, observed a posterior osteophyte (spur) also in the intervertebral joints between the 5th and 7th cervical vertebrae, and diagnosed a suspicion of ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (O.P.L.L.), and on the 19th of the same month admitted the Plaintiff to the said hospital in order to administer physical therapy; Defendant 2, who was serving as head of the Neurosurgery Department of the said hospital, determined that the Plaintiff could not be cured by physical therapy and, in order to treat it fundamentally, performed an anterior cervical fusion operation on the Plaintiff on 4.2. of the same year (an operation in which the skin on the anterior side of the neck is incised, the intervertebral disc between the 6th cervical vertebra and the 7th cervical vertebra is removed, and a bone graft is inserted in its place; hereinafter referred to as the surgery in this case); a herniated intervertebral disc refers to a state in which the intervertebral disc cannot withstand external force, tears the capsule surrounding it, and herniates, and it usually herniates posteriorly, compresses the spinal nerve root, and causes neurological disorders; when the symptoms are severe, the posteriorly herniated intervertebral disc (disc) is removed; in performing the surgery in this case, Defendant 2 used a “modified △△△-□□□ method for cervical spondylosis,” which was a modification by Mayfield, Benjamin, and others of the anterior cervical fusion method for cervical intervertebral disc disease originally developed by △△△ and □□□ in 1955, so as to remove the cervical intervertebral disc and posterior osteophyte using an air drill; the surgical procedure for the Plaintiff was as follows: after the patient was placed under general anesthesia in the supine position, a skin incision of about 5 cm was made laterally along the wrinkle line from the midline of the neck toward the right side, and after reaching the anterior surface of the cervical spine along the anatomical space, the disc was roughly removed using a No. 15 surgical knife and a surgical instrument called disc forceps, and then, using a surgical microscope, the disc was completely removed with an air drill, after which a bone graft fusion operation was performed by inserting into that space a bone fragment taken from the patient’s iliac crest; however, immediately after the surgery in this case, upon awakening from anesthesia, the Plaintiff developed symptoms of incomplete paralysis of the limbs, including complete paralysis of the lower body, and Defendant 2 performed a computed tomography scan on the Plaintiff on 3. of the same month (the court below’s 4. appears to be a clerical error for 3.) and then performed a reoperation on 4. of the same month (the court below’s 3. appears to be a clerical error for 4.), but the position of the grafted bone was also normal, and no cause that could bring about paralysis was found (during the reoperation, blood coagulated in a space 5 mm anterior to the spinal cord was discovered and removed, but this was not a hematoma large enough to compress the spinal cord); the said symptoms of lower-body paralysis did not recover, and symptoms of incomplete paralysis of the limbs, including complete paralysis of the lower body, remained permanently in the Plaintiff; the final diagnosis for the Plaintiff was spinal atrophy at the 6th and 7th cervical vertebral level (focal atrophy accompanied by inadequate blood flow); the ossification diagnosed before the surgery in this case was not the cause of a sudden spinal cord lesion, and no trace of syringomyelia (a disease in which cavities form within the spinal cord and destroy the nerves) or the like that could have caused a spinal cord lesion before the surgery in this case was otherwise found in the Plaintiff; the causes of paralysis of the lower body due to spinal atrophy may be five types: ① traumatic, that is, caused by surgery, ② caused by bacterial infection, ③ caused by demyelination, ④ caused by vascular factors, and ⑤ of unknown cause (including cases caused by insufficient intravascular blood flow); among the above causes, in the case of ② bacterial infection, a prodromal symptom of a high fever appears; in the case of ③ demyelination, a prodromal symptom of first becoming unable to see appears; in the case of ④ vascular causes, prodromal symptoms such as systemic erythema and lupus appear, but the Plaintiff had none of these prodromal symptoms; however, the anterior spinal artery supplying blood to the cervical spine is an artery that branches downward along the center of the spinal cord from the vertebral arteries and joins with one to three radicular arteries, and if the above radicular arteries are compressed, arterial spasm or thrombosis may occur and spinal cord lesions may arise, and if the spinal cord or anterior spinal artery is damaged during surgery by surgical causes, symptoms such as motor paralysis and sensory disturbance are caused; it is known that the probability of severe complications occurring after surgery as in this case is less than 1 percent, and Defendant 2, since learning and performing the above surgical method in 1982, had performed the surgery in this case on about 50 patients before operating on the Plaintiff, and from after the surgery in this case until around 1991.12., had operated on about 70 patients, but the only case in which spinal paralysis like that in this case occurred was the Plaintiff’s case.\\n\\nb. Examining the evidentiary relationship selected by the court below based on the record, the above factual findings of the court below are acceptable, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality in the form of erroneous fact-finding due to violation of the rules governing the taking of evidence, as argued (even if one carefully examines, based on the record, the opinion evidence of the court below’s expert, Non-party 2, pointed out by the argument, it does not impede the above finding).\\n\\nIn general, in order to say that there is tort liability or liability for non-performance of an obligation due to a breach of the duty of care in medical practice, as in ordinary cases, the breach of the duty of care in the medical act, the occurrence of damage, and the existence of a causal relationship between the breach of the duty of care and the occurrence of damage must be premised, and this must be proved by the patient side asserting it. However, medical practice is a field requiring highly specialized knowledge, and in most cases the process of the medical treatment is such that only the physician, apart from the patient being able to know part of it, can know the rest, and the medical techniques for achieving the result of treatment depend on the physician’s discretion. Therefore, whether the direct cause of the occurrence of damage was due to medical negligence is a special matter that cannot possibly be ascertained by an ordinary person who is not an expert physician, and it is extremely difficult for the patient side to medically and completely prove the causal relationship between the physician’s breach of the duty of care in medical practice and the occurrence of damage. Thus, in a case like this one where, during treatment, a patient develops symptoms of incomplete paralysis of the limbs, including complete paralysis of the lower body, if the patient side, prima facie, proves a medical negligent act based on common sense of ordinary people in the course of a series of medical acts, and proves that no other cause could intervene between the result and the series of medical acts, namely, in a case where the circumstance that the patient had no health defect that could have caused such a result before the medical act has been proved, unless the side that performed the medical act proves that the result was not caused by medical negligence but by some entirely different cause, it is consistent with the ideal of the damages system, whose guiding principle is equitable and fair allocation of loss, to relax the burden of proof so that the causal relationship between medical negligence and the result may be presumed and liability for damages imposed (see Supreme Court Decision 93DA52402, decided 1995.2.10.). In light of the factual findings affirmed by the court below, the Plaintiff’s symptoms of incomplete paralysis of the limbs appeared immediately after the surgery in this case, and the final medical diagnosis of those symptoms was revealed to be spinal atrophy at the 6th and 7th cervical vertebral level due to insufficient blood flow, so that the affected area coincided with the surgical site of this case; throughout before and after the surgery in this case, no special cause or symptom that could bring about lower-body paralysis due to spinal atrophy was observed in the Plaintiff; furthermore, among the causes of lower-body paralysis due to spinal atrophy, in cases caused by bacterial infection, demyelination, and vascular factors, each specific prodromal symptom appears, but since the Plaintiff had none of these prodromal symptoms, only two possibilities remain, namely trauma or unknown cause; moreover, if the radicular arteries are compressed, arterial spasm or thrombosis may occur and spinal cord lesions may arise, and if the spinal cord or anterior spinal artery is damaged during surgery by surgical causes, symptoms such as motor paralysis and sensory disturbance may be caused, then even if the probability of complications occurring from an unknown cause other than a procedural mistake is known to be less than 1%, the Plaintiff’s symptoms of incomplete paralysis of the limbs must be presumed to have been caused either because Defendant 2, in the course of the procedure, excessively compressed or damaged the Plaintiff’s anterior spinal artery or radicular arteries with surgical instruments or the like, thereby causing spinal blood flow disturbance, or because of a mistake that damaged the spinal cord at the 6th or 7th cervical vertebral level of the Plaintiff.\\n\\nTherefore, the court below, in the above purport, found Defendant 2 negligent in the operation and held that Defendant 2 bears liability as a tortfeasor and that the Defendant corporation bears liability as Defendant 2’s employer; this is correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality in misapprehending the legal doctrine on the burden of proof in an action for damages arising from medical malpractice, as argued.\\n\\n2. As to Point 2\\n\\nThe court below, with respect to the Defendants’ argument that “the paralysis of the Plaintiff’s lower body was not caused by Defendant 2’s negligence in performing the surgery, but rather spinal paralysis naturally occurred on the basis of the Plaintiff’s latent spinal blood flow disturbance; or, in the Plaintiff’s case, cervical ossification, which is degenerative spondylosis, accompanies herniated cervical intervertebral disc, and because such degenerative disease accompanies the overall aging phenomenon of the body as well as the cervical spine, there is a possibility that vascular disease, such as arteriosclerosis, which is not clinically apparent, lies latent, and spinal paralysis caused by the above vascular disease is an unavoidable force under the level of modern medicine,” rejected it on the ground that even the Defendants’ cited evidence was insufficient to acknowledge it and that there was no other evidence to acknowledge it. Examining the record, the above judgment of the court below is correct, and it cannot be said that there is any error, as argued, in failing to determine the opinion evidence of the court below’s expert, Non-party 2. The argument also lacks merit.\\n\\n3. As to Point 3\\n\\nIn medical disputes, in light of the fact that entries in medical records and the like possessed by the physician side play an important role in fact-finding and legal determination, the act of falsifying medical records by the physician side constitutes an act of obstructing proof contrary to the principle of fairness between the parties or the principle of good faith, unless a substantial and reasonable explanation is offered for the reason for the falsification; and the court may, using this as one piece of material, make an adverse evaluation of the physician side according to free conviction.\\n\\nAs found by the court below, if, among the medical records (charts) of Defendant 2 and the resident Non-party 3, submitted at the evidentiary hearing on documentary evidence before the court of first instance concerning the medical records (charts) after the filing of this action, the entries in the medical records (chart) in the name of Defendant 2 finally prepared on 1987.3.16. (Plaintiff’s Exhibit No. 8-1) and the medical records (chart) in the name of resident Non-party 3 (Plaintiff’s Exhibit No. 8-10) were altered so that part of the diagnosis for the Plaintiff was additionally written over in black ballpoint pen, making the original diagnosis unidentifiable, then in this case where the Defendants have not offered a substantial and reasonable explanation for the reason for the falsification, this would clearly constitute an act of obstructing proof. Therefore, it was correct for the court below to use this as one piece of material for presuming Defendant 2’s procedural error in the surgery, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality, as argued, in misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning acts of obstructing proof. The argument also cannot be accepted.\\n\\n4. Accordingly, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing Defendants. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning litigation requirements is incorrect? (In case of dispute, according to precedents)
A: If, during an action seeking performance of the procedure for cancellation registration of a mortgage creation registration, the mortgage creation registration is cancelled on the ground of sale in an auction procedure, there is no longer a legal interest in seeking cancellation of the mortgage creation registration.
B: Where the expiration of the statute of limitations period for a claim by a final and conclusive judgment is imminent, a refiling action for the interruption of prescription has the benefit of suit, and in such case the court of the subsequent action must again examine whether all requirements for asserting the final and conclusive right are satisfied.
C: If the Plaintiff has an interest in seeking a declaration of non-existence of the Defendant’s liability for damages and sought such declaration in the principal action, even if the Defendant thereafter filed a counterclaim seeking performance of that liability for damages, such circumstance alone does not mean that the declaratory interest in the principal claim has extinguished and that the principal action has become inadmissible.
D: Even if there is a dispute over a specific right or legal relation, if the parties agreed not to institute an action, a suit brought in violation thereof lacks the interest in judicial protection.
E: The res judicata effect of a judgment dismissing an action extends to the defect in the litigation requirements determined in that judgment.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2002DA57904]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nIn a lawsuit seeking performance of the procedure for cancellation registration of a registration of establishment of a mortgage, where the registration of establishment of the mortgage has been cancelled on the ground of a sale by auction during the pendency of the action, it must be said that there is no longer any legal interest in seeking cancellation of the registration of establishment of the mortgage.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the registration of establishment of the mortgage at issue in this case, for which the Plaintiffs are seeking performance of the procedure for cancellation registration against the Defendant, was cancelled on 16. 10. 2002 on the ground of a successful bid during the pendency of the appeal, after the appellate judgment that partially upheld the Plaintiffs’ claim had been rendered; therefore, the Plaintiffs no longer have a legal interest in seeking cancellation of the registration of establishment of the mortgage at issue in this case, and accordingly, this action became unlawful as it lost its interest in the action during the pendency of the appeal, and the appellate judgment cannot be maintained as it is.\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the appellate judgment, but as this case is sufficiently ready for this Court to decide directly, we decide to render our own judgment pursuant to Article 437 of the Civil Procedure Act, and by cancelling the first-instance judgment that partially upheld the Plaintiffs’ claim, we dismiss this action and order that the total costs of litigation be borne by the Plaintiffs, and so judgment is rendered as follows by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

{"[2002DA70181]": "1. According to the reasons of the first-instance judgment cited by the court below, the court below, based on the evidence it admitted, found that the Plaintiff, in a suit against the Defendants, had filed with the Daegu District Court, Case No. 98GADAN27262, the same action as this lawsuit, seeking cancellation of the ownership transfer registration and the creation of a mortgage registration in the Defendants’ names concerning the land in question, and had obtained a judgment in its favor on 1999. 5. 19.; however, when the Defendants challenged the judgment and appealed, the Daegu District Court, as the appellate court, rendered judgment on 2001. 1. 17. in Case No. 99NA9514, and, on the ground that “it is difficult to view the Plaintiff as having acquired the substance as an organization as an association by being a separate natural village from Gangrim-dong located in Okpo-myeon, Dalseong-gun, Daegu, and by having a decision-making organ or an executive organ while having its own purpose and mission,” reversed the above first-instance judgment and dismissed the Plaintiff’s action, and after recognizing that the above judgment became final and conclusive on 2001. 4. 20., held that, since the Daegu District Court had, by the above 99NA9514 judgment, determined that the Plaintiff lacked substance as an organization and that judgment had become final and conclusive, the later court, too, as the court of a subsequent suit, had to make the same determination, and therefore concluded that the action in this case filed by the Plaintiff, who lacked capacity to be a party, was unlawful.\\n\\nAnd the court below, in response to the Plaintiff’s argument to the effect that the Plaintiff had existed as a separate association without juridical personality from before the above land survey confirmation, as being the same as “Gangrim-dong,” the person named in the land survey of the land before subdivision of the land in question, and thus was different from the Plaintiff in the prior suit, who denoted “Gangrim 2-ri” separated from the above “Gangrim-dong,” rejected that argument on the grounds that such contention was already precluded by the res judicata effect of the above final judgment in Case No. 99NA9514 and could no longer be raised, and then maintained as it stood the first-instance judgment dismissing this action.\\n\\n2. The res judicata effect of a judgment in a suit extends to the defect in the litigation requirements determined in that judgment, but where a party files the action again after curing such defect in the litigation requirements, it is not subject to such res judicata.\\n\\nHowever, according to the record, the Plaintiff, like the Plaintiff in the prior suit, filed the prior suit and this suit on the premise that it itself fell within the category of an association without juridical personality, as a natural village composed of residents living in Gangrim 2-ri, Okpo-myeon, Dalseong-gun, Daegu; that the reason the judgment in Case No. 99NA9514 dismissed the prior action was that: ① in order for a natural village as a community of residents living within an administrative district, namely a dong or ri, to have capacity to be a party as an association other than a juristic person under Article 48 of the former Civil Procedure Act, that natural village must possess the substance of a social organization acting independently, with the village residents as its members and with a decision-making organ and an executive organ in the form of representatives having its own purpose (see Supreme Court Decisions 92DA39532, rendered on 1993. 3. 9., 98DA33512, rendered on 1999. 1. 29., etc.), but there was no evidence sufficient to recognize that the Plaintiff had such substance; ② even if the Plaintiff had such substance, the decision to file the prior suit, or the selection of the representative as the executive organ, could not be said to have been made by attendance of a majority of the representatives of the households constituting the Plaintiff and by consent of a majority of the household heads present, so that the prior action was unlawful in any event; however, the residents living in the above Gangrim 2-ri, after the prior suit, held an extraordinary general meeting at the village hall on 2001. 9. 8. with more than half of all household heads present and unanimously resolved to file this action again while selecting the village head, Nonparty, as their representative (Exhibit A No. 4-4); moreover, in this suit the Plaintiff submitted as new evidence the “Gangrim 2-dong Village Association Bylaws” dated 1972. 1. 15. (Exhibit A No. 4-1) and the “registration number certificate” for the “Gangrim 2-dong Village Association” issued on 2000. 11. 21. (Exhibit A No. 4-2), and those bylaws specifically provided for the organization’s purpose of cooperating among members to create a prosperous village, as well as members, officers (dong chief, Saemaeul leader, women’s association president, general affairs officer, development committee member, youth association president), finances, meetings (regular general meeting, extraordinary general meeting), etc., thereby showing that it had a decision-making organ and an executive organ; and it can be seen that the above “Gangrim 2-dong” became “Gangrim 2-ri” pursuant to a county ordinance on 1988. 5. 1.\\n\\nIf that is so, the Plaintiff appears in substance to be the same as the above “Gangrim 2-dong Village Association,” as a natural village constituting a community of residents living in Gangrim 2-ri; in the suit after the prior action, the residents of Gangrim 2-ri held an extraordinary general meeting on 2001. 9. 8. and, not only cured the litigation requirement under ② among the grounds for dismissal of the prior action, but further, through post hoc organizational reorganization such as the holding of the above extraordinary general meeting and the selection of a representative, the Plaintiff can be viewed as having sufficiently cured even the litigation requirement under ①, namely the substance of a social organization that has a decision-making organ and an executive organ in the form of a representative and carries on independent activities with its own purpose.\\n\\nAnd in this case, in which the Plaintiff seeks performance of the procedure for cancellation of the registrations in the Defendants’ names concerning the land in question, if the Plaintiff’s capacity to be a party is recognized, whether the “Gangrim-dong” person named in the land survey of the land before subdivision is the same as the Plaintiff is a matter concerning the merits of this case, and whether the Plaintiff existed as a separate association without juridical personality even before the above land survey is likewise not determinative of the existence or absence of capacity to be a party as a litigation requirement; therefore, the court below should first have determined whether the Plaintiff currently has capacity to be a party as an association without juridical personality, and then, in proceeding to decide the merits, should have specifically examined whether such circumstances were established.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below denied the Plaintiff’s capacity to be a party solely on the basis of the res judicata effect of the prior judgment and concluded that the action in this case was unlawful; accordingly, it cannot be said that there was no error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal doctrine on the res judicata effect of a judgment in a suit and the capacity to be a party of an association without juridical personality, and by failing to conduct sufficient examination ex officio regarding the Plaintiff’s capacity to be a party, which is a matter subject to investigation ex officio. The ground of final appeal pointing out this issue is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the court below’s judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below, and it is so adjudged as per the disposition."}

{"[2011DA80449]": "We consider the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. On the first ground of appeal\\n\\nAn act of preservation of jointly owned property is a factual and legal act performed to prevent loss or damage to jointly owned property and to maintain its status quo, and the purport of allowing each joint owner to perform such an act of preservation independently is that such preservation acts often require urgency and are ordinarily also beneficial to the other joint owners (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 93DA54736, decided April 7, 1995). Where a joint contractor consortium that is a partnership under the Civil Act participated in a competitive bid and another competing company was selected as the successful bidder, a lawsuit filed by one member of the consortium asserting that the selection of the successful bidder is void and seeking a declaration of invalidity is a litigation act aimed at maintaining the status quo because the legal status or legally protected interest that the consortium has in relation to the competitive bid is at risk of being infringed, and thus this constitutes an act of preservation of jointly owned property.\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the judgment of the court below in light of the foregoing legal principle and the record, the consortium formed by the Plaintiff and Sun Engineering Comprehensive Architectural Firm Co., Ltd. to participate in the bid at issue (hereinafter referred to as the “Plaintiff Consortium”) may, absent special circumstances, be regarded as a partnership under the Civil Act as a joint contractor consortium, and the fact that the Plaintiff filed this action seeking a declaration of invalidity of the resolution (hereinafter referred to as the “Resolution at Issue”) by which, at the Defendant’s extraordinary general meeting, Junglim Architecture Comprehensive Architectural Firm Co., Ltd. and Yumin Engineering Comprehensive Architectural Firm Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Junglim Architecture, etc.”), who were competing companies, were selected as the successful bidders and the conclusion of the architectural design contract with Junglim Architecture, etc. was approved, is for the purpose of maintaining the status quo because the legal status or legally protected interest that the Plaintiff Consortium has in relation to the bid at issue is at risk of being infringed, and thus it constitutes an act of preservation of jointly owned property. Therefore, it cannot be deemed improper merely because the Plaintiff, as one member of the Plaintiff Consortium, filed this action alone.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, contrary to the above, held that this action does not merely prevent loss or damage to jointly owned property and maintain its status quo, but rather constitutes an inherent indispensable joint action as an act to actively accomplish the business purpose of the Plaintiff Consortium, and therefore the action filed only by the Plaintiff, as one member of the Plaintiff Consortium, is improper. In this determination by the court below, there is an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principle concerning acts of preservation of jointly owned property and inherent indispensable joint actions. The argument in the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n2. On the second ground of appeal\\n\\nIn an action for confirmation, the object of confirmation is not limited solely to the legal relationship between the parties; where, with respect to the legal relationship between one party and a third party or between third parties, there is a dispute between the parties concerning it, and uncertainty or risk is thereby created in relation to the legal relationship of one party, and confirming that legal relationship vis-à-vis the other party would be an effective and appropriate means of eliminating such uncertainty or risk regarding the legal relationship of the party, there is an interest in confirmation also with respect to the legal relationship between one party and a third party or between third parties (see Supreme Court Decision 96DA25449, 25456(participation), decided June 10, 1997; Supreme Court Decision 2006DA77272, decided February 15, 2008, etc.).\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the judgment of the court below in light of the foregoing legal principle and the record, depending on whether the Resolution at Issue, which selected Junglim Architecture, etc. as the successful bidders and approved the conclusion of the architectural design contract with Junglim Architecture, etc., is valid or void, the legal status or legally protected interest of the Plaintiff Consortium that participated in the bid at issue is directly affected; therefore, unless there are special circumstances such as Junglim Architecture, etc. having completed performance of their obligations under the architectural design contract, the Plaintiff may seek a declaration of invalidity of the Resolution at Issue in order to effectively and appropriately eliminate uncertainty or risk concerning the same, and in such case, if the Resolution at Issue is declared invalid, it is not necessary that the Plaintiff additionally satisfy the requirements that it must necessarily be selected as the successful bidder in the bidding procedure at issue or that there is a probability of being so selected.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, contrary to the above, held that even if the Resolution at Issue were invalid and the Plaintiff, etc. became the sole bidder participating in the bidding procedure at issue, absent any circumstance suggesting that the Defendant would hold a re-bid and would select the Plaintiff, etc. as the successful bidder in the bidding procedure at issue, merely seeking a declaration of invalidity of the Resolution at Issue would not enable the Plaintiff to assert against the Defendant the status or rights of a successful bidder, and therefore this action cannot be deemed a means to effectively and appropriately eliminate the existing uncertainty or risk in the Plaintiff’s legal status, and thus there is no interest in confirmation. In this determination by the court below, there is an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principle concerning the interest in confirmation. The argument in the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. On the third ground of appeal\\n\\na. Where the parties have agreed not to file suit even if a dispute arises over a particular right or legal relationship (hereinafter referred to as an “agreement not to sue”), a lawsuit filed in violation thereof lacks an interest in legal protection, and furthermore it is contrary to the principle of good faith, under which the parties and persons concerned in litigation must conduct litigation faithfully and in good faith (Civil Procedure Act, Article 1(2)) (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 92DA21760, decided May 14, 1993). Accordingly, where a lawsuit is filed in violation of an agreement not to sue, the court may determine ex officio whether the action is proper (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 79DA2066, decided January 29, 1980).\\n\\nUnlike the above, the argument in the grounds of appeal that it is unlawful for the court below to have determined ex officio whether this action violates an agreement not to sue and is thus improper, on the ground that it violated the principle of party presentation, cannot be accepted.\\n\\nb. Meanwhile, Article 136(1) of the Civil Procedure Act provides that “the presiding judge may, in order to clarify the litigation relationship, question the parties regarding factual or legal matters and may urge them to present proof,” and Article 136(4) provides that “the court shall afford the parties an opportunity to state their opinions on legal matters that are recognized as having clearly been overlooked by them.”\\n\\nAn agreement not to sue gives rise to a significant procedural effect, akin to a waiver by a litigant of the constitutionally guaranteed right to a trial, and is valid only if it concerns circumstances foreseeable at the time of the agreement (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 98DA63988, decided March 26, 1999). If there may be disagreement over whether it is effective or over the scope of its effect, the parties’ intent must be determined after reasonable interpretation. Therefore, even if the parties do not make the validity of the action an issue by disputing the effectiveness or scope of the agreement not to sue, in order for the court to hold ex officio that the action is improper on the ground that it violates the agreement not to sue, it must afford the parties an opportunity to state their opinions on such legal perspective, and it is also necessary to sufficiently examine the motive and circumstances leading to the agreement not to sue, the purpose to be achieved through that agreement, and the parties’ true intent. If the court, without doing so, recognizes the agreement not to sue ex officio and dismisses the action, this amounts to an unexpected judgment that inflicts an unforeseen blow on one party and constitutes a violation of the duty to clarify and a failure to properly conduct the necessary hearing.\\n\\nThe court below determined, in essence, that according to the written undertaking attached to the bid guidelines for this bid, it may be found that, in participating in the bidding procedure at issue, the Plaintiff Consortium agreed not to raise any objection to the company selection method established by the Defendant and to the result of selection of the successful bidder and the contracting party by the Defendant consortium general meeting, and to abide thereby; accordingly, the court held that the Plaintiff Consortium is deemed to have entered into an agreement not to sue with the Defendant concerning the Resolution at Issue, and that this action, brought in violation thereof, is improper.\\n\\nHowever, according to the record, the Defendant, up to the date on which oral argument in the court below was concluded, had never argued that the written undertaking submitted by the Plaintiff Consortium, which contained the above wording, constituted an agreement not to sue; rather, the Plaintiff and the Defendant disputed only whether the Plaintiff had the standing as a proper party and the interest in confirmation to file this action alone, and whether there existed any ground for invalidity in the Defendant’s measure selecting Junglim Architecture, etc. as the successful bidders. The court below never afforded the parties an opportunity to state their opinions on whether the wording of the above written undertaking constitutes an agreement not to sue, or whether, even though there is room to regard the bid as invalid because the bidder engaged in individual promotional acts and the like, which were the grounds agreed upon for invalidating the bid in this bidding process, the Defendant also agreed not to raise any objection even if it selected such bid participant as the successful bidder. Nor was sufficient examination conducted regarding the motive and circumstances leading to the submission of the above written undertaking, the purpose to be achieved through that written undertaking, or the parties’ true intent.\\n\\nNevertheless, in holding, merely on the basis of the wording of the above written undertaking, that an agreement not to sue had been formed between the Plaintiff Consortium and the Defendant concerning the Resolution at Issue and that this action is improper, the court below committed an error affecting the judgment by failing to properly conduct the necessary hearing in violation of the duty to clarify. The argument in the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nThe judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for a further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2018DA22008]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. A final judgment in favor of the Plaintiff has res judicata effect; therefore, where a party who has obtained a final judgment in its favor files against the other party an action for the same claim as in the prior action that resulted in the final judgment in its favor, the subsequent action lacks a benefit of protection of rights and is thus unlawful. However, exceptionally, where the expiration of the 10-year statute of limitations for a claim arising from a final judgment is imminent, an action to interrupt prescription has a benefit of lawsuit (see Supreme Court Decision 87DAKA1761 rendered on November 10, 1987; Supreme Court Decision 2005DA74764 rendered on April 14, 2006, etc.).\\nFurthermore, in such a case, since the judgment in the subsequent action must not conflict with the contents of the final judgment in the prior action that was in favor of the Plaintiff, the court in the subsequent action may not again review whether all requirements for asserting the finalized right are satisfied (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DA61557 rendered on October 28, 2010, etc.).\\n\\n2. The appellate court recognized the following facts by comprehensively considering the evidence it adopted. ① In or around December 1995, the Plaintiff concluded with the non-party an installment sales guarantee insurance contract (hereinafter, the “Guarantee Insurance Contract at Issue”) with the following terms: “insured party: Hyundai Motor Company (hereinafter, ‘Hyundai Motor’), insured amount: KRW 9,504,000, insurance period: from December 27, 1995 to December 26, 1997, guaranteed contents: payment guarantee for the obligation to pay installment payments for a Sonata automobile.” The Defendant jointly and severally guaranteed all obligations owed by the non-party to the Plaintiff under the Guarantee Insurance Contract at Issue. ② When the non-party failed to perform the obligation to pay installment payments on three occasions, Hyundai Motor claimed insurance proceeds from the Plaintiff under the Guarantee Insurance Contract at Issue, and on July 23, 1996, the Plaintiff paid Hyundai Motor KRW 7,600,951 as insurance proceeds. ③ The Plaintiff filed an action for reimbursement against the non-party and the Defendant in Seoul District Court Case No. 96GASO439231, obtained a judgment in its favor on April 8, 1997, which became final and conclusive around that time, and thereafter received KRW 2,337,933. ④ In order to extend the limitation period, the Plaintiff filed an action for reimbursement in Seoul Central District Court Case No. 2007GASO1135651 and on February 1, 2007, received an order for performance directing payment of “KRW 18,767,816 and, among that amount, money calculated at the rate of 18% per annum from June 30, 2006 until the day of payment on KRW 5,263,018,” which became final and conclusive as is on February 23, 2007.\\n\\nBased on these facts, the appellate court determined that the Defendant, jointly and severally with the non-party, is obliged to pay the Plaintiff reimbursement of KRW 18,767,816 and delay damages calculated on the principal amount of KRW 5,263,018 among that amount at the agreed interest rate of 18% per annum from June 30, 2006 until September 30, 2015 as sought by the Plaintiff, and thereafter at the rate of 15% per annum prescribed by the Act on Special Cases Concerning Expedition, etc. of Legal Proceedings from the following day until the day of full payment.\\n\\nFurthermore, with respect to the Defendant’s argument to the effect that “the Defendant does not know the non-party and did not conclude any joint surety agreement with the Plaintiff, and therefore does not bear liability under the Guarantee Insurance Contract at Issue,” the appellate court held that, in light of the fact that the existence of the above-mentioned claim for reimbursement had been established in the action for reimbursement filed by the Plaintiff against the Defendant in Seoul District Court Case No. 96GASO439231, the causes asserted by the Defendant in the present action filed to interrupt prescription would conflict with the res judicata effect of the final judgment and thus could not be reviewed.\\n\\nThe appellate court’s above determination follows the legal principles discussed above and contains no error such as misapprehension of the law, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Meanwhile, as noted above, the Supreme Court has consistently maintained the doctrine that where the expiration of the 10-year statute of limitations for a claim arising from a final judgment is imminent, a refiling action for interrupting prescription has a benefit of lawsuit. Such doctrine remains valid even now. There is no reasonable basis to hold that only in the case of a judicial claim should a one-time limitation be imposed, unlike other grounds for interrupting prescription such as seizure, provisional seizure, or acknowledgment, which are not limited to a single occurrence. Moreover, even where the obligation arises from a final judgment, if the debtor may be wholly or partially released from it through bankruptcy or rehabilitation procedures, it is balanced to permit the creditor to refile an action for interrupting prescription.\\nUpon review of the record, the present action, which is a refiling action for interrupting prescription, was filed on August 19, 2016, shortly before the lapse of 10 years from February 23, 2007, when the order for performance in the prior action (Seoul Central District Court Case No. 2007GASO1135651), which was in favor of the Plaintiff, became final and conclusive, and therefore has a benefit of lawsuit.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are borne by the losing party, and judgment is rendered as set forth in the Disposition. This judgment was unanimous except for the dissenting opinions of Justice Kim Chang-seok, Justice Kim Shin, Justice Kwon Soon-il, and Justice Park Sang-ok; there are supplemental opinions by Justice Kim So-young and Justice Min Yu-sook and supplemental opinions by Justice Kim Jae-hyung and Justice Jo Jae-yeon as to the majority opinion; and there is a supplemental opinion by Justice Kim Chang-seok as to the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n5. Dissenting opinion of Justice Kim Chang-seok, Justice Kim Shin, Justice Kwon Soon-il, and Justice Park Sang-ok\\n\\na. The majority opinion allows a refiling action for interrupting prescription on the premise that, if a creditor has not been repaid even though nearly 10 years have passed since the finalization of the judgment in its favor, the creditor has a benefit of protection of rights to file a subsequent action identical to the prior action in order to interrupt prescription.\\n\\nSuch majority opinion assumes as a matter of course that a claim finalized by judgment must not expire by prescription unless satisfied by payment, etc. This cannot be agreed to because it is contrary to the basic principles of the Civil Act, which provides for the extinction of claims and the statute of limitations, and to the principles of civil procedure that recognize the res judicata effect of a final judgment; the prior Supreme Court precedents followed by the majority opinion must be changed.\\n\\nb. The Civil Act provides for “extinction of claims” in Chapter 6 of Part I on claims, but there is no separate item in the part on real rights concerning extinction of real rights. In addition, the Civil Act provides for the “statute of limitations” in Chapter 7 of the General Provisions, and whereas the statute of limitations applies to all claims, it does not apply to most real rights, except superficies and easements, namely ownership, possessory rights, security interests in real property, etc. Claims, unlike real rights, which are absolute rights, are relative rights that seek the obligee’s cooperation in the performance of obligations from the other party in order to realize the right. Therefore, there is a need to extinguish the right and release the other party from the obligation not only when the other party’s cooperation is rendered and satisfaction is obtained, but also when no further cooperation can be expected. For this reason, the Civil Act contains provisions concerning performance, deposit, set-off, etc., by which claims are extinguished through satisfaction of the claim’s purpose, and provisions concerning the statute of limitations, by which claims are extinguished by the lapse of time regardless of whether the purpose of the claim has been achieved.\\n\\nThe Civil Act provides in Article 162(1) that “a claim shall be extinguished by prescription if it is not exercised for 10 years,” and Articles 163 and 164 specifically provide for claims that extinguish by a short, 3-year or 1-year prescription period. In addition, Article 766 of the Civil Act provides, with respect to a claim for damages arising from tort, in paragraph (1), that “if the victim or his or her legal representative does not exercise it for 3 years from the day on which he or she became aware of the damage and of the person who caused it, it shall be extinguished by prescription,” and in paragraph (2), that “the same shall apply even when 10 years have elapsed from the day of the tort.”\\n\\nWhen the statute of limitations is completed, the claim is extinguished. As seen above, a claim has, as its basic nature, temporality premised on “extinction,” and because the Civil Act also recognizes the extinction of unsatisfied claims, in interpreting and applying the statute of limitations, there is no normative basis for recognizing that unsatisfied claims must not be extinguished and that, for this purpose, the duration of existence must be extended until the claim is satisfied. Rather, the majority opinion’s view that extinction by prescription must be prevented until the claim is satisfied is contrary to the nature of claims and to the provisions of the Civil Act.\\n\\nc. The Civil Act sets the limitation period for extinction by prescription of claims in principle at 10 years, and for certain claims also provides a short-term prescription period of 1 year or 3 years. This reflects the realities of commercial transactions, where settlement within a short period has become customary, and the difficulty of preserving for a long period documentary evidence such as receipts for small claims that arise frequently in daily life, while also responding to the need to protect debtors by stabilizing legal relations at an early stage. However, if even for such claims it were interpreted that prescription can be extended indefinitely merely by obtaining a judgment every 10 years, the purpose of the short-term prescription system would be nullified. Not only that, Article 184(2) of the Civil Act provides that “the statute of limitations may not be excluded, extended, or aggravated by juristic act, but it may be shortened or mitigated,” and if a refiling action for interrupting prescription were allowed so as to recognize in substance an everlasting claim, this would also run counter to the purpose of that provision of the Civil Act.\\n\\nThe Civil Act, while providing the statute of limitations, also provides interruption of prescription. This is intended to achieve a balance of interests between creditors and debtors by pursuing early stabilization of legal relations while at the same time establishing a mechanism to protect the creditor’s rights. The grounds for interruption of prescription provided in Article 168 of the Civil Act—demand, seizure or provisional seizure, provisional disposition, and acknowledgment—do not permanently interrupt the progress of prescription, but instead, pursuant to Article 178 of the Civil Act, prescription begins anew from the time the ground for interruption terminates; in the case of a judicial claim, however, pursuant to Article 165(1) of the Civil Act, once the judgment becomes final and conclusive, even a claim subject to a short-term prescription period is uniformly granted a new 10-year prescription period. The Civil Act prescribes demand as a ground for interruption of prescription and, among such grounds, sets the prescription period that begins anew after interruption in the case of a judicial claim at 10 years; it does not provide that if judicial claims are repeated, the prescription is renewed perpetually rather than every 10 years. Nevertheless, allowing a refiling action for interrupting prescription has the result of causing a ground for interruption of prescription, which functions as a supplementary measure to balance interests between creditors and debtors, to block extinction by prescription itself, thereby reversing means and ends.\\n\\nThe Civil Act in Articles 162 et seq. provides that the “extinction by prescription” of claims is not exceptional or extraordinary, but is the natural and ordinary consequence of the temporality inherent in claims. In light of the purpose of the Civil Act in establishing the statute of limitations and interruption of prescription, it cannot be said that Articles 165(1), which sets the prescription period for claims finalized by judgment at 10 years, and 168(1), which provides “demand” as a ground for interruption of prescription, contemplate by infinite repetition and circulation claims that never extinguish. However, according to the majority opinion, even claims subject to the 1-year short-term statute of limitations may become claims that continue perpetually if a lawsuit is filed and a judgment is obtained periodically every 10 years. Such a conclusion cannot be said to be the result intended by our Civil Act, which has a statute of limitations system.\\n\\nd. The majority opinion allowing a refiling action for interrupting prescription also contains a problem that cannot be resolved with respect to res judicata.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court has stated that res judicata means not allowing a subsequent action that is identical to the subject matter of the prior action having res judicata effect (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DA41349 rendered on January 16, 2001, etc.), and because a final judgment in favor of the Plaintiff has res judicata effect, when the party who obtained the final judgment in its favor files again against the opposing party in the prior action an action for the same claim as in the prior action that resulted in the final judgment in its favor, the subsequent action is, absent special circumstances, unlawful because it lacks a benefit of protection of rights (see Supreme Court Decision 2017DA23066 rendered on November 14, 2017, etc.), thereby declaring the principle that the same filing by the party who obtained a final judgment in its favor lacks a benefit of protection of rights by virtue of the res judicata effect of the prior judgment.\\n\\nThe Civil Act likewise merely provides that, where a ground for interruption of prescription called a “judicial claim” has occurred with respect to a claim, prescription begins anew from the time the proceeding becomes final and conclusive, and contains no provision to the effect that, notwithstanding res judicata, a “judicial claim” may again be made with respect to a claim for which prescription has begun anew and thereby interrupt prescription. Rather, Article 170(1) of the Civil Act provides that if a judicial claim is dismissed as unlawful, it has no effect of interrupting prescription. Therefore, a refiling action for interrupting the statute of limitations is unlawful because there is already a final judgment in favor of the Plaintiff, and it should be understood that no further interruption of prescription is possible due to res judicata.\\n\\nNevertheless, the majority opinion states that, on the sole ground of the need that unsatisfied claims must not be extinguished by prescription, there is exceptionally a benefit of protection of rights where the completion of the statute of limitations is imminent even if there is a final judgment in favor of the Plaintiff. However, as discussed above, interpreting that unsatisfied claims must not be extinguished by prescription runs counter to the purpose of the statute of limitations. The majority opinion, which seeks to recognize a benefit of protection of rights on a premise different from that, is nothing more than reiterating the argument that claims must not be extinguished by prescription.\\n\\nIn addition, it is unclear when the “case where completion of the statute of limitations is imminent,” as stated by the majority opinion, is supposed to refer to. Is it the point when 2 years remain until completion of the prescription period, or when 1 year remains? If, as in current trial practice, judges differ in their determination of the imminence point, legal instability and judicial procedural costs will only increase. Moreover, according to the majority opinion, if completion of prescription is not imminent, even if the creditor files a lawsuit for the same purpose of interrupting prescription, there is no benefit of protection of rights due to the res judicata effect of the final judgment; but if completion of prescription becomes imminent, then a benefit of protection of rights arises at that time. However, res judicata is not a variable thing whose effect becomes weakened or extinguished as time passes, but rather is a judgment effect that is recognized permanently. It is logically impossible to explain why, due to such res judicata, the benefit of protection of rights in refiling, which was not originally recognized, suddenly becomes recognized on some day as time passes.\\n\\nUnder the Civil Procedure Act, a plaintiff who has already received a judgment of performance and thus has a valid title of execution is not recognized as having a legal interest to file the same lawsuit again. Since the Civil Act, by providing Article 170, presupposes the principles of the Civil Procedure Act and uses only a lawful judicial claim as a ground for interruption of prescription, it is logically consistent to regard a final judgment in favor of the Plaintiff as already existing, and therefore to regard a judicial claim as a ground for interruption of prescription that can no longer be asserted because of its res judicata effect.\\n\\ne. There is also the argument that, for the reason that the grounds for interruption of prescription prescribed in Article 168 of the Civil Act must always be applied in the same manner, if demand, seizure, provisional seizure, or acknowledgment may be made multiple times, then judicial claims must also be able to be made multiple times. However, acknowledgment among the grounds for interruption of prescription is the debtor’s expression of intent to perform its own obligation, so there is no reason to restrict it. By contrast, judicial claims, seizure, provisional seizure, and provisional disposition are procedural acts as grounds for interruption of prescription not based on the debtor’s intent; therefore, their effect should be recognized only when they are lawful procedural acts, and the Civil Act also provides for them in Articles 170 et seq. Just as a valid favorable judgment exists and the same lawsuit cannot be filed again, if a valid seizure, provisional seizure, or provisional disposition already exists, filing the same application repeatedly is unlawful and thus not allowed. The reason that, although a debtor’s property has been seized, only partial recovery results and seizure of other property is allowed is that, just as it is allowed to make the remaining claim after a judgment becomes final and conclusive on a claim expressly limited to part, this is properly recognized under procedural law. Also, because demand is not an act under procedural law, it is natural that repeated demand by a creditor cannot be prevented on the ground that it is unlawful; however, Article 174 of the Civil Act recognizes the effect of interruption of prescription by demand only when a judicial claim, etc. is made within 6 months. That is, Article 174 of the Civil Act firmly declares that, no matter how many times demand is made, the effect of interruption of prescription will not be repeatedly recognized. In this respect, it should be noted that not allowing a refiling action for interrupting prescription does not mean treating judicial claims differently from other grounds for interruption of prescription prescribed in Article 168 of the Civil Act.\\n\\nf. If allowing a refiling action for interrupting prescription leads to recognizing the existence of a claim that does not extinguish perpetually, it will also result in social problems, such as encouraging the proliferation and rampant operation of various debt collection agencies, thereby increasing the burden of debt borne by economically vulnerable persons who lack sufficient repayment capacity.\\n\\nIf the majority opinion is followed, it will result in allowing creditors, so long as they merely file a lawsuit every 10 years, to continuously collect debts from debtors and their families through assignment of claims and inheritance of debts, etc. Numerous statistics show the slight likelihood that long-overdue debts will be repaid. Even if the amount is not insignificant to an individual who has been repaid, we must not ignore the need to reasonably balance such benefit against the social costs arising from repeatedly filing lawsuits every 10 years and the pain debtors will suffer from debt collection.\\n\\nIf a claim cannot in any event be enforced by compulsory execution, there is also a need to extinguish it so as to free the creditor from the burden of refiling, to protect the debtor’s reliance on the extinction of the claim by prescription and thereby eliminate legal uncertainty, and to cut off the vicious cycle of repeated transfer of distressed claims and the resulting unjust debt collection, thereby protecting the economically vulnerable.\\n\\nIn addition, even if a refiling action for interrupting prescription is not allowed, the creditor can, by adding the 10-year prescription period newly added by interruption of prescription through a judicial claim to the basic statute of limitations period, collect the claim for a maximum period approaching 20 years or 15 years. At present, most property transactions are conducted electronically, making tracking easy; legal procedures such as property statement and property inquiry have been established to identify property subject to compulsory execution; and creditor revocation actions are also widely used. In light of these circumstances, the above period is by no means a short period for a creditor to exercise its rights. If that period is too short and there is concern that creditor protection may be insufficient, the reason lies in the fact that the Civil Act sets the prescription period for claims finalized by judgment at 10 years, and this is a matter for legislative consideration. To say that a refiling action for interrupting prescription will not be allowed is merely to interpret and apply, in accordance with its purpose, the system originally contemplated by the Civil Act; it is not to introduce a new system and thereby exempt malicious debtors from their obligations.\\n\\nIn this case, the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendant arose around July 1996. The Plaintiff filed suit in 1996, and the judgment in its favor became final and conclusive; then in 2007 it filed a second lawsuit and the order for performance became final and conclusive. The present action is the third lawsuit, filed in 2016, when another 10 years were about to pass from the finalization of the order for performance. Another 20 years have passed since the original claim arose. Even if another judgment is obtained and the prescription period is extended by 10 more years, what is the likelihood of receiving from the Defendant the principal amount of KRW 5,263,018 and delay damages thereon that were not received for the past 20 years? After another 10 years, a fourth lawsuit may be filed, and perhaps subsequent lawsuits may continue every 10 years against the Defendant’s heirs. Since it is said that prescription will not be completed if only a lawsuit is filed every 10 years, the Plaintiff may in practice know that repayment is difficult, but may nonetheless be in a situation where it must file a lawsuit every 10 years, even incurring costs because of regulatory violations or audit issues. It is clear that such a situation is undesirable in any respect.\\n\\ng. The Plaintiff in this case had already brought a lawsuit and obtained a final and conclusive order for performance having the same effect as a judgment, and near the time when 10 years had passed since then, filed the present action again to interrupt prescription. Because the present action is identical to the prior action in which the order for performance became final and conclusive, it lacks a benefit of protection of rights and is unlawful. Nevertheless, the appellate court’s judgment, which proceeded to decide the merits and upheld the Plaintiff’s claim, contains an error that affected the outcome of the judgment by misapprehending the law regarding the statute of limitations and interruption of prescription, res judicata of a final judgment, and the benefit of protection of rights; thus, it should be reversed.\\n\\nThe above sets forth the dissenting view against the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Supplemental opinion of Justice Kim So-young and Justice Min Yu-sook as to the majority opinion\\n\\na. The dissenting opinion is understood as meaning that once a final judgment has been obtained, no refiling action for interrupting prescription may thereafter be filed at all. However, as noted above, the precedents (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DA74764 rendered on April 14, 2006) have repeatedly held that “where the expiration of the 10-year statute of limitations for a claim arising from a final judgment is imminent, an action for interrupting prescription has a benefit of lawsuit.” Although the dissenting opinion argues that the precedents should be changed, the legal principle of the above precedents must be maintained.\\n\\nb. It cannot be said that allowing a refiling action for interrupting prescription runs counter to the purpose of the statute of limitations.\\n\\n(1) Under our Civil Act, the statute of limitations is not a system that “extinguishes claims that can no longer be expected to be performed by the debtor and thereby releases the debtor from liability” (the contention in section b of the dissenting opinion), but rather a system that achieves a balancing of interests between creditor and debtor by recognizing interruption of prescription. In this case, a claim that has been finalized by judgment remains unperformed, and the creditor is seeking through a lawsuit, as its own right, to interrupt prescription.\\nThe dissenting opinion is understood as meaning that, among the grounds for interruption of prescription prescribed in Article 168 of the Civil Act, acknowledgment (item 3) may be made multiple times, but with respect to demand (item 1), even judicial claims and applications for seizure, provisional seizure, or provisional disposition (item 2) cannot be filed repeatedly if there is a prior final judgment or prior seizure, etc. (section e of the dissenting opinion). However, as the dissenting opinion itself presupposes, the statute of limitations system under the Civil Act follows the provisions of Chapter 7 of the General Provisions of the Civil Act. The Civil Act provides for the prescription period, grounds for interruption, and their effects, but contains no provision limiting the number of times a ground for interruption may be invoked. Rather, as seen below, it contains provisions presupposing that prescription may be interrupted multiple times, and precedents have been established on that basis.\\n\\nInterruption of prescription falls within the creditor’s exercise of rights. An interpretation that restricts the exercise of rights without a statutory basis is not proper. The same is even more true for an interpretation that limits the scope of exercise only with respect to judicial claims, which are only part of the grounds for interruption of prescription that are identically provided for in the text of the statute.\\n\\n(2) Where property owned by the debtor has been validly seized but the execution results in recovery of only part of the claim and time passes, the creditor may again interrupt prescription by seizing other property of the debtor. Such pursuit of realization of rights is not prohibited.\\n\\nIf a creditor has demanded performance from the debtor but has not obtained voluntary performance and time passes, the creditor may again demand performance and thereby obtain the effect of interrupting prescription. However, demand is subject to the express limitation in Article 174 of the Civil Act, which provides that demand has no effect of interrupting prescription if a judicial claim, etc. is not made within 6 months; accordingly, where demand is repeated multiple times and a judicial claim, etc. is eventually made, the effect of interruption of prescription will arise, with respect to the time of the judicial claim, only retroactively at the time of the demand made within 6 months prior thereto (see Supreme Court Decision 87DAKA2337 rendered on December 22, 1987). Whether “demand,” a ground for interruption of prescription under the Civil Act, is an act under procedural law does not result in different treatment of whether the number of times it may be made is limited.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the reason that, in practice, repeated applications for interruption of prescription are difficult to find in provisional seizure cases, etc., is not that such provisional seizure is not allowed, but rather that, while the effect of execution preservation by provisional seizure continues, the effect of interruption of prescription by provisional seizure also continues (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DA11102 rendered on April 25, 2000, etc.), so there is no need to repeatedly seek provisional seizure for the purpose of interrupting prescription.\\n\\nc.
