Regarding the dissenting opinion section b, we fully agree with the portion to the effect that “the proliferation and rampant operation of debt collection agencies aggravates the suffering of economically vulnerable persons,” and the portion to the effect that “we should not turn a blind eye to the suffering of debtors caused by incessant collection, inheritance of debts, etc.” However, as seen below, this is an issue that should be addressed through other systems, or by setting more specific criteria for recognizing the benefit of protection of rights in a refiling action for interrupting prescription. We cannot agree with the dissenting opinion’s position that debtors can be protected merely by disallowing the refiling action for interrupting prescription itself.\\n\\n(1) The principal method by which a debtor in a state of insolvency can escape the debt is to use rehabilitation or bankruptcy procedures under the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act. Even a person of good faith may, in the course of economic life, fall into insolvency due to an unintended excessive debt burden; in such a case, the person may use individual rehabilitation procedures to repay only part of the debt and obtain discharge of the remainder, and if even that is difficult, escape the debt through individual bankruptcy procedures. Through such procedures, fairness among multiple creditors can also be pursued. Courts should help insolvent individuals use the above procedures to liquidate their debts within the legal framework and have an opportunity for economic recovery and rehabilitation.\\n\\nIn addition, the Civil Act has established systems of renunciation of inheritance and qualified acceptance with respect to the inheritance of a deceased parent’s debts. Courts should actively operate these systems so that young people are not discouraged by the hereditary transmission of debt.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Act on Registration of Loan Business and Protection of Financial Users, the Act on Fair Debt Collection, etc. (hereinafter, the “Debt Collection Act”), and other laws contain various provisions to protect debtors by preventing illegal debt collection practices by loan business operators and other debt collectors. In particular, the Debt Collection Act prohibits collection acts using deceit or force, and collection acts that undermine peace in private life by causing fear or anxiety, and even provides penal provisions therefor (see Articles 9 and 15 of the Debt Collection Act). Courts should strictly exercise criminal sanction authority against illegal debt collection practices by debt collectors. Furthermore, by broadly interpreting the duty of the State to endeavor to protect debtors or related persons from debt collectors who abuse debt collection rights or engage in illegal debt collection practices (see Article 3 of the Debt Collection Act), the State may also be assigned a heavy responsibility.\\n\\nThus, for a debtor of good faith who intends to perform an obligation borne through a final judgment, even if lacking means or capacity, systems already exist that encourage performance only within a reasonable procedure and scope and protect the debtor from excessive pressure by the creditor. Even so, by disallowing the refiling action for interrupting prescription itself, one should not deny the rights of a good-faith creditor who has had its rights recognized by a final judgment but has been unable to realize them, nor should one grant absolution to a debtor who, although burdened by an obligation through a final judgment, sometimes conceals property and refuses to perform the debt.\\n\\n(2) If the Supreme Court is to protect debtors, it should focus on establishing standards that allow the requirements for recognizing the benefit of protection of rights, which prior precedents present as the requirements for a refiling action for interrupting prescription, to be faithfully examined in each individual case.\\n\\nIndeed, trial judges are wisely providing relief to debtors who need protection by conducting concrete examinations in refiling cases for interrupting prescription with respect to the factor of whether “completion of the statute of limitations is imminent,” which is a requirement for determining the benefit of lawsuit. The dissenting opinion criticizes this by saying that “different judges will make different determinations and cause legal instability,” but the existence of a benefit of protection of rights must be determined by considering the specific circumstances of each individual case. Of course, it may be necessary for the Supreme Court to refine that standard more precisely and, by doing so, strive to provide predictability in adjudication.\\n\\nd. Returning to this case for examination.\\n\\n(1) The Plaintiff is a specialized guarantee institution whose business purpose includes the insurance business under the Insurance Business Act, such as guarantee insurance and credit insurance, and the collection of claims attendant thereto; in particular, it provides guarantee services necessary for various commercial transactions. Issuance of guarantee insurance policies for this automobile installment sale at issue and numerous other transactions, payment of insurance proceeds when an insured event occurs, and recovery from related persons of insurance proceeds paid in accordance with laws and agreements constitute the essential business of the Plaintiff.\\n\\nThe Plaintiff, after obtaining the final and conclusive judgment in the first lawsuit (Seoul District Court Case No. 96GASO439231) noted above, proceeded with compulsory auction proceedings against land owned by the Defendant, but due to the existence of senior lienholders, it received only about 6% of the claim by distribution. As the first lawsuit approached 10 years, the Plaintiff filed the second lawsuit in 2007, and because the Defendant did not contest the complaint, the order for performance became final and conclusive. In 2013, the Plaintiff discovered an insurance claim held by the Defendant as property and obtained an order for seizure and collection, but when the Defendant raised complaints alleging old age and deteriorating health, etc., the Plaintiff released the seizure. As the second lawsuit again approached 10 years, the Plaintiff filed the present lawsuit for interrupting prescription in 2016; in response, the Defendant has repeatedly made, from the first-instance court through the statement of grounds of appeal, the argument that the documents submitted by the Plaintiff concerning joint suretyship are forged documents, an argument barred by the res judicata effect of the final judgment in favor of the Plaintiff in the first lawsuit.\\n\\n(2) Examining these facts in light of the legal principles discussed above, there is no need, as the dissenting opinion asserts in this case, to prohibit the filing of a lawsuit as part of the performance of corporate duties, nor is there any necessity to extinguish the title of execution.\\n\\nIn the end, the present lawsuit was filed shortly before 10 years had elapsed from the time the above order for performance became final and conclusive, and therefore has a benefit of lawsuit.\\n\\nThe above sets forth the supplemental opinion as to the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Supplemental opinion of Justice Kim Jae-hyung and Justice Jo Jae-yeon as to the majority opinion\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion denying the filing of a new action to prevent completion of the statute of limitations for a claim that has received a final judgment cannot be accepted in our legal system. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\na. Viewing a claim as subject to the statute of limitations even when the right holder actively exercises the right is inconsistent with the nature of the statute of limitations and directly contradicts the provisions of the Civil Act.\\n\\nThe statute of limitations is a system under which, where the right holder is able to exercise the right but does not do so for a certain period, the legal effect of extinction of the right occurs. For the statute of limitations to be completed, the factual state of non-exercise of the right must continue for a certain period.\\n\\nA claim is extinguished by prescription if it is not exercised for a certain period (Civil Act Articles 162, 163, and 164). It is not that the right is extinguished merely because a certain period has passed; rather, continued non-exercise of the right during that period is another requirement for completion of prescription. When a fact contrary to the non-exercise of the right, which forms the basis of prescription, occurs, the running of prescription is interrupted. Article 168 of the Civil Act lists, as grounds for interruption of prescription, demand (item 1), seizure or provisional seizure, and provisional disposition (item 2), and acknowledgment (item 3). All these grounds were designated as grounds for interruption because they overturn the factual state of non-exercise of the right that forms the basis of prescription.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion would recognize completion of prescription for a claim finalized by judgment not on the basis of whether the state of non-exercise of the right continued for 10 years, but simply on whether 10 years have passed. This focuses only on one of the two requirements for completion of prescription, namely the “passage of a certain period,” and overlooks the other requirement, “non-exercise of the right,” and cannot be accepted.\\n\\nb. Allowing a refiling action for interrupting prescription does not run counter to the res judicata effect of the prior judgment.\\n\\n(1) The Civil Procedure Act sets forth, in Articles 216 and 218, the objective and subjective scope of res judicata, but provides nothing regarding the concrete meaning of res judicata, leaving that to interpretation. Res judicata is the binding force granted to a final judgment, and is generally understood to mean that “where the existence or non-existence of a right or legal relation being contested in litigation has already been litigated in a prior action between the same parties and there is a final judgment on it, the parties may not make assertions conflicting therewith, and the court also may not render a judgment conflicting therewith” (see Supreme Court Decision 89NU1308 rendered on October 10, 1989).\\n\\nThere is also no provision in law as to whether a subsequent action that is identical to the prior action in subject matter may not be filed because of the res judicata of the prior judgment. Therefore, this issue should be approached from the perspective of the general “benefit of lawsuit.” The Supreme Court’s consistent determination that “because a final judgment in favor of the Plaintiff has res judicata effect, when a party who has obtained a final judgment in its favor files again against the opposing party in the prior action an action for the same claim as in the prior action that resulted in the final judgment in its favor, the subsequent action is, absent special circumstances, unlawful because it lacks a benefit of protection of rights” (see Supreme Court Decision 2017DA23066 rendered on November 14, 2017, etc.) is in the same context. A subsequent action identical in subject matter to the prior action should in principle not be allowed because it would inevitably be decided in the same terms as the prior judgment under the res judicata effect of that prior judgment, and thus there is no practical benefit in recognizing it; however, exceptionally, if there is a need to file the subsequent action, the filing should be allowed because it has a benefit of protection of rights.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion takes the position that “by operation of res judicata, the filing of a subsequent action identical to the prior action is prohibited and an express provision is required to allow it,” but there is no clear basis for that view. This issue can be resolved by whether the filing of the subsequent action has a “benefit of protection of rights.”\\n\\n(2) As noted above, res judicata is recognized in order to avoid contradictory conclusions between the prior and subsequent actions and thereby prevent unnecessary litigation. If the filing of the subsequent action is necessary and does not result in a contradictory conclusion with the prior action, there is no reason to block the filing of the subsequent action on the ground of the res judicata of the prior judgment. A refiling action for interrupting prescription is the typical case.\\n\\nThe circumstances under which a creditor, despite having obtained a final judgment, fails to obtain satisfaction of the claim are truly diverse. There are not a few cases where the creditor cannot be blamed, such as where the debtor’s whereabouts are unknown or the creditor cannot locate property due to concealment of the debtor’s assets. Where satisfaction of the claim has not been obtained until the expiration of the 10-year statute of limitations for claims arising from a final judgment is imminent, the only way to interrupt prescription, absent special circumstances, is a “judicial claim.” In such cases, from the creditor’s standpoint, there is a need to file the same subsequent action again despite the prior favorable judgment.\\n\\nAgainst this, the dissenting opinion argues that to protect the debtor, the creditor’s benefit of protection of rights should be denied; however, this is difficult to accept. If a right exists, the principle is to protect it by law. The statute of limitations is a system that does not protect those who do not exercise their rights even though they are able to do so for a long period. Under the basic order of private law, a “creditor who seeks to exercise rights” should naturally be protected more than a “debtor who does not perform obligations.” If protection of rights is blocked by using the res judicata system, this is inconsistent with the purpose of the property-rights guarantee clause of our Constitution and the purpose of the res judicata system.\\n\\nc. It cannot be said that a “judicial claim,” as a ground for interruption of prescription, is limited to one occurrence.\\n\\n(1) The Civil Act provides in Article 165(1) that even claims finalized by judgment, if subject to a short prescription period, shall have a prescription period of 10 years; Article 168 provides three grounds for interruption of prescription: “① demand, ② seizure or provisional seizure, provisional disposition, ③ acknowledgment”; and it contains various other provisions concerning grounds for interruption of prescription. However, there is no provision prohibiting a refiling action for interrupting prescription. Like other grounds for interruption of prescription, “judicial claim” is not limited as to the number of times it may be made. As noted above, this issue should be resolved according to whether there is a benefit of protection of rights in filing the subsequent action in relation to the res judicata of the prior judgment.\\n\\n(2) The dissenting opinion argues that “since claims, which are relative rights, have temporality as their basic nature, the right must be extinguished even when no further cooperation can be expected from the debtor, and this is consistent with the purpose of the statute of limitations,” but this too is difficult to accept.\\n\\nA claim is a right to demand a certain act from the debtor, and has a different character from a real right, which is an exclusive right that directly controls a specific thing and thereby yields benefit, and which can be asserted against anyone. There is, however, no basis whatsoever for viewing temporality as a distinguishing feature separating claims from real rights. Real rights other than ownership are also subject to the statute of limitations, like claims, though only the periods differ (Civil Act Article 162(2)), and ownership may also be extinguished upon completion of acquisitive prescription.\\n\\nIn addition, the dissenting opinion’s premise that claims must be extinguished when “cooperation or performance can no longer be expected from the debtor” is also unfounded. If the creditor cannot expect cooperation from the debtor regarding performance of the obligation, it is the state’s inherent duty to realize the creditor’s rights through the procedure when the creditor files suit against the debtor and seeks compulsory execution based on a title of execution such as a final judgment. By the nature of claims, even where the purpose cannot be achieved without the debtor’s voluntary performance and performance cannot be compelled, damages for non-performance may still be claimed. In either case, it cannot be said that the creditor’s claim against the debtor is extinguished.\\n\\nIf there is no separate restriction, the law should be interpreted in a direction that protects rights. The interpretive theory that, because a claim is a relative right that may be asserted against a particular person, “even a debt finalized by judgment may be extinguished and discharged if 10 years pass without payment” cannot be justified.\\n\\n(3) There is no reason to reduce the protection afforded to a claim finalized by judgment as compared with a claim not finalized by judgment. So long as the creditor exercises its right, it is proper to protect that right in any event.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion presupposes that the provisions concerning interruption of prescription by judicial claim do not apply to claims finalized by judgment. This is unbalanced when compared with the application of those provisions to claims not finalized by judgment. In either case, where there is a judicial claim, the state of non-exercise of the right should be regarded as interrupted, yet the dissenting opinion would not recognize interruption of prescription through judicial claim for claims finalized by judgment, which is improper.\\n\\nd. Even if a refiling action concerning a claim finalized by judgment is allowed, there is room to conclude that it does not violate Article 184(2) of the Civil Act, which the dissenting opinion cites as one of its grounds.\\n\\nArticle 184(2) of the Civil Act provides that “the statute of limitations may not be excluded, extended, or aggravated by juristic act, but it may be shortened or mitigated.” This modifies the principle of freedom of juristic act so as to prevent exclusion, extension, or aggravation of prescription through a juristic act that produces legal effects as intended by the actor.\\n\\nEven if a claim subject to a short prescription period is finalized by judgment and its prescription period is set at 10 years, that is merely an effect under Article 165(1) of the Civil Act and has nothing to do with exclusion, extension, or aggravation of prescription by juristic act prohibited under Article 184(2) of the Civil Act.\\n\\nFurthermore, a judicial claim as a ground for interruption of prescription is not a juristic act either, so there is absolutely no room to view it as violating Article 184(2) of the Civil Act.\\n\\ne. In our Civil Act, the prescription period for ordinary claims and the prescription period for claims finalized by judgment are both 10 years, but in many countries claims finalized by judgment are subject to a longer statute of limitations than ordinary claims. The German Civil Code sets the prescription period for ordinary claims at 3 years (Article 195) while setting the prescription period for claims finalized by judgment at 30 years (Article 197(1)). France sets the prescription period for ordinary claims at 5 years (French Civil Code Article 2224) but, in principle, sets a 10-year prescription period for rights finalized by judgment (French Code of Civil Enforcement Procedure Article 111-4). The Principles of European Contract Law (PECL), announced by the Commission on European Contract Law to unify the contract laws of European countries, set the general prescription period for claims at 3 years (Article 14:201) while setting the prescription period for claims finalized by judgment at 10 years (Article 14:202(1)). In this way, even countries that set a long prescription period for claims finalized by judgment do not prohibit refiling actions to prevent completion of prescription.\\n\\nAlso, although in some systems judicial claims are designated not as grounds for interruption of prescription but as grounds for suspension of the originally running prescription period, once the judgment becomes final and conclusive pursuant to a judicial claim, the provisions relating to claims finalized by judgment apply, so there is not much substantive difference between a system in which judicial claims are grounds for suspension of the prescription period and one in which they are grounds for interruption.\\n\\nClaims finalized by judgment do not, unlike ordinary claims, carry the risk that the existence or amount of the claim becomes uncertain as time passes. Even though the Civil Act sets the prescription period for claims finalized by judgment at 10 years, just as for ordinary claims, it is not right to prohibit refiling actions to prevent completion of prescription. Since the creditor clearly demands performance of a claim whose existence is certain and the debtor also knows that the obligation must be performed, it accords with the notion of justice to give the creditor a means to prevent completion of prescription.\\n\\nf. The private law system has established through the insolvency system a means for debtors with much debt to escape obligations they cannot repay.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion worries that if a refiling action for interrupting prescription is allowed, an economically vulnerable debtor will be unable to escape the shackles of debt forever. However, the statute of limitations is not a system for protecting the economically vulnerable. Just as not all creditors are economically powerful, not all debtors are economically vulnerable. The statute of limitations is merely a system that, when the factual state of non-exercise of rights continues for a certain period, respects that factual state and recognizes the legal effect of extinction of the right. It is not consistent with the purpose of the statute of limitations to import into its operation a so-called “protection of the weak” theory by distinguishing between creditors as the strong and debtors as the weak.\\n\\nIn the private law system, the problem of excessive debt should not be resolved through the statute of limitations but through insolvency systems. A debtor can escape obligations that cannot be repaid through insolvency procedures.\\n\\nImmediately after the Civil Act came into force, the Bankruptcy Act, Composition Act, and Corporate Reorganization Act were enacted and implemented. From April 1, 2006, those laws were repealed and the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act has been in force, and thereafter personal insolvency systems have also been used increasingly actively. Even an individual may escape all or part of a debt through individual bankruptcy or individual rehabilitation procedures. If the debtor has died, there are also systems such as renunciation of inheritance by the heir so that the heir does not bear the debt, or qualified acceptance so that liability is limited to the inherited property. Debtors are provided with such avenues to escape excessive debt by using insolvency systems, etc. To seek to protect debtors by prohibiting refiling actions for interrupting prescription is not the right path.\\n\\ng. It has been pointed out that allowing refiling actions for interrupting prescription may create problems such as the risk of double execution, unnecessary litigation burdens arising from refiling, the possibility of debt collection by improper means, and the proliferation of various debt collection agencies.\\n\\nHowever, these points may be issues about how to determine the form and litigation costs of a refiling action for interrupting prescription, how far offensive and defensive methods should be allowed in litigation for the purpose of interrupting prescription, and how to strengthen protection of debtors or related persons under the Debt Collection Act, etc., when a debt collector abuses rights or engages in debt collection by unlawful means; they cannot be grounds for prohibiting refiling actions for interrupting prescription.\\n\\nRather, one should deeply consider whether the conclusion of the dissenting opinion—that once a creditor has actively exercised its right and obtained a final judgment, a refiling action for extending prescription is barred after 10 years even if satisfaction of the claim has not yet been obtained, and the claim is extinguished—accords with the legal sentiments of the general public, and what effect such a conclusion would have on the economic life of the public.\\n\\nThe above sets forth the supplemental opinion as to the majority opinion.\\n\\n8. Supplemental opinion of Justice Kim Chang-seok as to the dissenting opinion\\n\\na. Article 168(1) of the Civil Act provides that a judicial claim, that is, the filing of a lawsuit, constitutes a ground for interruption of prescription; Article 165(1) provides that “the prescription period for claims finalized by judgment shall be 10 years even if they are subject to a short prescription period”; and Article 178(1) provides that “when prescription is interrupted, the period of prescription that has elapsed until the interruption shall not be counted, and a new period shall run from the time the ground for interruption terminates,” while paragraph (2) provides that “prescription interrupted by a judicial claim shall begin anew from the time the trial becomes final and conclusive pursuant to the provisions of the preceding paragraph.”\\n\\nOn the premise of such provisions, the majority opinion says that, even if a claim finalized by judgment is allowed to file an action for interrupting prescription before the 10-year prescription period that newly began has elapsed, the effect of interruption of prescription under the above provisions arises repeatedly; the dissenting opinion says that such an interpretation gives claims finalized by judgment the character of a right that never extinguishes and therefore does not accord with the nature of claims or with the purpose of the statute of limitations system.\\n\\nb. Because the Civil Act does not contain an explicit provision as to whether, even after the 10-year prescription period that newly began has elapsed, filing an action for interrupting prescription before the expiration of that period causes the effect of interruption of prescription to arise repeatedly, this matter can ultimately be said to be entrusted to interpretation.\\n\\nHowever, the majority opinion and the supplemental opinions thereto (hereinafter collectively referred to simply as the “majority opinion”) state that if an action for interrupting prescription is filed before the prescription period of a claim finalized by judgment has elapsed, the creditor is clearly exercising its own right, and therefore the effect of completion of the statute of limitations should not be recognized. In addition, since a claim finalized by judgment already has its existence and scope clearly determined, it seems to view that there is no longer any reason to block the continued realization of the right in that respect because the difficulty of determining the existence and scope of the claim as time passes can no longer be affirmed.\\n\\nThe majority opinion can be said to adhere without limitation to the traditional view of the statute of limitations system. However, such an attitude cannot necessarily be regarded as self-evidently proper or justified. As examined in the dissenting opinion, it cannot be said to be an unavoidable interpretation theory under the current Civil Act.\\n\\nc. “Part III of the Principles of European Contract Law” sets the prescription period for claims finalized by judgment at 10 years (while providing a provision on the starting point of that prescription period to the same effect as Article 178(2) of our Civil Act), and recognizes attempted compulsory execution or acknowledgment as grounds for a new running of the prescription period concerning claims finalized by judgment, but recognizes judicial claims only as grounds for suspension of the originally running prescription period. Such an approach has been or will be adopted into the content of civil law in Germany and other European countries.\\n\\nThe attitude of the “Principles of European Contract Law” is understood as recognizing attempted compulsory execution or acknowledgment, which can be regarded as grounds indicating that effective realization of the claim is expected, as grounds for a new running of the prescription period concerning claims finalized by judgment, while not recognizing judicial claims, which cannot be regarded as such grounds, as grounds for a new running of the prescription period. This is entirely a perspective consistent with the dissenting opinion.\\n\\nIn conclusion, new perspectives on the statute of limitations system are gaining strength, and it is unnecessary to adhere only to the traditional view concerning the reasons for the existence of the statute of limitations system, namely “non-exercise of rights” or “difficulty in determining the existence or scope of the claim due to the passage of time.” In this respect, the grounds advanced by the majority opinion cannot be said to be sufficient, and rather the dissenting opinion may be seen as more persuasive.\\n\\nThe above sets forth the supplemental opinion as to the dissenting opinion."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding service is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: If, while a party was in custody during the pendency of the litigation, the court served a copy of the judgment by service by public notice, pursuant to the presiding judge’s order, at the party’s address, etc., without serving the copy of the judgment on the warden of the prison, etc., then this is defective in that it fails to satisfy the requirements for service by public notice, and is void.
B: Where a party who received a notice of hearing by service by public notice did not submit an answer or a preparatory brief, etc., and did not appear at the relevant hearing date, that party is not deemed to have admitted the adverse party’s allegations.
C: Where multiple litigation representatives conduct litigation for the same party, the court must serve a copy of the judgment on each of the multiple litigation representatives; however, in this case, the effect of service of a copy of the judgment on the party arises when it is first served on one of the litigation representatives, and the appeal period is also calculated from the time the copy of the judgment is first served on one of the litigation representatives.
D: Service by mail is permitted where personal service on the addressee is impossible, as is substitute service or service by leaving the document with an occupant, or where the party, etc. has not fulfilled the duty to report a change of place of service and the place of service cannot otherwise be ascertained from the materials appearing in the record alone.
E: Where there is a conflict of interests or opposing interests between the principal and the person who receives service on the principal’s behalf—namely, the principal’s office worker, employee, or cohabitant who has the intelligence to distinguish right from wrong—with respect to the litigation in question, service of litigation documents on behalf of the principal by the recipient agent is contrary to the principle prohibiting dual representation, and therefore substitute service cannot be effected on that recipient agent.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2009MA1029]": "1. The grounds for re-appeal are examined.\\n\\nArticle 185, paragraph (1) of the Civil Procedure Act provides, “When a party, legal representative, or litigation representative changes the place at which service is to be received, he or she shall immediately report that fact to the court.” Article 185, paragraph (2) of the same Act provides, “Documents to be served on a person who has not made the report under paragraph (1) may, where no other place for service can be ascertained, be sent to the place where service was previously received by the method prescribed by the Supreme Court Rules.” Article 51 of the Civil Procedure Rules provides, “The sending of documents pursuant to the provisions of Article 185, paragraph (2) of the Civil Procedure Act shall be by registered mail.” In light of the foregoing, the phrase “where no other place for service can be ascertained” in Article 185, paragraph (2) of the Civil Procedure Act should be construed to mean that service by sending via registered mail may be made only where, although there is no need to order the opposing party to correct the address or to investigate the resident registration record, etc. ex officio, the place for service cannot be ascertained even from materials available in the record (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005MA625 dated September 28, 2005).\\n\\nFurther, Article 187 of the Civil Procedure Act provides, “When service cannot be effected pursuant to the provisions of Article 186 of the Civil Procedure Act, the court clerk, etc. may send the documents by the method prescribed by the Supreme Court Rules, such as registered mail.” Service by sending via registered mail under the foregoing provision may be made where the place to which service is to be made, such as the addressee’s address, is known, but there is no person to receive substituted service, such as the addressee’s clerk, employee, or cohabitant, or all such persons are absent, so that not only service by delivery, which is the general method of service, but also substituted service and service by deposit under Article 186 of the Civil Procedure Act cannot be effected. Here, the place to which service is to be made means a lawful place of service where the addressee is actually likely to receive and review the court documents, such as the address, residence, business office, or office that constitutes the addressee’s actual base of life (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2004MA801 dated May 11, 2007).\\n\\n2. According to the record, the Re-appellant (Debtor, Appellant) stated his address in the application in this case, filed on February 12, 2007, as Imun-dong, Dongdaemun-gu, Seoul (hereinafter lot number 1 omitted), and when the court of first instance sent a notice of appearance to the above address for the purpose of hearing opinions, the Re-appellant received it and appeared at the hearing date for hearing opinions in the court of first instance; the court of first instance, on November 21, 2007, rendered a decision denying discharge, thereby disallowing the Re-appellant’s application in this case, and attempted to serve the written decision at the above address, but because service was not effected on the ground of “addressee absent” and “closed, no one present,” it ordered service by public notice on December 7, 2007; on January 23, 2009, the Re-appellant submitted a petition for appeal, listing the address as the above address and the place for service as the 3rd floor, Sinjeong 3-dong, Yangcheon-gu, Seoul (hereinafter lot number 2 omitted), addressee for service: Judicial Scrivener ○○; the court below served the summons for the hearing date at the above place for service, held the hearing date with the Re-appellant present, and then, on April 20, 2009, rendered a decision dismissing the appeal in this case; the court below attempted to serve the authenticated copy of the above decision on the Re-appellant at the above place for service, but service was impossible on April 23, 2009, on the ground of “addressee unknown”; on April 27, 2009, the Re-appellant again filed with the court below a report of the same place for service and addressee for service as above; however, the court below, without attempting service again at the above place for service or address, on May 14, 2009, sent the authenticated copy of the above decision by registered mail to the above place for service; thereafter, the Re-appellant submitted the petition for re-appeal in this case on May 25, 2009, and it is apparent that the presiding judge of the court below issued an order dismissing the petition for re-appeal on the ground that the Re-appellant, even after being served with the decision of the court below, submitted the petition for re-appeal only after the expiration of the one-week period for filing an immediate appeal, and thus it was unlawful.\\n\\nIf the circumstances are as such, then in light of the legal principles stated above, the court below should have attempted to serve the authenticated copy of the decision again at the above place for service or address reported by the Re-appellant, and only when service could not be effected there as well could it have effected service by sending via registered mail to the above place for service or address. It must be said that the court below erred in effecting service by sending via registered mail forthwith without reaching that point.\\n\\nNevertheless, the original order of the court below, which, premised on the legality of the above service by sending, held that the re-appeal in this case was unlawful as having been filed after the expiration of the re-appeal period, contains an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning service by sending. The argument in the grounds for re-appeal is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds for re-appeal, the original order is to be reversed, and the decision is rendered as stated in the order by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2011MA1335]": "The grounds for the re-appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. A party to a civil action must file an appeal within 2 weeks from the day on which a certified copy of the judgment is served pursuant to Article 396(1) of the Civil Procedure Act. Meanwhile, where a party has several litigation representatives, each of them represents the party pursuant to Article 93 of the Civil Procedure Act; therefore, in cases where several persons jointly exercise the power of representation, there is no room for Article 180 of the Civil Procedure Act, which provides for service upon one of them, to apply. Accordingly, the court must serve the certified copy of the judgment separately on each litigation representative. However, even in such a case, since all litigation representatives are in a position to receive service of litigation documents on behalf of the party, the effect of service of a certified copy of the judgment on the party arises ultimately when the certified copy of the judgment is first served on one of the litigation representatives. Therefore, where a party has several litigation representatives, the appeal period is computed from the time when the certified copy of the judgment is first served on one of the litigation representatives.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, upon review of the record of this case, the lower court’s order dismissing the appeal memorandum, on the ground that the re-appellant filed the appeal memorandum on 2011. 4. 27., after 2 weeks had elapsed from 2011. 4. 11., when the certified copy of the judgment was first served on one of the litigation representatives, is justifiable and can be upheld, and there is no error of violation of the Constitution, laws, orders, or rules that affected the judgment.\\n\\n2. Unless the appellant clearly indicates that the appeal is a restoration of a procedural act, the court is not necessarily required, before rendering a judgment dismissing the appeal, to inquire into whether grounds for restoration exist or to afford an opportunity to assert them (see Supreme Court Decision 80DA2315, decided June 23, 1981).\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, upon review of the record of this case, not only did the re-appellant fail to clearly assert, when filing the appeal memorandum, that it was a restoration of a procedural act, but there is also no room in the record to find that grounds for restoration exist; therefore, even if the lower court did not inquire into and determine whether grounds for restoration exist before issuing the order dismissing the appeal memorandum, there is no error of violation of the Constitution, laws, orders, or rules that affected the judgment.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the re-appeal is dismissed, and it is so decided in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[2019DA220618]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the following facts can be found.\\n\\na. On 2017. 9. 27., the Plaintiff filed the lawsuit in this case against the Defendant seeking payment of common area management fees for a shopping mall, etc. On 2017. 10. 11., the court of first instance issued an order recommending performance, and the Defendant, on 2017. 10. 18., received a certified copy of the order recommending performance at the Defendant’s address stated in the complaint and submitted an answer to the court of first instance on 2017. 10. 19.\\n\\nb. The Defendant was arrested and detained in Anyang Correctional Institution on 2017. 10. 20. The court of first instance held hearings twice, on 2017. 11. 16. and 2017. 12. 14., and concluded the proceedings. However, because service of the notice of hearing, etc. could not be made at the Defendant’s address due to no one being present at the premises, it was served by service through mailing, and the Defendant did not appear at the hearing dates.\\nThe court of first instance rendered a judgment on 2018. 1. 11. in favor of the Plaintiff’s claim, and because service of a certified copy of the judgment could not be made at the Defendant’s address due to no one being present at the premises, it was served by service by publication pursuant to the presiding judge’s order for service by publication, and the effect of service arose at 0:00 on 2018. 2. 10.\\n\\nc. The Defendant was released from Anyang Correctional Institution on 2018. 8. 19., obtained a certified copy of the judgment of the court of first instance on 2018. 8. 21., and submitted the appeal by restoration of the expired period in this case to the court of first instance on 2018. 9. 3. The lower court deemed this appeal by restoration of the expired period in this case unlawful and dismissed it.\\n\\n2. Effect of Service and Whether an Appeal by Restoration is Permissible Where a Certified Copy of a Judgment Is Served by Publication on a Detained Party\\na. In a situation where there is still no Supreme Court precedent concerning the interpretation of the relevant statute to be applied to a specific case in small-claims litigation, and numerous small-claims cases in which the interpretation of the same statute is at issue are pending in the lower courts, while cases showing divergent determinations depending on the panel are arising, if the Supreme Court were to conclude a case without ruling on statutory interpretation merely because it is a small-claims case, legal stability in the public’s daily life may be undermined. In such special circumstances, even if the requirement of being “a case in which a judgment contrary to Supreme Court precedent has been made,” which may be asserted as a ground of appeal in a small-claims case, is not satisfied, the Court may determine errors in the interpretation and application of substantive law in order to perform the Supreme Court’s essential function of unifying the interpretation of statutes (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DA1878, decided 2004. 8. 20.; Supreme Court Decision 2012DA48824, decided 2015. 3. 26.).\\n\\nb. Where a party is detained during the pendency of litigation, if the court, without serving the certified copy of the judgment on the warden of the correctional institution, etc. pursuant to Article 182 of the Civil Procedure Act, served it by service by publication at the party’s address, etc., then even if there is a defect in that the requirements for service by publication were not satisfied, the service is effective so long as service by publication was made pursuant to the presiding judge’s order.\\nSince the detained party does not bear the duty to report a change of the place of service prescribed in Article 185 of the Civil Procedure Act and was unable to comply with the appeal period due to service by publication that did not satisfy the requirements, the party, absent special circumstances, did not know of the service of the judgment without fault, and in such a case, it corresponds to when it was impossible to comply with the immutable period for a cause not attributable to the party, so an appeal by restoration may be filed within 2 weeks after such cause ceases to exist. Here, “the time when the cause ceases to exist” refers to the time when the party or litigation representative learns that the judgment was rendered and that the judgment was served by service by publication. In the ordinary course, it should be deemed that the party or litigation representative only learns that the judgment was served by service by publication when inspecting the case record or newly receiving a certified copy of the judgment (see Supreme Court en banc Order 84MA20, decided 1984. 3. 15.; Supreme Court Decision 96DA30427, decided 1997. 8. 22.).\\n\\nc. Examining the factual relations found above in light of these legal principles, the following conclusion is reached.\\nBecause the Defendant was detained in Anyang Correctional Institution during the pendency of the litigation, the court of first instance’s service of the certified copy of the judgment on the Defendant by service by publication at the Defendant’s address, without serving it on the warden of the correctional institution, had the defect that the requirements for service by publication were not satisfied, but the service was nevertheless effective. Since the Defendant, without fault, did not know of the service of the judgment of the court of first instance and thus was unable to comply with the appeal period for a cause not attributable to the Defendant, the Defendant may file an appeal by restoration within 2 weeks after the cause ceases to exist. The Defendant should be deemed to have learned, when obtaining the certified copy of the judgment of the court of first instance on 2018. 8. 21., that the judgment of the court of first instance had been rendered and that the judgment had been served by service by publication; therefore, the appeal by restoration in this case filed on 2018. 9. 3., within the 2-week appeal period from that time, is lawful.\\nNevertheless, the lower court dismissed the appeal by restoration in this case on the ground that the Defendant did not fall within the category of cases where the appeal period could not be complied with due to a cause not attributable to the Defendant. The lower court judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by going beyond the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning subsequent completion of procedural acts. The assertion in the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nSince the Defendant’s appeal is well-founded, the lower court judgment is reversed and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2020MEU11658]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Service of process is, in principle, personal service, in which service is made by delivering the process to the person to be served at that person’s address, residence, place of business, or office (Articles 178(1) and 183(1) of the Civil Procedure Act), but if the service authority is unable to meet the person to be served at such place, substituted service may also be effected on his or her clerk, employee, or cohabitant who is of sufficient intelligence to discern matters (Article 186(1) of the same Act).\\n\\nThe substituted service system presupposes, based on such person’s intelligence, objective status, and relationship with the principal, that even if the principal’s clerk, employee, or cohabitant, that is, the receiving agent, receives the litigation documents, there is a reasonable expectation, according to social norms, that the litigation documents will be delivered to the principal. There may be cases in which the same receiving agent simultaneously receives litigation documents on behalf of both parties to the litigation whose interests are adverse. In such a case, because it is not easy for the receiving agent to occupy a neutral position without a conflict of interest with either the Plaintiff or the Defendant, it is difficult to reasonably expect that the litigation documents will be properly delivered to both parties to the litigation. This also runs counter to the principle prohibiting dual representation under the main clause of Article 124 of the Civil Act, which is intended to protect the principal’s interests by avoiding the risk of a conflict of interest. Accordingly, unless there are special circumstances such as the consent of the parties to the litigation, the same receiving agent cannot simultaneously receive service of litigation documents on behalf of both parties to the litigation, and such substituted service should be deemed void (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on November 10, 2016, 2014DA54366).\\n\\n2. According to the reasoning of the first-instance judgment cited by the court below, in this case in which the Plaintiff filed a claim for divorce against the Defendant, the first-instance court issued a decision recommending settlement to the effect that the Plaintiff and the Defendant divorce each other (hereinafter referred to as the “Decision in this case”), and the authenticated copy of the Decision in this case was simultaneously served on behalf of the Plaintiff and the Defendant by the nonparty, who is the adult child and cohabitant of the Plaintiff and the Defendant.\\n\\n3. The above factual relationship is examined in light of the legal principles set forth above.\\n\\nThe nonparty simultaneously received service of the authenticated copy of the Decision in this case on behalf of the Plaintiff and the Defendant, who are the two parties to the litigation whose interests are adverse, and it is difficult to reasonably expect that the nonparty would properly deliver the litigation documents to both the Plaintiff and the Defendant, whose interests conflict. Therefore, unless there are special circumstances such as the nonparty having obtained the Defendant’s consent, the nonparty’s simultaneous receipt of service of the authenticated copy of the Decision in this case on behalf of the Plaintiff and the Defendant is an unlawful service and thus void.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below held that the nonparty’s substituted service of the authenticated copy of the Decision in this case as the Defendant’s cohabitant was valid for the reasons stated in its judgment, and determined that this litigation ended upon the finality of the Decision in this case. In the court below’s judgment there is an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning substituted service. The ground of appeal asserting this point is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the dispositive part."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding the prohibition of duplicate filing is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, in accordance with case law)
A: Of the two victims of the same traffic accident, A, during the pendency of an action for payment of insurance proceeds concerning A's own damages, filed against insurer Company A by subrogating the insured C, who was the tortfeasor, B separately files against the same Company A an action for payment of insurance proceeds concerning B's own damages by subrogating the same C; such action does not constitute a duplicate filing.
B: Even when a creditor's subrogation action (prior action) is pending before the court, if another creditor of the same debtor brings a later action based on the creditor's subrogation right with respect to the same subject matter, if the prior action is withdrawn or dismissed by the conclusion of oral argument in the later action, the later action does not constitute a duplicate filing.
C: If, during the pendency of an action to set aside a fraudulent act brought by creditor A, another creditor B brings an action to set aside the same fraudulent act, it does not constitute a duplicate filing.
D: An action for performance of a debt brought by a creditor against a debt assumer (prior action) and an action for declaratory judgment of nonexistence of the debt of the original debtor against the creditor brought by the debt assumer (later action) are different from each other in their relief sought and cause of action; therefore, even if the later action is brought during the pendency of the prior action, it does not constitute a duplicate filing.
E: A settlement concluded in litigation proceedings that were continued despite being a duplicate filing and overlooked as such is null and void ab initio.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2001DA22246]": "1. The facts found by the court below are as follows.\\n\\na. With respect to 1,240㎡ of field land and the house thereon, which were owned by the Plaintiff (hereinafter referred to as “the real property at issue”), a registration establishing a mortgage, with a maximum secured amount of KRW 100 million, the debtor as the Plaintiff, and the mortgagee as Nonparty 1, was completed on July 13, 1995, on the basis of a mortgage creation agreement dated July 10, 1995 (hereinafter referred to as “the mortgage creation registration at issue”); thereafter, on the basis of an assignment of claim, a supplementary registration of transfer of the mortgage, making the mortgagee the Defendant, was completed on May 12, 1998.\\n\\nb. In the first-instance proceedings of this case, the Plaintiff sought cancellation of the mortgage creation registration at issue, asserting that the secured debt of the above mortgage was a debt owed by Nonparty 2 to Nonparty 1 and had been extinguished by payment, but lost.\\n\\nc. Before the Plaintiff filed this action, the Defendant applied for a voluntary auction concerning the real property at issue, and in that auction procedure, the person who purchased the real property at issue at auction paid the purchase price in full and, after the first-instance judgment was rendered, on December 4, 2000, the registration of transfer of ownership was completed, and the mortgage creation registration at issue was cancelled.\\n\\nd. Accordingly, on March 5, 2001, the Plaintiff changed the relief sought in the court below so that it would read: “It is confirmed that the debt in the amount of KRW 100 million, based on an agreement around July 10, 1995, owed by Nonparty 2 to the Defendant, does not exist.”\\n\\ne. Meanwhile, when, on January 18, 2001, at the distribution date in the voluntary auction procedure concerning the real property at issue, the Plaintiff denied the claim of the Defendant, who had demanded distribution without an enforceable authenticated copy, the Defendant, on January 22, 2001, filed with the Busan District Court Eastern Branch an action for determination of claim against the Plaintiff, asserting that “the Plaintiff concurrently assumed the debt of KRW 100 million owed by Nonparty 2 to Nonparty 1 and, in addition, completed the registration of the mortgage creation registration at issue with that debt as the secured obligation,” and seeking payment of KRW 100 million and the delay damages thereon; a duplicate of the complaint was served on the Plaintiff on January 29, 2001.\\n\\n2. The court below, after recognizing the above facts, held that the Plaintiff’s action in this case seeking confirmation of nonexistence of debt and the above action for determination of claim brought by the Defendant against the Plaintiff are a case in which only the positions of plaintiff and defendant have been reversed, but the parties and the claims are all identical; and that because, after the above action for determination of claim had been pending, the Plaintiff changed the relief sought and the effect of lis pendens arose with respect to the action in this case seeking confirmation of nonexistence of debt, this action constitutes duplicative litigation and is therefore unlawful.\\n\\n3. However, this action is an action for confirmation that the debt owed by Nonparty 2 to the Defendant does not exist, and the above action for determination of claim brought by the Defendant against the Plaintiff is an action for performance of a monetary obligation based on the ground that the Plaintiff concurrently assumed the debt owed by Nonparty 2 to the Defendant, and because the relief sought and the cause of action are different, the court below erred in holding that this action constitutes duplicative litigation. Nevertheless, with respect to the mortgage creation registration at issue, the Defendant’s action for determination of claim seeking payment of KRW 100 million against the Plaintiff is already pending, and the Plaintiff may, in that action, dispute that the Defendant does not have a claim of KRW 100 million against the Plaintiff or Nonparty 2 by seeking a judgment dismissing the claim; thus, there is no benefit in separately seeking confirmation against the Defendant that the debt of KRW 100 million owed by Nonparty 2 to the Plaintiff does not exist. Therefore, the Plaintiff’s action in this case seeking confirmation of nonexistence of debt lacks an interest in confirmation and is unlawful, so the court below’s conclusion dismissing this action is, in result, correct, and the grounds for appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, the burden of litigation costs is determined as stated in the order, and it is so adjudged."}

{"[2007DA84352]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to Ground 1 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nAccording to the judgment of the court below, the court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found the following facts: the Plaintiff lent money to Non-party 1 and others on four occasions by taking as security frozen marine products owned by them; the Defendant-Intervenor (hereinafter referred to as the “Intervenor”), while taking custody of the frozen marine products owned by Non-party 1 and others, had its manager, Non-party 2, execute a joint and several suretyship on behalf of the Intervenor for the above loan debts owed by Non-party 1 and others to the Plaintiff (hereinafter referred to as the “Joint and Several Suretyship Agreement at Issue”); and then, in response to the Defendant’s and the Intervenor’s assertion that the Joint and Several Suretyship Agreement at Issue does not constitute an act concerning the Intervenor’s business and therefore was concluded by Non-party 2 without authority and is thus ineffective against the Intervenor, the court below held that the Joint and Several Suretyship Agreement at Issue was a suretyship for the loan debts of marine-product sellers who had been storing frozen marine products with the Intervenor, and that, as it also served the purpose of maintaining the Intervenor’s business relationship with them, it cannot be said to be unrelated to business; accordingly, it determined that Non-party 2, the Intervenor’s manager, had lawful authority to execute the Joint and Several Suretyship Agreement at Issue.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the above fact-finding and determination by the court below are reasonable and persuasive, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the existence and scope of agency authority, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. With respect to Ground 2 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. According to the judgment of the court below, the court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found the facts stated in the opinion and then, in response to the Defendant’s and the Intervenor’s assertion that the Joint and Several Suretyship Agreement at Issue should be excluded from effect because it was a breach of fiduciary duty on the part of Non-party 2 and the Plaintiff knew or could have known of this, rejected that assertion on the ground that, although it was acknowledged that Non-party 2 submitted a board resolution approving the guarantee (joint and several suretyship) bearing the signature and seal of Non-party 4, who was not serving as a director at the time, in relation to the joint and several suretyship agreements for the remaining shipper-creditors excluding Non-party 3, such circumstance alone is insufficient to establish that the Plaintiff knew or could have known that Non-party 2’s act of suretyship in this case was a fiduciary breach, and that there was otherwise no evidence sufficient to support such a finding.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the above measures taken by the court below are reasonable and persuasive, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality, such as inadequate judicial examination or violation of the rules of evidence evaluation, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nB. Furthermore, in response to the Defendant’s and the Intervenor’s assertion that, because there was no valid board resolution by the Intervenor regarding the act of suretyship in this case and the Plaintiff knew or could have known of this fact, the Joint and Several Suretyship Agreement at Issue is void, the court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, recognized that Non-party 2, at the time of the Joint and Several Suretyship Agreement at Issue, submitted a board resolution approving the guarantee bearing the engraved nameplate and corporate seal of Non-party 5, the Intervenor’s representative director; and that, in the corporate registry transcript of the Intervenor that the Plaintiff received when it began entering into joint and several suretyship agreements with the Intervenor, Non-party 4 was registered as a director; and then rejected the Defendant’s and the Intervenor’s above assertion on the ground that, even if the board resolution attached to the Joint and Several Suretyship Agreement at Issue bore the signature and seal of Non-party 4, who had resigned as director more than 1 year earlier, the Plaintiff appears to have had no choice but to believe that the above board resolution had been validly formed, and that there was otherwise no evidence whatsoever sufficient to establish that the Plaintiff knew or could have known that the Intervenor had not held a board meeting for approval at that time.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the above measure by the court below is also reasonable and persuasive, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality, such as inadequate judicial examination or violation of the rules of evidence evaluation, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. With respect to Ground 3 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nIn an action to avoid a fraudulent act, the term “beneficiary” refers to the counterparty to the debtor’s act of disposing of property, and even a person who actually purchased property from the debtor at market price falls within the meaning of the beneficiary here. Moreover, an act by which a debtor converts his or her only asset, real property, into cash, which is easily consumed, etc., is, absent special circumstances, a fraudulent act against creditors, and not only is the debtor’s intent to defraud presumed, but the burden of proving that the beneficiary was not in bad faith when purchasing or receiving the property lies on the beneficiary (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DA26550, decided July 22, 2005). Meanwhile, in recognizing that the beneficiary was in good faith at the time of the fraudulent act, objective and convincing evidentiary materials must support such recognition, and one must not readily conclude that the beneficiary was in good faith at the time of the fraudulent act based solely on the debtor’s unilateral statement or statements that amount merely to conjecture by a third party (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DA5710, decided April 14, 2006).\\n\\nAccording to the judgment of the court below, the court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found the following facts: the Intervenor, in July 2002, while insolvent with debts of approximately KRW 9.7 billion and having the Real Property at Issue as its only asset, completed the registration of transfer of ownership in the Defendant’s name on July 31, 2002, based on a sale dated July 8, 2002; thereafter, the registration of establishment of a mortgage right by Shinhan Bank Co., Ltd. and the respective registrations of leasehold rights by Woojin Trading Co., Ltd. and Non-party 6 concerning the Real Property at Issue were cancelled; at that time, the Intervenor’s shareholders consisted of Non-party 4 holding 41.7%, Najin Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Najin Industrial”) holding 36.6%, and Non-party 8 and relatives of Non-party 4 holding 21.7%; the Defendant’s shareholders consisted of Najin Industrial holding 29.17%, Non-party 4 holding 26.15%, and Non-party 7 holding 3.85%; Najin Industrial’s shareholders consisted of Non-party 4 holding 52.18%, Non-party 5 holding 5.45%, and Non-party 7 and relatives of Non-party 4 holding 43%; Non-party 5 concurrently served as the Intervenor’s representative director, Najin Industrial’s representative director and manager, and the Defendant’s director, while Non-party 4 concurrently served as the Defendant’s representative director, Najin Industrial’s director, and the Intervenor’s representative director, thus resulting in overlapping appointments among the executive officers of the Intervenor, Najin Industrial, and the Defendant; and, in fact, Non-party 4, the de facto manager of Najin Industrial, took the lead in relation to the sale of the Real Property at Issue and other major management matters of the Intervenor and the Defendant. On that basis, the court below held that the Intervenor’s execution of a contract to transfer the Real Property at Issue, its only asset, to the Defendant, which had a special relationship with it, while in an insolvent state, constitutes, absent special circumstances, a fraudulent act done with intent to harm the Plaintiff as a creditor, and that the Defendant’s bad faith as beneficiary is presumed; meanwhile, it determined that circumstances such as the Intervenor’s having used all of the proceeds from the sale of the Real Property at Issue to repay debts to some creditors, or the Defendant’s and the Intervenor’s having tried for years to dispose of the Real Property at issue at an appropriate price, or the Defendant’s business need to purchase the Real Property at Issue, are insufficient to rebut the presumption of the Intervenor’s intent to defraud or the Defendant’s bad faith as beneficiary.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles and record discussed above, the court below’s fact-finding and determination are reasonable and persuasive, and there is no illegality, such as misapprehension of legal principles or factual error due to violation of the rules of evidence evaluation, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court decision cited in the grounds of appeal concerns a different case and is not appropriate for application to this case.\\n\\n4. With respect to Ground 4 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. Since each creditor who satisfies the requirements for a Creditor’s Right of Revocation may, in his or her own right, revoke the debtor’s act of disposing of property and seek restoration to the original state, where multiple creditors file actions for revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration to the original state either simultaneously or at different times, these actions do not constitute duplicative litigation. Moreover, the mere fact that one creditor obtained a favorable judgment and that judgment became final and conclusive in an action for revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration to the original state concerning the same fraudulent act does not mean that another creditor’s later-filed identical claim lacks an interest in legal protection; rather, only when property or value has actually been restored on that basis does another creditor’s claim for revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration to the original state lose its interest in legal protection to the extent it overlaps with that restoration (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2003DA19558, decided July 11, 2003; Supreme Court Decision 2004DA67806, decided May 27, 2005). Accordingly, where multiple creditors file actions for revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration to the original state and multiple lawsuits are pending, judgments ordering revocation of the fraudulent act and restoration to the original state must be rendered in each action according to the creditor’s claim. Even where the beneficiary (including a subsequent transferee; the same applies hereinafter) must make value compensation, the order should not direct payment only within the scope of allocating the value to be returned by the beneficiary among the creditors in proportion to each creditor’s claim amount; rather, it must order return of the full amount of each creditor’s preserved claim within the scope of the value that the beneficiary is to return. Although, when judgments ordering return of the full amount that the beneficiary must compensate are rendered and become final and conclusive in multiple lawsuits, the beneficiary may be exposed to the risk of returning value twice, if the beneficiary has returned all or part of the amount he or she must compensate to one creditor, the beneficiary may refuse double payment to the other creditors within that extent by means such as filing an objection to enforcement of the claim (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DA51457, decided November 25, 2005).\\n\\nIn the same vein, the court below’s measure of partially granting the Plaintiff’s claim in this case for revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration to the original state, within the limit of KRW 2,798,442,020, which is the remainder after subtracting the secured amount of the senior mortgage and the lease deposit amounts from the value of the Real Property at Issue, is proper, and there is no illegality, such as misapprehension of legal principles, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nB. Since the Creditor’s Right of Revocation is a right that essentially serves to relatively revoke, as between the creditor and the beneficiary or subsequent transferee, the debtor’s fraudulent act and to restore property that has left the debtor’s responsible assets so that the creditor may carry out compulsory execution, it should be understood that, where restoration to the original state is effected by value compensation, the counterparty to performance must be the creditor.\\n\\nThe court below’s measure ordering the Defendant, as beneficiary, to make value compensation to the Plaintiff, as creditor, is in accordance with the above legal principles and is proper, and there is no illegality, such as misapprehension of legal principles, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court decision cited in the grounds of appeal concerns a different case and is not appropriate for application to this case.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices in attendance, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[91DA41187]": "As to the grounds for final appeal asserted by counsel for the Plaintiff, the court below dismissed the action as an improper filing duplicative of Suwon District Court Seongnam Branch 90GAHAP215 (Seoul High Court 91NA6896).\\n\\nWhere, during the pendency before the court of a creditor’s subrogation action brought by a creditor against a third-party debtor by subrogating the debtor, an action is filed between the debtor and the third-party debtor containing the same object of litigation as the creditor’s subrogation action, the two actions are the same action, and the later-filed action shall be deemed an improper action filed in violation of the principle prohibiting duplicative filing; however, in such case, the criterion for distinguishing the prior action and the later action shall depend on the temporal order of the commencement of the pendency of litigation (see this Court’s decisions rendered on 1989.4.11., 87DAKA3155; 1990.4.27., 88DAKA25274, 25281), and where there is an additional amendment of the action, the effect of the pendency of the additional action shall arise when the written statement is served on the opposing party or handed over at the hearing date.\\n\\nHowever, in Case 90GAHAP215 above, it is clear that Intervenor 1 and Intervenor 2, as plaintiffs, subrogated the Defendant in this case and claimed insurance proceeds from the Plaintiff in this case by means of the preparatory brief dated 1990.7.2., and it should be deemed that the effect of the pendency of litigation arose only upon service of this written statement on the opposing party or upon its handover at the hearing date; by contrast, the record shows that the complaint in this case was served on the Defendant on 1990.4.17., before the effect of the aforementioned pendency of litigation arose, and thus pendency of litigation commenced. If so, even assuming that the object of litigation in the action additionally amended in Case 90GAHAP215 above and the object of litigation in this case are identical, this case cannot be said to fall under the later-filed action of the action additionally amended in Case 90GAHAP215 above. The court below, on the contrary, erred in holding that this action constituted the later-filed action and dismissing the action as stated above.\\n\\nIn addition, in Case 90GAHAP215 above, the Defendant’s insurance claim right arising from the death of Nonparty 1 is being subrogated, whereas in this case, confirmation of the nonexistence of the Defendant’s insurance claim right arising from the injuries of Nonparty 2 and 11 others is being sought; where there are multiple victims of the same traffic accident and one of them, by subrogating the insured, is making a claim for insurance proceeds against the insurer with respect to that victim’s own portion of damages, the fact that another victim, by subrogating the insured, makes a separate claim for insurance proceeds with respect to another victim’s portion of damages cannot be said to constitute duplicative filing; in such a case, an independent insured event arises for each victim, and the object of litigation concerning the right to claim insurance proceeds cannot be said to be identical.\\n\\nThe judgment of the court below, by misapprehending the legal principles on duplicative litigation and thereby committing an illegality affecting the judgment, is erroneous, and the arguments pointing out this point are well-founded.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the operative part."}

{"[94DA59028]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nRegarding Point 1\\n\\nWhen a judicial settlement is entered in the record, that record has the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment, and res judicata arises between the parties; therefore, unless it is revoked or altered by an action for retrial, the parties may not assert claims contrary to the purport of the settlement (see Supreme Court en banc decision of 1962. 2. 15., 4294MINSANG914; decision of 1981. 2. 24., 80DA1838; decision of 1992. 11. 27., 92DA8521, etc.). The lower court’s determination to this effect is proper, and it cannot be said that the judgment below contains any illegality of misapprehension of legal principles as argued. The Supreme Court decision cited by the appellant, namely the decision of 1957. 12. 26., 4290MINSANG638, etc., has been altered by the above en banc decision and cannot be relied upon in this case. The argument is without merit.\\n\\nRegarding Points 2 and 3\\n\\nAccording to the record, the lower court’s factual findings and selection of evidence concerning the points identified in the argument (including the rejection of the result of the examination of Non-Party 1 as a party, which is consistent with the point that Settlement No. 1 referred to in the judgment was revoked or rescinded by Settlement No. 2 referred to in the judgment) are all convincing, and it cannot be said that in the process there was any illegality in violation of the rules of evidence resulting in erroneous factual findings.\\n\\nIf the factual circumstances are as finally and conclusively determined by the lower court, even though after Settlement No. 1 referred to in the judgment was formed between the Nongdong Agricultural Cooperative Association and Non-Party 1 and Non-Party 2, Settlement No. 2 referred to in the judgment, which is inconsistent and in conflict with Settlement No. 1, was again formed between the said association and Non-Party 1, since Settlement No. 1 was entered in the record and res judicata arose in the same manner as a final and conclusive judgment, it cannot be said that Settlement No. 1 was naturally extinguished or altered by Settlement No. 2, nor further that the ownership transfer registration in the name of Non-Party 1 referred to in the judgment, completed by execution of the record of Settlement No. 1, and the respective ownership transfer registrations in the names of the Defendants based thereon, became void (see Supreme Court decision of 1994. 7. 29., 92DA25137). In addition, even a judgment on a suit filed in violation of the principle prohibiting duplicate litigation, or a settlement reached in the course of such litigation, cannot be said to be automatically void if it has become final and conclusive (see Supreme Court decision of 1968. 4. 16., 68DA122). The lower court’s determination to this effect is proper, and it cannot be said that the judgment below contains any illegality such as misapprehension of legal principles as argued. All of the arguments are without merit.\\n\\nRegarding Point 4\\n\\nThe lower court determined that the provisional registration and ownership transfer registration in the name of Non-Party 2 concerning the real property in this case were valid because they were not completed to secure his claim against Non-Party 1, but were completed by execution of the record of Settlement No. 1 referred to in the judgment; and upon review of the record, the above finding and determination by the lower court appears correct, and it cannot be said that the judgment below contains any illegality as argued.
