question: Which of the following statements concerning setoff and the setoff defense is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) Which of the following statements concerning setoff and the setoff defense is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: Where the principal obligor has previously waived the defense against the claim for provision of security against the entrusted surety, the entrusted surety may set off its debt to the principal obligor by using the prior reimbursement claim as the active claim.
B: Where the defendant alleged two or more counterclaims by way of a setoff defense, but the court recognized only one of those counterclaims and rejected the setoff defense as to the remainder on the ground that the remaining counterclaims did not exist, the scope of res judicata with respect to the determination that the counterclaims do not exist cannot exceed the balance of the passive claim after setoff has been completed.
C: In calculating the debtor's liability for damages arising from a tort or nonperformance of an obligation, where it is necessary to limit the debtor's liability in order to achieve equitable allocation of loss, if the debtor raises a setoff defense with a counterclaim held against the creditor, the setoff must be made against the amount of damages after the limitation of liability.
D: A third-party debtor who has a counterclaim that was eligible for setoff against the debtor before service on the third-party debtor of an order of seizure and assignment of claims may, after service of that order, assert setoff against the assignee creditor.
E: A defendant who, in the court of first instance of the earlier-filed action, submitted a setoff defense and thereby obtained a determination on the merits by the first-instance judgment, but later withdrew the setoff defense in the appellate court, is not permitted, pursuant to the principle prohibiting a subsequent suit, to separately bring an action based on a claim identical to that active claim.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2001DA81245]": "1. With respect to Ground 1 of Appeal on Points of Law\\n\\nIf setoff were permitted by treating a claim subject to a right of defense as the active claim and offsetting it against another obligation (passive claim), the result would be that, by one party’s declaration of intention to set off, the other party would lose the opportunity to exercise its right of defense; therefore, such setoff cannot be permitted. In particular, the right to prior reimbursement under Article 442 of the Civil Act that a commissioned surety has against the principal debtor has attached to it, as a right of defense, the right to demand provision of security prescribed in Article 443 of the Civil Act, and accordingly setoff using it as the active claim cannot be permitted (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on November 13, 2001, 2001DA55222, 55239). However, since Article 443 of the Civil Act is a default rule, if the principal debtor has, in advance, waived the right of defense to demand provision of security, the surety may set off the debt owed to the principal debtor by using the right to prior reimbursement as the active claim (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on January 31, 1989, 87DAKA594).\\n\\nThe court below, in response to the Defendant’s defense that Article 13 of the corporate bond guarantee insurance agreement concluded among the Plaintiff, Asia Motors Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Asia Motors”), and the Defendant constitutes an agreement waiving the right of defense prescribed in Article 443 of the Civil Act, so that setoff using the instant right to prior reimbursement as the active claim is valid, found as follows: the Plaintiff and Asia Motors (hereinafter referred to as “the Plaintiffs, etc.”) issued guaranteed corporate bonds for which the Defendant guaranteed payment from around May 1995 and around March 1996, and in that process concluded the instant corporate bond guarantee insurance agreement with the Defendant by means of a contract form prepared by the Defendant; Article 8 of the instant corporate bond guarantee insurance agreement provides that “the Plaintiffs, etc. shall provide the Defendant, together with a power of attorney for completion, with a blank checking account check or bank-accepted promissory note for the protection of the Defendant’s claim”; Article 13 provides that “when bankruptcy, commencement of composition proceedings, or an application for commencement of company reorganization proceedings is filed against the Plaintiffs, etc., the Plaintiffs, etc. shall lose the benefit of time, and the Defendant may thereupon exercise its right to prior reimbursement by demanding immediate payment from the Plaintiffs, etc. of the promissory note amount or check amount collected pursuant to Article 8 and enforcing security rights, etc.”; and, when concluding the instant corporate bond guarantee insurance agreement, the Plaintiffs, etc. delivered to the Defendant, pursuant to the above Article 8, a blank checking account check with both the face amount and date of issuance left blank, together with the power of attorney for completion. Based on these findings, the court below held: first, there is no express provision in the instant corporate bond guarantee insurance agreement stating that the Plaintiffs, etc. waive, with respect to the Defendant’s right to prior reimbursement, rights of defense such as the right to demand discharge from liability; second, the meaning of the phrase in the above Article 13, “thereupon ... may exercise the right to prior reimbursement,” appears only to mean that, if an application for commencement of company reorganization proceedings is filed against the Plaintiffs, etc., the Plaintiffs, etc. lose the benefit of time, so that the Defendant may immediately exercise the right to prior reimbursement, and it cannot be concluded that the Plaintiffs waived rights of defense such as the right to demand discharge from liability; third, even where the principal debtor has provided security for the reimbursement obligation to the surety, if sufficient security is not provided, the surety cannot avoid the exercise of the right to prior reimbursement, and, in light of the fact that in auction proceedings concerning real property secured by the principal debtor, a surety is permitted to file for distribution based on the right to prior reimbursement, it cannot be concluded that enforcement of security rights based on the right to prior reimbursement is not permitted at all; therefore, the mere fact that the Defendant may enforce the security rights provided by the Plaintiffs, etc. cannot be deemed to mean that the Plaintiffs, etc. waived rights of defense such as the right to demand discharge from liability; fourth, because the Plaintiffs, etc. may revoke the instruction for payment of the blank checks provided as security for the exercise of the right to prior reimbursement while asserting rights of defense such as the right to demand discharge from liability against the Defendant, the mere fact that the Plaintiffs provided blank checks to the Defendant as security for the reimbursement obligation and delivered powers of attorney necessary for filling in the blanks cannot be taken as a definitive basis to conclude that they waived rights of defense such as the right to demand discharge from liability; and fifth, since the instant corporate bond guarantee insurance agreement between the Plaintiffs, etc. and the Defendant was concluded pursuant to standard terms and conditions prepared by the Defendant, unless it is clear whether the provisions of the instant corporate bond guarantee insurance terms and conditions constitute a waiver by the Plaintiffs, etc. of rights of defense such as the right to demand discharge from liability, the rights of defense such as the right to demand discharge from liability cannot, under Article 5(1) and (2) of the Act on the Regulation of Standardized Contracts, be construed as waived to the detriment of the customer Plaintiffs, etc. On the above grounds, the court below rejected the Defendant’s defense. The above determination of the court below is proper, and there is no error of law, such as misapprehension of the legal principles regarding Articles 8 and 13 of the instant corporate bond guarantee insurance agreement, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. With respect to Ground 2 of Appeal on Points of Law\\n\\nAccording to the record, at the date for examination of claims in the company reorganization proceedings against the reorganized company Kia Motors Co., Ltd., it may be seen that the receiver of the reorganized company Kia Motors Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the “Receiver”) disallowed certain claims filed by some creditors of the corporate bonds guaranteed by the Defendant on the ground of the Defendant’s exercise of its right of recourse or the guarantor institution’s acknowledgment of the principal debt (the Receiver, where creditors of the corporate bonds guaranteed by the Defendant filed claims, disallowed not only the claims of those creditors but also the portion of the claims filed by the Defendant, on the ground of duplicate filing, etc., and later withdrew the disallowance of the creditors’ claims). However, for setoff based on the commissioned surety’s right to prior reimbursement to be valid, there must have been, in advance, a waiver by the principal debtor of the right of defense to demand provision of security prescribed in Article 443 of the Civil Act. Accordingly, the admission or denial of the reorganized claims made after the Defendant’s declaration of intention to set off based on the instant right to prior reimbursement cannot be deemed to constitute an express waiver of the right of defense concerning the right to demand provision of security that would validate the Defendant’s setoff. Moreover, according to the record, the Defendant had been paying insurance proceeds under the installment sales guarantee insurance at the request of the Plaintiffs, but, from around December 23, 1997, refused payment of the insurance proceeds on the ground of setoff based on the right to prior reimbursement under the instant corporate bond guarantee insurance agreement; the Plaintiffs’ staff objected and repeatedly urged the Defendant to pay the insurance proceeds; and the Receiver requested the Defendant, around May 21, 1998, to pay the insurance proceeds. In light of these circumstances, it would be difficult to view the Plaintiffs as having implicitly waived the right of defense to demand provision of security prescribed in Article 443 of the Civil Act.\\n\\nAlthough the court below rejected the argument concerning an agreement to waive the right of defense to demand provision of security prescribed in Article 443 of the Civil Act, it did not separately rule on the argument that such right of defense had been waived. Nevertheless, it is reasonable to view the above determination of the court below as including the purport of rejecting the argument that the foregoing right of defense had been waived. Moreover, since the ground of appeal asserting express or implied waiver of the right of defense to demand provision of security prescribed in Article 443 of the Civil Act cannot be accepted, it cannot be said that the judgment below is unlawful in a manner affecting the result of the judgment due to incomplete examination or omission of a ruling.\\n\\n3. With respect to Ground 3 of Appeal on Points of Law\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Defendant had been paying insurance proceeds under the installment sales guarantee insurance at the request of the Plaintiffs, but, from around December 23, 1997, refused payment of the insurance proceeds on the ground of setoff based on the right to prior reimbursement under the instant corporate bond guarantee insurance agreement; the Plaintiffs’ staff objected and repeatedly urged the Defendant to pay the insurance proceeds; the Receiver, on May 21, 1998, the day after the period for filing reorganized claims, requested the Defendant to pay the insurance proceeds; and the Receiver notified the Defendant on November 13, 1998 and December 2, 1998 that the setoff based on the instant right to prior reimbursement was invalid and that a supplementary filing should be made for the reorganized claims, but the Defendant did not make such supplementary filing by December 28, 1998, the date of the second meeting of interested parties. In light of these circumstances, the court below correctly rejected the Defendant’s argument, holding that even though the Defendant’s instant right to prior reimbursement had been extinguished by failure to file it with the reorganization court, it cannot be said to violate the principle of good faith and fair dealing, the principle of fairness, commercial morality, or the sense of justice for the Plaintiff to deny the effect of the setoff based on the instant right to prior reimbursement and further to seek payment of the instant insurance proceeds from the Defendant. There is no error of law, such as misapprehension of legal principles concerning the principle of good faith and fair dealing, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. With respect to Ground 4 of Appeal on Points of Law\\n\\nThe case where a judgment fails to state reasons, which is an absolute ground for appeal under Article 424(1)6 of the Civil Procedure Act, refers to a case where the judgment contains no reasons at all or omits part of the reasons, or where any part of the reasons is unclear so that it is uncertain how the court found the facts and interpreted and applied the law to arrive at the conclusion (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on March 3, 1995, 92DA55770).\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Plaintiff’s claim in this case is a claim for insurance proceeds based on installment sales guarantee insurance contracts concluded between purchasers who bought automobiles, etc. on installment from the Plaintiffs and the Defendant, with the Plaintiffs as the insured. Around September 1996, the Plaintiff concluded with the Defendant an agreement concerning a “comprehensive agreement on installment sales guarantee insurance for automobiles,” and, where the Plaintiff sold automobiles to customers and received the purchase price in installments, had the customers conclude installment sales guarantee insurance with the Defendant and submit the guarantee insurance policies to the Plaintiff for the purpose of securing the claim for installment payments (Asia Motors also concluded, in August 1994 and July 1995, with the Defendant, respectively, comprehensive agreements on installment sales guarantee insurance for automobiles and construction machinery in the same form). Accordingly, the customers concluded with the Defendant installment sales guarantee insurance contracts providing that the policyholder be the relevant customer and the insured be the Plaintiff or Asia Motors, and that, if grounds such as a delay in installment payments by the customers under the installment sales contracts with the Plaintiffs for two or more installments arose, the Defendant would pay the installment principal and default interest, etc.; thereafter the customers submitted the guarantee insurance policies to the Plaintiffs, etc. When an insured event occurred, such as the customers’ being in arrears for two or more installments under the installment sale contracts, the Plaintiffs, etc. claimed payment of the insurance proceeds from the Defendant on the basis of the guarantee insurance policies issued by the Defendant, and the Defendant had been paying insurance proceeds to the Plaintiffs, etc. under the installment sales guarantee insurance contracts. However, when applications for commencement of company reorganization proceedings or composition proceedings were filed against the Plaintiffs, etc. after September 1997, the Defendant, from December 23, 1997 to May 19, 1998, declared setoff against the insurance debt owed to the Plaintiffs, etc. under the installment sales guarantee insurance contracts, using as the active claim its claim for reimbursement based on the right to prior reimbursement under the instant corporate bond guarantee insurance agreement concluded with the Plaintiffs, etc. (including Kia Motec Co., Ltd.), and thereby did not pay the insurance proceeds of KRW 96,164,961,592, which are the amount claimed in this case. The Plaintiff then brought this action on the ground that such setoff was unlawful. It is also apparent from the record that, in the first-instance proceedings in this case, it was undisputed that the Defendant declared setoff with respect to the above amount among the insurance proceeds claimed by the Plaintiffs from the Defendant under the installment sales guarantee insurance contracts. Up to the proceedings in the court below, the Plaintiff and the Defendant disputed only the legality of the setoff exercised by the Defendant based on the instant right to prior reimbursement; they did not dispute at all whether the individual insurance claim, which constitutes the cause of action in this case, was specifically identified, or whether the passive claim subject to setoff by the Defendant was specifically identified.\\n\\nThe court below, in the reasons for its judgment, set forth findings of fact regarding the conclusion of the above-described comprehensive agreement on installment sales guarantee insurance for automobiles between the Plaintiffs, etc. and the Defendant, the contents of the installment sales guarantee insurance contracts concluded on that basis between the Plaintiffs’ installment-sale customers and the Defendant, the Defendant’s exercise of the right of setoff based on the instant right to prior reimbursement and the contents thereof, and the circumstances leading the Plaintiff to bring this action. Accordingly, the Plaintiff’s claim in this case can be generally identified as the amount, among the insurance proceeds claimed by the Plaintiffs from the Defendant on the ground of the occurrence of an insured event under the installment sales guarantee insurance contracts, which the Defendant, from December 23, 1997 to May 19, 1998, had treated as the passive claim while making declarations of setoff using as the active claim its claim for prior reimbursement under the instant corporate bond guarantee insurance. Since this does not constitute a case where the statement of reasons is unclear to the extent that it is impossible to know what the cause of action in this case is, the ground of appeal asserting that the judgment below is unlawful for failure to state reasons cannot be accepted.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged unanimously by the participating Justices."}

{"[2012DA107662]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the grounds for appeal against Defendant Hanla Co., Ltd.\\n   a. Argument concerning the rejoinder of set-off in litigation\\n   (1) A plea of set-off as a method of defense in litigation is ordinarily made as a kind of preliminary defense on the premise that the existence of the passive claim is established; it does not definitively produce its effect upon the manifestation of intent to set off in litigation, but the effect of set-off under substantive law arises only when the court makes a substantive determination on the set-off, including the existence of the passive claim, in the relevant litigation (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DA3329 rendered on March 28, 2013).\\n   When, in response to such a defendant’s plea of set-off in litigation, the plaintiff again raises a rejoinder of set-off in litigation in order to extinguish the defendant’s active claim, if the court rejects the defendant’s plea of set-off in litigation for reasons unrelated to the plaintiff’s rejoinder of set-off in litigation, there is no need to determine the plaintiff’s rejoinder of set-off in litigation; and if the court determines that the defendant’s plea of set-off in litigation is well-founded, then the plaintiff’s claim claim, which is the passive claim, and the defendant’s active claim will be deemed to have been extinguished to the extent of equal amounts at the time when set-off became possible, and thus the defendant’s active claim, which is the object of set-off by the plaintiff’s rejoinder of set-off in litigation, will not exist within that extent, so that there is likewise no need to determine the plaintiff’s rejoinder of set-off in litigation. In addition, if the plaintiff has other claims against the defendant besides the claim claim that is the subject matter of the lawsuit, the plaintiff may assert such claims in the relevant litigation by way of an additional change of claim or file a separate action.\\n   In that event, the plaintiff’s rejoinder of set-off in litigation generally has no interest in being allowed. Therefore, it is reasonable to view that the plaintiff’s raising of a rejoinder of set-off in litigation against the defendant’s plea of set-off in litigation is not permitted absent other special circumstances (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DA95964 rendered on June 12, 2014). The same applies where the plaintiff asserts two claims, the defendant raises a plea of set-off in litigation using one of those claims as the passive claim, and the plaintiff again raises a rejoinder of set-off in litigation using the other one of the above claim claims as the active claim.\\n   (2) According to the reasoning of the lower judgment and the record, the lower court determined that (a) the KRW 439,398,688 damage claim in lieu of repair after use inspection, belonging to the first-instance co-defendant The P&D Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “The P&D”), whose rights the Plaintiff exercises by subrogation, was extinguished, retroactively from the time each defect arose, to the extent of equal amounts by the declaration of intent to set off dated May 24, 2011, in which Defendant Hanla Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Defendant Hanla”) used its claim for the balance of the construction price in this case of KRW 214,313,428 as the active claim, and then, (b) only thereafter, through the preparatory brief dated May 8, 2012 and the application for change of the statement of grounds for appeal and appellate relief dated June 12, 2012, the Plaintiff newly asserted a set-off against Defendant Hanla’s claim for the balance of the construction price in this case, as the passive claim, against the damage claim in lieu of repair before use inspection, and recognized that copies of the written submissions containing such declaration of intent to set off by the Plaintiff were served on Defendant Hanla on May 9, 2012 and June 12, 2012, respectively, and then rejected the Plaintiff’s above plea of set-off in litigation, taking the view that Defendant Hanla’s claim for the balance of the construction price in this case, which is the passive claim the Plaintiff seeks to set off, had already been extinguished by the earlier set-off defense using the very same claim of Defendant Hanla as the active claim.\\n   (3) Examining the reasoning of the lower judgment in light of the evidence lawfully admitted, the lower court’s determination appears to be based on the legal principles stated above, and there is no illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles on the concurrent performance relationship, the timing of set-off eligibility, set-off in litigation, the principle of good faith, and the principle of equity, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n   b. Argument concerning set-off before limitation of the amount of damages liability\\n   (1) When calculating the amount of damages owed by a debtor for tort or nonperformance of obligation, it is necessary to limit the debtor’s liability in order to ensure equity in the burden of loss, and when the debtor raises a plea of set-off with a counterclaim against the creditor, set-off must be made against the amount of damages after such limitation of liability.\\n   (2) The lower court, citing the reasons as stated in its opinion, determined that set-off by Defendant Hanla’s claim for the balance of the construction price in this case must be made against the amount, after limitation of liability under the principle of equity or the principle of good faith, among the damage claim in lieu of repair against Defendant Hanla held by The P&D, which the Plaintiff exercises by subrogation, and accordingly found that the liability-limited amount of damages and Defendant Hanla’s balance of the construction price in this case were extinguished to the extent of equal amounts.\\n   (3) The lower court’s determination conforms to the above legal principles, and there is no illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the timing when set-off becomes possible and the object of set-off, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. Regarding the grounds for appeal against Defendant Seoul Guarantee Insurance Co., Ltd.\\n   a. The claim for the defect repair guarantee deposit that the residents’ representative council has against the defect repair guarantee company based on the former Housing Act (before amendment by Act No. 8974 of March 21, 2008) and the former Enforcement Decree of the Housing Act (before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 22254 of July 6, 2010), and the right to claim damages in lieu of defect repair that the employer has against the contractor based on Article 28(1) of the former Framework Act on the Construction Industry (before amendment by Act No. 10719 of May 24, 2011) and Article 667 of the Civil Act, etc., are separate rights whose grounds for recognition, parties to the legal relationship, and contents of liability are different from one another.\\n   Therefore, even where the residents’ representative council receives an assignment from the sectional owners of the claim for damages in lieu of repair against the seller, as recognized under the Act on the Ownership and Management of Condominium Buildings (hereinafter referred to as the “Condominium Buildings Act”), and, by subrogating the seller who is the employer under the Condominium Buildings Act, claims damages in lieu of repair as defect liability against the contractor, who is the builder, and at the same time directly claims the defect repair guarantee deposit against the defect repair guarantee company as the guarantee creditor under the defect repair guarantee contract, the contractor’s obligation to pay damages in lieu of repair to the employer and the defect repair guarantee company’s obligation to pay the defect repair guarantee deposit to the residents’ representative council cannot be regarded as being in a relationship of imperfect joint and several obligations.\\n   However, the contractor’s obligation to pay damages in lieu of repair to the employer and the defect repair guarantee company’s obligation to pay the defect repair guarantee deposit to the residents’ representative council may partially overlap in the defects they cover, and to the extent of such overlap they ultimately exist for the repair of the same defects; therefore, if the residents’ representative council later obtains judgments in its favor in both the damages claim in lieu of repair by subrogating the employer and the suit for the defect repair guarantee deposit against the defect repair guarantee company, and then exercises either of those rights and actually receives money equivalent to the repair costs for the defects, thereby achieving the purpose of defect repair within the scope related to the defects for which that money was paid, the other right may be said to be extinguished (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DA23160 rendered on September 13, 2012). However, if the employer’s claim for damages in lieu of repair against the contractor is set off by the contractor’s claim against the employer, that circumstance alone does not mean that the purpose of the right concerning defect repair held by the residents’ representative council based on the former Housing Act and subordinate statutes has been achieved, and thus it has no effect on the claim for the defect repair guarantee deposit that the residents’ representative council has against the defect repair guarantee company.\\n   b. In light of these legal principles, in the present case, even though the Plaintiff received an assignment from the sectional owners of this apartment of the damage claim in lieu of repair against The P&D, subrogated The P&D, and claimed damages against Defendant Hanla, who is the contractor, and additionally directly sought the defect repair guarantee deposit from Defendant Seoul Guarantee Insurance as the guarantee creditor under each defect repair guarantee contract in this case, it cannot be said that the damages liability of Defendant Hanla and the obligation of Defendant Seoul Guarantee Insurance to pay the defect repair guarantee deposit are in a relationship of imperfect joint and several obligations.\\n   Therefore, even if, as stated above, part of the damages liability in lieu of repair or damages liability arising from nonperformance of defect repair borne by Defendant Hanla as contractor toward The P&D was extinguished by set-off with Defendant Hanla’s claim for the balance of the construction price in this case against The P&D, it cannot be said that the purpose of defect repair or damages in lieu thereof against the Plaintiff has been achieved; thus, that effect does not affect at all the obligation of Defendant Seoul Guarantee Insurance to pay the defect repair guarantee deposit to the Plaintiff, the residents’ representative council, under each defect repair guarantee contract in this case.\\n   And because the obligation extinguished by the above set-off is Defendant Hanla’s obligation to The P&D, not Defendant Hanla’s defect repair liability toward the Plaintiff under the former Housing Act and subordinate statutes, which is the principal obligation under each defect repair guarantee contract in this case, even under Article 434 of the Civil Act, which permits a surety to assert against the creditor a set-off based on the principal obligor’s claim, it cannot be said that Defendant Hanla’s defect repair liability toward the Plaintiff is reduced or that Defendant Seoul Guarantee Insurance’s guaranty liability toward the Plaintiff under each defect repair guarantee contract in this case is reduced.\\n   c. Nevertheless, contrary to this, the lower court erroneously determined that KRW 214,313,428 of Defendant Hanla’s damages liability in lieu of repair toward the Plaintiff, or damages liability arising from nonperformance of defect repair, as the principal obligor under each defect repair guarantee contract in this case, was extinguished by Defendant Hanla’s above set-off, and on that premise held that the above amount should be deducted from the defect repair guarantee deposit that Defendant Seoul Guarantee Insurance must pay to the Plaintiff. Accordingly, the lower court’s determination contains illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the legal nature of the employer’s claim for damages in lieu of repair against the contractor and the residents’ representative council’s claim for the defect repair guarantee deposit under the former Housing Act and subordinate statutes and the defect repair guarantee contract, and the difference between them. The grounds for appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, among the lower judgment, the part against the Plaintiff concerning Defendant Seoul Guarantee Insurance is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination; the remainder of the appeal is dismissed; and the costs of appeal incurred between the Plaintiff and Defendant Hanla shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged as ordered, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

{"[2021DA275741]": "The Court determines the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Whether the case constitutes duplicative litigation or violates the prohibition on refiling (Ground of Appeal No. 2)\\n\\na. Where, at the time a defense of setoff was raised, an action based on the same claim as the active claim had already been separately filed and was pending, it is desirable for the trial court to attempt severance, transfer, or joinder of pleadings so as to hear and determine the prior and later actions at the same opportunity, thereby preventing conflict or inconsistency with res judicata and at the same time promoting judicial economy; however, it cannot be deemed that, absent special circumstances, a claim of setoff in litigation, using as the active claim a claim pending in a separate action, is impermissible (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2000DA4050, rendered on April 27, 2001). Likewise, after raising a defense of setoff in the first-filed action, it is also possible, while that action is pending, to separately file an action or a counterclaim based on the same claim as the active claim.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 267(2) of the Civil Procedure Act provides, “A person who withdraws an action after a final judgment on the merits has been rendered may not bring the same action.” This is a provision of a punitive nature enacted for the purpose of preventing the unjust situation in which the court’s efforts expended on adjudication are rendered futile by withdrawal of the action and the same dispute is raised again, thereby abusing the litigation system (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2018DA259213, rendered on May 7, 2021). However, unlike the withdrawal of an action, which becomes effective only with the consent of the other party after the other party has submitted preparatory pleadings or made statements or arguments at a preparatory hearing on the merits, a defense of setoff as a means of defense in litigation is a kind of provisional defense made on the premise that the existence of the passive claim is ascertained, and it may be withdrawn without the other party’s consent; in such case, under the principle of disposition, the court may not adjudicate thereon (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2011DA23323, rendered on July 14, 2011). Therefore, even if, in the court of first instance in the first-filed action, a defense of setoff was raised and the merits were adjudicated in the first-instance judgment, and thereafter the defense of setoff was withdrawn in the appellate court, this is merely a withdrawal of a means of defense in litigation, and the prohibition on refiling under Article 267(2) of the Civil Procedure Act does not apply; accordingly, an action based on the same claim as the active claim may be separately filed.\\n\\nb. According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\nThe Defendant filed against the Plaintiff an action for payment of the construction price under the construction contract at issue (hereinafter referred to as the “prior action”). In the court of first instance in the prior action (Busan District Court 2017GASO505896), the Plaintiff raised a defense of setoff with a claim for damages in lieu of repair of defects as the active claim, but the court of first instance in the prior action, on September 5, 2017, rejected the Plaintiff’s defense of setoff on the ground that proof regarding the existence of defects and the like was insufficient, and rendered a judgment entirely in favor of the Defendant. The Plaintiff, after separately filing on April 5, 2018, the present action against the Defendant seeking damages in lieu of repair of defects in the construction at issue, withdrew the above defense of setoff at the second oral argument date in the appellate court of the prior action (Busan District Court 2017NA56896).\\n\\nc. If these factual circumstances are examined in light of the legal principles stated above, even though the Plaintiff had already raised, in the prior action, a defense of setoff with the claim for damages in lieu of repair of defects as the active claim, it is also permissible for the Plaintiff to separately file the present action based on the same claim as the above active claim while the prior action was pending. In addition, even if the Plaintiff, after receiving an adjudication on the merits concerning the defense of setoff in the court of first instance in the prior action, withdrew the defense of setoff in the appellate court thereof, this does not render the claim for damages in lieu of repair of defects no longer actionable.\\n\\nAccordingly, the argument that the filing of the present action constitutes duplicative litigation prohibited by Article 259 of the Civil Procedure Act or violates the prohibition on refiling under Article 267(2) of the Civil Procedure Act, and that therefore the present action should have been dismissed, is unfounded; there is no error in the court below’s proceeding to adjudicate the merits and rendering judgment while overlooking a defect in the litigation requirements, which is a matter to be examined ex officio.\\n\\n2. Whether the rules of evidence were violated in calculating the amount of damages (Ground of Appeal No. 1)\\n\\nThe court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence cited in its decision, found that defects existed in the building at issue and that a total of 83,154,169 won (including the cost of temporary works for defect repair) would be required for repair of those defects, and then, taking into account all circumstances revealed in the pleadings, limited the amount of damages in lieu of repair of defects to 66,523,335 won, which is 80% of the above repair cost, in accordance with the principle of fairness or the principle of good faith.\\n\\nIf the record is reviewed in accordance with the relevant legal principles, the above determination by the court below does not contain any error affecting the judgment by violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the probative force of a final and conclusive judgment, or by insufficiency of reasons, etc.\\n\\n3. Whether it contravenes res judicata concerning the defense of setoff (Ground of Appeal No. 3)\\n\\na. Article 216(1) of the Civil Procedure Act provides, “A final and conclusive judgment shall have res judicata only as to what is included in the text of the judgment.” Thus, as a general rule, res judicata does not extend to determinations in the reasons for judgment, while, as an exception, paragraph (2) provides, “A determination as to whether the claim asserted as a setoff is established shall have res judicata only to the extent of the amount against which setoff was asserted.” The reason why res judicata is recognized for the court’s determination regarding a claim of setoff, even though it is a determination in the reasons for judgment, is that if res judicata were not recognized with respect thereto, a dispute over the existence or nonexistence of the plaintiff’s claim would later be transformed into a dispute over the existence or nonexistence of the active claim that is brought in another action, so that the opposing party to the setoff claim would not only be subject to disadvantage by the person asserting setoff exercising that active claim twice, but there would also be a risk that the prior judgment on the existence or nonexistence of the plaintiff’s claim, rendered on the premise of the determination regarding the setoff claim, would ultimately become meaningless; this is intended to prevent such result (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2004DA17207, rendered on July 22, 2005; Supreme Court Decision 2016DA46338, 46345, rendered on August 30, 2018).\\n\\nb. According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the Plaintiff, in the court of first instance in the prior action, raised a defense of simultaneous performance based on the right to claim repair of defects or the right to claim damages in lieu of repair of defects concerning the construction at issue, and a defense of setoff with the above damages claim as the active claim; thereafter, in the appellate court, the Plaintiff withdrew the above defense of setoff. The appellate court in the prior action rendered a judgment partially sustaining the Defendant’s claim for the construction price, and in the reasons for that judgment, it rejected only the Plaintiff’s above defense of simultaneous performance and did not adjudicate on the withdrawn defense of setoff. It can also be ascertained that the appellate judgment in the prior action became final and conclusive as rendered.\\n\\nc. If such is the case, the appellate judgment in the prior action does not have res judicata with respect to the Plaintiff’s defense of setoff; therefore, the court below’s determination, which partially upheld the Plaintiff’s claim for damages in lieu of repair of defects, is not erroneous for misapprehending the legal principles concerning res judicata of setoff, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are assessed against the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[73DA518]": "The grounds of appeal advanced by the Plaintiff’s counsel are examined (the supplemental statement of grounds of appeal having been filed after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal, only to the extent that it supplements the grounds of appeal filed within the period).\\n\\nHowever, according to the contents of the preparatory brief dated 1972.9.28 submitted by the Defendant’s counsel and stated at the third oral argument in the court below, it is clear that the Defendant made an expression of intent to set off, against the claim assigned in this case of Non-Party Dongjin Construction Limited Partnership Company, which was the obligor of the claim assigned in this case, a damages claim in an amount equal thereto. The fact that the original judgment, while purporting to examine the Defendant’s defense of setoff, held that on 1970.5.4, when the said Non-Party company and others refused performance of defect repair sought by the Defendant as stated in the original judgment, the obligation to perform defect repair was converted into an obligation to pay damages, and that the Defendant’s damages claim, which fell due on that date, and the claim of the said Non-Party company assigned in this case were already in a state ripe for setoff before 1970.5.8, when the order of assignment in this case was served on the Defendant, so that at that time both claims were extinguished within the extent of their equal amount, is plainly a determination concerning the Defendant’s above expression of intent to set off. Therefore, the argument that, on the contrary assumption that the Defendant never made any expression of intent to set off, the original judgment is erroneous for incomplete deliberation is improper; moreover, the original judgment’s determination concerning setoff is correct, and it cannot be deemed unlawful for having misunderstood the legal doctrine of setoff.\\n\\nIn an attachment of claims and assignment order, the Supreme Court Decision rendered on 1972.12.26. in 72DA2117, to the effect that, after an assignment order has been served on the third-party debtor, even if that third-party debtor had, before service of the order, a counterclaim that was ripe for setoff against the debtor, it cannot set off that counterclaim against the debtor’s claim assigned by the order, conflicts with the determination above and is hereby overruled.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the appellate litigation shall be borne by the losing party; it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of all Justices as stated in the operative part."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the creditor’s revocation right and a lawsuit to revoke a fraudulent act are correct? (In the event of a dispute, according to case law) (a) The requirement of prejudice to creditors must be satisfied not only at the time of the act of disposition but also at the close of oral argument in the first-instance trial of the lawsuit to revoke the fraudulent act. (b) In exercising the creditor’s revocation right, the burden of proving the lapse of the exclusion period rests with the opposing party in the lawsuit to revoke the fraudulent act. (c) Where a creditor exercises by subrogation the debtor’s creditor’s revocation right, whether the filing period has been observed shall be determined with reference to the creditor in question. (d) Where one creditor has obtained a final and binding judgment in a claim for revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration to the original condition, and has completed the restoration of property or value based on that judgment, a claim for revocation of the fraudulent act and restoration to the original condition brought by another creditor concerning the same fraudulent act lacks an interest in legal protection to the extent it overlaps therewith.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2000DA73049]": "The appeal is dismissed. The costs of appeal shall be borne by the Defendant."}

{"[2003DA19558]": "1. Judgment of the Court Below\\n\\nThe court below held that, in a creditor’s revocation action, because the creditor’s revocation and restoration to original condition are effective for the benefit of all creditors, where one creditor first files a creditor’s revocation action against the beneficiary and obtains a final and conclusive judgment of victory, it is not an action with a legal interest in protection for another creditor to file the same action again; accordingly, in this case, since the Korea Technology Finance Corporation filed against Defendant 1 and Defendant 2, with the Daegu District Court Case No. 2000GAHAP4092, an action seeking, on the ground that each of the sales contracts at issue constituted a fraudulent act, cancellation of the sales contracts and performance of compensation by value, and a judgment in favor was rendered on January 16, 2001 and became final and conclusive, the Plaintiff’s action against Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 was dismissed as unlawful for lack of a legal interest in protection.\\n\\nFurthermore, the court below held that, where a fraudulent act is committed with respect to real property on which a mortgage has been established, a fraudulent act is constituted only within the extent of the balance obtained by deducting the amount of the secured debt of the mortgage from the value of the real property; thus, when the mortgage registration is canceled after the fraudulent act, the fraudulent act may be revoked and compensation by value sought within the limit of the balance obtained by deducting the amount of the secured debt of the mortgage from the value of the real property. On the premise that, where there is a claim for compensation by value from multiple creditors exceeding the limit for which the beneficiary should be liable, the creditor’s claim for compensation by value for the portion exceeding the balance obtained by deducting the amount of the secured debt of the mortgage to be borne by the relevant real property from the value of the real property is unlawful, the court below fixed the amount of the secured debt to be deducted from the value of the real properties in Schedule 1 and 2 at 33,239,351 won, and the amount of the secured debt to be deducted from the value of the real property in Schedule 3 at 40,059,468 won, respectively, and then, since the Korea Technology Finance Corporation had already obtained a judgment ordering, against Defendant 1, cancellation of the fraudulent act and compensation by value within the respective scope of 94,414,399 won (127,653,720 - 33,239,351) and, against Defendant 2, 113,786,532 won (153,846,000 - 40,059,468), to the extent of deducting the above secured debt amounts from the values of the above real properties, and that judgment had already become final and conclusive, there remained no balance obtained by deducting the secured debt amounts from the values of the real properties in Schedule 1, 2, and 3, and thus held that, on this point as well, the Plaintiff’s above claims against Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 were unlawful.\\n\\n2. Judgment of This Court\\n\\nThe essence of the court below’s holding is that, where one creditor first files against the beneficiary an action for creditor’s revocation and restoration to original condition and obtains a final and conclusive judgment in his or her favor, it is unlawful for another creditor to file the same action because there is no legal interest in protection.\\n\\nHowever, since each creditor who satisfies the requirements for the creditor’s revocation right may, as his or her own right, revoke the debtor’s act of disposing of property and seek restoration to original condition, where each creditor simultaneously or at different times files an action for creditor’s revocation and restoration to original condition, such actions do not constitute duplicate litigation; moreover, even if one creditor, with respect to the same fraudulent act, seeks creditor’s revocation and restoration to original condition, obtains a judgment in his or her favor, and that judgment becomes final and conclusive, this alone does not cause the same claim of another creditor filed thereafter to lose its legal interest in protection, and only when recovery of the property or value has been completed on that basis should the other creditor’s claim for creditor’s revocation and restoration to original condition be deemed to lack a legal interest in protection to the extent overlapping therewith (see Supreme Court Decision 99DA6180, rendered July 28, 2000; Supreme Court Decision 2001DA49043, rendered October 12, 2001).\\n\\nThe record contains no material to acknowledge that Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 paid the compensation by value pursuant to the above final and conclusive judgment to the Korea Technology Finance Corporation and that restoration to original condition was thereby effected.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below erred in law affecting the judgment by holding that the Plaintiff’s action against Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 was unlawful for lack of a legal interest in protection merely because the Korea Technology Finance Corporation had obtained and made final and conclusive a judgment in its favor against Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 seeking, on the ground that each of the sales contracts at issue concerning the above real properties constituted fraudulent acts, cancellation of the contracts and performance of compensation by value. In an action for revocation of a fraudulent act, the court below misapprehended the legal principles concerning the legal interest in protection.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the portion of the judgment below dismissing the action against Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for a further trial and determination of this portion, and the judgment is rendered as ordered, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2007DA63102]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to Ground 1 of the appeal\\nIn the exercise of a creditor’s right of revocation, the creditor’s “day of knowledge of the cause for revocation,” which is the starting point of the preclusive period, means the day on which the creditor came to know that the debtor had engaged in a fraudulent act while knowing that he would harm the creditor. It is not enough merely to know that the debtor performed an act of disposition of property; it is also necessary to know the existence of the specific fraudulent act and further to know that the debtor had the intent to defraud (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DA3262, rendered on September 29, 2000). Meanwhile, the burden of proving the lapse of that preclusive period rests on the opposing party in a creditor’s revocation action.\\n\\nIn the court below, the Defendant argued that the Plaintiff knew the cause for revocation of the gift at issue by no later than around March 23, 2000, for the following reasons, and therefore the action at issue, filed on September 16, 2003, was improper due to the lapse of the preclusive period. That is, before bankruptcy, Nara Comprehensive Finance Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Nara Comprehensive Finance”) already knew, from the Financial Structure Improvement Agreement dated February 26, 1998 and from the press conference held by Non-Party 1 on June 15, 1998, that the shares at issue would be gifted to the Defendant; moreover, through the company reorganization proceedings thereafter and through the council of creditor banks led by Hanil Bank, as well as in the process of enforcing the security rights over the real property located in Chungmuro additionally provided by Non-Party 1, it had again confirmed the fact of the gift of the shares at issue.\\n\\nIn response, the court below held that there was no evidence to support a finding that Nara Comprehensive Finance knew, at the time of the above Financial Structure Improvement Agreement, that such agreement had been concluded; further, that the mere fact that such agreement had been concluded or that Non-Party 1 held the above press conference does not allow a finding that a gift agreement concerning the shares at issue had been concluded; that even if Nara Comprehensive Finance had received other collateral from Non-Party 1 besides the shares at issue, it cannot automatically be recognized that Nara Comprehensive Finance thereby came to know that Non-Party 1 had gifted the shares at issue to Hanil Synthetic Fiber; that neither the fact that the investigation report prepared by Korean Credit Information was placed at the court and made available for inspection by interested persons in the company reorganization proceedings concerning Hanil Synthetic Fiber, nor the fact that a reorganization plan concerning Hanil Synthetic Fiber was approved, permits a finding that Nara Comprehensive Finance knew around that time that the gift agreement at issue had been concluded; and that the evidence submitted by the Defendant and the testimony of witness Non-Party 2 at the court below were insufficient to establish the facts alleged by the Defendant, and that there was otherwise no evidence to support such finding.\\n\\nAccording to the facts found by the court below, the gift agreement at issue, which is the subject of the fraudulent conveyance revocation, was concluded on September 22, 1998; therefore, Nara Comprehensive Finance could not have known of the existence of the gift agreement at issue at the time of the Financial Structure Improvement Agreement or the press conference held prior thereto. Also, according to the record, the investigation report prepared by Korean Credit Information in the company reorganization proceedings and the draft reorganization plan prepared by Hanil Synthetic Fiber do not state the specific details of the agreement, such as the parties, date, and subject matter of the gift agreement at issue; accordingly, it cannot be recognized that Nara Comprehensive Finance learned the specific contents of the gift agreement at issue through that investigation report or reorganization plan.\\n\\nThe court below’s judgment to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of law regarding the preclusive period or its method of proof, violation of the rules of evidence, error in fact-finding due to incomplete examination, or violation of the duty to explain, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. With respect to Ground 2 of the appeal\\na. In a fraudulent conveyance, the meaning of the debtor’s legal act harming the creditor is that it causes a reduction in the debtor’s total assets; that is, the debtor’s act of disposing of property reduces those assets, thereby causing insufficiency in the common security for claims or making the common security, already in a state of insufficiency, even more insufficient, so that the creditor can no longer be fully satisfied. Even if a claim is accompanied by personal security such as joint and several suretyship, it is not to be included in the debtor’s active assets.\\n\\nAlso, even if one of the joint and several sureties for a particular claim gifts property to another joint and several surety so that there is no change in the total liable assets of the debtors that a particular creditor may pursue, if the surety who made the gift has seen his assets reduced and, as a result, there has been insufficiency in the common security for the general creditors including that particular creditor, or that insufficiency has become more serious, the fraudulent nature of the gift cannot be denied.\\n\\nMeanwhile, since the requirement of fraudulent intent must be satisfied not only at the time of the act but also at the time when the creditor exercises the right of revocation (that is, at the closing of oral argument in the trial on the merits of the fraudulent conveyance revocation action), even if the act of disposition was harmful to the creditor at the time it was made, if the debtor thereafter recovers solvency or the debt is reduced so that it no longer harms the creditor at the time the right of revocation is exercised, the creditor’s right of revocation is extinguished because there is no need to preserve the responsible assets by means of the creditor’s right of revocation. However, Article 240(2) of the former Corporate Reorganization Act (before repeal by Act No. 7428 on March 1, 2005) provides that “the reorganization plan shall not affect the rights that a reorganization creditor or a reorganization secured creditor has against the company’s guarantor or other person who bears the debt together with the company, or the security provided by a person other than the company for the benefit of the reorganization creditor or reorganization secured creditor.” Therefore, it cannot be said that the debt of a person who jointly and severally guaranteed the company’s obligation is naturally extinguished merely because the company’s reorganization claim has been extinguished.\\n\\nAccordingly, the court below’s rejection of the Defendant’s argument—namely, that since the gift agreement at issue was an agreement between Non-Party 1, a joint and several surety for Nara Comprehensive Finance, and Hanil Synthetic Fiber, it cannot be recognized as fraudulent, or that as all reorganization claims against Hanil Synthetic Fiber were extinguished, Non-Party 1’s joint and several suretyship debt was also wholly extinguished, and the fraudulent nature of the gift agreement at issue therefore disappeared—and its recognition of the fraudulent nature of the gift agreement at issue, is proper in conclusion. There is no illegality in misapprehension of law regarding fraudulent intent as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nb. Fraudulent intent means that, when the debtor performs a legal act, he knows that it harms the creditor. Here, “knows” does not mean intention or desire, but merely recognition is sufficient. Ultimately, fraudulent intent means recognizing the fact that, due to insufficiency of common security, there arises a risk that the creditor will have difficulty receiving payment of the claim; and such recognition need exist only in relation to general creditors, and it is not necessary that there be recognition that a specific creditor is being harmed (see Supreme Court Decision 97DA57320, rendered on May 12, 1998).\\n\\nThe Defendant’s argument that there was no fraudulent intent because Non-Party 1 concluded the gift agreement at issue by donating his property in the sole belief that he would rehabilitate the Hanil Group and thereby promote the interests of all creditors including Nara Comprehensive Finance is based on the premise that fraudulent intent is “intention or desire,” not mere recognition, and is therefore improper in itself. The Supreme Court Decision 2000DA50015, rendered on May 8, 2001, cited by the Defendant, concerns a different matter and is not appropriate for application to this case.\\n\\nAccording to the record, at the time of the gift agreement at issue, Non-Party 1 bore joint and several suretyship debts totaling KRW 1,541.5 billion to several financial institutions and was in excess of liabilities. If so, it is sufficient to recognize that at the time of the gift agreement at issue, Non-Party 1 recognized the fact that, because of insufficiency of common security, there would arise a risk that general creditors would have difficulty receiving payment of their claims. Therefore, the court below’s judgment recognizing Non-Party 1’s fraudulent intent is proper, and there is no illegality in misapprehension of law regarding fraudulent intent as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. With respect to Ground 4 of the appeal\\nAs to the Defendant’s argument that, because of the gift at issue, Nara Comprehensive Finance’s claim could be realized to a greater extent, thereby making it more advantageous to Nara Comprehensive Finance, the gift agreement at issue does not constitute a fraudulent act, the court below determined that it is difficult in fact to regard Nara Comprehensive Finance as having obtained greater benefit from the gift agreement at issue. It may be said that such holding of the court below includes a determination rejecting the argument that Nara Comprehensive Finance’s seeking revocation of the gift agreement at issue, despite having obtained a benefit of KRW 5.5 billion in the company reorganization proceedings of Hanil Synthetic Fiber initiated by the gift agreement at issue, violates the principle of good faith; and even if not, in light of the factual findings and the record as stated by the court below, it is also difficult to regard the Plaintiff’s fraudulent conveyance revocation action at issue as violating the principle of good faith. Therefore, it cannot be said that the judgment below contains an illegality of omitting a determination that affected the result of the judgment.\\n\\n4. With respect to Ground 5 of the appeal\\nAs a rule, restoration following the revocation of a fraudulent act must be effected by return of the property itself, and only exceptionally, where such return is impossible or extremely difficult, may it be effected by return of the value. The term “where return of the property itself is impossible or extremely difficult” does not refer merely to cases where return of the property itself is absolutely or physically impossible, but to cases where, in light of the rules of experience in social life or the concept of transactions, the creditor cannot expect performance to be realized from the beneficiary or subsequent transferee (see Supreme Court Decision 97DA58316, rendered on May 15, 1998). Changes in the value of shares due to changed circumstances are included in the ordinary attributes of shares, and because there is no change in the nature or content of the shares themselves, they cannot serve as a ground for value compensation.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, there is no evidence to support a finding that return of the shares at issue themselves is impossible or extremely difficult, and the court below’s determination is proper that, merely because certain mortgage rights over real property owned by Hanil Resort were canceled after the gift agreement at issue, or because the value of the shares at issue increased due to the passage of time and the like, ordering return of the property itself cannot be deemed to result in an unfair outcome by requiring return of portions not originally included in the responsible assets. There is no illegality in misapprehension of law regarding the method of restoration as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged, by unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2021DA309231]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nIn the exercise of the creditor’s right of revocation, the “day on which the creditor became aware of the cause for revocation,” which is the starting point of the preclusive period, means the day on which the creditor became aware of the requirements for the creditor’s right of revocation, that is, the day on which the creditor became aware that the debtor had committed a fraudulent act while knowing that it would prejudice the creditor. At this time, in order to conclude that the creditor became aware of the cause for revocation, it is not sufficient merely to know that the debtor engaged in an act of disposing of property; the creditor must also know the existence of the specific fraudulent act and, further, the fact that the debtor had the intent to prejudice creditors. The fact that the objective elements of the fraudulent act were known cannot be presumed to mean that the cause for revocation was known, and the burden of proof regarding the lapse of the preclusive period lies with the opposing party in the lawsuit to revoke the fraudulent act (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 2013DA79320 decided on March 27, 2014, 2016DA272311 decided on April 10, 2018, etc.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, where the Plaintiff, a public corporation established under the National Health Insurance Act, exercises the creditor’s right of revocation against the debtor’s legal act by using a claim against the debtor as the preserved claim, with respect to the starting point of the preclusive period, whether the Plaintiff knew of the cause for revocation shall, barring special circumstances, be determined based on the awareness of the employee in charge of the collection and preservation, etc. of the preserved claim; therefore, if the employee in charge recognized not only the fact of the debtor’s act of disposing of property but also the existence of the specific fraudulent act and the fact that the debtor had the intent to prejudice creditors, then the Plaintiff may likewise be deemed to have known of the cause for revocation at that time (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 2015DA247707 decided on June 15, 2017, 2018DA222747 decided on July 20, 2018, etc.).\\n\\n2. The course of the case and the lower court’s determination\\n\\na. According to the reasons stated in the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n1) Non-Party 1 was indicted around July 2016 on charges including violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (fraud), to the effect that “a person who was not a pharmacist conspired to establish and operate a pharmacy and received payment of medical care benefit costs from the Plaintiff by claiming medical care benefit costs as if the pharmacy had been lawfully established,” and in around September 2017 a judgment became final and conclusive that found all of the charges against Non-Party 1 guilty.\\n\\n2) Meanwhile, the Jongno Branch Office of the Plaintiff made a decision to recover the medical care benefit costs against Non-Party 1 around the end of July 2016.\\n\\n3) Around August 2016, Non-Party 1 completed registration of the transfer of ownership, based on a sales contract concluded in April 2016 for the real properties at issue owned by Non-Party 1 (hereinafter referred to as “the sales contract in this case”), in favor of Non-Party 2, who was Non-Party 1’s maternal uncle.\\n\\n4) Among the premium assessment points calculated against Non-Party 1 under the National Health Insurance Act, the points assessed on property were 365 points as of August 2016, but were changed to 22 points as of September 2016. In response to Non-Party 1’s question regarding the reason for the change in points as above, an employee of the Plaintiff in charge of civil complaints replied, “As the real properties at issue were sold and adjustment was made, the date of change in ownership is confirmed as August 19, 2016.” \\n\\n5) In around October 2017, Non-Party 2 sold the real properties at issue to the Defendant, who was Non-Party 2’s younger sister and Non-Party 1’s mother, and completed registration of the transfer of ownership with respect to the real properties at issue in around November 2017.\\n\\nb. The lower court’s determination\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its judgment, the lower court held that, at the latest around September 2016, when the points assessed on Non-Party 1’s property were changed, the Plaintiff knew that Non-Party 1 had concluded the sales contract in this case while knowing that it would prejudice the creditor, namely the Plaintiff, and determined that this action, filed after one year had elapsed from that time, was unlawful because it was filed after the preclusive period for a creditor’s revocation action had expired, and thus dismissed the action in this case.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\na. However, in light of the legal principles discussed above, the lower court’s determination is difficult to accept.\\n\\n1) As stated above, in creditor’s revocation actions brought by the State (Supreme Court Decision 2015DA247707 decided on June 15, 2017) or the Korea Deposit Insurance Corporation, which is a corporation established pursuant to law (Supreme Court Decision 2018DA222747 decided on July 20, 2018), the Supreme Court held that the “day on which the creditor became aware of the cause for revocation,” which is the starting point of the preclusive period, must be determined based on the awareness of the employee in charge of the collection and preservation, etc. of the claim. Nevertheless, the lower court’s view that such precedents cannot apply merely because the Plaintiff is a special public corporation administering national health insurance affairs, on account of the scale and particularity of the State’s civil service organization, is not proper.\\n\\n2) At the time when the premium assessment points changed due to the transfer of ownership of the real properties at issue, which had been owned by Non-Party 1, the Plaintiff likely had, in addition to its main office, regional headquarters and branch offices, and at its main office, regional headquarters, or branch offices, separate departments or employees in charge of the assessment and collection, etc. of insurance premiums under the National Health Insurance Act and separate departments or employees in charge of the assessment and collection, etc. of unjust enrichment amounts or collected amounts.\\n\\nIn such a case, even if the employee in charge of calculating premium assessment points or assessing premiums knew of the fact that Non-Party 1 had concluded the sales contract in this case, it cannot be said that the employee in charge of the collection and preservation, etc. of the claim arising from the decision to recover the medical care benefit costs recognized not only such fact of property disposition but also the existence of the specific fraudulent act and the fact that the debtor had the intent to prejudice creditors.\\n\\n3) In addition, there are no circumstances from which it can be found that an employee of the Plaintiff in charge of the collection and preservation, etc. of the preserved claim had an occasion to examine Non-Party 1’s premium assessment point changes or whether there had been an act of disposing of property, and through such examination became aware of the cause for revocation.\\n\\nb. Accordingly, the lower court should have determined the day on which the Plaintiff became aware of the cause for revocation after examining who was the Plaintiff’s employee in charge of the collection and preservation, etc. of the Plaintiff’s preserved claim, and whether that employee had recognized not only the fact of the debtor’s act of disposing of property but also the existence of the specific fraudulent act and the fact that the debtor had the intent to prejudice creditors. Nevertheless, the lower court, instead, determined that the Plaintiff became aware of the cause for revocation around September 2016 solely for the reasons stated in its judgment, and thus dismissed the action in this case by determining that the action was filed in around November 2018, after the one-year preclusive period had elapsed, and was therefore unlawful. The lower court’s determination contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the starting date of the preclusive period in a lawsuit to revoke a fraudulent act or the intent to prejudice creditors. The ground of appeal pointing out this issue is meritorious.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, without examining the remaining grounds for appeal, the lower court judgment is reversed and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court who participated in the case."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning fraudulent procurement of a judgment is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: Where the Plaintiff falsifies the Defendant's address so that a copy of the complaint and the authenticated copy of the judgment in favor of the Plaintiff are served by service by publication, the Defendant may obtain relief by filing an appeal with restoration of the time limit or an action for retrial after the appeal period has elapsed.
B: Where the Plaintiff falsifies the Defendant's address so that a copy of the complaint and an authenticated copy of a judgment in favor of the Plaintiff rendered without oral argument are sent to that address and received by a third party other than the Defendant, thereby being treated as served, the Defendant may obtain relief by filing an appeal.
C: Compulsory execution based on a fraudulently procured final and conclusive judgment shall be deemed to constitute a tort only in cases where the judgment was rendered in a state in which the parties' fundamental procedural rights were fundamentally infringed or where grounds for retrial exist in the final and conclusive judgment, etc., and where it is manifestly contrary to justice to respect the effect of the final and conclusive judgment, such that it cannot be overlooked.
D: With respect to a creditor who, despite having received repayment of part of a loan, concealed that fact and filed a lawsuit for the entire amount of the loan, obtained a final and conclusive judgment in his favor, and then received the amount of the judgment through compulsory execution, the debtor may seek restitution of unjust enrichment on the ground that the amount corresponding to the partially repaid sum constitutes enrichment without legal cause, without going through retrial proceedings, etc.
E: If compulsory execution based on a fraudulently procured final and conclusive judgment constitutes an abuse of rights, the defendant to that judgment (the execution debtor) may seek exclusion of the execution by means of an action for objection to a claim.

supporting_precedents: {"[2004DA8005]": "We consider the grounds of appeal (a statement of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing a statement of grounds of appeal shall be considered only to the extent that it supplements the grounds of appeal).\\n\\nIf a duplicate of the complaint and a certified copy of the judgment, etc. were served by means of service by public notice, then, unless special circumstances exist, the Defendant is deemed, without negligence, not to have known of the service of the judgment; in such a case, the Defendant falls under the situation where he or she was unable to comply with a non-extendable period for reasons not attributable to him or her, and may file an appeal by way of subsequent completion within 2 weeks after the cause ceased to exist (or within 30 days if, at the time the cause ceased to exist, he or she was abroad). Here, the phrase “after the cause ceased to exist” does not refer merely to the time when the party or litigation representative learned that there had been a judgment, but further refers to the time when the party or litigation representative learned that the judgment had been served by means of service by public notice; and, unless there are other special circumstances, in ordinary cases the party or litigation representative should be deemed to have learned that the judgment had been served by means of service by public notice only when he or she inspected the case record or newly received a certified copy of the judgment (see Supreme Court Decisions rendered on August 22, 1997, 96DA30427, and on September 5, 2000, 2000MEU87, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the record, when the Defendant learned that registration of transfer of ownership had been made in the Plaintiff’s name with respect to each of the forest lands in this case, which had originally been owned by the Defendant, the Defendant filed, on 2001. 10. 10., an action for cancellation against the Plaintiff in Uijeongbu District Court Case No. 2001GADAN52117, alleging that the registration of transfer of ownership in the Plaintiff’s name had been completed without cause by forged documents; the fact that attorney Lee Joong-kwang, who had been the Defendant’s litigation representative, received from the Plaintiff, during the pendency of the said action, a preparatory brief dated 2002. 9. 13. stating that there had been the first-instance judgment in this case, together with copies of the first-instance judgment in this case submitted as evidence attached thereto, an application for permission of service by public notice, replies to factual inquiries, and other documents from which the process leading to service by public notice could be ascertained; the fact that the first-instance judgment in this case states, “Defendant currently whereabouts unknown, last address Seoul (detailed address omitted)”; and the fact that, on the hearing date of 2002. 11. 20. in the said case No. 2001GADAN52117, the Defendant appeared for examination of the party himself/herself and, on the premise that he/she was aware of the first-instance judgment in this case and the documents from which the process leading to service by public notice could be ascertained, made a statement to the effect that such service by public notice was improper, can be ascertained; thus, there is much room to view that the Defendant knew, at least before 2002. 11. 20., that the first-instance judgment in this case had been rendered and that the judgment had been served by means of service by public notice.\\n\\nAlso, according to the record, the Defendant’s address stated in the first-instance judgment in this case was a place where the Defendant had once lived, the forest lands in this case that are the subject of the claim for registration of transfer of ownership in this case are real property owned by the Defendant, and the said address and the real property have nothing to do with the deceased Non-Party 2, who had the same name as the Defendant and whose resident registration number was (resident registration number omitted); in light of this, it is evident that the party to the first-instance judgment in this case is not Non-Party 2, who has the same name, but the Defendant, and even if the
