Looking back at the record, the circumstances under which the joint-name deposit was opened in this case appear to be as follows: the Plaintiff, the aforementioned Non-Party 1, and Non-Party 3 agreed that Non-Party 3 would sell one unit of a row house to the Plaintiff for KRW 17,200,000, and that, in lieu of the Plaintiff paying that amount to Non-Party 3, the Plaintiff would pay it directly to Non-Party 1 as repayment of Non-Party 3’s debt to Non-Party 1; and that Non-Party 1 would cooperate in the cancellation of the notice registration completed in connection with the lawsuit he had filed regarding the said row house, and, as security for that duty of cooperation, would deposit KRW 14,000,000 in joint name with the Plaintiff at a bank, while, with the intent of securing the Plaintiff’s cooperation regarding a demand for return of the jointly deposited amount in the event that he cooperated in the cancellation of the notice registration, the Plaintiff would also deposit KRW 16,000,000 together; and it appears that, pursuant to this agreement, the joint-name deposit in the amount of KRW 30,000,000 at the Defendant Bank was opened in this case (Exhibits A No. 1, A No. 2-1, 2, A No. 3-5, etc.), and if that is so, then the depositor of the KRW 16,000,000 claimed by the Plaintiff in this case should be deemed to be the Plaintiff, but as the Plaintiff merely agreed with Non-Party 1 and the Defendant Bank that the procedure for demanding return of the said deposit would be jointly undertaken by the Plaintiff and Non-Party 1, the suit for return of this deposit cannot be said to be an indispensable joint action.\\n\\nTherefore, the court below, with respect to the interest claim portion of the said deposit, may, after proceeding to the merits, examine whether the requirements concerning the joint return-demand procedure have been satisfied and, if such requirements are lacking, may dismiss that portion of the claim on that ground; however, it cannot dismiss the action itself on the ground that the Plaintiff’s claim on this portion lacks standing as a proper party.\\n\\n5. Meanwhile, according to the record, after the judgment in Seoul Civil District Court case 88GAHAP53642 became final and conclusive, the Plaintiff again instituted this action and, with Non-Party 1 and the Defendant Bank as joint defendants, sought against Non-Party 1 a ruling requiring him, with the Plaintiff, to carry out the deposit-demand procedure regarding the said deposit of KRW 16,000,000, and, against the Defendant Bank, on the premise that the Plaintiff and Non-Party 1 must jointly follow the deposit-demand procedure, supplemented the cause of action by making the above claim against Non-Party 1 together and sought payment of KRW 16,000,000; as a result, it is apparent that in the first instance a judgment in favor of the Plaintiff was rendered against Non-Party 1 and that this part of the judgment has already become final and conclusive. If that is the case, this should properly be viewed as a change in circumstances after the judgment in the prior action became final and conclusive, and therefore the res judicata effect regarding the defect in the litigation requirements finally determined in the prior action does not extend to this action.\\n\\n6. If so, the judgment of the court below contains legal error in misapprehending the legal nature of deposit claims opened in joint name and the doctrine of res judicata, and in failing to conduct a sufficient examination, and the arguments are well founded.\\n\\nAccordingly, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and, pursuant to the proviso of Article 388 of the Civil Procedure Act, the case is remanded to the court below, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as stated in the order."}

{"[96DA23238]": "Before examining the grounds of appeal, this Court examines ex officio.\\n\\nUpon review, since the lawsuit in this case is an action seeking performance of the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of termination of the title trust with respect to real property for which ownership-transfer registration has been made in the joint ownership of the Defendant, the First-Instance Defendants Bang Heon-yong, Bang Hyo-seop, Bang O-bong, and the non-party Bang Hyo-jeong, among five persons, it is an action concerning property held in joint ownership and thus constitutes an indispensable joint suit of a special nature (see Supreme Court Decision 83DAKA850, rendered on October 25, 1983); accordingly, not only must all joint owners be made Defendants, but the matter must be conclusively determined uniformly as to all joint owners, and therefore neither an admission of claim by some of the joint owners nor a withdrawal of the action against some of the joint owners can be permitted.\\n\\nHowever, looking at the course of this case, the Plaintiff filed this action not only against the Defendant, the First-Instance Defendants Bang Heon-yong, Bang Hyo-seop, and Bang O-bong, who are the registered titleholders of the joint ownership registration at issue, but also against the heirs of the non-party Bang Hyo-jeong, who is likewise a registered titleholder; when Bang Heon-yong, Bang Hyo-seop, Bang O-seop, and Bang Jeong-seok, the First-Instance Defendant and one of those heirs, admitted the claim, the Plaintiff withdrew the action against the remaining Defendants among those heirs, and the court of first instance, also overlooking the point that this action is an indispensable joint suit, treated the above admission of claim and withdrawal of action as valid and rendered judgment only against the remaining Defendant, Bang Hyo-beom; the appellate court below likewise adjudicated only the appeal by Defendant Bang Hyo-beom.\\n\\nHowever, where some of the joint owners of real property have died, unless there is a special agreement among the joint owners, the heirs of the deceased joint owner do not succeed to the status of joint owner; rather, this Court’s view is that the relevant real property vests in the joint ownership of the surviving joint owners if there are two or more surviving joint owners, and vests in the sole ownership of the surviving joint owner if there is one surviving joint owner (see Supreme Court Decision 93DA39225, rendered on February 25, 1994). Therefore, even in this case, in which the non-party Bang Hyo-jeong, one of the registered titleholders, has died, the scope of the joint owners who should be made adverse parties in the action would differ depending on whether such a special agreement existed among the registered titleholders; nevertheless, both the court of first instance and the appellate court below overlooked this point and did not examine it at all. Furthermore, they regarded the admission of claim by some of the joint owners and the withdrawal of the action against some of the joint owners as valid and rendered judgment only against the Defendant (provided, however, that if the heirs of the non-party Bang Hyo-jeong are not joint owners, the withdrawal of the action against those heirs is permissible); accordingly, the appellate judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the nature of a suit relating to property held in joint ownership, which is an indispensable joint suit, and furthermore by failing to properly examine the scope of the joint owners.\\n\\nTherefore, the appellate judgment can no longer be maintained, and without the need to examine the grounds of appeal, it is reversed and remanded to the appellate court below for further trial and determination, and the opinion of the participating Justices being in agreement, judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

question: In the lawsuit filed by shareholders A and B against Company A seeking a judgment confirming the nullity of the shareholders’ meeting resolution by which director D was elected at Company A’s shareholders’ meeting, which of the following statements are correct? (In case of dispute, according to case law) (a) If a judgment confirming the nullity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution becomes final and binding, its effect extends to third parties other than the parties, so that third parties also cannot contest it; therefore, as a rule, Company A cannot admit the claim in the above lawsuit. Nevertheless, if such an admission of the claim is made, then, by reason of the effect erga omnes and the demands of legal stability, the effect of the record of admission also extends to third parties. (b) If shareholder C properly intervened as a co-litigant during the pendency of the first instance litigation, the period for appeal by the plaintiffs against the first instance judgment runs individually from the time a certified copy of the judgment is served on A, B, and C, respectively, but the judgment does not become final and binding until the appeal period expires as to all of A, B, and C. (c) If only A appeals from the first instance judgment in which the plaintiffs lost, the finality of the judgment is blocked as against both A and B, the entire case is transferred to the appellate court, and it becomes the scope of adjudication in the appellate trial. (d) In the above lawsuit, the person to represent Company A is the person currently registered as the representative director and performing that duties, and the same applies even if that representative director is a director appointed by the resolution that is the subject of the above action for confirmation of nullity.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2004DA28047]": "1. As to the Plaintiff’s present lawsuit seeking confirmation of the invalidity of the resolution of the Defendant Company’s extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated 1998. 9. 8., it is plainly apparent from the record that, on 2002. 1. 4., a mediation was reached between the Plaintiff, the Defendant Company, and the non-party, who was the representative director and the intervenor in the mediation, and a mediation record was prepared to the following effect: “(1) The Plaintiff, the Defendant, and the intervenor in the mediation confirm that all resolutions of the Defendant Company’s extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated 1998. 9. 8. (agenda items: dismissal and appointment of officers, change of trade name, change of head office location, etc.) are either null and void or nonexistent. (2) The Plaintiff shall lawfully convene and hold a board of directors meeting by 2002. 1. 14. for the purpose of convening the Defendant Company’s extraordinary general meeting of shareholders (the agenda items of which are the same as those of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated 1998. 9. 8.), and shall lawfully convene and hold the said extraordinary general meeting of shareholders by 2002. 1. 31. (3) If the Plaintiff delays the procedures under paragraph (2) above, the Plaintiff shall thereupon step down from the position of representative director and director of the Defendant Company, agree to transfer his position to the non-party, the intervenor in the mediation, and shall no longer raise any objection to the resolutions of the Defendant Company’s extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated 1998. 9. 8. (4) The Plaintiff waives the remainder of his claims. (5) The litigation costs and mediation costs shall be borne by each party.” It is also plainly apparent from the record that, on 2002. 12. 11., the Plaintiff filed an application with the court of first instance for the designation of a hearing date, asserting that the above mediation record was invalid; however, the court of first instance declared the termination of the lawsuit on the ground that, even if a company-related action has ended by mediation between the parties, it cannot be said that such mediation is automatically invalid merely for that reason alone, and further that, even if a hearing date were designated and the matter examined, no ground for invalidity of the above mediation record would otherwise be found to exist.\\n\\n2. The appellate court, based on the evidence it admitted, found the facts stated in its reasoning and then held that, at the time of the mediation in this case, the Plaintiff, the Defendant Company, and the non-party, in the absence of the resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated 1998. 9. 8., intended to newly convene and hold a lawful board of directors meeting and shareholders’ meeting under the responsibility of the Plaintiff, the former representative director whose term had expired, and to accept the resolutions adopted thereat, but, in the event that the convening procedures were not properly carried out, they would no longer dispute the validity of the resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated 1998. 9. 8.; accordingly, it held that the mediation containing such content cannot be concluded to be automatically invalid, and upheld the judgment of the court of first instance, which rejected the Plaintiff’s application for designation of a hearing date and regarded this lawsuit as terminated by the establishment of the mediation in this case.\\n\\n3. However, the appellate court’s above determination is difficult to accept.\\n\\na. If a judgment confirming the nonexistence or invalidity of a resolution of a shareholders’ meeting, or cancelling such a resolution, becomes final and conclusive, its effect extends to third parties other than the parties, so that third parties too cannot challenge it. Therefore, in an action disputing defects in a resolution of a shareholders’ meeting, no acceptance of claim, or settlement or mediation purporting to confirm the nonexistence or invalidity of such resolution, may be made; even if an acceptance of claim or settlement or mediation containing such content were made, the record of acceptance or the settlement/mediation record would be without effect (see Supreme Court Decision 92NU14908 rendered on 1993. 5. 29.), and thus paragraph (1) of the mediation clause in this case, which clearly contains confirmation of the nonexistence or invalidity of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders’ resolution dated 1998. 9. 8., is difficult to recognize as effective.\\n\\nb. The appellate court deemed paragraph (1) of the mediation clause in this case to be merely a means for resolving the dispute between the Plaintiff and the non-party over the validity of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders’ resolution dated 1998. 9. 8. by again lawfully convening and holding a board of directors meeting and a shareholders’ meeting under the Plaintiff’s responsibility, and viewed the essence as lying in the agreement not to further dispute the validity of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders’ resolution dated 1998. 9. 8. if the Plaintiff fails properly to carry out the procedures for convening a new shareholders’ meeting, and on that basis held the mediation in this case to be valid; however, once a mediation is reached to the effect that the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders’ resolution dated 1998. 9. 8. is null and void or nonexistent, the new resolution adopted at the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders that the Plaintiff will convene and hold on that premise is not, as the appellate court stated, merely something that the Plaintiff and the non-party “mutually accept,” with the issue of its validity thereby concluded, but rather its validity or lawfulness may again become an issue in relation to third parties. Therefore, the mediation in this case cannot be deemed valid based solely on the circumstances described by the appellate court.\\n\\nc. Ultimately, the appellate court’s determination above contains an error of law by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the possibility of mediation in litigation contesting the validity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution, and therefore the Plaintiff’s argument to that effect, raised as the first ground of appeal, is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Accordingly, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the appellate court is reversed, and the case is remanded to the appellate court, and judgment is rendered as set forth in the main text."}

{"[2020DA284977]": "1. Ex officio determination on the form of joinder of parties\\n\\nThis action is an action seeking a declaration of the nonexistence or nullity of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, and under the main clause of Article 190 of the Commercial Act, which is applied mutatis mutandis by Article 380 of the Commercial Act, a judgment granting the claim is effective even against third parties. Where such an action is brought jointly by multiple persons, the effect of the judgment in favor of one of the co-litigants extends to the other co-litigants, and therefore the necessity of a uniform determination is recognized among the co-litigants under procedural law. In addition, in light of the exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing provisions concerning company-related litigation under the Commercial Act (Articles 186 and 188 of the Commercial Act), which also presuppose a uniform determination between the parties, and considering the parties’ intentions and litigation economy, this constitutes a mandatory joint litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies.\\n\\nAccording to such legal principles, the lower court judgment, which proceeded on the premise that the action in this case jointly brought by the Plaintiffs constituted mandatory joint litigation, is proper, and there is no error in misapprehending the law concerning the form of joinder of parties.\\n\\n2. Determination on the grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. According to the reasons stated in the lower court judgment, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\nThe Defendant is a stock company established for the purpose of real estate development business, etc., and the Plaintiffs are shareholders of the Defendant.\\n\\nNon-party 1, who is listed in the shareholder register as holding 2,000 shares, obtained permission from the court to convene an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders and held an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders on 2012. 5. 25. At the said meeting, a resolution was adopted to continue the company and restore the Defendant, which had been deemed dissolved, to its pre-dissolution status, and a resolution was adopted to appoint Non-party 2 and others as officers following the expiration of the terms of office and death of the existing officers. At the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders held on 2015. 5. 22., a resolution was adopted to reappoint Non-party 2 and others as officers following the expiration of the terms of office of the existing officers, and at the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders held on 2015. 12. 2., a resolution was adopted to dismiss the existing auditor and appoint a new auditor.\\n\\nB. The Plaintiffs alleged that the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders held on 2012. 5. 25. was convened by Non-party 1 or Non-party 2, who had no authority to convene it, and that there was a defect in that the proxy forms of some shareholders were forged and the quorum for resolution was not met, so the resolutions were nonexistent or void, and that the extraordinary general meeting resolutions held on 2015. 5. 22. and 2015. 12. 2., which were based thereon, were also nonexistent or void.\\n\\nIn response, the lower court determined that the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders held on 2012. 5. 25. was convened by Non-party 1, who, as a shareholder listed in the shareholder register, was entitled to exercise shareholder rights, and therefore it could not be said to have been convened by a person lacking authority to convene. The lower court further determined that Non-party 2 had been duly authorized by some shareholders to exercise voting rights and had participated in the resolutions of the general meeting as their agent, so the quorum for resolution was satisfied. Furthermore, the lower court did not accept the Plaintiffs’ claims regarding the extraordinary general meeting resolutions of 2015. 5. 22. and 2015. 12. 2. premised on the nonexistence or nullity of the above resolutions.\\n\\nC. Reviewing the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in the lower court’s determination, such as failing to conduct the necessary examination of evidence as alleged in the grounds of appeal, violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehending the relevant legal principles such as the authority to convene a general meeting of shareholders, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are to be borne by the losing party, and judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition. In this judgment, apart from the separate opinions of Justices Lee Gi-taek, Park Jeong-hwa, Kim Seon-su, and Lee Heung-gu concerning the form of joinder of parties, the supplementary opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Min Yu-sook, and No Tae-ak on the majority opinion, and the supplementary opinion of Justice Lee Gi-taek on the separate opinion, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous.\\n\\n4. Separate opinion of Justices Lee Gi-taek, Park Jeong-hwa, Kim Seon-su, and Lee Heung-gu concerning the form of joinder of parties\\n\\nA. The main clause of Article 190 of the Commercial Act provides, “A judgment declaring nullity of incorporation or revocation of incorporation shall also be effective against third parties.” Accordingly, in an action for nullity or revocation of incorporation of a company, a judgment granting the claim is effective even against third parties. The above provision is applied mutatis mutandis to various company-related litigation under the Commercial Act, so that in actions for nullity of merger (Article 240), actions for nullity of share exchange (Article 360-14(4)), actions for nullity of share transfer (Article 360-23(4)), actions for revocation of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders (Article 376(2)), actions for confirmation of the nullity or nonexistence of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders (Article 380), actions for revocation or alteration of an improper resolution of the general meeting of shareholders (Article 381(2)), actions for nullity of issuance of new shares (Article 430), actions for nullity of capital reduction (Article 446), etc., judgments granting the claim have erga omnes effect.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that, where multiple persons jointly bring an action in such company-related litigation under the Commercial Act, in which a judgment dismissing the claim is not effective against third parties but a judgment granting the claim is effective against third parties (hereinafter referred to as “company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect”), this constitutes mandatory joint litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies. However, such litigation should be regarded as ordinary joint litigation, which is the principle form of joinder of parties. Since the necessity of a uniform determination, which is a requirement of mandatory joint litigation, cannot be recognized, there is no reason or necessity to apply Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act to strictly unify the litigation materials and litigation progress and thereby restrict the parties’ dispositive rights or rights concerning litigation procedure. Specific reasons are set forth below.\\n\\nB. Before engaging in a full discussion of the issue, I will first examine the current provisions, structure, and relevant legal principles of the Civil Procedure Act concerning ordinary joint litigation, mandatory joint litigation, and the method of trial, and clarify from what perspective the separate opinion discusses the issue.\\n\\n1) Joinder of parties is a form of litigation in which multiple plaintiffs or defendants participate in a single litigation procedure. Article 65 of the Civil Procedure Act provides, with respect to the requirements for joinder of parties, that “Where the right or obligation that is the object of the litigation is common to several persons, or has arisen from the same cause in fact or in law, such persons may become parties as co-litigants. The same shall also apply where the right or obligation that is the object of the litigation is of the same kind and arises from causes of the same kind in fact or in law.” Joinder of parties can be divided into ordinary joint litigation, in which the co-litigants need not prevail or lose together, and mandatory joint litigation, in which they must prevail or lose together.\\n\\n2) Article 66 of the Civil Procedure Act provides, “A litigation act by one of the co-litigants, or the opposing party’s litigation act in relation thereto, and a matter concerning one of the co-litigants shall not affect the other co-litigants.”\\n\\nIn general, the parties, as subjects of rights and obligations, may independently file and conduct litigation. Even where multiple persons become parties jointly, the case is merely one in which matters that may be resolved through separate litigation are consolidated into a single procedure for joint examination, and there is no reason why the independent status and authority each party has when litigating individually should be specially restricted merely because they are in joinder of parties. Therefore, even in joinder of parties, each party conducts litigation at its own responsibility, without assistance or interference from other co-litigants, and is responsible only for its own litigation acts. Article 66 of the Civil Procedure Act provides that, as such, ordinary joint litigation in which the status of each co-litigant is independent is the principle form of joinder of parties.\\n\\n3) Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act provides that a “joinder of parties in which the object of the litigation must be uniformly determined for all co-litigants” is mandatory joint litigation, and it establishes special rules of trial so that the result of adjudication among the co-litigants can be uniformly determined. Paragraph (1) of Article 67 provides, “A litigation act by one of the co-litigants shall be effective only for the benefit of all,” and paragraph (2) provides, “A litigation act by the opposing party against one of the co-litigants shall be effective against all co-litigants.” Under the above provisions, litigation acts by one party that benefit all, such as assertions or submission of evidence for victory, extend to all co-litigants, while unfavorable litigation acts, such as admissions, have no effect unless all parties do them together, thereby unifying the litigation materials for all parties. The effect of dispositional acts concerning the subject matter of litigation, such as waiver of claim, acknowledgment of claim, and judicial settlement, is also limited. Next, paragraph (3) provides, “Where there is a reason to suspend or stay the proceedings against one of the co-litigants, such suspension or stay shall be effective against all.” In addition, separate oral argument for co-litigants is not permitted, a single judgment must be rendered against all co-litigants, and if some co-litigants file an appeal, finality of the judgment is blocked as to all and the entire case is transferred to the appellate instance, so that the litigation proceeds in a unified manner in all respects (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DA44615, 44622, rendered on 2003. 12. 12.; Supreme Court Decision 2008DA50691, rendered on 2010. 4. 29., etc.).\\n\\nWhen Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies in this way, the litigation materials are unified among the co-litigants (common assertions and evidence), and the progress of the litigation (common oral argument, judgment, and instance) is also unified, so that the result of adjudication among the co-litigants is uniformly determined. On the other hand, if even one of the litigation materials or the progress of litigation is not unified, uniform determination of the adjudication result is not guaranteed.\\n\\n4) To summarize the above legal principles, joinder of parties has the following features: ① ordinary joint litigation is the principle; ② only where there is a “necessity of uniform determination” does it become mandatory joint litigation; and ③ in mandatory joint litigation, the special trial rules of Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act are applied to uniformly determine the result of adjudication.\\n\\nThe separate opinion raises the question of whether company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect falls within mandatory joint litigation in which a uniform determination is necessary, under the premise of respecting the existing structure and legal principles concerning the form of joinder of parties, that is, the issue in step ② above. It is not discussing the legislative-theoretical or policy discussion concerning step ①, namely, which form of joinder is preferable, or whether mandatory joint litigation should be recognized even where a uniform determination is not necessary, nor is it discussing step ③, namely, what method of trial is more appropriate for mandatory joint litigation.\\n\\nTherefore, the argument that it is smooth and natural for the parties to prevail or lose together where the right or obligation that is the object of the litigation is common among co-litigants may be a discussion concerning step ①, that is, a discussion that the principle form of joinder of parties should be regarded as mandatory joint litigation, or that the scope of recognition of mandatory joint litigation should be broadened, contrary to the current provisions of the Civil Procedure Act. However, it cannot serve as a valid basis for regarding company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as mandatory joint litigation under the current system and legal principles concerning joinder of parties. Further, discussion concerning the method of trial under Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act is also a discussion concerning step ③, premised on the litigation falling within mandatory joint litigation, and differs from the separate opinion in the level on which the discussion is made. Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act merely provides procedural means for uniformly determining the litigation when a case falls within mandatory joint litigation requiring uniform determination among co-litigants. The argument that Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act should be applied among co-litigants because it is reasonable or desirable is nothing more than reversing the logical order or altering the concept of mandatory joint litigation.\\n\\nC. The principal bases for viewing company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as ordinary joint litigation are as follows.\\n\\n1) The principle form of joinder of parties is ordinary joint litigation in which the status of each co-litigant is independent. Only exceptionally, where substantive law or procedural law requires the object of litigation to be uniformly determined, can it be regarded as mandatory joint litigation.\\n\\n(a) As noted above, under our Civil Procedure Act, ordinary joint litigation in which the status of each co-litigant is independent is the principle form of joinder of parties. This is clear from the structure of the provisions on joinder of parties in the Civil Procedure Act, namely, that Article 66 on the independence of the status of co-litigants comes first and that Article 67 and following are special provisions to Article 66, establishing special trial rules for certain types of joinder of parties (mandatory joint litigation, preliminary and alternative joint litigation), as well as from the fact that ordinary joint litigation is the procedural expression of the principle of private autonomy, the basic principle of civil law that regulates legal relationships under private law according to the free will of individuals and at their own responsibility.\\n\\n(b) If one departs from this principle and deems the case to be mandatory joint litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies, as noted above, various restrictions are imposed on the parties’ independent status and authority concerning the conduct of litigation, such as restrictions on the effect of litigation acts and on the freedom to dispose of the subject matter of litigation. To justify such restrictions, the requirements for mandatory joint litigation prescribed by Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, namely, the case where “the object of the litigation must be uniformly determined for all co-litigants,” must be satisfied.\\n\\nFor this, either the parties must, under substantive law, be unable to exercise alone the power to manage and dispose of property rights, so that joint litigation is compelled and the result of adjudication must also be consistent, or it must be the case that multiple persons can litigate individually but, under procedural law, because the judgment received by one party affects the other parties, if the results of judgments differ among them, their effects conflict or collide, so that there is a need for uniform determination under substantive or procedural law.\\n\\nWhere there is no need for uniform determination under law among co-litigants, and it merely appears logical or practically desirable that they prevail or lose together, this cannot be deemed mandatory joint litigation. The most typical example is where a creditor brings an action against the principal debtor and the guarantor. It may be substantively appropriate and logical to render consistent judgments on whether the debt has been paid as between the principal debtor and the guarantor, but that alone does not make it mandatory joint litigation. The principal debtor who asserted and proved payment may prevail, while the guarantor who did not raise the defense that the principal debtor paid may lose. In the same vein, Supreme Court precedents have held that where uniform determination under law is not required, such as in claims against multiple joint and several obligors or actions seeking cancellation of successive registrations of transfer of ownership, it does not constitute mandatory joint litigation (see Supreme Court Decision 4287MINSANG204, rendered on 1955. 2. 10.; Supreme Court Decision 70DA232, rendered on 1971. 2. 9., etc.).\\n\\n2) In company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, the necessity of uniform determination under substantive law is not recognized. This is because, under the erga omnes effect provisions, the objective of unifying the legal relationship under substantive law can be sufficiently achieved, making other means unnecessary, and because applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act cannot be regarded as an effective and appropriate means for unifying legal relationships under substantive law.\\n\\n(a) As a rule, the res judicata effect of a judgment extends only to the parties and the persons prescribed in Article 218 of the Civil Procedure Act, such as successors after the closing of oral argument. The one-sided erga omnes effect provisions concerning company-related litigation are exceptions to the principle of relativity of res judicata and expand the effect of judgments to third parties in order to uniformly determine corporate legal relationships surrounding the company, such as those involving shareholders, counterparties to transactions, and other interested persons.\\n\\nFor example, even if a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders has a ground for nullity, each shareholder may freely choose whether to file an action for confirmation of nullity of the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, and among them, shareholder A may receive an adverse judgment while shareholder B, who files later, may receive a favorable judgment. In such a case, if the same shareholders’ meeting resolution is null as to shareholder B but valid as to shareholder A and the remaining shareholders who did not file the action or other interested persons, confusion would arise in corporate legal relationships. Therefore, Article 380 of the Commercial Act applies the main clause of Article 190 mutatis mutandis so that the favorable judgment received by shareholder B is recognized as having erga omnes effect, allowing the corporate legal relationship to be handled uniformly.\\n\\nThe one-sided erga omnes effect provisions concerning company-related litigation (the main clause of Article 190 of the Commercial Act and Articles 240, 380, 430, etc. of the Commercial Act, which apply it mutatis mutandis) were established because, as noted above, in company-related litigation, joint litigation is not compelled (hereinafter referred to as “litigation joinder”), so the results of adjudication may not be unified for all. They were enacted in order to uniformly determine the substantive legal relationship surrounding the corporate body. In company-related litigation, if a judgment denying the validity of incorporation of the company, merger, resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, issuance of new shares, etc. is rendered, the substantive legal relationship is uniformly regulated in accordance with such one-sided erga omnes effect provisions.\\n\\n(b) Where, under substantive law, the power to manage and dispose of property rights jointly belongs to multiple persons and cannot be disposed of unilaterally by a party, the result of litigation must also be consistent for all; otherwise, resolution of the dispute becomes impossible. Therefore, litigation joinder is compelled, all persons must necessarily become parties and file a single action, an action in which all persons are not parties is not permitted, and it is dismissed as improper for lack of standing to sue or be sued, and a consistent conclusion must be reached by a single judgment. Such a type of litigation is called “inherent mandatory joint litigation.” Actions for partition of co-owned property, and actions concerning the bankruptcy estate where there are multiple trustees in bankruptcy, are examples (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DA44615, 44622, rendered on 2003. 12. 12.; Supreme Court Decision 2006DA14363, rendered on 2008. 4. 24., etc.). Where litigation joinder is compelled and only a single action is permitted against all parties, applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act and rendering a single uniform judgment may be regarded as an appropriate means for effectively resolving the dispute.\\n\\n(c) By contrast, in company-related litigation, litigation joinder is not compelled, so the parties may each file separate actions or may choose not to file an action. Therefore, even if the results of judgments are made consistent only among co-litigants, the purpose of unifying substantive legal relationships through adjudication cannot be achieved.\\n\\nAs noted above, the action for confirmation of nullity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution will serve as an example. Since litigation joinder is not compelled in an action for confirmation of nullity of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, shareholders A and B may jointly file an action, shareholder C may file a separate action later, and shareholder D may choose not to file an action. Even if, in such a case, A and B’s joint action is treated as mandatory joint litigation and a single uniform judgment is rendered, there is no way to make its result consistent with C’s later separate action, so after A and B lose, C may still prevail. In the case of D, who did not file an action, there is not even a judgment. Thus, even if A and B’s litigation is deemed mandatory joint litigation, there is no way to make the result consistent for those who filed separate actions such as C and those who did not file such as D.\\n\\nIn company-related litigation, uniformity of the substantive legal relationship can be sufficiently achieved by giving the favorable judgment of C erga omnes effect not only against the losing A and B but also against D and others who did not file an action, in accordance with the one-sided erga omnes effect provisions. Other means are unnecessary, and treating A and B’s litigation as mandatory joint litigation cannot be regarded as an effective or appropriate means for unifying the substantive legal relationship.\\n\\n(d) The Civil Procedure Act as amended in 2002 newly introduced preliminary and alternative joinder of parties as a type of joinder and expressly allowed the previously unpermitted one-sided independent intervention action, applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act to all of those procedures by analogy (Articles 70 and 79 of the Civil Procedure Act). These types of litigation primarily concern matters where multiple claims are legally incompatible with one another, and in such cases, because litigation joinder is not compelled and there are no provisions that can unify the substantive legal relationship, the contents of judgments on each claim may conflict with one another under substantive law, and the party could suffer disadvantages such as being unable to exercise a right despite its existence or bearing obligations twice. The purpose of introducing these types of litigation and applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act by analogy was to classify such cases into categories, establish a special procedural system capable of reaching judgments free from substantive legal inconsistency, and allow the parties to use such a procedural system if they so desire.\\n\\nThis has no relation to company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect. In company-related litigation, as noted above, there are one-sided erga omnes effect provisions for the uniform regulation of substantive legal relationships, so regardless of whether the party claims it in separate actions or in joinder of parties, even if the results of the judgments differ, the parties suffer no disadvantage (the legal relationship is regulated according to the favorable judgment), and no separate procedural system or measure is needed to protect the parties’ interests. Therefore, from the purpose of the above amendment to the Civil Procedure Act, no necessity can be derived for applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act to company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect.\\n\\n3) In company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, even if the results of judgments differ among co-litigants, there is no possibility that the effects of the judgments will conflict with one another, and therefore it cannot be said that conflicting or colliding judgments arise; accordingly, there is no procedural need for a uniform determination.\\n\\n(a) Where the effect of a judgment received by one of the parties extends to the other parties, and if the results of judgments among them differ such that the effects of the judgments conflict and the dispute cannot be resolved, there is a need to unify the adjudicative result among the parties. Such litigation must have unified adjudication regardless of whether the parties file separate actions or, by chance, jointly file an action, and if it is a joinder of parties, it constitutes mandatory joint litigation requiring a uniform determination. This type of litigation is called “quasi-mandatory joint litigation.”\\n\\nThe representative example of quasi-mandatory joint litigation is where the effect of a judgment is extended comprehensively to a certain range of interested persons regardless of the outcome of the judgment. For example, in rehabilitation proceedings, a judgment in an action concerning the determination of rehabilitation claims and secured rehabilitation claims is effective against all rehabilitation creditors, secured rehabilitation creditors, shareholders, and equity holders (Article 176(1) of the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act). Where multiple objectors have filed actions objecting to a judicial decision on the determination of claims concerning the same claim, if the court renders a favorable judgment for one and an adverse judgment for another, the effects of the two judgments extend to all rehabilitation creditors, secured rehabilitation creditors, shareholders, and equity holders and thereby conflict with one another. Therefore, if the objectors jointly file such an action, it should be treated as mandatory joint litigation and a single uniform judgment should be rendered, and even if the objectors each file an action separately, the oral arguments must necessarily be consolidated and the matter must proceed as joint litigation (for this purpose, the time for commencement of oral argument is limited until the period during which another action of objection may be filed; see Article 171(4) and (5) of the same Act).\\n\\nThe same applies where multiple litigation administrators file an action. For example, in an action by a creditor exercising subrogation, if the debtor is aware of the fact that the action was filed, the res judicata effect extends to the debtor under Article 218(3) of the Civil Procedure Act (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 74DA1664, rendered on 1975. 5. 13.). Therefore, if multiple creditors each file an action and the debtor is aware of this fact, and different outcomes result, the effects of each judgment extend to the debtor and conflict with each other. To prevent this, if an action by a creditor exercising subrogation is pending, other creditors must intervene in that action and filing a separate action is not permitted as duplicative litigation (see Supreme Court Decision 87DAKA1618, rendered on 1988. 9. 27.; Supreme Court Decision 2013DA30301, 30325, rendered on 2015. 7. 23., etc.). If multiple creditors jointly file an action, or if they become co-litigants through intervention in the litigation, it should be regarded as mandatory joint litigation and a single uniform judgment should be rendered (see Supreme Court Decision 91DA23486, rendered on 1991. 12. 27., etc.).\\n\\nBy contrast, if the parties file separate actions and different judgment results are acceptable, then even if they jointly file the action, it cannot be regarded as mandatory joint litigation. For example, where joint and several creditors A and B each file an action against the debtor, joint and several creditor A may prevail, but joint and several creditor B may lose because payment is found. Therefore, even if A and B jointly file an action, uniform determination is not required, and it constitutes ordinary joint litigation.\\n\\n(b) However, in company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, even if different judgments are rendered among the parties, there is no problem of conflicting or colliding judgments. Unlike types of litigation in which the effect of the judgment extends comprehensively regardless of whether the outcome is favorable or unfavorable, because erga omnes effect is recognized only for a plaintiff’s favorable judgment, the effects of favorable and unfavorable judgments do not conflict with each other.\\n\\nFor example, even if shareholder A files an action for confirmation of nullity of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders and receives an adverse judgment, shareholder B may file the same action and obtain a favorable judgment, and A’s adverse judgment does not impede B’s success. If B prevails, the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders is uniformly treated as null against all interested persons, including the company and shareholders, pursuant to the erga omnes effect, and the same applies to A, who lost. The company cannot assert that the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders is valid only as to A. Thus, even if A, who received an adverse judgment, is also bound by the erga omnes effect of B’s favorable judgment, and the effects of the two judgments as to A appear to conflict, such conflict is resolved pursuant to the one-sided erga omnes effect provisions and no problem arises.\\n\\nEven where shareholders A and B jointly file an action, the problem of conflicting or colliding judgments does not arise. Even if there is an adverse judgment against A and a favorable judgment against B, because B’s favorable judgment has erga omnes effect, the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders becomes null against all interested persons, including A, who lost. Furthermore, because this problem is the same whether the action is filed separately or jointly as noted above, it cannot be said that conflicting or colliding judgments arise only in the case of joinder of parties.\\n\\nNor can separate actions and joinder of parties be treated differently merely because a judgment is rendered separately for A and B in separate actions, while a single judgment is rendered for A and B in joinder of parties. A joint action by A and B is a subjective consolidation of the action between A and the company and the action between B and the company, and a litigation relationship arises separately between each of A and B and the opposing party. Even if a single formal judgment is rendered against A and B, it is no different from a judgment having been rendered separately for each litigation relationship.\\n\\nIn the case of joinder of parties, it cannot be said that A’s unfavorable judgment against him is meaningless merely because A receives the benefit of B’s favorable judgment, which is rendered together in a single judgment. The judgment against A is a valid judgment with formal finality and res judicata that terminates the litigation. That is why the one-sided erga omnes effect provisions were established, in order to resolve conflict between the two judgments and uniformly regulate the substantive legal relationship. The majority opinion, conversely, says that because the one-sided erga omnes effect provisions apply to company-related litigation, an unfavorable judgment cannot be rendered at the same time as a favorable judgment in joinder of parties, but this misunderstands the chronological and logical order. Furthermore, even if A and B are disputing defects in the same resolution of the general meeting of shareholders in joinder of parties and it is logical to reach a consistent conclusion, as noted above in 1), logical consistency alone does not justify recognizing the necessity of uniform determination under law.\\n\\nThus, in company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, the necessity of uniform determination under procedural law among co-litigants cannot be recognized. The majority opinion, which views the necessity of uniform determination as arising only when the parties file separate actions and may receive different judgments, but not when they happen to file jointly, lacks logical consistency.\\n\\n4) If company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect is treated as mandatory joint litigation, not only are the parties’ dispositive powers and rights concerning litigation procedure unduly restricted, but it may also run counter to litigation economy. There is no problem in treating it as ordinary joint litigation, and rather the litigation procedure becomes simpler and litigation economy can be promoted.\\n\\nOf course, this may be one basis, in legislative-theoretical terms, for considering one form rather than the other—ordinary joint litigation or mandatory joint litigation—as the principle form of joinder of parties [this corresponds to step ① in paragraph B.4)], but it is not related to whether a particular type of litigation falls within mandatory joint litigation requiring “a necessity of uniform determination under law.” It is mentioned only additionally to explain that there is no problem in treating this type of litigation as ordinary joint litigation and, indeed, that the litigation relationship may become simpler.\\n\\n(a) As noted above in paragraph B, Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act imposes various restrictions on the parties’ right to conduct litigation in order to unify the litigation materials and the progress of litigation in mandatory joint litigation and thereby render a uniform judgment. I will examine this in more detail.\\n\\nFirst, unfavorable acts such as admissions, waiver of claim, acknowledgment of claim, and settlement are ineffective unless all co-litigants do them together (Article 67(1) of the Civil Procedure Act). Where A and B jointly file an action, even if A makes admissions regarding some factual matters in order to obtain a prompt judgment through examination limited to the issues, the admissions are ineffective unless B agrees. Nor is it permitted for A to end the litigation against A by first waiving his own claim. Meanwhile, because a litigation act by the opposing party against one co-litigant is effective against all regardless of whether it is beneficial or unfavorable (Article 67(2)), if A fails to appear on the hearing date but B does appear, the hearing date may proceed, the opposing party may present new assertions and proof at that hearing date, and all such litigation acts are effective against A even though A was not involved.\\n\\nComplex issues also arise regarding appeals. According to case law, in mandatory joint litigation, if A and B both receive adverse judgments and A does not appeal, intending to accept the judgment, but B appeals, finality of the judgment as to A is blocked, the case is transferred to the appellate instance, and A becomes a “mere party in the appellate instance,” who is neither appellant nor appellee in the appellate proceedings (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA33002, rendered on 1995. 1. 12., etc.). However, it is questionable whether the Civil Procedure Act contemplates a third-party status in the appellate instance who is neither appellant nor appellee. Since there is no provision in the Civil Procedure Act on what degree of litigation authority such a person has in the appellate instance if he is neither appellant nor appellee, whether he may file an incidental appeal, whether he must bear litigation costs, or whether he may appeal from the appellate judgment, etc., Moreover, in the above example, even if A, who received an adverse judgment and has no intention to appeal, seeks to withdraw the action, it is impossible unless the opposing party consents, so it cannot be said that he may be treated as a party in the appellate instance merely because he can withdraw the action.\\n\\nIn this way, a party to mandatory joint litigation is restricted in dispositive powers and is subject to many limitations in conducting litigation. To depart from the principle of ordinary joint litigation and impose such restrictions on the parties’ procedural status, there must be a clear legal basis justifying it. As noted above, in company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, it is difficult to say that there is a substantive or procedural necessity sufficient to justify such restrictions by requiring a uniform determination of judgment among co-litigants.\\n\\n(b) Even if company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect is treated as ordinary joint litigation, there is no problem, and rather the litigation procedure becomes simpler and litigation economy can be promoted.\\n\\nAssuming a case in which shareholders A and B file an action for confirmation of nullity of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, I will explain it by treating it as ordinary joint litigation. Co-litigants A and B may each conduct the litigation and receive judgments accordingly. A and B may each freely perform unfavorable acts such as admissions, withdrawal of the action, waiver of claim, and withdrawal of appeal, and these have effect only as to that party. As a result, if A loses the will to conduct the litigation, A may leave the litigation early by, for example, withdrawing the action alone or waiving the claim with the opposing party’s consent, and only B, who intends to conduct the litigation, remains as a party, thereby lightening the litigation procedure.\\n\\nIf A and B received adverse judgments in the first instance and only B appeals, the adverse part as to A becomes separately final and is not transferred to the appellate instance. B may independently conduct the litigation and obtain a favorable judgment in the appellate instance, and A’s adverse judgment does not impede B’s success. The litigation relationship becomes much simpler without having to rely on unclear and unnatural legal theories such as the “mere party in the appellate instance” discussed above.\\n\\nEven in ordinary joint litigation, oral argument and evidence-taking are conducted at a common hearing date, and judgment is also rendered together. Under the principle of common evidence, evidence submitted separately by co-litigants may serve as material for fact-finding for the other co-litigants even without mutual invocation, and the judge’s state of conviction is also shared. Therefore, even in ordinary joint litigation, unless there are special circumstances such as only one of the co-litigants making an admission, in most cases the court renders a consistent judgment, and the likelihood of an unnatural judgment reaching different conclusions for different parties on the same issue is slim.\\n\\nThus, even if treated as ordinary joint litigation, there are no adverse side effects to worry about; on the contrary, the parties’ dispositive powers can be respected, and practical advantages exist, such as simplification of the litigation procedure and promotion of litigation economy by making only the appellant who intends to conduct the litigation the party in the appellate instance.\\n\\n5) It cannot be said that the provisions on exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing under the Commercial Act presuppose that the consolidated action is mandatory joint litigation.\\n\\nThe Commercial Act provides that company-related litigation falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the district court having jurisdiction over the location of the company’s principal office, and that where multiple company-related litigations concerning the same matter are pending, the court must consolidate and hear them together (see Articles 186 and 188 of the Commercial Act. The above provisions apply mutatis mutandis to all company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect). These provisions may be understood as aiming to have such cases heard together in a single procedural framework, since duplicate hearings by multiple courts on the same matter are not desirable in terms of litigation economy and a company may have difficulty responding simultaneously to multiple actions. As noted above, even in ordinary joint litigation, because of the principles of common hearing and common evidence, the same conclusion is often reached, and to that extent, unification of the result of adjudication may also be promoted.\\n\\nThere is no basis for viewing the above exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing provisions as provisions presupposing a uniform determination of the result of adjudication beyond such purpose. In company-related litigation as well, if a judgment is first rendered in one action due to differences in filing time, etc., the cases may be at different instances and cannot be consolidated, and in such a case, even if the plaintiff loses in the earlier action, a different plaintiff may win in the later action, so a uniform determination of the result of adjudication is not guaranteed. Furthermore, where multiple litigations with overlapping issues and parties are pending, courts often consolidate the hearings in order to reach a consistent conclusion (for example, where actions are separately filed against joint tortfeasors, or where multiple creditors separately file actions to avoid fraudulent conveyances, or where a creditor separately files actions against the principal debtor and the guarantor, etc.), but the fact that cases are consolidated does not make them mandatory joint litigation. Thus, the provisions on exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing cannot serve as grounds for viewing company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as mandatory joint litigation.\\n\\nD. The form of joinder of parties is an important issue that is also related to the status of parties in the appellate instance, and the Supreme Court needs to clarify it to prevent confusion in judicial practice.\\n\\nIn this case, the Plaintiffs jointly appointed litigation counsel and conducted the litigation from the first instance, so the form of joinder of parties does not bring a practical difference in the result of the litigation. However, the form of joinder of parties is, as noted below, an important issue related not only to the method of trial or the result of litigation, but also to “to whom the status of party is recognized in the appellate instance.” Who is a party in the appellate instance and whether a co-litigant who did not appeal becomes a party in the appellate instance are matters arising from the time the appellate procedure begins. If this is not clarified, confusion will arise in the entire process of the appellate instance, and doubts will also arise as to the legality of the judgment rendered through such procedure. Since the issue of parties falls within the requirements for litigation, a judgment that omits a party to the litigation or mistakenly treats a non-party as a party is always unlawful. This means that a party who has the right to participate in the litigation is excluded from the litigation procedure, or an incorrect party is involved in the litigation; it is not merely an incorrect description of the parties in the judgment. Even in final appeal, it is a matter to be examined ex officio regardless of the grounds of appeal, and it cannot be said that the unlawfulness is cured merely because it did not bring a practical difference in the result of the judgment.\\n\\nIt cannot be said that prior Supreme Court decisions and judicial practice have, like the majority opinion, viewed company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as mandatory joint litigation. There is no Supreme Court decision expressly stating such legal principle, and the only statement was made as obiter dictum in the Supreme Court Decision 4291MINHANG231, rendered on 1959. 2. 19., during the operation of the former Civil Procedure Act before the enactment of the Civil Procedure Act in 1960, where it was mentioned that an action for confirmation of nullity of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders brought by multiple persons constituted mandatory joint litigation. Rather, more recent Supreme Court Decisions 2003DA69355, rendered on 2004. 12. 9.; 2005DA54265, rendered on 2006. 7. 13.; and 2015DA27699, rendered on 2015. 8. 13. excluded from the parties in the Supreme Court proceedings those plaintiffs among the joint plaintiffs in the lower court judgment who did not appeal. Not only that, but even in administrative appeal litigation in which a judgment annulling or declaring void an administrative disposition, or declaring illegality of a failure to act, has one-sided erga omnes effect (Article 29(1) and Article 38 of the Administrative Litigation Act), many Supreme Court decisions likewise excluded from the parties in the Supreme Court proceedings those plaintiffs who did not appeal against the lower court judgment (Supreme Court Decision 2010DU13463, rendered on 2012. 8. 23.; Supreme Court Decision 2012DU1006, rendered on 2014. 3. 13.; Supreme Court Decision 2012DU5572, rendered on 2014. 8. 20.; Supreme Court Decision 2018DU54163, rendered on 2018. 11. 29.; Supreme Court Decision 2019DU60486, rendered on 2020. 3. 12.; Supreme Court Decision 2020DU37215, rendered on 2020. 7. 9.; Supreme Court Decision 2020DU49423, rendered on 2020. 12. 24.). Conversely, it is difficult to find any judgment in such types of litigation that recognized plaintiffs who did not appeal as parties in the Supreme Court proceedings. This treated the part concerning the non-appealing party as having become separately final, clearly on the premise of ordinary joint litigation.\\n\\nThe majority opinion merely states that company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect is mandatory joint litigation, without saying whether this had been the Supreme Court’s prior position or whether this judgment changes the existing position. If the above judgments omitted parties in the Supreme Court proceedings even though the Supreme Court had previously regarded such litigation as mandatory joint litigation, then those judgments would have unlawfully excluded parties who were in a position to participate in the litigation, and there would exist a ground for retrial analogous to Article 451(1)3 of the Civil Procedure Act (where there is a defect in the legal representative’s authority, litigation representative’s authority, or the granting of authority necessary for the agent to perform litigation acts; see Supreme Court Decision 95JAENU91, rendered on 1997. 8. 29., etc.). If not, and if the above judgments treated the litigation as mandatory joint litigation but excluded the plaintiffs who did not appeal from the parties, then they created a third type of litigation different from the previously recognized mandatory joint litigation. If, as in the above judgments, the Supreme Court had treated such litigation as ordinary joint litigation and the majority opinion changes the existing position through this judgment, the majority opinion should have made that intention clear.\\n\\nSince judicial practice concerning company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect is not clear in this way, there is a great need, in this case, to clarify what form of joinder of parties it is in order to prevent confusion in judicial practice.\\n\\nE. Under the principles established by the current Civil Procedure Act, joinder of parties relations can be resolved, and there is not a great need to recognize an exception; accordingly, an unnecessary interpretive theory should be avoided.\\n\\nIt cannot be denied that, where the right or obligation that is the object of litigation is common or arises from a common cause, it is logical and natural for co-litigants to prevail or lose together. However, under our Civil Procedure Act, the principle form of joinder of parties is ordinary joint litigation, and, as noted above, unless a uniform determination is required “under law” among co-litigants, the fact that it is logically or practically desirable to prevail or lose together does not make it mandatory joint litigation. To regard such a type of litigation as mandatory joint litigation, there must be a clear logical basis for recognizing an exception to the principle, but it cannot be said that sufficient arguments have previously been made for this, and no basis sufficient to recognize an exception can be found no matter how one examines it.\\n\\nWhere multiple persons are involved in a single legal relationship, if the effect of the judgment received by one person does not extend to the others and the dispute cannot be resolved unless all are parties, that is inherent mandatory joint litigation. Conversely, where the effect of the judgment received by one person extends to the others so that the results of litigation should not differ whether multiple persons each file actions or happen to file jointly, that is quasi-mandatory joint litigation. It is clear that company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect falls under neither category. In such cases, unification of the adjudication result among co-litigants can be sufficiently achieved through common hearings and common evidence in ordinary joint litigation, and there is no reason or necessity sufficient to apply Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act and strictly unify the litigation materials and litigation progress.\\n\\nLegal principles must be consistently applicable regardless of whether the matter is large or small. Even if a principle functions without issue in most cases, it cannot be a correct legal principle if it fails to function properly in some cases. In company-related litigation, even if most cases proceed as a single integrated litigation because co-litigants jointly appoint litigation counsel, etc., if this is not compelled, there may always be cases where a party seeks to conduct the litigation independently. In the former case, the fact that imposing the restrictions of Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act on the parties is not unreasonable cannot make this a justified legal principle. The scene where the legal principle concerning joinder of parties actually makes a difference is the latter case, where a party wishes to conduct the litigation independently, and even in that case, the legal principle concerning joinder of parties must be able to be justified consistently.\\n\\nIt is also not reasonable to treat separate actions differently from joint litigation merely because it is rare for different judgments to be rendered separately in separate actions. Even where the parties each file actions and the cases are mostly consolidated pursuant to the provisions on consolidated hearing, consolidation may be impossible because the actions are at different instances, or because another case was overlooked, separate actions may become finally decided with different contents. In such cases as well, there is no problem, and the substantive legal relationship is governed according to the erga omnes effect of the favorable judgment. One cannot find the view that there is a procedural problem with the later-rendered judgment and that a ground for retrial exists. Yet the majority opinion’s logic that, because of the provisions on consolidated hearing, the result of adjudication must be uniformly determined cannot serve as a valid basis capable of encompassing cases where consolidated hearing is impossible or not carried out.\\n\\nF. Turning to this case.\\n\\nThe action in this case is an action jointly brought by two Plaintiffs seeking confirmation of the nonexistence or nullity of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders. According to the legal principles stated above, this action constitutes ordinary joint litigation.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court appears to have proceeded with the trial on the premise that the action jointly brought by the Plaintiffs was mandatory joint litigation. There is an error in the lower court judgment in that it misapprehended the legal principles concerning the form of joinder of parties. However, as a result of the Plaintiffs jointly appointing litigation counsel and conducting the litigation, it does not appear that such error of the lower court affected the result of the judgment. The determination on the grounds of appeal is the same as in the majority opinion.\\n\\nThus, although I agree with the majority opinion in concluding that there is no ground to reverse the lower court judgment, I set forth my reasons differently and therefore state this as a separate opinion.\\n\\n5. Supplementary opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Min Yu-sook, and No Tae-ak on the majority opinion\\n\\nIn company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, where multiple persons become plaintiffs jointly, judicial practice regards such litigation as mandatory joint litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies. The Supreme Court Decision 4291MINHANG231, rendered on 1959. 2. 19., was a case concerning the former Civil Procedure Act before the enactment of the Civil Procedure Act and stated as obiter dictum that an action for confirmation of nullity of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders brought by multiple persons constitutes mandatory joint litigation. Thereafter, although the form of joinder of parties was not at issue and therefore the legal principles were not expressly articulated, the courts proceeded on the premise that such litigation was mandatory joint litigation. The prevailing academic view is also the same, not only in the field of civil procedure but also in company law. Such judicial practice is based on the necessity of uniform determination under procedural law, and, together with the purpose of the provisions on consolidated hearing under the Commercial Act, its validity can still be recognized even when the parties’ intentions and litigation economy are taken into account. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\nA. Whether a case falls within mandatory joint litigation is a matter for the courts to determine through interpretation, and there is no absolute standard or normative inevitability.\\n\\nArticle 67 of the Civil Procedure Act defines mandatory joint litigation as “joinder of parties in which the object of the litigation must be uniformly determined for all co-litigants” and sets forth special rules of trial. However, because there is no provision specifically determining what cases are ones in which “the object of the litigation must be uniformly determined for all co-litigants,” this must ultimately be determined by the court through interpretation. As also mentioned in the separate opinion, precedents and academic opinion classify mandatory joint litigation into “inherent mandatory joint litigation,” in which the parties cannot independently exercise substantive rights or perform obligations and therefore must conduct the litigation jointly and the result of adjudication must also be uniformly determined, and “quasi-mandatory joint litigation,” in which individual litigation is possible but, once it becomes joint litigation, the result of adjudication must be uniformly determined among the parties; this likewise has been recognized through interpretation of the law, not directly derived from Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act.\\n\\nAmong inherent mandatory joint litigation, there are cases in which the law expressly requires multiple persons to be parties jointly (for instance, where a third party files an action for nullity or revocation of marriage, the spouses must be joined as co-defendants under Article 24(2) of the Family Litigation Act), or cases in which the dispute cannot be resolved unless the parties jointly exercise rights or perform obligations (for instance, the purpose of partition of co-owned property cannot be achieved by a partition action only among some co-owners), in which the necessity of uniform determination among the parties can readily be recognized. There are also many cases where this is unclear, such as actions for performance concerning jointly owned or co-owned property. There is also the view that, in addition to the attribution of the power to manage and dispose as the criterion for recognizing inherent mandatory joint litigation, the scope of recognition of inherent mandatory joint litigation should be broadened by considering the unified resolution of disputes and balancing the interests of the parties. Even within ordinary joint litigation, there are various types, from cases in which the right or obligation that is the object of litigation is common between the parties or there is a substantive-law relationship of interdependence, so that it appears necessary for the co-litigants to prevail or lose together, to cases where the relevance is weak, and there is also the view that the former should be viewed as quasi-mandatory joint litigation to promote uniform determination.\\n\\nThus, there exists a broad spectrum of joinder of parties, from inherent mandatory joint litigation, where the necessity of uniform determination among co-litigants is clearly recognized, to ordinary joint litigation, where it is not. Quasi-mandatory joint litigation, in which joint litigation is not compelled but, once joint litigation arises, there is a procedural necessity for uniform determination, may be said to be positioned nearer to mandatory joint litigation among them.\\n\\nWhere it is unclear whether a certain type of litigation is ordinary joint litigation or mandatory joint litigation, the court must determine the matter by comprehensively considering the nature of the right that is the object of the litigation, the substantive and procedural provisions applicable thereto, whether the litigation may be assessed as closer to mandatory joint litigation or ordinary joint litigation, and the interests of the parties involved and litigation economy. There is no absolute boundary or standard here, and there is no logical necessity or normative requirement that anything not falling within the typical types of mandatory joint litigation must be regarded as ordinary joint litigation. In this respect, it is difficult to agree with the basic premise of the separate opinion that, in litigation for resolving disputes among multiple parties, ordinary joint litigation must necessarily be the principle and mandatory joint litigation an exceptional form departing from this principle. Moreover, even if ordinary joint litigation is the principle form of joinder of parties, the necessity of uniform determination referred to in mandatory joint litigation need not be interpreted in a rigid and narrow manner in every instance.\\n\\nUltimately, the question of in what cases the necessity of uniform determination is recognized, and whether it should be recognized relatively broadly or narrowly, must be left to the interpretation of the courts.\\n\\nB. Company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect recognizes the necessity of uniform determination under procedural law.\\n\\n1) Company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, such as in this case, falls within quasi-mandatory joint litigation requiring uniform determination under procedural law. This is because, where multiple persons jointly file an action, if one loses and the other wins, the effect of the favorable judgment extends also to the losing person, causing procedural-law inconsistency or conflict between the two judgments.\\n\\nFor example, where shareholders A and B jointly file an action for confirmation of nullity of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, if shareholder A loses and shareholder B wins and the judgment becomes final, not only A’s adverse judgment but also the effect of B’s favorable judgment extends to A, so that both judgments with mutually inconsistent contents have effect against A. To prevent such conflict or collision of judgments, it is desirable to treat the action jointly filed by A and B as quasi-mandatory joint litigation requiring uniform determination under procedural law.\\n\\nThe separate opinion states that, pursuant to the erga omnes effect of B’s favorable judgment, the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders becomes uniformly null against all interested persons and the same applies to A, so no conflict or collision of judgments arises. However, this merely means that the company treats the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders as null as to A as well, and it cannot be denied that conflict or collision arises between the two judgments under procedural law.
