The main clause of Article 190 of the Commercial Act, which provides one-sided erga omnes effect, is merely the basis on which the effect of B’s favorable judgment may extend to A, and it is not a procedural-law basis for construing the effect of A’s adverse judgment as having been extinguished.\\n\\n2) Even if, as the separate opinion states, the problem of conflicting or colliding judgments can be resolved pursuant to the one-sided erga omnes effect provisions, if the case is treated as ordinary joint litigation and the outcome may differ for each co-litigant, then the adverse judgment rendered together with the favorable judgment becomes meaningless. In the above joint action by A and B, if A loses and B wins and the judgment becomes final, because the effect of B’s favorable judgment extends to A under the one-sided erga omnes effect provisions, A, despite having lost, ultimately wins as a result, and in the end A’s adverse judgment becomes meaningless. There is no reason for the court, while rendering a single judgment for A and B, to render such a meaningless judgment against A, and it is difficult to find necessity for doing so in joinder of parties.\\n\\nIf A and B each file separate actions and A loses first (even under the consolidated hearing provisions discussed in paragraph C below, there may be cases where consolidation is impossible due to differences in filing time, etc.), B may still prevail because the erga omnes effect is not recognized as to A’s adverse judgment. In such a case, until B’s favorable judgment is rendered, A’s adverse judgment has res judicata preventing the repetition of conflicting claims or arguments, so it cannot be said to be useless, and there is no way for the court hearing A’s action to prevent conflicting or colliding judgments by considering whether B later files suit. However, in the case of joinder of parties, because A and B are jointly adjudicated in a single judgment as above, the court can prevent meaningless judgments by rendering a uniform judgment as to A and B. Thus, cases where a single judgment is rendered through joinder of parties and cases where separate judgments are rendered through individual litigation cannot be treated identically.\\n\\nIn this respect as well, it is reasonable to treat company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as mandatory joint litigation and to unify the results of adjudication.\\n\\nC. Even in light of the purpose of the provisions on exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing under the Commercial Act, it is reasonable to view company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as mandatory joint litigation.\\n\\nIn the example above, shareholders A and B may file separate actions because joint litigation is not compelled. In such a case, even if A loses first, if B prevails in a separate litigation, A will be bound by both the adverse judgment received by him and the favorable judgment received by B. This is because there is no basis for compelling parties to litigate jointly and because erga omnes effect is not recognized as to adverse judgments in order to protect the rights and procedural participation of other shareholders (if only one shareholder received an adverse judgment, and thereafter all shareholders could no longer dispute the validity of the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, the harm could be severe in cases where a person colludes with the company or lacks the ability to conduct litigation and files the action). Even in such a case, it cannot be denied that procedural-law conflict or collision arises between the two judgments affecting A.\\n\\nTo prevent such a result, the Commercial Act provides that company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the district court having jurisdiction over the location of the company’s principal office, and that where multiple actions concerning the same matter are filed, the court must hear them jointly (see Articles 186 and 188 of the Commercial Act. The above provisions apply mutatis mutandis to all company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect). This is intended to have all actions filed in the same court regarding the same matter consolidated and to render a uniform judgment. Ultimately, these provisions of the Commercial Act also presuppose that the result of adjudication in company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect will be uniformly determined, so interpreting such litigation as mandatory joint litigation accords with the legislative purpose of those provisions.\\n\\nThe separate opinion states that if A and B each file separate actions and A can lose while B can win, then to say that uniform determination is necessary only when A and B jointly file the action lacks logical consistency. However, even where A and B each file separate actions, the court generally consolidates A and B’s actions and proceeds as joint litigation pursuant to the consolidated hearing provisions, and cases in which consolidation is impossible because of differences in instance caused by differences in filing time, etc., are exceptional. Therefore, the separate opinion’s criticism by comparison with cases in which A and B receive separate judgments through separate litigation is not appropriate.\\n\\nD. Even if company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect is treated as mandatory joint litigation and the parties’ procedural status is thereby somewhat restricted, it cannot necessarily be said that the parties’ procedural rights are unduly infringed or that it runs counter to litigation economy.\\n\\n1) Company-related litigation in which one-sided erga omnes effect is recognized is litigation challenging the company’s corporate acts, such as resolutions of the general meeting of shareholders, mergers, share exchanges/transfers, or issuance of new shares. Whether shareholders file actions jointly or the actions they separately file are consolidated for hearing, the shareholders who filed actions concerning the same matter share the same interest in the subject matter of litigation with the common purpose of extinguishing the effect of resolutions of the general meeting of shareholders, etc. In judicial practice as well, co-litigants mostly jointly appoint litigation counsel or proceed as a single unit through a selected party on the same purpose and interest, and this case is no different. That is also why it is difficult to find precedents that have considered and decided this type of joint litigation as being within ordinary joint litigation or mandatory joint litigation.\\n\\nIn joinder of parties, the parties unite and cooperate to achieve a common purpose, and they need to restrain other co-litigants’ litigation acts from operating against them legally or factually. If Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies, favorable acts such as appearance on the hearing date and submission of assertions and evidence by one party are effective against all co-litigants, and unfavorable litigation acts are ineffective unless all do them together. This accords with the parties’ will to obtain victory, and even if it somewhat restricts the independent authority of the parties concerning the litigation procedure, it cannot be said to be unreasonable.\\n\\nIn company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, judicial settlement, compromise, and conciliation containing acknowledgment of claim or acceptance of the claim are not possible (see Supreme Court Decision 92NU14908, rendered on 1993. 5. 27.; Supreme Court Decision 2004DA28047, rendered on 2004. 9. 24., etc.). A party who has no intention to prevail, that is, who wishes to waive the claim or not appeal from an adverse judgment, may withdraw the action and leave the litigation (in quasi-mandatory joint litigation, the consent of the other co-litigants is not required for withdrawal of the action; see Supreme Court Decision 2011DU13729, rendered on 2013. 3. 28., etc.). Furthermore, even if only some of the losing plaintiffs appeal and finality of the judgment is blocked as to all plaintiffs and the case is transferred to the appellate instance (it is practically difficult to assume a case where the company, as defendant, does not appeal as to some plaintiffs when the plaintiffs prevail), plaintiffs who do not appeal and have no intention to conduct litigation in the appellate instance will merely have the possibility that the first-instance judgment may be favorably changed depending on the litigation conduct of other co-litigants; they do not bear an obligation to conduct the litigation or bear the litigation costs of the appellate instance, and they may withdraw the action as stated above. Therefore, even if Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act is applied to company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect and the parties’ dispositive powers concerning the subject matter of litigation are somewhat restricted, this cannot be regarded as unreasonable.\\n\\n2) Treating company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as mandatory joint litigation does not run counter to litigation economy. If Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies, the opposing party and the court can examine the litigation in a unified manner by treating all assertions and evidence as either effective against all or ineffective, without distinguishing them by co-litigant, which makes the responsive litigation and the processes of hearing and determination much simpler. Even if the service of documents and similar procedures take more time in order to proceed with litigation involving multiple parties together, the court may appropriately exercise its case-management powers to prevent delay. If one of the co-litigants dies, company-related litigation usually involves a litigation representative, so the litigation does not become suspended (Article 238 of the Civil Procedure Act), and even if not, the court may ex officio issue an order to continue the proceedings and remove the suspended state (Article 244 of the Civil Procedure Act).\\n\\n3) Ultimately, even if company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect is treated as mandatory joint litigation and the parties’ procedural status is somewhat restricted, it cannot be said that the parties’ procedural rights are unduly infringed or that it runs counter to litigation economy.\\n\\nE. There is no need to recognize the necessity of changing the currently established judicial practice.\\n\\n1) The Civil Procedure Act, wholly amended in 2002, newly introduced preliminary and alternative joinder of parties as a type of joinder of parties (Article 70 of the Civil Procedure Act), and broadened the scope of permitted independent intervention by allowing one-sided independent intervention, which had previously not been allowed (Article 79 of the Civil Procedure Act). The recent Supreme Court en banc Decision 2012DA46170, rendered on 2019. 10. 23., taking into account the purpose of this amendment to the Civil Procedure Act, changed the prior precedent that regarded overlapping claims of the plaintiff and intervenor in succession by transfer of rights as ordinary joint litigation and held that Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies. These types of litigation do not compel joint filing among the parties, and the judgment’s effect does not extend between the co-litigants or between the parties to the main action and the intervenor, so they were previously treated as ordinary joint litigation. Nevertheless, where the claims are substantively incompatible, if the results of the litigation differ, the parties may in effect lose their rights or bear obligations twice. Accordingly, Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act came to be applied in order to resolve such disputes once, without contradiction, and to protect the parties’ interests.\\n\\nAs noted above, there are also diverse views regarding the criterion for recognizing inherent mandatory joint litigation, and there is also the view that where, in co-ownership-related litigation or an action for confirmation of ownership against multiple persons, or claims against multiple joint and several debtors, uniform determination among co-litigants is theoretically or logically required, such cases should be treated as quasi-mandatory joint litigation and uniform determination should be promoted. As to in what cases the uniform determination of the result of adjudication should be deemed necessary and Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applied, there is no absolute standard or normative requirement, and it cannot be said that applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act necessarily disadvantages the co-litigants or runs counter to litigation economy. Taking these various aspects into account, judicial practice that has regarded company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as mandatory joint litigation can still be regarded as valid, and there is no need to change it.\\n\\n2) The separate opinion mentions judgments that did not list the plaintiffs who did not appeal as parties to the Supreme Court judgment where only some of the joint plaintiffs in the lower court judgment appealed in company-related litigation, and states that it is clear that the Supreme Court had previously premised such litigation on being ordinary joint litigation. However, all of those cases involved plaintiffs who lost in the lower court and some plaintiffs who appealed and whose appeal was dismissed, and because the form of joinder of parties or who the parties were was not at all at issue, those cases never declared a precedent legal principle on this issue. As mentioned above, it has been the prevailing academic view to regard company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as quasi-mandatory joint litigation, the issue had never previously been raised, and judicial practice has accepted it as established legal principle. It cannot be said, on the basis of those judgments, that the Supreme Court had taken the opposite position in the past or that its position had been unclear. However, I note that in future judicial practice, care should be taken in proceeding with the case so that, where only some of the parties to quasi-mandatory joint litigation appeal, the co-litigants who did not appeal should be treated as parties in the appellate proceedings.\\n\\nFor the reasons stated above, I express this supplementary opinion on the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. The supplementary opinion of Justice Lee Gi-taek on the separate opinion is as follows.\\n\\nAs a related issue, I examine the form of joint trial and the structure of the action for revocation of a trial decision in cases where two or more persons jointly file a petition for an invalidation trial concerning the same patent right under Article 139(1) of the Patent Act.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court Decision 2007HU1510, rendered on 2009. 5. 28., held that, once a trial decision invalidating a patent becomes final, that patent becomes invalid even in relation to third parties, that is, based on the erga omnes effect of a patent invalidation trial decision, if two or more persons jointly file a petition for an invalidation trial concerning the same patent right, this constitutes quasi-mandatory joint trial, and then held that if the patent holder who lost in that trial files an action for revocation of the trial decision against only one of the joint petitioners, finality of the trial decision is also blocked as to the other joint petitioners. However, the above judgment is not proper for the following reasons and needs to be changed in future cases.\\n\\nA. No necessity of uniform determination under law is recognized among joint petitioners for trial.\\n\\nWhere multiple persons each separately file a petition for an invalidation trial concerning the same patent right, the result of the trial may differ depending on the assertions and proof of each petitioner. For example, if A and B each file an invalidation petition concerning the same patent right, A may receive a dismissal trial decision while B may receive an invalidation trial decision. At that time, because erga omnes effect is recognized for B’s invalidation trial decision and the patent becomes invalid against all persons including A (Article 133(3) of the Patent Act), no problem arises from conflicting or colliding invalidation and dismissal trial decisions. Even if the dismissal trial decision becomes final first in one case, another pending trial case that was filed earlier is not barred by Article 163 of the Patent Act in relation to the final dismissal trial decision, so there is no obstacle to rendering an invalidation trial decision in that pending case (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009HU2234, rendered on 2012. 1. 19.). However, if the invalidation trial decision becomes final first, the patent right is retroactively invalidated and the pending invalidation petition of another person is dismissed as improper due to the extinction of the subject matter of the trial.\\n\\nEven where A and B did not each separately file invalidation petitions but jointly filed an invalidation petition (Article 139(1) of the Patent Act), or where their separately filed invalidation petitions were consolidated (Article 160 of the Patent Act), no necessity is recognized, as above, for the trial decision to be uniformly determined between A and B.\\n\\nB. Since patent trials are subject to ex officio examination, the applicability of Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act premised on the adversarial principle is not at issue.\\n\\nAs mentioned in the separate opinion, in civil litigation where the adversarial principle is the rule, each party conducts litigation at its own responsibility, without assistance or interference from other co-litigants, and is responsible only for its own litigation acts. Under this principle, the results of judgments may differ among co-litigants, so Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, in mandatory joint litigation, partially modifies the adversarial principle and the dispositive principle to unify the litigation materials (assertions and evidence) among co-litigants so that the result of adjudication may be uniformly determined.\\n\\nHowever, patent trials are governed not by the adversarial principle but by ex officio examination. In patent trials, the tribunal may examine grounds not requested by the parties (Article 159(1) of the Patent Act), and may take evidence ex officio (Article 157(1) of the Patent Act).\\n\\nSince quasi-mandatory joint litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies is also, basically, a procedure governed by the adversarial principle, the court cannot base its determination on facts not asserted or proved by any co-litigant. However, in patent trials, the examiner is not bound by the parties’ assertions and proof and may examine and determine even facts not asserted by any party. Naturally, no separate measure is needed to unify the litigation materials among joint petitioners.\\n\\nThus, in patent trial proceedings governed by ex officio examination, there is no reason to import the concept of mandatory joint litigation premised on the adversarial principle. The above Supreme Court decision overlooked the fundamental differences between civil litigation and patent trial proceedings, between the adversarial principle and ex officio examination, and the procedural status of Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, namely that it is a provision applying to adversarial proceedings.\\n\\nC. Because patent trials and actions for revocation of patent trial decisions are separate proceedings with no appellate-instance linkage, the legal principles concerning appeals in mandatory joint litigation cannot be applied as they are.\\n\\nThe above Supreme Court decision, after viewing a joint patent invalidation trial brought by two or more persons as quasi-mandatory joint trial, drew the conclusion that if the patent holder files an action for revocation of the invalidation trial decision against only one of the joint petitioners, the finality of the trial decision is also blocked as to the remaining joint petitioner. As already noted in the separate opinion, prior precedents held that where an appeal is filed only by some of the co-litigants in mandatory joint litigation, the judgment as to the remaining co-litigants who did not appeal is also blocked from becoming final and is transferred to the appellate instance, and the co-litigants who did not appeal also become parties in the appellate instance; the above Supreme Court decision appears to have applied this legal principle concerning appeals in mandatory joint litigation to patent trials and actions for revocation of trial decisions.\\n\\nHowever, the above legal principle concerning appeals in mandatory joint litigation presupposes an appellate-instance linkage within the litigation, such as between the first and second instance or between the second instance and the final appeal, and serves the purpose of ensuring that, where an appeal is filed only against some of the co-litigants, all co-litigants retain party status to the end and the result of adjudication is unified for all co-litigants. There is no basis for extending this legal principle to different proceedings, such as where an administrative action is filed after an administrative trial or where an action for administrative appeal is filed after an administrative disposition. Patent trials are administrative trial proceedings, and an action for revocation of a trial decision is an administrative action concerning it. They are separate proceedings with different adjudicative bodies and different procedural laws, and there is no appellate-instance linkage between them, so a person who is not made a defendant in an action for revocation of the trial decision cannot become a party to that action. For example, if A and B jointly file a petition for invalidation trial against C and receive an invalidation trial decision, and C files an action for revocation of the trial decision naming only A as defendant, B cannot become a party to the revocation action. There is no basis for saying that the trial decision as to B is also blocked from becoming final, because no action for revocation of the trial decision has been filed against B, and B is not even a party to the revocation action.\\n\\nIn mandatory joint litigation, even if C appeals only against A among the winning A and B, the effect of the appeal extends to B, blocking finality of the judgment as to B as well and transferring the case to the appellate instance, where B also becomes a party. If the above Supreme Court decision regarded patent trial and actions for revocation of trial decisions as having an appellate-instance linkage and applied the above legal principle as is, then even if C filed an action for revocation of the trial decision only against A, the effect of filing the action should have extended to B as well, and B should have been regarded as a party to the revocation action. In any event, the above Supreme Court decision incorrectly applied the legal principles concerning appeals in mandatory joint litigation.\\n\\nD. According to the above Supreme Court decision, the procedural rights of joint petitioners are unduly infringed.\\n\\nAccording to the above Supreme Court decision, where A and B jointly file an invalidation petition and receive an invalidation trial decision, even if the patent holder files an action against only one of A and B, finality of the trial decision as to the other is also blocked. As a result, the patent holder may file an action only against A, who is less capable of conducting litigation among A and B, exclude B from the litigation procedure, and easily obtain a favorable judgment. B will believe that the invalidation trial decision as to him has become final because the period for filing an action against the trial decision has expired, but as a result of A’s action for revocation of the trial decision, which proceeded without B being included, B’s own trial decision will also be revoked. This not only infringes B’s procedural rights, but also gives the patent holder the opportunity to arbitrarily choose the opposing party in litigation merely because A and B’s invalidation petitions were filed as a joint trial, which is not proper.\\n\\nIf A and B each filed invalidation petitions concerning the same patent right and received an invalidation trial decision, the patent holder should of course file an action for revocation of the trial decision against both A and B. If the patent holder files the action only against A, the trial decision as to B becomes final upon expiration of the filing period, and the patent becomes invalid against all pursuant to the erga omnes effect of the invalidation trial decision; the action against A lacks standing to seek judicial relief and should be dismissed as improper. It cannot be said that this is particularly unfavorable or unreasonable to the patent holder.\\n\\nE. The above discussion is not directly related to the majority opinion or the separate opinion concerning company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect. It is only because the legal principles in the above Supreme Court decision also stem from a misunderstanding of the form of joint trial or Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act that I have pointed it out here as well.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I express this supplementary opinion on the separate opinion."}

{"[82DAKA1810]": "1. We examine ground (1) of the Defendant’s litigation representative’s grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAn action for a declaration of non-existence of a company’s resolution of a general meeting or an action for a declaration of nullity thereof are both the same in that they seek to have it determined that the effect of a legally valid resolution does not presently exist; therefore, even if the Plaintiffs are seeking a declaration of nullity with respect to a resolution of a general meeting that can only be regarded as legally non-existent, it is proper to construe this as an action seeking a declaration of nullity in the sense of a declaration of non-existence.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below acknowledged that the Defendant Company’s extraordinary members’ meeting dated 1981.6.1. in this case was convened and held by Non-party 1, Non-party 2, Non-party 3, Non-party 4, Non-party 5, and Non-party 6, who were not legitimate members of the Defendant limited liability company, without lawful convocation procedures, and that at such meeting a resolution was adopted appointing Non-party 1 as director and representative director, Non-party 2, Non-party 3, Non-party 4, and Non-party 5 as directors, and Non-party 6 as auditor, and thereafter accepted the Plaintiffs’ action seeking a declaration that the above resolution is void.\\n\\nIn my view, the above members’ meeting was not convened by a lawful convener and was merely an assembly held by persons who were not legitimate members, so that it cannot be regarded in law as a members’ meeting of the Defendant Company or as existing resolutions thereof; however, since it is clear that the court below interpreted the present action for a declaration of nullity as having the meaning of an action for a declaration of non-existence and accepted it, this is proper, and the argument that, unless it is brought as an action for a declaration of non-existence, the present action for a declaration of nullity is unlawful and must be dismissed is without merit.\\n\\n2. We examine ground (2) of the same grounds of appeal.\\n\\nIn an action in which a party asserts that a company’s resolution appointing directors is void or non-existent and seeks a declaration of nullity or non-existence of that resolution, the person who is to represent the company is the person who is currently registered as representative director and is performing that office, and even if that representative director was appointed as a director by the resolution that is the subject of the action seeking a declaration of nullity or non-existence, there is no change in the fact that he is the person who can represent the company in that action.\\n\\nIn such a case, there may be a question whether, if the resolution is finally determined to be void or non-existent, the action for declaration of nullity or non-existence regarding the resolution, conducted by the director appointed by that resolution as the company’s representative, is the result of having been conducted by a person lacking representative authority; however, according to Commercial Act Article 380 (which is applied mutatis mutandis to limited liability companies pursuant to Article 578 of the same Act), Article 190 of the same Act is applied to an action seeking a declaration of nullity of a resolution, and Article 190 of the same Act provides that the effect of a judgment declaring incorporation null and void does not affect rights and obligations between the company and its members and third parties arising before the judgment becomes final and conclusive. Accordingly, it is clear that even if a judgment declaring the nullity of the resolution becomes final and conclusive in an action seeking a declaration of nullity of a director-appointment resolution, such judgment has no effect whatsoever on the litigation acts performed by the director appointed by that resolution as the company’s representative before the judgment becomes final and conclusive. In addition, since the provision of Commercial Act Article 380 above is also applied mutatis mutandis to an action for a declaration of non-existence of a resolution (see this Court’s Decision of 1982.9.14. rendered in 80DA2425), in an action for a declaration of non-existence of a director-appointment resolution, the effect of the judgment on the litigation acts of the director appointed by that resolution is the same as in the case of a declaration of nullity.\\n\\nThe view of this Court’s Decision of 1963.4.25. rendered in 62DA836, which held, contrary to the above view, that in an action seeking a declaration of nullity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution appointing directors, a director appointed by that resolution cannot represent the company, is hereby overruled.\\n\\nIf that is so, even if Non-party 1, the representative director who represented the Defendant limited liability company in this action for a declaration of nullity of the resolution, was appointed as a director by the members’ meeting resolution that is the subject of the action for a declaration of nullity and has completed registration thereof, he is, according to the reasoning set forth above, qualified to conduct this action on behalf of the Defendant Company; therefore, this action is lawful, and the argument to the contrary—that this action, in which the representative director appointed by the resolution that is the subject of nullity was representing the Defendant Company, is unlawful—is without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, the costs of appeal are assessed against the losing party, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the order by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices."}

question: Which of the following explanations regarding judicial compromise and mediation is incorrect? (Where there is dispute, according to precedents)
A: Unless there are grounds in the pre-litigation settlement record equivalent to grounds for the inherent nullity of a final and conclusive judgment, even if its contents violate mandatory law, that settlement record cannot be deemed void.
B: Where the settlement record contains a lapse-of-effect clause stating, "This compromise in this case shall be void if the actual owner of the real property involved in this case raises an objection," the effect of the compromise is extinguished when that condition is satisfied.
C: A mediation clause to the effect that "the judgment subject to retrial and the first-instance judgment shall each be reversed" is inherently void.
D: In the mediation procedure for partition of co-owned property at the court before which the action is pending, if the co-owners reach an agreement on partition in kind of the co-owned land and the agreed matters are entered in the record, the co-ownership relationship is extinguished immediately, and the effect arises that new legal relations are created for each co-owner in accordance with that agreement.
E: Where there has been a final and conclusive decision recommending settlement, rendered in a prior action between the same parties, concerning the existence or nonexistence of the legal relationship disputed in the litigation, a party's assertion to the contrary is not admitted.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2002DA44014]": "The Court examines the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. As to Points 1 and 2\\nEven if the subject matter of the prior and subsequent actions is not identical, if the subject matter of the subsequent action is one that is directly opposite to, and contradicts, the legal relationship confirmed in the prior action, then in such a case the res judicata of the judgment in the prior action extends to the subsequent action (see Supreme Court Decision 93DA52488, rendered on March 24, 1995), and because a pre-suit settlement record has the same effect as a final judgment and thus res judicata arises between the parties, unless the pre-suit settlement in this case, under which the Plaintiff agreed to implement, in favor of the Defendant, the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of termination of the trust with respect to each of the lands at issue, has been revoked by means of a quasi-retrial, the Plaintiff’s demand for implementation of the cancellation registration procedure, alleging that the registration of transfer of ownership completed on the basis of that pre-suit settlement is void due to lack of cause, is to deny the right to claim registration of transfer of ownership confirmed by the pre-suit settlement and therefore conflicts with its res judicata.\\n\\nMoreover, a claim for registration of transfer of ownership for the recovery of true registered title is, where a person has already had a registration evidencing ownership in his or her own name or has acquired ownership by operation of law, permitted as a means of recovering the true registered title in lieu of seeking cancellation of the registration against the current registered title holder, and both a claim for registration of transfer of ownership based on recovery of true title permitted in lieu of cancellation registration and a claim for cancellation registration of a void registration are each aimed at recovering the registered title of the true owner, and since both claims have the same legal basis and nature as a claim for removal of interference based on ownership, their substantive purpose is identical; thus, even though the former takes the form of transfer registration and the latter the form of cancellation registration, the subject matter of litigation must be regarded as substantially identical (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 99DA37894, rendered on September 20, 2001). In this case, the Plaintiff’s claim for registration of transfer of ownership for the recovery of true title is a claim made in lieu of a claim for cancellation registration of the registration of transfer of ownership completed on the basis of the pre-suit settlement in this case, and therefore, in substance, the subject matter of litigation is the same as that of the claim for cancellation registration; accordingly, the res judicata of the pre-suit settlement in this case must also be deemed to extend to the claim for registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of recovery of true title.\\n\\nOn the same purport, the lower court’s determination that, with respect to the Plaintiff’s alternative claim seeking implementation of the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of recovery of true title with respect to the lands at issue or implementation of the procedure for cancellation registration of the registration of transfer of ownership based on the conciliation record in this case, unless the pre-suit settlement in this case has been revoked by a quasi-retrial, disputing the validity of the registration of transfer of ownership based thereon is contrary to, and conflicts with, the res judicata of the pre-suit settlement and is therefore impermissible, is proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality such as incomplete deliberation, insufficiency of reasoning, or misapprehension of the legal principles concerning res judicata, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. As to Point 3\\nBecause a pre-suit settlement record has the same effect as a final judgment and thus res judicata arises between the parties, unless there exists a ground for absolute nullity of a final judgment, even if its contents violate mandatory provisions, that is merely a defect in the pre-suit settlement, and setting it aside through quasi-retrial proceedings is a separate matter; therefore, one may not assert that the settlement record is void (see Supreme Court Decisions 86DAKA2275, rendered on October 13, 1987, 99DA67703, rendered on March 10, 2000, etc.), and the ground of appeal asserting that the pre-suit settlement in this case is void as an act contrary to social order, having been effected by active collusion by Non-party 2, who was the representative of the Defendant clan, in the breach of trust by Non-party 1, who was the representative of the Plaintiff clan, cannot be accepted.\\n\\nThe lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality such as insufficiency of reasoning or omission of a determination affecting the result of the judgment, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the appellate costs shall be borne by the Plaintiff, who is the losing party. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

{"[2010DA97846]": "We examine Grounds of Appeal Nos. 1 and 2 together.\\n\\n1. Since the legal relationship that is the subject of conciliation or judicial settlement concerns private interests and thus must be one that the parties may freely dispose of, conciliation or judicial settlement concerning matters that, by their nature, cannot be disposed of by the parties at their discretion cannot be permitted, and even if conciliation or judicial settlement were concluded with respect thereto, it would be without effect and therefore null and void ab initio.\\n\\nMoreover, even where, in the restoration registration procedure for cancellation, there is a third party having an interest in the registration and his consent is required, unless that third party, in relation to the holder of the registration right, is under a substantive law obligation to give such consent, there is no reason for him to comply with the request for consent (see Supreme Court Decisions 78DA2040, decided November 13, 1979, and 2003DA35567, decided February 27, 2004, etc.).\\n\\n2. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, ① the Non-party, who was the owner of the land in this case, had, for the purpose of securing his debt for the price of goods owed to the Plaintiff, completed in favor of the Plaintiff the registration of creation of a mortgage with the Cheongju District Court on July 30, 1993, Receipt No. 21423 (hereinafter referred to as the “registration of creation of the mortgage in this case”); ② the Non-party filed a lawsuit against the Plaintiff seeking cancellation of the registration of creation of the mortgage in this case before the Cheongju District Court, Case No. 2004GADAN12196, on the ground that the statute of limitations on the said debt for the price of goods had expired, and obtained a judgment in his favor on January 13, 2005, and the Plaintiff filed an appeal (Cheongju District Court Case No. 2005NA511) and a final appeal (Supreme Court Case No. 2005DA48567) therefrom, but both were dismissed and the first-instance judgment became final and conclusive as is (hereinafter the said appellate judgment referred to as the “Judgment Subject to Retrial”); ③ the Non-party completed, on March 29, 2006, in favor of the Defendant, with respect to the land in this case, the registration of creation of a mortgage and the registration of creation of a superficies, respectively, and thereafter, on the following day, March 30, 2006, completed the registration of cancellation of the registration of creation of the mortgage in this case based on the above final and conclusive judgment; ④ thereafter, the Plaintiff, on October 27, 2008, filed an action for retrial against the Non-party with respect to the Judgment Subject to Retrial (Cheongju District Court Case No. 2008JAENA12), and in that retrial case, on August 21, 2009, a conciliation (hereinafter referred to as the “conciliation in this case”) was reached stating, “1. The Judgment Subject to Retrial and the first-instance judgment are each revoked. 2. The Non-party waives the claim in this case. 3. The Non-party shall implement the procedure for restoration registration of the registration of creation of mortgage in this case in favor of the Plaintiff. 4. The total litigation costs shall be borne by each party.”; and ⑤ the Plaintiff, contending that, upon the formation of the conciliation in this case, the Judgment Subject to Retrial and the first-instance judgment lost their effect and, accordingly, the cancellation of the registration of creation of the mortgage in this case was void for lack of underlying cause, filed this action against the Defendant seeking consent to the restoration of the above cancellation registration.\\n\\n3. In light of the foregoing facts and the legal principles stated above, the conciliation provision in the conciliation in this case stating that “the Judgment Subject to Retrial and the first-instance judgment are each revoked” concerns a right relationship that is not, as the object of a constitutive judgment of the court, one that the Plaintiff and the Non-party may freely dispose of, and thus must be deemed null and void ab initio; the final and conclusive Judgment Subject to Retrial and first-instance judgment cannot be said to have been revoked by that conciliation provision, which is null and void ab initio; nor do the remaining conciliation provisions cause the effect of those judgments to be extinguished ipso jure; therefore, the registration of cancellation of the registration of creation of the mortgage in this case based on those judgments is not a registration void for lack of underlying cause, and accordingly the Defendant does not bear a substantive law obligation to consent to the restoration of the cancellation of the registration of creation of the mortgage in this case.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, without determining the effect of the Judgment Subject to Retrial and the first-instance judgment, which were the cause of the above cancellation registration, simply held that, in light of the circumstances under which the mortgage right in this case was cancelled and the circumstances under which the conciliation in this case was formed, the mortgage right in this case was unlawfully cancelled, and therefore that the Defendant had a duty to consent to the restoration registration of such cancellation; the judgment of the court below thus erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the effect of the conciliation in this case reached in the retrial procedure and the requirements for the establishment of the duty to consent to restoration registration, thereby affecting the conclusion of the judgment.\\n\\nThe Defendant’s argument pointing this out as a ground for final appeal is well-founded (the Plaintiff may seek a determination on the petition for retrial by filing an application with the retrial court for designation of a date on the ground that the said conciliation provision stating that the Judgment Subject to Retrial and the first-instance judgment are revoked is null and void ab initio, and according to the record, the Plaintiff appears already to have filed such an application with the retrial court on that ground).\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2011DU1917]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. a. Article 268(1) of the Civil Act provides that “A co-owner may demand partition of the co-owned property,” thereby recognizing the freedom of partition of co-owned property. Under Article 269(1) of the Civil Act, partition of co-owned property is, in principle, effected by agreement among the parties, and only when no agreement is reached among the co-owners may a co-owner demand partition of the co-owned property from the court. Therefore, where an agreement on partition has been reached among the co-owners, it is not permissible to maintain an already filed action for partition of co-owned property [see Supreme Court Judgment dated November 14, 1967, 67DA1105; Supreme Court Judgment dated January 12, 1995, 94DA30348, 30355, etc.].\\n\\nSince partition of co-owned property by agreement is effected in an area governed by private autonomy and the principle of freedom of contract, the parties may freely and arbitrarily choose the method of partition by agreement.\\n\\nOn the other hand, in partition of co-owned property by judgment, under Article 269(2) of the Civil Act, the court must partition the co-owned property in kind, and may order an auction of the property only where partition in kind is impossible or where partition in kind would cause a manifest decrease in its value. In addition, an action for partition of co-owned property by judgment, that is, an action for partition of co-owned property, does not result in the court determining the rights and legal relations that have become the subject of dispute between the parties; rather, in lieu of agreement, the court, in its discretion and by a reasonable method, abolishes the existing legal relationship, namely the co-ownership relationship, among the co-owners and creates an appropriate future legal relationship. Therefore, the parties need not specifically identify the method or content of partition when seeking partition of co-owned property; it is sufficient simply to seek partition of the co-owned property. Even if a party seeks partition by specifying in detail the method or content of partition, such specification has only the meaning of a proposal to the court, and the court is not bound thereby [see Supreme Court Judgment dated December 29, 1969, 68DA2425; Supreme Court Judgment dated November 12, 1991, 91DA27228, etc.].\\n\\nb. Conciliation includes the parties’ disposition of the rights and legal relations that are the subject of dispute, and thus conciliation concerning matters over which the parties cannot freely dispose is invalid even if it is formed [see Supreme Court Judgment dated July 26, 2007, 2006MEU2757, 2764, etc.]. On the other hand, conciliation is not limited to the rights or legal relations that are the subject matter of the litigation, and the parties may, if necessary, include other rights or legal relations as the subject of conciliation [see Supreme Court Judgment dated September 29, 2011, 2011DA48902, etc.].\\n\\nc. Where an action for partition of co-owned property is filed and, while the litigation is pending, an agreement on partition of the co-owned property is reached among the parties, the action for partition of co-owned property seeking partition by judgment loses its legal interest; however, since the substantive-law rights and legal relations related to the action for partition of co-owned property, namely the rights and legal relations concerning shares, are freely disposable by the parties, if there is a possibility that an agreement on partition of co-owned property may be reached among the parties while the action is pending, it is, of course, possible for the court seized of the case to issue an order of referral to conciliation and thereby have the parties reach conciliation directly or through a conciliation judge or a conciliation committee, thereby bringing the dispute to an end.\\n\\nHowever, such conciliation does not itself target the subject matter of the action for partition of co-owned property and does not substitute for the court’s determination in that action; in essence, it is no different from partition of co-owned property by agreement among the parties. Accordingly, such conciliation cannot be said to have constitutive effect equivalent to that of partition of co-owned property by judgment, namely, the extinction of the existing co-ownership relationship and the creation of a new ownership relationship immediately upon the finalization of a judgment of partition in kind rendered by the court after considering all circumstances of the case. It must be deemed impermissible, even through conciliation proceedings, to create by agreement between the parties, without going through the court’s adjudicative process, a legal change that the law permits to occur exceptionally through a judgment of partition under certain restrictions.\\n\\nTherefore, even if, in the litigation proceedings or conciliation proceedings for partition of co-owned property, an agreement on partition in kind concerning co-owned land is reached among the co-owners and conciliation is formed by entering the agreed terms into the record, such circumstance alone does not mean that, as in the case of partition of co-owned property by judgment, the co-ownership relationship is extinguished immediately and a new legal relationship is created for each co-owner pursuant to that agreement. Rather, it should be deemed that the parties acquire ownership as a right effective against all only when, after completing the land subdivision procedure in accordance with the agreement among the co-owners, they register the transfer of the other co-owner’s share in the portion to be held separately by each party.\\n\\n2. a. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below and the record, it can be seen that: ① the rice paddy of 1,947 square meters at (Address 1 omitted), Seocho-gu, Seoul (hereinafter referred to as the “land before partition”) was jointly owned by the Plaintiff and 7 others; ② in or around July 2003, the Plaintiff and Nonparties 1 and 2 filed an action for partition of co-owned property against the remaining co-owners concerning the land before partition; ③ on July 6, 2004, the co-owners subdivided the land before partition into a rice paddy of 973 square meters at (Address 1 omitted), Seocho-gu, Seoul (hereinafter referred to as the “First Land”) and a rice paddy of 974 square meters at (Address 2 omitted) (hereinafter referred to as the “Second Land”), and on July 12, 2004, at the conciliation date in the above action for partition of co-owned property, agreed to partition the land before partition into the First Land and the Second Land, with the Plaintiff and Nonparties 1 and 2 co-owning the Second Land and the remaining co-owners co-owning the First Land, and further agreed that the co-owners would each complete the registration procedure for transfer of ownership based on the above partition of co-owned property with respect to their respective portions, and conciliation (hereinafter referred to as the “conciliation in this case”) was formed by the court entering the agreed terms into the record; ④ while the Plaintiff had not completed the registration of transfer of ownership pursuant to the conciliation in this case, on October 12, 2006, a decision to commence compulsory auction was rendered at the request of the Korea Credit Guarantee Fund, a creditor of the Plaintiff, with respect to the Plaintiff’s share in the First Land (hereinafter referred to as the “share in this case”), and the share in this case was sold for KRW 90,000,000 in the compulsory auction proceedings on July 13, 2007; ⑤ the Defendant, on January 7, 2010, issued the disposition in this case imposing and notifying the Plaintiff of capital gains tax in the amount of KRW 5,415,220 for the year 2007 attributable to the transfer of the share in this case.\\n\\nb. The court below held, in response to the Plaintiff’s argument that, because the conciliation in this case was formed, the Plaintiff no longer has any rights in the First Land (which would mean that the above compulsory auction would ultimately have been an unlawful auction proceeding concerning a share owned by another person), that although the conciliation in this case was formed with respect to the land before partition, the owner of the share in this case remains the Plaintiff so long as the Plaintiff has not transferred the share in this case to the remaining co-owners in accordance with the conciliation in this case, and therefore the disposition in this case made by the Defendant on the premise that the share in this case belonged to the Plaintiff is lawful.\\n\\nc. In light of the legal principles and the record discussed above, the court below’s determination is just and persuasive, and there is no illegality, such as a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning conciliation on partition of co-owned property or the effect of the conciliation record, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged. The opinions of the Justices participating in this judgment were unanimous except for the dissenting opinion of Justice Min Il-young.\\n\\n4. The dissenting opinion of Justice Min Il-young is as follows.\\n\\na. Before presenting the dissenting opinion, it is first necessary to organize the issues. In short, even conciliation concerning partition of co-owned property may take various forms. First, one can think of a method exactly identical to a judgment ordering partition in kind, namely, a method of “dividing part of the co-owned real property into the ownership of one party and part into the ownership of another party.” Next, one can think of a method of dividing as above, but separately fixing the time when the effect of partition of co-owned property takes place, for example by making the effect conditional upon reciprocal performance such as registration and payment of an equalization payment between the parties in order to adjust their interests, etc. (the so-called mixed form of pure partition in kind and price compensation). If conciliation is formed in the latter method, it should be followed accordingly, and the dissenting opinion does not differ from the majority opinion even in such a case. The problem is the former case. The majority opinion considers that even in such a case, the effect of a change in real rights arises only when subdivision and registration are effected as agreed between the parties, and I cannot agree with such a view. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\nb. An action for partition of co-owned property is a so-called formal formative action, and unlike ordinary formative actions, conciliation may be formed in its conciliation proceedings, and a formative judgment ordering partition in kind constitutes a “judgment” as provided in Article 187 of the Civil Act.\\n\\nArticle 28 of the Civil Conciliation Act provides that “conciliation is formed by entering the matters agreed upon between the parties into the record,” Article 29 of the same Act provides that “conciliation has the same effect as judicial settlement,” and Article 220 of the Civil Procedure Act provides that “when settlement, waiver of claim, or admission is entered in the trial record or preparatory hearing record, such record has the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment.” Accordingly, in the conciliation proceedings concerning partition of co-owned property, where conciliation is formed in the form of partition in kind, it is a logically natural interpretation to regard the conciliation record as having the same effect as the above formative judgment and as constituting a “judgment” as provided in Article 187 of the Civil Act.\\n\\nc. Article 186 of the Civil Act provides that “with respect to a legal act concerning real property, the creation, transfer, or extinction of a real right shall take effect only upon registration.” Under the majority opinion, conciliation concerning partition of co-owned property is merely an agreement among the co-owners, and such agreement ultimately constitutes a “legal act” as provided in Article 186 of the Civil Act.\\n\\nWhen the provisions of Article 28 and Article 29 of the Civil Conciliation Act and Article 220 of the Civil Procedure Act are considered together, judicial settlement and conciliation do not differ in legal effect. However, the Supreme Court, with respect to judicial settlement, until around 1961 regarded its legal nature as simultaneously a private-law agreement and an agreement under procedural law, and held that even if the settlement terms are entered in the record and thus have the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment under procedural law, if there is a ground for invalidity or rescission under private law, then unlike a final and conclusive judgment, the procedural effect is also void ab initio or loses its effect, and in such a case a hearing and determination could be sought by an application for designation of a date in the civil case that had ended upon settlement, and an action for performance based on confirmation of invalidity or invalidity or lapse could also be filed separately [see Supreme Court Judgment dated September 15, 1955, 4288MINSANG229; Supreme Court Judgment dated December 26, 1957, 4290MINSANG638]. Thereafter, as Article 431 of the Civil Procedure Act (currently Article 461) was amended by Act No. 706 on September 1, 1961, making quasi-retrial available with respect to a settlement record as well, the Supreme Court, in its en banc judgment dated February 15, 1962, 4294MINSANG914, changed the above Supreme Court Judgment 4288MINSANG229 and Supreme Court Judgment 4290MINSANG638 and held that no argument contrary to the purport of the settlement may be made unless the settlement is rescinded or modified by quasi-retrial; since then, it has made clear that judicial settlement is a pure procedural act and, unlike private-law settlement, cannot be rescinded on the ground of fraud or mistake, thereby clarifying that its legal nature is a procedural act [see Supreme Court Judgment dated May 31, 1962, 4293MINJAE6; Supreme Court Judgment dated May 15, 1979, 78DA1094, etc.]. Furthermore, conciliation too is explained to have the legal nature of a procedural act for the same reason as judicial settlement [see Supreme Court Judgment dated February 17, 2005, 2004DA55087, etc.].\\n\\nIn general, a judgment of performance or declaratory judgment in an action for performance or action for declaration, where the existence or non-existence of a duty of performance is at issue, does not constitute a “judgment” as provided in Article 187 of the Civil Act [see Supreme Court Judgment dated March 23, 1971, 71DA234, etc.], and it is the established precedent of the Supreme Court that, even when conciliation or judicial settlement is formed with such content, Article 186 of the Civil Act rather than Article 187 of the Civil Act must likewise be applied [see Supreme Court Judgment dated September 8, 1964, 64DA165; Supreme Court Order dated October 8, 1969, 69GEU15; Supreme Court Judgment dated March 13, 2001, 99DA56345, etc.]. By contrast, a formative judgment ordering partition in kind in an action for partition of co-owned property, which is a formal formative action, constitutes a “judgment” as provided in Article 187 of the Civil Act; where conciliation is formed with the same content of partition in kind, such conciliation is merely a procedural act, not a private-law legal act among the co-owners. Therefore, such procedural act cannot be interpreted as a “legal act” as provided in Article 186 of the Civil Act.\\n\\nd. The majority opinion states that because conciliation that brings about a change in legal relations solely by agreement among the parties without going through the court’s adjudicative process in a case concerning partition of co-owned property cannot be permitted, even if conciliation is formed in that regard, the effect of a change in real rights arises only upon registration. However, I cannot readily agree with such reasoning.\\n\\nUnder Articles 30 and 32 of the Civil Conciliation Act, a “decision in lieu of conciliation” made by a judge in charge of conciliation has, when the parties do not file an objection to it or when any filed objection is withdrawn or dismissed and the decision becomes final and conclusive, the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment, just like a judicial settlement record (Article 34(4) of the same Act; Article 220 of the Civil Procedure Act). The essential nature of such a “decision in lieu of conciliation” is that it is, in the final analysis, a judgment rendered ex officio by the judge in charge of conciliation, considering all circumstances, in cases where no agreement has been reached between the parties or the content of the reached agreement is not appropriate. In this respect, when the parties do not file an objection to it or the objection is withdrawn or dismissed and the decision becomes final and conclusive, the decision has the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment. Thus, it takes the same structure as a partition judgment rendered by the judge in charge of a co-owned property partition case after considering all circumstances, whereupon if the parties do not appeal or the appeal is withdrawn or dismissed and the judgment becomes final and conclusive, it operates as a final and conclusive judgment. Therefore, according to the logic of the majority opinion, a decision in lieu of conciliation, since it is not an agreement between the parties but has gone through the court’s adjudicative process, should, once final and conclusive, be recognized as having the effect of a change in real rights without registration, just like a partition judgment concerning co-owned property.\\n\\nHowever, the majority opinion considers that even when a decision in lieu of conciliation that effects partition in kind becomes final and conclusive, the effect of a change in real rights arises only when registration is completed under Article 186 of the Civil Act. Yet, this ultimately treats the two differently even though, as noted above, the essential nature of a decision in lieu of conciliation is that it is a judgment that has gone through the court’s adjudicative process and takes the same structure as a partition judgment concerning co-owned property, and I find it difficult to discover any rational basis for such differential treatment.\\n\\nIn short, such a decision in lieu of conciliation is a judgment that has gone through the court’s adjudicative process and constitutes a “judgment” as provided in Article 187 of the Civil Act; when it becomes final and conclusive, it should be understood that the effect of acquisition of a real right arises without registration. Furthermore, in view of the legislative purpose of the conciliation system, which seeks to equate the two by allowing a “decision in lieu of conciliation” to “stand in lieu of conciliation,” and in view of the fact that when a decision in lieu of conciliation becomes final and conclusive or when conciliation is formed, both have the effect of judicial settlement, it should likewise be deemed that a conciliation formed to partition in kind and the conciliation record embodying it constitute a “judgment” as provided in Article 187 of the Civil Act.\\n\\ne. The majority opinion states that, although an action for partition of co-owned property has been filed at first, if there is a possibility that an agreement on partition of co-owned property may be reached between the parties during the continuation of the litigation, the court seized of the case may issue an order of referral to conciliation and thereby have conciliation formed between the parties in the conciliation proceedings, and that such conciliation is not directed at the subject matter of the action for partition of co-owned property itself, so its effect is not essentially different from partition of co-owned property by agreement.\\n\\nWhere an agreement on partition has been reached among the co-owners, filing an action seeking registration of transfer of ownership concerning the divided portion or seeking confirmation of ownership is a separate matter, but the previously filed action for partition of co-owned property loses its legal interest and becomes improper [see Supreme Court Judgment dated January 12, 1995, 94DA30348, 30355, etc.]. Accordingly, if, during the pendency of an action for partition of co-owned property, an agreement on partition has been reached, it is of course possible to change the subject matter of litigation of the formally formative action that has thus become improper into an action for performance or an action for declaration concerning the divided portion determined in the agreement, and to conciliate the changed subject matter of litigation. However, such conciliation is now conciliation in an action for performance or an action for declaration, and is no longer conciliation in a formal formative action.\\n\\nHowever, even if, during the pendency of an action for partition of co-owned property, which is a formal formative action, an agreement on partition has been reached, or the case has been referred to conciliation in a state where such agreement may be reached, it cannot immediately be concluded from that circumstance alone that the subject matter of litigation in that action has been changed into the subject matter of litigation of an action for performance or an action for declaration. This is because, in order to change the subject matter of litigation, as a rule the procedure for amendment of claim by written submission must be followed pursuant to Article 262 of the Civil Procedure Act. Therefore, if a case is referred to conciliation in an action for partition of co-owned property without the subject matter of litigation being changed into an action for performance, etc., and conciliation is formed as it stands, it cannot be said that the subject matter of litigation in the conciliation and the subject matter of litigation in the action for partition of co-owned property are different from one another. Moreover, if the conciliation terms take exactly the same form as a partition judgment concerning co-owned property, it is even more difficult to recognize a difference in the subject matter of litigation.\\n\\nf. I think the majority opinion may also have considered that, if acquisition of a real right under Article 187 of the Civil Act is recognized even though registration has not been completed according to the content of the conciliation after conciliation on partition of co-owned property has been formed, this could harm transactional security under our legal system, which does not recognize the public faith of registration. However, this problem also arises in the case of a partition judgment concerning co-owned property. Therefore, if one seeks to prioritize transactional security, the fundamental measure would be not to deny the effect of a change in real rights by conciliation, but rather to deny the effect of a change in real rights by a partition judgment concerning co-owned property.\\n\\ng. In conclusion, if, in an action for partition of co-owned property, conciliation is formed in the form of partition in kind, assigning specific portions of co-owned real property to the respective co-owners, the conciliation record has the same effect as a partition judgment concerning co-owned property and constitutes a “judgment” as provided in Article 187 of the Civil Act, so the effect of a change in real rights should be understood to arise when the conciliation is formed.\\n\\nHowever, looking at the conciliation terms in this case, while they divide specific portions of the co-owned real property subject to conciliation into the respective ownership of the Plaintiff and others, they further add a clause requiring subdivision and registration of transfer of ownership for the portions thereby owned; such subdivision and registration clauses are merely superfluous recitations that merely emphasize prudent voluntary performance between the parties, because even without them the parties would of course be required to carry out such procedures. They cannot be viewed as specifying the timing of the effect of the change in real rights. In that respect, they are different in nature from the clause requiring reciprocal performance of registration of transfer and payment of equalization money, as set forth at the outset of the dissenting opinion.\\n\\nThe court below held otherwise, and this is a misjudgment caused by a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning conciliation on partition of co-owned property or the effect of the conciliation record. Therefore, the Plaintiff’s appeal, which points out this error, should be granted.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state that I cannot concur with the majority opinion."}

{"[2012DA29557]": "We decide on the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Grounds of appeal concerning the claim relating to deposit money\\n\\nA. Where a debt has no fixed due date, the debtor bears liability for delay from the day after receiving a demand for performance (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on 1988. 11. 8., 88DA3253), whereas, on the other hand, where a nominative claim has been assigned, the assignee cannot assert the claim against the debtor until the requirements for assertion against the debtor are satisfied. Accordingly, if the assignee of a claim with no fixed due date files an action against the debtor seeking performance, and during the pendency of that action notice of assignment is given to the debtor, then, absent special circumstances, the debtor bears liability for delay from the day after such notice of assignment is delivered.\\n\\nIn the same purport, the court below’s order for payment of delay damages from the day after the notice of assignment of the deposit claim, as stated in item ① of the lower judgment, was proper, and there is no error such as misapprehension of law regarding the nature of the deposit claim, violation of the rules of evidence, or incomplete trial, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nB. The Defendant argues as a ground of appeal that the settlement recommendation decision rendered on 2009. 9. 7. and stated in the lower judgment was intended to completely and finally terminate the dispute between the Plaintiff and the Defendant, and therefore the Plaintiff’s claim regarding the above deposit claim is contrary to the purport of the final and conclusive settlement recommendation decision. However, the claim in this case is based not on the assignment dated 2008. 10. 9., which was confirmed invalid in the above settlement recommendation decision, but on the assignment dated 2009. 10. 12., and thus the argument of this ground of appeal cannot be accepted. The remaining grounds of appeal merely dispute the selection and weighing of evidence and the fact-finding, which are within the exclusive province of the court below, and therefore cannot constitute lawful grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Grounds of appeal concerning the claim relating to expropriation compensation\\n\\nA. If no objection is filed within the prescribed period to a decision recommending settlement, that decision has the same effect as a judicial settlement (Civil Procedure Act Article 231). A judicial settlement has the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment and has constitutive effect; accordingly, once a settlement is reached, the rights and obligations relationship based on the prior legal relationship is extinguished, and at the same time a new legal relationship in accordance with the judicial settlement is validly formed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2008. 2. 1., 2005DA42880). If there is a final and conclusive decision recommending settlement in a prior action between the same parties concerning the existence or nonexistence of a right or legal relationship being disputed in litigation, the parties may not assert a position contrary thereto, and the court may not render a determination conflicting therewith. On the other hand, unless the plaintiff, when filing an action seeking performance of part of a divisible claim, expressly states that the remainder is reserved and only the balance is claimed, the res judicata of a final and conclusive judgment or judicial settlement regarding that partial claim extends to the remaining balance claim as well (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2008. 12. 24., 2008DA6083, 6090).\\n\\nB. According to the reasons of the lower judgment and the record, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n\\n1) When Non-party 2 made a will on 2001. 10. 16., bequeathing his own 1/2 share in the real property at issue to the Defendant and Non-party 1, who were the remaining children excluding the Plaintiff, each in equal 1/2 shares, and then died, the Defendant and Non-party 1 completed ownership transfer registrations, based on the bequest, for each 1/4 share in the real property at issue, pursuant to that will.\\n\\n2) In the prior suit filed by the Plaintiff against the Defendant, the Plaintiff, as a principal claim, sought performance of the procedure for ownership transfer registration based on inheritance recovery with respect to a 1/12 share of the real property at issue, on the ground of inheritance recovery following the invalidity of the will in this case, while, in the alternative, the Plaintiff sought performance of the procedure for ownership transfer registration based on return of the legally reserved portion with respect to a 1/24 share of the real property at issue. During the pendency of the appeal to the Supreme Court in the prior suit, the real property at issue was expropriated by Bucheon City, and Non-party 1 and the Defendant received a total of KRW 673,322,000 as expropriation compensation.\\n\\nAccordingly, separately from the prior suit, the Plaintiff filed an action against the Defendant seeking payment of the amount corresponding to the Plaintiff’s legally reserved portion out of the expropriation compensation received by the Defendant. On 2008. 2. 14., the court rendered a judgment to the effect that “the Defendant shall pay to the Plaintiff KRW 56,110,166 and amounts calculated thereon at the respective rates of 5% per annum from 2005. 12. 2. to 2008. 1. 3., and 20% per annum from the following day until the day of full payment,” and once that judgment became final and conclusive, the Plaintiff, using that judgment as a title of execution, applied for compulsory execution against other real property owned by the Defendant and received distribution in the auction proceedings.\\n\\n3) After remand in the prior suit, in Case Nos. 2008NA33087 and 2008NA33094 (consolidated) before the Seoul High Court, the Plaintiff changed the claim from a claim for ownership transfer registration to a claim for monetary payment as a substitute claim arising from expropriation, and, as a principal claim, sought payment of KRW 243,389,340, corresponding to the Plaintiff’s inheritance share, and delay damages thereon, on the premise that the Defendant had no inheritance right; and, in the alternative, sought payment of a total of KRW 168,330,498, consisting of the amount corresponding to the Plaintiff’s inheritance share and the amount assigned from Non-party 1, and delay damages thereon, on the premise that the will in this case was invalid.\\n\\nDuring the pendency of that action, a decision recommending settlement in this case became final and conclusive, fully terminating all procedural legal relationships, with the following terms between the Plaintiff and the Defendant: “① The will in this case has no effect, and it is acknowledged that the Plaintiff and the Defendant are equal heirs of Non-party 2. ② The Defendant shall pay KRW 50,000,000 to the Plaintiff (the amount remaining after deducting from the amount that the Defendant appears to have paid on behalf of the Plaintiff, from among the amount other than the legally reserved portion out of the inherited share the Defendant would return to the Plaintiff if the will in this case were invalid, certain portions of capital gains tax and resident tax) by 2009. 10. 30.; provided that, if the Defendant fails to pay said amount by the above due date, the Defendant shall additionally pay delay damages calculated on the unpaid amount at the rate of 20% per annum from the day following the above due date until the day of full payment,” and so forth.\\n\\n4) In this action, the Plaintiff seeks, on the premise that the Plaintiff inherited a 1/3 share of the real property at issue due to the invalidity of the above will, payment of the unpaid amount remaining after deducting from the amount corresponding to the Plaintiff’s inheritance share out of the compensation received by the Defendant the amounts received by the Plaintiff pursuant to the settlement recommendation decision and the amounts distributed in the above auction proceedings (claim ⑤ stated in the lower judgment), as well as payment of statutory interest under Article 748(2) of the Civil Act on the Plaintiff’s above unpaid amount and the respective amounts received (claims ⑥ through ⑧ stated in the lower judgment), together with delay damages thereon.\\n\\nC. Examining the foregoing factual relationship in light of the legal principles stated above, the monetary claim sought by the Plaintiff by changing the claim in the prior suit and the respective claims relating to expropriation compensation sought in this action, as well as the claim for delay damages thereon, are claims with the same subject matter of litigation, and, by the constitutive effect of the settlement recommendation decision in this case, the prior legal relationship concerning the portion corresponding to the Plaintiff’s inheritance share out of the expropriation compensation for the real property at issue, which is inherited property, is extinguished and a new legal relationship according to the settlement recommendation decision is formed. Therefore, absent special circumstances such as the express indication in the “Indication of Claim” section of the settlement recommendation decision in this case that a part of the Plaintiff’s monetary claim, which is a divisible claim, is reserved, the Plaintiff may not assert a position contrary to the final and conclusive settlement recommendation decision in this case with respect to the legal relationship concerning the portion corresponding to the Plaintiff’s inheritance share out of the above expropriation compensation.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Plaintiff’s respective claims in this part relating to expropriation compensation conflict with the res judicata of the final and conclusive settlement recommendation decision in this case and therefore should have been dismissed without further examination on the merits.
