Nevertheless, the court below granted the Plaintiff’s claims in this part. Accordingly, this lower judgment contains an error that affected the conclusion of the judgment by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the res judicata of a final and conclusive decision recommending settlement, and the argument in the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the Defendant’s remaining grounds of appeal concerning the claims relating to expropriation compensation, the portion of the lower judgment against the Defendant concerning each claim relating to expropriation compensation and the delay damages thereon is reversed. Since the case as to this portion is sufficiently ready for direct adjudication by the Supreme Court, the Court will itself render judgment; accordingly, the first-instance judgment concerning this portion is vacated and the Plaintiff’s corresponding claims are dismissed, the Defendant’s remaining appeal is dismissed, and the total costs of litigation are divided into two, with one half to be borne by the Plaintiff and the remainder by the Defendant, and the judgment is rendered unanimously by the Justices involved as stated in the disposition."}

{"[92DA56056]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (the grounds stated in the supplemental appellate brief submitted after the expiration of the period shall be considered only within the scope of supplementing them).\\n\\n(1) As to Point 1,\\nIn light of the facts found, the court below held that the judicial compromise reached between the non-party and the non-party Nongdong Agricultural Cooperative Association in this case was a compromise subject to a condition subsequent that would become void if the Plaintiff, who is the beneficial owner of the real property in this case, raised an objection, and that since it is evident that the Plaintiff has raised an objection by filing this lawsuit, the effect of the said compromise has lapsed, and therefore the transfer registration of ownership under the name of the said non-party, which was completed on the basis of the void compromise record, and each registration under the names of the Defendants effected on that basis are registrations that are void for lack of cause; this determination is in accordance with this Court’s precedents holding that, even in a judicial compromise, it is possible to agree that the effect of the compromise shall lapse upon a third party’s objection, and that upon fulfillment of such condition subsequent, the effect of the compromise naturally extinguishes (see 1965. 3. 2. rendered judgment 64DA1514; 1988. 8. 9. rendered judgment 88DAKA2332, etc.), and is therefore proper. The argument that the lower court judgment contains an error of law regarding the lapse of a judicial compromise or the opposability against a third party in good faith is difficult to accept.\\n\\n(2) As to Point 2,\\nIn the preparatory brief dated 1989. 12. 5., the Defendants argued that, according to the Plaintiff’s assertion, title trust had been created with respect to 20 parcels of land, including the land in this case, in favor of the Nongdong Agricultural Cooperative Association, and that “as to the non-party who received the transfer of ownership from the title trustee or any subsequent third party, a trust claim cannot be asserted regardless of good faith or bad faith.” Thereafter, according to the contents of the preparatory brief dated 1991. 6. 13., the Defendants merely reorganized and argued their foregoing position by stating that “the registration under the name of the said non-party should be deemed a title trust by the Plaintiff to the said non-party, and since ownership thereof belongs externally to the said non-party, acquisition of the land in this case from him was proper,” and it does not appear that they argued that the registration under the name of the said non-party, which is void for lack of cause, is valid because it conforms to the substantive legal relationship. Therefore, it cannot be said that the court below erred by misunderstanding the Defendants’ argument in determining according to the later reorganized argument. Even if it were assumed that the foregoing argument had remained as it was and that there was an argument that the registration under the names of the said non-party and thereafter is valid because it conforms to the substantive legal relationship, once the court below determined that the transfer registration of ownership completed from the said association to the said non-party was void for lack of cause by reason of the lapse of the said compromise, even if the Plaintiff had, before the said compromise, title-trusted the land to the said association or the non-party, the registration under the name of the said non-party transferred from the said association cannot be said to conform to the substantive legal relationship, and ultimately the argument that it is a valid registration conforming to the substantive legal relationship must also be rejected. Accordingly, the argument that the lower court judgment contains an error of law regarding a valid registration conforming to the substantive legal relationship, or an omission of judgment on such argument, cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(3) As to Point 3,\\nUpon examination of the record, the court below, by comprehensively considering the cited evidence, recognized that the waiver of objection stated in B Exhibit No. 1-15, 1-17 and A Exhibit No. 5-3 pertained to the three parcels, including (Addresses 1 through 3 omitted), and rejected the evidence supporting the Defendants’ assertion that the documentary evidence, etc., and the object of the waiver of objection also included the land in this case; this is persuasive, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in violation of the rules of evidence by violating the rules of experience as alleged. Meanwhile, the Plaintiff’s objection provided for in paragraph 9 of the judicial compromise reached between the said non-party and the said association appears to refer to the factual state in which the Plaintiff raises an objection, and therefore the court below’s rejection of the Defendants’ defense of the statute of limitations on the ground that the right of objection cannot be said to be a claim extinguished by a ten-year prescriptive period is also persuasive. Even if the said objection were deemed to be an objection as the exercise of a right, it appears to refer to the exercise of rights pursuant to the agreement, as stated in the lower court judgment, in the sale dated 1977. 4. 8. between the Plaintiff and the said non-party, namely, the agreement that if the said non-party violated the agreement whereby, within one month from the date on which it received registration with respect to the lands listed in the attached schedule to the lower court judgment, the Plaintiff would repay the debt of 117,050,000 won borne by the Plaintiff, and the balance of the purchase price after deducting the said debt, namely 500,000,000 won, would be paid to the Plaintiff by 1979. 12. 30., and the remaining 468,410,000 won by 1980. 12. 30., the said sales contract would be void and the registration under the name of the said non-party would be cancelled; but, as stated by the court below, the said non-party received registration on 1979. 5. 26., and the filing of this lawsuit, recognized as the Plaintiff’s objection provided for in the said judicial compromise, was made on 1988. 12. 7., so it is clear that ten years had not elapsed from 1979. 6. 26., which was one month from the date of registration, until the time of the said objection, and thus the court’s action in rejecting the Defendants’ argument that the right of objection was extinguished by the failure to object for ten years is correct; accordingly, the lower court’s determination as above cannot be said to contain any error of law that affected the outcome of the judgment, any misapprehension of the parties’ arguments, or any illegality in failing to exercise the right to clarification. Neither of the arguments can be accepted.\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the judges who participated."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning intervention in support under the Civil Procedure Act is incorrect? (If there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Under the Civil Procedure Act, with respect to an application for intervention in support, the court seised of the case must decide whether to permit intervention, regardless of whether any party has filed an objection.
B: In ordinary litigation, even if the party being supported withdraws the action without the consent of the quasi-joint intervenor, the withdrawal is valid; however, in an action for retrial, even if the party being supported withdraws the retrial action, it is ineffective unless the quasi-joint intervenor consents.
C: In quasi-joint intervention, because among the procedural acts of the party being supported, those that are unfavorable to the intervenor are ineffective, if the intervenor files an appeal, the party being supported cannot withdraw the appeal or waive the appeal.
D: If an intervenor who has not filed an appeal submits a written submission after the expiration of the time limit for the party being supported to submit a statement of reasons for final appeal, and asserts matters that were not asserted in the statement of reasons for final appeal lawfully submitted by the party being supported, this cannot be regarded as an assertion of grounds for final appeal submitted within the lawful time limit.
E: If, after a third party has purchased land from the Defendant but before completing registration, a Plaintiff who has placed a provisional attachment on real property registered in the Defendant's name files an action against the Defendant for a loan claim, and the third party, on the ground that the Plaintiff's claim sued upon is a fictitious claim and that the Defendant intends to cause the Plaintiff to prevail by admitting the factual allegations asserted by the Plaintiff, seeks to intervene in support on the Defendant's side in the loan claim action, such intervention is not permitted.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2000DA59333]": "The appeal is dismissed. The costs of appeal shall be borne by the Intervenor Supporting the Defendant."}

{"[2014DA13044]": "The grounds for final appeal shall be determined (with respect to the written submissions filed after the expiration of the period for filing the grounds for final appeal, only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\n1. As to Ground 2 of the grounds for final appeal\\n\\nIn light of the relevant statutes and the record, the court below, a collegiate division of the District Court, proceeded to adjudicate this case on the premise that it had appellate jurisdiction over the first-instance judgment rendered by a single judge of the District Court. Such action was in accordance with Article 32(2) of the Court Organization Act, etc., and is proper, and there is no illegality such as a violation of appellate-instance jurisdiction, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n2. As to the argument under Ground 1 and Ground 5 of the grounds for final appeal to the effect that there was no benefit of appeal\\n\\nThe benefit of appeal is a requirement for appeal and is a matter subject to ex officio review by the court; accordingly, a party’s argument on this point merely urges the court to exercise its authority ex officio, and even if it is not addressed, it cannot serve as a ground for final appeal on the basis of omission of determination [see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 1990. 4. 27. rendered in 88DAKA25274, 25281 (intervention), Supreme Court Decision 1994. 11. 8. rendered in 94DA31549, etc.]. An appeal may be brought only against a judgment that is adverse to the appellant, and whether a judgment is adverse to the appellant must be determined, based on the operative part of the judgment, as of the time the appeal is filed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 1994. 11. 4. rendered in 94DA21207).\\n\\nAccording to the record, in the first instance of the action for retrial in this case, the Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor (the retrial Plaintiff, hereinafter referred to as the “Plaintiff”) received a judgment against the Defendant (the retrial Defendant, hereinafter referred to as the “Defendant”) that fully granted the retrial petition of the auxiliary intervenor, vacated the judgment subject to retrial, and disallowed compulsory execution based on the notarial deed of the promissory note in this case. Thus, in light of the foregoing legal principles, the first-instance judgment was adverse to the Defendant, so it is clear that the Defendant had a benefit of appeal.\\n\\nAccordingly, the argument in this part of the grounds for final appeal, to the effect that the Defendant had no benefit of appeal or that the court below omitted its determination thereon, cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. As to Ground 4 of the grounds for final appeal\\n\\nWhen a party files an objection to auxiliary intervention, the court must decide whether to permit the intervention (Article 73(1) of the Civil Procedure Act). However, even if the court adjudicates this by a final judgment rather than by a decision, it is not unlawful (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 1962. 1. 11. rendered in 4294MINSANG558), and the same applies where, in the case of a third party whose rights are affected by the judgment having made auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity, a party files an objection to such intervention. In addition, because a judgment must set forth its conclusion in the operative part in order to make the court’s determination clear, even if the propriety of the matter is determined in the reasons for the judgment, if there is no statement in the operative part, then, absent special circumstances, the ruling thereon must be regarded as omitted; and where there is an omission of a ruling, the litigation as to that part remains pending in that instance and therefore is not a proper subject of appeal, so an appeal as to that part is improper (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2007. 11. 16. rendered in 2005DU15700).\\n\\nAccording to the record, when the Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor in a joint-litigation capacity (hereinafter referred to as the “Intervenor”) submitted an application for auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity to the court of first instance on 2013. 3. 14., the Defendant filed an objection by submitting a preparatory brief on 2013. 3. 22. to the effect that the Intervenor’s auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity should not be permitted. Nevertheless, the first instance did not, at either a hearing date or outside a hearing date, decide whether to permit the Intervenor’s auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity, and in the operative part of the first-instance judgment, it likewise made no determination on this point. Thereafter, when the Defendant appealed the first-instance judgment, the court below found that the Intervenor’s application for auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity was improper and rendered a judgment dismissing it.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing facts and the legal principles stated above, it must be said that the first instance omitted a ruling on whether to permit the Intervenor’s intervention, and thus this part remained pending before the first instance and was not a proper subject of appeal. Nevertheless, the court below overlooked this and, mistakenly regarding this part as a matter for adjudication, found the Intervenor’s application for intervention to be improper and rendered a judgment dismissing it. Such action by the court below contains an error that affected the outcome of the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning omission of a ruling and the subject of appeal. The argument in the grounds for final appeal pointing out this issue has merit.\\n\\n4. As to Ground 3 of the grounds for final appeal\\n\\na. When a bankruptcy trustee conducts litigation concerning the bankruptcy estate, the debtor whose rights are affected by the judgment may make not only ordinary auxiliary intervention but also auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity (see Supreme Court Decision 2012. 11. 29. rendered in 2011DA109876).\\n\\nMeanwhile, in auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity under Article 78 of the Civil Procedure Act, Article 67(1) of the Civil Procedure Act concerning necessary joinder of parties, namely the provision that “in cases of joinder of parties in which the subject matter of the litigation must be determined uniformly for all joint litigants, a procedural act by one of the joint litigants has effect only for the benefit of all,” applies mutatis mutandis. Accordingly, the procedural acts of the party being assisted have effect only for the benefit of all, and acts adverse to the auxiliary intervenor in a joint-litigation capacity have no effect (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2013. 3. 28. rendered in 2011DU13729).\\n\\nHowever, retrial as provided in Article 451 of the Civil Procedure Act is an extraordinary method of objection by which, where a final judgment has a serious defect falling under a ground for retrial, a party seeks to have that judgment vacated and to obtain a retrial of a case that has already concluded. Its principal purpose is to exclude the effects of a judgment, such as res judicata, formative effect, and enforceability, that a final judgment possesses (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009. 5. 14. rendered in 2006DA34190). Unlike the withdrawal of an ordinary action, the withdrawal of an action for retrial is an act that causes the loss of the opportunity to challenge a final judgment and thereby prevents the exclusion of the effect of the final judgment any further; accordingly, as a procedural act directly related to the effect of the judgment, it is an act adverse to an auxiliary intervenor in a joint-litigation capacity to whom the effect of the final judgment extends. Therefore, after an auxiliary intervenor in a joint-litigation capacity has intervened in an action for retrial, even if the party being assisted withdraws the action for retrial, such withdrawal is ineffective unless the auxiliary intervenor in a joint-litigation capacity consents. The same applies where the party being assisted filed the action for retrial or where an ordinary auxiliary intervenor filed it. In particular, where an ordinary auxiliary intervenor files an action for retrial, even if the party being assisted has the authority to withdraw the action for retrial as against the ordinary auxiliary intervenor, such authority cannot be exercised so as to adversely affect an auxiliary intervenor in a joint-litigation capacity; thus, it cannot be said that the filing of the action for retrial becomes void or improper because of the withdrawal of the action for retrial by the party being assisted.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the court below’s judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained. Namely, (1) in the case subject to retrial, the Intervenor had filed against the Defendant, in Seoul Southern District Court Case No. 2009GADAN45362, an action to object to claim seeking exclusion of enforceability of the notarial deed of the promissory note in this case issued by the Intervenor to the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as the “case subject to retrial”), and while that case was pending in the first instance, the Intervenor was declared bankrupt; accordingly, the Plaintiff succeeded to the litigation as bankruptcy trustee and, on 2010. 9. 7., received a partially favorable judgment subject to retrial, which, after the appellate and final appellate proceedings, had already become final and conclusive upon the Plaintiff’s withdrawal of appeal. (2) The Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor, who had intervened by auxiliary intervention in the case subject to retrial, filed the action for retrial in this case seeking, inter alia, vacatur of the judgment subject to retrial on 2012. 7. 27. (3) Thereupon, on 2013. 3. 14., the Intervenor submitted an application for auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity to the court of first instance, and that application was served on the Plaintiff’s and Defendant’s counsel on 2013. 3. 20. (4) Then, on 2013. 3. 21., the Plaintiff submitted to the court of first instance a notice of withdrawal of action stating that the action for retrial in this case was withdrawn.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing facts and the legal principles stated above, so long as the effect of the judgment subject to retrial received by the Plaintiff, as bankruptcy trustee, extends to the debtor, the Intervenor must be deemed to have properly made auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity in the action for retrial in this case. Therefore, even if thereafter the Plaintiff, as the party being assisted, withdrew the action for retrial in this case, such withdrawal is an act adverse to the Intervenor and is ineffective, and it cannot be said that the filing of the action for retrial in this case became void or improper as a result.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, for the reasons stated in its holding, found that the action for retrial in this case became improper due to the Plaintiff’s withdrawal of the action for retrial and dismissed it. Such action by the court below, it must be said, contains an error of law concerning the effect of withdrawal of an action for retrial where there is auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity, and concerning Article 76(2) of the Civil Procedure Act, etc.\\n\\nb. However, for the following reasons, the action for retrial in this case must be dismissed as improper; therefore, the above error of the court below cannot be said to have affected the outcome of the judgment.\\n\\nThe proviso to Article 451(1) of the Civil Procedure Act provides that where a party has asserted a ground for retrial by appeal or, knowing of such ground, has failed to assert it, an action for retrial may not be filed. Here, the phrase “knowing of such ground but failing to assert it” includes not only cases where, despite knowing that a ground for retrial existed, the party filed an appeal but failed to assert the ground in the appellate court, but also cases where no appeal was filed and the judgment became final and conclusive as it stood (see Supreme Court Decision 1985. 10. 22. rendered in 84HU68, Supreme Court Decision 1991. 11. 12. rendered in 91DA29057, etc.). A ground for retrial such as omission of determination will, absent special circumstances, be deemed to have become known to the party upon service of a certified copy of the judgment (see Supreme Court Decision 1989. 5. 23. rendered in 88NU5570, etc.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, ordinary auxiliary intervention is intervention for the purpose of assisting the party being assisted on the premise of the procedural status at the time of intervention, and therefore, depending on the stage of the litigation at the time of intervention, the intervenor cannot perform an act that the party being assisted could not perform (see the proviso to Article 76(1) of the Civil Procedure Act). Although an auxiliary intervenor in a joint-litigation capacity is also granted a status akin to that of a necessary co-litigant under Articles 78 and 67 of the Civil Procedure Act in that the effect of the judgment extends to it, it is originally not a party but rather has the character of an auxiliary intervenor; thus, in this respect, it must be regarded as the same as an ordinary auxiliary intervenor.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the court below’s judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained: (1) in the case subject to retrial mentioned above, a judgment subject to retrial partially favorable to the Plaintiff was rendered on 2010. 9. 7., and a certified copy of the judgment was served on 2010. 9. 10. on the Plaintiff personally and on the Defendant’s counsel; (2) thereupon, the Plaintiff and the Defendant did not appeal, and only the Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor filed an application for joint-litigation intervention and at the same time appealed, but the Plaintiff withdrew the appeal on 2010. 11. 17.; (3) the appellate court in the case subject to retrial, on 2011. 4. 20., held that the Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor’s application for joint-litigation intervention and the appeal based thereon were both improper, and that, even if the case subject to retrial were viewed as one in which neither the Plaintiff nor the Defendant appealed and the Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor filed an appeal as an auxiliary intervenor, the litigation had ended by the Plaintiff’s withdrawal of appeal; accordingly, it rendered a judgment dismissing the Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor’s application for joint-litigation intervention and appeal and declaring that the litigation had ended because the judgment subject to retrial became final and conclusive on 2010. 9. 25.; (4) the Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor appealed therefrom, but received a judgment dismissing the appeal on the ground that the conclusion of the appellate judgment was proper; and (5) the Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor filed the action for retrial in this case on 2012. 7. 27., alleging only the omission of determination in the judgment subject to retrial as to the “litigation trust argument” and the “novation argument” as grounds for retrial, and thereafter the Intervenor made auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing facts and the legal principles stated above, the Plaintiff must, absent special circumstances, be deemed to have become aware of the ground for retrial based on omission of determination asserted by the Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor upon service of a certified copy of the judgment subject to retrial. Since the Plaintiff did not file an appeal against the judgment subject to retrial, and the appeal filed by the Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor was withdrawn, causing the judgment subject to retrial to become final and conclusive as it stood, the Plaintiff could no longer file an action for retrial on the ground of such omission of determination. Furthermore, insofar as the Plaintiff, as the party being assisted, could not file an action for retrial, the Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor likewise could not file an action for retrial on the ground of such omission of determination, and the same applies even if the Intervenor made auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity in this action for retrial. Ultimately, the action for retrial in this case alleged as grounds for retrial only grounds that do not constitute proper grounds for retrial, and therefore it is improper.\\n\\nc. Accordingly, the argument in this part of the grounds for final appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, without addressing the remaining grounds for final appeal to the effect that the court below erred in dismissing the Intervenor’s application for auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity despite its being proper, the part of the court below’s judgment dismissing the application for auxiliary intervention in a joint-litigation capacity is reversed, the remaining final appeal is dismissed, and with respect to the costs of appeal, the Plaintiff’s auxiliary intervenor shall bear the portion arising from the auxiliary intervention, and the Intervenor shall bear the remainder, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who deliberated on the case."}

{"[2015DU36836]": "1. First, we examine whether the appeal in this case is lawful.\\n\\na. Even where an intervention in support of a party made by an intervenor in an administrative litigation case does not fall under intervention by a third party as provided in Article 16 of the Administrative Litigation Act, in light of the nature of administrative litigation, including the fact that the effect of the judgment extends to the intervenor, such intervention may be regarded as a quasi-joint-party intervention in support of a party as provided in Article 78 of the Civil Procedure Act. Since Article 67(1) of the Civil Procedure Act concerning necessary joinder, namely, the provision that “where, in a common action in which the object of the litigation must be uniformly determined as to all co-litigants, the litigation act of one of the co-litigants is effective only for the benefit of all,” applies mutatis mutandis to quasi-joint-party intervention in support of a party under Article 78 of the Civil Procedure Act, the litigation acts of the party supported by the intervenor are effective only for the benefit of all, and anything disadvantageous to the quasi-joint-party intervenor has no effect. Therefore, where the intervenor files an appeal, the party supported by the intervenor may not withdraw or waive the appeal (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 70NU35, rendered July 28, 1970; Supreme Court Decision 2011DU13729, rendered March 28, 2013).\\n\\nMeanwhile, under the Civil Procedure Act, when a party raises an objection to an application for intervention in support of a party, the court seized of the case must decide whether to permit the intervention; however, if a party pleads or makes statements at a preparatory hearing without raising an objection, the party loses the right to raise an objection (Articles 73(1) and 74 of the Civil Procedure Act), and may continue to perform litigation acts even without a decision by the court seized of the case granting intervention in support of a party.\\n\\nb. According to the record, ① the Defendant’s supporting intervenor (hereinafter referred to as the “Intervenor”) filed an application for intervention in support of a party on 2014. 6. 18. while the first-instance proceedings in this case were pending; ② although, on the same day, the court of first instance sent the Plaintiff a request for submission of comments on the Intervenor’s application for intervention in support of a party, and the Plaintiff received it the following day, the Plaintiff pled at the first hearing date of the first instance held on 2014. 6. 26. without filing any objection to the Intervenor’s application for intervention in support of a party; ③ accordingly, the court of first instance, without expressly deciding whether to grant or deny the Intervenor’s application for intervention in support of a party, allowed the Intervenor to perform litigation acts in this case as a Defendant’s supporting intervenor, and from that time onward the Intervenor has continued to perform litigation acts as the Defendant’s supporting intervenor; and ④ the Intervenor appealed on 2015. 1. 19., which was within the appeal period, but the Defendant submitted a written waiver of appeal on 2015. 1. 21.\\n\\nc. Examining the above factual relationship in light of the legal principles discussed above, since the effect of the judgment in this case also extends to the Intervenor, the Intervenor may be regarded as occupying the status of a quasi-joint-party intervenor in support of a party, and because the Intervenor lawfully filed an appeal within the appeal period, even if the Defendant, who is the party supported by the intervenor, thereafter submitted a written waiver of appeal, such waiver of appeal has no effect against the Intervenor’s interests. Accordingly, the appeal in this case filed by the Intervenor is lawful.\\n\\n2. Next, we determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\na. Whether the land in this case had been an ancillary facility of the Boseong Sea Dike since around the completion of the Boseong Sea Dike in 1937\\n\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in its opinion, determined that, although the land in this case was “miscellaneous land” at the time of the completion of the Boseong Sea Dike around 1937, it only became submerged and came to serve as the water-storage basin of the Boseong Sea Dike as the water level of the inland water surface inside the dike rose due to the construction of the internal embankment around 1986.\\n\\nThe portion of the grounds for appeal challenging this factual finding by the court below is, in substance, nothing more than criticism of the selection and assessment of evidence, which belong to the free evaluation of evidence by the court of fact, and therefore cannot be accepted.\\n\\nb. Whether, in its current state, the land in this case qualifies as a “water-storage basin used for farmland conservation or agricultural production” and thus is subject to approval for “use for a purpose other than the intended purpose” under Article 23 of the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act\\n\\n(1) Article 61(1) of the former National Land Planning and Utilization Act (before amendment by Act No. 11922 of 2013. 7. 16.; hereinafter referred to as the “National Land Planning Act”) provides: “When granting a development act permit, where the Mayor of a Special Metropolitan City, the Mayor of a Metropolitan City, the Mayor of a Special Self-Governing City, the Governor of a Special Self-Governing Province, the head of a Si, or the head of a Gun has, pursuant to paragraph 3, consulted in advance with the head of the relevant administrative agency regarding approval, permit, authorization, license, consultation, release, report, or examination, etc., under each subparagraph below concerning that development act, such matters shall be deemed to have received the relevant approval, permit, authorization, license, consultation, release, report, or examination, etc.” and item 4 thereof provides for “approval for use of agricultural production infrastructure facilities for a purpose other than the intended purpose under Article 23 of the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act.”\\n\\nArticle 23(1) of the former Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act (before amendment by Act No. 14480 of 2016. 12. 27.; hereinafter referred to as the “Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act”), which is cited by the above provision of the National Land Planning Act, and Article 31(2) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act (before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 28028 of 2017. 5. 8.), enacted pursuant thereto, provide that a person who intends to use agricultural production infrastructure facilities or water resources managed by the Korea Rural Community Corporation for a purpose other than their original purpose must obtain approval from the Korea Rural Community Corporation.\\n\\nHere, “agricultural production infrastructure facilities” means “facilities such as reservoirs, pumping stations, underground water use facilities such as wells, drainage stations, intake weirs, irrigation channels, drainage channels, water-storage basins (water-storage basins: ponds), roads (including farm roads such as agricultural and fishing villages roads under Article 4 of the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Road Improvement Act; the same applies hereinafter), sea dikes, embankments (embankments: levees), and their auxiliary facilities, installed through agricultural production infrastructure improvement projects or otherwise used for farmland conservation or agricultural production, as well as farming facilities such as production, processing, storage, and distribution facilities for agricultural, forestry, fishery, and livestock products” (Article 2 subparagraph 6 of the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act).\\n\\nFurthermore, the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act, in Chapter III, Section 2, under the title “Management of Agricultural Production Infrastructure Facilities,” provides in Articles 16 through 24 for the managers of agricultural production infrastructure facilities, registration, methods of management, approval for use for a purpose other than the intended purpose, and so forth. In other words, when an implementer of an agricultural production infrastructure improvement project completes the project, he or she manages the agricultural production infrastructure facilities installed through that project; however, “agricultural production infrastructure facilities installed through agricultural production infrastructure improvement projects implemented by the State” and “agricultural production infrastructure facilities managed by a local government or a landowner, for which that local government or landowner requests the Minister of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs to have the Korea Rural Community Corporation take over and manage them” may be taken over and managed by the Korea Rural Community Corporation according to the Minister of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs’ decision (Article 16(1), Article 16(2), first sentence, items 1 and 2). Accordingly, a person who manages agricultural production infrastructure facilities (hereinafter referred to as the “manager of agricultural production infrastructure facilities”) must register the agricultural production infrastructure facilities he or she manages with the competent administrative agency (Article 17), must exercise due care in management by, for example, establishing and improving safety management plans, taking measures such as replacement and repair of facilities, and conducting safety inspections and detailed safety inspections (Article 18(1) and (2)), and has the authority to approve use for a purpose other than the intended purpose and to collect expenses under certain requirements (Article 23).\\n\\n(2) In light of the language, structure, and content of these relevant provisions, the term “agricultural production infrastructure facilities” under the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act is a concept encompassing not only various facilities installed through agricultural production infrastructure improvement projects under the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act and used for farmland conservation or agricultural production, but also various facilities created by other means and used for farmland conservation or agricultural production. However, it is appropriate to construe Articles 17 and following of the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act concerning the management of agricultural production infrastructure facilities as applying only to cases involving a manager of agricultural production infrastructure facilities who has acquired management authority pursuant to Article 16 of the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act. Accordingly, the cases in which approval from the Korea Rural Community Corporation for “use for a purpose other than the intended purpose” of agricultural production infrastructure facilities is required under Article 23(1) of the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act are limited to ① cases in which the Korea Rural Community Corporation, as the implementer of an agricultural production infrastructure improvement project, manages the agricultural production infrastructure facilities installed through the project after completing the project, and ② cases in which the Korea Rural Community Corporation takes over management authority from the State, a local government, or a landowner for agricultural production infrastructure facilities installed or managed by that entity, pursuant to the Minister of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs’ decision.\\n\\nFurthermore, “registration of agricultural production infrastructure facilities” under Article 17 of the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act is merely intended as a factual basis for the competent administrative agency to supervise the management affairs of the manager of agricultural production infrastructure facilities, and as materials for the convenience of the execution of administrative affairs and proof of facts; therefore, the registration itself cannot be regarded as having the effect of granting management authority over the agricultural production infrastructure facilities.\\n\\n(3) The court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it accepted, found that the Boseong Land Improvement Association, the predecessor of the Intervenor’s Boseong Branch, carried out construction work in around 1986 to install the internal embankment of the Boseong Sea Dike, and as the water level of the inland water surface inside the dike rose, the land in this case, which had previously been miscellaneous land, only then became submerged and became the water-storage basin of the Boseong Sea Dike; nevertheless, the Boseong Land Improvement Association or the Intervenor did not compensate the owner of the land for the loss, nor did they register the land as agricultural production infrastructure facilities, and only when the Plaintiff applied to the Defendant for a development act permit on 2012. 12. 26., and around that time the Defendant requested the Intervenor to consult on approval for use of agricultural production infrastructure facilities for a purpose other than the intended purpose, did the Intervenor then register the land in this case with the Governor of Jeollanam-do in around January 2013 as the water-storage basin of the Boseong Sea Dike. The record also shows no allegation or proof that the Intervenor acquired management authority over the land in this case in the manner prescribed by Article 16 of the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act.\\n\\n(4) Examining the matter in light of the content and legal principles of the above statutes, the land in this case functions in fact as a water-storage basin, an ancillary facility of the Boseong Sea Dike, and therefore there is room to regard it as agricultural production infrastructure facilities under the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act; accordingly, the portion of the court below’s ruling that the land in this case does not fall under agricultural production infrastructure facilities under the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act is not appropriate. However, if the Intervenor did not acquire management authority over the land in this case in the manner prescribed by Article 16 of the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act, then the land in this case is not subject to approval from the Intervenor for use of agricultural production infrastructure facilities for a purpose other than the intended purpose under Article 23(1) of the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act, and thus is not a subject regarding which prior consultation with the head of the relevant administrative agency is required pursuant to Article 61(1), item 4 of the National Land Planning Act when granting a development act permit. Therefore, the disposition in this case, which denied the development act permit solely on the premise that consultation with the Intervenor was necessary for the Plaintiff, the owner of the land in this case, and that the Intervenor refused such consultation, is unlawful.\\n\\n(5) Ultimately, the court below’s conclusion that the disposition in this case is unlawful on the premise that the Intervenor does not hold management authority over the land in this case is acceptable, and there is no error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning agricultural production infrastructure facilities under the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act, as asserted in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nHowever, because this judgment results in the first-instance judgment that annulled the disposition in this case becoming final and conclusive, the Defendant must again render a disposition on the Plaintiff’s application for a development act permit in this case in accordance with the purport of the judgment of annulment (Article 30(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act). At that time, a proper review should be conducted as to whether the Plaintiff’s project plan is appropriate and whether the other requirements for a development act permit are satisfied. On the other hand, if, as the Intervenor contends, maintaining and managing the land in this case in its current state is essential for maintaining the function of the Boseong Sea Dike, the Intervenor should now expropriate the land in this case and lawfully acquire management authority over agricultural production infrastructure facilities under the Agricultural and Fishing Villages Improvement Act.\\n\\nc. Abuse of rights and whether there was submergence\\n\\nIt is clear from the record that the grounds for appeal on this point are arguments raised by the Intervenor for the first time at the stage of final appeal, and therefore they cannot constitute lawful grounds for appeal against the judgment below.\\n\\nFurthermore, even upon further examination, whether the former owners of the land in this case waived their rightful authority to use and derive benefit from it, or whether the land became State-owned through submergence, was not a ground for disposition originally stated by the Defendant when making the disposition in this case, and therefore cannot be used as a lawful ground for the disposition in this case at the final appeal stage. In addition, submergence refers to a case in which a certain parcel of land becomes State-owned by operation of law if it meets the requirements of a national river or public waters prescribed by law (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 99DA11687, rendered December 8, 2000), and the mere fact that the land in this case, located inside a sea dike, became submerged due to a rise in water level and in fact became a water-storage basin does not mean that it constitutes submergence. Accordingly, all of the Intervenor’s arguments on this point are without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the appeal costs shall be borne by the Intervenor. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

{"[2019DU40611]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the Defendant’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\na. Ground 1 of final appeal\\n\\nThe court below, after finding the facts as stated in its reasoning with respect to the disciplinary cause of “obstruction of the pilot implementation of single-crew operation” against Plaintiffs 6, 7, 8, and 9, held that the disciplinary cause was not established because it could not be said that the order of official duties was disrupted by the acts of the above Plaintiffs, and there was no evidence to support the finding that the honor and prestige of the Defendant’s auxiliary intervenor (hereinafter referred to as the “Intervenor”) were impaired or that the Intervenor suffered property damage.\\n\\nReviewing the reasons for the judgment of the court below in light of the record, there is no error in the court below’s above determination, such as failing to decide as alleged in the grounds of appeal, or, without conducting the necessary examination, violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nb. Ground 2 of final appeal\\n\\nThe court below held that each disciplinary action against Plaintiffs 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 was void as it exceeded the limits of disciplinary discretion, for the reasons stated in its reasoning.\\n\\nReviewing the reasons for the judgment of the court below in light of the record, there is no error in the court below’s above determination, such as failing to decide as alleged in the grounds of appeal, or, without conducting the necessary examination, violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\n2. Regarding the grounds for final appeal of the Intervenor\\n\\na. Grounds 1 and 2 of final appeal\\n\\n1) The grounds of appeal on this part assert that the 24-hour warning strike conducted by the National Railroad Workers’ Union to which the Plaintiffs belonged on 2014. 2. 25. (hereinafter referred to as “the strike in this case”) is an industrial action lacking legitimacy, and therefore the act of participating in the strike in this case constitutes a disciplinary cause.\\n\\n2) The Intervenor filed an appeal against the part of the judgment of the court below that revoked the retrial decision concerning Plaintiffs 4 and 5. However, according to the record, it is clear that the Intervenor disciplined Plaintiffs 4 and 5 only on the ground that they engaged in “assault on the head of the business office in relation to rotational transfer,” and did not discipline them on the ground that they participated in “the strike in this case,” and the Intervenor did not even allege in this lawsuit that “Plaintiffs 4 and 5 participated in the strike in this case.”\\n\\nUltimately, the grounds of appeal on this part are unrelated to the legitimacy of the discipline of Plaintiffs 4 and 5 appealed by the Intervenor, and thus cannot be accepted as such.\\n\\nHowever, the grounds of appeal on this part may be regarded as the grounds of appeal asserted by the Intervenor with respect to the portion appealed by the Defendant. Accordingly, ex officio, we examine whether this statement of grounds of appeal was filed within the filing period.\\n\\n3) a) Even where the defendant’s auxiliary intervention in an administrative litigation case by the Intervenor does not fall under the intervention of a third party under Article 16 of the Administrative Litigation Act, in light of the nature of administrative litigation, including the fact that the effect of the judgment extends to the Intervenor, such intervention constitutes an auxiliary intervention in the nature of a co-litigation provided in Article 78 of the Civil Procedure Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DU13729, rendered on Mar. 28, 2013).\\n\\nIf an Intervenor who has made an auxiliary intervention in the nature of a co-litigation lawfully files an appeal and submits a statement of grounds of appeal within the period for submitting such statement, the submission of the statement of grounds of appeal is lawful even if the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal of the supported party who did not file an appeal has expired (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DU30069, rendered on Nov. 29, 2012).\\n\\nMeanwhile, an Intervenor who has made an auxiliary intervention in the nature of a co-litigation may submit a statement of grounds of appeal concerning the portion for which the supported party filed an appeal without the Intervenor itself filing an appeal; however, in such a case, whether the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal has been complied with must be determined by reference to the supported party. Therefore, if an Intervenor who has not filed an appeal submits a statement of grounds of appeal after the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal of the supported party has expired, it cannot be deemed to have been submitted within the lawful period. This legal principle likewise applies to assertions of grounds of appeal, so even if an Intervenor who has not filed an appeal asserts in a written submission filed after the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal of the supported party has expired matters not asserted in the duly filed statement of grounds of appeal of the supported party, such assertions cannot be regarded as assertions of grounds of appeal submitted within the lawful period.\\n\\nWhere the Intervenor and the supported party who made auxiliary intervention in the nature of a co-litigation each file an appeal separately by distinguishing the portions of the court below’s judgment against which they are dissatisfied, as to the “portion disputed only by the supported party,” the Intervenor is in the position of an “Intervenor who has not filed an appeal.” Therefore, with respect to the “portion disputed only by the supported party,” if the Intervenor asserts new matters not asserted in the supported party’s statement of grounds of appeal after the period for submitting the supported party’s statement of grounds of appeal has expired, such assertion cannot be regarded as an assertion of grounds of appeal submitted within the lawful period.\\n\\nb) The record reveals the following circumstances.\\n\\n(1) On 2016. 1. 19., while this lawsuit, in which the Plaintiffs sought revocation of the retrial decision granting relief from unfair disciplinary action, etc. against the Defendant, was pending in the court of first instance, the Intervenor submitted an application for auxiliary intervention in support of the Defendant. The court of first instance, with respect to that application, caused the Intervenor to participate in this lawsuit and engage in litigation acts as an auxiliary intervenor supporting the Defendant without going through the third-party intervention procedure prescribed in Article 16 of the Administrative Litigation Act, and from that time onward the Intervenor continued to engage in litigation acts as an auxiliary intervenor supporting the Defendant.\\n\\n(2) The Defendant filed an appeal against the portion of the retrial decision in the judgment of the court below concerning Plaintiffs 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10, and the Intervenor filed an appeal against the portion of the retrial decision concerning Plaintiffs 4 and 5, thereby placing the Intervenor in the position of an “Intervenor who has not filed an appeal” with respect to the Plaintiffs appealed by the Defendant.\\n\\n(3) Among the Plaintiffs, the persons for whom participation in the strike in this case constitutes a disciplinary cause are only Plaintiffs 6, 7, 8, and 10; with respect to those Plaintiffs, the Intervenor is, as noted above, merely an “Intervenor who has not filed an appeal.”\\n\\n(4) The petition of appeal submitted by the Intervenor contains no statement of grounds of appeal concerning Plaintiffs 6, 7, 8, and 10, and the Intervenor, when submitting the statement of grounds of appeal, asserted to the effect that the fact of participation in the strike in this case constitutes a disciplinary cause; however, this statement of grounds of appeal was submitted after the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal had expired when measured against the supported party.\\n\\n(5) Meanwhile, the Defendant, who is the supported party, did not allege in the petition of appeal or the statement of grounds of appeal that the fact that Plaintiffs 6, 7, 8, and 10 participated in the strike in this case constitutes a legitimate disciplinary cause.\\n\\nc) Reviewing these circumstances in light of the legal principles stated above, the grounds of appeal on this part asserted by the Intervenor, who stands in the position of an auxiliary intervenor in the nature of a co-litigant, are unrelated to the portion appealed by the Intervenor and concern the portion appealed by the supported party, namely the Defendant. Ultimately, since this corresponds to a case where the Intervenor submitted new grounds of appeal after the period for submitting the Defendant’s statement of grounds of appeal had expired, the assertion of grounds of appeal on this part cannot be deemed to have been submitted within the lawful period.\\n\\nb. Ground 3 of final appeal\\n\\nThe court below, with respect to the disciplinary cause of “assault on the head of the business office in relation to rotational transfer” concerning Plaintiffs 4 and 5, held that it did not constitute a disciplinary cause on the ground that the act was a protest against a personnel measure in violation of a collective bargaining agreement and was an activity within the legitimate scope that union members may engage in.\\n\\nReviewing the reasons for the judgment of the court below in light of the record, there is no error in the court below’s above determination, such as misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning recognition of a disciplinary cause as alleged in the grounds of appeal, or violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the appellate costs shall be borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[93DA39850]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. As to Point 1\\n\\nA person who is in a position to effect supplementary intervention may, even if he or she did not effect supplementary intervention in the first-instance proceedings, file an appeal simultaneously with an application for intervention within the period for filing an appeal by the party to be assisted (see Article 66(3) of the Civil Procedure Act); meanwhile, since a party loses the right to object when he or she pleads without objection to supplementary intervention or makes a statement in preparatory proceedings (Article 68 of the Civil Procedure Act), where a supplementary intervenor who did not participate in the first instance files an appeal simultaneously with an application for intervention, unless there is an objection from the party to be assisted or the opposing party to the supplementary intervenor’s application for intervention, the appellate court need not, ex officio, investigate whether the supplementary intervenor satisfies the requirements for intervention in order to determine the existence of the right of appeal, which is a lawful requirement for the appeal.\\n\\nThe argument premised on a contrary view cannot be accepted.\\n\\n2. As to Point 2\\n\\nThe court below was correct in rejecting the Plaintiff’s allegation that the Plaintiff purchased the land at issue from Defendant Bongam-dong Housing Construction Association and also had the building at issue newly constructed by contracting it out at his own expense to the Defendants’ supplementary intervenor, and there is no illegality therein, such as misinterpretation of the resolution of the Defendants’ association’s management committee dated 1982.6.25., as argued, or mistake of fact due to violation of the rules of evidence, or misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the nature of the auxiliary facilities or welfare facilities prescribed in Article 33(2) of the Housing Construction Promotion Act; accordingly, all of the arguments are without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the appeal shall be borne by the losing Plaintiff, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the selected party system is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: Unless there is an agreement limiting the effect to a certain instance at the time of the selection of the selected party, the effect of the selection continues until the termination of the litigation.
B: If a person who is in a relationship with a number of persons such that he or she could be a co-litigant, but who does not share the principal methods of attack and defense and thus has no common interest, is selected as a selected party, and the court overlooks the defect in such qualification and a judgment against that person becomes final and conclusive, this constitutes a ground for retrial under the Civil Procedure Act.
C: A selected party, as a party who has received comprehensive authority from the persons selecting him or her to conduct the litigation, may perform all litigation acts for all of the persons selecting him or her unless otherwise agreed.
D: Where the common interest is extinguished because the suit as to the part concerning the selected party himself or herself is withdrawn or the judgment becomes final and conclusive, the selected party loses that qualification as a matter of course.
E: Under the Civil Procedure Act, where among several parties selected there is a person who has died or lost his or her qualification, the remaining selected party conducts litigation acts for all.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2001DA10748]": "The judgment of the lower court is reversed, and the case is remanded to the collegiate division of the Seoul District Court, main court."}

{"[2005DA10470]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nA plurality of persons having a common interest may designate a designated party; in such a case, the term “common interest” means that the multiple persons are in a relationship in which they may be co-litigants with one another and also share the principal means of attack and defense, and therefore it cannot be said that there is a common interest merely because the rights and obligations of the multiple persons are of the same kind and the causes of their occurrence are of the same kind, and the designation of a designated party should not be permitted (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 97DA362, decided July 25, 1997).\\n\\nHowever, where, among multiple persons, a person who is in a relationship in which he or she may be a co-litigant but does not share the principal means of attack and defense and thus does not have a common interest was designated as a designated party, and the court overlooked the defect in such qualification as designated party and a judgment against him or her became final and binding, as to whether such circumstances fall under the ground for retrial provided in Article 451(1) item 3 of the Civil Procedure Act, namely, “where there is a defect in the authority of a statutory representative, litigation representative, or the grant of authority necessary for an agent to perform litigation acts,” to fall under the above ground for retrial, it must be the case that an unauthorized agent performed substantive litigation acts on behalf of the principal as an agent, or that, due to a defect in authority, the principal or his or her litigation representative was unable to perform substantive litigation acts (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 92JAEDA259, decided December 22, 1992), and in such a case, if the designator himself or herself made the act of designation granting the authority to conduct the litigation to the designated party, who is one of the co-litigants in the relevant action, then the designator was not deprived of the opportunity to perform substantive litigation acts or lawfully participate in the relevant action, so even if there was no common interest with the designated party, such circumstances should be viewed as not falling under the above ground for retrial. This legal principle likewise applies not only where a judgment against the designated party became final and binding, but also where the designated party admitted the claim and the record of admission became final and binding.\\n\\nAccording to the record, in the action for registration of transfer of ownership, Suwon District Court 89GAHAP5730, which is the subject of the quasi-retrial in this case, the Plaintiff clan (Defendant in the quasi-retrial, hereinafter referred to simply as the “Plaintiff”) alleged that “the forest land in Buk-ri, Namsa-myeon, Yongin-si (parcel number 1 omitted) (hereinafter referred to as ‘the forest land at issue’) was, on December 11, 1970, and the forest land in the same ri (parcel number 2 omitted) was, on January 21, 1971, each title-trusted to the persons in whose names the registration of preservation of ownership stood,” and sought, as against Nonparty 1, Nonparty 2 {a person with the same name as Defendant 19 (Defendant in the quasi-retrial, hereinafter referred to simply as the “Defendant”)}, Nonparty 3, Nonparty 4, Defendant 19, and Defendants 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, and 18, who were the registered titleholders and heirs of the deceased Nonparty 5, with respect to the forest land at issue, and as against Nonparty 6 and 24 others, who were the registered titleholders or their heirs, with respect to the forest land in the above (parcel number 2 omitted), performance of the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of termination of the title trust as of May 22, 1989; in that case, all of the co-defendants designated Nonparty 6 as the designated party, and it can be seen that the said Nonparty 6 admitted the claim of the Plaintiff clan.\\n\\nOn the basis of such factual circumstances, the court below held that, among the case subject to the quasi-retrial, the part concerning the forest land at issue and the part concerning the forest land in the above (parcel number 2 omitted) merely involved rights that were of the same kind and causes of occurrence that were of the same kind, and did not fall within a case in which the principal means of attack and defense were common, so there could be no finding of a common interest; accordingly, if Nonparty 6, one of the co-defendants with respect to the forest land in the above (parcel number 2 omitted), became the designated party for the defendants with respect to the forest land at issue and admitted the claim of the Plaintiff clan regarding the forest land at issue, then, as to the defendants with respect to the forest land at issue, the opportunity to participate in the litigation procedure was excluded, and therefore this constituted a ground for retrial by analogy to a case where there is a defect in the authority of a statutory representative, litigation representative, or the grant of authority necessary for an agent to perform litigation acts.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principle, the reasoning of the judgment of the court below, to the effect that there was a defect in the qualification as designated party because there was no common interest between the designated party, Nonparty 6, and the defendants regarding the forest land at issue in the case subject to the quasi-retrial, is well-founded and acceptable (however, it should be added that it was not appropriate for the court below, in determining the existence of a common interest, to rely on the ownership dispute between the Plaintiff clan and the clan of the Hyeongjochamui-gong branch of the Nonparty 7 family, a circumstance that had not been mentioned at all in the case subject to the quasi-retrial). Nevertheless, in this case, where it is acknowledged that the defendants regarding the forest land at issue themselves designated the said Nonparty 6 as the designated party at that time, the court below erred in law by holding that such a defect in the qualification as designated party also constitutes a ground for retrial, and it is clear that such illegality affected the result of the judgment.\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal advanced by the Plaintiff, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for a new trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2006DA28775]": "The Court examines ex officio.\\n\\nBecause the designated party provided for in Article 53 of the Civil Procedure Act must be selected from among several persons having a common interest, where the common interest ceases to exist, as when the action as to the designated party himself is withdrawn or the judgment becomes final and conclusive, the designated party should be deemed to naturally lose the status of designated party.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Plaintiff filed the present action against Defendant 1, Defendant (Designated Party) 2, and eight persons, and among the above eight persons, at first instance Defendant (Designated Party) 2 was selected as the designated party and had him conduct the litigation; a judgment fully granting the Plaintiff's claim was rendered at first instance. Defendant (Designated Party) 2 filed an appeal only as to the portion concerning the designating party Defendant 1, and did not file an appeal as to the portion concerning the designated party himself and the remaining designating parties, so that the first-instance judgment became final and conclusive as is. Under the above facts found, since the portion of the first-instance judgment concerning Defendant (Designated Party) 2 himself became final and conclusive and thereby the common interest ceased to exist, Defendant (Designated Party) 2 should be deemed to have lost the status of designated party with respect to Defendant 1; therefore, the appeal in this case filed by Defendant (Designated Party) 2 in the status of designated party with respect to Defendant 1 is unlawful and thus improper.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by Defendant (Designated Party) 2, and the judgment is rendered as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[94MA2452]": "We consider the grounds for the petitioners’ re-appeal.\\n\\n1. As can be seen from the reasons stated in the original order and the record, the petitioners, as Plaintiffs, filed a civil action for damages against Nonparty 1 and 9 others as Defendants in the Suncheon Branch of the Gwangju District Court. Thereafter, among the petitioners, Petitioners 2, 3, and 1 submitted an application for appointment of a selected party, appointing the said Petitioner 1 as the selected party \"with respect to the first-instance litigation proceedings,\" and thereafter additionally appointed Petitioner 4 as a selected party so that he or she would conduct the first-instance litigation. When the said court rendered and served a judgment on 1993.4.8. dismissing all claims of Plaintiffs (selected parties) Petitioners 1, 4, 5, 6, and 7 (hereinafter referred to as the first-instance Plaintiffs), the appeal in this case was filed on 1993.5.3. It can be seen that the presiding judge of the lower appellate court, on 1994.11.2., ordered that the unpaid amount of service fees of KRW 228,800 be cured within 7 days, and served the said order for cure on the first-instance Plaintiffs excluding Petitioners 3 and 2, among the petitioners, on the ground that they were selected parties (the said Petitioners 5 and 6 were served on Petitioner 1, their legal representative, on the ground that they were minors), and when no payment of service fees was made within that period, dismissed the appeal petition in this case.\\n\\n2. Where the expenses necessary for service of the appeal petition have not been prepaid, this may be regarded as a state in which service of the appeal petition is impossible, and the presiding judge of the appellate court may designate a reasonable period and order that the defect be cured within that period, and if no cure is made within that period, may issue an order dismissing the appeal petition. Moreover, it cannot be deemed unlawful that the presiding judge of the appellate court issued the order dismissing the appeal petition without paying the service expenses in advance out of the national treasury and disbursing them, or that the order dismissing the appeal petition did not state the names and addresses of the individual parties. Therefore, the argument to the contrary is without merit.\\n\\n3. Where a large number of persons having a common interest have designated a party, the selected party may conduct the litigation for the whole group until the conclusion of the relevant litigation, and matters such as appeals must also be brought by such party; however, since the designation of a party may be revoked or altered prospectively by the agreement of the whole group, it shall also be permissible to designate a party from the outset for the purpose of having him or her retain party status limited to a particular instance.\\nHowever, considering that the system of selected parties is intended, in litigation involving multiple parties, to simplify and streamline litigation procedures and thereby promote the efficient progress of litigation, and that the original purport of the system is for the selected person to conduct the litigation as a party until the conclusion of the litigation, even where, as in this case, the written designation submitted at the first instance contains the case title and then states the phrase \"with respect to the first-instance litigation proceedings\" or \"to conduct the first-instance litigation proceedings,\" unless there are special circumstances, the above wording, together with the case title, should be regarded as identifying the case in which the selected party is designated; accordingly, it shall be reasonable to interpret the effect of such designation as continuing until the conclusion of the litigation, rather than being limited to the first-instance litigation.\\nIf so, as stated above, the order of the presiding judge of the appellate court requiring cure of the prepaid service fees in this case was served upon Plaintiffs (selected parties) Petitioners 1 and 4, and Petitioners 5, 6, and 7, who were the selected parties designated by the selecting parties Petitioners 2 and 3, so the said order for cure must be regarded as having been lawfully served upon all appellants; therefore, it is lawful for the presiding judge of the appellate court to have dismissed the appeal petition on the ground that no cure was made within the period during which cure was ordered, and the argument criticizing this is without merit.\\n\\n4. In addition, among the Defendants in the said civil action for damages, Nonparties 1, 2, and 3 did not dispute the first-instance Plaintiffs’ allegations, yet the argument that rendering a judgment against the first-instance Plaintiffs dismissing all of their claims constitutes an omission of judgment is a contention that the first-instance Plaintiffs lost at trial. Further, the remaining arguments, such as the contention that this appeal was filed in anticipation of an immediate appeal against the first-instance court’s refusal to reopen oral argument and against the dismissal of a petition for additional judgment, although the petitioners had filed an application for reopening oral argument regarding the conclusion of the first-instance oral argument, because the first-instance court rendered judgment; and that it was unlawful for the presiding judge of the appellate court to review the appeal petition in this case even though there had been no ruling yet on the above immediate appeal against the refusal to reopen oral argument, are either not valid grounds for a lawful re-appeal against the order dismissing the appeal petition in this case or are merely independent views, and thus cannot be accepted.\\n\\n5. Therefore, all re-appeals are dismissed, and it is so ordered by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning a provisional disposition suspending the performance of duties of a director of a stock company and appointing an acting director are correct? (If there is a dispute, according to case law) (a) Where there is a provisional disposition with a director of a stock company as the respondent, suspending the performance of that director’s duties and appointing an acting director, the provisional disposition order merely suspends the director’s performance of duties and does not deprive the director of status or qualification. (b) A provisional disposition suspending the performance of duties of a director of a stock company and appointing an acting director, by its nature, has effect not only between the parties but also in relation to third parties; therefore, an act done in violation of the provisional disposition is void even in relation to third parties. (c) If, while an acting representative director has been appointed pursuant to a provisional disposition order deciding to suspend the performance of duties of the representative director of a stock company and appoint an acting director, the successor to the person whose duties were being performed is newly elected pursuant to a resolution of a general meeting of shareholders lawfully convened, that successor may lawfully represent the stock company. (d) If a director elected by a general meeting of shareholders whose validity is disputed regarding the effect of the resolution resigns from the office of director and is again elected as a director at a new general meeting of shareholders, an application for a provisional disposition suspending the performance of duties against that director on the ground that the earlier resolution of the general meeting of shareholders is void cannot be granted.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2018DA249148]": "1. Judgment on the Grounds of Appeal\\n\\nA. Where there is a provisional injunction, with a director or auditor of a stock company as the respondent, suspending the performance of duties and appointing a person to act on behalf of such director or auditor, the provisional injunction decision merely suspends the performance of duties of the director or auditor and does not deprive the director or auditor of status or qualification (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 87DO145, rendered on August 18, 1987). Therefore, absent special circumstances, it cannot be said that the term of office of the director or auditor is automatically suspended or extended for the duration that the provisional injunction decision remains in force. Furthermore, although a provisional injunction decision of the foregoing nature, by its nature, is effective not only between the parties but also against third parties (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2013DA39551, rendered on March 27, 2014), this merely limits the validity of acts of performing duties and does not affect the running of the term of office of the director or auditor.\\n\\nB. According to the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts can be known.\\n\\n1) The Plaintiff was appointed as an auditor of the Defendant at the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders on December 1, 2014 (hereinafter referred to as “the general meeting of shareholders in this case”), which was convened by Nonparty 1, etc., who were shareholders of the Defendant, upon obtaining the court’s permission to convene an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders.\\n\\n2) On March 13, 2015, the Plaintiff filed the present action against the Defendant, etc., who denied the Plaintiff’s status as auditor, seeking a declaration that the Plaintiff holds the status of auditor of the Defendant (the Plaintiff maintained the “claim for confirmation of auditor status” as the principal claim while adding the first and second alternative claims during the pendency of the action at first instance), and on April 1, 2015, the Plaintiff requested the Defendant in writing to execute an employment agreement for auditor pursuant to the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders in this case.\\n\\n3) The court below prior to remand, following the former Supreme Court precedents, held that because no employment agreement had been concluded between the Plaintiff and the Defendant, the Plaintiff had not acquired the status of auditor even though there had been a resolution appointing the Plaintiff as auditor at the general meeting of shareholders in this case, and accordingly dismissed the Plaintiff’s principal claim for confirmation of auditor status.
