Against this, the Plaintiff filed an appeal.\\n\\n4) On March 23, 2017, the Supreme Court, by a unanimous opinion of the en banc full bench, changed the former Supreme Court precedents by holding that where there is a resolution of appointment by a general meeting of shareholders and acceptance by the person appointed, the status of director or auditor is acquired regardless of whether a separate employment agreement has been concluded. Accordingly, because there had been a resolution appointing the Plaintiff as auditor at the general meeting of shareholders in this case and the Plaintiff had accepted the appointment as auditor by requesting the Defendant to conclude an employment agreement, the Supreme Court upheld the Plaintiff’s appeal and reversed and remanded the entirety of the judgment of the court below prior to remand on the ground that the Plaintiff should be regarded as having acquired the status of auditor.\\n\\n5) On June 7, 2018, the court below dismissed the principal claim portion of the present action on the ground that, even if the Plaintiff had acquired the Defendant’s auditor status from April 1, 2015, when the Plaintiff requested the conclusion of an auditor employment agreement, the regular general meeting of shareholders concerning the final accounting period within three years thereafter was concluded on March 23, 2018, and the Plaintiff’s term as auditor had expired, and a successor auditor had been validly appointed at the said regular general meeting of shareholders; therefore, absent evidence that the said regular general meeting of shareholders did not exist or was void or that its resolution had been canceled, the Plaintiff’s claim for confirmation of auditor status was merely a request for confirmation of a past legal relationship and thus lacked a legal interest in confirmation.\\n\\n6) Meanwhile, on February 4, 2015, the court issued a decision suspending the performance of duties concerning Nonparty 2, who had been the Defendant’s former auditor, and on the 12th day of the same month issued a decision appointing an acting person for auditor duties (hereinafter referred to as “the provisional injunction decision in this case”); thereafter, on June 7, 2017, in consideration of the purport of the remand judgment in this case, etc., the court ex officio canceled the provisional injunction decision in this case.\\n\\nC. The foregoing factual circumstances shall be examined in light of the legal principles discussed above.\\n\\nEven if the Plaintiff was unable in fact to perform duties as auditor while an acting person had been appointed under the provisional injunction decision in this case, it cannot be said that this caused the Plaintiff’s term of office to be suspended or extended for the duration that the provisional injunction decision in this case remained in force. No different conclusion is warranted merely because the Defendant’s articles of incorporation provide for one auditor. Nor can it be said that it would violate the principle of good faith for the Defendant, which had effectively denied the Plaintiff’s assumption of office as auditor, now to assert the expiration of the Plaintiff’s term.\\n\\nAccordingly, the court below’s determination that the Plaintiff’s term of office ran from April 1, 2015 and expired upon the conclusion of the Defendant’s regular general meeting of shareholders on March 23, 2018, contains no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the effect of a provisional injunction decision suspending the performance of duties and appointing an acting person, whether the provision regarding the number of auditors under the Commercial Act and the articles of incorporation was violated, or whether the principle of good faith was violated.\\n\\n2. Determination ex officio\\n\\nA. Whether the court has a duty to clarify concerning the legal interest in confirmation in this case\\n\\nAt the time the Plaintiff filed the present action, and even at the time the Supreme Court rendered the remand judgment intended to uphold the Plaintiff’s claim for confirmation of auditor status, there still remained a sufficient term of office as auditor. However, during the proceedings before the court below, the Plaintiff’s term of office expired and a successor auditor was appointed, so the Plaintiff’s claim for confirmation of auditor status became a request for confirmation of a past legal relationship. Nonetheless, even with respect to a past legal relationship, where it is recognized that obtaining a declaratory judgment concerning that legal relationship is an effective and appropriate means to remove danger or uncertainty concerning current rights or legal status, there exists a legal interest in seeking confirmation. Therefore, in such a case, the court below should not immediately dismiss the claim as improper merely on the ground that the former claim for confirmation of auditor status has become a request for confirmation of a past legal relationship, but should clarify whether the Plaintiff has a legal interest or necessity in seeking confirmation of a past legal relationship in order to remove danger or uncertainty concerning current rights or legal status, and should give the Plaintiff an opportunity to state opinions on that issue or to amend the relief sought. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) Generally, a past legal relationship cannot be the subject of an action for confirmation; however, where it constitutes the premise of a current or potential dispute among interested persons, and seeking confirmation of the past legal relationship itself can be an effective and appropriate means of resolving the related dispute in one stroke, a legal interest in confirmation is exceptionally recognized (see Supreme Court Decisions 94MEU1447, rendered on March 28, 1995; 95MEU694, rendered on November 14, 1995; etc.).\\n\\nIn this case, even though the Plaintiff’s term of office expired and a successor auditor was appointed by the time the case reached the court below, it cannot be said that there was no dispute between the parties concerning the Plaintiff’s rights or legal relationship, or that legal uncertainty or danger had disappeared. This is because the Plaintiff filed the present action after being denied auditor status by the Defendant, and the Defendant has continued to dispute this up to the final appeal proceedings in the case. If, in such a case, there is always deemed to be no legal interest in confirmation and a decision on the merits cannot be made, this may result in the court effectively refusing to adjudicate despite the existence of a substantive dispute between the parties. In practice, side effects may also arise, such as the opposing party intentionally delaying the litigation in order to avoid an adverse determination on the merits.\\n\\nFurthermore, in this case, whether the Plaintiff held the status of auditor of the Defendant, a stock company, may affect other rights or legal status of the Plaintiff premised thereon. For example, since an auditor has a claim for remuneration against the company pursuant to Articles 388 and 415 of the Commercial Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DA214202, rendered on August 27, 2015; etc.), the Plaintiff may assert against the Defendant claims for damages arising from not having received remuneration during the term of office as auditor. Also, if the Plaintiff’s damage was caused by the intentional act or gross negligence of the Defendant’s representative director, then under Article 401 of the Commercial Act, the representative director personally becomes jointly and severally liable with the Defendant for damages. Accordingly, even though it is a past legal relationship, obtaining a confirmation judgment with res judicata effect concerning the existence or absence of the Plaintiff’s auditor status, which is the subject matter of the principal claim in this case, can be an effective and appropriate means of more fundamentally resolving the foregoing subsequent disputes.\\n\\nWhether the Plaintiff held the status of auditor of the Defendant may also become a preliminary issue in a subsequent lawsuit seeking monetary payment and be examined and determined. However, such circumstance does not constitute a ground for wholly denying the legal interest in confirmation regarding the principal claim in this case. Requiring the parties and the court to repeatedly undergo assertion and proof by the parties, and examination and determination by the court, on the same issue in related disputes is not consistent with judicial economy.\\n\\n2) Article 136(4) of the Civil Procedure Act provides, “The court shall give the parties an opportunity to state their opinions on matters of law that are deemed to have been clearly overlooked by the parties.” Therefore, where there exists a legal matter clearly overlooked by the parties due to negligence or misunderstanding, or where there are legal contradictions or ambiguities in the parties’ assertions, the court shall actively exercise its power to clarify and give the parties an opportunity to state opinions; if it neglects to do so, it is unlawful as it has failed to fulfill its duty to clarify or point out matters (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 94DA34265, rendered on July 11, 1995; Supreme Court Decision 2009DA83599, rendered on February 11, 2010; etc.).\\n\\nIn a case such as this one, where at the time of filing as well as at the time of the remand judgment there still remained a sufficient term of office as auditor and the Plaintiff sought a declaration that he presently held the status of auditor, but where a change in circumstances occurred during the proceedings before the court below, namely expiration of the term and appointment of a successor auditor, the court below should have clarified whether there was a legal interest or necessity in seeking confirmation that the Plaintiff had held the status of auditor of the Defendant for a certain period in the past in order to remove danger or uncertainty concerning current rights or legal status, and should have given the Plaintiff an opportunity to state opinions on that issue or to amend the relief sought. Then, if the Plaintiff, in response to such clarification, amended the relief sought, the court should have rendered a decision accordingly and thereby sought one-time resolution of the dispute. This is because, in light of the progress of the litigation in this case, it is reasonable to regard the Plaintiff, absent special circumstances, as having an intention to obtain, rather than a judgment of improper dismissal for maintaining the former claim as is, even a confirmation judgment concerning the past auditor status that may affect current rights or legal status. In addition, such clarification by the court is based on matters that have been sufficiently asserted and proved between the parties from first instance through the remand judgment, and thus falls within the range that the Defendant could logically have foreseen; it cannot therefore be said that the Defendant would be specially prejudiced thereby.\\n\\n3) Legal interest in confirmation is a special interest in an action for confirmation and, from a state and public interest perspective, is the principle controlling the use of useless litigation. However, in this case, since examination and determination on the merits have already been conducted from the first instance through the final appeal proceedings, there is little practical benefit in the court below revisiting the existence or absence of legal interest in confirmation in order to control the use of useless litigation and reduce the burden arising from the court’s decision on the merits. Rather, if the former claim for confirmation of auditor status, on which substantive determination has already been made through the remand judgment by the final appeal, is dismissed as improper on the ground that there is no legal interest in confirmation, the problem arises that the litigation procedure ends while it remains unclear what the court’s final determination concerning the subject matter of the action is. This runs counter to the inherent function and role of judicial procedure, which must finally and uniformly resolve legal disputes.\\n\\n4) Ultimately, in this case, the court below should have clarified to the Plaintiff whether he intended to seek confirmation that he had held the status of auditor of the Defendant for a certain period in the past, and whether it was necessary thereby to remove danger or uncertainty concerning current rights or legal status, and should have given him an opportunity to state opinions on that issue or to amend the relief sought.\\n\\nB. Sub conclusion\\n\\nThe court below, merely on the ground that the former claim seeking confirmation of current auditor status had become a claim concerning a past legal relationship due to the expiration of the term, etc., dismissed the principal claim as improper for lack of a legal interest in confirmation without clarifying to the Plaintiff whether he intended to seek confirmation that he had held the status of auditor for a certain period in the past, or giving him an opportunity to state opinions. As explained above, the judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the legal interest in confirmation in an action for confirmation and the scope of the duty to clarify.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further examination and determination. It is so adjudged, with the concurrence of all participating Justices, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[80DA2424]": "1. First, we consider the appeals filed by Applicants 1, 2, 4, 3, 5, and 6, who are the successors in litigation of the deceased Non-party 1.  \\nThe above Applicants did not state the grounds of appeal in the petition of appeal, and they also did not submit a statement of grounds of appeal within the prescribed period.\\n\\n2. Next, we examine the grounds of appeal by Applicant 7.  \\n(1) With respect to Points 1, 2, 3, and 6  \\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below found that Non-party 2, who was the representative director of the Respondent Company Hanil Jesa Industry Co., Ltd. (hereinafter, referred to as the Respondent Company), entered into an agreement with Non-party Se Kyung Mulsan Co., Ltd. (hereinafter, referred to as the Non-party Company) around 1972.9.20, in order to overcome financial difficulties, to the effect that the Non-party Company would operate the Respondent Company with its funds, and that if Non-party Seongeop Corporation, having been transferred from the Korea Development Bank and with foreclosure proceedings pending, resolved the overdue principal and interest debt of approximately 124 million won by repayment, the shares of the Respondent Company would be owned in the ratio of 60 to the Non-party Company and 40 to the Respondent Company, as stated in the judgment; that at that time, Non-party 2, having been entrusted by the shareholders with stock certificates, seals, and blank assignment certificates in preparation for the need to procure funds in the course of operating the company, had been delegated authority to provide the shares as security by means such as pledge and security assignment; that, upon a request from the Non-party Company to transfer the shares in order to perform the obligations under the above agreement and to overcome the financial difficulties of the Respondent Company, he, on 1972.10.18, delivered the stock certificates for 13,200 shares, corresponding to 60% of the total number of issued shares (including part of his own shares, and all of the shares of the remaining shareholders other than Applicant 7 and Non-party 3), together with seals of the shareholders or blank assignment certificates, so as to have the form of transfer of stock certificates not bearing the shareholders’ name seal in the endorsement section, and that the Non-party Company used them to complete the form of share transfer; that the Non-party Company, while in de facto management of the Respondent Company, on 1973.3.9 repaid the above overdue principal and interest and auction expenses totaling 145,411,841 won to Non-party Seongeop Corporation, and obtained from the auction court an order revoking the decision to commence auction and a decision dismissing the application for auction; and that on 1973.4.20 it transferred 2,000 shares among the above shares to another party, leaving the remaining 11,200 shares, and the court below, on that basis, determined that the above shares were transferred to secure the claim of the Non-party Company in the event that the Non-party Company repaid the above overdue principal and interest or injected operating funds for the Respondent Company, and therefore the Non-party Company should be deemed, as a matter of law, to be in the status of a full shareholder until it is repaid the secured claim and the shares are restored; and thus it held that the resolution at the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders convened on 1973.11.15 with the permission of the Chuncheon District Court by the Non-party Company in the capacity of a minority shareholder, appointing the above Respondent 2, Respondent 3, Respondent 4, and Non-party 4 as directors and Respondent 5 as auditor, and the resolution of the board of directors held on the same day selecting Respondent 2 as representative director, were all lawful. The record shows that the above factual findings and determination of the court below are proper, and there is no illegality such as insufficient examination or violation of the rules of evidence as argued. The evidence pointed out in the grounds of appeal that was not expressly rejected by the court below is clearly intended to have been rejected in the text of the judgment below, and even if the above 13,200 shares were not allocated in equal proportion according to the number of shares held by the shareholders, such circumstance alone does not affect the validity of the share transfer in this case for security purposes; and since a resolution of the shareholders’ meeting and the affixation of the company representative’s seal on the stock certificate are not requirements for share transfer, even if, as argued, there was no lawful resolution of the shareholders’ meeting in entering into the above agreement, or some of the stock certificates of the above shares did not bear the company representative’s seal, that would have no effect whatsoever on the above determination of the court below. In the end, the argument merely attacks the judgment below on the premise of evidence that was lawfully rejected by the court below and an independent view of the matter, and thus cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(2) With respect to Point 4  \\nAccording to the facts determined by the court below, Respondent 2, appointed as director and representative director by the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders and board resolution dated 1973.6.5 of the Respondent Company, Respondent 3 and Respondent 4, appointed as directors, and Respondent 5, appointed as auditor, all resigned on 1973.10.4, prior to the filing of the present application for provisional disposition, and the registration of such resignations was completed; and the above Respondents were again appointed as officers in the same positions by the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders and board resolution dated 1973.11.15. Therefore, in the present case seeking a provisional disposition suspending performance of duties, as the right to be preserved, it may be alleged that there are defects in the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders and board resolution dated 1973.11.15 that appointed the above Respondents to their present officer positions, but it cannot be alleged that there were defects in the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders and board resolution dated 1973.6.5, which have no relation thereto. The determination of the court below to this effect is proper, and there is no illegality as argued. Accordingly, the argument lacks merit.\\n\\n(3) With respect to Point 5  \\nThe determination by the court below that, in the present provisional disposition seeking to determine a temporary status under Article 714, paragraph (2) of the Civil Procedure Act, the persons who may be the Respondents are, by their nature, Respondent 2, Respondent 3, Respondent 4, and Respondent 5, who are the directors, representative director, or auditor of the Respondent Company and who, according to Applicant 7’s own assertion, are in positions conflicting therewith, and that the Respondent Company itself does not have the capacity to be a Respondent, is proper (see Supreme Court Decision 62DA820, decided 1963.2.7; Supreme Court Decision 71DA2351, decided 1972.1.31). However, the court below did not, for this reason, revoke the part of the provisional disposition order concerning the Respondent Company and dismiss Applicant 7’s application for a provisional disposition against the Respondent Company, and it did not, as argued, revoke the part of the provisional disposition order concerning the other Respondents on the main ground of such reason. The argument arises from a misunderstanding of the purport of the judgment below, and cannot be accepted. As to the part of the grounds of appeal that alleges error in the court below’s determination regarding the existence of the right to be preserved, it is as stated above in (1).\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals by the Applicants are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties, and it is so adjudged in the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as set forth in the order."}

{"[92DA5638]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nOnce a provisional injunction suspending the performance of duties of the representative director and appointing an acting representative director has been granted, even if the representative director is thereafter removed and a new representative director is appointed, unless the provisional injunction order is revoked, the authority of the acting representative director validly continues to subsist, whereas the newly appointed representative director shall not have authority as representative director, regardless of the legality of the resolution appointing him or her. Meanwhile, such provisional injunction, by its nature, has effect not only between the parties but also against third parties; therefore, a juristic act performed by a newly appointed representative director in the capacity of a company representative in violation of such provisional injunction is ultimately invalid even in relation to third parties (see this Court’s decision dated 1991.12.24. rendered in 91DA4355), and at such time, the counterparty who entered into a juristic act with a representative director lacking authority in violation of such provisional injunction cannot assert the validity of such juristic act on the ground that he or she acted in good faith.\\n\\nThe appellate court’s determination to the same effect is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality in the form of an erroneous interpretation of the legal principles concerning the effect of a provisional injunction suspending the performance of duties of the representative director and appointing an acting representative director, as pointed out in the grounds of the appeal. The argument is without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[92DA5638]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nOnce a provisional disposition has been made suspending the performance of duties of the representative director and appointing a person to act on his behalf, even if the representative director is thereafter dismissed and a new representative director is appointed, so long as the provisional disposition order is not revoked, the authority of the acting person validly continues, whereas the newly appointed representative director does not have authority as representative director regardless of the lawfulness of the resolution appointing him. Meanwhile, since the above provisional disposition, by its nature, has effect not only between the parties but also against third parties, any juridical act performed by the newly appointed representative director in the capacity of the company representative contrary to the above provisional disposition is ultimately void even as against third parties (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on December 24, 1991, 91DA4355), and at this time, the counterparty who engaged in a juridical act with a representative director lacking representative authority in violation of the above provisional disposition cannot assert the validity of such juridical act on the ground that it was in good faith.\\n\\nThe lower court’s determination to the same purport is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality of misapprehending the legal principle concerning the effect of the provisional disposition suspending the duties of the representative director and appointing a person to act on his behalf, as pointed out in the arguments. The arguments are without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the judges involved, as set forth in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning preparation, conspiracy, and attempt are correct? (where there is a dispute, according to case law) (a) If A participated in B's commission of the offense of preparatory robbery in the form of aiding and abetting, A cannot be punished as an aider and abettor to the offense of preparatory robbery. (b) Under the Criminal Act, in order to say that there is an agreement on the commission of a crime for the establishment of the offense of conspiracy, it is insufficient merely to externally express or communicate the resolve to commit a crime; objectively, it must be clearly recognized as preparatory conduct for the execution of a specific crime, and substantial danger must be recognized in that agreement. (c) In the case of an abandonment attempt, both the upper and lower limits of the statutory punishment are reduced by one-half, whereas in the case of a frustrated attempt, depending on the degree of danger of infringement of the legal interest, the punishment may either not be reduced or only the lower limit of the statutory punishment may be reduced by one-half. (d) Where acts of preparation or conspiracy, which are punished before the commencement of execution, are involved, the concept of an abandonment attempt cannot be recognized; therefore, even if the offense is discontinued at the preparatory stage, the provisions on an abandonment attempt cannot apply. (e) If A, recognizing that the victim was in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, had sexual intercourse with the victim with the intent to exploit that condition, but from the time of commencement of execution the victim was in fact not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, then if, based on the circumstances A recognized at the time of the act, a reasonable person objectively judged that there was a risk that the result of quasi-rape would occur, an impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is established.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2018DO16002]": "We decide on the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Course of the Case\\n\\na. The Military Prosecutor indicted the Defendant on the following charge of rape.\\n\\nAt around 22:30 on April 17, 2017, while drinking alcohol with the Defendant’s wife and the Victim at his home, after the Defendant’s wife fell asleep first at around 01:00 the next day and the Victim also entered the master bedroom at around 02:00, the Defendant followed the Victim inside, touched the Victim’s breasts while she was lying down, inserted his hand into her panties and touched her genitals, and then, after blocking the Victim’s mouth as she twisted her body and made noises to escape the situation, taking off her pants and panties, had sexual intercourse once and raped her.\\n\\nb. The court of first instance granted the Military Prosecutor’s motion to amend the indictment by adding, as an alternative charge, the following allegation of quasi-rape.\\n\\nAt the date, time, and place stated in subparagraph a. above, the Defendant, by the above method, had sexual intercourse once with the Victim, who was intoxicated and lying down. By doing so, the Defendant raped the Victim by taking advantage of her inability to resist.\\n\\nc. The court of first instance, on the grounds that it could not readily conclude, based solely on the evidence submitted by the Military Prosecutor, that there had been violence or intimidation sufficient to render resistance impossible or markedly difficult, found the principal charge of rape not guilty in the reasoning and found the alternative charge of quasi-rape guilty. Only the Defendant appealed.\\n\\nd. The lower court granted the Military Prosecutor’s motion to amend the indictment by adding, as an alternative charge, the following allegation of attempted quasi-rape.\\n\\nAt the date, time, and place stated in subparagraph a. above, although the Defendant could not rape the Victim, who was not actually so intoxicated as to be unable to resist and was in a state of inability to resist, because the Victim was believed to be so severely intoxicated as to be in a state of inability to resist, the Defendant, by the above method, had sexual intercourse once with the Victim, who was lying down. By doing so, the Defendant attempted to rape the Victim by taking advantage of her inability to resist, but the attempt was not completed.\\n\\ne. The lower court found the portion of quasi-rape that had been held guilty in the court of first instance not guilty in the reasoning, on the ground that the evidence submitted by the Military Prosecutor alone was insufficient to recognize that the Victim was, at the time of this case, in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, and found guilty of the impossible attempt portion of quasi-rape added as an alternative charge. However, it deleted from the factual allegations the portion stating, “after blocking the Victim’s mouth as she twisted her body and made noises to escape the situation,” on the ground that this was an erroneous entry.\\n\\nf. Only the Defendant filed a final appeal with respect to the guilty portion. As grounds for the final appeal, the Defendant argues as follows: 1) there was no intent for quasi-rape; 2) because the Victim was in fact not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and thus engaged in sexual intercourse without infringing sexual self-determination, there was no possibility of the result of quasi-rape or risk of infringement of a protected legal interest, and therefore impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is not established. We decide on these matters in order.\\n\\n2. Grounds of Appeal Alleging No Intent for Quasi-Rape\\n\\na. 1) Article 297 of the Criminal Act provides, “A person who rapes another by violence or intimidation shall be punished by imprisonment for a fixed term of not less than 3 years.” Article 299 provides, “A person who commits sexual intercourse or indecent conduct by taking advantage of another’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist shall be punished in accordance with Articles 297, 297-2, and 298.” Since the Criminal Act punishes, by analogy to rape, the act of sexual intercourse by taking advantage of a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, rather than by means of violence or intimidation, the intent for quasi-rape means an inner will to recognize that the victim is in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and that sexual intercourse is being committed by taking advantage of such state, and to tolerate the possibility of the occurrence of the constitutive result.\\n\\n2) Where the Defendant denies intent, which is a subjective element of the constituent elements of the offense, the criminal intent itself cannot be proved objectively; therefore, by the nature of things, it must be proved by proving indirect facts or circumstantial facts that are related to the criminal intent. In determining what constitutes relevant indirect facts or circumstantial facts at this point, one must do so by rationally assessing the connected state of facts based on normal rules of experience and with careful observation and analytical ability (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DO8645, decided February 23, 2006). Meanwhile, conditional intent, which is a type of intent, requires recognition of the possibility of the occurrence of the criminal facts and, further, an inner will to tolerate the risk of the occurrence of the criminal facts. Whether the actor tolerated the possibility that the criminal facts would occur must be inferred from the actor’s psychological state by considering the form of the actor’s externally manifested conduct and the circumstances of the conduct, without relying on the actor’s statements, while taking into account how an ordinary person would evaluate the possibility that the relevant criminal facts would occur (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2004DO74, decided May 14, 2004; Supreme Court Decision 2016DO15470, decided January 12, 2017).\\n\\n3) In addition, recognition of criminal facts must reach the level of proof beyond a reasonable doubt (Article 359(2) of the Military Court Act; Article 307(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act), but the selection and weighing of evidence conducted as a premise for factual determination, and the probative value of evidence, belong to the free evaluation of the trial court of fact (Article 360 of the Military Court Act; Article 308 of the Criminal Procedure Act). This means that it is within the judge’s free evaluation of evidence to select and use the necessary evidence among the evidence having evidentiary capacity and to assess the substantive value of the evidence in recognizing the facts. Therefore, unless a judge rejects sufficiently probative evidence without reasonable grounds or, conversely, adopts and uses evidence that plainly contradicts objective facts without any reasonable grounds, thereby violating the rules of logic and experience, the judge may, based on free evaluation of evidence, adopt evidence and recognize facts (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2007DO1755, decided May 29, 2008; Supreme Court en banc Decision 2013DO11650, decided August 20, 2015).\\n\\nb. The lower court, for the reasons stated in its opinion, determined that the Defendant had intent for quasi-rape. The ground of appeal on this point merely disputes such factual findings of the lower court and criticizes the lower court’s choice of evidence and evaluation of probative value, which belong to the free evaluation of the trial court of fact. Even in light of the following circumstances discernible from the lower court’s reasoning and from the evidence lawfully admitted and examined above, namely, the circumstances in which the Defendant, the Defendant’s wife, and the Victim drank together; the respective amounts of alcohol consumed by the Defendant and the Victim; the situation in which the Victim, even if she had not reached a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, was intoxicated after drinking for a long time beyond her capacity, entered the master bedroom, and lay down; the Victim’s condition when the Defendant commenced the act of quasi-rape; and the content of the text messages exchanged between the Defendant and the Victim after the offense, it was proper for the lower court to recognize that the Defendant had intent for quasi-rape. There is no error in the lower court’s judgment, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, that violates the rules of logic and experience, exceeds the limits of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehends the legal principles on intent for quasi-rape.\\n\\n3. Grounds of Appeal Alleging That Impossible Attempt of Quasi-Rape Is Not Established\\n\\na. Article 300 of the Criminal Act punishes attempts of the offense of quasi-rape. In addition, Article 27 of the Criminal Act provides, “A person shall be punished when, although the occurrence of the result is impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, there is danger. However, the punishment may be mitigated or remitted,” thereby punishing impossible attempts.\\n\\nAccordingly, where the Defendant, believing that the Victim was in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and, with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state, had sexual intercourse with the Victim, but the Victim was in fact not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, then, due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, the occurrence of the constitutive result prescribed in the offense of quasi-rape was impossible from the outset, and it cannot be said that such result actually occurred. Since the Defendant commenced the execution of quasi-rape but the offense did not reach consummation, an attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is established. Because, from the standpoint of an ordinary person objectively evaluating the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time of the act, there was a risk of the result of quasi-rape occurring, impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is established (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DO8105, decided December 8, 2005; Supreme Court Decision 2015DO7343, decided August 13, 2015).\\n\\nb. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) Impossible attempt as provided in Article 27 of the Criminal Act refers to a case in which the actor has criminal intent and has engaged in conduct that can be regarded as commencement of execution, but due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, there is from the outset no possibility of satisfying the constituent elements. However, although fulfillment of the constituent elements is impossible as a result, if the conduct is dangerous, it is punished as impossible attempt. Impossible attempt differs from factual mistake in that the actor mistakenly believes that a fact that does not actually exist does exist.\\n\\n2) The Criminal Act provides in Article 25(1), “When a person has commenced the execution of a crime but has failed to complete the act or the result has not occurred, the person shall be punished as an attempt,” thereby providing for a thwarted attempt, and in Article 26, “When an offender voluntarily ceases the act commenced for execution or prevents the occurrence of the result caused by such act, the punishment shall be mitigated or remitted,” thereby providing for an abandoned attempt. A thwarted attempt or abandoned attempt is distinguished from impossible attempt, because, when the act of commencement of execution is viewed, there was a possibility that the intended completed offense would be established, and thus there was a possibility that the constitutive result could occur.\\n\\n3) The “mistake as to the means or object of execution” prescribed in Article 27 of the Criminal Act means that, due to the nature of the means of conduct or object of conduct attempted by the actor, occurrence of the result is impossible from the outset. And “impossibility of occurrence of the result” should be understood to mean that the offense cannot be completed because of the original impossibility of the means or object of execution.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the “danger” constituting a requirement for impossible attempt, which is distinguished from an impossible offense, should be determined by objectively considering, from the standpoint of an ordinary person, the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time of the act, and asking whether there was a possibility of the occurrence of the result (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 77DO4049, decided March 28, 1978; Supreme Court Decision 2005DO8105, decided December 8, 2005).\\n\\n4) The offense of quasi-rape prescribed in Article 299 of the Criminal Act is an offense established by committing sexual intercourse by taking advantage of another person’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, and its protected legal interest is the sexual self-determination of a person who cannot exercise sexual self-defense due to mental or physical circumstances (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 98DO3257, decided May 26, 2000). Because a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist must exist in the victimized person, the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape is a “person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” And the act corresponding to the constituent elements is “committing sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” If sexual intercourse is committed against a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist by taking advantage of such state, the constituent elements are satisfied and the offense of quasi-rape is consummated.\\n\\nIf the Defendant believed that the Victim was in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and had sexual intercourse with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state, but the Victim was in fact not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist from the beginning of the commencement of execution, it may be said that, due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, there was no possibility of consummation of the offense of quasi-rape from the outset. In such a case, if, from the standpoint of an ordinary person objectively considering the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time of the act, there was a risk that the result of quasi-rape would occur, thereby infringing the sexual self-determination of a person who cannot exercise sexual self-defense due to mental or physical circumstances, impossible attempt is established.\\n\\nc. Examining the reasoning of the lower court judgment in light of the legal principles above, this case corresponds to a situation in which the Defendant had sexual intercourse with the Victim with intent for quasi-rape, but the Victim was in fact not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, so that the occurrence of the result of quasi-rape was impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, and, from the standpoint of an ordinary person objectively considering the circumstances recognized by the Defendant, there is danger because there was a possibility of the occurrence of the result. Although some portions of the reasoning of the lower court judgment are not entirely proper, the lower court’s conclusion that impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is guilty is proper. There is no error in the lower court’s judgment, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles on impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition. In this judgment, the opinions of the Justices were unanimous except for the dissenting opinion of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Ahn Chul-sang, and Kim Sang-hwan on whether impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is established; there are also supplementary opinions by Justices Park Sang-ok, Park Jeong-hwa, and Kim Seon-su in support of the majority opinion, and supplementary opinions by Justices Min Yu-sook and No Jeong-hee.\\n\\n5. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Ahn Chul-sang, and Kim Sang-hwan\\n\\na. 1) Article 13 of the Criminal Act (Intent) provides, “An act that does not recognize the facts constituting an element of a crime shall not be punished.” Here, the “facts constituting an element of a crime” means the objective constituent elements, which are external indicia in the constituent elements of offenses prescribed in the Criminal Act, namely, the actor, object, act, result, etc. By contrast, the psychological or mental state belonging to the actor’s inner self is called a subjective constituent element, of which intent is the typical example. Since Article 13 of the Criminal Act provides that, for a willful offense to be established, the actor must have recognition of the actor, object, act, result, etc. that are objective constituent elements, where the constituent elements require a special mode of conduct, such as “violence or intimidation” in rape or “taking advantage of a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist” in quasi-rape, the actor must also recognize the existence of such circumstances.\\n\\n2) The Criminal Act provides in Chapter 32 of Part II the “Offenses of Rape and Indecent Acts.” The offenses prescribed in this Chapter are all crimes that involve infringement of an individual’s sexual freedom or sexual self-determination, and their basic constituent elements are the offense of rape (Article 297) and the offense of forcible indecent assault (Article 298). Rape is an offense established by raping another person by violence or intimidation. Rape means sexual intercourse with another person by making resistance impossible or markedly difficult through violence or intimidation. Sexual intercourse broadly means an unlawful act of satisfying sexual desire, but here it means insertion of the male genital organ into the female genital organ. In the offense of rape, the act constituting the offense is rape, its special mode of conduct is “violence or intimidation,” the object is a person, and the constitutive result is sexual intercourse. The offense of quasi-rape (Article 299) is an offense established by committing sexual intercourse by taking advantage of another person’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist; the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor, etc. (Article 302), is an offense established by committing sexual intercourse by deceit or force against a minor or a person with diminished mental capacity; and the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor (Article 305) is an offense established by committing sexual intercourse with a person under 13 years of age. The offense of quasi-rape differs from the rape offense, which is the basic constituent element of offenses under Chapter 32 of the Criminal Act, in its objective constituent elements, in that its special mode of conduct is taking advantage of a person’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist; the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor, etc. (Article 302), in that its object is a minor or a person with diminished mental capacity and its special mode of conduct is the use of deceit or force; and the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor (Article 305), in that its object is a person under 13 years of age and that it is established even if violence or intimidation, deceit or force are not used as the means of the offense. However, like the offense of rape, they all share the protected legal interest of infringement of sexual self-determination, that is, they all require the occurrence of the constitutive result of sexual intercourse.\\n\\nb. Article 27 of the Criminal Act (Impossible Offense) provides, “A person shall be punished when, although the occurrence of the result is impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, there is danger. However, the punishment may be mitigated or remitted.” The “impossible offense” referred to in the heading of this provision means a case in which, by the nature of the criminal act, there can absolutely be no possibility of the occurrence of the result or of infringement of the protected legal interest (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 98DO2313, decided October 23, 1998; Supreme Court Decision 2007DO3687, decided July 26, 2007). Here, a “mistake as to the means of execution” means a case in which execution has been commenced, but, although the means chosen by the actor cannot, by its nature, actually cause the intended result to occur, the actor, due to ignorance or error, assumes the possibility of consummation of the relevant constituent act. And a mistake as to the object means a case in which the actor, although due to the nature of the object of conduct chosen by the actor the object is defective or placed in a state in which it cannot be infringed and thus cannot actually cause the intended result to occur, assumes the possibility of consummation of the relevant constituent act due to ignorance or error. Meanwhile, in Article 27 of the Criminal Act, “impossibility of occurrence of the result” is a concept that includes not only the impossibility of completion of the offense but also the impossibility of realization of the offense. If judgment is made at the ex post facto point after the act has been completed, all forms of attempted offense prescribed in the Criminal Act can be seen as situations in which the result did not occur; thus, if one does not distinguish between “non-occurrence of the result,” that is, the fact that the result did not actually occur, and “impossibility of occurrence of the result,” that is, the impossibility of realizing the offense, a thwarted attempt and an impossible attempt cannot be distinguished. In other words, the “impossibility of occurrence of the result” in Article 27 of the Criminal Act is a concept strictly distinguishable from “non-occurrence of the result,” which is revealed at the stage of factual determination.\\n\\nAlthough the heading of this provision is “impossible offense,” its content concerns the punishable impossible offense, namely “impossible attempt.” Impossible attempt means a case in which, by the nature of the act, there is no possibility in any case that the constituent elements will be realized, but punishment is imposed as an attempt offense because of “danger.” The precedents take the position that, as the standard for determining impossible attempt, danger should be assessed by considering, from an objective standpoint, whether there was a possibility of the occurrence of the result based on the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time of the act (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 77DO4049, decided March 28, 1978; Supreme Court Decision 2005DO8105, decided December 8, 2005). On this basis, the Supreme Court held, ① in a case where the Defendant tried to kill the Victim by making her drink decoction mixed with pesticide made from “chowpuri” or “bujja,” that the Defendant’s act fell under a case in which the occurrence of the result was impossible due to a mistake as to the means of execution, but that punishment as attempted murder was proper because there was danger (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2007DO3687), and ② in a case in which an indictment was brought for attempted quasi-forcible indecent assault after nighttime intrusion into a residence, that because the Victim had already died when the Defendant intruded into the Victim’s residence, the Defendant’s act fell under a case in which the occurrence of the result was impossible due to a mistake as to the object, but that, because there was danger, the lower court properly found the Defendant guilty of impossible attempt of quasi-forcible indecent assault after intrusion into a residence (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DO5355, decided July 11, 2013).\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of Article 27 of the Criminal Act is that, because realization of the constituent elements in the manner intended by the actor was objectively impossible from the outset, the actor would in principle not be subject to punishment even as an attempt offender; however, in exceptional cases that satisfy the danger requirement from a normative perspective, the actor should be treated as an attempt offender and made subject to criminal punishment. For this reason, whether the occurrence of the result is impossible under Article 27 of the Criminal Act must be judged not by the actor who mistook the means or object of execution, but by whether there is a probability of the occurrence of the result under any condition, when the meaning of the act itself is viewed from the standpoint of an insightful ordinary person. Accordingly, where there is a probability of the occurrence of the result under certain conditions but, because of the circumstances at the time of the act, the result did not occur, it is not an impossible attempt but only a thwarted attempt.\\n\\nc. 1) First, we examine the course of this case. The gist of the original charge in this case is that “the Defendant, at around 02:00 on April 18, 2017, at the master bedroom of his home, touched the Victim’s breasts while she was lying down, blocked the Victim’s mouth, took off her pants and panties, and had sexual intercourse once, thereby raping her.” In response, the Defendant denied the offense at the first instance trial, arguing that although it was true that the Victim was intoxicated at the time of the offense as stated in the indictment, the sexual intercourse was consensual. The Military Prosecutor then added an alternative charge alleging that “at the date, time, and place above, the Defendant touched the Victim’s breasts while she was intoxicated and lying down, took off her pants and panties, and had sexual intercourse once, thereby raping her by taking advantage of her inability to resist.” The court of first instance found the principal charge not guilty in the reasoning on the ground that there was no proof of the criminal facts concerning violence or intimidation, and found the alternative charge of quasi-rape guilty.\\n\\nOnly the Defendant appealed the first instance judgment, and defense counsel filed a statement of reasons for appeal, disputing that there was no proof of the crime with respect to the allegation that the Defendant took advantage of the Victim’s inability to resist. The Military Prosecutor then additionally cited, in the alternative, Articles 300, 299, and 297 of the Criminal Act, which are the applicable provisions for the offense of attempted quasi-rape, with respect to the offense of quasi-rape found guilty in the first instance. This means that, even if the Victim was not in a state of inability to resist as the Defendant alleged, the Defendant had intent for quasi-rape, and thus the offense of attempted quasi-rape (impossible attempt) could be established. The lower court accepted the Military Prosecutor’s argument and held that, although there was insufficient evidence to recognize that the Victim was, at the time of this case, in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, and therefore this fell under a case in which the proof of the criminal facts was lacking, so long as the Defendant had intent for quasi-rape, it constituted impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape.\\n\\n2) The Defendant was indicted for the offense of rape and the offense of quasi-rape among the “offenses of rape and indecent acts” prescribed in Chapter 32 of Part II of the Criminal Act. Rape and quasi-rape are result offenses that require the occurrence of a constitutive result, and also offenses of infringement that require actual infringement of the protected legal interest. Therefore, whether the constitutive result of rape or quasi-rape occurred must be determined based on whether sexual intercourse took place, that is, whether the protected legal interest, the individual’s sexual self-determination, was infringed. In this case, both the court of first instance and the lower court recognized that sexual intercourse, which is the constitutive result of the offenses of rape and quasi-rape, took place. However, the court of first instance only found that there was no evidence that the special mode of conduct of rape, namely “violence or intimidation,” had been used, and the lower court only found that there was no evidence that sexual intercourse had been committed by the special mode of conduct of quasi-rape, namely “taking advantage of a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” As to the point that the Victim’s sexual self-determination was infringed by the sexual intercourse, there is no doubt. Then, does this case truly correspond to a case in which the occurrence of the result is impossible under Article 27 of the Criminal Act, that is, a “case in which, by the nature of the criminal act, there can absolutely be no possibility of the occurrence of the result or of infringement of the protected legal interest” (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2007DO3687)? It should be answered in the negative. This case is not a matter to be discussed in the domain of attempts.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that where the Defendant believed that the Victim was in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and, with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state, had sexual intercourse with the Victim, but the Victim was in fact not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, then, due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, the occurrence of the result of quasi-rape was impossible and the result corresponding to the constituent elements of quasi-rape did not actually occur, but because, from the standpoint of an ordinary person objectively considering the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time of the act, there was a risk of the result of quasi-rape occurring, impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is established. However, because the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape is a person, there is no mistake as to the object in the sense that the object could not be the subject of realization of the constituent elements from the outset in this case. Further, there was no mistake as to the identity of the object in the Defendant’s selection of the Victim as the object of sexual intercourse. Although the majority opinion states as if the Defendant also had a “mistake as to the means of execution,” it gives no explanation as to in what respect there was a mistake as to the means of execution in this case. It is erroneous for the majority opinion to hold that this case falls under a case in which the occurrence of the result of quasi-rape, namely infringement of the Victim’s sexual self-determination by sexual intercourse, was impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution.\\n\\nThe majority opinion views the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape as a “person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” However, Article 299 of the Criminal Act provides that “A person who commits sexual intercourse or indecent conduct by taking advantage of another’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist shall be punished in accordance with Articles 297, 297-2, and 298,” and thus punishes “committing sexual intercourse or indecent conduct” against a “person” by “taking advantage of a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” That is, taking advantage of a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist corresponds to the special mode of conduct of the constituent elements as a method of offense, and the object of the constituent act is a person. This point becomes clearer when compared with Article 297 of the Criminal Act, which provides, “A person who rapes another by violence or intimidation shall be punished by imprisonment for a fixed term of not less than 3 years.” The part in Article 297 corresponding to “by violence or intimidation” in Article 299 is the part “by taking advantage of another’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” It is the same for both rape and quasi-rape that the sexual intercourse, which is the constituent act and also the constitutive result, occurs when the victim is placed in a state in which resistance is impossible. The difference is only that rape makes resistance impossible by “violence or intimidation,” whereas quasi-rape “takes advantage of” an already existing state of inability to resist. The view of the majority opinion is an interpretation that goes beyond the text of the penal provision.\\n\\nThe majority opinion holds that, because it was ex post facto confirmed that the Victim was not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist at the time the Defendant attempted the offense, it was impossible for the Defendant to take advantage of the Victim’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, and therefore the occurrence of the result of the offense of quasi-rape was impossible from the outset. However, does this case truly correspond to a case in which the occurrence of the result is impossible, as prescribed in Article 27 of the Criminal Act, that is, a case in which, by the nature of the criminal act, there can absolutely be no possibility of the occurrence of the result or of infringement of the protected legal interest? The majority opinion’s concern and legal construction are worth hearing, but an affirmative answer cannot readily be given. As seen above, the “impossibility of occurrence of the result” in Article 27 of the Criminal Act is a concept that includes not only the impossibility of completion of the offense but also the impossibility of realization of the offense, and thus is different from the concept of “non-occurrence of the result,” meaning that the result did not actually occur. In this case, the court of first instance found the offense of quasi-rape guilty. The lower court found that the evidence was insufficient to recognize the offense of quasi-rape as guilty. The Military Prosecutor additionally cited, in the alternative, at least impossible attempt of quasi-rape in case the offense of quasi-rape was found not guilty. It has already been observed that the legislative purpose of Article 27 of the Criminal Act was not intended for such a case. This case is merely a matter of whether the evidence is sufficient with respect to the special mode of conduct that constitutes the constituent elements of the offense of quasi-rape for which the Military Prosecutor seeks application.\\n\\n3) In conclusion, the majority opinion confuses the issue of conformity to the constituent elements or satisfaction of the constituent elements with the meaning of impossibility of occurrence of the result under Article 27 of the Criminal Act. If one follows the majority opinion, it would amount to saying that if the Defendant’s conduct fails to satisfy the constituent elements of the offense charged by the prosecutor, that corresponds to a case in which the occurrence of the result is impossible, and it would lead to the conclusion that even where the prosecutor fails to prove the facts constituting the elements of the offense prescribed in the applicable provision stated in the indictment, as in this case, the Defendant may be punished as an impossible attempt offender. Such a theory of interpretation cannot be accepted because it would completely hollow out the principle of legality in criminal law, the fundamental principle of modern criminal law.\\n\\nd. Nevertheless, the lower court, unlike this, held that attempted quasi-rape, which was charged as an alternative count, was established based solely on the circumstances stated in its opinion. This lower court judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles on impossible attempt under Article 27 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state my dissent from the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Concurring Opinion by Justices Park Sang-ok, Park Jeong-hwa, and Kim Seon-su on the Majority Opinion\\n\\nI would supplement the majority opinion’s grounds and offer several views regarding the criticism in the dissenting opinion.\\n\\na. 1) Penal statutes must be strictly construed and applied according to their text, and no analogical interpretation may be made arbitrarily in a manner unfavorable to the Defendant. However, even in construing penal statutes, teleological interpretation taking into account the legislative purpose and objective of the statute, and its legislative history, is not excluded so long as it does not go beyond the ordinary meaning of the statutory text (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2007DO2162, decided June 14, 2007; Supreme Court Decision 2009DO13332, decided May 13, 2010). Furthermore, examining the legislative purpose of a penal statute, its overall content, and structure, and finding a reasonable interpretive standard that shapes or limits the type of conduct corresponding to the constituent elements by the understanding and judgment of an ordinary person properly equipped with the ability to distinguish things, is also an act of interpreting and applying the law and does not violate the principle of legality in criminal law (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2001DO3531, decided November 13, 2001).\\n\\n2) The majority opinion distinguishes impossible attempt from thwarted attempt or abandoned attempt based on whether there is “impossibility of occurrence of the result” as prescribed in Article 27 of the Criminal Act, and distinguishes impossible attempt from non-punishable impossible offense based on whether there is “danger.”\\n\\na) The forms of crime that the Criminal Act fundamentally regulates are those satisfying the objective constituent elements and the subjective constituent elements, and among them the objective constituent elements involve the performance of a certain act or the occurrence, as a result of that act, of a certain infringement upon the legal interest that the Criminal Act seeks to protect, and that a normative causal relation and objective attribution between such act and result are recognized. Therefore, an attempted offense under the Criminal Act, like a completed offense, has intent as to the realization of a specific constituent element as a subjective constituent element, but it may be regarded as a reduced form of offense in which the objective constituent elements are not completed and the requirements for the establishment of the offense are reduced.\\n\\nb) Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act provides, “When a person has commenced the execution of a crime but has failed to complete the act or the result has not occurred, the person shall be punished as an attempt,” thereby providing for a thwarted attempt, and Article 26 provides, “When an offender voluntarily ceases the act commenced for execution or prevents the occurrence of the result caused by such act, the punishment shall be mitigated or remitted,” thereby providing for an abandoned attempt. An act that has commenced execution is punished as a thwarted attempt or an abandoned attempt because, although the constitutive result of actual infringement or endangerment of the protected legal interest has not occurred, there was commencement of execution and a possibility that the result would occur. Accordingly, a thwarted attempt or abandoned attempt may be said to be an attempt offense in which realization of the constituent elements was possible, that is, the occurrence of the result was possible, but the offense did not reach completion.\\n\\nc) Originally, an impossible offense means a case in which the actor has criminal intent and has engaged in conduct that appears externally to be commencement of execution, but, by the nature of the act, the occurrence of the result is impossible, that is, a case in which, because there is no possibility of realization of the constituent elements, the offense in principle is not established. However, as a legislative decision on whether to subject impossible offenses to criminal punishment, Article 27 of the Criminal Act, under the heading of impossible offense, provides, “A person shall be punished when, although the occurrence of the result is impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, there is danger. However, the punishment may be mitigated or remitted,” thereby exceptionally punishing impossible attempts that involve danger. The “impossibility of occurrence of the result” prescribed in Article 27 of the Criminal Act is an essential marker of impossible attempt, and the content of the constitutive result does not change depending on whether it is an impossible attempt or a thwarted attempt or abandoned attempt. Therefore, there is no basis for interpreting the “occurrence of the result” in Article 27 of the Criminal Act differently from the “occurrence of the result” in Articles 25(1) and 26 of the Criminal Act, and because an impossible attempt is also a type of attempt offense, the “impossibility of occurrence of the result” in Article 27 of the Criminal Act must be interpreted to mean that the offense could not reach completion because there was no possibility from the outset that the constituent elements would be satisfied.\\n\\nd) The Supreme Court held, in a case where the Defendant, intending to kill his husband, mixed pesticide into cabbage soup and made him drink it, but the Victim spat out the soup, that, although the Defendant’s act fell under a case in which the occurrence of the result was impossible due to a mistake as to the means of execution, it was proper to punish it as attempted murder because there was danger, and that the lower court’s failure to examine whether the Defendant’s act fell under either case was unlawful (see Supreme Court Decision 83DO2967, decided February 14, 1984). The Supreme Court also held that, in a case where the Defendant, believing that the Victim was in a state of mental incapacity, inserted his finger into the Victim’s genitalia, but the Victim was in fact not in a state of mental incapacity, the Defendant’s act made the occurrence of the result of attempted quasi-forcible quasi-rape impossible due to a mistake as to the object, and danger was recognized, so there is a high likelihood that impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is established (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO7343, decided August 13, 2015).\\n\\nThrough such decisions, the Supreme Court made clear that thwarted attempt and impossible attempt are distinguished, and that impossible attempt is established, from the outset of commencement of execution, when fulfillment of the constituent elements is ultimately impossible but danger exists.\\n\\nb. The dissenting opinion states that, because the offense of quasi-rape is a result offense that requires the occurrence of a constitutive result and an offense of infringement that requires actual infringement of the protected legal interest, whether the constitutive result occurred must be determined based on whether sexual intercourse took place, that is, whether the protected legal interest, the individual’s sexual self-determination, was infringed; therefore, since the Victim’s sexual self-determination was infringed by sexual intercourse, which is the constitutive result of the offense of quasi-rape, there is no room for impossible attempt. Furthermore, it states that the majority opinion confuses the issue of conformity to the constituent elements or satisfaction of the constituent elements with cases in which the occurrence of the result is impossible. However, the above criticism in the dissenting opinion is not proper for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) The offense of quasi-rape under Article 299 of the Criminal Act is consummated when a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist is sexually intercourse with by taking advantage of such state. Sexual intercourse with a person who is not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist is neither the object nor the constitutive act of the offense of quasi-rape; therefore, even if sexual intercourse has occurred, it cannot be said that the offense of quasi-rape has reached completion. If the Defendant had sexual intercourse with the Victim with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of the Victim’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, but the Victim was in fact not in such a state, then, at the time of commencement of execution, because of a mistake as to the means or object of execution, the constituent elements could not be satisfied, and thus the offense of quasi-rape could not be completed; accordingly, the issue is whether impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is established. Once the Defendant has commenced execution with intent for quasi-rape, it is in principle obvious, given the logic of criminal theory, that the conduct becomes subject to criminal evaluation.\\n\\n2) The dissenting opinion contends that “sexual intercourse” itself is the constitutive result of the offenses of rape and quasi-rape, but this is contrary to the Criminal Act’s system of separately prescribing rape and quasi-rape as distinct constituent elements. In rape and quasi-rape, the result of infringement of sexual self-determination, which is the protected legal interest, is not produced by the sexual intercourse itself alone, but only when combined with a separate act of the perpetrator or the victim’s state, etc., that infringes the victim’s right of self-determination. Therefore, the dissenting opinion appears to confuse “act,” which corresponds to one of the objective constituent elements, with “consummation,” which means the occurrence of the constitutive result.\\n\\nc. The dissenting opinion states that, because the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape is “a person,” it cannot be said that there was a mistake as to the object in this case, and that the majority opinion, which interprets the object of the act as “a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist,” goes beyond the textual scope of the penal provision. It also states that the majority opinion did not explain in what respect there was a mistake as to the means of execution.\\n\\n1) The Criminal Act provides in Chapter 32 of Part II the “Offenses of Rape and Indecent Acts,” explicitly prescribing as the object of the act in the offense of rape (Article 297) “a person,” as the object of the act in the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor, etc. (Article 302) “a minor or a person with diminished mental capacity,” and as the object of the act in the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor (Article 305) “a person under 13 years of age.” By contrast, the offense of quasi-rape prescribed in Article 299 of the Criminal Act is an offense of sexual intercourse by taking advantage of another person’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, and “by taking advantage of” means that the actor recognizes a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and that, because of such state, sexual intercourse became easier. Therefore, the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape must be understood as “a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” Because one must take advantage of “another person’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist,” the object of the act can only be interpreted as a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist. This is because one does not take advantage of another person other than the sexual partner’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist. Since the majority opinion systematically and logically interprets Article 299 of the Criminal Act within the ordinary meaning and scope of such wording, we cannot agree with the dissenting opinion that the majority opinion goes beyond the wording of the penal provision.\\n\\n2) The “mistake as to the means of execution” prescribed in Article 27 of the Criminal Act refers to the impossibility or unsuitability of means, meaning that, by the method of conduct attempted by the actor, the occurrence of the result is impossible from the outset. A “mistake as to the object” refers to the impossibility or unsuitability of the object, meaning that the object of the conduct attempted by the actor cannot be the object that satisfies the constituent elements. As seen above, the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape is “a person in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist,” and the act corresponding to the constituent elements is “committing sexual intercourse by taking advantage of a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.” In the offense of quasi-rape, that the Victim is in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist is not only a characteristic of the object but also a premise of the means of execution. If the Defendant believed that the Victim was in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and had sexual intercourse with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state, but the Victim was in fact not in such a state, then this corresponds to a case in which, because of the impossibility or unsuitability of the method of conduct or the object of conduct attempted by the Defendant, there was no possibility from the outset that the offense of quasi-rape could reach completion. Since, as above, the mistake as to the means of execution and the mistake as to the object cannot be clearly distinguished, and distinguishing whether the case is a mistake as to the means or a mistake as to the object does not affect the conclusion that “the occurrence of the result is impossible,” there is no practical benefit in making the distinction. Therefore, the dissenting opinion’s criticism that the majority opinion does not explain in what respect the Defendant had a mistake as to the means of execution, or that the Defendant had no mistake as to the object on the premise that the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape is simply “a person,” is incorrect.\\n\\nd. The dissenting opinion states that, according to the majority opinion, the conclusion would be reached that any conduct that does not satisfy the constituent elements of a crime is always an impossible offense and may be punished as an attempt offense if there is danger, and that this theory of interpretation would completely hollow out the principle of legality in criminal law. However, the above criticism in the dissenting opinion is not proper for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) The majority opinion does not mean that impossible attempt is established for all acts not satisfying the constituent elements; it means that the punishability of impossible attempt under Article 27 of the Criminal Act must be determined only where the constituent elements cannot be satisfied from the outset because of a mistake as to the means or object of execution.\\n\\n2) An impossible attempt under criminal law, like other attempt offenses, also requires intent for realization of a specific constituent element as a subjective constituent element, and conditional intent suffices. Such subjective constituent element forms part of the criminal facts and requires strict proof beyond a reasonable doubt; if the prosecutor’s proof does not reach the level that creates such conviction, the matter must be decided in the Defendant’s favor (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2012DO231, decided June 28, 2012; Supreme Court Decision 2017DO12649, decided December 22, 2017).
