Therefore, if the Defendant’s intent, which is a subjective constituent element, cannot be recognized, there is no need to consider whether impossible attempt was established in the first place.\\n\\n3) Article 27 of the Criminal Act provides that a person shall be punished when, although the occurrence of the result is impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, there is danger, thereby exceptionally recognizing the establishment of a punishable impossible attempt. The majority opinion merely means that impossible attempt can be established only in cases where such requirements for impossible attempt are satisfied, and does not purport to extend impossible attempt to cases where the occurrence of the result is impossible for reasons other than a mistake as to the means or object of execution, or to cases where there is no danger.\\n\\n4) Article 29 of the Criminal Act provides, “The crimes punishable as attempts shall be prescribed in each relevant article,” meaning that an attempt is punished only where there is a punishment provision, and impossible attempt is punished only where there is danger, as provided in Article 27 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\n5) Accordingly, it cannot be said that the majority opinion’s logic hollow out the principle of legality in criminal law.\\n\\ne. Article 13 of the Criminal Act provides, “An act that does not recognize the facts constituting an element of a crime shall not be punished,” and the majority opinion and the dissenting opinion agree that the “facts constituting an element of a crime” means the objective constituent elements, which are external indicia in the constituent elements of offenses prescribed in the Criminal Act, namely, the actor, object, act, result, etc.\\n\\nHowever, the dissenting opinion concludes that, in this case, impossible attempt is not in issue because it is not a case of “mistake as to the means or object” under impossible attempt, and that the Defendant is simply not guilty. If the meaning of “impossibility of occurrence of the result due to a mistake as to the means or object,” which is a requirement of impossible attempt under Article 27 of the Criminal Act as assumed by the dissenting opinion, is limited to cases in which the actor thought the object was a person but it was actually not a person, then in a case where the Defendant saw the Victim lying down, believed that the Victim was in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, and had sexual intercourse with the Victim with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state, but the Victim had already died at the time of commencement of execution, impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape would be established, whereas if the Victim was alive but in fact not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, the conclusion would be not guilty. Such a conclusion is difficult to accept for the following reasons. First, once the Defendant has commenced conduct of having sexual intercourse with the Victim with intent for quasi-rape, whether the Victim was dead at that time or alive but not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist cannot be a reason affecting intent for quasi-rape. Second, from the standpoint of objectively existing facts at the time of commencement of execution, the circumstance that the Victim was dead and the circumstance that the Victim was alive but not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist are the same in that there was no possibility of realizing the constituent elements of the offense of quasi-rape and therefore consummation could not be reached; yet there is no rational reason to treat them differently by recognizing impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape only in the former case. Third, if a not-guilty verdict were rendered on the ground that the Victim was not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and therefore there was no conformity to the constituent elements, that would amount to protecting the sexual self-determination of a deceased victim more strongly than that of a living victim, which is unreasonable.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state the concurring opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Concurring Opinion by Justices Min Yu-sook and No Jeong-hee on the Majority Opinion\\n\\na. This case concerns a situation in which only the Defendant filed a final appeal against the lower court’s recognition of impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape. Therefore, whether the offense of quasi-rape is consummated is not subject to review in the final appeal, and only the issue of whether impossible attempt is established is in dispute. With respect to the distinction between thwarted attempt and impossible attempt, and between impossible offense and impossible attempt, and the relationship between the problem of satisfaction of the constituent elements and impossibility of occurrence of the result, I proceed on the premise of what the previous concurring opinion on the majority opinion discussed, and below I will supplement only the elements of the offense of quasi-rape to the extent necessary to show that the establishment of an attempted offense of quasi-rape in this case is clear.\\n\\nb. Regarding intent for quasi-rape and commencement of execution\\n\\n1) Impossible attempt is a form of attempt offense, and the establishment of an attempt offense requires intent and commencement of execution, while also requiring incompletion of the offense.\\n\\n2) Article 299 of the Criminal Act provides that a “person who commits sexual intercourse by taking advantage of another person’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist” shall be punished for quasi-rape. “Mental incapacity” means a state in which a person cannot make a judgment regarding sexual conduct because of mental disorder or impaired consciousness, and “inability to resist” means a state in which psychological or physical resistance is impossible or markedly difficult due to reasons other than mental incapacity. “Taking advantage of” means recognizing that the victim is in such a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and using it as a means to facilitate sexual intercourse. Therefore, intent for quasi-rape is recognized where the Defendant has commenced execution with a definite intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of the Victim’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, having recognized such state, or with conditional intent to the effect that it does not matter even if sexual intercourse is committed by taking advantage of such state.\\n\\n3) Commencement of execution of a crime is recognized when conduct that corresponds to the constituent elements or conduct closely linked to such conduct is begun. In the case of the offense of quasi-rape, for example, if the Defendant undresses a sleeping Victim, lowers his own pants, and touches the Victim’s genitalia, then at that point he has begun conduct that can be regarded as a means of sexual intercourse, with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by taking advantage of the Victim’s inability to resist, and commencement of execution of the offense of quasi-rape can be recognized (see Supreme Court Decision 99DO5187, decided January 14, 2000). The Supreme Court has held in such a case that even if the Victim woke up because the Defendant performed the above acts, there is no obstacle to the establishment of attempted quasi-rape.\\n\\n4) As the majority opinion has examined, the Defendant’s ground of appeal that there was no intent for quasi-rape in this case lacks merit. Also, in light of the factual circumstances found by the lower court based on evidence lawfully admitted, it can be sufficiently recognized that the Defendant engaged in conduct that can be regarded as commencement of execution of quasi-rape. Although the dissenting opinion does not expressly state so, it appears to assume this. If so, the Defendant’s conduct must be regarded as an attempted offense of quasi-rape unless it constitutes a non-punishable impossible offense.\\n\\nc. Regarding whether sexual intercourse and the establishment of an attempted offense are mutually exclusive\\n\\n1) Nevertheless, I think the reason the dissenting opinion questions the establishment of the attempt offense itself is largely because sexual intercourse occurred in this case. A summary of the dissenting opinion’s argument on this point is as follows. In this case, the constitutive result of sexual intercourse occurred, and the Victim’s sexual self-determination was infringed by the sexual intercourse. Therefore, this does not correspond to a case in which the occurrence of the result is impossible under Article 27 of the Criminal Act, and it is not a matter to be discussed within the domain of attempts.\\n\\nIn this way, the dissenting opinion says that, while the constitutive result occurred, neither the completed offense nor even an attempt offense is established, and while stating that impossible attempt is not established, it remains silent on whether a thwarted attempt is established. To point out the logical inconsistency of the dissenting opinion, we first examine the relationship between sexual intercourse and the completion of the offense or consummation.\\n\\n2) A Korean dictionary explains the meaning of “sexual intercourse” as “illicit sexual relations” or “sexual relations, usually with someone other than one’s spouse.” As can be seen from this, although the term “sexual intercourse” contains a negative connotation, it is generally understood not to include the meaning of coercive elements or sexual relations against the other party’s express or implied will. Therefore, directly linking sexual intercourse with infringement of sexual self-determination creates confusion between the act or the factual result of the act and infringement of the protected legal interest, and thus they need to be used distinctly. On this premise, reconsidering the constituent elements of rape and quasi-rape, rape and quasi-rape do not punish sexual intercourse itself, but instead define and punish as crimes sexual intercourse when it is carried out by a method that infringes the victim’s sexual self-determination, such as suppressing the victim’s will to refuse by violence or intimidation. Therefore, even if sexual intercourse took place as the Defendant intended or desired, rape or quasi-rape cannot be said to have been consummated unless the sexual intercourse was committed by violence or intimidation or by taking advantage of the victim’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist.\\n\\nThis sort of case, in which the completion of the offense is denied due to lack of causation even though what the Defendant aimed for or desired was realized, is often discussed in the context of extortion and fraud. In the case of extortion, if the Defendant used violence or intimidation with extortionate intent but the Victim was not actually frightened and instead disposed of property for another reason, then the Defendant obtained the intended result of acquiring property, but extortion is not evaluated as consummated. The same is true in the case of fraud, where the Defendant engaged in deceptive conduct with intent to obtain property but the Victim, without falling into error, delivered property for another reason. This is because causation between the Defendant’s violence or intimidation, etc. and the Victim’s act of disposal is denied. In rape and quasi-rape as well, even if the result intended or desired by the Defendant occurred, an attempted offense can be established due to lack of causation. Incompleteness of the offense means that the constitutive result did not occur, and it is not determined by whether the actor achieved his purpose.\\n\\n3) Further, one may ask whether, unless sexual intercourse is committed by the Defendant’s violence or intimidation or by conduct taking advantage of a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, there is no infringement or danger of infringement of the Victim’s sexual self-determination, and thus even an attempt offense cannot be established. However, we must consider whether this question is perhaps based on a prejudice that forcing sexual intercourse on a victim is impossible unless there is violence or intimidation sufficient to render resistance impossible or markedly difficult, or unless such a state is used.\\n\\nIn the offense of quasi-rape, interpreting “a state of inability to resist” as a state in which resistance is absolutely impossible or markedly difficult is influenced by the need to balance with the position of the narrowest interpretation, which most strictly requires a degree of violence or intimidation in establishing rape (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DO2001, decided April 23, 2009). One of the long-standing grounds for limiting violence or intimidation to the narrowest scope in rape is the notion that, unless the degree is such that resistance is impossible or markedly difficult, rape against the victim’s will is impossible. However, this is not very different from a leap to the conclusion that, if the victim did not resist with all possible effort, the victim consented to sexual intercourse and therefore there was no infringement of the victim’s sexual self-determination, by arbitrarily interpreting the victim’s will. There is a wide gap between the two situations. In everyday life, too, we often fail to respond properly to unexpected attacks, unlike what we would rationally imagine in ordinary circumstances. Even if an act of attack is minor when viewed objectively and ex post facto, the specific circumstances at the time may cause serious fear or psychological or physical paralysis or confusion. Moreover, one must not make the mistake of demanding only the victim to make a rational and desirable choice in an absurd and abnormal criminal situation and then blaming the victim for failing to do so. In other words, even sexual intercourse not carried out by the degree of violence or intimidation or by taking advantage of a state of inability to resist required by the Criminal Act and by the Supreme Court through interpretation of the criminal norms governing rape and quasi-rape may still actually infringe the victim’s sexual self-determination in many cases. And the possibility of that is greater the more strictly the constitutive act is interpreted.\\n\\nReturning to this case, as noted above, the only issue in this case is whether impossible attempt of the offense of quasi-rape is established. Therefore, if, because of the Defendant’s mistake, sexual intercourse by taking advantage of the Victim’s inability to resist was objectively impossible, but, when objectively assessed in light of the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time, there was a risk of consummation, the establishment of impossible attempt is recognized. And this is also affirmed where the Defendant commenced execution with intent for quasi-rape but did not reach sexual intercourse. Yet if, instead, one says that because sexual intercourse was realized as the Defendant desired, there was no risk of infringement of the Victim’s sexual self-determination, that can only be called an inversion of the proper order of analysis. In conclusion, the majority opinion’s interpretation based on the constituent elements of the offense of quasi-rape under criminal law and the requirements for impossible attempt accords with the principle of legality in criminal law.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state the concurring opinion to the majority opinion."}

{"[2018DO5475]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the case and issues\\n\\na. The defendant was indicted on the charged facts of assault and attempted aggravated bodily injury: “On or about December 23, 2016, he assaulted Victim Person Not Indicted 1 and, on the same day, stabbed Victim Person Not Indicted 2 in the chest with a kitchen knife, which was a dangerous object, but Victim Person Not Indicted 2 pushed the defendant’s hand away with his hand, tearing only the victim’s clothing and resulting in an attempt.”\\nThe court of first instance applied Article 260(1) of the Criminal Act to the assault allegation among the above charged facts against the defendant and found him guilty, selecting imprisonment, and applied Article 258-2(3), (1), and Article 257(1) of the Criminal Act to the attempted aggravated bodily injury allegation and found him guilty. The statutory punishment for the assault offense selected by the court of first instance is “imprisonment for not more than 2 years,” and the statutory punishment for attempted aggravated bodily injury is “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years.” Thereafter, the court of first instance, after mitigating the attempted aggravated bodily injury offense pursuant to Article 25(2) and Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act (the term of punishment for attempted aggravated bodily injury became imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years), imposed aggravation for concurrent offenses on the punishment prescribed for the more severe offense of attempted aggravated bodily injury; however, because the term obtained by adding together the upper limits of attempted aggravated bodily injury and assault (7 years) was lower than the term obtained by aggravating by one-half of the upper limit of attempted aggravated bodily injury (7 years and 6 months), it determined the punishment to be imposed within the combined range (imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 7 years). And within the range of the punishment to be imposed, it sentenced the defendant to imprisonment for 8 months, suspended for 2 years, and ordered probation and 120 hours of community service.\\nThe defendant appealed the judgment of the court of first instance on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence. The court below dismissed the defendant’s appeal.\\n\\nb. Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act provides that “The punishment of an attempt may be mitigated from that of a completed offense.” A case in which the statute provides that the punishment “may be mitigated” as above is called discretionary mitigation. When a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, precedents have held to the effect that “it is not erroneous for the court below not to mitigate by law pursuant to such ground of discretionary mitigation” (see Supreme Court Decisions 91DO985 rendered on June 11, 1991, 2005DO6120 rendered on September 29, 2005, 2014DO15131 rendered on February 12, 2015, etc.), thereby taking the position that even if a ground for discretionary mitigation exists, whether to mitigate is within the court’s discretion. And if mitigation for a determinate term of imprisonment is decided, the current practice of the courts is to reduce both the upper limit and the lower limit of the term of punishment by one-half pursuant to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act.\\nHowever, there is a question whether it is proper for the court to decide in its discretion whether to mitigate when a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized. In addition, it is said that the method of mitigating both the upper limit and the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half in the case of discretionary mitigation is also improper. More specifically, in this case, it is said that the court of first instance maintained by the court below erred in reducing both the upper limit and the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half when it mitigated the attempted aggravated bodily injury offense pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act. Therefore, the issue in this case is whether the current interpretive theory regarding discretionary mitigation is valid.\\n\\n2. Meaning of discretionary mitigation\\n\\nSentencing is divided into stages such as checking the statutory punishment, determining the punishment to be imposed, and determining the sentence. When sentencing, a judge must determine the sentence only within the range of the punishment to be imposed formed through aggravation and mitigation of the statutory punishment, taking into account sentencing conditions (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DO8376 rendered on September 11, 2008, etc.).\\nArticle 25 of the Criminal Act provides that a person shall be punished as an attempted offender if the execution of a crime has been commenced but the act has not been completed or the result has not occurred (paragraph 1), and that the punishment for an attempt may be mitigated from that of a completed offense (paragraph 2). Mitigation of punishment pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act is a type of mitigation by law and is distinguished from extenuating mitigation (Criminal Act, Article 53), which is mitigation in the exercise of judicial discretion. As to mitigation by law, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act provides the method of mitigation according to the type of punishment. What constitutes grounds for mitigation by law and whether mitigation must be made when such grounds are recognized are separately and specifically provided in the Criminal Act and special statutes. Such mitigation provisions are phrased in the statutory text as “the punishment shall be mitigated” or “the punishment may be mitigated”; cases phrased as “shall be mitigated” are called mandatory mitigation, and cases phrased as “may be mitigated” are called discretionary mitigation. Mitigation of punishment pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act falls under discretionary mitigation.\\nIn the case of mandatory mitigation, if the existence of a ground for mitigation is recognized, mitigation by law pursuant to Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act must be made; whereas in the case of discretionary mitigation, even if the existence of a ground for mitigation is recognized, the judge may or may not mitigate by law pursuant to Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act. Furthermore, once the existence of a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized and the judge accordingly mitigates the term of imprisonment by law, both the upper limit and the lower limit are reduced by one-half pursuant to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act. The interpretation of current precedents and practice remains valid. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\na. The Criminal Act specifically prescribes the method, content, and grounds of mitigation by law, and its meaning is also clear.\\nThe Criminal Act sets the statutory punishment corresponding to conduct that falls under the elements of a crime, and through aggravation and mitigation by law, as well as extenuating mitigation, it provides that the final punishment to be imposed is to be determined. In other words, the punishment to be imposed is solely the result of a judge’s application of law based on legal provisions. Whereas extenuating mitigation is to reduce punishment solely by the judge’s discretion, mitigation by law is to reduce punishment when the grounds for mitigation prescribed by the Criminal Act are recognized, and whether the method of mitigation is extenuating mitigation or mitigation by law, the method of mitigation must follow Article 55 of the Criminal Act according to the type of punishment. Mitigation by law is classified into mandatory mitigation, in which mitigation must be made when the existence of a ground for mitigation is recognized, and discretionary mitigation, in which mitigation may or may not be made even if the existence of a ground for mitigation is recognized. If the statute provides that punishment may be mitigated or exempted, either mitigation or exemption from punishment may be chosen.\\nSpecifically, the grounds for mandatory mitigation or reduction of punishment prescribed by the Criminal Act are termination attempt (Article 26), the provisions of special parts concerning voluntary surrender at the stage of preparation or conspiracy (Articles 90, 101, 111(3), 120, 175, 213), false testimony, false accusation, and confession and voluntary surrender (Articles 153, 154, 157), and the familial relationship between the receiver of stolen property and the principal offender (Article 365(2)). The grounds for mandatory mitigation are deafness and muteness (Article 11) and aider and abettor (Article 32(2)). The grounds for discretionary reduction or exemption are excessive self-defense (Article 21(2)), excessive emergency evacuation (Article 22(3)), excessive self-help (Article 23(2)), impossible attempt (Article 27), subsequent concurrent offenses (Article 39(1)), and voluntary surrender and confession (Article 52). The grounds for discretionary mitigation are mental and physical disorder (Article 10(2)), impeded attempt (Article 25(2)), organization of a criminal organization (Article 114), and release of a kidnapped person (Article 324-6). Meanwhile, in the en banc Decision 2017DO14609 rendered on April 18, 2019, the Supreme Court confirmed that even when mitigating punishment under Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act for concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act concerning mitigation by law applies, and thus when mitigating a determinate term of imprisonment, it cannot be mitigated to less than one-half of that term.\\n\\nb. In light of the principle of nulla poena sine lege, the current precedents and practice regarding discretionary mitigation are faithful to the text and conform to the system of the Criminal Act.\\nThe principle of nulla poena sine lege requires that crimes and punishments be prescribed by law in order to protect the freedom and rights of individuals from arbitrary exercise of the state’s punitive power. In light of that purpose, interpretation of penal statutes must be strict, and interpretation beyond the possible meaning of the language in a manner unfavorable to the defendant is not permitted under the prohibition on expansive interpretation, which is part of the principle of nulla poena sine lege (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO17847 rendered on March 10, 2016, etc.). When interpreting statutes, systematic and logical methods of interpretation may be used, taking into account legislative intent and purpose, legislative and amendment history, harmony with the overall legal order, and the relationship with other statutes, but if the text itself is composed of relatively clear concepts, in principle there is no need to use such interpretive methods, or their use is necessarily limited. This is even more so in the interpretation of penal statutes to which the principle of nulla poena sine lege applies (see en banc Supreme Court Decision 2015DO8335 rendered on December 21, 2017).\\nThe Criminal Act expresses mandatory mitigation of punishment in the text as “shall be mitigated,” while in the case of discretionary mitigation, like extenuating mitigation, it expresses the punishment in the text as “may be mitigated.” The words “may” denote the possibility or general ability of some proposition and include the meaning that it “may not” be done. In light of the meaning of the phrase “may,” the legislator, in cases of discretionary mitigation, has allowed punishment to be mitigated or not mitigated depending on the circumstances, and has conferred that authority or discretion on the judge. Such an interpretation is not only natural in terms of the text, but also close to everyday language usage and readily understandable to anyone. So long as it accords with the text and the legislator’s intent, it does not constitute analogical interpretation prohibited under the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\nMeanwhile, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act prescribes the method of mitigation by law according to the type of punishment, and Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act provides that “When reducing determinate imprisonment or determinate penal detention, the term shall be reduced by one-half.” It is clear from the text that, when reducing a determinate term of imprisonment, not only one of the “minimum term” or “maximum term” is reduced by one-half, but the “term of punishment,” that is, both the maximum and minimum statutory terms, are reduced by one-half. Since the punishment to be imposed becomes the final standard for the sentence, its scope must be strictly determined according to law, and unless there is a separate express provision, it is not possible to recognize other grounds for mitigation of a different nature that do not fall within the grounds for aggravation or mitigation enumerated in Article 56 of the Criminal Act (see en banc Supreme Court Decision 2017DO14609 rendered on April 18, 2019). Accordingly, in the case of mitigation by law for a determinate term of imprisonment, methods such as reducing only either the maximum term or the minimum term by one-half, or mitigating beyond one-half, instead of reducing both the maximum and minimum terms as provided in Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act, cannot be permitted under the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\nc. The Criminal Act distinguishes discretionary mitigation from mandatory mitigation, and precedents and practice clearly distinguish the two.\\nAs noted above, most grounds for mitigation by law are grounds related to the requirements for the establishment of a crime, such as satisfaction of the elements of an offense, unlawfulness, or culpability, or are grounds related to the degree of illegality or the degree of infringement of the protected legal interest. The legislator, after designating important matters related to the establishment and punishment of crimes as requirements for mitigation by law, has classified and prescribed them as mandatory mitigation or discretionary mitigation, comprehensively considering the general effect or importance that such requirements have on the establishment of crimes or determination of the scope of punishment.\\nConsidering the purpose of distinguishing and prescribing grounds for mandatory mitigation and grounds for discretionary mitigation as above, their legal effects must also be clearly distinguished. For example, impeded attempt, in which execution of the crime has been commenced but completion of the criminal act has not been achieved due to external circumstances, is prescribed as discretionary mitigation, whereas termination attempt, in which execution of the crime has been commenced but the act is voluntarily discontinued or the result is prevented before completion, is prescribed as mandatory mitigation; accordingly, their legal effects must be clearly distinguished. The legal evaluation of cases in which the offender commenced execution to realize the unlawful act and thereby created a risk of infringement of a legal interest but then made efforts to return to legality on his or her own (termination attempt), and cases in which the offender’s intent to realize the unlawful act remains unchanged but the result of infringement of the legal interest did not occur due to external factors (impeded attempt), must inevitably differ significantly. Under current practice and precedents, in the case of termination attempt, both the upper and lower limits of the statutory punishment are reduced by one-half, whereas in the case of impeded attempt, depending on the degree of risk created to the legal interest, mitigation of the statutory punishment may not be made or both the upper and lower limits may be reduced by one-half, and the choice is left to the judge’s discretion. However, if, unlike this, one interprets the minimum term of the statutory punishment as being reduced by one-half in both termination attempt and impeded attempt, and the maximum term of the statutory punishment as being reduced by one-half only in the case of termination attempt and not reduced in the case of impeded attempt, one ignores the need for legal evaluation of termination attempt and impeded attempt as well as the judge’s case-specific evaluation according to individual circumstances, thereby rendering meaningless the legislative purpose of distinguishing mandatory mitigation from discretionary mitigation.\\nd. There is no error in the current practice that if there is no need to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed, there is no need to bother with discretionary mitigation.\\nThe Criminal Act provides, with respect to the order of application when grounds for aggravation and mitigation of punishment coexist, that aggravation by the principal provision of the special part, aggravation under Article 34(2), aggravation for recidivism, mitigation by law, aggravation for concurrent offenses, and extenuating mitigation are applied in that order (Article 56), and the punishment to be imposed is calculated through the process of aggravation and mitigation according to this order. Discretionary mitigation is a type of mitigation by law, and when the existence of the relevant ground for mitigation is recognized, whether to actually perform the corresponding mitigation should be independently determined by considering the weight the ground for mitigation such as diminished capacity, attempt, or voluntary surrender has in the act’s unlawfulness or the illegality of the result, and the degree to which it affected the offense. However, to assess the extent to which the relevant ground for discretionary mitigation occupies in the unlawfulness of the act or illegality of the result of the offense, consideration of other sentencing conditions will inevitably be necessary.\\nIn addition, it cannot be legally or logically wrong for a judge, in the process of determining the punishment to be imposed, to decide whether to apply discretionary mitigation while mentally envisioning the final sentence, taking into account sentencing conditions for the defendant. Sentencing, that is, determination of punishment, consists of the process of selecting the type of punishment based on the statutory punishment, then aggravating or mitigating it to determine the punishment to be imposed, and then determining the specific sentence within the range of that punishment to be imposed. Mitigation by law is provided in Article 55 of the Criminal Act, together with sentencing conditions (Article 51), voluntary surrender and confession (Article 52), extenuating mitigation (Article 53), selection of punishment and extenuating mitigation (Article 54), and the order of aggravation and mitigation (Article 56), in Part 1, Chapter 3, Section 2, “Sentencing.” Discretionary mitigation is mitigation by law within the process for sentencing. In sentencing, considerations of sentencing conditions are indispensable for a judge to decide matters in which discretion is granted to the judge, such as the selection of punishment or extenuating mitigation. It is difficult to imagine a judge selecting the type of punishment or deciding whether to apply extenuating mitigation without considering sentencing conditions. Therefore, once the legislature has conferred on the judge discretion or authority regarding discretionary mitigation, it is in fact difficult for the judge, in deciding whether to mitigate, to completely exclude consideration of other sentencing conditions and to deliberate solely on the ground for discretionary mitigation.\\nIn current practice, even if there is a ground for discretionary mitigation, the method of not bothering to apply discretionary mitigation unless it is necessary to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed has been accepted. However, this practice does not mean that the sentence is first determined and then the question of discretionary mitigation is decided. As noted above, since the legislature has conferred discretionary mitigation on the judge’s discretion or authority, the judge necessarily cannot avoid considering other sentencing conditions apart from the ground for discretionary mitigation in deciding whether to apply discretionary mitigation, and in that process may to some extent mentally sketch the sentence. Accordingly, current practice can be understood to mean that, within this process of judgment, there is no practical benefit to bothering with discretionary mitigation unless it is necessary to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed, and thus it is sufficient to consider it as a sentencing factor or sentencing condition under the sentencing guidelines. If there is no need to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed, it should not be deemed unlawful for the current practice not to bother with discretionary mitigation.\\ne. A judge is granted broad discretion from the point a guilty verdict is affirmed to the point of determining the sentence, and the judge’s discretion regarding discretionary mitigation is one of them and cannot be regarded as improper.\\nThe Criminal Act prescribes that one offense may be punished by several types of punishment and then leaves it to the court to determine the type of punishment to be applied to the defendant (Article 54). Most penal provisions, except for treason (Criminal Act, Article 93), which prescribes only death, prescribe as principal punishments two or more of the types of punishment set forth in Article 41(1) through (8) of the Criminal Act (death, imprisonment for life, penal detention for life, determinate imprisonment, determinate penal detention, deprivation of qualifications, suspension of qualifications, fine, detention, and petty fine), thereby conferring on the judge the authority to select the type of punishment most suitable for the case and the defendant. The legislature prescribed various types of punishment and a broad range of sentencing for individual crimes and then made the judge first select the type of punishment and determine the specific sentence within the range of the punishment to be imposed. This is because the legislature could not predefine in advance a proper sentence that takes into account all sentencing conditions for each individual offense, so it granted the judge considerable discretion starting with the selection of the type of punishment.\\nFurthermore, a judge may mitigate the punishment when there are grounds to consider circumstances of the offense with respect to the punishment to be imposed after all aggravation and mitigation by law have been made (Criminal Act, Article 53). This is called judicial mitigation, extenuating mitigation, or mitigation in consideration of circumstances, and is the final mitigation applied when, even after all mitigation by law has been made, a sentence lower than the punishment to be imposed must be imposed (see Supreme Court Decision 91DO985 rendered on June 11, 1991, etc.), functioning as a device to correct cases in which the statutory punishment or the punishment to be imposed after aggravation and mitigation by law is excessively severe.\\nUltimately, the judge determines the sentence within the range of the punishment to be imposed, considering all sentencing conditions and referring to the sentencing guidelines of the Sentencing Commission.\\nAs such, examining the concrete sentencing process that a judge carries out to determine the sentence after the facts constituting the offense are found guilty reveals that the judge is granted broad discretion. This is a measure chosen for objective, reasonable, and specifically appropriate sentencing by fully considering all sentencing conditions in each individual case, from the selection of the type of punishment to the determination of the sentence. Considering these wide-ranging discretions granted to the judge, it cannot be said to be unreasonable to interpret that the judge has the authority or discretion to decide whether to mitigate with respect to discretionary mitigation. The need for and method of proper control of such judicial discretion are separate issues.\\n\\nf. There is no need to uniformly define the legal effect of discretionary mitigation.\\nEven if the existence of a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, there are cases in which applying mitigation by law pursuant to that ground would instead offend the notion of justice. There are cases where a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized but mitigation pursuant thereto is deemed appropriate not to be made, such as cases where, even though the offense is an attempt and the constitutive result did not occur, a result of grave severity nearly identical to a completed offense has occurred (for example, in homicide, where the victim did not die but remained in a coma for a long period or became a vegetative patient), or cases where the offense was committed while in a diminished capacity state but mitigating punishment on account of diminished capacity would be inappropriate. In other words, the Criminal Act’s provision that punishment “may be mitigated” means that even if a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, there may be cases where mitigation pursuant thereto is necessary and cases where it is not necessary, so that where the effect of reducing unlawfulness of the act or result due to discretionary mitigation is minimal or the degree of reduction of the offender’s culpability is low, punishment may be imposed with a heavier punishment to be imposed without mitigation. And the authority or discretion to make that judgment is conferred on the judge. There is no need to interpret it so as to produce a uniform legal effect without considering these various situations.\\n\\n3. Resolution of this case\\n\\na. For the reasons stated in its opinion, the court below affirmed the first-instance judgment that found both the assault offense and attempted aggravated bodily injury offense guilty and, with respect to attempted aggravated bodily injury, mitigated punishment for attempt pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act and then reduced both the upper and lower limits of the term by one-half pursuant to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act, and then determined the punishment to be imposed after aggravation for concurrent offenses. In light of the legal principles noted above, the above measures of the court below are lawful.\\n\\nb. Meanwhile, the argument to the effect that the court below’s sentencing determination is unlawful because it did not reflect the settlement with Victim Person Not Indicted 1 ultimately amounts to an argument of inappropriateness of sentence. However, according to Article 383(4) of the Criminal Procedure Act, a final appeal on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence is allowed only in cases in which the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or penal detention for not less than 10 years has been imposed. In this case, where a lighter sentence than that was imposed on the defendant, arguments to the effect that the sentence is too severe and improper or that probation and the community service order should be reduced do not constitute lawful grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the final appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition. Except for the separate opinion of Justice Lee Gi-taek, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there is a concurring opinion of Justice Lee Gi-taek to the separate opinion.\\n\\n5. Justice Lee Gi-taek’s separate opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. The following is the face of our criminal trials.\\n\\n(1) Defendants who committed the same offense and have the same grounds for aggravation and mitigation of punishment are punished with different punishments to be imposed.\\n(2) In a guilty judgment, the sentence corresponding to the disposition is determined first, and then the punishment to be imposed, which is the range of the sentence, is determined.\\n(3) It is lawful to set the punishment to be imposed for a defendant’s same offense at 3 years to 30 years, and it is also lawful to set it at 4.5 months to 3 years and 9 months.\\n(4) When aggravation for concurrent offenses is imposed among several offenses with different punishments, which offense’s prescribed punishment is aggravated depends on the judge’s discretion.\\n(5) Even when the sentence is set at the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed, an appeal may be filed on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence.\\n(6) In order to accept the appellate ground of inappropriateness of sentence and impose a lighter punishment than in the first instance, the part applying the law to determine the punishment to be imposed must be revised.\\nThe current face of criminal trials as described in (1) through (6) above appears even without applying extenuating mitigation under Article 53 of the Criminal Act, and it should be regarded not merely as undesirable but as unlawful. Nevertheless, the majority opinion seeks to continue such trials, whereas the separate opinion seeks to correct them and conduct proper trials. Below, the problems arising under the current practice regarding discretionary mitigation as in the majority opinion are identified, and solutions thereto are proposed.\\n\\nb. In the Criminal Act, the provision that punishment “may be mitigated” as a ground for mitigation of punishment is called discretionary mitigation in practice. The current practice of the courts understands the above text as conferring on the judge authority or discretion to mitigate or not mitigate. Because of such authority or discretion, in the case of discretionary mitigation, the punishment to be imposed exists in two forms. Taking the attempted aggravated bodily injury offense under Article 258-2(3), (1), and Article 257(1) of the Criminal Act (imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years) as an example, if the punishment is mitigated pursuant to Article 25(2) and Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act, the punishment to be imposed appears in the form of “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years”; if the punishment is not mitigated, the punishment to be imposed appears in the form of “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years.” Current practice allows the judge to determine the punishment to be imposed by choosing one of those two forms depending on whether to apply discretionary mitigation, and then to determine the sentence within that range. Since whether to mitigate is within the judge’s discretion, in effect sentencing is conducted within the combined range of the two, that is, imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years.\\nThe new interpretive theory based on the correct understanding of discretionary mitigation argued below in the separate opinion (hereinafter the “new interpretive theory”) is as follows. In the case of attempted aggravated bodily injury, the statement in Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act that the punishment “may be mitigated” means that the sentence may be determined across both the range “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years,” in which mitigation is made pursuant to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act, and the range “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years,” in which no mitigation is made, which ultimately means that the punishment to be imposed is determined as “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years,” combining the two ranges. As a result, the same conclusion is reached as if only the lower limit of the statutory punishment is reduced by one-half while the upper limit is left unchanged, but this is the result of combining the above two ranges and does not mean that the upper limit is not mitigated.\\nFrom the standpoint of the legal effect of discretionary mitigation, current practice can be called an “election discretion” because one of two punishments to be imposed is selected, whereas the new interpretive theory can be called “automatic determination” because the same legal effect (the punishment to be imposed) always arises.\\nMeanwhile, before its amendment by Act No. 15982 on December 18, 2018, Article 10(2) of the former Criminal Act provided mandatory mitigation of punishment for a person with diminished capacity, but with the amendment of that statute, mitigation of punishment for a person with diminished capacity was changed to discretionary. Claims of diminished capacity and the determination thereof are frequently at issue in practice, so the importance of the interpretive theory regarding discretionary mitigation has increased as a result of the amendment of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nc. The current practice regarding discretionary mitigation has understood that when there is a ground for mandatory mitigation, mitigation by law is always made, but when there is a ground for discretionary mitigation, it is “not necessary to mitigate unless needed to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed.” Taking attempted aggravated bodily injury as an example, as noted above, depending on whether the judge mitigates for attempt, two forms of punishment to be imposed are possible, such as “imprisonment from 6 months to 5 years” and “imprisonment from 1 year to 10 years.” However, because mitigation is limited to cases where the sentence is lower than the punishment to be imposed and is “needed to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed,” in the end the judge is made to determine the sentence first, then if the sentence is less than 1 year apply mitigation, and if the sentence is 1 year or more not apply mitigation. As seen in the above example, “where needed to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed” means where the sentence is lower than the punishment to be imposed before mitigation, and this means that discretion as to whether to mitigate is ultimately a sentencing consideration. The process of determining the punishment to be imposed and sentencing should be distinguished. According to the majority opinion seeking to maintain the current practice, the following problems arise.\\n\\n1) Current practice does not faithfully reflect the actual decision-making process of judges in criminal trials.\\nIn the case of attempted aggravated bodily injury, according to current practice, depending on whether attempt mitigation is applied, two punishments to be imposed are possible: imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years, and imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years. Current practice in effect determines the sentence within the range of imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years, and then notes in the judgment whether mitigation has been applied depending on which of the two punishments to be imposed the sentence falls into. According to the wording of the judgment, the process consists of two stages: discretionary selection of the punishment to be imposed and determination of the sentence. However, this differs greatly not only from the actual decision-making process of judges handling criminal trials, but also from decision-making in our everyday life.\\nFor example, in an everyday situation, if one is to purchase an item by first choosing either the range of “300,000 won to 700,000 won” or the range of “500,000 won to 1,000,000 won,” and then purchasing within the chosen range, a reasonable person would think this is equivalent to being able to purchase within the entire range of “300,000 won to 1,000,000 won.” One would not first determine one of the two ranges and then think of purchasing within that range. Nevertheless, in the above example, the current practice is to choose the range “300,000 won to 700,000 won” from the ranges “300,000 won to 700,000 won” and “500,000 won to 1,000,000 won,” and then purchase an item worth 600,000 won within that range, whereas the new interpretive theory is to directly purchase an item worth 600,000 won within the combined range of “300,000 won to 1,000,000 won.” Judges handling actual criminal trials also do not in fact think in the unnecessary two-stage structure of deciding whether to apply discretionary mitigation and then selecting the sentence accordingly as in current practice; rather, taking into account the fact that grounds for discretionary mitigation exist, they determine the sentence within the combined range of the above two punishments to be imposed (in the case of attempted aggravated bodily injury, imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years). Thus, current practice, while failing to reflect the actual decision-making process of judges, adopts an unnecessary two-stage judgment structure that does not conform to reality.\\nBy contrast, the new interpretive theory directly determines the sentence within the combined range of the above two ranges by setting as the punishment to be imposed a range in which only the lower limit of the statutory punishment is reduced by one-half. This is consistent with the actual decision-making process of judges.\\n\\n2) Current practice is contrary to the structure of judicial reasoning and violates Article 56 of the Criminal Act.\\nThe structure of judicial reasoning is no different from a judge’s structure of reasoning. A judge reaches a conclusion by determining the arguments and facts of the parties that may affect the result of the trial in a legal, logical, and systematic order of reasoning. In other words, once the judicial reasoning structure is followed, the conclusion (the disposition) is automatically derived. Here, arguments and facts that may affect the conclusion are called “legal requirements,” the result of applying law thereto is called the “legal effect,” and the legal, logical, and systematic order of reasoning can be called the “reasoning structure.” A trial is the process of deriving the legal effect corresponding to the legal requirements according to the reasoning structure. Changing or modifying the order in which legal requirements are determined as established in the reasoning structure cannot be permitted. In civil cases, after determining the cause of action and defenses, the court determines a rejoinder, but depending on how the rejoinder is decided, the court cannot retroactively revise its determination of the cause of action or defenses. Furthermore, after the disposition is determined, revising the determination of the cause of action or defenses again is even less permissible.\\nIn criminal trials, if the judge finds the facts constituting the offense through evidence examination, the judge determines the punishment to be imposed through the process of applying the relevant statutes, and then determines the sentence within that range. Application of the law means first identifying the statutory provision applicable to the relevant facts and checking the statutory punishment, and then, pursuant to Article 56 of the Criminal Act, aggravation and mitigation are applied in the following order: “1. aggravation by the principal provision of the specific part; 2. aggravation under Article 34(2); 3. aggravation for recidivism; 4. mitigation by law; 5. aggravation for concurrent offenses; 6. extenuating mitigation,” thereby determining the punishment to be imposed. Within the range of the punishment to be imposed thus determined, the judge determines the sentence by considering all sentencing conditions for the defendant. Since this process is the reasoning structure for determining the sentence, which may be called the final conclusion of a criminal trial, failure to follow or going against this process cannot be permitted. However, as noted above, current practice limits discretionary mitigation to situations where “the sentence is lower than the punishment to be imposed,” which is no different from first determining the final sentence and then deciding or modifying whether mitigation by law regarding discretionary mitigation should apply, thereby adjusting the punishment to be imposed to fit the sentence. The process of reasoning regarding the punishment to be imposed and the sentence under current practice is no different from the proposition that when a set of legal effects (no mitigation) resulting from applying the legal requirements (attempt, etc., grounds for discretionary mitigation) do not conform to the conclusion (sentence), those legal effects can be differently applied in the exercise of discretion (mitigation applied). This is logically improper, and making the determination of mitigation by law after first determining the sentence violates Article 56 of the Criminal Act, which prescribes the order of aggravation and mitigation of punishment, and is unlawful.\\nUnder the new interpretive theory, however, if a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the same legal effect, namely a changed punishment to be imposed, always arises, so the problem of deciding or revising the determination of mitigation by law according to the sentence in contravention of the structure of criminal adjudication does not occur.\\n\\n3) Current practice is contrary to the principle of nulla poena sine lege in that the punishment to be imposed becomes unclear when grounds for discretionary mitigation are recognized.\\nThe principle of nulla poena sine lege provided in Article 12(1) of the Constitution has as its core content the requirement that crimes and punishments be prescribed by formal statutory law enacted by the legislature; furthermore, even if prescribed by formal statutory law, it requires that the elements of the offense be clearly defined so that anyone can foresee what conduct the relevant provision seeks to punish and what punishment attaches thereto, and thus decide his or her own conduct accordingly (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DO3600 rendered on November 14, 2003). Under the principle of nulla poena sine lege, not only crimes but also punishments must be clearly prescribed by law. Since a judge determines the sentence within the range of the punishment to be imposed derived through aggravation and mitigation prescribed by law on the statutory punishment set by the penal provision, matters concerning aggravation and mitigation of punishment for deriving the punishment to be imposed, as well as the provisions concerning the statutory punishment, must be clearly prescribed by law, and interpretation thereof must likewise be clear so as to ensure the foreseeability of punishment.\\nHowever, even though it has been clearly established through adjudication that a ground for discretionary mitigation of punishment exists, if the application of that ground is determined solely at the judge’s discretion, this in effect leads to a result contrary to the principle of clarity, a derivative principle of nulla poena sine lege. If a ground for mitigation of punishment is prescribed by law and exists, yet whether to mitigate is interpreted as a judge’s discretion (the so-called “OX discretion”), and no standard is provided regarding the reasonable scope and exercise of such discretion, the defendant is effectively unable to know the range of punishment to be imposed for his or her act, and it opens the door to arbitrariness in the judge’s determination of the punishment to be imposed, thereby violating the principle of clarity under nulla poena sine lege. In the example of attempted aggravated bodily injury, the defendant is placed in an unstable situation, not knowing whether he or she will be punished by the punishment to be imposed of “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years” or “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years.” Furthermore, if one assumes a case in which a person commits attempted robbery under Article 342 and Article 333 of the Criminal Act while in a diminished capacity and then voluntarily surrenders (the choice of exemption is excluded from consideration; the same applies hereinafter), the statutory punishment for robbery is “imprisonment for not less than 3 years and not more than 30 years,” and depending on how many times the judge applies mitigation by law due to the three grounds for discretionary mitigation—diminished capacity, attempt, and voluntary surrender—four different forms of punishment to be imposed may arise. Specifically, if no discretionary mitigation is applied at all, the punishment to be imposed becomes “imprisonment for not less than 3 years and not more than 30 years,” whereas if all three grounds for discretionary mitigation above are applied, it becomes “imprisonment for not less than 4.5 months and not more than 3 years and 9 months,” showing that the deviation in the punishment to be imposed based solely on the judge’s discretion is excessively large.\\nMeanwhile, in the example of attempted aggravated bodily injury, if attempt mitigation is not applied, the range of the punishment to be imposed is “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years,” whereas if attempt mitigation is applied, the range becomes “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years,” making it possible to impose a sentence between 6 months and 1 year. Considering that the punishment to be imposed means the final range from which the sentence can be determined after aggravation and mitigation of punishment, the punishment to be imposed, which serves as the final standard for the sentence, should be interpreted so as to include the area in which a sentence can be imposed, namely “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and less than 1 year.” Nevertheless, according to current practice, in the above example the judge may, solely at his or her discretion, choose not to apply attempt mitigation, in which case the “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and less than 1 year” portion is excluded from the range of the punishment to be imposed; such current practice regarding discretionary mitigation is an interpretation that renders the punishment to be imposed unclear and is therefore improper in violation of nulla poena sine lege.\\nAs noted above, while the determination of the punishment to be imposed is a matter of application of law, the part of determining the sentence through extenuating mitigation is a matter of sentencing. Discretionary mitigation is one of the mitigation by law rules that affects the determination of the punishment to be imposed and is not a matter of sentencing. However, current practice wrongly treats discretionary mitigation as a matter of de facto sentencing rather than a matter of application of law, and the result appears in the form of a violation of nulla poena sine lege as noted above.\\nUnder the new interpretive theory, however, one punishment to be imposed corresponding to the ground for discretionary mitigation is clearly determined, thereby guaranteeing the defendant foreseeability of punishment and conforming to nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\n4) Current practice, in that it causes differences in the punishment to be imposed by the judge’s discretion for defendants who committed the same offense, may amount to discrimination without a reasonable basis.\\nThis interpretation, under which the very range of the punishment to be imposed differs according to the judge’s discretion even though the same offense has been committed, is a result that is difficult for the general public to accept, and recognizing different legal effects through the judge’s discretion even though the same legal requirements have been satisfied also runs counter to the general principles of law and the principle of nulla poena sine lege. For example, if two defendants are sentenced in the same courtroom on the same day for attempted aggravated bodily injury, the judge may say to one defendant, “Because attempt is recognized in your case, I will apply discretionary mitigation, so the punishment to be imposed is between 6 months and 5 years of imprisonment,” and to the other defendant, “Although attempt is recognized in your case, I will not apply discretionary mitigation, so the punishment to be imposed is between 1 year and 10 years of imprisonment.” Furthermore, if both of the above defendants are found to be in a diminished capacity state and to have voluntarily surrendered, the gap in the punishment to be imposed may widen to between “imprisonment for 1 year to 10 years” and “imprisonment for 1.5 months to 1 year and 3 months.” Current practice, under which such differences in the punishment to be imposed may arise between defendants who are charged with the same offense and for whom the same grounds for mitigation are recognized, depending on the judge’s discretion regarding whether to apply discretionary mitigation, is an interpretation of law that cannot be accepted under the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\nSetting aside the fact that the actual sentence varies depending on specific sentencing conditions, it is proper that the punishment to be imposed as the legal effect should be applied identically to defendants who fall under the same legal requirements of attempted aggravated bodily injury. It is likewise improper that, under current practice as described above, the possibility remains that different punishments to be imposed may be applied depending on the judge’s discretion among defendants who share the same legal requirements, because this is no different from enabling discrimination without a reasonable basis.\\nFurthermore, according to Article 56 of the Criminal Act, aggravation for concurrent offenses is to be applied after mitigation by law, but even where the offense subject to aggravation is determined by comparison of punishments rather than by the nature or character of the offense, the offense subject to aggravation for concurrent offenses may differ. For example, if one assumes the commission of theft under Article 329 of the Criminal Act (imprisonment for not more than 6 years or a fine not exceeding 10 million won, with imprisonment selected) and attempted fraud under Article 352 and Article 347(1) of the Criminal Act (imprisonment for not more than 10 years or a fine not exceeding 20 million won, with imprisonment selected), under current practice the offense subject to aggravation for concurrent offenses may be theft or attempted fraud depending on whether attempt mitigation is applied to the attempted fraud. However, no reasonable explanation is possible for the basis on which such a difference arises.\\n\\n5) The phrase “may” cannot be interpreted as conferring on the judge discretion or authority to decide whether to mitigate.\\nThe majority opinion argues that, in light of the text “may,” it is proper to interpret it as meaning “discretion or authority to mitigate or not.” However, the phrase “may” expresses various meanings depending on context, such as conjecture, ability, possibility, or permission, but at its core converges on the meaning of “potential or actual possibility.” And unlike cases where the object of “may” is, by its nature, one in which a yes-or-no choice must be made, such as permission or confiscation, in the case of discretionary mitigation the object is a numerical range, so it is also textually proper that the result of its application appears as a changed numerical range. Therefore, it cannot be said that, as the majority opinion contends, interpreting it as meaning the judge’s discretion or authority is proper in textual interpretation. It is proper to interpret it from the standpoint of possibility, and further proper to interpret it from the standpoint of a range encompassing all such possibilities.\\nArticle 38(1)2 of the Criminal Act concerning aggravation for concurrent offenses provides that “where the punishments prescribed for each offense are of the same kind, other than death, imprisonment for life, or penal detention for life, the term or amount shall be increased by up to one-half of the longest term or highest amount prescribed for the most serious offense, but the aggregate term or amount of punishment prescribed for each offense shall not be exceeded. However, petty fines and petty fines, confiscation and confiscation may be cumulatively imposed.” The prevailing view and practice interpret the phrase “may be cumulatively imposed” in the proviso not as meaning “they may or may not be cumulatively imposed,” but as meaning that “petty fines and petty fines, confiscation and confiscation are not aggravated but are cumulatively imposed.” No view can be found that the judge has discretion not to cumulatively impose them. In addition, Article 55(2) of the Criminal Act provides that “If there are multiple grounds for mitigation by law, mitigation may be repeated,” but the meaning of “may” here is also understood as opening the possibility of repeated mitigation, not as meaning that the judge may, in his or her discretion, either repeatedly mitigate or not. For example, if a deaf-mute person commits termination attempt of homicide, since both deafness and muteness and termination attempt are mandatory grounds for mitigation, the practice is to repeatedly apply mitigation for each ground, and this is not interpreted to mean that whether to repeat mitigation is within the judge’s discretion. And Article 398(2) of the Civil Act provides that “if the predetermined amount of damages is unjustly excessive, the court may reasonably reduce it,” but the Supreme Court has held to the effect that “it was erroneous for the court to recognize the full amount of the predetermined amount of damages without any reduction even though the predetermined amount of damages was unjustly excessive, without properly examining whether the predetermined amount of damages was excessive” (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DA19051 rendered on February 26, 2009).\\nThus, the mere fact that the phrase “may” is used in the statutory text does not always mean that discretion or authority is conferred on the judge. In this respect, the majority opinion’s argument that, by interpreting the phrase “may be mitigated,” the judge is granted discretion to mitigate or not mitigate has lost its principal basis. These provisions set out together with the provisions on discretionary mitigation in the General Part of the Criminal Act, as well as the textual interpretation of the “may” in the above Civil Act provision, clearly show that the core grounds of current practice regarding discretionary mitigation are not valid.\\n\\n6) Current practice treats discretionary mitigation as the judge’s discretion, yet it has not engaged in any discussion of control over that discretion to ensure it is properly exercised.\\nThere can be no dispute that even discretionary matters are unlawful if they are deviated from or abused. When an administrative disposition is a matter of administrative discretion, discussions to properly control the discretion are active, discretionary rules setting out the reasonable scope and standards of discretion have been enacted and implemented, and considerable precedents concerning deviation from and abuse of discretionary power have accumulated. Even with sentencing discretion, there have long been numerous discussions for the proper exercise of discretion. Moreover, after the Sentencing Commission was launched and sentencing guidelines were implemented, in-depth discussions on sentencing discretion have continued through the establishment and revision of sentencing guidelines.\\nHowever, there is no discussion whatsoever regarding the judge’s discretion or authority over discretionary mitigation. Since the range of the punishment to be imposed varies depending on whether discretionary mitigation is applied, if this is regarded as the judge’s discretion, it would correspond to one of the most important discretions in criminal procedure; therefore, in light of the seriousness of its effect, there should rightly be discussion on reasonable exercise and control thereof. For example, in a case where a person commits attempted homicide under Article 254 and Article 250(1) of the Criminal Act and then voluntarily surrenders, there should be standards and scope for proper control of discretion regarding discretionary mitigation, such as whether attempt mitigation should or should not be applied depending on whether injury occurred or the degree of injury, or whether voluntary surrender mitigation should not be applied if the offender surrendered only after the offender had been identified and an arrest warrant issued, but should be applied if the offender surrendered before being identified. However, there is no discussion whatsoever concerning control of the judge’s discretionary power regarding discretionary mitigation. It is difficult to understand that the judge is granted discretion or authority concerning the determination of the punishment to be imposed, which is an important process leading to the conclusion of a criminal trial, yet nothing is discussed about it.\\nDiscretionary mitigation, being a type of mitigation by law, must be carried out before aggravation for concurrent offenses and extenuating mitigation, and thus is not a matter to be decided in relation to specific sentencing by the judge’s discretion. Nevertheless, it is wrong for current practice to leave the decision whether to mitigate pursuant to discretionary mitigation, which is a ground for mitigation by law, to the judge’s discretion and yet exercise no control over that discretion.\\nUnder the new interpretive theory, however, once a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the corresponding legal effect is automatically determined immediately, so discussion of control over discretion regarding discretionary mitigation is unnecessary. Perhaps the reason there has been no discussion to date concerning control over discretion in discretionary mitigation is that judges in practice are actually deciding in the same way as the new interpretive theory, namely by determining the punishment to be imposed within the combined range of the range in which mitigation has been applied and the range in which it has not; thus, discussion of control over discretion was not originally necessary.\\n\\n7) Current practice provides a theoretical basis that justifies the court’s omission of a determination on the defendant’s argument.\\nThe Supreme Court has held that “According to Article 52 of the Criminal Act, it is clear that voluntary surrender is not a ground for mandatory mitigation or exemption from punishment; therefore, the assertion regarding voluntary surrender is merely a matter affecting sentencing and cannot be said to constitute a reason that must be stated in a guilty judgment under Article 323 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and thus even if the court below made no determination on the defendant’s above argument, it cannot be said that there is illegality of omission of determination” (see Supreme Court Decisions 87DO945 rendered on July 7, 1987, 98DO492 rendered on April 28, 1998, etc.). In other words, precedents have interpreted the decision whether to apply discretionary mitigation as being solely within the judge’s discretion, and as a result they hold that even if the court omits a determination on the defendant’s assertion concerning a ground for discretionary mitigation, it is not unlawful. In practical terms, this can be understood to mean that there is not even a need to examine whether the ground for discretionary mitigation exists.\\nThis stands in contrast to the above Supreme Court Decision 2007DA19051 concerning the predetermined amount of damages under Article 398(2) of the Civil Act. Although the wording in both provisions is similar, namely “may be reduced” and “may be mitigated,” there is a Supreme Court decision holding that failure to reduce the predetermined amount of damages is unlawful, whereas with respect to discretionary mitigation there is a Supreme Court decision holding that because the judge has discretion as to whether to mitigate, it is not unlawful to fail to determine the assertion. It is not easy to accept that the Supreme Court’s ruling in a civil matter regarding similar wording is stricter than its ruling in a criminal matter.\\nGrounds for discretionary mitigation such as voluntary surrender, diminished capacity, and attempt are factors that bring about changes in the punishment to be imposed and are important grounds that greatly affect the determination of the sentence. In practice, a defendant or defense counsel who raises such grounds in court believes that they will significantly affect the final sentence depending on whether such grounds exist and makes great efforts to prove them. However, to say that whether mitigation is applied for such grounds for discretionary mitigation depends solely on the judge’s discretion, so that even if proof succeeds the corresponding legal effect may not arise and even omission of a determination or no examination at all is not unlawful, is a conclusion that is difficult for a defendant and defense counsel to accept. Moreover, if the defendant argues discretionary mitigation but the first-instance judgment makes no determination regarding it, the defendant cannot know whether the asserted ground for discretionary mitigation was found not to exist, or whether the ground existed but mitigation was not applied due to sentencing considerations, and furthermore cannot know what procedural efforts should be made in the second instance. Meanwhile, there is also practice in which the first instance accepts the defendant’s argument and applies discretionary mitigation, but the second instance renders a judgment not applying discretionary mitigation without explanation, and according to the precedents noted above, such a judgment is not unlawful. Thus, this practice, which is difficult for a defendant and defense counsel to accept, is being carried out with the support of precedent. Current practice in this form cannot but be said to constitute a serious obstacle to the defendant’s right of defense.\\nThis wrongful appearance of practice stems from the perception that whether to apply discretionary mitigation is a matter of the judge’s discretion. However, under the new interpretive theory, once a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the court must make a determination reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half, and failure to do so becomes unlawful. Therefore, an argument concerning a ground for discretionary mitigation naturally falls under the statement of facts constituting the reason for aggravation or mitigation of punishment under Article 323(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, and a determination thereon must be expressly stated in the guilty judgment. This can be naturally corrected through the new interpretive theory.\\nA considerable number of scholars, while regarding discretionary mitigation as within the court’s discretion as in current practice, also consider it proper to state a determination in the reasons for a guilty judgment pursuant to Article 323(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act with the intent of carefully considering the party’s argument and ensuring the objectivity of the judgment. There are also many practitioners who concur with this view.\\nMeanwhile, as will be discussed below, although diminished capacity was changed from mandatory mitigation to discretionary mitigation by the 2018 amendment to the Criminal Act, most current practice appears to expressly state the determination even when the defendant’s claim of diminished capacity is not accepted.
