This attitude of practice is not only entirely proper, but also reveals a latent awareness of the problems in current practice regarding discretionary mitigation.\\n\\n8) According to current practice, a logically difficult problem arises in relation to the defendant’s appeal against a judgment that imposed the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed without discretionary mitigation.\\nAs an example in the attempted aggravated bodily injury offense, assume that the defendant confessed to the offense and wished to have the statutory minimum sentence of 6 months’ imprisonment imposed within the range of punishment to be imposed after attempt mitigation, but the court of first instance, without applying attempt mitigation, imposed the minimum sentence of 1 year’s imprisonment within the range of “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years.” In such a case, the issue is on what grounds the defendant, who wanted a sentence of 6 months’ imprisonment, could appeal. First, one might argue that the defendant could raise violation of law as a ground for appeal by pointing out that attempt mitigation was not applied; however, as noted above, precedents take the position that whether to apply discretionary mitigation is a matter of judicial discretion and that failure to mitigate is not unlawful, so even if violation of law is asserted as a ground for appeal, it is difficult to have it accepted. If accepted, this would also negate the current practice regarding discretionary mitigation. Next, one might argue that the appeal may be filed on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence. However, because the first instance imposed the lowest sentence within the range of the punishment to be imposed, it rendered the most favorable judgment to the defendant within the scope of sentencing discretion, so an appeal against such a first-instance judgment on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence is logically not proper. The substance of the defendant’s appeal against the above first-instance judgment would be an objection to the part that did not apply attempt mitigation, which is a discretionary mitigation. However, as current practice wrongly understands discretionary mitigation as the judge’s discretion lacking control over discretion, there is no ground of appeal that can effectively express the defendant’s intention to object to a judgment that imposed the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed without discretionary mitigation.\\nFurthermore, a serious contradiction also arises in appellate proceedings. In the above example, suppose the appellate court determines that the sentence of 1 year’s imprisonment is excessive and quashes it and imposes 6 months’ imprisonment. In such a case, the question is for what reason the appellate court will quash the first-instance judgment. According to the precedential view that whether to apply discretionary mitigation is a matter of judicial discretion, the first-instance judgment cannot be quashed on the ground of violation of law, and since the quashing is based on the determination that the sentence in the first-instance judgment is excessive, it may be considered proper to quash it on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence. To regard this as a matter of legal misinterpretation or violation of law would also be tantamount to acknowledging the error of current practice. Therefore, current practice appears to quash the first-instance judgment on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence in such cases. However, in order for the appellate court to quash the first-instance judgment that imposed 1 year’s imprisonment, which is the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed without attempt mitigation, and then impose 6 months’ imprisonment, the appellate court must newly apply attempt mitigation by modifying the part applying the law in the first-instance judgment when drafting the new appellate judgment. In the end, there is a difference in the application of law between the first-instance and appellate judgments, which creates a contradiction with the fact that the ground for quashing is inappropriateness of sentence. The appellate court’s determination in such cases is in substance no different from viewing the first-instance judgment as having an error of violation of law. This problem is also the result of wrongly understanding discretionary mitigation as judicial discretion.\\nThe phrase commonly encountered in practice, “legal suspension of sentence is impossible,” is an expression based on the range of the punishment to be imposed stated in the judgment, but premised on current practice regarding discretionary mitigation, this phrase becomes highly inaccurate as well. Taking the case of homicide under Article 250(1) of the Criminal Act (death penalty, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for not less than 5 years) and voluntary surrender as an example, according to current practice, even if the fact of voluntary surrender, which is a ground for discretionary mitigation, is recognized, the court may not mitigate and may omit any mention thereof in the judgment. According to such a judgment, because the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed is 5 years’ imprisonment, suspension of sentence becomes impossible. However, in fact, if mitigation based on voluntary surrender is applied and the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed becomes 2 years and 6 months’ imprisonment, suspension of sentence becomes possible. In other words, it means that legal suspension of sentence is not impossible. Under current practice, which does not state in the judgment the determination when mitigation is not applied even though a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, whether grounds such as suspension of sentence can be asserted as inappropriateness of sentence may be a separate issue, but from the judgment alone it is difficult even to know whether such an argument is legally available, and one must necessarily review the litigation record to know. It would mean that one should not simply trust the punishment to be imposed stated in the judgment, and one wonders whether this is truly consistent with our trial practice.\\nUnder the new interpretive theory, however, there is no room for such confusion. Once a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the effect of changing the punishment to be imposed always arises; if such action is not taken, it is a violation of law, and if such action is taken, only inappropriateness of sentence is at issue. Whether a ground of appeal based on inappropriateness of sentence, including suspension of sentence, is legally available can be clearly known from the wording of the judgment alone, and only at the stage of determining whether the claim will be accepted is it necessary to examine the litigation record.\\n\\n9) According to current practice, there may arise a problem in which the range of the punishment to be imposed is segmented, creating a gap where a sentence cannot be selected between the highest and lowest points of the punishment to be imposed.\\nUnder the current Criminal Act, the range of determinate imprisonment is not less than 1 month and not more than 30 years, and when aggravated, a sentence up to 50 years may be imposed; however, under the former Criminal Act before amendment by Act No. 10259 on April 15, 2010 (hereinafter the “former Criminal Act”), the range of imprisonment was not less than 1 month and not more than 15 years, and when aggravated, a sentence up to 25 years could be imposed. Taking, as an example, the offense of robbery causing death under the former Article 338 of the former Criminal Act, as amended by Act No. 5057 on December 29, 1995 and before its amendment by Act No. 10259, the statutory punishment is life imprisonment or determinate imprisonment for not less than 10 years; if determinate imprisonment is selected, under the former practice the range of the punishment to be imposed varies depending on whether discretionary mitigation is applied for voluntary surrender. If voluntary surrender mitigation is not applied, it becomes “imprisonment for not less than 10 years and not more than 15 years”; if voluntary surrender mitigation is applied, it becomes “imprisonment for not less than 5 years and not more than 7 years and 6 months.” In the end, for the above defendant, depending on whether voluntary surrender mitigation is applied, a sentence ranging from a minimum of 5 years’ imprisonment to a maximum of 15 years’ imprisonment could be imposed, but the problem is that the area of “more than 7 years and 6 months and less than 10 years” cannot be imposed. While it is understandable that a sentence of 5 years or 15 years may be imposed in determining the sentence, it is hard to accept that 8 years or 9 years cannot be imposed. In the above example, if recidivism aggravation is imposed up to twice the maximum and minimum terms of the punishment for robbery causing death pursuant to Article 3 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Specific Violent Crimes (hereinafter the “Specific Violent Crime Act”), or if additional discretionary mitigation grounds such as juvenile delinquency are added, or if extenuating mitigation is also applied, the gap between the minimum and maximum of the punishment to be imposed becomes even larger. The same applies to the current Criminal Act. Under the current Criminal Act as well, this applies where the lower limit of determinate imprisonment exceeds 15 years. If recidivism aggravation is imposed pursuant to Article 3 of the Specific Violent Crime Act, the same problem arises if there is an offense with a lower limit of the statutory punishment exceeding 12 years and 6 months. Put differently, it is no different from having a penal provision with a statutory punishment of, for example, “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 5 years, or imprisonment for not less than 8 years and not more than 15 years.”\\nUnder the new interpretive theory, however, in the case of discretionary mitigation the punishment to be imposed is the range obtained by reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half, so the problem of segmentation of the range of the punishment to be imposed and the resulting sentencing gap does not arise as described above.\\n\\n10) Current practice obscures the legislative intent behind the legislature’s establishment of a stepwise system of mitigation by law.\\nThe Criminal Act, while establishing a system of mitigation of punishment according to the degree of illegality and the degree of culpability, etc., distinguishes and treats differently, in order of lighter criminal responsibility: (1) mandatory mitigation, (2) discretionary mitigation, and (3) cases with no ground for mitigation.\\nCurrent practice either applies mitigation for discretionary mitigation at the judge’s discretion and treats it the same as mandatory mitigation, or does not apply it and treats it the same as cases with no ground for mitigation. Taking attempted aggravated bodily injury as an example, in the former case the punishment to be imposed becomes imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years, thus becoming the same as mandatory mitigation; in the latter case it becomes imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years, thus becoming the same as when there is no ground for mitigation. Such interpretation renders meaningless the purpose and legislative choice of the Criminal Act’s mitigation system. Something that was divided into three categories in law has been reduced to two through interpretation. The majority opinion, while claiming that mandatory mitigation and discretionary mitigation are clearly distinguishable, can be said to be undermining that distinction itself.\\nUnder the new interpretive theory, however, differences in the punishment to be imposed according to each ground for mitigation are clearly revealed. In the example of attempted aggravated bodily injury, in case (1) the punishment is imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years, in case (2) imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years, and in case (3) imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years.\\n\\n11) Before amendment by Act No. 15982 on December 18, 2018, Article 10(2) of the former Criminal Act provided that “The act of a person whose ability under the preceding paragraph is deficient due to mental and physical disorder shall be mitigated,” thereby prescribing diminished capacity as a ground for mandatory mitigation. Accordingly, if the defendant asserted diminished capacity, a determination thereon had to be stated in the judgment, and if diminished capacity was recognized, mitigation by law pursuant to Article 55 of the Criminal Act had to be made. However, the current Article 10(2) of the Criminal Act, as amended above, provides that “The act of a person whose ability under the preceding paragraph is deficient due to mental and physical disorder may be mitigated,” thereby prescribing diminished capacity as a ground for discretionary mitigation. According to current practice regarding discretionary mitigation, the above amendment to the Criminal Act should naturally have brought a significant change to the practice concerning diminished capacity. That is, even if the defendant asserts diminished capacity, the court need not make a determination thereon, and even if diminished capacity is recognized, if there is no need to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed according to the sentence, the punishment need not be mitigated.\\nHowever, current practice regarding diminished capacity appears to operate in a manner not very different from when it was a ground for mandatory mitigation. Even if the defendant’s claim of diminished capacity is not accepted, the determination is stated in the judgment, and even where diminished capacity is recognized, the general practice appears to be to mitigate by law even when it is not a case requiring lowering the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed. Such practice is consonant in part with the new interpretive theory. This aspect of practice concerning diminished capacity may be said to be an example showing that current practice regarding discretionary mitigation is not based on legal or logical grounds but is the result of simply inheriting a mistaken custom.\\n\\nd. Discretionary mitigation should be newly interpreted as follows.\\n\\n1) As noted above, since the meaning of “may” can be interpreted in multiple ways, it should be interpreted as closely as possible in conformity with the legislator’s intent. “May” should be understood to mean that the sentence can be determined across both the “range in case of mitigation” and the “range in case of no mitigation.” In other words, taking into account that both mitigation and no mitigation are possible, the punishment to be imposed should be determined by combining the ranges of the two cases. Then the range between the upper limit of the range where no mitigation is applied and the lower limit of the range where mitigation is applied becomes the range of punishment to be imposed for discretionary mitigation. Put simply, it may also be understood that only the lower limit of the statutory punishment is mitigated. Taking attempted aggravated bodily injury as an example, the statement that attempt mitigation may “mitigate the punishment” means that the sentence may be determined across both the range “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years,” in which attempt mitigation has been applied, and the range “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years,” in which it has not been applied, which means that the punishment to be imposed is determined as “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years.” In the end, it can be said that only the lower limit, namely 1 year, is reduced by one-half while the upper limit, namely 10 years, is left unchanged.\\nUnder the discretionary mitigation method according to the new interpretive theory, the area obtained by combining the mitigated range and the non-mitigated range is automatically determined as the punishment to be imposed without room for judicial discretion, and accordingly the range of the punishment to be imposed is viewed as the upper limit of the non-mitigated range and the lower limit of the mitigated range. The result is the same as reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half. Although extremely exceptional, if discretionary mitigation is viewed as “election discretion,” the problem of segmentation of the punishment to be imposed and the resulting gap, as noted above, cannot be resolved. On the other hand, the new interpretive theory, by taking the form of reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half in the end, leaves no room for such a problem and is simpler and clearer.\\nMeanwhile, according to the new interpretive theory regarding discretionary mitigation, in cases of offenses for which the lower limit of the statutory punishment is not prescribed, even if mitigation is applied, the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed can no longer be lowered, so the punishment to be imposed does not change, but the grounds for mitigation must be stated in the part applying the law in the judgment as a process leading to the sentence.\\nThe foregoing discussion has centered for convenience on determinate imprisonment, but the same discussion applies to other types of punishment such as fines.\\n\\n2) When the legal requirements corresponding to grounds for discretionary mitigation such as diminished capacity, attempt, or voluntary surrender are satisfied, according to the interpretation of the wording that the punishment “may be mitigated,” the legal effect noted above arises, namely that only the lower limit of the statutory punishment is reduced by one-half. If the existence of a ground for discretionary mitigation, that is, the legal requirements, is recognized, the above legal effect naturally arises, so there is no room for judicial discretion to intervene in whether to mitigate. Therefore, if the existence of the legal requirements corresponding to grounds for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the corresponding legal effect always arises, and since that legal effect makes a difference in the range of the punishment to be imposed, whenever a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized the court must always include a notation to that effect in the part applying the law. The same applies even if the defendant does not assert a ground for discretionary mitigation. Furthermore, since grounds for discretionary mitigation always have the effect of lowering the punishment to be imposed, if the defendant asserts a ground for discretionary mitigation, the guilty judgment must state a determination thereon pursuant to Article 323(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\n3) As above, with the new understanding of discretionary mitigation, it is necessary to newly understand the grounds for mitigation that have traditionally been contrasted as mandatory mitigation and discretionary mitigation. As noted above, discretionary mitigation has the effect of lowering only the lower limit, whereas mandatory mitigation has the effect of lowering both the upper and lower limits. In the case of mandatory mitigation, when the relevant ground is recognized, the effect arises that not only is a sentence lower than the lower limit within the statutory punishment permitted, but also the upper limit of the statutory punishment is reduced by one-half so that no sentence above that may be imposed. By contrast, in the case of discretionary mitigation, since the degree of reduction of culpability is considered smaller than in the case of mandatory mitigation, a sentence lower than the lower limit of the statutory punishment may be imposed, but all sentences within the original range of the statutory punishment may also be imposed. When understood in this way, the traditional distinction between mandatory mitigation and discretionary mitigation becomes terminologically inappropriate in that once the requirements for a ground for mitigation are satisfied, the corresponding legal effect naturally arises. Accordingly, what was traditionally called mandatory mitigation appears proper to call “upper-and-lower-limit mitigation,” while discretionary mitigation appears proper to call “lower-limit mitigation.” It is my view that the current practice with several problems, as noted above, has become entrenched in part because of the erroneous use of the term “discretionary” mitigation.\\n\\n4) I have thus examined the content of the new interpretive theory on discretionary mitigation. But on reflection, the new interpretive theory is not materially different from current practice. It is, in fact, not new at all.\\nFirst, there is no difference between current practice and the new interpretive theory in that the punishment to be imposed means the final range from which the judge can select the sentence. Current practice allows the judge to determine whether to apply discretionary mitigation, and accordingly the mitigated range and the non-mitigated range each become punishments to be imposed; but because the judge can determine the sentence within both the mitigated and non-mitigated ranges, this is no different from the new interpretive theory, which regards the combined range of the two as the punishment to be imposed.\\nNext, the rule is that if a legal requirement is recognized, the corresponding legal effect follows, and the new interpretive theory seeks to create for discretionary mitigation the same logical structure as this general rule. Current practice understands the legal effects of other grounds for aggravation and mitigation as “automatic determination,” but only discretionary mitigation as “election discretion”; the new interpretive theory interprets the legal effects of all grounds for aggravation and mitigation as “automatic determination.” From the perspective of trial practice, there is nothing at all new.\\n\\ne. 1) The majority opinion says that the current practice of “there is no need to bother with discretionary mitigation if there is no need to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed” does not mean that the sentence is determined and then the decision whether to apply discretionary mitigation is made, and therefore the practice is not erroneous.\\nHowever, according to current practice, the sentence must inevitably be determined before the punishment to be imposed is fixed. The practice that “there is no need to bother with discretionary mitigation if there is no need to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed” has been used for a long time and can be confirmed in court training materials from the past and present, and under this practice, whether to apply discretionary mitigation is decided depending on whether it is necessary to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed in light of the sentence. But the need to lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed means that the sentence is lower than the punishment to be imposed, so without determining the sentence one cannot know whether the lower limit needs to be lowered. In the end, under current practice, one has no choice but to determine the sentence before fixing the punishment to be imposed in order to decide whether discretionary mitigation applies. Moreover, precedents support the current practice in which whether to apply discretionary mitigation is determined in the process of deciding the sentence by holding that the assertion of voluntary surrender, which is a ground for discretionary mitigation, is merely a sentencing factor (see the above Supreme Court Decision 98DO492, etc.). Furthermore, the sentencing guidelines established by the Sentencing Commission recommend that “where a sentencing factor constituting a ground for discretionary mitigation by law exists and the recommended sentencing range reflecting it is lower than the statutory punishment, it should be considered as either a ground for mitigation by law or a ground for extenuating mitigation,” which means adjusting the punishment to be imposed to fit the recommended sentencing range and is in substance the same as current practice. Therefore, the majority opinion that current practice does not first determine the sentence and then decide whether to apply discretionary mitigation is not valid.\\nMeanwhile, the fact that there is no discussion at all in current practice regarding discretion over discretionary mitigation shows that judges handling practice actually determine the punishment to be imposed for discretionary mitigation, like the new interpretive theory, within the combined range of the mitigated and non-mitigated ranges. The reason current practice has been able to remain unchanged without much sense of problem despite being wrong is not because current practice can be construed as in the manner of the majority opinion, but because judges, in their actual work, avoid judgments according to current practice and instead decide in the same way as the new interpretive theory, thereby avoiding the problems that would arise if current practice were followed as is.\\n2) The majority opinion says that, when mitigation by law is applied for a determinate term of imprisonment, a method that reduces only either the upper limit or the lower limit by one-half, rather than reducing both the upper and lower limits by one-half as provided in Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act, cannot be permitted under the principle of nulla poena sine lege. If the majority opinion above understood the separate opinion to mean that the upper-limit portion of Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act is not applied, I clarify that this is a misunderstanding.\\nAs explained in detail above, the separate opinion means that in the case of discretionary mitigation, because mitigation by law is applied pursuant to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act, the sentence may be determined across both the range in which both the upper and lower limits are reduced by one-half and the range in which no mitigation is applied, and this ultimately appears as the same result as reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment by one-half while leaving the upper limit unchanged. In other words, this is merely a shorthand expression of the result obtained by combining both the case in which mitigation by law under Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act is applied and the case in which it is not applied; it does not recognize a mitigation by law that reduces only the minimum term by one-half contrary to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act.\\n3) The majority opinion says that, from the point a guilty finding is made to the point of determining the sentence, the judge is granted broad discretion, such as in selecting the type of punishment, and that the judge’s discretion regarding discretionary mitigation is only one of them.\\nFor example, in the case of theft under Article 329 of the Criminal Act, because imprisonment and fines are provided as alternatives, selection of the type of punishment is inevitable in determining the sentence, and before that selection, the same punishment to be imposed is always indicated. However, in current practice regarding attempted aggravated bodily injury, if attempt mitigation is not applied, the range of imprisonment for not less than 6 months and less than 1 year is excluded from the punishment to be imposed for that defendant from the outset. In the former case, the same punishment to be imposed is applied to all defendants, whereas in the latter case the punishment to be imposed differs depending on the defendant. In this respect, the problem of selecting the type of punishment and the problem of discretionary mitigation are entirely different matters.\\n4) As noted above in item 7) of section c., there is a view that, while maintaining current practice, the claim of a ground for discretionary mitigation should be regarded as falling under the “statement of facts constituting the reason for aggravation or mitigation of punishment” in Article 323(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act and that a determination thereon should be expressly stated. However, precedents have steadfastly maintained the position that even if the court omits a determination on the defendant’s argument concerning a ground for discretionary mitigation, it is not unlawful, and as noted above in item 7) of section c., current practice regarding discretionary mitigation provides a theoretical basis for justifying the court’s omission of a determination on the defendant’s argument. While a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, under current practice the occurrence of the legal effect of changing the punishment to be imposed is uncertain; maintaining that practice and at the same time requiring that determinations on arguments regarding grounds for discretionary mitigation be expressly stated seems logically difficult.\\nEven if current practice regarding discretionary mitigation were maintained but changed so that determinations on arguments regarding grounds for discretionary mitigation had to be stated, various difficulties are foreseeable. If, as a result of examination of the defendant’s argument, a ground for discretionary mitigation such as voluntary surrender is not recognized, there would be no particular problem. However, the problem arises when the ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized but the judge decides not to mitigate. In particular, it would be difficult to distinguish and state the reasons why one defendant is mitigated and another is not. And because the process of fixing the punishment to be imposed and the sentencing for determining the concrete sentence must be distinguished, it would be desirable to explain the determination on whether to mitigate by referring to circumstances other than sentencing conditions, but that is very difficult. In the end, in order to avoid such difficulties, practice will be operated in the direction of always mitigating pursuant to Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act once a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, which would completely undermine the distinction between discretionary mitigation and mandatory mitigation and damage the purpose of the Criminal Act’s separate provisions for discretionary and mandatory mitigation.\\nThis problem can be confirmed by looking at recent practice involving claims of diminished capacity mentioned above in item 11) of section d. Looking more concretely at practice after diminished capacity was changed from mandatory mitigation to discretionary mitigation, one can readily find cases in which the defendant’s argument is rejected because diminished capacity is not recognized, cases in which diminished capacity is recognized and mitigation for diminished capacity is applied, and cases in which mitigation for diminished capacity is applied even though the case is not one requiring lowering the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed. However, it is difficult to find a case in which diminished capacity is recognized but mitigation for diminished capacity is not applied and the reason is stated in the judgment. Such operation of practice is no different from deciding whether to mitigate depending on whether diminished capacity is recognized, and thus is in substance the same as mandatory mitigation. If, while maintaining current practice in this way, determinations on arguments for discretionary mitigation are required to be stated in the judgment, there is a high possibility that it will in practice operate in the same way as mandatory mitigation, making it difficult to distinguish between the two.\\n5) Most issues of statutory interpretation encountered in trials concern legal requirements, and in such cases which legal effect is granted depends on which view is chosen. Put differently, the gains and losses of legal effect hinge on how the boundaries of the legal requirements are drawn. There are things to “gain” and “lose.”\\nHowever, broadly speaking, the issue of discretionary mitigation addressed in this judgment is not wrong to describe as a discussion about, while in substance agreeing on the range of punishment that may be imposed on the defendant, which interpretation is legally and logically better for expressing that in the judgment. It might be more appropriate to call this a discussion about improving the practice of drafting criminal judgments. Through the new interpretive theory, many of the problems of current practice can be resolved, and it is difficult to find new legal or practical problems arising from it. I do not understand what the insistence on maintaining the current practice of drafting criminal judgments, which cannot even clearly communicate the range of the punishment to be imposed, is intended to preserve. It is difficult to know precisely what the majority opinion opposes and for what reason.\\n\\nf. As above, examining the problems raised in the beginning based on the new interpretive theory of discretionary mitigation, one can see that all problems are naturally resolved as follows.\\n\\n1) According to the new interpretive theory, whenever a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the effect is that the lower limit of the statutory punishment is reduced by one-half, so defendants who committed the same offense and have the same grounds for aggravation and mitigation of punishment are always punished by the same punishment to be imposed. If a ground for mitigation by law is recognized, the legal effect is always the same, so the punishment to be imposed is likewise determined identically.\\n\\n2) According to the new interpretive theory, unlike current practice, whether to apply mitigation by law to a ground for discretionary mitigation is not decided at the judge’s discretion; rather, because the effect of changing the punishment to be imposed always arises, discretionary mitigation is not limited as in current practice to cases where the sentence is lower than the punishment to be imposed, and furthermore there is no room for the judge, after determining the sentence, to go back and add discretionary mitigation in the part applying the law when the sentence does not correspond to the punishment to be imposed.\\n\\n3) Under current practice, if there are several grounds for discretionary mitigation—for example, if voluntary surrender and diminished capacity are added to attempted robbery—multiple punishments to be imposed may appear, such as “imprisonment for not less than 3 years and not more than 30 years,” “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and 6 months and not more than 15 years,” “imprisonment for not less than 9 months and not more than 7 years and 6 months,” and “imprisonment for not less than 4.5 months and not more than 3 years and 9 months.” Under the new interpretive theory, however, when there are multiple grounds for discretionary mitigation as above, the lower limit is repeatedly reduced by one-half, so the punishment to be imposed is always “imprisonment for not less than 4.5 months and not more than 30 years.”\\n\\n4) According to Article 56 of the Criminal Act, mitigation by law must be applied before aggravation for concurrent offenses. Under current practice, however, even where the most serious offense subject to aggravation among several offenses in a concurrent-offense relationship is determined by comparison of punishments rather than by the nature or character of the offense under Article 38(1) of the Criminal Act, the offense with the highest punishment may vary depending on the judge’s discretion regarding discretionary mitigation; but under the new interpretive theory, if a ground for discretionary mitigation is recognized, the lower limit of the statutory punishment is always reduced by one-half and the same punishment to be imposed results, so based on this, the offense with the highest punishment subject to aggravation for concurrent offenses is always consistently determined.\\n\\n5) As noted above, according to current practice there arise cases in which, even when a sentence equal to the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed is imposed, an appeal on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence must be allowed. Under the new interpretive theory, however, if a ground for discretionary mitigation exists, the punishment to be imposed always includes the full maximum range within which the judge can determine a specific sentence, and because the sentence is determined within the range of the punishment to be imposed expanded in this way to all possible areas, if the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed has been imposed, it necessarily means that the most favorable punishment possible has been imposed on the defendant. Accordingly, in such cases there is no room for an appeal on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence, and it is evident that such an interpretation conforms to the structure of our criminal procedure. As noted above, the phrase “legal suspension of sentence is impossible” can also be highly inaccurate under current practice regarding discretionary mitigation.\\n\\n6) According to current practice, if the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed without discretionary mitigation is imposed at first instance, the appellate court may impose a lower sentence than the first instance, and to do so it must modify the part applying the law in the first-instance judgment in order to apply discretionary mitigation and lower the lower limit of the punishment to be imposed. However, under the new interpretive theory, as noted above, discretionary mitigation always has the same legal effect, so the situation in which the part applying the law in the first-instance judgment is modified simply to accept an appeal on the ground of inappropriateness of sentence and newly apply discretionary mitigation does not occur.\\n\\ng. I will examine the court below’s determination in light of the new interpretive theory concerning discretionary mitigation.\\nThe court of first instance, according to current practice regarding discretionary mitigation, applied attempt mitigation, which is discretionary mitigation, to the attempted aggravated bodily injury offense pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act, and then mitigated it pursuant to Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act. As a result, the punishment to be imposed for attempted aggravated bodily injury became imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 5 years, and based on that term, the punishment to be imposed was determined after aggravation for concurrent offenses.\\nHowever, according to the new interpretive theory regarding discretionary mitigation, attempt mitigation for attempted aggravated bodily injury should be applied by “Article 25(2) and Article 55(1)3 of the Criminal Act” (lower-limit mitigation only), thereby using as the basis for aggravation for concurrent offenses the term in which only the lower limit of the punishment for attempted aggravated bodily injury is reduced by one-half (imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years); but because the term obtained by adding together the upper limits of attempted aggravated bodily injury and assault (12 years) is lower than the term obtained by aggravating by one-half the upper limit of attempted aggravated bodily injury (15 years), the punishment to be imposed should be determined within the combined range (imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 12 years), and the sentence should be determined within that punishment-to-be-imposed range.\\nThe court below’s judgment, which failed to correct the above error of the court of first instance, contains an error of misunderstanding the legal principles concerning discretionary mitigation; however, because the punishment to be imposed that the court of first instance, maintained by the court below, used as the standard for sentencing falls within the range of the punishment to be imposed under the new interpretive theory and is not unfavorable to the defendant, the above error does not appear to have affected the judgment in the end. The determination regarding the defendant’s grounds for final appeal is the same as in the majority opinion.\\nIn this way, I concur with the majority opinion in concluding that there is no ground for quashing the judgment below, but because my reasoning differs, I state this in a separate opinion.\\n\\n6. Justice Lee Gi-taek’s supplementary opinion on the separate opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. The issue in this case is whether the current practice regarding discretionary mitigation, including attempt mitigation under Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act, is valid. Because current practice treats attempt mitigation the same as other discretionary mitigation, the separate opinion discussed the new interpretive theory on discretionary mitigation generally without distinguishing attempt mitigation from other discretionary mitigation. However, as will be discussed below, attempt mitigation has certain differences from other discretionary mitigation in relation to “mitigation of punishment.” In other words, other discretionary mitigation concerns, as discussed in the separate opinion, the meaning of the “mitigation of punishment” provision in determining the “range of the punishment to be imposed” on the premise of the statutory punishment prescribed in the penal provision, whereas attempt mitigation concerns the meaning of the “mitigation of punishment” provision in determining the “statutory punishment for an attempted offense,” which is not prescribed in the individual penal provision. Below, I will examine the legal structure of punishing attempted offenses.\\nCurrent practice and the prevailing academic view understand the attempt under Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act (hereinafter simply the “attempt”) as, in principle, punishing it with the same statutory punishment as the completed offense, but merely a ground for discretionary mitigation under paragraph 2 of the same Article. However, the above understanding of attempt under current practice is wrong. An attempt is a separate offense distinguished from a completed offense, has its own statutory punishment, and that statutory punishment is properly understood to be the range obtained by reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment for the completed offense by one-half.\\nFirst, the subject of punishment as an attempt is determined by the provision “The offenses punishable as attempts shall be prescribed in each principal provision” in Article 29 of the Criminal Act and the provision “Attempts under Article ___ above shall be punished” in the specific parts of the Criminal Act. Next, the elements of an attempted offense are determined by combining the provision in Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act—“When the execution of a crime has been commenced but the act has not been completed or the result has not occurred, the offender shall be punished as an attempted offender”—with the elements-of-offense provisions for completed offenses in the specific parts of the Criminal Act. And the statutory punishment for an attempted offense is determined by combining the provision in Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act—“The punishment of an attempt may be mitigated from that of a completed offense”—with Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act regarding the meaning of mitigation and the statutory punishment provisions for completed offenses in the specific parts of the Criminal Act. For example, the offense of attempted homicide under Article 254 and Article 250(1) of the Criminal Act is determined, in combination with Article 25(1) and (2) of the Criminal Act, to have the attempt-specific elements and statutory punishment stating that “a person who has commenced the execution of an act of killing another and whose result has not occurred shall be punished by death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for not less than 2 years and 6 months.”\\nThe specific reasons why a new understanding of the punishment of attempted offenses is needed are as follows. For convenience, I will discuss it centered on result crimes.\\n1) Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act provides that “When the execution of a crime has been commenced but the act has not been completed or the result has not occurred, the offender shall be punished as an attempted offender.” In the case of an attempt, punishment cannot be imposed based solely on Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act, nor can an attempted offender be punished based only on the punishment provision for the completed offense. The elements of an attempted offense are completed only when the punishment provision for the completed offense and Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act are combined, and only then do they have legitimacy as the basis for punishing an attempted offense. Taking the offense of attempted homicide under Article 254 and Article 250(1) of the Criminal Act as an example, the provision in Article 254 that “attempts under the preceding four Articles shall be punished” becomes the basis for punishing attempted homicide, and the provision in Article 250(1) that “a person who kills another...” and the provision in Article 25(1) combine to complete the elements of attempted homicide, namely, “when a person has commenced the execution of an act of killing another and the result of death has not occurred.” The concept of attempt as an element of offense becomes clear only through Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act.\\n2) Like the elements of offense, the statutory punishment for an attempted offense should also be understood as being determined by combining the punishment provision for the completed offense and Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act. Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act provides that “The punishment of an attempt may be mitigated from that of a completed offense,” and according to the new interpretive theory on discretionary mitigation, the statutory punishment for an attempted offense is determined as the range obtained by reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment for the completed offense by one-half.\\nCurrent practice understands Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act concerning punishment for attempts as a provision of discretionary mitigation. That is, it interprets that an attempted offender is, in principle, punished with the same statutory punishment as the completed offense, but punishment may or may not be mitigated pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act. However, there is no textual basis for punishing an attempt with the same statutory punishment as the completed offense. Moreover, although there is an obvious difference in the illegality of the result between a completed offense and an attempted offense, the fact that their statutory punishments are the same has an aspect that is hard to accept in criminal law doctrine. Furthermore, considering that there are countless offenses for which attempts are not punishable, it is improper to regard the statutory punishment for an attempt as, in principle, identical to that of the completed offense.\\n3) The legislature used a legislative technique of concisely and efficiently prescribing the elements and statutory punishment of attempted offenses in the General Part, but current practice mistakenly takes this mode of expression as discretionary mitigation. Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act provides that “When the execution of a crime has been commenced but the act has not been completed or the result has not occurred, the offender shall be punished as an attempted offender”; Article 25(2) provides that “The punishment of an attempt may be mitigated from that of a completed offense”; Article 29 provides that “The offenses punishable as attempts shall be prescribed in each principal provision”; and the specific parts of the Criminal Act prescribe the punishment for attempted offenses in the form that “attempts under Article ___ above shall be punished.” Such a form of provision reflects the legislature’s use of a legislative technique in which, instead of separately and complexly prescribing the elements and statutory punishment for attempts for each offense, the general rule for punishing attempts is prescribed in the General Part, and then the offenses punishable as attempts are designated in the specific parts so that the relevant elements and statutory punishment are automatically completed. If the current Criminal Act merely provided in Article 254 that “attempts under the preceding four Articles shall be punished” concerning attempted homicide, the elements and statutory punishment of the attempt would be automatically completed; without such a legislative technique, it would have been necessary to separately prescribe the elements and statutory punishment for every attempted offense.\\nIn other words, instead of separately and complexly prescribing the elements and statutory punishment of attempts for each offense, the Criminal Act places in Article 25 of the General Part common provisions for attempts as to elements of offense (paragraph 1) and statutory punishment (paragraph 2), and then combines them with the individual provisions on completed offenses so that the elements and statutory punishment of attempts are derived. In addition, it is proper to view the legislature as having expressly indicated through such a form of provision that the statutory punishment for attempts is reduced only in the lower limit by one-half from that of the completed offense. If the statutory punishment for an attempted offense had been prescribed individually, it would have been very difficult to express such legislative intent. Therefore, the current practice of viewing the statutory punishment for an attempt as, in principle, identical to that of the completed offense, but merely capable of discretionary mitigation under Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act, is not valid.\\nBased on this new understanding of attempts, it can be seen that the legislature classifies offenses with respect to attempts as follows: (i) offenses for which attempts need not be punished because they are minor offenses do not have attempt punishment provisions; (ii) where punishment is necessary for the danger of result occurrence caused by commencement of execution even though the constitutive result has not occurred, attempt punishment provisions are provided and the offense is punished by a statutory punishment obtained by reducing only the lower limit of the statutory punishment for the completed offense by one-half pursuant to Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act; and (iii) where the offense is an attempt but strong punishment is required, as in the precedent cases discussed below, the statutory punishment for the attempt is separately specified so that the application of Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act is excluded.\\n4) The statutory punishment refers to the range of punishment generally evaluating the typical unlawfulness of each element of offense as prescribed by the legislature in each element of offense. In other words, once the elements are satisfied, the scope of punishment predetermined by the legislature is determined, and that is the statutory punishment. Then any setting or alteration of the range of punishment resulting from the element of attempt should all be regarded as part of the determination of the statutory punishment. It is not appropriate to view this, as current practice does, as a ground for mitigation of punishment after determination of the statutory punishment. Furthermore, under the principle of prohibition against double evaluation, matters constituting signs of the elements of the offense must not be considered again in the sentencing process. The circumstance that the execution of a crime was commenced but the result did not occur and the offense remained an attempt is a sign of the elements of an attempted offense, so understanding this as a ground for mitigation by law may amount to double evaluation, and such legal interpretation should be avoided unless unavoidable.\\n5) The Supreme Court has traditionally held to the effect that “where a special statute such as the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (hereinafter the ‘Specific Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act’) expressly prescribes the statutory punishment for an attempt to a specific offense in the same manner as the completed offense (e.g., Article 5-4(6), Article 11(1), etc.), mitigation of punishment for attempt under Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act is not permitted” (see Supreme Court Decisions 87DO1635 rendered on September 22, 1987, 2000DO3947 rendered on November 14, 2000, 2010DO11620 rendered on November 25, 2010, etc.). However, according to current practice, since the statutory punishment for an attempted offense and a completed offense is basically the same and Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act merely means that an attempted offense may be mitigated at the judge’s discretion, even if a special statute expressly provides that an attempt is punished with the same statutory punishment as the completed offense, this merely confirms the principle that “the statutory punishment for a completed offense and an attempt is the same,” and it is difficult to find a basis for interpreting this as excluding the mitigation provision for attempts in the General Part of the Criminal Act. Therefore, according to current practice, the discretionary mitigation provision in Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act should naturally apply to attempt punishment provisions in the above special statutes as well. In the end, the attitude of the above Supreme Court precedents and current practice contradict each other and are difficult to harmonize.\\nHowever, according to the new understanding that the statutory punishment for an attempted offense is recognized as above, the statutory punishment for the attempt is determined by combining the statutory punishment for the completed offense and Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act; but if the special statute separately specifies the statutory punishment for the attempt, there is no longer any need for the interpretive process of law to fix the statutory punishment, so Article 25(2) of the Criminal Act, which serves to fix the statutory punishment, has no room to operate. In this way, the above Supreme Court precedents can be explained consistently and harmoniously through the new understanding of attempts.\\n6) In short, Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act prescribes the elements of an attempted offense, and paragraph 2 prescribes its statutory punishment. To say, without express statutory basis, that the statutory punishment for an attempt is the same as that for the completed offense is an interpretation contrary to nulla poena sine lege. Before Article 25 of the Criminal Act operates, there is neither the elements of an attempted offense nor its statutory punishment.\\n\\nb. As a related matter, I would like to make one point regarding subject-matter jurisdiction.\\nIt is proper to interpret that the phrase “cases corresponding to death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or penal detention with a minimum term of 1 year or more” subject to the collegiate panel under Article 32(1)3 of the Court Organization Act means cases in which the lowest among the alternative punishments enumerated as statutory punishment is imprisonment or penal detention with a minimum term of 1 year or more, and that it does not include cases in which a lighter punishment such as a fine is provided as an alternative punishment rather than imprisonment or penal detention. The reasons are as follows.\\n1) The Court Organization Act, while in principle vesting the trial power of district courts and their branches in a single judge, exceptionally requires a collegiate panel to try the cases listed in each subparagraph of Article 32(1), and, in the interest of taking caution in handling serious cases in which the statutory punishment is severe, it designates as within the collegiate panel’s jurisdiction “cases corresponding to death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or penal detention with a minimum term of 1 year or more” (subparagraph 3 of the same paragraph). Current practice takes the position that if the statutory punishment provides imprisonment with a minimum term of 1 year or more, even if a fine is provided as an alternative punishment, the case is within the collegiate panel’s jurisdiction. According to this, Article 16(1) of the Act on Special Measures for Registration, etc. of Real Estate Ownership Transfer (hereinafter the “Act on Registration of Real Estate Ownership Transfer”) provides that a person who prepares a false certificate or obtains a certificate by false means, etc., shall be punished by “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years, or a fine of not less than 10 million won and not more than 100 million won,” so a violation of Article 16(1) of the Act on Registration of Real Estate Ownership Transfer falls under the jurisdiction of the collegiate panel. The offense of riot under Article 115 of the Criminal Act also has a statutory punishment of “imprisonment or penal detention for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years, or a fine not exceeding 15 million won,” and thus is within the collegiate panel’s jurisdiction.\\n2) However, the phrase “cases corresponding to death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or penal detention with a minimum term of 1 year or more” subject to the collegiate panel under Article 32(1)3 of the Court Organization Act should be determined solely on the basis of the statutory punishment itself, which can be said to be the stage before selection of the type of punishment. The above current practice appears to focus on the fact that even if a fine is provided as the statutory punishment, if imprisonment is selected, the term becomes 1 year or more, but subject-matter jurisdiction should be determined based on the statutory punishment. Since a fine is lighter than “imprisonment or penal detention with a minimum term of 1 year or more,” it cannot be viewed as satisfying the above requirement. Therefore, it is proper to interpret the collegiate panel’s jurisdiction only where the lightest available punishment among the statutory punishments, that is, the lowest among the alternative punishments enumerated as statutory punishment, is imprisonment or penal detention with a minimum term of 1 year or more; accordingly, where a lighter fine is prescribed as an alternative punishment, it is proper to regard the case as within the jurisdiction of a single judge. In the case of the above violation of Article 16(1) of the Act on Registration of Real Estate Ownership Transfer or riot, since a fine may be selected, it is proper to regard the case as within the jurisdiction of a single judge.\\n3) And according to the new understanding of attempted offenses, the statutory punishment for an attempt is the same as the reduction by one-half of only the lower limit of the completed offense’s statutory punishment, and jurisdiction over an attempted offense should be based on the statutory punishment for the attempt. Taking the offense of attempted destruction of public goods under Article 143 and Article 141(2) of the Criminal Act as an example, the statutory punishment for destruction of public goods is “imprisonment for not less than 1 year and not more than 10 years,” and the statutory punishment for attempted destruction of public goods is “imprisonment for not less than 6 months and not more than 10 years,” so while destruction of public goods falls within the collegiate panel’s jurisdiction, attempted destruction of public goods is properly regarded as within the jurisdiction of a single judge.\\n\\nI hereby state the supplementary opinion to the separate opinion as above."}

{"[75DO1549]": "Judgment on the Grounds for the Prosecutor’s Appeal\\n\\nSince it should be understood that the “offense of another” in the provision of Article 32(1) of the Criminal Act, which states that a person who aids another’s offense shall be punished as an accessory, refers to a case in which the principal offender has commenced the commission of the offense in order to realize it, accessory liability can arise only where there has been a commencement of execution by the principal offender; and where the principal offender has remained merely at the preparatory stage without reaching commencement of execution, the act of assistance thereto cannot be punished as accessory liability, except where such act becomes co-principal liability for preparation.\\n\\nThis is because, in terms of the concept of the constituent elements of a crime, the act of execution of a preparatory offense is an unstructured and indefinite act, and the act of an accessory is likewise unstructured and indefinite; and because Article 28 of the Criminal Act provides that where a conspiracy or preparatory act for a crime has not reached commencement of execution, it shall not be punished unless there is a special statutory provision, thereby prohibiting unjust analogical or expansive interpretation of the constituent elements of a crime that would arise from punishment of a preparatory offense, it is not possible to directly include within the concept of an independent constituent offense the provisions in the Specific Part of the Criminal Act punishing preparatory offenses, and this interpretation is also consistent with the principle of nulla poena sine lege. Therefore, in light of the spirit of the Criminal Act as a whole, it is a reasonable interpretation to regard accessory liability as not being established at the preparatory stage.\\n\\nThe ground of appeal that the preparatory offense of robbery in this case is a crime corresponding to an independent constituent offense under the Criminal Act is, as stated above, an untenable independent view; and even if the purport of the judgment of the court below differs somewhat from this, it is proper in that it denied the establishment of accessory liability for a preparatory offense, and the ground of appeal disputing this is without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[99DO424]": "1. Regarding the first ground of appeal by the court-appointed defense counsel\\nArticle 28 of the Criminal Act provides that when a conspiracy or preparatory act for an offense has not reached the commencement of execution, it shall not be punished unless there is a special provision of law; Article 182(2) of the Customs Act provides that a person who has made preparations with the intent to commit a customs evasion offense, etc. prescribed in Article 180 shall be punished, together with an attempted offender, in the same manner as the principal offense; and Article 6(7) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes provides for aggravated punishment, under certain requirements, of a person who has committed an offense prescribed in Article 182 of the Customs Act. This is because customs offenses, including customs evasion offenses, have a significant effect on the national economy, have the characteristics of profit-making offenses equipped with organization, expertise, intelligence, and internationality, and because, in terms of the possibility or risk of infringement of legal interests, there is not a substantial difference between completion and attempt, or between attempt and preparation; accordingly, the provisions punishing preparatory acts are established solely for the purpose of achieving the legislative objective of the Customs Act and for maintaining order and public welfare, and are not intended, without rational basis, to discriminate a particular person from the general public or to specially crack down on customs evasion offenses, etc. different from other specific offenses such as tax evasion offenses under the Punishment of Tax Offenders Act; therefore, the above provisions concerning the preparatory offense of customs evasion cannot be deemed to violate the principle of equality under Article 11 of the Constitution or the principle of guaranteeing basic human rights under Article 10 of the Constitution.\\n\\n2. Regarding the second ground of appeal by the court-appointed defense counsel and the first and second grounds of appeal by the Defendant\\nA comparison of the judgment of the court below and the evidence expressly stated in the first-instance judgment as cited by the court below with the record shows that the court below rightly found that the Defendant, etc. on 1998. 2. 17. executed a contract with a Chinese non-party limited liability company for the import of 1,000 tons of mung beans, and also submitted that contract as it was when applying on the 25th of the same month for advance review of the taxable price, but in fact decided to evade the customs duties corresponding thereto by paying the Chinese company an amount additionally equivalent to 10% of the imported quantity, importing that much additional quantity, and not filing an import declaration with respect to that portion, and thereafter, by July 7 of the same year, imported and cleared through customs 330 tons of mung beans in three installments and attempted to import the remaining 770 tons; and there is no illegality in fact-finding due to violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\nMeanwhile, according to Article 9-2(1) of the Customs Act, a person obligated to pay customs duties shall, at the time of filing an import declaration, declare to the head of the customs office the price of the relevant goods in accordance with the Presidential Decree; however, Article 9-15 of the same Act provides that when a person who is required to file a tax declaration has doubts concerning matters forming the basis for the determination of the taxable value, he/she may, before filing a price declaration, apply to the Commissioner of the Korea Customs Service or the head of the customs office for prior examination by preparing the documents prescribed by the Presidential Decree, and that when the head of the customs office recognizes that, in the case where the person obligated to pay customs duties files a tax declaration by such advance examination report, the relevant person obligated to pay and the applicant for advance examination are identical and the imported goods and the declaration of taxable value are identical to the contents of the advance examination report, the taxable value shall be determined according to the contents of the advance examination report unless there is a special reason prescribed by the Presidential Decree. Therefore, it is appropriate to regard the act of falsely declaring the taxable value and obtaining in advance an advance examination report on the taxable value by attaching a contract stating a lower quantity and price of goods to be imported, and applying for prior examination of the taxable value for all scheduled imported quantities, as an external preparatory act for the realization of the customs evasion offense. In this purport, the court below correctly held that the preparatory offense of customs evasion prescribed in Article 182(2) of the Customs Act applies to the remaining 770 tons, excluding the 330 tons of mung beans actually imported and cleared through customs by the Defendant, etc., and applied Article 6(7) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the preparatory offense of customs evasion.\\nAlso, upon examining the record, the fact that the validity period of the above advance examination report on taxable value was entered as until 1998. 8. 25. does not mean that it was impossible for the Defendant, etc. to actually import the remaining 770 tons of mung beans; moreover, no circumstance is recognized that the Defendant, etc. voluntarily abandoned such import, and furthermore, desistance offense means a case in which, after commencement of the execution of a crime, the person voluntarily ceases the act, and in the case of punishing an act of conspiracy/preparation before commencement of execution, the concept of desistance offense cannot be recognized (see Supreme Court Decision 91DO436, rendered on 1991. 6. 25.), so the argument in the grounds of appeal on this point also cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Regarding the Defendant's third ground of appeal\\nIn a case such as this, where a sentence of imprisonment of less than 10 years was imposed, the argument that the sentencing is too severe and therefore unjust cannot constitute a lawful ground of appeal.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and 55 days out of the detention after the appeal are included in the principal sentence, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the order by unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning accomplices is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: The intent required of an aider and abettor regarding the principal offender, etc. need not involve awareness of the specific content of the crime realized by the principal offender; conditional intent or foresight is sufficient, but this is not inconsistent with the point that awareness of the unlawfulness of the principal offender’s act, etc. is required.
B: The legal principle that the general provisions of the Criminal Act concerning accomplices cannot be applied to reciprocal offenses applies not only to reciprocal offenses that are necessary accomplice offenses, but also to cases in which, in terms of the statutory elements, the offense is structured so that it can be committed by a single person but is merely carried out in the form of a reciprocal offense.
C: If a person who does not have the status relationship of being engaged in business conspired with a person who has such a status relationship and committed the crime of occupational breach of trust, the accomplice without such status relationship must, pursuant to the proviso of Article 33 of the Criminal Act, be punished by the sentence prescribed for the crime of simple breach of trust.
D: For the formation of co-principal liability, the common intent to jointly engage in the act is insufficient if it merely consists of recognizing another person’s criminal act and tolerating it without preventing it; it must instead consist of becoming united to carry out a specific criminal act by common intent and, by using the acts of another person, carrying one’s own intent into execution.
E: In order for aider and abettor liability to be established, the act of assistance must be closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime; therefore, if a person merely assisted an act that is not closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime, aider and abettor liability does not arise.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2000DO576]": "Judgment on the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. The gist of the reasoning of the judgment below is as follows.\\n\\nA. The gist of the criminal facts against the Defendants found by the court below is that: \"The Defendants, (1) together with Nonparty 1, the crew members of the regular cargo vessel Pegasus Pride, and trailer driver Nonparty 2, etc., after resolving that the said crew members would each invest KRW 20,000,000 to purchase goods in Japan and then import them without declaration by using the said vessel, whereupon Nonparty 1 proposed to the Defendants that he was going to smuggle goods from Japan and asked them to purchase the smuggled goods, and proposed to Nonparty 2 to transport them, thereby obtaining each of their consent and then sequentially conspiring, and thereafter, when Nonparty 1, etc. purchased camcorders, etc. in Japan, loaded them on the said vessel, and entered Busan Port, Nonparty 2 used his own trailer to clandestinely remove them from the pier, then met Defendant 1 on the road and transferred them to the vehicle driven by Defendant 1, thereby importing camcorders, etc. without an import declaration as stated in Attached Table 1 of the List of Crimes appended to the judgment below; and (2) together with Nonparty 3, the crew members of Meristar, a vessel belonging to Namseong Shipping Co., Ltd., and the said Nonparty 2, etc., after resolving that the said crew members would purchase liquor in Japan and then import it without declaration by using the said vessel and, if it were smuggled into the country, Nonparty 2 would clandestinely remove it from the pier and sell it to the Defendants, thereby sequentially conspiring, and thereafter, when Nonparty 3, etc. purchased liquor in Japan, loaded it on the said vessel, and entered Busan Port, Nonparty 2 used his own trailer to clandestinely remove it from the pier, then met Defendant 1 on the road and transferred it to the vehicle driven by Defendant 1, thereby smuggling liquor without an import declaration as stated in Attached Table 4 of the List of Crimes appended to the judgment below.\"\\n\\nB. The Defendants have consistently denied the offenses from the investigative authorities to the proceedings in the court below, asserting that although they purchased liquor or camcorders, etc. from Nonparty 2 or Nonparty 1, etc., they had never conspired in advance with them in the smuggling offenses or participated therein at all. As to this, the court below, comparing the evidence lawfully examined and admitted by the trial court with the record, determined that it was sufficiently established that the Defendants, together with Nonparty 1, etc. or Nonparty 3, etc., committed the smuggling offenses by acting as one entity with a common intent and by using the acts of different persons, and thus recognized and punished the Defendants as co-principals of the smuggling offenses stated in its holding.\\n\\n2. As to the grounds of appeal concerning the misapprehension of the legal principles on co-principal liability\\n\\nIn order for co-principal liability to be established, there must, as a subjective requirement, be a common intent to jointly engage in the offense, and, as an objective requirement, execution of the offense through functional control over the act based on a common intent; the common intent as a subjective requirement is not satisfied merely by recognizing another person's offense and yet failing to stop it and tolerating it, but must consist of becoming one entity for the purpose of committing a particular criminal act with a common intent and thereby carrying out one's own intent by using the acts of another person (see Supreme Court Decisions 95DO2461, rendered January 26, 1996, 97DO3297, rendered June 26, 1998, and others).\\n\\nAccordingly, in order to punish the Defendants in this case as co-principals of the smuggling offenses stated in the judgment below, it is not enough to show only that the Defendants knew in advance of and tolerated the smuggling offenses of Nonparty 1, etc. or Nonparty 3, etc.; at least the Defendants' intent must have reached the point where it could be evaluated as intending to become one entity with them for the smuggling offenses and to execute their own intent to smuggle by using their acts.\\n\\nHowever, no matter how closely the record is examined, it is difficult to find sufficient materials to conclude that the Defendants expressed an intent, for the smuggling offenses, to become one entity with Nonparty 1, etc. or Nonparty 3, etc. and to carry out their own intent to smuggle by using their acts. Rather, according to the record, the Defendants, a married couple engaged in the business of selling imported goods, received a proposal from Nonparty 1, a crew member of Pegasus Pride, that he would bring goods such as camcorders from Japan and asked them to sell them, and responded, \"Since orders for camcorders are already coming in from Seoul, and I cannot sell any because I do not have any, bring them and I will sell them.\" Thereafter, when the crew members including Nonparty 1 smuggled in camcorders, etc. from Japan, took them out of the pier through Nonparty 2, met them at a rendezvous place, received the goods, paid the price at a price predetermined according to the then market price, and thereafter disposed of them elsewhere at a profit, and in the meantime trailer driver Nonparty 2 recommended that they also purchase liquor, so they began purchasing liquor smuggled in by the crew members of Meristar, including Nonparty 3; and unlike the camcorders, etc., they did not directly contact the crew members regarding the liquor, but negotiated the price with Nonparty 2, paid the price to Nonparty 2, received the liquor, and disposed of it.\\n\\nIf, as above, what the Defendants did in relation to the smuggling offenses in this case was merely to agree, after being asked by Nonparty 1 whether they would sell camcorders, etc. smuggled in from Japan, to sell them, or after being urged by Nonparty 2 to also purchase liquor, to agree to that, and thereafter, when the crew members smuggled goods in, to pay the price, receive the goods, and dispose of them to others, then it cannot be said that this constituted sharing the acts of execution of the smuggling offenses in this case or that the Defendants had the common intent required for the establishment of co-principal liability. The Defendants' statement that they would sell the goods if they were smuggled in can only be viewed as an expression of intent to acquire the goods or to mediate their sale if the goods were smuggled in, and cannot be viewed as an expression of an agreement to jointly commit the smuggling offenses.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below determined that the Defendants conspired with Nonparty 1, etc. or Nonparty 3, etc. and committed the smuggling offenses in this case, and recognized and punished the Defendants as co-principals of the smuggling crimes stated in its holding. This is an error of law as to the requirements for the establishment of co-principal liability, or an illegality of finding facts without evidence in violation of the rules of evidence. The portion of the grounds of appeal pointing out this issue has merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the judgment below and, in order to have the case retried and redetermined, remand it to the court below. The decision is rendered with the concurrence of the Justices participating in the case, and is so ordered."}

{"[2018DO10047]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Fraud against Victim Nonparty 1\\n\\nThe lower court found the fraud against Victim Nonparty 1 among the facts charged in this case to be guilty. Looking at the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the evidence duly admitted, there is no error in the lower court’s determination, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in that it did not conduct the necessary examination and thereby went beyond the limits of the free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehended the legal doctrine on the crime of fraud.\\n\\n2. Breach of Trust in the Course of Business\\n\\na.
