Claim of misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning accomplice and status\\n\\n(1) The crime of breach of trust in the course of business is established when a person who is in a position to handle another’s affairs in the course of business acquires a property gain, or causes a third person to acquire such gain, by an act in violation of that person’s duty, thereby causing damage to the principal. In terms of being in a position to handle another’s affairs, this is an aggravated provision for the crime of ordinary breach of trust, and thus it is a case where there is a difference in the severity of punishment by reason of a status relationship. Accordingly, if a person who does not have such a status relationship of a duty in the course of business conspired with a person having such a status relationship and committed the crime of breach of trust in the course of business, then, with respect to the accomplice without such status relationship, punishment must be imposed under the proviso of Article 33 of the Criminal Act with the punishment prescribed for ordinary breach of trust. In such a case, the status offense of breach of trust in the course of business is established at least against the accomplice without such status relationship under the main text of the same Article, but only in sentencing is the statutory punishment for ordinary breach of trust, rather than the heavier punishment, applied (see Supreme Court Decision 86DO1517, decided October 28, 1986; Supreme Court Decision 2010DO6507, decided September 9, 2010, etc.).\\n\\n(2) The facts charged in this part are that the Defendant conspired in the act of breach of trust in the course of business by Nonparty 1, who was in the position of handling another’s affairs in the course of business, with respect to Victim Nonparty 2; therefore, as to the Defendant, who does not have the status relationship of a duty in the course of business, the crime of breach of trust in the course of business, which is a status offense, is established at least under the main text of Article 33 of the Criminal Act, but in sentencing the statutory punishment for ordinary breach of trust must be applied under the proviso of Article 33 of the Criminal Act. Nevertheless, the lower court applied only Articles 356, 355(2), and 30 of the Criminal Act to the breach of trust in the course of business in this case, and selected imprisonment from among the statutory punishments under Article 356 of the Criminal Act applicable to the crime of breach of trust in the course of business; therefore, the lower court judgment misapplied the law by failing to apply the proviso of Article 33 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\n(3) However, because the lower court determined the punishment to be imposed by aggravating the punishment prescribed for the crime of fraud against Victim Nonparty 1, which is in a relation of concurrent crimes with the above crime of breach of trust in the course of business and is more serious in terms of gravity than the crime of breach of trust in the course of business, the error in the lower court judgment seen in (2) above does not affect the result of the judgment. The ground of appeal on this point is ultimately without merit.\\n\\nb. Remaining arguments\\n\\nThe lower court recognized the breach of trust in the course of business among the facts charged in this case as guilty. Looking at the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the legal doctrine seen above and the evidence duly admitted, there is no error in the lower court’s determination, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in that it did not conduct the necessary examination and thereby went beyond the limits of the free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehended the legal doctrine on the crime of breach of trust in the course of business.\\n\\n3. Claim of improper sentencing\\n\\nAccording to Article 383(4) of the Criminal Procedure Act, an appeal may be taken on the ground of improper sentencing only in cases where death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or confinement for 10 years or more has been imposed. Therefore, in this case, in which a lighter sentence than that was imposed on the Defendant, the argument that the sentence is too severe and therefore improper is not a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Defendant’s appeal is without merit, and it is ordered to dismiss it; accordingly, the Court renders judgment as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2020DO7866]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Summary of the aiding-and-abetting portion of the facts charged in this case, concerning a violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Prevention of Illegal Trafficking in Narcotics, etc. (hereinafter, the “Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act”)\\nThe Defendant, knowing that the non-indicted person used so-called a “borrowed-name bank account” in order to evade tracking by investigative authorities, nevertheless, at the request of the non-indicted person, while purchasing cannabis on 4 occasions by depositing the purchase price for cannabis into a borrowed-name account under the name of a third party by means of deposit without a passbook, aided and abetted the non-indicted person’s act of concealing the source and attribution relationship of illicit proceeds, etc. for the purpose of obstructing an investigation into the discovery of narcotics offenses.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the court below\\nThe court below reversed the first-instance judgment, which had found the above facts charged guilty, and found the Defendant not guilty for the following reasons.\\nIn the type of offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc.” prescribed in Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act, where the offense requires the existence of another person’s mutually opposing act in order to be committed, leaving aside the question whether a person in such mutually opposing relationship may become an instigator or co-principal where he or she actively participates in the entire process of the “concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc.” offense or instigates the offense, if the person merely performed the mutually opposing act in accordance with the request, etc. of the offender (the principal offender), the accomplice provisions of the general provisions of the Criminal Act cannot be applied to punish that person together with the offender (the principal offender) who committed the “concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc.” offense.\\nThe Defendant’s mutually opposing act as the purchaser of cannabis (depositing the purchase price into a borrowed-name bank account while purchasing cannabis) is an indispensable element of the non-indicted person’s offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc.”; therefore, it is not appropriate to apply the accomplice provisions of the general provisions of the Criminal Act to the Defendant’s act and punish the Defendant together with the non-indicted person, who is the principal offender and also the cannabis seller, and there are no circumstances indicating that the Defendant actively participated in the non-indicted person’s violation of the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act.\\n\\n3. Supreme Court determination\\nHowever, the above determination of the court below cannot be accepted.\\n\\na. The general provisions of the Criminal Act concerning accomplices cannot be applied to reciprocal offenses that require the existence of mutually opposing acts by 2 or more persons (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of 2004. 10. 28. 2004DO3994). This legal principle presupposes reciprocal offenses, which are necessary accomplices, in which the constituent elements of the punishment provision itself require the existence of mutually opposing acts by 2 or more persons. It cannot be said that this legal principle applies where the constituent elements are structured in a form that can be committed by a single person, but are merely carried out in the form of a reciprocal offense.\\n\\nb. Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act criminally punishes, as the offense of concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc., “a person who, for the purpose of obstructing an investigation into the discovery of narcotics offenses or the source of illicit proceeds, etc. or evading confiscation of illicit proceeds, etc., conceals or disguises the nature, location, source, or attribution relationship of illicit proceeds, etc.” Among such acts, the act of “concealing or disguising the source or attribution relationship of illicit proceeds, etc.” means an act of concealing or disguising facts concerning the cause of acquisition as if the illicit proceeds, etc. were lawfully acquired, or an act of concealing or disguising facts concerning attribution as if the illicit proceeds, etc. were not attributed (see Supreme Court Decision of 2014. 9. 4. 2014DO4408).\\nAccordingly, because the act of “concealing or disguising the source or attribution relationship of illicit proceeds, etc.” prescribed in Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act does not require, in the constituent elements of the punishment provision itself, the existence of mutually opposing acts by 2 or more persons, the accomplice provisions of the general provisions of the Criminal Act apply to the act of participating in such act by the principal offender.\\n\\nc. Article 32(1) of the Criminal Act provides: “A person who aids and abets another’s crime shall be punished as an accessory.” Aiding and abetting refers to a supportive act that, with knowledge of the principal offender’s specific preparation for or facts of the offense, makes the act of execution possible, promotes, or facilitates it, or to an act that, before the principal offender’s criminal act is completed, strengthens or increases the infringement of the legal interest by the principal offender, namely an act closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of 2012. 8. 30. 2012DO6027).\\nIn addition, an accessory must have the so-called “intent to aid and abet” to aid the principal offender’s execution and the “principal offender’s intent” as to the fact that the principal offender’s act is an act corresponding to the constituent elements (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision of 2021. 9. 9. 2017DO19025). With regard to the intent to aid and abet and the principal offender’s intent required for the establishment of an accessory to the principal offender’s offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc.” under the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act, this means, for example, that a cannabis purchaser, while purchasing cannabis from the principal offender who is a cannabis seller, deposits the cannabis sale price under the name of a third party into a borrowed-name account at the request of the cannabis seller, and must recognize that such act is unlawful as aiding the principal offender’s execution. Of course, the principal offender’s intent required in an accessory need not include awareness of the specific details of the crime realized by the principal offender, and conditional awareness or foresight is sufficient (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of 2005. 4. 29. 2003DO6056), but this does not conflict with the requirement that awareness of the unlawfulness of the principal offender’s crime, etc. is necessary (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision of 2021. 9. 9. 2017DO19025).\\n\\nd. The court below should have examined whether the Defendant’s act constituted aiding and abetting the violation of the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act arising from the principal offender, the non-indicted person’s act of “concealing or disguising the source or attribution relationship of illicit proceeds, etc.” as prescribed in Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act, and whether the Defendant had the intent to aid and abet.\\nNevertheless, the court below found the Defendant not guilty on the ground that the accomplice provisions of the general provisions of the Criminal Act do not apply to the Defendant who purchased cannabis and deposited the purchase price without a passbook into a borrowed-name bank account. The judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principle concerning the establishment, etc. of an accessory to the offense of violating the Narcotics Trafficking Prevention Act through concealment and disguise of illicit proceeds, etc., and by failing to conduct the necessary examination, and the grounds of appeal pointing this out are justified.\\n\\n4. Scope of reversal\\nFor the reasons stated above, the not guilty portion of the judgment of the court below must be reversed. Where, among several criminal facts charged as concurrent offenses, the court below rendered a guilty verdict for some and a not guilty verdict for others, and the prosecutor appealed only the not guilty portion, while neither the Defendant nor the prosecutor appealed the guilty portion, the guilty portion becomes final upon lapse of the appeal period, so even if the appeal as to the not guilty portion is meritorious, only the not guilty portion must be reversed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of 2007. 6. 28. 2005DO7473). Since the portions concerning the offense of violating the Act on the Management of Narcotics, etc. (cannabis), arising from cannabis sale, cannabis smoking, and attempted cannabis sale, which are in a concurrent-offense relationship with the not guilty portion of the judgment of the court below, were found guilty by the court below and neither the Defendant nor the prosecutor appealed them, they became final; therefore, the scope of reversal of the judgment of the court below is limited to the not guilty portion.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nThe not guilty portion of the judgment of the court below is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for rehearing and determination on that portion. It is so adjudged unanimously by the Justices as stated in the dispositive part."}

{"[2020DO7866]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Summary of the portion of the facts charged in this case constituting aiding and abetting a violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Prevention of Illicit Trade in Narcotics, Etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Narcotics Trade Prevention Act”)\\nThe Defendant, while knowing that the non-indicted person used a so-called “borrowed-name bank account” in order to evade tracing by investigative authorities, purchased cannabis on four occasions by depositing, at the request of the non-indicted person, the purchase price for cannabis into a nominee account in the name of a third party by cash deposit, and thereby aided the non-indicted person in concealing the source and relation of attribution of illicit profits, etc. for the purpose of obstructing an investigation into the detection of narcotics-related crimes.\\n\\n2. The lower court’s determination\\nThe lower court, for the following reasons, reversed the first-instance judgment that had found the above facts charged guilty and held the Defendant not guilty.\\nIn the type of offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc.” prescribed in Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act, where the commission of the offense necessarily requires another person’s reciprocal act, apart from the issue of whether a person in a reciprocal relationship may be an instigator or co-principal by actively participating in the principal offender’s offense, such as by being involved in the entire process of the offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc.” or by instigating the offense, if a person merely performed a reciprocal act in accordance with the request, etc. of the offender (principal offender), the provisions on complicity in the General Part of the Criminal Act cannot be applied to punish such person as an accomplice of the offender (principal offender) who committed the act of “concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc.”\\nThe reciprocal act of the Defendant, a purchaser of cannabis (depositing the purchase price into a borrowed-name bank account while purchasing cannabis), is an indispensable element of the non-indicted person’s offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc.”; therefore, it is not appropriate to apply the provisions on complicity in the General Part of the Criminal Act to the Defendant’s act and punish the Defendant together with the non-indicted person, who was both the principal offender and the cannabis seller, and there are no circumstances suggesting that the Defendant actively participated in the non-indicted person’s violation of the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s determination\\nHowever, the above determination of the lower court cannot be accepted.\\n\\na. The provisions of the General Part of the Criminal Act concerning complicity cannot be applied to reciprocal offenses that require the existence of reciprocal acts by two or more persons (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2004DO3994, decided October 28, 2004). This principle presupposes reciprocal offenses, which are necessary accomplice offenses requiring, in the elements of the offense itself, the existence of reciprocal acts by two or more persons. It cannot be said that the principle concerning reciprocal offenses applies merely because, although the offense is structured in a form that can be committed alone in terms of the elements of the offense, it happens to be committed in the form of a reciprocal offense.\\n\\nb. Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act criminally punishes, as the offense of concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc., “a person who conceals or disguises the nature, location, source, or relation of attribution of illicit profits, etc., for the purpose of obstructing an investigation into the detection of narcotics-related crimes or the source of illicit profits, etc. or evading confiscation of illicit profits, etc.” Among such conduct, the act of “concealing or disguising the source or relation of attribution of illicit profits, etc.” means an act of concealing or disguising facts concerning the cause of acquisition so as to make illicit profits, etc. appear to have been lawfully acquired, or an act of concealing or disguising facts concerning attribution so as to make illicit profits, etc. appear not to be attributed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2014DO4408, decided September 4, 2014).\\nAccordingly, since the act of “concealing or disguising the source or relation of attribution of illicit profits, etc.” prescribed in Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act does not, in the elements of the offense itself, require the existence of reciprocal acts by two or more persons, the provisions on complicity in the General Part of the Criminal Act apply to acts of participating in such conduct by the principal offender.\\n\\nc. Article 32(1) of the Criminal Act provides, “A person who aids another person’s crime shall be punished as an accessory.” Aiding and abetting means, with knowledge of the principal offender’s concrete preparation for or facts of the offense, an act of support that makes the execution possible, promotes, or facilitates it, or an act that, before the principal offender’s criminal act has ended, strengthens or increases the infringement of legal interests by the principal offender; it refers to an act closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2012DO6027, decided August 30, 2012).\\nIn addition, an accessory must have the so-called “intent to aid,” namely the intent to aid the principal offender’s execution, and the “intent of the principal offender” as to the fact that the principal offender’s act constitutes an act falling under the elements of the offense (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2017DO19025, decided September 9, 2021). As to the intent to aid and the principal offender’s intent required for the establishment of an accessory to the offense of “concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc.” under the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act, this means, for example, that when a purchaser of cannabis buys cannabis from the principal offender who is the cannabis seller and, at the request of the cannabis seller, deposits the cannabis purchase price into a nominee account in the name of a third party, the purchaser must recognize that such act is unlawful as it aids the principal offender’s execution of the offense. Of course, the principal offender’s intent required for an accessory need not involve recognition of the concrete content of the crime realized by the principal offender, and conditional awareness or foresight is sufficient (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2003DO6056, decided April 29, 2005), but this does not contradict the requirement that there be recognition of the unlawfulness of the principal offender’s offense, etc. (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2017DO19025, decided September 9, 2021).\\n\\nd. The lower court should have examined whether the Defendant’s act constituted aiding and abetting a violation of Article 7(1) of the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act by the principal offender, the non-indicted person, through the act of “concealing or disguising the source or relation of attribution of illicit profits, etc.,” and whether the Defendant had the intent to aid.\\nNevertheless, the lower court held that the provisions on complicity in the General Part of the Criminal Act did not apply to the Defendant, who purchased cannabis and deposited the purchase price by cash deposit into a borrowed-name bank account, and thus found the Defendant not guilty. The lower court judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment, etc. of an aider and abettor to a violation of the Narcotics Trade Prevention Act resulting from an act of concealment and disguise of illicit profits, etc., and by failing to conduct the necessary examination, and the argument in the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Scope of reversal\\nFor the reasons stated above, the not-guilty portion of the lower court judgment must be reversed. Where, among several criminal facts charged as concurrent offenses, the lower court separately rendered a guilty judgment on some and a not-guilty judgment on others, and the prosecutor appealed only the not-guilty portion while neither the Defendant nor the prosecutor appealed the guilty portion, the guilty portion becomes final upon expiration of the appeal period; therefore, even if the appeal as to the not-guilty portion is well-founded, only the not-guilty portion must be reversed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DO7473, decided June 28, 2007). The portions of the lower court judgment concerning the offense of violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. (cannabis) resulting from the sale and purchase of cannabis, cannabis smoking, and attempted sale of cannabis, which are in concurrent-offense relation with the not-guilty portion of the lower court judgment, were found guilty by the lower court, and since neither the Defendant nor the prosecutor appealed them, they became final; therefore, the scope of reversal of the lower court judgment is limited to the not-guilty portion.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nAccordingly, the not-guilty portion of the lower court judgment is reversed and this case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination on that portion, and the judgment is rendered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2022DO15537]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Relevant legal principles  \\n“Aiding and abetting” refers to an act of assistance that, by knowing the principal offender’s specific preparation for or facts of the offense, makes the execution act possible, promotes it, or facilitates it, or to an act that, before the principal offender’s criminal conduct is completed, strengthens or increases the infringement of the legal interest by the principal offender, that is, an act closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime. An aider and abettor must have both the so-called intent to aid, namely the intent to aid the principal offender’s execution, and the principal offender’s intent as to the fact that the principal offender’s act is an act falling under the constituent elements of the offense; and because it is a crime established subordinately to the principal offender, a causal relationship is required between the aiding act and the realization of the principal offender’s crime. In order for aiding and abetting to be established, the aiding act must be closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime and must be capable of being evaluated as having actually contributed to the realization of the principal offender’s crime, such as by causing the principal offender to realize a concrete risk or by increasing the opportunity to bring about the criminal result. Where the act merely assisted conduct not closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime, aiding and abetting is not established (see Supreme Court en banc Decision rendered on September 9, 2021, 2017DO19025, Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 16, 2021, 2015DO12632, etc.).\\n\\n2. Lower court determination  \\nThe lower court determined that the operators of Baksa-bang created the Telegram group described in the opinion (hereinafter referred to as the “Mission Room”) and, by ordering the so-called “real-time search ranking challenge” by which participants in the Mission Room would cause a specific search term to appear as a real-time trending search term by simultaneously entering a specific search term on the Internet portal Naver at specific times (2019. 12. 1. 20:00, 21:00, 22:00, 23:00 and 2019. 12. 2. 00:00, 01:00, 02:00, 03:00, 08:00, 21:00), caused an unspecified number of Telegram users to participate in the Mission Room at the designated times, and then, around 2019. 12. 2. 21:20, posted obscene materials concerning the victim, the non-indicted person, in the Mission Room; and, in relation thereto, the court found that the Defendant, while recognizing the operators of Baksa-bang’s intent to distribute obscene materials concerning the victim, the non-indicted person, entered search terms on four occasions from 2019. 12. 1. 21:00 to 2019. 12. 2. 00:00 in accordance with their instructions with the intent to facilitate the same, and by posting and certifying the fact of the searches in the above Mission Room and the channel related to Baksa-bang, facilitated the act of distributing obscene materials for children and juveniles by the operators of Baksa-bang and thereby aided and abetted it.\\n\\n3. Supreme Court determination  \\na. According to the legal principles examined above, in order for aiding and abetting to be established, not only must there be the intent to aid, namely the intent to aid the principal offender’s execution, and the principal offender’s intent as to the fact that the principal offender’s act is an act falling under the constituent elements of the offense, but also the relevant act must be closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime and must be capable of being evaluated as having actually contributed to the realization of the principal offender’s crime, such as by causing the principal offender to realize a concrete risk or by increasing the opportunity to bring about the criminal result; accordingly, it is difficult to recognize the establishment of aiding and abetting merely because a person performed or was involved in an act not closely related to the realization of the principal offender’s crime. In light of the reasoning of the lower court judgment and the evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court, the lower court’s determination cannot be upheld for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) As to the total of four searches listed in the attached schedule of offenses of the lower court judgment, it is acknowledged that, for some of those searches, the time gap between the time the search terms were announced in the “Mission Room” and the time the Defendant searched was quite short (items 2 and 3), or the time gap between the announced designated search time and the time the Defendant searched was quite short (items 1 and 4). However, such circumstances cannot immediately be said to constitute indirect facts supporting the proposition that the Defendant recognized that the “real-time search ranking challenge” was being carried out as a means of realizing the crime of distributing obscene materials concerning the victim, the non-indicted person, by the operators of Baksa-bang, or that the Defendant actually participated in the “Mission Room.” In other words, from the investigative stage to the trial, the Defendant consistently stated that he conducted the searches in this case out of curiosity after reading a post concerning the non-indicted person in “△△,” and submitted evidence related to “△△” consistent therewith; ① the evidence related to “△△” submitted by the Defendant clearly shows a situation in which the same keyword was repeatedly searched, without any particular reason or explanation, starting approximately 30 minutes before the time when the Mission Room announced the search keyword for item 2 of the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court judgment; and ② even according to the evidence submitted by the prosecutor, it can be seen that the first certification by a participant had already been completed approximately 10 minutes before the time when the Mission Room announced the search keyword for items 1 and 3 of the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court judgment. This shows circumstances indicating that the search terms listed in the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court judgment were being widely searched across various websites and multiple chat rooms, including “△△,” which was unrelated to Baksa-bang, even before the instructions of the operators of Baksa-bang; if so, it is difficult to exclude the possibility that the Defendant searched them after seeing them on other sites such as “△△” rather than in the “Mission Room,” as he contended, and the possibility that the operators of Baksa-bang also issued the instructions listed in the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court judgment in the sense of riding on the above widespread existing search state. This is even more so in light of the fact, as recognized in the first-instance judgment, that the victim, the non-indicted person, was a person who became famous by appearing in the ○○ program, that at that time numerous posts actually related to the non-indicted person were being uploaded on △△ and the like, and that the Defendant also ordinarily liked □□ music and had applied for the above ○○ program. Therefore, the time gap between the Defendant’s search time and the time the search terms were announced in the Mission Room or the announced designated search time is difficult to regard as having significant meaning in relation to the facts charged in this case.\\n\\n2) Even in light of the fact that there were approximately 2,700 participants in the “Mission Room,” whereas approximately 12,000 people searched for the “non-indicted person” on Naver from 2019. 12. 1. to 2019. 12. 2., it is difficult to exclude the possibility that they searched for it through various routes and motives unrelated to the posting and search instructions of the operators of Baksa-bang, rather than pursuant thereto. In particular, in the absence of any evidence to acknowledge that the chat room the Defendant entered through △△ and the “Mission Room” described in the facts charged in this case are the same, the mere fact that the Defendant searched for the same phrase as the search term announced in the “Mission Room” at a time close to a particular point in time, or certified some search screen in the chat room he entered, cannot justify the inference that he knew of the content of the instructions, such as the real-time search ranking challenge posted in the “Mission Room” by the operators of Baksa-bang, and acted pursuant thereto. The Defendant himself also consistently asserted, in substance, that “as a fan of the non-indicted person, he searched after seeing rumors about the non-indicted person posted on △△ and the controversy surrounding their truthfulness.” If the Defendant had known the contents of the instructions in the “Mission Room” and searched in accordance with those instructions, it would be possible to infer that he would have participated in all real-time search ranking challenges, if only to avoid being forcibly expelled as posted; yet the Defendant, apart from the searches listed in the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court judgment, additionally searched for the “non-indicted person” seven times until around 03:30 on 2019. 12. 2. at times unrelated to the designated search times announced in the “Mission Room,” and except for that, he does not appear to have entered the relevant search terms at the designated search times announced in the “Mission Room.” Even considering that most of the Defendant’s search times make it difficult to conclude that they were related to the designated search times announced in the “Mission Room,” it cannot be said that the Defendant participated in the real-time search ranking challenge according to the instructions of the “Mission Room”; rather, in light of the fact that, even under such circumstances, he was not forcibly expelled from the chat room, it is difficult to exclude the possibility that the chat room in which the Defendant participated was not the “Mission Room” opened by the operators of Baksa-bang, and this constitutes circumstances inconsistent with the facts charged in this case and indirect facts supporting the Defendant’s assertion.\\n\\n3) As such, inasmuch as it is difficult to find that the Defendant participated in the “Mission Room” and thereby recognized the instructions and announcements of the operators of Baksa-bang, or that he knew, from the search terms alone, that they were for the criminal act of “distributing obscene materials for children and juveniles,” it is difficult to conclude that there was, with respect to the facts charged in this case, the intent to aid and abet, much less the principal offender’s intent concerning the distribution of obscene materials for children and juveniles. Furthermore, adding to the above search circumstances the fact that the operators of Baksa-bang distributed obscene materials for children and juveniles only at a point approximately 21 hours to 24 hours after the Defendant’s search times listed in the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court judgment, the act of merely entering search terms encountered through various routes at the time in question, as in this case, rather than actively participating in the operators’ “Mission Room” and entering search terms and certifying in accordance with its instructions, may be viewed as having been merely utilized in the real-time search ranking challenge, etc. that the operators of Baksa-bang initiated with the intent to entice persons interested in the fact that a specific search term was then a hot issue into the “Mission Room” and thereby promote the sale of obscene materials, and it is difficult otherwise to acknowledge a close relationship or causal relationship between each of the Defendant’s acts and the realization of the principal offender’s crime, or to conclude that each of the Defendant’s acts actually contributed to the realization of the principal offender’s crime.\\n\\nb. Nevertheless, the lower court found the facts charged in this case guilty solely on the grounds stated in the opinion. In so doing, the lower court erred by violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning aiding and abetting, and such error affected the judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion  \\nTherefore, the lower court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. Accordingly, the judgment is rendered as stated in the order, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Of A, who has one of the following <CRIMINAL_RECORDS>, if A is indicted on November 10, 2023, for one or more of the following <CRIMINAL_FACTS>, and those <CRIMINAL_FACTS> are found to be true, which of the following statements is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents) <CRIMINAL_RECORD> Ⓐ On April 10, 2023, at the Seoul Central District Court, he was sentenced to a fine of 5,000,000 won for habitual theft, and that judgment became final on April 18, 2023. Ⓑ On May 10, 2023, at the Seoul Central District Court, he was sentenced to imprisonment for 6 months for theft, and that judgment became final on May 18, 2023. <CRIMINAL_FACTS> ㉠ Habitually, around February 10, 2023, at X convenience store, he took one mobile phone owned by victim M and stole it [habitual theft]. ㉡ Around March 8, 2023, at Y coffee shop, he lied to victim N, saying, “There is a virtual asset that will be listed on a famous virtual asset exchange within a few days, and if you invest money in me, you can obtain a profit of several hundred times or more,” and around March 10, 2023, received 10,000,000 won from victim N and thereby defrauded him [fraud]. ㉢ Around June 10, 2023, at Z entertainment bar, he struck victim O on the cheek several times and kicked the victim’s leg with his foot, assaulting the victim [assault].
A: If A, who has a criminal record, is indicted for the ㉠ offense, and it is recognized that the ㉠ criminal fact and the Ⓐ criminal fact were committed by the same habitual pattern, a judgment of dismissal of prosecution under Article 326, item 1, of the Criminal Procedure Act must be rendered.
B: If A, who has a criminal record, is indicted for the ㉠ offense, even if it is recognized that the ㉠ criminal fact and the Ⓑ criminal fact were committed by the same habitual pattern, a judgment of dismissal of prosecution under Article 326, item 1, of the Criminal Procedure Act cannot be rendered.
C: If A, who has a criminal record, is indicted for the ㉡ offense, it is in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the Ⓐ offense, for which the judgment has become final.
D: If A, who has a criminal record, is indicted for the ㉡ and ㉢ offenses, since the ㉡ offense is in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the Ⓑ offense, for which the judgment has become final, the court must, when rendering a judgment simultaneously on the ㉡ and ㉢ offenses, sentence one punishment for the ㉡ offense and one punishment for the ㉢ offense, respectively.
E: If A, who has a criminal record, is indicted for the ㉡ and ㉢ offenses, even when the punishment is reduced for the ㉡ offense under Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act concerning statutory mitigation applies, and when reducing a fixed-term imprisonment, it cannot be reduced to less than one-half of the term.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DO7864]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nEven if the criminal facts for which a final judgment has been rendered and the criminal facts committed before the pronouncement of the judgment of fact in that final judgment can be evaluated as falling under a single comprehensive offense as a habitual offender, in order for the res judicata effect of that final judgment to extend even to the criminal facts committed before that time, the defendant concerned must have been indicted and punished as a habitual offender in that final judgment; if the defendant was punished only for the basic constituent offense and not as a habitual offender, then even if the criminal facts for which the final judgment was rendered and the criminal facts committed before that time are comprehensively considered and are thus determined to constitute a single comprehensive offense as a habitual offender only at that point, it cannot be deemed that the res judicata effect of that final judgment extends to the criminal facts committed before the pronouncement of the judgment of fact (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2001DO3206 rendered on September 16, 2004).\\n\\nIn the same purport, the lower court’s determination that it did not render a judgment of dismissal for the crime of fraud in this case is correct, and there is no illegality such as a misapprehension of law as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and part of the number of days of detention after the appeal is to be included in the principal sentence for each of the offenses set forth in Paragraph 1 of the holding, and the judgment is rendered as ordered, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2006DO7864]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nEven if the criminal facts for which a final judgment has been rendered and the criminal facts committed before the pronouncement of the fact-finding judgment in that final judgment may be evaluated as constituting a habitual offense and thus a comprehensive single offense, in order for the res judicata effect of that final judgment to extend to the criminal facts committed before that time, in that final judgment the defendant in question must have been indicted and punished as a habitual offender; where the defendant was only punished for an offense comprising the basic constituent elements, not for a habitual offense, even if the criminal facts for which the final judgment was rendered and the criminal facts committed before that time are combined and only then determined to all correspond to a comprehensive single offense as a habitual offender, the res judicata effect of that final judgment cannot be deemed to extend to the criminal facts committed before the pronouncement of the fact-finding judgment (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2001DO3206, decided September 16, 2004).\\n\\nOn the same reasoning, the appellate court's determination not to render a judgment of dismissal of prosecution with respect to the criminal facts of the fraud offense in this case is correct, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of law, as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and part of the number of days of detention after the appeal is credited toward the principal punishment for each offense in Paragraph 1, and the judgment is rendered as ordered, with the unanimous opinion of the judges participating."}

{"[2014DO469]": "We determine the grounds for final appeal (the statements in a supplemental statement of grounds for final appeal submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds for final appeal has elapsed shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\nIn light of the wording and legislative purpose, etc. of the latter part of Article 37 and Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, where an offense that has not yet been adjudicated could not be adjudicated together with an offense for which judgment has already become final and conclusive, it is reasonable to interpret that the relation of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act cannot arise, and that a sentence may not be imposed, reduced, or exempted by considering equity with a case in which the offenses are adjudicated together under Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DO9948 rendered on October 27, 2011; Supreme Court Decision 2012DO9295 rendered on September 27, 2012). Meanwhile, where several offenses that have not yet been adjudicated were committed before and after the judgment became final and conclusive, if the offenses committed before the judgment became final and conclusive could not be adjudicated together with the offenses for which judgment had already become final and conclusive, it cannot be said that the relation of concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act is recognized between those several offenses as if no final and conclusive judgment existed, and that Article 38 of the Criminal Act applies; therefore, a sentence can only be separately determined and imposed for each offense committed before and after the judgment became final and conclusive (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DO2351 rendered on June 10, 2011).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the offenses of violating the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. (psychotropic drugs) committed on January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012 in this case were committed before the judgment sentencing the Defendant to imprisonment for 8 months, suspended for 2 years, for the same offense at the Seoul Central District Court became final and conclusive on February 29, 2012; however, separate from the above prior conviction, the Defendant has another prior conviction in which the Seoul Central District Court sentenced him to imprisonment for 1 year, suspended for 2 years, for the same offense, etc., and which became final and conclusive on November 26, 2011, and the offenses for which judgment became final and conclusive on February 29, 2012 were committed before the judgment became final and conclusive on November 26, 2011, so it can be seen that the offenses for which judgment became final and conclusive on February 29, 2012 and the offenses of January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012 in this case could not, from the outset, be adjudicated together.\\n\\nTherefore, no relation of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act can arise between the offenses for which judgment became final and conclusive on February 29, 2012 and the offenses of January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012 in this case, and Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, which requires consideration of equity with a case in which the offense and the offense for which judgment has become final and conclusive are adjudicated together when imposing a sentence for an offense that has not yet been adjudicated among concurrent offenses, has no room for application here. Nor does it follow that, as if the judgment that became final and conclusive on February 29, 2012 did not exist, the relation of concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act is recognized between the offenses of January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012, which were committed before the above judgment became final and conclusive, and the remaining offenses committed after the above judgment became final and conclusive, and that Article 38 of the Criminal Act applies. Therefore, a sentence can only be separately determined and imposed for the offenses of January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012 and the remaining offenses in this case.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court correctly determined that no relation of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act can arise between the offenses for which judgment became final and conclusive on February 29, 2012 and the offenses of January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012 in this case. However, the lower court, on the premise that the relation of concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act is recognized between the offenses of January 5, 2012 and January 17, 2012 in this case, which were committed before the above judgment became final and conclusive, and the remaining offenses committed after the above judgment became final and conclusive, determined and imposed a single sentence for all of the offenses in this case, which contains illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nTherefore, without reaching the Defendant’s grounds for final appeal, the lower court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court, and it is so adjudged as follows by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2017DO14609]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Procedural History and Issues\\n\\na. On December 9, 2016, the Defendant was convicted by the Daejeon High Court of the offense of violating the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropics) and sentenced to imprisonment for 4 years on the factual finding that “from March 11, 2015, to August 7, 2015, he sold psychotropic drugs on 33 occasions.” That judgment became final by the Supreme Court’s decision dismissing the appeal on February 10, 2017 (hereinafter referred to as “the prior conviction in this case”).\\n\\nb. While the above trial was still pending before the Daejeon High Court, on November 22, 2016, this indictment was filed against the Defendant at the Gongju Branch of the Daejeon District Court on the counts of violating the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropics), alleging the following facts (hereinafter referred to as “the offense in this case”): “in early October 2015, he sold psychotropic drugs once, and on November 8, 2015, he attempted to sell psychotropic drugs once but failed.” The offense in this case constitutes the sale and attempted sale of psychotropic drugs; accordingly, Article 58(1) 3 and Article 58(3), Article 58(1) 3 of the Narcotics Control Act apply, and the statutory punishment is life imprisonment or imprisonment for not less than 5 years.\\n\\nc. The latter sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act provides that “an offense committed before the final judgment of an offense for which a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier has been imposed and an offense committed before the finality of that judgment shall be concurrent offenses.” Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act provides that “where there is an offense among concurrent offenses that has not yet been adjudicated, a sentence shall be imposed for that offense, taking into account equity with the case where that offense and the offense for which judgment has become final are adjudicated at the same time. In such case, the sentence may be mitigated or remitted.” Article 55(1) 3 of the Criminal Act provides that “when mitigating a determinate term of imprisonment or confinement, the term shall be reduced to one-half thereof.”\\n\\nd. The trial court selected determinate terms of imprisonment for the offense in this case, found that the offense in the prior conviction in this case and the offense in this case were in the relation of concurrent offenses under the latter sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act (hereinafter referred to as “latter-part concurrent offenses”), and, pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, applied Article 55(1) 3 of the Criminal Act to grant statutory mitigation. It then applied, in sequence, the aggravation for concurrent offenses under the former sentence of Article 37 and Article 38(1), and discretionary mitigation, and within the range of the sentence to be imposed thus calculated (imprisonment from 1 year and 3 months to 11 years and 3 months), sentenced the Defendant to imprisonment for 1 year and 6 months.\\n\\ne. The appellate court reversed the trial court judgment and sentenced the Defendant to imprisonment for 6 months for the following reasons. That is, where, as in this case, the offense falling within latter-part concurrent offenses committed before the judgment imposing a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier becomes final is subject to a statutory minimum sentence, and where the sentence prescribed for that offense and the sentence prescribed for the offense whose judgment has become final are the “same type of sentence other than death, life imprisonment, or life confinement” as provided in Article 38(1) 2 of the Criminal Act (hereinafter referred to as “the issue at hand”), then in mitigating punishment pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, no limit may be imposed on the extent of mitigation. Therefore, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act concerning statutory mitigation does not apply, and the sentence should be determined fairly and appropriately in consideration of equity with the case where punishment is imposed as former-part concurrent offenses under the former sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act (hereinafter referred to as “former-part concurrent offenses”).\\n\\nUltimately, the appellate court selected determinate terms of imprisonment for the offense in this case, found it to be in the relation of latter-part concurrent offenses with the offense in the prior conviction in this case, applied the former sentence of Article 37 and Article 38(1) of the Criminal Act to aggravate punishment for concurrent offenses, then applied Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act to mitigate punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses, and thereafter applied discretionary mitigation.\\n\\nf. The gist of the prosecutor’s grounds for appeal is that, when mitigating punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses pursuant to the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, the statutory mitigation method under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act must be followed.\\n\\ng. The issue in this case is whether, when mitigating punishment pursuant to the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act for latter-part concurrent offenses for which a statutory minimum sentence has been set, as in the present issue, in the case of imprisonment it should be deemed possible to mitigate only within one-half of the term of imprisonment by applying Article 55(1) 3 of the Criminal Act, or whether the application of Article 55(1) 3 of the Criminal Act should be excluded so that mitigation below one-half of the term of imprisonment is possible.\\n\\n2. The Supreme Court’s Determination\\n\\na. According to existing Supreme Court precedents, even when mitigating punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act concerning statutory mitigation applies, and when mitigating a determinate term of imprisonment, mitigation below one-half of the term is not allowed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DO6627, decided December 21, 2006). These Supreme Court precedents are sound and should be maintained going forward. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\nb. 1) Sentencing is divided into stages such as confirmation of the statutory punishment, determination of the sentence to be imposed, and determination of the sentence to be pronounced. When imposing a sentence, a judge must determine the sentence to be pronounced only within the range of the sentence to be imposed, formed through aggravation and mitigation of the statutory punishment, while considering sentencing factors; this also applies to latter-part concurrent offenses (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DO8376, decided September 11, 2008).\\n\\nArticle 56 of the Criminal Act prescribes the order of aggravation and mitigation when causes for aggravation and mitigation of punishment coincide in the following order: “1. aggravation under the main text of each respective provision, 2. aggravation under Article 34(2), 3. repeat-offender aggravation, 4. statutory mitigation, 5. aggravation for concurrent offenses, 6. discretionary mitigation.” Since statutory mitigation is to be applied first and discretionary mitigation last, where there is a cause for statutory mitigation, it must be applied before discretionary mitigation; discretionary mitigation is applied when, even after such statutory mitigation has been fully applied, the range of the sentence to be imposed is to be eased so as to pronounce a lower sentence (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 91DO985, decided June 11, 1991, and 2005DO6120, decided September 29, 2005). Where Article 55 and Article 56 of the Criminal Act apply to an offense with a statutory minimum sentence, the mitigated minimum is maintained even after statutory mitigation and discretionary mitigation.\\n\\n2) In light of the above provisions of the Criminal Act, since the sentence to be imposed becomes the final standard for the sentence to be pronounced, its scope must be strictly determined according to law, and unless there is a separate express provision, no mitigation ground of a different nature from the causes for aggravation and mitigation listed in Article 56 of the Criminal Act may be recognized.\\n\\nThere are statutory mitigation and judicial mitigation, namely discretionary mitigation. Aside from discretionary mitigation, all mitigation prescribed in various provisions of the law falls within the single framework of statutory mitigation. Accordingly, mitigation prescribed in the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act naturally constitutes statutory mitigation. The wording “the sentence may be mitigated or remitted” in the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act is no different from other statutory grounds for mitigation. If Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act were to be understood as establishing a new type of mitigation, then, with respect to it, a different extent or method of mitigation from ordinary statutory mitigation would have to be provided, and the order of mitigation should also have been separately prescribed; yet no such provision exists. Unless the extent, method, or order of mitigation is otherwise provided, it is entirely natural to view Articles 55 and 56 of the Criminal Act, which are general provisions on the method of statutory mitigation, as applicable even to latter-part concurrent offenses.\\n\\nc. The problem of latter-part concurrent offenses arises because, although the offense and the offense whose judgment has become final could have been adjudicated together as former-part concurrent offenses, they were not, and thus the defendant may be disadvantaged compared with the case of simultaneous adjudication. However, how latter-part concurrent offenses should be handled is fundamentally a matter of legislative policy. Whether to consider this at the sentencing stage, whether to consider it at the execution stage, and, if considered at either stage, how it is to be considered, all must follow the legislature’s intent.\\n\\nSince the enactment of the Criminal Act until it was amended by Act No. 7623 on July 29, 2005, into its present form, Article 39 had provided in paragraph 1 that “where there is an offense among concurrent offenses that has not yet been adjudicated, a sentence shall be imposed for that offense,” and in paragraph 2 that “where there are several judgments under the preceding paragraph, they shall be executed according to the example of the preceding Article.”\\n\\nAlthough the current Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act aims to eliminate disparities in punishment between latter-part concurrent offenses and former-part concurrent offenses, it does not state that, where there is an offense among concurrent offenses that has not yet been adjudicated, one should “determine the total sentence within the range of the sentence to be imposed calculated by applying Article 38 of the Criminal Act to that offense and the offense whose judgment has become final, and then pronounce, as the sentence for the offense not yet adjudicated, the remainder after deducting the sentence for the offense whose judgment has become final from that total sentence,” or that one should “pronounce, as the sentence for the offense not yet adjudicated, a sentence such that the total of the sentences pronounced for that offense and the offense whose judgment has become final falls within the range of the sentence to be imposed calculated by applying Article 38 of the Criminal Act to both offenses.” Rather, by providing that a sentence is to be imposed for the offense not yet adjudicated “taking into account equity with the case where that offense and the offense whose judgment has become final are adjudicated at the same time,” the legislature adopted a flexible legislative form enabling the court to determine a reasonable and appropriate sentence, taking into account that determining the total sentence or limiting the range of the sentence to be imposed in the manner described above could amount to a second adjudication of the offense whose judgment has already become final, thereby potentially violating the principle against double jeopardy, and could unduly restrict the range of the sentence that may be imposed for latter-part concurrent offenses sentenced later, making it impossible or extremely difficult to determine a reasonable and appropriate sentence corresponding to responsibility (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2006DO8376, etc.).\\n\\nDuring the above legislative amendment process, there was a proposed amendment to include in the current Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act a provision that “mitigation may be made even below the mitigation limit under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act,” thereby enabling mitigation without a lower limit, but it was not ultimately adopted. In other words, although the legislative process presented the view that the application of Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act should be excluded when mitigating latter-part concurrent offenses, that view was not accepted. In light of this, it is not only consistent with textual and systematic interpretation to regard mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses as one form of ordinary statutory mitigation and to require compliance with Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act in mitigating latter-part concurrent offenses, but it also accords with teleological interpretation considering the legislature’s intent and legislative history.\\n\\nd. Meanwhile, the introductory sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act provides that “where there is an offense among concurrent offenses that has not yet been adjudicated, a sentence shall be imposed for that offense, taking into account equity with the case where that offense and the offense whose judgment has become final are adjudicated at the same time.” This merely expresses the intent to determine punishment by taking equity into account at the sentencing stage, rather than at the execution stage as had previously been done for latter-part concurrent offenses, and cannot be understood as declaring that, for latter-part concurrent offenses, mitigation may be made without any restriction on the extent of mitigation so as to achieve perfect equity with simultaneous adjudication.\\n\\nThat is, the provision that a sentence shall be imposed “taking into account equity with the case where that offense and the offense whose judgment has become final are adjudicated at the same time” declares the principle that the court shall impose a sentence for latter-part concurrent offenses within the range of the sentence to be imposed, taking into account equity with the case where the offense whose judgment has become final and the latter-part concurrent offense are adjudicated together, thereby presenting an additional consideration relevant to sentencing under Article 51 of the Criminal Act. This means that, in the case of latter-part concurrent offenses, if in the sentencing process the resulting punishment is deemed inequitable compared with punishing the offense whose judgment has become final together with the latter-part concurrent offense, the punishment must, as far as possible, be made equitable through mitigation or exemption from punishment as provided in the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act. If, in light of sentencing discretion, it is considered impossible to reach an equitable result by mitigation alone, exemption from punishment suffices. Whether to mitigate or exempt punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses is, in principle, a matter that the court adjudicating the offense may determine at its discretion (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2006DO8376, etc.). Therefore, there is not much need to view the law as permitting a sentence outside the lower limit of the sentence to be imposed, contrary to the significant principle that even when mitigating offenses with a statutory minimum, a certain minimum must be maintained. It is also difficult to say that a judge’s sentencing discretion is seriously infringed or that appropriate sentencing becomes impossible.\\n\\ne. It cannot be categorically said that, in mitigating punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses, maintaining a lower limit for the term of punishment is disadvantageous to the defendant, or that not maintaining such a lower limit is advantageous to the defendant. If, after eliminating the lower limit of punishment so that the sentence to be imposed becomes continuous up to exemption from punishment, the sentence is determined, then this would run counter to the purpose of the law, which, while requiring that a sentence for latter-part concurrent offenses be imposed taking into account equity with the case where the offense is punished together with the offense whose judgment has become final, allows not only mitigation but also exemption from punishment, and may in fact produce a disadvantageous result for the defendant. If Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act is applied to mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses, then after mitigation the sentence is determined within the range of the sentence to be imposed, that is, with a lower limit of punishment maintained; at that time, if it is considered inequitable compared with punishing the offense together with the offense whose judgment has become final, the court will choose exemption from punishment rather than pronouncement of sentence, because such exemption is more favorable to the defendant than pronouncing a sentence with the lower limit removed.\\n\\nf. Exemption from punishment is not the case where the sentence to be imposed is “0.” The fixation of the sentence to be imposed is carried out at a stage prior to pronouncement of sentence, whereas exemption from punishment means that although the offense is established and the power to punish has arisen, punishment is not imposed for certain reasons; in other words, it is a guilty judgment but no sentence is pronounced, so it does not presuppose a sentence to be imposed. Also, the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act regarding latter-part concurrent offenses provides that “in such case, the sentence may be mitigated or remitted,” and does not provide that “in such case, the sentence may be mitigated and remitted,” so it is clear from the wording that mitigation and exemption from punishment are not compatible. Therefore, if one chooses mitigation, one cannot reflect the result of exemption from punishment. But if one accepts that there is no lower limit for mitigation, then no meaning remains for separately providing exemption from punishment apart from mitigation.\\n\\n3. Resolution of this Case\\n\\nIn light of these legal principles, the appellate court, having selected determinate imprisonment from among the statutory punishment of life imprisonment or imprisonment for not less than 5 years and having decided to mitigate punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses and to apply discretionary mitigation, should have aggravated and mitigated punishment in the order prescribed by Article 56 of the Criminal Act—namely, mitigation pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act (Article 56 4), aggravation for concurrent offenses (Article 56 5), and discretionary mitigation (Article 56 6)—and, in doing so, should have mitigated in accordance with Article 55(1) 3 of the Criminal Act to “one-half of the term of that punishment,” and thus should have determined the Defendant’s sentence within the range of the sentence to be imposed, namely imprisonment from 1 year and 3 months to 11 years and 3 months.\\n\\nNevertheless, contrary to this, the appellate court, on the erroneous premise that Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act does not apply when mitigating punishment prescribed by Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act for latter-part concurrent offenses, sentenced the Defendant to imprisonment for 6 months, which fell below the statutory lower limit of the sentence to be imposed as described above. There is error in the appellate court’s judgment in misapprehending the legal principles concerning mitigation of punishment prescribed in Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, thereby affecting the judgment. The prosecutor’s grounds of appeal pointing out this issue are well-founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appellate judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the appellate court for further proceedings and determination. It is so adjudged as set forth in the disposition. In this judgment, apart from the dissenting opinions of Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Ahn Cheol-sang, Kim Seon-soo, and Justice Lee Ki-taek, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there is a supplemental opinion to the majority opinion by Justices Park Sang-ok, Min Yoo-sook, and Lee Dong-won.\\n\\n5. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Ahn Cheol-sang, and Kim Seon-soo\\n\\na. When mitigating punishment under Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act for latter-part concurrent offenses under the latter sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act (“an offense committed before the final judgment of an offense for which a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier has been imposed and an offense committed before the finality of that judgment”), does Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act, which prescribes the limit of statutory mitigation, apply?\\n\\nIn interpreting statutes, if neither wording nor system gives clear priority to one of two possible interpretations, the purpose and orientation of the statute become more important. Considering not only the wording and system of the statute at issue in this case but also its purpose, when mitigating latter-part concurrent offenses, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act should not apply, and it should be understood that mitigation may be made to a sentence lower than “one-half of the term of that punishment,” which is the lower limit of statutory mitigation. In contrast, it is difficult to agree with the majority opinion that Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act applies even to mitigation under Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\nb. First, as to the wording of the statute, there is no reason to apply Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act concerning statutory mitigation to the case of latter-part concurrent offenses.\\n\\nArticle 39(1) of the Criminal Act is a provision concerning how to determine the sentence to be pronounced for latter-part concurrent offenses. The introductory sentence of this provision declares that, for offenses among concurrent offenses not yet adjudicated, “a sentence shall be imposed taking into account equity with the case where they are adjudicated at the same time,” and the latter sentence additionally provides that “in such case, the sentence may be mitigated or remitted.” It imposes on the judge the duty to impose a sentence for latter-part concurrent offenses while necessarily considering equity, and declares the principle that the defendant should not be disadvantaged, but may be granted mitigation or exemption from punishment if necessary. Here, “mitigation” is provided together with “exemption from punishment” as a means of considering equity with the case where latter-part concurrent offenses are adjudicated together. The latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act supplements the preceding phrase “a sentence shall be imposed for that offense, taking into account equity,” and the meaning of the introductory sentence cannot be narrowed or limited on the basis of the wording of the latter sentence.\\n\\nOther mitigation provisions in statutes outside this provision (for example, Article 153 of the Criminal Act provides that “where a person who has committed the offense in the preceding Article confesses or surrenders before the trial or disciplinary action regarding the stated case becomes final, the sentence shall be mitigated or remitted”) allow, where a ground for mitigation exists, mitigation or exemption from punishment as its effect. In such cases, the “sentence” subject to mitigation refers either to the statutory punishment or, where there are other statutory grounds for mitigation, the “sentence to be imposed” after mitigation pursuant thereto.\\n\\nBy contrast, Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act sets forth in its introductory sentence the requirement that there be “an offense among concurrent offenses not yet adjudicated” and the effect that follows from that requirement, namely that “a sentence shall be imposed for that offense, taking into account equity with the case where it and the offense whose judgment has become final are adjudicated at the same time,” and then in the latter sentence provides that by that method the sentence may be “mitigated or remitted.” Apart from Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, no mitigation provision with such wording and structure can be found even upon examining both the Criminal Act and special criminal statutes.\\n\\nThe most important principle in interpreting the provision on latter-part concurrent offenses under the latter sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act is that the defendant should not suffer disadvantage merely because the offense is adjudicated in separate proceedings, as compared with the case where the offense whose judgment has become final and the latter-part concurrent offense are adjudicated together. The principle of proportionality between crime and punishment, which requires an appropriate balance between crime and punishment, and the principle of culpability, which requires punishment to be based on culpability and proportional thereto, are basic principles of criminal responsibility. The exceptional and independent form of the provision concerning latter-part concurrent offenses is based on the demand that the court adjudicating latter-part concurrent offenses, when punishing such offenses, discover a sentence consistent with the principle of proportionality and the principle of culpability so that the defendant is not disadvantaged merely because the offense is tried in separate proceedings, compared with the case where the offense whose judgment has become final and the latter-part concurrent offense are adjudicated together.\\n\\nIn light of this independent form and content of the provision and its legislative purpose, “a sentence shall be imposed taking into account equity” means that the sentence may be mitigated within an appropriate range, or exemption from punishment may be granted, and at this time Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act should be understood not to apply. If, when mitigating pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, one were to deem it subject to the limitations of Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act, the result could be inequitable.\\n\\nMoreover, since the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act does not expressly provide that Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act is to be applied as the method of mitigation, whether that provision applies in the case of latter-part concurrent offenses is left to interpretation. Even though Article 56 of the Criminal Act provides that discretionary mitigation follows statutory mitigation in the order of mitigation, it is difficult to say that it declares a principle that all statutory mitigation must preserve a lower limit. There is no rational reason to leave a gap in the range of the sentence to be imposed between the lower limit and exemption from punishment by imposing a lower limit on mitigation, when exemption from punishment is available in order to provide the court with the broadest possible means to determine a sentence taking into account equity. Even if one interprets that there is no lower limit for mitigation of latter-part concurrent offenses, there is no problem in terms of consistency within the criminal law system.\\n\\nIn short, while mitigation directed at the statutory punishment or the sentence to be imposed is properly construed as mitigation subject to Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act, the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act should be construed as confirming the content of the introductory sentence and, at the same time, as providing a separate means of equity for which the sentence may be mitigated within an appropriate range or punishment may be remitted, and thus as mitigation not subject to Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nc. Applying Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act to latter-part concurrent offenses produces highly unreasonable results, such as unexpected disadvantage to the defendant.\\n\\nIf, in mitigation pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, the mitigation method of “one-half of the term of punishment prescribed for each offense or the amount” prescribed in Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act applies, and the lower limit of mitigation is maintained even after statutory mitigation and discretionary mitigation, then this would not accord with the purpose of ensuring that, in latter-part concurrent offenses, the defendant is not disadvantaged merely because the offense is punished in separate proceedings compared with the case where the offense is punished together with the offense whose judgment has become final. Such an interpretation runs counter to the constitutional principles of equality and culpability. Where, among multiple offenses in a concurrent-offense relationship, the sentence discovered by considering equity with simultaneous punishment is not so low as to justify exemption from punishment, but is even lower than the lower limit of the sentence to be imposed after statutory mitigation, sentencing in accordance with the purpose of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act becomes impossible, thereby infringing the judge’s sentencing authority and violating culpability, as well as the principle of proportionality.\\n\\nIf several offenses with statutory minimum sentences were punished simultaneously, Article 38(1) of the Criminal Act would apply, and only the maximum term or maximum amount prescribed for the most serious offense would be aggravated by up to one-half. However, if the same offenses are punished in separate proceedings and, as the majority opinion asserts, a sentence lower than the lower limit of the sentence to be imposed cannot be pronounced, the defendant may be excessively punished. In such a case, because the sum of the lower limits of the sentence to be imposed for the offense whose judgment has become final and the sentence to be imposed for the latter-part concurrent offense becomes the new lower limit, punishment different from that in simultaneous punishment is unavoidable merely because the offenses are punished in separate proceedings.\\n\\nIn a case such as this, where the defendant has a prior conviction for an offense punishable by life imprisonment or imprisonment for not less than 5 years and is again indicted for the same offense, for the latter-part concurrent offense the court must either sentence him to imprisonment for 2 years and 6 months or more (or 1 year and 3 months or more if discretionary mitigation is also applied) or exempt him from punishment.
