If the court chooses the mitigated lower limit of punishment, the defendant will receive harsher punishment than in the case of simultaneous punishment, because the sum of the lower limits of the sentence to be imposed for the offense whose judgment has become final and the sentence to be imposed for the latter-part concurrent offense becomes the new lower limit. By contrast, if the court exempts punishment to avoid this result, the defendant receives more favorable treatment than in the case of simultaneous punishment, which leads to the irrational result that the defendant is treated more favorably without any justification compared with simultaneous punishment. Such a result, merely by maintaining a lower limit on statutory mitigation, causes the punishment range for the defendant to differ according to the prosecutor’s charging method without any rational reason, and thus irrationally discriminates between defendants punished simultaneously and defendants punished in separate proceedings, violating the principle of equality and the principle of culpability.\\n\\nThe appellate court, in addition to considering equity with the offense in the prior conviction in this case, for which the defendant received and finalized a sentence of imprisonment for 4 years, also took into account that the offense in this case, while identical to the offense in the prior conviction in terms of criminal method and type of drug involved, involved fewer than one-tenth of the number of offenses or profits obtained, and only about one-eighth of the amount of drugs handled, and that the investigative authorities, after investigating all 35 narcotics offenses committed by the defendant, prosecuted only the offenses involving 33 occasions first without special circumstances and separately indicted the offense in this case; as a result of considering these various circumstances, the appellate court determined that the punishment appropriate to the defendant’s responsibility for the offense in this case was imprisonment for 6 months.\\n\\nSuch sentencing judgment by the appellate court should be respected. If Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act is construed, as the majority opinion does, to apply to latter-part concurrent offenses, the appellate court’s sentencing authority is infringed as the court becomes unable to pronounce the punishment most appropriate to the defendant’s responsibility for the offense in this case. Even if the appellate court could choose exemption from punishment or suspend the execution of the sentence, the result remains the same: it cannot impose a sentence of imprisonment for 6 months that fits the responsibility, which leads to an unfair outcome. A principle that the lower limit of statutory mitigation must be maintained should not force the judge to determine punishment contrary to culpability.\\n\\nd. In light of the legislative history and legislative purpose, it is desirable to interpret Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act flexibly.\\n\\nThe legislature’s purpose in amending Article 39 of the Criminal Act by Act No. 7623 on July 29, 2005 was to ensure that, in the case of latter-part concurrent offenses, the defendant would not suffer disadvantage merely because the offense was punished in separate proceedings, and that a sentence consistent with the principle of proportionality between crime and punishment and the principle of culpability would be found. Before the amendment, Article 39 of the Criminal Act provided in paragraph 1 that “where there is an offense among concurrent offenses not yet adjudicated, a sentence shall be imposed for that offense,” and in paragraph 2 that “where there are several judgments under the preceding paragraph, they shall be executed according to the example of the preceding Article.” The Supreme Court interpreted this to mean that “execution according to the example of Article 38(1) 2 does not mean that each sentence pronounced by those judgments is reduced and executed pursuant to that provision, but rather that the terms of imprisonment pronounced by the respective judgments are aggregated and executed within the term-of-imprisonment range obtained by adding one-half to the maximum term prescribed for the most serious offense among the concurrent offenses according to that provision” (see Supreme Court Decision 67CHO6, dated March 6, 1967). As a result, by effectively executing each sentence in full, there arose the irrationality that, in the case of latter-part concurrent offenses, the defendant was punished more severely than in former-part concurrent offenses for reasons not attributable to the defendant’s responsibility, such as separate indictment, and to resolve this at the sentencing stage the provision was amended into the current Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nIn Austria and Switzerland, the system adopted is to determine an aggregate sentence matching the sentence that would have been imposed if the finalized offense and the latter-part concurrent offense had been punished simultaneously, and then, for the latter-part concurrent offense, to impose an additional sentence by deducting the sentence already imposed for the prior conviction from the aggregate sentence (Article 31(1) of the Austrian Criminal Code, Article 49(2) of the Swiss Criminal Code). Germany, too, imposes a new subsequent aggregate sentence for the offense whose judgment has become final and the latter-part concurrent offense, as if they were punished simultaneously (Articles 55(1), 53, and 54 of the German Criminal Code). These legislative examples show an intention not to disadvantage the defendant merely because the latter-part concurrent offense was punished in separate proceedings, and the purpose of our Criminal Act amendment is the same.\\n\\nAt the time of amendment to our Criminal Act, the original proposal was to determine one aggregate sentence within the range of the sentence to be imposed calculated by applying Article 38 of the Criminal Act to the latter-part concurrent offense and the offense whose judgment had become final, and then to impose an additional sentence for the latter-part concurrent offense. However, in our Criminal Act, Article 38(1) 2 with respect to determinate imprisonment merely states that one may increase “the maximum term or maximum amount prescribed for the most serious offense by up to one-half, but not exceed the aggregate of the maximum terms or amounts prescribed for each offense,” and does not separately determine punishment for individual offenses. Practical problems were also raised, namely that it is difficult to determine an aggregate sentence because it is difficult to obtain sentencing materials again concerning the offense whose judgment has become final. Reflecting such circumstances, the legislature adopted a rule declaring the principle that even in the case of latter-part concurrent offenses equity with the case of simultaneous trial must be maintained, but instead of introducing a method of re-determining the aggregate sentence, it adopted the method of “mitigation or exemption from punishment.” However, the fact that the method of determining the aggregate sentence and then determining the sentence for latter-part concurrent offenses was not adopted does not mean that the necessity of preventing disadvantage to the defendant merely because the offense is tried in separate proceedings was overlooked; rather, that legislative purpose should be respected.\\n\\nDuring the deliberations on the amendment to the Criminal Act, a proposal to add the phrase “(when mitigating or exempting punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses) mitigation may be made even below the mitigation limit under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act” was not ultimately adopted. However, in light of the above legislative purpose and legislative history, it is difficult to say that, merely because the legislature did not expressly specify the method of mitigation, the intention was to require application of Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act in the case of this kind so that the sentence could not be mitigated below the lower limit of the sentence to be imposed, thereby punishing the defendant more disadvantageously than in the case of simultaneous punishment of latter-part concurrent offenses.\\n\\ne. Even from the perspective of constitutional interpretation, Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act should not be applied to latter-part concurrent offenses.\\n\\nThe authority to determine, in adjudicating concrete disputes, the meaning, content, and scope of application of statutes or statutory provisions—that is, the authority to interpret and apply statutes—is an essential component of judicial power, and interpreting statutes so that they are harmonized with constitutional norms is a fundamental principle in statutory interpretation and application. Where multiple interpretations of a statutory provision are possible, a judge should, in principle, choose the interpretation consistent with the Constitution, that is, a constitution-conforming interpretation (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DU10289, decided February 12, 2009; Constitutional Court En Banc Decision 89HEONMA38, decided July 21, 1989, etc.).\\n\\nThe legislature cannot exercise unlimited legislative discretion in defining conduct as a crime and imposing punishment. When comparing punishments for crimes similar in criminal nature and protected legal interests, if it is manifest that the justice and balance of the punishment system are substantially lost, the provision is unconstitutional not only for violating the basic constitutional principle guaranteeing human dignity and worth but also for violating the principle of equality (see Constitutional Court En Banc Decision 2008HEONBA9, 43, etc.). The balance of the punishment system and the principle of equality mean that crimes similar in criminal nature and protected legal interests must, within a reasonable range, be punished with similar statutory punishments (see Constitutional Court En Banc Decisions 2006HEONGA7, decided June 29, 2006; 2012HEONBA275, decided September 26, 2013; 2015HEONBA225, decided December 29, 2016, etc.).\\n\\nIf, in the process of interpreting the wording of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, both an interpretation affirming and an interpretation denying the application of Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act are possible, then an interpretation that results in harsher or more favorable punishment merely because the offense is punished in separate proceedings compared with the case where the offense whose judgment has become final and the latter-part concurrent offense are punished together would infringe the justice of the punishment system and violate the constitutional basic principles guaranteeing human dignity and worth as well as the principle of equality; therefore, such interpretation should be avoided and a constitution-conforming interpretation should be adopted.\\n\\nThere are also limits, grounded in the principle of proportionality between crime and punishment and the principle of culpability, on legislation concerning punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses. If latter-part concurrent offenses are interpreted as the majority opinion does, then in order to realize these principles of criminal law, a new legislative measure must be enacted so that no disadvantage is suffered merely because the case is tried in a separate proceeding, compared with the case where latter-part concurrent offenses are adjudicated together. There is no reason to take the difficult path when there is a method of statutory interpretation that can easily escape an unconstitutional situation without departing from the possible meaning of the wording.\\n\\nMeanwhile, even if one were to interpret that, for latter-part concurrent offenses with a statutory minimum sentence, mitigation pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act may be made below the mitigation limit prescribed by Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act and pronounced, that would be an interpretation favorable to the defendant and thus would not violate the principle of nulla poena sine lege, nor is there any reason to construe it strictly. The request that criminal statutes be strictly construed is intended to prevent arbitrary interpretation and application of the law to the disadvantage of the public; it is not intended to prohibit interpretation in a way that is not unfavorable to the public and is reasonable, so long as the legislative spirit is not undermined (see Supreme Court En Banc Decision 78DO246, decided April 25, 1978, etc.).\\n\\nf. In light of these legal principles, the appellate judgment should be examined.\\n\\nThe appellate court selected determinate terms of imprisonment for the offense in this case, for which the statutory punishment is life imprisonment or imprisonment for not less than 5 years, and found that it was in the relation of latter-part concurrent offenses with the offense in the prior conviction in this case. It then applied the former sentence of Article 37 and Article 38(1) of the Criminal Act to aggravate punishment for concurrent offenses. Thereafter, applying Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, it mitigated punishment; in doing so, it did not apply Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act, and, taking into account equity with the case where the offense would be punished as former-part concurrent offenses, it determined the sentence and, after discretionary mitigation, ultimately sentenced the Defendant to imprisonment for 6 months. Although there is an inappropriate aspect in the order in which the law was applied, the appellate court did not err in a way that affected the conclusion of the judgment, such as by misapprehending the legal principles concerning mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses. Therefore, the appeal should be dismissed.\\n\\nThese are the reasons for dissenting from the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek\\n\\na. The majority opinion construes the provision “the sentence may be mitigated or remitted” in the latter sentence of Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, in imposing punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses for which a statutory minimum sentence is set, as having a segmented meaning in which one must choose between “mitigation” and “remission,” so that in the case of mitigation the sentence may be mitigated only within the range prescribed by Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act, and if one wishes to mitigate to a lower sentence, punishment must be remitted. However, I cannot agree with the majority opinion’s segmented interpretation of the meaning of “mitigated or remitted.”\\n\\nThe Criminal Act uses the provisions “the sentence may be mitigated or remitted” in Articles 21 (self-defense), 22 (necessity), 23 (self-help), 27 (impossible offense), 39 (latter-part concurrent offenses), 52 (voluntary surrender), etc., and uses the provisions “the sentence shall be mitigated or remitted” in Articles 26 (abandoned offense), 153 (confession of perjury, voluntary surrender), 157 (confession of false accusation, voluntary surrender), etc. The legal effect of “mitigated or remitted” is a matter not limited to latter-part concurrent offenses like the present case; rather, it is a general issue that applies whenever the Criminal Act or special criminal statutes contain provisions on “mitigation or remission” of punishment. Of course, it concerns only one type of punishment after the choice of the type of punishment has been made under Article 54 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nBelow, I will examine the legal effect of “mitigation or remission.” For convenience of discussion, however, I will not consider discretionary mitigation when mentioning the lower limit of punishment by mitigation.\\n\\nb. Provisions on “mitigation or remission” of punishment function to determine the modified sentence to be imposed. First, it is clear that mitigation determines the range of the sentence to be imposed, and further, because there are no separate provisions concerning different requirements or effects for “remission” that differ from those for other ranges of the sentence to be imposed, remission likewise falls within the ordinary range of the sentence to be imposed.\\n\\nProvisions on “mitigation or remission” of punishment present to the judge the range of the sentence to be imposed as modified by those provisions as the limit of sentencing, and it is proper to view the legal effect as meaning a single integrated domain. Once the choice of the type of punishment has already been made, there is no reason or necessity for a provision that changes the range of punishment to require the judge to choose anew between two separate domains.\\n\\nExemption from punishment is a type of guilty judgment in which the offense is established but no punishment is imposed, and it is a case where the defendant’s sentencing responsibility is at the level of “0.” In other words, exemption from punishment may be understood as setting the sentence to be imposed at “0.” If exemption is understood in this way, then when “mitigation or remission” is applied to a statutory punishment with a minimum limit, the lower limit of the sentence to be imposed is set at “0.” Since there can be only one lower limit of the sentence to be imposed, once the lower limit is set at “0” by remission, there is no need to refer to the general provision of Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act in order to confirm the lower limit of punishment resulting from “mitigation or remission.” In this case, because the upper limit of the sentence to be imposed is not separately provided in the individual statutory provision that prescribes “mitigation or remission,” reference must be made to Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nIf the meaning of “mitigation or remission” is understood as above, then where “mitigation or remission” is provided together with “mitigation,” it should be understood as a single integrated concept, not as a segmented meaning. Accordingly, the range of the sentence to be imposed by “mitigation or remission” has a lower limit of “0” and an upper limit of one-half of the maximum term or amount, with no room for a gap in between.\\n\\nAlthough not directly relevant to this part of the discussion, I add the following to avoid misunderstanding. Unlike the case of “shall mitigate or remit,” where the wording is “may mitigate or remit,” the range of the sentence to be imposed in the event of no such action also includes the range before mitigation or remission (that is, the statutory punishment or sentence to be imposed before mitigation or remission), so naturally the maximum term does not change. Current practice is the same.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 56 of the Criminal Act prescribes the order of aggravation and mitigation, but does not expressly provide for “mitigation or remission.” If the legal effect of “mitigation or remission” is understood as above, then “mitigation or remission” may be regarded as falling under “statutory mitigation” under Article 56 4 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nc. Where a statutory minimum is set, if the legal effect of “mitigation or remission” is not understood, as above, as a single integrated concept in which the sentence to be imposed continuously ranges from “0” to the upper limit, but instead, as the majority opinion does, “mitigation or remission” is understood in a segmented sense, it results in an unjustified gap in the range of the sentence to be imposed between “0” and the lower limit mitigated under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) The legislature presents judges with a certain kind and range of punishment proportionate to responsibility for all crimes, and judges determine a specific sentence corresponding to the principle of individual act responsibility and the preventive purpose of punishment within the range of the sentence to be imposed for each offense. Punishment appropriate to responsibility exists as a certain range of responsibility or judgment within the range of the sentence to be imposed; if there is a gap between the upper and lower limits of the sentence to be imposed, the range of punishment appropriate to responsibility cannot be properly determined, which is contrary to culpability.\\n\\nThere is no case in which a gap exists between the lower and upper limits of the statutory punishment for any offense prescribed in the Criminal Act or in special criminal statutes. For example, one cannot find legislative examples where the statutory punishment is “imprisonment for up to 3 years, or imprisonment for between 7 and 15 years,” and it is probably self-evident that such legislation would be impossible. The legislature, too, knows all too well that a gap in a certain range between the lower and upper limits of punishment is inconsistent with responsibility and may permit sentencing that does not accord with responsibility, and therefore legislates so as not to create any gap between the lower and upper limits of punishment. Also, under the current criminal justice system, there is no case where the lower and upper limits of the sentence to be imposed are separated by a gap even when punishment is aggravated or mitigated. Yet the only area in which continuity between the lower and upper limits is severed and a gap arises is the case of “mitigation or remission” of punishment. The legislature permitted judges to “mitigate or remit” punishment so as to impose punishment appropriate to responsibility; it could never have intended that “mitigation or remission” would create a gap between the lower and upper limits of punishment. The majority opinion is essentially no different from enacting a statute that leaves a gap in the statutory punishment.\\n\\n2) “Mitigation or remission” of punishment is a matter of determining the degree and amount of punishment. However, in ordinary social understanding, it is difficult to imagine leaving a gap of a certain range in the middle of the question of degree and amount. Even if such a gap were created, there would be almost no case in which it could be accepted in ordinary social understanding.\\n\\nFor example, can one imagine a situation in which, when an employer negotiates wages with workers, the wage must be set either at 55 million won or more, or at 50 million won or less, and the amount between 50 million won and 55 million won can absolutely not be set? If a school teacher, when assigning exam scores to students on a scale from 0 to 100, says that scores between 70 and 80 can never be assigned, could that truly be considered normal? Can one even imagine a legal order in which the state, when imposing taxes on taxpayers, sets taxes of at least 500,000 won but less than 750,000 won at 500,000 won, and taxes of at least 750,000 won but less than 1,000,000 won at 1,000,000 won, so that taxes between 500,000 won and 1,000,000 won cannot be recognized? In light of ordinary social common sense, such a situation is impossible.\\n\\nThe same is true for “mitigation or remission” of punishment. If “mitigation or remission” is understood in the segmented sense, as the majority opinion does, then where a statutory minimum is set, a judge can only determine the sentence to be pronounced within the sentence-to-be-imposed range with “0” or with a lower limit mitigated within one-half of the punishment as the lower limit, and cannot pronounce a sentence between “0” and that lower limit mitigated by statute. A gap arises in the sentence-to-be-imposed range within a certain band, and even if the judge, after reviewing the various sentencing factors prescribed in Article 51 of the Criminal Act, concludes that a sentence between “0” and that statutory mitigated lower limit is most appropriate to responsibility, the judge cannot pronounce that sentence. The judge is forced either to pronounce a sentence not less than the lower limit mitigated within one-half or to exempt punishment. It is self-evident that such a result is unreasonable in ordinary social understanding.\\n\\nd. Let us apply the foregoing discussion to this case. In this case, the statutory punishment is “life imprisonment or imprisonment for not less than 5 years.” According to the majority opinion, if the judge selects determinate imprisonment and then aggravates punishment for concurrent offenses and, pursuant to statutory mitigation, “mitigates or remits,” the judge will have to exempt punishment or determine the sentence within the range of the sentence to be imposed of imprisonment for 2 years and 6 months or more (the upper limit is not separately mentioned because it is not an issue in this case). The judge can choose only one of “0” or “imprisonment for 2 years and 6 months or more.” From the standpoint that “mitigation or remission” is a single integrated concept, the lower limit of the sentence to be imposed for each offense in this case becomes “0” by virtue of exemption from punishment, and there is no gap up to the upper limit.\\n\\nViewing the above result, from the standpoint of criminal policy it cannot possibly be said that understanding “mitigation or remission” as a single integrated concept so as not to create a gap in the sentence to be imposed is an interpretation or application of the law unfavorable to the public, nor can it be said to unnecessarily strengthen the state’s punitive power by granting judges excessive sentencing discretion. It simply makes the criminal justice order a rational legal order in accordance with natural principle.\\n\\ne. When a judge is deliberating between imprisonment for 3 years and exemption from punishment, which citizen would say, “Why not make it 1 year or 2 years?” Is there any lawyer who can explain that the judge’s deliberation is unavoidable?\\n\\nThe parts of the world and of life that need to be regulated by legal order are made law; one cannot make into law what does not exist in the world. In matters of degree and amount, there is no world in which a gap exists in the middle.\\n\\nf. Examining the reasons of the appellate judgment in light of the above legal principles and the evidence adopted by the appellate court, the appellate court, after finding that the offense in this case was in the relation of latter-part concurrent offenses with the offense in the prior conviction in this case, applied the former sentence of Article 37 and Article 38(1) of the Criminal Act to aggravate punishment for concurrent offenses, then applied Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act to mitigate punishment, and, without applying Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act, determined the sentence while considering equity with the case where punishment is imposed as former-part concurrent offenses, and after discretionary mitigation finally sentenced the Defendant to imprisonment for 6 months. Although there is an inappropriate aspect in the order in which the law was applied, the appellate court’s judgment does not contain an error that affected the conclusion of the judgment, such as misapprehending the legal principles concerning mitigation of punishment for latter-part concurrent offenses. Therefore, the appeal should be dismissed.\\n\\nThis is the reason for setting forth the dissenting opinion against the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Supplemental Opinion of Justices Park Sang-ok, Min Yoo-sook, and Lee Dong-won on the Majority Opinion\\n\\na. Statutory mitigation, as used in the Criminal Act, does not itself denote a special type of mitigation. Rather, it refers to all cases, except for discretionary mitigation, where the Criminal Act or other statutes provide for mitigation of punishment. The dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Ahn Cheol-sang, and Kim Seon-soo (hereinafter referred to as “the dissenting opinion”) seeks to bolster its basis by pointing out that there is no express provision requiring Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act to be applied as the method of mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses. The dissenting opinion appears to affirm that mitigation other than mitigation of latter-part concurrent offenses generally constitutes statutory mitigation, but one can hardly find any case in which a dissenting opinion that recognizes statutory mitigation includes an express provision in the relevant individual article requiring application of Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act. Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act is not applied because the individual provision expressly provides for its application; rather, on the premise that cases where the Criminal Act or other statutes provide for mitigation of punishment, other than discretionary mitigation, all fall under statutory mitigation, it is prescribed that such mitigation shall be made under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act. In the case of discretionary mitigation, although the Criminal Act does not expressly say so, it is understood by interpretation to be a mitigation method similar to statutory mitigation. Therefore, it is not appropriate to build an argument on the basis that there is no provision requiring mitigation under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Act for latter-part concurrent offenses.\\n\\nb. If mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses were not statutory mitigation but an independent form of mitigation, there must follow an explanation that coherently, within the Criminal Act system, shows how that mitigation differs from statutory mitigation.\\n\\nThe mitigation of latter-part concurrent offenses discussed by the dissenting opinion includes not only mitigation of the lower limit but also mitigation of the upper limit, yet there is no explanation whatsoever as to the upper limit. It is necessary to explain by what method the upper limit is mitigated, and whether mitigation of the upper limit is the same as statutory mitigation. If mitigation of the upper limit is the same as statutory mitigation, then the dissenting opinion must also explain on what basis the upper limit is mitigated in the same manner as statutory mitigation despite claiming that it is not statutory mitigation, and why, unlike the lower limit, it follows the method of statutory mitigation.\\n\\nIn addition, with respect to aggravation and mitigation of punishment, explanation is needed regarding the order of aggravation and mitigation under Article 56 of the Criminal Act. It is necessary to explain at which stage mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses is carried out, particularly its order relative to discretionary mitigation. Under the dissenting opinion’s logic, discretionary mitigation itself might not be necessary in cases of latter-part concurrent offenses, so an explanation is also needed as to whether discretionary mitigation is separately recognized. If discretionary mitigation is unnecessary, an explanation is also needed as to why the most fundamental and ultimate method of mitigation under the Criminal Act, namely discretionary mitigation, is excluded without basis.\\n\\nWhile there may be no difference between the majority opinion and the dissenting opinion on the fundamental distinction between exemption from punishment and pronouncement of punishment, under the dissenting opinion it is difficult to explain the independent meaning of providing for exemption from punishment, in addition to providing for mitigation of punishment as a method to impose a sentence taking into account equity with the case where the offense is adjudicated together with the offense whose judgment has become final in cases of latter-part concurrent offenses.\\n\\nc. Judicial sentencing discretion is granted within the range of the sentence to be imposed, and the dissenting opinion does not appear to take a different view, but when the dissenting opinion says that the majority opinion excessively infringes the judge’s sentencing discretion with respect to latter-part concurrent offenses, it is speaking about the question of how to determine the range of the sentence to be imposed and then invoking the judge’s sentencing discretion, which is an issue at the next stage; this is deeply improper. Under the dissenting opinion, one may misunderstand as if judges have sentencing discretion notwithstanding the sentence to be imposed, and that the majority opinion’s limitation of the range of the sentence to be imposed infringes the judge’s sentencing discretion.\\n\\nd. In determining punishment, the notion of imposing punishment taking equity into account necessarily presupposes that punishment is imposed taking equity into account within the range of the sentence to be imposed. The dissenting opinion also does not seem to take the position that taking equity into account means that the same punishment as in simultaneous adjudication must be imposed. If the offense whose judgment had become final and the offense of latter-part concurrent offenses had both been before the court, what sentence would have been imposed is something that the court trying the latter-part concurrent offense could not know and cannot impose a corresponding sentence with certainty. Where it appears that determining the sentence for latter-part concurrent offenses within the fixed range of the sentence to be imposed would be inequitable compared with simultaneous adjudication, the law has provided a basis for mitigation so that the sentence can be determined by changing the sentence to be imposed. Furthermore, where mitigation alone is clearly insufficient to avoid inequity, exemption from punishment is allowed. For that reason, the above Supreme Court Decision 2006DO8376 said that the Criminal Act provisions concerning latter-part concurrent offenses adopted a flexible legislative form enabling the court to determine a reasonable and appropriate sentence. A judge trying latter-part concurrent offenses must exempt punishment, rather than merely mitigate it, if setting the sentence with a lower limit of mitigation for a defendant punished as latter-part concurrent offenses would be so disadvantageous, compared with simultaneous punishment, as to violate the principle of equality or culpability.\\n\\nIt is difficult to accept how such an interpretation of mitigation for latter-part concurrent offenses could violate the principle of equality or culpability.\\n\\nFurthermore, according to the dissenting opinion, the sentencing and execution under the former Article 39(1) and (2) of the Criminal Act, under which, unlike the current law, neither mitigation nor exemption from punishment was possible for latter-part concurrent offenses, would be even more contrary to culpability and equality. If so, it would mean that until the above statutory provisions were amended, the Supreme Court had never once raised an objection and had continued to render judgments contrary to culpability and equality, which is also unacceptable. As noted above, one must remember that how latter-part concurrent offenses should be handled fundamentally depends on legislative policy.\\n\\nThis concludes the supplemental opinion on the majority opinion."}

{"[2017DO7287]": "The Court examines ex officio.\\n\\nSince the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act provides that “an offense for which a judgment imposing a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or a heavier punishment has become final and binding, and an offense committed before the final and binding judgment” shall constitute concurrent offenses, an offense for which a fine judgment or a summary order has become final and binding cannot constitute concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the court below found that the theft offenses and fraud offenses for which each of the summary orders stated in the judgment had become final and binding, and each of the offenses stated in the judgment committed before the date on which each of the above summary orders became final and binding, were in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, and accordingly determined separate punishments for each of the offenses stated in the judgment committed before the date on which each of the above summary orders became final and binding and each of the offenses stated in the judgment committed after the date on which each of the above summary orders became final and binding, thereby sentencing the Defendant to three punishments.\\n\\nHowever, in light of the legal principles set forth above, the offenses stated in the judgment committed by the Defendant before and after the final and binding of each of the above summary orders cannot constitute concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, and all are in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, so one punishment should have been imposed thereon. Nevertheless, the court below determined otherwise; therefore, there is illegality that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal doctrine of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning offenses of negligence and aggravated offenses by result are correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) (a) Under the Criminal Act, the offense of special obstruction of the performance of public duties causing bodily injury is an improper aggravated offense by result that includes not only cases where the serious result was not foreseen despite foreseeability, but also cases involving intent. (b) In a negligent offense, unconscious negligence is a case in which there is no awareness whatsoever of the possibility of the occurrence of the result, and it shall be regarded as negligence liability as a normative reality, namely, carelessness in failing to recognize the occurrence of the result. (c) With respect to an accident that occurred while a construction company, during construction work, had the installation work of a tower crane subcontracted to a specialist and the tower crane was being installed, if A, the site agent of the construction company, did not have actual authority to direct and supervise the installation work of the tower crane so as to manage and control it, he cannot be deemed to have been negligent in violation of the duty of care in the course of business. (d) If A, with intent to kill A, set fire to the house where A was sleeping, and the fire reached the ceiling of the master bedroom in A's house, but A woke up and got out of the house, thereby failing to achieve the purpose of killing, then A is punished as an attempted offender of arson of an inhabited building resulting in death. (e) Where a person instigated assault, but the person instigated went beyond this and committed homicide, the instigator becomes an accessory by instigation to the offense of assault; however, in such a case, if the instigator had negligence or foreseeability with respect to the result of the victim's death, it becomes an ideal concurrence of an accessory by instigation to the offense of assault and negligent homicide.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2005Do3108]": "All appeals are dismissed."}

{"[2007Do10058]": "We determine the grounds of appeal (the statements in the supplemental statement of grounds of appeal submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal has elapsed are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. As to the first ground of appeal\\nUnder Article 9(1) of the Act on the Punishment of Sexual Violence Crimes and Protection of Victims Thereof, not only a person who commits the crime of special rape as prescribed in Article 6(1) of the same Act, but also where special rape remains at the attempted stage, if the victim thereby suffers injury, the crime of special rape resulting in bodily injury is established; and the punishment provision for an attempt under the above Article 9(1) prescribed in Article 12 of the same Act applies to cases where the offense of special rape inflicting injury, which is prescribed together with the offense of special rape resulting in bodily injury in Article 9(1), remains at the attempted stage, that is, where a person who commits or attempts special rape, with intent to cause injury to the victim, attempts to injure the victim but the attempt fails.\\nConsidering the evidence cited in the judgment below as a whole, the court below found that the Defendant, by placing an electroshock device, which is a dangerous object, against the victim’s waist and assaulting the victim in an attempt to rape her, only to the extent of an attempt, and thereby causing the victim injuries such as a contusion to the face requiring approximately 2 weeks of treatment, and the court below further found that this constituted the consummated offense of special rape resulting in bodily injury under the Act on the Punishment of Sexual Violence Crimes and Protection of Victims Thereof. In light of the record and the legal principles stated above, that determination is proper, and there is no illegality such as an error of law regarding the doctrine of an attempted offense of a consequential aggravated offense, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. As to the second ground of appeal\\na. As to whether the medical certificate has evidentiary admissibility\\nExcept where the entries in the trial transcript are due to an obvious clerical error or mistake, matters entered in the trial transcript as procedural acts on the trial date must be proved by the transcript alone, and its probative force is absolute in that contrary proof by materials other than the trial transcript is not permitted (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DO6557 rendered on December 22, 2005; Supreme Court Decision 2002DO2134 rendered on July 12, 2002, etc.).\\nAccording to the record, it can be seen that at the first hearing date of the first instance, the Defendant consented to the admission of the medical certificate submitted by the prosecutor, and that fact is stated in the list of evidence; and since there is no material showing that such entry was the result of an obvious clerical error or mistake, the ground of appeal challenging the evidentiary admissibility of the above medical certificate contrary to the entry in the list of evidence is not accepted.\\nb. As to the injury count and the credibility of the medical certificate\\nThe arguments disputing the lower court’s determination regarding the injury count and the credibility of the medical certificate ultimately complain of the selection and weighing of evidence and the finding of facts, which are within the exclusive province of the lower court as the trier of fact, and therefore all cannot be accepted; nor is any illegality such as a violation of the rules of evidence, insufficiency of deliberation, or error of law otherwise apparent in the lower court judgment. The Supreme Court decisions pointed out in the grounds of appeal concern different matters from this case and are not appropriate for invocation here.\\n\\n3. As to the third ground of appeal\\nExamining the evidence admitted by the court below in light of the record, it is recognized that the Defendant possessed an electroshock device without obtaining permission from the competent chief of police, and therefore the lower court’s determination that the Defendant violated the Control of Firearms, Swords, Explosives, Etc. Act is proper; the Defendant’s argument criticizing this point cannot be accepted, and no illegality such as insufficiency of deliberation or error of law is otherwise apparent in the lower court judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and with the concurrence of all participating Justices of the Supreme Court, it is decided as set forth in the disposition that a part of the period of detention after appeal shall be included in the principal sentence."}

{"[83Do3007]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to the prosecutor’s grounds for final appeal against Defendant 1, the terms “a person who, by reason of the mental and physical disorder under Article 10 of the Criminal Act, lacks the ability to distinguish things or to decide his or her will” and “a person whose such ability is weak” both refer to a person in a state of mental and physical disorder; the difference between the two lies only in the difference in degree of the severity of the disorder, and they mean, in one case, a person who, due to mental disorder, lacks the ability to distinguish right from wrong or good from evil in matters, or to act according to what has been so distinguished, and, in the other case, a person whose mental disorder has not reached the degree of depriving him or her of such ability, but whose ability has been markedly diminished. According to the facts established by the first-instance judgment as upheld by the court below and the evidence cited therein, at the time of the offenses in this case, Defendant 1, due to schizophrenic symptoms and an uncontrollable impulse toward arson, committed eight successive acts of arson over only 6 days while in a state of weakened ability to discern things or decide his will; therefore, the court below’s action in upholding the first-instance judgment that recognized the Defendant as a person of diminished capacity and punished him by applying Article 10(2) of the Criminal Act is proper, and there is no illegality in misapprehending the legal principles on diminished capacity or in misapprehending the facts. Accordingly, the ground of final appeal is without merit.\\n\\n2. With respect to Defendant 1’s grounds for final appeal,\\nTaken together, the evidence cited in the first-instance judgment as upheld by the court below is sufficient to recognize the arson of the hotel stated in item 1.(a) of the first-instance judgment, and there is no material to find that Defendant’s consistent confession from the time of the police investigation through the second trial date in the first-instance court lacked voluntariness or that the content of the confession lacked truthfulness and is therefore unreliable; nor can any illegality of insufficient deliberation or misapprehension of legal principles be found in the court below’s action. Thus, the ground of final appeal can only be said to lack merit.\\n\\nMeanwhile, examining from the record the Defendant’s age, character and conduct, intelligence and environment, relationship with the victim, motive for the offense, means and result, and circumstances after the offense, which serve as materials for sentencing, the court below’s action in upholding the first-instance court’s determination of the Defendant’s sentence appears reasonable, and there is no reason to deem it excessively heavy and improper. Accordingly, the ground of final appeal on this point is also without merit.\\n\\n3. With respect to the grounds for final appeal of Defendants 2 and 3,\\n(1) Taken together, the evidence cited in the first-instance judgment as cited by the court below is sufficient to recognize the facts constituting the offense of occupational negligence causing death or injury by the Defendants, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality of misapprehension of legal principles in the course by which the court below reached this conclusion.\\n\\nAccording to what the court below lawfully found, the Defendants, as the president and maintenance manager of each hotel, had a duty of care in the course of their duties to ensure that, if a fire occurred, type A fire doors blocking stairways and corridors so that the fire would not spread would always open and close automatically, and that type B fire doors (emergency doors) on each floor would be managed so that guests could promptly escape and evacuate and would open as they were whenever merely pushed from inside toward the outside escape direction; and to manage the facilities so that in the event of a fire the detector, receiver, main alarm bell, and local alarm bell notifying every floor and each room would operate perfectly and normally immediately. Nevertheless, they neglected this duty, and on the ground that false alarms occurred frequently, they turned off the local alarm bell switch of the receiver, which was the automatic fire detection and alarm equipment, and sealed over it with Scotch tape, and caused employees, on the ground that it spoiled the business appearance, to keep the type A fire doors installed on each floor open by securing them with wooden props from around 06:00 to 24:00 every day; and they kept the type B fire doors (emergency doors) leading to the outdoor emergency staircase fastened, for reasons such as preventing theft, by fitting the steel plate hook attached to the door into the long latch attached to the building, so that in an emergency a person making a hurried escape could not open them by pushing them as they were without removing the steel plate hook, thereby making them fail to fulfill their function as escape routes. The Defendants’ breach of duty would, as a result, in the event of a fire in the building, prevent the fire from being promptly reported to guests and others, make the prevention of spread to the upper and lower floors from the point of ignition inadequate, and also prevent guests and others from being promptly evacuated outdoors through the emergency exits; this is plainly apparent from experience and thus was sufficiently foreseeable.\\n\\nIn offenses of negligence, the intellectual element of blameworthiness means awareness of the possibility of the occurrence of the result; conscious negligence has such awareness, while unconscious negligence does not even have such awareness itself, but in the former responsibility arises of course, and even in the latter, negligence liability generally exists as normative liability for carelessness in not recognizing the occurrence of the result. Therefore, in light of the facts finally established in the preceding sentence, the argument that the Defendants had no negligence causally related to the occurrence of the result, or that there was no subjective foreseeability of the result and no possibility of expecting the actor to avoid the result, is an arbitrary view and cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(2) The first-instance judgment cited by the court below held, as to Defendant 2, that Defendant 2, as the private proprietor of the hotel, in overall control of the management and administration of the hotel, not only had the duty of care stated in the first half of subparagraph (1) above regarding Defendant 3, but also had the duty of care in the course of duties to prevent the occurrence and spread of fire accidents by confirming and directing and supervising Defendant 3 to take the measures stated therein; and this action of the court below is proper. Therefore, even if the circumstances advanced in the argument existed, they could not be grounds for relieving the Defendant of liability, and thus the ground of final appeal is also without merit.\\n\\n4. In the end, as the prosecutor’s final appeal against Defendant 1 and the respective final appeals of the Defendants are all without merit, they are each dismissed, and it is so adjudged as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[93Do1873]": "We jointly determine the grounds of appeal by the Defendant and his counsel.\\n\\nWhere a person who instigated another to commit bodily injury or serious bodily injury thereby instigated the person so instigated, but the person so instigated went beyond that and actually committed murder, the instigator will generally be liable as an instigator of the offense of bodily injury or serious bodily injury; however, in such a case, where the instigator had negligence or foreseeability with respect to the result of the victim’s death, liability as an instigator of the offense of bodily injury resulting in death may be imposed.\\n\\nThe court of original instance, on the same purport, and based on each piece of evidence recited in the first-instance judgment cited by the court below, found that, in order to retaliate against the victim, who had been interfering with the Defendant’s business on every occasion and had been threatening him, the Defendant, after being introduced to the person not party to the case who had previously been serving as the victim’s bodyguard but later became estranged, provided KRW 5,000,000 under the name of an advance payment and thereby instigated that person to inflict serious bodily injury on the victim so as to prevent him from carrying on his activities; that the said person not party to the case then stabbed the victim all over his body with a knife and killed him; and that, in light of the circumstances at that time, the Defendant could have foreseen that if serious bodily injury were inflicted, the victim might die, and then convicted the Defendant as an instigator of the offense of bodily injury resulting in death, and such disposition is just and well-founded, and there is no illegality in it, such as incomplete deliberation or error in fact-finding due to violation of the rules of evidence evaluation, or error of law concerning the instigator of the offense of bodily injury resulting in death, as alleged. All arguments are without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and part of the period of detention after the filing of the appeal is credited toward the principal sentence, and judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[94Do2842]": "The grounds of appeal submitted by the Defendants and their counsel are considered together.\\n\\n1. With respect to ground of appeal No. 1 raised by counsel for Defendant 1\\n\\nAlthough the offense of special obstruction of the performance of official duties resulting in injury is originally a result-aggravated offense, it is not a true result-aggravated offense punishable only in cases where the serious result was not foreseen despite foreseeability thereof, but rather an improper result-aggravated offense that includes not only cases where the serious result was not foreseen despite foreseeability thereof, but also cases involving intent (see Supreme Court Decision 90DO765, rendered on 1990.6.26.). However, it cannot be deemed that, because a result-aggravated offense thus includes cases in which a serious result is intentionally caused, even in cases where there exists a provision that punishes intentional offenses more severely, the offender cannot be punished with the punishment prescribed for intentional offenses. A result-aggravated offense is a crime in which the punishment is aggravated even when the actor did not foresee the serious result; if even in cases where the serious result is intentionally caused, the offense were to be treated as a result-aggravated offense and thus could not be punished with the punishment prescribed for the intentional offense that is punished more severely, the result would be that it is punished more lightly by being charged as a result-aggravated offense. Therefore, where a separate constituent element providing for heavier punishment has been established for cases in which a serious result is intentionally caused, it must naturally be punished with the punishment prescribed in that heavier-punishment constituent element, and where the punishment for a result-aggravated offense is heavier, it should be possible to punish it with the punishment prescribed for the result-aggravated offense. Therefore, in the case of an improper result-aggravated offense in which a serious result is intentionally caused through the basic offense, if the serious result corresponds to a separate constituent element, it must be deemed to stand in a relation of ideal concurrence between the result-aggravated offense and the intentional offense as to the serious result (see Supreme Court Decision 90DO670, rendered on 1990.5.8.).\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal doctrine, the court below's measure of maintaining in full the first-instance judgment, which convicted the criminal facts under item “2. (b)” as stated in the first-instance judgment against Defendant 1 as a case of ideal concurrence between the offense of special obstruction of the performance of official duties resulting in injury and the offense of violating Article 3(2)1 of the Act on the Punishment of Violences, etc. and Article 257(1) (Injury) of the Criminal Act, is proper, and there is no error of misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning result-aggravated offenses and ideal concurrence. The portion of the grounds of appeal pointing this out is without merit.\\n\\n2. With respect to ground of appeal No. 2 raised by counsel for Defendant 1 and the ground of appeal by Defendant 1\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the record, the judgment below’s determination that Defendant 1 was not in a state of mental and physical loss or diminished mental and physical capacity at the time of the second offense stated in the first-instance judgment is proper, and there is no error in fact-finding due to a violation of the rules of evidence or due to incomplete deliberation, and upon examining the sentencing conditions shown in the record of this case, the determination of the sentence imposed on the Defendant is also appropriate. The portion of the grounds of appeal pointing this out is likewise without merit.\\n\\n3. With respect to the grounds of appeal by Defendant 2 and his counsel\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the record, it is proper that the court below maintained the first-instance court’s measure of finding Defendant guilty of the criminal facts stated in the relevant part of the judgment by comprehensively considering the evidence cited in that judgment, and there is no error of violating the rules of evidence or of failing to conduct a full hearing, and the point of mere factual error does not constitute a lawful ground of appeal in this case in which Defendant was sentenced to imprisonment for 3 years. All grounds of appeal are unacceptable.\\n\\n4. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, and 30 days out of the period of detention after appeal are to be credited toward the principal sentence in the first-instance judgment against the Defendants, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the disposition by the agreement of the participating Justices."}

question: Which of the following explanations concerning crimes protecting the judicial function of the State is incorrect? (If there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Criminal intent for the crime of false accusation may be recognized not only in cases where the informant reports facts that he is certain are false, but also in cases where he reports facts without being certain that they are true.
B: Even if a person reported false facts to a public office for the purpose of causing another person to receive criminal punishment, if the facts are such that, as an offense subject to complaint, the complaint period has elapsed and prosecution cannot be instituted, and this is clear from the contents of the report itself, the crime of false accusation is not established.
C: Where the falsely reported fact could have been the subject of criminal punishment at the time of the false accusation, the crime of false accusation is established, and even if precedents are later changed so that such fact does not become a criminal offense, it does not affect the already established crime of false accusation unless there are special circumstances.
D: If A, having appeared as a witness at the 9th trial date of Case A and having made a false statement, had the witness examination procedure end as it was without any withdrawal or correction, and thereafter A again appeared at the 21st trial date, was informed that the effect of the previous oath remained in force, and, while testifying, admitted that the statement made at the previous date was a false statement and made a statement to the effect of withdrawing it, then the crime of perjury is not established against A.
E: If Defense counsel A, in order to obtain a reduced sentence for A, repeatedly transferred money from A's bank account to a bank account in the name of Company B and then received it back, and thereafter obtained only the remittance records among them and submitted them to the court together with a false assertion that 200 million won had been repaid, the crime of fabrication of evidence is not established against A.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2010DO7525]": "The guilty portion of the lower court judgment and the acquittal portion concerning the charge of instigation of perjury are reversed, and this case is remanded to the Gwangju High Court. The remainder of the Prosecutor’s appeal is dismissed."}

{"[2015DO15398]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. The crime of false accusation is established when, for the purpose of causing another person to receive criminal punishment or disciplinary action, false facts are reported to a public office or public official (Article 156 of the Criminal Act). Although the crime of false accusation incidentally also protects the interest of an individual in not being unjustly punished or disciplined, its primary protected legal interest is the proper exercise of the State’s criminal justice authority or disciplinary authority (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DO2712, rendered on 2005. 9. 30.).\\n\\nIn order for an act of reporting “false facts” for the purpose of causing another person to receive criminal punishment to constitute the crime of false accusation, the reported facts themselves must be capable of being subject to criminal punishment; thus, even if false facts were reported, false accusation is not established if, at the time of the report, those facts themselves do not constitute a criminal offense (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DO558, rendered on 2007. 4. 13.). However, where the falsely reported facts could have been subject to criminal punishment at the time of the false accusation, the risk of impairing the proper exercise of the State’s criminal justice authority and the risk of infringing the individual’s legal stability against unjust punishment have already arisen; therefore, the crime of false accusation is consummated, and even if the precedent is later changed so that such facts are no longer deemed criminal, it does not affect an already established crime of false accusation absent special circumstances.\\n\\n2. a. The lower court found the charged facts of this case guilty on the following grounds, holding that the contents of the Defendant’s complaint constituted false facts, that the Defendant also knew of these circumstances, and that, at the time of the false accusation, the facts reported by the Defendant themselves could have been the cause of criminal punishment.\\n\\n(1) The Defendant was a director of Non-party 1 Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Non-party 1 Company”), and on 2014. 1. 9., he submitted to the civil petitions office of the Busan District Prosecutors’ Office a complaint against Non-party 3, who was the representative of Non-party 2 Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Non-party 2 Company”), stating: “The Defendant purchased ○○○○Ville (room number 1 omitted) and (room number 2 omitted) from the side of the accused Non-party 3 on 2009. 9. 2., but since the accused Non-party 3 double-sold them to another person, please punish him.” Thereafter, when making a statement as the complainant on 2014. 2. 6. at the office of the investigation division of the Busan District Prosecutors’ Office, the Defendant stated: “For the progress payment of KRW 150,000,000 for the interior finishing work of ○○○○Ville, which Non-party 1 Company had contracted from Non-party 2 Company and carried out, I agreed with Non-party 3 on 2009. 9. 1. to the construction price of KRW 90,000,000 and received two units of ○○○○Ville as the method of repayment. Nevertheless, since Non-party 3 did not transfer these to me and sold them to another person around 2014. 1., please punish him.” (hereinafter referred to as “the complaint in this case”).\\n\\n(2) The Defendant asserted that he agreed with Non-party 3 on the construction price for this construction work at KRW 90,000,000 and that, if Non-party 3 could not pay it, he would instead receive two units of ○○○○Ville as payment in kind; however, the Defendant has failed to submit objective materials concerning the contents of the work he performed, the progress rate, or the amount of completed work accordingly. Rather, the work performed by the Defendant consisted only of some paint work and fence work, and the construction price was only KRW 6,500,000; it appears that the Defendant received the full KRW 6,500,000 from Non-party 3, and that the creditor-debtor relationship between the two was fully settled.\\n\\n(3) Before the complaint in this case, the Defendant had filed a criminal complaint against Non-party 3 in relation to this construction work on suspicion of fraud, but on 2009. 12. 24., Non-party 3 was acquitted on appeal on the ground that the amount of construction payment to be received by the Defendant was only KRW 6,500,000, unlike the amount claimed to the investigative authorities (KRW 500,000,000) (Busan District Court 2009NO1085), and that judgment became final and conclusive as is when the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 2010. 4. 29. (Supreme Court 2010DO482).\\n\\n(4) Pursuant to the Defendant’s complaint in this case, Non-party 3 was investigated by the prosecution as a suspect regarding the above complaint facts.\\n\\n(5) At the time of the complaint in this case and the investigation, Supreme Court precedent held that “where a debtor who concluded a reservation for substitute performance concerning real property as security for a claim disposes of the real property agreed to be delivered in substitution, the crime of breach of trust is established” (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2000DO4293, rendered on 2000. 12. 8.); however, by a judgment of the Supreme Court en banc rendered on 2014. 8. 21., the Supreme Court changed its precedent and held that breach of trust is not established in such a case (Supreme Court en banc Decision 2014DO3363).\\n\\nb. The lower court’s determination is proper in light of the legal principles set forth above. There is no error in the lower court’s determination in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the crime of false accusation, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Defendant’s appeal is without merit, and is therefore dismissed. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

{"[2018DO1818]": "The Court examines ex officio.\\n\\n1. Even if a person reported false facts to a public office for the purpose of causing another person to receive criminal punishment, where the facts are, as an offense subject to complaint, such that prosecution cannot be instituted because the complaint period has expired and this is clear from the contents of the report itself, there is no risk of misleading the duties of the relevant state agency; therefore, in such a case, the offense of false accusation is not established (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 98DO150 rendered on 1998. 4. 14.).\\nMeanwhile, according to the provisions of Articles 354 and 328 of the Criminal Act, fraud committed between lineal blood relatives, spouses, cohabiting relatives, cohabiting family members, or their spouses shall be exempted from punishment, and between relatives other than such persons, prosecution may be instituted only upon complaint. In addition, under Article 230(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, the complaint period is 6 months from the day the offender is known.\\nHere, “knowing the offender” means, from the standpoint of an ordinary person, knowing the facts of the crime and the offender to the extent that the person entitled to file a complaint can do so, and “knowing the facts of the crime” means that the person entitled to file a complaint has a definitive awareness of the factual circumstances that there was harm from a crime falling under an offense subject to complaint (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2001DO3106 rendered on 2001. 10. 9.).\\n2. The gist of the charges in this case is as follows.\\na. Defendant 1 was sentenced to imprisonment for 2 years and 4 months for an offense in violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, etc. (psychotropic substances), etc., and while he was incarcerated in ○○ Prison after the sentence became final, he instigated his biological older sister, Defendant 2, to falsely accuse him of fraud to the ○○ District Prosecutors' Office, △△ Branch Office, in order to be transferred to △△ Prison where his family was living.\\nb. Defendant 2 accepted this and, around 2015. 11. 30., drafted a false complaint to the effect that “Defendant 1 borrowed 50,000,000 won on 2012. 10. 1. and has not yet repaid it, so please punish him for fraud,” and submitted the complaint by mail to ○○ District Court, △△ Branch Court on the same day, and around 2015. 12. 3., caused a public official belonging to △△ Branch Court whose name is unknown to file the above complaint with the ○○ District Prosecutors' Office, △△ Branch Office, thereby falsely accusing Defendant 1.\\n3. a. Even according to the statement of the charges in this case, since the Defendants are biological siblings, the fraud case for which Defendant 2 complained against Defendant 1 falls within a case in which prosecution may be instituted only if Defendant 2 files a lawful complaint.\\nb. However, according to the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n(1) Defendant 2, in accordance with the instigation of false accusation as stated in the charges against Defendant 1, drafted a complaint stating that “the accused, Defendant 1, borrowed 50,000,000 won from the complainant, Defendant 2, on 2012. 10. 1. with the promise to open a coffee shop in □□ and repay the money, and was to repay it by 2015. 10. 1., but because he is currently serving his sentence at ○○ Prison and is not fulfilling the promise, I was compelled to file this complaint,” and attempted to file it with the △△ Police Station, but was refused by the police officer in charge of receiving filings on the ground that the Defendants were relatives.\\n(2) Accordingly, Defendant 2 submitted the above complaint by mail to ○○ District Court, △△ Branch Court, and around 2015. 12. 3., a public official belonging to △△ Branch Court whose name is unknown filed the above complaint with the ○○ District Prosecutors' Office, △△ Branch Office.\\n(3) Defendant 2, during her statement as complainant in the investigation conducted at the △△ Police Station pursuant to the above complaint, stated, in essence, that “my younger brother, Defendant 1, said that if I lent him the money necessary to open a coffee shop in □□, he would repay it by around 2012. 10., so I lent him a total of 50,000,000 won, consisting of 30,000,000 won around 2012. 3. and 20,000,000 won around 2012. 9.; however, he did not open the coffee shop and did not repay it even by October, so on 2012. 10. 1. I asked him to prepare a loan certificate. Accordingly, Defendant 1 prepared a loan certificate stating that he would repay 50,000,000 won by 2015. 10. 1.”\\n(4) Defendant 1 likewise, during police and prosecutorial interrogation as a suspect, made statements consistent with Defendant 2’s above police statement, and stated that, at the time he borrowed money from Defendant 2, he had almost no property in his own name and that he was correct in saying that he had neither the intention nor the ability to repay the money.\\nc. Examining Defendant 2’s complaint and her statements to the police as above in light of the legal principles set forth earlier, it appears from the contents of the report itself that, at the time Defendant 2 received a loan certificate from Defendant 1 on 2012. 10. 1., she knew that Defendant 1 had not used the above money for opening the coffee shop, which had been the purpose when he borrowed the money in the first place, and that he lacked the ability to repay.\\nTherefore, as of around 2012. 10. 1., Defendant 2 had a definitive awareness that she had suffered harm from a fraud offense to an extent sufficient to file a complaint against Defendant 1, so the complaint period began to run around that time, and there is considerable room to conclude that by 2015. 12. 3., when the complaint was filed with the ○○ District Prosecutors' Office, △△ Branch Office, that complaint period had already expired. If viewed in this way, Defendant 2’s false complaint of fraud would fall under a case where it is clear from the contents of the report itself that prosecution could not be instituted because the complaint period had expired, and thus the offense of false accusation would not be established; as a result, Defendant 1’s offense of instigating false accusation would also not be established.\\nd. Nevertheless, the court below, without conducting any particular examination as to whether Defendant 2’s complaint period had expired, found both the charge of instigating false accusation against Defendant 1 in this case and the charge of false accusation against Defendant 2 guilty. In this determination by the court below, there is error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the complaint period for an offense subject to complaint and the establishment of the offense of false accusation.\\n4. Therefore, without omitting judgment on the Defendants’ grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for a new trial and determination, and accordingly, the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as set forth in the disposition."}

{"[2020DO2642]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Summary of the Facts Charged\\nThe Defendant, while meeting the client, Non-party 1, at ○○ Prison located in ○○ City (address omitted) around April 2018, advised him to the effect that “if it is made to appear that all of the money received from Non-party 2 Company (hereinafter referred to as the ‘Non-party 2 Company’) has been returned, a reduction in sentence may be obtained. Since there is no money to return, there is a method of depositing money into the Non-party 2 Company’s account and then receiving it back, repeating this and revolving the funds.” Non-party 1 accepted this. Upon hearing through Non-party 1’s acquaintance, Non-party 3, words to the effect that “as a result of contacting the Non-party 2 Company side, it seems likely that if money is sent, it can be received back again,” the Defendant caused Non-party 3 to have Non-party 1’s older sister, Non-party 4, transfer funds to a △△ Bank account in the name of Non-party 2 Company. Non-party 4, around May 18, 2018, transferred 70,000,000 won to the △△ Bank account in the name of Non-party 2 Company, and then immediately received back the above 70,000,000 won from the Non-party 2 Company side into a □□ Bank account in Non-party 4’s name; thereafter, by the same method, she deposited 50,000,000 won on May 24, 2018, 30,000,000 won on May 30, 2018, 20,000,000 won on June 1, 2018, 60,000,000 won on June 7, 2018, 70,000,000 won on June 14, 2018, 20,000,000 won on June 26, 2018, and 30,000,000 won on June 29, 2018, each into the △△ Bank account in the name of Non-party 2 Company, and then immediately received them back into the □□ Bank account in Non-party 4’s name, and around that time faxed the deposit materials thus falsely created to the Defendant.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Defendant, notwithstanding that he had not returned any money at all to the Non-party 2 Company side as stated above, asserted that Non-party 1 had returned in full the 350,000,000 won received from the Non-party 2 Company side, and around June 20, 2018, submitted to the appellate trial panel in Non-party 1’s case one consolidated voucher received from Non-party 4 as above and five deposit confirmation certificates (total returned money: 300,000,000 won), and thereafter, on June 25, 2018, submitted to the same panel a written brief stating, to the effect that Non-party 1 had returned in full the brokerage compensation received and therefore should receive a reduction in sentence, and around July 2, 2018, further submitted two deposit confirmation certificates (total returned money: 50,000,000 won) to the same panel.\\n\\nBy doing so, the Defendant, in collusion with Non-party 3, fabricated sentencing evidence concerning Non-party 1’s criminal case and used the fabricated evidence.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the Lower Court\\nFor the reasons stated in its opinion, the court below held that “evidence concerning a criminal case or disciplinary case” in Article 155(1) of the Criminal Act includes not only materials relating to whether a crime is established but also materials relating to sentencing, and that the Defendant, in collusion with Non-party 1, etc., caused meaningless deposit and withdrawal entries to arise between Non-party 4 and Non-party 2 Company by remitting funds to a bank account in the name of Non-party 2 Company and then receiving them back again, and thereafter extracting only the deposit records, which were part of the entire transaction records, and submitting them to the court as sentencing materials, constituted an act of creating novel and spurious materials that possess content and value conforming to false factual elements, as evidence created to prove the nonexistent fact that “Non-party 1 returned 350,000,000 won to Non-party 2 Company and Non-party 2 Company received all of it,” and thus constituted “forgery” of evidence, and accordingly found the facts charged in this case guilty.\\n\\n3. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\nA. The term “evidence” in the offense of forgery of evidence under Article 155(1) of the Criminal Act means all materials deemed relevant to the investigative agency, court, or disciplinary authority’s confirmation of whether the State’s power to punish or disciplinary power exists with respect to another person’s criminal case or disciplinary case (see Supreme Court Judgment dated June 28, 2007, 2002DO3600, etc.). Therefore, not only materials concerning whether a crime or disciplinary cause is established, but also materials helpful in recognizing mitigating or aggravating circumstances relating to punishment or discipline, are included in the evidence prescribed by this provision.\\n\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in its opinion, held that “evidence concerning a criminal case or disciplinary case” under Article 155(1) of the Criminal Act includes sentencing materials; this is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misunderstanding the law concerning the scope of “evidence,” the object of forgery in the offense of forgery of evidence.\\n\\nB.
