Summary of the Facts Charged  \\nThe gist of the facts charged in this case is as follows.  \\nThe Defendant was an inside director of B Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “B”), a liquor company, and had been engaged in liquor supply transactions with the Victim. The Defendant, having filed a civil action against the Victim seeking payment of liquor prices, received and held KRW 4,700,000 on September 30, 2019, remitted by the Victim to an account in the name of B managed by the Defendant, during the civil dispute. However, the above amount was money the Victim had intended to remit to Co., Ltd. C, and was remitted to the Defendant by mistake of account number, and the Defendant was obligated to return the above amount after being notified by the Victim through text message on October 1, 2019 that the above amount had been remitted by mistake. Nevertheless, without any agreement with the Victim concerning set-off and settlement, the Defendant unilaterally set off and settled KRW 1,108,310, being the amount of the liquor-price claim asserted by the Defendant, and then refused to return the money and embezzled it.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the Court Below  \\nThe court below held that, with respect to the money mistakenly remitted by the Victim to the Defendant, so long as a custodial relationship under the principle of good faith is recognized between the Defendant and the Victim, the Defendant could not unilaterally set off such money as with money entrusted by limiting its purpose or use; accordingly, it judged the facts charged in this case to be guilty on the ground that the Defendant’s act constitutes “refusal of return,” an element of the crime of embezzlement, and that the intent of unlawful acquisition is also recognized.\\n\\n3. Judgment of the Supreme Court  \\na. Since “refusal of return” as prescribed in Article 355(1) of the Criminal Act means an act of expressing an intention to exclude the owner’s rights over the thing held in custody, in order for “refusal of return” to constitute embezzlement, it is insufficient that a person who keeps another’s property in custody merely refused to return it; by comprehensively considering the reason for the refusal to return and the subjective intentions, the refusal to return must be such that it may be viewed as equivalent to an act of embezzlement. The intent of unlawful acquisition in the crime of embezzlement refers to the intention of a person who keeps another’s property in custody to dispose of it as if he or she were the owner, without just title, contrary to the purpose thereof; therefore, even if return is refused, if there is a justifiable reason for the refusal to return, it cannot be said that there was intent of unlawful acquisition (see Supreme Court Decision 98DO126 dated July 10, 1998, Supreme Court Decision 2000DO637 dated September 4, 2002, Supreme Court Decision 2014DO11552 dated February 26, 2015, etc.).\\n\\nb. Examining the following circumstances, as discernible from the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, in light of such legal principles, the Defendant’s act of refusing to return the portion corresponding to B’s claim against the Victim among the money remitted to the account in B’s name by the Victim’s mistake may be viewed as an exercise of a valid right of set-off; accordingly, it is difficult to accept as is the court below’s determination that the Defendant’s refusal to return constitutes an act of embezzlement and that the intent of unlawful acquisition is recognized.\\n\\n(1) Where money has been mistakenly remitted to and deposited in a deposit account by error, a custodial relationship under the principle of good faith is established between the recipient and the remitter (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DO891 dated December 9, 2010, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2017DO17494 dated July 19, 2018, etc.); however, absent special circumstances, this alone does not mean that the money remitted by mistake by the remitter is identical to money expressly entrusted by the entrustor with a specified purpose and use, nor can it be evaluated that the recipient’s exercise of a set-off right against the remitter is contrary to the original intent of the entrustment on the ground that the remitter entrusted the recipient with affairs involving the receipt and payment of money.\\n\\n(2) In light of the progress of the related civil case, B appears to have held a claim for payment of goods corresponding to the amount of the refusal to return against the Victim as of the time of the refusal to return described in the facts charged in this case. There also appears to be no material or circumstances suggesting that, at that time, the above claim for payment of goods of B and the Victim’s claim for return of unjust enrichment were not in set-offable relation, or that B’s exercise of the right of set-off constituted a violation of the principle of good faith or an abuse of rights.\\n\\n(3) The Defendant returned, on the day after the remittance, the remainder of the KRW 4,700,000 mistakenly remitted, excluding the amount corresponding to B’s above claim for payment of goods in the amount of KRW 1,108,310, and even with respect to the KRW 1,108,310, appears to have sufficiently made clear to the Victim, who requested its return, the intention to exercise the right of set-off using B’s above claim for payment of goods as the automatic claim. In this manner, when examining the reason for and subjective intention behind the Defendant’s refusal to return the money corresponding to the amount of the above claim for payment of goods, it is difficult to conclude that the Defendant refused to return it with intent of unlawful acquisition.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below judged the facts charged to be guilty by regarding the Defendant’s refusal to return as equivalent to an act of embezzlement in the crime of embezzlement and recognizing the intent of unlawful acquisition. The judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the act of embezzlement and the intent of unlawful acquisition in the crime of embezzlement and by failing to conduct the necessary review.\\n\\n4. Conclusion  \\nThe judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[80DO306]": "In considering the grounds of appeal submitted by each defense counsel for the Defendants and by Defendant G himself (including supplemental grounds in part), for convenience in this judgment all of the above grounds of appeal shall collectively be referred to as the “Grounds of Appeal,” and they shall be considered item by item, broadly divided in the following order.\\n\\nBelow\\n\\nSection 1. Illegality in overlooking the order dismissing the prosecution\\nSection 2. Procedural illegality\\n1. Violation of the principle of accusation and adjudication\\n2. Violation of “public trial”\\n3. Illegality of limiting examination\\n4. Illegality of ordering withdrawal from the courtroom\\n5. Illegality in witness examination procedure\\n6. Illegality in opening the proceedings without counsel\\n7. Deprivation of the right to counsel\\n8. Deficiency in the trial transcript and deprivation of the rights of inspection and copying\\n9. Infringement of the independence of the trial\\nSection 3. Issue of “voluntariness” regarding the suspect-interrogation record prepared by the prosecutor\\nSection 4. Illegality concerning the constituent elements of the offense\\n1. Purpose of “subversion of the Constitution”\\n2. “Riot”\\n3. “Participation”\\n4. “Killing”\\n5. Commencement of execution and time of consummation of the crime of insurrection\\n6. “Concealment of evidence”\\nSection 5. Illegality concerning co-principal liability for the offense of murder\\nSection 6. Illegality concerning abandonment of attempt\\nSection 7. Grounds negating illegality\\n1. Lawful act\\n(1) Theory of the “right of resistance”\\n(2) Legitimate performance of official duty\\n(3) Order of a superior\\n2. Justifiable act\\n3. Necessity\\n(1) In the case of Defendant A\\n(2) In the case of Defendant C\\nSection 8. Grounds negating criminal responsibility\\nSection 9. Improper severity of sentence\\nSection 10. Conclusion\\nSection 11. Separate opinions\\n1. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Min Mun-gi\\n2. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Yang Byeong-ho\\n3. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Im Hang-jun\\n4. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Kim Yun-haeng\\n5. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Jeong Tae-won\\n6. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Seo Yun-hong\\n\\nSection 1. Illegality in overlooking the order dismissing the prosecution\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, it is argued that, even based on the facts stated in the indictment, there is no statement of specific facts concerning the purpose of subverting the Constitution, the riotous acts, and the contents of the conspiracy, which are constituent elements of the crime of insurrection, or concerning the division of execution in the co-principal offense of murder; thus, because the facts charged are not specified, an order dismissing the prosecution should have been entered pursuant to Article 373(1)4 of the Military Court-Martial Act, but the lower court overlooked this and thereby erred in misunderstanding the above legal principles. We shall first consider this point.\\n\\nUpon review, this point was already lawfully considered by the lower court. In addition, the facts charged against the Defendants, as organized from the indictment in this case and the applications to amend the indictment made on two occasions, are sufficiently specified on their face to be recognized as the relevant offenses, and it is admitted that they are specifically stated. Further, as to the murder of Defendant C, the indictment clearly charges co-principal liability by conspiracy; accordingly, in that case, the omission of facts concerning the division of execution in co-principal liability cannot be deemed a defect. Therefore, this argument is without merit.\\n\\nSection 2. Procedural illegality\\n\\n1. Violation of the principle of accusation and adjudication\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, it is argued that, according to the indictment and the application to amend the indictment, Defendant G was prosecuted for killing T and U with the purpose of subverting the Constitution, but the lower judgment found Defendant G to have killed six persons, namely B, T, V, W, X, and U; this, it is argued, is a violation of the principle of accusation and adjudication and thus a violation of law. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, according to the application to amend the indictment lawfully granted at the first trial date in the lower court (trial transcript p. 1458), it is clear, as argued, that Defendant G was prosecuted for having killed T and U, among the six deceased persons in this case, for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. However, in the reasoning of the lower judgment, in the conclusion portion concerning the facts of the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose, the court stated: “From around 19:40 to 20:05 on the same day, former President B, ..., the said T, ..., the said V, ..., the said W, the said X, and the said U were each caused to die, thereby the Defendants jointly murdered the above victims for the purpose of subverting the Constitution.” This appears, on its face, to have committed the illegality alleged. Nevertheless, the lower court had previously stated that, on October 26, 1979, around 19:40, Defendant G, after the other Defendants had fired at the above deceased persons, received at around 20:05 that day an instruction from Defendant E to carry out a confirmation shot on persons not yet fully dead and agreed to participate in that killing. Not only that, but the lower court also stated that, with respect to the shooting pursuant to that instruction, it was done by firing “one shot at the said W lying fallen, two shots at the said V, two shots at the said T groaning, and one shot at the said U lying fallen and groaning.” In view of this point, although the expression in the conclusion portion of the lower judgment is somewhat inaccurate, it is still recognized that the lower court judged within the scope of the prosecution. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n2. Violation of “public trial”\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the court-martial of first instance, at the second trial date on December 8, 1979, conducted the defense counsel’s statements and questioning of Defendant A in closed session without satisfying the prescribed requirements, and also, at the ninth trial date on December 18, 1979, effectively prohibited public access and proceeded with Defendant A’s final statement without even entering a decision of closure; thus, it is argued that the closed proceedings were plainly illegal in their grounds and procedure. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, according to the record (trial transcript p. 223), at the second trial date on December 8, 1979, during the defense counsel’s cross-examination of Defendant A, the court ordered a closed proceeding on the ground that “Defendant A, as former Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, has performed important duties concerning foreign intelligence and domestic security intelligence, security affairs pertaining to state secrets, insurrection, foreign relations, the investigation of crimes prescribed in the National Security Act, the Anti-Communist Act, and similar laws, and the coordination and supervision of intelligence and security affairs, and the content of the defendant’s statements in this court pursuant to the defense counsel’s cross-examination substantially includes matters that may interfere with the security or public order of the State.” It then proceeded in camera thereafter. This was based on Article 67 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which provides that “the oral proceedings and judgment in trial shall be public; provided, however, that where public order may be disturbed, morals harmed, or where necessary for military secrecy, the military court may decide not to hold them publicly.” Even in light of the record, the reason is fully understandable. Therefore, the first-instance court’s measure was proper and cannot be said to have been mistaken. Accordingly, this portion of the argument is without merit.\\n\\nFurther, whether any stage of the trial proceedings was public is to be recorded in the trial transcript pursuant to Article 85(2)5 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which prescribes the entries in the trial transcript. Article 89 of the same Act provides that “matters recorded in the trial transcript as procedural acts on a trial date are proved by that transcript alone.” Thus, the public or private nature of the proceedings on December 18, 1979, the ninth trial date in the first instance, can be established only by the trial transcript in this case. The first-instance ninth trial transcript (trial transcript p. 769) states in the column for “public or private” that the trial was “public in court.” Therefore, it can be recognized that the proceedings on that date were conducted in a public courtroom. Accordingly, this argument also lacks merit.\\n\\n3. Illegality of limiting examination\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the first instance and the lower court, though under Article 344 of the Military Court-Martial Act they could limit examination only to the extent that the essential rights of parties to the litigation were not harmed, nevertheless restricted examination and statements whenever specific references were to be made in the course of examining Defendant A concerning the motive and purpose of this act, the domestic political situation immediately before the act, and the inevitability of the act, and also frequently imposed limitations during the examination of Defendants E and F; this, it is argued, constituted a grave infringement of the Defendants’ and counsel’s right of defense beyond the permissible bounds of examination restriction. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review of the first-instance and appellate trial transcripts, it can be recognized that the first instance and the lower court afforded the above Defendants necessary and sufficient opportunities to make statements, and that each defense counsel was granted the necessary right to examine the Defendants and other parties to the litigation; further, it is sufficiently recognized that each defense counsel had necessary and sufficient opportunities to defend the Defendants, which were realized, and that each Defendant had a full opportunity to make final statements. In particular, in the case of Defendant A, from the content of the Defendant’s statements in response to examinations by the prosecutor, defense counsel, and legal officer in the first-instance and appellate courts, as well as the supplemental statement of reasons for appeal submitted by Defendant A himself (trial transcript p. 1695), and the statements of reasons for appeal and grounds of appeal submitted by his counsel, it can be recognized that the defense content alleged by the appellant is sufficiently reflected. Therefore, the contrary argument lacks merit.\\n\\n4. Illegality of ordering withdrawal from the courtroom\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, when questioning Defendant C and others at the third trial date on December 10, 1979, the first-instance court, invoking Article 343(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, ordered Defendant A to withdraw from the courtroom on the ground that he could not make sufficient statements in Defendant A’s presence; this, it is argued, was done without just cause solely upon the application of the prosecutor, and furthermore, when Defendant C’s statement ended in that case, Defendant A, who had been withdrawn, should have been brought back into the courtroom and informed of the substance, and Defendant A should have been allowed to question Defendant C directly, but instead the proceedings were simply closed without Defendant A being brought back into the courtroom that day; this is said to be illegal. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, according to the first-instance third trial transcript, before the examination of Defendant C at the said third trial date, the first-instance court, ex officio, ordered the remaining Defendants including Defendant A to withdraw from the courtroom on the ground that they were deemed unable to make sufficient statements in the presence of co-defendants (trial transcript p. 237). This measure was based on Article 343(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, which provides that “the presiding judge may order the defendant to withdraw and be questioned when, on his own motion or upon application by the prosecutor, the defendant is deemed unable to make sufficient statements in the presence of another defendant or ....” In light of the record, this was reasonable. It is true, as argued, that after Defendant C’s statement ended at that date, the proceedings were closed without Defendant A being brought back into the courtroom. However, according to the first-instance fourth trial transcript, when the first-instance court resumed and, at the fourth trial date, the legal officer informed the parties in the courtroom, which included all defendants in this case including Defendant A and all their counsel, of the substance of the previous court hearing on Defendant C, and asked the parties for their views, the parties stated that they had no particular opinion; this is clearly shown in the record (trial transcript p. 318). Further, according to the first-instance sixth trial transcript, it is clearly shown in the record that Defendant A’s assigned counsel O and Y cross-examined Defendant C on behalf of Defendant A (trial transcript pp. 518, 520). Therefore, this argument lacks merit.\\n\\n5. Illegality in witness examination procedure\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, first, according to the witness examination record of Z adopted by the lower court, it is clear that Defendant A was not allowed to participate in the examination of that witness. This, it is argued, violated the law guaranteeing a defendant’s right to participate in witness examination and, through that, the right of cross-examination. Second, it is argued that, in examining witnesses, there was no service of summons by the prescribed procedure under Articles 106 through 108 of the Military Court-Martial Act; moreover, in some cases, witnesses were made to wait in advance before the prosecutor had even applied for evidence, and then were taken up and examined immediately upon application; this, it is argued, was not only a procedural violation but a grave illegality depriving the Defendants and their counsel of the opportunity to prepare for cross-examination. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, first, according to the first-instance trial record, at the eighth trial date at which all the Defendants in this case and their counsel were present, regarding witness Z who failed to appear, the first-instance court instructed the legal officer that he would conduct the examination outside the courtroom and ordered the attendance of the relevant persons (trial transcript p. 707). Thereafter, on December 17, 1979, legal officer AA examined the witness at the Army Headquarters Judge Advocate General’s Office, where Defendant C and his counsel and the counsel for Defendants A and D were present (trial transcript p. 749). In the manner of that witness examination, it cannot be said that Defendant A was not notified and thus was denied an opportunity to participate. Moreover, the witness’s testimony primarily concerned the criminal facts of Defendant C, so it cannot be said that there was any illegality in the procedure. In addition, according to the same trial record, at the ninth trial date resumed on December 18, 1979, the first-instance court, after the legal officer informed the courtroom that witness Z had been examined, presented the substance and asked the parties for their opinions; the parties stated that they had no particular opinion, as clearly shown in the record (trial transcript p. 771). Therefore, even if there were a mistake as alleged, the Defendants and their counsel stated at the evidence examination that they had no particular opinion, so the mistake would be cured by waiver of the right to object (see Supreme Court decisions dated May 20, 1962, 4294HYEONGSANG127; July 4, 1967, 67DO613; and April 8, 1975, 74DA3323). Accordingly, this part of the argument is without merit.\\n\\nSecond, according to the first-instance trial record, after the first-instance court selected eight witnesses at the sixth trial date, it examined the two selected witnesses who appeared at the seventh trial date (trial transcript p. 571), and at the eighth trial date it newly selected nine witnesses present at the court and examined those witnesses and the five witnesses selected earlier who appeared (trial transcript p. 629). Also, one witness examination was conducted outside the courtroom by legal officer AA on December 17, 1979, all of which is clear from the relevant trial transcripts and witness examination records. Under the proviso of Article 192 of the Military Court-Martial Act, witnesses present in court may be examined without summons, so it cannot be illegal that the nine present witnesses were not summoned. Nor can it necessarily be faulted that those witnesses were examined immediately upon application. As to the remaining witnesses, although summons procedures should have been taken, no trace of the issuance of summons can be found in the record (except that the trial transcripts state that they were summoned and appeared). However, after examining those witnesses and the witness outside the courtroom, the first-instance court afforded the Defendants and their counsel the opportunity to state their opinions in court or at the next trial date, and they stated that they had no particular opinion. Moreover, it is clearly shown in the record that the Defendants and their counsel conducted sufficient and necessary cross-examination of those witnesses. Therefore, the defect of non-issuance of summons cannot be said to be a case affecting the outcome of the judgment, and this portion of the argument also cannot be accepted.\\n\\n6. Illegality in opening the proceedings without counsel\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, in military court cases, counsel is mandatory under Articles 62 and 315 of the Military Court-Martial Act, and therefore proceedings cannot be opened without counsel’s appearance. Nevertheless, on January 22, 1980, at the first trial date, as a measure under Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act rather than severance of trial, the lower court opened proceedings with only Defendants C and G present and without the appearance of Defendants A, E, and F and their counsel, and is alleged to have illegally examined matters concerning the motives and circumstances of the co-defendants’ offenses. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review of the appellate trial record, after notifying Defendants A, E, and F and their counsel that the first trial date was set for January 22, 1980 (trial transcript pp. 1007, 1009-1011, 1019-1021, 1024, 1040-1044), the court later re-designated and notified the trial date as January 23, 1980 (trial transcript p. 1381). Then, at the first trial date on January 22, 1980, the court, pursuant to Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act, deemed that some of the Defendants including Defendants A, E, and F need not appear at trial and did not order their appearance, but proceeded with the hearing with only Defendants C and G present (trial transcript p. 1383). Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act is only the provision that in appellate proceedings under the Military Court-Martial Act, the appeal instance is not a de novo trial of the first instance, but rather a post hoc review of specific factual and legal issues in the first-instance judgment, and thus as a rule the defendant need not appear at appellate trial dates. It is not a provision allowing only some co-defendants to appear selectively, as in this case, and excusing the appearance of the others. Therefore, the above measure of the appellate court was mistaken. However, at the continued second trial date on January 23, 1980, the legal officer informed the substance of the important matters of the previous trial hearing (trial transcript p. 1469), and thereafter sufficient opportunity for cross-examination was afforded. Moreover, the record shows that the first instance had already conducted sufficient hearings on the matters alleged in the appeal grounds, and at the first appellate trial date there is no indication that new matters were examined on that point. Accordingly, the error was not such as to affect the outcome of the judgment. The Supreme Court decisions cited by the appellant are not apt to this case. Thus, this argument also cannot be accepted.\\n\\n7. Deprivation of the right to counsel\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, the Defendants’ lineal family members and spouse have, under Article 59 of the Military Court-Martial Act, an independent right to appoint counsel. Thus, even if the defendant himself refuses to argue, the right of counsel appointed by the lineal family members and spouse does not extinguish. Nevertheless, counsel AB and others appointed by Defendant A’s lineal family members and spouse were denied entry into the courtroom by military police serving as courtroom order personnel pursuant to the judge’s order at the first-instance fifth trial date on December 12, 1979, and it is argued that thereby their right to counsel was deprived, and that the court committed illegality in failing to decide on the objection to this point. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, even if, pursuant to Article 59(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, the defendant’s lineal family members and spouse may independently appoint counsel, the appointing party is one who independently exercises the appointing right of the principal, so the effect of the appointment extends to the principal, and the principal must be understood as being able to revoke the appointment. In this case, according to the first-instance fourth trial transcript, while the hearing at the fourth trial date proceeded under the participation of privately retained counsel including attorneys AB and others appointed by Defendant A’s mother and spouse, Defendant A stated, “From now on, I refuse the defense by the private defense team for this defendant.” At that time the legal officer informed him of the fact that “the military court requires counsel and, if the privately retained counsel must be dismissed, the military court must decide to appoint assigned counsel.” Defendant A then stated, “Please appoint assigned counsel for this defendant; I will revoke all privately retained counsel for myself.” This is clearly shown in the record (trial transcript pp. 346-347). Therefore, the above private counsel were lawfully revoked, and the fact that they were later denied entry to the courtroom as counsel at the first-instance fifth trial date on December 12, 1979, cannot be regarded as deprivation of the right to counsel. Nor can it be said that any illegality occurred merely because the objection thereto was not decided. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n8. Deficiency in the trial transcript and deprivation of the rights of inspection and copying\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, even if the Military Court-Martial Act does not have a provision like Article 54 of the Criminal Procedure Act that trial transcripts must be promptly prepared within five days after each trial date, considering Articles 89 (probative force of the trial transcript), 86 (special provisions concerning the trial transcript), and 64 (inspection and copying of documents and evidence), etc., the trial transcript in military court proceedings should also be prepared before the next trial date or, at the latest, before the factual hearing ends. Nevertheless, it is argued that the first instance and the appellate court did not promptly prepare the trial transcripts, thereby effectively depriving counsel of the right under Article 64 of the Military Court-Martial Act to inspect and copy the transcripts, etc. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, the Military Court-Martial Act does not contain a provision like Article 54 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which sets a statutory period for preparing trial transcripts. Of course, military court trial transcripts must also be prepared promptly, but one cannot definitively say by when they must be completed. In particular, even the statutory period set by the Criminal Procedure Act is only a directive provision, and merely failing to complete the transcript within that period cannot by itself be regarded as rendering the trial transcript void. Therefore, no fault can be found with respect to the timing of preparation of the first-instance and appellate trial transcripts; nor can it be said that there was illegality in depriving the right of inspection and copying of transcripts. The gist of the argument is that it concerns the defendants’ right of defense. Upon review of the first-instance and appellate trial records in this case, it is recognized that the defendants’ right of defense was fully protected; accordingly, this argument cannot be accepted.\\n\\n9. Infringement of the independence of the trial\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the first instance and appellate court pressed ahead with the hearing as though there were a fixed, predetermined schedule under the aforementioned unlawful procedures infringing the defendants’ right of defense and right to counsel, and that even during the hearing, there were cases in which notes of contact from outside were publicly and repeatedly handed to the judges through the back door behind the judges’ bench; this, it is argued, violated Article 102 of the Constitution and Article 28 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which guarantee judicial independence. We consider this argument.\\n\\nAs to the arguments alleging that the above first-instance and appellate trial procedures were illegal, we have already found them to be without merit. Even in light of the record, it is not recognized that the factual hearings in the first instance and appellate court were pressed ahead under some fixed schedule as alleged. Rather, the record only shows that the first instance conducted sufficient factual hearings eight times across the second through ninth trial dates, and the appellate court did so three times across the first through third trial dates, while ensuring the defendants’ right of defense and right to counsel. No other illegality is found. Furthermore, there is absolutely nothing in the record suggesting that contact notes were delivered to the judges during the hearing, and especially whether their content infringed judicial independence is wholly unknown. This point is too abstract and fabricated to require further discussion. Therefore, the argument lacks merit.\\n\\nSection 3. Issue of “voluntariness” regarding the suspect-interrogation record prepared by the prosecutor\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the suspect-interrogation records concerning the Defendants prepared by the prosecutor were merely an extension of the records prepared by the military police investigators because, at the time of the prosecutor’s interrogation, the Defendants were physically and mentally exhausted by numerous acts of torture at the joint investigation headquarters under martial law, and in particular Defendant A made statements involuntarily, under the prosecutor’s earnest persuasion, while his consciousness was dim due to aggravation of his chronic liver disease; or because the prosecutor conducted the interrogation at the place where the military judicial police had investigated after receiving the case, under a state in which access and communication with counsel and family were completely prohibited, and the record content was the same as the military judicial police records except for legal refinement, so that it lacked “voluntariness.” It is argued that the lower court nevertheless used this as evidence of guilt, thereby committing an error of law concerning evidentiary capacity or a defect for failure to provide reasons, and also erred by omitting consideration of the grounds of appeal. We consider this argument. (This point is related to the argument below that the fact-finding violated the rules of evidence, and for convenience it is considered separately.)\\n\\nUpon review, in general, the absence of voluntariness in a statement means that the person being interrogated by an investigative authority did not make the statement under free conditions because of threats, torture, or other means. The determination of voluntariness is made within a reasonable scope by the free conviction of the judge without violating the rules of experience. It suffices that the adjudicating panel makes a reasonable judgment in all respects of the litigation process—namely, the preparation and content of the document, the defendant’s explanation and demeanor, the prosecutor’s elucidations, and the testimony of witnesses involved in the preparation of the document. On that basis, the record shows the following:\\n\\n(1) In the prosecutor’s direct examination of Defendant A at the second trial date in the first instance:\\nQ: “When the prosecutor investigated, I wrote the record and made you verify it item by item, did I not?”\\nA: “Yes.”\\nQ: “After confirming the contents, you signed and affixed your seal, did you not?”\\nA: “Yes.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 210)\\n\\n(2) During the prosecutor’s direct examination of Defendant A at the third trial date in the first instance:\\nQ: “During the prosecutor’s investigation, was there any instance in which you made a statement under compulsion or threat?”\\nA: “I said, please write it as it was.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 247)\\nAnd:\\nQ: “When the prosecutor investigated, was there any threat or coercion?”\\nA: “No.”\\nQ: “You reviewed the record prepared at that time, confirmed the contents, and signed and affixed your seal, did you not?”\\nA: “Yes.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 256)\\n\\n(3) During the cross-examination of Defendant A by defense counsel AC at the first appellate trial date:\\nQ: “Looking at the prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation record concerning the defendant, it says that during a conversation at the curb in front of the entrance you nodded your head and thought you would kill T, and where was that record prepared?”\\nA: “I do not know the exact location, but the prosecutor came to the Joint Investigation Headquarters and took the record for two days.”\\nQ: “Was there no investigation at the Prosecutor’s Office?”\\nA: “There was. 1398-1400)\\n\\n(4) During the cross-examination of Defendant F by his counsel Y at the fifth trial date in the first instance:\\nQ: “When you were investigated before the prosecutor, did you tell the record as you said?”\\nA: “Yes.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 435)\\n\\n(6) Through the hearings in the first instance and appellate court, there is no statement to be found that the Defendants were particular, as for Defendants C, D, E, and G, they were investigated on two occasions and the statements on both occasions are consistent.\\n\\n(8) In the trial hearings in the first instance and These facts are apparent from the record. Therefore, the lower court’s use of them as evidence of guilt was proper, and there is no illegality as alleged. Accordingly, this part of the argument lacks merit.\\n\\nAnd although Defendant C’s counsel AC raised this point in the statement of grounds of appeal submitted, the lower court’s failure to decide it was mistaken (trial transcript p. 1128); however, since the argument is plainly without merit as above, the mistake could not have affected the outcome of the judgment. Therefore, this point also lacks merit.\\n\\nSection 4. Illegality concerning the constituent elements of the offense\\n\\n1. Purpose of “subversion of the Constitution”\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, the “subversion of the Constitution” prescribed in Article 91 of the Criminal Act, as the purpose element of the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection, ultimately means everything that unlawfully destroys the State’s political basic order itself. The political basic order of our country is, needless to say, a liberal democratic political system; therefore, only acts that substantially or formally destroy the principle of popular sovereignty and the people’s fundamental freedoms and equality would constitute subversion of the Constitution. Accordingly, the overthrow of a specific government or cabinet, or an act of shouting slogans of overthrow, or whether the means of overthrowing is violence, or the killing of a specific constitutional organ as a natural person and the planning of succession or improvement thereof, would not fall under this.\\n\\nFirst, in the case of Defendant A, the Yushin system, by its establishment and continuance alone, was not only an illegal criminal state in which sovereignty was usurped, but its content and operation produced a continuing condition that destroyed the political basic order of a democratic state. Therefore, for Defendant A, the killing of the President, a natural person, was unavoidably done according to a plan long prepared for the restoration of democracy. Even if not so, since after this offense he intended to enact a democratic constitution and organize the National Assembly and Government by democratic methods, there was no purpose to subvert the Constitution.\\n\\nSecond, in the case of Defendant C, it is difficult to conclude, merely because he killed T, the head of the Presidential Security Service, who was not even a state organ established by the Constitution, that he had a purpose of “subverting the Constitution” like the co-defendants; and as to Defendant C, neither his own statement nor his external behavior can be said to show a purpose of “subverting the Constitution.”\\n\\nThird, in the case of Defendant D, he merely thought that only a few persons would be killed and the President abducted in this offense, and the killing of security officer V and the like, which he admits was done pursuant to the order of his superior, would not amount to subversion of the Constitution. Moreover, Defendant A’s explanation also states that he reached this offense in order to restore liberal democracy, so it cannot be said that there was a purpose to “subvert the Constitution.”\\n\\nFourth, in the case of Defendants E, F, and G, the Defendants were merely security guards or drivers of the Central Intelligence Agency restaurant and, having no choice, blindly and mechanically carried out the orders of Defendant D, the chief responsible person there. They could not even imagine the specific harm and consequences. In particular, Defendant G did not know of the murder of the President or even of its plan. Nevertheless, the lower court found, contrary to Defendant C’s explanation, that the facts it held satisfied the purpose of “subverting the Constitution,” and as to the other Defendants, it found that they had carried out riots or killings with the purpose of “subverting the Constitution,” on the ground that they knew a state of national upheaval had occurred. It is argued that this was a fact-finding without evidence (including corroboration required by strict proof), a violation of the rules of evidence contrary to logic and experience, a failure of hearing (especially concerning the specific method after the act), and a defect for lack of reasons (because there were no factual statements that could constitute a purpose to subvert the Constitution); or that the legal principles concerning the purpose of “subversion of the Constitution” in the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection were misunderstood. We consider this argument.\\n\\n(1) First, we examine the legal principles concerning the purpose of “subversion of the Constitution.”\\n\\nArticle 91 of the Criminal Act provides: “In this Chapter, ‘purpose of subverting the Constitution’ means any of the following: 1. abolishing the functions of the Constitution or laws without following the procedures prescribed by the Constitution or laws; 2. overthrowing, by force, a state organ established by the Constitution or making the exercise of its functions impossible.” Thus it defines “subversion of the Constitution.” This ultimately means unlawfully destroying the political basic order prescribed by the present Constitution or laws. As argued, it does not necessarily have an extra-legal meaning, and certainly does not mean changing to a communist, monarchical, or dictatorial system. Of course, as argued, killing only a natural person who is a specific state organ, or planning his succession, does not fall under it. Further, since the crime of insurrection is a crime with a specific purpose, the general principles concerning crimes with specific purpose apply. The purpose belongs to matters requiring strict proof and must be direct, but it cannot be said that it requires a desire or will for the result to occur, nor does it require definite knowledge; a conditional awareness is sufficient (see Supreme Court decision dated April 2, 1968, 68DO61).\\n\\n(2) Next, we examine the lower court’s factual findings on this point regarding the Defendants.\\n\\n(A) Part concerning Defendant A\\n\\nThe lower judgment stated the following as the facts of Defendant A’s “purpose of subverting the Constitution”: “While performing his duties as Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, Defendant A’s plans for stabilizing the political situation repeatedly failed, exposing his incompetence in carrying out his duties, and after being reprimanded by former President B, rumors of a dismissal for taking responsibility circulated, causing him to feel insecure in his position. Meanwhile, although he resented the President’s greater trust in T, then head of the Presidential Security Service, who was junior to him and younger, despite T’s arrogant attitude and interference in matters beyond his authority, ... he planned to seize power after killing the President, and, for secrecy, independently devised the concrete plan for the act ... after assassinating the President, he planned to declare martial law on the ground of national security and public disorder, to use the authority and organizational power of the Central Intelligence Agency to take control of the martial law forces and suppress the situation by force, to constitute a revolutionary committee that would oversee legislative, judicial, and executive powers, to assume the chairmanship himself and secure a basis of power, and then to run for President.” Examining the important basis of this conclusion from the evidence lawfully admitted and cited by the lower court:\\n\\n(a) Defendant A’s statements\\n\\n1) “Q: Why did you call the Army Chief of Staff and ... to the vicinity of the accident site?\\nA: I lured them from the outset for use after the act; after the act, I would come immediately, keep the Army Chief with me and constantly remain in contact so that he could not entertain other thoughts. When martial law is declared, he will, as martial law commander, handle the situation, so I had called him in advance to sever his contact with the outside and to verify the progress of the situation directly.”\\n(Same purport in the prosecutor’s record p. 10 and trial transcript pp. 197, 542)\\n\\n2) “Q: Explain in detail the course of the assassination of the President.\\nA: ... On the same day, around 16:30, arriving at my office, ... lying down on the bed there, I was for a long time imagining what would happen after the act ... continuing to imagine ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 3-4; trial transcript p. 197 uses the phrase “revolutionary plan”)\\n\\n3) “Q: Same as above.\\nA: At around 17:40, after hearing that C, the Chief Secretary of the Blue House, had arrived, I came down to the first floor and entered the reception room. The first words of Chief Secretary C were, ‘The Agency has had a hard time and the Republican Party fellows have ruined everything,’ so I said casually, ‘There is nothing we can do. From now on, when AY’s acting administration is launched, we will have to attach them one by one,’ and ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 4)\\n\\n4) “Q: Same as above.\\nA: Sitting again with C on the curb at the right front gate of that entrance, continuing the conversation, after hearing Chief Secretary C say first, ‘That friend T, the chief, is so hard-line and troublesome. He listens only to one or two opposition-party fellows and rushes to report to the President,’ ... I had already resolved to remove the President and T ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 4-5; trial transcript p. 198 to the same effect)\\n\\n5) “Q: Same as above.\\nA: ... Then, at around 18:50, the President and T arrived ... and dinner began ... The President asked me, ‘How is the New Democratic Party operation?’ so I said, ‘Because of the Republican Party announcement, everything has been ruined. The fellows who said they would resign have all turned hard-line. As far as I can see, it will be difficult for the AY acting administration system to be launched for the time being. The mainstreams have become hard-line, so it will be somewhat noisy.’”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 5)\\n\\n6) “Q: But you departed for the Namsan Intelligence Agency. How did you enter Army Headquarters?\\nA: ... I took Chief Secretary C alone into the adjacent restroom ... and said, ‘You must remove the signboard of the Martial Law Command as soon as possible and change it to the Revolutionary Committee signboard.’”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 17-18)\\n\\n7) “Then why did you also kill Chief Secretary T?\\nA: In order for me to carry out the act, I could only achieve the purpose by dealing together with the obstacle T and the escort officers. The content was that after assassinating the President, I would first keep security with Chief Secretary C, who always attended, ... lure military strongmen to the area ... and, after convening an emergency cabinet meeting and declaring nationwide emergency martial law, control the situation by manipulating the Martial Law Commander and gradually transform the Martial Law Command into a Military Revolutionary Committee ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 25-26; trial transcript p. 209 to the same effect)\\n\\n11) “Q: Same as above.\\nA: And in order to complete the revolutionary task as quickly as possible, I planned to dissolve the National Assembly, disband the existing political parties, and form a Revolutionary Committee, whose chairman would be me and vice-chairman the Army Chief of Staff, composed only of military officers; and, in order to supervise this, in constituting the Revolutionary Council, I would be chairman, the Prime Minister vice-chairman, and the revolutionary committee members would be the principal Army commanders of the corps level or above, principal Navy commanders of fleet commander level or above, principal Air Force commanders of operations commander level or above, and all ministers at governor level or above, ... Also, the Revolutionary Council would oversee legislation and administration, and as subsidiary organs it would establish under it a Revolutionary Court and Revolutionary Prosecutor’s Office, the latter composed jointly of innovative prosecutors and military prosecutors, and the court would be composed of prominent generals from the military ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 26-27; trial transcript pp. 216, 542 to the same effect)\\n\\n12) “Q: What is the meaning of revolution?\\nA: The destruction of the existing order.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 229)\\n\\n(b) Defendant C’s statements\\n\\n1) “Q: State, to the best of your knowledge, the relationship between T, the chief of the security service, and A.\\nA: ... In my view, the two seemed to have been secretly maneuvering to gain the President’s trust.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 41; trial transcript p. 242 to the same effect)\\n\\n2) “Q: State what you know about the proposed reorganization of intelligence key posts.\\nA: ... Since around May of this year, I remember that A, perhaps because he felt insecure about his position, said to me, ‘A person should leave a position cleanly when leaving it, so since you, brother, know best, if I should leave my position or if you notice anything displeasing to the President, please tell me, and I will cleanly resign.’”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 43-44; trial transcript p. 244 to the same effect)\\n\\n3) “Q: What was the atmosphere in the banquet hall?\\nA: ... The President said, ‘The Busan situation is something the New Democratic Party is involved in; everyone is making a fuss for nothing ...’ and said, ‘I know the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency has worked hard too, but we need to collect more accurate information,’ while A continued to look gloomy ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 46-47)\\n\\n4) “Q: What did you hear from A in the restroom of the Army Chief of Staff’s office?\\nA: I heard A say, ‘First declare martial law, take control of the situation, and lead it toward a military revolution.’”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 75)\\n\\nTaking these together with the other lawfully admitted evidence cited by the lower judgment, the above reasoning is fully understandable.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Defendant A strongly argued in this respect that the so-called Yushin system, in its establishment and continuation, destroyed the political basic order of the democratic state, so this offense was solely for “restoring democracy.” His explanation was gradually systematized as this case proceeded and, as well expressed in the supplemental statement of reasons for appeal submitted by Defendant A himself (trial transcript pp. 1694-1710), appears fairly persuasive.\\n\\nHowever, it is acknowledged that the current Constitution contains some non-democratic provisions as pointed out in the argument, but the current Constitution also declares that our country is a democratic republic and that sovereignty resides in the people, and it provides for the fundamental rights of the people including the guarantee of human rights, and it is unquestionably a democratic constitution in its essence, with separation of the three powers. Therefore, the argument that the Yushin Constitution itself usurped sovereignty or destroyed the political basic order of the democratic state and that it itself was a state of insurrection is excessively exaggerated and merely dogmatic, having no value for consideration. Moreover, as to the claim that the offense was for “restoring democracy,” this is plainly fictitious from the circumstances noted above. We further examine this point using the evidence lawfully cited in the lower judgment.\\n\\nDefendant A was appointed Director of the Central Intelligence Agency on December 4, 1976, and it is clear from the record that he held that office for about 2 years and 10 months until the time of the offense, handling 639 cases involving violations of emergency measures (trial transcript p. 219), etc.\\n\\n(a) Defendant A’s statements\\n\\n1) “Q: As to the reason for martial law...\\nA: ‘The Soviet Union kept AD’s movements secret for a week; why can’t we keep ours secret for several days?’ ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 17)\\n\\n2) “Q: You held a countermeasure meeting regarding the Y.H. incident, did you not?\\nA: Yes. In the New Democratic Party, amidst the female workers, the labor bureau chief of the New Democratic Party slashed his abdomen with a razor blade ...\\nThe female workers were forming a group for suicide by jumping ... I instructed the police to cast a net.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 217)\\n\\n(b) Defendant C’s statements\\n\\n1) “Q: Is it true that A strongly insisted on the enactment and implementation of Emergency Measure No. 10 and that you heard him say so?\\nA: Yes. It was during the New Democratic Party convention last May, at the chairmanship election, that the Central Intelligence Agency was working to make AE the party chairman ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 41)\\n\\n3) “Q: Same as above.\\nA: After the duties of New Democratic Party chairman AF were suspended and AY was judicially determined to be acting chairman, ... Therefore, Defendant A’s explanation is difficult to accept.\\n\\n(b) Part concerning Defendant C\\n\\nAccording to the evidence lawfully admitted and cited by the lower court:\\n\\n(a) Defendant C’s statements\\n\\n1) “Q: Explain in detail how A assassinated T and the President.\\nA: ... When I was given orders, I had to participate because I thought everything had been arranged in advance between the chief and Park, the section chief.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 197)\\n\\n2) “Q: ... State the circumstances of your participation in the offense.\\nA: ... At that time, a car carrying the President was parked in front of the east entrance of the old building, and I thought the chief might harm the President inside, but ... on the other hand, I participated in the offense because I thought it might be good for my own future if this succeeded.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 201)\\n\\n3) “Q: When A assassinated the President and the suspects shot the security guards, what situation did you think would arise?\\nA: I also worried that a coup d’état against the State would be launched and confusion would follow.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 202-203; however, this is denied at trial transcript pp. 366, 429)\\n\\n4) “Q: What did you think at the hospital?\\nA: I was waiting, thinking that the big thing had already happened and that the chief would handle everything properly.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 210)\\n\\nThese serve as grounds for recognizing that the above Defendants had the purpose of “subverting the Constitution.”\\n\\n(e) Part concerning Defendant G\\n\\nAccording to the evidence lawfully admitted and cited by the lower court:\\n\\n(a) Defendant D’s statements\\n\\n1) “Q: Tell us about the course of executing the offense.\\nA: ... Again, because I was curious about the scene, I told G, a guard waiting in the lounge who was quick on his feet, ‘Arm yourself and follow me,’ and then G, armed with an M16, followed ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 111)\\n\\n2) “Q: ... At that time, G sufficiently knew what had happened in ‘na,’ didn’t he?\\nA: Since a gunshot was heard where the President was having dinner, and since I and E were carrying guns and I saw the President’s guards and the driver lying there shot in the kitchen, I thought he would have sufficiently inferred that the President’s personal safety was in danger.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 138)\\n\\n(b) Defendant E’s statements\\n\\n1) “Q: State the circumstances of the offense up to the point where G was made to perform the confirmation killing on the security guards, etc.\\nA: ... Section chief D said, ‘Tell G to go inside and shoot them all dead cleanly,’ so I immediately conveyed D’s instruction to G, who was nearby ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 182; trial transcript p. 358 to the same effect)\\n\\n2) “Q: You instructed G to perform the confirmation killing, and G allegedly asked, ‘What happened to grandfather and the chief?’ Is that true?\\nA: I do not remember well. In my memory, I do not think I heard such words.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 187, 190)\\n\\n(c) Defendant G’s statements\\n\\n1) “Q: State the circumstances by which you came to be in the waiting room of the new building guard at Gungjeong-dong on October 26, 1979.\\nA: ... I went to the waiting room and was resting when a radio message came that the President had arrived.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 218; trial transcript p. 372)\\n\\n2) “Q: After the President arrived, ... state in detail the course up to the point when you heard gunshots.\\nA: ... E came and asked for the gun, so ... I took out one M15 submachine gun and one magazine containing 15 rounds and took them out, and shortly afterward F also took out a pistol and went out. At that time, I thought it strange why they were taking guns ... Gunshots rang out loudly from the direction of the Gungjeong-dong restaurant.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 218-219)\\n\\n3) “Q: Even in ordinary times, are there cases where you are armed with a submachine gun while on guard duty?\\nA: ... Since I worked in the new building, that was the first time.\\nQ: Did you see the driver F arming himself?\\nA: I did not.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 219)\\n\\n4) “Q: After hearing the gunshots, how did you act?\\nA: ... Section chief D ... instructed, ‘You need not worry; if the security guards rush over from the Blue House side, shoot them dead,’ and then, looking at me, he said, ‘You come with me.’”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 221; trial transcript p. 374 to the same effect)\\n\\n(g) Statement of first-instance witness AJ\\n\\n“Q: Did you see G at that time?\\nA: It seemed as if he was on duty.\\nQ: Didn’t you hear anything then?\\nA: G muttered to himself, ‘The die is cast.’”\\n(Trial transcript p. 668)\\n\\nThese are accepted as sufficient grounds for recognizing that the above Defendant also had the purpose of “subverting the Constitution.”\\n\\n(3) Therefore, the lower court’s factual findings on this point are proper. As noted above, it cannot be said that the Defendants, in this offense, lacked conclusive awareness or conditional awareness of unlawfully destroying the political basic order prescribed by the present Constitution or laws, and it cannot be said that they merely killed a natural person who was a specific constitutional organ. Nor can it be said that the purpose was not direct; moreover, in the case of Defendant A, the post-offense formation of a government was also specifically planned.\\n\\nAccordingly, as no illegality alleged in the appeal is found in the lower judgment, all arguments are without merit.\\n\\n(4) However, with respect to this point, Supreme Court Justices Min Mun-gi and Yang Byeong-ho have separate opinions concerning all six Defendants, Justice Seo Yun-hong has a separate opinion concerning Defendants C, E, F, and G, and Justices Im Hang-jun and Jeong Tae-won have separate opinions concerning Defendants E, F, and G, as set forth in Section 11 below.\\n\\n2. “Riot”\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, the insurrectionary act under Article 87 of the Criminal Act is punished according to the degree of participation in the riot when the act was committed for the prescribed purpose. In such case, “riot” means a combination of a number of persons with some organization that uses violence or intimidation to the extent of disturbing the peace of a locality, and such riot must bear a means-end relationship to the purpose of insurrection. However, first, the Defendants in this case cannot be said to constitute a combination of a number of persons with any organization; second, it cannot be found at all that they used the above violence or intimidation, nor did they reach the degree of disturbing the peace of a locality; and third, although the Defendants’ acts as found by the judgment below cannot be said to bear a means-end relationship to the purpose of subverting the Constitution, the lower court recognized the facts as found and punished them for murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection. It is argued that this constitutes misinterpretation of law concerning “riot” in the crime of insurrection, violation of the rules of evidence, and failure of hearing. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, “riot” as an element of Article 87 of the Criminal Act means a number of persons combining to commit violence or intimidation. In such case, the combination of many persons requires some degree of organization, but the number cannot be specified. Also, the degree of violence or intimidation must be such as to disturb the peace of a locality; when that degree is reached, the offense is consummated, and when it is not reached, it becomes an attempt.\\n\\nFurther, as argued, the riot must, of course, bear a means-end relationship to the purpose of insurrection. In this case, even when reviewing the evidence lawfully cited by the lower court in light of the record, the lower court’s factual findings on this point are proper. In this offense, initially, the leader Defendant A sequentially combined with E and F, and Defendant D with E, and E with G, and so on, as is clear from the lower court’s reasoning. That is enough to constitute a number of persons for the execution of a riot. (And according to Defendant A’s initial intention, to achieve the purpose of subverting the Constitution in this case, Defendant C was to be brought in as a cooperating force, the Army Chief of Staff was to be drawn in by persuasion or intimidation, and the extensive organizational power of the Central Intelligence Agency was to be used.) The above Defendants easily combined based on their positions, trust, and personal relationships as recognized from the record, and their division of roles was clearly determined, so it may be recognized as organized. The gunfire, etc. described in the lower judgment constitutes violence or intimidation as a riot. (Whether the gunfire after that also provides material to view it as a riot is considered in item 5 below.) However, it cannot be said that this reached the extent of disturbing the peace of a locality (the lower court also held it to be an attempt on the same grounds). On the other hand, according to the record, some of the Defendants were preparing for a gun battle with the Blue House security guards after the above gunfire, and further clashes between military units due to cooperation or opposition were anticipated; if it had come to that, it would undoubtedly have been sufficient to disturb the peace of a locality. In light of the purpose to subvert the Constitution as discussed above, it cannot be denied that the riot in this case bore a means-end relationship to the purpose of insurrection. Meanwhile, the lower judgment found and punished Defendant C as an attempted major participant in the insurrection, and Article 87(2) of the Criminal Act defines a “major participant” broadly to include, for example, those responsible for supply, accounting, liaison, communications, sanitation, general affairs, and similar duties. Defendant C’s original mission falls within a major role in this insurrection case, and it is possible for such a major role to involve no violence or intimidation at all.\\n\\nTherefore, since no illegality alleged in the appeal is found in the lower judgment, all arguments are without merit.\\n\\nHowever, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi, Im Hang-jun, and Kim Yun-haeng have separate opinions concerning all six Defendants, and Justices Yang Byeong-ho and Seo Yun-hong have separate opinions concerning Defendant C, as set forth in Section 11 below. Also, ex officio, although it is recognized that the lower court properly treated the acts of Defendants A, D, E, F, and G as imaginary concurrence between murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection, there are differing opinions by Justices Min Mun-gi, Im Hang-jun, and Kim Yun-haeng on this point (see Section 11).\\n\\n3. “Participation”\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, Defendant C was not in a hierarchical status of superior and subordinate with Defendant A as a “state official” and thus cannot be said to have joined a group for carrying out the insurrectionary acts in this case. Moreover, there was no conspiratorial agreement regarding mutual communication in the group for carrying out insurrection. Nevertheless, the lower court held that Defendant C joined the group when he received instructions from Defendant A, the leader, to keep security, as if he had joined the group. This, it is argued, was a fact-finding without evidence, or there was a failure of hearing and contradiction in reasons, and it violated the Supreme Court precedent on co-principal liability (Decision dated November 30, 1956, 4288HYEONG145). We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, as determined in the above items (purpose of subverting the Constitution and riot), Defendant C also clearly participated in this insurrection. Reviewing the evidence lawfully cited by the lower court in light of the record, one can recognize Defendant C’s original acts concerning the attempted major participation in insurrection (security maintenance, prohibition of troop movement from the Blue House, recommendation of martial law declaration, etc.), and these were indispensable for carrying out the insurrectionary acts in this case. As such, they themselves provide important factual material for the alleged participation, and considering the evidence cited by the lower court, the lower court’s factual findings on this point are proper. The fact that Defendant C was not in the hierarchical status alleged vis-à-vis Defendant A, the leader, cannot be said to obstruct the above factual findings. Also, as expressed in Defendant A’s statement to the prosecutor that after the assassination of the President, “Please explain in detail the course of the suspect’s conduct after that,” and Defendant A said, “Immediately thereafter, as I came out onto the floor, I encountered Chief Secretary C standing there, and when I said, ‘I will do it if I do it. It is all over now. Please keep security tight,’ Chief Secretary C asked back, ‘What did you say?’ so I said, ‘You should say that the President fainted from overwork, or say something appropriate,’ and Chief Secretary C answered, ‘Anyway, I understand,’ so I thought Chief Secretary C had completely understood” (Prosecutor’s record pp. 12-13), Defendant C cannot be said not to have had sufficient communication of intent with Defendant A while agreeing to perform the original mission. Therefore, the lower judgment contains no illegality alleged in the appeal, and this argument also lacks merit.\\n\\nHowever, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, and Seo Yun-hong have separate opinions as set forth in Section 11 below.\\n\\n4. “Killing”\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, in light of the record in this case, the deceased T’s gunshot wound, inflicted by Defendant A’s gunfire progressing from the front of the right shoulder joint toward the lower left, was a fatal wound; and Defendant G fired two shots only after T had already died. Also, the deceased U died from a fatal gunshot wound to the front of the right chest wall and a gunshot wound to the right scapular area, causing cardiac injury and death by cardiac tamponade; afterward, Defendant G fired one shot causing a blind-ended wound to the right buttock, which had no relation to U’s fatal injury. Nevertheless, the lower judgment found Defendant G guilty and punished him for the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose. It is argued that this violated the rules of evidence by finding facts of killing without evidence or misunderstood the legal principles of murder. We consider this argument.\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the lower judgment, the lower court recognized as to Defendant G responsibility for the killing of two of the six deceased persons in this case, T and U. According to the entries in the autopsy reports and on-site inspection report for T and U in the investigation record, the deceased T had wounds ㉮ blind-ended wound to the front of the right shoulder joint, ㉯ blind-ended wound to the left abdomen, ㉰ blind-ended wound to the left flank, and ㉱ through-and-through wound of the right wrist; among these, the gunshot wound located centrally at the right shoulder joint was the fatal wound, believed to have been caused by a small-caliber pistol shot. The deceased U had wounds ㉮ blind-ended wound to the front of the right chest wall, ㉯ blind-ended wound to the lateral left chest wall, ㉰ blind-ended wound to the lower left chest wall, ㉱ blind-ended wound to the right scapular area, ㉲ blind-ended wound to the right buttock, and ㉳ through-and-through wound at the right iliac crest; among these, the gunshot wound to the front of the right chest wall and the gunshot wound to the right scapular area were fatal wounds, and it is presumed that he fell because of them. (However, it was not established which gunshot caused the fatal wound.) Thus, parts of the record support the argument. However, among the various lawfully admitted pieces of evidence cited by the lower court:\\n\\n(1) Defendant C’s statements\\n(a) “Q: Then state the circumstances by which you came to conduct the confirmation killing.\\nA: Following E into the room, I fired one shot at a person lying at the entrance to the security guards’ waiting room, and then two shots at a person lying face down on the opposite side of the waiting room. At that time, I heard a groaning sound of ‘ugh’ from the banquet hall side, and after firing one shot at the fat person (Security Guard U) lying on his back with his face toward the sky, AJ, AK, AL, etc. were lying face down ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 224; however, at p. 375 and p. 1450, he says he did not hear that groaning sound and did not see the left hand move)\\n\\n(b) “Q: As to Chief of the Security Service T, did you not shoot him knowing perfectly well that he was still alive?\\nA: Yes, that is correct.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 225)\\n\\n(2) Defendant C’s statements\\n“Explain in detail the course by which A assassinated T and the President.\\nA: ... Immediately afterward, curious, I entered the room used as the banquet hall, and while someone was looking into the room holding a pistol, I heard the words ‘T is not dead yet’ ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 49; trial transcript p. 258)\\n\\n(3) Defendant E’s statements\\n(a) “Q: State the circumstances from the shooting of the President’s guards, etc. up to the point where the President was taken to the hospital.\\nA: ... When I looked into the banquet room, I saw two legs, so I cried ‘don’t move,’ and looked inside, where Chief of Security Cha Chi-cheol was lying with his eyes open, and it seemed that his hand was still moving ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 180-181; trial transcript p. 356)\\n\\n(b) “Q: When you told D that the President had been injured and gone to the hospital, what did you talk about?\\nA: When I said he had been transported, the person inside asked, ‘How is it?’ so I thought he was talking about Chief T, and when I said, ‘I’m not sure whether he was injured or dead,’ he seemed to speak to G and said to clean it up completely.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 504)\\n\\n(4) Statement of first-instance witness AS\\n(a) “Q: Was Chief of Security T there?\\nA: As I was trying to get out of there, the chief of security was by the door, so I tried to help him up, but he said he did not think he could get up, so I just went out. AI guided me to a side room, and I kept hearing groaning sounds from somewhere ...”\\n(Trial transcript p. 577)\\n\\n(b) “Q: Did you touch Chief T’s body or look at him carefully?\\nA: I looked at his face and touched only his hand. It seemed he was waving by the door, so I touched his hand, and when I tried to help him up, he said, ‘I don’t think I can get up.’”\\n(Trial transcript p. 586)\\n\\n(5) Statement of first-instance witness AI\\n“Q: Did you see Chief T lying down at that time?\\nA: I saw him. After I carried the President out, I saw him lying on the left side.\\nQ: What was Chief T saying then?\\nA: I do not know whether he saw me, but he was calling ‘AZ, AZ.’\\nQ: So what did you do?\\nA: At that time, as I was coming out with the female guest next to me, I tried to help him up ...”\\n(Trial transcript p. 663)\\n\\n(6) Statement of first-instance witness AJ\\n(a) “Q: Then did you hear groaning sounds from U and Lee Jeong-o?\\nA: ... Hearing cries of ‘Aigoo, aigoo,’ I saw that it was Security Guard U.”\\n(Trial transcript pp. 666-667)\\n\\n(b) “Q: Judging from the location where he was lying in the kitchen at that time, who would have been the first person to catch the eye of someone coming from the living room?\\nA: Security Guard U.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 667)\\n\\n(c) Statement of first-instance witness AK\\n“Q: What did the fat security guard say at that time?\\nA: He said, ‘Save me.’\\nQ: Was he groaning until before G fired?\\nA: Yes, before he fired.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 691)\\n\\nTaking these together with the other lawfully admitted evidence cited by the lower judgment, it can be sufficiently recognized from the record that T and U were alive until immediately before the shock caused by Defendant G’s action and were completely killed by that gunfire. In murder, the object is a living person, and whether the victim had the capacity to survive is irrelevant. Where independent acts clearly caused the result of death, there is no inconsistency in punishing each act as a consummated offense. Therefore, no illegality such as alleged can be found in the lower court’s factual findings or reasoning process. Accordingly, this argument lacks merit.\\n\\nHowever, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi, Im Hang-jun, Jeong Tae-won, and Seo Yun-hong have separate opinions as set forth in Section 11 below.\\n\\n5. Commencement of execution and time of consummation of the crime of insurrection\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, the crime of insurrection becomes consummated when a riot is initiated for the purpose of subverting the Constitution and the riot reaches consummation, regardless of whether the purpose of subverting the Constitution has been attained. In this case, if the President, his chief of security, and the escort guards were murdered for the purpose of subverting the Constitution, that would amount to a riot sufficient to disturb the peace of a locality, and the crime of insurrection would have reached consummation regardless of whether the constitutional-subversion purpose was achieved. Therefore, Defendant C’s conduct in this insurrection is a post-offense act not punishable, or otherwise the execution had not yet commenced. Nevertheless, the lower court found Defendant C guilty of attempted major participation in insurrection. It is argued that the lower court misunderstood the legal principles concerning the commencement of execution and consummation of the crime of insurrection, or committed violations of the rules of evidence and contradiction in reasons. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, it is true, as argued, that the crime of insurrection may be consummated after the group action as a riot has begun, regardless of whether the purpose of territorial usurpation or subversion of the Constitution has been achieved. However, the riot must have reached the extent of disturbing the peace of a locality before consummation occurs. In this case, the riotous acts described in the lower judgment alone cannot be said to have reached the extent of disturbing the peace of a locality, so it is not proper to say that the crime of insurrection in this case was consummated. Further, as for the concept of violence or intimidation as riot conduct, this is the broadest possible concept, and the conduct of preparing for or assisting such acts is comprehensively understood as riot. In this case, the state of armed guarding by Defendant F pursuant to Defendant C’s instructions at the Seoul District Army Hospital, the state of surveillance by Central Intelligence Agency personnel who did not know what was happening at Namdaemun and Seoul Station pursuant to the instructions of the deceased Park Heung-ju, who was a first-instance defendant, and the state of waiting of security vehicles at Army Headquarters, together with the facts discernible from the record by other lawfully cited evidence of the lower judgment—namely, (i) the state of security guards at the Gungjeong-dong restaurant of the Central Intelligence Agency after the gunfire there, in preparation for the approach of Blue House security guards (Prosecutor’s record pp. 110, 221; trial transcript pp. 329, 374), (ii) the surveillance state of Defendant A, as in Defendant A’s prosecutor statement: “Q: If the Army Chief of Staff and the second assistant director of the Central Intelligence Agency did not listen, A: After the act, I would persuade them, bring them to the side of the revolution, and if they still did not listen, I would intimidate or detain them and make them follow as I intended. So I kept close by them and monitored them ...” (Prosecutor’s record p. 11), and the consciousness of Defendant A and C as in “Chief Secretary C hesitated a little on the phone, then said, ‘All right, I will go there’ (I felt at that time that Chief Secretary C thought I had taken the Army Chief as a hostage and was consenting)’” (Prosecutor’s record p. 16), collectively show that the riot did not end after the Gungjeong-dong restaurant gunfire but continued. In particular, Defendant G’s confirmation killing took place after Defendant C had participated in the insurrection, so it cannot be said that Defendant C merely participated in an unpunishable post-offense act. Also, the appellate court’s measure of regarding the riot as having commenced execution when the riotous act began is proper.
