Therefore, the lower judgment has no illegality such as alleged, and this argument lacks merit.\\n\\nHowever, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi and Yang Byeong-ho have separate opinions as set forth in Section 11 below.\\n\\n6. “Concealment of evidence”\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, it is argued that, as the elements of the offense of concealment of evidence, only where the objective requirement that the evidence concern another person’s criminal or disciplinary case and the subjective requirement of intent to conceal it are satisfied can the act be punished. Yet Defendant H did not know that the items in question were evidence used in the offense of killing the former President and T’s party, and also had no intent whatsoever to conceal those items. Nevertheless, the lower court upheld the first-instance finding of guilt for concealment of evidence against Defendant H. It is argued that this violated the rules of evidence or constituted a failure of hearing or a misunderstanding of the legal principles concerning concealment of evidence. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, it is true, as argued, that the offense of concealment of evidence is constituted when a person subjectively recognizes evidence relating to another person’s criminal or disciplinary case and conceals it. Reviewing the various pieces of evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court in light of the record:\\n\\n(1) Defendant H:\\n(a) “I knew that the President had come to the banquet room while I was working as a guard at the scene of the offense.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 244; trial transcript p. 380)\\n\\n(b) “Because gunshots kept sounding loudly from the banquet room side, I became anxious, and G suggested that we should do our own security, so I armed myself with an M16 rifle ... Shortly afterward, AK, the cook from the other building, entered with his face as white as paper, so when I asked what happened, he said the lights suddenly went out and shots were fired from all directions, and he was lying face down on the kitchen floor.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 245)\\n\\n(c) In response to the question, “When did you know that President Park and the security guards had been killed in the shooting incident on the evening of October 26?”, he said: “The next day, around 05:00, while I was sleeping, I woke up and heard the news of the President’s absence from the radio in the waiting room in front of the room, and learned of it.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 243)\\n\\n“I heard the news on October 27, 1979, around 05:00, that the President was absent and the Prime Minister would act, and I thought it would be a big matter if the President passed away.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 382)\\n\\n“In response to the question whether he thought the above news was related to the gunshots of the previous day, he answered that because he heard the gunshots he thought it was related. Also, when asked what he understood the meaning of ‘absence’ to be, he answered that he understood it to mean that he had died.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 441)\\n\\n(d) “Regarding how I received the pistol, etc. from E, E gave me two pistols held in both hands and told me that there was aluminum foil in the kitchen, so I should wrap them in aluminum foil, take the shovel in the basement of the new building, and bury them somewhere in the garden.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 242)\\n\\n(e) In response to the question of where he thought the guns had come from, he said: “The moment I received them from E, I thought they must be the ones used in the gun battle that had taken place in the old building of the guesthouse on the evening of October 26, but since I was told to do it, I carried it out as instructed.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 243)\\n\\n(2) Defendant E stated: “Around 07:00, being concerned that the pistols and other items used in the offense might be discovered, I gave the guard H the pistol I had placed in the desk drawer and the security guard’s pistol hidden under the blanket, and ordered him to go into the kitchen, wrap them in aluminum foil, and bury them in the garden with the shovel in the basement.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 184)\\n\\nConsidering the other evidence together, the first-instance court’s factual finding and legal application regarding concealment of evidence as upheld by the lower court against Defendant H are proper, and it cannot be said that the rules of evidence were violated as alleged, or that there was a failure of hearing or misunderstanding of the legal principles. Therefore, this argument lacks merit.\\n\\nSection 5. Illegality concerning co-principal liability for the offense of murder\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, the lower court held that Defendant C conspired with Defendant A to kill T. However, co-principal liability is, in essence, based on two or more persons jointly, in mutual cooperation, executing their common criminal intent, and to commit a crime with the intention of acting jointly requires not only a communication of intent but also a concrete disclosure of the contents, means, and method of that conspiracy. In addition, beyond such communication of intent, there must be a fact of joint execution as an objective constituent element. Further, in its original form co-principal liability is principally a form of execution co-principal liability, while conspiracy co-principal liability is a ceremonial form in which a person participates only in the conspiracy and does not perform the constituent facts at all, yet is held to the same criminal responsibility as the executor. It arose in actual judicial practice as a theory of accomplice liability where the substantive principal plans the crime behind the scenes and causes subordinates or persons under his control to carry out the execution, making it impossible to treat it as mere instigation or aiding and abetting. Therefore, mere awareness of the crime or communication of intent is insufficient; the word “conspiracy” means a fairly high degree of consultation such as discussing the execution of the crime and determining even the role of the executor. As to a conspirator who does not undertake the execution act, there must be a subjective intent to realize his own crime through the executor. In this case, the conversation or behavior between Defendants A and C in the garden at the restaurant cannot by itself be definitively taken as a proposal to commit murder jointly or as assent thereto, and even the lower court’s explanation cannot be taken to imply that there was intent to kill or communication of such intent; nor is there evidence to support it. Moreover, Defendant C, unlike Defendant A, did not share the execution role when Defendant A killed the chief of security; rather, it appears that he attempted to restrain Defendant A from committing murder. Nevertheless, the lower court recognized Defendant C as a co-principal in the offense of murder and punished him accordingly. In any event, this is far removed from Defendant C’s explanation or Defendant A’s statements. It is argued that the lower court thus found facts without evidence, violated the rules of evidence, and committed a defect for lack of reasons and failure of hearing; and further, it misunderstood the law concerning co-principal liability and omission crimes. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, since the lower court clearly applied conspiracy co-principal liability to Defendant C concerning the murder of the deceased T, there is no need to consider further the arguments premised on execution co-principal liability. It is a precedent of this Court that in co-principal liability, even if one does not directly participate in the execution after conspiring to commit the offense, one cannot avoid co-principal liability for the acts carried out by other co-conspirators (Supreme Court decisions dated June 24, 1955, 4288HYEONG145; September 19, 1967, 67DO1027; April 20, 1971, 71DO496). In conspiracy co-principal liability, conspiracy means communication of intent among two or more persons to cooperate and realize their common criminal intent. As argued, the conspirator who does not undertake the execution act must have a subjective intent to realize his own crime through the executor; of course, but it is not necessarily required that he be the substantive principal behind the scenes who plans the crime and causes a subordinate or controllable person to carry it out.\\n\\nIn this case, reviewing the evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court in light of the record, the lower court’s factual findings and reasoning on this point are proper. However, if one quotes the important evidence recognized from the record:\\n\\n1. Defendant C’s statements\\n\\n(1) “Q: Explain in detail your relationship with T while you were serving as chief secretary.\\nA: ... I was displeased with Chief T’s overbearing conduct. As to me, since I had taken office as chief secretary on December 22, 1978, ... ① not long after that, although I formally visited T’s office to pay my respects on assuming office, T never returned the visit, which I found insulting. Also, ② when I was going to report to him, etiquette required that he come upstairs to my office if he had something to say, but instead T always had a guard call me down to the first-floor waiting room, and I felt that T was somewhat arrogant and too strong in personality ... T had such a strong sense of authority that during his tenure he never even once came to my office. And ③ when the President inspected the Government Complex or attended meetings and used the guest elevator ... T would sometimes tell me to use a different elevator that was waiting. ② Even in work reporting matters, I ordinarily would receive approval immediately with the documents if the President came to work each day, but T would wait in the office before the President arrived and go in first to report, interfering with my obtaining approval, or when I or a minister was waiting to receive approval, T would contact the guard at the entrance to the President’s office and instruct him not to let me in because he had business to see the President, making me wait and then going in to report first ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 36-39; trial transcript pp. 240-241 to the same effect)\\n\\n(2) “Q: Same as above.\\nA: ... T also frequently engaged in abuses of authority by involving himself in political operation matters that were not even his work, collecting intelligence and reporting it to the President ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 39; trial transcript p. 240 to the same effect)\\n\\n(3) “Q: Same as above.\\nA: ... In addition, he was arrogant and rude even toward me, an elder, ministers, the Speaker of the National Assembly, or senior military figures, never adding the honorific ‘nim’ when addressing anyone ... In light of these points, my relationship with T was one that could not coexist, and I was thinking of having him step down by making a proposal to the President someday.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 40; trial transcript p. 241 to the same effect)\\n\\n(4) “Q: State, to the best of your knowledge, the relationship between T, the chief of the security service, and A.\\nA: ... After being scolded by the President for ... the reason, A noticed that it was due to T’s manipulation and his anger reached the extreme.”\\n(5) “Q: From when did you and A start criticizing T together, and what was the content?\\nA: From about two months after I objected, and whenever I met A, it was mainly about T’s arrogant and rude behavior and especially that he was deeply involved in political matters and, with hard-line statements and proposals only, caused the President to hesitate in his decisions.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 43; trial transcript p. 243 to the same effect)\\n\\n(6) “Q: What did you talk about with Bureau Chief Kim after arriving at Gungjeong-dong?\\nA: When I said, ‘A fellow like a thing sitting in clear water and constantly muddying the water—how can work be done? We should get that fellow (meaning T) today ...,’ I said, ‘He listens to only one or two of the opposition fellows and rushes over to tell the President, and he’s hard-line and troublesome,’ and when Bureau Chief Kim said, ‘Shall we take that fellow out today?,’ I just nodded silently ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 45; however, at trial transcript pp. 247 and 1391 he denies it, saying he heard such words countless times and never nodded)\\n\\n(7) “Q: ... When A said, ‘Please take care of what happens after this, brother,’ what did it mean when you nodded your head?\\nA: It was agreement to remove T, because A and T were usually extremely ill-disposed toward each other, and I too always had dissatisfaction with T. As to the words ‘please take care of it,’ I thought that if you explained well to the President and made the President understand A’s true intention, A’s life at least could be saved, so I agreed.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 63; at trial transcript p. 249 he states that he did say something like that during the prosecutor’s investigation)\\n\\n(8) “Q: What was your state of mind when A left the banquet table?\\nA: ... As time passed ... A’s gloomy expression and the conversation held in front of the entrance ... came to mind ... and it is true that I felt uneasy and impatient.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 64-65; however, at trial transcript p. 254 he denies the purport)\\n\\n(9) “Q: When A ... tapped your side, what did you think?\\nA: ... I thought at last that something big was happening.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 65)\\n\\n(10) “Q: What did you hear from A in the restroom of the banka office of the Army Chief of Staff?\\nA: As soon as I went in, I said to A, ‘How could you do that even to the President?’ ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 75; on this point Defendant A’s statements also coincide = Prosecutor’s record p. 17, though in trial transcript it appears as “to the President” or “the President”)\\n\\n2. Defendant A’s statements\\n\\n(1) “Q: What was your relationship with former Blue House Security Chief T?\\nA: It is true that T, beyond his proper duty of security work, intruded into political matters and other broad affairs and had hard-line positions in opinions and assertions, so I constantly thought of him as objectionable. Also, even though T was a junior officer and younger than me, he would sometimes offend me by arrogant and rude behavior toward me or elders.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 22)\\n\\n(2) “Q: State, to the best of your knowledge, the ordinary relationship between Chief C and Security Chief T.\\nA: Two or three weeks after Chief C took office, I visited the chief’s office and heard him vent his dissatisfaction with Chief T, saying ‘I’ll have to settle this with that guy or find some way,’ and thereafter I several times heard him express great dissatisfaction due to disagreements and trivial disputes with Chief T ... I can conclusively say that the relationship between the two was not fundamentally a good one.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 30; trial transcript pp. 199-200 to the same effect, and at the time he is said to have said, “When a colonel and a captain fight, you must scold the colonel, so please endure it.”)\\n\\n(3) “Q: Explain in detail the course of the assassination of the President.\\nA: ... When I looked at Chief C’s expression while saying, ‘Shall I get rid of that guy?,’ he kept nodding, so I understood that he agreed; then when I said, ‘Please take care of what happens after this, brother,’ he again nodded, and I understood that he was agreeing ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 5; however, at trial transcript pp. 199, 542, 1510, etc., this is partly denied)\\n\\n(4) “Q: Have you been accustomed to saying ‘get rid of him’ as a habit?\\nA: As far as I remember, saying that I would get rid of Chief T was the first time that day.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 542)\\n\\n(5) “Q: What if Chief C had objected to your proposal to eliminate T?\\nA: I would have just brushed it off by saying it was a joke, and I would have died together at the scene of the President’s assassination.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 11; trial transcript p. 200 to the same effect)\\n\\nIn light of this, it cannot be said that there was no communication of intent between Defendant C and Defendant A to cooperate and jointly realize the intent to kill the deceased T. Nor can it be said that Defendant C had no intent to realize his own murderous intent toward T through Defendant A. In particular, Defendant A’s act of accepting the imminent timing of the offense as described above and his act of leaving the scene during the gunfire can be viewed as aiding acts for Defendant A’s criminal execution. Therefore, the lower court’s factual findings and reasoning on this point are all proper, and there is no illegality such as alleged. Accordingly, this argument lacks merit.\\n\\nHowever, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, Kim Yun-haeng, and Seo Yun-hong have separate opinions as set forth in Section 11 below.\\n\\nSection 6. Illegality concerning abandonment of attempt\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, the lower court’s holding, in relation to the attempted major participation in insurrection against Defendant C, that the facts of “opposition by the Prime Minister and the Ministers of Home Affairs and Justice” cannot necessarily be said to constitute the reason for the failure of the insurrection, and that the fact of “pressure by Blue House Chief Secretary Z” cannot be said to be a decisive obstacle to insurrection, and in addition there is no evidence to support these points; whereas in fact Defendant C, if he had wanted to help Defendant A after 23:00 that day, could have done so, but instead it was clear that he had him arrested of his own accord. Nevertheless, the lower court found him guilty of attempted major participation in insurrection. It is argued that there was a violation of the rules of evidence, failure of hearing, and misunderstanding of the law concerning abandonment of attempt, and also that the lower court failed to determine the defense on the above purport and thus committed a defect for lack of reasons. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, if the various pieces of evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court are examined in light of the record, the lower court’s action on this point is proper. Therefore, the above argument is plainly without merit. However, if one identifies the important basis of the lower court’s measure below:\\n\\n1. Defendant C’s prosecutor statement\\n\\n(1) “Q: Explain in detail the words exchanged and atmosphere at the Minister of National Defense’s office.\\nA: Around 21:40 that day, at the Minister of National Defense’s office ... when I said to the Prime Minister, ‘If you are going to declare emergency martial law, shouldn’t you convene the cabinet meeting?’ he said, ‘Of course,’ and then asked, ‘What shall we state as the reason for martial law? Shall we say the President has passed away? Shall we say he is absent?’ So I said, ‘If we say emergency martial law is declared from 00:00 on the 27th due to the President’s absence, wouldn’t that do?’ But the Prime Minister said, ‘Would the public accept it if we say only absence? You need to say some reason the public can accept; the cabinet ministers must know some substance in order to exchange opinions, must they not?’ Then A, who was beside us, objected saying, ‘Absence won’t do. It must be stated that martial law is being declared because the domestic security situation is bad.’ The Prime Minister objected, saying, ‘There were no demonstrations in the country, and Busan, where martial law has been declared, is quiet, so we cannot use such a reason; how can we keep the President’s absence from the public? It will be difficult to maintain secrecy all the way, and first the cabinet ministers will not accept it.’ Then A said, ‘Why not? The Soviet Union did not announce AD’s movements for over a week, so why can’t we keep secrecy for two or three days?’ When the Prime Minister said, ‘Then can Bureau Chief Kim or Chief Secretary C explain the reason at the cabinet meeting?’, A said, ‘Yes, I can,’ but I objected, saying, ‘That will not do. We are not cabinet ministers, so we cannot enter.’”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 55-57; trial transcript pp. 269 and following to the same effect)\\n\\n(2) “Q: How did you feel in the atmosphere at that time?\\nA: Yes, I felt that the cabinet ministers were showing a rather strong reaction, stronger than I had expected.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 57-58)\\n\\n(3) “Q: What was the attitude of the cabinet ministers at that time?\\nA: My thought that, as expected, the cabinet ministers had come under A’s control and were within his sphere of influence was completely mistaken, because I got the impression that the cabinet ministers were reacting against A’s assertions.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 76)\\n\\n2. Defendant A’s prosecutor statement\\n\\n(1) “Q: After going up to the Ministry of National Defense, what did you do?\\nA: I was inside the Minister of National Defense’s office ... Chief Secretary C was seated with me ... The chief secretary Z said, ‘As I was coming, reporters were gathered near the Government Complex and seem to have noticed something,’ so I instructed Assistant Vice-Director AH to strictly control domestic reporting and to tell Assistant Director AM to control any foreign reporters so that they would not notice and send out reports ...”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 18-19)\\n\\n(2) “Q: After going up to the Ministry of National Defense, what did you do?\\nA: ... When the Minister of Culture and Public Information asked, ‘We should inform the public of the reason for the martial law declaration, but what shall we announce?’, I said, ‘Wouldn’t it be enough to say only that an emergency situation has arisen in the country and martial law is being declared?’ Then the Prime Minister said, ‘We have to give cabinet ministers an explanatory statement for the declaration of emergency martial law, so what shall we say?’ ... After much back and forth we could not reach a conclusion, and at around 23:30 the Prime Minister said, ‘Please have Chief Secretary C attend the cabinet meeting and explain.’ Chief Secretary C said, ‘Prime Minister, please do it. Wouldn’t it be enough to explain that the reason for martial law declaration is the President’s absence?’ and refused to attend, saying he was not a cabinet minister. ... Suddenly, when I looked at the chief secretary’s seat, it was empty. While I was wondering about this, around 00:30 that same day, a person who seemed to be an employee of the Minister of National Defense’s annex office came and said the chief secretary was looking for me, so when I entered the annex room at the entrance to the minister’s office, two military police officers there arrested me.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record pp. 18-20)\\n\\n(3) “Q: What do you think was the reason this offense failed?\\nA: In the end, security was not maintained, and Chief Secretary C, whom I trusted most, changed his mind too quickly.”\\n(Prosecutor’s record p. 30)\\n\\n3. Statement of first-instance witness Z\\n\\n“Q: Who called Defendant C at that time?\\nA: I did. When I said, ‘Why aren’t you talking? You should talk, shouldn’t you?’, he seemed to give an affirmative answer, and it seemed as though he told me to let him see the minister, so I went to the Minister of National Defense and said, ‘Please come and see,’ I think.”\\n(Trial transcript p. 755)\\n\\nTaking these together with the other evidence, the lower court’s factual findings and reasoning are proper, and there is no violation of the rules of evidence, failure of hearing, or misunderstanding of law as alleged. The failure to consider the defendant’s explanation is not such as to affect the outcome of the judgment. Therefore, there is no defect for lack of reasons. Accordingly, this argument lacks merit.\\n\\nSection 7. Grounds negating illegality\\n\\n1. Lawful act\\n\\n(1) Theory of the “right of resistance”\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, the “right of resistance,” which has been discussed under natural law by many scholars and is now generally recognized by modern constitutional theory as having even an actual positive-law basis, should be recognized as a natural right with or without express constitutional provision. It is the right that ultimately applies, whether passive, active, violent, or nonviolent, when no other means of remedy exists, for the maintenance of the constitutional order of liberal democracy and the protection of fundamental human rights. In this case, the Yushin system, in its establishment and operation, was an anti-democratic legal order and an anti-human-rights system, so in restoring it, no other lawful remedial procedure was possible institutionally or practically. Therefore, Defendant A and D’s offenses in this case fall within the exercise of the above “right of resistance.” It is argued that the lower court rejected this application, thereby misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the right of resistance and lawful acts prescribed in Article 20 of the Criminal Act, and that Supreme Court decision 74DA3323 dated April 8, 1975, should be changed. We consider this argument.\\n\\nThis Court has previously held, in substance, that “the assertion of the so-called right of resistance is a claim to rights within a supra-positive natural-law order that disregards the existing positive legal order, and under that premise it is interpreted as an attempt to justify acts disregarding the existing constitutional order. Within the scope of positive law premised on the existing constitutional order, the exercise of judicial power charged with maintaining the State’s legal order cannot accept an argument that invokes a supra-legal concept of right to justify acts contrary to the current positive law by disregarding the existing constitutional order.”\\n\\nOn the other hand, even if one accepts the argument that, in constitutional theory of modern constitutional liberal democratic states, the so-called right of resistance as a natural right arising from natural law should be recognized as an existing right whether or not it is prescribed in the Constitution or other positive law, as long as that right of resistance does not have a basis in positive law and rests only on natural law, a judge cannot invoke it as a judicial norm. Moreover, even among scholars who acknowledge the existence of the right of resistance today, their views differ widely as to the content of its concrete concept or its requirements for establishment, so it cannot be said to be unified; in the end it cannot escape being called a vague and abstract concept. Even several legislative examples that declare the existence of the right of resistance in the Constitution have different specific requirements from one another. Since in our Constitution and laws there is no provision concerning the right of resistance at all (the argument that the Preamble’s reference to “the April 19 revolution, etc.” does not constitute a provision on the right of resistance), we cannot but hesitate all the more to adopt and apply this theory as a standard for adjudication at the present stage in our country. Therefore, there is no need to change the above precedent of this Court, and the argument that there is an error of law in the lower court on this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\nHowever, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi and Im Hang-jun have separate opinions (see Section 11 below).\\n\\n(2) Legitimate performance of official duty\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, the facts found in the lower judgment concerning attempted major participation in insurrection against Defendant C—namely, security maintenance, prohibition of troop deployment, report to the Prime Minister, and recommendation to the Ministers of Home Affairs and Justice to declare martial law and the reasons therefor—were all the best measures to deal with an emergency situation, an unexpected national crisis that fell upon him as Chief Secretary to the President, and therefore constitute legitimate performance of official duty under Article 20 of the Criminal Act. Nevertheless, it is argued that the lower court overlooked this point, committing an error of law concerning lawful acts and a failure of hearing, and also omitting consideration of the grounds of appeal submitted by that Defendant’s counsel. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review of the record, the above argument is nothing more than a false explanation offered by Defendant C in order to escape responsibility for the attempted major participation in insurrection charge against him. Rather, the above acts by Defendant C are all recognized as actions taken to actively join, respond to, and support the offense of Defendant A, the leader of the insurrection. Therefore, there is no error of law or failure of hearing by the lower court on this point. And since there is no error of law or failure of hearing on this point, even if the grounds of appeal on this point were omitted from the lower judgment, it could not be said to have affected the judgment. In the end, this argument is without merit.\\n\\n(3) Order of a superior\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the acts found by the lower court against Defendant D were acts in accordance with orders given by co-defendant A as Director of the Central Intelligence Agency and thus constitute lawful acts under Article 20 of the Criminal Act. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, a public official, in performing duties, is under no authority by a superior to order a subordinate to commit a criminal act or other unlawful act. Also, while a subordinate has a duty to obey lawful orders from a superior within the organization, when the order is clearly unlawful or illegal, it cannot be regarded as an official directive order, and therefore there is no duty to follow it. Accordingly, this argument is plainly without merit.\\n\\n2. Justifiable defense\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, when the so-called “Busan-Masan incident” arose as a national resistance against the denial and infringement of popular sovereignty under the Yushin Constitution and emergency measures, and while the authorities were attempting to respond with indiscriminate massacre of the people, the Defendants reached the offense in this case as a last resort to defend the present unlawful infringement upon the lives and property of the sovereign people. It is argued that this constitutes self-defense and thus lacks unlawfulness; moreover, Defendant A had advanced such an explanation from the investigative authorities through the conclusion of the lower proceedings, but the lower court failed to fully hear this point or omitted to decide it. We consider this argument.\\n\\nAs repeatedly stated above, Defendant A’s act in this case, namely the murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrectionary leadership committed to kill the President and seize power through insurrection, has no obstacle to formation. Nevertheless, the Defendant argues that, based on the date of the offense, within a few days a popular uprising such as the so-called “Busan-Masan incident” would occur in Seoul, and that President Park would have ordered firing upon the people, so he committed this act because he intended to save the likely sacrificed lives, bodies, and property of the people, that is, to defend against the present unlawful infringement upon the legal interests of the people and the State.\\n\\nHowever, according to the record, on October 19, 1979, the Defendant who had visited the scene and returned as the then Director of the Central Intelligence Agency on October 17 and 18, 1979, when asked at the first-instance trial, “Were there any people who died in the Busan-Masan incident?”, answered, “As far as I know, there were none” (trial transcript p. 227).\\n\\nThen even if expansion of the so-called Busan-Masan incident were anticipated, one could not conclude that not only injury to body or destruction of property but also necessarily the sacrifice of many lives would occur. Moreover, the allegation of the expansion of the Busan-Masan incident and of the President’s alleged order to fire is merely the Defendant’s own assertion, and there is no objective material supporting it. In this case, such an explanation is ultimately either fabricated falsehood by the Defendant or merely a fanciful inference about an uncertain future situation. Therefore, there is no evidentiary material establishing facts that satisfy the requirements for self-defense under Article 21(1) of the Criminal Act. Hence, the argument that the lower court overlooked this point lacks merit. And even if further hearing were conducted on this point, the possibility of obtaining materials to support it is slim in this case, so it cannot be said that there was a failure of hearing. Moreover, since no such illegality by the lower court exists, even if the lower judgment omitted consideration of this point, it could not be an illegality affecting the judgment. Accordingly, all of the above arguments are without merit.\\n\\n3. Necessity\\n\\n(1) Among the grounds of appeal, as in the domestic political situation at the time of October 26 noted in the above self-defense argument, Defendant A reached the offense in this case unavoidably to avoid the existing danger to the life, body, and freedom of numerous people. This constitutes necessity and thus lacks unlawfulness. Nevertheless, it is argued that the lower court overlooked this point and also failed to fully hear the argument, and further committed an illegality by omitting its determination. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, for the same reasons already stated in the section on self-defense above, it is clear that this argument also lacks merit.\\n\\n(2) Among the grounds of appeal, Defendant C maintained security, prohibited troop movement to the Blue House, and recommended declaration of martial law because he feared that if the fact that the head of state had been lost were leaked externally, it would lead to bloodshed from a gun battle among our own troops and give the North Korean regime an opportunity to provoke an invasion. Accordingly, these acts were unavoidable to avoid the present danger to the lives of many people and military/police personnel, and thus constitute necessity. Nevertheless, it is argued that the lower court overlooked this, misunderstood the law regarding necessity, and also omitted its determination despite Defendant C consistently maintaining this explanation in the first instance and appellate court, thereby committing a defect for lack of reasons. We consider this argument.\\n\\nAs noted in another section above, this Court has already held that the lower court’s measure recognizing Defendant C’s above conduct (security maintenance, prohibition of troop movement from the Blue House, recommendation of martial law declaration, etc.) as constituting attempted major participation in insurrection is proper. This argument, even if those acts constitute the acts found in the lower judgment and the offense of major participation in insurrection, contends that they are exempt from unlawfulness because they were acts to avoid “present danger” to the lives of many people and military/police personnel caused by bloodshed from mutual gunfire among our own troops and the opportunity for the North to provoke an invasion.\\n\\nTherefore, we examine whether Defendant C at that time truly had the intent to avoid such danger, that is, the “intent of necessity.” Looking at the record:\\n\\nFirst, if the Defendant truly had the intent to avoid the above danger, then at minimum he should have told the truth to the then Prime Minister AO, who would naturally become acting President, and should have discussed countermeasures, yet he did not do so and instead falsely reported that the President had died from A’s accidental bullet. This shows that the intent to participate in A’s insurrection came before the intent to avoid the danger.\\n\\nSecond, if the Defendant truly had the intent to avoid the above danger, he could have consulted with Lieutenant General AN, commander of the Capital Defense Command and Deputy Director of the Presidential Security Service, who at that time commanded the formidable Capital Defense Command, and arrested or shot A through a small-scale operation; yet he did not do so. This shows that the intent to participate in A’s insurrection came before the intent to avoid the danger.\\n\\nThird, on the afternoon of the day of the offense, around 19:43, immediately after A finished the shooting and left, asking him to keep security and take care of the aftermath, the Defendant seized the pistol that had been held by co-defendant E and carried it while visiting the military hospital, the Blue House, the Army Headquarters banka, the Ministry of National Defense, etc. Therefore, if he truly had the intent to avoid the above danger, then he could have killed A when meeting and conversing with him at the Army Headquarters banka or in the Ministry of National Defense office, yet he did not do so. This indicates that the intent to participate in A’s insurrection came before the intent to avoid the danger.\\n\\nThen even if one assumes that the situation at that time was one of the present danger alleged, as long as no necessity intent can be recognized, necessity in this case cannot be recognized. Therefore, the argument that the lower court erred in law on this point lacks merit, and even if the lower court’s reasoning on this defense were omitted, it would not be an error affecting the judgment. Thus the arguments of omitted determination and lack of reasons also lack merit.\\n\\nSection 8. Grounds negating criminal responsibility\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, because Central Intelligence Agency personnel were in a more rigid superior-subordinate relationship than an army, with the Director at the apex, they had no room to determine whether a superior’s order was unlawful or to choose whether to execute it. Accordingly, Defendants D, E, F, G, and H, who acted in special circumstances where they could not refuse their superior’s orders, are said to have engaged in compelled acts or acts where no reasonable alternative existed, and thus cannot be punished. Nevertheless, it is argued that the lower court misunderstood the law concerning compelled acts and the absence of reasonable alternatives, thereby overlooking these grounds negating criminal responsibility. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, the first instance held that public officials, in performing duties, are obligated to obey their immediate superior’s official orders, but are not obligated to obey clearly unlawful orders. Also, although it may be an unwritten rule among Central Intelligence Agency personnel that they must absolutely obey superior orders, that alone cannot make the clearly and flagrantly unlawful acts constituting the offenses found in this case into compelled acts or acts where lawful conduct cannot be expected. There is no other material showing that, at the time of the offense, the Defendants were unable to make free decisions because they were subjected to force that could not be resisted or threats that could not be prevented, nor that they were under special circumstances in which they could not refuse an unlawful order from a superior and thus lawful conduct could not reasonably be expected. The lower court so held, and the appellate court also stated that it maintained the first-instance view. Reviewing the record, it is easy to recognize that in light of the time and place of the offense, if the above Defendants had not been motivated by the desire for the so-called “share” they expected to receive in return for participating in this revolutionary act, they would have had enough time and spatial environment to refuse the superior’s order and escape from the scene. Thus the lower court’s judgment is all the more proper. Therefore, this argument lacks merit.\\n\\nSection 9. Improper severity of sentence\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal, Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act provides that improper severity of sentence may be raised as a ground of appeal. However, since that article conflicts with Article 8 of the Constitution guaranteeing human dignity and Article 9 of the Constitution concerning equality of the people, in conjunction with Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and is therefore void, the Defendants sentenced to the death penalty should be allowed to appeal on the ground of improper severity of sentence. Considering the motive and purpose of the Defendants’ offenses in this case, the domestic political situation before and after the offenses, and their personal circumstances, as well as the fact that in more modern civilized countries many have already abolished the death penalty as punishment, and even theoretically the view favoring abolition is far superior, it is argued that the lower court’s imposition of the death penalty was excessively severe and thus improper. We consider this argument.\\n\\nUpon review, military courts are special courts established for special purposes and objectives, unlike ordinary courts. Even if there is inequality between their treatment of defendants and that of ordinary courts, this is understood to have been anticipated by the Constitution and laws from the outset. Therefore, Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act cannot be regarded as an unconstitutional provision violating Articles 8 and 9 of the Constitution. Accordingly, the argument developed on the premise of such unconstitutionality lacks merit.\\n\\nHowever, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi and Im Hang-jun have separate opinions (see Section 11 below).\\n\\nSection 10. Conclusion\\n\\nAs seen above, there are separate opinions by (i) Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, and Kim Yun-haeng as to part of Defendant A’s grounds of appeal; (ii) Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, Kim Yun-haeng, and Seo Yun-hong as to part of Defendant C’s grounds of appeal; (iii) Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, and Kim Yun-haeng as to part of Defendant D’s grounds of appeal; and (iv) Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, Kim Yun-haeng, Jeong Tae-won, and Seo Yun-hong as to part of Defendants E, F, and G’s grounds of appeal (which have already been set out in detail in each relevant section). Nevertheless, according to the majority opinion, those grounds of appeal are without merit, and as to the other grounds of appeal, all participating Justices are unanimous that they lack merit. Accordingly, all appeals by the Defendants are dismissed. Also, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as to Defendant H, pursuant to Article 57 of the Criminal Act, all days of pretrial detention in the appellate instance before this judgment is pronounced shall be credited against the principal sentence, and judgment is rendered as stated in the operative part.\\n\\nSection 11. Separate opinions\\n\\n1. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Min Mun-gi\\n\\nI consider the grounds of appeal submitted by counsel alleging an error of law concerning the legal principles of insurrection.\\n\\nThe insurrection at issue in this case is inherently a crime with a strong political coloration, and in reality it is accompanied by regime change, so a view of the political situation cannot be avoided.\\n\\nAs declared by the acting President AO, who succeeded the President who became vacant due to the offense of this case (October 26, 1979), through the confirmation declaration (November 10, 1979), the creation of a new constitution as a nationwide consensus is a milestone historical fact, a significant political decision of the people having undeniable prospectivity, an unwritten rule supported by the people’s legal conviction, and a binding force governing the political situation. However, because this consensus conflicts with the Yushin system and constitutes its true nature, it is clearly impossible without going beyond that system. Therefore, the very existence of nationwide consensus practically means the abolition of the Yushin system itself (today’s political development is proof of this), and because this consensus cannot be said to have been achieved simultaneously with the fate of former President B, the Yushin system becomes, in legal logic, a system that shared the fate of the late President Park.\\n\\nTo help understanding, by way of example: if, in transforming the democratic order into a monarchical system, one were charged with insurrection, but a nationwide consensus was reached to change the Constitution into a monarchical constitution, then one could not punish the act as insurrection as it is. Since that consensus means the abolition of the democratic system, after the consensus, insurrection cannot mean a demand for democracy and certainly cannot mean a demand for monarchy; thus, one may not convict as insurrection merely because after consensus one seeks monarchy. The reason is that the protected legal interest differs because the constitutive basis differs, so the systems can no longer be regarded as the same as the constitutional order.\\n\\nThis case is exactly the same as that example, so the same legal principle applies.\\n\\nGiven the appellate judgment’s application of Article 87(1) and (2), Article 89, and Article 88 of the Criminal Act to all Defendants, and the purport explained as the reason, it is clear that all were treated as crimes with the purpose of subverting the Constitution. Moreover, according to Defendant A’s statements, which the lower court recognized as the leader, the purpose of the offense, as expressed, was to remove former President Park, the core of the Yushin system, terminate that system, and restore the democratic system. This cannot be denied on the record, and it is consistent with the original explanation. If one follows the lower judgment’s findings, the appellate court found that the Defendants killed the President and others as described in the judgment with the purpose of forcibly transforming the Yushin system, and considering the course of the litigation, it is clear that the trial was conducted after a nationwide consensus to amend the Constitution had already formed. Therefore, in this situation, because the basis of the act at the time of the offense and the basis at the time of trial are different, as explained above, this is a political situation that cannot be punished supra-legally. Thus, apart from whether the offense should be viewed as another crime, it cannot be punished as insurrection.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower judgment left a legal error affecting the conclusion (which would have been correct if under the Yushin system), and the attempted-opinion supporting it is the same.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, the argument is well-founded in conclusion, and I do not proceed to other claims.\\n\\nFinally, in the alternative, I state my agreement with and incorporation by reference of the opinions of Justices Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, and Kim Yun-haeng.\\n\\n2. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Yang Byeong-ho\\n\\nI consider together the first, second, and third points of the appeal by Defendant A’s counsel I, the appeal grounds of AB, and the appeal grounds of AP for 17 persons.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons in the lower judgment, Defendant A, while serving as Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, saw his plans to stabilize the political situation, which he himself drafted and implemented, repeatedly fail, exposing his incompetence in performance of duties, and after being reprimanded by President B, rumors of dismissal for responsibility circulated, making him feel insecure in his position. Meanwhile, although the President disliked the arrogant and overreaching attitude and interference by Chief T of the Presidential Security Service, who was his junior officer, he resented the President’s greater trust in T. From around an unknown date in April 1979, he planned to kill the President and seize power, independently devised the concrete plan for the act to maintain secrecy, chose the appropriate time, and decided to kill the President and others. After assassinating the President, he would declare martial law on the ground of national security and disturbance of public order, and using the authority and organizational force of the Central Intelligence Agency, take control of the martial law forces and suppress the situation by force, form a revolutionary committee overseeing legislative, judicial, and executive powers, become chairman himself and secure a base of power, and then run for President. The lower court recognized the facts of murder with insurrectionary purpose by finding that from 19:40 to around 20:05 on October 26, 1979, as found in the judgment, the President and others were shot to death.\\n\\nHowever, in determining whether Defendant killed the President for the purpose of subverting the Constitution, reviewing the evidence the lower court adopted and considered in support of the insurrectionary-murder facts, the only relevant materials are the statements of the Defendant and co-defendant C in the first-instance and appellate military court, and the statements in the suspect-interrogation records prepared by the military prosecutor for the Defendant and C. Among them, Defendant’s statements in the first-instance and appellate court (including the supplemental statement of appeal grounds) and the statements in the suspect-interrogation records prepared by the prosecutor indicate that this act of October 26 was done to abolish the undemocratic Yushin system for the lifetime rule of President B and to restore liberal democracy, the founding ideology and national policy; that the core of the Yushin system was President Park, and as long as he was there the Yushin system could not be changed; that democratic restoration was desired by all the people; that challenge and resistance to the Yushin system were widespread in the public mind; that the Busan-Masan incident immediately before the case was a good example; and that even though it spread to Seoul and the five major cities nationwide, the President would directly order firing as a countermeasure, forcing enormous sacrifices of the nation and people. In view of the President’s strong desire to remain in power and his character of never retreating, the Defendant says that in this desperate situation there was no way to prevent this tragedy, so he was compelled to kill and remove the person because the restoration of liberal democracy and the sacrifice of the President’s life were fatefully connected. At the same time, he calls this act a revolution, saying that it was to eliminate the Yushin order, and that the revolutionary task was to declare martial law first to restore the situation, form a revolutionary committee and carry it out according to the basic organization and constitutional procedures, and that he intended to amend the Constitution through proper constitutional revision procedures.\\n\\nIn short, he says that he killed natural person B, the President, for the restoration of democracy, and that the other steps were to be taken through proper and lawful procedures. And he insists that he is a soldier and revolutionary, but that if soldiers take power it becomes dictatorship, and that he is not morally degraded enough to trample on the President’s grave, so he certainly did not make a revolution for the purpose of becoming President.\\n\\nOn this basis, we consider the Defendant’s above statement as a confession and examine whether there is corroborating evidence. According to the statements of co-defendant C in the first-instance and appellate military court and the statements in the suspect-interrogation records prepared by the military prosecutor regarding C, there is a statement that on the day of the incident, at around 22:25, in the restroom of the Army Headquarters banka, Defendant said that martial law should first be declared and the signboard changed to Revolutionary Committee, and nothing else appears in the record that could serve as supporting material. Therefore, among Defendant’s confession, only the part about declaring martial law, revolution, or the Revolutionary Committee has corroboration, and this becomes the issue. We then need to know what Defendant meant by “revolution.” As noted above, Defendant said this revolution meant abolishing the Yushin order. In addition, he says that declaring martial law and forming a revolutionary committee were necessary steps or organs in the process of restoring order and steering the political situation in the right direction. No material is found to conclude that his reference to revolution was one without reference to constitutional or legal procedures and thus precisely for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. Moreover, in our country, many people call the events of April 19, 1960, the “April 19 Revolution,” so the use of the term revolution is easily overused in reality. In view of this, whether the “revolution” spoken of by Defendant truly meant transforming the State’s governing apparatus must be examined more carefully, and it is too hasty to simply conclude, from the use of the words “revolution or Revolutionary Committee,” that he planned to overthrow the State’s basic order. This appears appropriate.\\n\\nThere is no material to support the lower court’s finding that Defendant intended to take control of the martial law forces by using the authority and organizational force of the Central Intelligence Agency and suppress the situation by force, or that he intended to seize power. And the fact that Defendant planned to form a Revolutionary Committee overseeing legislative, judicial, and executive powers, become chairman himself, secure a base of power, and then run for President is indeed a confession appearing in similar words in the statements in the suspect-interrogation records prepared by the prosecutor, but there is no corroborating evidence for it. On the contrary, those records include a statement that he intended to establish a constitutional drafting committee, have it research and draft a constitution desired by the people, submit it to a referendum, and, after confirmation, hold elections under the new constitution. This is no different from saying that constitutional revision would be done according to current constitutional procedures, and thus does not constitute abolition of the functions of the Constitution without following constitutional procedures.\\n\\nAgain, according to those records, in conducting the elections the presidential candidates could be AO, Prime Minister, and AQ AR, and the Defendant himself would decide whether to run depending on circumstances. Even if one accepts that statement as it is, it is doubtful whether the fact that he recommended those persons as presidential candidates or that he would decide whether to run himself depending on the situation can be immediately concluded to be overthrow by force or making the exercise of the functions of a state organ established by the Constitution impossible. Further, even if the Defendant caused C to bring the Prime Minister to the Army Headquarters banka and induced the Prime Minister to declare emergency martial law after a cabinet meeting, if one follows the Defendant’s own statement, that would have been according to proper procedure.\\n\\nMoreover, the purpose of subverting the Constitution means unlawfully abolishing or extinguishing the functions of the Constitution or laws and destroying or overthrowing by force the basic organs of governance and other constitutional organs of the State. In this case, the lower court, in its reasoning, characterized the Defendant’s claim that the act was for the restoration of democracy as a pretext: taking advantage of the time when constitutional revision work based on nationwide consensus after the President’s death was being actively pursued in the government and National Assembly, and the democratization movement was widespread among all sectors of the people, he had no other choice but to kill and remove the President, natural person B, who was an obstacle to the restoration of democracy, and that he was disguising an unlawful plan to overthrow the government by violence and seize power under the guise of restoring liberal democracy. To find as fact that he committed the offense for the purpose of unlawfully destroying the State’s basic governing organization and seizing power, there must of course be precise evidence on this point. In addition, if, as the judgment below says, he used the authority and organizational force of the Central Intelligence Agency to control the martial law forces, one must explain by what authority, organization, and method a non-military agency like the Central Intelligence Agency sought to control the martial law forces. Also, if he intended to suppress the situation by force and form a Revolutionary Committee overseeing legislative, judicial, and executive powers, one must clearly state whether he intended to suppress the people’s will and the State organs by force and lead the situation toward the seizure of power, or overthrow and abolish the National Assembly, courts, and government, so that the Revolutionary Committee itself would exercise all three powers. And if he intended to secure a base of power and then run for President, one must specify whether this meant not through organizing a political party and building support, but through martial law or emergency measures to prohibit all opposing opinions, or through force and other coercive means to gain people’s support rather than through the free exercise of the people’s choice under the constitutional election system.\\n\\nIf one simply reasons that, because he killed the President, he must necessarily have done so for the purpose of subverting the Constitution by overthrowing the government, that appears to reflect a very naive and simplistic way of thinking. The President is an organ of the national government; the President is not the government itself. Also, before discussing the President’s noble position, one must first regard the duties he bears as more important, and the President too is merely one public official among those serving the entire people and responsible to the people.\\n\\nThe facts found by the lower court proceed by assuming that the Defendant had a personal grievance against the President and planned to kill him, and then concluding that it was murder with the purpose of subverting the Constitution. But if it was a personal grievance, that is a reason that could support the Defendant’s claim that he intended to kill the natural person who was the President. In addition, the reasoning appears inconsistent on its face, showing a defect of contradiction.\\n\\nIn this situation, the lower court, without considering these several points, conclusively held that the Defendant committed murder with insurrectionary purpose. This amounts either to a case of factual error without evidence or in violation of the rules of evidence, and in this case, where the crucial issue is whether it was merely the killing of a natural person holding the office of President or whether it was a murder with purpose of subverting the Constitution, the court should at least have further examined the facts and evidence. Failing to do so and broadly finding the facts amounts to a failure of hearing and defect for lack of reasons. Since that affects the judgment, the grounds of appeal are meritorious.\\n\\nI consider together the grounds of appeal points 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6 submitted by Defendant C’s counsel AC, point 2 of the grounds of appeal by J Kim Hong-jae, and point 1 of the grounds of appeal by L.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons in the lower judgment, since Defendant C was appointed Chief Secretary to the President, he had long expressed dissatisfaction together with A regarding T’s arrogant and overreaching attitude and interference in authority, and had shown an intent to remove T. Then, on the day in question at around 17:50, when he arrived at the Central Intelligence Agency’s Gungjeong-dong restaurant to receive the President and sat with A on the curb in the garden in front of the restaurant entrance, during conversation he vented complaints such as saying, “That chief T fellow is so hard-line and troublesome,” and received from A the suggestion “Shall we get rid of that fellow today,” while recognizing that it meant killing T as the explosion of long-accumulated feelings, and consented thereto, thereby conspiring with A to kill T. Thereafter, although A repeatedly left the banquet table and even went outside for 15 minutes and came back, showing that the time for execution of the offense was imminent, he tolerated it; then at around 19:40 that same day, as a signal A lightly struck him with his right hand while saying, “Please take care of the President,” and fired a pistol at T. To facilitate the offense, Defendant C left the scene, thereby jointly with A killing T.\\n\\nHowever, even if one carefully examines the evidence the lower court adopted, there is not the slightest trace of material supporting the conclusion that the Defendant and A conspired by communicating intent to kill Security Chief T of the President. According to the statements of the Defendant and A in the first-instance and appellate court, as well as the statements in the prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation records, it can be recognized that at around 17:50 on the day of the incident, Defendant, who had come early to the Central Intelligence Agency’s Gungjeong-dong restaurant to receive the President, sat with A on the curb in front of the restaurant entrance and was talking when Defendant said, “T, the chief, is so hard-line and troublesome,” and A replied, “Shall we get rid of that guy today?” The lower court seems to have taken this to mean that the Defendant had received from A the proposal to “get rid of that guy today” and, knowing that it meant killing T, consented, and therefore should be regarded as having mutually conspired to kill T. However, the phrase “get rid of” cannot possibly, between persons like the Defendants who are not gangsters but national officials, be interpreted as meaning “kill,” and there is no material showing that the Defendant understood it as meaning that T would be killed. The prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation records do contain a statement that the Defendant nodded silently at the time, but this cannot be taken as more than a look of “ah, is that so?” and not as an indication of will to do so or a manifestation of consent to “do that.” Moreover, to conclude that a conspiracy to kill was formed by a casual exchange of words during a short period while waiting in the garden in front of the restaurant entrance for the President’s arrival, where people in charge of the restaurant were passing back and forth, is contrary to our experience and logic. The fact that the Defendant had a strong dissatisfaction with T’s arrogant conduct and abuse of authority, and that he had the same position as A in this respect, does not become a motive to conspire to kill T.\\n\\nThe fact that he had facial expressions in the banquet hall, that he knew A had left the banquet table several times, that he left the scene after A fired a pistol at T and at that time recognized that T was groaning and still alive, and that he said to A in the Army Headquarters banka restroom, “Why did you do that even to the President?”, may have some reason or point of inconsistency, but even setting that aside, even if those facts were recognized as they are, apart from whether he could be liable as an omission offender or accomplice, they cannot serve as material establishing that he jointly conspired with A and jointly killed in that murder. The Defendant did not share the execution act for the killing, as the lower court’s reasoning says, and there is no material to show that he had a subjective intent to realize his own crime through the executor A. It is clear from the record that A killed T because T was a person who would be a decisive obstacle to the achievement of the purpose of killing President B.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court recognized Defendant as a conspiracy co-principal in the killing of T. This constitutes a grave factual error without evidence or in violation of the rules of evidence, and also a misunderstanding of the law concerning conspiracy co-principal liability, which affected the judgment. Therefore, the grounds of appeal are meritorious.\\n\\nI consider together points 9 and 11 of the grounds of appeal by Defendant C’s counsel AC and point 2 of the grounds of appeal by L.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons in the lower judgment, on the same day at around 19:43, Defendant C heard A say in front of the restaurant entrance, “It’s all over now. Please keep security tight,” and, as the only high-ranking state official to have witnessed A’s killing of the President, knowing that the security maintenance was an important mission that would determine the direction of the constitutional order in view of the influence attached to his position, he replied, “I understand,” agreeing to perform that duty according to the leader A’s order to maintain security. Thereafter, in order to maintain security for the offense and to use it later if the situation turned adverse as a pretext that he himself had tried to save the President, at around 19:55 that day he transported the President’s remains to the Seoul District Army Hospital and had the duty military doctor diagnose them, confirmed that “death had occurred five minutes earlier,” yet concealed the fact that the patient was the President and went to the Blue House Presidential Chief Secretary’s office, where he told the summoned chief secretaries AT and others, and Deputy Director of the Presidential Security Service, Army Lieutenant General AN, that “something has happened to the President and the chief T cannot now direct the troops, so strengthen the guard and closely control any rash actions; troop deployment from the Security Service is unnecessary.” Thereby he gained time to achieve the offense. At around 20:50, when he arrived there, he also told Prime Minister AO, who was then present, that “in the banquet hall, A and T fought and, in the end, the President died from a shot accidentally fired by A,” falsely reporting that A had intentionally killed the President. When asked by Ministers of Home Affairs and Justice AU and AV, he merely answered that “the President was injured,” thereby continuing to conceal A’s killing of the President. At around 21:10, after again receiving a telephone call from A ordering him to bring the Prime Minister, he went with the Prime Minister and the Ministers of Home Affairs and Justice to the Army Chief of Staff’s office in the Army Headquarters banka at around 21:30, saw A and then Minister of National Defense AW and major generals gathered there, and thought A had already taken control of the military. He then lied to the Minister of National Defense and others, saying, “The President has become absent; the incident happened because Chief T was too hard-line,” and proposed that they should bring the Prime Minister and restore order, thus inducing the declaration of martial law. At around 22:40, when in the Minister of National Defense’s office A, seated with the Prime Minister and other cabinet ministers, emphasized security maintenance and, in declaring emergency martial law, proposed that the reason should not be the President’s death but rather domestic security problems, Defendant C supported this and proposed as a compromise that martial law be declared on the ground of the President’s absence. At around 23:30, when the Prime Minister and the Ministers of Home Affairs and Justice showed no sign of agreeing with A and Blue House chief secretary Z urged him to explain the circumstances of the President’s absence at the cabinet meeting, Defendant concluded that A’s assertion would not be adopted, changed his attitude, and at around 00:30 the next day told the Minister of National Defense and the Army Chief of Staff that “A is the person who killed the President,” causing A to be arrested; thus the insurrectionary riot for the purpose of subverting the Constitution was not completed and the matter remained an attempt, which the lower court recognized as attempted major participation in insurrection.\\n\\nHowever, the facts found by the lower court mean that after A killed the President in the restaurant and came out of the entrance asking Defendant to keep security tight and take care of the aftermath, the court found Defendant’s later conduct to constitute attempted major participation in insurrection. The major mission he was handling was understood to include security maintenance. Upon review, Defendant was in a situation where, in the terrifying atmosphere of an unexpected shootout in which A suddenly shot and killed the President and others, he could hardly be expected to do anything other than answer “I understand” to a request to maintain security. The transportation of the President’s remains to the Seoul District Army Hospital, the emergency summoning of the President’s chief secretaries and the deputy director of the security service, and the notice to the Prime Minister and ministers to come to the Blue House may have involved concealment or false reporting, but in the sense that he did take his own steps to inform the high-level relevant officials of the event despite A’s request to maintain security, one may say that he did not properly perform the mission in question.\\n\\nInsurrection requires a person who riots for the purpose of usurping the territory or subverting the Constitution. As seen from the facts found in the lower judgment, the acts involving violence after the killing were confined to conduct after the request “please only keep security regarding this now that it’s all over.” In this case, the evidence adopted by the lower court reveals that A, together with Army Chief of Staff AX and Assistant Vice-Director AH, whom he had made wait in the main building of the restaurant, went to the Army Headquarters banka, emphasized security, and monitored the movements of major military officials and cabinet ministers—facts entirely unknown to the Defendant. Also, A called the Blue House again and said, “The work is all done; why are you still there? The Minister of National Defense is here too, so bring the Prime Minister to the Army Headquarters banka,” and the Prime Minister and ministers of Home Affairs and Justice went there. A’s act of emphasizing security to the Prime Minister and other cabinet ministers and inducing martial law declaration was merely a process to calmly proceed with restoring order after the killing of the President and others and to achieve the purpose of the planned act. There is no evidentiary material showing that the act itself was a riot or that the riot continued until he was arrested. And the fact that Defendant thought A had taken control of the military after enticing the Army Chief of Staff and went to the Army Headquarters banka can only mean that he thought A had taken control of the military without any riot. Defendant said there that declaring emergency martial law on the ground of the President’s absence would be better, and while watching how things developed he took the opportunity to have A arrested. Thus, after the killing of the President and others, the riot ended, and there were no subsequent riotous acts; one cannot say there was a continuing riot. Even if one assumed that the riot was continuing, there is no evidence that Defendant participated in it or engaged in conspiratorial acts.\\n\\nAccordingly, there is no room to recognize Defendant’s attempted major participation in insurrection, which presupposes involvement in riot. Nevertheless, the lower court found and applied that offense. This is either a factual mistake in violation of the rules of evidence or a misunderstanding of law or defect for lack of reasons that affected the judgment. Therefore, the grounds of appeal are meritorious.\\n\\nI consider together point 1 of the grounds of appeal by Defendant D’s counsel N, point 3 of the grounds of appeal by counsel O for Defendants E and F, and point 3 of the grounds of appeal by counsel P for Defendant G.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons in the lower judgment, at around 19:00 on the day of the incident, when Defendant A left the banquet table with the President and T in the restaurant and put one pistol prepared in advance in the second-floor bedroom of the main office into his pants watch pocket and was entering the banquet table, at around 19:10 in the old building garden adjacent to the restaurant he instructed Defendant D and first-instance defendant Park Heung-ju, saying, “I will take care of it today, so be prepared. I will handle the President and others directly, so as soon as you hear gunshots, pick three smart men and deal with the security guards,” and informed them that the Army Chief of Staff and the second assistant director were in the office, thereby urging them to solidify their will to participate in the offense, and received a promise from Defendant D that he would finish preparations within 30 minutes. Then, at around 19:15 in the west garden of the restaurant, Bureau Chief Kim Sun-ho instructed Defendants F and E, saying, “This is an order from the chief. If things go well today, you will get a share. When the chief fires from inside, shoot the security guards in the kitchen,” and received their assent. Defendant C, in the guard waiting room opposite the restaurant, received from Defendant D instructions to shoot the security guards if they came from the Blue House, and also, at around 20:05, received from Defendant E instructions to fire a confirmation shot at persons in the restaurant who were not yet fully dead. Defendant C then entered the security guards’ waiting room inside the restaurant, saw the guards being shot, recognized that this was a state of national upheaval, and agreed to participate according to the instruction. Thus each Defendant sequentially conspired to participate in killings for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. According to the same conspiracy, when at around 19:40 the sound of Defendant A’s pistol shot was heard as a signal, Defendant D fired his pistol toward the security guards in the waiting room in front of the restaurant entrance; Defendants E and F, together with Park Heung-ju, fired their pistols toward the President’s driver and security guards in the kitchen of the restaurant; and Defendant G, at around 20:05, carrying an M16 rifle, fired at the security guards lying in the restaurant waiting room and kitchen, as well as T groaning in the banquet table, thereby Defendant D, E, F, and G also jointly with Defendant A killed the President and others for the purpose of subverting the Constitution.\\n\\nHowever, even if one carefully examines the evidence adopted by the lower court against the record, the offense plan in this case, as mentioned in the lower judgment, was independently devised by Defendant A for security reasons, and the words “I will take care of it today” said to Defendant D and first-instance defendant Park Heung-ju were first spoken to those two persons at around 19:10 that day. If at that time A gave the instruction that “I will take care of the President and others directly, so as soon as gunshots are heard, you take care of the security guards,” the natural meaning would be that they should cooperate in killing the President and others. Even if Defendant D knew that killing the President would bring about state upheaval, in this case there is no record showing any other particular instruction regarding the purpose of the act or other matters. Therefore, it would be a leap of logic inconsistent with our experience and logic to conclude that the Defendants participated in and carried out a killing of natural person B, the President, rather than a killing for the purpose of subverting the constitutional organ itself, the President, by force or making the exercise of its powers impossible. Even if Defendant D knew that the Army Chief of Staff and the second assistant director of the Central Intelligence Agency were in the main office at the time, that alone cannot change the conclusion.\\n\\nDefendants E and F were those who received from Defendant D the instruction to “shoot the security guards in the kitchen when gunshots are heard” (according to the record, they are recognized as having received instruction to drive the security guards into the kitchen and return fire if the guards shot), and Defendant D said, “If today goes well, you will get a share.” However, those words were not spoken by A but were an independent remark by Defendant D. Even if the restaurant guards or drivers, no more than that, thought that getting a share would mean advancement or something major, and even if they knew that the Army Chief of Staff and the second assistant director of the Central Intelligence Agency were present, or even thought that this was a coup d’état bringing about upheaval against the State, that would merely reflect the Defendants’ awareness or thoughts in a system in which they blindly obeyed a superior’s directive. There is no basis for recognizing that “coup d’état” means the purpose of subverting the Constitution here, and such thoughts alone cannot constitute evidence of mutual conspiracy.\\n\\nDefendant G, further down the chain, was the one who received from E the instruction to perform a confirmation killing on persons in the restaurant who had not yet died. It is shown that he did not think a state upheaval had occurred at the time, and he denies having ever muttered to himself that “the die is cast,” and there is no evidentiary material to the contrary.\\n\\nAccordingly, not only Defendant G, but also Defendants E and F and Defendant D are properly viewed as unrelated to murderous acts for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. Yet the lower court recognized all of those Defendants as co-principals in murder with the purpose of subverting the Constitution. This cannot be denied to be a factual error without evidence or in violation of the rules of evidence, and this affected the judgment. Therefore, the grounds of appeal are meritorious.\\n\\n3. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Im Hang-jun\\n\\nAccording to the appellate judgment, the lower court held that the acts of the Defendants other than Defendant C H corresponded to both the crime of murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88 of the Criminal Act and the crime of attempted insurrection under Article 87 of the Criminal Act, and that the two offenses are in imaginary concurrence; and it held that Defendant C’s acts corresponded to both murder and attempted insurrection. However, the lower court’s above holdings contain the following unlawful grounds:\\n\\n(1) In this case, the Defendants cannot be regarded as a combination of a number of persons sufficient to constitute a riot under Article 87 of the Criminal Act, and therefore cannot be subjects of the crime of insurrection under Article 87.
