Criminal law merely provides that the constituent act of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is “intrusion,” and its punishment is imprisonment for not more than 3 years or a fine not exceeding 5,000,000 won, which is higher than the legislative examples in other countries such as Germany, and it is regulated as a non-complaint-based offense. Considering the essence of criminal law and its regulatory content, together with the social and normative meaning inherent in the concepts of shared dwelling and intrusion, the concept of “intrusion” in the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling should be understood to already include, in itself, the legal assessment of an act that entails a risk of serious infringement upon the legal interest of peace of the dwelling that exceeds the socially tolerable scope, or an act whose harm to society is significant; therefore, only when it can be evaluated as an act subject to regulation by criminal law can it be punished as the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling. However, where an act of entering a shared dwelling pursuant to the consent of one co-occupant can be evaluated as part of, and as an accompanying act to, the ordinary act of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-occupant who consented to the entry, it is difficult to regard such act as one involving a risk of serious infringement of the legal interest of peace of the dwelling that cannot be resolved by other norms or social control measures, or as one whose harm to society is significant. If, due to an outsider’s entry into a shared dwelling, another co-occupant’s separate legal interest, such as bodily freedom, is infringed and the infringement constitutes a separate crime, it is sufficient to punish that separate crime, and the Criminal Act already contains penal provisions for such cases. Criminally punishing even such cases as the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling would be an excessive intervention by the state’s punitive power, disregarding the diversity and special nature of social relationships arising from shared dwelling and the possibility of self-regulation, and would be improper.\\n\\nC) Between co-occupants, the value of protection of the legal interests each enjoys in the shared dwelling is equal, so even where the peace of a co-occupant’s dwelling is infringed by an outsider’s entry into the shared dwelling, recognizing the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling against the outsider would also be improper in that it would prioritize only the legal interest of the co-occupant who refused the outsider’s entry, and disregard the legal interest of another co-occupant who consented to the outsider’s entry.\\n\\nD) Even where an outsider’s entry into a shared dwelling pursuant to the consent of one co-occupant can be evaluated as part of, and as an accompanying act to, the ordinary act of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-occupant who consented to the entry, it may become an issue whether the co-occupant who consented to the outsider’s entry can also be punished as an accomplice to the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling. However, as noted above, since a co-occupant cannot be punished for the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling absent departure from the shared life relationship or the existence of any legal basis or other justifiable reason to prohibit his or her entry into the shared dwelling, in such a case only the outsider who entered the shared dwelling pursuant to the co-occupant’s consent could be punished for the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling; but so long as the outsider’s entry can be evaluated as part of, and as an accompanying act to, the ordinary act of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-occupant who consented to it, such a conclusion does not accord with the reality of shared life or with the general societal understanding, and it is improper even in light of the subsidiary nature of criminal punishment. In particular, the impropriety becomes even clearer if one considers the case where one co-occupant actively encouraged the outsider’s entry and they entered the dwelling together.\\n\\n3) A) According to the record of this case, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n(1) Non-Indicted Person 1, a co-occupant of the apartment at issue, went out around May 19, 2018, the day of the offense in this case, and asked her mother and younger sibling, the victim Non-Indicted Person 2, to take care of the child, and the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 was staying in the apartment at issue at the time of the offense.\\n\\n(2) Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, without knowing that Non-Indicted Person 1 had gone out, visited the apartment at issue together with Defendant 1, with the aim, according to their assertion, of reconciling Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 and of meeting their granddaughter. However, the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 fastened the chain latch installed on the entrance door so that the Defendants could not enter and did not open the door. Then Defendant 1, a co-occupant of the apartment at issue, damaged the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the apartment at issue, and Defendant 2 also joined in that conduct. Thereafter, the Defendants entered the apartment at issue together.\\n\\nB) We examine these facts in light of the foregoing legal principles. In entering the apartment at issue, Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 can be viewed as having joined in entering the apartment at issue in response to the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s justifiably unwarranted prohibition of entry, which was entrusted to her by another co-occupant, Non-Indicted Person 1, even though Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 entered the shared dwelling of Defendant 1, who was their son and a co-occupant of the apartment at issue. Although Defendant 1, in the process, exercised physical force by damaging the chain latch installed on the entrance door, and Defendant 2 also joined in that conduct and thus jointly committed the offense of damage to property, Defendant 1’s conduct can be seen as a means, without departing from the shared life relationship, to enter and use the place of common life as a co-occupant in response to a prohibition of entry made without justifiable reason, and Defendant 2’s conduct is, in substance, merely joining in and riding on Defendant 1’s conduct. If so, the act of Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 in entering the apartment at issue can, in its entirety, be evaluated as part of, and as accompanied by, the act of Defendant 1, a co-occupant, in entering and using the apartment at issue; therefore, it must be viewed that the crime of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) is not established as to Defendant 2 and Defendant 3.\\n\\nC) Nevertheless, the lower court found this portion of the facts charged guilty. The lower court judgment contains error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the law regarding the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling. The Defendants’ grounds for appeal pointing out this error are well-founded.\\n\\n5. Scope of reversal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated above, the portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) concerning Defendant 2 must be reversed. And the remaining guilty portion as to Defendant 2 is in the relation of concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the reversed portion, so because one punishment must be imposed and the judgment must be reversed together, ultimately all guilty portions concerning Defendant 2 in the lower court judgment must be reversed.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds for appeal by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, we reverse the guilty portion concerning Defendant 2 and the portion concerning Defendant 3 in the lower court judgment, and remand this part of the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and dismiss the appeals by the prosecutor and Defendant 1 respectively, and so we render the judgment as stated in the dispositive part. In this judgment, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous except for the separate opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek and the dissenting opinions of Justice Jo Jae-yeon, Justice Min Yoo-sook, and Justice Lee Dong-won, and there are supplementary opinions by Justice Kim Seon-su and Justice Cheon Dae-yeop to the majority opinion, and a supplementary opinion by Justice Min Yoo-sook to the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n7. Separate opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek on each portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) as to the Defendants\\n\\nThe issue in this case is whether Defendant 1, whose status as a co-occupant of the apartment at issue is disputed, and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, who received his consent, entering the apartment at issue in contravention of the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s outwardly manifested intention to prohibit entry, constitutes the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling. On this point, the majority opinion discusses whether the Defendants’ act of entering the apartment at issue falls within the ordinary manner of use by co-occupants, etc., as the standard for determining whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established. In contrast, the separate opinion intends to discuss whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established as to the Defendants through interpretation of the true intention of the victim Non-Indicted Person 2, who expressed an intention to prohibit the Defendants’ entry.\\n\\nA. Diversity of interpretations as to whether the act was contrary to the resident’s intention\\n\\n1) A) We examine the matter in light of the legal principle of Supreme Court en banc decision of September 9, 2021, 2020DO12630. The meaning of “intrusion,” the constituent act of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling, means “entering a dwelling in a manner that harms the state of de facto peace enjoyed by the resident in the dwelling,” and, as a general rule, whether the act falls within this meaning is determined based on the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the act at the time of entry.\\n\\nB) However, whether the act constitutes intrusion is fundamentally a matter of interpreting the resident’s intention. If a person enters a dwelling in a manner that harms the state of de facto peace, it is generally interpreted as contrary to the resident’s intention.\\n\\n2) Whether the actor’s entry is contrary to the resident’s intention must be determined by rationally interpreting the resident’s true intention, while specifically considering the objective circumstances at the time of entry. It may be said that, as a general rule, whether it is contrary to the resident’s intention is determined based on the intention outwardly manifested, but there may be cases where it may be determined differently depending on concrete factual circumstances such as the situation at the time of entry. Ultimately, the interpretation as to whether it is contrary to the resident’s intention is a matter within the domain of fact-finding.\\n\\n3) Where the resident explicitly expressed an intention to prohibit entry, entry into the dwelling in violation of that intention will generally be regarded as intrusion. For example, if the resident explicitly tells a door-to-door salesperson trying to enter the house, “Please do not come in,” and the salesperson nevertheless enters the house, that is clearly contrary to the resident’s intention and constitutes intrusion.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the resident’s intention regarding prohibition of entry usually has a reason. Even in determining whether an act is contrary to the resident’s intention, there are cases where the true intention can be ascertained only by knowing the reason the resident prohibited entry. In such cases, if one interprets the matter simply on the basis of the outwardly expressed intention to prohibit entry and concludes that the act is contrary to the resident’s intention, an improper conclusion may result. This can unjustifiably expand the scope of punishability for the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling. That is why the resident’s true intention is important in determining whether the act was contrary to the resident’s intention.\\n\\nEven if the resident explicitly expressed an intention to prohibit entry, there may be a premise or background to such intention. For example, one may consider a case where the resident decided whether to allow entry based on a status or qualification that permits entry. In such a case, if a person with the status or qualification that permits entry entered, it cannot be regarded as intrusion, but if a person without such status or qualification entered, it can be regarded as intrusion. For example, in the case of believers of a certain religion, there is a prayer space for clergy whose entry is permitted. In such a case, if a believer enters the clergy’s prayer space, it cannot be regarded as intrusion, but if a person other than a believer enters, it must be regarded as intrusion. If, in a company, an employee enters an office where only its officers and employees are permitted to enter for the reason of protecting trade secrets, it cannot be regarded as intrusion; however, if a retired employee or an officer or employee of a competitor enters, it must be regarded as intrusion.\\n\\nHowever, even where the resident has decided whether to allow entry on the premise of a status or qualification as above, there may be cases in which there is a dispute as to that status or qualification.\\n\\nFor example, one may consider a case where the resident believed that A was a person who could not enter and prohibited entry, but later A’s status or qualification was confirmed and it was found that A was a person who could enter. In such a case, since the premise fact prohibiting A’s entry did not exist, A cannot be viewed as having entered contrary to the resident’s intention.\\n\\nAs in the example above, in the case of believers, there is a prayer space for clergy whose entry is permitted. Suppose A tries to enter the above prayer space, and the clergy prevent A from entering the prayer space on the belief that A is not a believer, but A comes into the prayer space. Later it is confirmed that A is a believer. In this case, can the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling be established against A?\\n\\nAs another example, suppose there is an office where trade secrets are stored and entry is permitted only to the officers and employees of a company. A tries to enter the above office, and the manager of the office prevents A from entering because he believes that A is not an officer or employee of the company, but A nonetheless enters the above office. Later it is confirmed that A is an officer or employee of the company. In this case, can the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling be established against A?\\n\\nIn each of the above examples, if one bases the matter on the true intention of the clergy or office manager, finding the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling against A based solely on the outwardly manifested intention would fail to grasp the true intention to prohibit entry. Since the premise fact prohibiting A’s entry did not exist from the outset, A’s entry into the prayer space or office cannot be viewed as contrary to the clergy’s or office manager’s intention. In the above examples, according to the true intention of the clergy or office manager, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling should not be deemed established against A.\\n\\nB. Determination on whether each crime of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) is established against the Defendants\\n\\n1) Premise for discussion\\n\\nThe issue in this case is whether Defendant 1, whose status as a co-occupant of the apartment at issue is disputed, and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, who received permission to enter from him, entering the apartment at issue in contravention of the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s outwardly manifested intention to prohibit entry, constitutes the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling.\\n\\nIn this case, the basic premise of the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s intention to prohibit the Defendants from entering the apartment at issue can be seen as the fact that Defendant 1 is not a co-occupant of the apartment at issue.\\n\\nIn order to interpret the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s true intention to prohibit the Defendants from entering the apartment at issue, it is necessary first to examine whether Defendant 1 is a co-occupant of the apartment at issue.\\n\\nBelow, we will examine the factual circumstances of this case, determine whether Defendant 1 is a co-occupant of the apartment at issue, and then interpret the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s true intention regarding the Defendants’ entry into the apartment at issue to determine whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established against the Defendants.\\n\\n2) Factual circumstances of this case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record of this case, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\nA) Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 are husband and wife by law, married on September 5, 2015. There is one child between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1, and they have lived in the apartment at issue since around August 15, 2016.\\n\\nB) Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 frequently argued over the sale of a newly built apartment from around January 2018. Defendant 1 fought with Non-Indicted Person 1 on April 9, 2018 and left the apartment at issue with some of his belongings. Defendant 1 went to the apartment at issue on April 13, 2018, fought again with Non-Indicted Person 1, and left the home. Thereafter, Non-Indicted Person 1 unilaterally changed the password for the entrance door to the apartment at issue and also installed a chain latch on the entrance door.\\n\\nC) Through a mobile phone messenger, Defendant 1 asked Non-Indicted Person 1 on April 17, 2018 and April 19, 2018 to tell him the password for the front entrance of the apartment at issue. Around May 4, 2018, Defendant 1 went to the apartment at issue and asked Non-Indicted Person 1 to open the door, but Non-Indicted Person 1 refused.\\n\\nD) Non-Indicted Person 1, a co-occupant of the apartment at issue, went out around May 19, 2018, the day of the offense in this case, and asked her mother and younger sibling, the victim Non-Indicted Person 2, to take care of the child, and the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 was staying in the apartment at issue at the time of the offense.\\n\\nE) Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 visited the apartment at issue together with Defendant 1 without knowing that Non-Indicted Person 1 had gone out. However, the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 refused the Defendants’ entry into the apartment at issue. Then Defendant 1, a co-occupant of the apartment at issue, damaged the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the apartment at issue, and Defendant 2 also joined in that conduct. Thereafter, the Defendants entered the apartment at issue together.\\n\\nF) Non-Indicted Person 1 filed a complaint for divorce with the court around June 28, 2018, after the incident in this case, and a divorce mediation between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 was established on September 4, 2018.\\n\\n3) Whether Defendant 1 is a co-occupant of the apartment at issue\\n\\nA) The crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established where a person other than the resident intrudes into a dwelling. The dwelling that is the object of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is limited to one occupied by another person. Where one of the co-occupants who lives in a shared dwelling together with another person is the actor, the relevant shared dwelling does not become the object of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling. However, where it can be recognized that the co-occupant departed from the shared life relationship or lost the factual relation of control and management over the dwelling, the relevant dwelling falls within the object of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling. Whether a co-occupant departed from the shared life relationship or lost the factual relation of control and management over the shared dwelling must be determined individually, considering concrete circumstances such as the relationship among co-occupants, the circumstances leading to the dispute among co-occupants, and the circumstances by which the person left the shared dwelling.\\n\\nMeanwhile, there may be cases where entry into a shared dwelling is prohibited on legal grounds, such as where one co-occupant applies to the court for an injunction prohibiting entry into the shared dwelling against another co-occupant and receives a court order for an injunction prohibiting entry, or where one co-occupant, pursuant to the 「Special Act on the Punishment, etc. of Domestic Violence Crimes」 (hereinafter referred to as the “Domestic Violence Punishment Act”) or the 「Special Act on the Punishment, etc. of Child Abuse Crimes」 (hereinafter referred to as the “Child Abuse Punishment Act”), receives a temporary measure order for “eviction from the dwelling, etc.” or “prohibition of approach within 100 meters of the dwelling” (Article 29(1)1 and 2 of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act; Article 19(1)1 and 2 of the Child Abuse Punishment Act). Such cases can be viewed as cases where the co-occupant departed from the shared life relationship or lost the factual relation of control and management over the shared dwelling.\\n\\nB) We examine the above factual circumstances in light of the foregoing legal principles.\\n\\nAt the time of this case, it is difficult to deem that there was an explicit agreement between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 to terminate the marital relationship and for Defendant 1 to leave the apartment at issue and live elsewhere, or that the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 had broken down. In such a situation, the mere fact that Defendant 1 took some of his belongings out of the apartment, or that Non-Indicted Person 1 unilaterally changed the password for the entrance door and prevented Defendant 1 from entering, does not justify recognizing that Defendant 1 departed from the shared life relationship in the apartment at issue or lost control and management over it. Accordingly, Defendant 1 must be deemed to have maintained the status of a co-occupant of the apartment at issue at the time of this case.\\n\\n4) Interpretation of the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s true intention\\n\\nA) Based on the above factual circumstances, let us examine the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s true intention in prohibiting the Defendants from entering the apartment at issue.\\n\\nB) In light of the relationship among the Defendants and Non-Indicted Person 1 and the victim Non-Indicted Person 2, as recognized from the above factual circumstances, and the circumstances surrounding the dispute in this case, it is reasonable to view the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 as having prohibited the Defendants’ entry because she believed that the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 had broken down and that Defendant 1 had lost the status of co-occupant of the apartment at issue and therefore could not enter the apartment at issue without the consent of Non-Indicted Person 1. Apart from the above circumstances, no other separate circumstance can be found in the record that would have motivated or justified the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 in prohibiting Defendant 1 or Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, who received his consent, from entering the apartment at issue.\\n\\nC) The premise fact of the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s intention to prohibit entry into the apartment at issue against the Defendants can be viewed as that the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 had broken down and that Defendant 1 was no longer a co-occupant of the apartment at issue and therefore could not enter the apartment at issue without the consent of Non-Indicted Person 1. However, as noted above, it is difficult to recognize that the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 had broken down, or that Defendant 1 departed from the shared life relationship in the apartment at issue or lost control and management over it.\\n\\nIf so, even if the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 outwardly expressed an intention to prohibit the Defendants from entering the apartment at issue, it is reasonable to see the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s true intention as that, had the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted Person 1 not broken down, and had Defendant 1 not departed from the shared life relationship in the apartment at issue or lost control and management over it, she would not have prohibited the Defendants from entering the apartment at issue. Therefore, since the Defendants’ entry into the apartment at issue cannot be deemed to have been made contrary to the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s intention, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling cannot be recognized as established against the Defendants. Furthermore, even if the Defendants damaged the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the apartment at issue in the process of entering the apartment at issue, this can be regarded as the minimum exercise of physical force necessary to enter the apartment at issue, and therefore such circumstance does not affect whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established against the Defendants.\\n\\n5) Determination on the grounds for appeal by the prosecutor and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\nFor the above reasons, each portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) against the Defendants must all be judged not guilty.\\n\\nThe conclusion of the lower court judgment that found the portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) concerning Defendant 1 not guilty is proper. Therefore, there is no error, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in that it violated the rules of logic and experience and exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehended the law regarding the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling.\\n\\nHowever, the lower court judgment that found the portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) concerning Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 guilty contains error in fact-finding, by violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence in determining whether it was contrary to the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s intention, or misapprehending the law regarding intrusion. The Defendants’ grounds for appeal pointing out this error are well-founded.\\n\\nC. Subconclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the portions of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) concerning Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 in the lower court judgment must be reversed. And because the above reversed portion and the remaining guilty portion as to Defendant 2 are in the relation of concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, one punishment must be imposed and the judgment must be reversed together; therefore, all guilty portions concerning Defendant 2 in the lower court judgment must be reversed. Without examining the remaining grounds for appeal by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, the guilty portion concerning Defendant 2 and the portion concerning Defendant 3 in the lower court judgment must be reversed, and this part of the case must be remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and the appeals by the prosecutor and Defendant 1 must each be dismissed.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state that I cannot concur with the majority opinion.\\n\\n8. Dissenting opinion of Justices Jo Jae-yeon, Min Yoo-sook, and Lee Dong-won on each portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) as to the Defendants\\n\\nA. Summary of the dissent\\n\\nThrough this en banc decision, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that the protected legal interest of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is not the “right to residence,” but the “de facto peace of the dwelling.” The same applies to shared dwellings.\\n\\nWhere a co-occupant present in the dwelling has prohibited entry, but a person enters the shared dwelling by violent means or through an abnormal route, in light of the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the act at the time of entry, the conduct clearly harms the state of peace of the co-occupant present in the dwelling and thus constitutes an act of intrusion, so the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established. The same is true even if the intruder is a co-occupant who has left the home on his or her own, or an outsider who received consent from that co-occupant.\\n\\nWe cannot agree with the majority opinion’s view that even if the actor enters a dwelling he or she occupies or manages jointly in a manner that harms the de facto peace of another co-occupant, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is not constituted.\\n\\nB. Premise for discussion\\n\\n1) First, I would make clear the relationship between this case and the Supreme Court en banc decision of September 9, 2021, 2020DO12630. This case is premised on the legal opinion of the Supreme Court 2020DO12630 en banc decision, but differs in factual circumstances and legal issues.\\n\\nIn the Supreme Court 2020DO12630 en banc decision, the issue is whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established for “an act of peacefully entering a dwelling pursuant to the consent of the resident present in the dwelling.” The issue is the evaluation of the “presumed contrary intention of a co-occupant absent from the dwelling.” This case concerns “an act in which a resident who has left the dwelling on his or her own and can no longer enter by ordinary means enters the dwelling by using violence notwithstanding the prohibition of entry by a co-occupant present in the dwelling.” The issue is the evaluation of an “act that infringes the de facto peace of a co-occupant present in the dwelling.”\\n\\n2) I turn to the increased need to protect the peace of the dwelling and the need for concrete and individualized regulation of shared dwelling relationships.\\n\\nA) With changes in modern social life and residential life, the need to protect the peace of the dwelling has further increased. In modern society, as the development of mass media and information and communications means increased the possibility of infringement upon the secrecy of private life, the importance of protecting privacy came to be emphasized further, and the need to protect the peace of the dwelling as a condition for protecting the secrecy of private life became greater. That is, because when residential space is invaded there is a high possibility that privacy will be infringed, the possibility of infringement upon the peace of the dwelling at this stage also increased significantly. Moreover, with the deepening of urbanization, individual residential space has been limited to narrow spaces, and the concern over infringement upon the peace of the dwelling by outsiders’ entry has become more serious than in the past, greatly increasing the need for protection.\\n\\nB) Most citizens form family relationships by reason of marriage or the like, or otherwise share one residential space jointly for economic reasons, etc. Due to urbanization and density, many citizens live in multi-family housing. Meanwhile, the concept of dwelling also includes elevators, common stairways, and corridors inside multi-family housing such as single-family houses for multiple households, multi-unit housing, row houses, and apartments (see Supreme Court decision of August 20, 2009, 2009DO3452, etc.). In modern society, where most citizens have the status of co-occupants with respect to residential space, the relationship of status among co-occupants, the modes in which the legal interests enjoyed by co-occupants within the shared dwelling conflict with one another, and the need for regulation thereof are highly diverse. Regulation of shared dwelling relationships must be carried out individually, examining concrete circumstances such as the circumstances of formation of the shared dwelling, its form, and the relationships among co-occupants.\\n\\n3) The issue of whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established in a shared dwelling arises when legal interests among co-occupants conflict. As the saying goes, “Every unhappy family is unhappy for its own reason,” the modes of infringement of legal interests among family members and the need to protect the peace of the dwelling also vary within a single residential space called a family home. However, to regulate this uniformly and abstractly on the ground of shared dwelling or co-occupant status and discuss in a single line whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established is not correct legal regulation of diverse dispute situations. Moreover, even where there exists legislation regulating shared dwellings, whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established against a co-occupant or outsider is a matter to be determined by individually and concretely examining the internal relationship among co-occupants and the relationship with outsiders under that legislation, and it is not right to set in advance a uniform and abstract standard for that determination.\\n\\nUltimately, whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established in a shared dwelling must be determined concretely and individually, comprehensively considering “freedom of residence,” “protection of marriage and family life,” “the legislative purpose and intent of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling,” “the specific content and legal nature of the protected legal interest of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling,” and “the meaning of intrusion and its criteria for determination,” all of which are guaranteed by the Constitution.\\n\\nC. Whether a co-occupant can be punished for the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling\\n\\n1) The crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is a crime concerning individual legal interests, and where there are multiple persons residing in the dwelling, infringement of the protected legal interest must be determined based on the peace of the dwelling enjoyed by each resident.\\n\\nA) A shared dwelling is both one’s own dwelling and another person’s dwelling as well. Therefore, if one co-occupant engages in conduct that harms another co-occupant’s peace of the dwelling, infringement of the protected legal interest of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling arises.\\n\\nB) The Constitution, in the preamble to Article 16, guarantees freedom of residence as a fundamental right by providing that “all citizens shall not be infringed in their freedom of residence.” The Constitution also, in Article 36(1), provides that “marriage and family life shall be formed and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and equality between the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this,” thereby placing marriage and family under special protection of the State. Since marriage and family life are realized through the place called residence, freedom of residence functions to secure the fundamental rights concerning marriage and family life by guaranteeing the spatial domain of marriage and family life.\\n\\nBecause residential space is the center of private life and is inseparably connected with personality, unless its inviolability is guaranteed, the private sphere, which is the minimum condition for human happiness, cannot be protected (see Constitutional Court decision of September 24, 2020, 2018HEONBA171, en banc panel decision). Since residence is the place where private life is centered, unless its inviolability is guaranteed, the safety of an individual’s life, body, and property is also difficult to protect. Therefore, freedom of residence guaranteed by the Constitution takes the individual residing in the dwelling as the subject of the fundamental right, and the fundamental right concerning marriage and family life is also guaranteed on the basis of the individual who enters into marriage and forms a family. The crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is a provision that specifically protects freedom of residence guaranteed by the Constitution as a fundamental right, and because it also indirectly protects marriage and family life guaranteed by the Constitution, the subject of the legal interest protected by the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is likewise the individual resident. This legal nature of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling must remain unchanged even in internal relationships among co-occupants.\\n\\nC) The cases cited for reference by the majority opinion cannot be cited because they concern different matters from the issue in this case. That is, Supreme Court decision of April 27, 1982, 81DO2956, and Supreme Court decision of December 27, 2012, 2010DO16537, were both cases indicted for the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling, etc. on the premise that the act was an entry by a person without the authority to reside or possess, but after trial, it was found that the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling, etc. was not established because the circumstances of co-residence or lawful title to possession were recognized; these were not cases in which the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the act was by a method that harms the peace of the dwelling of another co-possessor or co-occupant.\\n\\n2) The majority opinion says that even if one co-occupant entered in a manner that harmed the peace of the co-occupant who prohibited his or her entry, that is the ordinary form of use of a shared dwelling.\\n\\nHowever, the majority opinion is contrary to the content and legal nature of the protected legal interest of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling, the meaning and criteria of determination of intrusion, and it errs in treating as compatible the co-occupant’s “ordinary form of use of the shared dwelling” and the “manner of act that harms the state of de facto peace,” which are incompatible.\\n\\nA) The majority opinion also acknowledges the principle that the constituent act of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling, “intrusion,” means entering a dwelling in a manner that harms the state of de facto peace enjoyed by the resident in the dwelling, and that whether it falls within that meaning is determined based on the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the act at the time of entry.\\n\\nIf so, even a co-occupant who enters a shared dwelling by violent means or through an abnormal route, such as by damaging a locking device, enters in a manner that harms the state of peace of the other co-occupant when viewed objectively and outwardly, and thus constitutes an act of intrusion.\\n\\nB) An act of entry by a manner that harms the state of de facto peace cannot coexist with the ordinary form of use of a shared dwelling.\\n\\nTo be included in the ordinary form of use of a shared dwelling mutually tolerated among co-occupants, each person must possess a key to the locking device or share the password so that each co-occupant can unlock the locking device and open the door by using that key or password and enter the dwelling.\\n\\nThe attitude of a co-occupant who leaves the home on his or her own and then repeatedly conflicts and uses violence with another co-occupant while disputing the use of the dwelling or the ownership attribution cannot be regarded as the ordinary form of use of a shared dwelling. It is difficult to impose on the co-occupant remaining in the home a burden to tolerate such conduct. If minor children are being raised in that home, the need to prohibit violent entry is even greater.\\n\\nIn that situation, if the resident feels threatened in peace and changes the locking device to prohibit the other party’s entry, thereby rendering ordinary entry impossible for the co-occupant who left the home, and that co-occupant then uses means harmful to peace, such as damage or use of violence, to enter the shared dwelling, that is an act of intrusion that exceeds the limits of use of the shared dwelling.\\n\\nC) As the majority opinion itself acknowledges, the content and scope of the use mutually tolerated among co-occupants must be examined individually according to the circumstances by which the shared dwelling was formed, the form and nature of the shared dwelling, and the relationships among the co-occupants. Mere status as a co-occupant does not require that the resident’s acts of entry into and use of the shared dwelling always be tolerated.\\n\\n3) According to the majority opinion, the period until a person departs from co-occupant status is left in a regulatory vacuum, which is improper.\\n\\nA) The majority opinion denies the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling so long as one remains in the status of a co-occupant. Although the majority opinion says that the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling can also be recognized against a co-occupant if there are “special circumstances,” it says that such special circumstances are “where the person has departed from shared life or lost de facto control and management.” However, a person who has departed from shared life or lost de facto control and management is no longer included in “co-occupant.” This is merely a tautology about the meaning of co-occupant. Therefore, the majority opinion appears to be a view that denies the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling against a co-occupant almost without exception. If the true intent of the majority opinion is different, it should explicitly state the standards and scope of the determination of “special circumstances.”\\n\\nB) The majority opinion says that the content and scope of acts of using a shared dwelling mutually tolerated among co-occupants must be determined individually according to internal co-occupant relationships, but at the same time, on the premise of a peaceful and ordinary shared dwelling, it excludes from the protected scope of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling, on the ground that the actor is a co-occupant, acts of entry that harm the state of peace of another co-occupant until the co-occupant departs from the shared life relationship or status as a co-occupant. However, depending on the circumstances by which the shared dwelling was formed, and the form and nature of the shared dwelling, etc., the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling can be established even before a co-occupant departs from status as a co-occupant.\\n\\nC) Rather, as can be seen from many judicial precedents, cases in which the issue is whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established among co-occupants arise during the process in which the shared dwelling relationship collapses (the stage before departure from the shared life relationship, where status as a co-occupant is still recognized), that is, when a dispute arises among co-occupants and one side repeatedly leaves and re-enters the dwelling, causing conflict and confrontation, so that the resident has no choice but to change the key or password of the locking device in order to protect the peace of the dwelling.\\n\\nIn particular, in cases such as this one, where the marital relationship between spouses collapses and the process leading to divorce takes various forms in each specific case, in many instances the family community, including the spouses, is engulfed in conflict and confrontation, and serious violence also occurs. There is a period that has not yet led to dissolution of the shared dwelling, but during which it is difficult to endure shared life.\\n\\nD) The dissenting opinion’s purport is that the interpretation of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling should be made in a direction that actively responds to violence arising in the process of the dissolution of the shared life relationship and protects the peace and safety of its members.\\n\\n4) It is difficult to agree with the majority opinion’s linking of “justifiable reason” as a basis for denying the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling.\\n\\nA) The majority opinion says that where a co-occupant, without legal basis or other justifiable reason, prohibits another co-occupant’s entry, even if entry is made by resorting to violence, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is not established. It cites the reasons that the act is “in response to the prohibition of entry” and “a means to use it in accordance with the purpose of the shared dwelling.”\\n\\nThis is akin to requiring that the victim have legal basis or a corresponding justifiable reason, and reaches the conclusion that the existence of the crime is to be determined by sorting out the rights relation before the act of intrusion.\\n\\nHowever, established Supreme Court precedents take the position that even if a person is the right holder, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling or unlawful entry into a structure is established where the person intrudes into a dwelling or structure as a means of self-help by exercising the right.\\n\\nIf, in the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling, which protects “the peace of the dwelling” and punishes acts infringing it, the criterion is whether “the victim’s act of prohibiting entry had legal basis,” that would not accord with the established position of the Supreme Court.\\n\\nB) Furthermore, even if “justifiable reason” may be considered, whether the prohibition of entry is justified must be determined only after examining the overall process of the dispute and the circumstances leading to the prohibition of entry, and that is a matter of fact-finding that can be determined through trial in the fact-finding court.\\n\\nThe justification of individual acts arising in the course of a dispute among co-occupants, especially in the process of dissolving a marital community, cannot be determined solely by fragmentary circumstances at a specific point in time. There is concern whether, by looking only at the resulting measure of “prohibition of entry,” one is concluding that the victim lacks justification and the defendant’s entry is allowed.\\n\\nC) The case imagined by the majority opinion, where “one co-occupant prohibits the other’s entry without justifiable reason,” may be a hypothetical example discussed in criminal law theory texts, but it is far removed from real disputes (an example is sometimes mentioned of a wife locking the door because she is displeased that her husband is trying to come home late at night with drinking companions), and this should be pointed out again.\\n\\n5) The majority opinion excessively minimizes the independent value of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling and does not accord with the recent legislative amendment trend.\\n\\nA) The majority opinion says that where, in the process of entry by co-occupants, separate legal interests such as another co-occupant’s bodily freedom are infringed, punishment may be imposed for the corresponding offense, and that is sufficient; however, this fails properly to grasp the significance of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling or treats it lightly.\\n\\nB) The reason freedom and peace of the dwelling are protected by penal sanctions is that anyone can expect the greatest possible safety while inside his or her own dwelling, and the State actively protects that expectation. This is a basic right, like the gatekeeper standing at the very front among other fundamental freedoms such as bodily freedom, and an expectation and demand toward the State. The view that one can just punish the conduct as assault, damage, etc. fails to properly understand the weight of the value each individual expects from freedom and peace of the dwelling.\\n\\nThe crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling aims to protect the peace and safety of the dwelling, and because it functions to prevent infringement upon life, body, and property that may occur within the dwelling through control of entry into the dwelling, there is a need to independently protect the legal interest protected by the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling. Therefore, where the entry by one co-occupant or an outsider infringes the legal interest of another co-occupant’s de facto peace of the dwelling, punishment should be imposed for the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling, and further, where in the course of or after entry the life, body, property, etc. of another co-occupant are separately infringed, it is proper to punish for the offense constituted by infringement of that legal interest.\\n\\nC) Today, threats to the peace of the dwelling can arise not only from outsiders but also from co-occupants such as family members.\\n\\nIn particular, in most cases where the spouse remaining in the dwelling is raising minor children, violent acts of entry inflict serious harm on the welfare of the minor children, regardless of the circumstances of the dispute or the attribution of responsibility.\\n\\nIn the past, under the notion that “criminal law does not intervene in domestic disputes,” there was a period when domestic disputes were thought to be best resolved autonomously within the family, with the state’s punitive power intervening only subsidiarily. However, this attitude led to a refusal of protection against domestic violence and became a cause of crimes within the family, and in reflection thereof, the 「Act on the Prevention of Domestic Violence and Protection of Victims, etc.」 and the Domestic Violence Punishment Act were enacted, enabling the State to actively intervene in domestic violence.\\n\\nFurthermore, in response to criticism that prevention of violence and protection of victims within the home are still insufficient, the Domestic Violence Punishment Act was amended by Act No. 17499 on October 20, 2020, and took effect on January 21, 2021, to improve and supplement deficiencies. The amended Act included the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling in Chapter 36, Part II of the Criminal Act among domestic violence crimes [Article 2(3)(sa)]. The family members subject to the Domestic Violence Punishment Act are spouses, lineal ascendants and descendants, and cohabiting relatives [Article 2(2)(ga) through (da)], whose scope nearly coincides with co-occupants. Accordingly, not only the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling and the crime of refusal to leave prescribed in Chapter 36, Part II of the Criminal Act, but also the attempt thereof, are included in domestic violence crimes under the Domestic Violence Punishment Act.\\n\\nUnlike the majority opinion, the legislation, through amendment of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act, is taking an active regulatory stance to severely punish acts by co-occupants that harm the physical and mental peace of other family members.\\n\\nD. Whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established where an outsider who received the consent of one of the co-occupants enters a shared dwelling in a manner that harms the state of peace of another co-occupant\\n\\n1) The majority opinion denies the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling on the ground that the outsider’s entry into the shared dwelling, even in a manner that harms the state of peace of the co-occupant present in the dwelling, was based on the consent of another co-occupant, but this is also improper.\\n\\nIf an outsider suppresses a co-occupant present in the dwelling’s prohibition of entry by violent means and enters the shared dwelling, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established, and the establishment of the crime cannot be denied merely because the outsider received the consent of one of the co-occupants.\\n\\nThe substance of “an outsider’s entry pursuant to the consent of a co-occupant,” expressed abstractly by the majority opinion, is that the outsider, together with the co-occupant, overcomes by violent means the prohibition of entry by the co-occupant present in the dwelling and intrudes into the shared dwelling.\\n\\n2) A legal-interest conflict arising within a shared dwelling among co-occupants, even if it is an internal relationship between them, is different: an outsider’s intrusion into the shared dwelling is itself conduct meeting the elements of the offense and must be independently punished.\\n\\nAn outsider’s act of entering a shared dwelling has no relation whatsoever to the ordinary acts of use of the shared dwelling among co-occupants. The outsider recognized that the resident prohibited entry, yet overpowered that prohibition and forced entry. There is no basis for evaluating this as a conflict of legal interests within the internal relationship among co-occupants; rather, denying the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling on the ground of the consent of another co-occupant results in disregarding the independent status as legal-interest holder of the co-occupant who prohibited the outsider’s entry.\\n\\n3) Furthermore, the reasons the majority opinion cites to justify the outsider’s intrusion are also not correct.\\n\\nA) It is a proper exercise of the state’s punitive power to punish a person who commits conduct satisfying the elements of Article 319(1) of the Criminal Act within the statutory range. If an outsider’s act of entering a shared dwelling satisfies the elements of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling, it must be punished within the statutory range. The majority opinion says that even though the conduct satisfies the elements of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling established by the legislature, it would further distinguish the seriousness of the infringed legal interest or require social harm as an additional element, but it does not provide grounds for that. Furthermore, the act of an outsider entering a shared dwelling in a manner that harms the state of de facto peace in disregard of another co-occupant’s opposition is, in itself, an infringement of a legal interest beyond the socially tolerable scope, and thus the harm to society is also significant.\\n\\nB) The fact that the statutory maximum penalty for the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling under the Criminal Act is 3 years’ imprisonment, and that it is regulated as a non-complaint-based offense, is within the scope of the legislature’s power to form legislation, and it is difficult to find a logical connection to the issue in this case.\\n\\nFurthermore, with respect to the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling, the Swiss Penal Code (Article 186), the Japanese Penal Code (Article 130), and the Chinese Criminal Law (Article 245) also set the statutory maximum penalty at 3 years’ deprivation of liberty or imprisonment, which is the same as the statutory maximum penalty prescribed by our Criminal Act, and it is also inappropriate to limit the scope of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling by formally and arithmetically comparing the statutory penalties prescribed by some other countries’ criminal laws with those prescribed by our Criminal Act (the circumstances that an outsider’s act of entering a shared dwelling was pursuant to the consent of a co-occupant can be sufficiently taken into account in sentencing, if necessary, by individually considering the concrete circumstances).\\n\\nThe 「Act on the Punishment of Stalking Crimes」, which is scheduled to take effect on October 21, 2021, sets the statutory maximum penalty at 3 years’ imprisonment even where a person commits “waiting or watching” in a dwelling, etc., a place of daily life, or nearby, that is, even where a person commits conduct that does not rise to “intrusion” into a dwelling, etc. [Article 18(1), Article 2(1)(b)].\\n\\nC) Whether to define a certain offense as a complaint-based offense is a matter of legislative policy taking into account the victim’s intention or feelings, and in light of this case and most cases of punishment for unlawful entry into a dwelling where investigation is initiated by the victim’s complaint or report, our Criminal Act cannot justify an outsider’s act of entering a shared dwelling on the ground that the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is not a complaint-based offense.\\n\\nD) Since the value of the legal interest each co-occupant enjoys in the shared dwelling is equal, it should be equally protected even where the peace of a co-occupant’s dwelling is infringed by an outsider’s act of entering the shared dwelling. The conflict between the majority opinion and the dissent stems from differing criteria for balancing interests in situations where legal interests among co-occupants conflict. The dissent takes the position that the legal interest of freedom and peace of the dwelling, which should be protected from force and the dominance of the majority, should be given greater priority. The majority opinion says that in this case, punishing the outsider would improperly disregard the legal interest of the co-occupant who sided with him or her; however, the judgment whether to balance legal interests and whether punishment is proper or improper must be distinguished.\\n\\nE. Determination in this case\\n\\n1) Facts found relating to “justifiable reason”\\n\\nThe majority opinion stated that there was “no legal basis or other justifiable reason for the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 to prohibit Defendant 1’s entry.”\\n\\nA) The majority opinion seems to have reached that conclusion on the grounds that Non-Indicted Person 1 changed the password for the apartment entrance door and installed a chain latch on April 13, 2018, and did not tell Defendant 1 the password for the entrance door, and that the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 did not open the door at the time of the offense in this case.\\n\\nHowever, in a series of events that unfolded starting about a month before the offense in this case, one cannot determine the matter based only on those fragmentary circumstances; only by also considering the circumstances under which Non-Indicted Person 1 changed the password and the context in which the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 engaged in such conduct at the time of the offense can one determine whether there was justifiable reason.\\n\\nB) Since this point was not an issue even up to the lower court, we are compelled to examine the facts recognized in the record based on evidence not rejected by the lower court, including Non-Indicted Person 1’s statement at the first-instance trial, and point out the impropriety of the majority opinion.\\n\\n(1) Defendant 1 had a conflict with Non-Indicted Person 1 over the sale of a newly built apartment, and around April 9, 2018, said, “Live by yourself. Tell the child that father is not around,” and took clothes (including winter and summer clothes) and shoes, etc., and left the apartment at issue. Then, the next day, he entered the apartment at issue, took bankbooks in his own name, and left again. (The fact that Defendant 1 left home on his own on that date was also recognized by the lower court.)\\n\\n(2) On April 13, 2018, Defendant 1 came to the apartment at issue and, arguing with Non-Indicted Person 1 that he wanted to live separately and requesting that some of the lease deposit for the apartment at issue be returned, smashed the cup he was holding. As a result, Non-Indicted Person 1 reported to the police at 112, and the police even came to the apartment at issue. The victim Non-Indicted Person 2 was also present at the scene at that time. Thereafter, Non-Indicted Person 1 changed the password for the entrance door and installed a latch on the entrance door.\\n\\n(3) Since Defendant 1 left the apartment at issue on April 9, 2018 and was staying at Defendant 2 and Defendant 3’s residence, Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 were also aware that Defendant 1 was living separately.\\n\\nC) The circumstances regarding the situation on the day of the offense in this case are as already recognized by the lower court.\\n\\n(1) The Defendants went to the apartment at issue on the day of the offense without any prior contact, rang the doorbell, and then cursed when the entrance door was not opened. The victim Non-Indicted Person 2, who knew the prior course of events, did not open the door and told the Defendants through the interphone to come when Non-Indicted Person 1 returned home. The Defendants then made a disturbance, banging on the door and demanding it be opened, and when the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 opened the door a little and fastened the latch, Defendant 2, while demanding that the door be opened, stuck his foot in through the open door gap so that the door could not be closed and kept shaking the doorknob, and Defendant 1 inserted his hand through the open gap in the entrance door and struck the chain latch several times. The latch attached to the entrance door of the apartment at issue could be released only by closing the door, but the Defendants prevented the door from being closed as above, making it impossible to release the latch. In the process, Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 jointly engaged in such conduct and caused the latch to come off the door.\\n\\n(2) As soon as the latch came off and the door opened, the Defendants rushed into the apartment at issue (Defendant 1, in the process, pushed the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 standing in front of the entrance door and was convicted of assault, and that judgment became final). At that time, the mother of Non-Indicted Person 1, who was staying in the apartment at issue, was startled and fell down in shock because the Defendants suddenly came into the apartment, and immediately thereafter she went into the master bedroom with the child and locked the door. Thereafter, both sides confronted each other across the master bedroom door.\\n\\nD) In light of this series of events, it cannot be categorically said that the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s “prohibition of entry” at the time of the offense lacked justifiable reason, nor can it be used as a basis to justify the Defendants’ entry.\\n\\nE) The separate opinion says that the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s true intention would not have prohibited the Defendants from entering the apartment at issue if Defendant 1 had not departed from the shared life relationship in the apartment at issue or lost control and management over it.\\n\\nThis separate opinion likewise interprets intention in a manner detached from the circumstances and content of the dispute in this case recognized by the record, the circumstances under which Non-Indicted Person 1 changed the password of the apartment entrance door and installed the latch, and the specific situation in which the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 prohibited the Defendants’ entry.\\n\\n2) Whether the crime of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) is established against Defendant 1\\n\\nA) The lower court found Defendant 1 not guilty of the portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) on the ground that Defendant 1 was a co-occupant of the apartment at issue.\\n\\nB) As noted above, Defendant 1 fought with Non-Indicted Person 1, left the shared dwelling on his own and began living separately, and while Non-Indicted Person 1 allowed him to enter, he entered, took bankbooks, or fought with Non-Indicted Person 1 and left the shared dwelling again. After Non-Indicted Person 1 changed the entrance door password, Defendant 1 requested entry several times before reaching the offense in this case.\\n\\nDefendant 1, notwithstanding the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s refusal to allow entry, used violent means, such as damaging the latch, overpowered the victim Non-Indicted Person 2, and entered the apartment at issue.\\n\\nC) Considering in the aggregate the circumstances by which Defendant 1 left home on his own and the separation began, and the circumstances by which the victim’s side initially did not block Defendant 1’s entry but later, as the dispute and conflict continued, changed the locking device on the entrance door and prohibited Defendant 1’s entry, Defendant 1’s act of entering the apartment at issue constitutes, even in light of the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the act, a clear harm to the de facto peace of the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 and exceeds the scope of use as a co-occupant, and thus is not permitted. There was justifiable reason for the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 to block Defendant 1’s entry, and the crime of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) can be recognized as established against Defendant 1.\\n\\nThe crime of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) cannot be denied merely on the ground that Defendant 1 did not depart from the status of co-occupant.\\n\\nD) Nevertheless, the lower court found this portion of the facts charged not guilty. The lower court judgment contains error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the law regarding the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling. The prosecutor’s grounds for appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n3) Whether the crime of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) is established against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\nA) The conduct of Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 in using violent means against the victim Non-Indicted Person 2, overpowering that victim who refused their entry, and entering the apartment at issue constitutes, even in light of the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the act, a clear harm to the de facto peace of the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 and therefore the crime of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) is established against the said Defendants. Even if their entry was pursuant to the consent of Defendant 1, a co-occupant, this does not affect the establishment of the offense.\\n\\nB) The lower court’s judgment, which upheld the first-instance judgment finding Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 guilty of the portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling), contains no error, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in that it violated the rules of logic and experience and exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehended the law regarding the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling.\\n\\nF. Subconclusion\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, each portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) as to the Defendants must all be found guilty. Accordingly, the portion of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint unlawful entry into a dwelling) concerning Defendant 1 in the lower court judgment must be reversed. Meanwhile, because the reversed portion and the remaining crimes found guilty by the lower court as to Defendant 1 are in the relation of concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act and one punishment must be imposed, ultimately all portions concerning Defendant 1 in the lower court judgment must be reversed and this part of the case remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and the appeals by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 must each be dismissed.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, I state that I cannot concur with the majority opinion.\\n\\n9. Supplementary opinion of Justices Kim Seon-su and Cheon Dae-yeop on the majority opinion\\n\\nIn the majority opinion, the present issues were examined from the perspective of the ordinary form in which co-occupants use a shared dwelling under mutual tolerance. As a result, it was determined that where one co-occupant, without legal basis or justifiable reason, unilaterally physically obstructs or prohibits another co-occupant’s act of entering the place of common life, such as by locking the door, even if the other co-occupant exercises physical force to解除, in effect, the barrier to entry in response and thereby enter the place of common life, that can be evaluated merely as a means for the co-occupant to enter and use the shared dwelling, and if the outsider’s entry, together with that, can be evaluated as part of, and as an accompanying act to, the ordinary act of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-occupant who consented to it, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is likewise not established.\\n\\nBelow, we will further clarify the purport of the majority opinion on each issue in this case, supplement its grounds, and express our views on the points raised by the dissenting opinion.\\n\\nA. Meaning and limits of the shared life relationship within a shared dwelling\\n\\nResidence means both the physical and objective environment constituting human life and a subjective and socio-psychological environment. Various ideas and perceptions regarding the meaning and role of residence, and cultural differences in residence experienced by each individual, appear as differences in views of residence.\\n\\nA shared dwelling refers to a form of cooperative residence formed by mutual co-occupants, and does not in itself mean a complete community. A shared dwelling may be equipped with each person’s private residential space, or it may consist solely of communal residential space for all co-occupants, and it is not fixed, but rather is also a concept of an open space that can change based on mutual agreement, custom, and circumstances.\\n\\nShared residence is a form of residential culture in which the independence and communality of people sharing life and values are harmonized; the degree of bonding among co-occupants constituting the shared dwelling, the stage of life, is diverse, and the boundary between single-person residence and shared residence is not always clear. A typical example is that the meaning of shared dwelling or shared residence in a traditional family community and the meaning in a modern shared dwelling form such as a share house in an urban setting are different. Shared residence is a residential culture that maintains the fundamental value of residence in which individual dignity is realized while tolerating restrictions on rights as private space and accepting a life of coexistence as co-occupants sharing the same residential space. The extent to which each person’s private sphere exists within the shared dwelling is determined by mutual agreement and the form and custom of residence, as well as the general social perception thereof. Such shared residence begins only when a single residential space accepts a life of sharing and coexistence. Nevertheless, differences in views of residence among co-occupants, and different perceptions of the boundary between the private sphere and the common sphere, constantly create tension.\\n\\nEven in the case of the family, the most basic residential community, conflict among family members may be caused by, for example, a parent arbitrarily entering a room used exclusively by a child and whether that constitutes an invasion of the private sphere within the shared dwelling. In such a case, if the child unilaterally declared the room to be its complete private sphere and prohibited the parents from entering, it is not easy to conclude that the legal evaluation of the parents’ entry into that room should be different. In particular, in the issue of applying the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling, it would be even more difficult to affirm this in light of the subsidiary nature of criminal punishment. On the other hand, even if a space is premised on mutual tolerance and agreement for complete private use for a specific purpose, such as a bathroom, where a person invades it by entering through an abnormal method, it would be difficult to easily deny the unlawfulness of the intrusion merely because it is an entry by a co-occupant into a space within the shared dwelling. In the case of a residential form in which personal space is mixed within the entire shared dwelling that has been made communal, conflicts over the boundary between private space and common space can become even more intense.\\n\\nAs such, because a shared dwelling contains multifaceted relationships between the individual and the residential community, one cannot completely exclude the individual private sphere and space, but the area recognized as common space functions as a space in which mutual shared time and life are experienced and communicated in an open rather than closed space. Within it, each co-occupant must refrain from planning a life that uses it only as his or her own independent space; if one is unwilling to endure this, one must dismantle the shared dwelling relationship or depart from the shared dwelling, and once such dissolution or departure has occurred, one can no longer assert rights and duties attendant to the shared dwelling or shared residence.\\n\\nThe communal communication and participation of co-occupants within a shared dwelling is a process of using the space as a residential community together and sharing values. In order to make the space one that balances personal privacy and communal life, it is necessary to identify and agree on what space each individual occupies and what space is shared with others. Above all, what is important is that co-occupants understand and tolerate the meaning of the residential community and the limits of the private sphere and life within it, and have the attitude and mutual respect to live together within it.\\n\\nThe majority opinion’s view and conclusion on each issue in this case are based on the understanding of the meaning and limits of the shared life relationship within a shared dwelling as above.\\n\\nB. Whether a co-occupant can be punished for the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling\\n\\n1) As interpreted from the wording of Article 319(1) of the Criminal Act, the object of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is a dwelling occupied by a person other than the actor, that is, another person; and where one of the co-occupants is the actor, the dwelling shared with another person does not fall within the object of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling unless there are special circumstances such as departure from the shared life relationship or loss of de facto control and management over the dwelling.\\n\\n2) A shared dwelling is, for one co-occupant, his or her own dwelling, and at the same time, in relation to the other residents, also has the status of another person’s dwelling. Because of this dual nature of the shared dwelling, each co-occupant enjoys in the shared dwelling the legal interest of the de facto peace of the dwelling, while in relations among co-occupants, the legal interests each enjoys are necessarily subject to certain limitations, and it must be viewed that the co-occupants tolerated these circumstances while forming the shared dwelling relationship. Each co-occupant freely entering the place of common life during the period of co-residence is the ordinary form of use of the shared dwelling as a co-occupant and is a basic part of the shared dwelling relationship that each co-occupant must tolerate. Therefore, absent special circumstances, among co-occupants, no one may prohibit another co-occupant from entering, and one’s free entry notwithstanding that does not establish the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling.\\n\\n3) However, exceptional cases in which a co-occupant’s entry into the shared dwelling may, in relation to another co-occupant, fall within special circumstances constituting the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling cannot be excluded. The majority opinion does not deny even such exceptional possibility.\\n\\nFirst, where, under concrete facts such as the circumstances and form of shared residence, its progress, and its current status, a co-occupant is recognized as having departed from the shared dwelling, that may be regarded as a case where such special circumstances exist.\\n\\nNext, where one co-occupant applies to the court for an injunction prohibiting entry into the shared dwelling against another co-occupant and receives a court order for an injunction prohibiting entry, or where one co-occupant is a domestic violence offender and receives, pursuant to the Domestic Violence Punishment Act, a temporary measure order such as “eviction from the dwelling, etc.” or “prohibition of approach within 100 meters of the victim or family member, or of the dwelling, workplace, etc.” (Article 29(1)1 and 2), or where one co-occupant is a child abuse offender and receives, pursuant to the Child Abuse Punishment Act, a temporary measure order for eviction from the dwelling, etc. or prohibition of approach within 100 meters of the dwelling, etc. (Article 19(1)1 and 2), if a person enters the shared dwelling in violation of such legally based prohibition, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling may be considered established. This can be viewed as a case where there are special circumstances such that de facto control and management over the dwelling has been lost.\\n\\n4) Unless there are such special circumstances or equivalent circumstances, a co-occupant cannot prohibit another co-occupant from entering the place of common life. This is because excluding another co-occupant from the shared dwelling without justifiable reason, even though that person enters in order to use the place of common life, is impermissible. If a co-occupant who has been prohibited from entry without justifiable reason enters the place of common life in response, and the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is deemed not established, then even if there had been physical force in the form of locking the door and the like before such entry, thereby blocking entry itself and having the purpose of解除ing that obstruction, that conduct itself may be punishable as a separate matter, but the entry into the place of common life does not constitute the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling.\\n\\nOf course, even before lawful procedures such as the above injunction against entry are taken, in exceptional situations where protection of peace of the dwelling is necessary from a co-occupant, for example where the shared dwelling functions as a refuge protecting another co-occupant and the minor child under his or her protection from one co-occupant’s serious domestic violence or child abuse, if one co-occupant exercises physical force and forcibly enters, etc., it may, depending on the concrete facts, be recognized as an act of intrusion.
