This is because the freedom of a co-occupant to enter a shared dwelling presupposes a residential space as a tool for realizing human dignity; therefore, if a shared dwelling or a specific space within it has lost the function of shared dwelling for realizing such human dignity and is functioning only as a refuge under circumstances where one co-occupant’s violence and a serious danger to the life or bodily safety of another co-occupant, who is the victim, is imminent or has arrived, then in substance there may be special circumstances requiring protection of the other co-occupant’s peace of the dwelling.\\n\\nIn this regard, unlike what the dissenting opinion points out, the majority opinion cannot be viewed as contrary to the purpose of the 2020. 10. 20. amendment to the Domestic Violence Punishment Act, which included the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling among domestic violence crimes. The majority opinion’s purpose also respects and accords with the amendment’s purpose of preventing domestic violence and protecting victims. Furthermore, the Domestic Violence Punishment Act sets forth special rules concerning criminal procedures for certain crimes involving domestic violence, and even if the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is included among domestic violence crimes, that only means that where an act involving physical, mental, or property damage among family members is committed by the method of unlawful entry into a dwelling, it falls within the scope of the law; it does not mean that an act of entering a dwelling that does not constitute unlawful entry into a dwelling is to be characterized and punished as unlawful entry into a dwelling merely because it caused physical, mental, or property damage to a family member in the process. Whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established in the internal relationship among co-occupants constituting a family community, the traditional form of shared dwelling, is simply a matter to be determined under the foregoing legal principles by examining the substance of the case under concrete facts. Without considering that substance, one cannot uniformly characterize and punish the conduct as unlawful entry into a dwelling merely because there was an exercise of physical force in the course of a co-occupant’s entry into the shared dwelling.\\n\\nMoreover, the family members who are the requirements for the application of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act mean spouses, lineal ascendants and descendants, and cohabiting relatives, etc.; in this case, the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 who prohibited Defendant 1’s entry can hardly be deemed to fall within this, so it is not appropriate to use this as a basis for the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n5) A) The majority opinion, premised on the case where one co-occupant, lacking any legal basis or other justifiable reason to prohibit the entry of another co-occupant, nonetheless prohibits that other co-occupant’s entry itself by unilateral force, discussed whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established against the co-occupant who entered in response to such impermissible prohibition. The majority opinion is not intended to deny entirely the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling even where one co-occupant has a legal basis or other justifiable reason to prohibit the other co-occupant’s entry, but the other co-occupant ignores it and enters in a manner that harms the de facto peace of the dwelling.\\n\\nThe purport of the majority opinion is that, in relation to disputes among co-occupants, a balanced and careful approach is required when determining whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established against one of them. This is because it is not proper, even where facts or legal procedures exist that can correct disputes among co-occupants and the disorder of their shared dwelling form—such as recognition of departure from the shared dwelling, or deprivation of de facto control and management over the shared dwelling pursuant to a court’s injunction against entry or temporary measures such as prohibition of approach—to immediately criminalize a co-occupant’s entry into the shared place of life without such procedures. The crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is an offense punishable even if the victim withdraws the intention to punish, and if the State intervenes hastily through criminal statutes amid disputes among co-occupants, it may in some cases reach a point from which the causal relationship that formed the shared dwelling cannot be restored. Considering that a shared dwelling, the basic place where everyday life is conducted, is a place where human dignity is routinely realized for any co-occupant, it is also necessary to exercise greater caution in depriving anyone of rights or status concerning it.\\n\\nB) As to this case, the majority opinion held, on the premise that Defendant 1 had not departed from the shared life relationship in the apartment at issue and that no court decision such as an injunction against entry or temporary measures such as prohibition of approach had been issued against Defendant 1, so that no “special circumstances” existed permitting Non-Indicted Person 1, a co-occupant, or the victim Non-Indicted Person 2, to whom management of entry into the apartment at issue was entrusted by Non-Indicted Person 1, to prohibit Defendant 1’s entry, that the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s unilateral use of force to prohibit Defendant 1’s entry was impermissible, and that even if Defendant 1, in response, exercised physical force such as damaging the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the apartment at issue in order to enter the apartment at issue, this was merely a means for Defendant 1 to enter the shared dwelling, the apartment at issue, and thus the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is not established against Defendant 1. In this case, the majority opinion’s purport is that this does not constitute an exceptional situation in which the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established even though the actor is a co-occupant, and therefore it is not a case for applying exceptional doctrine premised on such a situation.\\n\\nC) The dissenting opinion, based on the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s and Non-Indicted Person 1’s statements, etc., newly found facts concerning the justifiable reason for the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s measure prohibiting Defendant 1’s entry, and then stated that one cannot categorically say that the victim Non-Indicted Person 2’s “prohibition of entry” at the time of this case lacked justifiable reason.\\n\\nHowever, the dissenting opinion is problematic in that it made the above determination based on a factual relation not recognized by the lower court. The majority opinion, premised on the facts recognized by the lower court, concluded that, in light of the circumstances at the time of entry, the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 had no legal basis or other justifiable reason to take measures prohibiting Defendant 1’s entry [meanwhile, from the record, Defendant 1 stated at the investigative agency that he was expelled from home on April 13, 2018 (Vol. 1, p. 50 of the evidentiary record); we add that it is also doubtful whether the dissenting opinion’s fact-finding based on the statements of the opposing party, the victim Non-Indicted Person 2 or Non-Indicted Person 1, is persuasive].\\n\\n6) A) The dissenting opinion says that if one co-occupant enters the shared dwelling in a manner that harms the peace of the co-occupant who prohibited his or her entry, then this cannot be regarded as the ordinary form of use of a shared dwelling and goes beyond the normal limits of use of a shared dwelling.\\n\\nHowever, just as the fact that a resident exercised some physical force while entering a dwelling does not mean that the resident’s conduct becomes the act of a person other than the resident intruding into the dwelling, the fact that a co-occupant exercised physical force in response to a unilateral prohibition of entry by another co-occupant, in order to解除 that prohibition while entering the place of common life, does not mean that the nature of the entry changes into intrusion. Entry into the shared dwelling is the most basic premise of use of the shared dwelling pursuant to the shared dwelling relationship, and there is separately a penal provision punishing the physical force exercised.\\n\\nB) The dissenting opinion also deliberately ignores or overlooks the problem of the prior measure by another co-occupant in this case, who without legal basis or justifiable reason blocked and prohibited one co-occupant’s entry itself by unilateral force. The act of a co-occupant physically obstructing and prohibiting another co-occupant’s entry into the shared dwelling can itself be evaluated as an act that preemptively infringes the other co-occupant’s peace of the dwelling, and, if one imagines a case where the blocked co-occupant has nowhere else to stay, it does not conform to social common sense to evaluate and punish as intrusion the act of overpowering that unilateral blocking measure and entering the dwelling on the premise that it was justified.\\n\\nIn this case, although it is a matter where the wife resided in the shared dwelling and the husband had left and sought to re-enter, if one imagines the reverse, namely, a case where the husband uses the temporary absence of the wife from the shared dwelling to change the key or password of the entrance-door locking device so that she cannot come in, and then the wife, together with her parents in her natal family, damages or解除s the locking device and enters the home, then under the dissenting opinion, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling would also have to be regarded as established in that case, but such a conclusion cannot readily be accepted by anyone.\\n\\nIf even in such a case the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling were deemed established and criminally punished, it could lead to a harsh conclusion against the weaker co-occupant who was expelled from the shared dwelling.\\n\\nC) The dissenting opinion says that if the majority opinion were to use, in the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling—which protects the peace of the dwelling as a legal interest and punishes acts infringing it—the criterion of “whether the victim’s act of prohibiting entry had legal basis,” it would not accord with the established Supreme Court position that “even if a person is the right holder, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling or unlawful entry into a structure is established where the person intrudes into a dwelling or structure as a means of self-help by exercising the right.”\\n\\nThe Supreme Court decision mentioned by the dissenting opinion is understood as concerning a case in which, among disputing parties in a conflict over the exclusive attribution of rights concerning residence or occupancy over a dwelling or structure, the party who had already lost possession entered the dwelling or structure by using self-help as a means of exercising rights to regain it, and in such general cases there is no particular theory in saying that the above position of the Supreme Court is proper.\\n\\nHowever, the issue in this case—whether, in a shared dwelling relationship that continues without interruption or severance due to unilateral departure, etc., and where each co-occupant’s freedom and peace of entry into and use of the shared dwelling is guaranteed, a co-occupant’s act of entering in response to another co-occupant’s entry prohibition without justifiable reason constitutes the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling—is different in substance from the above case in which the Supreme Court recognized the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling or unlawful entry into a structure on the basis that even a right holder cannot resort to self-help. Therefore, the doctrine of the above Supreme Court decision cannot be applied as is. This is because, within a shared dwelling under facts where departure from the shared dwelling relationship is not recognized, each co-occupant can enjoy freedom and peace of residence in which personal dignity is realized, while each co-occupant’s exercise of rights associated with the shared use of the dwelling is accompanied by restrictions and mutual tolerance of the existence and exercise of rights by other co-occupants is required.\\n\\nAgain, the majority opinion is addressing whether, in light of the ordinary form of use of the shared dwelling by co-occupants, when a co-occupant, as a resident, seeks to enter the dwelling in accordance with the ordinary method of entry as a normal form of use of the dwelling, another co-occupant unilaterally prohibits that entry without legal basis or other justifiable reason, the co-occupant seeking to enter the dwelling can be punished for the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling.\\n\\nC. Whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established where an outsider who received the consent of one of the co-occupants enters a shared dwelling in a manner that harms the state of peace of another co-occupant\\n\\n1) The crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is a crime concerning individual legal interests, and even if the resident has no legal right or authority to reside in the dwelling, if the control and management over that dwelling is factually peaceful, it is protected by criminal law. Even in the case of a shared dwelling, each co-occupant residing in the shared dwelling is in the position to enjoy from outside the protected legal interest of the peace of the dwelling.\\n\\nOn the other hand, in the case of a shared dwelling, the legal interests of peace of the dwelling held by each co-occupant may conflict with each other, so each co-occupant is necessarily subject to certain limitations on the legal interest of peace of the dwelling enjoyed in the shared dwelling due to the relationship with other co-occupants, and it must be deemed that the co-occupants mutually tolerated such circumstances while forming the shared dwelling relationship.\\n\\nThe content and scope of ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life mutually tolerated by each co-occupant must be examined individually and concretely according to the form and nature of the shared dwelling and the circumstances by which the shared dwelling was formed, etc. A co-occupant inviting an outsider and allowing that outsider to enter the shared dwelling is one of the ordinary forms in which a co-occupant uses a shared dwelling. For example, if in a family one spouse invites his or her parents or colleagues to the house, this can be seen in light of ordinary life relations as an ordinary form of use of the shared dwelling as a co-occupant. Therefore, an outsider’s entry into the shared dwelling pursuant to the invitation or consent of one co-occupant can, absent special circumstances, be evaluated as part of, and as an accompanying act to, the co-occupant’s entry into and use of the place of common life. On the other hand, where the outsider’s entry into the shared dwelling cannot be regarded as conduct accompanying or subsumed within ordinary use of the shared dwelling as a co-occupant, but rather where an outsider enters the shared dwelling against the opposition of another co-occupant merely because one co-occupant consented, the matter must be viewed differently.\\n\\nThus, whether an outsider’s entry into a shared dwelling pursuant to the consent of one co-occupant constitutes the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling in relation to another co-occupant who objects to that entry cannot be evaluated uniformly. The criteria for evaluation may be whether, from the standpoint of the co-occupant who consented to the outsider’s entry, the outsider’s entry can be evaluated as an act accompanying the co-occupant’s ordinary use of the shared dwelling, and from the standpoint of the other co-occupant, whether it can be evaluated as within the tolerable range. The specific determination will be sufficient if, by comprehensively considering the nature of the shared dwelling relationship, agreements or regulation among co-occupants, and other related factual circumstances, a rational conclusion fitting the case is reached.\\n\\n2) The above legal principles and evaluation criteria can likewise be applied where an outsider, pursuant to the consent of one co-occupant, enters that co-occupant’s shared dwelling and thereby harms the state of de facto peace of another co-occupant.\\n\\nThat is, even in such a case, one must examine whether this can be evaluated as part of, and as an accompanying act to, the co-occupant’s entry into and use of the place of common life, and whether the other co-occupant, in light of the nature of the relevant shared dwelling relationship, should tolerate it within a certain range, and then determine whether the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is established.\\n\\nAs noted above, just as the nature of an entry act by a co-occupant entering the place of common life does not change into an act of intrusion merely because some physical force was exercised in the process of entering the shared dwelling in response to a unilateral blocking measure by another co-occupant, the logic and subsidiarity of criminal punishment—that the physical force exercise should be regulated by a separate penal provision punishing it—must likewise apply to an outsider who acted accompanying the ordinary use of the shared dwelling by the co-occupant.\\n\\n3) The dissenting opinion says that where an outsider who received the consent of one co-occupant, as in this case, exercises physical force to harm the de facto peace of another co-occupant in order to enter the shared dwelling, the person must be punished for the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling.\\n\\nFirst, as examined above, it cannot be the correct interpretation and application of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling in relation to a shared dwelling to uniformly punish as unlawful entry into a dwelling the existence of a manner of act that harms the de facto peace of another co-occupant, merely because there was such a manner in the process of entry by a co-occupant into the shared dwelling and by an outsider accompanying that entry under the co-occupant’s consent.\\n\\nFurthermore, the fact that a co-occupant physically obstructs and prohibits another co-occupant’s entry into the shared dwelling itself can be evaluated as a preemptive infringement upon the other co-occupant’s peace of the dwelling, and, considering a case where the blocked co-occupant has nowhere else to stay, it is likewise as noted above that evaluating as intrusion, and punishing, the act of overcoming and entering on the premise that such unilateral blocking was justified, does not accord with social common sense. In this case, even though Non-Indicted Person 1, a co-occupant, or the victim Non-Indicted Person 2, to whom management of entry into the apartment at issue was entrusted by Non-Indicted Person 1, had no special circumstances permitting them to prohibit entry by Defendant 1, who was another co-occupant not having departed from the shared dwelling relationship at that time, they physically obstructed and prohibited Defendant 1’s entry, causing Defendant 1, in order to enter the apartment at issue, to exercise physical force such as damaging the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the apartment at issue. Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, in the position of the parents-in-law of Non-Indicted Person 1 and the parents of Defendant 1, joined in Defendant 1’s conduct and entered together as an accompanying act, which can, in its entirety, be evaluated as part of, and as accompanying, Defendant 1’s act of entering and using the apartment at issue as a shared dwelling.\\n\\nThe majority opinion, on the premise of such a situation, holds that in light of the legal principles of mutual restrictions on rights and the duty to tolerate arising from the shared dwelling relationship, the entry by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 can receive the same evaluation as the entry by Defendant 1, a co-occupant.\\n\\nWhether the dissenting opinion means that in cases where physical force was used in the course of an outsider’s entry into a shared dwelling, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling must uniformly be established, or that the same should be regarded as true in this case, the majority opinion does not view either as a proper legal principle or conclusion.\\n\\n4) The dissenting opinion also argues that the majority opinion is insufficient in protecting the legal interest of freedom and peace of residence that should be protected from force and the dominance of the majority.\\n\\nHowever, this misunderstands the purport of the majority opinion. Repeatedly stated, the majority opinion premises a situation in which one co-occupant enters the place of common life in a shared dwelling as conduct within the scope mutually tolerated by co-occupants as co-occupants, and an outsider’s entry likewise occurs in connection with ordinary use together with that co-occupant’s consent. Even in such cases, if the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is deemed established in relation to the co-occupant who prohibited entry without justifiable reason, the legal interest of the ordinary peace of the dwelling enjoyed by co-occupants in the shared dwelling is unjustly negated by another co-occupant’s unilateral exercise of force. That is precisely an infringement of the legal interest of freedom and peace of residence by one party’s force and dominance, and an acceptance of it.\\n\\n5) The majority opinion’s comparison of the statutory punishment for the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling under the Criminal Act with the cases of other countries that define unlawful entry into a dwelling as a non-complaint-based offense is intended to point out that, in light of the punishment and regulatory structure of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling under the Criminal Act, punishing an outsider for unlawful entry into a dwelling even though entry into a shared dwelling pursuant to the consent of one co-occupant can be evaluated as part of, and as an accompanying act to, the ordinary act of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-occupant who consented to it, would constitute excessive exercise of the state’s punitive power.\\n\\nIn relation to this point, the majority opinion’s purport is that excessive state intervention into the private sphere through the state’s punitive power can inevitably create side effects that prevent the autonomy of the private sphere and the development of civil, family, and domestic legal principles and institutions, so caution is needed. Even though the need for protection of socially vulnerable persons by the State in private spheres, including the family, is increasing day by day, this is also why it is difficult to readily extend the application of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling in the direction of broadening the scope of criminal statutes and criminal punishment.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, we express this supplementary opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n10. Supplementary opinion of Justice Min Yoo-sook on the dissenting opinion\\n\\nA. Summary of the supplementary dissenting opinion\\n\\nI will forecast the impact of this en banc decision on future trials and the interpretive theory of related statutes.\\n\\nB. Changes in the requirements for recognizing “departure from the shared dwelling relationship”\\n\\nBecause the majority opinion denies the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling against a co-occupant, whether a person has departed from the status of co-occupant will become an important criterion in determining the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling.\\n\\nThere is no established criterion for recognizing whether a co-occupant has departed from that status, and it must be determined individually according to the factual relationship recognized in each concrete case. There is not yet any Supreme Court precedent that has articulated the criterion.\\n\\nWhere the marital community is dissolved by divorce and one spouse leaves the shared dwelling, it is clear that that spouse has departed from the status of co-occupant. However, departure from the status of co-occupant does not occur only when the causal relationship that formed the shared dwelling relationship is dissolved or the title to possession of the residence is lost.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court upheld a lower court that recognized the defendant’s conduct of tearing off the lock from the entrance door and entering the home as unlawful entry into a dwelling, where the defendant left home due to family discord and lived separately for about 5 months, handed the entrance-door key to his wife through a marriage broker, and thereafter did not request the return of the key, even though the defendant, as tenant, had left some of his belongings in the house (see Supreme Court decision of September 15, 1995, 94DO3336).\\n\\nSince the majority opinion finds the grounds for denying the establishment of the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling against a co-occupant in the “ordinary form of use of a shared dwelling” and the “restrictions on legal interests that co-occupants should mutually tolerate,” the criterion for determining whether one has departed from the shared dwelling relationship should also be found there going forward. And that determination must be made concretely and individually based on the facts recognized as a result of hearing circumstances such as the circumstances and duration leading the co-occupant to live separately, the circumstances under which the co-occupant remaining in the home took measures prohibiting the other party’s entry (such as changing the password), and the subsequent responses of both sides.\\n\\nC. Relationship with the Domestic Violence Punishment Act\\n\\nAs stated in the dissenting opinion, under the amended Domestic Violence Punishment Act effective January 21, 2021, the crimes of unlawful entry into a dwelling (Article 319(1) of the Criminal Act), refusal to leave (Article 319(2) of the Criminal Act), special unlawful entry into a dwelling (Article 320 of the Criminal Act), and the attempt of each of the above crimes (Article 322 of the Criminal Act) arising among family members who are co-occupants also fall within the “domestic violence crimes” under that Act [Article 2(3)(sa)].\\n\\nAlso, judicial police officers who dispatch to the scene upon receiving a report of a domestic violence crime have been amended to conduct not only suppression of the violent act and separation of the domestic violence offender and the victim, but also criminal investigation, including arrest of a flagrant offender pursuant to Article 212 of the Criminal Procedure Act (Article 5(1), item 1 and item 1-2).\\n\\nThe conclusion, pursuant to the majority opinion, that the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling is not established against a co-occupant should be understood as limited to cases prosecuted under the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling under the Criminal Act. It appears that the majority opinion does not deny that where other provisions exist under statutes, those statutes must be followed.\\n\\nEven if a co-occupant uses violent means to overcome another co-occupant’s refusal and enters the common dwelling, even if such conduct cannot be characterized as unlawful entry into a dwelling under the Criminal Act according to the majority opinion, it falls within the domestic violence crimes defined by the amended Domestic Violence Punishment Act, and under the Domestic Violence Punishment Act, investigative agencies that receive a report of domestic violence have the authority and duty to dispatch to the scene and conduct criminal investigations, including arresting the domestic violence offender as a flagrant offender. For such conduct, temporary measures such as eviction from the victim or family member’s dwelling, etc. or prohibition of approach within 100 meters [Article 29(1)1 and 2], victim protection orders with the same content [Article 55-2(1)1 and 2], temporary protection orders [Article 55-4(1)], and protection disposition orders restricting acts of approaching the victim or family member [Article 40(1)1] may be issued. If a co-occupant enters the residence in violation of such disposition, etc., it constitutes the offense of non-performance of protective disposition, etc. under Article 63 of the same Act and is subject to criminal punishment. Conduct violating temporary measures, etc. as above is an act of entering despite “a court measure prohibiting entry into the shared dwelling,” and even according to the majority opinion, the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling under the Criminal Act would separately be established.\\n\\nIf the majority opinion were to mean that “because a co-occupant’s use of violent means to overcome another co-occupant’s refusal and enter the common dwelling does not constitute unlawful entry into a dwelling under the Criminal Act, it also does not fall within the domestic violence crimes defined by the Domestic Violence Punishment Act,” then the purpose of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act amendment would be completely nullified by the majority opinion. This is because, although the Domestic Violence Punishment Act was amended to expressly include within the crime of unlawful entry into a dwelling in Chapter 36, Part II of the Criminal Act, in order to protect family members who suffer harm from violent acts of unlawful entry into a dwelling even if they are family members, that would be excluded by interpretation from domestic violence crimes.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, I state this supplementary opinion to the dissenting opinion."}

{"[2021DO15507]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Summary of the charged facts of this case\\nAt around 00:55 on 2019. 9. 25., the Defendant resolved to enter the victim’s home, because he wanted to talk with the victim, Non-Indicted Person, who had been his romantic partner about 7 months earlier, in the underground parking lot on the 2nd basement level of the apartment at issue. Accordingly, in the underground parking lot on the 2nd basement level of the apartment at issue, the Defendant entered the common entrance door of the entrance connected to the building in which the victim’s home was located by inputting the password that he had learned through the victim during their relationship, and took an elevator to go up to the floor where the victim’s home was located. Upon reaching in front of the front door of the victim’s home, the Defendant attempted to enter the victim’s home for about 1 minute by repeatedly pressing the front-door password, and when the victim asked, “Who is it?”, he fled and came out through the exit of the underground parking lot of the apartment at issue. In this manner, the Defendant entered the common areas of the apartment at issue and intruded upon the residence of the victim and the residents living in the same building as the victim.\\n\\n2. The court below’s determination\\nThe court below rejected the Defendant’s grounds for appeal as follows, and left undisturbed the first-instance judgment that found the charged facts of this case guilty.\\na. The stairs, corridors, and elevators, which are common areas in a multi-unit residential building, are included in “dwelling,” the object of the offense of intrusion upon habitation.\\nb. Since it cannot be deemed that the victim presumptively consented to the Defendant’s entry from the underground parking lot of the apartment at issue to the entrance connected to the building in which the victim’s home is located (hereinafter referred to as the “entrance at issue”), or that she actually consented upon knowing of the Defendant’s entry on the day in question, the argument that the legal doctrine concerning the presumptive consent of residents living in the same building as the victim is limited on the premise that the victim’s consent existed cannot be accepted.\\nc. Even if the Defendant mistakenly believed that the victim had given presumptive consent, there was no justifiable reason for that mistake.\\nd. The Defendant’s act of entering the entrance at issue constituted intrusion upon the residence of the victim and the residents living in the same building as the victim, and even if the Defendant did not actually enter the victim’s home, the offense would have been completed.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s determination\\na. Relevant legal principles\\n1) The offense of intrusion upon habitation protects the factual peace and quiet of habitation as its legal interest. Since intrusion, which is the constituent act of the offense of intrusion upon habitation, must be interpreted in relation to the protected legal interest of the offense, intrusion means entering a dwelling in a manner that disturbs the factual state of peace and quiet enjoyed by the resident in the dwelling, and whether it constitutes intrusion is, in principle, to be determined based on the objectively and externally manifested manner of conduct at the time of entry. If entering a dwelling in a manner that disturbs the factual peace and quiet, it would, absent special circumstances, be contrary to the resident’s will; however, it cannot be immediately deemed to constitute intrusion solely on the basis of the resident’s subjective circumstance that the mere act of entering the dwelling itself is contrary to the resident’s will (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2020DO12630, decided on 2021. 9. 9., etc.). Therefore, in order to recognize that it constitutes intrusion, it is not sufficient merely that it is contrary to the resident’s will; when objectively and externally assessed by comprehensively considering the form and use/nature of the dwelling, the state of control and management over outsiders’ entry, and the circumstances and manner of entry, it must reach the point of disturbing the factual peace and quiet of the dwelling.\\n2) Common areas such as elevators, common stairs, and corridors inside multi-unit housing such as a detached house for multiple households, multi-unit housing, row housing, and apartments also constitute “another person’s dwelling,” the object of the offense of intrusion upon habitation, because there is a need to protect the factual peace and quiet of the residents’ habitation therein (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DO4335, decided on 2009. 9. 10., etc.). Even when determining whether an outsider who is not a resident’s entry into common areas of a multi-unit residential building constitutes intrusion upon habitation against the residents of that building, whether the common area is not a space open to the general public, but is a part necessarily appurtenant to the exclusive portion of each household or unit used as a dwelling, and whether control and management of outsiders’ entry is contemplated by the residents or the manager so that there is a need to protect the factual peace and quiet of the residents’ habitation therein, and whether the residents of the multi-unit residential building or the manager ordinarily controlled and managed outsiders’ entry into that place, together with the outsider’s purpose and circumstances of entry, the manner of entry, and the time of entry, must be comprehensively considered, and the issue must be judged objectively and externally from the perspective of whether the factual state of peace and quiet of the dwelling was infringed.\\nAccordingly, even in the case of entering the common entrance of an apartment or other multi-unit residential building, if entry is possible only by inputting into the entrance door a password given only to residents and the manager because the area is necessarily appurtenant to the exclusive portion of each unit used as a dwelling, or if there exist circumstances externally showing that unauthorized entry by outsiders is controlled and managed, such as signs indicating the purpose of controlling outsiders’ entry or the presence of a security guard, and if an outsider, even while recognizing this, has no consent from the resident or manager regarding entry and, in light of the relationship with the resident or the necessity of entry, enters the common entrance without the resident or manager’s knowledge by arbitrarily inputting or manipulating the password without justifiable reason, etc., then, when comprehensively considering the purpose and circumstances of entry, the manner of entry, and the time of entry, if it can be viewed as a mode of conduct that disturbs the factual peace and quiet of the residents of the multi-unit residential building, it will constitute intrusion upon habitation against the residents of the multi-unit residential building.\\nb. Determination\\n1) According to the evidence duly admitted by the court below, the following facts and circumstances can be ascertained.\\na) In order to reach the victim’s home from the underground parking lot of the apartment at issue, one must enter by inputting the password given to the resident or manager into the common entrance door installed at the entrance at issue, and then use the elevator, etc.\\nb) At the time of the offense at issue, the Defendant entered the building of the apartment in which the victim’s home was located by inputting the password of the said common entrance door, which he had known while dating the victim for about 2 months. However, since about 7 months had passed after the Defendant and the victim briefly dated and then quarreled and broke up, and while the victim was refusing to meet the Defendant, the Defendant, without any prior contact with the victim, entered the building in which the victim’s home was located through the entrance at issue in the manner described above during late-night hours when the victim and her child were sleeping, used the elevator to reach in front of the victim’s home, and attempted to enter the victim’s home by repeatedly pressing the password of the front door of the victim’s home for about 1 minute. When the victim said, “Who is it?”, the Defendant, startled, fled without even facing the victim. According to the victim’s statement, at that time the victim was in a situation of fearing the Defendant and refusing to meet him to the extent of stating that she was “frightened that the Defendant suddenly came to the house without any contact, and if the front door had opened, it seems that she would have been sexually assaulted in front of her child.”\\n2) Examining these facts in light of the relevant legal principles set forth above, it is appropriate to view the Defendant’s act of, as charged in this case, unlawfully entering the entrance of the apartment at issue and the area in front of the victim’s front door during late-night hours as an act that disturbs the factual peace and quiet of the residents living in the same building as the victim. The reasons in detail are as follows.\\na) The entrance at issue that the Defendant entered is a part necessarily appurtenant to the exclusive portion used as the victim’s dwelling, and the manager or residents of the apartment at issue ordinarily controlled and managed outsiders’ entry into the common area beyond the entrance door through the installation of a common entrance door with a password. The Defendant was not a resident of the apartment at issue, and in the past, while dating the victim, he had only entered temporarily in the capacity of visiting the victim’s home and had not entered the apartment at issue for a long period of about 7 months before this case.\\nb) Taking advantage of the fact that he learned the password while previously dating the victim, the Defendant, without going through any procedure such as obtaining permission to visit from the victim, unlocked the entrance door by unlawfully inputting the password of the common entrance door during late-night hours, and entered the inside of the entrance, which is a space whose entry is permitted only to the apartment manager or residents, and even in front of the victim’s front door. Considering these circumstances together, the Defendant appears to have had the intent to secretly enter the victim’s dwelling.\\nc) The reasons asserted by the Defendant, such as the fact that he had briefly dated the victim in the past and learned the password of the common entrance door at the entrance at issue through the victim, alone, make it difficult to recognize that, considering the relationship between the Defendant and the victim and the usage status of the apartment at issue at the time of the Defendant’s entry, there was actual or implied consent by the victim or the manager of the apartment at issue; furthermore, it cannot be deemed that there was a justifiable reason for the Defendant to engage in the above conduct or that it otherwise falls under a case where unlawfulness is excluded.\\n3) Although the court below, in finding the charged facts of this case guilty, had deficiencies in the reasoning of its judgment in that it determined that the conduct constituted intrusion merely on the basis that actual or implied consent of the victim could not be recognized, that is, on the basis that the conduct was contrary to the victim’s will, without determining whether the Defendant’s conduct was a mode of conduct that disturbs the factual state of peace and quiet of the dwelling, the conclusion is proper, and there is otherwise no error in the court below’s determination such as violation of the rules of logic and experience, going beyond the limits of free evaluation of evidence, or misunderstanding of the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon habitation or implied consent, or mistake of fact underlying such consent.\\n4. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged, with the concurrence of all Justices participating."}

question: A lives separately from his uncle, A. One day, A secretly entered A’s vacant house and stole a laptop owned by A’s friend B and being kept by A, as well as A’s passbook and driver’s license. Using the stolen passbook, A went to a nearby automated teller machine and, using a password he happened to learn, transferred KRW 1,000,000 from A’s account to his own account. While A was returning after transferring the money, A presented the stolen driver’s license of A in response to a police officer’s request to present identification during a police stop-and-identification check. Thereafter, A withdrew the transferred money and handed it over to his friend B, who knew the circumstances. Which of the following correctly combines the correct statements (○) and the incorrect statements (×) regarding this matter? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents) (a). Since there is a familial relationship between A and the possessor, A cannot be prosecuted for theft unless A’s complaint exists with respect to the theft of the laptop. (b). With respect to A’s offense of fraud by use of a computer, etc., since the financial institution for the account in A’s name cannot be regarded as the victim, the act of A transferring KRW 1,000,000 from A’s account to his own account is subject to the special rule for offenses between relatives. (c). Receiving stolen property is established against B, who received the money from A. (d). A’s presentation of A’s driver’s license in response to the police officer’s request to present identification does not constitute the offense of unlawful use of an official document because a driver’s license does not perform the function of proving identity. (e). If A had been unable to withdraw the transferred money, it would constitute an attempt of the offense of fraud by use of a computer, etc.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2000DO1985]": "The judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the collegiate panel of the Seoul District Court, Headquarters."}
{"[2004DO353]": "The appeal is dismissed."}

{"[2006DO2704]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. An electronic funds transfer transaction between financial institutions conducted through a computer or other information-processing device is a transaction method that, through the correspondent banking relationship between financial institutions, effectuates payment and receipt between financial institutions or between customers using financial institutions, without the actual exchange of funds. Accordingly, where a defendant, without authority, uses a computer or other information-processing device to transfer part of the deposit balance in an account at a financial institution with which the holder of the deposit account transacts to an account in that name opened at another financial institution with which the defendant transacts, the deposit-return claim of the holder of the deposit account against the financial institution with which that holder transacts has no reason to be affected by such act. Therefore, the financial institution with which the account is maintained remains liable for the obligation to return the deposit to the holder of the deposit account, while, under the correspondent banking relationship, it additionally incurs the settlement obligation to the other financial institution in an amount equivalent to the transferred funds resulting from the funds transfer, and thus becomes exposed to the risk of having to make double payment of the obligation equivalent to the transferred deposit.\\n\\nAccordingly, where a defendant who stole a deposit passbook owned by a relative inserts the passbook into an automated teller machine installed at the financial institution with which that relative transacts and manipulates it so as to transfer the deposit balance in the account in the relative’s name to an account in the defendant’s name opened at another financial institution with which the defendant transacts, the victim of the offense is the financial institution with which that relative transacts, which is placed at risk of having to make double payment of the obligation equivalent to the transferred deposit. And it cannot be deemed that the financial institution that is the direct party to the funds transfer transaction and the principal bearer of the risk of double payment is not the victim of such offense of fraud by use of computer, etc., merely because the damage arising from such offense may ultimately be shifted to the deposit holder, the relative, through the exemption clause in the terms and conditions of the transaction or through application of the doctrine concerning a quasi-possessor of a claim. Therefore, in such a case, the special provision for offenses among relatives, which presupposes an offense committed among relatives, cannot be applied.\\n\\nIn this case, where the Prosecutor indicted the defendant by specifying as the victim of the computer, etc. fraud offense at issue the Goheung Agricultural Cooperative, because the defendant stole a deposit passbook owned by his paternal grandfather, the Non-Indicted Person, and transferred 570,000 won from the deposit balance in the account under the Non-Indicted Person’s name at that Agricultural Cooperative to an account in the defendant’s name at Kookmin Bank by inserting the passbook into an automated teller machine and manipulating it, the lower court, on the ground that the victim of the offense was the defendant’s paternal grandfather, the Non-Indicted Person, reversed the first-instance court, which had found the charges guilty, and, applying the special provision for offenses among relatives, sentenced the defendant to exemption from punishment. This contains an error of law in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the scope of the victim in the offense of fraud by use of computer, etc. and the scope of application of the special provision for offenses among relatives, and since this is clearly material to the judgment, it cannot be upheld as is.\\n\\n2. Therefore, the portion of the lower court judgment exempting punishment is reversed, and this case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination of this part. The judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, as stated in the operative part."}

{"[2006DO4127]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. In a co-principal relationship in which two or more persons jointly participate in the commission of a crime, conspiracy is not required by law to take any particular form; it is sufficient if two or more persons conspire and, with the intent to jointly participate in a certain crime and bring about that crime, there is merely a union of intent. Thus, even if there was no process of overall collusion, a conspiratorial relationship is established if the union of intent is formed sequentially or tacitly among several persons, and once such conspiracy is formed, even a person who was not directly involved in the acts of execution bears criminal liability as a joint principal for the acts of the other conspirators (see Supreme Court Decision 98DO30, decided March 27, 1998; Decision 2005DO8507, decided January 26, 2006, etc.).\\n\\nExamining the judgment of the court below and the evidence admitted by the first instance court cited by the court below in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the court below recognized the facts as stated in its holding, and then, by comprehensively considering the various circumstances set forth in its holding, found that the Defendant had the intent to commit each of the crimes in this case and that liability as a co-principal was also established, and thus properly found all of the factual allegations of attempted fraud and fraud by use of computers, etc. charged against the Defendant to be guilty.\\n\\nThere is no illegality in the judgment of the court below, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in that it violated the rules of evidence or erred in fact-finding without fully examining the case, or misconstrued the legal principles concerning the establishment of co-principal liability by conspiracy.\\n\\n2. Article 347-2 of the Criminal Act provides that a person who obtains property benefits, or causes a third person to obtain such benefits, by inputting false information or an unlawful command into an information-processing device, or by causing information processing through inputting or altering information without authority, shall be punished. Accordingly, where an employee of a financial institution, by using a computer terminal, inputs false information as if money had been deposited into a specified account designated by the other conspirators, thereby causing the money to be deposited into that account, the completion of such deposit procedure shall be deemed to have resulted in the acquisition of a property benefit that could in the future be withdrawn from that account; therefore, the crime of fraud by use of computers, etc. prescribed in Article 347-2 of the Criminal Act is completed, and even if such deposit was later canceled and could not actually be withdrawn, that cannot be said to affect the already established crime of fraud by use of computers, etc.\\n\\nThe court below punished, as the completed offense of fraud by use of computers, etc. prescribed in Article 347-2 of the Criminal Act, the act of the person not indicted, an employee at the Bongpyeong Agricultural Cooperative YP branch, who, in accordance with the instructions of the Defendant and other conspirators, completed a deposit into a specified account by means of a resource-less remittance using the computer terminal installed at that branch of the agricultural cooperative; this is proper as it accords with the foregoing legal principles.\\n\\nThere is no illegality in the judgment of the court below in that it misconstrued the legal principles concerning the timing of completion of the crime of fraud by use of computers, etc.\\n\\n3. In this case, in which a sentence of imprisonment of less than 10 years was imposed on the Defendant, an argument to the effect that the sentence of the court below is too severe cannot constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudicated in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[80DO131]": "We examine the grounds of the Prosecutor’s final appeal.\\n\\nThe court below affirmed the first-instance judgment dismissing the instant public prosecution on the ground that, after finding as a fact that the accused, at around 19 : 00 on 1978. 8. 8. at a precious-metal processing factory operated by Non-Indicted 1 at 49, Jongno 4-ga, Jongno-gu, Seoul, stole six diamonds owned by Non-Indicted Hong Sang-yeol, with a total market value of 1,380,000 won, which Non-Indicted 1 had been keeping after receiving a request for processing from Non-Indicted Hong Sang-yeol, Non-Indicted 1 was the accused’s nephew (the son of Non-Indicted 2, the accused’s sister), and the accused and Non-Indicted 1 were in the familial relationship prescribed in Article 328(2) of the Criminal Act as applied mutatis mutandis by Article 344 of the Criminal Act; that the provision on offenses between relatives does not regulate the relationship between the owner of the damaged property and the offender, but rather regulates the relationship between the possessor of the damaged property, who is the direct victim of the larceny offense, and the offender; and therefore the instant larceny offense should ultimately be deemed subject to the application of the provision on offenses between relatives; however, since the victim, Non-Indicted 1, had not filed a complaint against the accused, the instant public prosecution constituted a prosecution instituted without the complaint required by Articles 344 and 328(2) of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nHowever, larceny is a crime established by trespassing upon possession of property, so the possessor of the property becomes the victim of the larceny offense; but since larceny, by trespassing upon the possessor’s possession, harms the owner of the property, the owner of the property also should be regarded as a victim of larceny.\\n\\nAccordingly, the provision on offenses between relatives in Article 328(2) of the Criminal Act as applied mutatis mutandis by Article 344 of the Criminal Act applies only where both the offender and the owner and possessor of the damaged property are in the familial relationship prescribed in that provision; and where only the larceny offender and the owner of the damaged property are in a familial relationship, or only the larceny offender and the possessor of the damaged property are in a familial relationship, it would be reasonable to view that the provision does not apply.\\n\\nHowever, in this case, if the accused has the familial relationship prescribed in the above provision only in relation to Non-Indicted 1, the possessor (holder) of the instant damaged property, and has no familial relationship prescribed in the above provision with Non-Indicted Hong Sang-yeol, the owner of the instant damaged property, then Article 328(2) of the Criminal Act as applied mutatis mutandis by Article 344 of the Criminal Act cannot be applied to the accused; thus, the lower court, by applying the provision on offenses between relatives to the accused and affirming the first-instance judgment dismissing the prosecution, erred by misapprehending the legal principle on the protected legal interest of larceny and on offenses between relatives and thereby affecting the conclusion of the judgment.\\n\\nTherefore, the grounds of appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, the original judgment is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as stated in the disposition."}

question: A woman A, wearing a short skirt and using the escalator in a subway station, was filming her underwear and body for about 1 minute by inserting a mobile phone camera under her skirt, when she was discovered by A. A police officer who responded after receiving A's report received the mobile phone from A by voluntary submission. Which of the following statements regarding this is correct? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents)
A: If A had been arrested as a flagrant offender at the scene of the above crime, since, in the ordinary case, it cannot be construed that he had the intention to voluntarily submit items proving his culpability at the place where a flagrant offender is arrested, and since urgent seizure is possible pursuant to Article 216(1)2 of the Criminal Procedure Act with respect to a person arrested as a flagrant offender, seizure by voluntary submission is not permitted.
B: If, when the police officer received the mobile phone from A by voluntary submission, he did not clearly confirm from A the scope of the voluntary submission as to which of the information contained in the mobile phone was being submitted, information that can be used as indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence concerning the motive and circumstances of the offense, the means and method, and the time and place, cannot be included among the objects of seizure.
C: If A had sent the above recording to A, this would correspond to providing the recording to another person, and the crime of Violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (filming by use of camera, etc. and distribution, etc.) would separately be established.
D: Even if, after A filmed A, a certain period of time had elapsed and the above video information had been entered into main memory, if the filmed video information was forcefully terminated by the user without being permanently stored in the form of an electronic file, etc., it constitutes an attempt of the crime of Violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (filming by use of camera, etc. and distribution, etc.).
E: Even if a police officer obtains a seizure and search warrant, seizes another storage medium from A's house, and accesses the cloud linked to that storage medium in order to secure as evidence the illegal filming video stored there, electronic information stored on a remote server must be included among the objects to be seized under the seizure and search warrant.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2010DO10677]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Article 14-2(1) of the former Act on the Punishment of Sexual Crimes and Protection of Victims, etc. (the version prior to its amendment, by Act No. 10258 on Apr. 15, 2010, to the Act on the Protection of Victims of Sexual Crimes, etc.) provides, “A person who, by using a camera or other mechanical device having a similar function, photographs another person’s body that may arouse sexual desire or cause a sense of shame against that person’s will, or who distributes, sells, leases, or publicly displays or screens such photographs, shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 5 years or by a fine not exceeding 10 million won.” Among such acts, the “photographing by using a camera, etc. offense” should be deemed completed when the image information concerning the subject has been input into the film or storage device inside the camera or other mechanical device having a similar function. Meanwhile, devices such as digital cameras or mobile phones equipped with video-recording functions, which have emerged with the recent development of technological civilization, often employ a method in which, even before the recorded image information is stored in the form of an electronic file, etc. by the user or others, once recording begins, the image information of the recorded subject is immediately input into and temporarily stored in the main memory, such as RAM (Random Access Memory), inside the device, and is then stored in a secondary storage device, etc. inside the device upon a later storage instruction. If video recording was made by using a camera, etc. device adopting such a storage method, the offense is already completed when, after a certain time has elapsed following the recording, the image information is input into the main memory, etc. inside the device; it cannot be deemed to have remained at the attempt stage merely because the recorded image information was forcibly terminated by the user without being permanently stored in the form of an electronic file, etc.\\n\\n2. The gist of the facts charged in this case is that “the Defendant, at around 08:55 on Sep. 28, 2009, stood behind the Victim, who was wearing a short black skirt, inside the transfer escalator at Jongno 3-ga Station on Seoul Subway Line 1, and, with a camera phone in his possession, photographed by video the body parts under the skirt that could cause sexual humiliation, against the Victim’s will.” The first instance court, in light of the admitted evidence, found that the Defendant had attempted to video-record, with the camera phone, the body parts under the Victim’s skirt as described above, but upon being discovered by a police officer during the recording, terminated the recording without pressing the save button on the camera phone and thereby failed to complete the recording, so that the offense remained at the attempt stage, and thus there was no proof that the offense had been completed; accordingly, it acquitted the portion of the facts charged alleging completion of the offense. The appellate court, on the same ground, found the above determination by the first instance court to be proper and affirmed it as is.\\n\\nHowever, examining the evidence admitted by the first instance court and upheld by the appellate court in light of the legal principles stated above, if the Defendant began video recording using a mobile phone and a certain amount of time elapsed, then even if he was discovered by a police officer during the recording and terminated the recording without pressing the save button, there is a very strong basis for viewing the photographing by using a camera, etc. offense as already completed. Nevertheless, the appellate court, on the sole ground that the Defendant terminated the recording without pressing the save button during the above video recording, concluded that the photographing offense had not been completed and thereby affirmed the first instance judgment, which had acquitted the Defendant on the completed-offense point among the facts charged in this case. In so doing, the appellate court either misunderstood the legal principles concerning the “time at which the photographing offense is completed,” which constitutes an element of the offense under the relevant punitive statute, or failed to conduct the necessary examination, or there is a contradiction in the reasons for judgment, and thus its judgment is unlawful. The grounds for final appeal raising this point are well-founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2015DO13726]": "The Court determines the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. On the Prosecutor’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\nA. Any person caught in flagrante delicto while the offense is being committed or immediately after its commission may be arrested without a warrant (Article 212 of the Criminal Procedure Act). To arrest a person caught in flagrante delicto, there must be, in addition to the punishability of the act, the contemporaneity of the offense, temporal immediacy, and the obviousness of the offender and the offense, the necessity of arrest, namely, a fear of flight or destruction of evidence (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 98DO3029, decided January 26, 1999), and whether the requirements for such arrest of a person caught in flagrante delicto are satisfied shall be determined on the basis of the circumstances at the time of arrest; it may be said that the investigative authority has considerable discretion in making that determination. Therefore, unless, in light of the circumstances at the time of arrest, the investigative authority’s determination regarding such requirements is found to be manifestly unreasonable under the rules of experience, the investigative authority’s arrest of a person caught in flagrante delicto should not be deemed unlawful (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2012DO8184, decided November 29, 2012).\\n\\nWhere the Prosecutor or a judicial police officer arrests a suspect as a person caught in flagrante delicto pursuant to Article 212 of the Criminal Procedure Act, he/she may, if necessary, conduct seizure, search, and inspection without a warrant at the place of arrest; however, where it is necessary to continue the seizure of the items seized in this manner, a seizure warrant shall be requested without delay within 48 hours from the time of arrest (Article 216(1)2 and Article 217(2)). And where the Prosecutor or a judicial police officer, at a crime scene during or immediately after the commission of the offense, is unable to obtain a judge’s warrant due to urgency, he/she may conduct seizure, search, or inspection without a warrant; in such case, a warrant must be obtained without delay thereafter (Article 216(3)). Provided, however, under Article 218 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the Prosecutor or a judicial police officer may seize without a warrant items left behind by a suspect, etc., or items voluntarily submitted by the owner, possessor, or custodian; accordingly, even at the place of arrest of a person caught in flagrante delicto or at a crime scene, items voluntarily submitted by the possessor, etc. may be seized without a warrant pursuant to the above provision, and in such case the Prosecutor or the judicial police officer need not obtain a warrant thereafter.\\n\\nB. Of the facts charged in this case, the gist of the count of violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. (psychotropic substances) dated June 1, 2014 is that “the Defendant, upon the proposal of Non-Indicted Person 1, concealed about 6.1 kg of methamphetamine divided into 7 plastic bags on his body around May 29, 2014, boarded a barge at ○○ Port, China, and entered △△ Port, Geoje City, at around 16:15 on June 1 of the same year, thereby, in conspiracy with Non-Indicted Person 1, etc., smuggling in about 6.1 kg of methamphetamine.”\\n\\nThe court below held, on the reasoning set forth in its opinion, that a prosecutorial investigator searched the interior of the barge after receiving a report, arrested the Defendant, who had been hiding, as a person caught in flagrante delicto of violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. (psychotropic substances) due to methamphetamine smuggling, and then seized the methamphetamine by voluntary submission after searching the place of arrest and receiving the methamphetamine found; however, at the time of arrest, the methamphetamine, which was evidence of the methamphetamine smuggling offense, had not yet been discovered, and mere intelligence that methamphetamine was being smuggled was insufficient to recognize the obviousness of the offense among the requirements for arrest of a person caught in flagrante delicto; and even if the arrest as a person caught in flagrante delicto were lawful, the investigative agency violated due process by seizing the methamphetamine and failing to obtain a post-seizure search-and-seizure warrant, and because the Defendant did not himself indicate where the methamphetamine was, and it was not discovered at the very place where he had been hiding, even though the investigative agency adopted the form of voluntarily receiving the methamphetamine from the Defendant who had already been subdued by an arrest of a person caught in flagrante delicto, it could not be regarded as a lawful voluntarily submitted item; accordingly, the seized methamphetamine and the secondary evidence in this case, such as the expert report collected on that basis, are illegally obtained evidence or secondary evidence of illegally obtained evidence and lack admissibility, and the remaining evidence submitted by the Prosecutor alone is insufficient to establish the above facts charged, and thus found the Defendant not guilty.\\n\\nC. However, the court below’s determination on this part cannot be accepted for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) According to the reasons of the court below’s judgment and the evidence lawfully admitted by the first-instance court, as maintained by the court below, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n(A) Around May 29, 2014, the prosecutorial investigators received information that the Defendant was smuggling methamphetamine while entering the country illegally on a barge (Ship Name 2 omitted) towed by (Ship Name 1 omitted), and searched the above barge, which had arrived at △△ Port at around 16:15 on June 1.\\n\\n(B) Prosecutorial investigator Non-Indicted Person 2 discovered the Defendant, who was hiding on a shelf in the ship’s stores warehouse during the search, and made him slowly come down, then asked where the methamphetamine had been placed, but received no answer; and when another prosecutorial investigator who was searching another place inside the barge happened to shout, “The item is here; I found it,” the Defendant was arrested at around 16:30 as a person caught in flagrante delicto of methamphetamine smuggling and illegal entry, etc.\\n\\n(C) Non-Indicted Person 2 immediately presented to the Defendant about 6.1 kg of methamphetamine that had been found and explained, “If methamphetamine is voluntarily submitted, it can be seized without a warrant, and if it is seized, it cannot be returned voluntarily; if it is not voluntarily submitted, it must be seized after obtaining a warrant,” and asked whether there was an intention to voluntarily submit it; he then obtained the Defendant’s consent, accompanied by the words, “I know that much as well,” and seized the methamphetamine, and on the same day at the Prosecutor’s Office prepared a voluntary submission confirmation and obtained the Defendant’s signature and seal. The Prosecutor has not obtained a post-seizure warrant for the seized methamphetamine and is keeping it to date.\\n\\n(D) On April 29, 2010, the Defendant was sentenced to 7 months’ imprisonment for violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. (psychotropic substances) due to methamphetamine sale, etc., and completed the execution of that sentence on May 17 of the same year, and in total has been punished 6 times for the same kind of offense.\\n\\n(2) Examining these facts in light of the above legal principles, since the prosecutorial investigator discovered methamphetamine near the place where he found the Defendant inside the barge while the Defendant had boarded the barge and was in the midst of, or immediately after, committing the offense of smuggling methamphetamine while entering illegally, and immediately arrested the Defendant, this was a lawful arrest of a person caught in flagrante delicto, and it cannot be said that, in the circumstances at the time of arrest, the Defendant did not correspond to a person caught in flagrante delicto who smuggled methamphetamine while entering illegally or that the prosecutorial investigator’s determination in this regard was manifestly unreasonable under the rules of experience.\\n\\nAnd in light of the fact that the prosecutorial investigator informed the Defendant of the meaning and effect of voluntary submission before seizing the methamphetamine; the fact that the Defendant himself had several prior criminal punishments for the same kind of offense such as methamphetamine sale, and thus appears to have sufficiently known that if he voluntarily submitted the seized methamphetamine, it would be seized and not returned; the fact that there is no material to show that the Defendant denied the methamphetamine-related offense at the time of arrest; and the fact that there are no circumstances whatsoever suggesting that the prosecutorial investigator deceived or threatened the Defendant in order to obtain the voluntary submission of the methamphetamine, the Defendant, as the possessor of the methamphetamine, is deemed to have voluntarily submitted it, and thus the seizure of that methamphetamine is also lawful.\\n\\n(3) Nevertheless, the court below, solely on the grounds stated in its opinion, held that the prosecutorial investigator’s arrest of the Defendant as a person caught in flagrante delicto of methamphetamine smuggling was unlawful, and that the seized methamphetamine was not a lawful voluntarily submitted item, and therefore that the methamphetamine and the secondary evidence of this case based thereon lacked admissibility as illegally obtained evidence or secondary evidence thereof; accordingly, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principles regarding the lawful requirements for arrest of a person caught in flagrante delicto and the seizure of voluntarily submitted items under Article 218 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and thereby affected the judgment. The Prosecutor’s ground for final appeal pointing out this issue has merit.\\n\\nD. Therefore, the portion of the court below’s judgment concerning the count of violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. (psychotropic substances) dated June 1, 2014 must be reversed; and because the counts of violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. (psychotropic substances) dated March 30, 2011, April 25, 2011, and early June 2011, as well as the count of violation of the Immigration Control Act, all of which the court below found guilty, are in a relation of concurrent crimes under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, they must be reversed together.\\n\\n2. On the Defendant’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\nUnder Article 383(4) of the Criminal Procedure Act, an appeal on the ground of improper sentencing is permitted only in cases in which death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or confinement for not less than 10 years has been imposed, and thus in this case, where a lighter sentence than that was imposed for the count of violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. (psychotropic substances) dated August 3, 2009, the argument that the sentence is too severe and unjust or that there was an error of insufficient hearing of sentencing factors does not constitute a lawful ground for final appeal. Therefore, the Defendant’s ground for final appeal in this respect cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without addressing the remainder of the Defendant’s and Prosecutor’s grounds for final appeal, we reverse the portions of the court below’s judgment concerning the counts of violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. (psychotropic substances) dated March 30, 2011, April 25, 2011, early June 2011, and June 1, 2014, and the count of violation of the Immigration Control Act, remand this part of the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and dismiss the Defendant’s appeal concerning the portion of the court below’s judgment on the count of violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. (psychotropic substances) dated August 3, 2009, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2018DO1481]": "We determine the grounds for appeal (the defendant’s supplementary statement of grounds for appeal and opinion statement submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal has elapsed shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. Regarding the defendant’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nExamining the reasons for the lower court’s judgment in light of the evidence duly admitted, the lower court properly found guilty, among the facts charged in this case, of the assault charge, the violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (filming using a camera, etc.) arising from each act of filming (excluding the acquittal portion), and the attempted violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (filming using a camera, etc.) arising from the display of the filmed material. There is no error, such as a violation of the rules of logic and experience and thus exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nIn addition, under Article 383, item 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, an appeal on the ground of unfair sentencing is permitted only in cases where the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or penal detention for not less than 10 years has been imposed. Therefore, in this case, in which a lighter sentence than that was imposed on the defendant, the argument that the order to attend a course is excessive does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n2. Regarding the prosecutor’s grounds for appeal\\n\\na. As to the part concerning the violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (filming using a camera, etc.) arising from the provision of filmed material\\n\\nArticle 14, paragraph 1 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Sexual Crimes Punishment Act”) punishes the act of “photographing, against another person’s will, that person’s body, which may arouse sexual desire or cause shame, by using a camera or other device having similar functions, or distributing, selling, leasing, providing, or publicly displaying or screening the photographed material.”\\n\\nThat Article 14, paragraph 1 of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act punishes not only the act of photographing but also the act of distributing, selling, leasing, providing, or publicly displaying or screening the photographed material is because, in light of the social problem that photographs of another person’s body, which may arouse sexual desire or cause shame, are rapidly and widely disseminated through the internet and other information and communications networks, causing immense harm and suffering to victims, it is intended to punish the person who disseminates such material, whose culpability or blameworthiness can be said to be no less than that of the act of photographing, in the same manner as the photographer (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2016DO6172, rendered October 13, 2016).\\n\\nThe “provision” separately enumerated from “distribution” in Article 14, paragraph 1 of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act means a gratuitous transfer act that does not amount to “distribution,” namely, a gratuitous transfer to a “specific one person or a small number of persons” without an intent to “distribute” (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DO16676, rendered December 27, 2016).
