However, as noted above, in light of the fact that Article 14, paragraph 1 of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act punishes not only the act of photographing but also the act of distributing, selling, leasing, providing, or publicly displaying or screening the photographed material in order to protect victims by preventing the dissemination of such material, it is proper to view the victim who was the subject of the photographing as not included in the “specific one person or a small number of persons” who are the counterpart to “provision” under Article 14, paragraph 1 of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act.\\n\\nAccordingly, unless there are other special circumstances, the act of delivering the photographed material to the victim himself or herself cannot be said to constitute “provision” under Article 14, paragraph 1 of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act.\\n\\nWhile the lower court found the defendant guilty of the act of photographing, using a camera, the victim’s body, which may arouse sexual desire or cause shame, against the victim’s will, among the facts charged in this case, it found not guilty, for the reasons stated in its opinion, of the part concerning the violation of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act (filming using a camera, etc.) arising from the defendant’s act of transmitting one of those photographs to the victim’s mobile phone. The lower court’s above determination is in accordance with the foregoing legal principles and is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, such as misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning “provision” under Article 14, paragraph 1 of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act.\\n\\nb. As to the remaining parts\\n\\nThe prosecutor appealed the entire lower court judgment, but as to the acquittal parts other than the part concerning the violation of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act (filming using a camera, etc.) arising from the provision of filmed material, and as to the guilty parts, there is no statement of lawful grounds for appeal in the petition of appeal, and there is likewise no statement of grounds for objection in the statement of grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as per the disposition, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court involved."}

{"[2019DO4938]": "We consider the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Summary of the facts charged\\n\\na. The Defendant, from 2017. 6. 28. to 2017. 9. 2., as stated in items 1 through 7 of the attached crime list indicated in the lower court’s judgment, photographed with the camera of a mobile phone (hereinafter referred to as “the mobile phone at issue”) the bodies of victims of unknown identity in a manner capable of arousing sexual desire or causing shame, against their will (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “No. 1–7 offenses”).\\n\\nb. At around 00:13 on 2017. 9. 4., the Defendant approached from behind a victim wearing a short skirt who was waiting for the pedestrian signal in front of a crosswalk near Goyang-si (address omitted), and secretly photographed her legs with the mobile phone at issue (hereinafter referred to as the “No. 8 offense”).\\n\\n2. The lower court’s determination\\n\\nThe lower court reversed the first-instance judgment that had found the Defendant guilty of the portion concerning the No. 1–7 offenses and acquitted him, on the grounds that the Defendant had only voluntarily submitted the video of the No. 8 offense recorded at the place where he was discovered, and that it could not be deemed that he intended to submit the videos of the No. 1–7 offenses contained in the mobile phone at issue as well; that the No. 1–7 offenses were not related to the No. 8 offense; and that the investigative authorities, while searching the mobile phone at issue, did not guarantee the Defendant’s right to participate and did not deliver a list of the seized electronic data, among other reasons.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\na. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nWhere an investigative authority receives, by voluntary submission from a suspect, a medium containing electronic information and seizes it without clearly confirming which of the information stored therein is being submitted, only electronic information related to the criminal suspicion that motivated the voluntary submission and having at least minimal value to prove it may be the object of seizure; information that can also be used as indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence concerning the motive and circumstances of the offense, the means and method, and the time and place thereof may also be included therein. Where an investigative authority receives, by voluntary submission from a suspect, a medium containing a mixture of electronic information related to the criminal suspicion and electronic information unrelated thereto, and searches, copies, and prints out the information in an office or elsewhere, it must guarantee the opportunity for the suspect or defense counsel to participate and deliver a list specifying the seized electronic information; however, even if such measures were not taken, unless the suspect’s procedural rights were not substantially infringed in light of the nature and content of the process in which the procedural violation occurred, the seizure and search cannot be deemed unlawful (see Supreme Court en banc Decision rendered on 2021. 11. 18., 2016DO348).\\n\\nb. According to the reasons of the lower court’s judgment and the evidence lawfully admitted, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n1) A police officer who was dispatched upon receiving the 112 report from the victim of the No. 8 offense voluntarily received the mobile phone at issue from the Defendant at the scene, seized it without a warrant, and voluntarily accompanied the Defendant to the police substation office. The seizure record prepared at that time states: “The victim pointed to the mobile phone possessed by the person under suspicion and claimed that he had taken a picture of her back; the person under suspicion also admitted to having taken the picture; accordingly, as the mobile phone used in the crime was requested to be voluntarily submitted, it was voluntarily submitted and seized in response thereto.”\\n\\n2) The police officer who voluntarily accompanied the Defendant examined the mobile phone at issue at the police substation, but the video recorded as the No. 8 offense had been deleted before the Defendant voluntarily submitted it and could not be found, and videos depicting the bodies of several women whose names were unknown were discovered. At that place, the Defendant prepared a written statement to the effect that, in addition to the No. 8 offense, he had secretly photographed women on several occasions.\\n\\n3) While interrogating the suspect, the police officer showed printouts of the videos recorded in the No. 1–7 offenses, and the Defendant stated specifically the time and place where they were filmed.\\n\\nc. Determination\\n\\n1) Since the Defendant did not clearly indicate the scope of the electronic information contained in the mobile phone at issue at the time he voluntarily submitted it, only electronic information related to the criminal suspicion that motivated the voluntary submission and having at least minimal value to prove it may be the object of seizure. The videos concerning the No. 1–7 offenses were recorded over a period of a little more than two months, from 2017. 6. 28. to 2017. 9. 2., and are close in time to 2017. 9. 4., the date of the No. 8 offense; moreover, like the No. 8 offense, they were recorded with the mobile phone at issue in public places such as bus stops, subway stations, and in front of crosswalks. By their nature, the above offenses leave ample room to suspect habituality or to suspect that they are a series of acts arising from the manifestation of sexual preference or tendency, and the video of each offense is in a relationship such that it may be used as evidence concerning the motive and circumstances of the offense, the means and method, and the time and place thereof, vis-à-vis one another. The videos of the No. 1–7 offenses are evidence related to the criminal suspicion regarding the No. 8 offense that motivated the voluntary submission.\\n\\n2) The police officer examined the voluntarily submitted mobile phone at the place where the Defendant was present and discovered videos other than the No. 8 offense; therefore, it may be deemed that the Defendant participated in the search.\\n\\n3) During the suspect interrogation, the police officer presented the videos of the No. 1–7 offenses, and the Defendant easily recognized when and where those videos were taken and made specific statements thereabout. Even though a list specifying the seized electronic information was not delivered to the Defendant, it is difficult to view, in light of the nature and content of the process in which the procedural violation occurred, that his procedural rights were substantially infringed.\\n\\n4) Therefore, the printouts and CD containing file copies of the videos recorded in the No. 1–7 offenses were generated from electronic information lawfully seized by voluntary submission and are admissible in evidence; accordingly, the lower court’s determination acquitting the Defendant of that portion of the offenses contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the scope of voluntary submission of electronic information contained in an information storage medium. The ground of appeal pointing this out has merit.\\n\\n4. Scope of reversal\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, the acquittal portion of the lower court’s judgment must be reversed. Since the reversed portion is in a concurrent-offense relationship under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the remaining conviction portion and a single punishment must be imposed, the entire lower court’s judgment must be reversed.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the lower court’s judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices as stated in the order."}

{"[2022DO1452]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Determination on the Prosecutor’s Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in its opinion, found that there was no proof of a crime with respect to the portions of the facts charged in this case set forth in No. 1 and Nos. 7 through 11 of Crime Table 2 in the lower-court judgment, concerning violations of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (hereinafter the “Sexual Violence Punishment Act”) (filming, distribution, etc. using cameras, etc.), and therefore acquitted the Defendant of those portions. Examining the reasons of the lower-court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in the lower court’s determination that violated the rules of logic and experience, exceeded the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misunderstood the legal principles concerning the exclusionary rule of illegally obtained evidence.\\n\\n2. Determination on the Defendant’s Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nA. Determination on the Fraud Offense Portion\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in its opinion, found the fraud portion among the facts charged in this case guilty. Examining the reasons of the lower-court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, there is no error in the lower court’s determination that violated the rules of logic and experience, exceeded the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misunderstood the legal principles concerning the exclusionary rule of illegally obtained evidence, etc.\\n\\nIn addition, the assertion that there was an illegality of mistaken fact-finding in the fraud portion concerning Victim B in the lower-court judgment is being raised for the first time at the Supreme Court level, although the Defendant did not assert it as a ground for appeal nor did the lower court treat it as a matter subject to ex officio review; therefore, it does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\nB. Determination on the Portion of the lower-court judgment set forth in Nos. 2 through 6 of Crime Table 2, concerning violations of the Sexual Violence Punishment Act (filming, distribution, etc. using cameras, etc.)\\n\\n1) Summary of the facts charged in this portion\\n\\nFrom around March 7, 2018 to around October 6, 2019, on five occasions, the Defendant, using a mobile phone camera, filmed, against their will, the bodies of victims that could arouse sexual desire or shame.\\n\\n2) The lower court’s determination\\n\\nThe lower court found this portion of the facts charged guilty for the following reasons.\\n\\nA) The police searched, copied, and printed photographs and videos relating to illegal filming offenses, which had no specific and individual connection to the fraud offense that motivated the voluntary submission, from the mobile phone voluntarily submitted by the Defendant, who was under investigation on suspicion of fraud; this constitutes an unlawful seizure and search in violation of the warrant requirement and the principle of due process.\\n\\nB) However, the police lawfully obtained from the court a seizure and search warrant for the Defendant’s suspicion of illegal filming, and, with the Defendant’s right to participate ensured, lawfully conducted the seizure and search procedures, and seized from the C cloud linked to a mobile phone separate from the voluntarily submitted mobile phone the illegal-filming photographs and videos corresponding to the results of the offense in this portion of the facts charged. These are newly collected pieces of evidence different from the photographs and videos discovered in the voluntarily submitted mobile phone.\\n\\nC) Criminal acts caused by illegal-filming materials have the nature of significantly infringing upon the victim’s personal rights, and are also subject to confiscation; therefore, there is a substantial need to protect victims by promptly seizing and searching them so as to timely block the possibility of distribution of illegal-filming materials.\\n\\nD) Accordingly, as to the police seizure protocol and detailed list of electronic information prepared pursuant to the execution of the seizure and search warrant (evidence list Nos. 34 and 36), the investigative report setting forth the circumstances thereof (evidence list No. 40), each investigative report recording the contents of calls with Victims D and E after the seizure and search execution (evidence list Nos. 51, 104, and 112), and the text message from Victim D (evidence list No. 52), the exception doctrine to the exclusionary rule of illegally obtained evidence applies, and evidentiary admissibility is recognized.\\n\\n3) The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\nHowever, the foregoing determination of the lower court cannot be sustained for the following reasons.\\n\\nA) In light of the spirit of due process and the warrant requirement embodied in the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, the wording used by a judge in issuing a seizure and search warrant to specify the “items to be seized” must be strictly construed, and it is not permissible to expansively construe or analogically construe it in a manner unfavorable to the person subject to seizure, etc. (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DO763, decided March 12, 2009, etc.).\\n\\nStorage media containing electronic information to be seized are distinguished from computers or other information-processing devices, such as computers, hard disks, and mobile phones, located at the place to be searched as stated in the seizure and search warrant, and remote servers, etc. connected to computers or other information-processing devices through an information and communications network and not located at the place to be searched (hereinafter “remote servers”), in terms of location, administrator, and storage capacity. In order to seize and search electronic information stored on a remote server, procedures are required in which a computer or other information-processing device is used to access the remote server through an information and communications network and the electronic information stored thereon is downloaded to the computer or other information-processing device or displayed on a screen; thus, there is a difference in the method of seizure and search compared with electronic information stored on the computer or other information-processing device itself. Because electronic information stored on a remote server and electronic information stored on a computer or other information-processing device differ in content or quality, the scope of electronic information obtainable by seizure and search and the degree of infringement upon fundamental rights resulting therefrom also differ.\\n\\nTherefore, in order for investigative authorities to seize and search electronic information stored on a remote server in addition to electronic information stored on a computer or other information-processing device located at the “place to be searched” stated in the seizure and search warrant, the electronic information stored on the remote server must be separately specified in the “items to be seized” stated in the seizure and search warrant. If the “items to be seized” stated in the seizure and search warrant list only electronic information stored on a computer or other information-processing device, then electronic information stored on a remote server cannot be seized by using a computer or other information-processing device.\\n\\nB) From the reasons for the lower-court judgment and the lawfully admitted evidence, the following facts can be ascertained. (1) On December 23, 2020, while investigating the Defendant on suspicion of fraud against Victim F, the police, with the Defendant’s consent, used the Defendant’s mobile phone to confirm bank transaction records and call records, messages related to debts, and mobile phone messenger conversation records. When the Defendant deleted the mobile phone messenger conversation records during a break, the police requested the Defendant and received the mobile phone as a voluntary submission.\\n\\n(2) While searching the voluntarily submitted mobile phone, the police discovered photographs and videos suspected to be illegal-filming materials in the camera folder, and by contacting the women believed to be the victims, confirmed that they had not consented to the taking of the photographs and videos.\\n\\n(3) On February 18, 2021, the police obtained from the Incheon District Court a seizure and search warrant (hereinafter the “Seizure and Search Warrant in this Case”) stating the “items to be seized” as “computer hard disks and external storage media containing image and video files judged to have secretly captured the bodies of women,” the “place to be searched” as the Defendant’s residence, namely “H Building, Unit H, Yeonsu-gu, Incheon,” and the “offense facts” as “violations of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (filming, distribution, etc. using cameras, etc.), etc.”\\n\\n(4) On February 21, 2021, the police discovered and seized at the Defendant’s residence a mobile phone separate from the voluntarily submitted mobile phone (hereinafter the “mobile phone in this case”), and, using the fact that the mobile phone in this case was logged into the C account, confirmed illegal-filming materials concerning Victim E in the C cloud and then seized four videos and three photographs related to the offense set forth in Nos. 2 through 6 of Crime Table 2 in the lower-court judgment by downloading selected files.\\n\\n(5) The police prepared a seizure protocol and detailed list of electronic information concerning the above seized items (evidence list Nos. 34 and 36), and prepared an investigative report stating that illegal-filming materials were discovered as a result of searching the C cloud linked to the mobile phone in this case (evidence list No. 40). Thereafter, the police and a public prosecutor’s assistant examiner prepared each investigative report recording calls with Victims D and E, who stated that they had not consented to being filmed (evidence list Nos. 51, 104, and 112), and received a text message of the same content from Victim D (evidence list No. 52).\\n\\nC) The lower court, premising that the execution of the Seizure and Search Warrant in this Case was lawful, found this portion of the facts charged guilty on the ground that the evidence in paragraph (5) above acquired through that execution had evidentiary admissibility.\\n\\nHowever, examining the foregoing factual circumstances in light of the legal principles stated above, the seizure and search of the illegal-filming photographs and videos stored in the C cloud by using the mobile phone in this case while executing the Seizure and Search Warrant in this Case was unlawful, and the evidence in paragraph (5) above lacks evidentiary admissibility. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) The “items to be seized” stated in the Seizure and Search Warrant in this Case include “computer hard disks and external storage media containing image and video files judged to have secretly captured the bodies of women,” and the “place to be searched” is stated as the Defendant’s residence. Unless the “items to be seized” stated in the Seizure and Search Warrant in this Case specify electronic information stored on a remote server, the “items to be seized” stated in the Seizure and Search Warrant in this Case are limited to electronic information stored on computer hard disks and external storage media at the Defendant’s residence.\\n\\n(2) Nevertheless, the police accessed the C cloud, which constitutes a remote server, by using the mobile phone in this case while it was logged into the C account, and seized the illegal-filming materials found in the C cloud. Ultimately, the police seizure exceeded the scope of seizure permitted by the Seizure and Search Warrant in this Case, and is unlawful in violation of the principles of due process and the warrant requirement.\\n\\n(3) Therefore, the illegal-filming materials collected under the Seizure and Search Warrant in this Case constitute illegally obtained evidence lacking evidentiary admissibility, and the seizure protocol, etc. revealing the execution circumstances of the Seizure and Search Warrant in this Case, as well as the statements of related persons collected by presenting illegally obtained evidence, also constitute secondary evidence based on illegally obtained evidence and thus lack evidentiary admissibility.\\n\\nD) In the end, in this case, it is difficult to view the facts charged in this portion as having been proven beyond a reasonable doubt by the remaining evidence alone, excluding the evidence lacking evidentiary admissibility.\\n\\nE) Nevertheless, the lower court found this portion of the facts charged guilty. The lower-court judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the effect of the seizure and search warrant and the exclusionary rule of illegally obtained evidence. The Defendant’s ground for appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Scope of Reversal\\n\\nThe portion of the lower-court judgment concerning violations of the Sexual Violence Punishment Act (filming, distribution, etc. using cameras, etc.) set forth in Nos. 2 through 6 of Crime Table 2 in the lower-court judgment must be reversed for the reasons stated above. And among the reversed portion, the fraud portion for which a single sentence was imposed in a concurrent offense relationship under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the portion of the lower-court judgment concerning violations of the Sexual Violence Punishment Act (filming, distribution, etc. using cameras, etc.) set forth in No. 6 of Crime Table 2 in the lower-court judgment must also be reversed. In the end, the guilty portion of the lower-court judgment must be reversed in its entirety.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without addressing the Defendant’s remaining grounds for appeal, we reverse the guilty portion of the lower-court judgment against the Defendant and dismiss the Prosecutor’s appeal, and by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, render the judgment as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following is the correct combination of the true (○) and false (×) statements concerning concurrence of offenses? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents) (a) Where, through one act of deception, property is fraudulently obtained from multiple victims, each victim gives rise to an independent offense of fraud, and each offense of fraud stands in a relationship of ideal concurrence, even if the intent is singular and the method of commission is the same. (b) Where a person who was entrusted by a thief with the safekeeping of stolen goods, knowing that they are stolen goods, receives and keeps them and then disposes of them at will, such embezzling act is merely a non-punishable subsequent act of the offense of stolen goods and does not constitute a separate offense of embezzlement. (c) If pecuniary damage is caused to a company by arbitrarily preparing and delivering a settlement agreement in the company’s name, the offense of forging a private document and the offense of uttering such document, and the offense of occupational breach of trust, are in a relationship of real concurrence. (d) When a document jointly signed and sealed by two or more persons named as makers is forged by a single act, it constitutes an ideal concurrence of offenses of forging a document corresponding to the number of persons named as makers. (e) Where a person who has received a final and conclusive judgment of conviction thereafter commits a separate subsequent offense, and a retrial is commenced with respect to the final and conclusive judgment of conviction, concurrent offenses as provided in the latter sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act are established between the subsequent offense and the prior offense for which the retrial judgment has become final and conclusive.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2003DO8219]": "1. Even if a person who, having been entrusted by a thief with the safekeeping of stolen property, receives and keeps the property knowing the circumstances and thereafter disposes of it at his own discretion, the offense of receiving and keeping stolen property is established, and because the owner’s right to recover his property has already been infringed, the subsequent act of embezzlement is merely a non-punishable subsequent act and does not separately constitute the offense of embezzlement (see Supreme Court Decision 76DO3067 rendered on November 23, 1976).\\n\\n2. Based on the evidence it admitted, the lower appellate court found that, although the Defendant, in the beginning of September 2002, when he received a request from a person not named in the indictment to sell one Goryeo celadon mandarin-duck-shaped incense burner, which was stolen property, for KRW 250,000,000, had a duty of care in the course of business to ascertain whether the above incense burner was stolen property, he negligently failed to do so and received the above incense burner, thereby keeping stolen property; and that thereafter, on November 29, 2002, while borrowing money from Jin Jeong-u, he provided the above incense burner then being kept as security. After recognizing these facts, the lower appellate court determined that the Defendant’s act of disposing of the above incense burner, which was stolen property and which he had kept through negligence in the course of business, is included in the punishable evaluation of the offense of negligent safekeeping of stolen property in the course of business and does not separately constitute embezzlement. The lower appellate court’s determination is proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality such as misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning the non-punishable subsequent act in the offense of stolen property.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as follows by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2008DO5634]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Determination on the Part Concerning Dismissal of Prosecution\\n\\nIn the case of the relationship of ideal concurrence under Article 40 of the Criminal Act, the binding force of a final and conclusive judgment on one offense also extends to the other offenses (see Supreme Court Decisions 91DO643, rendered June 25, 1991, and 91DO2642, rendered December 10, 1991, etc.), and here, one act means that, apart from legal evaluation, from the perspective of social common sense, the act is evaluated as one as a state of natural existence (see Supreme Court Decision 86DO2731, rendered February 24, 1987).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below and the record, the gist of the count of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Breach of Trust) among the facts charged in this case is that, “The Defendant is a person who worked as the head of the development planning team of the victim, Nonparty 1 Construction. While Nonparty 1 Construction had failed to perform the memorandum of understanding executed on April 22, 2005 between Nonparty 1 Construction and Nonparty 2 Construction, and was being demanded by Nonparty 2 Construction to return the agreed amount and penalty, on June 28, 2005, at the office of Nonparty 1 Construction, when the nonparty who had prepared on behalf of Nonparty 2 Construction an agreement stating that ‘Nonparty 1 Construction shall compensate Nonparty 2 Construction by paying double the down payment of 500 million won, and shall pay 500 million won as the first installment by June 29, 2005 and 500 million won as the second installment by July 6, 2005’ requested that the Defendant affix the corporate seal of Nonparty 1 Construction to the agreement, the Defendant, in violation of his duty to prepare the agreement by following the normal approval procedure, such as obtaining the representative director’s approval, affixed the corporate seal of Nonparty 1 Construction to the said agreement and then handed it over to the said nonparty, thereby causing Nonparty 2 Construction to obtain a property benefit exceeding by 500 million won the agreed amount originally to be received, and causing Nonparty 1 Construction to additionally bear a property debt of 500 million won in excess of the agreed amount originally to be returned, thereby inflicting property damage equivalent thereto.” Meanwhile, it is ascertainable that, with respect to the act of preparing and using the agreement dated June 28, 2005 described in the above facts charged, the Defendant was notified, on October 13, 2006, by the Suwon District Court of a summary order imposing a fine of 500,000 won for forgery of a private document and uttering thereof, and that the said summary order became final and conclusive around that time.\\n\\nIf so, the facts constituting the offense of forgery of a private document and uttering thereof in the final and conclusive summary order and the above facts charged that the Defendant arbitrarily prepared and delivered the same agreement and thereby caused property damage to the company are such that the objective factual relationship constitutes one act, and thus this is a case where one act falls under several offenses and is in the relationship of ideal concurrence prescribed in Article 40 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nOn the same purport, the court below’s determination that the binding force of the above final and conclusive summary order also extends to the above facts charged is proper, and there is no illegality such as a misapprehension of the law as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Determination on the Part Concerning Acquittal\\n\\nThe appellate court may investigate and determine only within the extent of the appeal filed on the grounds of appeal; therefore, the statement of reasons for appeal must specify the grounds for appeal and contain a specific and explicit statement of reasons as to which point of the judgment below violated which law and how. Where the statement of reasons for appeal submitted by the appellant merely states, without such specific and explicit statement of reasons, that the judgment below is in violation due to factual error or misapprehension of legal principles, and does not at all assert specific reasons as to which evidentiary disposition violated the rules of evidence, or what misapplication of law exists and in what respect it is improper, it cannot be regarded as a lawful statement of grounds for appeal (see Supreme Court Decision 99DO5513, rendered April 21, 2000, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Prosecutor, when filing the appeal, submitted a petition of appeal that briefly stated only “entirety” in the column for the scope of appeal and “there is illegality affecting the judgment due to violation of the rules of evidence and misunderstanding of legal principles” in the column for the grounds of appeal; and thereafter, the statement of reasons for appeal did not set forth any grounds for appeal concerning the acquittal part. In light of the foregoing legal principles, it is difficult to view that a lawful ground for appeal was submitted with respect to the acquittal part; accordingly, the Prosecutor’s appeal as to this part is without merit.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is adjudged as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court involved."}

{"[2014DO16980]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n1. Concerning the grounds of appeal by Defendant 1\\nA. Concerning the point of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Fraud)\\n(1) The amount of gain referred to in Article 3 of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes means the amount of gain from a single offense or the aggregated amount of gain in cases where a comprehensive single offense is established, and does not mean the sum of the amounts of gain for multiple offenses punishable as concurrent offenses (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2000DO28, decided March 24, 2000); where, by means of separate acts of deception against multiple victims, property benefits have been fraudulently obtained from each of them, even if the criminal intent is single and the method of offense is the same, the protected legal interests of each victim are independent, so such acts cannot be regarded as a comprehensive single offense, and separate offenses of fraud are established for each victim (see Supreme Court Decision 93DO743, decided June 22, 1993). However, where there are circumstances indicating that the protected legal interests of the victims may be regarded as identical, such as where the victims constitute a single business partnership, the offenses of fraud against them may also be viewed as a single offense in the aggregate, notwithstanding that there are multiple victims (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2011DO769, decided April 14, 2011). Furthermore, where property benefits are fraudulently obtained from multiple victims by a single act of deception, multiple offenses of fraud are established for each victim, and the relationship among them should be regarded as one of ideal concurrence (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2010DO9330, decided January 13, 2011).\\n(2) The court below, based on a comprehensive examination of the evidence cited in the judgment, found: ① that the victims, Non-indicted Persons 1, 2, and 3, owned each a one-third share in the forest land of 10,860 square meters at Mangu-ri, Tanhyeon-myeon, Paju-si, (Address 1 omitted), and the forest land of 972 square meters in the same ri, (Address 2 omitted) (hereinafter referred to as the “Mangu-ri real property”); ② that the victims entered into a sales contract with Defendant 1 concerning the Mangu-ri real property on August 2, 2011, and, in accordance with the contents of that sales contract, entered into a contract for the establishment of a mortgage with Non-indicted Person 4 concerning the said real property on September 5, 2011; and, after so finding, held that it was reasonable to view the protected legal interests as identical because, rather than separately deceiving the co-owners who had a common interest in disposing of each ownership share in the Mangu-ri real property simultaneously and in bulk and thereby causing each of the victims to establish separate mortgages over their respective co-owned shares, a single mortgage was established over the entirety of the said real property. Accordingly, it upheld the trial court, which had found the relevant charge of the indictment to be guilty on the ground that Defendant 1’s act in this part constituted an act of fraudulently obtaining property benefits in the amount of 700 million won, the maximum secured amount of the mortgage established on the Mangu-ri real property, from the victims in the aggregate, and thus fell under the offense of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Fraud).\\n(3) However, the court below’s determination cannot be accepted as it stands for the following reasons.\\nAccording to the record: ① on May 29, 1962, Non-indicted Persons 2 and 1, and Non-indicted Person 5 completed registration of transfer of ownership, each for a one-third share in the Mangu-ri real property, on the ground of sale dated May 10, 1962; ② on September 24, 2009, Victim Non-indicted Person 3 completed registration of transfer of shares, on the ground of inheritance by agreement and partition dated July 5, 2002, with respect to Non-indicted Person 5’s aforementioned one-third share in the Mangu-ri real property; ③ the victims met Defendant 1 and others together at a judicial scrivener’s office and entered into a sales contract for the Mangu-ri real property with the purchase price set at 1.43 billion won, and each of the victims separately signed and sealed the sales contract and the contract for establishment of mortgage, etc.; and ④ Victim Non-indicted Person 1 stated in the Prosecutor’s Office, in rebuttal to the explanation of co-defendant 2 at the court below, who had said, “I asked Victim Non-indicted Person 1 for help and thus decided not to prepare the documents for release of the mortgage establishment to the victims,” that “the Mangu-ri real property was jointly owned by three persons, so it was a situation where [he/she] could not give permission alone.”\\nAs such, taking into comprehensive consideration the circumstances in which the victims acquired their respective co-owned shares in the Mangu-ri real property, the fact that the victims met Defendant 1 together and exercised, each for himself/herself, the power to dispose of his/her own co-owned share, and the absence of any other circumstance indicating that the protected legal interests are identical, such as the victims constituting a single business partnership, each victim’s protected legal interest is independent; accordingly, separate offenses of fraud are established for each victim, and the act of Defendant 1 and others in fraudulently obtaining each property benefit from the victims at the same time and place may, in social common sense, be evaluated as a single act, so the relationship between the above offenses of fraud is one of ideal concurrence.\\n(4) Nevertheless, the court below, solely for the reasons stated in its judgment, regarded each offense of fraud against the victims by Defendant 1 as a single offense in the aggregate and charged it as a violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Fraud). Thus, the court below’s determination contains an error that affected the conclusion of the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the amount of gain prescribed in Article 3 of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes and the count of offenses in fraud. Defendant 1’s assertion in this part of the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\nB. Concerning the point of violation of Article 40(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act\\nThe gist of this part of Defendant 1’s grounds of appeal is that Defendant 1’s retained counsel submitted a notice of appointment and a motion to reopen arguments on November 19, 2014, the day before the date of pronouncement of the judgment by the court below, but the court below only listed the name of the court-appointed counsel in the judgment and did not list the name of the retained counsel; therefore, the court below’s judgment is unlawful for violating Article 40(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, which provides that “the name of the counsel shall be stated in the judgment.”\\nHowever, since the court below listed the name of the court-appointed counsel as of the date of conclusion of arguments, it cannot be said to have violated Article 40(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, nor can it be said that this affected the conclusion of the judgment.\\nC. Concerning the remaining grounds of appeal by Defendant 1, excluding the claim of inappropriate sentencing\\nWhere a person deceives another for the purpose of borrowing money from a third party or receiving goods on credit and causes the other person’s real property to be mortgaged in favor of the third party, the property benefit thereby acquired is the benefit of being able to use the other person’s real property as security for transactions with that third party (see Supreme Court Decisions 84DO119, decided April 10, 1984, and 96DO384, decided March 22, 1996, etc.), and the value thereof (amount of gain) is, in principle, equivalent to the maximum secured amount within the market value of the real property (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DO137, decided April 25, 2000).\\nExamining the reasons for the court below’s judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence duly admitted by the court below and the trial court upheld by the court below, the court below’s determination that, for the reasons stated in its judgment, the remaining charges in this case, except for the part concerning Defendant 1’s violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Fraud), are guilty is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the calculation of the amount of gain in the offense of fraud, or any violation of the rules of logic and experience, thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n2. Concerning the Prosecutor’s grounds of appeal\\nFor the reasons stated in its judgment, the court below found Defendant 2 not guilty on the ground that the facts charged against Defendant 2 were not proven.\\nExamining the reasons for the court below’s judgment in light of the record, the above determination of the court below is proper and can be accepted, and there is no illegality such as violation of the rules of logic and experience, thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehension of the relevant legal principles, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n3. Scope of reversal\\nFor the reasons examined above, the part of the court below’s judgment concerning Defendant 1’s violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Fraud) must be reversed. However, since the court below punished the remaining part concerning Defendant 1 as concurrent offenses, the entire part of the court below’s judgment concerning Defendant 1 must be reversed.\\n4. Conclusion\\nTherefore, omitting the determination on Defendant 1’s claim of inappropriate sentencing, the part of the court below’s judgment concerning Defendant 1 is reversed, and this case, insofar as it concerns that part, is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; the Prosecutor’s appeal is dismissed; and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2018DO20698]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Procedural History\\na. The gist of the facts charged in this case is as follows.\\n1) The Defendant, habitually, stole a total of 21 credit cards or debit cards belonging to the victims over 20 occasions from around 2016. 10. 3. to around 2017. 10. 28., and, during the same period, stole cash totaling 111,360,900 won belonging to the victims over 46 occasions at an ATM by using the cards stolen as above. In this way, after being sentenced to imprisonment with prison labor more than twice and after the execution of such sentence had been completed or remitted, the Defendant again, within 3 years, habitually committed larceny.\\n2) During the same period as in paragraph 1) above, the Defendant used another person’s stolen credit card on 26 occasions.\\nb. With respect to the Defendant, the following retrial judgments became final in relation to offenses committed before the facts charged in this case.\\n1) The Defendant, habitually, was sentenced by the Busan District Court on 2003. 10. 13. to 2 years of imprisonment with prison labor for violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Act on the Aggravated Punishment of Specific Crimes”) and other offenses, on the factual basis that from 2003. 2. 9. to 2003. 8. 16. he stole credit cards and withdrew and stole cash by using the stolen credit cards, and the judgment became final on 2003. 12. 13. The Constitutional Court held that, among the statutory provisions applied in the above judgment, the portion concerning Article 329 of the Criminal Act in Article 5-4(1) of the former Act on the Aggravated Punishment of Specific Crimes (as amended by Act No. 10210 on 2010. 3. 31., hereinafter the same) was unconstitutional, etc. (Constitutional Court en banc decision of 2015. 2. 26., 2014HEONGA16, etc.). The Defendant petitioned for a retrial of the above judgment, and after the indictment was amended at the same court to habitual larceny, he was sentenced to 2 years of imprisonment with prison labor and appealed, but on 2016. 12. 22. the appellate court rendered a judgment dismissing the appeal, and on 2016. 12. 30. the above retrial judgment became final (hereinafter referred to as “the first retrial judgment in this case”).\\n2) The Defendant was sentenced by the Busan District Court on 2001. 8. 31. to 1 year and 6 months of imprisonment with prison labor for violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment of Specific Crimes and other offenses, and the judgment became final on 2001. 12. 5. Through retrial proceedings, on 2018. 4. 27. the same court rendered a judgment of dismissal of prosecution as to habitual larceny, which was the amended facts charged, and sentenced him to 1 year and 6 months of imprisonment with prison labor as to the remaining facts charged, namely, violation of the Specialized Credit Finance Business Act, and the above retrial judgment became final on 2018. 8. 10. (hereinafter referred to as “the second retrial judgment in this case”).\\nc. The lower court, after the above retrial judgments became final, on 2018. 12. 6. rendered a judgment of conviction on all of the facts charged in this case, and on the premise that the offenses in the final second retrial judgment in this case and the offenses charged in this case were not in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act (hereinafter referred to as “concurrent offenses under the latter part”), it did not reduce or exempt the punishment pursuant to Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act.\\nd. The gist of the Defendant’s grounds for appeal is as follows.\\n1) The res judicata effect of the final first retrial judgment in this case extends to the offenses of theft committed on 2016. 10. 3. among the offenses that, as offenses in a comprehensive single offense (habitual offense), are in a relationship with the offenses of the first retrial judgment, and therefore a judgment of dismissal of prosecution should be rendered.\\n2) Since the offenses in the final second retrial judgment in this case and the offenses charged in this case are in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part, Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act should be applied.\\n3) Because the act by which the Defendant withdrew cash using a card in the name of a person not charged in the prosecution was not use in accordance with the original manner of use of a credit card or debit card, the offense of violation of the Specialized Credit Finance Business Act is not established.\\n4) The sentence imposed on the Defendant (5 years of imprisonment with prison labor) is excessively severe.\\n\\n2. On the assertions concerning res judicata and concurrent offenses under the latter part\\nThe issues in this part are what the temporal scope of the res judicata effect of a retrial judgment is, and whether concurrent offenses under the latter part are established between the offense for which the retrial judgment imposing imprisonment or a heavier punishment has become final and the offense committed before such retrial judgment became final. Because these issues are closely related to whether the effect of the judgment subject to retrial continues after the decision to commence retrial becomes final and whether amendment of the indictment to add facts charged in the retrial proceedings is permissible, we first examine those matters and then determine, in order, res judicata and concurrent offenses under the latter part.\\n\\na. We examine the special nature of retrial proceedings.\\n1) The Criminal Procedure Act provides retrial as one of the special proceedings in Part 4 and limits the grounds on which retrial may be petitioned by exhaustively enumerating them (Article 420), and the Constitutional Court Act permits retrial of a final conviction based on a law or provision thereof that has been held unconstitutional (Article 47(4)). Retrial is an exceptional, extraordinary remedy that reexamines factual determinations that became final at that level or through appeal (see Supreme Court en banc decision of 2005. 9. 28., 2004MO453, etc.), and it is designed to roll back the legal stability maintained by the finality of the judgment and to realize concrete justice where there is a serious defect in a final judgment (see Supreme Court Decision of 2019. 2. 28., 2018DO13382; Constitutional Court en banc decision of 2011. 6. 30., 2009HEONBA430, etc.).\\nThe Criminal Procedure Act allows only so-called beneficial retrial, which is for the benefit of the accused, by providing that “retrial may be petitioned for the benefit of the person who received the sentence” as to a final conviction and a judgment dismissing appeal or final appeal (Articles 420 and 421(1)). Further, reflecting the principle of beneficial retrial, it provides that “in retrial, a sentence more severe than the sentence of the original judgment may not be imposed” (Article 439 of the Criminal Procedure Act). This purports to permit retrial for the realization of substantive justice, while retrial must also be conducted within a scope that does not impair the accused’s legal stability, for the accused’s benefit (see Supreme Court Decision of 2018. 2. 28., 2015DO15782, etc.).\\n2) Under the Criminal Procedure Act, retrial proceedings are distinguished into the procedure for examining whether retrial should be commenced and the adjudicatory procedure after the decision to commence retrial becomes final. In the retrial-commencement procedure, the court determines only whether there exists any ground for retrial provided in the Criminal Procedure Act, etc., and the substantive question of whether the ground for retrial is capable of affecting the judgment subject to retrial may not be considered (see Supreme Court Order of 2008. 4. 24., 2008MO77). Meanwhile, a petition for retrial does not have the effect of suspending execution of sentence (Article 428 of the Criminal Procedure Act), and even when a decision to commence retrial is made upon finding the petition for retrial well-founded, execution of sentence may be suspended only by order (Article 435(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act); it is not automatically suspended thereby. In light of the nature of the procedure for examining whether retrial should be commenced, its scope of determination, and the effect of the decision to commence retrial, the mere fact that the retrial adjudication proceedings are pending after the decision to commence retrial becomes final with respect to a final conviction, etc. cannot negate the existence or effect of the final judgment, and the previous final judgment loses its effect only when the decision to commence retrial becomes final, the court reexamines the case, renders a retrial judgment, and that retrial judgment becomes final (see Supreme Court Order of 2005. 9. 28., 2004MO453; Supreme Court Decision of 2017. 9. 21., 2017DO4019, etc.).\\n3) Once the decision to commence retrial becomes final, the court must again adjudicate according to its level, except as provided in Article 436 of the Criminal Procedure Act (Article 438(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act). Retrial adjudication proceedings are not a subsequent procedure to the previous litigation that reviews whether the original judgment was proper; they are a completely new litigation procedure that adjudicates the case itself anew from the beginning (see the above 2015DO15782 decision, etc.). However, this means that the retrial court must determine the guilt or innocence of the case subject to retrial and determine the sentence without being bound by the contents of the judgment subject to retrial, under the restriction of the principle of beneficial retrial; it does not mean that all laws applicable to ordinary proceedings apply in the same way to retrial adjudication proceedings, which are an extraordinary remedy. Laws governing ordinary proceedings may apply to retrial adjudication proceedings only to the extent that they do not contradict the purpose and nature of retrial as an extraordinary remedy. In light of the purpose and nature of retrial and the special rules concerning the principle of beneficial retrial and retrial adjudication proceedings in the Criminal Procedure Act, except in special circumstances, the prosecutor may not amend the indictment in retrial adjudication proceedings so as to add facts charged separate from the case subject to retrial, and it is also not permissible to consolidate and hear separately pending criminal cases under ordinary procedure with the case subject to retrial.\\n\\nb. We examine retrial adjudication proceedings and res judicata.\\nWhere a person who received a final conviction for a habitual offense (hereinafter, the offense committed earlier and subject to retrial is referred to as the “prior offense”) thereafter committed offenses by the same habitual propensity (hereinafter, the offenses committed later are referred to as the “subsequent offense”), and retrial has been commenced with respect to the final conviction, the res judicata effect of the retrial judgment does not extend to the subsequent offense even if the subsequent offense by the same habitual propensity was committed before the retrial judgment on the judgment subject to retrial was rendered. The reasons are as follows.\\n1) A habitual offense refers to a type of offense in which repeated criminal acts are punished more severely when the offender who performed acts falling under the basic elements of the offense has the habitual propensity to repeatedly commit such criminal acts, namely, the actor-related attribute of habituality. It has long been the view consistently held by the Supreme Court that where a person with such habituality commits multiple offenses repeatedly, all of them should be treated not as separate offenses to be punished as concurrent offenses, but as one offense called a habitual offense, because that accords with the essence of habitual offenses and the legislative purpose of the aggravated punishment provisions for habitual offenses (see many cases, including Supreme Court en banc decision of 2004. 9. 16., 2001DO3206). Therefore, if, among several factual bases constituting a comprehensive single offense as a habitual offense, a person is prosecuted as a habitual offender for some of them and a judgment of conviction becomes final, and thereafter new prosecution is instituted for the remaining offenses committed before the factual trial judgment in that final judgment was rendered, such new prosecution corresponds to a renewed prosecution for the same case as the case in which the final judgment was rendered, and a judgment dismissing prosecution must be rendered for such prosecution (Article 326 subparagraph 1 of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\nMeanwhile, because the temporal scope of the effect of instituting prosecution in a habitual offense must be based on the time of pronouncement of judgment, which is the latest point at which factual adjudication is possible, the effect of instituting prosecution and the res judicata effect of the judgment extend only to acts done up to that time (see Supreme Court Decisions of 1999. 11. 26., 99DO3929, 99GAMDO97, etc.). Therefore, where there is a final conviction for another offense committed by the same habitual propensity between a series of offenses committed through habituality in a habitual offense, the unity of the prior and subsequent offenses is severed by that final conviction, and they become separate offenses lacking identity (see Supreme Court Decisions of 2000. 3. 10., 99DO2744; 2017. 4. 28., 2016DO21342, etc.). This is because the factual offenses before and after the final conviction could not possibly be tried simultaneously.\\n2) In retrial adjudication proceedings, because it is not permissible to amend the indictment by adding the subsequent offense to the facts charged in the prior offense, that is, the facts charged in the judgment subject to retrial, or to additionally institute prosecution and then consolidate it with the case subject to retrial for trial, there is no possibility of factual adjudication of the subsequent offense in retrial adjudication proceedings. Further, because the finality of the decision to commence retrial alone does not extinguish the effect of the judgment subject to retrial in retrial adjudication proceedings, the judgment subject to retrial remains valid as a final judgment, and therefore the unity of the prior offense and the subsequent offense committed before and after the judgment subject to retrial is severed by the judgment subject to retrial, becoming separate habitual offenses lacking identity. Accordingly, the effect of instituting prosecution for the prior offense does not extend to the subsequent offense, and the res judicata effect of the retrial judgment on the prior offense does not extend to the subsequent offense.\\n3) The Criminal Procedure Act imposes no limitation on the timing of a petition for retrial (see Article 427, etc.). If the res judicata effect of a retrial judgment were to extend to all offenses committed by the same habitual propensity as the prior offense before the retrial judgment was rendered, then offenses committed between the rendition of the retrial-eligible judgment for the prior offense and the rendition of the retrial judgment, despite having had no possibility of simultaneous trial, would all become unpunishable, which would create a gap in punishment and run counter to equity.\\nWhere, before a retrial judgment on the prior offense is rendered, a judgment on the subsequent offense is rendered and becomes final first, the effect of instituting prosecution for the subsequent offense does not extend to the prior offense. This is because, when the subsequent offense is prosecuted or tried, the judgment subject to retrial exists validly, and in the proceeding for the subsequent offense, the unity between the prior offense and the subsequent offense is severed by the final conviction in the judgment subject to retrial, so they should be regarded as separate habitual offenses. However, if, conversely, the retrial judgment is rendered and becomes final before the judgment on the subsequent offense, and the res judicata effect of the retrial judgment on the prior offense is held to extend to the subsequent offense, then whether res judicata extends would differ depending on the accidental circumstance of which judgment becomes rendered and final first among the retrial judgment on the prior offense and the judgment on the subsequent offense, resulting in an inequitable outcome.\\nc. We examine retrial adjudication proceedings and concurrent offenses under the latter part.\\n1) Where a person who received a final conviction later committed separate subsequent offenses, and retrial has been commenced with respect to the final conviction, even if the subsequent offense was committed before the retrial judgment on the judgment subject to retrial became final, concurrent offenses under the latter part are not established between the subsequent offense, for which no judgment has yet been rendered, and the prior offense for which the retrial judgment has become final. The reasons are as follows.\\na) In light of the wording and legislative purpose of the latter part of Article 37 and Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, where an offense for which no judgment has yet been rendered could not be tried simultaneously with an offense for which a judgment has already become final, a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part cannot be established, and under Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act, the sentence cannot be reduced or exempted in consideration of equity with a simultaneous trial. Therefore, where several offenses for which no judgment has yet been rendered were committed before and after the finalization of judgment, even if the offenses committed before finalization could not be tried simultaneously with the offenses for which judgment has already become final, it cannot be said that a relationship of concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act is recognized among the several offenses as though no final judgment existed, such that Article 38 of the Criminal Act applies; rather, separate sentences must be determined and imposed for the respective offenses committed before and after finalization of judgment (see Supreme Court Decision of 2014. 3. 27., 2014DO469, etc.).\\nb) If, where the retrial judgment becomes final before the judgment on the subsequent offense is rendered, concurrent offenses under the latter part are to be deemed established for the subsequent offense on the basis of the retrial judgment, the retrial court must have been able to render judgment simultaneously on the subsequent offense. However, because the subsequent offense for which no judgment has yet been rendered could not be tried together with the prior offense that became the subject of retrial in the retrial adjudication proceedings and simultaneously judged, concurrent offenses under the latter part are not established between the subsequent offense and the prior offense for which the retrial judgment became final, and the sentence cannot be reduced or exempted in consideration of equity with a simultaneous trial.\\nc) If, where the judgment on the subsequent offense becomes final first and the retrial court renders a retrial judgment on the prior offense, the prior offense cannot be treated as an offense committed before finalization of judgment on the basis of the final conviction for the subsequent offense so as to deem concurrent offenses under the latter part established. This is because, at the time the judgment on the subsequent offense was rendered, the judgment subject to retrial on the prior offense existed and had become final, and thus the prior offense for which the judgment subject to retrial became final and the subsequent offense could not have been judged simultaneously. Nevertheless, if, where the retrial judgment becomes final before the judgment on the subsequent offense, the subsequent offense is formally treated on the basis of the retrial judgment as an offense committed before finalization of judgment so as to deem concurrent offenses under the latter part established, then an inequitable result arises in which whether concurrent offenses under the latter part are established depends on the accidental circumstance of which judgment becomes final first among the retrial judgment on the prior offense and the judgment on the subsequent offense.\\n2) By contrast, Supreme Court Decision of 2013. 9. 12., 2012DO12190, and Supreme Court Decision of 2016. 2. 18., 2015DO17440, etc., which held to the effect that where a person who received a judgment subject to retrial thereafter committed separate subsequent offenses and the retrial judgment on the judgment subject to retrial became final before the judgment on the subsequent offense, concurrent offenses under the latter part are established between the subsequent offense and the offense in the retrial case for which the retrial judgment became final, are modified to the extent that they conflict with this decision.\\nd. Examining this case in light of these legal principles, the following is determined.\\n1) The first retrial judgment in this case became final, but at the time the first retrial judgment in this case was rendered, the judgment subject to retrial existed validly as a final judgment, so the offenses in the first retrial judgment in this case and the theft offenses on 2016. 10. 3. among the facts charged in this case are severed and become separate habitual offenses lacking identity, and the retrial court for the first retrial judgment in this case also had no possibility of simultaneously trying the theft offenses on 2016. 10. 3. among the facts charged in this case. Therefore, the res judicata effect of the first retrial judgment in this case does not extend to the theft offenses on 2016. 10. 3. among the facts charged in this case. Although there is some inaccuracy in the lower court’s reasoning, the lower court’s determination that the res judicata effect of the final first retrial judgment in this case does not extend to the theft offenses on 2016. 10. 3. among the facts charged in this case does not contain, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, an error of misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the res judicata effect of a final judgment.\\n2) Because the offenses charged in this case by the Defendant fall within the category in which they could not have been adjudicated simultaneously with the final offenses in the second retrial judgment in this case, concurrent offenses under the latter part cannot be established between the two offenses. Accordingly, the lower court’s determination, which did not apply Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act to the offenses charged in this case, contains no error of misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the establishment of concurrent offenses under the latter part, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. On the remaining grounds for appeal\\nThe lower court found the Defendant guilty by applying the Specialized Credit Finance Business Act to the act by which the Defendant withdrew cash using a card in the name of a third party, for the reasons stated in its opinion. Examining the reasons of the lower-court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, the lower-court judgment contains no error such as misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning the offense of violation of the Specialized Credit Finance Business Act, as alleged in the Defendant’s grounds for appeal.\\nMeanwhile, under Article 383 subparagraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, an appeal on the ground of improper sentencing is permitted only in cases in which the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment with prison labor or imprisonment for 10 years or more has been imposed; therefore, in this case where a lesser sentence was imposed, the argument that the sentence is unfair does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as stated in the operative part. With the exception that Justices Kim Jae-hyeong and Lee Dong-won filed dissenting opinions, the views of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there are supplemental opinions to the majority opinion by Justices Kwon Soon-il, Park Sang-ok, and Noh Jeong-hee, as well as a supplemental opinion to the dissenting opinion by Justice Kim Jae-hyeong.\\n\\n5. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyeong and Lee Dong-won\\na. We examine the special nature of retrial proceedings.\\n1) Although retrial proceedings are special litigation proceedings, their character as special litigation clearly appears only before the decision to commence retrial becomes final, whereas at the stage after the decision to commence retrial becomes final and the case is retried, and with respect to the effect of the retrial judgment, they are no different from ordinary proceedings.\\nIn retrial adjudication proceedings after the decision to commence retrial becomes final, the case itself is tried anew from the beginning in order to render a new judgment that extinguishes the finality of the judgment subject to retrial. Article 438(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that the retrial court must adjudicate again according to its level. “Adjudicate again according to its level” means adjudicating again according to the ordinary procedure for that level provided by the Criminal Procedure Act. Only cases specially provided by law are excluded, such as exclusion of the rule suspending the trial proceedings for a defendant with an irreversible mental and physical disability and the rule for an order dismissing prosecution for a deceased defendant, as well as exceptions to the principle requiring the defendant’s appearance at trial (Articles 438(2) and (3) of the Criminal Procedure Act), and matters that cannot naturally be permitted in light of the nature of retrial adjudication, such as withdrawal of prosecution (see Supreme Court Decision of 1976. 12. 28., 76DO3203). Therefore, once retrial has commenced and reached a finalized stage, the acts permitted in the corresponding level of ordinary proceedings in relation to the retrial case should be regarded as permissible.\\n2) As above, if the litigation acts permitted in the corresponding level of ordinary proceedings may also be performed in retrial adjudication proceedings after the decision to commence retrial becomes final, then amendment of the indictment to add the facts charged of another case to the retrial case or consolidation with another ordinary case for joint adjudication is also permissible. This is because the Criminal Procedure Act merely provides that the petition for retrial is under the jurisdiction of the court that rendered the original judgment (Article 423), and does not contain any express provision prohibiting amendment of the indictment or consolidated hearing.\\na) Even if the facts constituting the subsequent offense are added in retrial adjudication proceedings by amendment of the indictment or consolidation, it does not in itself result in a consequence contrary to the principle of beneficial retrial. In such a case, within the scope not contrary to the principle of beneficial retrial, a sentence appropriate to the retrial case is determined, and then a sentence appropriate to the subsequent offense is determined, and a single sentence is imposed; and it cannot necessarily be said that the sentence determined through such a process is heavier than the sentence in the judgment subject to retrial and therefore necessarily contrary to the principle of beneficial retrial. In other words, where a single sentence is imposed through consolidation of a retrial case and an ordinary case, punishment is imposed on both the retrial case and the ordinary case together, so whether the prohibition on disadvantageous alteration is violated cannot be determined by simply comparing that sentence with the sentence of the judgment subject to retrial. In such a case, the statutory punishment for the other case, reasons for aggravation or mitigation of punishment, the sentencing factors under Article 51 of the Criminal Act, and other circumstances must be comprehensively and substantively considered to determine whether the sentence imposed in the retrial judgment has been altered to the detriment of the accused (see Supreme Court Decision of 2004. 11. 11., 2004DO6784, etc.).\\nb) Where a judgment imposing a single sentence on several factual bases becomes final and, among them, only some of the factual bases are found to have grounds for a petition for retrial, a decision to commence retrial is formally made even for the factual bases for which there are no grounds for retrial, but the examination as to that part is limited to the extent necessary for sentencing (see Supreme Court Decision of 1996. 6. 14., 96DO477, etc.).\\nThe above decisions, etc. merely purport that where a single judgment is rendered and becomes final as to several factual bases in a relationship of concurrent offenses, the court should refrain from examining factual bases for which there are no grounds for retrial; they are not directly related to whether a retrial case may be jointly examined and determined together with subsequent offenses that have not yet become final.\\nc) In civil proceedings, there is no need to consolidate a new claim into a retrial action. Because civil proceedings are proceedings that adjudicate by cause of action, it suffices to file a separate action concerning the new claim. There is no difference between filing a separate action and obtaining a decision thereon, and consolidating it into a retrial action and obtaining a decision thereon. By contrast, criminal proceedings are different from civil proceedings in that they are not proceedings that adjudicate by offense. The basic form of criminal proceedings is not to separately determine and add the individual sentences for offenses found guilty among several offenses, but to determine one overall sentence for the offenses found guilty. Therefore, there is a significant difference between dividing offenses belonging to one habitual offense into part as a retrial case and part as an ordinary case, on the one hand, and adding facts charged to a retrial case or consolidating an ordinary case so as to conduct one trial, on the other. Considering this difference between civil and criminal proceedings, it is more suitable to the structure of criminal proceedings to permit addition of facts charged to, or consolidation of, an ordinary case with a retrial case.\\nd) If another case is consolidated with a retrial case or another factual basis is added by amendment of the indictment, and later the petition for retrial is withdrawn, only the consolidated or added factual basis remains, and the ordinary trial procedure according to the corresponding level may be conducted with respect thereto. Therefore, it does not appear that unnecessary procedural confusion would arise therefrom.\\n\\nb. We examine res judicata.\\n1) Where a person who received a judgment subject to retrial for a prior habitual offense thereafter committed a subsequent offense based on the same habitual propensity, if the decision to commence retrial as to the judgment subject to retrial became final and, without the two cases being jointly tried, the retrial judgment was rendered and became final first, its res judicata effect should be deemed to extend to the subsequent offense case. The reasons are as follows.\\n2) Article 13(1) of the Constitution provides that “all citizens shall not be punished repeatedly for the same crime,” thereby proclaiming the “principle of double jeopardy prohibition.” This principle is the constitutional declaration of the “principle of ne bis in idem,” namely that once a judgment becomes final, the same case may not be tried again, as a binding principle on the state’s penal power, and is intended to guarantee fundamental rights of the people, especially bodily liberty, by preventing the state from repeatedly exercising penal power over the same criminal act (see Constitutional Court en banc decision of 2001. 5. 31., 99HEONGA18, etc.). Where there is a final conviction for part of offenses in a comprehensive single offense such as a habitual offense, the effect of that final judgment extends to all remaining offenses in the comprehensive single offense, but the temporal scope of res judicata, that is, the standard point for determining until when the factual offenses are covered by res judicata, is determined on the basis of the latest point at which factual adjudication is possible, namely the time of pronouncement of judgment (see Supreme Court Decision of 2008. 7. 24., 2008DO5068, etc.). Meanwhile, for a case in which a decision to commence retrial has become final, the court must adjudicate again according to its level, and “adjudicate again” here means not reviewing whether the judgment subject to retrial was proper, but trying the case itself anew from the beginning (see Supreme Court Decision of 2013. 1. 24., 2010DO14282, etc.). Once a retrial judgment concerning the prior offense becomes final, the effect of the judgment subject to retrial is extinguished; therefore, the standard point to which the res judicata effect of the retrial judgment extends is not the time the judgment subject to retrial was rendered, but the time the retrial judgment was rendered, which is the latest point at which factual adjudication is possible in retrial proceedings (see, by analogy, Supreme Court Decision of 1993. 2. 12., 92DA25151, concerning civil cases, etc.).\\n3) In light of the above legal principles, the effect of a final retrial judgment concerning the prior offense extends, as of the time the retrial judgment is rendered, which is the latest point at which another case may be heard in retrial proceedings, to other offenses that arose before that point and are in a relationship of a comprehensive single offense. Once the decision to commence retrial as to the prior offense has already become final, factual adjudication on the subsequent offense may also be conducted in retrial proceedings through procedures such as amendment of the indictment; thus, deeming the res judicata effect of the retrial judgment concerning the prior offense to extend to the subsequent offense does not produce improper results such as creating a gap in punishment.\\n4) The majority opinion, while examining whether the retrial court could have tried the subsequent offense, views the offenses in the retrial case and the subsequent offense as still separate habitual offenses blocked by the judgment subject to retrial, which remains in force as a final judgment until the retrial judgment becomes final.
