However, this view establishes an exception unfavorable to the defendant by limiting the effect of the retrial judgment to the time of pronouncement of the judgment subject to retrial, without any express provision excluding the general principle that the effect of a final judgment extends to offenses committed up to the time of factual judgment and the principle of double jeopardy prohibition under Article 13(1) of the Constitution. The court, after completing the examination of the retrial case according to the ordinary trial procedure, renders the retrial judgment as the final judgment, and it is difficult to find legal grounds for treating the effect of such retrial judgment differently from the effect of a judgment rendered through ordinary proceedings.\\nThe majority opinion states that, on the premise that the judgment subject to retrial formally remains valid until the retrial judgment becomes final, the prior offense and the subsequent offense in the retrial case are divided by the judgment subject to retrial and become separate habitual offenses lacking identity, so the effect of instituting prosecution for the prior case does not extend to the subsequent offense. However, the retrial court adjudicates the case anew from the beginning on the premise that the finality of the judgment subject to retrial will be extinguished; it does not adjudicate on the premise that the finality of the judgment subject to retrial will be maintained. Nevertheless, the logic that the prior offense and the subsequent offense become separate habitual offenses on the premise that the judgment subject to retrial formally remains valid cannot escape the criticism of being excessively formalistic and schematic.\\n5) The retrial of the Defendant is based on the Constitutional Court’s decision that the portion concerning Article 329 of the Criminal Act in Article 5-4(1) of the former Act on the Aggravated Punishment of Specific Crimes, which merely raised the statutory penalty while prescribing the same elements as those of a crime under the Criminal Act, is unconstitutional (Constitutional Court en banc decision of 2015. 2. 26., 2014HEONGA16, etc.). Since the commencement of retrial for the Defendant can be viewed as attributable not to the Defendant’s fault but to the state’s legislative error, even if the Defendant thereby becomes unable to be punished, that should be regarded as an unavoidable result that must be borne. Nevertheless, it is difficult to agree with the majority opinion, which emphasizes the need to punish the Defendant and seeks to limit the effect flowing from finalization of the retrial judgment.\\n6) Where the prosecutor first prosecutes a fraud offense viewing it as a simple offense, and then additionally prosecutes habitual fraud, which is a comprehensive single offense, but in the course of the trial it is revealed that all of the factual bases of the offenses prosecuted before and after constitute a single offense of habitual fraud in a comprehensive sense, it would ordinarily be an appropriate handling faithful to the Criminal Procedure Act’s provisions for the prosecutor to file a motion to amend the indictment by adding to the factual basis of the first prosecuted case the factual basis stated in the additionally prosecuted indictment and by changing the offense name and applicable provisions accordingly to habitual offense, and to withdraw the prosecution as to the additionally prosecuted case. However, the prosecutor’s additional prosecution itself may be understood to include the purport of seeking punishment of all of the factual bases of the offenses prosecuted before and after as one comprehensive single offense, and in substance there is no significant difference from amendment of the indictment by adding facts charged, etc. Therefore, where the filing of the additionally prosecuted indictment is clearly explained, by interpretation, as adding and supplementing matters omitted from the first-prosecuted indictment among the acts constituting the comprehensive single offense and as changing the offense name and applicable provisions to those of the comprehensive single offense, and it becomes clear that it is not a duplicate prosecution of one offense, the prosecution should be deemed to have been amended by the additional prosecution, and a substantive determination should be made as to all of the factual bases of the offenses prosecuted before and after; there is no need to render a judgment dismissing prosecution as to the additional prosecution (see Supreme Court Decision of 1999. 11. 26., 99DO3929, 99GAMDO97).\\nIn light of the above legal principles, in a case such as this one, even if there was no issue of double prosecution at the time the subsequent offense case was prosecuted, once retrial proceedings have been commenced for the prior offense case during the trial of the subsequent offense case, allowing ordinary trial proceedings to proceed separately in both cases is tantamount to tolerating the defendant being prosecuted twice for one offense in a relationship of a comprehensive single offense and leaving two judgments to be rendered. Therefore, the two cases should be consolidated, or the factual basis of the subsequent offense case should be added to the factual basis of the prior offense case, so that they are determined in one proceeding. This is the most desirable way of proceeding with the trial to resolve the problem of double prosecution that arose unpredictably because of retrial.\\nThe majority opinion, if it were to view the unity of the prior offense and the subsequent offense as maintained, would fall into circular reasoning that because that would amount to double prosecution, the unity of the offenses must be deemed not maintained. This not only allows the court to render two judgments without correcting the problem of double prosecution arising from one offense, but also shifts to the defendant the disadvantage caused by an unclear institutional problem; this is difficult to accept in light of the ideals and procedure of criminal litigation.\\n7) Whether the res judicata effect of the final judgment extends to the remaining case, when a judgment is first rendered and becomes final in either the retrial case or the subsequent offense case, may be understood to depend on whether there was a possibility of trying the other case in the trial proceedings of the case rendered and finalized first. If so understood, the conclusion as to whether res judicata extends does not unreasonably differ depending on which judgment among the retrial case concerning the prior offense and the subsequent offense case became final first.\\nConsider the case where the judgment in the subsequent offense case became final first and thereafter the retrial court renders a retrial judgment. If the decision to commence retrial as to the prior offense case had not become final by the time the factual trial judgment in the subsequent offense case was rendered, then there was no possibility of trying the prior offense in the proceeding for the subsequent offense, so there is no room for the res judicata effect of the final judgment on the subsequent offense to extend to the retrial case. However, if the decision to commence retrial as to the prior offense case had become final before the factual trial judgment in the subsequent offense case was rendered, then the prior offense case could have been factually adjudicated in one proceeding by consolidating it in the proceeding for the subsequent offense case, and there is no reason to conclude that the res judicata effect of the final judgment on the subsequent offense does not extend to the retrial case.\\nThus, if one examines whether the two cases actually could have been tried in one proceeding through consolidation, amendment of the indictment, etc., and determines whether res judicata extends accordingly, the irrationality pointed out by the majority opinion does not arise.\\nc. We examine concurrent offenses under the latter part.\\n1) Where a person who received a judgment subject to retrial thereafter committed separate subsequent offenses, and the decision to commence retrial as to the judgment subject to retrial became final and the retrial judgment became final first, if the subsequent offense case could have been jointly tried and adjudicated together in the retrial adjudication proceedings, then concurrent offenses under the latter part are established between the subsequent offense, for which no judgment has yet been rendered, and the prior offense in the final retrial judgment. In the same purport, the conclusions of Supreme Court Decision of 2013. 9. 12., 2012DO12190, and Supreme Court Decision of 2016. 2. 18., 2015DO17440, etc., which recognized the establishment of concurrent offenses under the latter part, are entirely just and should be maintained. The reasons are as follows.\\n2) Article 37 of the Criminal Act defines as concurrent offenses under the latter part “an offense for which a judgment imposing imprisonment with prison labor or a heavier punishment has become final and an offense committed before that judgment became final,” and the first sentence of Article 39(1) provides: “Where among concurrent offenses there is an offense for which no judgment has been rendered, a sentence shall be imposed for that offense in consideration of equity with the case where that offense and the offense for which judgment has become final are adjudicated at the same time.” These provisions of the Criminal Act impose on the court adjudicating concurrent offenses under the latter part a duty to determine the sentence in consideration of equity so that the defendant is not disadvantaged merely because the offenses are being tried in separate proceedings, as compared with a case where the offense for which judgment has become final and the concurrent offense under the latter part are adjudicated together.\\n3) In light of the above legal principles, where the retrial judgment becomes final before the judgment in the subsequent offense case, the court adjudicating the subsequent offense case must, so long as it is clear that the subsequent offense was committed before the retrial judgment imposing imprisonment with prison labor or a heavier punishment became final, determine the sentence for the subsequent offense in consideration of equity with simultaneous trial, by viewing it as being in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part with the offense in the final retrial judgment. The majority opinion, contrary to this, interprets the law so as to deny the establishment of concurrent offenses under the latter part against the defendant without an express provision, and it is difficult to find a proper basis for that.\\nThe premise for viewing the subsequent offense as being in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part with the offense in the retrial judgment, where the retrial judgment becomes final before the judgment in the subsequent offense case, is that the retrial court could have simultaneously adjudicated the subsequent offense. Since the retrial adjudication proceedings may jointly try and simultaneously adjudicate the case concerning the subsequent offense after the decision to commence retrial becomes final, it is natural to treat the subsequent offense as an offense committed before finalization of the retrial judgment and thus in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part with the offense in the retrial judgment.\\n4) Whether concurrent offenses under the latter part are established between an offense for which no judgment has yet been rendered and an offense for which judgment has already become final, when a judgment is first rendered and becomes final in either the prior offense case or the subsequent offense case, may sufficiently be understood to depend on whether the other case’s offense could have been simultaneously adjudicated in the trial proceedings of the case whose judgment was rendered and finalized first. If so understood, the conclusion as to whether concurrent offenses under the latter part are established does not unreasonably differ depending on which judgment among the retrial case concerning the prior offense and the subsequent offense case became final first.\\nConsider the case where the judgment in the subsequent offense case became final first and the court then renders a retrial judgment on the prior offense in the retrial case. If the decision to commence retrial as to the prior offense had not become final by the time the judgment in the subsequent offense case became final, then the prior offense could not have been adjudicated simultaneously in the proceedings of the subsequent offense case, and therefore the prior offense cannot be viewed, on the basis of the final judgment in the subsequent offense case, as being in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part with the subsequent offense. However, if the decision to commence retrial as to the prior offense became final before the judgment in the subsequent offense case became final, then the prior offense could have been simultaneously adjudicated by consolidating it in the proceedings for the subsequent offense case, and in that case a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part is established between the subsequent offense and the prior offense.\\nThus, if one examines whether the offense in the other case could actually have been simultaneously adjudicated in the trial proceedings of the judgment rendered and finalized first, and determines whether concurrent offenses under the latter part are established accordingly, the problems pointed out by the majority opinion do not arise.\\nd. We examine the lower court’s determination in light of these legal principles.\\n1) The Defendant was sentenced by the Busan District Court to 2 years of imprisonment with prison labor for violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment of Specific Crimes and other offenses, and the judgment became final on 2003. 12. 13., and the decision to commence retrial thereon was made on 2016. 6. 14. and became final around that time, thereby commencing retrial proceedings. The first instance of the retrial proceedings sentenced the Defendant to 2 years of imprisonment with prison labor on 2016. 8. 18., and the first retrial judgment in this case became final on the 30th of the same month when the appellate court rendered a judgment dismissing the appeal on 2016. 12. 22. However, even if an amended factual basis is no different in substance from the prior factual basis and resembles an additional new prosecution, the indictment may also be amended at the appellate stage (see Supreme Court Decision of 2017. 9. 21., 2017DO7843, etc.). Therefore, with respect to the theft offenses on 2016. 10. 3. among the facts charged in this case, which were committed by the same habitual propensity as the offenses in the retrial case, the appellate court in the retrial proceedings could have conducted factual adjudication through amendment of the indictment, etc. Accordingly, the res judicata effect of the first retrial judgment in this case should be deemed to extend to the theft offenses on 2016. 10. 3. among the facts charged in this case.\\nNevertheless, the lower court, on the erroneous premise that the res judicata effect of the retrial judgment does not extend to the subsequent offense, determined that the res judicata effect of the first retrial judgment in this case does not extend to the theft offenses on 2016. 10. 3. among the facts charged in this case. In that respect, the lower court’s determination contains an error of misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning res judicata, which affected the judgment. The Defendant’s argument on this point is well founded.\\n2) The Defendant was sentenced by the Busan District Court on 2001. 8. 31. to 1 year and 6 months of imprisonment with prison labor for violation of the Specialized Credit Finance Business Act and other offenses, and the judgment became final on 2001. 12. 5.; the decision to commence retrial thereon was made on 2017. 2. 16. and became final around that time; accordingly, the second retrial judgment in this case, which sentenced the Defendant to 1 year and 6 months of imprisonment with prison labor on 2018. 4. 27., became final on 2018. 8. 10. The retrial court concerning the second retrial judgment in this case could have consolidated and simultaneously adjudicated this case; therefore, the offenses in the facts charged in this case committed before the second retrial judgment in this case became final should be viewed as being in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part with the offenses in the final second retrial judgment in this case, and Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act should have been applied. Nevertheless, the lower court determined that there was no relationship of concurrent offenses under the latter part and did not apply Article 39(1) of the Criminal Act. In that respect, the lower court’s determination contains an error of misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning concurrent offenses under the latter part, which affected the judgment. The Defendant’s argument on this point is also well founded.\\n3) Therefore, the lower-court judgment must be reversed and the case remanded to the lower court for further fact-finding and determination. This is why we dissent from the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Supplemental Opinion to the Majority Opinion by Justices Kwon Soon-il, Park Sang-ok, and Noh Jeong-hee\\na. The dissenting opinion states that, after the decision to commence retrial becomes final, retrial proceedings at the retrial adjudication stage are no different from ordinary proceedings, and therefore it is possible in retrial adjudication proceedings to add the facts charged of the subsequent offense case to the facts charged of the prior offense case or to consolidate the two cases. However, this is not only a formalistic interpretation that disregards the purpose of retrial and the special nature of retrial proceedings, but also does not accord with the provisions and legislative intent of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n1) The Criminal Procedure Act, reflecting the purpose and intent of retrial and the special nature of retrial proceedings, expressly provides special rules regarding retrial proceedings, including retrial adjudication proceedings. Unlike ordinary proceedings, which are commenced by an indictment filed by the prosecutor, retrial is initiated by a petition for retrial by a person entitled to petition for retrial as provided by law, where there is a ground for retrial enumerated by law (Articles 420, 424, etc. of the Criminal Procedure Act). In retrial proceedings, even when a petition for retrial is filed for a deceased person or a person with an irreversible mental and physical disability, or when a person who received a conviction dies or becomes a person with an irreversible mental and physical disability before the retrial judgment, the trial proceedings are not suspended, and adjudication may be conducted even if the defendant does not appear (Articles 438(2) and (3) of the Criminal Procedure Act). In addition, under the Criminal Procedure Act, the petitioner for retrial may withdraw the petition and thereby terminate the retrial proceedings, although he or she may not petition for retrial again on the same ground (Article 429). Furthermore, petitions for retrial may also compete across different levels of instance (Article 436 of the Criminal Procedure Act; Article 169 of the Criminal Procedure Rules).\\nAs such, retrial proceedings differ in purpose from ordinary proceedings, and accordingly retrial proceedings are special litigation proceedings with different commencement, termination, and structure from ordinary proceedings. Therefore, this special nature of retrial proceedings must be considered not only at the stage of commencing retrial but also at the stage of retrial adjudication.\\n2) Article 438(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that, for a case in which the decision to commence retrial has become final, the court shall again adjudicate “according to its level.” However, this cannot be construed to mean that all contents of the ordinary proceedings under the Criminal Procedure Act are applied to retrial proceedings, which are special litigation; rather, whether they apply must be determined individually in light of the purpose and structure of the proceedings.\\nThe Supreme Court has long held that, under Article 255(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, prosecution may be withdrawn before the pronouncement of the first-instance judgment, but if the first-instance judgment on the relevant facts charged had already been rendered long ago and became final and retrial proceedings are pending thereon, prosecution may not be withdrawn in retrial proceedings (see Supreme Court Decision of 1976. 12. 28., 76DO3203). In addition, the Supreme Court has held that, where a final, indivisible judgment imposing a single sentence on several factual bases in a relationship of concurrent offenses finds grounds for retrial only as to some of the factual bases, a decision to commence retrial must formally be made for the entire judgment because it is a judgment imposing a single sentence, but by the very nature of the retrial system as an extraordinary remedy, as to the factual bases for which there are no grounds for retrial, the effect of the decision to commence retrial is merely to formally include them in the subject of adjudication, and the retrial court cannot retry and overturn the conviction as to those facts; rather, it may hear them only to the extent necessary for sentencing, because a new sentence must be determined only as to that part (see Supreme Court Decision of 1996. 6. 14., 96DO477, etc.). This means that even if grounds for retrial are recognized as to some factual bases for which a single sentence was imposed in a relationship of concurrent offenses, the court cannot newly adjudicate guilt or innocence as to other factual bases without grounds for retrial, and only hearing necessary for sentencing may be conducted to redetermine the sentence; that accords with the nature and legislative intent of the retrial system. In determining whether laws concerning ordinary proceedings apply to retrial proceedings, the nature and legislative intent of the retrial system, and legal stability, must be fully considered.\\n3) Retrial is an extraordinary remedy to correct errors in final judgments for the benefit of the person who received the conviction, where there is a ground for retrial enumerated by law. This means that retrial is permitted for the realization of substantive justice, but it must be conducted within a scope that does not harm the defendant’s legal stability, and it does not merely mean that a sentence heavier than the prior judgment cannot be imposed in retrial proceedings (see Supreme Court Decision of 2015. 10. 29., 2012DO2938, etc.). In retrial adjudication proceedings, which adjudicate facts charged for which there are grounds for retrial after the decision to commence retrial becomes final, allowing other facts charged to be added or consolidated through amendment of the indictment, etc., so that they are tried together, may substantially infringe the defendant’s right of defense because it imposes on the defendant an additional burden of defense with respect to facts charged that the person entitled to petition for retrial did not place within the scope of retrial. Accordingly, adding or consolidating new facts charged other than the case subject to retrial in retrial proceedings and trying them together is contrary to the nature of the retrial system and the principle of beneficial retrial.\\n4) Even in civil proceedings, it is not permitted to add a new claim by consolidating it into a retrial action (see Supreme Court Decision of 2009. 9. 10., 2009DA41977, etc.). Criminal litigation is a procedure requiring legal stability and formal certainty, and it is reasonable to regard the addition or consolidation of new facts charged to a retrial case in criminal retrial proceedings as impermissible.\\nb. The dissenting opinion states that the retrial court adjudicates the case anew from the beginning on the premise that the finality of the judgment subject to retrial will be extinguished; the supplemental opinion by Justice Kim Jae-hyeong to the dissenting opinion states that, once the decision to commence retrial becomes final, the effect of the judgment subject to retrial is temporarily lost or placed in a fluid state in retrial proceedings; and therefore they assert that the judgment subject to retrial should not be treated as validly existing in retrial adjudication proceedings. However, for the following reasons, we cannot agree with the above view.\\n1) The proposition that a case in which the decision to commence retrial has become final is to be adjudicated again according to its level, and the question of whether the effect of the judgment subject to retrial is lost before the retrial judgment becomes final after the decision to commence retrial, are not logically necessary relations. In the retrial system, the distinction between the retrial-commencement stage and the retrial-adjudication stage, or whether the effect of the judgment subject to retrial continues to exist before the retrial judgment becomes final after the decision to commence retrial, can be viewed as a matter of legislative policy. The Criminal Procedure Act merely provides that, for a case in which the decision to commence retrial has become final, the court shall again adjudicate according to its level (Article 438(1)), and does not provide that the effect of the judgment subject to retrial is extinguished by the decision to commence retrial. Rather, it provides that, even if a decision to commence retrial is made upon finding the petition for retrial well-founded, execution of the sentence under the judgment subject to retrial may be suspended at the court’s discretion (Article 435(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act). This provision is construed as providing for discretionary suspension of execution on the premise that the effect of the judgment subject to retrial continues until the retrial judgment becomes final, so that execution of the sentence is in principle possible. It cannot be interpreted as a provision that, once the decision to commence retrial becomes final, other effects of the judgment subject to retrial are extinguished but only its executory force remains.\\n2) The meaning that the effect of the judgment subject to retrial is temporarily lost or placed in a fluid state is unclear. Such an interpretation is contrary to the provisions of our Criminal Procedure Act and contrary to the principles of legal stability and formal certainty in criminal procedure.\\n3) The majority opinion’s reasoning for why the res judicata effect of the final retrial judgment does not extend to the subsequent offense does not mean that the court adjudicating the subsequent case after the retrial judgment became final should treat the judgment subject to retrial as if it still validly exists, or that two final judgments are recognized in one case. Even if the effect of the judgment subject to retrial is not lost merely by the decision to commence retrial becoming final, the retrial court may still conduct retrial adjudication and render a retrial judgment without being bound by its contents. It cannot be said, by treating the judgment subject to retrial as still validly remaining while the retrial court reexamines and judges the prior case from the beginning in retrial proceedings, that this is contradictory or contrary to the presumption of innocence.\\nThe majority opinion states that, before the retrial judgment becomes final, the retrial court cannot recognize the res judicata effect of the retrial judgment on the subsequent offense because, due to the existence of the judgment subject to retrial, the retrial court must view the offenses in the retrial case and the subsequent offense as separate habitual offenses and cannot simultaneously try the subsequent offense. After the retrial judgment becomes final, only the retrial judgment remains validly existing, but it is only difficult to recognize the res judicata effect of the retrial judgment on the subsequent offense.\\nc. The dissenting opinion states that, where the decision to commence retrial as to the prior offense case becomes final before the factual trial judgment in the subsequent offense case is rendered, since the prior offense case and the subsequent offense case can be tried and adjudicated in one proceeding through procedures such as consolidation in the proceeding for the subsequent offense case, no irrationality arises as to whether res judicata extends and whether concurrent offenses under the latter part are established depending on which judgment among the retrial case concerning the prior offense and the subsequent offense case became final first.\\nHowever, even if, as the dissenting opinion suggests, the prior offense case could be tried together in the proceeding for the subsequent offense case, if one imagines the many cases in which retrial has not even been commenced for the final conviction concerning the prior offense before the factual trial judgment in the subsequent offense case is rendered, it cannot be said that no irrationality arises in that whether res judicata extends and whether concurrent offenses under the latter part are established depends on which judgment among the retrial case and the subsequent offense case became final first. In other words, it is not appropriate to discuss the somewhat exceptional situation where the decision to commence retrial as to the prior offense case becomes final before the factual trial judgment in the subsequent offense case.\\nd. Justice Kim Jae-hyeong’s supplemental opinion to the dissenting opinion states that there is room to view the first retrial judgment in this case and the theft offenses on 2016. 10. 3. among the facts charged in this case, when taken together, as a single offense, as this may amount to recognizing habituality too easily, and that a stricter examination of habituality could be a more direct solution.\\nIn larceny, habituality refers to a habit of repeatedly committing theft offenses, and whether such habituality exists is determined by comprehensively considering the presence or absence of prior convictions of the same kind, the number of offenses in the case, the period, motive, means and method, etc. (see Supreme Court Decision of 2009. 2. 12., 2008DO11550, etc.). Whether habituality is recognized, and the temporal scope of the res judicata effect of a final judgment or whether the final judgment severs the unity of the factual offenses before and after it, are separate issues with different requirements and effects.\\nFor the above reasons, I supplement the reasoning of the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Supplemental Opinion to the Dissenting Opinion by Justice Kim Jae-hyeong\\na. Res judicata (res judicata) originates from the principle that no one should be permitted to examine again a matter already adjudicated. Because res judicata arises only when a judgment becomes final, it may be said to be the effect of a final judgment. Once a judgment becomes final, the parties may no longer contest it through ordinary procedures, and it may be corrected only through the retrial procedure prescribed by law, and only where there is a very serious defect in the final judgment.\\nRetrial proceedings are procedures that remove the finality of the judgment subject to retrial and retry the case itself. In criminal procedure, once the decision to commence retrial becomes final, the effect of the judgment subject to retrial is temporarily lost in relation to retrial adjudication proceedings, and when the retrial judgment becomes final, the effect of the judgment subject to retrial is conclusively extinguished. Once the decision to commence retrial becomes final, the effect of the judgment subject to retrial is in a fluid state, as if the first-instance judgment had been appealed, and it should not be treated in retrial adjudication proceedings as if the judgment subject to retrial still validly exists.\\nA criminal defendant is presumed innocent until a conviction becomes final (Article 27(4) of the Constitution, Article 275-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act). It is clear that once the decision to commence retrial becomes final, it is the retrial judgment, not the judgment subject to retrial, that becomes the final judgment. Treating the judgment subject to retrial as if it still validly exists in retrial adjudication proceedings also contravenes the presumption of innocence for a defendant whose retrial proceedings are pending after the decision to commence retrial has become final.\\nThe majority opinion states that because the retrial court in retrial adjudication proceedings cannot negate the existence and effect of the judgment subject to retrial, the unity of the offenses in the case subject to retrial and the subsequent offense is severed by the judgment subject to retrial, which is the final judgment, and they become separate habitual offenses lacking identity, so the res judicata effect of the retrial judgment does not extend to the subsequent offense. This means that the court adjudicating the subsequent case must determine that the unity of the offenses in the case subject to retrial and the subsequent offense is severed, as if the judgment subject to retrial validly still exists.\\nHowever, it is contradictory for the retrial court, while reexamining and determining the prior case from the beginning in retrial adjudication proceedings, to regard the judgment subject to retrial concerning the prior case as validly remaining as a final judgment. Once the decision to commence retrial becomes final, the retrial court is freed from the constraints arising from the final judgment and may newly determine the facts and law in the relevant case. Treating the judgment subject to retrial as a final judgment in retrial adjudication proceedings is improper because it produces the result that the same factual offense is, on the one hand, recognized as an offense before a final judgment and, on the other hand, newly adjudicated as to that factual offense.\\nEven after the retrial judgment becomes final and the effect of the judgment subject to retrial has already been conclusively extinguished, it should not be treated in another criminal trial proceeding as if the judgment subject to retrial still validly exists as a final judgment. There cannot be two final judgments in one case. This is a principle common to retrial in criminal proceedings, civil proceedings, and administrative proceedings.\\nIn criminal cases, once a conviction becomes final, the prior conviction may become the basis for aggravation of repeated offenses (a person who, as provided in Article 35(1) of the Criminal Act, “having received imprisonment with prison labor or a heavier punishment, commits an offense punishable by imprisonment with prison labor or a heavier punishment within 3 years after the completion or remission of the execution thereof”) or a disqualifying prior conviction for a suspended sentence (an offense committed during the period from the finalization of a judgment imposing imprisonment with prison labor or a heavier punishment until 3 years after the completion or remission of its execution, as provided in the proviso to Article 62(1) of the Criminal Act). At that time, once a conviction in retrial becomes final, the retrial judgment becomes the new final conviction, and the judgment subject to retrial should not be treated as a final conviction. The court adjudicating the subsequent offense should also not treat the judgment subject to retrial concerning the prior offense as a valid judgment.\\nAlthough Article 435(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that execution of sentence may be suspended when the decision to commence retrial is made, this is an exceptional provision concerning the executory force of a judgment and cannot serve as a basis for regarding the judgment subject to retrial as validly existing in retrial adjudication proceedings. Because the decision to commence retrial recognizes that there is a serious defect in the final judgment due to limited grounds prescribed by law, the rule is that once the decision to commence retrial becomes final, the effect of the judgment subject to retrial is extinguished. In the retrial-commencement procedure, the court must determine only whether there exists a ground for retrial provided in the Criminal Procedure Act, and may not consider the substantive question of whether the ground for retrial is capable of affecting the judgment subject to retrial (see Supreme Court Order of 2008. 4. 24., 2008MO77). Even if the decision to commence retrial becomes final, this special provision allows the court to determine whether to suspend execution of sentence by considering the effect of the ground for retrial on the judgment subject to retrial, on the premise that there may be cases where suspension is convenient for execution of sentence.\\nIn short, in retrial adjudication proceedings, the judgment subject to retrial should not be regarded as valid, and once the decision to commence retrial becomes final, the effect of the judgment subject to retrial should be deemed temporarily lost. There is no legal basis for viewing the res judicata effect of the final retrial judgment as not extending to the subsequent offense, where in criminal proceedings the retrial judgment is rendered and becomes final first. Even if punishment is necessary, an exception concerning the effect of a judgment cannot be recognized without any basis in the Constitution or law.\\nb. In larceny, habituality refers to a habit of repeatedly committing theft offenses, and whether habituality exists must be determined by comprehensively considering the presence or absence of prior convictions of the same kind, the number of offenses in the case, the period, motive, means, and method, etc. (see Supreme Court Decision of 2009. 2. 12., 2008DO11550, etc.). Where there are multiple offenses in which habituality is manifested, one cannot group all of them together and deem them a single comprehensive offense without considering factors that serve as criteria for recognizing a comprehensive single offense, such as the protected legal interest among the offenses, the appearance and method of the acts, whether the intent was singular or renewed, and temporal and spatial proximity, etc.\\nThe offense in the first retrial judgment in this case is that, from 2003. 2. 9. to 2003. 8. 16., the Defendant stole credit cards and withdrew cash and stole it. The offense among the facts charged in this case, for which res judicata is at issue because it was committed before the first retrial judgment in this case became final, is that around 2016. 10. 3. the Defendant stole credit cards and withdrew cash and stole it.\\nAlthough the offense in the first retrial judgment in this case and the theft offenses on 2016. 10. 3. among the facts charged in this case involve similar methods of offense—targeting unspecified middle-aged women, winning their trust by pretending to have an accidental encounter, then stealing credit cards, etc., and withdrawing cash or receiving cash advances—and the number of offenses is large, it is questionable whether these offenses, which occurred with a temporal gap of more than 13 years, should be viewed as a comprehensive single offense in which the same habituality is recognized. Where the temporal gap between offenses is so long and a long period has passed, habitual offenses may perhaps be recognized by period of offenses, but viewing both the offense in the first retrial judgment in this case and the theft offenses on 2016. 10. 3. among the facts charged in this case as one offense may be regarded as recognizing habitual offenses too easily. A more rigorous examination of habituality, taking into account factors such as temporal and spatial proximity, may be a more direct solution. If one intends to punish both the habitual offense committed around 2003 and the habitual offense committed around 2016, it is natural to interpret the two habitual offenses as separate habitual offenses. If habituality is not recognized, the res judicata effect of the first retrial judgment in this case does not extend to the theft offenses on 2016. 10. 3. among the facts charged in this case.\\nc. The purpose of Article 420 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which provides that a petition for retrial may be filed for the benefit of the person who received a final conviction, is to correct serious errors in fact-finding in a final conviction and thereby remedy violations of human rights suffered by an innocent and blameless defendant (see Supreme Court en banc decision of 2015. 5. 21., 2011DO1932, etc.). Retrial proceedings are procedures for realizing concrete justice, but retrial must be conducted within a scope that does not harm the defendant’s legal stability (see Supreme Court Decision of 2015. 10. 29., 2012DO2938, etc.). In other words, because retrial proceedings are a system established for the benefit of the defendant, the defendant should not suffer disadvantage because of the retrial trial.\\nThe grounds for retrial under Article 420 of the Criminal Procedure Act may be classified into types such as: ① where the evidence of the original judgment is revealed to be false (subparagraphs 1 through 4), ② where new evidence is discovered (subparagraph 5), ③ where the judgment forming the basis (premise) of the original judgment is changed (subparagraph 6), and ④ where there is a manifest defect in the original judgment or in the investigative procedure (subparagraph 7). All of these grounds for retrial apply only to cases with such serious defects that the finality of the original judgment cannot be recognized as is (see Constitutional Court en banc decision of 2011. 6. 30., 2009HEONBA430, etc.), and they do not involve any cause attributable to the defendant.\\nIn cases such as the present Defendant’s, a petition for retrial may be filed against a final conviction based on a law or provision thereof that has been held unconstitutional (Article 47(4) of the Constitutional Court Act), but this too is because the law is unconstitutional, not because it is a cause attributable to the defendant. The commencement of retrial for the Defendant is due not to the Defendant’s fault but to the state’s legislative mistake. There is no other reason or basis for giving the Defendant a disadvantage because of retrial.\\nThe majority opinion, by emphasizing only the special nature of retrial trials, does not permit amendment of the indictment or consolidated trial in retrial adjudication proceedings and, with respect to the effect of the retrial judgment, limits the scope of the effect, thereby causing disadvantage to the defendant because of the retrial trial. Since there is no particular fault on the part of the defendant and the majority opinion merely emphasizes the need to punish the defendant, it is difficult to agree with it, as it also runs counter to the very nature of the retrial system, which exists for the benefit of the defendant.\\nd. It is necessary to actively interpret and operate the Criminal Procedure Act so that separate offenses of the same kind habitually committed, which are described in the facts charged in the judgment that is the subject of retrial, may also be tried together by adding facts charged or by consolidating cases in retrial adjudication proceedings.\\nIn the absence of a provision in the Criminal Procedure Act prohibiting addition of facts charged or consolidation of cases in retrial adjudication proceedings, an interpretation beneficial to the defendant is desirable. If the subsequent offense committed by the defendant is based on the same habituality as the prior offense, it is in principle a comprehensive single offense under substantive law, so the defendant should be able to be tried in one proceeding. Even if the subsequent offense committed by the defendant is a separate offense under substantive law from the prior offense, the defendant has an interest in being tried simultaneously as concurrent offenses. Because the prosecutor may add the subsequent offense in the retrial proceedings as facts charged, there is no gap in punishment for the subsequent offense committed by the defendant. Interpreting the law so as to prevent trial of the subsequent offense in retrial adjudication proceedings shifts responsibility for the prosecutor’s neglect of the duty to prosecute the subsequent offense onto the defendant.\\nIn particular, in this case the Defendant’s retrial was commenced because the provision of the former Act on the Aggravated Punishment of Specific Crimes that merely prescribed the same elements as those of a crime under the Criminal Act while increasing only the statutory punishment was held unconstitutional, so this is a case in which it is highly likely that the Defendant will be convicted by merely changing the applicable provision. In such a case where conviction is highly likely, there is no substantive reason to interpret the special nature of retrial adjudication proceedings as precluding punishment together with the subsequent offense. On the other hand, when there is a high likelihood of being found guilty again in the retrial judgment, the defendant’s interest in being punished together with another offense is very great.\\nThe simplest solution is to view as triable together the separate offenses of the same kind habitually committed, which are described in the facts charged in the judgment subject to retrial. Since simultaneous trial and punishment are possible in retrial adjudication proceedings in this way, the res judicata effect of the retrial judgment naturally extends to the subsequent offense, and on the basis of the final retrial judgment, the offense subject to retrial and the subsequent offense may be recognized as concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act. This interpretation also accords with the purpose of Article 438(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, which provides that the retrial court must again adjudicate according to its level.\\nThe majority opinion interprets retrial adjudication proceedings so as to prevent trial of the subsequent offense, and as a result concludes that there is no possibility of hearing the subsequent offense, so the res judicata effect of the retrial judgment does not extend to the subsequent offense; and because there is no possibility of simultaneous judgment on the subsequent offense, it does not reduce the subsequent offense under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act on the basis of the final prior offense. Such a view is not only unfair, because it too easily recognizes an exception unfavorable to the defendant to the general doctrines concerning final judgments and res judicata and, more broadly, the general doctrine concerning the establishment of concurrent offenses under the latter part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, despite a simple and easy solution being available, but is also difficult to regard as legally justified.\\nThis concludes the supplemental opinion to the dissenting opinion."}

{"[87DO564]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nWhere a document bears two or more persons as the name-holders of its execution, one document is constituted for each name-holder (see this Court, Judgment of July 12, 1977, 77DO1736; Judgment of March 2, 1956, 4288HYEONGSANG343), and therefore, where a document jointly signed by two or more persons is forged, as many offenses of forgery of a document are constituted as there are name-holders of execution; and since the act of forging such a jointly signed document is, by natural observation or in social common sense, a single act, the aforesaid multiple offenses of forgery of a document should be deemed to fall under the offense of ideal concurrence provided in Article 40 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nAccordingly, the court below, on this view, having found that the offense of forging the part in the name of non-indicted Park Seung-ha of the consent form stated in the judgment below, for which the Defendant received a final judgment of conviction, and the offense of forging the part in the name of non-indicted Mun Pil-geun of the same consent form, which is the facts charged in this case, constitute offenses in ideal concurrence, and, on the premise that, since a final judgment of conviction had been rendered with respect to the part in the name of Park Seung-ha, the effect of that judgment also extends to the facts of this case, which are in a relationship of ideal concurrence with it, rendered a judgment of dismissal of prosecution against the Defendant, is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the number of offenses of forgery of a document, as alleged. The precedents cited are not appropriate to this case. The argument is without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the Justices who participated concur in the decision, so judgment is rendered as ordered."}

question: Which of the following statements is incorrect? (Where there is dispute, according to precedents)
A: It cannot be said that Party A defamed A by posting on Party A's SNS profile status message statements such as “No contact with school violence offenders” after Party A reported that A had committed school violence against Party A's daughter, and measures such as “prohibition of contact and retaliatory acts” were imposed on A.
B: Since the victims of the crime of defamation or the crime of insult include not only natural persons but also “juridical persons” and “associations without legal personality,” a county, which is a local government, may also be a victim of the crime of defamation or the crime of insult.
C: In the so-called insult by collective designation, where the content of the insult is difficult to interpret as being directed at a specific individual belonging to that group, and where criticism by collective designation is diluted when it reaches individual members so that it does not reach the extent of affecting the social evaluation of each individual member, it is, as a rule, understood that insult against each individual member is not established.
D: The act of merely impersonating another person and posting an article on an internet bulletin board by masquerading as if it were written directly by that person does not constitute an act of revealing facts about that person or a statement of facts, and therefore does not constitute the offense of Violation of the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc. (Defamation).
E: Under Article 310 of the Criminal Act, for unlawfulness to be excluded, even if there is no proof that the stated fact is true, the actor must have believed it to be true and there must also have been reasonable grounds for such belief.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2012DO13189]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. The court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found the alternative count in this case guilty, namely, that the Defendants posted writings such as “Christian-obsessed shills, those ○○○○ crackpot bastards,” “professional demonstrator ○○○○ lackeys,” and “you puny bastards” on the Agora discussion forum of the Internet portal site Daum, thereby publicly insulting the victim, the person not named in the indictment, who was a member of “○○○○.”\\n\\n2. However, the court below’s determination is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nIn the so-called insult by collective reference, if the content of the insult is difficult to construe as being directed at a specific individual belonging to that group, and if the criticism by collective reference is such that, as it reaches the individual members, the degree of censure is diluted and is not assessed as reaching the level of affecting the social evaluation of each individual member, then insult against each individual member cannot be said to be established. However, where the number of members is so small that the remarks may be regarded as being directed at each individual member, or where, in light of the surrounding circumstances at the time, the remarks may be regarded as referring to individual members within the group, each individual member within the group must be deemed to have been specified as the victim; as concrete standards therefor, the size of the group, the nature of the group, and the victim’s position within the group may be considered (see Supreme Court Decision 2002DA63558 rendered on September 2, 2003).\\n\\nAccording to the record, “○○○○” is a café created on the Internet portal site Naver by persons opposing illegal, radical, and violent demonstrations; anyone can relatively easily join as a member by going through the procedure of answering simple questions presented by the café. At the time of this case, the number of members had reached approximately 36,000. The members mainly engage in activities by freely exchanging opinions through the café bulletin board, and in that process they use only IDs or nicknames, so that their personal identifying information is not disclosed. The victim was a regular member of “○○○○” at the time of this case and later became its operator, but the writings at issue do not contain expressions that can be viewed as referring to a specific member of “○○○○,” including the victim.\\n\\nGiven these circumstances, there is ample room to view the writings at issue posted by the Defendants as being directed generally at the members of the Internet café “○○○○,” such that, as applied to the victim who was merely one of its individual members, the degree of censure was diluted and did not reach the level of affecting the victim’s personal social evaluation. Meanwhile, it is also difficult to conclude that the Defendants had the intent to insult the victim, who was merely one of the members of “○○○○.”\\n\\nIf so, the court below, by giving the reasons stated in its judgment, found the alternative count against the Defendants guilty; in so doing, it erred in law regarding insult by collective reference and thereby affected the outcome of the judgment, and the argument in the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the portion of the court below’s judgment concerning the alternative count against the Defendants cannot escape reversal, and accordingly the portion concerning the principal count must also be reversed. Thus, the portion of the court below’s judgment concerning the Defendants is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court participating in this case."}

{"[2014DO15290]": "1. Prior to determining the grounds of appeal concerning the portions of violation of the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc. (defamation) and insult against Goheung County, the Court examines ex officio.\\n\\nA. The external honor, which is an evaluation of a person’s value that the Criminal Act seeks to protect by punishing the crime of defamation or the crime of insult, is a personal legal interest; and the State or local governments, as exercisers of public power that bear responsibility and duty to protect or realize the fundamental rights of the people, are merely the addressees of fundamental rights and not the subjects thereof. Matters related to their policy decisions or performance of duties must always be subject to broad public monitoring and criticism, and such monitoring and criticism can be properly carried out only when freedom of expression concerning them is fully guaranteed. Therefore, the State or local governments cannot be the subjects of external honor protected by penal means in relation to the people, and accordingly cannot be victims of the crime of defamation or the crime of insult.\\n\\nB. For the reasons stated in the judgment, the court below determined that the Defendant, by posting on the internet homepage of the Goheung County Office a written statement containing false content for the purpose of slandering Goheung County or by posting a written statement expressing contempt toward Goheung County, defamed and insulted Goheung County, and accordingly left undisturbed the first-instance judgment that found all portions of the facts charged in this case concerning violation of the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc. (defamation) and insult against Goheung County guilty.\\n\\nHowever, in light of the legal principle seen above, although Goheung County, as a local government, cannot be a victim of the crime of defamation or the crime of insult, the court below, premised on the erroneous view that a local government can also be such a victim, determined that the above crimes were established against Goheung County; thus, the court below’s judgment contains an error that misapprehended the legal principles concerning the victim of the crime of defamation and the crime of insult and thereby affected the judgment.\\n\\n2. The Court determines the grounds of appeal concerning the portion of insult against the non-indicted person.\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment, the court below determined that the writing posted by the Defendant on the Goheung County Office homepage expressed a contemptuous intent toward the non-indicted person individually, who is the County Governor of Goheung County, and that the crime of insult against the non-indicted person was therefore established, and further determined that the Defendant’s act could not be deemed to be widely permitted in light of social norms or to fall under any ground excluding unlawfulness; accordingly, it left undisturbed the first-instance judgment that found the portion of insult against the non-indicted person among the facts charged in this case guilty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons for the court below’s judgment on the basis of the evidence, the above judgment of the court below contains no error that affected the judgment by mistaking the facts in violation of the rules of logic and experience, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning grounds excluding unlawfulness of the crime of insult.\\n\\n3. The portions of the court below’s judgment concerning each violation of the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc. (defamation) and each insult against Goheung County are reversed for the foregoing reasons, but since the first-instance judgment affirmed by the court below imposed one punishment on the ground that the above portions and the remaining criminal facts were in a relation of concurrent offenses or ideal concurrence under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, the court below’s judgment is ultimately reversed in its entirety.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without addressing the remaining grounds of appeal, the Court reverses the court below’s judgment and remands the case to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2017DO607]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. The gist of the facts charged in this case is as follows: “The Defendant changed the nickname used in an Internet community ‘○○○○○ ○○○’ subscribed to under the Defendant’s name to ‘□□□□,’ which is the nickname used by the victim on the Internet portal site ‘△△△,’ and then impersonated the victim and, by masquerading as though the posts had been directly written by the victim, posted the instant each post on the ‘◇◇’ bulletin board of the said community, thereby publicly stating false facts and damaging the victim’s reputation.” \\n\\nThe court below, on the grounds as stated in its opinion, found the above facts charged guilty, holding that the Defendant’s act constituted defamation under Article 70(2) of the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Information and Communications Network Act”).\\n\\n2. However, the judgment of the court below is difficult to uphold for the following reasons.\\n\\nArticle 70(2) of the Information and Communications Network Act provides: “Any person who, with the intent to defame another person, publicly reveals false facts through an information and communications network and thereby damages the reputation of another person shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 7 years, suspension of qualifications for not more than 10 years, or a fine not exceeding 50 million won.” Here, “reveals facts” means a report or statement concerning concrete facts in the past or present, whether temporally or spatially. Therefore, in order to apply the above provision to an act of posting a post on a website with the intent to defame a certain person, the relevant post must contain a report or statement of concrete facts concerning that person. A mere act of impersonating that person and posting a post by masquerading as though it had been directly written by that person does not constitute an act of revealing facts about that person, and thus the above provision cannot be applied in relation to that person (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO10112, decided March 24, 2016).\\n\\nAccording to the foregoing legal principle, even if, in this case, the Defendant impersonated the victim and posted each post by masquerading as though they had been directly written by the victim, such act does not constitute an act of revealing facts about the victim and therefore does not amount to defamation under Article 70(2) of the Information and Communications Network Act.\\n\\nNevertheless, the judgment of the court below, which found the instant facts charged guilty solely for the reasons stated in its opinion, contains an error of misapprehending the legal principle concerning Article 70(2) of the Information and Communications Network Act.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the lower court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged as ordered, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2019DO12750]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Determination on the Prosecutor’s grounds for final appeal\\nThe lower court, with respect to the portion of the charges in this case concerning violation of the Child Welfare Act, found that there was no proof of the crime, quashed the first-instance judgment that had found the Defendant guilty, and entered a judgment of acquittal. Reviewing the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the lower court did not err by exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the “emotional abuse acts that harm a child’s mental health and development” prescribed in Article 17, item 5, of the Child Welfare Act.\\n\\n2. Determination on the Defendant’s grounds for final appeal\\na. Article 70, paragraph 1, of the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc. (hereinafter the “Information and Communications Network Act”) provides: “Any person who, with the purpose of slandering another person, publicly reveals facts via an information and communications network and thereby damages the reputation of another person shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 3 years or by a fine not exceeding 30 million won.” In order for a crime under this provision to be established, the victim must be identified and facts must be revealed so as to defame the victim. Here, to reveal facts means to reveal facts that are sufficiently specific to the extent that the social value or evaluation of a particular person may thereby be infringed; although it is not necessary that specific facts be expressly stated directly in order for such requirement to be satisfied, at a minimum the specific expression must be such that such facts can be directly inferred therefrom. In addition, to say that the victim has been identified, when the content of the expression is viewed together with the surrounding circumstances, the expression must be such that it is possible to recognize whom it points to (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 82DO1256 dated November 9, 1982; Supreme Court Decision 2011DO6904 dated August 18, 2011; Supreme Court Decision 2011DO11226 dated March 27, 2014). Meanwhile, when distinguishing whether a particular expression is a fact or an opinion, it must be determined by considering the ordinary meaning and usage of the language, provability, the context in which the words at issue were used, the social situation in which the expression was made, and other overall circumstances (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 97DO2956 dated March 24, 1998).\\n\\nb. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\nIn 2017, the Defendant’s daughter, the person outside the prosecution, and the victim were attending the same class in the third grade at XX Elementary School. On June 30, 2017, while claiming that the victim had bullied the person outside the prosecution, the Defendant’s side filed a school violence report with XX Elementary School.\\nAround July 7, 2017, the principal imposed a preliminary measure ordering the victim to be suspended from attendance for 5 days. On July 12, 2017, the XX Elementary School School Violence Countermeasures Autonomous Committee, on the premise that there had been school violence by the victim against the person outside the prosecution, resolved to approve the principal’s preliminary measure and ordered the victim, as to the victim student: prohibition of contact with the victim student and of retaliatory acts (from July 13, 2017 to September 30, 2017), 3 hours of service at school, 2 hours of special education for the student, and 2 hours of special education for the guardian (hereinafter the “resolution in this case”). On July 13, 2017, the principal implemented the measures pursuant to the resolution in this case against the victim.\\nThereafter, around mid-July 2017, the Defendant posted, on the profile status message of his KakaoTalk account, the words “No contact with school violence offenders!!!” and three fist-shaped emoticons (hereinafter the “status message in this case”).\\n\\nc. The following circumstances can be ascertained from the foregoing facts.\\nThe status message in this case, consisting of the words “No contact with school violence offenders!!!” and three fist-shaped emoticons, does not reveal the factual basis underlying the expression. The term “school violence offender” is an expression that adds the suffix “offender” meaning a person who has committed a crime to the term “school violence,” and is a collective expression referring to a “person who has committed school violence”; the Defendant merely used “school violence offender” itself as the object of the expression and did not refer to any specific person as a “school violence offender.” Considering the reality of our society, in which school violence has emerged as a serious problem, and the Defendant’s status as a parent of an elementary school child, it cannot be concluded that, merely because the Defendant used the term “school violence offender,” he was referring to an actual school violence incident. The word “contact prohibition” is ordinarily understood to mean “do not make contact,” and there is also no evidence proving that the fact that a measure of “prohibition of contact with the victim student (the person outside the prosecution)” had been imposed through the resolution in this case, etc. was known to the classmates of the victim or their parents.\\nd. When the foregoing circumstances are examined in light of the legal principles stated above, it cannot be said that, by posting the status message in this case, the Defendant revealed specific facts sufficient to lower the victim’s social value or evaluation by describing the victim’s school violence incident or the measures imposed on the victim as a result of that incident.\\nNevertheless, the lower court held that the Defendant defamed the victim by posting the status message in this case, thereby revealing specific facts sufficient to lower the victim’s social value or evaluation, and found the portion of the charges in this case concerning a violation of the Information and Communications Network Act (defamation) guilty. In the guilty portion of the lower court judgment, there is an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning defamation prescribed in Article 70, paragraph 1, of the Information and Communications Network Act. The Defendant’s argument on this point in the grounds for final appeal is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nWithout addressing the remaining grounds for the Defendant’s final appeal, we reverse the guilty portion of the lower court judgment and remand this part of the case to the lower court for further trial and determination, and dismiss the Prosecutor’s final appeal. Accordingly, the Court renders judgment as ordered, by unanimous opinion of the Justices."}

{"[92DO3160]": "The Court determines the grounds of appeal by counsel for the Defendant.\\n\\n1. Summary of the facts charged recognized by the first-instance judgment upheld by the judgment below\\n\\nThe Defendant, as a city bus driver of Non-Indicted Company 1 Co., Ltd., located in Guro-gu, Seoul ([hereinafter omitted]), and as the head of the labor union of the said company, took office as the head of the labor union of the said company on April 1, 1991. In the course of confirming the manner in which the former labor union head, Victim Non-Indicted Person 2, had handled union business during his term of office, the Defendant found somewhat unclear portions in the supporting materials and, for the purpose of informing the union members of such fact and thereby excluding the victim from the competition in future union head elections, on or about April 20, 1991, prepared and posted a large placard on the wall of the dispatch room within the said company, using imitation paper sheets, stating: “With respect to athletic uniforms, we purchased them at the outrageously high price of KRW 18,000, although they could have been purchased for KRW 10,000 per set” (hereinafter referred to as the “athletic-uniform-related placard”); “With respect to flood-disaster relief money, the branch received reports from our members on the status of flood damage and paid flood-disaster relief money, but former branch head Non-Indicted Person 2 did not even announce such fact and secretly paid KRW 50,000 each to members who had not suffered any damage at all” (hereinafter referred to as the “flood-disaster-relief-money-related placard”); and “With respect to union dues, farewell money, and congratulatory and condolence money, former officeholder Non-Indicted Person 2 irregularly paid union dues from July 1, 1988, when he executed the duties, until the present, but did not pay a single won in farewell money or congratulatory and condolence money” (hereinafter referred to as the “farewell-money etc.-related placard”), and by causing other union members to read the same, publicly stated facts and thereby damaged the victim’s reputation. The first instance applied Article 307(1) of the Criminal Act to the above recognized facts and rendered a judgment of conviction against the Defendant.\\n\\n2. Summary of the reasons of the judgment below\\n\\nIn response to the argument by counsel for the Defendant in the court below that the Defendant lacked intent to defame and that the Defendant’s act constituted truthful facts solely concerning the public interest or was not contrary to social norms, the court below held that, although some aspect of the circumstances in which the Defendant had the said placard posted may be seen as reflecting an intent to serve the union, in light of the contents described and the means used, it could not be found that the Defendant lacked intent to defame in the act at issue in this case, and that it could not be deemed to fall under a case of truthful facts solely concerning the interests of the union members or to constitute an act not in violation of the law because it was not contrary to social norms. Accordingly, the court rejected counsel’s argument and dismissed the Defendant’s appeal.\\n\\n3. The Court’s determination\\n\\na. Since Article 310 of the Criminal Act provides that “Where the act under Article 307(1) is truthful facts solely concerning the public interest, punishment shall not be imposed,” even if a person publicly states facts and thereby damages another’s reputation, where such facts concern the public interest and the facts are stated for the purpose of serving the public interest, if the truth of such facts is proven, unlawfulness is excluded and the act is not punished. The above provision of the Criminal Act should be understood as seeking harmony between the two conflicting legal interests of protection of an individual’s honor as a personality right and guarantee of the just freedom of expression under Article 21 of the Constitution. Therefore, taking into account the harmony and balance between these two legal interests, even if there is no proof that the stated facts are true, where the actor believed those facts to be true and had reasonable grounds to so believe, unlawfulness should be deemed absent (see Supreme Court Decision 4294HYEONGSANG12, rendered on May 17, 1962; Supreme Court Decision 85DAKA29, rendered on October 11, 1988, etc.). In such case, whether the stated facts concern the public interest must be determined objectively in light of the contents and nature of the facts themselves, and if the actor’s principal purpose was to serve the public interest, the application of Article 310 of the Criminal Act cannot be excluded merely because there were incidentally other private motives (see Supreme Court Decision 88DO899, rendered on February 14, 1989).\\n\\nb. We first examine whether the facts stated by the Defendant concern the public interest.\\n\\nUpon reviewing the relevant evidence in comparison with the record, it may be found that the Defendant was elected on March 21, 1991, through an election, as the branch head (hereinafter referred to as the union head) of the branch of Non-Indicted Company 1 Co., Ltd. of the Seoul Bus Branch of the National Automobile Labor Union Federation, with a term of office of 3 years, and took office on April 1. Previously, the results of the union’s operation or accounting audit had not been disclosed, and there had been misunderstandings and dissatisfaction among the union members. Accordingly, at the time of the union head election, the Defendant had pledged to disclose all union operations. It may also be found that the union officers, from April 8, 1991 through April 12, 1991, conducted an accounting audit openly pursuant to the Branch Operating Rules (trial record, pages 57 through 75), as a result of which, as the court below also found, they discovered, among the business handled by Victim Non-Indicted Person 2, the former union head, during his tenure as union head, portions, as stated in the placard at issue, where supporting materials showing disbursement of union funds were lacking or gave rise to doubt, and that the placard was posted mainly for the purpose of informing the union members thereof; and that the union officers who conducted the accounting audit strongly requested the Defendant to disclose the results of the accounting audit. It is difficult to find that the principal motive for the Defendant’s posting of the said placard was, as stated in the facts charged, to exclude the said Non-Indicted Person 2 from the union head election to be held thereafter (other than the unilateral assertion of the said Non-Indicted Person 2 contained in the statement prepared by the prosecutor, there is no evidence supporting this point).\\n\\nTherefore, the facts stated in the said placard concern whether union funds were properly disbursed during the period in which the said Non-Indicted Person 2 served as union head, and when objectively determined in light of their contents and nature, it is appropriate to deem them to fall under “matters concerning the public interest” as provided in Article 310 of the Criminal Act. Even if the manner of expression in the said placard did not take the form of a simple accounting-audit result report but instead took the form of criticizing the performance of duties by the said Non-Indicted Person 2, the former union head, since the Defendant, as union head, posted the said placard mainly for the purpose of informing the union members of the above facts, it may be deemed to have been for the public interest.\\n\\nEven if the place where the Defendant posted the said placard was the dispatch room to which the general public could enter, as recognized from the relevant evidence and the record, considering that the dispatch room was mainly used as a waiting room for driver members and that it was difficult for all members, including drivers working on a two-shift system per day, to gather in one place, posting the placard in the dispatch room may also have been the most effective method of informing all union members of the above facts. Therefore, it cannot be said that the Defendant’s act was not for the public interest merely because the Defendant posted the placard in such a place.\\n\\nc. Next, we examine whether the facts stated by the Defendant are true.\\n\\nAccording to the relevant evidence and the record, including the testimony of First-Instance Witness Non-Indicted Person 3 and Court-Below Witness Non-Indicted Person 4, which were not rejected by the court below, the photographs of the said placard filed in the investigation record (pages 13 and 14), the respective written statements prepared by Non-Indicted Person 5 and Non-Indicted Person 6 (pages 48 and 50), the simplified tax invoices (page 49), the receipts (page 51), and the respective entries in the documents concerning the disbursement of flood-disaster relief money (pages 52 through 69), the grounds on which the Defendant learned of the facts stated in the said placard as a result of the union officers’ open accounting audit may be recognized as follows: (1) with respect to the “athletic-uniform-related placard,” Non-Indicted Person 5, a union member, stated that he purchased on the market at KRW 10,000 a set of athletic uniforms having the same trademark and fabric as the athletic uniforms the union had already purchased at KRW 18,000 per set, differing only in color and design, and brought the item for comparison, whereupon it was found to be of the same quality (the Defendant displayed the athletic uniform purchased by the said Non-Indicted Person 5 together with the placard and made it public);
