{"[91DO1566]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. The Defendant’s act of changing the use of the building in this case, which is a neighborhood living facility, to use it as a church without permission from the mayor or county governor, was not something that first became punishable only from 1987; rather, it is clear that even at the time when the Defendant commenced the above act of changing the use on 1985.9.1., it was an act in violation of Article 54(1), the main text of Article 5(1), and Article 48 of the Building Act then in force and was punishable. In addition, Article 16 of the Criminal Act provides that a person who, in respect of his own act, mistakes that it does not constitute a crime by virtue of a statute shall not be punished only where there is a justifiable reason for such mistake; this does not refer to mere ignorance of the law, but means that where an act is generally a criminal act, yet in the particular case the person mistakenly recognizes it as an act permitted by statute and thus not constituting a crime, and there is a justifiable reason for such recognition, he shall not be punished. Therefore, the circumstance that the Defendant did not know that the act in this case was subject to permission under the Building Act is merely simple ignorance of the law, and in particular does not constitute a case in which he affirmatively and mistakenly recognized it as an act permitted by statute and thus not constituting a crime; thus, it cannot be said to be an act resulting from a mistake of law. This argument is without merit.\\n\\n2. In this case, in which a sentence of a fine was imposed on the Defendant, the reason of improper sentencing does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal. This argument is without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, since the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous that the appeal be dismissed, the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (×) concerning evidence? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) (a) To examine “a written item that is physical evidence,” the procedures of reading aloud, notifying the contents, or inspection, which are methods of examining documentary evidence, and the procedure of presentation, which is the method of examining physical evidence, must be carried out together. (b) A photograph of the injured area submitted as evidence of injury is non-statement evidence, and the hearsay rule does not apply. (c) Since “a statement prepared during the investigative process,” which is subject to Article 312(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act, means one prepared in an investigative office under the involvement of an investigative agency after the investigation has begun, a statement prepared by a suspect at a place other than the investigative office at the request of the investigative agency does not constitute a statement prepared during the investigative process. (d) If, after the prosecutor has summoned in advance, without special circumstances, and interviewed a person whom the prosecutor intends to request and examine as a witness on the trial date, that witness testifies in court to matters unfavorable to the defendant, the witness’s in-court testimony can be found credible only if it is ensured that the prosecutor did not influence the witness’s in-court testimony through coaxing or pressure, or by leading or suggesting answers, etc., during the pre-examination interview process.

supporting_precedents: {"[2007DO3906]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the assertion that the principle of indictment-only was violated\\n\\nWhen the prosecutor petitions for a summary order, he must submit to the court, at the same time as the petition for the summary order, the documentary evidence and exhibits necessary for issuing the summary order (Criminal Procedure Rules Article 170). This is because the summary procedure is a trial based on written examination, and therefore an exception to the principle of indictment-only is recognized; accordingly, it cannot be said that the principle of indictment-only was violated merely because the documentary evidence and exhibits were submitted to the court concurrently with the petition for the summary order. Nor can it be said that, even after a request for formal trial against the summary order was filed, the fact that the court retained the documentary evidence and exhibits without returning them to the prosecutor rendered the procedure of the indictment, which had already been lawfully instituted prior thereto, unlawful.\\n\\nThe judgment of the court below to the same effect is proper, and, as argued in the grounds for appeal, there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principle concerning the principle of indictment-only, violation of the principle of due process under Article 12(1) of the Constitution, or violation of Article 254(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act and Article 61 of the Rules on the Administrative Affairs of Prosecutorial Cases.\\n\\n2. Regarding the assertion that the petition for a summary order was unlawful\\n\\nThis part of the argument was raised only at the stage of this Court and therefore does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal. Moreover, even upon examination of the record, the offense subject to the petition for a summary order in this case is the offense of violation of the Act on the Punishment of Violent Acts, etc. (night-time and joint injury), and the applicable provisions are Article 2(2) and Article 2(1) of the Act on the Punishment of Violent Acts, etc., and Article 257(1) of the Criminal Act, so that it is capable of being the subject of a summary order; accordingly, this ground of appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Regarding the assertion that the photographs taken of the injured part of the non-party person are inadmissible\\n\\nA. The reason Article 55(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act grants the defendant the right to inspect or copy the trial record is to ensure the accuracy of the record by giving the defendant an opportunity, through inspection or copying of the trial record, to confirm whether the contents of the declarant’s statement correspond to the contents of the recorded minutes, and thereby to fully guarantee the defendant’s right of defense (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DO3282, rendered on October 10, 2003). Therefore, even if the defendant did not inspect or copy the trial record at a time of his choosing, such as before the next trial date, if he inspected or copied it before the conclusion of oral argument, the defendant’s right under Article 55(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act to request inspection or copying of the trial record cannot be deemed infringed absent special circumstances, such as where the delay in inspection or copying hindered the exercise of the defendant’s right of defense, and the trial record must be deemed admissible as evidence of guilt.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the defendant inspected and copied the trial record of the first trial date held on April 18, 2005, on which the first trial date held on October 19, 2004, had been recorded. It can be seen that the court of first instance, at the second trial date on December 16, 2004, informed the defendant, by reference to the trial record of the first trial date, of the gist of the main matters concerning the proceedings at the first trial date, and concluded oral argument on December 8, 2005. If such are the circumstances, then even if the defendant had requested inspection and copying of the first trial record on December 13, 2004, before the second trial date in the court of first instance, and was unable to inspect or copy it, there is no indication that this caused any hindrance to the exercise of the defendant’s right of defense. Accordingly, the first trial record may be used as evidence of guilt, and therefore the argument in the grounds for appeal—that because the above first trial record cannot be used as evidence of guilt, the evidentiary examination of the “photographs taken of the injured part of the non-party person” made at that trial date is also invalid and thus those photographs cannot be used as evidence of guilt—is without merit.\\n\\nB. Even if, as argued in the grounds for appeal, there were any illegality in the procedure by which the investigative authorities arrested the defendant in flagrante delicto, the “photographs taken of the injured part of the non-party person” were not evidence collected from the defendant, and thus cannot be deemed illegally collected evidence. This ground of appeal is also without merit.\\n\\nC. The “photographs taken of the injured part of the non-party person” are non-testimonial evidence, to which the hearsay rule does not apply; therefore, the ground of appeal asserting that the hearsay rule should apply on the premise that the photographs are testimonial evidence cannot be accepted.\\n\\nD. The expression of consent to evidence stipulated in Article 318 of the Criminal Procedure Act may be revoked or withdrawn until the completion of the evidentiary proceeding; however, once the evidentiary proceeding has been completed, revocation or withdrawal is not recognized, and therefore evidentiary capacity already acquired prior to revocation or withdrawal is not lost (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DO2611, rendered on June 25, 2004). Upon examination of the record, it can be seen that the defendant consented at the first trial date in the court of first instance to use the above photographs as evidence, and that the court of first instance thereby completed the evidentiary examination of those photographs. Accordingly, even if the defendant, at the court below, revoked or withdrew the expression of consent to evidence regarding the above photographs, as argued in the grounds for appeal, the evidentiary capacity of the above photographs is not lost. This ground of appeal is also without merit.\\n\\nE. Therefore, the court below’s measure recognizing the evidentiary capacity of the “photographs taken of the injured part of the non-party person” is proper, and there is no illegality such as a violation of Article 55(3), Article 307, Article 310-2, Article 312(1), or Article 318(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, Article 12(1) of the Constitution, or Article 61 of the Rules on the Administrative Affairs of Prosecutorial Cases, as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n4. Regarding the assertion that the defendant did not inflict injury on the non-party person\\n\\nUpon examination of the evidence lawfully admitted and examined by the court of first instance, as cited by the court below, by reference to the record, the court below’s measure of finding the facts charged in this case guilty—that the defendant grabbed the victim, the non-party person, by the collar, pushed and pulled him, and thereby inflicted on the victim an injury of an unspecified number of days for treatment consisting of abrasions to the neck and chest areas—is proper, and there is no illegality, such as a violation of the rules of evidence and logic, as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as per the order, with the concurrence of all participating Justices."}

{"[2013DO2511]": "The Court determines the grounds for appeal (the statements in the respective supplemental appellate briefs submitted by the Defendants after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds for appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. Determination of the Defendants’ grounds for appeal and the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal related thereto\\n\\nA. As to the argument regarding the principle of indictment-only\\n\\nAs a general rule, when a prosecutor institutes a prosecution, the indictment must not attach documents or other objects that may create prejudice in the court regarding the case, nor may it cite their contents (Criminal Procedure Rules Article 118(2)). However, whether this principle against indictment by reference has been violated must be determined specifically in the particular case by considering, in light of the type and content of the offense stated in the indictment, the contents of the documents or other objects attached to or cited in the indictment, and whether, in addition to the matters required by law, the facts stated in the indictment may create prejudice in the judge and hinder the judge from grasping the substance of the criminal facts (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009. 10. 22., 2009DO7436).\\n\\nThe lower court determined that, although the indictment in this case cited written materials and photographs to be submitted as evidence, such citations were for the purpose of specifying the facts charged for each violation of the National Security Act in this case or concerned part of the objective and subjective constituent elements, and that the cited portions did not hinder the Defendants’ exercise of their defense rights nor create prejudice in the judge or hinder the judge from grasping the substance of the criminal facts, and thus could not be regarded as violating the principle against indictment by reference.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the principle against indictment by reference as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nB. As to the argument regarding the illegality of the seizure and search execution procedure and the resulting admissibility of evidence\\n\\n(1) The lower court, after comprehensively considering the circumstances as found in its reasoning, determined that it could not be deemed that the Defendants were in a de facto state of detention at the time of execution of the seizure and search warrant for the office of the National Intelligence Service investigator against Non-party 1 Co., Ltd. (hereinafter “Non-party 1 Company”). Examining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the record, the lower court’s above factual finding and determination are proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in omitting a determination on necessary matters or in misunderstanding the legal principles regarding the guarantee of the right to participate in the execution of a seizure and search warrant or the legality of such execution.\\n\\n(2) In addition, the lower court determined that, because the columns “place and person/body to be seized, searched, and inspected” in the seizure, search, and inspection warrant of this case stated the residence of Defendant 1 and the body of Defendant 1, even though the above warrant had been presented and the seizure and search of Defendant 1’s body had been completed, the seizure and search of Defendant 1’s residence could not yet be deemed to have commenced, and on such reasons as stated in its reasoning, the act of the National Intelligence Service investigators in executing the seizure and search of Defendant 1’s residence pursuant to the above warrant was not unlawful. Examining this in light of the record, the lower court’s above determination is acceptable as proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the warrant principle, etc.\\n\\n(3) Furthermore, the lower court determined that, at the time of the seizure and search of Defendant 3’s residence, the investigator in charge notified Non-party 2, who was Defendant 3’s wife and was stated as a co-suspect in the seizure and search warrant, of the fact of execution of the warrant and then presented the warrant, and considering, among other things, the circumstances that, at the time of execution, the seizure and search of the office of Non-party 1 Company jointly operated by Defendant 3 took place simultaneously and Defendant 3 participated in the seizure and search of that office, Defendant 3’s right to participate in the seizure and search of the residence was not substantively infringed. Examining the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the warrant principle, etc.\\n\\n(4) Furthermore, the lower court determined that the “result of execution of restrictive measures on communications concerning e-mail,” which the trial court inspected, was directed at the contents of electronic mail that Defendant 1 sent and received in real time, obtained and recorded pursuant to the court’s warrant permitting restrictive measures on communications, and that Criminal Procedure Act Articles 219 and 123, concerning execution of warrants and the participation of the person in charge, do not apply to the execution procedure of the above permit; and it recognized the admissibility of the inspection result on the grounds, inter alia, that the trial court directly inspected in the inspection procedure whether the original electronic mail was identical to the printout. Examining this in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the legal nature of restrictive measures on communications concerning e-mail or the identity of electronic evidence.\\n\\nC. As to the argument regarding infringement of the right to a public trial and the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal related thereto\\n\\n(1) The latter sentence of Article 27(3) of the Constitution provides, “Any accused person shall have the right to a speedy and public trial in the absence of exceptional circumstances where a trial may be held in camera as provided by law.” Thus, it declares that the criminal defendant’s right to a public trial is guaranteed as a fundamental right. Article 109 of the Constitution and Article 57(1) of the Court Organization Act provide that trials and judgments shall be public, but that the hearing may be non-public by decision when there is a risk of harming national security, public peace and order, or good morals and manners. Article 57(2) of the Court Organization Act provides that a decision prohibiting public access concerning the hearing of a trial shall be pronounced stating the reasons. In light of the purport of these provisions, if a decision was made to prohibit public access to the hearing of a trial even though there was no ground for prohibition of public access under Article 109 of the Constitution and Article 57(1) of the Court Organization Act, such decision prohibiting public access would infringe the Defendant’s right to a public trial, and the testimony of a witness taken through that procedure would have no admissibility as evidence. This is not altered even if the defense counsel’s right of cross-examination was guaranteed (see Supreme Court Decision 2005. 10. 28., 2005DO5854), and the same applies even where the reason for the decision prohibiting public access is unknown, such as where no pronouncement of a decision prohibiting public access was made.\\n\\nAccording to the record, it can be seen that at the fourth trial date of the first instance, the trial court conducted the witness examination of Non-party 3 without pronouncing a decision prohibiting public access, and that the examination was conducted in a non-public state. In light of the above legal principles, there was a procedural illegality infringing the Defendants’ right to a public trial in the witness examination procedure for Non-party 3; thus, the witness examination record for Non-party 3, a piece of evidence collected in that procedure, cannot be used as evidence of guilt against the Defendants.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court’s action in upholding the first-instance judgment, which otherwise used the witness examination record for Non-party 3 as evidence of guilt, contains an error in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the principle of public trial and the admissibility of evidence. However, examining the relevant evidence in light of the record, even excluding the witness examination record for Non-party 3, which lacks admissibility as evidence, the remaining evidence admitted by the lower court—namely, various documents including the “organizational status report,” the respective in-court statements of witness Non-party 4, Non-party 5, and the National Intelligence Service investigators, and the images of each on-site photograph, as well as the respective entry and exit records of Defendant 1, Defendant 2, and Defendant 5—sufficiently establishes the points of spy activity for the purpose of execution and special intrusion/escape among the facts charged in this case that the lower court found guilty. Therefore, the lower court’s conclusion finding this part of the facts charged guilty is proper, and ultimately the above error by the lower court cannot be deemed to have affected the judgment.\\n\\n(2) Meanwhile, Criminal Procedure Act Article 56 provides, “Matters entered in the trial record as procedural acts on the trial date shall be proved only by that record.” Therefore, insofar as the first-instance trial record of the 26th hearing states that the trial court, after pronouncing a decision prohibiting public access, conducted the witness examination procedure for the above investigators in a non-public state, proof or rebuttal by means other than the trial record regarding whether such decision prohibiting public access was pronounced is not permitted. In the same context, the lower court’s action determining that each of the above witnesses’ in-court statements had admissibility as evidence is proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the principle of public trial.\\n\\n(3) Furthermore, the lower court recognized, based on the trial record, the fact that at the fourth trial date of the first instance, in the witness examination procedure for Non-party 6, and at the fifth trial date, in the partial witness examination procedure for Non-party 7 and the witness examination procedure for Non-party 8, the trial proceeded non-publicly without pronouncing a decision prohibiting public access, and determined that the in-court statements of such witnesses lacked admissibility as evidence. The lower court’s determination on this point follows the above legal principles and is proper, and there is no illegality, such as failure to fully deliberate, as argued in the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal.\\n\\nD. As to the argument concerning the integrity and identity of documents printed from seized information storage media, and the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal related thereto\\n\\n(1) In order to use as evidence the character information stored by input into a seized computer disk or other similar information storage medium (hereinafter referred to only as “information storage medium”) or its printout (hereinafter referred to as “printed document”), the identity between the contents stored in the original information storage medium and the printed document must be recognized, and for this purpose, the circumstance that the original information storage medium was not altered from the time of seizure until the time of document output, that is, integrity, must be secured. In particular, in the case of a document printed from a medium that “hard-copied” or “imaged” the data stored on the storage medium in lieu of the original information storage medium, not only must the identity of the data between the original information storage medium and the “hard-copied” or “imaged” medium be recognized, but also the mechanical accuracy of the computer used in the process of verification, the reliability of the program, and the operator’s professional technical ability and accuracy at each stage of input, processing, and output must be secured (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 2007. 12. 13., 2007DO7257). In this case, as a matter of principle, the fact that the printed document and the data stored in the information storage medium are identical, and that the original information storage medium was not altered until the time of document output, shall be proved by the method of receiving from the party subjected to seizure/search a written confirmation signed to the effect that the hash values of the original information storage medium and the “hard-copied” or “imaged” medium are identical and submitting it to the court; however, where proof by such method is impossible or markedly difficult, the integrity and identity may also be recognized by testimony of investigators or experts who participated in a series of procedures such as seizure, sealing, unsealing, “hard-copying,” or “imaging” of the original information storage medium, by proving circumstances such as the identical hash values between the original information storage medium and the “hard-copied” or “imaged” medium or that the original information storage medium remained sealed from the time of initial seizure until submission of evidence and was not altered at all, or by a method in which the court compares the data stored in the original and the printed document submitted as evidence. It cannot be said that proof must necessarily be made only by means such as playback of video recordings of the seizure and search process.\\n\\n(2) According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court, based on the following circumstances recognized through the respective testimonies of the National Intelligence Service investigators who executed the seizure and search of the office of Non-party 1 Company or the residences of the Defendants, and the experts who participated in the “imaging” procedure at the National Intelligence Service office, namely: the National Intelligence Service investigators seized the respective information storage media indicated in the lower court’s reasoning in the presence of the Defendants or their family members and employees, then sealed them after obtaining the participants’ signatures; when the National Intelligence Service duplicated data stored in some information storage media by the “imaging” method, the seal status was checked, unsealed, and resealed after obtaining signatures from the Defendants or the above experts; and these persons signed to the effect that the hash values of the original information storage media and the hash values of the files created through the “imaging” work were identical; together with the circumstance that the trial court conducted an inspection with the participation of both the Defendants and the Prosecutor and defense counsel, and in that inspection process verified that the hash values produced in the inspection were identical to the hash values produced during “imaging” while a write-protection device was attached at the time of seizure and search, or verified that the character information of the files created through the “imaging” work and the printed documents were identical; and the circumstance that, in the case of some information storage media, the court confirmed the existence, inside the sealed envelope of the portion concerning the inspection result carried out by the lower court, of a previously unsealed envelope that appears to have been signed by the expert who participated in the “imaging” process as an expert on electronic information—all taken together, the lower court determined that the printed documents submitted as evidence, as stated in its reasoning, were not only identical to the contents stored in the original seized information storage media, but also that the original information storage media had not been altered until the time of document output, and therefore the printed documents could be used as evidence.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s determination is acceptable as proper, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the method or degree of proof for the integrity, identity, and reliability of electronic evidence. Furthermore, there is also no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in the lower court’s action rejecting the Defendants’ argument to the effect that the above information storage media, etc. had been manipulated by investigative agencies or that the Defendants did not own or possess such information storage media.\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, as to the MP3 file submitted as evidence concerning the point of praise and encouragement arising from possession of enemy-related expressive materials by Defendant 2, the lower court determined that the file could not be used as evidence, and acquitted on this part of the facts charged, on the grounds that, according to the trial court’s inspection result, traces of access to the hard disk on which the above MP3 file was stored appeared at a time after the seizure and search had begun, and even according to the testimony of the National Intelligence Service investigator who was in charge of the seizure and search at the time, no reasonable explanation was revealed regarding the circumstances of such access.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the record, the lower court’s determination is acceptable as proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning admissibility of evidence or in exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nE. As to the application of the hearsay rule\\n\\n(1) When the character information stored by input into an information storage medium by the Defendant or a person other than the Defendant, or its printout, is used as evidence, it is in substance not greatly different from a written statement prepared by the Defendant or the non-Defendant or a document recording that person’s statement, and in light of the possibility of manipulation after seizure and during the printing process, and the fact that the opportunity for cross-examination is not fundamentally guaranteed, the hearsay rule applies to the truth of its contents. Therefore, as a general rule, such evidence may be used only when the authenticity of its formation is proved by the statement of its maker or declarant pursuant to Criminal Procedure Act Article 313(1). However, where the fact to be proved is not the truth of the contents of the character information stored in the information storage medium but the existence of such character information itself, the hearsay rule does not apply (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decisions 99DO2317 dated 1999. 9. 3. and 2010DO3504 dated 2013. 2. 15.). Furthermore, when a certain statement is used as direct evidence of the criminal facts, even if that statement constitutes hearsay evidence, it does not necessarily become hearsay evidence when it is used as circumstantial evidence of the very fact that such statement was made or of indirect facts unrelated to the truth of the statement (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 99DO1252 dated 2000. 2. 25.).\\n\\n(2) According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court determined that, in the case of communication by exchanging documents with members of an anti-state organization, where the facts charged relate to having received instructions from an anti-state organization and having searched for and collected state secrets, if the received instructions and the state secrets searched for and collected exist in the form of documents, or if the object of the provision of convenience is documents, the truth of the contents of the documents is not at issue; rather, the very existence of documents containing such contents is evidence, and therefore the hearsay rule does not apply to such facts charged, and the printed documents submitted as evidence concerning that part of the facts charged have admissibility as evidence.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, most of the contents of the printed documents submitted as evidence for this part of the facts charged fall within the category where, in relation to the facts to be proved, the issue is not whether the contents of the documents are true, but the very existence of character information containing such contents is evidence. Therefore, the above determination by the lower court is proper and acceptable within that scope.\\n\\nHowever, among the contents of the above printed documents, some include contents such as “○○○ (Defendant 5) is active as a political affairs special advisor, etc. under the chairman of the election countermeasures committee of the △△ Party,” and contents reporting the Defendants’ own experiences and activities. In such cases, in relation to the “search and collection” of state secrets, which is the fact to be proved, whether the Defendants actually engaged in such experiences and activities, that is, whether the contents of the documents are true, becomes an issue, and there is room for application of the hearsay rule. Thus, it was erroneous for the lower court to conclude broadly that the hearsay rule does not apply even to the parts of the entire printed documents that describe the Defendants’ own experiences and activities. However, these document contents constitute only a very small part of the entire set of documents submitted as evidence, and according to the evidence, including the lawful in-court statement of witness Non-party 4 adopted by the first instance, together with the contents of most of the document contents that the lower court properly determined were not subject to the hearsay rule, even excluding from the evidence of guilt the parts of the printed documents concerning the Defendants’ actual experiences and activities, there is sufficient basis to recognize this part of the facts charged as guilty. Therefore, the lower court’s conclusion finding each part of these facts charged guilty is proper and acceptable. Accordingly, the above error by the lower court cannot be deemed to have affected the outcome of the judgment.\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, according to the reasons of the lower court judgment, with respect to Defendant 1, Defendant 2, and Defendant 5’s special intrusion/escape and meeting, the court below can be seen to have relied, as one of the indirect facts supporting a guilty finding, on the fact that files containing contents such as “To Mr. Non-party 9: regarding the 2011 interview, I think it would be preferable to conduct it in Beijing with Non-party 9 and Mr. ▽▽ from January 30 to February 1” had been “saved” on Defendant 1’s computer.\\n\\nExamining this in light of the above legal principles, if one seeks to prove that Defendant 1 and Defendant 5 actually met with North Korean operatives at that time, as described in the contents, the truth of the document contents is at issue, and the hearsay rule would apply. However, the fact itself that a file containing such contents was stored on Defendant 1’s computer is unrelated to the truth of the contents and constitutes an indirect fact for proving this part of the facts charged. Therefore, the hearsay rule cannot be said to apply even in such a case. The lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the hearsay rule or the granting of admissibility as evidence.\\n\\nF. As to the admissibility of photographs taken overseas\\n\\n(1) Any person has the freedom not to have his or her face or appearance arbitrarily photographed; however, such freedom is not guaranteed without limitation, and to the extent necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, reasonable restrictions may be imposed within that scope. Where investigative agencies photograph in the course of investigating crime when the offense is currently being committed or has just been committed, there is a need and urgency to preserve evidence, and the photograph is taken by a generally permitted and reasonable method, the mere fact that the photography was conducted without a warrant does not necessarily make it unlawful (see Supreme Court Decision 99DO2317 dated 1999. 9. 3.).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court, the video recording of Defendant 1, Defendant 2, and Defendant 5 meeting with North Korean operatives in Japan or China was made because there was a need to preserve evidence of the Defendants’ meetings, and it can be seen that the Defendants were photographed while meeting with members of an anti-state organization or immediately before or after such meetings, and the locations of the photography were public places such as roads used by vehicles, the street in front of a restaurant, or the hotel front desk. Accordingly, such photography was not conducted by a method beyond what is generally permitted and reasonable, nor can it be deemed unlawful as a coercive disposition without a warrant. Therefore, under such circumstances, the lower court’s determination that the above photography was not unlawful and its recognition of the admissibility of the photographs capturing the 6mm tape video, as stated in its reasoning, are proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the scope of application of the warrant principle or the legal principles concerning the right of portrait.\\n\\n(2) Meanwhile, according to the reasons of the lower court judgment, it can be seen that the lower court rejected the Defendants’ argument that the above video-captured photographs should be denied admissibility as illegally obtained evidence infringing the foreign territorial sovereignty that ought to be guaranteed under international law and violating the international criminal judicial cooperation procedures, and used them as evidence of guilt.\\n\\nAlthough the filming constituted an investigative act for the collection of evidence and the place of filming was within the territory of Japan or China rather than Korea, considering that the person filmed was a Korean national and that, as stated above, the filming was conducted by a generally permitted and reasonable method in a public place and thus cannot be said to be a coercive disposition, such circumstances do not constitute grounds for denying the admissibility as evidence of the evidence obtained through the filming act. In the end, the lower court’s action recognizing the admissibility of the above photographs is proper, and there is no illegality, such as misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the scope of application of the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence, as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nG. As to the argument concerning the “overseas residence” requirement under Criminal Procedure Act Article 314\\n\\n“Overseas residence” under Criminal Procedure Act Article 314 is not satisfied merely because the person who is to give a statement is simply located abroad; exceptionally, the requirement can be satisfied only where there are circumstances making it impossible to have that person appear in court even if all possible and reasonable means are used (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decisions 2007DO10004 dated 2008. 2. 28. and 2011DO1013 dated 2011. 7. 14.). Although, in general, whether the requirement is satisfied is determined through procedures such as confirming the whereabouts and dispatching a summons, such procedures are not always necessary; in some cases, even if such procedures are not followed, if the court can recognize circumstances making it difficult to expect that person to be examined in court, the requirement must be deemed satisfied (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 2001DO5666 dated 2002. 3. 26.).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, Non-party 10 is a person who left North Korea after working as an operative of the External Liaison Department, the predecessor of North Korea’s Bureau 225, which is in charge of operations against South Korea, and after giving a statement at the National Intelligence Service on 2011. 6. 15. regarding his experiences from when he had worked as an operative, he has since his move to Japan around 2011. 7. 22. remained in a state where his residence or whereabouts are unknown except for communication by e-mail. At the time of his statement at the National Intelligence Service, he expressed his plan to move, and also stated that after moving he would find and submit materials related to his statement; the investigative agency, after confirming Non-party 10’s departure from the country, repeatedly requested his appearance as a witness via his e-mail address, which was his only contact information, together with a notice upon entry into the country, but Non-party 10 clearly indicated through a handwritten statement that he refused to testify.\\n\\nIn addition, when the circumstances that, even under the criminal judicial assistance treaty concluded between Korea and Japan, it is impossible to forcibly apprehend Non-party 10 and bring him to this court, are comprehensively considered, even if Non-party 10’s whereabouts were confirmed and a summons were sent, it would be difficult to expect that he would appear in court as a witness. Therefore, even if measures such as confirming his Japanese address and dispatching a witness summons were not fully taken, the “overseas residence” requirement under Criminal Procedure Act Article 314 must be deemed satisfied. In the same sense, the lower court’s determination recognizing the admissibility of the statement record of Non-party 10 on the basis that it satisfied not only the “overseas residence” requirement but also that his statement was proved to have been made under circumstances of special reliability is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the requirements for granting admissibility of evidence under Criminal Procedure Act Article 314 or in failing to fully deliberate.\\n\\nH. As to the argument regarding the installation of shielding facilities\\n\\nUnder Article 17 of the National Intelligence Service Employees Act, an employee of the National Intelligence Service has a duty not to divulge secrets acquired in the course of duty (paragraph 1), and where an employee intends, as a witness pursuant to law, to testify concerning matters of official secrets, prior permission from the Director of the National Intelligence Service must be obtained (paragraph 2); where the Director of the National Intelligence Service permits testimony under paragraph 2, the court may take appropriate measures, such as non-public testimony, to protect official secrets (paragraph 6).\\n\\nAccording to the record and the reasons of the lower court judgment, it can be seen that, at the 26th trial date in the first instance, during each witness examination of the National Intelligence Service investigators, the trial court pronounced a decision that the witnesses’ personal information and the witness examination procedure would be conducted non-publicly, and proceeded with the witness examination in a state where shielding facilities were installed so that the Defendants or their counsel could not see the appearance of the National Intelligence Service employees, and only the bench could see them. In light of the purport of the above provisions, the contents of the testimony concerned the circumstances of the witnesses having photographed the meeting between Defendant 1, etc. and the North Korean operative in China or Japan, and thus concerned matters of official secrets of the National Intelligence Service employees. Therefore, the trial court’s measure of installing shielding facilities to protect such secrets should be regarded as part of the “appropriate measures for the protection of official secrets.”\\n\\nFurthermore, even if, due to the installation of such shielding facilities, defense counsel could not see the witness during cross-examination, in light of the fact that detailed cross-examination was conducted regarding the above photographing circumstances, and the above witnesses answered relatively in detail regarding matters other than portions relating to some official secrets, it cannot be said that the defense counsel’s defense rights were substantively infringed or that the legitimacy of the judgment itself became impossible to recognize, and thus this cannot be deemed an illegality affecting the judgment (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DO3983 dated 2007. 6. 1.). The lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the guarantee of the defense counsel’s right of cross-examination, the principle of direct examination, or the scope of application of the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence.\\n\\nI. As to the argument concerning the method of examination of documentary evidence\\n\\nUnder Criminal Procedure Act Article 292 and Criminal Procedure Rules Article 134-6, when documentary evidence is examined, the applicant, in principle, shall read it aloud, but when the presiding judge deems it necessary, the applicant may be directed to state its gist in lieu thereof, and when inspection by reading is deemed more appropriate than other methods, examination may be conducted by presenting the documentary evidence and allowing it to be read. Meanwhile, under Criminal Procedure Act Article 292-2(1), when examining physical evidence, the applicant shall present it.\\n\\nIn light of the purport of these provisions, to examine the so-called “written document as physical evidence,” which is originally physical evidence but also has the nature of documentary evidence, the procedures for examination of documentary evidence—reading, disclosure of contents, or inspection—and the procedure for examination of physical evidence—presentation—must be carried out together. Therefore, as a rule, the evidentiary applicant must be made to read the document while presenting it, or in lieu thereof, disclose or inspect its contents.\\n\\nThe lower court determined that the first-instance court had adopted as evidence the books allegedly possessed by Defendant 1 and Defendant 3 as enemy-related expressive materials, and that in light of the circumstances that evidence examination was conducted by presentation and disclosure of contents for those books, the examination method was not unlawful and the admissibility of the books could not be denied. The lower court’s factual findings and determinations are proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the scope of recognition of admissibility as evidence.\\n\\nJ. As to the argument concerning the point of execution for the purpose of attaining the objective (spy activity), and the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal related thereto\\n\\n(1) The “state secret” prescribed in Article 4(1)2(b) of the National Security Act is limited to cases where the secret is any fact, object, or knowledge that is not already widely known to the general public domestically through lawful procedures, etc., and whose being kept secret or unconfirmed vis-à-vis an anti-state organization in matters such as politics, economy, society, or culture is in the interest of the Republic of Korea; and where disclosure of its contents is likely to cause a danger to national security, thereby having substantial value warranting secret protection. This has been the Supreme Court’s settled view since the en banc Decision 97DO985 dated 1997. 9. 16. While interpreting the general meaning of “state secret” in this limited manner, and considering that the above provision not only limits the subject of the act to “a member of an anti-state organization or a person who received instructions therefrom,” but also makes it a constituent element that the act be “an act for the purpose of carrying out the objective of an anti-state organization,” thereby imposing limitations in terms of the subject and manner of the act, it cannot be said that the provision violates the principle of definiteness required by the principle of nulla poena sine lege to the extent of being unconstitutional.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the issue of how to punish a certain crime, namely the choice of the type and range of the statutory penalty, is a matter to be determined by the legislature after comprehensively considering not only the nature of the crime and the protected legal interest, but also our history and culture, the circumstances of the times at the time of legislation, the value judgments and legal sentiments of the general public, and criminal policy aspects for crime prevention. Accordingly, broad legislative discretion or freedom of formation should be recognized in this area. Therefore, unless the statutory penalty for a crime is so excessively harsh in comparison with the nature of the crime and the responsibility of the actor that it markedly loses balance within the penal system, or departs from the degree necessary to achieve the original purpose and function of punishment for that crime, and thus clearly violates the principle of equality or proportionality, it should not be readily concluded to be unconstitutional (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decisions 2012NO4637 dated 2012. 9. 27. and 2009DO13197 dated 2012. 10. 25.).\\n\\nExamining this in light of such legal principles, the mere circumstance that, unlike Article 11 of the Military Secrets Protection Act, which provides for a statutory penalty of imprisonment for not more than 10 years for the act of searching for and collecting military secrets, the statutory penalty for Article 4(1)2(b) of the National Security Act, which is the punitive provision in this case, provides for death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for not less than 7 years, does not mean that the above provision prescribes excessively severe punishment in violation of the principle of responsibility, nor can it be said to be a provision that violates the principle of equality because its statutory penalty has lost balance within the penal system. Nor can it be deemed to substantially infringe the judge’s authority to determine and decide sentencing.\\n\\n(2) Furthermore, in order to fall under “state secret” within the above legal provision, the relevant information must, as noted above, not belong to facts, objects, or knowledge already publicly known. Whether such matters are publicly known should be determined by considering various circumstances, such as the degree of development of mass media or communication means like newspapers and broadcasting, the scope of readers and listeners, and the subject of publication, and by the standard of whether it can be judged that an anti-state organization or a person who received instructions therefrom no longer needs to search for, collect, confirm, or verify it. Whether disclosure poses a substantial risk should be determined according to sound common sense and social norms, taking into account the status of confrontation between the Republic of Korea and North Korea or other anti-state organizations and security matters at the time the secret was collected (see, inter alia, Supreme Court en banc Decision 97DO985 dated 1997. 9. 16.).\\n\\nApplying this legal principle, the lower court, for the reasons stated in its reasoning, determined as follows: as to the part of the facts charged that the first-instance judgment found guilty and which was maintained, on the premise that the contents of the relevant documents were facts or knowledge not publicly known and, if disclosed, there was a risk of causing danger to national security, thus constituting “state secrets,” Defendant 1, Defendant 3, and Defendant 5 were recognized as having “searched for and collected” such secrets as “a member of an anti-state organization or a person who received instructions therefrom”; whereas, as to the part of the facts charged that maintained the acquittal of the first-instance judgment or reversed the guilty portion of the first-instance judgment and was found not guilty, the contents of the relevant documents were deemed not to constitute “state secrets” on the grounds that they were facts or knowledge already publicly known through media reports, etc. at the time of search and collection, or merely subjective predictions or opinions based thereon.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the respective grounds for appeal by the above Defendants and the Prosecutor, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the scope of “state secrets” or “search and collection” or in exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nK. As to Defendant 4’s point of providing convenience (guilty part)\\n\\nArticle 3 of the former Act on Inter-Korean Exchange and Cooperation (before amendment by Act No. 7539 on 2005. 5. 31.) provides: “With respect to acts for the purpose of exchange and cooperation between South Korea and North Korea, such as movement, trade, cooperative projects, and provision of communication services between South Korea and North Korea, this Act shall apply in preference to other laws within the scope recognized as justifiable.” The phrase “other laws” here includes the National Security Act, but for the preferential application to apply, the act of a resident of South Korea contacting a resident of North Korea by meeting, communication, or other means must be an act “for the purpose of inter-Korean exchange and cooperation” and be “recognized as justifiable” or fall “within the scope of the purpose of the above Act,” and whether it falls thereunder must be determined objectively by comprehensively considering the circumstances leading to such act, whether reporting, etc. was made as prescribed by the same Act, and the conduct before and after the act (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DO6310 dated 2012. 10. 25.).\\n\\nThe lower court, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, upheld the first-instance judgment that found Defendant 4 guilty of this part of the facts charged, on the grounds that Defendant 4’s act, in around June 2005, of taking the lead in creating and providing the Internet Chosun press information base (KPM) site to Joseon Media, an organization under Chongryon, an anti-state organization, posed a risk of endangering the existence and security of the Republic of Korea or the free democratic basic order, and that the mere circumstance that Defendant 4 had previously obtained approval from the Ministry of Unification for contact with residents could not render his act justifiable under the above Act.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above factual findings and determinations are proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence or in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the scope of the offense of providing convenience.\\n\\nL. As to the points of receipt of money and valuables, special intrusion/escape, meeting/communication contact, possession/distribution of enemy-related expressive materials, and provision of convenience (each guilty part)\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the evidence admitted by the first-instance judgment cited by the lower court (excluding, however, the witness examination record for Non-party 3 discussed above) and the record, the lower court’s determination that all of the respective facts charged in this part were guilty for the reasons stated in its reasoning is proper, and there is no illegality, such as failure to fully deliberate by misunderstanding the legal principles asserted in the grounds for appeal, or in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the scope of granting admissibility as evidence, or in exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nM. As to the remaining grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe Defendants’ remaining grounds for appeal concern violations of law that do not affect the outcome of the judgment, or they challenge the selection and weighing of evidence and factual findings, or they are matters not raised as grounds for appeal before and are asserted only for the first time in the statement of grounds for appeal, and thus do not constitute lawful grounds for appeal. Furthermore, even upon ex officio review, no illegality as argued in the grounds for appeal can be found in the lower court judgment.\\n\\n2. Determination of the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nA. As to the point of constituting an anti-state organization, special intrusion/escape, and meeting (not guilty part)\\n\\nThe lower court, on the premise that where the constitution of an anti-state organization or special intrusion/escape and meeting is the fact to be proved, the truth of the contents stated in the documents becomes an issue, and therefore the contents of printed documents whose authenticity of formation has not been proved by the maker cannot be used as evidence directly proving the relevant facts charged, upheld the first-instance judgment that acquitted the Defendants on the ground that the evidence related to this part, namely the existence of the documents, the in-court statement of witness Non-party 4, and records concerning the Defendants’ entry and exit, alone were insufficient to prove the crime for each of these parts of the facts charged.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in violating logic and empirical rules and thereby exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nB. As to the points of possession/distribution of enemy-related expressive materials and provision of convenience (each not guilty part)\\n\\nIn order to be recognized as enemy-related expressive materials under Article 7(5) of the National Security Act, the contents of the expressive materials must be affirmative and aggressive, threatening the existence and security of the state and the free democratic basic order, which are the protected legal interests of the National Security Act. Whether such subversive character exists in the expressive materials must be determined by comprehensively considering not only the overall contents of the expressive materials but also the motive for their creation, the manner of the expression itself, external related matters, and the circumstances at the time of the expressive act (see, inter alia, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2010DO1189 dated 2010. 7. 23. and Supreme Court Decision 2012DO7455 dated 2012. 10. 11.).\\n\\nThe lower court, comprehensively considering circumstances such as that the expressive materials as stated in its reasoning that Defendant 1 and Defendant 4 possessed or distributed, or that Defendant 4 posted, were videos that did not use expressions sympathetic to North Korea’s assertions or doctrines, or were posted by citing domestic press materials, determined that they cannot be viewed as affirmative and aggressive materials threatening the existence and security of the state and the free democratic basic order, and that Defendant 4’s conduct in this part cannot be deemed to have had the purpose of subversive activity, and on such grounds acquitted all of the respective facts charged in this part.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning enemy-related expressive materials or the purpose of subversive activity under the National Security Act, or in violating logic and rules of experience and thereby exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nC. As to the point of sympathizing with enemy activity\\n\\nAs an element of the offense of praising or sympathizing with the activities of an anti-state organization, etc. under Article 7(1) of the National Security Act, “sympathizing” means to respond to or join the activities of an anti-state organization, etc. by making assertions of the same content as the propaganda, incitement, and activities of an anti-state organization, etc., or by engaging in conduct consistent therewith, and such act of “sympathizing” must reach the level of presenting a clear danger that can cause substantial harm to the existence and security of the state or the free democratic basic order (see, inter alia, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2003DO758 dated 2008. 4. 17. and Supreme Court Decision 2010DO3504 dated 2013. 2. 15.).\\n\\nThe lower court upheld the first-instance judgment that acquitted this part of the facts charged on the grounds that, in light of the gist of the declaration in which Defendant 3 is said to have participated, and the social discussion and circumstances at the time of the declaration, the mere circumstance that Defendant 3 engaged in search and collection of state secrets around that time does not make Defendant 3’s participation in the declaration such that it can be evaluated as praising, encouraging, or propagandizing the activities of an anti-state organization, etc., and thus cannot be said to present a clear danger that can cause substantial harm to the existence and security of the state or the free democratic basic order.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning sympathy with enemy activity or in violating logic and rules of experience and thereby exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nD. As to the point of communication contact (not guilty part)\\n\\nThe offense of meeting/communication, etc. under Article 8(1) of the National Security Act is constituted when, while knowing that the existence and security of the state or the free democratic basic order are threatened, one makes contact by meeting, communication, or other means with a member of an anti-state organization or a person who received instructions therefrom, and such meeting, etc. presents a clear danger of causing substantial harm to the existence and security of the state or the free democratic basic order (see, inter alia, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2003DO758 dated 2008. 4. 17. and Supreme Court Decision 2010DO6310 dated 2012. 10. 25.).\\n\\nThe lower court, comprehensively considering circumstances such as that the documents as stated in its reasoning cannot be regarded as core technology of a vehicle number recognition system received from a member of an anti-state organization or as materials related to the economy, military, diplomacy, etc. of the Republic of Korea, determined that Defendant 1’s act of exchanging documents containing such contents does not present a danger to the existence and security of the Republic of Korea or the free democratic basic order, and on such grounds acquitted this part of the facts charged.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above determination is proper, and there is no illegality, as argued in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning communication contact or in violating logic and rules of experience and thereby exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nE. As to the remaining grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe lower court, with respect to some of the so-called overseas photographs, recognized admissibility as evidence, and with respect to the remaining photographs denied such admissibility, and then upheld the first-instance judgment that found some of the facts charged concerning special intrusion/escape and meeting guilty on the grounds that, even excluding such evidence lacking admissibility, the other evidence as stated in its reasoning, taken together, was sufficient to recognize the related criminal facts. Therefore, the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal disputing the lower court’s determination on the admissibility of the above photographs concern matters not affecting the outcome of the judgment and cannot constitute lawful grounds for appeal.\\n\\nMeanwhile, under the interpretation of Criminal Procedure Act Article 383(4), the Prosecutor cannot assert as grounds for appeal that the lower court’s sentencing is too lenient or that the lower court violated the rules of evidence in recognizing the factual premise for sentencing against the Defendant’s interest. Therefore, this too cannot constitute lawful grounds for appeal (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 2005DO1952 dated 2005. 9. 15.).\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the Court dismisses both the Defendants’ appeal and the Prosecutor’s appeal, and renders the judgment as per the order by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2020DO15891]": "The grounds of appeal (the defendant’s supplemental appellate brief submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal shall be considered only to the extent that it supplements the grounds of appeal) are determined.\\n\\n1. Regarding the defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nThe Constitution proclaims, in the latter sentence of Article 12(1), the principle of due process, and guarantees in Article 27 the right to trial. In order to implement these principles substantively, the Criminal Procedure Act adopts as its basic principles the adversarial system and the trial-centered principle, under which the substantive examination of a criminal case must be conducted in an open courtroom through the offensive and defensive activities of both the prosecutor and the defendant, and the principles of direct examination and evidence-based adjudication, under which the finding of the facts charged must be based only on evidence directly examined in the presence of the judge. Accordingly, after a prosecution is instituted, all authority over the criminal procedure concerning that case belongs to the court seized of the case presiding over it, and the suspect who was the subject of the investigation assumes the status of a defendant, a party equal to the prosecutor, and exercises the right of defense (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009DO7436, decided October 22, 2009, and Supreme Court Decision 2009DO10412, decided April 28, 2011).\\n\\nIn light of these basic principles of the Criminal Procedure Act, where a person whom the prosecutor has requested and examined as a witness on the trial date is, without special circumstances, summoned in advance to the investigative authority and interviewed, and thereafter the witness makes a statement in court unfavorable to the defendant, the witness’s in-court testimony may be relied upon only if it is guaranteed that the prosecutor did not influence the witness’s in-court testimony through persuasion, pressure, leading responses, or suggestion during the pre-examination interview. Even if the prosecutor may interview a witness in advance as needed for the preparation of witness examination, the possibility cannot be ruled out that the witness may be coached or guided through a unilateral advance interview, without the court’s or the defendant’s participation, and thereby make distorted statements in court. The circumstance that there was no persuasion or pressure upon the witness must be proved by the prosecutor through the witness’s testimony or materials recording the witness’s in-court testimony or the interview process, thereby revealing the time, reasons, method, and specific content of the advance interview.\\n\\nB. Summary of the facts charged in this part and the course of the proceedings\\n\\n1) The summary of the amended facts charged in this part is that the defendant, from around October 2000 to around May 2011, in connection with his duties, received bribes totaling at least KRW 51,600,345 from Person 1 in the form of credit card usage payments, gift certificates, borrowed-name mobile phone usage payments, charges for drinks, money, and the like, and at the same time, by using his status as a public official, received bribes in the same amount in connection with arranging matters belonging to the duties of another public official.\\n\\n2) The first-instance court held: ① with respect to the portion of the receipt of gift certificates among the receipt of bribes from around June 2009 to around May 2011, which falls within the ten-year statute of limitations counted backward from the date of indictment, the proof of the receipt was insufficient; and with respect to the portion of the receipt of borrowed-name mobile phone usage payments, the receipt was recognized, but the credibility of Person 1’s in-court testimony in the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case was rejected, and proof of the connection with official duties and quid pro quo could not be deemed sufficient based on the remaining evidence alone, and therefore acquitted the defendant; and ② with respect to the remaining portions of the receipt of bribes, it held that the statute of limitations had expired and dismissed the case on the merits.\\n\\n3) By contrast, the appellate court held: ① with respect to the parts of the acceptance of bribes in connection with mediation involving credit card usage payments, borrowed-name mobile phone usage payments, charges for drinks on May 19, 2009, and money, Person 1’s in-court testimony in the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case and Person 1’s appellate in-court testimony regarding the borrowed-name mobile phone were credible, and therefore found the defendant guilty on the ground that he received money or property benefits as consideration for mediation and that criminal intent was established; and with respect to the receipt of gift certificates and the charges for drinks on February 26, 2009 and March 25, 2009, it held that there was no proof of the crime and acquitted the defendant on the merits; and ② with respect to the portion of simple bribery, it held that the connection with official duties could not be recognized and acquitted the defendant on the merits.\\n\\nC. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\nHowever, the appellate court’s determination cannot be accepted.\\n\\n1) According to the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na) On July 26, 2019, at the second pretrial preparation hearing in the first instance, the prosecutor requested Person 1 as a witness, and on August 13, 2019, at the first trial date, the first-instance court adopted Person 1 as a witness and conducted the examination of Person 1 in closed session on September 24, 2019, at the fifth trial date.\\n\\nBefore the examination of Person 1 was conducted, however, the prosecutor summoned Person 1 and interviewed Person 1, including by having Person 1 confirm the contents of the prosecutorial statement record.\\n\\nIn the first-instance witness examination, Person 1 testified, unlike his prosecutorial statement, with respect to the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case, which was his bribery-giving case in or around 1998, that “Person 2 discussed the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case by, for example, asking the defendant what would happen to Person 2, and the defendant told him that Person 1 himself also seemed to be a subject of investigation, and shortly thereafter a search and seizure of his office was conducted.”\\n\\nb) On June 17, 2020, at the first trial date in the appellate court, the prosecutor again requested Person 1 as a witness, and on the same day the appellate court adopted Person 1 as a witness and conducted the examination of Person 1 in closed session on August 19, 2020, at the second trial date.\\n\\nAs in the first instance, however, the prosecutor in the appellate court summoned Person 1 before the examination of Person 1 was conducted and interviewed Person 1, including by having Person 1 confirm the contents of the first-instance in-court testimony and the prosecutorial statement record. During the interview, Person 1 even asked the prosecutor about matters he would testify to.\\n\\nThereafter, in the appellate witness examination, Person 1 testified, unlike his prosecutorial statement, with respect to the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case, that “the apartment permitting and licensing process carried out by Person 3 Co., Ltd., where Person 1 worked, was the issue, and at that time Person 2, then head of the relevant division in Yongin City, was a friend of mine, and because he consulted me saying that he was being investigated for bribery, I asked the defendant for help, and later I received a message from the defendant that I too was a subject of investigation, and at that time a search and seizure took place at my office and I was investigated at the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office for about 48 hours.”\\n\\nIn addition, after the prosecutor’s advance interview, Person 1 testified in the appellate witness examination, unlike his first-instance in-court testimony, with respect to the borrowed-name mobile phone, that “distinguishing it from the provision of other money or property benefits, the borrowed-name mobile phone was not provided purely for the reason of helping the defendant or simply lending a mobile phone.”\\n\\n2) These factual circumstances are examined in light of the legal principles stated above. The prosecutor summoned and interviewed Person 1 before the witness examination on two occasions, in the first instance and in the appellate court. During the interview process, Person 1 not only confirmed the contents of his prosecutorial statement record and his first-instance in-court testimony, but even asked the prosecutor about matters he would testify to in court. And in the witness examination that followed immediately thereafter, he changed his prior statements regarding the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case and the borrowed-name mobile phone, and with respect to the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case he made increasingly specific statements unfavorable to the defendant. In such circumstances, it is difficult to exclude the possibility that, before Person 1 testified in court in the first instance and in the appellate court, he changed his prior statements to statements consistent with the facts charged under the influence of persuasion, pressure, leading responses, or suggestion by the investigative authority during the process of being summoned and interviewed by the prosecution. Therefore, unless the prosecutor proves through the witness’s testimony or otherwise that he did not influence Person 1’s in-court testimony through persuasion or pressure during the pre-examination interview process, it is difficult to recognize the credibility of Person 1’s in-court testimony regarding the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case and Person 1’s appellate in-court testimony regarding the borrowed-name mobile phone, which formed the basis of the appellate court’s guilty finding contrary to the first instance.\\n\\n3) Nevertheless, the appellate court, without conducting any specific review as to the timing, reasons, method, or content of the prosecutor’s advance interview, recognized the credibility of Person 1’s in-court testimony regarding the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office case and Person 1’s appellate in-court testimony regarding the borrowed-name mobile phone, and found guilty the portions of the facts charged for acceptance of bribes in connection with mediation involving credit card usage payments, borrowed-name mobile phone usage payments, charges for drinks on May 19, 2009, and money.\\n\\nThis appellate judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the determination of the credibility of the in-court testimony of a witness who had undergone an advance interview by the prosecutor, and by failing to conduct the necessary review. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well founded.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Prosecutor’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment, the appellate court held that, with respect to the parts concerning Person 4 and Person 5 among the facts charged in this case, each violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Specific Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act”) (bribery) had not been proved or the statute of limitations had expired, and therefore found not guilty or dismissed the case on the merits, and held that, with respect to the parts concerning Person 1 among the violations of the Specific Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act (bribery) arising from acceptance of bribes in connection with mediation, the receipt of gift certificates and the charges for drinks on February 26, 2009 and March 25, 2009 had not been proved, and therefore acquitted the defendant on the merits. Examining the reasons of the appellate judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the appellate court did not err by violating the rules of logic and experience and going beyond the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, nor by misapprehending the legal principles concerning improper solicitation in the third-party bribery offense, the establishment of the offense of improper action after receipt of a bribe, the connection with official duties in bribery offenses, or the statute of limitations.\\n\\n3. Scope of reversal\\n\\nAmong the appellate judgment, the guilty portion of the part concerning the violation of the Specific Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act (bribery) related to Person 1 must be reversed for the reasons stated above, and the portions acquitting on the merits among the part concerning the violation of the Specific Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act (bribery) related to Person 1, which stand in comprehensive concurrence and ideal concurrence with that guilty portion, must also be reversed together.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without addressing the remaining grounds of appeal of the defendant, the guilty portion of the appellate judgment (including the portions acquitted on the merits) is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the appellate court for further trial and determination. The remainder of the Prosecutor’s appeal is dismissed, and accordingly, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision, judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2022DO9510]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1.
