As to the charges concerning violation of the restriction on methods of intra-party primary election campaigning in relation to recruiting responsible party members\\nThe court below, for the same reasons as stated in its opinion, found this part of the indictment not guilty, holding that the acts of recruiting responsible party members committed by Defendants 1, 3, 4, and 5 could not be regarded as intra-party primary election campaigning.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment, there is no error affecting the judgment by violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning “campaigning in a primary election.”\\n\\n2. As to the charges concerning intra-party primary election campaigning by a person who cannot engage in primary election campaigning\\nThe court below, as noted above, held this part of the indictment not guilty on the ground that, since the acts of recruiting responsible party members could not be regarded as intra-party primary election campaigning, this part of the indictment was also not guilty.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment, there is no error affecting the judgment by violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of violation of the Public Official Election Act.\\n\\n3. As to the charges concerning pre-election campaigning\\nThe court below, for the same reasons as stated in its opinion, held that the method of pre-election campaigning described in this part of the indictment and made the subject of trial was merely “the method of appealing for support of Defendant 1 orally,” and that the placards, business cards, name tags, etc. were merely statements of the factual circumstances attendant upon the above oral appeal for support; and even if these were regarded as having been stated as separate methods of pre-election campaigning, they did not constitute “election campaigning,” and thus found this part of the indictment not guilty.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment, there is no error affecting the judgment by violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of violation of the Public Official Election Act and failing to conduct the necessary examination.\\n\\n4. As to the charges concerning the receipt and provision of money and valuables in relation to intra-party primary election campaigning and election campaigning\\nThe court below, for the same reasons as stated in its opinion, held that Defendants 1, 5, and 4 could not be deemed to have provided or received benefits in connection with election campaigning, and thus found this part of the indictment not guilty.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment, there is no error affecting the judgment by violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning “election campaigning” and “primary election campaigning.”\\n\\n5. As to the evidentiary admissibility of the party membership application forms\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\n1) Article 18(2) item 7 of the former “Personal Information Protection Act” (before its partial amendment by Act No. 16930 on February 4, 2020; hereinafter the same) provided that where the personal information controller deems it necessary “for the investigation of crimes and the institution and maintenance of public prosecution,” it may use personal information for a purpose other than the original purpose or provide it to a third party, except where there is a risk of unduly infringing the interests of the data subject or a third party. However, this applies only where the “personal information controller” is a “public institution” and does not apply to corporations, organizations, individuals, etc. (proviso to Article 18(2), and Article 2 items 5 and 6, of the former “Personal Information Protection Act”). In addition, the phrase “where there is a special provision in another Act” under Article 18(2) item 2 of the former “Personal Information Protection Act” should be construed, according to its plain meaning, as limited to cases where individual statutes specifically provide that personal information may be disclosed; therefore, a general provision such as Article 199(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, under which an investigative agency may inquire of public offices and other public or private organizations and request a report on necessary matters, does not fall thereunder. If Article 199(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act were included in “where there is a special provision in another Act” under Article 18(2) item 2 of the former “Personal Information Protection Act,” it would not only defeat the legislative intent and purpose of Article 18(2) item 7 of the former “Personal Information Protection Act,” which allows investigative agencies to receive personal information from public institutions only under certain restrictions, but would also likely bypass the constitutional principle of warrant requirement and due process.\\n2) The “person who processes or has processed personal information” who is the subject of the duty under Article 59 item 2 of the Personal Information Protection Act is not limited to the “personal information controller” under Article 2 item 5, but includes a person who “processes” or “has processed” “personal information” under Article 2 item 1, by the means under Article 2 item 2, which he or she learned in the course of business (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO8766, decided March 10, 2016).\\n\\nB. Determination\\nThe court below, for the same reasons as stated in its opinion, held that the act by Defendants 5 and 4 of arbitrarily submitting to the investigative agency, without the consent of the author, the party membership application forms they had processed for Defendant 1 constituted an act prohibited by Article 59 item 2 of the Personal Information Protection Act, that Article 18(2) item 2 or item 7 of the former Personal Information Protection Act could not apply, and that although it constituted illegally obtained evidence, it was not a case where evidentiary admissibility should exceptionally be recognized; accordingly, it did not recognize the admissibility of the party membership application forms and the evidence related thereto.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment, there is no error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning illegally obtained evidence, Article 59 item 2 of the Personal Information Protection Act, and Article 18(2) item 7.\\n\\n6. As to the evidentiary admissibility of the “written statement”\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\nSince Article 312(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that Articles 312(1) through (4) of the Criminal Procedure Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to the evidentiary admissibility of a written statement prepared during the investigative process by the defendant or a person other than the defendant, the legal principle that, for the evidentiary admissibility of a protocol in which a prosecutor or judicial police officer recorded the statement of a person other than the defendant, it must have been “prepared in accordance with lawful procedures and methods” also applies to the evidentiary admissibility of a written statement prepared during the investigative process by a person other than the defendant. Meanwhile, when a prosecutor or judicial police officer requests the appearance of a person who is not a suspect and examines him or her, the purport of Articles 221(1) and 244-4(1) and (3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, which require that the process of examination be recorded by entering in the protocol or recording on a separate written document the time of arrival at the place of examination, the time when the examination began and ended, and other matters necessary to confirm the progress of the examination process, and then filing it in the investigative record, as in the case of examining a suspect, is to institutionally guarantee procedural legality in that process by making transparent the process by which the investigative agency obtains testimonial evidence from the person examined during the examination process. Therefore, even where the investigative agency, as necessary for the investigation, has a person other than the suspect prepare and submit a written statement, the procedure must be complied with; accordingly, if a person other than the defendant prepared a written statement during the investigative process but the investigative agency did not take appropriate measures, such as recording in the written statement or on a separate written document the matters necessary to confirm the progress of the examination process and then filing it in the investigative record, thereby violating the procedure prescribed in Articles 244-4(1) and (3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, then, unless there are special circumstances indicating that the institutional guarantee of procedural legality in the process of obtaining testimonial evidence was not infringed, it cannot be said that the written statement was prepared during the investigative process “in accordance with lawful procedures and methods,” and its evidentiary admissibility cannot be recognized (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2013DO3790, decided April 23, 2015).\\nIn light of these provisions and wording of the Criminal Procedure Act and their legislative purpose, the “written statement prepared during the investigative process” subject to Article 312(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act means a document prepared after the investigation has begun under the involvement of the investigative agency, or prepared for the purpose of being submitted during the investigative process in relation to an investigation already commenced; so long as its substance falls thereunder in light of various circumstances such as the time and circumstances of preparation, it does not matter what it is called or whether it was prepared at a particular place.\\n\\nB. Determination\\nThe court below, for the same reasons as stated in its opinion, held that, insofar as a police officer visited the residence and workplace of the person who prepared the party membership application forms, questioned the circumstances of their preparation, and then required the preparation of a written statement and received it, Article 312(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act should apply, and therefore the evidentiary admissibility of the above evidence, which did not comply with the procedure prescribed in Article 244-4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, could not be recognized; and it rejected the prosecutor’s argument that, unlike this, since the written statement was not prepared at a police station but was received by visiting the place desired by the preparer, the provisions concerning the above procedures do not apply.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment, there is no error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning whether Article 312(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act applies, or whether Articles 221(1) and 244-4(1) and (3) of the Criminal Procedure Act apply.\\n\\n7. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and it is so adjudged as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court participating in the case."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding illegally obtained evidence is correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: Evidence obtained by an investigative agency by seizing and searching, without a warrant, electronic information that exceeds the scope of the electronic information subject to seizure from an information storage medium voluntarily submitted is inadmissible as illegally obtained evidence, and even if a seizure and search warrant is later issued or the defendant or defense counsel agrees to use it as evidence, its illegality is not cured.
B: When an investigative agency interrogates a suspect and fails to advise the suspect in advance of the right to remain silent, the statement of that suspect is inadmissible even if the voluntariness of the statement is recognized; however, this means only that it cannot be used as evidence of guilt against the suspect who was not advised of the right to remain silent, and therefore it may be used as evidence of guilt against that suspect's co-offender.
C: Compulsory urine collection conducted without the suspect's consent for the purpose of collecting criminal evidence is an investigative method that causes the suspect physical pain or disability, gives rise to shame or humiliation, and infringes human dignity and worth, and therefore is not permitted even if a seizure and search warrant is lawfully issued by a judge pursuant to Article 215 of the Criminal Procedure Act.
D: Inspections such as opening, sample collection, and component analysis of goods conducted in the customs clearance inspection procedure for import and export goods are for the purpose of proper customs clearance of import and export goods, and customs officers may conduct such inspections without a seizure and search warrant, but in order for an investigative agency to obtain possession of goods that a customs officer possesses or keeps in the course of duty for customs inspection, a warrant must be obtained in advance or afterward.
E: A work log bearing traces of practice for document forgery can be used, when public and private interests are balanced, as evidence of guilt to prove the defendant's litigation fraud, but if that work log was stolen by a third party and the victim of the litigation fraud acquired it by paying consideration, it cannot be used as evidence of guilt.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2008DO1584]": "1. Upon examination of the record, the business log in this case itself was prepared by the employee in charge by recording the contents of work performed day by day at the site and in the office by the Defendant’s company, Subok Construction Co., Ltd., and the reverse side thereof is nothing more than traces left from prior practice for the forgery of each document in this case, such as the 1996. 2. 25. Taejeonsa New Construction Contract (hereinafter referred to as the “New Construction Contract”), the 1998. 2. 25. Taejeonsa New Construction Additional Construction Contract (hereinafter referred to as the “Additional Contract”), and the 1999. 11. 27. Agreement, and therefore it cannot be regarded as an expression of free personality rights relating to the sphere of the Defendant’s private life; and since it appears to be indispensable evidence for criminally prosecuting the Defendant for the series of offenses leading to forgery of private documents, uttering of forged private documents, and litigation fraud, even if it was stolen by a third party and the victim side of such litigation fraud, etc. paid consideration in order to submit it to the investigative authorities as evidentiary material, for the realization of the public interest, submission of the business log in this case as evidence of a crime must be permitted, and even if this results in an infringement of the Defendant’s private sphere, this constitutes a restriction on fundamental rights that the Defendant must endure.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court’s action of using it as material for factual determination on the premise that the business log in this case had evidentiary capacity is correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as a misapprehension of legal principles concerning evidentiary capacity under the Criminal Procedure Act, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Upon examining the judgment of the lower court and the evidence adopted in the first-instance judgment cited by the lower court in light of the record, the lower court’s recognition of the following circumstances, namely, ① that traces of prior practice for the forgery of each document in this case appear on the reverse side of the business log in this case, ② that the handwritten additions on the reverse side of the above business log are recognized as being very similar to the Defendant’s handwriting, ③ that Subok Construction Co., Ltd., which is listed as a party to the New Construction Contract prepared on 1996. 2. 25., was a company established only on 1997. 12. 10., and that the agreement submitted by the Defendant when he filed, on 2000. 10. 11., an application for a provisional disposition against Taejeonsa seeking prohibition of construction and prohibition of change of the building owner’s name contains, in the agreement, the name of Non-Indicted Person 1, the representative of Taejeonsa, as transferee, incorrectly written as “Baek Jae-joong,” and other circumstances giving rise to doubt as to the manner of preparation of each document in this case in light of the form of the documents, ④ that the aggregate construction price of approximately 600,000,000 won stated in the New Construction Contract and the Additional Contract is a significantly larger amount than the total construction cost of approximately 320,000,000 won according to the appraisal result concerning construction costs revealed in the civil action filed by the Defendant against Taejeonsa, and that although the agreement provides that if the entire unpaid construction price is not paid within 6 months, the name of the building owner shall be reverted to the Defendant, the amount of the unpaid construction price had not been specified at all as of the time of its preparation, and furthermore, when the wording is interpreted literally, the content is irrational in that if even a very small amount of the construction price is not paid by the payment deadline, the name of the building owner can only be transferred to the Defendant, ⑤ that the business log in this case was found, among the portions of some of it, to contain traces of practice for the forgery of each document in this case on the reverse side of what Non-Indicted Person 2, who had been an employee of the company operated by the Defendant, brought in its entirety from the Defendant’s company in order to file a separate civil action against the Defendant and, while examining the evidence, discovered; that it was not submitted as evidentiary material in the said lawsuit because it was discovered after the claim for performance of procedures for change of the building owner’s name, which the Defendant filed against Taejeonsa on the basis of each document in this case, was finally and conclusively won by the Defendant; and that the prosecution initially rendered a non-prosecution disposition as to the Defendant’s alleged forgery of private documents, etc. in this case, but, upon the additional submission of the reverse side of the business log in this case as evidentiary material, reopened the investigation and brought this indictment, and in light of all these circumstances, the action of upholding the first-instance judgment that recognized that each document in this case had been forged by the Defendant is acceptable as correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as a violation of the rules of evidence or an incomplete examination, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. According to the factual findings lawfully recognized by the lower court, although there was in fact no agreement between the Defendant and Non-Indicted Person 1, who was the representative of Taejeonsa, that if the construction price were not paid, the name of the owner of Taejeonsa’s temple building would be transferred to the Defendant, the Defendant filed a lawsuit against Taejeonsa seeking performance of procedures for change of the building owner’s name and submitted the above-forged documents in this case as evidentiary material; accordingly, it is recognized that the Defendant had the fraudulent intent to acquire ownership of the Taejeonsa temple building under construction through the judgment in that civil action.\\n\\nIn the same purport, the lower court’s action of upholding the first-instance judgment that found this portion of the indictment guilty is correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as a misapprehension of legal principles concerning the fraudulent intent in the crime of litigation fraud, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. Upon examining the judgment of the lower court and the evidence lawfully adopted by the lower court in light of the record, the lower court, on the premise that the procedure for instituting the prosecution regarding the indictment for fraud against Non-Indicted Person 2 did not violate the provisions of law, correctly found this portion of the indictment, namely, that the Defendant deceived Non-Indicted Person 2 and obtained money from him, guilty, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as a misapprehension of legal principles concerning procedural conditions under the Criminal Procedure Act, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n5. The lower court, upon determining that it is recognized that the Defendant falsely accused Non-Indicted Person 2 in light of the factual findings stated in the judgment and recognized by the evidence adopted in the first-instance judgment maintained by the lower court, upheld the first-instance judgment that found this portion of the indictment guilty; upon examining the record, such action by the lower court is also correct and acceptable, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as a violation of the rules of evidence or an incomplete examination, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n6. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[2008DO8213]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. As to the Defendant’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\nUnder Article 7(5) of the National Security Act, “purpose” does not require an active desire or definitive awareness with respect to acts such as praise or encouragement, and conditional awareness is sufficient; thus, if a person recognizes that, objectively viewed, the content of the expressive material contains subversiveness, such as siding with the activities of an anti-state organization, and further has conditional awareness that such an act may become a subversive act, the constituent elements are satisfied (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2004DO3212 rendered on August 30, 2004), and, on the other hand, the selection and exclusion of evidence and factual determination belong to the exclusive province of the trier of fact so long as they do not contravene logic and the rules of experience.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal doctrine and the record, the court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence it adopted, determined for the reasons stated in its judgment that the Defendant had a subversive purpose in acquiring and possessing the subversive expressive materials stated in Count 1, subparagraphs (a) and (h), and that the Defendant participated in a prohibited assembly and obstructed traffic as stated in Count 2, and such determination is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning subversive purpose or factual error resulting from violation of the rules of evidence.\\n\\n2. As to the Prosecutor’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\nIf a document recording or setting forth a suspect’s statement was prepared during the course of investigation by an investigative agency, then even if it takes the form of a “statement protocol, statement, or written confession,” it cannot be distinguished from a suspect interrogation protocol (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2004DO3588 rendered on September 3, 2004), and, on the other hand, the suspect’s right to remain silent guaranteed by the Criminal Procedure Act is based on the constitutional right against self-incrimination, that is, the right not to be compelled to make statements adverse to oneself in criminal proceedings; therefore, when an investigative agency interrogates a suspect without first informing the suspect of the right to remain silent, the suspect’s statement must be denied evidentiary admissibility as unlawfully obtained evidence, even if the voluntariness of the statement is recognized (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 92DO682 rendered on June 23, 1992).\\n\\nThe court below found that the Prosecutor, on August 16, 2006, applied for an arrest warrant against Non-indicted Person 1 on charges of violating the National Security Act, and on August 18, 2006, obtained an arrest warrant from the Seoul Central District Court, and that the facts constituting the offense in the arrest warrant included that Non-indicted Person 1 had violated the National Security Act by conspiring with accomplices linked thereto, etc.; that thereafter, while interrogating Non-indicted Person 1 as a suspect, the Prosecutor questioned him regarding the organization and activities with accomplices, but Non-indicted Person 1 refused to make statements; that the Prosecutor, after indicting Non-indicted Person 1 in custody for violation of the National Security Act, etc. on September 12, 2006, summoned Non-indicted Person 1 again on September 19, 2006, and, while questioning him regarding the organization and activities with the Defendant and other accomplices, prepared the above statement protocol in the form of a general statement protocol rather than in the form of a suspect interrogation protocol; and then held that, even if the above statement protocol concerning Non-indicted Person 1 took the form of a statement protocol, its content is substantially the same as that of a suspect interrogation protocol recording a suspect’s statement, and yet there is no material in the record establishing that, in hearing Non-indicted Person 1’s statement, the Prosecutor had previously informed Non-indicted Person 1 of the right to remain silent; therefore, even if voluntariness of the statement is recognized, it is inadmissible as unlawfully obtained evidence and cannot be used as evidence of the Defendant’s guilt, and further, based on the remaining evidence submitted by the Prosecutor alone, it is insufficient to find the above facts charged, namely that the Defendant, in conspiracy with Non-indicted Person 2, Non-indicted Person 1, and others, disseminated Juche ideology at universities around November 2005 and formed the central leadership of a nationwide unified organization for cultivating Juche ideology adherents, and for that purpose systematically produced and distributed study CDs on Juche ideology, etc. at universities and, by studying and discussing them, praised and concurred in subversive activities, and there is no other evidence sufficient to establish this.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and it is so adjudicated by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2014DO8719]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. The part concerning violation of the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropic) arising from the importation of philopon on 2011. 6. 27.\\n\\na. The Constitution declares the principles of due process and warrant requirement with respect to search and seizure by providing that “no person shall be searched or seized except as provided by law” (the latter sentence of Article 12, paragraph 1 of the Constitution), and that “when a person is arrested, detained, searched, or seized, a warrant issued by a judge upon the request of a prosecutor shall be presented in accordance with due process of law. Provided, however, that where a person is caught in flagrante delicto, or where there is concern that a person who has committed an offense punishable by imprisonment for not less than 3 years may flee or destroy evidence, a warrant may be requested ex post facto” (paragraph 3 of the same Article).\\n\\nThe Criminal Procedure Act contains provisions that concretize the principles of due process and warrant requirement with respect to search and seizure. According to those provisions, when necessary for criminal investigation, a prosecutor may, only with respect to matters for which there are circumstances sufficient to suspect that the suspect has committed an offense and that may reasonably be recognized as related to the case, conduct seizure, search, or inspection pursuant to a warrant applied for to and issued by a judge of the district court (Article 215, paragraph 1). When, at a crime scene during or immediately after the commission of an offense, it is urgent and a judge’s warrant cannot be obtained, seizure, search, or inspection may be conducted without a warrant, but in such case a warrant must be obtained ex post facto without delay (Article 216, paragraph 3). In addition, the Criminal Procedure Act adopts the principle of statutory authorization of compulsory dispositions and provides that compulsory dispositions necessary for investigative agencies’ activities of discovering and securing offenders and collecting and preserving evidence may not be taken unless there is a special provision in the Criminal Procedure Act (Article 199, paragraph 1).\\n\\nIn the case of seizure and search by investigative agencies, the principles of due process and warrant requirement prescribed by the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act must be observed unless they fall within an exception permitted by law. Where, in the course of inspecting imported and exported goods, customs officials discover that narcotics are concealed or there is such suspicion, the prosecutor may request the head of customs to take the necessary measures in order to prevent dispersal of the narcotics, if the prosecutor has secured a sufficient surveillance system and needs to take them out of the country or bring them into the Republic of Korea for investigation, and the head of customs may take the necessary measures to comply with that request (Article 4, paragraph 1 of the Special Act on the Prevention of Illicit Trafficking in Narcotics, etc.). However, if such measures constitute seizure or search by investigative agencies, the warrant requirement principle applies.\\n\\nOf course, inspections such as opening, sampling, and component analysis conducted in the customs clearance inspection procedure for imported and exported goods are investigations for the purpose of proper customs clearance, etc. of imported and exported goods, and thus cannot be deemed compulsory dispositions by investigative agencies; therefore, customs officials may carry out such inspections without a warrant for seizure or search. Where a customs official voluntarily submits goods in his or her official possession or custody for customs clearance inspection to an investigative agency, even if the owner’s consent was not obtained, such goods cannot be said to have been seized unless the investigative agency acquired possession by force (see Supreme Court Decision 2013. 9. 26. rendered 2013DO7718). However, an act of opening and inspecting specific imported or exported goods and acquiring possession of their contents as part of measures pursuant to Article 4, paragraph 1 of the Special Act on the Prevention of Illicit Trafficking in Narcotics, etc., unlike the above-mentioned case of conducting an investigation for the purpose of proper customs clearance, etc. of imported and exported goods, is a seizure or search that constitutes criminal investigation, and it is appropriate to view that a warrant must be obtained before or after such act.\\n\\nb. According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the evidence duly admitted, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n(1) The prosecutor obtained information that the Defendant intended to import philopon by air express cargo transiting through the United States from Mexico, and, with the cooperation of the U.S. investigative authorities and the Incheon Airport Customs, had the said express cargo brought into the country under surveillance and delivered [this is called “controlled delivery”], and intended to arrest the Defendant as an offender when he or she received it.\\n\\n(2) A customs officer belonging to the Narcotics Investigation Division of Incheon Airport Customs brought the express cargo that had arrived at Incheon Airport to his or her office without going through the ordinary customs clearance procedure.\\n\\n(3) When philopon was discovered in the said express cargo, the investigative prosecutor seized it without a warrant in the form of having the customs officer voluntarily submit the express cargo containing the philopon, and then conducted controlled delivery with a substitute cargo.\\n\\n(4) As the said cargo was not delivered as the consignee unknown at the address stated on the waybill, the investigative prosecutor, with the cooperation of transport operators, waited for the recipient at the place where the cargo was stored, but the recipient did not appear and delivery failed.\\n\\nc. The court below maintained the first-instance judgment that acquitted this part of the indictment for the following reasons. ① Although the above acts constituted seizure and search by investigative agencies for the purpose of collecting evidence of specific criminal facts from the outset, a warrant was not issued before or after, and thus the warrant requirement was violated. ② Evidence obtained through the unlawful seizure and search, including the seized items, the seizure report, and the appraisal report on the seized items, all lacked admissibility, and the remaining evidence alone was insufficient to recognize the facts charged.\\n\\nIn light of the reasoning of the judgment below and the evidence duly admitted, there is a part in the reasoning of the judgment below that insufficiently determined the role of the customs officer, but the court below’s determination is based on the legal principles set forth above and is proper. There is no error in the court below’s determination in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the admissibility of seized items.\\n\\n2. The remaining part concerning violation of the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropic) arising from the importation of philopon, sale of philopon, and receipt thereof\\n\\nThe court below maintained the first-instance judgment that acquitted this part of the indictment on the ground that there was no proof of the crime. In light of the evidence duly admitted and the reasoning of the judgment below, the court below’s determination is proper. The judgment below contains no error that exceeds the bounds of free evaluation of evidence in contravention of logic and the rules of experience.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nThe prosecutor’s appeal is without merit, and it is dismissed. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court who participated, as ordered."}

{"[2016DO348]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. With respect to the Defendant’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe recognition of criminal facts must reach the level of proof beyond a reasonable doubt (Article 307(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act), but the selection and weighing of evidence, and the probative value of evidence, made as a premise to fact-finding fall within the free evaluation of the court of fact (Article 308 of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment, the court below found that the Defendant, as stated in the criminal facts in the judgment of the court below, photographed the victim Nonindicted 1’s genitalia with a mobile phone at his own home on December 11, 2014, against the victim’s will, and accordingly rejected the ground of appeal alleging factual error and misapprehension of law and affirmed the first-instance judgment.\\n\\nThe argument in the grounds for appeal is, in substance, merely a challenge to the court below’s fact-finding, that is, a criticism of the court below’s selection and weighing of evidence and assessment of probative value, which are matters within the free evaluation of the court of fact. Moreover, even upon examining the reasons for the judgment of the court below in light of the foregoing legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, the court below’s determination is not erroneous, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in that it misconstrued the law concerning intent or violated the principle of trial-centered adjudication, or departed from the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the laws of logic and experience.\\n\\n2. With respect to the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\n\\n1) Method of seizure of electronic information pursuant to voluntary submission\\n\\nToday, the business of individuals or corporations can hardly be maintained without information processing devices equipped with computers, servers, or storage media, and various storage media on which electronic information is stored (hereinafter referred to as “information storage media”) are mostly large in capacity, so they broadly contain information regarding an individual’s daily life or corporate management unrelated to the criminal suspicion under investigation. Since seizure and search of such electronic information by investigative authorities are highly likely to infringe the secrecy and freedom of privacy, the right to informational self-determination, property rights, and the like, they must not be conducted in a comprehensive manner, but must be conducted within the minimum scope necessary for the purpose of the investigation in accordance with the principle of proportionality. As a matter of principle, seizure and search of electronic information by investigative authorities must be conducted only by collecting, as printed documents, the portions related to the criminal suspicion that was the basis for issuance of the warrant, or by copying the relevant files onto an information storage medium carried by the investigative authorities; and seizure and search by directly removing the information storage medium itself or by removing all electronic files contained in the storage medium to the investigative authority’s office or other external location in the form of hard copy or imaging, etc. (hereinafter referred to as a “copy”) may exceptionally be permitted only where, due to on-site circumstances or the massive volume of electronic information, the method of printing or copying within a defined scope is impossible or it is recognized as markedly difficult to achieve the purpose of seizure, such as where a long time is required to obtain the relevant information or technical measures by specialized personnel are necessary (see Supreme Court en banc Decision dated July 16, 2015, 2011MO1839, etc.).\\n\\nThe foregoing legal principles likewise apply to the seizure of voluntarily submitted items that constitute information storage media (Article 218 of the Criminal Procedure Act). This is because seizure of voluntarily submitted items differs only in that the investigative authority’s acquisition of possession over the seized item is made in accordance with the submitter’s intent, whereas the investigative purpose premised on criminal suspicion and the effect of seizure are the same as in the case of a warrant. Therefore, when an investigative authority receives, by voluntary submission, an information storage medium containing electronic information in relation to a particular criminal suspicion and seizes the electronic information stored therein, as a matter of principle it should seize only printed matter, etc. of the electronic information related to the criminal suspicion that prompted the submission. However, only where, due to on-site circumstances or the massive quantity of electronic information and the difficulty of searching it, the method of printing or copying within a defined scope is impossible or is recognized as markedly difficult to achieve the purpose of seizure, may the information storage medium itself or a copy thereof exceptionally be voluntarily submitted and seized.\\n\\n2) Subject matter and scope of seizure of electronic information pursuant to voluntary submission\\n\\na) Intent of the voluntary submitter\\n\\nAn information storage medium and the electronic information stored therein are conceptually and functionally distinct, each having independent value and utility, and are distinguishable from each other. Moreover, because the legality of seizure of voluntarily submitted electronic information is based solely on the submitter’s free intent to submit, when an information storage medium or its copy containing both electronic information related to the criminal suspicion and electronic information unrelated thereto is voluntarily submitted to an investigative authority, the submitter may individually specify the electronic information to be submitted and seized or limit its scope. Since the scope of voluntary submission of electronic information within an information storage medium may vary according to the submitter’s intent in this way, the investigative authority receiving such voluntary submission must ascertain from the submitter the scope of the electronic information subject to voluntary submission so as to clearly specify the scope of seizure. Furthermore, in light of the importance of electronic information within information storage media from the perspective not only of due process, the principle of warrant, and the principle of proportionality that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to realize, but also the protection of secrecy and freedom of privacy, the right to informational self-determination, and property rights, a declaration of intent by a person submitting an information storage medium that is intended to designate the electronic information contained therein or limit the scope of submission must be strictly construed, and it is impermissible for an investigative authority to infer the uncertain intent of the submitter at will.\\n\\nAccordingly, where an investigative authority can readily confirm the submitter’s intent but receives, without such confirmation, a voluntarily submitted information storage medium containing both electronic information related to a particular criminal suspicion and electronic information unrelated thereto, it cannot be treated as though all electronic information stored in that information storage medium was voluntarily submitted and seized. In such a case, the issue is how to specify, in accordance with the voluntary submitter’s intent, the scope of the electronic information subject to seizure.\\n\\nb) Electronic information related to the criminal suspicion that prompted the seizure pursuant to voluntary submission\\n\\nAn investigative authority may seize only evidentiary articles or items believed to be subject to forfeiture, limited to those that may be recognized as relevant to the facts of suspicion (Articles 219 and 106 of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\n\\nAccordingly, when an investigative authority seeking to seize electronic information seizes an information storage medium and the electronic information stored therein by means of voluntary submission, if, due to reasons such as the failure to properly confirm the submitter’s intent regarding the specific scope of submission, the subject matter and scope of seizure of electronic information pursuant to the voluntary submitter’s intent are unclear or cannot be ascertained, only electronic information that is related to and minimally valuable for proving the criminal suspicion that prompted the voluntary submission is subject to seizure. At this time, electronic information related to the criminal suspicion includes not only the criminal suspicion itself or acts directly related to the offense having the same basic factual relationship, but also information that may be used as indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence to prove the motive and process of the offense, the means and methods of the offense, and the time and place of the offense. However, such relevance is recognized only where there is a concrete and individualized nexus, considering comprehensively the content of the criminal suspicion that prompted the voluntary submission and seizure, the subject matter of the investigation, the course of the investigation, and the process of voluntary submission; relevance cannot be found merely because the criminal suspicion concerns an offense of the same kind or a similar offense (see Supreme Court Decision 2021DO2205 dated August 26, 2021, etc.).\\n\\nc) Scope of seizure of voluntarily submitted electronic information in cases of offenses such as illegal filming\\n\\nWhen determining whether electronic information is related to the criminal suspicion, it is necessary to examine whether there is a concrete and individualized nexus based on the content and nature of the criminal suspicion and the process of voluntary submission. In particular, in cases of illegal filming offenses using a smartphone, which is a mobile phone having both camera functions and information storage functions, because of the nature of the offense, habituality of the act may be suspected or it may be suspected that the act was committed as part of a series of offenses arising from the manifestation of sexual preference or tendency, and where there is a likelihood that direct evidence of the offense remains in the smartphone in the form of image files or video files, there is a high probability that strong indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence related thereto may be discovered in electronic information of the same type stored therein. In such circumstances, such indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence can be recognized as having a concrete and individualized nexus with the criminal suspicion. In this way, illegal recordings containing electronic information of a nature that significantly infringes the personality rights of the victim who was the subject of the offense are generated by the criminal act and are also subject to forfeiture; thus, there is a substantial need to promptly seize and search the relevant electronic information from the voluntarily submitted mobile phone so as to timely block the possibility of distribution of the illegal recording and protect the victim. Furthermore, in such cases, because the types of electronic information that constitute indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence and are subject to forfeiture and seizure and search can be relatively clearly specified as image files or video files, etc., there is little possibility that the seizure and search will lead to the seizure and search of all irrelevant private electronic information, and therefore there is more room to recognize relevance more broadly.\\n\\nd) Scope of seizure of electronic information where a person other than the suspect voluntarily submits an information storage medium owned and managed by the suspect\\n\\nWhere a third party, such as a victim who is not the suspect, voluntarily submits an information storage medium owned and managed by the suspect, even if such voluntary submission and the ensuing seizure by the investigative authority are lawful, it must be interpreted more restrictively so that only electronic information having a concrete and individualized nexus with the criminal suspicion that prompted the voluntary submission is subject to seizure. Where the subject of voluntary submission is a holder or custodian rather than the owner, and the submission may significantly infringe the owner’s secrecy of privacy or other personality interests, special consideration for the owner’s legal interests, who did not consent to the voluntary submission, is necessary together with the necessity of the seizure and search pursuant to voluntary submission (see Supreme Court Decisions 98DO968 dated September 3, 1999; 2008DO1097 dated May 15, 2008; 2013DO7718 dated September 26, 2013, etc.), because if all matters concerning the personality interests of the suspect, such as secrecy and freedom of privacy and the right to informational self-determination, are stored in an information storage medium owned and managed by the suspect individually, and seizure and search are permitted without limitation, the suspect’s personality interests may be significantly infringed. Therefore, even if the third party who made the voluntary submission indicates an intent to submit, in a single batch, electronic information beyond the scope in which a concrete and individualized nexus with the criminal suspicion that prompted the submission is recognized, unless special circumstances exist such that the third party has disposal authority over all electronic information in the information storage medium or the suspect’s intent to consent thereto may be inferred, the scope of electronic information that the investigative authority may lawfully seize without a warrant through such voluntary submission must be regarded as limited to electronic information related to the criminal suspicion.\\n\\n3) Guarantee of the suspect’s right to participate during the search, copying, and printing of electronic information, and delivery of an inventory of seized electronic information\\n\\nWhere an investigative authority receives, by voluntary submission, an information storage medium or a copy thereof containing both electronic information subject to seizure and electronic information not subject to seizure, and moves the information storage medium, etc. to the investigative authority’s office or elsewhere to search, copy, or print it, due process and the principle of warrant must be observed in such series of procedures by guaranteeing the opportunity for participation to the party subject to seizure and search prescribed in Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act (hereinafter referred to as the “person subjected to seizure”) or his or her counsel, and by preparing and delivering an inventory specifying the file details of the seized electronic information, and by taking appropriate measures to prevent arbitrary copying, etc. of electronic information unrelated to the criminal suspicion. If such measures were not taken, then, unless there are special circumstances such as where the person subjected to seizure explicitly indicated an intention not to participate, or where, in light of the nature and content of the intent and process of voluntary submission or of the manner and content of the process in which the procedural violation occurred, it cannot be said that the purpose of guaranteeing participation in the procedure to the person subjected to seizure was substantially infringed, the seizure and search cannot be regarded as lawful, and the same is true even if the investigative authority copied or printed only the electronic information related to the criminal suspicion from the information storage medium or copy thereof (see the above Supreme Court en banc Decision 2011MO1839, Supreme Court Decision dated November 17, 2020, 2019MO291, etc.). Furthermore, where a victim or other third party voluntarily submits, without a warrant, an information storage medium owned and managed by the suspect, it is difficult to regard the actual person subjected to seizure, namely the suspect, as having consented to the investigative authority’s unrestricted search of all the electronic information therein; and even when the suspect himself or herself makes the voluntary submission, considering that the suspect’s right to participate, etc. must be guaranteed, unless there are special circumstances, appropriate measures to guarantee the suspect’s procedural rights must be taken in accordance with Articles 219, 121, and 129 of the Criminal Procedure Act, such as by guaranteeing the suspect’s right to participate and delivering an inventory of the seized electronic information.\\n\\n4) Necessary measures and procedures when irrelevant information is discovered during the process of searching voluntarily submitted information storage media\\n\\nAs seen above, the investigative authority’s arbitrary search, copying, or printing of electronic information beyond the scope of electronic information subject to seizure from a voluntarily submitted information storage medium is, in principle, an unlawful seizure and search and therefore cannot be permitted. If, before the seizure and search of electronic information has concluded, electronic information related to a separate criminal suspicion is incidentally discovered during a lawful search of electronic information related to the criminal suspicion, the investigative authority must cease any further additional search and may lawfully seize and search such information only upon obtaining a separate seizure-and-search warrant from the court for the separate criminal suspicion. Therefore, evidence obtained by the investigative authority through seizure and search without a warrant of electronic information exceeding the scope subject to seizure from a voluntarily submitted information storage medium constitutes illegally obtained evidence, and its illegality is not cured even if a warrant is later issued by the court or the Defendant or counsel consents to its use as evidence.\\n\\nB. Determination\\n\\n1) According to the reasons for the judgment of the court below and the evidence lawfully admitted, the following facts can be found.\\n\\na) As found by the court below, the Defendant committed the offense of photographing the victim Nonindicted 1’s genitalia at his home against the victim’s will on December 11, 2014 (hereinafter referred to as the “2014 offense”). Victim Nonindicted 1 immediately reported the damage to the police, stating that videos and photographs taken by the Defendant were stored in two mobile phones owned by the Defendant (an iPhone and a Samsung mobile phone) that he had taken from the Defendant’s home, and voluntarily submitted them as evidentiary items of the offense.\\n\\nb) The police officers seized the two mobile phones without a warrant, but they did not separately confirm with Victim Nonindicted 1 the intent regarding the scope of submission, such as whether the intention was to submit all electronic information stored in the mobile phones, including the videos and photographs.\\n\\nc) The Defendant provided the password for one mobile phone (the iPhone) to the police and participated in the file imaging process, whereas for the other mobile phone (the Samsung mobile phone), he effectively refused to provide the password and did not participate in the process of restoring and extracting the stored video files. The police, after confirming the 2014 offense against Victim Nonindicted 1 through the video files stored in the former mobile phone (the iPhone), while searching the latter mobile phone (the Samsung mobile phone) for additional video evidence of the 2014 offense, discovered 30 videos and photographs showing two other men, not Victim Nonindicted 1, sleeping on a bed, and someone holding their genitalia with his hand, etc., and after confirming their contents, copied them to a CD.\\n\\nd) The police summoned Victim Nonindicted 1, investigated the identity, etc. of the two men appearing in the above videos, learned that they were Victim Nonindicted 2 and Nonindicted 3, and through additional investigation became aware that the Defendant had committed the offense of touching the victims’ genitalia and recording the above videos around December 2013 while Victim Nonindicted 2 and Nonindicted 3 were asleep in an intoxicated state (hereinafter referred to as the “2013 offense”).\\n\\ne) Thereafter, the police obtained a seizure-and-search warrant and seized, as evidentiary items, the CD on which the electronic information of the 2013 offense videos had been copied.\\n\\n2) Examining the above factual relationship in light of the legal principles set forth above, when Victim Nonindicted 1 submitted the Defendant’s mobile phones to the police as evidentiary items, he did not clearly state the scope of submission of the electronic information contained therein, and the officers in charge also did not go through a confirmation procedure with the submitter regarding that matter. In such circumstances, it falls under a case where the submitter’s intent regarding the scope of submission of the electronic information contained in the mobile phones is unclear or cannot be ascertained. Accordingly, it is reasonable to construe restrictively that the scope of electronic information in the mobile phones lawfully seized through voluntary submission is limited to electronic information having a concrete and individualized nexus with the Defendant’s 2014 offense itself, which prompted the voluntary submission and seizure. In light of this, the videos concerning the Defendant’s 2013 offense, which occurred at a considerable interval from the time of the offense and involved a victim and a mobile phone used in the offense that were entirely different, are difficult to regard, even under the legal principles on related evidence having a concrete and individualized nexus, including the indirect evidence and circumstantial evidence discussed above, as electronic information having a concrete and individualized nexus with the criminal suspicion that prompted the seizure pursuant to voluntary submission (the 2014 offense). Therefore, since the investigative authority obtained them without a prior warrant, they lack admissibility as evidence, and this conclusion is not altered even though the seizure procedure was later carried out after obtaining a seizure-and-search warrant.\\n\\n3) Although there are some parts of the reasons for the judgment of the court below that are not entirely appropriate, the conclusion of the court below, which reversed the first-instance judgment that found the 2013 offense guilty and rendered an acquittal, is acceptable on the grounds that, even if the video discovered in relation to the 2013 offense is illegally obtained evidence and was seized after a seizure-and-search warrant was later obtained, it lacks admissibility as evidence of the 2013 offense, and derivative evidence based thereon also lacks admissibility as evidence. There is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misconstruing the legal principles concerning limiting the scope of submission of electronic information according to the submitter’s intent in the seizure of voluntarily submitted items of information storage media, or the requirements for recognizing the admissibility of evidence of voluntarily submitted electronic information.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, all appeals are dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as per the order by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2018DO6219]": "We determine the grounds for appeal (and other written opinions, etc. submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the petition of grounds for appeal, to the extent that they supplement them).\\n\\n1. Compulsory urine collection is an act of obtaining, storing, and collecting urine by using force against a suspect, inserting a catheter through the urethra into the bladder and then expelling the urine within the body when the suspect does not voluntarily submit urine. Compulsory urine collection by an investigative agency for the purpose of collecting criminal evidence not only involves direct physical intervention in the suspect’s body, but may also cause physical pain or impairment to the suspect, or may give rise to a sense of shame or humiliation. Accordingly, it should be regarded as being permitted under lawful procedure as a last resort only where it is deemed unavoidable for criminal investigation, taking into account whether the suspect is under suspicion of a crime and whether that crime is serious, whether the criminal suspicion can be clarified through analysis of the urine components, whether it is necessary to obtain urine from the suspect’s body in order to collect criminal evidence, and whether proof would be difficult by means other than urine collection. At such time, urine must be collected by a doctor, nurse, or other skilled medical professional, in a place equipped with medical devices and facilities suitable for urine collection, in a manner that entails little risk of harming the suspect’s body and health and minimizes the suspect’s sense of humiliation, etc.\\n\\nAn investigative agency may, for the purpose of collecting criminal evidence, collect a suspect’s urine without the suspect’s consent by obtaining a court-issued warrant for expert examination and as a “disposition necessary for an expert examination” prescribed in Article 221-4(1) and Article 173(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act (where it is necessary to confine the suspect in a hospital, etc., a warrant for expert examination and confinement must be obtained from the court pursuant to Article 221-3 of the Criminal Procedure Act); however, it may also do so by means of seizure and search under Articles 219, 106(1), and 109 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Even in such seizure and search cases, the investigative agency must, in principle, lawfully obtain and execute a seizure and search warrant from a judge pursuant to Article 215 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nWhere urine is collected by means of seizure and search, if, notwithstanding the investigative agency’s efforts to secure the suspect’s urine, which is the object of seizure, there are circumstances under which voluntary accompaniment cannot be expected, such as where the suspect does not agree to or resists moving to a nearby hospital emergency room or other place suitable for urine collection, the investigative agency is permitted to exercise the minimum necessary physical force in order to take the suspect to a place suitable for urine collection. This should be regarded as falling within the “disposition necessary for the execution of a seizure and search warrant” prescribed in Articles 219 and 120(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act. Otherwise, because compulsory urine collection pursuant to the procedure established to minimize the risk of harming the suspect’s body and health and to minimize the suspect’s sense of humiliation would be impossible, there would be no way to achieve the purpose of the seizure warrant.\\n\\n2. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the evidence duly admitted, the following facts can be found.\\n\\nA. A prosecutor belonging to the Busan District Prosecutors’ Office, upon application by a police officer belonging to the Busan Metropolitan Police Agency, and based on information that the Defendant had administered methamphetamine (hereinafter referred to as “Philopon”) in early August 2017, applied to the Busan District Court for a seizure, search, and inspection warrant and, on 2017. 8. 10., obtained from the judge in charge of warrants a seizure, search, and inspection warrant (hereinafter referred to as “the warrant in this case”) with respect to a suspicion of violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. In the “items to be seized” section of the warrant in this case, “30 cc of the suspect’s urine, approximately 80 strands of hair, tools for unlawful use of narcotics,” etc. were included, and in the “places to be searched/inspected” section, “the suspect’s actual residence [Busan, Haeundae-gu, (address omitted)],” etc. were included. The Defendant has a history of being punished several times for the offense of violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, Etc. (psychotropics) due to Philopon administration.\\n\\nB. On 2017. 8. 28. at around 11:10, a police officer presented the warrant in this case to the Defendant at (address omitted), Busan, Haeundae-gu, and searched the residence, seizing four used syringes as evidence.\\n\\nC. Although the police officer, pursuant to the warrant in this case, demanded that the Defendant submit urine and hair, the Defendant used abusive language and steadfastly refused. The police officer persuaded the Defendant for about 3 hours, but when the Defendant continued to refuse and engaged in self-harm, the officer subdued him, handcuffed and tied him with a rope, and forcibly took him to the emergency room of OO Medical Center.\\n\\nD. When the Defendant also refused voluntary submission of urine at the emergency room of OO Medical Center, the police officer, at around 15:30 on the same day, had a paramedic collect 30 cc of urine from the Defendant’s body and seized it. As a result of testing the seized urine with a simple reagent (MET), a positive reaction for Philopon was obtained.\\n\\n3. The above factual circumstances are examined in light of the legal principles set forth above.\\n\\nIt can be seen that the facts charged against the Defendant were serious and that there was a clear criminal suspicion based on objective facts. Despite the police officer’s prolonged persuasion, the Defendant refused to voluntarily submit urine and resisted execution of the seizure warrant lawfully issued by the judge. Judging that it would be difficult to achieve the investigative purpose by other means, the police officer forcibly took the Defendant to the nearby hospital emergency room, which was a place suitable for urine collection, in order to collect the Defendant’s urine, the object of seizure, and had a paramedic, under a doctor’s instructions, collect urine from the Defendant’s body; in that process, the exercise of force against the Defendant did not exceed the minimum necessary level. It is appropriate to view such action by the police officer as a “disposition necessary for the execution of a seizure warrant” prescribed in Articles 219 and 120(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, and therefore as permissible.\\n\\nAccording to Article 10(1) and Article 10-2(1) items 2 and 3, and paragraph (2), etc. of the Police Officials’ Duty Execution Act, a police officer may use police equipment such as handcuffs, ropes, police batons, and shields, within necessary limits, by reasonably judging the situation when there are substantial grounds deemed necessary for the protection and defense of his or her own life and body or those of others, and for restraining resistance to the execution of official duties, during the performance of duties. In this case, the police officer’s use of handcuffs and ropes, in the course of taking the Defendant to the emergency room of OO Medical Center in order to execute the seizure warrant, to restrain the Defendant who was resisting the execution of official duties and to prevent the risk of self-harm, was lawful as the use of police equipment permitted under the Police Officials’ Duty Execution Act.\\n\\nFor the same reason, the lower court’s determination that the execution of the seizure warrant with respect to the Defendant’s urine was lawful contains no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, of finding facts in violation of the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or of misunderstanding the legal principles concerning execution of a seizure warrant.\\n\\n4. According to Article 383(4) of the Criminal Procedure Act, an appeal on the ground of unfair sentencing may be filed only in cases where the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or custody for 10 years or more has been imposed. Therefore, in this case where a lighter sentence than that was imposed on the Defendant, the argument that the sentence is too severe and therefore unfair does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n5. Since the Defendant’s appeal is without merit, it is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Supreme Court Justices, as stated in the dispositive part."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the admissibility of documentary hearsay evidence is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: If a witness, even after the criminal judgment related to himself had become final and binding, refused without justifiable reason to testify in court, so that the Defendant was unable to cross-examine him, then even if the Defendant caused the witness’s refusal to testify, a document recording that witness’s statement at the investigative agency does not fall under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act’s “where a statement cannot be made due to any other similar reason,” and thus has no evidentiary admissibility.
B: The phrase “an interrogation protocol of a suspect prepared by a prosecutor” in Article 312(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act means not only an interrogation protocol of the Defendant in question, but also an interrogation protocol prepared by a prosecutor with respect to another Defendant or suspect who is in a co-offender relationship with the Defendant in question, and “co-offender” in this context includes a counterpart offender.
C: A protocol recording the contents of an examination of a suspect or reference person who became the Defendant, conducted by a tax official in charge of tax offense investigations, constitutes a statement prepared by a Defendant or a person other than the Defendant, or a document recording such statement, and therefore its admissibility as evidence must be determined pursuant to Article 313 of the Criminal Procedure Act.
D: In an insurance fraud case, a “reply to a request for review of whether inpatient medical treatment was appropriate, etc., from the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service,” which states the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service’s opinion on the appropriateness of inpatient medical treatment based on the materials sent to it by the investigative agency, does not constitute a document continuously and mechanically recording the details of office processing, and therefore does not fall under “a document prepared under particularly trustworthy circumstances” under Article 315(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act.
E: A protocol in which a hearsay statement is recorded is admissible as evidence when it satisfies the requirements of Article 312 or Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act and the requirements of Article 316 of the Criminal Procedure Act.
label: A

{"[2017DO12671]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nDocuments that continuously and mechanically record, from time to time, the details of affairs entrusted to oneself, such as commercial books, ship logs, medical charts, or cashbooks and the like, regardless of whether criminal facts are found, are documents that exist to prove the details of the handling of affairs, and therefore their admissibility as evidence is recognized as a matter of course under Article 315(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act. Moreover, in light of the legislative intent of Article 315 of the Criminal Procedure Act to recognize the admissibility of such documents as a matter of course because, due to the mechanical repetitiveness of the work, there is little room for falsification to intervene, and because, in view of the nature of the document, a high degree of reliability is recognized such that there is no need for cross-examination or, even if the person who prepared it is summoned, it would have no significance beyond the submission of a written document, and further taking into comprehensive account the structure and purport of the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act concerning the hearsay rule, as well as the wording “other” in the provision of Article 315(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, which treats the documents set forth in Article 315(1) and (2) of the Criminal Procedure Act as examples of “documents prepared under especially reliable circumstances,” the phrase “other documents prepared under especially reliable circumstances” prescribed in Article 315(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act means “documents for which there is circumstantial assurance of a high degree of reliability to such an extent that the question whether an opportunity for cross-examination must be afforded is not even at issue,” by analogy to the official documentary evidence and ordinary business documents enumerated in Article 315(1) and (2) of the Criminal Procedure Act (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2015DO2625, rendered July 16, 2015, etc.).\\n\\nAccordingly, a document that is not one continuously and mechanically recording the details of affairs, but instead contains content expressing some opinion related to whether criminal facts are found, cannot be deemed to fall under the written instrument that has admissibility as evidence as a matter of course prescribed in Article 315(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act; therefore, the “Reply to the Request for Review Regarding Whether Inpatient Treatment, etc. Was Appropriate” prepared by the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service, which contains the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service’s expression of its opinion on the appropriateness of inpatient treatment based on the materials forwarded by an investigative agency in a so-called insurance fraud case, does not fall under the “other documents prepared under especially reliable circumstances” of Article 315(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the court below, on the premise that the reply to the request for review regarding whether inpatient treatment, etc. was appropriate prepared by the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service does not fall under the “other documents prepared under especially reliable circumstances” prescribed in Article 315(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, and concluding that the above reply did not satisfy the requirements for recognition of admissibility as hearsay evidence and therefore rejecting its admissibility as evidence, was proper. There is no illegality, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in that it violated the rules of logic and experience, exceeded the bounds of the free evaluation of evidence, or misunderstood the legal principles concerning Article 315(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the Disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2018DO13945]": "The grounds for appeal are determined.\\n\\n1. Overview of the case\\n\\na. Summary of the charged facts in this case\\n\\nIf a person is not a narcotics handler, he/she shall not sell, possess, manage, etc. methamphetamine, a psychotropic drug (also known as Philopon, hereinafter referred to as “Philopon”), and the Defendant is not a narcotics handler.\\n\\nAt around 19:10 on 2017. 3. 27., on the street in front of □□ Station located on △△-ro, ○○○-gu, Goyang-si, the Defendant sold Philopon by delivering about 41.5 g of Philopon to Non-indicted Party 1 after agreeing to receive 6.4 million won from Non-indicted Party 1.\\n\\nb. Progress of the related case concerning Non-indicted Party 1\\n\\n1) Non-indicted Party 1 was indicted on 2017. 4. 24. for violation of the Act on the Control of Narcotics, etc. (psychotropic), on the charged facts that he/she sold Philopon, etc. on a total of 11 occasions, and the court of first instance sentenced him/her to 4 years of imprisonment on 2017. 10. 13. Among those, the criminal facts related to the charged facts of this case are the part stating: “Non-indicted Party 1, at around 19:10 on 2017. 3. 27., on the street in front of □□ Station located on △△-ro, ○○○-gu, Goyang-si, agreed to pay 6.4 million won to ‘◇◇◇◇’ (the Defendant’s nickname), received about 41.5 g of Philopon from him/her, purchased it, and thereafter possessed it for sale (sale and possession).”\\n\\n2) Non-indicted Party 1 appealed the judgment of the court of first instance, and the appellate court, after granting the prosecutor’s amendment of the indictment, reversed the judgment of the court of first instance on the ground of the prosecutor’s amendment of the indictment on 2018. 1. 31. and sentenced him/her to 4 years of imprisonment. The criminal facts related to the charged facts of this case as recognized by the appellate court under the amended charged facts are the part stating: “Non-indicted Party 1, at around 19:10 on 2017. 3. 27., on the street in front of □□ Station located on △△-ro, ○○○-gu, Goyang-si, while waiting for Non-indicted Party 2 with about 41.5 g of Philopon to be sold to Non-indicted Party 2 in his/her possession, was arrested by the police officer and the attempt remained unconsummated (attempted sale).”\\n\\n3) Non-indicted Party 1 filed a final appeal against the appellate court judgment, but on 2018. 5. 15. the Supreme Court rendered a judgment dismissing the final appeal.\\n\\nc. Progress of Non-indicted Party 1’s refusal to testify in this case\\n\\n1) Non-indicted Party 1 appeared as a witness at the 5th trial date of the court of first instance on 2017. 11. 24., but refused to take the oath and testify. Non-indicted Party 1 stated that the reason for refusing to take the oath and testify was that his/her related case was pending before the appellate court at present. Non-indicted Party 1 also appeared as a witness at the 7th trial date of the court of first instance on 2018. 1. 17. and refused to take the oath and testify.\\n\\n2) On 2018. 2. 7., the court of first instance acquitted the Defendant on the ground that the offense was not proved, and the prosecutor appealed.\\n\\n3) The prosecutor again requested Non-indicted Party 1 as a witness in the lower appellate court. Non-indicted Party 1 appeared at the 2nd trial date of the lower appellate court on 2018. 6. 19. and, stating “I refuse to take the oath because I have determined to refuse to take the oath,” refused to take the oath and testify.\\n\\nd. The lower appellate court’s determination\\n\\n1) Each refusal to testify by Non-indicted Party 1 at the court of first instance constituted a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify under Article 148 of the Criminal Procedure Act and does not fall under “when a person required to make a statement at trial preparation or at trial is unable to make a statement due to death, disease, residence abroad, unknown whereabouts, or any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\n2) Because Non-indicted Party 1’s refusal to testify in the lower appellate court occurred after his/her related case had become final and binding, the right to refuse to testify under Article 148 of the Criminal Procedure Act is not recognized, and under Article 150 of the Criminal Procedure Act, a person refusing to testify must explain the grounds for refusal, but Non-indicted Party 1 merely said, “I have determined to refuse to take the oath.” Therefore, Non-indicted Party 1’s refusal to testify cannot be viewed as a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify.
