Such a case does not fall under “when a person required to make a statement is unable to make a statement due to death, disease, residence abroad, unknown whereabouts, or any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and thus the statement record and suspect interrogation record concerning Non-indicted Party 1 prepared by the prosecutor (hereinafter collectively referred to as “the prosecution records concerning Non-indicted Party 1”) are not admissible as evidence. Even if viewed otherwise, it cannot be said that Non-indicted Party 1’s statement before the prosecution was made in a particularly trustworthy state pursuant to the proviso of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and therefore they are not admissible as evidence.\\n\\n3) The seizure of Non-indicted Party 1’s mobile phone by the police and the prosecution was unlawful, and therefore the audio files and transcripts of the calls between the Defendant and Non-indicted Party 1 obtained thereby are not admissible as evidence.\\n\\ne. Summary of the prosecutor’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\nThe lower appellate court’s determination is erroneous in violation of the relevant laws concerning the rules of evidence for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) When a witness refuses to testify without justifiable grounds, such case falls under “when a person required to make a statement is unable to make a statement due to death, disease, residence abroad, unknown whereabouts, or any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Since, prior to the 7th trial date of the court of first instance, the part of the criminal facts of the related case concerning Non-indicted Party 1 stating “purchased Philopon from the Defendant” was excluded from the charged facts through amendment of the indictment, Non-indicted Party 1’s refusal to testify at the 7th trial date of the court of first instance was not a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify. In addition, because Non-indicted Party 1’s refusal to testify in the lower appellate court occurred after the judgment in his/her related case became final and binding, it was not a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify. However, because Non-indicted Party 1’s statement before the prosecution in the related case was made in a particularly trustworthy state, the prosecution records concerning Non-indicted Party 1 are admissible as evidence.\\n\\n2) The seizure by the police of Non-indicted Party 1’s mobile phone was lawful as a seizure of voluntarily submitted items. Even if it cannot be viewed as a seizure of voluntarily submitted items and is therefore unlawful, once the prosecutor obtained a seizure and search warrant for the mobile phone and followed the procedure of seizure, there was a new and separate seizure procedure distinct from the police seizure, and there was no independent ground of illegality; thus, the causal relationship with the illegality at the police stage was severed. Accordingly, the audio files and transcripts of the calls between the Defendant and Non-indicted Party 1 obtained from the mobile phone are admissible as evidence.\\n\\n2. Determination on the admissibility of the prosecution records concerning Non-indicted Party 1\\n\\na. Admissibility arising from refusal to testify at the court of first instance\\n\\nArticle 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides: “In cases under Articles 312 or 313, when a person required to make a statement at trial preparation or at trial is unable to make a statement due to death, disease, residence abroad, unknown whereabouts, or any other equivalent cause, the record and other documents (including information in the form of text, photographs, videos, etc. written or stated by the accused or a person other than the accused, which is stored on a computer disk or any similar information storage medium) may be used as evidence. However, this shall apply only when it is proved that such statement or preparation was made in a particularly trustworthy state.” By so providing, it cites, as a ground by which hearsay evidence whose authenticity is not proved by the statement of the original declarant, etc. may exceptionally be admitted as evidence, the circumstance that the person is “unable to make a statement due to death, disease, residence abroad, unknown whereabouts, or any other equivalent cause.” Compared with the former Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act prior to amendment by Act No. 5054 on 1995. 12. 29., which prescribed “when unable to make a statement due to death, disease, or other causes,” and the former Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act prior to amendment by Act No. 8496 on 2007. 6. 1., which prescribed “when unable to make a statement due to death, disease, residence abroad, or other causes,” the current Criminal Procedure Act more strictly limits the scope of such exceptions; this reflects the intent to strengthen the elements of direct examination and trial-centered adjudication. Meanwhile, the Criminal Procedure Act guarantees that anyone may refuse to testify regarding matters that may give rise to concern that he/she, his/her relatives, etc. would be subject to criminal prosecution or indictment or would receive a guilty judgment (Article 148), and further provides that lawyers, patent attorneys, notaries public, certified public accountants, tax accountants, scriveners, physicians, Korean medicine doctors, dentists, pharmacists, druggists, midwives, nurses, persons in religious office, or persons who formerly held such offices may refuse to testify regarding matters concerning another person’s secrets known in connection with entrusted duties (main text of Article 149), thereby guaranteeing a witness the right to refuse to testify in certain circumstances. In light of the wording and amendment purpose of the current Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act and the content of the provisions concerning the right to refuse to testify, when a witness who appears in court lawfully exercises the right to refuse to testify pursuant to Articles 148 and 149 of the Criminal Procedure Act and refuses to testify, such case does not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009DO6788 rendered on 2012. 5. 17.).\\n\\nAs argued by the prosecutor, merely because the indictment was amended in the related case, it is difficult to view that, when Non-indicted Party 1 appeared as a witness at the 7th trial date of the court of first instance in this case, he/she had no right to refuse to testify in the event of concern that a fact subject to a guilty judgment under Article 148 of the Criminal Procedure Act might be revealed. The lower appellate court’s determination that Non-indicted Party 1’s refusal to testify at the court of first instance constituted a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify pursuant to Article 148 of the Criminal Procedure Act and therefore did not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act is in accordance with the above legal principles, and, as argued in the grounds for final appeal, there is no error in violation of the law concerning the rules of evidence.\\n\\nb. Admissibility arising from refusal to testify in the lower appellate court\\n\\n1) Where a reference witness who has made statements to an investigative agency refuses to testify at trial so that the Defendant cannot cross-examine him/her, even if the refusal was not a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify, unless there are special circumstances such as that the Defendant caused the witness’s refusal to testify, it must be regarded as not falling under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Therefore, just as in the case where a witness lawfully exercises the right to refuse to testify and refuses to testify, a document recording that witness’s statement to an investigative agency is not admissible as evidence. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\na) In order to realize the due process required by the Constitution, the Criminal Procedure Act adopts the substantive principle of direct examination and the hearsay rule, under which the formation of judicial conviction regarding the substance of the case must be accomplished through evidentiary examination in which cross-examination of original evidence is guaranteed in the presence of the judge. The substantive principle of direct examination, an element of trial-centered adjudication, is the principle that only evidence directly examined in the presence of the judge may serve as the basis of judgment, the original evidence closest to the fact to be proved must serve as the basis of judgment, and the use of substitutes for original evidence should not be permitted absent special circumstances. A judge can form a fresh and accurate conviction concerning the case by directly examining original evidence in court, and by affording the Defendant an opportunity to state direct opinions on the original evidence, the court can discover the substantive truth and realize a fair trial (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2017DO16593-1 rendered on 2019. 3. 21.).\\n\\nAccordingly, the court must ensure that such substantive direct examination principle and hearsay rule faithfully function as the principal and substantive governing principles throughout the criminal procedure and the course of hearing, and their exceptions must be limited to the minimum extent necessary as prescribed by the Criminal Procedure Act so that the right to a fair and public trial and the presumption of innocence, which arise from direct examination and trial-centered adjudication, are not substantially infringed or rendered hollow (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2010DO12 rendered on 2011. 11. 10.).\\n\\nArticle 310-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides: “Except as provided in Articles 311 through 316, no document recording a statement in place of a statement at trial preparation or at trial, or any statement containing the statement of another person made outside trial preparation or trial, may be used as evidence.” In this way, it declares the so-called hearsay rule, under which statements of persons who directly experienced the facts must be directly presented to the court and substitutes therefor in the form of statements or documents may not be presented, and limits cases in which admissibility as evidence is recognized as exceptions to the hearsay rule to Articles 311 through 316.\\n\\nIn addition, Articles 312 and 313 provide exceptions recognizing admissibility only when strict requirements are satisfied for documentary evidence such as statements of reference persons, including that the right of cross-examination is guaranteed; and Article 314 provides the requirements for exceptionally recognizing admissibility without the statement of the person required to make the statement in cases under Article 312 or 313 when such person is unable to make a statement.\\n\\nAs noted above, the exceptions to the hearsay rule must be limited to the minimum necessary. Since Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides yet another exception to the requirements that must be satisfied for hearsay evidence to be exceptionally admissible, those requirements themselves being exempted, its scope of application must be interpreted even more narrowly.\\n\\nb) Prior to the amendment by Act No. 8496 on 2007. 6. 1., Article 312(1) of the former Criminal Procedure Act provided: “A record prepared by a prosecutor of the statement of a suspect or a person other than a suspect, and a record prepared by a prosecutor or a judicial police officer of the results of an inspection may be used as evidence when the authenticity of its formation is acknowledged by the original declarant’s statement at trial preparation or at trial. However, a record prepared of a statement by a suspect who has become the accused may be used as evidence notwithstanding the accused’s statement at trial preparation or at trial, only when the statement was made in a particularly trustworthy state.” Article 313(1) provided the same effect with respect to a statement record concerning a reference person prepared by a judicial police officer. The Criminal Procedure Act as amended on 2007. 6. 1. provides in Article 312(4): “A record prepared by a prosecutor or a judicial police officer of the statement of a person other than the accused may be used as evidence when it is prepared in accordance with lawful procedure and method, when it is proved by the original declarant’s statement at trial preparation or at trial, by videotaped recording, or by any other objective method that the record contains the same content as that stated before the prosecutor or judicial police officer, and when the Defendant or defense counsel was able to question the original declarant concerning the contents thereof at trial preparation or at trial. However, this shall apply only when it is proved that the statement recorded therein was made in a particularly trustworthy state.”\\n\\nArticle 312(4) of the current Criminal Procedure Act, in addition to the requirement under the former Criminal Procedure Act that the authenticity of the original declarant’s statement be recognized, further added, as a requirement for admitting the evidence, “when the Defendant or defense counsel was able to question the original declarant concerning the contents thereof at trial preparation or at trial,” that is, the Defendant’s right of cross-examination must be guaranteed, thereby declaring that a statement record concerning a reference person for whom the Defendant’s right of cross-examination was not guaranteed is not, in principle, admissible as evidence. The guarantee of the right of cross-examination must be substantive and effective, not merely formal and procedural.\\n\\nAlso, with respect to the exceptions under which hearsay evidence may exceptionally be admitted without the original declarant’s statement, Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act has repeatedly been revised in the direction of further strictly limiting the scope of such exceptions, changing from “when unable to make a statement due to death, disease, or other causes,” to “when unable to make a statement due to death, disease, residence abroad, or other causes,” and again to “when unable to make a statement due to death, disease, residence abroad, unknown whereabouts, or any other equivalent cause,” as noted above (see the above en banc Decision 2009DO6788).\\n\\nAs such, the purpose of the amendments to the Criminal Procedure Act, which have strengthened the Defendant’s right of cross-examination and further strictly limited the exceptions to the hearsay rule, must also be an important consideration when determining whether Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act applies to a refusal to testify that is not recognized as a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify.\\n\\nc) The Supreme Court, in accordance with the content of these provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act and the purpose of their amendments, has confirmed through several precedents that the satisfaction of the requirements of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which sets forth exceptions to the principles of direct examination and the hearsay rule, must be strictly examined.\\n\\nFirst, with respect to the “disease” prescribed in Article 314, the Court held that it must be a serious illness to such an extent that even clinical examination or out-of-court examination is impossible during the period in which the trial is pending (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DO3619 rendered on 2006. 5. 25.). With respect to “residence abroad,” the Court held that it is insufficient merely that the original declarant is abroad; there must be circumstances in which the person required to make a statement cannot be brought to court to make a statement even by exhausting all possible and reasonable means, such as taking every possible measure to have him/her appear in court and testify; and if an international mutual legal assistance treaty has been concluded with the relevant country, one must first examine whether the witness can be summoned through mutual legal assistance procedures, and even where the witness cannot be summoned, procedures such as requesting the foreign court to conduct witness examination by mutual legal assistance must be followed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2015DO17115 rendered on 2016. 2. 18.). In addition, to fall under “unknown whereabouts,” it held that mere inability to serve a summons is insufficient; even after conducting an investigation into whereabouts through a request for location tracing, the whereabouts must still remain unconfirmed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2010DO2602 rendered on 2010. 9. 9.).\\n\\nIn this manner, the “death, disease, residence abroad, unknown whereabouts” prescribed in Article 314 must be recognized only where, due to personal physical reasons of the individual or limitations of place or distance arising from appearance in court, or circumstances in which appearance cannot be notified, etc., it is objectively clear that it is physically impossible for the witness to appear in court or, even if he/she appears, impossible to make a statement. However, a refusal to testify that does not amount to a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify cannot readily be regarded as falling within such a case where it is impossible to make a statement in court to the extent that it can be deemed equivalent to “death, disease, residence abroad, unknown whereabouts.”\\n\\nUltimately, if Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act were applied merely because, as argued by the prosecutor, there was a refusal to testify that did not amount to a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify, that would deprive the Defendant of the opportunity for cross-examination and expand the scope of exceptions to the hearsay rule, thereby effectively allowing consequences unfavorable to the Defendant. Such an interpretation of the Criminal Procedure Act runs counter to the purpose of the Criminal Procedure Act, which, as noted above, adopts and strengthens the substantive direct examination principle and the hearsay rule in order to establish trial-centered adjudication, as well as to the attitude of Supreme Court precedents based thereon.\\n\\nd) The Supreme Court already stated in the en banc Decision 2009DO6788 rendered on 2012. 5. 17. that where a witness who appeared in court lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify and refused to testify, such case does not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nComparing the case where a witness lawfully exercises the right to refuse to testify and the case where the refusal is not a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify, there is no difference in that the Defendant’s right of cross-examination is not guaranteed. Whether a witness’s refusal to testify is a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify is a matter arising within the sphere of the witness, which is unrelated to the Defendant, and as far as the Defendant is concerned, the right of cross-examination guaranteed by the Criminal Procedure Act must be secured regardless of whether the witness is a person entitled to refuse to testify or not.\\n\\nThat the applicability of the phrase “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, an exception to the hearsay rule, would vary depending on the accidental circumstance of whether the witness has a right to refuse to testify would create grave instability in the Defendant’s procedural status in criminal proceedings.\\n\\nMoreover, because in some cases it is not easy to clearly determine whether a witness has justifiable grounds for refusing to testify, differentiating the admissibility of the witness’s statement record prepared by an investigative agency according to whether the witness lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify may even undermine the stability of criminal procedure.\\n\\ne) However, where there are special circumstances such as that the Defendant caused the witness’s refusal to testify, there is no reason to exclude the application of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. If even such a case were regarded as not falling under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, it would run counter to the purpose of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which sets forth exceptions to the substantive direct examination principle and the hearsay rule that the formation of judicial conviction on the substance of the case must be achieved through evidentiary examination in which cross-examination of original evidence is guaranteed in the presence of the judge, and it would also not accord with the concept of justice.\\n\\nf) If a case in which a witness’s refusal to testify cannot be regarded as a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify is deemed to fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, then where a reference person made a statement unfavorable to the Defendant during the investigation and later refuses to testify in court, an innocent Defendant may instead end up being unjustly criminally punished.\\n\\nThat a witness, notwithstanding the absence of the right to refuse to testify, effectively evades testifying and thus cannot reproduce before the Defendant statements made to an investigative agency raises suspicion that the statements made at the investigative agency may have been false. Therefore, where a witness refuses to testify without justifiable grounds, there is a strong need to examine the truthfulness of the statement made to the investigative agency through cross-examination.\\n\\nArticle 161(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides: “Where a witness refuses to take an oath or testify without justifiable grounds, a fine for negligence not exceeding 500,000 won may be imposed by decision,” thereby establishing a sanction for a witness’s refusal to take an oath or testify without justifiable grounds, and the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Specific Violent Crimes, the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes, the Act on the Protection of Specific Crime Informants, etc., and others provide provisions concerning measures for the safety and protection of witnesses. As to refusal to testify without justifiable grounds, measures to induce testimony should be devised through the enactment or amendment of related statutes, such as introducing effective sanctions or improving the witness protection system; this is not a matter to be resolved by interpreting the scope of application of exceptions to the hearsay rule expansively.\\n\\n2) In this case, since the judgment in the related case became final and binding before the lower appellate court’s witness examination date, and Non-indicted Party 1 refused to testify in the lower appellate court without explaining the grounds for refusal in accordance with Article 150 of the Criminal Procedure Act, Non-indicted Party 1’s refusal to testify in the lower appellate court cannot be regarded as a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify. In addition, there is no special circumstance indicating that the Defendant caused Non-indicted Party 1’s refusal to testify. Therefore, because Non-indicted Party 1’s refusal to testify in the lower appellate court does not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause,” an exception to the hearsay rule prescribed in Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the prosecution records concerning Non-indicted Party 1 are not admissible as evidence.\\n\\nThe lower appellate court’s determination is based on the legal principles stated above, and, as argued in the grounds for final appeal, there is no error in violation of the law concerning the rules of evidence.\\n\\n3. Determination on the lawfulness of the seizure of the mobile phone and the admissibility of the audio files, etc. stored therein\\n\\nThe lower appellate court, for the reasons stated in its opinion, determined that ① the seizure of Non-indicted Party 1’s mobile phone at the police stage cannot be viewed as a lawful seizure of voluntarily submitted items, ② the seizure of Non-indicted Party 1’s mobile phone at the prosecution stage likewise cannot be viewed as a lawful seizure of voluntarily submitted items, and even if the prosecutor obtained and executed a seizure and search warrant for the mobile phone, it is difficult to view that the causal relationship with the prior illegal situation was severed, and accordingly rejected the admissibility of the audio files and transcripts obtained from Non-indicted Party 1’s mobile phone.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, there is no error in the lower appellate court’s determination in violation of the law concerning the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as stated in the order. In this judgment, the opinions of the justices participating were unanimous except for the separate opinion of Justice Park Sang-ok, and there are supplementary opinions by Justice Kwon Soon-il and Justice Kim Seon-su on the majority opinion.\\n\\n5. Separate opinion of Justice Park Sang-ok\\n\\na. The majority opinion states that even where a witness cannot be regarded as having lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify, such case does not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, unless there are special circumstances such as that the Defendant caused the witness’s refusal to testify. However, because such determination of the majority opinion is contrary to legal principles, I cannot agree. Nor is the reasoning of the majority opinion necessary to resolve this case. Below, I will refute the problems of the majority opinion in order.\\n\\nb. Where a witness cannot be regarded as having lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify, it should be viewed as falling under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\n1) The Supreme Court has already determined by an en banc decision that when a witness lawfully exercises the right to refuse to testify and refuses to testify, such case does not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act (Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009DO6788 rendered on 2012. 5. 17.).\\n\\nThat en banc decision clearly stated that only when a witness lawfully exercises the right to refuse to testify and refuses to testify does the case not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and that the basis is that the witness lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify. Such Supreme Court en banc decision is entirely proper.\\n\\nThe majority opinion takes the position that the same should apply where the witness cannot be regarded as having lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify, and cites the following grounds: ① the purpose of the Criminal Procedure Act, which has developed in the direction of establishing trial-centered adjudication by adopting and strengthening the substantive direct examination principle and the hearsay rule, should be considered; ② there is no difference between the case where the right to refuse to testify is lawfully exercised and the case where the exercise is not lawful, in that the Defendant’s right of cross-examination is not guaranteed in either case; and ③ the problems arising when non-lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify is treated the same as lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify should be resolved by legislation.\\n\\nHowever, the grounds cited by the majority opinion are not only insufficient but also contain various logical defects. I will examine the problems of the majority opinion in order.\\n\\n2) I fully agree that trial-centered adjudication should be established in accordance with the purpose of the substantive direct examination principle and the hearsay rule. However, direct examination and trial-centered adjudication must be harmonized with the ideal of discovering the substantive truth in criminal proceedings. The reason our Criminal Procedure Act declares the hearsay rule while also providing Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, an exception thereto, is that excessively strict restrictions on the admissibility of hearsay evidence should not obstruct the discovery of the substantive truth, which is the guiding principle of criminal procedure. Therefore, when interpreting Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the ideal of discovering the substantive truth must be considered together with the direct examination principle and trial-centered adjudication, and no one of them should be unilaterally prioritized.\\n\\nAs also stated in the above en banc decision, compared with the former Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act before amendment by Act No. 8496 on 2007. 6. 1., which provided “when unable to make a statement due to death, disease, residence abroad, or other causes,” the current Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act more strictly limits the scope of its exceptions, reflecting the intent to strengthen the elements of direct examination and trial-centered adjudication. However, the above en banc decision did not determine that, based solely on the wording and amendment purpose of the current Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, a case where a witness lawfully exercises the right to refuse to testify and refuses to testify does not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. After examining the wording and amendment purpose of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act together with the provisions concerning the right to refuse to testify, that en banc decision expressly stated, “the Criminal Procedure Act guarantees a witness the right to refuse to testify when certain grounds exist,” and then held, “it shall be considered that where a witness who appears in court lawfully exercises the right to refuse to testify pursuant to Articles 148 and 149 of the Criminal Procedure Act and refuses to testify, such case does not fall under ‘when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause’ under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act.” In addition, as a premise for applying such legal principles, it expressly stated “that the attorney appeared as a witness at the 6th trial date of the lower appellate court, explained that the content to which he/she was to testify concerned another person’s secret learned in connection with entrusted duties from the defendant company, and after hearing from the presiding judge that he/she could refuse to testify, refused to testify.” In other words, the above en banc decision reached that conclusion on the ground of guaranteeing the witness’s right to refuse to testify.\\n\\nIf the majority’s logic were followed, there would have been no need in the above en banc decision to specifically invoke the lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify. It would have sufficed to simply hold that when a witness refuses to testify, the case does not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. The majority opinion misapprehends the purport of the above en banc decision.\\n\\n3) The majority opinion cites as grounds that there is no difference between the case where the right to refuse to testify is lawfully exercised and the case where it is not lawfully exercised, because in both cases the Defendant’s right of cross-examination is not guaranteed. However, this is not an appropriate ground. That is because Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act fundamentally presupposes situations in which the Defendant’s right of cross-examination is not guaranteed. On the premise that the right of cross-examination is not realized, the question is whether, for a specific individual situation, it should be regarded as falling under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. The circumstance cited by the majority opinion is meaningful only in the situation where the applicability of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act is at issue; it has no meaning when actually determining whether the provision applies. Rather, where a witness without the right to refuse to testify disregards the court’s summons and obstinately refuses to appear and testify, making execution of the warrant of arrest impossible, it should be considered to fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act; however, there is no essential difference between that case and the case where a witness directly appears in court and refuses to testify without justifiable grounds, since in both cases the witness is refusing to testify in court. There is no reason whatsoever to treat these two cases differently.\\n\\nThe significance of the case where a witness lawfully exercises the right to refuse to testify and refuses to testify is markedly different, for purposes of applying Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, from the case where a witness refuses to testify without the right to refuse to testify.\\n\\na) The Criminal Procedure Act, the representative statute governing criminal justice, imposes on all citizens the duty to appear as witnesses and testify for the discovery of truth (Article 146). On the other hand, it seeks harmony with the objectives and ideals pursued by the procedural law, as well as with the fundamental rights or interests of witnesses and other public values that may be in tension or conflict with them. The various systems and detailed procedural provisions established by the Criminal Procedure Act concerning witness examination are all devices for realizing due process within this balance and harmony of values, rights, and interests. With respect to witness examination, the Criminal Procedure Act imposes upon witnesses a truthfulness obligation through serious and solemn procedural provisions and imposes punishment for perjury when it is violated. Meanwhile, for witnesses who, despite not being parties to the proceedings against themselves, bear the duty to appear in court, take an oath, and state facts they have experienced, the Criminal Procedure Act establishes, in certain cases, a system of the right to refuse to testify, allowing silence in place of a statement. That is, it recognizes the right to refuse to testify in relation to statements likely to give rise to concern that the person himself/herself, his/her spouse or relatives, legal representatives, and guardians/supervisors may be subject to criminal prosecution or indictment or may receive a guilty judgment, and in relation to statements concerning another person’s secrets known by persons in certain professions such as lawyers, physicians, and persons in religious office, or by persons who formerly held such professions, in connection with entrusted duties (Articles 148 and 149). The system of the right to refuse to testify grants the witness the right to refuse to fulfill the duty to testify (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2008DO942 rendered on 2010. 1. 21.).\\n\\nThe duty to appear as a witness and testify serves the discovery of substantive truth, an important ideal of the Criminal Procedure Act. Only when the Criminal Procedure Act, yielding this fundamental ideal of discovering substantive truth, grants a right to refuse to testify in certain circumstances is the duty to testify exempted. In particular, the right to refuse to testify under Article 148 of the Criminal Procedure Act is grounded in the privilege against self-incrimination under Article 12 of the Constitution. In order to substantively guarantee this right to refuse to testify, the Supreme Court’s en banc Decision 2009DO6788 held that where the right to refuse to testify is lawfully exercised, Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act does not apply. Where a witness lawfully exercises the right to refuse to testify, even at the expense of the ideal of discovering substantive truth, all admissibility of his/her statements to investigative agencies is denied. If, even in such a case, it is deemed to fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, then the exercise of the right to refuse to testify, which is granted as a justifiable ground for being unable to testify, becomes meaningless because it would bring about the same result as if the statements made to the investigative agency were made in court in the same form. Moreover, to avoid such a result, the witness would have no choice but to testify, which would in effect compel testimony. This is contrary to the purposes of Article 12 of the Constitution and Articles 148 and 149 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nOn the other hand, when a witness refuses to testify, he/she has voluntarily appeared in court and clearly expressed the will to refuse testimony, so absent special circumstances sufficient to reverse such will, it is an even clearer ground that his/her statement cannot be heard than the grounds of disease, residence abroad, or unknown whereabouts expressly set forth in Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Therefore, irrespective of whether the witness’s refusal to testify is a lawful exercise of the right to refuse to testify or an actual evasion of testimony despite no right to refuse to testify, it is logical to regard all such cases as falling under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. However, as noted above, the Supreme Court, through the above en banc decision, adopted a restrictive interpretation of a witness’s refusal to testify where the witness had the right to refuse to testify, taking into account the purpose of legally guaranteeing the right to refuse to testify.\\n\\nIn other words, excluding the application of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act where the right to refuse to testify is lawfully exercised is intended to protect the witness’s right to refuse to testify, not the Defendant.\\n\\nBy contrast, a witness without the right to refuse to testify has a duty to testify. He/she also has a duty to state the truth, and if that duty is violated, he/she is punished for perjury. Such a person cannot be treated the same as one who unlawfully refuses to testify in breach of that duty. In such a situation of non-performance, the ideal of discovering substantive truth under the Criminal Procedure Act should not be compromised. A person who has abandoned a citizen’s duty cannot be granted the power to nullify statements made during the investigation.\\n\\nb) Even when viewed from foreign examples, the majority opinion’s logic is unpersuasive.\\n\\nThe German Federal Court of Justice permits reading of records prepared during investigation where a person without the right to refuse to testify nevertheless refuses to testify in trial proceedings. In Japan, if a witness refuses to testify, regardless of whether he/she has a right to refuse to testify, where the determination not to testify is firm and the likelihood of changing one’s mind and testifying is low, it is regarded as “inability to make a statement,” and admissibility is recognized for the records prepared by investigative agencies. The U.S. Supreme Court, based on the accused’s right under the Sixth Amendment to confront witnesses, views the evidence as inadmissible if the opportunity for cross-examination was not guaranteed.\\n\\nAs such, the issue of whether to recognize admissibility as an exception to the hearsay rule where the right to refuse to testify was lawfully exercised or not may be regulated differently according to the legislative policy of each country. Rather, Germany and Japan, both civil-law countries like Korea, allow records prepared by investigative agencies to be used as evidence when a witness without the right to refuse to testify refuses to testify. The United States takes a different view based on the accused’s right to confront witnesses expressly stated in the Sixth Amendment, and because the American investigative and trial systems based on the jury system differ from ours, the various problems that will be discussed below do not arise even if it is so viewed. By contrast, in Korea, the Defendant’s right of cross-examination is not a constitutionally guaranteed right but a statutory right recognized by the Criminal Procedure Act (see Constitutional Court en banc Decision 2011HEONBA108 rendered on 2013. 12. 26.). The guarantee of the right of cross-examination and the limitation of admissibility are matters of legislative policy and statutory interpretation, and they must be recognized only within the scope that can be harmonized with the various ideals recognized under our Criminal Procedure Act system.\\n\\nAccordingly, the majority opinion’s logic—that because a case where the right to refuse to testify is lawfully exercised does not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the same should apply to cases not recognized as lawful exercise of the right—is weak in its grounds.\\n\\n4) The majority opinion states that the problems that may arise under the majority’s view can be resolved by legislation. However, this attitude of the majority opinion cannot be agreed with, because it not only disregards the various problems that may arise under the current criminal procedure system, but also goes beyond the role and authority of the court exercising judicial power.\\n\\na) If the majority opinion is followed, it is easy to foresee at least the following serious problems.\\n\\n(1) In numerous cases currently pending before the courts, defendants will, after indicating non-consent to the investigative agency statements of victims and other reference persons, attempt to induce or threaten them to refuse to testify against them. In particular, since under current law there is no provision punishing or sanctioning a defendant’s act of inducing a witness to refuse to testify, such acts will occur indiscriminately. Even if a witness refuses to testify without justifiable grounds, only a fine for negligence not exceeding 500,000 won may be imposed (Article 161(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act), so even as a witness, he/she will be tempted to refuse to testify without much hesitation. It is entirely possible that a defendant may promise to pay the fine or offer money or valuables in excess thereof to induce refusal to testify. In addition, the current legal provisions concerning witness safety measures mentioned by the majority opinion are limited in their application to only certain specific crimes and cannot serve as a solution for voluntary refusal to testify induced by persuasion.\\n\\nThe duty to testify imposed by the Criminal Procedure Act on citizens will, overnight, be reduced to a subject of barter. This phenomenon will be especially pronounced in cases involving bribery, violations of the Political Funds Act, narcotics and organized violence crimes, sexual offenses, property crimes, cases in which there is no physical evidence from the outset or where the reference person’s statement is decisive evidence, crimes concerning social legal interests or state legal interests, or abstract endangerment offenses where no actual infringement of a legal interest need occur. In numerous sexual offenses for which the complaint-based prosecution rule has been abolished, attempts to obtain acquittals by causing refusal to testify will become rampant, thereby producing results contrary to the purpose of abolishing the complaint-based prosecution rule. Criminal proceedings will degenerate into a tool for civil recovery of damages.\\n\\n(2) The majority opinion holds that, exceptionally, where there are special circumstances such as that the Defendant caused the witness’s refusal to testify, the case falls under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. However, what exactly is meant by the Defendant having caused the witness’s refusal to testify is highly unclear. Even if this were interpreted to include cases where the Defendant induces or threatens a witness to refuse to testify, it would still not be easy to prevent the phenomenon described above, in which defendants induce or threaten witnesses to refuse to testify.\\n\\nIt may be foreseeable to some extent that a witness who has the right to refuse to testify will appear in court and refuse to testify. However, whether a witness without the right to refuse to testify will refuse to testify cannot be known at all until he/she actually appears in court and refuses to testify. In cases where the Defendant’s persuasion or threats have intervened in relation to refusal to testify, the fact that the witness appeared in court and actually refused to testify means that the Defendant’s persuasion or threats succeeded. In other words, a witness who refused to testify due to the Defendant’s persuasion, having already been promised or received economic compensation, etc., would have no reason to state truthfully that such persuasion occurred; and a witness who refused to testify due to the Defendant’s threats would not truthfully state that threats were made out of concern for harm to himself/herself or his/her family. Ultimately, it will be extremely difficult to uncover in the instant criminal case the fact that the witness refused to testify due to the Defendant’s persuasion or threats. Then, even under the majority opinion’s exceptional interpretation, cases in which the Defendant induces the witness to refuse to testify by persuasion or threats in order to deny the admissibility of the witness’s statement to investigative agencies will still remain widespread.\\n\\n(3) Perjury is also likely to become a dead letter. For a witness who fears punishment for perjury, refusing to testify and bearing only a fine for negligence not exceeding 500,000 won is the rational choice. It is unrealistic to expect refusal of a promise of money or valuables exceeding the amount of the fine when offered by the defendant. As a result, aside from the crime of false accusation perjury, cases punished as perjury will in effect disappear. A neutral third party who has no interest in either the Defendant or the victim, such as a person who happened to witness another person’s sexual offense, a traffic accident, or an act of violence, can, if he/she appears in court, sees the Defendant or victim, or is influenced by the attitude of persons concerned in the gallery, choose to refuse to testify and thereby easily be completely freed from the duties and burdens arising from his/her accidental experience as a citizen. As a result, even statements truthfully made to investigative agencies without any hindrance will become unusable as evidence, and not only the discovery of substantive truth but also results manifestly contrary to justice will arise.\\n\\n(4) According to the majority opinion, investigative agencies will no longer have reason to actively pursue location tracing of witnesses or execute warrants of arrest. If the investigative agency that received a request for location tracing actively traced the witness and caused him/her to appear, or actively executed a warrant of arrest and caused the witness to appear, but the witness then refused to testify, the admissibility of the witness’s statement to the investigative agency would be denied. On the other hand, if location tracing or execution of the warrant of arrest is handled passively and the witness is found to have unknown whereabouts or the warrant of arrest becomes unexecutable, the witness’s statement to the investigative agency would be granted admissibility. Thus, the more diligently the investigative agency attempts location tracing or execution of a warrant of arrest for a witness, the higher the likelihood that the admissibility of the statement to the investigative agency will be denied, and accordingly it is more likely that the agency will handle its work in a formalistic and passive manner.\\n\\n(5) The purpose of the investigative agency in interviewing a reference person is to determine whether there is criminal suspicion and decide whether to indict, and after indictment to faithfully maintain the prosecution. Until now, investigative agencies have conducted investigations without anticipating that a witness would refuse to testify without justifiable grounds in court. In cases where a witness refuses to testify without justifiable grounds, because admissibility may be granted to the witness’s record prepared by the investigative agency, in order to prevent a guilty judgment from being rendered contrary to the contents of his/her statement at the investigative agency, the witness had no choice but to take the stand bearing the burden of perjury and reverse the statement made at the investigative agency. Accordingly, investigative agencies have faithfully interviewed reference persons on the premise that the record would be admissible, left the statement in a record, and conducted investigations so that, even if the witness reversed the statement made at the investigative agency in court, guilt could still be established based on the content of the record.\\n\\nHowever, if the majority opinion is followed, since a witness may refuse to testify in a manner favorable to the Defendant without any sanction other than bearing a fine, investigative agencies in the future will have no choice but to investigate on the premise that the witness will refuse to testify without justifiable grounds. A not insignificant amount of time passes from when the reference person makes a statement to the investigative agency until he/she is summoned as a witness in court, and during that time various circumstances may affect the witness’s decision whether to testify or refuse to testify. The witness-victim’s feelings of harm may also be greatly diminished. Since investigative agencies cannot predict whether a witness will refuse to testify in the future, it is sufficient to collect physical evidence and interview reference persons, and when the statements are deemed credible and the criminal suspicion is recognized, to indict. If, during trial, a witness refuses to testify in a manner favorable to the Defendant, it is not merely that testimony cannot be obtained; the record containing content unfavorable to the Defendant will also lose admissibility, and conversely, if the witness does not refuse to testify and instead testifies unfavorably to the Defendant, that testimony can be used as evidence. Ultimately, there will be no practical need for investigative agencies to prepare records of reference persons’ statements. If all witnesses in a case refuse to testify, the result in that case will be that there is no statement evidence at all. Now, once a witness refuses to testify, there is no need even to examine the reason, and his/her statement record will no longer be recognized as evidence. Whether a witness has the right to refuse to testify will matter only for deciding whether to impose a fine in the event of refusal to testify; otherwise, there will be no legal difference.\\n\\nAs such, the future investigative and trial practice according to the majority opinion does not fundamentally accord with the Criminal Procedure Act system, which recognizes reference persons’ statement records at the investigative stage as statement evidence. One must seriously consider whether this truly reflects the essence of direct examination and trial-centered adjudication pursued by our Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\n(6) Under the majority opinion’s interpretation, the means available to a prosecutor under the current criminal procedure system to prepare for a witness’s refusal to testify will be the evidence preservation procedure prescribed in Article 184 of the Criminal Procedure Act. The prosecutor is likely to use the evidence preservation procedure at the investigative stage, arguing that there are circumstances in which it would be difficult to use evidence unless it is preserved in advance, in order to prevent statements of reference persons that critically affect guilt or innocence from losing admissibility for the entirely unexpected reason of refusal to testify in court. However, it will not be easy for the prosecutor to prove the necessity of evidence preservation in a situation where it is impossible to know at all whether the witness will refuse to testify in the future, and it is doubtful whether a request for evidence preservation can be granted merely on the ground of concern over refusal to testify. Even if the request is granted and witness examination is conducted, it will be difficult to avoid criticism that this runs counter to the direct examination principle and trial-centered adjudication by the court of first instance.\\n\\nb) Such problems can arise immediately if a judgment is rendered according to the majority opinion. Nevertheless, the majority opinion attempts to shift responsibility to the legislature by saying that these problems should be resolved by legislation.\\n\\nHowever, changes that create such serious problems in criminal trial and investigative procedures must be made by legislation, not by court judgment. This is because legislative procedures can collect opinions from various citizens, including relevant agencies, and, after in-depth review of the various problems that may be caused thereby, can establish flexible and realistic specific rules. In addition, they can minimize social shock from abrupt changes by allowing a grace period for implementation and can build various human and institutional conditions for prior response. If the Supreme Court renders judgment according to the majority opinion, the public and society will be forced overnight to bear entirely unexpected rapid changes and problems. More seriously, while legislation to resolve the problems will inevitably proceed slowly, refusal-to-testify situations by witnesses will arise frequently until legislation supplementing the interpretation under the majority opinion is enacted, and investigative and criminal trial procedures will fall into a prolonged state of confusion, with the resulting damage borne entirely by the people.\\n\\nIt is doubtful whether it is necessary for the Supreme Court to render a judgment according to the majority opinion, declaring the legal principles of the majority opinion without any prior preparatory procedure and thereby causing enormous confusion in investigative and trial procedures and then passing the responsibility to the National Assembly to resolve it through legislation.\\n\\nAs noted above, whether to grant admissibility to a statement made to an investigative agency where a witness cannot be regarded as having lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify is a matter of legislative policy and an issue of interpretation of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Such statutory interpretation must be harmonized with the entirety of our criminal justice order. If one interprets a case where a witness cannot be regarded as having lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify as not falling under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, thereby causing the serious problems in investigative and trial procedures described above and necessitating various legislative measures to resolve them, this itself proves that such interpretation does not accord with our legal order. It is beyond the role and authority of the judiciary to render a judgment based on a statutory interpretation that cannot be harmonized with the entirety of the legal order, while telling the legislature to change the rest of the legal order to fit that interpretation.\\n\\nI cannot help but point out that a more careful approach and normative interpretation are needed, in the hope that the concern that the legal principles declared according to the majority opinion may cause great confusion throughout criminal justice and have serious repercussions on society and the public is merely a false alarm.\\n\\n5) By contrast, as before, if Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act is not applied when the right to refuse to testify is lawfully exercised pursuant to Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009DO6788, and is applied only when the right to refuse to testify cannot be regarded as lawfully exercised, there is no problem. The matters raised by the majority opinion are all either not logically sound or capable of resolution under the existing interpretation of the law.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that if the applicability of the phrase “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, an exception to the hearsay rule, varies depending on the accidental circumstance of whether the right to refuse to testify exists, this creates grave instability in the Defendant’s status in criminal procedure. However, the grounds of “death, disease, residence abroad, unknown whereabouts” expressly set forth in Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act are all matters that regulate the existence of accidental circumstances unrelated to the Defendant. Accordingly, the majority opinion’s above concern is not valid.\\n\\nIn addition, the majority opinion says that because in some cases it is not easy to determine whether a witness has justifiable grounds for refusing to testify, it is improper to differentiate the determination of admissibility according to whether the witness lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify. However, the significance of the right to refuse to testify has already been examined in detail above, and if it is difficult to determine whether there are justifiable grounds for refusal to testify, then it is appropriate to interpret broadly that the right to refuse to testify exists; therefore, the majority opinion’s above point is also unpersuasive.\\n\\nThe majority opinion says that where a reference person made a statement unfavorable to the Defendant during the investigation and later refused to testify in court, an innocent Defendant may instead end up being unjustly criminally punished. That is, because the statement made to the investigative agency may be false, it appears to mean that admissibility cannot be granted to the statement to the investigative agency merely because the witness refused to testify without justifiable grounds. However, the problem feared by the majority opinion can be resolved through the requirement provided in the proviso of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act: “However, this shall apply only when it is proved that such statement or preparation was made in a particularly trustworthy state.”\\n\\nThe Supreme Court interprets the meaning of the proviso to Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act as “when there is little room for falsehood to intervene in the content of the statement or in the preparation of the record or document, and concrete and external circumstances are proved that assure the credibility and voluntariness of the contents of the statement.” Specifically, in order for a court to recognize admissibility under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, it is not enough that no obvious procedural illegality appears in the course of preparing the statement or record, or that there are no concrete circumstances calling the voluntariness of the statement into question; beyond that, there must be concrete and external circumstances sufficiently assuring the credibility and voluntariness of the statement even without undergoing verification through cross-examination in court, such that if the court forms a conviction of guilt based thereon, it can still be evaluated as not contrary to the principle of trial by evidence (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2011DO6035 rendered on 2014. 8. 26.). In addition, because Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides another major exception allowing admissibility without even the opportunity for cross-examination of the original declarant, etc., despite the exception to fundamental principles such as direct examination in cases of unknown whereabouts of a reference person, proof that the reference person’s statement or preparation was made “in a particularly trustworthy state” is not satisfied merely by showing a probability thereof; it must reach the level of excluding reasonable doubt (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2013DO12652 rendered on 2014. 2. 21.).\\n\\nAs such, the Supreme Court requires very strict requirements in recognizing a “particularly trustworthy state.” Ultimately, the matters feared by the majority opinion can be fully resolved by excluding the admissibility of statement evidence through strict determination regarding whether a “particularly trustworthy state” is recognized.\\n\\nDepending on the case, for example, if at an investigative agency a face-to-face examination between the Defendant and the reference person is conducted in the presence of counsel and the questioning and rebuttal of them proceed in depth, so that the investigation is faithfully carried out, and, together with various other circumstances, the reference person’s statement is recognized as having been made in a particularly trustworthy state, there may be cases in which granting admissibility to statement evidence and allowing the judge to assess its probative value according to free evaluation of evidence is consistent with the criminal procedure ideal of discovering the substantive truth. Otherwise, treating refusal to testify without justifiable grounds as not falling under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act and uniformly denying admissibility would be tantamount to blocking all paths from the outset without even identifying the path to the substantive truth in a concrete case, which is unfair.\\n\\n6) As noted above, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009DO6788 adopted a restrictive interpretation that where a witness lawfully exercises the right to refuse to testify and refuses to testify, the case does not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, considering the purpose of legally guaranteeing the right to refuse to testify. Therefore, the above en banc decision can be understood as taking the position that when a witness cannot be regarded as having lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify, the case falls under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause.” Ultimately, the interpretation of the majority opinion changes the above precedent.\\n\\nPrecedent should be changed with caution. This is so even though the institutional possibility of changing precedent is open and it is anticipated that the public will accept changes in legal relations resulting therefrom. Only then is legal stability secured and can the public use precedent as a guide for decision-making and conduct, so that precedent truly has normative force. Where, absent any change in statutory provisions, Supreme Court precedent has accumulated for a long period in a certain direction regarding interpretation, greater caution is required in changing that precedent. To alter an accumulated line of precedent, there must be circumstances so great that the view has become markedly contrary to the sense of justice due to changes in the times and circumstances, or that it has significantly departed from the purpose of the statutory provision, and the change must possess far greater value than maintaining it so that sacrificing legal stability is justified; it is not the solution to alter an accumulated line of precedent merely because a new legal view appears somewhat better or more rational. Yet in this case, there is no reason to change the doctrinal holding of Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009DO6788. Since the rendering of that en banc decision, there has been no meaningful change in the statutory provisions to date, nor have the times or circumstances changed. Following the doctrinal holding of that en banc decision has not become markedly contrary to the sense of justice or significantly beyond the purpose of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Rather, as noted above, if the precedent is changed according to the majority opinion, enormous problems difficult for the public to bear will arise. It cannot even be said that the majority opinion is somewhat better or more rational than the legal principles of the above en banc decision.\\n\\nThe majority opinion has not presented any clear reason to change precedent.\\n\\nc. Moreover, as noted above, the majority opinion is not only unsound but is also unnecessary for resolving this case. In this case, even if the judgment according to the majority opinion is not made, the prosecution records concerning Non-indicted Party 1 should still be deemed inadmissible as evidence. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\nWhere a witness lawfully exercises the right to refuse to testify so that the statement record of his/her statement at an investigative agency does not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act and thus is not admissible as evidence, if the prosecutor later requests examination of that same witness again on the ground that the reason for refusal to testify has ceased to exist due to a subsequent circumstance, such request should be permitted only when the purpose is not to grant admissibility to the statement made at the investigative agency but, irrespective of that statement, solely to directly hear the witness’s in-court statement concerning the substantive truth of the case in the trial court. At that time, even if the witness again refuses to testify in the same manner as before despite the cessation of the reason for refusal, admissibility should not be recognized for the statement made at the investigative agency that has already been denied admissibility. If, even in such a case, one were to regard the matter as falling under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act on the ground that the reason for refusal to testify has ceased, thereby allowing admissibility to be granted to the statement made at the investigative agency that had already been denied admissibility, this would not only run counter to the original purpose of guaranteeing the witness’s right to refuse to testify, but would also create grave instability in the status of the witness and the Defendant in criminal procedure due to accidental circumstances such as the extent of the investigative agency’s evidence request or the progress of the trial. This is the same as the case where, after a witness makes a statement in court denying the authenticity of a statement record prepared by the investigative agency and admissibility is denied, the prosecutor again requests the witness in order to establish the authenticity of that statement record, which cannot be allowed.\\n\\nIn short, when a witness lawfully exercises the right to refuse to testify and refuses to testify, the case does not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, so the statement record of the reference person prepared by the investigative agency concerning that witness is not admissible as evidence, and even if the witness later appears in court again at the time when the reason for refusal has ceased and again refuses to testify, admissibility of his/her statement record as a reference person cannot thereafter be recognized under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nd. The grounds for appeal are determined according to these legal principles.\\n\\nThe lower appellate court determined that, although Non-indicted Party 1 refused to testify in the lower appellate court without justifiable grounds, this does not fall under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and thus the prosecution records concerning Non-indicted Party 1 are not admissible as evidence; even if viewed otherwise, it cannot be said under the proviso of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act that Non-indicted Party 1’s statement before the prosecution was made in a particularly trustworthy state, and therefore it is not admissible as evidence.\\n\\nHowever, according to the legal principles discussed above, because Non-indicted Party 1 lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify and refused to testify at the court of first instance, the prosecution records concerning Non-indicted Party 1 are denied admissibility, and even if Non-indicted Party 1 appeared again as a witness in the lower appellate court and refused to testify without justifiable grounds, admissibility cannot be granted again. Therefore, although the lower appellate court erred in proceeding to determine whether Non-indicted Party 1’s refusal to testify in the lower appellate court fell under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, its conclusion denying admissibility of the prosecution records concerning Non-indicted Party 1 is proper.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the lower appellate court rejected the admissibility of the audio files and transcripts obtained from Non-indicted Party 1’s mobile phone, and there is no error in that part of the lower appellate court’s determination in violation of the law concerning the rules of evidence as argued in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nUltimately, because the lower appellate court’s determination contains no error affecting the judgment in violation of the law concerning the rules of evidence as argued in the grounds for final appeal, the appeal should be dismissed.\\n\\ne. Although I agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion of this case that the appeal should be dismissed as above, because the specific reasons leading to the conclusion differ, I state this in a separate opinion.\\n\\n6. Supplementary opinions of Justices Kwon Soon-il and Kim Seon-su on the majority opinion\\n\\na. The separate opinion states that Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009DO6788 can be viewed as taking the position that when a witness cannot be regarded as having lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify, such case falls under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and thus the interpretation of the majority opinion changes the above precedent.\\n\\nHowever, the above en banc decision concerned a case where a witness lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify under Article 149 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and the present case, in which the witness cannot be regarded as having lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify, is different in its facts. The above en banc decision was limited to determining the issue in a case where the witness lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify.\\n\\nSince the 2007 amendment to the Criminal Procedure Act, the Supreme Court has not yet determined whether, where a witness cannot be regarded as having lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify, a document recording that witness’s statement prepared by an investigative agency has admissibility as evidence. After the above en banc decision, academic opinion has been divided between the view that the same interpretation should apply to the issue in this case and the view that it should not, and lower-court precedents are also divided. This judgment clarifies the scope of application of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, thereby serving to resolve the practical confusion that had existed in lower courts.\\n\\nIn order to fall under the “any other equivalent cause” in “death, disease, residence abroad, unknown whereabouts, or any other equivalent cause” prescribed in Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the case must be one, as the majority opinion notes, where it is physically impossible for the witness to appear in court or where it is objectively clear that, even if he/she appears, he/she cannot make a statement. A witness who is to testify about the facts of an offense in which he/she was involved may be punished for that offense if he/she testifies truthfully, so Article 148 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides for the right to refuse to testify by concretizing the privilege against self-incrimination guaranteed by Article 12 of the Constitution. In this situation, even when a person is in a position where he/she may be criminally punished by testifying and exercises the right to refuse to testify guaranteed by the Constitution and law, it is not recognized as a case in which “it is objectively clear that the person cannot make a statement in court”; therefore, a witness who, though free from fear of criminal punishment by testifying, is not recognized as having the right to refuse to testify, has even less room to fall under the case in which “it is objectively clear that the person cannot make a statement in court.” Rather, the above en banc decision’s view that where the right to refuse to testify is lawfully exercised the case does not fall under the “any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act can be said to presuppose as a logical matter that a case where the exercise of the right to refuse to testify is not lawful likewise does not fall under that cause.\\n\\nb. The separate opinion states that, when interpreting Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, one must consider not only the direct examination principle and trial-centered adjudication but also the ideal of discovering substantive truth, and that no one of them should be unilaterally prioritized. This appears to indicate concern that, if the majority opinion is followed, the discovery of substantive truth in criminal trials may be impeded.\\n\\nThe direct examination principle, trial-centered adjudication, and the ideal of discovering substantive truth should be viewed not as being in antagonistic relations or as one possessing a value superior to the others, but as being in a complementary relationship. A judge can form a fresh and accurate conviction about the case by directly examining original evidence in court, and by affording the Defendant an opportunity to state direct opinions on the original evidence, the ideal of discovering substantive truth can be realized. In other words, the direct examination principle and trial-centered adjudication are the most effective means for reaching substantive truth. Of course, there may be points at which the two ideals conflict, and in such cases it may be necessary to choose which ideal should be given greater weight.\\n\\nHowever, a case in which a reference person who has made a statement to an investigative agency refuses to testify without justifiable grounds in court so that the Defendant cannot cross-examine him/her cannot readily be said to correspond to such a situation. There may be various reasons why a reference person who has made a statement to an investigative agency refuses to testify without justifiable grounds despite having a duty to testify. If the reference person does not make clear in court that the statement made to the investigative agency was true and does not give the Defendant an opportunity to cross-examine, this means that he/she is evading testimony so as not to bear the risk of perjury, and such a statement can hardly be regarded as likely to contain objective truth.\\n\\nIn addition, with respect to the majority opinion’s concern that where a reference person made a statement unfavorable to the Defendant during the investigation and later refused to testify in court, an innocent Defendant may instead end up being unjustly criminally punished, the separate opinion states that this can be sufficiently resolved through a strict determination of whether it falls under the “particularly trustworthy state” in the proviso of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. As the separate opinion properly points out, in order to recognize admissibility by applying the proviso to Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, it is not enough that no obvious procedural illegality appears in the course of preparing the statement or record, or that there are no concrete circumstances calling the voluntariness of the statement into question; beyond that, there must be concrete and external circumstances sufficiently assuring the credibility and voluntariness of the statement even without undergoing verification through cross-examination in court, such that if the court forms a conviction of guilt based thereon, it can still be evaluated as not contrary to the principle of trial by evidence. However, even though the Criminal Procedure Act provides various provisions for securing a witness’s appearance and testimony, if the investigative agency that obtained the reference person’s statement during investigation failed to make that reference person testify in court, such circumstance alone can hardly be viewed as satisfying the condition of guarantee of credibility for the hearsay statement. This is because the judge cannot form a fresh and accurate conviction through the original statement, and it results in deprivation of the Defendant’s opportunity for cross-examination.\\n\\nIn other words, even where a witness cannot be regarded as having lawfully exercised the right to refuse to testify, the principles of direct examination and trial-centered adjudication must be carried through, and that is precisely the path by which one can more closely approach substantive truth.\\n\\nc.
