The separate opinion points out the problems that may be feared if judgment according to the majority opinion is rendered.\\n\\n1) The separate opinion states that, if the majority opinion is followed, the phenomenon of defendants persuading or threatening witnesses will occur indiscriminately. The majority opinion views special circumstances such as that the Defendant caused the witness’s refusal to testify as falling under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Accordingly, where a defendant induces or threatens a witness to refuse to testify, there remains a path for admissibility to be granted under the proviso of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nNevertheless, the separate opinion states that because it is extremely difficult to uncover the fact that the witness refused to testify due to the Defendant’s persuasion or threats, cases in which defendants persuade or threaten witnesses will still remain widespread. However, because the burden of proving guilt under the Criminal Procedure Act rests on the prosecutor, the fact that such proof is not easy does not constitute a circumstance to be considered when determining the existence of admissibility.\\n\\n2) The separate opinion states that power cannot be granted to a person who has abandoned the duty to testify to nullify statements made during the investigation. However, rather, a person who refuses to testify in court without justifiable grounds is unable to reproduce before the Defendant the statements made to the investigative agency and to respond to cross-examination, and cannot repeat the same content as the statement made to the investigative agency even while bearing the risk of punishment for perjury, so his/her statement to the investigative agency should also be excluded at the stage of examining whether it is admissible.\\n\\nIn addition, ensuring that the witness can testify in court by preparing in advance and responding effectively so that the witness’s statement made during the investigation is not nullified is the role and duty of the prosecutor in charge of maintaining the prosecution. If the prosecutor cannot elicit the witness’s testimony, the record prepared by the investigative agency concerning that witness cannot be used as evidence, and this is merely the natural consequence contemplated by the Criminal Procedure Act. Unless there are circumstances such as that the Defendant caused the witness’s refusal to testify, the circumstance of the witness’s non-performance of the duty to testify cannot become a reason to abandon procedural justice, namely guaranteeing the Defendant’s right of cross-examination.\\n\\n3) The separate opinion states that the ground of “inability to execute the warrant of arrest” concerning a witness falls under “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and that there is no reason to treat the issue in this case differently because it is essentially no different in that testimony in court is refused. However, if a witness obstinately refuses to appear in court but in fact appears in court by virtue of the coercive force of the warrant of arrest, he/she may be likely to testify without refusing to testify; therefore, the mere inability to execute the warrant of arrest against a witness cannot be evaluated the same as the case where the witness appears in court and refuses to testify in the presence of the Defendant.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the separate opinion states that under the majority opinion, if investigative agencies do their utmost in location tracing of a witness or execution of a warrant of arrest and the witness appears in court and then refuses to testify, admissibility of the statement to the investigative agency is denied, whereas if location tracing or execution of the warrant of arrest is handled passively and the witness is found to have unknown whereabouts or the warrant of arrest becomes unexecutable, admissibility is granted; thus, investigative agencies have no reason to actively perform location tracing or execute warrants of arrest. However, as the separate opinion itself notes, the Supreme Court, when determining grounds such as unknown whereabouts or inability to execute a warrant of arrest, views it as necessary for the prosecutor to prove that, despite making possible and sufficient efforts to secure the witness’s appearance in court, the witness’s appearance in court ultimately became impossible. Therefore, if the investigative agency did not do its utmost in location tracing or execution of the warrant of arrest, such grounds would not initially be recognized as unknown whereabouts or inability to execute a warrant of arrest, and admissibility of the statement to the investigative agency could not be recognized. In addition, even if there is concern that the investigative agency may appear to have done its utmost despite neglecting location tracing or execution of the warrant of arrest, expanding interpretation of the issue in this case to include “when a person is unable to make a statement due to any other equivalent cause” under Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act because of such concern would be to confuse the primary and the secondary.\\n\\nd. While the separate opinion acknowledges that the determination on the issue in this case is a matter of interpretation of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, it states that the majority opinion’s interpretation goes beyond the role and authority of a court exercising judicial power and is a change that causes serious problems in criminal trials and investigative procedures, and therefore such change should be made by legislation, not by judgment. It further states that if judgment is rendered according to the majority opinion, the public and society will bear entirely unexpected abrupt changes and problems.\\n\\nHowever, as the separate opinion itself acknowledges, the issue in this case is a matter of interpretation of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Since, as a matter of legislative technique, that provision generally and abstractly refers to “any other equivalent cause,” it is the judiciary’s own role and duty to clearly interpret its meaning.\\n\\nAs noted above, because judgments adopting differing views are in fact being rendered in lower courts, the Supreme Court cannot indefinitely evade determining the issue in this case. Rather, waiting only for legislation to be enacted would mean that the Supreme Court is failing to discharge its duty to provide uniform statutory interpretation.\\n\\nThere are many examples where legislation supplementing a legal principle announced by the Supreme Court has followed thereafter. If, because no legislation has first been enacted to supplement the legal principle that the Supreme Court is to announce, the Court does not announce that legal principle, then the Supreme Court would not be fulfilling its responsibility for final statutory interpretation. Since the issue in this case is one of interpreting Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the court must do its utmost to declare the correct legal principle. In this case, the view of the majority opinion by no means goes beyond the role and authority of a court exercising judicial power, nor does it intervene in legislation.\\n\\ne. The separate opinion assumes, while noting that the problem concerning this issue may be regulated differently according to each country’s legislative policy, that our criminal procedure system, like those of Germany and Japan, belongs to the civil-law tradition, and cites the fact that Germany and Japan allow the contents of records prepared by investigative agencies to be used as evidence when a witness without the right to refuse to testify refuses to testify. However, because our Criminal Procedure Act fundamentally adopts an adversarial procedural structure and has developed in a direction strengthening it further, it is no longer appropriate to limit the interpretation of our Criminal Procedure Act within the framework of the civil-law tradition.\\n\\nIn addition, the separate opinion points out, to the effect that whereas the Defendant’s right of cross-examination is guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution’s Sixth Amendment, in Korea it is a statutory right recognized by the Criminal Procedure Act, and therefore must be viewed fundamentally differently. However, because the Defendant’s right of cross-examination is clearly recognized as a statutory right under our Criminal Procedure Act, it is only natural that interpretive theory should develop in a direction that respects it.\\n\\nf. The separate opinion states that the majority opinion’s legal principle concerning the issue in this case is not necessary for resolving this case. However, the issue in this case was the main subject of dispute between the prosecutor and the Defendant in the lower appellate court, the lower appellate court also determined it directly, and the core of the prosecutor’s grounds for final appeal likewise concerns this issue. Nevertheless, for the Supreme Court not to express its view on this issue would not only mean that it makes no determination on the issue most principally disputed by the parties, but would also not be the proper attitude for the Supreme Court to take in the situation where academic opinion and lower-court determinations are divided, as noted above.\\n\\nIt is entirely understandable that the separate opinion is concerned about the possible negative aspects of the legal principles according to the majority opinion that may affect criminal procedure, but in light of the capabilities and level of our society, it is expected that the legal principles set forth in the majority opinion will greatly contribute to realizing the ideals of criminal justice.\\n\\nThe foregoing sets forth the supplementary opinion on the majority opinion."}

{"[2022DO8824]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. As to the grounds of appeal by Defendant 1\\n\\nA. Actual transaction and joint commission\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment, the lower court found Defendant 1 guilty of the facts charged. Examining the reasons for the lower-court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, the lower court’s determination contains no error that affected the judgment by violating the rule of logic and experience and thus exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the relevant legal principles.\\n\\nB. Sentencing\\n\\nAccording to Article 383 subparagraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, an appeal on the ground of unfair sentencing is permitted only in cases in which the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or confinement for not less than 10 years has been imposed. In this case, in which a lighter punishment than that was imposed on Defendant 1, the argument to the effect that the punishment is too severe and therefore unjust does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n2. As to the grounds of appeal by Defendant 2\\n\\nA. Actual transaction and joint commission\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment, the lower court affirmed the first-instance judgment, which found Defendant 2 guilty of the facts charged (except for the acquittal portion). Examining the reasons for the lower-court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, this lower-court determination contains no error that affected the judgment by violating the rule of logic and experience and thus exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nB. Evidentiary admissibility of the interrogation record of a person suspected of a tax offense\\n\\n1) Relevant legal principles\\n\\nJudicial police officers or special judicial police officers are vested, pursuant to the Constitution, the Criminal Procedure Act, and other statutes and regulations, with the authority to take broad measures restricting fundamental rights in order to protect the life, body, property, etc. of the people; therefore, even where the nature of the competent duties is similar to or equivalent to investigative duties, unless there is an express provision, the public officials in charge of such duties cannot be lightly construed as falling within the category of judicial police officers or special judicial police officers.\\n\\nArticle 197 of the former Criminal Procedure Act (before its amendment by Act No. 16924 on February 4, 2020) provides that the persons who shall perform the duties of special judicial police officers in the field of taxation and the scope of those duties shall be prescribed by statute. Pursuant thereto, the former Act on Persons Who Perform the Duties of Judicial Police Officers and the Scope of Their Duties (before its amendment by Act No. 17929 on March 16, 2021; hereinafter referred to as the “former Judicial Police Duties Act”) specifically enumerated special judicial police officers but expressly included only “customs officials engaged in the investigation of customs offenses pursuant to the Customs Act,” and did not include “tax officials in charge of tax offense investigations” (former Judicial Police Duties Act, Article 5 subparagraph 17). Moreover, under the current statutes, the legal nature of tax offense investigations basically falls within administrative procedure; therefore, although relevant statutes such as the Act on Procedure for the Punishment of Tax Offenses grant tax officials in charge of tax offense investigations the authority to conduct seizure and search and to interrogate suspects or persons of reference, and thus the contents and substance of such duties are similar to investigative procedures, and although in cases where a complaint is filed with the investigative authorities on that basis there is an aspect in which the matter is transferred to criminal procedure, unless there are special circumstances to the contrary, such matters cannot be regarded as part of criminal procedure.\\n\\nTherefore, a record prepared by a tax official in charge of a tax offense investigation, setting forth the contents of the interrogation of a suspect or person of reference who has become a defendant, cannot be viewed in the same manner as a record prepared by a prosecutor, judicial police officer, or other investigative authority; accordingly, whether it has evidentiary admissibility cannot be determined under Article 312 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Rather, as it constitutes a statement or a document recording a statement made by the defendant or by a person other than the defendant, evidentiary admissibility is recognized under Article 313 of the Criminal Procedure Act only when the authenticity of its formation is proved according to the statements of the maker or declarant at the preparatory hearing or trial date, and further only when the statement was made under circumstances particularly worthy of credit. Here, “circumstances particularly worthy of credit” means a case in which, at the time the record was prepared, there was little possibility of the intervention of falsehood in the contents of the statement or in the preparation of the record or document, and there are concrete and external circumstances ensuring the credibility and voluntariness of the contents of the statement; in determining whether there are “circumstances particularly worthy of credit,” the infringement or violation of the essential contents of procedural provisions concerning the preparation of an interrogation record, such as notice of the right to refuse to make a statement, the right to receive assistance from an attorney, and the right to inspect, raise objections, and state opinions, specifically provided in the Act on Procedure for the Punishment of Tax Offenses and the Presidential Decree, Enforcement Rules, and official directives based thereon (Investigation Affairs Processing Regulations), must also be considered.\\n\\n2) Determination\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment, the lower court affirmed the first-instance judgment, which found Defendant 2 guilty of the facts charged (except for the acquittal portion), premised on the recognition of evidentiary admissibility of “each interrogation record of the persons suspected of tax offenses concerning the Defendants” under Article 313 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nExamining the reasons for the lower-court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, there is no error in this lower-court determination that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning whether a tax official qualifies as a special judicial police officer.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and it is so adjudged, with the concurrence of the participating Justices, as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning appeals is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Even though defense counsel indicated an intention to question the Defendant at the appellate trial, the presiding judge’s measure of not allowing defense counsel to question the Defendant at all constitutes a violation of the laws governing litigation procedure and falls under a ground for final appeal.
B: In a case in which only the Defendant appealed, even if the appellate court found some of the criminal facts recognized by the court of first instance to be not guilty and nevertheless imposed on the Defendant the same sentence as the court of first instance, this does not violate the principle prohibiting disadvantageous modification.
C: Where the Defendant did not appeal the first-instance judgment in which guilt was affirmed, or appealed only on the ground of improper sentence, and the prosecutor also appealed only on the ground of improper sentence, and the appellate court accepted the prosecutor’s appeal, reversed the first-instance judgment, and imposed a higher sentence than that judgment, the Defendant cannot assert new grounds such as factual error or violation of laws and regulations as grounds for final appeal.
D: Where, with respect to an appellate judgment that acquitted the Defendant of some of the concurrent crimes and convicted the Defendant of some of the concurrent crimes, only the prosecutor filed a final appeal as to the acquittal portion, when reversing it in the final appeal, only the acquittal portion must be reversed.
E: Where, with respect to the first-instance judgment, the Defendant filed a leapfrog appeal and the prosecutor filed an appeal, and these were concurrent, the Defendant’s leapfrog appeal loses its effect; therefore, even if the Defendant’s leapfrog appeal satisfied all the lawful requirements as an appeal, such as compliance with the appeal period, and even if the Defendant had an intention to challenge the first-instance judgment in the appellate trial, effect as an appeal cannot be given to the Defendant’s leapfrog appeal.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2005DO7473]": "We review the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nWhere, in a case prosecuted as concurrent offenses, the court below renders a judgment of guilty as to some of the criminal facts and a judgment of not guilty as to the remainder, and the prosecutor appeals only the not-guilty portion while neither the defendant nor the prosecutor appeals the guilty portion, the guilty portion becomes final upon the expiration of the appeal period, so even if the appeal as to the not-guilty portion has merit, only the not-guilty portion must be reversed (see Supreme Court en banc decision rendered on January 21, 1992, 91DO1402). However, where, in a case prosecuted as concurrent offenses, the court below renders a judgment of guilty as to some of the criminal facts and a judgment of not guilty as to the remainder, and the defendant appeals the guilty portion while the prosecutor appeals the not-guilty portion, finality of the entire judgment of the court below is blocked and the case is transferred to the appellate instance; therefore, even if the defendant’s appeal as to the guilty portion lacks merit, if the prosecutor’s appeal as to the not-guilty portion has merit, because a single sentence must be imposed on the defendant, not only the not-guilty portion but also the guilty portion must be reversed together (see Supreme Court en banc decision rendered on June 20, 2002, 2002DO807).\\n\\nIn addition, the principle prohibiting disadvantageous modification means that, in a case appealed by the defendant or a case appealed for the defendant’s benefit, a heavier sentence than that imposed by the judgment of the court below may not be imposed in order to secure the defendant’s right of appeal; thus, it does not apply where, as a result of appeals by both the defendant and the prosecutor, the prosecutor’s appeal is accepted and the entire judgment of the court below is reversed so that the entire sentence for the defendant must be determined anew. Nor, merely because the case constitutes concurrent offenses, is the question whether a disadvantageous modification has occurred to be determined separately for each individual offense.\\n\\nIn this case, as to the offense of abortion upon request in the course of business, the Criminal Act provides that a sentence of imprisonment and a sentence of suspension of qualifications must be imposed cumulatively; the first instance court found the defendant guilty of murder, abortion upon request in the course of business, and violation of the Medical Service Act (solicitation of patients for profit), and sentenced the defendant to imprisonment for 3 years, suspension of execution for 4 years, and suspension of qualifications for 3 years; the court below prior to remand found the defendant guilty only of murder and abortion upon request in the course of business, and found the defendant not guilty of the violation of the Medical Service Act (solicitation of patients for profit), and sentenced the defendant to imprisonment for 2 years and 6 months, suspension of execution for 3 years, and suspension of qualifications for 1 year; the defendant appealed as to the guilty portion, and the prosecutor appealed as to the not-guilty portion; and when the Supreme Court determined that the defendant’s appeal lacked merit and accepted only the prosecutor’s appeal, reversing and remanding the not-guilty portion as having the purport of guilt, it is clear from the record that the court below after remand, while finding the defendant guilty of all charges, sentenced the defendant to imprisonment for 3 years, suspension of execution for 4 years, and suspension of qualifications for 2 years.\\n\\nIn response, the defendant again appeals and argues that, as to the offense of abortion upon request in the course of business, the Supreme Court dismissed the defendant’s appeal and thereby that part became final, so the court below after remand could not increase the term of suspension of qualifications; therefore, the sentence imposed by the court below after remand violates the principle prohibiting disadvantageous modification. However, as seen above, in this case both the defendant and the prosecutor appealed, and the prosecutor’s appeal was accepted so that the entire judgment of the court below prior to remand was reversed; accordingly, this is a case in which the court below after remand had to determine anew the entire sentence for the defendant, and it is not a case to which the principle prohibiting disadvantageous modification applies.\\n\\nAccordingly, the judgment of the court below sentencing the defendant to imprisonment for 3 years, suspension of execution for 4 years, and suspension of qualifications for 2 years cannot be said to contain, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, an error of law regarding the prohibition on disadvantageous modification.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court sitting in the case."}

{"[2017DO16593-1]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case and the Issues\\nA. The Defendants, as herbal pharmacists, conspired with the non-party and caused the non-party, who did not possess herbal pharmacist qualifications, to open a herbal medicine pharmacy and sell diet herbal medicine; and Defendant 1 was indicted for violations of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act on the facts that, at the herbal medicine pharmacy he had opened, he compounded herbal medicine without following the compounding method prescribed by the Minister of Health and Welfare and sold it to customers by courier delivery after receiving only telephone consultations, all without a prescription from a doctor of Korean medicine.\\nB. The court of first instance found the Defendants guilty and sentenced each to a fine of KRW 10,000,000. In response, Defendant 2 appealed solely on the ground of unfair sentencing, while Defendant 1 did not appeal, and the prosecutor appealed against the Defendants on the ground of unfair sentencing.\\nC. The court below accepted the prosecutor’s ground of appeal, reversed the judgment of the court of first instance, and sentenced Defendant 1 to imprisonment for 6 months, suspended for 1 year, and Defendant 2 to a fine of KRW 20,000,000. The Defendants filed a final appeal against the judgment of the court below, alleging that the court below erred in fact-finding in a manner contrary to logic and experience, failed to conduct the necessary review, or misunderstood the law; and Defendant 2 additionally alleged unfair sentencing as a ground of appeal.\\nD. The issue in this case is whether, where the Defendants did not appeal or appealed only on the ground of unfair sentencing, and the prosecutor appealed on the ground of unfair sentencing, and the appellate court accepted only the prosecutor’s ground of appeal and reversed the judgment of the court of first instance by rendering a judgment itself, thereby imposing a higher sentence, the Supreme Court’s established precedents, which declare the so-called “legal principle concerning limitation of grounds for final appeal” (hereinafter referred to as the “doctrine of limitation on grounds of appeal”), should be changed in light of whether new grounds, such as violation of laws and regulations, that were not made the subject of adjudication because the Defendants did not assert them as grounds of appeal in the appellate court, may be raised as grounds for final appeal.\\n2. Doctrine of Limitation on Grounds of Appeal\\nA. Relevant provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act\\nThe current Criminal Procedure Act, amended by Act No. 1500 on December 13, 1963, provides that if the prosecutor or the defendant is dissatisfied with the appellate judgment, he or she may file a final appeal to the Supreme Court (Article 338(1), Article 371), and it prescribes the grounds that the appellant may assert as grounds for final appeal against the appellate judgment as follows: “1. Where there is a violation of the Constitution, statutes, orders, or rules that affected the judgment; 2. Where there is abolition or alteration of punishment, or pardon, after the judgment; 3. Where there are grounds for a retrial; 4. Where, in a case in which death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment or penal detention for not less than 10 years was imposed, there is a mistaken finding of material fact that affected the judgment, or there is a manifest reason to recognize that the determination of punishment is extremely unfair” (Article 383).\\nB. Supreme Court precedents\\n1) Early on, the Supreme Court held that, unless the defendant had appealed against a first-instance judgment that recognized the same criminal facts as those recognized by the appellate court, the defendant could not assert as grounds for final appeal a claim of omission of review or a claim of factual mistake caused by violation of the rules of evidence against the first-instance judgment (see Supreme Court Decision 66DO16, rendered on February 22, 1966). Thereafter, in cases where only the prosecutor appealed against the first-instance judgment solely on the ground of unfair sentencing and the appellate court, finding the prosecutor’s appeal well-founded, reversed the first-instance judgment and imposed a higher sentence than before (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 91DO1796, rendered on December 24, 1991, and 2009DO579, rendered on May 28, 2009), and in cases where both the defendant and the prosecutor appealed against the first-instance judgment solely on the ground of unfair sentencing, but the appellate court dismissed the defendant’s appeal, accepted the prosecutor’s appeal, reversed the first-instance judgment, and imposed a higher sentence on the defendant (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DO12387, rendered on January 14, 2010), the Court held that the defendant could not raise new grounds such as factual mistake or violation of statutes as grounds for final appeal.\\nAlso, in a case where only the defendant appealed against the first-instance judgment solely on the ground of unfair sentencing, and the appellate court dismissed the defendant’s appeal because the claim lacked merit (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 87DO1561, rendered on December 8, 1987), as well as in cases where the appellate court accepted that claim, reversed the first-instance judgment, and imposed a lighter sentence than before (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 90DO2376, rendered on November 27, 1990), and in cases where the appellate court, citing another reason overlooked by the first instance, reversed the first-instance judgment ex officio while imposing the same sentence as the first instance (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2008DO10924, rendered on January 30, 2009), the Court held that the defendant could not raise new arguments on final appeal such as factual mistake caused by violation of the rules of evidence or misunderstanding of the law in the appellate judgment.\\nAccordingly, the Supreme Court has held that, because final appeal is a subsequent review of appellate judgments, matters that were not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court do not fall within the scope of review in final appeal, and therefore the defendant may not assert as lawful grounds for final appeal any reason other than those raised as grounds for appeal in the appellate court or those made the subject of adjudication ex officio by the appellate court (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DO9919, rendered on November 10, 2011).\\n2) The doctrine limiting grounds for final appeal derives from the structure of final appeal as a subsequent review, as discussed below, and has long been recognized as an indispensable element for maintaining the function of final appeal under the hierarchical review system. Since it was declared as a legal doctrine by the Supreme Court when the provisions on grounds for final appeal in the Criminal Procedure Act were established in their present form, it has been accepted over a long period, without particular criticism, not only in practice but also in academia, as one of the representative doctrines.\\nIn that process, although there were some modifications depending on the specific circumstances of each case—such as who among the prosecutor or the defendant appealed, what grounds were asserted in the appeal among factual mistake, violation of statutes, and unfair sentencing, whether the appeal was dismissed or accepted as a result of the appellate proceedings, and whether, after reversal by the appellate court, either ex officio or by acceptance of the appeal, a higher sentence was imposed—the original intent that reasons not asserted as grounds for appeal or not made the subject of adjudication ex officio by the appellate court cannot constitute lawful grounds for final appeal remained consistently maintained.\\n3. Grounds for the Doctrine Limiting Grounds for Appeal\\nA. The Structure of Final Appeal as a Subsequent Review\\n1) Under the Criminal Procedure Act, the appellant or defense counsel must submit a statement of grounds for final appeal to the appellate court within the prescribed period, and the statement must specify the reasons by citing facts contained in the trial record and the appellate court’s examination of evidence (Article 379(1) and (2)). As a general rule, the appellate court must adjudicate only on the grounds included in the statement of grounds for final appeal (main text of Article 384), and if there are grounds for final appeal, it must reverse the appellate judgment by a judgment (Article 391). Even when reversing, the principle is to remand or transfer the case so that the appellate court may re-examine and determine the case, and rendering judgment itself is permitted only exceptionally (Articles 393 through 397). In addition, because the final appellate court must determine the propriety of the appellate judgment on the basis of the litigation materials up to the appellate stage, as of the time of pronouncement of the appellate judgment (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 90DO2225, rendered on November 27, 1990), it cannot conduct new evidentiary examinations except in cases specifically provided by law, including ex officio investigation; moreover, facts or evidence that emerge after the appellate judgment cannot be used, even if attached to the statement of grounds for final appeal, etc. (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DO4894, rendered on October 14, 2010).\\nTaken together, the above provisions and doctrines show that final appeal is a subsequent review of appellate judgments, and thus only matters that were made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court may be examined for their propriety within the scope of the grounds for final appeal. As a result, reasons other than those asserted by the appellant as grounds for appeal or made the subject of adjudication ex officio by the appellate court cannot be used as grounds for final appeal, and including them again within the scope of review in final appeal would be contrary to the structure of final appeal as a subsequent review. In this respect, the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal is the consequence of the Criminal Procedure Act’s provision that final appeal is a subsequent review.\\n2) Meanwhile, final appeal is a subsequent review and, at the same time, in principle, a review limited to issues of law (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2002MO265, rendered on December 3, 2002). That is, findings of fact and determination of punishment in adjudication are made in the fact-finding courts, and the original function of final appeal is to ensure uniform interpretation and application of the law. However, if the fact that final appeal is a subsequent review were to allow, without restriction, appeals merely on the ground that the fact-finding judgment was erroneous, the number of final appeals would be excessive, overburdening the processing of cases in final appeal and risking failure to faithfully perform the functions of a subsequent review and a review limited to issues of law, as well as failure to fully provide relief to defendants through such review. In particular, in order for judgments in final appeal, as a review limited to issues of law, to serve as precedents that present standards for interpretation and application of the law to lower courts and establish standards of punishment, thereby carrying out the task of maintaining the legal order of our society, it is necessary to guarantee the function of final appeal so that proper determinations can be made therein. Furthermore, although there may be a demand under the three-tier system to allow defendants to complain of injustice as much as possible and to guarantee opportunities for appeal so that they can continue to contest the case until the end, it cannot be said that providing three opportunities for review on legal aspects to every case automatically guarantees the right to a trial “by judges established by the Constitution and laws” under Article 27(1) of the Constitution (see, e.g., Constitutional Court en banc Decision 90HEONBA25, rendered on June 26, 1992).\\nAccordingly, in order to appropriately distribute judicial resources according to the nature and function of the lower courts and the final appellate court, prevent unnecessary final appeals, and promote procedural economy, limiting the grounds for final appeal so as to confine the matters that may actually become the subject of review in final appeal is also reasonable at the constitutional level (see, e.g., Constitutional Court en banc Decision 2010HEONBA90, rendered on May 31, 2012). In this sense, the hierarchical review system is a matter of rationally distributing the limited adjudicative capacity of the courts with respect to protection of rights through the judiciary, and also a matter of how to reconcile the conflicting demands of properness and promptness of adjudication; in principle, it falls within the legislative discretion of the legislature (see, e.g., Constitutional Court en banc Decision 97HEONBA37, rendered on October 30, 1997).\\nThe doctrine limiting grounds for appeal restricts the scope of matters that may substantially become the subject of review in final appeal by treating as unlawful even if the defendant files a final appeal on the basis of new matters such as violation of statutes, which were not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court because the defendant did not appeal or appealed only on the ground of unfair sentencing. As discussed above, this is the result of a legislative decision that selected the system of subsequent review and a review limited to issues of law among several alternative forms of operation of the hierarchical review system. In particular, even though the defendant has been given an opportunity for factual and legal review by a judge in the first-instance criminal trial procedure for every case and has been given an opportunity to appeal the first-instance judgment, taking into account circumstances such as the fact that the defendant did not actively contest the matter in the appellate court, it also constitutes a statutory restriction adopted to promote promptness of trial and procedural economy and to realize efficient operation of the hierarchical review system within the scope compatible with proper adjudication, relief of the defendant, and guarantee of the right of defense in each individual case; its reasonableness is thus also recognized.\\nB. Uniform Interpretation and Application of Laws and Ex Officio Adjudication\\n1) Under the Criminal Procedure Act, the appellate court may adjudicate ex officio on causes that affected the first-instance judgment even if they are not included in the statement of grounds for appeal (Article 364(2)), and the final appellate court may adjudicate ex officio in cases under Article 383, subparagraphs 1 through 3, of the Criminal Procedure Act even if they are not included in the statement of grounds for final appeal (proviso of Article 384). In particular, the final appellate court’s ex officio adjudication may be exercised even where the defendant did not file a final appeal and only the prosecutor filed a final appeal on other grounds, against an appellate judgment that erroneously convicted the defendant through misinterpretation or misapplication of the law, and it is clear that the prosecutor’s final appeal was not filed for the defendant’s benefit (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2001DO6730, rendered on March 15, 2002).\\nThe ex officio adjudicatory power of the final appellate court and the appellate court is intended to correct, to the maximum extent, errors such as violations of statutes in lower court judgments. Thus, through the appellate court’s ex officio adjudicatory power, even if the defendant did not assert grounds of appeal and did not properly contest the first-instance judgment, if there is an error that affected the judgment due to factual mistake or violation of statutes, the appellate court may correct it; and the final appellate court, if there remains illegality in the appellate judgment itself—for example, where the appellate court overlooks the illegality of the first-instance judgment and renders a judgment dismissing the appeal, or where there is an illegality in the application of law inherent in an appellate judgment reversing the first-instance judgment and rendering judgment itself—may ultimately correct it by broadly utilizing ex officio adjudication.\\n2) As above, regarding errors that are deemed to correspond to matters subject to ex officio adjudication by the exercise of ex officio adjudicatory power established across the two tiers of appellate review under the Criminal Procedure Act, there is a mechanism by which even matters that did not become part of the appellate court’s subject of adjudication because the defendant did not appeal or did not assert them as grounds for appeal can be corrected to the extent possible in a direction favorable to the defendant. Through this, the functions of final appeal as a subsequent review and a review limited to issues of law, as well as the defendant’s relief, are further strengthened.\\nC. Relationship with Guarantee of the Defendant’s Procedural Rights\\n1) The Criminal Procedure Act adopts the adversarial principle, the principle of trial-centeredness, and the principle of immediacy and evidentiary adjudication, under which substantive review of a defendant’s case is to be conducted in an open courtroom by the prosecution and the defendant through both parties’ offensive and defensive activities, and the finding of the charged facts must be based only on evidence directly examined before the judge (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009DO7436, rendered on October 22, 2009). The principle of substantive immediacy, one element of trial-centeredness, is the principle that only evidence directly examined before the judge may be used as the basis for adjudication, that the original evidence closest to the fact to be proven must be used as the basis for adjudication, and that, in principle, use of substitutes for original evidence should not be permitted. Through direct examination of original evidence in the courtroom, the judge can form a fresh and accurate conviction regarding the case, and by giving the defendant an opportunity to directly state opinions on the original evidence, the truth can be discovered and a fair trial realized (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DO4994, rendered on November 24, 2006).\\nFrom this perspective, the procedure in the court of first instance, where all arguments and evidentiary examinations by the parties are substantially conducted before the judge, is the principal procedure implementing the principle of substantive immediacy and trial-centeredness under the Criminal Procedure Act; however, because the provisions concerning first-instance trial procedure apply mutatis mutandis to appellate proceedings unless otherwise provided (Article 370), the appellate court may also, within a limited scope, be viewed as proceeding under such principles.\\nBy contrast, under the Criminal Procedure Act, final appeal is allowed to be decided without oral argument based on the petition of final appeal, the statement of grounds, and other litigation records (Article 390(1)), and even if oral proceedings are conducted, the defendant need not be summoned (Article 389-2), showing a marked procedural difference.\\nViewing the differences in the review procedures between the first instance and the appellate/final appellate stages in light of the spirit of trial-centeredness and substantive immediacy discussed above, if the defendant, without appealing a reason by which the court of first instance examined facts before the judge and rendered judgment and applied the law, or if the defendant appealed only on the ground of unfair sentencing, thereby showing an attitude of accepting the determination regarding whether the offense was established, then it must be deemed impermissible for the defendant to file a final appeal alleging that the relevant determination was erroneous.\\n2) Meanwhile, sentencing is a discretionary determination made within a reasonable and proper scope by comprehensively considering, on the basis of the statutory punishment, the matters constituting sentencing conditions set forth in Article 51 of the Criminal Act; in our criminal procedure, which adopts trial-centeredness and immediacy, there exists an original sphere of the first instance even with respect to sentencing determinations, and the appellate court, as a continuation of proceedings with a subsequent-review character added to the first instance, should also be regarded as having its own sentencing discretion distinct from that of the first instance (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2015DO3260, rendered on July 23, 2015).\\nIn light of the fact that sentencing is, in principle, a discretionary determination, when the appellate court accepts the prosecutor’s appeal regarding unfair sentencing, reverses the first-instance judgment, and imposes a higher sentence, it should be viewed as an inevitable result arising from repeated review by different courts, each exercising its own authority over the same subject of adjudication, namely sentencing factors, within the hierarchical review system. Therefore, it is difficult to view the fact that the sentencing determination between the first instance and the appellate court changed in a manner unfavorable to the defendant as a changed circumstance that could affect the validity of the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal based on the structure of subsequent review, etc.\\n4. Determination in This Case\\nA. Regarding the defendants’ grounds of appeal alleging violation of the rules of evidence, omission of review, and misunderstanding of the law\\nIn light of the doctrine discussed above and the circumstances leading to the defendants’ final appeal, the defendants’ above grounds of appeal are matters that were not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court and are newly asserted in the final appellate court; therefore, they are not lawful grounds for final appeal.\\nB. Regarding the remaining grounds of appeal by Defendant 2\\nAccording to Article 383, subparagraph 4, of the Criminal Procedure Act, an appeal on the ground of unfair sentencing is permitted only in cases in which death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment or penal detention for not less than 10 years was imposed; therefore, in this case, in which a fine was imposed on the defendant, arguments that the determination of punishment is unfair or that the appellate judgment contains factual mistake and illegality in omission of review concerning the conditions of sentencing do not constitute lawful grounds for final appeal.\\n5. Conclusion\\nTherefore, we dismiss all final appeals and render judgment as stated in the text of the decision. In this judgment, the opinions of the judges in attendance were unanimous except for the separate opinions of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Lee Ki-taek, Kim Jae-hyung, and Kim Seon-su, and the separate opinion of Justice Cho Hee-dae; there is also a supplementary opinion by Justice Min Yoo-sook to the majority opinion, and a supplementary opinion by Justice Lee Ki-taek to the separate opinions of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Lee Ki-taek, Kim Jae-hyung, and Kim Seon-su.\\n6. Separate Opinion of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Lee Ki-taek, Kim Jae-hyung, and Kim Seon-su\\nA. Specification of the Issue in this Case Concerning the Doctrine Limiting Grounds for Appeal\\n1) The doctrine limiting grounds for appeal in this case is intended to restrict the scope of lawful grounds for appeal at the first stage of examining grounds for appeal by holding that, with respect to matters that were not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court because the defendant did not assert them as grounds for appeal in the appellate court, even if they correspond to grounds for final appeal set forth in each item of Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act, they cannot be used as grounds for final appeal.\\nThe majority opinion, based on abstract and general doctrines such as the structure of final appeal as a subsequent review, the ex officio adjudicatory powers of the appellate court and the final appellate court, and the ideals of trial-centeredness and substantive immediacy, argues that the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal should apply uniformly to all cases, without considering at all the specific circumstances of concrete cases, such as who was the appellant, what the content of the specific grounds of appeal was, what the outcome of the appellate proceedings was, and what effect it had on the defendant.\\nHowever, in a case such as Defendant 1’s, where only the prosecutor appealed the first-instance judgment on the ground of unfair sentencing and the defendant did not appeal, and the appellate court accepted the prosecutor’s appeal and imposed a harsher sentence than the first instance; or in a case such as Defendant 2’s, where both the defendant and the prosecutor appealed the first-instance judgment only on the ground of unfair sentencing, but the appellate court dismissed the defendant’s appeal, accepted only the prosecutor’s appeal, reversed the first-instance judgment, and imposed a harsher sentence (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “cases of this case”), the majority’s position that the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal should also apply to such cases contains, as discussed below, numerous problems not only doctrinally but also in relation to the necessity of relief for defendants and the maintenance of the function of final appeal.\\n2) Therefore, even if one assumes that the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal is deeply related to the hierarchical review system, the structure and role of each tier, etc., and has a long historical origin, so that its validity is in principle recognized and the need to maintain it remains, it should be reconsidered whether it is proper to extend its application even to the situations of this case. Delineating the boundary line as to how far the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal should be applied is the issue in this case. However, it should also be pointed out that even if it is deemed that the limitation on grounds for appeal under that doctrine does not apply in certain situations, the limitation on grounds for appeal under Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act still naturally applies.\\nB. The Majority Opinion’s Grounds and Their Problems\\n1) The principal points presented by the majority opinion as grounds for the view that the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal should also apply to the situations of this case may be summarized as follows: ① Final appeal is a subsequent review of appellate judgments and should examine only the propriety of matters that were made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court, within the scope of the grounds for final appeal. ② If final appeals were permitted, the burden of handling cases would become excessive, creating a risk that the court would not faithfully perform its original function as a final appellate court and provide relief for defendants. ③ Based on trial-centeredness and substantive immediacy, there is an opportunity for sufficient review by judges at the fact-finding stage, and an opportunity to appeal the first-instance judgment is provided. ④ Through the exercise of ex officio adjudicatory power, even matters that were not part of the appellate court’s subject of adjudication can be corrected as much as possible to remedy erroneous lower court determinations and relieve the defendant.\\n2) The fact that final appeal is a subsequent review means only that the appellate judgment becomes the subject of review in final appeal, and that grounds for final appeal are therefore limited to matters concerning that judgment. From that alone, it cannot be said that only matters that the defendant asserted as grounds for appeal in the appellate court, or that the appellate court expressly adjudicated by making them the subject of adjudication ex officio, can constitute grounds for final appeal.\\nIt is recognized that there is a need to exclude some cases from the scope of review in final appeal in order to maintain the function of final appeal, but limiting final appeals uniformly without considering the concrete circumstances of each case up to the point of final appeal, and thereby excluding even cases with a strong need for relief, excessively restricts the defendant’s right to final appeal.\\nSecuring a proper trial result through faithful and careful review in the fact-finding courts, by implementing trial-centeredness, etc., is a prerequisite that must be satisfied before final appeals can be strictly limited through the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal. It is inappropriate to use such general doctrines as grounds to justify limiting grounds for appeal without any argument as to whether such conditions have been met. In particular, even if there are devices to maintain properness of the trial at the first instance and ample opportunities to correct errors in the judgment through appellate proceedings, if such errors remain in the trial result even after the appellate stage, the defendant must be substantially guaranteed an opportunity for final appeal so that such errors can be corrected to the maximum extent in the final appellate proceedings. From this perspective, ex officio adjudicatory power also has limited value as a ground for supporting the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal, because whether to exercise it is determined by discretion.\\n3) Ultimately, there is no shortage of deficiencies in the grounds presented by the majority opinion for the proposition that the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal should be uniformly applied to all cases, including this case, without considering concrete circumstances.\\nOn that premise, we examine the legal and policy grounds for deeming it proper to exclude the cases of this case from the scope of application of the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal.\\nC. Occurrence of a Material Change in Circumstances\\n1) Even if rendered by a lower court, a final judgment in a criminal case is presumed for the time being to be proper until it is overturned through a formal appeal procedure by a higher court and loses its effect. Accordingly, unless special circumstances exist, the defendant also proceeds with the litigation expecting that the first-instance judgment’s conclusion on guilt or innocence and its reasons will be maintained by the higher court. Meanwhile, under the Criminal Procedure Act, if the defendant is dissatisfied with a first-instance judgment finding guilt, he or she may freely appeal (Article 338(1), Article 357). However, the outcome in the appellate court may change depending on various procedural factors, such as differences in legal views among judges, the difficulty of the case or of determining the grounds of appeal, and the degree of advocacy or pleading ability of the parties. Accordingly, it is realistically difficult for a defendant, who is not a lawyer, to predict the result in advance when deciding whether to appeal.\\nIn addition to these circumstances, considering the fact that the defendant bears various costs in appealing and responding to proceedings, and that such costs increase especially as the reasons for challenge become more complex and numerous, and considering that the conclusion on sentencing or detention in the first-instance judgment is an important factor in deciding whether to appeal, it is reasonable to view that if the defendant accepts the conclusion of a first-instance judgment finding guilt and, unless special circumstances exist, believes that the conclusion will be maintained on higher appeal, then even if there are errors in detailed determinations such as factual mistake, violation of statutes, or unfair sentencing, the defendant would not each time file an appeal asserting such reasons.\\n2) If the defendant did not appeal a first-instance judgment finding guilt, or appealed passively only on the ground of unfair sentencing, and the prosecutor appealed only on the ground of unfair sentencing, but the appellate court accepted the prosecutor’s appeal, reversed the first-instance judgment, and imposed a higher sentence, then this may be viewed as a material change in the circumstances on which the defendant relied when deciding whether to appeal. Such a change occurred in the course of the appellate court, which is the higher court, correcting the first-instance court’s erroneous determination concerning sentencing, and thus it was not only difficult to foresee when the defendant decided whether to appeal, but the defendant cannot be said to bear responsibility for the cause of its occurrence.\\nTaking these circumstances together, it is proper to allow a defendant, who had suspended asserting grounds such as factual mistake or violation of statutes at the time of appeal by accepting the conclusion of the first-instance judgment, to file a final appeal on those grounds after the sentence is increased in the appellate court. Even if the grounds asserted by the defendant as grounds for final appeal are new matters that were not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court, it cannot be said that the defendant’s conduct in filing a final appeal on those grounds is improper as inconsistent with the conduct at the time of appeal. It is also difficult to characterize this as a frivolous final appeal. Rather, even in such cases, limiting grounds for final appeal by reference to the time when the decision whether to appeal was made excessively restricts the defendant’s right to final appeal and is unjust.\\n3) The cases of this case are also instances where there was a material change in circumstances compared with the time when the defendant decided whether to appeal. Therefore, unlike the cases cited above, there is no reason to treat them differently, and it should be permitted to assert as grounds for final appeal new reasons that were not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court. The majority opinion, which insists on applying the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal even to the cases of this case, overlooks the fact that, in the course of the appellate proceedings, there was a material change in the circumstances that formed the basis for deciding whether to appeal, for reasons not attributable to the defendant.\\nD. Adverse Change in the Dispositive Portion of the Judgment\\n1) If a lower court’s judgment is not adverse to the defendant, the defendant cannot have the right to appeal against it (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DO4866, rendered on September 15, 2005). Whether a first-instance judgment is adverse to the defendant who has standing to appeal must be determined based on the dispositive portion of the judgment; therefore, even if the defendant is dissatisfied with the reasons for the judgment, there is no benefit in appealing, and the defendant cannot file a challenge merely seeking correction of those reasons (see, e.g., Constitutional Court Decision 92MO21, rendered on March 4, 1993, and Supreme Court Decision 93DO1091, rendered on July 29, 1994). Even a defendant who has been found guilty cannot, under the current Criminal Procedure Act, appeal merely to point out factual mistakes or violations of statutes in the reasons while being satisfied with the content of the dispositive portion, such as the sentence imposed in the first-instance judgment, and seek correction thereof.\\nThe matter in which a defendant is most concerned in a criminal trial is the dispositive portion of the judgment, namely the final conclusion regarding whether the offense is established and the severity of the sentence. The defendant’s defensive efforts in the litigation focus on this, and even when deciding whether to appeal a judgment finding guilt, the propriety of the sentence appearing in the dispositive portion of the judgment and its accompanying effects, such as detention, are key considerations. By contrast, the propriety of the procedural legality of the litigation, or of detailed determinations on fact-finding or application of law in the reasons for judgment, is merely a secondary consideration as the basis supporting the conclusion shown in the dispositive portion.\\nIn this respect, with regard to the appeal system, the dispositive portion of a judgment is qualitatively different from the reasons for the judgment in that it is the core that generally determines the defendant’s possibility and intent to appeal, as well as the specific content and scope of the grounds for appeal. Even when determining whether an appeal is lawful and the permissible scope of the grounds for appeal, the two must be treated differently, and the dispositive portion of the judgment must primarily serve as the standard. Therefore, when the dispositive portion of the judgment has been changed to the defendant’s detriment compared with the previous tier, and the defendant does not accept it and files an appeal, the permissible scope of the grounds for appeal that support it should also be recognized as broadly as possible, insofar as they are capable of contesting the propriety of the dispositive portion. This accords with the intent of recognizing the defendant’s right to appeal as a procedural means of defense against unfavorable judicial outcomes.\\n2) The cases of this case are ones in which the defendant accepted the dispositive portion of the first-instance judgment, had no active intent to appeal so long as that conclusion was maintained, and even if the defendant had been dissatisfied with factual findings or application of law in the reasons for judgment, appealing was not permitted; then, when the appellate judgment changed the dispositive portion unfavorably, a new benefit or necessity to appeal arose. Accordingly, even in filing a final appeal, if there are new reasons such as violations of statutes in the reasons for judgment, those should be allowed to be asserted so that the error in the appellate judgment can be fully contested.\\nApplying the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal even to the cases of this case would place excessive emphasis on the reasons for judgment, as opposed to the dispositive portion of the appellate judgment, as the criterion for determining whether to appeal, and would tilt too far toward the reasons for judgment as the specific content of the grounds for final appeal, thereby reversing the order of importance, given the legal and qualitative difference that exists between the dispositive portion and the reasons for judgment as factors determining the possibility of exercising the right to appeal and the intent to do so.\\n3) The majority opinion states that, because the Criminal Procedure Act recognizes the ex officio adjudicatory power of the final appellate court (Article 384) and the appellate court (Article 364(2)), even if the defendant’s opportunity for final appeal is restricted by the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal, the defendant can still be relieved from erroneous lower court judgments and a substantively proper outcome can be secured by the court’s ex officio correcting such errors. However, as discussed above, because ex officio adjudication is activated at the discretion of the final appellate court, it cannot be viewed as a sufficient means for the defendant’s relief when compared with relief through adjudication of grounds for final appeal, which is a mandatory subject of adjudication.\\nE. Reverse and Decide the Case Itself After Reversal, and the Subject of Adjudication in the Appellate Court\\n1) Under the Criminal Procedure Act, when the appellate court recognizes that an appeal against the first-instance judgment is well-founded or reverses the judgment by ex officio determination, it is in principle to render judgment anew on the defendant’s case itself (proviso of Article 361-4(1), Article 364(2), Article 364(6)). In such a case, if the defendant’s case is found guilty, the reasons for the judgment must again set out, in addition to the determination of the grounds for appeal that caused the reversal, the facts constituting the crime, summary of evidence, application of law, and determination of punishment as the basis for the guilty finding (Article 323(1) and (2), Articles 369, 370).\\nIn light of the above provisions, even the appellate court, which basically determines the propriety of the first-instance judgment centered on the grounds for appeal, may, when it determines that the first-instance judgment is erroneous and reverses it while rendering judgment itself, be regarded as having become, as in the first instance, a court of fact and law together. In the cases of this case as well, the appellate court newly determined not only the sentencing matter that caused the reversal but also the underlying factual findings and application of law, and these fall within the appellate court’s own determinations. Even if the contents of the factual findings and application of law are the same as, or cite, those of the first-instance judgment, there is no reason to view them differently. At that point, a ground for final appeal pointing out errors in factual findings or application of law set forth in the reasons of the appellate judgment concerns matters that became the subject of adjudication in the appellate court, not the assertion of new matters unrelated thereto.\\n2) A subsequent review means a post hoc review of the propriety of the original judgment itself, based on the grounds for appeal submitted, with the original judgment itself as the subject of adjudication. The essential feature distinguishing a subsequent review from other adjudicatory structures, such as a second-instance review or a full rehearing, lies in whether the subject of adjudication is the original judgment itself or the defendant’s case itself, and whether the method of adjudication is to review only on the basis of the existing litigation materials, using the time of the original judgment as the standard. Therefore, the mere fact that final appeal is a subsequent review cannot be the basis for concluding, as the majority opinion argues, that the matters a defendant may use as grounds for final appeal are limited to those that were argued as grounds of appeal in the appellate court or made the subject of adjudication by ex officio activation. As discussed above, matters concerning factual findings and application of law included in the appellate judgment’s determinations may also belong to matters that became the subject of adjudication in the appellate court, and such an interpretation does not contradict the structure of final appeal as a subsequent review.\\n3) If final appeal is a subsequent review, and the subject of adjudication is not understood as the entirety of the appellate judgment, unfair results will arise even in other similar cases.\\nFor example, if in the first instance the defendant is entirely acquitted on the premise of a certain interpretation of law, then, as discussed above, the defendant has no benefit in appealing and appeal itself is not permitted. If only the prosecutor appeals on the ground concerning that interpretation of law, and the appellate court accepts that ground, reverses the acquittal, and imposes punishment, then if the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal is consistently enforced, the non-appealing defendant may not file a final appeal on the grounds of factual mistake or other violations of statutes in the appellate judgment. However, considering that the defendant was legally not permitted even to appeal and therefore had no opportunity to argue factual mistake or other violations of statutes as grounds of appeal regarding the charged conduct, and that the determination on whether the offense was established was itself changed unfavorably to the defendant in the appellate court, it would be difficult for anyone to readily accept such a conclusion. This in the end proves that the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal is difficult to generalize and apply even to cases involving special circumstances such as those in this case.\\nF. Balance with Cases in which the Sentence in the Appellate Court Is Compared with the Sentence Imposed in the First Instance\\n1) Although the composition and operation of an appeal system based on hierarchical review are matters of legislative policy, the constitutional principles of the rule of law, the due process clause of Article 12(1) of the Constitution, and the right to demand a fair trial under Article 27(1) of the Constitution are intended to guarantee the defendant’s right of defense in criminal trials; therefore, this intent must also be maintained in appellate proceedings, and so long as the current structure of criminal appellate review is basically regarded as a full rehearing, the content of the defendant’s right of defense in the appellate court should, in essential respects, be regarded as the same as in the first instance (see, e.g., Constitutional Court en banc Decision 92HEONMA44, rendered on November 30, 1995).\\nIn particular, in a case like this one, where the appellate court’s reversal and own disposition effectively extinguish the effect of the first-instance judgment and the appellate court’s review continues from the state immediately before the first-instance judgment was pronounced, the full-rehearing character is even clearer in that the appellate court rendered a new judgment on the substance of the defendant’s case by reference to the time of pronouncement of the appellate judgment.\\nTherefore, just as when the defendant appeals a first-instance judgment that was unfavorable to him or her, the defendant should also be guaranteed, against an appellate judgment that was changed unfavorably to him or her, the opportunity to actively defend himself or herself by freely contesting in the next tier, i.e., final appeal, grounds such as violations of statutes that affected the appellate judgment, regardless of whether he or she actively contested them during the immediately preceding appellate proceedings.\\n2) Even in the cases of this case, if the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal is applied so that the scope of review in final appeal of the appellate judgment differs depending on whether the defendant appealed the first-instance judgment, there remains a possibility of unreasonable situations that are difficult to accept in common sense.\\nFor example, suppose that the defendant was first sentenced to a severe punishment of suspended execution of imprisonment in the first instance, and then actively appealed while asserting all grounds of factual mistake, violation of statutes, and unfair sentencing that affected the first-instance judgment, but the appeal was dismissed. In that case, the defendant would have had the opportunity to exercise appellate rights twice in total by again filing a final appeal on grounds such as violations of statutes that affected the appellate judgment. By contrast, if, as in this case, the defendant was sentenced in the first instance to a lighter punishment such as a fine, accepted it, did not appeal the first-instance judgment, or passively appealed only on the ground of unfair sentencing, and then in the appellate court was sentenced to a severe punishment such as suspended execution of imprisonment because the prosecutor’s appeal on unfair sentencing was accepted, application of the current doctrine limiting grounds for appeal would prevent the defendant from even asserting grounds such as violations of statutes that affected the appellate judgment as grounds for final appeal, thereby effectively depriving the defendant of any opportunity to exercise appellate rights at all. That is, if the court rendered an accurate sentencing judgment in the first-instance stage corresponding to the substance of the defendant’s case, the defendant would have had an opportunity to seek review twice under the former scenario; but if, despite the same ultimate conclusion on sentencing, such sentencing was imposed at the appellate stage because of an error in the first-instance sentencing determination, an unreasonable situation arises in which the defendant has no opportunity whatsoever to seek review to correct it.\\nThis is a result far removed from the expectation or common understanding of the average person, who would expect at least one opportunity to challenge an unfavorable judicial outcome in a higher court and defend oneself. It not only infringes the defendant’s right of defense in the litigation procedure, but, especially in view of the fact that such a situation arises from an erroneous lower court determination, it cannot be accepted even from the standpoint of justice and equity.\\n3) The majority opinion states that, since the first instance and the appellate stage conduct faithful and careful review under the ideals of trial-centeredness and substantive immediacy, limiting the scope of grounds for final appeal in cases such as this does not infringe the right to appeal. Securing a proper trial result through faithful and careful review in the lower courts is a prerequisite that must necessarily be satisfied in order to introduce the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal. However, our litigation reality still does not satisfy such conditions to a satisfactory degree. The fact that too many cases are brought to the final appellate court because defendants are dissatisfied with the results of lower court judgments and seek review is itself evidence of this point. Therefore, in cases such as this one, where the application of the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal can be viewed as unjust, there remains a strong need to moderate it.\\nG. Unnecessary Appeals and Increased Review Burdens\\nIf the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal is maintained as is, a defendant who accepts a first-instance judgment finding guilt nevertheless bears the burden of filing an appeal strategically when the prosecutor appeals on the ground of unfair sentencing, in order to avoid being deprived of the opportunity to contest the matter in final appeal should a material change in circumstances arise during the appellate proceedings. In particular, in such a case, it is not enough simply to file a notice of appeal and submit a statement of grounds for appeal at an appropriate level; rather, because the defendant must assume a situation in which the propriety of the appellate judgment’s contents will be actively contested in final appeal, the defendant must carefully examine the reasons for the first-instance judgment and extract all errors in fact-finding, violations of statutes, and errors in sentencing determinations that affected it, then formulate those as grounds for appeal. The burden is thus significant.\\nThe appellate court also, in reality, will have to proceed as if there were a dispute in a case in which the procedure was initiated only by the prosecutor’s appeal on unfair sentencing, while the defendant had accepted the first-instance judgment and had no active request or need for relief, and in order ultimately to dismiss both parties’ appeals, it must make determinations rejecting each of the grounds of appeal submitted by the defendant.\\nTherefore, if the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal is strictly enforced in the cases of this case, it will induce strategic behavior by defendants, and the procedure will operate without regard to the original purpose or objective of the hierarchical review system and appeal system, which is to provide relief for rights and correction of erroneous judgments; moreover, it will cause side effects in the form of unnecessary costs and burdens related to litigation procedures for both the defendant and the appellate court. In the end, this doctrine cannot be an appropriate means to prevent frivolous appeals.\\nH. Conclusion\\n1) In short, where a defendant convicted at first instance did not appeal or appealed only on the ground of unfair sentencing, and the appellate court accepts the prosecutor’s appeal on unfair sentencing, reverses the first-instance judgment, and renders its own judgment while imposing a higher sentence, even if the reason was not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court, it should be recognized as a lawful ground for final appeal. Applying the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal even to the cases of this case overlooks special circumstances such as the material change in circumstances that was difficult to foresee when the defendant decided whether to appeal, the fact that under the Criminal Procedure Act the possibility and intent of appeal are determined by the dispositive portion of the judgment, yet the dispositive portion was changed unfavorably in the appellate court, the fact that the contents of the judgment rendered by reversal and own disposition in the appellate court are the appellate court’s own determinations, the need to prevent an imbalance in the guarantee of appellate rights depending on the outcomes in the first instance and appellate courts, and the fact that it induces unnecessary appeals and is unsuitable as a means to reduce review burdens. Accordingly, despite the existence of a practical basis for the defendant to file a final appeal and exercise the right of defense, depriving the defendant of that opportunity in substance results in unexpected detriment to the defendant. This also contravenes the spirit of the Constitution, which provides the right to trial as a fundamental right and guarantees due process.\\nThe doctrine limiting grounds for appeal is based on the hierarchical review system and the structure and role of each tier, as well as the defendant’s procedural status corresponding thereto, and the validity of that doctrine itself is recognized. However, unlike Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act, it is recognized through systematic interpretation of the relevant provisions without any express provision, and as a result, the defendant’s opportunity to exercise the right of final appeal prescribed by the Criminal Procedure Act is greatly restricted.
