In light of these points, where, as in this case, applying that doctrine to a concrete case causes unreasonable results that do not accord with its original purpose, or where special circumstances exist such as contradiction to the essence of guaranteeing appellate rights according to the tiers, and thus it is not appropriate to apply it as is, excluding its application is the balanced interpretation.\\nAccordingly, in this case as well, precedents holding that a defendant may not file a final appeal on matters not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court, including Supreme Court Decisions 91DO1796, rendered on December 24, 1991, 2001DO191, rendered on March 13, 2001, 2006DO2860, rendered on September 8, 2006, and 2009DO579, rendered on May 28, 2009, as well as all judgments to the same effect, should be changed to the extent inconsistent with the view of this judgment.\\n2) With respect to a first-instance guilty judgment, the defendant who does not appeal or appeals only on the ground of unfair sentencing is saying, “I will accept the first-instance judgment if the sentence is not increased.” By no means is the defendant dividing the first-instance judgment into the part concerning guilt and the part concerning sentencing and saying that he or she finally accepts the former. Nor is there any way to accept the latter while disputing only the former.\\n3) In this case, in light of the doctrine discussed above and the circumstances leading to the defendants’ final appeal, among the grounds asserted as grounds for appeal by Defendant 1, grounds concerning violations of law such as Article 20(1) of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act or the requirements for joint principal liability concerning status offenses were newly raised in final appeal, but since they fall under Article 383, subparagraph 1, of the Criminal Procedure Act, they are lawful grounds for final appeal. However, the defendants’ grounds for appeal alleging that the appellate court’s factual findings concerning whether they participated in the act of opening the pharmacy by an unqualified person were erroneous due to violation of the rules of evidence and omission of review do not fall under the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal for the reasons above, but they are in substance nothing more than complaints of errors in the fact-finding authority of the appellate court and therefore do not correspond to any of the grounds for final appeal set forth in Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and thus cannot be lawful grounds for final appeal.\\n4) Meanwhile, even a pharmacist who conspires to assist in the act of opening a pharmacy by a person who is not a pharmacist or herbal pharmacist falls under joint principal liability for violation of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2003DO2971, rendered on July 11, 2003).\\nIn light of the above doctrine and the evidence adopted by the appellate court, the appellate court’s determination that Defendant 1’s participation, in conspiracy with the non-party, in the act of opening a pharmacy by an unqualified person constituted a violation of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act and was guilty is proper. There is no error such as misunderstanding the application of law concerning Article 20(1) of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act or the requirements for joint principal liability concerning status offenses.\\n5) Defendant 2’s remaining grounds of appeal asserting that the sentencing is unfair do not constitute lawful grounds for final appeal under Article 383, subparagraph 4, of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\nAlthough we share the majority opinion’s conclusion that all final appeals should be dismissed, we set forth the above as a separate opinion because our reasons differ.\\n7. Separate Opinion of Justice Cho Hee-dae\\nA. The majority opinion holds that, based on the structure of final appeal as a subsequent review, etc., even if the ground asserted by the appellant as a ground for final appeal concerns a violation of statutes, etc. prescribed in Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act, if it is a matter not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court, it is not a lawful ground for final appeal. However, it is difficult to agree with this majority opinion.\\nB. The above-mentioned “doctrine limiting grounds for appeal” of the majority opinion has no basis in the Criminal Procedure Act or any other related statutes. Even from the perspective of the structure of final appeal as a review limited to issues of law and the policy demand for limiting grounds for appeal, there is no need to recognize this separate doctrine limiting grounds for appeal beyond the provisions of Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act. I will examine this specifically below.\\n1) Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act, under the title “Grounds for Final Appeal,” provides that “where the following grounds exist, they may be used as grounds for final appeal against the judgment below,” and enumerates: where there is a violation of the Constitution, statutes, orders, or rules that affected the judgment (subparagraph 1), where there is abolition or alteration of punishment, or pardon, after the judgment (subparagraph 2), where there are grounds for a retrial (subparagraph 3), and where, in a case in which death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment or penal detention for not less than 10 years was imposed, there is a mistaken finding of material fact that affected the judgment, or there is a manifest reason to recognize that the determination of punishment is extremely unfair (subparagraph 4).\\nAs seen above, Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act requires only two things as conditions for a person entitled to final appeal to lawfully file a final appeal: that it concerns the judgment below, and that it falls under one of the grounds set forth in subparagraphs 1 through 4. Beyond those two requirements, it cannot be said, as the majority opinion asserts, that it is additionally required that the matter have been made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court because it was either asserted by the appellant as a ground for appeal or made the subject of ex officio adjudication by the appellate court. Viewing that such a requirement is included goes beyond the range of possible interpretation based on the wording of the provision.\\nMoreover, even upon examining the Criminal Procedure Act and other statutes, there is no basis provision at all that can be seen as supporting the majority opinion’s doctrine limiting grounds for appeal as described above.\\n2) The majority opinion argues that the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal is a logical consequence of adopting the structure of final appeal as a subsequent review, and takes this as the main basis for limiting grounds for appeal by that doctrine.\\nHowever, in the system of the Criminal Procedure Act, when final appeal is distinguished from a second-instance review or a full rehearing and is called a subsequent review, it presupposes matters mainly concerning whether the appellant is compelled to submit a statement of grounds for final appeal (Article 379(1)), and on that premise whether the appellate court adjudicates the grounds included in the statement (Article 384), reviews the propriety of the original judgment based on the evidence examined up to the original instance and the submitted litigation records, and, if grounds for final appeal exist, reverses the original judgment and remands the case for retrial (Article 379(2), Articles 390 through 397). Thus, the mere fact that final appeal adopts a subsequent-review structure does not lead to the conclusion that the scope or requirements of the grounds for final appeal to be set forth in the statement of grounds are limited to certain types of factual or legal issues, or limited to specific matters linked to the subject of adjudication in the original judgment, such as matters asserted as grounds for appeal or made the subject of ex officio adjudication by the appellate court.\\nWhether to structure final appeal under the Criminal Procedure Act as a review limited to issues of law or as a fact review, and on that basis how to set the specific scope and type of grounds for final appeal that the appellant may assert, should be regarded as a matter of the legislature’s legislative discretion regarding the hierarchical review system and appeal system. Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act specifically defines the scope of grounds for final appeal based on a legislative decision that comprehensively considered various matters to be taken into account in the legislative process, such as the function and structure of final appeal and the burden of case handling. The majority opinion’s doctrine limiting grounds for appeal is nothing more than a strained interpretive theory that, by invoking matters already considered by the legislature, namely the function and structure of final appeal, narrows the scope of lawful grounds for final appeal expressly provided in the Criminal Procedure Act without legal basis. This violates the constitutional principle of separation of powers by infringing the legislature’s power to shape the system of hierarchy of courts with the Supreme Court as the highest court under the Constitution (Article 102), and it unfairly restricts the defendant’s right to final appeal, which is the concrete realization of the constitutional right to demand a trial (Article 27(1)).\\n3) Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act, while in principle limiting grounds for final appeal that may be asserted to matters concerning violations of statutes, etc., such as where there is a violation of the Constitution, statutes, orders, or rules that affected the judgment (subparagraph 1), exceptionally permits grounds for final appeal concerning factual findings only in the case of a defendant who has received a severe sentence and only where there is a need for greater protection of the defendant’s interests (subparagraph 4). Article 384 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which prescribes the ex officio adjudicatory power of the final appellate court, also confirms that the reasons for exercising that power are limited to the grounds in Article 383, subparagraphs 1 through 3, thereby confirming that the subject of review in final appeal is in principle limited to matters concerning violations of statutes. By contrast, the grounds that may become grounds for appeal include not only violations of statutes but also a wide range of reasons spanning legal and factual issues, such as illegality in litigation procedures, factual mistake, and unfair sentencing (Article 361-5). Here, violation of statutes means a case in which, on the premise of the facts found by the original judgment, the law was misapplied thereto; a case in which the original court’s factual findings themselves were erroneous and, as a result, the application of law thereto was erroneous does not fall within this category (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 81DO2111, rendered on September 22, 1981).\\nIn this way, final appeal, as a review limited to issues of law, has as its essential function to finally correct, through adjudication, errors of violations of statutes in the original judgment, thereby overcoming the state of illegality or legal confusion that arises when the determinations of several lower courts differ from one another on legal issues. This is intended to enable the sole highest court to have final adjudicative authority concerning interpretation and application of the law, thereby maintaining uniformity in interpretation and application of the law throughout the country, and to provide relief for the defendant’s rights infringed by erroneous interpretation and application of the law by lower courts. It is the inherent authority and duty of final appeal, which cannot be abandoned, as a legislative decision concerning the hierarchical review system and appeal system, for the final appellate court to perform such functions and roles as the final adjudicatory body on legal issues.\\nTherefore, grounds for final appeal alleging violations of statutes, etc. prescribed in Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act should always be regarded as lawful grounds for final appeal. The majority opinion’s doctrine limiting grounds for appeal holds that even with respect to such grounds concerning legal issues, lawfulness depends on whether they were concretely made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court, which is difficult to accept because it is contrary to the function and role of the final appellate court as a review limited to issues of law.\\n4) The majority opinion argues that even if grounds for final appeal concerning legal issues are limited by the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal, the final appellate court can strengthen its function as a review limited to issues of law by exercising ex officio adjudicatory power over the illegality in lower court judgments and correcting such errors.\\nHowever, ex officio adjudication under Article 384 of the Criminal Procedure Act is not an obligation of the final appellate court but a power, and whether to exercise it depends on the discretion of the final appellate court. Accordingly, as to matters subject to ex officio adjudication, not only must the illegality be affirmed, but explicit determinations are made only in exceptional cases where the final appellate court itself recognizes the need to reverse the original judgment in order to correct it; thus in most cases there is no way to know whether the final appellate court properly exercised ex officio adjudicatory power. In this respect, the ex officio adjudication of the final appellate court is insufficient as a means of strengthening a review limited to issues of law when compared with adjudication of grounds for final appeal, which are mandatory subjects of adjudication, and is therefore insufficient to rationalize the majority opinion’s doctrine limiting grounds for appeal.\\n5) From the standpoint of proportional balance between the institutional costs and efforts invested in criminal procedure and the benefits obtained if final appellate review is permitted, it may be desirable from the public interest perspective for the appeal system to be used not diffusely but concentrated on resolving issues that significantly affect the public’s legal life. Under a hierarchical review system in which several lower courts and a single highest court coexist, if limiting the scope of grounds for final appeal that may become the subject of final appellate review reduces the burden of case handling in final appeal, the final appellate court will be able to more faithfully perform its original function.\\nHowever, even if such a public-interest demand or need exists, the means must still conform to the original function of final appeal as a review limited to issues of law. As a means to achieve this purpose, the Criminal Procedure Act has already enacted Article 383, which strictly limits, in principle, the grounds that may be used as grounds for final appeal to matters concerning violations of the Constitution, statutes, orders, or rules that affected the judgment, namely matters involving pure legal issues. This is a necessary and reasonable measure, in line with the essence and function of the hierarchical review system, under which lower courts are, in principle, courts of fact and final appeal is a court of law, in order to appropriately distribute judicial resources between lower courts and the final appellate court, prevent unnecessary final appeals, and promote procedural economy by limiting the grounds that the appellant may invoke as grounds for final appeal, in principle, to matters concerning violations of statutes that affected the judgment. By contrast, the majority opinion’s doctrine limiting grounds for appeal excludes, in some cases, even grounds concerning clear violations of statutes from the subject of final appellate review merely because they were not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court; this is contrary to the function and role of final appeal as a review limited to issues of law, and as a means to attain this purpose, the means and the end are reversed.\\n6) The reason the Supreme Court has in the past derived a separate doctrine limiting grounds for appeal not found in Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act appears to stem from a concern that if the fact-finding by judges in fact-finding courts is treated as a lawful ground for final appeal merely because it was made without clear evidence or is unclear whether it reached the level of arbitrariness or caprice, or if reasons that are in substance nothing more than disputes over facts as part of the fact-finding court’s exclusive authority are treated as lawful grounds for final appeal concerning violation of statutes, the scope of cases to be reviewed by the final appellate court would be unnecessarily expanded, potentially impairing the original function of the final appellate court as a review limited to issues of law.\\nOriginally, the selection and evaluation of evidence, which are the basis of fact-finding, falls within the exclusive authority of the fact-finding court, and so long as the fact-finding court’s determination does not exceed the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in accordance with logic and experience, it cannot be immediately concluded that such determination itself constitutes a violation of statutes as prescribed in Article 383, subparagraph 1, of the Criminal Procedure Act; and, absent special circumstances, challenging only the selection of evidence and fact-finding by the original court without pointing out specific violations of logic or experience is merely an assertion of factual mistake and cannot be a lawful ground for final appeal (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2007DO1755, rendered on May 29, 2008).\\nHowever, the Supreme Court has treated as lawful grounds for appeal cases in which, despite the fact that fact-finding is within the exclusive authority of the fact-finding court, the Court has determined that whether the criminal facts are established must conform to logic and experience, and that rejecting evidence with sufficient probative value without reasonable grounds or, conversely, adopting and using evidence plainly contrary to objective facts without basis exceeds the bounds of free evaluation of evidence and constitutes a violation of statutes (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 4287HYEONGSANG135, rendered on October 5, 1954; 84DO554, rendered on May 29, 1984; 95DO535, rendered on May 9, 1995; 2004DO2221, rendered on June 25, 2004; 2007DO1950, rendered on May 10, 2007; 2010DO12728, rendered on January 27, 2011; 2015DO17869, rendered on October 13, 2016; 2016DO12460, rendered on November 9, 2017; 2018DO7709, rendered on October 25, 2018, etc.). Even though, with respect to fact-finding, only in cases where, pursuant to Article 383, subparagraph 4, of the Criminal Procedure Act, “in a case in which death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment or penal detention for not less than 10 years was imposed, there is a mistaken finding of material fact that affected the judgment” does it constitute a lawful ground for final appeal, the Supreme Court has similarly applied the above doctrine even in cases where such severe punishment was not imposed.\\nThe Supreme Court’s adoption of such a dual stance appears to reflect the practical need that, while recognizing that fact-finding is originally within the exclusive authority of the fact-finding court and that the Supreme Court is a court of law, the final appellate court, as the final instance, cannot simply ignore erroneous conclusions caused by factual mistakes of the fact-finding court.\\nHowever, with respect to the exclusion of illegally obtained evidence (Article 308-2), exclusion of involuntary confessions (Article 309), corroboration of confessions (Article 310), the hearsay rule and its exceptions (Articles 310-2 through 316), and similar specific rules of evidence under the Criminal Procedure Act, a ground asserting that the evidence forming the basis of conviction was found to be unreliable and that the facts were wrongly found, without specifying the circumstances and basis of violation of the concrete evidentiary provisions, and vaguely citing logic and experience, is in essence a matter of fact rather than law. This is especially so where the defendant, having been subjected to an unfavorable trial up to the appellate stage, seeks, as much as possible, to contest even the fact-finding in the appellate court. This is even more so where the defendant did not make such arguments in the appellate court but, after receiving an unfavorable judgment, asserts them for the first time as grounds for final appeal. Accordingly, such grounds should not be recognized as lawful grounds for final appeal under Article 383, subparagraph 1, of the Criminal Procedure Act. If such cases were to be deemed to constitute grounds for final appeal concerning violation of statutes, this would not only contravene the function and role of the Supreme Court, established as a court of law within the hierarchical review system, and the wording and legislative purpose of Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act, but would also encourage unnecessary and useless final appeals, thereby increasing the burden of case handling in final appeal.\\nTherefore, the Supreme Court should not cling to a separate doctrine limiting grounds for appeal derived from its existing erroneous precedents and practice; rather, it should faithfully function as a court of law by strictly determining whether the case falls under one of the grounds for final appeal set forth in the items of Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Otherwise, treating cases that are merely factual issues as lawful grounds for final appeal while holding that even grounds concerning violation of statutes are not lawful if they were not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court is a reversal of means and ends.\\nC. In short, Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act contains an express provision regarding the scope of grounds for final appeal, and the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal advocated by the majority has no basis whatsoever in the Criminal Procedure Act or other related statutes, nor can its validity be recognized on the ground of the structure of final appeal as a subsequent review or the policy need to secure the proper function of final appeal. It is wholly unacceptable because it contravenes the purport of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, as well as the function and role of final appeal as a review limited to issues of law. Therefore, when final appeal is filed under Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act on grounds such as violations of statutes that affected the judgment, it should always be deemed a lawful ground for final appeal, regardless of whether the matter was made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court. The function of final appeal should be resolved by interpreting the above provision more strictly and limiting the scope of grounds for appeal to grounds concerning pure violations of statutes.\\nAccordingly, all judgments to the same effect, including Supreme Court Decision 87DO1561, rendered on December 8, 1987, and Supreme Court Decision 2009DO579, rendered on May 28, 2009, which held that a matter is not a lawful ground for final appeal merely because it was not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court despite falling under the grounds set forth in the items of Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act, should all be overruled.\\nD. Applying this doctrine to the defendants’ grounds for final appeal:\\n1) Among the defendants’ grounds for final appeal, the argument that the appellate court, contrary to logic and experience, found facts incorrectly or failed to conduct the necessary review beyond the bounds of free evaluation of evidence is, in substance, a challenge to the appellate court’s selection of evidence and fact-finding and, absent special circumstances, is merely an assertion of factual mistake and is not a lawful ground for final appeal.\\n2) Even a pharmacist who conspires to participate in the act of opening a pharmacy by a person who is not a pharmacist or herbal pharmacist falls under joint principal liability for violation of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2003DO2971, rendered on July 11, 2003).\\nApplying the above doctrine, the appellate court’s determination, based on the reasons stated in its opinion, that Defendant 1, who is a pharmacist, conspired to participate in the act of opening a pharmacy by the non-party, an unqualified person, and thus committed a violation of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act, is proper. There is no error such as a violation of the application of law concerning Article 20(1) of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act or the requirements for joint principal liability concerning status offenses.\\n3) Defendant 2’s remaining grounds for final appeal concerning sentencing are not lawful grounds for final appeal under Article 383, subparagraph 4, of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\nAlthough we share the majority opinion on the conclusion that all appeals must be dismissed in this case, we differ as to the reasons and therefore state this as a separate opinion.\\n8. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Min Yoo-sook to the Majority Opinion\\nA. Put simply, the gist of the separate opinion of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Lee Ki-taek, Kim Jae-hyung, and Kim Seon-su (hereinafter “Separate Opinion 1”) is that: ① a defendant who has been found guilty in the first-instance judgment makes different judgments regarding whether to appeal to contest guilt, and the scope of asserting grounds such as factual mistake or violation of statutes as grounds for appeal, depending on whether he or she is satisfied with the sentence shown in the dispositive portion; and ② respecting such judgment by the defendant, it is proper to broadly accept new grounds as lawful grounds for final appeal when there has been a material change in circumstances, such as where the prosecutor’s ground of appeal regarding unfair sentencing was accepted in the appellate court and the sentence was increased. However, I cannot agree with this argument because it emphasizes only the defendant’s position, does not accord with the basic structure of our criminal procedure and the basic ideals of the review procedure, and lacks sufficient legal basis.\\n1) Under the Criminal Procedure Act, after the prosecutor’s opening statement based on the indictment has concluded, the defendant must state whether he or she admits the charged facts (Articles 285 and 286(1)), and the subsequent trial proceedings advance according to the defendant’s position regarding guilt or innocence, such as admission or denial of the charged facts. Thus, a defendant who disputes the charged facts actively exercises the right of defense against the prosecution’s allegations in both factual and legal aspects, and the first-instance court, based on that, renders a final conclusion on guilt or innocence and sentencing after sufficient review. In other words, our criminal procedure does not allow, at the first stage, a so-called “pre-indictment plea procedure,” which may exist only in foreign procedures, in which the determination of sentencing and the admission of the charged facts are linked so that the defendant can obtain a favorable sentence; rather, the procedure leading to judgment is structured to proceed sequentially, premised on the determination of guilt or innocence, to the determination concerning sentencing factors under Article 51 of the Criminal Act. In light of this, Separate Opinion 1’s stance—that the scope of reasons that may be asserted to contest guilt in the subsequent final appellate proceedings may vary depending on the defendant’s subjective assessment of whether he or she is satisfied with the sentence in the first-instance judgment and whether the sentence was unfavorably changed in the appellate judgment—is inconsistent with the basic structure of our criminal procedure.\\n2) In light of the litigation structure and procedural dynamics of the current Criminal Procedure Act, which aims at the adversarial principle, trial-centeredness, and substantive immediacy, and the dynamic and developmental nature of litigation procedures, the above situations regarded by Separate Opinion 1 as a material change in the litigation procedure cannot be said, even when compared with other cases to which the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal applies, to constitute an unexpected detriment requiring recognition of a special exception to the application of that doctrine. Unless Separate Opinion 1 can present a convincing and clear basis as to why a different interpretation should be made only in such cases while concurring with the basic purpose of the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal, its validity is difficult to maintain.\\n3) In addition, the circumstances pointed out by Separate Opinion 1—namely that the dispositive portion of the judgment was unfavorably changed in the appellate court, that the appellate court states the reasons for a guilty finding when reversing and rendering judgment itself, that there is an imbalance in opportunities for appeal compared with the case where the increased sentence was imposed in the first instance, and that the burden is increased by unnecessarily inducing the defendant to appeal—are also insufficient, in light of the litigation structure and basic ideals concerning review procedures adopted by our Criminal Procedure Act, as grounds for changing or overruling the precedent concerning the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal that has been consistently maintained.\\nB. Separate Opinion 1 and the separate opinion of Justice Cho Hee-dae (hereinafter “Separate Opinion 2”) state that, even if final appeal is a subsequent review, there is insufficient positive-law basis to narrowly interpret the scope of grounds lawfully assertable on final appeal as limited to matters that were made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court, as the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal suggests.\\nHowever, the phrase “matters that were made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court” can be understood as matters the appellate court made the subject of review and determination in the litigation procedure, and the Criminal Procedure Act generally requires the appellate court to adjudicate the reasons included in the statement of grounds for appeal (Article 364(1)) and exceptionally to determine matters made the subject of ex officio adjudication (Articles 361-4(1), 364(2)). The expression “matters that were made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court” in the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal is based precisely on this. Therefore, the argument that the basis for the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal, which limits grounds for appeal on the basis of the structure of final appeal as a subsequent review, etc., is insufficient is difficult to accept.\\nC. Separate Opinion 2 takes the position that, although final appeal, as a review limited to issues of law, should in principle include all grounds concerning violations of statutes within its subject of review, only when the circumstances and basis of violation of specific evidentiary rules under the Criminal Procedure Act are specified should it be regarded as lawful grounds for final appeal.\\nHowever, our Criminal Procedure Act, before prescribing concrete rules of evidence such as the rule excluding illegally obtained evidence (Article 308-2), sets forth, in Article 307, the principle of evidentiary adjudication, and in Article 308, the principle of free evaluation of evidence as the basic principles of evidentiary law. A ground for final appeal asserting that the appellate court’s evaluation of evidence and fact-finding violated the rules of logic and experience and exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence, thus amounting to violation of the rules of evidence, is precisely a point out of violation of those evidentiary provisions. In the same vein, the Supreme Court has treated such matters as violations of statutes under Article 383, subparagraph 1, of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\nAlso, insofar as a case violating the principle of evidentiary adjudication or free evaluation of evidence constitutes a lawful ground for final appeal as a matter of violation of statutes, the burden of case handling that the final appellate court bears in the process of adjudicating such matters inevitably increases to some extent. The doctrine limiting grounds for appeal reflects this circumstance, and one cannot help emphasizing that it was an unavoidable measure introduced to secure the function and role of the final appellate court as the highest court.\\nD. In many cases, even if the defendant ostensibly asserts violation of statutes as a ground for final appeal, the final appellate court often must determine specific factual relationships in order to adjudicate it. If no review or determination concerning those factual relationships was made at the original instance, then by reason of its characteristics as a subsequent review and a review limited to issues of law, the final appellate court finds it difficult to determine the propriety of that ground of appeal.\\nEven in light of the concrete determinations in this case, Separate Opinion 1 and Separate Opinion 2, while considering that matters not made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court may in principle become the subject of final appeal, held that the defendants’ ground of appeal alleging violation of the rules of evidence or omission of review concerning whether they participated in the act of opening a pharmacy by an unqualified person was, in substance, a challenge to fact-finding, which is the exclusive authority of the original court, and therefore was unlawful without proceeding to the merits.\\nIn light of this, even if the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal were changed or overruled, as Separate Opinion 1 or Separate Opinion 2 contends, thereby outwardly expanding the scope of reasons the defendant may use as grounds for final appeal, there would in reality not be many matters that actually fall under the grounds for final appeal prescribed in the items of Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act and are worth adjudicating in the final appellate court. That is, the practical benefit of changing the doctrine, etc., should be viewed as small.\\nI set forth the above as a supplementary opinion to the majority opinion.\\n9. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek to the Separate Opinion of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Lee Ki-taek, Kim Jae-hyung, and Kim Seon-su\\nA. Separate Opinion 1 states that, in opposition to the majority opinion, the existing doctrine limiting grounds for appeal should not apply to the cases of this case. However, in addition, even where the defendant actively appealed a first-instance judgment finding guilt while asserting as grounds of appeal the reasons set forth in each item of Article 361-5 of the Criminal Procedure Act, such as factual mistake or violation of statutes in the sense of innocence, if the defendant’s appeal is dismissed in the appellate court and only the prosecutor’s appeal on unfair sentencing is accepted, resulting in a higher sentence (hereinafter referred to as “active appeal cases”), I believe such cases should be excluded from the scope of application of the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal. The reasons are as follows.\\nB. Separate Opinion 1 points out that, in light of the developmental and dynamic nature of criminal trials, there may be special circumstances in concrete cases depending on how proceedings progress in the lower courts, such that the propriety or necessity of limiting grounds for appeal should be evaluated differently, and that whether the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal applies should be determined differently in light of such special circumstances. The main logic leading to the conclusion that the cases of this case should be excluded from the application of the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal may be summarized as follows.\\n1) First, when comparing the time of final appeal with the time of appeal, there has been a material change in the circumstances forming the basis for decisions regarding whether to appeal, etc. Because there was a change in circumstances in which the result of the first-instance judgment, which formed the basis for the defendant’s decision whether to appeal, was unfavorably changed in the appellate court, it is appropriate that, when deciding whether to file a final appeal and the grounds therefor, the defendant may do so based on the appellate judgment as changed.\\n2) Because the dispositive portion of the judgment is the key factor in determining the possibility of appeal and whether there is an intent to appeal, the propriety and scope of the limitation on grounds for final appeal should also be determined based on it. Thus, even if the defendant was satisfied with the dispositive portion of the first-instance judgment and had complaints only with the reasons for the judgment under the Criminal Procedure Act, appeal contesting those reasons was not permitted and the defendant did not appeal; if, thereafter, the prosecutor’s grounds of appeal regarding unfair sentencing were accepted in the appellate court and the dispositive portion changed unfavorably, it is proper to allow the defendant to file a final appeal actively asserting factual mistake, violation of statutes, and other errors in the reasons for judgment that had been held in reserve.\\n3) When the appellate court accepts the prosecutor’s appeal on unfair sentencing and reverses the judgment while rendering judgment itself, that is an appellate court’s own determination. At that point, the appellate court makes a new determination not only regarding sentencing, which was the cause of reversal, but also regarding the underlying factual findings and application of law, and therefore grounds for final appeal pointing out factual mistake and violation of statutes in an appeal against the appellate judgment should be regarded as concerning matters made the subject of adjudication in the appellate court.\\n4) Furthermore, there is a risk of imbalance in opportunities for appeal depending on the concrete case. For example, under the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal, even if the sentence imposed on the defendant in the appellate judgment is identical in all cases as suspended execution of imprisonment, if such sentence was imposed in the first instance and the defendant, from the outset, appealed and contested by asserting factual mistake and violation of statutes as grounds for appeal, the defendant ultimately has two opportunities to appeal up to final appeal; but if, by chance, a lighter sentence such as a fine was imposed in the first instance, the defendant accepted the judgment and later, only in the appellate court, the above sentence was imposed, then because final appeal is restricted, an unreasonable result arises in which the defendant effectively has no opportunity to appeal at all.\\n5) Finally, the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal increases the burden of review in the appellate court contrary to expectation. Even if the defendant intends to accept the first-instance judgment, if the prosecutor appeals on the ground of unfair sentencing, the defendant will respond by appealing while asserting all reasons such as factual mistake and violation of statutes as grounds of appeal, taking into account that grounds for final appeal will be limited in the future. As a result, the appellate court bears the burden of reviewing and determining those grounds for appeal.\\nC. However, such reasoning appears to remain largely valid even when the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal is applied to active appeal cases. Although active appeal cases are somewhat distinguishable from the cases of this case in that the defendant has actively contested both the dispositive portion and the reasons of the first-instance judgment, such circumstances are not an essential element warranting a different evaluation of the two in delineating the boundary of application of the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal. Rather, even in active appeal cases, the standard determining whether to appeal and, concomitantly, the content and scope of the grounds of appeal to be asserted remains the first-instance judgment before reversal in the appellate court, just as in the cases of this case. Furthermore, even in such cases, the defendant decides whether to appeal on the assumption that the conclusion of the first-instance judgment will be maintained in the appellate court. On that premise, once, as in the cases of this case, there arises after that point a situation in which the first-instance judgment loses effect and is replaced by an appellate judgment with more unfavorable content, as the changed circumstance forming the basis of the decision regarding whether to appeal, it is logically consistent to allow even in active appeal cases the defendant to file a final appeal once again, using new grounds such as factual mistake or violation of statutes that had not been asserted as grounds of appeal, based on the changed circumstances in the appellate court.\\nD. As pointed out in Separate Opinion 1, the defendant’s greatest concern in criminal trials is the propriety of the guilty or not-guilty determination and sentence reflected in the dispositive portion of the judgment. The greater the defendant’s dissatisfaction with the dispositive portion of the judgment, the greater the possibility of appeal, and accordingly, the broader the scope of grounds of appeal the defendant will seek to make the subject of dispute. Meanwhile, if the procedure continues due to the defendant’s appeal, the defendant bears additional substantial costs or burdens, which increase as the number of grounds for appeal increases or their content becomes more complex, lengthening the review period. Accordingly, even if the defendant appeals against the first-instance judgment, it is reasonable to expect that the defendant will assert as grounds of appeal only some factual mistakes or violations of statutes that merit priority among several reasons, and will reserve the remainder unless a more unfavorable situation arises. Such judgment by the defendant is the result of a rational choice of conduct in exercising the right of appeal in the direction most beneficial to himself or herself, and is a universal and natural response in situations where his or her interests intersect in social life, while also conforming to the purpose of the Criminal Procedure Act in recognizing the defendant’s right of appeal as a remedy. Therefore, if thereafter the appellate court dismisses all grounds of appeal asserted by the defendant, accepts the prosecutor’s grounds of appeal concerning unfair sentencing, reverses the first-instance judgment, and imposes a harsher sentence, thereby changing the existing situation more unfavorably to the defendant, it is proper to allow the defendant, even in active appeal cases where he or she had already asserted grounds such as factual mistake and violation of statutes from the time of appeal, to file a final appeal on the basis of the new grounds of factual mistake and violation of statutes that had been held in reserve, thereby affording the defendant an opportunity to defend his or her own interests.\\nE. The Criminal Procedure Act generally limits the subject of adjudication in the appellate court to matters included in the statement of grounds for appeal (Article 364(1)), and requires a defendant who has filed a notice of appeal to submit the statement of grounds for appeal to the appellate court within 20 days from the date the court notifies receipt of the trial record (Article 361-3(1)). Accordingly, defendants in active appeal cases bear the burden of examining and analyzing grounds such as factual mistake and violation of statutes that affected the judgment, and of preparing and submitting a statement of grounds for appeal within such a relatively short period. However, unlike the determination of whether to accept the conclusion of the judgment, such as unfair sentencing, it is not easy for the defendant to legally determine the propriety of the specific factual findings and application of law stated in the reasons for the judgment. Thus, in the process of drafting the statement of grounds for appeal, it appears inevitable that some grounds of factual mistake or violation of statutes that might constitute grounds for appeal will be incorrectly judged or omitted by the defendant. Although such omissions are attributable to the defendant’s negligence, it is proper to allow the defendant to file a final appeal asserting such omitted grounds of factual mistake and violation of statutes. Leaving plainly erroneous judgment contents intact, even though there remains an opportunity to correct them through final appeal, does not conform to the purpose or objective of the hierarchical review system, which is properness of adjudication and maintenance of trust. In particular, if the appellate court accepts the prosecutor’s grounds of appeal on unfair sentencing, reverses the first-instance judgment, but merely increases the sentence while overlooking the first-instance court’s erroneous factual findings and application of law, there is already reason to view that such illegality exists in the appellate judgment itself, and the need to exclude the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal and allow such reasons to be asserted as grounds for final appeal is even greater.\\nF. Taking these circumstances together, when the appellate court accepts the prosecutor’s appeal on unfair sentencing and the defendant receives an unfavorable appellate judgment compared with the first-instance judgment, there is no rational reason to treat the case differently depending on whether the defendant appealed at the earlier stage of objection, asserted only unfair sentencing as a ground of appeal, or asserted comprehensively even factual mistake and violation of statutes. Active appeal cases should also be excluded from the scope of application of the doctrine limiting grounds for appeal.\\nFor the above reasons, I state this supplementary opinion to Separate Opinion 1."}

{"[2020DO10778]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Since the main text of Article 296-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, Article 370, and Article 296-2(1) provides that “the prosecutor or defense counsel may, in sequence after the completion of the examination of evidence, question the defendant on matters necessary concerning the facts charged and circumstances,” defense counsel’s right to examine the defendant is a procedural right of defense counsel. Meanwhile, where the prosecutor or defense counsel conducts an examination of the defendant at the appellate trial, the presiding judge may restrict all or part of such examination if it is deemed to duplicate the examination of the defendant at the first instance or to be unnecessary for determining the propriety of the grounds for appeal (Article 156-6(2) of the Rules on Criminal Procedure), but may not impair the essential rights of defense counsel (see Articles 370 and 299 of the Criminal Procedure Act). Therefore, when defense counsel expresses an intention to examine the defendant, the presiding judge must take measures to allow the defendant to be examined, and if, notwithstanding defense counsel’s expression of intent to examine the defendant, no examination of the defendant whatsoever is permitted to defense counsel, this impairs the essential right relating to defense counsel’s right to examine the defendant and constitutes a violation of laws and regulations concerning litigation procedure.\\n\\n2. According to the record, counsel for the defendant in the court below, upon the completion of the examination of evidence at the 2nd hearing date on June 17, 2020, expressed to the presiding judge an intent to examine the defendant; however, it can be ascertained that the presiding judge disallowed the examination of the defendant, ordered defense counsel to submit the matters to be asserted in a summary brief of arguments, closed the pleadings, and rendered judgment at the 3rd hearing date on July 15, 2020.\\n\\n3. Examining the above facts in light of the foregoing legal principles, the judgment of the court below, which closed the pleadings and rendered judgment without proceeding with the examination of the defendant despite defense counsel’s expression of intent to examine the defendant, contains an error of violating laws and regulations concerning litigation procedure. The grounds of appeal pointing out this point are well taken.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds for appeal, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for a new trial and determination, and so, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, we render the judgment as stated in the dispositive part."}

{"[2021DO1282]": "We examine the grounds of final appeal (limited to the extent that the statement in the supplemental brief of final appeal submitted after the expiration of the filing period for the statement of grounds of final appeal supplements the grounds of final appeal).\\n\\n1. Article 368 of the Criminal Procedure Act concerning the “prohibition against disadvantageous modification” provides that, in cases appealed by the Defendant and in cases appealed for the Defendant’s benefit, no sentence more severe than the sentence of the original judgment may be imposed, and this provision applies mutatis mutandis at the final appeal stage pursuant to Article 399 of the Criminal Procedure Act. This principle of prohibition against disadvantageous modification was adopted by the legislature as a policy consideration to prevent the exercise of the Defendant’s right of appeal from being chilled by concern that a sentence more severe than that imposed by the original judgment may be imposed in the appellate trial. In light of the fact that the wording of the above statutory provision prohibits only a change to “a sentence more severe than the sentence of the original judgment,” and that the appellate court is not necessarily bound by the circumstances or views on which the lower court based its determination of sentence, it cannot be said that, in a case appealed only by the Defendant, the appellate court violated the principle of prohibition against disadvantageous modification merely because it found some of the criminal facts recognized by the lower court not guilty while still imposing on the Defendant the same sentence as that imposed by the lower court (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2002DO5679, rendered February 11, 2003).\\n\\nMeanwhile, where, in a final appeal filed only by the Defendant, the Supreme Court quashes the original judgment and remands the case to the appellate court, the principle of prohibition against disadvantageous modification also applies in relation to the original judgment before remand, and the lower court after remand may not impose a sentence more severe than the original judgment before remand that was quashed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 92DO2020, rendered December 8, 1992).\\n\\n2. We examine the above legal principles in light of the record. According to the record, the original judgment before remand imposed imprisonment for 4 years with respect to the breach of trust portion (as indicated in the original court’s decision 2017GODAN2343) and the fraud portion (as indicated in the original court’s decision 2017GODAN682 and 2017GODAN800), and, as only the Defendant filed a final appeal therefrom, the Supreme Court rendered a judgment quashing those portions of the original judgment and remanding the case to the appellate court. Thereafter, the original court after remand, in accordance with the purport of the quashing and remand, found the breach of trust portion not guilty and found only the remaining fraud portion guilty, and imposed thereon imprisonment for 4 years, the same sentence as in the original judgment before remand. So long as no sentence more severe than that in the original judgment before remand was imposed, there is no error in the original court’s determination after remand that violated the principle of prohibition against disadvantageous modification or misconstrued the legal doctrine concerning the binding force of the remand judgment. The argument in the grounds of final appeal disputing this is without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and it is adjudged as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices of the Supreme Court."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning seizure and search are incorrect? (In cases of dispute, pursuant to case law) (a) If the person subject to seizure expressly indicated to the investigative agency that he would not participate in the execution of the seizure/search warrant, then, except in special circumstances, it is permissible not to separately guarantee his defense counsel an opportunity to participate in the execution of the seizure/search warrant. (b) If, after the investigative agency has selectively seized information related to the alleged crime and is retaining the remaining information unrelated thereto without deleting, discarding, or returning it, then, as to the portion unrelated to the alleged crime, it has unlawfully seized and searched electronic information beyond the scope of electronic information subject to seizure without a warrant, and such illegality cannot be deemed cured merely because a seizure/search warrant was later issued by a court or because the defendant or defense counsel consented to its use as evidence. (c) The term "an information storage medium belonging to the suspect's ownership or management," for which the right of participation should be guaranteed not only to the person subject to seizure who voluntarily submitted the information storage medium but also to a suspect who is not the voluntary submitter, means a case in which the suspect, at the time of the seizure/search or up to a temporally proximate time, actually controlled and managed the information storage medium and possessed and exercised exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information within that information storage medium, and did not otherwise transfer or relinquish it to a third party according to his own intent, so that the suspect can be evaluated as the substantive person subject to seizure with respect to the electronic information stored in that information storage medium. (d) Whether a person qualifies as the substantive person subject to seizure must be determined on the basis of the externally and objectively recognizable factual condition at the time of the seizure/search; thus, if the suspect or any other third party had, in the past, been involved in the use of that information storage medium or the creation or use of individual electronic information, or if they are the data subject identified by electronic information created in the course thereof, then they must be treated as the party substantively subjected to seizure and search. (e) If, while voluntarily submitting a mobile phone, the suspect voluntarily provided the investigative agency with the ID and password for accessing cloud services or the like, with the intent of submitting to the investigative agency electronic information stored not in the mobile phone but in remote locations managed by a third party such as the cloud, then the electronic information stored in the cloud or the like may be regarded as having been voluntarily submitted.

supporting_precedents: {"[2020DO10729]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. a. When investigative agencies execute a warrant of seizure and search, the person from whom items are seized or the defense counsel may participate in its execution (Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act). Even where, in the course of a seizure and search of storage media, it is impossible to print and duplicate within the scope fixed, or where exceptional circumstances are recognized in which it is markedly difficult to accomplish the purpose of seizure, and the storage media containing electronic information, hard copies, or imaging and other forms (hereinafter referred to as the “duplicate copy”) are moved to the investigative agency’s office, etc. for duplication, examination, and printing, the principles of warrant issuance and due process must still be observed by guaranteeing the opportunity for the person from whom items are seized or the defense counsel to participate and by taking appropriate measures to prevent arbitrary duplication, etc. of electronic information unrelated to the alleged facts. If such measures were not taken, then, unless there are special circumstances such as where the side of the person from whom items were seized explicitly indicated an intention not to participate in the above procedures or process, or where it cannot be said that the purpose of guaranteeing participation in the procedure was substantially infringed in light of the nature and content of the process in which the procedural violation occurred, the seizure and search cannot be said to be lawful. The same applies even where the investigative agency duplicated and printed only the electronic information related to the alleged facts from the storage media or the duplicate copy (see Supreme Court en banc Decision dated 2015. 7. 16. in 2011MO1839, Supreme Court Judgment dated 2017. 9. 21. in 2015DO12400, etc.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, the defense counsel’s right to participate, as provided in Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act, is an inherent right granted to the defense counsel for the protection of the person from whom items are seized. Therefore, even if the person from whom items were seized explicitly indicated to the investigative agency an intention not to participate in the execution of the warrant of seizure and search, the defense counsel must, unless special circumstances exist, be separately guaranteed an opportunity to participate in the execution of the warrant of seizure and search by being notified in advance of the time and place of execution pursuant to Articles 219 and 122 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nb. Article 308-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “evidence collected in violation of lawful procedures shall not be admissible as evidence.” This explicitly sets forth the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence in order to realize the constitutional ideal of guaranteeing the fundamental human rights of the people by suppressing unlawful acts in investigative processes, including unlawful seizure and search, and preventing their recurrence (see Supreme Court Judgment dated 2013. 3. 14. in 2010DO2094, Supreme Court Judgment dated 2019. 7. 11. in 2018DO20504, etc.). Article 12 of the Constitution declares the principles of due process and warrant issuance with respect to seizure and search in order to guarantee fundamental human rights, and the Criminal Procedure Act inherits this and establishes specific standards concerning seizure and search procedures so as to harmoniously realize the ideals of discovering substantive truth and protecting individual rights. Since it is necessary to firmly maintain the normative force of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act and to suppress unlawful acts in investigative processes, evidence collected not only in violation of lawful procedures but also secondary evidence obtained on the basis thereof should be regarded as having been secured without lawful procedures prepared for the protection of fundamental human rights and, in principle, cannot be used as evidence for conviction.\\n\\nHowever, uniformly denying evidentiary admissibility merely because evidence was collected without following the procedures prescribed by law does not accord with the purposes of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act. This is because the realization of legitimate punitive power through the discovery of substantive truth is also an important goal and ideal that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to achieve through criminal procedure. If the investigative agency’s procedural violation does not amount to an infringement of the substantive content of due process, and rather it is an exceptional case in which excluding evidentiary admissibility would be evaluated as producing a result contrary to the intent of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act in establishing procedural provisions for criminal procedure so as to seek harmony between the principle of due process and the discovery of substantive truth and thereby realize criminal justice, the court should find that such evidence may be used as evidence for conviction. Whether this applies must be determined by comprehensively and holistically examining all circumstances relating to the procedural violation committed in the course of the investigative agency’s collection of evidence, namely, the purport of the procedural provision, the content and degree of the violation, the specific circumstances and avoidability of the violation, the nature of the rights or legal interests that the procedural provision seeks to protect and the degree of infringement, the relationship between such rights or legal interests and the defendant, the relationship between the procedural violation and the collection of evidence, and the investigative agency’s awareness and intent. Since this legal principle applies equally to secondary evidence obtained on the basis of evidence collected without lawful procedures, secondary evidence may also be used as evidence for conviction in exceptional cases by comprehensively and holistically considering all circumstances relating to the collection of secondary evidence, focusing on whether the causal relationship between the collection of evidence without procedure and the collection of secondary evidence has been attenuated or severed (see Supreme Court en banc Decision dated 2007. 11. 15. in 2007DO3061, Supreme Court en banc Decision dated 2015. 1. 22. in 2014DO10978, Supreme Court Judgment dated 2019. 7. 11. in 2018DO20504, etc.).\\n\\n2. a. The gist of the charged facts at issue in this case is as follows.\\n\\nThe Defendant, at an unknown time in or before 2019, in the restroom of “○○ Singing Practice Room” located in Uijeongbu-si (address omitted), attached, by using tape, a small camera wrapped in vinyl to the outside of a trash can inside the toilet stall there, attached a portable battery connected to the above camera to the inside of the trash can, and then pressed the record button, thereby filming the buttocks and genitals of an unidentified female who was using the toilet in that restroom; in addition, from around 2013 to around 2019, the Defendant filmed the victims using the toilet in restrooms on a total of 296 occasions as set forth in numbers 1 through 296 of the crime list table cited in the judgment below. In this way, the Defendant, by using a camera or any other mechanical device with a similar function, filmed the body of another person that may arouse sexual desire or cause shame, against that person’s will.\\n\\nb. The lower court, for the following reasons, found that this portion of the charged facts fell under a case in which the facts constituting the offense were not proven, and thus reversed the first-instance judgment that had found the Defendant guilty and held him not guilty.\\n\\n1) The investigative agency violated due process by executing the warrant of seizure and search on 2019. 10. 30. in the investigative agency’s office by searching, duplicating, and printing the storage media, without having previously notified the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel of the time and place of execution.\\n\\n2) Considering that the Defendant was then in custody and the importance of the participation procedure prescribed in Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the above violation of due process was serious in degree.\\n\\n3) Therefore, video capture printouts, etc. collected through the unlawful seizure and search cannot be used as evidence pursuant to Article 308-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and the Defendant’s confession is also a product based on those pieces of evidence or the only evidence for this portion of the charged facts, so it cannot be used as evidence of guilt pursuant to Article 308-2 or Article 310 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\n3. The lower court’s above determination cannot be accepted as is for the following reasons.\\n\\na. According to the reasoning of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n1) A judicial police officer affiliated with the Gyeonggi Uijeongbu Police Station, Police Lieutenant Nonparty 1, on 2019. 10. 25. at around 09:00, removed from the Defendant’s residence to the police station, by way of taking them out, one computer main unit owned by the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as the “computer at issue”) and one Galaxy Note8 mobile phone (hereinafter referred to as the “mobile phone at issue”), on the basis of the search, seizure, and inspection warrant dated 2019. 10. 24. issued by a judge of the Uijeongbu District Court (hereinafter referred to as the “warrant at issue”).\\n\\n2) At that time, the Defendant handwrote a “V” mark and signed and affixed his thumbprint on the portions of the confirmation forms for removal of the original for the computer at issue and the mobile phone at issue stating, “I participated in the process of sealing the digital device and storage media and confirmed that there was no problem with the sealing; I was notified that I may participate in the process of unsealing, obtaining the duplicate copy, and searching, duplicating, and printing the digital device, storage media, or duplicate copy; and I will not participate in the above process.”\\n\\n3) In the first police interrogation of the suspect immediately thereafter, the Defendant stated, “Since 4 to 5 years ago, I installed a hidden camera purchased online in trash cans in restrooms of PC rooms, singing rooms, etc. and filmed women’s genitals, etc., and stored the videos on the hard disk of the computer at issue.”\\n\\n4) Police Sergeant Nonparty 2, affiliated with the Gyeonggi Uijeongbu Police Station, searched the hard disk of the computer at issue on 2019. 10. 25., discovered a number of video files that appeared to have been filmed by the Defendant with a hidden camera, prepared an investigative report to that effect, and attached thereto photographs of the folder screen where the video files were stored.\\n\\n5) Meanwhile, the Prosecutor filed an application for an arrest warrant against the Defendant on 2019. 10. 25., and a judge of the Uijeongbu District Court, after appointing Attorney Nonparty 3 as the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel on 2019. 10. 26., conducted a pre-arrest suspect interrogation of the Defendant and issued the arrest warrant.\\n\\n6) In the second police interrogation of the suspect on 2019. 10. 29., the Defendant stated, “From around 2011 to around 2019, I installed hidden cameras in the restrooms of six places in total, including the places of offense stated in the charged facts at issue in this case, such as PC rooms, hospitals, and singing rooms, and filmed other persons’ bodies,” while specifying the places of offense by year.\\n\\n7) Police Lieutenant Nonparty 1, Police Sergeant Nonparty 4, and Police Corporal Nonparty 2, affiliated with the Gyeonggi Uijeongbu Police Station, each took charge of one of the three hard disks built into the computer at issue and searched them in their office on 2019. 10. 30., then captured the playback scene of the illegal filming video they each found (one scene per video file) and printed it together with the captured image of the corresponding video file information (all such printouts are hereinafter referred to as the “printouts at issue”).\\n\\n8) However, the investigative agency did not give advance notice to the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel concerning the above search and duplication of the computer at issue and the procedure for creation of the printouts at issue, and neither the Defendant nor the above court-appointed defense counsel participated in those procedures.\\n\\nb. In light of the foregoing legal principles, when examining the above factual relationship, even if the Defendant indicated to the investigative agency an intention not to participate in the process of searching, duplicating, and printing the computer at issue, the investigative agency should have provided the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel with an opportunity to participate in the above procedure by notifying him in advance of the time and place of execution before searching, duplicating, and printing the storage medium, namely, the computer at issue, in the investigative agency’s office on 2019. 10. 30.; yet it did not do so. Therefore, the lower court’s determination that the investigative agency executing the warrant at issue violated the seizure procedure is proper, and there is no illegality in the lower court’s above determination that violated no rules of logic or experience, did not exceed the limits of free evaluation of evidence, and did not misapprehend the legal principles regarding the nature of the defense counsel’s right to participate.\\n\\nc. 1) However, when all of the following circumstances ascertainable through the above factual relationship and the record are comprehensively considered, the above procedural violation by the investigative agency does not amount to an infringement of the substantive content of due process, and rather there is ample room to view this as an exceptional case in which excluding the admissibility of evidence collected through the execution of the warrant at issue would produce a result contrary to the intent of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act in establishing procedural provisions regarding criminal procedure so as to seek harmony between the principle of due process and the discovery of substantive truth and thereby realize criminal justice.\\n\\na) On 2019. 10. 25., the investigative agency, after confirming from the Defendant, who was then the only person entitled to participate as the person from whom items were seized, that he did not wish to participate in the process of searching, duplicating, and printing the computer at issue, began the search of the computer at issue. At the time of the search, the Defendant had already stated that “illegal filming videos are stored on the hard disk of the computer at issue.”\\n\\nb) By the time the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel was appointed, it appears that the investigative agency had already carried out the search of the computer at issue to some extent and had identified at least the location of the folder where the seized electronic information was stored.\\n\\nc) The Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel had not inquired of the investigative agency about the status of execution of the warrant at issue, nor had he requested participation in the process.\\n\\nd) At the time of execution of the warrant at issue, there was no established precedent or internal guideline of the investigative agency that the defense counsel appointed or selected after the commencement of the seizure and search procedure had to be separately notified in advance notwithstanding the person from whom items were seized having waived or refused participation.\\n\\ne) In the course of executing the warrant at issue, the investigative agency seized videos that the Defendant had recorded, through hidden cameras installed in restrooms of PC rooms, singing rooms, etc. since around 2011, of the bodies of hundreds of victims, and indicted him for 296 of those acts (the charged facts at issue in this case). The Defendant confessed to all of those offenses in the investigative agency and in court.\\n\\n2) If so, the lower court should have carefully determined, by comprehensively considering the circumstances of the seizure and search pursuant to the warrant at issue, the provisions relating to seizure procedures for electronic information in force at the time of execution of the warrant at issue, the probative purpose of the seized evidence, the circumstances that led to the procedural violation and the investigative agency’s awareness and intent regarding it, and the content and nature of the offense in this case, whether this case falls under an exception to the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court, based solely on the reasons stated in its opinion, concluded that the evidence collected through the seizure and search pursuant to the warrant at issue could not be used as evidence of guilt and found the charged facts at issue in this case not guilty. In this respect, the lower court erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the exception to the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence and by failing to conduct the necessary examination. The Prosecutor’s ground for appeal pointing out this error is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the portion of the lower court judgment finding not guilty is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for retrial and reconsideration of this portion, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2020DO14654]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Summary of the charges at issue\\n\\nThe Defendant, ① from around 2018. 1. 2. to around 2018. 12. 10., committed sexual abuse acts such as sexual harassment causing sexual humiliation against each of the 14 child and juvenile victims in the Attached Sheet of the judgment of the court below, “Amended Crime List I,” and at the same time produced obscene materials by using them; ② on 2019. 3. 1., distributed obscene materials using children and juveniles by transmitting photographs taken of the victim’s genital area, etc.; and ③ from around 2018. 6. 14. to around 2019. 1. 5., possessed a total of 229 items of obscene materials using children and juveniles.\\n\\n2. Judgment concerning the seizure pursuant to the warrant in this case\\n\\nA. The judgment of the court below\\n\\nThe court below, based on the reasons stated in its holding, determined that the procedure by which the mobile phone in this case, etc., owned by the Defendant, was seized from the Defendant’s residence pursuant to the warrant in this case was not unlawful, such as by violating the warrant principle or infringing the Defendant’s right to participate in the seizure and search proceedings.\\n\\nB. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\n\\n(1) Article 215(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides: “When necessary for a criminal investigation, the prosecutor may conduct seizure, search, or inspection by a warrant issued upon application to a judge of a district court, limited to property for which there are circumstances sufficient to suspect that the suspect committed the offense and which may be recognized as related to the case concerned.” Accordingly, if separate evidence unrelated to the criminal facts that formed the ground for issuance of the warrant is seized, such evidence cannot, in principle, be used as evidence of guilt. However, in the case of an offense that was the object of the seizure and search, or an offense related thereto, the results of such seizure and search may be used as evidence of guilt. A “crime related to the criminal suspicion stated in a seizure and search warrant” means a crime that has an objective connection with the suspected facts stated in the seizure and search warrant and a personal connection between the person subject to the warrant and the suspect. Among such crimes, “objective connection” with the suspected facts means a case directly related to the suspected facts themselves stated in the seizure and search warrant or to an offense having the same basic factual relationship as such facts; however, it may also be recognized where the evidence can be used as indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence to prove the motive and background of the offense, the means and method of the offense, the time and place of the offense, etc. At this time, objective connection should be recognized only where, taking into comprehensive consideration the content of the suspected facts stated in the seizure and search warrant, the object of the investigation, and the course of the investigation, there is a concrete and individual relationship, and such connection should not be deemed to exist merely because the suspected facts and the offense are of the same kind or similar. And the personal connection with the suspect refers to the offense of the person stated in the seizure and search warrant, but it may also be recognized in criminal cases against accomplices such as co-principals, instigators, and indirect principals, as well as necessary accomplices (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DO13489, decided 2017. 1. 25.; Supreme Court Decision 2017DO13458, decided 2017. 12. 5., etc.).\\n\\n(2) According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n(a) The police, based on the results of seizure and search regarding the Defendant’s Facebook account through which the victim communicated, confirmed that the subscriber to the access IP address of the account through which the offender conversed with the victim via Facebook Messenger was Non-Indicted Person 1 (the Defendant’s mother). The police further confirmed that Non-Indicted Person 2 (the Defendant’s father) and Non-Indicted Person 3 (the Defendant’s younger brother) were residing together on the resident registration record of Non-Indicted Person 1. At the time, the Defendant was residing at the above Facebook access location, but because his resident registration address was different, he did not appear on Non-Indicted Person 1’s resident registration record. The police, after identifying Non-Indicted Person 3 as the suspect, applied for a seizure and search warrant, and the judge of the district court issued the instant warrant as requested by the police.\\n\\n(b) In the instant warrant, the Defendant’s younger brother, “Non-Indicted Person 3,” is specified and stated as the suspect of the crime; “a.
