Therefore, with respect to a criminal case at first instance, since the district court main court and the district court branch court are separate courts under procedural law and are in an equal relationship, each sharing a certain territorial jurisdiction, the distribution of jurisdiction between the district court main court and the district court branch court is not merely a division of administrative affairs within the district court, as carried out between the district court main court and its branch court, but must be regarded as a distribution of territorial jurisdiction under procedural law. Therefore, unless there are special circumstances making it impossible to conclude that territorial jurisdiction at first instance is recognized for the district court main court pursuant to Article 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, territorial jurisdiction at first instance cannot be deemed to be recognized for the district court main court merely because territorial jurisdiction at first instance is recognized for the district court branch court.\\n\\nExamining the record in accordance with the foregoing legal principle, since Jindo-gun, Jeollanam-do, the place of the offense in this case, falls within the jurisdiction of the Haenam Branch Court of the Gwangju District Court, in this case in which the prosecutor filed an indictment with the Gwangju District Court main court, which is the court of first instance, on the ground that the Gwangju District Court main court also had territorial jurisdiction at first instance by reason of the place of the offense, it is proper that the court below, on the ground that territorial jurisdiction at first instance by reason of the place of the offense in this case exists only in the Haenam Branch Court of the Gwangju District Court, and that the jurisdictional district of a district court branch court cannot be interpreted as naturally included in the jurisdictional district of the district court main court, affirmed as it stood the first-instance judgment that had rendered a declaration of lack of jurisdiction with respect to this case. There is no illegality in that judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the distribution of jurisdiction between the district court main court and the district court branch court, etc.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged as stated in the Disposition, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning a request for adjudication is incorrect? (In case of dispute, according to judicial precedents)
A: If a request for adjudication is filed, the running of the Statute of Limitations for prosecution is suspended until the adjudication decision becomes final and conclusive, and the prosecutor who instituted the prosecution by the court’s decision to institute prosecution may amend the indictment so long as the identity of the charges is recognized, but may not withdraw the prosecution.
B: A request for adjudication may be withdrawn until the court renders its decision, and the effect of such withdrawal does not extend to other joint persons entitled to request.
C: Where, after the period for filing a request for adjudication has elapsed, a supplementary brief for request for adjudication is submitted and facts of accusation not originally subject to the request for adjudication are added as the subject of the request for adjudication, the request for adjudication as to the portion added in that supplementary brief is contrary to the legal form and thus unlawful.
D: With respect to a case for which a decision dismissing a request for adjudication has become final and conclusive, prosecution is barred except where other important evidence is discovered; here, a “case for which a decision dismissing a request for adjudication has become final and conclusive” means only a case that became the subject of a decision dismissing the request for adjudication after the court in charge of the request for adjudication actually conducted review and made a determination on the possibility and necessity of instituting prosecution.
E: If a complainant in prison submitted a request for adjudication to the warden of the prison, or to a person acting on behalf of the warden’s duties, within the period for filing a request for adjudication, then even if that request for adjudication did not reach the chief prosecutor of the district prosecutor’s office, or the chief of the branch office, to which the prosecutor who rendered the non-prosecution disposition belongs, within the above period, it shall be deemed to have been lawfully submitted.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2012DO14755]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. As to the argument alleging misapprehension of legal principles concerning the scope to which the effect of the restriction on prosecution extends\\n\\nArticle 262, paragraph 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides, “The court shall, within 3 months from the date it receives the petition for adjudication, render a decision in accordance mutatis mutandis with the procedure for an appeal, according to the classification of the following subparagraphs. In this case, it may examine evidence when necessary. 1. If the petition violates the legal form or is groundless, it shall dismiss the petition. 2. If the petition is well-founded, it shall decide to institute prosecution for the case.” Paragraph 4 of the same Article provides, “No appeal may be taken from a decision under paragraph 2. A case for which a decision under paragraph 2, subparagraph 1, has become final and conclusive may not be prosecuted except where other important evidence has been discovered.”\\n\\nThus, the fact that the latter sentence of Article 262, paragraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that a case for which a decision dismissing a petition for adjudication has become final and conclusive may not be prosecuted except where other important evidence has been discovered, on the one hand, takes into account that if a prosecutor were freely permitted to institute prosecution even though a decision dismissing a petition for adjudication has become final and conclusive by a court’s determination, the suspect could be left in an excessively prolonged state of uncertainty and judicial manpower and budget could be wasted on cases in which the possibility of a guilty verdict is low, thereby restricting the prosecutor’s institution of prosecution in cases where a decision dismissing a petition for adjudication has become final and conclusive; on the other hand, it takes into account that, since a court’s decision in a petition-for-adjudication case is not recognized as having the effect of res judicata, wholly prohibiting a prosecutor’s institution of prosecution merely on the ground that a decision dismissing a petition for adjudication has become final and conclusive, even where clear evidence proving the facts charged as guilty has been discovered, would result in a consequence contrary to justice.\\n\\nIn light of the above provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act and the legislative intent thereof, the “case for which a decision under paragraph 2, subparagraph 1, has become final and conclusive” referred to in the latter sentence of Article 262, paragraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act should be construed as meaning only a case that actually underwent a hearing and determination concerning the possibility and necessity of prosecution in the court in charge of the petition-for-adjudication case and thus became the subject of a decision dismissing the petition for adjudication.\\n\\nAccordingly, a case that was not the subject of a decision dismissing a petition for adjudication cannot be said to be a “case for which a decision under paragraph 2, subparagraph 1, has become final and conclusive” referred to in the latter sentence of Article 262, paragraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and this cannot be viewed differently even if the case that was not the subject of a decision dismissing a petition for adjudication was included in the complainant’s complaint.\\n\\nThe court below, on the ground that the facts charged in each criminal fact set forth in serial numbers 1 through 23 of the schedule (1) in the judgment of Changwon District Court Case 2011GODAN2541 were not included in the facts charged in the non-prosecution decision dated June 10, 2010, issued by the Changwon District Prosecutors’ Office in Case 2010HYEONGJE6745, which was the subject of the hearing and determination for the decision dismissing the petition for adjudication in this case, did not accept the Defendant’s argument that “the portion of this prosecution was unlawful because, although the decision dismissing the complainant Nonparty’s petition for adjudication concerning the above criminal facts became final and conclusive, this prosecution was instituted without other important evidence.”\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the above determination by the court below is proper. There is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the scope of the prohibition on prosecution provided in Article 262, paragraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act or failure to conduct the necessary hearing.\\n\\n2. As to the argument alleging misapprehension of legal principles concerning the intent of unlawful appropriation in the crime of embezzlement\\n\\nExamining the evidence duly admitted and examined by the court below and the first instance court, the court below properly found the facts charged in serial numbers 5 through 12 of the crime list set forth in the judgment of Changwon District Court Case 2010GODAN3078 and serial numbers 3 through 28 of schedule (1) set forth in the judgment of Changwon District Court Case 2011GODAN2541 to be guilty for the reasons stated in its judgment. There is no illegality such as violating the rules of logic and experience, thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehending the legal principles concerning the intent of unlawful appropriation in the crime of embezzlement.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the Justices of the Supreme Court participating in this case unanimously render the judgment as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[88DO2428]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal advanced by the Defendant’s counsel.\\n\\nWith respect to Point 1,\\n\\nAccording to Article 260 of the Criminal Procedure Act, when there is a decision subject to adjudication under Article 262(1)2 of the same Act, the institution of prosecution shall be deemed to have been made with respect to that case; therefore, thereafter, just as in ordinary trial proceedings, amendment of the charge and the applicable statutory provisions is possible so long as the basic factual relations are identical, and this legal principle is not altered by the fact that Article 263 of the Criminal Procedure Act has opened the way for a petition for adjudication only with respect to offenses under Articles 123 through 125 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court’s permission of the additional amendment of the charge and applicable statutory provisions for quasi-forcible indecent assault, which stands in an ideal concurrence relationship with the cruel treatment brought to adjudication in this case, and its treating the same as within the scope of adjudication, is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of law as alleged.\\n\\nWith respect to Point 2,\\n\\nAccording to the evidence cited in the first-instance judgment affirmed by the lower court, all of the facts constituting the offense in this case against the Defendant may be recognized; therefore, there is no illegality in violation of the rules of evidence as alleged in the lower court’s judgment.\\n\\nWith respect to Point 3,\\n\\nIn the case of a judgment in which a sentence of imprisonment for less than 10 years and a sentence of suspension of qualifications have been imposed, as in this case, the contention that the sentence is improper cannot constitute a lawful ground for final appeal under the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nAll of the arguments are without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and among the days of detention after the filing of the appeal, a part is counted toward the term of imprisonment, and the judgment is rendered as ordered, with the opinions of the judges in attendance being in agreement."}

{"[97MO30]": "We review the grounds for the Re-appellant’s re-appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the portion filed after the period for filing an application for adjudication\\nUpon examination of the record, it is clear that in the application for adjudication filed with the court below on October 9, 1996, the Re-appellant specified only the act of making donations on March 5, 1996 and on the 23rd of the same month, and the act of publicizing false facts about the opposing candidate C through speeches and election campaign materials, as the subjects of the application for adjudication; and that only in the supplemental statement of application for adjudication filed with the court below on December 12, 1996 did the Re-appellant add as the subject of the application for adjudication the reported facts of the complaint, namely, the act of distributing business cards bearing the false career description of “D Central Committee Member” on February 9, 1996 and on the 10th of the same month, the act of sending New Year’s cards in or around late December 1995, the act of selling by unattended self-service the booklet “E” at Sosa Catholic Church on February 25, 1996, and the act of distributing envelopes containing business cards and “E,” etc. at a snack bar located in Songnae-dong, Sosa-gu, on the 26th of the same month. If the circumstances are as such, the application for adjudication filed on October 9, 1996 cannot be said to include the portion added in the supplemental statement of application for adjudication, and, according to the record, the supplemental statement of application for adjudication was filed after the time limit for filing an application for adjudication prescribed by Article 273(1) of the Public Official Election and Prevention of Election Fraud Act, as is clearly evident from the chronology; therefore, the application for adjudication concerning the portion added in the supplemental statement of application for adjudication is contrary to legal form and thus improper.\\nAlso, even if the act of sending New Year’s cards in or around late December 1995 were recognized as constituting the charged facts as alleged, it would be difficult to regard it as falling under the subjects of an application for adjudication enumerated in Article 273(1) of the Public Official Election and Prevention of Election Fraud Act. Therefore, the application for adjudication regarding the above reported facts is also improper as being directed to an offense that does not fall within the subject matter of an application for adjudication.\\nIn the end, the court below’s determination dismissing the application for adjudication with respect to each of the above reported facts is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error therein. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n2. Regarding the donation act on March 5, 1996\\nFirst, according to the reasons stated in the decision of the court below, the court below found that it could not recognize the fact that the suspect distributed the “E” booklet, priced at 5,000 won, free of charge at the date, time, and place stated in the judgment, but only found that he sold the same booklet at 1,000 won per copy; and upon comparing the record and examining it, there is no basis to find a factual error due to violation of the rules of evidence.\\nAnd where there is an application for adjudication regarding the propriety of a prosecutor’s disposition not to institute prosecution, the court may dismiss the application for adjudication if, even though the prosecutor’s non-prosecution disposition of no suspicion is unlawful, it is recognized in light of the various circumstances shown in the record that the case is one for which a non-prosecution disposition of suspension of indictment would be appropriate (see Supreme Court Decision 94MO33 dated June 24, 1995, Supreme Court Decision 96MO1 dated March 11, 1996, Supreme Court Decision 96MO53 dated July 16, 1996, etc.). The court below further determined that the suspect’s above act constitutes a donation act prohibited by the Public Official Election and Prevention of Election Fraud Act, so the prosecutor’s non-prosecution disposition of no suspicion on this point was erroneous; however, on the other hand, according to the statements of F and G, the publicity director F, as a result of inquiring of the election management committee, heard the reply that there might be a problem if the booklet were distributed free of charge, and misunderstood this to mean that it would be sufficient merely to sell it for a fee, thereby engaging in the above donation act. Taking this into account, the court below determined that the above suspected facts were appropriate for a non-prosecution disposition of suspension of indictment. In light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the court below’s determination is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error as argued. This argument also lacks merit.\\n\\n3. Regarding each donation act on March 23, 1996 and on the 25th of the same month\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the decision of the court below, the court below determined that there was no evidence to recognize that the suspect directly distributed the “E” and “J” booklets to H and I at the date, time, and place stated in the judgment, or manifested an intention to distribute them, and that there was also no evidence to recognize that the suspect was involved in the fact that H and I brought the party-member booklet from the district party office; and upon comparing the record and examining it, such determination by the court below is proper, and there is no error therein as argued. This argument also lacks merit.\\n\\n4. Regarding each act of publicizing false facts through speeches and statutory election campaign materials\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the decision of the court below, after the court below selected and weighed the evidence as stated in the judgment, it determined that with respect to the portion concerning C’s United States permanent residency, and the portion concerning campaign contribution money, the suspect cannot be regarded as having recognized that the contents publicized were objectively false; that with respect to the portion concerning collusion with the K regime, there is no evidence to show that the facts stated are false facts; and that with respect to the portions concerning being a liar and illicit accumulation of wealth, the factual elements of the statements are so vague and broad that they cannot be said to be facts whose objective truth can be verified, and it is appropriate to view them as a subjective evaluation of the other party’s honesty. Accordingly, it determined that the prosecutor’s non-prosecution disposition on the ground of no suspicion with respect to each of those portions was not erroneous, and that the application for adjudication thereon lacked merit. Upon comparing and reviewing the record, the court below’s above determination is understandable, and there is no basis for finding any error therein. The argument on this point also lacks merit.\\n\\n5. Therefore, the re-appeal is dismissed, and it is so ordered by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[98MO127]": "We consider the grounds for reappeal.\\n\\nAccording to the provisions of Article 260, paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, a person who has filed a complaint for offenses under Articles 123 through 125 of the Criminal Act must, within 10 days from the day on which he received notice from the prosecutor that prosecution will not be instituted, file in writing a petition for adjudication through the chief prosecutor or branch chief prosecutor of the district prosecutor's office to which that prosecutor belongs, and Article 262, item 1 of the same Act provides that when a petition violates the legal form or is groundless, the petition shall be dismissed; according to the record, the re-appellant received notice from the prosecutor on 1998. 7. 24. that prosecution would not be instituted, and it is clear that the petition for adjudication in this case was received by the Incheon District Prosecutors' Office on 8. 6. of the same year, after 10 days had elapsed therefrom, and the court below dismissed the petition for adjudication in this case, one of the reasons being that it was unlawful because it had been filed after the filing period had expired.\\n\\nThe second ground for reappeal is to the effect that, at the time the re-appellant prepared the petition for adjudication in this case, the re-appellant, as an inmate, had prepared and submitted the petition for adjudication to a correctional officer at the Incheon Detention Center on 8. 1. of the same year, within the period for filing a petition for adjudication, and therefore the period should be deemed to have been complied with; however, since there is no special provision in the Criminal Procedure Act such as Article 344, paragraph 1 with respect to a petition for adjudication, the petition for adjudication must reach the chief prosecutor or branch chief prosecutor of the district prosecutor's office to which the prosecutor who made the non-prosecution disposition belongs within the period prescribed by Article 260, paragraph 2 of the same Act, and even if a complainant in custody submitted the petition for adjudication to the warden of the prison or a person acting on his duties within that period, so long as the petition for adjudication did not reach the chief prosecutor or branch chief prosecutor of the district prosecutor's office to which the prosecutor who made the non-prosecution disposition belongs within the above period, this cannot be regarded as the filing of a lawful petition for adjudication. In the end, the decision of the court below dismissing the petition for adjudication in this case is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality therein. The argument is without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, without need to determine the first ground for reappeal, the reappeal is dismissed, and by the unanimous opinion of the participating justices, it is so decided as stated in the operative part."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning special criminal procedures are all correct? (In case of dispute, according to precedents) (a) Once the chief of a police station has issued a notice disposition for an offense subject to a notice disposition, since the offender who pays the fine in accordance with the notice disposition is afforded an opportunity to be exempted from criminal prosecution and criminal punishment, until the fine payment period specified in the notice disposition expires, the chief of a police station, as a matter of principle, may not request a summary trial, and the prosecutor may not institute a prosecution for the same offense subject to a notice disposition. (b) In summary trial proceedings, a suspect interrogation protocol prepared by a judicial police officer in accordance with lawful procedure and method is admissible as evidence even if the defendant, who had been the suspect, does not admit its contents; corroborating evidence for a confession is not required, but the confession exclusionary rule still applies. (c) A summary order becomes effective upon service of the written judgment on the defendant, and even where defense counsel exists, it is not necessarily required that a copy of the summary order be served on defense counsel; therefore, the period for filing a formal trial request must be calculated from the date of notice of the summary order to the defendant. (d) The principle of prohibition against increasing the type of punishment prescribed in Article 457-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act applies unchanged, even in a case where a case for which only the defendant requested a formal trial and another case are jointly tried and thereafter punished as concurrent offenses, and the same applies to an appeal from a first-instance judgment that imposed a fine in a case where only the defendant requested a formal trial. (e) Where multiple acts corresponding to the same offense name are continuously committed over a certain period under a single and continuous intent, and the protected legal interest harmed is also the same, so that the offenses are in the relationship of a comprehensive single offense, if a summary order has become final and conclusive with respect to part of such offenses, the res judicata of the summary order extends, based on the time of issuance of the summary order, not only to offenses that constitute part of the comprehensive single offense committed before that time, but also to other offenses in the relationship of ideal concurrence with them.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2017DO13409]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. The Act on Punishment of Minor Offenses provides in Chapter 3, as “Special Provisions for Punishment of Minor Offenses,” for notice disposition concerning offending acts (Article 7), payment of the penalty surcharge (Articles 8 and 8-2), and handling of persons who fail to comply with the notice disposition, etc. (Article 9). A person who has received a notice disposition of a penalty surcharge from the chief of the police station shall pay the penalty surcharge within 10 days from the date of receipt of the notice disposition document, and a person who has not paid the penalty surcharge within the above period shall pay the amount increased by 20/100 of the notified penalty surcharge within 20 days from the day following the last day of the above period (Article 8, paragraphs (1) and (2)). With respect to a person who has failed to pay the penalty surcharge within the payment period under Article 8, paragraph (2) of the Act on Punishment of Minor Offenses, the chief of the police station shall request a summary trial without delay (Article 9, paragraph (1), subparagraph 2), and even if a summary trial is requested, if, before the pronouncement thereof, the defendant pays the amount increased by 50/100 of the notified penalty surcharge and submits documentary proof thereof, the chief of the police station shall cancel the request for summary trial (Article 9, paragraph (2)). A person who has paid the notified penalty surcharge in this way shall not be punished again for that offending act (Article 8, paragraph (3), Article 9, paragraph (3)).\\n\\nIn light of the content of the foregoing provisions and the legislative purpose of the notice disposition, the penalty surcharge system under the Act on Punishment of Minor Offenses is one that provides, for offending acts, a special exception to punishment whereby, if the penalty surcharge is paid pursuant to the notice disposition by the chief of the police station prior to criminal procedure, prosecution is not instituted against the person who pays it, and thus differs from court trial procedures in institutional purpose and legal nature (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2012DO6612, decided September 13, 2012). In addition, even if the offender fails to comply with the notice disposition, the principle of exclusive prosecutorial power is exceptionally recognized, and the chief of the police station’s request for summary trial enables the case to be handled simply, swiftly, and properly without going through trial proceedings, thereby promoting litigation economy; moreover, by allowing the offender to avoid criminal punishment if the penalty surcharge is paid before the pronouncement of the summary trial, it affords the offender an opportunity to be exempted from criminal prosecution and criminal punishment.\\n\\nTherefore, once the chief of the police station has issued a notice disposition concerning an offending act, in order to protect the offender’s procedural status as described above, as a general rule the chief of the police station may not request a summary trial until the payment period for the penalty surcharge set forth in the notice disposition has expired, and the prosecutor likewise may not institute a public prosecution for the same offending act.\\n\\n2. The court below determined as follows. In the fraud case of the first instance, 2017GODAN387, in which the defendant obtained food by deception without the intent or ability to pay the price and thereby defrauded the provider, the chief of the police station issued a notice disposition concerning the same offending act as the facts charged, and the prosecutor instituted a public prosecution in that fraud case before the penalty surcharge payment period had expired. Such institution of public prosecution corresponds to a case where the procedure is void for violation of the provisions of law, and the public prosecution must therefore be dismissed.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the legal principles set forth above, the determination of the court below is proper. There is no error in the determination of the court below, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning notice disposition and summary trial under the Act on Punishment of Minor Offenses.\\n\\n3. The prosecutor’s appeal is without merit, and is therefore dismissed. It is so adjudged unanimously by the Justices of the Supreme Court, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2017MO1557]": "The grounds for re-appeal are examined.\\n\\nArticle 452 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that notice of a summary order shall be effected by service of the written judgment on the prosecutor and the defendant; therefore, a summary order takes effect upon service of the written judgment on the defendant, and even where defense counsel exists, it is not necessarily required that a copy of the summary order be served on defense counsel. Accordingly, the period for filing a request for a formal trial must be computed from the date on which the summary order was notified to the defendant (see Supreme Court Decision 2016MO2711 dated December 2, 2016).\\n\\nEven if the defendant, believing that defense counsel would submit the request for a formal trial, failed to submit the request for a formal trial within the lawful period for requesting a formal trial on his or her own, that does not fall within a case where the defendant failed to request a formal trial within the period for requesting a formal trial due to a cause not attributable to the defendant or the representative (see Supreme Court Decision 2006MO658 dated January 12, 2007).\\n\\nThe court below, after recognizing the fact that a copy of the summary order in this case was served on Re-appellant 1 on February 3, 2017 and on Re-appellant 2 on February 22 of the same month, respectively, then upheld the first-instance decision that dismissed the petition for restoration of the right to request a formal trial on the ground that, although the counsel for the re-appellants filed, on March 22, 2017, a petition for restoration of the formal-trial request right together with a request for a formal trial after seven days had elapsed from the date of notice of the summary order to the re-appellants, it could not be deemed, in light of the circumstances stated in its reasoning, that the re-appellants’ failure to request a formal trial within the lawful period for requesting a formal trial was attributable to a cause not attributable to the re-appellants or their representative, and that there was no other material to recognize this.\\n\\nExamining these factual circumstances in light of the legal principles stated above, the above determination of the court below is proper. There is no error in violation of the Constitution, statutes, orders, or rules that affected the judgment, as alleged in the grounds for re-appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, all re-appeals are dismissed, and it is so decided as stated in the order, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2020DO355]": "The Court examines the matter ex officio.\\n\\n1. Article 457-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides, “With respect to a case in which the defendant has filed a petition for a formal trial, the court shall not impose a punishment of a more severe type than the punishment prescribed in the summary order.” and thus establishes the principle prohibiting an increase in the type of punishment in cases of a petition for a formal trial. The above principle prohibiting an increase in the type of punishment also applies, as it stands, to the case for which the defendant filed a petition for a formal trial, even where that case is consolidated and tried together with another case and thereafter adjudicated as concurrent crimes (see Supreme Court Decision 2019DO15700, rendered on January 9, 2020).\\n\\n2. According to the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. On September 5, 2019, the Seoul Central District Court, in case No. 2019GODAN1760 of that court concerning the defendant (hereinafter referred to as the “First Case”), found the defendant guilty of each offense of fraud, injury, and interference with business, and sentenced the defendant to imprisonment for 1 year and 2 months.\\n\\nb. On November 26, 2018, the Seoul Central District Court issued a summary order imposing a fine of KRW 3,000,000 on the defendant for the offenses of assault and insult, and thereafter, in case No. 2019GOJEONG1468 of that court (hereinafter referred to as the “Second Case”), in which the defendant’s petition for restoration of a formal trial was granted, the court found the defendant guilty of each of the above offenses on September 26, 2019 and sentenced the defendant to a fine of KRW 3,000,000.\\n\\nc. On December 12, 2019, the lower court, on the ground that the appellate case in the First Case and the appellate case in the Second Case had been consolidated, set aside all of the above first-instance judgments, then found the defendant guilty of each of the above offenses and selected imprisonment for each offense, and after applying an aggravated punishment for recidivism and an aggravated punishment for concurrent crimes, sentenced the defendant to imprisonment for 1 year and 2 months within the range of the punishment to be imposed.\\n\\n3. If the foregoing factual relationship is examined in light of the legal principle stated above, the Second Case is a case in which only the defendant filed a petition for a formal trial; accordingly, in accordance with the principle prohibiting an increase in the type of punishment, it was not permissible to select imprisonment, which is a punishment of a more severe type than the fine in the summary order, for each of the offenses, and furthermore, even if the Second Case was consolidated and tried together with the First Case at the appellate stage and adjudicated as concurrent crimes, imprisonment should not have been imposed for the Second Case. Nevertheless, in the appellate trial of the Second Case, the lower court selected imprisonment, which is a punishment of a more severe type than the fine in the summary order, for each offense, and then, through aggravation for concurrent crimes, etc., imposed a single term of imprisonment on the defendant for each offense in the First Case and each offense in the Second Case. The lower court judgment contains an error in violating the principle prohibiting an increase in the type of punishment set forth in Article 457-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without examining the grounds for appeal, the Court reverses the lower court judgment and remands the case to the lower court for further trial and determination, and so it renders a judgment in accordance with the operative part by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2020DO3705]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Where a judgment has become final and conclusive with respect to part of an offense constituting a crime of continuous concurrence, the res judicata effect of the final judgment extends, as of the time of the pronouncement of the judgment by the trial of facts, and where a summary order has become final and conclusive, as of the time of the issuance of the summary order, to offenses committed prior thereto (see Supreme Court Decision 94DO1318, dated August 9, 1994, and Supreme Court Decision 2009DO39, dated February 26, 2009, etc.). In addition, the res judicata effect of a final judgment on one offense among offenses in concurrent offense relations in an apparent concurrence also extends to the other offenses (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DO10233, dated February 23, 2007, etc.). Therefore, where a judgment has become final and conclusive, or a summary order has become final and conclusive, with respect to part of an offense constituting a crime of continuous concurrence, and the offense committed prior thereto, as of the time of the pronouncement of the trial-court judgment or the issuance of the summary order, not only falls within part of the crime of continuous concurrence but also constitutes another offense in concurrent offense relations with it, the res judicata effect of the final judgment or summary order also extends, as stated above, to the other offense in concurrent offense relations (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DO6273, dated November 23, 2006).\\n\\n2. For the reasons stated in the judgment, the court below determined that the portions of the facts charged in this case corresponding to items 1 through 7 of Attached Table 1 of the crime list in the judgment below, namely, violations of the Act on Special Cases concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Violence Crimes (obscene acts by use of communications media), items 2 through 8 of Attached Table 2 of the crime list in the judgment below, namely, violations of the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc. (defamation), and items 1 through 4 of Attached Table 3 of the crime list in the judgment below, namely, insult, fell under “where there is a final and conclusive judgment” under Article 326 subparagraph 1 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and therefore ruled in the main text or reasons that the prosecution was dismissed. Examining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in that the court below failed to conduct the necessary examination, thereby violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the bounds of the free evaluation of evidence, or misunderstood the legal principles concerning concurrent offense relations.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Prosecutor filed an appeal against the entire judgment below, but did not state in the petition of appeal or the statement of grounds for appeal any reasons for objection with respect to the conviction portion.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning preservation of evidence under Article 184 of the Criminal Procedure Act (A) and a petition for witness examination under Article 221-2 (B) is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: A may not be petitioned before the suspect or defendant has been formally booked in a criminal case.
B: A matter that constitutes suspect interrogation cannot be petitioned by the A method, and even if the suspect is interrogated by the A method and the contents of that interrogation include a statement concerning another accomplice, if that accomplice had not been formally booked at the time of the interrogation, the effect of preservation of evidence concerning that accomplice cannot be recognized.
C: When a judge conducts witness examination under the A procedure, the prosecutor, suspect, or defense counsel must be notified in advance of the date and place of the witness examination and given an opportunity to participate in the witness examination; however, even if no opportunity to participate was given, if the defendant and defense counsel agreed that the witness examination record may be used as evidence and, without any special objection, it was lawfully subjected to evidentiary examination, the said witness examination record is admissible.
D: Even where a reference person who made a voluntary statement to a prosecutor or judicial police officer is likely to make a statement at the trial date different from the prior statement, and where that statement is recognized as indispensable to proving the offense, the prosecutor may petition a judge for examination of that person as a witness pursuant to the B procedure only before the first trial date.
E: A witness examination record conducted under the procedures of A and B is admissible pursuant to Article 311 of the Criminal Procedure Act.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[79DO792]": "We consider the grounds for appeal by the Prosecutor.\\n\\n(1) It is proper to hold that preservation of evidence under Article 184 of the Criminal Procedure Act may not be requested before the defendant or suspect has even been formally booked in a criminal case, and that matters falling under the examination of a suspect may not be requested by way of preservation of evidence. According to the records of this case, the application for preservation of evidence concerned the time when the co-defendant in the court below was a suspect (see the cover sheet of the application record and the petition in 78CHO87), but the contents of the examination state that the same co-defendant was examined as a witness.\\n\\nThis constitutes an unlawful direct examination of the suspect as a witness regarding the facts suspected against himself, and therefore it lacks evidentiary admissibility against that co-defendant; moreover, even if the examination contains statements concerning another accomplice, if that accomplice was also not formally booked at the time of the examination, the effect of preservation of evidence concerning that accomplice cannot be recognized. In this case, since the court below properly found that the defendant had not been formally booked at the time of the above preservation of evidence, the legal determination of the court below to the foregoing effect is proper, and there is no misapprehension of the legal principle concerning preservation of evidence.\\n\\nAccordingly, the argument criticizing this point is without merit.\\n\\n(2) The reasoning given by the court below for not finding the defendant guilty of the offense of uttering an altered private document is also persuasive, and there is no error therein contrary to the rules of experience or logic.\\n\\nThus, the judgment of the court below is proper, and as the Prosecutor's appeal is without merit, it is dismissed, and it is adjudged as stated in the disposition in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the judges concerned."}

{"[79DO792]": "We consider the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal.\\n\\n(1) It is reasonable to say that preservation of evidence under Article 184 of the Criminal Procedure Act cannot be requested before the defendant or suspect has even been criminally booked, and that matters corresponding to examination of a suspect cannot be requested by way of preservation of evidence. According to the record of this case, the application for preservation of evidence concerned the period when the co-defendant in the court below was a suspect (see the cover sheet of the application record and the petition in 78CHO 87), and, looking at the content of the examination, it is stated that the same co-defendant was examined as a witness.\\n\\nThis constitutes an unlawful direct examination of the suspect as a witness regarding his own suspected facts, and is unlawful, so that it has no evidentiary admissibility against the same co-defendant; moreover, even if there are statements concerning another accomplice among the content of the examination, if that accomplice also had not been criminally booked at the time of the examination, the effect of preservation of evidence concerning that accomplice cannot be recognized. In this case, the fact that the Defendant had not been booked at the time of the above preservation of evidence was lawfully recognized by the court below, so the legal judgment of the court below to the above effect is proper, and there is no misapprehension of the legal principles concerning preservation of evidence.\\n\\nTherefore, the argument criticizing this point is without merit.\\n\\n(2) The court below’s statement of reasons for not recognizing the Defendant as guilty of the offense of uttering a falsified private document is also persuasive, and there is no error therein contrary to the rules of experience or logic.\\n\\nAccordingly, the judgment of the court below is proper, and since the Prosecutor’s appeal is without merit, it is dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[86DO1646]": "1. Determination on the First Point of the Grounds of Final Appeal by the Defendant and Counsel\\nEven if the co-defendant in the court below and the Defendant were in a relationship of exchanging bribes and thus were in a relationship of necessary accomplices, the prosecutor may, where necessary in order to preserve evidence against the Defendant in advance at the investigation stage, petition a judge to examine the co-defendant in the court below as a witness (see this Court’s 1966.5.17. rendered 66DO276 judgment; 1966.6.28. rendered 66DO482 judgment; 1968.12.17. rendered 67DO1067 judgment, etc.). According to the record, it is persuasive that the judge of the Seoul Criminal District Court determined that it was necessary to examine the co-defendant in the court below as a witness in order to preserve evidence against the Defendant in advance, and, upon the prosecutor’s petition, examined the co-defendant in the court below as a witness. However, where a judge conducts witness examination as an evidence-preservation procedure under Article 184 of the Criminal Procedure Act, unlike in the case of witness examination under Article 221-2 of the same Act, it should be deemed necessary, pursuant to Article 163 of the same Act, to give the prosecutor, suspect, or defense counsel advance notice of the date and place of the witness examination and an opportunity to participate therein (see this Court’s 1965.12.10. rendered 65DO826 judgment). According to the record, it is true, as the Defendant asserts, that in examining the co-defendant in the court below as a witness, the judge of the Seoul Criminal District Court did not give the Defendant an opportunity to participate in the witness examination; however, it is clear that the Defendant and defense counsel, at the first-instance court hearing (the 4th trial date), consented that the above witness examination record concerning the co-defendant in the court below could be used as evidence and that the evidence was duly examined without any particular objection. Accordingly, the above witness examination record must be deemed to have been given admissibility as evidence regardless of whether the witness examination procedure was unlawful. In the end, the argument to the effect that the above witness examination record lacks admissibility as evidence is without merit.\\n\\n2. Determination on the Second Point of the Same Grounds of Final Appeal\\nWhen, at the 9th trial date of the first instance, the prosecutor requested an amendment regarding the part of the 1st trial transcript in which the Defendant’s statement was recorded and stated an objection as to the accuracy of the entries in the trial transcript, counsel expressed an opinion to the effect that the entries in that trial transcript were accurate. However, the presiding judge of the first instance determined that the prosecutor’s request was well-founded and ordered the court clerk present to amend the entries in the 1st trial transcript as requested by the prosecutor, and the court clerk present re-entered the contents of the Defendant’s statement in the amended form in the 9th trial transcript. It is clear from the record that, in subsequent questioning, the Defendant stated to the same effect as recorded in the 1st trial transcript. If so, the result is that two trial transcripts containing different contents with respect to the same matter coexist. In such a case, the two trial transcripts should be regarded as having the same probative force, so that there can be no superiority or inferiority in their probative force. Therefore, when the contents of the two trial transcripts are contradictory, which trial transcript’s contents are to be regarded as true is a matter of assessing the probative force of the trial transcript and can only be left to the free conviction of the judge. Accordingly, it cannot necessarily be deemed unlawful that the first-instance judgment or the judgment below used as evidence of guilt the contents of the 9th trial transcript of the first instance as amended. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n3. Determination on the Third Point of the Same Grounds of Final Appeal\\nWith respect to the 3rd interrogation record of the suspect concerning the co-defendant in the court below prepared by the prosecutor and the testimony of witness Ha Heung-ye at the first-instance court hearing, in light of the results of the evidentiary examination at the first instance and in the court below, it is recognized that the statements of the co-defendant in the court below and Ha Heung-ye were made voluntarily; thus, this argument is also without merit.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Fourth Point of the Same Grounds of Final Appeal\\nComparing the evidence adopted by the judgment below and the first-instance judgment cited by the judgment below with the record and reviewing them, it can be fully recognized that the Defendant, at around 19:00 on 1985.6.26., received 4,500,000 won in cash as a bribe in connection with his official duties from the co-defendant in the court below at the cafeteria of the Security Headquarters Investigation Unit 2, and it cannot be said that the judgment below violated the rules governing the weighing of evidence and unlawfully found facts without relying on evidence. The argument is also without merit.\\n\\n5. Ultimately, since the Defendant’s final appeal is without merit, the participating Justices are unanimous in deciding to dismiss it, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

{"[94HEONBA1]": "1. Overview of the Case and Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nA. Overview of the Case\\n\\nOn 1993. 7. 31., the Petitioner was indicted in the criminal case 93GOHAP1570 for special obstruction of the execution of official duties resulting in death, etc., before the Seoul Criminal District Court. Prior to that, on the 29th of the same month, that court, in case 93CHO3657, examined as a witness under Article 221-2(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, upon the prosecutor’s request, the Petitioner’s non-party witness Shin ◯-gyun, who had witnessed the case. The prosecutor submitted the record so prepared as evidence in the said criminal case, and the court decided to admit it as evidence.\\n\\nAccordingly, while the said criminal case was pending, the Petitioner, on the ground that Article 221-2(2) and (5) of the Criminal Procedure Act, which formed the basis for the examination of witness Shin ◯-gyun, did not guarantee the defendant’s right of cross-examination, but the record prepared at that time was nevertheless admissible in evidence under Article 311 of the Criminal Procedure Act, contended that, as a result, the said provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act infringed Article 12(1) and (4), Article 27(1), (3), and (4), and Article 37 of the Constitution, which guarantee due process of law, the right to assistance of counsel, the right to a fair trial, the right to a public trial, and the right to be presumed innocent, and that whether they were unconstitutional was a prerequisite to the judgment in the case. On that basis, in case 93CHO4943 before the same court, the Petitioner filed a motion for a request for adjudication on whether the said provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act were unconstitutional. When the Petitioner’s motion was dismissed on 1993. 12. 20., and the order of dismissal was served on the Petitioner on the 27th of the same month, the Petitioner filed the present constitutional complaint on 1994. 1. 8. pursuant to Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act.\\n\\nB. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe subject matter of review in this case is whether Article 221-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act (hereinafter the “Act”) (added by Act No. 2450 on 1973. 1. 25.) paragraph (2) (hereinafter “the paragraph (2) at issue”) and the portion of paragraph (5) concerning paragraph (2) (hereinafter “the paragraph (5) at issue”) are unconstitutional.\\n\\nArticle 221-2 (Request for Examination of Witness)  \\n(2) Where a person who has voluntarily made a statement to a prosecutor or judicial police officer pursuant to the provisions of the preceding Article is likely to make a statement different from the previous statement at the trial date, and where such statement is deemed indispensable for proving the offense, the prosecutor may, only before the first trial date, request a judge to examine such person as a witness.  \\n(3), (4) Omitted.  \\n(5) Where the judge deems that there is no impediment to the investigation, the judge may allow the defendant, suspect, or counsel to participate in the examination of a witness upon a request under paragraph (1) or (2).  \\n(6) Omitted.\\n\\n2. The Petitioner’s Arguments and the Opinions of Interested Parties\\n\\nA. Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\n(1) Because the provisions at issue prescribe a system that confers evidentiary admissibility, depending on whether they are unconstitutional or not, the outcome of the related trial may differ. Accordingly, the prerequisite to judgment is satisfied.\\n\\n(2) Considering Article 12(1) and (4) and Article 27(1), (3), and (4) of the Constitution together, it is clear that our Constitution guarantees the right to receive a “fair trial.” In criminal trial proceedings, the right to examine witnesses against oneself is an essential and core element of the right to a fair trial. The statutory provisions at issue violate the constitutional right to a fair trial by recognizing evidentiary admissibility for testimony and the record thereof in witness-examination proceedings conducted without providing an opportunity for cross-examination, and moreover they contravene Article 37 of the Constitution, which provides that when fundamental rights are restricted by law, the essential content of such rights may not be infringed.\\n\\nB. Grounds for the Court’s Rejection of the Request for Referral\\n\\n(1) In order for the prerequisite to judgment to exist, the provisions at issue must be such that, depending on whether they are unconstitutional, the court in charge of the case would render a different judgment. However, in the above criminal trial against the Petitioner, if the Petitioner were found not guilty, the probative value of the pre-trial witness-examination record would be rejected, and thus there would be no prerequisite to judgment; and even if the Petitioner were found guilty, the same result could be reached solely on the basis of the testimony given by Shin ◯-gyun at the trial date in the criminal procedure, which had the same substance as that recorded, excluding the above pre-trial witness-examination record. Therefore, there would likewise be no prerequisite to judgment in that case.\\n\\n(2) The pre-trial witness-examination procedure for Shin ◯-gyun was conducted with the participation of the Petitioner and his counsel, Attorney Yu Seon-ho, and with cross-examination. In addition, Shin ◯-gyun later appeared again as a witness for the defense at the 4th trial date in the said criminal procedure and was examined sufficiently by defense counsel; the substance of his testimony was also largely the same as the substance of his testimony in the pre-trial witness-examination procedure. Accordingly, the Petitioner was not deprived of his “right to a fair trial.”\\n\\nC. Opinion of the Prosecutor General\\n\\nThe legislature has broad legislative discretion with respect to systems conferring evidentiary admissibility in criminal procedure. Our Criminal Procedure Act separately prescribes, according to the type of evidence, the methods and standards for conferring evidentiary admissibility, while also providing exceptional provisions that confer evidentiary admissibility on evidence prepared under certain conditions or circumstances even without a separate act of conferring evidentiary admissibility. The provisions at issue were enacted within the scope of the legislature’s legislative discretion and do not infringe the Petitioner’s fundamental rights.\\n\\n3. Judgment\\n\\nA. Judgment on Procedural Admissibility\\n\\nArticle 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act provides that “where a motion to request an adjudication on whether a statute is unconstitutional under Article 41(1) is dismissed, the party who made such motion may file a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court.” Article 41(1) of the Constitutional Court Act provides that “where whether a statute violates the Constitution becomes a prerequisite to judgment, the court in charge of the case shall, by decision ex officio or upon motion by a party, request the Constitutional Court to adjudicate on the constitutionality thereof.” Therefore, a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act may be filed only when whether the statutory provision subject to review violates the Constitution has become a prerequisite to judgment in the related case.\\n\\nHere, the term “judgment” means a judgment regardless of form, such as a judgment, decision, or order, and regardless of whether it concerns the merits or the procedural aspects of the case (see Constitutional Court Decision 91HEONGA3, rendered on 1994. 2. 24.), and includes not only final judgments that definitively conclude a stage of litigation but also interlocutory judgments. This is because when a judge, as a court, must make a judicial determination, and when the conclusion of that determination would differ depending on whether a certain statutory provision is unconstitutional, the principle of rule of law and the purport of Article 111(1)1 and Article 107(1) of the Constitution, which confer upon the Constitutional Court the power to adjudicate the constitutionality of statutes, require that the court first request the Constitutional Court to adjudicate on the constitutionality of the statute and then decide the case in accordance with the Constitutional Court’s decision.\\n\\nTherefore, even if a court’s decision to admit evidence under Article 295 of the Act is not a judgment that definitively concludes the case, it shall itself be deemed a judgment within the meaning of Article 107(1) of the Constitution and Articles 41(1) and 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act, as a judicial determination by a court.\\n\\nIn addition, for a certain statutory provision to be deemed a prerequisite to judgment, it means a case in which, depending on whether the provision is unconstitutional, the conclusion of the judgment changes or the legal meaning concerning the content and effect of the judgment changes (see Constitutional Court Decisions 92HEONBA22, rendered on 1994. 12. 29.; 93HEONBA33, rendered on 1995. 5. 25., etc.). Although the paragraph (2) and the paragraph (5) at issue are not statutory provisions directly applied to the court’s decision on the admissibility of evidence in the related case, they affect the admissibility of the record that became the subject of the decision on admissibility of evidence, and thus depending on whether they are unconstitutional, they determine the result of the decision on admissibility of evidence, namely, whether the court may or may not admit the record as evidence. If so, the constitutional complaint in this case, in which the provisions at issue are made the subject of review, is lawful (from this perspective, the fact that at a later trial date the right of cross-examination was guaranteed in the witness-examination procedure, or the post hoc fact that even without the pre-trial witness-examination record there was sufficient evidence to find the defendant guilty, or the fact that cross-examination was actually conducted in the pre-trial witness-examination procedure for Shin ◯-gyun, are facts that have no effect on the conclusion of the court’s decision on admissibility of evidence and therefore have no bearing on the determination of the prerequisite to judgment in this case).\\n\\nB. Due Process under the Constitution and Principles of Criminal Procedure\\n\\n(1) Due Process under the Constitution and the Right to a Trial\\n\\nThe latter sentence of Article 12(1) of the Constitution of the Republic of Korea provides that “no person shall be arrested, detained, searched, seized, or interrogated except as provided by law, and no person shall be punished, subjected to security measures, or forced labor except as provided by law and through due process of law,” thereby adopting the principle of due process as a constitutional principle. This principle of due process has substantive meaning, in that both the formal procedures and the substantive content prescribed by law must be proper and possess rationality and legitimacy. Particularly when applied in connection with criminal procedure, it must be understood as declaring the basic principle that the entirety of criminal procedure must be regulated from the perspective of guaranteeing fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court Decision 92HEONGA8, rendered on 1992. 12. 24.).\\n\\nThe Constitution also provides in Article 27(1) that “all citizens shall have the right to receive a trial according to law by judges established by the Constitution and laws,” and in Article 27(3) that “all citizens shall have the right to a speedy trial. Criminal defendants shall have the right to a public trial without delay unless there is a sufficient reason to the contrary,” thereby guaranteeing the right to a fair, speedy, and public trial. This right to a trial includes not only the right to receive a trial according to law in the sense that both the laws governing trial procedures and the substantive laws to be applied in trial must be constitutional, but also the right to receive a fair trial by excluding secret trials and by having proceedings and judgment under the supervision of the public.\\n\\nIncluded within this right to a fair trial is the right to receive a trial in which all evidentiary materials are examined and stated in the presence of the judge in a prompt and public courtroom, and the defendant is guaranteed the opportunity to attack and defend against them; that is, in principle, a trial in which adversarial proceedings and oral argument are guaranteed and the parties are fully guaranteed the rights of attack and defense, such as answering the indictment and proving and rebutting it (see Constitutional Court Decisions 95HEONGA5, rendered on 1996. 1. 25.; 93HEONBA26, rendered on 1994. 4. 28., etc.). If so, in relation to the rules of evidence in criminal trials, the negative substantive truth principle is constitutionally guaranteed. In other words, as a criminal defendant, a person enjoys not merely the status of an object of punishment in criminal procedure, but the status of a party to the procedure who forms and maintains that procedure, and in criminal procedure has a constitutional right to enjoy a procedure in which the principle of “equality of arms” is guaranteed vis-à-vis the prosecutor.\\n\\nHowever, it cannot be said that the Constitution prescribes all specific content of the right to a fair trial. This is because the task of concretizing the content of the fair trial procedures guaranteed by the Constitution is primarily a task for the legislature. Nevertheless, the legislature, in regulating criminal procedure, has legislative limits in that it cannot create trial procedures that disregard elements which are constitutionally non-waivable, such as by producing the result of reducing a criminal defendant to a mere object of punishment. Therefore, under procedural law concerning criminal procedure, it is not constitutionally permissible to allow the collection and examination of evidence by methods or procedures lacking rationality and legitimacy, while disregarding the demands of the negative substantive truth principle and placing one-sided emphasis only on the demand to punish offenders. Such a result would violate the principle of due process and the right to a fair trial.\\n\\n(2) The Legal Nature of the Witness-Examination System before the First Trial Date\\n\\n(a) The current Act, in principle, requires investigation to be conducted by voluntary investigation, while coercive investigation is exceptionally permitted only where there are special provisions (Article 199(1) of the Act). Even where the evidence highly probative of proving an offense depends on a third person’s statement, a prosecutor or judicial police officer may first request that person to appear and may only hear a voluntary statement from that person (Article 221 of the Act). However, where, despite the fact that the third person’s statement is indispensable to the investigation, the third person does not comply with the request to appear or to make a statement, or where there is a concern that the third person will make a statement at trial different from the voluntary statement made at the investigative agency, there is a need, exceptionally, to secure the third person’s statement coercively, or to secure in advance the probative value or evidentiary admissibility of the statement made by the third person at the investigative agency.\\n\\nThe “witness-examination procedure before the first trial date” prescribed in Article 221-2 of the Act, which is at issue in this case, is a system established by the Act precisely to meet the above need. Such witness examination may be requested by the prosecutor only before the first trial date, and the grounds for the request are limited to: ① where a person clearly deemed to know facts indispensable to the investigation of a crime refuses the request of the prosecutor or judicial police officer to appear or to make a statement (paragraph (1) of the same Article), and ② where a person who has voluntarily made a statement to a prosecutor or judicial police officer is likely to make a statement at the trial date different from the previous statement and where such statement is deemed indispensable for proving the crime (paragraph (2) of the same Article). Of these grounds, the ground set forth in paragraph (1) is for promoting the progress of the investigation, whereas the ground set forth in paragraph (2), which is the subject of review in this case, may be said to be for the preservation of evidence.\\n\\nOur law also provides a separate general system for preserving evidence, namely the evidence preservation procedure prescribed in Article 184 of the Act. Unlike the above witness-examination procedure, the evidence preservation procedure may be requested not only by the prosecutor but also by the defendant, suspect, or his/her counsel (hereinafter “the defendant, etc.”), and the grounds for the request are broadly defined as cases where, if evidence is not preserved in advance, it will be difficult to use such evidence due to circumstances (inevitability and urgency). Here, circumstances in which evidence is difficult to use are interpreted, in the case of a witness, as meaning cases in which examination is difficult due to death, a long trip, etc.\\n\\nAs will be seen below, the first-trial-date witness-examination system is characterized by the fact that the defendant, suspect, or counsel is only partially and restrictively guaranteed the right to participate in the examination procedure, and yet the record prepared in that procedure is automatically conferred evidentiary admissibility.\\n\\n(b) It may be seen that similar systems to our pre-trial witness-examination request system exist in foreign countries as well, but there is a fundamental difference in that foreign systems do not automatically confer evidentiary admissibility on the record of the witness examination, as ours does.\\n\\nThe Japanese Code of Criminal Procedure provides that where a person clearly deemed to have knowledge indispensable to the investigation of a crime refuses to appear or to make a statement in response to an inquiry under Article 223(1) (Article 226), or where a person who voluntarily made a statement in an inquiry by a public prosecutor, public prosecutor’s assistant, or judicial police officer pursuant to Article 223(1) is likely to, under pressure at the trial date, make a statement different from the one previously made, and where such person’s statement is deemed indispensable for the establishment of the crime (Article 227), the public prosecutor may request the judge to examine that person as a witness only before the first trial date, and in such witness-examination procedure, where the judge deems that there is no risk of obstructing the investigation, the judge may allow the defendant, suspect, or counsel to be present at the examination (Article 228(2)). Thus, the Japanese pre-trial witness-examination system is, in terms of requirements and procedure, almost similar to our pre-trial witness-examination system. However, in Japan, first, Article 37(2) of the Constitution of Japan provides that “criminal defendants shall be afforded full opportunity to examine all witnesses,” making it a major premise that, with respect to witnesses examined ex officio by the court or upon a party’s request, an adequate opportunity for cross-examination must be provided; and a record prepared in the pre-trial witness-examination procedure may be used as evidence only where the declarant has died, has a mental or physical impairment, is of unknown whereabouts, or is staying abroad and therefore cannot testify at the pretrial or trial date, or where the declarant has made a statement at the pretrial or trial date different from the previous statement (Article 321(1)1). In contrast, in our country, the record prepared in the pre-trial witness-examination procedure may, as a matter of course, be used as evidence, which means that, compared with Japan, there is a major difference in terms of evidentiary effect.\\n\\nGermany also has a system similar to our pre-trial witness-examination system. First, the German Code of Criminal Procedure provides in Article 162 that where the prosecutor deems an investigative act by a judge necessary (this investigative act is interpreted as including witness examination), the prosecutor shall request a district court judge to conduct it; and in Article 168c(2) and (3), when the judge examines a witness or expert, the prosecutor, suspect, and counsel shall be allowed to participate, but where the suspect’s participation would endanger the purpose of the investigation, the suspect may be excluded from the hearing (according to the second sentence of paragraph (3), this provision applies only when there is a concern that the witness will not tell the truth in the presence of the suspect). Thus, the German system prescribes more relaxed requirements and procedures than our pre-trial witness-examination system. However, the German Code of Criminal Procedure provides in Article 250 the principle that examination of witnesses, etc. in the trial proceedings may not be replaced by records of prior examinations or other written statements, and provides exceptions thereto in Article 251 and the following provisions. Under Article 251, concerning records prepared in the pre-trial witness-examination procedure, only where the witness, expert, or co-suspect has died or become mentally ill or his/her residence within the country cannot be ascertained, where the witness, expert, or co-suspect’s attendance at the trial date is being hindered for a long period or indefinitely by illness, old age, or other insurmountable obstacle, where the importance of the witness’s or expert’s statement in view of the significance of the statement makes it impossible to expect the witness’s or expert’s attendance at the trial date due to a long-distance trip, or where the prosecutor, counsel, and defendant consent to reading it, may the record of the prior examination by a judge be read and thereby substitute for the examination of the witness, expert, or co-suspect. Accordingly, in Germany, the record prepared in the pre-trial witness-examination procedure may be used as evidence only under the above specific requirements for substitution by reading, and this evidentiary effect is a major difference from our system, which provides that records of pre-trial witness examinations may always be used as evidence.\\n\\nIn the United States, because criminal procedure is carried out through a thoroughly trial-centered and party-centered system, it is difficult for there to exist an evidence preservation system conducted before the first trial date with the suspect’s side excluded from participation.\\n\\nC. Unconstitutionality of the Portion of Article 221-2(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act Concerning Paragraph (2)\\n\\nArticle 221-2(5) of the Act, while providing for the defendant’s, suspect’s, or counsel’s right to participate in the pre-trial witness-examination procedure, states that “where the judge deems that there is no impediment to the investigation, the judge may allow the defendant, suspect, or counsel to participate in the examination of a witness upon a request under paragraph (1) or (2),” thereby making it a matter of the judge’s discretion whether the defendant, etc. may participate in the witness-examination procedure under paragraph (2) of the same Article. This provision, as compared with the party’s right to participate in and examine witnesses in the ordinary witness-examination procedure, restrictively prescribes the content of that right. In other words, under Article 163(1), which governs ordinary witness examination, the prosecutor, defendant, or counsel may participate in witness examination. Paragraph (2) of the same Article provides that the date and place of witness examination shall be notified in advance to the persons who may participate pursuant to the preceding paragraph, thereby comprehensively guaranteeing the party’s right to participate and to examine.\\n\\nHowever, according to the latter sentence of Article 311 of the Act, the Act automatically confers evidentiary admissibility on records prepared in the above witness-examination procedure. Therefore, when such a record is submitted as evidence in the trial proceedings, even if the defendant who was unable to participate in the above witness-examination procedure requests examination of the original declarant in order to impeach the credibility of the statement, there is no guarantee that such request will necessarily be granted. This, in effect, has the meaning of depriving the defendant, etc. of the opportunity to cross-examine the witness.\\n\\nMeanwhile, as to the interpretation of the above provision, the Supreme Court has held that “in the evidence preservation procedure under Article 184 of the Act, where the suspect and counsel are not notified in advance of the time and place of witness examination and are not given an opportunity to participate in the witness examination, there is no evidentiary admissibility; and since witness examination under Article 221-2 of the Act is also witness examination conducted before the first trial date and is no different in that evidentiary admissibility is automatically recognized under Article 311 of the Act, the court, in view of that balance, should, when conducting witness examination under paragraph (5), unless it is recognized that there is a special impediment to the investigation, give the defendant, suspect, or counsel an opportunity to participate” (see Supreme Court Decision 92DO1751, rendered on 1992. 9. 22.). Thus, the Court interprets the provision so as to allow the defendant, etc. to participate in the pre-trial witness-examination procedure as broadly as possible. Nevertheless, even under such interpretation, the possibility remains that where there is a “special impediment to the investigation,” the participation of the defendant, etc. in the procedure may be excluded, and thus there remains room for the defendant, etc. to be deprived of the right of cross-examination.\\n\\nAccordingly, a question arises whether Article 221-2(5) of the Act, which only restrictively guarantees the party’s right to participate and to examine witnesses in a witness-examination procedure where a record with automatic evidentiary admissibility is prepared, infringes the principle of due process and the Petitioner’s right to a trial.\\n\\nIn my view, the phrase in paragraph (2) at issue, “where a person who has voluntarily made a statement to an investigative agency is likely to make a statement at the trial date different from the previous statement,” or, as interpreted by the Supreme Court, the phrase “where there is a special impediment to the investigation,” may be understood to mean a case where, if witness examination is conducted with the participation of the defendant, etc., there is a greater possibility that the witness will make a statement contrary to the truth due to threats or inducements by the suspect or defendant side, thereby making it difficult to ascertain the truth for the punishment of offenders. In such a case, excluding the participation of the defendant, etc. from the procedure would allow the witness to testify freely and candidly as to the facts known to him or her, and if evidentiary admissibility is conferred on the witness-examination record prepared at that time, it cannot be denied that this would greatly assist the maintenance of the prosecution and the active ascertainment of truth in criminal procedure.\\n\\nHowever, these legislative purposes alone are insufficient to justify or rationalize paragraph (5) at issue, which provides for the possibility of depriving the defendant, etc. of participation in the procedure and of the opportunity for cross-examination. Testimonial evidence by nature is highly susceptible to errors entering into the declarant’s memory or expression, and the content conveyed may differ from the declarant’s intent depending on the examiner’s method or skill of examination. The most basic control mechanism to correct this is the opposing party’s right of cross-examination.
