In order to guarantee this substantively and actively, the Act does not stop at guaranteeing the right of cross-examination directly in order to impeach the probative value of the testimony in the trial proceedings or pretrial preparation proceedings (Article 161-2(1) of the Act), but goes further and limits the evidentiary admissibility of hearsay evidence so that the right of cross-examination may also be exercised in the process of conferring evidentiary admissibility (see Article 310-2 and following of the Act).\\n\\nIn general, testimonial evidence corresponding to the facts charged can possess true evidentiary value only when it is given in the presence of the person disadvantaged thereby and when, through impeachment by cross-examination, contradictions or irrationalities in the content of the testimony are revealed. Conferring automatic evidentiary admissibility on testimonial evidence that has not undergone such verification or has not been afforded such an opportunity may to some extent assist the function of punishing offenders, but it may also seriously impede the discovery of substantive truth. Therefore, the fact that there is a concern that a statement made to an investigative agency may later be recanted when witness examination is conducted before the defendant, etc. actually means that there is an even greater need to guarantee the defendant, etc. the right of cross-examination; such circumstance cannot be a reason to exclude the defendant, etc. from participating in the procedure. Even if the possibility of recantation is attributable to threats or inducements by the defendant or suspect side, for such cases it would be a proper measure consistent with the principle of due process to establish a system that allows appropriate protective measures for the witness’s safety, etc. to be taken (for example, Article 7 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment of Specific Violent Crimes may be cited as a legislative example), thereby adopting a system that restricts the fundamental rights of the people to a lesser degree.\\n\\nIf so, paragraph (5) at issue excessively restricts the defendant’s rights of attack and defense, and neither by its own content nor even under the Supreme Court’s restrictive interpretation can its rationality or legitimacy as a necessary legislative means to achieve its legislative purpose be recognized. In the end, paragraph (5) at issue infringes the constitutional principle of due process and the Petitioner’s right to a fair trial, which guarantee the status of the defendant, etc. as a party in criminal proceedings.\\n\\nD. Unconstitutionality of Article 221-2(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act\\n\\n(1) Unconstitutionality of the Paragraph (2) at Issue in Relation to the Paragraph (5) at Issue\\n\\nAs a principle, where a certain statutory provision among the provisions subject to constitutional review is declared unconstitutional, other provisions of the same statute that are not so declared retain their validity. However, exceptionally, there are cases in which, beyond the provision declared unconstitutional, other provisions or the entire statute must also be declared unconstitutional. Such cases include where the remaining provisions that remain constitutional do not have legally independent meaning, or where the unconstitutional provision has such an extremely close relationship with the remaining provisions that, in an overall and comprehensive sense, the two form an inseparable unity. This is the case where, if only the unconstitutional provision were declared unconstitutional, the meaning and legitimacy of the entire provision would be lost.\\n\\nThis is because when a certain statutory provision is a core constituent part of a system, and declaring it unconstitutional would destroy the internal balance of the entire system and distort the legislature’s intent, it is appropriate to declare unconstitutional not only that provision but also the remaining parts.\\n\\nIn my view, the right of cross-examination of testimonial evidence is a core content of the right to a fair trial in criminal procedure. As seen above, the witness-examination procedure under paragraph (2) at issue is a procedure that prescribes the coercive collection of testimonial evidence. Therefore, paragraph (5) at issue, which prescribes the right to participate in and to cross-examine in that witness-examination procedure, should be regarded as a core constituent part of the witness-examination procedure under paragraph (2) at issue.\\n\\nThis is because, if paragraph (5) at issue is found unconstitutional, the internal balance of the entire witness-examination procedure under paragraph (2) at issue would collapse, and the legislature’s intent in establishing that system would be distorted. Accordingly, since there is no need to leave paragraph (2) at issue valid while declaring paragraph (5) unconstitutional, it is proper to declare paragraph (2) unconstitutional together with paragraph (5).\\n\\n(2) The Inherent Unconstitutionality of Paragraph (2) at Issue\\n\\nUnder the Constitution, all citizens have the right to a fair, speedy, and public trial (Article 27(1) and (3) of the Constitution). In light of the guarantee of fairness in trials and the principle of trial-centered proceedings, a judge, who is the adjudicatory authority, should not intervene, as far as possible, in the investigative stage prior to the trial date unless there is a need to guarantee fundamental rights of the people (such as the issuance of an arrest warrant, etc.) or other necessary and unavoidable circumstances (such as preservation of evidence). In the case of the provisions at issue, they are not for guaranteeing fundamental rights, and unlike the case under Article 221-2(1) of the Act, there is no necessity or inevitability for a judge to intervene in advance.\\n\\nIn addition, the latter sentence of Article 12(1) of our Constitution provides that no person shall be punished “except through due process of law.” The criminal procedure is the procedure by which the State protects the people from the State’s unjust and arbitrary exercise of the punitive power by implementing a proper procedure for guaranteeing the fundamental rights of the defendant, etc. in realizing the State’s penal power, namely, a procedure that assures fundamental fairness. Our Criminal Procedure Act, in order to realize constitutional due process in the determination of evidence and fact-finding in criminal procedure, provides, as a principle, for the principle of free evaluation of evidence (Article 308). Here, the principle of free evaluation of evidence does not mean arbitrary assessment of evidence and fact-finding by a judge, but rather the fact-finding process according to the judge’s rational free conviction; thus, for the judge’s proper free conviction, it is premised on the existence of conditions under which the parties, as the subjects of the procedure, freely submit all evidence favorable to each of them and actively engage in proof, while the judge can also freely evaluate evidence from an objective standpoint.\\n\\nParagraph (2) at issue, as its requirements indicate, aims to secure evidence at the investigative stage where a person who has voluntarily made a statement to a prosecutor or judicial police officer is likely to make a statement at the trial date different from the previous statement and where such statement is deemed indispensable for proving the crime. However, examining the requirements of paragraph (2) at issue, one can see that the applicant for the witness-examination procedure under paragraph (2) at issue is limited to the prosecutor, and that, unlike the evidence preservation procedure under Article 184 of the Act, which is another evidence preservation procedure, urgency is not included among the requirements, such as cases where the witness’s death, long-distance travel, or other circumstances would make the witness-examination procedure at the trial date significantly difficult, or cases where evidence would be difficult to use unless preserved in advance. If so, the evidence preservation contemplated by paragraph (2) at issue appears not to be evidence preservation to meet the need for rapid preservation of evidence due to urgent investigative necessity, but evidence preservation in a broader sense intended to facilitate investigative activities by conferring coercive force upon investigative agencies’ activities.\\n\\nHowever, in order to realize such legislative purpose, the effect of restricting fundamental rights under the witness-examination procedure prescribed in paragraph (2) at issue cannot be said to be anything other than excessive relative to that legislative purpose. The latter sentence of Article 311 of the Act provides that the record prepared in the procedure under paragraph (2) at issue has the same evidentiary admissibility as a statement made during pretrial preparation or at trial. This means that if one testifies as a witness in the procedure under paragraph (2) at issue, that testimony may be used as evidence immediately even without appearing at pretrial preparation or trial and making a direct statement in the presence of the judge. Such a witness-examination system seeks, on the sole ground that a voluntary statement was made at the investigative stage but there is a concern that a different statement will be made in court, to have the prosecutor once again obtain evidence in the same investigative stage by having a judge examine the witness in advance. This restricts the witness from freely testifying in the presence of the judge at trial and also restricts the judge from forming conviction based on evidence directly examined in court at the trial date, and in the end it will cause a defect in ensuring the authenticity of value judgments on evidence by allowing the judge to form conviction directly from the contents of the witness-examination record made without direct judicial examination.\\n\\nMeanwhile, where the judge who conducts the witness examination under Article 221-2(4) of the Act and the judge (court) who directly tries the case after indictment are different, it is difficult for the judge to form a true conviction based on witness demeanor (demeanor evidence), etc. In particular, if the witness is an important witness whose testimony at trial is likely to be recanted from statements made to the investigative agency and whose testimony is indispensable for proving the offense, the court must necessarily directly observe the demeanor evidence. In addition, although the grounds corresponding to paragraph (2) at issue must be explained in writing by the prosecutor when requesting witness examination, a judge who was not involved in the investigation of the case would find it difficult to virtually disregard the opinion of the prosecutor who directly investigated or directed the investigation of that case. Therefore, such witness-examination procedure is an exceptional system and there is also a concern that it may be abused.\\n\\nFinally, the right of cross-examination of the defendant or counsel must be substantive and effective, not merely formal and procedural. However, if it is said that before the first trial date there is no right for counsel to inspect or copy the litigation documents, then even if counsel, etc. participate in the procedure under paragraph (2) at issue, it would be difficult to conduct effective cross-examination; and if counsel, etc. cannot properly conduct such cross-examination, this will ultimately affect the judge’s formation of conviction.\\n\\nThis seriously impairs the basic content of trial-centered proceedings or the principle of free evaluation of evidence, which are the procedural expression in criminal procedure of due process and the right to a fair trial guaranteed by the Constitution, and severely restricts fairness and rationality in forming the judge’s proper free conviction. In the end, it cannot be denied that it results in a significant impairment of the constitutionally guaranteed independence of judges.\\n\\nTherefore, establishing the provisions of the witness-examination procedure under paragraph (2) at issue, which entail such a serious restriction on fundamental rights as their legal effect, cannot be said to have rationality or necessity based merely on the legislative purpose of facilitating investigative activities. In other words, paragraph (2) at issue is an overbroad legislative measure because, compared with the public interest it seeks to achieve through its legislative purpose, it employs far greater restrictions on fundamental rights as a means.\\n\\nUltimately, paragraph (2) at issue, by putting forward only the demand for punishment of offenders and allowing evidence collection and examination through excessive legislative means, is likely to obstruct the judge’s rational and fair free evaluation of evidence and to infringe the constitutionally guaranteed independence of judges. Consequently, it violates the Constitution as contrary to the principle of due process and the right to a fair trial.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, since Article 221-2(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act and the portion of paragraph (5) concerning paragraph (2) of the same Article are unconstitutional, the decision is rendered as stated in the dispositive part.\\n\\nThis decision follows the agreement of the remaining participating Justices, except for the separate dissenting opinions of Justices Kim Jin-woo and Shin Chang-eon, as set forth below in 5 and 6, and the dissenting opinion of Justice Kim Yong-jun on Article 221-2(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act and on the portion of paragraph (5) of the same Article concerning paragraph (2), as set forth below in 7.\\n\\n5. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Kim Jin-woo\\n\\nI dissent from the majority opinion that Article 221-2(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act and the portion of paragraph (5) concerning paragraph (2) of the same Article are unconstitutional, for the following reasons.\\n\\nA. As the majority opinion asserts, where the defendant’s rights of attack and defense are excessively restricted without justifiable reason, this contravenes the principle of due process, which particularly means that the entire criminal procedure should be regulated from the perspective of guaranteeing fundamental rights, and infringes the right to a trial, which includes the right to a fair trial in which all evidence is examined and stated in the presence of the judge in an open courtroom and the defendant is guaranteed the opportunity to attack and defend against it. In particular, the defendant’s right of cross-examination of testimony adverse to the defendant is a means that has a particularly important meaning among the defendant’s methods of attack and defense. Therefore, any restriction on it without justifiable reason infringes the defendant’s right to a fair trial and also contravenes the principle of due process. Accordingly, if the witness who was examined under the procedure prescribed by the provisions at issue is not given an opportunity for cross-examination to the defendant, etc. in that procedure or even in the trial proceedings, and yet unlimited evidentiary admissibility is recognized for the witness-examination record prepared through that procedure, the result may, in principle, be to infringe the defendant’s right to a fair trial and contravene the principle of due process.\\n\\nB. Therefore, I examine whether the provisions at issue restrict the defendant’s right of cross-examination without justifiable reason.\\n\\n(1) The witness-examination procedure before the first trial date under Article 221-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act is a procedure aimed at securing, in advance, the evidentiary admissibility of the statements of eyewitnesses or victims by preserving such statements as evidence, because if a person who gave a statement to an investigative agency as a reference witness later recants that statement in court, the reference-witness statement record becomes worthless. Where a prosecutor or other investigative agency uses the evidence preservation procedure under Article 184 of the Criminal Procedure Act, depending on the case, there may be cases where, when witnesses, etc. are examined in the presence of the suspect, there is a possibility that statements contrary to the truth will be made due to threats, inducements, or fear of retaliation by the suspect side. In such cases, there is a need to exclude the suspect’s presence or cross-examination in particular and to secure the statements necessary for revealing substantive truth while relieving the witness’s fear, etc.; the independent meaning of the witness-examination procedure under the provisions at issue in relation to the evidence preservation procedure prescribed in Article 184 of the Criminal Procedure Act lies in such necessity. In particular, as crimes today become more organized, sophisticated, and ferocious, the need to protect victims and witnesses of cases from threats or harm by suspects is increasing, and the importance of this system is likewise increasing.\\n\\n(2) Among the provisions at issue, paragraph (5) entrusts to the discretion of the presiding judge whether the defendant and counsel may participate in the same witness-examination procedure and, further, whether the right of cross-examination may be exercised, even when there is no impediment to the investigation. However, by interpreting this provision so that the defendant, etc. are to be allowed to participate in witness examination so long as there is no impediment to the investigation, that is, by means of constitutional interpretation, there is ample room to operate the discretionary provision as a mandatory provision. Moreover, the provisions at issue do not block the path to cross-examining the witness even in the trial proceedings.\\n\\n(3) Furthermore, even where the defendant, etc. are inevitably excluded from the witness-examination procedure, because the judge, who is not the subject of the investigation, can preside over the witness-examination procedure from a neutral and professional standpoint so that the authenticity of the testimony may be secured, it cannot be said that in this procedure the defendant, etc. are reduced entirely to mere objects of investigation and criminal punishment.\\n\\n(4) In addition, since the procedure under the provisions at issue is a procedure conducted as part of the investigation, it is not necessary that an opportunity for cross-examination always be afforded in that procedure as in the trial proceedings.\\n\\n(5) And paragraph (2) among the provisions at issue clearly limits the requirements for requesting a witness examination under the witness-examination procedure before the first trial date to the case where “a person who has voluntarily made a statement is likely to make a statement at the trial date different from the previous statement and where such statement is deemed indispensable for proving the crime.” This requirement should also be strictly construed so that the abstract risk of recantation alone is insufficient and it is satisfied only when there is a rational basis in light of specific circumstances. If so, the witness-examination procedure under the provisions at issue can be used only where there is justifiable reason in the investigation.\\n\\n(6) Therefore, the witness-examination procedure itself under the provisions at issue cannot be said to contravene the constitutionally guaranteed due process or infringe the right to a fair trial, which is one aspect of the right to a trial, merely because it deprives the defendant of the opportunity for cross-examination of a witness without justifiable reason. For this reason, Japan, Germany, and France also adopt systems similar to the witness-examination procedure under the provisions at issue.\\n\\nC. Rather, the issue is whether the latter sentence of Article 311 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which recognizes the evidentiary admissibility of witness-examination records prepared in the procedure under the provisions at issue regardless of whether an opportunity for cross-examination was afforded even in the trial proceedings, infringes the right to a fair trial or contravenes the principle of due process. This is because, if evidence adverse to the defendant (hearsay evidence) is admitted as evidence and the defendant is punished on the basis of such evidence even though the defendant or counsel was not given an opportunity without justifiable reason to impeach that evidence through cross-examination, then this infringes the defendant’s right to a fair trial and contravenes due process.\\n\\n(1) First, where participation of the defendant, etc. in the witness-examination procedure before the first trial date is permitted and the defendant, etc. were able to dispute the authenticity of the witness’s testimony, there is no problem in recognizing evidentiary admissibility for the witness-examination record.\\n\\n(2) Where the witness is summoned again in the trial proceedings and an opportunity for cross-examination is afforded to the defendant, it cannot be said to be unconstitutional to grant evidentiary admissibility. Needless to say, this is the case where the witness, when summoned again in the trial proceedings, testifies in the same terms as the witness-examination record. Even where the summoned witness in the trial proceedings testifies in court contrary to the contents recorded in the witness-examination record, the issue is merely one of probative value, and even if evidentiary admissibility is recognized for the witness-examination record, it cannot be said on that ground alone that the defendant’s right to a trial has been infringed or that due process has been violated.\\n\\n(3) Where the witness has died, is in critical condition, or is otherwise unable to appear in the trial proceedings for other equivalent justifiable reasons, and the defendant is unable to exercise the right of cross-examination of the witness in the trial proceedings, the defendant cannot impeach the authenticity of the testimony recorded in the witness-examination record through cross-examination of that witness. However, in relation to the defendant’s right of cross-examination regarding records or written statements prepared by a prosecutor or judicial police officer, the Constitutional Court has already declared, with respect to Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which provides that “when a person required to make a statement at pretrial preparation or at trial cannot make a statement due to death, illness, or other reasons, the record or other document may be used as evidence. Provided, that such record or document shall be limited to those made under circumstances in which the statement or preparation was particularly reliable,” that “the reasons in which the necessity to recognize an exception to [hearsay evidence] lies are limited to justifiable reasons, and even in cases of such necessity, the application is limited to reasonable conditions, so that its scope of application remains within a rational minimum; therefore, it cannot be said that it essentially infringes, emasculates, or directly violates the right to a fair public trial and the right to be presumed innocent, and it is consistent with due process, and thus does not violate the Constitution” (Constitutional Court Decision 93HEONBA26, rendered on 1994. 4. 28.).\\n\\nIf, with respect to records or other statements prepared by a prosecutor or judicial police officer, the Constitution presents no problem in recognizing evidentiary admissibility under certain requirements when the statement or preparation was made under circumstances particularly trustworthy, then the witness-examination record prepared pursuant to the procedure prescribed by the provisions at issue was prepared in the presence of an independent, neutral, and professionally competent judge, thereby ensuring authenticity in its formation, and the statement was made under circumstances of relatively high trustworthiness. Accordingly, even where the witness cannot testify in the trial proceedings due to death, illness, or other unavoidable justifiable reasons, and therefore the defendant, etc. are not given an opportunity for cross-examination, the validity of recognizing evidentiary admissibility for such witness-examination record is greater than in the case of Article 314 of the Criminal Procedure Act. In such a case, even if evidentiary admissibility is recognized for the witness-examination record, it cannot be said to infringe the right to a fair trial or contravene due process.\\n\\n(Also, in this regard, one must consider the function of the provisions at issue in protecting witnesses from criminal organizations with formidable structures such as the mafia. That is, in the case of witnesses concerning formidable organized crime, it is necessary under certain requirements to allow trial testimony to be replaced by a witness-examination record prepared in the presence of a judge before the first trial date. In such a case, the restriction on the defendant’s, etc. right of cross-examination is justified by the judge’s supplementary function in this regard and by the need to protect the witness from the latent dangers posed by organized criminal groups.)\\n\\n(4) However, even where there is no such unavoidable justifiable reason, if the defendant, etc. are not given an opportunity in the courtroom to cross-examine the witness who testified in the procedure prescribed by the provisions at issue, and therefore cannot exercise the right of cross-examination of that witness, then recognizing evidentiary admissibility for the witness-examination record severely restricts the defendant’s right to a trial, and there is no public-interest reason sufficient to justify it. Accordingly, even in such cases, the latter sentence of Article 311 of the Criminal Procedure Act, by recognizing evidentiary admissibility for the pre-trial witness-examination record under the provisions at issue, excessively restricts the defendant’s right to a trial, which includes the right to a fair public trial, and I believe this violates the Constitution.\\n\\nD. As seen above, I think that what should be examined first is not the unconstitutionality of the witness-examination procedure itself under the provisions at issue, which in my view does not infringe due process or the right to a trial, but rather the unconstitutionality of the latter sentence of Article 311 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which confers evidentiary admissibility without any limitation on the witness-examination record prepared under the provisions at issue. Nevertheless, the majority opinion that the provisions at issue themselves are unconstitutional merely because evidentiary admissibility is conferred under the latter sentence of Article 311 of the Criminal Procedure Act on the witness-examination record prepared under the provisions at issue, even though the right of cross-examination was not afforded in the trial proceedings, seems to reverse the source of the problem.\\n\\nE. For the foregoing reasons, I dissent from the majority opinion that the provisions at issue themselves must be declared unconstitutional without first examining the unconstitutionality of the latter sentence of Article 311 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Shin Chang-eon\\n\\nA. Discovery of Substantive Truth and the Witness-Examination Request System\\n\\nOur criminal procedure system fundamentally adopts a party-centered litigation structure, and accordingly, even though the prosecutor and the defendant are both parties in the trial proceedings, this by no means means that the prosecutor, who bears the grave duty of realizing the State’s punitive power such as criminal investigation, prosecution, and direction of execution of punishment as a representative of the public interest, and the defendant, who is an offender, occupy completely identical positions in all procedures or must be treated in exactly the same way within the current criminal procedure structure.\\n\\nCriminal procedure is not a private procedure for resolving disputes between offenders and victims, but a public-interest procedure for realizing the State’s punitive power through punishment of offenders; therefore, discovery of substantive truth is the most important guiding ideology and highest objective of criminal procedure.\\n\\nThe provisions at issue, in such a public-interest dimension of eradicating crime through discovery of substantive truth, recognize the prosecutor’s right to request witness examination only in exceptional cases, before the first trial date and mainly at the investigative stage, where a reference witness indispensable to proving the crime is highly likely to recant, at the trial stage, the statements made at the investigative stage due to threats, inducements, or settlement by the suspect side. The majority opinion, which views this as an unconstitutional provision that infringes the constitutional principle of due process guaranteeing the criminal defendant’s status as a party and the right to a fair trial and further impairs judicial independence, is excessively formalistic and superficial.\\n\\nB. Investigative Procedure and Guarantee of the Right of Cross-Examination\\n\\nGenerally, even in the investigative procedure, the constitutional principle of due process should be observed in order to faithfully protect the human rights of the related parties. In the witness-examination request procedure, where the legal requirements are satisfied, it is allowed by judicial determination, namely by a judge’s review of the requirements followed by summoning of the reference witness (witness) and witness examination. However, unlike trial proceedings, in the investigative procedure the principles of trial-centered impeachment or party-centered litigation structure cannot be strictly applied in principle because of the demands of promptness and secrecy, and accordingly the guarantee of the right of cross-examination for the suspect, etc. is not necessarily required.\\n\\nFrom this perspective, the majority opinion’s assertion that, although the witness-examination request system under our Criminal Procedure Act has the legitimacy of its legislative purpose, the effect of restricting fundamental rights is excessive relative to that legislative purpose because the suspect side’s right of cross-examination is not guaranteed procedurally, and further that it obstructs the judge’s rational and fair free evaluation of evidence and thereby infringes the constitutionally guaranteed independence of judges, is a biased view that fails to correctly grasp the essence of criminal investigation and investigative procedure.\\n\\nC. Constitutionality of the Witness-Examination Request System\\n\\nAccording to Article 221-2(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act, where the judge examines a witness and deems that there is no impediment to the investigation, the judge may allow the suspect, etc. to participate; and even where that is not the case, the suspect side may request evidence preservation or later apply to examine the witness again in the trial proceedings and conduct cross-examination. Therefore, it cannot be said that the suspect side’s right of cross-examination has been deprived. Moreover, the recognition of evidentiary admissibility for the witness-examination record is also justified because, as a record of statements made in the presence of a judge, its formation is authentic and it is supported by high circumstantial guarantees of trustworthiness (see Supreme Court Decision 4288HYEONGSANG308, rendered on 1956. 2. 17.); our Criminal Procedure Act recognizes it as an exception to the hearsay rule. This merely means that the record is qualified to be submitted as evidence in court and used as a basis for fact-finding; whether it has concrete value as evidence, that is, whether it has probative value, is ultimately determined by the judge’s free evaluation of evidence, and therefore there is no possibility whatsoever that it infringes judicial independence.\\n\\nAlso, if, as the majority opinion’s logic holds, the suspect side’s right of cross-examination is a very important core element in the witness-examination request procedure, it should suffice to declare only paragraph (5) unconstitutional, and the assertion that paragraph (2) must also be declared unconstitutional is nothing short of an incomprehensible leap in logic. This is because, if the suspect side’s right of cross-examination is guaranteed by declaring paragraph (5) unconstitutional, the core constitutional defect asserted by the majority opinion is itself cured, and the procedural legitimacy and systemic validity of the witness-examination request system under paragraph (2) would be significantly strengthened.\\n\\nD. Foreign Legislative Examples\\n\\nThe above witness-examination request system is by no means unique to Korea. The Japanese Code of Criminal Procedure (Articles 227 and 228) also contains provisions almost identical to ours. In addition, Article 321(1)1 of the Criminal Procedure Act recognizes the evidentiary admissibility of witness-examination records as an exception to the hearsay rule, and the Supreme Court of Japan has repeatedly upheld constitutionality in response to claims that the above provisions are unconstitutional because they exclude the suspect side’s right to participate.\\n\\nThe German Code of Criminal Procedure recognizes the prosecutor’s authority to compel the appearance of reference witnesses (Article 161a), and separately provides a judicial investigative-act system (richterliche Untersuchunghandlung), similar to ours, whereby a judge examines witnesses upon the prosecutor’s request (Article 162). Moreover, when the judge examines a witness, if the suspect’s participation would endanger the purpose of the investigation, the judge may exclude the suspect from participation (Article 168c(3)), thereby restricting the right of cross-examination in a manner similar to ours. This clearly shows that the witness-examination request system is an indispensable system for achieving the public purpose of the proper realization of the State’s punitive power, regardless of whether the right of cross-examination is guaranteed.\\n\\nE. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, taking into account the prosecutor’s substantive status in the criminal procedure system as representative of the public interest and the director of the investigation, the provisions at issue are unavoidable provisions necessary to effectively cope with crime trends that are becoming more sophisticated, organized, and ferocious, to eradicate crime, and thereby to secure the peace and order of the State and society and realize judicial justice. They cannot be said to violate the Constitution.\\n\\n7. Opinion of Justice Kim Yong-jun on the Dissenting Opinion regarding Article 221-2(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act and on the Portion of Paragraph (5) of the Same Article Concerning Paragraph (2)\\n\\nI dissent from the majority opinion that Article 221-2(2) of the Act (hereinafter abbreviated as “paragraph (2)”) is unconstitutional, and I agree with the majority’s conclusion that the portion of paragraph (5) of the same Article (hereinafter abbreviated as “paragraph (5)”) concerning paragraph (2) is unconstitutional, but I differ with respect to the reasons. Accordingly, I state my opinion as follows.\\n\\nA. Criminal Procedure and the Principle of Due Process\\n\\nThe essential task of criminal procedure is to concretely realize the State’s punitive power required by criminal substantive law. As a basic premise for this, it is required that the truth of the matter be clarified clearly and accurately by discovering objective truth concerning the facts underlying the criminal trial. This demand is called substantive truth doctrine in criminal procedure. Substantive truth doctrine, positively, demands punishment of offenders, that is, punishment without omission of those who are guilty (positive substantive truth doctrine), while negatively, it demands non-punishment of the innocent, that is, that innocent persons not be punished (negative substantive truth doctrine). The Act expressly reaffirms the principle of presumption of innocence declared in Article 27(4) of the Constitution (Article 275-2), while placing the burden of proof regarding the facts charged on the prosecutor; it also requires that findings of fact be based on evidence (Article 307); and, in order to exclude confessions and hearsay evidence lacking voluntariness or reliability, it denies or restricts their evidentiary admissibility (Articles 309 and 301-2), and adopts the corroboration rule requiring corroborative evidence for confessions unfavorable to the defendant (Article 310). In this way, the Act provides various institutional safeguards to prevent innocent persons from being punished, focusing on the negative aspect of substantive truth doctrine.\\n\\nUltimately, the Act, when the demand for positive substantive truth doctrine conflicts with the demand for negative substantive truth doctrine, gives priority to the latter and thus makes negative substantive truth doctrine the guiding principle of criminal procedure.\\n\\nSuch negative substantive truth doctrine, which is the guiding principle of criminal procedure, is not merely a legislative policy choice made through the exercise of legislative discretion at the level of ordinary legislation, but is the inevitable result of the reflection of the constitutionally guaranteed principle of due process in criminal evidence law. In other words, the latter sentence of Article 12(1) of our Constitution codifies the principle of due process as an independent constitutional principle by providing that “no person shall be arrested, detained, seized, searched, or interrogated except as provided by law, and no person shall be punished, subjected to security measures, or forced labor except as provided by law and through due process of law.” The principle of due process has substantive meaning in that both the formal procedures and the substantive content prescribed by law must be proper and possess rationality and legitimacy. It is not applied only within the limited scope of criminal procedure restrictions prescribed by constitutional provisions, but broadly applies to all legislative and administrative acts, whether or not related to restrictions on fundamental rights as state action; and, particularly when applied in relation to criminal procedure, it must be understood as the basic principle that regulates the entirety of criminal procedure from the perspective of guaranteeing fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court Decision 92HEONGA8, rendered on 1992. 12. 24.). Therefore, in relation to the rules of evidence in criminal trials, it inevitably manifests itself as the spirit of negative substantive truth doctrine. Accordingly, in criminal procedure, allowing the collection and examination of evidence by methods or procedures lacking rationality and legitimacy, while disregarding the demands of negative substantive truth doctrine and placing sole emphasis on the demand to punish offenders, violates the principle of due process and is not constitutionally permissible.\\n\\nB. The Legal Nature of the Witness-Examination System before the First Trial Date\\n\\nThe Act, while in principle requiring investigation to be conducted by voluntary investigation, permits coercive investigation only exceptionally when the Act contains special provisions (Article 199(1)). However, where there is a third person clearly deemed to know facts indispensable to the investigation of a crime, a prosecutor or judicial police officer may request that person to appear and may hear a statement from him or her (Article 221). Yet such requests for appearance or statements by investigative agencies are not coercive, so if the third person does not comply with the request to appear or to make a statement, it is necessary to secure the statement with the aid of a judge; and even if the third person made a voluntary statement to the investigative agency, if he or she makes a different statement at trial, the probative value of the statement made to the investigative agency is markedly weakened. Moreover, if the third person makes a statement denying even the voluntariness of the statement or the authenticity of the formation of the statement record, there is a concern that the evidentiary admissibility of the statement record itself may be denied. Therefore, in preparation for this, there is a need to secure in advance the probative value or evidentiary admissibility of the statement.\\n\\nThe “first-trial-date witness-examination procedure” prescribed in Article 221-2 of the Act, which is at issue in this case, is precisely the system established by the Act to meet the above need. Under this procedure, only the prosecutor may request witness examination before the first trial date, and the grounds for the request are limited to: ① where a person clearly deemed to know facts indispensable to the investigation of a crime does not comply with the request of the prosecutor or judicial police officer to appear or to make a statement and thus refuses to appear or to make a statement (paragraph (1)), and ② where a person who has voluntarily made a statement to a prosecutor or judicial police officer is likely to make a statement at the trial date different from the previous statement and where such statement is deemed indispensable for proving the crime (paragraph (2)). Of these, the grounds set forth in paragraph (1) are for promoting the progress of the investigation, while the grounds set forth in paragraph (2), which are the subject of review in this case, may be said to be for the preservation of evidence.\\n\\nHowever, although the first-trial-date witness-examination procedure is based on Article 221-2 of the Act, which is located in Chapter 1 of Part II of the Criminal Procedure Act concerning investigative procedure, and although the judge is required to send the documents concerning the witness examination to the prosecutor when the witness has been examined (paragraph (6) of the same Article), thereby leaving some room to view it as a coercive investigative measure by an investigative agency with the aid of the court, on the other hand, considering that the procedure is presided over by a judge who has the same authority as the court or presiding judge with respect to witness examination and is conducted by the method of witness examination, and that the record of witness examination prepared in that procedure is automatically granted evidentiary admissibility (latter sentence of Article 311 of the Act), it is understood essentially as a witness-examination procedure possessing the character of evidence preservation.\\n\\nC. Whether the Provisions Subject to Review in This Case Are Unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Article 221-2(2) of the Act\\n\\n(a) This provision is a rule that enables the prosecutor to secure in advance the probative value of the statement or the evidentiary admissibility of the statement record as evidence preservation through witness examination before the first trial date, in order to prevent in advance the difficulties in maintaining the prosecution that would arise where a reference witness indispensable to maintaining the prosecution made a statement indispensable for proving the crime at the investigative agency but later recanted the content of that statement and made a different statement at trial. This is intended to properly realize the State’s punitive power, and because it reflects the demands of positive substantive truth doctrine, which is one of the important principles that cannot be overlooked in criminal procedure, the content of the provision itself, which allows the prosecutor to request evidence preservation from the court on the basis of the possibility of recanting statements indispensable to proving the crime, is based on rational and legitimate reasons and grounds, and therefore cannot be said to violate the constitutional principle of due process or to infringe the people’s right to a trial.\\n\\n(b) Of course, under paragraph (5), participation of the defendant, suspect, or counsel (hereinafter “the defendant, etc.”) in the witness-examination procedure is only restrictively allowed, and in the case of evidence preservation procedures, the Act expressly provides that the defendant, etc. may, with permission from the judge, inspect or copy the documents and evidence relating to the evidence-preservation measure (Article 185). However, in the case of the first-trial-date witness-examination procedure, because the defendant’s right to inspect and copy the documents prepared in that procedure is not expressly prescribed, there is room for the prosecutor, the only party to the criminal procedure on the prosecution side, to be able to use the evidence preserved in that procedure. In that sense, a question may be raised as to the rationality and legitimacy of the first-trial-date witness-examination system.\\n\\nHowever, the first problem is a matter to be resolved by determining the constitutionality of the portion of paragraph (5) concerning paragraph (2), which restricts the defendant’s etc. participation in the witness-examination procedure (as noted above, if the first-trial-date witness-examination procedure is viewed as a witness-examination procedure having the character of evidence preservation by a judge, then if the exception in paragraph (5) concerning paragraph (2), which restricts the defendant’s etc. participation in the witness-examination procedure, is held unconstitutional, the defendant’s etc. right to participate as parties and to examine witnesses will be guaranteed pursuant to the rule governing the witness-examination procedure). There is no reason to relate this to the constitutionality of paragraph (2) itself or of the first-trial-date witness-examination system itself. The second problem, too, if participation by the defendant, etc. in the witness-examination procedure is guaranteed, need not be related to the constitutionality of paragraph (2), because, unlike the evidence-preservation procedure, even if the right to inspect and copy is not expressly prescribed, the defendant, etc. may still submit the witness-examination record as evidence in the trial proceedings by, for example, requesting transmission of the documents concerning the first-trial-date witness examination. Accordingly, this point too is merely related to the guarantee of participation by the defendant, etc. in the witness-examination procedure and there is no reason to relate it to the constitutionality of paragraph (2).\\n\\n(c) On this point, the majority opinion argues that if the portion of paragraph (5) concerning paragraph (2), which is a core component of the first-trial-date witness-examination procedure, is found unconstitutional, the internal balance of the entire first-trial-date witness-examination procedure under paragraph (2) collapses, thereby distorting the legislature’s intent in establishing that system, and therefore paragraph (2) should also be declared unconstitutional together.\\n\\nOf course, if the portion of paragraph (5) concerning paragraph (2) is held unconstitutional, the defendant’s etc. right to participate in the witness-examination procedure and right of cross-examination would naturally be guaranteed, and it cannot be denied that, as a result, the first-trial-date witness-examination procedure under paragraph (2) would in practice substantially overlap with the ordinary evidence-preservation procedure and thus would no longer have special independent significance as an evidence-preservation system. However, the Constitutional Court does not have the authority to declare such a system unconstitutional merely because it, in fact, performs the same function as another ordinary system and thus has no separate independent significance or need to continue to exist. The abolition or modification of such a system is a matter entrusted to the legislature. In some cases, if only the statutory provision judged to be unconstitutional is declared unconstitutional and related other statutory provisions are left in place, and those other provisions produce an opposite result that the legislature never intended, the scope of the unconstitutionality declaration may need to be expanded to the extent necessary to prevent distortion of the legislature’s intent. However, it is clear that this case does not fall within such a situation. Therefore, the majority opinion’s argument is not persuasive.\\n\\n(d) The majority opinion also argues that the first-trial-date witness-examination procedure under paragraph (2) itself is unconstitutional because it seriously impairs the basic content of trial-centered proceedings or the principle of direct examination, which are the criminal-procedure expression of the principle of due process or the right to a fair trial.\\n\\nHowever, the principle of free evaluation of evidence merely means that the probative value of evidence is not prescribed by law but left to the free judgment of the judge. It does not apply when determining whether evidence has evidentiary admissibility. Therefore, even if the latter sentence of Article 311 of the Act automatically grants evidentiary admissibility to records prepared in the first-trial-date witness-examination procedure, this cannot be viewed as prescribing an exception to the principle of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nWhat the majority opinion calls “trial-centered proceedings” appears to refer to the principle of direct examination. Even if the participation of the defendant, etc. in the first-trial-date witness-examination procedure is guaranteed, granting evidentiary admissibility automatically to the record prepared in that procedure would constitute an exception to the principle of direct examination. However, the Act broadly recognizes exceptions to the principle of direct examination in addition for the discovery of substantive truth and for procedural economy. Representative examples include automatically granting evidentiary admissibility to records of statements made by the defendant or by persons other than the defendant during pretrial preparation or at trial, and to records of inspections or expert examinations by the court or a judge, as well as to records prepared in evidence preservation procedures (Article 311 of the Act).\\n\\nAs seen above, paragraph (2) is intended to properly realize the State’s punitive power and reflects the demands of positive substantive truth doctrine, one of the important principles that cannot be overlooked in criminal procedure. Therefore, even if records prepared in this procedure are automatically granted evidentiary admissibility, this is, like records of statements made at trial, an exception to the principle of direct examination on proper and rational grounds, and cannot be said to seriously impair the basic content of the principle of direct examination, which is the criminal-procedure expression of due process or the right to a fair trial.\\n\\n(e) Moreover, since the first-trial-date witness-examination can only be requested by the prosecutor, there may be a question whether this violates the principle of equality in criminal procedure. However, the defendant, etc. may also use the ordinary evidence-preservation procedure when evidence preservation is necessary (where, as prescribed as the ground for requesting evidence preservation in Article 184(1) of the Act, “if evidence is not preserved in advance it will be difficult to use such evidence,” this is interpreted to include not only situations where witness examination is difficult because of death, long-distance travel, etc., but also situations where there is a concern that the witness will make a statement different from the previous statement). Since the same purpose as the first-trial-date witness-examination may be achieved through that procedure, it is difficult to say that the fact that only the prosecutor is allowed to use the first-trial-date witness-examination procedure in addition to the ordinary evidence-preservation procedure for the purpose of evidence preservation directly violates the constitutional principle of equality.\\n\\n(f) In the end, paragraph (2) is for the proper realization of the State’s punitive power, and its content is rational and legitimate, so it cannot be said to violate the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) The Portion of Article 221-2(5) of the Act Concerning Paragraph (2)\\n\\n(a) The above portion of the provision allows the judge, at his or her discretion, to permit the defendant, etc. to participate in the first-trial-date witness-examination procedure under paragraph (2) only when the judge deems that there is no impediment to the investigation. Thus, it restricts only to a limited extent the defendant’s etc. opportunity to participate in the witness-examination procedure under paragraph (2). However, as noted above, the Act automatically grants evidentiary admissibility to records prepared in such witness-examination procedure (Article 311). Therefore, when such a record is later submitted as evidence in the trial proceedings, even if the defendant who did not participate in the witness-examination procedure requests examination of the original declarant in order to impeach the credibility of the witness’s statement, there is no guarantee that such request will necessarily be accepted. As a result, the opportunity for the defendant, etc. to cross-examine the witness may be deprived.\\n\\nAs to the interpretation of the above provision, the Supreme Court held that “in the evidence preservation procedure under Article 184 of the Act, if the suspect and counsel are not notified in advance of the time and place of witness examination and thus are not given an opportunity to participate in the witness examination, there is no evidentiary admissibility (see Supreme Court Decision 91DO2337, rendered on 1992. 2. 28.); and since witness examination under Article 221-2 of the Act is also witness examination before the first trial date and is no different in that evidentiary admissibility is automatically recognized under Article 311 of the Act, the court, in view of that balance, should, when conducting witness examination under paragraph (5), unless it is recognized that there is a special impediment to the investigation, give the defendant, suspect, or counsel an opportunity to participate” (see Supreme Court Decision 92DO1751, rendered on 1992. 9. 22.), thereby requiring that participation in the first-trial-date witness-examination procedure by the defendant, etc. be allowed as broadly as possible. Yet even under such interpretation, where there is a special impediment to the investigation, the defendant, etc. inevitably cannot participate in the witness-examination procedure, and thus there remains room for the defendant’s etc. right of cross-examination to be deprived.\\n\\n(b) Here, a question naturally arises whether it is truly rational and legitimate in criminal procedure to allow, in the case of a special impediment to the investigation, the defendant, etc. to be deprived of the right to cross-examine the witness. This is because doing so amounts to tolerating to a certain extent the result of contravening the demands of negative substantive truth doctrine, which is the basic guiding principle of criminal procedure, while pursuing the discovery of positive truth.\\n\\nOf course, even if negative substantive truth doctrine in criminal procedure is based on the constitutional principle of due process and has value superior to positive substantive truth doctrine, if a system plays a significant role in realizing positive substantive truth doctrine while causing only a minor impediment to the realization of negative substantive truth doctrine, the rationality and legitimacy of that system cannot be denied. However, even if a system plays an important role in discovering substantive truth, if it significantly impedes the defendant’s exercise of the right of defense and thereby substantially conflicts with the demands of negative substantive truth doctrine, it cannot be said to be consistent with the principle of due process.\\n\\n(c) Therefore, it is necessary to further examine how much the exclusion of the defendant’s etc. participation in the witness-examination procedure on the ground of a special impediment to the investigation aids the discovery of substantive truth, and correspondingly how much it may obstruct the realization of negative substantive truth doctrine by depriving the defendant’s etc. of the opportunity to cross-examine the witness.\\n\\nThe phrase “where there is an impediment to the investigation,” as a requirement for excluding the defendant’s etc. participation in the witness-examination procedure under the above portion of the provision, may be understood to mean a case where allowing the defendant, etc. to participate in witness examination would make it difficult to discover substantive truth because the witness, under threats or inducements by the defendant side, may make a statement contrary to the truth. In such a case, if the defendant, etc. are not allowed to participate in the witness-examination procedure, the witness will be able to testify as he or she knows the facts, in a calm state of mind, and it cannot be denied that the record of witness examination prepared in that procedure, because it is immediately granted evidentiary admissibility, will greatly assist the maintenance of the prosecution and the discovery of substantive truth in criminal procedure.\\n\\nHowever, on the other hand, the result of excluding the defendant’s etc. participation in the witness-examination procedure and thereby depriving them of the opportunity for cross-examination, which leads to a result contrary to negative substantive truth doctrine, is by no means light. Testimonial evidence is generally highly susceptible to errors entering into the declarant’s memory or expression, and the content conveyed may differ from the declarant’s intent depending on the examiner’s method or skill. The most fundamental control mechanism for correcting such errors is the opposing party’s right of cross-examination. The Act, in order to impeach the probative value of testimony in witness-examination procedures, not only guarantees the right of cross-examination (Article 161-2(1), Article 163) but also, further, takes the guarantee of the right of cross-examination as the theoretical basis for limiting the evidentiary admissibility of hearsay evidence, thereby actively and substantively guaranteeing the right of cross-examination even through the process of conferring evidentiary admissibility. In the end, the guarantee of the right of cross-examination, in accordance with the demands of negative substantive truth doctrine, forms the most basic framework in relation to the discovery of substantive truth through testimonial evidence in criminal procedure. In particular, the defendant’s etc. right of cross-examination is a core element of the right of defense; therefore, unless there are unavoidable circumstances in which the opportunity to exercise it cannot be afforded (such as the death or illness of the original declarant under Articles 314 and 316 of the Act), guaranteeing it to the maximum extent is consistent with the constitutional principle of due process. In particular, since the first-trial-date witness-examination procedure under paragraph (2) concerns statements indispensable for proving the offense, the need to ensure that the defendant, etc. necessarily participate in the procedure so that cross-examination may be conducted is even more pressing.\\n\\n(d) In general, testimonial evidence consistent with the facts charged can acquire true evidentiary value only when it is given in the presence of the defendant, etc., who will suffer disadvantage from it, and when, after being impeached by cross-examination, the content of the statement is not recanted and no contradictions or irrationalities are revealed. If such a process has not been undergone, allowing testimonial evidence to have evidentiary admissibility as is may to some extent assist the function of punishing offenders, but it will seriously impede the realization of negative substantive truth doctrine. Therefore, when a witness makes statements different from those made to the investigative agency because the defendant, etc. participate in the witness examination, that fact only means that the need to guarantee the defendant’s etc. right of cross-examination increases even more; it cannot be a reason to exclude the defendant’s etc. from participating in the witness-examination procedure. Even if the possibility that the witness will make a statement different from the previous one is due to threats or inducements by the defendant or suspect side, in such cases, under Article 297 of the Act, the court can have the defendant leave the courtroom, have the witness testify, then have the defendant re-enter the courtroom, notify him or her of the gist of the testimony, and afford an opportunity for cross-examination. To prepare for situations where even such measures would not make it possible to expect free testimony from the witness, institutional arrangements should be established to allow necessary and appropriate safety measures for witness protection (for example, safety measures for witnesses prescribed in Article 7 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment of Specific Violent Crimes), which would be a reasonable measure consistent with the principle of due process. To allow, on the basis of such circumstances alone, room for deprivation of the defendant’s etc. right of cross-examination is a wholesale retreat from the demands of negative substantive truth doctrine, and its rationality and legitimacy cannot be recognized.\\n\\n(e) In the end, the above portion of the Act’s provision cannot but be said to violate the fundamental constitutional principle of due process by unjustly distorting criminal procedure without justifiable basis and by allowing room for deprivation of the defendant’s etc. right of cross-examination.\\n\\n26. 12. 1996."}

question: A, while preparing for a divorce action due to discord with her husband A, who had a severe drinking habit and pathological jealousy, asked B, A’s driver, to kill A. At A’s request, B strangled and killed A, who was drunk and asleep. The prosecutor indicted B for murder and A for instigating murder, and the court is conducting a joint trial of A and B. Which of the following statements are incorrect? (Where there is dispute, follow case law.) (a) If A, in an interrogation of a suspect by a judicial police officer, admitted the instigation, but denies it in court, the suspect interrogation record prepared by the judicial police officer concerning A, in which A denied the contents, may be used as rebuttal evidence to impeach A’s in-court testimony, insofar as voluntariness is recognized. (b) If W, B’s friend, appears in court and testifies that B told him, “I killed A,” W’s testimony cannot be used as evidence of B’s guilt so long as B, the original declarant, is appearing in court. (c) If both A and B are confessing to the charged facts, but there is no other evidence corroborating the confessions, A and B must be acquitted. (d) If A confesses in court to instigating the murder of A, A’s statement may be used as evidence of B’s guilt. (e) Even if the court of first instance, in sentencing A, did not specify the fact that B strangled and killed A, if there are special circumstances showing that A’s right of defense or A’s counsel’s right of defense was not essentially infringed, it is not a violation of law that affected the judgment.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2005DO2617]": "1. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below held that the trial court’s judgment acquitting the defendant was proper on the ground that the victim Nonparty 1’s statements to the police and in the trial court of first instance, which were consistent with the facts charged, were hard to believe, and that the medical certificate concerning Nonparty 1 prepared by Physician Nonparty 2 and Nonparty 2’s statement in the trial court of first instance alone were insufficient to recognize the facts charged; upon examining the record, the court below’s fact-finding and determination are proper, and there is no illegality in the misapprehension of facts in violation of the rules of evidence evaluation as alleged in the grounds of final appeal.\\n\\n2. The interrogation record of the suspect concerning the defendant, prepared by a judicial police officer and submitted by the prosecutor as material of guilt, has no evidentiary value once the defendant denies its contents; however, unless there are circumstances sufficient to arouse suspicion that it was not prepared voluntarily, it may be used as counterevidence to impeach the defendant’s statement in court. In addition, it is clear pursuant to Article 318-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act that impeachment evidence is not evidence to establish the facts of the crime and therefore need not undergo strict evidentiary examination, but evidentiary examination thereof in court as impeachment evidence is necessary (see Supreme Court Decision 95DO1333 rendered on January 26, 1996, Supreme Court Decision 97DO1770 rendered on February 27, 1998, etc.); meanwhile, in light of the purport of Article 132(1) of the Criminal Procedure Rules, which prescribes the method of evidentiary motions, even in the submission of impeachment evidence, the relationship between the evidence and the fact to be proved and the purpose of proof, etc. must be specifically indicated in advance, in that the opposing party must be given an opportunity in advance to devise means of attack and defense concerning it; therefore, the opposing party must be informed in advance which part of the statement is to be challenged by which part of the evidence whose probative value is to be disputed.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the prosecutor submitted the interrogation record of the suspect concerning the defendant, prepared by a judicial police officer, as evidence of guilt, and the defendant admitted its authenticity and voluntariness but denied its contents, so it became inadmissible; the prosecutor did not state, at the time of submission of evidence or thereafter in the trial court of first instance, the evidentiary purpose that the above interrogation record of the suspect was impeachment evidence, but stated that purport in the statement of reasons for appeal made in the court below; although evidentiary examination thereof as impeachment evidence was not conducted in court, impeachment evidence is not evidence to establish the facts of the crime and therefore need not undergo strict evidentiary examination; although evidentiary examination of the above interrogation record of the suspect as impeachment evidence was not conducted, it was in any event submitted to court and evidentiary examination was conducted; the procedure for evidentiary examination of the above interrogation record of the suspect as impeachment evidence would ultimately be by the prosecutor stating the evidentiary purpose, etc., and then, after giving the defendant’s side an opportunity to inspect it, hearing its opinion, and, in light of the circumstances that such procedure can be seen to have been largely carried out up to the court below, the above interrogation record of the suspect should be deemed usable as impeachment evidence against the defendant’s in-court statement.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below held that, in order to use the above interrogation record of the suspect as impeachment evidence against the defendant’s in-court statement, as a general rule, the evidentiary purpose that it is for impeaching the defendant’s in-court statement must be specified, and evidentiary examination must be conducted in court as impeachment evidence; however, although the prosecutor submitted the above interrogation record of the suspect as evidence at the first trial date in the court of first instance, he did not specify in the evidentiary purpose that it was for impeaching the defendant’s in-court statement, and no evidentiary examination thereof was conducted in court as impeachment evidence, so the court below determined that the above interrogation record of the suspect could not become impeachment evidence against the defendant’s in-court statement; as examined above, such action of the court below contains an error of law in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the admissibility of impeachment evidence or the method of its examination.\\n\\nHowever, even if the above interrogation record of the suspect can be used as impeachment evidence against the defendant’s in-court statement, this cannot be deemed to have diminished the probative value of the defendant’s in-court statement denying the facts charged, and, as determined in Paragraph 1, since there is no evidence to recognize the facts charged, such error does not affect the result of the judgment and therefore cannot be viewed as an illegality constituting a ground for reversal of the judgment; accordingly, the ground of final appeal pointing this out is without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and it is adjudged as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court participating."}

{"[81DO2422]": "We decide on the grounds of appeal filed by the Defendant’s counsel, Attorney Kang An-hui.\\n\\n1. We examine the first ground of appeal.\\n\\nThe so-called simplified trial procedure prescribed by Article 286-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act is a trial procedure adopted, in cases other than those to be tried by the collegiate division of a district court and its branch court as a court of first instance, when the Defendant confesses the facts charged in open court; it consists, inter alia, of special provisions concerning the admissibility of evidence (Article 318-3 of the Criminal Procedure Act) and the simplification of the evidence-taking procedure (Article 297-2 of the same Act). A confession of the facts charged should be understood as being sufficient if the Defendant admits the facts stated in the indictment and further does not state facts constituting grounds for unlawfulness or for exclusion of responsibility; it should not be understood as requiring a statement explicitly admitting guilt.\\n\\nHowever, according to the entries in the transcript of the first hearing of the first instance in this case, the Defendant, in response to the question from the participating prosecutor, “Did the Defendant receive a request from the co-defendant at first instance to escort Nonindicted 1, a stowaway, to Busan, and, while knowing that he was a stowaway, facilitate his stowaway departure and thereby aid and abet it?”, answered, “The co-defendant at first instance is the Defendant’s daughter, so she merely carried out the matter by telling the Defendant to take Nonindicted 1 and deliver him to Nonindicted 2” (Record, p. 27), and it is clear that he is not making a statement denying the offense; the purport of the Defendant’s above answer, when the entirety of the Defendant’s statements in open court are considered, is construed as admitting the criminal facts stated in the indictment in this case against the Defendant while merely denying the motive for the offense, namely that it was done at the request of the Defendant’s daughter. Therefore, the first-instance decision that determined this case should be tried under the simplified trial procedure is proper, and there is no error of law in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the simplified trial procedure. The argument to the contrary, that the purport of the above answer should be construed as denying criminal intent and that, even if such a statement does not actively deny criminal intent, the confession prescribed in Article 286-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act must explicitly admit guilt as to the facts charged, so that the Defendant’s statement as set forth in the foregoing first part cannot constitute a clear statement admitting guilt and affirming criminal responsibility as to the facts charged in this case, and therefore the above decision cannot escape illegality, is nothing more than an independent view and cannot be accepted.\\n\\n2. We examine the second ground of appeal.\\n\\nAs a general matter, the establishment of the principal offender forms part of the elements of accessory liability for instigation and accessory liability for aiding and abetting, and, in order for instigation or aiding and abetting to be established, it is a prerequisite, as a matter of course flowing from the principle of dependence of accomplice liability, that the criminal act of the principal offender be first recognized. Therefore, even in stating the facts of instigation or aiding and abetting, all facts constituting the offense of the principal offender must be stated, and a statement of the facts of instigation or aiding and abetting that lacks such description cannot be said to be a statement of facts constituting a crime. The first-instance judgment maintained by the appellate court states the Defendant’s criminal facts as follows: “On December 21, 1978, at around 15:00, at the waiting room of Jeju Airport located in Jeju City, the Defendant received a request from the co-defendant at first instance to escort Nonindicted 1, a stowaway, to Busan, and, while knowing that he was a stowaway, took Nonindicted 1 to the entrance of the waiting room of the domestic passenger terminal at Busan Port and handed him over there to Nonindicted 2, thereby causing Nonindicted 1 to depart by sea as in the preceding paragraph, facilitating his stowaway departure and thereby aiding and abetting it.” However, not only is there no finding whatsoever as to the criminal facts of Nonindicted 1, who appears to be the principal offender, but the phrase “causing Nonindicted 1 to do as in the preceding paragraph” written in the judgment form refers to a preceding paragraph that is not even set forth in the judgment, which plainly shows that there is no statement of facts constituting a crime. Accordingly, the appellate judgment upheld the first-instance judgment, which did not contain the reasons to be stated in a conviction, and thereby there is an error of law in failing to provide reasons, and this error clearly affected the outcome of the judgment. Therefore, the ground of appeal is well taken in this respect.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the judgment below is reversed, and, for the purpose of having the case heard and decided again, the case is remanded to the Collegiate Division of the Jeju District Court, and judgment is rendered as follows, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[90DO1939]": "1. Determination on each of the Defendants’ first grounds of appeal.  \\nAccording to the record, it is clear not only that, at the third trial date in the first instance, the Defendants each admitted the genuineness of the formation of each interrogation protocol of suspects prepared by the prosecutor concerning themselves, and even admitted that the statements recorded in each such protocol were made voluntarily, but also that the Defendants, while being investigated by the prosecutor, all gave detailed statements concerning each of the facts charged in this case and the factual circumstances related thereto. In light of the Defendants’ educational background, career, occupation, degree of intelligence, and the like, it cannot be said that each of the Defendants’ statements recorded in each interrogation protocol of suspects prepared by the prosecutor concerning the Defendants was not made voluntarily. Accordingly, the argument contesting the admissibility of evidence of each interrogation protocol of suspects concerning the Defendants prepared by the prosecutor is without merit.\\n\\n2. Determination on each of the Defendants’ second grounds of appeal, the defense counsel’s ground of appeal concerning Defendant A, the third ground of appeal concerning Defendant C, and the first ground of appeal concerning Defendant D.  \\nWhen the evidence adopted by the first-instance judgment cited by the court below is examined in comparison with the record, the count of robbery causing injury against Defendant A, the counts of robbery causing death against Defendants C and D, the counts of aggravated robbery and aggravated theft against Defendant D, and the counts of aggravated theft against Defendant E may all be sufficiently recognized. Moreover, the appellate court’s judgment cannot be deemed to contain any illegality that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning co-principal liability or causation, or by erroneously finding facts in violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the argument. Therefore, all of the arguments are without merit.\\n\\n3. Determination on the defense counsel’s first ground of appeal concerning Defendant C and the ground of appeal concerning Defendant E.  \\nSince the statement of a co-defendant who is an accomplice is not included in the “defendant’s confession” provided in Article 310 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the statement of a co-defendant who is an accomplice may not only be used as evidence to establish criminal facts against another co-defendant, but the respective statements of co-defendants who are accomplices may also serve as mutual corroborating evidence (see Supreme Court Decisions 85DO951, rendered on July 9, 1985; 86DO1773, rendered on October 28, 1986; 87DO973, rendered on July 7, 1987; 87DO1020, rendered on December 22, 1987, and others). Accordingly, the argument to the effect that the appellate judgment erred in its understanding of the legal principles concerning corroborating evidence for a confession is also not acceptable.\\n\\n4. Determination on the defense counsel’s second ground of appeal concerning Defendant C.  \\nThe court below acquitted Defendant C of the count of robbery causing injury among the facts charged in this case on the ground that there was no proof of the criminal facts; therefore, it is clear that the argument criticizing the appellate judgment on the premise that the court below also found this count guilty is without merit.\\n\\n5. Determination on the defense counsel’s fourth ground of appeal concerning Defendant C and the second ground of appeal concerning Defendant D.  \\nIn view of the various circumstances appearing in the record that constitute sentencing conditions, such as the age, conduct, intelligence, and environment of the above Defendants, their relationship with the victims, the motive, means, and result of each offense, and the circumstances after the offenses, even taking into account the mitigating circumstances asserted by defense counsel, the sentencing imposed by the court below on the above Defendants appears appropriate, and there is no manifest reason to conclude that the sentencing is grossly unjust. Accordingly, this argument is also without merit.\\n\\n6.
