Therefore, all appeals by the Defendants are dismissed, and it is unanimously decided by the judges participating in the case that some of the days of detention after appeal shall each be credited toward the principal sentence in the judgment below, and judgment is rendered as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[92DO917]": "1. We shall consider together the grounds of appeal by Defendants A and C, and the first point of the grounds of appeal by Attorney D (court-appointed) and Attorneys B and E (retained), counsel for Defendant A.\\n\\nUpon examining, from the record, the evidence adopted in the first-instance judgment as affirmed by the court below, the criminal facts of each Defendant as stated in the judgment below are fully established, and there is no illegality in the court below’s fact-finding process, such as violation of the rules of evidence, insufficiency of deliberation, or erroneous understanding of the law, as alleged.\\n\\nThe confessions of a defendant under Article 310 of the Criminal Procedure Act do not include the statements of a co-defendant who is a co-offender, and with respect to such statements of a co-defendant, the defendant’s right to cross-examine is guaranteed, so that they have independent evidentiary admissibility; this is this Court’s consistent view (see Supreme Court Decisions 85DO951, rendered on March 9, 1985; 85DO691, rendered on June 25, 1985; and 87DO973, rendered on July 7, 1987). Accordingly, it cannot be faulted as unlawful that the court below relied on the statements of the other co-defendants as evidence in finding the criminal facts of Defendant A.\\n\\nThe record further shows that, in the evidentiary examination proceedings at first instance, the Defendants admitted the authenticity and voluntariness of each interrogation record of a suspect prepared by the prosecutor and the judicial police officer acting in the capacity of a judicial police officer for each Defendant, and there are no grounds to suspect, as alleged, that the Defendants’ statements before the investigative authorities were made under coercion such as torture; nor is the contention that the statements made in court by the other Defendants concerning Defendant A’s crime were obtained through the prosecutor’s torture and threats anything more than an assertion wholly unsupported by the record.\\n\\nAll of the contentions are without merit.\\n\\n2. We shall consider the second point of the grounds of appeal by Attorney B and E, counsel for Defendant A.\\n\\nA joint principal offense requires, as a subjective element, conspiracy and, as an objective element, division of the acts of execution at the scene; however, such division of the acts of execution does not necessarily mean only that the acts of execution are specifically divided simultaneously at the same place, but it is sufficient if they can be deemed to have a cooperative relationship with each other in terms of time or place.\\n\\nAccording to the facts stated in paragraph 1.(1) of the judgment below, Defendant C among the Defendants climbed over the wall of the victim’s house and opened the gate to allow Defendants A and F to enter, after which Defendants F and C opened and entered the front door with a screwdriver and, each holding one of two kitchen knives found there, all of the Defendants entered the main room, threatened the victims with the knives, tied their hands, and searched the wardrobe drawers to take jewelry and cash by force. Therefore, even if Defendant A did not personally open the door or hold a kitchen knife as alleged, since he acted together with the other Defendants and cooperated in the commission of the offense as stated in the judgment below, it should be deemed that he divided the acts of execution at the scene.\\n\\nThe contention that the judgment below is unlawful for lack of reasoning and for erroneous understanding of the law concerning the joint commission of robbery is without merit.\\n\\n3. We shall consider points 3 and 4 of the same grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe nighttime housebreaking robbery under Article 334(1) of the Criminal Act is a compound offense of housebreaking and robbery, and since the housebreaking precedes temporally, it is to be deemed that the execution of this offense has been commenced at the time of housebreaking. Likewise, in the case of the robbery by a group acting in concert while carrying a deadly weapon prescribed in Article 334(2), where the robbery is committed by entering a dwelling at night, it is proper to regard the execution as having commenced at the time of housebreaking.\\n\\nAccording to the facts stated in paragraph 1.(3) of the judgment below, the Defendants, having arrived at the house of victim G at night with the intent to take property by force, Defendant C entered through the bars beside the entrance, and Defendant F, while tearing off the kitchen window screen and entering, fled upon thinking that they had been discovered by the victim’s father-in-law, who coughed deliberately, and thus failed to accomplish their purpose. According to the facts stated in paragraph 1.(1) of the judgment below, the Defendants arrived at the house of victim H at night, Defendant C climbed over the wall and opened the gate, the remaining Defendants entered the house, and at the moment Defendant F held a kitchen knife in the kitchen and entered the room, the emergency bell sounded and they fled, thus failing to accomplish their purpose. Therefore, since the Defendants, as above, entered a dwelling at night, they had commenced the execution of the special robbery offense and should be punished as attempted offenders, and it goes without saying that Defendant A, as a Defendant who acted together at the scene, must bear the same criminal liability. The court below’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality, such as lack of reasoning or erroneous understanding of the law concerning attempt of special robbery, as alleged. Accordingly, this contention is also without merit.\\n\\n4. We shall consider the fifth point of the same grounds of appeal.\\n\\nWhen a thief assaults or threatens a police officer for the purpose of evading arrest, it constitutes quasi-robbery and obstruction of performance of official duties, and the two offenses are in a relationship of ideal concurrence; however, when a robber assaults a police officer for the purpose of evading arrest, robbery and obstruction of performance of official duties are in a relationship of real concurrence, not ideal concurrence.\\n\\nThe contrary contention is without merit as an independent view.\\n\\n5. We shall consider the sixth point of the same grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the facts in paragraph 2.(1) of the judgment below, while the Defendants were committing robbery, Defendants C and A dragged victim I into a small room in an attempt to rape her, forcibly removed her panties and touched her genitals, but failed to accomplish their purpose because the victim pleaded that she had abdominal pain as she had recently undergone surgery. Since they attempted to rape a victim who had already fallen into a state of fear during the continuation of the robbery, the execution of rape should be deemed to have commenced; and in light of the contents of the relevant evidence, including the victim’s statement, the reason the Defendants discontinued the sexual intercourse was not pity for the victim, but rather that they considered there to be an impediment to committing rape due to the victim’s physical condition. Thus, under ordinary experience, this is nothing more than a case where the offense was discontinued due to an external circumstance that impeded the commission of the rape, and it must be deemed to lack voluntariness, which is a requirement for an abandoned offense.\\n\\nThe court below’s determination not to apply the mitigation or exemption provision for an abandoned offense is proper, and there is no illegality, such as lack of reasoning or erroneous understanding of the law, as alleged. Accordingly, this contention is also without merit.\\n\\n6. We shall consider together point 7 of the same grounds of appeal, the grounds of appeal by Defendant F, the point of inappropriate sentencing among the remaining Defendants’ grounds of appeal, and point 2 of the grounds of appeal by counsel for the Defendants, Attorney D.\\n\\nUpon examining the various circumstances constituting the conditions for sentencing appearing in the record, such as the Defendants’ age, character and conduct, intelligence and environment, their relationship with the victims, the motive, means, and result of the offense, and the circumstances after the offense, the court below’s determination of sentence for the Defendants appears appropriate, and there are no manifest reasons to conclude that the determination of sentence is extremely heavy and unfair. Accordingly, all contentions on this point are without merit.\\n\\n7. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as follows, by the unanimous opinion of the judges involved."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning trial proceedings are correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) (a) If the defendant failed to appear on the first trial date in the appellate instance, appeared on the second trial date, but again failed to appear on the third trial date, and the court proceeded with the trial proceedings in the presence only of the defendant's defense counsel and the prosecutor, closed the arguments, and then pronounced a judgment dismissing the defendant's appeal on the fourth trial date, this is lawful as a measure under Article 365 of the Criminal Procedure Act. (b) In first-instance trial proceedings, if the defendant's whereabouts cannot be ascertained for six months from the receipt of a report of failure of service on the defendant, the case may be tried without the defendant's statement in accordance with the Supreme Court Rules; however, in cases punishable by death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or penal detention for a term exceeding 10 years, the case may not be tried without the defendant's statement. (c) The opportunity to state the final opinion need only be given to the defendant or defense counsel; therefore, even if the presiding judge, immediately after defense counsel's final argument, designated and notified the date for pronouncement of judgment, thereby closing the arguments and pronouncing judgment without giving the defendant an opportunity to state a final opinion, this is an act of discretion within the scope of the presiding judge's power to direct the proceedings and cannot be regarded as a violation of the law in the procedural proceedings. (d) Whether to reopen closed arguments is, in principle, a matter within the court's discretion; however, if the appellate court did not grant a motion for reopening of arguments filed by defense counsel appointed after the close of arguments, this corresponds to a case in which there is illegality due to incomplete hearing. (e) Whether to admit an evidentiary application is within the court's discretion, so with respect to the court's evidentiary decision neither an ordinary appeal nor an immediate appeal may be taken; rather, an objection may be raised only when the evidentiary decision violates statutes and regulations, and it may also be used as a ground for appeal only when, as a result, there has been a mistaken finding of facts affecting the judgment.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2018DO327]": "Examining the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nArticle 303 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “after hearing the prosecutor’s opinion, the presiding judge shall give the defendant and the defense counsel an opportunity to state their final opinions.” Accordingly, the opportunity to state final opinions must be given to both the defendant and the defense counsel. Such opportunity to state final opinions is a procedural right of the defendant and the defense counsel, and since it is the last opportunity for the defendant and the defense counsel to assert disputes over facts or favorable sentencing factors, concluding the trial and rendering judgment without giving the defendant or the defense counsel an opportunity to state final opinions constitutes a violation of the laws and regulations concerning the procedural process (see Supreme Court Decision 75DO1010, rendered November 11, 1975, and others).\\n\\nAccording to the record of this case, ① the court below concluded the trial on November 1, 2017, at the first trial date, and the trial transcript of that trial date states that the defendant made a statement to the effect of “I hope for leniency” as his final opinion; ② after the conclusion of the trial, the court below rendered a judgment on December 11, 2017, at the second trial date, dismissing both the defendant’s and the prosecutor’s appeals; ③ however, the defense counsel for the defendant filed an objection to the record with the court below on December 15, 2017, on the ground that the presiding judge had designated and notified the date of judgment immediately after the defense counsel’s final argument, thereby preventing the defendant from being afforded an opportunity to make a final statement, and the court below, on December 16, 2017, accepted this objection and corrected the trial transcript of the first trial date by deleting the portion stating that the defendant had said he hoped for leniency.\\nIf so, it must be said that the court below concluded the trial and rendered judgment without giving the defendant an opportunity to state his final opinion, and therefore the judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the outcome of the judgment by violating the laws and regulations concerning the procedural process. The ground of appeal asserting this point is well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below shall be reversed and the case shall be remanded to the court below for a new trial and determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[86DO769]": "We consider together the grounds for appeal by the Defendant and his counsel.\\n\\nComparing the evidence admitted in the first-instance judgment cited by the court below with the record, the court below’s disposition recognizing the criminal facts stated in the judgment against the Defendant as guilty is proper, and there is no illegality of factual misapprehension caused by violation of the rules of evidence in the course thereof (the Defendant denied some of the facts of the offense in the first instance, but has admitted them all by the time of the court below).\\n\\nWhether to reopen argument after it has been concluded is a matter within the court’s discretion, and the court below did not err by failing to grant the motion for reopening of argument filed by counsel appointed after the close of argument; there is thus no illegality of incomplete examination.\\n\\nIn addition, in light of the various circumstances constituting the conditions for sentencing as seen from the record, it cannot be found that the determination of the punishment against the Defendant is grossly improper.\\n\\nEach of the arguments lacks merit.\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and pursuant to Article 57 of the Criminal Act and Article 24 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning Expedition, etc. of Legal Proceedings, a portion of the period of detention after the filing of the appeal shall be reckoned, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the institution of public prosecution and amendment of the indictment is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedent)
A: Even if the prosecution was instituted without specifying the defendant, if the defendant and defense counsel did not raise an objection and proceeded with the trial, the defect in the prosecution is cured.
B: Even where, because the time, place, means, and object of the offense differ among the criminal facts, they are recognized as multiple criminal facts, those multiple criminal facts may be pleaded alternatively or in the alternative.
C: In the case of a comprehensive single offense, in determining whether to grant leave to amend the indictment, rather than examining, for each individual count constituting the comprehensive single offense, whether it is identical to the former one, the focus should be on whether the amended facts, viewed as a whole, fall within the category of a comprehensive single offense; that is, whether they may be regarded as a case in which the same kind of offense is repeatedly committed under a single and continuous criminal intent and the protected legal interest harmed is also the same.
D: Even where, as a result of an amendment to the indictment, the case no longer qualifies as a case subject to a citizen participation trial, the court must continue the citizen participation trial; however, the court may decide to have the case tried by the collegiate division of the main branch of the District Court without a citizen participation trial, and no appeal lies against such decision.
E: Even if, without the intent and ability to perform repayment, the defendant was prosecuted for having defrauded money from the victim, if it is recognized, without going through the procedure for amendment of the indictment, as the fact that the defendant caused the victim to be introduced to a third party, borrowed the same amount of money, and thereby obtained a property benefit by causing the victim to assume a surety obligation therefor, there can be no illegality.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DO514]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe court below, while presenting the doubts stated in its reasoning, and on the ground that, in a situation where such doubts had not been reasonably explained, the evidence submitted by the Prosecutor alone could not conclude that each of the charged facts against the Defendants was guilty, rendered a judgment of not guilty as to the amended charged facts in the court below against Defendants 1, 2, and 3, and maintained, as it was, the first-instance judgment that had rendered a judgment of not guilty as to Defendant 4; and, when the relevant evidence is examined in light of the record, the court below’s such determination is persuasive, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality of mistake of fact due to violation of the rules of evidence evaluation, as asserted in the grounds of appeal. The court below, having found that the statement of the non-indicted person, which the Prosecutor presented as the most powerful evidence, lacked credibility as a whole, determined all of the charged facts against the Defendants to be not guilty; it did not render a judgment of not guilty as to all of the charged facts on the ground that the statement of that person did not conform to some of the charged facts that are in the relationship of a single continuing offense, without even examining the remaining charged facts. Therefore, it cannot be said that the court below’s judgment violated the legal doctrine on a single continuing offense and failed to conduct a complete examination. The argument in the grounds of appeal disputing this cannot be accepted.\\n\\nWith respect to each of the charged facts against Defendant 1, which are in the relationship of a single continuing offense, the court below did not permit the amendment of the indictment that changed, as stated in item 8 of Attached Table 1 to the judgment of the court below (Status of Amounts Received by Defendant 1), the time of delivery of money from the previously stated “around the latter part of January 2002” to “around the early part of February 2002,” and the place of delivery of money from the previously stated “an unnamed teahouse near Seodaemun Police Station located in Migeun-dong, Seodaemun-gu, Seoul” to “the duty office of the Criminal Section of Seodaemun Police Station located in Migeun-dong, Seodaemun-gu, Seoul,” respectively, and, as stated in item 15 of the same table, changed the time of delivery of money from the previously stated “around the latter part of September 2002” to “around the middle of September 2002,” and the place of delivery of money from the previously stated “an unnamed teahouse near Seodaemun Police Station located in Migeun-dong, Seodaemun-gu, Seoul” to “the duty office of the Criminal Section of Seodaemun Police Station located in Migeun-dong, Seodaemun-gu, Seoul,” respectively. In a single continuing offense, in light of the fact that the withdrawal of the previous charged facts and the addition of new charged facts through amendment of the indictment are possible, in determining whether to grant permission for amendment of the indictment, rather than examining, for each individual charged fact constituting the single continuing offense, whether it is identical to the previous one, the focus should be on whether the amended charged facts, taken as a whole, fall within the category of a single continuing offense, that is, whether they can be regarded as repeated commission of the same kind of offense under a single and continuing criminal intent and as corresponding to the same protected legal interest. In this case, the above charged facts in issue, despite the changes in the time and place of delivery of money, still retain their character as the so-called offense of receiving bribes in the form of monthly payments, and it is clear that they constitute a single continuing offense together with the other charged facts; therefore, the court below’s failure to permit the amendment of the indictment with respect to the above charged facts contains an illegality of misapprehending the legal doctrine on amendment of an indictment.\\n\\nHowever, on the other hand, if permission were granted for the amendment of the indictment with respect to the above charged facts, the evidentiary relationship concerning the amended charged facts also appears to be not much different from that concerning the previous charged facts, and, just as there is insufficient evidence to acknowledge the previous charged facts, there also appears to be insufficient evidence to acknowledge the amended charged facts, and no other evidence appears capable of proving the amended charged facts. (Although Defendants 1 and 2 admit that they received some money from the non-indicted person, as the court below properly determined, the fact that the above Defendants admitted receiving money and the charged facts of this case differ in the name or purpose of the money received and are separate criminal facts that are mutually compatible, so it is difficult to regard the above Defendants as admitting some of the charged facts in this case.) If the circumstances are such, then even if the court below had permitted the amendment of the indictment with respect to the above charged facts and had conducted an examination concerning the amended charged facts, it is clear that it would ultimately have rendered a judgment of not guilty with respect to the amended charged facts; therefore, the illegality of the court below in not permitting the amendment of the indictment with respect to the above charged facts cannot be deemed to have affected the result of the judgment (see Supreme Court Decision 1999. 5. 14. 98DO1438), and accordingly the argument in this part of the grounds of appeal also cannot be accepted.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the participating Justices are unanimous, so judgment is rendered as follows."}

{"[2008DO11813]": "We decide together on the grounds of appeal by the Defendant and the court-appointed defense counsel.\\n\\n1. The institution of a public prosecution is the prosecutor’s juridical procedural act by which the prosecutor requests the court to adjudicate a specified criminal case. Article 254(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”) provides that, when instituting a prosecution, the bill of indictment shall be submitted to the competent court, and Article 254(3) of the same Act provides that such bill of indictment shall state certain matters, including the defendant’s name and other matters identifying the defendant, the name of the offense, the facts constituting the charge, and the applicable provisions of law. Article 266 of the Act provides that, when a prosecution has been instituted, a duplicate of the bill of indictment shall be served on the defendant or defense counsel without delay. The Criminal Procedure Act adopted, with respect to the institution of a prosecution, the above-mentioned written-form principle and strict formal acts because judicial review by the court commences upon the institution of a prosecution, thereby clarifying the subject of the requested adjudication and ensuring the defendant’s right to defense. Accordingly, the submission of a bill of indictment in accordance with such strict form and procedure is an essential element for the establishment of the procedural act of instituting a prosecution; therefore, where there is a material violation of form in the institution of a prosecution, the procedure for instituting the prosecution shall be deemed to fall under a case where it is void in violation of the provisions of law. Such defect is not cured merely because the Defendant and defense counsel did not raise an objection and proceeded with the trial in response to a prosecution instituted in violation of the above procedure.\\n\\n2. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the records of this case, a prosecution was initially instituted against the Defendant for the criminal facts set forth in Items 1, 2, and 4 of the first-instance judgment and for the sale of Philopon on August 26, 2007 (hereinafter referred to as “the sale act in this case”); while the first instance was pending, on May 9, 2008, the prosecutor filed an application for permission to amend the indictment (hereinafter referred to as “the application for amendment in this case”) adding, in the alternative, the act of brokering the sale and purchase of Philopon on August 30, 2007 (hereinafter referred to as “the brokering act in this case”) to the facts charged regarding the sale act in this case; the first-instance court granted the application for amendment in this case, but on the 13th trial date on June 13, 2008, it revoked the order granting the application for amendment in this case on the ground that there was no identity between the sale act in this case and the brokering act in this case; thereupon, the prosecutor, on the spot, stated that the application for amendment in this case would substitute for the bill of indictment regarding the brokering act in this case, and made a statement maintaining the prosecution based on the application for amendment in this case, to which the Defendant and defense counsel stated that they had no objection; on August 13, 2008, as the first-instance judgment was rendered, a not-guilty verdict was entered with respect to the sale act in this case, and guilt was found with respect to the remaining criminal facts, including the brokering act in this case; the Defendant argued in the lower court that there had been a mistake in fact concerning the brokering act in this case, but that argument was not accepted, so the Defendant’s appeal was dismissed, and the prosecutor’s appeal regarding the above not-guilty portion was also dismissed; the application for amendment in this case contained only the facts charged regarding the brokering act in this case and the wording requesting permission for the application for amendment in this case, and did not state the Defendant’s name, other matters identifying the Defendant, or the applicable provisions of law, and the application for amendment in this case was not served on the Defendant or defense counsel, nor were the case-number assignment and case-distribution procedures for a new institution of prosecution gone through. Each of the above facts is acknowledged.\\n\\n3. In light of the foregoing legal principles, the institution of the prosecution regarding the brokering act in this case was effected not only on the basis of the application for amendment in this case, which failed to satisfy the formal requirements prescribed in Article 254 of the Act, but also by the prosecutor’s oral statement at the trial date that the application for amendment in this case would substitute for the bill of indictment without procedures such as service of a duplicate of the bill of indictment. Thus, it is appropriate to regard the procedure for instituting such prosecution as having a material violation of form to the extent that it is void in violation of the provisions of law, and it cannot be viewed that the defect was cured merely because the Defendant and defense counsel did not raise an objection thereto. Accordingly, with respect to the facts charged concerning the brokering act in this case, a judgment dismissing the prosecution should have been rendered.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court, premised on the legality of the institution of prosecution regarding the brokering act in this case, recognized the facts charged for that part as guilty. In doing so, it erred by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the method of instituting a prosecution, and such error affected the outcome of the judgment. Therefore, the ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded. However, since the facts charged concerning the brokering act in this case and the remaining facts charged found guilty are in a concurrent-offenses relationship under the former sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, the guilty portion of the lower court judgment cannot avoid reversal in its entirety.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the guilty portion of the lower court judgment is reversed, and this case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination on that part, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2018DO1481]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined (the Defendant’s supplementary statement of grounds for final appeal and written opinion submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds for final appeal shall be considered to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\n1. Regarding the Defendant’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\nExamining the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below in light of the evidence lawfully admitted, the court below’s determination that the portions of the facts charged in this case concerning assault, the portions concerning violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (filming using a camera, etc.) arising from each act of filming (excluding the acquitted portion), and the portion concerning attempted violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (filming using a camera, etc.) arising from the display of recorded materials were guilty is proper. There is no error therein, such as, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nIn addition, under Article 383 subparagraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, final appeal may be taken on the ground of improper sentencing only in cases in which death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or custody for not less than 10 years has been imposed. Therefore, in this case, in which a lighter sentence was imposed on the Defendant, the assertion to the effect that the order to attend lectures is excessive does not constitute a lawful ground for final appeal.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Prosecutor’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\na. Regarding the portion concerning violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (filming using a camera, etc.) arising from the provision of recorded materials\\n\\nArticle 14(1) of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Sexual Crimes Punishment Act”) punishes the act of “photographing, against the will of another person, the body of another person that may cause sexual desire or humiliation by using a camera or other device with a similar function, or distributing, selling, leasing, providing, or openly displaying or screening the photographed material.”\\n\\nThe reason why Article 14(1) of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act punishes not only the act of photographing but also the act of distributing, selling, leasing, providing, or openly displaying or screening photographed materials is to protect victims by preventing the dissemination of photographed materials; in light of the social problem that photographed materials depicting another person’s body that may arouse sexual desire or shame are rapidly and widely disseminated through the internet and other information and communications networks, thereby causing enormous damage and suffering to victims, the culpability and blameworthiness of the person who disseminates the photographed materials can be said to be as great as that of the photographer (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2016DO6172, decided October 13, 2016).\\n\\n“Providing,” which is separately listed from “distributing” in Article 14(1) of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act, means a gratuitous transfer that does not amount to “distribution,” namely, gratuitously transferring to a “specific one person or a small number of persons” without intent to “distribute” (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DO16676, decided December 27, 2016). However, as seen above, given that Article 14(1) of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act punishes not only the act of photographing but also the act of distributing, selling, leasing, providing, or openly displaying or screening photographed materials in order to protect victims by preventing the dissemination of such materials, it is reasonable to view that the victim who was the subject of the photographing is not included among the “specific one person or a small number of persons,” who are the recipients of “providing” as referred to in Article 14(1) of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act.\\n\\nAccordingly, the act of delivering photographed materials to the victim personally cannot be said to constitute “providing” under Article 14(1) of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act, absent other special circumstances.\\n\\nWhile the court below found the Defendant guilty of the act in the facts charged of photographing, against the victim’s will, the victim’s body that could cause sexual desire or humiliation by using a camera, it found not guilty of the portion concerning violation of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act (filming using a camera, etc.) arising from the Defendant’s act of transmitting one of the photographs to the victim’s mobile phone, on the grounds stated in its reasoning. The court below’s determination as above is in accordance with the legal principles previously stated and is proper, and there is no error therein, such as misapprehending the legal principles concerning “providing” under Article 14(1) of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nb. Regarding the remaining portions\\n\\nThe Prosecutor filed a final appeal against the entire judgment of the court below, but with respect to the remaining acquitted portions and the guilty portions of the judgment of the court below, excluding the portion concerning violation of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act (filming using a camera, etc.) arising from the provision of recorded materials, the petition for final appeal contains no lawful statement of grounds for final appeal, and the statement of grounds for final appeal likewise contains no statement of reasons for objection.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all final appeals are dismissed, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[84DO312]": "We examine the Defendant’s grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. If one compares the reasons of the judgment of the court below with the record, the gist of the charged facts in this case is that the Defendant, on two occasions at the home of the victim Heo Ok-ryeon, at around 11:00 on 1981.10.28. and at around 14:00 on 11.25. of the same year, deceived the said victim by falsely stating that he would promptly repay the money after temporarily borrowing it despite having no intention or ability to repay, and thereby obtained a total of 480,000 won from her by fraud; whereas the gist of the criminal facts found by the court below as to the Defendant is that at the same time and place the Defendant told the same victim a falsehood to the effect that if the victim would either lend him money directly or enable him to borrow money from others through the victim’s introduction, he would promptly repay it, thereby deceiving her, and through the person thus deceived, borrowed a total of 480,000 won from two persons, namely the unindicted persons Kim Il-sun and Kim Do-sun, while causing the victim Heo Ok-ryeon to bear a guaranty debt therefor and thereby obtaining pecuniary gain. Thus, as the argument points out, there are some differences between the charged facts and the facts found by the court below regarding the source of the damaged funds or the details of the loss suffered by the victim, and there was also no amendment procedure to the indictment; however, if the charged facts of this case are compared with the criminal facts found by the court below, the amount of money borrowed by the Defendant is identical in both cases, totaling 480,000 won, and the manner of deception is also identical in that he falsely stated, despite having no intention or ability to repay, that he would repay it within a short period of time, and even with respect to the nature of the damage suffered by the victim Heo Ok-ryeon, although there is a formal difference such as a decrease in active assets or an increase in passive assets, substantively the amount of damage is identical at 480,000 won; therefore, there is no difference whatsoever in the basic fact that the Defendant deceived the victim and fraudulently obtained money. Accordingly, the facts found by the court below cannot be said to have departed from the identity of the charged facts in this case. Moreover, since it is clear that at the court below the Defendant admitted that he borrowed the funds in this case from Kim Il-sun and Kim Do-sun with the introduction and guaranty of the victim Heo Ok-ryeon, it cannot be said that the court below, by recognizing such facts without amendment of the indictment, caused the Defendant any disadvantage in his defense; therefore, the above measure of the court below cannot be deemed unlawful for having misapprehended the legal principle of no accusation and no disadvantage as argued. Accordingly, this ground of appeal is without merit.\\n\\n2. However, the court below, in recognizing the criminal facts of this case against the Defendant, cited as evidence some of the Defendant’s statements from the police stage through the court below, the respective statements of the unindicted persons Heo Ok-ryeon and Kim Hwa-sun at the police, prosecution, or trial stage, and the respective statements of the lower-court witnesses Kim Il-sun and Kim Do-sun. Yet, unless the Defendant confesses, the presence or absence of intent regarding deception and fraudulent appropriation, which are the subjective constituent elements of the offense of fraud, can only be determined by comprehensively considering all objective circumstances such as the Defendant’s financial resources, environment, occupation, and economic activities before and after the offense. Even upon careful examination of the content of all the above evidence cited by the court below, it concerns only the fact that the Defendant borrowed the funds at issue, and it is insufficient as material to recognize objective circumstances from which it may be inferred that the Defendant lacked the ability to repay the borrowed funds or had the intent to fraudulently obtain them by means of deception; and there is no other evidence to support such a finding. In other words, while consistently denying any intent to deceive or defraud, the Defendant has defended himself to the effect that he had sufficient intention and ability to repay both at the time of the borrowing in this case and now, but that only the timing of repayment has been somewhat delayed due to the occurrence of unexpected circumstances such as an unexpected traffic accident. If one considers in combination the testimony in court of the first-instance and court below witness Heo Ok-ryeon, the testimony in court of the first-instance witness Kim Hwa-sun, the contents of the written statements made at the prosecution and police, as well as the testimony of the lower-court witnesses Kim Il-sun and Kim Do-sun, the Defendant originally lived in a family with considerable property and bought a taxi to operate a driving business, and his father also possessed considerable real estate and engaged in shiitake mushroom cultivation, so that their life was fairly comfortable; thus, he was regarded as having sufficient repayment ability even before this case and had been engaging in financial transactions with Heo Ok-yeon and Kim Hwa-sun. Then, when a traffic accident occurred, because of handling it and repairing the vehicle, he borrowed the funds in this case from the unindicted persons Kim Il-sun and Kim Do-sun with the guaranty of the complainant Heo Ok-ryeon, repaid one portion thereof according to the agreement, while the remainder was delayed, but after the complaint in this case all amounts were repaid by the Defendant or his father. As for the creditor Kim Il-sun, he in fact had also received repayment of one portion of the claim in this case from the Defendant and believed that the Defendant had repayment ability, but the guarantor Heo Ok-ryeon, for reasons unknown, filed this complaint; and the other creditor Kim Do-sun also learned of the complaint only later. In light of the continuous money-dealing relationship between the Defendant and the complainant Heo Ok-ryeon established by the above evidence, the property status of the unmarried Defendant and his father, the amount of the borrowed funds in this case, and the motives and circumstances of the delay in repayment of the debt, and other relevant circumstances, there is no reason not to accept the Defendant’s above defense.\\nIf so, although the Defendant’s above conduct amounts merely to a temporary delay in performance of one portion of a debt, the court below erred in finding, without evidence, that the Defendant had intent to deceive and fraudulently obtain property; therefore, the ground of final appeal criticizing this is well-founded, and the judgment of the court below cannot escape reversal.\\n\\n3. Accordingly, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below, and so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the judges participating."}

question: Entertainer A, around 08:00 on 2023. 3. 9., while driving his passenger car, which was covered by comprehensive automobile insurance, on a highway, struck the curb on the left side of the road, and as a result of the impact, sustained an injury requiring six weeks of treatment himself and caused an injury requiring eight weeks of treatment to B, who was in the front passenger seat and was in a de facto marital relationship with him. A and B got out of the passenger car immediately after the accident but soon lost consciousness, and were transported to a hospital in that state. When B regained consciousness, B, out of concern that A’s entertainment activities might be affected, made a false statement to Police Officer P that B had been driving the above passenger car and caused the traffic accident. Which of the following statements regarding this is correct? (If there is a dispute, according to precedent)
A: Although P sought to investigate whether B, who had been found near the driver’s seat and transported to the hospital, had driven under the influence, when B did not regain consciousness, and P received, by voluntary submission, from Nurse A a portion of the blood that A had drawn from B for treatment purposes and seized it without a warrant, the seizure procedure violates due process.
B: B was indicted for the crime of violation of the Road Traffic Act (driving under the influence) and the crime of violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents (injury), and at the first trial date B and B’s counsel objected to the reply to the request for blood examination as evidence; however, if, at the third trial date, while B was absent, B’s counsel consented to its being used as evidence, then the above consent to evidence is effective.
C: After B received a final judgment of conviction for the crime of violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents (injury), and then broke up with A, if B petitions for a retrial by submitting as evidence a mobile phone photograph of A driving at the time of the above traffic accident, which B had concealed, this falls under the “when clear evidence establishing innocence has been newly discovered” clause in Article 420, item 5, of the Criminal Procedure Act.
D: Even if A cannot be prosecuted for the crime of violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents (injury) because the above passenger car was covered by comprehensive automobile insurance, B’s act of helping A escape may constitute the crime of harboring a criminal.
E: Even if B’s act of making a false statement to P constitutes the crime of harboring a criminal, B is not punishable because, at the time of the offense, B was in a de facto marital relationship with A.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2000DO4078]": "The judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the Panel Division of the Chuncheon District Court, Main Branch."}

{"[2003DO4533]": "1. The offense of harboring a criminal prescribed in Article 151 of the Criminal Act refers to an act that, by means other than concealing a criminal, renders the functioning of criminal justice, such as investigation, trial, and the execution of punishment, difficult or impossible, and there is no restriction whatsoever on the means thereof; moreover, since the above offense is a danger offense, it does not require that a result actually hindering the functioning of criminal justice be brought about, the so-called “a person who has committed an offense” in Article 151, paragraph 1, of the Criminal Act includes a person who is under suspicion of a crime and is the subject of investigation (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 81DO1931, decided January 26, 1982; Supreme Court Decision 93DO3080, decided March 3, 1995; Supreme Court Decision 2000DO4078, decided November 24, 2000, etc.), and furthermore, if a person is caused to flee while recognizing that he or she is a person who has committed an offense punishable by a fine or more severe punishment, the offense of harboring a criminal is established even if that person was not yet the subject of investigation at that time. Meanwhile, the so-called “another person’s criminal case” in Article 155, paragraph 1, of the Criminal Act concerning the offense of destruction of evidence shall be deemed to include even cases that may become criminal cases in the future, even if no investigation procedure has yet commenced at the time of the act of destruction (see Supreme Court Decision 82DO274, decided April 27, 1982).\\nExamining the judgment of the court below and the evidence adopted in the first-instance judgment cited by the court below in light of the above legal doctrine and the record, it can sufficiently be found that the Defendant, while recognizing that Non-Indicted 1 was a person who had committed an offense punishable by a fine or more severe punishment, had the accident vehicle, which was the evidence of this case, removed and repaired on the day of the incident, and caused Non-Indicted 1 to flee abroad. Therefore, the court below’s action of affirming as is the first-instance judgment that found all of the criminal facts in this case guilty is correct, and there is no illegality, such as misapprehension of facts in violation of the rules of evidence or misunderstanding of the legal principles concerning the offense of harboring a criminal or the offense of destruction of evidence, by failing to conduct the necessary examination.\\n\\n2. In addition, Article 151, paragraph 2, and Article 155, paragraph 4, of the Criminal Act provide that when a relative, family head, or family member living together commits the offense of harboring a criminal, the offense of destruction of evidence, etc. for the person concerned, he or she shall not be punished; a person in a de facto marital relationship cannot be deemed a relative under the Civil Act and therefore does not fall under the relative referred to in the above provisions (see Supreme Court Decision 80DO485, decided April 22, 1980; Supreme Court Decision 2001DO2514, decided June 29, 2001, etc.).\\nThe court below’s action of rejecting the Defendant’s argument on the same ground is correct, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of the legal principles concerning Article 151, paragraph 2, and Article 155, paragraph 4, of the Criminal Act.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2005MO472]": "The reasons for the re-appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. On Ground 1 of the reasons for re-appeal\\n\\nA. Article 420, item 5 of the Criminal Procedure Act (hereinafter referred to as “the provision at issue”) provides, as one of the grounds for retrial, that “where clear evidence newly discovered proves, for a person who has been sentenced to conviction, an acquittal or dismissal of prosecution, or, for a person who has been sentenced to punishment, exemption from punishment or a crime lighter than the crime recognized by the original judgment.” This is what is known, even among the grounds for retrial, as a “new evidence” ground for retrial, which concerns the emergence of new evidence after the finalization of a judgment, and it requires, first, that “new evidence has been discovered” (the newness of the evidence) and, second, that the newly discovered evidence “constitutes clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc.” (the manifestness of the evidence).\\n\\nIn the provision at issue, the phrase “where evidence newly discovered proves an acquittal, etc.” means evidence that was not discovered in the proceedings of the final judgment subject to retrial, or, even if discovered, could not be submitted, and refers to the time when such evidence is newly discovered or only then becomes capable of being submitted. Since the provision at issue does not limit the scope of by whom the newness of the evidence is to be determined, the subject of that determination cannot be confined to the court. However, retrial is an exceptional and extraordinary remedy that reexamines facts finalized through proceedings at the relevant instance or after careful fact-finding through appeal; thus, if evidence that the Defendant could have submitted in the proceedings before the finalization of the judgment were also included, the finality of the judgment could easily be denied depending on the timing chosen by the Defendant for submitting evidence, thereby undermining the legal stability of criminal adjudication and, contrary to the constitutional intent of designating the Supreme Court as the final court, resulting in retrial being allowed as a fourth instance. Accordingly, where the Defendant petitions for retrial, if there was negligence in failing to submit such evidence during the proceedings of the final judgment subject to retrial, it is reasonable to interpret that such evidence is excluded from the “evidence newly discovered” under the provision at issue (see Supreme Court Decision of October 31, 1963, 63RO6, Supreme Court Decision of June 11, 1966, 66MO24, Supreme Court Decision of February 11, 1987, 86MO22, Supreme Court Decision of November 8, 1995, 95MO67, Supreme Court Decision of January 16, 1997, 95MO38, Supreme Court Decision of August 11, 1999, 99MO93, etc.).\\n\\nIn addition, in determining whether evidence constitutes “clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc.,” the court should not consider only the newly discovered evidence independently and in isolation and decide whether to commence retrial based solely on its evidentiary value; rather, among the evidence on which the court that rendered the final judgment subject to retrial based its fact-finding, those that are organically and closely related to, and contradictory with, the newly discovered evidence must be considered and evaluated together. If, as a result, there is recognized a high degree of probability such that the final judgment of conviction subject to retrial cannot be maintained as it stands, then such new evidence shall be deemed “clear evidence” under the provision at issue. If the court were to evaluate and determine manifestness by considering only the newly discovered evidence independently and in isolation, retrial would be allowed only where the evidence itself has clear evidentiary value sufficient to establish acquittal, etc., and the grounds for retrial would be unduly restricted. This is because it would run counter to the purpose of the retrial system, which provides, as one of the grounds for retrial, for the “new discovery of clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc.” in order to reexamine the matter under a changed evidentiary landscape brought about by new evidence and thereby search for substantive truth.\\n\\nBy contrast, Supreme Court Decision of November 5, 1990, 90MO50, Supreme Court Decision of September 10, 1991, 91MO45, and Supreme Court Decision of August 11, 1999, 99MO93, etc., which determined whether evidence was “clear evidence warranting an acquittal” based only on the evidentiary value of the newly discovered evidence, are changed to the extent they conflict with the above legal principles.\\n\\nB. The lower court held, in substance, that in the record of the case subject to retrial, the court that rendered the judgment subject to retrial found the facts of the offense that the Re-appellant (Defendant, hereinafter referred to as “the Re-appellant”) raped the victim while carrying a dangerous weapon, etc., as guilty, while assuming that the offender in this case was azoospermic; however, after the judgment subject to retrial became final, semen test results on the Re-appellant revealed that the Re-appellant was not azoospermic, and therefore the judgment subject to retrial had a ground for retrial falling under the provision at issue. In response to the Re-appellant’s argument, the lower court held that the semen test results could not be regarded as evidence that could not have been submitted in the proceedings of the judgment subject to retrial, and moreover that they could not be regarded as clear evidence warranting an acquittal, and thus determined that the above ground for retrial did not exist.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court’s decision in light of the foregoing legal principles, the lower court, first, in determining whether the case fell under “where evidence newly discovered proves an acquittal,” should have first considered whether evidence that the Re-appellant was not azoospermic had not been discovered in the proceedings of the judgment subject to retrial, and then, if it was found that the Re-appellant had discovered and knew of such evidence at that time but failed to submit it intentionally or negligently, it should have determined that such evidence could not be regarded as new evidence constituting a ground for retrial under the provision at issue. However, without even examining whether the semen test results had not been discovered in those proceedings, the lower court simply determined that they did not constitute evidence that could not be submitted, and in doing so misconstrued the legal principles concerning the newness requirement of evidence under the provision at issue, thereby failing to fully examine whether the evidence had been discovered and whether the Re-appellant intentionally or negligently failed to submit it. Second, whether evidence constitutes “clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc.” should have been assessed by considering together the evidence among those on which the court that rendered the judgment subject to retrial based its fact-finding that are organically and closely related to, and contradictory with, the semen test results; instead, the lower court erred by excluding such evidence and determining manifestness solely on the evidentiary value of the semen test results.\\n\\nHowever, the evidence relied upon by the Re-appellant as the ground for retrial, namely the semen test results showing that he was not azoospermic, when considered together with the evidence organically and closely related thereto, included among the evidence on which the final judgment subject to retrial was based in the record of the case subject to retrial, the reply to the request for forensic appraisal from the Director of the National Forensic Service and the investigative report of the prosecutorial officer. The content of the above appraisal reply was that a positive reaction for semen was found in a specimen collected from the victim’s body, but spermatozoa were not detected, and the above investigative report stated that, in light of such appraisal reply, the offender was presumed to be azoospermic. However, the reasons why there was a positive reaction for semen but spermatozoa were not detected, as in the above appraisal reply, may include causes other than azoospermia, such as various factors relating to the condition of the collected specimen or its preservation process that caused spermatozoa to be lost. Accordingly, the above appraisal reply alone cannot establish that the offender was necessarily azoospermic, and the above investigative report, which merely speculates as one of several possibilities and contains nothing more than conjecture, cannot be recognized as having any particular evidentiary value. The above semen test results, which are merely materials capable of proving that the Re-appellant was not azoospermic, do not possess evidentiary value such that, even when the foregoing evidence is considered together, a high degree of probability is recognized to the extent that the final judgment subject to retrial in this case cannot be maintained as is. Ultimately, they do not constitute clear evidence warranting an acquittal in this case.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court’s determination that the semen test results concerning the Re-appellant do not fall under the grounds for retrial prescribed in Article 420, item 5 of the Criminal Procedure Act is proper in conclusion.\\n\\n2. On Ground 2 of the reasons for re-appeal\\n\\nArticle 420, item 7 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides as a ground for retrial that “where it is proved by a final judgment that the judge who participated in the original judgment, the preceding-instance judgment, or the investigation on which that judgment was based, or the prosecutor or judicial police officer who participated in the institution of prosecution or the investigation on which such prosecution was based, committed a crime in connection with his or her official duties.” This applies only where there is a separate final judgment or a substitute proof for the final judgment prescribed in Article 422 of the Criminal Procedure Act concerning the point that the original judgment was obtained through the criminal act of such public official (see Supreme Court Decision of August 29, 1996, 96MO72, Supreme Court Decision of May 11, 2006, 2004MO16, etc.).\\n\\nIn light of this legal principle, in this case, the lower court’s decision, which held that there was no ground for retrial under Article 420, item 7 of the Criminal Procedure Act because there was no separate final judgment or substitute proof for the final judgment prescribed in Article 422 of the Criminal Procedure Act concerning the point that the final judgment subject to retrial was obtained through the criminal act of a judicial police officer involved in the investigation, is proper, and there is otherwise no error such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the grounds for retrial under Article 420, item 7 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the re-appeal is dismissed, and it is so ordered.\\n\\nIn this Decision, with respect to the interpretation of the phrase “where clear evidence newly discovered proves an acquittal, etc.,” which is a ground for retrial prescribed in Article 420, item 5 of the Criminal Procedure Act, in addition to the separate opinions of Justices Kim Young-ran, Park Si-hwan, Kim Ji-hyeong, Park Il-hwan, Kim Neung-hwan, and Jeon Su-an regarding “where evidence newly discovered,” and the separate opinions of Justices Kim Young-ran, Park Si-hwan, Kim Ji-hyeong, Park Il-hwan, and Kim Neung-hwan regarding the method of determining whether evidence is “clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc.,” the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there is a supplementary opinion by Justices Yang Seung-tae, Lee Hong-hoon, and Ahn Dae-hee on the majority opinion.\\n\\n4. Separate opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran, Park Si-hwan, Kim Ji-hyeong, Park Il-hwan, Kim Neung-hwan, and Jeon Su-an on “where evidence newly discovered”\\n\\nA. The majority opinion is that, among the grounds for retrial prescribed in the provision at issue, the evidence warranting an acquittal, etc. must be newly discovered not only by the court but also by the Defendant who petitioned for retrial.\\n\\nHowever, I think it is correct to view whether evidence warranting an acquittal, etc. under the provision at issue falls under the phrase “where evidence newly discovered” as being determined according to whether it was newly discovered and became known by the court that reviews whether to commence retrial, rather than by the Defendant who petitions for retrial. The reasons for this view are as follows.\\n\\n(1) The grounds for retrial prescribed in the provision at issue are unique to criminal procedure. In civil litigation and the like, where the binding force of a final judgment is recognized, as to causes arising before the closing of argument at the fact-finding stage, the factual and legal relations are fixed based on the evidence submitted up to that point (the so-called “temporal scope of res judicata”), and it is not, in principle, permitted for a party to submit later evidence that existed before but was not submitted and thereby dispute the factual and legal relations (the so-called “preclusion effect” or “bar effect”). However, the grounds for retrial prescribed in the provision at issue allow, even after the prior judgment has become final, the newly submitted evidence not presented in that proceeding to impeach the already finalized fact-finding, irrespective of whether such evidence existed before the finalization of that judgment. In other words, unlike civil litigation and the like, which are based on adversarial proceedings and impose on the parties the responsibility to submit all evidence necessary for fact-finding up to the fact-finding stage and thereafter do not recognize a right to submit new evidence, it is not difficult to see that the purpose of the provision at issue is not to extend the temporal scope of the res judicata effect of a final judgment in criminal trials by, under certain requirements even after final judgment, denying the preclusion effect of failure to submit evidence.\\n\\nEven in criminal procedure, the need to promote legal stability by recognizing substantive finality following final judgment cannot be denied. Nevertheless, in criminal proceedings imposing punishment such as deprivation of human life or restrictions on bodily freedom, if it is revealed that the judgment convicting the Defendant contained an obvious factual error, then, if the opportunity to correct it were barred solely on the basis of substantive finality following final judgment, irreparable violations of the Defendant’s human rights would result. Since the ultimate goal of criminal procedure should fundamentally lie in maximally protecting the Defendant’s human rights and discovering the substantive truth, the need to provide relief to a person who may have been punished without guilt must necessarily be considered from a perspective entirely different from that in civil litigation and the like, and within that scope the demand for legal stability must also yield to some extent. The grounds for retrial prescribed in the provision at issue are, above all, most urgently required precisely in the above respect, and this purpose must be fully reflected in the interpretation of that provision.\\n\\n(2) The majority opinion maintains the prior Supreme Court precedents that evidence warranting an acquittal, etc. under the provision at issue must be evidence newly discovered and learned by the court as well as by the Defendant who petitioned for retrial.\\n\\nAccording to this majority opinion, the evidence prescribed as a ground for retrial in the provision at issue is insufficient if it is only evidence newly discovered and learned by the court; it must also be evidence that the Defendant who petitioned for retrial did not discover in the proceedings of the final judgment subject to retrial and then newly discovered and learned thereafter. Accordingly, even if the court that rendered the judgment subject to retrial was completely unaware of the evidence and only came to know of it after the judgment became final, evidence that the Defendant had discovered in the prior proceedings and could have submitted but failed to submit is excluded from the “newly discovered” evidence referred to here.\\n\\nHowever, as the majority opinion itself presupposes, the provision at issue merely states “where evidence newly discovered proves an acquittal, etc.,” and thus, as a matter of text, does not limit the scope of what must be newly discovered by whom. To interpret, as the majority opinion does, that the evidence must have been newly discovered by the court and also newly discovered by the Defendant who petitioned for retrial is clearly a construction unfavorable to the Defendant, and unless there is a clear basis in the Criminal Procedure Act, one should not readily construe the grounds for retrial in a manner unfavorable to the Defendant. Moreover, according to the supplementary opinion of the majority, discussed below, if a court recognizes newness merely because it newly discovered testimony or written statements reflecting testimony that changed before and after final judgment, this would contradict the purpose and basic spirit of Article 420, items 1 and 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which allow retrial only where prior evidence has been proven false by a final judgment. However, the grounds for retrial under Article 420, items 1 and 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act are both so-called “error-type” (Falsa) grounds for retrial, in that if documentary evidence, physical evidence, testimony, or expert opinions submitted as evidence in the proceedings of the prior judgment subject to retrial are proved by a final judgment to have been forged, altered, or false, such fact itself constitutes a serious defect in the final judgment, and the purpose is to nullify the prior proceedings and proceed entirely anew in order to cure that defect, regardless of whether it affected the determination of guilt or innocence. By contrast, the grounds for retrial under the provision at issue are the only so-called “new evidence” (Nova) grounds for retrial, intended to correct an erroneous substantive fact-finding that led to a final conviction. Since the two differ entirely in purpose and perspective, even if new evidence differs from old evidence only in content, it cannot be interpreted that, in order to have newness constituting a ground for retrial under the provision at issue, it must necessarily satisfy the requirements for the grounds for retrial under Article 420, items 1 and 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nRather, a petition for retrial based on the grounds prescribed in the provision at issue is allowed solely for the benefit of a person who has been sentenced to a final conviction, and the content of that retrial petition is to seek a retrial of the fact-finding that convicted the Defendant. Considering that such fact-finding was made by the court that rendered the judgment subject to retrial based on the contents verified by the evidence materials submitted up to that time, whether the evidence is “newly discovered” under the provision at issue should be determined on the basis of whether it differs from the contents perceived by the court through the evidence materials on which it based the fact-finding of guilt in the proceedings of the final judgment subject to retrial.\\n\\n(3) The majority opinion, despite there being no express textual basis in the provision at issue, cites as the reason for constraining the evidence referred to in that provision as above only to evidence that the Defendant did not discover or, even if discovered, could not submit, that if evidence the Defendant could have submitted in the proceedings before final judgment were also included, the finality of the judgment could easily be denied depending on the timing chosen by the Defendant for submitting evidence, thereby undermining the legal stability of criminal trials.\\n\\nHowever, as seen in paragraph (1) above, while the finality of judgments cannot be denied from the standpoint of legal stability, recognizing the grounds for retrial prescribed in the provision at issue is intended to realize the ultimate goal of criminal adjudication, namely the protection of the Defendant’s human rights, by opening a way for the Defendant to impeach the fact-finding in a criminal trial even after final judgment, and within that scope the demand for legal stability must also step back to some extent. For that reason, I think that, by emphasizing only the aspect of legal stability and thereby construing the meaning of new evidence under the provision at issue restrictively, the purpose of that provision is not properly reflected.\\n\\nMoreover, in general, limiting the temporal scope in which the binding force of a final judgment is recognized to the fact-finding stage and not permitting a party to later submit evidence that was not submitted before and thereby dispute the facts is understood to be based on the idea that, under adversarial proceedings, the burden of submitting all evidence necessary for fact-finding lies with the party who bears the burden of allegation and proof in the litigation, so that any party who fails to fulfill that responsibility must suffer the disadvantage. However, in criminal proceedings, only the prosecutor bears the burden of proving the charged offense, and the Defendant is merely in the position of being able to submit evidence necessary to impeach the evidence submitted by the prosecutor; furthermore, the Defendant does not bear the responsibility to submit such evidence. The provision at issue, taking into account the specificity of criminal procedure, also presupposes that the Defendant has only the right, and not the responsibility, to submit impeachment evidence necessary up to the fact-finding stage, by allowing the Defendant to submit new evidence even after final judgment and thereby denying the so-called preclusion effect following final judgment. Yet if one interprets that the Defendant may no longer submit it as new evidence on the ground that, although the Defendant could have discovered and submitted it in the prior proceedings, there was a fault attributable to intentional or negligent failure to do so, that would amount to recognizing a preclusion effect whereby the Defendant, despite having had the responsibility to submit such evidence in the prior proceedings, lost the right to submit it as new evidence because of neglect. This directly denies the law of the burden of proof in criminal procedure and conflicts with the purpose of the provision at issue, which excludes the finality of judgments, and therefore cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(4) It must not be overlooked that, by excessively restricting the “newness of evidence” prescribed in the provision at issue, even where some evidence is new and satisfies the requirement of “manifestness of evidence,” it may nonetheless fail to be recognized as a ground for retrial on the basis of the Defendant’s fault as envisioned by the majority opinion, thereby producing a result that is markedly contrary to the notion of justice.\\n\\nFor example, one can imagine a case where the Defendant who petitions for retrial discovered clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc. in the proceedings of the final judgment subject to retrial, but due to carelessness failed to submit it, and the court that rendered that final judgment could have examined the evidence ex officio if only it had exercised slightly greater care. Even in such a case, according to the majority opinion, the evidence would be denied newness and retrial would not be commenced. However, this result is difficult to defend against criticism that, rather than realizing justice through the discovery of substantive truth for an innocent person who should plainly be acquitted, it shifts the responsibility only to the retrial petitioner and denies relief procedures for the protection of human rights, while also excessively emphasizing only the superiority of legal stability through final judgment and thereby unduly restricting retrial.\\n\\nIn addition, in actual criminal trial proceedings, there may well be cases in which it is clearly revealed that, due to ignorance, distress, rashness, and other various reasons, the Defendant falsely confessed to the charged facts on behalf of the true offender and the judgment became final on that basis. As for such a Defendant, leaving aside the question of criminal liability under the Criminal Act for harboring the offender, etc., even where there are materials capable of clearly proving the Defendant’s innocence, such as statements in which the Defendant retracts a false confession made in the prior proceedings after the judgment became final, or statements in which the true offender confesses after the judgment became final that the crime was his or her own, according to the majority opinion all such evidence would inevitably be denied newness on the ground that the Defendant intentionally failed to submit it in the prior proceedings, and if the result of a judgment based on a false confession must thereby be maintained as is, that would be contrary to substantive truth and thus inconsistent with substantial justice. Of course, as the majority opinion points out, substantive truth must be pursued through careful and faithful fact-finding within the scope of instances and appeals, and the legal peace and order formed by final judgments must be respected as a result. The Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, in order to realize this within ordinary criminal proceedings, ensure that the Defendant is presumed innocent and may receive the assistance of counsel, and they pursue discovery of substantive truth through the operation of strict rules of evidence. However, in special cases such as the example above, correcting the result of such a final judgment would instead conform to the ideals of realizing justice through discovery of substantive truth, which the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act pursue, and to the purpose of the retrial system.\\n\\n(5) As for the point that, due to the grounds for retrial prescribed in the provision at issue, retrial should not, as feared by the majority opinion, be allowed as a fourth instance contrary to the constitutional intent of designating the Supreme Court as the final court, I do not differ in principle from the majority opinion.\\n\\nHowever, the provision at issue sets “where clear evidence proving an acquittal, etc. is newly discovered” as a ground for retrial, and while the retrial procedure concerns only the fact-finding in the final judgment and is still within the realm of fact trials, the Supreme Court being the final court appears to mean that, premised on a finalized factual relationship, it functions in principle as a court of law (Article 383, item 3 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “where there are grounds for petitioning for retrial” may be asserted as a ground for appeal; however, this merely allows the Supreme Court to serve as the subject of review on appeal because requiring a retrial petition to be filed only after waiting for final judgment, despite grounds for retrial having arisen after the judgment of the appellate court, would run counter to judicial economy, and it is nothing more than an additional function the Supreme Court performs for convenience in lieu of the fact-finding function of the appellate court within that limit, so it cannot be included in the inherent function of the Supreme Court as the court of final appeal), and merely determining whether evidence is new by whether the court perceived it in the prior proceedings, and thereby allowing, even after final judgment, only the question of fact-finding to be reopened, cannot be said to contravene the constitutional intent of designating the Supreme Court as the final court.\\n\\nThat said, even if the majority opinion’s intent is that the retrial procedure, due to the grounds for retrial prescribed in the provision at issue, may function in substance as a fourth instance after the Supreme Court and thereby create a risk of abuse of the retrial system, I think that concern may be unnecessary. Even if one takes the position that whether evidence is new should be determined according to whether the court perceived it in the prior proceedings, that alone does not mean the grounds for retrial prescribed in the provision at issue are established; rather, the requirement that the evidence be manifest must also be satisfied for retrial grounds to exist. Therefore, if some evidence is new but not such as to control fact-finding to the extent that the final judgment cannot be maintained as is, the expansion of retrial grounds can be sufficiently prevented through examination of the manifestness of the evidence. In other words, even in a case such as the example cited in the supplementary opinion of the majority below, where a witness who testified in the proceedings of the judgment subject to retrial reverses prior testimony or position, even if newness is recognized for such evidence, in order for manifestness to be further recognized, a high degree of probability must exist to the extent that the final judgment of conviction subject to retrial cannot be maintained as is.
