In the absence of special circumstances, reversed testimony, etc. would be subject only to free evaluation of evidence and manifestness would be denied, so it could not become evidence constituting grounds for retrial under the provision at issue. In this way, determining the grounds for retrial prescribed in the provision at issue through examination of whether the evidence is manifest may avoid, in some cases, the markedly unjust result noted in paragraph (4) above by preventing the retrial grounds from being restricted through a formal determination of whether the evidence is new and thereby failing to commence retrial, and it also accords with the ideal of the retrial system, which prescribes the emergence of new evidence as one of the grounds for retrial in order to provide relief to an innocent person.\\n\\nB. Applying this legal principle to this case, the semen test results concerning the Re-appellant, which he asserts constitute grounds for retrial under the provision at issue, were discovered after the final judgment subject to retrial became final, and are therefore new as to the court; accordingly, they fall under “where evidence newly discovered” in the provision at issue. By contrast, the lower court’s decision, which held that the semen test results could not be regarded as evidence that could not have been submitted in the proceedings of the judgment subject to retrial, contains an error in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the newness of evidence under the provision at issue.\\n\\nC. However, since I agree with the majority opinion that the above test results cannot be regarded as clear evidence warranting an acquittal, I ultimately concur with the conclusion that this re-appeal must be dismissed, but because I differ from the majority opinion on the newness of the evidence, I state this as a separate opinion.\\n\\n5. Separate opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran, Park Si-hwan, Kim Ji-hyeong, Park Il-hwan, and Kim Neung-hwan on the method of determining whether evidence is “clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc.”\\n\\nA. The majority opinion states that it was erroneous for prior Supreme Court precedents to determine whether evidence constitutes “clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc.” solely by reference to the evidentiary value of the newly discovered evidence, and that the evidentiary value should be assessed together with the old evidence on which the court that rendered the final judgment subject to retrial based its fact-finding; however, it further states that among those, only the evidence organically and closely related to, and contradictory with, the newly discovered evidence should be considered and evaluated together.\\n\\nHowever, I think that, when determining whether evidence constitutes “clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc.,” it is not proper to restrict the scope of evaluation of the old evidence as the majority opinion does, but rather to consider and comprehensively assess the newly discovered evidence together with all old evidence adopted by the final judgment subject to retrial in its fact-finding. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) First, if, as the majority opinion does, one interprets that the new evidence should not be considered independently and in isolation when determining whether it constitutes “clear evidence” warranting an acquittal, etc., then, since the retrial grounds referred to in the provision at issue lie in the reconsideration of the fact-finding in the final judgment upon the discovery of evidence warranting an acquittal, etc., there is no need to limit the scope, as the majority opinion does, to only those old pieces of evidence among the evidence adopted by the final judgment subject to retrial that are organically and closely related to, and contradictory with, the new evidence.\\n\\n(2) Furthermore, the majority opinion merely states that among the old evidence adopted by the final judgment subject to retrial for its fact-finding, only those organically and closely related to, and contradictory with, the newly discovered evidence should be considered and evaluated together with the new evidence, but provides no criterion whatsoever for that determination. Also, from the standpoint of the newly discovered evidence, the old evidence adopted for the fact-finding in the final judgment subject to retrial is not only closely related to the event subject to the final judgment with the new evidence, but may also be viewed as contradictory because it supports a different result, making the distinction unclear. Since the closeness of the relationship or the contradiction between the newly discovered evidence and the old evidence adopted by the final judgment will in practice have to be determined specifically and individually in each case, whether the evidence constitutes clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc. should, as a matter of practical reasonableness, be determined by the court comprehensively considering together the new evidence and the evidence adopted by the final judgment according to each case.\\n\\nB. Applying this legal principle to this case, it is erroneous for the lower court to have determined, without comprehensively evaluating together the above semen test results and the old evidence adopted by the final judgment subject to retrial for fact-finding, that the semen test results alone cannot be regarded as clear evidence warranting an acquittal. However, the above semen test results submitted by the Re-appellant are merely materials capable of proving that the Re-appellant is not azoospermic, and as seen in the majority opinion, the reply to the request for expert examination from the Director of the National Forensic Service and the investigative report of the prosecutorial officer alone cannot establish that the offender was necessarily azoospermic. Therefore, they cannot be recognized as having any special evidentiary value. Moreover, when considering together the old evidence adopted by the final judgment subject to retrial for its fact-finding, or the circumstances recognized thereby—namely, that the fingerprints lifted from the railing of the victim’s house, which was the offender’s entry route, matched the Re-appellant’s fingerprints, and that tools of the same type as those used in the offense were found at the Re-appellant’s residence, etc.—this case cannot be regarded as one in which, even when those pieces of evidence are comprehensively evaluated together with the above semen test results, a high degree of probability is recognized to the extent that the final judgment of conviction can no longer be maintained as is.\\n\\nC. As stated above, I concur with the majority opinion in the conclusion that this re-appeal must be dismissed, but because I differ in the reasons, I state this as a separate opinion.\\n\\n6. Supplementary opinion of Justices Yang Seung-tae, Lee Hong-hoon, and Ahn Dae-hee on the majority opinion\\n\\nA. On the “newness of evidence” under the provision at issue\\n\\n(1) Prior Supreme Court precedent has stated the view that evidence constituting grounds for retrial under the provision at issue must be new not only to the court but also to the petitioner for retrial, and that, however, where the Defendant who petitioned for retrial was negligent in failing to submit it, it is excluded from “where evidence newly discovered.” The majority opinion maintained this view. In response, the separate opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran, Park Si-hwan, Kim Ji-hyeong, Park Il-hwan, Kim Neung-hwan, and Jeon Su-an (hereinafter “the separate opinion”) states that whether a case falls under “where evidence newly discovered” should be determined according to whether it was newly discovered and became known by the court that reviews whether to commence retrial, rather than by the Defendant petitioning for retrial.\\n\\nHowever, the separate opinion, by example of cases where the Defendant retracts a confession, may lead to the view that even where, for example, a witness who testified at the time of final judgment reverses prior testimony or position, the evidence should be regarded as newly discovered from the standpoint of the court, and newness should therefore be recognized. Yet such a result, as discussed below, is improper because it would hollow out the newness requirement of evidence by determining whether grounds for retrial under the provision at issue exist solely through the manifestness requirement, thereby disregarding the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act or shaking the foundation of the instance system in connection with the ground of appeal in Article 383, item 3 of the Criminal Procedure Act, namely “where there are grounds for petitioning for retrial.” Therefore, I think an interpretive theory that may lead to such a result is not proper.\\n\\n(2) Before discussing whether recognizing newness in cases where the Defendant retracts a confession or where a witness who testified at the time of final judgment reverses prior testimony or position truly accords with the guarantee of the Defendant’s human rights, I wish to point out that this is clearly an interpretation contrary to the current Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nArticle 420 of the Criminal Procedure Act enumerates the grounds for retrial in a limited manner, and items 1 and 2 of the same Article, unlike the provision at issue, treat as grounds for retrial only cases where it is proved by a final judgment that documents or physical evidence used as evidence for the original judgment were forged or altered, or that testimony, expert opinions, etc. were false.\\n\\nIn light of the purpose of Article 420 and items 1 and 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, even if testimony of a witness that changed before and after final judgment or a written statement embodying such testimony is newly submitted as evidence, if one were to regard it, in formal terms, as newly discovered evidence and therefore as falling under the grounds for retrial prescribed in the provision at issue, that would run counter to the basic spirit of those provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act, which intended to allow retrial only exceptionally where prior evidence has been proved false by a final judgment. Not only that, where such written statements or the like differ from the past only in the form of the evidence, without any substantive difference, and merely change to contradictory content or attitude, it is proper to regard them as being of the same nature as the existing testimony, etc. already discovered at the time of final judgment and subjected to substantive review, and thus not as new evidence.\\n\\nAccordingly, to the contrary, recognizing newness for retracted or changed testimony that has not been proven false by a final judgment merely because it is new to the court, and thereby allowing retrial, would be difficult to defend against criticism that it artificially formalizes the newness requirement of evidence, hollowing it out, and thus unduly expands the grounds for retrial contrary to the purpose of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nMoreover, considering that retrial is an exceptional extraordinary remedy that reexamines facts finalized through careful fact-finding in ordinary criminal trial proceedings, that our courts currently subject testimonial evidence to strict review before adopting it as evidence for conviction, and the reality of Korean criminal justice, where the Defendant’s statements and those of witnesses often change, recognizing retracted testimony as a ground for retrial would not so much ensure the Defendant’s human rights in substance as impose unnecessary review on the courts and burden their work, and in some cases would clearly expose witnesses, including victim witnesses, who testified in the proceedings of the final judgment, to persistent inducement and threats, thereby seriously infringing legal stability in the criminal justice system.\\n\\nThe separate opinion cites the case of a false confession and argues that, as an exceptional case for an unjustly accused Defendant, newness should be recognized for the retraction of a confession. However, in order to recognize that a confession is false, there must be new evidence proving the falsity of that confession, and the Defendant could sufficiently seek retrial on the basis of that new evidence. In other words, since one cannot posit a case where a mere retraction of a confession alone is immediately recognized as a false confession, the view that an unjustly accused Defendant may fail to be relieved if newness is denied merely because the confession was retracted is nothing but an unnecessary fear.\\n\\nThe separate opinion further explains that even if newness is recognized for the retraction of a confession, retrial will not be readily accepted through examination of the manifestness requirement. However, as this Decision states, once newness is recognized, the court will evaluate and determine, together with evidence among the evidence on which the final judgment relied that is closely related to, and contradictory with, the new evidence, whether it is clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc.\\n\\nThis ultimately means that if a confession is retracted, the court receiving the retrial petition must review the relevant record, examine all evidence attached thereto, and then determine whether the grounds for retrial exist. As noted above, this would require a futile judicial review even for a mere retraction of a confession, i.e., a retraction of a confession unsupported by evidence capable of proving it, leading to waste of procedure. And it would induce the Defendant, who peacefully endures the execution of punishment, to retract the confession, thereby causing serious instability in the criminal justice order.\\n\\n(3) The Criminal Procedure Act prescribes as grounds for appeal “where there is a violation of the Constitution, law, orders, or rules that affected the judgment (Article 383, item 1 of the Criminal Procedure Act)” or “where there was a serious mistake of fact in a case in which the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or detention for 10 years or more (hereinafter referred to as ‘imprisonment, etc. for 10 years or more’) was imposed, and such mistake affected the judgment, or where there is a manifest reason to acknowledge that the determination of punishment is grossly unfair (Article 383, item 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act).” This means that, because the probative value of evidence in criminal procedure belongs to the free evaluation of the judge (Article 308 of the Criminal Procedure Act), the proceedings are divided into first instance, appellate instance, and final appeal, and unless the case is one in which imprisonment, etc. for 10 years or more was imposed, matters concerning fact-finding are to be sufficiently examined and finalized at the first-instance and appellate stages, while the scope of review in final appeal is limited to violations of law.\\n\\nHowever, if, as the separate opinion does, evidence warranting an acquittal, etc. under the grounds for retrial in the provision at issue is deemed to be sufficient if it is new to the court, and the petitioner is allowed to newly submit evidence that could have been submitted through the appellate instance, especially statements purporting to alter prior testimony or statements, and newness is thereby recognized, the retrial court will be forced, in order to examine manifestness, to newly determine the probative value of the prior evidence related to that evidence, which not only runs counter to judicial economy but also contradicts the basic spirit of the Criminal Procedure Act, which leaves determinations of evidentiary value to the free conviction of the first-instance and appellate judges and limits later stages to review of legal violations where imprisonment, etc. for 10 years or more has not been imposed.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 383, item 3 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides “where there are grounds for petitioning for retrial” as one of the grounds for appeal. This provision appears to have been enacted because requiring a retrial petition only after waiting for final judgment, even though grounds for retrial arose before final judgment, would run counter to judicial economy and to the notion of justice. However, if, as the separate opinion does, newness is recognized where the petitioner newly submits on appeal evidence that could have been fully submitted through the appellate instance, the Supreme Court, like the retrial court, would have to newly determine the evidentiary value of the prior evidence in order to examine manifestness, which would run counter to the basic spirit of the Criminal Procedure Act, which limits the Supreme Court to review of legal violations. Furthermore, if appeal is filed by claiming as new evidence material that is of no evidentiary value whatsoever, and if newness is allowed such that the Supreme Court must re-determine the evidentiary value of the prior evidence, then evidence or materials that merely purport to dispute fact-finding could be asserted as grounds for appeal, which is highly improper.\\n\\nIn light of the purpose of Article 383, item 3 of the Criminal Procedure Act and the policy ideal of criminal justice—namely, efficient allocation of judicial resources through strengthening the functions of the first and second instances as fact-finding courts and the final appeal as a court of law—it is proper that, independently of examination of the manifestness requirement, in which evaluation of fact-finding must inevitably be involved, the newness requirement of evidence should function substantively in the grounds for retrial prescribed in the provision at issue. At that level, it will be possible to effectively filter out improper grounds for appeal that are merely intended to criticize the fact-finding of the trial court via the retrial grounds by interpreting that even for a Defendant petitioning for retrial, the requirement of newness of evidence must be satisfied.\\n\\n(4) The separate opinion also criticizes the majority opinion for excessively limiting the newness of evidence by the court and the Defendant both as the standard, thereby unduly restricting the opportunity to discover substantive truth through retrial and neglecting human rights protection.\\n\\nThe legal maxim that “even if 10 offenders escape, one innocent person must not be punished” symbolizes the propositions of discovery of substantive truth and protection of human rights, which are the fundamental starting points of democratic criminal procedure, and it requires no elaboration that our criminal procedure also exists on that foundation. This ideal must be shared by all who operate the criminal justice process and cannot be the private property of any particular person or group. The majority opinion does not ignore that ideal; rather, it seeks, within the bounds that do not infringe the principle, to find a harmonious point of contact with legal stability, another great principle of the rule of law, by preventing the essential effect of judgments, which are indispensable elements of judicial proceedings, from being undermined or judicial order from being disturbed by indiscriminate retrial procedures.\\n\\nOnce a judgment becomes final, the case that was the object of its review is concluded and can no longer be contested. Retrial is a procedure that returns the case to the status of one in which the final judgment had not existed and reexamines it; it is an extremely exceptional and extraordinary remedy that overturns the effect of a final judgment. Because of that exceptional and overthrowing nature, retrial proceedings are commenced in most cases when, after judgment, a ground arises that clearly reveals from the judgment itself that the judgment can no longer be maintained (Article 420, items 1 through 4, 6, and 7 of the Criminal Procedure Act). However, the Criminal Procedure Act also provides, as a retrial ground of a different nature, for the case where clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc. is newly discovered. This is understood to mean that, although facts finalized after judgment cannot in principle be contested, where new evidence suggests that there is a serious error in the judgment comparable to other retrial grounds, the law specially prescribes it as a retrial ground based on the above ideals of discovery of substantive truth and protection of human rights. The reason the provision expressly sets the newness and manifestness of evidence as requirements for commencement of retrial is precisely this; it is not the intent of the provision to easily make already finalized judgments subject to retrial merely because additional evidence exists.\\n\\nOur criminal procedure is, in principle, based on adversarial proceedings, and evidence examination is not driven ex officio. Materials not submitted or pointed out in court by the prosecutor or Defendant are difficult for the court to know and difficult to use as evidence. If, in such a system, whether evidence constituting a retrial ground has been “newly discovered” were judged only by the court, then even evidence already known by the Defendant would, insofar as it was not submitted in court during the trial, fall within that category. Ultimately, the meaning of “new” would be determined by whether the Defendant had previously submitted it, which would not only be inconsistent with the text but also, in effect, reduce the newness requirement to a mere shell.\\n\\nIn addition, in criminal procedure the burden of proving guilt lies with the prosecutor, and the Defendant is in the position of defending against it. Although defending against the charged facts is fundamentally the Defendant’s right, and many legal powers are granted to the Defendant to secure that right of defense, it cannot be denied that the Defendant also has a duty to cooperate with the trial proceedings for the discovery of substantive truth. In that respect, where the Defendant already knew of the evidence and could have submitted it but failed to do so negligently, that constitutes a failure to fulfill that duty. Just as, in the case of appeal, even if the appeal period expires without the Defendant’s knowledge, restoration of the right to appeal is not recognized unless the failure was due to a cause for which the Defendant or the representative cannot be held responsible (Article 345 of the Criminal Procedure Act), the prior precedents’ attitude of denying newness in such cases cannot be said to be improper.\\n\\nThe separate opinion worries that, if newness is limited as in the majority opinion, protection of human rights through discovery of substantive truth will be insufficient. However, cases in which the Defendant knows of the existence of decisive evidence warranting acquittal and can submit it, yet fails to submit it without any obstacle, are difficult to imagine, so in almost all such cases relief would be available on the ground that there was an obstacle. As noted above, the concerns of the separate opinion are, in my view, overly theoretical and nothing more than unnecessary fear. The majority opinion seeks to prevent the impairment of judicial justice by futile procedures that require the court to regard as “newly” discovered all materials the Defendant submits that were not presented in court and then, further, to go through the process of assessing their evidentiary value based on the record. Even if a trial is conducted only once, it is important that the ideal of human rights protection be faithfully and thoroughly realized within that proceeding; repeated and duplicated trials do not necessarily produce better results.\\n\\n(5) In this way, the separate opinion concerning newness is an interpretation that goes beyond the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act and is close to creating law. Rather than substantially guaranteeing the Defendant’s human rights, it only creates the risk of shaking the foundations of the criminal justice system.\\n\\nB. On the method of determining “manifestness of evidence” under the provision at issue\\n\\n(1) The provision at issue merely prescribes, as a ground for retrial, the case where “clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc. for a person sentenced to conviction” is newly discovered; it does not separately prescribe by what method such clear evidence is to be evaluated and determined. The majority opinion, as the method of determination, departs from the view of prior precedents, which held that only the newly discovered evidence should be considered independently and in isolation and whether it is clear enough to commence retrial should be determined solely by its evidentiary value, and instead adopts the view that among the old evidence on which the court that rendered the final judgment subject to retrial based its fact-finding, those organically and closely related to, and contradictory with, the newly discovered evidence should be considered and evaluated together.\\n\\nThe purpose of the provision at issue is that, because the newly discovered evidence was not considered at all in the fact-finding of the final judgment, the final judgment should be retried in light of the newly discovered evidence to determine whether it can be maintained. Such retrial would proceed by the court comparing and evaluating, in light of the newly discovered evidence, whether the fact-finding based on the old evidence in the final judgment was proper. However, if the court were to examine and determine manifestness by considering only the newly discovered evidence independently and in isolation, the new evidence would necessarily be limited to being capable, by itself, of proving acquittal, etc., regardless of the old evidence adopted by the final judgment. Also, whether acquittal, etc. can be recognized inevitably depends on comparing and evaluating the new evidence with the old evidence to see whether there is an error or contradiction in the fact-finding of the final judgment. Yet determining whether to commence retrial solely from the new evidence itself also runs counter to the logic of the process of determining whether retrial grounds under the provision at issue exist.\\n\\nNevertheless, prior precedents adopted such a view regarding the manifestness requirement under the provision at issue, and it cannot be denied that this led to an overly restrictive scope of retrial grounds falling under the provision at issue. This also conflicts with the purpose of the retrial system, which, unlike the remaining grounds for retrial in Article 420 of the Criminal Procedure Act, is based on the emergence of new evidence and is intended to ensure that, by having an opportunity to revisit the fact-finding and evidentiary relationships of the final judgment under changed evidentiary circumstances, no Defendant who has been unjustly punished remains. For these reasons, the majority opinion has changed the prior precedents. Accordingly, the determination of whether evidence constitutes clear evidence warranting an acquittal, etc. should be made by considering together and evaluating the newly discovered evidence and the old evidence that formed the basis of the fact-finding in the final judgment. However, because the factual relationship recognized by the final judgment was established through careful fact-finding at the relevant instance or on appeal, and retrial is an exceptional and extraordinary remedy against it, and because retrial is divided into the retrial commencement procedure and the subsequent trial procedure, it is proper that the evidence to be reexamined by the court receiving the retrial petition in deciding whether to commence retrial be limited to those among the old evidence forming the basis of the fact-finding in the final judgment that are organically and closely related to, and contradictory with, the newly discovered evidence.\\n\\n(2) If, as a result of considering together and comparing and evaluating the newly discovered evidence and those among the old evidence forming the basis of the fact-finding in the judgment subject to retrial that are organically and closely related to, and contradictory with, it, a high degree of probability is recognized to the extent that the final judgment of conviction subject to retrial cannot be maintained as is, beyond merely casting doubt on the justice of that final judgment, then such new evidence constitutes “clear evidence” under the provision at issue.\\n\\nIt may not be easy to define in a single way how far the result of such comparison and evaluation must go in order to exceed the level of merely casting doubt on the validity of the final judgment and to be considered clear enough to warrant an acquittal, etc. However, since this problem broadly falls within the area of fact-finding in criminal procedure, it is necessary to infer indirectly, at least to some extent, the degree of conviction required for the evidence to be considered clear enough to warrant an acquittal, etc. under the provision at issue, by comparing it with the situation in which a Defendant appeals and contests fact-finding already made at the fact-finding stage under the Criminal Procedure Act, thereby raising the question of whether the appellate court will maintain the conviction.\\n\\nIn the proceedings before final judgment, the Defendant is presumed innocent until a guilty judgment becomes final (Constitution Article 27, paragraph 4; Article 275-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act), and in that judgment fact-finding must be based on evidence and the finding of criminal facts must reach proof beyond a reasonable doubt (Article 307 of the same Act), while the probative value of evidence is subject to the free evaluation of the judge (Article 308 of the same Act). With respect to the first-instance judgment, the Criminal Procedure Act provides as grounds for appeal “where there is a violation of the Constitution, law, orders, or rules that affected the judgment” or “where there was a mistake of fact that affected the judgment” (Article 361-5, items 1 and 14), thereby allowing the appellate court to review the propriety of the fact-finding in the first-instance judgment. Meanwhile, unlike the grounds for appeal, the Criminal Procedure Act provides as grounds for final appeal only “where there is a violation of the Constitution, law, orders, or rules that affected the judgment” (Article 383, item 1), and, except in exceptional cases such as “where there are grounds for petitioning for retrial” or “where in a case in which the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or detention for 10 years or more was imposed, there was a serious mistake of fact affecting the judgment or there is a manifest reason to acknowledge that the determination of punishment is grossly unfair” (Article 383, items 1, 3, and 4), it does not in principle allow, as a ground for final appeal, arguments criticizing fact error in the appellate judgment unless they fall under Article 383, item 1.\\n\\nBy contrast, retrial targets judgments that were finalized as guilty after careful fact-finding at the relevant instance or on appeal, and therefore differs in plane from final appeal, which reviews whether there were violations of the Constitution, law, etc. affecting the appellate judgment in an unfinalized state. Also, as in the wording of the provision at issue, newly discovered evidence must not only be capable of supporting “acquittal or dismissal of prosecution” for the final judgment of conviction, but must also be “clear” enough for that recognition. Thus, it differs structurally from final appeal, which examines, from the perspective of whether there is a violation of the Constitution, law, etc., whether the criminal facts were proven beyond a reasonable doubt under the principle of the presumption of innocence. Therefore, the result of comparing and evaluating the newly discovered evidence together with the old evidence that is closely related to, and contradictory with, it must be such that it can go beyond the mere dispute over the relative strength of probative value between evidence supporting or impeaching the indictment within the range of the judge’s free conviction, and reach the question of whether the final judgment of conviction can be maintained as is. At that point, if the validity of the final judgment is merely doubtful, that means the result of the evaluation and determination may differ depending on the court receiving the retrial petition, and thus it cannot be regarded as clear enough to warrant an acquittal, etc. Only when, beyond that level, a high degree of probability is recognized to the extent that maintaining the final judgment as is would be contrary to the purpose of the retrial system—namely, the relief of an innocent person through discovery of substantive truth—and to the ideal of criminal justice of realizing justice through such discovery, can it be considered clear enough to warrant an acquittal, etc., and only then may retrial be commenced.\\n\\n(3) The separate opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran, Park Si-hwan, Kim Ji-hyeong, Park Il-hwan, and Kim Neung-hwan is that the court receiving the retrial petition must comprehensively re-evaluate the newly discovered evidence together with the old evidence adopted as the basis for fact-finding in the judgment subject to retrial.\\n\\nUnlike civil retrial, criminal retrial has a separate procedure for reviewing whether to commence retrial and the trial procedure concerning the case subject to retrial after the decision to commence retrial. Accordingly, the court receiving the retrial petition need only proceed with fact investigation and related procedures limited to the extent necessary for deciding whether the retrial petition has merit, and among the old evidence that formed the basis of fact-finding in the judgment subject to retrial, it need only examine those within the scope organically and closely related to, and contradictory with, the grounds for retrial; a full reexamination of the case subject to retrial can be conducted in the trial procedure that follows after the decision to commence retrial becomes final, together with the prosecutor’s additional proof and the defense’s impeachment activities, according to the relevant instance. In this respect, the separate opinion’s view that even old evidence unrelated to the grounds for retrial must be fully reexamined is not only an unnecessary duplication of review that causes waste in criminal justice, but also contrary to the bifurcated structure of retrial under the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nThe above is stated as a supplementary opinion on the majority opinion."}

{"[2013DO3]": "The Court examines the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe subject of consent to evidence prescribed in Article 318 of the Criminal Procedure Act is the prosecutor and the defendant, who are the parties to the litigation, and defense counsel may only present opinions regarding consent to evidence on behalf of the defendant; accordingly, defense counsel may not consent to the use of evidence against the defendant’s expressed intent. Therefore, where, at a trial date at which the defendant is present, an opinion is stated that there is no consent to the use of evidence, even if thereafter, at a trial date at which the defendant is not present, only defense counsel appears and reverses the prior position to consent to the use of evidence, such consent shall be deemed ineffective unless there are special circumstances.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the following facts can be ascertained. That is, on September 9, 2009, at the first trial date of the first instance and the first hearing, the defendant and defense counsel appeared together, and the trial record states that, among the evidence submitted by the prosecutor, an opinion was stated that there was no consent to the use as evidence of the complaint, each police statement report concerning Non-Indicted 1 and Non-Indicted 2, and each written confirmation prepared by Non-Indicted 3 and Non-Indicted 4 (hereinafter referred to as “the evidence in this case”). Thereafter, because the defendant did not appear at trial dates, the court of first instance, after procedures such as a request to investigate whereabouts, issued on February 22, 2012, a decision ordering that service of process upon the defendant be effected by public notice service, and at the 13th trial date on April 5, 2012, which proceeded in the defendant’s absence, only privately retained defense counsel appeared and consented to the use as evidence of most of the evidence that had previously been objected to. Accordingly, the court of first instance, after conducting an evidentiary examination of the evidence in this case to which defense counsel, as above, reversed the prior position and consented to the use as evidence, and by comprehensively considering them together with other evidence, found the charged facts of this case against the defendant to be guilty. And the appellate court set aside the judgment of the court of first instance on the ground that the sentence was excessive, rendered a new judgment, and, by citing as it stood the summary of evidence in the judgment of the court of first instance, found the charged facts of this case to be guilty.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles set forth above, when the course of the proceedings as described above is considered, the opinion of non-consent to evidence expressed at the first trial date and the first hearing of the first instance must be regarded as either having been stated by the defendant himself or having been made by defense counsel “on behalf of” the defendant, and in either case it has the effect of the defendant himself expressing an opinion of non-consent. Then, defense counsel’s reversal of that position and consent to the use as evidence at the 13th trial date of the first instance was contrary to the defendant’s expressed intent and, unless otherwise special circumstances exist, is ineffective. Moreover, because the evidence in this case is hearsay evidence, it lacks admissibility unless the authenticity of its formation, etc. is recognized by the original declarant’s statement at the trial date, etc. Accordingly, although the evidence in this case could not be used as evidence, the court of first instance used it as evidence to establish the charged facts of this case and found the defendant guilty, and the appellate court likewise, by relying on the result of the evidentiary examination conducted by the court of first instance, found the charged facts of this case guilty; this is unlawful. Ultimately, the appellate court judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the subject and effect of consent to evidence.\\n\\nAccordingly, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal raised by the defendant, the Court shall reverse the appellate court judgment and remand the case to the appellate court for further trial and decision, and hereby renders judgment as stated in the Disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[98DO968]": "We adjudicate the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. On the first point\\n\\nThe gist of the facts charged in this case is that, at around 17:00 on July 19, 1995, the Defendant, while in an intoxicated state with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.09% on a road located in Sangseo-ri, Useong-myeon, Gongju-si, drove a cargo truck with the vehicle registration number omitted, crossed the center line, and collided with a Pride passenger car and a Grandeur passenger car traveling in the opposite lane, thereby causing five victims riding in the said passenger cars to suffer injuries requiring approximately 2 to 6 weeks of treatment.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below and the record, with respect to the trial court’s adoption of the National Scientific Investigation Institute’s reply to the request for blood examination as evidence and its finding of the Defendant’s intoxicated state, defense counsel argued that the police, without going through proper legal procedures such as obtaining the Defendant’s consent or a warrant issued by a judge, arbitrarily drew blood from the Defendant’s body, who was unconscious due to the traffic accident in this case, and requested an examination by the National Scientific Investigation Institute; therefore, the said reply to the request for blood examination, which was obtained, had serious defects in the manner of collection and thus lacked evidentiary capacity, and furthermore, even though it could not be guaranteed that the blood subject to examination was the Defendant’s blood, the trial court committed an error by finding, based on the said reply to the request for blood examination, that the Defendant drove under the influence of alcohol at the time of the traffic accident in this case. The court below, based on the testimony of the witness Non-Party Person in the court below and the record, found that a police officer, at the Gongju Medical Center, attempted to draw blood from the Defendant, for whom breath alcohol testing was difficult, in order to investigate whether he had driven under the influence at the request of the victim’s side; however, the Defendant, who had been transported there and was receiving emergency treatment at the time due to the accident in this case, was completely unconscious, and his family members were not present at the scene, and that, just then, a nurse at the said medical center drew the Defendant’s blood for treatment purposes, whereupon the police officer asked the nurse and received a portion of the drawn blood, delivered it to the traffic accident processing team, and used it for the purpose of determining the blood alcohol concentration. On the basis of the above facts found, the court below held that although the result of the examination obtained by using a small amount of the Defendant’s blood, which was drawn by a nurse at a hospital according to the necessity of treatment in a situation where the consent of the Defendant or his family could not be obtained, cannot be said to be evidence obtained by lawfully complying with all procedures, the degree of illegality thereof and the degree of infringement thereby on the Defendant’s bodily safety and human dignity did not reach the level that would require exclusion of that evidence; accordingly, it determined that the reply to the request for examination arising from the blood draw should be deemed to have evidentiary capacity, dismissed the Defendant’s appeal, and affirmed the judgment of the trial court.\\n\\nWith respect to whether there was any procedural illegality in the police officer’s seizure of a portion of the Defendant’s blood, which had been drawn by the nurse for treatment purposes, after receiving it from the nurse for the purpose of determining intoxication, Article 218 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “a prosecutor or judicial police officer may seize, without a warrant, articles abandoned by a suspect or any other person, or articles voluntarily submitted by the owner, possessor, or custodian,” and the main text of Article 112, which is applied mutatis mutandis pursuant to Article 219 of the same Act, provides only that “a lawyer, patent attorney, notary public, certified public accountant, tax accountant, scrivener, physician, oriental medical doctor, dentist, pharmacist, druggist, midwife, nurse, or person engaged in a religious office, or a person who was engaged in such office, may refuse seizure of matters concerning another person’s secrets among articles possessed or kept upon entrustment in the course of such person’s duties.” Apart from this, under the Criminal Procedure Act and other laws and regulations, there is no special procedural restriction concerning the investigative agency’s seizure, for investigative purposes, of blood drawn by a medical practitioner for treatment purposes; therefore, if a medical practitioner voluntarily submitted a patient’s blood drawn for treatment purposes to an investigative agency, the patient’s consent is not necessarily required for the use of that blood as evidence, unless there exist special circumstances such as infringement of the patient’s privacy, confidentiality, or other personality-related legal interests. Accordingly, according to the facts lawfully found by the court below, the police officer appears to have voluntarily received and seized a portion of the Defendant’s blood that had already been drawn for treatment purposes from the nurse; thus, unless there are special circumstances indicating that, at the time, the nurse lacked authority to voluntarily submit the blood to the police officer on behalf of Gongju Medical Center, as the possessor and custodian of the blood, or on behalf of the attending physician, even if the seizure procedure was carried out without the consent of the Defendant or the Defendant’s family and without a warrant, it cannot be said that there was any illegality in violation of due process.\\n\\nTherefore, in the end, the conclusion of the court below, which recognized the evidentiary capacity of the reply to the request for blood examination using the said blood, is proper, and it cannot be said that there was any error of law such as misapprehension of legal principles as pointed out in the grounds of appeal. This argument is without merit.\\n\\n2. On the second point\\n\\nWhile recognizing the evidentiary capacity of the said reply to the request for blood examination, the court below stated that “even if, arguendo, the said evidence were evidence to be excluded as illegally obtained evidence, and thus the negligence of driving under the influence of alcohol could not be recognized, the fact that the traffic accident in this case occurred due to the Defendant’s negligence in crossing the center line is recognized, as will be seen below, and since even a traffic accident caused solely by crossing the center line is not deemed to have resulted in a sentence that is too severe as imposed by the court below, the error in the determination related to the said drunk driving cannot be said to have had any effect on the maintenance of the prosecution or the determination of the sentence in the judgment of the court below against the Defendant; therefore, the Defendant’s above argument is, in this respect as well, without merit in the end.” This is a hypothetical determination made on the assumption that the evidentiary capacity of the said reply to the request for blood examination is not recognized, but, as stated above, since the court below’s determination recognizing the evidentiary capacity of the said reply to the request for blood examination is proper, the ground of appeal criticizing that hypothetical determination cannot constitute a lawful ground of appeal.\\n\\n3. On the third point\\n\\nExamining the reasons for the judgment of the court below and the reasons for the judgment of the trial court cited by the court below in comparison with the record, the court below’s recognition of the Defendant’s negligence in crossing the center line is proper, and it cannot be said that there was any error of misapprehension of facts due to a violation of the rules of evidence, as asserted in the grounds of appeal. This argument is also without merit.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the judges participating, as stated in the disposition."}

question: Party A and A are brothers who do not live together, and A went missing. In around January 2023, Party A, as the court-appointed absentee property administrator for A, received KRW 700 million in expropriation compensation deposited in favor of A. Thereafter, in around March 2023, the court changed the absentee property administrator for A from Party A to B. Nevertheless, Party A neither informed B of the existence of the deposited money nor handed it over. After B learned of these facts in around May 2023, B obtained permission from the court concerning the exercise of the right to file a complaint in around June 2023 and then immediately filed a complaint with the investigative agency against Party A for the offense of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Breach of Trust) concerning these facts. Which of the following statements are incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents) (a) While Party A, B, and Party A's older sister C were gathered together and talking, B recorded the conversation among the three persons using the voice-recording function of his mobile phone for the purpose of collecting evidence, and such recording act falls under Article 16(1) of the Protection of Communications Secrets Act and is unlawful. (b) B, as the absentee property administrator for A, having obtained permission from the court concerning the exercise of the right to file a complaint regarding criminal acts against A's property, which was the object of administration, qualifies as a lawful person entitled to file a complaint as A's legal representative. (c) After Judicial Police Officer P, having obtained an arrest warrant for Party A for the offense of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Breach of Trust), discovered Party A, who had parked a vehicle in the parking lot in front of his house, and arrested Party A pursuant to the arrest warrant while searching Party A's vehicle, such act is lawful under Article 216(1) No. 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act. (d) If Party A injured Judicial Police Officer P by colliding with him with Party A's vehicle during the arrest process described in item (c), then the offense of special obstruction of the execution of official duties causing injury and the offense of special injury are established against Party A, and the two offenses are in a relation of ideal concurrence. (e) If Party A were A's non-cohabiting son and B's complaint had been filed on December 20, 2023, then the court must, with respect to Party A's offense of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Breach of Trust), render a judgment dismissing the public prosecution pursuant to Article 327(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DO4981]": "We examine the Prosecutor’s grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nThe provision in Article 3(1) of the Protection of Communications Secrets Act, which states, “No one shall record or listen to a conversation between other persons that has not been made public,” means that a third party who did not originally participate in the conversation may not record statements made between the persons holding that conversation. In the case of a conversation among three persons, where one of them records the conversation, the statements of the other two persons cannot be said to be a “conversation between other persons” in relation to the recorder; therefore, such recording conduct cannot be deemed to violate Article 3(1) of the Protection of Communications Secrets Act.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below in this case, the court below held, with respect to the facts charged that “the Defendant, around 12:30 on July 9, 2005, at the office of ‘(name of company omitted),’ recorded a conversation between Non-Indicted Persons 1 and 2 that had not been made public by using a small tape recorder while Non-Indicted Persons 1 and 2 were together,” that the Defendant merely recorded the content of a mutual conversation among the above three persons as one party to the conversation, and did not record a conversation between Non-Indicted Persons 1 and 2 as a third party; thus, the case fell within the situation where one party to a conversation records the content of the conversation without the other party’s knowledge and did not violate Article 3(1) of the Protection of Communications Secrets Act, and on that same ground maintained the first-instance judgment.\\n\\nExamining the reasons for the judgment of the court below in comparison with the above legal principles and the record, the court below’s decision to acquit the Defendant on this part of the facts charged on the ground that it did not constitute a crime is acceptable, and there is no illegality in that decision, such as misapprehension of the law or violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as per the Disposition in unanimous agreement of the Justices of the Supreme Court who participated."}

{"[2008DO7311]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nIn a non-genuine aggravated-result offense, in which aggravated punishment is imposed when a serious result is intentionally caused through the underlying offense, if the act of intentionally causing the serious result corresponds to a separate constituent offense and there is a provision punishing the intentional offense more severely than the punishment prescribed for the aggravated-result offense, then the intentional offense and the aggravated-result offense should be regarded as standing in a relationship of ideal concurrence (see Supreme Court Decision 94DO2842, decided January 20, 1995; Supreme Court Decision 96DO485, decided April 26, 1996, etc.), but where, as above, there is no provision punishing the intentional offense more severely, the aggravated-result offense is construed to be in a special relationship to the intentional offense, so only the aggravated-result offense is established and the intentional offense, which is in a relationship of concurrence of statutory provisions with it, cannot be viewed as separately constituting a crime. Accordingly, where a public official executing official duties is intentionally injured by carrying a dangerous object, only the offense of aggravated obstruction of the performance of official duties resulting in injury is established, and it cannot be viewed as separately constituting the offense of violation of the Act on the Punishment of Violences, etc. (injury by a group, with a deadly weapon, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the record, as to the facts charged in this case that the Defendant, while driving a passenger car, struck the police officer conducting the drunk-driving crackdown with the passenger car, a dangerous object, in order to evade the drunk-driving enforcement, thereby obstructing the performance of official duties by that police officer and causing injury to that police officer, it is clear that the Prosecutor instituted the prosecution on the view that the Defendant’s act constituted the offense of violation of the Act on the Punishment of Violences, etc. (injury by a group, with a deadly weapon, etc.) and the offense of aggravated obstruction of the performance of official duties resulting in injury, and that the two offenses were in a relationship of ideal concurrence.\\n\\nIn this regard, the court below held that the Defendant’s act constituted only the offense of aggravated obstruction of the performance of official duties resulting in injury, and that the offense of violation of the Act on the Punishment of Violences, etc. (injury by a group, with a deadly weapon, etc.) was absorbed into the offense of aggravated obstruction of the performance of official duties resulting in injury and did not separately constitute a crime; thus, it found the Defendant not guilty of the offense of violation of the Act on the Punishment of Violences, etc. (injury by a group, with a deadly weapon, etc.). In light of the foregoing legal principle and the record, the above determination of the court below is proper, and there is no error such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the number of crimes, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2013DO7754]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nAccording to Articles 361 and 328 of the Criminal Act, the offense of embezzlement between direct lineal blood relatives, spouses, cohabiting relatives, cohabiting family members, or their spouses shall have its punishment exempted, and among other relatives, prosecution may be instituted only upon complaint. Even in cases where the offense of embezzlement under the Criminal Act is aggravated and punished under Article 3(1) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the \"Special Act\"), its nature remains unchanged, and since there is no express provision in the Special Act excluding the application of Articles 361 and 328 of the Criminal Act concerning the special rule of relatives, Article 361 of the Criminal Act applies as is to offenses in violation of Article 3(1) of the Special Act.\\n\\nEven according to the facts charged in this case, the victim is the defendant's cousin, so the offense in violation of the Special Act in this case arising from embezzlement is, in light of the legal principle stated above, a case in which prosecution may be instituted only upon complaint, and in this case, the period for filing a complaint is six months from the day the offender became known pursuant to Article 230(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act; therefore, a complaint filed after the lapse of that period is procedurally improper and has no effect. Accordingly, before making a determination of guilt or innocence with respect to the facts charged in this case, the court below should have examined whether the victim's complaint in this case was filed within six months from the day the offender became known, and if it was found to have been filed after the lapse of that period, it should have rendered a judgment dismissing the prosecution pursuant to Article 327(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below did not take the above measures and merely upheld the first-instance judgment that had found the facts charged in this case guilty; thus, this appellate judgment contains an illegality that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principle concerning the application of the special rule of relatives in offenses in violation of the Special Act and by failing to conduct the necessary examination. The argument in the grounds for appeal pointing out this point is well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, without considering the remaining grounds for appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; accordingly, the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2015DO364]": "We review the grounds of appeal (the statements in each supplemental brief of grounds of appeal submitted by Defendant B after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement said Defendant’s grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. As to Defendant B\\n(a) Regarding the grounds of appeal disputing the amendment of the indictment\\nIf the prosecutor’s application for leave to amend the indictment falls within the scope of the identity of the facts charged, the court must grant it pursuant to Article 298(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 99DO375 rendered on April 13, 1999). And if the social factual relationship forming the basis of the facts charged is identical in its essential points, it shall be deemed that the identity of the facts charged remains intact; in determining such identity of the essential factual relationship, the court must, in light of the function of the identity of such facts, base its assessment on the defendant’s conduct and the social factual relationship thereof, while also taking normative elements into account (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 93DO2080 rendered on March 22, 1994). In addition, because the structure of criminal appellate proceedings is not exclusively limited to a character as post-review, amendment of the indictment at the appellate stage is also possible; therefore, the mere fact that the appellate court granted such amendment does not mean that the defendant was deprived of the opportunity to receive the first-instance judgment, thereby infringing the right to receive a trial according to law guaranteed by the Constitution, or that the defendant suffered a disadvantage in exercising the right of defense during the course of the trial (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 94DO3297 rendered on February 17, 1995).\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below together with the foregoing legal principles and in light of the record, the lower court’s determination granting the prosecutor’s application for leave to amend the indictment, which changed the date and time of the offense stated in item 2 of the list of offenses attached to the first-instance judgment concerning Defendant B, contains no error in law by misapprehending the legal principles concerning amendment of the indictment, the presumption of innocence, or the specification of the facts charged, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n(b) Regarding the grounds of appeal disputing the admission of illegally collected evidence\\n(1) (a) When necessary for the investigation of a crime, a judicial police officer may, only in relation to matters for which there exist circumstances sufficient to suspect that the suspect committed the offense and which may be recognized as related to the case in question, apply to a prosecutor, and by a warrant issued by a judge of the district court upon the prosecutor’s request, conduct seizure, search, or inspection (Article 215(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\n\\nAs an exception to such prior warrant principle, a judicial police officer may, when necessary in arresting or detaining a suspect, conduct seizure, search, or inspection at the place of arrest without a warrant (Article 216(1)2 of the Criminal Procedure Act); however, if it is necessary to continue the seizure of the articles seized thereby, an application for a seizure and search warrant must be made without delay (Article 217(2) of the same Act). Also, where, at the scene of the crime during the commission of the offense or immediately thereafter, there is urgency such that a warrant from a judge of the court cannot be obtained, seizure, search, or inspection may be conducted without a warrant, and in such case a warrant must be obtained afterward without delay (Article 216(3) of the same Act).\\n\\n(b) Further, in order for a judicial police officer, etc. who possesses an arrest warrant to arrest a suspect, the arrest warrant must be presented to the suspect at the time of arrest, and the gist of the criminal facts concerning the suspect, the reason for the arrest, and that the suspect may retain counsel must be explained, and the suspect must be given an opportunity to make an explanation in defense (Article 200-5 of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\n\\nAs a general rule, such presentation or notice of the arrest warrant must be made in advance, before resorting to physical force for the arrest; however, where a fleeing suspect is chased and caught, or a suspect resisting with violence is subdued by force, it may be done in the course of catching or subduing the suspect, or, if that is not feasible, immediately after the suspect has been caught or subdued (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2007DO10006 rendered on February 14, 2008).\\n\\n(c) Meanwhile, Article 308-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “evidence collected in violation of lawful procedures shall not be admissible as evidence.” In order to guarantee basic human rights, the Constitution, which declares the foundation of due process and the warrant principle concerning compulsory dispositions, and the Criminal Procedure Act, which has inherited such principles and provides specific standards regarding seizure, search, and inspection so as to harmoniously realize the ideals of substantive truth ascertaining and protection of individual rights, must retain their normative force. Accordingly, evidence collected without following the procedures for seizure, search, and inspection prescribed by the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, as well as secondary evidence obtained on the basis thereof, constitutes evidence collected without lawful procedures established for the protection of basic human rights and, in principle, cannot be used as evidence of guilt (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2007DO3061 rendered on November 15, 2007).\\n\\nFurthermore, in light of the importance of the warrant principle as above, the illegality of evidence unlawfully collected in violation of the procedure concerning the warrant principle is not cured merely because a warrant was later issued by the court with respect to such evidence, or because the defendant or defense counsel consented to its use as evidence (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DO10092 rendered on January 28, 2010).\\n\\n(2) The reasons of the judgment below and the record, including the evidence lawfully admitted, reveal the following facts.\\n1) An arrest warrant was issued against said Defendant on suspicion of selling Philopon, etc.\\n2) On July 17, 2013, narcotics investigators belonging to the Prosecutors’ Office, who were judicial police officers, commenced procedures to arrest said Defendant, including lying in wait near said Defendant’s residence. The investigators confirmed that at the time a woman appearing to be the Defendant’s cohabitant and others were residing together at the Defendant’s residence.\\n3) On July 18, 2013, at around 6:45 p.m., in the parking lot in front of the Gimhae Sports Park tennis courts, said Defendant was finally arrested in the course of fleeing after abandoning his vehicle while driving it in order to evade arrest by the investigators, and immediately thereafter he was presented with the arrest warrant by the investigator, informed of the matters prescribed in Article 200-5 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and afforded an opportunity to explain.\\n4) Immediately after arresting said Defendant, the investigators searched the vehicle without a separate seizure and search warrant and seized Philopon, marijuana, and the like; meanwhile, they continuously searched said Defendant’s residence, which was about 2 kilometers away from that place, and seized swords in said Defendant’s possession; thereafter, on July 21, 2013, a seizure and search warrant was issued for the seized articles.\\n5) Said Defendant and defense counsel agreed to use as evidence the seizure record concerning the seized articles (hereinafter referred to as “the seizure record of this case”) and the photographs of the seized articles (hereinafter referred to as “the photographs of the seized articles of this case”) at the fourth trial date in the first instance of this case.\\n6) The lower court found all of the facts charged, including the facts charged for violation of the Act on the Control of Firearms, Swords, Explosives, Etc., guilty as to said Defendant, and treated the seizure record of this case and the photographs of the seized articles, etc. as corroborative evidence for said Defendant’s confession.\\n\\n(3) Examining these factual circumstances in light of the above provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act and the legal principles, the following conclusion follows.\\n(a) The presentation and notice of the arrest warrant made immediately after the investigators arrested said Defendant pursuant to a warrant previously issued appear lawful. Furthermore, the investigators’ search of the vehicle in which said Defendant was riding during the arrest process and their seizure of Philopon, marijuana, and the like therefrom may be regarded as lawful pursuant to Article 216(1)2 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\nAlthough there are some inappropriate parts in the reasons of the judgment below, there is no error in the portion of the lower court’s determination reaching such conclusion, affecting the judgment, by misapprehending, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, the legal principles concerning Miranda warnings, exclusion of illegally collected evidence, entrapment investigation, etc.\\n(b) However, the investigators’ search of said Defendant’s residence and seizure of swords without a separate seizure and search warrant cannot be regarded as lawful for the following reasons.\\n1) When the investigators commenced the search of said Defendant’s residence, the arrest of said Defendant had already been completed, and considering that the place where said Defendant was arrested and said Defendant’s residence were about 2 kilometers apart, said Defendant’s residence cannot be regarded as the “place of arrest.”\\nAccordingly, the seizure and search of said Defendant’s residence cannot be deemed lawful seizure and search under Article 216(1)2 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n2) Considering that an arrest warrant had been issued against said Defendant on suspicion of selling Philopon, etc., and that narcotics had been discovered at the scene of arrest, the investigators appear to have searched said Defendant’s residence in order to seize narcotics that said Defendant might additionally possess. However, with only such circumstances, it is difficult to deem that, when the investigators commenced the seizure and search, it was manifest that said Defendant possessed narcotics at his residence; moreover, as to the swords, it appears that the investigators did not even have a clue regarding their possession, and thus said Defendant’s residence cannot be regarded as a crime scene where there were clearly existing incriminating circumstances of “during the commission of the offense or immediately thereafter” with respect to possession of narcotics or swords (see Supreme Court Decision 2001DO300 rendered on May 10, 2002; Supreme Court Decision 2009DO14884 rendered on February 9, 2012). In addition, although a third party was cohabiting at said Defendant’s residence at the time, and thus there was a risk that, if said Defendant’s arrest became known, the narcotics in the residence could be concealed by accomplices, etc., considering that an arrest warrant had already been previously issued against said Defendant on suspicion of selling Philopon, etc., it is also difficult to hastily conclude that there was such urgency that there was no temporal leeway to obtain in advance a seizure and search warrant for said Defendant’s residence.\\nAccordingly, the seizure and search of said Defendant’s residence cannot be regarded as lawful seizure and search under Article 216(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act either.\\n3) Ultimately, in this case, where there are no circumstances sufficient to conclude that said Defendant clearly and voluntarily consented, on the basis of his own free will, to the seizure and search of his residence, it is proper to deem that the swords were unlawfully seized without a warrant and thus lack admissibility, and that the seizure record of this case and the photographs of the seized articles, which are secondary evidence based thereon, likewise lack admissibility. And it cannot be otherwise deemed merely because a seizure and search warrant for said swords was issued afterward, or because said Defendant or defense counsel consented to the use of the seizure record of this case and the photographs of the seized articles as evidence.\\n(c) Nevertheless, the lower court erred by determining that said swords and the seizure record of this case and photographs of the seized articles relating thereto were admissible, and as a result, used them as corroborative evidence for said Defendant’s confession and found guilty the portion of the facts charged concerning violation of the Act on the Control of Firearms, Swords, Explosives, Etc. against said Defendant.\\nAccordingly, the lower court’s determination on this point contains an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning exclusion of illegally collected evidence and corroborative evidence for a confession. The grounds of appeal alleging this is well-founded.\\n\\n(c) Regarding the grounds of appeal disputing some of the facts charged and the calculation of the amount subject to forfeiture\\nThe recognition of criminal facts must be proven to a degree beyond reasonable doubt (Article 307(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act), but the selection and exclusion of evidence and the determination of probative value made as a premise for fact-finding fall within the free evaluation of the facts-finding court (Article 308 of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in the judgment, determined that: (1) said Defendant sold or attempted to sell Philopon to W, provided Philopon to S, possessed marijuana, and conspired with co-defendant A to import Philopon; and on that basis found guilty all of the facts charged stated in the lower court’s judgment, including the above facts; and (2) ordered, as against said Defendant, forfeiture of the amount stated in the judgment, being the aggregate value of the remaining narcotics other than the imported Philopon, etc., which had been seized.\\n\\nThe portion of the grounds of appeal disputing the lower court’s fact-finding is, in substance, nothing more than criticizing the lower court’s determination on the selection and probative value of evidence, which falls within the free evaluation of the facts-finding court. And even upon examining the reasons of the lower court’s judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence (excluding, however, the seizure record of this case, etc., which lack admissibility), the lower court’s determination contains no error affecting the judgment by, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning entrapment investigation or forfeiture under the proviso to Article 67 of the Narcotics Control Act.\\n\\n(d) Regarding the grounds of appeal asserting that the sentence is unfair\\nEven upon examining the various circumstances pertaining to sentencing reflected in the record, such as said Defendant’s age, character and conduct, environment, motive, means and result of each of the offenses in this case, and the circumstances after the offenses, the lower court’s sentence against said Defendant cannot be deemed grossly unfair.\\n\\n(e) Scope of reversal\\nThe portion of the judgment below concerning said Defendant’s violation of the Act on the Control of Firearms, Swords, Explosives, Etc. must be reversed, and because one sentence was imposed in the court below on the ground that that portion stood in concurrent offense relationship under the former sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the remaining guilty portions concerning said Defendant, the entire portion of the judgment below concerning said Defendant must ultimately be reversed.\\n\\n2. As to Defendant A\\nThe grounds of appeal alleging that the lower court’s imposition of a severe sentence on Defendant A is unlawful because it violates the principle of estoppel against a state agency are, in the end, a claim that the lower court’s determination of the sentence is unfair. However, under Article 383(4) of the Criminal Procedure Act, an appeal on the ground of unfair sentencing is permitted only in cases where the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or confinement for not less than 10 years has been imposed; therefore, in this case, in which a lighter sentence was imposed on said Defendant, the foregoing assertion, as well as the assertion that the sentence determined by the lower court is too severe and therefore unfair, does not constitute lawful grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAnd the remaining grounds of appeal asserted by said Defendant concern matters that the Defendant did not assert as grounds for appeal in the court below and were not matters made subject to adjudication by the lower court ex officio, and therefore do not constitute lawful grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the portion of the judgment below concerning Defendant B is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination of that portion; and Defendant A’s appeal is dismissed. It is so adjudged, by unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[2021DO2488]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal (a petition filed after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds for final appeal shall be considered only to the extent that it supplements them).\\n\\n1. Summary of the facts alleged in the indictment and the lower court’s determination\\n\\na. The gist of the facts alleged in the indictment in this case is as follows.\\n\\nThe Defendant and the victim are sisters who do not live together. The Defendant, as the court-appointed administrator of the victim’s absentee property, received the expropriation compensation deposited for the victim in the amount of 1,374,349,100 won. Thereafter, the court changed the administrator of the victim’s absentee property from the Defendant to Attorney Non-Party. While serving as the victim’s administrator of absentee property, the Defendant had a duty, under the duty of care of a good manager, to preserve, use, and improve the victim’s property for the victim, and, in the event that the Defendant was changed and lost that position, had a duty to enable the newly appointed administrator of absentee property to properly ascertain, preserve, and manage the victim’s property. Nevertheless, in violation of those duties, the Defendant neither informed the newly appointed administrator of absentee property of the existence of the deposited money nor transferred it, thereby obtaining pecuniary benefit and causing pecuniary loss.\\n\\nb. The lower court found that the institution of prosecution in this case was lawful for the following reasons and found the facts alleged in the indictment in this case guilty. Under Article 361 and Article 328(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, in this case where a complaint is required in order to institute prosecution, Non-Party, the victim’s administrator of absentee property appointed by the court, obtained permission from the court to exercise the right to file a complaint and filed a complaint against the Defendant. Since Non-Party qualifies as the victim’s legal representative and is a lawful person entitled to file a complaint, the institution of prosecution in this case is lawful.\\n\\n2. Determination on the grounds of appeal alleging that the procedure for instituting prosecution is void\\n\\na. Where an administrator of absentee property appointed by the court obtains permission from the court to exercise the right to file a complaint with respect to a criminal act concerning the property of the absentee who is the object of such administration, the administrator of absentee property must be regarded as a legal representative provided for in Article 225(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act and as a lawful person entitled to file a complaint. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) The Criminal Procedure Act provides that “the legal representative of the victim may file a complaint independently” (see Article 225(1)).
