Nevertheless, the court below, overlooking the aforesaid illegality in the first instance, held that the evidence investigation in the first instance was lawful, and, based on the evidence examined and admitted by the first instance, rejected the Defendant’s ground of appeal regarding factual error; furthermore, ex officio, on the ground of improper sentencing, it quashed the first-instance judgment while citing as they were the evidence indicated in the first-instance judgment and rendered a guilty judgment. Consequently, the judgment of the court below contains an error of law in misunderstanding the legal principle concerning the validity of procedural acts conducted without defense counsel in a case requiring mandatory defense counsel.\\n\\nHowever, even if the trial proceedings were unlawful because they were conducted in the absence of defense counsel or without defense counsel appearing in a case requiring mandatory defense counsel, it cannot be deemed that all procedural acts validly performed in other proceedings, apart from the procedural acts in those proceedings, are also rendered void (see Supreme Court Decision 90DO646 dated June 8, 1990). Therefore, where the facts constituting the offense can be recognized by comprehensively considering other evidence that has been lawfully examined, such illegality cannot be said to have affected the judgment.\\n\\nAccordingly, we examine the evidence adopted by the court below as proof of guilt regarding the count of rape causing injury among the facts charged in this case.\\n\\nThe testimony of witness Non-Party Person in the first-instance courtroom cannot, as noted above, be used as evidence, and furthermore, the written statements of the victim, Non-Party Person, recorded in the prosecution and the police are not agreed by the Defendant to be used as evidence; therefore, under Articles 312 and 313 of the Criminal Procedure Act, they may be used as evidence only when their authenticity of formation is acknowledged or proven by the statements of the original declarant, Non-Party Person, in pretrial preparation or at the trial date. However, since the second hearing in the first instance is void as stated above, these written statements, whose authenticity of formation was stated in that proceeding, cannot be said to have evidentiary admissibility under Articles 312 and 313 of the same Act.\\n\\nHowever, in such a case, if a person required to make a statement in pretrial preparation or at the trial date is unable to testify due to death, illness, residence abroad, or other reasons, there may be cases in which it may be used as evidence pursuant to Article 314 of the same Act. Yet, according to the record, Non-Party Person, although summoned as a witness on the trial date at the court below, did not appear on the ground that she was about to give birth; and absence from the trial date for such a reason cannot, absent special circumstances, be said to fall under a case where the person is unable to testify due to death, illness, residence abroad, or other reasons, and thus it cannot be said to have evidentiary admissibility under Article 314 of the same Act. In addition, the Defendant has consistently denied the offense from the time of the police investigation through the courtroom of the court below, so the Defendant’s statements in the prosecution, the first instance, and the courtroom of the court below cannot support recognition of the count of rape causing injury in this case, and the other evidence is all merely circumstantial evidence and cannot be said to be sufficient to establish it.\\n\\nUltimately, the court below, with respect to the count of rape causing injury in this case, committed an illegality by misunderstanding the legal principle concerning the validity of procedural acts conducted without defense counsel in a case requiring mandatory defense counsel, or by finding facts in violation of the rules of evidence evaluation, and such illegality clearly affected the judgment.\\n\\n3. Meanwhile, the court below also adopted the same evidence with respect to the count of unlawful confinement among the facts charged against the Defendant, found the Defendant guilty, and adjudged the Defendant guilty of rape causing injury and unlawful confinement as substantive concurrent offenses. Where the Defendant has been convicted of multiple offenses as substantive concurrent offenses, if there exists a ground for reversal as to one of those offenses, the entire judgment must be reversed; therefore, ultimately, the judgment of the court below cannot avoid reversal in its entirety.\\n\\n4. Accordingly, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and a new determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the judges participating in the decision, as set forth in the Disposition."}

question: A, a public official with authority to grant building permits, received 20,000,000 won in bribes from C, a building contractor, in connection with a building permit for a building, under the aid and abetment of B, the person in charge of practical affairs. Thereafter, A gave B 2,000,000 won out of the 20,000,000 won as a gratuity, spent 4,000,000 won as necessary expenses for the building permit, and deposited the remaining 14,000,000 won in a bank. When the building permit was later refused, C demanded the return of the entire amount of the bribe he had given to A. A withdrew the 14,000,000 won that had been deposited, on the grounds that he had given 2,000,000 won to B as a gratuity and spent 4,000,000 won as expenses, and returned only that money to C. Which of the following statements concerning this is correct? (If there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: The 2,000,000 won gratuity that A gave to B cannot be collected from A.
B: Since the 4,000,000 won in necessary expenses that A expended in connection with the building permit cannot be regarded as having been actually acquired by A, it cannot be collected from A.
C: The 14,000,000 won that A returned to C cannot be collected from C.
D: If C is indicted for the offense of bribery-giving and a final conviction is rendered, the statute of limitations for prosecution for A's offense of acceptance of bribes is suspended from the time the above criminal case against C is indicted until the time it becomes final.
E: If B leaves for the United States for the purpose of evading punishment for aiding and abetting the offense of acceptance of bribes, the statute of limitations for prosecution for A, a co-offender, for the offense of acceptance of bribes is also suspended during B's period of flight.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2011DO9585]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined (the statements in the supplementary appellate brief filed after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds for final appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\n1. As to the grounds for final appeal by Defendant 2\\n\\na. The portion concerning the subject of bribery acceptance\\n\\nThe offense of accepting bribes under Article 129(1) of the Criminal Act applies when a public official receives a bribe in connection with his or her duties; even if the public official does not directly receive the bribe but causes the bribe-giver to give the bribe to another person, if there exists a relationship such that, in light of social norms, the other person’s receipt of the bribe can be evaluated as equivalent to the public official’s direct receipt of the bribe, such as where the other person received the bribe as the public official’s messenger or agent, the offense of accepting bribes under Article 129(1) of the Criminal Act is established. This legal principle likewise applies where officers and employees of a specialized maintenance project management company deemed to be public officials cause, in connection with their duties, a specialized maintenance project management company or some other third party rather than themselves to give or receive bribes (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DO5506, decided May 13, 2010, among others).\\n\\nThe court below, in light of the various circumstances as stated in its holding, upheld the first-instance judgment that applied Article 129(1) of the Criminal Act to Defendant 2, who was the representative director of Non-indicted Company 1 Co., Ltd., a specialized maintenance project management company under the Act on the Maintenance and Improvement of Urban Areas and Dwelling Conditions for Residents (hereinafter the “Urban Improvement Act”), on the ground that, in the process of receiving bribes from construction companies by disguising a service contract between construction companies and consulting companies, the construction companies deposited the bribes into the accounts of consulting companies such as Non-indicted Company 2 Co., Ltd. and Non-indicted Company 3 Co., Ltd., which were the nominal counterparties to the service contract, and that, in light of social norms, this can be evaluated as equivalent to Defendant 2’s direct giving of bribes.\\n\\nIn light of the evidence duly admitted by the court below and the foregoing legal principle, the above determination by the court below is proper and acceptable, and there is no error of law that violated logic and empirical rules and went beyond the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or that misunderstood the legal principles concerning the subject of bribery acceptance.\\n\\nb. The portion concerning the amount of bribes and the calculation of the amount to be collected\\n\\nWhere a public official has expended expenses necessary to receive a bribe, such expenses are merely incidental costs of the bribery acceptance and therefore do not constitute items to be deducted from the value of the bribe or from the amount to be collected (see Supreme Court Decision 99DO1638, decided October 8, 1999; Supreme Court Decision 2003DO4293, decided July 15, 2005, among others). If a person who received money or property as a bribe independently used all or part of such money or property for such expenses, this is merely a consumption of property acquired by the offender, and the amount corresponding to such expenses must also be collected from the bribe recipient (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DO4378, decided August 21, 2008, among others). Meanwhile, where several persons jointly received a bribe, to collect its value, only the money or property actually distributed and received must be individually collected, and where the money or property received cannot be individually ascertained, it must be collected equally; and not only co-principals but also instigators or accessories may qualify as joint recipients of a bribe (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DO794, decided March 9, 2001; Supreme Court Decision 2003DO6738, decided October 27, 2004, among others). However, in the case of an instigator or accessory who is not a co-principal, whether he or she qualifies as a joint recipient must be determined by considering the relationship with the principal offender, the circumstances and degree of participation in the offense, the existence of any prior agreement regarding the distribution of the bribe, the intent of the bribe-giver, and the proportion that the money or property acquired by the accessory or instigator bears to the total amount of the bribe received. And if the person who received the bribe gave part of the bribe to an instigator or accessory who is not a joint recipient under the title of a gratuity for services or the like, this is merely the expenditure of incidental costs attendant upon the receipt of a bribe or an act of consumption of the bribe, and the entire amount of the bribe received must be collected from the bribe recipient.\\n\\nThe court below, in light of the various circumstances as stated in its holding, premised that the service contracts between the construction companies and the consulting companies in this case were wholly mere instruments for Defendant 2’s receipt of bribes, and thus that the entire amount of the service fees was provided as bribes. On that basis, it determined that the subject who received the bribes by disguising the service contracts in this manner was Defendant 2, and that Defendant 1, the co-defendant in the court below, the first-instance co-defendant 1, and the like, who aided Defendant 2’s bribery acceptance, were not persons who jointly received and distributed the bribes together with Defendant 2; therefore, even if part of the bribes received by Defendant 2 was used for Defendant 1 and others as a fee for services or the like, or was used to pay value-added tax under the nominal service contracts, this was merely incidental expense related to Defendant 2’s bribery acceptance and could not be deducted from the amount of bribes to be collected from Defendant 2.\\n\\nAlthough the statement of reasons by the court below is somewhat lacking in detail, the conclusion of the court below that the entire amount of the bribes stated in its holding must be collected from Defendant 2 is proper and acceptable, and there is no error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the calculation of the amount of bribes and the amount to be collected, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, or by omitting to make a determination on the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nc. The portion concerning the relevance to official duties in bribery cases\\n\\nThe court below determined, for the reasons stated in its holding, that Defendant 2’s act of receiving money from construction companies under the pretext of being selected as the implementer had a relevance to the duties of a maintenance project manager, namely, “consultation related to the selection of a contractor.” Comparing the relevant provisions of the Urban Improvement Act with the reasons of the court below’s judgment, the above determination by the court below is proper and acceptable, and there is no error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the relevance to official duties in bribery cases, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n2. As to the grounds for final appeal by Defendant 1\\n\\nIn light of the evidence duly admitted by the court below and the reasons of the court below’s judgment, the court below’s determination that Defendant 1 aided Defendant 2’s bribery acceptance offense in connection with the Munsan Seonyu District maintenance project is proper and acceptable, and there is no error that violated logic and empirical rules and went beyond the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nThe remaining argument in the grounds for final appeal is premised on the non-recognition of Defendant 2’s bribery acceptance offense; however, as noted above, the court below’s judgment that found Defendant 2 guilty of the bribery acceptance offense is proper and there is no reason to set it aside, and thus Defendant 1’s argument in this part of the grounds for final appeal is without merit.\\n\\n3. As to the grounds for final appeal by the Prosecutor\\n\\na. The portion concerning whether joint principal offender status is established\\n\\nA joint principal offender under Article 30 of the Criminal Act is established only when the subjective and objective requirements are satisfied, namely, a common intent to act jointly and the execution of the crime through functional control of the act based on that common intent (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DO235, decided April 26, 2007, among others).\\n\\nThe court below, in light of the various circumstances as stated in its holding, upheld the first-instance judgment that found the charged facts in this part not guilty on the ground that Defendant 1 could not be conclusively deemed to have participated in the offense to such an extent that functional control through essential contribution to Defendant 2’s bribery acceptance offense could be recognized, and therefore Defendant 1 could not be regarded as a joint principal offender in the bribery acceptance offense.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principle, the above determination by the court below is proper and acceptable, and there is no error that misapprehended the legal requirements for the establishment of joint principal offender status.\\n\\nb. The portion concerning the relevance to official duties in bribery cases\\n\\nWhether money or property acquired by a public official constitutes a bribe should be determined by taking into account all circumstances, including the content of the public official’s duties, the relationship between the duties and the person providing the money or property, whether there exists a special personal relationship of friendship between the two parties, the amount of the money or property, and the circumstances and timing of the receipt of the money or property; the same applies to officers and employees of a specialized maintenance project management company deemed to be public officials pursuant to Article 84 of the Urban Improvement Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DO2590, decided September 25, 2008, among others).\\n\\nThe court below, in light of the various circumstances as stated in its holding, upheld the first-instance judgment that acquitted Defendant 2 on the charged facts concerning Defendant 2’s receipt of the money stated in its holding from Defendant 3, an executive of Non-indicted Company 4 Co., Ltd., a demolition company, during the process of withdrawing from the project area in which Defendant 2 had been active in order to be selected as the maintenance project manager, on the ground that such receipt appears to have been made pursuant to an agreement with Non-indicted Company 4 Co., Ltd. and unrelated to Defendant 2’s status as a maintenance project manager, and that there was no evidence to support the charged facts that Defendant 2 received a bribe from Defendant 3 in connection with the duties of a maintenance project manager.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principle, the above determination by the court below is proper and acceptable, and there is no error that misapprehended the legal principles concerning the relevance to official duties in bribery cases.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals by Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 and the Prosecutor’s appeal against the Defendants are dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as set forth in the order, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2012DO4842]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. The Criminal Procedure Act provides in Article 248(1) that “an indictment shall not have effect on any person other than the person designated by the prosecutor as the Defendant,” and in Article 253(1) that “the statute of limitations shall be suspended by the institution of prosecution and shall run from the time when a judgment dismissing the prosecution or a judgment of violation of jurisdiction becomes final,” and, in paragraph (2) of the same Article, that “the suspension of the statute of limitations under the preceding paragraph with respect to one of the accomplices shall also have effect on the other accomplices and shall run from the time when the judgment in the case concerned becomes final.”\\nAs such, the Criminal Procedure Act provides that, in order to ensure fairness in punishment among accomplices, the institution of prosecution against one accomplice also suspends the statute of limitations for the other accomplices; however, it contains no provision whatsoever concerning the concept or type of such accomplices. Therefore, in interpreting “accomplice” under Article 253(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, one must comprehensively consider the legislative purpose of the above provision, namely fairness in punishment among accomplices, the fundamental idea of the Criminal Procedure Act of proper realization of the State’s punitive power, and the perspective of systematic harmony with substantive law, such as the Criminal Act, which regulates the objects of the State’s exercise of punitive power; in particular, because the above provision creates an exception extending the personal scope of the effect of the institution of prosecution, it must, in principle, be strictly interpreted and must not be expansively interpreted to the detriment of the Defendant (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DO15137, decided on 2012. 3. 29.).\\nA person in a so-called reciprocal offense relationship, such as between the offense of giving a bribe and the offense of receiving a bribe, is doctrinally called a necessary accomplice; however, such a relationship merely requires the existence of mutually corresponding acts, and each person realizes his or her own constituent elements and is punished under separate penal provisions, so it is essentially different from persons who are in an accomplice relationship in which two or more persons jointly realize the common constituent elements by acting in concert, and between persons in a reciprocal offense relationship, the provisions on accomplice liability in the General Part of the Criminal Act do not apply to each other’s acts (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DO6969, decided on 2014. 1. 16.).\\nIn light of these points, “accomplice” as used in Article 253(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act should be interpreted as not including a person in a reciprocal offense relationship such as between the offense of giving a bribe and the offense of receiving a bribe.\\n\\n2. According to the reasoning of the judgment of the court below and the record, on 2011. 6. 29. the prosecutor instituted prosecution against the Defendant on the ground that “the Defendant, in conspiracy with Non-indicted 1, on 2005. 2. 3., gave 60,000,000 won to Non-indicted 2, saying that it should be delivered to Non-indicted 3, a public official in charge of reserve land at Bucheon City Hall, so that the reserve land in this case could be purchased cheaply.” Meanwhile, on 2006. 1. 10., prosecution was instituted against Non-indicted 1, Non-indicted 2, and Non-indicted 3 respectively for the offense of giving a bribe to a third party, the offense of receiving a bribe from a third party, and the offense of violating the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (bribery), and on 2007. 4. 20., the Seoul High Court rendered guilty judgments sentencing Non-indicted 1 to 1 year of imprisonment, Non-indicted 2 to 1 year and 6 months of imprisonment, and Non-indicted 3 to 3 years of imprisonment; it can be seen that the guilty judgment against Non-indicted 1 became final on 2007. 4. 27. upon expiration of the period for appeal, and the guilty judgments against Non-indicted 2 and Non-indicted 3 became final on 2007. 7. 27. when their appeals were dismissed.\\nAccording to these facts, the prosecution in this case was instituted 6 years and 147 days after the Defendant’s act was completed, so even if the period of suspension of the statute of limitations, which is 1 year and 107 days calculated on the basis of the date on which the guilty judgment against Non-indicted 1, who is in an accomplice relationship with the Defendant, became final, is excluded, the prosecution was instituted after the 5-year statute of limitations period for the offense in this case had elapsed.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the judgment of the court below, which held that the prosecution in this case against the Defendant was instituted after 5 years had already elapsed even after excluding the period during which the statute of limitations was suspended due to the institution of prosecution against Non-indicted 1, who is an accomplice, from the time when the Defendant’s act was completed, is in accordance with the aforementioned legal principles and is proper, and there is no illegality in it as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning accomplices under Article 253(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and it is adjudged as follows, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2016DO21536]": "We examine the grounds for appeal (the statements in the supplemental statement of grounds for appeal filed after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds for appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. Determination on the grounds for appeal of Defendant 1\\n\\na. The act of donating political funds is an act of financial support for political activity, and a bribe is an unlawful consideration for a public official’s official acts; the two are distinct concepts. Even if valuables were exchanged under the name of political funds and the procedures prescribed by the Political Funds Act were followed, if such exchange is not in the nature of support for the politician’s overall political activities but has the substance of a quid pro quo for a public official-politician’s official acts, by providing valuables in expectation of favorable acts in relation to a specific and concrete official act of the public official who is a politician, or as a reward therefor, bribery is recognized. In determining the bribery character of the provision of valuables, the status and official authority of the other party, the prior relationship between the provider of the valuables and the other party, whether the provider of the valuables had ordinarily made donations and the timing, recipient, amount, and frequency of such donations, the amount of the valuables provided, and the motive and circumstances of the provision of the valuables, etc. must be comprehensively considered (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered June 12, 2008, 2006DO8568).\\n\\nThe court below found guilty the bribery receipt portion related to Nonparty Company 1 and the portion violating the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (bribery) among the facts charged in this case against Defendant 1. That is, the money received by the above Defendant from First-instance Co-defendant 3 and Defendant 2 has the character of a bribe received in relation to the official duties of a member of the National Assembly.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the evidence duly admitted by the court below and the trial court, the court below’s determination is proper. There is no error in the court below’s determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in that it did not violate the rules of logic and experience and exceed the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehend the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of acceptance of bribes.\\n\\nb. Where a public official has expended expenses necessary for receiving a bribe, such expenses are merely incidental costs of bribery and do not fall under items to be deducted from the value of the bribe and the amount of collection (see Supreme Court Decision rendered October 8, 1999, 99DO1638). The portion received as a gratuity by a person other than the subject of receiving the bribe, or the portion used as expenses pursuant to a service contract formally concluded for the purpose of receiving the bribe, is nothing more than an incidental cost of bribery (see Supreme Court Decision rendered November 24, 2011, 2011DO9585). Since receiving a bribe means receiving valuables with the intent to permanently retain them, if a person received them without knowing that they were a bribe and, upon learning that they were a bribe, immediately returned them, or if the briber unilaterally left the bribe and the recipient had no choice but to temporarily keep it with the intent to return it later upon an opportunity, and then returned it, then it cannot be said that a bribe was received. However, if the Defendant first demanded the bribe and received money from the briber, the Defendant is recognized as having had the intent to permanently retain the entirety of the money received (see Supreme Court Decision rendered March 29, 2007, 2006DO9182).\\n\\nThe court below determined, with respect to the portion violating the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (bribery) among the facts charged in this case against Defendant 1, that the receipt of a bribe with respect to the full amount of KRW 70,000,000 received by the above Defendant was established for the following reasons: (1) In or around August 2014, Defendant 1 requested a sponsorship fund from First-instance Co-defendant 3 through Defendant 2. (2) First-instance Co-defendant 3 transferred KRW 77,000,000 (including KRW 7,000,000 in value-added tax) to Nonparty Company 2, the ostensible counterparty to the service contract, on October 17, 2014, and informed Defendant 3 and Defendant 2 thereof; on the same day, Defendant 3 reported to Defendant 1 that KRW 70,000,000 had been transferred. (3) Defendant 1 instructed Defendant 3 to “deliver it in cash, excluding fees and expenses,” and Defendant 1 received a total of KRW 55,000,000 in cash from among it. (4) Even if KRW 15,000,000 out of the above KRW 70,000,000 was not actually delivered to Defendant 1, KRW 10,000,000 thereof was expenses provided to Nonparty Company 2, and the remaining KRW 5,000,000 was expenses incurred in the process of converting it into cash, and thus merely expenses incurred in order to deliver the bribe, so they cannot be deducted from the value of the bribe.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the evidence duly admitted by the court below and the trial court, the court below’s determination is proper. There is no error in the court below’s determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in that it did not violate the rules of logic and experience and exceed the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehend the legal principles concerning the calculation of the amount of bribe in the offense of acceptance of bribes.\\n\\n2. Determination on the grounds for appeal of Defendant 2\\n\\nThe phrase “receives money or valuables, entertainment, or other benefits under the pretext of making a request or arranging matters concerning a case or affair handled by a public official” as provided in Article 111 of the Attorney-at-Law Act means receiving valuables under the pretext of mediating between a public official and a client with respect to a case or affair handled by the public official. Where the character of receiving valuables under the pretext of making a request concerning a case or affair handled by a public official and the character of receiving valuables as consideration for labor or convenience merely related to a case or affair handled by a public official are inseparably combined, the entirety must be regarded as having been received under the pretext of making a request concerning a case or affair handled by a public official (see Supreme Court Decisions rendered April 29, 2005, 2005DO514; December 22, 2005, 2005DO7771, etc.). The same applies where valuables under the pretext of making a request concerning a case or affair handled by a public official and valuables as consideration for an act unrelated thereto are received in an inseparably combined manner without the amounts being distinguished.\\n\\nHowever, where the receipt of such valuables occurred on multiple occasions and, as to each act, there is room to view differently whether there was consideration under the pretext of making a request concerning a case or affair handled by a public official, it is only necessary to determine whether each act is related to the pretext of request (Supreme Court Decision rendered January 12, 2012, 2011DO12642 held to that effect with respect to the offense of bribery, and the same applies to the offense of violating the Attorney-at-Law Act).\\n\\nThe court below found that Defendant 2 received a total of KRW 96,700,020 from Nonparty Company 1 over five occasions, without separately distinguishing the amounts, as valuables under the pretext of making a request concerning a matter handled by a public official and as consideration under the pretext of service fees related to M&A with Nonparty Company 3, and determined that the offense of violating the Attorney-at-Law Act was established with respect to the entire amount received by Defendant 2 because the above two characteristics were inseparably combined in the funds received, and ordered collection of the full amount.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the evidence duly admitted by the court below and the trial court, it is difficult to view the funds received by Defendant 2 as allowing a different conclusion as to whether, for each act, there was consideration under the pretext of making a request concerning a matter handled by a public official, or to distinguish the consideration under the pretext of a request from the consideration for the M&A-related services with Nonparty Company 3. Accordingly, the court below’s determination that the offense of violating the Attorney-at-Law Act is established with respect to the entirety of the amount received by Defendant 2 from Nonparty Company 1 and ordering collection of that amount contains no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in that it did not violate the rules of logic and experience and exceed the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehend the legal principles concerning collection.\\n\\n3. Determination on the grounds for appeal of Defendant 3\\n\\nIn light of the evidence duly admitted by the court below and the trial court, the court below’s determination that all of the facts charged in this case against Defendant 3 were guilty is proper. There is no error in the court below’s determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in that it did not fully conduct the necessary examination and instead violated the rules of logic and experience and exceeded the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehend the legal principles concerning the intent of the offense of acceptance of bribes and the establishment of aiding and abetting. Further, the court below, which upheld the trial court’s imposition of a fine cumulatively on Defendant 3, did not err, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, by infringing human dignity and worth, the right to pursue happiness, the right to equality, or the freedom of the person, or by violating the principle prohibiting double punishment and the principle of responsibility.\\n\\n4. Determination on the grounds for appeal of the Prosecutor\\n\\nIn criminal trials, the burden of proof for the facts charged rests with the Prosecutor. To find guilt, there must be evidence having probative force such that the judge can be convinced that the facts charged are true beyond a reasonable doubt. Therefore, absent such evidence, even if the Defendant is suspected of guilt, the Defendant must be found not guilty in his or her favor (see Supreme Court Decision rendered February 24, 2006, 2005DO4737, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below reversed the trial court judgment, which found guilty the portion concerning acceptance of third-party bribery in the amount of KRW 1,000,000 in or around December 2013 among the facts charged in this case against Defendant 2, on the ground that the crime was not proven, and rendered a judgment of acquittal. In light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the court below’s determination is proper, and there is no error in that it did not violate the rules of logic and experience and exceed the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehend the relevant legal principles.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAll appeals by the Defendants and the Prosecutor are dismissed. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[85DO1350]": "We examine the grounds of appeal advanced by defense counsel.\\n\\nAccording to the evidence cited in the judgment of the first instance, which the court below affirmed, the facts found therein were lawfully recognized, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in misapprehending the facts in violation of the rules of evidence as alleged. Further, if the factual relationship is as determined by the court below, it is clear that the defendant’s conduct falls under the offense of acceptance of bribes; accordingly, the court below’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality in the form of a misapprehension of law concerning the offense of acceptance of bribes as alleged.\\n\\nWhere money received as a bribe is deposited in a bank, such act of deposit shall be deemed an act of disposal of the bribe; therefore, even if the bribe recipient thereafter returned to the bribe giver money in the same amount, this cannot be regarded as a return of the bribe itself. In such a case, the value thereof shall be collected from the bribe recipient; accordingly, the court below’s order of collection against the defendant is proper, and there is no illegality in the form of a misapprehension of law concerning collection as alleged.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is adjudged as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the judges participating."}

question: A sold to the voice-phishing scammer B, on 2023. 2. 12., for KRW 1,000,000, a deposit passbook with no balance for a deposit account opened in his own name at X Bank, one debit card linked to the said account, and one OTP card, without knowing that they would be used in a fraud offense. Thereafter, on 2023. 2. 13., B called A and, while impersonating a prosecutor, said, “If you transfer the money to A, who is a financial law expert, I will verify any criminal connection and then return it,” and A, having been deceived thereby, transferred KRW 10,000,000 to the said account around 11:20 on 2023. 2. 14.; and A, around 11:50 on the same day, used the debit card linked to the said account, which he had separately made and had in his possession, and arbitrarily withdrew KRW 3,000,000 of that amount. Regarding this, the prosecutor filed an indictment on the ground that A, by arbitrarily withdrawing KRW 3,000,000 from the fraud proceeds, embezzled B's property primarily and A's property alternatively. However, part of the page seal had been affixed to the reverse side of page 1 of the indictment, but the remaining page seal had not been affixed to the front side of page 2, and there was no page seal from the reverse side of page 2 to the last page. Which of the following statements concerning this is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: After A deposited KRW 10,000,000 into the account in the name of A, A is in the position of holding the said KRW 10,000,000 for the benefit of A.
B: A's act of arbitrarily withdrawing KRW 3,000,000 from the fraud proceeds constitutes the crime of embezzlement against B.
C: If A were an accomplice to B's fraud offense, then the act of arbitrarily withdrawing KRW 3,000,000 from the fraud proceeds does not constitute the crime of embezzlement against A.
D: Even if the indictment lacks the prosecutor's page seal, so long as the form and content of the indictment are recognized as being continuous and its identity is recognized, and it is recognized as having been prepared by the same prosecutor, the indictment cannot be regarded as a document without legal effect.
E: If, in the appellate trial concerning A, a judgment of not guilty is rendered on all counts of the indictment and the prosecutor files an appeal therefrom, then if the alternative count part must be reversed in the Supreme Court trial, the principal count part, which stands in the relationship of the same entity with it, also inevitably must be reversed together.
label: B

{"[2019DO16259]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. To institute public prosecution, an indictment must be submitted to the court with jurisdiction (Article 254(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act). Documents prepared by a public official shall bear a cross-seal or a measure equivalent thereto (Article 57(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act). Here, “documents prepared by a public official” include indictments prepared by a prosecutor (see Supreme Court Decision of October 25, 2007, 2007DO4961; Supreme Court Decision of September 27, 2012, 2010DO17052).\\n\\n“Cross-sealing” is the seal of the document preparer, and where a single document consists of multiple sheets, it is the stamping across the overlapping portions between each sheet of the document. This is intended to ensure that, after the document has been prepared, no part of it has been omitted or replaced. Therefore, even if the indictment bears no cross-seal of the prosecutor, so long as the form and content of the indictment are recognized as continuous and integral, and it is recognized that the same prosecutor prepared it, the indictment cannot be said to be a document without effect in violation of Article 57(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act. The institution of public prosecution by submission of such an indictment cannot be said to fall under the case where the procedure is void for violation of statutory provisions (Article 327 item 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\n\\n2. The court below, ex officio, set aside the first-instance judgment that found the facts charged in this case guilty for the following reasons and dismissed the public prosecution in this case.\\n\\nAlthough part of the cross-seal remains on the reverse side of page 1 of the indictment in this case, the rest of the cross-seal is not on the front side of page 2, and there is no cross-seal from the reverse side of page 2 to the last page of Appendix [Crime List 2]. In principle, supplementation of such a defect should be permitted only in the first instance. Even where there is a transfer of the prosecuting prosecutor, supplementation of the defect cannot be recognized. So long as part of the cross-seal remains on the reverse side of page 1 of the indictment in this case, the defect cannot be supplemented. The court should not require supplementation of the defect. The prosecution in this case falls under the case where the procedure for instituting public prosecution is void for violation of statutory provisions (Article 327 item 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\n\\n3. However, it is difficult to accept the judgment of the court below as it stands.\\n\\na. The record reveals the following facts.\\n\\n1) The indictment in this case consists of 3 pages of the main text, 1 page of Appendix [Crime List 1], and 3 pages of Appendix [Crime List 2], for a total of 7 pages. The main text and Appendix [Crime Lists] are all included without omission. The page numbers of the main text are also consecutively indicated at the lower right of the main text as “1/3,” “2/3,” and “3/3.”\\n\\n2) The name seal and signature of the prosecuting prosecutor are affixed to page 1 of the main text of the indictment in this case. It appears that the same prosecuting prosecutor prepared the indictment, and there is no material whatsoever to find that a different prosecutor prepared the indictment in this case.\\n\\n3) On page 1 of the main text of the indictment in this case, under the title “Indictment,” it states, “The prosecution is instituted as follows.” Thereafter, under the heading “I. Information Concerning the Defendant,” the defendant’s name, resident registration number, age, occupation, residence, registered domicile, name of the offense, and applicable statutory provisions are set forth in order.\\n\\n4) On page 2 of the main text of the indictment in this case, the remaining “Information Concerning the Defendant” sets forth, in order, whether the defendant is detained and the defense counsel. Thereafter, under the heading “II. Facts Charged,” the facts charged are set forth on pages 2 and 3 of the main text as follows.\\n\\n“1. (omitted) He possessed the material knowing that it was child and juvenile pornography. 2. (omitted) From around August 9, 2018 to around August 20 of the same month, he sold the videos in this case on a total of 9 occasions for a total of KRW 45,000, thereby selling child and juvenile pornography for profit as set forth in Appendix Crime List 1. 3. (omitted) The defendant, around 19:11 on August 9, 2018, (omitted) from around that time to around August 20 of the same month, as set forth in Appendix Crime List 2, received a total of KRW 940,000 on a total of 147 occasions and distributed, sold, rented, or openly displayed obscene videos.”\\n\\n5) The facts charged were drafted integrally for each offense so as to conform to the elements of the offenses of violation of the Act on the Protection of Children and Youth Against Sexual Abuse (possession of obscene materials), violation of the Act on the Protection of Children and Youth Against Sexual Abuse (production, distribution, etc. of obscene materials), and violation of the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc. (distribution of obscene materials), according to the name of the offense and applicable statutory provisions.\\n\\n6) In the attached Appendix [Crime List 1], the serial numbers are from 1 to 9, and the dates and times of the offenses are set forth from around August 9, 2018 to around August 20, 2018, thus matching the content of “Crime List 1” cited in Paragraph 2 of the facts charged. Appendix [Crime List 1] forms an integral part of the main text of the indictment in this case.\\n\\n7) In Appendix [Crime List (List of Obscene Materials Distributed by the Suspect) 2], the serial numbers are from 1 to 147, and the dates and times of the offenses are set forth from 19:11:37 on August 9, 2018 to 17:07:04 on August 20, 2018, thus matching the content of “Crime List 2” cited in Paragraph 3 of the facts charged. Appendix [Crime List (List of Obscene Materials Distributed by the Suspect) 2] also forms an integral part of the main text of the indictment in this case.\\n\\nb. When these facts are examined in light of the legal principles stated above, the form and content of the indictment in this case are recognized as continuous and integral, and it may be recognized that the same prosecuting prosecutor prepared it. Even if the prosecuting prosecutor’s cross-seal is absent, the indictment in this case is valid; therefore, the institution of public prosecution by submission of the indictment in this case cannot be said to fall under the case where the procedure is void for violation of statutory provisions (Article 327 item 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below, by contrast, held that the procedure for instituting public prosecution by submission of the indictment in this case fell under the case where it is void for violation of statutory provisions, on the ground that the indictment in this case bore no cross-seal of the prosecuting prosecutor, and rendered a judgment dismissing the public prosecution. The judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning omission of the cross-seal on the indictment and the effect of instituting prosecution. The prosecutor’s assertion of this ground of appeal is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court as indicated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the following case is correct? (In case of dispute, according to precedents) The Chief of the Tax Office imposed a tax disposition on A, who constitutes a secondary taxpayer under the Framework Act on National Taxes, with respect to B Corporation’s delinquent national taxes (hereinafter referred to as “the tax disposition at issue”). The filing period for an administrative lawsuit to assert the illegality of the tax disposition at issue has elapsed. However, one year later, the Constitutional Court, in a constitutional complaint case filed by B, decided that the provision of the Framework Act on National Taxes that served as the basis for the tax disposition at issue was unconstitutional (hereinafter referred to as “the unconstitutional decision at issue”). The Chief of the Tax Office attached the deposit claim in A’s name, on the basis of the National Tax Collection Act, which was validly in force at the time pursuant to the tax disposition at issue, in order to collect the delinquent amount and deficiency amount (including additional tax) that A had been in arrears with.
A: Since the provision of the Framework Act on National Taxes that served as the basis for the tax disposition at issue was declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court, the tax disposition at issue is a disposition lacking legal basis and is therefore void ab initio; accordingly, although the filing period has elapsed, bringing an administrative lawsuit seeking confirmation of its nullity is lawful.
B: The statutory provision that was the subject of the unconstitutional decision is the basis of the tax disposition at issue, and even if the retroactive effect of the unconstitutional decision is recognized, there is no risk of undermining legal stability; therefore, the retroactive effect of the unconstitutional decision also extends to A.
C: If, before the unconstitutional decision at issue, A had brought an administrative lawsuit seeking revocation of the tax disposition at issue and had already lost with final and conclusive effect, then because the unconstitutional decision at issue constitutes a ground for retrial under Article 75(7) of the Constitutional Court Act, A may petition for retrial.
D: The defect constituting a ground for revocation in the prior disposition, namely the tax disposition at issue, is succeeded to by the subsequent delinquent tax disposition, namely the attachment disposition.
E: If the statutory provision that served as the basis for the imposition of tax is declared unconstitutional, then, because of the binding force of the unconstitutional decision, it is no longer permitted to commence or continue a new delinquent tax collection disposition for the enforcement of the tax claim after the unconstitutional decision. A delinquent tax collection disposition made in violation of the effect of such unconstitutional decision is, by that reason alone, so seriously and objectively manifestly defective as to be void ab initio.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2010DU10907]": "The grounds of appeal are considered together.\\n\\n1. In order for a defective administrative disposition to become automatically void, the defect must be grave enough to violate an important part of the relevant law and must be objectively clear; in determining whether the defect is grave and obvious, the purpose, meaning, and function of the relevant legal provision must be examined teleologically, and the special features of the specific case itself must also be reasonably considered (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc judgment dated 1995. 7. 11. in 94NU4615, and Supreme Court en banc judgment dated 2006. 3. 16. in 2006DU330).\\nMeanwhile, Article 47(1) of the former Constitutional Court Act (prior to amendment by Act No. 10546 on 2011. 4. 5., hereinafter referred to as the “former Constitutional Court Act”) provides that “a decision that a statute is unconstitutional shall bind the courts, other state agencies, and local governments.” In light of the binding force of such a decision of unconstitutionality and the systemic demand of the legal order that takes the Constitution as the supreme norm, it is reasonable to view that state agencies and local governments may not make a new administrative disposition on the basis of a statutory provision declared unconstitutional, and that even a subsequent disposition based on legal relations already formed before the decision of unconstitutionality may not be permitted if it creates or expands a new unconstitutional legal relationship.\\nAccordingly, where the statutory provision that served as the basis for the imposition of taxes has been declared unconstitutional, even if the tax assessment disposition based thereon was made before the decision of unconstitutionality, and the period for filing a lawsuit against that tax assessment disposition has already elapsed so that the tax claim has become final, and even if no separate decision of unconstitutionality has been rendered with respect to the provision itself that served as the basis for collection dispositions to enforce that tax claim, it is no longer permissible, after such decision of unconstitutionality, to commence or continue a new collection disposition to enforce the tax claim; furthermore, a collection disposition made in violation of the effect of such decision of unconstitutionality must be deemed, for that reason alone, to be grave and objectively obvious in its defect and therefore void ab initio.\\nAccording to the reasons of the first-instance judgment, as partially cited by the court below, the facts are as follows: on 1997. 10. 22., the Defendant made a tax imposition disposition (hereinafter referred to as the “tax assessment disposition at issue”) against the Plaintiff concerning the delinquent national taxes of Kyungsung Co., Ltd., on the ground that the Plaintiff fell under a secondary taxpayer under Article 39(1)2(c) of the former Framework Act on National Taxes (prior to amendment by Act No. 5579 on 1998. 12. 28., hereinafter referred to as the “former Framework Act on National Taxes”); the Constitutional Court, by its decision dated 1998. 5. 28. in 97HEONGA13, declared that Article 39(1)2(c) of the former Framework Act on National Taxes was in violation of the Constitution; and thereafter, the Defendant, on the basis of the National Tax Collection Act then validly in force pursuant to the tax assessment disposition at issue, seized a deposit claim in the name of the Plaintiff on 2005. 10. 11. in order to collect the amount in arrears and the amount of deficiency (including additional taxes) then delinquent by the Plaintiff (hereinafter referred to as the “seizure disposition at issue”).\\nOn the premise of these facts, the court below held that, in light of the fact that after a decision of unconstitutionality, from the perspective of the remedy of citizens’ rights, it must not be allowed to leave the state of application of an unconstitutional statute as it is or to permit additional acts by state agencies for the final execution of an unconstitutional statute, the seizure disposition at issue made after the decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision serving as the basis for the tax assessment disposition at issue constituted an additional act by the Defendant for the final execution of the tax assessment disposition at issue and thus fell under an administrative disposition void ab initio.\\nIn light of the above legal principles and the record, although there is an improper point in part of the court below’s reasoning, the conclusion of the court below that the seizure disposition at issue is void ab initio on the premise that, after a decision of unconstitutionality, additional acts by state agencies for the final execution of an unconstitutional statute may not be permitted, is proper. There is no illegality that affected the outcome of the judgment due to misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the grounds for automatic nullity of a seizure disposition made after a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision underlying a tax assessment disposition, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged. Except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Ahn Dae-hee, Shin Young-chul, and Kim Yong-deok, the opinions of the participating Justices were in accord.\\n\\n2. The dissenting opinions of Justices Ahn Dae-hee, Shin Young-chul, and Kim Yong-deok are as follows.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that, in light of the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality under Article 47(1) of the former Constitutional Court Act and the systemic demand of the legal order that takes the Constitution as the supreme norm, even if there is a decision of unconstitutionality only with respect to the provision underlying the tax assessment disposition and no decision of unconstitutionality with respect to the provision underlying the collection disposition based on that tax assessment disposition, a collection disposition first made after the decision of unconstitutionality pursuant to a tax assessment disposition made before the decision of unconstitutionality is, for that reason alone, grave and objectively obvious in its defect and therefore void ab initio. However, I cannot concur with this majority opinion for the following reasons.\\nFirst, if an administrative agency made an administrative disposition on the basis of a provision of a statute and thereafter the Constitutional Court declared that provision unconstitutional, then the administrative disposition would, as a result, be equivalent to one made without legal basis and thus would have a defect, albeit retroactively; however, as a general rule, the circumstance that a statute violates the Constitution cannot be said to be objectively obvious before there is a decision of unconstitutionality by the Constitutional Court, and therefore, absent special circumstances, such a defect constitutes only a ground for revocation of the administrative disposition, not a ground for automatic nullity (see, e.g., Supreme Court judgment dated 1994. 10. 28. in 92NU9463, and Supreme Court judgment dated 2009. 5. 14. in 2007DU16202).\\nAlso, where separate acts for a specific administrative purpose are carried out in stages, it cannot be said that the defect in the prior disposition is automatically succeeded by the subsequent disposition, except where the prior disposition has a defect that makes it void ab initio or nonexistent (see, e.g., Supreme Court judgment dated 1961. 10. 26. in 4292HAENGSANG73, and Supreme Court judgment dated 2001. 11. 27. in 98DU9530).\\nIf the foregoing established Supreme Court precedents are taken as the premise, the tax assessment disposition at issue and the seizure disposition at issue are separate administrative dispositions; thus, except where the prior disposition, namely the tax assessment disposition at issue, is void ab initio, the validity of the seizure disposition at issue, being a subsequent collection disposition, cannot be challenged on the ground of any defect in the tax assessment disposition at issue. Moreover, as stated above, the tax assessment disposition at issue may be regarded as a valid disposition.\\nSecond, under Article 47 of the former Constitutional Court Act concerning the effect of a decision of unconstitutionality, a decision that a statute is unconstitutional binds the courts, other state agencies, and local governments (paragraph (1)); however, a statute or statutory provision declared unconstitutional loses its effect from the date of the decision, but, in the case of a criminal statute or a statutory provision, it is in principle retroactively deprived of effect (paragraph (2)); accordingly, it is reasonable to interpret the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality on state agencies and local governments as having effect only within the scope to which the effect of unconstitutionality extends.\\nHowever, a collection disposition, such as a seizure disposition, is a separate administrative disposition from the tax assessment disposition, and the provisions underlying the tax assessment disposition are not directly applied; only the provisions concerning collection dispositions are applied. Therefore, the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provisions underlying the tax assessment disposition is unrelated to, and does not extend to, the collection disposition.\\nFurthermore, where, with respect to a tax assessment disposition made in the past, the retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality is limited and it is viewed that such effect does not extend thereto, the relevant tax assessment disposition should be regarded as valid and not unconstitutional; accordingly, the collection disposition based on that tax assessment disposition is also not unconstitutional and cannot be said to violate the binding force of the decision of unconstitutionality. Therefore, in order to halt the progression of collection proceedings based on a tax assessment disposition, as in the case of criminal statutes, separate legislation is necessary, such as establishing a procedure to exclude the effect of the tax assessment disposition by extending the scope of the effect of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision underlying the tax assessment disposition, or restricting the progress of collection proceedings.\\nNevertheless, if, as the majority opinion does, the scope of binding force is construed to extend to the point of prohibiting the progress of collection proceedings concerning a valid tax assessment disposition, thereby substantially denying the effect of the tax assessment disposition in question and causing it to disappear in fact, then it may be pointed out that this excessively expands the scope of binding force and consequently does not accord with the purport of the main clause of Article 47(2) of the former Constitutional Court Act, which limited the retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality.\\nThird, when compared with certain foreign legislative examples, in Germany, retroactive effect is in principle recognized for a decision of unconstitutionality, but it is understood that such retroactive effect does not extend to legal relationships already finally determined at the time of the decision of unconstitutionality; moreover, there is an express statutory provision to the effect that no enforcement act may be taken pursuant to the statutory provision declared unconstitutional. The majority opinion ultimately means that Korea's relevant provisions should be interpreted and applied like those of Germany, which has such an express provision; however, in Korea, where no such express provision exists, it is difficult to accept such an interpretive theory as it stands.\\nAccordingly, so long as the tax assessment disposition, being the prior disposition, has no ground for automatic nullity and the provisions underlying the collection disposition based on the tax assessment disposition remain valid, the collection disposition cannot be deemed unlawful merely because the Constitutional Court has rendered a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision underlying the tax assessment disposition.\\nIn light of this legal principle, the tax assessment disposition at issue has no ground for automatic nullity, and the provisions underlying the seizure disposition at issue, which constitutes a subsequent collection disposition based on that tax assessment disposition, remain valid; absent an express provision, as seen in some foreign legislative examples, excluding the enforceability of an unconstitutional statute, the seizure disposition at issue cannot be regarded as void ab initio.\\nNevertheless, the court below held that the seizure disposition at issue, made after the decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision underlying the tax assessment disposition at issue, was void ab initio, relying only on the reason that, after a decision of unconstitutionality, from the perspective of the remedy of citizens’ rights, it must not be allowed to leave the state of application of an unconstitutional statute as it is or to permit additional acts by state agencies for the final execution of an unconstitutional statute. Accordingly, this judgment of the court below contains illegality that affected the outcome of the judgment by misapprehending, inter alia, the legal principles concerning the grounds for automatic nullity of a seizure disposition made after a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision underlying a tax assessment disposition. Therefore, the judgment of the court below must be reversed."}

{"[4292HAENGSANG73]": "Where independent acts are carried out in stages for a certain administrative purpose, except where there exist grounds that would naturally render the prior act void, it cannot be said that the defect of illegality in the prior act is naturally succeeded to by the subsequent act. In the present case, according to Article 11 of the Education Tax Act before amendment, it provided that Education Tax, being a national tax, could not be levied on the portion falling short of a certain amount as certain income; and according to Article 15(1) of the same Act, it provided that local Education Tax shall be levied on income on which Education Tax, being a national tax, is not levied pursuant to the provisions of Article 11 of the same Act; and, considering in conjunction Article 15(2) and (3) and Article 4 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, since it is provided that, where there is income other than certain income, local Education Tax may be levied by taking, as the tax base, the total income amount or the gross total income amount of that income and the amount based on assets or the standard of living calculated according to certain standards, it is not only a literal interpretation that, even for the same person, both national Education Tax and local Education Tax may be concurrently imposed, but also, if income that had not been subject to taxation is newly discovered, then if such income is an income amount on which national Education Tax may be levied, national Education Tax should be additionally levied thereon, and local Education Tax cannot be levied thereon. However, such an improper measure cannot be said to constitute a ground for voidness ab initio, but is to be construed as merely a ground for revocation; whereas the record clearly shows that the Plaintiff objected to the Defendant’s disposition imposing local Education Tax on the ground that the assessed tax amount was excessive, and that the Defendant rendered a ruling correcting the same, and, on the premise that that ruling had become final and conclusive, made the present disposition for collection of delinquent taxes, the Plaintiff has not raised any defect with respect to the delinquent-tax collection disposition itself, and is contesting the present delinquent-tax collection disposition on the ground of the so-called defect in the already final and conclusive taxation disposition itself, as is clear from the Plaintiff’s claim itself; therefore, the Plaintiff’s claim, which contests the subsequent delinquent-tax collection disposition on the ground of a defect in the prior taxation disposition as aforesaid, is improper, but despite that, the court below, on a contrary premise, upheld the Plaintiff’s claim, and the original judgment is improper, without the need to determine the other grounds of appeal."}

{"[92NU9463]": "We shall determine together the first and second points of the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below duly found that the non-party Korea Light Semiconductor Co., Ltd., in obtaining a loan from the non-party Korea Exchange Bank on 1989.5.17., had provided the machinery involved in this case as security by way of security assignment; that the Defendant, on 1990.4.3., for the collection of the Value-Added Tax, Corporate Tax, and Defense Tax imposed on the said company, attached the machinery in this case pursuant to Article 42(1) of the former Framework Act on National Taxes (prior to its amendment by Act No. 4277 of 1990.12.31.); and that, with respect to the Plaintiff, who paid the company’s debt to the said Korea Exchange Bank and acquired the rights to the said machinery, the proviso to the said provision to the effect that only property subject to security assignment may not be attached one year before the payment deadline for the said national taxes (more precisely, the part of the proviso reading “one year before”) is unconstitutional, and therefore the said attachment disposition is void. As to that argument, the court below held that it lacks merit because, first, no constitutional ruling has been rendered with respect to the said proviso, and second, even if such a constitutional ruling were rendered, the defect in the said disposition cannot be deemed so grave and obvious as to render it void.\\n\\n2. If, after an administrative disposition has been issued on the basis of a statute, the Constitutional Court declares the statute that constituted the basis for the administrative disposition unconstitutional, then, in consequence, the said administrative disposition would be deemed to have been made without any legal basis and thus to be defective. However, in order for a defective administrative disposition to be void as a matter of course, the defect must not only be grave but also obvious. Generally, before a constitutional decision of unconstitutionality by the Constitutional Court, the circumstance that a statute violates the Constitution cannot objectively be said to be obvious. Accordingly, absent special circumstances, the ground that the statute constituting the basis of an administrative disposition violates the Constitution before a constitutional decision by the Constitutional Court may serve only as a premise for an action seeking revocation of that administrative disposition, and is not a ground for automatic nullity. If, contrary to the above, an administrative disposition based on an unconstitutional statute were generally deemed void as a matter of course, this would result in a serious threat to legal stability, and even in light of the principle of the rule of law, it would have to be regarded as improper.\\n\\nFurther, whether an administrative disposition based on an unconstitutional statute is void as a matter of course is a question separate from the retroactive effect of a constitutional decision; even if retroactive effect of a constitutional decision is recognized, it cannot be said that an administrative disposition based on an unconstitutional statute becomes void as a matter of course. Rather, for an administrative disposition whose period for filing an action for revocation has already elapsed and whose finality has thereby arisen, the retroactive effect of a constitutional decision should be deemed not to extend. Therefore, where an action seeking a declaration of nullity is brought against an administrative disposition on the ground that the statute constituting its basis is unconstitutional, the court, absent other special circumstances, should dismiss the said action seeking a declaration of nullity without needing to determine whether the statute is unconstitutional. Accordingly, the court below’s determination that the Defendant’s attachment disposition in this case cannot be deemed void as a matter of course merely because the relevant provision of the said Framework Act on National Taxes is unconstitutional is proper in light of the legal principles stated above, and it cannot be said to contain an illegality such as the alleged misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the retroactive effect of a constitutional decision or the automatic nullity of an administrative disposition. All the arguments are without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. The judgment is rendered as follows by unanimous agreement of the Justices involved."}

{"[92NU9463]": "The first and second grounds of appeal are examined together.\\n\\n1. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below properly found that Non-party Hanguk Gwang Semiconductor Co., Ltd., in obtaining a loan from Non-party Korea Exchange Bank on 1989.5.17., had provided the machinery at issue in this case as transfer security as collateral, and that the Defendant, on 1990.4.3., seized said machinery pursuant to Article 42(1) of the former Framework Act on National Taxes (as amended by Act No. 4277 on 1990.12.31.) for the collection of value-added tax, corporate tax, and defense tax against said company; and, with respect to the Plaintiff, who had discharged the company’s debt to said Korea Exchange Bank and received the rights to said machinery, the court below held that the proviso to the above provision to the effect that only the property subject to transfer security that became the object of security could not be seized within 1 year before the due date for payment of the above national taxes (more precisely, the portion of the above proviso stating “1 year earlier”) was unconstitutional, and therefore the said seizure disposition was void. As to that contention, the court below held that there had been no decision of unconstitutionality with respect to the provision of the above proviso, and further that even if a decision of unconstitutionality were rendered, the defect in the said disposition could not be deemed to be grave and obvious so as to make it void, and accordingly held that the above argument was without merit.\\n\\n2. If, after an administrative disposition has been issued on the basis of a statute, the Constitutional Court declares the statute that formed the basis of that administrative disposition unconstitutional, then, as a result, such administrative disposition would be regarded as having been made without legal basis and thus as defective. However, for a defective administrative disposition to be void as a matter of course, the defect must not only be grave but also obvious; and, generally, before the Constitutional Court renders a decision of unconstitutionality, the circumstance that a statute violates the Constitution cannot objectively be said to be obvious. Therefore, it is reasonable to view the ground that the relevant statute forming the basis of an administrative disposition violates the Constitution before the Constitutional Court’s decision of unconstitutionality as, absent special circumstances, merely a premise for an action to revoke that administrative disposition, and not a ground for voidness as a matter of course. If, contrary to the above, an administrative disposition based on an unconstitutional statute were generally deemed void as a matter of course, this would result in a substantial threat to legal stability and, in light of the principle of the rule of law, cannot be said to be proper.\\n\\nIn addition, whether an administrative disposition based on an unconstitutional statute is void as a matter of course is a matter separate from the retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality; even if retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality is recognized, it cannot be said that an administrative disposition based on an unconstitutional statute becomes void as a matter of course. Rather, it should be understood that the retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality does not extend to an administrative disposition whose finality has arisen after the period for filing an action for revocation has already elapsed. Therefore, in a case where an action seeking confirmation of invalidity is brought against an administrative disposition on the ground that the statute forming the basis of that administrative disposition is unconstitutional, the court should, absent other special circumstances, dismiss the above action seeking confirmation of invalidity without needing to determine whether the statute is unconstitutional. Accordingly, the court below’s determination that the Defendant’s seizure disposition in this case cannot be deemed void as a matter of course merely because the relevant provision of the above Framework Act on National Taxes is unconstitutional is proper in light of the foregoing legal principles, and there is no illegality, such as the alleged misunderstanding of the law concerning the retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality or the voidness as a matter of course of an administrative disposition. All arguments are without merit.\\n\\n3. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. The participating Justices being in agreement, it is so adjudged as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[99HEONBA66]": "1. Outline of the Case and Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nA. Outline of the Case\\n\\n(1) 99HEONBA66 Case\\n\\nPetitioner Im ○ Hong received on 1995. 8. 31. from the Head of Yongsan-gu Office, Seoul Metropolitan City, a disposition imposing an Excess Land Ownership Charge of 222,405,750 won, and filed an administrative lawsuit with the Seoul High Court seeking revocation thereof (96GU2936), but it was dismissed on 1996. 11. 6. The Petitioner appealed to the Supreme Court against this judgment of dismissal (96NU18458), but the appeal was dismissed on 1997. 7. 11., and the above judgment became final. As the former Act on the Ownership Ceiling on Land, which served as the basis for the imposition of the Excess Land Ownership Charge, was declared unconstitutional by our Constitutional Court on 1999. 4. 29., the Petitioner filed an action for retrial with the Seoul High Court (99JAENU357) and applied for a referral of a constitutional review regarding Article 75(7) of the Constitutional Court Act, which grants an opportunity for retrial to a person who has filed a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act while not granting such an opportunity to a person who has not filed such a constitutional complaint, alleging that it was unconstitutional (99A310); however, that court, on 1999. 7. 9., dismissed the retrial request and also dismissed the application for referral as without merit. Accordingly, the Petitioner received service of the decision dismissing the application for referral of a constitutional review on 1999. 7. 21., and on 1999. 7. 29. filed the constitutional complaint in this case pursuant to Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act.\\n\\n(2) 99HEONBA67 Case\\n\\nPetitioner Im ○ Hong received on 1994. 8. 31. from the Head of Yongsan-gu Office, Seoul Metropolitan City, a disposition imposing an Excess Land Ownership Charge of 171,166,090 won, and filed an administrative lawsuit with the Seoul High Court seeking revocation thereof (95GU26560), but it was dismissed on 1998. 1. 15. The Petitioner appealed to the Supreme Court against this judgment of dismissal (98DU3921), but the appeal was dismissed on 1998. 5. 22., and the above judgment became final. As the former Act on the Ownership Ceiling on Land, which served as the basis for the imposition of the Excess Land Ownership Charge, was declared unconstitutional by our Constitutional Court on 1999. 4. 29., the Petitioner filed an action for retrial with the Seoul High Court (99JAENU326) and, while asserting that Article 75(7) of the Constitutional Court Act, which defines the scope of retrial requests, violates the principle of equality and is therefore unconstitutional, applied for a referral of a constitutional review of the said provision (99A311); however, that court, on 1999. 7. 9., dismissed the Petitioner’s above action for retrial and also dismissed the above application as without merit.
