Summary of the Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\nThe provisions of the Act at issue treat the Petitioners as potential criminals regardless of the risk of recidivism and allow their DNA identification information to be collected for use in identifying perpetrators of crimes whose occurrence in the future is uncertain, thereby infringing freedom of the body, the right to informational self-determination, human dignity and worth, the right to pursue happiness, personality rights, and the freedom and privacy of private life, and violating the prohibition against double punishment and the presumption of innocence, and, in particular, by applying them even where comparatively minor crimes such as bodily injury, trespass into a residence, and refusal to leave premises resulted in a suspended sentence rather than an actual sentence, they violate the principle of proportionality. The provisions of the Act at issue also infringe the right to equality in that they discriminate without reasonable basis between persons who committed crimes subject to DNA collection and persons who committed crimes other than the relevant crimes.\\n\\nThe collection-warrant provision at issue violates the warrant principle because it lacks substantive requirements for a judge to determine in issuing a collection warrant, such as the risk of recidivism.\\n\\nWith respect to the collection-by-consent provision at issue, in Petitioner Seo ○ Mun’s case, there was no guide at all regarding refusal to collection and consent, and because the procedure of seeking written consent was not followed, the DNA collection cannot be deemed to have been based on genuine voluntary consent.\\n\\nThe deletion provision at issue, by providing that DNA identification information is deleted only when convicted prisoners, etc. die, in effect allows DNA identification information to be recorded in the database indefinitely and therefore violates the principle of proportionality.\\n\\nThe Addenda provision at issue retroactively applies the Act at issue even to the Petitioners whose sentences had already become final and who were confined, thereby violating the principle against retroactive legislation; it also excessively expands the scope of persons subject to the Act retroactively, thereby infringing the trust of persons whose sentences had already become final and violating the principle of proportionality; and it unreasonably discriminates against, and thereby infringes the right to equality of, persons who had already been sentenced for offenses subject to collection at the time the Act at issue came into force and whose custodial term had already been fully served and who had been released from detention.\\n\\n4. Determination on Procedural Admissibility\\n\\nThe main text of Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act provides that a person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power may file a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court. However, if the exercise or non-exercise of public power has no effect whatsoever on the legal status of the person seeking to file a constitutional complaint, then, since there is in the first place no possibility or danger of infringement of fundamental rights, filing a constitutional complaint against such exercise of public power is not permitted (Constitutional Court 1999. 5. 27. 97HEONMA368; Constitutional Court 1999. 6. 24. 97HEONMA315).\\n\\nBelow, we examine, by challenged provision, those portions of the instant petition in which defects in the procedural requirements are at issue.\\n\\na. Possibility of infringement of fundamental rights by the collection-warrant provision at issue\\n\\nThe collection-warrant provision at issue is a provision requiring that, where the person subject to collection of a DNA sample does not consent to collection, a DNA sample be collected upon obtaining a warrant from a judge of the competent district court. It is not a provision that infringes the fundamental rights of the person subject to collection of a DNA sample, but rather a provision that concretizes the constitutional warrant principle. The collection-warrant provision at issue states only “a warrant issued upon application to a judge of the competent district court” and otherwise does not separately prescribe the requirements for issuance of a warrant, but requirements such as the “risk of recidivism” asserted by the Petitioners are more directly related to Article 5(1) of the Act at issue than to the collection-warrant provision at issue, and therefore it is difficult to view the collection-warrant provision at issue itself as likely to violate the warrant principle, which requires a warrant issued after a judge’s specific determination.\\n\\nAccordingly, because the fundamental rights of Petitioners Kim ○ Ho, No ○ Min, Kim ○ Su, Cheon ○ Seok, Kim ○ Ho, Kim ○ Hwan, and Kim ○ Young cannot be said to have been directly infringed by the collection-warrant provision at issue, nor can it be said that any effect arose in their legal status, the above Petitioners’ petitions concerning the collection-warrant provision at issue are inadmissible.\\n\\nb. Possibility of infringement of fundamental rights by the DNA analysis, recording, and management provision at issue\\n\\nThe DNA analysis, recording, and management provision at issue merely prescribes a method of processing the work by stating that “the Prosecutor General and the Commissioner of the National Police Agency may delegate or entrust the following duties to a person or institution designated by Presidential Decree.”\\n\\nAccordingly, because it cannot be said that Petitioner Kim ○ Ho’s fundamental rights are directly infringed by the DNA analysis, recording, and management provision at issue, nor can it be said that any effect arose in his legal status, the petition concerning it is inadmissible.\\n\\n5. Determination on the Merits\\n\\na. Legislative background and main content of the Act in this case\\n\\nDiscussion on the establishment of a criminal DNA database began already in the mid-1990s, and on 2006. 8. 1., the Government submitted to the National Assembly a bill on the collection and management of DNA profiling information, but it was discarded due to the expiry of the term of the 17th National Assembly. Thereafter, as a series of violent crimes attracting public attention occurred one after another, the necessity of establishing a DNA identification information database again emerged in order to promptly apprehend offenders and to enhance crime-prevention effects; the National Assembly enacted the Act on the Use and Protection of DNA Identification Information on 2009. 12. 29. and introduced a DNA identification information database system enabling the collection of DNA identification information for use in criminal investigations, etc.\\n\\nDNA means deoxyribonucleic acid, a chemical substance containing information on the life phenomena of organisms (Article 2(1) of the Act at issue). Through DNA samples that are the subject of DNA analysis, such as blood, saliva, hair, and buccal mucosa (Article 2(2) of the same Act), DNA analysis (Articles 2(3) and (4) of the same Act), which examines and analyzes specific base-sequence regions that do not contain genetic information in DNA for the purpose of personal identification (introns, so-called junk DNA), and obtains DNA identification information expressed as combinations of a series of numbers or symbols, a DNA identification information database is established as a collection systematically recording DNA identification information so that the information can be individually accessed or searched (Article 2(5) of the same Act).\\n\\nThe cases in which a DNA sample may be collected are broadly divided into collection from convicted prisoners, etc. (Article 5 of the same Act), collection from suspects under detention and persons subject to treatment and custody protected under the Act on the Treatment and Custody of Offenders (Article 6 of the same Act), and collection from crime scenes (Article 7 of the same Act). The subject crimes are typified as arson, murder, kidnapping and enticement, crimes of rape and indecent assault, theft and robbery (including quasi-robbery), assault, intimidation, trespass into a residence / refusal to leave premises, damage to property, arrest, confinement, coercion, bodily injury, extortion, organizing a criminal organization, obstruction of official duties, obstruction of auction/bidding, crimes concerning narcotics, etc. (each item of Article 5(1) of the same Act). Although the warrant principle is adopted when a DNA sample is collected from a convicted prisoner or a detained suspect, the sample may also be collected without a warrant only where the person concerned gives written consent (Article 8 of the same Act).\\n\\nThe administration of matters relating to DNA identification information is divided between the Prosecutor General and the Commissioner of the National Police Agency, who are to operate their respective databases in linkage (Article 4 of the same Act). The Prosecutor General and the Commissioner of the National Police Agency may delegate or entrust the tasks of analyzing DNA samples and recording DNA identification information in the database, and of managing the database, to a person or institution designated by Presidential Decree (the DNA identification information officer) (Article 10(1) of the same Act), and matters necessary in this regard are to be prescribed by Presidential Decree, which provides as follows: when a DNA sample is collected from a person subject to collection, the prosecutor or judicial police officer sends the DNA sample to the DNA personal-information manager (Article 10(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act); the DNA personal-information manager reviews the enclosed consent form of the person concerned (or the warrant) and the sample collection confirmation form to verify whether there is any irregularity, and then enters the person’s identifying information into the DNA personal-information management system. At this time, the person concerned is assigned a unique identification code (barcode), and after the personal-information manager prints and attaches the same barcode to the sample, the sample is sent to the DNA identification information officer (the Chief of the Scientific Investigation Planning Division of the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office or the National Forensic Service) (paragraph (2) of the same Article). The DNA identification information officer receives only a sample bearing the unique barcode and no personal information, and designates the person to analyze the sample. The analyst separates DNA from the sample and obtains DNA identification information by marking as a series of numbers the analysis information on short tandem repeats (STRs), which are short sequences of repeated nucleotides (the units constituting nucleic acids) in introns. The DNA identification information officer verifies the analysis data concerning the DNA identification information obtained from the analyst, confirms whether there is any irregularity, and then records and manages the information in the DNA identification information database. The DNA identification information officer may search DNA identification information or report the results thereof for the recording of new DNA identification information, criminal investigations or identification of deceased persons, inquiries of facts in criminal trials by a court, or comparison among databases (Article 11(1) of the same Act).\\n\\nThe DNA identification information officer shall delete, ex officio or upon application by a relative, the DNA identification information recorded in the database from samples collected pursuant to Article 5 or 6 when a convicted prisoner, etc. is acquitted in a retrial, or a judgment of dismissal of prosecution or decision of dismissal of prosecution becomes final (Article 13(1) of the same Act), or when a suspect under detention receives a disposition such as a finding of no suspicion from a prosecutor (paragraph (2)1 of the same Article) or a judgment of acquittal, dismissal of prosecution, etc. becomes final from a court (paragraph (2)2 of the same Article), or when a convicted prisoner, etc. or detained suspect dies (paragraph (3) of the same Article). In addition, where a sample is collected from a crime scene, etc. pursuant to Article 7 of the same Act and the identity is later revealed with respect to the recorded identification information, it shall be deleted (Article 13(4) of the same Act). If the identification information is deleted as above, the fact shall be notified to the person concerned or the applicant within 30 days (paragraph (5) of the same Article).\\n\\nb. Determination concerning the collection provisions at issue\\n\\n(1) Fundamental rights restricted\\n\\nFreedom of the body under Article 12(1) of the Constitution means freedom from the body’s stability being infringed by physical force or mental danger from outside, and freedom to engage in bodily activity voluntarily and autonomously (Constitutional Court 1992. 12. 24. 92HEONGA8; Constitutional Court 2005. 5. 26. 99HEONMA513 et al.). The specific methods of collecting a DNA sample are collection from the buccal mucosa or from hair including the roots; where collection by the above methods is impossible or manifestly difficult, collection is by means of secretions or bodily fluids (Article 8(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act in this case). If so, the act of collecting a DNA sample may be deemed to impair bodily stability, and therefore the collection provisions at issue restrict freedom of the body.\\n\\n(2) Whether freedom of the body is infringed\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of the collection provisions at issue, which collect DNA samples from persons convicted of certain crimes in order to overcome the difficulty of apprehending offenders and conducting post hoc management under existing investigative methods in violent crimes, by introducing a DNA identification information database system that secures and manages in advance the DNA identification information of persons who committed violent crimes, thereby promptly apprehending offenders, early excluding innocent suspects from the investigative line, and additionally enhancing crime-prevention effects, is legitimate, and collecting DNA samples from convicted persons for certain crimes in order to record and manage their DNA identification information in the database is an appropriate means to achieve the legislative purpose.\\n\\nThe offenses of bodily injury while carrying a deadly weapon, rape, etc. causing injury, rape causing injury, arson, and the like have a higher risk of recidivism than other crimes, so there is a greater need to record and manage the DNA identification information of persons who committed such offenses in the database. Where a person subject to collection does not consent to collection of a DNA sample, collection is subject to a warrant issued by a judge (Article 8(2) of the Act in this case), and in the case of collection by consent, the person must be informed in advance that he or she may refuse collection and written consent must be obtained (paragraph (3) of the same Article); at the time of collection, the person must be informed of the reason for collection and the type and method of the sample to be collected (paragraph (8) of the same Article); and, when collecting DNA samples, priority is given to collection from the buccal mucosa or hair including the roots, and only where the above methods are impossible or manifestly difficult are bodily parts, secretions, or bodily fluids from which DNA can otherwise be collected taken, thereby minimizing infringement of the body or reputation of the person subject to collection (Article 9 of the same Act; Article 8 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act). Even though the risk of recidivism is not separately prescribed as a requirement for collection, it can sufficiently be considered in practice at the stage where the judge determines the necessity and considerable grounds for issuing a collection warrant. In light of the foregoing, the requirement of minimal impairment is satisfied.\\n\\nFurthermore, the degree of restriction on freedom of the body imposed by the collection provisions at issue is slight to the extent that it can be experienced even in everyday life and does not entail external injury or a decline in physiological functions, and therefore it cannot be said to be greater than the public interest in contributing to criminal investigation and crime prevention; accordingly, the balance of interests is also recognized.\\n\\nTherefore, the collection provisions at issue cannot be deemed to infringe the Petitioners’ freedom of the body in violation of the principle of proportionality.\\n\\n(3) Whether the right to equality is infringed\\n\\nThe collection provisions at issue result in differential treatment between criminals who committed offenses subject to DNA sample collection and criminals who committed offenses not subject to such collection. However, the relevant offenses under the collection provisions at issue—violations of the Punishment of Violences, etc. Act, violations of the Special Act on the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Violence Crimes, rape causing injury, arson, and the like—are offenses that are subject to aggravated punishment because of the dangerousness of the method and means of commission, compared with offenses not subject to DNA sample collection, or are offenses constituting violent crimes of a serious character in the form of conduct or in the nature of the offense. In particular, offenses such as bodily injury while carrying a deadly weapon, rape, etc. causing injury, rape causing injury, and arson are statistically offenses with a high possibility of recidivism in the future; accordingly, there is a rational basis for designating persons who committed such offenses as a class subject to DNA sample collection for future criminal investigations and crime prevention. Therefore, the collection provisions at issue cannot be said to violate the principle of equality.\\n\\nc. Determination concerning the collection-by-consent provision at issue\\n\\nThe collection-by-consent provision at issue provides that DNA samples may be collected without a warrant when the person subject to collection consents, thereby restricting freedom of the body. Because collection of a DNA sample may be carried out by consent in place of the requirement that collection be made by judicial warrant, the issue is whether allowing such a restriction on freedom of the body by consent violates the warrant principle and the principle of due process and thereby infringes freedom of the body.\\n\\nWhere a DNA sample is collected by consent, the person must be informed in advance that collection may be refused, and written consent must be obtained (the second sentence of Article 8(3) of the Act in this case). Moreover, if there is no consent, collection must necessarily be carried out by a warrant issued by a judge; therefore, it is difficult to view the provision itself, which allows DNA sample collection by consent, as a means to evade the warrant principle or as contrary to the warrant principle and the principle of due process. Extending beyond prior notice that collection may be refused in order to secure voluntary consent, the question of to what extent matters to be notified before consent should be prescribed falls within the area of legislative discretion, and the fact that additional items for notice are not prescribed cannot lead to the conclusion that the collection-by-consent provision at issue itself violates the principle of due process.\\n\\nAccordingly, the collection-by-consent provision at issue cannot be deemed to infringe freedom of the body in violation of the warrant principle and the principle of due process.\\n\\nd. Determination concerning the deletion provision at issue\\n\\n(1) Fundamental rights restricted\\n\\nThe general personality right derived from the first sentence of Article 10 of the Constitution, which provides for human dignity and worth and the right to pursue happiness, and the right to informational self-determination guaranteed by the freedom and privacy of private life under Article 17 of the Constitution, are rights of the data subject to determine for himself or herself when, to whom, and to what extent information about oneself will be disclosed and used. In other words, they refer to the right of the data subject to determine on his or her own the disclosure and use of personal information. Personal information protected by the right to informational self-determination means all information that characterizes an individual’s personality subjectivity, such as the individual’s body, beliefs, social status, and identity, and enables the individual’s identity to be identified. In addition, acts such as investigation, collection, storage, processing, and use of such personal information all in principle constitute restrictions on the right to informational self-determination (see Constitutional Court 2005. 7. 21. 2003HEONMA282 et al.).\\n\\nDNA identification information is information obtained through DNA analysis for the purpose of personal identification and expressed as combinations of a series of numbers or symbols; it constitutes personal information under Article 2(1) of the Personal Information Protection Act, as information concerning a living individual that cannot identify a specific individual by that information alone but can easily identify the individual when combined with other information. The deletion provision at issue restricts the right to informational self-determination by providing that, unless there is a special reason, DNA identification information, which is personal information, may be recorded and managed in the database until the person’s death. Meanwhile, the right to human dignity, the right to pursue happiness, personality rights, and the freedom and privacy of private life are among the constitutional grounds invoked for the right to informational self-determination, and unless there are special circumstances, a determination as to whether those fundamental rights are infringed is made together by determining whether the right to informational self-determination has been infringed; accordingly, they are not separately addressed.\\n\\n(2) Whether the right to informational self-determination is infringed\\n\\n(a) Depending on the type and nature of personal information, the purpose of collection, the form of use, the method of information processing, and the like, the impact and degree of infringement that the restriction on the right to informational self-determination has on personality rights or freedom of private life will differ. Therefore, in determining whether the restriction on the right to informational self-determination is justified, such factors and the importance of the public interest pursued must be considered.\\n\\nGenerally speaking, with respect to sensitive personal information approaching human dignity, the inner core of personality, or the intimate private sphere, such as religious beliefs, physical or mental disabilities, and sexual life, the permissibility of restriction should be strictly examined. By contrast, basic information such as names and job titles, which, so long as a person lives in community with others, must be identified and communicated among others, is information naturally exposed in the sphere of social life and information that the State cannot avoid accumulating and using to a certain extent in order to properly perform its functions. Unless such information serves as an identifier for access to other dangerous information or is used in combination with other personal information to extract a person’s overall or partial personality image, it is difficult to say that such information is always subject, by its very nature, to strict protection.\\n\\nOn the other hand, when information is held and managed in an automated computer system, there is a high risk that unauthorized access to information, combination of information, transmission of information, and information sharing through collaboration can occur very easily without temporal or spatial limitation. If exposed to such risks, even the justification for holding the information itself may become fragile. Therefore, the scope of information processed in this manner should be reduced as much as possible, and the holding institution has the duty to take certain measures to protect personal information from such risks (Constitutional Court 2005. 7. 21. 2003HEONMA282 et al.).\\n\\n(b) Legitimacy of purpose and appropriateness of means\\n\\nSince convicted prisoners, etc. who committed crimes with a relatively high risk of recidivism compared to other crimes cannot know when they may again commit the same kind of crime, they may be said to have a risk of recidivism while they are alive. Accordingly, the deletion provision at issue, which aims to contribute to criminal investigations and crime prevention by managing the DNA identification information recorded in the database until the death of convicted prisoners, etc., has a legitimate legislative purpose and an appropriate means.\\n\\n(c) Minimal impairment\\n\\nArticle 3(2) of the Act in this case provides that the DNA identification information to be recorded in the database shall not include information or personal details other than those necessary for personal identification, thereby limiting recording to the minimum necessary information. In fact, the method of analyzing DNA identification information uses the technique of analyzing STRs; the STR analysis technique identifies whether individuals match by finding whether the number of repeated fragments composed of DNA base sequences in the intron region, which does not contain genetic information in DNA (so-called junk DNA), is the same, and DNA identification information is merely a series of numbers, from which genetic information about any individual’s genetic characteristics cannot be confirmed and which serves only to confirm whether the person is the same individual. Therefore, the DNA identification information recorded in the database is less likely to leak personal information and cannot be seen as sensitive information that, in itself, may have a serious impact on personal dignity and personality rights; it can be said to be minimum information containing only what is necessary for personal identification.\\n\\nThe Act in this case provides that when a DNA identification information officer records DNA identification information in the database, the collected DNA sample and the DNA extracted therefrom shall be discarded without delay (Article 12(1)), and that where a convicted prisoner, etc. is acquitted in a retrial, or a judgment or decision of dismissal of prosecution becomes final, the DNA identification information recorded in the database shall be deleted (Article 13(1)).\\n\\nUnder Articles 3 and 4 of the Enforcement Decree of the Act in this case, a DNA personal-information manager who manages personal details and identification codes of individuals is designated separately from the DNA identification information officer who manages DNA identification information, thereby establishing an institutional mechanism that makes identification impossible with DNA identification information alone. Moreover, for the management and operation of the database, a DNA Identification Information Database Management Committee is established to deliberate matters concerning the collection, transport, storage, and disposal of DNA samples, matters concerning the methods of DNA analysis, procedures, and standardization of analysis technology, and matters concerning the notation of DNA identification information, recording in the database, and deletion (Article 14 of the Act in this case); and the DNA identification information officer is prohibited from using DNA samples or DNA identification information obtained in the course of duties for purposes other than the duty, or from providing or divulging them to others, and criminal punishment is imposed for violations (Articles 15 and 17(3) of the same Act). In addition, criminal punishment is imposed where DNA identification information is unlawfully accessed or received, or where reported DNA identification information is used for purposes other than the duty or provided or divulged to others (Article 17(4) of the same Act), and the DNA identification information officer is required to take necessary measures, such as security devices, in the database to prevent recorded information from being leaked or arbitrarily altered, deleted, or lost (Article 14(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act), thereby providing provisions concerning personal information protection to prevent misuse or abuse of DNA identification information.\\n\\nGiven the foregoing minimality of DNA identification information, and the fact that the Act contains provisions on personal information protection in relation to deletion of DNA-related materials and information and the operation of the database, even if the deletion provision at issue provides that DNA identification information shall be recorded in the database until the death of convicted prisoners, etc., it is difficult to say that it violates the principle of minimal impairment.\\n\\n(d) Balance of interests\\n\\nAs noted above, considering that DNA identification information has characteristics such as neutrality and restriction of user subject, even if the Petitioner’s DNA identification information is recorded in the database throughout his life pursuant to the deletion provision at issue, the disadvantage actually suffered by the Petitioner cannot be said to be substantial. On the other hand, the public interest that the Prosecutor General and the Commissioner of the National Police Agency can achieve by using the DNA identification information they store and computerized, as noted above, for identification in future criminal investigations, etc., is important and must be considered greater than the disadvantage suffered by the Petitioner. Therefore, the principle of balance of interests is not violated.\\n\\n(e) Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the deletion provision at issue cannot be deemed to infringe the right to informational self-determination of persons subject to DNA identification information recording in violation of the principle of proportionality.\\n\\ne. Determination concerning the search-and-report provision at issue\\n\\n(1) Fundamental rights restricted\\n\\nThe DNA identification information officer may search DNA identification information or report the results thereof, under the search-and-report provision at issue, when new DNA identification information is being recorded in the database (item 1), when it is for a criminal investigation or identification of a deceased person (item 2), when a court makes an inquiry of facts in a criminal trial (item 3), or when comparison among databases is necessary (item 4); because this constitutes use of personal information, the search-and-report provision at issue also restricts the right to informational self-determination.\\n\\n(2) Whether the right to informational self-determination is infringed\\n\\nWhen new DNA identification information is recorded in the database, it is necessary to verify whether there are additional offenses; searching for criminal investigations is itself the legislative purpose of the Act in this case; there are cases where a search is needed for comparison with the DNA identification information of identified persons for the identification of deceased persons; there are cases where, in conducting a criminal trial, a court needs to search DNA identification information for reasons such as identification; and because the Prosecutor General and the Commissioner of the National Police Agency each manage databases, there are cases where searches are needed for comparison between the two databases for criminal investigations, etc. Accordingly, the legislative purpose of the search-and-report provision at issue, which enables search and reporting of DNA identification information in such cases, is legitimate, and searching and reporting DNA identification information in such cases is an appropriate means.\\n\\nThe search-and-report provision at issue limits the grounds on which DNA identification information may be searched and reported; when the results of a search are reported, it requires that the purpose, author, name of the inquirer, and date and time of preparation be specified (Article 11(2) of the Act in this case); and it imposes criminal punishment where DNA identification information is used for purposes other than the duty or provided or divulged to others (Articles 17(3) and (4) of the same Act), thereby minimizing possible damage arising from the use of personal information and not violating the principle of minimal impairment. Also, like the deletion provision at issue, the public interest in criminal investigations and the like is greater than the Petitioners’ actual disadvantages, and therefore the balance of interests is also satisfied.\\n\\nAccordingly, the search-and-report provision at issue cannot be deemed to infringe the right to informational self-determination of persons subject to DNA identification information recording in violation of the principle of proportionality.\\n\\nf. Determination concerning the Addenda provision at issue\\n\\n(1) Issue\\n\\nThe Addenda provision at issue provides that, as to persons who, as of the effective date of the Act in this case, are already confined after having been sentenced to an actual term of imprisonment or confinement or more for offenses subject to DNA sample collection, DNA samples may also be collected and DNA identification information may be recorded and managed in the database.\\n\\nThe collection of DNA samples and the collection and use of DNA identification information, including collection, recording, search, and reporting of DNA identification information, may be regarded as criminal dispositions whose purpose is criminal investigation and crime prevention. The first sentence of Article 13(1) of the Constitution strictly prohibits the enactment of retroactive criminal elements and the retroactive aggravation of punishment. Therefore, it is first necessary to examine what the legal nature of the collection and use of DNA identification information is, and depending on that legal nature, whether the prohibition on retroactive legislation applies becomes an issue; it also becomes an issue whether the Addenda provision at issue, by excessively enlarging the scope of application retroactively and thereby applying the Act in this case, infringes the Petitioners’ freedom of the body and right to informational self-determination in violation of the principle of proportionality by infringing the trust of persons whose sentences have already become final.\\n\\n(2) Legal nature of the collection and use of DNA identification information\\n\\nAccording to the traditional general theory concerning criminal sanctions, punishment means sanctions imposed essentially on the premise of responsibility for the actor’s past illegality, whereas security measures refer to dispositions such as deprivation and restriction of liberty imposed in place of or in addition to punishment in order to prevent crime through the rehabilitation of offenders and prevent future danger based on the actor’s future dangerousness, thereby protecting society. Thus, punishment is a sanction whose main purpose is retribution for past illegality within the limits of responsibility, while security measures are sanctions intended to prevent crime on the premise of future risk of recidivism. Meanwhile, today the forms of punishment and security measures have diversified, and the boundary between punishment and security measures has become blurred with the emergence of new criminal sanctioning tools, so there is also an aspect in which it is not proper simply to apply the dichotomous logic of “retribution for past acts - social prevention according to risk of recidivism” as in the past (Constitutional Court 2012. 12. 27. 2010HEONGA82 et al.).\\n\\nThe collection and use of DNA identification information is intended to secure and manage in advance the DNA identification information of persons who committed crimes with a high risk of recidivism, promptly apprehend offenders, prevent additional harm, early exclude innocent suspects from the investigative line, and further enhance crime-prevention effects; its main purposes are criminal investigation and crime prevention. The act of collecting a DNA sample from a person subject to collection in order to obtain DNA identification information is carried out by the consent of the person concerned or by warrant and restricts the freedom of the body of the person concerned, but, as seen above, the degree of restriction is slight, temporary, and one-time only. The series of acts necessarily following the collection act—analysis of the collected sample and collection, recording, search, and reporting of DNA identification information—are imposed in addition to the sentence and have a crime-prevention effect through the deterrent effect arising from psychological pressure on convicted prisoners, etc., but they do not directly further restrict the freedom of the body of the person concerned.\\n\\nIf so, the act of collecting DNA samples and the series of acts involving collection, recording, search, and reporting of DNA identification information can be viewed as having the character of security measures imposed in order to prevent crime and protect society by rehabilitating offenders and preventing future danger based on the actor’s future dangerousness, in that they have a crime-prevention effect through deterrence arising from psychological pressure on convicted prisoners, etc.\\n\\n(3) Whether the prohibition on retroactive legislation is violated\\n\\nUnlike punishment, security measures are based on the actor’s future risk of recidivism, and because the imposition of security measures is determined according to the assessment of the risk of recidivism at the time of trial rather than at the time of the act, it is proper and reasonable in principle to view retroactive application of the law in force at the time of trial as permissible. However, given that the category of security measures is broad and their forms are diverse, it should not be uniformly concluded, merely because they fall within security measures, that the principle against retroactive legislation applies or does not apply, and it must not be permitted to render the principle of non-retroactivity of punishment a dead letter through the indirect method of security measures. Therefore, even for security measures, where they have a strong punitive character and deprive freedom of the body or restrict freedom of the body to an extent equivalent to deprivation, the application of the prohibition on retroactive legislation accords with the rule of law and the principle of nulla poena sine lege (Constitutional Court 2012. 12. 27. 2010HEONGA82 et al.).\\n\\nAs noted above, the legislative purpose of the Act in this case is criminal investigation and crime prevention, and the collection and use of DNA identification information may restrict the right to informational self-determination but does not deprive or directly restrict freedom of the body as imprisonment does, nor does it impose restrictions on freedom equivalent to or in place of punishment, nor impose any restriction on the general conduct of the person subject to collection. In addition, to minimize restrictions on fundamental rights of the person subject to collection, the Act in this case provides that DNA identification information shall contain only the minimum necessary information, and for the protection of personal information it provides various rules such as separation of the DNA personal-information manager and the DNA identification information officer, establishment of the DNA Identification Information Database Management Committee, prohibition on use, provision, or divulgence of DNA identification information outside the purpose of duty and punishment for violations, and database security devices.\\n\\nIf so, the collection and use of DNA identification information, including the collection of DNA samples and the collection, recording, search, and reporting of DNA identification information, is not traditional punishment, but rather aims at a public interest in protecting the people by contributing to criminal investigation and crime prevention, and does not control the actual conduct of the person concerned through DNA identification information. Therefore, the Addenda provision at issue does not have punitive effect. Accordingly, even if the collection and use of DNA identification information partially possesses the character of a security measure with crime-prevention effects, it is a non-punitive security measure distinct from punishment and is not subject to the principle against retroactive legislation; and because the public-interest purpose arising from retroactive application is greater than the loss suffered by the person concerned through retroactive application, it is not contrary to the principle against retroactive legislation to apply the Act in this case even to persons who, at the time the Act in this case came into force, had already received and had finalized an actual sentence of imprisonment or confinement for offenses subject to DNA sample collection and are confined.\\n\\nTherefore, the Addenda provision at issue cannot be said to violate the principle against retroactive legislation.\\n\\n(4) Whether the principle of proportionality is violated\\n\\nIn order to effectively deal with the risk of recidivism of criminals, even in the case of persons who, before the enforcement of the Act in this case, had already received and had finalized an actual sentence and are confined, the need to secure their DNA identification information in advance is recognized; and in terms of increasing the efficiency and utility of the DNA identification information database, the Addenda provision at issue, which applies the provisions of the Act in this case to persons who, before the enforcement of the Act in this case, had already received and had finalized an actual sentence and are confined, has a legitimate purpose and the means are also appropriate.\\n\\nApplying the Addenda provision at issue not to all persons with prior convictions but only to persons who, having received and had finalized an actual sentence of imprisonment or confinement or more, are confined, retroactively applying the provisions of the Act in this case only to them, can be said to fall within the scope of legislative discretion because it is a factor that can be rationally taken into account in exercising legislative discretion, such as the seriousness of the crime and the status of completion of sentence, and therefore does not violate the principle of minimal impairment.\\n\\nBecause the collection and use of DNA identification information has the character of a security measure aimed not only at criminal investigation but also at future crime prevention, whether a person is subject to DNA identification information collection is determined based on the point in time at which the DNA identification information is collected. In addition, as examined above, considering that DNA identification information has characteristics such as neutrality, minimality, and restriction of user subject, even if a person who had already had his sentence finalized and was confined before the enforcement of the Act in this case had an expectation that he would not be subject to it, the value of protecting that trust cannot be said to be large. On the other hand, it cannot be said that the possibility of recidivism of the subject crime differs depending on whether the Act in this case was enforced before or after, and the public interest in more effectively achieving the purpose of the DNA identification information database system by applying the Act in this case also to existing convicted prisoners, etc. who committed subject crimes with a high risk of recidivism for the purpose of criminal investigation and crime prevention must be considered relatively greater. Therefore, the balance of interests is also satisfied.\\n\\nIf so, the Addenda provision at issue cannot be deemed to infringe, in violation of the principle of proportionality, the freedom of the body and the right to informational self-determination of persons who, before the enforcement of the Act in this case, had their sentences finalized and are confined.\\n\\n(5) Whether the right to equality is infringed\\n\\nThe Addenda provision at issue applies the collection provisions, etc. only to persons among prior offenders who have been sentenced to an actual sentence of imprisonment or confinement or more and whose sentence has become final and who were confined at the time the Act in this case came into force, while excluding from the subject persons whose execution of sentence has already ended and who have been released from detention, thereby discriminating between persons serving sentence and persons whose sentence has ended. However, persons who had already been released at the time the Act in this case came into force can be said to have a lower risk of recidivism than persons currently confined, since a considerable period of time has elapsed since the offense; and retroactively collecting DNA samples and recording DNA identification information even from persons who have peacefully carried on social life after release appears excessive. Therefore, unlike persons whose execution of sentence has already ended and who have been released from detention, the Addenda provision at issue, which allows application of the collection provisions, etc. only to persons who are confined, has a rational basis for the discrimination and cannot be said to infringe the right to equality.\\n\\ng. Determination concerning the Petitioners’ other arguments\\n\\n(1) Whether the principle prohibiting double punishment is violated\\n\\nThe “punishment” referred to in Article 13(1) of the Constitution means, in principle, punishment as the State’s execution of its penal power against a crime, and not every sanction or disadvantageous disposition taken by the State can be included in “punishment” (Constitutional Court 2003. 7. 24. 2001HEONGA25; Constitutional Court 2012. 12. 27. 2011HEONBA89).\\n\\nThe collection of DNA samples and the collection, recording, search, and reporting of DNA identification information are intended to protect society by preventing future danger and therefore have a purpose and function different from punishment; accordingly, they cannot be said to constitute corporal punishment or reputational punishment as another punishment in addition to punishment, and cannot be regarded as “punishment” within the meaning of Article 13(1) of the Constitution.\\n\\nTherefore, the provisions of the Act at issue cannot be said to violate the principle prohibiting double punishment.\\n\\n(2) Whether the principle of presumption of innocence is violated\\n\\nThe Petitioners are persons who already have final judgments of conviction; therefore, the principle of presumption of innocence no longer applies to them, and because DNA samples are collected and the results are stored and managed in the database on the basis of the fact of guilt, the provisions of the Act at issue do not run counter to the principle of presumption of innocence. Therefore, the provisions of the Act at issue cannot be said to violate the principle of presumption of innocence.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, among the petitions filed by Petitioners Kim ○ Ho, No ○ Min, Kim ○ Su, Cheon ○ Seok, Kim ○ Ho, Kim ○ Hwan, and Kim ○ Young, the petitions regarding the collection-warrant provision at issue and Petitioner Kim ○ Ho’s petition regarding the DNA analysis, recording, and management provision at issue are all dismissed as inadmissible; and the remaining petitions of the above Petitioners and the petitions of Petitioners Seo ○ Hun, Ahn ○ Wook, Seo ○ Mun, and Kim ○ Gyu are all dismissed as without merit, and the decision is made as stated in the operative part. The opinions of the remaining participating Justices are unanimous, except for the dissenting opinion of Justices Kim I-su, Lee Jin-seong, Kang Il-won, and Seo Gi-seok on the collection provisions at issue as in 7 below; the dissenting opinion of Justice Kim I-su on the deletion provision at issue and the Addenda provision at issue as in 8 below; the dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Chang-jong and Jo Yong-ho on the collection-by-consent provision at issue as in 9 below; and the supplementary opinion to the opinion of the Court by Justices Lee Jeong-mi, Lee Jin-seong, Kim Chang-jong, and Seo Gi-seok on the deletion provision at issue as in 10 below.\\n\\n7. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim I-su, Lee Jin-seong, Kang Il-won, and Seo Gi-seok on the Collection Provisions at Issue\\n\\nWe conclude that the collection provisions at issue infringe the Petitioners’ freedom of the body and are unconstitutional; we state our view as follows.\\n\\nBecause the collection provisions at issue concern convicted prisoners, etc. whose sentences have been imposed and finalized, the main purpose of the Act in this case related to the collection provisions at issue is to use them in future criminal investigations, and there must exist individual grounds showing a high likelihood that the person subject to collection will commit crimes again in the future. This is because collecting DNA samples from persons with no risk of recidivism does not accord with such legislative purpose.\\n\\nHowever, the collection provisions at issue do not prescribe any risk of recidivism as a requirement for collecting DNA samples, and allow collection of DNA samples solely because a person committed a particular crime. Although the recidivism rates of offenders who committed bodily injury while carrying a deadly weapon, rape, etc. causing injury, and rape causing injury among the crimes subject to the collection provisions at issue are higher than those of ordinary crimes, the difference cannot be said to be large; and in the case of violations of the Punishment of Violences, etc. Act due to trespass into a residence, damage to property, etc., the nature of the offense is relatively minor and the risk of recidivism cannot be said to be high. The risk of recidivism is not a matter that can be schematically generalized based merely on a particular criminal record; it is a matter that must be determined for each offender by comprehensively evaluating various circumstances such as the offender’s occupation and environment, his or her conduct before the offense in question, the motive and means of the offense, the circumstances after the offense, and signs of remorse.\\n\\nUltimately, because the collection provisions at issue do not prescribe at all the requirement of the actor’s risk of recidivism and uniformly allow DNA samples to be collected from convicted prisoners, etc. who committed particular crimes, they violate the principle of minimal impairment; and because the disadvantage suffered by convicted prisoners, etc. from the collection provisions at issue, which lack a provision concerning the risk-of-recidivism requirement, is by no means small compared with the public interest sought through those provisions, they also violate the principle of balance of interests.\\n\\nTherefore, the collection provisions at issue violate the principle of proportionality and infringe the Petitioners’ freedom of the body.\\n\\n8. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Kim I-su on the Deletion Provision at Issue and the Addenda Provision at Issue\\n\\nI conclude that the deletion provision at issue and the Addenda provision at issue infringe the right to informational self-determination and are unconstitutional; I state my view as follows.\\n\\na. Deletion provision at issue\\n\\nThe deletion provision at issue, with respect to DNA identification information once recorded in the database, provides that it shall be deleted only when convicted prisoners, etc. die, unless there is a special reason such as a court’s judgment of acquittal, thereby in effect allowing retention of DNA identification information without limitation of time. This, as seen below, violates the principle of proportionality and infringes the Petitioners’ right to informational self-determination.\\n\\n(1) Legitimacy of purpose and appropriateness of means\\n\\nIt can be accepted that the deletion provision at issue, by recording and managing the DNA identification information of convicted prisoners, etc. with a risk of recidivism in the database during their lifetime, is an appropriate means to achieve the legitimate legislative purpose of future criminal investigation and crime prevention.\\n\\n(2) Minimal impairment\\n\\nThe deletion provision at issue presupposes that convicted prisoners, etc. who committed the subject crimes continue to have a risk of recidivism while they are alive. However, as shown by foreign research results indicating that in fact 52% of criminals reoffend within 6 years and that after 15 years the risk of recidivism becomes the same as for persons without a criminal record, if a person subject to the measure does not reoffend and a considerable period has elapsed, the risk of recidivism will have decreased accordingly. Nevertheless, the deletion provision at issue does not devise a proper time limitation by, for example, setting a fixed period and reviewing whether the recorded DNA identification information should be deleted, or by deleting it uniformly after a certain period has elapsed; instead, it uniformly provides that DNA identification information shall be recorded and managed until the death of the person subject to the measure, which imposes an excessively excessive restriction for achieving the legislative purpose and thus violates the principle of minimal impairment. In particular, in the case of juvenile offenders, it is excessively harsh to have their DNA identification information stored in the database and searchable for their entire lives because of offenses committed while their ability to discern right from wrong was still immature, and thereby to brand them socially as prior offenders of the subject crime, thereby hindering their sound reintegration into society and reformation.\\n\\nMoreover, among the subject crimes, some offenses such as violations of the Punishment of Violences, etc. Act due to trespass into a residence or damage to property are relatively minor in nature, and accordingly the risk of recidivism cannot be said to be high. Nevertheless, the deletion provision at issue applies uniformly once a conviction for the subject crimes becomes final, without any consideration of the seriousness of the crime and the consequent risk of recidivism, so that, for example, even in the case of a person sentenced to a suspended sentence for a subject crime whose nature is relatively minor and whose risk of recidivism is not large, the harsh result arises that DNA identification information is retained until that person’s death merely because he or she committed the subject crime. Moreover, compared with the registration of personal information for sexual violence offenders such as rape offenders, for whom the Special Act on the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Violence Crimes limits the registration period to 20 years even though the nature of the offense is more serious than some of the above-mentioned offenses and the risk of recidivism is not significantly different, this is markedly unbalanced.\\n\\nIn addition, although DNA identification information has characteristics such as neutrality, minimality, and restriction of user subject, as stated in the majority opinion, the possibility that the information content may still be distorted cannot be ruled out; even if DNA analysis targets only the intron region of DNA (junk DNA), it may be used to determine race, sex, or family relationships; and with future advances in science and technology, the possibility of obtaining new information from the above intron region or DNA identification information alone that cannot be foreseen at the current level of science and technology cannot be completely excluded. In such a situation, if DNA identification information is retained in the form of a computer file for an indefinite long period until the person subject to the measure dies, problems such as leakage, misuse, and contamination of information are all the more likely to arise.\\n\\nTherefore, the deletion provision at issue also violates the principle of minimal impairment in that it did not adopt a sufficiently possible and less intrusive means, such as differentiating the management period according to the seriousness of the subject crime and the consequent risk of recidivism.\\n\\n(3) Balance of interests\\n\\nIt is clear that the public interest pursued by the deletion provision at issue—crime prevention and criminal investigation—is important. Also, in general, it cannot be said that persons subject to registration suffer a serious disadvantage merely because DNA identification information is retained for a long period.\\n\\nHowever, because the deletion provision at issue uniformly requires DNA identification information to be retained until the death of the person subject to the measure, without considering the type of offense or the subject person’s risk of recidivism, an imbalance may arise between the public interest exceptionally achieved in the case of a subject who does not reoffend for a long period and the private interest infringed; and if risks such as leakage and misuse of information become actualized during the long-term retention process, the actual disadvantage suffered by the subject, such as being branded a prior offender of the subject crime, is by no means small. In light of these circumstances, it is difficult to say that the balance of interests is satisfied.\\n\\nb. Addenda provision at issue\\n\\n(1) Whether the principle against retroactive legislation is violated\\n\\nThe Addenda provision at issue provides that the Act in this case is to be applied retroactively even to persons who, as of the effective date of the Act in this case, already had their sentences finalized and were confined. The collection and use of DNA identification information, including the collection of DNA samples from prisoners whose sentences have already been imposed, is a kind of security measure imposed in addition to punishment based on the actor’s future risk of recidivism, for the purposes of criminal investigation and crime prevention, and it is clear that this restricts the person’s freedom of the body and right to informational self-determination.\\n\\nThe precedents of our Constitutional Court interpret the latter sentence of Article 12(1) and the first sentence of Article 13(1) of the Constitution as being limited to prescribing the principle of nulla poena sine lege and the principle against retroactive punishment (the principle against retroactive legislation), and in particular Article 13(1), first sentence, is construed as strictly prohibiting the enactment of retroactive criminal elements and the retroactive aggravation of punishment (see Constitutional Court 1996. 2. 16. 96HEONGA2 et al.). From this perspective, punishment is a sanction whose main purpose is retribution for past illegality within the limits of responsibility, whereas security measures are sanctions intended to prevent crime on the premise of future risk of recidivism; although the boundary between the two is becoming blurred today, they have essentially different legal characters. Accordingly, the principle against retroactive legislation applies to punishment or punitive security measures that, because they are strongly punitive in character, deprive freedom of the body or restrict freedom of the body to an extent equivalent to deprivation, whereas it does not apply to non-punitive security measures distinct from punishment (see Constitutional Court 2012. 12. 27. 2010HEONGA82 et al.), and the majority opinion adopts the same position.\\n\\nThe above view is based on a dichotomous logic that punishment and security measures are distinct because they differ in essence and purpose, and thus holds that the principle against retroactive legislation applies only to punishment or punitive security measures. However, recently, with the emergence of new forms of security measures such as the DNA identification information database system at issue, personal-publication systems, and location-tracking electronic device attachment systems, not only has it become difficult to distinguish between punishment and security measures, but in modern times punishment itself no longer pursues only retribution for past illegality and also pursues the purposes of general prevention and special prevention through the offender’s resocialization; and considering that the above new types of security measures also undeniably have the aspect of harmful or oppressive criminal sanctions by the State, the distinction between the two has become considerably relativized rather than absolute.\\n\\nFor this reason, the principle of nulla poena sine lege today should be viewed not merely as a principle required only for “punishment,” but as a principle equally required for all coercive State interventions into or dispositions concerning the individual’s sphere of liberty in a broad sense. The fundamental purpose of the principle against retroactive legislation derived from the principle of nulla poena sine lege is not merely to protect citizens from unjust infringement through formal punishment, but to protect them from all forms of infringement by State public power that intrudes upon citizens’ freedom and legal life in an unpredictable manner. If so viewed, security measures, whether punitive or non-punitive, are no different from punishment in that they are criminal sanctions by the State for crime; therefore, they can never be exempt from the scope of application of the principle against retroactive legislation.\\n\\nAccordingly, if the new Act is applied, pursuant to the Addenda provision at issue, to secure DNA identification information even from persons who had already committed subject crimes before the enforcement of the Act in this case and are confined under a final judgment, this is contrary to the principle against retroactive legislation because a criminal sanction not in existence at the time of the act is retroactively imposed by after-the-fact legislation.\\n\\n(2) Whether the principle of proportionality is violated\\n\\nFurthermore, even if, as the majority opinion states, the principle against retroactive legislation does not apply to non-punitive security measures, the Addenda provision at issue, when comprehensively considering the fundamental purport of the constitutional provisions strictly prohibiting the enactment of retroactive criminal elements and the retroactive aggravation of punishment (Article 12(1), Article 13(1)), the basis for defining the retroactive effect’s scope of application in the Addenda provision at issue, and the unconstitutionality of the provisions relating to the collection and use of DNA identification information, cannot but be seen as excessive in that it allows the Act in this case to be applied retroactively even to persons who, as of the effective date of the Act in this case, already had their sentences finalized and were confined.\\n\\nFirst, the fact that the Addenda provision at issue contemplates retroactive application even to persons whose sentences have already become final and who are confined appears to have taken into account the convenience of execution, namely, that it is easier to collect DNA samples from such persons, rather than any special criminal-policy basis or necessity to apply the law retroactively only to them. However, these persons are serving their sentences while relying on the expectation that the criminal sanctions for the crimes they committed have already been finalized through the final judgment, and the Addenda provision at issue, by leaning toward execution convenience and accordingly providing for retroactive application of the Act in this case even to them, harms their trust and legal stability. This is difficult to justify even considering that the degree of infringement of fundamental rights by the collection and use of DNA identification information is relatively light and considering the legislative purpose of criminal investigation and crime prevention.\\n\\nIn particular, persons who have been confined for a long period after a final judgment for a subject crime can be said to have such trust even more strongly; yet the Addenda provision at issue did not devise a more less intrusive means, such as limiting the persons subject to retroactive application to those who had been confined after a final judgment for a subject crime within a certain period before the enforcement of the Act in this case, for example within 3 or 5 years, but instead uniformly expanded the subject to all confined persons with final judgments for the subject crime, thereby also violating the principle of minimal impairment.\\n\\nMoreover, even if one accepts, as the majority opinion does, that, due to the nature of security measures aimed at future crime prevention, the persons subject to collection of DNA identification information are to be determined by reference to the time of collection, the Addenda provision at issue uniformly provides for retroactive application to all confined persons who committed the subject crimes without any measure or procedure at the time of collection for determining whether there is a risk of recidivism for the individual subject, which is the core requirement for imposing security measures. This is inconsistent with the nature of security measures and is improper.\\n\\nFurthermore, considering that the collection provisions at issue and the deletion provision at issue are unconstitutional for violating the principle of proportionality, it must also be deemed impermissible to retroactively expand the scope of collection of DNA samples and retention of DNA identification information under those provisions.\\n\\nNo matter how important the public interest in criminal investigation and crime prevention, which is the legislative purpose of the Act in this case, may be, the Addenda provision at issue, by permitting the collection of DNA samples and the retention of DNA identification information even with respect to persons who had already committed crimes before the DNA identification information database system under the Act in this case came into existence and whose sentences had become final and who were confined, cannot be said to satisfy the balance of interests in light of the fact that, although the disadvantage suffered by the person concerned is not large, the degree of infringement of trust in legal stability is by no means light.\\n\\n(3) Conclusion\\n\\nThe Addenda provision at issue not only contravenes the principle against retroactive legislation prescribed by the first sentence of Article 13(1) of the Constitution, but also excessively infringes the trust of persons who, as of the effective date of the Act in this case, already had their sentences finalized and were confined, and thus violates the principle of proportionality and is unconstitutional.\\n\\nThe Addenda provision at issue is in line with the recent trend toward the introduction and expansion of various forms of criminal sanctions being implemented under the banner of strong responses to violent crimes, including sexual violence crimes, for crime prevention and efficient suppression of crime. In our society today, violent crimes rooted in contempt for life and materialism are occurring frequently, and victims and their families suffer pain and wounds that cannot be erased for life; considering the public demand for safety from violent crime, there can be no argument about the need for a thorough response to such violent crimes. However, not only is it highly doubtful whether these measures in fact achieve sufficient crime-prevention and suppression effects as expected, but indiscriminate retroactive application is likely to undermine the fundamental values of respect for human rights and legal stability guaranteed by our Constitution. I therefore must emphasize that I deeply worry about the trend of excessive criminal-justice absolutism, including the frequent retroactive legislation of such criminal sanctions.\\n\\n9. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim Chang-jong and Jo Yong-ho on the Collection-by-Consent Provision at Issue\\n\\nWe believe that Petitioner Seo ○ Mun’s petition concerning the collection-by-consent provision at issue should be dismissed as inadmissible because there is no possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.\\n\\nThe collection-by-consent provision at issue provides that, if the person subject to collection consents, a DNA sample may be collected without a warrant, while also providing that the person subject to collection must be informed in advance, before the consent to collection is obtained, that he or she may refuse collection, and that written consent must be obtained.\\n\\nThe collection-by-consent provision at issue is merely a provision creating an exception that, in principle, a DNA sample may be collected from the person subject to collection only by warrant, but if the person subject to collection consents in advance, the sample may also be collected without a warrant.\\n\\nEven under the collection-by-consent provision at issue, the person subject to collection does not bear an obligation to necessarily consent to the request for consent to DNA sample collection, and because the person is entirely free not to consent to sample collection, no disadvantage arises immediately merely because he or she did not consent to sample collection. In other words, if the person subject to collection does not consent to collection, sample collection cannot be forcibly carried out against his or her will; only compulsory collection by warrant is possible. Therefore, it is difficult to say that the person subject to collection’s fundamental rights are directly infringed or restricted by the collection-by-consent provision at issue.\\n\\nOf course, if the person subject to collection does not consent to sample collection, the prosecutor may forcibly collect the sample by a warrant obtained by applying to a judge of the district court, but this is merely the legal effect arising from application of the collection-warrant provision at issue and is not a direct infringement of fundamental rights by the collection-by-consent provision at issue.\\n\\nAlthough as a practical matter it may appear that there is a tendency first to confirm with the person subject to collection whether he or she consents to sample collection and then, if consent is given, to collect the sample without a warrant, and if not, to obtain a warrant and collect the sample, according to the collection-warrant provision at issue, the prosecutor is not required, as an indispensable prior procedure for requesting a sample collection warrant, to first confirm with the person subject to collection whether he or she consents to sample collection. Even considering that the prosecutor may immediately apply for a sample collection warrant without first going through the procedure of asking the person subject to collection whether he or she consents to sample collection, it is easily clear that the collection-by-consent provision at issue is not a provision that directly infringes or restricts the person subject to collection’s fundamental rights.\\n\\nUltimately, Petitioner Seo ○ Mun’s petition concerning the collection-by-consent provision at issue should be dismissed as inadmissible because there is no possibility that his fundamental rights are infringed.\\n\\n10. Supplementary Opinion to the Opinion of the Court by Justices Lee Jeong-mi, Lee Jin-seong, Kim Chang-jong, and Seo Gi-seok on the Deletion Provision at Issue\\n\\nAlthough we do not conclude that the deletion provision at issue violates the Constitution, we think that legislation should be improved by limiting the retention period of DNA identification information, and thus state our view as follows.\\n\\nThe deletion provision at issue provides that DNA identification information is deleted only when convicted prisoners, etc. die. However, if a person subject to the measure does not reoffend and a considerable period of time passes, the risk of recidivism is lowered accordingly; and retention-related problems such as leakage and misuse due to long-term storage of information are likely to occur, while a subject who does not reoffend for a long time may be said to suffer relatively greater private disadvantage from the retention of DNA identification information. Therefore, a legitimate question can be raised as to whether it is really necessary to uniformly retain DNA identification information for all convicted prisoners, etc. until death.\\n\\nIn light of the characteristics of DNA identification information, we agree with the majority’s conclusion that the disadvantage actually suffered by the Petitioners is not large and that, considering the public-interest purpose of the DNA identification information database system, it is difficult to say that the deletion provision at issue clearly infringes the Petitioners’ right to informational self-determination to such an extent as to be unconstitutional.\\n\\nHowever, because there remains some doubt as to whether it is necessary to retain DNA identification information uniformly for all convicted prisoners, etc. until death, and because, taking into account the seriousness of the crime, the risk of recidivism, the need for crime prevention, and the balance with the private interest infringed by social stigma, it would be more desirable to legislate so that DNA identification information may be deleted in the case of subjects within an appropriate scope who have not reoffended for a certain period, in order to minimize restrictions on the people’s fundamental rights, we think that legislation should be improved accordingly."}

{"[2013HEONMA517]": "[Appendix] Relevant Provisions\\n\\nGame Industry Promotion Act (enacted by Act No. 7941 on April 28, 2006)  \\nArticle 1 (Purpose) This Act aims to contribute to the development of the national economy and the improvement of the quality of the cultural life of the people by creating the foundation for the game industry and by providing for matters concerning the use of games, thereby promoting the game industry and establishing a sound game culture for the people.\\n\\nArticle 2 (Definitions) The terms used in this Act are defined as follows:  \\n10.
