{"[2016HEONMA1124]": "1. Case Summary\\n\\nThe Petitioner was, on 2015. 11. 26., sentenced by the Seoul Northern District Court to 6 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 2 years, for the crime of violation of the Act on Special Cases concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (indecent conduct in a crowded public place), and the appeal and final appeal therefrom were both dismissed, thereby rendering the above judgment final. By virtue of the finality of the above judgment, the Petitioner became a person subject to registration of personal information under Article 42(1) of the Act on Special Cases concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes.\\n\\nOn 2016. 12. 23., the Petitioner filed the constitutional complaint in this case, alleging that the part of Article 42(1) of the Act on Special Cases concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes, namely, “a person whose conviction for an offense under Article 11 has become final shall become a person subject to registration of personal information,” infringes his fundamental rights.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether the part of Article 42(1) of the former Act on Special Cases concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (wholly amended by Act No. 11556 on 2012. 12. 18., and as in force before amendment by Act No. 14412 on 2016. 12. 20.; hereinafter referred to as the “Sexual Crimes Punishment Act”) stating that “a person whose conviction for an offense under Article 11 has become final shall become a person subject to registration of personal information” infringes the Petitioner’s fundamental rights, and the content of the provision under review (the underlined portion below) and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision Under Review]\\n\\nFormer Act on Special Cases concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes\\n(wholly amended by Act No. 11556 on 2012. 12. 18., and as in force before amendment by Act No. 14412 on 2016. 12. 20.)\\n\\nArticle 42 (Persons Subject to Registration of Personal Information) (1) A person whose conviction has become final for any crime under Article 2(1)3 or 4, Article 2(2) (limited to Article 2(1)3 or 4), Articles 3 through 15, or Article 2(2)2 of the Act on the Protection of Children and Juveniles from Sexual Abuse (hereinafter referred to as “registered sexual crimes”), or a person against whom a public disclosure order has become final pursuant to Article 49(1)4 of the same Act, shall become a person subject to registration of personal information (hereinafter referred to as a “person subject to registration”); provided, however, that this shall not apply to a person who has been sentenced to a fine for a crime under Article 11(5) of the Act on the Protection of Children and Juveniles from Sexual Abuse.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nAct on Special Cases concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes\\n(enacted by Act No. 10258 on 2010. 4. 15.)\\n\\nArticle 11 (Indecent Acts in Crowded Public Places) A person who commits an indecent act against another person on public transportation, at performance or assembly venues, or in any other place where people are densely concentrated shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 1 year or by a fine not exceeding 3 million won.\\n\\nArticle 13 (Obscene Acts Using Communication Media) A person who, for the purpose of arousing or satisfying his or her own or another person’s sexual desire, causes words, sounds, writings, pictures, images, or objects that arouse sexual humiliation or disgust to reach the other party through telephone, mail, computers, or other communication media shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 2 years or by a fine not exceeding 5 million won.\\n\\nAct on Special Cases concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes\\n(as amended by Act No. 14412 on 2016. 12. 20.)\\n\\nArticle 42 (Persons Subject to Registration of Personal Information) (1) A person whose conviction or summary order has become final for any crime under Article 2(1)3 or 4, Article 2(2) (limited to Article 2(1)3 or 4), Articles 3 through 15, or Article 2(2)2(a) or (d) of the Act on the Protection of Children and Juveniles from Sexual Abuse (hereinafter referred to as “registered sexual crimes”), or a person against whom a public disclosure order has become final pursuant to Article 49(1)4 of the same Act, shall become a person subject to registration of personal information (hereinafter referred to as a “person subject to registration”); provided, however, that this shall not apply to a person who has been sentenced to a fine for crimes under Articles 12 and 13 and crimes under Article 11(3) and (5) of the Act on the Protection of Children and Juveniles from Sexual Abuse.\\n\\n3. Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\nThe provision under review infringes the right to informational self-determination because, even in the case of committing the relatively minor offense of violation of the Act on Special Cases concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (indecent acts in crowded public places) (hereinafter referred to as the “offense of indecent acts in crowded public places”), it designates all such offenders without exception as persons subject to registration of personal information, without reflecting differences in unlawfulness and the possibility of recidivism.\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court, in its decision of 2016. 3. 31. in 2015HEONMA688, held unconstitutional the part of Article 42(1) of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act stating that “a person whose conviction for an offense under Article 13 has become final shall become a person subject to registration of personal information.” The offense of indecent acts in crowded public places, like the crime of obscene acts using communication media provided in Article 13 of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act, does not fall under a specified violent crime under the Act on the Punishment of Specific Violent Crimes and is a relatively minor sexual offense. Nevertheless, the provision under review treats, without rational reason, a person whose conviction for the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places has become final differently from a person whose conviction for the crime of obscene acts using communication media has become final, by causing the former to become a person subject to registration of personal information, and thus infringes the right to equality.\\n\\n4. Decision\\n\\nA. Fundamental Rights Restricted\\n\\nThe general personality right derived from the first sentence of Article 10 of the Constitution, which provides for human dignity and worth and the right to pursue happiness, and the right to informational self-determination guaranteed by the right to privacy and freedom under Article 17 of the Constitution, are rights by which the data subject may autonomously decide when, to whom, and to what extent information about himself or herself is to be disclosed and used. In other words, it means the right of the data subject to decide autonomously regarding the disclosure and use of personal information. Personal information protected by the right to informational self-determination can be said to be any information that identifies the individuality of a person, such as matters characterizing that person’s personality-subject status, including the person’s body, beliefs, social status, and status, and that enables identification of that person’s identity. Acts of investigation, collection, storage, processing, use, and the like directed at such personal information all, in principle, constitute restrictions on the right to informational self-determination.\\n\\nThe provision under review restricts the right to informational self-determination because it prescribes a person whose conviction for the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places has become final as a person subject to registration of personal information and thereby serves as the basis for the collection, storage, processing, and use of the relevant offender’s personal information.\\n\\nB. Whether the Right to Informational Self-Determination Is Infringed\\n\\n(1) Legitimacy of Purpose and Suitability of Means\\n\\nThe provision under review is intended to deter recidivism of sexual crimes, thereby protecting potential victims and the community from sexual offenders, guaranteeing an individual’s sexual self-determination, and promoting social defense; it is also intended to prevent social confusion through efficient investigations, such as the prompt apprehension of sexual offenders. Therefore, the legitimacy of the legislative purpose is recognized. Requiring a person who has committed a specified sexual offense to submit certain personal information to a state agency, which then preserves and manages it, makes it foreseeable that if the person subject to registration commits a sexual offense again, he or she can be easily apprehended, thereby deterring sexual crimes, and, if recidivism actually occurs, contributes to enhancing the efficiency and promptness of the investigation thereinto. Accordingly, the provision under review constitutes a suitable means for achieving the above legislative purpose.\\n\\n(2) Minimum Restriction\\n\\n(a) The offense of indecent acts in crowded public places is established when a person commits an indecent act against another person on public transportation, at performance or assembly venues, or in any other place where people are densely concentrated, and has steadily increased since its introduction with the enactment of the “Act on the Punishment of Sexual Crimes and the Protection of Victims, etc.” on 1994. 1. 5.\\n\\nAlthough fundamental measures such as continuous dialogue and education for sexual offenders must be steadily sought in order to deter and eradicate sexual crimes, considering on the other hand that fundamental improvement in socio-cultural spheres, such as the lack of specialized personnel and facilities and the correction of distorted sexual awareness, requires much time and effort, systematically managing a certain range of information on a person whose conviction for the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places has become final by designating him or her as a person subject to registration of personal information can be an effective and practical method of preventing recidivism.\\n\\n(b) The Act on the Effacement, etc. of Criminal Records provides for the creation, management, and deletion of criminal records (register of convicted persons, card index of convicted persons, criminal records data) and investigative records data. However, the above records contain only a narrower range of personal information than the provision under review, and because changes in already created information are not immediately reflected, they cannot continuously ensure accuracy. Accordingly, it is difficult to regard ordinary criminal investigation records or criminal records alone as capable of achieving the same effect as the registration provision, which seeks to deter recidivism of sexual crimes and enhance investigative efficiency.\\n\\nIn addition, there are a series of security disposition systems designed to prevent recidivism of sexual crimes, such as the probation system under the Act on Special Cases concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (Article 16), the medical treatment and custody system under the Act on Medical Treatment and Custody, etc. (Article 2(1), etc.), and the so-called electronic anklet system under the Act on Probation and Electronic Monitoring, etc. for Specific Criminal Offenders (Article 5(1), etc.). However, these systems differ from the provision under review in terms of their scope of application or their subjects, and it is also difficult to assert that the fundamental rights-restricting effects of each measure are lighter than the fundamental rights-restricting effects caused by the provision under review; thus, they cannot be recognized as less restrictive means substituting for the personal information registration system.\\n\\n(c) The provision under review does not prescribe that whether to register personal information may be determined differently according to the gravity of the criminal responsibility of each individual actor who committed the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places. In the case of the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places, although in individual cases the manner of the act or the degree of unlawfulness may appear differently, the essence as a sexual crime infringing the victim’s sexual self-determination does not change because it is established when, in a place where the public is densely concentrated and is open to the general public and where access to the victim is easy, one exploits a state in which the victim cannot readily resist or avoid and engages in an act that arouses sexual humiliation or disgust. Therefore, it is difficult to view the legislature’s failure to distinguish the need for deterrence and prevention according to individual cases as imposing unnecessary restrictions for the achievement of the legislative purpose.\\n\\n(d) Ultimately, it is difficult to see that there exists another less restrictive means for the effective achievement of the legislative purpose of the provision under review, and the provision under review is within the scope necessary for achieving the purpose; therefore, the minimum restriction is satisfied.\\n\\n(3) Balance of Legal Interests\\n\\nThe fact that a person becomes a person subject to registration of personal information under the provision under review does not, in itself, hinder the social reintegration of the person subject to registration or brand the person with the social stigma of being a convicted offender. Considering that the registration information may be distributed only to a limited range of persons, such as prosecutors or the heads of police agencies at each level, for the limited purpose of preventing crimes related to registered sexual crimes and conducting investigations (Article 46(1) of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act), and considering that a person engaged in or having been engaged in the registration, preservation, and management of the personal information of a person subject to registration is subject to criminal punishment if he or she divulges registration information learned in the course of duty (Articles 48 and 50(1)1 of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act), the private interest infringed by the provision under review cannot be said to be substantial. On the other hand, it is evident that the public interest in preventing recidivism of sexual offenders and in social defense achieved through the provision under review is of great importance.\\n\\nTherefore, the balance of legal interests is satisfied in that the public interest achieved is greater than the private interest restricted by the provision under review (see Constitutional Court 2014. 7. 24. 2013HEONMA423 et al.).\\n\\n(4) Conclusion\\n\\nThe provision under review does not infringe the Petitioner’s right to informational self-determination in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\nC. Decision on the Petitioner’s Other Arguments\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues, in substance, that the provision under review infringes the right to equality because, although the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places, like the crime of obscene acts using communication media, is a relatively minor sexual offense, the provision under review treats, without rational reason, a person whose conviction for the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places has become final differently from a person whose conviction for the crime of obscene acts using communication media has become final by causing the former to become a person subject to registration of personal information.\\n\\nHowever, under the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act as amended on 2016. 12. 20., “a person sentenced to a fine for the crime of obscene acts using communication media” was excluded from persons subject to registration of personal information (proviso to Article 42(1)). This reflects a comprehensive consideration of various factors, including the manner of commission and the protected legal interest of each offense, the social situation at the time of legislation, the legal sentiment of the general public, and criminal policy aspects for the actual state and prevention of crime, and there is a rational reason for treating the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places differently. Furthermore, even under the amended Sexual Crimes Punishment Act, a person sentenced to imprisonment for the crime of obscene acts using communication media still falls under persons subject to registration of personal information; thus, it is difficult to view there as being any discriminatory treatment between the Petitioner, who was sentenced to imprisonment for the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places, and such a person. Therefore, the provision under review cannot be said to infringe the Petitioner’s right to equality.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, since the petition for adjudication on the provision under review is without merit, it shall be dismissed, and it is so decided as stated in the disposition. In this decision, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous except for the dissenting opinions of Justice Lee Jin-sung and Justice Kim I-soo, as set forth in 6. below.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinions of Justice Lee Jin-sung and Justice Kim I-soo\\n\\nUnlike the majority opinion, we are of the view that the provision under review violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringes the Petitioner’s right to informational self-determination.\\n\\nAlthough the provision under review takes prevention of recidivism by sexual offenders as one of its principal legislative purposes, it does not require “risk of recidivism” at all in selecting persons subject to registration. Statistically, it is difficult to deny that sexual crimes have been on an annual upward trend; however, according to the recent crime analysis statistics of the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office, it cannot be empirically proven that, compared to other crimes, sexual crimes have a markedly higher recidivism rate among offenders with prior convictions for the same kind of offense. Nevertheless, the provision under review, which provides that a person whose conviction for the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places has become final shall naturally become a person subject to registration of personal information, excessively broadens the scope of persons subject to registration and, in that it results in imposing restrictions unnecessary for the achievement of the legislative purpose by causing even those for whom risk of recidivism is not recognized to become persons subject to registration, runs counter to the minimum restriction requirement.\\n\\nIn individual cases, the manner in which the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places is committed may vary, and the responsibility and degree of unlawfulness of the actor who engaged in such conduct may also vary; this should be regarded as one of the important factors in determining the necessity of preventing recidivism by the actor or the necessity of social defense. However, according to the provision under review, once conviction for the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places becomes final, the person is unconditionally subject to registration even in cases where the unlawfulness or responsibility is judged to be relatively slight. Therefore, the provision under review also runs counter to the minimum restriction requirement in that it did not reduce the registered sexual crimes by considering the characteristics of the manner of the act or the degree of unlawfulness.\\n\\nIt is evident that the public interest pursued by the provision under review is important. However, due to the provision under review, with respect to those who committed the offense of indecent acts in crowded public places and for whom no risk of recidivism is recognized, there may arise an imbalance between the public interest exceptionally achieved and the private interest infringed, and thus it is difficult to recognize the balance of legal interests.\\n\\nAccordingly, the provision under review violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringes the Petitioner’s right to informational self-determination (see the dissenting opinion among Constitutional Court 2014. 7. 24. 2013HEONMA423 et al.)."}

{"[2017HEONBA479]": "1. Case Overview\\n\\na. The Petitioner is a person who was sentenced on 2013. 7. 26. to 5 years’ imprisonment and 5 years’ suspension of qualifications for the offense of Violation of the National Security Act (Detection and Collection of State Secrets), etc. (Supreme Court 2013DO2511), and who completed service of the sentence at XX Prison on 2016. 7. 17.\\n\\nb. The Petitioner fell within the category of a person subject to a security surveillance disposition under the Security Surveillance Act, and although under Article 6 of the Security Surveillance Act he had a duty to report, after release, the fact of release and the fact of changes in residence among matters previously reported, he failed to report them without justifiable grounds, and was indicted for the offense of Violation of the Security Surveillance Act.\\n\\nc. During the pendency of the first instance, the Petitioner filed an application for a request for adjudication on the constitutionality of the Security Surveillance Act, Articles 2, 3, 6(1), 6(2), and 27(2), but on 2017. 11. 1. the application was dismissed (Seoul Western District Court 2017CHOGI606), and on the same day he was sentenced to a fine of 1,000,000 won (Seoul Western District Court 2017GODAN1171). Thereafter, on 2017. 11. 30. he filed this constitutional complaint.\\n\\n2. Object of Review\\n\\nThis case concerns the Petitioner’s violation of the duty to report after release and the duty to report changes under Article 6(1) and (2) of the former Security Surveillance Act, so the object of review is limited to the relevant portions thereof. Articles 2 and 3 of the Security Surveillance Act are provisions defining the persons subject to a security surveillance disposition and the offenses to which the Act applies, and since the Petitioner does not separately argue that these are unconstitutional, they are excluded from the object of review.\\n\\nAccordingly, the object of review in this case is whether the following provisions are unconstitutional: the portion concerning the duty to report after release in the main clause of Article 6(1) of the former Security Surveillance Act (wholly amended by Act No. 4132 on 1989. 6. 16. and before amendment by Act No. 16928 on 2020. 2. 4.) (hereinafter, the “Post-Release Reporting Provision”); the portion concerning the main clause of Article 6(1) of the former Security Surveillance Act in Article 27(2) of the Security Surveillance Act (wholly amended by Act No. 4132 on 1989. 6. 16.) (hereinafter, the “Penalty Provision for Violation of the Duty to Report After Release”), together with the Post-Release Reporting Provision, the “Post-Release Reporting Provision and Penalty Provision for Violation”; the main clause of Article 6(2) of the Security Surveillance Act (wholly amended by Act No. 4132 on 1989. 6. 16.) (hereinafter, the “Change-Reporting Provision”); and the portion concerning the main clause of Article 6(2) in Article 27(2) (hereinafter, the “Penalty Provision for Violation of the Duty to Report Changes”), together with the Change-Reporting Provision, the “Change-Reporting Provision and Penalty Provision for Violation,” and whether all of the foregoing provisions, taken together, are in violation of the Constitution (hereinafter, the foregoing provisions collectively, the “Reviewed Provisions”). The Reviewed Provisions and related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Reviewed Provisions]\\n\\nFormer Security Surveillance Act (wholly amended by Act No. 4132 on 1989. 6. 16. and before amendment by Act No. 16928 on 2020. 2. 4.)\\n\\nArticle 6 (Reporting by Persons Subject to a Security Surveillance Disposition) (1) Before release from a prison, juvenile prison, detention house, police lockup, military prison, or guardhouse (hereinafter, “correctional facilities, etc.”), a person subject to a security surveillance disposition shall, pursuant to the Presidential Decree, report the expected place of residence and other matters prescribed by Presidential Decree to the chief of the police station having jurisdiction over the expected place of residence through the head of the correctional facility, etc., and shall, within 7 days after release, report the fact of release to the chief of the police station having jurisdiction over the expected place of residence. (The latter sentence omitted.)\\n\\nSecurity Surveillance Act (wholly amended by Act No. 4132 on 1989. 6. 16.)\\n\\nArticle 6 (Reporting by Persons Subject to a Security Surveillance Disposition) (2) After release from correctional facilities, etc., when there is any change in the matters reported under paragraph (1), the person subject to a security surveillance disposition shall, within 7 days from the date of the change, report the changed matters to the chief of the competent police station. The Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\na. The Change-Reporting Provision imposes on a person subject to a security surveillance disposition who has been released (hereinafter, the “subject”) a duty to report any changes when there is a change in the matters reported pursuant to Article 6(1) of the Security Surveillance Act. However, because it is unclear as to which of the various reporting items under Article 6(1) the duty to report changes is imposed when a change occurs, it violates the principle of clarity. Moreover, as to the item in Article 6(1) of “the expected place of residence and other matters prescribed by Presidential Decree,” what falls within that item cannot be predicted from the wording of the statute alone; this violates the principle against blanket delegation.\\n\\nb. Article 9 of the same Enforcement Decree, which requires that two personal guarantors be secured when making the report of the fact of release under the Post-Release Reporting Provision, imposes an obligation without statutory delegation or beyond the scope of such delegation, and is unconstitutional.\\n\\nc. The Security Surveillance Act originated in the former Public Security Act, which in turn stemmed from the Provisional Probation Act for ideological offenders during the Japanese colonial period, and the present Security Surveillance Act serves the purpose of suppressing and controlling individual freedom of thought. Even if some extent of information collection from the subject is acknowledged as necessary, requiring reports even of matters constituting private life and personal information, such as family and friendship relations, occupation before admission, the financial status of the person and the family, religion, and military service status, which are unrelated to the determination of the risk of recidivism, and selecting criminal punishment rather than administrative sanctions such as fines as a sanction for failure to comply with a reporting duty that is merely an administrative cooperation duty, is excessive regulation contrary to Article 37(2) of the Constitution. Therefore, the Reviewed Provisions violate the petitioner’s privacy and freedom of private life and the right to self-determination over personal information.\\n\\nd. Although the subject and a person who has actually been subjected to a security surveillance disposition are fundamentally different in whether they have been assessed for risk of recidivism, the Reviewed Provisions impose on the subject a reporting duty and penal sanctions in the same manner as on a person who has been subjected to a security surveillance disposition. In addition, while treatment custody, probation, and security surveillance are all security measures aimed at preventing recidivism, security surveillance is the only one that imposes various reporting duties and penal sanctions on a subject who has not yet been assessed for risk of recidivism. Thus, since they treat essentially the same group differently, the Reviewed Provisions also violate the principle of equality.\\n\\ne. In this respect, the Reviewed Provisions also infringe freedom of thought and violate the principle of due process, the principle of proportionality between culpability and punishment, and the substantive principle of legality in criminal punishment.\\n\\n4. Holding\\n\\na. Reporting system for subjects, etc.\\n\\nA subject means a person who has been sentenced to imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment, and whose total sentence term is 3 years or more, for an offense subject to security surveillance under the Criminal Act, the Military Criminal Act, or the National Security Act, such as espionage, insurrection, or crimes benefiting the enemy, and who has served all or part of the sentence (Articles 2 and 3 of the Security Surveillance Act; hereinafter, the Security Surveillance Act and its Enforcement Decree, regardless of legislative history, are each referred to as the “Act” and the “Enforcement Decree”).\\n\\nA subject must report before and after release, and also report any changes after release. First, before release from correctional facilities, etc. where the sentence is being served, the subject must report the expected place of residence and other matters prescribed by Presidential Decree to the chief of the police station having jurisdiction over the expected place of residence through the head of the correctional facility, etc. (Article 6(1) of the Act). Second, after release, the subject must report the fact of release to the chief of the police station having jurisdiction over the expected place of residence within 7 days (Article 6(1) of the Act). Third, when there is any change in the matters reported under the foregoing paragraph (1) after release, the subject must report the changed matters to the chief of the competent police station within 7 days from the date of change (Article 6(2) of the Act).\\n\\nA security surveillance disposition is imposed on a person among the subjects who, for sufficient reasons to recognize that there is a risk of again committing an offense subject to security surveillance, requires observation for the prevention of recidivism (Article 4(1) of the Act). A request for a security surveillance disposition is made by a prosecutor submitting a request for disposition to the Minister of Justice, and the decision on a security surveillance disposition is made by the Minister of Justice through deliberation and resolution by the Security Surveillance Disposition Review Committee established to deliberate and decide matters concerning such disposition (see Articles 7, 8, 12(1), and 14(1) of the Act). The period of a security surveillance disposition is 2 years, and the Minister of Justice may renew the period upon a prosecutor’s request, through the resolution of the Security Surveillance Disposition Review Committee (Article 5 of the Act). Meanwhile, even if the period of a security surveillance disposition is not renewed, a person who has received such disposition is again managed as a subject after the period ends (see Article 11(6) of the Act).\\n\\nA person who has received a security surveillance disposition (hereinafter, the “person under security surveillance”) shall, within 7 days from the date of notice of the decision imposing the security surveillance disposition, report to the chief of the competent police station, through the head of the district police unit or police substation having jurisdiction over the place of residence, the registered domicile, residence, name, date of birth, sex, resident registration number, family and cohabitants’ circumstances and friendship relations, occupation, monthly income, financial status of the person and the family, religion and affiliated organizations, the police station that received the report by the subject, and the date of report, etc. (Article 18(1) of the Act). If there is any change in such reported matters, the changed matters shall likewise be reported within 7 days through the same method (Article 18(3) of the same Article). In addition, the person under security surveillance is subject to various reporting duties, such as reporting, through the head of the district police unit or police substation in the same manner, to the chief of the competent police station by the end of each month that is every third month counted from the month in which notice of the decision imposing the security surveillance disposition was received, on the main activities during the preceding 3 months, the personal information of other subjects communicated or meeting with him or her, and the date, place, and content thereof (Article 18(2) of the same Article), and criminal punishment follows for violation thereof (Article 27(2) of the Act).\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Minister of Justice may issue a decision not to impose a security surveillance disposition (hereinafter, the “exemption decision”) if the subject satisfies certain requirements, such as having established compliance with the law and having a fixed residence and occupation (Article 11(1) of the Act). A person who has received such exemption decision is relieved from the duties of a subject or a person under security surveillance under the Act from that time forward (Article 11(6) of the same Article).\\n\\nb. Organization of the issues\\n\\n(1) The Reviewed Provisions impose a reporting duty regarding information concerning the private sphere of the subject, such as the fact of release and changes in expected place of residence, and provide for criminal punishment in case of nonperformance, thereby restricting the subject’s freedom and privacy of private life. Since the personal information collected in this manner is communicated to the chief of the competent police station by the head of the correctional facility, etc., or used in the future when a request for and decision on a security surveillance disposition are made, the right to self-determination over personal information is also restricted. Because there are differences in content between the Post-Release Reporting Provision and Penalty Provision for Violation, and the Change-Reporting Provision and Penalty Provision for Violation, we examine in order whether the above provisions violate the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n(2) Unlike treatment custody and probation, the Reviewed Provisions also impose a reporting duty on subjects who have not yet been subjected to a security surveillance disposition, and provide that violation thereof will be subject to criminal sanctions identical to those imposed on persons under security surveillance. Accordingly, we also examine whether the Reviewed Provisions, by imposing a reporting duty on the subject and punishing violation with criminal sanctions, treat the same as different or different as the same, in comparison with persons under security surveillance under the Security Surveillance Act and treatment custody/probation, thereby violating the principle of equality.\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, with respect to the Change-Reporting Provision, we first examine whether the provision of Article 6(1) that merely defines the subject’s reporting items as “the expected place of residence and other matters prescribed by Presidential Decree” delegates to the Presidential Decree without setting specific standards in the Act, thereby violating the principle against blanket delegation, in the part concerning the Change-Reporting Provision. The Petitioner also argues that the Change-Reporting Provision requires the subject, when there is a change in the reporting items under paragraph (1) after release from correctional facilities, etc., to report the changed matters, but that Article 6(1) imposes on the subject the duty to report, before release, matters such as the expected place of residence; after release, the fact of release; and, where the Minister of Justice has provided a place of residence, that place of residence as the expected place of residence, so the object of change-reporting is unclear and contrary to the principle of clarity. However, because it is clear from the wording of the Act that a change in the reporting items set forth in Article 6(1) gives rise to the object of change-reporting, we do not separately determine whether the principle of clarity has been violated.\\n\\n(4) The Petitioner argues that the portion of Article 9 of the Enforcement Decree requiring the signatures and seals of two personal guarantors when reporting after release is unconstitutional because it was imposed without statutory delegation or beyond the scope of such delegation. However, because this argument is a constitutional challenge to the Enforcement Decree provision, we do not determine it.\\n\\n(5) The Petitioner argues that the Reviewed Provisions also violate the principles of due process, proportionality between culpability and punishment, and the substantive principle of legality in criminal punishment. However, this is no different from an argument that the Reviewed Provisions violate the principle against excessive restriction under Article 37(2) of the Constitution, so we do not separately determine it.\\n\\nc. Determination on the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation\\n\\n(1) Whether the principle against excessive restriction is violated\\n\\n(a) Precedent of the Constitutional Court\\n\\nOn 2001. 7. 19., in Decision 2000HEONBA22, the Constitutional Court held that the corresponding portion of the main clause of Article 6(1) and the corresponding portion of Article 27(2), having the same purport as the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation, were constitutional on the ground that they did not violate the principle against excessive restriction, etc. The gist of the precedent is as follows:\\n\\n“Article 6(1), main clause, latter part, which imposes on the subject the duty to report the fact of release to the chief of the police station having jurisdiction over the expected place of residence within 7 days after release and provides for punishment upon violation, and Article 27(2), are justified in their legislative purpose in light of the fact that the Constitution of Korea accepts security measures and contains provisions thereon, and the fact that the Act provides for a security surveillance disposition in order to prevent the subject’s recidivism and promote a sound return to society.\\n\\nThe reporting under the above provisions, compared with the notice of the occurrence of the subject under Article 6(3) of the Act by the head of the correctional facility, etc. and the notice of release under Article 8 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, and the pre-release report under Article 6(1), main clause, first sentence, of the Act by the subject, differs in subject, timing, method, and purpose in a formal sense; and in a substantive sense as well, the ‘post-release report’ is an important procedure to the extent that it may be said to be the starting point for determining whether to impose a security surveillance disposition, and if it is not recognized, there is a possibility of infringing the privacy and freedom of the subject or his or her family in order to accomplish the legislative purpose of the Act. In these respects, it is an appropriate means to achieve the legislative purpose of the Act.\\n\\nIn addition, in light of the content of the post-release reporting duty, the inconvenience to the subject can by no means be said to be great, nor can it be said that an unnecessary and excessive reporting duty has been imposed again on the people merely for the convenience of the chief of the competent police station in performing his or her duties or administrative convenience; moreover, in view of the public interest underlying the reporting duty, the disadvantage to the subject or infringement of fundamental rights cannot be said to be substantial. As to the 7-day reporting period, in light of the content of the reporting duty, the period is sufficient for the subject to return to the expected place of residence after release and report; and considering that Article 18 requires a person under security surveillance to report to the chief of the competent police station within 7 days from the date of notice of the decision imposing the security surveillance disposition, the period cannot be said to have been set too short. Finally, as for the punishment for nonperformance of the post-release reporting duty, offenses subject to security surveillance are offenses that directly and seriously affect the protection of the democratic system, the maintenance of social order, and the existence and freedom of the people; the Act prescribes the above reporting duty precisely in order to identify subjects who have served all or part of a sentence with a total term of 3 years or more of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment for such offenses and to secure the factual basis for determining whether a security surveillance disposition is necessary, such as the risk of recidivism; and the ultimate legislative purpose of the Act lies in the safety of the State and the peace and security of society. In light of these points, the punishment prescribed by this Act cannot be directly compared with punishment under other statutes. Moreover, the relevant portion of Article 27(2) provides imprisonment and a fine as alternative penalties, and the term of punishment is also prescribed as ‘not more than 2 years,’ so that a short-term sentence is possible. Thus, the statutory penalty cannot be regarded as exceptionally severe compared with other statutes, and therefore it cannot be said to violate the principle of minimum infringement or proportionality of interests. Accordingly, the above statutory provisions do not violate the principle against excessive restriction.”\\n\\n(b) Whether there is a need to change the precedent\\n\\nThe reasoning of the above precedent remains valid, and there are no special changes in circumstances or necessity that would warrant a different conclusion in this case from the precedent. Accordingly, we maintain the precedent as is in this case.\\n\\nIn addition, the subject system is intended to lay the foundation for management to impose a security surveillance disposition on those among persons who have committed offenses infringing national legal interests and who are judged to pose a risk of recidivism. To qualify as a subject, a person must have been sentenced to a term of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment totaling 3 years or more for an offense subject to security surveillance or a concurrent offense thereof, and must have completed service of the sentence; thus, the types of offenses and the gravity of culpability are limited. On the other hand, the Post-Release Reporting Provision merely requires reporting of the fact of release in order to ensure the accuracy of information about the subject, so the effect of restricting fundamental rights therefrom is not serious. Therefore, it does not violate the principle of minimum infringement merely because it does not make the risk of recidivism a requirement for imposing the duty.\\n\\nFurthermore, whether a violation of an administrative ordinance should be sanctioned by an administrative order fine, on the view that it merely poses an indirect risk of disturbing administrative order, or by an administrative criminal penalty, on the view that it directly infringes administrative objectives and the public interest, is a matter that fundamentally falls within the legislative discretion of the legislature, which is to decide in consideration of all circumstances (see Constitutional Court 2005HEONMA373; Constitutional Court 2010HEONBA86). Here, since offenses subject to security surveillance largely consist of serious crimes, and crimes that undermine state security and order are, by their nature, committed covertly, management of such offenders after release is necessary to prevent recidivism; and in light of the fact that securing the subject’s compliance with the reporting duty is important as a measure to obtain the basic data for that purpose, the method of sanctioning violation of the reporting duty with an administrative order fine is insufficient, and since effective enforcement cannot be expected because coercive investigative measures cannot be mobilized to detect nonperformance of the reporting duty, it cannot be said that the Penalty Provision for Violation of the Duty to Report After Release is excessive in choosing criminal punishment as the means of sanction.\\n\\n(c) Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation do not infringe the petitioner’s freedom and privacy of private life or the right to self-determination over personal information in violation of the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n(2) Whether the principle of equality is violated\\n\\n(a) Discrimination from persons under security surveillance\\n\\nWhether a person falls within the category of subject is uniformly determined, regardless of the existence of a risk of recidivism, by whether the aggregate sentence term for certain offenses or concurrent offenses thereof is at least a certain period, whereas a security surveillance disposition is imposed on a person who, for sufficient reasons to recognize a risk of again committing an offense subject to security surveillance, requires observation for the prevention of recidivism (Article 4 of the Act). Accordingly, the Act, for subjects, requires the reporting of the subject’s personal information and matters necessary to determine the risk of recidivism for the purpose of securing basic materials for a security surveillance disposition to prevent recidivism, whereas, for persons under security surveillance who have already been judged to pose a risk of recidivism and have been subjected to a security surveillance disposition, it imposes a duty to report matters necessary for guidance and supervision to prevent recidivism. In this respect, there is a difference in nature between subjects and persons under security surveillance, and the Act also makes some difference in the content of reporting duties in light of this.\\n\\nConsidering that the Act imposes reporting duties appropriate to subjects and persons under security surveillance respectively, the imposition of such reporting duties itself cannot be regarded as irrational; that the difference in status between subjects and persons under security surveillance does not necessarily imply that subjects must be prescribed a reporting duty entirely different in content; and that it is difficult to say that the reporting duty of subjects and the reporting duty of persons under security surveillance differ with respect to the need for the administrative agency to secure relevant data through reporting, it cannot be said that imposing a “reporting duty” on both subjects and persons under security surveillance and subjecting violations to the same statutory penalty violates the principle of equality.\\n\\n(b) Discrimination from treatment custody and probation\\n\\nThe Act on Treatment and Custody, Etc. (hereinafter, the “Treatment and Custody Act”) distinguishes between treatment-custody subjects (Article 2) and persons subject to treatment custody who have received a court judgment of treatment custody among such subjects (Article 16(1)), and imposes no duty on treatment-custody subjects before the pronouncement of a treatment-custody judgment. The Act on Probation, Etc. (hereinafter, the “Probation Act”) does not even contemplate the concept of a subject before it is decided that probation will be imposed from the outset. By contrast, the Act regards a person who satisfies the statutory requirements under Articles 2 and 3 of the Act as a subject by operation of law, without a separate determination by the court, and imposes a reporting duty; in this respect, there is discriminatory treatment of subjects under the Act.\\n\\nHowever, treatment custody is aimed at preventing recidivism and promoting return to society by providing appropriate protection and treatment to a person who has committed a criminal act in a state of mental or physical disability, in a state of drug, alcohol, or other substance addiction, or in a state of mental sexual disorder, and who requires treatment in a treatment-custody facility and poses a risk of recidivism (see Treatment and Custody Act Articles 1, 2, 16, etc.). Probation under the Probation Act is a system that implements probation as a substitute for punishment, especially a substitute for deprivation of liberty, whereby a convicted offender or delinquent juvenile is allowed to live a normal and free life in the community for a certain period instead of being confined in a correctional facility such as a prison or juvenile training school, while being subject to the guidance and supervision of a probation officer (see Probation Act Articles 1, 3, 33, etc.). By contrast, security surveillance and the subject system aim to prevent recidivism by persons who have committed offenses such as espionage or insurrection that infringe national legal interests, and to promote a sound return to society, and thus differ in purpose and objective.\\n\\nAs such, the reason why the scope and requirements of persons subject to reporting duties, and the sanctions for violation, differ between security surveillance and treatment custody/probation lies in the differences in the purpose and objective of each system, their legal nature, and the status of the subject and the content of the disposition, so there is a rational basis for the discriminatory treatment.\\n\\n(c) Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation do not violate the principle of equality.\\n\\nd. Determination on the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation\\n\\n(1) Whether the Change-Reporting Provision violates the principle against blanket delegation\\n\\n(a) Standard of review\\n\\nArticle 75 of the Constitution provides that “the President may issue Presidential Decrees concerning matters delegated to him by law, with specific scope defined therein,” thereby indicating the basis for delegated legislation and its scope and limits. The phrase “with specific scope defined by law” means that the basic matters concerning the contents and scope to be prescribed in subordinate legislation such as Presidential Decrees must already be specified in the law in a concrete and clear manner so that anyone can predict, from the statute itself, the general outline of the content to be prescribed in the Presidential Decree, etc. (see Constitutional Court 2010HEONBA385, et al.).\\n\\n(b) Determination\\n\\n1) The reason the Act imposes a reporting duty on the subject is to prevent recidivism by the subject, who is a security offender, and to promote a sound return to society by securing data to determine the risk of recidivism in post-release life, thereby maintaining the safety of the State and the peace and security of society. In view of this preventive nature, there is a need to delegate to subordinate legislation the specific matters the subject must report, so that flexible responses can be made to social changes.\\n\\n2) In determining whether predictability exists, one must not determine it by looking at a single specific provision alone, but must comprehensively and organically consider all relevant statutory provisions, and must conduct a concrete and individual review according to the nature of the target statute (see Constitutional Court 2013HEONBA173). The reporting matters under the Change-Reporting Provision and Article 6(1) of the Act are information necessary to determine whether the subject poses a risk of recidivism; therefore, it is sufficiently predictable that the reporting matters delegated to the Presidential Decree under Article 6(1) of the Act would include information about occupation, assets, family and friendship relations, etc., necessary to ascertain the subject’s living environment and conduct. Meanwhile, Article 18(1) of the Act specifies as matters to be reported by the person under security surveillance “the subject’s family and friendship relations, occupation, financial status of the person and the family, religion and affiliated organizations, etc.” Considering that a security surveillance disposition is imposed on a person among the subjects who is recognized as posing a risk of recidivism, this provision also enables one to anticipate the content of the reporting matters to be performed by the subject.\\n\\n3) Taking these points together, even though Article 6(1) of the Act delegates to the Presidential Decree matters other than the expected place of residence, the Change-Reporting Provision cannot be said to violate the principle against blanket delegation.\\n\\n(c) Conclusion\\n\\nThus, the Change-Reporting Provision does not violate the principle against blanket delegation.\\n\\n(2) Whether the principle against excessive restriction is violated\\n\\n(a) Dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Seok-tae, Kim Ki-young, Moon Hyung-bae, and Lee Mi-sun\\n\\n1) Security surveillance disposition and persons subject thereto\\n\\nA “person under security surveillance,” who has been subjected to a security surveillance disposition because a risk of recidivism has been recognized, must report the matters prescribed in Article 18(1) to the chief of the competent police station and, if there is any change in those matters, must make a change report (paragraph (3)). Article 3 of the Act defines a “person subject to a security surveillance disposition” at the stage before a security surveillance disposition is made, and Article 6(1) of the Act and Article 6(1) of the Enforcement Decree require reporting of content almost identical to the reporting items of a person under security surveillance. Article 6(2) of the Act makes reporting of changes in the above reporting items obligatory, and Article 27(2) of the Act prescribes the same statutory penalty for violations of the reporting duty by persons under security surveillance and for violations of each of the above reporting duties by subjects.\\n\\nA request for a security surveillance disposition is made by a prosecutor submitting a request for disposition to the Minister of Justice (Articles 7 and 8(1) of the Act), and the Minister of Justice makes the security surveillance disposition through the resolution of the Security Surveillance Disposition Review Committee (Articles 12(9) and 14 of the Act). The period of a security surveillance disposition is 2 years, and the Minister of Justice may renew the period through a resolution of the Security Surveillance Disposition Review Committee upon a prosecutor’s request (Article 5 of the Act). By contrast, the status of a subject continues without time limitation unless the person satisfies the requirements such as establishing compliance with the law and receives an exemption decision not to impose a security surveillance disposition (Article 11(1) of the Act). Even if a person has received a security surveillance disposition and has become a person under security surveillance, if the disposition is not renewed or the renewal disposition is revoked by a court, the person again becomes a subject unless he or she separately receives the above exemption decision, and thus continues to bear the reporting duty prescribed in Article 6(2) of the Act. In practice, the above exemption decision is not actively used, and even if there is such a decision, the Minister of Justice may revoke it upon a prosecutor’s request (Article 11(3) and (4) of the Act). Moreover, the number of cases in which a person reaches a security surveillance disposition upon a prosecutor’s request is far smaller than the number of cases in which the status of subject continues without time limitation while the determination of recidivism risk is deferred.\\n\\n2) Justification of legislative purpose and suitability of means\\n\\nBefore deciding whether to commence a security surveillance disposition against a person sentenced to a term of imprisonment totaling 3 years or more for offenses subject to security surveillance, etc., there is a need to confirm the subject’s residence, etc. and secure data for deciding whether to request a security surveillance disposition; thus, imposing on the subject a duty to report changes in the matters reported under Article 6(1) and punishing violation thereof satisfies the justification of legislative purpose and suitability of means.\\n\\n3) Minimum infringement\\n\\nA) The essence of a security surveillance disposition is a security measure, and a security measure is a special preventive measure devised to achieve social defense and the offender’s sound return to society in cases where punishment alone is insufficient to eliminate the danger of the offender’s future recidivism (see Constitutional Court 2014HEONBA475). The risk of recidivism is the core of a security measure, and the security-measure-related demand of the principle of legality in criminal punishment embodied in Article 12(1) of the Constitution, which provides that “no person shall be punished, subjected to a security measure, or forced labor without law and due process,” implies that “if there is no risk of recidivism, there is no security measure” (see Constitutional Court 88HEONGA5, et al.).\\n\\nHowever, the Change-Reporting Provision imposes on persons who, merely because they are subjects, are not or are only slightly at risk of recidivism and therefore cannot be subjected to a security surveillance disposition, a duty to report changes, and provides for criminal punishment in case of violation, thereby imposing duties and sanctions similar in degree to those imposed on persons under security surveillance. In light of the very purpose of setting up the category of subjects, namely “the prevention of recidivism and promotion of a sound return to society of persons under security surveillance through security surveillance dispositions against persons recognized as posing a risk of recidivism,” imposing such duties and sanctions even on subjects with no or low recidivism risk violates the security-measure-related request of the principle of legality that no security measure may be imposed where there is no risk of recidivism, and produces restrictions not necessary to achieve the legislative purpose, thus contravening the principle of minimum infringement (see Constitutional Court 2014HEONMA340, et al.).\\n\\nSince the subject is not in a state in which risk of recidivism has been recognized, the reporting duty imposed on the subject is merely a kind of administrative cooperation duty. Even if such duty is not smoothly fulfilled and information necessary for assessing the risk of recidivism is not provided, the chief of the competent police station merely bears the burden of collecting the information himself or herself, and the assessment of recidivism risk is not rendered impossible. Nevertheless, punishing a subject who fails to report changes by imprisonment for not more than 2 years or a fine not exceeding 1,000,000 won, just as in the case of violation of the reporting duty by a person under security surveillance, is to prescribe a penalty that is excessively severe in relation to culpability.\\n\\nB) After release, if there is any change in the reporting items under Article 6(1), the subject must report within 7 days, but the duty to report changes prescribed in Article 6(2) has no terminal point. As a result, even though the subject is not a person under security surveillance, the subject bears a reporting duty indefinitely, without even reflecting the fact that the risk of recidivism diminishes after a certain period without recidivism. Even if offenses subject to security surveillance have the characteristic of being capable of being committed under long-term planning, indefinite collection of data for the purpose of assessing recidivism risk cannot be justified. To this end, one should respond by examining the actual circumstances of offenses and prescribing an ample period, but one cannot justify or permit an absolute indefinite measure without any upper time limit.\\n\\nEven for a person under security surveillance against whom a security surveillance disposition has been imposed because a risk of recidivism has been recognized, the period of the disposition is statutorily fixed at 2 years, and to renew that period, the Minister of Justice must, through the resolution of the Security Surveillance Disposition Review Committee, decide to renew it. The Supreme Court has held that “risk of recidivism,” as a requirement for security surveillance disposition, means the likelihood of again committing an offense subject to security surveillance in the future, and that this must be determined by comprehensively considering various circumstances such as the type and nature of the offense subject to security surveillance previously committed, the offender’s conduct during the execution of the sentence, post-sentence social activities and attitude, living environment, and conduct; and that when making a decision to renew the period of a security surveillance disposition, there must be a recognized “need to continue security surveillance to prevent recidivism of the offense subject to security surveillance despite the existing security surveillance, as of the time of renewal” (Supreme Court 2016. 8. 24. 2016DU34929).\\n\\nHowever, in the case of the subject, although no determination of recidivism risk has been made, the subject is, as noted above, subject to a reporting duty almost identical to that of a person under security surveillance, and if it is violated, criminal punishment with the same statutory penalty as that applicable to a person under security surveillance is prescribed; furthermore, unlike a person under security surveillance, the subject bears the reporting duty indefinitely without any periodic review of recidivism risk for disposition period and renewal decisions. Thus, this is even harsher than the position of a person under security surveillance whose recidivism risk has been recognized.\\n\\nBecause the institutional design for subjects and persons under security surveillance is structured in this way, it is understood that among those sentenced to imprisonment for 3 years or more for offenses subject to security surveillance, etc. and who have served such sentence, the number of persons who, as subjects, bear reporting duties, etc. is far greater than the number of persons who, upon a prosecutor’s request, become persons under security surveillance. In the end, regulation of the subject, who has not yet been found to pose a risk of recidivism and should remain in a temporary and provisional state for proper judgment in security surveillance disposition, is set at a degree similar to that in which a security surveillance disposition has been issued, thereby producing the irrational result of preempting an effect similar to that of a security surveillance disposition even though there has in fact been no final disposition.\\n\\n4) Balance of legal interests\\n\\nTaking the foregoing into account, imposing on a subject who has already completed execution of the sentence for an offense subject to security surveillance and has thus paid the price for past crimes, a reporting duty of excessive scope indefinitely, regardless of recidivism risk, for the public interest of deciding whether to commence a security surveillance disposition, and criminally punishing the subject with the same penalty as a person under security surveillance in case of violation, excessively restricts their fundamental rights in relation to the public interest to be achieved, and therefore also violates the balance of legal interests.\\n\\n5) Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation infringe the petitioner’s freedom and privacy of private life and the right to self-determination over personal information in violation of the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n(b) Constitutional inconsistency opinion of Justices Yoo Nam-seok and Lee Eun-ae\\n\\n1) The determination on the justification of legislative purpose and the suitability of means is the same as in the above dissenting opinion regarding the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation.\\n\\n2) Minimum infringement\\n\\nIn order for the chief of the competent police station to know accurate information about the subject, such as the subject’s actual place of residence, after the subject’s release, it is necessary to require the subject to report any changes each time they occur after release; therefore, it is not contrary to the principle of minimum infringement merely because the duty to report changes does not require recidivism risk as a condition.\\n\\nHowever, whereas the Post-Release Reporting Provision requires only the fact of release to be reported and thus the duty arises only once, the Change-Reporting Provision imposes a duty to report, within 7 days, any change in the previously reported information such as the expected place of residence after release, but there is no upper limit on the duration of that duty, so the subject, even though not a person under security surveillance, bears a reporting duty indefinitely. Even taking into account the characteristic that offenses such as espionage, insurrection, and treason under the Criminal Act, the Military Criminal Act, and the National Security Act, and offenses such as collection and detection of secrets that infringe national legal interests can be committed under long-term planning, indefinite collection of data for determining recidivism risk cannot be justified. Therefore, leaving aside the point that one could respond by examining the actual circumstances of offenses and prescribing an appropriate period, or by preparing a procedure for renewal of the period during which the subject bears the reporting duty if the administrative agency deems it necessary, an absolute indefinite measure with no upper time limit cannot be justified or permitted.\\n\\nMeanwhile, because a security surveillance disposition is imposed on persons among the subjects who pose a risk of recidivism, “subject” may be said to be a person in a “temporary” status who may become a person under security surveillance depending on the presence or absence of recidivism risk. If so, the principle should be that only when a subject is recognized as posing a risk of recidivism should the person be subjected to a security surveillance disposition, and otherwise should be able to escape the provisional status of “subject.” However, the Change-Reporting Provision makes it the rule that the subject bears an indefinite duty to report changes.\\n\\nIn addition, the subject is always placed in an unstable state in which the administrative agency empowered to impose a security surveillance disposition may at some point make such a disposition, and there is also the problem that the burden of the administrative agency’s failure to judge the subject’s recidivism risk is instead shifted to the subject.\\n\\nAlthough a subject can be relieved from the reporting duty if he or she receives an exemption decision, that exemption is also determined by the Minister of Justice through deliberation and resolution by the Security Surveillance Disposition Review Committee under the Ministry of Justice, just as in the procedure for commencement of a security surveillance disposition, so the procedure is cumbersome, and an exemption decision already made may be revoked at any time by the Minister of Justice upon a prosecutor’s request if it is deemed that the person has “ceased to meet the requirements for exemption” (Article 11(4) of the Act), so this is insufficient to cure the unconstitutionality of a duty to report changes imposed with no upper time limit. Furthermore, because such remedial measure is nothing more than an “exception” under the present reporting system, which in principle requires continued assumption of the reporting duty, it cannot fundamentally resolve the problem of the current system, which makes the continuance of the duty to report changes the rule from the outset.\\n\\nThus, even if the necessity of imposing a duty to report changes is recognized, the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation, which impose on the subject a duty to report changes with no upper time limit, violate the principle of minimum infringement in that they place the subject in an unstable status for an excessively long period.\\n\\n3) Balance of legal interests\\n\\nThe Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation impose on a subject who has completed service of the sentence for an offense subject to security surveillance and has been released from prison a reporting duty carrying criminal punishment for an excessive period, for the public interest of deciding whether to commence a security surveillance disposition. This excessively restricts the subject’s fundamental rights in relation to the public interest to be achieved and therefore also violates the balance of legal interests.\\n\\n4) Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation infringe the petitioner’s freedom and privacy of private life and the right to self-determination over personal information in violation of the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n5) Decision of constitutional inconsistency and order of temporary application regarding the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation\\n\\nThe unconstitutionality of the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation lies in the fact that, once there is any change in the reporting items under Article 6(1) of the Act, such as the expected place of residence, the subject is imposed a duty to report within 7 days, yet the statute does not prescribe an upper limit on the reporting duty period, thereby requiring the subject to bear the reporting duty indefinitely. The legislature can eliminate the unconstitutionality of the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation by prescribing, within a reasonable period appropriate for determining the subject’s risk of recidivism, an upper limit on the reporting duty period, taking into account, inter alia, that the risk of recidivism decreases as time passes.\\n\\nHowever, if the Constitutional Court were to render a simple unconstitutional decision on the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation and their effect were to be lost immediately, the duty to report changes would immediately disappear even in cases where imposing such duty on the subject would be justified, and difficulties may arise in achieving the legislative purpose due to such legal vacuum.\\n\\nTherefore, it is proper to render a decision of constitutional inconsistency with respect to the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation and to order temporary application until the legislature enacts remedial legislation. The legislature must enact remedial legislation by no later than 2023. 6. 30.; if remedial legislation is not enacted by then, the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation shall lose effect from 2023. 7. 1.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, with respect to the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation, if the dissenting opinions of Justices Lee Seok-tae, Kim Ki-young, Moon Hyung-bae, and Lee Mi-sun are combined with the constitutional inconsistency opinion of Justices Yoo Nam-seok and Lee Eun-ae, the quorum required for a finding of unconstitutionality is satisfied. Therefore, it is declared that the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation do not violate the Constitution, and that the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation are not in conformity with the Constitution, and the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation shall continue to apply until the legislature enacts remedial legislation before 2023. 6. 30.; if no remedial legislation is enacted by that date, the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation shall lose effect from 2023. 7. 1. However, as to the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation, there is the separate dissenting opinion below in Section 6 by Justices Lee Seok-tae, Kim Ki-young, Moon Hyung-bae, and Lee Mi-sun, and as to the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation, there is the separate dissenting opinion below in Section 7 by Justices Lee Sun-ae, Lee Jong-seok, and Lee Young-jin.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Lee Seok-tae, Kim Ki-young, Moon Hyung-bae, and Lee Mi-sun on the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation\\n\\nUnlike the majority opinion, we think that the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation violate the principle against excessive restriction and infringe the petitioner’s freedom and privacy of private life and the right to self-determination over personal information. Accordingly, we state our dissent as follows.\\n\\na. Justification of legislative purpose; suitability of means\\n\\nThe same as the majority opinion on the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation.\\n\\nb. Minimum infringement\\n\\n(1) Although the essence of a security surveillance disposition is a security measure and the risk of recidivism is the core of a security measure, the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation uniformly impose the post-release reporting duty even on persons who, merely because they are subjects, are not or are only slightly at risk of recidivism and therefore cannot be subjected to a security surveillance disposition, and provide for criminal punishment if they violate it. This violates the request of the principle of legality in criminal punishment concerning security measures that no security measure may be imposed where there is no risk of recidivism, and produces restrictions not necessary to achieve the legislative purpose, thereby contravening the principle of minimum infringement (see Constitutional Court 2014HEONMA340, et al.). In this way, since the subject is not in a state in which recidivism risk has been recognized, the reporting duty imposed on the subject is merely a kind of administrative cooperation duty; nevertheless, punishing it by imprisonment for not more than 2 years or a fine not exceeding 1,000,000 won is to prescribe a penalty excessively severe in relation to culpability.\\n\\n(2) Furthermore, even in terms of the need to secure information for determining whether a subject poses a risk of recidivism, these provisions contravene the principle of minimum infringement. When a subject arises, the head of the correctional facility, etc. prepares and sends to the chief of the police station having jurisdiction over the expected place of residence a notice containing the expected place of residence after release (notice of occurrence, Article 6(3) of the Act, Article 10(1) of the Enforcement Decree). Before release, the subject must prepare 5 copies of a report setting forth former registration address, family registry address, residence, resident registration number, family and friendship relations, occupation before admission, the financial status of the person and the family, educational background and career, religion and affiliated organizations, military service status, expected date of release, expected place of residence after release and expected date of arrival there, summary of the facts of the offense subject to security surveillance, and prior convictions, and submit them to the head of the correctional facility, etc. (pre-release reporting duty, Article 6(1) of the Act, Article 6(1) of the Enforcement Decree). Two months before the expected date of release, the head of the correctional facility, etc. sends the above pre-release report submitted by the person subject to a security surveillance disposition to the chief of the police station having jurisdiction over the expected place of residence (pre-release notice, Article 6(2) of the Enforcement Decree, Article 5(3) of the Enforcement Rules). Immediately after the subject’s release, the head of the correctional facility, etc. notifies the chief of the police station having jurisdiction over the expected place of residence of the expected date of release, the expected place of residence after release and the expected date and time of arrival, the quality of conduct, health condition, and whether ideological conversion has occurred, etc. (notice upon release, Article 8(1) of the Enforcement Decree). Therefore, it can be said that after the subject is released, the chief of the competent police station sufficiently knows the information concerning the subject’s expected place of residence and expected date and time of arrival, as well as the data regarding the request for a security surveillance disposition that can be secured around that time. Since the number of new subjects arising at local competent police stations is not very large and Article 11 of the Enforcement Decree provides for status reports regarding subjects, while defining as reportable matters to the chief of the competent police station cases where whereabouts are unknown or the subject has fled, it is not difficult to confirm the actual residence of a person subject to probation on the basis of already secured data. Accordingly, the legislative purpose can be sufficiently achieved by a method more lenient than imposing a reporting duty and criminal punishment.\\n\\nc. Balance of legal interests\\n\\nTaking the foregoing into account, imposing on a subject a reporting duty of excessive scope, more than necessary, and criminally punishing matters that are merely a kind of administrative cooperation duty, for the public interest of deciding whether to commence a security surveillance disposition, excessively restricts their fundamental rights in relation to the public interest to be achieved, and therefore also violates the balance of legal interests.\\n\\nd. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation infringe the petitioner’s freedom and privacy of private life and the right to self-determination over personal information in violation of the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n7.
