Dissenting Opinion of Justices Lee Sun-ae, Lee Jong-seok, and Lee Young-jin on the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation\\n\\nWe consider that, for the same reasons as the majority opinion on the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation above, the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation do not violate the principle of equality, and furthermore, for the following reasons, do not violate the principle against excessive restriction and therefore do not infringe the petitioner’s freedom and privacy of private life and the right to self-determination over personal information. Accordingly, we state our opinion.\\n\\na. Justification of legislative purpose and suitability of means\\n\\nThe Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation are intended to continuously and systematically manage subjects, prevent them from again committing offenses subject to security surveillance, and promote the subjects’ sound return to society, and to impose a security surveillance disposition on those who, among them, pose a risk of recidivism and require observation for the prevention thereof; thus, like the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation, the legitimacy of purpose is recognized. Meanwhile, in order to impose a security surveillance disposition when there are sufficient grounds to recognize that a subject poses a risk of again committing an offense subject to security surveillance, it is necessary that the chief of the competent police station, even after the subject’s release, accurately grasp matters concerning the subject’s actual place of residence, etc. Therefore, it contributes to the achievement of the legislative purpose that the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation require the subject, even after reporting under Article 6(1), to report to the chief of the competent police station whenever there is any change in the subject’s personal information and information concerning post-release circumstances, and punish violations with criminal sanctions; thus, suitability of means is also recognized.\\n\\nb. Minimum infringement\\n\\n(1) Unlike the Post-Release Reporting Provision, which requires only the fact of release to be reported and thus involves performance of the duty only once, the Change-Reporting Provision imposes a duty to report whenever there is any change in the previously reported information such as the expected place of residence after release, yet does not set an upper limit on the duration of that duty. It is true that the degree of restriction on fundamental rights is relatively greater. However, offenses subject to security surveillance are offenses that directly and seriously affect the protection of the democratic system, the maintenance of social order, and the existence and freedom of the people; accordingly, in determining whether the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation violate the principle of minimum infringement, the special importance of suppressing recidivism for offenses subject to security surveillance must be taken into account.\\n\\nAlthough the subject may be inconvenienced by having to report any changes in former registration address, family registry address, residence, family and friendship relations, financial status, educational background and career, religion and affiliated organizations, summary of the facts of the offense subject to security surveillance, and prior convictions that were previously reported pursuant to Article 6(1) each time they change, such duty is limited to changes in matters already reported, and if the public interest underlying the above duty to report changes is also taken into account, the reporting content required of the subject by the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation is essential to achieve the legislative purpose, and the degree of restriction on the subject’s fundamental rights resulting from performance of that duty cannot be said to be excessive.\\n\\nIn addition, in order to effectively manage and suppress the subject’s possibility of recidivism by identifying subjects at risk of recidivism and imposing a security surveillance disposition, it is essential to continuously manage the subject, including ensuring the subject’s compliance with the duty to report changes under the Change-Reporting Provision and updating information concerning the subject’s actual place of residence, etc. Moreover, offenses subject to security surveillance such as espionage, insurrection, treason, and detection/collection of secrets under the Criminal Act, the Military Criminal Act, and the National Security Act have the characteristic that they can be committed under long-term planning, so the period during which the reporting duty under the Change-Reporting Provision is imposed generally needs to be long, and if the duty period were uniformly capped, there is a concern that the legislative purpose would be difficult to achieve.\\n\\nMeanwhile, a subject can receive from the Minister of Justice a decision not to impose a security surveillance disposition if certain requirements such as having established compliance with the law and having a fixed residence and occupation are satisfied, and a person who has received such an exemption decision is relieved of the duties as a subject from that time (Articles 11(1) and 11(6) of the Act). Accordingly, the reporting duty borne by the subject under the Change-Reporting Provision is not perpetual, and imposing the duty to report changes with the point at which such a law-abiding subject receives an exemption decision as the upper limit is for the purpose of effectively suppressing recidivism by the subject, and is a sufficiently acceptable and reasonable restriction.\\n\\n(2) Furthermore, for the same reasons as in the majority opinion on the Post-Release Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation above, it cannot be said that the fact that the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation do not make recidivism risk a requirement when imposing the duty to report changes on the subject, or that choosing criminal punishment as the sanction for violation of the duty to report changes, directly results in a violation of the principle of minimum infringement, and the statutory penalty for the Penalty Provision for Violation of the Duty to Report Changes cannot be said to be excessive.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation do not violate the principle of minimum infringement.\\n\\nc. Balance of legal interests\\n\\nThe subject may indeed find it burdensome to report each change arising under the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation. However, the public interest achieved by compelling performance of the reporting duty is the safety of the State, the peace and security of society, and social defense, which are very important. Since the above disadvantage to the subject cannot be said to outweigh that public interest, the above provisions do not violate the balance of legal interests.\\n\\nd. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the Change-Reporting Provision and the Penalty Provision for Violation do not infringe the petitioner’s freedom and privacy of private life and the right to self-determination over personal information in violation of the principle against excessive restriction."}

{"[2019HEONBA520]": "1. Case Overview\\n\\na. The petitioner was the director of a child-care center established pursuant to the Infant Care Act. On 2018. 3. 30., the Mayor of Jeju City issued an order to close the child-care center operated by the petitioner on the ground that “from around 2010. 9. to around 2017. 8., the petitioner fraudulently obtained and appropriated a total of KRW 164,258,660, including child care teacher personnel expenses (allowances) and basic child care fees, by falsely registering child care teachers.”\\n\\nb. Thereafter, from 2018. 11. 21. to 2021. 11. 20., the Mayor of Jeju City publicly disclosed on the Internet homepage of the Ministry of Health and Welfare and elsewhere the above violation, the contents of the disposition, as well as the name and address of the child-care center operated by the petitioner and the name of the petitioner, who was both the representative and director (hereinafter referred to as “the public disclosure at issue”).\\n\\nc. The petitioner filed a lawsuit seeking revocation of the public disclosure at issue (Jeju District Court 2018GUHAP6090) and, while that lawsuit was pending, filed an application requesting referral for adjudication on the constitutionality of statutes regarding Article 49-3 of the Infant Care Act, Article 25-7 and Article 25-8 of the former Enforcement Decree of the Infant Care Act, which are the provisions forming the basis for the public disclosure at issue; however, on 2019. 11. 20., that application was denied and dismissed (Jeju District Court 2018A1118).\\n\\nd. Accordingly, the petitioner filed this constitutional complaint on 2019. 12. 16., asserting that Article 49-3 of the Infant Care Act is contrary to the Constitution.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nAlthough the petitioner has designated the entirety of Article 49-3 of the Infant Care Act as the subject matter of adjudication, the subject matter is limited to the part applicable to the petitioner. Therefore, the subject matter of this case is whether Article 49-3(1)1 of the former Infant Care Act (as amended by Act No. 13321 on 2015. 5. 18. and before its amendment by Act No. 17785 on 2020. 12. 29.; hereinafter, regardless of its history, referred to as the “Infant Care Act”) is contrary to the Constitution. The provision subject to adjudication and related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision Subject to Adjudication]\\n\\nFormer Infant Care Act (as amended by Act No. 13321 on 2015. 5. 18. and before its amendment by Act No. 17785 on 2020. 12. 29.)\\n\\nArticle 49-3 (Public Disclosure of Facts of Violation) (1) The Minister of Health and Welfare, the Mayor of a Special Metropolitan City or Metropolitan City, the Governor of a Do, or the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head shall publicly disclose the violation, the contents of the disposition, the name of the relevant child-care center, the name of its representative, the name of the director of the child-care center (only where the director is not the same person as the representative), and other matters prescribed by Presidential Decree as necessary to distinguish the relevant child-care center from other child-care centers, with respect to a child-care center that has received an administrative disposition under Article 45 or Article 45-2 and falls under any of the following cases. Provided, That in the case of subparagraph 1, public disclosure shall be made only where the amount is at least the amount prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Welfare.\\n1. Where subsidies were received or used in violation through false or other improper means\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nFormer Infant Care Act (as amended by Act No. 12068 on 2013. 8. 13. and before its amendment by Act No. 17785 on 2020. 12. 29.)\\n\\nArticle 45 (Closure of Child-Care Centers, etc.) (1) Where a person who establishes and operates a child-care center (hereinafter in this Article referred to as the “operator”) falls under any of the following subparagraphs, the Minister of Health and Welfare, the Mayor of a Special Metropolitan City or Metropolitan City, the Governor of a Do, or the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head may order the suspension of operation of the child-care center for up to one year or may order the closure of the child-care center. In such case, where a person under the control and supervision of the operator, such as a child-care worker, commits an act falling under subparagraph 4, it shall be deemed to be an act committed by the operator (this shall not apply where the operator has not neglected due care and supervision to prevent such act).\\n1. Where subsidies were received or used in violation through false or other improper means\\n\\nInfant Care Act (as amended by Act No. 10789 on 2011. 6. 7.)\\n\\nArticle 45-2 (Imposition of Penalty Surcharges) (1) Where the Minister of Health and Welfare, the Mayor of a Special Metropolitan City or Metropolitan City, the Governor of a Do, or the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head must order the suspension of operation of a child-care center because the operator of the child-care center falls under any subparagraph of Article 45(1), and such suspension would cause severe inconvenience to infants and young children and their guardians or would otherwise likely harm the public interest, a penalty surcharge not exceeding KRW 30 million may be imposed in lieu of the disposition of suspension of operation of the child-care center.\\n\\nFormer Enforcement Rules of the Infant Care Act (as amended by Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Welfare No. 92 on 2011. 12. 8. and before its amendment by Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Welfare No. 788 on 2021. 3. 30.)\\n\\nArticle 38 (Administrative Dispositions Concerning Child-Care Centers) (1) The detailed standards for administrative dispositions concerning child-care centers under Article 45(1) of the Act shall be as stated in Attached Table 9.\\n(2) Where the administrative disposition under paragraph (1) corresponds to suspension of operation, the Special Self-Governing Province Governor, Mayor, County Governor, or District Head may increase or reduce the period of suspension of operation under paragraph (1) within the extent of one-half, taking into consideration the motive, content, and frequency of the violation, and where the period is increased, the total period of suspension of operation may not exceed one year.\\n\\nFormer Enforcement Rules of the Infant Care Act (as amended by Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Welfare No. 355 on 2015. 9. 18. and before its amendment by Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Welfare No. 805 on 2021. 6. 30.)\\n\\nArticle 39-2 (Amount Subject to Public Disclosure) “Where the amount prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Welfare” in the proviso to the part of Article 49-3(1) of the Act other than the subparagraphs means any of the following cases:\\n1. Where subsidies received or used in violation through false or other improper means are KRW 3 million or more for a single violation\\n2. Where the cumulative amount of subsidies received or used in violation through false or other improper means is KRW 2 million or more due to two or more violations in the most recent three years\\n\\n3. The Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\na. The petitioner was subjected not only to administrative dispositions of closure of the child-care center and suspension of qualification as a director, but also to criminal punishment, on the ground that the petitioner had fraudulently received child-care center subsidies. Nevertheless, the provision subject to adjudication infringes the petitioner’s right to be forgotten, by publicly disclosing the petitioner’s acts of violation and the contents of the disposition, thereby making the petitioner forget past wrongs and pursue new happiness.\\n\\nb. Unlike operators of child-care centers who fraudulently receive or divert subsidies, there is no system of public disclosure of facts of violation for persons who commit similar offenses, such as construction business operators who violate the “Act on the Management of Subsidies,” or public officials who embezzle public funds or accept bribes. Accordingly, the provision subject to adjudication infringes the petitioner’s equality right by creating a social special status of “a person who operated a child-care center and received subsidies improperly and was subjected to a closure disposition of the child-care center.”\\n\\nc. The provision subject to adjudication infringes the petitioner’s privacy and freedom of private life by publicly disclosing to an indefinite and numerous public that there is a person who operated a child-care center and was subjected to a closure disposition of the child-care center after improperly receiving subsidies.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Procedural Requirements\\n\\nAs the provision subject to adjudication is the legal basis for the public disclosure at issue, at the time of the petition in this case there was room for the conclusion of the judgment in the case on the merits to differ depending on its constitutionality, and therefore the precondition for trial was recognized. However, as of 2021. 11. 20., after the petition in this case, the public disclosure at issue ended upon the expiration of the period; accordingly, the petitioner no longer has a legal interest in seeking revocation of the public disclosure at issue, and the constitutionality of the provision subject to adjudication no longer serves as a precondition for the judgment in the case on the merits.\\n\\nNevertheless, even where the precondition for trial is absent, the Constitutional Court may exceptionally proceed to a merits determination in order to fulfill its mission as guardian of the constitutional order where constitutional clarification is urgently required or where there is a risk that the infringement of fundamental rights by the relevant provision may recur (see Constitutional Court 2002HEONBA3 decided on 2003. 6. 26.). As the issue of public disclosure of facts of violation under the provision subject to adjudication is of interest to all operators of child-care centers and there is a risk that infringements of fundamental rights resulting therefrom may recur, yet no constitutional clarification on this matter has been provided, we recognize the need for constitutional clarification as to whether the provision subject to adjudication is unconstitutional and proceed to a merits determination.\\n\\n5. Determination on the Merits\\n\\na. Overview of the System of Public Disclosure of Facts of Violation\\n\\n(1) Legislative History\\n\\nThe Minister of Health and Welfare, the Mayor of a Special Metropolitan City or Metropolitan City, the Governor of a Do, or the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head (hereinafter referred to as the “Minister of Health and Welfare, etc.”) may impose an order to suspend the operation of a child-care center, an order to close it, or a penalty surcharge disposition where the operator of a child-care center has received subsidies or diverted subsidies through false or other improper means (Articles 45 and 45-2 of the Infant Care Act). Where the amount of subsidies fraudulently received or diverted by a child-care center that has received such administrative disposition is at least the amount prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Welfare, the Minister of Health and Welfare, etc. shall publicly disclose the facts of the violation (provision subject to adjudication).\\n\\nThe system of public disclosure of the facts of violation by child-care centers that have received subsidies from the State or a local government and fraudulently received or diverted them, and for which an order of suspension of operation, an order of closure, or a penalty surcharge disposition has been imposed, was first introduced on 2013. 6. 4., when the Infant Care Act was amended by Act No. 11858, for the purpose of promoting transparent operation of child-care centers by their operators and ensuring the right of guardians of infants and young children to choose child-care institutions. At the time of introduction, it was provided that the Minister of Health and Welfare, etc. could determine whether to make a public disclosure by taking into account the motive, degree, frequency, and result of the violation, and thus it was stipulated as discretionary public disclosure; however, when amended by Act No. 13321 on 2015. 5. 18., it was changed into a mandatory public disclosure provision like the provision subject to adjudication, but the requirements were limited so that public disclosure could be made only where the amount of subsidies received or diverted through false or other improper means was KRW 3 million or more for a single violation, or where the cumulative amount was KRW 2 million or more due to two or more violations in the most recent three years, and it remains so to this day.\\n\\n(2) Content\\n\\nThe information disclosed includes the violation, the contents of the disposition, the name of the relevant child-care center, the name of its representative, the name of the director of the child-care center (only where the director is not the same person as the representative), the type of child-care center, the address, and other matters necessary to distinguish it from other child-care centers [provision subject to adjudication; Article 25-7(1) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Infant Care Act (as amended by Presidential Decree No. 26525 on 2015. 9. 15. and before its amendment by Presidential Decree No. 29805 on 2019. 6. 4.; hereinafter the same shall apply)], and the period of disclosure is three years for facts of violation corresponding to closure of a child-care center, and a period corresponding to twice the suspension period applicable to facts of violation corresponding to suspension of operation of a child-care center or a penalty surcharge (where the suspension was replaced by a penalty surcharge, referring to the period of suspension replaced by the penalty surcharge) (Article 25-8(4) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Infant Care Act). However, since the period of suspension of operation is up to one year (Article 38(1) and (2) of the former Enforcement Rules of the Infant Care Act), public disclosure concerning a child-care center that received an order of suspension of operation may last up to two years.\\n\\nThe place of disclosure is the homepage of the Ministry of Health and Welfare or each local government, and disclosure may additionally be made on the homepage of institutions related to child care, such as the information disclosure system or a comprehensive child-care support center (Article 25-8(4) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Infant Care Act). Where it is recognized that additional public disclosure is necessary, such as where the violation subject to public disclosure is serious or where the violation subject to public disclosure has been repeated, additional disclosure may be made in a newspaper or by broadcast (paragraph (5) of the same Article).\\n\\nWhere the Minister of Health and Welfare, etc. publicly discloses facts of violation, the Minister of Health and Welfare, etc. shall notify in writing the person subject to public disclosure, such as the representative of the child-care center decided to be disclosed, that he or she is subject to public disclosure, and shall give an opportunity to submit opinions (Article 49-3(3) of the Infant Care Act; Article 25-8(2) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Infant Care Act).\\n\\nb. Organization of Issues\\n\\n(1) The general personality right derived from Article 10 of the Constitution includes the right concerning a person’s reputation (see Constitutional Court 2002HEONMA425 decided on 2005. 10. 27.). If information about the representative of a child-care center, etc. who received subsidies or diverted subsidies through false or other improper means is publicly disclosed pursuant to the provision subject to adjudication, the social evaluation of the person subject to public disclosure may be infringed; accordingly, the provision subject to adjudication restricts the general personality right derived from Article 10 of the Constitution.\\n\\nPersonal information that is protected by the right to self-determination over personal information may be described as all information that enables the identification of an individual’s identity, as matters characterizing the subjectivity of the individual’s personality, such as the individual’s body, beliefs, social status, or status (see Constitutional Court 2007HEONMA1092 decided on 2009. 9. 24.), and is not necessarily limited to information belonging to the intimate sphere or the private sphere of the individual, but also includes personal information formed in public life or already disclosed. Acts such as investigation, collection, storage, processing, and use of such personal information all, in principle, constitute a restriction on the right to self-determination over personal information (see Constitutional Court 2008HEONMA257 decided on 2009. 10. 29.).\\n\\nBecause the provision subject to adjudication makes the name, type, address, and the name of the representative or director of a child-care center, etc. that received subsidies or diverted subsidies through false or other improper means known to an indefinite and numerous public, regardless of the will of the representative or director of the child-care center, it restricts the person subject to public disclosure’s right to self-determination over personal information.\\n\\n(2) Meanwhile, the petitioner contends that the provision subject to adjudication infringes the right to be forgotten derived from Article 10 of the Constitution and the secrecy and freedom of private life under Article 17 of the Constitution; however, insofar as we determine whether the provision infringes the personality right and the right to self-determination over personal information, which are the fundamental rights most closely related to and primary in this case, we do not separately determine these claims.\\n\\nThe petitioner also contends that the provision subject to adjudication infringes the petitioner’s equality right by creating a social special status of “a person who operated a child-care center and received subsidies improperly and was subjected to a closure disposition of the child-care center.” However, the social status under Article 11(1) of the Constitution means a status occupied in society over a long period of time and accompanying a certain social evaluation (see Constitutional Court 93HEONBA43 decided on 1995. 2. 23.), and it is difficult to view the petitioner as having acquired such social status due to the closure disposition of the child-care center. Moreover, this part of the argument is ultimately no different from the argument that the provision subject to adjudication infringes the petitioner’s personality right and right to self-determination over personal information by publicly disclosing the facts of violation; accordingly, we do not separately determine this issue either.\\n\\n(3) Therefore, below we examine whether the provision subject to adjudication violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringes the petitioner’s personality right and right to self-determination over personal information.\\n\\nc. Whether the Principle of Prohibition of Excessive Restriction Is Violated\\n\\n(1) Legitimacy of Purpose and Appropriateness of Means\\n\\nSubsidies provided to operators of child-care centers under the Infant Care Act are intended for the State or local governments to support the costs so that child-care centers, which are institutions for infant and young child care, can safely and healthily protect and nurture infants and young children and provide education suited to the developmental characteristics of infants and young children. Corrupt acts of fraudulently receiving or diverting such subsidies are directly linked to the quality of infant and young child care, and the resulting disadvantages are wholly transferred to infants and young children; hence, there is a great need to eradicate them. The provision subject to adjudication is intended to give child-care center operators a sense of alertness to prevent similar violations, and to provide guardians of infants and young children with information about child-care centers that have committed violations, thereby ensuring their right to choose child-care institutions and ultimately protecting the mind and body of infants and young children and fostering them through sound education into healthy members of society; therefore, its legitimacy of purpose is recognized.\\n\\nIf the provision subject to adjudication requires public disclosure of facts of violation concerning child-care centers that received subsidies or diverted subsidies through false or other improper means, it can promote transparent operation of child-care centers by causing their operators to use subsidies properly in accordance with their purpose, and can provide practical assistance to guardians of infants and young children in choosing child-care institutions; therefore, appropriateness of means is also recognized.\\n\\n(2) Minimum Impairment\\n\\n(a) With the expansion of women’s participation in society and the shift to nuclear families, the importance of child-care centers, which are institutions that protect and nurture infants and young children entrusted by guardians, has increased, and accordingly the State and local governments greatly expanded financial support for them as part of policies to secure the public nature of infant and young child care. However, as subsidies related to the operation of child-care centers increased, child-care centers that exploited loopholes in the policy to receive subsidies unlawfully or to use them for purposes other than intended also increased.\\n\\nFraudulent receipt and diversion of subsidies are directly connected to the morality of child-care center operators and, in turn, may lead to inadequate child-care environments; therefore, there is a significant need to allow guardians of infants and young children to know of such matters. However, the existing system did not provide a means of supplying guardians of infants and young children with information regarding child-care centers that violated the law, in addition to suspension of operation, closure, or imposition of penalty surcharges. In cases where a child-care center received an order of suspension of operation or closure due to fraudulent receipt or diversion of subsidies, the center could again be established and operated after the suspension period ended or after five years had passed from the order of closure, and where a penalty surcharge disposition was imposed in lieu of suspension of operation, the child-care center could continue to operate; thus, guardians of infants and young children chose child-care centers without knowing that there had been a violation.\\n\\nThe former Infant Care Act before amendment by Act No. 11858 on 2013. 6. 4. and before amendment by Act No. 13321 on 2015. 5. 18. provided that the Minister of Health and Welfare, etc. could publicly disclose facts of violation by child-care centers in order to curb fraudulent receipt and diversion of subsidies by taking into account the motive, degree, frequency, and result of the violation; however, as the decision whether to disclose was left to the discretion of the administrative agency, only a small number of child-care centers were actually publicly disclosed, and the number of child-care centers fraudulently receiving or diverting subsidies and the scale of such subsidies continued to increase. Accordingly, the purpose of having such a provision in the Infant Care Act was not sufficiently achieved.\\n\\nTherefore, in order to ensure the transparent operation of child-care centers and to effectively guarantee the right of guardians of infants and young children to choose child-care institutions, it was necessary to publicly disclose the list of child-care centers that fraudulently received or diverted subsidies, and thus a discretionary public disclosure system was introduced in 2013; however, as it did not produce any significant results, a mandatory public disclosure system like the provision subject to adjudication was introduced.\\n\\n(b) The provision subject to adjudication does not designate all child-care centers that fraudulently received or diverted subsidies as subject to disclosure, but rather limits the subject to cases where the amount of subsidies received or diverted through false or other improper means is KRW 3 million or more for a single violation, or where the cumulative amount is KRW 2 million or more due to two or more violations in the most recent three years (Article 39-2 of the former Enforcement Rules of the Infant Care Act). The information publicly disclosed pursuant to the provision subject to adjudication is limited to information of public value that guardians of infants and young children must minimally receive in order to choose a child-care center, such as the violation, the contents of the disposition, the name of the child-care center, and the names of the representative and director, and no personal information that may hinder daily life, such as the private address or telephone number of the person subject to disclosure, is disclosed (provision subject to adjudication; Article 25-7(1) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Infant Care Act). The period of disclosure is also limited to three years in cases of violations corresponding to an order of closure of a child-care center, and to a period corresponding to twice the period of suspension of operation in cases of violations corresponding to suspension of operation (since the period of suspension of operation is up to one year, the period of disclosure is up to two years) (Article 25-8(4) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Infant Care Act; Article 38(1) and (2) of the former Enforcement Rules of the Infant Care Act).\\n\\n(c) Although the provision subject to adjudication provides that facts of violation shall mandatorily be publicly disclosed when the requirements are met, the suspension of operation, order of closure, or penalty surcharge disposition that serves as the premise for public disclosure is stipulated as discretionary (Articles 45 and 45-2 of the Infant Care Act), and therefore specific equity may be achieved in the prior disposition process according to the content and seriousness of the facts of violation, etc.\\n\\n(d) In addition, the Infant Care Act provides that the Minister of Health and Welfare, etc., before implementing public disclosure, must notify the person subject to disclosure in writing that he or she is subject to disclosure and must grant an opportunity to submit materials explaining the matter or to appear and state opinions (Article 49-3(3) of the Infant Care Act; Article 25-8(2) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Infant Care Act), thereby also establishing a mechanism to minimize the infringement of fundamental rights by ensuring the procedural rights of the person subject to disclosure.\\n\\n(e) Taking the foregoing circumstances together, the provision subject to adjudication satisfies the requirement of minimum impairment.\\n\\n(3) Balance of Interests\\n\\nAlthough the person subject to disclosure suffers the disadvantage that the fact of his or her legal violation is publicly disclosed externally for a certain period of time due to the provision subject to adjudication, this cannot be viewed as more serious than the public interest of ensuring the substantial operation of the subsidy system in order to promote the healthy growth of infants and young children and guarantee the right of guardians of infants and young children to choose child-care institutions. Accordingly, the provision subject to adjudication also satisfies the balance of interests.\\n\\n(4) Conclusion\\n\\nThe provision subject to adjudication does not infringe the petitioner’s personality right and right to self-determination over personal information in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, since the provision subject to adjudication is not contrary to the Constitution, the Court, with the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating, renders the decision as stated in the order."}

question: Which of the following is the correct combination of the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (×) regarding the right to a trial? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents.) (a) Even if a statute provides that a lawsuit seeking revocation of a disciplinary disposition by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court against a judge shall be tried by the Supreme Court as a single-instance trial, this can be deemed reasonable because it is intended to promote the promptness of adjudication in light of the status of a judge and the special nature of disciplinary proceedings against judges; therefore, it cannot be said that the judge’s right to a trial is thereby infringed. (b) Since seized articles exist for the benefit of the prosecutor who seeks to prove the facts charged, the act of investigative authorities arbitrarily disposing of articles seized in the course of an arrest of a flagrant offender, but without the defendant’s waiver of ownership, cannot be deemed to infringe the defendant’s right to a fair trial. (c) Since extradition proceedings are inherently criminal-procedure in nature, and criminal procedure as a trial procedure naturally includes procedures for challenge to a higher court, a statutory provision that places extradition review under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Seoul High Court and does not recognize a procedure for challenge to the Supreme Court infringes the extraditable person’s right to a trial. (d) Because granting the defendant a right of access to the trial procedure concerning medical treatment and custody is deemed necessary in order to more effectively secure the defendant’s rights, the “right of the defendant himself or herself to request medical treatment and custody” is also included within the scope of protection of the right to a trial.

{"[2009HEONBA34]": "1. Overview of the Case and Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nA. Overview of the Case\\n\\n(1) The Petitioner was serving as a Presiding Judge of the Seoul ○○ District Court. The Supreme Court Judges Disciplinary Committee (hereinafter referred to as the “Committee”) held a disciplinary committee meeting concerning the Petitioner on 2007. 10. 5. and, on the ground that the Petitioner, disregarding repeated instructions to restrain himself through oral warnings and written warnings by the chief judge of the court to which he belonged, persistently repeated, over a period of 6 months from 2007. 2. 20. and on more than 20 occasions, assertions that went beyond the limits of legitimate expression of opinion as a judge, not only inside the court but also to outside news media, and expressed himself in extreme terms, thereby determining that the Petitioner’s conduct fell under the “case where a judge damages his dignity or tarnishes the prestige of the court” prescribed in Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges, and rendered a disciplinary decision of suspension for 2 months (hereinafter referred to as “the disciplinary decision in this case”); and the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, on 2007. 10. 12., imposed, pursuant to the above disciplinary decision, a disciplinary disposition of suspension for 2 months on the Petitioner as of the 18th of the same month.\\n\\n(2) Accordingly, the Petitioner instituted an action for confirmation of nullity and revocation of the disciplinary disposition under Supreme Court case No. 2007CHU127, and, during the pendency of the above action, filed with the Supreme Court an application for referral of a constitutional review of statutes (2008A20) with respect to Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges, which prescribes the grounds for disciplinary action against judges, and Article 27 of the same Act, which provides that an action challenging a disciplinary disposition against a judge shall fall under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and be tried in a single instance; however, when the Supreme Court dismissed both the above claim and the application for referral on 2009. 1. 30., the Petitioner filed the constitutional complaint review in this case on 2009. 2. 26.\\n\\nB. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues that Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges is unconstitutional insofar as it applies to a judge’s expressive acts; however, in light of the fact that the Petitioner takes as the ground of unconstitutionality that the relevant statutory provision, by using vague concepts, infringes the freedom of expression of judges in violation of the principle of clarity and the principle against excessive restriction, it is reasonable to view this as disputing not the court’s interpretation and application of the statute with respect to the said statutory provision, but the unconstitutionality of the statutory provision itself.\\n\\nAccordingly, the subject matter of review in this case is whether Article 2, Item 2 and Article 27 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges (as amended by Act No. 5642 on 1999. 1. 21. and before amendment by Act No. 10578 on 2011. 4. 12.) are unconstitutional, and the contents of the provisions subject to review in this case and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Review]\\n\\nFormer Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges (as amended by Act No. 5642 on 1999. 1. 21. and before amendment by Act No. 10578 on 2011. 4. 12.)  \\nArticle 2 (Grounds for Disciplinary Action) The grounds for disciplinary action against a judge shall be as follows:\\n\\n2. Where a judge damages his dignity or tarnishes the prestige of the court\\n\\nArticle 27 (Procedure for Objection) ① Where the respondent intends to object to a disciplinary disposition, he shall, within 14 days from the date on which he became aware that the disciplinary disposition was made, file with the Supreme Court a petition for revocation of the disciplinary disposition without going through prior proceedings.\\n\\n② The Supreme Court shall adjudicate the case on the petition for revocation under paragraph (1) in a single instance.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nFormer Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges (as amended by Act No. 8058 on 2006. 10. 27. and before amendment by Act No. 10578 on 2011. 4. 12.)  \\nArticle 4 (Judges Disciplinary Committee) ① A Judges Disciplinary Committee shall be established in the Supreme Court in order to deliberate and decide disciplinary cases concerning judges.\\n\\n② The Committee shall consist of one chairperson and 6 members, and 3 substitute members shall be appointed.\\n\\nFormer Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges (as amended by Act No. 5642 on 1999. 1. 21. and before amendment by Act No. 10578 on 2011. 4. 12.)  \\nArticle 7 (Request for Disciplinary Action and Commencement of Disciplinary Deliberation) ① The Committee’s deliberation on disciplinary action shall be commenced upon a request for disciplinary action by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, Justices of the Supreme Court, or, with respect to the judge concerned, the Director General of the Court Administration Office, the Dean of the Judicial Research and Training Institute, the Chief Judges of the respective courts, or the Director of the Court Library, who have supervisory authority over judicial administration affairs pursuant to the Court Organization Act.\\n\\nArticle 24 (Committee’s Decision on Disciplinary Action) Upon conclusion of the deliberation, the Committee shall make one of the following decisions:\\n\\n1. Where there are grounds for disciplinary action and it is deemed reasonable to impose a disciplinary disposition thereon, a decision to impose an appropriate disciplinary disposition by comprehensively considering the seriousness of the grounds for disciplinary action, the respondent’s work performance, merits, remorse, and all other circumstances. Provided, That where it is deemed reasonable not to impose a disciplinary disposition, a decision of no action may be made.\\n\\n2. Where the grounds for disciplinary action are not recognized, a decision of no fault\\n\\nArticle 26 (Disciplinary Disposition and Execution) ① The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court shall impose and execute a disciplinary disposition in accordance with the Committee’s decision.\\n\\n② When the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court imposes a disciplinary disposition, he shall publish it in the Official Gazette.\\n\\n2. Summary of the Petitioner’s Claims and the Court’s Reasons for Dismissing the Application for Constitutional Review\\n\\nA. Summary of the Petitioner’s Claims\\n\\n(1) Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges provides for the imposition of a disciplinary disposition by making vague concepts such as “damage to dignity” or “tarnishing of prestige” the constituent elements of the offense; when the said statutory provision is applied to a judge’s expressive acts, and to a judge’s expressive acts criticizing the judiciary from within, it excessively and broadly restricts a judge’s freedom of expression, thereby violating the constitutional principle of clarity and the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n(2) Article 27 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges, by providing that an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge shall be adjudicated in a single instance by the Supreme Court, which is a court of law, discriminates against judges without reasonable basis as compared with other professionals such as prosecutors, attorneys, law professors, doctors, certified public accountants, tax accountants, and architects who challenge disciplinary dispositions, and deprives judges of the opportunity for fact-finding and application of law by judges, thereby infringing the right to equality and the right to receive a trial by judges.\\n\\nB. Summary of the Court’s Reasons for Dismissing the Application for Constitutional Review\\n\\n(1) Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges, by providing as grounds for disciplinary action against a judge “where a judge damages his dignity or tarnishes the prestige of the court,” uses abstract terms such as “damage to dignity” and “tarnishing of prestige,” but a judge, who is a legal expert, can without difficulty know what conduct falls thereunder; therefore, the said provision does not contravene the principle of clarity. Furthermore, the said provision is intended to achieve the objective of securing public trust in judges, and cannot be said to excessively restrict the constitutional right of judges to freedom of expression.\\n\\n(2) Article 27 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges is based on a public interest demand for prompt handling of disciplinary cases against judges in light of the special status of judges exercising judicial power, and does not infringe the constitutional principle of equality or the right to file a petition for trial.\\n\\n3. Determination on the Merits\\n\\nA. Judges’ Disciplinary System\\n\\nArticle 106, paragraph 1 of the Constitution provides that “A judge shall not be removed from office except by impeachment or a sentence of imprisonment without labor or heavier punishment, and shall not be suspended from office, have his salary reduced, or suffer any other adverse disposition except by disciplinary action.” Thus, while limiting removal from office of judges and thereby guaranteeing the status of judges, which is essential to the independence of trials, it also permits adverse dispositions such as suspension by disciplinary action in order to secure the dignity and faithful performance of duties as a judge.\\n\\nAccording to the Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges, which regulates discipline of judges, the grounds for disciplinary action are where a judge violates his official duties or neglects his duties, or where a judge damages his dignity or tarnishes the prestige of the court (Article 2); the types of disciplinary dispositions are suspension, reduction in salary, and reprimand (Article 3); and the deliberation and decision on disciplinary cases are made by the Judges Disciplinary Committee (Article 4).\\n\\nThe Judges Disciplinary Committee is established in the Supreme Court, consists of one chairperson, 6 members, and 3 substitute members (Article 4); the chairperson is appointed from among the Justices of the Supreme Court, the members are appointed by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, one each from among 3 judges, a lawyer, a law professor, and another person of broad learning and experience, and the substitute members are each appointed from among judges (Article 5); the Committee’s deliberation on disciplinary action is commenced by a request for disciplinary action by ① the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, ② Justices of the Supreme Court, or ③, with respect to the judge concerned, the Director General of the Court Administration Office, the Dean of the Judicial Research and Training Institute, the Chief Judges of the respective courts, or the Director of the Court Library, who have supervisory authority over judicial administration affairs pursuant to the Court Organization Act (Article 7); and where the Committee, with the attendance of a majority of members and with the consent of a majority of the members present, renders a decision to impose a disciplinary disposition (Articles 23 and 24), the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court shall impose and execute the disciplinary disposition according to the Committee’s decision (Article 26).\\n\\nWhere the respondent intends to object to a disciplinary disposition, he shall, within 14 days from the date on which he became aware that the disciplinary disposition was made, file with the Supreme Court a petition for revocation of the disciplinary disposition without going through prior proceedings, and the Supreme Court shall adjudicate this in a single instance (Article 27). At the time of the enactment of the Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges, no separate procedure for objection to disciplinary dispositions against judges was provided, thereby giving rise to doctrinal debate as to whether prior proceedings by petition and administrative litigation were available by analogy to state public officials; this was legislatively resolved when the Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges was amended by Act No. 5642 on 1999. 1. 21. and Article 27 newly established the above objection procedure.\\n\\nB. Whether Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges Is Unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Whether it Violates the Principle of Clarity\\n\\nArticle 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges, as a ground for disciplinary action against a judge, provides for “where a judge damages his dignity or tarnishes the prestige of the court,” and uses abstract terms such as “damage to dignity” and “tarnishing of prestige”; the issue is whether the use of such terms violates the constitutional principle of clarity and infringes freedom of expression.\\n\\nThe principle of clarity means the principle of prescribing laws and regulations in clear terms so as to give fair notice to the addressees of the norm, that is, the subjects of regulation, of the contents of the regulation in advance and thereby provide guidance for future conduct, and at the same time to give objective standards for judgment to law-enforcement authorities so as to prevent discriminatory or arbitrary interpretation and enforcement of the law; it is a principle required of all legislation restricting fundamental rights based on the principles of democracy and the rule of law (see Constitutional Court 2010. 10. 28. 2008HEONMA638, Decisions Collection 22-2, Part II, 216, 228). Whether a legal norm is clear may be determined depending on whether the legal norm gives fair notice to the addressee so that the meaning and content of the law can be known, thereby providing predictability, and whether it sufficiently regulates the content for the agencies interpreting and enforcing the law so that arbitrary interpretation or enforcement is excluded; in other words, whether predictability and exclusion of arbitrary law enforcement are secured. Since the meaning and content of a legal norm are concretized by an interpretive method that comprehensively considers not only the wording but also the legislative purpose, legislative intent, legislative history, and the systematic structure of the legal norm, whether a legal norm violates the principle of clarity ultimately depends on whether an interpretive standard that can rationally ascertain the meaning and content thereof can be derived through the above interpretive method (see Constitutional Court 2009. 5. 28. 2006HEONBA109 et al., Decisions Collection 21-1, Part II, 545, 561). Further, the requirement that a law and regulation as a conduct norm for the addressee be clear does not mean that every ordinary citizen must clearly understand its meaning; it is sufficient if the average person in society can understand its meaning and be informed of the risk of violation, and in the case of laws and regulations applicable only to persons residing in a particular status, occupation, or region, the standard should be the average person among those persons.\\n\\nThe legislative intent of Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges is, taking into account that a judge has legal and ethical obligations to ensure that, as the subject of judicial power that guarantees fundamental human rights and realizes judicial justice, he does not engage in conduct contrary to fairness and neutrality, regardless of whether inside or outside his official duties, and to gain the trust and respect of the people by protecting the independence of judicial power, the authority of the courts, and the honor of judges as a member of the court, to secure public trust in the courts and judges by causing judges to exercise caution in words and conduct likely to undermine public trust in the judge himself as well as in the court as a whole.\\n\\nMeanwhile, in dictionary terms, “dignity” refers to the combination of one’s status and position, and means the dignity or grace a person should have, or the lofty and elevated impression possessed by a thing; “prestige” means dignity and trust; and “damage” or “tarnish” means to diminish or impair the above dignity or prestige.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court has held, with respect to the meaning of “dignity” that a public official must maintain under Article 63 of the State Public Officials Act, which imposes on public officials a duty to maintain dignity, that it means “personality appropriate to carrying out duties as the agent of the sovereign people” (see Supreme Court 1998. 2. 27. Decision 97NU18172, Supreme Court Reports 1998. 4. 1. (55), 926), and with respect to the meaning of “dignity as a teacher” under Article 61, paragraph 1, Item 3 of the Private School Act, which prescribes grounds for disciplinary action against teachers at private schools, has held that it means “personality appropriate to carrying out duties as an educator to the people” (see Supreme Court 2000. 6. 9. Decision 98DU16613, Supreme Court Reports 2000. 8. 1. (111), 1666).\\n\\nTaking the above legislative intent, the dictionary meaning of the terms, and the court’s statutory interpretations in analogous cases together, the phrase in Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges, “where a judge damages his dignity or tarnishes the prestige of the court,” may be interpreted to mean “where a judge engages in conduct that is inappropriate to the personality suitable for exercising judicial power entrusted by the sovereign people, or engages in conduct that impairs the dignity of the court, thereby causing concern that public trust in the court and judges will be undermined.” And what specific conduct falls thereunder should be determined based on the average judge, the addressee of the said statutory provision; in light of the fact that judges are professionals who pass the state-certified bar examination and receive highly specialized education and possess not only expert knowledge of law but also a high level of moral and ethical cultivation, the average judge, including the Petitioner, can sufficiently foresee this.\\n\\nAccordingly, Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges cannot be said to fail to provide guidance for conduct to the addressee or to permit arbitrary interpretation or enforcement by law-enforcement authorities; therefore, it does not violate the principle of clarity.\\n\\n(2) Whether it Violates the Principle Against Excessive Restriction\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues that Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges, by restricting judges’ freedom of expression on the premise of vague concepts such as “damage to dignity” and “tarnishing of prestige,” necessarily suppresses expressive acts by judges for internal judicial reform, etc., by restricting together all expressions that should not be restricted due to the ambiguity, abstraction, and comprehensiveness of those concepts, and thus violates the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\nThe above argument is that there is a loss of proportionality between the legislative purpose of Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges and the means employed, namely, that it infringes fundamental rights by setting an excessively broad and comprehensive scope of application beyond what is necessary to achieve the legislative purpose. Ultimately, the issue is whether the scope of application of the said statutory provision is excessively broad and comprehensive so as to infringe a judge’s freedom of expression in violation of the constitutional principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\nUpon examination, although the said statutory provision uses abstract terms such as “damage to dignity” and “tarnishing of prestige,” as noted above, its scope of application cannot be said to be so vague or unclear that it is impossible to sufficiently foresee what specific conduct falls thereunder.\\n\\nA judge, too, as a holder of fundamental rights, should be guaranteed freedom of expression; however, a judge’s freedom of expression may be restricted to maintain fairness and neutrality in the exercise of judicial power by the courts and judges and to secure public trust therein, and the grounds for disciplinary action prescribed in Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges restrict only conduct that damages a judge’s dignity or tarnishes the prestige of the court in order to achieve such purpose. Even in expressive acts by judges for internal judicial reform, etc., the mere fact that such expressive act was made does not in itself become a ground for discipline under the said statutory provision; only where, considering all circumstances such as the time and place of the expressive act, the content and method of the expression, and the counterparty to the act, it falls under conduct that damages a judge’s dignity or tarnishes the prestige of the court, does it become a ground for disciplinary action.\\n\\nAccordingly, Article 2, Item 2 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges is not so excessively broad or comprehensive in its scope of application as to excessively restrict a judge’s freedom of expression; therefore, it does not violate the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\nC. Whether Article 27 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges Is Unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Whether it Infringes the Right to Petition for Trial\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues that Article 27 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges, by providing that an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge shall be adjudicated in a single instance by the Supreme Court, which is a court of law, deprives judges of the opportunity for fact-finding and application of law by judges, thereby infringing the constitutional right to receive a trial by judges.\\n\\nUpon examination, Article 27, paragraph 1 of the Constitution provides that “All citizens shall have the right to a trial in accordance with the law by judges qualified under the Constitution and the law,” and a trial is a series of processes whose essential content consists of fact-finding concerning a concrete case and the interpretation and application of law thereto; thus, guaranteeing the right to receive a trial by judges means guaranteeing the right to receive a trial in which judges determine the facts and interpret and apply the law (see Constitutional Court 2002. 2. 28. 2001HEONGA18, Decisions Collection 14-1, 98, 103). Furthermore, in order to guarantee the right to petition for trial prescribed in Article 27, paragraph 1 of the Constitution, concrete formation of the right to petition for trial by the legislature is inevitable, and therefore the legislature is accorded broad legislative discretion (see Constitutional Court 2009. 2. 26. 2007HEONBA8, Decisions Collection 21-1, Part I, 45, 52-53), and the multi-tiered court system also, as a matter of how to harmonize the two conflicting demands of the properness and promptness of trial while reasonably allocating limited judicial resources with respect to judicial protection of rights, is in principle a matter belonging to the legislature’s freedom of formation (see Constitutional Court 2007. 7. 26. 2006HEONMA1447 et al.).\\n\\nBecause disciplinary procedures against judges have a large impact on the general public, they need to be concluded promptly, and a disciplinary disposition by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court against a judge is, unlike other administrative dispositions, subject, as a prior stage to the disposition, to deliberation and decision by the quasi-judicial procedure of the Judges Disciplinary Committee. Moreover, unlike the case of a disposition refusing reappointment of a judge or a disposition refusing appointment, etc., in which the status of the judge is determined to be lost by the disposition, in the case of a disciplinary disposition the judge’s status continues to be maintained even if the disposition is received, so there is a much stronger need to resolve the objection procedure expeditiously, and taking into account the difficulty in practice of trying a case against the Chief Justice’s disposition from the first instance in the lower courts, the legislature provides that an action to revoke the Chief Justice’s disciplinary disposition against a judge shall be adjudicated in a single instance by the Supreme Court. This can be recognized as rational, as the legislature sought promptness of trial in consideration of the special status of judges who independently exercise judicial power and the special characteristics of disciplinary procedures against judges.\\n\\nAnd when the Supreme Court adjudicates an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge in a single instance, unlike other trials as a court of law that do not involve fact-finding as a court of final appeal, there is no restriction on the scope of review, so fact-finding also falls within the Supreme Court’s authority; thus, it cannot be said that the opportunity for fact-finding by a judge has been deprived.\\n\\nAccordingly, even if Article 27 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges provides that the Supreme Court shall adjudicate in a single instance an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge, this is a legislative act within the legislature’s proper discretion, and it cannot be said that the legislative discretion was exercised in a manifestly unreasonable or arbitrary manner; therefore, it cannot be said to violate Article 27, paragraph 1 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Whether it Infringes the Right to Equality\\n\\nUnlike the fact that an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against other professionals such as prosecutors, attorneys, law professors, doctors, certified public accountants, tax accountants, and architects is subject to a three-tier court system, Article 27 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges provides that an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge shall be adjudicated in a single instance by the Supreme Court, thereby treating judges differently from other professionals.\\n\\nHowever, considering that the deliberation and decision on disciplinary action against a judge are made by the Judges Disciplinary Committee, in which judges constitute the majority, through quasi-judicial procedures such as statements of opinion and submission of evidence by the respondent and the complainant requesting disciplinary action, appraisal, examination of witnesses, and inquiry of facts (Articles 14 and 16 of the Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges); that in the case of discipline against judges there is no severe disciplinary disposition that changes the status relationship itself, such as removal from office, dismissal, or discharge; that judges are persons who independently exercise judicial power and thus need their status to be stabilized as soon as possible; and that an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge can only be conducted by a judge who has the same status as the disciplined person, there is a rational basis for this differential treatment, and it cannot be said to infringe the Petitioner’s constitutional right to equality.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, since Article 2, Item 2 and Article 27 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges do not violate the Constitution, the decision is made as stated in the order by the unanimous opinion of the remaining participating Justices, except for the supplementary opinions of Justice Lee Dong-heub and Justice Mok Young-jun regarding Article 27 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges as set forth in 5. below.\\n\\n5. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Lee Dong-heub and Justice Mok Young-jun\\n\\nWe agree with the conclusion of the majority opinion that Article 27 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges does not violate the Constitution, but we express the following supplementary opinion because, as follows, the said statutory provision is insufficient to substantially guarantee the right to petition for trial under Article 27, paragraph 1 of the Constitution, and legislative improvement is appropriate.\\n\\nIn order to guarantee the right to petition for trial prescribed in Article 27, paragraph 1 of the Constitution, concrete formation of the right to petition for trial by the legislature is inevitable, and thus the legislature is accorded broad legislative discretion; however, such legislative discretion also has limits and must be exercised within the bounds that do not contravene constitutional provisions or constitutional principles. Meanwhile, Article 103 of the Constitution provides that “Judges shall adjudicate independently according to their conscience and in accordance with the Constitution and the law,” thereby declaring the judicial independence of judges as a constitutional principle, and judicial independence includes not only independence from external pressure or influence but also autonomous adjudication independent from internal pressure or influence within the court. Therefore, when the legislature enacts legislation to guarantee the right to petition for trial under Article 27, paragraph 1 of the Constitution, it must ensure the right to receive a trial by a “judge independent from pressure or influence within the court.” Accordingly, although the formation of the multi-tiered court system concerning an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge belongs to the legislature’s freedom of formation with respect to the right to petition for trial, if the disciplined person is not afforded an opportunity to receive a trial regarding the disciplinary disposition by a judge independent from pressure or influence within the court, it cannot be said that the right to petition for trial under Article 27, paragraph 1 of the Constitution is substantially guaranteed.\\n\\nUpon examination, the multi-tiered court system is, in principle, a matter belonging to the legislature’s freedom of formation, and an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge has the special characteristic that both the parties and the adjudicating person are judges, and the subject matter of the lawsuit is the legality of the Chief Justice’s disciplinary disposition, so it must ultimately go through a trial by the Supreme Court, which is the court of final appeal; therefore, it cannot be said that Article 27 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges, which provides that an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge shall be adjudicated in a single instance by the Supreme Court, is an unconstitutional law that has gone beyond the limits of legislative discretion.\\n\\nHowever, the Judges Disciplinary Committee, which deliberates and decides whether to discipline a judge, has all 7 members appointed by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, and among them judges constitute the majority with 4 members, including a Justice of the Supreme Court who serves as chairperson, and because the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court is in a position to direct and supervise judges with respect to judicial administration affairs (Article 9, paragraph 1 of the Court Organization Act), there is a possibility that the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court may greatly influence the decision-making of the committee members when deciding whether to discipline a judge in the Judges Disciplinary Committee. Moreover, since the trial of the Supreme Court is participated in by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court and the Justice of the Supreme Court who is the chairperson of the Judges Disciplinary Committee, if an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge is tried in a single instance by the Supreme Court, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court and the Justice who is the chairperson of the Judges Disciplinary Committee will inevitably be able to influence the outcome of the trial, and thus there is concern that judicial review of the disciplinary disposition is in fact not conducted independently from internal influence. Therefore, in order to substantially guarantee the disciplined judge’s right to petition for trial, it is necessary to reduce the influence of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court in the disciplinary disposition procedure or to guarantee a trial by a court on which the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court and the Justice who is the chairperson of the Judges Disciplinary Committee do not exert influence in the objection procedure against the disciplinary disposition.\\n\\nAs a means to reduce the influence of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court in the disciplinary disposition procedure, one may consider, as seen in the legislative examples of advanced foreign countries, limiting the Chief Justice’s authority to appoint committee members by structuring the Judges Disciplinary Committee so that judges do not comprise a majority, and so that judge-members, other than the chairperson, are elected as representatives by each level of judges, such as chief judges, district court judges, and high court judges, while non-judge members are nominated by outside institutions.\\n\\nAs a means to guarantee a trial by a court on which the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court and the Justice who is the chairperson of the Judges Disciplinary Committee do not exert influence in the objection procedure against the disciplinary disposition, one may consider making an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge subject not to a single-instance system by the Supreme Court, but to a two-instance system. Although the Supreme Court is the highest-level court composed of Justices including the Chief Justice, and therefore even an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge cannot ultimately avoid being tried by the Supreme Court, it is because at least one opportunity should be afforded for a trial regarding the disciplinary disposition by a judge who is not the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court or a member of the Judges Disciplinary Committee.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that the legislature’s choice to make an action to revoke a disciplinary disposition against a judge subject to single-instance review by the Supreme Court can be recognized as rational because disciplinary procedures against judges need to be concluded promptly due to their great impact on the general public, are carried out through the deliberation and decision of the Judges Disciplinary Committee, which is a quasi-judicial procedure, and because judges continue to retain their status even if disciplined, there is a strong need to resolve the objection procedure as soon as possible, and it is difficult in practice to conduct a trial from the first instance in the lower courts against a disposition by the Chief Justice.\\n\\nHowever, what greatly affects the general public is the conduct of the judge that constitutes a ground for discipline, not the disciplinary procedure against the judge itself, so it cannot be said that the disciplinary procedure needs to be concluded promptly because of its influence on the public. Rather, in light of the Constitution’s intent to guarantee the status of judges, careful handling rather than prompt handling should be considered more important in discipline of judges; and since the Supreme Court, being primarily a court of law, has a structure more suitable for the application of law than for fact-finding, it is necessary, for a thorough hearing on the existence or nonexistence of the facts constituting the disciplinary grounds, for an action to revoke the disciplinary disposition to be heard in a lower court with a structure more suitable for fact-finding. Even if the respondent in the above action to revoke is the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, who has supervisory authority over judicial administration affairs concerning judges, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court as the respondent in the above action to revoke is merely the subject of an administrative disposition and has no official relevance to judges who exercise judicial power through trial; moreover, the influence of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court is greater in the Supreme Court, where the Chief Justice participates directly in the trial, than in lower courts, so it may also be viewed as more desirable for the guarantee of the disciplined person’s right to petition for trial that the lower courts conduct the trial in such an action.\\n\\nAccordingly, although Article 27 of the former Act on Disciplinary Proceedings Against Judges does not rise to the level that it should be declared unconstitutional, it appears insufficient to guarantee the disciplined judge’s right to petition for trial; therefore, we wish to point out that the legislature should make efforts to improve the legislation by taking into account the above-mentioned measures and the like so as to reduce the influence of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court in disciplinary procedures against judges."}

{"[2011HEONMA351]": "1. Overview of the Case and Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\na. Overview of the Case\\n\\n(1) On 2010. 11. 20., while the Petitioner was being arrested in flagrante delicto on charges of preparation for robbery and preparation for arson of an inhabited building, inside a ○○ store located at 355-1, ○○-dong, Wonmi-gu, Bucheon, the Petitioner voluntarily submitted to a police officer affiliated with the Gyeonggi Bucheon Wonmi Police Station one plastic water bottle, one fruit knife, one school bag, and one disposable lighter (hereinafter referred to as “the seized items in this case”), which the police officer seized. In this process, the police officer also received from the Petitioner one pack of psychiatric medication in the Petitioner’s possession (quantity unknown) and one Taekwondo handbook (hereinafter referred to as “the entrusted items in this case”) and kept them in custody.\\n\\n(2) The Petitioner was indicted before the Bucheon Branch of the Incheon District Court under 2011GOHAP36 and 2011GAMGO4 (consolidated) for preparation for robbery and preparation for arson of an inhabited building, and medical treatment and custody was also requested. As a result of the hearing, on 2011. 7. 22., with respect to the charge of preparation for robbery, it was found to fall under a case where proof of the crime was absent, and with respect to the charge of preparation for arson of an inhabited building, it was found to fall under a case where punishment was not permissible under Article 10, paragraph (1) of the Criminal Act, and thus judgments of acquittal were each rendered. However, determining that there was a risk of recidivism, a judgment was rendered that the Petitioner be subjected to medical treatment and custody. Against this, the prosecutor appealed (Seoul High Court 2011NO2195), but the appeal was dismissed and the above judgment became final and conclusive.\\n\\n(3) During the first-instance trial, around 2011. 4. 22., the Petitioner filed a request for inspection regarding the fruit knife among the seized items in this case in order to dispute acquittal on the charge of preparation for robbery, and came to learn that the Respondent, under the direction of the investigating prosecutor around 2010. 12. 20., had destroyed all of the seized items in this case, and that at that time the entrusted items in this case had also been destroyed together.\\n\\n(4) Accordingly, on 2011. 5. 18., the Petitioner filed an application for appointment of state-appointed counsel to file the present constitutional complaint adjudication, and the state-appointed counsel thus appointed filed this constitutional complaint adjudication on 2011. 7. 5., seeking revocation of the Respondent’s act of destroying the seized items in this case on the ground that it infringed the Petitioner’s right to a fair trial, etc., and seeking a confirmation of unconstitutionality of omission on the ground that the Petitioner’s property right was infringed by the omission of failing properly to keep the entrusted items in this case.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues that the Respondent’s act of destroying “the entrusted items in this case” constitutes a case in which the State, which must guarantee an individual’s property right, failed to discharge its duty to act and thereby infringed the Petitioner’s property right, and thus seeks a confirmation of unconstitutionality regarding that omission. However, an omission that may become the subject of a constitutional complaint refers to a case where the subject of public power is under a duty to act derived from the Constitution, and that duty to act is specially and concretely prescribed such that the holder of a fundamental right may request an administrative act, yet the subject of public power neglects that duty (Constitutional Court 1996. 11. 28. 92HEONMA237, Court Cases 8-2, 600, 606). In the present case, the duty to keep the entrusted items in this case cannot be evaluated as a duty to act derived from the Constitution.
