Accordingly, the Respondent’s act of destroying the entrusted items in this case cannot be regarded as an act by omission, and thus the petition for adjudication on this point is construed as seeking a confirmation of unconstitutionality of the act of destroying the entrusted items in this case itself.\\n\\nIf so, the subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether the Respondent’s act of destroying the seized items in this case on 2010. 12. 20. (hereinafter referred to as “the act of destroying the seized items in this case”) and the act of destroying the entrusted items in this case around that time (hereinafter referred to as “the act of destroying the entrusted items in this case”) each infringe the Petitioner’s fundamental rights, and the contents of the relevant statutory provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Relevant Statutory Provisions]\\n\\nCriminal Procedure Act (enacted by Act No. 341 on 1954. 9. 23.) Article 218 (Seizure Without Warrant) A prosecutor or a judicial police officer may seize without a warrant things abandoned by a suspect or any other person, or things voluntarily submitted by the owner, possessor, or custodian.\\n\\nCriminal Procedure Act (amended by Act No. 7496 on 2007. 6. 1. and before amendment by Act No. 10864 on 2011. 7. 18.)\\nArticle 219 (Provisions Applied Mutatis Mutandis) The provisions of Articles 106, 107, 109 through 112, 114, 115(1) main clause, 2, 118 through 135, 140, 141, 333(2), and 486 shall apply mutatis mutandis to a seizure, search, or inspection by a prosecutor or judicial police officer under this Chapter. Provided, That in making dispositions pursuant to Articles 130 and 132 through 134, a judicial police officer shall follow the direction of a prosecutor.\\n\\nCriminal Procedure Act (enacted by Act No. 341 on 1954. 9. 23.)\\nArticle 130 (Custody and Disposal of Seized Articles)\\n(2) Seized articles that are likely to pose a danger may be destroyed.\\n\\n2. Summary of the Parties’ Arguments\\n\\na. Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\n(1) Because the Respondent’s act of destroying the seized items without the Petitioner’s consent prevented important evidence from being used as evidence of acquittal, it infringed the Petitioner’s right to a fair trial. Furthermore, although the seized items in this case posed no likelihood of danger, the Respondent arbitrarily destroyed them; this infringed the Petitioner’s property right.\\n\\n(2) Although the Respondent was responsible for keeping the entrusted items in this case with the duty of care of a good manager, the Respondent violated that duty and destroyed them; this constituted an infringement of the Petitioner’s property right by the State, which must guarantee an individual’s property right, in violation of its duty.\\n\\nb. Summary of the Respondent’s Arguments\\n\\nWhen preparing the suspect interrogation report against the Petitioner, the Respondent asked the Petitioner whether the Petitioner intended to have the seized items in this case returned, confirmed from the Petitioner that there was no intention to receive them back, and obtained a waiver of ownership, thereby destroying the seized items in this case. At the time the waiver of ownership regarding the seized items in this case was obtained, the Respondent also asked whether there was an intention to receive the entrusted items in this case back together, and the Petitioner stated that there was no intention to receive them back, and thus they were destroyed together with the seized items in this case.\\n\\nAs such, because both the destruction of the seized items in this case and the entrusted items in this case were carried out after obtaining the Petitioner’s intention to waive ownership, they are lawful, and therefore the claim that the above acts infringed the Petitioner’s fundamental rights is without merit.\\n\\n3. Determination on Admissibility\\n\\na. Petition for Adjudication Concerning the Act of Destroying the Entrusted Items in this Case\\n\\nWhether an administrative act constitutes a factual act involving the exercise of public power that is subject to a constitutional complaint must be determined individually by comprehensively considering the concrete circumstances at the time the act was carried out, such as the relationship between the administrative authority and the other party, the other party’s intent, degree of involvement, and attitude toward the factual act, the purpose and background of the factual act, and whether measures of command or coercion under statutes could be invoked (Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2003HEONMA87, Court Cases 17-1, 437, 446).\\n\\nAccording to the record in this case, the entrusted items in this case had no relation whatsoever to the crime, no seizure report or list of seized items had been prepared for them, and the Respondent also argues that there was no intention to seize them. In light of these circumstances, the entrusted items in this case were not items seized on the basis of the police officer’s intention to seize, but merely simple entrusted items that the Petitioner voluntarily submitted at the recommendation of the police officer and that the Respondent kept in custody; therefore, the act of destroying the entrusted items in this case cannot be regarded as a power-based factual act unilaterally carried out by the Respondent from a superior position.\\n\\nAccordingly, the act of destroying the entrusted items in this case is merely a simple non-power-based factual act and cannot be regarded as an exercise of public power subject to a constitutional complaint; therefore, the petition for adjudication on this point is inadmissible.\\n\\nb. Petition for Adjudication Concerning the Act of Destroying the Seized Items in this Case\\n\\n(1) Since a constitutional complaint is a system for remedying infringements of the people’s fundamental rights, it is in principle necessary for there to be an interest in the protection of rights both at the time of filing the petition for adjudication and at the time of decision in order for the petition for constitutional complaint adjudication to be lawful (Constitutional Court 2008. 7. 31. 2004HEONMA1010, Court Cases 20-2, 236, 247). Here, the act of destroying the seized items in this case ended around 2010. 12. 20., and as a result of the court’s hearing, after the filing of the petition for constitutional complaint adjudication in this case, on 2011. 7. 22. a judgment of acquittal was rendered pursuant to the latter part of Article 325 of the Criminal Procedure Act with respect to the charge of preparation for robbery, on the ground that it fell under a case where proof of the crime was absent; the prosecutor appealed against this, but the appeal was dismissed and the above judgment became final and conclusive as rendered. As a result, for the Petitioner, who had sought to prove acquittal on the charge of preparation for robbery through inspection of the seized items in this case, the subjective purpose has already been achieved. Therefore, this petition for adjudication lacks an interest in the protection of subjective rights in the first place.\\n\\nHowever, because constitutional adjudication also serves the function of safeguarding the objective constitutional order, even where an interest in the protection of subjective rights has been extinguished due to a change in circumstances occurring during the continuation of adjudication, if there is a risk that such an act of infringing fundamental rights may be repeated in the future, or if the resolution of the dispute concerned is a matter of importance for the maintenance and protection of the constitutional order such that constitutional clarification thereof has significant meaning, then exceptionally an interest in adjudication may be recognized (see, e.g., Constitutional Court 2008. 7. 31. 2004HEONMA1010, Court Cases 20-2, 236, 247-248).\\n\\n(2) First, as to the risk of repetition.\\n\\nArticle 219 and Article 130(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act provide that “seized articles that are likely to pose a danger may be destroyed,” thereby establishing the basis for the investigative authorities to destroy seized articles. However, in investigative practice, in the course of applying the above statutory provisions, cases occasionally occur in which seized articles that pose no likelihood of danger are destroyed before the case is concluded. The fact that lawsuits for damages against the State are frequently filed due to unlawful destruction of seized articles by investigative authorities supports this.\\n\\nIn particular, the Respondent argues that the destruction was justified because a waiver of ownership had been prepared regarding the seized items in this case. Even in light of the above arguments and the tenor of the Respondent’s response, there remains a possibility that the act of destroying seized articles like this case may be repeated. Furthermore, according to the investigation report submitted by a judicial police officer affiliated with the Gyeonggi Bucheon Wonmi Police Station in this case to a judicial police officer, it states, “Since the suspect and the suspect’s brother say that they have no intention to receive back the seized articles, and there is a risk of loss, etc. during custody, we intend to destroy them.” Considering this, it can still be said that there remains a risk that the act of destroying seized articles like this case may be repeated, as investigative authorities arbitrarily interpret the requirements for destruction of seized articles according to convenience, such as inconvenience in custody.\\n\\n(3) Next, as to the significance of constitutional clarification.\\n\\nThe unlawful destruction of seized articles is a very important matter from the perspective of a defendant who seeks to prove his or her innocence through evidentiary examination of the seized articles, in that it may infringe the defendant’s right to a fair trial, especially where the defendant’s ability to defend is already weak; accordingly, constitutional clarification of the requirements and limitations for destruction of seized articles has significant meaning for the protection of the constitutional order. Therefore, issuing a declaration of unconstitutionality with respect to an act of destroying seized articles such as in this case is necessary to clarify the requirements and limits of destroying seized articles and to reaffirm that the exercise of public power must be carried out in accordance with due process, thereby correcting the practice whereby destruction of seized articles has been abused and preventing seized articles from being destroyed based on convenient and arbitrary judgments.\\n\\nAlso, what the Petitioner seeks to dispute through the constitutional complaint adjudication in this case is not a mere dispute over interpretation and application of law, but rather a dispute over the fact that, in interpreting the statutory provisions forming the basis for the destruction of seized articles, the Respondent overlooked or misunderstood the effect of the relevant fundamental rights and thereby unconstitutionally interpreted and applied those statutory provisions, infringing the right to a fair trial.\\n\\nTherefore, because an act of destroying seized articles such as in this case carries a risk of repetition in the future, and because constitutional clarification thereof is important for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order, this petition for adjudication satisfies the interest in protection of rights.\\n\\n4. Whether the Act of Destroying the Seized Items in this Case Is Unconstitutional\\n\\na. Requirements for Destroying Seized Articles\\n\\n(1) “Seized articles” means evidentiary articles seized by an investigative agency or a court pursuant to statutes, articles believed to be subject to confiscation (Article 106(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act; hereinafter, when only the article number is stated without the name of the statute, it refers to a provision of the Criminal Procedure Act), postal items (Article 107), evidentiary articles submitted pursuant to an order for submission, articles subject to confiscation (Article 106(2)), or voluntarily submitted articles and abandoned articles (Article 108). Most seizures are directed at evidentiary articles or articles subject to confiscation.\\n\\n(2) Since the ultimate purpose of seizure is to collect and preserve evidentiary articles or articles subject to confiscation so that they may later be used as evidence in trial proceedings or be confiscated, seized articles, in principle, must be preserved and kept in custody in the same condition, state, and form as at the time of seizure until the judgment becomes final and conclusive. Therefore, the seizing authority must, with the care of a good manager, promptly and appropriately keep seized articles in custody until they are returned, etc.\\n\\n(3) However, depending on the seized article, there are cases in which disposition is required even before investigative or litigation procedures have ended. This is called treatment of seized articles before conclusion of the case, and disposal by destruction of seized articles (Article 130(2) and (3)) is one such method.\\n\\nAn investigative agency or a court may destroy seized articles that are likely to pose a danger (Articles 130(2) and 219). In addition, seized articles whose production, manufacture, possession, ownership, or distribution is prohibited by statute and that are likely to rot or are difficult to keep in custody may be destroyed with the consent of the owner or other authorized person (Articles 130(3) and 219).\\n\\nHere, however, interpretive questions may arise as to what kind of items “seized articles that are likely to pose a danger” under Article 130(2) means. Yet because seized articles are mostly items that will become evidence, and they are closely related to the fundamental rights of the person from whom they were seized, such as property rights, and especially because, in the case of destruction of seized articles under this provision, rules on notice to interested persons do not apply (see Article 135), thereby causing serious restrictions on the fundamental rights of the person from whom the items were seized, the meaning of seized articles in this provision must be strictly construed. In other words, “seized articles that are likely to pose a danger” under Article 130(2) should be interpreted to mean seized articles such as explosives and poisonous substances that can harm human life, body, health, or property, and whose custody itself is extremely dangerous and very difficult to maintain until the final judgment is rendered. Therefore, even a weapon or dangerous object, which is one of the aggravating elements under the Criminal Act, cannot be considered a seized article that is likely to pose a danger here if its custody itself poses no danger.\\n\\nb. Whether the Act of Destroying the Seized Items in This Case Is Unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Organization of the Issues\\n\\n(a) The Petitioner argues that, even though the seized items in this case posed no likelihood of danger, the Respondent’s act of destroying them is unconstitutional because it infringed the Petitioner’s property right. However, under the Civil Act, the owner of a thing may waive ownership of that thing at any time, and such declaration of waiver of ownership is a unilateral act without a counterparty; upon the declaration of waiver, ownership is extinguished immediately, and the owner of the thing can no longer exercise any further property rights over it. This legal principle applies equally to waiver of ownership over seized articles, and therefore a person who waives ownership of seized articles can no longer exercise property rights over those seized articles; accordingly, there is no room to say that the suspect’s property right is infringed merely because the investigative agency arbitrarily destroyed seized articles for which the suspect, as the person from whom the items were seized, had waived ownership. Therefore, insofar as the Petitioner submitted a waiver of ownership regarding the seized items in this case to the Respondent and thereby waived ownership of the seized items in this case, the act of destroying the seized items in this case does not infringe the Petitioner’s property right.\\n\\n(b) Meanwhile, Article 27(1) of the Constitution provides that “All citizens shall have the right to be tried according to the law by judges qualified under the Constitution and the laws,” and Article 27(3) provides that “All citizens shall have the right to a speedy trial. In criminal proceedings, the accused shall have the right to a public trial without delay, except when there is a just cause.” Thus, it guarantees the right to a fair and speedy public trial. The right to request a trial includes not only the right to a trial according to law in the sense that both the laws governing trial procedures and the substantive law applied at trial must be constitutional, but also the right to a fair trial by excluding secret trials and having proceedings and judgments under the watch of the general public. Included within this right to a fair trial is the right to receive a trial in which all evidentiary materials are examined and presented in the presence of a judge in a speedy and public courtroom, and in which the defendant is guaranteed an opportunity to attack and defend against them; that is, in principle, a trial in which adversarial proceedings, oral argument, and the principle of evidentiary adjudication are guaranteed so that the parties are fully guaranteed the right to attack and defend, such as by responding to the charges and making proof and counterproof.\\n\\nIn criminal procedure having the above trial structure of adversarial proceedings and oral argument, the defendant’s right to request evidence (Article 294) cannot but be a very important right not only for guaranteeing the defendant’s defense rights but also for discovering the substantive truth.\\n\\nIn this matter, the Petitioner attempted to prove innocence through evidentiary examination of the fruit knife among the seized items in this case, but was restricted in exercising defense rights because the item had already been destroyed and thus evidentiary examination could not be conducted. Ultimately, the issue is whether the Respondent’s act of destroying the seized items in this case violated the right to a trial provided in Article 27 of the Constitution, and more specifically, the “right to a fair trial,” in violation of the principle of due process.\\n\\n(2) Whether the Right to a Fair Trial Was Infringed\\n\\n(a) In principle, seized articles are to be kept in custody until the case is concluded. One reason is that most seized articles are evidentiary articles, and therefore there is a need to preserve their evidentiary value as it is until the case is concluded. Of course, in criminal procedure, the prosecutor bears the burden of proof regarding the charges, and seizure during investigation is generally carried out as part of obtaining physical evidence for the prosecutor to prove the charges; therefore, seized articles will often have great evidentiary value for the prosecutor, who bears the burden of proving the charges. However, it cannot be concluded that the preservation of seized articles is solely for the prosecutor’s convenience in proving the case in criminal procedure. In criminal procedure, the defendant also has the right to request evidence to prove facts favorable to him or her, and since seized articles can be used not only to prove the charges but also as materials favorable to the defendant (such as counterevidence and sentencing materials), if the seized articles are destroyed and no longer exist even though the defendant wishes to prove facts favorable to him or her through evidentiary examination of the seized articles, this would infringe the defendant’s right to a fair trial, including the right to request evidence.\\n\\n(b) Therefore, destruction of seized articles before conclusion of the case must be strictly restricted. Specifically, Article 130(3) allows destruction only for “seized articles whose production, manufacture, possession, ownership, or distribution is prohibited by statute and that are likely to rot or are difficult to keep in custody,” with the consent of the owner or other authorized person, and Article 130(2) provides that other seized articles may be destroyed only “when they are likely to pose a danger” (the meaning of “when they are likely to pose a danger” was already examined above). Here, for general seized articles other than those under Article 130(3), if they do not fall under the grounds set forth in Article 130(2), it must be interpreted that destruction is not permitted even if the person from whom the items were seized has waived ownership or given consent. Otherwise, allowing general destruction of seized articles based on waiver of ownership or consent would render meaningless the principle of statutory reservation in criminal procedure, which requires criminal procedure as the process for realizing the State’s punitive power to be subject only to procedures prescribed by law.\\n\\nIn the present case, the Respondent destroyed the seized items in this case on the ground that they were likely to pose a danger. However, in light of the nature, form, and other characteristics of the seized items in this case, it is clear that they are items for which custody until the final judgment itself cannot be considered dangerous and that there is no inconvenience whatsoever in keeping them in custody. Nevertheless, arbitrarily destroying the seized articles solely on the ground that there was a waiver of ownership, unrelated to the requirements for destruction of seized articles prescribed by law as above, violates the due process principle as the principle of statutory reservation for restriction of fundamental rights, is therefore unconstitutional, and infringed the Petitioner’s right to a fair trial.\\n\\n(c) Even if the Respondent’s argument is construed as an argument based on Articles 29 and 48 of the Rules on Prosecutorial Affairs of Seized Articles (as amended by Ministry of Justice Ordinance No. 720 on 2010. 9. 10.) that when a waiver of ownership has been prepared, destruction of seized articles is possible regardless of the grounds in Article 130(2), that argument is not valid for the following reasons.\\n\\nArticle 48(1) of the above Rules provides that seized articles in respect of which ownership has been waived shall vest in the national treasury, and paragraph (2) of the same Article provides that the provisions of Article 29 shall apply mutatis mutandis to the disposition of seized articles vested in the national treasury pursuant to paragraph (1). Article 29 of the above Rules provides that, in the case of articles subject to confiscation, where they are “valueless, or even if valuable, ① they are dangerous objects, ② automobiles, vessels, aircraft, or construction machinery cannot be sold at public auction due to age, damage, etc., or ③ there are other reasonable grounds requiring destruction or disposal,” the prosecutor shall destroy them.\\n\\nHowever, as emphasized above, seized articles are to be kept in custody until the judgment becomes final and conclusive because they are used as evidence in the trial process, and Article 29 of the above Rules also merely provides that articles subject to confiscation (construed as seized articles on which confiscation has been ordered by judgment) may be destroyed. Therefore, even in the case of seized articles subject to waiver of ownership to which Article 29 applies mutatis mutandis pursuant to Article 48(2) of the above Rules, they should be interpreted as being capable of destruction only at a stage equivalent to articles subject to confiscation, that is, only when they have not been confiscated but the judgment has become final and the case has concluded so that there is no longer any possibility of use as evidence. It cannot be said that the legislative purpose of the above Rules was to permit destruction merely on the ground that custody is inconvenient, even before the judgment becomes final, by obtaining a waiver of ownership. Ultimately, the act of destroying the seized items in this case also cannot be regarded as having been carried out in accordance with the requirements and procedures prescribed in the above Rules.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the petition for adjudication on the act of destroying the entrusted items in this case is dismissed as inadmissible, and the act of destroying the seized items in this case is confirmed, in declaratory terms, to be unconstitutional because it is contrary to the principle of due process and infringes the Petitioner’s right to a fair trial.\\n\\nThis decision is based on the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, except for the dissenting opinion regarding the act of destroying the seized items in this case, as stated in Section 6 below by Justice Kim I-su, Justice Kim Chang-jong, and Justice Ahn Chang-ho.\\n\\n6. Opinion of Justice Kim I-su, Justice Kim Chang-jong, and Justice Ahn Chang-ho Dismissing the Portion Concerning the Act of Destroying the Seized Items in This Case\\n\\nWe agree with the majority opinion that the petition for adjudication concerning the act of destroying the seized items in this case lacks an interest in the protection of subjective rights, and that where constitutional clarification is necessary for certain reasons, an interest in the protection of rights may exceptionally be recognized. However, we determine that the act of destroying the seized items in this case does not fall within the exceptional case in which an interest in the protection of rights is recognized, and therefore state our opinion as follows.\\n\\na. Cases in Which an Exceptional Interest in the Protection of Rights Is Recognized\\n\\n(1) Even where there is no interest in the protection of subjective rights, cases in which an exceptional interest in the protection of rights is recognized are those where there is a risk that a power-based factual act, etc. will be repeated in the future, or where the matter is important for the maintenance and protection of the constitutional order such that constitutional clarification thereof has significant meaning (see Constitutional Court 1994. 7. 29. 91HEONMA137, Court Cases 6-2, 122, 134).\\n\\n(2) “Risk of repetition of the infringing act” requires not merely an abstract or theoretical possibility, but a concrete risk (see Constitutional Court 1994. 7. 29. 91HEONMA137, Court Cases 6-2, 122, 134). Accordingly, “risk of repetition of the infringing act” means that a power-based factual act, etc. is generally and continuously carried out such that a concrete risk of repetition is recognized, and where such acts, etc. are carried out individually and exceptionally, it cannot be said that there is a risk of repetition of the infringing act.\\n\\nFirst, where the statutory basis for a power-based factual act, etc. grants discretion to an administrative agency or is open to various interpretations, the Constitutional Court recognizes a “risk of repetition of the infringing act” in the following cases.\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court recognizes a “risk of repetition of the infringing act” where power-based factual acts, etc. carried out by an administrative agency: ① are generally and continuously carried out directly on the basis of administrative rules such as directives or guidelines related to statutes granting discretion to the administrative agency (see Constitutional Court 1998. 10. 29. 98HEONMA4, Court Cases 10-2, 637, 645; Constitutional Court 2003. 12. 18. 2001HEONMA163, Court Cases 15-2, 562, 572; Constitutional Court 2006. 6. 29. 2004HEONMA826, Official Gazette No. 117, 938, 941; Constitutional Court 2010. 10. 28. 2009HEONMA438, Official Gazette No. 169, 1956, 1960, etc.); ② are continuously and repeatedly carried out under the perception that they fall within the broad discretionary scope of statutes, without direct basis for individual acts, or have continued as a practice (see Constitutional Court 1999. 5. 27. 97HEONMA137, Court Cases 11-1, 653, 661; Constitutional Court 2002. 7. 18. 2000HEONMA327, Court Cases 14-2, 54, 60; Constitutional Court 2006. 7. 27. 2005HEONMA277, Court Cases 18-2, 280, 285; Constitutional Court 2009. 9. 24. 2007HEONMA738, Court Cases 21-2, 725, 732; Constitutional Court 2011. 12. 29. 2009HEONMA527, Court Cases 23-2, 840, 846, etc.). In other words, the precedents of the Constitutional Court recognize a “risk of repetition of the infringing act” where, in an area perceived as acts within the discretionary scope under statutes, an administrative agency repeatedly carries out power-based factual acts, etc. generally and continuously on the basis of administrative rules such as directives or guidelines, or by administrative practice, etc.\\n\\nNext, where the content of the relevant statutes is clear and admits no other interpretation or room for discretion, two situations may be considered. First, if an administrative agency generally and continuously repeats power-based factual acts, etc. in accordance with the clear content of the statutes, a “risk of repetition of the infringing act” may be recognized as above (see Constitutional Court 1995. 7. 21. 92HEONMA144, Court Cases 7-2, 94, 103; Constitutional Court 1998. 8. 27. 96HEONMA398, Court Cases 10-2, 416, 426; Constitutional Court 2011. 5. 26. 2009HEONMA341, Court Cases 23-1, 201, 207). However, where, as in this case, an administrative agency performs a power-based factual act, etc. in contravention of clear statutory content, it is exceptional for the administrative agency, whether intentionally or negligently, not to recognize the unlawfulness and to perform a power-based factual act, etc. in violation of the clear statutory content. Thus, while there may be an abstract possibility of infringement, it cannot be said that there is concretely a “risk of repetition of the infringing act.”\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, a case in which constitutional clarification has significant meaning refers to a case that, apart from the case at hand, has general and important meaning such that clarification thereof is necessary for the maintenance and protection of the constitutional order. Where an administrative agency, in interpreting the applicable law, overlooks or misunderstands the effect of fundamental rights on statutory provisions and thereby unconstitutionally interprets and applies the statutory provisions, the need for constitutional clarification is recognized. However, where the matter is simply one of interpretation and application of law, that is, a question of legality as to whether the administrative agency’s act conforms to what the law prescribes, the need for constitutional clarification is not recognized (see Constitutional Court 2003. 2. 27. 2002HEONMA106, Court Cases 15-1, 223, 238-239).\\n\\nConstitutional clarification concerning a power-based factual act should be recognized only where a general constitutional meaning can be extracted from the case. Even if it is an assessment of a factual act that occurred in a one-time and specific situation, if a general constitutional meaning can be attributed thereto, the need for constitutional clarification may be recognized (see Constitutional Court 2006. 6. 29. 2005HEONMA703), but where an administrative agency generally and continuously interprets and applies the relevant laws constitutionally, and yet one of its members in an exceptional situation commits an unlawful act due to a clear misunderstanding of the law, then aside from evaluating that act as unlawful, there is no need to assign general constitutional meaning and provide constitutional clarification.\\n\\nb. Determination on the Act of Destroying the Seized Items in This Case\\n\\n(1) First, we examine whether there is a risk that the act of destroying the seized items in this case will be repeated. The phrase “seized articles that are likely to pose a danger” in Article 130(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, the basis for general destruction of seized articles, means seized articles such as explosives and poisonous substances that can harm human life, body, health, or property, and whose custody itself is extremely dangerous and very difficult to maintain until the final judgment is rendered. It is clear from the wording of the provision that the fruit knife, etc. among the seized items in this case do not fall under “seized articles that are likely to pose a danger.” Accordingly, the act of destroying the seized items in this case should be regarded as a power-based factual act that unlawfully applied a statute whose wording is clear and admits no other interpretation or room for discretion. Since it is exceptional for an investigative agency to knowingly or negligently perform a manifestly unlawful act without recognizing its unlawfulness, even if there is an unlawful act of destroying seized articles, it can be said to have been carried out individually and exceptionally, but not generally and continuously.\\n\\nThe majority opinion refers to the possibility of repetition of the infringing act on the ground that unlawful destruction of seized articles such as the act of destroying the seized items in this case may occasionally occur. However, as noted above, a “risk of repetition of the infringing act” requires not merely an abstract or theoretical possibility, but a concrete risk. The mere fact that an unlawful act of destroying seized articles may occur individually and exceptionally does not mean that there is a concrete risk of repetition of the infringing act.\\n\\nMoreover, the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office, which is in charge of overall direction regarding disposition, etc. of seized articles, reconfirmed that interpreting the fruit knife, etc. among the seized items in this case as “seized articles that are likely to pose a danger” under Article 130(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act and destroying them is unlawful, and through an instruction dated 2012. 11. 21., it caused prosecutors’ offices nationwide to thoroughly comply with the relevant provisions so that cases like the act of destroying the seized items in this case would not occur.\\n\\nIf so, the act of destroying the seized items in this case is clearly contrary to the content of the statute, and cannot be regarded as having been knowingly or negligently repeated generally and continuously by the police or prosecution under the belief that it fell within the scope of the statute, nor as having continued as a practice. In light of the clarity of the statutory text and the measures taken by the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office, a “risk of repetition of the infringing act” cannot be recognized.\\n\\n(2) Next, we examine whether the matter is important for the maintenance and protection of the constitutional order. As noted above, a case in which constitutional clarification has significant meaning refers to a case that, apart from the case at hand, has general and important meaning such that clarification thereof is necessary for the maintenance and protection of the constitutional order. Here, the seized items in this case do not fall under “seized articles that are likely to pose a danger” under Article 130(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, and even if the person from whom they were seized has waived ownership or consented thereto, it is clear, even by interpretation of the Rules on Prosecutorial Affairs of Seized Articles (Articles 48(2) and 29), that they cannot be destroyed before the judgment becomes final and conclusive. At the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office level as well, through a constitutional interpretation of “seized articles that are likely to pose a danger” under Article 130(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, it pointed out the unlawfulness of the act of destroying the seized items in this case and took measures to prevent recurrence of this type of destruction of seized articles. If so, the act of destroying the seized items in this case is one in which, due to misunderstanding of the statute, the statute was interpreted and applied unlawfully in a manner different from ordinary constitutional interpretation and application, and it is individual and exceptional. Therefore, it cannot be said to be a case that, apart from the case at hand, has general and important meaning such that clarification thereof is necessary for the maintenance and protection of the constitutional order. Rather, the act of destroying the seized items in this case is a matter of misinterpretation and misapplication of law and must be understood as falling under “a matter of interpretation and application of law” and “a matter of illegality.”\\n\\nAccordingly, an act of destroying seized articles like in this case should be subjected to a legality determination through a court judgment. Where the act of destroying seized articles was carried out unlawfully, the defendant, etc. would be able to confirm the unlawfulness of the act and seek monetary compensation through a civil claim for damages against the State, etc. Also, in criminal trials, the court will make a determination in relation to the burden of proof. Since the prosecutor bears the burden of proof with respect to the charges, if the seized articles have been destroyed and no longer exist, the prosecutor alone bears the disadvantage in proof, and the defendant has no duty to actively present them as counterevidence. In other words, the defendant need only make arguments to the extent that the judge may harbor doubt as to the charges the prosecutor seeks to prove by means of the destroyed seized articles, and in such a case the prosecutor bears the burden of actively proving the charges through evidence other than the seized articles. Furthermore, if such unlawful destruction of seized articles is attributable to the actor’s intent, the actor may become subject to criminal punishment for offenses such as destruction of evidence or damage to public goods, and ultimately the overall legal judgment regarding the unlawfulness of the act of destroying seized articles will be made by a court judgment.\\n\\n(3) Therefore, the act of destroying the seized items in this case does not present a “risk of repetition of infringement,” and it cannot be said to be a matter requiring constitutional clarification because it is important for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order. Accordingly, the petition for adjudication concerning the act of destroying the seized items in this case lacks not only an interest in the protection of subjective rights but also any exceptionally recognized interest in the protection of rights, and therefore is inadmissible and must be dismissed."}

{"[2019HEONGA24]": "[Appendix] Related Provisions\\n\\nAct on Medical Treatment and Custodial Care, etc. (as amended by Act No. 17510 of October 20, 2020)\\n\\nArticle 2 (Persons Subject to Treatment and Custodial Care) ① In this Act, “person subject to treatment and custodial care” means a person who falls under any of the following items, who needs treatment at a treatment and custodial care facility and who poses a risk of recidivism.\\n\\n1. A person with a mental or physical disorder who is not punishable pursuant to Article 10(1) of the Criminal Act or whose punishment may be mitigated pursuant to paragraph (2) of the same Article, and who has committed a crime punishable by imprisonment without labor or a heavier punishment\\n\\n2. A person who has a habit of ingesting, inhaling, smoking, or injecting narcotics, psychotropic drugs, cannabis, or other substances or alcohol that are likely to be abused or cause harm, or who is addicted thereto, and who has committed a crime punishable by imprisonment without labor or a heavier punishment\\n\\n3. A person with a psychosexual disorder having sexual perversions, such as pedophilia or sexual sadism, and who has committed a sexual violence crime punishable by imprisonment without labor or a heavier punishment\\n\\nArticle 4 (Prosecutor’s Petition for Treatment and Custodial Care) ② When petitioning for treatment and custodial care for a person subject thereto, the prosecutor shall take into consideration a diagnosis or expert appraisal by a specialist in psychiatry, etc. However, with respect to a person subject to treatment and custodial care under Article 2(1)3, the prosecutor shall petition for treatment and custodial care after obtaining a diagnosis or expert appraisal by a specialist in psychiatry, etc.\\n\\n③ When petitioning for treatment and custodial care, the prosecutor shall submit a petition for treatment and custodial care to the competent court. As many duplicate copies as there are persons against whom the petition for treatment and custodial care is made shall be attached to the petition.\\n\\n④ The petition for treatment and custodial care shall state the following matters:\\n\\n1. The name of the person against whom the petition for treatment and custodial care is made and other matters by which such person can be identified\\n\\n2. The facts constituting the cause of the petition\\n\\n3. The applicable provisions of law\\n\\n4. Other matters prescribed by Presidential Decree\\n\\n⑤ The prosecutor may petition for treatment and custodial care until the conclusion of oral arguments in the appellate instance of a case in which prosecution has been instituted.\\n\\nArticle 7 (Independent Petition for Treatment and Custodial Care) The prosecutor may petition only for treatment and custodial care, without instituting prosecution, in any of the following cases:\\n\\n1. Where the suspect falls under Article 10(1) of the Criminal Act and thus cannot be punished\\n\\n2. Where, in an offense that may be considered only upon complaint or accusation, there is no such complaint or accusation, or it has been withdrawn, or where, in an offense that may not be considered against the express will of the victim, the victim has expressed that he or she does not wish punishment or has withdrawn the expression of willingness to be punished\\n\\n3. Where, with respect to the suspect, a decision not to institute prosecution has been made pursuant to Article 247 of the Criminal Procedure Act\\n\\nArticle 12 (Judgment, etc. on Treatment and Custodial Care) ① The court shall try the treatment and custodial care case and, when it finds the petition well-founded, shall sentence treatment and custodial care by judgment, and when it finds it unfounded or when it renders an acquittal in the defendant’s case for a cause other than lack of mental capacity or renders a death sentence, shall dismiss the petition by judgment.\\n\\n② The judgment in the treatment and custodial care case shall be rendered simultaneously with the judgment in the defendant’s case. However, this shall not apply where, pursuant to Article 7, prosecution was not instituted and only treatment and custodial care was petitioned.\\n\\n③ The reasons for the judgment ordering treatment and custodial care shall specifically state the facts constituting the requirements, the gist of the evidence, and the applicable provisions of law.\\n\\n④ Where there are grounds under each item of Article 326, items 1 through 4 of Article 327, or each item of paragraph (1) of Article 328 of the Criminal Procedure Act in the defendant’s case (excluding, in item 2, cases where the corporation that is the defendant has ceased to exist), the court shall also render a judgment or order dismissing the petition in the treatment and custodial care petition case. The same shall also apply where there are such grounds in the treatment and custodial care petition case.\\n\\nArticle 16 (Contents of Treatment and Custodial Care) ① A person sentenced to treatment and custodial care (hereinafter referred to as “a person subject to treatment and custodial care”) shall be confined in a treatment and custodial care facility and be subject to measures for treatment.\\n\\n② The period during which a person subject to treatment and custodial care is confined in a treatment and custodial care facility may not exceed the period classified as follows:\\n\\n1. A person falling under Article 2(1)1 or 3: 15 years\\n\\n2. A person falling under Article 2(1)2: 2 years\\n\\nArticle 18 (Order and Method of Execution) Where treatment and custodial care and punishment are cumulatively imposed, treatment and custodial care shall be executed first. In this case, the period of execution of treatment and custodial care shall be included in the period of execution of the punishment.\\n\\nArticle 32 (Probation) ① When a person subject to treatment and custodial care falls under any of the following items, probation under the Act on Probation, etc. (hereinafter referred to as “probation”) shall commence.\\n\\n1. When the treatment and custodial care for the person subject to treatment and custodial care has been provisionally terminated\\n\\n2. When the person subject to treatment and custodial care is entrusted to a legal representative, etc. to receive treatment outside a treatment and custodial care facility\\n\\n3. When, with respect to a person subject to treatment and custodial care whose period under each item of Article 16(2) or the extended period under paragraph (3) of the same Article (hereinafter referred to as “the period of treatment and custodial care”) expires, the Treatment and Custodial Care Deliberation Committee under Article 37 reviews the case and decides that probation is necessary, at the time the period of treatment and custodial care expires\\n\\n② The period of probation shall be 3 years."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning freedom of religion is incorrect? (In case of dispute, according to precedents)
A: The act by the Commander of the Army Training Center of compelling recruits to attend one of the Protestant, Buddhist, Catholic, or Won Buddhist religious events held at the religious facilities within the Army Training Center favors a particular religion and thus violates the principle of separation of religion and state.
B: Since conscientious objection to military service is based on an earnest hope and determination for the peaceful coexistence of humankind, a provision of the ｢Military Service Act｣ that compels performance of military service for conscientious objectors who have not been specially exempted from military service does not restrict the freedom of religion of the relevant religious person, even when applied to a person who refuses military service on the basis of religious belief.
C: The act of the Commissioner of the Statistics Korea, while conducting the face-to-face interview survey of the Population and Housing Census, of requiring respondents through the responsible enumerators to answer the survey items asking whether they have a religion and, if so, what specific religion it is, is one of the survey matters to be used as basic data for statistics and is not intended to impose disadvantages on the ground that one believes in a particular religion or to compel conduct contrary to religious conviction.
D: A statutory provision that also imposes a duty to file a report on the establishment of an elderly care facility operated by a religious organization as part of relief activities and punishes violations thereof does not infringe freedom of religion, because in elderly care facilities of a certain size or larger, the degree of harm from safety accidents or human rights violations may increase, so it is necessary to impose the reporting duty without exception.
E: A statutory provision that, for a person who has been subjected to a disciplinary confinement measure, prohibits attendance at religious rites or religious events, except for religious activities through religious counseling during the period of the disciplinary confinement measure, does not infringe the freedom of religion of the relevant inmate, because such disadvantage cannot be said to outweigh the public interest in maintaining order in detention through compliance with discipline.

supporting_precedents: {"[2014HEONMA45]": "1. Summary of the Case\\n\\na. The Petitioner was sentenced to 3 years’ imprisonment for the crime of rape resulting in injury, and that sentence became final and conclusive (Wonju Branch Court of Chuncheon District Court 2011GOHAP38, Chuncheon Division of Seoul High Court 2012NO24).\\n\\nb. The Petitioner, at XX Prison, from 2013. 11. 10. to 2013. 11. 21., was suspected of noncompliance with orders and obstruction of duties, and, as a person subject to disciplinary action, was placed under investigative confinement (hereinafter referred to as “the investigative confinement disposition in this case”), during which he was restricted in outdoor exercise, educational training, and participation in group events.\\n\\nc. On 2013. 11. 22., because the above charges were found to be substantiated, the Petitioner was subjected to a 25-day confinement to a disciplinary cell disposition (hereinafter referred to as “the disciplinary-cell disposition in this case”), and the disciplinary-cell disposition in this case was executed from 2013. 11. 10., with 12 days of the investigative confinement disposition in this case counted toward the period, until 2013. 12. 4.; additionally, from 2013. 11. 22. to 2013. 12. 4., the Petitioner was also subjected to suspension of participation in group events, restriction on reading newspapers, restriction on watching television, restriction on use of self-purchased items, suspension of work, restriction on telephone calls, restriction on writing, restriction on receipt and dispatch of correspondence, restriction on visits, and suspension of outdoor exercise.\\n\\nd. Accordingly, alleging that Article 108 of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates, which prescribes the types of disciplinary sanctions, infringes human dignity and value, the right to trial, freedom of expression, and the like, the Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint on 2014. 1. 21.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court shall comprehensively determine the gist of the Petitioner’s claims, without being bound by the relief sought as stated in the petition, and may ex officio ascertain the subject matter of review by investigating the fundamental rights alleged to have been infringed and the exercise of public power alleged to be the cause of the infringement (see Constitutional Court 2002HEONMA90, 2003. 5. 15.).\\n\\nAlthough the Petitioner and state-appointed counsel have designated Article 108 of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates, which prescribes the types of disciplinary sanctions, as the subject matter of review, they in substance argue that the statutory provisions prescribing that, during the investigation period, treatment restrictions such as suspension of outdoor exercise, suspension of educational training, and suspension of participation in group events are to be imposed, and that, during the confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell period, treatment restrictions such as suspension of participation in group events, restriction on reading newspapers, restriction on watching television, restriction on use of self-purchased items, restriction on telephone calls, restriction on writing, restriction on receipt and dispatch of correspondence, restriction on visits, and suspension of outdoor exercise are to be imposed, infringe the Petitioner’s fundamental rights and are therefore unconstitutional.\\n\\nArticle 108 of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates merely enumerates the types of disciplinary sanctions, whereas Article 110(2) of the same Act provides that, if a person subject to disciplinary action is separately confined during the investigation period, all or part of the treatment allowing contact with other persons, such as visits, receipt and dispatch of correspondence, telephone calls, outdoor exercise, work, educational training, and participation in group events, may be restricted, and the main text of Article 112(3) of the same Act provides that a person who has received a confinement-to-a-disciplinary-cell disposition shall be subject, during that period, to treatment restrictions, including suspension of participation in group events. Accordingly, taking into account the gist of the Petitioner’s claims, the subject matter of review in this case is changed ex officio to the relevant portions of Article 110(2) and the main text of Article 112(3) of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates (see Constitutional Court 2011HEONMA201, 2013. 2. 28.; Constitutional Court 2012HEONMA623, 2014. 8. 28., et al.).\\n\\nTherefore, the subject matter of review in this case is whether ① Article 110(2) of the former Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates (completely amended by Act No. 8728 on 2007. 12. 21., and before amendment by Act No. 13235 on 2015. 3. 27.) (hereinafter referred to as “the investigation provision at issue in this case”), and ② the portion concerning Article 108 items 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13 of the main text of Article 112(3) of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates (completely amended by Act No. 8728 on 2007. 12. 21., hereinafter referred to as “the Sentence Execution Act”) (hereinafter referred to as “the confinement provision at issue in this case”) are in violation of the Constitution by infringing the Petitioner’s fundamental rights. The content of the provisions subject to review and the related provisions is as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Review]\\n\\nFormer Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates\\n(completely amended by Act No. 8728 on 2007. 12. 21., and before amendment by Act No. 13235 on 2015. 3. 27.)\\n\\nArticle 110 (Investigation of Persons Subject to Disciplinary Action) (2) The warden may restrict all or part of the treatment allowing contact with other persons, such as visits, receipt and dispatch of correspondence, telephone calls, outdoor exercise, work, educational training, and participation in group events, if the person subject to disciplinary action falls under any of the items of paragraph (1).\\n\\nAct on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates\\n(completely amended by Act No. 8728 on 2007. 12. 21.)\\n\\nArticle 112 (Execution of Disciplinary Sanctions) (3) A person who has been subjected to the disposition under Article 108, item 14, shall, during that period, also be subject to the treatment restrictions under items 4 through 13 of the same Article.
