Therefore, there is no other effective remedy available to the Petitioner apart from filing a constitutional complaint (see Constitutional Court 1995. 7. 21., 92HEONMA144, Court Reports 7-2, 94, 102; Constitutional Court 1998. 10. 29., 98HEONMA4, Court Reports 10-2, 637, 644; Constitutional Court 2006. 6. 29., 2004HEONMA826, Official Gazette 117, 938, etc.).\\n\\nIn addition, since the Petitioner was released on 2005. 3. 31. and the infringing act against the Petitioner has ended, even if a determination of unconstitutionality is made regarding the act of collecting urine, rights relief for the Petitioner is impossible, so the subjective interest in protection of rights has already been extinguished; however, even if a constitutional complaint is of little help to subjective rights relief, if there is a risk that such infringing act may be repeated in the future and the elucidation of the issue has significant constitutional meaning, the interest in adjudication may be recognized (see Constitutional Court 1997. 11. 27., 94HEONMA60, Court Reports 9-2, 675, 688; Constitutional Court 2001. 7. 19., 2000HEONMA546, Court Reports 13-2, 103, 108; Constitutional Court 2001. 8. 30., 99HEONMA496, Court Reports 13-2, 238, 244; Constitutional Court 2002. 7. 18., 2000HEONMA327, Court Reports 14-2, 54, 60; Constitutional Court 2006. 6. 29., 2004HEONMA826, Official Gazette 117, 938, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the materials in this case, urine collection is carried out regularly and repeatedly at detention centers or prisons for narcotics offenders upon admission and once a month or once per quarter, so it has significant constitutional meaning in its clarification, and therefore the interest in adjudication may be recognized.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Merits\\n\\nA. Overview of the Narcotics Reaction Test\\n\\n(1) Statutory Basis\\n\\n(a) Article 17-2(1) of the Prison Administration Act (Physical Examination, etc.) provides that “correctional officers may inspect the bodies, clothing, personal effects, cells, and workplaces of inmates when necessary for the safety and maintenance of order of prisons, etc.,” thereby allowing physical examinations of inmates, and since collecting urine from inmates for the narcotics reaction test is likewise one form of the above physical examination, that provision constitutes the statutory basis for the collection of urine in this case.\\n\\n(b) Meanwhile, the narcotics reaction test through urine collection in correctional facilities is generally carried out pursuant to the Minister of Justice’s directive dated 1989. 8. 26. (Correction 01250-11529), which ordered the use of the T.B.P.E. reagent test for the management of inmates convicted of psychotropic-substance-related offenses, and the directive dated 1990. 5. 1. (Correction 01250-5623), which ordered that the T.B.P.E. reagent test be conducted at least once a month and that the results of processing be reported.\\n\\n(2) Contents\\n\\nThe persons subject to the narcotics reaction test through urine collection are inmates such as narcotics offenders, persons who, before admission, had worked at entertainment establishments, persons who had frequent overseas travel such as crew members of foreign-going vessels, and persons with other narcotics-related criminal records, for whom narcotics reaction testing is deemed necessary because there is a likelihood of narcotics use; it is generally conducted once when newly admitted to detention centers and prisons and once a month, and, exceptionally, it is also conducted when necessary. The testing method is to have the inmate collect urine in a paper cup in a place where others cannot see and submit it, and then to drop 0.3cc of sodium borate and 0.5㎖ of T.B.P.E. reagent into 3 to 5cc of it and confirm whether it turns red within 1 to 3 minutes (positive reaction); each time the test is conducted, the timing and result are recorded in the health examination register, reported to the Corrections Agency and the Ministry of Justice, and if the result is positive, a request is made to the relevant agency for an in-depth examination such as serum testing or hair testing.\\n\\nB. Constitutional Limits on Urine Collection\\n\\n(1) The Collection of Urine in This Case and the Petitioner’s Fundamental Rights\\n\\nIf, as the Petitioner argues, he was compelled without any statutory basis to undergo urine collection to which he was under no duty, then the issue would be whether there was an infringement of the general right to freedom of action [the freedom not to do what one does not want to do (the act of collecting urine in a paper cup and submitting it), the freedom not to disclose one’s physical condition or information to the outside] guaranteed by the dignity and value of the human being and the right to pursue happiness under Article 10 of the Constitution, and of the freedom of the person guaranteed by Article 12 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Relationship with the Warrant Principle\\n\\nArticle 12(3) of the Constitution provides, with respect to arrest, detention, seizure, or search, that a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s request be presented in accordance with lawful procedure, thereby guaranteeing the warrant principle at the constitutional level, and this warrant principle refers to the principle that coercive measures necessary for investigation may not be taken without a warrant issued by a judge (Constitutional Court 1997. 3. 27., 96HEONGA11, Court Reports 9-1, 245, 258).\\n\\nThe collection of urine in this case is conducted for the purpose of maintaining safety and order in correctional facilities and is not a measure necessary for investigation; moreover, it is one that causes the person subject to testing, such as the Petitioner, to collect and submit urine in a paper cup, so the cooperation of the party is unavoidable, and it could not be called a coercive measure (see Constitutional Court 1997. 3. 27., 96HEONGA11, Court Reports 9-1, 245, 258).\\n\\nAccordingly, the collection of urine in this case cannot be said to be a coercive measure requiring a judicial warrant, and therefore the fact that urine was collected in the above manner within detention centers and other correctional facilities without a judicial warrant cannot be said to violate the warrant principle under Article 12(3) of the Constitution.\\n\\n(3) Whether the Principle of Prohibition of Excessive Restriction Was Violated\\n\\nEven if the collection of urine in this case from the Petitioner, a narcotics offender, is inevitable for the safety and maintenance of order within the correctional facility on the basis of Article 17-2 of the Prison Administration Act, it must not infringe the essential content of fundamental rights or violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction, which refers to the legitimacy of the purpose, the appropriateness of the means, the minimum necessary infringement, and the balance of legal interests.\\n\\nConsidering that one of the characteristics of narcotics is addictiveness and that most narcotics offenders are repeat offenders or more, there is always a risk that narcotics will be brought into the correctional facility or that narcotics offenders will consume them, and in such case not only would the purpose of correction concerning the relevant inmate be fundamentally undermined, but another accident may occur due to harm to other inmates. Since such possibilities and risks always exist, regular inspections of inmates who may have access to narcotics, such as narcotics offenders, can enable early detection of the bringing in and consumption of narcotics; by making all inmates aware that regular inspections are conducted, attempts to bring in narcotics can be blocked in advance; and from the inmates’ perspective as well, abandoning attempts to bring in narcotics increases the possibility of complying with the original correctional purpose such as rehabilitation education. In this respect, conducting the narcotics reaction test through urine collection on a regular basis is highly contributory to the safety and maintenance of order within correctional facilities and to the correctional purpose, and thus the legitimacy of the purpose is recognized.\\n\\nIn addition, whether narcotics have been brought in can be confirmed through inspection of clothing, personal effects, cells, and workplaces and through visual observation of the outside of the body or body cavities, etc.; however, this also cannot be done perfectly (such inspections may also infringe inmates’ fundamental rights, and inspection of body cavities, etc., rather has a greater likelihood of infringing fundamental rights), and since whether they have been consumed cannot be determined by visual inspection, the appropriateness of the means is also recognized in the narcotics reaction test through urine collection.\\n\\nFurthermore, the collection of urine in this case is carried out through the cooperative acts of the persons subject to testing, such as the Petitioner, and there are no sanctioning means such as disciplinary punishment for failure to comply. It is conducted within a short time (1 to 3 minutes) by a simple method (dropping sodium borate and T.B.P.E. reagent into the paper cup into which urine has been collected), and the result can be known immediately. In this respect, the principle of minimum infringement can also be said to have been observed.\\n\\nLastly, the collection of urine in this case imposes on the Petitioner and other persons subject to testing the disadvantage that they must regularly collect and submit urine excreted from their own bodies, that is, the restriction of self-determination over their bodies and the limitation of private interests such as having to do something they do not want to do; however, as seen above, the increase in the feasibility of realizing the correctional purpose with respect to the persons subject to testing (which also has the aspect of an increase in private interests) and the public interest of safety and maintenance of order within correctional facilities are far greater, and thus the balance of legal interests is also satisfied.\\n\\nAccordingly, the collection of urine in this case from the Petitioner, a narcotics offender, does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the constitutional complaint seeking a determination of unconstitutionality regarding the collection of urine in this case from the Petitioner, a narcotics offender, is dismissed as inadmissible with respect to the Respondent, the Minister of Justice, because the subjectivity of the exercise of public power is not recognized, and with respect to the Respondent, the Warden of Daegu Prison, it is held that the above urine collection was carried out within the scope of restriction on fundamental rights, and thus is dismissed as lacking merit; and it is so decided by the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating."}

{"[2012HEONBA302]": "1. Summary of the Case\\nThe Petitioner left the country on June 9, 2005, while under investigation on suspicion of fraud, reentered the country on November 22, 2011, and was indicted on April 30, 2012, on suspicion of fraud (Seoul Western District Court No. 2012GODAN837). On May 7, 2012, the Minister of Justice prohibited the Petitioner’s departure for a period of 6 months from May 7, 2012 to November 6, 2012, on the ground that the Petitioner was pending criminal trial, pursuant to Article 4(1)1 of the Immigration Control Act.\\n\\nAccordingly, on May 22, 2012, the Petitioner filed a lawsuit against the Minister of Justice in the Seoul Administrative Court seeking revocation of the above departure prohibition disposition (No. 2012GUHAP16466), and at the same time filed an application for a request for a constitutional review of laws concerning Article 4(1)1 of the Immigration Control Act, which provides that departure may be prohibited for a person pending criminal trial (Seoul Administrative Court No. 2012A1748). When this was dismissed on July 27, 2012, the Petitioner filed the constitutional complaint in this case on August 21, 2012.\\n\\n2. Subject of Review\\nThe subject of review in this case is whether Article 4(1)1 of the Immigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 10863 on July 18, 2011) is contrary to the Constitution, and its content is as follows.\\n\\n[Provision Subject to Review]\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 10863 on July 18, 2011)\\nArticle 4 (Prohibition of Departure) (1) The Minister of Justice may prohibit the departure of a national falling under any of the following subparagraphs for a period not exceeding 6 months.\\n1. A person pending criminal trial\\n\\n3. Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments\\nAlthough the prohibition of departure against a person pending criminal trial substantially constitutes a coercive measure in criminal procedure, the provision subject to review allows the Minister of Justice to arbitrarily prohibit departure without a warrant issued by a judge, and thus violates the constitutional principle of warrant requirement. While permitting the Minister of Justice to prohibit the departure of a defendant, who is one party to criminal procedure, upon the request of a prosecutor, who is the other party to criminal procedure, the provision subject to review does not provide for prior notice to the defendant or an opportunity for a hearing, and therefore also violates the constitutional principle of due process. Furthermore, the provision subject to review violates the constitutional principle of presumption of innocence by imposing the disadvantage of departure prohibition on a person whose guilt or innocence has not yet been finally determined and who is still pending criminal trial, and because departure is prohibited when there is evidence favorable to the person abroad, the collection and submission of evidence are fundamentally blocked, so that the Petitioner cannot engage in attack and defense on an equal footing with the prosecutor, thereby infringing the Petitioner’s right to a fair trial and freedom to leave the country.\\n\\n4. Determination on Admissibility\\nSince the period of departure prohibition against the Petitioner had already expired after this constitutional complaint was filed, even if the Constitutional Court were to render a decision of unconstitutionality with respect to the provision subject to review, the Petitioner would no longer be able to obtain relief in the relevant case, and thus it is difficult to conclude that the Petitioner still has a protected interest in the relief of rights. However, as the essence of a constitutional complaint is not only the relief of individual rights but also the guarantee of the constitutional order, even if a constitutional complaint does not aid subjective relief of rights, the interest in adjudication may be recognized where there is a risk that such an act of infringement will be repeated, or where resolution of the relevant dispute is an essential matter for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order and its constitutional elucidation is of significant importance (see Constitutional Court Decision of Mar. 25, 2004, 2002HEONBA104, etc.).\\n\\nIn this case, whether the provision subject to review is unconstitutional is an important constitutional issue related to the freedom to leave the country among the freedom of residence and movement, and no clarification thereof has yet been made by the Constitutional Court. Furthermore, departure prohibition dispositions based on the provision subject to review are continuing to be made, so the same type of issue may repeatedly arise in the future. Accordingly, since its constitutional elucidation has significant importance for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order, the interest in adjudication is exceptionally recognized.\\n\\n5. Determination on the Merits\\nA. Whether the warrant requirement is violated\\nArticle 12(3) of the Constitution declares the warrant requirement, and the warrant requirement is a principle derived from the due process principle of Article 12(1) of the Constitution, according to which, in relation to criminal procedure, coercive measures such as arrest, detention, seizure, and search must be based on a warrant issued by a judge whose status is guaranteed (see Constitutional Court Decisions of May 31, 2012, 2010HEONMA672; Dec. 27, 2012, 2010HEONMA153). However, a departure prohibition decision by the Minister of Justice under the provision subject to review is merely an administrative disposition that restricts the freedom to leave the country of a national pending criminal trial, and cannot be regarded as a coercive measure directly involving physical force against the body to which the warrant requirement applies. Therefore, the provision subject to review cannot be deemed to violate the warrant requirement under Article 12(3) of the Constitution.\\n\\nB. Whether the due process principle is violated\\nSince the due process principle under Article 12 of the Constitution applies not only to criminal procedure but to all state action in general (see Constitutional Court Decision of July 24, 2003, 2001HEONGA25), even where, as in this case, the Minister of Justice restricts the freedom to leave the country by means of an administrative disposition against a person pending criminal trial, the constitutional due process principle must be observed. Among the important procedural requirements derivable from the due process principle are the giving of appropriate notice to the party and the granting of an opportunity to submit opinions and materials. However, the specific procedures and the extent to which they are required by this principle can only be determined on a case-by-case basis by comparing various factors such as the nature of the matter being regulated, the rights and interests of the relevant parties, the value to be enhanced by implementing the procedure, the efficiency of state action, the costs involved in the procedure, and opportunities for objection (see Constitutional Court Decisions of July 24, 2003, 2001HEONGA25; Oct. 4, 2007, 2006HEONBA91).\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues, in essence, that the provision subject to review violates the due process principle because it permits the prosecutor, who is one party in criminal procedure, to request departure prohibition against the defendant, while it does not even provide a rule on prior notice to a person pending criminal trial and thereby deprives such person of an opportunity for a hearing.\\n\\nThe departure prohibition decision under the provision subject to review is intended to prevent flight abroad by a person pending criminal trial and thereby secure the State’s power to punish, and thus requires speed and secrecy by its nature. However, if the Minister of Justice were required, when making a departure prohibition decision, to give prior notice to the person subject to departure prohibition or to conduct a hearing, it would be difficult to exclude the possibility that the person subject to departure prohibition might flee abroad before the decision in order to evade the State’s power to punish, and this would greatly risk hindering the achievement of the purpose of the departure prohibition system, namely securing the State’s power to punish. Furthermore, the Immigration Control Act provides that when the Minister of Justice has prohibited departure, written notice stating the grounds and period thereof shall be given immediately (Article 4-4(1)), thereby guaranteeing the relevant person subject to departure prohibition an opportunity to prepare a defense and to object, and it also guarantees sufficient opportunities for the person subject to departure prohibition to state opinions or submit materials through an objection or administrative litigation.\\n\\nAs such, since the person subject to departure prohibition is afforded an opportunity to later challenge the departure prohibition decision and is thereby guaranteed procedural participation, it is difficult to conclude that the provision subject to review violates the due process principle merely because it does not provide for prior notice to the person subject to departure prohibition or an opportunity for a hearing.\\n\\nC. Whether the presumption of innocence is violated\\nThe presumption of innocence provided in Article 27(4) of the Constitution means that a defendant or suspect must not be treated as a guilty person before a guilty judgment becomes final, thereby being subjected to tangible or intangible disadvantages in legal and factual respects. Here, disadvantages mean disadvantages as the effect of a finding of guilt, that is, disadvantages imposed on the basis of guilt by way of social reproach or other punitive discriminatory treatment (see Constitutional Court Decisions of May 26, 2005, 2002HEONMA699, etc.; Jan. 28, 2014, 2012HEONBA298).\\n\\nThe provision subject to review merely allows the Minister of Justice to prohibit departure when there is a risk that a person pending criminal trial may flee abroad in order to evade the State’s power to punish. Even if a defendant who is at risk of flight abroad suffers the disadvantage of being prohibited from departing for a certain period, it is difficult to regard this as the disadvantage as the effect of a finding of guilt that is prohibited by the presumption of innocence, namely an attempt to impose social reproach or punitive sanctions on a person pending criminal trial on the basis of guilt. Therefore, the provision subject to review cannot be deemed to violate the presumption of innocence.\\n\\nD. Whether the freedom to leave the country is infringed\\n(1) Standard of review\\nThe freedom of residence and movement under Article 14 of the Constitution is the freedom to freely determine one’s place of residence and sojourn without state interference, and it functions to increase the effectiveness of other fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution by promoting the enhancement of personality in all fields of life, such as politics, economy, society, and culture. The freedom of residence and movement includes the freedom of overseas travel and overseas emigration, namely the freedom to determine freely one’s place of sojourn and residence abroad, and this necessarily includes the freedom to leave the country in order to sojourn or reside in a foreign country, as well as the freedom to enter the country, namely the freedom to discontinue residence or sojourn abroad and return to the Republic of Korea (see Constitutional Court Decision of Oct. 28, 2004, 2003HEONGA18).\\n\\nBy providing that the Minister of Justice may prohibit departure for a period not exceeding 6 months against a person pending criminal trial, the provision subject to review restricts the freedom to leave the country, which is part of the freedom of residence and movement, and therefore must comply with the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction under Article 37(2) of the Constitution (see Constitutional Court Decision of Oct. 28, 2004, 2003HEONGA18).\\n\\n(2) Legitimacy of the legislative purpose and appropriateness of means\\nThe provision subject to review, which seeks to realize the discovery of substantive truth and judicial justice by preventing flight abroad by a person pending criminal trial and thereby securing the State’s power to punish, has a legitimate legislative purpose, and allowing the departure of a person pending criminal trial to be prohibited for a certain period also contributes to achieving that legislative purpose, so the appropriateness of means is also recognized.\\n\\n(3) Minimal impairment\\nAs non-detention investigations and trials have increased pursuant to the principle of investigation and trial without detention under the Criminal Procedure Act, the number of defendants who flee abroad while pending criminal trial is increasing every year, and as a result, obstacles to the realization of the State’s power to punish are arising, such as the trial proceedings being practically suspended and remaining as cases pending indefinitely, or enforcement of punishment becoming difficult. In such circumstances, where it is recognized as necessary to prevent flight abroad by a person pending criminal trial who is not in custody, it is necessary to permit departure prohibition for a certain period.\\n\\nThe Enforcement Rule of the Immigration Control Act provides basic principles for departure prohibition, stating that departure prohibition shall be imposed only within the minimum necessary scope, shall not be imposed merely for the convenience of official duties or for the purpose of imposing administrative sanctions on a person who has received criminal punishment or administrative punishment, and shall be imposed only when the person subject to departure prohibition is deemed to possess a valid passport (Article 6). It further requires the Minister of Justice, when deciding whether to prohibit departure for a person pending criminal trial, to consider such basic principles of departure prohibition, the criminal facts, age, family relations, and the possibility of flight abroad of the person subject to departure prohibition (Article 6-5(1)), and thus requires the Minister to determine whether to prohibit departure by examining concrete circumstances such as whether the defendant has ties or a business base abroad, and whether departure is frequent. Meanwhile, in order for the head of a relevant agency to request departure prohibition, the grounds for the request and the intended period of departure prohibition must be specified, and materials substantiating the fact that the person concerned is a person pending criminal trial and the grounds for the necessity of departure prohibition must also be attached (main text of Article 2(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act, Article 6-4(1) of the Enforcement Rule).\\n\\nIn practice as well, departure prohibition under the provision subject to review is operated in a very limited manner. In 2012, the number of non-detention defendants in criminal trial cases was 319,545, while the number of requests for departure prohibition under the provision subject to review was 734, and only 714 of those resulted in a departure prohibition decision.\\n\\nFurthermore, when the Minister of Justice has made a departure prohibition decision, absent special circumstances such as a risk of serious harm to national security or the public interest, the Minister must immediately notify the person concerned in writing of the grounds and period, etc. (Article 4-4(1) of the Immigration Control Act). In addition, a person whose departure has been prohibited may file an objection with the Minister of Justice against the departure prohibition decision within 10 days from the date on which the person was notified of the decision or from the date on which the person learned of the fact (Article 4-5(1)), and if the objection is dismissed, a means of obtaining relief of rights through administrative litigation is also provided. Of course, it is also possible to file administrative litigation directly without going through the objection procedure, and where it is recognized that there is an urgent necessity to prevent irreparable harm that would be caused by departure prohibition, there is also the possibility of departing after filing a revocation suit and obtaining a decision suspending the execution of the departure prohibition disposition.\\n\\nIn addition, the Minister of Justice must immediately lift departure prohibition when the grounds for departure prohibition have ceased to exist or when it is recognized that departure prohibition is no longer necessary (Article 4-3(1) of the Immigration Control Act), and if a citizen suffers damage because the head of the agency that requested departure prohibition does not request the Minister of Justice to lift departure prohibition even though the grounds therefor have ceased to exist, a claim for state compensation may also be made. The provision subject to review limits the period of departure prohibition against a person pending criminal trial so that, in principle, it may not exceed 6 months.\\n\\nSince various measures have been established to minimize the restriction of fundamental rights of a person pending criminal trial in this way, the provision subject to review does not violate the principle of minimal impairment.\\n\\n(4) Balance of legal interests\\nThe disadvantage suffered by a person pending criminal trial due to the provision subject to review is the prohibition of departure for a certain period, whereas the public interest obtained through the provision subject to review is significant, namely realizing the discovery of substantive truth and judicial justice by preventing flight abroad by a person pending criminal trial and thereby securing the State’s power to punish. Accordingly, the balance of legal interests is also satisfied between the public interest sought to be achieved by the provision subject to review and the private interest being restricted.\\n\\n(5) Conclusion\\nThe provision subject to review does not infringe the Petitioner’s freedom to leave the country in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\nE. Whether the right to a fair trial is infringed\\nThe right to a fair trial guaranteed by Article 27(1) of the Constitution includes the right to receive a trial in which the adversarial principle and oral argument principle are guaranteed so that the parties are sufficiently guaranteed the right to attack and defend, such as by responding to the charges and presenting proof and counterproof (see Constitutional Court Decisions of Apr. 28, 1994, 93HEONBA26; Nov. 25, 2010, 2009HEONBA57). The Petitioner argues, in essence, that the provision subject to review infringes the right to a fair trial by restricting the defense rights of the defendant, since it makes it difficult for the defendant to collect and submit evidence abroad where evidence favorable to the defense may exist. However, the provision subject to review merely allows the Minister of Justice to prohibit a defendant’s departure, and cannot be said to be directly related to the exercise of the defendant’s rights of attack and defense, nor can the right to a fair trial be understood as including the right to go abroad to collect evidence.\\n\\nTherefore, it cannot be said that the provision subject to review restricts the defendant’s exercise of the rights of attack and defense and thereby infringes the Petitioner’s right to a fair trial.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\nSince the provision subject to review does not violate the Constitution, the decision is rendered as stated in the order by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, excluding the dissenting opinion of Justice Lee Jung-mi and Justice Lee Jin-sung as set forth in 7. below.\\n\\n7. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Lee Jung-mi and Justice Lee Jin-sung\\nUnlike the majority opinion, we believe that the provision subject to review violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringes the Petitioner’s freedom to leave the country, and therefore state our opinion as follows.\\n\\nA. Legitimacy of the legislative purpose and appropriateness of means\\nAs stated by the majority opinion, the provision subject to review, which permits the prohibition of departure by a person pending criminal trial for a certain period, seeks to realize the discovery of substantive truth and judicial justice by preventing flight abroad by a person pending criminal trial and thereby securing the State’s power to punish, and thus its legislative purpose is legitimate, and the appropriateness of means is also recognized.\\n\\nB. Minimal impairment\\nBecause the Minister of Justice’s departure prohibition decision restricts the freedom to leave the country, which is an important constitutional fundamental right that the people must enjoy for enhancement of personality through observation abroad and occupational activities, exchange of various information, and formation of personality free from cultural prejudice (see the dissenting opinion to Constitutional Court Decision of Oct. 28, 2004, 2003HEONGA18), it is necessary to permit it only for the minimum period in cases where it is unavoidable for securing the State’s power to punish.\\n\\nIn today’s world, where conducting economic activities or daily life across borders has become common, even a person pending criminal trial may have a need to depart, such as where the person has a main base of life or business base in a foreign country or must travel abroad for work, and there is ample room for different determinations as to whether departure should be prohibited depending on concrete circumstances such as the type and nature of the offense, the degree of reproach, the risk of flight abroad, etc. However, the provision subject to review allows departure to be prohibited merely on the ground that the person is pending criminal trial, and thus has the potential to excessively restrict the fundamental rights of a non-detention defendant for whom a strong need to depart is requested. This is even more so in the case of a non-detention defendant who frequently travels abroad for work, insofar as the person may suffer disadvantages that interfere with livelihood. Even in light of the statistics showing that the Minister of Justice’s approval rate for requests for departure prohibition against persons pending criminal trial exceeds 97%, it is difficult to conclude that the Minister of Justice considers the concrete circumstances of persons pending criminal trial when deciding whether to prohibit departure.\\n\\nFurthermore, the Immigration Control Act allows the period to be extended where it is recognized that departure prohibition must continue beyond the 6-month maximum period of departure prohibition (Article 4-2), but it does not impose any special limitation on the number of extensions. As a result, the Minister of Justice may repeatedly extend the period of departure prohibition without limitation on the number of times, thereby causing serious restrictions on the freedom to leave the country of a person pending criminal trial by prohibiting departure for periods ranging from as short as several months to as long as several years until a guilty or not guilty judgment becomes final.\\n\\nThe departure prohibition of a person pending criminal trial must be limited to the minimum necessary for the realization of the State’s power to punish. Specifically, other methods that are less restrictive of fundamental rights while still achieving the legislative purpose appear to be fully conceivable, such as: a measure of strictly prohibiting departure under explicit statutory additional requirements, such as where there is a high risk of flight abroad or where the person fails to appear on the trial date; a measure of prohibiting departure for a period not exceeding 1 month or limiting the number of extensions, as is done for persons whose departure is prohibited for criminal investigation purposes; a measure enabling prior judicial control, such as requiring the competent trial panel, which knows best about the relevant case, to submit its opinion on whether departure should be permitted by considering various circumstances such as the defendant’s charged facts, the possibility of destruction of evidence, the defendant’s attitude, the necessity of departure, and whether entry into the country is guaranteed; or a measure limiting departure prohibition to cases in which the defendant is indicted for a serious offense according to the gravity of the offense.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that relief of rights may be obtained through objection or administrative litigation, but the objection procedure prescribed in Article 4-5 of the Immigration Control Act is a self-remedy procedure by the Minister of Justice, who is the subject of the departure prohibition decision, and thus cannot be regarded as highly effective. In fact, in light of the fact that only 3 out of a total of 86 objections from 2010 through 2012 were granted, it can be seen that the possibility of relief through objection is slight. Furthermore, in the case of filing administrative litigation such as a suit to revoke a departure prohibition disposition, it cannot be excluded that dismissal may occur on the ground that the period of departure prohibition has elapsed during the litigation and that there is no standing to sue, because litigation takes a relatively long time; thus, this also cannot be regarded as an effective remedy.\\n\\nAccording to statistics, although cases of departure prohibition for criminal investigation account for more than half and constitute a high proportion, cases of departure prohibition on the ground that a person is pending criminal trial also account for 5 to 10% of the total number of departure prohibition cases, showing that the number is by no means small. As for foreign legislative examples, apart from methods such as refusal to issue a passport to a person suspected of a serious crime, surrender or invalidation of an issued passport, there are few legislative examples, like ours, in which the Minister of Justice decides departure prohibition for a person pending criminal trial.\\n\\nIf so, even a person pending criminal trial should, in principle, be guaranteed freedom to leave the country where the smooth progress of the trial can be ensured, and therefore the provision subject to review, which allows departure prohibition throughout the trial period, violates the principle of minimal impairment.\\n\\nC. Balance of legal interests\\nThe provision subject to review imposes serious disadvantages amounting to interference with livelihood on persons pending criminal trial who must depart for work, and also restricts for a certain period the freedom to leave the country, which is an important constitutional fundamental right, for other persons pending criminal trial; thus, it excessively restricts the fundamental rights of persons pending criminal trial compared with the public interest of preventing flight abroad and ensuring the smooth progress of trials that the provision subject to review seeks to achieve. Accordingly, the provision subject to review also violates the principle of balance of legal interests.\\n\\nD. Conclusion\\nIf so, the provision subject to review violates the Constitution because it infringes the Petitioner’s freedom to leave the country in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction."}
