Outline of the Case\\n\\n(1) Case 96HEONBA28\\n\\nPetitioner Jeon ○ Hwan was arrested on 3 Dec. 1995 on charges including rebellion, and was indicted for the crimes of rebellion, insurrection, and violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes; Petitioner Jeong Ho-yong was arrested on 31 Jan. 1996 on suspicion of insurrection, and was indicted for the crimes of insurrection and violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes; and Petitioners Heo ○ Su and Heo ○ Pyeong were each arrested on 31 Jan. 1996 on suspicion of insurrection, and were indicted for the crimes of insurrection and rebellion, and the above cases were pending before the 30th Criminal Division of the Seoul District Court. In view of the progress of the proceedings in the above cases, the Petitioners filed a motion for a declaration of unconstitutionality as to whether Articles 70(1) and 73 of the former Criminal Procedure Act (as in force before amendment by Act No. 5054 of 29 Dec. 1995, hereinafter referred to as the “Act”), which are the provisions serving as the basis for the court’s ex officio issuance of warrants, violate Article 12(3) of the Constitution, which provides that “... when ... arresting or detaining ... a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application shall be presented,” on the ground that it was impossible to conclude the trial by the expiration dates of their respective detention periods (Petitioner Jeon Du-hwan: 2 June 1996; Petitioners Jeong Ho-yong, Heo Sam-su, and Heo Hwa-pyeong: 30 July 1996), and that, since the said court had already issued, on 15 May 1996, separate detention warrants against Petitioners I ○ Woo and No ○ Woo regarding criminal facts among the facts charged that were not stated in the detention warrant, it was expected that it would also issue, ex officio, detention warrants against them regarding the criminal facts among the facts charged that were not stated in the detention warrant. However, when the said court on 16 May 1996 dismissed each of the Petitioners’ motions for referral for a constitutional review, they filed this constitutional complaint adjudication on 27 May of the same month pursuant to Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act.\\n\\n(2) Cases 96HEONBA31 and 96HEONBA32\\n\\nPetitioner I ○ Woo was arrested on 17 Nov. 1995, and Petitioner No ○ Woo on 16 Nov. of the same month, each on suspicion of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (acceptance of bribery), and each was indicted on 5 Dec. 1995 for the said crimes, etc. When the detention periods for the above Petitioners expired on 16 May 1996 and 15 May of the same month, respectively, after two renewals, the Presiding Judge of the 30th Criminal Division of the Seoul District Court issued, on 10 May 1996, detention warrants pursuant to Articles 70 and 73 of the Act with respect to the criminal facts among the facts charged against the above Petitioners other than those stated in the detention warrant. Accordingly, the above Petitioners filed a quasi-appeal against each detention warrant issued on 10 May 1996, and filed a motion for referral for a constitutional review with the 23rd Criminal Division of the Seoul District Court (96CHO1852, 1830) on the ground that Articles 70(1) and 73 of the Act, which served as the basis for the issuance of the above warrants, violate Article 12(3) of the Constitution, which provides that “when arresting, detaining ... a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application shall be presented,” but when the said court on 18 May 1996 dismissed each of the above Petitioners’ motions, they filed this constitutional complaint adjudication on 29 May of the same month pursuant to Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act.\\n\\nb. Subject of Review\\n\\nThe subject of review in this case is whether the phrase in Articles 70(1) and 73 of the Act, “a detention warrant shall be issued when ... arresting or detaining a defendant,” is in violation of the Constitution. The content of each of the above provisions is as follows [Although the Petitioners stated in the petitum of the petition for review that they sought a constitutional review of the entirety of Article 73 of the Act, in substance they are seeking review on the ground that the portion of the above provision relating to the detention (arrest, detention) of a defendant is unconstitutional, and thus the subject of review is determined as above].\\n\\nAct Article 70 (Grounds for Detention) ① The court may detain a defendant if there is a reasonable ground to suspect that the defendant has committed a crime and if any one of the following grounds exists.\\n\\n1. Where the defendant has no fixed residence\\n2. Where there is a risk that the defendant may destroy evidence\\n3. Where the defendant may flee or there is a risk that the defendant may flee\\n\\nAct Article 73 (Issuance of Warrant) A summons shall be issued when summoning a defendant, and a detention warrant shall be issued when arresting or detaining a defendant.\\n\\n2. The Petitioners’ Arguments and the Opinions of Interested Institutions\\n\\na. The Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\nThe main text of Article 12(3) of the Constitution provides that “when arresting, detaining, searching, or seizing, a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application shall be presented in accordance with due process of law.” This is a provision intended to guarantee the fundamental rights of the people against unjust infringement of human rights by all public authority, including judges, and it therefore means not only that the warrant-issuing authority must be a judge and that no person may be subjected to arrest, detention, seizure, or search without a warrant, but also that a judge may issue a warrant only upon the prosecutor’s application. Our Constitution has provided the same purport since the Fifth Amendment Constitution of 26 Dec. 1962.\\n\\nAccordingly, the provisions subject to review in this case, which permit a court to issue a warrant even without the prosecutor’s application, are provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act enacted under the Constitution that had merely provided for “a judge’s warrant” with respect to the issuance of warrants, and have remained in force without being amended to conform to the above Fifth Amendment Constitution; they are therefore unconstitutional statutory provisions.\\n\\nb. Grounds for Dismissal of the Motion for Referral for Constitutional Review and Summary of the Opinion of the Chief Prosecutor of the Seoul District Prosecutors’ Office\\n\\nThe phrase in the main text of Article 12(3) of the Constitution, “... upon the prosecutor’s application ...,” clearly provides that, in order for arrest, detention, etc. to be carried out by an investigative agency, the procedure of an application by a prosecutor must be followed, and that no investigative agency other than a prosecutor may apply for the issuance of a detention warrant; it does not provide that the prosecutor’s application is required even in cases where a judge, at the trial stage, issues a warrant ex officio and detains a person. This is clear from the very nature of the warrant principle.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the provisions subject to review in this case are intended to ensure the defendant’s appearance in court, eliminate obstruction of the proceedings caused by flight and destruction of evidence, thereby making possible the collection and preservation of evidence for the discovery of the substantive truth, and realize the State’s punitive power specifically determined through the trial procedure, and thus do not violate the constitutional principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\n3. Judgment\\n\\na. Article 12(3) of the Constitution provides that “... when ... detaining ... a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application shall be presented ...,” and the above provision may literally be interpreted, as the Petitioners argue, as providing that the issuance of a detention warrant must always be preceded by an application by a prosecutor, regardless of whether it is the pretrial investigative stage or the trial stage. On the other hand, it may also be interpreted as providing that, in detaining a suspect at the investigative stage, a warrant must be obtained from a judge, and that at that time only a prosecutor among the investigative agencies may apply for the warrant. Which of the above interpretations accords with the purport of the Constitution will ultimately be determined in light of the essence of the warrant principle and the history of the adoption of the above constitutional provision.\\n\\nb. Article 12(1) of the Constitution provides that “All citizens shall enjoy freedom of the person. No person shall be arrested, detained, searched, or interrogated except as provided by law, and no person shall be punished, subjected to security measures, or forced labor except as provided by law and through due process of law.” The first sentence of the above provision declares freedom of the person, and the second sentence provides that, where freedom of the person is infringed, the principle of due process must be observed.\\n\\nAlthough freedom of the person, together with freedom of thought, is the basis of all fundamental rights, it has historically often been infringed upon by the State, especially in the form of the exercise of punitive power. Therefore, after declaring the principle of due process in Article 12(1), the Constitution lists in Article 12(2) through (7) several principles of particular importance among those that may be derived from the principle of due process. Among them, Article 12(3) of the Constitution, which is the provision relevant to this case, declares the warrant principle by providing that “when arresting, detaining, searching, or seizing, a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application shall be presented in accordance with due process of law....”\\n\\nThe warrant principle is the principle that, in relation to criminal procedure, coercive measures such as arrest, detention, and seizure may not be taken unless pursuant to a warrant issued by a judge whose status is guaranteed by judicial independence; therefore, the essence of the warrant principle lies in the fact that coercive measures infringing freedom of the person must be based only on a warrant issued, after concrete review, by a neutral judge.\\n\\nWhether at the investigative stage or at the trial stage, there will inevitably be cases where coercive measures such as detention cannot be avoided for the needs of investigation or trial. However, from the standpoint of the suspect or defendant subject to such coercive measures, a serious infringement of fundamental rights will occur. Therefore, the Constitution declares the warrant principle as a means of protecting the fundamental rights of the people from abuse of coercive measures. In particular, among coercive measures, in the case of coercive measures by investigative agencies, as opposed to those by the court, which has the status of a neutral adjudicator (the structure of criminal procedure in our country is, in principle, an adversarial structure; see Constitutional Court Decision 92HEONMA44, decided on 30 Nov. 1995), the more public power is exercised overtly for the purpose of finding the offender and securing evidence, the greater the possibility of infringing the fundamental rights of the people. Thus, the significance of the warrant principle is great in that it prevents abuse of coercive measures by investigative agencies and promotes the protection of human rights through prior and judicial restraint by judges over rights infringements by investigative agencies (in this respect, the legal character of warrants issued ex officio by a court and detention warrants issued upon application by an investigative agency does not differ. That is, the former is understood to have the character of a command order, while the latter has the character of an authorization).\\n\\nc. However, Article 12(3) of the Constitution provides that “... when ... detaining ... a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application ...,” as though the prosecutor’s application were required for the issuance of every detention warrant. Such a provision, with respect to the issuance of detention warrants, was not present in the original Constitution, which merely provided that “an arrest, detention, or search shall require a judge’s warrant” (Article 9), but was first introduced in the Fifth Amendment Constitution of 26 Dec. 1962 through the provision that “... when detaining ... a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application shall be presented” (main text of Article 10(3)). Although there are some differences in wording, the same content has continued through the current Constitution.\\n\\nThe reason why the Fifth Amendment Constitution added the requirement of a “prosecutor’s application” with respect to the issuance of detention warrants can be understood in connection with the amendment of the Criminal Procedure Act of 1 Sept. 1961.\\n\\nAt the time the Criminal Procedure Act was first enacted (Act No. 341 of 23 Sept. 1954), the provision concerning applications for warrants by investigative agencies stated that “where there is a reasonable ground to suspect that a suspect has committed a crime and there exists one of the grounds set forth in subparagraphs of Article 70(1), a prosecutor or judicial police officer may obtain a detention warrant from the competent district court judge and detain the suspect” (main text of Article 201(1)), thereby granting the power to apply for warrants not only to prosecutors but also to judicial police officers. However, by the amendment to the Criminal Procedure Act of 1 Sept. 1961 (Act No. 705), this was amended to provide that “where there is a reasonable ground to suspect that a suspect has committed a crime and there exists one of the grounds set forth in subparagraphs of Article 70(1), a prosecutor may obtain a detention warrant from the competent district court judge and detain the suspect” (main text of Article 201(1)), thereby limiting the person who may apply for a warrant to a prosecutor. This amendment to the Criminal Procedure Act was reflected in the constitutional amendment of 1962.\\n\\nAccordingly, the purport of the Fifth Amendment Constitution in adding the requirement of a “prosecutor’s application” with respect to the issuance of warrants was to establish the prosecutor’s power to direct investigations over other investigative agencies, and thereby to prevent the harmful effects of human rights violations arising from warrant applications by investigative agencies other than prosecutors, which had frequently occurred in the past. Therefore, it is reasonable to interpret the phrase “prosecutor’s application” in Article 12(3) of the current Constitution not as meaning that a prosecutor’s application is required for the issuance of every warrant, but as limiting the person who may apply for a warrant at the investigative stage to a prosecutor. In other words, the purport is to prevent indiscriminate applications for warrants by other investigative agencies and reduce the possibility of infringing the fundamental rights of the people by requiring that warrant applications at the investigative stage pass through a prosecutor, who is a legal expert.\\n\\nd. Taking a comprehensive view of the essence of the warrant principle and the history of Article 12(3) of the Constitution as discussed above, the warrant principle is derived from the provisions of Article 12(1) and (3) of the Constitution, and among them, the purport of Article 12(3) of the Constitution in providing that “... when ... detaining ... a warrant issued by a judge upon the prosecutor’s application ...” is understood to lie in especially emphasizing the warrant principle at the investigative stage and at the same time limiting the person who may apply for a warrant at the investigative stage to a prosecutor (the constitutional basis for the issuance of warrants at the trial stage lies in Article 12(1) of the Constitution).\\n\\nOtherwise, interpreting the purport of Article 12(3) of the Constitution as requiring the prosecutor’s application even for the issuance of warrants at the trial stage would lead to the result that the investigative agency, which is the object of judicial restraint intended to protect freedom of the person, would control the judge, who is the subject of judicial restraint, and would rather run counter to the essence of the warrant principle.\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court’s holding in Decision 96HEONMA256, decided on 28 Nov. 1996, that “after a prosecution is instituted in court, ... under the Criminal Procedure Act, the authority concerning the defendant’s detention belongs solely to the judge, and the prosecutor has no authority even similar to the prosecutor’s right to request a detention warrant in order to detain a suspect ...” was also to the same effect.\\n\\nAccordingly, the provisions subject to review in this case do not violate Article 12(3) of the Constitution, and they also do not appear to violate any other part of the Constitution.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, since the portion of Articles 70(1) and 73 of the Act stating that “a detention warrant shall be issued when ... arresting or detaining a defendant” does not violate the Constitution, the decision is made as stated in the disposition, except for the separate opinion of Justice Cho Seung-hyeong regarding the wording of the disposition in 5. below, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices.\\n\\n5. Separate Opinion of Justice Cho Seung-hyeong Regarding the Wording of the Disposition\\n\\nI think that in the wording of the disposition, the phrase “The portion of Article 70(1) and 73 of the former Criminal Procedure Act (...) stating that ‘a detention warrant shall be issued when ... arresting or detaining a defendant’ does not violate the Constitution” should properly be replaced with “the petition is dismissed.”\\n\\nThe reason is that, as explained in detail in the separate opinions regarding the wording of the disposition in each of the cases of a constitutional complaint concerning Article 75(1)1 of the Military Criminal Act in 92HEONBA45, a constitutional complaint concerning Article 52(1)3 of the former Housing Construction Promotion Act in 93HEONBA62, a constitutional complaint concerning Article 62(3) of the former Tax Reduction and Exemption Regulation Act in 94HEONBA7·8 (consolidated), a constitutional complaint concerning Article 20(1) of the Special Measures Act on the Arrangement of Requisitioned Property in 95HEONBA22, and a constitutional complaint concerning Article 3 of the Small Claims Trial Act in 94HEONBA28, decided by our Court on 26 Oct. 1995, there is no need to issue, despite the absence of binding force under Article 75(7) and Article 47 of the Constitutional Court Act, a decision of constitutionality. In this case, since the people have filed the petition alleging unconstitutionality, there is no need to state in the disposition the word “constitutional,” which was not even sought by the people, merely because the conclusion cannot be accepted, that is, because it is constitutional and thus has no practical effect.\\n\\n27 Mar. 1997."}

question: Bar Examination, 13th Session, Public Law Multiple-Choice Question 8. Which of the following is the correct combination of the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (×) regarding the pardon system? (In case of dispute, according to precedents) (a) The President may grant amnesty, commutation of sentence, or restoration of rights as provided by law, and under the Act on the Pardon, etc., when general amnesty, general commutation of sentence, or general restoration of rights is granted, the consent of the National Assembly must be obtained. (b) Under the Act on the Pardon, etc., when the Minister of Justice submits to the President a recommendation for special amnesty, commutation of sentence for a specified person, and restoration of rights, it must undergo review by the Pardon Review Committee, and when the President grants special amnesty, commutation of sentence for a specified person, and restoration of rights, the consent of the National Assembly is not required. (c) Restoration of rights shall not be granted to a person whose execution of sentence has not yet been completed or who has not been exempted from execution. (d) Because an individual convict has no subjective right to demand special amnesty or commutation of sentence, there is no constitutional duty to act or statutory duty on the President, the Minister of Justice, etc. to grant special amnesty to, or commute the sentence of, a convict.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2005HEONMA111]": "1. Summary of the Case  \\nThe Petitioner, who is confined in Gwangju Prison, was sentenced by the Gwangju High Court on 1997. 9. 10. to imprisonment for 10 months, suspended for 2 years, for violation of the Act on the Regulation of Illegal Checks, etc., and the said sentence became final on 11. 25. of the same year. However, because there was a prior fact that a sentence of a fine of 2,000,000 won had been imposed on the Petitioner and had become final, on 1997. 9. 10. the Gwangju High Court separately sentenced the Petitioner to imprisonment for 6 years for the crime of forging an official document, etc.  \\nThe Petitioner, alleging that, according to Criminal Act Article 37 as amended by Act No. 7077 on 2004. 1. 20., even among several offenses for which judgments have not become final, if there is an offense for which a judgment imposing a fine has become final, one sentence is to be imposed, and thus it is a provision favorable to the defendant because it results in a lighter sentence than when separate sentences are imposed, but that it is not being applied to the Petitioner, whose judgment has already become final and who is serving a term of imprisonment, and asserting that the inaction of not taking measures such as legislation or special amnesty and commutation to relieve cases like the Petitioner violates Articles 11 and 13, etc. of the Constitution, filed the constitutional complaint in this case.\\n\\n2. Decision  \\na. Part of the petition concerning legislative inaction  \\nThe Constitutional Court’s jurisdiction over constitutional complaints concerning legislative inaction is, as established precedent of our Court, recognized only in a limited manner in cases where, although the Constitution expressly delegates legislation for the guarantee of fundamental rights, the legislature has failed to implement it, or in cases where, by constitutional interpretation, a specific person acquires a concrete fundamental right and thereby the State’s duty to act or duty to protect arises, yet the legislature has taken no legislative measures at all (Constitutional Court, 1998. 5. 28., 96HEONMA44, Reports 10-1, 687, 692, etc.).  \\nHowever, the status of a prisoner against whom a judgment imposing imprisonment, etc. has become final and that of a defendant whose sentence has not become final are different, and under Criminal Act Article 37 prior to its amendment by Act No. 7077 on 2004. 1. 20., there is no express constitutional legislative delegation requiring legislation to establish a system to relieve the Petitioner, who received separate sentences rather than one sentence because among several offenses for which judgments had not become final there was an offense for which a judgment imposing a fine had become final, nor can it be said, by constitutional interpretation, that the legislature’s duty to act or duty to protect the Petitioner’s fundamental rights through such legislation arose.  \\nTherefore, this part of the petition, premised on the existence of the legislature’s legislative duty, does not satisfy the requirements for a constitutional complaint concerning legislative inaction and is inadmissible.\\n\\nb. Constitutional complaint concerning inaction in special amnesty or commutation  \\nIn the case of a constitutional complaint against inaction by administrative power, it is permissible only where the subject of public power is specifically and concretely prescribed with a duty to act deriving from the Constitution, and on that basis the holder of a fundamental right may demand an administrative act, yet the subject of public power neglects that duty; therefore, a mere general allegation that one suffered harm because of inaction in violation of a duty would be an inadmissible constitutional complaint (Constitutional Court, 1991. 9. 16., 89HEONMA163, Reports 3, 505, 513; 2002. 12. 18., 2002HEONMA52, Reports 14-2, 904, 908; 2003. 6. 26., 2002HEONMA484, Reports 15-1, 802, 807, etc.).  \\nHowever, according to the Act on Amnesty, special amnesty and commutation for a specific person are effected only when the prosecutor who directed the execution of the sentence and the superintendent of the prison where the prisoner is confined report to the Prosecutor General, the Prosecutor General applies to the Minister of Justice for submission, the Minister of Justice submits it to the President, and the President acts thereon; thus, since an individual prisoner does not have a subjective right to demand special amnesty or commutation, there exists no duty to act or legal duty derived from the Constitution requiring the President, the Minister of Justice, etc. to grant the Petitioner special amnesty or commutation (see Constitutional Court, 1995. 3. 23., 93HEONMA12, Reports 7-1, 416, 422).  \\nAccordingly, the mere fact that the Petitioner was not granted special amnesty or commutation cannot be regarded as non-exercise of public power subject to constitutional adjudication; thus, this part of the petition fails to satisfy the requirements for a constitutional complaint concerning inaction by administrative power and is inadmissible.\\n\\n3. Conclusion  \\nTherefore, as the constitutional complaint in this case is entirely inadmissible and falls within a case where the defects cannot be cured, it is decided, pursuant to Article 72(3)4 of the Constitutional Court Act, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, to dismiss it, and the decision is rendered as follows.  \\n2005. 2. 22."}

question: Which of the following explanations concerning the requirements for admissibility of an adjudication on a dispute over authority is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: The chairperson of the Agenda Adjustment Committee under the National Assembly Act does not fall under a state organ that may file an adjudication on a dispute over authority as prescribed by the Constitution and the Constitutional Court Act, and therefore legal capacity as a party in an adjudication on a dispute over authority is not recognized.
B: Under the current legal system, which contains no statutory provision permitting “third-party litigation standing” in an adjudication on a dispute over authority, a petition for adjudication on a dispute over authority filed by National Assembly members alleging that their right of consent was infringed in the conclusion of a contract that would become a burden on the State in addition to the budget is improper for lack of standing as petitioner.
C: A petition for adjudication on a dispute over authority may be filed only when the respondent’s disposition or omission has infringed, or presents a significant risk of infringing, the petitioner’s authority conferred by the Constitution or by law, and here “disposition” means only something of legal significance and must be an act that may specifically affect the petitioner’s legal status.
D: As a requirement for admissibility of a petition for adjudication on a dispute over authority, “omission” does not mean a mere de facto omission, but means failure to perform despite the existence of a constitutional or statutory duty to act.
E: Regardless of whether an act of a state organ constitutes the exercise of its independent power conferred on that state organ by the Constitution and laws, if such act of a state organ is subject to restrictions by another state organ, the possibility that the authority referred to in an adjudication on a dispute over authority is infringed may be recognized.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2004HEONRA3]": "1. Outline of the Case and Subject of Adjudication\\n\\nA. Outline of the Case\\n\\n(1) On 2004. 11. 12., the Respondent Government submitted the Draft Act Amending the Act on Local Education Autonomy (hereinafter referred to as the “Autonomy Bill”) and the Draft Act Amending the Local Education Subsidy Grant Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Grant Bill”), and these bills were referred to the National Assembly Education Committee on the 15th of the same month.\\n\\nThe stated purpose of the Autonomy Bill was to amend Article 39(1) of the then Act on Local Education Autonomy (hereinafter referred to as the “former Autonomy Act”), which provided that the State bear the expenses related to compulsory education and merely allowed local governments to bear part of the expenses for compulsory middle school education, so as to change the entities bearing the expenses related to compulsory education to the State and local governments.\\n\\nThe stated purpose of the Grant Bill was to re-adjust the support structure for local education finance in accordance with the full implementation of compulsory education for middle schools; specifically, ① to amend Article 11(1) of the then Local Education Subsidy Grant Act (hereinafter referred to as the “former Grant Act”), which provided that compulsory education expenses be covered by grant funds and transfers from local education grants and, with respect to teachers’ salaries at public schools other than compulsory education institutions, that local governments cover part thereof (provided that the Seoul Metropolitan Government cover the full amount) from transfers from the general account of the relevant local government, so as to cover compulsory education expenses with grant funds and transfers from the general account of local governments; and ② to amend Article 11(2) of the former Grant Act, which uniformly provided that an amount equivalent to 36/1,000 of the total local tax of the relevant city/province be appropriated as a transfer to the Special Account for Educational Expenses for the purpose of raising financial resources for education expenses, so as to distinguish between the Seoul Metropolitan Government and other local governments and, in the case of the former, to appropriate an amount equivalent to 10/100 of the total metropolitan city tax in the general account budget and transfer it to the Special Account for Educational Expenses.\\n\\n(2) On 2004. 11. 22., the Petitioner filed with the Constitutional Court a petition for an adjudication on a competence dispute, against the Respondent Government, seeking confirmation that ① the Respondent Government’s submission of the above amended bills (Article 39 of the Autonomy Bill, Articles 11(1) and 11(2) of the Grant Bill) and ② the laws amended thereby all infringe the Petitioner’s authority and are furthermore void, on the ground that the above amended bills violated Article 31(3) of the Constitution, which provides for the State’s bearing of expenses for compulsory education, Article 117(1) of the Constitution, which guarantees local autonomy, and Article 113(2) of the Local Autonomy Act, which guarantees sound management of local finances, thereby infringing or threatening to infringe the Petitioner’s autonomous fiscal authority.\\n\\n(3) The above amended bills submitted by the Respondent Government were each referred to the National Assembly Education Committee, placed on the agenda of the 7th Education Committee meeting of the 250th National Assembly (regular session), and underwent review reports and substitute debate; however, on 2004. 11. 25., at the 9th Education Committee meeting of the same National Assembly, it was resolved not to submit the above amended bills to the plenary session, but to adopt the corresponding amended bills (alternative bills) as committee bills, and on 2004. 12. 8., each was resolved in the plenary session of the National Assembly as committee bills, and on 2004. 12. 30., the partially amended Act on Local Education Autonomy (amended by Act No. 7252, hereinafter referred to as the “Act on Local Education Autonomy”) and the Local Education Subsidy Grant Act (amended by Act No. 7251, hereinafter referred to as the “Grant Act”) were promulgated, respectively.\\n\\n(4) Accordingly, on 2005. 4. 4., the Petitioner applied to amend the subject of the instant petition so that the “Respondent Government” be corrected to “the Respondent Government and the National Assembly,” stating that the subject of the instant adjudication petition includes not only the Respondent Government’s submission of the above amended bills but also the above amended laws resulting therefrom, and the Constitutional Court granted this on the 11th of the same month.\\n\\nB. Subject of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject of adjudication in this case is whether ① the Respondent Government’s act of submitting the Autonomy Bill and the Grant Bill to the 250th National Assembly (regular session) on 2004. 11. 12. infringes the Petitioner’s authority and, furthermore, is void; and whether ② the Respondent National Assembly’s provision in Article 39(1) of the Act on Local Education Autonomy (Act No. 7252) that the State and local governments shall bear the expenses related to compulsory education, the provision in Article 11(1) of the Grant Act (Act No. 7251) that compulsory education expenses shall be covered by grant funds and transfers from the general account of local governments, and the provision in Article 11(2) 3 that, distinguishing between the Seoul Metropolitan Government and other local governments, in the case of the Seoul Metropolitan Government, an amount equivalent to 10/100 of the total metropolitan city tax shall be appropriated in the general account budget and transferred to the Special Account for Educational Expenses, infringes the Petitioner’s authority and, furthermore, is void.\\n\\nThe contents of the relevant provisions and related provisions of the Act on Local Education Autonomy and the Grant Act are as follows.\\n\\nAct on Local Education Autonomy, Article 39 (Expenses for Compulsory Education, etc.) ① Salaries of teachers engaged in compulsory education and other expenses related to compulsory education shall be borne by the State and local governments in accordance with the Local Education Subsidy Grant Act.\\n② Expenses related to education other than compulsory education under paragraph (1) shall be borne by the State, local governments, and parents, etc. in accordance with the Local Education Subsidy Grant Act.\\n\\nSupplementary Provisions\\nThis Act shall enter into force on January 1, 2005.\\n\\nGrant Act, Article 11 (Burden of Local Governments) ① Expenses required for education and academic affairs in cities and provinces shall be borne by the Special Account for Educational Expenses of the relevant local government; provided, however, that expenses related to compulsory education shall be covered by grant funds and transfers from the general account under paragraph (2) among the financial resources of the Special Account for Educational Expenses, and expenses related to education other than compulsory education shall be covered by grant funds, transfers from the general account under paragraph (2), tuition fees, admission fees, etc. among the financial resources of the Special Account for Educational Expenses.\\n② For the establishment, operation, and improvement of the educational environment of public schools, each city/province shall appropriate the following amounts in the general account budget for each fiscal year and transfer them to the Special Account for Educational Expenses. The same shall apply where there is an increase or decrease by means of a supplementary budget.\\n1. An amount corresponding to the local education tax under Article 260-3 of the Local Tax Act\\n2. An amount corresponding to 45/100 of the tobacco consumption tax (excluding provinces)\\n3. The Seoul Metropolitan Government: an amount corresponding to 10/100 of the total metropolitan city tax (excluding the amount corresponding to a purpose tax under Article 6(1) 2 of the Local Tax Act), metropolitan cities and Gyeonggi Province: an amount corresponding to 5/100 of the total metropolitan city tax or provincial tax (excluding the amount corresponding to a purpose tax under Article 6(2) 2 of the Local Tax Act), and other provinces: an amount corresponding to 36/1,000 of the total provincial tax\\n\\nSupplementary Provisions\\n① (Effective Date) This Act shall enter into force on January 1, 2005.\\n② (Term of Validity) The amended provisions of Articles 3 and 11 shall remain effective until December 31, 2006.\\n\\n2. The Grounds for the Petitioner’s Petition and the Respondents’ Answers\\n\\nA. Grounds for the Petition\\n\\n(1) Although our Constitution does not expressly state so, the entity that bears the cost of compulsory education is, of course, the State, and since the establishment of the Republic of Korea, educational finance policy has been consistently maintained on that premise. The former Autonomy Act and the former Grant Act, amended on 2001. 12. 19., also, under the principle that the State bears the salaries of teachers engaged in compulsory education institutions (main text of Article 39(1) of the former Autonomy Act), merely provided that, until December 31, 2004, part of the expenses related to compulsory middle school education would temporarily be borne by local governments (proviso to Article 39(1) of the former Autonomy Act, Supplementary Provisions 2 and 3).\\n\\nAccordingly, even though the State should naturally bear the salaries of middle school teachers from 2005. 1. 1., when compulsory middle school education is fully implemented, the Respondents, through the Act on Local Education Autonomy and the Grant Act, are causing local governments continuously to bear all or part of the salaries of middle school teachers, which are expenses for compulsory education; this violates Article 31(3) of the Constitution concerning the compulsory education system, Article 117(1) of the Constitution concerning the guarantee of local autonomy, and the provisions and spirit of the education-related statutes.\\n\\nIn addition, the Grant Act distinguishes between the Seoul Metropolitan Government and other local governments and, only in the case of the former, requires that an amount equivalent to 10/100 of the total metropolitan city tax be appropriated in the general account budget and transferred to the Special Account for Educational Expenses; this violates the principle of equality.\\n\\nIf the salaries of teachers at middle schools, which are compulsory education institutions, are forcibly borne by transfers from the general account, the Petitioner will, to that extent, be constrained in autonomously budgeting for the welfare of residents.\\n\\n(2) As the主体 of education, the State not only exercises substantive plenary authority over major educational policies such as the establishment of secondary schools and the curriculum and content of education, but also, since the legal status of teachers at national and public schools is that of national public officials, the State should naturally bear the salaries of such teachers.\\n\\nEven in the 1960s, when national finances were poor, the State adhered to the principle that teachers at compulsory education institutions should be salaried by the State and also bore one-half of the salaries of teachers at non-compulsory education institutions. The fact that, even after the national budget has increased beyond comparison and after secondary schools were completely converted to compulsory education after 2005, the State will not bear the salaries of teachers at compulsory education institutions is contrary to the spirit of the Constitution and to the consistent educational policy of the past 50 years.\\n\\n(3) The Respondent Government’s act of submitting the bills and the laws amended thereby infringe the Petitioner’s autonomous fiscal authority granted by the Constitution and the Local Autonomy Act, and are void.\\n\\nB. The Respondent Government’s Answer\\n\\n(1) This case concerns matters of local government affairs relating to education and academic affairs, and therefore the Superintendent of the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education, not the Seoul Metropolitan Government, should be the party to the adjudication on a competence dispute.\\n\\n(2) The bills submitted by the Government were decided by the 250th National Assembly (regular session) Education Committee not to be referred to the plenary session, and instead the alternative bills adopted as committee bills became the basis of the amended laws; moreover, the Petitioner’s autonomous fiscal authority can be infringed not by the bills but only by laws as amended and promulgated, and the authority to amend laws resides in the National Assembly, so it was erroneous to designate the Government as the opposing party.\\n\\n(3) There is no constitutional provision or principle that the State must bear the expenses for compulsory education, and local governments may be made to bear such expenses by statute. The reason the State has borne most of the expenses for compulsory education thus far is that local autonomy was not properly implemented and local governments lacked the ability to bear the expenses; now that local autonomy has been invigorated and central authority is being transferred to local governments, local governments should also bear the expenses for compulsory education.\\n\\n(4) According to Article 9(2) 5 of the Local Autonomy Act, educational affairs and the establishment, operation, and supervision of public schools such as middle schools are inherent affairs of local governments, and therefore, as a matter of principle, their financial resources should be procured and borne by local governments; the mere fact that teachers have the status of national public officials does not mean that the State must bear their salaries.\\n\\n(5) The autonomous fiscal authority asserted by the Petitioner is too abstract to be regarded as a concrete authority, and under the amended provisions, the nationwide total amount borne by local governments decreases compared to the previous system; the same applies in the Petitioner’s case, so it cannot be said that the Petitioner’s authority is infringed.\\n\\nC. The Respondent National Assembly’s Answer\\n\\nIt is substantially the same as the Respondent Government’s answer.\\n\\n3. Determination on Procedural Requirements\\n\\n(1) The Respondents contend that, because this case concerns a competence dispute over the affairs of a local government relating to education and academic affairs, the Superintendent of the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education, not the Seoul Metropolitan Government, should be the party to the adjudication on a competence dispute. However, the essence of the competence dispute in this case lies in how financial burdens relating to education and academic affairs are to be allocated in the relationship between the State and local governments, and the Petitioner’s intent in seeking adjudication is that the Seoul Metropolitan Government, as a local government, had its power to formulate budgets infringed by the Respondents’ acts; therefore, this competence dispute cannot be said to fall under “a competence dispute concerning the affairs of a local government relating to education and academic affairs under Article 2 of the Act on Local Education Autonomy” as provided in Article 62(2) of the Constitutional Court Act. Accordingly, the Respondents’ argument is without merit.\\n\\n(2) Article 61(1) of the Constitutional Court Act provides, “Where there is a dispute concerning the existence or scope of authority, the relevant State institution or local government may file a petition for an adjudication on a competence dispute with the Constitutional Court.” However, paragraph (2) provides, “A petition for an adjudication under paragraph (1) may be filed only where the Respondent’s disposition or omission has infringed, or there is a manifest danger of infringing, the Petitioner’s authority granted by the Constitution or by law.” Therefore, to file a petition for an adjudication on a competence dispute, there must be a disposition or omission by the Respondent.\\n\\nHere, since “disposition” is limited to that which has legal significance, an act that is not likely to specifically affect the Petitioner’s legal status cannot be deemed a “disposition,” and a petition for an adjudication on a competence dispute targeting such an act is not permissible.\\n\\nEven if the Government submits a bill, in order for it to become law it must go through numerous procedures in the National Assembly, and whether to accept the bill is entirely within the authority of the legislature, which exclusively holds the constitutional legislative power. Accordingly, the Government’s act of submitting a bill is merely a preliminary preparatory act for legislation and cannot be regarded as an act having legal significance so as to become an independent subject of an adjudication on a competence dispute.\\n\\nTherefore, the portion of the petition disputing the Respondent Government’s act of submitting the Autonomy Bill and the Grant Bill to the 250th National Assembly (regular session) on 2004. 11. 12. is procedurally improper.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Merits\\n\\nA. Interpretation of the Constitutional Provisions Concerning the Bearing of Expenses for Compulsory Education\\n\\nArticle 31(2) of the Constitution provides only that “All citizens shall be obligated to ensure that their children receive at least primary education and the education prescribed by law,” and Article 31(3) provides only that “Compulsory education shall be free,” and therefore a conclusion that the State, as the central government, must bear the expenses for compulsory education cannot be directly derived from the above constitutional text.\\n\\nThat does not mean, however, that by the nature of compulsory education the State, as the central government, must bear all costs. Originally, education, by its origin, stems from private education such as freedom of religious education and parents’ right to educate their children; moreover, centralized, uniform domination of education is far removed from the essence and ideal of education, and instead autonomous educational administration through participation by residents such as parents can be regarded as more desirable. Our Constitution also constitutionally guarantees local education autonomy through Article 31(4) and Article 117(1), and the Constitutional Court has also attributed to such local education autonomy the three constitutional values of democracy, local autonomy, and educational autonomy (Constitutional Court 2000. 3. 30. 99HEONBA113, Court Decisions 12-1, 359, 368-3698; 2002. 3. 28. 2000HEONMA283, Court Decisions 14-1, 211, 223). Such constitutional guarantees are realized through specific statutes on education via Article 31(6) of the Constitution.\\n\\nThe same applies to public education, at the core of which lies compulsory education. The guarantee that compulsory education shall be free is intended to guarantee equal educational opportunities to all children, which in turn requires that human and material facilities and resources be evenly provided throughout the country so as to meet the needs of all those subject to compulsory education. This does not necessarily mean, however, that it must be prescribed as an affair of the central government. If schools can be established in each local unit to meet demand and an educational system suited to local conditions can be implemented, then the average guarantee of compulsory education may rather better accord with the ideal of local education autonomy.\\n\\nThus, as a matter of principle, there is no reason that, whether for general education or compulsory education, the right to receive such education must be controlled and administered by the central government.\\n\\nThe constitutional provision on free compulsory education is merely a command to shift the burden of the cost of compulsory education from the direct burden of parents to the burden of the entire community, and is neutral as to how that public burden should be constituted. It is difficult to regard Articles 31(2) and 31(3) of the Constitution as directly commanding how the financial resources for such public burden are to be secured.\\n\\nRather, Article 31(4) of the Constitution provides that educational independence, professionalism, and political neutrality “shall be guaranteed as prescribed by law,” and paragraph (6) provides that fundamental matters concerning “the educational system and its operation, and educational finance” shall be prescribed by law, thereby delegating to the legislature matters other than those directly provided by the Constitution concerning the formation of the educational system and educational finance system (see Constitutional Court 1992. 11. 12. 89HEONMA88, Court Decisions 4, 739, 774-775). As the Constitution thus delegates the formation of education-related systems to the legislature, the legislature may, taking into account various factors and circumstances such as the fiscal conditions of the central and local governments and the level of compulsory education, devise and select among various policy measures for the enhancement of education and educational finance; and the legislature’s policy judgment and discretion in this regard are broadly recognized.\\n\\nB. Evaluation of the Revised Method of Bearing Compulsory Education Expenses\\n\\n(1) Perspective of Evaluation\\n\\nThere may be various discussions from educational and fiscal perspectives as to the relative advantages and disadvantages of the central government bearing the expenses for compulsory education and local governments bearing them. And in that regard, one should not discuss the matter abstractly and uniformly apart from the form of state in each country (whether it is a federal state or not, and what the relationship is between central and local governments), the education system and legal system, and the structure and condition of finances.\\n\\nFrom a principled standpoint, if local education autonomy is desirable, and if local education autonomy is adopted as a system, then local education finance is also desirable to be procured locally. If local governments are the主体 of education, educational finance should also be procured by local governments so that educational autonomy can be fully realized without dependence on or interference from the central government.\\n\\nHowever, since it is a common phenomenon in countries around the world that it is difficult to expect local governments to bear local education finance perfectly, the central government bears a certain responsibility to provide the conditions for education. Therefore, the question is how to distribute burdens and authority between the central and local governments, given the reality that local government finances are insufficient, so as to faithfully guarantee opportunities for public education.\\n\\n(2) Article 39(1) of the Act on Local Education Autonomy\\n\\nArticle 39(1) of the Act on Local Education Autonomy provides that expenses related to compulsory education, including teachers’ salaries for those engaged in compulsory education, shall be borne by the “State and local governments.” The specific content is delegated to the Grant Act, but the possibility of shared burden between the central government and local governments is established in this provision.\\n\\nAs seen above, the constitutional provisions relating to compulsory education, namely Article 31(1) through (3) of the Constitution, and Article 117(1) of the Constitution, which guarantees local autonomy, do not directly lead to the conclusion that the State, as the central government, must bear all compulsory education expenses. Accordingly, the mere fact that Article 39(1) of the Act on Local Education Autonomy contemplates the possibility of local government burden does not violate the above constitutional provisions.\\n\\nThis provision, which declares the possibility of fiscal burden by local governments, is also consistent with the system of local autonomy and the ideal of local education autonomy. If local autonomy is being invigorated and central authority is being transferred to the local level, it is natural that related fiscal burdens formerly borne by the central government are also transferred to local governments. The fact that the central government has borne compulsory education expenses over the past 50 years is related to the circumstances that local autonomy had not been properly implemented and that local governments, due to their low financial self-reliance, lacked the ability to bear such expenses. Although current circumstances have not greatly changed, seeking to broaden the fiscal burden of the local level in step with the pursuit of local education autonomy is not, in principle, wrong so long as this does not render hollow the constitutional command or purpose of free compulsory education.\\n\\n(3) Article 11(1) and Article 11(2) 3 of the Grant Act\\n\\nNext, the issue is whether the method and content of financial procurement specifically prescribed in the above provisions of the Grant Act are arbitrary and clearly contrary to the intended purpose of the Constitution’s delegation, which provides for free compulsory education and the statutory reservation of educational finance. The purpose of the delegation regarding compulsory education finance ultimately comes down to forming a financial system that can evenly and substantively guarantee the right to receive compulsory education. Accordingly, only where the right to receive compulsory education is rendered hollow or is significantly impeded by the method and content prescribed in the above provisions, in terms of substantive education finance stability and, from the perspective of fairness vis-à-vis others, nationwide average equality, can they be said to be unconstitutional.\\n\\nUpon examination: first, Article 11(1) of the Grant Act provides that compulsory education expenses shall be borne by the Special Account for Educational Expenses of local governments. Since revenues and expenditures are managed by an account independent of the general account of local governments, it is guaranteed that local governments cannot arbitrarily divert the revenues of this special account to purposes other than education.\\n\\nSecond, because compulsory education expenses are covered by grant funds from the national treasury and by transfers borne by local governments from their general budgets, the State is not recognized as bearing no responsibility at all with respect to compulsory education expenses, but is obligated to bear a certain part thereof. The State must appropriate such grants for local education in the national budget each fiscal year (Article 9(1) of the Grant Act).\\n\\nThird, examination of the criteria, method, and content for payment of grants shows that they substantially guarantee the stability of educational finance and nationwide average equality to a considerable degree. One structural characteristic of educational finance in our country is that the proportion of rigid expenses such as labor costs among educational expenses is overwhelmingly high (based on the 2005 expenditure budget, labor costs account for 65.6%, and school operation costs 14.4%); by statutory prescription of the criteria for grant payment with respect to items accounting for most compulsory education expenses, such as teachers’ labor costs, school operation costs, and costs for opening new schools (Article 2(1), Article 5(1), Article 6(1), Article 7(1) of the Grant Act, Article 4(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, and Attached Table 1), it guarantees stable procurement of compulsory education finance on a nationwide basis under the same standards. Meanwhile, because labor costs account for most compulsory education expenses, educational finance can be stabilized only when the total scale of educational finance increases accordingly as labor costs increase. However, where there is a significant fluctuation in labor cost requirements, the State is required to adjust the grant rate of grants (Article 4 of the Grant Act), and even in measuring the standard financial demand amount, there is a teacher labor-cost add-on item so that if the number exceeds the standard number of teachers, the amount increases by the number of excess teachers, and there are also provisions to address this. Furthermore, where there is a special educational finance demand, the State is to provide special grants. Special grants are to be provided when there is a special fiscal demand due to a national policy project related to education, when there is a special local educational issue demand, or when fiscal demand arises or fiscal revenue decreases due to a disaster (Article 5-2 of the Grant Act).\\n\\nFourth, the Petitioner argues that it is unfair to set, only for the Seoul Metropolitan Government, the ratio of the amount of the relevant city/province tax to the total amount to be appropriated each fiscal year in the general account budget and transferred to the Special Account for Educational Expenses at 10/100, higher than that of other local governments; however, in light of the Seoul Metropolitan Government’s high level of local fiscal self-reliance, this is a reasonable and appropriate differential treatment. Moreover, the share of the relevant city/province tax transfer, which is the only item that establishes such differential treatment based on fiscal self-reliance, in the Special Account for Educational Expenses is extremely low. Despite its high fiscal self-reliance, the Seoul Metropolitan Government still relies on the central government for about half of its total educational resources.\\n\\nTherefore, in conclusion, Article 11(1) and Article 11(2) 3 of the Grant Act fall far short of the level necessary to speak of a violation of the Constitution, whether from the perspective of securing stable educational finance or from the perspective of guaranteeing nationwide average equality.\\n\\nC. Determination on the Petitioner’s Other Arguments\\n\\n(1) The Petitioner argues that, as the主体 of education, the State substantially exercises plenary authority over major educational policies such as the establishment of secondary schools and the curriculum and content of education, and therefore the State should bear the salaries of teachers.\\n\\nPursuant to the delegation under Article 31(6) of the Constitution, the State, as the central government, regulating fundamental matters concerning the educational system by statute is not only its authority but also its duty. The State’s certain regulatory and supervisory powers over education and schools are intended to substantively guarantee the right to receive education and are one of the essential elements of the public education system, and are also recognized to a certain extent even in the legal system for private education. In addition, such authority of the State does not conflict with the ideal of local education autonomy. The State determines the basic conditions and structure of education and schools, and local educational institutions carry out concrete educational activities and administration within that framework; thus the two are harmonized.\\n\\nLooking at the current educational legal system concerning elementary and secondary education, the State prescribes by statute the basic matters for creating educational conditions, such as the types of schools, their establishment, and educational finance (Framework Act on Education Articles 7 and 11, Elementary and Secondary Education Act Articles 2, 4, and 12, Act on Local Education Autonomy Articles 38 and 39, etc.), and also prescribes by statute standards for educational content, such as teachers’ qualifications, curriculum, school year system, classes, and inspection and approval of textbook materials (Elementary and Secondary Education Act Articles 21, 23, 24, 26, 27, 29, etc.). It also establishes the educational administration system by granting supervisory authority over schools to the State or local governments (Framework Act on Education Article 17, Elementary and Secondary Education Act Articles 6 and 7, etc.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, looking at the authority of local governments or local educational institutions concerning education, the establishment, operation, and supervision of schools are regarded as autonomous affairs of local governments (Local Autonomy Act Article 9(2) 5(a), Framework Act on Education Article 11, Elementary and Secondary Education Act Article 12), and the Superintendent of Education and the Education Committee have various authorities concerning educational autonomy, such as the formulation or review and resolution of educational budgets, enactment of educational rules, operation of the curriculum, and supervisory authority over public and private schools (Act on Local Education Autonomy Article 8(1), Article 22, Elementary and Secondary Education Act Articles 6 and 7, etc.). The State assists local education finance (Act on Local Education Autonomy Articles 39 and 41(1)), and has certain supervisory authority over local educational institutions (Act on Local Education Autonomy Articles 47 and 48).\\n\\nThis legal system reflects the ideas and institutions of the current educational legal system, which cannot abandon either the State’s authority and responsibility for public education or local education autonomy; it is not intended to allow the State to exercise substantive plenary authority over education. The State’s determination of the basic conditions and structure of education and schools, and its exercise of supervisory authority to a certain extent, is simply a natural and universal phenomenon for fulfilling its educational responsibility, and therefore cannot justify requiring the central government to bear all educational financial resources. Even if it is true that the central government is interfering more than necessary in the content of education or the operation of schools, that issue must be separately considered in terms of whether such aspects are unconstitutional in light of the legal theory of local education autonomy; it cannot be directly converted into a question of educational finance burden.\\n\\n(2) The Petitioner argues that, since the legal status of teachers at national and public schools is that of national public officials, the State should also bear their salaries.\\n\\nTeachers at national elementary and secondary schools established by the State and teachers at public elementary and secondary schools established by local governments are all educational public officials and thus specific-category national public officials (Article 2(2) 2 of the State Public Officials Act). Only educational public officials working at public universities and junior colleges are specific-category local public officials (Article 2(2) 2 of the Local Public Officials Act).\\n\\nThus, making elementary and secondary teachers national public officials regardless of whether the school is national or public can also be seen as intended to secure nationwide average equality of public education conditions. If teachers are divided into national public officials and local public officials according to the entity that established the school, and their qualifications, appointment, remuneration, status guarantees, and service relations are regulated differently, the legal system concerning teachers, who are the human agents of education, will be bifurcated. Of course, if the overall level of local autonomy is high and local education autonomy is also realized at a high level so that local governments can independently establish and operate schools without special assistance from the central government, it would be possible to independently regulate the appointment, remuneration, and status guarantees of the teachers belonging to them. However, under the current level of local autonomy and in a situation where dependence of local education finance on the central government is high, if teachers at public schools are classified and separately regulated as local public officials, there is rather a risk that, in terms of qualifications, remuneration, and status guarantees of teachers, they will be subjected to disadvantageous differential treatment compared with teachers who are national public officials. Such a situation may create problems for guaranteeing the average level and fairness of public education conditions.\\n\\nThe current legal system uniformly regulates teachers’ qualifications, appointment, remuneration, status guarantees, and service relations through the Educational Public Officials Act, on the premise that making elementary and secondary teachers national public officials and regulating them under the same legal relations nationwide is beneficial to the guarantee of teachers’ status and position and contributes to the equal guarantee of public education.\\n\\nThus, not only is there a legitimate reason for making teachers national public officials, but the status or not of teachers is not a matter directly connected to the burden of educational finance. In a situation where the ideal of local education autonomy and the ideal of guaranteeing public education are intertwined, the status of teachers may run on the same track as the burden of educational finance, but it may also not. While it is not unnatural for the State to support most of teachers’ salaries through local education subsidy grants and to make teachers national public officials, it is also possible to make teachers local public officials while the State, depending on the circumstances of local finances, bears their salaries.\\n\\n(3) The Petitioner also argues that, although educational affairs are separated from the affairs of local governments and authority is granted to education-autonomy bodies, local governments have no authority over education, and therefore it is unjust to require local governments to bear educational expenses from their general resources.\\n\\nHowever, as seen above, the establishment, operation, and supervision of schools are autonomous affairs of local governments, and local governments are granted supervisory authority over schools. In addition, when a Superintendent of Education intends to submit a bill concerning matters related to the general account of a local government to the Education Committee, he or she must consult in advance with the mayor/governor of the city/province (Act on Local Education Autonomy Article 8(3) 2), and when preparing an expenditure budget covered by transfers from the local government’s general account, must consult in advance with the head of the local government (Article 11(4) of the Grant Act). Thus, the operation of local education is itself an affair of the local government, and the local government also has certain authorities such as supervisory authority over education and the right to consult on educational budgets.\\n\\nAbove all, the question of how to distribute resources other than national subsidies between local governments and local educational institutions in order to realize local education autonomy is a matter of legislative policy. It is possible to allow local educational institutions direct procurement by recognizing taxing power in them, or to require them to be covered by transfer revenues from the general account of local governments. This is also linked to various circumstances, especially the question of how the national tax system should be structured, and so long as it does not amount to rendering the procurement of local education resources hollow and thereby infringing the right to receive education, it is likewise a matter of policy choice.\\n\\n(4) The Petitioner further argues that, over the past 50 years, a legal system under which the State bears the salaries of compulsory education institutions has continued, creating a reliance thereon; and, on the eve of full implementation of compulsory middle school education, the Government used the circumstance that it would be difficult to bear the salaries of public middle school teachers immediately to temporarily require local governments to bear part of them for three years, but contrary to its promise, it changed the very principle that the State bears the burden, which violates the principle of protection of trust.\\n\\nHowever, statutes may generally be amended at any time due to changes in actual circumstances or changes in legislative policy (Constitutional Court 2002. 11. 28. 2002HEONBA45, Court Decisions 14-2, 704, 713), and a vague expectation that a legal relationship which has continued in the same form for a long period will continue in the future is difficult to regard as constitutionally protected trust. Moreover, as compulsory middle school education was expanded, the Government merely maintained, temporarily, the portion previously borne by local governments, considering that it would be burdensome on the State’s fiscal operation to bear in full even the salaries of some middle school teachers previously borne by local governments. Therefore, when balancing the value of protection of trust against the public interest objective to be realized through the new legislation, it cannot be said to violate the principle of trust.\\n\\nD. Whether There Has Been an Infringement of Authority\\n\\nThe subject of adjudication in a competence dispute is “whether the Petitioner’s constitutional or statutory authority has been infringed by the Respondent’s disposition or omission” (Article 61(2) of the Constitutional Court Act). In this case, what is subject to determination on the merits is the Respondent National Assembly’s legislative act, and the issue is whether it is unconstitutional. As seen above, there is no violation of constitutional provisions concerning education and local autonomy, and therefore an infringement of the Petitioner’s authority resulting therefrom is not recognized.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nBecause the petition for adjudication against the Respondent Government is procedurally improper, it is dismissed; and because the petition for adjudication against the Respondent National Assembly lacks merit, it is rejected. Accordingly, by the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating, the Court renders the decision as set forth in the order."}
