{"[98HEONRA3]": "1. Outline of the Case and the Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nA. Outline of the Case\\n\\nUpon assuming office as President on 1998. 2. 25., President Kim Dae-jung, who had been elected in the 15th Presidential Election held on 1997. 12. 18., transmitted to the National Assembly on the same day, inter alia, the motion for consent to the appointment of Kim Jong-pil, who is not a party to this petition, as Prime Minister. The Respondent convened the 189th Extraordinary Session of the National Assembly by setting the session period from the same day to the same year’s 3. 2. in order to process the above motion for consent to appointment, etc., at 14:00 on the same day, but it could not be opened due to the absence of members of the Grand National Party, and the extraordinary session thereafter continued to be deadlocked because of confrontation between the ruling and opposition parties.\\n\\nThen, at around 15:21 on 1998. 3. 2., the First Plenary Session of the 189th Extraordinary Session of the National Assembly was opened with members of both the ruling and opposition parties present, and at around 15:44 on the same day the Respondent placed on the agenda the “matter of consent to the appointment of the Prime Minister (Kim Jong-pil),” and immediately thereafter the voting of the National Assembly members commenced by secret ballot pursuant to Article 112(5) of the National Assembly Act. However, from around 15:50, members of the National Assembly belonging to the New Politics National Congress and the United Liberal Democrats, asserting that members belonging to the Grand National Party were casting blank ballots, obstructed the vote by blocking the ballot distribution table and ballot box, and accordingly, between members belonging to the Grand National Party who insisted on the continuation of the vote and members belonging to the New Politics National Congress and the United Liberal Democrats who demanded suspension of the vote or a revote, verbal altercations and physical scuffles broke out throughout the chamber, rendering the chamber so disorderly that the progress of the vote was difficult. The Respondent declared a recess at around 16:05, then declared the resumption of the session at around 16:08, but normal voting did not take place as the vote was again interrupted at around 16:21 and 16:24. At around 22:00 on the same day, a floor leaders’ meeting among the above three parties was held in the Speaker’s office to break the impasse, but the agreement broke down. The Respondent returned to the plenary chamber at around 22:40 and urged the members who had not completed voting to vote by 23:00, but the resumption of voting failed, and as midnight passed on the same day, the session was automatically adjourned, and the session period of the 189th Extraordinary Session of the National Assembly also expired. Thereafter, upon the application for preservation, etc. of ballot boxes under the names of representative members of the ruling and opposition parties, the ballot boxes, etc. in which 201 National Assembly members (155 belonging to the Grand National Party, 40 belonging to the New Politics National Congress, and 6 belonging to the National United Party) had completed voting were sealed.\\n\\nThe Petitioners alleged that, during the voting process on the motion for consent to the appointment of the Prime Minister on 1998. 3. 2., the Respondent, although the voting procedure had been lawful, infringed their voting authority as National Assembly members over the motion for consent to appointment by not counting the votes and not proclaiming the voting result, and on 1998. 3. 26. filed the present petition for adjudication on a dispute over powers against the Respondent.\\n\\nB. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether the Respondent, by not proceeding with the counting procedure and not proclaiming the voting result with respect to the vote on the “matter of consent to the appointment of the Prime Minister (Kim ○-pil)” (hereinafter referred to as the “motion for consent to appointment”), which was placed on the agenda of the First Plenary Session of the 189th Extraordinary Session of the National Assembly opened on 1998. 3. 2. (hereinafter referred to as the “plenary session at issue”), infringed the Petitioners’ right to vote on the motion for consent to appointment.\\n\\n2. Summary of the Parties’ Allegations\\n\\nA. The Petitioners’ Allegations\\n\\n(1) A National Assembly member’s right to vote or right to decide on a bill is a power granted to National Assembly members by Article 49 of the Constitution and Articles 109 and 111 of the National Assembly Act, and this power includes not only the authority to participate in voting but also the right to state opinions regarding the relevant agenda item, the right to confirm the voting result, and the like.\\n\\n(2) With respect to the motion for consent to appointment placed on the agenda of the plenary session at issue, voting proceeded by secret ballot pursuant to the National Assembly Act, but because of obstruction of voting by members belonging to the New Politics National Congress and the United Liberal Democrats, the process of suspending and resuming voting was repeated several times. However, the Respondent acknowledged the legality of the voting and repeatedly called for order maintenance and normal voting, and from around 22:40 on that day it had announced 23:00 as the deadline for completion of voting, and by then 201 National Assembly members, corresponding to more than two-thirds of the incumbent National Assembly members, had completed voting. If so, except for certain members who had abandoned voting while obstructing the vote, it should be deemed that the voting had concluded, and under Article 113 of the National Assembly Act, the Respondent, who is under a duty to proclaim the result when voting has ended, should naturally have declared the end of voting, proceeded with the counting procedure, and proclaimed the voting result. Nevertheless, the Respondent did not fulfill his duty prescribed in the National Assembly Act, and because of such omission by the Respondent, the Petitioners could no longer confirm the result of their vote on the motion for consent to appointment; ultimately, the Petitioners’ right to vote was infringed.\\n\\nB. The Respondent’s Allegations\\n\\n(1) The Petitioners merely seek relief on the ground that their powers were infringed by the Respondent’s omission, and since there is no dispute between the Petitioners and the Respondent concerning the attribution of powers, this petition is unlawful.\\n\\n(2) Since National Assembly members and the Speaker of the National Assembly are not State organs that may file a petition for adjudication on a dispute over powers, this petition is unlawful.\\n\\n(3) The Petitioners’ right to decide on a bill is not infringed merely because the voting result was not proclaimed, and even in a situation where voting was suspended and normal voting could not proceed due to a show of force between the ruling and opposition parties, the Respondent exerted his best efforts to proceed with normal voting and to achieve a political settlement; therefore, even if the Petitioners’ right to decide on the bill was infringed, responsibility cannot be attributed to the Respondent.\\n\\n3. Decision\\n\\nWe examine whether the petition in this case is lawful.\\n\\nA. The Respondent argues that, not only are National Assembly members and the Speaker of the National Assembly not State organs that may file a petition for adjudication on a dispute over powers, but also there is no dispute between the Petitioners and the Respondent concerning the attribution of powers, and thus this petition is unlawful.\\n\\nHowever, National Assembly members and the Speaker of the National Assembly qualify as State organs that may be parties to an adjudication on a dispute over powers (Constitutional Court 1997. 7. 16. 96HEONRA2, Collection of Decisions 9-2, 154), and according to Article 61(2) of the Constitutional Court Act, an adjudication on a dispute over powers may be requested when the Respondent’s disposition or omission has infringed, or poses a substantial risk of infringing, the authority of the Petitioner granted by the Constitution or laws. The petition in this case is one in which the Petitioners, who are National Assembly members, dispute against the Respondent, the Speaker of the National Assembly, that the Respondent infringed their voting authority by omitting to proceed with the counting procedure and proclaim the voting result with respect to the motion for consent to appointment; therefore, it satisfies the grounds for a petition for adjudication on a dispute over powers, and the above argument is not persuasive.\\n\\nB. As noted above, an adjudication on a dispute over powers may be requested when the Petitioners’ powers have been infringed, or there is a substantial risk of infringement, by the Respondent’s disposition or omission; and an adjudication on a dispute over powers alleging that the Petitioner’s powers were infringed by the Respondent’s omission is permitted only when the Respondent has a duty to act arising under the Constitution or laws, but nevertheless fails to fulfill such duty.\\n\\nIn this case, the subject matter of adjudication is whether the Respondent infringed the Petitioners’ voting authority by omitting to proceed with the counting procedure and proclaim the voting result with respect to the vote by National Assembly members on the motion for consent to appointment in the plenary session at issue. Accordingly, we examine whether the Respondent indeed had a duty to act to proceed with the counting procedure and proclaim the voting result as above.\\n\\nC. Article 10 of the National Assembly Act provides that the Speaker of the National Assembly shall represent the National Assembly, organize proceedings, maintain order, and supervise affairs, and the various provisions of Chapter 6 of the National Assembly Act grant the Speaker broad authority with respect to the overall session procedure, including convening, preparation of the agenda, referral of bills to standing committees and placement on the plenary session agenda, speeches and debates, and voting. Therefore, as to the proceedings of the National Assembly, in principle, authority and responsibility may be said to vest in the Speaker.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 113 of the National Assembly Act provides that “when voting has ended, the Speaker shall proclaim the result.” A National Assembly member’s vote is a composite act that determines the will of the National Assembly, which is a collegiate body, and since it is formally finalized by proclamation of the voting result, the above provision requiring proclamation of the voting result when voting has concluded is understood to confer upon the Speaker both authority and duty. In addition, because proclamation of the voting result is impossible without a counting procedure, it may be said that proceeding with the counting procedure when voting has concluded is the Speaker’s natural authority and duty even if there is no express provision on this matter. However, the Speaker’s duty to proceed with the counting procedure and proclaim the voting result, as above, presupposes that voting has concluded normally. It cannot be said that such duty is recognized even where voting was unlawfully conducted in clear violation of the National Assembly Act provisions concerning the voting method, or where voting cannot otherwise be regarded as having concluded normally.\\n\\nIn short, where voting has proceeded lawfully and concluded normally, the Speaker is deemed to have a duty to proceed with the counting procedure and proclaim the voting result.\\n\\nD. If so, whether the duty to act as asserted by the Petitioners can be recognized as having been imposed on the Respondent ultimately depends on whether the vote on the motion for consent to appointment in the plenary session at issue was in fact lawfully conducted and whether that vote concluded normally; we therefore examine this point.\\n\\nAccording to the records and evidence in this adjudication, as already noted in A. above under 1., voting by secret ballot began and proceeded at around 15:46 on 1998. 3. 2., and from around 15:50 members of the National Assembly belonging to the New Politics National Congress and the United Liberal Democrats, asserting that members belonging to the Grand National Party were casting blank ballots, demanded suspension and nullification of the vote and a revote, while members belonging to the Grand National Party insisted on the continuation of voting; confrontations without any room for compromise, including verbal altercations and physical scuffles, continued for several hours. At around 22:00 on the same day, a floor leaders’ meeting among the above three parties was held in the Speaker’s office to break the impasse, but the agreement ended in failure; the confrontation and differences between the ruling and opposition parties were ultimately not resolved, and as midnight passed the plenary session at issue was automatically adjourned, and it is found that 201 out of 299 incumbent National Assembly members had completed voting by that time.\\n\\nHowever, with regard to voting procedures, the National Assembly Act does not regulate every matter exhaustively, but sets forth only the basic and important matters in Articles 109 through 114. Even upon reviewing these provisions, it remains difficult to determine clearly whether the above vote on the motion for consent to appointment was indeed lawfully conducted and concluded normally. Furthermore, there are no National Assembly rules supplementing the National Assembly Act in this regard, nor does there appear to be any established parliamentary practice of the National Assembly (neither the Petitioners nor the Respondent alleges any parliamentary practice in this regard).\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 64 of the Constitution guarantees the autonomy of the National Assembly by providing that the National Assembly may enact rules concerning proceedings and internal discipline within the bounds not contrary to law, and may make autonomous decisions regarding qualifications review, discipline, and expulsion of members. As the representative organ of the people and the legislative body, the National Assembly has broad autonomy with respect to the operation of the National Assembly, including its proceedings and internal discipline; accordingly, unless there is a defect in its proceedings or legislative process that clearly violates the Constitution or laws, that autonomy must be respected in light of the principle of separation of powers and the status and function of the National Assembly (Constitutional Court 1997. 7. 16. 96HEONRA2, Collection of Decisions 9-2, 154). Therefore, it is not desirable for another State organ to intervene in and assess the propriety of the National Assembly’s judgment on matters within the scope of such autonomy, and the Constitutional Court is no exception.\\n\\nIn the present case, since there is no clear provision in the National Assembly Act regarding the lawfulness of the voting procedure for the motion for consent to appointment, and there is room for controversy, the handling of the various issues surrounding that voting procedure is a matter within the scope of the National Assembly’s autonomy, and thus could have been resolved autonomously through compromise and adjustment between the opposing ruling and opposition parties. However, even the floor leaders’ meeting among the three parties convened for this purpose ended in failure, as noted above.\\n\\nUnder these circumstances, the final authority to determine the voting procedure at issue should ultimately be deemed reserved to the Speaker of the National Assembly, that is, the Respondent, who is vested as the representative of the National Assembly with overall and comprehensive authority and responsibility over the proceedings (see Article 76(2) of the National Assembly Act). The Respondent has discretion to choose among various possible measures, such as how to view the effect of the vote already cast, whether to regard the vote as having been suspended, or instead to treat the vote as concluded and proceed with the counting procedure, whether to hold a revote, or whether to defer all such judgments and continue urging dialogue and compromise between the ruling and opposition parties. Such autonomous authority over proceedings recognized in the Respondent is broadly a type of autonomy of the National Assembly, and since it cannot be said that the Respondent’s failure to proceed with the counting procedure and proclaim the voting result under such a controversial factual situation clearly violated the Constitution or laws, other State organs must respect this. Therefore, it is not desirable for the Constitutional Court to independently judge whether the vote in the plenary session at issue concluded normally, and as a result it cannot be recognized that the Respondent had a duty to proceed with the counting procedure and proclaim the voting result. If such recognition were made, it would mean rejecting the Respondent’s autonomous judgment by a legal judgment of the Constitutional Court, thereby failing to respect the autonomy of the National Assembly.\\n\\nE. If so, it cannot be said that the Respondent had a duty to act to proceed with the counting procedure and proclaim the voting result with respect to the vote on the motion for consent to appointment, and unless such duty to act is recognized, an adjudication on a dispute over powers challenging infringement of powers by the Respondent’s omission is not permitted; therefore, this petition is unlawful.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nSince the Petitioners’ petition is unlawful, it is dismissed, and a decision is rendered as stated in the disposition. In this decision, except for the separate opinion of Justices Jeong Kyeong-sik and Shin Chang-eon set forth in 5. below regarding the statement of reasons, the opinions of the remaining Justices were in accord.\\n\\n5. Separate Opinion of Justices Jeong Kyeong-sik and Shin Chang-eon\\n\\nWe concur with the majority opinion in concluding that the petition in this case is unlawful and must therefore be dismissed, but as we differ from the majority opinion in the reasoning leading to that conclusion, we set forth our view below.\\n\\nWe consider that a National Assembly member cannot lawfully file a petition for adjudication on a dispute over powers against the President or the Speaker of the National Assembly.\\n\\nA. We already explained in detail, in Constitutional Court decision 90HEONRA1 rendered on 1995. 2. 23., which was a case of a dispute over powers between National Assembly members and the Speaker of the National Assembly, our view that National Assembly members or parliamentary groups within the National Assembly cannot be petitioners in an adjudication on a dispute over powers (Collection of Decisions 7-1, 140). Thereafter, in Constitutional Court decision 96HEONRA2 rendered on 1997. 7. 16., we consistently maintained the above view while pointing out the legislative deficiency in the current system of adjudication on disputes over powers (Collection of Decisions 9-2, 154, 166-168). The gist is as follows.\\n\\n(1) Article 111(1) item 4 of the Constitution, as one of the matters under the jurisdiction of the Constitutional Court, provides for “adjudication on disputes over powers between State organs, between State organs and local governments, and between local governments.” The adjudication system for disputes over powers under the above provision is a system designed to protect the constitutional order by enabling the Constitutional Court to adjudicate, where there is a dispute concerning the existence or scope of powers between a State organ or local government exercising public authority and another State organ or local government, thereby clarifying the limits of those powers and duties, promoting the smooth performance of State functions, and maintaining checks and balances among powers. Based on the above constitutional provision, Article 61 of the Constitutional Court Act provides: “(1) When there is a dispute concerning the existence or scope of powers between State organs, between State organs and local governments, or between local governments, the relevant State organ or local government may file a petition for adjudication on a dispute over powers with the Constitutional Court. (2) A petition under paragraph (1) may be filed only when the Respondent’s disposition or omission has infringed, or poses a substantial risk of infringing, the Petitioner’s powers granted by the Constitution and laws.” Article 62, which prescribes the types of adjudication on disputes over powers, enumerates in paragraph (1) item 1 “adjudication on disputes over powers between State organs” as “adjudication on disputes over powers among the National Assembly, the Government, the courts, and the National Election Commission.”\\n\\n(2) In light of the purpose of the above adjudication system for disputes over powers, the phrase “disputes over powers between State organs” in Article 111(1) item 4 of the Constitution means disputes concerning powers between equal organs exercising State power that the Constitution has distributed in accordance with the people’s sovereignty and the principle of separation of powers so as to maintain mutual checks and balances. Thus, Article 62(1) item 1 of the Constitutional Court Act, by prescribing “adjudication on disputes over powers between State organs” as “adjudication on disputes over powers among the National Assembly, the Government, the courts, and the National Election Commission,” may be understood as clearly and concretely specifying the above constitutional provision by enumerating the National Assembly, the Government, and the courts, which exercise the State’s legislative, executive, and judicial powers, and the National Election Commission, which handles election administration.\\n\\n(3) Therefore, organs not enumerated in Article 62(1) item 1 of the Constitutional Court Act, or organs at various levels within the enumerated organs, cannot be parties to an adjudication on a dispute over powers even if they are in a position to make sovereign dispositions, and disputes concerning powers within the above enumerated State organs cannot be the subject of an adjudication on a dispute over powers. Consequently, in the case of the National Assembly, under the current system of adjudication on disputes over powers, only the National Assembly as a State organ may be the party and pursue adjudication on a dispute over powers, and members of the National Assembly or parliamentary groups, which are constituent members of the National Assembly or partial organs thereof, cannot file a petition for adjudication on a dispute over powers against the Speaker of the National Assembly, who is another organ within the National Assembly.\\n\\n(4) If interpreted according to our view, however, there will be no legal remedy to ascertain and resolve claims, as in this case, that the authority as a National Assembly member has been infringed. The Constitution expressly guarantees a multi-party system (Article 8(1)), and since the National Assembly of our country was established, there have always been confrontations between the ruling party and the opposition parties, and between the majority party and the minority party; in the case of bills or agenda items in which each side’s policies and interests are sharply opposed, there have often been disputes within the National Assembly due to defects in the deliberation or voting procedures, yet the National Assembly Act contains no provision for resolving these matters. In light of the nature of an organ lawsuit under the Administrative Litigation Act, which allows such a suit only in cases prescribed by law and only by persons prescribed by law, and in light of the current system of administrative litigation (Article 45 of the Administrative Litigation Act), this is a clear legislative deficiency, and legislation should be enacted as soon as possible. However, in order to remedy this legislative deficiency, expanding the scope of parties to an adjudication on a dispute over powers in contravention of the allocation of jurisdiction between the Constitutional Court and the courts concerning organ lawsuits (see Articles 2 and 62 of the Constitutional Court Act, and Article 3 item 4 of the Administrative Litigation Act) and the express provisions of Article 62 of the Constitutional Court Act may be thought to reverse the proper order of means and ends in problem-solving.\\n\\nB. Since we cannot regard there as having been any special change in circumstances requiring a change to the views expressed in the above two decisions to date, we maintain the above view that National Assembly members or parliamentary groups cannot be parties to an adjudication on a dispute over powers, and therefore consider that this petition, filed in the name of National Assembly members rather than the National Assembly, is unlawful."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning directness, an admissibility requirement for a constitutional complaint adjudication, is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Since statutes, as a general rule, infringe fundamental rights only through concrete enforcement acts as an intermediary, an individual who has suffered an infringement of fundamental rights is, first of all, required, by the nature of a constitutional complaint, to pursue relief for the infringement of fundamental rights through the method of ordinary litigation by targeting that enforcement act.
B: A provision of the Act on the Performance of Duties by Police Officers that prescribes the requirements for the use of water cannon, etc. presupposes a concrete enforcement act, namely the police’s water-spraying act at an assembly or demonstration site, and therefore directness of the infringement of fundamental rights is not recognized.
C: A provision of the Enforcement Rule of the Judicial Scriveners Act that provides that the total number of clerical staff for a judicial scrivener shall not exceed 5 does not directly bring about the effect of dismissing clerical staff, and therefore directness of the infringement of fundamental rights is not recognized.
D: A provision of the Prosecutors Disciplinary Act that prescribes the composition of the members of the Prosecutors Disciplinary Committee does not recognize directness of the infringement of fundamental rights because that Act contemplates a separate disciplinary disposition.
E: A provision of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and the Treatment of Inmates that grants the prison warden discretion to open correspondence does not recognize directness of the infringement of an inmate’s fundamental rights because it presupposes a concrete enforcement act, such as the prison warden’s act of checking prohibited items.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2005HEONMA833]": "1. Outline of the Case\\n\\na. The Petitioner registered as a judicial scrivener pursuant to the Judicial Scrivener Act on 2003. 4. 1. and has, since that same day, opened a judicial scrivener office in Gunsan-si and employed 5 office staff members.\\n\\nb. The Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint on 2005. 9. 2., alleging that, in order to protect the rights and interests of clients who entrust cases to him, he should assign office staff by area of work and faithfully perform his duties, and that, in order to prevent overwork of the office staff, he should employ a few more office staff members, but that, pursuant to Article 23(4) of the Judicial Scrivener Act and Article 37(5) of the Enforcement Rules of the same Act, he is unable to employ more than 5 office staff members, thereby infringing the Petitioner’s constitutionally guaranteed right to equality and other rights.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether Article 23(4) of the Judicial Scrivener Act and Article 37(5) of the Enforcement Rules of the same Act are unconstitutional, and the contents of the relevant provisions are as follows.\\n\\nJudicial Scrivener Act, Article 23 (Office Employees)\\n① A judicial scrivener may employ office employees.\\n\\n④ The number of office employees under paragraph 1, hiring, and other necessary matters shall be determined by Supreme Court Rules.\\n\\nEnforcement Rules of the Judicial Scrivener Act, Article 37 (Office Employees)\\n⑤ The total number of office employees of a judicial scrivener (including members of a joint office and members of a judicial scrivener joint corporation, as well as judicial scriveners who are not members) shall not exceed 5.\\n\\n3. Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\na. Whether a judicial scrivener uses office employees as auxiliary personnel for the performance of his duties, and how many office employees he uses, fall within the private sphere and are not matters for State intervention under the constitutional principles such as the market economic order prescribed by our Constitution. Therefore, the above provisions restrict the Petitioner’s freedom to pursue his occupation or business.\\n\\nb. Even if the legislative purpose of the provisions subject to adjudication in this case is taken into account, namely, to prevent office employees from improperly soliciting cases and receiving money or valuables, etc., since they limit the number to a very small number of 5, rather than 10 or 15, they violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction, such as the appropriateness of the means for achieving the legislative purpose and the minimum impairment of rights.\\n\\nc. Under the current statutes and regulations, among independent professional occupations, only judicial scriveners are subject to a statutory limitation on the number of office employees; this is discriminatory treatment of judicial scriveners alone among professional occupations, and thus infringes the right to equality and other rights.\\n\\n4. Review of the Requirements for Admissibility\\n\\na. Legal Relevance\\n\\n1) Judicial Scrivener Act, Article 23(4)\\n\\nThe fundamental rights of the Petitioner must be directly infringed by the exercise of public power. Since enforcement acts include legislative acts, where a statutory provision contemplates the implementation of subordinate norms for the concretization of that provision, the directness of the relevant statute is denied.\\n\\nThe Judicial Scrivener Act, Article 23(4), which is the subject matter of adjudication in this case, merely delegates detailed matters concerning office employees to Supreme Court Rules by providing that “the number of office employees, hiring, and other necessary matters shall be determined by Supreme Court Rules,” and therefore it is difficult to regard the Petitioner’s fundamental rights as having been directly infringed by that statutory provision; accordingly, directness cannot be recognized.\\n\\n2) Article 37(5) of the Enforcement Rules of the Judicial Scrivener Act\\n\\nThe public power referred to as the subject matter of a constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act means all public power, including legislative power and executive power, and orders and rules promulgated by the judiciary may also become the subject of a constitutional complaint when they directly infringe fundamental rights without awaiting any separate enforcement act.\\n\\nThe Petitioner, who is a judicial scrivener, alleges that he is unable to employ more than 5 office employees under the Enforcement Rules of the Judicial Scrivener Act and is thereby deprived of freedom of business, and that he is receiving discriminatory treatment compared to other professional occupations to which no restriction on the employment of office employees applies, and therefore his right to equality is infringed; accordingly, the Petitioner has self-relatedness. Moreover, since the Petitioner’s rights are directly restricted under the said provision of the Enforcement Rules without the intermediation of any separate enforcement act, the requirements of directness and presentness of the infringement of fundamental rights are also satisfied.\\n\\nb. Filing Period\\n\\nThe filing period for a constitutional complaint based on a statute or regulation is: ① where, upon the statute’s coming into force, the infringement of fundamental rights occurs, the constitutional complaint must be filed within 90 days from the date on which the statute became known to have entered into force, and within 1 year from the date the statute entered into force (Constitutional Court 1999. 4. 29., 96HEONMA352 et al., Court Reports 11-1, 477, 496); ② where, after the statute has entered into force, a circumstance falling under that statute first arises and the infringement of fundamental rights occurs, the constitutional complaint must be filed within 90 days from the date on which the occurrence of that circumstance became known (Constitutional Court 1996. 8. 29., 94HEONMA113, Court Reports 8-2, 141, 153), and within 1 year from the date on which that circumstance arose (Constitutional Court 1998. 7. 16., 95HEONBA19 et al., Court Reports 10-2, 89, 101).\\n\\nOn 1994. 12. 30., the Enforcement Rules of the Judicial Scrivener Act (Supreme Court Rule No. 1327) were amended, and the total number of office employees of a judicial scrivener was made unable to exceed 5 (Article 35(1) of the above Rules); thereafter, on 1996. 12. 31., when the same Rules were amended by Supreme Court Rule No. 1425, the contents of that provision remained the same, while only the article number was changed to Article 37(5), and it has continued in force to the present.\\n\\nIn addition, the provision of the current Judicial Scrivener Act, Article 23(4), stating that “the number of office employees, hiring, and other necessary matters shall be determined by Supreme Court Rules,” has, since 1990. 1. 13., when the Judicial Scrivener Act (Act No. 4200), Article 21(2), provided that “the number of office employees, hiring, and other necessary matters shall be determined by Supreme Court Rules,” remained substantively unchanged and has continued in force to the present, with only the article number having been changed thereafter to Article 23(4).\\n\\nAccording to the judicial scrivener registration certificate and business registration certificate submitted by the Petitioner, the Petitioner acquired the qualification of judicial scrivener and began practicing as a judicial scrivener from 2003. 4. 1., after the Judicial Scrivener Act and the Enforcement Rules thereof, which are the subject matter of this constitutional complaint, had already entered into force; this corresponds to a case where, after the statute has entered into force, a circumstance falling under that statute first arose and the infringement of fundamental rights occurred. In other words, it must be said that the Petitioner first began to suffer an infringement of his fundamental rights under the provisions of this statute only when he began practicing as a judicial scrivener from 2003. 4. 1.\\n\\nThen, it is manifest from the reverse calculation that this constitutional complaint was filed only on 2005. 9. 2., after 1 year had elapsed from 2003. 4. 1., which is the point in time when, after the statute subject to adjudication had entered into force, a circumstance falling under that statute first arose; accordingly, it is untimely and thus unlawful.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the Petitioner’s request for adjudication is not only filed after the expiration of the filing period, but, in particular, the part concerning Article 23(4) of the Judicial Scrivener Act is an unlawful petition lacking directness; therefore, it is dismissed, and this is decided unanimously by all participating Justices as follows.\\n\\n2005. 9. 27.\\n\\nPresiding Justice Kwon Seong\\n\\nJustice Song Injun\\n\\nJustice Jo Daehyeon"}

{"[2018HEONMA1100]": "1. Case Overview\\n\\na. The Petitioners are specialists in obstetrics and gynecology.\\n\\nb. On August 17, 2018, the Minister of Health and Welfare, while partially amending the Rules on Administrative Dispositions Relating to Medical Affairs, added, under [Attached Table] Administrative Disposition Standards (related to Article 4), 2. Individual Standards, a. Where a medical practitioner violates the Medical Service Act and the Enforcement Decree of the Medical Service Act, 32) in the case of having engaged in unethical medical practice, “‘d) where a person caused an abortion in violation of Article 270 of the Criminal Act’” as a subject to a 1-month suspension of qualification disposition.\\n\\nc. The Petitioners filed the constitutional complaint in this case on November 13, 2018, alleging that it is unconstitutional because imposing a suspension of qualification disposition by defining “where a person caused an abortion in violation of Article 270 of the Criminal Act” as unethical medical practice violates the principle of clarity, the principle against blanket delegation, and the limits on legislative delegation, and infringes upon the Petitioners’ freedom of conscience.\\n\\n2. Determination\\n\\nIn order for a statute or a statutory provision to be subject to a constitutional complaint, it must directly infringe basic rights in and of itself, without waiting for a specific act of execution. This is because laws and regulations generally come to infringe basic rights only through a concrete act of execution, and, first, due to the nature of constitutional complaint proceedings, relief procedures for infringement of basic rights are to be pursued by means of general litigation against such act of execution. Even if a law or regulation univocally prescribes that a specific act of execution is to be performed, so long as a remedial procedure against that act of execution is provided, the mere circumstance that the content of the law or regulation is univocal cannot be deemed to make the law or regulation itself automatically subject to constitutional complaint review (see Constitutional Court decision of July 25, 2013, 2012HEONMA934; Constitutional Court decision of February 27, 2014, 2012HEONMA904, etc.).\\n\\nLooking at this case, the provision under review prescribes that, where a medical practitioner causes an abortion in violation of Article 270 of the Criminal Act, the Minister of Health and Welfare shall suspend the qualification for 1 month; however, the infringement of basic rights alleged by the Petitioners does not arise directly from the provision under review, but becomes actual only when there is a concrete act of execution, namely, the Minister of Health and Welfare’s disposition of suspension of qualification, and separate remedial procedures such as administrative litigation are provided with respect to the above suspension disposition.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, this petition for review in this case is improper, and thus, pursuant to Article 72(3)4 of the Constitutional Court Act, it is dismissed as inadmissible; therefore, by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices, the decision is rendered as stated in the operative part."}
