The Claimant’s Arguments  \\nA. The Claimant was unable to visit suspect Yun XX-hyeon due to the Respondents’ denial of visitation in this case, and as a result, lost the opportunity to assist the above suspect, and direct disadvantage was caused to the exercise of the above suspect’s right of defense. The denial of visitation in this case infringed not only the above suspect’s right of access and communication with counsel, but also the Claimant’s constitutional fundamental right of access and communication with counsel.  \\nB. Since a detention warrant is sought within 48 hours after a suspect is arrested, the right of a suspect to immediately receive assistance from counsel must be guaranteed during that period as well, and considering that the period immediately before the warrant review hearing is the time when the assistance of counsel is most needed, the Visitation Hours Provision in this case, which limits counsel visitation hours to public officials’ working hours, violates the principle of prohibition against excessive restriction and infringes the Claimant’s right of access and communication with counsel.  \\nMoreover, where an arrested suspect is housed in a police detention cell, Article 7(1) of the Rules on Defense Counsel Visitation and Participation, etc. and Article 37(1) of the Rules on Detention and Escort of Suspects apply, so that counsel visitation is permitted even outside the working hours under the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials. Accordingly, because an unreasonable discrimination arises in the exercise of defense counsel’s right of access and communication depending on whether the suspect is confined in a detention center or housed in a detention cell, the Visitation Hours Provision in this case infringes the Claimant’s right to equality.  \\n\\n4. The Visitation and Communication System between Suspects/Defendants and Defense Counsel  \\nA. Constitutional Basis  \\nThe main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution provides that “any person who is arrested or detained shall have the right to prompt assistance of counsel.” The Constitutional Court has held: “Even in the case of a suspect who is not detained, the right to the assistance of counsel is a natural content recognized under the constitutional principles of a rule-of-law state and due process contained in our Constitution, and Article 12(4) of the Constitution also separately and expressly provides for this in order to particularly emphasize the importance of the right to the assistance of counsel for persons under physical restraint.” (see Constitutional Court 2004. 9. 23. 2000HEONMA138). In this manner, a suspect or defendant (hereinafter, “suspect or defendant” shall be referred to as “suspect, etc.”) is recognized as having the right to the assistance of counsel regardless of whether he or she is arrested or detained.  \\nIn order for a suspect, etc. to sufficiently exercise the right of defense, he or she must be able to consult sufficiently on all factual and legal issues through visitation and communication with defense counsel or a “person who intends to become defense counsel” (hereinafter, defense counsel or a “person who intends to become defense counsel” shall be referred to as “defense counsel, etc.”). With respect to visitation and communication between a suspect, etc. and defense counsel, etc., matters are provided in Article 34 and Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, Article 84(1) and (2), and Article 85 of the Execution of Sentences Act, etc., and these provisions concretize the right to the assistance of counsel guaranteed by the Constitution as above. Among them, Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act expressly provides that a “person who intends to become defense counsel” also has the right to visit and communicate with a suspect, etc.  \\n\\nB. Meaning of “Under Physical Restraint” and “Person Who Intends to Become Defense Counsel”  \\n(1) Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “a defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel may visit a defendant or suspect who is under physical restraint.” Here, “a defendant or suspect who is under physical restraint” means not only a suspect, etc. detained pursuant to a detention warrant, but also a suspect, etc. arrested pursuant to an arrest warrant or arrested by emergency arrest or as a person caught in flagrante delicto, and it should be understood to presuppose deprivation of physical liberty in whatever form.  \\n(2) Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act expressly provides that not only defense counsel but also a “person who intends to become defense counsel” has the right to visit and communicate with a suspect, etc. Here, “a person who intends to become defense counsel” should be understood to include not only a person who has been requested to be appointed as defense counsel but has not yet filed a notice of appointment of defense counsel, but also a person who seeks to act as defense counsel on his or her own. It is difficult to say that, in a state where physical liberty is suppressed and communication with the outside is severed, a suspect, etc. can decide and carry through his or her own intention without being conscious of investigative authorities, and if the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” were permitted only when the suspect, etc. expressly indicates an intention to receive the assistance of counsel, this could result in the existence of the right of visitation and communication being substantially determined by the will of the investigative authorities.  \\nThe Supreme Court, in a case where an attorney not appointed as defense counsel expressed an intention to exercise the right of visitation and communication with respect to a suspect arrested, but it was not confirmed what the suspect’s intention was, held that “even where a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having a possibility of becoming defense counsel, he or she may not be restricted from visiting a defendant or suspect under physical restraint on the ground that he or she is not a ‘defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel’ as prescribed in Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act” (see Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.).  \\n\\nC. Subject Authorized to Determine Whether to Permit Visitation  \\nThe Execution of Sentences Act aims to promote the correction and rehabilitation of convicted prisoners and their sound return to society, and to prescribe matters necessary concerning the treatment and rights of prisoners and the operation of correctional institutions (Article 1). Accordingly, Part II of the Execution of Sentences Act regulates the treatment of prisoners, and matters concerning the treatment of prisoners, such as confinement of prisoners, visitation, exchange of correspondence and telephone communication, maintenance of safety and order, discipline and rewards/punishments, and special protection for female prisoners and pregnant women, are vested in the authority of the heads of prisons and detention centers. Meanwhile, the Execution of Sentences Act is a statute that applies to the premises of correctional institutions and to other places where correctional officers are guarding prisoners and where the control of correctional officers is required (Article 3). In light of the legislative purpose, regulatory content, scope of application, etc. of the Execution of Sentences Act, when there is an application for visitation by a prisoner, this concerns a matter of treatment of prisoners; therefore, if the place is a space where the guarding and control of prisoners by correctional officers is required, it is in principle the warden of the prison or detention center, or the correctional officer entrusted by such warden, who determines whether to permit it.  \\nHowever, Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “a prosecutor or judicial police officer shall, upon application by a suspect or his or her defense counsel, legal representative, spouse, lineal relative, brother, or sister, allow defense counsel to visit the suspect or allow defense counsel to participate in the interrogation of the suspect unless there is a justifiable ground,” thereby establishing a special provision to the above principle and making the prosecutor or judicial police officer determine whether to permit such visitation when there is an application for visitation by defense counsel during the interrogation of a suspect.  \\nArticle 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act, however, regulates the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel and the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” without making any distinction between them; therefore, even where a “person who intends to become defense counsel” applies for visitation pursuant to Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act during the interrogation of a suspect, the subject who determines whether to permit it should also be the prosecutor or judicial police officer, and such interpretation is consistent with the content of Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act.  \\n\\n5. Determination on Whether the Requirements for Adjudication Are Satisfied  \\nA. Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case  \\n(1) Existence of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case  \\nA constitutional complaint may be filed when fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution are infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power (Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act); therefore, in order to file a constitutional complaint, there must first be a fact of “exercise or non-exercise of public power” that caused the infringement of fundamental rights, and where there is no fact at all of exercise or non-exercise of public power that is subject to constitutional complaint, the petition is unlawful (see Constitutional Court 2004. 11. 25. 2004HEONMA178; Constitutional Court 2014. 3. 31. 2014HEONMA239).  \\nHere, as seen above, the Respondent Prosecutor merely informed the correctional officer of the fact that the Claimant had applied for visitation, and even though the Claimant continued to stay in the prosecutor’s office in order to visit suspect Yun XX-hyeon after the correctional officer in charge denied visitation between the Claimant and the suspect, the Respondent Prosecutor did not take measures such as allowing the visitation to take place in the prosecutor’s office or in a separately prepared counsel visitation room.  \\nSince the Respondent Prosecutor’s failure to take any further measures after the correctional officer’s notice of denial of visitation can be assessed as substantially equivalent to denying the Claimant’s application for visitation (see Constitutional Court 1991. 7. 8. 89HEONMA181; Supreme Court Decision 89MO37 dated 1990. 2. 13.; Supreme Court Decision 91MO24 dated 1991. 3. 28.), the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case exists as an exercise of public power subject to a constitutional complaint.  \\n(2) Whether the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights is recognized - Whether the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” can be regarded as a constitutional fundamental right  \\n(a) Organization of the issue  \\nBecause the Claimant was not appointed as defense counsel for suspect Yun XX-hyeon, with respect to the constitutional complaint against the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, only whether the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” was infringed is at issue.  \\nA constitutional complaint is a system by which a “person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed” petitions the Constitutional Court for adjudication in order to obtain relief from that infringement; therefore, for the constitutional complaint against the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case to be lawful, the right allegedly infringed by the Claimant, namely the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” must not only be recognized as a statutory right but must further be recognized as a constitutional fundamental right.  \\n(b) Constitutional Court precedents  \\nThe Constitutional Court, in its decision rendered on 2003. 3. 27., 2000HEONMA474, for the first time recognized the core part of the right to assistance of counsel as a constitutional fundamental right, and also took the same position in its decision 2016HEONMA503 rendered on 2017. 11. 30.; the gist of the decision 2016HEONMA503 is as follows:  \\n“[T]he right of a suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel can be concretely realized in the mutual relationship between them and defense counsel. The right of a suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel can become solid through the guarantee of the right of defense counsel to assist them, whereas if the right of defense counsel is not guaranteed, it may become a mere empty shell. The core part of the right of defense counsel to assist a suspect or defendant, without which it becomes a dead letter for them to receive the assistance of counsel, stands in a relationship of mutual complementarity with the constitutional fundamental right of the suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel. Therefore, in order to practically secure the right of a suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel, the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist the suspect and defendant must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right.”  \\n(c) Determination  \\n1) Article 27(4) of the Constitution provides that “a criminal defendant shall be presumed innocent until a conviction becomes final and conclusive,” thereby declaring the principle of presumption of innocence. This principle of presumption of innocence originates from the constitutional ideal that has the respect for human dignity as its ultimate goal and seeks to protect the status of suspects, etc., who are in an unfavorable position, so that their disadvantages in criminal proceedings are limited to the minimum necessary. Detention is a system recognized only when there are especially unavoidable reasons with respect to suspects, etc., but the detention system is susceptible to abuse by investigative or trial authorities merely for the convenience of investigation or trial, and while in a detained state, the right to remain silent prescribed in Article 12(2) of the Constitution may not be effectively guaranteed. Accordingly, in order to remove the various harms arising from the situation of physical restraint with respect to suspects, etc. who are presumed innocent and to ensure that detention is not improperly used beyond its original purpose, the main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution guarantees as a fundamental right the right of a person under physical restraint to receive the assistance of counsel as stated above (see Constitutional Court 1995. 7. 21. 92HEONMA144).  \\nThe reason for and necessity of recognizing, as a constitutional fundamental right, the right of a detained suspect, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel applies equally to arrested suspects, etc.  \\n2) The main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution clearly provides that, upon being arrested or detained, a person has the right to prompt assistance of counsel, thereby making clear that suspects, etc. have the right to receive the assistance of counsel even before counsel is appointed. The right of a suspect, etc. who has not yet appointed defense counsel to receive the assistance of counsel is concretized through the appointment of defense counsel; the right of a suspect, etc. to appoint defense counsel is the starting point and the most basic component of the right to receive the assistance of counsel, and is a right that cannot even be limited by law (see Constitutional Court 2004. 9. 23. 2000HEONMA138). Accordingly, the right of visitation and communication with a “person who intends to become defense counsel” that a suspect, etc. has for purposes of appointing defense counsel must also be protected as a constitutional fundamental right.  \\n3) In order for a suspect, etc. to appoint defense counsel, a relationship of trust must be formed between the suspect, etc. and the “person who intends to become defense counsel,” and for this purpose, sufficient consultation must be conducted through visitation and communication with the “person who intends to become defense counsel.” In this way, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” is intended to solidify the right of a suspect, etc. to appoint defense counsel and receive assistance from that counsel; if it is not guaranteed, the right of the suspect, etc. to receive sufficient assistance from defense counsel through the appointment of counsel will inevitably become meaningless. Accordingly, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” is a core part for assisting a suspect, etc., and stands in a relationship of mutual complementarity with the constitutional fundamental right of the suspect, etc. to visit and communicate with a “person who intends to become defense counsel.”  \\n4) Therefore, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” as a core right for assisting a suspect, etc., must also be guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right in order to practically secure the right of a suspect, etc. to receive the assistance of a “person who intends to become defense counsel.” Accordingly, this part of the petition seeking a constitutional determination on the ground that the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case infringed the Claimant’s constitutional fundamental right, namely the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” also satisfies the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.  \\n(3) Whether an exception to the principle of subsidiarity is recognized  \\nA constitutional complaint must be filed only after all procedures have been exhausted where there is a remedy procedure under other laws (proviso to Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act); however, where the claimant failed to take a prior remedy procedure due to a mistake based on justifiable grounds not attributable to his or her disadvantage, or where there is little possibility that the right will be remedied through the prior remedy procedure, or where it is objectively uncertain whether the right-concretization procedure is permitted, making it impossible to expect performance of the prior remedy procedure, it is recognized as a lawful petition as an exception to subsidiarity (see Constitutional Court 1989. 9. 4. 88HEONMA22; Constitutional Court 2008. 5. 29. 2007HEONMA712, etc.).  \\nHowever, since the subject who finally determines the Claimant’s application for visitation with suspect Yun XX-hyeon is the Respondent Prosecutor, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case falls under “dispositions concerning detention by a prosecutor and dispositions concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc. under Article 243-2” that are subject to quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Nevertheless, the Claimant filed the present constitutional complaint without first filing a quasi-appeal seeking revocation of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act.  \\nThe Supreme Court, however, has held that even a quasi-appeal seeking revocation of a denial of visitation by an investigative agency must have a legal interest, and that where the purpose sought to be achieved through the quasi-appeal during the pendency of the case has already been achieved or where the interest has been lost due to the lapse of time or other circumstances, the quasi-appeal becomes unlawful for lack of interest (see Supreme Court Decision 98MO121 dated 1999. 6. 14.; Supreme Court Decision 2014MO686 dated 2014. 4. 15.), yet has not presented specific criteria therefor. Accordingly, if the Claimant were to file a quasi-appeal seeking revocation of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, which ended on the day of the incident, it is objectively uncertain whether the court would deem legal interest to be lacking or would proceed to a merits determination, and thus this is a case where it is difficult to expect the Claimant to have exhausted the prior remedy procedure.  \\nAccordingly, this part of the petition should be recognized as a lawful petition as an exception to subsidiarity.  \\n(4) Sub-conclusion  \\nAs above, the petition concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case targets an exercise of public power subject to constitutional complaint, the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights is recognized, an exception to the principle of subsidiarity is also recognized, and all other requirements for lawfulness are satisfied; thus, it is lawful.  \\n\\nB. The Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case  \\nArticle 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act limits the subject matter of constitutional complaints to acts of public power by providing that a person whose fundamental rights have been infringed by the “exercise or non-exercise of public power” may file a constitutional complaint.  \\nAccording to the record, at the time of the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case, the Respondent Prosecutor handed over the physical custody of suspect Yun XX-hyeon to the Respondent Correctional Officer so that he could have dinner and rest in the detention room, but it is recognized that an interrogation of the suspect was scheduled even at night, and thus it may be said that the interrogation of the above suspect was ongoing. In addition, the Claimant at that time applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for counsel visitation.  \\nAs seen above, where there is an application for visitation by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect, the prosecutor or judicial police officer must determine whether to permit it; accordingly, it must be said that a correctional officer who escorted the suspect to the investigative agency is not vested with the authority to permit or restrict such visitation.  \\nArticle 118 of the “Operational Guidelines on the Management of Prisoners” (Ministerial Instruction of the Ministry of Justice No. 1077, 2015. 1. 13.), which was in force at the time of this case, provided that where there is an application for defense counsel visitation with a prisoner outside the institution who is being escorted out, the escorting correctional officer is to conduct the visitation between the escorted prisoner and defense counsel through certain procedures, such as obtaining permission from the warden. However, that provision applies to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. where the warden of the prison or detention center, or a correctional officer delegated by them, determines whether to permit it, and cannot be said to apply to cases, such as this one, where an application for visitation by defense counsel, etc. is made during the interrogation of a suspect, and the prosecutor or judicial police officer determines whether to permit it.  \\nUltimately, in this case, because it cannot be said that the Respondent Correctional Officer had the authority to determine whether to permit visitation between the Claimant and suspect Yun XX-hyeon, the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case does not constitute an “exercise of public power” that is made subject to constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act.  \\n\\nC. The Visitation Hours Provision in this case  \\nThe main text of Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act provides that “a person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power may ... file a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court,” which means that only a person whose own fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been currently and directly infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power may file a constitutional complaint. Therefore, if the exercise of public power has no effect whatsoever on the legal status of the person seeking to file a constitutional complaint, then there is no possibility or danger of infringement of fundamental rights in the first place, and filing a constitutional complaint against such exercise of public power is not permitted (see Constitutional Court 1999. 5. 27. 97HEONMA368; Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2012HEONMA630, etc.).  \\nThe Visitation Hours Provision in this case is a provision that applies to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. where the warden of the prison or detention center determines whether to permit it, and it cannot be said to apply to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect where the prosecutor or judicial police officer determines whether to permit it; accordingly, it must be said that the denial or restriction of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect cannot be based on that provision. In practice as well, the police and prosecutors impose no time restrictions whatsoever on visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect [see Article 7 of the “Rules on Defense Counsel Visitation and Participation, etc.” (Korean National Police Agency Instruction No. 882, 2018. 8. 13.), Article 37(2) of the “Rules on Detention and Escort of Suspects” (Korean National Police Agency Instruction No. 883, 2018. 8. 13.), Article 2(6) and Article 8 of the “Guidelines on the Operation of Defense Counsel Participation in Suspect Interrogation” (Korean Supreme Prosecutors’ Office guidelines, amended 2017. 12. 4.), and Article 230 of the “Guidelines on Defense Counsel Visitation and Communication with Suspects” (Seoul Central District Prosecutors’ Office Rule No. 230, 2017. 8. 30.)].  \\nAs seen above, the Claimant applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for visitation with suspect Yun XX-hyeon, against whom interrogation was continuing, and therefore the Visitation Hours Provision in this case does not apply here, nor did the Respondent Prosecutor at the time deny the above visitation application by applying that provision. Accordingly, this part of the petition lacks self-relatedness for purposes of the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.  \\n\\n6. Determination on Whether the Prosecutor’s Denial of Visitation in this Case Infringed Fundamental Rights  \\nA. Whether the Claimant’s right of access and communication was restricted  \\nAs seen above, the Claimant applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for visitation and remained in the prosecutor’s office, but due to the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case ultimately could not visit suspect Yun XX-hyeon and left the prosecutor’s office; accordingly, it is reasonable to view the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case as having restricted the Claimant’s right of access and communication with the above suspect.  \\nHowever, according to the record, suspect Yun XX-hyeon did not raise an objection to the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, visited with another attorney twice the following day, and that attorney personally appeared and responded at the pre-detention suspect interrogation hearing. Nevertheless, even if the suspect did not indicate an intention to visit and communicate with a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” if a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having a possibility of becoming defense counsel, visitation with the suspect must be permitted (see Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.); moreover, the Claimant had even been entrusted by suspect Yun XX-hyeon’s family and intended to visit the suspect, so at the time of the visitation application there was sufficient possibility that the Claimant would become defense counsel for the above suspect; and the person claiming infringement of fundamental rights caused by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is not suspect Yun XX-hyeon but the Claimant. In light of these circumstances, the facts recognized above are not factors to be considered in determining whether the Claimant’s fundamental rights were infringed by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case.  \\n\\nB. Whether the Claimant’s visitation application was exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication  \\nBecause the right of access and communication of defense counsel, etc. must be exercised within the limits that do not infringe the original purpose of the physical restraint system, attempts by defense counsel, etc. to visit a suspect, etc. beyond the limits that can realistically be guaranteed in light of the concrete temporal and spatial circumstances do not constitute a proper exercise of the right of access and communication and cannot be permitted (see Constitutional Court 2009. 10. 29. 2007HEONMA992; Supreme Court Decision 2006MO657 dated 2007. 1. 31.; Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.).  \\nHowever, in this case, since suspect Yun XX-hyeon was scheduled to continue being interrogated at night on that day, it appears that measures could have been taken to permit visitation and communication between the Claimant and the above suspect in the prosecutor’s office or in a separately prepared counsel visitation room before the interrogation, and thus in light of the concrete temporal and spatial circumstances at the time of the visitation application, no specific circumstances are discernible showing that the Claimant, who intended to become defense counsel, attempted to abuse the exercise of visitation and communication with the suspect beyond the limits realistically guaranteeable or beyond the original purpose of the physical restraint system.  \\nAccordingly, the Claimant’s visitation application must be deemed to have been exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication guaranteed to a “person who intends to become defense counsel.”  \\n\\nC. Whether it was based on the Constitution or statutes  \\n(1) In the case where visitation actually takes place between a person arrested or detained and defense counsel, etc., “free visitation,” that is, “visitation in which confidentiality regarding the content of the conversation is fully guaranteed and the parties may converse freely without any restriction, influence, pressure, or improper interference,” is not of a nature that can be restricted under any pretext (see Constitutional Court 1992. 1. 28. 91HEONMA111). However, this means only that such is the case where visitation actually takes place between a person arrested or detained and defense counsel, etc.; it does not mean that no restriction whatsoever may be imposed on visitation itself with defense counsel, etc. The right to the assistance of counsel and the right of visitation and communication with counsel, which is one component thereof, may, like all other constitutional fundamental rights, be restricted not only by the Constitution but also by law when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare (see Constitutional Court 2011. 5. 26. 2009HEONMA341; Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2015HEONMA243), and the same shall apply to the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel.”  \\n(2) As seen above, the Respondent Prosecutor temporarily handed over the physical custody of suspect Yun XX-hyeon to the correctional officer in charge so that he could have dinner and rest in the detention room, but since a night interrogation of the above suspect was planned, it may be said that the investigation or interrogation of the above suspect was continuing.  \\nAlthough the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel, etc. may be restricted not only by the Constitution but also by law, neither the Constitution nor laws such as the Criminal Procedure Act contain a provision allowing restriction or refusal where there is an application for visitation by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect. This is to ensure, in light of the importance of the right of access and communication held by a suspect, etc., that the right of access and communication held by defense counsel, etc. is also guaranteed to the maximum extent.  \\nThe Visitation Hours Provision in this case, which is delegated by Article 41(4) of the Execution of Sentences Act, restricts visitation and communication between a suspect and defense counsel, etc. by limiting visitation by prisoners to working hours pursuant to the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials; however, as seen above, that provision applies to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. where the warden of the prison or detention center determines whether to permit it, and does not apply to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect where the prosecutor or judicial police officer determines whether to permit it, and thus it must be said that visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. cannot be denied or restricted on the basis of that provision.  \\nAccordingly, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case was made without the basis of the Constitution or statutes.  \\n\\nD. Sub-conclusion  \\nUltimately, the Claimant’s visitation application concerning suspect Yun XX-hyeon was exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication guaranteed to a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” and furthermore the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case was made without the basis of the Constitution or statutes; therefore, it infringed the Claimant’s right of access and communication.  \\n\\n7. Conclusion  \\nAccordingly, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case should be found unconstitutional and revoked; however, since the denial of visitation has already ended, we shall, for declaratory purposes and to prevent repetition of the same or similar infringement of fundamental rights, make a determination that it is unconstitutional. The petition regarding the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case and the Visitation Hours Provision in this case is unlawful in its entirety and shall therefore be dismissed, and it is so decided as stated in the order. The concurrence of the remaining participating Justices was reached, except for the dissenting opinion by Justices Cho Yong-ho, Lee Eun-ae, and Lee Jong-seok regarding the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case as stated in Section 8 below.  \\n\\n8. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Cho Yong-ho, Lee Eun-ae, and Lee Jong-seok on the Prosecutor’s Denial of Visitation in this Case  \\nWe are of the view that the constitutional complaint concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is also unlawful and should be dismissed, and we state our opinion as follows.  \\n\\nA. Possibility of Infringement of Fundamental Rights  \\n(1) A constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act may be filed only by a person whose “fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution” have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power. Therefore, a constitutional complaint alleging infringement of a right based merely on statute, rather than on a constitutional fundamental right, is unlawful.  \\n(2) In the Constitutional Court’s decision 2012HEONMA610 rendered on 2015. 7. 30., three Justices presented the following separate opinion:  \\n“Guaranteeing the right to the assistance of counsel means sufficiently and substantively guaranteeing the activities of defense counsel aimed at assisting the person arrested, etc. Thus, the Criminal Procedure Act recognizes, as concrete means for substantively guaranteeing the right to the assistance of counsel, the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel (Article 34), defense counsel’s right to inspect and copy investigative and litigation records (Articles 35 and 266-3), and defense counsel’s right to participate in various procedures such as investigation and trial (Articles 121, 163, 243-2, etc.).  \\nThe reason special rights such as the right to inspect and copy records or the right of visitation and communication are recognized for defense counsel is that they all originate from the purpose of faithfully guaranteeing the right of a person arrested, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel, and it cannot be viewed as a right recognized in order to guarantee defense counsel’s own fundamental rights. Defense counsel exercises the ‘right to assist as defense counsel’ recognized in the Criminal Procedure Act for the benefit of the person arrested, etc. as an assistant to the person arrested, etc., not for the protection of his or her own fundamental rights. Therefore, the ‘right to assist as defense counsel’ should be viewed as a statutory right recognized as a result of the legislator concretely shaping it through individual statutes such as the Criminal Procedure Act in order to faithfully guarantee the constitutional fundamental right of a person arrested, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel.  \\nFrom this perspective, the Constitutional Court has long held that the constitutional right of visitation and communication with defense counsel is a fundamental right concerning personal liberty limited only to suspects and defendants, and that defense counsel’s own right of visitation and communication with a suspect or defendant cannot be regarded as a constitutional right, but is merely a right guaranteed only by Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act; accordingly, it dismissed a constitutional complaint filed by defense counsel on the ground that there was no possibility of infringement of fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court 1991. 7. 8. 89HEONMA181).”  \\nFor the reasons stated in the above separate opinion, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” is also merely a statutory right specifically formed through individual statutes such as the Criminal Procedure Act as an indirect and incidental effect arising from recognizing the “right to receive the assistance of counsel” of a person arrested, etc. as a fundamental right, and cannot be viewed as an “independent fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution.”  \\n(3) The majority opinion relies on the Court’s majority opinions in Constitutional Court 2000HEONMA474 decided on 2003. 3. 27. and Constitutional Court 2016HEONMA503 decided on 2017. 11. 30., which held that “in order for the right of a suspect, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel to be practically secured, the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist the suspect, etc. must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right,” and reasons that the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” should also be guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right because it is a core right for assisting a suspect, etc., and if it is not guaranteed, the right of a suspect, etc. to receive sufficient assistance from counsel becomes meaningless.  \\nIt is true that through visitation counsel can grasp the status of a detained suspect, etc. and devise appropriate responses accordingly, explain the meaning of the facts of suspicion or the charges, consult about countermeasures by hearing the opinions of the suspect, etc. thereon, and provide comfort to a suspect, etc. who is in a legally and psychologically anxious state, thereby restoring psychological stability and enabling the suspect, etc. to effectively exercise the right of defense within the criminal procedure (see Constitutional Court 2009. 10. 29. 2007HEONMA992). It is also true that through visitation and communication between a “person who intends to become defense counsel” and a suspect, etc., such advice, consultation, and comfort to the suspect, etc. are possible to some extent. However, when a “person who intends to become defense counsel” visits and communicates with a suspect, etc., because the point at which it is confirmed whether the suspect, etc. will actually retain the attorney and receive assistance from him or her has not yet been reached, the main purpose may be seen as the person’s own retention activities rather than assistance to the suspect, etc.; and the disadvantage suffered by the “person who intends to become defense counsel” due to inability to visit the suspect, etc., namely the disadvantage resulting from failure to obtain a criminal case retention, is merely an indirect, factual, and economic interest (see Constitutional Court 2004. 4. 29. 2002HEONMA756).  \\nMeanwhile, as stated by the majority opinion, it is reasonable to view not only a person who has been requested to be appointed as defense counsel but has not yet filed a notice of appointment as defense counsel, but also a person who seeks to act as defense counsel on his or her own, as falling within the meaning of “a person who intends to become defense counsel,” and the Supreme Court has also held that “even where a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having a possibility of becoming defense counsel, he or she may not be restricted from visiting a defendant or suspect under physical restraint on the ground that he or she is not a ‘defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel’ as prescribed in Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act” (see Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.). If the meaning of “a person who intends to become defense counsel” is interpreted as above, the right of visitation and communication of such a person should be viewed as a right recognized to that person regardless of the suspect’s or defendant’s will, at the stage before assisting the suspect, etc.  \\nIn light of the above circumstances, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” cannot be viewed as standing in a relationship of mutual complementarity with the right of a suspect, etc. to receive assistance, and it cannot be concluded that, unless it is elevated and guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right, the right of a suspect, etc. to receive sufficient assistance from counsel becomes meaningless. Therefore, even if one adopts the view that the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist a suspect, etc. must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right, there is no need, as in the majority opinion, to understand the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” as well as a constitutional fundamental right.  \\n(4) Ultimately, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” which the Claimant alleges was infringed by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, cannot be regarded as a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution; accordingly, the Claimant’s constitutional complaint against the denial of visitation is unlawful because there is no possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.  \\n\\nB. Subsidiarity  \\n(1) Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “if there is an objection to a disposition concerning detention, seizure, or the return of seized articles made by a prosecutor or judicial police officer, or to a disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc. under Article 243-2, a petition may be filed with the court having jurisdiction over the place where the duties are performed, or with the court corresponding to the prosecutor’s public prosecutors’ office to which the prosecutor belongs, for revocation or alteration of the disposition.”  \\nAn act by an investigative agency denying visitation between a suspect and defense counsel, etc. falls under a “disposition concerning detention” or a “disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc.” subject to quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and therefore not only the suspect or defense counsel but also a “person who intends to become defense counsel” may challenge it by filing a quasi-appeal pursuant to that provision (see Supreme Court Decision 89MO37 dated 1990. 2. 13.; Supreme Court Decision 91MO24 dated 1991. 3. 28.; Supreme Court Decision 2006MO656 dated 2007. 1. 31., etc.).  \\nA constitutional complaint may not be filed unless all procedures have been exhausted where there is a remedy procedure under other laws (proviso to Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act), and the Constitutional Court has held that where a constitutional complaint is filed without going through such a procedure despite the availability of a quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act, it is unlawful for failure to exhaust the lawful remedy procedure prescribed by other laws (see Constitutional Court 2007. 5. 31. 2006HEONMA1131).  \\n(2) The Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case constitutes a “disposition concerning detention” or a “disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc.” subject to a quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Nevertheless, the Claimant filed the present constitutional complaint without seeking revocation or alteration of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case through the quasi-appeal procedure.  \\nThe majority opinion held that, because the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case ended on the day of the incident, if the Claimant were to file a quasi-appeal seeking revocation thereof, it would be objectively uncertain whether the court would proceed to a merits determination, and thus it is difficult to expect the Claimant to have exhausted the prior remedy procedure; on that basis, it concluded that the constitutional complaint concerning the denial of visitation was lawful as an exception to subsidiarity.  \\nHowever, after the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, the Claimant was unable to visit suspect Yun XX-hyeon or participate in the interrogation of the suspect, and ultimately was not retained as defense counsel for the above suspect. In addition, with respect to the above suspect, a detention warrant was issued and he was prosecuted while in custody. There is nothing in the record to suggest any circumstance that would lead a court to find legal interest to be lacking or extinguished if the Claimant filed a quasi-appeal against the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case. The Supreme Court has decided on the merits on the premise that legal interest exists even when a defense counsel’s participation was denied during the interrogation of a suspect and the interrogation procedure had ended (see Supreme Court Decision 2008MO793 dated 2008. 9. 12.); the same should apply where visitation is denied during the interrogation of a suspect.  \\nAccordingly, even if the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case has already ended, the Claimant may challenge it by filing a quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act; thus, the Claimant’s constitutional complaint regarding the denial of visitation in this case fails to satisfy the subsidiarity requirement and is unlawful.  \\n\\nC. Conclusion  \\nThe right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” which the Claimant alleges was infringed by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, cannot be said to be a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution, and therefore the Claimant’s petition regarding the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case lacks the possibility of infringement of a fundamental right. Moreover, because the Claimant did not go through the quasi-appeal procedure under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the subsidiarity requirement is also not satisfied.  \\nAccordingly, the constitutional complaint concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is unlawful in any event and must be dismissed."}

Case Overview\\n\\nA. 2020HEONGA1\\n\\nThe petitioner for referral, Park ○○ (a foreigner), is a foreign national of the Arab Republic of Egypt who entered the Republic of Korea on 2018. 7. 21. with tourist/transit (B-2) status and remained in the Republic of Korea after the period of stay granted to him had expired.\\n\\nThe Head of the Suwon Immigration and Foreigners Office, on 2018. 10. 17., pursuant to Article 51(3) of the Immigration Control Act, placed the above petitioner for referral under emergency protection, and on 2018. 10. 18., pursuant to Article 46(1) No. 3, No. 8, Article 11(1) No. 8, and Article 17(1) of the same Act, issued a deportation order against the above petitioner for referral and, at the same time, pursuant to Article 63(1) of the same Act, issued a detention order.\\n\\nAccordingly, the above petitioner for referral filed an action seeking cancellation of the above deportation order and detention order (Suwon District Court 2019GU-DAN6240), and during the pendency of that case applied for a request to refer the matter for adjudication on the constitutionality of Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act, etc. (Suwon District Court 2019A4057). The referring court, having granted the application insofar as it concerned Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act, referred the constitutional review of this case on 2020. 1. 23.\\n\\nB. 2021HEONGA10\\n\\nThe petitioner for referral, Jha ○○ (a foreigner), is a foreign national of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh who entered the Republic of Korea on 2017. 5. 13. with short-term business (C-3-4) status and, after applying for refugee status recognition on 2017. 8. 7., was additionally granted other (G-1-5) status.\\n\\nThe Head of the Seoul Immigration and Foreigners Office, on 2017. 11. 22., on the ground that the above petitioner for referral had entered the country by fraudulent invitation, issued a deportation order against the above petitioner for referral pursuant to Article 46(1) No. 2 and No. 3, Article 7-2 No. 2, and Article 11(1) No. 3 and No. 4 of the Immigration Control Act and, at the same time, pursuant to Article 63(1) of the same Act, issued a detention order.\\n\\nAccordingly, the above petitioner for referral filed an action seeking cancellation of the above deportation order and detention order (Seoul Administrative Court 2018GU-DAN54708), and during the pendency of that case applied for a request to refer the matter for adjudication on the constitutionality of Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act, etc. (Seoul Administrative Court 2018A12518). The referring court, having granted the application insofar as it concerned Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act, referred the constitutional review of this case on 2021. 2. 9.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe subject matter of this case is whether Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.) (hereinafter referred to as the “provision subject to review”) violates the Constitution. The provision subject to review and the relevant provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision Subject to Review]\\n\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.)\\n\\nArticle 63 (Detention and Release from Detention of a Person Subject to a Deportation Order) (1) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may detain in a detention facility a person subject to a deportation order until such person can be repatriated when immediate repatriation outside the Republic of Korea is impossible for reasons such as the absence of a passport or lack of transportation.\\n\\n[Relevant Provisions]\\n\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 10282 on 2010. 5. 14.)\\n\\nArticle 2 (Definitions) The meanings of the terms used in this Act are as follows:\\n\\n11. The term “detention” means enforcement activity by which an immigration control official takes and confines a person who has reasonable grounds to be suspected of falling under a person subject to deportation under any item of Article 46(1) in an alien detention room, alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice, for the purpose of deporting such person.\\n\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.)\\n\\nArticle 46 (Persons Subject to Deportation) (1) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may deport outside the Republic of Korea an alien falling under any of the following items in accordance with the procedures prescribed in this Chapter.\\n\\n2. An alien who has violated Article 7-2 or an alien who entered the Republic of Korea through acts such as fraudulent invitation prescribed in that Article\\n\\n3. A person whose ground for denial of entry, falling under any item of Article 11(1), is discovered or arises after entry\\n\\n8. A person who has violated Article 17(1) or (2), Article 18, Article 20, Article 23, Article 24, or Article 25\\n\\nArticle 63 (Detention and Release from Detention of a Person Subject to a Deportation Order) (2) Where the period of detention under paragraph (1) exceeds 3 months, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office shall obtain prior approval from the Minister of Justice every 3 months.\\n\\n(3) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office shall promptly release a person from detention if prior approval under paragraph (2) is not obtained.\\n\\n(4) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may release a person from detention if it becomes manifest that the person subject to a deportation order cannot be repatriated for reasons such as denial of entry from another country.\\n\\n(5) Where the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office releases a person from detention pursuant to paragraph (3) or (4), he or she may attach restrictions on residence or other necessary conditions.\\n\\nArticle 66 (Revocation of Temporary Release from Detention) (1) Where a person temporarily released from detention falls under any of the following items, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may revoke the temporary release from detention and take measures for detention again.\\n\\n1. Where it is deemed that the person has absconded or is likely to abscond\\n\\n2. Where the person fails to comply with a summons without justifiable grounds\\n\\n3. Where the person violates conditions attached to the temporary release, other than the matters prescribed in Items 1 and 2\\n\\n(2) Where the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office revokes the temporary release from detention pursuant to paragraph (1), he or she may issue a revocation document of temporary release from detention and forfeit all or part of the security deposit to the National Treasury.\\n\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 15492 on 2018. 3. 20.)\\n\\nArticle 65 (Temporary Release from Detention) (1) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may, ex officio or upon request of the detainee (including his or her surety or legal representative, etc.), temporarily release the detainee from detention by requiring the deposit of a security deposit not exceeding 20 million won and attaching restrictions on residence or other necessary conditions, after considering the detainee’s circumstances, reasons for request for release, assets, and other matters.\\n\\n3. Grounds for the Referring Court’s Request for Constitutional Review\\n\\nA. The provision subject to review does not set an upper limit on the detention period, thereby rendering the detainee unable to predict at all when he or she will be released, which itself causes serious mental pressure. Permitting detention without a time limit merely for the administrative purpose of facilitating execution of a deportation order emphasizes only administrative convenience and uniformity, and thus violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person.\\n\\nB. Detention under the Immigration Control Act restricts freedom of the person as it is equivalent to “arrest or detention” in criminal procedure. Therefore, it should be subject to strict warrant principle; yet the provision subject to review allows the physical restraint of an alien subject to a deportation order without a court warrant, and thus violates the warrant principle.\\n\\nC. In light of the fact that no third independent and neutral institution or judicial body is involved at all in the stage of commencement or extension of detention; that the detainee may file an objection against the detention order with the Minister of Justice, and detention may be extended only with the Minister of Justice’s approval, but the Minister of Justice is merely the supervisory authority over the administrative agency that issues and executes detention orders, so it cannot be said that ex post remedies or control procedures by an external neutral and objective institution are secured; and that there is no provision in the Immigration Control Act requiring that the person concerned be given an opportunity to present opinions before issuance of a detention order under the provision subject to review, the provision subject to review violates the principle of due process.\\n\\n4. Judgment\\n\\nA. Alien detention system under the Immigration Control Act\\n\\n(1) Detention under the Immigration Control Act means “enforcement activity by which an immigration control official takes and confines a person who has reasonable grounds to be suspected of falling under a person subject to deportation under Article 46(1) of the Immigration Control Act in an alien detention room, alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice, for the purpose of deporting such person” (Article 2 No. 11 of the Immigration Control Act). Detention under the Immigration Control Act includes “detention for the determination of a person subject to deportation” prescribed in Article 51 and “detention for the execution of a deportation order” prescribed in the provision subject to review.\\n\\n(2) According to the provision subject to review, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may detain an alien subject to a deportation order (hereinafter referred to as a “person subject to deportation”) in an alien detention room, alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice (hereinafter referred to as a “detention facility”) until such person can be repatriated when immediate repatriation outside the Republic of Korea is impossible for reasons such as the absence of a passport or lack of transportation. Detention under the provision subject to review is intended to secure the execution of a deportation order where a deportation order has been issued upon determining that an alien falls under a person subject to deportation, but immediate execution is impossible, and is distinguished from detention under Article 51 of the Immigration Control Act, which secures the physical presence of an alien in order to examine whether the alien falls under a person subject to deportation.\\n\\nThe provision subject to review states that detention is permissible “until such person can be repatriated,” and thus, in the wording of the statute, imposes no limitation on the detention period; instead, where the period of detention exceeds 3 months, prior approval from the Minister of Justice must be obtained every 3 months, and if such approval is not obtained, detention must be released (Article 63(2) and (3) of the Immigration Control Act). In addition, a person detained in a detention facility pursuant to the provision subject to review may file an objection with the Minister of Justice (Article 63(6) and Article 55 of the Immigration Control Act), and the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may, ex officio or upon request of the detainee, temporarily release the detainee from detention by requiring the deposit of a security deposit not exceeding 20 million won and attaching restrictions on residence or other necessary conditions, after considering the detainee’s circumstances, reasons for request for release, assets, and other matters (Article 65(1) of the Immigration Control Act).\\n\\nB. Issues and Standard of Review\\n\\n(1) Detention under the provision subject to review is a compulsory measure by which a person subject to deportation is taken and confined in a detention facility in order to secure execution of a deportation order when immediate execution of the deportation order is impossible, and thus restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person (see Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29). Therefore, the issue in this case is whether the provision subject to review infringes freedom of the person by violating the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction, which is the limiting principle on restriction of fundamental rights, and the principle of due process under Article 12 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Immigration control administration is state administration that promotes the national interest and security by appropriately controlling and adjusting the entry and exit of nationals and foreigners and the stay of foreigners. Among matters relating to immigration control, matters concerning the entry and domestic stay of foreigners are necessary for performing the functions of a sovereign state and lie within the domain of broad policy discretion (see Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2003HEONMA87; Constitutional Court 2014. 4. 24. 2011HEONMA474 et al.). Detention under the provision subject to review, which is carried out to secure execution of a deportation order, may be regarded as part of immigration control administration.\\n\\nHowever, freedom of the person under Article 12(1) of the Constitution is the most fundamental minimum freedom necessary to realize human dignity and value, and serves as the premise for the guarantee of all fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court 2020. 9. 24. 2017HEONBA157 et al.). By its nature, it is a human right, and whether it is recognized does not vary depending on whether one has lawful status of stay in the country. Therefore, a strict standard of review must be applied to whether the provision subject to review infringes freedom of the person.\\n\\nC. Constitutional Opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon\\n\\n(1) Whether the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction is violated\\n\\n(a) Legitimacy of purpose and appropriateness of means\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of the provision subject to review is to appropriately control and adjust the entry, exit, and stay of foreigners, thereby promoting national security and order, by taking and confining persons subject to deportation in a detention facility until they can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea so that deportation orders may be executed easily and efficiently. Such legislative purpose is legitimate, and taking and confining persons subject to deportation in a detention facility until they can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea is an effective means of securing execution of a deportation order; thus, appropriateness of means is also recognized.\\n\\n(b) Minimum infringement and balance of interests\\n\\nHowever, the provision subject to review fails to satisfy the minimum infringement requirement and the balance of interests requirement for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) Detention under the provision subject to review is a compulsory measure temporarily and provisionally taken to secure execution when a deportation order cannot be executed immediately upon issuance (see Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29). Yet the provision subject to review merely provides that a person subject to deportation may be detained until such person can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea, and does not set an upper limit on the detention period, thereby making indefinite detention possible.\\n\\nDetention by which a person subject to deportation is temporarily and provisionally confined in a specific place for the purpose of executing a deportation order can, by its very nature, be deemed justified only when the person is confined within a reasonable period necessary for the execution of the deportation order. However, according to the provision subject to review, for example, where the detainee has applied for refugee status recognition under the Refugee Act or has filed an objection to a decision of non-recognition of refugee status, etc., so that the deportation order cannot be executed until the related procedures are completed (see Article 62(4) of the Immigration Control Act), or where the detainee has filed an action for cancellation, etc. against the deportation order or civil or criminal disputes are pending, making execution of the deportation order practically difficult, the detention period may be extended indefinitely depending on the progress of those procedures. In addition, the provision subject to review permits continued detention without any limitation on the period until repatriation becomes possible even where repatriation is impossible because entry is denied by another country. Long-term or indefinite detention of a person subject to deportation even where the deportation order cannot be executed within a considerable period exceeds the limits of a temporary and provisional compulsory measure and seriously restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person. Furthermore, detention without an upper limit on duration causes serious mental pressure in itself, regardless of the actual length of detention, because the detainee cannot predict at all when he or she will be released (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Jin-seong, Kim I-su, Kang Il-won, Lee Seon-ae, and Yoon Nam-seok in Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29).\\n\\nDetention under the provision subject to review has a substantive limitation in purpose, in that it may not be ordered for any purpose other than securing execution of a deportation order; and it has a temporal limitation in that it may be temporary only for the minimum period necessary until repatriation is possible and the period of detention may not be extended for other purposes (see Supreme Court Decision 99DA68829, decided on 2001. 10. 26.). Although the average detention period until an actual person subject to deportation is repatriated is only a little over 10 days, and cases in which long-term detention exceeding one year becomes an issue are only few. However, such limitations naturally derive from the nature of detention as a temporary and provisional measure, and whether the normative concept of “the minimum period necessary until repatriation becomes possible” must be limited to a considerable period is not taken into account here. Therefore, notwithstanding the above interpretive limitations, the provision subject to review, which does not set an upper limit on detention period, still leaves the problems arising from the absence of such an upper limit unresolved, in that long-term or indefinite detention is possible, and even where execution of the deportation order is impossible for reasons not attributable to the detainee, the person may still be detained for a long period until actual repatriation if “immediate repatriation is impossible.”\\n\\nMeanwhile, there may be cases where there is no objective reason making repatriation impossible, but the detainee does not cooperate with repatriation, making it impossible to execute the deportation order promptly; however, non-cooperation with repatriation alone cannot justify indefinite detention. If execution of the deportation order is delayed due to the detainee’s refusal to cooperate, that refusal may be taken as a reason for extending the detention period; however, as the immigration authorities in charge of repatriation must faithfully carry out repatriation work by removing obstacles delaying repatriation, they cannot keep detaining the person until repatriation is realized merely because the detainee does not cooperate with repatriation.\\n\\n2) Therefore, even if the appropriate upper limit on the detention period is left aside, at the very least the law must clearly specify that upper limit so as to prevent harm arising from unreasonable prolongation or uncertainty of the detention period. Permitting detention without a time limit merely for the administrative purpose of efficient execution of a deportation order emphasizes only administrative convenience and uniformity, and excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person. It is difficult to regard foreigners who were not able to choose voluntary departure for various reasons or who were unable to depart voluntarily and therefore were apprehended and detained as having, in effect, a “freedom to depart,” so the infringement of fundamental rights due to the absence of an upper limit on detention period cannot be deemed mitigated on the ground that a person subject to deportation is free to depart at any time and thus escape from being a detainee (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Jin-seong, Kim I-su, Kang Il-won, Lee Seon-ae, and Yoon Nam-seok in Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29).\\n\\nLooking to international standards and foreign legislation, many countries set an upper limit on the period when detaining a person subject to a deportation order. The “Directive 2008/115/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on common standards and procedures in Member States for returning illegally staying third-country nationals” (so-called “EU Returns Directive for Irregular Migrants”) requires Member States to prescribe in domestic law an absolute maximum period of detention in order to curb unnecessary long-term detention and respect the basic human rights of foreigners subject to deportation; it strengthens control over prolonged detention by providing that the initial detention period may not exceed 6 months and may be extended exceptionally, but the extension period shall be at most 12 months. Accordingly, EU Member States have enacted domestic laws establishing detention requirements and procedures that are equal to or stricter than the standards set forth in the above directive and have set upper limits on detention periods. For example, France provides by law that detention may be ordered up to a maximum of 90 days only where effective custody is difficult for a foreigner whose repatriation is reasonably possible and other measures to ensure effective execution are insufficient. Germany provides by law that detention for deportation may be ordered up to 6 months, but even upon extension may not exceed a maximum of 12 months. Taiwan and South Africa also limit by statute the detention period for persons subject to deportation to a maximum of 100 days or 120 days, respectively. The reason why international standards and other legislative examples set upper limits on detention periods is that detention with no fixed duration may cause serious human rights violations.\\n\\nThe period required until repatriation in the actual process of executing a deportation order may vary depending on whether the person subject to deportation cooperates and on the circumstances of the Republic of Korea or the receiving country. One may argue from this point that the provision subject to review necessarily had no upper limit on the detention period; however, considering that detention under the provision subject to review is a temporary and provisional measure taken for the purpose of executing a deportation order and that many countries, as noted above, set upper limits on detention periods for persons subject to deportation, it cannot be said that it is impossible to set a reasonable upper limit on the detention period necessary to execute a deportation order.\\n\\n3) If an upper limit is set on the detention period, and repatriation is delayed so that the period exceeds that upper limit, detention of the person subject to deportation must be released. In such a case, it may be argued that the person subject to deportation who has been released may go into hiding or be exposed to crime. However, this is merely a vague and potential possibility that has not yet materialized, or a concern that exaggerates some situations; thus, based only on such vague assumptions, it is difficult to justify measures that seriously restrict freedom of the person, such as “detention without any upper limit on duration.” One cannot conclude that a foreigner who committed a crime in the Republic of Korea will abscond or commit crimes again if released from detention. Moreover, among persons subject to deportation there may be not only foreigners who committed crimes and were sentenced to punishment, but also foreigners who merely violated administrative regulations concerning entry or stay. Treating all such persons as potential fugitives or potential criminals and detaining them without any time limit is an excessive measure (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Jin-seong, Kim I-su, Kang Il-won, Lee Seon-ae, and Yoon Nam-seok in Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29).\\n\\nThere may be concern that if an upper limit is imposed on the detention period, the detainee could exceed that upper limit through a cancellation action against the deportation order or by applying for refugee status recognition, etc.; however, such cases can be minimized through institutional improvements such as having the courts give priority and focus to such cases, expediting refugee status examination and decisions, or preventing abuse of refugee status applications.\\n\\nFurthermore, securing execution of a deportation order is possible through various means other than detention under the provision subject to review. For example, execution of a deportation order may be secured through means substituting for detention, such as restricting the residence of a person subject to deportation until departure requirements are met or requiring periodic reporting of residence, designating a guarantor or requiring payment of an appropriate security deposit, or continuously observing or supervising the person subject to deportation through supervisors, etc. Therefore, in order to secure execution of a deportation order, it is not inevitable to adopt a method that excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person, such as detention without an upper limit on duration.\\n\\n4) Meanwhile, the current procedures and operation of the Immigration Control Act are insufficient, by themselves, to properly control the detention period and thereby mitigate excessive restrictions on freedom of the person.\\n\\nFirst, the detainee may request temporary release from detention from the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office under the Immigration Control Act, and the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may temporarily release the detainee from detention ex officio (Article 65 of the Immigration Control Act). However, unless there are circumstances such that the detainee has won a cancellation action against the deportation order, etc., whether to grant temporary release from detention is entirely within the discretion of the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office (see Article 65 of the Immigration Control Act and Article 6 of the Regulations on Handling Temporary Release from Detention). It is highly likely to be carried out for administrative convenience rather than through a substantive review of the necessity of detention. According to the result of the fact inquiry dated 2021. 7. 1. to the Minister of Justice in Case 2020HEONGA1 and the reference materials submitted by the Minister of Justice on 2022. 9. 5., while the average number of cases of temporary release from detention during the five years from 2013 to 2017 was 120 per year and the average number during the three years from 2018 to 2020 was 131 per year, temporary release from detention in 2021 surged to 461 cases; the sharp increase in requests for temporary release from detention and grants thereof in 2021 appears to have been due to difficulties in infection control within detention facilities caused by the spread of COVID-19, and administrative convenience appears to have been the main reason. Article 63(4) of the Immigration Control Act provides that the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may release a person from detention where it becomes manifest that the person subject to deportation cannot be repatriated for reasons such as denial of entry from another country, but this too is entirely within the discretion of the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office. In light of these points, it is difficult to regard the temporary release from detention system as functioning as a device that can supplement the problem of having no upper limit on the detention period.\\n\\nIn addition, the Immigration Control Act provides for objections to detention orders and a system of prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extensions of detention periods; however, as will be discussed below, these are merely procedures conducted by the Minister of Justice, who is the supervisory authority over the administrative agency issuing and executing detention orders, and thus cannot be considered effective enough to supplement the problem of not setting an upper limit on the detention period. In particular, according to the reference materials submitted by the Minister of Justice on 2021. 7. 21. and 2022. 9. 5., the rate of disapproval of extensions was 4.9% in 2017, 6.7% in 2018, 6.4% in 2019, 4.0% in 2020, and 9.4% in 2021, with an average disapproval rate of only 6.28% over the past five years, making it impossible not to question the effectiveness of the extension approval system.\\n\\n5) Taking the above circumstances together, although means exist for securing execution of a deportation order other than indefinite detention in a detention facility, the provision subject to review allows the detainee to be detained without any upper limit on duration, which exceeds the minimum necessary to achieve the legislative purpose and excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person.
