Outline of the Case\\n\\nThe Petitioner is a foreign national of Nepalese nationality who entered the Republic of Korea on 1997. 9. 30. with a short-term commercial visa and, after the expiration of the period of stay, remained in the country illegally without departing. While staying illegally, the Petitioner married a national of the Republic of Korea and changed the status of stay to a marriage residence visa on 2007. 1. 30., and has been staying.\\n\\nOn 2013. 1. 24., the Petitioner applied to the Minister of Justice for simplified naturalization pursuant to Article 6 of the Nationality Act. However, on the ground that the Petitioner had previously stayed illegally and had a criminal record for which the judgment became final and conclusive on 2014. 2. 27. after having been sentenced to a fine of 5,000,000 won for obstruction of business, obstruction of performance of official duties, and an offense in violation of the Act on Assemblies and Demonstrations, the Minister of Justice rendered, on 2014. 3. 11., a disposition denying the Petitioner’s naturalization, on the ground that the Petitioner did not satisfy the requirement under Article 5, item 3 of the Nationality Act that “conduct be upright.”\\n\\nThe Petitioner filed a lawsuit with the Seoul Administrative Court seeking revocation of the above disposition (Seoul Administrative Court 2014GUHAP6524), and during the pendency of that lawsuit filed an application for referral for a constitutional review of statutes regarding Article 5, item 3 of the Nationality Act, but when it was dismissed (Seoul Administrative Court 2014A2001), the Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint petition on 2014. 10. 10.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject matter of this adjudication is whether Article 5, item 3 of the Nationality Act (as amended by Act No. 8892 on 2008. 3. 14.) is unconstitutional, and the provision under review and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision under Review]\\n\\nNationality Act (as amended by Act No. 8892 on 2008. 3. 14.)\\n\\nArticle 5 (Requirements for General Naturalization) In order for a foreigner to obtain permission for naturalization, he or she shall satisfy the following requirements, except in cases falling under Article 6 or Article 7.\\n\\n3. That conduct be upright\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nNationality Act (as amended by Act No. 10275 on 2010. 5. 4.)\\n\\nArticle 4 (Acquisition of Nationality by Naturalization) (1) A foreigner who has never acquired the nationality of the Republic of Korea may acquire the nationality of the Republic of Korea by obtaining permission for naturalization from the Minister of Justice.\\n\\n(2) Upon receiving an application for permission for naturalization, the Minister of Justice shall examine whether the applicant satisfies the requirements for naturalization under Articles 5 through 7, and then grant naturalization only to a person who satisfies those requirements.\\n\\n(3) A person who has obtained permission for naturalization pursuant to paragraph (1) shall acquire the nationality of the Republic of Korea at the time the Minister of Justice grants such permission.\\n\\n(4) Matters necessary concerning the application procedures, examination, and other matters under paragraphs (1) and (2) shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n\\nArticle 5 (Requirements for General Naturalization) In order for a foreigner to obtain permission for naturalization, he or she shall satisfy the following requirements, except in cases falling under Article 6 or Article 7.\\n\\n1. To have had a domicile in the Republic of Korea continuously for at least 5 years\\n\\n2. To be an adult under the Civil Act of the Republic of Korea\\n\\n3. (omitted)\\n\\n4. To have the ability to maintain livelihood by relying on his or her own assets or skills, or on family members with whom he or she maintains a common livelihood\\n\\n5. To possess the basic qualities as a national of the Republic of Korea, such as proficiency in the Korean language and understanding of Korean customs\\n\\nArticle 6 (Requirements for Simplified Naturalization) (1) A foreigner falling under any of the following items who has had a domicile in the Republic of Korea continuously for at least 3 years may obtain permission for naturalization without satisfying the requirement under Article 5, item 1.\\n\\n1. A person whose father or mother was a national of the Republic of Korea\\n\\n2. A person born in the Republic of Korea whose father or mother was born in the Republic of Korea\\n\\n3. A person who was an adult under the Civil Act of the Republic of Korea at the time of adoption as an adopted child of a national of the Republic of Korea\\n\\n(2) A foreigner whose spouse is a national of the Republic of Korea and who falls under any of the following items may obtain permission for naturalization without satisfying the requirement under Article 5, item 1.\\n\\n1. A person who has had a domicile in the Republic of Korea continuously for at least 2 years while married to that spouse\\n\\n2. A person who, after marrying that spouse, has passed 3 years and has had a domicile in the Republic of Korea continuously for at least 1 year while married\\n\\n3. A person who has not met the period under item 1 or item 2, but while having a domicile in the Republic of Korea while married to that spouse, was unable to maintain normal married life due to the death, disappearance, or any other cause for which he or she is not responsible, has completed the remaining period under item 1 or item 2, and is recognized as appropriate by the Minister of Justice\\n\\n4. A person who has not satisfied the requirements under item 1 or item 2, but is raising, or must raise, a minor child born from the marriage with that spouse, has completed the period under item 1 or item 2, and is recognized as appropriate by the Minister of Justice\\n\\nArticle 7 (Requirements for Special Naturalization) (1) A foreigner falling under any of the following items who has a domicile in the Republic of Korea may obtain permission for naturalization without satisfying the requirements under Article 5, items 1, 2, or 4.\\n\\n1. A person whose father or mother is a national of the Republic of Korea; provided, however, that a person adopted as an adopted child after becoming an adult under the Civil Act of the Republic of Korea shall be excluded\\n\\n2. A person who has rendered special meritorious service to the Republic of Korea\\n\\n3. A person who possesses highly outstanding ability in a specific field such as science, economy, culture, or sports, and is recognized as likely to contribute to the national interest of the Republic of Korea\\n\\n(2) The standards and procedures for determining persons falling under paragraph (1), items 2 and 3, shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n\\n3. Summary of the Petitioner’s Argument\\n\\na. The provision under review violates the principle of statutory reservation because it leaves the determination criterion for “upright conduct,” one of the requirements for naturalization permission, entirely to the administrative agency without setting such criterion by statute.\\n\\nb. The provision under review also violates the principle of clarity because the meaning of “upright conduct” cannot be ascertained from the text of the provision alone.\\n\\nc. Since the vagueness of the requirements for naturalization permission causes foreigners who fear denial of their naturalization applications to be constrained in all of their actions, the provision under review infringes the Petitioner’s general freedom of action and the right of the Petitioner’s family members to pursue happiness, and infringes the right to equality by discriminating against the Petitioner, without reasonable grounds, from Koreans or foreigners who have not applied for naturalization.\\n\\n4. Judgment\\n\\na. General Naturalization System\\n\\n(1) Article 2, paragraph 1 of the Constitution provides, “The requirements for becoming a national of the Republic of Korea shall be prescribed by Act,” thereby delegating the requirements for nationality to legislation, and the Nationality Act enacted upon such delegation provides for acquisition of nationality by birth, acquisition of nationality by acknowledgment, and acquisition of nationality by naturalization as grounds for acquisition of nationality.\\n\\nAmong them, “naturalization” is a system whereby the State accepts a person as a national by granting permission to a person who, regardless of the requirements for acquisition of innate nationality by birth, satisfies the requirements prescribed by the domestic law of that State and has applied for acquisition of nationality in accordance with the procedures prescribed by that State. A foreigner who has never acquired the nationality of the Republic of Korea may acquire the nationality of the Republic of Korea by obtaining permission for naturalization from the Minister of Justice, and the Minister of Justice may, after examining whether the person satisfies the requirements for naturalization, grant naturalization only to a person who satisfies those requirements (Article 4 of the Nationality Act).\\n\\n(2) Naturalization consists of general naturalization, simplified naturalization, and special naturalization. General naturalization requires: ① having had a domicile in the Republic of Korea continuously for at least 5 years; ② being an adult under the Civil Act of the Republic of Korea; ③ upright conduct; ④ the ability to maintain livelihood; and ⑤ possessing the basic qualities as a national of the Republic of Korea, such as proficiency in the Korean language and understanding of Korean customs (Article 5 of the Nationality Act).\\n\\nSimplified naturalization applies to a person whose father or mother was a national of the Republic of Korea, a person born in the Republic of Korea whose father or mother was born in the Republic of Korea, a person who was an adult under the Civil Act of the Republic of Korea at the time of adoption as an adopted child of a national of the Republic of Korea, and a foreigner whose spouse is a national of the Republic of Korea. Except that the requirement ① necessary for general naturalization is shortened, the remaining requirements ② through ⑤ must be satisfied in the same manner (Article 6 of the Nationality Act).\\n\\nSpecial naturalization applies to a person whose father or mother is a national of the Republic of Korea, a person who has rendered special meritorious service to the Republic of Korea, or a person who possesses highly outstanding ability in a specific field such as science, economy, culture, or sports and is recognized as likely to contribute to the national interest of the Republic of Korea. A person who currently has a domicile in the Republic of Korea may be naturalized without satisfying ①, ②, and ④ among the requirements for general naturalization (Article 7 of the Nationality Act).\\n\\nRegardless of whether it is general naturalization, simplified naturalization, or special naturalization, naturalization may be granted only when requirement ③, upright conduct, and requirement ⑤, possessing the basic qualities as a national of the Republic of Korea, such as proficiency in the Korean language and understanding of Korean customs, are satisfied.\\n\\n(3) Nationality determines the qualifications of a national, and a person who acquires it becomes a sovereign while at the same time becoming subject to the State’s personal governing authority. Therefore, permission for naturalization is an act by which the legal status of a national is comprehensively established by granting nationality of the Republic of Korea to a foreigner, and considering the form and wording of the provision serving as the basis for permission for naturalization, as well as the content and characteristics of permission for naturalization, the Minister of Justice has discretion as to whether to grant naturalization even if the applicant for naturalization satisfies the requirements for naturalization (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DU19069, decided 2010. 7. 15.; Supreme Court Decision 2010DU6496, decided 2010. 10. 28.).\\n\\nb. Whether the Provision under Review Is Unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Organization of the Issues\\n\\nThe provision under review uses the abstract and comprehensive concept of “upright conduct” as a requirement for permission for naturalization, and thus the issue arises whether such a provision violates the principle of clarity.\\n\\nThe Petitioner also argues that the provision under review violates the principle of statutory reservation because it leaves the determination criterion for “upright conduct” entirely to the administrative agency without setting such criterion by statute. However, this is nothing other than saying that the concept of “upright conduct” is not clear.\\n\\nThe Petitioner further argues that the provision under review infringes foreigners’ general freedom of action and the right of their family members to pursue happiness, and infringes the right to equality by discriminating, without reasonable grounds, between foreigners who intend to apply for naturalization and foreigners or Koreans who do not. However, the provision under review prescribes the requirements for permission for naturalization, which grants nationality of the Republic of Korea to foreigners, and is not directly related to foreigners’ general freedom of action or the right of their family members to pursue happiness. Foreigners who do not apply for naturalization or Koreans are not persons seeking naturalization, and thus do not raise the issue of discrimination with persons who seek to apply for naturalization.\\n\\nAccordingly, only whether the provision under review violates the principle of clarity will be examined below.\\n\\n(2) Whether the Principle of Clarity Is Violated\\n\\n(A) All statutes must be clear, because from the standpoint of legal stability they serve as standards for the application of law by the administration and the judiciary. If the meaning and content of legal norms are uncertain, legal stability and predictability cannot be secured, and arbitrary interpretation and enforcement of the law by law-enforcement authorities become possible. However, the degree of clarity is not required to be the same for all statutes, and may differ depending on the nature of each statute or provision and the background or circumstances under which each statute was enacted. As a general principle, where a provision has an imposing character, the principle of clarity is required more strictly than where it has a beneficial character, and in criminal-related statutes governed by the principle of nulla poena sine lege, in particular, the degree of clarity is heightened and a stricter standard is applied. In addition, statutory provisions ordinarily have generality and abstraction, and therefore some use of universal or general concepts is inevitable as a matter of legislative technique. Thus, whether clarity is satisfied is determined by whether a reasonable interpretation is possible, considering the purpose for which the relevant statute was enacted and its relation to other norms; and if the meaning can be clarified through judicial supplementation and interpretation in light of the legislative intent, overall system, and content of the relevant provision, it cannot be said that clarity is lacking even in such a case (see Constitutional Court Decision 2001HEONBA9, decided 2001. 10. 25.; Constitutional Court Decision 2013HEONBA172, etc., decided 2014. 8. 28.; Constitutional Court Decision 2014HEONBA156, decided 2015. 3. 26.).\\n\\n(B) “Naturalization” is a system by which nationality of the Republic of Korea is granted to a foreigner who has never acquired the nationality of the Republic of Korea. Since a person who acquires nationality becomes the sovereign of the State while at the same time becoming subject to the State’s personal governing authority, the State, in prescribing the requirements for naturalization under which foreigners are accepted as new members of the national community, considers in various respects whether they are suitable for the national order and social order.\\n\\nAs one of such requirements for naturalization, the provision under review is intended to determine whether a foreigner, in being accepted as a new member of the national community, possesses sound character and qualities that enable him or her to harmonize with the existing national order and members of society. Considering even the point that broad discretion is recognized for the State in deciding whether to grant naturalization, the use in the provision under review of a somewhat general and value-evaluative concept such as “upright conduct” has an unavoidable aspect.\\n\\nThe fact that the United States prescribes “good moral character,” the United Kingdom “good character,” France “bonnes vie et moeurs” (good conduct and morals), and Japan “good conduct” as one of the requirements for permission for naturalization, and that various legislative examples use indeterminate concepts related to personality or character as one of the requirements for permission for naturalization, may also be seen as arising from these characteristics of the naturalization system.\\n\\nMeanwhile, “conduct” is a term often used when evaluating outwardly manifested behavior in light of the general moral notions of society, and lexically refers collectively to character and behavior. “Upright” means neat and proper in attire, bearing, and the like. Thus, “upright conduct” is generally understood to mean that a person’s character and behavior are neat and proper.\\n\\nIn addition, courts generally have held that “upright conduct” means conduct with character that, when various circumstances such as the foreigner’s sex, age, occupation, family, career, and criminal record are comprehensively considered, presents no obstacle to recognizing the person as a member of our national community and accepting him or her as one of the sovereigns.\\n\\nTaking together the legislative intent of the provision under review, the dictionary meaning of the terms, and judicial interpretations, “upright conduct” in the provision under review can be construed to mean “having character and behavior such that there is no obstacle to accepting the applicant for naturalization as a new member of the Republic of Korea,” and it may be anticipated that what specific cases fall under this will be determined by comprehensively considering various circumstances such as the applicant’s sex, age, occupation, family, career, and criminal record. In particular, as to the criminal record, it may be anticipated that consideration will not be limited merely to whether or not there was an act of committing a crime, but will comprehensively include various circumstances such as the content of the crime, the degree of punishment, the circumstances at the time of and after the crime, and the period from the date of the crime to the time of the naturalization disposition.\\n\\nTherefore, it cannot be said that the interpretation of the provision under review is so unclear that it impairs the foreseeability of those subject to the norm or causes arbitrary enforcement by law-enforcement agencies, and thus it cannot be deemed to violate the principle of clarity.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, since the provision under review does not violate the Constitution, it is so decided as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices."}
