proceedings (Daejeon District Court Seosan Branch 2009GODAN775), and on its own motion referred this constitutional review of law with respect to Article 56 of the Management of Mountainous Districts Act.\\n\\n(2) Case 2010HEONGA26\\n\\n(a) The defendant in the underlying case, ○○ Comtec Co., Ltd., was indicted on the facts charged that “Han ○Yeop, the head of its Personnel and General Affairs Team, on January 29, 2008, at the Suwon Immigration Office in Guun-dong, Gwonseon-gu, Suwon-si, in applying for certificates of visa issuance for 15 persons including Chinese national Wang ○Mae, falsely applied for the certificates of visa issuance in order to have them enter the country by submitting certificates of employment, dispatch orders, letters of guarantee, etc. containing false statements to the effect that they had worked for more than 6 months, although they had in fact never worked for ○○ Comtec Optoelectronics Co., Ltd., a local corporation.” (Suwon District Court 2009GODAN3493).\\n\\n(b) During the pendency of the first-instance proceedings, the requester for referral applied for a request for constitutional review with respect to Article 99-3 of the Immigration Control Act, and the court accepted the application and referred this constitutional review of law.\\n\\n(3) Case 2010HEONGA75\\n\\n(a) A summary order was sought against the defendant in the underlying case, ○○ Housing Co., Ltd., on the facts charged that “around July 2006, in the course of expanding a factory from July 6, 2007 to around March 2008 after obtaining permission for factory expansion, its employee, Oh ○Sang, in relation to the business of the company, unlawfully altered the form and quality of 480㎡ of forest land in Sokchang-ri, Susin-myeon, Dongnam-gu, Cheonan-si, by piling natural stones and paving with asphalt concrete so as to use it as a materials storage yard.” (Daejeon District Court Cheonan Branch 2009GOYAK11881).\\n\\n(b) The court referred the case to trial proceedings (Daejeon District Court Cheonan Branch 2009GODAN1534), and on its own motion referred this constitutional review of law with respect to Article 56 of the Management of Mountainous Districts Act.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe provisions subject to review in this case provide that where an agent, employee, or worker of a corporation (hereinafter referred to as “employee, etc.”) commits an unlawful act in relation to the business of the corporation, the corporation shall be punished together with the employee, etc.\\n\\n(1) Cases 2010HEONGA19 and 75\\n\\nThe subject matter of review in this case is whether the portion of Article 56 of the Management of Mountainous Districts Act (enacted by Act No. 6841 on December 30, 2002) that states, “Where the agent, employee, or worker of a corporation commits an act in violation of Article 53, item 1, or Article 54, item 1, in relation to the business of the corporation, a fine under the relevant Article shall also be imposed on the corporation” is contrary to the Constitution, and the content of the above provision subject to review (the underlined portion below) and the related provisions is as follows.\\n\\n[Provision Subject to Review]\\n\\nManagement of Mountainous Districts Act (enacted by Act No. 6841 on December 30, 2002) Article 56 (Dual Punishment Provision) Where the representative of a corporation, or the agent, employee, or worker of a corporation or individual commits an act in violation of Articles 53 through 55 in relation to the business of the corporation or individual, the offender shall be punished, and a fine under the relevant Article shall also be imposed on that corporation or individual.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nManagement of Mountainous Districts Act (as amended by Act No. 8852 on February 29, 2008) Article 53 (Penalties) Any person falling under any of the following subparagraphs shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 7 years or by a fine not exceeding 50 million won. In this case, imprisonment and a fine may be cumulatively imposed. <AMENDED_2007_1_26>\\n1. A person who, in violation of the first sentence of Article 14 (1), converts mountainous district land without obtaining permission for conversion of mountainous district land, or who converts mountainous district land by obtaining permission for conversion of mountainous district land by false or other wrongful means\\nArticle 54 (Penalties) Any person falling under any of the following subparagraphs shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 5 years or by a fine not exceeding 30 million won. <AMENDED_2007_1_26>\\n1. A person who, in violation of the latter sentence of Article 14 (1), converts mountainous district land without obtaining a change permit, or who converts mountainous district land by obtaining a change permit by false or other wrongful means\\nArticle 14 (Permission for Conversion of Mountainous District Land) (1) A person who intends to convert mountainous district land shall, as prescribed by Presidential Decree, obtain permission from the Administrator of the Korea Forest Service, specifying the intended use, and the same shall also apply where the person intends to change the permitted matters. Provided, however, that where a person intends to change minor matters prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry for Food, Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, such change may be made by report to the Administrator of the Korea Forest Service. <AMENDED_2007_1_26_2008_2_29>\\n\\n(2) Case 2010HEONGA26\\n\\nThe subject matter of review in this case is whether the portion of Article 99-3 of the Immigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 7406 on March 24, 2005) that states, “Where the representative of a corporation, or the agent, employee, or other worker of a corporation or individual commits an act in violation under Article 94, item 2-3, in relation to the business of the corporation or individual, a fine under the relevant Article shall also be imposed on the corporation or individual” is contrary to the Constitution, and the content of the above provision subject to review (the underlined portion below) and the related provisions is as follows.\\n\\n[Provision Subject to Review]\\n\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 7406 on March 24, 2005) Article 99-3 (Dual Punishment Provision) Where the representative of a corporation, or the agent, employee, or other worker of a corporation or individual commits any violation falling under any of the following subparagraphs in relation to the business of the corporation or individual, the offender shall be punished, and a fine under the relevant Article shall also be imposed on that corporation or individual.\\n1. A violation under Article 94, item 2-3\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 6745 on December 5, 2002) Article 94 (Penalties) Any person falling under any of the following subparagraphs shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 3 years or imprisonment without prison labor, or by a fine not exceeding 20 million won.\\n2-3. A person who violates Article 7-2\\n\\nArticle 7-2 (Prohibition of False Invitation, etc.) No person shall do any of the following acts for the purpose of causing a foreigner to enter the country.\\n2. An act of falsely applying for a visa or certificate of visa issuance, or an act of brokering such application <ARTICLE_ADDED_2001_12_29>\\n\\n2. Summary of the Reasons for the Request for Constitutional Review by the Requesting Courts\\n\\nThe gist of the reasons for the request for constitutional review by the requesting courts is as follows.\\n\\nThe provisions subject to review in this case provide that where employees, etc. employed by a corporation commit a violation in relation to the business of the corporation, the corporation, as the employer, shall be punished immediately for such criminal act of the employees, etc., regardless of whether the corporation, as the employer, has any fault. This is contrary to the principle of responsibility derived from the principle of a rule-of-law state and the principle of nulla poena sine lege, by imposing punishment without inquiring into responsibility for another person’s crime.\\n\\n3. Determination on the Admissibility Requirements\\n\\nThe provisions subject to review in this case were already amended by adding exculpatory provisions, and the supplementary provisions thereto did not contain any transitional provision to the effect that the application of penalties for criminal acts committed before the enforcement of the amended Act shall be governed by the former provisions (Management of Mountainous Districts Act, Act No. 10331 of May 31, 2010; Immigration Control Act, Act No. 10282 of May 14, 2010), but the effective date thereof has not yet arrived (Management of Mountainous Districts Act: December 1, 2010; Immigration Control Act: November 15, 2010).\\n\\nAccordingly, the provisions subject to review in this case are currently directly applicable to the underlying cases, and if these provisions are declared unconstitutional, the basis for punishment of the above defendants will disappear, and a judgment of acquittal will be rendered on the facts charged in each underlying case. If so, the disposition of the trial in the underlying case will differ depending on whether the above provisions are unconstitutional, and therefore these provisions satisfy the prerequisite for adjudication in relation to the underlying cases.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Merits\\n\\na. The provisions subject to review in this case provide that, if it is established that employees, etc. employed by a corporation committed a certain unlawful act, the corporation that employed such employees, etc. shall also immediately be subject to the fine prescribed in the penal provision applicable to the employees, etc.\\n\\nIn other words, the provisions subject to review in this case do not prescribe as a requirement for punishment of the corporation whether the corporation participated in the criminal act of the employees, etc. or whether it violated its duty of care in supervision thereof, nor do they otherwise prescribe any possibility of exculpation of the corporation. Ultimately, if employees, etc. commit a certain act, the corporation is immediately punished together with such employees, etc., as the employer, without at all asking whether the corporation has any fault regarding such criminal act of the employees, etc.\\n\\nb. Punishment is a sanction for a crime, and its essence is censure for conduct negatively evaluated by the legal order. Even if a consequence negatively evaluated by the legal order has occurred, if the occurrence of such consequence is not attributable to anyone’s fault, punishment cannot be imposed on anyone merely because the negative consequence occurred. The principle of responsibility in criminal punishment, namely that “punishment cannot be imposed on a person without responsibility,” is a basic principle of criminal law, a principle inherent in the constitutional principle of a rule-of-law state, and at the same time a principle derived from the purport of Article 10 of the Constitution; and the principle of responsibility applies to corporations as it does to natural persons.\\n\\nHowever, under the provisions subject to review in this case, even where the corporation has exercised due care in appointment and supervision with respect to the violation by employees, etc. and has no fault, punishment would necessarily be imposed on the corporation. As such, the provisions subject to review in this case impose criminal punishment on the corporation merely because employees, etc. employed by the corporation committed a criminal act in relation to the business, without at all addressing the corporation’s independent responsibility for the result of the act committed by the employees, etc., namely the corporation’s decision-making and conduct structure that serves as the basis for censure regarding the criminal act of the employees, etc. This is the imposition of punishment for another person’s crime without inquiring into responsibility, and therefore violates the principle of responsibility derived from the constitutional principle of a rule-of-law state and the principle of nulla poena sine lege (see Constitutional Court 2008HEONGA14, decided on July 30, 2009, Collection of Cases 21-2, 77).\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, since the provisions subject to review in this case are contrary to the Constitution, the Court decides as follows by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices except for Justice Lee Gong-hyeon’s separate opinion of unconstitutionality in 6 below, Justice Jo Dae-hyeon’s dissenting opinion in 7 below, and Justice Lee Dong-heub’s dissenting opinion in 8 below.\\n\\n6. Separate Opinion of Justice Lee Gong-hyeon That the Provisions Are Unconstitutional\\n\\na. Whether they are unconstitutional as punishment of a person without responsibility\\n\\nA corporation is a legally constituted fictitious entity and in reality acts through its employees. Therefore, if criminal responsibility is to be attributed to the corporation on the ground that it has an inherent risk of harming the public interest or may cause serious harm to society by means of undue exercise of economic power, the conduct of the employee in question must be regarded as conduct of the corporation. If criminal responsibility is attributed to the corporation even for conduct of employees that cannot be regarded as conduct of the corporation, despite the absence of any fault on the corporation’s part, such as involvement in the conduct or fault in appointment and supervision, it amounts to imposing punishment on a person without responsibility and thus violates the principle of responsibility. Accordingly, the issue is whether the conduct of an employee in a certain position within the hierarchical structure of the corporation can be regarded as conduct of the corporation. Acts performed within the scope of authority by an organ or employee who is in a position to determine the corporation’s management policy or major intentions or to manage and supervise the corporation’s overall affairs, or by an agent delegated full authority by such a person, may be identified with the acts of the corporation.\\n\\nMeanwhile, as persons whose acts can be identified with the acts of the corporation, not only the representative stated in the register but also an organ or employee who is in a position to determine the corporation’s management policy or major intentions or to manage and supervise the corporation’s overall affairs, or an agent delegated full authority by such a person, should be included.\\n\\nAccordingly, since an organ or employee who is in a position to determine the corporation’s management policy or major intentions or to manage and supervise the corporation’s overall affairs, or an agent delegated full authority by such a person, is a person who externally expresses the corporation’s intention and internally manages and supervises the corporation’s overall affairs, his or her conduct can be regarded as conduct of the corporation, and thus attributing criminal responsibility to the corporation for a criminal act committed by a person in such a position in relation to the corporation’s business cannot be said to violate the principle of responsibility. Therefore, the part of the provisions subject to review in this case concerning an agent, employee, or other worker who is in the above-mentioned position does not violate the Constitution.\\n\\nBy contrast, the part of the provisions subject to review in this case concerning other agents, employees, or workers, as the majority opinion on unconstitutionality determined, does not prescribe as an element of the offense any responsibility such as the corporation’s involvement in the criminal act of such persons or fault in appointment and supervision, but instead provides that, if a certain criminal act by such persons is established, such persons are punished and the corporation is automatically punished as well. This amounts to imposing punishment on a corporation that bears no fault, and therefore should be regarded as violating the principle of responsibility.\\n\\nb. Whether the principle of proportionality between responsibility and punishment is violated\\n\\nWhere a person, such as the representative of a corporation, who can be identified with the acts of the corporation commits a criminal act in relation to the business of the corporation and the corporation is punished, or where the corporation is punished under the doctrine of joint criminality because it conspired with employees, etc. or facilitated or condoned the violation, it may be evaluated as consistent with the principle of proportionality between responsibility and punishment even if the statutory punishment for the actor and the corporation is the same.\\n\\nHowever, even if acts produce the same result, depending on the mode of the act there may be cases that are difficult to accept in light of the protected legal interest and the nature of the offense under the principle of proportionality between crime and punishment. For example, between intentional conduct and negligent conduct, the degree of responsibility arising therefrom should be determined differently under the principle of proportionality. Thus, even if the provisions subject to review in this case are regarded as provisions punishing corporations that are negligent in appointment and supervision with respect to agents, employees, or other workers other than those agents, employees, or other workers prescribed by the provisions subject to review in this case who are in a position to determine the corporation’s management policy or major intentions or to manage and supervise the corporation’s overall affairs, and agents delegated full authority by such persons, it is difficult to regard the punishment of a corporation that is only negligent with the same statutory punishment as the principal offender who acted intentionally as an imposition of punishment proportionate to each party’s responsibility (see Constitutional Court 2008HEONGA14, decided on July 30, 2009, Collection of Cases 21-2, 77, 89-94).\\n\\nc. Interim conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the part concerning agents, employees, or other workers who are in a position to determine the corporation’s management policy or major intentions or to manage and supervise the corporation’s overall affairs, or agents delegated full authority by such persons, among the agents, employees, or other workers prescribed by the provisions subject to review in this case, does not violate the Constitution, whereas the part concerning other workers does violate the Constitution.\\n\\n7. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Jo Dae-hyeon\\n\\nHuman beings are autonomous actors who think and judge for themselves, regulate their own conduct, and bear responsibility. All persons, as autonomous actors with dignity and value, are responsible only for their own conduct, are not punished for the conduct of others, and are not punished for causes for which they are not responsible (the principle of responsibility).\\n\\nA corporation, too, has an independent subjectivity distinct from its members (officers and employees) and acts autonomously, and since a corporation must also comply with the legal order, it is proper that a corporation, as an autonomous actor, bears responsibility for its business activities in accordance with the principle of responsibility. Because a corporation systematically utilizes the abilities of many persons, the scope, scale, and influence of its activities may surpass the limits of individual activity, and as a result the sphere of corporate activity has spread to all areas of modern society. Accordingly, unlawful acts in relation to corporate business have become more frequent and the scale of damage has become large, so the need to punish corporations is also increasing. If an unlawful act in relation to corporate business is based on the intention of the corporation (its business policy), it is necessary to regard the corporation itself as the offender and punish it, and even where the duty to supervise officers and employees has been neglected, corresponding sanctions are necessary.\\n\\nHowever, punishing the corporation together with its officers and employees for their unlawful acts can be recognized only where the business activities of the officers and employees can be regarded as acts of the corporation, or where the corporation has a duty to direct and supervise the officers and employees. Since the corporation’s duty to direct and supervise its officers and employees is recognized only where the officers and employees are engaged in the corporation’s business, criminal punishment of the corporation for an unlawful act committed by its officers and employees even when such unlawful act is unrelated to the corporation’s business cannot but be regarded as violating the principle of responsibility.\\n\\nWhere the officers and employees of a corporation commit an unlawful act in relation to the corporation’s business, it can be said that the corporation used the conduct of the officers and employees to commit the unlawful act, or that it failed to prevent the unlawful act in the course of business because it did not fulfill its duty to direct and supervise the officers and employees. Therefore, punishing the corporation together with the officers and employees for their unlawful acts cannot easily be said to violate the principle of responsibility. However, where the officers and employees of a corporation commit an unlawful act unrelated to the corporation’s business, the corporation cannot be regarded as owing a duty to direct and supervise the officers and employees, and in such a case, punishing the corporation together with the officers and employees would be contrary to the principle of responsibility and thus unconstitutional.\\n\\nYet all of the provisions subject to review in this case provide that where officers and employees of a corporation commit an unlawful act in relation to the corporation’s business, the corporation shall also be punished by a fine. Since this punishes the corporation where it failed to prevent the unlawful act in the course of business because it did not fulfill its duty to direct and supervise the officers and employees, it is difficult to see it as contrary to the principle of responsibility.\\n\\nAs noted above, although the provisions subject to review in this case were later amended so that the corporation is not punished where it has not neglected reasonable care and supervision to prevent the unlawful act in the course of business by officers and employees, such amendment merely made clear that punishment is imposed only where the corporation is negligent in direction and supervision with respect to the unlawful act in the course of business by officers and employees. Even if such statutory amendment had not been made, attributing responsibility to the corporation only for unlawful acts in relation to the corporation’s business among the unlawful acts of officers and employees would not be contrary to responsibility.\\n\\n8. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Lee Dong-heub\\n\\nI think that the provisions subject to review in this case are not contrary to the principle of responsibility that “punishment cannot be imposed on a person without responsibility,” and therefore are not contrary to the Constitution, for the following reasons.\\n\\nAs today’s industrial society becomes highly organized, corporate activities and social influence increase, and the resulting anti-social infringements of legal interests increase as well, so stronger sanctions are required. In such cases, however, merely punishing the corporate employee who actually committed the violation makes it difficult to expect a crime-prevention effect, and because social blame is directly directed at the corporation, which is the subject to which the benefits arising from the employee’s violation accrue, a direct sanction against the corporation, in addition to the violating employee, is necessary. In addition, such violations are, in most cases, committed for the benefit of the corporation rather than solely for the individual benefit of the employee or due to the employee’s lack of ethics; in fact, they often result from tacit instructions, condonation, or neglect by a corporate organ or middle manager, or from a failure in appointment or supervision over the relevant employee. Yet, due to the complex and decentralized structure of corporate business, it is difficult to clearly identify where responsibility lies, and more broadly, such violations may be seen as resulting from defects in the corporate operating system or decision-making structure that are insufficient to supervise the prevention of such violations. Therefore, it is appropriate that the corporation also bear direct criminal responsibility for them.\\n\\nConsidering the special nature of corporate crimes and the need to punish corporations, recent arguments have also been advanced that independent criminal responsibility should be recognized for corporations regardless of the actor, or that various effective sanctioning measures should be established for corporations in addition to fines. In the United States, where the history of criminal punishment for corporate crimes is long, the mainstream case law position regarding dual punishment provisions for corporate employers is that, where (1) there is a negligent or intentional violation by an employee of the corporation, (2) the violation falls within the scope related to business, and (3) the act was done for the benefit of the corporation, the corporation is directly subjected to punishment on the basis of so-called respondeat superior.\\n\\nMeanwhile, in relation to dual punishment provisions for corporate employers and the principle of responsibility, the Supreme Court has held that “in light of the principle of self-responsibility in punishment, it is reasonable to view the above dual punishment provision as applicable only where the corporation has neglected a considerable duty of care or supervision in relation to the business in which the violation occurred, and …” (Supreme Court Decision 2009DO5824 rendered on February 25, 2010), and that “the purpose is to invigorate the effectiveness of regulation by strongly presuming fault, even if not strict no-fault liability, in the case of corporations or individuals, etc. as employers, while also imposing the burden of proof on the employer …” (Supreme Court Decision 2005DO2733 rendered on June 9, 2005). Thus, it is reasonable to understand that the Supreme Court has consistently held that the liability of a corporate employer is based on negligence in appointment and supervision of employees, while presuming such negligence in relation to the employees’ violation.\\n\\nIn Japan, which, like us, has dual punishment provisions for punishing employers in special administrative criminal statutes, the prevailing view and the position of the Supreme Court regarding dual punishment provisions for corporate employers are that, with respect to the violations of their agents, employees, or other workers, the existence of negligence is presumed in that, as a corporate employer, the person failed to exercise the necessary care to prevent unlawful acts, such as appointment, supervision, and other measures for the actor, and that, unless the corporation proves that it exercised such care, it cannot be exempted from criminal responsibility.\\n\\nExamining the matter, the provisions subject to review in this case provide that if an employee, etc. of a corporation commits a violation in relation to the business of the corporation, a fine under the relevant Article shall also be imposed on the corporation. Even by the wording, the scope of the corporation falling under the elements of the offense does not include corporations entirely unrelated to the criminal act of the employee, but is limited to cases where there is a “violation” by an employee in relation to the “business” of the relevant corporation. Thus, “fault in appointment and supervision of employees by the corporate employer” can be inferred as a subjective element of the offense connecting the corporation’s “business” and the employee’s “violation.” Since such a subjective element can be construed as above even if not expressly stated in the text, the provisions subject to review in this case do not violate the principle of responsibility in punishment when interpreted on that premise.\\n\\nTherefore, even though the wording of the provisions subject to review in this case does not expressly state “fault in appointment and supervision of employees of the corporation or other grounds for attribution,” it is within the scope of textual interpretation to construe them as punishing only where such grounds for attribution exist, and it is judged that such construction is permissible under a constitutional interpretation of statutes (see Constitutional Court 2008HEONGA14, decided on July 30, 2009, Collection of Cases 21-2, 77, 94-96).\\n\\nAccordingly, the provisions subject to review in this case cannot be regarded as violating the principle of responsibility that “punishment cannot be imposed on a person without responsibility.”"}

Outline of the Case\\nGang○Cheol, the representative director of Co., Ltd. ○○ C&C, was indicted on the following facts charged, received a summary order imposing a fine of 3,000,000 won from the Seoul Northern District Court, filed a request for a formal trial, and the case (Seoul Northern District Court 2012GODAN2703) is pending.\\n“The Defendant obtained an order for the construction of a new factory of Co., Ltd. ○○ located at Lot 1, Block A4, ○○ Complex, ○○-dong, Deokjin-gu, Jeonju-si, from Co., Ltd. ○○, and subcontracted the structural frame, plastering, civil engineering, and equipment/firefighting portions to Gim○Cheon. Gim○Cheon, however, did not pay the total wages of 25,316,669 won of Choe○Ho, who worked at the above construction site from 2010. 11. 22. to 2011. 6. 30., within 14 days from the date of retirement, which was the date on which the ground for payment arose, without any agreement with Choe○Ho to extend the payment due date; thus, although the Defendant, as the immediate contractor, was jointly and severally liable with Gim○Cheon to pay the total wages of 25,316,669 won of the worker Choe○Ho employed by Gim○Cheon, he failed to perform such obligation.”\\nThe petitioning court, stating that there are substantial grounds to recognize that the portion concerning Article 44-2(1) in Article 109(1) of the Labor Standards Act violates the principle of clarity, etc., and is unconstitutional, made this ex officio constitutional review reference on 2013. 2. 21.\\n2. Object of Review\\nThe object of review in this case is whether the portion concerning Article 44-2(1) of the former Labor Standards Act (amended by Act No. 8561 of July 27, 2007, and before amendment by Act No. 10719 of May 24, 2011) in Article 109(1) of the Labor Standards Act (amended by Act No. 8561 of July 27, 2007) (hereinafter referred to as “the statutory provision at issue”) is unconstitutional. The contents of the provision under review and the related provisions are as follows.\\n[Provision under Review]\\nLabor Standards Act (amended by Act No. 8561 of July 27, 2007)\\nArticle 109 (Penalties) ① Any person who violates Article 36, Article 43, Article 44, Article 44-2, Article 46, Article 56, Article 65, or Article 72 shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 3 years or by a fine not exceeding 20,000,000 won.\\n[Related Provisions]\\nLabor Standards Act (wholly amended by Act No. 8372 of April 11, 2007)\\nArticle 36 (Settlement of Money and Valuables) When a worker dies or retires, the employer shall pay wages, compensation, and all other money and valuables within 14 days from the time the grounds for payment arise. Provided, That where special circumstances exist, the due date may be extended by agreement between the parties.\\nArticle 43 (Payment of Wages) ② Wages shall be paid on a fixed date at least once every month. Provided, That this shall not apply to wages, allowances, or other payments equivalent thereto that are paid temporarily, or to wages prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\nFormer Labor Standards Act (amended by Act No. 8561 of July 27, 2007, and before amendment by Act No. 10719 of May 24, 2011)\\nArticle 44-2 (Joint and Several Liability for Wage Payment in the Construction Industry) ① Where, in the construction industry, there are two or more tiers of contracts for work under Article 2, item 8, of the Framework Act on the Construction Industry (hereinafter referred to as “construction contract”), and where a subcontractor who is not a construction business operator under Article 2, item 5, of the same Act fails to pay wages (limited to wages arising from the relevant construction work) to the workers employed by him or her, the immediate contractor shall be liable jointly and severally with the subcontractor for the payment of the wages of the workers employed by the subcontractor.\\nLabor Standards Act (amended by Act No. 8561 of July 27, 2007)\\nArticle 109 (Penalties) ② No prosecution may be instituted, contrary to the explicit intention of the victim, against a person who violates Article 36, Article 43, Article 44, Article 44-2, Article 46, or Article 56.\\nFormer Framework Act on the Construction Industry (amended by Act No. 8477 of May 17, 2007, and before amendment by Act No. 10719 of May 24, 2011)\\nArticle 2 (Definitions) The terms used in this Act are defined as follows:\\n5. “Construction business operator” means a person who carries on the construction business after registration, etc. pursuant to this Act or other Acts.\\n8. “Contract for work” means a contract, regardless of whether it is called a prime contract, subcontract, entrustment, or otherwise, under which one party agrees to complete construction work and the other party agrees to pay consideration for the result of the work.\\nFormer Framework Act on the Construction Industry (amended by Act No. 5965 of April 15, 1999, and before amendment by Act No. 10719 of May 24, 2011)\\nArticle 25 (Restriction on Qualifications of Contractors, etc.) ① An ordering party or contractor shall award a contract or subcontract to a construction business operator registered in an industry corresponding to the contents of the construction work.\\n3. Summary of the Grounds for the Constitutional Reference by the Petitioning Court\\nThe statutory provision at issue violates the principle of clarity because it is unclear whether “where a subcontractor fails to pay wages to the workers employed by him or her,” which is the requirement for the occurrence of the immediate contractor’s joint and several liability, includes cases where the subcontractor fails to pay wages within 14 days from the worker’s death or retirement, and because it is unclear by when the immediate contractor’s joint and several liability must be performed.\\nThe statutory provision at issue unconditionally imposes criminal liability on the immediate contractor, without inquiring whether the immediate contractor recognized the worker’s death or retirement or the amount of wages to be paid, or the timing of such recognition, where the worker employed by the subcontractor dies or retires and the wages are not paid within 14 days from such death or retirement; therefore, it violates the principle of self-responsibility or the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n4. Decision\\nA. Whether it violates the principle of clarity under the principle of legality in criminal law\\n(1) The principle of legality in criminal law, guaranteed through Articles 12 and 13 of the Constitution, means that crimes and punishments must be prescribed by law, and the principle of clarity derived from such principle of legality in criminal law requires that the constituent elements be clearly prescribed so that anyone can foresee what conduct the law intends to punish and what the punishment therefor will be, and thereby determine his or her own conduct accordingly. However, even though the constituent elements of a penal provision must be clear, this does not mean that all constituent elements must be defined by simple descriptive concepts; rather, even if somewhat broad concepts requiring supplementary interpretation by judges are used, if, by the ordinary method of interpretation, the provision is so framed that a person of sound common sense and ordinary legal sentiment can ascertain the protected legal interest of the penal provision and the prohibited conduct, etc., it is not contrary to the clarity required by the Constitution for penal provisions. And whether foreseeability exists with respect to a penal provision should not be determined only by considering the particular provision alone, but by comprehensively and systematically examining all relevant statutory provisions in an organic manner, and should be reviewed concretely and individually according to the nature of each statute at issue (Constitutional Court 2011. 10. 25. 2010HEONGA29).\\n(2) Considering that the Labor Standards Act imposes on the employer the duty to pay wages on a fixed date at least once every month (main clause of Article 43(2)) and the duty to pay wages within 14 days from the time the ground for payment arises when the worker dies or retires (main clause of Article 36), and punishes the non-performance of both duties (Article 109(1)), these duties to pay wages each have independent significance, and since, in cases where the employer, who is the subcontractor, fails to perform them, there is no difference in the necessity of recognizing the immediate contractor’s joint and several liability in order to promote the stability of the livelihoods of workers and their families, “where a subcontractor fails to pay wages to the workers employed by him or her” in the statutory provision at issue is interpreted to include both cases where the subcontractor fails to pay wages on the fixed date set each month and thereby fails to perform the duty under the main clause of Article 43(2) of the Labor Standards Act, and cases where, although the worker has died or retired, wages are not paid within 14 days from the time the ground for payment arises and thereby the duty under the main clause of Article 36 of the Labor Standards Act is not performed.\\nAlso, considering that the statutory provision at issue imposes on the immediate contractor joint and several liability with the subcontractor for wage payment when the subcontractor fails to pay wages to the workers, the immediate contractor’s liability under the statutory provision at issue means that, where the subcontractor’s duty to pay wages is not performed, the immediate contractor, jointly and severally with the subcontractor, bears the duty to pay wages with the same content as the subcontractor’s duty, and such immediate contractor’s duty to pay wages arises respectively when the subcontractor fails to pay wages on the fixed date set each month and when, although the worker has died or retired, wages are not paid within 14 days from the time the ground for payment arises, and must be performed immediately upon arrival of the time for performance.\\nMeanwhile, considering that, for a subcontractor’s failure to perform the duty to pay wages to constitute the crime under Article 109(1) and Article 36 of the Labor Standards Act or the crime under Article 109(1) and Article 43(2) of the Labor Standards Act, the subcontractor must have intent (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DO14693, decided October 27, 2011), even where the immediate contractor’s duty to pay wages, which arises on the premise that the subcontractor failed to perform the duty to pay wages, is not performed pursuant to the statutory provision at issue, for such immediate contractor’s non-performance to be punished under the statutory provision at issue, it is required that the immediate contractor had intent with respect thereto, that is, awareness of the existence of the duty to pay wages borne by him or her.\\nAs such, since a person of sound common sense and ordinary legal sentiment can sufficiently know in what cases the immediate contractor is punished under the statutory provision at issue, the statutory provision at issue cannot be seen as violating the principle of clarity under the principle of legality in criminal law.\\nB. Whether it violates the principle of self-responsibility\\n(1) The right of self-determination or general freedom of action derived from the right to pursue happiness prescribed by Article 10 of the Constitution presupposes respect for a rational and responsible person’s decisions and choices regarding his or her own fate, while assuming that he or she bears responsibility therefor on his or her own (Constitutional Court 2011. 9. 29. 2010HEONMA68). As the limiting logic of such right of self-determination, the principle of self-responsibility functions as the basis for bearing responsibility, while at the same time functioning as the principle of delimitation of responsibility, meaning that one is not responsible for what one did not decide or could not decide, and that the scope of responsibility is limited to the results of one’s own decisions or to portions causally related thereto (Constitutional Court 2013. 5. 30. 2012HEONBA195).\\n(2) The statutory provision at issue imposes on the immediate contractor the duty to pay wages jointly and severally with the subcontractor when the subcontractor fails to perform the duty to pay wages, and punishes the immediate contractor’s failure to perform such duty to pay wages. Thus, punishing the immediate contractor under the statutory provision at issue is to hold the immediate contractor responsible for the failure to perform the duty to pay wages borne by the immediate contractor himself or herself, and not to hold him or her responsible for another person’s failure to perform a duty, such as that of the subcontractor.\\nIn addition, the statutory provision at issue imposes on the immediate contractor, who is not the employer, the duty to pay wages jointly and severally with the subcontractor, who is the employer, and provides that the immediate contractor shall be punished if he or she knowingly fails to perform such duty immediately, without granting any grace period for performance of the duty. This is to hold the immediate contractor responsible, for the fault of having caused an abstract risk of non-performance of the subcontractor’s duty to pay wages by committing an unlawful act in construction contracting, namely, subcontracting construction work to a person whose construction business registration has not been made and whose financial capacity, etc. for the construction work has not been verified, and to hold him or her responsible when such risk materializes because the subcontractor actually fails to perform the duty to pay wages. And even where the immediate contractor’s failure to perform the duty to pay wages falls within the constituent elements of the statutory provision at issue, the immediate contractor may also be exempted from punishment if he or she performs the duty to pay wages before the judgment of the first instance is rendered and the worker’s side’s intention not to wish for the immediate contractor’s punishment is confirmed.\\nTherefore, it cannot be seen that the statutory provision at issue violates the principle of self-responsibility by imposing on the immediate contractor the duty to pay wages jointly and severally with the subcontractor and punishing the immediate contractor’s non-performance of such duty without granting a separate grace period for performance of the duty, because it would hold the immediate contractor responsible for what he or she did not decide or could not decide, or impose responsibility beyond the scope of the immediate contractor’s responsibility.\\nC. Whether it violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction\\n(1) The issue of what conduct is to be defined as a crime and how it is to be punished, namely, the establishment of crimes and the selection of the type and scope of statutory punishment, is a matter to be determined by the legislature by comprehensively considering not only the social maliciousness of the act, the nature of the crime, and the protected legal interest, but also various factors such as our history and culture, the circumstances at the time of legislation, the general public’s values and legal sentiment, and the criminal policy aspect for crime prevention; this is an area in which broad legislative discretion should be recognized (Constitutional Court 2012. 8. 23. 2011HEONGA22).\\n(2) The statutory provision at issue not only imposes on the immediate contractor the duty to pay wages jointly and severally with the subcontractor, but further provides that the immediate contractor’s failure to perform such duty shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 3 years or by a fine not exceeding 20,000,000 won.\\nPunishing the immediate contractor’s failure to perform the duty to pay wages compels the immediate contractor to pay wages when the subcontractor has not paid wages, and is a suitable means for achieving the legitimate legislative purpose because it is intended to secure the payment of wages, which are the basic means of livelihood for workers and their families, and thereby promote the stability of their lives.\\nMeanwhile, in the reality of construction contracting relationships in which immediate contractors mainly subcontract construction work to persons whose construction business registration has not been made for economic purposes, it cannot be said that the legislative purpose of the statutory provision at issue can be sufficiently achieved merely by imposing no sanction on the immediate contractor’s failure to perform the duty to pay wages, or by imposing only administrative sanctions such as administrative fines; therefore, punishing the failure to perform the immediate contractor’s duty to pay wages cannot be said to be an excessive regulation beyond the scope necessary to achieve the legislative purpose. And the statutory provision at issue places no restriction on the minimum punishment, thereby allowing a punishment commensurate with the actor’s responsibility to be imposed.\\nAlso, the disadvantage suffered by a person who is criminally punished under the statutory provision at issue cannot be said to be greater than the public interest achieved through the statutory provision at issue.\\nTherefore, it cannot be seen that the statutory provision at issue violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n5. Conclusion\\nSince the statutory provision at issue does not violate the Constitution, the decision is made as ordered, by the unanimous opinion of all Justices involved."}

{"[2013HEONGA15]": "1. Summary of the Case and Subject Matter of Adjudication  \\na. Summary of the Case  \\n(1) The defendant corporation in the underlying case, Stock Company ○○, is the shipowner of the tugboat ○○, a vessel registered in Seosan City, and the barge □□, a barge for aggregate extraction; and it was indicted on the following charge: “Kim ○-cheol, the master of the above vessels, in connection with the business of the defendant, on or about February 27, 2009, on or about March 9, 2009, and on or about March 10, 2009, navigated the □□ vessel loaded with aggregate, etc. so as to exceed the load line from Seongap Cadastral Parcel No. 49 in Wonbuk-myeon, Taean-gun, Chungcheongnam-do, to the unloading site located at San 1-209, Gagok-ri, Songsan-myeon, Dangjin-gun, Chungcheongnam-do, and on or about March 25, 2009, navigated the □□ vessel loaded with aggregate, etc. so as to exceed the load line from the dredging area of the Pyeongtaek-Dangjin Harbor route located in Pyeongtaek City to the above unloading site, thereby transporting cargo in excess of the load line.” The case is currently pending trial (Daejeon District Court Seosan Branch 2009GODAN548).  \\n(2) On April 22, 2013, the referring court, finding substantial grounds to conclude that the portion of Article 84(2) of the former Ship Safety Act (as amended by Act No. 8221 on January 3, 2007, and before amendment by Act No. 9871 on December 29, 2009) stating that “if the master has committed an act in violation of paragraph (1) in connection with the business of the shipowner, the shipowner shall also be punished by the fine under the same paragraph” is contrary to the Constitution, referred this constitutional review ex officio.  \\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Adjudication  \\nThe subject matter of this case is whether the portion of Article 84(2) of the former Ship Safety Act (as amended by Act No. 8221 on January 3, 2007, and before amendment by Act No. 9871 on December 29, 2009) stating that “if the master has committed an act in violation of paragraph (1) in connection with the business of the shipowner, the shipowner shall also be punished by the fine under the same paragraph” (hereinafter referred to as the “statutory provision at issue”) is contrary to the Constitution; and the text of the provision subject to review (the underlined portion below) and the related provisions are as follows.  \\n\\n[Provision Subject to Review]  \\nFormer Ship Safety Act (as amended by Act No. 8221 on January 3, 2007, and before amendment by Act No. 9871 on December 29, 2009)  \\nArticle 84 (Penal Provisions)  \\n(2) When the master has committed an act in violation of paragraph (1) in connection with the business of the shipowner, the shipowner shall also be punished by the fine under the same paragraph, in addition to punishing the master.  \\n\\n[Related Provisions]  \\nShip Safety Act (as amended by Act No. 8221 on January 3, 2007)  \\nArticle 84 (Penal Provisions)  \\n(1) When a shipowner, master, or ship officer commits any of the following acts, they shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 1 year or by a fine not exceeding 10,000,000 won.  \\n9. When passengers or cargo are transported in excess of the load line in violation of the provisions of Article 27(2)  \\n\\nFormer Ship Safety Act (as amended by Act No. 8852 on February 29, 2008, and before amendment by Act No. 11690 on March 23, 2013)  \\nArticle 27 (Marking of Load Line, etc.)  \\n(1) A shipowner falling under any of the following subparagraphs shall mark the load line in accordance with the standards prescribed and publicly notified by the Minister of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs: Provided, That for submersible vessels and other vessels prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs, the marking of the load line may be omitted.  \\n1. Vessels engaged in international voyages  \\n2. Vessels whose length, determined by the method prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs (hereinafter referred to as “vessel length”), is at least 12 meters  \\n3. Vessels with a vessel length of less than 12 meters that fall under any of the following items  \\na. Passenger vessels  \\nb. Vessels transporting dangerous goods in bulk in accordance with the provisions of Article 41  \\n(2) No person shall transport passengers or cargo in excess of the load line marked pursuant to paragraph (1).  \\n\\n2. Summary of the Reasons for the Constitutional Referral by the Referring Court  \\nThe statutory provision at issue imposes punishment on another person’s crime without inquiring into whether that person bears responsibility therefor; accordingly, it is contrary to the principle of liability derived from the principle of a rule-of-law state and the principle of nulla poena sine lege.  \\n\\n3. Decision  \\na. The statutory provision at issue provides that, if a master employed by a shipowner has committed an act in violation, the shipowner shall immediately be subject, as well, to the punishment prescribed for the master in the penal provision.  \\nIn other words, the statutory provision at issue does not prescribe, as a requirement for punishing the shipowner, whether the shipowner participated in the master’s criminal act or whether the shipowner breached any duty of care to supervise the master’s conduct; nor does it otherwise prescribe any possibility for the shipowner to be exempted from liability. Ultimately, if the master commits a certain act, the shipowner is punished in the same manner as the master without any inquiry whatsoever into whether the shipowner is at fault for the master’s crime.  \\n\\nb. Punishment, as a sanction for crime, is, in its essence, condemnation of conduct negatively evaluated by the legal order.  \\nEven if a result negatively evaluated by the legal order has occurred, if the occurrence of such result is not attributable to anyone’s fault, punishment may not be imposed on anyone merely because a negative result has occurred.  \\nThus, the principle of liability in relation to punishment, namely that “punishment cannot be imposed on one who bears no responsibility,” is a basic principle of criminal law and is at the same time a principle inherent in the constitutional principle of a rule-of-law state and a principle derived from the purport of Article 10 of the Constitution.  \\nHowever, under the statutory provision at issue, even where the shipowner has exercised due care in selection and supervision in relation to the master’s violation and is without fault, punishment must nevertheless be imposed on the shipowner.  \\nIn this way, the statutory provision at issue, without at all prescribing the shipowner’s decision-making and conduct structure that forms the basis for condemnation concerning the master’s criminal act, that is, the shipowner’s independent responsibility for the result of the act committed by the master, imposes criminal punishment on the shipowner merely because the master employed by the shipowner committed a criminal act in connection with the business; this constitutes imposing punishment for another person’s crime without inquiring into whether that person bears responsibility therefor, and therefore contravenes the principle of liability derived from the constitutional principle of a rule-of-law state and the principle of nulla poena sine lege (see Constitutional Court 2008HEONGA10, decided on July 30, 2009, Constitutional Court Reports 21-2(I), 64).  \\n\\n4. Conclusion  \\nAccordingly, since the statutory provision at issue is contrary to the Constitution, the Court unanimously decides as stated in the Disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the principle prohibiting retroactive legislation is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: A provision of the former Special Act on the Improvement of Air Quality in the Seoul Metropolitan Area, which requires an owner operating a specific diesel vehicle equipped with an emission reduction device to return the emission reduction device when, after the amendment of the provision, a separate factual requirement of "cancellation of vehicle registration for scrapping or export, etc." is satisfied, constitutes non-genuine retroactive legislation.
B: A provision of the Commercial Building Lease Protection Act that extended the period for a commercial building tenant to exercise the right to demand contract renewal from 5 years to 10 years, and a supplementary provision of the same Act providing that this amended provision applies to leases renewed after the enforcement of the amended Act even if the lease was concluded before the enforcement of the amended Act, constitute genuine retroactive legislation and violate the principle prohibiting retroactive legislation.
C: A supplementary provision of the former Government Employees Pension Act that provides that, except in cases of "negligence unrelated to official duties" and "negligence while following a lawful official order of a superior officer to whom the official belongs," if a public official is sentenced during service to imprisonment without labor or heavier punishment for a cause arising during service, retirement benefits, etc. shall be reduced, and that the amended provision applies from the following year, does not constitute genuine retroactive legislation.
D: Among the ordinances of the United States Army Military Government in Korea promulgated on 1945. 9. 25. and 1945. 12. 6., respectively, the provision that rendered wholly void all transactions concluded with respect to property owned by Japanese nationals after 1945. 8. 9., and the provision that caused the property subject thereto to belong wholly to the United States Army Military Government in Korea retroactively as of 1945. 9. 25., both fall within exceptions to the principle prohibiting retroactive legislation and thus do not violate the Constitution.
E: A supplementary provision of the Criminal Act, which applies retroactively to the detriment of a person sentenced to a fine of at least KRW 100 million by making the lower limit of the term of detention in a workhouse more severe, from the first indictment filed after the effective date, violates the principle of non-retroactivity of punishment.
label: B
