On Point 1\\n\\nThe “Act on the Restoration of Honor and Compensation, etc. for Persons Related to the Democratization Movement” (hereinafter the “Act”), enacted for the purpose of restoring honor and providing compensation to persons sacrificed in connection with the democratization movement and their surviving family members, defines “Democratization Movement” in Article 2(1), while defining in the main text of Article 2(2) that “persons related to the democratization movement (hereinafter referred to as ‘related persons’)” means persons who fall under any one of the following items and who have been deliberated and decided by the “Deliberation Committee for the Restoration of Honor and Compensation for Persons Related to the Democratization Movement” (hereinafter the “Committee”) pursuant to Article 4, and the items in Article 2(2) list as such persons “(a) a person who died or went missing in connection with the democratization movement, (b) a person who suffered injury in connection with the democratization movement, (c) a person who was recognized as having suffered from a disease prescribed by Presidential Decree due to the democratization movement or as having died from its aftereffects, and (d) a person who received a conviction, dismissal from office, or academic disciplinary action on account of the democratization movement.”\\n\\nFurthermore, Articles 4 and following of the Act establish the Committee under the Prime Minister in order to deliberate and decide on restoration of honor and compensation payments, etc. for related persons and their surviving family members, and assign to the Committee the functions of deliberating and deciding whether persons fall under related persons and their surviving family members (hereinafter “related persons, etc.”), determining the disability grades of related injured persons, deliberating and deciding on and paying compensation payments, etc. for related persons, etc., and deliberating and deciding on matters necessary for the restoration of honor of related persons, etc. Articles 10, 11, 13, etc. of the Act further provide procedural rules concerning payment of compensation payments, medical aid payments, livelihood support payments (hereinafter “compensation payments, etc.”) by the Committee: a person seeking to receive compensation payments, etc. as a related person, etc. must apply to the Committee for payment thereof; the Committee must determine whether and in what amount the compensation payments, etc. are to be paid within 90 days from the date it receives the application; and a related person, etc. who is dissatisfied with the Committee’s determination may apply to the Committee for reconsideration within 30 days from the date the written determination is served.\\n\\nIn light of the purpose and content of the foregoing provisions, the items of Article 2(2) of the Act merely abstractly prescribe types of harm connected with the democratization movement; therefore, even when Article 2(1), which defines Democratization Movement, is taken into account, those provisions alone cannot be said to immediately determine the recipients of compensation payments, etc. under the Act, and only after deliberation and decision by the Committee can a person be finally determined to be a recipient of compensation payments, etc. Accordingly, since such a decision by the Committee constitutes an administrative disposition that directly affects the rights and obligations of the people, if, in response to an application seeking payment of compensation payments, etc. as a related person, etc., the Committee renders a decision dismissing the payment of compensation payments, etc. by not recognizing all or part of the requirements for related-person status, the applicant may file a suit against the Committee seeking revocation of that decision and thereby become a person eligible to receive compensation payments, etc.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 17 of the Act merely provides that “a lawsuit concerning the payment of compensation payments, etc. under this Act may be filed only after a decision by the Committee to pay or dismiss compensation payments, etc. has been made; however, this shall not apply where 90 days have elapsed from the date an application for payment of compensation payments, etc. was filed,” but it does not prescribe the form of the lawsuit concerning payment of compensation payments, etc. However, since the lawsuit concerning payment of compensation payments, etc. referred to in the first sentence of the above provision means a lawsuit seeking to challenge a decision by the Committee dismissing payment in whole or in part with respect to an application for payment of compensation payments, etc., it should be understood to mean the revocation action discussed above. Although the latter sentence permits the filing of such a lawsuit without going through that decision when 90 days have elapsed from the date an application for payment of compensation payments, etc. was filed, this is merely construed as having the purport of providing that, for the prompt relief of rights of related persons, etc., where a decision on whether to pay compensation payments, etc. has not been received within that period, one may regard there as having been a decision refusing payment and immediately file a revocation action against the Committee in court; it cannot be construed as meaning that the provision restricts a revocation action seeking revocation of a disposition concerning payment of compensation payments, etc., or that it permits a person who has not been determined by the Committee to be a related person, etc. to directly file an action for performance against the State seeking payment of compensation payments, etc.\\n\\nIn the same vein, the court below, having found that the instant action, in which the Plaintiff sought revocation of the disposition by which the Committee partially dismissed the application for payment of compensation payments, etc., was lawful, and having rejected the Defendant’s defense on the merits that the Plaintiff should have sought performance of payment of compensation payments against the State, was correct, and there is no illegality of misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the dispositive nature of the Committee’s decision or the form of litigation, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe judgment cited in the grounds of appeal does not concern the interpretation or application of the law applicable to this case, and therefore cannot be invoked to assert that the lower court judgment violated precedent.\\n\\n2. On Point 2\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the first-instance judgment cited by the court below, the deceased, while attending Seoul National University, had been wanted for leading protests opposing military training and resisting the authoritarian regime and for possessing subversive leaflets related to the National Democratic Youth and Students Federation Incident, and was arrested by investigative authorities around 1972; at that time, the investigative authorities inflicted torture upon the deceased, including beating him en masse, with the intent of fabricating him as a spy and eliciting a confession, as a result of which four of the deceased’s teeth, including the front teeth and molars, were broken. Thereafter, the deceased not only lost weight to such an extent that even his friends could not recognize him, but also developed symptoms such as convulsions of the facial muscles and generalized paralysis—such as the sudden twisting of the limbs, opening of the mouth, and dislocation of the jaw downward while walking or speaking—so that he could not walk properly and would often collapse in the street, and he died on 1993. 10. 8. If so, the deceased falls under Article 2(2)(b) of the Act, i.e., “a person who suffered injury in connection with the democratization movement,” as sought by the Plaintiff, and not only loss of teeth but also symptoms such as generalized paralysis constitute injuries eligible for compensation payments, etc.\\n\\nThe lower court’s determination to the same effect was correct, and there is no illegality of misapprehending the legal doctrine. The grounds of appeal asserting that the lower court judgment is unlawful for misapprehending the legal doctrine while disputing the lower court’s weighing of evidence and fact-finding do not constitute valid grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are assessed against the losing party, and judgment is rendered as ordered.\\n\\nIn this judgment, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous except for the dissenting opinions of Justice Kim Hwang-sik, Justice Kim Ji-hyung, and Justice Lee Hong-hoon on the determination with respect to Point 1 of the grounds for appeal; there is a supplementary opinion by Justice Jeon Su-an on the majority opinion and a supplementary opinion by Justice Lee Hong-hoon on the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n4. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Kim Hwang-sik, Justice Kim Ji-hyung, and Justice Lee Hong-hoon\\n\\na. The majority opinion held, in substance, that the right to receive compensation payments, etc. prescribed by the Act does not arise directly by virtue of the Act’s provisions but arises only upon a decision from the Committee that one is a related person, etc. entitled to receive compensation payments, etc. under the Act; therefore, such a decision by the Committee constitutes an administrative disposition that directly affects the rights and obligations of the people, and thus, where a person applied to receive compensation payments, etc. but the Committee rendered a decision dismissing payment in whole or in part because it did not recognize all or part of the requirements for related-person status, the applicant must obtain relief in the form of an appeal litigation against the Committee seeking revocation of that decision.\\n\\nHowever, we cannot agree with such a view of the majority opinion, and we believe that in such a case the applicant should file a party litigation against the State seeking payment of compensation payments, etc. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) First of all, the interpretation should faithfully adhere to the text of Article 17 of the Act.\\n\\nArticle 17(1) of the Act, under the heading [Doctrine of Prior Determination], provides: “A lawsuit concerning the payment of compensation payments, etc. under this Act may be filed only after a decision by the Committee to pay or dismiss compensation payments, etc. has been made. Provided, however, that this shall not apply where 90 days have elapsed from the date an application for payment of compensation payments, etc. was filed.”\\n\\nThus, Article 17(1) of the Act uses the expression “a lawsuit concerning the payment of compensation payments, etc.” in its first sentence. The majority opinion takes the view that the meaning of the above wording should be understood as “a lawsuit seeking revocation of the Committee’s decision to pay or dismiss compensation payments, etc.” However, if this is directly applied to the statutory text, the first sentence of Article 17(1) would be intended to provide that “a lawsuit seeking revocation of the Committee’s decision to pay or dismiss compensation payments, etc. under this Act may be filed only after a decision by the Committee to pay or dismiss compensation payments, etc. has been made,” which is an extremely awkward provision. If the legislature had intended to regulate such content through the above article, its purport would amount to no more than the meaning that “appeal litigation may be filed only after the administrative disposition that is its object has been made.”\\n\\nI do not think the legislature enacted this provision merely to confirm such an obvious proposition. It is not difficult to infer that the fact that Article 17 is explicitly labeled [Doctrine of Prior Determination] from the title itself indicates that it was intended to set forth a meaning different from mere confirmation. If one considers that the legislature would have had no reason to include such a meaningless provision in Article 17, the meaning of the “lawsuit concerning the payment of compensation payments, etc.” mentioned in that provision can only be understood as “a lawsuit seeking payment of compensation payments, etc.”\\n\\nBy way of reference, the former State Compensation Act (as in force before its full amendment by Act No. 6310 on 2000. 12. 29, hereinafter the same) also provided in the first sentence of Article 9 that “a lawsuit for damages under this Act may be filed only after a decision to pay or dismiss compensation by the Compensation Deliberation Council has been made,” thereby establishing a doctrine of prior compensation determination. However, as to the meaning of this provision, the Supreme Court has already held that “going through the decision of the Compensation Deliberation Council referred to in the above provision is merely a prerequisite before filing a claim for state compensation, and therefore the decision of the Compensation Deliberation Council cannot be said to be an administrative disposition” (see Supreme Court Decision 80NU317 rendered on 1981. 2. 10). Compared with such an interpretive precedent, the textual meaning of the doctrine of prior determination established by Article 17 would become even clearer.\\n\\nIn addition, in various statutes regulating public-law benefit relationships, such as the Public Officials Pension Act, the Military Personnel Pension Act, the National Pension Act, the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act, and the Act on the Honorable Treatment and Support of Persons of Distinguished Service to the State, it is well known from existing precedents and from literature that, if a person files an application seeking payment of such benefits and is refused, the applicant must obtain relief not by immediately filing a party litigation seeking payment of those benefits, but by filing an appeal litigation against such a refusal disposition. Nevertheless, it is also an undeniable fact that such statutes do not contain a separate provision like Article 17 concerning a doctrine of prior determination.\\n\\nBy contrast, a statute that contains a doctrine of prior determination like Article 17 is the “Act on Compensation, etc. for Persons Related to the Gwangju Democratization Movement” (hereinafter only the “Gwangju Democratization Movement Compensation Act”). The substance of the doctrine of prior determination prescribed in Article 17 is identical to the provisions on prior determination under the Gwangju Democratization Movement Compensation Act, and not only the functions of the Committee but also the procedures for applying for compensation payments, etc. and the overall structure are nearly similar. With respect to applications for payment of compensation payments, etc. under the Gwangju Democratization Movement Compensation Act, which has such a similar structure, the Supreme Court has held that the form of litigation in the case of objecting to a decision by the Compensation Deliberation Committee on an application for compensation payments, etc. under the Gwangju Democratization Movement Compensation Act should be regarded not as appeal litigation but as party litigation with the State as defendant (see Supreme Court Decision 92NU3335 rendered on 1992. 12. 24). If so, with respect to statutes having similar structures, the existing precedents’ interpretive approach to statutory provisions of identical content should, absent special circumstances, maintain a consistent position. Under the majority opinion, it is unclear whether the intent is to substantively alter the existing Supreme Court precedent concerning the Gwangju Democratization Movement Compensation Act, or whether, despite identical wording, the doctrine of prior determination under the Gwangju Democratization Movement Compensation Act and the doctrine of prior determination under Article 17 must be interpreted differently so that the existing Supreme Court precedent concerning the Gwangju Democratization Movement Compensation Act remains intact while the majority opinion applies only to cases such as this one concerning compensation payments, etc. for persons related to the democratization movement. I cannot dispel the feeling of confusion.\\n\\nIn addition, the latter sentence of Article 17(1) of the Act cannot be overlooked. According to the latter sentence, where 90 days have elapsed from the date an application for payment of compensation payments, etc. was filed, a lawsuit may be filed “even without a decision by the Committee.” It is a legitimate question whether it is not extremely awkward and unnatural to interpret this as allowing an appeal litigation to be filed even though no administrative disposition exists that is the object of objection, or to deem a disposition subject to appeal litigation to exist even though the Committee has made no decision at all.\\n\\nMoreover, despite Article 17 of the Act, if there were provisions that expressly allowed an administrative appeal to be filed against the Committee’s decision itself, or that contemplated or presupposed the filing of a lawsuit seeking revocation, etc. of such a decision, then another interpretation might be possible; however, no such provision can be found in the Act.\\n\\nThe majority opinion appears to rely most strongly on the fact that Article 2(2) of the Act defines “a person related to the democratization movement” as “a person among those falling under any one of the following items who has been deliberated and decided by the Deliberation Committee for the Restoration of Honor and Compensation for Persons Related to the Democratization Movement under Article 4,” so that it is insufficient merely to fall under “(a) a person who died or went missing in connection with the democratization movement, (b) a person who suffered injury in connection with the democratization movement, (c) a person who was recognized as having suffered from a disease prescribed by Presidential Decree due to the democratization movement or as having died from its aftereffects, and (d) a person who received a conviction, dismissal from office, or academic disciplinary action on account of the democratization movement” prescribed in the items of Article 2(2); rather, one must further undergo “deliberation and decision by the Committee.” However, whether a person can receive compensation payments, etc. prescribed by the Act will depend on whether that person falls under the categories set forth in the items of Article 2(2), and the ultimate authority to adjudicate such matter naturally belongs to the court. Therefore, whether by appeal litigation or by party litigation, if a court can render judgment on whether a person is a democratization-movement-related person as prescribed by the Act, the legislative purpose appears to be sufficiently achieved. Accordingly, the contents of Article 2(2) of the Act are not intended to require that compensation payments, etc. can be received only after necessarily going through the Committee’s deliberation and decision, despite the result of a court judgment; rather, the provision that the person is one “deliberated and decided upon by the Committee” in Article 2(2) should be understood merely as referring to the doctrine of prior determination prescribed in Article 17 of the Act, that is, the Committee’s prior procedure as a preliminary review for payment of compensation payments, etc., and should not be read beyond that as having any more decisive meaning.\\n\\nUltimately, if the Act did not contain the provision of Article 17 concerning the doctrine of prior determination, there may be room for the majority opinion’s view that litigation concerning payment of compensation payments, etc. should follow the form of appeal litigation. However, given that the Act does contain such a provision concerning the doctrine of prior determination, which is difficult to find in other statutes, it should be regarded as the legislature having attached special significance to the doctrine of prior determination, that is, as evincing the true intent to allow relief of rights in the form of party litigation immediately after going through prior review such as the Committee’s decision or after the lapse of a certain period for prior review.\\n\\n(2) Another point is to view the matter from the perspective of what is more purposive from the standpoint of the party seeking relief through administrative litigation.\\n\\nAdministrative litigation has as its purpose remedying infringement of the rights or interests of the people by revoking or altering unlawful dispositions, etc. by administrative agencies, or by confirming their validity, invalidity, or existence, and properly resolving disputes concerning public-law legal relationships or the application of law, thereby performing functions such as judicial control over administration and expansion of relief for rights and interests. Meanwhile, Article 3 of the Administrative Litigation Act broadly classifies administrative litigation into four types, thereby typifying them so that the people may select the form of litigation most appropriate to their circumstances of rights and interests infringement and to the purpose of administrative litigation, etc. Therefore, in cases where the form of litigation is at issue, as in this case, it should be rationally determined by comprehensively considering the purpose and functions of the Administrative Litigation Act discussed above, as well as which form of litigation can serve as the most effective and appropriate means for resolving the infringement of the people’s rights and interests.\\n\\nHowever, one cannot help but point out that the majority opinion raises questions as to whether it is truly faithful to the most fundamental request sought to be achieved by the remedies prescribed by the Administrative Litigation Act. This is because, under the majority opinion, there is a possibility that disputes will not be resolved once and for all from the standpoint of the party bringing the lawsuit, but may recur. To be specific, if one imagines a case in which an applicant applies for payment of compensation payments, etc. under the Act, but the Committee renders a decision dismissing all or part of the application, then under the majority opinion the applicant must seek revocation of the Committee’s decision dismissing all or part of the application. If, at that point, the court renders a judgment revoking the Committee’s total or partial dismissal decision and that judgment becomes final and binding, but the Committee, in accordance with the judgment, revokes the total dismissal decision and issues only a partial allowance decision, or revokes the partial dismissal decision and again determines compensation in an amount less than that sought by the applicant, so that the applicant remains unsatisfied, the applicant would have to file yet another lawsuit against the Committee seeking revocation of the partial dismissal decision concerning compensation payments. Thus, under the majority opinion, when a party objects to the Committee’s decision regarding payment of compensation payments, etc., multiple administrative lawsuits may be filed, and depending on the case, disputes over compensation payments, etc. may revolve repeatedly. From the standpoint of judicial economy and prompt resolution of disputes, this would not be desirable for the relief of the people’s rights and interests.\\n\\nBy contrast, if party litigation is used, the applicant may file a lawsuit with the court seeking payment of compensation payments, etc. without being bound by the Committee’s dismissal decision on compensation payments, etc. and without contesting that decision itself. Moreover, the court, without being bound by the matters found and determined in the Committee’s decision to pay compensation payments, etc., can freely determine whether the person concerned falls under related-person status, the degree of injury, the amount of compensation payments, etc., so that the dispute can be resolved in substance in a single proceeding. Therefore, party litigation would be the most effective and appropriate means to remedy the infringement of the people’s rights and interests.\\n\\nb. As seen above, whether from the perspective of statutory interpretation or from the standpoint of the purposiveness of litigation procedure, I cannot agree with the majority opinion’s view that litigation concerning payment of compensation payments, etc. to persons related to the democratization movement, as in this case, must take the form of appeal litigation. Accordingly, if a person who applied for payment of compensation payments, etc. wishes to challenge the Committee’s decision concerning payment of compensation payments, etc., that person must immediately file a lawsuit seeking payment of compensation payments, etc., and since the right to compensation payments, etc. held by related persons, etc. is a public-law right specially recognized by the Act, a lawsuit concerning payment of such compensation payments, etc. should be brought by way of party litigation under Article 3(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below rejected the Defendant’s defense on the merits that, because a lawsuit concerning payment of compensation payments, etc. prescribed by the Act must be brought by way of party litigation with the State as defendant, and because the Plaintiff filed this action against the Committee as defendant, the instant action is unlawful, on the ground that it was possible for the Plaintiff to file an appeal litigation directly against the Committee.\\n\\nSince the court below’s determination contains an error of law in misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning decisions regarding persons related to the democratization movement, the Defendant’s grounds of appeal to that effect are well-founded. Therefore, the judgment of the court below should be reversed, and I dissent from the majority opinion.\\n\\n5. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Jeon Su-an on the Majority Opinion\\n\\nJustice Jeon Su-an seeks to supplement the majority opinion through criticism of the dissenting opinion.\\n\\na. The dissenting opinion, despite the Act’s provision that related persons are those among the persons falling under any one of the items of Article 2(2) who have been deliberated and decided upon by the Committee, interprets, contrary thereto, that persons falling under any one of the said items directly qualify as related persons, thereby treating the Committee’s decision as a mere prior review and regarding the above provision as nothing more than a procedural rule for prior review. However, I think such a view in the dissenting opinion is an interpretation that does not accord with the text and purport of the Act’s provision defining related persons in that manner.\\n\\n(1) What the Act seeks to do is not to immediately pay compensation payments, etc. merely on the basis that a person falls under Article 2(2), but rather to determine, through the Committee’s ex post review, whether a person is a person related to the democratization movement and whether the surviving family members qualify, and only where that is recognized to restore honor or pay compensation payments, etc.\\n\\nSince the Act treats separately, on the one hand, persons who may be deliberated upon as recipients of compensation payments, etc. and, on the other hand, persons who may receive compensation payments, etc. after the Committee’s deliberation and decision, the status or expectation of a person who may be deliberated upon as a recipient of compensation payments, etc. is abstract and uncertain and cannot be said to be a concrete right. It is a leap of logic to say that, merely because there is a possibility of becoming a recipient of compensation payments, etc., one should be deemed to have a direct right to claim payment and thereby be able to demand it. As the majority opinion notes, the reason the Act contains detailed provisions concerning the Committee’s composition and duties, the procedure for filing payment applications with the Committee, and the Committee’s decisions and the procedures for objection thereto appears to be because it contemplates that a concrete right to claim payment of compensation payments, etc. arises through the Committee’s deliberation and decision.\\n\\nBecause the Committee’s deliberation and decision cannot be regarded as a mere prior procedure that must be completed before the exercise of the right to claim payment of compensation payments, etc., when the Committee deliberates and decides, it should be regarded as having exercised its review authority granted thereunder; and where it does not determine whether and in what amount compensation payments, etc. are to be paid within 90 days, it should be regarded as having exercised its review authority in a manner rejecting the application.\\n\\n(2) Since the items of Article 2(2) of the Act that prescribe related persons only set forth types of harm connected with the democratization movement, a person cannot be finally determined to be a recipient of compensation payments, etc. under the Act merely by falling under those items; only when it is established that the person is connected with the democratization movement prescribed in Article 2(1) of the Act can that person finally be determined to be a recipient of compensation payments, etc. However, the democratization movement prescribed in Article 2(1) of the Act refers to activities, after 1964. 3. 24., that contributed to the realization of the ideals and values pursued by the Constitution and to the establishment of a democratic constitutional order, and to the recovery and enhancement of the people’s freedom and rights by resisting authoritarian rule that disturbed the free democratic basic order and infringed the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution. Thus, activities from 1964. 3. 24. to the present, as well as future activities, may fall within its scope, making it extremely broad. Moreover, the content of activities that may be recognized as democratization movement is also quite abstract and comprehensive, so it is not easy to know whether a certain activity qualifies as a democratization movement.\\n\\nThus, unless the Committee specifically examines what the democratization movement prescribed in Article 2(1) of the Act is and whether the acts performed by the applicant fall within it, it is difficult to regard the applicant as immediately qualifying as a person eligible for compensation. Ultimately, since the concepts set forth in Article 2 of the Act alone do not readily identify the recipients of compensation payments, etc. under the Act, it is necessary to confer substantive review functions upon the Committee and have it first decide whether there is a connection with the democratization movement and whether the person becomes a recipient of compensation payments, etc.\\n\\n(3) The dissenting opinion cites the fact that, with respect to applications for payment of compensation payments, etc. under the Gwangju Democratization Movement Compensation Act, the Supreme Court held that the form of litigation in the case of objecting to a decision by the Compensation Deliberation Committee on an application for compensation payments, etc. under the Gwangju Democratization Movement Compensation Act should be regarded not as appeal litigation but as party litigation with the State as defendant, and asserts that the interpretation of the doctrine of prior determination under Article 17 of the Act, whose content and structure are similar to the doctrine of prior determination under the Gwangju Democratization Movement Compensation Act, should likewise be the same.\\n\\nHowever, the Gwangju Democratization Movement Compensation Act differs from the Act applicable to this case in the object of application and the text of its provisions, and therefore the interpretation thereof cannot be said to be valid in this case as well. In addition, considering the reasoning concerning the litigation structure discussed above, and the differences in litigation costs and the allocation of the burden of proof in party litigation and appeal litigation, as discussed below, it is rather more reasonable to regard the form of litigation in the case of objecting to the Committee’s decision on an application for compensation payments, etc. under the Gwangju Democratization Movement Compensation Act as appeal litigation rather than party litigation.\\n\\n(4) Therefore, taking into account the text and purport of the Act’s provision defining related persons as above, as well as the procedural meaning and substantive function of the Committee’s deliberation and decision in examining whether a person qualifies as a related person, it is appropriate to regard the Committee’s deliberation and decision not as a mere prior procedure but as a disposition made by an administrative agency in a position of public authority, and the procedure for challenging the Committee’s decision should be regarded as appeal litigation.\\n\\nb. The dissenting opinion states that if, as in the majority opinion, one interprets the lawsuit challenging the Committee’s decision as appeal litigation, there is a possibility that the dispute will not be resolved once and for all through litigation but may recur, whereas if such litigation is viewed as party litigation, the dispute can be resolved substantively through litigation; therefore, the theory of party litigation would be the most effective and appropriate means for remedying the infringement of the people’s rights and interests. However, such a view in the dissenting opinion is not persuasive for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) First, even if one adopts the theory of appeal litigation, in most cases the dispute will in substance be resolved in one proceeding, so the result will not differ from that of adopting the theory of party litigation. This is because, if a court renders a judgment revoking all or part of the Committee’s dismissal decision, the judgment will state in its reasons why the decision was unlawful, and the Committee, in accordance with the reasoning of the administrative judgment, to which binding force attaches, will recognize the person as a related person and then calculate and pay compensation payments, etc. prescribed by law; thus, most disputes concerning payment of compensation payments, etc. will in substance be resolved in a single proceeding.\\n\\nHowever, in some limited cases, disputes may recur, but this is an unavoidable phenomenon arising because the current Administrative Litigation Act does not recognize a mandatory action.\\n\\nMoreover, this problem is not limited to payment of compensation payments, etc. under the Act; it may also generally arise in cases of benefits under various social security-related statutes, including claims for various benefits under the Public Officials Pension Act, the Military Personnel Pension Act, the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act, the National Pension Act, and the Act on the Honorable Treatment and Support of Persons of Distinguished Service to the State. So far, precedents have not simply regarded administrative agencies’ decisions concerning benefits under various social security-related statutes as merely internal acts of the administrative agency on the ground that such problems exist; rather, in almost all such cases, they have treated them as administrative dispositions and, if dissatisfied, have required the party to contest them by appeal litigation seeking revocation. In such statutes too, this is because the administrative agency’s investigation and confirmation are necessary regarding the constituent facts of the claim to benefits and the amount of the benefits, and because there is room for the administrative agency to exercise discretion in making the decision. Considering, as noted above, that the Act grants the administrative agency primary authority to determine what constitutes a democratization movement and whether the applicant’s death or injury is related to a democratization movement, there is no reason to treat the payment of compensation payments, etc. under the Act differently from benefits under other social security-related statutes.\\n\\nIf, to the contrary, all disputes arising from public-law benefit claims under all social security-related statutes are to be resolved by party litigation merely because of the problems pointed out in the dissenting opinion, this would not only disregard the provisions of the Administrative Litigation Act and the theoretical attempts distinguishing appeal litigation from party litigation, but also run counter to the accumulated trend that has continuously sought to derive, through careful study of the text and legislative intent of each individual administrative law provision, the form of administrative litigation or the concept of administrative disposition most appropriate to the statute in question.\\n\\n(2) From the perspective of the burden of proof or litigation costs in administrative litigation, appeal litigation may in fact be more favorable to the people than party litigation; therefore, the assertion that party litigation is the most effective and appropriate means of remedying infringement of rights and interests is also not valid.\\n\\nIn appeal litigation, the burden of proving the legality of an administrative disposition lies with the administrative agency. Thus, even where, in response to an application for payment of compensation payments, etc. asserting that one is a person related to the democratization movement, the Committee, acting as an expert and making policy-oriented considerations while also conducting procedures such as collection of materials ex officio, renders a decision dismissing all or part of the application, the Committee must itself prove in the lawsuit seeking revocation of that decision that the decision was proper. By contrast, if one adopts the theory of party litigation, the burden of proof for matters such as collection of materials and the burden of legal argument will fall on the applicant, placing the applicant in a more disadvantageous position than under the theory of appeal litigation.\\n\\nAs an incidental matter, compared with adopting the theory of appeal litigation, adopting the theory of party litigation may increase the applicant’s burden of litigation costs such as filing fees.\\n\\nc. As seen above, the various arguments by which the dissenting opinion criticizes the majority opinion from the standpoint of the theory of party litigation are not valid. In short, it should be made clear that, as in the majority opinion, the proper means of challenge to a Committee decision dismissing all or part of an application for compensation payments, etc. by a person related to the democratization movement is appeal litigation, which is not only sound in law but also an effective and appropriate means of relief for the applicant.\\n\\n6. Supplementary Opinion to the Dissenting Opinion by Justice Lee Hong-hoon\\n\\nJustice Lee Hong-hoon seeks to supplement the dissenting opinion by adding the following arguments.\\n\\nFirst, the majority opinion presupposes that the Committee’s decision constitutes an “administrative disposition that directly affects the rights and obligations of the people.” However, when one examines the effect of the Committee’s decision as contemplated by the Act, one cannot but question the majority opinion’s view.\\n\\nArticle 18(2) of the Act provides: “Where the applicant consents to a decision on payment of compensation payments, etc. under this Act, the decision shall be deemed to have resulted in a judicial compromise under the provisions of the Civil Procedure Act with respect to the damage suffered in connection with the democratization movement.” Accordingly, if the applicant consents to the Committee’s decision to pay compensation, it is deemed that a judicial compromise has been formed; but if the applicant does not consent, the Committee’s decision to pay compensation produces no legal effect whatsoever vis-à-vis the applicant. Thus, the Act contemplates that the effect of the Committee’s decision to pay compensation ultimately depends on whether the party consents. It is questionable whether a Committee decision that, in itself, has no binding force and only acquires binding force upon the party’s consent can be regarded as an “administrative disposition that directly affects the rights and obligations of the people.”\\n\\nAn administrative disposition that is the subject of so-called appeal litigation must be a public-law act of an administrative agency that, with respect to a specific matter, orders the establishment of a right or the assumption of an obligation pursuant to law, or otherwise causes legal effects, thereby directly bringing about a change in the concrete rights and obligations of the people; acts that do not directly alter the legal status of interested parties cannot be the subject of appeal litigation. Even from this perspective, the Committee’s decision should be deemed not an independent administrative disposition subject to appeal litigation but merely a prerequisite for seeking payment of compensation payments, etc.\\n\\nAs the dissenting opinion appropriately states, this Court has already held that a decision of the Compensation Deliberation Council referred to in the first sentence of Article 9 of the former State Compensation Act, which established a doctrine of prior compensation determination, is not an administrative disposition but merely a prerequisite. However, Article 15(1) of the former State Compensation Act (Consent of Applicant and Payment of Compensation) provided that “an applicant who has received a compensation decision shall, without delay, file a claim for payment of compensation with the State or local government, attaching his or her written consent to that decision,” thereby requiring the consent of the party for the decision of the Compensation Deliberation Council to take effect, and this was a strong ground for concluding that the Compensation Deliberation Council’s decision could not be regarded as an administrative disposition subject to appeal litigation. Likewise, the content of Article 18(2) of the Act, which makes the effectiveness of the Committee’s decision depend on the party’s consent, is a strong ground for concluding that the Committee’s decision does not constitute an administrative disposition.\\n\\nNext, in light of the fact that Articles 7 through 9 of the Act and the Presidential Decree prescribe the concrete basis for calculation, standards of payment, amount, and method of payment for compensation payments, medical aid payments, livelihood support payments, etc., the Act should be interpreted as recognizing that, if the applicant does not follow the Committee’s decision, the applicant has a direct right to claim performance of compensation payments, etc. And since such a right to claim payment of compensation payments, etc. is a public-law right, I think that a lawsuit seeking such payment can only be brought by way of party litigation prescribed in Article 3(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act, which is a lawsuit concerning a public-law legal relationship.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, while dissenting from the majority opinion, I present this supplementary opinion to the dissenting opinion."}

A housing reconstruction redevelopment project association under the Act on the Improvement of Urban Areas and Residential Environments (hereinafter referred to as the “Urban Improvement Act”) (hereinafter referred to as the “reconstruction association”) is a public corporation that implements a housing reconstruction project under the Urban Improvement Act under the supervision of the competent administrative agency (Article 18 of the Urban Improvement Act) and, within the scope of its purpose, has the status of an administrative subject that performs certain administrative acts according to the provisions of statutes.
