supporting_precedents: {"[2005DU8269]": "1. We examine the grounds for appeal asserted by the Defendant Korea Racing Authority.\\n\\na. Whether the revocation of the licenses of the jockey and trainer in this case constitutes an administrative disposition\\n\\nThe term “administrative disposition,” which is subject to an administrative lawsuit, means an act under public law by which an administrative agency, an organ belonging thereto, or a public body that has been delegated or entrusted with administrative authority pursuant to statutes, exercises public authority that directly affects matters relating to the rights and duties of the people; even if such act restricts the rights of the other party, it cannot be called an administrative disposition unless it is an act of an administrative agency, an organ belonging thereto, or a public body to which authority has been delegated (see Supreme Court Order dated 1999. 11. 26., 99BU3, Supreme Court Order dated 2004. 3. 4., 2001MU49, etc.).\\n\\nThe lower court held that the Defendant Korea Racing Authority is a corporation established pursuant to the Korea Racing Authority Act for the purpose of contributing to the promotion of horse breeding and the development of livestock production through the fair conduct and smooth dissemination of horse racing; that, according to the said Act, with respect to its duties it is subject to the supervision of the Minister of Agriculture and Forestry (at the time of the revocation of the license in this case, before the Korea Racing Authority Act was amended by Act No. 6400 on 2001. 1. 29., it was the Minister of Culture and Sports); that when it intends to establish or amend rules concerning matters relating to the conduct of horse racing, it must obtain approval from the Minister of Agriculture and Forestry; and that it must obtain approval from the Minister of Agriculture and Forestry for its business plan and budget. However, this is nothing more than a provision establishing the basis upon which the State may guide and supervise it in light of the importance and public nature of the horse racing business; and the mere existence of such provisions does not mean that the revocation by the Defendant Korea Racing Authority of the trainer’s and jockey’s licenses can be characterized as a public-law power relationship. Rather, even under the Korea Racing Authority Act and the Defendant Korea Racing Authority’s Rules for Conducting Horse Racing and the Enforcement Rules thereunder, no basis can be found for concluding that the Defendant Korea Racing Authority is delegated or entrusted with administrative authority by the State; there is no provision requiring that remedies against decisions made by the Defendant Korea Racing Authority be sought through administrative appeals or administrative litigation; and a person who wishes to train or ride a racehorse must obtain a trainer’s or jockey’s license from the Defendant Korea Racing Authority, while all necessary matters concerning the requirements for and revocation of such license may be determined by the Defendant Korea Racing Authority. Taking all of this into account, the granting or revocation by the Defendant Korea Racing Authority of a trainer’s or jockey’s license is nothing more than conferring on, or depriving, a person recognized as having outstanding ability of qualifications to perform certain functions and roles in horse racing from the position of exclusive organizer of horse races; accordingly, it should be regarded not as an exercise of administrative authority entrusted by the State or other administrative agency, but as a disciplinary or sanctioning measure within an organization carried out in a general private-law legal relationship.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principle, the lower court’s determination as above is proper, and it does not contain any illegality, as argued in Ground 1 of the grounds for appeal, in misapprehending the law on administrative dispositions and thereby erring in its determination regarding the filing period for an action for revocation and the grounds for invalidity of an administrative disposition.\\n\\nb. Whether there was an abuse of disciplinary authority\\n\\nWhere an employment rule or disciplinary rule provides for disciplinary grounds and stipulates that multiple levels of discipline may be imposed for the same ground, the selection of which disciplinary measure among them is to be imposed lies within the discretion of the person vested with disciplinary authority. However, such discretion is not arbitrary or expedient discretion of the disciplinary authority, and because a balance deemed reasonable according to social norms is required between the disciplinary ground and the disciplinary measure, the imposition of a harsh sanction for a minor disciplinary ground must be deemed invalid as an abuse of disciplinary authority (see Supreme Court Decision dated 1991. 12. 13., 90DA18999, etc.). This standard for determining an abuse of disciplinary authority should likewise apply where the Korea Racing Authority imposes sanctions such as revocation or suspension of a license upon a trainer or jockey who has been licensed by it.\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the lower court judgment on this point in light of the foregoing legal principle and the record, the lower court’s determination that the Plaintiff, while associating with former fellow jockey Non-Party 1, etc., received hospitality such as meals, alcohol, and side dishes from Non-Party 2 and others who were horse-racing customers, constituted undesirable conduct as a trainer and jockey and thus fell within the ground for sanction under the Rules for Conducting Horse Racing as a case of impairing dignity; but that, on the other hand, according to the evidence admitted, it appears highly likely that, from the Plaintiff’s standpoint, he was exploited by Non-Party 1 without properly knowing the circumstances before and after, and it does not appear that he committed any improper act, such as providing horse-racing information to horse-racing customers, in the process; therefore, even considering that the integrity and fairness of trainers and jockeys are essential to ensuring the fairness of horse racing, the Defendant Korea Racing Authority’s selection of the revocation of the Plaintiff’s trainer’s and jockey’s licenses, which is the most severe among the sanctions that could be imposed on the Plaintiff, constitutes an abuse of disciplinary authority in light of social norms and is therefore void, is proper and can be accepted. Accordingly, this lower court judgment does not contain any illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the law concerning abuse of discretion in disciplinary or sanctioning measures, as argued in Ground 2 of the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. We examine the grounds for appeal asserted by the Plaintiff against the Defendant Korea Racing Authority.\\n\\na. The nature of the race cooperation payment and the entity obligated to pay it\\n\\nAccording to the facts lawfully found by the lower court based on the evidence it admitted, the Defendant Korea Racing Authority, within the scope of the budget approved by the Minister of Agriculture and Forestry, pays prize money to horse owners according to the results of horse racing, and also pays subsidies to horse-owner associations and to trainer/jockey associations; horse owners entrust racehorse management to trainers and pay part of the prize money and subsidies each month under the title of entrusted management fees, etc.; and trainers in turn conclude riding contracts with jockeys and pay part of the prize money and subsidies. Based on this, it was found that the Plaintiff also, on 1999. 7. 31., entered into a riding contract with Trainer Lee Yong-jun and agreed to receive race-riding fees, etc. in the event that the Plaintiff entered a race and received prize money.\\n\\nTaking into account the foregoing facts, together with the horse-racing operation structure and the prize money/subsidy payment system, the content and effect of the riding contract as shown in the record (the riding contract between the Plaintiff and the trainer appears to have already been terminated before the revocation of the licenses of the jockey and trainer in this case), the mere circumstance that the race cooperation payment ordinarily received by jockeys has the nature of basic living expenses and welfare expenses does not mean that it is, in substance, wages paid to the jockey as an employee belonging to the Defendant Korea Racing Authority, or that it is money that can naturally be received from the Defendant Korea Racing Authority merely because one holds the status of a jockey.\\n\\nThe lower court judgment to the same effect is proper, and it does not contain any illegality, as argued in Grounds 1 and 2 of the grounds for appeal, in misapprehending the law concerning race cooperation payment or in failing to conduct a full examination.\\n\\nb. Whether a tort was established\\n\\nEven if the assessment of a disciplinary measure imposed by an employer upon an employee is ultimately found to have deviated from or abused discretionary power and the disciplinary measure is therefore held void, if the matter merely amounts to a misinterpretation by the disciplinary committee members, who are not legal experts, of the relevant statutes concerning the degree of severity of discipline, then it cannot be said that those disciplinary committee members who erred in assessing the discipline were negligent such that tort liability may be imposed. Further, if, in light of the objective circumstances at the time the employer imposed an adverse measure such as dismissal upon an employee, the degree of the employee’s misconduct, the circumstances leading to the adverse measure, and similar factors, it was not unreasonable for the employer to determine that the misconduct constituted grounds for an adverse measure against the employee under the employment rules or collective agreement, and if the adverse measure was imposed through the prescribed lawful procedure, then the employer must be deemed to have fulfilled the duty of care required when imposing an adverse measure on the employee; accordingly, even if the adverse measure was later held void by the court, there can be no intent or negligence warranting tort liability (see Supreme Court Decision dated 1996. 4. 23., 95DA6823, etc.). This legal principle likewise applies in determining whether the revocation of the licenses of the jockey and trainer in this case, whose structure may be regarded as similar to an adverse measure such as dismissal of an employee, constitutes a tort.\\n\\nThe lower court rejected the Plaintiff’s claim for damages on the ground that the Defendant Korea Racing Authority’s determination that there were grounds for sanction against the Plaintiff and its revocation of the jockey’s and trainer’s licenses was merely a misassessment of the severity of discipline, and that it could not be said that there was intent or negligence warranting tort liability. This is proper in light of the foregoing legal principle and the record. Accordingly, the assertion in Ground 3 of the grounds for appeal that the lower court judgment on this point is unlawful for misapprehending the law concerning the establishment of a tort is without merit.\\n\\n3. Meanwhile, the Plaintiff also filed an appeal regarding the portion of the lower court judgment adverse to the Plaintiff with respect to the President of the Defendant Korea Racing Authority, but no statement of grounds for appeal was submitted within the statutory period, and the petition of appeal also contains no statement of grounds for appeal.\\n\\n4. Therefore, both the Plaintiff’s appeal and the Defendant Korea Racing Authority’s appeal are dismissed, and the costs of appeal are to be borne by each losing party, respectively. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2011DU11570]": "We shall determine together the grounds of appeal filed by the Defendant and the Defendant’s auxiliary intervenor (hereinafter referred to as the “Intervenor Association”).\\n\\n1. On the grounds of appeal alleging misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the legal character of the disposition approving the establishment of the association in this case\\nThe Housing Reconstruction Improvement Project Association under the Act on the Improvement of Urban Areas and Residential Environments (hereinafter referred to as the “Urban Improvement Act”), enacted by Act No. 6852 on December 30, 2002 and enforced on July 1, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as the “Reconstruction Association”), comes into existence as a juristic person by obtaining approval for the establishment of the association from the competent administrative agency after satisfying the requirements and procedures prescribed by the relevant statutes, such as obtaining consent for the establishment of the association from the owners of land and buildings within the improvement zone, and by registering thereafter (Article 16(2), Article 16(5), and Article 18 of the Urban Improvement Act). And the Reconstruction Association established through such procedures has the status of an administrative entity that performs certain administrative acts in accordance with the statutes, within the scope of the purpose of implementing the “housing reconstruction project” under the Urban Improvement Act in the improvement zone under the supervision of the competent administrative agency.\\n\\nTherefore, the disposition approving the establishment of an association made by the administrative agency on the basis of the Urban Improvement Act and other relevant statutes should be regarded as having the character not merely of a supplementary act to the act of establishing an association by private persons, but rather as a type of constitutive disposition granting the status of an administrative entity (a public juristic person) that has the authority to carry out a housing reconstruction project under the Urban Improvement Act, if the statutory requirements are met (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DA60568, decided September 24, 2009; Supreme Court Decision 2008DA95915, decided November 26, 2009, etc.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 3 of the Supplementary Provisions of the Urban Improvement Act (December 30, 2002), under the heading “General Transitional Measures,” provides that “dispositions, procedures, and other acts carried out pursuant to the provisions concerning reconstruction under the former Urban Redevelopment Act, the Temporary Measures Act on the Improvement of Residential Environment for Urban Low-Income Residents, and the Housing Construction Promotion Act (hereinafter referred to as the ‘former statutes’) at the time this Act enters into force shall be deemed to have been carried out pursuant to the provisions of this Act.” In addition, the main text of Article 10(1) thereof, under the heading “Transitional Measures concerning the Establishment of Associations,” provides that “an association that obtained approval for establishment pursuant to the former statutes shall be deemed to have been established as a juristic person under this Act by registering at the location of its principal office pursuant to the provisions of Article 18(2) of the main text.”\\n\\nIn light of the content and purport of the above provisions, even if the administrative agency rendered the disposition approving the establishment of an association to a Reconstruction Association under the former statutes, namely the former Housing Construction Promotion Act (the version before it was wholly amended into the Housing Act by Act No. 6916 of May 29, 2003; hereinafter referred to as the “Housing Construction Promotion Act”), after the Urban Improvement Act entered into force and the relevant Reconstruction Association completed registration of establishment pursuant to Article 10(1) of the Supplementary Provisions of the Urban Improvement Act, the Reconstruction Association should be regarded as an administrative entity (a public juristic person), and it is reasonable to view the above disposition approving the establishment of an association as being deemed, pursuant to Article 3 of the Supplementary Provisions of the Urban Improvement Act, to be a type of constitutive disposition, so that the propriety of that disposition may be challenged by an action for administrative litigation (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DA95915, decided November 26, 2009, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below, based on the evidence it admitted, found that the Defendant rendered the disposition approving the establishment of the association in this case on February 21, 2003 with respect to the Intervenor Association, and that the Intervenor Association completed registration of establishment on September 1, 2003 after the Urban Improvement Act entered into force, and then held that the Urban Improvement Act also applies to the Intervenor Association pursuant to Article 10 of the Supplementary Provisions of the Urban Improvement Act and that the Plaintiffs may seek, through an action for administrative litigation against the Defendant, a declaration of nullity of the disposition approving the establishment of the association in this case, thereby rejecting the Defendant’s preliminary defense.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the above determination by the court below is justifiable and acceptable, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the legal character of the disposition approving the establishment of an association, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. On the allegations of misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the nullity by operation of law of an administrative disposition\\nEven if, pursuant to Article 3 of the Supplementary Provisions of the Urban Improvement Act, the legal character of the disposition approving the establishment of an association under the Housing Construction Promotion Act is deemed to be that of a constitutive disposition, this concerns only the disposition approving the establishment of an association that was validly established under the Housing Construction Promotion Act, and it cannot be said that a disposition approving the establishment of an association that was void under the Housing Construction Promotion Act becomes valid due to the enforcement of the Urban Improvement Act. Therefore, if the act of establishing an association, which was the underlying act for the disposition approving the establishment of an association under the Housing Construction Promotion Act, is void and thus the disposition approving it is void, then even if such disposition is thereafter deemed a constitutive disposition due to the enforcement of the Urban Improvement Act, it remains proper to regard it as still void.\\n\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in its judgment, determined that the reconstruction resolution in this case was void, and then held that the disposition approving the establishment of the association in this case, which was based on that reconstruction resolution, was also void because its defect was serious and objectively obvious.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, although there may be some inadequacy in the reasoning stated by the court below, it is justifiable and acceptable in conclusion that the court below held the disposition approving the establishment of the association in this case to be void, and there is no illegality affecting the judgment due to misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the nullity by operation of law of an administrative disposition, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, or due to other defects such as inadequacy of reasons.\\n\\n3. On the grounds of appeal alleging misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the criteria and timing for determining the validity of the reconstruction resolution in this case\\nThe court below, based on the evidence it admitted, found the facts as stated in its judgment, and then held that the reconstruction resolution document in this case not only contains no provision even stating that matters concerning the sharing of expenses are subject to the articles of association, but also that, even if the reconstruction resolution was reached through the process asserted by the Defendant and the Intervenor Association, as long as there was no clear explanation thereof because the reconstruction resolution document omitted any explicit statement concerning the sharing of expenses, it is difficult to view the reconstruction resolution as valid merely because such facts had been explained in advance through various procedures and the members were thus able to know their content; furthermore, the reconstruction resolution document and the articles of association in this case contain only the calculation method for the liquidation payment to be borne by members due to project implementation (liquidation payment = price of the land and buildings allocated - price of the former land and buildings), and do not specifically provide for the appraisal method and valuation date for the price of the land and buildings allocated and the former land and buildings, or the timing and method of payment of the liquidation payment, and accordingly rejected the Defendant’s and the Intervenor Association’s argument that the reconstruction resolution in this case was valid.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the above determination by the court below is justifiable and acceptable, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the criteria and timing for determining the validity of a reconstruction resolution, failure to conduct the necessary examination, or violation of the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. On the allegation of misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the cure of defects\\nIn administrative litigation, whether an administrative disposition is unlawful must be determined on the basis of the laws and factual circumstances existing at the time of the administrative disposition, and as a general rule it is not affected by the repeal or amendment of laws or changes in factual circumstances after the disposition. In addition, the cure of a defective administrative act is, in principle, impermissible in light of the nature of administrative acts and the rule of law; and even when, exceptionally, it is permitted in order to avoid futile repetition of administrative acts and to ensure legal stability for the parties, it must be recognized purposively according to specific circumstances within the scope that does not infringe the rights or interests of the people (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DU2579, decided August 26, 2010, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below rejected the Defendant’s and the Intervenor Association’s argument that, since after the first-instance judgment it obtained amended consents from 215 out of 272 owners of land, etc. within the improvement zone in this case, exceeding three-fourths thereof, the defect in the disposition approving the establishment of the association in this case had been cured, on the grounds that the disposition approving the establishment of an association prescribed by the Urban Improvement Act and other statutes has the character of a constitutive disposition, and that if cure of the defect were recognized in this case, there would be a substantial risk of infringing the predictability and legal stability of the legal relationships surrounding the housing redevelopment improvement project.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the above determination by the court below is justifiable and acceptable, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the cure of a defective administrative act, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal, insofar as they arise from the auxiliary intervention, shall be borne by the Intervenor Association, and the remainder by the Defendant. It is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, as stated in the disposition.\\n\\n[[Attachment] List of Plaintiffs: omitted]"}

{"[2015DA34444]": "1. Outline of the case\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na. The Plaintiff is a person who, after obtaining from the Defendant approval for the hiring of a judicial scrivener’s clerk, was hired and worked as a clerk at the office of Judicial Scrivener Nonparty 1 from 2013. 12. 5.\\n\\nb. Before being hired and working as a clerk at the office of Judicial Scrivener Nonparty 1, from 2013. 10. 15. to the 29th of the same month, the Plaintiff worked at the office of Judicial Scrivener Nonparty 2 without obtaining approval from the Defendant for the hiring of a judicial scrivener’s clerk, and hired clerk Nonparty 3 to engage in improper solicitation of cases, etc. Accordingly, on 2014. 3. 31., the Defendant convened the Judicial Scrivener’s Clerk Disciplinary Committee (hereinafter referred to as the “Disciplinary Committee”) and, on the ground that the Plaintiff’s above acts fell under the disciplinary grounds set forth in Article 4, Items 2 through 5 of the Defendant’s Disciplinary Rules for Judicial Scrivener’s Clerks (hereinafter referred to as the “Disciplinary Rules”), imposed on the Plaintiff a disciplinary disposition of 3 months’ suspension of service, and notified the Plaintiff thereof around that time.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, when the Plaintiff continued to work as a clerk at the office of Judicial Scrivener Nonparty 1, the Defendant again convened the Disciplinary Committee on 2014. 6. 2. and, on the ground that “the Plaintiff, by failing to comply with the disciplinary disposition of 3 months’ suspension of service, fell under the disciplinary grounds set forth in Article 4, Items 1, 2, and 4 of the Disciplinary Rules,” made a decision, pursuant to Article 37(6) of the Rules on Judicial Scriveners, to revoke the approval for hiring a clerk so that the Plaintiff could no longer be employed and work at the office of Judicial Scrivener Nonparty 1 (hereinafter referred to as “the revocation of approval for hiring in this case”), and notified Judicial Scrivener Nonparty 1 and the Plaintiff thereof around that time.\\n\\nd. On 2014. 6. 24., the Plaintiff filed this lawsuit with the Busan District Court against the Defendant, seeking a declaration that “the revocation of approval for hiring in this case is void.”\\n\\n2. The parties’ arguments, and the judgments of the first instance court and the court below\\na. The Plaintiff argued, inter alia, that the latter part of Article 37(6) of the Rules on Judicial Scriveners, which is the basis for the revocation of approval for hiring in this case (the part providing that “the local district association of judicial scriveners to which the person belongs shall revoke the approval for hiring if the judicial scrivener’s clerk has committed an act deemed to hinder the performance of duties as a judicial scrivener’s clerk,” hereinafter referred to as “the Rule provision at issue in this case”), exceeded the scope of delegation under the parent statute, the Judicial Scriveners Act, Article 23(4), and thus violated the principle of reservation by statute and was void; and that the revocation of approval for hiring in this case, based on the void Rule provision at issue in this case, was also void.\\n\\nb. The first instance court (Civil Division of the Busan District Court) rendered a judgment dismissing the Plaintiff’s claim on the ground that the Rule provision at issue in this case did not exceed the limits of delegated legislation and that there were no other procedural or substantive defects in the revocation of approval for hiring in this case. The court below (Civil Division of the Busan High Court) also rendered a judgment dismissing the Plaintiff’s appeal on the same grounds.\\n\\n3. We examine ex officio whether the selection of the litigation method is appropriate.\\na. Relevant legal principles\\n1) “Disposition,” which is the subject of an appeal litigation, means the exercise or refusal of public authority as the enforcement of law regarding specific facts performed by an administrative agency, and other equivalent administrative acts (Article 2(1)1 of the Administrative Litigation Act). Whether an act by an administrative agency can be the subject of an appeal litigation cannot be determined abstractly and generally; in a concrete case, it must be determined individually by considering the contents and purpose of the relevant statutes and regulations, the subject, content, form, and procedure of the act, the substantive connection between the act and the disadvantages suffered by interested persons such as the other party, and the principles of administration under the rule of law, as well as the attitudes of the administrative agency or interested persons related to the act (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2008DU167, rendered on 2010. 11. 18.). In addition, whether a disposition has a legal basis under statutes and whether the procedure for disposition prescribed by the Administrative Procedures Act was observed are factors to be considered at the stage of determining whether the disposition at issue is lawful on the merits, and are not factors to be considered at the stage of reviewing the procedural requirements for litigation (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DU60617, rendered on 2016. 8. 30.).\\n\\n2) The addressee of an adverse disposition, as a person whose direct personal interest has been infringed, is recognized as having standing to sue (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2015DU47492, rendered on 2018. 3. 27.). Even if a person is not the direct addressee of an administrative disposition, standing to seek the revocation of the disposition is recognized where that person has an interest individually, directly, and concretely protected by the statutory provisions serving as the basis for the administrative disposition or by related statutes and regulations (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DU9651, rendered on 2007. 12. 27.; Supreme Court Decision 2012DU19496, 19502, rendered on 2015. 7. 23.; etc.).\\n\\n3) Where a case that should have been brought as an appeal litigation under the Administrative Litigation Act is mistakenly filed as a civil action, if the court seized of the case also has jurisdiction over the appeal litigation, unless it is obvious that the litigation requirements for an appeal litigation are not satisfied, such as where the prior-instance procedure has not been gone through or the filing period has elapsed, and therefore the case would be inadmissible in any event even if brought as an appeal litigation, the court must exercise its authority to explain so as to allow the Plaintiff to change the action into an appeal litigation and then examine and determine the case in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the Administrative Litigation Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2019DA264700, rendered on 2020. 1. 16.; etc.).\\n\\nb. Whether the measures relating to approval for hiring a clerk by a local district association of judicial scriveners constitute an administrative disposition\\n1) Article 23 of the Judicial Scriveners Act regulates the hiring of clerks by judicial scriveners, prescribes the grounds for disqualification from hiring a clerk in each item of paragraph (2), and in paragraph (4) provides that “the number of clerks, their hiring, and other necessary matters shall be prescribed by Supreme Court Rules.” Pursuant to that delegation, Article 37 of the Rules on Judicial Scriveners enacted by the Supreme Court provides for an application for approval for hiring a clerk by a judicial scrivener (paragraphs (1) and (2)), the examination procedure by the local district association of judicial scriveners to which the judicial scrivener belongs (paragraphs (3) and (8)), and the procedure for filing an objection with the chief judge of the competent district court when approval for hiring is refused (paragraphs (4) and (7)); and paragraph (6) provides that the local district association of judicial scriveners to which the judicial scrivener belongs shall revoke the approval for hiring if the judicial scrivener’s clerk falls under any of the items of Article 23(2) of the Act or has committed an act deemed to hinder the performance of duties as a judicial scrivener’s clerk.\\n\\n2) A measure by which the local district association of judicial scriveners “refuses approval for hiring,” in response to an application for approval for hiring a clerk by a judicial scrivener, or a measure by which, after having once granted approval for hiring, it “revokes approval for hiring” on the basis of Article 37(6) of the Rules on Judicial Scriveners, should be regarded as a “disposition” subject to an appeal litigation, because it constitutes the exercise or refusal of public authority as the enforcement of law regarding specific facts performed by a local district association of judicial scriveners, which is a public corporation. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\nA) Under the Judicial Scriveners Act, judicial scriveners must obligatorily join the local district association of judicial scriveners established within the jurisdiction of the district court having jurisdiction over the location of their office (Article 28), and are subject to the supervision of the local district association of judicial scriveners to which they belong, the Korean Association of Judicial Scriveners, and the chief judge of the district court having jurisdiction over the location of their office (Article 32). A local district association of judicial scriveners is a corporation whose establishment is compulsory for each jurisdiction of the district court for the maintenance of the dignity of judicial scriveners, the improvement of their work, and the handling of affairs concerning guidance and liaison among members (Article 52), and the Korean Association of Judicial Scriveners is a corporation that must be established by federation of local district associations of judicial scriveners for the purpose of handling affairs concerning the registration of judicial scriveners, etc. (Article 62). The enactment and amendment of the articles of association of a local district association of judicial scriveners require the approval of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, and the local district association of judicial scriveners is subject to the supervision of the Korean Association of Judicial Scriveners and the chief judge of the district court having jurisdiction over its location (Articles 53 and 61).\\n\\nB) Originally, approval for hiring a clerk by a judicial scrivener was an affair performed by the chief judge of the competent district court [see Article 35 of the former Enforcement Rules of the Judicial Scriveners Act (as in force before amendment by Supreme Court Rule No. 1452 on 1996. 12. 31.)], but it was transferred to local district associations of judicial scriveners through the Supreme Court Rules in 1996. Under the Rules on Judicial Scriveners, when the local district association of judicial scriveners to which a judicial scrivener belongs grants approval in response to an application for approval for hiring a clerk, it must report that fact to the chief judge of the competent district court without delay after approval; and when it refuses an application for approval for hiring a clerk, it must notify the judicial scrivener who filed the application for approval for hiring a clerk, stating the reason therefor (Article 37(3)). A person whose application for approval for hiring a clerk has been refused may file an objection with the chief judge of the competent district court within 1 month from the date of receipt of the notification, and if the chief judge of the district court finds the objection well-founded, the chief judge must order the local district association of judicial scriveners to grant approval for hiring, and the local district association of judicial scriveners must grant such approval without delay (Article 37(4) and Article 21(3)). The authority to impose disciplinary dispositions on judicial scriveners belongs to the chief judge of the competent district court, and if a judicial scrivener hires a clerk without approval from the local district association to which he or she belongs, this constitutes “a violation of the Judicial Scriveners Act or the Supreme Court Rules under the Judicial Scriveners Act” and falls under the grounds for discipline (Article 48(1)1 of the Judicial Scriveners Act).\\n\\nC) Requiring a judicial scrivener to obtain approval from the local district association of judicial scriveners in order to hire a clerk is intended to prevent misconduct by judicial scrivener’s clerks and secure public trust in the profession of judicial scriveners by preliminarily examining whether that person falls under any of the grounds for disqualification set forth in the items of Article 23(2) of the Judicial Scriveners Act. Approval for hiring a judicial scrivener’s clerk was originally a state affair performed by the chief judge of the competent district court, who had supervisory authority over judicial scriveners, and was later transferred to local district associations of judicial scriveners; nevertheless, even thereafter the chief judge of the competent district court receives reports of approvals for hiring from the local district association of judicial scriveners and directly handles objections, thereby supervising the propriety of the local district association’s performance of its duties. In addition, if a judicial scrivener violates the Judicial Scriveners Act or the Rules on Judicial Scriveners with respect to hiring a clerk, he or she may be disciplined by the chief judge of the competent district court; accordingly, the judicial obligation imposed on judicial scriveners to hire a clerk only after obtaining approval from the local district association of judicial scriveners is a public-law obligation enforced by the Judicial Scriveners Act.\\n\\nD) In light of the legal nature and history of the system of approval for hiring a judicial scrivener’s clerk, and the fact that the system provides for an objection to the chief judge of the competent district court as a remedy against refusal of approval for hiring, the approval for hiring a judicial scrivener’s clerk by a local district association of judicial scriveners cannot be regarded merely as an internal legal matter between the local district association of judicial scriveners and the affiliated judicial scrivener, nor as an inherent affair of the local district association of judicial scriveners; rather, it must be regarded as the performance of a state affair delegated to it, namely supervision of judicial scriveners. Accordingly, the local district association of judicial scriveners is a public corporation whose establishment and membership by judicial scriveners are compulsory by law for the performance of affairs concerning supervision of judicial scriveners, and, at least with respect to approval for hiring a judicial scrivener’s clerk, it must be regarded as the subject of the exercise of public authority (see Constitutional Court full bench Decision 2017HEONMA759, rendered on 2019. 11. 28.; etc.).\\n\\n3) If a local district association of judicial scriveners refuses an application for approval for hiring a clerk by a judicial scrivener, or revokes approval for hiring for a person who has been employed after obtaining approval for hiring, not only does the judicial scrivener, as the counterparty, suffer the disadvantage of being unable to hire that person as a clerk, but that person also suffers the disadvantage of being unable to be hired and work as a judicial scrivener’s clerk. The fact that Article 37(4) of the Rules on Judicial Scriveners provides for an objection procedure can be understood as intended to protect not only the interests of the judicial scrivener who applied for approval for hiring, but also the interests of the person who seeks to become a clerk. Accordingly, with respect to a disposition by a local district association of judicial scriveners refusing approval for hiring a clerk or a disposition revoking such approval, standing to challenge it must be recognized not only for the judicial scrivener who is the addressee of the disposition, but also for the person who thereby becomes unable to become a clerk.\\n\\nc. We examine the foregoing facts in light of these legal principles.\\n1) The revocation of approval for hiring in this case constitutes a “disposition” that is the subject of an appeal litigation under the Administrative Litigation Act, and although the Plaintiff is not the direct addressee of the revocation of approval for hiring in this case, the Plaintiff suffered the disadvantage of no longer being able to be hired as a clerk by Judicial Scrivener Nonparty 1 as a result thereof; therefore, the Plaintiff should not have filed a civil action against the Defendant, but should have filed an appeal litigation under the Administrative Litigation Act seeking revocation of, or a declaration of invalidity of, the revocation of approval for hiring in this case.\\n\\n2) If this case is an appeal litigation under the Administrative Litigation Act, the panel of the Busan District Court, which is the court of first instance, and the panel of the Busan High Court, which is the court below, also have jurisdiction over the trial at the first instance and appellate stages, so there is no issue of lack of jurisdiction. In addition, because the Plaintiff filed this lawsuit on 2014. 6. 24. after receiving notification of the revocation of approval for hiring in this case dated 2014. 6. 2. around that time, the filing period for a revocation action was observed, and there are no circumstances that would indicate failure to satisfy any other litigation requirements for a revocation action. Accordingly, the court below should have exercised its authority to explain so as to allow the Plaintiff to change the action into a revocation action under the Administrative Litigation Act and should have examined and determined, in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the Administrative Litigation Act, whether the revocation of approval for hiring in this case was a lawful disposition.\\n\\n3) Nevertheless, the court below, overlooking the fact that the revocation of approval for hiring in this case constitutes a disposition subject to an appeal litigation, dismissed the Plaintiff’s appeal while, on the premise that this lawsuit is a civil action, proceeding to a determination on the merits and upholding the first instance court’s conclusion that there were no procedural or substantive defects in the revocation of approval for hiring in this case. The judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning dispositions subject to appeal litigation and the method of litigation, and by failing to conduct the necessary examination.\\n\\n4. We determine the grounds for appeal.\\na. A subordinate statute or regulation under a statute, absent delegation by statute, may not change or supplement the contents concerning an individual’s rights and obligations, or establish new matters not provided for by statute; however, where the contents of an enforcement decree or enforcement rule of a statute merely expressly state what is interpretatively possible under the parent statute by examining the legislative purpose of the parent statute and the related provisions as a whole in an organic and systematic manner, or where they are intended to specify matters on the basis of the purpose of the parent statute, they cannot be regarded as going beyond the regulatory scope of the parent statute, and therefore cannot be deemed void merely because the parent statute does not contain a provision expressly delegating such matters (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DU19526, rendered on 2014. 8. 20.; etc.).\\n\\nb. The court below held that, in light of the fact that Article 23(4) of the Judicial Scriveners Act broadly delegates matters to be specified by Supreme Court Rules concerning the hiring of judicial scrivener’s clerks so that flexible responses can be made to changing socio-economic circumstances, and in light of the fact that, even if the Rule provision at issue in this case contains somewhat abstract aspects, it is necessary for securing the public nature and professionalism of judicial scrivener affairs, which is the legislative purpose of the system of approval for hiring judicial scrivener’s clerks, and its meaning can be specified and clarified through judicial interpretation, the Rule provision at issue in this case cannot be regarded as having exceeded the scope of delegation under the parent statute.\\n\\nc. Examining the content, structure, and legislative purpose of the relevant provisions in light of the foregoing legal principles, the foregoing judgment of the court below does not contain the error alleged in the grounds for appeal, namely, misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the principle of reservation by statute and the limits of delegated legislation, affecting the judgment.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nTherefore, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for further proceedings and determination. It is so adjudged, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2016DA252478]": "We determine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Overview of the Case and the Issue\\n\\nA. According to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n(1) On February 23, 2006, the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City decided and publicly notified a city management plan concerning the installation, maintenance, and improvement of roads, which are urban planning facilities, in order to expand the roads around the Southeastern Metropolitan Distribution Complex.\\n\\n(2) On June 2, 2011, the Plaintiff obtained from the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City designation as the project implementer and approval of the implementation plan for the “Jangji Bridge Intersection Grade-Separation Facility Construction” (hereinafter referred to as “the instant Project”), which is a project to make three-dimensional the road connecting the Songpa Interchange of the Seoul Outer Ring Expressway and Seongnam-si, in accordance with the above city management plan decision.\\n\\n(3) Of the total project area of 6,669㎡ for the instant Project, the land owned by the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as “the instant Land”) consists of 19 parcels totaling 4,186㎡ (12 parcels, 1,097㎡ under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport + 7 parcels, 3,089㎡ under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Defense).\\n\\n(4) On August 6, 2014, the Plaintiff entered into a sale agreement with the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport with respect to 12 parcels totaling 1,097㎡ among the instant Land under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, and paid the purchase price of 1,649,453,340 won on August 21, 2014; on September 26, 2014, the Plaintiff entered into a sale agreement with the Minister of National Defense with respect to 7 parcels totaling 3,089㎡ among the instant Land under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Defense, and paid the purchase price of 5,409,966,660 won on the same day.\\n\\n(5) At the time the approval of the implementation plan for the instant Project and the above sales agreements were concluded, “Wirye Jungang-ro,” a city planning facility road connecting Songpa-gu Jangji-dong 545 as the starting point and extending to Songpa-gu Jangji-dong 647, was installed on the instant Land and in use; the instant Project is a project whose purpose is to install, beneath the existing road left intact on the ground, a grade-separated intersection (an underground roadway 4 lanes wide, 19 m wide, and 1,275 m long).\\n\\nB. The issue in this case is whether, because a new public facility, namely the “Jangji Bridge Intersection Grade-Separation,” was installed through the implementation of the instant Project, the instant Land, which is an existing public facility on which an above-ground road had already been installed, should vest free of charge in the Plaintiff, who is the implementer, pursuant to Article 65(1) of the National Land Planning and Utilization Act (hereinafter referred to as the “NLPUA”), and therefore whether the Defendant must return to the Plaintiff, as unjust enrichment, the purchase price received under the above sales agreements.\\n\\n2. Whether the Plaintiff falls under an administrative agency prescribed in Article 65 of the NLPUA\\n\\nA. Under Article 65 of the NLPUA, if a person who has obtained a development activity permit (hereinafter referred to as the “implementer of a development project”) is an administrative agency, then where that person newly installs a public facility or installs a public facility to replace an existing public facility, notwithstanding the State Property Act and the Public Property and Commodity Management Act (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “State/Public Property Acts”), the newly installed public facility shall vest free of charge in the managing authority of the facility, and the existing public facility shall vest free of charge in the implementer of the development project (paragraph (1)). If the implementer of the development project is not an administrative agency, then the public facility newly installed by that person shall vest free of charge in the managing authority of the facility, and a public facility whose use is abolished by the development activity may, notwithstanding the State/Public Property Acts, be transferred free of charge to the implementer of the development project within the extent corresponding to the cost of installing the newly installed public facility (paragraph (2)). Where an administrative agency in charge of granting a development activity permit intends to grant a development activity permit that includes matters concerning the vesting of public facilities under paragraphs (1) and (2), it shall hear in advance the opinion of the managing authority to which the relevant public facility belongs (main text of paragraph (3)).\\n\\nMeanwhile, under Article 99 of the NLPUA, where a new public facility is installed or a public facility to replace an existing public facility is installed by a city or county planning facility project, Article 65 shall apply mutatis mutandis.\\n\\nB. In light of the wording, content, and structure of the above provisions, and considering the following circumstances as well, where the Plaintiff obtained a development activity permit or approval of the implementation plan for a city or county planning facility project in order to newly install a public facility or install a public facility to replace an existing public facility and thereby became the implementer of the development project, the Plaintiff may be regarded as “a case in which the implementer of the development project is an administrative agency” as prescribed in Article 65(1) of the NLPUA.\\n\\n(1) The Plaintiff, a public entity (local public corporation) established with full investment by Seoul Metropolitan City pursuant to the Local Public Enterprises Act, may be regarded as an administrative agency delegated by Seoul Metropolitan City with the authority to implement Seoul Metropolitan City’s development projects through its establishment and related acts [Article 2(1)(b) of the Administrative Procedures Act].\\n\\n(2) While Article 65(1) and (2) of the NLPUA provide that the existing public facility shall vest free of charge where the implementer of the development project is an administrative agency, they distinguish that where the implementer of the development project is not an administrative agency, the existing public facility may be transferred free of charge, and this distinction reflects consideration of the legal status of the project implementer, the degree of public nature of the project, and the extent of involvement of the traditional supervisory administrative agency (see Constitutional Court, full bench decision of March 26, 2015, 2014HEONBA156).\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 86(5) and (7) of the NLPUA provide that, in order for a person other than the Mayor of a Metropolitan City, the Mayor of a Special Metropolitan City, the Governor of a Special Self-Governing Province, the head of a Si or Gun, or the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport to be designated as the implementer of a city or county planning facility project, such person must, in principle, satisfy the requirements prescribed by Presidential Decree regarding the area of land owned by such person and the ratio of consent from landowners, but that in the case of the State, local governments, public institutions prescribed by Presidential Decree, and other persons prescribed by Presidential Decree, it is not necessary to satisfy the above land ownership and consent requirements. Article 96(4)(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the National Land Planning and Utilization Act, pursuant to such delegation, provides that local public corporations and local public agencies under the Local Public Enterprises Act are among those who need not satisfy the above land ownership and consent requirements in order to be designated as the implementer of a city or county planning facility project.\\n\\nThe purpose of the NLPUA and its subordinate statutes in prescribing land ownership and consent requirements as conditions for designating a private person as the implementer of a city or county planning facility project is to supplement the public nature of a city or county planning facility project implemented by a private person and to control unilateral expropriation by a private person (see Supreme Court Decision of July 11, 2017, 2016DU35120), and the NLPUA and its subordinate statutes already contain a special provision so that when a local public corporation implements a city or county planning facility project, it is treated not as a private person but equivalently to the case in which the State or a local government implements such project.\\n\\n(3) Similar to Article 65(1) of the NLPUA, Article 97(1) and (2) of the Act on the Improvement of Urban Areas and Residential Environments (hereinafter referred to as the “Urban Improvement Act”), which provides for a system of free vesting and transfer of new improvement infrastructure facilities and existing improvement infrastructure facilities, also distinguishes between the case in which “the mayor, the head of a county, etc. or the Korea Land and Housing Corporation, etc.” implements an improvement project and the case in which “a project implementer other than the mayor, the head of a county, etc. or the Korea Land and Housing Corporation, etc.” implements an improvement project. Article 2(10) of the Urban Improvement Act defines “the Korea Land and Housing Corporation, etc.” as “the Korea Land and Housing Corporation established pursuant to the Korea Land and Housing Corporation Act or a local public corporation established pursuant to the Local Public Enterprises Act to carry out housing projects,” thereby treating the case in which a local public corporation implements an improvement project equivalently to the case in which the mayor, the head of a county, etc. implements an improvement project.\\n\\n(4) Article 65(1) and (2) of the NLPUA clearly distinguish between “a case in which the person who has obtained the development activity permit is an administrative agency” and “a case in which the person who has obtained the development activity permit is not an administrative agency.” Therefore, before obtaining the development activity permit, it must already be established whether the person is or is not an administrative agency. Likewise, even where Article 65 is applied mutatis mutandis pursuant to Article 99 of the NLPUA, it must already be established whether the person is or is not an administrative agency before being designated as the implementer of a city or county planning facility project. Accordingly, in a case where, “by being designated as the implementer of a city or county planning facility project, the person only then acquires the status of an administrative agency entrusted with administrative authority,” such implementer must be deemed not to fall under “an administrative agency” prescribed in Article 99 and Article 65(1) of the NLPUA.\\n\\nC. Although the court below stated some inappropriate reasoning in holding that the Plaintiff falls under an administrative agency prescribed in Article 65(1) of the NLPUA, its conclusion is proper, and there is no error such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the meaning of “administrative agency” prescribed in Article 65(1) of the NLPUA, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n3. Whether Articles 99 and 65(1) of the NLPUA apply to the instant Project\\n\\nA. Articles 65(1) and (2) of the NLPUA do not apply to all development projects for which a development activity permit has been obtained (including cases where such permit is deemed to have been obtained), but apply only to so-called “complex-type development projects” targeting a project area of a large size, and the existing public facility becomes an object that may vest in or be transferred to the project implementer free of charge when it falls within the case where its use is abolished by the implementation of the relevant development project. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Other than the NLPUA, laws that provide for the free vesting of newly installed public facilities and the free vesting/transfer of existing public facilities (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “free vesting/transfer system for new and existing public facilities”) include the Urban Improvement Act, the Urban Development Act, the Housing Site Development Promotion Act, the Housing Act, and the Act on the Promotion of Industrial Sites and Development, etc.; all of these concern “complex-type development projects” involving a large area. As a matter of principle, the implementer of a complex-type development project acquires land within the project area for consideration, such as by purchasing or expropriating it, but the free vesting/transfer system for new and existing public facilities is a special exception concerning the acquisition and disposition of State/public administrative property among those lands. In the case of State/public general property, the implementer of the development project must go through the procedure of acquiring it for consideration, such as by purchase or expropriation.\\n\\n(2) In a complex-type development project, from the standpoint of securing publicness and recovering development gains, the implementer is required to formulate a project plan that expands public facilities such as roads and parks within the project area. The “free vesting system for new public facilities” has its legislative purpose in achieving the task of “smooth securing and efficient maintenance and management of public facilities” by considering that the development project creates demand for new public facilities in the project area, directly imposing on the implementer of the development project the duty to install new public facilities, and at the same time causing them to vest free of charge in the managing authority of the State or local government, thereby enabling the managing authority to secure ownership of the newly installed public facilities and then maintain and manage them efficiently so as to suit public use (see Constitutional Court, full bench decision of March 26, 2015, 2014HEONBA156). Through this, the scale of existing public facilities may be expanded, their location may be adjusted, and new public facilities that did not previously exist may be installed.\\n\\n(3) The “free vesting/transfer system for existing public facilities” has its legislative purpose in compensating, at least in part within a reasonable scope, for the property loss or costs incurred by the implementer of the development project as a result of the newly installed public facility vesting free of charge in the managing authority (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of April 13, 2007, 2006DU11149).\\n\\nIn order for the free vesting or transfer of an existing public facility to the implementer of a development project to serve as compensation for loss or costs, it must be premised that the implementer acquires economic value equivalent to the land value by using the existing public facility as the site for the relevant development project and can later dispose of or monetize it, for example by selling it, and this is impossible without the abolition of the use of the existing public facility. Therefore, for the free vesting of an existing public facility under Article 65(1) of the NLPUA to occur, it must be a case in which “the use of the existing public facility is abolished by the implementation of the relevant development project,” just as is clearly provided in Article 65(2).\\n\\n(4) Where the implementer of a development project adjusts the route, for example by straightening an existing road, or expands the width of a road, the straightened or expanded road should vest in the road managing authority, but the site of the existing road no longer needed due to the straightening should vest in the implementer so that it can be used for the development project. For this, under the State/Public Property Acts, the road managing authority of the existing road must decide to abolish its use and transfer the road site to the implementer, and the implementer must go through a series of steps, such as dedication and acceptance, in order to have the new road vest in the road managing authority.\\n\\nThe free vesting/transfer system for new and existing public facilities also has its legislative purpose in streamlining and enhancing the efficiency of the handling of related administrative affairs by causing the effect of changes in ownership of new and existing public facilities to arise directly by operation of law at the time of completion of the development project, rather than through individual legal acts, without the need to go through such a series of steps.\\n\\n(5) Article 65(3) of the NLPUA provides that where an administrative agency intends to grant a development activity permit that includes matters concerning the vesting of public facilities under paragraphs (1) and (2), it shall “hear the opinion of the managing authority” to which the relevant public facility belongs in advance. Since this merely provides for an “opinion-hearing procedure” and not the “consent or consultation” of the managing authority to which the existing public facility belongs, the fact that such opinion-hearing procedure was not followed does not exclude the existing public facility from the object of free vesting/transfer (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of June 25, 2009, 2006DA18174).\\n\\nUnder the State/Public Property Acts, administrative property may not be sold or disposed of unless its use has been abolished, and the abolition of use of administrative property may be made only by the managing authority or the general administrative authority of the relevant administrative property (Articles 22, 27, and 40 of the State Property Act; Articles 11 and 19 of the Public Property and Commodity Management Act). In the free vesting/transfer system for new and existing public facilities, the provision allowing an administrative agency in charge of development project authorization to grant development project authorization including matters concerning the abolition of use and free vesting/transfer of existing public facilities without the consent of the managing authority of the existing public facility may be viewed as reflecting the consideration that, through the implementation of a complex-type development project, public facilities are expanded as a whole and the public interest is promoted, so the gains and losses of the individual administrative property managing authority are not important. If this “special nature of a complex-type development project” is not premised, it is difficult to justify, under the order of the State/Public Property Acts, an administrative agency granting development project authorization deciding to abolish the use of administrative property without the consent of the managing authority or general administrative authority of the existing public facility.\\n\\n(6) In a case that is not a complex-type development project, the land necessary for the implementation of the development project must be acquired for consideration by the project implementer, with payment of the price (compensation), pursuant to a private-law contract or public-law procedures, even if the project involves the installation of public facilities (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of October 25, 2018, 2017DU56476).\\n\\nB. We examine the facts found above in light of these legal principles.\\n\\nThe instant Project is not a “complex-type development project” targeting a project area of a large size, and moreover is merely a project that simply adds a grade-separated intersection beneath the existing public facility (Wirye Jungang-ro) without abolishing its use; therefore, it does not constitute a development project to which Articles 99 and 65(1) of the NLPUA apply.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, first, held that the instant Project is a development project to which Articles 99 and 65(1) of the NLPUA apply, solely on the ground that the existing road installed above the instant Land and the grade-separated intersection newly installed beneath the instant Land are public facilities under the NLPUA, and that the instant Land vests free of charge in the Plaintiff, the implementer of the development project; then, second, concluded that the above sales agreements entered into between the Plaintiff and the Defendant concerning the instant Land are null and void in contravention of Articles 99 and 65(1) of the NLPUA, and held that the Defendant is obliged to return to the Plaintiff the aggregate purchase price of 7,059,420,000 won as unjust enrichment without legal cause.\\n\\nThese holdings of the court below contain an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the “free vesting/transfer system for new and existing public facilities” under the NLPUA. The ground of appeal pointing out this issue is well taken.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning a stay of execution under the Administrative Litigation Act are all incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) (a) Even if a revocation action, which is the principal action, has been filed, and even if it is dismissed on the ground that the act that is the subject matter of the action is not a disposition, a stay of execution is permitted in light of the purpose of the stay-of-execution system based on an urgent necessity, etc. (b) Among the requirements for a stay of execution, the burden of allegation and prima facie showing with respect to the likelihood of seriously affecting public welfare lies with the applicant for the stay-of-execution order. (c) Unless there are special circumstances, the ground for revocation of a stay-of-execution decision must have arisen after the stay-of-execution decision became final and conclusive. (d) If it has been confirmed by a final judgment on the merits that the sanction disposition is lawful, then it should not result in the addressee of the sanction disposition being subjected to less sanction than in the case where a stay of execution was not effected through a provisional stay of execution.
