{"[2005MU16]": "We examine the grounds for the re-appeal.\\n\\n1. Basic Facts\\n\\nAccording to the record, the following facts may be recognized.\\n\\na. On 2003. 11. 5., the non-party, with respect to three parcels of land located about 68 m from the entrance gate of Gumi Elementary School and about 54 m from the boundary line (fence), namely Gumi-si Wonpyeong-dong 147-9, 10, and 375-13 in the same dong, which were located within the relative purification zone among the school environmental sanitation purification zones prescribed in Article 5(1) of the former School Health Act (as amended by Act No. 7396 of 2005. 3. 24. and before such amendment; hereinafter the same) and Article 3(1) of the former Enforcement Decree of the School Health Act (as amended by Presidential Decree No. 18771 of 2005. 3. 31. and before such amendment; hereinafter the same; hereinafter referred to as the \"purification zone\"), applied to the Superintendent of the Gyeongsangbuk-do Gumi Office of Education for deliberation on prohibited acts and facility exemption within the purification zone, pursuant to the proviso to Article 6(1) of the School Health Act and Article 4 of the Enforcement Decree of the School Health Act, in order to construct a theater (a multiplex movie theater, hereinafter \"the theater at issue\") on the land at issue, and the Superintendent of the Gyeongsangbuk-do Gumi Office of Education, after deliberation by the School Environmental Sanitation Purification Committee on 2003. 11. 20., issued a disposition denying the application of the non-party (hereinafter referred to as \"the original disposition at issue\").\\n\\nb. When the non-party filed an administrative appeal against the applicant on 2003. 12. 3., seeking revocation of the original disposition at issue, the applicant, on 2004. 1. 3., rendered an adjudication revoking the original disposition at issue in accordance with the resolution of the Gyeongsangbuk-do Administrative Appeals Commission (hereinafter referred to as \"the adjudication at issue\").\\n\\nc. When 160 parents of students at Gumi Elementary School, including the Respondents, filed an administrative lawsuit against the applicant on 2004. 1. 17. in Daegu District Court Case No. 2004GUHAP482, seeking revocation of the adjudication at issue, and filed an application in the same court, Case No. 2004A237, seeking suspension of execution of the adjudication at issue, the said court, on 2004. 5. 20., in the matter of the said application for suspension of execution, issued a decision stating that \"the effect of the adjudication at issue shall be suspended until the judgment is rendered in Daegu District Court Case No. 2004GUHAP482\" (hereinafter referred to as \"the decision on suspension of execution at issue\") (Record p. 573), and the said decision became final and conclusive as it stood at that time.\\n\\n2. The Holding of the Court Below\\n\\nThe court below, after taking together the materials submitted to show prima facie proof, found: (1) that the land at issue is located about 68 m from the entrance gate of Gumi Elementary School, a nearby school, and about 54 m from the boundary line (fence), so that it is a place designated as a relative purification zone among the purification zones; but that it is located in the central commercial district of Gumi-si, between Road No. 2 and Road No. 3, and is also close to Gumi Station; that Road No. 2, near the land at issue, is a bustling area of Gumi-si, and the merchants' association designated it as Munhwa-ro (Culture Road), affixing large bronze plates to the pavement at every intersection so that it could be easily recognized as Munhwa-ro, and it is crowded with many young people; that the roads connecting Road No. 2, Road No. 3, and Roads No. 2 and 3 are one-way roads; that in light of the location of nearby bus stops, road conditions, and the location of the entrance gate of Gumi Elementary School, the fire road adjoining the front of the theater building at issue is not the main route to and from school for the students of Gumi Elementary School, but is merely used as a commuting route by some of the students of Gumi Elementary School (about 25 students, or about 3.3% of the entire 763 students); that the Gumi Elementary School Steering Committee stated the opinion that the theater at issue is thought not to have a direct influence on the students, but that prudence should be exercised in the method of promoting and posting movie promotional materials; that the Gumi Munhwa-ro Development Council and the head of the Gumi Cultural Center each submitted petitions stating that they hoped a multiplex theater would be constructed as soon as possible so that the area could be transformed into a bright and wholesome street of culture, or that they hoped it would be newly constructed because the multiplex theater would greatly contribute to the development of Gumi popular culture as well as culture and the arts; that most parents of Gumi Elementary School students, nearby merchants, and local residents support the construction of the theater and expect expansion of cultural facilities in Gumi-si and the resulting revitalization of the economy, whereas the Gyeongbuk Citizens' Coalition for Safe Living Practice filed a petition stating that theater operation should be prevented because the surrounding roads of the land at issue are narrow and, if vehicles rush out simultaneously after the theater screening ends, traffic congestion may occur in the surrounding area, and there is a concern that posters and phrases with sexually suggestive content that children should not see may be posted in large numbers around the school; and that the Constitutional Court, on 2004. 5. 27., in Constitutional Court Case No. 2003HEONGA1 and 2004HEONGA4 (consolidated), in the case requesting a constitutional review of Article 6(1) item 2 of the School Health Act, rendered a decision that the portion concerning universities among the \"theater\" portion of the main text of Article 6(1) item 2 of the School Health Act, which prohibits theater operation in school purification zones, violates the Constitution because it infringes the freedom of occupation of persons who wish to operate theaters within purification zones, the freedom of art and expression of theater operators, and the right to pursue happiness regarding the enjoyment of culture of students who wish to use theaters, and that the portion concerning kindergartens, elementary schools, middle schools, and high schools is not in conformity with the Constitution for the same reason, and further ordered that with respect to the above non-conforming portion, the application of the statutory provision be suspended until the legislature amends it; that, accordingly, the Ministry of Education and Human Resources Development, in accordance with the purport of the above Constitutional Court decision of incompatibility with the Constitution, gathered opinions from related agencies and others, gave legislative notice of the amended bill on 2004. 7. 19., and submitted it to the National Assembly around 2004. 10.; that 160 parents of students at Gumi Elementary School, including the Respondents, filed a lawsuit seeking revocation of the adjudication at issue against the applicant on 2004. 1. 17. in Daegu District Court Case No. 2004GUHAP482, but thereafter most of the remaining parents, excluding the Respondents, withdrew their lawsuits or their children had already graduated from Gumi Elementary School or transferred to other schools; and that the non-party received a permit for new construction of the theater building at issue from the Mayor of Gumi on 2004. 12. 31. Having recognized each of these facts, the court below then held in (2) that the land at issue is located in the central commercial district of Gumi-si and close to Gumi Station, and that the fire road adjoining the front of the theater building at issue cannot be regarded as the main route to and from school for the students of Gumi Elementary School; and that, in view of the location of the theater building at issue and the surrounding circumstances, the opening time of the theater and the time difference between the opening of the theater and the school commuting times of the students of Gumi Elementary School, the possibility that theater operation in the theater building at issue would adversely affect the study and school health and sanitation of the students of Gumi Elementary School appears slight, whereas the disadvantage to the non-party, such as infringement of property rights resulting from the issuance of a prohibition disposition with respect to the application for exemption for theater operation, appears to be very great; and that, when these points are taken together with the purport of the above Constitutional Court decision of incompatibility with the Constitution, the contents of the amended bill submitted to the government in accordance therewith, the fact that most parents of students at Gumi Elementary School and local residents, excluding the Respondents and the intervenors in support thereof, desire the construction of the theater, and the development benefits that the construction of the theater would bring to the surrounding area, a concern arose that suspending the execution of the adjudication at issue after the decision on suspension of execution at issue became final and conclusive would have a serious impact on public welfare, and thus maintained as is the first-instance decision ordering revocation of the decision on suspension of execution at issue.\\n\\n3. This Court's Determination\\n\\nThe above holding of the court below cannot be accepted for the following reasons.\\n\\nThe ground for revocation of a decision on suspension of execution prescribed in Article 24(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act must, absent special circumstances, have arisen after the decision on suspension of execution became final and conclusive, and among such grounds, the phrase \"when suspension of execution has a serious impact on public welfare\" refers not to the possibility of infringement of the general and abstract public interest, but to the probability of causing serious harm to the concrete and individual public interest related to the relevant decision on suspension of execution (see Supreme Court Decision 2004MU6, rendered on 2004. 5. 17., etc.).\\n\\nThe court below cited, as grounds for revoking the decision on suspension of execution at issue, that \"the land at issue is located in the central commercial district of Gumi-si and close to Gumi Station; that the fire road adjoining the front of the theater building at issue cannot be regarded as the main route to and from school for the students of Gumi Elementary School; and that, in view of the location of the theater building at issue and the surrounding circumstances, the theater's opening time and the time difference between the students' school commuting times, the possibility that theater operation in the theater building at issue would adversely affect the study and school health and sanitation of the students of Gumi Elementary School appears slight, and that the disadvantage to the non-party, such as infringement of property rights resulting from the issuance of a prohibition disposition with respect to the application for exemption for theater operation, appears to be very great\"; however, it is clear that such reasons did not arise only after the decision on suspension of execution at issue became final and conclusive, and therefore, absent special circumstances, they cannot be deemed grounds for revoking the decision on suspension of execution at issue. Moreover, the record does not show that there was proof of such special circumstances, nor can it be said that such reasons alone caused the decision on suspension of execution at issue to have a serious impact on public welfare or that the ground for suspension has ceased to exist.\\n\\nIn addition, the court below cited, as grounds for revoking the decision on suspension of execution at issue, that \"most parents of students at Gumi Elementary School and local residents, excluding the Respondents and the intervenors in support thereof, desire the construction of the theater, and the development benefits that the construction of the theater would bring to the surrounding area\"; however, the mere circumstance that most parents of students at Gumi Elementary School and local residents, excluding the Respondents and the intervenors in support thereof, desire the construction of the theater at issue does not mean that the ground for the decision on suspension of execution at issue has disappeared, and even if the construction of the theater at issue is halted by the decision on suspension of execution at issue and thereby has an adverse effect on the local economy, this is merely an indirect and collateral interest, and it is difficult to view this as a case where there is a probability of causing serious harm to the concrete and individual public interest related to the decision on suspension of execution at issue.\\n\\nNext, the court below cited, as grounds for revoking the decision on suspension of execution at issue, the Constitutional Court's decision of 2004. 5. 27. in Cases No. 2003HEONGA1 and 2004HEONGA4 (consolidated), which held that \"the portion concerning each school prescribed in Article 2 of the Higher Education Act among the 'theater' portion of the main text of Article 6(1) item 2 of the School Health Act violates the Constitution; the portion concerning each school prescribed in Article 2 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act among the 'theater' portion of the main text of Article 6(1) item 2 of the School Health Act (hereinafter referred to as the 'statutory provision subject to constitutional review') is not in conformity with the Constitution; and courts and other state agencies and local governments shall suspend the application of this portion of the statutory provision until the legislature amends it,\" as well as the government's amended bill to the School Health Act submitted in accordance with that decision. The gist of the portion of the Constitutional Court's reasoning relevant to this case, namely the portion concerning each school prescribed in Article 2 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, is as follows: \"1. Because theater facilities have the character of harmful environments, the statutory provision subject to constitutional review, which prevents theater facilities from being operated within purification zones, is an appropriate means to achieve the legislative purpose. 2. The proviso to Article 6(1) of the School Health Act recognizes exceptions to the general prohibition of the statutory provision subject to constitutional review; thus, on the premise that exceptions are recognized in cases where there is no adverse effect on study and school health and sanitation, prohibiting theaters within purification zones cannot be regarded as unconstitutional. 3. However, the statutory provision subject to constitutional review presupposes a certain range of purification zones absolutely prohibiting the operation of all theaters; in the case of performance halls and movie theaters installed by the State, local governments, or nonprofit organizations such as cultural foundations, performance halls under the Performances Act for the purpose of performances of artistic works including pure art or dedicated venues for children and youth, and dedicated movie theaters under the Motion Pictures Promotion Act for pure art or for children and youth, it is difficult to deny that, even if they are located within purification zones, they are not so much harmful environments for elementary, middle, and high school students as facilities having the character of being beneficial for the cultural growth of these students and are highly likely to be used in a desirable direction; yet the statutory provision subject to constitutional review, which does not recognize at all the possibility of permitting such types of theaters as exceptions to the prohibition and uniformly prohibits them, is an unconstitutional provision.\" In other words, the statutory provision subject to constitutional review, which prohibits all theaters within absolute purification zones, is an unconstitutional provision, but the prohibition of theaters, as in this case, within relative purification zones on the premise that exceptions are recognized under the proviso to Article 6(1) of the School Health Act in cases where there is no adverse effect on study and school health and sanitation, cannot be regarded as unconstitutional. Further, the amended bill to the School Health Act submitted by the government to the National Assembly after the above Constitutional Court decision (Record p. 491) also fully reflects the purport of the above Constitutional Court decision (the amended bill was enacted by the National Assembly and promulgated as Act No. 7396 on 2005. 3. 24.), and therefore it cannot be said that, after the decision on suspension of execution at issue became final and conclusive, the above Constitutional Court decision and the government's submission of the above amended bill caused the decision on suspension of execution at issue to have a serious impact on public welfare or that the ground for suspension had ceased to exist.\\n\\nAccordingly, even when all of the reasons cited by the court below are taken together, it cannot be said that the grounds for revocation arose after the decision on suspension of execution at issue became final and conclusive. Nevertheless, the court below held that, after the decision on suspension of execution at issue became final and conclusive, a concern arose that suspending the execution of the adjudication at issue would have a serious impact on public welfare; thus, the decision of the court below contains illegality affecting the outcome of the trial by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the grounds for revocation of a decision on suspension of execution prescribed in Article 24 of the Administrative Litigation Act. The argument in the grounds for re-appeal pointing out this point is well founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds for re-appeal, the decision of the court below shall be reversed, and the case shall be remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so decided by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court involved, as stated in the order."}

{"[2006MU89]": "Administrative Litigation Act Article 23(2) provides that, “where, in the event an action for revocation is filed, it is recognized that there is an urgent need to prevent irreparable damage that may arise due to the administrative disposition, etc. or the continuation of its execution or procedure, the court where the merits action is pending may, upon application by a party or ex officio, order the suspension in whole or in part of the effect of the disposition, etc. or its execution or the continuation of the procedure,” and this is applied mutatis mutandis to actions for confirmation of invalidity, etc. under Article 38(1) of the same Act; therefore, a stay of execution of an administrative disposition requires, as its condition, that a merits action such as an action for revocation or an action for confirmation of invalidity be filed and pending.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Re-appellant filed as the merits action the “action for confirmation of invalidity, etc. of the claim concerning the disposition approving the change in the implementation of the housing reconstruction project made on February 9, 2006 against the Intervenor by the Respondent (Seoul Administrative Court Case No. 2006GUHAP20600),” and additionally filed the present application for stay of execution seeking suspension of the effect of the above disposition; however, it can be ascertained that the merits action, Seoul Administrative Court Case No. 2006GUHAP20600, was dismissed by judgment on March 21, 2007 and became final and conclusive on April 12, 2007. Accordingly, the present application for stay of execution is manifestly defective in that the merits action was not pending before the court and thus failed to satisfy the requirements for application, and therefore the present Re-appeal is unlawful.\\n\\nTherefore, the Re-appeal is dismissed as inadmissible, and it is so decided as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2020DU34070]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\nA. The Plaintiff is an organization established with veterans who fall under the categories of combat-disabled veterans and service-disabled veterans as members, pursuant to Article 3 subparagraph 1 of the Act on the Establishment of Organizations for Persons of Distinguished Service to the State, etc., and is deemed a small and medium enterprise, in relation to, among others, the promotion of purchase of small and medium enterprise products and the operation of the competition system among small and medium enterprises (Articles 4 through 12) prescribed in Chapter 2 of the Act on Facilitation of Purchase of Small and Medium Enterprise Products and Support for Their Market Access (hereinafter referred to as the “Market Support Act”), pursuant to Article 33(1) subparagraph 2 of the Market Support Act. The Defendant is an agency entrusted by the Minister of SMEs and Startups, pursuant to Article 34(2) of the Market Support Act, with duties such as determining whether there is direct production, issuing certificates of direct production confirmation, revoking direct production confirmation, and conducting hearings.\\n\\nB. Based on Article 6, etc. of the Rules on Profit-Making Businesses of Organizations for Persons of Distinguished Service to the State, etc., the Plaintiff designated its Gyeonggi Provincial Branch, subordinate to the Plaintiff, as the business operator for the cleaning service business within Gyeonggi Province, and on 2011. 1. 11. received direct production confirmation from the Defendant for building cleaning services designated as a product subject to competition among small and medium enterprises, and registered the business office of the Gyeonggi Provincial Branch as “Production Plant 32” in the above direct production confirmation (valid period: 2011. 1. 11.~2013. 1. 10.). Thereafter, the Plaintiff received direct production confirmation two more times for building cleaning services, using the business office of the Gyeonggi Provincial Branch as the production plant (valid periods: 2012. 3. 22.~2014. 3. 21. and 2014. 3. 31.~2016. 3. 30.).\\n\\nC. On 2014. 7. 23., the Defendant issued a disposition against the Plaintiff to revoke, as of 2014. 8. 8., all direct production confirmations that the Plaintiff had obtained for products whose validity periods were then still remaining, pursuant to the part concerning Article 11(3) and Article 11(2) subparagraph 3 of the Market Support Act (hereinafter referred to as the “first direct production confirmation”), and the reason given was that the first direct production confirmation was revoked (hereinafter referred to as the “first revocation disposition”). The reason stated was that “the Gyeonggi Provincial Branch subordinate to the Plaintiff submitted the above direct production confirmation certificate and entered into cleaning service contracts regarding public institutions such as Hwaseong-si and, within Hwaseong-si, the Hwaseong-si Public Health Center and the Hwaseong U&I Center, but caused the subcontractor, Daehan Sangigun Gyeonggi Hwaseong Business Office Co., Ltd., to perform the above cleaning services” (hereinafter referred to as the “violation at issue”).\\n\\nD. The Plaintiff, being dissatisfied with the first revocation disposition, filed an administrative appeal on 2014. 7. 24. and a cancellation lawsuit on 2014. 7. 30. (hereinafter referred to as the “prior cancellation lawsuit”), while applying for a stay of execution in each case. Pursuant to the sequential stay-of-execution decisions rendered by the Central Administrative Appeals Commission and by the first, second, and third instance courts in the cancellation lawsuit, the effect of the first revocation disposition was stayed from 2014. 8. 5. to 2019. 2. 18. (however, for 15 days during that period, a stay-of-execution decision was not obtained). However, the administrative appeal was ultimately dismissed, and in the prior cancellation lawsuit as well, a judgment dismissing the claim was rendered and became final and conclusive (Supreme Court 2018DU61611 decided on 2019. 2. 18.), thereby causing the stay-of-execution decisions to lose effect. Meanwhile, all of the Plaintiff’s direct production confirmations that the Defendant had designated as subjects of revocation at the time of the first revocation disposition all expired during the stay-of-execution period in this case.\\n\\nE. On 2019. 4. 30., the Defendant notified the Plaintiff that it would revoke, as of 2019. 5. 7., all of the direct production confirmations listed in attached Table 1 of the first-instance judgment, among the direct production confirmations obtained by the Plaintiff through applications filed during the stay-of-execution period in this case and currently still having validity periods remaining (hereinafter referred to as the “second direct production confirmation”) (hereinafter referred to as the “disposition at issue”). The disposition document states as follows.\\n\\n<TABLE0>\\n\\n2. Lower Court’s Determination and Issues\\nA. Lower Court’s Determination\\nThe lower court assumed that, unlike the first revocation disposition, the disposition at issue was a direct production confirmation revocation disposition whose ground for disposition was the original defect in the second direct production confirmation, namely, that the application for the second direct production confirmation violated the part concerning Article 11(2) subparagraph 3 of Article 11(5) of the Market Support Act, which provides that when direct production confirmation for all products has been revoked on a ground prescribed in Article 11(2) subparagraph 3, no application for confirmation of direct production for all products may be filed for six months from the date of revocation. The lower court then held that, since the first revocation disposition could not be executed during the stay-of-execution period in this case, the Plaintiff’s application for the second direct production confirmation made during that period could not be deemed to violate the above provision, and even if the judgment against the Plaintiff in the prior cancellation lawsuit became final and conclusive, the above application could not retroactively be deemed to violate the above provision; accordingly, the disposition at issue was unlawful because its grounds for disposition were not established.\\n\\nB. Issues\\nThe issues are: ① whether the Defendant may change the object of revocation of direct production confirmation from “direct production confirmation for all products for which the validity periods were still remaining at the time of the first revocation disposition” to “direct production confirmation for all products for which the validity periods are still remaining at the time when the first revocation disposition became executable” (whether authority to issue a changed disposition is recognized), and ② if such authority to issue a changed disposition exists, whether the disposition at issue constitutes such a changed disposition (interpretation of the grounds for disposition).\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s Determination\\nA. Relevant provisions of the Market Support Act and its subordinate statutes\\n(1) The Market Support Act, for the purpose of contributing to the enhancement of the competitiveness and stabilization of management of small and medium enterprises by promoting the purchase of small and medium enterprise products and supporting their market channels (Article 1), provides as follows. The Minister of SMEs and Startups may designate as products subject to competition among small and medium enterprises products that are directly produced or provided by small and medium enterprises and are recognized as requiring market expansion (Article 6(1)). The head of a public institution shall, in principle, conclude procurement contracts for competitive products in accordance with competitive bidding among small and medium enterprises (Article 7(1)). This is intended to promote the purchase of small and medium enterprise products and support their market channels, and at the same time, in procurement contracts concluded in this manner, to foster domestic small and medium enterprises and ensure the effective operation of the competition system among small and medium enterprises by prohibiting small and medium enterprises from purchasing the relevant products from large enterprises, subcontractors, foreign companies, etc., and supplying them as their own, and by requiring direct production.\\n\\nA small and medium enterprise intending to conclude a product procurement contract by way of competition among small and medium enterprises must obtain confirmation from the head of a public institution as to whether it directly produces the product (main text of Article 9(1)). However, if necessary, the head of a public institution or a small and medium enterprise intending to supply products to a public institution may apply to the Minister of SMEs and Startups for confirmation as to whether the relevant product is directly produced (Article 9(3)); in such case, the Minister of SMEs and Startups shall confirm whether the product is directly produced and notify the result to the relevant small and medium enterprise, and may issue to the small and medium enterprise confirmed to be directly producing the product a document certifying such fact by specifying its validity period (hereinafter referred to as the “direct production confirmation certificate”) (Article 9(4)). A small and medium enterprise that has obtained such direct production confirmation certificate may participate in competitive bidding among small and medium enterprises without separately obtaining confirmation from the head of a public institution as to whether it directly produces the product (proviso to Article 9(1)). The Minister of SMEs and Startups may investigate whether a small and medium enterprise that has received direct production confirmation satisfies the standards for direct production confirmation and whether it is actually performing direct production (Article 11(1)). If the investigation reveals that the small and medium enterprise “delivered products not directly produced, such as by subcontract production, after concluding a supply contract with the head of a public institution,” the direct production confirmation for all products obtained by the small and medium enterprise shall be revoked (the part concerning Article 11(2) subparagraph 3 in Article 11(3), hereinafter referred to as the “provision serving as the basis of this case”). When direct production confirmation is revoked pursuant to the provision serving as the basis of this case, the small and medium enterprise may not apply for confirmation as to whether it directly produces any product for six months from the date on which the direct production confirmation was revoked (the part concerning Article 11(2) subparagraph 3 in Article 11(5) subparagraph 3, hereinafter referred to as the “new application restriction provision”), and when the direct production confirmation of a small and medium enterprise that has concluded a procurement contract is revoked, the head of a public institution shall, in principle, rescind or terminate all or part of the contract concluded with that small and medium enterprise (Article 11(6), hereinafter referred to as the “existing contract rescission provision”).\\n\\n(2) According to the Enforcement Rule of the Act on Facilitation of Purchase of Small and Medium Enterprise Products and Support for Their Market Access, the validity period of a direct production confirmation certificate is two years from the date of issuance (Article 5(4)), and when revoking direct production confirmation, the products for which direct production confirmation is revoked must be clearly identified (Article 8(1)).\\n\\nB. Relevant legal principles\\n(1) Since law is, in principle, a universally valid norm of society having the same binding force upon an unspecified number of persons, in interpreting it one must clarify the standard meaning of the law so that it has objective validity, and, insofar as possible, maintain consistency that can be accepted by everyone so as not to impair legal stability. Meanwhile, because statutes are usually enacted with universal and typical cases in mind, when applying statutes to various cases arising in social reality, interpretation is also required so as to reach the most appropriate solution for the specific case. In short, the goal of legal interpretation must be to find concrete validity within the bounds that do not undermine legal stability. To this end, the principle is to interpret as faithfully as possible to the ordinary meaning of the words used in the statute, while additionally employing systematic and logical methods of interpretation that take into account the legislative intent and purpose of the statute, legislative history, harmony with the entire legal order, and the relationship with other statutes, thereby arriving at a sound interpretation that meets the above demands of legal interpretation (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DA81035 rendered on 2009. 4. 23.).\\n\\n(2) If a stay-of-execution decision is rendered under Article 23 of the Administrative Litigation Act, no measures may be taken to realize the disposition during the stay period set forth in the operative part of the decision (see Supreme Court Decision 2002DA48023 rendered on 2003. 7. 11.). In particular, if there is a stay-of-execution decision suspending the effect of the disposition, the status during the stay period set forth in the operative part of the decision becomes the same as the original status as if there had been no disposition (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DU17543 rendered on 2007. 3. 29.).\\n\\nThe effect of a stay-of-execution decision continues until the period specified in the operative part of the decision, and expires prospectively upon the expiration of that period (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DU25498 rendered on 2017. 7. 11.). Since the purpose of a stay-of-execution decision is to prevent such damage by temporarily suspending execution of the relevant disposition until judgment on the merits, on the condition that there is an urgent need to prevent irreparable harm from the execution of the disposition and that it will not otherwise have a serious effect on the public welfare, the effect of a stay-of-execution decision does not retroactively cease even if the plaintiff who filed the administrative appeal receives a final and conclusive judgment against it in the merits action.\\n\\nHowever, even if a stay-of-execution decision is rendered with respect to a disposition in administrative dispute proceedings concerning a sanction disposition, if in the merits the relevant disposition is ultimately confirmed lawful, causing the stay-of-execution decision to lose effect and allowing the sanction disposition to be executed again, the disposition agency must take necessary measures so that the relevant sanction disposition is executed at a level equivalent to the case where there had been no stay-of-execution decision in the first place. Because a stay of execution is merely a provisional measure to secure effective relief in administrative dispute proceedings, if it is confirmed by a final judgment on the merits that the relevant sanction disposition is lawful, the outcome must not be such that the addressee of the sanction disposition receives a lesser sanction, compared with the case where no stay of execution had been granted, by means of the provisional stay of execution (see the purport of Supreme Court Decision 2013DU25498 rendered on 2017. 7. 11.). Conversely, if the addressee of the disposition could not obtain a stay-of-execution decision, but in the merits action it is confirmed that the relevant sanction disposition was unlawful and a judgment revoking it becomes final and conclusive, the disposition agency must take necessary measures to eliminate the unfavorable consequences caused to the addressee by that sanction disposition (see the purport of Supreme Court Decision 2016DU52019 rendered on 2019. 1. 31.).\\n\\n(3) Where an administrative agency has issued a disposition in writing, in principle, the content of the disposition must be determined according to the wording of the disposition document. However, where there are special circumstances, such as when it is unclear from the wording of the disposition document alone what disposition the administrative agency made, the content of the disposition may also be interpreted differently from the wording of the disposition document by considering other circumstances, such as the process leading to the disposition, the true intent of the disposition agency, and the attitude of the other party before and after the disposition (see Supreme Court Decisions 2009DU18035 rendered on 2010. 2. 11., 2012DU20571 rendered on 2013. 7. 12., etc.).\\n\\nC. Whether authority to issue a changed disposition is recognized\\n(1) Before determining this issue, we would like to present a brief example. A small and medium enterprise that received direct production confirmation entered into a supply contract with the head of a public institution and then supplied products not directly produced by itself. The competent administrative agency issued the first revocation disposition, revoking the direct production confirmation for all products of the small and medium enterprise whose validity periods were still remaining at the time, pursuant to the provision serving as the basis of this case. In response, the small and medium enterprise filed a cancellation lawsuit against the first revocation disposition, and a stay-of-execution decision was rendered. However, in the end, a judgment against the small and medium enterprise became final and conclusive, the stay of execution lost effect, and the revocation disposition became executable. Yet all or part of the direct production confirmations whose validity periods were still remaining at the time of the first revocation disposition expired during the stay-of-execution period, and the list of direct production confirmation products whose validity periods were still remaining at the time of the first revocation disposition differs from the list of direct production confirmation products whose validity periods were still remaining at the time when the revocation disposition became executable.\\n\\nIn such a case, the competent administrative agency must be deemed to have authority, within a reasonable period from the time when the first revocation disposition became executable, to issue a disposition changing the object of revocation of direct production confirmation from all products whose validity periods were still remaining “at the time of the first revocation disposition” to all products whose validity periods are still remaining, based on “the time when the first revocation disposition became executable or a time close thereto.” Such a changed disposition is identical to the first revocation disposition in that it takes the fact that the small and medium enterprise supplied products not directly produced and the provision serving as the basis of this case as the ultimate “fact constituting the cause of the disposition” and “legal basis,” respectively, and merely changes the object of revocation of direct production confirmation in order to ensure the effectiveness of the sanction.\\n\\n(2) The specific reasons why such authority to issue a changed disposition is recognized are as follows.\\n\\n(a) The competition system among small and medium enterprises and the direct production confirmation system based thereon provide only small and medium enterprises that have received direct production confirmation with qualifications to participate in public institution procurement bidding, etc., while restricting competition in the market in order to improve the quality of procurement goods and protect and foster competitive small and medium enterprises. Therefore, if this is not strictly enforced, there is a concern that the system itself may become a dead letter (see Constitutional Court en banc decision 2016HEONBA353 rendered on 2018. 11. 29.). The Market Support Act, with respect to a small and medium enterprise that, despite receiving direct production confirmation, delivered products not directly produced, requires revocation of direct production confirmation for all products (the provision serving as the basis of this case), restricts applications for direct production confirmation for six months from the date of revocation (new application restriction provision), and causes the head of a public institution to, in principle, rescind or terminate all or part of the contracts concluded with that small and medium enterprise (existing contract rescission provision), thereby excluding it from competitive bidding among small and medium enterprises for six months. This reflects the fact that there is a significant public need to strictly maintain the direct production confirmation system.\\n\\n(b) If a stay-of-execution decision is rendered in administrative dispute proceedings concerning a direct production confirmation revocation disposition pursuant to the provision serving as the basis of this case, the relevant small and medium enterprise may continue to enjoy the benefits arising from the direct production confirmation that became the subject of revocation during the stay-of-execution period, and the existing contract rescission provision or the new application restriction provision will not apply.\\n\\nEven if, in the merits action, the small and medium enterprise loses and the judgment becomes final and conclusive, causing the stay of execution to lose effect and allowing the revocation disposition to be executed again, by that time some or all of the direct production confirmations that still had a two-year validity period at the time of the disposition may have already expired during the stay-of-execution period, while the direct production confirmations newly obtained during the stay-of-execution period may still remain valid. If the competent administrative agency were unable to change the object of revocation of direct production confirmation to all products whose validity periods are still remaining based on the time when the revocation disposition became executable or a time close thereto, then the relevant small and medium enterprise would be able to continue participating in competitive bidding among small and medium enterprises based on direct production confirmations for all products it holds at that time even after the revocation disposition becomes executable. As a result, the sanction effect intended by the provision serving as the basis of this case, which is to revoke direct production confirmation for all products held by the addressee and thereby prevent participation in competitive bidding among small and medium enterprises, would not be achieved. In addition, compared with an addressee of a disposition who did not obtain a stay-of-execution decision and therefore suffers the disadvantage of having direct production confirmation for all products held at the time of execution of the revocation disposition revoked, this would result in a benefit being conferred on the addressee who obtained a stay-of-execution decision.\\n\\nD. Whether the disposition at issue constitutes a changed disposition\\n(1) Examining the facts above in light of these legal principles leads to the following conclusion.\\n\\n(a) The first revocation disposition dated 2014. 7. 23. was stayed by sequential stay-of-execution decisions until 2019. 2. 18. (excluding the 15-day period during which a stay-of-execution decision was not obtained). During the stay-of-execution period, the new application restriction provision did not apply in relation to the first revocation disposition, and therefore the Plaintiff’s direct production confirmation application made during that period and the Defendant’s second direct production confirmation with respect thereto cannot be deemed unlawful. On 2019. 2. 18., the judgment against the Plaintiff in the prior cancellation lawsuit became final and conclusive, causing the stay-of-execution decision to lose effect and the first revocation disposition to become executable again; however, this has effect only prospectively, and the Plaintiff’s second direct production confirmation application lawfully made during the stay-of-execution period and the Defendant’s second direct production confirmation with respect thereto do not become retroactively unlawful.\\n\\n(b) However, when the circumstances below are taken together, the disposition at issue should be understood not as a separate direct production confirmation revocation disposition from the first revocation disposition, on the ground of the original defect in the second direct production confirmation, but as a disposition that shares with the first revocation disposition the same “fact constituting the cause of the disposition” and “legal basis,” while merely changing the products subject to revocation of direct production confirmation in order to secure the effectiveness of the sanctions under the first revocation disposition.\\n\\n① In this case, the first revocation disposition dated 2014. 7. 23. was to revoke the Plaintiff’s direct production confirmation for all products whose validity periods were still remaining as of the time of the disposition, that is, the first direct production confirmation. However, during the stay-of-execution period in this case, the Plaintiff continued to maintain, until each product’s validity period expired, the existing procurement contract relations already concluded on the basis of the first direct production confirmation for all products that were within their validity periods as of the time of the above first revocation disposition, and also enjoyed the benefits under the Market Support Act relating to the first direct production confirmation, including participation in competitive bidding among small and medium enterprises. In addition, even during the stay-of-execution period, the Plaintiff applied for and received direct production confirmation for new products without restriction, and continued to receive the benefits under the Market Support Act arising from the second direct production confirmation until the time when the judgment against it became final and conclusive in the prior cancellation lawsuit and the stay-of-execution decision lost effect.\\n\\n② On 2019. 2. 19., the Defendant notified the Plaintiff that, because the judgment against the Plaintiff in the prior cancellation lawsuit had become final and conclusive, the first revocation disposition had become executable, and that the remaining period, excluding the 15 days during which a stay-of-execution decision was not obtained within the six-month restriction period set forth in the new application restriction provision, would run again from 2019. 2. 18. to 2019. 8. 2. This indicates that the new application restriction provision did not apply during the stay-of-execution period in this case when the Plaintiff’s second direct production confirmation application was filed.\\n\\n③ Thereafter, on 2019. 4. 30., the Defendant issued the disposition at issue, setting the planned effective date of the disposition at 2019. 5. 7., and revoking all direct production confirmations for all products of the Plaintiff whose validity periods were still remaining as of that time. Comparing the contents of the first revocation disposition and the disposition at issue, the only difference lies in the list of products subject to revocation of direct production confirmation, reflecting the difference in the list of the Plaintiff’s direct production confirmation products whose validity periods were still remaining as of each disposition date. In light of the above sequence of circumstances, the disposition at issue may be regarded as a measure taken to secure the effectiveness of the first revocation disposition.\\n\\n④ The disposition document for the disposition at issue states, “Revocation restriction period: from the date of the Supreme Court judgment (2019. 2. 18.) to 2019. 8. 2. (Friday).” The Defendant may also be deemed, through the disposition document, to have acknowledged that the new application restriction provision could not be applied during the stay-of-execution period in this case when the Plaintiff’s second direct production confirmation application was filed. Accordingly, it is difficult to regard the disposition at issue as having taken the Plaintiff’s second direct production confirmation application’s alleged violation of the new application restriction provision as the ground for disposition.\\n\\n(2) Insofar as the disposition at issue is understood as a changed disposition as above, if the Plaintiff’s violation at issue is recognized, as was determined in the final and conclusive judgment in the prior cancellation lawsuit, then the disposition at issue must be deemed to have established its grounds for disposition.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court concluded that the disposition at issue was based on the original defect of the second direct production confirmation and held that such grounds for disposition were not established in light of the effect of the stay-of-execution decision. In so doing, the lower court erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning direct production confirmation revocation dispositions based on the part concerning Article 11(2) subparagraph 3 in Article 11(3) of the Market Support Act, as well as the legal principles concerning the interpretation of administrative dispositions, and by failing to conduct the necessary trial, thereby affecting the judgment. The grounds for appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nThe Defendant’s appeal is meritorious. Accordingly, the lower court judgment is reversed and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. It is so decided by the unanimous opinion of the Justices."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the National Assembly Act is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: When seeking the consent of the National Assembly in order to arrest or detain a member of the National Assembly, the judge of the competent court shall submit a request for consent to arrest to the Government before issuing the warrant, and the Government, after receiving it, shall without delay attach a copy thereof and request the National Assembly to consent to the arrest.
B: A member of the National Assembly may be a member of two or more standing committees, and each floor leader of a negotiating group shall become a member of the National Assembly Steering Committee. Provided, however, that the Speaker of the National Assembly may not be a member of a standing committee.
C: A standing committee member of the National Assembly shall not engage in profit-making activities related to the duties of the standing committee under his or her jurisdiction. Provided, however, that this shall not apply where, after review by the National Assembly Ethics Review Advisory Committee, permission has been granted by the chairperson of the Ethics Review Advisory Committee.
D: Since the proviso to Article 50(1) of the Constitution, which provides that meetings of the National Assembly may not be made public when a majority of the members present agree or when the Speaker deems it necessary for the security of the State, also applies to National Assembly subcommittees, the provision of the National Assembly Act that permits a subcommittee meeting to be closed by resolution of the National Assembly subcommittee cannot be said to be an unconstitutional provision violating the principle against excessive restriction.
E: When a member of the National Assembly introduces a motion demanding the release of a member who has been arrested or detained, a request stating the reasons thereto, signed jointly by at least one-fourth of the total number of members of the National Assembly, shall be submitted to the Speaker of the National Assembly.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2007HEONBA17]": "1. Overview of the Case and Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nA. Overview of the Case\\n\\n(1) The National Assembly Special Committee on Follow-up Measures to the Decision of Unconstitutionality of the Special Measures Act for the Construction of a New Administrative Capital and on Balanced Regional Development established the Subcommittee on Follow-up Measures for the New Administrative Capital (hereinafter referred to as “the Subcommittee in this case”), and the Subcommittee in this case held seven meetings from January 10, 2005 to February 17 of the same year, during which some meetings of the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th meetings were conducted in closed session.\\n\\n(2) On February 8, 2006, the Petitioners requested the Speaker of the National Assembly to disclose, from among the minutes of the six closed sessions among the seven meetings held by the Subcommittee in this case, information concerning ① the list of attendees of the Subcommittee for each meeting, ② the content of each attendee’s remarks, and ③ the list of members who voted for and against the decision; thereupon, the Secretary-General of the National Assembly, on March 10, 2006, disclosed the list of attendees for each meeting, but decided, pursuant to the proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act and Article 9(1) of the Act on Disclosure of Information by Public Agencies, to withhold the content of each attendee’s remarks and the list of members who voted for or against the decision.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, the Petitioners filed an administrative lawsuit seeking revocation of the Secretary-General of the National Assembly’s above-mentioned decision not to disclose information (Seoul Administrative Court 2006GUHAP26578), and, during the pendency of the said lawsuit, filed an application for a referral for constitutional review of laws (Seoul Administrative Court 2006A1820), asserting that the proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act (as amended by Act No. 6266 of February 16, 2000), which provides that meetings of subcommittees may be closed by resolution, violates Article 50(1) of the Constitution and infringes the Petitioners’ right to know; however, when the application was dismissed on January 24, 2007, they were served with the written decision on February 8, 2007 and filed the constitutional complaint in this case on March 6, 2007.\\n\\nB. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether the proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act (as amended by Act No. 6266 of February 16, 2000), Article 118(4) of the National Assembly Act (as amended by Act No. 4385 of May 31, 1991), and Article 9(1) of the Act on Disclosure of Information by Public Agencies (wholly amended by Act No. 7127 of January 29, 2004, hereinafter referred to as the “Information Disclosure Act”) are unconstitutional, and their text and the relevant provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions under Review]\\n\\nNational Assembly Act (as amended by Act No. 6266 of February 16, 2000) Article 57 (Subcommittees)\\n⑤ Meetings of subcommittees shall be open to the public. However, they may be closed by resolution of the subcommittee.\\n\\nNational Assembly Act (as amended by Act No. 4385 of May 31, 1991) Article 118 (Distribution and Publication of Minutes)\\n④ The contents of meetings not opened to the public shall not be published. However, when it is determined by resolution of the plenary session or by the decision of the Speaker that the ground under the proviso to paragraph (1) has ceased to exist, such contents may be published.\\n\\nAct on Disclosure of Information by Public Agencies (wholly amended by Act No. 7127 of January 29, 2004) Article 9 (Information Subject to Non-Disclosure)\\n① Information held and managed by public agencies shall be subject to disclosure. However, information falling under any of the following subparagraphs may not be disclosed.\\n\\n1. Information prescribed as confidential or non-disclosable by other statutes or by orders delegated by statute (limited to National Assembly Rules, Supreme Court Rules, Constitutional Court Rules, National Election Commission Rules, Presidential Decrees, and ordinances)\\n2. Information concerning national security, defense, unification, foreign relations, and other matters, where disclosure is deemed likely to significantly harm the national interest\\n3. Information where disclosure is deemed likely to cause a significant hindrance to the protection of life, body, or property of the people\\n4. Information related to ongoing trials and matters concerning the prevention of crime, investigation, institution and maintenance of public prosecution, execution of criminal punishment, correctional treatment, and security dispositions, where disclosure is deemed to significantly impede the performance of such duties or likely infringe the right of a criminal defendant to a fair trial\\n5. Information concerning audit, supervision, inspection, examination, regulation, bidding contracts, technological development, personnel management, decision-making processes, or internal review processes, etc., where disclosure is deemed likely to significantly impede the fair performance of duties or research and development\\n6. Information concerning matters about individuals, such as names and resident registration numbers, contained in the relevant information, where disclosure is deemed likely to infringe upon the secrecy or freedom of private life of individuals. However, the following information concerning individuals shall be excluded:\\n   a. Information that may be inspected pursuant to statutes and regulations\\n   b. Information prepared or obtained by public agencies for the purpose of publication, which does not unduly infringe upon the secrecy and freedom of private life of individuals\\n   c. Information prepared or obtained by public agencies, where disclosure is deemed necessary for the public interest or for the relief of individual rights\\n   d. The name and position of a public official who performed duties\\n   e. Where disclosure is necessary for the public interest, the name and occupation of an individual to whom the State or a local government has entrusted or commissioned part of its duties pursuant to statutes\\n7. Information concerning the management or business secrets of a corporation, organization, or individual (hereinafter referred to as “corporations, etc.”), where disclosure is deemed likely to significantly harm the legitimate interests of corporations, etc. However, the following information shall be excluded:\\n   a. Information that is necessary to disclose in order to protect human life, body, or health from harm arising from business activities\\n   b. Information that is necessary to disclose in order to protect the property or livelihood of the people from unlawful or improper business activities\\n8. Information where disclosure is deemed likely to confer an advantage or disadvantage on a specific person through real-estate speculation, hoarding, or cornering, etc.\\n\\n[Relevant Provision]\\n\\nConstitution Article 50 (Principle of Open Proceedings)\\n① Meetings of the National Assembly shall be open to the public. However, they may not be open to the public when a majority of the members present so approve or when the Speaker deems it necessary for the security of the State.\\n② Matters concerning publication of the content of meetings not opened to the public shall be determined by statute.\\n\\n2. Summary of the Petitioners’ Arguments, Reasons for the Court’s Dismissal of the Application for Constitutional Review, and Opinions of Interested Institutions\\n\\nA. Summary of the Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\nThe principle of open proceedings of the National Assembly and the right to know of the people are core values of democracy and principles or rights of superior status; therefore, there must be a rational justification for restricting them, and even where there exists a necessity for non-disclosure, such restriction must be confined to the unavoidable minimum. Since the provisions under review allow meetings of a subcommittee to be closed by resolution of the subcommittee and thereby permit refusal to disclose the contents of the meeting, they violate the principle of openness of National Assembly meetings prescribed in Article 50(1) of the Constitution, infringe the people’s right to know, and also violate the principle against excessive restriction under Article 37(2) of the Constitution.\\n\\nB. Summary of the Reasons for the Court’s Dismissal of the Application for Constitutional Review\\n\\nIt is desirable that meetings of subcommittees of the National Assembly be disclosed to the public as much as possible; however, if meetings of subcommittees are disclosed, there is also a high possibility that politically promotional statements and voting made with the electorate in mind will be made, thereby causing substantive debate or conclusions desirable from the standpoint of the State as a whole to be sacrificed, and there is also a negative aspect in that it becomes difficult to perform the original function of eliciting political compromise while protected from social pressure.\\n\\nIn light of the principle of open proceedings, the purpose of establishing subcommittees, and their functions, etc., a decision by a subcommittee to close a meeting should be limited to cases where there are substantial grounds to deem that, if the contents of the statements and votes of the attendees concerning matters at the review stage of the subcommittee before the plenary session are disclosed in advance, it would significantly impede the fair performance of the committee’s duties; and, insofar as the statutory provision under review is interpreted in that manner, it should be regarded as seeking an appropriate harmony between the people’s right to know and the smooth operation of the subcommittee, and thus cannot be regarded as an unconstitutional provision that violates the principle of openness of National Assembly meetings or excessively infringes the people’s right to know.\\n\\nC. Summary of the Speaker of the National Assembly’s Opinion\\n\\n(1) The portion of the constitutional complaint concerning Article 118(4) of the National Assembly Act and Article 9(1) of the Information Disclosure Act, for which the Petitioners had not filed an application for a referral for constitutional review of laws, cannot be the subject of a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act, and is therefore inadmissible.\\n\\n(2) The proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act is a provision setting forth an indispensable exception for the purpose of promoting the smooth operation of subcommittees, and thus cannot be regarded as an unconstitutional provision contrary to the principle of openness of National Assembly meetings.\\n\\n(3) Meetings of subcommittees are, in principle, open to the public, and even where non-disclosure is exceptionally necessary, the procedure of a resolution by the members is required; and, pursuant to the proviso to Article 118(4) of the National Assembly Act, even where a meeting is closed, if it is determined by resolution of the plenary session or by the Speaker that the ground for non-disclosure has ceased to exist, such content may be published. Accordingly, the proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act cannot be said to be an unconstitutional provision that excessively restricts the people’s right to know and thereby violates the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n3. Determination on the Procedural Requirements for Adjudication\\n\\nA constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act may be filed only when an application for a referral for constitutional review of the constitutionality of a statute has been made and that application has been dismissed; therefore, if the petitioner did not apply for a referral for constitutional review of a particular statutory provision and thus there was no court decision dismissing such application, the petition for adjudication in that part is inadmissible for failure to satisfy the requirements for adjudication (Constitutional Court 1994. 4. 28. 89HEONMA221, Case Reports 6-1, 239, 256-257; Constitutional Court 2000. 7. 20. 98HEONBA74, Case Reports 12-2, 68, 76-77).\\n\\nLooking at the application for referral for constitutional review of laws submitted by the Petitioners attached to the records of this case, in filing the application for constitutional review, the Petitioners challenged only the constitutionality of the proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act, and did not challenge the constitutionality of Article 118(4) of the National Assembly Act or Article 9(1) of the Information Disclosure Act; accordingly, in the court’s decision dismissing the application for referral for constitutional review, only the proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act was addressed.\\n\\nIf so, the portion of the petition for adjudication concerning Article 118(4) of the National Assembly Act and Article 9(1) of the Information Disclosure Act is inadmissible without the need for further determination.\\n\\nAccordingly, the merits will hereinafter be determined only with respect to the proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Merits\\n\\nA. The Principle of Open Proceedings of the National Assembly and the Right to Know\\n\\n(1) Our Constitution proclaims the principle of open proceedings of the National Assembly in the main text of Article 50(1), stating that “Meetings of the National Assembly shall be open to the public.” This includes the freedom of attendance and reporting and the disclosure of minutes, etc. The principle of open proceedings originates from the democratic demand of putting into practice National Assembly operations based on the public will by disclosing the contents of proceedings and the activities of members to the people; only when debates and policy-making processes in the National Assembly are disclosed can the people, as sovereign, monitor and criticize legislative activities, and fairness in decision-making can be secured. Moreover, information is provided so that the people may understand the agenda and express opinions thereon, and real opportunities to participate in the process of national decision-making are afforded, thereby contributing to the formation of the people’s political will. Accordingly, the principle of open proceedings of the National Assembly is an indispensable element in representative democratic politics for enhancing public participation in state affairs through disclosure of public information and securing transparency in the administration of state affairs.\\n\\nIn light of the purport of these constitutional provisions, the people have the right to demand disclosure of the legislative process from the National Assembly as part of the right to know guaranteed by the Constitution, and with respect to the proceedings of the National Assembly, it may be said that they have a general right to request disclosure of information regardless of the existence or absence of direct legal interest.\\n\\n(2) However, the principle of open proceedings and the right to know are not absolute and may of course be limited by Article 21(4) of the Constitution, a clause of constitutional reservation, and by Article 37(2) of the Constitution, a general clause of statutory reservation (see Constitutional Court 1989. 9. 4. 88HEONMA22 et al., Case Reports 1, 190), and the general right to request disclosure of information derived from the right to know is likewise subject to the same. The proviso to Article 50(1) of the Constitution, which provides that “they may not be open to the public when a majority of the members present so approve or when the Speaker deems it necessary for the security of the State,” creates an exception to the principle of open proceedings and constitutes a constitutional reservation regarding the principle of open proceedings and the right to know. The proviso to the same paragraph does not place any restriction on the grounds for non-disclosure in cases where meetings are closed to the public by a “majority of the members present,” thereby recognizing the discretion of the National Assembly regarding whether proceedings are open.\\n\\nB. Relationship Between Article 50(1) of the Constitution and Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act, and Their Interpretation\\n\\n(1) Subcommittees established in the National Assembly are created under Article 57 of the National Assembly Act for the specialized and efficient examination of bills and other agenda items, and perform specific and substantive review of bills, preparation of amendments, and the foundational work for committee drafts.\\n\\nToday, as the center of National Assembly functions has shifted from the plenary session to committees and the National Assembly is being operated in a committee-centered manner, and given the reality that substantive deliberation on bills and other agenda items is conducted in committees, the principle of open proceedings of the National Assembly proclaimed in the main text of Article 50(1) of the Constitution also applies to committee meetings (see Constitutional Court 2000. 6. 29. 98HEONMA443 et al., Case Reports 12-1, 886, 896-898), and it should of course be regarded as applying to subcommittee meetings as well. Accordingly, the provision in the main text of Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act that “meetings of subcommittees shall be open to the public” merely confirms the principle of open proceedings of the National Assembly proclaimed in the main text of Article 50(1) of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Just as the principle of open proceedings in the main text of Article 50(1) of the Constitution applies to committees and subcommittees, it is also appropriate to view the provision concerning exceptional closure of meetings in the proviso to the same paragraph as applying not only to plenary sessions but also to committees and subcommittees.\\n\\nIf meetings of subcommittees were disclosed without exception, in some cases a member might focus on politically promotional statements and voting with an eye toward his or her own constituency, thereby distorting or narrowing the role as a representative of the people. In addition, there is no denying the risk that, in the process of handling bills, political expression free from various interest groups or social pressures may be adversely affected, and especially in the case of economic bills, merely disclosing the discussion process of the bill itself may unexpectedly affect the economy; moreover, disclosure of all statements and votes may rather risk undermining the essence of politics as a process of legitimate adjustment and compromise.\\n\\nThe proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act, inheriting the purport of the proviso to Article 50(1) of the Constitution, which allows autonomous judgment by the members of the meeting regarding whether meetings of the National Assembly are open to the public, also enables the subcommittee to reasonably determine whether to open a meeting by comprehensively considering various circumstances, such as the nature of the subcommittee’s work, the characteristics of the agenda items under review, the advantages and disadvantages of opening the meeting, and prior parliamentary practice (see Constitutional Court 2000. 6. 29. 98HEONMA443 et al., Case Reports 12-1, 899-900).\\n\\nIn other words, the proviso to the same paragraph is not a provision separately granting the subcommittee an inherent autonomous power, but merely reflects, in the case of subcommittees as well, the purport of the proviso to Article 50(1) of the Constitution, which constitutes a constitutional reservation regarding the principle of open proceedings of the National Assembly and the right to know.\\n\\n(3) In addition, Article 54 of the National Assembly Act provides that resolutions of committees shall be adopted by a majority of the full membership and a majority of the members present, and since this provision applies mutatis mutandis to subcommittees pursuant to Article 57(7) of the National Assembly Act, a procedural requirement of a majority of the members present must be satisfied for a resolution by a subcommittee to close a meeting, which may be seen as consistent with the constitutional provision that imposes procedural control by requiring a majority of the members present for a resolution to close a meeting of the National Assembly. Meanwhile, pursuant to Article 57(7), Article 71, and the proviso to Article 118(4) of the National Assembly Act, if it is determined after a decision to close a meeting that the ground for non-disclosure has ceased to exist, the contents of the meeting may be published by resolution of the subcommittee or by the decision of its chairperson.\\n\\nIn other words, the proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act does not relax the grounds and procedures for closing a meeting, etc., compared with the requirements for non-disclosure prescribed by the Constitution; thus, there is no room to view it as contrary to the principle of proportionality implicated when fundamental rights are restricted by statute. If the National Assembly Act were to broaden the non-disclosure area of subcommittees beyond what is prescribed by the proviso to Article 50(1) of the Constitution concerning non-disclosure of proceedings of the National Assembly, there would be room for a constitutional review as to the justification for restricting fundamental rights by statute; however, it should be regarded as not giving rise to any constitutional issue for the National Assembly Act to prescribe the non-disclosure requirements for subcommittee meetings more strictly than those prescribed by the Constitution and thereby to expand and carry out the constitutional principle of open proceedings, or, as in the proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act, to prescribe such requirements at a level equivalent to that of the constitutional provision.\\n\\n(4) Ultimately, the proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act merely carries over, as it is, to subcommittee meetings the content of the proviso to Article 50(1) of the Constitution, which prescribes the requirements for non-disclosure as an exception to the principle of open proceedings of the National Assembly; therefore, it cannot be said to violate Article 50(1) of the Constitution by infringing the people’s right to know regarding meetings of the National Assembly, nor can it be regarded as an unconstitutional provision that violates the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the Petitioners’ petition for adjudication concerning Article 118(4) of the National Assembly Act and Article 9(1) of the Information Disclosure Act is dismissed as inadmissible, and the proviso to Article 57(5) of the National Assembly Act does not violate the Constitution; accordingly, it is so decided with the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning Article 5 of the State Compensation Act is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: The term “public structure” means tangible objects or material facilities devoted by the State or a local government to a specific public purpose, and includes cases in which the State or a local government manages them on the basis of ownership, leasehold rights, or other authority, but does not include cases in which they are actually managed.
B: The term “defect in the installation or management of a public structure” means that a public structure devoted to a public purpose is in a condition that does not possess the safety it ordinarily should have according to its intended use.
C: The term “defect in the installation or management of a public structure” also includes cases in which, in the use of a public structure for a public purpose, the condition and degree of use exceed a certain limit and thereby cause damage to a third party beyond the limit that is expected to be tolerated under social norms.
D: If, after the installation of a road, a defect arises in its safety for passage, which is its original purpose, due to the conduct of a third party, the mere fact that the road has such a defect should not be used hastily to recognize a defect in the preservation of the road, and the existence or absence of a defect should be determined by individually and concretely examining whether, despite the possibility of removing such a defect and restoring it to its original condition by comprehensively considering all circumstances such as the structure of the road, the locational environment, and the conditions of use, it was left unattended.
E: Flooding of a river caused by rainfall with a 600-year or 1,000-year recurrence interval, exceeding the design flood level established on the basis of rainfall with a 100-year recurrence interval, is a force majeure disaster lacking foreseeability and avoidability, and liability cannot be imposed on the managing authority of the public structure.
