{"[94DA45302]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons given in the judgment of the court below, the court below, after recognizing the facts found and stated on the basis of the evidence cited, premised as follows: the accident in this case was caused by the Korea Motorsports Federation, under the non-party incorporated association Korea Society Sports Promotion Association, having forced through an automobile race at the planned site for the stadium in this case, which is owned by Defendant City, without installing sufficient safety facilities to the extent that the automobile race could be held safely, and by Defendant City also having left it unattended; consequently, the accident was caused by allowing the planned site for the stadium in this case to be used as an automobile-race venue in a state in which it lacked the safety that such an automobile-race venue should generally have. The court further held that, although the planned site for the stadium in this case was merely vacant land on which no scheduled facilities had been installed at the time of the accident and thus did not qualify as the so-called public thing in the doctrinal sense, namely a corporeal object directly provided by the State or a public body for a public purpose, since it had already been determined before the accident in this case to be a planned site for a stadium, it constituted the \"public structure\" prescribed in Article 5 of the State Compensation Act as the so-called planned public structure; and also, in this case, where Defendant City, the managing entity of the planned site for the stadium in this case, granted permission for its use as an automobile-race venue, Defendant City should have managed the planned site for the stadium in this case so as to have the degree of safety sufficient to hold the automobile race safely, but the accident in this case occurred at the planned site for the stadium in this case, which is a \"public structure,\" due to a defect in management arising from Defendant City's negligence in that regard; therefore, Defendant City, as its manager, is liable under Article 5 of the State Compensation Act to compensate the damage suffered by the Plaintiffs as a result of the accident in this case.\\n\\nTherefore, we shall examine whether the planned site for the stadium in this case is a \"public structure\" prescribed in Article 5, paragraph 1 of the State Compensation Act.\\n\\nThe above \"public structure\" refers to corporeal property or physical facilities devoted by the State or a local government to a specific public purpose (see the judgment of this Court rendered on 1981. 7. 7. in 80DA2478), and property devoted to a specific public purpose is not limited to public property directly provided for the free use of the general public, but also includes public property provided for use by the administrative entity itself, and includes not only cases where the State or a local government manages it on the basis of ownership, leasehold, or other authority, but also cases where it is managed de facto.\\n\\nHowever, according to the record, the planned site for the stadium in this case was merely designated as a planned site for a stadium while the non-party Industrial Base Development Corporation was carrying out a land readjustment project in the Ansan area; thereafter, although ownership transfer registration was completed in the name of Defendant City on 1989. 8. 28., it remained vacant land on which no facilities had been installed by the time of the accident in this case and was in a state in which public use had not commenced. In that state, as stated in the judgment of the court below, it was merely granted, at the request of the Korea Motorsports Federation, permission for use for the automobile-race meeting hosted by that Federation; Defendant City had not directly provided the planned site for the stadium in this case for use by the general public, and Defendant City also had not managed the safety facilities necessary for the automobile race, such as barriers installed on the land in this case by the Korea Motorsports Federation. Therefore, neither the planned site for the stadium in this case nor the above safety facilities installed thereon can be said to constitute the above \"public structure,\" and the judgment of the court below, which held otherwise and recognized Defendant City's damage liability as above on the premise that it was the above \"public structure,\" erred by misapprehending the legal principle concerning the \"public structure\" prescribed in Article 5 of the State Compensation Act, and such error affected the judgment.\\n\\nThe argument pointing out this point is well-founded.\\n\\nAccordingly, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below, and the Justices participating in the decision are unanimous; it is so adjudged as stated in the order."}

{"[97DA3194]": "1. Part Dismissing the Appeal\\n\\nAccording to the record, in this case the court of first instance rendered a judgment partially granting and partially dismissing the Plaintiffs’ claims, and both the Plaintiffs and the Defendant appealed with respect to their respective losing portions; it is clear that the appellate court, in the disposition and the reasons, adjudicated only the portion in which the Defendant lost under the judgment of the court of first instance, and did not adjudicate the portion in which the Plaintiffs lost. Therefore, the appellate court must be regarded as having omitted adjudication with respect to the portion on which the Plaintiffs lost at the court of first instance, and the Plaintiffs’ appeal concerning this portion has no subject matter and is unlawful, and thus cannot escape dismissal.\\n\\n2. We examine the grounds of appeal concerning the remaining portion that is not dismissed.\\n\\nA defect in the installation or management of a road should be specifically determined in accordance with social norms by comprehensively considering all circumstances, such as locational conditions including the road’s location, the road’s structure, traffic volume, traffic conditions at the time of an accident, the conditions of road use and its original purpose of use, and the location and form of the physical defect; where, after the installation of a road, a defect has arisen in the safety of passage, which is its original purpose, due to the act of a third party, the mere fact that such a defect exists on the road should not hastily lead to recognition of a defect in the preservation of the road, and the existence or absence of a defect must be determined by individually and specifically examining, in light of all circumstances including the structure of the relevant road, the locational environment, and the conditions of use, whether, despite the possibility of removing such defect and restoring it to its original condition, it was left unattended (see this Court’s Judgment rendered on 1992. 9. 14., 92DA3243).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the lower court judgment, the lower court, by comprehensively considering the evidence presented, found that Non-party Kim Gang-yeong, at around 10:30 on 1995. 11. 21., while driving a Pride passenger car on a two-lane national road located in Sam-ri, Nongong-myeon, Dalseong-gun, Daegu, which was possessed and managed by the Defendant, fell onto the first lane of the road in the opposite direction, and that a U-shaped iron pipe, 120 cm in length and 2 cm in diameter, lying there, was rebounded by the rear tire of a Galloper passenger car of unknown plate number and pierced the front windshield of Kim Gang-yeong’s passenger car, causing the iron pipe to stab his neck and resulting in his death from an open skull fracture, etc.; it recognized that, if such iron pipe had been lying on the above road, it could in the first instance be viewed as a defect in the management of the road, but, according to the evidence presented, a vehicle for the shift change of the personnel on duty at the overloading vehicle checkpoint operated by the Defendant passed the accident site between 09:57 and 10:08 on the day of the accident (33 to 22 minutes before the accident occurred) yet failed to discover the above iron pipe, and it determined that it was practically impossible for the Defendant to patrol the broad national road under its management at shorter intervals and remove fallen objects one by one, and thus held that the Defendant had no liability for damages as prescribed by Article 5(1) of the State Compensation Act. Upon review against the record, the above factual findings of the lower court are acceptable, and if the facts are as such, the lower court’s determination is also acceptable. It cannot be said that the lower court judgment contains any illegality, such as violation of the rules of evidence or misapprehension of the law, as alleged. All arguments lack merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, among the Plaintiffs’ appeal, the portion concerning the part as to which the lower court omitted adjudication is each dismissed, the remainder of the Plaintiffs’ appeal is dismissed in its entirety, and the costs of the appeal shall be borne by the losing parties, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the judges participating."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the following case are incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) An A startup enterprise, pursuant to the Small and Medium Enterprise Start-up Support Act, seeks to apply to Mayor A for approval of its factory establishment plan. Article 47 of the Act provides that, when Mayor A approves a factory establishment plan, with respect to a permit to occupy a river under Article 33 of the River Act, matters on which Mayor A has consulted with the river occupancy permit authority shall be deemed to have been granted the permit. (a) In order for A to be deemed to have been granted a permit to occupy a river, when applying for the above approval of the factory establishment plan, A must submit the documents necessary for the permit to occupy a river by the deadline separately prescribed by the river occupancy permit authority. (b) As to matters on which consultation has been reached between Mayor A and the river occupancy permit authority, it is deemed that the permit to occupy a river was granted at the time the consultation was concluded. (c) The river occupancy permit authority, when requested to consult by Mayor A, shall not respond to the consultation in violation of the River Act and its statutes and regulations, and with respect to procedures such as deliberation and hearing of opinions necessary for a permit to occupy a river, such procedures are followed only where there is an express statutory provision that those procedures are also to be followed in cases of deemed authorization/permission. (d) If a permit to occupy a river is deemed to have been granted, the river occupancy permit authority shall take necessary measures, including management and supervision, under the relevant statutes, as if it had directly granted the permit to occupy a river.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2020DU42569]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Relevant provisions and legal principles\\n\\nA. Article 33 of the Act on Assistance to Small and Medium Enterprise Startups (hereinafter referred to as the “SME Startup Act”) provides as follows regarding approval of business plans. A person starting a business who intends to engage in manufacturing may prepare a business plan in accordance with the Presidential Decree and conduct business with the approval of the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head (hereinafter referred to as the “Mayor, etc.”) therefor (Article 33(1), first sentence). The Mayor, etc. shall notify whether approval is granted within 20 days from the date of receipt of the application for approval of the business plan, and if such notification is not made within 20 days, approval shall be deemed to have been granted on the day following the day on which 20 days have elapsed (Article 33(3)). The purport of Article 33(3) of the SME Startup Act concerning the processing period for approval of a business plan and deemed approval is to promote the establishment of small and medium enterprises and foster their growth base by forcing simplification of the approval procedure for startup business plans and expeditious processing, thereby promoting the construction of a sound industrial structure through the sound development of small and medium enterprises (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DU23785 rendered on 2013. 3. 14.).\\n\\nThe main clause of Article 21(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, pursuant to the delegation under Article 18 of the Act on the Handling of Civil Petitions (hereinafter referred to as the “Civil Petitions Processing Act”), provides that “where the head of an administrative agency deems that it is difficult to process a civil petition within the processing period due to unavoidable circumstances, the processing period may be extended once within the scope of the processing period for that civil petition.” However, Article 3(1) of the Civil Petitions Processing Act provides that “with respect to civil petitions, except where there are special provisions in other Acts, the matters shall be governed by this Act.”\\n\\nB. Taking the content and structure of these provisions, as well as the legislative purpose, into comprehensive consideration, Article 33(3) of the SME Startup Act regarding the processing period and deemed approval of a civil petition for an application for approval of a business plan must be deemed to fall under the “where there are special provisions in other Acts” as provided in Article 3(1) of the Civil Petitions Processing Act. Therefore, the Mayor, etc. who has received an application for approval of a business plan has no discretion to arbitrarily extend the processing period pursuant to the main clause of Article 21(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Civil Petitions Processing Act, and if approval or disapproval is not notified within 20 days from the date of receipt of the application for approval of the business plan, a disposition approving the relevant business plan is deemed to have been made on the day following the day on which 20 days have elapsed, pursuant to Article 33(3) of the SME Startup Act.\\n\\nMeanwhile, according to Article 35(1) and (4) of the SME Startup Act, when the Mayor, etc. approves a business plan, with respect to the relevant permits and licenses prescribed in each item of paragraph (1), matters on which consultation has been conducted with the head of the competent administrative agency are deemed to have obtained such relevant permits and licenses. The legislative purpose of this system of deemed permits and licenses is to simplify administrative procedures by unifying the window for the smooth implementation of the intended business, and it is not intended to exclude review of whether the intended business satisfies the substantive requirements for permits and licenses under the relevant statutes. Therefore, only with respect to matters on which prior consultation has been conducted with the competent administrative agency before the Mayor, etc. approves the business plan, does the effect of deeming the relevant permit or license to have been granted arise when the business plan approval disposition is made (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2018DU43095 rendered on 2018. 10. 25.).\\n\\nEven if, without prior consultation on matters concerning the relevant permits and licenses, the business plan approval disposition is deemed to have been made on the day following the day on which the 20-day processing period prescribed in Article 33(3) of the SME Startup Act has elapsed, the entrepreneur merely acquires the status of having received a business plan approval disposition under the SME Startup Act, and does not acquire the status of having received the relevant permits and licenses as well. Therefore, the entrepreneur must separately go through the procedure of applying to the competent administrative agency for the relevant permits and licenses necessary to establish the factory. If, after the entrepreneur has applied for a development activity permit under the Act on the Planning and Use of National Territory necessary to establish the factory, a refusal disposition is rendered and its effect becomes final and no longer contestable due to reasons such as the lapse of the period for filing a lawsuit, the Mayor, etc. may also, ex officio, revoke the business plan approval disposition under the SME Startup Act on the ground that the establishment of the factory is objectively impossible (see Supreme Court Decision 2019DU31839 rendered on 2020. 7. 23.).\\n\\n2. Determination in this case\\n\\nA. The court below determined that, on 2018. 7. 14., the day following the day on which 20 days had elapsed from the date of the Plaintiff’s application for approval of the business plan, the effect arose that a business plan approval disposition had been made pursuant to Article 33(3) of the SME Startup Act, and that the disposition in this case dated 2018. 8. 3., premised on the Defendant’s ability to arbitrarily extend the processing period, was unlawful.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the judgment below is proper, and there is no error of law in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the processing period for approval of a business plan and the deemed approval system prescribed in Article 33(3) of the SME Startup Act.\\n\\nB. The Defendant contends that the disposition in this case dated 2018. 8. 3. is proper as a disposition that, ex officio, cancels or revokes the business plan approval disposition for which the deemed effect arose on 2018. 7. 14. However, according to the clear wording of the written disposition for the disposition in this case dated 2018. 8. 3. (Exhibit A No. 1), it is evident that the disposition in this case is a “refusal disposition” regarding the Plaintiff’s application for a business plan, and not a “cancellation/revocation disposition” of a business plan approval premised on the fact that a business plan approval disposition had already been made; therefore, the Defendant’s argument cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Defendant’s appeal is without merit and is dismissed, and the costs of the appeal are borne by the losing party. Accordingly, it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Supreme Court Justices."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning administrative planning is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: If, in formulating and deciding an administrative plan, an administrative entity omits a matter that ought properly to have been included among the considerations in balancing interests, that administrative planning decision constitutes an abuse or excess of discretion.
B: Under the former Urban Planning Act, a resident who owns land, etc. within an urban planning area has a statutory or legal-principle right to request the person with authority to draft the urban plan to do so.
C: Under the Industrial Sites and Development Act, a person who, as the landowner of land within an industrial complex under an industrial complex development plan, intends to install facilities conforming to the industrial complex development plan and move in, has no statutory or legal-principle right to request the industrial complex designating authority to amend the industrial complex development plan.
D: A management disposition plan established by a housing reconstruction improvement project association pursuant to the Act on the Maintenance and Improvement of Urban Areas and Dwelling Conditions for Residents constitutes a binding administrative plan.
E:
Under the former National Land Use Management Act, where refusing an application for amendment of a national land use plan by a person in a legal position to file, within a certain future period, an application seeking a certain administrative disposition by equipping the facilities, etc. prescribed by the relevant statutes, practically results in a refusal of the administrative disposition itself, the applicant is recognized as having the right to apply for a change in the national land use plan.

A: 
B: 
C: 
D: 
E:

{"[2007DA2428]": "Before addressing the grounds for appeal, the Court examines ex officio.\\n\\n1. A housing reconstruction and improvement project association under the Act on the Maintenance and Improvement of Urban Areas and Dwelling Conditions for Residents (hereinafter referred to as the “Urban Improvement Act”) (hereinafter referred to as a “reconstruction association”) is a public-law corporation (Article 18 of the Urban Improvement Act) that implements a housing reconstruction project under the Urban Improvement Act under the supervision of the competent administrative agency, and as such has the status of an administrative entity that performs certain administrative acts in accordance with what is prescribed by statutes within the scope of its purpose. And a management and disposal plan established by a reconstruction association in the status of an administrative entity pursuant to Article 48 of the Urban Improvement Act determines matters concerning the attribution of rights in land or structures created as a result of the implementation of the maintenance project and matters concerning the allocation of expenses among members, thereby directly and concretely affecting the proprietary rights and obligations of the members, etc.; accordingly, it constitutes a binding administrative plan and an independent administrative disposition made by the reconstruction association (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 94DA31235, rendered on February 15, 1996, and Supreme Court Decision 2005DU11951, rendered on September 6, 2007, etc.).\\n\\nHowever, because a management and disposal plan becomes effective only when the reconstruction association prepares a draft management and disposal plan on the basis of the status of the members’ applications for allotment, then goes through the association’s general meeting resolution thereon and the public inspection procedure for owners of land, etc., and thereafter obtains authorization and public notice from the competent administrative agency (Article 24, paragraph 3, item 10, Article 48, paragraph 1, and Article 49 of the Urban Improvement Act), the association’s general meeting resolution on the draft management and disposal plan is one of the procedural requirements leading to the administrative disposition known as the management and disposal plan, and if it is unlawful and thus ineffective, the management and disposal plan becomes defective.\\n\\nAccordingly, a lawsuit against the administrative entity, namely the reconstruction association, disputing the validity, etc. of the association’s general meeting resolution on the draft management and disposal plan is a lawsuit concerning the existence or validity of a procedural requirement leading to an administrative disposition, and because it concerns a public-law legal relationship that directly affects whether the administrative disposition is unlawful depending on the outcome of the lawsuit, it constitutes a party suit under the Administrative Litigation Act.\\n\\nAnd such a lawsuit may, before authorization and public notice of the management and disposal plan, prevent a defective management and disposal plan from proceeding to the stage where it is authorized and publicly notified and becomes effective as an administrative disposition by obtaining a judgment confirming the nullity of the unlawful general meeting resolution and submitting it as materials to the competent administrative agency or by causing the reconstruction association to prepare a new lawful draft management and disposal plan and undergo the general meeting resolution again; further, even if the management and disposal plan is authorized and publicly notified notwithstanding a judgment confirming the nullity of the general meeting resolution, the dispute may be resolved promptly by utilizing the judgment and evidence from the action for confirmation of nullity of the general meeting resolution as litigation materials in an administrative appeal action disputing the validity of the management and disposal plan. Therefore, prior to authorization and public notice of the management and disposal plan, it must be permitted.\\n\\nHowever, once the competent administrative agency authorizes and publicly notifies the management and disposal plan, the management and disposal plan acquires effect as an administrative disposition; accordingly, the validity of the management and disposal plan must be challenged by way of an administrative appeal action seeking revocation or confirmation of nullity of the management and disposal plan on the ground of defects in the general meeting resolution, and, absent special circumstances, it should be deemed impermissible to separately sever only the portion concerning the general meeting resolution, which is merely one of the procedural requirements leading to the administrative disposition, and file an action for confirmation disputing its validity.\\n\\nTo the extent that Supreme Court Decision 2004DA13694, rendered on July 22, 2004, which held, contrary to the foregoing, that an action for confirmation of nullity of a general meeting resolution on a draft management and disposal plan of a redevelopment association under the Urban Redevelopment Act (repealed by Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the Act on the Maintenance and Improvement of Urban Areas and Dwelling Conditions for Residents, Act No. 6852, December 30, 2002) is a civil action and that, even after authorization and public notice of the management and disposal plan, nullity of the general meeting resolution may still be sought by lawsuit, and the Supreme Court decisions to the same effect are inconsistent with the view of this judgment, all such decisions are hereby modified accordingly.\\n\\n2. According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the record, it is apparent that the lawsuit in this case was filed on March 11, 2005, before authorization and public notice of the management and disposal plan, seeking against the Defendant, a reconstruction association under the Urban Improvement Act, a declaration of nullity of the general meeting resolution on the draft management and disposal plan; as seen above, this constitutes a party suit under the Administrative Litigation Act, and therefore the court of exclusive jurisdiction at first instance in this case is the Seoul Administrative Court.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court of first instance and the court below proceeded to adjudicate on the merits, overlooking that this case was filed with the Seoul Central District Court in violation of exclusive jurisdiction; thus, the determinations of the court of first instance and the court below contain an error of law in misunderstanding the legal doctrine on party suits under the Administrative Litigation Act and violating the provisions concerning exclusive jurisdiction.\\n\\nMeanwhile, since on March 18, 2005, after this lawsuit was filed, the competent administrative agency authorized and publicly notified the management and disposal plan in this case, it may be said that it is no longer possible to separately seek only a declaration of nullity of the general meeting resolution. However, in light of the possibility that, after transfer, the case may be changed to an action for revocation of the management and disposal plan with permission from the administrative court, it is difficult to deem that circumstance alone to amount to a case in which, after transfer, this lawsuit clearly becomes improper and must be dismissed; accordingly, it is appropriate to transfer this case to the court with jurisdiction (see Supreme Court Decision 95DA28960, rendered on May 30, 1997, and Supreme Court Decision 2007DA25261, rendered on July 24, 2008, etc.).\\n\\n3. Therefore, without addressing the grounds for appeal, the Court, ex officio, sets aside the judgment below, reverses the judgment of first instance, and transfers the case to the court with jurisdiction for further proceedings and determination, and so, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, renders judgment as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[2016DU44186]": "The grounds of appeal are considered (the statements in a supplemental statement of grounds of appeal submitted after the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal are considered within the scope of supplementing the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Right to Request Amendment of the Industrial Complex Development Plan (Point 1 of the Grounds of Appeal)\\n\\na. The Act on Industrial Location and Development (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) was enacted for the purpose of contributing to the sound development of the national economy by promoting balanced national land development and sustainable industrial development through the smooth supply of industrial sites and the rational allocation of industry (Article 1), and regulates industrial complexes. Under this Act, an industrial complex includes a tract of land designated and developed in accordance with a comprehensive plan in order to collectively install facilities installed on land for industrial facilities and residential, cultural, environmental, park and green space, medical, tourism, sports, welfare facilities, etc. related thereto, as well as education, research, office, support, information processing, and distribution facilities, for the purpose of improving the functions of these facilities (Article 2, Item 8 of the Act).\\n\\nThe authority to designate and alter a national industrial complex belongs to the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport (Article 6(1) of the Act), and the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport must formulate an industrial complex development plan in order to designate a national industrial complex (Article 6(3) of the Act). The authority of the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport may be delegated in whole or in part to a Mayor/Provincial Governor, a Mayor/County Governor/District Head, or the head of a subordinate agency, as prescribed by Presidential Decree (Article 49 of the Act), and the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport has delegated the authority concerning the amendment of the development plan for a national industrial complex to the Mayor/Provincial Governor [Article 49(1) Item 1 of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on Industrial Location and Development (hereinafter referred to as the “Enforcement Decree”)].\\n\\nMeanwhile, according to Article 11(1) of the Act, Article 13(1) of the Enforcement Decree, Article 16(1) Items 3 and 6 of the Act, etc., a person who intends to install facilities suitable for an industrial complex and move in, and an owner, etc. of land within an industrial complex, may prepare an industrial complex development plan and request the industrial complex designating authority to designate the area as a national industrial complex, etc. Such “facilities suitable for the industrial complex development plan” include waste treatment facilities [Article 16(1) Item 3 of the Act, Article 2(9) sub-item (a) of the Act], and the industrial complex development plan includes a land use plan and a major infrastructure plan, etc., which are the main subjects of regulation under the Act on the Planning and Use of National Territory (Article 6(5) Item 6 of the Act).\\n\\nWhere an industrial complex is designated pursuant to a request for designation as a national industrial complex, etc., the person who requested the designation may be designated as the project implementer (Article 11(3) of the Act). On the other hand, if the industrial complex designating authority determines that it is not appropriate to designate the area for which designation of an industrial complex has been requested as an industrial complex, the authority shall notify the person who made the request of the reason therefor, or select and notify an appropriate alternative site among other industrial complexes under development by the State or a local government (Article 13(6) of the Enforcement Decree). Furthermore, where the industrial complex designating authority intends to designate an industrial complex or alter important matters prescribed by Presidential Decree, it must give public notice thereof and hear opinions from residents and relevant experts, etc., and where such opinions are found to be valid, they shall be reflected (Article 10 of the Act). Such important matters include changes to the land use plan and major infrastructure plan that are included in the contents of the industrial complex development plan (Article 7(1) Item 3 of the Enforcement Decree).\\n\\nb. As above, the statutes concerning industrial sites recognize for persons who intend to install facilities suitable for an industrial complex and move in, and for landowners, the authority to formulate an industrial complex development plan related to the designation of an industrial complex, and also contain provisions guaranteeing procedural rights for interested persons not only with respect to the designation of an industrial complex but also with respect to its alteration. In addition, industrial complexes include numerous infrastructure facilities and other urban planning facilities, etc., and under the interpretation of the Act on the Planning and Use of National Territory, it is understood that the owner of land for urban planning facilities is recognized as having a statutory or logical right to request changes, etc. to the relevant urban/county management plan (see Supreme Court Decision 2014DU42742, decided March 26, 2015). In light of the purpose of the constitutional guarantee of property rights, it may be deemed justified to recognize such procedural rights and right to apply in favor of the landowner. It is appropriate to hold that this legal principle may likewise apply where, after an industrial complex has already been designated, a person who is the owner of land within the industrial complex and intends to install facilities suitable for the industrial complex development plan and move in requests an amendment of the existing plan.\\n\\nTherefore, a person who, as the owner of land within an industrial complex under the industrial complex development plan, intends to install facilities suitable for the industrial complex development plan and move in has a statutory or logical right to apply to the industrial complex designating authority or an agency delegated with authority by it for an amendment of the industrial complex development plan, and a refusal to grant such application must be regarded as an administrative disposition subject to an administrative appeal action.\\n\\nc. According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the record, the Plaintiff owned the project site within the industrial complex at issue, which had originally been designated as green land under the industrial complex development plan, and it can be seen that the Plaintiff filed an application with the Defendant requesting that the industrial complex development plan for the project site be amended from the original green land designation to waste treatment facility land in order to carry on a waste treatment business on the project site (hereinafter referred to as “the application in this case”).\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above, since the Defendant’s refusal of the application in this case may be deemed an administrative disposition, the judgment of the court below, which proceeded to decide the merits on that premise, is proper. There is no error in the court below’s determination, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misconstruing the legal principles regarding the nature of a disposition.\\n\\n2. Illegality of the Disposition in This Case (Point 2 of the Grounds of Appeal)\\n\\na. Interpretation of an Administrative Disposition\\n\\n(1) Where an administrative agency has made a disposition in writing, unless there are special circumstances such as ambiguity in the wording of the written disposition, it must be determined what disposition was made according to the wording. Even though the wording of the written disposition alone clearly shows what disposition the administrative agency made, it may not be expansively interpreted to include another disposition different from the wording of the written disposition by taking into consideration other circumstances, such as the circumstances leading to the disposition or the attitude of the other party after the disposition (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2016DU42449, decided October 13, 2016).\\n\\n(2) According to the reasoning of the judgment below, the Defendant, on April 10, 2015, issued the disposition in this case, refusing the application in this case on the ground that “under the land use plan of the industrial complex development plan in this case, the project site in this case is designated as green land, so the location of a waste landfill is not permitted, and amending the development plan to convert the green land into land for waste treatment facilities is also not permitted” (hereinafter referred to as “the ground for the disposition in this case”).\\n\\n(3) The court below erred in determining, contrary to the above, that the ground for the disposition in this case was that “if the application in this case is accepted, the green space ratio prescribed by the former Integrated Guidelines on the Development of Industrial Sites (as in effect before amendment by Notice of the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport No. 2015-650 dated September 8, 2015) would decrease, which would have a negative effect on maintaining that ratio.”\\n\\nb. Presentation of the Grounds and Reasons for an Administrative Disposition\\n\\n(1) When an administrative agency makes a disposition, it must, in principle, present the grounds and reasons therefor to the party concerned (Article 23(1) of the Administrative Procedures Act). Where the agency makes a disposition refusing a permit, etc. sought by a party and presents reasons to the extent that the party can know the grounds therefor, the disposition cannot be deemed unlawful merely because the grounds and reasons for the disposition were not specifically stated (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DU8912, decided May 17, 2002). Here, the expression “where reasons are presented” means a case in which, by comprehensively considering the contents stated in the written disposition, the relevant statutes, and the overall process leading to the disposition, it is recognized that the party concerned could sufficiently understand, at the time of the disposition, on what grounds and for what reasons the disposition was made, and thus had no particular impediment in proceeding to administrative relief procedures in contesting it (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DU20362, decided December 10, 2009).\\n\\n(2) In order to say that the Defendant, in refusing the application in this case seeking amendment of the existing industrial complex development plan, presented reasons, it should have enabled the party concerned to know the substantive reasons for the refusal, such as that granting the application would violate statutes or that no change in circumstances warranting amendment of the existing plan was recognized.\\n\\n(3) As seen above, the written disposition in this case merely notified the result of a simple refusal of the application without any substantive content. Even if one examines the overall process leading to the disposition in this case as shown in the record, no circumstance can be found indicating that the Plaintiff knew or could know the precise reason why the application in this case was denied. Thus, insofar as the Plaintiff argued in this lawsuit by incorrectly identifying the ground for the disposition, and the courts also proceeded with the proceedings based on the incorrectly identified ground for the disposition up to the court below, it cannot be said that the Plaintiff had no impediment in proceeding to administrative relief procedures in contesting the disposition. In such circumstances, the disposition in this case must be deemed unlawful as one made without presenting the grounds and reasons.\\n\\nAlthough the judgment below erred in its reasoning by misconstruing the legal principles concerning the interpretation of an administrative disposition and the presentation of the grounds and reasons for a disposition, its conclusion that the disposition in this case was unlawful and therefore upholding the Plaintiff’s claim is ultimately proper. Such error by the court below did not affect the outcome of the judgment.\\n\\n3. Whether Additional Grounds for an Administrative Disposition May Be Asserted (Point 3 of the Grounds of Appeal)\\n\\nIn an administrative appeal action seeking revocation of an administrative disposition, the agency may not assert, as grounds for the disposition, separate facts that are not identical in basic factual relation to the reasons originally presented as the grounds for the disposition (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DU10883, decided April 15, 2005, etc.).\\n\\nIn this lawsuit, the Defendant additionally asserted, as grounds for the refusal disposition in this case, that “there is no urgent need to secure new waste facility land within the industrial complex in this case.” However, insofar as the reasons originally presented by the Defendant as the basis for the disposition are deemed to have no substantive content, the above additional reason is not even subject to a determination as to whether it is identical in basic factual relation thereto, and ultimately, additional grounds for the disposition cannot be asserted at the litigation stage.\\n\\nAccordingly, it was not appropriate for the court below to regard even the above additional reason as a ground for the disposition in this case and to determine the legality of the disposition. However, as seen above, insofar as the conclusion of the court below that the disposition in this case was unlawful is proper, such error by the court below does not affect the outcome of the judgment. The grounds of appeal on this point are also not accepted.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Defendant’s appeal is without merit and is therefore dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2020DU34346]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case and Issues\\na. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below and the record, the following circumstances can be ascertained.\\n(1) The Plaintiff operates “□□□□ Park,” a funeral facility complex consisting of a funeral hall, cemetery, tree burial grounds, an ossuary, and the like, in the area of Gyeonggi, ○○eup, △△ri (lot number 1 omitted).\\n(2) The Plaintiff formulated a business plan to install and operate a crematorium as an “urban and county planning facility” on 4,995 square meters (hereinafter referred to as the “land at issue”) out of five parcels, including Gyeonggi, ○○eup, △△ri (lot number 2 omitted), which adjoin the site of □□□□ Park, after being designated as the implementing entity of the urban and county planning facility project, and on 2018. 5. 10. proposed to the Defendant the drafting of a change to the urban and county management plan.\\n(3) Approximately one-half of the land at issue is designated as a “conservation management area” under Article 36(1) of the Act on the Planning and Use of National Territory (hereinafter referred to as the “National Land Planning Act”), and the remainder is designated as a “planned management area” under the same provision. Approximately 150 m from the land at issue is the military apartment housing of the neighboring military unit, and approximately 360 m away is the village hall of △△◇ri.\\n(4) On the ground that the land at issue is only 2 to 3 km from the main downtown core of ○○eup, that there are villages, a military unit, and military apartment housing nearby, and that it is an area in which the resident population is continuously increasing due to the rise in development of rural housing sites, so that the surrounding residential environment is likely to deteriorate, the Defendant, on 2018. 5. 25., issued the disposition at issue refusing the Plaintiff’s proposal for drafting.\\nb. The issue in this case is whether the disposition at issue contains a defect of deviation from or abuse of the Defendant’s discretion concerning the drafting of the urban and county management plan.\\n\\n2. Relevant Provisions and Legal Principles\\na. Under the National Land Planning Act, infrastructure means facilities that must be basically supplied for urban communal life, but which require public intervention in decisions on their location, installation, and management because of their strong public nature or external economies. Article 2 of the National Land Planning Act provides “health and sanitation facilities such as funeral facilities” as one of the infrastructure items [subparagraph 6 (b)], and defines “urban and county planning facilities” as facilities determined by an urban and county management plan among infrastructure facilities (subparagraph 7), and “urban and county planning facility project” as a project to install, improve, or upgrade urban and county planning facilities (subparagraph 10). Rule 8(1) of the Rules on the Determination, Structure, and Installation Standards of Urban and County Planning Facilities, delegated under Article 43(2) of the National Land Planning Act, provides that, when making a determination on urban and county planning facilities, environmental, ecosystem, and natural landscape damage shall be minimized.\\nMeanwhile, according to Article 36(1) 2 (a) and (c) of the National Land Planning Act, a “conservation management area” means an area that needs to be preserved for the protection of the natural environment, forest protection, prevention of water pollution, securing green space, and conservation of the ecosystem, but that is difficult to designate and manage as a natural environment conservation area in light of its relationship with surrounding land-use zones, etc.; and a “planned management area” means an area expected to be incorporated into an urban area or an area in which limited use and development is to be made in consideration of the natural environment, and that requires planned and systematic management.\\nb. An administrative plan is set as a standard of activity to realize a certain order at a certain point in the future by comprehensively coordinating relevant administrative means based on professional and technical judgment in order to achieve a specific administrative objective. Since the National Land Planning Act and other relevant statutes stipulate only abstract administrative objectives and procedures, and do not contain any special provisions regarding the contents of administrative plans, the administrative body has broad discretion in the drafting and determination of specific administrative plans. However, such discretion in formation is not unlimited; it is subject to the limitation that the relevant public and private interests must be compared and balanced. Where, in drafting and determining an administrative plan, the administrative body does not conduct such balancing of interests at all, or omits matters that should properly be included among the subjects of consideration in the balancing of interests, or where it did conduct the balancing of interests but lacks legitimacy and objectivity, it must be deemed illegal as a deviation from or abuse of discretion (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DU1893, rendered on 2007. 4. 12., etc.).\\nThe discretionary determination by an administrative agency concerning requirements that require predictions of uncertain situations and ripple effects to arise in the future, such as “effects on the natural environment and living environment,” should be broadly respected unless its content is markedly unreasonable or there are circumstances such that, when contrasted with opposing interests or values, it is clearly contrary to the principle of equity or proportionality. In such a case, the fact alone that an appraisal opinion differing in part from the administrative agency’s original forecast or assessment has been presented should not readily lead to the conclusion that the administrative agency’s determination is unlawful (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DU55490, rendered on 2017. 3. 15., etc.). In addition, in this context, the development project itself should not be separately taken as the object of review for its effects on the living environment and natural environment; rather, based on the existing surrounding living environment and natural environment, the subject of review should be whether, if the relevant development project is additionally realized, it is likely to cause what total and cumulative adverse effects on the surrounding environment (see Supreme Court Decision 2020DU36007, rendered on 2020. 7. 23., etc.).\\n\\n3. Determination in this Case\\na. The circumstances seen above are examined in light of the relevant legal principles and provisions. Since the land at issue is designated as a conservation management area and a planned management area under the National Land Planning Act, unless there are special circumstances making it difficult to conclude that, due to changes in circumstances after designation, the forest and green space have already been damaged to such an extent that recovery is impossible and there is no longer any need to maintain the existing planning restrictions, the Defendant’s discretionary determination refusing the drafting of an urban and county management plan to install a crematorium on the land at issue as an urban and county planning facility should be broadly respected, on the view that the need to preserve its natural environment remains high. In addition, in a situation where the Plaintiff is already operating a memorial park consisting of a funeral hall, cemetery, ossuary, and the like, it is not easy to conclude that the total and cumulative impact on the living environment of residents living in nearby villages and military apartment housing would not be very great if a crematorium were additionally installed and operated there. Therefore, even considering the circumstances stated by the court below, such as the public necessity for installing a crematorium, it is difficult to conclude that the disposition at issue refusing the Plaintiff’s proposal for drafting lacked legitimacy and objectivity and thus constituted a deviation from or abuse of discretion.\\nb. Nevertheless, the court below determined that the disposition at issue contained a defect of deviation from or abuse of discretion solely on the basis of the circumstances as stated in its holding. The judgment of the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning administrative plans and the standards for determining deviation from or abuse of discretion, and by failing to conduct the necessary deliberation.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so decided, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the case are correct? (In case of a dispute, according to case law) The Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport approved a project under the Act on the Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects (hereinafter referred to as the “Land Compensation Act”) for a project to develop sports facilities within an urban park, using as the site a large tract of land owned by A located within the jurisdiction of A Metropolitan City, which A Metropolitan City was promoting; and, since consultation with A did not reach agreement, A Metropolitan City, as the project implementer, went through an expropriation award by the Central Land Expropriation Committee. (a). Even if there is a defect amounting to a ground for revocation in the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport’s project approval under the Land Compensation Act, A cannot file an administrative lawsuit seeking revocation of the expropriation award on the ground that the project approval was unlawful and the period for filing a lawsuit has expired. (b). A may file an objection with the Central Land Expropriation Committee within 30 days from the date on which A received the authenticated copy of the expropriation award, and when the Central Land Expropriation Committee finds that the expropriation award is unlawful or improper, it may cancel all or part of it or order A Metropolitan City to change the amount of compensation. (c). If A has gone through the objection procedure but wishes to challenge again, A may file an administrative lawsuit against the Central Land Expropriation Committee’s ruling on objection within 90 days from the date on which A received the written ruling. (d). If A files an administrative lawsuit against the expropriation award without going through the objection procedure, A must file the lawsuit within 60 days from the date on which A received the authenticated copy of the award. (e). In an administrative lawsuit concerning increase or decrease of compensation money, when the person filing the lawsuit is A, A Metropolitan City shall be the defendant, and when the person filing the lawsuit is A Metropolitan City, A shall be the defendant.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2008DU1504]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\nArticle 85(1), first sentence, of the Act on the Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects (hereinafter referred to as the “Public Works Act”) provides that where a project operator, landowner, or interested party is dissatisfied with an expropriation adjudication by the Central Land Expropriation Committee or a local Land Expropriation Committee, such party may institute an administrative action within 60 days from the date of receipt of the written adjudication, and where an objection has been filed, may institute an administrative action within 30 days from the date of receipt of the written adjudication on the objection.\\n\\nIn light of the textual content of Article 85(1), first sentence, of the Public Works Act as stated above, the fact that Articles 83 and 85 of the Public Works Act provide that an objection to the Central Land Expropriation Committee is an optional procedure, and the fact that the proviso to Article 19 of the Administrative Litigation Act provides that an adjudication on an administrative appeal may be subject to an action for revocation only where the adjudication itself contains an inherent illegality, it should be deemed that, when instituting an action for revocation in dissatisfaction with an expropriation adjudication, even if an objection procedure has been gone through, the action must be brought against the Central Land Expropriation Committee or the local Land Expropriation Committee that rendered the expropriation adjudication, seeking revocation of the expropriation adjudication; however, where the ground is that the adjudication on the objection itself contains an inherent illegality, the action for revocation of the objection adjudication may be brought against the Central Land Expropriation Committee that rendered the objection adjudication.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, on the ground that, where an objection adjudication by the Central Land Expropriation Committee has been gone through in dissatisfaction with an expropriation adjudication, in an administrative action seeking revocation of the expropriation adjudication itself, only the Central Land Expropriation Committee that rendered the objection adjudication has standing to be sued, dismissed the portion of the action seeking revocation of the expropriation adjudication against the Defendant Central Land Expropriation Committee that rendered the expropriation adjudication. The judgment of the court below contains an error affecting the conclusion of the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the subject matter of litigation and standing to be sued in the case of instituting an action for revocation in dissatisfaction with an expropriation adjudication. The portion of the grounds of appeal pointing out this issue is well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, the part of the judgment below concerning the claim for revocation of the expropriation adjudication against the Defendant Central Land Expropriation Committee, and the part against the Defendant Republic of Korea that need to be conclusively determined together therewith, are reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2009DU11607]": "1. We examine the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal (with respect to the contents of the supplemental explanation of grounds of appeal submitted after the period for filing a statement of grounds of appeal has expired, only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal stated in the petition of appeal).\\nSince the court of final appeal may investigate and determine only within the extent of the appeal filed on the grounds of appeal, the statement of grounds of appeal must specify the grounds of appeal and set forth concrete and explicit reasons as to which points of the judgment of the court below violated what laws and regulations; therefore, where the statement of grounds of appeal submitted by the appellant does not contain such concrete and explicit statement of reasons as above, it can only be treated as if no statement of grounds of appeal had been filed (see Supreme Court Decision 97DA55126 rendered on March 27, 1998, Supreme Court Decision 2004DA25185 rendered on March 9, 2006, etc.).\\nAccording to the record, the court below rendered a judgment dismissing the portion of the action seeking confirmation of invalidity in this case while, on the other hand, granting the Plaintiff’s claim seeking revocation of the expropriation award in this case, and it can be seen that the Plaintiff filed an appeal only with respect to the dismissal portion of the judgment of the court below. However, in the petition of appeal containing the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal, grounds of appeal are stated only with respect to the portion of the court below’s determination that granted the Plaintiff’s claim for revocation of the expropriation award in this case; accordingly, such statement of grounds of appeal fails to specify the grounds of appeal and to set forth concrete and explicit reasons as to which point of the judgment of the court below, which dismissed the action on the portion seeking confirmation of invalidity in this case, violated what laws and regulations, and thus cannot be deemed a lawful statement of grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. We examine the Defendant’s grounds of appeal.\\nAccording to the reasoning of the judgment of the court below, the court below found that the paddy field of 2,017㎡, lot No. 423-7, Bucheong-dong, Nonsan-si, owned by the Plaintiff, was subdivided on September 22, 2006 into a paddy field of 1,911㎡, lot No. 423-7, same dong, and a paddy field of 106㎡, lot No. 423-16, same dong; that the Head of the Daejeon Regional Land Management Office, when issuing on February 14, 2007 the notice of approval of the second amended project implementation plan at issue, stated in the land itemized statement attached thereto (No. 2882) that 141㎡ out of the Plaintiff-owned paddy field of 2,017㎡, lot No. 423-7, Bucheong-dong, Nonsan-si, would be expropriated and 124㎡ would be used; that the Defendant, on November 23, 2007, made the expropriation award at issue providing for expropriation with respect to the said paddy field of 106㎡, lot No. 423-16 (hereinafter referred to as the “land subject to expropriation”), and use with respect to 124㎡ out of the said paddy field of 1,911㎡, lot No. 423-7 (hereinafter referred to as the “land subject to use”); and then, the court below held that “141㎡ out of the paddy field of 2,017㎡, lot No. 423-7, Bucheong-dong, Nonsan-si,” stated in the notice of approval of the second amended project implementation plan at issue had a different lot number and area from the said paddy field of 106㎡, lot No. 423-16, which was already subdivided at the time of the notice and was the land subject to expropriation at issue, and thus could not be regarded as a lawful notice with respect to the land subject to expropriation at issue; and further, in light of the fact that the land subject to expropriation amounted to only 141㎡, approximately 7% of the total land area of 2,017㎡, and the land subject to use amounted to only 124㎡, approximately 6%, the contents of the said notice alone could not be deemed to represent the land subject to expropriation and the land subject to use at issue, or to have specified the objects thereof, and thus the said notice was invalid as a disposition with grave and obvious defects; and the expropriation award at issue based on such invalid notice was also unlawful.\\nHowever, the above determination of the court below is difficult to accept.\\nIf, in the public notice of permission for an urban planning project, the notice of land items is omitted, or, in granting project approval, the procedure for publicizing the particulars of the land to be expropriated or used is omitted, this constitutes a procedural illegality and may be a ground for revocation that can be contested at the project-approval stage prior to the expropriation-award stage, but it is difficult to further regard it as a grave and obvious defect that would render the project approval itself void; accordingly, on the basis of such illegality, one cannot seek revocation of the expropriation-award disposition or seek confirmation of invalidity (see Supreme Court Decision 87NU1141 rendered on December 27, 1988, Supreme Court Decision 2000DU5142 rendered on October 13, 2000, etc.).\\nAccording to the factual findings recognized by the court below and the record, the Head of the Daejeon Regional Land Management Office issued on May 24, 2004 a notice of approval of the implementation plan for the Chungnam Central Area Water Supply Project at issue, and in the said notice it was stated that 140㎡ out of the Plaintiff-owned paddy field of 2,017㎡, lot No. 423-7, would be incorporated as the site for the buried water pipeline; thereafter, a decision was made to incorporate only 106㎡ of the said land, and Korea Water Resources Corporation, the project implementer, applied for cadastral subdivision of the said 106㎡, whereby on September 22, 2006 lot No. 423-16 was assigned to the said 106㎡; the property survey sheet attached to the compensation plan notice received by the Plaintiff around early September 2006 stated that Korea Water Resources Corporation would use 122㎡ of the said lot No. 423-7 land and would subdivide 106㎡ thereof under lot No. 423-16 of the same dong and expropriate it; the land schedule prepared on September 26, 2006 also stated that the said lot No. 423-16 land of 106㎡ was the land subject to expropriation and that 124㎡ out of the said lot No. 423-7 land was the land subject to use; meanwhile, the said notice dated May 24, 2004 and the notice of approval of the first amended project implementation plan at issue dated June 5, 2006 by the Head of the Daejeon Regional Land Management Office lost effect because no application for adjudication was filed within the project period, and the notice of approval of the second amended project implementation plan at issue had effect as a new notice of approval of the implementation plan.\\nIn light of the foregoing factual relations and the legal principles examined above, the Head of the Daejeon Regional Land Management Office erred in issuing the notice of approval of the second amended project implementation plan at issue by stating, without noticing that the land subject to expropriation at issue had already been subdivided, that 141㎡ out of the paddy field of 2,017㎡, lot No. 423-7, would be expropriated and 124㎡ would be used, but the fact that the area of the expropriation and use portions amounted to only a very small part of the total area of the said lot No. 423-7 land cannot be deemed a grave and obvious defect that would render the said notice itself void.\\nNevertheless, the court below determined that the notice of approval of the second amended project implementation plan at issue was void and ordered revocation of the expropriation award at issue; in so doing, the court below erred by misunderstanding the legal principles regarding a notice of approval of a project implementation plan, and such error affected the judgment, and the Defendant’s argument pointing this out is well taken.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the portion of the judgment of the court below unfavorable to the Defendant is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination of this portion; the Plaintiff’s appeal is dismissed; and the costs of appeal with respect to this portion shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: Which of the following statements is correct based on the facts below? (In cases of dispute, according to precedent) ◦ A, as a person operating a lodging business under the Public Health Control Act, received on 2022. 1. 5. from B, the head of the competent district office, a disposition suspending business for 3 months (hereinafter referred to as “the disposition at issue”) and filed an action seeking revocation of the disposition (hereinafter referred to as “the action at issue”). ◦ The action at issue was closed for oral argument in the appellate instance on 2023. 12. 7. ◦ A ground: A arranged prostitution for lodgers (the original ground for the disposition dated 2022. 1. 5.). ◦ B ground: A arranged obscene acts for lodgers. ◦ The A ground and the B ground concern matters that occurred at the time of the disposition at issue and have the same basic factual relation.
A: Since the time for determining whether the disposition at issue is unlawful is the time of the disposition, the court may determine the unlawfulness of the disposition at issue only on the basis of materials known to the administrative agency at the time of the disposition at issue, and, unlike this, may not synthesize all materials submitted up to the close of oral argument in fact-finding proceedings to identify the objective facts that existed at the time of the disposition and determine the unlawfulness of the disposition at issue on the basis of those facts.
B: Even after 2023. 12. 7., so long as it is before the pronouncement of judgment, B may change the ground for the disposition at issue from the A ground to the B ground.
C: Even if B changes only the statutory basis for the disposition without changing the A ground stated at the time of the disposition at issue, this should be regarded as a change of the ground for the disposition, and the same applies even where changing the statutory basis for the disposition is tantamount to making a separate disposition.
D: Whether A has standing as plaintiff is determined as of the close of oral argument in the fact-finding instance, so if, as of 2023. 12. 7., A was recognized as having standing as plaintiff, then even if A later lost the legal interest to seek revocation of the disposition at issue in the final appeal proceedings, the action does not become procedurally improper. If A was recognized as having legal interest at the close of oral argument in the fact-finding instance, then even if legal interest does not survive in the final appeal proceedings, the action does not become procedurally improper.
E: Although the disposition at issue was revoked by a final and conclusive judgment of the court on the ground that the A ground was not recognized, B’s making a disposition with the same content on the basis of the B ground conflicts with the binding force of the final and conclusive judgment.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2004DU7924]": "The grounds of appeal are examined (supplemental grounds submitted after the period has elapsed shall be considered only within the scope of supplementing them).\\n\\n1. With respect to Grounds 1 and 2 of the Grounds of Appeal\\n\\nAn “administrative disposition” that is the subject of an administrative appeal action means an act of an administrative agency in the sphere of public law that directly affects the specific rights and duties of the people by, as to a specific matter, ordering the establishment of rights or the assumption of obligations, or by causing other legal effects; and it must be individually determined according to the extent to which the requirements for establishment or effectiveness are satisfied in respect of its subject, content, procedure, and form (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2003DU10251, 10268 rendered on November 26, 2004).\\n\\nThe court of original instance determined that the act by which the Defendant Minister of Information and Communications reviewed the requirements and accepted the request for international registration application of a satellite network by the Defendant’s auxiliary intervenor (hereinafter referred to as the “Intervenor”) and the application for international registration of a satellite network made to the International Telecommunication Union on that premise (hereinafter referred to as the “registration application in this case”) are conceptually distinct; that the registration application in this case is merely an application act made by the above Defendant, who is the competent radio administration authority, to the International Telecommunication Union pursuant to the radio regulations of the International Telecommunication Union in order to secure satellite orbits and frequencies, which are international common resources, as resources of the Republic of Korea, and is not an act directly directed toward the people as the counterparty; and that, even if the Plaintiff suffers disadvantages, such as being unable to use a portion of the frequencies assigned to the Plaintiff, if the Defendant Minister of Information and Communications allocates, pursuant to Article 41(2) of the former Radio Waves Act (before its amendment by Act No. 7815 of December 30, 2005; hereinafter referred to as the “former Radio Waves Act before partial amendment”), the secured frequencies to the Intervenor, who requested the registration application in this case, this can become an issue only when the satellite orbit and frequencies are actually secured through the international satellite network registration procedure prescribed by the above radio regulations; and that, at the stage of the registration application such as in this case, it does not affect the rights and duties of the people at all, and therefore the registration application in this case cannot be deemed an administrative disposition subject to an action for revocation under the Administrative Litigation Act.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles set forth above and the purport of the relevant statutes, the above determination by the court of original instance is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the administrative disposition that is the subject of an administrative appeal action, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nIn addition, Ground 2 of the Grounds of Appeal, premised on the proposition that the registration application in this case constitutes an administrative disposition, is without merit without need for further examination, insofar as the registration application in this case does not constitute an administrative disposition.\\n\\n2. With respect to Ground 3 of the Grounds of Appeal\\n\\nEven a third party who is not the direct addressee of an administrative disposition has standing to sue, that is, the qualification to file an administrative lawsuit seeking revocation or confirmation of invalidity of the disposition, if he or she has suffered an infringement of interests protected by law due to the relevant administrative disposition; the “interests protected by law” referred to here mean individual, direct, and concrete interests protected by the statutory provisions serving as the basis for the relevant disposition and related statutes; and since standing to sue is one of the requirements for an action, it must subsist not only at the time of conclusion of oral argument in the fact-finding court but also in the Supreme Court, and if it is lacking, the action shall be unlawful (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2000DU7155 rendered on November 10, 2000; Supreme Court Decision 2004DU6716 rendered on July 28, 2006).\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Plaintiff was designated under the former Comprehensive Cable Broadcasting Act (before its full amendment by Act No. 5926 of February 8, 1999) as a transmission network operator whose business includes the provision of transmission line facilities for comprehensive cable broadcasting transmission, and under the former Radio Waves Act (before its full amendment by Act No. 6197 of January 21, 2000; hereinafter referred to as the “former Radio Waves Act before full amendment”) and the former Radio Waves Act before partial amendment, obtained each permission to establish a radio station using the frequency band in this case from the Defendant Head of the Seoul Regional Office of Posts and Telecommunications, etc.; however, it can be understood that, thereafter, by around June 2003, before the conclusion of oral argument in the court of original instance, the effects of all such permissions to establish radio stations were extinguished because the said permissions were revoked due to arrears in usage fees or became null upon expiration of their validity periods. Examining the relevant statutes, one cannot consider that the mere designation as a transmission network operator gives rise to a right to use the frequency band in this case, and where a frequency designation was received upon obtaining permission to establish a radio station, that frequency band may be used; however, as the effects of the permissions to establish radio stations received by the Plaintiff were all extinguished as stated above, the status enabling the Plaintiff to use the frequency band in this case has ceased to exist, and therefore it cannot be said that the Plaintiff has interests protected by law in relation to the frequency band in this case. Accordingly, even if the Defendant Head of the Seoul Regional Office of Posts and Telecommunications rendered the disposition of permission to establish the experimental station in this case to the Intervenor with respect to a portion of the frequency band in this case, it cannot be said that the Plaintiff has standing to sue seeking revocation thereof.\\n\\nAlthough the reasoning of the court of original instance is somewhat inappropriate, the conclusion that the Plaintiff has no legal interest and therefore lacks standing to sue is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of the legal principles concerning a third party’s standing to sue, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. With respect to Ground 4 of the Grounds of Appeal\\n\\nWhen the radio regulations of the International Telecommunication Union, Resolution 528 of the 1992 World Administrative Radio Conference (hereinafter referred to as “WARC-92 Resolution 528”), and the relevant provisions of the former Radio Waves Act before full amendment are taken together, even if the use purposes of the frequency band in this case are prescribed in the radio regulations of the International Telecommunication Union for various purposes of equal priority, what use is to be given priority domestically is a matter of the inherent authority of our country’s radio administration authority regarding radio policy; therefore, even if, under the radio regulations of the International Telecommunication Union, the priority of wireless CATV transmission service and satellite DAB (Digital Audio Broadcasting, hereinafter referred to as “DAB”) service is the same, it cannot be deemed a violation of the above radio regulations that the Defendant Minister of Information and Communications, who is the radio administration authority of the Republic of Korea, gave priority to the DAB service as the use purpose of the frequency band in this case in the conditions attached to the public notice on the frequency allocation in this case (Public Notice of the Ministry of Information and Communications No. 1997-50; hereinafter the same), and it cannot be deemed that the Defendant Minister of Information and Communications violated WARC-92 Resolution 528 by providing, in the conditions attached to the public notice on the frequency allocation in this case, that up to the maximum upper 60 MHz of the frequency band in this case shall be immediately returned when DAB is introduced in the future, in accordance with frequency policy.\\n\\nThe court of original instance’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of legal principles, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. With respect to Ground 5 of the Grounds of Appeal\\n\\nAccording to the relevant provisions of the former Radio Waves Act before partial amendment, frequency allocation means determining the use purpose of a specific frequency, and frequency assignment means granting a specific person the right to use a specific frequency; therefore, when a radio administration authority assigns a specific frequency to a specific person, it must assign it for the use purpose determined in the frequency allocation, and if it intends to assign it for a different use purpose, it must first change the frequency allocation.\\n\\nThe court of original instance determined that the frequency band in this case had already been allocated, by the public notice on the frequency allocation in this case, with priority for DAB use over wireless CATV transmission use; and that the Intervenor’s use of the S-band portion of the frequency band in this case, which is part of the frequency band in this case, for leasing a DAB satellite network constitutes the eventual use of the S-band portion of the frequency band in this case for DAB, and thus is use for the purpose determined in the public notice on the frequency allocation in this case, so there is no reason to undergo a procedure for changing the frequency allocation for the S-band portion of the frequency band in this case.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant statutes and the record, the above determination by the court of original instance is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of legal principles, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n5.
