With respect to Ground 6 of the Grounds of Appeal\\n\\nIn light of the relevant provisions of the current Radio Waves Act, etc., the “change of frequency allocation” prescribed in Article 6 of the former Radio Waves Act before partial amendment means changing the determined use purpose of a specific frequency, the “frequency recovery” means revoking all or part of a frequency assignment, a frequency designation, or approval for the use of frequencies, and the “frequency reassignment” means recovering frequencies and substituting therefor a frequency assignment, frequency designation, or approval for the use of frequencies; thus, even if the Defendant Minister of Information and Communications announced the frequency band in this case as being for a public telecommunications business as part of the introduction of the DAB business with respect to the S-band portion of the frequency band in this case, that alone cannot be deemed a change of frequency allocation, frequency recovery, or reassignment prescribed in Article 6 of the former Radio Waves Act before partial amendment.\\n\\nThe court of original instance’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of legal principles, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2009DU11843]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. On the corrective order  \\nWhen the Fair Trade Commission issues a corrective order under Article 25(1) of the Act on Fair Transactions in Subcontracting (hereinafter referred to as the “Subcontracting Act”), it shall not merely determine whether there was a violation of Article 13, such as the accrual and delayed payment of subcontract consideration; it must further determine whether the consequences of the violation were continuing up to that time, and even if there was a violation of law, if the consequences of the violation no longer exist, regardless of the reason, including the non-occurrence of the obligation to pay subcontract consideration, payment, set-off, settlement, or the like, then there is no room to issue a corrective order directing the correction of such consequences (see Supreme Court Decision 2001DU3099, rendered November 26, 2002). Meanwhile, in administrative litigation, whether an administrative disposition is unlawful must be determined on the basis of the statutes and factual state as of the time of the administrative disposition, and the court may, by comprehensively considering not only the materials known to the administrative agency at the time of the administrative disposition but also all materials submitted by the time the hearing in fact-finding proceedings is concluded, determine the objective facts existing at the time of the disposition and judge the unlawfulness of the disposition on the basis of those facts (see Supreme Court Decisions 80NU412, rendered December 8, 1981, and 92NU19033, rendered May 27, 1993, among others).\\n\\nIn light of these legal principles, the lower court’s determination that the Defendant’s corrective order in this case, issued against the violation at issue, is unlawful because the consequences of the violation of the Subcontracting Act had already been corrected, is correct, and even if the Defendant, for the reasons alleged, did not know at the time of the corrective order in this case that the violation had been corrected, no different conclusion may be drawn. The argument in the grounds of appeal on this point is without merit.\\n\\n2. On the imposition of the penalty surcharge  \\nAlthough the imposition of a penalty surcharge under the Subcontracting Act has a punitive character, it is basically imposed to deprive the violator of the unlawful economic benefit obtained through the violation of the Subcontracting Act, and Article 55-3(1) of the Monopoly Regulation and Fair Trade Act, as applied mutatis mutandis by the Subcontracting Act, also takes this into account by providing that, in imposing a penalty surcharge, not only the content and degree, period, and number of the violation, but also the amount of the benefit obtained through the violation, among other matters, shall be considered; accordingly, the amount of the penalty surcharge must be in balanced proportion not only to the degree of illegality, which is determined based on the specific form of the relevant violation, but also to the amount of the benefit derived therefrom, and if such balance is lost, it may constitute a deviation from and abuse of discretionary power in violation of the principle of proportionality (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DU6206, rendered February 9, 2001).\\n\\nAs the lower court held, prior to the imposition of the penalty surcharge in this case, the Plaintiff had voluntarily corrected a substantial portion of the violating acts subject to the surcharge, so that the benefits obtained through those violating acts had also largely ceased to remain; yet, in calculating the penalty surcharge in this case, such circumstances were not considered at all. Taking this into account, the lower court determined that, even considering the content and degree, period, and number of the violating acts, the imposition of the penalty surcharge in this case was excessively heavy and therefore constituted a deviation from and abuse of discretionary power. In light of the foregoing legal principles and the provisions of the relevant statutes and notices concerning the calculation process of the penalty surcharge in this case, the lower court’s above determination is persuasive, and, contrary to the grounds of appeal, there is no illegality in misconstruing the legal nature of the penalty surcharge or the legal principles concerning the discretionary power to impose a penalty surcharge.\\n\\n3. Conclusion  \\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the appeal costs are to be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged as per the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated in the case."}

{"[2015DU48235]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the binding effect and res judicata of a judgment of revocation (Defendant’s first ground of appeal)\\n\\nA. (1) Article 30(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act provides, “A final judgment that cancels a disposition, etc. shall bind the administrative agency that is a party to the case and any other relevant administrative agency with respect to that case.” The “binding effect” of such a final judgment of revocation is recognized in a judgment in which a claim for revocation is granted, and it operates to impose upon the administrative agency that is a party to the case and any other relevant administrative agency a duty to act in accordance with the purport of the final judgment. By contrast, the “res judicata” prescribed by Articles 216 and 218 of the Civil Procedure Act, which are applied mutatis mutandis to administrative litigation pursuant to Article 8(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act, operates to preclude a later action whose subject matter is identical to that of the earlier action in which res judicata has attached, and at the same time, even where the subject matter of the later action is not identical to that of the earlier action, to preclude in the later action assertions contrary to the judgment in the earlier action when the determination regarding the subject matter of the earlier action becomes a prerequisite issue in, or is in a contradictory relationship with, the later action (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2013DA19083, rendered on 28 November 2013).\\n\\n(2) The binding effect of a final judgment of revocation extends to the operative part of the judgment and to the determination on the specific grounds of illegality of the disposition, etc. that formed the premise thereof; however, even if the prior disposition was revoked by a judgment, the making of a new disposition on grounds different from those of the prior disposition does not contravene the binding effect. Whether the grounds are the same grounds or different grounds in this context must be determined according to whether identity is recognized in the basic factual relations with the grounds for the prior disposition that were held unlawful in the final judgment, and whether the basic factual relations are identical is determined by focusing on the concrete facts before legal evaluation of the grounds for disposition and by considering whether the underlying social factual relations are, in their essential points, the same (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2003DU7705, rendered on 9 December 2005). In addition, because the unlawfulness of an administrative disposition is determined based on the statutes and facts as of the time the administrative disposition was made, the disposition-making administrative agency that was a party to the final judgment may, of course, make a new disposition by relying on new grounds that arose after the prior disposition (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2011DU14401, rendered on 27 October 2011), and insofar as the grounds for the new disposition constitute different grounds that are not identical in the basic factual relations to the grounds for the prior disposition, making a new disposition by relying on such grounds does not contravene the binding effect of the final judgment even if those grounds already existed at the time of the prior disposition and the party knew of them.\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, the res judicata of a final judgment of revocation extends only to the operative part of that judgment, and also only to the determination itself regarding the existence or nonexistence of unlawfulness of the administrative disposition that was the subject matter of the action; therefore, where the earlier action and the later action have different subject matters, the res judicata of the final judgment in the earlier action does not extend to the later action (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 95NU5820, rendered on 26 April 1996).\\n\\nB. According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the evidence adopted by the court below, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n\\n(1) Plaintiff Shinmi Transportation Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Plaintiff Shinmi Transportation”) owns 101 taxis, including the 70 vehicles listed in Attached List 1, and Plaintiff Juho Transportation Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Plaintiff Juho Transportation”) owns 101 taxis, including the 23 vehicles listed in Attached List 2, and each is engaged in the general taxi transport business.\\n\\n(2) On 22 May 2008, the Defendant, on the ground that “the Plaintiffs operated a total of 48 taxis in November 2007 in the form of a subcontracting system (25 vehicles for Plaintiff Shinmi Transportation and 23 vehicles for Plaintiff Juho Transportation), thereby causing other persons to manage the passenger automobile transport business,” issued to the Plaintiffs an order to reduce the number of vehicles with respect to each of the above taxis pursuant to Article 13(1) and Article 76(1)13 of the former Passenger Automobile Transport Business Act (as in effect before it was wholly amended by Act No. 8980 of 21 March 2008), etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “prior disposition”).\\n\\n(3) The Plaintiffs filed a lawsuit seeking revocation of the prior disposition in Seoul Administrative Court Case No. 2008GUHAP22549, and on 9 July 2009, that court rendered a judgment in favor of the Plaintiffs revoking the prior disposition on the ground that it was difficult to regard the operation of the Plaintiffs’ 48 taxis as constituting the use of another’s name. The Defendant appealed to the Seoul High Court in Case No. 2009NU22623, but the appellate court concluded the pleadings on 27 January 2010 and rendered a judgment dismissing the appeal on 10 February of the same year. The Defendant then filed an appeal to the Supreme Court, but it was dismissed on 27 May 2010, and around that time the above judgment in favor of the Plaintiffs became final and conclusive (hereinafter the above final and conclusive judgment in favor of the Plaintiffs is referred to as the “final judgment in this case”).\\n\\n(4) Thereafter, on 22 March 2013, the Defendant, against the Plaintiffs, issued an order to reduce the number of vehicles with respect to each of the vehicles listed in Attached Lists 1 and 2 pursuant to Article 12(1) and Article 85(1)13 of the Passenger Automobile Transport Business Act, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “disposition in this case”), on the ground that “the Plaintiffs, from 3 July 2006 to 14 September 2010, leased the Plaintiffs’ vehicles to Non-party 1 on a total of 263 occasions by receiving each month a fixed rental fee per vehicle, and Plaintiff Shinmi Transportation, by the same method, leased its vehicles to Non-party 2 on a total of 233 occasions from around March 2007 to 30 September 2010, to Non-party 3 on a total of 294 occasions from around April 2007 to 30 September 2010, and to Non-party 4 on 79 occasions from around July 2007 to 31 December 2008, thereby causing Non-party 1 and Non-party 2, Non-party 3, and Non-party 4 (hereinafter referred to as ‘Non-parties 2 et seq.’) to manage the passenger automobile transport business.”\\n\\nC. Based on the above facts, the court below premised that ① whether the same subject matter to which res judicata extends is involved should be determined on the basis of the basic factual relations of the violation that became the object of the sanction, while also considering normative elements; and that the temporal scope of res judicata should be viewed as the time of conclusion of oral argument in the fact-finding trial of the administrative litigation; and then held that ② since the conduct of using another’s name prohibited by Article 12(1) of the Passenger Automobile Transport Business Act is, by the nature of its elements, expected to be repeated as similar conduct, where a transport business operator continuously caused the use of another’s name with respect to the same vehicle for a certain period, this constitutes, in aggregate, a single violation, so the part of the prior disposition and the part of the disposition in this case based on the use of another’s name with respect to the same vehicle should be regarded as having the same basic factual relations; and ③ since each vehicle listed in paragraphs 1 and 2 of Attached List 3 (hereinafter referred to as the “overlapping vehicles at issue”) was also subject to reduction in the prior disposition, and the disposition in this case took as its grounds for disposition the use of another’s name before 27 January 2010, which was the date of conclusion of oral argument in the appellate trial of the final judgment in this case, the part of the disposition in this case relating to the overlapping vehicles at issue was unlawful as it contravened the binding effect or res judicata of the final judgment in this case.\\n\\nD. However, in light of the legal principles set forth above and the following circumstances discernible from the reasoning of the judgment below and the reasoning of the first-instance judgment cited by the court below, the court below’s determination cannot be accepted as is.\\n\\n(1) At the time of the disposition in this case, the Defendant specified the period of the violation with respect to the overlapping vehicles at issue, as stated in the column “Period of Use of Another’s Name” for the relevant vehicle in paragraphs 1 and 2 of Attached List 3. However, in the case of the vehicles listed as item numbers 2, 4, 7, and 9 in paragraph 1 of Attached List 3 and item numbers 3, 5, 6, and 7 in paragraph 2 thereof, the violation that was the object of the disposition includes the use of another’s name that took place in November 2007, which was the object of the prior disposition, and the part of the grounds for disposition in this case concerning the use of another’s name during the above period for some of the overlapping vehicles at issue that were the object of the prior disposition should be regarded as having the same basic factual relations as the grounds for the prior disposition; therefore, in issuing the disposition in this case, the Defendant’s inclusion of this part as well in the violation would contravene the binding effect of the final judgment in this case.\\n\\n(2) However, with respect to the remaining parts of the grounds for disposition in this case, excluding the use of another’s name during the above period that was the object of the prior disposition, it is appropriate to conclude, when focusing on the concrete facts before legal evaluation, that because the period differs from that of the grounds for the prior disposition, identity in the basic factual relations is not recognized; accordingly, even if the Defendant relied on those violation acts as grounds for the disposition in this case, this does not contravene the binding effect of the final judgment in this case.\\n\\n(3) Moreover, the res judicata of the final judgment in this case extends only to the determination itself regarding the existence or nonexistence of unlawfulness of the prior disposition, which was the subject matter of that action, and does not extend to this action in this case, which has a different subject matter and targets the disposition in this case.\\n\\nE. Nevertheless, the court below, on reasons such as those stated in its holding, determined that all parts of the disposition in this case concerning the overlapping vehicles at issue were unlawful because they violated the binding effect or res judicata of the final judgment in this case, on the ground that in the case of the use of another’s name prohibited by Article 12(1) of the Passenger Automobile Transport Business Act, the question of identity in the basic factual relations should be determined mainly on the basis of legal and normative elements such as the expected repetition of the act. In this judgment below, there is an error that affected the outcome of the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the binding effect or res judicata of a final judgment. The Defendant’s ground of appeal on this point is well-founded.\\n\\n2. Regarding whether there was use of another’s name (Plaintiffs’ ground of appeal and Defendant’s second ground of appeal)\\n\\nA. Regarding whether there was use of another’s name by Non-party 1 (Plaintiffs’ ground of appeal)\\n\\n(1) The main text of Article 12(1) of the Passenger Automobile Transport Business Act provides, “A transport business operator shall not permit another transport business operator or a person who is not a transport business operator to manage the passenger automobile transport business by using all or part of the business vehicle, for consideration or free of charge.”\\n\\nIn light of the content of this provision and its legislative purpose, in order to fall under conduct of using another’s name under the Passenger Automobile Transport Business Act, it must be recognized that a person who is not a transport business operator, by using the transport business operator’s name and while excluding that transport business operator, independently managed the passenger automobile transport business, and if the person merely caused the operation of individual vehicles under the general direction and supervision of the transport business operator, this does not fall under the above conduct of using another’s name (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DO4129, rendered on 24 September 2009).\\n\\nFurthermore, in determining whether a person who is not a transport business operator, by excluding the transport business operator, independently managed the passenger automobile transport business and thereby engaged in conduct of using another’s name, one is not bound by outward factors such as who is named as the insured member in the mutual aid association for the vehicle or who is named as the employer in the employment contract with the relevant driving personnel. Rather, more important criteria than such outward factors are: the circumstances under which the person who is not a transport business operator came to use the vehicles and the content of the agreement accompanying that use; who in substance exercises the authority to direct and supervise matters such as assignment of vehicles to driving personnel, operation, days off, training, and the amount of transport revenue to be remitted; who ultimately bears the risk of profit and loss arising from the operation of the vehicles; and who in substance bears the wages of the driving personnel and the costs of operating the vehicles, such as premiums for the four major social insurance schemes, fuel costs, and repair costs.\\n\\n(2) According to the reasoning of the judgment below, the court below found the following: ① Non-party 1, after leasing a total of 29 taxis from the Plaintiffs at a fixed monthly or daily price, recruited transport personnel on his own; ② Non-party 1 set up an office in Gwangmyeong-si, (address omitted), received the applicants’ documents required for hiring, and personally executed employment contracts with some of the transport personnel; ③ Non-party 1 exercised authority to make decisions concerning assignment of taxis to the recruited transport personnel, the amount of transport revenue to be remitted, and vacations; ④ Non-party 1 separately prepared and kept vehicle allocation logs and daily operation logs, apart from the Plaintiffs; ⑤ Non-party 1 agreed to pay the agreed amount to the Plaintiffs even in cases where the taxis could not operate because the recruited transport personnel were absent from work; ⑥ the Plaintiffs separately classified and managed materials recording the daily LPG usage fees and deposit amounts of the regular transport personnel belonging to them and those of the transport personnel recruited by Non-party 1; and ⑦ the Plaintiffs did not pay wages to the transport personnel recruited by Non-party 1, and did not in substance bear the four major social insurance premiums by deducting them from the LPG subsidy. On the basis of such circumstances, the court below determined that, even if the Plaintiffs had executed employment contracts with the transport personnel recruited by Non-party 1, those contracts appeared to have been formally prepared without any actual intent to conclude employment contracts and to have been made to evade enforcement, etc.; and that Non-party 1, while the Plaintiffs’ direction and supervision were excluded, independently managed the taxi transport business by using the Plaintiffs’ names.\\n\\n(3) Examining the reasoning of the judgment below in light of the legal principles set forth above, the above determination of the court below is proper, and there is no error, as asserted in the grounds of appeal, in that it went beyond the bounds of free evaluation of evidence by contravening the rules of logic and experience or misapprehended the legal principles concerning conduct of using another’s name.\\n\\nB. Regarding whether there was use of another’s name by Non-party 2 and others (Defendant’s second ground of appeal)\\n\\n(1) According to the reasoning of the judgment below, the court below held that ① unlike Non-party 1, Non-party 2 and others did not establish separate offices and executed employment contracts in the dispatch office of Plaintiff Shinmi Transportation; ② there was no evidence that Non-party 2 and others separately prepared books such as vehicle allocation logs; ③ Non-party 2 and others did not receive taxis from any transport business operators other than Plaintiff Shinmi Transportation; and ④ while the number of taxis provided by Plaintiff Shinmi Transportation to Non-party 2 and others totaled 64, the number of transport personnel recruited and managed by Non-party 2 and others was less than half of the number recruited and managed by Non-party 1. On such grounds, the court below determined that the part of the disposition in this case concerning the vehicles listed in paragraph 3 of Attached List 3 was unlawful because it was difficult to conclude that Non-party 2 and others, while excluding Plaintiff Shinmi Transportation, independently managed the passenger automobile transport business.\\n\\n(2) However, according to the reasoning of the judgment below, it can be ascertained that ① Non-party 2 and others, like Non-party 1, also leased taxis from the Plaintiffs by paying a certain amount to the Plaintiffs and recruited transport personnel; ② Non-party 2 and others exercised authority to make decisions regarding taxi assignment and vacations for the recruited transport personnel; and ③ the Plaintiffs separately managed materials regarding the daily LPG usage fees, etc. of the transport personnel recruited by Non-party 2 and others, and did not pay wages to those transport personnel and did not in substance bear the premiums for the four major social insurance schemes.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles set forth above, based on such factual relations, ① Non-party 2 and others, too, may be viewed as having leased taxis from the Plaintiffs and then themselves bearing the risk of profit and loss arising from their operation, and as having managed those transport personnel; ② Plaintiff Shinmi Transportation appears not to have made any substantial distinction in the terms of lease or management structure when leasing taxis to Non-party 1 and to Non-party 2 and others; and ③ the number of times and the period during which Non-party 2 and others leased taxis from Plaintiff Shinmi Transportation were also substantial, so there is ample room to conclude that Non-party 2 and others, like Non-party 1, independently managed the taxi transport business while excluding the direction and supervision of Plaintiff Shinmi Transportation.\\n\\nMoreover, even if, as the court below held, Non-party 2 and others did not establish separate offices or prepare books necessary for management, such as vehicle allocation logs, the nature of the taxi transport business carried out through use of another’s name means that it cannot be said that there was any particular hindrance to actually managing the business, and Article 12(1) of the Passenger Automobile Transport Business Act does not make the borrowing of vehicles from several transport business operators a requirement for conduct of using another’s name; therefore, the circumstances pointed out by the court below are not of such a nature as to determine whether Non-party 2 and others independently managed the passenger automobile transport business while excluding Plaintiff Shinmi Transportation.\\n\\n(3) Nevertheless, the court below determined, solely for the reasons stated in its holding, that Non-party 2 and others did not engage in conduct of using another’s name; thus, in this determination by the court below, there is an error that affected the outcome of the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning conduct of using another’s name prescribed by Article 12(1) of the Passenger Automobile Transport Business Act and by failing to conduct the necessary deliberation. The Defendant’s ground of appeal on this point is also well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the part of the judgment below adverse to the Defendant is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination of that part; and all of the Plaintiffs’ appeals are dismissed. Accordingly, the judgment is rendered as stated in the operative part by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating.\\n\\n[[Attachment 1] List: Omitted]\\n[[Attachment 2] List: Omitted]\\n[[Attachment 3] List: Omitted]"}

{"[2021DU34756]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below and the record, the following circumstances may be found.\\n\\nA. From around April 2019, the Plaintiffs installed the container at issue on the land at issue and began using some of it as offices, a restaurant, and restrooms, and renting out the remainder as a warehouse.\\n\\nB. On 2019. 4. 29., the Defendant gave prior notice to the Plaintiffs that it would issue a corrective order for restoration to the original condition on the ground that the installation of the container at issue without obtaining a building permit constituted a violation of Article 11 of the former Building Act (the version before amendment by Act No. 16380 on 2019. 4. 23.; hereinafter referred to as the “Building Act”), and notified them to submit any opinions by 2019. 5. 14.\\n\\nC. On 2019. 5. 14., the Plaintiffs submitted to the Defendant an opinion requesting that the portion of the container at issue used as a warehouse not be regarded as an unlawful facility and that it be reviewed once again, while stating that they would restore to the original condition by 2019. 6. 30. the portion of the container at issue used as offices, a restaurant, and restrooms, and would submit supporting materials.\\n\\nD. On 2019. 5. 20., the Defendant, on the ground that the container at issue constituted a building under Article 2(1)2 of the Building Act but had been constructed without obtaining a building permit under Article 11 of the same Act, ordered restoration to the original condition pursuant to Article 79 of the Building Act, and warned that if restoration to the original condition was not carried out within the above period, the container at issue would be removed through administrative vicarious execution (hereinafter referred to as “the disposition at issue”).\\n\\nE. On 2019. 6. 10., the Plaintiffs filed with the Defendant a report of the erection of a temporary building concerning the erection of the container at issue on the land at issue. However, on 2019. 6. 25., the Defendant rejected the above report, on the ground that the container at issue constituted a building under Article 2(1)2 of the Building Act and therefore a building permit under Article 11 of the Building Act was required.\\n\\n2. Whether the addition/change of the grounds for disposition is permitted (Ground of Appeal No. 2)\\n\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nIn an administrative action seeking the revocation of an administrative disposition, the agency making the disposition may add or change other grounds only to the extent that the grounds originally relied upon for the disposition and the basic factual relationship are identical. Whether such basic factual relationship is identical is determined by focusing on the concrete facts prior to the legal evaluation of the grounds for disposition, and by whether the underlying social factual relationship is identical in essential respects; therefore, the fact that the added or changed ground already existed at the time of the disposition, or that the party knew of that fact, cannot be said to make it identical to the original grounds for disposition (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DU19021 dated 2011. 11. 24., etc.).\\n\\nWhere the agency making the disposition, without changing the specific facts stated at the time of the disposition, merely adds or changes only the statutes and regulations serving as the basis for the disposition, this does not amount to the addition of a new ground for disposition, and thus the administrative agency may determine the legality of the disposition by applying the statutes and regulations added or changed after the disposition to the specific facts stated at the time of the disposition (see Supreme Court Decision 87NU632 dated 1987. 12. 8., etc.). However, where changing the statutory basis for the disposition is tantamount to making a separate disposition for which identity with the prior disposition cannot be recognized, it is not permitted (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DU28106 dated 2011. 5. 26., etc.).\\n\\nB. The court below’s determination\\n\\nThe court below held that, although the Defendant originally made the disposition at issue on the ground of “violation of Article 11 of the Building Act,” the addition at the appellate stage of “violation of Article 20(3) of the Building Act” as a ground for disposition merely adds the statutory basis for the disposition to the same factual situation, and thus does not constitute the addition of a new ground for disposition and is permissible.\\n\\nC. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\nHowever, examining the factual relationship above in light of the relevant legal principles, it is reasonable to regard the Defendant’s addition at the appellate stage of a violation of Article 20(3) of the Building Act as a ground for disposition as the addition of a new ground for disposition whose basic factual relationship is not identical to the original grounds for disposition, and thus as impermissible. Therefore, the above determination of the court below is difficult to accept as it stands. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) The original ground for disposition in the disposition at issue was that “although the container at issue constitutes a building under Article 2(1)2 of the Building Act, it was constructed in violation of Article 11 of the Building Act,” whereas the added ground for disposition was that “although the container at issue constitutes a temporary building, it was erected in violation of Article 20(3) of the Building Act without filing a report of erection.”\\n\\nThe Building Act separately provides the procedures and requirements, etc. for a building permit for a “building” (Article 11(1)) and for a report of erection for a “temporary building” (Article 20(3)). A “building” means, among the structures fixed to land, those having a roof and pillars or walls, and offices, performance halls, stores, garages, warehouses, and other items installed in structures elevated above the ground attached thereto as prescribed by Presidential Decree (Article 2(1)2), and a person intending to construct such a building must obtain a permit under Article 11(1) of the Building Act. By contrast, a temporary building that does not satisfy the element of being fixed to land among the requirements for a building, and therefore does not constitute a “building” under the Building Act, may in principle be installed without a building permit or a building report; however, Article 20(3) of the Building Act regulates certain temporary buildings that require control of risks akin to those of buildings as subject to a report of erection (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DU35116 dated 2018. 1. 25.).\\n\\nIn the case of a building permit, the permit-granting authority must verify compliance with the Korean Building Code pursuant to Article 25 of the Framework Act on Building (Article 11(4) of the Building Act), and must confirm whether the relevant building satisfies the requirements prescribed by the building statutes and regulations, namely, the site and roads for the building (Chapter IV), the structure and materials of the building, etc. (Chapter V), the building requirements for each area and district (Chapter VI), and the standards concerning building equipment (Chapter VII). By contrast, with respect to a temporary building subject to a report of erection, most of the provisions concerning such building requirements do not apply [Article 20(5) of the Building Act; Article 15(6) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Building Act (the version before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 30145 on 2019. 10. 22.)]. In addition, a temporary building does not require a separate commencement report or approval for use in addition to the report of erection (Article 21(1) and Article 22(1) of the Building Act), and even if a report of erection is filed, related permits and approvals are not deemed to be granted, unlike in the case of a building permit; accordingly, there is also a difference from a building subject to a building permit in that the administrative agency may not refuse to accept the report of erection of a temporary building on the ground that the requirements for related permits and approvals are not satisfied (see Supreme Court Decision 2017DU75606 dated 2019. 1. 10.).\\n\\nIn view of the above distinction under the Building Act between buildings and temporary buildings, and the differences in the procedures and requirements for building permits and reports of erection, the original ground for disposition in the disposition at issue and the ground added by the Defendant at the appellate stage differ in the content of the violating act, and accordingly the procedures to be followed to eliminate the unlawful state, the building standards, and the degree of permissibility are different; thus, the underlying social factual relationship cannot ultimately be deemed identical.\\n\\n2) The reason why it is interpreted that asserting separate facts for which identity of the basic factual relationship is not recognized as grounds for disposition is not permitted is to realize substantive rule of law by guaranteeing the opposing party’s right of defense against the administrative disposition and to protect the opposing party’s trust in the administrative disposition (see Supreme Court Decision 2001DU8827 dated 2003. 12. 11., etc.).\\n\\nIn light of the factual relationship above, the Defendant’s addition, at the appellate stage of this litigation, of a ground for disposition on the premise, unlike at the time of the disposition, that the container at issue constitutes a temporary building infringes the Plaintiffs’ right of defense; therefore, even from this standpoint, it is difficult to view the addition or change of the grounds for disposition as permitted.\\n\\n3) Nevertheless, the court below held that the Defendant’s addition in this litigation of a violation of Article 20(3) of the Building Act as a ground for disposition was permissible, and determined that the disposition at issue was lawful on the basis of the added ground. The court below’s determination contains an error of law by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the limitation on the addition or change of grounds for disposition, and the ground of appeal pointing out this issue is well founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without addressing the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for a new hearing and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[98DU17043]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding Issue 1\\n\\nArticle 8(1) of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Acquisition of Land for Public Works and the Compensation Therefor (hereinafter referred to as the Public Land Compensation Act) provides that the project operator shall establish and implement relocation measures for persons who lose their means of livelihood by providing land, etc. necessary for the implementation of a public works project. Where relocation measures are established for persons who provided land, etc. for the implementation of a project under the Housing Site Development Promotion Act, such relocation measures are deemed to confer upon those who cooperated in the public works project a legal interest in being able to demand an opportunity for special allocation, and therefore a right to apply for special allocation is recognized for them; accordingly, an act by the project operator refusing a person who requests special sale allocation on the ground that the above provision applies, even if such refusal was made in the form of a response to a civil petition, constitutes a refusal disposition subject to an administrative action seeking revocation (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 94NU11279, rendered on October 12, 1995, and Supreme Court Decision 96NU18014, rendered on March 28, 1997).\\n\\nIn addition, if the project operator has the duty to establish and implement relocation measures, and has established and announced a relocation measures plan in performance of that duty, then seeking revocation of an administrative disposition that rejected, on the ground that the applicant was not a person subject to relocation measures, a person who applied for selection while claiming to be a person subject to relocation measures also has the meaning of obtaining confirmation that he or she is a person subject to relocation measures; and since the project operator’s confirmation and determination constitute requirements for acquiring a specific right to receive a right to purchase housing sites or a right to move into apartments, etc. under the relocation measures, even if the relocation measures work already established and implemented has in reality been completed, and the project has been completed so that there are no longer any detached housing sites for relocation measures to be allotted within the project district in this case, the legal interest in determining rights such as the right to claim compensation remains, and therefore, on that ground alone, it cannot be said that the Plaintiff lacks a legal interest in seeking revocation of the refusal disposition in this case.\\n\\nAlthough there are some inappropriate aspects in the reasoning stated in the judgment of the court below, it is correct in its conclusion that there is a legal interest, and there is no illegality in the misunderstanding of the legal principles concerning administrative dispositions or legal interest as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe argument in the grounds of appeal on this point is not accepted.\\n\\n2. Regarding Issue 2\\n\\na. An administrative agency may add or change another ground for disposition only within the extent that the identity of the basic factual relations is recognized, but this is permitted only until the conclusion of oral argument in fact-finding proceedings (see Supreme Court Decision 98DU16675, rendered on February 9, 1999).\\n\\nThe argument in the grounds of appeal advanced by the Defendant—that because the Plaintiff filed a belated relocation measures application after the application period for relocation measures or the prescribed implementation period for relocation measures had all elapsed, the Plaintiff had no right to apply for relocation measures, and the project operator therefore could not be deemed to bear any legal duty to accept it and provide housing sites or apartments—is not only a new argument not made in the court below, but also lacks identity of the basic factual relations with the ground for the disposition in this case, namely that the Plaintiff was not an owner of a house within the project district, and therefore cannot constitute a lawful ground of appeal.\\n\\nThe grounds of appeal on this point likewise cannot be accepted.\\n\\nb. In light of the purport of each provision of Articles 5(1) and 5(5) and Article 8(1) of the Public Land Compensation Act, a house owner should be understood not as a person who has title outwardly, but as a person who has actual power of disposition; nor can it be said that proof of such actual power of disposition is excluded by means of reliable materials other than the certified copy of the building register (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 96NU14067, rendered on February 11, 1997, and Supreme Court Decision 91NU8692, rendered on April 24, 1992).\\n\\nAccording to the record, it can be seen that the Plaintiff purchased the house in this case on December 18, 1979, before the Defendant’s official announcement of the planned housing site development district, and thus possessed actual power of disposition; accordingly, the Plaintiff must be deemed to fall within the persons eligible for the supply of relocation housing sites.\\n\\nThe court below’s finding and determination to the same effect are proper, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the selection of persons subject to relocation measures, etc., as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe argument in the grounds of appeal on this point is also not accepted.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the Defendant. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the case below are correct? (Where there is a dispute, the answer is based on precedents.) The A Metropolitan City Council adopted a proposed amendment to the Ordinance on the Management and Operation of Administrative Property of A Metropolitan City, which provides that tenants who have been granted a use permit for administrative property owned by A Metropolitan City may transfer, be transferred, or sublease that administrative property, pursuant to the Public Property and Goods Management Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Public Property Act”). The Minister of the Interior and Safety instructed the Mayor of A Metropolitan City to request reconsideration on the ground that the above proposed amendment violates the Public Property Act. (a) Under the Public Property Act, a person who has been granted a use permit for administrative property shall not allow another person to use or profit from that administrative property; therefore, the above proposed amendment, which permits tenants to transfer, be transferred, or sublease the administrative property for which they have received a use permit, violates higher-ranking law. (b) A resident of A Metropolitan City may lawfully bring an action against the Mayor of A Metropolitan City seeking a declaration of invalidity of the resolution on the ordinance bill. (c) If the Mayor of A Metropolitan City fails to comply with the Minister of the Interior and Safety’s instruction to request reconsideration, the Minister of the Interior and Safety may bring an action in the Supreme Court against the A Metropolitan City Council seeking a declaration of invalidity of the resolution on the ordinance bill. (d) If the Mayor of A Metropolitan City requests reconsideration from the A Metropolitan City Council, but the A Metropolitan City Council re-adopts the bill in its original form, even if part of the above proposed amendment violates the Public Property Act and its effect is therefore not recognized, the entire effect of the resolution on the reconsidered proposed amendment is not denied.

supporting_precedents: {"[2016CHU5162]": "1. Re-adoption of the ordinance bill at issue and outline of its main contents  \\nWhen the entries in Exhibits A-2-1 through A-2-2 are comprehensively considered together with the entire purport of the pleadings, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. On April 26, 2016, the Defendant resolved to adopt the “Ordinance Bill for the Protection of the Electromagnetic-Wave Vulnerable Classes of the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education” (hereinafter referred to as “the ordinance bill at issue”) and transmitted it to the Superintendent of the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education on April 28, 2016. On May 11, 2016, the Plaintiff Minister of Education demanded that the Defendant reconsider Article 5, Article 6(1), and Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the ordinance bill at issue (hereinafter referred to as “the provisions of the ordinance bill at issue”). According to the provisions of the ordinance bill at issue, the Superintendent of the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education may designate electromagnetic-wave safe zones and prohibit the installation of base stations within designated electromagnetic-wave safe zones and recommend the removal of already installed base stations; this is said to run counter to Article 19, Article 19-2, Article 21, and Article 72, etc. of the Radio Waves Act concerning the establishment of wireless stations, as well as Article 47-2 of the Radio Waves Act, etc., which prescribe measures for the protection of the human body from electromagnetic waves. However, the Defendant re-adopted the ordinance bill at issue as originally proposed on October 18, 2016, thereby confirming it.\\n\\nb. The ordinance bill at issue contains the following provisions.\\n\\n(1) The ordinance bill at issue aims to protect the electromagnetic-wave vulnerable classes by designating and operating kindergartens and elementary schools, etc. in Gyeonggi Province as electromagnetic-wave safe zones (Article 1).\\n\\n(2) The Superintendent of the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education shall designate kindergartens and elementary schools in Gyeonggi Province as electromagnetic-wave safe zones (main clause of Article 5(1)). Provided, however, that a mixed-use building in the same building that houses other persons, organizations, or institutions using that building shall be excepted if it does not exceed the human body protection standards for electromagnetic waves under Article 47-2(1) of the Radio Waves Act (proviso of Article 5(1)). Furthermore, the Superintendent of the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education may designate “children’s and juveniles’ facilities” as electromagnetic-wave safe zones if deemed necessary (Article 5(2)).\\n\\n(3) No person may install a base station in an electromagnetic-wave safe zone (Article 6(1)).\\n\\n(4) The Superintendent of the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education may recommend the removal of base stations installed before the enforcement of this ordinance, taking into account electromagnetic wave risks, etc. (Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions).\\n\\n2. Determination on the Defendant’s preliminary defense on the merits  \\nWith respect to the filing of this action by the Plaintiff Minister of Science, ICT and Future Planning together with the Plaintiff Minister of Education, the Defendant argues that this violates Article 172(8) of the Local Autonomy Act, which allows the Minister of the Interior and Safety to bring an action before the Supreme Court where the matter re-adopted by a local council concerns two or more ministries.\\n\\nIf it is determined that a matter re-adopted by a local council violates statutes, the competent Minister may direct the head of the local government to file an action before the Supreme Court or may file such action directly (Article 172(4) of the Local Autonomy Act). Provided, however, that where the re-adopted matter relates to two or more ministries, or where the competent Minister is unclear, the Minister of the Interior and Safety may direct reconsideration or the filing of an action, or may file an action directly and apply for a decision suspending execution (Article 172(8) of the Local Autonomy Act). This merely means that, in cases where the competent ministry is duplicated or the competent Minister is unclear, the Minister of the Interior and Safety may, at his or her discretion and as necessary for litigation, substitute for and exercise the authority of the competent Minister; it is not intended to exclude the authority of the competent Minister in all cases and to vest such authority exclusively in the Minister of the Interior and Safety alone. Accordingly, the Defendant’s preliminary defense on the merits is not accepted.\\n\\n3. Scope of application of Article 5 of the ordinance bill at issue  \\nArticle 5(1) of the ordinance bill at issue provides that the subjects for designation as electromagnetic-wave safe zones are “kindergartens and elementary schools in Gyeonggi Province, and children’s and juveniles’ facilities,” and Article 2(2) of the ordinance bill at issue defines children’s and juveniles’ facilities as “facilities exclusively for children and juveniles aged 18 or under.” Before determining whether the ordinance bill at issue is invalid, it is necessary, as a premise, to clearly define the meaning of “children’s and juveniles’ facilities.”\\n\\nIn light of the fact that Article 5 of the ordinance bill at issue places the designation of electromagnetic-wave safe zones within the affairs under the jurisdiction of the Superintendent of the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education, the subjects of application of Article 5(1) of the ordinance bill at issue must be limited to the scope within which the Superintendent may provide guidance and supervision under education-related statutes. Accordingly, the “kindergartens and elementary schools” referred to in the above provision should not be understood as referring to all kindergartens and elementary schools, but should be limited to public and private kindergartens over which the Superintendent may provide guidance and supervision under education-related statutes (see Article 18(1) of the Early Childhood Education Act) and public and private elementary schools (see Article 6 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act). In addition, the “children’s and juveniles’ facilities” referred to in the above provision must likewise be “facilities exclusively for” children and juveniles over which the Superintendent’s guidance and supervision is possible; accordingly, they may be understood to mean public and private educational facilities, etc. under Article 2 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act and the like, other than kindergartens and elementary schools (hereinafter referred to as “children’s and juveniles’ educational facilities”).\\n\\n4. Whether the provisions of the ordinance bill at issue fall within matters subject to ordinance enactment  \\na. A local government shall administer affairs concerning the welfare of residents, manage property, and enact regulations concerning autonomy within the scope of statutes (Article 117(1) of the Constitution). According to Articles 22 and 9 of the Local Autonomy Act, matters for which a local government may enact an ordinance are limited to autonomous affairs, which are the inherent affairs of the local government, and affairs entrusted as an entity to the local government under individual statutes. Matters concerning affairs entrusted as an organ, in which state affairs are entrusted to the head of a local government or the affairs of a higher-level local government are entrusted to the head of a lower-level local government, do not in principle fall within the scope of ordinance enactment. In determining whether affairs that statutes prescribe to be handled by the head of a local government are autonomous affairs or affairs entrusted as an organ, the form and purport of the relevant statutory provisions should be considered first; in addition, whether the nature of the affairs requires uniform nationwide handling and who bears the costs and ultimate responsibility should also be considered (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DU12153, decided April 11, 2013, etc.).\\n\\nb. Article 9(2)2(d) of the Local Autonomy Act exemplifies “protection of the elderly, children, persons with mental and physical disabilities, juveniles, and women, and the promotion of welfare” as “autonomous affairs” of local governments. The provisions of the ordinance bill at issue provide that, in order to protect the health and safety of children and juveniles in Gyeonggi Province from the harmfulness of electromagnetic waves, the Superintendent of the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education shall designate kindergartens, elementary schools, and children’s and juveniles’ facilities as electromagnetic-wave safe zones and prohibit the installation of base stations there. This may be understood as prescribing matters concerning the protection of children and juveniles that are not prescribed by the Radio Waves Act. Accordingly, the affairs prescribed in the ordinance bill at issue correspond to autonomous affairs under Article 9(2)2(d) of the Local Autonomy Act. In addition, the designation by the ordinance bill at issue of kindergartens and elementary schools in Gyeonggi Province as electromagnetic-wave safe zones is also consistent with Article 9(2)5(a) of the Local Autonomy Act, which prescribes the installation, operation, and guidance of kindergartens and elementary schools, etc. as autonomous affairs, and also accords with Article 20(9) of the Act on Special Cases concerning the Local Autonomy of Education, which prescribes affairs concerning school health and the purification of the school environment as affairs of the Superintendent.\\n\\nFurthermore, the provisions of the ordinance bill at issue were enacted for the purpose of protecting the health of children and juveniles in Gyeonggi Province within the extent that does not undermine the purpose and effect of Article 47-2 of the Radio Waves Act, which requires the establishment of human body protection standards for electromagnetic waves. Their primary subjects of application are the “kindergarten and elementary school” facilities under the management and supervision of the Superintendent. Accordingly, the provisions of the ordinance bill at issue may be viewed as regulating matters that can be autonomously regulated according to the characteristics of each region and thus as prescribing matters concerning autonomous affairs. The Plaintiffs’ argument that the above provisions concern state affairs and exceed the scope of ordinance-making power is not accepted.\\n\\n5. Whether the provisions of the ordinance bill at issue violate statutes  \\na. According to Articles 22 of the Local Autonomy Act and 4(3) of the Framework Act on Administrative Regulations, when a local government enacts an ordinance, if the content concerns restrictions on the rights of residents or the imposition of obligations, or if it concerns penalties, there must be a delegation by statute. An ordinance that prescribes matters restricting the rights of residents or imposing obligations without statutory delegation has no effect (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2010DU19270, decided November 22, 2012, etc.).\\n\\nHowever, there is no statutory restriction as to the manner in which statutes delegate matters to ordinances. The local council, which is the body vested with the power to enact ordinances, is the representative organ of residents who possess regional democratic legitimacy through elections. Article 117(1) of the Constitution guarantees local governments comprehensive autonomy. Accordingly, delegation by statute to an ordinance need not necessarily define the scope in a specific manner as with delegation by statute to a regulatory order. Even where a statute broadly delegates matters concerning the rights and obligations of residents to be prescribed by ordinance without specifically defining the scope, a local government may enact by ordinance matters concerning the rights and obligations of residents within the extent that they do not violate statutes (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DU947, decided September 8, 2006; Constitutional Court en banc Decision 92HEONMA264, 279, decided April 20, 1995, etc.).\\n\\nb. The freedom to choose an occupation guaranteed by Article 15 of the Constitution includes not only the freedom to freely choose one’s desired occupation, but also the freedom of occupational performance and freedom of business, which together constitute the freedom of occupation concerning how one conducts business (see Constitutional Court en banc Decision 2011HEONBA18, decided November 24, 2011). In addition, the freedom of contract derived from the general freedom of action includes not only the freedom of a party to decide by his or her own will whether to conclude a contract, and if so, with what content, with what counterparty, and in what manner, but also the freedom not to conclude a contract if one does not wish to do so, that is, the freedom not to be compelled by law or by the State to conclude an unwanted contract (see Constitutional Court en banc Decision 97HEONMA345, decided October 29, 1998). However, such freedom of occupation and freedom of contract may be restricted by law only to the extent necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare pursuant to Article 37(2) of the Constitution (see Constitutional Court en banc Decision 2000HEONBA35, decided January 31, 2002; Constitutional Court en banc Decision 2000HEONMA764, decided December 18, 2002, etc.).\\n\\nc. Meanwhile, Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the ordinance bill at issue provides that the Superintendent of the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education may recommend the removal of already installed base stations. This, as non-authoritative administrative guidance, cannot be viewed as restricting the rights of residents or imposing obligations.\\n\\nArticle 5 and Article 6(1) of the ordinance bill at issue are provisions that, when the Superintendent of the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education designates kindergartens, elementary schools, etc. as electromagnetic-wave safe zones, no person may install a base station there; thus, they may be seen as restricting the “freedom of business” of the base-station installer and the “freedom of contract” of the counterparty thereto.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles seen above, Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the ordinance bill at issue is effective even without statutory delegation, whereas Article 5 and Article 6(1) of the ordinance bill at issue are effective only if there is statutory delegation.\\n\\nd. We examine whether there is statutory delegation with respect to Article 5 and Article 6(1) of the ordinance bill at issue.\\n\\n(1) As seen above, Article 5 of the ordinance bill at issue designates kindergartens, elementary schools, and children’s and juveniles’ educational facilities, as well as mixed-use buildings in which they are located that exceed the human body protection standards for electromagnetic waves, as subjects for designation as electromagnetic-wave safe zones.\\n\\nPublic kindergartens, public elementary schools, and public children’s and juveniles’ educational facilities are all schools and facilities established and operated by local governments (see Article 7 of the Early Childhood Education Act and Article 3 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act) and thus constitute public property of the local government. Furthermore, Article 94-2(2) of the Act on the Management of Public Property and Articles provides that a local government may enact and operate matters concerning the management, disposition, revenue, and expenditure of public property and articles by ordinance or rule.\\n\\nThe Elementary and Secondary Education Act applies to national and public as well as private elementary schools, kindergartens, and national/public and private children’s and juveniles’ educational facilities other than kindergartens and elementary schools (see Articles 2 and 3). Article 11 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act provides that all citizens may use facilities of national schools, etc. in accordance with the decision of the head of the school, within the extent that school education is not hindered, and that facilities of public and private schools, etc. may be used as prescribed by municipal and provincial education regulations. In Gyeonggi Province, the “Rules on the Opening and Use of Facilities of Each Level of School Below High School in Gyeonggi Province” have been enacted and are in force, and Article 2(1) of those Rules provides that the heads of public and private schools shall open school facilities.\\n\\n(2) The portions of Article 5 and Article 6(1) of the ordinance bill at issue concerning public kindergartens, public elementary schools, and public children’s and juveniles’ educational facilities may be based on Article 94-2(2) of the Act on the Management of Public Property and Articles, which delegates matters concerning the management of public property, etc. to ordinances, as the statutory basis for delegation. In addition, the portions concerning public and private elementary schools and public and private children’s and juveniles’ educational facilities may be based on Article 11 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, which delegates matters concerning the use of facilities, etc. of public and private schools to education regulations (the portions concerning public elementary schools and public children’s and juveniles’ educational facilities may be based on the above two statutory provisions).\\n\\n(3) However, with respect to the portions of Article 5 and Article 6(1) of the ordinance bill at issue concerning “private kindergartens and mixed-use buildings owned or managed by private persons,” which are neither public property of a local government nor subjects to which the Elementary and Secondary Education Act applies, there exists no statutory provision delegating to ordinances so as to permit restrictions on the freedom of business of the base-station installer and the freedom of contract of the counterparty thereto in relation to the installation of base stations.\\n\\ne. Ultimately, Article 5 and Article 6(1) of the ordinance bill at issue prescribe matters concerning restrictions on the rights of residents with respect to private kindergartens and mixed-use buildings without statutory delegation, and therefore their validity cannot be recognized. The Plaintiffs’ argument pointing this out is correct.\\n\\n6. Where part of an ordinance bill violates statutes  \\nThe ordinance bill at issue is unlawful because part of it violates statutes; however, in such a case, excluding the effect of only part of the resolution would, in consequence, amount to altering the overall contents of the resolution and would infringe the inherent authority of the local council, which is the deciding body. Moreover, excluding the effect of only part of the resolution carries the risk that the overall contents of the resolution may be altered into something different from the local council’s original intent. In addition, where a request for reconsideration is made, even if the objection pointed out in the request concerns only part of the resolution, the entire resolution loses effect, and only the re-adoption takes effect as a new resolution. Accordingly, a request for reconsideration or a request for reconsideration with modification concerning only part of the resolution is not permitted. Taking these points together, even where only part of the re-adopted content is unlawful rather than the entirety thereof, the Supreme Court must deny the validity of the entire resolution (see Supreme Court Decision 92CHU31, decided July 28, 1992, etc.).\\n\\n7. Conclusion  \\nThe ordinance bill at issue is unlawful because part of it violates statutes, and the re-adoption of the ordinance bill at issue is denied effect in its entirety. Accordingly, the Plaintiffs’ claim seeking exclusion of the effect of the re-adoption of the ordinance bill at issue is well-founded and is granted; litigation costs shall be borne by the losing party. Therefore, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, it is adjudged as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following correctly combines the statements concerning defective administrative acts that are correct (○) and incorrect (×)? (In cases of dispute, according to case law) (a) Even if the administrative agency that issued the administrative act had no particular defect at the time of issuance and there is no separate legal basis under the individual statute for withdrawal, if there is a significant public interest necessity after issuance, it may withdraw the administrative act prospectively after balancing public and private interests. (b) As a general rule, an administrative agency may cancel all or part of a defective administrative act retroactively, but where there is justifiable reason, such as where the party's reliance deserves protection, it may cancel it prospectively. (c) If the defect in the beneficial administrative disposition to be canceled is attributable to the party's application act by concealment of facts or other fraudulent means, the party cannot invoke the reliance interest regarding the disposition; however, if the administrative agency does not consider this, it constitutes a deviation from or abuse of discretionary power. (d) Curing a defect in an administrative act is, in principle, not permitted from the standpoint of the nature of the administrative act or the rule of law, but exceptionally, in order to avoid needless repetition of administrative acts and for the legal stability of the parties, not only substantive defects but also procedural defects may be cured.

supporting_precedents: {"[2017DU31064]": "The grounds of appeal (the statements in each preparatory brief submitted after the period for filing the petition for appeal and in the supplemental brief of grounds of appeal shall be considered to the extent they supplement the grounds of appeal) are examined.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case and Issues\\n\\nA. According to the reasons stated in the judgment below and the evidence duly adopted by the court below, the following facts and circumstances may be found.\\n\\n1) The Defendant established a plan concerning the “Solar Power Generation Facility Installation Project within △△△△△△△△ in Gwangju Metropolitan City” (hereinafter referred to as “the Project”) to install solar power generation facilities at the sanitary landfill located in ○○-dong, Buk-gu, Gwangju Metropolitan City, and around 2015. 7. 31. publicly announced the investment solicitation guidelines for the Project (hereinafter referred to as “the Guidelines”) in order to promote the Project.\\n\\n2) In response, a total of five consortia, including the tentatively named “Green Eco-Friendly Energy Co., Ltd.” composed of LG CNS Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “LG CNS”), Korea East-West Power Co., Ltd., and SK Securities Co., Ltd. (which was established as the Plaintiff on 2015. 12. 10.; hereinafter, regardless of whether before or after its establishment, collectively referred to as “the Plaintiff”), and the tentatively named “Bitgoeul Unjeong Solar Power Plant Co., Ltd.” composed of SDN Co., Ltd., SPV Co., Ltd., and the Defendant-intervenor (hereinafter referred to as “Bitgoeul Unjeong”), submitted investment solicitation proposals.\\n\\n3) After a certain review through the Korea Environment Corporation, the Defendant selected the Plaintiff as the preferred negotiation bidder for the Project and Bitgoeul Unjeong as the next-ranked negotiation bidder on 2015. 11. 16.\\n\\n4) Meanwhile, on 2011. 12. 12., the Commissioner of the Public Procurement Service imposed on LG CNS a three-month restriction on qualification to participate in bids on the ground that, in connection with bidding, award, or the conclusion or performance of a contract, an employee of LG CNS had bribed a public official of the Korean Intellectual Property Office from around 2008 to around 2009. LG CNS filed a lawsuit seeking revocation of the disposition restricting qualification to participate in bids, but a judgment dismissing the claim was rendered and became final and conclusive (Supreme Court Decision 2014DU7435 rendered on 2015. 12. 10.). Accordingly, an effect arose that LG CNS’s qualification to participate in bids was restricted pursuant to the relevant statutes from 2015. 12. 11. to 2016. 3. 2.\\n\\n5) Upon learning that LG CNS’s qualification to participate in bids was restricted from 2015. 12. 11. to 2016. 3. 2., the Defendant, on 2016. 2. 29., notified the Plaintiff of a decision to exclude the Plaintiff from the status of preferred negotiation bidder on the ground that, pursuant to Section 7.2 of the Guidelines, it was determined that continuing negotiations with the Plaintiff would not be desirable (hereinafter referred to as “the Decision Excluding the Status of Preferred Negotiation Bidder”).\\n\\n6) On 2016. 3. 29., after informing SDN Co., Ltd. and the representative of Bitgoeul Unjeong that it had decided to proceed with negotiations with Bitgoeul Unjeong, the next-ranked negotiation bidder, in relation to the Project, the Defendant executed an implementation agreement concerning the Project with Bitgoeul Unjeong on 2016. 7. 27. and designated Bitgoeul Unjeong as the project implementer for the Project on 2016. 7. 28.\\n\\nB. The issues in this case are what is the applicable statute underlying the Project, whether the Decision Excluding the Status of Preferred Negotiation Bidder constitutes a disposition subject to administrative appeal litigation, whether the Plaintiff is recognized to have a legal interest in challenging this decision and filing an action for revocation, and whether there are procedural or substantive defects in this decision warranting its revocation.\\n\\n2. With respect to the Defendant’s ground of appeal No. 2 and the argument concerning the applicable statutes among the grounds of appeal of the Defendant-intervenor\\n\\nA. The former Act on Public-Private Partnerships in Infrastructure (before amendment by Act No. 14044 on 2016. 3. 2.; hereinafter referred to as “the PPP Act”) defines “social infrastructure” as “facilities that serve as the basis for various productive activities, facilities that enhance the utility of such facilities or promote convenience for users, and facilities that increase convenience in the lives of the people, and that fall under any one of the following items,” and enumerates the subject facilities in each item (Article 2, subparagraph 1); defines “social infrastructure project” as “a project concerning the establishment, expansion, improvement, or operation of social infrastructure” (Article 2, subparagraph 2); and defines “private investment project” as “a project proposed by the private sector pursuant to Article 9 or a social infrastructure project implemented by the project implementer under subparagraph 7 pursuant to the master plan for social infrastructure facilities projects under Article 10” (main clause of subparagraph 5).\\n\\nThus, the PPP Act merely provides that certain social infrastructure may be implemented in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the PPP Act, and it does not expressly contain any “priority application provision” stating that projects in which private investors install and operate social infrastructure must be carried out only pursuant to the PPP Act. Therefore, it is difficult to view the PPP Act as purporting to disallow private investment projects based on other individual statutes, in addition to private investment projects under the PPP Act. Accordingly, so long as other individual statutes permit private investment projects in other forms, it is proper to view that the administrative agency has discretion to promote private investment projects in other forms based on individual statutes other than the PPP Act, and the same applies even where the subject facility constitutes social infrastructure under the PPP Act and the private investment project method under the PPP Act is available.\\n\\nB. According to the reasons stated in the judgment below and the evidence duly adopted by the court below, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n1) The full text of the Defendant’s announcement around 2015. 7. 31. states: “Pursuant to Article 26 of the Act on the Promotion of the Development, Use, and Diffusion of New and Renewable Energy and Article 7 of the Public Property and Commodity Management Act, we hereby publicly announce the request for investment proposals to promote the ‘Solar Power Generation Facility Installation Project within △△△△△△△△.’”\\n\\n2) The Guidelines expressly state that the basis for the facility use-and-profit permission period is “Article 7 of the Public Property and Commodity Management Act (donation and acceptance), Article 21 (period of use-and-profit permission), and Article 26 of the Act on the Promotion of the Development, Use, and Diffusion of New and Renewable Energy (lease, etc. of state property and public property)” (Section 3.1), and stipulate that the method of promoting the project is “full burden by the private proposer and a similar BTO method (※ A similar BTO method means a method by which, after constructing the facility, the facility is donated pursuant to the Public Property and Commodity Management Act and permission to use and profit the facility is granted)” (Section 3.2); they further provide that Article 7(9) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on Public-Private Partnerships in Infrastructure shall be “applied mutatis mutandis” with respect to the evaluation of investment solicitation proposals and the announcement of negotiation candidates (Section 9.5), and that Article 13 of the PPP Act shall be “applied mutatis mutandis” with respect to the designation of the project implementer (Section 9.6).\\n\\nC. Examining these factual relations in light of the foregoing legal principles, although the subject facility of the Project falls under social infrastructure under the PPP Act [new and renewable energy facilities under Article 2, subparagraph 1, item (mu) of the PPP Act and Article 2, subparagraph 3 of the Act on the Promotion of the Development, Use, and Diffusion of New and Renewable Energy], it is clear that the Defendant decided to promote the Project not by way of a private investment project under the PPP Act but by way of donation and acceptance and permission for use and profit under the Public Property and Commodity Management Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Public Property Act”). Therefore, whether each disposition or measure taken by the Defendant while promoting the Project is lawful, in principle, should be determined according to whether the standards and procedures prescribed by the Public Property Act, which serves as the basis law, were complied with, and the PPP Act cannot be applied absent an express basis in the relevant statutes.\\n\\nD. Nevertheless, the court below held that the PPP Act applies to the Project. The judgment below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the basis law applicable to private investment projects. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. With respect to the Defendant’s ground of appeal No. 3 and the argument concerning dispositional nature among the grounds of appeal of the Defendant-intervenor\\n\\nA. The “disposition” that is the subject of administrative appeal litigation means “the exercise or refusal of public authority as an enforcement of law concerning concrete facts by an administrative agency, and other equivalent administrative acts” (Article 2(1)(i) of the Administrative Litigation Act). Whether an act of an administrative agency may be the subject of administrative appeal litigation cannot be determined abstractly and generally; in a specific case, it must be determined individually by considering the content and purpose of the relevant statutes and regulations, the subject, content, form, and procedure of the act, the substantive nexus between the act and the disadvantage suffered by the other party and other interested persons, and the principle of administration under the rule of law and the attitude of the administrative agency or interested persons concerning the act (en banc Supreme Court Decision 2008DU167 rendered on 2010. 11. 18.). In addition, whether a certain disposition has a legal basis under statutes, or whether the disposition procedures prescribed by the Administrative Procedures Act were complied with, is a factor to be considered at the stage of determining whether the relevant disposition is lawful on the merits, and not a factor to be considered at the stage of examining litigation requirements (Supreme Court Decision 2015DU60617 rendered on 2016. 8. 30.).\\n\\nB.
