Under the Public Property Act, “public property” means “property listed in each item of Article 4(1) that belongs to a local government by burden borne by the local government, donation and acceptance, or by statutes” (Article 2, subparagraph 1), and the head of a local government may accept property listed in each item of Article 4(1) from a person intending to donate such property to the local government, pursuant to the Presidential Decree (Article 7(1)). In addition, the head of a local government may permit the use or profit from administrative property to the extent that such use or profit does not impede the purpose or use of such property (Article 20(1)); in such case, as a general rule, a general competitive bidding process is required, but “where permission for free use and profit is granted to a donor under the proviso to Article 7(2) and his or her heirs or other universal successors,” the permission may be granted by nominated competitive bidding or by the sole-source method (Article 20(2), subparagraph 2).\\n\\nC. Synthesizing the content and system of the provisions of the Public Property Act and the relevant legal principles, in the process in which the head of a local government promotes a private investment project on the basis of the Public Property Act by accepting donation of public property and granting permission for use and profit, both the act of receiving public proposals and selecting the preferred negotiation bidder through a certain review at the preliminary stage for designating the project implementer, and the act of excluding the already selected preferred negotiation bidder from that status, constitute acts of setting, or depriving, a status by which permission for use and profit of public property under the Public Property Act may be preferentially granted after negotiation on the detailed terms of the private investment project; accordingly, both must be regarded as administrative dispositions subject to administrative appeal litigation. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) In some cases, the head of a local government promotes a private investment project on the basis of the Public Property Act by having a private investor install specified facilities and donate them, and then granting permission for use and profit of public property so that the investor may operate the facilities free of charge for a certain period and earn profits. The Guidelines in this case may be viewed as having publicly announced, in advance, the internal administrative plan and standards for disposition (Article 20 of the Administrative Procedures Act) by presenting the detailed matters necessary to promote the Project while the Defendant was promoting the Project as a private investment project based on the Public Property Act. According to the Guidelines, the Project proceeds in the order of proposal solicitation → proposal review → selection of the preferred negotiation bidder → negotiation → execution of the implementation agreement and designation of the project implementer → approval of the implementation plan → construction of facilities → donation of facilities → permission for use and profit of public property → management and operation. In this method of progression, only the donation of facilities and the permission for use and profit of public property are matters directly regulated by the Public Property Act, while the remainder were prescribed in the Guidelines by the Defendant by reference to the progression method of a private investment project under the PPP Act.\\n\\n2) Here, the selection of the preferred negotiation bidder is not the final act in a series of administrative processes but rather an intermediate act; thus, the question arises whether it should indeed be characterized as a disposition subject to administrative appeal litigation. It is not necessary to recognize internal or intermediate acts in a series of administrative processes as dispositions in all cases; they must be determined individually and concretely in consideration of the particular nature of each administrative act. To make internal or intermediate acts separately challengeable as subjects of administrative appeal litigation apart from the final act, there must be recognized, on the one hand, the need for early and effective resolution of disputes, and on the other hand, the need to secure early finality of legal relations through the filing period and preclusive effect, as well as the smooth execution of administration, by viewing such acts as dispositions.\\n\\n3) In the course of a local government head promoting a private investment project on the basis of the Public Property Act, not only the permission for use and profit concerning public property donated to the local government, but also the preferential granting or deprivation of the opportunity to become the counterparty to such permission for use and profit, constitute an exercise of public authority based on the Public Property Act.\\n\\n4) In the case of a competing applicant who failed to be selected as the preferred negotiation bidder after a certain review of a proposal submitted in response to a public solicitation, there is a need to enable such applicant to challenge the decision selecting the preferred negotiation bidder at an early stage by means of administrative appeal litigation. If the head of a local government were to complete negotiations with the preferred negotiation bidder regarding the detailed terms of the private investment project and then finish both the donation and acceptance and the permission for use and profit of public property before allowing an interested third party to challenge the permission for use and profit of public property by means of administrative appeal litigation, effective relief of rights may become difficult; moreover, after a series of administrative processes has already substantially progressed, cancelling all subsequent procedures on the ground of defects at the earlier stage of the decision selecting the preferred negotiation bidder could impede the smooth execution of administration. Furthermore, if the decision selecting the preferred negotiation bidder is regarded as a disposition, a measure by the administrative agency revoking or withdrawing it ex officio must also be regarded as a disposition.\\n\\n5) The Supreme Court has, in cases of designation of a preferred negotiation bidder or withdrawal of such designation in a private investment project implemented on the basis of the PPP Act, rendered merits decisions on the premise that such acts constitute dispositions (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DU9181 rendered on 2010. 9. 30., Supreme Court Decision 2011DU27599 rendered on 2013. 9. 26., etc.).\\n\\nD. The court below, premised on the view that the Decision Excluding the Status of Preferred Negotiation Bidder made on 2016. 2. 29. in the course of the Defendant’s promotion of the private investment project on the basis of the Public Property Act constitutes a disposition subject to administrative appeal litigation, proceeded to examine and determine the existence of procedural and substantive defects on the merits. The judgment below is based on the foregoing legal principles and contains no error, such as misapprehending the law on dispositional nature, as alleged in the ground of appeal (hereinafter, the Defendant’s Decision Excluding the Status of Preferred Negotiation Bidder dated 2016. 2. 29. shall be referred to as “the Disposition”).\\n\\n4. With respect to the Defendant’s ground of appeal No. 1\\n\\nThe court below, taking the position that the counterparty to the Disposition was the Plaintiff and that the Plaintiff had a legal interest in seeking revocation of the Disposition, proceeded to examine and determine the case on the merits.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in the judgment below, as alleged in the ground of appeal, in that it misapprehended the legal principles concerning the Plaintiff’s standing to sue in an action for revocation.\\n\\n5. With respect to the Defendant’s ground of appeal No. 4 and the argument concerning procedural defects among the grounds of appeal of the Defendant-intervenor\\n\\nA. The court below held that, because the PPP Act applies to the Project, there was a procedural defect in that the Defendant failed to conduct a hearing pursuant to Article 48 of the PPP Act before making the Disposition, and that therefore the Disposition is unlawful and must be revoked.\\n\\nB. As pointed out in Section 2 above, the court below erred in holding that the PPP Act applies to the Project. In addition, it cannot be said that, while a head of a local government is promoting a private investment project on the basis of the Public Property Act, there is always a duty to conduct a hearing in order to make a disposition depriving a party of the status of preferred negotiation bidder. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) Under Article 21(1) and (4) and Article 22(1), (3), and (4) of the Administrative Procedures Act, where an administrative agency makes a disposition imposing obligations on, or restricting the rights and interests of, a party, it must, in advance, notify the party, etc. of matters such as the “title of the disposition,” “the facts giving rise to the intended disposition, the content of the disposition, and the legal basis,” “the effect that opinions may be submitted in response and the method of handling if no opinion is submitted,” “the name and address of the opinion-submission agency,” and “the deadline for submission of opinions”; the deadline for submission of opinions must be set by taking into account a reasonable period necessary for submitting opinions; and even where other statutes, etc. do not mandate a hearing or the holding of a public hearing, the party, etc. must be given an opportunity to submit opinions; provided, however, that prior notice of the disposition or hearing of opinions may be omitted only where there are “reasonable grounds to find that, by the nature of the disposition concerned, hearing opinions is markedly difficult or clearly unnecessary.” Accordingly, if an administrative agency makes an injurious administrative disposition without providing the party with such prior notice or an opportunity to submit opinions, then, unless it falls within the exceptional cases where prior notice or hearing of opinions is not required, the disposition is unlawful and cannot avoid revocation (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2016DU41811 rendered on 2016. 10. 27.).\\n\\nThe reason the Administrative Procedures Act provides for prior notice and hearing of opinions when an administrative agency makes a disposition imposing obligations on, or restricting the rights and interests of, a party is to substantively guarantee the exercise of the defense rights of the recipient of an unfavorable disposition (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DU33339 rendered on 2018. 3. 13.).\\n\\n2) In light of the content and system of the Administrative Procedures Act, where an administrative agency makes a disposition imposing obligations on, or restricting the rights and interests of, a party, it is in principle sufficient to provide prior notice under Article 21(1) of the Administrative Procedures Act and an opportunity to submit opinions under Article 22(3), and there is a duty to conduct a hearing only where other statutes, etc. specifically require a hearing or where the administrative agency deems it necessary.\\n\\n3) Neither the Public Property Act nor the Guidelines prepared by the Defendant contain any provision requiring that a hearing be conducted in every case where a disposition is made ex officio revoking or withdrawing the decision selecting the preferred negotiation bidder and depriving that bidder of its status.\\n\\nC. Accordingly, the judgment below, which found a procedural defect in that no hearing was conducted on the premise that the PPP Act applies to the Disposition, contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning hearing of opinions and hearings under the Administrative Procedures Act. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n6. With respect to the Defendant’s ground of appeal No. 5 and the argument concerning substantive defects among the grounds of appeal of the Defendant-intervenor\\n\\nA. Even if the agency issuing the disposition had no particular defect at the time of the disposition, and even if there is no separate legal basis for withdrawing it after the disposition, where there has arisen a change in circumstances such that it is no longer necessary to maintain the original disposition, or where a serious public interest necessity has arisen, the disposition may be withdrawn by a separate disposition that extinguishes its effect. However, in the case of revoking or withdrawing a beneficial disposition, since this would infringe the vested rights already granted to the citizen, even if there are grounds such as revocation, the exercise of such revocation authority, etc. must be determined in comparison and balancing against the disadvantages suffered by the counterparty, and only where there is a serious public interest necessity or a need to protect the interests of a third party that would justify infringing vested rights; if the disadvantages suffered by the counterparty due to the disposition far exceed the public interest necessity, it is beyond the limits of discretion and impermissible (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DU12648 rendered on 2009. 11. 12., etc.).\\n\\nB. The court below held that the disadvantage suffered by the Plaintiff is markedly greater than the public interest necessity that the Defendant sought to achieve through the Disposition, based on the following circumstances, and therefore found the Disposition unlawful as an abuse or excess of discretion.\\n\\n1) LG CNS is merely one investor in the Plaintiff. Due to the Disposition, not only the Plaintiff’s other investors excluding LG CNS but also the Defendant-intervenor, which is a participant in the construction, are suffering damage.\\n\\n2) The restriction on LG CNS’s qualification to participate in bids under the State Contracts Act, imposed by the Commissioner of the Public Procurement Service, was a disposition made on 2011. 12. 12. on the ground of bribery in 2008 and 2009.\\n\\n3) The date of the Disposition, 2016. 2. 29., is only two days before 2016. 3. 2., the expiration date of the restriction on LG CNS’s qualification to participate in bids under the State Contracts Act. After 2016. 3. 2., LG CNS may bid without restriction even on government-funded public works ordered by the State and local governments.\\n\\nC. However, the foregoing judgment of the court below is difficult to accept as it stands for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) Article 31(4) of the Act on Contracts to Which a Local Government Is a Party, which is applied mutatis mutandis to contracts for public property and commodities pursuant to Article 97(1) of the Public Property Act, provides: “A person whose qualification to participate in bids has been restricted pursuant to paragraphs (1) through (3) shall be restricted from participating in all bids conducted by each local government during the restricted period. The same shall apply to a person whose qualification to participate in bids has been restricted under other statutes.” In addition, the main clause of Article 92(10) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Act on Contracts to Which a Local Government Is a Party (before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 26491 of 2015. 8. 19.) provides: “If the person who won a bid is subject to a restriction on qualification to participate in bids pursuant to paragraph (1) before the conclusion of the contract, the head of a local government or the contract officer shall not conclude the contract with that successful bidder.”\\n\\nAnd Section 4.1 of the Guidelines provides, with respect to the qualifications of the proposer, that “a person who, as of the deadline for receipt of business proposals, is subject to sanctions as an improper contractor under the Act on Contracts to Which the State Is a Party, the Act on Contracts to Which a Local Government Is a Party, or the Act on Public-Private Partnerships in Infrastructure, or under notices/statutes by the competent authority or the ordering agency, shall not be allowed to become a proposer under the public solicitation or an investor (including a prospective investor).”\\n\\nConsidering the content and system of these provisions, together with the legislative purpose of the qualification restriction system, which aims to secure faithful performance of contracts concluded by the State and at the same time prevent disadvantages to the State in advance by excluding for a certain period persons who engage in acts disturbing fair bidding and contracting order from participation, the intent of the Defendant in setting forth the disqualifying grounds for a proposer under the public solicitation or an investor (including a prospective investor) should be understood not as merely excluding persons who have been subject to qualification restriction dispositions under various statutes only at the bidding stage, but as excluding them even at the negotiation stage, which is preparatory to contract conclusion and the conclusion of the contract.\\n\\nAccordingly, if, after selection as the preferred negotiation bidder, the effects of restriction pursuant to a disposition restricting qualification to participate in bids arise, the Defendant should not conclude an implementation agreement (contract) with that preferred negotiation bidder during the restriction period, and should not even conduct negotiations, which are preparatory steps for concluding the implementation agreement; the same applies where the effects of restriction pursuant to a disposition restricting qualification to participate in bids arise with respect to an investor. However, whether, in a case where the effects of restriction pursuant to a disposition restricting qualification to participate in bids arise after selection as the preferred negotiation bidder, it is sufficient to temporarily suspend or hold in abeyance the negotiations until the restriction period expires, or whether the status of the preferred negotiation bidder itself must be deprived, cannot be uniformly determined, and must be individually decided in the specific case by comparing and balancing the relevant public and private interests in accordance with the legal principles governing limitations on ex officio revocation or withdrawal of beneficial dispositions.\\n\\nIn this case, after the selection of the preferred negotiation bidder on 2015. 11. 16., LG CNS, while partially conducting negotiations with the Defendant for concluding the implementation agreement as the representative of the LG CNS consortium, lost the related lawsuit and the effect of qualification restriction arose from 2015. 12. 11.; upon learning that LG CNS concealed this fact from the Defendant for about two months without promptly notifying it, the Defendant compared and balanced the relevant public and private interests and determined that merely suspending or holding in abeyance negotiations during LG CNS’s qualification restriction period would not sufficiently give effect to the legislative purpose of the qualification restriction system, and that it was necessary to deprive the Plaintiff of the status of preferred negotiation bidder. There is no error in this determination by the Defendant in violation of the provisions of the relevant statutes or the relevant legal principles.\\n\\n2) Since there is also Bitgoeul Unjeong, the next-ranked negotiation bidder, in addition to the Plaintiff, the preferred negotiation bidder, among the negotiation candidates for the Project, it is necessary to consider the interests of the next-ranked negotiation bidder as well.\\n\\n3) The reason there was an approximately four-year temporal gap between the time the effect of the disposition restricting LG CNS’s qualification to participate in bids arose and the time of LG CNS’s improper conduct is that, in the course of the revocation lawsuit against the said disposition, its effect was suspended by a court decision staying execution granted upon LG CNS’s application. In addition, the fact that the Defendant made the Disposition only two days before the expiration date of the aforementioned disposition restricting qualification to participate in bids had an unavoidable aspect in that LG CNS concealed that fact for about two months, and after learning of that fact, the Defendant carefully reviewed whether to issue the Disposition through prior notice and opinion-submission procedures, which took time. Therefore, based on these circumstances alone, it is also difficult to conclude that the Disposition was unnecessary or that the Defendant abused or exceeded its discretion as to the timing of the administrative disposition by making the Disposition belatedly.\\n\\nD. Nevertheless, the court below held otherwise and, relying only on the circumstances noted above, found that the Disposition was unlawful as an abuse or excess of discretion. The judgment below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning withdrawal of beneficial dispositions. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n7. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for a new trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Supreme Court Justices who participated, as stated in the dispositive part."}

{"[2019DU39611]": "We determine the grounds for appeal (the statements in the supplemental brief filed after the expiration of the period for filing the petition for final appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. Summary of the Case and Issues\\n\\na. According to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n1) The Plaintiff is a foundation corporation that was granted permission for establishment on 2016. 1. 13., with projects such as the discovery and support of athletic talent as its purpose business.\\n\\n2) The Defendant revoked the incorporation permission in this case against the Plaintiff on 2017. 3. 20. on the grounds that, first, since large corporations had involuntarily contributed capital due to criminal acts committed by public officials in the course of the Plaintiff’s establishment, there existed an original defect requiring revocation of the incorporation permission granted to the Plaintiff; and, second, because even in the course of the Plaintiff’s operation after its establishment, Nonparty 1 had pursued private interests, the very existence of the Plaintiff was harmful to the public interest, based on the legal doctrine of ex officio revocation of administrative dispositions and Article 38 of the Civil Act.\\n\\nb. The issues in this case are whether the two grounds for disposition stated by the Defendant in the revocation disposition of the incorporation permission in this case are justified, that is, whether: ① there was an original defect in the incorporation permission so that it is permissible to revoke ex officio the incorporation permission granted to the Plaintiff on that ground; and ② grounds prescribed in Article 38 of the Civil Act arose in the course of operation after establishment so that it is permissible to revoke the incorporation permission granted to the Plaintiff on that ground.\\n\\n2. Whether ex officio revocation of the incorporation permission is permissible on the ground of an original defect in the incorporation permission\\n\\na. 1) Where the administrative agency that issued an administrative act finds that the act is defective, it may, even without a separate legal basis, revoke it on its own. However, when revoking a beneficial administrative disposition, only where, after comparing and balancing the public interest necessity to revoke it and the disadvantages such revocation would impose on the party, such as infringement of vested rights, protection of trust, and stability of legal life, the public interest necessity is sufficiently strong to justify the disadvantages that the party would suffer, may the revocation be made. Furthermore, if the defect in a beneficial administrative disposition is attributable to an application made by the party through concealment of facts or other fraudulent means, the party should be deemed to have known that the benefit conferred by the disposition was unlawfully obtained and to have anticipated the possibility of revocation; therefore, the party itself cannot invoke the interest in trust regarding the disposition, and even if the administrative agency did not consider this, it cannot be deemed an abuse of discretion (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of 2014. 11. 27., 2013DU16111).\\n\\n2) Although an administrative trial is not bound by the findings of fact in a criminal trial, since facts found guilty in a final criminal judgment concerning the same factual relationship constitute powerful evidentiary material, unless there are special circumstances making it difficult to adopt the factual findings of the criminal trial in light of other evidence submitted in the administrative trial, facts contrary thereto cannot be recognized (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of 2012. 5. 24., 2011DU28240).\\n\\nb. The court below determined as follows.\\n\\n1) In the process of establishing the Plaintiff, Nonparty 2, former President, Nonparty 3, former Senior Secretary for Economic Affairs of the Blue House, Nonparty 1, and others conspired and abused the President’s authority to coerce contributions, and accordingly large corporations contributed a total of 269 hundred million won as the Plaintiff’s capital; such conduct constitutes a legal act voidable as a manifestation of intent under duress.\\n\\n2) Therefore, even though the Plaintiff did not satisfy the requirement of establishing a financial foundation capable of carrying out the intended business, the incorporation permission granted by the Defendant while overlooking this fact must be deemed to have a serious defect; and since the public interest necessity to eliminate the result of unlawful exercise of public power and restore the legal order by revoking the incorporation permission granted to the Plaintiff is far greater than the private interests infringed upon thereby against the Plaintiff and its officers and employees, the revocation disposition of the incorporation permission in this case does not violate the principle of protection of trust or the principle of proportionality, and so forth.\\n\\nc. In light of the point that, in the related criminal trial, it was determined that the conduct of Nonparty 3, Nonparty 1, and others demanding from large corporations contributions for the establishment of the Plaintiff did not easily qualify as the notification of harm constituting an element of the crime of coercion (see Supreme Court en banc Decision of 2019. 8. 29., 2018DO13792), the portion of the court below’s holding that the contribution by large corporations constituted a manifestation of intent under duress is not appropriate.\\n\\nHowever, in light of the point that, in the related criminal trial, it was determined that the conduct of Nonparty 2, former President, Nonparty 3, Nonparty 1, and others in conspiracy in the process of establishing the Plaintiff, by abusing the authority of public officials and causing large corporations to contribute a total of 269 hundred million won, constituted the crime of abuse of authority as conduct making another do an act for which there is no duty (see the above en banc Decision 2018DO13792 and Supreme Court en banc Decision of 2019. 8. 29., 2018DO14303), the Defendant’s granting of permission for the Plaintiff’s establishment while overlooking the fact that a crime committed in the performance of official duties by a public official had intervened in the process of the Plaintiff’s establishment was seriously defective; therefore, the public interest necessity to revoke the incorporation permission granted to the Plaintiff and thereby eliminate the result of unlawful exercise of public power and restore the legal order must be deemed far greater than the private interests infringed upon thereby against the Plaintiff and its officers and employees.\\n\\nAccordingly, the conclusion of the court below that the revocation disposition of the incorporation permission in this case satisfied the requirements for ex officio revocation of a beneficial administrative disposition and was lawful is justified and acceptable. There is no illegality in the court below’s determination, such as misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning ex officio revocation of a beneficial administrative disposition or the probative value of related criminal judgments as argued in the grounds for final appeal, or, contrary to logic and the rules of experience, exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence and thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n3. Whether revocation of the incorporation permission under Article 38 of the Civil Act is permissible\\n\\na. Article 38 of the Civil Act provides, “When a corporation carries on a business other than its purpose, violates the conditions of incorporation permission, or otherwise commits an act harmful to the public interest, the competent authority may revoke its permission,” thereby setting out grounds for revocation of incorporation permission concerning non-profit corporations. Here, the phrase that a non-profit corporation “has committed an act harmful to the public interest” means a case where an organ of the corporation, in the execution of its duties, commits an act infringing the public interest, or where the general meeting of members adopts such a resolution. In addition, Article 38 of the Civil Act is a provision intended to address the case where, although the business that the corporation intended at the time of its establishment was not harmful to the public interest, it later became harmful to the public interest due to a change in circumstances; and in light of the fact that revocation of a corporation’s incorporation permission is a sanctioning disposition that dissolves the corporation and ultimately extinguishes its legal personality (Article 77(1) of the Civil Act), in order to fall under the case of “committing an act harmful to the public interest” prescribed in Article 38 of the Civil Act, the purpose business or the existence itself of the relevant corporation must be deemed harmful to the public interest, or the act of the relevant corporation must directly and concretely infringe the public interest; and, taking into comprehensive consideration the content of the purpose business, the manner and degree of unlawfulness of the act, the degree and circumstances of the infringement of the public interest, etc., it must be a case where ordering the extinction of the relevant corporation is indispensably required as a sanction to remove the unlawful state of public-interest infringement and restore the proper legal order (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of 2014. 1. 23., 2011DU25012).\\n\\nb. The court below determined as follows.\\n\\n1) In the course of the Plaintiff’s operation after its establishment, Nonparty 1 contributed property to the Plaintiff or, although not being an officer or employee of the Plaintiff, in fact controlled and managed the Plaintiff; and, while Nonparty 2, former President, and Nonparty 1 were in conspiracy, Nonparty 4, the Plaintiff’s standing director and secretary-general, and Nonparty 5, an employee of the Plaintiff, acting according to Nonparty 1’s instructions, demanded 75 hundred million won from the ○○ Group under the pretext of additional support funds for the Plaintiff’s business, received 70 hundred million won, and demanded 89 hundred million won from the △△△△ Group; this was not merely a personal deviation by Nonparty 4, etc., but must be deemed to fall under “the Plaintiff having committed an act harmful to the public interest,” which is a ground for revocation of incorporation permission prescribed in Article 38 of the Civil Act.\\n\\n2) Even considering the disadvantages that the Plaintiff and its officers and employees may suffer if the incorporation permission granted to the Plaintiff is revoked, since revoking the incorporation permission granted to the Plaintiff is indispensably required in order to eliminate the unlawful state of public-interest infringement and restore the proper legal order, the revocation disposition of the incorporation permission in this case does not violate the legal doctrine concerning Article 38 of the Civil Act, and so forth.\\n\\nc. In light of the point that, in the related criminal trial, the conduct of Nonparty 4 and Nonparty 5, officers and employees of the Plaintiff, in demanding 75 hundred million won from the ○○ Group under the pretext of additional support funds for the Plaintiff’s business and receiving 70 hundred million won, and their conduct in demanding 89 hundred million won from the △△△△ Group, was determined to constitute a violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (receipt of bribes by a third party and demand for bribes by a third party) committed in conspiracy with Nonparty 2, former President, and Nonparty 1 (see the above en banc Decision 2018DO13792), and so forth, the above determination by the court below is acceptable. There is no illegality in the court below’s determination, such as misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning Article 38 of the Civil Act or the probative value of related criminal judgments as argued in the grounds for final appeal, or, contrary to logic and the rules of experience, exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence and thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[90NU1359]": "The grounds of appeal of the Defendant and the Defendant Auxiliary Intervenor (hereinafter referred to as the Intervening Company) (the Defendant’s supplemental grounds of appeal stated in the supplemental statement of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal, only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal) are determined as follows.\\n\\n(1) With respect to the argument that there is illegality in misapprehending the legal principle concerning the “justifiable cause” under the proviso of Article 18(3) of the Administrative Appeals Act\\n\\nWhen a third party who is not the addressee of an administrative disposition files an administrative appeal as an interested person, even if he or she did not file the petition for adjudication within the petition period (180 days from the date on which the disposition was made) prescribed in the main clause of Article 18(3) of the Administrative Appeals Act, unless there are special circumstances under which the petition for adjudication could have been filed within the adjudication petition period, it is deemed that there was justifiable cause for failing to comply with the period prescribed in the proviso to that provision, and thus the petition is not subject to the limitation period for filing a petition for adjudication; this is the precedent of this Court (see, inter alia, this Court Decisions 83NU59 rendered on 1983.7.12.; 86NU473 rendered on 1986.11.11.; 88NU29 rendered on 1988.9.27.; 88NU5150 rendered on 1989.5.9., etc.).\\n\\nThe court below, based on the evidence cited by it, found the following: On 1987.5.16., at the request of the Intervening Company, the Defendant rendered, with respect to five existing operating routes each having Daegu as the origin and Uiseong, Gibori, Jibo, Yecheon, and Onhye, respectively, as the destination in the northern North Gyeongsang area, an approval disposition for a change in the business plan (hereinafter referred to as the disposition at issue) to the effect that, with each destination as the origin, Daegu, the origin, would be made a stopping point, the operating route would be extended, the destination would be Busan, and the stopping points would be partially changed as stated in the judgment of the court below; the Intervening Company commenced operation pursuant to the disposition at issue on 1988.2.12. and began publicizing the fact of operation to the general public around that time; the Plaintiffs, without knowing at all that the disposition at issue had been made, only learned of the fact that the disposition at issue had been made after obtaining and viewing, on 1988.2.18., a publicity material concerning the Intervening Company’s commencement of operation, and then, as third parties interested in the disposition at issue, filed an administrative appeal with the Minister of Transportation on 1988.4.11.; and when, on 1988.5.17., the Minister of Transportation dismissed the administrative appeal as improper on the ground that it had been filed after the expiration of the adjudication petition period, the Plaintiffs received the adjudication document on the 20th of that month and filed this action with the court below on 1988.7.6. Having so found, the court below held that although it is plainly evident from the reverse calculation that the administrative appeal filed by the Plaintiffs was filed after the 180 days prescribed in the main clause of Article 18(3) of the Administrative Appeals Act had elapsed from the date on which the disposition at issue was made, in this case the Plaintiffs only came to know of the fact of the disposition through the Intervening Company’s external publicity, and that in such a case there must be deemed to be justifiable cause for failing to comply with the above 180-day petition period, and accordingly rejected the Defendant’s defense going to the merits.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the court below’s findings of fact and judgment are justified and acceptable, and there is no illegality in misapprehension of law as pointed out in the argument. The line of argument criticizing the judgment below from a contrary view cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(2) With respect to the argument that there is illegality in misapprehending the legal principle concerning route licenses and approval of changes to business plans under the Motor Vehicle Transportation Business Act\\n\\nA. Under Article 3(1) of the Motor Vehicle Transportation Business Act (as in effect prior to the amendment of 1989.12.30.) and Article 2 item 1 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act (as in effect prior to the amendment of 1987.7.24.), among motor vehicle transportation businesses, route passenger motor vehicle transportation business is subdivided into city bus transportation business, express bus transportation business, and intercity bus transportation business. Under Article 4(1) of the same Act, a person who intends to operate a motor vehicle transportation business shall submit a business plan and obtain a license from the Minister of Transportation. According to Article 10(1), Article 10(2), Article 11, and Article 12 of the Enforcement Rules of the same Act (as in effect prior to the amendment of 1987.9.19.), a person who intends to apply for a route passenger motor vehicle transportation business license shall, together with the application form, submit a business plan stating nine matters necessary for the operation of the relevant business, such as the operating route (origin, stopping points, and destination), as listed in each item of Article 12(1) of the same Enforcement Rules, and a proposed route and route map stating three matters, such as the names and lot numbers of the origin and destination, as listed in each item of Article 11(1) of the same Enforcement Rules. Under the respective provisions of Article 4(2) and Article 6 of the same Act, Article 13(1) and Article 13-2 of the Enforcement Rules of the same Act (as in effect prior to the amendment of 1987.9.19.), and Article 14(1) of the Enforcement Rules of the same Act (as in effect prior to the amendment of 1989.3.29.), the Minister of Transportation, in licensing a motor vehicle transportation business, is to determine the route and grant the license after examining whether the business plan is appropriate to the transportation demand and transport capacity supply of the relevant route or business area and whether facilities and the like required for the relevant business are provided. Meanwhile, under Article 13(1) of the same Act, a person who has already obtained a motor vehicle transportation business license must obtain approval from the Minister of Transportation when intending to change the business plan; however, minor matters prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry of Transportation are to be reported to the Minister of Transportation. Under Article 21(1) of the same Enforcement Rules based thereon (as in effect prior to the amendment of 1987.9.19.), a person who intends to obtain approval of a change in the business plan with respect to matters stated in the business plan under Article 12 of the above Enforcement Rules pursuant to the main clause of Article 13 of the Act shall submit the prescribed application form to the Minister of Transportation. {Under Article 69(1) of the same Act and Article 9(1) items 1 and 5 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act (as in effect prior to the amendment of 1987.7.24.), the authority concerning motor vehicle transportation business licenses other than express bus transportation business licenses and approvals of changes to business plans is delegated to the Governors.} Article 2 item 1 of the Guidelines for Processing Licensing and Approval Affairs under the Motor Vehicle Transportation Business Act (Ministry of Transportation Directive No. 823), based on Article 13-2 of the Enforcement Rules of the same Act (as in effect prior to the amendment of 1987.9.19.), defines a route as “a section in which the origin, stopping points, and destination distances are specified and along which route passenger motor vehicle transportation operators and route freight motor vehicle transportation operators may operate,” and the main clause of item 2 of the same Article defines an operating route as “a section in which operations are conducted by setting the distance from the origin to the stopping points and destination and the number of trips within the licensed route.”\\n\\nAccordingly, when the above provisions and the purport of the provisions concerning motor vehicle transportation businesses and approval of changes to business plans are considered together, the operating route included in an intercity bus transportation business plan means only the origin, stopping points, and destination within the licensed route. Therefore, where changing the origin, stopping points, or destination causes the route originally licensed to be exceeded, it cannot be done by approval of a change to the business plan, and such approval of a change to the business plan should in substance be regarded as corresponding to a license for a new passenger motor vehicle transportation business.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the court below’s judgment, the court below, taking together the respective provisions of Article 3(1), Article 4(1) and (2), and Article 13(1) of the Motor Vehicle Transportation Business Act as in effect at the time of the disposition at issue, reasoned that in the case of route passenger motor vehicle transportation business, one obtains a business license for a certain route and thereby may establish various operating routes within that route, so that the establishment or extension of a route can be done only by a business license, whereas changes or extensions of operating routes within the licensed route can be done only by approval of a change to the business plan; and then, based on the undisputed facts and the cited evidence, held that the intercity bus transportation business license held by the Intervening Company covered only five routes consisting of Daegu as the origin and Uiseong, Gibori, Jibo, Yecheon, and Onhye in the northern North Gyeongsang area as the respective destinations, and the route with Daegu as the origin, Yeongcheon as the stopping point, and Jinbo as the destination, and the route with Chungbuk Danyang as the origin, Yeongju, Andong, Uiseong, Yeongcheon, and the expressway as stopping points, and Busan as the destination, which it had acquired by transfer from the non-party Guksin Passenger Co., Ltd. on 1986.11.14.; therefore, while it appears that it possesses a route license for the section from the northern North Gyeongsang area, which is the origin, to Daegu, and for the expressway operating section from Yeongcheon to Busan among the sections whose operating route was extended by the disposition at issue, it does not possess a route license for the expressway operating section from the Seo-Daegu Interchange to Yeongcheon; and, given that a route must specify the distances from the origin to the stopping points and destination, and in light of the distinction under the Road Act between national roads and expressways, it is clear that the route between Daegu and Yeongcheon held by the Intervening Company is not an expressway, the court below held that the portion of the operating route extension in the disposition at issue, by going beyond the scope of the licensed route, concerns a matter that cannot be allowed by approval of a change to the business plan unless a license for the establishment or extension of the route for that section precedes it, and that it is therefore unlawful.\\n\\nThe court below considered the operating route included in the intercity transportation business plan to mean the origin, stopping points, and destination within the licensed route, and held that an extension or change of an operating route within an already licensed route may be effected by approval of a change to the business plan, whereas an extension or change of an operating route in the absence of a route license constitutes, in substance, a new transportation business license, so that the establishment or extension of a route for a section without a route license cannot be effected by approval of a change to the business plan unless a route license precedes it; this is correct. However, as noted above, the disposition at issue merely changes the respective destinations, with respect to the five prior operating routes each having Daegu as the origin and Uiseong, Gibori, Jibo, Yecheon, and Onhye in the northern North Gyeongsang area as the respective destinations, so that each respective destination becomes the origin, Daegu, the origin, becomes a stopping point, the operating routes are extended, the destination becomes Busan, and the stopping points are partially changed as stated in the judgment of the court below; and it is clear from the record that it is not a disposition that consolidates and changes the route license with Daegu as the origin, Yeongcheon as the stopping point, and Jinbo as the destination held by the Intervening Company, or the route license with Chungbuk Danyang as the origin, Yeongju, Andong, Uiseong, Yeongcheon, and the expressway as stopping points, and Busan as the destination, which the Intervening Company acquired by transfer from the non-party Guksin Passenger Co., Ltd. on 1986.11.14. Therefore, it was erroneous to hold that the defect of lack of route in the disposition at issue was cured merely because the Intervening Company held the route license for the Danyang-Busan section, which was not the subject of the disposition at issue.\\n\\nHowever, among the dispositions at issue, the route between Daegu and Busan, which is the section whose operating route was extended, was an extension of an operating route without a route license, and therefore the disposition at issue should be viewed as having approved by way of approval of a change to the business plan something that does not fall within the category of approval of a change to the business plan, and thus should be held unlawful. The court below, however, in that the Intervening Company had route licenses for other sections among the Daegu-Busan section whose operating route was extended by the disposition at issue but did not possess a route license for the expressway operating section from Daegu to Yeongcheon, held that the disposition at issue was ultimately unlawful because it extended and changed the operating route without a route license, and in that respect it is ultimately correct; accordingly, the above error cannot be said to have affected the outcome of the judgment.\\n\\nB. The Intervening Company’s grounds of appeal, to the effect that since the authority over motor vehicle transportation business licenses other than express bus transportation business licenses and approvals of changes to business plans was fully delegated by the Minister of Transportation to the Governors, it is the administrative practice of Governors not to strictly distinguish between route licenses and approvals of changes to business plans even in the case of changes or extensions of operating routes involving the establishment or extension of a route, and therefore the Governor’s disposition concerning changes or extensions to intercity bus operating routes should be assessed by examining the substance rather than the form of the disposition, so that if it is a mere change or extension of an operating route within an already licensed route it should be seen as approval of a change to the business plan, while if it is a change or extension of an operating route into an area without a route it should be seen as having simultaneously effected not only approval of a change to the business plan but also a license for the establishment or extension of the route, and therefore even if there was no route license for the expressway section between Daegu and Yeongcheon in the disposition at issue, because the content of the approval disposition specifies the distances from the origin, stopping points, and destination, which are elements of a route, so as to operate the expressway section between the Seo-Daegu Interchange and Yeongcheon, the above approval disposition should be deemed to include a route license for the above section, and even if not, because changes to operating routes include changes to stopping points, the portion of the disposition at issue extending the operating route of the expressway from the Seo-Daegu Interchange to Yeongcheon should be viewed as having been made as an approval disposition of a change to the business plan changing the stopping point from a national road to an expressway, are all premised on the assumption that the Danyang-Busan route license acquired by the Intervening Company from the non-party Guksin Passenger Co., Ltd. cures the defect of lack of route in the Daegu-Busan route among the disposition at issue.\\n\\nHowever, as already explained above, since it has been established that the above Danyang-Busan route license held by the Intervening Company cannot cure the defect of lack of route in the disposition at issue, the above grounds of appeal are without merit, without the need for further consideration.\\n\\n(3) With respect to the argument that there is illegality in misapprehending the legal principle concerning the cure of defects in administrative acts\\n\\nAs to the argument that the defect of lack of route was cured because, on 1989.11.16., while this case was pending before the court below, the Defendant granted the Intervening Company a route license with Daegu as the origin, the Seo-Daegu Interchange, the expressway, Sinpyeong, the expressway, and Busan as the destination, the court below rejected this argument on the ground that whether an administrative disposition is lawful must be determined based on the circumstances at the time of the disposition, and that recognizing a post hoc cure of a defective administrative disposition is not permissible from the standpoint of the nature of administrative acts or the rule of law.\\n\\nFrom the standpoint of the nature of administrative acts or the rule of law, not only is the cure of a defective administrative act in principle impermissible, but even where it is allowed, it must be determined teleologically according to the specific circumstances within the range that does not infringe the rights and interests of the people (see this Court Decision 82NU420 rendered on 1983.7.26.). In light of the fact that the defect concerning the disposition at issue relates to the contents of the administrative disposition and that a new route license was granted after this action was filed, the court below’s judgment not recognizing the cure of the defect is justified, and there is no illegality in misapprehension of law as pointed out in the argument. The line of argument criticizing the judgment below from a contrary view cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(4) With respect to the argument that there is illegality in misapprehending the legal principle concerning public welfare under Article 28(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act;\\n\\nEven if the disposition at issue is unlawful, the extension of the operating route pursuant thereto has greatly contributed, since the beginning of 1988, to transportation convenience for residents of the northern Daegu area and the northern North Gyeongsang area, so closing the route would result in a manifestly contrary outcome to public welfare; therefore, in response to the Defendant’s argument that a judgment on grounds of circumstances should be rendered pursuant to Article 28(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act, the court below rejected it on the ground that, in order to render such a judgment, the cancellation of the administrative disposition must fall within the category of being manifestly unsuitable to public welfare, and although inconvenience to passengers using the extended route is expected from the cancellation of the disposition at issue, such inconvenience is expected to remain a temporary phenomenon due to various countermeasures that the Defendant can take, and thus the requirements for a judgment on grounds of circumstances are not satisfied.\\n\\nSince a judgment on grounds of circumstances is a system recognized only exceptionally for the maintenance of public welfare, its application must be limited under extremely strict requirements; and in determining whether the requirement that it be not manifestly suitable to public welfare is met, the necessity of canceling or changing an unlawful and improper administrative disposition and the manifestly harmful consequences to public welfare that may arise from such cancellation or change must be compared and weighed to determine whether it applies. Considering various circumstances appearing in the record, such as the need to establish order concerning the motor vehicle transportation business, to prevent excessive competition among transportation companies, to protect the vested interests of the Plaintiffs, and the countermeasures that the Defendant can take after cancellation of the disposition at issue, it cannot be said that cancellation of the disposition at issue falls within the category of being manifestly unsuitable to public welfare.\\n\\nThe court below’s determination is correct, and there is no illegality in misapprehension of law as pointed out in the argument; thus this ground of appeal is also without merit.\\n\\n(5) Accordingly, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne separately by the losing Defendant and the Defendant Auxiliary Intervenor, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the judges concerned as set forth in the Disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning disclosure of information under the Act on the Disclosure of Information by Public Agencies (hereinafter referred to as the “Information Disclosure Act”) is incorrect? (Where there is any dispute, according to case law)
A: Even taking into account that state funding for private universities is limited, temporary, and localized, it cannot be said that listing private universities as one of the public institutions subject to the duty of disclosure under the Enforcement Decree of the Information Disclosure Act is contrary to the constitutional principle of guaranteeing university autonomy or exceeds the scope of delegation under the parent Act, namely the Information Disclosure Act.
B: In a lawsuit seeking revocation of a disposition refusing disclosure of information, if a public institution submits the requested information to the court as evidence, etc., and causes a copy thereof to be delivered or served on the requester through the court, thereby resulting in disclosure of the information to the requester, such disclosure may be regarded as disclosure under the Information Disclosure Act.
C: A third party who has been notified that information related to him or her has been requested for disclosure may, within 3 days from the date of receipt of that notice, request the relevant public institution not to disclose it, and even if such request for nondisclosure has been made, when the public institution decides to disclose, it must, without delay, notify in writing by clearly stating the reasons for the disclosure decision and the date of disclosure.
D: Since a requester has a statutory right to apply for disclosure by designating a specific method of disclosure, if a public institution decides to disclose by a method other than the method applied for by the requester, this constitutes a partial refusal disposition with respect to the part concerning the method of disclosure among the request for disclosure of information, and the requester may challenge it by an administrative appeal action.
E: If a person who has requested disclosure of information and received notice of the decision on whether to disclose the information again requests disclosure of the relevant information without justifiable grounds, the public institution that received the request for disclosure of information may close the request after comprehensively considering the nature of the information subject to the disclosure request, the substantive similarity and relevance to the prior request, and the circumstances making it unavoidable to give the same response as to the prior request, and must inform the requester of the fact that the request has been closed.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2004DU2783]": "Upon examining the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Article 2 subparagraph 3 of the former Act on Disclosure of Information by Public Agencies (those prior to the full amendment by Act No. 7127 on January 29, 2004; hereinafter referred to as the \"Information Disclosure Act\") provides that \"public agencies\" means the State, local governments, government-invested institutions under Article 2 of the Framework Act on the Management of Government-Invested Institutions, and other institutions prescribed by Presidential Decree; and Article 2 subparagraph 1 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act (those prior to the amendment by Presidential Decree No. 18312 on March 17, 2004; the same shall apply hereinafter) includes schools at all levels established under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, the Higher Education Act, and other Acts among the institutions prescribed by Presidential Decree. Accordingly, private universities came to fall under public agencies subject to the duty of information disclosure.\\n\\nThe determination of the agencies subject to the duty of information disclosure falls within the legislature's power of legislative formation, and accordingly the legislature designated such agencies as public agencies in Article 2 subparagraph 3 of the Information Disclosure Act. The term \"public agencies\" is construed not as being limited to State agencies, but as including local governments, government-invested institutions, and also institutions that play important roles or functions in the interests of the entire community. In light of the purpose of information disclosure, the public nature of education, and the commonality between public and private schools, as well as various circumstances such as the State's financial support and subsidies for private universities, even considering that State funding for private universities is limited, temporary, and local, Article 2 subparagraph 1 of the Enforcement Decree of the Information Disclosure Act, in listing private universities as one of the public agencies subject to the duty of information disclosure, cannot be deemed to have exceeded the scope of delegation under the parent statute, the Information Disclosure Act, nor can private universities be deemed to have the character of public agencies only within the scope of State funding.\\n\\nThe court below's determination to the same effect is justifiable, and there is no illegality, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the validity, etc. of Article 2 subparagraph 1 of the Enforcement Decree of the Information Disclosure Act.\\n\\n2. In light of the purpose, provisions, and purport of the Information Disclosure Act, there can be said to be no special restriction on the purpose of a request for information disclosure; therefore, unless there are special circumstances such as seeking disclosure solely for the purpose of harassing the Defendant, a request for information disclosure cannot be deemed contrary to the principle of good faith or to constitute an abuse of rights (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DO1370, rendered September 23, 2004). On the same reasoning, the court below's determination that the Plaintiff's request for information disclosure in this case cannot be deemed contrary to the principle of good faith or to constitute an abuse of rights is justifiable, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principles on violation of the principle of good faith and abuse of rights, or omission to decide.\\n\\n3. The court below rejected the Defendant's contention that the information for which the Plaintiff sought disclosure could not be disclosed because it would be difficult to separate it from information of other persons, on the ground that, upon examining the materials for which the Plaintiff requested disclosure, it would be easy to determine for whom those materials were intended, and if such determination were difficult, then all related information could be disclosed, and the Information Disclosure Act does not separately provide such circumstances as grounds for refusing disclosure.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant statutes and the record, this determination of the court below is justifiable, and there is no illegality in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the specific identification of information subject to disclosure.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing Defendant, and it is so adjudged as per the Disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2016DU44674]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. In order for an act by which an administrative agency refuses to carry out an act in accordance with the application made by a citizen’s affirmative application act to constitute an administrative disposition subject to an administrative appeal action, the applied-for act must be the exercise of public authority or an administrative act equivalent thereto, the refusal must bring about some change in the legal relationship of the applicant, and the citizen must have a statutory or equitable right to request the issuance of such act (see Supreme Court Decision 96NU14036, decided July 10, 1998; Supreme Court Decision 2007DU1316, decided October 11, 2007, among others). Whether a right to apply exists, which is a prerequisite for recognizing the dispositional nature of the refusal act, is determined in the abstract by examining whether such a right to apply is recognized for the general public through the interpretation of the relevant statutes, and whether a particular person’s application can be granted in a concrete case is a matter to be determined on the merits of the lawsuit (see Supreme Court Decision 95NU12460, decided June 11, 1996; Supreme Court Decision 2007DU20638, decided September 10, 2009, among others).\\n\\n2. Article 10(1)2 of the former Act on Disclosure of Information by Public Institutions (before amendment by Act No. 11991 on August 6, 2013; hereinafter referred to as the “Information Disclosure Act”) provides that a person requesting disclosure of information (hereinafter referred to as the “applicant”) may make the request by submitting an information disclosure request form stating “the contents of the information requested for disclosure and the method of disclosure,” etc., and Article 14(1)4 of the Enforcement Decree of the Information Disclosure Act (before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 24837 on November 13, 2013; hereinafter referred to as the “Enforcement Decree”) provides, as one method of information disclosure, the method of “duplicating the file and sending it by e-mail” with respect to “information held and managed in electronic form.” Meanwhile, Article 15 of the Information Disclosure Act provides that “Where a public institution is requested by an applicant to disclose information held and managed in electronic form in electronic form, it shall comply with the applicant’s request except where it is significantly difficult in light of the nature of the relevant information” (paragraph 1), and that “Where an applicant requests disclosure in electronic form of information not held and managed in electronic form, the information may be converted into electronic form and disclosed unless it would cause a significant hindrance to the normal performance of duties or there is a concern that the nature of the relevant information would be impaired” (paragraph 2).\\n\\nAs such, the Information Disclosure Act allows an applicant to request information disclosure while also designating the method of disclosure, and where disclosure in electronic form is requested for information in electronic form, the public institution is, in principle, under a duty to comply with such request. Furthermore, even with respect to information in non-electronic form, if disclosure in electronic form is requested, it may, according to discretionary judgment, be converted into electronic form and disclosed. Since this is intended to faithfully guarantee the people’s right to know, which is the purpose of the Information Disclosure Act, by promoting the efficient use of information and enhancing the convenience of the applicant, the applicant must be regarded as having a statutory right to request information disclosure by designating a specific method of disclosure.\\n\\nAccordingly, if a public institution discloses the information that is the subject of the disclosure request, but decides to disclose it by a method other than the method requested by the applicant, such decision must be regarded as a partial refusal disposition with respect to the part concerning the method of information disclosure among the information disclosure request, and the applicant must be regarded as being able to challenge it through an administrative appeal action.\\n\\n3. According to the reasoning of the lower court judgment and the reasoning of the first-instance judgment partly cited by the lower court, the lower court recognized that, while the Plaintiff was working in the Automotive Administration Division of Namyangju-si, the Plaintiff requested that the Defendant disclose, by sending them through an information and communications network in the form of electronic files, the information stated in the judgment (hereinafter referred to as the “information at issue”), such as expenditure approval forms and supporting documents (copies of credit cards, etc.) and the records management register; and that the Defendant sent the notice at issue to the Plaintiff, stating that the Plaintiff should directly visit the office of the Automotive Administration Division of Namyangju-si to receive the information at issue.\\n\\nThe lower court held that, considering the purpose of the right to request information disclosure prescribed in the Information Disclosure Act and the manpower and costs expended by public institutions due to information disclosure, a public institution need only disclose information in a manner that allows the holder of the right to request information disclosure to access the disclosed information with ease, and is not always under a duty to disclose information in the manner requested by the holder of the right to request information disclosure; and that the notice at issue was made in a manner allowing the Plaintiff to access the information at issue with ease, so it could not be regarded as a refusal disposition on the request for information disclosure, and therefore the present lawsuit filed by the Plaintiff was inadmissible as seeking to revoke a refusal disposition that does not exist.\\n\\nHowever, in light of the legal principles stated above, the notice at issue did not adopt the method of transmitting the information in the form of electronic files through an information and communications network, which was the method of information disclosure requested by the Plaintiff, but instead required direct visit and receipt or inspection. Therefore, it must be regarded as a partial refusal of the Plaintiff’s information disclosure request and as an administrative disposition subject to administrative appeal action.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court should have proceeded to the merits, examined whether any of the information requested for disclosure by the Plaintiff was information held and managed in electronic form, and whether providing such information in electronic form would be significantly difficult in light of the nature of the information or would risk causing a significant hindrance to the Defendant’s normal performance of duties, and then determined whether the Plaintiff’s claim was well-founded.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court dismissed the present lawsuit on the ground that the notice at issue was not a refusal disposition; thus, it erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning administrative dispositions subject to administrative appeal action, thereby affecting the conclusion of the judgment.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the lower court judgment is reversed, and this case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated, as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the effects arising from a change in an administrative disposition are correct? (In cases of dispute, according to case law.) (a) Where a business change permit is granted in a manner that substantially changes the essential part of a district heating and cooling business permit, the original district heating and cooling business permit loses its effect unless there are special circumstances. (b) Where the prior disposition remains in force to the extent not changed by the subsequent disposition, and the subsequent disposition has effect to the extent that it changes part of the content of the prior disposition, revocation of the subsequent disposition may be sought on the ground of a cause for revocation existing only in the prior disposition. (c) If there is a correction disposition that increases the tax base and tax amount of the original tax assessment disposition, the original disposition is absorbed into the correction disposition, thereby losing its independent existence value. (d) Where, after an original administrative surcharge imposition disposition, a disposition is made reducing the amount of the administrative surcharge, the reduction disposition is not an independent administrative surcharge imposition disposition separate from the original disposition, but in substance merely a disposition bringing about the favorable result of partial revocation of the original administrative surcharge, and therefore is not the subject of an independent appeal litigation. (e) Where a business suspension disposition is changed in a manner favorable to the business operator, the original business suspension disposition is absorbed into the changed disposition and loses its independent existence value.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2004DU9302]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\nWhere an administrative agency, pursuant to the Food Sanitation Act and its subordinate statutes, has imposed an administrative sanction on a business operator and then renders a disposition changing that disposition in favor of the business operator (hereinafter, the initial disposition is referred to as the “Original Disposition,” and the later disposition as the “Amended Disposition”), the Original Disposition is not extinguished by the Amended Disposition, but exists from the outset as a disposition with its contents amended in favor of the business operator. Accordingly, where a revocation is sought on the ground that the administrative sanction, as amended in favor by the Amended Disposition, is unlawful, the object of such revocation action is the Original Disposition as amended, and not the Amended Disposition; and whether the period for filing suit has been observed must also be determined on the basis of the Original Disposition as amended, and not the Amended Disposition.\\n\\nAccording to the factual findings affirmed by the court below and the record, the Defendant, on 2002. 12. 26., rendered the Original Disposition in this case, namely a three-month business suspension disposition against the Plaintiff; and when the Plaintiff filed an administrative appeal thereagainst, the adjudicating authority, on 2003. 3. 6., rendered an implementation ruling of partial dismissal (partial grant) stating that “the Defendant’s three-month business suspension disposition against the Plaintiff made on 2002. 12. 26. shall be changed to a disposition imposing an administrative surcharge in lieu of a two-month business suspension.” The certified copy of that ruling was delivered to the Plaintiff on 2003. 3. 10. The Defendant, in accordance with the purport of the above ruling, on 2003. 3. 13. (although the court below states 2003. 3. 12., this appears to be an error) rendered the subsequent Amended Disposition in this case, to the effect of changing the three-month business suspension disposition to an administrative surcharge of KRW 5.6 million, thereby rendering a disposition that changed the Original Disposition in a manner favorable to the Plaintiff. It is also evident that, while filing this action on 2003. 6. 12., the Plaintiff seeks in the prayer the revocation of the disposition imposing an administrative surcharge dated 2003. 3. 13.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principle stated above, in this action seeking revocation on the ground that the imposition of the administrative surcharge, being an administrative sanction whose contents were changed in favor by the subsequent Amended Disposition in this case, is unlawful, the above prayer must be understood as seeking revocation of the disposition imposing an administrative surcharge dated 2002. 12. 26., which, by the subsequent Amended Disposition in this case, has existed from the outset as amended in favor of the Plaintiff; and this action, which seeks revocation of the Original Disposition as changed by the subsequent Amended Disposition pursuant to the implementation ruling of partial dismissal (partial grant), must also be brought within 90 days from the date on which the certified copy of the administrative appeal decision was served. The judgment of the court below, which held this action unlawful on the ground that the Plaintiff filed this action after 90 days had elapsed from the date on which the certified copy of the above ruling was served, is proper, and the grounds for final appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2006DU3957]": "We decide on the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. As to Ground 1 of the grounds for final appeal\\n\\nWhere the administrative agency that imposed an administrative disposition finds that the disposition is defective, it may revoke or modify it on its own even in the absence of any separate legal basis (see Supreme Court Decision 85NU664, rendered on February 25, 1986, and Supreme Court Decision 2003DU4669, rendered on May 25, 2006, among others); and, in the case of an order imposing a penalty surcharge, where the administrative agency, after having imposed such order on the person obligated to pay, reduces the amount of the penalty surcharge on the ground that the original order is defective, such reduction order has legal effect only with respect to the reduced portion of the penalty surcharge, and it is not a separate and independent penalty-surcharge imposition order distinct from the original imposition order, but in substance a modification of the original imposition order, and since it is an order that brings about a result favorable to the person obligated to pay, namely partial revocation of the penalty surcharge, the original imposition order is not thereby wholly extinguished; and where, in challenging the portion that still remains unrepealed and is alleged to be unlawful even after the reduction order, the object of the administrative litigation is the portion of the original imposition order that remains unrepealed by the reduction order, and the reduction order itself is not the object of the administrative litigation.
