This legal principle shall likewise apply even where a ground of illegality exists in the reduction order itself, unless there are special circumstances requiring recognition of a separate means of litigation therefor.\\n\\nThe court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence admitted, recognized the facts as stated in the opinion, and in light of the circumstances, including that a suit is pending in the Seoul High Court under Case No. 2005NU489 regarding the administrative litigation concerning the penalty-surcharge imposition order in the amount of 14,369,000,000 won, which is the portion remaining unrepealed out of the original penalty-surcharge imposition order in the amount of 17,820,000,000 won, held that there are no special circumstances warranting recognition of an action regarding the principal and alternative claims in this case, which seek, separately, confirmation of invalidity or revocation of the reduction order itself, and therefore determined that the Plaintiff’s principal and alternative claims in this case are procedurally improper.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principle and the record, the court below’s such disposition is proper, and there is no illegality arising from an error of law regarding the subject matter of litigation in a partial reduction order for a penalty surcharge, as asserted in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 2 of the grounds for final appeal\\n\\nWhere the administrative agency reduced the amount of a penalty surcharge on the ground that the original imposition order was defective, but the portion still remaining unrepealed even after such reduction order is challenged as unlawful, the question of what constitutes the object of such administrative litigation is a matter subject to ex officio judicial review and is not subject to the application of the principle of protection of trust as to the acts of the administrative agency; accordingly, the argument in the grounds for final appeal on this point likewise cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and the costs of final appeal shall be borne by the losing party; and the judgment is rendered as follows, by unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2012DU12822]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to the Plaintiffs’ grounds for appeal\\n\\nA. (1) Article 22-2(1) of the former Framework Act on National Taxes (as amended by Act No. 9911 on 2010. 1. 1., and before that amendment, hereinafter the same) provides: “A correction that increases the tax amount initially finalized pursuant to the provisions of tax statutes shall not affect the rights and obligations relationship concerning the tax amount initially finalized as prescribed by this Act or the tax statutes.”\\n\\nWhere there is a disposition of increased correction, the original return or decision is absorbed into the disposition of increased correction and thereby loses its independent value of existence; therefore, in principle, only the disposition of increased correction becomes the subject of adjudication in an administrative appeal action, and the taxpayer may also assert in that administrative appeal action the grounds of illegality concerning the original return or decision. Nevertheless, in light of the wording of the above provision and the legislative purpose thereof—namely, to restrict challenges to the tax amount in the original return or decision that can no longer be contested due to the lapse of the objection period or the correction request period even if there is a disposition of increased correction—it should be said that, with respect to a tax amount that can no longer be contested due to the expiration of the objection period or the correction request period, revocation cannot be sought, and revocation may be sought only within the scope of the tax amount increased by the disposition of increased correction (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2009. 5. 14., 2006DU17390; Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2011. 4. 14., 2010DU9808; Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2012. 3. 29., 2011DU4855, etc.).\\n\\n(2) Meanwhile, Article 45-2(1) of the former Framework Act on National Taxes, as amended by Act No. 8830 on 2007. 12. 31. and before the amendment by Act No. 10405 on 2010. 12. 27. (hereinafter referred to as the “pre-amendment provision”), provides: “A person who has submitted a tax base return within the statutory filing deadline may, where any of the following items applies, request the head of the competent tax office to determine or correct the tax base and tax amount of the national tax initially reported and amended reported (in cases where there is a decision or correction under each tax statute, the tax base and tax amount after such decision or correction shall mean the tax base and tax amount after such decision or correction) within three years after the statutory filing deadline (in cases where there is a decision or correction under each tax statute, this means the period for filing an objection, a request for examination, or a request for trial).”\\n\\nHowever, Article 45-2(1) of the former Framework Act on National Taxes before amendment by Act No. 8830 on 2007. 12. 31. prescribed the correction request period as three years regardless of whether there had been a decision or correction by the tax authority, and Article 45-2(1) of the Framework Act on National Taxes as amended by Act No. 10405 on 2010. 12. 27. also allows a correction request period of three years with respect to the originally reported tax base and tax amount, although a correction request must be made within 90 days with respect to the tax base and tax amount increased thereby in cases where there is a decision or correction by the tax authority. The fact that, through several amendments to the Framework Act on National Taxes, the three-year correction request period for the originally reported tax base and tax amount has been maintained is intended to secure the taxpayer’s procedural rights and interests. The fact that the pre-amendment provision adopts a legislative form in which, in principle, a correction request may be made for three years with respect to the originally reported tax base and tax amount, and in exceptional cases the correction request period is limited to the period for filing an objection, a request for examination, or a request for trial (hereinafter referred to as the “objection, etc. period”), may likewise be understood as having the same purpose. Therefore, the “case where there is a decision or correction under tax statutes” in which the correction request period is limited to the objection, etc. period under the pre-amendment provision should be construed as limited to exceptional cases appropriate to the purpose of the correction request system as described above.\\n\\nEven if there is a disposition of decreased correction, such disposition cancels part of the original return or decision and is not independent from the original return, etc., and thus an objection, etc. against the disposition of decreased correction is not permitted; accordingly, it cannot be viewed as a “case where there is a decision or correction under tax statutes” in which the taxpayer’s correction request period is restricted.\\n\\nMeanwhile, in cases where there is a disposition of increased correction, the original return, etc. is absorbed into the disposition of increased correction; however, since both a correction request and an administrative appeal action against a taxation disposition are challenge measures that share the same purpose of determining the existence of the proper tax base and tax amount, the taxpayer may contest the disposition of increased correction by an administrative appeal action within the prescribed appeal period, and may also contest it by a correction request within the correction request period (see Supreme Court en banc Decision rendered on 2013. 4. 18., 2010DU11733). However, allowing a taxpayer who has submitted a tax base return within the statutory filing deadline to contest, in a single challenge procedure, a decision or correction as the challenged disposition is for the sake of litigation economy or the protection of the taxpayer’s rights and interests, and is not intended to restrict the taxpayer’s right to request correction; nor is it reasonable to view that the taxpayer’s exercise of the right to request correction, which is a separate means of challenge concerning the original return, etc., is restricted merely because the tax authority has made a decision or correction while the correction request period for the original return, etc. remains open. Moreover, the legislative purpose of the pre-amendment provision, which seeks the prompt stabilization of tax legal relations, can be sufficiently achieved by limiting only the exercise of the right to request correction concerning the newly increased tax base and tax amount.\\n\\nIn light of the amendment history of the Framework Act on National Taxes regarding this correction request system, the purpose of the correction request system, and relevant legal principles, etc., even if a taxpayer who has submitted a tax base return within the statutory filing deadline did not contest, within the prescribed appeal period, a disposition resulting from a decision or correction subsequently made by the tax authority, that has no effect on the exercise, within the three-year correction request period, of the right to request correction concerning the originally reported tax base and tax amount; and the “case where there is a decision or correction under tax statutes” in which the correction request period is limited to the objection, etc. period under the pre-amendment provision means only the portion of the tax base and tax amount increased by the decision or correction of the tax authority.\\n\\nB. The court below, for the reasons stated in its reasoning, determined that, at the time of commencement of the inheritance in this case, the shares in the real property in this case registered in the joint names of the deceased Non-Party 2 and the Plaintiffs, unlike the registered names, were owned by the decedent, the deceased Non-Party 1, and that it is difficult to recognize that the shares under the name of Non-Party 2 were title-trusted.\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the judgment below in light of the evidence duly admitted, there is no illegality in the above determination of the court below that affected the judgment by misapprehending the law on the destruction of the presumption of registration, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. With respect to the Defendant’s grounds for appeal\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the part of the judgment below against the Plaintiffs is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination of that part. The Defendant’s appeal is dismissed. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning administrative legislation is incorrect? (If there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: Where the legislature, with respect to matters delegated by statute, establishes the general outline and then re-delegates specific matters within that scope to subordinate statutes, subdelegation is permitted.
B: When an official notice has a general and abstract character, it will fall under an administrative legislation in the form of a statutory rule or an administrative rule; however, when it has the character of directly regulating, by itself and without mediation of any other enforcement act, the specific rights and duties of the public or legal relations, it falls under an administrative disposition.
C: Without legislative delegation, it is contrary to the principle of statutory taxation to provide, by administrative legislation such as orders or rules, matters concerning taxation requirements, or to establish interpretive provisions that analogize or expand the contents prescribed by statute.
D: Examining the meaning of Article 40, Articles 75 and 95 of the Constitution, even if authorization by legislation enacted by the National Assembly delegates to an administrative agency, by statute or otherwise, the specific scope is defined, the constitutional form of delegated legislation should be regarded as limited, because the relevant administrative agency does not have independent authority to create law.
E: The Act on the Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects delegates to the Enforcement Rule specific standards concerning the calculation of compensation amounts for acquisition by agreement, and within the scope of that delegation, the relevant Enforcement Rule provides that, where there are buildings, etc. on the land, the land shall be appraised on the assumption that there are no buildings, etc.; such Enforcement Rule, in conjunction with the provisions of the above Act, has external binding force.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2005DU2506]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. As to Ground 1 of the final appeal\\n\\na. When a certain public notice has a general and abstract character, it shall correspond to a legislative rule or an administrative rule; however, when it has the character of directly regulating specific rights and obligations or legal relationships of the public by itself, without the medium of any other enforcement act, it shall correspond to an administrative disposition (see Supreme Court Decision 2003MU23 dated October 9, 2003).\\n\\nThe court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it adopted, recognized the facts as stated in its opinion, and then held, to the effect that: ① the List of Covered and Non-Covered Drugs and the Table of Maximum Reimbursement Prices (as amended by Ministry of Health and Welfare Public Notice No. 2002-46, hereinafter referred to as the “Public Notice at issue”) specifically sets and establishes the specific upper limit amount of drug costs that the National Health Insurance subscribers or the National Health Insurance Corporation must pay, or that medical care institutions may be reimbursed for, with respect to specific drugs of a specific pharmaceutical company; ② as long as there is the act of dispensing the drug and claiming the cost, the Public Notice at issue is applied without the intervention of any special enforcement act by the administrative agency; ③ in light of the fact that a change in the ceiling price of a specific drug may directly change the amount of drug costs that the National Health Insurance subscribers or the National Health Insurance Corporation must pay, or that medical care institutions may be reimbursed for, it may be deemed that the Public Notice at issue, without the medium of any other enforcement act, has the character of directly regulating the legal relationships of the National Health Insurance subscribers, the National Health Insurance Corporation, medical care institutions, and the like; accordingly, it corresponds to an administrative disposition subject to an administrative appeal action. Examining the relevant statutes and the foregoing legal principles in light of the record, the above determination of the court below is just and persuasive, and there is no violation of the rules of evidence or error in the interpretation of law regarding the dispositive character of a public notice, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nb. The court below held that, pursuant to the delegation under Article 39(2) and (3) of the National Health Insurance Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”), Article 10(1) of the Rules on the Standards for Medical Care Benefits under the National Health Insurance (Ministry of Health and Welfare Ordinance No. 207 of December 31, 2001, hereinafter referred to as the “Medical Care Benefits Rules”), which prescribes the necessary matters concerning the standards for medical care benefits such as the method, procedure, scope, ceiling, and exclusion of medical care benefits, not only provides that drug manufacturers such as the Plaintiffs have the right to apply for a determination as to whether new drugs, etc. that have not been determined as covered benefits or non-covered benefits for the Defendant are subject to medical care benefits, but also grants, under Article 12(1) of the Medical Care Benefits Rules, the right to apply for an adjustment even with respect to the ceiling price of drugs already publicly notified as covered-benefit drugs; that Article 13(2)(4) of the Criteria for Determination and Adjustment of Undetermined Acts, etc. pursuant to the delegation under Article 14 of the Medical Care Benefits Rules (Ministry of Health and Welfare Public Notice No. 2001-65 of December 5, 2001, hereinafter referred to as the “Adjustment Criteria”) provides that, when the Defendant adjusts the ceiling price of drugs already publicly notified, the transaction price of drugs supplied by the drug manufacturer to a specific wholesaler may be used as adjustment material; that Articles 4 and 6 of the Criteria for Determination of Purchase Amount for Drugs and Medical Materials (Ministry of Health and Welfare Public Notice No. 2001-66 of December 5, 2001, hereinafter referred to as the “Determination Criteria”), which prescribe the criteria, procedures, and other necessary matters for the calculation of drugs and medical materials pursuant to the delegation under Article 24(3) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act, provide that, in certain cases, for the purpose of calculating the purchase price of drugs used for medical care benefits and adjusting the ceiling price of drugs, the Defendant may also designate suppliers of drugs (including manufacturers of drugs such as the Plaintiffs, who are the original suppliers of the drugs) as subjects of periodic and ad hoc post-management, verify the transaction details with medical care institutions, and require the submission of relevant materials such as documents, written records, and evidentiary materials if necessary, and that suppliers of drugs shall maintain itemized sales ledgers for drugs included in the public notice on drug ceiling prices, accurately stating the transaction date, counterparty, transaction quantity, and total transaction amount, and shall bear the duty to comply with the Defendant’s post-management; that if, by the Public Notice at issue, the ceiling price of the Plaintiffs’ drugs at issue is reduced, ① National Health Insurance subscribers or the National Health Insurance Corporation will receive a benefit because the amount of drug costs to be paid may be reduced, but ② on the other hand, medical care institutions, even if they purchase the drugs at issue from suppliers such as the Plaintiffs at a price higher than the ceiling price, cannot receive reimbursement from the National Health Insurance subscribers or the National Health Insurance Corporation for the portion of the purchase price exceeding the ceiling price, and therefore, in providing medical care benefits, they may exclude those drugs and dispense other drugs with the same or similar ingredients whose purchase price falls within the range of the ceiling price (medical institutions, public health centers, etc.), or exclude them from transaction items (pharmacies), thereby being able to receive reimbursement for all such costs, and since the choice of drugs is within their authority and they can themselves change the demand, the possibility that their actual interests will be impaired is almost nonexistent; and ③ however, as to the pharmaceutical companies, namely the Plaintiffs, supplying the drugs at issue to medical care institutions, if the ceiling price of those drugs is reduced, then if they maintain the supply price to medical care institutions above the ceiling price, the medical care institutions will not purchase those drugs, and thus the supply price must inevitably be reduced to within the range of the ceiling price; accordingly, they are directly affected by the reduction in the ceiling price and their interests are infringed. Taking these points together, the Plaintiffs shall be deemed to enjoy direct and specific interests protected by the statutes forming the basis for the public notice on drug ceiling prices, such as the Act, the Enforcement Decree of the Act, and the Medical Care Benefits Rules, with respect to the drugs at issue they supply; and by the Public Notice at issue, the Plaintiffs, as the ceiling price of the drugs at issue they manufacture and supply is reduced, shall be deemed to have suffered an infringement of legal interests protected by the aforementioned statutes and regulations. Therefore, the court below held that the Plaintiffs have standing as plaintiffs to seek revocation of the Public Notice at issue. Examining the relevant statutes and the record, the above determination of the court below is just, and there is no violation of the rules of evidence or error in the interpretation of law regarding standing of a party, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 2 of the final appeal\\n\\nThe court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it adopted, recognized the facts as stated in its opinion, and then, pursuant to the relevant provisions such as the Act, the Enforcement Decree of the Act, the Medical Care Benefits Rules, the Adjustment Criteria, and the Determination Criteria, held that the Defendant, as a general rule, calculates the weighted average price by drug item (the amount obtained by dividing the total purchase amount by the total purchase quantity) on the basis of the actual purchase price data submitted by medical care institutions and the actual purchase prices of medical care institutions confirmed through management of medical care institutions and drug suppliers designated as subjects of post-management, and adjusts the ceiling price of covered-benefit drugs (Article 13(2)(1) of the Adjustment Criteria); and that, where it is confirmed that a drug manufacturer supplied a drug to a specific wholesaler at a substantially lower price than the average transaction price with other wholesalers, this may be used as adjustment material for the ceiling price (Article 13(2)(4) of the Adjustment Criteria). On that premise, the court below further held that, if the Defendant confirmed, as stated in its opinion, that the Plaintiffs supplied the drugs at issue to specific wholesalers at substantially lower prices than the average transaction price with other wholesalers, the Defendant should use, as adjustment material, the actual purchase prices of medical care institutions that received the drugs at issue from the specific wholesalers, the total quantity and total amount of each corresponding drug supplied by the Plaintiffs directly to medical care institutions or through wholesalers, the respective transaction quantities and transaction amounts at the specific wholesalers and at all wholesalers subject to investigation, the ratio occupied by the quantity and amount transacted by the wholesalers subject to investigation among the total transaction quantity and transaction amount of the corresponding drugs, the regional distribution of the wholesalers subject to investigation, and the like, together with the actual purchase price data ordinarily submitted to it by medical care institutions for the corresponding drugs and the transaction details confirmed for the enterprises subject to management, and should adjust by calculating the ceiling price for each corresponding drug in a manner reflecting the discount rates of the specific enterprise subject to investigation and the remaining wholesalers; however, the Defendant, based only on the discount rates of the supply prices to 4 to 9 wholesalers for the Plaintiffs’ drugs at issue, uniformly calculated the reduction rate of the ceiling price by deducting from the highest discount rate among the wholesalers subject to investigation the average discount rate of the remaining enterprises (provided that, if it is 5% or more, the ceiling is 5%) and the basic markup rate of 10%, respectively, by the method of determining it (hereinafter referred to as the “Adjustment Formula”), and with respect to the three drugs among the drugs at issue for which the comparison-by-content method was used, again calculated the reduction rate on the premise of the amount estimated by the aforementioned Adjustment Formula and thereby reduced the ceiling price of the drugs at issue; and that this not only failed to conform to the purport of the relevant statutes and regulations and the various provisions, but also was inevitably deemed to have substantially lost its reasonableness in light of social norms. Accordingly, the court below held that, with respect to the portion of the Public Notice at issue concerning the ceiling prices of the drugs at issue, the Defendant deviated from and abused its discretionary power in reducing the ceiling price, and thus there was illegality.\\n\\nExamining the relevant statutes and the record, the above determination of the court below is just, and there is no violation of the rules of evidence or error in the interpretation of law regarding the method for adjusting the ceiling price prescribed in Article 13 of the Adjustment Criteria or regarding deviation from or abuse of discretion, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n3. As to Ground 3 of the final appeal\\n\\nWhere an administrative disposition is illegal, the general rule is to revoke it, and exceptionally, where revoking or altering such illegal disposition would rather be manifestly contrary to the public welfare, a judgment dismissing the claim on grounds of circumstances, which does not allow revocation, may be rendered; and as to such a judgment based on circumstances, even if there is no explicit assertion by the parties, the court may, ex officio, determine it on the basis of the various circumstances appearing in the record. However, whether the requirement that it be “manifestly contrary to the public welfare” is satisfied should be determined by comparing and balancing the necessity to revoke or alter the illegal administrative disposition and the public-welfare-disrupting situations that may arise from such revocation or alteration (see Supreme Court Decisions 98DU4061 rendered on May 8, 1998, and 99DU9674 rendered on January 19, 2001, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it adopted, recognized the facts as stated in its opinion, and then held that although, if the portion of the Public Notice at issue concerning the ceiling prices of the drugs at issue were revoked, there might be inconvenience due to the settlement of the insured persons’ out-of-pocket payments related to the drugs at issue, it is difficult to deem that such revocation would directly and significantly affect the finances of the health insurance system or cause enormous disruption in the operation of the health insurance system; accordingly, revoking the portion of the Public Notice at issue concerning the ceiling prices of the drugs at issue cannot be said to fall under a case that is manifestly contrary to the public welfare.\\n\\nExamining the foregoing legal principles in light of the record, the above determination of the court below is just and persuasive, and there is no violation of the rules of evidence or error in the interpretation of law regarding the requirements for a judgment based on circumstances, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the final appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged as per the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2011DA104253]": "1. As to Grounds for Appeal Nos. 1 and 3\\n\\na. Article 68(3) of the Act on Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects (hereinafter referred to as the “Public Works Act”) delegates specific standards regarding the calculation of compensation for acquisition by agreement to the Enforcement Rule of the same Act, and within the scope of such delegation, Article 22 of the Enforcement Rule of the Act on Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects provides that, where there are buildings, etc. on the land, the land shall be appraised on the assumption that such buildings, etc. do not exist; although in the form of an administrative rule, it has the function of specifically prescribing matters to become the content of the above Public Works Act and supplementing such content, and therefore, when combined with the provisions of the Public Works Act, it has external binding force (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on March 27, 2008, 2006DO3742, 3759).\\n\\nb. According to the evidence admitted by the court below, (1) the lands at issue owned by the Plaintiffs were subject to restrictions on use due to transmission towers and high-voltage transmission lines installed thereon by Korea Electric Power Corporation, (2) the Defendant acquired the above lands by agreement from the Plaintiffs in order to develop a national rental housing complex in the area surrounding the lands at issue, on the basis of the appraised value appraised by an appraisal institution, (3) at the time of the above acquisition by agreement, the Plaintiffs and the Defendant agreed that “where the sale price has been set and paid excessively or insufficiently due to intentional misconduct, negligence, or erroneous appraisal, etc., the shortfall or excess amount may be claimed from the other party, and the amount claimed by the other party shall be immediately paid or returned” (hereinafter referred to as the “agreement in this case”), (4) however, while calculating the compensation amount for acquisition by agreement under the Public Works Act with respect to the lands at issue, the Defendant, notwithstanding that under Article 22 of the Enforcement Rule of the Public Works Act, which has external binding force as stated above, the land should have been appraised on the assumption that there were no buildings, etc. where there were buildings, etc. on the land, appraised the lands at issue in the condition subject to restrictions from transmission towers and high-voltage transmission lines corresponding to buildings, etc., pursuant to Article 46-2(1) of the former Land Compensation Appraisal Guidelines of the Korea Association of Property Appraisers (as amended on February 14, 2003; the same shall apply hereinafter), which are appraisal standards not conforming to the standards for calculating compensation under the Public Works Act, thereby calculating the appraised value too low, and calculated the negotiated purchase price on that basis.\\n\\nIn light of the standards and procedures for calculating the sale price in acquisition by agreement of land, etc. for public works projects, the purport and content of specifically providing for the above agreement at the time of acquisition by agreement, and further the various circumstances that, if acquisition by agreement is not made, procedures for acquisition by expropriation and compensation for losses based on the appraised value are envisaged, it is reasonable to view that the agreement in this case applies not only where the appraisal value was erroneously calculated because the current condition or area of the land subject to acquisition by agreement was merely incorrectly appraised or because of a calculation error, etc., but also where the appraised value was erroneously calculated by applying appraisal standards not conforming to the standards for calculating compensation under the Public Works Act, and the negotiated purchase price was calculated on that basis.\\n\\nThe court below’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, of misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the legal nature of acquisition by agreement of land, etc. for public works projects and interpretation of contracts, or of exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience.\\n\\n2. As to Ground for Appeal No. 2\\n\\nEven if a judgment does not expressly state a concrete and direct determination on a matter alleged by a party, it cannot be said that there has been an omission to adjudicate if, in light of the overall purport of the reasons for the judgment, it can be understood that such allegation was either accepted or rejected (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on July 10, 2008, 2006JAEDA218, and Supreme Court Decision rendered on April 29, 2010, 2009DA88631).\\n\\nAlthough the reasons for the court below’s judgment do not expressly state a concrete and direct determination as to whether the Defendant’s underestimation of the negotiated purchase price falls under intentional misconduct, negligence, or erroneous appraisal, etc., the court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, determined that, in calculating the compensation amount for acquisition by agreement under the Public Works Act, the Defendant should have appraised the land on the assumption that there were no buildings, etc. where there were buildings, etc. on the land, in accordance with Article 22 of the Enforcement Rule of the Public Works Act, which has external binding force, but instead appraised the lands at issue in the condition subject to restrictions from transmission towers and high-voltage transmission lines corresponding to buildings, etc. pursuant to the former Land Compensation Appraisal Guidelines, which have no external binding force, and that such appraisal cannot be regarded as a proper appraisal of the land; furthermore, in light of circumstances such as the fact that, under Article 46-2(1) of the Land Compensation Appraisal Guidelines of the Korea Association of Property Appraisers, as amended on October 28, 2009, the appraisal standard was changed to provide that “the appraisal of land over which a high-voltage line passes in the airspace above the land (land under the line) shall be based on the condition that such restriction does not exist,” it is reasonable to view that, in this case, the Defendant underpaid the negotiated purchase price due to intentional misconduct, negligence, or erroneous appraisal, etc. and paid it, and thus the overall purport of such reasons for the judgment reveals that the court determined that where the appraised value was erroneously calculated by applying appraisal standards not conforming to the standards for calculating compensation under the Public Works Act, and the negotiated purchase price was calculated on that basis, this constitutes an erroneous appraisal prescribed in the agreement in this case; accordingly, there is no error of omission to adjudicate or insufficiency of reasons, etc. in the court below’s judgment.\\n\\n3. As to Ground for Appeal No. 4\\n\\nThe argument that the high-voltage transmission lines at issue do not fall under “buildings, etc.” under Article 22(2) of the Enforcement Rule of the Public Works Act is a new allegation of a fact not asserted in the court below, newly raised in the court of final appeal, and therefore cannot constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n4. As to Ground for Appeal No. 5\\n\\nIn order to deny the exercise of a right on the ground that it is contrary to the principle of good faith, the other party must have been induced to trust, or objectively, the other party must be in a position where it is reasonable to have trust, and the exercise of the right contrary to such trust must have reached a degree that cannot be tolerated in light of the concept of justice (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on November 29, 2007, 2005DA64552).\\n\\nIn the same context, the court below correctly determined that, even though the Plaintiffs filed a civil action several years after the negotiated purchase of the lands at issue had been made, it could not be deemed an exercise of rights contrary to the principle of good faith, and there is no error of law regarding the principle of good faith and sincerity.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged as per the Disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2013DU14238]": "We decide the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. A delegated order is permissible only where there is an individual delegation specifically defining the scope in a statute or superior order, and although the scope of such specific delegation varies depending on the type and nature of the object to be regulated and therefore no uniform standard can be set, at the very least the basic matters regarding the content and scope to be prescribed in the delegated order must be specifically provided so that anyone can foresee, in broad outline, the content to be prescribed in the delegated order from the relevant statute or superior statute; however, whether such foreseeability exists shall not be determined by considering only the delegation clause in question, but rather by comprehensively and organically considering the overall system, purport, and purpose of the statute to which the delegation clause belongs, the form and content of the delegation clause, and the related legal provisions, and moreover, it requires a specific and individual examination according to the nature of each regulated object (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DU7606, decided July 22, 2004, etc.). In addition, re-delegation without prescribing at all the matters delegated by statute is not permitted because it violates the principle prohibiting sub-delegation and also changes the content of the empowering statute concerning the form of enactment of a delegated order; however, re-delegation is permissible where the matters delegated are set out in broad outline and certain matters among them are again delegated, within a specified scope, to subordinate statutes (see Constitutional Court en banc Decision 2001HEONRA1, decided October 31, 2002, etc.).\\n\\nThe same legal principles apply where an ordinance, pursuant to the proviso to Article 22 of the Local Autonomy Act, after being delegated by statute matters concerning restrictions on residents’ rights or the imposition of duties, re-delegates them to a “rule” or “public notice” to be determined by the head of the local government.\\n\\nArticle 8(1) of the former Act on the Management and Use of Livestock Excreta (as amended by Act No. 12516 on March 24, 2014; hereinafter referred to as the “Livestock Excreta Act”) provides that “the Mayor, County Governor, or District Head (hereinafter referred to as the ‘Mayor, etc.’) may, for the preservation of the living environment of local residents or the protection of the quality of water sources, designate a certain area and restrict the raising of livestock in accordance with the ordinance of the relevant local government with respect to an area among the following subparagraphs that is deemed to require restriction on livestock raising,” and lists under each subparagraph “an area where the protection of the living environment is necessary as a densely populated residential area (subparagraph 1), a water source protection zone under Article 7 of the Water Supply and Waterworks Installation Act, a special countermeasure area under Article 38 of the Framework Act on Environmental Policy, and other areas comparable thereto where the conservation of the water environment is necessary (subparagraph 2), and an area exceeding the environmental standards under Article 12 of the Framework Act on Environmental Policy (subparagraph 3)” (hereinafter, the main text of Article 8(1) of the Livestock Excreta Act and each subparagraph thereof are collectively referred to as the “delegation provision”).\\n\\nPursuant to that delegation, the Ordinance on the Restriction of Livestock Raising in Gunwi-gun (hereinafter referred to as the “Ordinance at issue”) was enacted for the purpose of providing for necessary matters in order to contribute to the improvement of public health by maintaining a clean living environment through restricting the raising of livestock (Article 1), and Article 3(1) provides that “with respect to the restriction on the raising of livestock, the County Governor shall pre-designate and announce areas where the raising of livestock is prohibited” (hereinafter referred to as the “Ordinance provision at issue”), while paragraph (2) provides that “in areas announced pursuant to paragraph (1), livestock may not be raised without the permission of the County Governor.” Meanwhile, Article 5(2) provides that, when the County Governor receives an application for permission to raise livestock, the County Governor shall “investigate whether the livestock-raising site is likely to endanger the health and sanitation of nearby residents and residential stability, and shall obtain the opinion of the head of the competent public health center.”\\n\\nFurthermore, pursuant to the delegation in the Ordinance provision at issue, Article 4 subparagraph 3 of the Notice Designating Restricted Areas for Livestock Raising in Gunwi-gun (Gunwi-gun Public Notice No. 2011-10 of April 27, 2011; hereinafter referred to as the “Public Notice at issue”) provides that “an area within a straight-line distance of 200 m from the boundary line of a road (expressway, general national road, local road, county road), railway, or rural road to the outer wall of a livestock-raising facility building (provided, however, that for Korean cattle, an area within 100 m)” shall be one of the restricted areas for livestock raising (hereinafter referred to as the “Public Notice provision at issue”).\\n\\nThe delegation provision, by its wording, purports to delegate to local government ordinances matters concerning the designation of a certain area and the restriction on livestock raising in that area, as an area among those falling under each subparagraph of Article 8(1) of the Livestock Excreta Act and deemed to require restriction on livestock raising. Accordingly, the matters to be regulated by ordinance appear to include not only the detailed standards for such area designation, but also the method and procedure for such designation, and the restriction and lifting of restrictions on livestock raising within such area. The Ordinance at issue itself provides the timing and method of designation of the restricted area for livestock raising by requiring the County Governor, prior to a specific disposition such as restriction on livestock raising or its lifting, to pre-designate and announce the restricted area for livestock raising (Article 3(1)); it further concretely provides the meaning and effect of the restricted area for livestock raising by stipulating that livestock raising is not absolutely prohibited within the designated area and that livestock may be raised with the permission of the County Governor (Article 3(2)); and it also provides detailed procedures, such as requiring the County Governor, when granting such permission, to investigate whether there is a risk of harming the health and sanitation of nearby residents and residential stability and to hear the opinion of the head of the competent public health center (Article 5).\\n\\nAccording to the form, content, and system of each provision of the delegation provision, the Ordinance provision at issue, the Ordinance at issue including the Ordinance provision at issue, and the Public Notice provision at issue, the Ordinance at issue may be viewed as having itself prescribed the timing and method of designating the restricted area for livestock raising and the permission procedures for applications to raise livestock within the restricted area for livestock raising, while not directly setting the substantive standards for the designation of the restricted area for livestock raising and instead re-delegating this through the Ordinance provision at issue to the Public Notice at issue. However, the Livestock Excreta Act, through the delegation provision, prescribes that for “the preservation of the living environment of local residents or the protection of the quality of water sources,” restricted areas for livestock raising such as “densely populated residential areas, areas where the conservation of the water environment is necessary such as water source protection zones, and areas exceeding environmental standards” shall be designated, and therefore, from such content alone, the broad outline of the substantive standards can already be foreseen. Meanwhile, it is also recognized that the detailed content of the substantive standards regarding the designation of restricted areas for livestock raising needs to be regulated in accordance with the circumstances of each local government, based on specialized and technical judgment and policy considerations.\\n\\nTherefore, it is difficult to conclude that the Ordinance provision at issue, by not directly prescribing the substantive standards for the designation of the restricted area for livestock raising and delegating this to the Public Notice at issue, is contrary to the purport of the delegation in the delegation provision or violates the constitutional principle prohibiting blanket delegation or the principle prohibiting sub-delegation. \\n\\nHowever, the court below, unlike the foregoing, mistakenly understood that the purport of the delegation in the delegation provision was to delegate directly to the ordinance the prescription of even the substantive standards for the designation of the restricted area for livestock raising, and on that basis held that the Ordinance provision at issue, by exceeding the limit of delegation under the superior law, the delegation provision, and by causing the County Governor to determine matters that should have been prescribed in the ordinance, violated the constitutional principle prohibiting blanket delegation and was therefore void. In such reasoning of the court below, there was an error in misunderstanding the purport of the delegation provision and the legal principles concerning the constitutional principle prohibiting blanket delegation and the principle prohibiting sub-delegation.\\n\\n2. Meanwhile, apart from the validity of the Ordinance provision at issue, the Plaintiff challenged the validity of the disposition at issue on the ground that the Public Notice provision at issue, which was the basis of the disposition at issue, was void; and the court below, premising that the Public Notice provision at issue pursuant to the delegation thereunder was also void following the invalidity of the Ordinance provision at issue, held that the disposition at issue was unlawful. Accordingly, in relation to whether such conclusion of the court below is proper, we further examine whether the Public Notice provision at issue is valid and whether the disposition at issue is therefore unlawful.\\n\\nThe Public Notice at issue is an administrative rule that establishes the substantive standards for the restricted area for livestock raising pursuant to the sequential delegation under the delegation provision of the Livestock Excreta Act and the Ordinance provision at issue, and therefore it acquires effect as a regulatory order with externally binding force only to the extent that it does not exceed the limits of delegation under the superior statutes and regulations.\\n\\nTherefore, since the delegation provision sets out the broad outline of the substantive standards for the restricted area for livestock raising and, in doing so, prescribes the purpose of setting the restricted area as “the preservation of the living environment of local residents or the protection of the quality of water sources,” and the target areas as “densely populated residential areas, areas where the conservation of the water environment is necessary such as water source protection zones, and areas exceeding environmental standards,” the standards for designating restricted areas for livestock raising set forth in the Public Notice at issue must also conform to the purport of these provisions in the delegation provision.\\n\\nHowever, the standard for restricted areas for livestock raising prescribed in the Public Notice provision at issue, namely, “an area within a straight-line distance of 200 m from the boundary line of a road (expressway, general national road, local road, county road), railway, or rural road to the outer wall of a livestock-raising facility building (provided, however, that for Korean cattle, an area within 100 m),” includes not only roads under the Road Act but also railways and rural roads without considering the type, width, location, and surrounding environment of the road, and designates all areas within a considerable distance from such boundary line as restricted areas for livestock raising. Since this is difficult to regard as related to the preservation of the living environment of local residents or the protection of the quality of water sources, it does not conform to the purpose of setting the restricted area as stated in the delegation provision above; moreover, such areas near roads cannot be deemed to fall under any of the densely populated residential areas, areas where the conservation of the water environment is necessary, or areas exceeding environmental standards that the delegation provision envisions as restricted areas. Ultimately, the Public Notice provision at issue has unduly expanded the meaning of the terms used in the delegation provision beyond their scope, and therefore must be deemed to have exceeded the limits of the delegation.\\n\\nFurthermore, the Public Notice provision at issue designates, without exception, areas near roads as restricted areas for livestock raising merely because they are near roads, even in areas where there are no houses or facilities at all, or areas with almost no vehicular traffic, and thus can be seen as an unnecessary restriction in terms of the legislative purpose of the Livestock Excreta Act; and as to such areas, not only is the granting of new permission for livestock raising restricted, but under the Livestock Excreta Act an order to relocate existing livestock sheds, etc. in operation, and criminal punishment in case of noncompliance therewith, are also possible (Article 8(2), Article 50 subparagraph 1), and thus it appears capable of excessively infringing upon residents’ freedom of business and property rights. In light of these points, it also appears to violate the principle of proportionality in the restriction of fundamental rights.\\n\\nTherefore, the Public Notice provision at issue cannot be recognized as having regulatory effect because it exceeds the limits of delegation under the superior statutes and regulations or violates the principle of proportionality, and since it is difficult to find any other legal basis for the disposition at issue, the disposition at issue is unlawful.\\n\\nUltimately, although the court below erred in the legal principles as noted above, it is proper in that, premising the invalidity of the Public Notice provision at issue, it recognized the unlawfulness of the disposition at issue and accepted the Plaintiff’s claim in this case; therefore, it cannot be said that there was an error affecting the outcome of the judgment due to the legal-error argument asserted in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2013HEONBA183]": "1. Outline of the Case\\n\\na. Case 2013HEONBA183\\n\\nThe claimant is a corporation established for the purpose of conducting construction business, real estate business, and the like, and filed a corporate tax return for the fiscal year 2004 with the Head of the ○○ District Tax Office on 31 March 2005, calculating the assessed tax amount as KRW 13,120,315,697, and filed a corporate tax return for the fiscal year 2005 on 31 March 2006, calculating the assessed tax amount as KRW 0. On 30 March 2006, premised on the assumption that it qualified as a small and medium-sized enterprise prescribed in Article 25(1)1 of the former Corporate Tax Act (prior to its amendment by Act No. 8141 of 30 December 2006), the claimant filed an application with the Head of the ○○ District Tax Office to the effect that the deficit for the fiscal year 2005 be carried back and deducted within the limit of the corporate tax amount for the fiscal year 2004, and that approximately KRW 430 million be refunded.\\n\\nThe Head of the ○○ District Tax Office refunded KRW 4,313,391,340 to the claimant on 9 May 2006. However, the State, on the ground that the claimant was not a small and medium-sized enterprise engaged in construction business eligible to receive a corporate tax refund but was a real estate supply business operator, filed on 16 March 2011 a lawsuit seeking return of unjust enrichment to claim the return of the above refund. In that case, the court of first instance (Seoul Southern District Court 2011GAHAP4736) and the appellate court (Seoul High Court 2012NA60499) held that the claimant must pay the above refund and the delay damages thereon to the State.\\n\\nDuring the pendency of the above appellate litigation, the claimant applied for a request for a constitutional review, arguing that Article 2(3) of the former Restriction of Special Taxation Act (as amended by Act No. 6538 of 29 December 2001 and before its amendment by Act No. 8387 of 27 April 2007, hereinafter referred to as the “former Restriction of Special Taxation Act”), which provides that the classification of business types used in this Act shall be based on the Korean Standard Industrial Classification publicly notified by the Commissioner of Statistics Korea pursuant to Article 17 of the Statistics Act, without specifying in the Act the enterprises subject to carryback deduction of corporate tax deficits, is not only beyond the limits of delegated legislation but also violates the principle of statutory taxation requirements and the principle of clarity of taxation requirements; however, when that request was dismissed, the claimant filed the constitutional complaint in this case on 27 June 2013.\\n\\nb. Case 2013HEONBA202\\n\\nThe claimant entered into a contract with Stock Company ○○ Bank on 24 June 2002 and has been engaged in tasks such as the construction and operation of an online lottery (so-called Lotto lottery) system and the provision of related services; on 4 August 2003, it relocated its head office from Bangbae-dong, Seocho-gu, Seoul, to its current address in Cheonan-si. The claimant filed and paid corporate tax, treating approximately KRW 50 billion in corporate tax for the fiscal years 2003 through 2007 as reduced under the provision of the main clause of Article 63-2(1) of the former Restriction of Special Taxation Act (prior to its amendment by Act No. 6762 of 11 December 2002 and before its amendment by Act No. 7003 of 30 December 2003), which provides that corporate tax shall be exempted or reduced for 10 years where a corporation having its principal office in the Seoul Metropolitan Overcrowding Control Zone relocates to a region outside the Seoul Metropolitan Area.\\n\\nHowever, the Head of the □□ District Tax Office, on the ground that in the case of a corporation engaged in a consumer service business, it is excluded from the corporate tax reduction under the proviso to Article 63-2(1) of the above Restriction of Special Taxation Act, and that the claimant’s business type, being the lottery issuance business, falls under gambling establishment operation business, and gambling establishment operation business constitutes consumer service business, canceled the reduction in corporate tax and applied penalty taxes, and reassessed and notified the claimant of a total corporate tax amount of approximately KRW 66.8 billion for the fiscal years 2003 through 2007. Thereupon, the claimant filed a petition with the Board of Audit and Inspection for review of the above tax assessment disposition, obtained a reduction of approximately KRW 16.5 billion in additional tax for failure to pay, and then brought a lawsuit against the Head of the □□ District Tax Office seeking revocation of the remaining tax assessment disposition. In that case, the court of first instance (Daejeon District Court 2010GUHAP3055) and the appellate court (Daejeon High Court 2010NU2973) held that the claimant’s business type fell under “information processing and other computer operation-related business” under the Korean Standard Industrial Classification and rendered a judgment in favor of the claimant in full. However, the Supreme Court, on 16 January 2013, reversed the appellate judgment on the ground that the claimant’s business type constituted consumer service business (2011DU12856), and the appellate court after remand (Daejeon High Court 2013NU121) rendered, on 13 June 2013, a judgment against the claimant in accordance with the purport of the above Supreme Court judgment.\\n\\nWhile the appellate litigation after remand was pending, the claimant applied for a request for a constitutional review, arguing that Article 2(3) of the former Restriction of Special Taxation Act violates Article 59 of the Constitution, which provides the principle of taxation by law, and Article 75 of the Constitution, which prohibits blanket delegation; however, when that request was dismissed, the claimant filed the constitutional complaint in this case on 18 July 2013.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether Article 2(3) of the former Restriction of Special Taxation Act is in violation of the Constitution. The contents of the provision under review and the related provision are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision under Review]\\nFormer Restriction of Special Taxation Act (as amended by Act No. 6538 of 29 December 2001 and before its amendment by Act No. 8387 of 27 April 2007)\\n\\nArticle 2 (Definitions) (3) The classification of business types used in this Act shall, except where this Act contains special provisions, be based on the Korean Standard Industrial Classification publicly notified by the Commissioner of Statistics Korea pursuant to Article 17 of the Statistics Act.\\n\\n[Related Provision]\\nFormer Statistics Act (as amended by Act No. 5691 of 29 January 1999 and entirely amended by Act No. 8387 of 27 April 2007 before repeal)\\n\\nArticle 17 (Classification of Statistical Data) (1) When a statistical agency classifies statistical data in order to compile statistics, it shall do so according to the standard classification prepared and publicly notified by the Commissioner of Statistics Korea on the basis of international standard classifications. In preparing the standard classification, the Commissioner of Statistics Korea shall consult with the relevant agencies in advance.\\n\\n3. Claimants’ Arguments\\n\\na. Case 2013HEONBA183\\n\\nThe provision under review, in that it delegates the matter of “classification of business types,” which constitutes a legislative matter concerning taxation requirements or tax reduction requirements, to the Korean Standard Industrial Classification, which is a public notice lacking conspicuous clarity of content and is not a statutory ordinance enumerated in the Constitution, is not only beyond the limits of delegated legislation under the principle of legal reservation but also contrary to the principles of statutory taxation requirements and clarity of taxation requirements.\\n\\nb. Case 2013HEONBA202\\n\\nThe provision under review provides that matters concerning the classification of business types used in the former Restriction of Special Taxation Act shall follow the Korean Standard Industrial Classification prepared and publicly notified by the Commissioner of Statistics Korea. This ultimately has the result of delegating matters concerning the classification of business types excluded from corporate tax reduction to the Korean Standard Industrial Classification publicly notified by the Commissioner of Statistics Korea, which is not a statutory ordinance enumerated in the Constitution, and therefore violates the principle of taxation by law. In addition, the provision under review comprehensively delegates the classification of business types to the public notice of the Commissioner of Statistics Korea, a subordinate norm, without setting forth any provisions regarding foreseeable standards and scope, and thus also violates the prohibition on blanket delegation.\\n\\n4. Decision\\n\\na. Korean Standard Industrial Classification\\n\\nThe Korean Standard Industrial Classification was prepared based on the United Nations’ International Standard Industrial Classification in order to secure accuracy and comparability of industrial statistical data, and systematically categorizes the industrial activities mainly performed by production units according to their similarity. It is basically prepared for statistical purposes, but it is also widely applied mutatis mutandis as a standard for limiting the scope of application of the relevant statutes in general administrative and industrial policy-related legislation.\\n\\nSince its enactment on 1 March 1963, the Korean Standard Industrial Classification has been periodically revised to reflect revisions to the United Nations’ International Standard Industrial Classification and changes in domestic industrial structure and technology. The current system of the Korean Standard Industrial Classification classifies industries under 20 major categories into medium, minor, subdivision, and detailed subdivision categories, and such classification is based on the United Nations’ “International Standard Industrial Classification” system; as a matter of principle, it matches the international classification up to the subdivision level. However, where necessary, some items have been independently established in consideration of domestic circumstances.\\n\\nThe Korean Standard Industrial Classification currently reflects the characteristics of the industries of our country most effectively and classifies by encompassing almost all existing business types on the basis of reasonable standards, and accordingly it is evaluated as an accurate and authoritative standard with respect to the classification of business types. Accordingly, numerous tax-related statutes, including the provision under review, prescribe that the Korean Standard Industrial Classification shall be followed when classifying business types. The Supreme Court also, where the classification of business types arises in relation to tax imposition, etc., ordinarily determines, in accordance with the Korean Standard Industrial Classification, which business type a particular industrial activity falls under (Supreme Court Decision 85NU446 rendered on 10 March 1987; Decision 2010DU29192 rendered on 28 February 2013, etc.).\\n\\nb. Precedent of the Constitutional Court\\n\\nIn Decision 2005HEONBA59 rendered on 28 December 2006, the Constitutional Court held that the provision under review does not violate the principle of taxation by law or the prohibition on blanket delegation, and the gist of that decision is as follows.\\n\\n(1) Whether it is permissible to delegate legislative matters to the Korean Standard Industrial Classification, which is a public notice\\n\\nThe reason why, today, the legislative monopoly theory of Parliament has shifted to legislative centrism and administrative legislation is allowed within a certain scope lies in the increase in legislative demand in response to social change and in the functional separation of powers theory that the conventional formal separation of powers cannot address modern society. Considering these circumstances and examining the meanings of Articles 40, 75, and 95 of the Constitution, with respect to matters delegated by the National Assembly by legislation to administrative agencies within a specific scope, the relevant administrative agency acquires the authority to establish the law, and at that time the legislator may also choose the form of regulation, and thus the form of delegated legislation recognized by the Constitution should be understood as illustrative. Therefore, even if a statute delegates certain matters to administrative rules, those administrative rules may regulate only the delegated matters, and thus do not conflict with the principle of National Assembly legislation. However, because administrative rules do not require the strict enactment and amendment procedures required for statutory ordinances, in delegating legislation that restricts fundamental rights, the principle is to delegate to statutory ordinances, and where legislative delegation is made in the form of a public notice, etc., it is limited to matters that are professional and technical or minor matters and for which delegation is unavoidable by the nature of the work. Moreover, even for such matters, under the prohibition on blanket delegation, the delegation in a statute must be made with respect to matters specifically and individually limited.\\n\\nSince matters concerning special treatment such as tax reductions or heavy taxation directly affect the rights and obligations of the people, in statutes concerning tax special treatment it is desirable to delegate matters concerning the classification of business types to statutory ordinances such as presidential decrees, Prime Minister’s Ordinances, or ministerial ordinances. However, the classification of business types is the task of systematically categorizing all productive economic activities within a nation according to certain standards and principles, and such task requires highly professional and technical knowledge in the relevant field on the premise of economic and statistical concepts, and requires a great number of specialized personnel and a great deal of time. In addition, because the scope of the business types to be classified is vast, it is, as a matter of legislative technique, impossible for the legislator to identify the commonalities and differences among all business types and enumerate diverse business types one by one in the statute. Meanwhile, considering that the Korean Standard Industrial Classification best reflects the industrial structure of our country and is evaluated as the most authoritative material regarding the classification of business types, it is more rational and efficient to delegate to the Korean Standard Industrial Classification already publicly notified by the Commissioner of Statistics Korea rather than to delegate to the President or the heads of administrative ministries, whose capacity for judgment and expertise regarding the classification of business types is limited. In other words, the matters concerning the classification of business types delegated by the provision under review to the public notice of the Commissioner of Statistics Korea constitute professional and technical matters for which delegation is unavoidable by the nature of the work.\\n\\n(2) Whether there is a violation of the principle of taxation by law or the prohibition on blanket delegation\\n\\nEven where a statute recognizes the need to delegate legislation in the form of administrative rules such as a public notice because the matter is professional and technical or minor and delegation is necessary by the nature of the work, such delegation must not violate the prohibition on blanket delegation under Article 75 of the Constitution and must be made with respect to matters specifically and individually limited. Here, “within a specifically determined scope” means that the basic matters of the content and scope to be stipulated in subordinate norms should be prescribed in the statute as concretely and clearly as possible so that the general outline of the content to be prescribed in a presidential decree, etc. can be predicted from the statute itself. Whether predictability exists must not be judged only by a particular provision in question, but must be judged by comprehensively and organically considering the entire relevant legal provisions. Accordingly, even if the delegation provision itself does not clearly specify the specific scope of the delegation, if the intrinsic scope or limit of the delegation provision can be objectively and clearly determined in light of the overall structure of the statute and the relevant provisions, it cannot be regarded as a blanket delegation in blank form.\\n\\nSince the enactment of the Korean Standard Industrial Classification, numerous enforcement decrees and enforcement rules have been made that provide that the classification of business types listed in the individual provisions of various tax-related statutes shall follow the Korean Standard Industrial Classification when specifying those business types, and even in cases lacking such express provisions, the Supreme Court has, when classifying business types specifically, used the Korean Standard Industrial Classification as the standard. In light of these circumstances, even if the provision under review takes the form of comprehensively delegating the classification of business types to the Korean Standard Industrial Classification, this merely has the meaning of confirming the existing legal and institutional practice of classifying business types according to the Korean Standard Industrial Classification, and it cannot thereby be concluded that the predictability of the general public is infringed. Moreover, if one organically and systematically examines the dictionary meaning of the classification of business types, the academic achievements of related disciplines, Article 17 of the Statistics Act, which is the relevant legal provision, the International Standard Industrial Classification prepared by the United Nations, and other individual provisions of the Restriction of Special Taxation Act, the general outline of the content and scope to be stipulated in the Korean Standard Industrial Classification can be sufficiently predicted. Therefore, the provision under review does not violate the principle of taxation by law or the prohibition on blanket delegation.\\n\\nc. Determination\\n\\n(1) The prior precedent, which held that the provision under review not only has a necessity to delegate matters concerning the classification of business types, a legislative matter, to the Korean Standard Industrial Classification publicly notified by the Commissioner of Statistics Korea, but also does not violate the principle of taxation by law or the prohibition on blanket delegation, is proper, and there is no change in circumstances warranting a change in precedent in this case.\\n\\n(2) Claimant ○○ Co., Ltd. argues that, with only the provisions related to “construction business” and “real estate supply business” under the “Korean Standard Industrial Classification,” it is difficult to determine whether only a person who directly performs construction work qualifies as a “construction business operator,” or whether a person who did not directly perform construction work but carried out the work under his or her overall responsibility also qualifies as a “construction business operator,” and that this is contrary to the principle of clarity. However, the subject of a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act is the statute that serves as a premise for the judgment in the underlying case, and subordinate norms such as presidential decrees, ministerial ordinances, or administrative rules cannot be the subject of adjudication. Moreover, the grounds asserted by the claimant are merely matters relating to the interpretation of the Korean Standard Industrial Classification, and thus no separate determination is made with respect to this part of the claimant’s argument.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nSince the provision under review does not violate the Constitution, the decision is rendered as stated in the order. This decision was made by the unanimous opinion of the remaining Justices participating, except for the separate opinion of unconstitutionality conforming to the Constitution by Justices Park Han-cheol, Lee Jung-mi, and Lee Jin-seong as set forth in 6 below.\\n\\n6. Separate Opinion of Justices Park Han-cheol, Lee Jung-mi, and Lee Jin-seong: Unconstitutionality conforming to the Constitution\\n\\nBecause we do not agree with the majority opinion that the provision under review is consistent with the Constitution, we state the following opinion that it is unconstitutional but compatible with the Constitution.\\n\\na. The Constitution, in Article 40, declares the principle of National Assembly legislation, while in Articles 75, 95, 108, 113(2), and 114(6) it limitatively enumerates presidential decrees, Prime Minister’s Ordinances and ministerial ordinances, Supreme Court Rules, Constitutional Court Rules, National Election Commission Rules, etc. as statutory ordinances that may be issued upon delegation by statute. In addition, because our Constitution is a rigid constitution under which all expressions of state will, including statutes that conflict with it, cannot validly exist, legislative matters cannot be delegated to administrative rules such as public notices by way of statutes or lower legislative forms as an exception to constitutional principles.\\n\\nHowever, the provision under review states that “the classification of business types used in this Act shall, except where this Act contains special provisions, be based on the Korean Standard Industrial Classification publicly notified by the Commissioner of Statistics Korea pursuant to Article 17 of the Statistics Act,” thereby delegating matters concerning the classification of business types used in the Restriction of Special Taxation Act to the Korean Standard Industrial Classification prepared and publicly notified by the Commissioner of Statistics Korea, not to a statutory ordinance such as a presidential decree, Prime Minister’s Ordinance, or ministerial ordinance.\\n\\nThe Restriction of Special Taxation Act was enacted to prescribe matters concerning tax special treatment such as tax reductions or heavy taxation, and it distinguishes whether such reductions or heavy taxation apply according to business type; therefore, depending on how business types are classified under the Restriction of Special Taxation Act, the content and scope of the tax obligations of persons engaged in the relevant business type may differ. In other words, because the classification under the Restriction of Special Taxation Act may give rise to the effect of tax reduction or increase depending on the business type, matters concerning the classification of business types under the Restriction of Special Taxation Act are not merely a classification of business types, but belong to legislative matters directly affecting the rights and obligations of the general public, and thus delegation thereof should preferably be made to statutory ordinances such as presidential decrees, Prime Minister’s Ordinances, or ministerial ordinances.\\n\\nThe majority opinion argues that, after viewing the aforementioned forms of delegated legislation contemplated by the Constitution as illustrative, because the task of classifying all business types within a nation requires highly professional and technical knowledge in the relevant field and requires a great amount of manpower and time, a statute should also be permitted to delegate directly to administrative rules without delegating to statutory ordinances. However, the need for flexible response in professional and technical areas by delegation to administrative rules rather than statutory ordinances can be sufficiently addressed even by so-called constitutionally conforming step-by-step delegation. That is, while the statute delegates to statutory ordinances prescribed by the Constitution, and then the statutory ordinances again delegate, within a specifically determined scope, to administrative rules, the State can secure active governmental functions while conforming to the constitutional decision; it is not something that can be conveniently resolved by directly delegating to administrative rules.\\n\\nIn short, since the provision under review delegates regulatory matters concerning the rights and obligations of the people to administrative rules prepared and publicly notified by the Commissioner of Statistics Korea, rather than to statutory ordinances enumerated in the Constitution, it fails to satisfy the form of delegated legislation prescribed by the Constitution and cannot but be said to violate the Constitution.\\n\\nb. Meanwhile, Article 75 of the Constitution provides that “The President may issue presidential decrees concerning matters delegated by statute with specific scope ...,” thereby declaring the principle of specific and individual delegation. Accordingly, even where a statute recognizes the need to delegate legislation in the form of administrative rules such as a public notice because the matter is professional and technical or minor and delegation is necessary by the nature of the work, such delegation must not violate the prohibition on blanket delegation under Article 75 of the Constitution, and must be made with respect to matters specifically and individually limited; at a minimum, the basic matters of the content and scope to be stipulated in subordinate norms must be prescribed as concretely and clearly as possible by the statute so that anyone can predict the general outline of the content to be stipulated in a presidential decree, etc. from the statute itself (Constitutional Court 2007HEONBA74, 25 September 2008).\\n\\nHowever, other than requiring that the classification of business types follow the Korean Standard Industrial Classification publicly notified by the Commissioner of Statistics Korea, the provision under review does not set forth any concrete standards or policies regarding the basic matters of the content and scope to be stipulated in the public notice as a subordinate norm, but comprehensively delegates the regulation of the classification of business types to the Korean Standard Industrial Classification publicly notified by the Commissioner of Statistics Korea.
