and that the Plaintiff concluded on March 30, 2004, a sales contract (hereinafter referred to as “the sales contract at issue”) with the Defendant to purchase each of the lands at issue for KRW 32,535,106,400, and paid the down payment of KRW 3,253,510,640 on the same day and the balance of KRW 29,281,595,760 on May 31, 2004.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above, the Plaintiff’s assertion to the effect that, on the premise that the term attached by the Head of the Gangseo-gu Office when approving the housing construction project plan at issue, requiring the Plaintiff to purchase each of the lands at issue, was void or that such term subsequently lost its effect, the sales contract at issue concerning each of the lands at issue concluded by the Plaintiff in order to perform that term must also be deemed void, cannot be accepted without examining whether the term is effective or not; accordingly, the judgment of the court below, which rejected the Plaintiff’s assertion on the same basis, is proper, and there is no error of law such as misapprehension of legal doctrine concerning deviation from or abuse of discretion in an administrative act term, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Regarding the assertion that the sales contract at issue is void for violation of mandatory provisions\\n\\nA. Article 7(1) of the Supplementary Provisions of the former Act on the Maintenance and Improvement of Urban Areas and Dwelling Conditions for Residents (before amendment by Act No. 6893 on May 29, 2003; hereinafter referred to as the “former Urban Improvement Act”), under the heading “Transitional Measures Concerning Project Implementation Method,” provides that “matters being implemented pursuant to the approval of the project plan or the approval of project implementation under the former Act shall be governed by the former provisions.” In the case of a reconstruction project before the former Urban Improvement Act came into force, once approval of the project plan is obtained, as a matter of principle, the involvement of the administrative authority comes to an end, and the association members thereby acquire the right to receive a parcel allocation (the status of a person selected as an occupant) (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DU5369, decided June 15, 2007); and, in light of various circumstances, including the fact that the operation of the reconstruction association and the distribution of rights among the association members, as well as the method of transferring ownership of the newly constructed building or land, were originally envisaged to be carried out autonomously under the Civil Act and other general laws, it is difficult to find necessity or rationality for a reconstruction association that had already obtained approval of the project plan before the enforcement of the former Urban Improvement Act to carry out the remaining project according to the procedures or methods under the former Urban Improvement Act. However, Article 3 of the Supplementary Provisions of the former Urban Improvement Act, under the heading “General Transitional Measures,” provides that dispositions, procedures, and other acts conducted pursuant to the reconstruction-related provisions of the Housing Construction Promotion Act at the time of the enforcement of the former Urban Improvement Act (hereinafter referred to as the “former Act”) shall be deemed to have been conducted pursuant to the provisions of the former Urban Improvement Act, and Article 6 of the Supplementary Provisions of the former Urban Improvement Act, under the heading “Transitional Measures Concerning Residential Environment Improvement Projects,” provides that a reconstruction project being implemented after having obtained approval of the project plan or approval of project implementation under the former Act shall be deemed a housing reconstruction project under the former Urban Improvement Act; therefore, in the case of a reconstruction association, as to matters that do not fall under the “project implementation method” prescribed in Article 7(1) of the Supplementary Provisions of the former Urban Improvement Act, the main provisions of the former Urban Improvement Act or other supplementary provisions must be deemed applicable.\\n\\nArticle 65(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act provides: “Improvement infrastructure facilities newly installed by a project implementer other than a mayor, county governor, or Korea Housing Corporation, etc., through the implementation of a maintenance project shall vest gratuitously in the State or local government that is to manage such facilities, and improvement infrastructure facilities owned by the State or local government whose designated use is abolished by the implementation of a maintenance project shall be transferred gratuitously to the project implementer within the extent corresponding to the cost of installing the newly installed improvement infrastructure facilities.” This provision removes the room for claims of unconstitutionality or allegations of deviation from discretion by the administrative authority surrounding former Article 33(8) of the former Housing Construction Promotion Act (before amendment by Act No. 6655 on February 4, 2002; hereinafter the same), former Article 52(2) of the former Urban Planning Act (comprehensively amended by Act No. 6243 on January 28, 2000, and repealed by Act No. 6655 on February 4, 2002; hereinafter the same), etc., under which, when a private project implementer installed public facilities within a project district, the administrative authority was granted discretion to cause ownership of such public facilities and the land therefor to vest in the State or local government without any compensation; and, in consideration of the pecuniary loss suffered by a private project implementer due to improvement infrastructure facilities newly installed by the private project implementer gratuitously vesting in the managing authority pursuant to the first sentence of Article 65(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act, the latter sentence of the same paragraph was enacted so that, within the extent corresponding to the cost of installing the improvement infrastructure facilities newly installed by the private project implementer, the improvement infrastructure facilities owned by the State or local government whose designated use is abolished by the implementation of the maintenance project are transferred gratuitously to that private project implementer, thereby reasonably compensating for such pecuniary loss within a reasonable scope and more equitably and reasonably adjusting the property rights and obligations between the private project implementer and the State or local government. Accordingly, this is a provision that prescribes the substantive legal relationship concerning the transfer or vesting of improvement infrastructure facilities owned by the State or local government whose designated use is abolished by the implementation of a maintenance project, and cannot be regarded as a provision concerning the “project implementation method.” Therefore, where, after the enforcement of the former Urban Improvement Act, a private project implementer of a reconstruction project that had obtained approval of the project plan before the enforcement of the former Urban Improvement Act concludes a contract between the State or local government regarding the transfer or vesting of improvement infrastructure facilities owned by the State or local government whose designated use is abolished by the implementation of the maintenance project, the latter sentence of Article 65(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act should be deemed applicable.\\n\\nAnd in light of the legislative purpose of the latter sentence of Article 65(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act as stated above, this is a mandatory provision compelling gratuitous transfer of improvement infrastructure facilities whose designated use is to be abolished, within the extent corresponding to the cost of installing the improvement infrastructure facilities to be newly installed by the private project implementer (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DU6663, decided July 12, 2007); therefore, sales contracts, etc. concluded in violation of that provision between the project implementer and the State or local government are void.\\n\\nIn addition, whether improvement infrastructure facilities are to be transferred gratuitously or vested gratuitously is determined by Article 65(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act, and Article 65(3) of the former Urban Improvement Act merely provides that the approving authority shall hear the opinion of the managing authority in advance in order to coordinate interests, and Article 65(4) of the former Urban Improvement Act is also a procedural provision requiring the managing authority to be notified before completion of the maintenance project of the kinds and items of property to vest in or be transferred to the managing authority or the project implementer pursuant to paragraphs (1) and (2) of the same Article; therefore, the mere fact that the procedures under Article 65(3) and (4) of the former Urban Improvement Act were not followed does not mean that improvement infrastructure facilities whose designated use is abolished are not subject to gratuitous transfer, and the mere fact that such procedures were not followed does not justify treating a contract concluded in violation of Article 65(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act as valid (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DU1699, decided June 28, 2007). Moreover, the subject matter and price of a sales contract need not necessarily be specifically identified at the time the sales contract is concluded; it is sufficient if the means and standards by which they can be specifically identified even afterward are fixed in advance (see Supreme Court Decisions 92DA49447, decided June 8, 1993, and 2001DA7940, decided July 12, 2002, among others); thus, even if the cost of installing improvement infrastructure facilities to be newly installed by a private project implementer had not yet been determined at the time the sales contract was concluded, the parties may conclude a sales contract by providing means and standards for later specification of that cost, and if the private project implementer needs to acquire possessory and use rights over improvement infrastructure facilities whose designated use is to be abolished, it is entirely possible to acquire such possessory and use rights by concluding a sales contract through, for example, a method of deducting an amount corresponding thereto from the sale price on the basis of means and standards that enable future specification of the installation cost as described above; therefore, neither the fact that the cost of newly installed improvement infrastructure facilities had not yet been determined at the time the sales contract was concluded nor the fact that acquisition of possessory and use rights over improvement infrastructure facilities whose designated use is to be abolished is necessary can render valid a sales contract that, in substance, causes the private project implementer to purchase for consideration from the State or local government improvement infrastructure facilities whose designated use is abolished and which should instead be transferred gratuitously to the private project implementer.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the factual relations stated above, the statutory provision applicable to the sales contract at issue concluded between the Plaintiff and the Defendant after the enforcement of the former Urban Improvement Act is the latter sentence of Article 65(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act; and the sales contract at issue, under which the Plaintiff purchases for consideration from the Defendant the road and park portions of each of the lands at issue corresponding to the cost of the roads and parks newly installed by the Plaintiff, is void as it violates the mandatory provision in the latter sentence of Article 65(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act. Since there is no material in the record from which it can be seen that the portion of each of the lands at issue that becomes void as described above can be specified, in this case no part of the sales contract at issue can be held void only in part.\\n\\nThe judgment of the court below, which reached a different conclusion, erred by misapprehending the interpretation and application of Article 65(2) through (4) of the former Urban Improvement Act and the legal principles concerning the requirements for the validity of a sales contract, and such error affected the judgment. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\nB. The principle of good faith and fair dealing under the Civil Act is an abstract norm that a party to a legal relationship must not exercise rights or perform obligations in a manner contrary to equity or that betrays trust, in consideration of the other party’s interests; in order to deny the exercise of a right on the ground that it violates the principle of good faith and fair dealing, the other party must have been given grounds for trust, or objectively be in a state in which it is justified for the other party to have trust, and the exercise of the right contrary to such trust must have reached a degree that cannot be tolerated in light of the concept of justice.\\n\\nAbsent special circumstances, a person who has performed a legal act while knowing that it is void for violating statutes cannot be regarded as acting in violation of the principle of good faith, estoppel, or abuse of rights merely because that person asserts voidness on the ground of violation of a mandatory rule (see Supreme Court Decisions 95DA12217, decided May 10, 1996, and 2003DA19961, decided August 22, 2003, among others).\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the judgment below, the court below held that, before July 1, 2003, the enforcement date of the former Urban Improvement Act, former Article 33(8) of the former Housing Construction Promotion Act and former Article 52(2) of the former Urban Planning Act applied to the vesting of public facilities whose designated use is abolished by the implementation of a housing reconstruction project, so if the Plaintiff and the Defendant had concluded a sales contract concerning each of the lands at issue before June 30, 2003, its validity could not be denied; however, it further held that, since the Head of the Gangseo-gu Office attached, when approving the housing construction project plan at issue on May 6, 2002, the term that a sales contract concerning each of the lands at issue be concluded before the commencement report (the Plaintiff filed the commencement report on December 27, 2002), and since, thereafter, although there was a period of more than one year until the enforcement of the former Urban Improvement Act on July 1, 2003, the Plaintiff delayed by failing to conclude a sales contract concerning each of the lands at issue with the Defendant, the Plaintiff’s assertion that the sales contract at issue was concluded after July 1, 2003, and is therefore void for violating the former Urban Improvement Act, cannot be permitted under the principle of good faith and fair dealing.\\n\\nUpon review in light of the record, it was possible for the Defendant to conclude a sales contract concerning each of the lands at issue only after procedures such as a decision to abolish the designated use, approval by the city council, and appraisal-based determination of the sale price; when it was anticipated that considerable time would be required to conclude a sales contract with the Defendant and that this would impede the prompt progress of the project, the Plaintiff deposited KRW 27,535,140,000 with the Head of the Gangseo-gu Office on December 26, 2002, as a provisional sale price, and, with the approval of the Head of the Gangseo-gu Office, filed the commencement report on December 27, 2002, before proceeding with the construction; among each of the lands at issue, the lands listed in items 2 through 11 of the separate sheet attached to the reasoning portion of the judgment below, which had been used as roads, had already undergone a change in land classification to site before the above commencement report, whereas item 1 of the separate sheet attached to the reasoning portion of the judgment below, which had been used as a park, did not have a decision on abolition of designated use made until March 4, 2003, after the enforcement of the former Urban Improvement Act, and its land classification was changed to site only on August 1, 2003; and after the Plaintiff submitted an application for purchase concerning the lands at issue to the Defendant on August 18, 2003, the sales contract at issue was concluded on March 30, 2004, after going through procedures such as city council approval and appraisal. Apart from this, it is difficult to find in the record any circumstance suggesting that the Plaintiff delayed the conclusion of the sales contract by, without justifiable cause, refusing or delaying the Defendant’s request to conclude the sales contract in order to obtain application of the latter sentence of Article 65(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act. Then, on the basis of only the circumstances cited by the court below or stated above, it is difficult to conclude that, in concluding a sales contract with the Defendant concerning public facilities whose designated use is abolished by the implementation of the housing reconstruction project at issue, the Plaintiff gave the Defendant any trust that the former Article 33(8) of the former Housing Construction Promotion Act and former Article 52(2) of the former Urban Planning Act would apply, or that, objectively viewed, the Defendant had justifiable trust; nor can it be said that the Plaintiff’s assertion of the application of the latter sentence of Article 65(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act with respect to the sales contract at issue reached a degree that cannot be tolerated in light of the concept of justice. Accordingly, it cannot be said that the Plaintiff’s assertion that the sales contract at issue is void for violating the latter sentence of Article 65(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act is contrary to the principle of good faith and fair dealing.\\n\\nThe judgment of the court below, which reached a different conclusion, erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the principle of good faith and fair dealing, and such error affected the judgment. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the concurrence of the Justices of the Supreme Court as set forth in the disposition."}

{"[2008DA56262]": "The grounds of appeal shall be determined (the statements in the supplemental brief of grounds of appeal, filed after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal, shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. As to the legal character of the agreement in this case\\n\\nIn the case of a beneficial administrative disposition, even if there is no special statutory basis, a burden may be attached as an incidental condition thereto (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DO12837, rendered on March 25, 2004), and such burden may be unilaterally added by the administrative agency when making the administrative disposition, or, before attaching the burden, the administrative agency may consult with the other party and preliminarily determine the contents of the burden in the form of an agreement, and then attach it when making the administrative disposition.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below comprehensively considered the evidence it accepted and recognized the facts as stated in the judgment, and then held that, under the Road Act (as in force prior to its amendment by Act No. 4545 of March 10, 1993), the permission in this case was a so-called beneficial administrative disposition having the effect of conferring rights or benefits on the counterparty and falling within the discretionary act of the administrative agency, and that the instant agreement prescribed, mainly, the obligations to be performed by the Defendant on the premise that the Plaintiff, as the managing authority of the expressway, would in the future grant permission to the Defendant for the burying of oil pipelines in the expressway site and roadside area, and thus, in nature, was an agreement concerning the proposed conditions to be attached to the permission.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the foregoing determination by the court below is proper, and there is no error of law, such as a misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning conditions attached to an administrative act, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. As to whether the instant agreement has become ineffective\\n\\nIf the administrative agency, while making a beneficial administrative disposition that is a discretionary act, attaches a burden imposing certain obligations on the addressee of the disposition, such burden independently becomes an administrative disposition subject to administrative litigation. However, whether an administrative disposition is unlawful must be determined on the basis of the laws and regulations and factual circumstances existing at the time of the disposition, and is not affected by the repeal or amendment of the laws and regulations after the disposition or by changes in the factual circumstances (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DO1811, rendered on May 11, 2007, etc.). Therefore, the lawfulness of a burden attached by the administrative agency while making a discretionary beneficial administrative disposition must likewise be determined on the basis of the laws and regulations at the time of the disposition, and even if the burden was lawful on the basis of the laws and regulations at the time of the disposition, and even if, after the disposition, the statutory basis for the principal administrative disposition underlying the burden is amended so that the administrative agency can no longer attach incidental conditions, it cannot be said that the burden immediately becomes unlawful or that its effect ceases. Accordingly, even where the addressee of an administrative disposition entered into an agreement with the administrative agency regarding the burden to be attached to the administrative disposition in order to obtain a beneficial administrative disposition, and the administrative agency, while making the beneficial administrative disposition, attached the obligations under the agreement as a burden, even if the statutory basis for the principal administrative disposition underlying the burden is amended so that the administrative agency can no longer attach incidental conditions, the effect of the agreement made prior thereto does not immediately cease.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below held that, under Article 23(1)5 of the Enforcement Rule of the Road Act in force at the time the instant agreement was concluded, the act of installing oil pipelines in a roadside area within the limit not exceeding 15m from the road boundary line was prohibited as the act of newly constructing a structure or adding an object, and the act of installing oil pipelines in a roadside area exceeding 15m was permitted by obtaining permission from the Plaintiff; however, when the Enforcement Rule of the Road Act was amended by Ordinance of the Ministry of Construction No. 546 on February 1, 1994, pursuant to Article 24 Item 5 of the Enforcement Rule of that Act (as in force prior to its amendment by Ordinance of the Ministry of Construction and Transportation No. 209 on September 2, 1999), the installation of oil pipelines in a roadside area within the limit not exceeding 15m from the road boundary line became freely possible without requiring permission, and thus the part concerning the roadside area among the obligations under the instant agreement, which was an incidental condition attached to the road occupancy permit, lost its legal basis simultaneously with the amendment of the above Enforcement Rule and therefore ceased to have effect from that time.\\n\\nHowever, according to the foregoing legal doctrine, the instant agreement was an agreement that determined the content of the burden to be attached by the Plaintiff when granting the instant permission; therefore, by granting the instant permission on the condition that the instant agreement be observed, the Plaintiff attached a burden that the Defendant would be obligated to pay the cost of relocating the oil pipeline facilities in accordance with the content prescribed in the instant agreement. Accordingly, even if, by the amendment of the Enforcement Rule of the Road Act as stated above, the act of installing oil pipelines in a roadside area within the limit not exceeding 15m from the road boundary line under the instant permission was changed into an act that no longer required permission from the Plaintiff, and thus, after the enforcement of the above Enforcement Rule of the Road Act, the Plaintiff could no longer attach incidental conditions with respect to such act, the burden concerning the obligation to pay the cost of relocating the oil pipeline facilities in the roadside area under the instant permission, which was lawfully made under the former Enforcement Rule of the Road Act, does not lose its effect by the enforcement of the above Enforcement Rule of the Road Act. In addition, even after the former Enforcement Rule of the Road Act was amended on February 1, 1994, the act of installing oil pipelines in a roadside area exceeding 15m from the road boundary line still remained an act requiring permission from the Plaintiff; therefore, permission for the installation of structures within that roadside area remains a beneficial administrative disposition to which a burden may validly be attached.\\n\\nTherefore, the court below’s determination that the part concerning the roadside area among the obligations under the instant agreement lost its legal basis simultaneously with the amendment of the above Enforcement Rule and thereby ceased to have effect from that time is erroneous in that it misapprehended the legal doctrine concerning whether the instant agreement has become ineffective. The ground of appeal pointing out this issue has merit.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}
{"[97NU2627]": "The appeal is dismissed. The costs of the appeal shall be borne by the Plaintiff."}

{"[98DU8919]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. On the non-institution of suit agreement\\n\\nAs legally found by the court below, on 1995. 11. 15., when the Defendant redesignated the Plaintiff as a wholesale market corporation of the agricultural and marine products wholesale market located in Yongdu-dong, Dongdaemun-gu, Seoul, established by the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as the \"Cheongnyangni Market\"), the Defendant attached, as Item 2 of the conditions for designation, a proviso stating that \"even during the designation period, the establisher may not file any lawsuit or claim any compensation for losses in response to a transfer of the wholesale market corporation or an order to revoke the designation or to close it, in accordance with the policy of agricultural and marine products distribution.\" However, the portion concerning the non-institution of suit agreement cannot be permitted, because it targets legal relations under public law over which the parties cannot dispose of at will and constitutes a waiver, by agreement of the parties, of the right of action, which is a public right of a private person against the State (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 1961. 11. 2., 4293HAENGSANG60), and therefore the argument premised on the validity of such agreement is without merit.\\n\\n2. On deviation from or abuse of discretion\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, based on the evidence cited, found that the Plaintiff had been designated as the wholesale market corporation (former designation: designated wholesaler) of the agricultural and marine products wholesale market located in Yongdu-dong, Dongdaemun-gu, Seoul, established by the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as the \"Cheongnyangni Market\") from 1975. 11. 11. onward, and was redesignated by the Defendant on 1995. 11. 15. as a wholesale market corporation with the designation period set from 1995. 11. 11. to 1998. 11. 10., with a proviso stating that \"even during the designation period, the establisher may not file any lawsuit or claim any compensation for losses in response to a transfer of the wholesale market corporation or an order to revoke the designation or to close it, in accordance with the policy of agricultural and marine products distribution\"; that the Defendant, around 1980, decided to establish agricultural and marine products wholesale markets by district in the Seoul area, and, with respect to the northeastern district, finally decided, through consultations with related agencies including Guri City around 1991. 7., to establish an agricultural and marine products wholesale market in Inchang-dong, Guri City; that, accordingly, the Minister of Agriculture and Forestry, on 1997. 5. 31., incorporated six districts in the northeastern area of Seoul, including Dongdaemun-gu, into the opening area of the above wholesale market, while Guri City opened the Guri Agricultural and Marine Products Wholesale Market (hereinafter referred to as the \"Guri Wholesale Market\") in Inchang-dong, Guri City on the same year 6. 9., and then, on 1997. 8. 23., the Defendant, on the grounds that there had been a request from Guri City for revocation of the Plaintiff’s designation as a wholesale market corporation for the early revitalization of the Guri Wholesale Market, and also that it intended to improve the distribution structure for the northeastern district of Seoul and establish trade order by settling a transparent listing system, issued a disposition revoking the designation of the Plaintiff as a wholesale market corporation for the Cheongnyangni Market pursuant to the above designation conditions (hereinafter referred to as the \"Disposition in this case\"); that, meanwhile, on 1995. 10. 30., Guri City announced a designation plan for wholesale market corporations for the Guri Market, under which two corporations would be designated as wholesale market corporations for the fruit and vegetable category, and group commercial areas within the opening area and prominent merchants within Guri City would be selected in priority, and accordingly the Plaintiff, after prior consultation with the Guri City Wholesale Market Preparatory Task Force, took over Daedong Cheongwa Co., Ltd., which was preparing to move into the Guri Wholesale Market, and then on the same year 11. 30. applied for designation as a wholesale market corporation for the fruit and vegetable category, but Guri City, excluding the Plaintiff who had an existing commercial sphere, finalized the non-party Guri Cheongwa Co., Ltd. and Goryeo Cheongwa Co., Ltd., which had no experience whatsoever as wholesale market corporations, as the prospective designated entities for wholesale market corporations; that the Minister of Agriculture and Forestry, on 1997. 8. 7., took measures to restrain the Plaintiff’s business at the Cheongnyangni Market for the revitalization of the Guri Wholesale Market, but to date a considerable number of merchants at the Cheongnyangni Market are still engaged in business in the fruit and vegetable category, and the Plaintiff, while performing its duties as a wholesale market corporation, did not trade by means of consignment auction; and, after recognizing such facts, determined that, unlike the original plan for opening the Guri Wholesale Market, the Disposition in this case, which revoked the Plaintiff’s designation as a wholesale market corporation for the Cheongnyangni Market solely on the grounds that it was necessary to revitalize the Guri Wholesale Market and improve the distribution structure of the northeastern district of Seoul, and that the Plaintiff did not conduct consignment auction prescribed by law, while not designating the Plaintiff, who had operated as a wholesale market corporation in the existing commercial sphere for 22 years, was so harsh to the Plaintiff that, even considering the public interest purpose sought to be achieved thereby, it deviated from or abused the scope of discretion and was unlawful.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the foregoing factual findings by the court below are persuasive, and it cannot be said that there is any unlawfulness of misapprehending facts due to a violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged; furthermore, in light of the fact that the Cheongnyangni Market has not been closed and still remains in existence, that a wholesale market corporation is a substantive operator of a wholesale market and is indispensable in that wholesale market, and the various circumstances cited by the court below, the conclusion of the court below that, in relation to fruits and vegetables, the Disposition in this case, which revoked the designation of the Plaintiff as the wholesale market corporation for the Cheongnyangni Market, the Plaintiff being the sole lawful wholesaler in the Cheongnyangni Market except for the agricultural cooperative auction market, was an unlawful disposition constituting an abuse of discretion, is persuasive, and it cannot be said that there is any unlawfulness of an error of law regarding the scope of discretion, as alleged. The argument is also without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the final appeal shall be borne by the losing party; accordingly, it is adjudged as stated in the Disposition in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following explanations concerning administration under the rule of law is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Where a statute delegates matters of autonomous legislation to the articles of association of a public-law entity, the constitutional prohibition of blanket delegation legislation under Article 75 of the Constitution applies in principle, and even where delegation is made, if the matter relates to the rights and duties of the people, at least the basic and essential matters concerning the rights and duties of the people must be determined by the National Assembly.
B: The modern principle of legal reservation is understood as embodying not only the requirement that administrative action merely have a statutory basis, but also the requirement that, in areas of fundamental and important significance to the national community and its members, the legislator, as the representative of the people, must itself decide the essential matters.
C: A notice of exclusion from lawful union status is a grave infringing disposition that deprives a duly established labor union of its legal status, and as a matter that in principle must be prescribed by the legislator, the representative of the people, in a formal statute, legislation; to prescribe it by administrative legislation, there must necessarily be an explicit and specific delegation by statute.
D: Where, as with corporate income tax and comprehensive income tax, the taxpayer is imposed not only the duty to pay tax but also the duty to calculate and report the tax base and tax amount on its own, the basic matters necessary to fulfill the reporting duty, and the disadvantages the taxpayer will suffer in the event of non-performance of the reporting duty, etc., as the basic and essential content constituting the tax liability, must be prescribed by statute.
E: Cadets of the Army 3rd Military Academy may have their fundamental rights restricted more than ordinary citizens, but even in such a case, the constitutional principles governing restrictions on fundamental rights, such as the principle of legal reservation and the principle of proportionality, must be observed.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DU14476]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. As to Ground 1 of the appeal\\n\\nA. Portion alleging a misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the limits of quasi-retroactive legislation\\n\\nIn amending a statute, if the parties’ reliance on the continued existence of the former statute is reasonable and justified, and if the harm to, or infringement of the interests of the parties caused by the amendment of the statute is so grave that the public-interest purpose sought to be achieved by the new statute cannot justify the destruction of such reliance, the legislature must take appropriate measures to protect the parties’ reliance, such as by providing transitional provisions, and it would be impermissible to enact or apply the new statute as it is without such appropriate measures, because doing so would violate the principle of protection of reliance derived from the rule-of-law principle, which is a fundamental principle of the Constitution. In determining whether such a violation of the principle of protection of reliance exists, one must comprehensively compare and balance, on the one hand, the protected value of the infringed interest, the degree of severity of the infringement, the degree to which reliance has been impaired, and the manner of the infringement of reliance, and, on the other hand, the public-interest purpose sought to be realized through the new statute (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2003DU12899 rendered on 2006. 11. 16.).\\n\\nArticle 28(4) of the Urban and Residential Environment Improvement Act, as enacted by Act No. 6852 on 2002. 12. 30. and before amendment by Act No. 7392 on 2005. 3. 18. (hereinafter the “former Urban Improvement Act”), provided that, before applying for approval of project implementation, the project implementer (excluding the Mayor, County Governor, or housing corporation, etc.; hereinafter the same) was required to obtain in advance the consent of at least two-thirds of the landowners within the area of the rearrangement zone based on the area of land, and the consent of at least four-fifths of the owners of land, etc., with respect to the contents of the project implementation plan. However, Article 28(4) of the Urban and Residential Environment Improvement Act as amended by Act No. 7392 on 2005. 3. 18. (hereinafter the Urban and Residential Environment Improvement Act as amended as above is referred to as the “Amended Urban Improvement Act,” and when the Urban and Residential Environment Improvement Act is referred to simply regardless of the above amendment, it is referred to as the “Urban Improvement Act”) was amended to provide in its main clause that the project implementer must, before applying for approval of project implementation, obtain the consent of the owners of land, etc. in accordance with the articles of association, etc. Meanwhile, according to the reasons of the judgment below, the Defendant-intervenor, a redevelopment association established before the Amended Urban Improvement Act came into force (hereinafter the “Intervenor Association”), upon the amendment of the Urban Improvement Act as above, obtained the consent of at least one-half of its members and newly established an articles-of-association provision stating that “when applying for approval of project implementation, consent to project implementation shall be sought from the landowners of at least one-half of the area of land within the rearrangement zone and from at least two-thirds of the owners of land, etc.”; and the Plaintiffs, as members of the Intervenor Association, owned land comprising at least one-third of the total area of the redevelopment project site.\\n\\nIn light of the above factual circumstances and the contents of the relevant statutes, the Intervenor Association, while Article 28(4) of the former Urban Improvement Act was applicable, could apply for approval of project implementation only if it obtained the consent of landowners holding at least two-thirds of the area of land within the redevelopment zone, and thus the applicants, who owned land comprising at least one-third of that area, could, by exercising their right of consent at the time of application for approval of project implementation, restrict the implementation of the redevelopment project by the association in this case. However, after the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act came into force, depending on how the redevelopment association in this case prescribed in its articles of association the consent requirements at the time of application for approval of project implementation, the applicants could also lose the above existing status.\\n\\nNevertheless, the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act merely requires owners of land, etc., such as the applicants, to exercise their right of consent in accordance with what is prescribed in the articles of association of the association, which is the project implementer, in relation to the application for approval of project implementation; it does not deprive them of the right of consent itself. Even if the applicants’ existing status concerning the consent requirements at the time of application for approval of project implementation became unstable due to the enforcement of the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act, it is difficult to view this as a direct or serious infringement of the Plaintiffs’ property rights. Meanwhile, Article 16 of the Urban Improvement Act requires, in establishing an association for the purpose of a housing redevelopment project or an urban environment improvement project, the consent of at least four-fifths of the owners of land, etc., thereby imposing strict consent requirements for the very establishment of an association for the purpose of a housing redevelopment project, etc., which may affect the property rights of the owners of land, etc. However, once the association has been established through such strict consent requirements, there is a need, in the implementation of the project, to set consent requirements in a manner suited to the circumstances of the relevant association so as to enable prompt and efficient project implementation in accordance with the autonomous and democratic will of the members, and it appears that Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act was enacted to meet such public-interest requirements. In light of these circumstances, it is difficult to say that the necessity of protecting the Plaintiffs’ reliance on the continued existence of Article 28(4) of the former Urban Improvement Act is greater than the public interest sought to be achieved through the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act. Accordingly, it cannot be said that the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act violated the principle of protection of reliance in quasi-retroactive legislation.\\n\\nThe judgment below, which reached the same conclusion on this point, is proper, and there is no illegality affecting the outcome of the judgment due to any misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the limits of quasi-retroactive legislation, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nB. Portion alleging a misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the limits of delegated legislation and whether such limits were exceeded\\n\\nWhere a statute delegates matters of autonomous regulation to the articles of association of a public-law entity, etc., it is appropriate to view that the prohibition against blanket delegation legislation under Article 75 of the Constitution does not, in principle, apply. Meanwhile, even where a statute delegates autonomous matters to the articles of association, if the matter relates to the rights and obligations of the people, at least the basic and essential matters concerning the rights and obligations of the people must be determined by the National Assembly (see Constitutional Court Decision 2005HEONBA31 rendered on 2006. 3. 30.).\\n\\nIn light of the above legal principles and the contents of the relevant statutes, under the Urban Improvement Act, the project implementer has the authority to prepare the project implementation plan, and the administrative agency merely has the authority to approve it; therefore, the preparation of the project implementation plan by the association, which is the project implementer, is a matter having an autonomous-regulatory element. Since the preparation of the project implementation plan thus has an autonomous-regulatory element, the consent requirements of the owners of land, etc. at the time of the association’s application for approval of project implementation are also matters of autonomous regulation. Accordingly, even if the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act comprehensively delegates the consent requirements at the time of application for approval of project implementation to the articles of association of the association, the prohibition against blanket delegation legislation under Article 75 of the Constitution does not apply, and it cannot be said to violate that provision.\\n\\nMoreover, although the consent requirements of the owners of land, etc. at the time of the association’s application for approval of project implementation concern the project implementation plan, which affects the property-related rights and obligations of the owners of land, etc., those consent requirements are merely procedural requirements for prior control by the owners of land, etc. over the application for approval of project implementation and cannot be regarded as basic and essential matters concerning the property-related rights and obligations of the owners of land, etc.; thus, they cannot be said to fall within an area where the principle of statutory reservation or parliamentary reservation must necessarily be observed. Therefore, the main clause of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act cannot be said to violate the principle of statutory reservation or parliamentary reservation.\\n\\nThe judgment below on this point, which reached the same conclusion, is proper, and there is no illegality due to any misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the limits of delegated legislation and whether such limits were exceeded, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 2 of the appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the lower court determined that the legislative purpose of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act lies in promoting the expeditious implementation of projects by setting in the articles of association the consent requirements of members, etc. in a manner suited to the circumstances of the relevant association in the implementation of redevelopment projects, etc.; therefore, it premised that when setting the consent requirements of members, etc. in the articles of association, if those consent requirements are so unreasonable as not to properly reflect the actual intent of the members, etc., or if they deviate from the legislative purpose of Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act and are manifestly unfair, they may be deemed void. On that premise, the lower court determined that the amended articles-of-association provision in this case established by the Intervenor Association based on Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act set the consent requirements at the time of application for approval of project implementation as “the consent of landowners holding at least one-half of the area of land and the consent of at least two-thirds of the owners of land, etc.”. While this may be regarded as more lenient than the consent requirements under the former Urban Improvement Act, it does not appear manifestly improper as a consent requirement for determining or confirming the will of the association as a whole in a redevelopment project. The lower court further determined that, although the proviso to Article 28(4) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act requires, where the project implementer is a designated developer, the consent of landowners holding at least 50% of the area of land within the redevelopment zone and the consent of a majority of the owners of land, etc., that does not mean that a project implementer other than a designated developer must necessarily set, in the articles of association, the consent requirement at the time of application for approval of project implementation as requiring the consent of landowners holding at least two-thirds of the area of land.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant statutes and the record, the above determination by the lower court is proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality due to any misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the inherent limitations of the amended articles-of-association provision in this case, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. As to Ground 3 of the appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the lower court determined that Article 20(3) of the Amended Urban Improvement Act, in principle, requires that, when an association intends to amend its articles of association, it obtain the consent of a majority of its members and receive approval from the Mayor or County Governor; however, for items 2, 3, 4, 8, 12, and 15 among the matters to be stated in the articles of association under items 1 through 17 of paragraph (1) of the same Article, it requires the consent of at least two-thirds of the members, and for minor matters prescribed by Presidential Decree, the resolution of the general meeting may substitute for the consent of the members. The lower court then found no clear basis for treating matters concerning the consent of members, etc. at the time of application for approval of project implementation as matters requiring a significant amendment to the articles of association such that the consent of at least two-thirds of the members would be required. In light of those considerations, the lower court held that, in amending the articles of association so as to include matters concerning the consent requirements at the time of application for approval of the project implementation plan in a redevelopment project, the consent of at least two-thirds of the members cannot be said to be required, and that since the amendment to the articles of association to establish the amended articles-of-association provision in this case was made with the consent of a majority of the members, there can be no defect in the procedure for amending the articles of association or in the process of granting approval therefor.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant statutes and the record, the above determination by the lower court is proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality due to any misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the required quorum in the procedure for amending the articles of association with respect to the amended articles-of-association provision in this case, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. As to Ground 4 of the appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, it can be found that the Intervenor Association is an association that obtained approval for establishment on 2002. 7. 30. pursuant to Articles 12 and 13 of the former Urban Redevelopment Act (prior to its repeal by Act No. 6852 of 2002. 12. 30.) and completed registration of establishment on 2003. 2. 25. Since Article 3 of the Supplementary Provisions of the Urban Improvement Act, which came into force on 2003. 7. 1., provides that “dispositions, procedures, and other acts conducted pursuant to the provisions of the Urban Redevelopment Act, the Temporary Measures Act for Improvement of the Residential Environment of Urban Low-Income Residents, and the housing redevelopment-related provisions of the Housing Construction Promotion Act as of the time this Act enters into force shall be deemed to have been conducted pursuant to the provisions of this Act,” even if the original articles of association of the Intervenor Association did not contain provisions concerning the matters of “the timing and procedures for bearing the costs incurred in the rearrangement project, including construction costs, etc. (Article 20(1), Item 12 of the Urban Improvement Act)” and “the matters to be included in the contract with the contractor and the designer (Article 20(1), Item 15 of the Urban Improvement Act),” the former articles of association do not become void, and there is no basis for concluding that, when amending the articles of association to establish the amended articles-of-association provision in this case, an amendment to establish the matters under Article 20(1), Items 12 and 15 of the Urban Improvement Act must necessarily be made together. Accordingly, even if the Intervenor Association’s articles of association do not contain provisions concerning the matters under Article 20(1), Items 12 and 15 of the Urban Improvement Act, the entire articles of association of the Intervenor Association, including the amended articles-of-association provision in this case, cannot be deemed void.\\n\\nAlthough the reasoning set forth by the lower court on this point is somewhat insufficient, its conclusion is proper, and there is no illegality affecting the outcome of the judgment due to any misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the mandatory matters to be stated in the articles of association, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the Plaintiffs’ appeal is all dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing Plaintiffs, and it is so adjudged as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Supreme Court Justices."}

{"[2016DU32992]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following circumstances may be ascertained.\\n\\nA. Filing and Acceptance of the Plaintiff’s Establishment Report\\n\\n1) The Plaintiff was established on May 28, 1989, when teachers of national, public, and private schools nationwide were allowed to organize trade unions. At the time of establishment, Article 6 of the Plaintiff’s bylaws provided: “Members of this union shall be faculty and staff engaged in kindergartens, elementary schools, middle and high schools, universities, the Ministry of Education, and other educational institutions nationwide, excluding persons working for employers” (paragraph 1), and “Faculty and staff dismissed (dismissal, discharge, removal by authority, etc.) or excluded from appointment by the improper conduct of the Ministry of Education or municipal and provincial offices of education, or a foundation, may also become members” (paragraph 2), thus including not only “incumbent teachers” but also “dismissed teachers” within the qualifications for membership.\\n\\n2) Thereafter, in order to comply with universal international labor standards by guaranteeing the labor fundamental rights of teachers, which had until then been restricted, and, in respect of the plan to guarantee the labor fundamental rights of teachers agreed upon by the Tripartite Commission, to establish the scope of such guarantees and the structure of collective bargaining, Act No. 5727, the Act on the Establishment and Operation of Teachers’ Trade Unions, etc. (hereinafter the “Teachers’ Trade Union Act”) was enacted on January 29, 1999, and came into force on July 1, 1999, thereby permitting the establishment of teachers’ trade unions under positive law. The Teachers’ Trade Union Act provides certain special rules concerning teachers’ trade unions and, as to other matters, refers to the provisions of the Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act (hereinafter the “Trade Union Act”) (Article 14(1)). Since the proviso to Article 2, item 4, of the Trade Union Act provides that, in cases of “allowing persons who are not workers to join [(d)],” the organization shall not be deemed a trade union, membership by “persons who are not teachers,” such as dismissed teachers, was not permitted in teachers’ trade unions [Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act limits the statutory concept of “teacher” to “incumbent teacher” (main text), but provides in its proviso that “a person who has been dismissed and who has filed an application for relief from unfair labor practices with the Labor Relations Commission pursuant to the Trade Union Act shall be deemed a teacher until there is a re-hearing decision by the National Labor Relations Commission” (proviso). Meanwhile, the main text of Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act was partially amended by Act No. 17430 on June 9, 2020, in accordance with the purport of the Constitutional Court’s incompatible-with-the-Constitution decision (Constitutional Court, Decision of August 30, 2018, 2015HEONGA38, en banc); hereinafter, “Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act” refers to the provision prior to amendment].\\n\\n3) With the enactment and enforcement of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act containing the foregoing content, the Plaintiff convened a national delegates’ convention on June 27, 1999, and resolved to maintain Article 6, paragraph 1, of the bylaws in substance while deleting paragraph 2. On July 1, 1999, the Plaintiff filed an establishment report with the Defendant (who was then the “Minister of Labor” and, following the amendment of the Government Organization Act by Act No. 10339 on June 4, 2010, became the present “Minister of Employment and Labor”) and submitted the amended bylaws as above. Based on the amended bylaws submitted by the Plaintiff, the Defendant determined that there was no defect in the Plaintiff’s establishment requirements under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act and the Trade Union Act, accepted the establishment report on July 2, 1999, and issued the Plaintiff a certificate of report.\\n\\nB. First Corrective Order\\n\\n1) After accepting the establishment report, the Defendant confirmed that the Plaintiff’s bylaws’ supplementary provision Article 5 included the following: “Notwithstanding the provisions of Article 6, paragraph 1, of the bylaws, teachers who have been unfairly dismissed may become members” (paragraph 1), and “Among dismissed teachers who had been qualified for membership under the former bylaws, members who have not been reinstated, and members unfairly dismissed after the effective date of these bylaws, shall maintain their membership notwithstanding the provisions of Article 6, paragraph 1, of the bylaws” (paragraph 2).\\n\\n2) On February 12, 2010, the Defendant requested the Seoul Regional Labor Relations Commission to deliberate and decide on a corrective order with respect to matters in the Plaintiff’s bylaws deemed to violate labor-related statutes and regulations, and on March 10, 2010, the Seoul Regional Labor Relations Commission resolved that Article 9, the supplementary provision Article 5, and the like of the Plaintiff’s bylaws violated Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act (Seoul 2010 Decision No. 6). Accordingly, on March 31, 2010, the Defendant ordered the Plaintiff, pursuant to Article 14(1) of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act and Articles 21(1) and 21(3) of the Trade Union Act, to correct, by May 3, 2010, certain parts of the Plaintiff’s bylaws, including Article 55(4) and the supplementary provision Article 5 (hereinafter the “First Corrective Order”).\\n\\n3) On June 29, 2010, the Plaintiff filed an action seeking revocation of the First Corrective Order, alleging that it was unlawful, but the court rendered a judgment revoking only the part of the First Corrective Order concerning Article 55(4) of the Plaintiff’s bylaws and dismissing the claims regarding the remaining parts, including the supplementary provision Article 5. That judgment became final as rendered because both the Plaintiff’s appeal and appeal on points of law were dismissed (Seoul Administrative Court Judgment of November 5, 2010, 2010GUHAP27110; Seoul High Court Judgment of September 9, 2011, 2010NU43725; and Supreme Court Decision of January 12, 2012, 2011DU24231).\\n\\nC. Second Corrective Order\\n\\n1) On August 14, 2010, the Plaintiff amended its bylaws by deleting paragraph 1 of supplementary provision Article 5 and revising paragraph 2 to read: “A member who has been unfairly dismissed shall maintain membership notwithstanding the provisions of Article 6, paragraph 1, of the bylaws” (hereinafter, the revised supplementary provision Article 5 shall be referred to as the “Supplementary Provision at Issue”).\\n\\n2) On August 3, 2012, the Defendant requested the Seoul Regional Labor Relations Commission to deliberate and decide on a corrective order concerning the Plaintiff’s bylaws, and on September 3, 2012, the Seoul Regional Labor Relations Commission resolved that the portion of the Plaintiff’s bylaws corresponding to the Supplementary Provision at Issue violated Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act (Seoul 2012 Decision No. 7). Accordingly, on September 17, 2012, the Defendant ordered the Plaintiff to correct the Supplementary Provision at Issue by October 18, 2012, for the same reasons as the First Corrective Order (hereinafter the “Second Corrective Order”).\\n\\nD. Notice of Non-Recognition as a Trade Union under the Act\\n\\n1) On September 23, 2013, the Defendant, on the grounds that “despite having twice ordered correction of the bylaws permitting dismissed persons to join as members, the Plaintiff had failed to comply, and dismissed persons were in fact identified as joining and engaging in activities as members,” required, pursuant to Article 14(1) of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, Article 12(3) item 1 and Article 2(4) proviso (d) of the Trade Union Act, Article 9(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Establishment and Operation of Teachers’ Trade Unions, etc. (hereinafter the “Enforcement Decree of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act”), and Article 9(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act (hereinafter the “Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act”), that the Supplementary Provision at Issue be corrected in accordance with Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act by October 23, 2013, and that measures be taken so that dismissed persons who cannot become members do not join or engage in activities (hereinafter the “Request for Correction”). In the written request for correction, the Defendant specifically identified nine dismissed teachers who had joined and were engaging in activities as members of the Plaintiff and stated: “Please note that if the above deadline passes without compliance with the request for correction, notice will be given that the organization shall not be deemed a trade union under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act.”\\n\\n2) However, the Plaintiff did not comply with the Request for Correction, and accordingly, on October 24, 2013, the Defendant notified the Plaintiff, pursuant to Article 14(1) of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, Article 12(3) item 1 and Article 2(4) proviso (d) of the Trade Union Act, and Article 9(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act and Article 9(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act, that the Plaintiff “shall not be deemed a trade union under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act” (hereinafter, for brevity, a trade union established under the Trade Union Act or the Teachers’ Trade Union Act shall be referred to as a “statutory trade union,” and a trade union that is not a statutory trade union shall be referred to as a “non-statutory trade union.” The act of notifying that a trade union shall not be deemed a trade union under the Trade Union Act or the Teachers’ Trade Union Act shall be referred to as a “notice of non-recognition as a trade union,” and the notice of non-recognition as a trade union dated October 24, 2013, issued to the Plaintiff, shall be referred to as the “Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue”).\\n\\n3) On October 25, 2013, the Minister of Education sent each municipal and provincial office of education an official document titled “Request for Cooperation in Implementing Subsequent Measures and Notice of Dissolution of Suspension of Office Due to the ‘Notice that It Is Not a Labor Union’ for the Korean Teachers and Educational Workers Union.” The main content was that, following the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue, the Plaintiff had lost the status and authority as a trade union, such as the use of the name “trade union” and the right to collective bargaining, and therefore each municipal and provincial office of education was to implement subsequent measures such as: ① revocation of leave approval for full-time union officials and orders of reinstatement, ② eviction from offices provided to the Plaintiff and a request for return of office support subsidies, ③ loss of effect of previously concluded collective agreements after October 24, 2013, and suspension of ongoing collective bargaining, ④ prohibition on wage withholding for union dues, and ⑤ where members of the Plaintiff had participated as committee members in various committees pursuant to collective agreements, loss of committee qualification due to the lapse of the collective agreements, and to report the results of implementation to the Ministry of Education by December 2, 2013.\\n\\n2. Whether the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue Was Lawful (Grounds for Appeal Nos. 1 and 2)\\n\\nA. Relevant Statutory Provisions\\n\\n1) Under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, a person who intends to establish a teachers’ trade union must submit an establishment report to the Defendant (Article 4(2)), and matters concerning teachers’ trade unions not provided for in the Teachers’ Trade Union Act shall, except as otherwise provided in Article 14(2), follow the Trade Union Act (Article 14(1)).\\n\\n2) Under the Trade Union Act, a trade union means “an organization or federation thereof organized by workers as the principal body, autonomously united for the purpose of maintaining and improving working conditions and enhancing the economic and social status of workers” (main text of Article 2(4)); provided, however, that where it “allows persons who are not workers to join [(d)],” it shall not be deemed a trade union (proviso to Article 2(4); hereinafter, the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act, “Provided, however, that if any of the following applies, it shall not be deemed a trade union.” shall be referred to as the “Statutory Provision at Issue,” and the phrase “Provided, however, that if it allows persons who are not workers to join, it shall not be deemed a trade union,” including item (d), shall be referred to as “Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue”). Where a trade union to be established falls under any of the items of the proviso to Article 2(4), the administrative authority shall reject the establishment report (Article 12(3) item 1).\\n\\n3) Article 9(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act provides that matters concerning teachers’ trade unions not provided for in the Enforcement Decree of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act shall, except as otherwise provided in Article 9(2), follow the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act.\\n\\n4) Article 9(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act provides: “Where, after a trade union has been issued a certificate of report, a ground for rejection of the establishment report corresponding to Article 12(3) item 1 of the Trade Union Act arises, the administrative authority shall demand correction by specifying a period of 30 days, and if it is not complied with within that period, shall notify the relevant trade union that it shall not be deemed a trade union under the Trade Union Act.” (hereinafter the “Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue”).\\n\\nB. The Constitutional Principle of Statutory Reservation and the Limits of Administrative Legislation\\n\\n1) Article 37(2) of the Constitution provides: “The freedoms and rights of citizens may be restricted only by Act when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, and even when such restriction is imposed, the essential aspect of the freedom or right shall not be violated.” The rule of law under the Constitution takes the principle of statutory reservation as one of its core components, namely, the principle that administrative action requires a basis in formal legislation enacted by the National Assembly. Moreover, the principle of statutory reservation today is understood to include not merely the requirement that administrative action be based on statute, but also the requirement, in areas that have fundamental and important significance for the national community and its members, especially in areas related to the realization of fundamental rights of the people, that such matters not be left to administration but be decided by the legislature itself, i.e., the people’s representative. That is, it includes the principle of parliamentary reservation. Whether a given matter falls within the essential matters that the National Assembly itself must prescribe by formal legislation must be determined individually in concrete cases by considering the importance of the interests or values involved and the degree and method of regulation or infringement. The greater the importance of the regulated subject matter to the fundamental rights of the people, and the greater the need for public debate or reconciliation between conflicting interests, the greater becomes the need for direct regulation by statute enacted by the National Assembly. Therefore, fundamental and essential matters concerning the rights and obligations of the people must be determined by the National Assembly, and when restricting freedoms or rights guaranteed by the Constitution, at least the essential matters of such restrictions must be regulated by the National Assembly itself through legislation (see Supreme Court Decision of October 12, 2007, 2006DU14476; en banc Supreme Court Decision of August 20, 2015, 2012DU23808; and Constitutional Court, en banc decision of February 26, 2009, 2008HEONMA370, etc.).\\n\\n2) Article 75 of the Constitution provides: “The President may issue presidential decrees concerning matters delegated to him or her specifically by Act, and matters necessary to enforce Acts.” Accordingly, the President may issue presidential decrees only concerning matters specifically delegated by Acts and matters necessary for the enforcement of Acts; thus, enforcement decrees may provide only detailed matters delegated by the parent Act or matters necessary for the practical enforcement of the Act within the scope prescribed by the Act. Unless delegated by statute, they may neither alter or supplement the content concerning individual rights and duties prescribed by the Act nor provide new contents not prescribed by the Act (see Supreme Court Decision of September 28, 1990, 89NU2493; en banc Supreme Court Decision of January 24, 1995, 93DA37342, etc.).\\n\\nC. The Unconstitutionality of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue\\n\\nA notice of non-recognition as a trade union is a grave administrative disposition adverse to rights, depriving a lawfully established trade union of its legal status, and in principle is a matter that must be prescribed by the legislature itself, as the people’s representative, through formal legislation. In order to regulate this by administrative legislation, there must necessarily be an explicit and specific delegation by statute. However, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is invalid in itself because, without statutory delegation, it prescribes a notice of non-recognition as a trade union not provided for by statute and thereby essentially restricts the three labor rights guaranteed by the Constitution. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) A notice of non-recognition as a trade union should be regarded as a formative administrative disposition that definitively determines that a trade union, although lawfully established and in operation, is no longer a trade union under the Trade Union Act.\\n\\nThe Trade Union Act establishes a system of establishment report concerning trade unions, and in order to become a statutory trade union, one must not only satisfy the statutory establishment requirements but also complete the establishment report. Accordingly, a trade union under the Trade Union Act comes into existence by submitting an establishment report to the competent administrative authority and receiving a certificate of report from that authority (see Supreme Court Decision of December 11, 1979, 76NU189; Supreme Court Decision of June 28, 1996, 93DO855, etc.). For example, the mere fact that a trade union does not allow persons who are not workers to join does not immediately mean that it acquires the status of a statutory trade union, nor does allowing such persons to join immediately mean that it is not a statutory trade union. The provision in the Statutory Provision at Issue that “it shall not be deemed a trade union” does not itself have legal effect; it merely clarifies the criteria for determining whether it is a trade union under the Trade Union Act.\\n\\nThe administrative authority rejects the establishment report of an organization that does not satisfy the statutory establishment requirements, and such rejection is a refusal to accept the establishment report, thus constituting an administrative disposition directly affecting the legal status of the organization. In other words, an organization with a disqualifying factor shall not be deemed a trade union pursuant to the Statutory Provision at Issue, but such legal effect is realized only through the rejection of the establishment report as described above.\\n\\nA notice of non-recognition as a trade union is an administrative disposition by which the administrative authority, through the above procedure, authoritatively determines that a trade union lawfully established and in operation is no longer a trade union under the Trade Union Act. It is not merely a post hoc notice or confirmation that the organization has already become a non-statutory trade union by statute; rather, it is a formative act that causes it to become a non-statutory trade union by virtue of the notice. In other words, if a disqualifying factor arises in a statutory trade union, it does not become a non-statutory trade union immediately by the Statutory Provision at Issue; it becomes a non-statutory trade union only upon issuance of a notice of non-recognition as a trade union on that ground.\\n\\n2) The Trade Union Act provides special protection for trade unions established under the Trade Union Act. That is, a statutory trade union may acquire corporate personality (Article 6), may apply to the Labor Relations Commission for adjustment of labor disputes and relief from unfair labor practices (Article 7(1)), and may be exempt from taxes (Article 8). Above all, only a statutory trade union may use the designation “trade union” (Article 7(3)). Acceptance of a trade union’s establishment report grants it the legal status to enjoy the rights and benefits provided by the Trade Union Act by recognizing a trade union that meets the statutory establishment requirements as a statutory trade union, and a notice of non-recognition as a trade union deprives an already lawfully established trade union of such legal status on the ground that a disqualifying factor has arisen.\\n\\nA trade union that has received a notice of non-recognition can no longer use the designation “trade union,” and even if the employer commits an unfair labor practice, such as refusing collective bargaining, it cannot adequately respond, thereby suffering obstacles in its activities as a trade union. Of course, even if it becomes a non-statutory trade union, it does not lose its status as a trade union itself, so one may say that the general exercise of the three labor rights remains possible (see Supreme Court Decision of February 11, 1997, 96NU2125; Supreme Court Decision of December 27, 2016, 2011DU921; and Constitutional Court, en banc decision of March 29, 2012, 2011HEONBA53, etc.), but even so, practical restrictions and disadvantages cannot be avoided. The three labor rights can be substantively guaranteed only through trade unions, and it is difficult to expect a body that cannot even use the designation “trade union” to effectively exercise the three labor rights. Ultimately, although a notice of non-recognition formally appears merely to remove the special protection under the Trade Union Act, in substance it results in an essential restriction of the three labor rights guaranteed by the Constitution.\\n\\nArticle 33(1) of the Constitution provides: “Workers shall have the right to independent association, collective bargaining, and collective action for the improvement of working conditions,” thereby guaranteeing the three labor rights as fundamental rights. The three labor rights are not rights that can be realized only through state intervention in the form of legislation, but rather specific rights that may directly operate as legal norms by virtue of the constitutional provision alone, even without legislation. This can also be understood in the same dimension as Article 1 of the Trade Union Act, which provides that “This Act aims to guarantee the rights of workers to association, collective bargaining, and collective action under the Constitution, thereby maintaining and improving working conditions and enhancing workers’ economic and social status, and by fairly adjusting labor relations and preventing and resolving labor disputes, contributes to the maintenance of industrial peace and the development of the national economy.” In particular, the right of association among the three labor rights is the concretization of freedom of association in the sphere of labor (see Constitutional Court, en banc decision of March 29, 2012, 2011HEONBA53, etc.), and thus has, historically and conceptually, the nature of a liberty right; therefore, “freedom from the state” rather than “freedom granted by the state” should be emphasized more.
