Even if notice of non-recognition were prescribed by statute, if it were drafted so as to require uniform issuance without any limitation merely because a disqualifying factor arose, the majority opinion would presumably regard that statute as unconstitutional.\\n\\nIn short, as long as the law defines the concept of a trade union, clearly prescribes its statutory requirements and disqualifying factors, and provides a system of establishment report to implement them, even if the legislature has abolished the trade union dissolution-order system and has not separately enacted statutory provisions on notice of non-recognition, notice of non-recognition may be issued as ex officio revocation or withdrawal of the acceptance of the establishment report for the trade union, provided that a disqualifying factor has arisen. However, because acceptance of a trade union’s establishment report is a beneficial administrative disposition, certain restrictions apply under the doctrine limiting ex officio revocation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative acts. The issue is not the “possibility” of notice, but its “propriety.” In other words, the issue is in what cases notice of non-recognition may be issued.\\n\\n4) Ultimately, regardless of the validity or invalidity of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, even if that provision did not exist, notice of non-recognition as a trade union could be issued in the sense of withdrawing acceptance of the trade union’s establishment report, according to current statutory provisions and general principles of administrative law. Therefore, the significance of regarding the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue as invalid, as in the majority opinion, is diminished or lost, and the dispute can be resolved only by substantively determining the legality of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue. From this perspective, it would be appropriate to interpret the nature of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue affirmatively, namely that it prescribes the post hoc withdrawal procedure for the beneficial administrative disposition of accepting a trade union’s establishment report and is therefore not invalid. In other words, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is based on the Statutory Provision at Issue that where a disqualifying factor exists it “shall not be deemed a trade union,” and should be understood as prescribing a procedural aggravating requirement that the administrative authority must go through a corrective demand before notifying non-recognition. Regarding the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue as invalid would only remove the corrective demand procedure and thereby produce a result more unfavorable to the trade union.\\n\\nIf the legal nature of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue is viewed as withdrawal of the acceptance of a trade union’s establishment report, the issue in this case shifts from whether the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is valid to whether the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue is lawful when comparing and balancing the public interest sought through notice of non-recognition with the disadvantages borne by the Plaintiff. Such comparison and balancing of public and private interests is expressed by the principle of proportionality, and it is self-evident that the principle of proportionality must be observed even when issuing the adverse disposition of notice of non-recognition at issue. Therefore, it cannot be said that the mere circumstance that the Plaintiff allows dismissed teachers to join as members immediately satisfies the requirements for notice of non-recognition. Ultimately, the lawfulness of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue must be determined by comprehensively considering various circumstances, including the number of dismissed teachers within the Plaintiff, the influence of those dismissed teachers on the Plaintiff’s activities, whether the Plaintiff’s acceptance of dismissed teachers as members contravenes the constitutional order or impairs the essence of a trade union, the public interest achieved through notice of non-recognition against the Plaintiff, and the disadvantages suffered by the Plaintiff due to such notice.\\n\\nB. Whether the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue Was Lawful\\n\\n1) The Constitution guarantees freedom of association and, in particular, workers’ right of association. The right of association, collective bargaining, and collective action that compose the three labor rights each have independent significance and operate organically as an integral whole while pursuing the common goal of maintaining and improving working conditions. The formation and operation of a trade union constitute the exercise of this right of association itself and serve as the practical foundation for the substantive guarantee of labor basic rights. Therefore, workers should be free to organize or join trade unions unless special circumstances exist, and the system of establishment report prescribed by the Trade Union Act must be understood and operated within the bounds that do not unduly infringe the constitutional meaning and function of such trade unions.\\n\\nExcessive restriction of the right of association of trade unions turns resistance against that point into the immediate main objective of the organization, brings ideologically faithful and militant people to leadership, and tends to radicalize all policy directions as well. When a powerful obstacle stands in sight, the diverse opinions of members disappear and all efforts are concentrated on removing that obstacle. In order to prevent an organization from being buried in ideology, it is necessary to eliminate the room in which ideological issues may become matters of dispute. Providing a place where rational opinions can stand also helps establish a culture of dialogue and discussion characterized by diversity and flexibility.\\n\\n2) Excluding dismissed persons from trade union membership is contrary to the following universal global standards.\\n\\nAdvanced countries and the international community allow dismissed persons to join trade unions and do not deny the status of the relevant trade union merely because dismissed persons are members. It is not easy to find, other than in our country, a legal system that compels a person who was until then a fellow member to be excluded from a trade union merely because he or she was dismissed by the employer. This directly contravenes the essence and spirit of trade unions. Such universal global standards may be temporarily resisted, but in a healthy society they are standards that will eventually be reached.\\n\\nThe International Labour Organization (ILO), as of June 2020, designates 8 conventions in 4 areas concerning the most fundamental labor rights out of a total of 190 conventions as “Fundamental Conventions” and strongly recommends their ratification and observance by all member states. Among them, the Convention Concerning Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise (Convention No. 87) provides in Article 2: “Workers and employers, without distinction whatsoever and without previous authorization, have the right to establish and, subject only to the rules of the organization concerned, to join organizations of their own choosing.” This establishes as an international labor standard the principle of universal guarantee of the right of association without any discrimination or prior governmental authorization.\\n\\nIn fact, on March 26, 2014, the 320th Governing Body of the International Labour Organization adopted the 371st report of the Committee on Freedom of Association, which contained recommendations concerning the South Korean Government’s violation of freedom of association. There, the Committee stated that “the prohibition on union membership by dismissed persons under item (d) of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act [Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue] violates freedom of association.” Furthermore, in its 382nd report of June 17, 2017, the Committee on Freedom of Association, directly in relation to this case, presented the same view and recommended that it “again strongly urges the Korean Government to take the necessary measures to repeal without delay the relevant provisions of law prohibiting dismissed persons from becoming members, and to provide detailed information thereon.”\\n\\nMeanwhile, the European Union (EU), based on the Free Trade Agreement between the Republic of Korea and the European Union and its Member States, which entered into force in 2011, has continuously raised issues concerning the South Korean Government’s protection of labor fundamental rights, including by initiating dispute-settlement procedures on the ground that Korea’s efforts to ratify the ILO fundamental conventions are insufficient. More recently, on July 4, 2019, the European Union formally requested the South Korean Government to convene a panel of experts pursuant to Article 14(1) of Chapter 13 (Trade and Sustainable Development) of the said Free Trade Agreement, asserting that the South Korean Government violated the free trade agreement by infringing labor fundamental rights, and one of the principal violations cited was “denying the status of the relevant trade union because dismissed persons are members under item (d) of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act [Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue].”\\n\\nSince joining the International Labour Organization in 1991, Korea has ratified conventions in stages, taking into account their relationship with domestic law, but has still not ratified four conventions among the above 8 fundamental conventions, namely those concerning freedom of association and prohibition of forced labor (Nos. 29, 87, 98, and 105). However, on May 22, 2019, the Government (competent ministry: Ministry of Employment and Labor) announced that it would commence ratification procedures for 3 of those 4 conventions, including Convention No. 87, and follow-up work is now under way. Furthermore, the Government submitted to the 20th National Assembly a bill to amend the relevant laws to recognize trade union membership by unemployed and dismissed persons, and has again submitted a similar amendment bill to the 21st National Assembly.\\n\\n3) Based on the foregoing, the concrete circumstances of this case are as follows.\\n\\nMembership by dismissed teachers is a matter that, in light of the established international standards and the constitutional value of the right of association, should be recognized promptly through legislation and policy, not a matter to dismantle the very existence of a trade union through formal legal application. As related legislative and policy improvements are delayed, a solution must be sought through judicial determination in this case.\\n\\nThe dismissed teachers at issue in this case are 9 persons, a very small portion of the Plaintiff’s total membership of approximately 60,000, and there is no evidence that these 9 dismissed teachers influenced or are likely to influence the Plaintiff’s activities or autonomy. Rather, according to the record, among these 9 dismissed teachers, there appear to be none who are members of the Plaintiff’s main decision-making bodies, such as the delegates’ convention, central committee, or central executive committee. Meanwhile, the Plaintiff corresponds not to an enterprise-based trade union but to an industrial, occupational, or regional trade union. In the case of general workers who are not teachers, industrial, occupational, or regional trade unions may have dismissed persons as members (see Supreme Court Decision of February 27, 2004, 2001DU8568, etc.), because there is a need to guarantee the right of association in collective labor relations. In light of these circumstances, it is difficult to say that the Plaintiff’s having dismissed teachers as members contravenes the constitutional order or impairs the essence of a trade union.\\n\\nThe public interest achieved through the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue is also unclear. The Defendant refers to Article 31(6) of the Constitution, the principle of legal reservation regarding teachers’ status, and teachers’ status as servants of the whole people, and invokes the special morality and public trust required of teachers and teachers’ trade unions in light of the special nature of teachers’ status and the importance of their duties. Yet it is questionable whether excluding a trade union merely because existing members were dismissed truly accords with those values. On the other hand, the disadvantages suffered by the Plaintiff due to the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue are very substantial. Considering only what is explicitly prescribed in the Trade Union Act, a trade union that has received a notice of non-recognition can no longer use the designation “trade union” (Article 7(3)), cannot maintain corporate personality (Article 6), cannot apply to the Labor Relations Commission for adjustment of labor disputes or relief from unfair labor practices (Article 7(1)), and cannot be exempted from taxes (Article 8). In such circumstances, it goes without saying that the Plaintiff cannot properly function as a trade union. The Plaintiff should be regarded as having in substance lost the raison d’être and value of existence as a trade union by the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue.\\n\\nMeanwhile, with respect to the propriety of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue, although the notice-of-non-recognition system is clearly a system under current law, there is also room to consider whether this system is actually functioning and whether it has normative legitimacy. Even according to the Defendant’s position, it appears that the only notices of non-recognition actually issued by the Defendant until now were the notice dated October 20, 2009, to the Korean Government Employees’ Union and the notice dated October 24, 2013, at issue here. Yet considering that the notice-of-non-recognition system was introduced on April 15, 1988, on the ground that it would prevent trade unions lacking statutory requirements from existing (Presidential Decree No. 12429), the fact that there have been only two notices of non-recognition issued by the Defendant over more than 30 years suggests that the system has become defunct or has been applied arbitrarily and selectively. It appears that there are quite a few trade unions in our industry in which dismissed persons who are not incumbent workers maintain membership, and thus it cannot but be questioned whether the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue conforms to the principles of proportionality and equality.\\n\\n4) The Constitution aims for our people to build a free and cultural democratic welfare state and thereby contribute to lasting world peace and the common prosperity of humankind. To realize this constitutional ideal, the Framework Act on Education provides in Article 2 that “Education aims to enable all citizens, under the ideal of Hongik Ingan, to cultivate personality and acquire the qualities necessary for independent living and as democratic citizens, thereby enabling them to live a human life and contributing to the development of a democratic state and the realization of the ideal of common prosperity of humankind.” In particular, Article 6(1) provides that “Education shall be operated so as to fulfill its original purpose, and shall not be used as a means of propagating political, partisan, or personal bias.”\\n\\nYet today, education is centered on organized and institutionalized school education, and teachers carry out school education, which means that teachers have characteristics different from general workers who are employed by employers, provide labor, and receive wages and other consideration. Accordingly, the Teachers’ Trade Union Act prohibits all industrial action by teachers’ trade unions and their members (Article 8), prohibits all political activities by teachers’ trade unions (Article 3), and further broadly prohibits teachers’ political acts such as joining political parties and election campaigning under Article 51(1) of the Education Public Officials Act, Articles 78(1), 65 of the State Public Officials Act, Articles 55 and 58(1) of the Private School Act, Article 6 of the Political Parties Act, and Article 60(1) of the Public Official Election Act. Considering this current legal system, the activities of teachers’ trade unions are in practice limited to collective bargaining for the improvement of teachers’ working conditions, and the risk that politicization of teachers’ trade unions or resulting impairment of the public nature of education or the people’s right to receive education will occur is already blocked.\\n\\nIn light of these points, the issue of the lawfulness of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue, based on membership by dismissed teachers, should not be shifted to, or judged primarily by, questions of the importance of education or the special status of teachers. Our legal system is sufficiently institutionalized so that teachers’ trade unions do not run counter to the interests of the people as a whole, and our society is sufficiently resilient to accommodate membership by dismissed teachers in teachers’ trade unions.\\n\\n5) It is not something to encourage violation of law. Naturally, as long as positive law exists, it must be observed, and sanctions imposed on those who violate it are proper. However, if the sanction exceeds an appropriate level and restricts the organization’s very right of association, that is a different matter. Law is always lawful, but that does not mean it is valid in itself. Law cannot be self-purpose; its validity must be tested. Moreover, law cannot be eternal. There are cases where law is wrong from the beginning, and there are also cases where it becomes wrong over time as circumstances change.\\n\\nThe people have the freedom to express opposition to irrational statutes or systems. While one may file a petition for repeal or bring litigation seeking repeal for such improvement, it is not uncommon for mistaken law to be corrected in the process of disputing responsibility for a legal violation that occurs during that process.\\n\\nIn this case as well, the Plaintiff may be seen as not correcting the Supplementary Provision at Issue and not excluding the 9 dismissed teachers as a form of protest against an unjust trade union legal system. If the Plaintiff had merely wished to avoid the immediate sanction, it could have formally amended the bylaws or temporarily excluded the dismissed teachers. However, the Plaintiff did not do so. Rather, the Plaintiff has insisted on the value of trade unions and the improvement of the related legal system while bearing severe disadvantages not only in the action challenging the corrective order but also in this case. The Plaintiff is asserting “law,” not merely “statute.” In such a case, rather than denying the existence of the organization on that basis, the situation can be corrected through appropriate legal sanctions for the conduct at issue. Even if the issue in education, which greatly affects the lives of future generations, is the radical tendency or ideological bias of teachers’ organizations, it is desirable to find the proper course through the free marketplace of ideas and on the basis of the sound common sense and balance of the people, and I do not think it is a matter to be solved by restricting the right of association of the organization. Judicial determination should aim to resolve disputes and conflicts and achieve social integration through legal peace.\\n\\nC. Conclusion\\n\\nBecause a notice of non-recognition as a trade union means ex officio revocation or withdrawal of the acceptance of a trade union’s establishment report, the lawfulness of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue must be determined regardless of the validity of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue. In other words, one must examine whether the Plaintiff’s unlawful conduct is truly of a degree sufficient to deprive it of its status as a trade union. The core issue in this case lies here, and the normative significance of the judgment in this case can also be found here.\\n\\nThe Constitution guarantees workers’ right of association as a fundamental right. Trade unions are the basic foundation for the exercise of the three labor rights, and dismissed persons, unless they themselves become employers, cannot escape worker status and thus need the guarantee of the three labor rights. In the world, both currently and historically, it is difficult to find a legal system that excludes dismissed persons from trade unions. Allowing dismissed persons to join trade unions has already become a settled standard in the international community, and Korea is also moving in the same direction. Then the question in this case is how to evaluate the Plaintiff’s maintaining the membership status of dismissed teachers, notwithstanding Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue.\\n\\nIn this case, there is an opinion worthy of hearing that the notice of non-recognition issued against the Plaintiff, which has clearly violated the law and refused even the corrective order and corrective demand regarding that violation, is lawful and cannot be deemed unlawful simply because notice of non-recognition corresponds to withdrawal of the acceptance of the trade union’s establishment report. However, as noted above, the universal global standard has settled on allowing dismissed teachers to join teachers’ trade unions. This shows that, even considering the importance of education and the special status of teachers, there is no inevitable reason to disallow dismissed teachers from joining teachers’ trade unions. The fact that the Plaintiff accepts dismissed teachers as members does not by itself warrant depriving the Plaintiff of its very legal status as a trade union. The legitimacy of the Plaintiff as a trade union is a matter to be evaluated according to its activities, not according to whether dismissed teachers are members.\\n\\nIn short, the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue is unlawful not because the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is invalid, but because it is excessive in relation to the Plaintiff’s unlawful conduct. Therefore, the judgment of the court below, which held the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue lawful on a different premise, contains error affecting the judgment by misunderstanding the doctrine on limitations on withdrawal of beneficial administrative dispositions. The judgment below should be reversed.\\n\\nI also express a separate opinion because, although the conclusion that the judgment below should be reversed is the same as the majority opinion, the reason for reversal differs.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Lee Gitaek and Lee Dongwon\\n\\nA. On the Propriety of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue (Grounds for Appeal Nos. 1 and 2)\\n\\nThe main text of Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue, which applies to teachers’ trade unions pursuant to Article 14(1) of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, provides that if membership by persons who are not workers is allowed, it “shall not be deemed a trade union.” The Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue provides that, in such a case, the administrative authority shall demand correction and, if the trade union fails to comply within the period, “shall notify that it is not to be deemed a trade union.”\\n\\nWith respect to these provisions, the majority opinion states that a notice of non-recognition as a trade union deprives or restricts the legal protection afforded to a trade union already lawfully established, and that as a rule such matters must be prescribed by statute and, to be prescribed by administrative legislation, there must be an explicit and specific delegation by statute. However, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is invalid because it prescribes a notice of non-recognition as a trade union, which was not provided by statute, without statutory delegation; and the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue, based on that invalid provision, is unlawful.\\n\\nHowever, according to the above provisions, even a trade union whose establishment report has already been accepted can no longer be regarded as a trade union if it allows persons who are not workers to join, and unless such situation is corrected, the administrative authority must notify that it shall not be deemed a trade union. There is no room to interpret these clear and unambiguous statutes and regulations differently. In this case, from the time of the establishment report, the Plaintiff had, through its bylaws, fully allowed dismissed teachers to join as members; thus it falls under the main text of Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue, and it did not comply with the Defendant’s corrective demand in this regard. Accordingly, the Defendant’s notice of non-recognition to the Plaintiff pursuant to the above provisions is lawful. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) Law is a universal and valid norm of society that has the same binding force upon an unspecified and numerous public; therefore, in interpreting it, one must clarify the standard meaning of the law so that it has objective validity, and must maintain coherence insofar as possible so that legal stability is not undermined by achieving consistency acceptable to all. Even if one employs systematic and logical methods of interpretation taking into account the legislative intent and purpose, legislative history, harmony with the legal order as a whole, and relations with other statutes, the rule is that interpretation should remain faithful as far as possible to the ordinary meaning of the wording used in the statute, and if the statutory wording itself is composed of relatively clear concepts, other interpretive methods are in principle unnecessary or must be limited (see Supreme Court Decision of April 23, 2009, 2006DA81035; en banc Supreme Court Decision of January 17, 2013, 2011DA83431, etc.).\\n\\nArticle 75 of the Constitution provides: “The President may issue presidential decrees concerning matters delegated to him or her specifically by Act, and matters necessary to enforce Acts.” The purport is not that every presidential decree requires delegation by statute, but that the President may enact presidential decrees concerning specific methods, procedures, and other details for enforcing the law, except for matters that the Constitution requires to be regulated only by law, such as restrictions on the fundamental rights of the people (see Supreme Court Decision of January 11, 2007, 2004DU10432, etc.). An enforcement decree or enforcement rule may not, absent delegation by statute, alter or supplement contents concerning individual rights and duties or determine new matters not prescribed by the statute; however, if the contents of the enforcement decree or rule merely specify what is interpretively possible under the parent Act, when the legislative purpose of the parent Act and the entire related provisions are viewed organically and systematically, or if it merely concretizes the purport of the parent Act, it cannot be regarded as going beyond the scope of regulation of the parent Act, and thus cannot be deemed invalid merely because there is no direct delegation provision in the parent Act (see Supreme Court Decision of August 20, 2014, 2012DU19526; en banc Supreme Court Decision of February 16, 2017, 2015DO16014, etc.).\\n\\n2) The main text of Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act defines a “trade union” as “an organization or federation thereof organized by workers as the principal body, autonomously united for the purpose of maintaining and improving working conditions and enhancing workers’ economic and social status.” The Trade Union Act, while expressly stating that workers are the subject of a trade union as above, separately defines workers in Article 2(1) as persons who live on wages, salary, or other equivalent income regardless of occupation. Accordingly, a worker under the Trade Union Act means a person engaged in labor while being in a subordinate employment relationship with an employer and living on wages, etc. in return, and as long as there is such subordinate relationship with an employer, the form of the labor supply contract may be employment, contract for work, mandate, or a nameless contract and is immaterial (see Supreme Court Decision of June 13, 2019, 2019DU33712, etc.), but persons who are not workers under the Trade Union Act cannot organize a lawful trade union as prescribed by the Act (see Supreme Court Decision of May 26, 1992, 90NU9438, etc.).\\n\\nFurthermore, the phrase “an organization organized autonomously” as used in the main text of Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act means that, internally, workers must organize it by their own will and, externally, interference or intervention by the employer or any third party must be excluded in its operation. In this regard, the Statutory Provision at Issue enumerates “cases where participation by the employer or a person always acting on behalf of his or her interests is allowed [(a)],” “cases where the main part of expenses is assisted by the employer [(b)],” and “cases where membership by persons who are not workers is allowed [(d), main text],” and provides that such organizations shall not be deemed trade unions under the Trade Union Act.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 5 of the Trade Union Act permits workers to organize and join trade unions freely in the main text, but its proviso provides that matters concerning public officials and teachers shall be separately prescribed by law. Accordingly, the Teachers’ Trade Union Act prescribes matters concerning the establishment of teachers’ trade unions and special rules concerning the Trade Union Act as applied to teachers, and defines “teacher” in Article 2. This both sets the scope of teachers to whom the Teachers’ Trade Union Act applies and constitutes a mandatory provision limiting the organizers and membership qualifications of teachers’ trade unions. Therefore, teachers who may become members of teachers’ trade unions are limited in practice to those who are currently working as teachers or who have been dismissed but have filed an application for relief from unfair labor practice with the Labor Relations Commission and are before a re-hearing decision by the National Labor Relations Commission (see Supreme Court Decision of April 10, 2014, 2011DU6998; Supreme Court Decision of January 14, 2016, 2012DO10066, etc.), and no one else may become a member of a teachers’ trade union. If a teachers’ trade union allows persons without membership qualification as above to join, it falls under “allowing persons who are not workers to join” in the main text of Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue. Whether to limit “teachers” under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, as a rule, to teachers currently in office, or to open membership broadly even to holders of teaching credentials not yet appointed as teachers or dismissed teachers, may ultimately be a matter of legislative policy; but as seen above, current law clearly adopts the position of granting membership qualifications only to “teachers currently in office,” who have a direct and substantive interest in the activities of teachers’ trade unions. This aims to prevent non-teachers from interfering in the decision-making process of teachers’ trade unions and thereby affecting incumbent teachers’ working conditions and impairing the autonomy of teachers’ trade unions. Therefore, at least at present, in interpreting and applying this provision, “dismissed teachers” should be regarded as “third parties” who, if allowed to join, may rather impair the autonomy of teachers’ trade unions through improper interference or intervention.\\n\\n3) The Statutory Provision at Issue provides that where a statutory disqualifying factor exists, it “shall not be deemed a trade union,” and in the main text of Item (d) cites “allowing persons who are not workers to join.” Here, “shall not be deemed a trade union” means that it is to be regarded as not being a trade union. A statutory provision that says “shall be deemed” generally means a legal fiction that, unlike a presumption, does not permit rebuttal, or at least means that the provision directly has external effect. Accordingly, a trade union that allows membership by persons who are not workers can no longer be a trade union under the Trade Union Act, despite its name, and is merely what is called a “non-statutory trade union.” Even if the administrative authority overlooked this and accepted the establishment report, the legal effect arises and is maintained that it is deemed not to have been a trade union from the outset under the Statutory Provision at Issue; conversely, if after the establishment report has been accepted, membership by persons who are not workers is allowed, the effect of being deemed not to be a trade union arises post hoc and the status as a trade union under the Trade Union Act should be regarded as having been lost around that time. Such effect is based not on the fact that the Statutory Provision at Issue is a “definitional provision,” but on the fact that it is a “deeming provision.” In other words, where the requirements under the Statutory Provision at Issue are met, the resulting legal relationship is formed immediately, and this is the meaning of a deeming provision. The fact that the Statutory Provision at Issue is a definitional provision does not alter that deeming effect.\\n\\nWhat reinforces the view that the Statutory Provision at Issue should be understood as having direct external effect is that the proviso portion is connected with the main text portion of the same item to effectively prevent the loss of the workers’ status as the subject of the trade union or the loss of autonomy by the trade union. If a trade union falls under “cases where participation by the employer or a person always acting on behalf of his or her interests is allowed [(a)]” or “cases where the main part of expenses is assisted by the employer [(b)]”, then it has seriously lacked autonomy, an essential requirement for becoming a trade union under the Trade Union Act, and should not be granted the status of a statutory trade union; nor should it be viewed differently merely because its establishment report has already been accepted by the administrative authority. The interpretation derived in such cases under items (a) or (b) of the Statutory Provision at Issue should equally apply to main text item (d), “cases where persons who are not workers are allowed to join.” As noted above, item (d), like items (a) and (b), is designed to prevent a non-worker third party from impairing the autonomy of the trade union through improper interference or intervention. The Supreme Court’s holding in Decision of October 14, 1997, 96NU9829, that where the establishment report of an unqualified trade union is accepted, the company concerned lacks standing to contest the acceptance disposition itself in an administrative appeal action, but where the trade union that received the certificate of report specifically participates in a procedure permitted by law, such as filing an application for relief from unfair labor practice, it may directly assert and contest the lack of qualification of the trade union in that procedure, can also be understood in the same context.\\n\\nFurthermore, the Trade Union Act clearly states that protection under the Act is limited to “trade unions established under the Trade Union Act” (Articles 7(1) and 7(3)), and: ① the administrative authority shall, where an establishment report or bylaws require supplementation because of omissions in required entries, etc., demand supplementation within a period not exceeding 20 days as prescribed by Presidential Decree (Article 12(2)); ② it requires the administrative authority to reject the establishment report of an organization with a disqualifying factor under each item of the proviso to Article 2(4) (Article 12(3) item 1); ③ where the bylaws of a trade union violate labor-related statutes and regulations, the administrative authority may, with the resolution of the Labor Relations Commission, order correction thereof (Article 21(1)); a trade union subject to such corrective order shall in principle comply within 30 days (Article 21(3)), and where it violates this, a fine not exceeding 5 million won shall be imposed (Article 93 item 2). Thus, under the Trade Union Act, the administrative authority must reject the establishment report of an organization with a disqualifying factor and may order correction of a trade union with a disqualifying factor. Pursuant to the delegation in Article 12(2) of the Trade Union Act, Article 9(1) item 1 of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act provides as one of the grounds for demanding supplementation of a trade union’s establishment report that “the bylaws are not attached to the establishment report, or there are omissions or false statements in the establishment report or bylaws.” And among the words of Article 9(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act, which is the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, the part up to “the administrative authority shall demand correction by specifying a period of 30 days where a ground for rejection of the establishment report corresponding to Article 12(3) item 1 of the Act arises after the trade union has been issued a certificate of report” is either a verbatim repetition or an exact continuation of the contents of Article 12(3) item 1 and Article 21(1) and (3) of the Trade Union Act above.\\n\\nConsidering the contents and structure of these related provisions together, the Trade Union Act clearly states that persons who are not workers cannot be allowed to join in the case of trade unions already in operation after acceptance of their establishment reports, just as at the establishment stage. Therefore, in order to become a trade union under the Trade Union Act, one must satisfy the statutory requirements not only at the time of establishment but also after establishment, and there is no doubt that even a trade union that has already completed establishment report is no longer a lawful trade union once it allows persons who are not workers to join. In such a case, as in the above Supreme Court Decision 96NU9829, the administrative authority may not treat a group allowing persons who are not workers to join as a trade union; rather, treating it as a trade union is unlawful.\\n\\n4) Thus, the effect that it cannot be regarded as a trade union when membership by persons who are not workers is allowed is afforded by the Statutory Provision at Issue itself, namely the provision that it “shall not be deemed a trade union.”\\n\\nHowever, although the statutory provision is very clear in this regard, it may not be clear which specific trade union is currently a non-statutory trade union, when and for what reason it became a non-statutory trade union, etc., and this may create unnecessary confusion not only for the trade union itself but also for related interested parties. Therefore, the need arises for the administrative authority responsible for treating a trade union with a disqualifying factor as no longer a lawful trade union to issue a notice of non-recognition in order to clarify the relevant legal relations more clearly, and the provision concerning this is precisely the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue. In other words, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is a very natural executive order concerning the specific method and procedure for realizing the effect of becoming a non-statutory trade union under the Trade Union Act.\\n\\nHowever, the Trade Union Act and the Enforcement Decree not only provide a corrective order system for unlawful bylaws, etc., but also prescribe a corrective demand procedure regarding unlawful bylaws, etc., before a notice of non-recognition as a trade union is issued. This, too, can be seen as reasonable in the sense that it gives the administrative authority an opportunity to afford a trade union with a disqualifying factor an opportunity for autonomous correction to return to a lawful trade union. Therefore, if despite such an opportunity for correction the unlawful state persists without correction, the effect under the Statutory Provision at Issue is finally and definitively triggered, and at that time it is natural that not only interested parties such as the company concerned but also the administrative authority may take the position that the trade union with a disqualifying factor is no longer given protection under the Trade Union Act. In other words, a trade union with a statutory disqualifying factor becomes a non-statutory trade union under the provision that it “shall not be deemed a trade union,” but such effect remains abstract and potential while the procedures of corrective order and corrective demand are pending, and only becomes concrete and definitive when the trade union fails to comply with the corrective order and corrective demand regarding the disqualifying factor. The administrative authority then issues a notice of non-recognition to the trade union that has become a non-statutory trade union, indicating that it shall no longer be regarded as a trade union under the Trade Union Act.\\n\\nViewed this way, the part of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue stating that “if it is not complied with within that period, the administrative authority shall notify the relevant trade union that it shall not be deemed a trade union under the Trade Union Act” cannot be said to be contrary to the Trade Union Act or invalid, even though no specific delegation was made by the parent Act. As already noted above, although it is in principle true that an enforcement decree cannot, absent delegation by the parent Act, alter or supplement matters concerning individual rights and duties or determine new matters not prescribed by the parent Act, an enforcement decree may also prescribe matters necessary to execute the parent Act, and therefore it is not subject to the above limitation if it does not directly alter or supplement matters concerning individual rights and duties. Accordingly, it is fully permissible to provide regulations as necessary matters or guidelines for implementing the parent Act, so long as they do not go beyond the scope of the parent Act, and if the contents of the enforcement decree merely specify what is interpretively possible under the parent Act, when the legislative purpose of the parent Act and all related provisions are examined organically and systematically, or if they merely concretize the purport of the parent Act, they cannot be regarded as going beyond the scope of regulation of the parent Act.\\n\\nSpecifically, in light of the contents and structure of the related provisions seen above in section 3), when the administrative authority demands correction, etc. from a trade union with a statutory disqualifying factor but the trade union still fails to correct the defect, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, by requiring the administrative authority to notify that it shall not be deemed a lawful trade union under the Statutory Provision at Issue, merely forms part of the measures by which the legal effect that the trade union shall not be deemed a trade union under the Statutory Provision at Issue has already arisen and the administrative authority has adopted such position, is officially communicated. This is necessary not only for effective organization and management of trade unions by the administrative authority but also desirable from the standpoint of protecting and fostering trade unions so that they may continue to exist as organizations with autonomy and democracy. If it were held that the administrative authority, after a duly reported organization falls under a disqualifying factor under the items of the Statutory Provision at Issue and thus contravenes the essence of a trade union or lacks autonomy and democracy as a trade union, can do nothing beyond issuing a corrective order or corrective demand, then the law would be unable to prevent the proliferation of organizations that do not deserve and should not receive legal protection under the Trade Union Act yet nonetheless claim to be trade unions. Therefore, even though the Trade Union Act does not contain an explicit delegation to prescribe notice of non-recognition by enforcement decree, there is no reason why the administrative authority should be prohibited from announcing the fact that the effect under the above provision has arisen so that the statutory effect arising under the Statutory Provision at Issue can be implemented in reality, and the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue may be seen as having been prepared for precisely this purpose.\\n\\nHowever, the majority opinion states that the Statutory Provision at Issue is merely a criterion for determining a lawful trade union, and therefore the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, by prescribing notice of non-recognition, newly regulates a matter not prescribed or delegated by law and is invalid. Yet, as seen above, the Statutory Provision at Issue prescribes that where there is a disqualifying factor, it is not a lawful trade union, and thus it is a complete provision specifying both requirements and effects in itself. Therefore, notifying a trade union that has become non-statutory under such legal provision is nothing new and does not require special delegation. Nevertheless, the majority opinion assumes as if there were some defect or gap in the Statutory Provision at Issue and, on that basis, concludes that the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is an entirely new regulation lacking a legal basis or statutory delegation. This stance either overlooks that the Statutory Provision at Issue is complete in itself or is merely a convenient interpretive approach that arbitrarily narrows the meaning of the legal provision to reach the conclusion that the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue is invalid.\\n\\n5) Meanwhile, under Article 12(1) of the Trade Union Act, the administrative authority shall, when it receives an establishment report, issue a certificate of report within 3 days, except where supplementation is necessary because of omissions in entries in the establishment report or bylaws or where the organization to be established has a statutory disqualifying factor. Accordingly, even if a trade union receives a notice of non-recognition, if it corrects the disqualifying factor and files a new establishment report, it may restore its status as a lawful trade union within at most 3 days. In general, a disposition revoking a beneficial administrative act, such as revocation of a building permit, takes effect only upon the revocation disposition, and because the effect of the disposition is final, even if the addressee removes the reason for the disposition, one cannot be assured that the same beneficial disposition will be received again, and thus irreparable damage may be caused to the addressee. However, in the case of notice of non-recognition as a trade union, the effect that it shall no longer be deemed a trade union under the Statutory Provision at Issue has already arisen as a matter of fact, and the notice merely informs the organization that it cannot be recognized as a lawful trade union until its bylaws and organization are brought into conformity with the law, thereby urging it to return to legality; thus, it has characteristics different from an ordinary revocation of a beneficial administrative act, and the same applies to withdrawal. Taking these circumstances into account, it is not appropriate to be captivated by the view that a notice of non-recognition has an adverse nature and therefore should be avoided as much as possible. This is also so, as noted above, even if a trade union falls under “cases where participation by the employer or a person always acting on behalf of his or her interests is allowed [(a)]” or “cases where the main part of expenses is assisted by the employer [(b)]” among the items of the Statutory Provision at Issue, for in such a case the administrative authority should naturally take positive measures to notify that the body is a non-statutory trade union because it lacks autonomy and democracy as a trade union.\\n\\nThe adverse aspect of a notice of non-recognition under the Trade Union Act arises from the self-contradiction that a body which lacks not only the requirements of the Trade Union Act but also the administrative authority’s corrective order and corrective demand concerning them and thus has become an entity not deemed a trade union under the Statutory Provision at Issue is nonetheless refusing to return to a lawful trade union by satisfying the legal requirements anew, even though the path to recovery as a lawful trade union remains open. In other words, the issue is not one to be reframed as how to protect citizens from adverse administrative dispositions; rather, it is an issue arising because such a body makes a contradictory demand that it be treated as a trade union under the Trade Union Act as if the Statutory Provision at Issue did not exist, merely to selectively receive legal protection under the Act.\\n\\n6) As noted above, the Plaintiff became a non-statutory trade union under the Statutory Provision at Issue, not because of the notice of non-recognition under the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, and thus no special significance should be attached to the notice of non-recognition itself. Even if viewed differently, however, the notice of non-recognition issued by the Defendant against the Plaintiff can be regarded as lawful.\\n\\nAs is well known, the administrative authority that issued an administrative act may revoke it on its own even without a separate legal basis if the disposition is defective, and even if there was no particular defect at the time of the disposition and no separate legal basis for withdrawal after the disposition, it may withdraw it as a separate administrative act causing it to lose effect if there is a change in circumstances making it unnecessary to maintain the original disposition or if a significant public interest need arises. However, if the original administrative act was beneficial, there may be cases where such revocation or withdrawal is not permitted under the doctrine limiting revocation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative dispositions (see Supreme Court Decision of February 25, 1986, 85NU664; Supreme Court Decision of November 26, 2004, 2003DU10251, 10268, etc.).\\n\\nAcceptance of a trade union’s establishment report broadly corresponds to a beneficial administrative disposition that recognizes a trade union satisfying the establishment requirements prescribed in Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act as a statutory trade union, thereby granting the legal status to enjoy the rights and benefits prescribed by the Trade Union Act. Therefore, absent special grounds for limitation, the Defendant may issue a notice of non-recognition as a trade union in the sense of withdrawing post hoc the acceptance of a trade union’s establishment report, even without a separate regulatory provision under statute, and the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue may be understood as merely a precautionary and confirmatory statement of the withdrawing authority of the administrative authority, which naturally follows under the general principles of administrative law. This is consonant with the fact that Article 12(3) item 1 of the Trade Union Act provides that if, after reviewing whether a group submitting an establishment report falls under each item of the Statutory Provision at Issue, it is found to do so, the administrative authority shall reject the establishment report.\\n\\nThe purpose of the above provision is to prevent the proliferation of trade unions that lack substantive requirements as trade unions, thereby guaranteeing the workers’ independent and democratic exercise of the right of association. Accordingly, the administrative authority is given the authority to substantively examine whether the relevant organization falls under each item of the Statutory Provision at Issue (see Supreme Court Decision of April 10, 2014, 2011DU6998, etc.; however, according to the above Supreme Court Decision 2011DU6998, the substantive examination authority at the establishment report stage is not absolute but limited in part). Such substantive examination authority remains reserved to the administrative authority even after the establishment report has been accepted, as provided in Article 21 of the Trade Union Act, and the administrative authority may, as a result of such examination, take measures to return the trade union to a lawful state by issuing a corrective order, etc., against a trade union that has come to fall under a disqualifying factor of each item of the Statutory Provision at Issue. If such a trade union ultimately refuses to return to a lawful trade union, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, requiring the administrative authority to issue notice of non-recognition, merely describes the actual implementation of the above substantive examination authority possessed by the administrative authority.\\n\\nThis is so even when one normatively compares and evaluates the situations before and after the administrative authority accepts the establishment report of a disqualified organization as a trade union. If, in the course of substantively examining after receiving an establishment report whether the organization falls under each item of the Statutory Provision at Issue, the administrative authority discovers a disqualifying factor under one item and, because supplementation is not finally achieved, rejects the establishment report or refuses acceptance, such action is lawful based on Article 12 of the Trade Union Act above, and therefore the organization whose establishment report was refused will not be granted the legal effect of legal protection under the Trade Union Act or the status of a so-called lawful union. However, if in the same situation the administrative authority failed to discover the disqualifying factor and accepted the establishment report, but immediately thereafter discovered the disqualifying factor and, through the procedures prescribed in the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, issued a notice of non-recognition as a trade union, this is in substance the same situation as where the disqualifying factor was discovered before acceptance of the establishment report. Thus, it should be regarded as a lawful and appropriate measure to obtain a balanced result. By contrast, merely because the establishment report was accepted, it is not proper to set a far stricter standard of judicial review on the view that the substance of the organization changed and became materially different from its pre-acceptance nature, or that special legal protection must be given. Even if one accords significant meaning to the acceptance of the establishment report itself and recognizes the need to protect the organization’s vested rights or trust in that acceptance, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue does not permit immediate notice of non-recognition as soon as a disqualifying factor is found; instead, it specifies that a 30-day period must be set for corrective demand and that a notice of non-recognition shall be issued only if correction is not effected within that period. Therefore, even before notice of non-recognition, these measures alone should be deemed sufficient procedural safeguards to protect the organization’s vested rights or prior trust.\\n\\nMoreover, when revoking a beneficial administrative disposition, if the defect in the disposition arises from the party’s concealment of facts or other fraudulent acts in the application, the party is deemed to have known that the benefit obtained by the disposition was unlawfully acquired and thus could foresee the possibility of revocation; accordingly, the party cannot invoke the benefits of reliance, and the administrative authority does not commit an abuse or deviation of discretion by failing to consider such reliance (see Supreme Court Decision of April 12, 1991, 90NU9520, etc.). According to the facts found by the court below, the Plaintiff, at the time of establishment report, had bylaws allowing membership by dismissed teachers, yet submitted to the establishment report false bylaws from which such content had been deleted, thereby obtaining acceptance of the establishment report; thereafter, even though the Defendant confirmed this and issued corrective orders and corrective demands, the Plaintiff refused to comply. The record also shows that the Plaintiff has clearly indicated it has no intention in the future of satisfying the requirements for a trade union prescribed by the Trade Union Act. In other words, the Plaintiff from the outset did not satisfy the statutory requirements for a trade union, intentionally deceived the administrative authority into accepting its establishment report, received two corrective orders and one corrective demand because of that issue, refused correction, and has no intention of correcting it in the future. Considering these circumstances, the Plaintiff cannot contend that the grounds for disposition of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue impair its trust in the administration or legal stability. Rather, where the original establishment report was made from the outset by false or wrongful means, the administrative authority that later discovers this must, according to the wording of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, necessarily issue a notice of non-recognition, and even after such notice, the organization may at any time recover as a lawful trade union if it satisfies the statutory requirements; thus there is no room from the outset for discussion of the limitations on revocation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative acts or abuse or deviation of discretion.\\n\\nJustice Ahn Chulsang’s separate opinion is worth hearing as a legislative discussion from the standpoint that the notice-of-non-recognition system should not be abused, but it cannot be accepted as an interpretation of current law. The Statutory Provision at Issue does not provide an exception permitting recognition as a lawful trade union despite a disqualifying factor. Accordingly, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue provides an opportunity for correction but states that a trade union that does not comply “shall” be notified as a non-statutory trade union. Notice of non-recognition against a trade union with a disqualifying factor is inevitable unless there is a problem with the underlying corrective order or corrective demand. In this case, the lawfulness of the First Corrective Order was affirmed by a final Supreme Court judgment in the administrative litigation contesting it (Seoul Administrative Court Judgment of November 5, 2010, 2010GUHAP27110; Seoul High Court Judgment of September 9, 2011, 2010NU43725; Supreme Court Decision of January 12, 2012, 2011DU24231), and a final criminal conviction regarding noncompliance with that First Corrective Order was also affirmed by the Supreme Court (Seoul Southern District Court Judgment of December 1, 2011, 2011GODAN131; Seoul Southern District Court Judgment of July 26, 2012, 2011NO1798; Supreme Court Decision of January 14, 2016, 2012DO10066). In the constitutional complaint filed immediately after the Request for Correction at issue, the Constitutional Court held constitutional Article 2 of the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, which limits the scope of teachers to whom the Act applies to teachers currently employed in elementary and secondary schools, on the grounds that it does not infringe the right of association of the petitioner Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union and dismissed teachers (Constitutional Court en banc decision of May 28, 2015, 2013HEONMA671, etc.). In other words, it has already been repeatedly confirmed that the Plaintiff’s allowing dismissed teachers to join as members is unlawful. Allowing the Plaintiff’s claim of vested rights in these circumstances would mean abandoning regulation under current law.\\n\\n7) The grounds for disposition in this case are that the Plaintiff has bylaws allowing membership by dismissed teachers, that in fact 9 dismissed teachers are active as members of the Plaintiff, and that the Defendant, the administrative authority, demanded correction but the Plaintiff refused.\\n\\nFirst, at the time of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue, the fact that 9 dismissed teachers were active as members of the Plaintiff was undeniable, and since the Plaintiff also does not deny this, this alone is sufficient to uphold the lawfulness of the Notice of Non-Recognition at Issue.\\n\\nMoreover, the Plaintiff has formalized the above membership by dismissed teachers through the Supplementary Provision at Issue, that is, through its bylaws. Articles of incorporation or bylaws are the most basic and important basis for the establishment, existence, and activities of an organization, and are essential matters that identify its identity and maintain its character. The Plaintiff expressly allows membership by dismissed teachers in these very bylaws. Moreover, this is not merely a past or temporary matter, but an indication of an intention to continue allowing dismissed teachers to join as members in the future as well. It is a violation of law for a trade union to allow persons who are not workers to join and to act as members. If such a situation arises not temporarily due to a mere business error or the like, but pursuant to the express decision of the trade union, then such a trade union has itself abandoned being a trade union under the law. It is contradictory to say, with regard to one law, that one will not satisfy the requirements it prescribes but will still enjoy only the effects of that law. This is not merely a matter concerning the Trade Union Act. It is the same under every law, whether public law or private law, substantive law or procedural law. For example, one cannot accept the argument that one will not install the essential facilities required by the Medical Service Act but should nevertheless be granted the status of a hospital under the Medical Service Act. A legal order that permits such contradictory positions cannot exist in the first place.\\n\\nAgain, in this case the Plaintiff did not merely passively tolerate the membership of dismissed teachers. Nor was there a temporary situation in which dismissed teachers were members contrary to the Plaintiff’s true intention. By means of its official bylaws, the Plaintiff expressly permitted membership by persons who are not teachers, directly violating the establishment requirements under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act. Despite the Defendant’s repeated corrective orders and the final court judgments affirming the lawfulness of those orders, the Plaintiff asserted that its maintenance of the unlawful bylaws was justified, and it clearly indicated that it has no intention in the future of correcting the issue of membership by persons who are not teachers. Yet the Plaintiff still demands the status and protection of a trade union under the Teachers’ Trade Union Act. Such contradictory claims have always been and must always be rejected. One cannot, under a law that the organization rejects, recognize as lawful an organization that lacks the statutory requirements, merely because it wants the legal status and protection given when those requirements are met.\\n\\nJustice Ahn Chulsang’s separate opinion may be valid as a general theory, but it is not appropriate as an interpretive theory in this case. The Trade Union Act and its Enforcement Decree explicitly deny worker status under the Trade Union Act to dismissed persons, while recognizing certain exceptions related to unfair dismissal and providing corrective-order and corrective-demand systems to prevent unexpected unjust results, thereby giving even a post hoc opportunity for correction. The situation arising despite such clear legislative intent and consideration is not, as assumed in that separate opinion, a “counterintuitive unjust result”; it is merely a situation in which the trade union is not complying with current law. No interpretation different from the text is necessary in this case. Even if one were to deem such interpretation necessary, the same conclusion as Justice Ahn Chulsang’s separate opinion can be reached by other means, such as interpreting the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue as one of binding force rather than discretion, relaxing the effect of “deeming” under the Statutory Provision at Issue, judging the main text of Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue by reference to whether the trade union’s “autonomy” is impaired, or limiting the “joining” of persons who are not workers to new membership only. Nevertheless, that separate opinion rejects all such interpretive possibilities as contrary to clear statutory wording and uniquely claims that an interpretation different from the wording is needed only with respect to maintaining membership by dismissed union members. This position is difficult to distinguish from arbitrary and selective interpretation of the law premised on a predetermined conclusion.\\n\\n8) The majority opinion criticizes the current notice-of-non-recognition system as reviving, by presidential decree, the former law’s trade union dissolution-order system.\\n\\nHowever, the former law that existed when the dissolution-order system was in place defined trade unions and provided that, in cases of disqualifying factors such as permitting membership by persons who are not workers, “this shall not apply to the following cases.” This is significantly different from the current law’s provision that “if any of the following applies, it shall not be deemed a trade union.” The phrase “this shall not apply” is more negative in nature and it is not clear whether it generates an affirmative legal effect, whereas “shall not be deemed a trade union” should be understood as itself conferring an affirmative legal effect.\\n\\nAlso, the grounds for a dissolution order for a trade union were “where it is recognized that the labor-related statutes and regulations are violated or public interest is likely to be harmed,” whereas [former Trade Union Act (prior to amendment by Act No. 3966 of November 28, 1987), Article 32] the grounds for notice of non-recognition are, as prescribed by the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue, “where a ground for rejection of the establishment report corresponding to Article 12(3) item 1 of the Act arises,” namely “where any of the items of the proviso to Article 2(4) of the Act applies,” and ultimately mean “where a disqualifying factor arises so that the organization shall not be deemed a trade union” (Article 9(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act; Article 12(3) item 1 and Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act). Thus, the trade union dissolution-order system allowed dissolution of a relevant trade union for any violation of law, without considering the nature or seriousness of the violation, and even merely because there was a risk of harming the public interest, whereas the notice-of-non-recognition system strictly limits the grounds for notice to cases where, under the definitional provisions of the Trade Union Act, the organization cannot be recognized as a trade union, that is, cases where the organization cannot even be a subject of the law from the outset.\\n\\nAdding to this the point seen above that notice of non-recognition does not cause a body to become non-statutory only by virtue of the notice but merely informs post hoc that it has already become non-statutory under the Trade Union Act, the former dissolution-order system created a risk that the administrative authority could arbitrarily and improperly deprive or infringe a lawful trade union of its status, whereas under the current notice-of-non-recognition system the administrative authority merely informs an organization that has ceased to qualify as a trade union under the Trade Union Act, through the prescribed procedures, so that the effect already arising under the law can be clearly recognized; there is no room whatsoever for such unfair arbitrariness.\\n\\nThe legislature abolished the trade union dissolution-order system in order to prevent unjust infringement of trade unions’ right of association, not to guarantee the permanent existence of unlawful trade unions. The fact that the dissolution-order system was abolished does not mean that notice of non-recognition against a trade union lacking statutory requirements is prohibited.\\n\\nConsidering these circumstances together, the current notice-of-non-recognition system is already inherent in the Trade Union Act as an indispensable device for securing the effectiveness of the definitional provisions concerning trade unions. It cannot be placed on the same plane as the former trade union dissolution-order system or dismissed as a system that the executive arbitrarily revived after abolition by the legislature.\\n\\n9) What we have examined thus far shows that if an organization satisfies the requirements prescribed by the Trade Union Act, it becomes a lawful trade union; if it does not satisfy those requirements, it becomes a non-statutory trade union; and this is a legal effect directly given by the Statutory Provision at Issue itself. The administrative authority must reject the establishment report of an organization that does not meet the statutory requirements, and if such circumstances are discovered after the establishment report has already been accepted, it must induce correction through a corrective order and criminal punishment for noncompliance, and if correction still is not made, it must issue a notice of non-recognition through the corrective-demand procedure.\\n\\nThis is different from a situation where the law imposes a certain obligation but is silent on how to respond to its violation. The Trade Union Act and its Enforcement Decree clearly prescribe the effect of violation by providing that where the requirements for a trade union are not satisfied, “it shall not be deemed a trade union,” and further ensure the realization of that legal effect by prescribing rejection of establishment reports and notice of non-recognition.\\n\\nThus, there is absolutely no defect in this legal system. On the contrary, viewed from the statutory framework itself, the provision is complete and without any problem. Nevertheless, the majority opinion starts by assuming as a fundamental premise that there is a defect in this otherwise complete legal system. However, this case is not a constitutional review of a statute, nor does it concern legislative theory. In this case, only adjudication is at issue. The court need only interpret and apply the complete legal system as it stands and grant the resulting legal effects when the requirements are met. The majority opinion needlessly makes the issue more complicated. If one believes the law lacks legitimacy, one should request a constitutional review from the Constitutional Court or petition the National Assembly for amendment.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the majority opinion is also difficult to accept from the standpoint of legal methodology. The solution to this case should begin with the interpretation of the Statutory Provision at Issue, namely the provision that “it shall not be deemed a trade union.” However, that provision is extremely clear in stating that if the disqualifying factors prescribed by the Trade Union Act exist, it is no longer a lawful trade union. In other words, when the condition of falling under the disqualifying factors of the Trade Union Act is satisfied, the effect occurs that it is no longer a lawful trade union. There is no room for further interpretation of such a self-contained and complete provision. Any contrary view exceeds the limits of statutory interpretation. Nevertheless, the majority opinion intentionally disregards this clear literal meaning and avoids a clear interpretation, treating the provision as merely a criterion for a lawful trade union, and instead debates the validity of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue. Where there are a Constitution, a statute, and a presidential decree on a matter, and the validity of the presidential decree is at issue, one must first examine whether the presidential decree violates the statute, and if not, then whether it violates the Constitution, and whether the statute itself violates the Constitution. Moreover, the written notice of non-recognition at issue (Exhibit A No. 5) clearly cites, as the legal basis, both the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue (Article 9(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Trade Union Act) and Item (d) of the Statutory Provision at Issue (proviso to Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act). Therefore, the validity of the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue should basically be derived through interpretation of the Statutory Provision at Issue. One cannot judge the propriety of a presidential decree without first determining the meaning of the parent Act.\\n\\nThe majority opinion is also problematic in that it renders the Statutory Provision at Issue meaningless in cases where a disqualifying factor arises after establishment report has been accepted. If a disqualifying factor is found at the establishment-report stage of a trade union, then under the provision that “it shall not be deemed a trade union,” it cannot be recognized as a statutory trade union, so the administrative authority must reject the establishment report, and here the provision clearly has meaning. This is not much different even if one, as the majority opinion does, simply views the provision as a criterion for a lawful trade union. However, if a disqualifying factor arises after the establishment report has been accepted, then, if interpreted as the majority opinion does, the provision becomes meaningless. As noted above, under the general principles of administrative law, the administrative authority may revoke or withdraw existing administrative acts ex officio, and the same applies to acceptance of a trade union’s establishment report. In other words, even without the provision that “it shall not be deemed a trade union,” the administrative authority may ex officio revoke or withdraw the existing disposition accepting the establishment report of a trade union with a disqualifying factor. The majority opinion may oppose revocation or withdrawal in this case, but it would not deny the general principles concerning revocation or withdrawal of administrative acts or the Supreme Court’s established precedents based thereon. If, like the majority opinion, one denies the independent significance of the above provision and says it is merely a criterion for a lawful trade union, this ultimately means only that “where a disqualifying factor arises in a trade union, the existing disposition accepting the establishment report may be revoked or withdrawn ex officio,” which merely repeats an obvious matter and therefore leaves the provision without any substantive significance. Interpreting law contrary to its wording is unjust, and so too is interpreting actually existing law so as to render it meaningless.\\n\\nTo realize the constitutional principle of rule of law, finding the ideal legal order in concrete cases is one of the most important missions of the court. But this is not the court’s role alone. It is shared together with the National Assembly, the Government, and the Constitutional Court under the constitutional order. Accordingly, the legal order should be advanced through harmony with legislative enactments by the National Assembly, law enforcement and administrative legislation by the President and the executive branch, and constitutional review by the Constitutional Court. If the National Assembly has not amended the law, the President and the executive branch have not suspended law enforcement or improved the administrative legislation, and the Constitutional Court has recognized the constitutionality of such statutes and systems, that situation should properly be respected. For the court, by its own judgment, to overturn in one stroke the existing legal state formed and maintained by such statutes and systems is not desirable in method, even if the interpretation is ultimately in the right direction. This is all the more so if done while disregarding the clear wording of the statutes and the structure of a complete system. For the court to ignore an order established by constitutionally valid statutes and systems and unilaterally declare its own justice while compelling other state organs to follow it goes far beyond the limits of adjudication and is rather close to legislation. The majority opinion does not interpret law; it creates law itself. Even if the majority opinion ultimately points toward where our society should go, at least for the present it is difficult to accept its reasons and conclusion.\\n\\n10) In short, because law is a universal and valid norm of society, it should in principle be interpreted according to its wording, maintaining objective validity and consistency. The Trade Union Act defines a trade union as an organization composed of workers, and the Teachers’ Trade Union Act, which is a special act to the Trade Union Act, defines “teachers” who may become members of teachers’ trade unions while expressly excluding dismissed teachers. Furthermore, the Statutory Provision at Issue provides that if membership by persons who are not workers is allowed, “it shall not be deemed a trade union,” which applies both to trade unions in formation and to trade unions after establishment; accordingly, even if a trade union has already completed establishment report, once it allows persons who are not workers to join, the legal effect arises directly from the provision itself that it shall no longer be deemed a lawful trade union. In this regard, the Provision of the Enforcement Decree at Issue provides that for implementation of the Statutory Provision at Issue, the administrative authority shall demand correction from the trade union and, if it fails to comply, “shall notify that it shall not be deemed a trade union.” Therefore, if a trade union in operation after establishment is found to have allowed persons who are not workers to join and does not comply with the administrative authority’s corrective demand, the administrative authority must notify it of its non-statutory status without any room for discretion; if it fails to do so, it rather neglects its duty to ensure workers’ independent and democratic exercise of the right of association and is thereby acting unlawfully. There is no room to interpret such clear and complete statutes differently, and if there are parts of the current regulatory system and its content with which one cannot agree, that is a matter to be resolved through legislation.
