have different practical understandings and attitudes toward labor unions depending on their standpoint, one must never underestimate the normative significance of the fact itself that the Constitution, in Article 21, prohibits licensing of associations, and in Article 33 expressly guarantees the three labor rights including the right of association. Therefore, when interpreting a law such as the Trade Union Act, enacted for the purpose of “guaranteeing, under the Constitution, workers’ right of association, collective bargaining, and collective action in order to promote the maintenance and improvement of working conditions and the economic and social status of workers,” and its enforcement decree, one must ensure that the purpose of guaranteeing such right of association is not undermined, and that the three labor rights, including the right of association, are respected to the fullest extent.\\n\\nc) Meanwhile, Article 33(2) of the Constitution provides that public-official workers shall have the three labor rights only to the extent prescribed by Act. This is a provision considering the status of public officials and the characteristics of their duties, but it does not mean that the three labor rights of public officials are denied in principle; rather, it presupposes that certain categories of public officials have the three labor rights and delegates the concrete scope to law (see Constitutional Court full bench decision rendered on 88Hun-Ma5 on 1993. 3. 11., among others). The same applies to teachers who are public officials.\\n\\nThe Teachers’ Labor Union Act enacted pursuant to the above explicit constitutional delegation fundamentally has the character of a statute for guaranteeing teachers’ right of association, etc. In fact, the Teachers’ Labor Union Act applies mutatis mutandis the Trade Union Act except where there are special provisions in the Teachers’ Labor Union Act (Article 14), and is understood to have the status of a special act to the Trade Union Act for guaranteeing workers’ three labor rights.\\n\\nUltimately, despite the special form of regulation in the Constitution Article 33(2), etc. regarding public-official teachers, the interpretation of the Teachers’ Labor Union Act and its enforcement decree should likewise ensure that the purpose of guaranteeing the right of association described above is not undermined, and that teachers’ right of association is respected to the fullest extent possible.\\n\\nd) The same applies when determining whether the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, which establishes a notice of non-recognition system depriving a labor union of its status and thereby harming the right to continue existence, complies with the constitutional principle of statutory reservation. This is because notice of non-recognition as a labor union substantially restricts the right of association of a statutory labor union lawfully established and operating, and thus has strong relevance to fundamental rights.\\n\\n3) The disadvantage that the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue imposes on the fundamental right of association is very serious.\\n\\na) If the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue applies, the legal status of a labor union prescribed by the Trade Union Act is completely denied. Based on the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, the administrative authority uniformly notifies non-recognition as a labor union without considering at all the seriousness of the disqualifying ground or other specific circumstances. The disadvantages and harm suffered by the labor union and its members are plainly severe.\\n\\nb) Moreover, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue does not specifically regulate when and under what circumstances the administrative authority will exercise investigative authority for the application of the provision, what the effect of the notice of non-recognition is, or how the effectiveness of the notice is to be secured.\\n\\nAs a result, it is no exaggeration to say that both the exercise of the power to issue notice of non-recognition and subsequent enforcement are left to the arbitrary judgment of the administrative authority. Although the fact that the administrative authority has issued notice of non-recognition based on the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue only very rarely may show that the authority has exercised its power cautiously, it is also difficult to deny that the notice-of-non-recognition system contains the risk of arbitrary or excessive abuse depending on the position or interpretation of the executive branch.\\n\\n4) Nevertheless, it is difficult to find a legal delegation basis supporting the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue.\\n\\na) The greater the impact of administrative legislation on fundamental rights, the more explicitly that administrative legislation must be based on National Assembly legislation. However, as pointed out by the majority opinion, despite the clear fact that the notice of non-recognition provided in the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue restricts not only the constitutional right of association of each member of the labor union but also deprives it of its status as a statutory labor union recognized as the subject of enjoyment of the right of association, there is no express provision in the Act delegating the matters regulated by the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue.\\n\\nb) When the background of its introduction is also considered, it becomes even clearer that the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue was enacted without delegation by Act. The former labor union dissolution order system under the Trade Union Act before repeal not only had an express legal basis but also required the authority to be exercised cautiously upon obtaining a resolution of the Labor Relations Commission, whereas the notice-of-non-recognition system set forth in the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue has no express basis in law and, without any deliberation and resolution procedure by a neutral and fair committee, produces effects like the former dissolution order merely by declaration of the administrative authority.\\n\\nThe fact that the Executive branch in 1988 newly established the notice-of-non-recognition system through the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is a strong indication that it effectively disregarded the clear will of the “National Assembly” in 1987, which abolished the labor union dissolution order system after reflective consideration.\\n\\n5) I find it difficult to agree with the dissenting opinion that regards the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue as an enforcement decree of an Act.\\n\\na) The executive order for enforcement contemplated by Article 75 of the Constitution means an order enacted merely to enforce the contents of the law, that is, administrative legislation that prescribes detailed procedures or methods necessary to implement the law. An enforcement decree cannot prescribe new contents not provided by the law, nor new rights or duties of citizens. Assuming that the legislature has already provided the executive branch with concrete guidelines for conduct in the Act, the executive branch may only prescribe detailed rules for implementation within the scope of those guidelines. In other words, the executive branch is not given room to independently supplement or concretize the legislature’s intent contained in the Act through an enforcement decree.\\n\\nTherefore, in order for the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue to be evaluated as a lawful enforcement decree, there must first be a concrete regulation in the Act concerning the contents of the notice-of-non-recognition system. But is that truly the case? I will explain the reasons I cannot affirm it by dividing the discussion into separate parts.\\n\\nb) The dissenting opinion appears to understand the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue as lawful administrative legislation implementing the “definition provision of a labor union” prescribed in the Act, but this is difficult to accept because it does not accord with the universal understanding of a definitional provision.\\n\\n(1) Article 2 (Definitions) of the Trade Union Act, which includes the statutory provision at issue, states: “The definitions of the terms used in this Act shall be as follows.” And item 4 of that article defines “labor union” by stating: “‘Labor union’ means an organization or federation thereof organized by workers independently and voluntarily for the purpose of maintaining and improving working conditions and enhancing the economic and social status of workers. Provided, that where any of the following applies, it shall not be deemed a labor union.”\\n\\nGenerally, “definition” means “to clearly determine and state the meaning of a word or thing.” In legislative theory as well, a definitional provision is understood as a provision that clarifies the meaning of terms used in the relevant Act so as to prevent confusion and disputes in interpretation and application of the law, and that functions to concisely express statutory text by explaining in advance, in a single article, terms frequently used in the Act. Definitional provisions that explain the essential nature of an object and definitional provisions that positively or negatively enumerate part or all of an object are also not uncommon in various laws.\\n\\nThat is, Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act concretizes the essential nature of workers’ organizations whose collective right of association is guaranteed under Article 33(1) of the Constitution, and by defining labor unions, which are workers’ organizations that may receive protection under the Trade Union Act, it prescribes the substantive requirements. Among these, the main text prescribes, as one of the positive requirements for a statutory labor union, that workers must be the subject and must have been organized independently, and the statutory provision at issue enumerates, through its proviso items (a), (b), and (d), representative cases in which a workers’ organization may be judged to lack such subjectivity and autonomy.\\n\\n(2) The Trade Union Act, based on the criteria set forth in this definitional provision, that is, the substantive requirements, prescribes acceptance and return of labor union establishment reports, corrective orders for constitutions, and penalties for violations, according to the legislative purpose. In other words, the Trade Union Act provides that the administrative authority shall accept the establishment report of a labor union that satisfies the substantive requirements, but shall return the establishment report when a negative requirement is confirmed (Article 10(1), Article 12(1), Article 12(3) item 1), and provides, among other things, that if a labor union’s constitution or resolutions include content corresponding to a negative requirement and are therefore unlawful, the administrative authority may, upon obtaining a resolution of the Labor Relations Commission, order correction of the relevant constitution or resolution (Article 21). These are additional statutory provisions that separately regulate the content, procedures, and effects of prior and ex post review by the administrative authority on the assumption of the criteria set forth in the definitional provision of Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act, including the statutory provision at issue.\\n\\nIn the end, just as a statutory labor union cannot be recognized directly solely by Article 2(4) of the Trade Union Act, one cannot conclude that the loss of legal status as a statutory labor union is immediately finalized solely by the statutory provision at issue, which is merely part of the definitional provisions concerning labor unions. Likewise, just as the statutory provision at issue alone cannot be said to grant the administrative authority the power to accept or return a labor union’s establishment report, it is difficult to say that the administrative authority’s power to issue notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law is recognized based on the direct legal effect of the statutory provision at issue. The majority opinion is correct in this respect in saying that the statutory provision at issue merely clarifies the criteria for determining whether it is a labor union under the law.\\n\\nc) As above, because the Trade Union Act adopts the establishment-report system, in order to become a statutory labor union, a formal requirement, namely acceptance of the establishment report, is required in addition to the substantive requirements under the statutory provision at issue, etc. Therefore, as the dissenting opinion mentions, a labor union that satisfies the substantive requirements but has not completed establishment reporting cannot be said to be a statutory labor union, and a labor union that does not satisfy the substantive requirements may not be recognized as a statutory labor union even if it has been issued a certificate of report (see Supreme Court judgments rendered on 93DO855 on 1996. 6. 28., and on 96NU9829 on 1997. 10. 14., among others). However, this merely means that when issues arise such as qualifications for applying for relief from unfair labor practices under the Trade Union Act, the legal relationship can be finalized through substantive review of the requirements by the Labor Relations Commission and, ultimately, by the courts. To conclude from this that, because the legal effect of no longer being regarded as a statutory labor union arises immediately under the statutory provision at issue, the administrative authority may therefore issue notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law solely on the basis of the statutory provision at issue, would disregard the systematic understanding of the requirements for establishing a statutory labor union. Furthermore, if the administrative authority can make the abstract and potential legal effect under the statutory provision at issue concrete and final through corrective orders and corrective requests as a prior procedure for notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law, this is not very different from affirming the constitutive nature of the notice-of-non-recognition disposition.\\n\\nd) The dissenting opinion emphasizes that the statutory provision at issue takes the form of a deeming provision, saying it “shall not be deemed a labor union.” However, the expression “shall not be deemed” in the statutory provision at issue is a change from the expression “the foregoing shall not apply,” which was used in the definition provisions of the former Trade Union Act amended on 1963. 4. 17. and before the current Trade Union Act was enacted on 1997. 3. 13. It is not easy to confirm the legislature’s intent embedded in this legislative transition.\\n\\nNonetheless, it is too formalistic and hard to accept the view that during the period when the law was enacted using the expression “shall not be deemed” in the definitional provision of labor unions, a labor union already established and operating that met the negative requirements prescribed by the statutory provision at issue immediately became a non-statutory union as a matter of course, whereas during the period when the expression “the foregoing shall not apply” was used, no such immediate effect arose. Moreover, as noted above, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue had already existed before the definitional provision of labor unions adopted the form of “shall not be deemed.” In view of such legislative history, it is not appropriate to overemphasize merely the fact that the statutory provision at issue takes the form of a deeming provision and interpret the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue as merely cautious and confirmatory.\\n\\ne) Unlike the law’s specific regulation of the return system for labor union establishment reporting, it is necessary to give weight to the discriminatory situation where the law separately does not regulate the notice-of-non-recognition system. The legislative silence at the statutory level regarding the notice-of-non-recognition system can be seen as the result of the legislature’s intent.\\n\\n(1) The legislative policy for realizing the purpose of a definitional provision may vary. Grounds contrary to a definitional provision, the path and degree of violation, etc. can be diverse, and accordingly the degree to which the legislative purpose is infringed also varies, so the legislature will devise corresponding legislative policy. The fact that the labor union establishment-report return system is prescribed in law (Article 12(3) of the Trade Union Act) should also be viewed as the result of the legislature’s policy efforts to realize the legislative purpose of the definitional provisions concerning labor unions. It is difficult to view the return system as merely a simple implementation of the definitional provision.\\n\\n(2) If one pays attention to the fact that the legislature concretely formed the labor union establishment-report return system through the Act in this way, then if the legislature also intended to introduce a notice-of-non-recognition system, and especially if such legislative intent arose around the time it abolished the labor union dissolution order system, which had a function similar to the notice-of-non-recognition system, it is natural to think that the legislature would probably have separately established the basic outline of the notice-of-non-recognition system in the Act itself, namely the requirements and limits for the exercise of the administrative power of notice of non-recognition and the essential parts of its procedure and effects. This is because there are meaningful differences in the characteristics of the regulated objects, etc., between the labor union establishment-report return system and the notice-of-non-recognition system.\\n\\n(3) That is, at the labor union establishment-report stage, if the grounds set forth in item (d) of the statutory provision at issue are found to exist, the administrative authority must return the establishment report, and it need not separately examine whether the autonomy of the labor union has actually been impaired by allowing membership of persons who are not workers (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2011DU6998 on 2014. 4. 10., among others). This should be understood as aiming to clarify the scope of the administrative authority’s review and prevent arbitrariness, because at that stage the substance of the entity is still unclear and it is difficult to set the object and scope of a specific review for determining autonomy; thus, the system of reporting, which presupposes freedom to establish labor unions, might in practice be operated as a licensing system under the pretext of examining autonomy. However, where a labor union has already been lawfully established and is operating, its substance has been formed, and the actual impairment of labor union autonomy caused by permitting membership of persons who are not workers can be adequately examined through its specific organizational composition and activities. Even if disputes arise in the process or conclusion of that review, because the issue can be sufficiently corrected through judicial determination, the review in such a case does not pose a great risk of undermining the constitutional and legal purpose of autonomy of labor unions and freedom of establishment.\\n\\n(4) If the circumstances are as above, then the legislative silence at the statutory level regarding the notice-of-non-recognition system can be seen as resulting from the legislature’s clear intention or design, and the court needs to take this into significant consideration.\\n\\n6) The general legal principles concerning ex officio cancellation and withdrawal of beneficial administrative dispositions cannot be a sufficient basis to legislate a notice-of-non-recognition system through an enforcement decree without a clear legislative delegation.\\n\\na) Viewing ex officio cancellation or withdrawal of a beneficial administrative disposition as possible even without separate statutory grounds is not meant to recognize original administrative power free from statute; rather, it is the result of inferring a reasonable legislative intent that, if the legislature grants the administrative authority the power to issue a beneficial administrative disposition by law, the authorization provision implicitly includes the power to ex officio cancel or withdraw it when circumstances are found that make it difficult to maintain the already issued beneficial disposition. In ordinary cases, inferring the legislature’s reasonable intent in that way may be appropriate.\\n\\nb) However, taking into account the various circumstances mentioned above, such as the history of the legislature abolishing the labor union dissolution order system after reflective consideration, it is appropriate to view the legislature as not having granted the administrative authority the power to deprive a statutory labor union of its status by unilateral decision through notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law merely because grounds for return of the establishment report exist, via ex officio cancellation or withdrawal of the acceptance disposition of labor union establishment reporting.\\n\\nD. Meaning of regarding the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue as unconstitutional\\n\\n1) The majority opinion, recognizing the constitutional importance of judicial control over administrative legislation, focused on determining the matter based on Article 107(2) of the Constitution, viewing as central to the dispute the fundamental issue underlying the case: whether the relationship between National Assembly legislation and administrative legislation is constitutionally properly structured in light of the meaning of the Plaintiff’s claimed constitutional fundamental rights.\\n\\n2) In a democratic constitutional state, as a rule, state power should be exercised by law enacted by representatives of the people through democratic procedures, that is, by law embodying the will of the sovereign, or by administrative legislation concretized pursuant to a delegation by law. Only when the principle of statutory reservation is realized does “self-government by the people,” who willingly bind themselves by legitimate laws made by their elected representatives, become possible.\\n\\n3) The notice-of-non-recognition system under the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue was introduced through administrative legislation without confirmation of the will of the National Assembly, that is, without authorization by law, even though the disadvantages it imposes on the right of association of labor unions and their members are very serious. This violates the hierarchical relationship between National Assembly legislation and administrative legislation envisioned by the Constitution. In other words, regardless of whether the content itself is justifiable, the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue is administrative legislation that contravenes the constitutional principle of statutory reservation and thus cannot be used as the legal basis for measures restricting fundamental rights of citizens.\\n\\n4) As the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue, which contravenes the principle of statutory reservation, is declared invalid, the basis upon which the “administrative authority” can examine the qualifications of a labor union and completely deny the legal status of a labor union prescribed by the Trade Union Act is lost. Whether to grant legal basis for the notice-of-non-recognition system as designed by the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue should ultimately be dealt with by the National Assembly, the representative of the people. Whether it is proper to introduce a notice-of-non-recognition system at the statutory level, and if so, which state organ should determine a body to be a non-statutory union for what grounds and through what procedures, and what level of sanctions against a non-statutory union would be proportional, are matters that should ultimately be decided by the National Assembly through democratic procedures, after gathering diverse public opinions on the relevant constitutional provisions and after open debate and deliberation by interested parties, because that is precisely fully consistent with the constitutional principle of statutory reservation.\\n\\n5) I again wish to emphasize the significance of constitutional adjudication by the courts. Citizens’ claims grounded in the Constitution, especially fundamental rights, will not be able to be enforced without any restriction in all cases. However, if the court listens carefully and seriously to citizens’ claims grounded in fundamental rights—whether those claims are strong or weak—and consistently maintains the belief that the possibility of protecting citizens’ fundamental rights through the court’s adjudicatory process is always secured, then I believe the task of guaranteeing fundamental rights assigned to the courts by the Constitution will begin to be realized.\\n\\nE. The lower court’s misapprehension of the law on restrictions on addition and change of reasons for disposition\\n\\n1) I wish to note that the lower court and the dissenting opinion misunderstand the reason for the disposition in this case. “Ex officio cancellation” and “withdrawal” of a beneficial administrative disposition must be distinguished. Ex officio cancellation of an administrative disposition refers to an administrative disposition that retroactively extinguishes the effect of an administrative disposition validly formed in the first place, on the ground that the disposition had an unlawful defect; withdrawal of an administrative disposition refers to an administrative disposition that prospectively extinguishes all or part of the effect of an administrative disposition that had already acquired full effect because the legal requirements were met at the time of the disposition. As a rule, a “ground for cancellation” of an administrative disposition refers to a defect existing at the time the administrative disposition was formed, while a “ground for withdrawal” refers to a ground newly arising after the administrative disposition was formed that makes it impossible to maintain the effect of the disposition (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2015DU58195 on 2018. 6. 28., among others).\\n\\n2) The provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue applies when “a ground for return of an establishment report corresponding to Article 12(3) item 1 of the Trade Union Act arises after a labor union has been issued a certificate of report,” and in this case the Defendant issued a notice of non-recognition as a labor union under the law by applying the provision of the Enforcement Decree at issue on the ground that, after the issuance of the labor union establishment-report certificate, the grounds set forth in item (d) of the statutory provision at issue arose for the first time (hereinafter referred to as the “original reason for disposition”). Therefore, the notice of non-recognition at issue corresponds to “withdrawal,” which prospectively extinguishes the acceptance disposition of labor union establishment reporting on the ground of a subsequent circumstance.\\n\\n3) Nevertheless, the lower court accepted the Defendant’s litigation argument as it stood and determined that, at the time of the labor union establishment report, grounds already existed under item (d) of the statutory provision at issue, but the Plaintiff submitted a false constitution and the establishment report was accepted (hereinafter referred to as the “added reason for disposition”), thereby treating the notice of non-recognition at issue as a “cancellation” that retroactively extinguishes the acceptance disposition of labor union establishment reporting on the basis of an original defect. Since the original reason for disposition and the added reason for disposition described above do not share identity of the basic factual relationship, addition and change of reasons for disposition are not permitted from the standpoint of substantive rule of law and protection of the addressee’s trust, and the court cannot examine and determine the propriety of the added reason for disposition (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2000DU8684 on 2001. 9. 28., among others). Accordingly, the lower court’s determination also contains an error in misapprehending the legal principles on the restriction of addition and change of reasons for disposition.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, I state this supplementary opinion to the majority opinion."}

{"[2016DU60591]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Background of the Case\\n\\na. The Plaintiff was a cadet who entered the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon on 2014. 1. 10., completed the baccalaureate course, and graduated on 2016. 2. 24.\\n\\nb. In mid-2014. 11., the Plaintiff, while on overnight leave, shared and drank one bottle of soju with Non-Party 1; around 2015. 4., while having dinner with family, the Plaintiff drank about 2 to 4 shots of soju at the parents’ urging; in 2015. 8., during the summer vacation period, the Plaintiff drank about 4 to 5 shots of soju with a friend, Non-Party 2; and around 2015. 9., during the Chuseok holiday, the Plaintiff performed ancestral rites at home and partook of two glasses of Cheongju as ritual libation.\\n\\nc. On 2015. 11. 23., the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon Education Operation Committee, as a result of deliberation on the Plaintiff’s violation of the duty to maintain dignity (drinking), as referred by the Cadet Corps Committee, resolved to expel the Plaintiff. Accordingly, the Defendant, on 2015. 11. 24., issued the disposition at issue, imposing expulsion on the Plaintiff.\\n\\nd. The Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon is a military educational institution established pursuant to the Act on Establishment of the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon. The Superintendent may expel a cadet who falls under a cadet with extremely poor conduct, a cadet who does not comply with the rules that an officer cadet must observe, such as causing disorder in military discipline, a cadet with poor academic performance who is unlikely to graduate, a cadet who cannot complete the prescribed course due to disease or other physical or mental disability, or a cadet who has violated the school regulations (Article 18, paragraph 1 of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on Establishment of the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon). According to the subordinate document to the school regulations of the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon, the “Administrative Regulation for Officer Cadets” (hereinafter, the version before the amendment of 2015. 5. 19. shall be referred to as the “former Regulation,” and the version amended on 2015. 5. 19. and before the amendment of 2016. 3. 3. as the “Regulation”), it provides that “cadets may not drink alcohol” (former Regulation, Article 12, duty to maintain dignity), or that “cadets may not drink alcohol. However, if the cadet himself or herself must drink alcohol due to an unavoidable parent’s funeral/death anniversary, etc., approval from the Superintendent of Cadet Training must be obtained” (Regulation, Article 12, hereinafter, including the corresponding provision of the former Regulation, referred to collectively as the “no-drinking provision at issue”). A violation of the duty to maintain dignity is a “Class 1 incident,” and where such violation is committed repeatedly two or more times, expulsion is to be imposed in principle [former Regulation and Regulation, Article 61, subparagraph 1, item (a)].\\n\\n2. Holding of the court below\\n\\nThe court below determined that the expulsion disposition at issue was lawful for the following reasons.\\n\\na. The Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon is an educational institution established with the goal of cultivating elite officers equipped with leadership based on sound values and moral character, together with the basic qualities of a military expert. The Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon places the utmost importance on ensuring that its members have the qualifications of officers equipped with sound values and moral character, as well as a spirit of self-discipline and moderation, and for this purpose maintains the academy’s unique three-prohibition system (prohibition of drinking, smoking, and marriage). Since the no-drinking provision at issue does not appear, in light of the purpose of establishment or educational purpose of the academy and the purport of the delegation of the relevant statutes, to be unconstitutional, contrary to law, or manifestly unreasonable, a cadet who violates the duty to maintain dignity may be expelled under the no-drinking provision at issue.\\n\\nb. The Plaintiff enrolled in the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon while recognizing that the academy has its own unique three-prohibition system and fully aware that, as a result, some of the Plaintiff’s fundamental rights would be restricted, having decided to accept all of these restrictions. Nevertheless, as noted above, the Plaintiff clearly violated the no-drinking provision at issue.\\n\\nc. Unless the categories of incidents and disciplinary sanction standards prescribed in the Administrative Regulation for Officer Cadets are themselves unconstitutional or contrary to law, or unless there is no reasonable ground to recognize that the disciplinary sanction imposed according to the relevant sanction standard is manifestly unreasonable in light of the content and purport of the violation that became the cause of the disposition and the provisions of the relevant statutes, it is appropriate to regard a disciplinary sanction imposed according to the standards as, in principle, having been made within the scope of discretion. In addition to the circumstances that the Plaintiff violated the no-drinking provision at issue, considering comprehensively that even a person expelled from the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon may, if he or she so wishes, be appointed as an active-duty noncommissioned officer, and that if the person serves as an active-duty enlisted soldier, the period of military training received before expulsion is included in the period of service, thereby mitigating the disadvantage incurred by a cadet due to expulsion, the disadvantage that the Plaintiff will suffer from the expulsion disposition at issue cannot be said to be manifestly greater than the public purpose the Defendant seeks to achieve, and thus the expulsion disposition at issue cannot be deemed to have deviated from or abused discretion.\\n\\n3. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\n\\na. Article 10 of the Constitution guarantees the right to pursue happiness and the general freedom of action derived therefrom, and Article 17 of the Constitution guarantees privacy and freedom as fundamental rights. These fundamental rights may be restricted by law only when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare pursuant to Article 37, paragraph 2 of the Constitution, but even when restricted, the essential content of freedom and rights may not be infringed.\\n\\nMeanwhile, a cadet is in a special status relationship as a member of the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon, a special educational institution whose entire finances are borne by the State in order to produce military officers, and is enrolled in the military register of Army cadets and receives treatment equivalent to that of warrant officers from the day of entrance into the school (Article 3 of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on Establishment of the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon). Therefore, within the extent necessary to achieve its purpose of existence, the cadet’s fundamental rights may be more restricted than those of the general public; however, even in such cases, the constitutional principles governing restrictions on fundamental rights, such as the principle of legal reservation and the principle against excessive restriction, must be observed (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2012DU26401, rendered on 2018. 3. 22.).\\n\\nb. The Act on Establishment of the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon and its Enforcement Decree, the school regulations of the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon pursuant to the delegation thereof, and the Administrative Regulation for Officer Cadets establish matters that cadets must observe in order to achieve the purpose of establishment and educational objectives of the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon, and may prescribe disciplinary measures for conduct in violation thereof; such regulations should be respected as far as possible. On this premise, we examine whether the no-drinking provision at issue violates the principle against excessive restriction, a constitutional principle governing the restriction of fundamental rights.\\n\\nFirst, former Regulation, Article 12, subparagraph 1, provides that “cadets may not drink alcohol,” thereby imposing an unconditional duty of abstinence from alcohol on cadets, and Regulation, Article 12, subparagraph 1, provides that “cadets may not drink alcohol. However, if the cadet himself or herself must drink alcohol due to unavoidable circumstances such as a parent’s funeral/death anniversary, approval from the Superintendent of Cadet Training must be obtained,” thereby, in principle, imposing a duty of abstinence from alcohol on cadets while allowing drinking only in cases where there are unavoidable circumstances such as a parent’s funeral/death anniversary and approval from the Superintendent of Cadet Training is obtained. In order to achieve the purpose of establishment and educational objectives of the academy, it is of course necessary for the academy to prohibit or restrict acts such as drinking on campus, drinking during education, training, and official duties, and drinking in private activities while wearing cadet attire that identifies one’s status, as well as cases where, even when engaging in private activities without wearing cadet attire, the cadet’s dignity is impaired by causing social controversy as a result thereof. However, to go beyond this and require cadets to comply with an unconditional duty of abstinence from alcohol even in all aspects of their private life is to excessively restrict not only the cadets’ general freedom of action but also privacy and freedom.\\n\\nSecond, expulsion is the harshest disciplinary measure in that it deprives the cadet of enrollment status and extinguishes the status relationship as a cadet, and therefore should be imposed exceptionally only when there is a serious ground for discipline in light of the purpose of discipline, at least for educational necessity or maintenance of order within the academy. However, under Article 61 of the Administrative Regulation for Officer Cadets, drinking is a Class 1 incident as a violation of the duty to maintain dignity, and expulsion is the rule when such violation is committed repeatedly two or more times. Yet, the former Regulation and Regulation, Article 12, require cadets to comply with an unconditional duty of abstinence from alcohol even in all aspects of private life, while Article 61 uniformly provides that, without inquiring into whether a cadet’s drinking took place during education or training, the amount of drinking, the place of drinking, or the circumstances leading to the drinking, expulsion shall in principle be imposed upon two violations. Even in light of the purpose for which the academy implements the no-drinking system, this excessively infringes on cadets’ fundamental rights.\\n\\nUltimately, the no-drinking provision at issue, even when considering the special nature of cadet education, fails entirely to devise measures that minimize the restriction of fundamental rights, and thus excessively restricts cadets’ fundamental rights, such as the general freedom of action and privacy, and therefore must be deemed invalid.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, contrary to the foregoing, determined that the expulsion disposition at issue imposed by applying the no-drinking provision at issue to the Plaintiff was lawful. The judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the unconstitutionality, interpretation, and application, etc. of the no-drinking provision at issue. The ground of appeal pointing out this point is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for further proceedings and determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning minors are correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) (a) When appointing a special representative as the legal representative of a minor pursuant to Article 921 of the Civil Act, it is, as a rule, for the court to specify the content of the juristic act to be handled by the special representative and state it in the dispositive part of the adjudication. (b) Where a legal representative has permitted a minor to engage in a specific business, the legal representative may not revoke that permission. (c) If, at the time of the juristic act, a minor merely told the other party that he or she was an adult and did not actively use deception, the minor may rescind that juristic act. (d) Where a guardian of a minor is appointed as the legal representative of a minor, multiple guardians of a minor may be appointed for the minor's benefit. (e) Where a minor is subjected to sexual violence, the statute of limitations for a claim for damages arising therefrom does not run until the minor attains majority.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[71DA2045]": "With respect to the second and fifth grounds of appeal of Defendant’s litigation counsel Hong Seungman and the first ground of appeal of Choi Yunmo, the judgment below, taking into comprehensive account the contents stated in Plaintiff’s Exhibit No. 3 (copy of family register), Plaintiff’s Exhibit No. 4 (sales contract), and Plaintiff’s Exhibit No. 5 (certificate of seal impression), held that the Plaintiff was a male born on 1948. 8. 5. and was still a minor on 1968. 3. 26., when the sales contract for the forest land in question was concluded, and that it could be recognized that the sales contract in question was concluded without the consent of the legal representative, and that there was no counterevidence; examining the evidence relationship selected thereby and the process and content of fact-finding from the record, the above recognized facts can be accepted, so no error can be found in the judgment below in its assessment of the probative value of evidence, and its statement that there was no counterevidence may not be regarded otherwise than as having rejected, in the sense that the entries in Defendant’s exhibits Nos. 1 through 6 pointed out by the argument and the testimonies of Witness Non-parties 1 and 2 do not amount to evidence sufficient to overturn the presumption that the facts stated in Plaintiff’s Exhibit No. 3 are true; thus, there is no error in omitting a determination thereon. Nor can it be said that there was an error of insufficient deliberation on the ground that the appellate court did not urge the Plaintiff’s motion for age appraisal, did not order age appraisal ex officio, or did not exercise its right to clarification with respect to whether the date on which Defendant’s Exhibits Nos. 1, 2, and 3, etc. were delivered to the Defendant was before or after the Plaintiff attained majority; therefore, the above arguments are merely disputing the appellate court’s proper measures and cannot be accepted.\\n\\nWith respect to the fourth ground of appeal of the same Hong Seungman and the second ground of appeal of the same Choi Yunmo,\\nAs stated above, the judgment below recognized that the Plaintiff, at the time of concluding the sales contract for the forest land in question with the Defendant, was a minor and concluded the sales contract without the consent of the legal representative; thus the Plaintiff, being a minor, may rescind the sales contract, and therefore when the counterparty Defendant asserts that the Plaintiff, a minor, used fraudulent means prescribed in Civil Code Article 17 in order to exclude the minor Plaintiff’s right of rescission, the burden of proof for that assertion lies with the Defendant side, the party asserting it; in the present case, the Defendant submitted Defendant’s Exhibit No. 6 (the certificate of seal impression by which the Plaintiff became an adult) as one piece of proof, but since the Plaintiff submitted rebuttal evidence that the numerical portion of the year indicating majority was altered and that he himself had not altered it, the Defendant must, according to the principles of the burden of proof, bear the burden of proving that the alteration was made by the Plaintiff or a third party acting in collusion with the Plaintiff; therefore, in the same purport, the judgment below, which rejected the Defendant’s assertion that the Plaintiff used fraudulent means on the premise that the Plaintiff altered the certificate of seal impression, a required document for transfer registration of the forest land in question, on the ground that there was no proof thereof, is proper, and there is no error in shifting the burden of proof or violating the rules of evidence; furthermore, the phrase in Civil Code Article 17, “when a person lacking capacity caused another to believe him or her to be capable by fraudulent means,” means that the person lacking capacity actively used fraudulent means in order to cause the other party to believe that he or she is capable, and merely stating that one is capable cannot be said to constitute the use of fraudulent means referred to in that Article (see Supreme Court Decision 1954MINSANG77HO, decided 1955. 3. 31.); therefore, in the present case, even if the minor Plaintiff, at the time of the sales contract in question, himself stated that he was a company president, or even if a non-party present at the same table called the Plaintiff the president of Joongang Jeonseon Co., Ltd. to the counterparty Defendant, this alone would not fall under the case of using fraudulent means, so the judgment below, which judged in the purport of such view, is proper, and since the judgment below contains no illegality in the interpretation and application of law, the arguments cannot be accepted.\\n\\nWith respect to the third ground of appeal of the same Hong Seungman\\nThe court below, in the reasons for its judgment, held that since the Plaintiff had never served as a representative director of any company on 1968. 3. 26., when the sales contract for the forest land in question was concluded, the Defendant’s assertion premised on the Plaintiff having been the representative director of the company at the time of the conclusion of the sales contract in question is without merit, and that the provision of Civil Code Article 8 is without merit in this case where there is no assertion or proof whatsoever that a minor received permission to operate a business from his or her legal representative; moreover, because there is no room for the application of apparent representation as this case is not a sale of company property, the argument that there is a misunderstanding of Civil Code Article 8 regarding a minor’s permission to operate a business and of the law on apparent representation is merely an independent view and lacks merit.\\n\\nWith respect to the first ground of appeal of the same Hong Seungman and the third ground of appeal of the same Choi Yunmo,\\nAccording to the record, Defendant’s litigation counsel, at the hearing date of 1971. 5. 7. before the court below, by the preparatory brief received on 1971. 5. 6. deemed to have been stated (record 404 pages; the entry in the appellate court trial transcript deeming the answer statement is a clerical error for deeming the preparatory brief), asserted that “even if the Plaintiff’s contention is accepted, the fact that the Plaintiff attained majority on 1968. 8. 4. and that a considerable period elapsed until the filing of the present suit without any objection means that it is socially appropriate in general commercial practice to regard the Plaintiff as having implicitly ratified the sales contract in question,” and it is clear that the argument was made to the effect that the sales contract in question could be regarded as having been ratified after the Plaintiff became an adult; nevertheless, the court below did not make any determination thereon, which constitutes an error of omission of a determination that may affect the judgment, so the arguments on this point are well-founded and the judgment below cannot avoid reversal.\\n\\nTherefore, in accordance with Article 406 of the Civil Procedure Act, the judgment is rendered by the unanimous opinion of the participating judges as stated in the disposition."}

{"[96DA1139]": "We review the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. As to Ground 1\\nIn rejecting the Plaintiffs' assertion that the Defendant's deceased husband, Non-Party 1, had agreed in or around 1976 to return the land, etc. in this case as stated in the judgment to the Plaintiffs, the court below held that the evidence submitted by the Plaintiffs as set forth therein was insufficient to establish this fact. Although there is some inadequacy in the formulation of that holding, it can be understood as rejecting the assertion on the ground that all of the above evidence cannot be believed, and, upon review in light of the record, this is justifiable and persuasive; accordingly, it cannot be said that there was a serious violation of statutes, as alleged, in the court below's holding on this point, nor that there was illegality in violation of the Supreme Court precedents concerning the interpretation and application of Article 187 of the Civil Procedure Act. The precedents cited by the appellant are all cases whose specific facts differ from those of this case, and thus are not appropriate for direct application to this case. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 2\\nThe special representative system under Article 921 of the Civil Act is intended to prevent abuse of parental authority and to protect the interests of a minor by restricting the representative authority and consent authority of the person with parental authority and causing a special representative appointed by the court to exercise those rights, because when there is a conflict of interests between the person with parental authority and a person subject to that parental authority, or among persons subject to parental authority, it is difficult to expect the person with parental authority to exercise parental authority fairly. Accordingly, a special representative must be appointed individually with respect to a specific legal act in which interests conflict; therefore, an application for appointment of a special representative must specifically state the legal act to be handled by the special representative to be appointed, and the court, too, in issuing the ruling on such appointment, should in principle specify the legal act to be handled by the special representative and indicate it in the disposition of the ruling. The court cannot issue a ruling that broadly grants the special representative authority to handle any legal act that the minor should perform. Therefore, although it is not desirable for the court, in making a ruling appointing a special representative, merely to state in the disposition that a certain person is appointed as special representative for a minor without specifying the legal act to be handled by the special representative, even in such a case the authority of that special representative is limited to the specific legal act stated as the cause of the application in the application for appointment in that case, and as to other legal acts there is no authority to handle them, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nHowever, on the other hand, where registration of real estate has been completed, such registration is presumed to have been duly completed in terms of both cause and procedure unless special circumstances exist, and the same applies even where a registration of establishment of a mortgage in the name of another person has been completed by a special representative with respect to a minor's real estate in order to secure the debt of the person with parental authority; accordingly, a person asserting the invalidity of such registration of establishment of a mortgage must prove that the special representative completed the registration without authority.\\n\\nTurning to this case, as duly determined by the court below, with respect to the land in this case for which a registration of transfer of ownership had been completed in the name of the deceased Non-Party 2, who was the father of the Plaintiffs, a registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of donation was completed in the Plaintiffs' names on March 15, 1961, and thereafter registrations of establishment of a mortgage in the name of Chohung Bank, with the debtor being the above Non-Party 2, dated April 18, 1967 and September 28 of the same year, respectively, and registrations of establishment of a mortgage in the names of Non-Party 4 and Non-Party 5, with the debtor being Non-Party 3, the Plaintiffs' mother, dated August 21, 1968, were each completed, then even if Plaintiff 2 was a minor at the time of the mortgage registration in this case, the mortgage registration in this case concerning that Plaintiff's share is still presumed valid, and the burden of proving that the mortgage registration in this case was completed by an unauthorized special representative and is void rests on that Plaintiff asserting its invalidity. However, the mere statement in Exhibit A No. 1-1 (Decision) cited in the grounds for appeal is insufficient to establish that the mortgage registration in this case (particularly the registrations dated September 28, 1967 and August 21, 1968) was completed by a special representative without authority, and no other material can be found in the record to establish this; therefore, the mortgage registration in this case is still presumed to be a lawful registration.\\n\\nThe court below, with respect to the following assertion by Plaintiff 2, namely, that because Plaintiff 2 was a minor at the time of the mortgage registration in this case, his person with parental authority, the deceased Non-Party 2, in effecting an act in which interests conflict between himself and the above Plaintiff, applied to the court for appointment of a special representative to represent the above Plaintiff, obtained from the court a decision appointing a special representative for a broad act that did not specifically identify the act to be represented, and on that basis caused the special representative to enter into the mortgage contract on behalf of the above Plaintiff, and that the decision appointing a special representative targeting such a broad act is void, so that in the end the mortgage registration in this case was made by an unauthorized person and is therefore void for lack of cause, rejected that Plaintiff's assertion on the ground that even if the legal act to be represented was not specifically identified in making the decision appointing a special representative to represent an act involving conflicting interests, as claimed by the above Plaintiff, the decision of appointment cannot for that reason alone be void, nor can the specific legal act represented by the special representative necessarily be void, which is not without some inadequacy in the formulation thereof, but ultimately it is the same purport as the legal principle stated above. Therefore, the argument that the court below erred by misunderstanding the legal principle concerning the effect of the appointment of a special representative under Article 921 of the Civil Act cannot be accepted.\\n\\nFurthermore, if, by the decision in Exhibit A No. 1-1 above, the special representative was granted authority with respect to the establishment of the mortgage dated April 18, 1967, whose mortgagee is Chohung Bank, then the establishment of the above mortgage dated April 18, 1967 by Chohung Bank was lawful, and, if the above mortgage was lawful, even if the registration of establishment of a mortgage dated September 28, 1967 in the name of Chohung Bank, with the debtor being the above Non-Party 2, and the registration of establishment of a mortgage dated August 21, 1968 in the names of Non-Party 4 and Non-Party 5, with the debtor being Non-Party 3, the Plaintiffs' mother, were not each lawfully completed among the mortgage registrations in this case, the purchase at auction by Non-Party 1 of the land in this case in the non-judicial auction proceedings conducted upon enforcement of the security right of Chohung Bank, the secured creditor of the above mortgage dated April 18, 1967, would be lawful. The argument is without merit in any view.\\n\\n3. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed and the costs of appeal are borne by the losing parties, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

question: A loan claim of KRW 50,000,000 that A has against B has become extinguished by the statute of limitations. Which of the following explanations is incorrect? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, it is governed by precedents.)
A: If B, without knowing that the statute of limitations had been completed, paid A KRW 50,000,000 in discharge of the above debt, B cannot demand its return from A.
B: If C, before the completion of the statute of limitations, granted a mortgage over his own land X in order to secure the above claim of A against B, C may assert the completion of the statute of limitations for the above claim.
C: B's general creditor C may, to the extent necessary to preserve his own claim, exercise subrogation in B's stead and assert the completion of the statute of limitations for the above claim of A against B.
D: If the above claim of A against B could already have been set off against B's claim against A before the statute of limitations on the above claim had been completed, A may set off B's claim with the above claim.
E: If A filed an action against B for performance of the debt after the completion of the statute of limitations, but B did not assert the fact that the statute of limitations had been completed by the time the fact-finding proceedings were closed, the court shall consider the completion of the statute of limitations ex officio.
label: E
