The remaining appeal is dismissed."}

{"[2011DA109500]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Concerning the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nIf, in real property auction proceedings initiated by another creditor, real property owned by the debtor was sold at auction and the sale proceeds were distributed to a creditor holding a mortgage securing a debt for which the statute of limitations had already expired and were applied to satisfaction of that debt, and the debtor raised no objection until then, then, absent other special circumstances such as the debtor’s not knowing that the auction proceedings were underway, the debtor may be deemed to have waived the benefit of the statute of limitations as to the claim (see Supreme Court Decision 2001DA3580 dated June 12, 2001, Supreme Court Decision 2000DA25484 dated February 26, 2002, Supreme Court Decision 2010DA6345 dated May 13, 2010, etc.); meanwhile, waiver of the benefit of the statute of limitations is also possible with respect to part of a divisible obligation (see Supreme Court Decision 86DAKA2107 dated June 23, 1987).\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the lower court, for the reasons stated in its opinion, held that, because Green Gongyeong Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to simply as “Green Gongyeong”), the debtor in the auction proceedings at issue, raised no objection to the Defendant, who held a claim secured by a mortgage for which the statute of limitations had expired, receiving KRW 40,000,000 in distribution, Green Gongyeong must be deemed to have waived the benefit of limitations as to the remaining claim amount of KRW 26,666,666, excluding KRW 13,333,334 for which the Plaintiff, another creditor of Green Gongyeong, raised an objection by subrogating to Green Gongyeong; thus, the lower court’s determination that the Defendant did not obtain unjust enrichment in relation to this portion of the distributed amount is proper, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the law concerning waiver of the benefit of the statute of limitations, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Concerning the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nNot only claims arising from acts that constitute commercial transactions for both parties, but also claims arising from acts that constitute commercial transactions for only one party, fall within the category of commercial claims to which the five-year limitation period prescribed in Article 64 of the Commercial Act applies; such commercial transactions include not only basic commercial acts falling under each item of Article 46 of the Commercial Act, but also ancillary commercial acts performed by a merchant for the purpose of the merchant’s business (see Supreme Court Decision 93DA54842 dated April 29, 1994, Supreme Court Decision 2007DA91251 dated April 10, 2008, etc.); and acts performed by a company are presumed, absent proof to the contrary, to have been performed for its business purposes (Article 5(2) of the Commercial Act).\\n\\nMoreover, where the statute of limitations has expired, a general creditor of the debtor may not, in the capacity of creditor, independently invoke the statute of limitations; however, to the extent necessary to preserve the creditor’s own claim, the creditor may, by subrogating to the debtor, invoke the statute of limitations (see Supreme Court Decision 97DA22676 dated December 26, 1997, Supreme Court Decision 2005DA11312 dated March 30, 2007, etc.).\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the lower court judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the lower court held that Green Gongyeong, as a company and merchant, is presumed to have borrowed money from the Plaintiff for the purpose of its business, and thus the act constitutes a commercial transaction; and that the Defendant’s loan claim against Green Gongyeong, as a commercial claim, is subject to the five-year statute of limitations, which therefore expired around July 20, 2007; and that, at the distribution date in this case, the Plaintiff, by subrogating to Green Gongyeong, objected to KRW 13,333,334 of the Defendant’s claim against Green Gongyeong and thereby invoked the defense of expiration of the statute of limitations, so that the Defendant’s claim against Green Gongyeong was extinguished within the above scope, is proper, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the law concerning commercial claims, the statute of limitations, and creditor subrogation, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by each appellant. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2016DA258124]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Statute of Limitations Period and the Principle of Party Presentation\\nThe grounds of appeal with respect to this part assert that the Defendants argued the 10-year statute of limitations period under the Civil Act, but the lower court violated the principle of party presentation by applying the 5-year statute of limitations period under the Commercial Act.\\n\\nIn civil litigation procedure, the principle of party presentation applies to allegations and proof concerning the primary facts that serve as requirements for determining the legal effects of the creation, modification, and extinction of rights. Therefore, a defense of extinctive prescription, which extinguishes a right, becomes a subject of the court’s determination only when there is an allegation by the party in accordance with the principle of party presentation.\\n\\nHowever, in this case, an assertion as to which statute of limitations period applies is not an allegation concerning facts constituting the requirements that give rise to the legal effect of the extinction of a right, but merely an expression of an opinion on the interpretation or application of law. Since the principle of party presentation does not apply to such an assertion, the court is not bound by the party’s allegation and may determine the matter ex officio (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on March 27, 2008, 2006DA70929, 70936, etc.). Even where a party has asserted the statute of limitations period under the Civil Act, the court may apply the statute of limitations period under the Commercial Act ex officio. Accordingly, the above argument of the Plaintiff is not accepted.\\n\\n2. Statute of Limitations Period for the Claim for the Land Purchase Price\\nThe lower court first found that: ① the Plaintiff concluded an agreement on a business arrangement with Seohae Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Seohae Development”) and jointly operated a business of constructing and selling pension-type multi-family housing on the project site in and around Taean-gun, Chungcheongnam-do; and then ② determined that the Plaintiff’s sale of the instant Lands 1 and 2 to the Defendants was an act done by a merchant for business purposes, and that the 5-year statute of limitations period applies to the claim for the sale price.\\n\\nIn light of the contents and purpose of the agreement between the Plaintiff and Seohae Development, as discernible from the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the role performed by the Plaintiff pursuant to the agreement, and the contents of the sales contracts concluded by the Plaintiff with the Defendants, it can be found that the Plaintiff sold the above lands to the Defendants for a land development and sale project jointly operated with Seohae Development. Accordingly, the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendants for the sale price constitutes a claim arising from a commercial act prescribed in Article 64 of the Commercial Act, and the commercial statute of limitations applies thereto. The lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper and, contrary to the grounds of appeal, does not err by misapprehending the legal principles regarding business acts or the commercial statute of limitations.\\n\\n3. Statute of Limitations Period for the Claim for Site Development Costs\\nThe lower court determined that the Plaintiff’s claim for site development costs falls under “claims concerning work of the contractor” prescribed in Article 163(3) of the Civil Act, and that the 3-year short-term statute of limitations applies. In light of the contents of the agreement concerning site development costs relied upon by the lower court, the Plaintiff’s status, and the method of calculation of the site development costs, the Plaintiff’s claim for site development costs can be deemed a claim concerning the work of the contractor. Accordingly, the above determination of the lower court is proper and does not err by misapprehending the legal principles concerning Article 163 of the Civil Act, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. Waiver of the Benefit of Prescription and Acknowledgment of Debt, etc.\\nThe Plaintiff argued that he had agreed with Defendant 1 to change the due date for payment of the sale price, or that the Defendants waived the benefit of prescription regarding the sale price or site development costs debt, or acknowledged the debt, thereby interrupting the running of the statute of limitations. The lower court determined that the Plaintiff’s assertion could not be accepted merely on the grounds that: ① around July 28, 2004 and around April 19, 2010, the Plaintiff completed the registration of transfer of ownership or co-ownership shares for part of the instant Land 1 to the non-party, who is Defendant 1’s spouse; and ② around April 19, 2010, the Plaintiff completed the registration of transfer of co-ownership shares for part of the instant Land 2 to Defendant 2.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles, the reasons of the lower court judgment reveal no error in the lower court’s determination by going beyond the limits of the free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the starting point of the statute of limitations, waiver of the benefit of prescription, and acknowledgment of debt.\\n\\n5. Whether There Was a Violation of the Principle of Good Faith and an Abuse of Rights\\nThe Plaintiff argued that the Defendants’ defense of extinctive prescription constituted an abuse of rights or violated the principle of good faith, but the lower court rejected the above argument, determining that it is difficult to find circumstances such as the Defendants having made it impossible or substantially difficult for the Plaintiff to exercise his rights or interrupt the running of prescription before prescription had matured, or having acted in a manner that led the Plaintiff to believe that such measures were unnecessary.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the above determination of the lower court is proper. The lower court’s determination contains no error in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the principle of good faith or abuse of rights, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\nSince the Plaintiff’s appeal is without merit, all of it is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged, in unanimous opinion of the Supreme Court Justices involved, as set forth in the disposition."}

question:
A entrusted B with the authority to sell A’s X land at an appropriate price and also granted B authority of representation with respect thereto. Among the following explanations, which are correct? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law governs)

(a) If D, knowing that B, as A’s agent, had concluded a sales contract with C concerning X land and had received the intermediate payment, actively requested B to sell, and B then, as A’s agent, sold X land again to D and even completed registration of transfer of ownership, the sales contract between A and D is void, even if A was unaware of these facts. 

(b) If B, as A’s agent, while concluding a sales contract with C concerning X land, committed unlawful duress against C, C may avoid the sales contract with A only if A knew or could have known of these facts. 

(c) If B, as A’s agent, concluded a sales contract with C concerning X land, and C failed to pay the balance on the agreed date, then if B gave C a demand for performance by setting a reasonable period and C still failed to pay the balance within that period, B may rescind the above sales contract. 

(d) If B, as A’s agent, concluded a contract designating himself as the purchaser of X land without A’s permission, the contract is void, absent special circumstances.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2007DA74713]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Determination of the grounds of appeal concerning agency authority\\n\\nWhen an agent who has been granted authority to conclude a certain contract performs the legal act within the scope of such authority, the legal relationship that constitutes the cause of that agency authority (the underlying internal relationship) is, in principle, deemed to have achieved its purpose and terminated; and because the agency authority granted by legal act is extinguished upon termination of the legal relationship that is its cause (Civil Act Article 128), it cannot immediately be said that a person who concluded the contract as agent thereby has, in addition, all powers of disposition, including the right to receive the other party’s intention to rescind the concluded contract, etc. (see Supreme Court Decision of October 21, 1957, 4290MINSANG461, 462; Supreme Court Decision of April 28, 1987, 85DAKA971, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the lower court, the lower court, on the basis of the evidence admitted, found, as stated in its opinion, the profit-sharing agreement concerning the collection of scrap metal between the Plaintiff and the Non-party, the circumstances and contents of the scrap-metal collection contract with a contract amount of 60,000,000 won concluded with the Defendant by the Non-party on behalf of the Plaintiff (hereinafter referred to as “the contract at issue”), the process by which the Plaintiff remitted the above contract amount to the Defendant pursuant thereto, the separate scrap-metal collection contract with a contract amount of 200,000,000 won concluded with the Defendant by the Non-party on behalf of the Plaintiff, and the circumstances and contents of the establishment of security pursuant to that contract, as well as the process by which the said 200,000,000 won was thereafter returned to the Plaintiff; then, with respect to the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendant for return of the contract amount of 60,000,000 won, asserting rescission of the contract at issue by service of a duplicate of the complaint, the lower court, taking the above circumstances into comprehensive consideration, rejected the Defendant’s assertion that the other party to the contract was the Non-party, and presumed that the Defendant had an obligation to return the above contract amount to the Plaintiff; then, with respect to the Defendant’s defense that the Defendant had already returned the contract amount of 60,000,000 won at issue to the Non-party, the Plaintiff’s agent, the lower court found that the Defendant paid a total of 51,000,000 won to the Non-party from February 2, 2005 to March 11, 2005, in the name of returning the contract amount at issue, and that the remainder of 9,000,000 won, etc. was set off against the Defendant’s claim against the Non-party for construction payment of 15,000,000 won, and that the Defendant received the contract amount at issue from the Non-party after preparing and delivering a contract withdrawal statement stating that it had received the contract amount at issue from the Non-party; and although it also appeared that the Plaintiff’s representative director, without meeting the Defendant in person, had the Non-party, acting as agent, conclude with the Defendant a separate scrap-metal collection contract other than the contract at issue with a contract amount of 200,000,000 won, and that the amount under that contract was paid, the lower court rejected the Defendant’s defense concerning agency authority on the ground that, inasmuch as the mere fact that authority to conclude a contract involving receipt and payment of money had been granted does not necessarily mean that authority to receive the contract amount to be returned upon termination of the contract relationship was also granted, it is difficult to find, on the basis of such circumstances alone, that the Plaintiff had given the Non-party authority, on the Plaintiff’s behalf, to receive the contract amount at issue from the Defendant, and that there was no other proof by the Defendant to that effect.\\n\\nThe above determination by the lower court is based on the above legal principles and, in light of the record, is proper; and there is no error of law, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the scope of agency authority or the principle of party presentation, or mistake of facts due to violation of the rules governing the taking of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court Decisions cited in the grounds of appeal, namely, Supreme Court Decision of October 18, 1962, 62DA508, and Supreme Court Decision of July 2.2, 1969, 69DA548, concern different facts and are not appropriate for invocation in this case.\\n\\n2. Determination of the grounds of appeal concerning apparent representation\\n\\nApparent representation beyond authority referred to in Civil Act Article 126 arises when a person who presently has agency authority exceeds that authority; it does not arise even where some act of agency performed on behalf of the principal by a person who presently has no agency authority whatsoever exceeds agency authority that the person had already held in the past (see Supreme Court Decision of July 30, 1973, 72DA1631; Supreme Court Decision of March 27, 1979, 79DA234, etc.). On the other hand, where agency authority held in the past has ceased to exist and apparent representation is recognized under Civil Act Article 129, if there is an act of agency exceeding the authority of such apparent representation, apparent representation under Civil Act Article 126 may be established (see Supreme Court Decision of February 10, 1970, 69DA2149). In addition, in order to assert the effect of apparent representation, it is required that the other party believed that the self-styled agent had agency authority and that there was justifiable reason for such belief; the existence or absence of such justifiable reason must be determined by objectively observing all circumstances existing at the time the self-styled agent’s act of agency was performed (see Supreme Court Decision of July 7, 1987, 86DAKA2475).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the lower court, the lower court rejected the Defendant’s defense concerning apparent representation on the ground that, at the time the Defendant paid money in the name of returning the contract amount at issue, the Non-party had no authority whatsoever delegated by the Plaintiff and therefore no basic agency authority could be found to exist, and that, even considering only the circumstances that the Non-party was involved, as stated in the lower court’s opinion, in the formation and termination process of the contract at issue and the scrap-metal collection contract with a contract amount of 200,000,000 won, it is difficult to find that the Defendant had justifiable reason to believe that the Non-party had authority to receive the contract amount at issue on behalf of the Plaintiff; and, in light of the above legal principles and the record, the above determination by the lower court is acceptable, and there is no error of law, such as mistake of facts due to violation of the rules governing the taking of evidence or misapprehension of the legal principles concerning “justifiable reason” in apparent representation under Civil Act Article 126, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court Decision cited in the grounds of appeal, namely, Supreme Court Decision of July 8, 1997, 97DA9895, concerns different facts and is not appropriate for invocation in this case.\\n\\n3. Determination of the grounds of appeal concerning ratification\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the lower court, the lower court recognized that, while the Defendant, pursuant to a separate scrap-metal collection contract, paid 200,000,000 won to the Plaintiff and issued one promissory note in the amount of 200,000,000 won with the Non-party as payee, there was no evidence whatsoever proving that the Plaintiff, knowing that the Non-party was designated as payee on the above promissory note, failed to object; furthermore, even assuming that the Plaintiff did not object, the lower court also rejected the Defendant’s defense concerning ratification on the ground that such circumstances alone make it difficult to find that the Plaintiff ratified the Non-party’s unauthorized agency act of receiving the contract amount at issue of 60,000,000 won; and, in light of the record, the above determination by the lower court is proper, and there is no error of law, such as mistake of facts due to violation of the rules governing the taking of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the appellate costs shall be borne by the losing party. The judgment is rendered unanimously by the Justices participating, as stated in the operative part."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the organs of a juristic person under the Civil Act is correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Even if a director has expressed an intention to resign, if the juristic person does not consent, the effect of the resignation does not arise.
B: If there is a request by an interested person or the prosecutor concerning a matter in which the interests of the juristic person and the director conflict, the court shall appoint a temporary director.
C: Since an auditor is a necessary standing organ, the auditor’s name and address are mandatory matters in the articles of incorporation.
D: An acting officer may, with permission from the competent authority, perform acts that do not fall within the ordinary affairs of the juristic person.
E: Even if the juristic person has prescribed in the articles of incorporation the grounds and procedures for dismissal of a director, and the grounds for dismissal have actually occurred, and even if the relationship of trust between the juristic person and the director has not reached the point where it is no longer difficult to maintain, the juristic person may dismiss the director in accordance with the procedures prescribed in the articles of incorporation.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2023DA263537]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Outline of the case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. The Defendant is a foundation corporation established around March 3, 1993, with the land, buildings, and endowments of its affiliated private temple as basic assets for the purpose of managing the property of a Buddhist organization. The Plaintiff was appointed around January 19, 2021, as a director and chairperson of the Defendant.\\n\\nb. When the Plaintiff did not convene an extraordinary board meeting despite the continued requests by the Defendant’s directors and auditors to do so, the Defendant’s directors and auditors convened and held an extraordinary board meeting on March 23, 2022 (hereinafter referred to as “the extraordinary board meeting in this case”), and adopted a resolution removing the Plaintiff from the position of director, appointing Nonparty 1 as a new director, and appointing standing director Nonparty 2 as chairperson (hereinafter the portion of the resolution removing the Plaintiff shall be referred to as “the dismissal resolution in this case”).\\n\\nc. Under Article 8 of the Defendant’s articles of incorporation, the grounds for dismissal of officers are: “acts contrary to the purpose of the corporation” (Item 1), “disputes among officers, accounting fraud, or manifestly improper conduct” (Item 2), and “acts obstructing the affairs of the corporation” (Item 3); and under Article 11(2), where there is improper conduct in the performance of duties by a director, dismissal may be effected by a resolution of at least two-thirds of the incumbent directors, in accordance with the auditor’s audit result.\\n\\nd. The audit result reported at the extraordinary board meeting in this case pointed out, among other things, that the Plaintiff had caused disputes among the officers, had committed manifestly improper conduct such as defamation or use of violence, or had obstructed the Defendant’s affairs by refusing to affix his seal to the minutes of the regular board meeting. The Defendant’s board of directors approved this audit result report and then reached the dismissal resolution in this case.\\n\\ne. The Plaintiff contends that, since he had not engaged in any “improper conduct in the performance of duties” under Article 8 and Article 11(2) of the articles of incorporation, the dismissal resolution in this case has a substantive defect and is void. In response, the Defendant contends that the Plaintiff engaged in “improper conduct in the performance of duties,” such as causing disputes among officers, and that this falls within the grounds for dismissal prescribed in Article 8 of the articles of incorporation; therefore, the dismissal resolution in this case is substantively lawful and valid.\\n\\n2. The lower court’s determination\\n\\nWith respect to the Plaintiff’s assertion that the dismissal resolution in this case is defective and therefore void, the lower court, after stating the legal principle that if there is no separate disciplinary provision for officers and dismissal results in a serious status-related disadvantage, namely the immediate deprivation of the office of officer, then only when the officer’s conduct has reached a point where the relationship of trust between the corporation and the officer can no longer be maintained does a justifiable ground for dismissal exist, accepted the Plaintiff’s claim by holding that, for the reasons stated in its judgment, it is difficult to conclude that grounds for dismissal existed to such an extent that the relationship of trust between the Plaintiff and the Defendant could no longer be maintained, and thus the dismissal resolution in this case had a substantive defect.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\na. The legal relationship between a corporation and a director is one akin to mandate, based on trust. According to Article 689(1) of the Civil Act, a mandate agreement may be terminated by either party at any time. Therefore, in principle, a corporation may dismiss a director at any time even before the expiration of the director’s term of office. However, since these provisions of the Civil Act are default rules, a corporation may, by its autonomous rules, namely its articles of incorporation, separately provide for the grounds and procedures for dismissal of directors. Such provisions not only clarify the relationship between the corporation and the director, but also have the significance of guaranteeing the director’s status; thus, they cannot merely be regarded as cautionary provisions. Accordingly, where the articles of incorporation of a corporation contain provisions concerning the grounds for dismissal of a director, the corporation may not dismiss the director for reasons not prescribed in the articles of incorporation, unless special circumstances exist, such as a serious breach of duty by the director or inability to properly perform ordinary affairs (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DA41741 decided November 28, 2013).\\n\\nb. The necessity of respecting the articles of incorporation, which are the autonomous rules of a corporation, is required not only when a corporation dismisses a director for reasons not prescribed in the articles of incorporation, but also when it dismisses a director for reasons prescribed in the articles of incorporation. If a corporation has prescribed in its articles of incorporation the grounds and procedures for dismissal of a director and those grounds for dismissal have in fact occurred, the corporation may dismiss the director for that reason in accordance with the procedure prescribed in the articles of incorporation. At that time, it is not the case that, in addition to the requirement that the grounds for dismissal prescribed in the articles of incorporation have arisen, an additional requirement must be satisfied, namely that the relationship of trust between the corporation and the director has reached a point where it can no longer be maintained, before the corporation may dismiss the director. Depending on the type or content of the grounds for dismissal, there are cases in which the grounds for dismissal themselves already presuppose the breakdown of the relationship of trust between the corporation and the director, or in which it is appropriate to consider this in the course of determining whether such grounds have arisen; however, even in such cases, it is ultimately sufficient to determine whether the grounds for dismissal have arisen by interpreting and applying the articles of incorporation provision concerning the grounds for dismissal itself, and it is not the case that the breakdown of the relationship of trust between the corporation and the director must be treated as a separate requirement and its fulfillment determined.\\n\\nc. In light of such legal principles, the portion of the lower court’s reasoning stating that a justifiable ground for dismissal exists only when the relationship of trust between the corporation and the director has reached a point where it can no longer be maintained is erroneous. However, in light of the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, since it appears difficult to conclude that the Plaintiff committed improper conduct in the performance of duties, which constitutes grounds for dismissal prescribed in Article 8 and Article 11 of the Defendant’s articles of incorporation, and therefore that no grounds for dismissal under the articles of incorporation arose, the lower court’s conclusion that the dismissal resolution in this case had a substantive defect is just and can be upheld, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the dismissal of officers, etc., thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the final appeal are to be borne by the losing party; it is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[92DA749]": "1. As to the grounds of appeal by counsel for the Plaintiff, the court below, with respect to the validity of the board resolution dated 1989.3.25. of the Defendant appointing Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 as directors, held that, although Nonparty 3 and Nonparty 4, the directors who participated in the above board resolution, could not be regarded as having exercised valid voting rights because the board resolution dated 1988.6.27. appointing them as directors was void and they therefore had no qualification as directors of the Defendant foundation, nevertheless, even excluding them, all three persons, namely the Plaintiff and Nonparty 5 and Nonparty 6, who were then lawful directors of the Defendant foundation, attended the board meeting and the resolution was adopted with the consent of the above two persons, Nonparty 5 and Nonparty 6, so that the above board resolution ultimately satisfied both the quorum for attendance and the quorum for resolution prescribed by the articles of incorporation and was therefore lawful. Then, according to the entries in Exhibit A No. 4-17 and Exhibit B No. 3-5 and the testimony of the witness Nonparty 6, the court below found that the above Nonparty 6 had held both the office of director and the office of full-time director (which, unlike the other directors, entailed always being in charge of and handling the affairs of the Defendant foundation), but around 1989.3. he resigned from the office of full-time director and, at the board meeting held on 1989.3.25., intended also to resign from the office of director, but changed his mind upon persuasion by the other directors, and therefore at the board meeting on that day he still validly exercised his authority in the status of director, and accordingly rejected the Plaintiff’s contention that the above Nonparty 6 was not a director at the time of the board meeting.\\n\\nFrom the above evidence adopted by the court below and the entries in Exhibit A No. 4-19, 4-20 and Exhibit B No. 4-3, it can be seen that the above Nonparty 6, while serving as full-time director of the Defendant foundation juristic person, submitted a letter of resignation around the end of 1989.2., and that although he also expressed his intention to resign at the board meeting held on 3.25. of the same year, the resignation was not accepted by Director Nonparty 5, and therefore he attended the above board meeting and participated in its resolution.\\n\\nA director of a foundation juristic person may terminate the legal relationship by a unilateral manifestation of intent to resign to the juristic person, and such manifestation becomes effective when it reaches the organ authorized to receive it; it is not effective only upon the juristic person’s acceptance. Therefore, once the above Nonparty 6 submitted a letter of resignation, the effect arose upon that letter’s reaching the Defendant foundation juristic person, and whether it was accepted by the Defendant foundation juristic person does not affect the effectiveness of the resignation.\\n\\nIn addition, unless there are special circumstances, such as the above Nonparty 6 stating in his letter of resignation that he was resigning only from the office of full-time director, it is proper to construe the letter as intending to resign from all of his offices, and it was erroneous for the court below, without evidence of any other circumstance, to distinguish between the office of full-time director and the office of non-full-time director and find that the above Nonparty 6 resigned only from the former and not from the latter.\\n\\nFurthermore, according to the entry in Exhibit B No. 3-5 and the testimony of the witness Nonparty 6 in the court below, in adopting the resolution on 1989.3.25. appointing Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 as directors, Director Nonparty 5, the above Nonparty 6, Nonparty 3, and Nonparty 4 voted in favor, while the Plaintiff voted against. As the court below found, the above Nonparty 3 and Nonparty 4 were persons appointed by a void resolution and had no qualification as directors, and upon the resignation of the above Nonparty 6, only the Plaintiff and the above Nonparty 5 would remain as lawful directors of the Defendant foundation juristic person; meanwhile, according to the articles of incorporation (Exhibit A No. 2), the directors of the Defendant foundation juristic person are elected by the board of directors and take office upon approval by the Minister of Labor, and a board resolution is opened when a majority of the incumbent members are present and is adopted by a majority of those present. Accordingly, the resolution appointing directors dated 1989.3.25. was made with only the above Nonparty 5 in favor because the Plaintiff opposed it, and thus a defect in the manner of resolution, namely the approval of a majority or more, is ultimately established.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below contains illegality in that it erred in fact due to a violation of the rule governing the evaluation of evidence, and since this affected the result of the judgment, the argument is well founded.\\n\\n2. As to the grounds of appeal by counsel for the Defendant\\n\\nEven under the Civil Act, if the articles of incorporation of a nonprofit foundation juristic person require that, before a board meeting is held, a notice of convocation stating the agenda and other matters be sent in advance within a certain period, but a director who did not receive such notice did not attend because the procedures concerning such convocation notice were not followed, and if some directors prepared minutes as if a meeting had been held or if only some directors gathered and held a board meeting without actually holding such a meeting, then such a board resolution should be regarded as nonexistent or as null and void ab initio. In such a case, even if a director who did not receive lawful notice attended and cast a dissenting vote, that would not alter the conclusion that the board resolution is null and void ab initio, even if it had no effect on the formation of the board resolution (see Supreme Court Order 68MA1283, 1968.12.9.; Supreme Court Judgment 85NU973, rendered 1987.3.24.).\\n\\nThe court below, based on the evidence it adopted, found that on 1988.6.17., Nonparty 7, then the chairman of the Defendant foundation juristic person, resigned in order to take responsibility for poor management, and that at the direction of Nonparty 5, Nonparty 6, then a full-time director, prepared the minutes as if a board meeting had been held on 6.27. and as if Nonparty 3 and Nonparty 4 had been appointed as directors and Nonparty 5 as chairman, and as if a resolution had been adopted to relieve Nonparty 7 from the office of director, without going through the convocation-notice procedures prescribed by the articles of incorporation or even holding a board meeting, and that he then affixed the seal of the Plaintiff, which was kept in custody, to those minutes and completed the registration procedure. The court below then held that the above-found board resolution did not exist or was null and void ab initio, and further held that even if the Plaintiff, who at that time had not received convocation notice, had attended and cast a dissenting vote, this would not affect the formation of the board resolution, and even if the content of the resolution in fact conformed to the will of the director who was unable to attend, the board resolution would still remain invalid and would not become lawful.\\n\\nThe above determination by the court below is proper, and it cannot be said that there is an illegality of misapprehension of legal principles as alleged. The argument is without merit.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, among the portion of the judgment of the court below adverse to the Plaintiff, the part concerning the resolution of the Defendant board of directors dated 1989.3.25. is vacated and this part of the case is remanded to the court below, the Defendant’s appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the judges participating."}

question: Party A entrusted A with the task of providing Party A's X land as collateral and procuring a loan of KRW 200,000,000, and also conferred agency authority in relation thereto. A, after receiving from Party A an identification card, a seal stamp, etc., and forging documents, entered into a sales contract with Party B to sell X land to Party B for KRW 300,000,000, claiming to be Party A's agent. Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (X) with respect to this matter? (Each statement is independent, and where there is disagreement, according to case law)
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2017DA213838]": "The grounds for final appeal are determined, insofar as the statement in the supplemental statement of grounds for final appeal submitted after the expiration of the deadline for submitting the statement of grounds for final appeal supplements the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding Grounds 1 and 3 for Final Appeal\\n\\nCivil Act Article 134 provides, “A contract entered into by a person without authority of agency may be withdrawn by the other party as against the principal or the agent until the principal ratifies it. However, this shall not apply if, at the time of the contract, the other party knew of the lack of authority of agency.” The other party’s right of withdrawal prescribed in Civil Act Article 134 is a right granted to the other party in order to protect the other party who did not know that there was no authority of agency, in consideration of the fact that an act of unauthorized agency leaves the other party in an unstable position because its effect depends on whether the principal ratifies it. If the other party validly withdraws, the act of unauthorized agency becomes conclusively void, and thereafter the principal may not ratify the act of unauthorized agency. Meanwhile, the burden of assertion and proof as to the point that the other party knew that the agent lacked authority of agency lies with the principal disputing the effect of withdrawal.\\n\\nThe lower court determined that, before ratification of the act of unauthorized agency, the Plaintiffs had withdrawn the second contract entered into through the act of unauthorized agency, and that, insofar as it was insufficient to find that the Plaintiffs knew of Defendant 1’s lack of mental capacity and Defendant 2, etc.’s act of unauthorized agency at the time of the second contract, the portion of the second contract concerning Defendant 1 was conclusively void, and that it was difficult to view the parties as having entered into the second contract even had the above void portion not existed; thus, it held that the second contract was void in its entirety.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record, the above determination by the lower court is proper, and there is no illegality, as asserted in the grounds for final appeal, in that it went beyond the limits of the free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or in misunderstanding the legal principles regarding withdrawal or ratification of an act of unauthorized agency, incomplete deliberation, failure to exercise the right to clarify, or otherwise.\\n\\n2. Regarding Ground 2 for Final Appeal\\n\\nWhere, in performance of a contractual obligation, a party has rendered performance to the other party, but the contract does not have effect because it is void or rescinded, the parties may each claim against the other party the return of the performance they rendered as restoration to the status quo ante; in such a case, one of the core functions performed by the law of unjust enrichment prescribed in Civil Act Articles 741 et seq. is to legally support the duty of restoration (see Supreme Court Decision dated March 11, 2010, 2009DA98706). Since such a system of unjust enrichment, on the ground of the ideal of equity and justice, imposes on the enriched person the obligation to return where the enriched person’s property gain lacks a legal ground, if no benefit has in fact accrued to the enriched person, such person cannot be burdened with the obligation of return (see Supreme Court Decision dated September 8, 2011, 2010DA37325, 37332, and Supreme Court Decision dated December 29, 2016, 2016DA242273, among others).\\n\\nAccording to the record, Defendant 1 collapsed from cerebral hemorrhage and became unconscious on February 15, 2015, immediately after the conclusion of the first contract, and accordingly Defendant 2 and the non-party, Defendant 1’s son, entered into the second contract on behalf of Defendant 1; on the day the second contract was concluded, the Plaintiffs paid the down payment of KRW 110,000,000 to Defendant 2, and the said Defendant drew up and delivered to the Plaintiffs a receipt to the effect that he had received the above down payment.\\n\\nExamining the above factual relationship in light of the foregoing legal principles, the KRW 110,000,000 delivered by the Plaintiffs at the time of the second contract was merely paid to Defendant 2, and it cannot be deemed that the said money was paid to Defendant 1; nor can it otherwise be deemed that the said money actually accrued to Defendant 1, who was in a state of lacking mental capacity.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court, by contrast, upheld the Plaintiffs’ claim for return of unjust enrichment against Defendant 1 on the premise that Defendant 1 had benefited from the above money; thus, in the lower court’s determination there is illegality that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning unjust enrichment. The grounds for final appeal pointing this out are meritorious.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nThe portion of the lower court judgment that ruled against Defendant 1 is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination; Defendant 2’s final appeal is dismissed; and the costs of final appeal, among the appellate costs, incurred by Defendant 2’s final appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[81DAKA549]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, by comprehensively considering the partial testimony of each of the witnesses at the court below, non-party 1 and non-party 2, the result of inspection of the criminal case records in the first instance, and the whole purport of the oral argument, held that the Defendant, around 1980.7.25, stated to the Plaintiff that he would repay only one half of the total amount of KRW 4,890,000 used by his wife in the name of the Defendant, and thereby ratified, within the scope of that amount, the unauthorized agency act of the non-party; and it determined that the Defendant is obligated to pay to the Plaintiff one half of KRW 4,890,000, namely KRW 2,445,000, and interest thereon.\\n\\nRatification of an unauthorized agency act is an expression of intention aimed at causing the effect of an uncertain act performed by an unauthorized agent to arise directly to oneself, and, as a unilateral act that does not require the consent or approval of the unauthorized agent or the other party, no particular form is required; accordingly, it does not matter whether it is express or implied. On the other hand, ratification must be made with respect to the whole of the declaration of intention, and if ratification is made only with respect to part thereof or ratification is made after altering its contents, it should be construed as invalid unless the consent of the other party is obtained. The foregoing holding of the court below concerns the Plaintiff’s argument that “the Defendant also, on several occasions, requested reconciliation from the Plaintiff with respect to his wife’s acts, and even if the foregoing act of assuming liability was an unauthorized agency, he ratified it; in particular, on 1980.7.25, he ratified it by proposing to non-party 3, non-party 2, non-party 1, etc. that he would repay one half of the borrowed money.” The substance of the testimony of witness non-party 1, which the court below relied on as evidence, is that the Defendant called non-party 4, non-party 5, non-party 3, non-party 2, etc. on 1980.7.25 and said that he would repay only one half of his wife’s debt and asked them to convey this to the Plaintiff; the substance of the testimony of witness non-party 2 is that the Defendant had the witness call the Plaintiff by saying that he would pay back half, and that the Plaintiff said that if he were to receive anything, he would receive it all, but would not receive half; and (in addition, no materials concerning ratification can be discerned from the result of inspection of the records). In light of the Plaintiff’s own assertions or the contents of the evidence cited, it is not clear whether the declaration of intention to repay only the half allegedly proposed by the Defendant was intended as ratification, and further, if it was intended as ratification, how ratification concerning only part of the declaration of intention could take effect as ratification; thus, it cannot be said that the judgment below is free from unlawfulness in that it misconstrued the Civil Act regarding ratification. Accordingly, the appeal is well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is quashed, and the case is remanded to the Daegu High Court for further trial and determination; the judgment is rendered as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question:
A contract of sale with a retention-of-title agreement concerning chattel X owned by Seller A and Buyer B was concluded, and pursuant thereto A delivered the chattel X to B. Which of the following statements concerning this is correct? (Each statement is independent, and where there is dispute, according to case law)

(a) If B pays the full purchase price to A, ownership of the chattel X is transferred to B immediately without any separate expression of intention.  
(b) If, while one-half of the purchase price has been paid, the chattel X is incorporated into the Y building owned by Principal C by B, the contractor, and if C was unaware, without negligence, of the fact of the retention-of-title agreement between A and B, then A cannot make a claim for compensation against C.  
(c) If, while one-half of the purchase price has been paid, B disposes of the chattel X to D, who knows of this fact, and thereafter A learns of B’s unauthorized disposition and ratifies the act of disposition, then D acquires ownership of the chattel X from the time A ratifies it.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2009DA15602]": "The grounds of appeal are considered.\\n\\n1. With respect to Ground 1 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nIn order for a certain movable property to be recognized as having become accession to immovable property pursuant to Article 256 of the Civil Act, it must be determined comprehensively whether it has been attached and integrated to such an extent that it cannot be separated without damaging the movable property or incurring excessive expense, and whether, in terms of its physical structure, use, and function, it has independent economic utility apart from the existing immovable property and can become an object of separate ownership in transactions (see Supreme Court Decision dated May 16, 2003, 2003DA14959, 14966), and the legal doctrine concerning such accession to immovable property applies equally to cases of an extension to a building (see Supreme Court Decision dated October 25, 2002, 2000DA63110) as well as to cases of new construction of a building.\\n\\nIn light of the above legal doctrine, the lower court’s determination that, notwithstanding the Plaintiff’s retention of title, the steel products at issue, which were owned by the Plaintiff, were used in the extension and new construction of the factory buildings and thereby became accession to the factory buildings, so that the Defendant, as the owner of the factory buildings, became the owner of the steel products at issue, is proper, and there is no illegality arising from misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning accession as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. With respect to Ground 2 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nA. Article 261 of the Civil Act provides that, where acquisition of ownership by operation of law by accession is recognized under Articles 256 through 260 of the Civil Act, “the person who has suffered damage may claim compensation pursuant to the provisions concerning unjust enrichment.” In order for such a claim for compensation to be recognized, not only must the requirements under Article 261 of the Civil Act itself be satisfied, but all requirements for unjust enrichment must be satisfied as determined under the legal doctrine of unjust enrichment.\\n\\nB. Where, because contractual relations are connected between the parties to a contract, ownership is transferred sequentially by each performance, the performance based on the contractual relationship constitutes a legal cause; accordingly, the initial performer may not claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the final recipient of performance on the ground that the recipient received the performance without legal cause (see Supreme Court Decision dated December 26, 2003, 2001DA46730).\\n\\nIn contrast, where a sale is effected while ownership of the object of sale is reserved, ownership of the object of sale is not transferred until the full purchase price is paid and only possession is transferred; thus, even if the buyer resells and delivers the object, a third party does not validly acquire ownership (see Supreme Court Decision dated September 7, 1999, 99DA30534). Therefore, a third party cannot refuse the owner’s claim for return merely on the basis of performance under such contractual relationship, and if the third party validly acquired ownership due to accession or other reasons, the general rule is that the value thereof is to be returned to the owner as unjust enrichment. However, even where ownership of the object of sale is reserved, if the third party who repurchased it is recognized as having acquired it in good faith, such good-faith acquisition constitutes a legal cause enabling retention of the benefit, and thus the third party would not bear such obligation to return.\\n\\nC. Furthermore, where materials for which ownership has been reserved by the seller are used by the buyer, pursuant to a contract for work with a third party, in the construction of a building owned by the third party and thus become accession thereto, and the seller loses ownership, although such materials were not directly delivered from the buyer to the third party, they were provided to the third party through performance under the contract for work and therefore have the substance similar to the transfer of movable property by transaction; accordingly, it is reasonable to analogically apply to the claim for compensation based on such accession the legal doctrine concerning retention of benefit in good-faith acquisition discussed above.\\n\\nTherefore, where materials for which ownership has been reserved by the seller become accession through performance of a contract for work entered into between the third party and the buyer, there is no legal cause for refusing the claim for compensation; however, if the third party did not know, without negligence, of the fact that ownership of the materials provided under the contract for work had been reserved, then, as in the case of good-faith acquisition, it is reasonable to find that the third party has a legal cause to retain the benefit arising from the attribution of such materials, and thus the seller would not be able to make a claim for compensation therefor.\\n\\nD. In light of such legal doctrine, in this case, where the steel products at issue, for which ownership was reserved in favor of the Plaintiff, were used in the extension and new construction of the Defendant’s factory buildings by performance under the contract for work by the non-party corporation and thus became accession to the factory buildings, the mere circumstance that accession occurred through performance under the contract for work does not mean that the Defendant had a legal cause to retain the benefit concerning those materials; however, if it is recognized that the Defendant did not know, without negligence, the circumstance that ownership of the steel products at issue, which became accession to the Defendant’s factory buildings, had been reserved in favor of the Plaintiff, then it should be deemed that the Defendant had a legal cause to retain the benefit concerning those materials, and the claim for compensation based on unjust enrichment should be denied.\\n\\nE. Accordingly, the lower court’s determination rejecting the Defendant’s argument that the Plaintiff, being merely a third party in the supply contract between the Plaintiff and the non-party corporation, could not directly seek unjust enrichment from the Defendant, is proper, and the portion of the Defendant’s grounds for appeal disputing this is without merit. However, in this case, in which the Defendant asserts that it was in good faith with respect to the circumstance that ownership of the steel products at issue had been reserved in favor of the Plaintiff, the lower court decision that upheld the claim for compensation based on unjust enrichment without determining whether the Defendant was in good faith and whether there was negligence contains illegality in misapprehending the interpretation of Article 261 of the Civil Act and the legal doctrine of unjust enrichment and in failing to conduct the necessary examination, and such illegality clearly affected the judgment. Therefore, the portion of the grounds for appeal pointing out this issue is meritorious.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the lower court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2017DA3499]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Grounds of Appeal Nos. 1 and 2\\n\\nA. For a right to be transferred by a juristic act, there must be a disposition act by the right holder or a person authorized to dispose. Where a person lacking the right disposes of another’s right, the right is not transferred absent special circumstances. However, in such a case, it is also permissible for the right holder to ratify the disposition by the person lacking the right, in accordance with the principle of private autonomy that one may form one’s legal relations according to one’s own will. Such ratification must be made with knowledge that the disposition by the person lacking the right has occurred, may be express or implied, and the manifestation of intent may be made to either the person lacking the right or the other party thereto (see Supreme Court Decision rendered June 2, 1964, 63DA880, Supreme Court Decision rendered November 9, 2001, 2001DA44291, etc.).\\nIf the right holder ratifies the disposition by the person lacking the right, then, because the interest situation between the parties is similar to the case where the principal ratifies an unauthorized agency, Civil Act Articles 130 and 133, etc. concerning ratification of unauthorized agency may be applied by analogy to ratification by the person lacking the right. Accordingly, where a disposition by a person lacking the right is effected by contract, if the right holder ratifies it, the effect of that contract should, in principle, be deemed to vest in the right holder retroactively to the time the contract was concluded.\\n\\nB. According to the judgment of the lower court, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n(1) The Plaintiff is the owner of the 2,882 square meters of land in Pyeongtaek-si (address omitted) (hereinafter referred to as “the land at issue”), as the mother of Nonparty 1.\\n\\n(2) Nonparty 1 entered and worked for the Defendant Association around December 21, 2010, and Nonparty 2, who had been friends with Nonparty 1, entered the Defendant Association around February 20, 1993, worked as the manager of the Defendant’s ○○○ Branch, and resigned around August 14, 2013.\\n\\n(3) Nonparty 2 and Nonparty 1 conspired to forge and then use a loan transaction agreement and a mortgage agreement, etc. in the Plaintiff’s name, and thereby, on May 18, 2012, established and registered in the Defendant’s name, with the Plaintiff as debtor and the maximum secured amount of KRW 322,000,000, a mortgage over the land at issue (hereinafter referred to as the “First Mortgage Registration”), and borrowed KRW 230,000,000. Thereafter, the Plaintiff filed criminal complaints against Nonparty 2 and Nonparty 1 for forgery of private documents, fraud, etc., and they were convicted.\\n\\n(4) After the First Mortgage Registration was made, on May 21, 2012, notice of completion of registration was given to the Plaintiff, who was the person who established it, pursuant to the relevant statutes.\\n\\n(5) When the Defendant fell into arrears in paying interest on the KRW 230,000,000 secured loan under the First Mortgage Registration, the Defendant sent the Plaintiff, in late August 2012, a notice of impending loss of benefit of term concerning the loan debt, and as the arrears continued thereafter, the Defendant urged the Plaintiff to pay the loan interest and, on November 16, 2012, sent the Plaintiff a notice of intended execution of voluntary auction based on the First Mortgage Registration at issue; the Plaintiff personally received it on November 19, 2012.\\n\\n(6) On December 31, 2012, the Plaintiff personally visited the Defendant’s ○○○ Branch, hand-signed the relevant documents (loan transaction agreement, mortgage agreement), and then, with respect to the land at issue, obtained from the Defendant a mortgage registration with the Plaintiff as debtor and the maximum secured amount of KRW 16,800,000 (hereinafter referred to as the “Second Mortgage Registration”), and borrowed KRW 14,000,000, of which KRW 13,237,000 was paid as interest on the secured loan under the First Mortgage Registration.\\n\\nC. Based on the above acknowledged facts, it should be deemed that the Plaintiff learned, through various notices including the notice of completion of registration concerning the First Mortgage Registration, that Nonparties 2, etc., who lacked the right, had made the First Mortgage Registration and obtained the loan. Thereafter, the Plaintiff made the Second Mortgage Registration in the Defendant’s name with respect to the land at issue and borrowed KRW 14,000,000, paying most of it as interest on the secured loan under the First Mortgage; thus, this may be regarded as an implied acknowledgment that the effects of the First Mortgage Registration and the secured loan validly accrued to himself/herself. In this way, by ratifying the disposition by Nonparties 2, etc., who lacked the right, the Plaintiff must be deemed to have caused the effects of the First Mortgage Registration and the secured loan to accrue to the Plaintiff.\\n\\nD. The lower court accepted the Defendant’s defense concerning “ratification of unauthorized agency,” finding that the Plaintiff had manifested to the Defendant an intention to have the legal effects arising from the First Mortgage Registration attributed to the Plaintiff. Although the lower court’s determination mischaracterized “ratification of a disposition by a person lacking the right” as “ratification of unauthorized agency,” the conclusion accepting the Defendant’s defense of ratification is sustainable. There is no error in the lower court’s determination, such as misapprehending the law on ratification, that affected the judgment, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Ground of Appeal No. 3\\n\\nThe Plaintiff argues that the lower court erred in fact-finding by believing, as is, the false testimony of Nonparty 3, the manager of the Defendant’s ○○○ Branch. However, this argument ultimately challenges the selection and weighing of evidence and fact-finding, which fall within the exclusive province of the lower court as the trier of fact, and thus cannot be regarded as a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n3. Ground of Appeal No. 4\\n\\nThe Plaintiff argues that the lower court erred by omitting a determination, despite the Plaintiff’s contention that the Plaintiff concluded the Second Mortgage Registration and loan transaction agreement due to the deceptive conduct of Nonparty 3, rescinded the same on the ground of fraud, and accordingly the effect of ratification was also extinguished retroactively.\\n\\nIn light of the record, there are no circumstances indicating that the Plaintiff concluded the Second Mortgage Registration and loan transaction agreement due to the deceptive conduct of Nonparty 3; under such circumstances, the fact that the lower court did not expressly determine this point does not mean that the lower court judgment contains an error affecting the result of the judgment due to omission of a determination.\\n\\n4. Ground of Appeal No. 5\\n\\nThe Plaintiff argues that, because the Plaintiff suffered damage of KRW 230,000,000 in loan principal due to the tortious acts such as forgery of private documents by Nonparty 2, the Defendant, as his employer, is liable to compensate for it, so the secured obligation under the First Mortgage Registration has been extinguished in full and the First Mortgage Registration must be cancelled.\\n\\nHowever, the lower court rejected the Plaintiff’s argument premised on the proposition that Nonparty 2’s act of establishing the mortgage constituted a tort, holding that the act of establishing the First Mortgage no longer constituted a tort due to the Plaintiff’s ratification.\\n\\nEven if, through ratification of the disposition by the person lacking the right, the effects of the First Mortgage Registration and the secured loan are deemed to have accrued to the Plaintiff himself/herself, this cannot be regarded as a waiver of a claim for damages based on tort against Nonparties 2, etc. or a claim for damages based on the Defendant’s employer liability. Even considering that the Plaintiff filed a criminal complaint against Nonparties 2 and 1 for forgery of private documents, fraud, etc., it cannot be said that the Plaintiff waived such claim for damages.\\n\\nHowever, according to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, it can be found that, when Nonparties 2 and 1 conspired to make the First Mortgage Registration with respect to the land at issue and borrowed KRW 230,000,000, KRW 149,000,000 of that amount was used to repay the principal and interest of the existing mortgage-secured debt that had been established in the Defendant’s name over the land at issue and over the land owned by Nonparty 1, and as a result the existing mortgage was cancelled. Accordingly, the damage suffered by the Plaintiff due to the tortious acts of Nonparties 2, etc. cannot be regarded as KRW 230,000,000, which corresponds to the loan principal, nor is there any circumstance from which it can be deemed that the secured obligation under the First Mortgage Registration was extinguished in full. Although it may be said that the lower court misapprehended the law concerning the establishment of liability for damages arising from tort, the conclusion rejecting this part of the Plaintiff’s argument is proper, and therefore there is no illegality that affected the result of the judgment.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Plaintiff’s appeal is groundless and is dismissed, and the appellate costs shall be borne by the Plaintiff. It is so adjudged, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the disposition."}
{"[96DA14807]": "The appeal is dismissed. The costs of appeal shall be borne by the Defendant."}

question: On 2023. 4. 1., A entered into a sales contract with B concerning land X owned by A. Under this contract, A and B agreed that, on 2023. 8. 31., they would perform delivery of land X and the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership in exchange for payment of the full purchase price. Which of the following statements concerning this are incorrect? (Each item is independent, and in the event of a dispute, case law shall apply) (a) If B paid the purchase price to A on 2023. 8. 31., but the sales contract between A and B is void, then, absent special circumstances, the statute of limitations for B's claim against A for restitution of unjust enrichment equivalent to the purchase price runs from the time B paid the purchase price. (b) Even if B had not paid the purchase price by 2023. 8. 31., as long as the defense of simultaneous performance is recognized against A, the statute of limitations on A's claim against B for the purchase price does not run. (c) If A delivered land X to B and completed the registration of transfer of ownership on 2023. 8. 31., but B did not pay the purchase price, and thereafter A applied for a provisional attachment of B's claim against C in order to secure A's claim for the purchase price of land X, and the order was served on C on 2023. 10. 1. but B was not notified of the provisional attachment, the statute of limitations on A's claim against B for the purchase price is not interrupted. (d) If A delivered land X to B and completed the registration of transfer of ownership on 2023. 8. 31., but B did not pay the purchase price, and thereafter A's creditor A brought an action against B seeking payment of the purchase price by subrogating A, the statute of limitations on A's claim against B for the purchase price is not interrupted.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2010DA80930]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding Ground 1 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nA judicial claim has no effect of interrupting the statute of limitations where the action is dismissed, rejected, or withdrawn; however, even in such a case, if a judicial claim, participation in bankruptcy proceedings, seizure or provisional seizure, or provisional disposition is made within 6 months, the statute of limitations shall be deemed to have been interrupted by the initial judicial claim (Civil Act Article 170).\\n\\nMeanwhile, because the effect of the exercise of the creditor’s subrogation right accrues to the debtor, the effect of interruption of the extinctive prescription caused by the filing of a creditor’s subrogation action also arises for the debtor.\\n\\nAccording to the facts recognized by the court below, the late Non-Party 1, on February 25, 2005, brought an action against the Defendant, subrogating Non-Party 2, seeking performance of registration procedures for the transfer of ownership, based on restitution of unjust enrichment, with respect to each of the real properties listed in the attached schedule to the judgment of the court below (hereinafter referred to as “the Real Properties at Issue”); thereafter, on May 14, 2008, in the appellate instance thereof (Seoul High Court Case No. 2008NA20500), the action was dismissed on the ground that the preserved right was not recognized, and that judgment became final and conclusive on June 5, 2008; Non-Party 3, after a lapse of slightly more than 3 months therefrom, on September 19, 2008, filed against the Defendant, subrogating Non-Party 2, an action for registration of transfer of ownership concerning the said real properties on the same grounds, but on December 4, 2009, in the appellate instance thereof (Seoul High Court Case No. 2009NA66268), a conciliation was concluded between the Defendant and him to the effect that the right to be preserved did not exist (hereinafter referred to as “the Related Conciliation at Issue”); and accordingly, the Plaintiff, on December 17, 2009, again filed against the Defendant, subrogating Non-Party 2, an action seeking performance of registration procedures for the transfer of ownership concerning the said real properties on the same grounds, and the like.\\n\\nExamining this in light of the above legal principles, the extinctive prescription of Non-Party 2’s claim against the Defendant for registration of transfer of ownership concerning the Real Properties at Issue, based on restitution of unjust enrichment, must be deemed to have been interrupted by the filing of the creditor’s subrogation action by the late Non-Party 1, the first judicial claim, in accordance with the successive creditor’s subrogation actions filed by the late Non-Party 1, Non-Party 3, and the Plaintiff.\\n\\nThe judgment of the court below to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning interruption of extinctive prescription, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Regarding Ground 2 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe court below, in light of the terms of the Related Conciliation at Issue and the cause of action thereof, held that the determination as to the existence or non-existence of the legal relationship formed in the related conciliation was limited to the conclusion that the partnership funds claim between Non-Party 3 and Non-Party 2, asserted as the right to be preserved in the relevant creditor’s subrogation action, had been extinguished and did not exist, and that no determination was made as to the existence or non-existence of Non-Party 2’s claim against the Defendant for registration of transfer of ownership, based on restitution of unjust enrichment, concerning the Real Properties at Issue; therefore, it held that the action at issue, in which the Plaintiff, subrogating Non-Party 2, sought against the Defendant performance of registration procedures for the transfer of ownership concerning the Real Properties at Issue, based on restitution of unjust enrichment, does not conflict with the res judicata of the Related Conciliation at Issue.\\n\\nExamining this in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the above determination by the court below is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning the scope of res judicata, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Regarding Ground 3 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nExamining the facts recognized by the court below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, since the Plaintiff’s creditor’s subrogation action at issue cannot be deemed contrary to the principle of good faith and fair dealing, even if the court below did not expressly make a determination thereon, the result of the judgment is not affected. The judgment of the court below contains no illegality, such as an omission of determination or lack of reasons affecting the result of the judgment, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged as ordered, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2021DA301688]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Overview of the Case\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\nA. The Head of the Guro Tax Office, pursuant to Article 177-4(2) and (5) of the former Local Tax Act (prior to its full amendment by Act No. 10221 of March 31, 2010; hereinafter referred to as the “former Local Tax Act”), assessed and notified the Plaintiff, on February 10, 2003 and September 10, 2003, a total of 101,768,940 won in inhabitant tax on income for the year 2000 (including additional charges, payment deadlines: May 31, 2003 and December 31, 2003) (hereinafter referred to as the “Disposition in this Case,” and the above assessed inhabitant tax as the “Inhabitant Tax in this Case”).\\n\\nB. The Plaintiff departed from Korea on September 24, 2001, before the Disposition in this Case, and the Head of the Guro Tax Office, on July 1, 2003 and February 6, 2004, made a write-off disposition with respect to the Inhabitant Tax in this Case under Article 30-3(1)4 of the former Local Tax Act on the grounds of the Plaintiff’s insolvency and unknown whereabouts, etc.\\n\\nC. The Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan Government, who is the authority entitled to collect the Inhabitant Tax in this Case, seized the Plaintiff’s claim for return of insurance premiums against MetLife Insurance Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “MetLife”) on September 19, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Seizure in this Case”), then collected 24,800 won from MetLife, and released the above seizure on August 10, 2007.\\n\\nD. The Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan Government seized and collected the Plaintiff’s deposit claims against Kookmin Bank Co., Ltd., etc. on December 24, 2010, and released the seizure on December 31, 2010.\\n\\nE. The Plaintiff returned to Korea on June 24, 2015, and on July 24, 2015 paid to the Defendant 56,058,980 won, which was part of the Inhabitant Tax in this Case (hereinafter referred to as the “Payment in this Case”).\\n\\nF. The Plaintiff filed this action against the Defendant, seeking the return of the amount equivalent to the Payment in this Case, alleging that “the tax payment notice for the Disposition in this Case was not lawfully served and is therefore void ab initio, and the Payment in this Case was also made after the five-year extinctive prescription period for the right to collect local taxes had expired.”\\n\\n2. Determination on the First Ground of Appeal\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment below, the court of second instance determined that the burden of proof regarding the Plaintiff’s assertion that the tax payment notice for the Disposition in this Case was not lawfully served rested on the Plaintiff, and that, based solely on the evidence submitted by the Plaintiff, it was not proved that the tax payment notice had not been lawfully served.\\n\\nIn light of the reasons of the judgment below, together with the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in this determination of the court below, as alleged in this ground of appeal, in that it did not go beyond the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by contravening the rules of logic and experience, or in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the burden of proof as to service of a tax payment notice, thereby failing to conduct the necessary review.\\n\\n3. Determination on the Second Ground of Appeal\\nA. Relevant Legal Principles\\n1) The main clause of Article 30-3(2) of the former Local Tax Act provides that “where the head of a local government, etc. discovers other property that may be seized after making a write-off disposition, he/she shall promptly revoke such disposition and conduct delinquent tax collection proceedings.” Article 14(3) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Local Tax Act (prior to its full amendment by Presidential Decree No. 22395 of September 20, 2010) provides that “where the head of a local government, etc. revokes a write-off disposition pursuant to Article 30-3(2) of the former Local Tax Act, he/she shall promptly notify the taxpayer, etc. of such revocation.” According to the wording, structure, and purpose of these provisions, where the head of a local government, etc. has made a write-off disposition regarding local taxes and thereafter intends to carry out delinquent tax collection proceedings such as seizure, the existing write-off disposition must be revoked and that fact must be notified to the taxpayer, etc. prior to the delinquent tax collection proceedings, and delinquent tax collection proceedings taken without going through such procedures for revocation and notification of the write-off disposition shall, absent special circumstances, be unlawful.\\n\\n2) Meanwhile, Article 30-5(1) of the former Local Tax Act provides that “the right to collect local taxes shall be extinguished by prescription if it is not exercised for five years from the time when the right may be exercised,” and Article 30-6(1)4 of the same Act provides “seizure” as one of the grounds for interruption of prescription.
