Since seizure as a delinquent tax collection measure is an administrative disposition, even if there is a defect, unless the defect is so grave and obvious that the seizure cannot be regarded as null and void ab initio, the mere existence of such defect cannot negate the effect of interruption of prescription caused by the seizure.\\n\\nB. Specific Determination\\n1) Reviewing the reasons of the judgment below and the record in light of the above legal principles, the seizure in this case contains a procedural defect if the existing write-off disposition regarding the Inhabitant Tax in this case was not revoked before the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan Government carried out the Seizure in this Case and that fact was not notified to the Plaintiff, who is the taxpayer.\\n\\n2) However, under the former Local Tax Act applicable to this case, a write-off disposition for local taxes came to have only the meaning of the termination of delinquent tax collection proceedings, and the revocation of a write-off disposition also had only the meaning of an administrative procedure that restarts terminated delinquent tax collection proceedings (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2010DU25527, decided March 24, 2011), and, as noted above, the Plaintiff continued to stay abroad from the time of the write-off disposition until the Seizure in this Case was effected; thus, even if the write-off disposition had been revoked before the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan Government carried out the Seizure in this Case and that fact had been notified through service by publication or other means, it appears that the Plaintiff would not have been able to recognize the fact of revocation of the write-off disposition. Taking these circumstances together, it is difficult to view the seizure in this case as null and void ab initio merely because the existing write-off disposition was revoked before the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan Government carried out the Seizure in this Case and that fact was not notified to the Plaintiff, since the defect cannot be deemed grave and obvious, and the effect of interruption of prescription caused by the Seizure in this Case cannot be denied.\\n\\n3) Reviewing the reasons of the judgment below and the record in light of the relevant legal principles, the portion of the court below’s reasoning stating that it is not necessary to go through the procedure for revocation of the write-off disposition before the Seizure in this Case is not appropriate, but the conclusion that the effect of interruption of prescription caused by the Seizure in this Case may be recognized is correct, and there is no error in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the effect of interruption of prescription of a seizure that omitted the procedure for revocation of the write-off disposition.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Third Ground of Appeal\\nA. In attachment of claims under the Civil Execution Act, even where, at the time a creditor attaches the debtor’s claim against a third obligor, the attached claim does not exist because it has already been extinguished, etc., absent special circumstances, the running of the statute of limitations for the execution claim is interrupted by the execution of the attachment (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DA47330, decided January 29, 2014), and the same applies to attachment of claims as a delinquent tax collection measure.\\n\\nB. Reviewing the reasons of the judgment below and the record in light of the relevant legal principles, although some portions of the court below’s reasoning are not appropriate, the conclusion that the effect of interruption of prescription may be recognized in the Seizure in this Case even if the Plaintiff’s claim for return of insurance premiums against MetLife had already been extinguished by prescription is correct, and there is no error in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the effect of interruption of prescription of an attachment directed at an attached claim whose extinctive prescription had already been completed.\\n\\n5. Determination on the Fourth Ground of Appeal\\nWhere a creditor provisionally seizes a debtor’s claim against a third obligor for the preservation of a claim, it is reasonable to view that the effect of interruption of the statute of limitations arises with respect to the creditor’s claim even if the debtor is not notified of the fact of such provisional seizure (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DA8589, decided May 16, 2019), and the same applies to attachment of claims as a delinquent tax collection measure.\\n\\nOn the same grounds, the court below determined that, even if the Plaintiff was not notified of the fact of attachment at the time of the Seizure in this Case, the effect of interruption of prescription may be recognized in the Seizure in this Case. This determination of the court below is correct, and there is no error in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the effect of interruption of prescription of attachment of claims, etc.\\n\\n6. Determination on the Fifth Ground of Appeal\\nThe gist of this ground of appeal is that the payment of insurance premiums by MetLife to the Defendant does not constitute a ground for interruption of the extinctive prescription of the right to collect the Inhabitant Tax in this Case.\\n\\nHowever, since the court below determined that the Seizure in this Case falls under a ground for interruption of the extinctive prescription of the right to collect the Inhabitant Tax in this Case, the Plaintiff’s argument merely misunderstands the court below’s determination and is without merit.\\n\\n7. Conclusion\\nThe appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2023DA302920]": "We address the first and second grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. According to Civil Act Article 166(1), the statute of limitations runs from the time when the right accrues objectively and the right can be exercised, and it does not run while the right cannot be exercised. Here, the expression “cannot be exercised” means that there is a legal impediment to the exercise of the right, such as the fact that the time has not yet arrived or a condition has not been fulfilled; even if, in fact, one did not know of the existence of the right or of the possibility of exercising the right, or there was no negligence in not knowing such facts, such circumstances cannot be said to constitute a legal impediment (see Supreme Court en banc Decision dated 1992. 3. 31., 91DA32053, Supreme Court Decision dated 2010. 9. 9., 2008DA15865, and Supreme Court Decision dated 2023. 2. 2., 2022DA276307, etc.). Therefore, a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment equivalent to the sale price, based on the invalidity of a sales contract, accrues, absent special circumstances, when the purchase price is paid, and it can be exercised at the same time as its accrual; accordingly, the statute of limitations runs from that time.\\n\\n2. For the reasons stated in its opinion, the lower court determined that, under Article 65(2) of the former Urban and Residential Environment Improvement Act (before amendment by Act No. 13508 on 2015. 9. 1.), the subject matter and scope of improvement infrastructure transferred free of charge are determined after new improvement infrastructure has been installed and the installation costs thereof have been specifically ascertained; thus, until the installation costs incurred for the newly installed improvement infrastructure are ascertained, the Plaintiff cannot exercise the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment, and this can be regarded as a state of legal impediment. On that basis, the lower court rejected the Defendant’s defense based on the statute of limitations.\\n\\n3. However, the lower court judgment is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons for the lower court judgment and the record, it can be seen that the Plaintiff entered into the sales contract in this case with the Defendant on 2015. 8. 20., and paid to the Defendant a contract deposit of 417,419,820 won on the day of the contract and the balance of the purchase price of 3,756,778,400 won on 2015. 10. 16., respectively.\\n\\nThe Plaintiff is seeking restitution of unjust enrichment equivalent to the purchase price, alleging that the sales contract in this case is invalid; therefore, the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment asserted by the Plaintiff accrued when each of the above amounts was paid, and could be exercised at the same time. The statute of limitations also runs from that time. However, it is clear from the record that the Plaintiff filed this action only on 2021. 8. 27., after five years, which is the statute of limitations period prescribed by Local Finance Act Article 82(2), had elapsed from the above dates of payment. Then, in light of the legal principles stated above, there is room to view that the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment asserted by the Plaintiff was extinguished by the completion of the statute of limitations, and it is difficult to further view that there existed a legal impediment to the exercise of that right, such as the non-arrival of the period or non-fulfillment of a condition.\\n\\nThe lower court judgment, which, contrary to the above, found a legal impediment and rejected the Defendant’s defense based on the statute of limitations, erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the starting point of the statute of limitations, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the portion of the lower court judgment that ruled against the Defendant is set aside, and this part of the case is remanded to the lower court for further proceedings and determination. Accordingly, the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[90DA9797]": "With respect to the grounds of appeal by the Defendants’ litigation counsel\\n\\n1. The lower court, on the basis of the evidence it admitted, found that the deceased Choi Byeong-hui purchased, on 1964.9.24. (lunar calendar 8.19), the real property in this case and six other parcels of real property from the Defendants, and that the deceased Im No-seon, who is the father of the Plaintiffs, purchased the real property in this case from the said Choi Byeong-hui on the same day, and further found that there was an agreement on intervening registration between the said decedents and the Defendants with respect to the real property in this case; such findings of fact are proper, and there is no illegality of violation of the rules of evidence or error in the interpretation of the probative force of dispositive documents as asserted in the argument.\\n\\nThe lower court also, in response to the Defendants’ assertion that they had received no payment of the purchase price for the real property in this case from the said Im No-seon and therefore could not comply with the Plaintiffs’ claim for registration of transfer of ownership, rejected the Defendants’ argument by finding that the said Im No-seon had paid the entire purchase price to the Defendant Cho Seon-hui by 1964.12.3. (lunar calendar 10.30), the due date for payment of the balance of the purchase price of the real property, and that, even if not, the Defendants’ claim for the said purchase price had been extinguished by prescription on 1974.12.3., ten years after the said due date for payment of the balance; however, even upon examining the evidence adopted by the lower court as above, no material can be found to support the conclusion that the purchase price had all been paid, and therefore the lower court’s finding in this regard cannot but be said to be erroneous.\\n\\nNevertheless, the hypothetical determination that the claim for the purchase price was extinguished by prescription is proper, and thus the above error does not affect the result of the judgment. Even if the claim for the purchase price of the real property in this case is in a concurrent performance relationship with the claim for registration of transfer of ownership, the vendor may demand payment of that price at any time after the due date for payment of the purchase price, and the purchaser may merely refuse such payment until the purchaser receives tender of performance concerning the transfer registration from the vendor; therefore, it shall be deemed that the claim for the purchase price is subject to the running of prescription after the due date for payment. The argument ultimately lacks merit.\\n\\n2. Since a claim for registration of transfer of ownership is a claim under the law of obligations, it is subject to the ten-year statute of limitations; however, so long as the purchaser has received delivery of and is in possession of the real property that is the subject matter of the sale, the statute of limitations does not run regardless of whether the purchase price has been paid (see Supreme Court Decisions 76DA148, decided on 1976.11.6.; 79DA1799, decided on 1980.1.15.; 86DAKA2908, decided on 1988.9.13.).\\n\\nThe lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality of error in the interpretation of the law as asserted in the argument. The argument is without merit.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal are assessed against the losing parties, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices as stated in the Disposition."}

question:
A constructed the X building on the Y land owned by C and acquired it by original acquisition, then sold and delivered the X building to B in an unregistered and unpermitted state, and the ownership transfer registration in B’s name for the X building has not yet been completed. Of the following explanations, which are all correct? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, the precedents shall apply)

(a) If B, after paying the purchase price in full to A, sold the X building to D and delivered it, and A exercises a real right claim for return against D, D may assert against A his own right of possession and use.

(b) If B has paid the purchase price in full to A, B is recognized as having a legal status with respect to the X building as a customary real right equivalent to ownership or as de facto ownership.

(c) If B has paid the purchase price in full to A, and B already has a matured loan claim against C, and C, because A has no right to use the Y land, has brought against A a claim for return of unjust enrichment equivalent to rent for the Y land, A may set off the said claim of B, only to the extent of B’s share of the burden, by treating it as the active claim.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2011DA64782]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. The “third party” prescribed in the proviso to Article 548(1) of the Civil Act refers to a person who not only has acquired a new interest based on the legal effects arising from the rescinded contract, but has also acquired complete rights by registration, delivery, or the like (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 95DA49882 dated April 12, 1996).\\nHowever, a purchaser of an unregistered unauthorized building cannot acquire ownership of that building unless the ownership transfer registration is completed, cannot be said to have a customary real right equivalent to ownership, and it is also difficult to recognize, under current law, a comprehensive right or legal status called de facto ownership (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DA49000 dated October 27, 2006).\\nIn addition, the register of unauthorized buildings is prepared merely for the convenience of management concerning unauthorized buildings and is not prepared for the purpose of public notice of the rights relationship concerning them; therefore, the mere fact that a person is entered as the owner in the register of unauthorized buildings has no effect of acquiring ownership or any other right concerning the unauthorized building (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 92DA36274 dated January 26, 1993).\\nAccordingly, even if, before the sales contract concerning an unregistered unauthorized building was rescinded, a person repurchased the unauthorized building from the purchaser thereof and was entered as the owner in the register of unauthorized buildings, such person cannot be deemed to have acquired complete rights over the building, and therefore cannot be said to fall within the third party prescribed in the proviso to Article 548(1) of the Civil Act.\\n\\n2. Examining the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below in light of the record, the court below, on the grounds stated in its opinion, held that the Defendant was not a third party who acquired complete rights by registration, delivery, or the like, and therefore the Plaintiff may assert against the Defendant the effect of the rescission of the contract at issue; this is proper, and there is no illegality such as a misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the legal status of a purchaser of an unregistered unauthorized building or the scope of the third party under the proviso to Article 548(1) of the Civil Act, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[93DA21521]": "1. First, we examine the grounds for appeal by Plaintiff’s counsel.\\n\\na. As to Point 1\\n\\nUnder the provision of Article 126 of the Civil Act concerning apparent agency beyond authority, the term “third party” refers only to the person who became the direct counterparty to the relevant act of apparent agency, and the same should also apply when that provision is applied or analogically applied to bill acts such as endorsement (see this Court’s Decision 84DAKA2310, rendered on September 9, 1986). Also, the direct counterparty to an endorsement act on a promissory note refers only to the endorsee who acquired the note by that endorsement, and a person who thereafter acquired the note from that endorsee cannot be deemed a third party under Article 126 of the Civil Act. However, where the endorsement act satisfies the requirements for apparent agency in relation to the endorsee, who is the direct counterparty, it may separately be permitted for a subsequent acquirer of the note to invoke it (see this Court’s Decision 91DA3994, rendered on June 11, 1991).\\n\\nAccording to what the lower court lawfully found, the endorsement in Defendant’s name on the promissory note No. 1 in this case, naming the non-party Taeyang PR Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to only as “Taeyang PR”) as the endorsee, was forged by Non-party 1, who was serving as the executive director in charge of general affairs of Defendant, in collusion with Non-party 2, the representative director of Taeyang PR, beyond his authority, by using the corporate name plate for document dispatch and the seal of the representative partner that he had in his possession. Since Plaintiff did not acquire the note by direct endorsement and transfer from Defendant, but rather received a further endorsement from Taeyang PR, it is self-evident that apparent agency under Article 126 of the Civil Act cannot be established with respect to Non-party 1’s endorsement act. Unlike this, the lower court judgment, which did not accept Plaintiff’s argument that Non-party 1’s act of issuing the note constituted apparent agency under Article 126 of the Civil Act on the premise that Plaintiff itself fell within the category of a third party under Article 126 of the Civil Act, is proper, and the argument is without merit.\\n\\nb. As to Point 2\\n\\nAccording to the record, until the case reached the lower court, Plaintiff merely argued that the accounting staff of Defendant company or Non-party 1 had ratified, vis-à-vis Defendant, the endorsement made by Non-party 1 on promissory note No. 1 in this case and the endorsement made by Non-party 2 on the remaining promissory notes, but there is no trace of any argument that each such ratification satisfied the requirements for apparent agency, nor does Plaintiff make any concrete argument as to how the above ratification satisfied the requirements for apparent agency. Accordingly, the argument that the lower court judgment is unlawful for failing to determine the issue of apparent agency concerning the above ratification is without merit.\\n\\nc. As to Point 3\\n\\n(1) The lower court’s determination\\n\\nWith respect to Defendant’s liability for damages concerning promissory note No. 1 in this case, the lower court acknowledged that Non-party 1’s act of forging the endorsement in Defendant’s name on the above promissory note was not an act in the performance of his duties, but that, in light of all the circumstances, such as the content of the duties he performed as the executive director in charge of general affairs of Defendant company and the possession of the name plate and seal used, Non-party 1’s above act outwardly appeared to be an act closely related to his duties. Accordingly, the lower court held that Defendant, as the employer of Non-party 1, is obligated to compensate for damages in the amount of KRW 32,955,398, which is the amount of the bill discount, incurred by Plaintiff by acquiring the note whose endorsement had been forged by Non-party 1 as above. As to Defendant’s defense of set-off, the lower court held that Defendant company’s liability to Plaintiff for damages, as the employer of Non-party 1, and Taeyang PR’s liability to Plaintiff for damages arising from a tort related to the duties of its representative director, Non-party 2, are in a relationship of mutual quasi-joint and several liability, and that, as between Defendant company and Taeyang PR, the above liability for damages is an obligation that Taeyang PR must bear in full. The lower court further held that, when Plaintiff discounted the above note, it had Taeyang PR subscribe to a credit installment deposit in the amount of KRW 180,000,000 and received KRW 32,053,000, which it held on deposit, but that the above deposit contract was rescinded immediately on December 17, 1990, when the notes entrusted by Taeyang PR for discounting began to be dishonored, and that, since Defendant’s preparatory brief dated September 14, 1992, asserting set-off with respect to the claim for return of the principal paid into the above deposit, was served on Plaintiff’s counsel on the 18th of the same month, Plaintiff’s claim for damages against Defendant was extinguished within the limit of Taeyang PR’s claim for return of the deposit in the amount of KRW 32,053,000, and the lower court accepted such defense.\\n\\n(2) This Court’s determination\\n\\nThe lower court did not clearly state the ground on which Defendant could set off using Taeyang PR’s claim against Plaintiff as the active claim, but in light of the overall purport of the lower court judgment, the lower court appears to have applied Article 418(2) of the Civil Act, which provides that “where a solidary obligor having a claim subject to set-off does not effect set-off, another solidary obligor may set off only to the extent of that obligor’s burden share,” to this case.\\n\\nHowever, in order to apply the above provision, it must first be premised that a solidary obligor who has a claim against the creditor may set off that claim against its own obligation to the creditor. Also, even where another solidary obligor exercises the right of set-off under the above provision, the passive claim in such set-off remains the original obligation of the solidary obligor who was the original holder of the right of set-off (provided that, when the above obligation is extinguished, the obligation of the other solidary obligor who exercises the right of set-off is also extinguished as a result), and the obligation of the other solidary obligor who actually exercises the right of set-off to its creditor does not directly become the passive claim in the set-off. Therefore, the lower court should first have examined whether Taeyang PR’s obligation to Plaintiff could be subject to set-off, and only if it could be subject to set-off should it have accepted the same; yet the lower court, mistaking Plaintiff’s claim for damages against Defendant for the subject of set-off on the premise that Taeyang PR’s claim against Plaintiff could serve as the active claim for set-off, accepted the above set-off argument without examining and determining whether Taeyang PR’s obligation to Plaintiff could be subject to set-off. This cannot but be deemed an error in misunderstanding the law of set-off under Article 418(2) of the Civil Act and in failing to provide reasons.\\n\\nFurthermore, leaving aside the question of whether, in general, a set-off by one quasi-joint and several obligor has the effect of joint discharge or absolute effect even in relation to the other quasi-joint and several obligors, there is no burden share in the strict sense between quasi-joint and several obligors. Therefore, Article 418(2) of the Civil Act, which presupposes the existence of such burden share in the strict sense, should be understood as not applying to quasi-joint and several obligations. Accordingly, in quasi-joint and several obligations, even if one quasi-joint and several obligor has a claim against the creditor that is capable of set-off but does not effect set-off, another quasi-joint and several obligor cannot set off using that claim. In this respect as well, the lower court judgment committed an error in misunderstanding the legal principle that the above provision cannot be applied to quasi-joint and several obligations.\\n\\nOn the other hand, Plaintiff argued in the lower court that Taeyang PR, etc. had already caused all of the credit installment deposits they had paid to accrue to Plaintiff by violating the deposit contract, and therefore there was no obligation to return the paid credit installment deposits, so Defendant’s above set-off defense lacked merit (record, pp. 416, 429, etc.). Although the purport is not clear, if Plaintiff itself appropriated the above paid credit installment deposits to the satisfaction of its claim for damages against Taeyang PR, that could also affect the claim in this case; accordingly, the lower court would also need to clarify and determine this point. The argument has merit.\\n\\nd. As to Point 4\\n\\n(1) The facts found by the lower court with respect to the promissory notes in this case, other than the above promissory note No. 1, are as follows.\\n\\nThat is, Non-party 2, the representative director of Taeyang PR, engraved a corporate name plate bearing the name “Joseon Murak Limited Partnership Company,” in which only the syllable “yak” in Defendant company’s name, “Joseon Muyak Limited Partnership Company,” was changed to “rak,” and a seal of the representative partner in the name of Non-party 3, the representative partner of Defendant company, and used them to endorse the above remaining promissory notes Nos. 2 through 15 in the name of “Joseon Murak Limited Partnership Company, Representative Non-party 3,” then re-endorsed them to Plaintiff and obtained bill discounts. Non-party 4, Plaintiff’s sales manager, whenever discounting the above promissory notes, inquired of Non-party 5, Section Chief ○, and Non-party 6, a female employee, and others in Defendant company’s accounting department as to whether Defendant had endorsed them. However, Non-party 5, etc., having received instructions from Non-party 1, the executive director in charge of general affairs, to answer that Defendant company had endorsed the notes when inquiries were made about the authenticity of the endorsement in Defendant company’s name appearing on the notes that Taeyang PR had requested to be discounted, answered accordingly that the endorsement in Defendant company’s name on the above notes Nos. 2 through 15 was genuine, even though those notes were not entered in Defendant company’s bill ledger, and Non-party 4 discounted the notes, believing that the endorsements on each of the notes were genuine endorsements made by Defendant.\\n\\n(2) Based on the above factual findings, the lower court held that Defendant company’s staff, acting according to Non-party 1’s instructions, responded to inquiries without discovering the forged endorsement under the name of Joseon Murak Limited Partnership Company, which was similar to Defendant company’s name, on the notes Nos. 2 through 15, and that their response that the endorsement in Defendant company’s name on each note was duly made, even though the above notes were not entered in Defendant company’s bill ledger, constituted a tortious act of deceiving the other party by conveying false facts. The lower court further held that this was one cause of preventing Plaintiff company’s staff, who incorrectly believed the endorsement under the name of Joseon Murak Limited Partnership Company on each note to be an endorsement in Defendant company’s name, from discovering such mistake, and that since such conduct, in light of the duties of Non-party 1 and Defendant company’s accounting department staff, outwardly appeared to fall within their scope of duties, Defendant company is liable, as the employer of Non-party 1, etc., to compensate for the damages suffered by Plaintiff due to their tortious acts. However, the lower court held that no liability for damages could be imposed with respect to notes Nos. 11, 14, and 15, which Plaintiff did not present within the lawful presentment period, and further held that, even though Plaintiff’s staff should also have carefully examined the endorsement in the name of Joseon Murak Limited Partnership Company on the remaining notes and discovered that the endorsement name differed from Defendant company’s name, they failed to do so and instead discounted each of the above notes trusting only what Defendant company’s accounting staff said; such negligence by Plaintiff was one cause of the occurrence and expansion of the damage in this case. Accordingly, in determining the amount of damages Defendant company must compensate for with respect to the remaining promissory notes other than notes Nos. 11, 14, and 15, the lower court considered Plaintiff 70% negligent and ordered Defendant to compensate for only 30% of Plaintiff’s damages.\\n\\n(3) However, even if Plaintiff was negligent in mistaking the endorsement under the name of Joseon Murak Limited Partnership Company for an endorsement under Defendant company’s name, the above endorsement merely replaced the syllable “yak” in Defendant company’s name with the very similar syllable “rak,” so that unless one examined it carefully, it would be difficult to discover that fact. Moreover, in light of the fact that the address of the endorser or the name of its representative stated in the above endorsement corresponded to Defendant company’s actual address and the name of its representative, and in light of the fact that Plaintiff took steps to confirm with Defendant company when discounting the above notes, even considering that Plaintiff is a financial institution specializing in bill discounting, it would be difficult to say that Plaintiff’s above negligence was that serious. (According to the record, it can be seen that other financial institutions, in addition to Plaintiff, also discounted notes bearing endorsements in the name of Joseon Murak Limited Partnership Company forged by Non-party 2 in the same manner, believing them to be notes endorsed by Defendant.)\\n\\nMeanwhile, if one looks at the negligence on Defendant’s side as revealed in this case, the fact that Defendant’s employee answered that Defendant had endorsed the notes without confirming whether Defendant had actually endorsed the notes is intentional conduct or gross negligence close to intent, and the negligence of Defendant in failing to properly supervise such employees cannot be deemed light either. In comparison with such negligence by Defendant, the lower court’s view that Plaintiff’s negligence ratio was as high as 70%, more than twice Defendant’s negligence ratio, ultimately miscalculated the ratio of comparative negligence and led to a result that is manifestly contrary to equity; thus, the argument pointing out this point also has merit.\\n\\n2. Next, we examine the grounds for appeal by Defendant’s counsel.\\n\\nAs examined above, even if Plaintiff was negligent in mistaking the endorsement under the name of Joseon Murak Limited Partnership Company for an endorsement under Defendant’s name when discounting the promissory notes Nos. 2 through 15 in this case, and even if Defendant’s employees, in response to Plaintiff’s inquiry, mistakenly believed that the above notes had been endorsed in Defendant company’s name and answered that the endorsement was genuine, as long as Plaintiff acquired the notes in this case by believing such false responses from Defendant’s employees, a legal causal relationship between Plaintiff’s resulting damage and the unlawful acts of Defendant’s employees cannot be denied (see this Court’s Decisions 92DA46370, rendered on February 26, 1993, and 92DA54456, rendered on May 25, 1993). The lower court judgment, which reached the same conclusion, is proper, and no illegality as alleged can be found therein. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n3. Accordingly, Plaintiff’s appeal is meritorious, so the portion of the lower court judgment adverse to Plaintiff is reversed and this part of the case is remanded to the lower court; Defendant’s appeal is without merit, so it is dismissed; and the costs of this portion of the appeal shall be borne by the losing Defendant. The opinions of the participating Justices are unanimous, and the judgment is rendered as follows."}

{"[97DA42823]": "The judgment of the court below shall be reversed as to the portions against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, and this case shall be remanded to the Collegiate Division of the Principal Branch of the Busan District Court. The Plaintiff’s appeal and Defendant 1’s appeal shall both be dismissed. The costs of appeal as to the portions for which the appeals are dismissed shall be borne by each respective appellant."}

question: Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (X) regarding correction registration? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents)
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2012DA952]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. As to the grounds of appeal concerning the claim for cancellation of the sales reservation and restitution regarding the real properties listed in items 2 through 5, 7, 9, and 11 through 16 of the list appended to the judgment of the court below (hereinafter referred to as the “Attached List”)\\na. If a creditor’s action to revoke a fraudulent conveyance and claim restitution is upheld, the beneficiary or subsequent transferee bears the obligation to return the subject matter of the fraudulent conveyance to the debtor as restitution. If return of the original property is impossible or manifestly difficult, compensation in an amount equivalent to the value of the subject matter of the fraudulent conveyance must be made as performance of the duty of restitution. Here, the case where return of the original property is impossible or manifestly difficult does not mean only a case where return of the original property is absolutely and physically impossible, but refers to a case where, in light of the rules of experience in social life or commercial notions, the creditor cannot expect performance to be realized from the beneficiary or subsequent transferee (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 97DA58316, decided May 15, 1998).\\nWhere a provisional registration has been completed for real property owned by the debtor in order to preserve a right to demand transfer of ownership, the provisional registration itself does not give rise to the effect of ownership transfer, but if the final registration is later completed, the effect of a change in ownership arises retroactively to the time of the provisional registration, and as a result the creditor may be unable to obtain full satisfaction from the debtor’s property and may thereby be prejudiced (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 74DA334, decided February 10, 1975). Accordingly, the legal act constituting the cause of the provisional registration that harms the creditor is subject to cancellation as a fraudulent act, and if that legal act is revoked as a fraudulent act, the provisional registration holder, unless special circumstances exist, bears the duty to cancel the provisional registration, which is the obligation to return the original property, as restitution following such cancellation. Meanwhile, the claim for a change in a real right, which is the subject of priority preservation by means of a provisional registration, is, by its nature, not only a property right that may be transferred, but also a right whose publicity is secured by the provisional registration and, consequently, for which a method of public notice has been provided. Therefore, where such right is transferred, the transfer of the right recorded in the provisional registration may be effected in the form of an additional registration to the provisional registration, upon a joint application by the transferor and the transferee (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 98DA24105, decided November 19, 1998).\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, even if, after a provisional registration was completed in the name of the beneficiary based on a sales reservation constituting a fraudulent act, an additional registration of transfer of the provisional registration was completed in the name of a subsequent transferee, and further even if the final registration based on that provisional registration was completed, such additional registration merely indicates the transfer of the beneficiary’s right based on the sales reservation constituting the fraudulent act, and the status as beneficiary does not cease by virtue of such additional registration. Accordingly, the creditor may seek cancellation of the sales reservation constituting the fraudulent act against the beneficiary. And even if, as a result of the additional registration, performance of the duty to cancel the provisional registration, which is the beneficiary’s duty to return the original property, becomes impossible due to reasons such as the beneficiary’s lack of standing as a defendant in an action for cancellation of the provisional registration and the final registration, this does not warrant a different conclusion. Unless special circumstances exist, the beneficiary shall bear the duty to compensate the value as restitution with respect to the insufficiency of the common security of creditors arising from the provisional registration and the final registration.\\nBy contrast, Supreme Court Decision 2004DA70079, decided March 24, 2005, and the like, to the extent that they are contrary to the view of this judgment, are modified to that extent on the ground that, where a provisional registration completed by a sales reservation constituting a fraudulent act is transferred by an additional registration and the final registration based on that provisional registration is completed, the transferor of the right under that provisional registration cannot be a party defendant in a lawsuit for cancellation of the provisional registration and is not the nameholder of the final registration, and thus does not bear a duty to compensate value.\\nb. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the evidence lawfully admitted, (1) on September 13, 2006, with respect to the real properties listed in items 2 through 5, 7, 9, and 11 through 16 of the Attached List, owned by Non-Party 1, each provisional registration of the right to demand transfer of ownership in the name of Boeun General Timber Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Boeun General Timber”), based on the sales reservation dated August 31, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “sales reservation in this case”), was completed, and then on September 18, 2006, the registrar, ex officio and on the ground of discovery of error, completed each additional registration correcting the provisional registration holder to Defendant 1 and Boeun General Timber; (2) thereafter, as stated in the judgment of the court below, it can be seen that with respect to the said real properties, each additional registration of transfer of the provisional registration was completed in the name of each allottee or transferee, on the ground of sale or transfer of contract, and then the final registration based on each such provisional registration was completed.\\nc. Examining the foregoing factual relationship in light of the legal principles set forth above, in this case seeking cancellation of the sales reservation in this case on the ground that it constitutes a fraudulent act, the Plaintiff, as the creditor, may seek cancellation of the sales reservation against Defendant 1 and Boeun General Timber, who are beneficiaries of the sales reservation in this case, and even if performance of the duty to cancel the provisional registration in the names of the said beneficiaries is impossible, the Plaintiff may seek compensation in value from the said beneficiaries as restitution with respect to the insufficiency of the common security arising from the provisional registration and the final registration.\\nd. Nevertheless, the court below erred by determining, contrary to the foregoing, that because, with respect to the said real properties, additional registrations transferring the provisional registration were completed from Defendant 1 and Boeun General Timber to third parties such as allottees, and because they were not the nameholders of the final registrations, Defendant 1 and Boeun General Timber did not bear any duty to compensate value toward the creditor seeking revocation of the fraudulent act, and on that basis dismissed the claim for revocation of the fraudulent act and compensation in value concerning the said provisional registration.\\nAccordingly, the judgment below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning revocation of a fraudulent act and compensation in value in cases where a provisional registration completed by a fraudulent act has been transferred.\\n2. As to the grounds of appeal concerning the claim for cancellation of the sales reservation and restitution regarding the real properties listed in items 1, 8, and 10 of the Attached List\\na. A correction registration of a registered titleholder is not permitted beyond the scope in which the identity of the titleholder is recognized. However, even if a lawful correction registration is not made and, as a result of the application for correction registration being accepted, an unlawful correction registration is completed in which the identity of the titleholder is not recognized, if such registration has once been made and has come to represent the rights relationship of the titleholder after correction, and if that registration also conforms to the substantive relationship, such registration is valid (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 95DA2135, decided April 12, 1996). In such a case, since the effect of the correction registration does not operate retroactively and merely gives public notice of the acquisition of rights by the titleholder after correction, the registration before correction is also valid as a registration representing the rights relationship of the registered titleholder at the time before correction, unless it is a registration void due to absence of cause. Nor does the actual rights relationship of the registered titleholder before correction, which existed in fact prior to correction, retroactively disappear or become deemed not to have existed.\\nb. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the evidence lawfully admitted, (1) with respect to the real property listed in item 1 of the Attached List owned by Non-Party 1, on September 13, 2006, a provisional registration of the right to demand transfer of ownership in the name of the creditor Boeun General Timber, based on the sales reservation in this case, was completed, and then on September 18, 2006, the registrar, ex officio and on the ground of discovery of error, completed an additional registration correcting the provisional registration holder to the creditor Defendant 1 and Boeun General Timber; thereafter, on September 21, 2006, on the ground of application error, an additional registration correcting the provisional registration holder to the allottee, Non-Party 2, was completed, and then on February 7, 2007, the final registration in the name of Non-Party 2 based on the said provisional registration was completed; (2) with respect also to the real properties listed in items 8 and 10 of the Attached List owned by Non-Party 1, after a provisional registration of the right to demand transfer of ownership in the name of Boeun General Timber and an additional registration correcting the provisional registration holder to Defendant 1 and Boeun General Timber, in the same manner as above, were completed, on September 21, 2006, on the ground of application error, an additional registration correcting the provisional registration holder to the allottee, Non-Party 3, was completed with respect to the real property listed in item 8 of the Attached List, and an additional registration correcting the provisional registration holder to the allottees, Non-Party 4 and Non-Party 5, was completed with respect to the real property listed in item 10 of the Attached List, and then on February 6, 2007, each final registration in the names of Non-Party 3 and Non-Party 4 and Non-Party 5, respectively, based on each such provisional registration, was completed.\\nc. Examining the foregoing factual relationship in light of the legal principles set forth above, with respect to the said real properties, the correction registration correcting the provisional registration holder to each allottee, and the final registrations in the names of the respective allottees based thereon, although they are correction registrations and final registrations based thereon that go beyond the identity of the registered titleholder, are valid as registrations conforming to the substantive relationship of each allottee, who is the registered titleholder after correction. Meanwhile, such correction registrations do not operate retroactively and do not affect the existence or validity of the sales reservation in this case concluded prior thereto or the provisional registration of the right to demand transfer of ownership based thereon.\\nAccordingly, with respect to the said real properties, Defendant 1 and Boeun General Timber, having concluded the sales reservation in this case with Non-Party 1, the debtor, and having completed the provisional registration of the right to demand transfer of ownership, remain in the position of beneficiaries toward the Plaintiff, the creditor seeking revocation of the fraudulent act, notwithstanding the aforementioned unlawful correction registrations. Therefore, unless there are other circumstances, the Plaintiff may seek against Defendant 1 and Boeun General Timber revocation of the sales reservation in this case concerning the said real properties as a fraudulent act and restitution therefrom.\\nd. Nevertheless, the court below erred by determining, contrary to the foregoing, that since valid correction registrations conforming to the substantive relationship correcting the provisional registration holders to the respective allottees were completed with respect to the said real properties, the sales reservation in this case concerning the said real properties previously concluded no longer existed, and on that basis held that Defendant 1 and the bankruptcy trustee Defendant 4, who succeeded to the litigation of bankrupt Boeun General Timber, lacked the status of defendant in an action for revocation of a fraudulent act on the ground of nonexistence thereof.\\nAccordingly, the judgment below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning correction registrations of registered titleholders.\\n3. As to the grounds of appeal concerning the claim for cancellation of the sales reservation and restitution regarding the real property listed in item 6 of the Attached List, and the claim for cancellation of the mortgage creation contract and restitution regarding each real property listed in the Attached List\\nWhere a creditor files a lawsuit against the beneficiary seeking revocation of and restitution for a fraudulent act concerning the debtor’s real property, and during the pendency of the lawsuit the fraudulent act is rescinded or terminated and the property sought to be restored by revocation of the fraudulent act has already returned to the debtor, the purpose of the fraudulent act revocation lawsuit, unless special circumstances exist, has already been realized and there is no longer any interest in the protection of rights to be secured by that lawsuit (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2007DA85157, decided March 27, 2008). The same legal principle applies where, even before the fraudulent act revocation lawsuit is filed, the property sought to be restored by revocation of the fraudulent act has already returned to the debtor.\\nThe court below held that the sales reservation in this case concluded with respect to the real property listed in item 6 of the Attached List, the mortgage creation contract concluded on August 31, 2006 between Non-Party 1 and Boeun General Timber with respect to each real property listed in the Attached List, and the mortgage creation contract concluded on August 31, 2006 between Non-Party 1 and Defendant 1, Defendant 2, Defendant 3, Defendant 5, and Boeun General Timber, were all rescinded, waived, or terminated before the filing of this action, and that as a result the provisional registration of the right to demand transfer of shares and each registration of the creation of a mortgage had all been cancelled. Therefore, the court held that the Plaintiff had no interest in filing suit to seek revocation of and restitution for the said sales reservation and the said mortgage creation contracts.\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the record, the determination of the court below appears to be based on the foregoing legal principles, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the interest in legal protection in a fraudulent act revocation lawsuit.\\n4. Conclusion\\nTherefore, among the judgment below, the portion concerning the claim for cancellation of the sales reservation and restitution regarding the real properties listed in items 1 through 5 and 7 through 16 of the Attached List is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; all remaining appeals are dismissed; and the appellate costs incurred between the Plaintiff and Defendant 2, Defendant 3, and Defendant 5 shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[2016DA6309]": "The Court examines ex officio.\\n\\n1. A corrective registration refers to a registration that corrects or supplements the relevant portion of an existing registration so as to amend the matters of registration to conform to the substantive legal relationship, where there is an error or omission from the time of the registration in part of the existing registration and thus the registration does not originally correspond to the substantive legal relationship (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 2012DA118549, rendered June 27, 2013). For a corrective registration to be allowed, there must be identity or similarity between the registration before and after correction, and a corrective registration changing the titleholder before correction into a different titleholder after correction is not allowed because the identity of the registered titleholder is not recognized. Therefore, a corrective registration that changes sole ownership into co-ownership or co-ownership into sole ownership also results in a change of owner and thus causes the identity of the registered titleholder to be lost, and therefore cannot be allowed (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 95DA33214, rendered April 12, 1996).\\nHowever, where, with respect to real property that is in co-ownership in terms of the substantive legal relationship, a registration of preservation of ownership has been made in the name of sole ownership, or where, with respect to real property that is in sole ownership, a registration of preservation of ownership has been made in the form of co-ownership, the registration of preservation of ownership in the name of the registered titleholder concerning a portion of shares corresponding to the ownership portion of the true right holder among the registrations of preservation of ownership is void, and thus it must be cancelled and a registration of preservation of ownership by the true right holder concerning that portion must be made. In such a case, the true right holder may seek partial cancellation of the registration of preservation of ownership by action, and the court may order cancellation only with respect to that share; however, since partial cancellation of a registration of preservation of ownership is not allowed from the standpoint of registration technique, enforcement of such judgment is effected by way of a corrective registration changing sole ownership into co-ownership or co-ownership into sole ownership (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 94DA38403, rendered May 9, 1995). As such, a corrective registration in the sense of partial cancellation is allowed only within registration procedures, and in litigation procedures, seeking a corrective registration by action, in addition to seeking partial cancellation, is not allowed.\\nMoreover, where, with respect to joint property, a registration of preservation of ownership has been made in sole ownership in the name of one joint owner, because such registration of preservation of ownership is a registration void for lack of cause that does not conform to the substantive relationship (see Supreme Court Decision 69DA22, rendered December 29, 1970), the other joint owner may cancel such registration void for lack of cause by filing an action for cancellation of the registration of preservation of ownership against the joint owner who is the registered titleholder, and then apply anew for a registration of preservation of ownership in joint ownership.\\n\\n2. The alternative claim among the claims in this action seeks, on the ground that the real property listed in the attached schedule as stated in the judgment of the court below was registered by a registration of preservation of ownership in sole ownership in favor of the Defendant despite being in joint ownership between the Plaintiff and the Defendant in terms of the substantive legal relationship, performance of the procedure for a corrective registration changing the right holder of the registration of preservation of ownership from sole ownership by the Defendant to joint ownership by the Plaintiff and the Defendant, against the Defendant.\\nHowever, in light of the legal principles set forth above, a corrective registration changing sole ownership into joint ownership cannot be allowed because it results in a change of owner and thus causes the identity of the registered titleholder to be lost; moreover, a registration of preservation of ownership of joint property in sole ownership is not something to be dealt with by way of a corrective registration from the standpoint of registration technique. Accordingly, although the alternative claim among the claims in this action is, in any event, an impermissible and unlawful claim, the court below overlooked this and proceeded to the merits and examined and determined the case. The judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning corrective registration, etc.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without omitting the determination on the grounds of appeal, the portion of the judgment below concerning the alternative claim is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination on that portion, and it is so adjudged, with the concurrence of all Justices participating, as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[2016MA5579]": "The grounds for re-appeal are examined (the statements in the supplemental statement of grounds for re-appeal submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds for re-appeal has expired, to the extent that they supplement the grounds for re-appeal).\\n\\n1. Article 32(2) of the Real Estate Registration Act provides that, where a registration official discovers that an error in a registration or an omitted part is attributable to the registration official’s mistake, the registration must be corrected ex officio without delay; however, where there is a third party with an interest in the registration, the third party’s consent is required. Here, a “third party with an interest in the registration” means a holder of a registrable right who faces a risk of suffering loss by allowing a corrective registration that rectifies an error or omitted part existing in the prior registration; however, where there exists a registration that is incompatible with the registration to be corrected, the content of that registration is merely subject to correction, and there is no need separately to obtain the consent of the registrant by treating that registrant as a third party with an interest in the registration who is the counterparty to the request for consent (see Supreme Court Order of September 14, 2011, 2011MA1248).\\n\\nAnd a corrective registration is a registration that, where there is an error or omitted part in a portion of an existing registration from the time of registration and thus the registration does not originally conform to the substantive legal relationship, changes the registered matters so as to conform to the substantive legal relationship by correcting or supplementing the relevant portion of the existing registration; accordingly, even where there is an error such as omission of valid particulars or a typographical error in a registry record that has been computerized, it is also subject to corrective registration (see, e.g., Supreme Court Order of February 6, 2009, 2007MA1405). Therefore, where a registration official discovers that, with respect to a registry record that has been computerized, there is an error such as omission of valid particulars or a typographical error in the process of computerization, the registration official must, unless there is a third party with an interest in the registration, make a corrective registration ex officio pursuant to Article 32(2) of the Real Estate Registration Act without delay, and in such a case, the registrant of a right or the obligor for registration may independently file an application for corrective registration in the sense of urging the registration official to act ex officio.\\n\\n2. According to the reasons for the decision of the court below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na. The Korea National Housing Corporation constructed the ○○○○ Apartment complex, consisting of 23 buildings and 700 households, in Ichon-dong, Yongsan-gu, Seoul, around 1971 (hereinafter referred to as “the apartment complex at issue”), and the land located at Seoul, Yongsan-gu, (address 1 omitted), site 932.6㎡, (address 2 omitted), site 95.2㎡, (address 3 omitted), road 602㎡, (address 4 omitted), site 589.4㎡, and (address 5 omitted), site 1071.1㎡ (hereinafter referred to as “the land at issue”) is being used as a playground, roads, and the like for the apartment complex at issue.\\n\\nb. As to the land at issue, a registration of transfer of ownership was completed on December 31, 1971, in the names of the Applicant, Nonparty 1, Nonparty 2, and 698 others, totaling 701 persons, and in the co-owners column of the closed register for the land at issue, only the names and addresses of the above co-owners are stated, without separately indicating each co-ownership share.\\n\\nc. On March 26, 2001, when computerizing the register for the land at issue, the registration official entered the co-owners of the land at issue as the Applicant, Nonparty 1, Nonparty 2, and 698 others, and entered each co-owner’s share as 1/701.\\n\\nd. Meanwhile, the Applicant asserted that, according to the entries in the closed register for the land at issue, the co-ownership shares of Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2, who are husband and wife, should be treated as a total of 1/700 share, but that, due to the registration official’s mistake in the process of computerization, each of the co-ownership shares of the 701 co-owners was erroneously entered as 1/701 share; accordingly, the Applicant filed the application for corrective registration in this case, in the sense of urging the registration official to act ex officio, but the registration official issued a decision on January 21, 2016, dismissing the application for corrective registration in this case.\\n\\n3. Examining these facts in light of the legal principles discussed above, the following conclusion is reached.\\n\\na. Where, in the process of computerization, the relevant co-ownership shares of the co-owners were registered differently from the entries of the relevant co-ownership shares in the closed register due to the registration official’s mistake, the content of that registration is merely subject to correction, and there is no need separately to obtain the consent of the registrant by treating that registrant as a third party with an interest in the registration who is the counterparty to the request for consent; therefore, Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2, who are co-owners of the land at issue, do not fall under the category of third parties with an interest in the registration.\\n\\nb. (1) Where a registration of transfer of ownership has been completed, the registrant is presumed to have acquired ownership by a lawful cause of registration not only vis-à-vis third parties but also vis-à-vis the former owner (see, e.g., Supreme Court Judgment of September 24, 2004, 2004DA27273), and the shares of co-owners are presumed to be equal (Article 262(2) of the Civil Act). And when a registration official computerizes a real estate register, if, among the matters registered under the same priority number in the item column, the entry of the rights share of all co-owners is omitted, all co-owners must be calculated as having equal shares and computerized accordingly (see Supreme Court Registration Directives Nos. 1010 and 1567).\\n\\n(2) According to the entries in the closed register for the land at issue, it can be seen that the co-owners Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 have their addresses entered collectively only once, whereas the other co-owners each have their names and addresses entered separately.\\n\\nHowever, as long as the names of Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 are separately entered in the closed register for the land at issue and no co-ownership share is indicated, the 701 registrants, namely the Applicant, Nonparty 1, Nonparty 2, and 698 others, are presumed to co-own the land at issue, and the co-ownership shares of the 701 co-owners are presumed to be equal; therefore, based solely on the above circumstances, it cannot be concluded that the registration official’s entry, in the process of computerization, of the 701 co-owners as having equal shares (1/701 share) falls under a case in which an erroneous transcription was made due to the registration official’s mistake, which is a ground for ex officio corrective registration under Article 32(2) of the Real Estate Registration Act.\\n\\n(3) However, in light of the fact that the apartment complex at issue consists of 700 households and that the land at issue has been used as a playground, roads, and the like corresponding to the common areas of the apartment complex at issue, if the Applicant, when filing the application for corrective registration in this case in the sense of urging the registration official to act ex officio, submitted materials proving substantively that, at the time of the application for transfer of ownership dated December 31, 1971 in the above closed register, Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 were in a special relationship sufficient to constitute a common household, such as a marital relationship, or were in a relationship of jointly acquiring or owning a specific one household unit among the apartment units at issue, or that the other 699 co-owners were each the owners of 699 households among the apartment units at issue and that Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 had no rights whatsoever to the above 699 households, so that their share rights in the land at issue were merely the portion of one specific household unit, thereby proving that the total of the co-ownership shares belonging to Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 in the land at issue was equal to each of the co-ownership shares of the other 699 co-owners, then the co-ownership shares of Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2, totaling 1/700 share, could be construed as the meaning intended by the entries in the above closed register, and consequently it could be deemed that there was an error in the process of computerizing the register for the land at issue and that the case falls under the ground for ex officio corrective registration.\\n\\nHowever, according to the record, it is insufficient to conclude that the Applicant sufficiently submitted such materials at the time of filing the application for corrective registration in this case; furthermore, where an objection is raised on the ground that a decision or disposition by a registration official is improper, new facts or new evidence methods not asserted or submitted at the time of the decision or disposition cannot be used as grounds for objection (Article 102 of the Real Estate Registration Act; see Supreme Court Registration Directive No. 1411). Therefore, the Applicant cannot additionally submit such explanatory materials while filing this objection in this case against the above dismissal decision by the registration official.\\n\\n4. Accordingly, the decision of the court below, which reached the above conclusion, cannot be said, as alleged in the grounds for re-appeal, to contain illegality affecting the judgment due to misapprehension of the legal principles regarding Article 32(2) of the Real Estate Registration Act or otherwise.\\n\\n5. Therefore, the re-appeal is dismissed, and it is so decided, with the concurrence of all participating Justices."}

{"[2020DA299214]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. According to the findings of the court below, with respect to the real properties at issue, after the 'Jongdan Daesoon Jinrihoe Mokpo Branch' (hereinafter referred to as the 'existing Mokpo Branch') completed the registration of preservation of ownership in its name, the Plaintiff, around 2007~2008, completed the first supplementary registration of change in the indication of the registered titleholder in the name of 'Daemireukbongsimhoe' (as to some real properties, the supplementary registration of change in the indication of the registered titleholder was first made to 'Mireukbongsimhoe' and then again to 'Daemireukbongsimhoe'); thereafter, around 2018, the Defendant Jongdan Daesoon Jinrihoe Mokpo Branch (hereinafter referred to as the 'Defendant Branch') completed, under the name of 'Jongdan Daesoon Jinrihoe Mokpo Branch,' a supplementary registration of change in the indication of the registered titleholder for each item (hereinafter referred to as the 'second supplementary registration of change in indication'), and as to some of those real properties, the registration of transfer of ownership was completed in favor of the Defendant Foundation, Daesoon Jinrihoe Mokpo Branch Maintenance Foundation.\\n\\nThe court below premised that \"if the second supplementary registration of change in indication was made in a manner that impairs the identity of the registered titleholder, the Plaintiff, as the original registered titleholder, may seek against the Defendant Branch the cancellation of the second supplementary registration of change in indication,\" and then, finding that identity was not recognized between the Plaintiff, who was the existing registered titleholder, and the Defendant Branch, held that the Defendant Branch has the obligation to perform the procedure for cancellation registration with respect to the second supplementary registration of change in indication, and that the Defendant Foundation, Daesoon Jinrihoe Mokpo Branch Maintenance Foundation likewise has the obligation to cancel the registration of transfer of ownership it received from the Defendant Branch as to some of the real properties. Further, as to the Defendants' argument that the Plaintiff was not the true owner of the real properties at issue because it was a religious organization different from the existing Mokpo Branch, the court below rejected it on the ground that there was insufficient evidence to support that assertion.\\n\\n2. However, the determination of the court below is difficult to uphold for the following reasons.\\n\\na. If the supplementary registration of change in or correction of the indication of the registered titleholder is effected in a manner that impairs the identity of the registered titleholder, and the indication on the real estate registration certificate does not represent the actual ownership relationship, the true owner, by the rightful exercise of the right to demand exclusion of infringement, which is part of the content of ownership, may demand from the nominal owner shown in the register performance of the cancellation registration procedure for the supplementary registration of change in or correction of the indication, which constitutes an obstacle to that ownership; therefore, a person who seeks performance of the cancellation registration procedure for the registration of change in or correction of the indication of the registered titleholder of real property must prove that he or she is the original registered titleholder of the real property and the true owner (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2008. 12. 11. rendered in 2008DA1859).\\n\\nb. Examining the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below in light of this legal principle, the original registered titleholder of the real properties at issue is the 'existing Mokpo Branch,' and it would be the true owner. Accordingly, the Plaintiff bears the burden of proving both that it is the original registered titleholder of the real properties at issue and the true owner, that is, that it is the same organization as the existing Mokpo Branch, in whose name the registration of preservation of ownership, which is the main registration, was completed with respect to the real properties at issue, and that the second supplementary registration of change in indication impaired the identity of the registered titleholder.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, with respect to the Plaintiff's claim for cancellation registration, without properly examining whether the Plaintiff was the true owner, that is, whether the fact that it was the same organization as the existing Mokpo Branch had been proved, determined that the Plaintiff could seek against the Defendant Branch the cancellation registration for the second supplementary registration of change in indication merely on the ground that identity between the Plaintiff and the Defendant Branch was found not to be recognized, and instead, premised as if the burden of proving that the Plaintiff was not the true owner rested on the Defendants, rejected the Defendants' argument on the ground that there was no evidence to show that the Plaintiff was not the same organization as the existing Mokpo Branch; thus, in such determination of the court below, there is an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the requirements for the establishment of the right to claim cancellation registration of a registration of change in the indication of the registered titleholder and the allocation of the burden of proof, thereby failing to conduct the necessary trial and hearing.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged and decided, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, as set forth in the Disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning a title trust to which the 「Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder's Name」 applies is correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: In a three-party title trust by registration, where the title trustee disposes at will of the title-trusted real estate and a third party acquires ownership thereof, if the legal relationship between the seller and the title truster arising from the seller's duty to register transfer of ownership becoming impossible to perform, and the legal relationship between the title trustee and the seller arising from the title trustee's infringement of the seller's ownership, are each separately and individually adjusted by distinguishing them, this may run counter to the purpose of the restitution of unjust enrichment system.
B: In a three-party title trust by registration, if the title truster, without subrogating the seller, directly claims registration of transfer of ownership against the title trustee on the ground of restitution of unjust enrichment, the registration of transfer of ownership completed accordingly in the name of the title truster is void.
C: In a contract title trust, where the seller did not know of the title trust agreement, if the title trustee agreed to transfer the title-trusted real estate itself in lieu of returning the purchase funds to the title truster and, on that basis, had registration of transfer of ownership completed in the name of a third party designated by the title trustee, the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of that third party is valid.
D: In a contract title trust, where the seller did not know of the title trust agreement when entering into the sale contract with the title trustee but learned of it when registration of transfer of ownership was completed in the name of the title trustee, the sale contract between the seller and the title trustee becomes void retroactively.
E: In a contract title trust, where the seller knew of the title trust agreement, the sale contract concluded between the seller and the title trustee is void ab initio, and ownership of the relevant real estate remains vested in the seller; therefore, absent special circumstances, the title truster may claim registration of transfer of ownership from the seller.
label: A

{"[2010DA95185]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to Ground 1 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the judgment of the court below, the court below, citing the first-instance judgment, found the facts as stated therein and then determined that the Defendant had not purchased each of the real properties listed in Items 1 through 5 of the attached list (hereinafter referred to as the “real properties in this case”) from the Plaintiff, but had merely received the registration title in trust in order to avoid compulsory execution against the real properties in this case.\\n\\nIn light of the record, such factual findings and determination by the court below are justifiable and acceptable, and there is no error, as asserted in the grounds for appeal, in exceeding the limits of the free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or in failing to conduct the necessary deliberation.\\n\\n2. With respect to Ground 2 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nA. According to the reasoning of the judgment of the court below, the court below, citing the first-instance judgment, found the facts as stated therein and then determined that (Lot No. 1 omitted) farmland, 152 square meters, Anseok-dong, Hwaseong-si [hereinafter referred to as the “property (Lot No. 1 omitted)”], and (Lot No. 2 omitted) forest land, 1,884 square meters, Anseok-dong, Hwaseong-si [hereinafter referred to as the “forest land (Lot No. 2 omitted)”], are real properties title-trusted by the Plaintiff to the Defendant in the form of a two-party registration title trust, or real properties title-trusted by a non-party to the Defendant in the form of a three-party contract title trust, and that in the case of a two-party registration title trust or a three-party contract title trust, the registration in the name of the title trustee is void, so although the Defendant, as title trustee, bears the duty to cancel the registration or transfer the registration to the previous titleholder, namely the Plaintiff, the Defendant, as title trustee, arbitrarily disposed of the above real properties title-trusted to him and transferred them to a third party around August 18, 2001 and January 9, 2002, thereby causing the previous titleholder, namely the Plaintiff, to lose ownership, which constitutes a tort against the Plaintiff; accordingly, the court below determined that the Defendant is obligated to compensate the Plaintiff for the damage incurred by the Plaintiff as a result of the disposition of the above real properties, in the amount equivalent to the market value at the time when the above real properties were disposed of to a third party, namely 44,640,000 won, and delay damages thereon.\\n\\nB.
