However, such determination by the court below is difficult to accept as it stands for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) Where a title truster and a title trustee enter into the so-called contract title trust arrangement and the owner who entered into a sales contract, knowing the title trust agreement between the title truster and the title trustee, completes the registration of transfer of ownership of the relevant real property in the name of the title trustee pursuant to that sales contract, the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of the title trustee is void pursuant to the main clause of Article 4(2) of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder's Name, so ownership of the relevant real property remains with the owner who entered into the sales contract, and if the title trustee disposes of the real property for which he has completed the registration of transfer of ownership in his own name to a third party, such act constitutes a tort as an infringement of the seller’s ownership.\\n\\nHowever, an owner who has received the purchase price from the title trustee may, until he recovers title to the real property, refuse to perform the obligation to return the purchase price, which is in a relationship of simultaneous performance with the title trustee, pursuant to the principle of good faith or the main clause of Article 536(1) of the Civil Act; and where, in the so-called contract title trust, the title trustee’s act of disposition to a third party is validly finalized and recovery of title to the owner becomes impossible, the owner has no opportunity to perform the obligation to return the purchase price, which is in a relationship of simultaneous performance therewith. In addition, since the title truster has no contractual relationship of sale and purchase with the owner, a claim for registration of transfer of ownership against the owner is not permitted, and ultimately, the seller, who is the owner, cannot be said, absent special circumstances, to have suffered any damage due to the title trustee’s act of disposition.\\n\\n(2) In light of the foregoing legal principle, where a non-party made a so-called three-party contract title trust of the property (Lot No. 1 omitted) and the forest land (Lot No. 2 omitted) to the Defendant, the Plaintiff, as the seller, cannot, absent special circumstances, claim damages for tort against the Defendant, who is the title trustee, even if the Defendant arbitrarily disposed of the above real properties.\\n\\nNevertheless, without clearly stating whether the Plaintiff made a so-called two-party registration title trust of the property (Lot No. 1 omitted) and the forest land (Lot No. 2 omitted) to the Defendant, or whether a non-party made a so-called three-party contract title trust thereof to the Defendant, the court below found that the Plaintiff or the non-party made a so-called two-party registration title trust or three-party contract title trust of the above real properties to the Defendant, and then determined that, regardless of which of the two cases the Defendant’s subsequent arbitrary disposition of the above real properties by the title trustee falls under, it constitutes a tort against the Plaintiff, and that as a result the Plaintiff suffered damage equivalent to the market value at the time the Defendant disposed of the above real properties; in doing so, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principle regarding the occurrence of damage from a tort, and such error affected the judgment. The argument in the grounds for appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nThe portion of the judgment of the court below concerning the claim for payment of damages is reversed, and this portion of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, while the remaining appeal is dismissed; accordingly, it is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the judgment."}

{"[2011DA103472]": "The grounds of appeal are to be determined, insofar as the supplementary statement of grounds of appeal filed after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal supplements the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Part concerning the claim for registration of transfer of ownership of real property\\n\\na. As to the authenticity of documents\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the court below’s determination, for the reasons stated in its opinion, that the authenticity of A Exhibit No. 5-1, 3, 5, 7, 9 (each a fact confirmation statement) and A Exhibit No. 10-1 through 5 (each a memorandum of agreement performance) is established, is acceptable; and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the authenticity of dispositive documents, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, or violation of the rules of logic and experience or exceeding the bounds of the free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nb. As to the validity of the agreement to transfer ownership of real property\\n\\n(1) Based on the evidence it adopted, the court below found that, among the real properties listed in Attached List No. 1 to the judgment of the court below, the ownership transfer registrations in Defendant’s name had been completed for the real properties Nos. 1 through 13, 17 through 36, 41 through 48, 50 through 53, 58, 59, 68, and 69, as well as the real properties Nos. 60 through 66 on the same list, and the real properties Nos. 14 through 16 on the same list (hereinafter collectively referred to in this section as “the real properties at issue”); that Defendant, who was serving as the Head of Finance of the Plaintiff, instructed Monk Non-party 1, who belonged to the Plaintiff and was under his direction, and caused him to prepare, with the Plaintiff, three sets of memoranda of agreement performance and fact confirmation statements concerning the real properties at issue, on February 20, 2007, the 21st of the same month, and the 23rd of the same month; that Article 3 of each of the above memoranda of agreement performance stated, “The Plaintiff may at any time demand that the Defendant transfer ownership of the real property at issue, and the Defendant shall be discharged from the obligation by transferring ownership to a third party designated by the Plaintiff”; that Article 6 stated, “Taxes and public charges related to the real property at issue shall be borne by the Plaintiff”; and that each of the above fact confirmation statements stated, “Since the real property at issue cannot be registered for transfer of ownership, it was registered in Defendant’s name for convenience, but this is certainly because it is property owned by the Cheontae Order, and we confirm this,” and then held that Defendant agreed with the Plaintiff to transfer ownership of the real properties at issue to the Plaintiff as stated in Article 3 of each of the above memoranda of agreement performance; therefore, absent special circumstances, Defendant is obligated to perform the registration procedure for transfer of ownership of the real properties at issue to the Plaintiff pursuant to each of the above agreements, and rejected Defendant’s defense that the above agreements constitute a title trust agreement prescribed by the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name and are void under Article 3(1) and Article 4 of the same Act, for the reasons stated in its opinion.\\n\\n(2) However, the above determination of the court below is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nWhere, in purchasing real property, a title trust relationship is formed between the person who bears the purchase price in substance and the nominal holder, even if they agreed to transfer the title of ownership of the real property at the request of the person who bears the purchase price in substance, such agreement falls within the category of seeking the return of the title-trusted real property itself or the proceeds of its disposal on the premise of a title trust agreement that is void under the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name, and thus must also be regarded as void (see Supreme Court Judgment 2006DA35117 rendered on Nov. 9, 2006, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the above factual findings of the court below, the real properties at issue were acquired with the Plaintiff’s funds and were in substance owned by the Plaintiff, but the ownership transfer registrations were made in Defendant’s name for convenience and the taxes and public charges were to be borne by the Plaintiff, and thus a title trust relationship concerning them was formed between the Plaintiff and Defendant. Since the above title trust agreement is void under Article 4(1) of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name, the Plaintiff cannot demand the return of the above real properties themselves from Defendant.\\n\\nHowever, in Article 3 of each of the memoranda of agreement performance at issue, the Plaintiff and Defendant agreed, on the premise that the real properties at issue were properties title-trusted by the Plaintiff to Defendant, that Defendant would transfer title to a person designated by the Plaintiff at the Plaintiff’s request; and, in light of the legal principles discussed above, at least with respect to that portion of the agreement, this is nothing more than a promise to return the title-trusted real property itself on the premise that the void title trust agreement is valid through the form of a new agreement, and therefore it cannot but be deemed void as well.\\n\\nNevertheless, the judgment of the court below, which held that the agreement for return of the real properties at issue pursuant to each of the memoranda of agreement performance is valid, contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles regarding title trust in real property, and Defendant’s ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n2. Part concerning the claim for return of unjust enrichment\\n\\na. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below, based on the evidence it adopted and in sum, found that around May 2007, the Plaintiff could not acquire the real property listed as No. 49 in Attached List No. 1 in its own name because the real property (hereinafter referred to in this section as “the real property at issue”) was agricultural land, and thus caused Defendant, who was then the Plaintiff religious order’s Head of Finance, to purchase the above real property; that accordingly, Defendant received purchase funds from the Plaintiff, purchased the above real property owned by Non-party 2 for KRW 36,000,000 on May 9, 2007, and completed the ownership transfer registration thereto on May 21, 2007; and that on the same day, Defendant completed a registration of establishment of a mortgage over the above real property in favor of the Plaintiff with a maximum secured amount of KRW 50,000,000. Based on these findings, the court below held that, according to the above factual findings, the real property at issue was title-trusted by the Plaintiff to Defendant in the form of so-called contractual title trust, whereby the Plaintiff paid the purchase price to Defendant and caused Defendant to purchase it from Non-party 2; that where, after entering into a sale contract for real property with the owner without knowing that such a title trust agreement exists, ownership of the relevant real property is registered in the name of the trustee pursuant to that sale contract, the trustee acquires full ownership of the relevant real property notwithstanding the invalidity of the title trust agreement between the title truster and the title trustee, and the title trustee bears the obligation to return unjust enrichment equivalent to the purchase funds to the title truster; and that Defendant, knowing that the above title trust agreement was void due to the enforcement of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name, was a beneficiary in bad faith who received the above purchase funds, and therefore had the duty to return not only the purchase funds received but also the statutory interest thereon. On that basis, the court below held that Defendant is obligated to pay to the Plaintiff the above purchase price of KRW 36,000,000 and the statutory interest thereon at the rate of 5% per annum as prescribed by the Civil Act from May 22, 2007, which is after the date on which the above amount was provided and as sought by the Plaintiff, until July 6, 2010, the date on which the duplicate of the complaint in this case was served, and delay damages at the rate of 20% per annum as prescribed by the Act on Special Cases Concerning Expedition, etc. of Legal Proceedings from the following day until the date of full payment.\\n\\nb. The portion of the court below’s determination that, as stated above, the title trust agreement in this case is void, so that Defendant acquires full ownership of the real property at issue, while Defendant bears the obligation to return unjust enrichment equivalent to the purchase funds and the obligation to pay delay damages to the Plaintiff, is acceptable in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, and there is no illegality such as violation of the rules of logic and experience or exceeding the bounds of the free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehension of the legal principles concerning title trust in real property or unjust enrichment, or contradiction in the reasons for judgment, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nc. However, the portion of the court below’s determination concerning statutory interest cannot be accepted.\\n\\nAs to the point that the obligor to return unjust enrichment is a beneficiary in bad faith under Article 748(2) of the Civil Act, the burden of proof rests on the party asserting it. Also, “bad faith” here means, save for cases deemed to involve bad faith under Article 749(2) of the Civil Act, recognition that retention of one’s benefit lacks a legal cause; and the mere recognition that there are facts that make the retention of that benefit lacking a legal cause, that is, facts that constitute the requirements for the occurrence of the obligation to return unjust enrichment, is insufficient. Therefore, even if Defendant merely knew that the purchase funds at issue received by him were paid pursuant to a title trust agreement, absent additional circumstances such as knowledge that the title trust agreement was void under Article 4(1) of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name, it cannot readily be said that Defendant knew his retention of the money lacked a legal cause (see Supreme Court Judgment 2009DA24187, 24194 rendered on Jan. 28, 2010).\\n\\nRather, according to the record, even if, as a matter of law, Defendant is evaluated as having acquired full ownership of the real property at issue as noted above, the Plaintiff, as the title truster, appears to have possessed and used the real property at issue while recognizing itself as the owner of the real property at issue, and Defendant also appears likely to have continued, even after the ownership transfer registration was made in his name, to acknowledge the Plaintiff’s actual ownership without objecting to such possession and use by the Plaintiff. If so, it is difficult to conclude that Defendant, at the time he received the purchase funds from the Plaintiff on May 9, 2007, or when the ownership transfer registration was completed in his name on May 21, 2007, already knew that there was no legal cause for his retention of the purchase funds at issue and that he was obliged to return them, and there is room to view the matter as though, even after the registration, he still for a considerable period believed the title trust agreement concerning the acquisition of the real property at issue to be valid and assumed that he need not return the purchase funds.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below’s holding that Defendant is obligated to pay statutory interest at the rate of 5% per annum prescribed by the Civil Act on the unjust enrichment amount of KRW 36,000,000 for the period from May 22, 2007, which is after the date on which the above amount was provided and as sought by the Plaintiff, until the date of service of the duplicate of the complaint in this case, contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning a beneficiary in bad faith in the obligation to return unjust enrichment, or by failing to conduct the necessary examination as to whether Defendant acted in bad faith. The purport of the appeal on this point is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, among the parts of the judgment of the court below adverse to Defendant, the part concerning the claim for registration of transfer of ownership of real property and the part concerning statutory interest in the claim for return of unjust enrichment cannot be maintained as is; therefore, without needing to further examine Defendant’s other grounds of appeal, we reverse them, and remand this part of the case to the court below for further trial and determination. We also dismiss the remainder of Defendant’s appeal. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case, as set forth in the order."}

{"[2017DA257715]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Article 4 of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name (hereinafter referred to as the “Real-Name Registration Act”) provides that a title trust agreement (paragraph (1)) and a change in real rights in real estate effected by registration pursuant to a title trust agreement (main clause of paragraph (2)) shall be null and void, while the proviso to paragraph (2) provides that “provided, however, this shall not apply where, in a contract for acquiring a real right in real estate, the title trustee becomes one of the parties and the other party does not know the fact that there is a title trust agreement.”\\n\\nThe proviso to Article 4(2) of the Real-Name Registration Act is intended to protect the counterparty to a real estate transaction, and it deems valid the contract and the registration made pursuant thereto where the counterparty entered into a contract for acquiring a real right without knowing the fact that there was a title trust agreement (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2012DA202932, decided December 23, 2015). Where the title truster and the title trustee enter into a contract title trust agreement and the title trustee, as a party, concludes a sales contract for real estate with the seller, the validity of the contract and registration shall be determined based on the seller’s awareness at the time the sales contract is concluded, and even if the seller learned of the title trust agreement after the conclusion of the contract, such fact has no effect on the validity of the above contract and registration. There is no basis to regard a sales contract that was validly formed as above as being retroactively rendered void merely because of the accidental circumstance that the seller learned of the title trust agreement after the conclusion of the contract. If the seller were allowed to contest the validity of the sales contract on the ground that he or she learned of the title trust agreement after the conclusion of the contract, it would lead to the unfair result that the validity of the sales contract would depend on the seller’s choice.\\n\\n2. According to the judgment of the court below, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na. On September 23, 2015, the Plaintiff agreed to purchase from the Defendant the real estate listed in the attached list to the judgment of the first instance, owned by the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as the “Real Estate at Issue”), for KRW 150,000,000 (hereinafter referred to as the “Sales Contract at Issue”), and paid the Defendant a down payment of KRW 15,000,000 on the same day, while agreeing to pay the balance of KRW 135,000,000 on October 13, 2015, of which KRW 80,000,000 was to be assumed as the Defendant’s obligation to return the lease deposit.\\n\\nb. The non-party, who is the Plaintiff’s daughter, concluded the Sales Contract at Issue in the Plaintiff’s name in consideration of the fact that, if she concluded the Sales Contract at Issue in her own name, she would lose the benefits arising from being a first-time home buyer. At the time of the Sales Contract at Issue, the Plaintiff did not tell the Defendant of such circumstances. The non-party attended together with the Plaintiff when the Sales Contract at Issue was concluded, and the Plaintiff paid the down payment of KRW 15,000,000 withdrawn from the Shinhan Bank account of the non-party.\\n\\nc. Thereafter, on October 7, 2015, the Defendant notified the Plaintiff of rescission of the Sales Contract at Issue on the ground of a change in circumstances in that the Real Estate at Issue had become subject to reconstruction, and refused to perform it. While explaining the circumstances of concluding the sales contract to the Defendant, the Plaintiff stated that the Sales Contract at Issue had been concluded in the Plaintiff’s name for the benefit of the non-party.\\n\\nd. On October 13, 2015, the date for payment of the balance, the Plaintiff deposited with the Defendant the remaining KRW 55,000,000 after deducting from the balance of KRW 135,000,000 the KRW 80,000,000 lease deposit that the Plaintiff had agreed to assume.\\n\\n3. Examining the foregoing factual relations in light of the legal principles set forth above, the Defendant, at the time of concluding the Sales Contract at Issue, entered into the Sales Contract at Issue with the Plaintiff without knowing the fact of the title trust agreement between the Plaintiff and the daughter, the non-party; thus, the Sales Contract at Issue concluded between the Plaintiff and the Defendant is valid pursuant to the proviso to Article 4(2) of the Real-Name Registration Act. Whether the Defendant later became aware of the foregoing title trust agreement does not affect this conclusion. Accordingly, the Defendant is obligated to implement the registration procedure for transfer of ownership, based on the Sales Contract at Issue, with respect to the Real Estate at Issue, in favor of the Plaintiff.\\n\\nThe determination of the court below to the same effect is proper as it accords with the foregoing legal principles, and it contains no error of law by misconstruing the legal principles concerning the interpretation, etc. of Article 4(2) of the Real-Name Registration Act, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n4. The Defendant’s appeal lacks merit, and therefore it is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. Accordingly, the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices."}

{"[2018DA284233]": "We determine the grounds for appeal (the statements in each supplemental statement of grounds for appeal submitted after the deadline for submission of the statement of grounds for appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\na. On March 31, 2010, the Plaintiff concluded a sales contract with the non-party, the owner, with respect to the real estate at issue, and paid the entire purchase price of KRW 1 billion to the non-party by May 13, 2010. The non-party, pursuant to the title trust arrangement between the Plaintiff and the Defendant, completed the registration of transfer of ownership in the Defendant’s name with respect to the real estate at issue on May 17, 2010.\\n\\nb. On December 11, 2014, the Defendant borrowed KRW 500 million from Standard Chartered Bank Korea Limited (hereinafter referred to as “SC Bank”) and created the mortgage at issue over the real estate at issue in the maximum amount secured of KRW 600 million.\\n\\nc. The registration of the mortgage creation at issue had not been cancelled by the time of the conclusion of oral argument in the court below.\\n\\n2. The Judgment of the Court Below and the Issue\\na. The Plaintiff asserted that the Defendant, as the title trustee, created the mortgage at issue and obtained a loan, thereby obtaining a benefit equivalent to the amount of the secured obligation, and thereby causing damage to the Plaintiff in the same amount, and sought restitution of unjust enrichment against the Defendant.\\n\\nThe court below dismissed the Plaintiff’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment on the ground that, in the case of a title trust registration among three parties, both the title trust agreement and the registration of transfer of ownership made pursuant thereto are void, and ownership of the real estate remains with the seller; therefore, the person who suffered damage from the creation of the mortgage at issue is the non-party, who is both the seller and the owner, not the Plaintiff.\\n\\nb. The issue in this case is whether, in a title trust registration among three parties, where the title trustee disposes of the real estate by selling it to a third party or by creating a mortgage over the real estate, and the third party acquires rights in the real estate pursuant to Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name (hereinafter referred to as the “Real Estate Registration Act”), the title truster may directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee with respect to the benefit obtained by the title trustee in that process.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s Judgment\\na. Whether the title truster may directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee when the title trustee transfers title to the real estate to a third party in a title trust registration among three parties\\n\\nIn a title trust registration among three parties, when a registration of transfer of ownership is completed in the name of a third party on the grounds of the title trustee’s voluntary disposition, compulsory expropriation, or consultation acquisition of public land, the third party acquires ownership validly, absent special circumstances (Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act). As a result, the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership to the title truster becomes impossible to perform, so the title truster can no longer receive transfer of ownership of the real estate, while the title trustee acquires the proceeds from the disposal of the real estate or compensation money, etc. Precedents hold that the title trustee bears the obligation to return such proceeds from disposition or compensation money, etc. to the title truster as unjust enrichment (see Supreme Court Decision dated September 8, 2011, 2009DA49193, 49209; Supreme Court Decision dated September 10, 2015, 2015DA207235; Supreme Court Decision dated July 25, 2019, 2019DA203811, 203828, etc.). Such precedents are proper and should be maintained as they are. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) A title trust registration among three parties is where the title truster, while acquiring real estate from the owner, concludes a title trust agreement with the title trustee and then causes the registration of transfer of ownership of the relevant real estate to be made directly in the name of the title trustee by the owner.\\n\\nIn such a case, the title trust agreement is void pursuant to Article 4, Paragraph 1 of the Real Estate Registration Act, and therefore there is no direct legal relationship between the title truster and the title trustee with respect to the real estate. However, the title truster still has a claim for registration of transfer of ownership against the seller based on the sales contract, and the seller bears, to the title truster, the obligation to register transfer of ownership under the sales contract and, at the same time, may seek from the title trustee, as a claim for removal of interference based on ownership, the cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership or the restoration of the true registered title; and the title trustee is in the position of bearing, toward the seller, the obligation to cancel the registration of transfer of ownership or the obligation to register transfer of ownership based on the restoration of the true registered title. Thus, the title truster, the title trustee, and the seller in a title trust relationship among three parties each have contractual or legal rights and bear corresponding obligations with respect to the real estate. This accords with the purpose and intent of the Real Estate Registration Act, which is to have ownership and other real rights in real estate registered in the name of the actual right holder so as to conform to the substantive legal relationship.\\n\\nHowever, when a registration of transfer of ownership in the name of a third party is completed with respect to the real estate on the ground of the title trustee’s voluntary disposition, compulsory expropriation, consultation acquisition of public land, etc. (collectively, the grounds for transfer of ownership in these cases are hereinafter referred to as “the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.”), the rights and obligations that the title truster, title trustee, and seller have over the real estate, as seen above, are altered as the third party validly acquires ownership pursuant to Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act. In such a situation, the purpose of the Real Estate Registration Act—to have registration made in the name of the actual right holder so as to conform to the substantive legal relationship—can no longer be achieved.\\n\\nWhen, due to the application of the provision protecting third parties, changes arise in the contractual or legal rights and corresponding obligations that the title truster, title trustee, and seller have over the real estate, in adjusting the ensuing interests through restitution of unjust enrichment, it is necessary to consider not only the purpose and intent of the Real Estate Registration Act of realizing registration in the name of the actual right holder, but also the purpose of the restitution of unjust enrichment system, namely, that a person who has obtained a property benefit without legal cause should bear the duty to return it to the person who suffered loss by reason of that benefit, based on the ideals of fairness and justice.\\n\\n2) The title trustee is not a party to the real estate sales contract, nor a person who validly acquired ownership of the real estate, and thus has no right at all over the real estate. Yet, when the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and the valid transfer of ownership of the real estate to a third party occur pursuant to Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act, the title trustee, despite not being the owner of the real estate, obtains proceeds from disposition or compensation money, etc. in relation to the third party on the ground that it had held the title of ownership. However, because such benefit was obtained by the title trustee as the exchange value of the real estate, despite the title trustee not being the owner, it is a benefit without legal cause and must be returned to the rightful holder.\\n\\n3) Since the title truster has performed its obligation under the sales contract by paying the purchase price but has nonetheless failed to acquire ownership, the title truster is in a position to, after preserving its claim for registration of transfer of ownership against the seller, exercise subrogatorily the seller’s claim against the title trustee for cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership or the claim for registration of transfer of ownership based on restoration of the true registered title, thereby restoring the title in the seller’s name, and then demand the seller to perform registration of transfer of ownership to itself. However, when ownership of the real estate is validly transferred to a third party pursuant to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act, the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership to the title truster becomes impossible to perform; accordingly, the title truster suffers damage in that, although it has paid the purchase price to the seller, it loses the right to receive the ownership of the real estate, which is the counterperformance.\\n\\n4) Although the seller, at the request of the title truster, completed the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of the title trustee, the title trust agreement and the registration of transfer of ownership in the title trustee’s name become void, and the seller is thus in the position of having to recover the title to ownership of the real estate from the title trustee and complete registration of transfer of ownership to the title truster based on the sales contract. However, when there is the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership to the title truster becomes impossible to perform, as noted above. The Supreme Court, in a case where, before the Real Estate Registration Act was enforced, the seller, at the request of the title truster, transferred the title of registration to the title trustee, held that, where there is the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., it is difficult to deem the seller to be at fault for the conclusion or performance of the sales contract, and therefore it is not permitted under the principle of good faith for the title truster to seek restitution of the purchase price from the seller or require that a transfer registration of ownership be made anew in the title truster’s name on the ground of the fact that the title truster did not make the registration in its own name (see Supreme Court Decision dated March 15, 2002, 2001DA61654). Even after the Real Estate Registration Act was enforced, the same applies in the case where a title trust registration among three parties is made; namely, it is difficult to deem the seller to be at fault for the conclusion or performance of the sales contract, and even if the seller were at fault, it is still not permitted under the principle of good faith for the title truster, who caused the state of violation of the Real Estate Registration Act, to seek restitution of the purchase price from the seller or to claim damages for the impossibility of performance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership. The seller loses ownership of the real estate pursuant to Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., and no longer bears toward the title truster either the obligation to register transfer of ownership or liability for damages caused by impossibility of performance, while retaining the purchase price received from the title truster; therefore, it cannot be said that any economic loss occurs to the seller by reason of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.\\n\\n5) The benefit that the title trustee receives as consideration for the disposition act, etc. regarding the real estate is a benefit obtained by the title trustee as a result of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and the third party’s valid acquisition of ownership pursuant to Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act. The title truster had the right, in the first instance, to acquire ownership of the real estate through the seller but suffered damage in that, by reason of the third party’s valid acquisition of ownership as above, it can no longer acquire ownership of the real estate, even through the seller as an intermediary; meanwhile, the seller cannot be said to have suffered any economic loss to its property despite the third party’s valid acquisition of ownership as above. Considering these circumstances, the benefit that the title trustee obtained without legal cause by the disposition act, etc. of the real estate is, in social common sense, attributable to the damage suffered by the title truster and must be returned to the title truster.\\n\\n6) Even if, in this manner, where a third party acquires ownership of the real estate due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. in a title trust registration among three parties, the title trustee who obtained a benefit without legal cause is deemed to bear a direct obligation to return unjust enrichment to the title truster, this does not deprive the seller, a party to the title trust relationship among three parties, of rights or impose additional obligations on it; nor does it deprive the title trustee of rights or impose additional obligations on it, because the title trustee originally had no independent defense rights, etc. against the title truster or the seller; and nor does it confer unjust benefits or rights on the title truster.\\n\\nRather, if the legal relations arising from rescission of the contract or damages caused by impossibility of performance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership under the sales contract between the title truster and the seller in a title trust registration among three parties, and the legal relations of restitution of unjust enrichment or damages due to tort arising from the title trustee’s infringement of the seller’s ownership between the seller and the title trustee, are separately understood and the interests are adjusted individually, then depending on the concrete circumstances, there may be cases where a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment or a claim for damages is not recognized, or cases where it is recognized only in a limited manner due to comparative negligence or other grounds, resulting in insufficient compensation for the loss and at the same time the unforeseen obtaining of benefits. Permitting such a result runs counter to the purpose of the restitution of unjust enrichment system, which is grounded in the ideal of fairness.\\n\\n7) In a title trust registration among three parties, the title truster, title trustee, and seller understand that the sales contract has been fully performed and the legal relationship has ended, because the seller has received the purchase price from the title truster and transferred the title of registration to the title trustee pursuant to the three-party agreement, namely, the title trust agreement between the title truster and the title trustee and the agreement that the seller will transfer the title of registration to the title trustee at the request of the title truster. Thereafter, even if the title truster fails to acquire ownership of the real estate because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., so long as the seller is deemed not to be at fault for this, the seller retains the purchase price received from the title truster and suffers no economic loss. Even though a legal relationship arises among the title truster, title trustee, and seller requiring adjustment of interests due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., there is no need to draw the seller, who is in the above position, into the adjustment of interests caused by the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. The change in the rights and obligations among the title truster, title trustee, and seller arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. originates from the fact that the title trust agreement concluded between the title truster and the title trustee is void; therefore, the issue of adjusting the resulting interests should be resolved between the title truster and the title trustee, who are the parties to the title trust agreement, and there is no logically inevitable reason why the seller must intervene in this process. Even if the seller is brought into the adjustment of interests, the benefit such as the proceeds from disposition or compensation money obtained by the title trustee through the disposition act, etc. is, in substance, the same as if it were ultimately attributable to the title truster through the seller. Therefore, rather than unnecessarily involving the seller, it is reasonable to allow the title truster to exercise a direct claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee, because that more simply resolves the legal relationship.\\n\\nb. Whether the title truster may directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee when the title trustee creates a mortgage over the real estate in a title trust registration among three parties\\n\\nEven where the title trustee creates a mortgage over the real estate for a third party, the same view should apply as in the case where ownership of the real estate is transferred to a third party.\\n\\nWhen the title trustee creates a mortgage over the real estate for a third party, the third party validly acquires the mortgage right pursuant to Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act. In this case, the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership with respect to the real estate is not impossible to perform; therefore, the title truster may still, by subrogating the seller, receive transfer of ownership from the seller through registration of transfer of ownership based on restoration of the true registered title as to the title trustee’s real estate, etc., but that ownership would be subject to the mortgage right validly remaining in place as created by the title trustee. The title trustee, by creating the mortgage in favor of the third party, obtained a benefit equivalent to the amount of the secured obligation; the title truster suffered damage in that it could obtain only ownership with a diminished exchange value by the amount of the secured obligation even if the seller served as intermediary; meanwhile, the seller, having received the purchase price from the title truster and having thereby accomplished the purpose of the sales contract, suffers no substantive loss because it does not bear liability for damages in relation to transferring ownership with the mortgage remaining in place.\\n\\nAccordingly, when, in a title trust registration among three parties, the title trustee creates a mortgage over the real estate for a third party, the title trustee has obtained a benefit equivalent to the amount of the secured obligation under the mortgage and thereby caused corresponding damage to the title truster; therefore, the title trustee bears the duty to return that benefit to the title truster as unjust enrichment.\\n\\nc. Judgment in this case\\n1) As to the portion of the grounds of appeal by the Plaintiff concerning the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment (Grounds of Appeal Nos. 4 and 5)\\n\\nExamining the factual findings in paragraph 1 above in light of the legal principles set forth above, by causing the registration of creation of the mortgage at issue to be completed in favor of SC Bank, the Defendant, as title trustee, enabled SC Bank to validly acquire the mortgage right; the Defendant, as title trustee, obtained a benefit equivalent to the amount of the secured obligation of the mortgage through the real estate at issue, which was not its own; and the Plaintiff, as title truster, suffered damage in that it could obtain only ownership with a diminished exchange value by the amount of the secured obligation; therefore, the Defendant must return that benefit to the Plaintiff as unjust enrichment.\\n\\nContrary to this, the court below erred in dismissing the Plaintiff’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment in a title trust registration among three parties, thereby affecting the judgment. The Plaintiff’s assertion in this part of the grounds of appeal is well-founded.\\n\\n2) As to the portion of the grounds of appeal by the Plaintiff concerning the claim for delivery of shares (Grounds of Appeal Nos. 1, 2, and 3)\\n\\nThe court below dismissed this portion of the Plaintiff’s appeal, citing the first instance judgment, which held that there was no evidence of a title trust with respect to the shares listed in Attached List 2 to the judgment below (hereinafter referred to as the “Shares at issue”) between the Plaintiff and the Defendant, and that circumstances such as the Defendant’s having acted as a shareholder of Youngcheon Seal Tech Co., Ltd. were insufficient to conclude that the Plaintiff had title-trusted the Shares at issue to the Defendant and that the Defendant was merely a nominal shareholder.\\n\\nExamining the reasons for the judgment below in light of the record, the court below did not err in that judgment, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, by failing to conduct the necessary examination, thereby exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or by misapprehending the law regarding the distribution of the burden of proof, violating the principle of party presentation, or rendering a contradictory reasoning, etc., so as to affect the judgment.\\n\\n3) As to the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nThe court below recognized a title trust registration among three parties concerning the real estate at issue among the Plaintiff, the Defendant, and the non-party, and then upheld the Plaintiff’s claim seeking performance from the Defendant, as title trustee, by subrogating the non-party, as seller, for the registration procedure for transfer of ownership to restore true registered title in favor of the non-party.\\n\\nExamining the reasons for the judgment below in light of the record, the court below did not err in that judgment, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, by failing to conduct the necessary examination, thereby exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or by rendering contradictory reasoning, etc., so as to affect the judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nAccordingly, the part of the judgment below that ruled against the Plaintiff with respect to the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; the remainder of the Plaintiff’s appeal and the Defendant’s appeal are each dismissed; and judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition. In this decision, Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Park Jung-hwa, Kim Seon-su, Noh Tae-ak, and Lee Heung-gu filed a dissenting opinion on whether the Plaintiff may directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the Defendant. Other than that, the views of the participating Justices were unanimous, and Justice Jo Jae-yeon filed a supplemental opinion to the majority opinion, while Justices Park Jung-hwa and Noh Tae-ak filed supplemental opinions to the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n5. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Park Jung-hwa, Kim Seon-su, Noh Tae-ak, and Lee Heung-gu on the Issue\\nThe majority opinion states that, in a title trust registration among three parties, if the title trustee gained a benefit because title to the real estate was transferred from the title trustee to a third party or because a mortgage was created in favor of a third party, the title truster may directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee.\\n\\nHowever, even if, in a title trust registration among three parties, title is transferred to a third party through the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., and the title trustee thereby obtains a benefit such as proceeds from disposition or compensation money, etc. of the real estate, the title truster may not directly claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee. The Supreme Court Decision dated September 8, 2011, 2009DA49193, 49209, etc., which the majority opinion cites as precedents recognizing the title truster’s direct claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee, can no longer be maintained after the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act and must therefore be overruled. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\na. As to cases where ownership of the real estate is transferred to a third party through the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.\\n\\n1) After the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, there is no direct legal relationship between the title truster and the title trustee.\\n\\na) Under Article 4, Paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Real Estate Registration Act, in a title trust registration among three parties, the title trust agreement is void, and the registration of transfer of ownership in the title trustee’s name made thereby is also void. However, because the sales contract between the title truster and the seller is valid, the title truster merely acquires a claim for registration of transfer of ownership against the seller based on the sales contract and does not enter into any legal relationship with the title trustee. Therefore, in order for the title truster to exercise rights against the title trustee, the title truster must subrogate the seller. In other words, to preserve its claim for registration of transfer of ownership against the seller, it may only subrogate the seller to seek cancellation of the void registration of transfer of ownership completed in the title trustee’s name or to seek registration of transfer of ownership in the seller’s name on the ground of restoration of the true registered title. This legal principle does not change merely because the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. exists. Even if the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. occurs while the title truster is suing the title trustee by subrogating the seller, it cannot be said that, from that point, the title truster may no longer subrogate the seller and instead directly exercise rights against the title trustee.\\n\\nb) According to the majority opinion, until the title trustee engages in a disposition act, etc., the title truster could exercise rights against the title trustee only by subrogating the seller in order to preserve its claim for registration of transfer of ownership against the seller; but by the accidental circumstance that the title trustee engaged in a disposition act, etc., a claim against the title trustee that had not previously existed comes into being, allowing direct exercise of rights. This results in affirming a direct legal relationship between the title truster and the title trustee when the trust real estate is transformed into proceeds from disposition or compensation money, etc., thereby producing the same effect as validating the title trust.\\n\\n2) The person who suffers damage directly causally related to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. is the owner, namely, the seller, not the title truster. Therefore, the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment concerning the benefit obtained by the title trustee through the disposition act, etc. belongs to the seller.\\n\\na) Before the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, the title trust agreement was valid, and the registration in the title trustee’s name made pursuant thereto was recognized externally as ownership. Thus, if the seller transferred ownership to the title trustee in response to the title truster’s demand, the seller lost that ownership and its obligations as seller ended, while the title truster had only the legal relationship arising from the title trust agreement with the title trustee.\\n\\nHowever, after the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, as noted above, in a title trust registration among three parties, both the title trust agreement and the registration of transfer of ownership in the title trustee’s name made pursuant thereto are void; therefore, ownership of the real estate still remains with the seller, and the title truster is in the position of holding a claim for registration of transfer of ownership against the seller. Accordingly, if a third party validly acquires ownership through the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the seller loses ownership of the real estate. At that time, the title trustee’s obtaining of proceeds from disposition or compensation money, etc. merely because it had the title of ownership to the real estate constitutes the unlawful infringement of another’s right, causing that right to be lost and obtaining a benefit from that infringement; thus, it falls under what is called enrichment by infringement. Therefore, the title trustee must return the benefit obtained through the disposition act, etc. to the seller, who is the rightful owner.\\n\\nb) Precedents have also made clear that, in a case where a person without rights disposes of another person’s right to a third party, and the original right holder loses the right due to a provision protecting a good-faith third party, the right holder may claim restitution against the person without rights, treating what the latter received from the third party as consideration for the disposition as so-called enrichment by infringement (see Supreme Court Decision dated June 10, 2011, 2010DA40239; en banc Supreme Court Decision dated May 21, 2020, 2017DA220744, etc.). This legal principle should equally apply when the title trustee disposes of the trust real estate to a third party.\\n\\n3) Between the title truster and the title trustee, there exists no legal relationship involving a prestation without legal cause, expenditure of costs, or infringement of an exclusive right, which would justify directly recognizing a restitution of unjust enrichment relationship.\\n\\na) The title truster merely entrusted the title of registration to the title trustee pursuant to the title trust agreement, and did not directly make any prestation or expend any costs to the title trustee; nor does such prestation form part of the content of the title trust agreement. The title truster is merely a creditor of the seller, having purchased the real estate from the seller and paid the purchase price to the seller, and holding a claim for registration of transfer of ownership against the seller; such a claim is not a right that can be asserted against anyone other than the seller. Therefore, even if the title trustee, who is a third party and not a party to the contract, engages in a disposition act, etc., it merely infringes the seller’s ownership, and cannot be said to have infringed an exclusive right belonging to the title truster.\\n\\nFurthermore, even if, by the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the title truster’s claim for registration of transfer of ownership against the seller becomes impossible to perform, that does not mean that the claim held by the title truster against the seller is extinguished; the title truster still retains, against the seller, rights such as a claim for damages or rescission of the contract.\\n\\nThus, even if ownership of the trust real estate is transferred to a third party, no direct settlement relationship of prestation or compensation for infringement of rights arises between the title truster and the title trustee on that ground. Therefore, even if the seller loses ownership because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., and consequently the title truster’s claim for registration of transfer of ownership becomes impossible to perform, a restitution of unjust enrichment relationship cannot be said to arise directly between the title truster and the title trustee without including the seller.\\n\\nb) In a case where a title trust registration among three parties was made before the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, precedents held that even after the title trust agreement and the registration made pursuant thereto became void upon the lapse of the grace period prescribed by the Real Estate Registration Act, the title truster could not claim transfer of ownership against the title trustee, who is the registered title holder of the void registration, once ownership of the real estate had returned to the seller (see Supreme Court Decision dated November 27, 2008, 2008DA55290, 55306, etc.). Precedents also held that, in a title trust registration among three parties, the title truster is neither the owner of the real estate nor in a fiduciary relationship with the title trustee, so the title trustee cannot be said to be holding the title truster’s property; therefore, even if the title trustee disposes of the real estate at will, embezzlement is not constituted in relation to the title truster (see en banc Supreme Court Decision dated May 19, 2016, 2014DO6992, etc.). These precedents can be interpreted as having principally relied on the premise that there is no direct legal relationship between the title truster and the title trustee in a title trust registration among three parties.\\n\\n4) It cannot be categorically said that, due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the seller can definitively retain the purchase price received from the title truster or that the seller incurs no loss.\\n\\na) The majority opinion cites Supreme Court Decision dated March 15, 2002, 2001DA61654, which held that, if the seller transferred the title of registration to the title trustee at the request of the title truster, it is not permitted under the principle of good faith for the title truster to seek restitution of the purchase price from the seller or to require that a transfer registration of ownership be made in the title truster’s name on the ground that the title truster did not make the real-name registration, and states that, even after the Real Estate Registration Act was enforced, it is still not permitted under the principle of good faith for the title truster to seek restitution of the purchase price from the seller or claim damages for impossibility of performance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership. However, this is not proper. Supreme Court Decision 2001DA61654 held, on the premise that it was impossible to find fault in the seller who, before the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, complied with the title truster’s request at a time when title trust was valid, that it was not permitted under the principle of good faith for the title truster to seek restitution of the purchase price or transfer registration from the seller. However, once the Real Estate Registration Act was enforced and it became clear that the title trust agreement and the resulting real-right change are void, it is difficult to apply the legal principle of Supreme Court Decision 2001DA61654 as is to a case where a title trust registration among three parties was made. The majority opinion says that the title truster, having caused the state of violation of the Real Estate Registration Act, still cannot seek restitution of the purchase price or damages from the seller even after the Real Estate Registration Act was enforced; this is incorrect. A title trust relationship among three parties that violates the Real Estate Registration Act arises only because the seller has consented to it; it cannot arise by the title truster alone. This is clearly different from the case under the latter sentence of Article 4, Paragraph 2 of the Real Estate Registration Act, where the title trustee is one of the parties and the other party does not know of the existence of the title trust agreement, so the title trust agreement and the real-right change are not treated as void. In addition, unlike before the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, the title truster did not form any trust in the seller. Before the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, because the title trust agreement was valid, there was a need to protect the seller who believed that the sales contract had been validly concluded and terminated. However, after the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, since it is clear that the title trust agreement is void, there is no room for trust to be formed in the seller that the sales contract would be validly concluded and terminated, and no need to protect such trust. Problems between the title truster and the seller should be governed by the general legal principles relating to contracts, including Civil Act Article 390, and there is no room to apply the principle of good faith.\\n\\nb) Moreover, it is incorrect to deem, as the majority opinion does, that the seller incurs no loss because the seller need not, until it recovers the title from the title trustee, return the purchase price to the title truster or transfer ownership to the title truster. Damage in enrichment by infringement means the very fact that the possibility of enjoying the benefit exclusively allocated to the right holder has been fundamentally blocked by the infringing act; it does not require that the right holder suffered concrete or substantive loss. Further, it cannot be said that the seller, having lost ownership, suffers no damage. This is because the seller’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee is a statutory claim arising from the title trustee’s infringement of the seller’s ownership of the trust real estate.\\n\\nc) The restitution relationship between the seller and the title trustee and the sales contract relationship between the title truster and the seller are separate legal relationships. To say that, in the restitution relationship between the seller and the title trustee, one must consider whether the seller and the title truster retain or suffer loss of the purchase price, etc. presupposes that a valid title trust agreement existed between the title truster and the title trustee; this is not consistent with the purpose of the Real Estate Registration Act, which regards the title trust agreement as void.\\n\\n5) The title truster may exercise its contractual rights against the seller.\\nWhen, because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the title truster becomes unable to acquire the real estate, the title truster may obtain relief against the seller by exercising the right to rescind the contract and claim restitution to seek return of the purchase price, or by claiming damages for breach of contract. Because of the nature of a title trust registration among three parties, in which the seller receives the entire purchase price from the title truster and transfers the title of registration to the title trustee, unlike an ordinary sales contract the registration of transfer of ownership to the title trustee is void even after the seller has received the full purchase price and, at the request of the title truster, has performed the registration procedure for transfer of ownership to the title trustee; therefore, the seller still bears, toward the title truster, the obligation to register transfer of ownership with respect to the trust real estate, and has not completed performance of its obligations as seller. Accordingly, if the seller knowingly neglects that obligation and the obligation to register transfer of ownership becomes impossible to perform, the seller must bear responsibility for impossibility of performance toward the title truster. The seller bears liability for damages for breach of obligation under Civil Act Article 390 toward the title truster, and the title truster may rescind the contract under Civil Act Article 546 and claim restitution from the seller. The title truster may, by subrogating the seller, also exercise a claim for substitute performance concerning proceeds from disposition or compensation money, etc. against the title trustee, and may exercise the seller’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment. Depending on the degree of fault of the title truster or seller, etc., compensation for the loss may be insufficient; however, this may be due in part to what the title truster brought upon itself, and therefore cannot necessarily be said to be unjust. In this respect, the majority opinion, which proceeds on the premise that the title truster cannot seek restitution of the purchase price from the seller or claim damages for impossibility of performance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership, and instead must receive the full amount of the proceeds from disposition or compensation money, etc. from the title trustee, is not free from criticism that it overly protects the title truster.\\n\\n6) It is contrary to the purpose and intent of the Real Estate Registration Act to categorically hold that the seller is not at fault.\\n\\na) The majority opinion states that if the seller transferred the title of registration to the title trustee at the request of the title truster, it is difficult to deem the seller at fault for the conclusion or performance of the sales contract, or, even if the seller is at fault, the title truster’s seeking of restitution of the purchase price from the seller or damages for impossibility of performance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership is still not permitted; therefore, the title truster and title trustee must adjust their interests directly through restitution of unjust enrichment. The Supreme Court Decision 2001DA61654 cited by the majority opinion also held, in a title trust relationship formed before the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, in a case where the title truster, by subrogating the seller, claimed damages against the title trustee in the amount of the proceeds from disposition, that “because the seller is not at fault for the impossibility of performance, the title truster cannot, under the principle of good faith, demand restitution of the purchase price from the seller or require transfer registration to be made in the title truster’s name, and therefore the seller’s claim for damages against the title trustee is not recognized,” thereby holding that the seller bears no responsibility.\\n\\nb) However, such reasoning can no longer be applied after the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, which regards the title trust agreement as void from the outset. As the majority opinion itself notes, the Real Estate Registration Act was enacted for the purpose and intent of registering real rights such as ownership of real estate in the name of the actual right holder so as to conform to the substantive legal relationship. This Act was enacted on March 30, 1995, and has been enforced for approximately 25 years, during which it has become widely known among the public that, if a real estate title is not registered in the name of the actual right holder, such registration is void, and that title trust relationships violating this are subject to criminal punishment and are not legally protected, being subject to fines and charges for compulsion of performance. In such circumstances, the seller’s act of transferring title to the title trustee at the request of the title truster, while cooperating in or acquiescing in the title trust relationship of the title truster, is an act that disregards the Real Estate Registration Act and assists the title truster’s evasion of the law. Given these circumstances, to say that the court should find the seller not at fault or not liable for impossibility of performance merely because the seller complied with the title truster’s request is to neutralize the Real Estate Registration Act and constitutes a legal interpretation that departs from the purpose and intent of the Real Estate Registration Act to realize registration in the name of the actual right holder.\\n\\n7) Recognizing the title truster’s direct claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee when the title trustee has engaged in a disposition act, etc. is also contrary to the purpose and intent of the Real Estate Registration Act.\\n\\nWhen ownership of the real estate is transferred to a third party because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. in a title trust registration among three parties, it becomes fixed that the title truster cannot receive transfer of ownership of the real estate pursuant to the third-party protection provision of Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act. This third-party protection provision has the effect of limiting the purpose of the Real Estate Registration Act—which is to have registration made in the name of the actual right holder—in order to protect the third party who relied on the appearance formed by the title trust agreement and to ensure transactional security. Meanwhile, the Real Estate Registration Act contains no provision adjusting the interests among the title truster, title trustee, and seller where, as above, the trust real estate has been transferred to a third party and registration in the name of the actual right holder has become impossible; therefore, it is necessary to realize the purpose and intent of the Act through legal interpretation. However, if, as the majority opinion does, the title truster is allowed to claim restitution of unjust enrichment directly against the title trustee, it would have the effect of as if the title trust agreement were valid between the title truster and title trustee, enabling the title truster to easily recover the purchase price it had expended when transfer of registration to itself has become impossible. This is an interpretation that, while the purpose of the law is to require the title truster to register title in its own name as the actual right holder, nevertheless readily allows direct transfer of ownership registration in the real estate from the title trustee to the title truster, but then, when the law is violated, allows the loss to be recovered directly; it is in direct conflict with the position of the Real Estate Registration Act, which invalidates the title trust agreement and the resulting real-right change.\\n\\n8) The majority opinion mainly relies on the ground that recognizing a direct restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title trustee, who obtained an unjust benefit, and the title truster, who suffered property loss, accords with the ideals of fairness and justice and simplifies the adjustment of interests. However, this perspective of the majority opinion risks obscuring the requirements for the establishment of a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment and excessively expanding the scope in which such a claim can be recognized.\\n\\na) The ideals of fairness and justice said to underlie the restitution of unjust enrichment system are highly abstract concepts. A claim for restitution of unjust enrichment is a statutory claim arising not from the effect of a particular legal act but pursuant to the requirements prescribed by law, and the requirements of “benefit without legal cause” and “damage caused thereby” under Civil Act Article 741 are also not univocal concepts, so it is not easy in individual cases to determine whether the requirements for a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment are satisfied. If a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment is recognized merely on the ground that recognizing a restitution relationship between the person who suffered property loss and the person who obtained benefit accords with the ideals of fairness and justice and simplifies the adjustment of interests, it becomes difficult to determine in individual cases when such a claim can be recognized.\\n\\nb) As another example, suppose A enters into a contract to purchase movable property owned by B, pays the purchase price in full to B, but has not yet taken delivery, and C, who has incidentally obtained possession of B’s movable property, sells it to D and transfers possession as well, so that D acquires the movable property owned by B in good faith. In such a case, A may rescind the sales contract and claim restitution of the purchase price from B as restoration to the original state, and B may claim from C restitution of the consideration for disposing of B’s movable property as unjust enrichment. However, if a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment is deemed possible on the ground that it accords with the ideals of fairness and justice and simplifies the adjustment of interests, then A would also be able to seek direct restitution of unjust enrichment from C. Yet, in practice, a direct claim by A against C for restitution of unjust enrichment is rarely granted, on the view that such a right amounts merely to infringement of a claim right rather than infringement of an exclusive real right.\\n\\nTake another example. Suppose contracts are separately concluded whereby A sells his real estate to B, and B resells it to C, and the purchase price is paid in sequence from C to B and from B to A, but before the registration of transfer of ownership is made, A sells the real estate to D and completes the registration of transfer of ownership to D. In such a case, because the obligation to register transfer of ownership becomes impossible to perform under the sales contracts between A and B and between B and C, the creditors under each contract, namely B and C, will rescind their respective sales contracts and seek restitution from A and B, respectively, for their respective purchase prices. Even in this case, however, if one deems a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment possible on the ground that it accords with the ideals of fairness and justice and simplifies the adjustment of interests, then C would also be able to seek direct restitution of unjust enrichment from A in the amount corresponding to the consideration A obtained from the disposition of the real estate, disregarding the specific contractual relationships between A and B and between B and C. Yet even in such cases, claims by C have rarely been granted in practice.\\n\\nc) To recognize a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment in an individual case, there must be a substantive legal relationship forming the basis between the restitution creditor and the restitution obligor, namely, the existence of a prestation without legal cause, expenditure of costs, or infringement of an exclusive right. The same applies when the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. occurs in a title trust registration among three parties. The restitution relationship of unjust enrichment should be recognized between the seller, whose ownership was infringed, and the title trustee, who obtained proceeds from disposition or compensation money, etc. thereby, not between the title truster and the title trustee, who have no direct legal relationship, merely because it abstractly accords with the ideals of fairness and justice or because it simplifies adjustment of interests.\\n\\nd) The Supreme Court, in cases where the obtaining of benefits and the loss of rights are intertwined among multiple parties, has denied restitution of unjust enrichment on the ground that the parties were not direct contracting parties or were not parties to the restitution of the prestation itself. Supreme Court Decision dated July 22, 2005, 2005DA7566, 7573 held that, where a contract constituting the legal relationship between the promisor and the promisee in a contract for the benefit of a third party (the so-called underlying relationship) is rescinded, the settlement of that contractual relationship must be made between the promisor and the promisee, who are the parties to the contract, and therefore, absent special circumstances, even if the promisor has already performed to the third party, the promisor may not, on the basis of rescission or unjust enrichment, seek return from the third party. Supreme Court Decision dated December 26, 2003, 2001DA46730 held that, where one party to a contract, due to the instructions of the other contractual party, etc., shortened the performance process and directly rendered performance to a third party who has another contractual relationship with the other contractual party, such performance constitutes not only performance by the party to the contract to its counterparty, but also performance by that counterparty to the third party; therefore, one party to the contract cannot claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the third party on the ground that the third party received the prestation without legal cause. According to these precedents, restitution of unjust enrichment should also be denied in this case.\\n\\n9) Since the title trust agreement was rendered void by the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, the Supreme Court has, in sequence, altered in conformity with the legal principles of the Real Estate Registration Act those decisions rendered on the basis of legal relationships between the title truster and title trustee, where the title truster was treated as the substantive owner under a valid title trust made before the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act. Specifically, the title truster may not, against the title trustee, (i) claim registration of transfer of ownership of the real estate itself on the ground of restitution of unjust enrichment (see Supreme Court Decision dated November 27, 2008, 2008DA55290, 55306, etc.), (ii) claim registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of termination of title trust (see Supreme Court Decision dated January 26, 1999, 98DA1027; Supreme Court Decision dated October 23, 2008, 2008DA43693, etc.), or (iii) claim return of the real estate or cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of an agreement to return the real estate (see Supreme Court Decision dated November 9, 2006, 2006DA35117; Supreme Court Decision dated September 10, 2015, 2013DA55300, etc.). And in a title trust registration among three parties, since the title truster is not the owner of the real estate and there is no fiduciary relationship between the title truster and the title trustee, the title trustee cannot be regarded as a person holding the title truster’s property; thus, even if the title trustee disposes of the real estate at will, embezzlement is not constituted in relation to the title truster (see en banc Supreme Court Decision dated May 19, 2016, 2014DO6992, etc.).\\n\\nThese legal principles should also be consistently applied to the adjustment of interests among the title truster, title trustee, and seller arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.; accordingly, prior decisions, etc. cited by the majority opinion should be overruled.\\n\\nb. As to the case where the title trustee creates a mortgage over the real estate\\n\\nIn a title trust registration among three parties, when the title trustee creates a mortgage over the trust real estate, the legal relationship among the title truster, title trustee, and seller is basically the same as in the case, discussed above, where ownership of the real estate is transferred to a third party due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.\\n\\nIf the title trustee creates a mortgage over the real estate for a third party, the third party validly acquires the mortgage right (Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act). Even if the seller restores title through registration of transfer of ownership based on restoration of the true registered title with respect to the real estate, the seller obtains ownership subject to the mortgage right.
