The act of the title trustee, who is merely a person having the title of ownership without any right over the real estate, creating a mortgage for a third party over the real estate is an act that infringes the seller’s ownership; therefore, the title trustee bears the obligation to return the benefit obtained through creation of the mortgage to the seller as enrichment by infringement, or the obligation to pay damages under tort.\\n\\nOrdinarily, in a sales contract, the seller bears the obligation to perform a complete transfer of ownership registration of the object of sale free of restrictions or burdens (see Supreme Court Decision dated November 28, 2000, 2000DA8533, etc.). The same applies to the relationship between the title truster and the seller in a title trust registration among three parties. The fact that the title trustee created a mortgage over the real estate should not lead to any different conclusion. As a rule, the seller bears the obligation toward the title truster to transfer ownership of the trust real estate free of any security interest. If the seller transfers ownership of the real estate to the title truster without cancelling the mortgage created by the title trustee, that constitutes nonperformance of the obligation under the sales contract and gives rise to liability for damages to the title truster. However, the extent to which the seller may be held liable for breach of obligation may vary depending on the individual case.\\n\\nFurthermore, because the title truster, in relation to the seller, is in the position of having only a claim for registration of transfer of ownership with respect to the real estate under the sales contract and not ownership of the real estate itself, the title trustee’s creation of a mortgage over the real estate does not infringe any right of the title truster.\\n\\nTherefore, the title trustee bears the obligation to return unjust enrichment or the obligation to compensate for damages toward the seller, but does not bear the obligation to return unjust enrichment toward the title truster.\\n\\nc. Conclusion in this case\\nThe court below dismissed the Plaintiff’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the Defendant in the amount equivalent to the secured obligation under the mortgage at issue, on the ground that the damage caused by the creation of the mortgage at issue accrues to the non-party, the seller of the real estate at issue, and not to the Plaintiff. The court below’s judgment is proper. The court below did not err in its judgment, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, by violating the rules of logic and experience, exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, failing to conduct the necessary examination, misapprehending the law regarding unjust enrichment, or violating the duty to explain, etc., so as to affect the judgment. The Plaintiff’s appeal on this part should be dismissed.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, I cannot agree with the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Supplemental Opinion of Justice Jo Jae-yeon on the Majority Opinion\\na. The purpose of the Real Estate Registration Act\\nThe Real Estate Registration Act governs title trust agreements and resulting real-right changes on the premise that ownership of real estate vests in the actual right holder (see en banc Supreme Court Decision dated June 20, 2019, 2013DA218156).\\n\\nIn other words, while the Real Estate Registration Act provides that title trust agreements and the resulting real-right changes are void (Article 4, Paragraphs 1 and 2), it also imposes a penalty surcharge on the title truster as a sanction for violation and imposes a duty to register the real right concerning the title-trusted real estate in the title truster’s own name without delay, further providing that, if this is violated, a compulsion charge is imposed in addition to the penalty surcharge (Article 5, Paragraph 1, Item 1; Article 6). Because title trust agreements and the resulting real-right changes are void, the real rights in the real estate remain with the former registered title holder regardless of registration; accordingly, the title truster may exercise rights such as restoration of registration based on a legal relationship other than the title trust agreement, and furthermore bears the duty to remedy the inconsistency between the registration title and the substantive legal relationship.\\n\\nThus, while the Real Estate Registration Act invalidates the real-right changes effected through title trust agreements and the registrations made pursuant thereto, it does not prohibit the title truster from exercising rights such as restoration of registration on the basis of other legal relationships. Rather, by imposing administrative sanctions and criminal punishment on the title truster for the purpose of indirectly compelling the rectification of the inconsistency between the registration title and the substantive legal relationship and thereby eliminating the unlawful situation and ensuring the effectiveness of the Act (see Supreme Court Decision dated November 27, 2003, 2003DA41722; Supreme Court Decision dated June 28, 2016, 2014DU6456; en banc Supreme Court Decision dated June 20, 2019, 2013DA218156, etc.), the Act does not contain any provision extinguishing the title truster’s rights in the title-trusted real estate or depriving the title truster of the property benefit therefrom, nor any provision allowing the title trustee to retain the property benefit related to the title-trusted real estate. Meanwhile, although the Real Estate Registration Act imposes administrative sanctions and criminal punishment on the title truster and title trustee, it does not provide direct administrative sanctions against the seller, the former registered title holder, apart from the separate issue of general criminal liability such as aiding and abetting a violation of the Real Estate Registration Act.\\n\\nb. Significance of the restitution of unjust enrichment system\\nThe restitution of unjust enrichment system is one that imposes upon the beneficiary the duty to return the benefit where the beneficiary’s property gain lacks legal cause, based on the ideals of fairness and justice (see Supreme Court Decision dated March 13, 2008, 2006DA53733, 53740, etc.). It is a system intended to resolve contradictions that arise when, in a specific legal relationship between certain parties, a certain change in property value occurs and, though it may generally and formally appear to be legitimate, the change in property value between those parties conflicts, from a relative and substantive perspective, with another ideal of law, namely fairness, by ordering the acquirer of the property value to return the value (see en banc Supreme Court Decision dated June 25, 2015, 2014DA5531). In adjusting such improper changes in property value, classifying unjust enrichment according to substance and determining whether unjust enrichment has arisen can be a useful tool for identifying legal relationships concerning unjust enrichment concretely and clearly. However, in real legal relationships, unjust enrichment can appear in various forms based on diverse causes, and among them there may be cases not falling within a certain type of unjust enrichment or where it is not appropriate to apply the criteria for determining a type of unjust enrichment as they are. Therefore, in the end, whether unjust enrichment exists and the legal relationship for restitution of unjust enrichment must be determined in concrete cases according to the ideals of justice and fairness, and the issue of unjust enrichment should not be resolved only within the framework of a typified concept of unjust enrichment.\\n\\nc. Supplement to the majority opinion and rebuttal of the dissenting opinion\\n1) A restitution relationship of unjust enrichment may also arise between the title truster and the title trustee.\\n\\na) After the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, if a title trust agreement and the registration made pursuant thereto are effected, then pursuant to Article 4, Paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Real Estate Registration Act, the real-right change effected by the title trust agreement and the registration made pursuant thereto becomes void, so it may be said that no legal relationship concerning the trust real estate exists between the title truster and the title trustee. However, even in such a case, the title truster can realize, in its own name, registration of transfer of ownership concerning the trust real estate through the valid sales contract. Yet, when the title trustee engages in a disposition act, etc., the third party validly acquires the real right in the trust real estate in combination with Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act, and as a result the registration in the name of the actual right holder that the Real Estate Registration Act seeks cannot be realized or is restricted. Before the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the title truster could realize its registered title through the seller as intermediary, but once the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. occurs, a “new event” arises in relation to the attribution of ownership of the trust real estate, namely, the third party’s acquisition of ownership. Due to such a “new event,” the purpose of the Real Estate Registration Act—to realize registration in the name of the actual right holder through the seller—can no longer be achieved, while the rights and obligations existing before the occurrence of that event inevitably change. Because this change in legal relationship stems from the title trust agreement concluded between the title truster and the title trustee, a legal relationship requiring adjustment of the movement in property value also arises between the title truster and the title trustee.\\n\\nBecause the Real Estate Registration Act aims to realize registration in the name of the actual right holder for real estate, not to deprive the title truster of property rights, once it becomes impossible to realize registration in the name of the actual right holder due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act, recognizing a legal relationship of unjust enrichment between the title truster and title trustee cannot be considered equivalent to treating a title trust agreement and the resulting registration, which are void under the Real Estate Registration Act, as valid. It is unnecessary, even at the stage where the purpose of the Real Estate Registration Act can no longer be achieved, to deny the legal relationship between the title truster and title trustee that has emerged due to the occurrence of the “new event,” on the ground that the title trust agreement is void.\\n\\nb) Precedents hold that where the original right holder loses the right due to the disposition act of a person without rights, in accordance with the third-party protection provision, the benefit obtained by the person without rights must be returned to the original right holder as enrichment by infringement. This legal principle was declared in cases where the original right holder obtained no consideration in the process by which the person without rights became able to dispose of the relevant real estate. It should not be extended as-is to cases such as a title trust registration among three parties, where the original right holder, the seller, loses ownership because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. while, through the sales contract with the title truster, the seller receives the purchase price and is able to retain it, so that obtaining of benefits and loss of rights are closely intertwined among multiple parties. As noted above, although typifying unjust enrichment can allow one to identify, concretely and clearly, the legal relationship surrounding restitution of unjust enrichment, considering the purpose of the restitution of unjust enrichment system and the diversity of factual relationships in reality, it is not appropriate to identify the establishment of unjust enrichment or the legal relationship of restitution only within a particular type.\\n\\nc) The dissenting opinion says that, because the requirements for a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment are expressed in abstract concepts, it is not easy in an individual case to determine whether the requirements are satisfied; therefore, in order to recognize a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment, the existence of a substantive legal relationship forming the basis between the restitution creditor and the restitution obligor, namely, prestation without legal cause, expenditure of costs, or infringement of an exclusive right, etc., must be presupposed, and the same applies when the title trustee engages in a disposition act, etc. in a title trust registration among three parties. However, the cases cited by the dissenting opinion in support of this point are cases entirely unrelated to one another between a purchaser who bought a thing from the original owner and a person who infringed the original owner’s ownership, and the existing precedents cited by the dissenting opinion concern cases where performance was made to a third party under a contract for the benefit of a third party or pursuant to instructions for shortened performance, and the issue was whether return of the performance itself could be sought against the third party. By contrast, a title trust registration among three parties is a case in which, by reason of the title trust agreement between the purchaser/title truster and the title trustee and the registration made pursuant thereto, legal relationships surrounding registration title to the trust real estate are formed among the title truster, title trustee, and seller, and then those legal relationships are altered by the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. This is a different type of case from the examples given by the dissenting opinion and also not the same as the cases cited by the dissenting opinion. Therefore, it cannot be said that, merely because there is a similarity in that there exists a legal relationship among multiple parties concerning a specific object or prestation, the conclusion on whether restitution of unjust enrichment is established must also be the same. The change in rights and obligations arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. in a title trust registration among three parties is more complex than that arising merely from the disposition act of a person without rights, and because it originates from the title trust agreement and resulting registration that are legally void, the relationship between the title truster and the title trustee that caused such circumstances cannot be ignored.\\n\\n2) Where the title trustee engages in a disposition act, etc., the title trustee’s benefit without legal cause and the resulting damage to the title truster are recognized, and the requirements for a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment are satisfied.\\n\\na) Due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act, the title trustee obtains proceeds from disposition or compensation money, etc. without legal cause, despite not being the owner.\\n\\nb) Before the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the seller, as owner of the trust real estate, may demand restoration of title from the title trustee; however, if the title trustee engages in a disposition act, etc., the seller loses ownership of the trust real estate. At the same time, however, the seller is freed from the obligation to register transfer of ownership concerning the trust real estate, and moreover retains the purchase price received under the sales contract without bearing liability for damages for impossibility of performance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership, or at least the title truster is not permitted under the principle of good faith to seek return of the purchase price or demand performance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership from the seller. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Although the seller bears toward the title truster the obligation under the sales contract to register transfer of ownership, where that obligation becomes impossible to perform because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., absent special circumstances, it is difficult to deem the seller at fault for that impossibility of performance. This is because, in the series of events from the conclusion of the sales contract between the seller and the title truster, the registration of transfer of ownership in the title trustee’s name at the request of the title truster, and the impossibility of performance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership caused by the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the seller cannot be said to have violated the duty of care it owed under the sales contract toward the buyer, the “title truster.”\\n\\nMeanwhile, the title truster, who is the counterparty to the obligation to register transfer of ownership, actively intended the title trust agreement and registration prohibited by the Real Estate Registration Act, arranged for the title trustee, concluded the sales contract with the seller, and caused the seller and title trustee to create a registration inconsistent with the substantive relationship; moreover, even thereafter, despite having been able to avoid the consequence of impossibility of performance caused by the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. by subrogating the seller and cancelling the registration of transfer of ownership in the title trustee’s name and registering ownership in its own name, the title truster neglected to do so.\\n\\n(2) As above, because the seller cannot be deemed at fault for the impossibility of performance of the registration of transfer of ownership, and because it may be deemed a case where performance became impossible for a reason attributable to the creditor, namely, the title truster, the seller may retain the purchase price under Civil Act Article 538, Paragraph 1 and does not bear liability for damages toward the title truster for impossibility of performance. Even if the seller’s cooperation in violating the Real Estate Registration Act were deemed negligence regarding impossibility of performance, the title truster’s negligence regarding impossibility of performance, as seen above, is substantially heavier and greater in content and degree of breach of duty than that of the seller; therefore, it is not permitted under the principle of good faith for the title truster to assert that the seller is also at fault for impossibility of performance and thereby seek restitution of the purchase price or claim damages for impossibility of performance.\\n\\nSupreme Court Decision dated September 8, 2011, 2009DA49193, 49209 held that the lower court’s reasoning, which recognized the title truster’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee and held that the title truster could seek payment of compensation money concerning the trust real estate from the title trustee in order to preserve the rights arising from impossibility of performance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership toward the seller, was improper, thereby deciding on the premise that the title truster had no right against the seller arising from impossibility of performance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership. Supreme Court Decision dated September 10, 2015, 2015DA207235, and Supreme Court Decision dated July 25, 2019, 2019DA203811, 203828, concerning cases where title trust agreements and registrations were made after the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, can be understood as having repeatedly confirmed that the title truster has no right, as against the seller, to exercise any right arising from impossibility of performance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership, by holding that the legal principles of Supreme Court Decision 2009DA49193, 49209 could equally apply even where a title trust agreement among three parties was concluded and registration made pursuant thereto after the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act.\\n\\nc) Although the seller has received the purchase price from the title truster, the seller may refuse to return the purchase price and does not bear liability for damages caused by impossibility of performance, even if the obligation to register transfer of ownership toward the title truster becomes impossible to perform due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act; therefore, it cannot be said that the seller has suffered economic loss because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. Moreover, the title truster, having paid the purchase price to the seller based on the sales contract but becoming unable to receive transfer of ownership of the trust real estate because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., and being unable to obtain relief by seeking restitution of the purchase price or damages from the seller for impossibility of performance, has suffered direct damage because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.\\n\\nd) In this manner, because the title trustee obtained, through the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and Article 4, Paragraph 3 of the Real Estate Registration Act, a benefit equivalent to the proceeds from disposition of the real estate and thereby caused the title truster to lose the right to acquire ownership of the real estate, the requirements for the establishment of a restitution of unjust enrichment claim by the title trustee against the title truster are satisfied when the title trustee engages in the disposition act, etc. The claim for restitution of unjust enrichment concerning the benefit obtained by the title trustee through the disposition act, etc. belongs to the title truster.\\n\\n3) Recognizing the title truster’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee conforms to the principle of self-responsibility, which holds the title truster responsible for decisions made according to its own will, and is also a solution consistent with the principle of fairness in the process of adjusting interests.\\n\\na) The title truster should bear responsibility for its own decision-making because it has, through its own decisions, arranged for the title trustee, concluded the title trust agreement, concluded the sales contract with the seller, and proceeded with the transfer of registration under the title trust agreement.\\n\\nHowever, if, as the dissenting opinion argues, the seller may exercise a claim for damages or a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee, while the title truster may obtain relief by exercising the right to rescind the contract against the seller and seek return of the purchase price as restoration to the original state or claim damages for breach of obligation, this would make the seller bear the risk arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and even the risk of the title trustee’s insolvency, thereby shifting to the seller the risk that ought to be borne by the title truster, who actively caused the violation of the Real Estate Registration Act.\\n\\nb) Where there are multiple parties involved in a benefit without legal cause, in deciding how to allocate the legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment among the parties, the degree of legal defenses and risk burden the parties have in the original legal relationship should not differ, nor should they retain greater benefits than before or be deprived of rights.\\n\\nIn adjusting the interests arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. in a title trust registration among three parties, even if the title truster’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee is recognized, the legal defenses recognized in the legal relationship existing before the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. are neither taken away from the title truster, title trustee, and seller nor are additional risks imposed upon them.\\n\\nBy contrast, if the title truster claims damages for breach of obligation against the seller, it is conceivable that, due to comparative negligence or other reasons, the amount the title truster can obtain from the seller may be less than the purchase price the seller retains. This would allow the seller to retain an unexpected benefit because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., while depriving the title truster of an economic benefit, which is inconsistent with the ideals of fairness and the purpose of the Real Estate Registration Act.\\n\\nd. Summary\\nRecognizing, as the majority opinion does, the title truster’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee is by no means intended to protect the title truster in a title trust registration relationship among three parties. The Real Estate Registration Act invalidates the real-right changes concerning real estate effected through title trust agreements and the registrations made pursuant thereto, but where the title trustee engages in a disposition act, etc., it provides a third-party protection provision so that the real-right change with respect to the real estate may validly occur. Nevertheless, because the Real Estate Registration Act provides no rules regarding the resulting change in rights and obligations, the issue of adjusting interests arising from the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. must ultimately be resolved according to the law of restitution of unjust enrichment. Since the Real Estate Registration Act does not permit the title trustee to retain proceeds from the disposition of the trust real estate, the issue of returning such benefits is more directly and reasonably resolved between the parties to the title trust agreement, which is the original cause of the improper change in property value between the parties. Moreover, as noted above, because the requirements for the title truster’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee are satisfied, there is no need to drag the seller, who has acquired the purchase price and performed its obligations under the sales contract, back into the legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment.\\n\\nFor the reasons above, I supplement the reasoning of the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Supplemental Opinion of Justices Park Jung-hwa and Noh Tae-ak to the Dissenting Opinion\\na. Whether a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment may be recognized between the title truster and the title trustee in a title trust agreement rendered void by the Real Estate Registration Act\\n1) The majority opinion and the supplemental opinion to the majority opinion state that the Real Estate Registration Act aims to realize registration in the name of the actual right holder of the trust real estate, invalidates the real-right changes effected through title trust agreements and the registrations made pursuant thereto, but does not prohibit the title truster from exercising rights such as restoration of registration on the basis of other legal relationships, and does not deprive the title truster of property benefits.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion also has no reason to disagree that the Real Estate Registration Act invalidates title trust agreements and the resulting real-right changes while not prohibiting the title truster from exercising rights such as restoration of registration on the basis of other legal relationships and not depriving the title truster of property benefits.\\n\\nHowever, the dissenting opinion views differently from the majority opinion the method of adjusting the title truster’s registration restoration as the actual right holder and the property interests arising therefrom. That is, the dissenting opinion views the “other legal relationship” enabling the title truster to exercise rights such as restoration of registration, as set forth in the supplemental opinion to the majority opinion, as the “sales contract between the title truster and the seller,” and contends that, based on the legal effect arising therefrom, the restoration of rights in the name of the actual right holder and the adjustment of interests concerning the transformed asset must all be handled consistently and uniformly.\\n\\nBy contrast, the majority opinion states that the legal effect based on the sales contract between the title truster and the seller applies only when the trust real estate remains in the title trustee’s name, whereas when the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. results in a third party acquiring the trust real estate, interests may be adjusted not through the effect of the above contract but through the restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title truster and the title trustee.\\n\\n2) Because the sales contract between the title truster and the seller is valid, it must remain in force until the contract terminates. However, there is merely a difference in the legal effect arising therefrom depending on whether performance of the obligation is possible or impossible; the occurrence of a ground of impossibility of performance in a valid sales contract does not render it a juristic act void ab initio. Yet the majority opinion, when a ground of impossibility of performance arises while the sales contract remains in force, seeks to resolve the matter by bringing in the title trustee’s title trust agreement, which is separately void under the Real Estate Registration Act, excluding the seller, a party to the sales contract, and by framing the issue as a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title truster and the title trustee, while leaving intact the legal relationship based on the still-valid sales contract.\\n\\n3) From the perspective of the dissenting opinion, the third party’s acquisition of ownership caused by the title trustee’s disposition act, etc.—the “new event” referred to in the supplemental opinion to the majority opinion—is merely a ground of impossibility of performance in the sales contract between the title truster and the seller and is not a factor affecting the legal relationship between the title truster and title trustee formed by the title trust agreement, which was void from the outset.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion considers that the sales contract between the title truster and the seller has not yet terminated until the seller fully performs its obligations, so even if a ground of impossibility of performance arises in the process, the parties must resolve the issue according to the original sales contract. In other words, whether performance of the obligation is possible or impossible, the law should consistently be interpreted with the seller as the party.\\n\\nb. From this perspective, I would specifically rebut the majority opinion and its supplemental opinion, and supplement the reasoning of the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n1) The title truster is not a person entitled to claim restitution of unjust enrichment.\\n\\nThe title truster does not possess a legitimate right to claim restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee. The title truster is merely a creditor of the seller with a claim for registration of transfer of ownership based on sale and is not a person who acquired ownership, a real right; this right of the title truster does not change merely because a third party has acquired the trust real estate and the seller’s performance of its obligation has become impossible.\\n\\nSupreme Court Decision dated November 27, 2008, 2008DA55290, 55306, cited by the dissenting opinion, held that in a title trust registration among three parties the title truster cannot directly seek transfer registration against the title trustee, who is the registered title holder of the void registration, and cannot seek transfer registration of ownership on the ground of restitution of unjust enrichment, stating as its basis that the title truster is not the owner but merely has a claim for registration of transfer of ownership against the seller. In light of that reasoning, even where a third party acquires ownership because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., the title truster, not being the owner, should not be deemed able to seek restitution of proceeds from disposition, etc. from the title trustee as unjust enrichment.\\n\\n2) The majority opinion is, in substance, no different from recognizing the title trust agreement as valid.\\n\\na) The supplemental opinion to the majority opinion cites as the reason for recognizing a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title truster and the title trustee where the real estate is transferred to a third party because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. in a title trust registration among three parties, the fact that in a title trust registration among three parties, the obtaining of benefits and the loss of rights among the parties are closely interrelated, and that this presents special circumstances different from other cases of disposition by a person without rights. Ultimately, it says, one cannot avoid considering the relationship between the title truster and the title trustee.\\n\\nHowever, Article 4, Paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Real Estate Registration Act clearly provide that the title trust agreement and the resulting real-right change are void, and precedents likewise regard as void, in light of the purpose and intent of the Real Estate Registration Act, even the delegation agreement for the sale of real estate incidental to the title trust agreement, the title-trusted real estate and the agreement to return the proceeds from disposition based on the premise of title trust (see Supreme Court Decision dated November 9, 2006, 2006DA35117; Supreme Court Decision dated September 10, 2015, 2013DA55300, etc.). In a title trust registration among three parties as well, the title trust agreement between the title truster and the title trustee is void, and the legal relationship should be analyzed on the premise that no legal relationship exists between them, which accords with the purpose and intent of the Real Estate Registration Act. The fact that precedents do not allow the title truster, in a title trust registration among three parties, to directly claim registration of transfer of ownership of the real estate against the title trustee, and instead require the title truster to subrogate the seller and seek cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership or transfer registration based on restoration of the true registered title, and also hold that embezzlement is not constituted in relation to the title truster even if the title trustee disposes of the real estate at will, all stem from the premise that the title trust agreement between the title truster and title trustee is void and that no legal relationship exists between them.\\n\\nb) So long as the title trust agreement between the title truster and the title trustee is regarded as void, the legal relationship between the title truster and seller and the legal relationship between the seller and the title trustee are each independent and separate legal relationships that cannot affect one another. When the real estate is transferred to a third party because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., this only affects the legal relationship between the title truster and the seller, and the legal relationship between the seller and the title trustee, individually. Accordingly, as between the title trustee and the seller, there arises the issue of restitution of unjust enrichment due to the title trustee’s infringement of the seller’s ownership; and as between the title truster and the seller, there arises the issue of contractual breach because the seller becomes unable to perform its contractual obligation. Therefore, when the title trustee disposes of the real estate in a title trust registration among three parties, the structure is the same as the case addressed in Supreme Court Decision dated June 10, 2011, 2010DA40239, where a person without rights disposed of another person’s right to a third party, and the original right holder lost the right due to a provision protecting a good-faith third party. Just as a person without rights who must return the right to the rightful holder must return the consideration for the disposition to the rightful holder as unjust enrichment when the right is lost by disposing of it to a third party, the title trustee likewise bears responsibility to return the consideration for the disposition, etc., to the seller, who is the true owner of the real estate.\\n\\nc) Recognizing a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment merely because the real estate has been transferred to a third party due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. in a title trust registration among three parties, as the majority opinion does, is no different from creating a new legal relationship between the title truster and the title trustee. And the basis for that ultimately must be understood as presupposing that a valid title trust agreement existed between the title truster and the title trustee, that is, the validity of the title trust agreement.\\n\\nHowever, precedents after the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act have maintained an attitude of denying the presupposition of the validity of the title trust agreement or the construction of legal relationships based thereon. If, as the majority opinion does, the title truster’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee is recognized, this not only contradicts the consistent attitude of these precedents but also leads to the result of violating the Real Estate Registration Act.\\n\\nd) The supplemental opinion to the majority opinion states that the restitution relationship of unjust enrichment should not be examined only within a typified framework, but should be judged according to the ideals of fairness in concrete cases. There are many cases, besides title trust registration among three parties, in which the issue is whether a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment can be recognized, and in which the obtaining of benefits and the loss of rights are intertwined among multiple parties. However, in Supreme Court Decision dated December 26, 2003, 2001DA46730, and Supreme Court Decision dated July 22, 2005, 2005DA7566, 7573, etc., as examined in the dissenting opinion, the Court held that unjust enrichment cannot be recognized merely on the ground that the legal relationship involving multiple parties can be simply resolved among the parties or that it can accord with the principle of justice and fairness. Rather, where there is no substantive legal relationship between the parties that would justify recognizing a legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment such as a contract, direct restitution of unjust enrichment is not recognized. Yet the majority opinion alone, which seeks to recognize a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title truster and the title trustee in a title trust registration among three parties, can only be explained as having arisen from viewing the title trust agreement between the title truster and the title trustee as valid, despite the denial in the supplemental opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n3) The majority opinion’s grounds that it is not permitted under the principle of good faith for the title truster to seek restitution of the purchase price from the seller or demand performance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership lack rational persuasive force.\\n\\na) Precedents hold, with respect to the principle of good faith under civil law, that it is “an abstract norm stating that parties to a legal relationship must not exercise their rights or perform their obligations in a manner that offends fairness or betrays trust by considering the interests of the other party; in order to deny the exercise of a right on the ground of violation of the principle of good faith, the other party must have been given trust, or objectively be in a position where it is legitimate for the other party to have trust, and the exercise of the right against such trust must have reached a degree that cannot be tolerated in light of the concept of justice; moreover, absent special circumstances, a person who entered into a legal act while knowing that it violated the law and was void cannot be said to be acting contrary to the principle of good faith or the principle of estoppel, or to be abusing rights, merely because that person later asserts voidness on the ground of violation of mandatory law” (see Supreme Court Decision dated May 15, 2001, 99DA53490, etc.).\\n\\nb) Before the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, because title trust agreements and the resulting real-right changes were regarded as valid, if the seller at that time transferred the title of registration to the title trustee at the title truster’s request, the seller would have believed that it had thereby completed performance of its obligations under the sales contract, and such trust was legitimate. However, if, after the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, it is said that the title truster may again demand performance of contractual obligations such as seeking transfer registration of ownership or return of the purchase price from the seller on the ground that the title truster failed to restore the registration title, this would destroy the trust already formed in the seller. Therefore, before the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, there was a need to protect the trust of a seller who transferred title of ownership to the title trustee pursuant to a title trust agreement. For this reason, Supreme Court Decision dated March 15, 2002, 2001DA61654 held that, if the seller transferred the title of ownership to the title trustee at the request of the title truster before the Real Estate Registration Act was enforced, it is not permitted under the principle of good faith for the title truster to seek restitution of the purchase price from the seller or to require that a transfer registration of ownership be made again in the title truster’s name on the basis of the fact that the title truster failed, due to its own fault, to make the real-name registration until the grace period prescribed by law expired.\\n\\nHowever, such legal reasoning cannot be applied as it is after the Real Estate Registration Act was enforced. After the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, the fact that the title trust agreement and the resulting real-right change are void is obvious to both the title truster and the seller. Even if the seller transfers the title of ownership to the title trustee at the request of the title truster, that is void, so ownership of the real estate still remains with the seller; and because the sales contract with the title truster is valid, the seller must be understood to know that it still bears the obligation to register transfer of ownership toward the title truster. For the same reason, it cannot be said that the seller formed a trust that its contractual obligations had all been performed by transferring the title of ownership to the title trustee and that it would not thereafter receive a request for performance under the sales contract from the title truster. Even if the seller held such trust, it would contradict the mandatory provisions of the Real Estate Registration Act and cannot be regarded as a legitimate trust protected by the principle of good faith in civil law. Therefore, even though there are no circumstances warranting a finding that the seller had legitimate trust, the title truster’s claim against the seller under the sales contract cannot be restricted on the ground that it violates the principle of good faith.\\n\\nc) Whether there is legitimate trust deserving protection on the part of the seller in a title trust registration among three parties can be seen more clearly when compared with the position of the seller in a so-called contract title trust. The proviso to Article 4, Paragraph 2 of the Real Estate Registration Act provides that, in a contract for acquiring a real right in real estate, if the title trustee is one of the parties and the other party does not know that there is a title trust agreement, then the real-right change pursuant to the title trust agreement is not void. In a contract title trust, the good-faith seller would have believed that the sales contract was valid and transferred title of ownership to the title trustee; thus, trust was formed that it had thereby fully performed its obligations under the sales contract. Therefore, the Real Estate Registration Act also does not treat the real-right change in that case as void in order to protect such trust of the seller. By contrast, in a title trust registration among three parties, the Real Estate Registration Act does not provide a provision protecting trust for the seller, unlike the good-faith seller in a contract title trust; rather, criminal liability for aiding and abetting a violation of the Real Estate Registration Act may arise. This supports the view that a seller who knew of and cooperated in a void title trust agreement has no trust to protect.\\n\\nd) As the majority opinion does, categorically holding on the basis of the principle of good faith that the title truster’s claim against the seller for restitution of the purchase price or damages for impossibility of performance is uniformly impermissible not only deprives the title truster of its contractual rights from the outset, but may also cause legal confusion in resolving concrete future cases.\\n\\nThe supplemental opinion to the majority opinion cites, as grounds for saying that the title truster’s claim against the seller for restitution of the purchase price or damages due to impossibility of performance is not permitted under the principle of good faith, the circumstances that the seller bears no fault for the obligation to register transfer of ownership becoming impossible due to the title trustee’s disposition act, etc., or, even if the seller is at fault, the title truster’s fault in bringing about a title trust registration among three parties is much heavier than that of the seller. However, it is doubtful whether one can uniformly state that the seller has no fault or that the title truster’s fault is far greater than that of the seller in every title trust registration among three parties. Consider the following example. A seller, when a buyer hesitates to purchase real estate at a high price because of the burden of taxes and other costs, may encourage the buyer to use a title trust registration by saying that costs can be reduced, and may thereby sell the real estate at the desired price. Also, when a seller who urgently wishes to sell real estate cannot find a buyer, and after finding a suitable buyer, the buyer is unable to receive title in its own name or the title truster is in a situation where acquisition of ownership is difficult due to public-law restrictions on the trust real estate, the seller may step in, explain the method of title trust to the title truster, or actively arrange for the title trustee, and then persuade the buyer to entrust the registration title to the arranged title trustee. In such cases, can one really say that the principal party responsible for actively bringing about a title trust registration among three parties inconsistent with the substantive relationship is the title truster, and that the seller bears no fault or bears significantly less fault than the title truster? There may be various circumstances in which the title trust registration relationship among three parties is formed. As the majority opinion does, to categorically state without examining the concrete circumstances that the seller bears no fault or that the title truster’s fault is much heavier than the seller’s, and to thereby deprive the title truster of the claim against the seller for restitution of the purchase price or damages for impossibility of performance, cannot be the correct solution for all cases involving title trust registration among three parties, nor does it readily lead to a sound conclusion in concrete cases.\\n\\ne) In general, cases of title trust registration among three parties arise at the request of the title truster for the title truster’s benefit, and the title truster often bears greater fault than the seller. However, even in such cases, the title truster’s contractual position vis-à-vis the seller should not be uniformly deprived on grounds such as the principle of good faith advanced by the majority opinion. As in the dissenting opinion, the title truster’s contractual rights should be allowed or restricted based on general legal principles such as Civil Act Article 390, and the concrete circumstances of the title truster and the seller should be reflected within that framework. Let us examine more specifically. There may be cases where the title truster’s fault is assessed as heavy in a situation where the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership concerning the real estate has become impossible to perform. In such cases, the provision on comparative negligence in Civil Act Article 396 would apply, and the seller’s liability for damages arising from breach of obligation would be limited. Also, when viewed in light of the circumstances of the contract as a whole, there may be cases where the title truster’s fault is much heavier than the seller’s or where the title truster’s fault is so light that it cannot be said the seller is at fault, and thus it can be assessed that the impossibility of performance was not caused by any responsible reason attributable to the seller. In such cases, the seller would not bear liability for damages under Civil Act Article 390 nor would the title truster be recognized as having a right of rescission under Civil Act Article 546. Conversely, there may be cases where the title trust registration among three parties was arranged at the initiative of the seller, and the seller’s fault is far greater than the title truster’s. In such cases, the title truster would be recognized as having a claim for damages under Civil Act Article 390 or a right of rescission and a claim for restoration to the original state under Civil Act Articles 546 and 548.\\n\\nThe supplemental opinion to the majority opinion probably assumes that, because a direct claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee is recognized, the seller’s responsibility cannot again be recognized and therefore the seller’s responsibility is denied in a blanket manner. However, this can only be described as a reversal of the proper order of reasoning.\\n\\n4) Denying the title truster’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee does not produce a result contrary to the ideals of fairness.\\n\\na) The supplemental opinion to the majority opinion says that, if the title truster’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee is denied, the seller must bear the risk that the title truster should bear or the seller will retain the benefit that the title truster should have retained, and that this does not accord with the principle of fairness.\\n\\nHowever, when real estate is transferred to a third party because of the title trustee’s disposition act, etc. and the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership concerning the real estate becomes impossible to perform, the legal effect arises according to the separate legal relationships between the title truster and the seller, and between the seller and the title trustee. The dissenting opinion’s position is that the legal relationship arising from the sales contract between the title truster and the seller should be resolved consistently through the sales contract between the parties regardless of whether performance is possible, not that risk is shifted to the seller. Rather than considering even the risk of the title trustee’s and seller’s insolvency in performing the sales contract, it is more faithful to the legislative purpose of the Real Estate Registration Act to follow the original method. If, as the majority opinion does, one considers even the risk of insolvency of the contracting party or the title trustee, then the matter should be resolved even more by the ordinary method under the sales contract, not through the law of restitution of unjust enrichment.\\n\\nThe supplemental opinion to the majority opinion views the denial of the title truster’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee as contrary to the principle of fairness because the title truster’s ultimate purpose—acquisition of ownership of the trust real estate—has become impossible, and therefore the purchase price invested by the title truster should be returned to the title truster in accordance with the purpose of the title trust agreement. However, as above, an interpretation premised on the title trust agreement can no longer be accepted after the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act.\\n\\nb) Even if the title truster’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee is denied, it does not mean that there is no way for the title truster to recover the purchase price it paid.\\n\\nThe Civil Act does not separately provide for a claim for substitute performance as a consequence of impossibility of performance, apart from the creditor’s claim for damages and the right of rescission, but precedents recognize the claim for substitute performance by interpretation (see Supreme Court Decision dated May 12, 1992, 92DA4581, 4598, etc.). If the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership concerning the real estate becomes impossible to perform, the title truster may recover the purchase price by exercising a claim for substitute performance against the seller. If the real estate is transferred to a third party through expropriation, etc. and compensation money arises, or if the title trustee disposes of the real estate to a third party and proceeds from disposition arise, and if such compensation money or proceeds from disposition were transferred to the seller, the title truster may, by exercising the claim for substitute performance, seek return of the compensation money or proceeds from disposition against the seller. If the compensation money or proceeds from disposition have not been transferred to the seller but remain with the title trustee, the title truster may also seek, by exercising the claim for substitute performance, assignment by the seller of the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee (see Supreme Court Decision dated October 29, 1996, 95DA56910, etc.). The claim for substitute performance does not inquire whether there is any ground attributable to the debtor or creditor. Therefore, once the seller’s obligation to register transfer of ownership concerning the trust real estate becomes impossible to perform, the title truster may, without needing to examine fault, exercise the above claim for substitute performance against the seller and obtain compensation for the loss incurred by paying the purchase price.\\n\\nSince it is not the case that the title truster is entirely barred from recovering the purchase price it paid, it is not proper to recognize a legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment between the title truster and the title trustee, with whom it has no legal relationship whatsoever.\\n\\n5) Rather, recognizing a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment by the title truster against the title trustee results in a consequence contrary to the principle of self-responsibility and the ideals of fairness, and is therefore improper.\\n\\nIf, in a title trust registration among three parties, the title truster created an uncertain legal relationship by paying the purchase price in full to the seller while making a void title trust registration concerning the real estate purchased for its own benefit, then bearing the risk that may arise from that is consistent with the principle of self-responsibility if the title truster bears it itself. However, if the legal relationship of restitution of unjust enrichment between the title truster and the title trustee is recognized, the title truster can resolve the problem by seeking restitution of unjust enrichment from the title trustee, who is not even a party to the sales contract, without bearing the risk it created itself. This shifts the contractual risk assumed and performed by the title truster according to its own responsibility to a third party, the title trustee, and is contrary to the basic principles of contract law.\\n\\nc. After the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment cannot be recognized between the title truster and the title trustee in a void title trust agreement.\\n\\n1) Precedents have shown an attitude of not recognizing a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment when no substantive legal relationship exists between the two parties. Where the debtor under a contract can be sought to perform the obligation, relief is obtained through the debtor and a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against a third party is denied (Supreme Court Decision dated August 23, 2002, 99DA66564, 66571). In a contract for the benefit of a third party, even if performance has been rendered to the third party, if that performance has significance as performance in the legal relationship between the promisor and the promisee, restitution of unjust enrichment arises only between the promisor and the promisee, and the promisor cannot seek restitution of unjust enrichment from the third party (Supreme Court Decision dated July 22, 2005, 2005DA7566, 7573). Also, a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment arising from infringement of rights is recognized between the right holder and the person who infringed the right (Supreme Court Decision dated June 10, 2011, 2010DA40239).\\n\\nNevertheless, prior precedents recognize a direct restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title truster and the title trustee, despite the absence of any substantive legal relationship between them in a title trust registration among three parties. This is because prior precedents judged the legal relationship on the premise that a valid title trust agreement had been formed between the title truster and the title trustee. If title trust agreements and real-right changes had occurred before the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, the attitude of prior precedents could be understandable, because at that time title trust agreements and the resulting real-right changes were valid, and the legal relationship could be structured on that premise.\\n\\nHowever, the case is different when title trust agreements and resulting real-right changes occur after the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act. Because it is clear that the title trust agreement and resulting real-right change are void, the legal relationship in a title trust registration among three parties must be judged on the premise that there is no valid title trust agreement between the title truster and the title trustee. Between the title truster and the title trustee, no legal relationship exists; only the individual legal relationships between the title truster and the seller, and between the seller and the title trustee, exist, and there is no legal basis whatsoever for the title truster to exercise a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the title trustee, who is a party to a separate legal relationship.\\n\\nIn the end, recognizing a restitution relationship of unjust enrichment between the title truster and the title trustee amounts to following prior precedents premised on the validity of a title trust agreement between the title truster and the title trustee, and is therefore not suited to the situation after the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act.\\n\\n2) Although the custom of real estate title trust did not disappear even after the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act, the transactional environment surrounding real estate title trust changed because of various regulations, and it became widely known that real estate title trust agreements are void and difficult to protect legally, which greatly changed the people’s legal sentiment regarding them. As seen in the dissenting opinion, the Supreme Court has been changing legal doctrine on various issues in accordance with the purpose of the provisions of the Real Estate Registration Act. The same legal principles should also be applied to title trust registrations among three parties, and prior precedents based on logic from before the enforcement of the Real Estate Registration Act should not be followed in a way that creates confusion in the interpretation of the Real Estate Registration Act.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, I supplement the reasoning of the dissenting opinion and express my views on the majority opinion and the supplemental opinion to the majority opinion."}

question: A had a monetary claim for 100 million won against B, and B sold X real property, his only asset, to C and completed the ownership transfer registration in C’s name. Thereafter, A filed a lawsuit against C seeking revocation of the fraudulent act and restoration of the original state with respect to the sales contract for X real property. Which of the following is the correct combination of the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (X)? (Each statement is independent, and where there is dispute, case law governs)
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2004DA49532]": "1. Judgment of the Lower Court\\n\\na. Factual Background\\n\\nAccording to the judgment of the first instance cited by the lower court, Nonparty 1 entered into a sales contract with Nonparty 2 concerning the real property at issue, on which a mortgage had been established in favor of Nonparty Korea Housing Bank, and transferred ownership thereof; with respect to the real property at issue, Defendant Republic of Korea levied seizure on the ground of national tax arrears against Nonparty 2, and Defendant Korea Small and Medium Enterprises Bank made a provisional seizure with a claim against Nonparty 2 as the right to be preserved; in the foreclosure proceedings based on the mortgage on the real property at issue, a distribution schedule was prepared distributing the sale proceeds of the real property at issue by ranking Defendant Republic of Korea as third priority and Defendant Korea Small and Medium Enterprises Bank as fourth priority; thereafter, in the fraudulent act revocation lawsuit filed by the Plaintiff against Nonparty 2 in Incheon District Court Case No. 2000NA10697, a judgment was rendered, and became final around that time, revoking the sales contract concerning the real property at issue between Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 as a fraudulent act and, by way of compensation for value, ordering Nonparty 2 to pay the Plaintiff 50 million won and delay damages.\\n\\nb. Judgment of the Lower Court\\n\\nThe lower court, after determining that ① the Defendants were not subsequent transferees who had acquired the real property at issue, but merely provisional seizure creditors with claims against Nonparty 2 or persons entitled to distribution of delinquent national taxes, and thus interested parties who merely enjoyed an incidental benefit due to the accidental circumstance that the beneficiary, Nonparty 2, had acquired ownership of the real property at issue, so that, as against the Defendants, there is comparatively less need to protect transactional security or the stability of legal status than in the case of subsequent transferees; and that ② if it were held that the effect of the above judgment revoking the fraudulent act did not extend to creditors of the beneficiary who are merely interested parties and who did not engage in a new legal act with the beneficiary, then in the auction proceedings concerning the property that was the subject of the fraudulent act, the claims of the beneficiary’s creditors, who are merely interested parties, would take precedence over the return claim of the revoking creditor, with the result that, even though the revoking creditor had filed a fraudulent act revocation lawsuit against the beneficiary, Nonparty 2, and obtained a winning judgment, the judgment would be rendered ineffective, contrary to the purpose of recognizing the fraudulent act revocation system, concluded that the effect of the fraudulent act revocation judgment at issue, filed by the Plaintiff against the beneficiary, Nonparty 2, also extended to the Defendants, who are merely interested parties and who did not engage in a new legal act with the beneficiary, Nonparty 2, and further concluded that, pursuant to the fraudulent act revocation judgment at issue, within the limit of 50 million won, being the amount for which revocation and compensation for value were ordered in the judgment, among the real property at issue, restoration of the original property is deemed to have been realized, and therefore the property is restored to the liable assets of Nonparty 1; accordingly, it held that, within the scope of the above 50 million won among the amounts distributed to the Defendants, such amounts constitute benefits obtained without legal cause vis-à-vis the Plaintiff.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\n\\nHowever, the lower court’s determination concerning the effect of the fraudulent act revocation judgment is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nThe revocation of a fraudulent act is effective only relatively among the parties to the revocation action, and third parties other than the parties thereto are not affected by the revocation in their legal relations unless special circumstances exist to the contrary (see Supreme Court Decision 89DAKA35421 rendered on 1990. 10. 30., Supreme Court Decision 99DA9011 rendered on 2001. 5. 29.).\\n\\nSince subsequent transferees, etc. who acquired the real property subject to the fraudulent act through a new legal relationship are protected pursuant to the proviso of Article 406(1) of the Civil Act, recognizing only relative effect for the revocation of a fraudulent act is intended to adjust the interests of the creditor seeking revocation of the fraudulent act, the beneficiary, and third parties; and the scope of third parties to whom the effect of such revocation does not extend cannot be limited solely to subsequent transferees, etc. of the real property subject to the fraudulent act who newly engaged in a legal act concerning the subject real property based on the fraudulent act. However, even if the Defendants did not establish a new legal relationship with the beneficiary and merely seized or provisionally seized the real property at issue in order to secure claims they already held as creditors of the beneficiary, there is no basis whatsoever for granting the creditor seeking revocation of the fraudulent act a right to receive satisfaction from the sale proceeds of the property subject to the fraudulent act in priority over the Defendants, who are creditors of the beneficiary, so as to secure the effectiveness of the fraudulent act revocation judgment. Therefore, it cannot be said that the relative effect of the revocation of the fraudulent act is negated merely for the reasons stated by the lower court, and that the effect of the fraudulent act revocation judgment extends to the Defendants.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court judgment erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the effect of the revocation of a fraudulent act, thereby affecting the outcome of the judgment, and the ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal of the Defendants, the judgment of the lower court is reversed, and this case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination; the opinions of the participating Justices being unanimous, it is so adjudged as ordered."}

{"[2015DA224469]": "We determine the grounds for final appeal (the statements in the supplemental brief of final appeal submitted after the period for filing the petition for final appeal has elapsed, insofar as they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\n1. Article 252(1) of the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act (hereinafter referred to as the “DRBA”) provides: “When a decision to authorize the rehabilitation plan has been made, the rights of rehabilitation creditors, rehabilitation secured creditors, shareholders, and equity holders shall be changed in accordance with the rehabilitation plan.” Here, change of rights means that, by the decision to authorize the rehabilitation plan, the rights of rehabilitation creditors, etc. are substantively changed in accordance with the contents of that rehabilitation plan. This does not merely mean a change only in liability, as distinguished from debt, and thus is different in nature from the discharge under Article 251 of the DRBA with respect to rehabilitation claims and rehabilitation secured claims not recognized by the rehabilitation plan, etc. Therefore, when a decision to authorize the rehabilitation plan has been made, the rights of rehabilitation creditors, etc. are changed in accordance with the rehabilitation plan, so that the effect of a discharge of all or part of the debt arises; where a deferment of maturity has been granted, the maturity of the debt is extended accordingly; and where a rehabilitation claim or rehabilitation secured claim is converted into equity, such right is extinguished at the time of the authorization decision or at the time prescribed in the rehabilitation plan (see Supreme Court Decision 2002DA20964 rendered on March 14, 2003, etc.).\\nMeanwhile, the creditor’s right of revocation, being a right whose essence is to relatively avoid the debtor’s fraudulent act as between the creditor and the beneficiary or subsequent transferee and to restore property that has departed from the debtor’s liable assets so as to enable compulsory execution by the creditor, is extinguished when the necessity of preserving the liable assets no longer exists by virtue of the creditor’s right of revocation (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DA84352 rendered on April 24, 2008; Supreme Court Decision 2007DA63102 rendered on March 26, 2009). Accordingly, even if, in a creditor’s revocation lawsuit, a judgment ordering the revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration to the original state has become final and conclusive on the premise that the existence of the claim to be preserved has been recognized, if, before the restoration of property or value pursuant thereto is completed, the claim to be preserved is extinguished and the creditor can no longer enforce execution against the debtor’s liable assets, this constitutes a lawful ground of objection to a claim that excludes the executory force of the above judgment.\\n\\n2. According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the lawfully admitted evidence, the following facts may be found.\\na. Non-party 1, who is the father of the Plaintiffs, entered into a contract with the Plaintiffs on December 28, 2010, under which he donated to the Plaintiffs each a 1/2 share of each of the real properties indicated in the judgment below (hereinafter referred to as the “real properties at issue in this case”), and accordingly completed registration of transfer of shares in favor of the Plaintiffs on December 29, 2010.\\nb. On September 21, 2011, the Defendant filed an action against the Plaintiffs, Non-party 1, and Non-party 2 as co-defendants, seeking against Non-party 1 and Non-party 2 payment of KRW 3,209,584,666 in reimbursement money and delay damages on KRW 3,209,365,642 thereof, and seeking against the Plaintiffs revocation and restoration to the original state on the ground that the gift contract at issue in this case constituted a fraudulent act, using as the claim to be preserved the above reimbursement claim against Non-party 1.\\nIn that lawsuit, on July 19, 2012, a decision recommending settlement (hereinafter referred to as the “settlement-recommendation decision at issue in this case”) became final and conclusive, providing that: (1) Non-party 1 and Non-party 2 shall jointly and severally pay to the Defendant the above reimbursement money and delay damages; and (2) on the premise that, for the purpose of preserving the above claim against Non-party 1 (hereinafter referred to as the “reimbursement claim at issue in this case”), the gift contract at issue in this case is revoked as against the Plaintiffs within the limit of KRW 411,250,000 each, the Plaintiffs shall pay to the Defendant KRW 411,250,000 each as monetary compensation by July 12, 2012.\\nc. (1) Thereafter, rehabilitation proceedings were commenced with respect to Non-party 1 on May 28, 2013, and the Defendant filed, as a rehabilitation claim, the reimbursement claim at issue in this case based on the settlement-recommendation decision at issue in this case, and a total of KRW 3,569,624,605 consisting of principal and pre-commencement interest was admitted.\\n(2) Non-party 1 obtained a decision to authorize the rehabilitation plan on October 1, 2013 (hereinafter referred to as the “decision to authorize the rehabilitation plan at issue in this case”). According to the above rehabilitation plan, KRW 3,530,358,735, corresponding to 98.9% of the principal and pre-commencement interest among the Defendant’s rehabilitation claim, is to be discharged, the remaining KRW 39,265,870, corresponding to 1.1%, is to be repaid in cash, and post-commencement interest is to be discharged.\\n(3) Non-party 1 completed the performance of the obligation to repay the rehabilitation claim prescribed in the above rehabilitation plan and received a decision concluding the rehabilitation proceedings on November 4, 2013.\\n\\n3. The above factual relations are examined in light of the legal principles seen above.\\nThe Plaintiffs argued in the complaint that, after the settlement-recommendation decision at issue in this case became final and conclusive, by the decision to authorize the rehabilitation plan at issue in this case, part of the rehabilitation claim concerning the reimbursement claim at issue in this case was discharged and the remainder was repaid and thus all was extinguished, and therefore compulsory execution based on the settlement-recommendation decision at issue in this case, which uses the reimbursement claim at issue in this case as the claim to be preserved, should be disallowed.\\nIn the creditor’s revocation action brought by the Defendant against the Plaintiffs, who were the beneficiaries of the gift contract at issue in this case, a fraudulent act, using as the claim to be preserved the reimbursement claim at issue in this case against Non-party 1, the settlement-recommendation decision at issue in this case, which provides for payment of monetary compensation, became final and conclusive. However, as the decision to authorize the rehabilitation plan at issue in this case was made in the rehabilitation proceedings commenced thereafter with respect to Non-party 1, the rehabilitation claim concerning the reimbursement claim at issue in this case was substantively changed in accordance with the above rehabilitation plan. That is, the portion of the rehabilitation claim concerning the reimbursement claim at issue in this case that was to be discharged under the above rehabilitation plan was conclusively extinguished at the time of the decision to authorize the rehabilitation plan at issue in this case, and the remaining portion that was to be repaid in cash was conclusively extinguished by the subsequent repayment, and as a result the Defendant’s claim to be preserved, which was the premise of the settlement-recommendation decision at issue in this case concerning payment of monetary compensation due to the revocation of the fraudulent act, was also extinguished.\\nHowever, without determining the Plaintiffs’ above argument concerning the extinguishment of the reimbursement claim at issue in this case and the claim to be preserved based thereon, the court below held, on the sole ground that even if the reimbursement claim at issue in this case was discharged under Article 251 of the DRBA, it continued to exist as a natural obligation and was not substantively extinguished, that there existed no ground of objection to a claim for seeking exclusion of the executory force of the settlement-recommendation decision at issue in this case.\\nIf so, the court below’s determination contains illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the effect of change of rights under Article 252(1) of the DRBA and failing to conduct the necessary deliberation or omitting a determination. The ground of final appeal pointing this out is well taken.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the Court omits determination on the remaining grounds of final appeal, reverses the judgment below, and remands the case to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2016DA8923]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (the statements in a supplementary brief of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Regarding Ground of Appeal No. 1\\n\\nRevocation of a fraudulent act merely invalidates the juridical act between the debtor and the beneficiary in the relationship between the creditor and the beneficiary, and does not affect the legal relationship between the debtor and the beneficiary. Therefore, even if a real estate sales contract between the debtor and the beneficiary is revoked as a fraudulent act and, as restitution to the original status, the registration of transfer of ownership in the beneficiary’s name is cancelled and the debtor’s registered title is restored, the real estate is treated only as the debtor’s responsible property between the revoking creditor or the creditor and the beneficiary who are subject to the effects of revocation of the fraudulent act and restitution to the original status pursuant to Article 407 of the Civil Act; it does not mean that the debtor directly acquires the real estate and becomes the right holder (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DA2743, rendered on 2015. 11. 17.). Therefore, even if the debtor disposes of the real estate, whose registered title has been restored by revocation of the fraudulent act, to a third party, this is merely a disposition by a person without title and is ineffective (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DA217980, rendered on 2017. 3. 9.).
