In addition, a creditor who acquires a claim after the fraudulent act is a person who, at the time of acquisition of the claim, does not regard the property restored by revocation of the fraudulent act as the common security of creditors, and thus is not included among the creditors who are subject to the effects of revocation of the fraudulent act and restitution to the original status as prescribed by Article 407 of the Civil Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DA18502, rendered on 2009. 6. 23.).\\n\\nThe court below recognized the following facts: ① in the lawsuit for revocation of the fraudulent act filed by the creditor, a non-party person, the intervenor supporting the Plaintiffs, against the Defendant, a judgment was rendered and became final and conclusive, cancelling the sales contract at issue concluded with respect to each of the real properties at issue and ordering implementation of the procedure for the registration of cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership at issue; ② the non-party person completed the cancellation registration of the registration of transfer of ownership at issue (hereinafter referred to as “the cancellation registration at issue”) on the basis of the said final and conclusive judgment; ③ thereafter, the intervenor supporting the Plaintiffs completed, with respect to each of the real properties at issue, a registration of establishment of a mortgage with Plaintiff 2 as the creditor, a provisional registration of the right to claim transfer of ownership with the Plaintiff Presbyterian Church of Korea Busanbuk Church (hereinafter referred to as “the Plaintiff Church”) as the holder of the provisional registration right, and a registration of transfer of ownership and a registration of transfer of co-ownership with the Plaintiff Church as the owner or co-owner of the share, respectively; ④ thereafter, after the registration of transfer of ownership at issue had been completed, the voluntary auction proceedings for the real properties at issue commenced upon application by the transferee of the mortgage established before that registration and others, and the real properties were sold and distribution was carried out; and ⑤ after receiving the amount of the claim deposited in performance by the Defendant on behalf of the intervenor supporting the Plaintiffs, the non-party person did not participate in the distribution. Based on these facts, the court below determined that, in the voluntary auction proceedings for the real properties at issue, the surplus should be paid to the Defendant, who is in the position of the beneficiary, rather than to the Plaintiffs who acquired rights in the real properties at issue from the intervenor supporting the Plaintiffs, or to the intervenor supporting the Plaintiffs.\\n\\nAccording to the foregoing legal principles and upon examination of the record, the above determination by the court below is proper. There is no error affecting the judgment in that it misapprehended the relative effect of revocation of a fraudulent act and the formalism concerning changes in real rights in real property and the legal principles concerning the attribution of surplus under the Civil Execution Act. The Supreme Court precedents cited in the grounds of appeal differ in the facts and are not appropriate for application to this case.\\n\\nMeanwhile, because the above determination by the court below includes the purport of rejecting the Plaintiffs’ assertion that, if the surplus is to be restored to the beneficiary, the beneficiary must separately enforce attachment or seizure against the surplus distributed to the debtor, there is no error affecting the judgment in that the court below omitted a determination on the above assertion.\\n\\n2. Regarding Grounds of Appeal Nos. 2 and 3\\n\\nThe court below determined, for the reasons stated in its reasoning, that the Defendant agreed in the sales contract at issue to assume the secured obligation of the mortgage with the National Agricultural Cooperative Federation as the creditor in lieu of part of the purchase price, but that his failure to perform this cannot be said to constitute the Defendant’s breach of contract. Upon examination of the record, the above determination by the court below is proper. There is no error in that it exceeded the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience without conducting the necessary examination, or in that it misapprehended the legal principles concerning Article 588 of the Civil Act, or in that it neglected the duty to point out issues or the exercise of the right to give explanations concerning the agreed rescission of the sales contract or the special resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, etc.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[2017DA265815]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Course of the Case\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\na. On February 1, 2010, Non-party 1 entered into a sales contract with the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as “the sales contract at issue”) concerning each of the real properties listed in the attached list to the first-instance judgment, which were the only assets owned in Non-party 1’s name (hereinafter referred to as “the real properties at issue”), and on the 4th of the same month completed each ownership transfer registration in favor of the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as “the ownership transfer registrations at issue”) under Receipt No. 2892 at the Gimje Registry Office of the Jeonju District Court.\\n\\nb. (1) The Plaintiff is a creditor who, on July 25, 2011, filed an action against Non-party 1 seeking return of unjust enrichment on the ground, among others, that the Plaintiff’s funds were used in acquiring the real properties at issue, and who on May 2, 2013, in the appellate stage of that case, Gwangju High Court (Jeonju) Case No. 2012NA1042, received a judgment in the Plaintiff’s favor ordering payment of KRW 289,058,600 and delay damages thereon.\\n\\n(2) The Plaintiff, on July 25, 2011, filed an action against the Defendant with the Jeonju District Court, Case No. 2014GAHAP1804, seeking revocation of a fraudulent act and other relief; on January 16, 2014, in the appellate stage of that case, Gwangju High Court (Jeonju) Case No. 2013NA1544 (oral argument concluded on December 19, 2013), a judgment was rendered that “the first-instance judgment is reversed, the sales contract at issue is revoked, and the Defendant shall perform the procedure for cancellation registration of the ownership transfer registrations at issue in favor of Non-party 1,” and that judgment became final and conclusive as it was (hereinafter referred to as the “prior judgment”).\\n\\nc. However, on December 4, 2013, the Defendant completed, in favor of the Donggimje Agricultural Cooperative, and on January 17, 2014, in favor of Non-party 2, a mortgage creation registration on the real properties at issue, based on each mortgage creation contract dated respectively on those dates.\\n\\nd. (1) Accordingly, on March 24, 2014, the Plaintiff filed the present action with the Jeonju District Court, Case No. 2014GAHAP1804, seeking, as to the Donggimje Agricultural Cooperative, Non-party 2, and others, ① an expression of intent to consent to the procedure for cancellation registration of the ownership transfer registrations at issue and the performance of the procedure for cancellation registration of the mortgage creation registration based on the mortgage creation contract concluded between the Defendant and Non-party 2, and ② against the Defendant, in the alternative, compensatory damages on the grounds of impossibility of performance of the obligation ordered in the prior judgment or impossibility of enforcement of the prior judgment.\\n\\n(2) In the appellate instance, the Plaintiff withdrew the action against the Donggimje Agricultural Cooperative and Non-party 2, and as to the Defendant, amended the purport of the claim and the cause of action to seek: ① primarily, monetary compensation on the ground that the sales contract at issue had been revoked as a fraudulent act; ② in the first alternative, compensatory damages on the ground that the Defendant’s obligation to cancel the ownership transfer registration was impossible to perform or impossible to enforce; ③ in the second alternative, damages on the ground that the Defendant’s act of creating a mortgage was an unlawful act; and ④ in the third alternative, return of unjust enrichment.\\n\\nOn November 12, 2015, the appellate court rendered a judgment that: ① with respect to the primary claim and the first alternative claim, dismissed the action as inadmissible on the ground that, although the Plaintiff had filed an action seeking revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration therefrom and the prior judgment ordering return of the original property had become final and conclusive, seeking again monetary compensation or compensatory damages, which is not substantially different from monetary compensation, lacked an interest in legal protection; and ② with respect to the second and third alternative claims, dismissed them on the ground that the establishment of tort or unjust enrichment could not be acknowledged [Gwangju High Court (Jeonju) Case No. 2015NA231]. The Plaintiff’s appeal against this was also dismissed (Supreme Court Decision rendered March 24, 2016, 2015DA72262).\\n\\ne. On June 8, 2016, the Plaintiff filed the present action against the Defendant, seeking, on the ground that the sales contract at issue had been revoked as a fraudulent act, the performance by Non-party 1 of the procedure for ownership transfer registration concerning the real properties at issue as restoration therefrom.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\na. If a creditor’s claim for revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration to the original state is upheld, the beneficiary bears the obligation to return the subject matter of the fraudulent act to the debtor as restoration to the original state. If return in kind is impossible or manifestly difficult, the equivalent value of the subject matter of the fraudulent act must be compensated as performance of the obligation to restore to the original state. Here, the case where return in kind is impossible or manifestly difficult does not mean a case where return in kind is merely absolutely or physically impossible, but a case where, in light of the rules of experience in social life or the common understanding of transactions, the creditor cannot expect performance to be realized from the beneficiary or the subsequent transferee. Therefore, where, after ownership of real property has been transferred by a fraudulent act, a third party acquires a right such as a mortgage or a superficies over the real property, the creditor may seek compensation equivalent to its value from the beneficiary instead of return in kind, unless there are special circumstances, such as the beneficiary being able to restore the real property free from restrictions such as a mortgage and transfer it to the debtor. Even so, it does not follow that the creditor is not permitted to seek return in kind while bearing the risk or disadvantage himself. The creditor may, as a method of restoring to the original state, seek cancellation of the registration in the beneficiary’s name instead of value compensation, or may seek against the beneficiary the performance of the procedure for ownership transfer registration directly in favor of the debtor. In such case, the right to claim restoration to the original state becomes fixed, according to the creditor’s choice as of the time of the conclusion of oral argument in the fact-finding instance, as either return in kind or value compensation. If the creditor has once sought revocation of a fraudulent act and cancellation of the registration in the beneficiary’s name as restoration to the original state, and a judgment in the creditor’s favor has become final and conclusive, then even if, for any reason, it has become impossible to cancel the registration in the beneficiary’s name, the creditor may not again exercise the right to claim restoration to the original state against the beneficiary to demand value compensation or, as return in kind, to demand the performance of the procedure for ownership transfer registration directly in favor of the debtor; such a claim is not permissible for lack of an interest in legal protection (see Supreme Court Decision rendered December 7, 2006, 2004DA54978).\\n\\nb. In light of the foregoing legal principles, we examine the lower court’s determination. The Plaintiff filed an action for revocation of a fraudulent act against the Defendant, obtained a judgment in the Plaintiff’s favor revoking the sales contract at issue as a fraudulent act and ordering the Defendant to cancel the ownership transfer registrations at issue, and that judgment became final and conclusive. If so, the present action by which the Plaintiff again exercises the right to claim restoration to the original state following revocation of a fraudulent act and seeks that the Defendant perform the procedure for ownership transfer registration directly in favor of the debtor must be deemed inadmissible for lack of an interest in legal protection. Nevertheless, the lower court rejected the Defendant’s defense on the threshold issue that the present action is inadmissible for lack of an interest in legal protection, solely for the reasons stated in its holding. In doing so, the lower court erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the res judicata effect of a final and conclusive judgment and the interest in legal protection, thereby affecting the outcome of the judgment. The ground of appeal asserting this is meritorious.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nAccordingly, the lower court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for further proceedings and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices."}

question: 14th Korean Bar Examination, Civil Law, Multiple-Choice Question 12. Which of the following statements concerning graves are correct? (Do not consider the Act on Funeral Services, etc.; where there is a dispute, follow case law.)
A: (a) If the person entitled to protect and manage a grave dies and his direct descendants become co-heirs, and there is no agreement among them regarding succession to the right to protect and manage the grave, then, absent special circumstances, it is consistent with the content of customary law to view the eldest among the nearest-degree direct descendants as succeeding to it.
B: (b) Where a grave-site right is established by the landowner’s consent, even if, at the time the grave-site right was established, the landowner and the person entitled to protect and manage the grave made an agreement regarding the existence or scope of the duty to pay land use rent, the effect of that agreement does not extend to a person who purchased the land including the grave site in a voluntary auction procedure.
C: (c) A grave-site right is a customary real right that allows the use of land owned by another person within the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of protecting the grave and performing ancestral rites, and permits the exclusion of interference not only by third parties but also by the landowner.
D: (d) Even where the person entitled to protect and manage a grave unlawfully established a grave on another person’s land without the landowner’s consent, the grave-site right may be acquired by prescription.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2013DA17292]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. a. A grave-site right is a customary real right that enables the use of land owned by another person within the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of protecting the grave and performing ancestral rites therefor, and to exclude interference by the landowner or a third party (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 94DA15530, rendered on December 23, 1994, and Supreme Court Decision 2011DA63017, 63024, rendered on November 10, 2011). Here, a grave means a place where the corpse, remains, hair, etc. of a person are buried and the deceased is interred therein (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 91DA18040, rendered on October 25, 1991). A grave-site right, being a customary real right, is recognized only where the grave is equipped with a form by which its existence can be recognized from the outside, such as a burial mound, and is not recognized where it is laid flat or buried underground without an objectively recognizable appearance; therefore, by virtue of such characteristics, a grave-site right comes into existence without registration (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 96DA14036, rendered on June 14, 1996).\\n\\nThe Supreme Court has held that where a grave is established on land owned by another person with the owner’s consent for a long period, a grave-site right is acquired (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 4290MINSANG771, rendered on June 12, 1958, and Supreme Court Decision 99DA14006, rendered on September 26, 2000), and that where the person who established the grave transferred the land, a grave-site right is acquired unless there is a special agreement to relocate the grave (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 67DA1920, rendered on October 12, 1967), and has also held that even where a grave is established on land owned by another person without the owner’s consent, if the grave site is possessed peacefully and openly for 20 years, a grave-site right, which is a customary real right similar to superficies, is acquired by prescription, and that it is customary that such right may be asserted against a third party without registration (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 4290MINSANG539, rendered on October 31, 1957, and Supreme Court Decision 2011DA63017, 63024, rendered on November 10, 2011).\\n\\nb. From olden times, the Korean people revered their ancestors highly, and under the influence of such ancestor-worship, they sought out auspicious places to establish ancestral graves and regarded such places as sacred places where not only the corpses or remains of ancestors but also their spirits are believed to reside. In addition, an idea took root that descendants, as well as ordinary people, must respect such places as dignified places and must not damage them recklessly. Thus, under the influence of traditional culture that places importance on filial piety toward parents and ancestor worship, the basic method of burial and funeral in our society was “interment,” namely burying the corpse or remains in the ground.\\n\\nDuring the Joseon Dynasty, according to the principle of common ownership of forests, no private ownership was recognized with respect to the forested land where graves were mainly established, so when a grave was established on mountain land, protection was afforded, for so long as the grave existed, in the form of a private possessory right called so-called “grave-site possessory right” or “grave possessory right.”\\n\\nHowever, as a modern system of forest ownership came into being, legal disputes began to arise concerning graves established on land owned by others, and the Supreme Court, on the basis of the existence of a custom or practice whose content was the protection of land-use rights for the protection and service of graves, which was widely spread in our society and recognized on that basis, recognized a grave-site right, which is a land-use right for owning a grave, as a customary-law real right similar to superficies, and held that a grave-site right is acquired on the ground of the landowner’s consent or acquisitive prescription.\\n\\nc. As stated above, the Supreme Court has recognized the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right as one of the customary laws that has continued for a long time in our society, thereby legally protecting the social order concerning graves formed on the basis of factual relations that have continued for more than 20 years, and has confirmed and applied that, for a period of more than 50 years since January 1, 1960, the effective date of the Civil Act, the legal conviction of members of society regarding such custom has remained firm and unshaken.\\n\\nMeanwhile, with respect to the duration of a grave-site right acquired as above, the Supreme Court held that the provisions on superficies under the Civil Act are not applicable, and that if there are special circumstances such as an agreement between the parties, such agreement shall govern; absent such circumstances, the grave-site right continues to exist while the right holder continues to protect and serve the grave and the grave remains in existence (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 81DA1220, rendered on January 26, 1982, and Supreme Court Decision 2005DA44114, rendered on June 28, 2007).\\n\\n2. a. In the “Act on Funeral Services, etc.” effective from January 13, 2001 (hereinafter referred to, regardless of whether before or after amendment, as the “Funeral Services Act”), the legal regulation concerning graves changed, in that the Act imposed limits on the period for which graves may be established and contained provisions that do not recognize the acquisitive prescription of grave-site rights with respect to graves established after the Act came into force, thereby strengthening landownership. On the basis of such matters, as well as the fact that a grave-site right excessively restricts the ownership of landowners and impedes the efficient use of national land, and the fact that traditional public consciousness concerning funeral methods and burial culture is changing, such as an increase in the cremation rate, we examine the grounds of appeal that, along with changes in social members’ perception of grave-site rights and changes in the entire legal order concerning graves, the previous customary law on the acquisitive prescription of grave-site rights no longer accords with our legal order and has therefore become incapable of maintaining its legal effect.\\n\\nb. Even if a social norm created by repeated social practice has been approved as customary law, if members of society no longer have conviction regarding the legal binding force of such practice, or if, due to changes in the fundamental ideas governing society or the social order, it no longer accords with the overall legal order at the time when such customary law is to be applied, then such customary law is, of course, denied effect as a legal norm (see, inter alia, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2002DA1178, rendered on July 21, 2005).\\n\\nHowever, if the Supreme Court denies the effect of a customary law that it has long recognized as valid and supported by the legal conviction of members of society on the ground that, due to changes in the fundamental ideas or social order governing society, it no longer accords with the overall legal order, there is a risk of harming legal stability because this would shake at once the effect of past legal relationships formed over decades in reliance on the existing customary law. Therefore, in order to deny the legal normative effect of such customary law, a significant change must be clearly evident in the overall legal order surrounding the custom, together with a meaningful change in the perceptions, attitudes, or socio-cultural background of members of society that formed the basis of the Supreme Court precedents recognizing the effect of the customary law; unless such circumstances are clear, one must not hastily conclude that the existing customary law can no longer maintain its effect as a legal norm.\\n\\nc. First of all, the grounds of appeal to the effect that the Funeral Services Act extinguished or changed the customary law concerning a grave-site right or its acquisitive prescription are difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) The Funeral Services Act, which was entirely amended by Act No. 6158 on January 12, 2000, and came into force on January 13, 2001 [hereinafter “the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158)”], limits the period for establishing graves to 15 years and allows extensions of the period only up to three times, each for 15 years (Article 17(1) and (2)); and while it provides that, where the landowner exhumes a grave established without the landowner’s consent, the person with an interest in the grave may not assert against the landowner any right to use the land or any other right for the preservation of the grave (Article 23(3)), it expressly states, with respect to the time of application of those provisions, that they apply only to graves first established after the Act came into force (Addenda Article 2).\\n\\nThe Funeral Services Act, entirely amended by Act No. 8489 on May 25, 2007, and in force from May 26, 2008, contains provisions, like the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) before amendment, limiting the establishment period of graves and providing that the person with an interest in the grave may not assert rights such as the right to use land against a grave established without the landowner’s consent (Articles 19 and 27(3)); however, those provisions also expressly state that they apply only to graves first established after January 13, 2001, the date on which the pre-amendment Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) came into force (Addenda Article 2(2)).\\n\\nFurthermore, the Funeral Services Act, amended by Act No. 13660 on December 29, 2015, and enforced on the same day, limits the period for establishing graves to 30 years and provides that the period may be extended once for 30 years (Article 19(1) and (2)), and it likewise expressly states that the above limit on the establishment period of graves applies only to graves first established after January 13, 2001, the date of enforcement of the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158), which entirely amended the Burial Act (Addenda Article 2).\\n\\n(2) According to the above addenda provisions of the Funeral Services Act, the provisions limiting the establishment period of graves and providing that, where the landowner exhumes a grave established without the landowner’s consent, the person with an interest in the grave may not oppose the landowner, are expressly applicable only to graves established after the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158), and thus it cannot be said that the legal basis for the existence of a grave-site right with respect to graves established before the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) was lost by the enforcement of that Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2002DA53377, rendered on December 24, 2002).\\n\\nIn other words, the above provisions of the Funeral Services Act continue to allow the application of customary law concerning a grave-site right, as recognized by the Supreme Court, to graves established before January 13, 2001, the effective date of the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158). This also evidences that, as of January 12, 2000, when the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) was amended, and as of January 13, 2001, when it came into force, there was no change or extinction in the legal conviction of members of society regarding the custom recognizing a grave-site right or its acquisitive prescription with respect to graves established before the enforcement of that Act. If there had been a clear change in the fundamental ideas or social order governing society such that it became necessary to abolish or change the customary law concerning a grave-site right, there would be no reason not to enact legal regulations contrary to such customary law.\\n\\nd. Nor can it be readily said that there was a significant change in the overall legal order surrounding grave-site rights such that the previous customary law concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right no longer accords with the overall legal order whose supreme norm is the Constitution, or that its legitimacy and reasonableness can no longer be recognized.\\n\\n(1) Article 185 of the Civil Act provides, “No real right shall be created arbitrarily except by law or customary law,” thereby recognizing even under the current legal system the creation of real rights by customary law. Therefore, insofar as a limited real right called a grave-site right is recognized by customary law, the exercise of ownership rights over the portion of land serving as a grave site is inevitably restricted to the extent reasonably necessary for the protection and maintenance of the grave (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 99DA14006, rendered on September 26, 2000), and the fact that the owner of the grave acquires a grave-site right by prescription and thereby restricts the landowner’s exercise of rights cannot serve as a basis for denying completion of acquisitive prescription (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 94DA37912, rendered on February 28, 1995).\\n\\n(2) The acquisitive prescription system originally exists to maintain social order that has continued for a certain period, to provide relief from difficulties in preservation of evidence caused by the passage of time, and to exclude from legal protection those who do not exercise their own rights over a long period (see, inter alia, Supreme Court en banc Decision 98DA32175, rendered on March 18, 1999). In particular, legal stability is the most important basis supporting the system of acquisitive prescription (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 2009DA44327, rendered on May 27, 2010). That is, the acquisitive prescription system exists for reasons such as the maintenance of social order, relief from the difficulty of proof, and realization of litigation economy.\\n\\nIn the past, except where a person had a family burial mountain, most people did not own land on which they could establish graves, and there were hardly any cemeteries developed in Western societies or burial places provided by religious organizations; thus, in a situation where burial-centered funeral and burial culture was widespread, most people had no choice but to bury their ancestors’ corpses in other persons’ mountain land.\\n\\nLooking at the ordinary practice or actual situation regarding grave establishment, in most cases the person establishing the grave obtained express or at least implied consent from the landowner, but when establishing a grave on land owned by another person, it was very rare to prepare or keep documentary evidence such as a contract. Supreme Court precedents on the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right have an aspect of relieving such difficulties, because disputes requiring exhumation of graves frequently arose between parties who did not know the circumstances at the time the grave was established due to a change in land ownership, and in such cases it is practically impossible for the person asserting the grave-site right to prove that the landowner’s consent had been obtained; naturally, this accords with the very reason for the existence of the acquisitive prescription system.\\n\\nMoreover, because the landowner can, at any time during the long period of 20 years of prescription, exercise rights as owner, and because prescription can be interrupted under Articles 168 through 177 of the Civil Act, as applied mutatis mutandis by Article 247(2) of the Civil Act, by means such as demanding that the grave owner exhume the grave or demanding delivery of the possessed portion, it cannot be said that protection of the landowner is inadequate.\\n\\ne. Finally, even if there have been some changes in members’ awareness of traditional funeral methods or burial culture, such as an increase in the cremation rate, the burial-centered culture that formed the basis of a grave-site right still remains in our society, the establishment of private cemeteries is permitted, and there is no readily available material in the record from which it can be recognized that members of society’s legal conviction regarding the custom concerning a grave-site right has disappeared or that such practice has fundamentally changed.\\n\\nTherefore, the grounds of appeal asserting that the effect of the customary law concerning a grave-site right or its acquisitive prescription should be denied on the basis of changes in social members’ perception of traditional funeral methods or burial culture are likewise difficult to accept.\\n\\nf. Accordingly, the fact that, where a grave is established on land owned by another person, a grave-site right, which is a customary real right similar to superficies, is acquired by prescription if the grave site is possessed peacefully and openly for 20 years, has long been approved as a legal norm as a custom or practice that has continued over a long period, and such legal norm must be regarded as having remained in force until now with respect to graves established before January 13, 2001, the effective date of the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158).\\n\\n3. According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the reasoning of the first-instance judgment cited therein, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na. On the forest land of 14,257 square meters in Wonju (address omitted), jointly owned by the Plaintiff and Non-party 1 (hereinafter referred to as “the forest land at issue”), the following graves were established: ① in or around 1733, the grave marked (sa) on the attached map of the lower court, measuring 174 square meters, as the grave of Non-party 2, the progenitor of the ○○○ Clan △△△ Branch lineal descendants (hereinafter referred to as “the clan at issue”); ② in or around April 1987, the grave marked (ra) on the same map, measuring 100 square meters, as the grave of Non-party 3, a great-grandson of Non-party 2, and the grave marked (ba) on the same map, measuring 25 square meters, as the grave of Non-party 4, the third son of Non-party 2; ③ in or around spring of 1989, the grave marked (da) on the same map, measuring 95 square meters, as the grave of Non-party 5, the great-grandfather of Defendant 1; and ④ in or around November 1990, the grave marked (na) on the same map, measuring 90 square meters, as the grave of Non-party 6, the mother of Defendant 2.\\n\\nb. After each of the above graves was established and until the Plaintiff filed the present action, for more than 20 years, ① Defendant 1, as the eldest male-line descendant, protected and managed the graves marked (da), (ra), (ba), and (sa) and possessed each of those graves and their grave sites, and ② Defendant 2, as the son of Non-party 6, protected and managed the grave marked (na) and possessed that grave and its grave site.\\n\\n4. Based on those facts, the court below held that Defendant 1 acquired by prescription, pursuant to customary law, a grave-site right over each corresponding grave site with respect to the graves marked (da), (ra), (ba), and (sa), and that Defendant 2 similarly acquired by prescription, pursuant to customary law, a grave-site right over the grave site of the grave marked (na). In light of the legal principles examined above, the court below’s determination is proper, and there is no illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right or the effect of customary law, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the reason that the scope of a grave-site right must not exceed the area of possession of graves, etc. prescribed in Article 18(2) of the Funeral Services Act is an issue raised for the first time in the Supreme Court proceedings concerning a matter not asserted in the court below, and thus does not constitute a lawful ground of appeal.\\n\\n5. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal are borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged as per the order. In this judgment, other than the dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Yong-deok, Park Bo-young, Kim So-young, Kwon Soon-il, and Kim Jae-hyung concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right, the views of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there are the supplementary opinion of Justice Kim Shin and Justice Cho Hee-dae on the majority opinion, as well as the supplementary opinion of Justice Kim Jae-hyung on the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n6. The dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Yong-deok, Park Bo-young, Kim So-young, Kwon Soon-il, and Kim Jae-hyung concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right is as follows.\\n\\na. The Seoul High Court Decision of March 8, 1927, held that in Korea, a person who established a grave on land owned by another with the other’s consent acquires, for the purpose of owning it, a kind of real right similar to superficies over the land of another, and that even a person who established a grave on another’s land without obtaining that consent acquires, by prescription, a kind of real right similar to superficies over the land of another when the grave site is possessed peacefully and openly for 20 years, and that it is customary that such right may be asserted against a third party without proof or registration; thereby recognizing a grave-site right, and the Supreme Court has likewise held to the same effect.\\n\\nDuring the Joseon Dynasty, when there existed a custom concerning the use of land for the ownership of graves, no private or individual ownership was recognized with respect to the forests where graves were mainly established, and because the system of forest ownership in the modern sense was in the process of formation in Korea through the Japanese colonial period until around the time the current Civil Act came into force, members of society had little or no awareness of forest ownership rights, and the economic value of forest land was also not large. In light of the past situation, in which burial-centered funeral and burial culture was widespread, most people often had no choice but to bury their ancestors’ corpses in another person’s forest land, and express objection by the landowner to this was rare. Accordingly, the Seoul High Court and the Supreme Court, in cases where a grave was established in a form by which its existence could be recognized from the outside, such as a burial mound, or where forest land was transferred while such a grave existed, broadly construed the owner’s consent concerning the establishment and continuance of the grave and thereby held that a grave-site right existed; and, in the same vein, it may be said that even where a grave was established on land owned by another without the landowner’s consent, the courts allowed the acquisition of a grave-site right by the modern system of acquisitive prescription and recognized this as one of the customs.\\n\\nThat is, from the Joseon Dynasty, when Confucian culture that placed importance on filial piety toward parents and ancestor worship was dominant, through the period in which its influence remained, the method of burial in our society centered on “interment,” burying corpses or remains in the ground, and such tradition and custom formed the basis for the establishment of a grave-site right, as confirmed by the decisions of the Seoul High Court and the precedents of the Supreme Court.\\n\\nHowever, as will be discussed below, following the enforcement of the current Civil Act, the concept of land ownership, including forest land, and the private property system became established, and as the economic value of land increased, the awareness of landowners’ rights improved and the need for their protection grew; moreover, as the burial-centered burial culture relatively markedly faded, the socio-cultural basis that had recognized by custom even graves established without the landowner’s consent as subject to acquisitive prescription disappeared, and such custom no longer accorded with the overall legal order.\\n\\nb. Even if a custom or customary law as a social norm generated by repeated social practice has come to be approved and enforced as a legal norm by society’s legal conviction and recognition, if it is contrary to the overall legal order whose supreme norm is the Constitution, lacks legitimacy or reasonableness, or if, due to changes in the fundamental ideas or social order governing society, it no longer accords with the overall legal order at the time when such customary law is to be applied, it cannot be recognized as having legal effect as a source of law (see Supreme Court en banc Decisions 2001DA48781, rendered on July 24, 2003, and 2002DA1178, rendered on July 21, 2005).\\n\\n(1) After the period governed by the Former Civil Act ended, the Civil Act, the first modern general civil law created by our own hands, came into force on January 1, 1960, and it adopts, as its basic ideals, the principle of respect for private property rights and the principle of private autonomy. The preamble to Article 23(1) and Article 119(1) of the Constitution declare that the market economic order is based on the private property system and the principle of private autonomy with respect to economic activities (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2002DU8626, rendered on November 22, 2007), and the Civil Act reflects this constitutional spirit.\\n\\nArticle 211 of the Civil Act provides, as the content of ownership, “The owner shall have the right to use, profit from, and dispose of the object owned, within the limits of law.” In addition, with respect to acquisitive prescription for property rights other than ownership, Article 248 of the Civil Act provides, “The provisions of the preceding three Articles shall apply mutatis mutandis to the acquisition of property rights other than ownership,” and Article 245(1) of the Civil Act, applied mutatis mutandis pursuant to Article 248, provides, “A person who possesses immovable property peacefully and openly with the intention of owning it for 20 years shall acquire ownership thereof by registration,” thereby concretely shaping the content and limits of ownership in immovable property, which is a property right guaranteed by the Constitution (see Constitutional Court, en banc Decision 92HUNBA20, rendered on July 29, 1993).\\n\\nUnlike the Former Civil Act, Article 186 of the Civil Act provides, “The acquisition or loss of, or changes in, real rights in immovable property arising from a juristic act shall take effect only upon registration,” thereby adopting the so-called “formalism,” under which the effect of acquisition, loss, or changes in real rights in immovable property arising from a juristic act arises only when the publicity method of registration is satisfied. In line with this, the system of publicity for immovable property was gradually organized through the enforcement of the Act on Registration of Immovable Property. With the enforcement of the current Civil Act, the basic ideals of modern civil law, such as respect for private property rights, naturally became entrenched in our society, and the public’s awareness of land ownership rights greatly increased. By adopting the so-called “formalism” with respect to changes in real rights, it became necessary to be very cautious in recognizing immovable property rights that do not have a clear method of public notice such as registration, and to limit to extremely exceptional cases the recognition, against the will of the registered owner, of acquisitive prescription of ownership or property rights other than ownership in relation to immovable property.\\n\\n(2) Accordingly, the laws enacted thus far concerning graves, etc. have changed so as to reflect the principle of respect for ownership and private property rights, so that funeral and burial may be carried out in conformity with our overall legal order, including the Constitution and the Civil Act.\\n\\n(a) The “Rules on Cemeteries, Crematoriums, Burial and Cremation Control,” promulgated during the Japanese colonial period and first regulating graves (repealed by Addenda Article 2 of the Act on Burial, etc. and Graves, etc. promulgated on December 5, 1961, by Act No. 799; hereinafter the same), strictly regulated the establishment of new graves and made persons who recklessly buried corpses or remains in another person’s grave or in places other than a grave subject to criminal punishment. This may be said to have been based on an administrative purpose of cracking down on public morals disorder and sanitary harm concerning graves (see Supreme Court Decisions 4288MINSANG210, rendered on September 29, 1955, and 72DA2464, rendered on February 26, 1973), but it legally and clearly declared that burying a corpse recklessly on land owned by another is a criminal act that is prohibited and punishable.\\n\\n(b) The “Act on Burial, etc. and Graves, etc.”, which came into force on January 1, 1962, after the Civil Act came into force, and whose title was changed on December 31, 1968, by Act No. 2069 to “Act on Burial and Graves, etc.” and is, together with the changed Act, hereinafter referred to as the “Burial Act,” provides that the burial of corpses or remains may not be conducted in areas other than cemeteries, and that burial may not be conducted in another person’s cemetery unless a written consent from the installer is obtained (Article 4(1) and (4)), and criminally punishes those who violate this (Article 19(1)). Under the Burial Act, a provincial governor, etc. may, after giving public notice for a certain period, order the person who buried the corpse or remains or other person with an interest to exhume corpses or remains buried on land other than a cemetery or in another person’s cemetery without the consent of the installer (Article 16(1)), and with respect to graves without an interested person, the Act allowed the landowner, etc. to exhume them with the permission of the provincial governor, etc. (Article 16(2)).\\n\\nThus, while the Burial Act may also be said to have included the above provisions for public-law regulatory purposes, like the above-mentioned “Rules on Cemeteries, Crematoriums, Burial and Cremation Control,” it expressly stipulated by law that the place where a grave may be established is limited to a cemetery and that establishing a grave in a cemetery owned by another without the owner’s consent is prohibited as a crime.\\n\\n(c) Furthermore, the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158), which entirely amended the Burial Act and came into force on January 13, 2001, provides that the landowner, cemetery installer, or person with an interest may, with permission from the mayor, county governor, or district head having jurisdiction over the relevant grave, exhume the corpse or remains buried in a grave established on the land in question without the landowner’s consent, or in a grave established in a cemetery without the consent of the cemetery installer or person with an interest (Article 23(1)); and provides that the person with an interest in a grave established as above after the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act may not assert against the relevant landowner, cemetery installer, or person with an interest rights such as the right to use the land for the preservation of the grave (Article 23(3) and Addenda Article 2).\\n\\nLooking at the provisions of the above Funeral Services Act, unlike the former Burial Act, the landowner, etc. is allowed to exhume all graves established without his or her consent, thereby establishing a legal remedy by the direct interested party; and, by expressly stating that the person with an interest in a grave established on the land in question after the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act without the landowner’s consent may not assert against the landowner rights such as the right to use the land, the rights of the landowner are further strengthened.\\n\\nThis can be seen as actively reflecting the basic principles of modern civil law, namely the “principle of respect for private property rights” and the “principle of private autonomy,” by providing for private-law relations between the landowner and the person with an interest in the grave in order to ensure the effectiveness of the legal regime concerning graves, which had been limited to public-law regulation. Although the Funeral Services Act restricts the assertion of land-use rights with respect to graves established without the landowner’s consent after the enforcement of the Act, this seems merely to clarify that, where a grave had been established before the enforcement of the Act and land-use rights had already arisen, such rights are not retroactively denied nor do they automatically extinguish upon the enforcement of the Act; it cannot be viewed as taking the position that the basic principles expressly declared in the Funeral Services Act, namely the “principle of respect for private property rights” and the “principle of private autonomy,” must be denied merely because the grave was established before the enforcement of the Act.\\n\\n(3) (a) Originally, establishing a grave on land owned by another without the owner’s consent is unlawful because it constitutes an infringement of ownership by occupying and using the land without any title, and the above-mentioned statutes concerning burial expressly provide for the prohibition thereof. Although the Funeral Services Act contains provisions restricting a grave’s interested person from asserting land-use rights against the landowner with respect to graves established after its enforcement, the unlawfulness of the act of establishing a grave by infringing the landowner’s rights had already been confirmed by the Burial Act for about 40 years prior to the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act, even taking the period after the Civil Act came into force as the benchmark.\\n\\nNevertheless, to recognize the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right solely because possession has been peaceful and openly maintained for 20 years on the basis of such an unlawful act, there must be legitimacy and reasonableness that can be harmonized with the overall legal order.\\n\\n(b) Under Article 245(1) of the Civil Act, for acquisitive prescription of ownership in immovable property to be recognized, the possessor must not only possess peacefully and openly for 20 years but also have the intention to own. And because this provision is applied mutatis mutandis to other property rights under Article 248 of the Civil Act, in order for acquisitive prescription of another property right to be recognized, there must be substance amounting to the exercise of that property right and an intention thereto must be recognized.\\n\\nUnder Article 197(1) of the Civil Act, a possessor of an object is presumed to possess with the intention of owning; therefore, when the possessor asserts acquisitive prescription, the possessor does not bear the burden of proving the intention to own. Until 1997, the Supreme Court, relying on this presumption of intention to own, held that even where a possessor occupied land owned by another without authorization, such possession fell, absent special circumstances, under possession in one’s own right by virtue of the nature of the title.\\n\\nHowever, the en banc Supreme Court Decision 95DA28625, rendered on August 21, 1997, changed the prior view and held that whether a possessor’s possession is possession in one’s own right with the intention to own or possession on behalf of another without such intention is not determined by the possessor’s inner intent, but must be determined objectively and externally by the nature of the title from which the possession originated and by all circumstances related to the possession; and where it is proven that the possessor, at the commencement of possession, knowingly occupied without authorization immovable property owned by another, without any juristic act or other legal requirement that could serve as a cause for acquiring ownership, and aware that no such legal requirement existed, then, absent special circumstances, the possessor must be regarded as not having intended to exclude the other person’s ownership and possess the property; accordingly, the presumption of possession with the intention to own is rebutted, thereby denying acquisition of ownership by a bad-faith unauthorized possessor.\\n\\nAnd in order for acquisitive prescription of superficies over another person’s land for the ownership of a building or other structure to be recognized, in addition to the fact of possession of that land, it must be objectively shown and continuously maintained that such possession is not based on a lease or commodatum relationship but constitutes possession as a superficiary; the burden of proof rests with the party asserting acquisitive prescription, and whether such requirements exist is determined by comprehensively considering, in the individual case, the circumstances of the commencement of possession and the installation of the building or other structure, the relationship of consideration, the type and structure of the building or other structure, the subsequent relationship between the parties, and the state of use of the land, etc., and by examining whether there is substantive basis to regard the possession as possession as a superficiary (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 96DA7984, rendered on December 23, 1996).\\n\\nThus, after the above en banc decision was rendered on August 21, 1997, acquisitive prescription of ownership by unauthorized occupation was denied, and in light of the fact that the same legal principles must also apply to acquisitive prescription of other property rights, where a person, knowing that the landowner has not consented, establishes a grave on land owned by another without authorization, then, absent special circumstances, it cannot be said that the person who established the grave has the substance of having obtained the landowner’s consent to establish the grave or the intention to possess accordingly. Nevertheless, recognizing acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right with respect to such an unauthorized grave amounts in the end to recognizing a system of acquisitive prescription whose requirements differ from those for acquisitive prescription of ownership and other property rights.\\n\\n(c) Although acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right is recognized as one of the customs, in substance it is generally understood as reflecting the modern system of acquisitive prescription in the customary-law grave-site right. But it is questionable whether protecting bad-faith unauthorized possession only with respect to a grave-site right, by treating it differently from the requirements for acquisitive prescription of ownership or other property rights under the Civil Act, accords with the spirit of modern civil law, which respects private property rights and private autonomy, and with the purpose of the above en banc decision reflecting that spirit.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court views the formation and content of a grave-site right as being determined by the owner’s consent and an agreement with the owner; as noted above, however, in the case of an unauthorized grave, such an agreement with the owner does not exist and, furthermore, no such appearance exists at all, so there is no basis upon which a grave-site right can arise. Therefore, according to the requirements for acquisitive prescription regarding property rights other than ownership recognized by the Civil Act, acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right with respect to an unauthorized grave that lacks any basis for its formation is impossible; ultimately, the former custom allowing this is not in harmony with the acquisitive prescription system of the Civil Act.\\n\\nMoreover, with the enforcement of the Civil Act and the public notice of ownership of all land, including forest land, through the registry, anyone can identify the owner of forest land, and it is now a matter of ordinary legal common sense that the unauthorized use of another’s forest land without the owner’s consent or the installation of buildings or structures thereon constitutes an infringement of ownership and is not tolerable; this is no different merely because the structure is a grave.\\n\\nIt seems that the reason the system of acquisitive prescription has been recognized merely on the basis of factual possession of a grave site for 20 years is that it is not easy to prove, after the fact, the basis materials such as contracts that were not properly prepared during the grave-establishment process when disputes arise later. However, if a grave is established with the owner’s consent, a grave-site right arises immediately, and the existence or possibility of such consent is merely a matter concerning the formation of a grave-site right by consent, and in the end this is a matter of factual determination regarding the existence of such consent or interpretation of a declaration of intent. When a dispute arises concerning the existence of a grave-site right with respect to a grave that has existed peacefully and openly for more than 20 years, the fact that possession continued peacefully and openly over a long period or that the grave continued to exist provides a substantial basis for recognizing the probability that express or implied consent or permission had been obtained from the landowner around the time the grave was established; thus, in most cases, such consent or permission will be recognized. However, if, despite such fact-finding based on these circumstances, the grave is found to be bad-faith unauthorized possession, there will be no need to protect it, and, just as with acquisitive prescription of ownership, it is reasonable to deny acquisitive prescription based on bad-faith unauthorized possession, and allowing acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right within the scope and limits of the system of acquisitive prescription for other property rights recognized by the Civil Act would accord with the overall legal order of acquisitive prescription.\\n\\nIn addition, the Funeral Services Act allows the landowner to directly exhume graves established without the landowner’s consent, regardless of whether the time of establishment was before or after the Act’s enforcement; and, with respect to graves established after the enforcement of the Act, it declares that the person with an interest in the grave is completely barred from asserting rights such as the right to use the land against the landowner. As will be seen below, this reflects the disappearance of the legal conviction concerning the former custom that allowed acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right over unauthorized graves. In light of this, with respect to a grave that was unauthorizedly established and had not yet satisfied the prescription period for acquisitive prescription by the time the Funeral Services Act was enforced, the practical meaning of the possession that the person who established the grave has over the grave after the enforcement of the Act is difficult to regard as the same as before; thus, it is inappropriate to view continued unauthorized possession alone as resulting in the acquisition by prescription of a grave-site right, because this may conflict with the “principle of respect for private property rights” declared by the Funeral Services Act.\\n\\n(d) Moreover, with respect to the duration of a grave-site right, the Supreme Court interpreted that the Civil Act’s provisions on superficies are not to apply, and that if there are special circumstances such as an agreement between the parties, such circumstances shall govern; absent such circumstances, the grave-site right continues while the right holder continues to protect and serve the grave and the grave remains in existence (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decisions 81DA1220, rendered on January 26, 1982, and 2005DA44114, rendered on June 28, 2007), and, in view of the fact that payment of rent is not an element of superficies and that, absent an agreement concerning rent, rent cannot be claimed, it was said that even in the case of acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right, rent need not be paid (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA37912, rendered on February 28, 1995).\\n\\nHowever, recognizing the acquisitive prescription of an essentially perpetual and gratuitous grave-site right merely because there has been peaceful and open possession for 20 years despite the absence of the landowner’s consent not only excessively restricts the landowner’s ownership without any involvement or fault on the part of the landowner, but also does not allow the landowner even any compensation for the provision of the land; therefore, it may infringe the essential content of the constitutionally guaranteed property right, rendering ownership of land as a private property right nominal.\\n\\n(4) Considering the above circumstances in aggregate, although it may be said that recognizing acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right with respect to graves established without the landowner’s consent was a custom recognized in the past, reflecting the burial culture of an era when ownership of land such as forest land had not yet been established, such custom had, at least by the time the above en banc decision on acquisitive prescription of ownership was rendered and around the time the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) came into force on January 13, 2001, no longer accorded with the overall legal order, including the above constitutional provisions on property rights, the Civil Act provisions concerning the content of ownership and the requirements for acquisitive prescription, and the regulatory content of the Funeral Services Act, and had become unable to maintain legitimacy and reasonableness.\\n\\nd. Moreover, customary law refers to social norms generated by repeated social practice that come to be approved and enforced as legal norms by the legal conviction and recognition of society; therefore, even if a social norm created by repeated social practice has been approved as customary law, if members of society no longer have conviction regarding the legal binding force of such practice, such customary law inevitably loses its effect as a legal norm (see the above en banc Supreme Court Decision 2002DA1178).\\n\\n(1) As seen above, the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right, a customary real right, is closely related to the burial-centered funeral and burial culture that was prevalent in our society in the past. Such burial and funeral culture is based on a Confucian-centered culture that valued ancestor worship, a family system centered on extended families, and an agrarian society based on self-sufficiency. In addition, the social phenomenon that, in the past, most people had no choice but to bury their ancestors’ corpses in another person’s forest land, and that express objection by landowners to this was rare, may also be seen as one background.\\n\\n(2) However, our society has rapidly urbanized since the 1970s due to rapid industrialization and the ensuing economic growth, and in the course thereof the social environment changed greatly, with transportation and communications developing and the level of science, technology, and education improving; and the family form became generally a nuclear family composed of spouses and unmarried children. The agrarian, rural community society based on Confucian ethical notions, which was the background against which a grave-site right came to be recognized as customary, has substantially collapsed along with the urbanization and industrialization of our society as individualism and liberalism spread widely.\\n\\nUnlike before, as the development of forest land for housing complexes or industrial complexes has increased and transactions have become frequent, the economic value of forest land and the need to protect its ownership have increased, whereas graves established on forest land are seen not so much as objects of protection as major obstacles in the development or transaction of forest land. Furthermore, as burial-centered funeral and burial culture continued for a long time, the cemetery area nationwide continued to expand, damaging natural landscapes and the environment, causing a shortage of living space, and further impeding the efficient use of national land that is relatively narrow compared to the population.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, in order to prevent public health and sanitary harm, promote the efficient use of national land, and relieve the inconvenience of the people caused by the shortage of cemetery space and living space, the Burial Act was entirely amended and the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) was enforced from January 13, 2001, as noted above.\\n\\nThe Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) declared that the promotion of cremation is a duty of the State and local governments by requiring the State and local governments to devise and implement policies to promote cremation and the placing of ashes in columbaria in order to prevent damage to national land caused by the increase in cemeteries (Article 4), and thereafter, the Funeral Services Act, entirely amended by Act No. 8489 on May 25, 2007, required the State and local governments to devise and implement policies to promote cremation, the placement of ashes in memorial facilities, and natural burials, and additionally required local governments to have crematorium facilities capable of meeting local residents’ demand for cremation (Article 4(1) and (2)).\\n\\nIn particular, the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158), enforced on January 13, 2001, limited, in principle, the period for establishing graves in public and private cemeteries to 15 years, while allowing the relevant establishment period to be extended up to three times by 15 years each (Article 17(1) and (2)); and the Funeral Services Act, amended by Act No. 13660 on December 29, 2015, revised the above period of grave establishment to 30 years in principle and allowed one extension (Article 19(1) and (2)), but still limits the period in which establishment is allowed, including extensions, to 60 years.\\n\\nThese provisions of the Funeral Services Act reflect changes in the public’s consciousness concerning the former burial-centered funeral and burial culture, and, in response to those changes, the Act seeks to organize the cemetery system and diversify funeral and burial culture by encouraging cremation followed by placement of ashes in columbaria or burial in natural burial grounds or memorial facilities. Since the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act with such content, various funeral and burial facilities, such as crematorium facilities, columbaria, and natural burial grounds, have continuously expanded. Such changes in social awareness are also confirmed by the fact that the national cremation rate, which was only 19.1% on average nationwide in 1993, reached 76.9% on average nationwide in 2013, showing that new funeral methods and burial culture are taking root in our society.\\n\\nThat is, due to the establishment of national land-use plans for efficient use of national land, increased attention to environmental issues, and changes in the cemetery system, cremation has become widespread and natural burials have increased, so that the burial-centered funeral and burial culture in its traditional sense has been greatly weakened. In addition, due to improvements in national income, expansion of various funeral and burial facilities, and national support, the public’s perception of ancestor worship is moving away from emphasizing the outward aspect of graves and toward the spiritual aspect of ancestral rites and support.\\n\\n(4) Also, as seen above, the current Civil Act, which takes respect for private property rights as a basic ideal, came into force on January 1, 1960, and the system of publicity for immovable property was organized through the enforcement of the Act on Registration of Immovable Property, greatly strengthening the public’s awareness of land ownership rights; furthermore, because the Burial Act and the Funeral Services Act explicitly declared by law that establishing graves without the landowner’s consent is unlawful, and cremation, etc. became established as a new burial and funeral system, in light of the overall legal order including the Constitution, today it has become difficult to tolerate landownership being restricted by graves established without the landowner’s consent and without authorization, and it can further be said that people no longer expect protection for unauthorized graves.\\n\\nIn particular, as noted above, the Funeral Services Act provides that, with respect to graves unauthorizedly established after the enforcement of the Act, the person with an interest in the grave is completely barred from asserting rights such as the right to use the land against the landowner; this substantially denies the formation or acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right over unauthorized graves, and it can be said that the former custom allowing such acquisitive prescription no longer survives and has been abolished by the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act.\\n\\nSuch legislation abolishing the former custom would have been impossible unless it were based on the decline of the burial culture noted above and the public legal consciousness that does not tolerate unauthorized grave establishment; ultimately, this should be understood as reflecting the disappearance, by around the time of the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) on January 13, 2001, of the legal conviction concerning the former custom allowing acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right over unauthorized graves. Although the Funeral Services Act excludes claims of rights such as the right to use land against the landowner with respect to graves unauthorizedly established after its enforcement, this is merely to the effect that rights already established do not retroactively extinguish, and cannot be understood to mean that the legal conviction permitting the acquisition by prescription of a new grave-site right over an unauthorized grave after the enforcement of the Act remains intact.\\n\\n(5) Considering these circumstances in aggregate, although the former custom had recognized the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right in all cases where a grave was established on land owned by another without the owner’s consent, on the basis of traditional ancestor-worship and the practice of grave establishment, in light of the changed social realities, such as changes in the public’s perception of burial and funeral culture, changes in the burial and funeral system, and strengthened awareness of landowners’ rights, it can be said that the legal conviction held by members of our society concerning the custom of acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right has substantially declined, and that the practical disappearance of this legal conviction is reflected in the legislation of the Funeral Services Act.\\n\\ne. Therefore, the former custom that recognized, merely because there had been peaceful and open possession for 20 years despite the absence of the landowner’s consent, the acquisitive prescription of an essentially perpetual and gratuitous grave-site right, had, at least by the time the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) came into force on January 13, 2001, lost legitimacy and reasonableness as contrary to the overall legal order, including the Constitution respecting private property rights, and further lost its effect as a legal norm because members of our society no longer had conviction regarding the legal binding force of such custom. Accordingly, in the case of a grave for which the 20-year prescription period had not yet elapsed as of January 13, 2001, one cannot assert acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right by relying on the former custom concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right that had lost its effect as a legal norm.\\n\\nIn contrast, recognizing the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right for a person who, knowing that the landowner had not consented, unauthorizedly established a grave on another’s land is plainly to permit illegal bad-faith unlawful possession and further to protect continued unlawful acts as a permanent right; this not only conflicts with the legal principles of the above en banc decision, which declared that such unlawful possession would be excluded from acquisitive prescription and not legally protected, but also disregards the legal compliance spirit and matured legal consciousness of the people, who through sustained efforts without infringing others’ rights and in compliance with the Burial Act and Funeral Services Act have moved beyond burial-centered practices and achieved the current advanced burial and funeral culture; thus it runs contrary to the rule of law and the principles of justice and equity pursued by our society, and can no longer be justified under the name of practice or custom.\\n\\nHowever, this view does not deny the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right in every case where, as of January 13, 2001, the 20-year prescription period had not yet elapsed; it presupposes that, within the scope permitted by the current legal order, acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right may be recognized, like other property rights. That is, if a grave was established with consent from a person registered as the landowner, but it later turns out that such registration was invalid, and if, objectively and externally, the substance of possessing as a grave-site right holder can be recognized and such possession has been maintained peacefully and openly for 20 years, then the requirements of Article 248 of the Civil Act, applied mutatis mutandis from Article 245(1) of the Civil Act, may be satisfied, and acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right may be recognized.\\n\\nf. We examine the reasoning of the judgment below in light of the above legal principles.\\n\\n(1) Since the grave marked (sa) in this case was established around 1733 and the 20-year prescription period elapsed before January 13, 2001, the court below’s determination that it acquired a grave-site right by prescription pursuant to the former custom can be accepted.\\n\\n(2) However, it is clear that the 20-year prescription period had not elapsed before January 13, 2001 from the date of establishment of the grave marked (na) in this case, established by Defendant 2, and the graves marked (da), (ra), and (ba) in this case, established by Defendant 1; accordingly, the former custom concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right cannot be applied.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below held that the defendants acquired by prescription pursuant to the former custom, on the premise that the former custom concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right also applies to the above graves; this determination by the court below is erroneous. However, according to the record, at the time the above graves were established, the register for the forest land at issue showed the clan at issue as the owner, and thereafter it was revealed that the true owner was the Plaintiff. If the defendants established the above graves with the clan’s consent, there is room to recognize possession as a grave-site right holder; therefore, the court below should examine the specific circumstances under which the defendants came to establish the above graves and determine whether acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right under Article 248 of the Civil Act is possible.\\n\\nAccordingly, the judgment below on this point contains an error that affected the judgment by failing to conduct the necessary trial as a result of misapprehending the legal principles on the effect of customary law and the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right.\\n\\n(3) Therefore, the portion of the judgment below adverse to the Plaintiff as against Defendant 1 concerning the graves marked (da), (ra), and (ba), and the portion adverse to the Plaintiff as against Defendant 2, must be reversed.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state that I cannot concur with the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. The supplementary opinion of Justices Kim Shin and Cho Hee-dae on the majority opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. The dissenting opinion states that the former custom recognizing the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right, at least by the time the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) came into force on January 13, 2001, had lost legitimacy and reasonableness as contrary to the overall legal order, including the Constitution respecting private property rights, and had also lost its effect as a legal norm because members of our society no longer had conviction regarding the legal binding force of such custom; therefore, in the case of graves for which the 20-year prescription period had not yet elapsed as of January 13, 2001, one cannot assert acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right by relying on the former custom concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right that had lost its effect as a legal norm.\\n\\nHowever, the Supreme Court has long confirmed and applied the customary law concerning acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right on the basis of customs or practices whose content is the protection of land-use rights for the ownership of graves, and it is difficult to conclude that there was a significant change in the overall legal order, the fundamental ideas governing society, or the social order to the extent that the customary law concerning a grave-site right, whose effect as a legal norm has been firmly recognized as unshaken for so long, has lost its effect.\\n\\nb. First, we examine whether there was a meaningful change in the overall legal order surrounding the custom concerning acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right to the extent that it can be said that the customary law lost its effect as a legal norm.\\n\\n(1) Before the current Civil Act came into force, the Supreme Court held that where a grave was established on land owned by another without the owner’s consent, a grave-site right, which is a customary real right similar to superficies, is acquired by prescription if the grave site is possessed peacefully and openly for 20 years, and that it is customary that such right may be asserted against a third party without registration (see Supreme Court Decisions 4288MINSANG210, rendered on September 29, 1955, and 4290MINSANG539, rendered on October 31, 1957); and after the current Civil Act came into force, the Court also held that there was no need to abolish the Supreme Court decision that recognized the effect of customary law concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right (see Supreme Court Decision 63DA157, rendered on July 25, 1963).
