Thereafter, for nearly 50 years the Supreme Court repeatedly rendered decisions to the same effect, applying the customary law concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right to graves established before the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decisions 94DA37912, rendered on February 28, 1995, and 2011DA63017, 63024, rendered on November 10, 2011).\\n\\n(2) (a) Nor can it be said that there was a significant change in the legal regime concerning graves such as would affect the customary law concerning a grave-site right.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court held that even if a grave installer is punished pursuant to the “Rules on Cemeteries, Crematoriums, Burial and Cremation Control,” this has no effect on the acquisition of a grave-site right, which is a real right similar to superficies (see Supreme Court Decision 72DA2464, rendered on February 26, 1973); and it held that even where the chief of police may order exhumation under the above “Rules on Cemeteries, Crematoriums, Burial and Cremation Control,” this is for administrative purposes of cracking down on public morals disorder and sanitary harm concerning graves and thus has no effect on the acquisition of a grave-site right (see Supreme Court Decision 4288MINSANG210, rendered on September 29, 1955).\\n\\nThe Burial Act before its complete amendment by the Funeral Services Act did not contain an express provision disallowing a grave-site right recognized under customary law, and the Supreme Court held, among other things, that the scope of a grave-site right is not limited to the limited area of a grave prescribed by the Burial Act (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decisions 94DA28970, rendered on August 26, 1994, and 94DA15530, rendered on December 23, 1994), thereby making clear that the Burial Act, which was limited to public-law regulation, could not affect the content of the grave-site right recognized by customary law.\\n\\nFurthermore, Addenda Article 2 of the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) provides that Article 23(3), which states to the effect that, where a landowner exhumes a grave established without the landowner’s consent, the person with an interest in the grave may not assert acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right, which is a land-use right, against the landowner, applies only to graves first established after the Funeral Services Act came into force; thus, it does not exclude the application of the existing customary law to graves established before the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act.\\n\\nAs the Burial Act and similar statutes, which remained within the realm of public-law regulation, could not affect the acquisition of a private-law right, namely a grave-site right, and the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158), effective January 13, 2001, likewise does not exclude the application of the existing customary law to graves established before its enforcement, the mere enforcement of the Funeral Services Act, which contains provisions restricting the assertion of land-use rights with respect to graves established without the landowner’s consent, cannot be said to have extinguished the basis for the existence of the customary law concerning a grave-site right.\\n\\n(b) The Funeral Services Act has as its legislative purpose the prevention of public health and sanitary harm and the promotion of the efficient use of national land and public welfare by prescribing matters concerning burial methods such as burial and cremation and the installation, creation, and management of funeral and burial facilities such as cemeteries and crematoriums (Article 1). Although the Funeral Services Act contains provisions limiting the period for establishing graves and restricting the assertion of land-use rights with respect to graves established without the landowner’s consent in order to achieve and secure the effectiveness of such legislative purpose, it expressly states through its addenda that those provisions apply only to graves first established after January 13, 2001, when the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) came into force. In light of these provisions of the Funeral Services Act, the legislative attitude of the Act appears merely to aim at gradually resolving problems such as the shortage of cemeteries and the impediment to the efficient use of national land caused by grave establishment by regulating graves established after the enforcement of the Act, thereby promoting the efficient use of national land and public welfare; it cannot be viewed as intending to abolish at once the customary law concerning a grave-site right that had been recognized until the time of the Act’s enforcement and to resolve all practical problems caused by the increase and continuance of graves at once.\\n\\n(c) Therefore, it is difficult to say that, with respect to graves already established before January 13, 2001, the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) made the grave-site right by customary law or its acquisitive prescription no longer permissible; nor can it be concluded that a clear change in the overall legal order has emerged to the extent that the customary law concerning a grave-site right has changed or disappeared merely by reason of the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act.\\n\\n(3) (a) Since customary law is a social norm created by repeated social practice and approved and enforced as a legal norm by society’s legal conviction and recognition (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 80DA3231, rendered on June 14, 1983), the court is bound by the customary law so recognized and cannot arbitrarily deny its effect.\\n\\n(b) The customary law concerning a grave-site right is based on customs or practices grounded in the Korean people’s spirit of reverence and remembrance for their ancestors, and considering the special nature of “graves,” which are objects of ancestral rites and reverence, it cannot be said to lack legitimacy or reasonableness or to be contrary to the overall legal order merely because of the ideology of absolute ownership.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court long ago held that a grave is a place where the remains of ancestors are interred, and that descendants are of course obliged to preserve it and that even third parties must respect its dignity (see Supreme Court Decision 4291MINSANG770, rendered on October 8, 1959), and it also held that a person who acquires ownership of forest land where a grave is located has a duty of care to confirm whether he or she has acquired a legitimate title that can oppose the grave owner, who has a real right similar to superficies over the grave, when using or profiting from that forest land through construction or otherwise (see Supreme Court Decision 78DA2338, rendered on February 13, 1979).\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Criminal Act, in Chapter 12, “Crimes concerning Religion” of Part II, special provisions, prescribes the crime of grave exhumation (Article 160), and the Supreme Court has held that a “grave” that is the object of the crime of grave exhumation means a place where a human corpse, remains, hair, etc. are buried and are the object of ancestral rites, worship, or memorialization, and that even if it is unclear who the deceased was, if it is an object of ancestral rites, reverence, and religious etiquette and there is a person who protects and serves it, it falls within that concept (see Supreme Court Decision 89DO2061, rendered on February 13, 1990). According to this, infringement upon a grave that is the object of protection and service by the bereaved family constitutes, in criminal law, a criminal act.\\n\\nAs above, graves have a special nature that descendants or third parties such as landowners may not damage recklessly, and the grave-site right for the protection and service of a grave is also based on such an idea. Taking into account such attributes of graves and the characteristics of a grave-site right, the Supreme Court recognized the effect of a grave-site right as a real right that can exclude interference by the owner or a third party, and interpreted that if it is equipped with a form by which the existence of the grave can be recognized from the outside, such as a burial mound, the grave-site right is acquired without registration, and that the duration of the grave-site right also continues, absent special circumstances such as an agreement between the parties, so long as the grave continues to exist while the right holder continues to protect and serve it.\\n\\n(c) Meanwhile, for the following reasons, it cannot be said that the customary law recognizing a grave-site right or its acquisitive prescription lacks legitimacy or reasonableness to such an extent that it renders the landowner’s ownership nominal.\\n\\nIt is true that, as a result of the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right, the landowner’s rights are restricted, but this is a problem that inevitably arises once the system of acquisitive prescription is recognized. Nevertheless, the Supreme Court has held that a person who established a grave on land owned by another without the owner’s consent acquires, if he or she possesses the grave site peacefully and openly for 20 years, a real right similar to superficies over that land by prescription, and not ownership of it (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decisions 68DA1927, 1928, rendered on January 28, 1969), and it has held, by stating that a person who establishes and owns a grave on another’s land possesses that land only within the extent necessary for the preservation and management of the grave absent other special circumstances, that the intention to own is not presumed by the nature of such possession (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decisions 97DA3651, 3668, rendered on March 28, 1997), thereby fundamentally blocking the possibility of acquisitive prescription of ownership over the grave-site portion by the grave installer, etc. In other words, by recognizing only the right to use the land as the content of the grave-site right established through the system of acquisitive prescription, it prevents the landowner’s ownership from being completely lost even if a grave-site right is established.\\n\\nIn order to acquire a grave-site right by prescription, the law requires “peaceful” possession without using forcible conduct that is legally impermissible and “open” possession, not covert possession (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 96DA14036, rendered on June 14, 1996), so where a grave is established by a method that is utterly impermissible under law, acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right may not be recognized. In addition, it is of course possible for the landowner to obtain relief by claiming exhumation from the grave owner before the 20-year prescription period elapses after the grave is established.\\n\\nAlso, because a grave-site right is only a right to use another’s land within the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of protecting and serving the grave, construction of an extension to the grave, installation of stone monuments, or stone-wall works in front of the grave are not permitted unless such acts are within the scope strictly necessary for achieving the purpose of protecting and serving the ancestral grave, and the power to establish a new grave in addition to an existing one is also not recognized (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decisions 93DA210, rendered on July 16, 1993, and 92DA54944, rendered on April 12, 1994). As above, the landowner’s exercise of ownership over the portion of land serving as the grave site is restricted only within the extent reasonably necessary for the protection and management of the grave (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 99DA14006, rendered on September 26, 2000).\\n\\nIf the grave that is the subject of the grave-site right no longer exists or the descendants cease to protect and serve it, the right naturally extinguishes; thus, the grave-site right does not permanently restrict the landowner’s ownership either.\\n\\n(d) The effect of the en banc Supreme Court Decision 95DA28625, rendered on August 21, 1997, which held that, in the case of so-called “bad-faith unauthorized possession,” the presumption under Article 197(1) of the Civil Act that possession is with the intention to own is rebutted, cannot be said to have caused the customary law concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right to lose its effect.\\n\\nThat en banc decision denied acquisitive prescription of ownership under Article 245(1) of the Civil Act with respect to a bad-faith unauthorized possessor by holding that, where it is proven that the possessor, at the commencement of possession, knowingly occupied immovable property owned by another without authorization and without any juristic act or other legal requirement that could serve as the cause of acquisition of ownership, then, absent special circumstances, the possessor must be regarded as not intending to exclude the other person’s ownership and possess the property, thereby rebutting the presumption of possession with the intention to own; the purport of that holding can be seen as preventing the unreasonable result that the registered true owner of immovable property easily loses ownership due to the completion of acquisitive prescription by the possessor.\\n\\nHowever, the requirements for acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right, which is a customary-law real right acquired without registration and only for the right to use land for the ownership of a grave, cannot be viewed from exactly the same standpoint.\\n\\nThe current Civil Act adopts the so-called “formalism” whereby the acquisition or loss of, or changes in, real rights in immovable property arising from a juristic act take effect only when registration as a publicity method is completed; from this perspective, taking into account such matters as the fact that it would not be reasonable to say that a possessor intends to acquire immovable-property real rights such as ownership without registration, the above en banc decision held that the presumption of possession with the intention to own is rebutted where so-called “bad-faith unauthorized possession” is proven.\\n\\nBy contrast, when a grave has to be established because an ancestor dies suddenly in an unforeseeable situation, there are cases where the grave is established with the landowner’s express consent, but there are also many cases where the grave is established in a state where the landowner does not expressly object and tolerates it. If one also considers that a grave-site right is a real right under customary law that can be acquired without registration where there is consent from the landowner, the special nature of “graves,” which are objects of ancestral rites and reverence, and traditional values that prized justice and righteousness among neighbors, then it would accord with our legal sentiment and social reality to view most grave installers as having intended to establish graves under the landowner’s toleration rather than with the recognition that they were unlawfully infringing land ownership. In addition, if the protection and service of the grave continued for a long period of 20 years or more, it would be appropriate to preserve the social order formed concerning such grave.\\n\\nEven if a grave installer, etc. cannot prove the landowner’s consent, it is natural to recognize acquisitive prescription under certain requirements. If one denies acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right simply because there was no landowner’s consent and categorizes the matter as “bad-faith unauthorized possession,” this is tantamount to requiring the grave owner, after more than 20 years have passed since the grave was established, to prove the then landowner’s inner intent such as consent at the time of grave establishment, which is not materially different from denying acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right in practice. But it is questionable whether such a result accords with the practice and realities of grave establishment in our society or with the purport of recognizing a grave-site right as a customary-law real right.\\n\\nAccordingly, the requirements for acquisitive prescription of ownership based on the meaning of the registration system concerning immovable-property real rights must be clearly distinguished from the requirements for acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right, which is a customary real right that recognizes only the right to use the land for owning a grave and can be acquired without registration; it is difficult to view the legal principle of the above en banc decision as affecting the effect of the customary law concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right.\\n\\n(4) Therefore, it cannot be said that there was a meaningful change in the overall legal order surrounding the above custom to such an extent that the customary law concerning a grave-site right or its acquisitive prescription lost legitimacy or reasonableness in contravention of the overall legal order and accordingly could no longer maintain its effect as a legal norm.\\n\\nc. Next, we examine whether there was a significant change in the perceptions, attitudes, or socio-cultural background of members of society, which formed the basis of the Supreme Court precedents recognizing the effect of the customary law, to the extent that society’s members no longer had legal conviction regarding the customary law concerning acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right.\\n\\n(1) Since customary law, unlike written law, is a social norm created by repeated social practice that comes to be approved and enforced as a legal norm by the legal conviction and recognition of members of society, in order to recognize that customary law has lost its legal effect because society’s members have lost legal conviction, empirical materials such as a custom survey are required as a basis. However, there is no material in the record from which it can be recognized that, around the time the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) came into force on January 13, 2001, the legal conviction of members of society concerning the custom of a grave-site right based on burial culture, etc. had disappeared or that such practice had fundamentally changed.\\n\\n(2) The nationwide average cremation rate in 1999, before the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158) came into force on January 13, 2001, was only 30.3%, and the nationwide average cremation rate in 2000 was only 33.7%; thus, before the Funeral Services Act came into force, the traditional burial rate overwhelmingly exceeded the cremation rate as the burial and funeral method in Korea. Furthermore, even if the cremation rate rapidly increased after the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act due to national policies, etc., it cannot be concluded that the burial culture that had continued from the past has disappeared entirely or that there has been a change in the preference for burial, given that the demand for graves established for post-cremation burial is not negligible. Rather, under our legal system, which permits private cemeteries, the burial culture that forms the basis of a grave-site right must still be regarded as remaining in our society.\\n\\nNor can changes in burial and funeral culture be seen as directly leading to the disappearance of legal conviction regarding the customary law of a grave-site right. Separately from the perceptions of the current generation regarding burial and funeral culture or methods, the customary law concerning a grave-site right based on ancestor worship must still be regarded as continuing. For example, the tradition and practice of returning to one’s hometown during holidays such as Seollal and Chuseok—the so-called “great migration of the nation”—and visiting and tending ancestral graves is accepted as something entirely natural by our people. In this way, apart from changes in burial and funeral culture, the traditional perception of graves based on ancestor worship remains deeply rooted, which accords with our reality, and it can be seen that respect for and preservation of graves continue to be important matters for members of our society.\\n\\n(3) The Funeral Services Act, amended by Act No. 13660 on December 29, 2015, and enforced on the same day, increased the grave establishment period for graves established after January 13, 2001, the date on which the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158), which entirely amended the Burial Act, came into force, from 15 years to 30 years (Article 19(1) and Addenda Article 2); the reason for amending the Funeral Services Act in this way was to reflect belatedly the fact that the public was not sufficiently aware of the limit on grave establishment periods and that exhumation due to expiration of the grave establishment period could cause public resentment and inconvenience. In other words, with respect to exhumation arising from the expiration of the grave establishment period for graves established after the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act, the period was increased from 15 years to 30 years because administrative arrangements and social conditions in preparation for this were insufficient.\\n\\nIn light of the circumstances surrounding such amendments to the Funeral Services Act, even after a considerable period has passed since the Act’s enforcement, it is difficult to say that there has been a clear change in members of society’s perception regarding graves or the legal relationships surrounding them. Furthermore, if, following a change in Supreme Court precedent, graves established before the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act were also to be exhumed or relocated, it is questionable whether the resulting social and economic costs and various conditions could be borne, and it is not clear whether members of society would have tolerated such results.\\n\\n(4) Therefore, it cannot be said that there was a significant change in members of society’s perceptions, attitudes, or socio-cultural background regarding the customary law concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right.\\n\\nd. (1) Even if judicial review as to whether customary law applicable to past factual relations is legally effective is possible, if its legal effect is denied, the effect of past legal relationships formed over decades in reliance on the existing customary law would be shaken at once, creating a great risk of harming legal stability; therefore, one must judge very carefully.\\n\\nIn particular, if the effect of the customary law concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right is denied, it could retroactively extinguish a grave-site right that had already been established by completion of acquisitive prescription upon the lapse of the prescription period, thereby undermining legal stability regarding the norm of acquisitive prescription and the protection of the parties’ reliance based on the principle of good faith and fairness.\\n\\n(2) Also, as of the end of 1999, cemetery area is said to account for about 1% of the entire national territory, the number of graves is about 20 million, and about 170,000 new graves occur each year. According to this, one can infer that there would be a considerable number of graves for which the 20-year prescription period had not yet elapsed by January 13, 2001, the effective date of the Funeral Services Act (Act No. 6158). In light of these circumstances, if the effect of the customary law concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right were denied, there could be very serious social confusion due to the relocation and exhumation of graves; accordingly, the existence or non-existence of the effect of the above customary law must be determined with caution. Yet, as examined above, no clear circumstance is apparent from which it can be said that the customary law concerning a grave-site right can no longer maintain its effect as a legal norm.\\n\\ne. According to our traditional way of thinking, a grave is not merely a structure but a spiritual place where the spirit of an ancestor dwells, and while grief, respect, and other memories of the deceased remain in the minds of the living, it must be respected as a place of reverence that contains and reveals those memories. Based on this perception, the customary law described above has formed because the members of society have accumulated and rooted in themselves the recognition that graves must be respected. During the formation of such customary law, there was not the slightest idea of measuring graves in economic value. However, as a modern system of forest ownership formed, legal disputes concerning graves arose when some began to prioritize the economic value of not only land such as forest land where a grave site exists, but even the grave on it, over its spiritual value. If one applies the standard of the modern absolute nature of ownership to graves just as to ordinary structures, it may be difficult to easily reject claims seeking exhumation; nevertheless, the majority opinion’s point is that, even so, so long as the above requirements are met, one must not easily accept such claims, and it is presumed that the collective consciousness of our society, which formed and maintained the customary law concerning a grave-site right, is the basis for that stance. Even from the fact that the State cannot easily change such consciousness, which has been deeply rooted in the daily lives of members of society over a long period, through legislation such as the enforcement of the Funeral Services Act, as can be seen from the fact that the Act has been strongly enforced but amended several times, one can readily understand this. If so, even in the case of acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right, considering together the fact that only the right to use the grave site, and not ownership of it, is being asserted, and the spiritual value inherent in graves, attempts to apply the theory of acquisitive prescription of land ownership as it stands are not easily acceptable. However, even if one accepts the dissenting opinion to the effect that the balance between the view that land ownership of increasingly valuable forest land must be respected to the utmost and, correspondingly, the grave on it is merely an obstacle whose value should be reduced and whose exhumation should therefore be allowed as easily as possible, and the view that a grave is a sacred place with spiritual value that must not be compared simply to an ordinary structure that can be erected and dismantled easily and that exhumation must not be allowed so long as the ancestors’ breath remains alive in people’s memories, the purport of the majority opinion is that the balance has not yet tipped to the former.\\n\\nThe foregoing states the supplementary opinion on the majority opinion.\\n\\n8. With respect to the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right, Justice Kim Jae-hyung’s supplementary opinion on the dissenting opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. A grave-site right has functioned to legally guarantee traditional ancestor worship, while in modern society it is one of the causes impeding the efficient use of land. It can be said that a grave-site right performed a transitional role bridging the gap between traditional ancestor worship and the modern landownership system. However, a grave-site right cannot be said to be a rational institution. From the standpoint of either equity or efficiency, it is difficult to find a basis for maintaining the precedents concerning a grave-site right as they stand.\\n\\nI believe that the dissenting opinion, which seeks to revise the precedents concerning a grave-site right that conflict with the constitutional guarantee of property rights and the Civil Act’s provisions protecting ownership, is justified, and, in the sense of supplementing that opinion, I would like to add a few views.\\n\\nb. Where another person’s land is used in order to own a cemetery, i.e., a grave, the legal relationship of use may take various forms. If the parties concluded a commodatum, lease, or other use agreement concerning the land in order to own a grave, a creditor-debtor relationship arises according to the content of the contract, and if the parties agreed to establish a real right such as superficies, such a real right may arise. Therefore, the customary grave-site right recognized in Supreme Court precedents should be understood as one type of such diverse rights to use a cemetery.\\n\\nA claim may be established freely by the parties’ agreement in accordance with the principle of freedom of contract, but a real right is subject to the principle of numerus clausus and the publicity principle. A customary grave-site right is a customary-law real right that comes into existence without registration in order to own a grave on another person’s land. Since Article 185 of the Civil Act recognizes the creation of real rights by customary law while adopting numerus clausus, there is no legal obstacle to recognizing a grave-site right as a customary-law real right. Also, the existence of a grave, especially a burial mound (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 91DA18040, rendered on October 25, 1991), performs the function of public notice for a real right. Therefore, the customary grave-site right is not contrary to numerus clausus or the publicity principle.\\n\\nHowever, whether a grave-site right is recognized as a customary-law real right and whether the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right is also customary law are issues that must be distinguished. Recognizing a customary grave-site right as a real right does not mean that the cause of its origin or the requirements for its formation must be viewed as they have been in past precedents.\\n\\nc. During the Japanese colonial period, as a modern system of forest ownership formed, the continued existence of graves established on another’s forest land became an issue.\\n\\nThe precedent on the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right originates in the Seoul High Court Decision of March 8, 1927. That decision stated that not only where consent of the landowner was obtained, but also where a person established a grave on another’s land without such consent, if the grave site was possessed peacefully and openly for 20 years, the person acquired, by prescription, a kind of real right similar to superficies over the land of another, and that it is customary that this right may be asserted against a third party without proof or registration. Our Supreme Court also held to the same effect that where a grave is established on land owned by another without the owner’s consent, if the grave site is possessed peacefully and openly for 20 years, a grave-site right, which is a customary-law real right similar to superficies, is acquired by prescription; and as precedents accumulated, the acquisitive prescription of a customary grave-site right came to be understood as customary law.\\n\\nCustomary law must be such that a practice generated spontaneously in society is not merely observed as a ceremonial or moral norm, but is supported by society’s legal conviction or legal recognition so as to be followed by many people. Therefore, for customary law to be established, there must be a practice, and the legal community must generally recognize and approve that practice as a legal norm. However, even if there had been in the past a custom in our society recognizing a grave-site right as a right similar to ownership, there is no material that can support the conclusion that there was a custom concerning the acquisitive prescription of a customary grave-site right.\\n\\nRather, it appears that, in order to reduce disputes arising between the traditional concept of graves and the new system of forest ownership, the courts went so far as to transform the Civil Act’s provisions on acquisitive prescription and recognize acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right. Our society has long inherited a Confucian-centered culture that values filial piety toward parents and ancestor worship, the custom of venerating ancestors in auspicious places, geomancy, and the burial culture of interring corpses or remains in the ground. Before the Japanese colonial period, a modern forest ownership system had not formed, and even after the introduction of a modern landownership system, awareness of forest ownership remained minimal. Thus, it can be viewed that the courts, respecting traditional grave customs, recognized that a grave-site right could be acquired by prescription in order to protect cases where a grave was established on land owned by another without consent.\\n\\nThe precedent on the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right did not confirm a customary law existing generally in society; rather, in reality, it reflected the modern system of acquisitive prescription in the customary grave-site right, which arises when consent of the landowner is obtained. This is also clear from the fact that the requirements of a “20-year prescription period” and “peaceful and open possession” were necessarily derived from the Civil Act’s requirements for acquisitive prescription. Therefore, acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right should be viewed as the application or analogous application of acquisitive prescription provisions concerning property rights to a customary grave-site right.\\n\\nHowever, the Seoul High Court Decision, while referring to the acquisitive prescription provisions of the Former Civil Act, which are similar in content to the current Civil Act, omitted the requirement of an “intention to hold a property right,” corresponding to the “intention to own” required for acquisitive prescription of ownership. At the time, the graves for which the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right was at issue had been established before a modern ownership system for forest land had formed. Therefore, when a person possesses forest land owned by another in order to own a grave, it would have been difficult to posit an intention to possess the grave site with the forest landowner’s consent; accordingly, there is room to understand that, while the court imported the Civil Act’s acquisitive prescription provisions to recognize the acquisitive prescription of a customary grave-site right, it did not decide whether there was an “intention to hold a property right,” specifically an “intention to possess as a grave-site right holder.”\\n\\nHowever, such an attitude is no longer valid after the enforcement of the current Civil Act and the establishment of a modern forest ownership system and immovable-property registration system. If a person who established a grave on another’s land does not have “the intention to possess the grave site believing that consent of the landowner was obtained,” acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right cannot be recognized. In particular, according to the Supreme Court precedent that the presumption of intention to own is rebutted in cases of bad-faith unauthorized possession, acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right should in principle be denied where a grave is established on another’s land without authorization. Because this is explained in detail in the dissenting opinion, I do not repeat it here.\\n\\nd. Customary law is not fixed and immutable and inevitably changes according to changes in general social custom and the consciousness of the community. Therefore, the content and effect of customary law are necessarily affected by the social reality and legal order at the time of its application. If customary law no longer accords with the overall legal order, including constitutional provisions, at the time it is to be applied due to changes in the fundamental ideas or social order governing society, the court must make customary law conform to the current legal order by methods such as excluding portions inconsistent with the overall legal order. Also, even if it has been recognized as customary law by a court judgment, if its basis is not clear, narrowing its scope of application is also a task entrusted to the court. Therefore, the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right and its requirements for formation must also, from the current perspective, be interpreted and applied so as to conform to the overall legal order, including constitutional provisions on the guarantee of property rights, Civil Act provisions concerning the content of ownership and the requirements for acquisitive prescription, and the provisions of the Funeral Services Act concerning graves.\\n\\nUnder Article 245(1) of the Civil Act, for acquisitive prescription of ownership in immovable property to be recognized, the possessor must not only possess peacefully and openly for 20 years but also have the intention to own. Since this provision is applied mutatis mutandis to property rights other than ownership under Article 248 of the Civil Act, in order for acquisitive prescription of property rights other than ownership to be recognized, there must be an intention to hold such property right. If there is no intention to hold a property right, acquisitive prescription of that property right cannot be recognized merely because immovable property was possessed peacefully and openly for 20 years.\\n\\nIn order for acquisitive prescription of superficies over another person’s land for the ownership of a building on it to be recognized, in addition to the fact of possession of that land, it must be objectively shown and continuously maintained that such possession is not based on a lease or commodatum relationship but constitutes possession as a superficiary (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 92DA50904, rendered on September 28, 1993). Likewise, in order for acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right to be recognized, the possession of the person who established the grave must amount to “possession as a grave-site right holder.”\\n\\ne. In conclusion, in order to recognize the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right where a grave is established on land owned by another, not only must the grave site be possessed peacefully and openly for 20 years, but, corresponding to the requirement that the possessor of immovable property have the intention to own in acquisitive prescription of immovable-property ownership, the grave installer must have the intention to possess as a grave-site right holder, believing that consent of the landowner was obtained. Therefore, where a grave is established on land owned by another without consent, that is, in a case amounting to bad-faith unauthorized possession, absent special circumstances, it is difficult to say that the person who established the grave had the intention to possess as a grave-site right holder after obtaining the landowner’s consent; accordingly, acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right should be denied.\\n\\nThis conclusion is intended, as the dissenting opinion sets out in detail, to rationally regulate the legal relationship surrounding cemetery use in accordance with current perspectives in light of the constitutional guarantee of property rights, the Civil Act provisions concerning ownership and acquisitive prescription, and the content and purport of the Funeral Services Act. Problems arising from this interpretation can be resolved through matters such as the allocation of the burden of proof concerning bad-faith unauthorized possession.\\n\\nThe foregoing states the supplementary opinion on the dissenting opinion."}

{"[2017DA228007]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case and Issues\\nA. Outline of the Case\\nOn 400㎡ above the forest land at issue, the grave of the Defendant’s grandfather, who died around July 1940, and the grave of the Defendant’s father, who died around April 1961, are installed (hereinafter referred to as “the Graves at Issue”), and the Defendant has protected and managed the Graves at Issue to date. The Plaintiffs, after acquiring some of the co-ownership shares in the forest land at issue through auction around 2014, brought this action against the Defendant seeking payment of ground rent for the period after the date on which the Plaintiffs acquired ownership, based on the Defendant’s possession of the grave site of the Graves at Issue. In response, the Defendant argued that because it had peacefully and openly possessed the grave site of the Graves at Issue for more than 20 years and had acquired the grave site right by prescription, it had no obligation to pay ground rent.\\n\\nThe court below held that even where a grave site right is acquired by prescription, the landowner has the right to claim ground rent from the time of such claim, and accordingly partially granted the Plaintiffs’ claims. The Defendant filed a final appeal.\\n\\nB. Issue in This Case\\nThe issue in this case is whether, where a grave site right has been acquired by prescription, the holder of the grave site right is obligated to pay ground rent to the landowner.\\n\\n2. Existence of an Obligation to Pay Ground Rent Where a Grave Site Right Is Acquired by Prescription\\nA. Supreme Court Precedents on Grave Site Rights\\nThe Supreme Court has recognized the grave site right, a real right under customary law that entitles a person to use land owned by another for the purpose of owning a grave installed on that land, as a right to use land owned by another corresponding to the grave site. A grave site right is recognized within the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of protecting the grave and performing ancestral rites, and it is established without registration if it has a form from which the existence of the grave can be recognized from the outside, such as a burial mound (see Supreme Court 1962. 4. 26. decided 4294MINSANG1451, Supreme Court 1996. 6. 14. decided 96DA14036, etc.).\\n\\nA grave site right can arise where a grave is installed on another person’s land with the owner’s consent (see Supreme Court 2000. 9. 26. decided 99DA14006, etc.), and it also arises where a person who installed a grave on his or her own land transfers that land without a special agreement that the grave will be relocated (see Supreme Court 1967. 10. 12. decided 67DA1920, etc.). Furthermore, even where a grave is installed on another person’s land without the owner’s consent, if the grave site is possessed peacefully and openly for 20 years, a grave site right is acquired by prescription (see Supreme Court 1955. 9. 29. decided 4288MINSANG210, Supreme Court 2011. 11. 10. decided 2011DA63017, 63024, etc.; hereinafter such type of grave site right is referred to as “prescription-acquired grave site right”).\\n\\nAccording to the Act on Funeral Services, etc., which was wholly amended and enforced by Law No. 6158 of 2000. 1. 12. as the Act on Burial and Graves, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Burial Act”), after 2001. 1. 13., the effective date of that Act, the person with ties to a grave installed without the consent of the landowner cannot assert a right to use the land or any other right for the preservation of the grave against the landowner, etc. (Article 23(3), Addenda Article 2. The said Act was wholly amended by Law No. 8489 on 2007. 5. 25., and Article 23(3) was merely relocated to Article 27(3) while its content remained unchanged. Hereinafter, regardless of whether before or after amendment, it is referred to as the “Funeral Services Act.”). Accordingly, after the effective date of the Funeral Services Act, it became impossible to assert prescription acquisition of a grave site right with respect to a grave installed without the landowner’s consent. However, the Supreme Court confirmed that with respect to graves installed before the effective date of the Funeral Services Act, prescription acquisition of a grave site right remains in force as a long-standing practice or custom that continues to have legal normative force (see Supreme Court en banc decision of 2017. 1. 19. decided 2013DA17292. Hereinafter the above decision is referred to as the “2017 Grand Bench decision.”).\\n\\nB. Whether Ground Rent Must Be Paid Where a Grave Site Right Is Acquired by Prescription\\nEven if, before the effective date of the Funeral Services Act, a grave was installed on another person’s land and a grave site right was acquired by prescription by peacefully and openly possessing the grave site for 20 years, the holder of the grave site right must be deemed to have an obligation to pay ground rent from the date on which the landowner demanded ground rent for the grave site. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) In determining the content of a right recognized as customary law, it must be reasonably determined by considering the legal nature of the right, the purpose of its recognition, the balancing of interests between the parties, and harmony with the overall legal order. A prescription-acquired grave site right is a quasi-superficies right that arises not by agreement of the parties, and it may result in a de facto perpetual limitation on ownership of the land. Accordingly, it is consistent with equity to view the person who has acquired a grave site right by prescription as bearing an obligation to pay consideration for the use of the land to the landowner within a certain scope.\\n\\na) In the case of statutory superficies that arise by statute or customary law without agreement between the parties, the superficies holder must pay consideration for use of the land. Where statutory superficies arises for the ownership of a structure on the land pursuant to Article 305(1) and Article 366 of the Civil Act and Article 10 of the Act on Security for the Establishment of Rights in Provisional Registration, etc., the superficies holder must pay ground rent to the landowner. The Supreme Court has held that even where the same person owned both the land and the building, but the owner became different due to sale or other cause and the building owner acquired a customary-law statutory superficies, Article 366 of the Civil Act applies mutatis mutandis, and the superficies holder is obligated to pay ground rent (see Supreme Court 1996. 2. 13. decided 95NU11023, etc.). Furthermore, the Supreme Court, presupposing that there is an obligation to pay ground rent even with respect to a grave site right acquired where a person who installed a grave on his or her own land transferred the land without a special agreement to relocate the grave, analogically applied the provisions of the Civil Act concerning a claim for extinguishment of superficies (see Supreme Court 2015. 7. 23. decided 2015DA206850), and even where a right of way easement was acquired by prescription without requiring ground rent, it held that the owner of the dominant land must compensate the damage suffered by the owner of the servient land due to the installation and use of the road (see Supreme Court 2015. 3. 20. decided 2012DA17479).\\n\\nA prescription-acquired grave site right is a limited real right that arises by customary law without agreement of the parties. Although it restricts the exercise of ownership of land for the benefit of the holder of the grave site right, the parties cannot determine in advance whether ground rent will be paid or the amount thereof. In light of the nature of such prescription-acquired grave site right, the issue of the obligation to pay ground rent by a person who has acquired a grave site right by prescription should be determined by considering the provisions of law on statutory superficies and the purport of precedents recognizing obligations to pay ground rent, etc. in various cases where limited real rights arise without the landowner’s consent.\\n\\nb) Even if a grave is installed on another person’s land, the nature of possession does not presume an intent to possess as owner (see Supreme Court 1991. 3. 12. decided 90DA17507, etc.), and the right acquired by the holder of a grave site right through completion of prescription is not ownership of the land but merely a limited real right permitting use of another’s land, similar only to superficies (see Supreme Court 1969. 1. 28. decided 68DA1927, 1928, etc.). Nevertheless, because a grave site right does not extinguish so long as the grave remains and the grave continues to be protected and ancestral rites continue, the landowner’s ownership over the grave site may in practice be restricted perpetually. In many cases, the landowner cannot efficiently use the remaining land except for the grave site portion because of the grave.\\n\\nThe purpose of recognizing a grave site right under customary law is only to allow use of another person’s land to the extent necessary for protecting the grave and performing ancestral rites; it is not to protect only the interests of either the grave owner or the landowner. Therefore, it is necessary to rationally adjust the interests between the landowner and the holder of the grave site right by allowing the landowner, who must otherwise endure the above disadvantages due to a grave site right that arose against his or her will, to receive consideration for the use of the land within a certain scope.\\n\\n2) Taking into comprehensive consideration the historical and social background in which prescription-acquired grave site rights have long been recognized as customary law, the parties’ reliance on and legal stability regarding the existing factual relations formed around graves, the special nature of a grave site right as a customary-law right, the principle of reason and good faith and the purport of the Civil Act provisions on claims for increase or decrease in ground rent that concretize such values concerning continuing use relations of real property, it is proper to view that a person who has acquired a grave site right by prescription must pay ground rent from the date on which the landowner claims ground rent for the grave site.\\n\\na) During the Joseon Dynasty, pursuant to the principle of common ownership of forests, private ownership was not recognized over forest land, where graves were mainly installed. Even during the process of forming the modern forest-land ownership system through the Japanese colonial period, the members of society had little or very low awareness of rights over forest land, and the economic value of forest land was also slight. Meanwhile, despite the traditional burial-centered funeral culture, because there were no cemeteries as in Western societies, most people who did not own land on which to install graves had no choice but to bury their ancestors’ bodies in another person’s forest land.\\n\\nIn the traditional extended-family system and agricultural society, it was often the case that graves were installed with the express or at least implied consent of the forest-land owner in accordance with neighborly goodwill, but it was very rare for written evidence such as contracts to be left behind. Even where the landowner had not expressly consented to the installation of a grave, there were many cases where the owner tolerated the free use of the forest land in consideration of the value of the forest land and the special nature of graves. However, as time passed and the owners of the land and graves changed, disputes such as demands for exhumation arose between parties who did not know the circumstances at the time the grave was installed, and in many cases it was impossible for the grave owner to prove that the landowner had originally consented. The customary law on prescription acquisition of grave site rights that the Supreme Court has consistently confirmed and applied for more than 60 years, spanning before and after the enforcement of the Civil Act, resolved these difficulties and allowed graves to remain by respecting the long-standing factual relations formed around graves (see the 2017 Grand Bench decision).\\n\\nb) In light of the historical and social background and purpose of the customary law on prescription acquisition of grave site rights, when recognizing the obligation of the holder of a grave site right to pay ground rent, it is also necessary to respect the long-standing existing factual relations formed around graves and harmoniously protect the landowner’s interests as well as the holder’s reliance and legal stability.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court, on the premise that where a person who installed a grave on his or her own land transferred the land and thereby acquired a grave site right there is an obligation to pay ground rent, held that if, after the Supreme Court judgment on ground rent became final, the holder of the grave site right delays payment of ground rent for a considerable period due to a reason attributable to him or her and the overdue ground rent amounts to two years or more, the landowner may analogically apply Article 287 of the Civil Act and claim extinguishment of the grave site right (see Supreme Court 2015. 7. 23. decided 2015DA206850). Unless there are special circumstances, the same legal principle should apply to ground rent for a prescription-acquired grave site right.\\n\\nHowever, if one were to require a person who has acquired a grave site right by prescription to pay all ground rent retroactively from the time the grave was installed long ago merely because it cannot be proved that the landowner consented to free use of the land at the time the grave was installed, then the holder of the grave site right would have to pay the ground rent for the period after that time all at once upon the landowner’s claim for determination of ground rent, and if the holder does not pay it within a considerable period, the grave site right itself would be extinguished by the landowner’s claim for extinguishment. Such a result cannot be said to accord with the purport of recognizing prescription acquisition of a grave site right by customary law in order to respect the facts that have long continued concerning graves under the aforementioned historical and social background and to promote legal stability, and with the purport of the 2017 Grand Bench decision confirming again that prescription acquisition of a grave site right continues to have legal normative force.\\n\\nc) Although a grave site right is a real right similar to superficies, it was recognized based on our people’s ancestral reverence and traditions and customs unique to our society, and its content does not coincide with superficies under the Civil Act in terms of its creation, extinction, or changes. A prescription-acquired grave site right also conforms to the reason for the prescription system, which is to maintain a social order that has continued for a certain period, to provide relief from the preservation of evidence that becomes difficult with the passage of time, and to exclude from legal protection those who do not exercise their rights for a long period; therefore, the provisions or legal principles concerning superficies under the Civil Act cannot be applied as they are to the scope of the obligation to pay ground rent by a person who has acquired a grave site right by prescription.\\n\\nConsidering the special nature of a grave site right, the Supreme Court did not apply the legal principles regarding real rights under the Civil Act to a grave site right as they were. While adverse possession by bad-faith unauthorized possession is not recognized for acquisition of ownership by prescription (see Supreme Court en banc decision of 1997. 8. 21. decided 95DA28625, etc.), and while for acquisition of superficies by prescription, in addition to the fact of possession, there must be objective manifestation that such possession is as superficies holder, such as the existence of the landowner’s permission (see Supreme Court 1996. 12. 23. decided 96DA7984, etc.), with respect to a prescription-acquired grave site right, the Court held that, unlike prescription acquisition of property rights under the Civil Act, a grave site right can be acquired by prescription even where a grave is installed without the landowner’s consent (see Supreme Court 1957. 10. 31. decided 4290MINSANG539, Supreme Court 2011. 11. 10. decided 2011DA63017, 63024, etc.). Also, whereas under the Civil Act a possessor must register in order to acquire the property right even after adverse possession by prescription is completed (Civil Act Articles 245(1) and 248), a grave site right may be acquired without registration and may be asserted against third parties (see Supreme Court 1957. 10. 31. decided 4290MINSANG539, etc.), and as to the duration of existence, the Court held that, unless there are special circumstances such as an agreement between the parties, the grave site right continues so long as the holder continues to protect and perform ancestral rites for the grave and the grave remains, rather than following the provisions on superficies in the Civil Act (see Supreme Court 1982. 1. 26. decided 81DA1220, etc.). The scope of a grave site right is limited to the extent necessary to protect and perform ancestral rites, and even within the scope to which the grave site right extends, installing a new grave is not permitted (see Supreme Court 2001. 8. 21. decided 2001DA28367, etc.).\\n\\nd) Where no written law or customary law exists as the standard for adjudication in a given case, the judge must decide according to the principles of reason (Civil Act Article 1). The principles of reason are generally understood or interpreted as the norms of communal social life thought on the basis of human reason or common sense, general principles of law, social validity, equity, justice, etc., emphasizing social meaning. Also, rights must be exercised faithfully and in good faith (Civil Act Article 2). The principle of good faith and fair dealing is the principle that parties to a legal relationship must not exercise rights or perform obligations in a manner contrary to equity or trust, while considering the other party’s interests. In applying it to a concrete legal relationship, all specific circumstances such as the content of the other party’s interests, the relation between the right or obligation to be exercised or performed and the other party’s interests, and the reasonableness of the other party’s reliance must be considered (see Supreme Court 1989. 5. 9. decided 87DAKA2407, etc.).\\n\\nCivil Act Article 286 provides that, where ground rent has become unreasonable due to an increase or decrease in taxes or other burdens relating to the land or due to fluctuations in land value, either party may request such increase or decrease. The same provisions exist with respect to superficies, leasehold rights for deposit lease, and leases (Civil Act Article 312-2, Article 628), etc. According to those statutory provisions, even if ground rent has become unreasonable due to fluctuations in land value, etc., the effect of increasing or decreasing ground rent does not arise immediately when circumstances change without a party’s claim, nor may a party retroactively claim ground rent from the time the circumstances changed. This may be said to be a provision that embodies the principles of reason and good faith in continuing use relations concerning things, while regulating so that, when a party requests the other party to increase or decrease ground rent, the effect of increased or decreased ground rent arises prospectively, thereby promoting the interests and legal stability of the parties who have relied on the existing legal relationship.\\n\\nConsidering the special nature of the grave site right described above, together with the principles of reason and good faith and the fundamental purport of the above statutory provisions, where a holder of a grave site right peacefully and openly possessed the grave site for a long period without paying consideration and acquired the grave site right by prescription without objection by the landowner, it must be deemed that the holder of the grave site right bears an obligation to pay ground rent from the time the landowner claims consideration for the use of the land.\\n\\nC. Change of Precedent\\nTo the extent inconsistent with the above, Supreme Court 1992. 6. 26. decided 92DA13936, which stated that where a grave site right is acquired by prescription the obligation to pay ground rent arises simultaneously with the establishment of the grave site right, and Supreme Court 1995. 2. 28. decided 94DA37912, which held to the effect that the holder of a grave site right need not pay ground rent, are changed within the scope inconsistent with the view of this judgment.\\n\\n3. Decision in This Case\\nBased on the factual circumstances in section 1.A above, the court below held that even if the Defendant acquired the grave site right by prescription, it had an obligation to pay ground rent for the grave site from the day after the date on which a copy of the complaint in this case was served, on the premise that at least from the time the landowner claimed ground rent, the Defendant had an obligation to pay ground rent for the grave site.\\n\\nThis determination of the court below is proper in accordance with the legal principles stated above, and there is no error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the law on prescription-acquired grave site rights as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all final appeals are dismissed, and the costs of final appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged as per the dispositive part. This judgment includes separate opinions by Justices Lee Ki-taek, Kim Jae-hyung, and Lee Heung-gu, a dissenting opinion by Justices Ahn Cheol-sang and Lee Dong-won, and supplementary opinions to the majority opinion by Justices Park Sang-ok, Min Yoo-suk, Noh Jeong-hee, and Noh Tae-ak; otherwise, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous.\\n\\n5. Separate Opinion by Justices Lee Ki-taek, Kim Jae-hyung, and Lee Heung-gu on the Time Ground Rent Arises\\nA. Summary of the Separate Opinion\\nThe majority opinion holds that where a grave site right is acquired by prescription, the holder of the grave site right has an obligation to pay ground rent to the landowner from the date on which the landowner claims ground rent for the grave site.\\n\\nWe agree with the majority opinion in that the holder of a grave site right must pay ground rent to the landowner where the grave site right has been acquired by prescription, but we disagree with the part that says the obligation to pay ground rent arises from the time the landowner claims ground rent. Where a grave site right is acquired by prescription, it should be deemed that the holder of the grave site right has an obligation to pay ground rent to the landowner during the period in which the grave has been installed and the land has been possessed, and it cannot be said that the obligation to pay ground rent arises only when the landowner makes a claim for ground rent. However, because in this case, in which only the Defendant appealed, this issue does not affect the result, this opinion is a separate opinion.\\n\\nWe first examine the reason ground rent must be paid where a grave site right is recognized, and then present the grounds for deeming that ground rent arises from the time the grave is installed.\\n\\nB. Even if a Grave Site Right Is Recognized, Is It Permissible To Use Another Person’s Land for a Grave Without Paying Any Consideration?\\nA grave site right, being a right to use another person’s land by installing a grave, that is, a cemetery, on it, should, unless there is a special circumstance such as an agreement between the parties to use it free of charge, be viewed as for consideration, which accords with the overall legal order.\\n\\nThe Constitution guarantees property rights to all citizens and provides that their content and limitations shall be determined by law (Article 23(1) of the Constitution). Ownership is the most typical property right, and the owner has the right to use, profit from, and dispose of the thing (Civil Act Article 211). As remedies for infringement of ownership, the owner may claim return of the thing against a person who possesses the thing without lawful title (Civil Act Article 213), and may claim removal of interference or prevention thereof against a person who interferes with or is likely to interfere with ownership by means other than possession (Civil Act Article 214). In addition to these real-right claims, the owner may claim restitution of unjust enrichment for the benefit obtained by the possessor through possession or use of the thing (Civil Act Article 741), and may claim damages based on tort against a person who infringed ownership and thereby caused damage to the owner (Civil Act Article 750). Thus, ownership is the right to directly and exclusively control a thing, and is an absolute right or right in rem that may be asserted against anyone.\\n\\nWhere another person’s land is used, it is usual for the possessor to agree to pay consideration for the use of the land, such as rent or ground rent. Although it is possible for the landowner to establish superficies free of charge or conclude a loan-for-use agreement, this is mostly the case where there is a special personal relationship between the landowner and the possessor, and otherwise it cannot be said that the free use of another person’s land is the ordinary form.\\n\\nIn light of the constitutional principle of protection of property rights, the content and effect of ownership under the Civil Act, and ordinary transactional notions, where a possessor uses another person’s land for his or her own benefit, it must be deemed a use relationship for consideration requiring payment for the use of the land, unless there are special circumstances such as an agreement between the parties that it is free of charge.\\n\\nThe Civil Act provisions (Civil Act Article 366 proviso, Article 219, etc.) and Supreme Court decisions (Supreme Court 2015. 3. 20. decided 2012DA17479) that require the user of land to pay consideration such as ground rent or compensation for damages in the case of statutory superficies, a right of passage over surrounding land, or a right of way easement acquired by prescription, all rest on this notion. The fact that the Act on Funeral Services, etc., wholly amended by Law No. 6158 on 2000. 1. 12. and enforced from 2001. 1. 13., strengthened the landowner’s authority in legal relationships concerning graves may also be understood in the same context (especially Articles 23(1) and 23(3)). With respect to graves installed after the enforcement of the amended Act (the transitional provision in Addenda Article 2), prescription acquisition of a grave site right is not recognized (see the 2017 Grand Bench decision).\\n\\nSupreme Court 1992. 6. 26. decided 92DA13936, from the same perspective, stated that “even if a grave site right has been acquired by prescription, the holder of the grave site right has an obligation to pay ground rent to the landowner unless there are special circumstances, and that obligation arises simultaneously with the establishment of the grave site right.” This may be seen as applying to prescription-acquired grave site rights the obvious logic that where another person’s land is used, consideration must be paid. By contrast, Supreme Court 1995. 2. 28. decided 94DA37912, rendered thereafter, held the opposite, stating that “since payment of ground rent is not an element of superficies, and in the absence of an agreement concerning ground rent payment it cannot be claimed, it is proper to interpret that a prescription-acquired grave site right also need not pay ground rent.” That decision applied the legal principles on ground rent for contractual superficies to prescription-acquired grave site rights as they were, but because a prescription-acquired grave site right arises without agreement of the parties, the legal principles concerning contractual superficies cannot be applied as they are.\\n\\nThe two Supreme Court decisions differed, as above, on whether there is an obligation to pay ground rent in the case of a prescription-acquired grave site right. In principle, the approach of the above-mentioned 1992 Supreme Court decision, which affirmed the obligation to pay ground rent, is reasonable and should be maintained, and the above-mentioned 1995 Supreme Court decision should be abandoned.\\n\\nC. From When Does Ground Rent Arise in a Prescription-Acquired Grave Site Right?\\n1) A grave site right is a right to use another person’s land by installing a grave, that is, a cemetery, on it, and it should in principle be regarded as for consideration from the time the grave is installed. The majority opinion uses the logic that, assuming a prescription-acquired grave site right was originally free of charge, the holder of the grave site right has no obligation to pay ground rent until the landowner claims ground rent, and that when the landowner claims ground rent, the obligation to pay ground rent arises prospectively. However, there is no basis for viewing it as free of charge from the time the grave is installed until the landowner claims ground rent.\\n\\n2) First, if we refer to the legal principles on superficies or statutory superficies to organize how the legal relationship concerning ground rent would be formed when recognizing the obligation of the holder of a grave site right to pay ground rent, the following results.\\n\\nThe specific amount of ground rent may be determined by agreement of the parties or by the court upon a party’s claim (Civil Act Article 366 proviso), and if the ground rent thus determined becomes unreasonable due to changes in economic conditions such as an increase in land value, the parties may claim an increase or decrease in ground rent (Civil Act Article 286). In principle, a 10-year extinctive prescription applies to claims for ground rent (Civil Act Article 162(1)), but if the parties agreed to set it as a periodic payment for a period within one year, a 3-year short-term extinctive prescription applies (Civil Act Article 163(1)), and if it was determined by a court judgment, a 10-year extinctive prescription applies (Civil Act Article 165(1)).\\n\\nIf the holder of a grave site right fails to pay ground rent for two years or more, the landowner may claim extinguishment of the grave site right (Civil Act Article 287). However, until the landowner claims determination of ground rent in court and the amount of ground rent is finalized by judgment, the holder of the grave site right cannot be regarded as having delayed payment of ground rent, so a claim for extinguishment of the grave site right cannot be made (see Supreme Court 1994. 12. 2. decided 93DA52297). Only after a considerable period has passed after the judgment determining the amount of ground rent becomes final, and only if the holder of the grave site right has delayed payment of ground rent for two years or more, may the landowner claim extinguishment of the grave site right. Whether a “considerable period” has passed must be determined by comprehensively considering the nature of the grave site right, the purpose of land use, the circumstances, location, and area of installation of the grave, the reasons for delinquency in ground rent, the amount in arrears, and the parties’ attitudes.\\n\\nThere will probably be no substantial disagreement between the majority opinion and this separate opinion up to this point regarding the obligation of the holder of the grave site right to pay ground rent. The difference lies in when the obligation to pay ground rent arises, namely, whether it arises from the time the grave is installed or from the time the landowner claims ground rent.\\n\\n3) The legal relationship concerning ground rent for the above grave site right is generally the result of analogically applying the Civil Act provisions on superficies or statutory superficies to the grave site right. Likewise, the time at which the obligation to pay ground rent arises for a prescription-acquired grave site right should also be resolved by analogically applying the Civil Act provisions.\\n\\nThe grave site right performed a transitional role bridging the gap between the traditional ancestor-worship ideology and the modern landownership system. The Supreme Court referred to its basis as customary law, but in substance it combined the modern prescription-acquisition system with the customary grave site right that arises where the landowner gives consent, rather than merely confirming a customary law existing in society at large. This is also clear in that the requirements of a “20-year prescription period” and “peaceful and open possession” can only be understood as derived from the prescription-acquisition requirements under the Civil Act. Accordingly, the prescription acquisition of a grave site right should be understood as applying or analogically applying the prescription-acquisition provisions concerning property rights to customary grave site rights. Thus, a prescription-acquired grave site right has the character of a fictive customary-law right rather than customary law in the original sense.\\n\\nEven if a grave site right that arises through completion of prescription is a real right under customary law, it cannot be said that its specific content is also fixed by customary law as to whether there is an obligation to pay ground rent, when such obligation arises, whether a court determination of ground rent is required, or claims for increase or decrease in ground rent and extinguishment of the grave site right due to nonpayment of ground rent. In particular, among Supreme Court decisions, there coexisted, as noted in section 2.B above, the 1992 decision that a ground-rent payment obligation exists from the time of creation in the case of a prescription-acquired grave site right, and the 1995 decision that there is no ground-rent payment obligation, and neither of those can be called customary law.\\n\\nWhere there is a gap in the statutory provisions, the court may supplement the gap in the law by analogically applying legal norms concerning similar matters. For such analogy, there must be a commonality or similarity between a matter without legal regulation and a matter with legal regulation, and analogical application must be evaluated as justified in light of the system of legal norms, legislative intent and purpose, etc. (see Supreme Court 2020. 4. 29. decided 2019DA226135). Even if a right is recognized as customary law, where there is no custom concerning its specific content or such custom cannot be approved as customary law, the content of the right may likewise be supplemented by analogically applying legal norms concerning similar matters.\\n\\nThe most important legal norm for supplementing the specific content of a right under customary law is the law. Civil Act Article 1 establishes the order of sources of law in civil matters as law, customary law, and then the principles of reason, and this can also apply to situations where the content of a right under customary law must be supplemented. Moreover, laws enacted to rationally regulate legal relations have acquired legal approval from society members and may be regarded as norms possessing the “legal conviction or legal recognition of society members” required for customary law. Accordingly, to supplement portions of the content of a right under customary law that are not fixed by customary law, the court should first identify statutory provisions applicable to similar matters and seek a resolution through analogical application thereof.\\n\\nThe principles of reason are not a fixed content such as the essential law of things, the principle of things, or norms thought by human reason, but are extremely abstract terms used only when they seem most appropriate in light of the legal order as a whole or the spirit flowing within it, and they can appear as the standard for adjudication only when neither law nor customary law can serve as such standard. Law is a legal norm approved by the legislature that concretizes the principles of reason in article form in order to rationally regulate social relations. Because law precedes the principles of reason as the standard for adjudication, if there is a gap in customary law, the court may resolve it by analogically applying law, and should not decide otherwise by resorting to abstract principles of reason or the principle of good faith.\\n\\nThe former Supreme Court en banc decision of 2008. 11. 20. decided 2007DA27670 concerning the method of selecting the person who presides over ancestral rites, or the former Supreme Court en banc decision of 2005. 7. 21. decided 2002DA1178 concerning the qualifications of clan members, supplemented matters for which there was no customary law based on the principles of reason. However, because there were no statutory provisions concerning issues similar to the issues in those decisions, they could not be resolved by analogical application of law and had no choice but to be decided according to the principles of reason. In this case, because there are statutory provisions concerning similar matters, the situation differs from those Supreme Court decisions.\\n\\nIf there is no content fixed by customary law concerning ground rent for a prescription-acquired grave site right, legal norms concerning similar matters must be analogically applied. A grave site right is a real right similar to superficies that permits use of another person’s land and arises by customary law without agreement of the parties. The most similar form of such land-use relation is statutory superficies. Where statutory superficies arises pursuant to Civil Act Article 366, etc., the superficies holder must pay ground rent to the landowner “from the time the superficies arises.” Likewise, with respect to a land-use relation that arises through prescription acquisition of a grave site right, ground rent must be paid from the time the grave site right arises, just as in the case of statutory superficies (the Supreme Court 2012DA17479 decision discussed in section 2.B above may also be understood in this sense, in that it held that where a right of way easement is acquired by prescription, the owner of the dominant land must compensate the damage suffered by the owner of the servient land, just as in the case of a right of passage over surrounding land). However, once the prescription acquisition period for a grave site right is completed, its effect retroacts to the time the grave was installed and possession commenced (Civil Act Articles 247(1) and 248), and therefore the grave site right is deemed to have arisen from that time; ultimately, the holder of the grave site right must be deemed to have an obligation to pay ground rent from the time the grave was installed.\\n\\nThe majority opinion determines the time when the obligation to pay ground rent arises differently from statutory superficies, based on the principles of reason and the principle of good faith. In particular, the majority opinion analogically applies the Civil Act provisions on superficies or statutory superficies in all respects concerning whether an obligation to pay ground rent exists, the determination of ground rent, claims for increase or decrease in ground rent, and claims for extinguishment of superficies, yet as to the time when the obligation to pay ground rent arises, it alone determines the matter on the basis of the principles of reason and good faith in a manner entirely unsupported by the Civil Act.
