Applying the Civil Act provisions in some cases and the principles of reason and good faith in other cases with respect to the legal relationship concerning ground rent is excessively artificial. Even if this issue were to be decided according to the principles of reason, it is difficult to conclude that, among various possible times—such as the time the grave is installed, the time the prescription period is completed, the time the landowner later claims ground rent, or the time a lawsuit concerning ground rent is filed or a judgment fixing ground rent becomes final—one of them necessarily accords with the principles of reason. Even though a right called a grave site right has arisen, saying that no obligation to pay ground rent based on that right has arisen until the other party demands performance, and that there is a duty to pay consideration only upon the other party’s claim, lacks any basis in law and cannot even be called a “principle of reason.” Even in determining the time ground rent arises under a grave site right, the proper attitude is to respect to the maximum extent the purport of the legal norms governing land-use relations and to reach a conclusion that maintains the unity of legal norms.\\n\\n4) Where a grave is installed without authorization on another person’s land, an obligation to return unjust enrichment due to land use or liability for damages arising from tort arises, and prescription acquisition of a grave site right occurs while bearing such obligations. In this respect also, ground rent must be deemed to arise from the time the grave is installed.\\n\\nWhere it is proved that there was an agreement or consent between the landowner and the person who installed the grave regarding the use relationship of the grave site, the existence and amount of consideration for use are also determined according to the agreement, etc., and prescription acquisition of the grave site right is not in issue. Cases where a grave site right is acquired by prescription may be divided into two types: cases where a grave was installed without the landowner’s consent and cases where the existence of an agreement or consent cannot be determined because of the passage of time, etc.\\n\\nFirst, where a grave is installed without the landowner’s consent, it is clear that possession during the prescription period constitutes unauthorized possession. The grave owner must exhume the grave if the landowner so demands, and even if not, bears an obligation to return the benefit of use as unjust enrichment during the period in which the grave was installed and the grave site was possessed. There can be no disagreement that, before the prescription period for acquisition of the grave site right is completed, the grave owner is liable to return unjust enrichment. In this sense, it cannot be said that the use relationship is free of charge, since the grave owner bears an obligation to return consideration for land use to the landowner. Even if the grave owner is not actually paying consideration for land use to the landowner, this is nothing more than the grave owner’s failure to perform the obligation to return unjust enrichment. Whether the landowner has actually demanded restitution of unjust enrichment from the grave owner has no effect whatsoever on the establishment of the obligation to return unjust enrichment.\\n\\nOnce the 20-year prescription period passes and prescription acquisition of the grave site right is completed, the grave owner acquires the grave site right and, as a result, the landowner can no longer demand exhumation of the grave. However, such prescription acquisition should, as before, be viewed as occurring while the grave owner bears an obligation to return the benefit from land use. Because the effect of completion of prescription retroacts to the time when the grave was installed and possession commenced (Civil Act Articles 247(1) and 248), the person who acquires by prescription is deemed not to have been an unauthorized possessor from the outset but to have had a grave site right from the beginning, and as a result, the obligation to return unjust enrichment that arose during the prescription period merely changes into an obligation to pay ground rent.\\n\\nThe purpose of recognizing prescription acquisition of a grave site right under customary law is to enable graves to remain for the protection of the graves and the performance of ancestral rites. There is no basis for viewing this as going further to relieve unauthorized possessors from obligations to return unjust enrichment that already arose during the prescription period, or to convert a relationship that previously required payment for use into a free-of-charge use relationship. Even if a grave site right is acquired by prescription after a grave is installed without authorization and the prescription period has passed, the holder of the grave site right must be deemed to have an obligation to pay ground rent from the time the grave was installed.\\n\\nNext, even where it is unclear whether there was agreement or consent by the landowner, the conclusion cannot be different. When a landowner exercises against a possessor a real-right claim based on ownership, a claim for return of unjust enrichment, or a claim for damages arising from tort, the burden of proving lawful title to possess and use, that is, facts such as the existence of agreement or consent with the landowner, rests on the possessor. Therefore, if such proof cannot be made, the possessor must comply with the landowner’s claim as an unauthorized possessor.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that, in the past, when graves were installed on forest land, landowners often consented to free use or tolerated it even while knowing of it, and the purpose of recognizing prescription acquisition of a grave site right was to remedy the difficulty of proof in such cases, so viewing the holder of the grave site right as bearing an obligation to pay ground rent does not accord with that purpose. However, simply because a grave is installed and possessed for burial and ownership purposes, there is no basis for presuming that the possession is lawful based on the landowner’s consent or for shifting the burden of proving title to possess and use to the landowner. Whether the landowner consented is a matter of fact-finding or interpretation of intent, to be determined by considering various circumstances such as the location and circumstances of the grave’s installation, the relationship between the person who installed the grave and the landowner at the time, and the use relationship of the grave site over time. Recognizing agreement or consent with the landowner and following that is a separate matter (in which case prescription acquisition is not in issue); however, if the grave owner fails to prove the existence of agreement or consent with the landowner, then, as in the case of unauthorized possession, the grave owner bears the obligation to return unjust enrichment during the prescription period, and further, even after prescription acquisition of the grave site right, must be deemed to bear the obligation to pay ground rent from the time the grave was installed.\\n\\n5) The holder of a grave site right’s obligation to pay ground rent cannot be viewed as depending on whether the landowner claims ground rent. It is highly unfamiliar and unnatural in our legal order to recognize a ground-rent claim of the landowner against the holder of the grave site right while saying that the obligation to pay ground rent arises not at the time the claim arises, but only from the time the landowner’s claim.\\n\\nOriginally, a demand for performance presupposes the existence of a right and an obligation. Only where a certain right and the corresponding obligation have arisen can performance be demanded; it cannot be logically explained to demand performance where no right and obligation have arisen. A right to demand performance, one of the remedies for a claim, arises from the claim’s demandability and presupposes that the claim and the corresponding obligation have been established. The provisions on a demand for performance in the Civil Act also presuppose the establishment of the claim and the obligation. That is, Civil Act Article 387(2) provides that “if there is no time fixed for performance of the obligation, the obligor shall be liable for delay from the time when performance is demanded,” meaning that a demand for performance may be made on the premise that an obligation exists. The demand for performance against a joint and several obligor under Civil Act Articles 414 and 416 also presupposes the existence of joint and several obligations. The right to claim increase or decrease in ground rent (Civil Act Article 286), the right to claim increase or decrease in lease deposit (Civil Act Article 312-2), and the right to claim increase or decrease in rent (Civil Act Article 628) are merely rights to claim the “increase or decrease” of ground rent, etc. when the ground rent, etc. originally fixed becomes unreasonable due to changes in economic conditions; they are not rights that can “create” an obligation to pay ground rent, etc.\\n\\nThe landowner’s claim for ground rent against the holder of the grave site right arises from ownership of the land, but in the absence of a ground-rent claim, the landowner cannot demand performance of ground rent. Since a demand for performance of ground rent can be made only on the premise that a ground-rent claim exists, the time ground rent arises is unrelated to the demand for performance.\\n\\nThe majority opinion’s conclusion—that an obligation to return unjust enrichment and liability for damages due to tort arise while the land is being used without authorization for the installation or maintenance of a grave, that such obligations disappear upon prescription acquisition of a grave site right, and that ground rent arises upon the landowner’s demand for performance—is too awkward to accept.\\n\\n6) Even if it is deemed that there is an obligation to pay ground rent from the time the grave is installed, it cannot be said that there is a substantial risk of threatening the existence of the grave or undermining legal stability.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that if, in response to the landowner’s claim for ground rent, payment of past ground rent is required and nonpayment may result in extinguishment of the grave site right itself, legal stability would be harmed and this would not accord with the purpose of recognizing prescription acquisition of a grave site right.\\n\\nHowever, ground-rent claims are subject to extinctive prescription, and therefore, regardless of when the grave was installed, the ground rent to be paid by the grave owner is limited to a maximum of 10 years. Most grave sites are forest land, and the grave site right is limited to the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of protecting the grave and performing ancestral rites, so even taking the 10-year limitation into account, the total amount of ground rent does not appear to be large. As seen in section 3.2) above, until the landowner requests a court determination of ground rent and the amount is finalized by judgment, the holder of the grave site right cannot be regarded as having delayed payment of ground rent, and only if, after the judgment becomes final, the holder delays payment of ground rent for two years or more, may the landowner claim extinguishment of the grave site right. Therefore, even where the holder lacks the economic ability to pay ground rent, there is time to prepare for relocation of the grave, etc., from the time the claim is made by the landowner until the judgment becomes final and a considerable period passes, and the risk of being forced to move the grave on short notice is not substantial.\\n\\nThus, recognizing an obligation to pay ground rent even for the period before the landowner claims it cannot be said to be unfairly disadvantageous to the holder of the grave site right, and it does not appear likely to cause a mass extinguishment of grave site rights as feared by the majority opinion.\\n\\nD. View of This Case\\nIn this case, one of the Graves at Issue was installed in 1940 and the other around 1961 on the forest land at issue, and the prescription periods for acquisition of the grave site rights were completed around 1960 and 1981, respectively, and the Plaintiffs acquired co-ownership shares in the above forest land around 2014.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, the Defendant has an obligation to pay ground rent after the date on which the Plaintiffs acquired ownership, as claimed by the Plaintiffs. Nevertheless, the court below erred in holding that the Defendant has an obligation to pay ground rent only from the time the Plaintiffs demanded ground rent and in partially granting the Plaintiffs’ claims. However, in this case, in which only the Defendant filed a final appeal, the principle of prohibition of unfavorable alteration prevents the court below’s judgment from being altered to the Defendant’s disadvantage; therefore, the appeal is merely not accepted.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, this separate opinion reaches the same conclusion as the majority opinion in dismissing the final appeal, but because the reason differs from that of the majority opinion regarding the time when ground rent arises, this separate opinion is stated.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion by Justices Ahn Cheol-sang and Lee Dong-won\\nA. The majority opinion states that where a grave site right, a real right under customary law, is acquired by prescription, the holder of the grave site right has an obligation to pay ground rent to the landowner from the date on which the landowner claims ground rent for the grave site.\\n\\nHowever, if a grave was installed before the effective date of the Funeral Services Act, 2001. 1. 13., and the grave site was peacefully and openly possessed for 20 years and a grave site right was acquired by prescription, the holder of the grave site right should, unless there are special circumstances, be deemed not to have an obligation to pay ground rent to the landowner. The prior Supreme Court 1995. 2. 28. decided 94DA37912, which in principle denied the obligation of the holder of the grave site right to pay ground rent where a prescription-acquired grave site right is involved (hereinafter, “grave site right” refers to a prescription-acquired grave site right), is reasonable and should be maintained, and we cannot agree with the majority opinion seeking to change it. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) Because a grave site right is a real right under customary law, the content of customary law should be declared through investigation or confirmation of custom, and it is not proper for the court to determine that content through interpretation.\\na) The majority opinion, after presupposing that the court may determine whether a grave site right is for consideration or free of charge, states that it should be deemed for consideration in order to adjust the interests of the parties.\\n\\nCustomary law means that a social norm formed by repeated practices in society is approved and enforced as a legal norm by the society’s legal conviction and recognition and thus has the same effect as law. Since a grave site right is a real right recognized as such customary law, the content of the right must also be determined in accordance with customary law. Therefore, the court must investigate and confirm whether there exists custom or practice regarding ground rent in relation to grave site rights and the legal conviction of society members about it, and declare what the content of the customary law is. Determining the content of a grave site right through legal interpretation without proper investigation or confirmation of customary law, as in the majority opinion, is contrary to the nature and essence of customary-law rights discussed above, and amounts to the court arbitrarily determining the content of rights that should be set by custom without making efforts to confirm the content of custom.\\n\\nb) The fact that no custom with a content of for-consideration has ever been confirmed with respect to grave site rights so far is proof that grave site rights were free of charge under custom. It is correct to view the lack of indicia of for-consideration as because they were free of charge under custom, and not, conversely, to view the lack of indicia of free-of-charge use as because they were for consideration under custom; this is not the way lawyers reason. Moreover, as seen in section 2) below, in light of the purpose and background of recognizing prescription acquisition of grave site rights, it is natural and consistent with common sense to view grave site rights as having been free of charge under custom.\\n\\nThe above Supreme Court decision 94DA37912 held that there is no obligation to pay ground rent where a grave site right is acquired by prescription, and the decision has long been widely known since it was rendered, frequently cited in lower-court decisions, and has served as a Supreme Court precedent. On the other hand, the Supreme Court 1992. 6. 26. decided 92DA13936 decision affirming the obligation of the holder of a grave site right to pay ground rent has not played the role of precedent, and thus cannot be regarded as the Supreme Court’s prior interpretation. In the 2017 Grand Bench decision, whether prescription acquisition of a grave site right with respect to graves installed before the effective date of the Funeral Services Act remains effective after that date was fully discussed, and the Supreme Court clearly held that it remains a valid customary law. The majority opinion of the Grand Bench decision did not expressly state a position on whether the holder of a grave site right has an obligation to pay ground rent, but it should be viewed as presupposing the content of customary law in accordance with the above Supreme Court 94DA37912 decision and then recognizing the legal normativity of that customary law. This is so in light of the fact that the majority opinion expressly referred to the existing precedent on the duration of existence, which is one part of the content of the grave site right, to the effect that, unless there are special circumstances such as an agreement between the parties, the right continues so long as the holder continues to protect and perform ancestral rites and the grave remains, and in light of the fact that the dissenting opinion in the above Grand Bench decision stated that “the former custom that recognized prescription acquisition of a de facto perpetual and free-of-charge grave site right merely on the basis of 20 years’ peaceful and open possession without the landowner’s consent lost its force as a legal norm around the time the Funeral Services Act took effect,” thereby acknowledging that grave site rights were free of charge under custom without offering a contrary opinion.\\n\\nNevertheless, the majority opinion now seeks to change precedent by determining differently the content of a right under customary law that has thus far been accepted, on the ground that there is now a need to adjust the interests of the landowner and the holder of the grave site right, and this is inconsistent and contradicts what the 2017 Grand Bench decision premised.\\n\\nc) Even if it is regarded that the 2017 Grand Bench decision did not clearly state whether the content of a grave site right is for consideration or free of charge under customary law, there must be a need and justification for changing the precedent that has been maintained to date. However, no materials can be found supporting the existence of a custom that the grave site right is for consideration, and as seen in section 2) below, it is reasonable in legal interpretation and in light of common sense to view that there is no obligation to pay ground rent by the holder of a grave site right. Therefore, the majority opinion seeking to change the prior Supreme Court precedent is not proper.\\n\\n2) Even in light of the general legal principles concerning superficies, the differences between a grave site right and statutory superficies, and the purpose for which prescription acquisition of grave site rights has been recognized as customary law, it cannot be said that the holder of a grave site right has an obligation to pay ground rent.\\na) In principle, superficies do not permit a claim for payment of ground rent unless there is an agreement concerning ground rent. Even where there is a for-consideration agreement concerning ground rent, it can be asserted against third parties only if registered, and where it is not registered, it is a free-of-charge superficies and no right to claim increase in ground rent arises (see Supreme Court 1999. 9. 3. decided 99DA24874, etc.). This is because superficies are based on land use and do not require ground rent as an element. This is clearly distinguished from a lease, which requires rent as an element of formation (Civil Act Article 618). Accordingly, a for-consideration character cannot be directly derived from the fact that superficies is a right for using another person’s land.\\n\\nLikewise, with respect to a grave site right, a customary-law right similar to superficies, ground rent cannot be regarded as an essential requirement of the right. A grave site right arises and continues without registration, and there is also no means of public notice concerning ground rent. Nevertheless, there is insufficient legal basis for viewing that, after the prescription period for a grave site right is completed, an obligation to pay consideration for land use suddenly arises when the landowner so demands.\\n\\nb) Even according to the majority opinion, because the majority opinion says that the land is for consideration only from the date on which the landowner demands ground rent, it appears that the majority opinion itself presupposes that a grave site right without a demand for ground rent is free of charge.\\n\\nExcept in extraordinary cases such as when an abstract public-law claim for performance is converted into a concrete claim to receive performance, or the condition of a conditional right is fulfilled, the time of a fixed-term right arrives, or a formative right is exercised, it is difficult to find a legal principle supporting a change in the content of a right, such as when a free-of-charge legal relationship becomes a for-consideration legal relationship through the rights holder’s claim. Where no time for performance of an obligation is fixed, the obligor is liable for delay upon receiving a demand for performance (Civil Act Article 387(2)), but that concerns only liability for delay and not a change in the content of the right itself.\\n\\nUltimately, according to the majority opinion, a free-of-charge legal relationship concerning ground rent in a grave site right would be transformed into a for-consideration legal relationship by the unilateral declaration of intent of the landowner, which is understood as granting the landowner a kind of formative right. However, formative rights cannot be recognized without express statutory provisions, and our law has no such provision and no such custom has been confirmed to exist. The majority opinion refers to the principles of reason, the principle of good faith, or the right to claim increase or decrease in ground rent under Civil Act Article 286, but a formative right cannot be created on the basis of abstract principles of reason or good faith. The right to claim increase or decrease in ground rent under Civil Act Article 286 is, at the outset, a provision concerning for-consideration superficies with an obligation to pay ground rent, and where superficies is free of charge that provision does not apply (see Supreme Court 1999. 9. 3. decided 99DA24874); therefore, it is also not proper to analogically apply Civil Act Article 286 to a grave site right that is originally free of charge. The majority opinion is no different from the court creating a new formative right without any particular basis.\\n\\nAs the majority opinion acknowledged at the outset of its discussion, a grave site right is free of charge, and there is no basis for converting it into a for-consideration right. It is desirable to rationally adjust the interests between the parties to a legal relationship, but in doing so one should refrain from creating new legal principles. The content of a grave site right, originally free of charge, remains free of charge.\\n\\nc) Unlike superficies by agreement of the parties, the majority opinion points out that an obligation of the statutory superficies holder to pay ground rent to the landowner is recognized with respect to statutory superficies. However, there are express provisions on this in Civil Act Article 305(1), Article 366, etc. Precedents have also recognized an obligation to pay ground rent with respect to customary-law statutory superficies, because the right was regarded as similar to statutory superficies under the Civil Act and the provisions on statutory superficies were applied mutatis mutandis (see Supreme Court 1993. 6. 29. decided 93DA10781, etc.).\\n\\nA grave site right is a real right similar to superficies, but it differs in many respects from statutory superficies, including the content of the right, the method of public notice, and duration of existence. Because the holder of a grave site right may use another person’s land only within a reasonable scope necessary to achieve the purpose of protecting the grave and performing ancestral rites, the content and scope of the right are necessarily more limited than superficies under the Civil Act. Also, it is recognized only where the grave has a form from which its existence can be recognized from the outside, such as a burial mound; it is not recognized where there is no objectively recognizable outward appearance, such as a flat grave or secret burial, and because of such characteristics, a grave site right arises without registration (see Supreme Court 1996. 6. 14. decided 96DA14036, etc.). Furthermore, if there is an agreement between the parties, the duration of a grave site right follows that agreement; if there is no such agreement, it continues so long as the holder continues to protect and perform ancestral rites and the grave remains (see Supreme Court 1982. 1. 26. decided 81DA1220, etc.), and it does not follow the provisions on superficies under the Civil Act.\\n\\nAs such, because a grave site right, a real right under customary law, differs clearly from statutory superficies, there is no basis for applying the legal principles concerning statutory superficies to a grave site right as they stand.\\n\\nd) If there is an agreement on land use between the landowner and the person who installed the grave at the time of installation, that agreement prevails and prescription acquisition of a grave site right is not in issue. If, during the prescription period, the holder of the grave site right has paid ground rent to the landowner, even if the prescription period for the grave site right is completed, the holder of the grave site right should be understood as having acquired by prescription a for-consideration grave site right in that same state of payment. However, in most cases of prescription acquisition of a grave site right, during the prescription period the parties do not exchange ground rent, make claims, or enter into an agreement concerning ground rent.\\n\\nAs stated in the 2017 Grand Bench decision and the majority opinion, in Korea graves were often installed and their sites used free of charge under the landowner’s express consent or implied tolerance in the historical context of the former principle of common ownership of forests, the burial-centered funeral culture, the special nature of graves as objects of ancestral reverence, the normative awareness of ancestors regarding them, and the traditional value system that prized neighborly goodwill. However, as time passes and the owners of the land or graves change, disputes over grave sites arise, and it becomes virtually impossible to prove that the landowner consented.\\n\\nThe prescription system exists to maintain a social order that has continued for a certain period, to provide relief from the preservation of evidence that becomes difficult with the passage of time, and to exclude from legal protection those who fail to exercise their rights for a long period; in particular, legal stability is the most important basis supporting the prescription system. The reason prescription acquisition of a grave site right has been recognized as customary law is also to promote legal stability by protecting, as legal rights, the social order concerning graves formed on the basis of long-standing facts extending over 20 years or more (see the 2017 Grand Bench decision).\\n\\nConsidering the background and purpose behind the recognition of prescription acquisition of a grave site right as customary law, if possession of the grave site has continued peacefully and openly for more than 20 years without exchange or claim of ground rent, it is natural to view that the landowner implicitly tolerated the holder’s free use of the land, or at least that the holder has possessed the grave site on that understanding. Accordingly, the holder of the grave site right should be understood as acquiring a grave site right of the same content as the long-standing factual situation during the prescription period, namely a grave site right without an obligation to pay ground rent.\\n\\nThe majority opinion’s logic that something that was free of charge during the prescription period becomes for consideration after acquisition by completion of prescription is an interpretation that does not accord with the purpose of the prescription system, which is to protect a social order that has continued for a long time as a legal right. The Supreme Court 2015. 3. 20. decided 2012DA17479 decision mentioned by the majority opinion held that where a right of way easement is acquired by prescription, the owner of the dominant land must compensate the damage suffered by the owner of the servient land due to the installation and use of the road, but that decision mainly considered that a right of way easement is similar to a right of passage over surrounding land and that Civil Act Article 219(2) provides for the obligation of the owner of the land over which passage is exercised to compensate damage. A grave site right is a right under customary law and is entirely different in the nature of the right and the basis of its formation from a right of way easement or a right of passage over surrounding land under the Civil Act; and in the case of a right of way easement, the servient land is usually land located between a public road and a building site, whereas the land on which graves were installed was forest land with low utility value, and landowners often tolerated free use of the grave site. In light of these factors, the theory of that decision cannot be applied to a grave site right.\\n\\n3) Even if the obligation to pay ground rent is denied with respect to a grave site right, this does not infringe the landowner’s constitutionally guaranteed property rights or run counter to the overall legal order.\\na) Recently, the Constitutional Court, in its en banc decision of 2020. 10. 29. in Case 2017HEONBA208, clearly stated that prescription acquisition of a grave site right under customary law does not infringe the landowner’s property rights and held that such customary law does not violate the Constitution. The Constitutional Court considered that even if a grave site right is acquired by prescription, the grave site right is recognized only within the scope necessary for the protection and management of the grave, and if the protection and performance of ancestral rites cease, the grave site right is extinguished, so the limitation on the landowner’s property rights is limited in scope; and that recognizing ground rent or duration for a grave site right would allow a claim for extinguishment of the grave site right on the ground of delinquency in ground rent or a demand for relocation of the grave on the ground of the expiration of the period, thereby inevitably lowering the level of protection of the grave site right, complicating legal relations surrounding the grave site right, and causing serious infringement on the economic and emotional interests of the holder as well as results contrary to the good customs of our society, which has esteemed graves.\\n\\nAs the Constitutional Court properly held, denying ground rent with respect to a grave site right cannot be said to infringe the landowner’s property rights. The Constitution guarantees property rights, including ownership, but provides that their content and limits shall be determined by law and that the exercise of property rights shall conform to public welfare (Article 23(1) and (2) of the Constitution), so the protection of land ownership cannot be absolute. Since customary law also has the same force as law, the fact that land ownership is limited to some extent according to customary law concerning grave site rights can sufficiently be allowed even under the constitutional principle of protection of property rights.\\n\\nb) Even if a customary law has long been recognized as a legal norm, its force as a legal norm is denied if members of society no longer have confidence in the legal binding force of that custom or practice, or if, due to changes in the basic ideology or social order governing society, the customary law no longer conforms to the overall legal order at the time it should be applied (see Supreme Court 2005. 7. 21. decided 2002DA1178 en banc decision, etc.). However, if the Supreme Court were to deny the force of a customary law that has long been supported by the legal conviction of society members and recognized as valid, on the ground that changes in the basic ideology or social order make it inconsistent with the overall legal order, there is a risk of upsetting all legal relations from the past formed over decades in reliance on the existing customary law at once, thereby harming legal stability. Therefore, to deny the force of a customary law as a legal norm, a significant and clear change must be shown in the overall legal order surrounding that custom, together with the perception and attitude of society members or the social and cultural background that formed the basis of the Supreme Court precedent recognizing the customary law. Unless such circumstances are clear, one must not hastily conclude that the existing customary law can no longer retain force as a legal norm (see the 2017 Grand Bench decision).\\n\\nOur legal system recognizes prescription acquisition as a lawful means of acquiring rights in order to maintain social order, provide relief from evidentiary difficulties, and realize litigation economy. When acquisitive prescription based on adverse possession is completed, ownership itself is transferred free of charge, whereas in the case of a grave site right, it is merely the acquisition of a land use right rather than ownership. For prescription acquisition, possession of the grave site must be peaceful and open, and in view of the fact that prescription acquisition is recognized only when the landowner, despite being able to exercise rights at any time during 20 years, has not done so, it cannot be said that recognizing a free-of-charge grave site right runs counter to our overall legal order.\\n\\nThe interpretation like the majority opinion not only negates the significance of the prescription system but also opens the door to new disputes, and therefore cannot be considered a proper legal interpretation. As noted in section 1) above, there is no material showing that the prior custom concerning the content of grave site rights recognized as customary law has changed, and even though no significant change is evident in society members’ perceptions and attitudes, or in the basic ideology or social order governing society, surrounding this issue, simply excluding the application of customary law or changing its content by means of changing precedent is an hasty measure that can greatly undermine legal stability.\\n\\n4) Finally, as also mentioned in the Constitutional Court decision above, recognizing the holder’s obligation to pay ground rent with respect to a grave site right raises concern that disputes seeking exhumation of graves through claims for extinguishment of the grave site right due to arrears of ground rent will sharply increase. Whereas until now disputes have been about obtaining recognition of a grave site right, in the future they will take the form of disputes to extinguish a grave site right, eventually greatly damaging the good customs of our society, which has recognized prescription acquisition of a grave site right as a customary-law right. One cannot help but ask whether this was truly the form of grave site right that the Supreme Court intended to guarantee through the 2017 Grand Bench decision.\\n\\nB. As to the conclusion in this case\\nThe court below partially granted the Plaintiffs’ claim against the Defendant for ground rent in this case on the ground that the holder of a grave site right has an obligation to pay ground rent for the grave site to the landowner at least from the time the landowner claimed ground rent.\\n\\nHowever, the court below’s determination contains an error that affected the outcome by misapprehending the legal principles concerning ground rent for a grave site right, and therefore the judgment below must be reversed.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, we state that we cannot agree with the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Supplementary Opinion by Justices Park Sang-ok, Min Yoo-suk, Noh Jeong-hee, and Noh Tae-ak to the Majority Opinion\\nWe rebut, to the extent necessary, several issues raised by the separate opinion and the dissenting opinion, and supplement the reasoning of the majority opinion.\\n\\nA. Concerning the Separate Opinion\\n1) There can be no disagreement that the principle of protection of property rights under the Constitution and the content and effect of ownership under the Civil Act must be considered in determining the obligation of a person who has acquired a grave site right by prescription to pay ground rent. However, the separate opinion, based on the principle of protection of property rights under the Constitution, the content and effect of ownership under the Civil Act, and ordinary transactional notions, states that in our legal order the use relationship of another person’s land should in principle be regarded as a use relationship for consideration, and further uses this interpretation as the basis for the for-consideration nature of a prescription-acquired grave site right. It is difficult to readily agree with the above grounds cited by the separate opinion. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\nBecause a limited real right called a grave site right is recognized by customary law, the landowner’s exercise of ownership over the portion of land that has become the grave site must inevitably be restricted within the reasonable scope necessary for the protection and management of the grave (see Supreme Court 2000. 9. 26. decided 99DA14006, the 2017 Grand Bench decision, etc.). Nevertheless, the Constitutional Court held that the customary law concerning prescription acquisition of a grave site right does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and thus does not infringe the landowner’s property rights, considering the continuation of burial culture, the need to protect graves, the requirements for prescription acquisition due to the special nature of a grave site right, and the limited scope of property-right restriction, and further that the fact that there is in principle no obligation to pay ground rent does not make it an excessive restriction beyond the necessary degree (see Constitutional Court en banc decision of 2020. 10. 29. in Case 2017HEONBA208, etc.). If so, the principle of protection of property rights under the Constitution or the content and effect of ownership under the Civil Act cannot be regarded as sufficient grounds in determining the holder of a grave site right’s obligation to pay ground rent.\\n\\nAlso, even if it is usual today for a possessor using another person’s land to agree to pay consideration for the use of the land, such as rent or ground rent, as mentioned in the separate opinion, the landowner can still establish free-of-charge superficies or conclude a loan-for-use contract, and the Civil Act does not prescribe payment of ground rent as a requirement for the formation of superficies (Civil Act Article 279), so where no for-consideration agreement exists in a superficies establishment contract, it is treated as free of charge. Accordingly, one cannot uniformly say that a use relationship concerning land owned by another person should be regarded as a for-consideration use relationship unless there are special circumstances such as an agreement between the parties that it is free of charge, and one cannot as is apply to the land-use relationship of a prescription-acquired grave site right, which arises by customary law and in most cases does not permit an agreement concerning ground rent between the parties, the present-day transactional notion of a use relationship established by agreement.\\n\\nIf there is no provision in law concerning civil matters, customary law applies; if there is no customary law, the principles of reason apply (Civil Act Article 1). The principles of reason are understood or expressed as the norms of social common life thought on the basis of human reason or common sense, general principles of law, social validity, equity, and justice, and become the source of law, that is, the standard for adjudication, when there is no written law or customary law. In Supreme Court en banc decision of 2008. 11. 20. decided 2007DA27670, the Court held that because the Civil Act contains no provision concerning the method of determining the person who presides over ancestral rites under Article 1008-3, and the prior customary law that designated the eldest son among the co-heirs as the person presiding over ancestral rites had lost its force, the person presiding over ancestral rites must be determined according to the principles of reason under Civil Act Article 1. Supreme Court en banc decision of 2005. 7. 21. decided 2002DA1178 likewise held that because the prior customary law limiting the qualifications of clan members to adult males had lost its force, the qualifications of clan members must be supplemented by the principles of reason under Civil Act Article 1. In those en banc decisions, although the question of what result was proper when the principles of reason were applied was divided between the majority and minority opinions, there was agreement that the matter should be decided according to the principles of reason. The majority opinion, in deciding the issue in this case where there is neither written law nor customary law to serve as the standard for adjudication, has respected prior Supreme Court interpretations concerning grave site rights and, taking into account the constitutional principles governing the protection and limitation of property rights, as well as the content and purport of the relevant statutory provisions regulating ownership and use of land, has recognized the law in conformity with social validity and equity, namely the principles of reason.\\n\\n2) The separate opinion states that with respect to ground rent for a grave site right, the Civil Act provisions on statutory superficies must be analogically applied first, and that it is not correct to decide differently on the basis of the principles of reason. However, as the separate opinion itself notes, to analogically apply a legal norm, not only must there be a commonality or similarity between a matter without legal regulation and a matter with legal regulation, but analogical application must be evaluated as justified in light of the system of legal norms, legislative intent and purpose, etc. (see Supreme Court 2020. 4. 29. decided 2019DA226135), and it is difficult to evaluate as justified the direct analogical application of the Civil Act provisions concerning statutory superficies to the obligation to pay ground rent in a prescription-acquired grave site right for the following reasons.\\n\\nEven in written law, the law governing real rights, which regulates control relations over things, is an area more strongly influenced by each country’s historical traditions and social customs than other legal fields. Moreover, prescription acquisition of a grave site right is recognized by customary law for the protection and management of the special object called a grave, and the content of the right, including its requirements for creation and scope, duration of existence, and so forth, is not the same as rights under written law. As the majority opinion mentioned in reference to the 2017 Grand Bench decision, under the historical and social background of our people’s ancestral reverence, the principle of common ownership of forests, and the burial-centered funeral culture, landowners often tolerated free use of grave sites and did not object in light of the value of using forest land and the special nature of graves, and the courts have recognized prescription acquisition of a grave site right by respecting such factual relations that have formed over a long period around graves.\\n\\nWhen the court determines the concrete content of a grave site right that has not been fixed by customary law, it must also fully take into account the historical background in which the grave site right has been recognized as a customary-law right, the special nature of the right, and the need to prevent social confusion arising from changes in Supreme Court precedent. As carefully examined in the majority opinion above, the Supreme Court, in recognizing prescription acquisition of a grave site right as customary law, has not simply followed the Civil Act provisions concerning the scope to which a grave site right extends or its duration of existence; rather, it has derived concrete and reasonable interpretations. The obligation of the holder of a prescription-acquired grave site right to pay ground rent cannot be viewed from exactly the same perspective as in the case of statutory superficies. If, after installing a grave, a person possessed the grave site for a long period peacefully and openly without paying consideration and without objection by the landowner, and thereby acquired the grave site right by prescription, respecting such existing factual relations accords with the purport of the customary law concerning prescription acquisition of a grave site right, and it is rather natural that the scope of the obligation to pay ground rent of a person who acquires a grave site right by prescription under such background and requirements differs from cases governed by written law and its interpretation.\\n\\n3) The separate opinion states that because the holder of the grave site right bore obligations to return unjust enrichment or to pay damages during the prescription period, there is an obligation to pay ground rent from the time the grave was installed even after prescription acquisition. However, the legal relations after prescription acquisition do not necessarily have to be the same as those before prescription acquisition.\\n\\nIn the general and typical case of ownership where acquisitive prescription is in issue, the possessor bears an obligation to return unjust enrichment to the landowner corresponding to the benefit of land use during the prescription period, but once acquisitive prescription is completed and ownership is acquired, the retroactive effect of acquisitive prescription (Civil Act Article 247(1)) causes the effect of the acquisition of ownership to retroact to the time possession began. As a result, the possession during the prescription period becomes possession based on lawful title, and the obligation to return unjust enrichment to the landowner that arose during the prescription period disappears or is deemed never to have arisen retroactively.\\n\\nIn the case of a grave site right as well, during the period in which the prescription is running, the grave owner has no lawful title to possess the grave site and therefore owes the landowner either exhumation of the grave or an obligation to return unjust enrichment. However, once acquisitive prescription is completed and the grave site right is acquired, its effect retroacts to the time the grave was installed, and the possession of the grave site becomes lawful possession based on the grave site right from the outset, thereby extinguishing the obligation to return unjust enrichment premised on “unauthorized possession.”\\n\\nThe separate opinion states that once prescription acquisition of a grave site right is completed, the obligation to return unjust enrichment that had already arisen during the prescription period retroactively transforms into an obligation to pay ground rent. However, an obligation to return unjust enrichment premised on unauthorized possession and an obligation to pay ground rent premised on a lawful use relationship are different in nature. The obligation to return unjust enrichment is a claim-related relationship that arises only between the possessor and the landowner, whereas ground rent constitutes part of the content of a real right and, once determined by the court upon a party’s claim, is effective even against third parties such as a transferee of the land. The retroactive effect of completion of prescription may serve as the basis for retroactively extinguishing the obligation to return unjust enrichment that arose during the prescription period, but it cannot be said to serve as the basis for retroactively causing, from the commencement of possession, an obligation to pay ground rent that was not borne during the prescription period, or for converting the obligation to return unjust enrichment into an obligation to pay ground rent.\\n\\n4) The separate opinion states that it cannot be logically explained to demand performance when no right or obligation has arisen, and that in the absence of a ground-rent claim, the landowner cannot demand performance of ground rent. However, this rebuttal by the separate opinion criticizes the majority opinion on premises different from those of the majority opinion and is not valid, and it is difficult to agree that logically the arising of a claim must necessarily precede a demand for performance.\\n\\nAccording to the majority opinion, a person who has peacefully and openly possessed a grave site for 20 years without paying consideration and acquired a grave site right by prescription does not bear an obligation to pay ground rent until the landowner claims ground rent, but once the landowner claims ground rent, the obligation to pay ground rent arises. In legal orders to which written law applies, one can frequently see rights and obligations arising or being affected by the declaration of intent or unilateral act of one party to the legal relationship. For example, where no time for performance of an obligation is fixed, the creditor’s demand for performance gives rise to the debtor’s liability for delay (Civil Act Article 387(2)). Also, as mentioned by the majority opinion, when a superficies holder, a leasehold depositor, or a lessee exercises the right to claim increase or decrease in ground rent, deposit, or rent, the effect of increasing or decreasing ground rent, etc. arises, and the party bears an obligation to pay the increased or decreased amount from that time. Therefore, it cannot be said that it is illogical or unnatural for rights and obligations to arise when one party to the legal relationship makes a demand.\\n\\nB. Concerning the Dissenting Opinion\\n1) The dissenting opinion states that because a grave site right is a real right under customary law, the content of customary law should be declared through investigation or confirmation of custom, and it is not proper for the court to determine that content through interpretation. However, accepting this view of the dissenting opinion as it stands would lead to the conclusion that the Supreme Court can change its existing view concerning the content of a right recognized under customary law only through investigation and discovery of customary law, which cannot be accepted as is. Even if a prescription-acquired grave site right is a right recognized under customary law, the court should judge matters such as the existence or nonexistence of the obligation to pay ground rent, which is the issue in this case, by interpreting and applying customary law to the concrete case, and the Supreme Court should be able to change its view on the interpretation or application of customary law according to the general standards and principles of legal interpretation unless the content of the right under customary law was recognized on the basis of the existence of custom, etc.\\n\\nAlso, the dissenting opinion’s view that, unless a custom has been confirmed that a prescription-acquired grave site right is a right with for-consideration content, it should be viewed as free of charge, appears to merely analogically apply the legal principles on contractual superficies under the Civil Act and is difficult to regard as dealing with discovery and interpretation of customary law, so it is not easy to agree with it.\\n\\n2) As to prescription acquisition of a grave site right, the Chosun High Court appears to have first ruled on 1927. 3. 8. to the effect that “a person who, with another’s consent, installs a grave on land owned by that person acquires, for the purpose of owning it, a kind of real right similar to superficies over another person’s land, and even a person who installs a grave on another person’s land without that consent acquires by prescription a real right similar to superficies if he or she peacefully and openly possesses the grave site for 20 years, and it is customary that such right may be asserted against third parties without registration.” Since the prescription system is a modern legal institution that did not exist in the Joseon era, that Chosun High Court decision may be viewed as recognizing acquisition of a grave site right by prescription by combining custom concerning the protection of a land-use right for the protection and performance of ancestral rites with the modern prescription system. As similar Supreme Court precedents continued after liberation, the prescription acquisition of a grave site right came to be accepted as an established customary law.\\n\\nAs such, because a prescription-acquired grave site right was originally recognized not merely on the basis of custom alone but by combining it with the prescription system, there were parts concerning the specific content or scope of effect of the right where the existence of custom was not confirmed. In disputes between parties concerning a grave site right, the court cannot deny the right itself on the ground that the content of the right under customary law is not confirmed, so the Supreme Court has traditionally determined the content of a prescription-acquired grave site right based on interpretation of customary law and written law and on notions of equity.\\n\\nFor example, the Supreme Court held, with respect to the duration of a grave site right arising where a grave is installed with the landowner’s consent, that it is reasonable to interpret that, unless there are special circumstances such as an agreement between the parties, the grave site right continues so long as the holder continues to protect and perform ancestral rites and the grave remains (see Supreme Court 1982. 1. 26. decided 81DA1220, etc.), and applied this legal principle to prescription-acquired grave site rights as well. Regarding the effect of a grave site right, such as the scope to which the grave site right extends, the Supreme Court held that where multiple graves owned and managed by the same eldest son line are installed as a group, the grave site right recognized is for the protection and preservation of all the graves installed as a group, and therefore if some of those graves are relocated within the scope to which the grave site right extends, the effect of the grave site right remains intact for the relocated graves as well (see Supreme Court 1994. 12. 23. decided 94DA15530, etc.), while holding that even within the territorial scope to which the grave site right extends, the power to install a new grave in addition to the existing one is not included, and therefore it is not permitted to install a grave for the other spouse in the form of a dual grave on an existing grave installed when one spouse dies first (see Supreme Court 1997. 5. 23. decided 95DA29086, 29093, etc.). Furthermore, the Supreme Court held that even a combined grave in the form of a single grave is not permitted (see Supreme Court 2001. 8. 21. decided 2001DA28367, etc.). It is difficult to say that these decisions were made on the basis of the existence of custom.\\n\\n3) Supreme Court 1992. 6. 26. decided 92DA13936, which decided the issue in this case, held that the holder of a prescription-acquired grave site right has an obligation to pay ground rent from the time the grave site right arises unless there are special circumstances; meanwhile, Supreme Court 1995. 2. 28. decided 94DA37912 applied the legal principles concerning ground rent for contractual superficies to prescription-acquired grave site rights and held that, since payment of ground rent is not an element of superficies and ground rent cannot be claimed in the absence of an agreement concerning ground rent, it is reasonable to “interpret” that a prescription-acquired grave site right also need not pay ground rent. However, none of those decisions investigated or confirmed the existence of a custom or practice approved as a legal norm concerning whether a prescription-acquired grave site right is for consideration or free of charge. The 2017 Grand Bench decision also only held that prescription acquisition of a grave site right remains valid customary law with respect to graves installed before the effective date of the Funeral Services Act, but did not decide whether a grave site right thus acquired is a right with free-of-charge content under customary law. Aside from that, the Supreme Court has not previously confirmed whether there exists custom regarding the obligation to pay ground rent for a prescription-acquired grave site right, and rather, the existence of conflicting precedents as above concerning the issue in this case can be said to prove that no such customary law existed.\\n\\nC. Sixty or so years have passed since the Supreme Court recognized prescription acquisition of a grave site right under the current Civil Act as customary law, and Korea’s economic and social environment has changed greatly. With the enactment and enforcement of the Burial Act, the Funeral Services Act, etc., cremation and columbarium facilities and cemeteries have expanded, and the funeral culture is gradually shifting from burial to cremation; the social and cultural environment surrounding grave site rights has also continuously changed, such that for lawfully installed public and private cemeteries, payment of usage fees and maintenance fees has become normal. Because such changes in the social and economic circumstances surrounding grave site rights have made it unfair in light of social justice to maintain the prior use relationship as it was, it is reasonable to view that the holder of the grave site right must pay consideration for use of the grave site upon the landowner’s claim.\\n\\nMoreover, if it is viewed that the holder of a grave site right is obligated to pay ground rent from the time of the landowner’s demand, one can achieve a desirable result that accords with the overall legal order respecting the purport of customary law that has recognized prescription acquisition of grave site rights, promoting the continuity of graves and legal stability while preventing one-sided sacrifice by landowners and respecting private property rights.\\n\\nA holder of a grave site right that was acquired by prescription must pay ground rent from the time the landowner demands ground rent judicially or extrajudicially. If the holder fails to pay ground rent determined by the court upon a party’s claim for two years or more, the landowner should be able to claim extinguishment of the grave site right (Civil Act Article 287). However, if the amount of ground rent concerning the grave site right has not been determined by agreement of the parties or by court judgment, then even if the holder does not pay ground rent, it cannot be regarded as a delay in payment, and a claim for extinguishment of the grave site right is not permitted (see Supreme Court 1994. 12. 2. decided 93DA52297, etc.).\\n\\nTherefore, even where the holder of the grave site right lacks the economic ability to bear ground rent, the holder can take time to plan and prepare for relocation, etc., for at least two years from the time ground rent is demanded, and can avoid a situation in which an ancestral grave is forcibly exhumed on short notice. Meanwhile, where the landowner previously demanded ground rent, the holder of the grave site right must pay ground rent from the time of that demand, and if two years or more of ground rent determined by judgment is in arrears, the grave site right may eventually be extinguished pursuant to a claim for extinguishment of the grave site right. However, from the time the landowner demands ground rent, it cannot be said that the holder of the grave site right has a strong reliance on free use of the land, and such a result cannot be deemed unfair.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, we supplement the reasoning of the majority opinion."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding assumption of contract are correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2012DA41359]": "The grounds of appeal are examined (the statements in each supplemental brief of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the petition for final appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. The attachment of a claim is an order directed to the third-party obligor prohibiting payment to the debtor; thus, the debtor may not engage in acts such as extinguishing or reducing the claim and may not set up such acts against the creditor, but it does not have the effect of binding even the debtor’s disposition over the legal relationship that is the cause of the claim’s creation (see Supreme Court Decision 91DA29736, Nov. 12, 1991).\\n\\nHowever, in the case of contract assumption, which is a contract for the purpose of succeeding to the status of a contracting party, the contractual relationship between the transferor and the counterparty terminates because the transferor withdraws from the contractual relationship (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DA31990, Sept. 6, 2007), but the rights and obligations that the transferor held on the basis of the contractual relationship are succeeded to by the transferee as they are, while maintaining their identity. Therefore, where, after the transferor’s claim against the third-party obligor has been attached, contract assumption is effected to transfer the status of a party to the contract that is the cause of the claim’s creation, the transferee receives the claim in a state where its rights are restricted by the attachment; accordingly, it is reasonable to deem that the third-party obligor may not set up against the attaching creditor the fact that the contractual relationship between it and the transferor has terminated by virtue of the contract assumption.\\n\\n2. a. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n① Universe Housing Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Universe Housing”) sold to the Defendant on August 18, 2006 the basement level 6 through ground level 1 portion of a mixed-use residential and commercial building to be constructed in the area of (address omitted), Seongbuk-gu, Seoul, which the Defendant was to use as a large discount retail facility (hereinafter referred to as “the building portion in this case”), at a sale price of KRW 87,161,000,000 (value-added tax separate) (hereinafter referred to as “the sales contract in this case”), and received KRW 19.1 billion from the Defendant as a down payment on the day of the contract.\\n\\n② On May 25, 2007, Universe Housing, the Defendant-appellant’s auxiliary intervenor Saengbo Real Estate Trust Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Saengbo Real Estate Trust”), and Dongil Highvill Co., Ltd. and Dongil Construction Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Dongil Highvill” and “Dongil Construction,” respectively), which were the contractors for the construction work of the above mixed-use residential and commercial building, prepared a “Land Trust Project Agreement” providing that, for the performance of the above construction project, Universe Housing would entrust the project site for the above construction work to Saengbo Real Estate Trust, and that Saengbo Real Estate Trust would be in charge of sales and management work as the implementing entity of the above project; on June 29, 2007, Saengbo Real Estate Trust completed the registration of transfer of ownership on June 28, 2007, based on trust, with respect to the above project site, and made public the trust register.\\n\\n③ Universe Housing and Saengbo Real Estate Trust prepared a “Land Trust Project (Amended) Agreement” on November 15, 2007, partially modifying the contents of the above Land Trust Project Agreement, and then amended the trust register on April 17, 2008; there, the trust provisions included the following: “Universe Housing, etc. shall transfer or succeed the external status, including the name of Universe Housing, to Saengbo Real Estate Trust in accordance with the procedures under the project agreement in this case (Special Agreement Article 21), and if Universe Housing has made pre-sales before the conclusion of the trust agreement, Universe Housing shall take measures so that a succession agreement can be concluded between Saengbo Real Estate Trust and the pre-sold units simultaneously with the conclusion of the trust agreement, and the sale proceeds already received by Universe Housing shall be fully returned into Saengbo Real Estate Trust’s trust account (Special Agreement Article 22).”\\n\\n④ On June 10, 2008, the Defendant paid Universe Housing KRW 13.6 billion as the first interim payment.\\n\\n⑤ Based on an authentic copy of an enforceable judgment against Universe Housing, the Plaintiff obtained, on February 16, 2009, an order of attachment and collection with respect to KRW 2,392,885,368 out of Universe Housing’s above sale price claim against the Defendant, and the above order of attachment and collection was served on the Defendant on February 20, 2009.\\n\\n⑥ On February 17, 2010, the Defendant deposited KRW 13,585,386,618 as the second interim payment into Saengbo Real Estate Trust’s trust account.\\n\\n⑦ On April 15, 2010, Saengbo Real Estate Trust, the Defendant, Dongil Construction, and Universe Housing concluded a contract with respect to the building portion in this case, designating Saengbo Real Estate Trust as the seller and project developer, the Defendant as the buyer, Dongil Construction as the responsible completion contractor, and Universe Housing as the entrusting party, and partly modifying the sales contract in this case with respect to the payment of the down payment, interim payments, and balance (hereinafter referred to as “the sales contract in this case”).\\n\\nb. In light of the foregoing facts and the legal principles discussed above, the sales contract in this case constitutes a contract assumption, by which Universe Housing and Saengbo Real Estate Trust agreed to transfer the status of seller under the sales contract in this case from Universe Housing to Saengbo Real Estate Trust, and the Defendant consented thereto; accordingly, Universe Housing withdrew from the contractual relationship and the contractual relationship between Universe Housing and the Defendant terminated, but the rights and obligations that Universe Housing had under the sales contract in this case were succeeded to by Saengbo Real Estate Trust as they were, while maintaining their identity, and thus Saengbo Real Estate Trust would receive the sale price claim in a state where its rights were restricted by the order of attachment in this case. Therefore, the Defendant may not set up against the Plaintiff, who is the attaching creditor, the fact that the contractual relationship that was the cause of the claim’s creation between it and Universe Housing terminated by virtue of the above contract assumption.\\n\\nc. However, the court below denied the Plaintiff’s claim for collection money in this case, holding that, by the contract assumption, Universe Housing withdrew from the contractual relationship and was no longer in the status of seller, and that, accordingly, the attached claim, namely the sale price claim, was also extinguished; this is a misapplication of the legal principles concerning attachment of claims and contract assumption, and thus an erroneous determination.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court Decision 96DA53192, cited by the court below, concerns a different factual situation from this case and is not appropriate for citation in this case.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; it is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2020DA245958]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Judgment of the court below\\n\\nThe Plaintiff, while alternatively asserting the title that Bicotrip Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Bicotrip”) had, against the Defendant, succeeded to and acquired the claim for damages based on non-performance of the employment contract or tort acquired before November 4, 2015 (hereinafter referred to as “the damages claim at issue”) and the title that the Plaintiff had succeeded to and acquired it by virtue of the effect of the assumption of employment contracts attendant on the business transfer on November 4, 2015 (hereinafter referred to as “the business transfer at issue”), brought this action for the claim for damages at issue as a partial claim.\\n\\nThe court below, after recognizing the facts as stated in its reasoning, held that the damages claim at issue was either not included among the individual claims subject to the business transfer at issue or that there was a special agreement under the business transfer agreement at issue to exclude it from the transfer, and even assuming arguendo that the damages claim at issue was included among the individual claims subject to assignment under the business transfer agreement at issue, the requirements for opposability concerning individual assignment of claims were not met, and thus rejected all of the Plaintiff’s assertion of succession and acquisition regarding the damages claim at issue.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\n\\nHowever, the judgment of the court below is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\na. Assumption of a contract for the purpose of succession of status as a contracting party includes, in addition to the transfer of claims and obligations arising from the contract, the assignment of comprehensive rights and obligations arising from the contractual relationship, such as the right of rescission. If assumption of the contract is lawfully effected, the transferor withdraws from the contractual relationship, and after the assumption of the contract, unless there are special circumstances such as a reservation of the transferor’s discharge, no contractual relationship exists between the remaining party and the transferor, and the related claims and obligations also cease to exist. Such assumption of a contract is ordinarily effected by a tripartite contract concluded by agreement among the transferor, the transferee, and the remaining party, and where an agreement between two of the three parties concerned precedes, the effect arises only when the remaining party gives its consent or approval thereto (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DA88303, rendered on May 24, 2012).\\n\\nWhen such assumption of a contract is effected, the claims and obligations already arising under that contractual relationship are also transferred to the assignee, unless there are special circumstances such as a special agreement to exclude them from the subject of assumption. Assumption of a contract is not aimed at the transfer of individual claims and obligations, but rather at the comprehensive transfer of the status of a contracting party including multiple claims and obligations, and it becomes effective only through the involvement of all three contracting parties, whereas assignment of an individual claim is formed and becomes effective through the involvement of only the assignor and the assignee; thus, since the two differ in their legal nature and requirements, the requirements for opposability required in the assignment of an individual claim are not separately required in assumption of a contract. This legal principle applies equally to assumption of a contract attendant on a transfer of business under the Commercial Act.\\n\\nb. Upon examining the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n(1) Around November 18, 2015, Bicotrip entered into a business transfer agreement with the Plaintiff, which was incorporated on November 4 of the same year, with respect to the business segment for ticket issuance agency services, and the main contents thereof are as follows.\\n\\n① Assets subject to transfer and assumption\\n\\nAll assets listed below, as tangible and intangible assets owned or used by the transferor as necessary for, or in order to conduct, the ticket issuance agency business, shall be transferred to the transferee.\\n\\nTangible assets, intellectual property rights, claims (all accounts receivable, other claims, and rights held by the transferor against third parties in connection with the business in question), goodwill and customer relationships, business-related books and records, etc.\\n\\n② Excluded assets\\n\\nThe assets stated below shall be excluded from the subject of transfer and assumption, and shall continue to be retained by the transferor.\\n\\nAll cash and cash equivalents, all securities including stocks, government bonds, and public bonds and other marketable securities, deferred tax assets arising in connection with the business in question up to the closing date, shares of the transferor’s subsidiaries and all other equity interests in other business entities held by the transferor, intellectual property rights used or held for use in the transferor’s other business operations other than the business in question, and contracts to which the transferor is a party that are commonly related to the transferor’s other business operations other than the business in question\\n\\n③ Liabilities subject to transfer and assumption\\n\\nLiabilities arising before the closing of the transfer and assumption in connection with the business in question, which are fixed as of the time of the closing of the transfer and assumption\\n\\n④ Contracts subject to transfer and assumption\\n\\nThe transferor shall transfer to the transferee all written or oral contracts (including, but not limited to, sales contracts, insurance contracts, and employment contracts) concluded by the transferor with customers, business counterparts, and other third parties as necessary for the business in question or in connection with the business in question (the method of transfer shall be separately discussed and agreed upon by the parties).\\n\\n⑤ Employees subject to succession\\n\\nThe transferor shall transfer to the transferee all rights and obligations as employer with respect to the employees of the transferor, including the Defendant, and the transferee shall succeed thereto.\\n\\nThe working conditions for the employees subject to succession shall be the same as the working conditions being applied by the transferor to the employees subject to succession as of the closing date of the transfer and assumption, and, for the transferee’s succession to the employment relationship, the transferor shall cause the employees subject to succession to voluntarily resign from the transferor company as of the closing date of the transfer and assumption and to join the transferee company.\\n\\n(2) On March 1, 2016, the Plaintiff and the Defendant, pursuant to the business transfer agreement at issue, executed an annual salary employment contract under the same working conditions as those at Bicotrip, retroactively setting the commencement date of the employment contract as October 19, 2009.\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, while in charge of Bicotrip’s ticket purchasing agency duties pursuant to the employment contract with Bicotrip, the Defendant, from around October 2010 to around November 2015, received into a personal account in the Defendant’s name the money remitted by Bicotrip’s customers or business counterparts who requested ticket purchasing agency services and used it for personal purposes.\\n\\nc.
