Examining the above factual relations according to the legal principles stated earlier, the following conclusion follows.\\n\\n(1) Since the employment contract with the Defendant was included in the subject of the assumption of employment contracts attendant on the business transfer at issue, and the Defendant, as the remaining party, recognized the business transfer at issue and, after resigning from Bicotrip, accepted the assumption of the employment contract by entering into an employment contract with the Plaintiff under conditions identical to those of the previous employment contract while retroactively stating the contract period as the employment period under the previous employment contract, the status of employer was transferred to the Plaintiff as the assignee, and, unless there are special circumstances such as a special agreement to exclude the damages claim at issue, which had already arisen based on that employment contract relationship, from the subject of assumption, the damages claim at issue is also transferred to the Plaintiff, and it is not necessary to separately satisfy the requirements for opposability concerning individual assignment of claims.\\n\\n(2) In addition, under the business transfer agreement at issue, there was no provision excluding the damages claim at issue based on the employment contract from the subject of assumption, and only cash and cash equivalents existing at the time of the business transfer at issue were designated as excluded from transfer, and it is clear that the damages claim at issue cannot be regarded as cash and cash equivalents existing at the time of the business transfer at issue.\\n\\n(3) Therefore, the Plaintiff may be deemed to have acquired the damages claim at issue as the effect of the assumption of the employment contract attendant on the business transfer at issue.\\n\\nd. Nevertheless, the court below did not determine whether the Plaintiff acquired the damages claim at issue pursuant to the assumption of the employment contract attendant on the business transfer at issue, and instead, on the premise that the Plaintiff could exercise the damages claim at issue only if there had been an assignment of the individual claim attendant on the business transfer at issue, examined and determined only whether the damages claim at issue was included in the subject of individual assignment of claims under the business transfer agreement at issue, whether the requirements for opposability of that assignment were satisfied, and whether there was a special agreement excluding transfer. The judgment of the court below contains error that affected the judgment by omitting a determination on the factual issues required and by failing to fully examine the case through misapprehending the legal principles concerning the effect of assumption of a contract attendant on a business transfer, and the Plaintiff’s grounds for appeal pointing this out are well founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the Plaintiff’s remaining grounds for appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for a new trial and determination. It is so adjudged in unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: A entered into a construction contract with B concerning X house owned by B, and agreed that the construction price would be paid in a lump sum upon completion. Even though A completed the construction, B did not pay the construction price and demanded delivery of X house, and A is residing in X house while exercising a lawful possessory lien. The Y land, which is the site of X house, is owned by D. Which of the following statements are correct? (Each statement is independent, and if there is a dispute, the answer is governed by case law)
A: (a) If A incurred useful expenses with respect to X house, A may claim against B reimbursement, at B’s option, of either the amount expended or the increase in value, only if the increase in value of X house remains extant.
B: (a) If A incurred useful expenses with respect to X house, A may claim against B reimbursement, at B’s option, of either the amount expended or the increase in value, only if the increase in value of X house remains extant. (b) A does not bear toward D an obligation to return unjust enrichment equivalent to rent arising from the use and profit of Y land during the period A resided in X house.
C: (a) If a sale is effected in auction proceedings for X house based on A’s possessory lien, A’s possessory lien does not extinguish, just as in the case where a sale is effected in auction proceedings for X house filed by creditor B of B. (b) A does not bear toward D an obligation to return unjust enrichment equivalent to rent arising from the use and profit of Y land during the period A resided in X house.
D: (a) If a sale is effected in auction proceedings for X house based on A’s possessory lien, A’s possessory lien does not extinguish, just as in the case where a sale is effected in auction proceedings for X house filed by creditor B of B. (b) In auction proceedings filed by creditor B of B, if C purchases X house, it is permissible for creditor A of A to apply for an order of seizure and collection with respect to “the claim to be paid by C simultaneously with A’s delivery of X house to C.”
E: (a) If A incurred useful expenses with respect to X house, A may claim against B reimbursement, at B’s option, of either the amount expended or the increase in value, only if the increase in value of X house remains extant. (b) A does not bear toward D an obligation to return unjust enrichment equivalent to rent arising from the use and profit of Y land during the period A resided in X house. (c) In auction proceedings filed by creditor B of B, if C purchases X house, it is permissible for creditor A of A to apply for an order of seizure and collection with respect to “the claim to be paid by C simultaneously with A’s delivery of X house to C.”
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2005DA59963]": "Where a holder of the right of retention has used the retained building and its lot, unless special circumstances exist, he is under a duty to return to the owner a benefit equivalent to the rent; the same shall be true even where such use is necessary for the preservation of the retained building (see Supreme Court Decision 62DA294, decided on Aug. 31, 1962, and Supreme Court Decision 2004DA69420, decided on Jan. 26, 2006).\\n\\nThe judgment of the court of first instance cited by the court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found the following facts: Defendant D, pursuant to a construction contract with the Plaintiff, constructed the building at issue on land owned by the Plaintiff, but having not been paid the construction price, asked Defendant B, around Oct. 1998, to manage part of the building at issue, while around 2000, through E, asking Defendant C to manage the remaining part of the building at issue, permitting that part to be used as a used signboard shop and receiving a total of KRW 2,300,000 in return for such use; and from then until the present, Defendants B and C, while managing the building parts entrusted to them as above, have possessed and used the building at issue. It then held that, in a case such as this, where the Defendants inevitably possess and use the building in response to the Plaintiff’s nonpayment of the construction price, the Plaintiff seeking return of unjust enrichment arising therefrom must specifically allege and prove the actual benefit obtained by the Defendants; however, according to the above-recognized facts, it found that, apart from Defendant D having obtained a substantial benefit of KRW 2,300,000 received from Defendant C as a usage fee, there was no evidence to support the conclusion that Defendant D had any other actual benefit, or that the remaining Defendants had obtained any actual benefit whatsoever.\\n\\nHowever, if the factual relation is as found by the court of first instance, at least Defendant C, who is using the possessed part as a signboard shop, and Defendant D, who is indirectly using that part through him, would, even if such use is necessary for the preservation of the building at issue, be under a duty to return to the Plaintiff, the owner of the building and lot, a benefit equivalent to the rent for that part, and the rent-equivalent benefit in such case should be calculated not by the usage fee actually received by Defendant D from Defendant C, but by the rent objectively recognized by the results of a rental appraisal and the like.\\n\\nMeanwhile, according to the judgment of the court of first instance, Defendant B was asked by Defendant D to manage part of the building at issue and is stated to have possessed and used it, but nothing at all is specifically set forth as to how it was used; the court below should have further examined this point and then determined whether there was any actual benefit from the use of the possessed part (in addition, it should be pointed out that, although Defendant B’s whereabouts were unknown throughout the entire course of this litigation and all service documents to him were clearly served by publication, as is apparent from the record, the court below recognized, up to the close of oral argument in the trial on the merits, the fact that the said Defendant continued to possess and use the building at issue; this also constitutes a factual finding in violation of the rules of evidence).\\n\\nIf so, the judgment of the court below in this part contains an error in the interpretation of law regarding the duty to return benefits arising from the use of the retained property, or illegality in that it failed to fully examine the matter, and the ground of appeal pointing this out is well taken.\\n\\nTherefore, without considering the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below, and judgment is rendered as follows."}

{"[2010MA1059]": "The grounds for re-appeal shall be determined, and a supplemental statement of grounds for re-appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds for re-appeal shall be considered only to the extent that it supplements the grounds for re-appeal.\\n\\n1. Article 274(1) of the Civil Execution Act provides only that “auction based on a lien and auction conducted pursuant to the Civil Act, the Commercial Act, or other statutes shall be carried out in accordance with the examples of auction for execution of security interests,” and therefore, in an auction based on a lien conducted pursuant to Article 322(1) of the Civil Act, whether the so-called principle of extinguishment, under which encumbrances on the real property in question are extinguished and the purchaser acquires full ownership, or the so-called principle of assumption, under which the purchaser assumes the encumbrances on the real property in question, is to be adopted is not logically and necessarily derived according to whether the purpose of the auction lies in the collection of claims or merely in conversion into cash, but must be determined by comprehensively considering the purpose and objective and nature of the auction, the purpose of the substantive law on which the auction is based, and the interests of the creditor, debtor, owner, purchaser, and others surrounding the auction (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DA37908, rendered on October 29, 2009).\\n\\nArticle 91(2) and (3) and Article 268 of the Civil Execution Act provide that the principle of extinguishment applies in compulsory auction and auction for the execution of security interests, which account for most auctions, and on that premise, they also provide in detail for the final deadline for demands for distribution, notices to file claims, demands for distribution, distribution procedures, and the like; Article 322(1) of the Civil Act provides that “a lienholder may auction the thing subject to retention in order to receive performance of the claim”; thus, even in auction based on a lien, it is premised upon the existence of a creditor and a debtor and assumes an auction for the realization and satisfaction of a claim. On the other hand, there is no provision regarding the procedure for investigating and confirming the existence and content of encumbrances on the real property in question, which is deemed necessary if the principle of assumption is adopted, and no provision limiting the scope of the encumbrances to be assumed is also set forth; accordingly, if auction based on a lien is conducted on the principle of assumption, the legal status of the purchaser will be placed in a very unstable state. Considering together the fact that, depending on how the scope of the encumbrances to be assumed is set, adopting the principle of assumption may rather become disadvantageous to the lienholder, it is reasonable to view that auction based on a lien, like compulsory auction or auction for the execution of security interests, is conducted with extinguishment of encumbrances on the real property in question as a statutory sale condition, that demands for distribution by general creditors as well as preferential creditors are permitted, and that the lienholder may receive distribution in the same rank as general creditors. However, the execution court may, in light of the interests concerning the real property, decide through a change in sale conditions, contrary to the above statutory sale condition, to allow the purchaser to assume the encumbrances without extinguishing them.\\n\\nAnd since auction based on a lien is conducted on the principle of extinguishment, it extinguishes encumbrances on the real property in question, just as in the case of compulsory auction or auction for the execution of security interests. Therefore, unless the execution court separately decides through a change in sale conditions to have the purchaser assume the encumbrances without extinguishing them, the execution court need not state in the notice of the sale date or in the statement of the auctioned property that the encumbrances on the real property in question will not be extinguished and that the purchaser will assume them.\\n\\n2. According to the reasons for the decision of the lower court and the record, the execution court issued notices of each sale date around May 25, 2009 and around October 12, 2009, and the statement that the encumbrances, including limited real rights, on each real property of this case would not be extinguished by the sale and that the purchaser would assume them was not included in the contents of those notices; and, even when preparing the statement of the auctioned property concerning each real property of this case, the execution court entered in the column for “occupant of the real property and title to possession, and period during which possession may be had,” Seongeo 1, 2, and 3 as shop tenants, and Jade Construction as a person asserting a lien over each real property of this case, and in the “remarks” column entered only that “Jade Construction is a lienholder and auction petitioner, and there are notices of lien from Jeongho TLC and Tech One Co., Ltd., but the formation thereof is unclear”; it did not at all state that even if the respective real properties of this case were sold in the above auction proceedings, the encumbrances such as limited real rights established on the above real properties would not be extinguished and the purchaser would assume them. On that basis, the execution court viewed the auction proceedings of this case as having a serious error in that it failed to notify applicants for purchase and others of the existence of encumbrances to be assumed by the purchaser, and accordingly disallowed the sale.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles and factual relationship set forth above, unless the execution court in the auction proceedings of this case based on a lien made a change decision that the encumbrances on each real property of this case would not be extinguished and would be assumed by the purchaser, it was not required in the auction proceedings of this case to notify applicants for purchase and others of such fact by stating it in the notice of the sale date or in the statement of the auctioned property.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below maintained the execution court’s determination disallowing the sale of this case on the premise that the auction of this case based on a lien proceeded under the principle of assumption; thus, the decision of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning auction based on a lien.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the decision of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further review and determination, and it is so decided as ordered, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2014MA1407]": "The grounds of reappeal are examined.\\n\\nEven if a thing has property value, a right that lacks independence and therefore cannot itself be disposed of and converted into cash cannot be the object of execution (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 88DAKA3465, rendered on December 13, 1988).\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 91(5) of the Civil Execution Act, which is applied mutatis mutandis to auction procedures for exercising security rights pursuant to Article 268 of the same Act, provides that the purchaser shall be responsible for satisfying the claim secured by the lienholder’s lien. Here, the meaning of “being responsible for satisfying the claim” is that the burden on the real property is succeeded to, and it does not mean that a personal obligation is also assumed; therefore, the lienholder may only refuse to deliver the real property that is the object retained until the secured claim is satisfied, and may not demand payment of the secured claim from the successful bidder (see Supreme Court Decision 95DA8720, rendered on August 23, 1996).\\n\\nAccording to the record, (1) in the procedure for a compulsory auction of real property, Ulsan District Court 2013TAGYEONG13193, concerning the real property in this case owned by Non-party Edupower Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the “Non-party Company”), the third-party debtor purchased the property; (2) the debtor occupied the real property in this case while asserting that there remained construction payment to be received from the Non-party Company (hereinafter referred to as “the construction payment in this case”) and exercised a lien (hereinafter referred to as “the lien in this case”); (3) meanwhile, the creditor filed a lawsuit against the debtor seeking payment of construction payment in Busan District Court 2012GAHAP17175 and received a judgment wholly in favor of the creditor on April 4, 2013, and that judgment became final and conclusive on April 30, 2013; and (4) the creditor, on April 8, 2014, filed an application for the attachment and collection order at issue regarding “the claim to be paid by the third-party debtor upon the debtor’s delivery of the real property in this case to the third-party debtor,” based on the executory authentic copy of the above judgment.\\n\\nExamining these facts in light of the foregoing legal principles, (1) even if the debtor is the true lienholder with respect to the real property in this case, the debtor does not have a claim by which he may actively demand payment of the construction payment in this case from the third-party debtor, who is the purchaser, and may only refuse to deliver the real property in this case to the third-party debtor, who is the purchaser, until the construction payment in this case is satisfied; and (2) even though, in this manner, the debtor may receive payment of the construction payment in this case from the third-party debtor in the course of exercising the lien, this merely extinguishes the claim relating to the construction payment in this case and arises only from the power to retain the subject matter and refuse delivery under the lien in this case, and therefore the debtor’s authority with respect to such payment is independent of the lien in this case or the construction payment claim in this case, which is the secured claim, and cannot be separately disposed of or realized into cash, so it is appropriate to view it as having a nature that cannot be attached.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, contrary to this, wrongly determined that the above right of the debtor was attachable and maintained the first-instance order that granted the application for the attachment and collection order at issue; thus, the court below’s determination contains an error that affected the decision by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the attachability of claims subject to attachment. The assertion in the grounds of reappeal to that effect is well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, the order of the court below is reversed, but since this case is sufficient for this Court to decide directly, this Court will decide on the merits, revoke the first-instance order, and dismiss each of the applications for the attachment and collection order at issue; accordingly, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, it is so ordered."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding a surety obligation is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Even if one guarantees the principal obligation while the period of extinctive prescription for the principal obligation, which falls under the short-term extinctive prescription under each item of Article 163 of the Civil Act, has been extended to 10 years by a final judgment against the principal obligor, unless special circumstances exist, the period of extinctive prescription for the surety obligation is determined separately according to the nature of the surety obligation.
B: It is, in principle, only the bill obligation arising from that bill guarantee that a person who expressly provides a bill guarantee on a promissory note issued by another person bears.
C: Where the surety of one of several joint tortfeasors has satisfied the damages liability of the guaranteed person, the surety may exercise a right of reimbursement against the other joint tortfeasors, other than the guaranteed person, only to the extent of each party’s share of burden.
D: Where a surety has guaranteed an indeterminate obligation under the principal contract arising from a continuing contractual relationship, the surety obligation becomes fixed together with the obligation under the principal contract when the latter becomes fixed, regardless of the time of termination of the surety contract.
E: An agreement to assign only the suretyship claim separately from the principal claim is without effect.
label: D

{"[2007DA37530]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Determination of the Plaintiffs' grounds for appeal\\n\\na. Joint tortfeasors bear joint and several liability (quasi-joint and several obligation) in relation to the creditor, but there is an apportioned share among the joint tortfeasors inter se, and such share is determined according to the degree of each party's intent and negligence; accordingly, when one of the joint tortfeasors has paid in excess of his own share and thereby obtained joint discharge, he may exercise a right of reimbursement against the other joint tortfeasors in proportion to their respective shares (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on July 8, 2005, 2005DA8125; Supreme Court Decision rendered on January 27, 2006, 2005DA19378). Also, a finding of fact as to the degree of negligence of the parties whose negligence concurred in the tort, or the fixing of the ratio thereof, falls within the exclusive province of the trier of fact unless it is recognized as manifestly unreasonable in light of the principle of equity (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on July 8, 2005, 2005DA8125; Supreme Court Decision rendered on March 24, 2006, 2005DA48253).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the court below first found the facts as stated in its opinion and then held that, although the Defendants had a duty of care, when purchasing the government grain at issue, to confirm whether the grain to be purchased was illegally released government grain purchased by the government or whether it had been stored by Non-party 2, acting on behalf of Non-party 1, for sale, by methods such as confirming the source of the said government grain and inspecting the packaging condition, they were negligent in failing to do so; that such tortious purchase of government grain by the Defendants through business negligence and Non-party 1's intentional embezzlement of government grain were objectively related and thus constituted a joint tort against the victim, Jeollanam-do; and that, in light of the circumstances surrounding the acquisition of stolen goods by the Defendants, the process and result thereof, and the various other circumstances revealed in the arguments of this case, it was reasonable to determine the internal apportionment ratio between Non-party 1 and the Defendants, who were joint tortfeasors, as 85:15. In light of the above legal principles and the record, the foregoing fact-finding and determination by the court below are proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the law regarding the evaluation of the degree of negligence among joint tortfeasors or the apportionment share, or factual mistake, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nb. Where a surety for one joint tortfeasor has paid damages on behalf of the principal debtor, the surety may exercise a right of reimbursement against another joint tortfeasor other than the principal debtor only to the extent of that party's share (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on February 9, 1996, 95DA47176), and this principle likewise applies where a reimbursement surety, who has guaranteed the reimbursement debt owed by one joint tortfeasor to the surety who paid the said damages, pays that reimbursement debt on behalf of the principal debtor; thus, the reimbursement surety may exercise a right of reimbursement against another joint tortfeasor other than the principal debtor only to the extent of that party's share.\\n\\nIn light of the above legal principles and the record, the Korea Grain Association, an incorporated association (hereinafter referred to as the \"Korea Grain Association\"), from July 16, 2001 to August 30, 2001, as joint and several surety for Non-party 1, by paying in subrogation to Jeollanam-do the damages caused by Non-party 1's embezzlement of government grain, acquired a right of reimbursement against Non-party 1, the principal debtor, for the full amount paid by subrogation, while at the same time acquiring a right of reimbursement against the Defendants, who are the other tortfeasors, only to the extent of each one's share; and the Plaintiffs, on August 30, 2001, as joint and several sureties for the reimbursement debt owed by Non-party 1 to the Korea Grain Association arising from the said payment by subrogation, by paying in subrogation that reimbursement debt to the Korea Grain Association, acquired a right of reimbursement against Non-party 1, the principal debtor, for the entire amount paid by subrogation, while at the same time acquiring a right of reimbursement against the Defendants, who are the other tortfeasors, only to the extent of each one's share; and simultaneously, the Korea Grain Association's said claim for reimbursement against the Defendants was transferred to the Plaintiffs, under the doctrine of subrogation by the party who made payment, on the basis of the Plaintiffs' said right of reimbursement against the Defendants.\\n\\nThe court below, on the same reasoning, held that the Plaintiffs may exercise the Korea Grain Association's said reimbursement claim against the Defendants only to the extent of each one's share; such determination is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the law concerning the content and scope of the right of reimbursement, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. Determination of the incidental grounds for appeal by Defendant 1 and Defendant Jinwon Agricultural Cooperative (hereinafter referred to as \"Defendant Jinwon Agricultural Cooperative\")\\n\\na. According to the record, the Korea Grain Association, after fully compensating Jeollanam-do for the damage caused by Non-party 1's embezzlement of government grain, filed an action for payment of the assigned claim against the said Defendants in the Gwangju District Court Case No. 2003GAHAP10485, alleging that it had been assigned from Jeollanam-do the damage compensation claim against the said Defendants, and thereafter, on August 26, 2004, received a judgment dismissing all claims, and it can be ascertained that the said judgment became final and conclusive around that time; however, the claim at issue in this case by Plaintiff Naju Industrial Warehouse seeks, by way of subrogation under the doctrine of subrogation by the person who has made payment under Article 481 of the Civil Act, to exercise the reimbursement claim held by the Korea Grain Association against the Defendants, and thus the subject matter of litigation differs from that of the above final judgment, so this lawsuit cannot be said to violate the res judicata of the said final judgment.\\n\\nThe court below's judgment to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the law concerning res judicata or standing as a party, as alleged in the incidental grounds for appeal.\\n\\nb. In light of the record, the court below's calculation of the scope of Defendant 1's and Defendant Jinwon Agricultural Cooperative's obligation to reimburse Plaintiff Naju Industrial Warehouse for the reimbursement money as KRW 7,926,294, corresponding to one-fifth of 15% of KRW 264,209,800, which is the sale price of the 5,023 sacks of government grain purchased by the said Defendants (KRW 264,209,800 × 0.15 × 1/5), is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the law concerning calculation of damages or factual mistake, as alleged in the incidental grounds for appeal.\\n\\nc. The extinctive prescription period for the right of reimbursement that a surety of one joint tortfeasor who has compensated the victim for damages holds against that joint tortfeasor or another joint tortfeasor is ten years, as with ordinary claims, and the starting point is the time when the right of reimbursement arises, that is, when the surety actually pays the damages to the victim (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on January 11, 1994, 93DA32958; Supreme Court Decision rendered on June 11, 1999, 99DA3143).\\n\\nThe court below, on the same reasoning, properly rejected the Defendants' argument that a 3-year short extinctive prescription period applies to the reimbursement claim at issue of Plaintiff Naju Industrial Warehouse, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the law concerning extinctive prescription of the right of reimbursement, as alleged in the incidental grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all of the Plaintiffs' appeal and the incidental appeal by Defendant 1 and Defendant Jinwon Agricultural Cooperative are dismissed, and the costs of appeal and the costs of incidental appeal shall be borne by the respective losing parties; accordingly, the Court renders judgment as stated in the disposition with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2011DA76105]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Since a guarantee obligation is an independent obligation separate from the principal obligation, the statute of limitations period for the guarantee obligation and that for the principal obligation are separately determined according to the nature of each obligation (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2010DA28031, rendered on 2010. 9. 9.). Also, where a person guarantees the principal obligation after the statute of limitations period for the principal obligation, which falls under the short statute of limitations in each item of Article 163 of the Civil Act, has been extended to 10 years by a final judgment against the principal debtor, unless special circumstances exist, there is no room to apply the short statute of limitations under each item of Article 163 of the Civil Act to that guarantee obligation, and depending on its nature, a statute of limitations period of 10 years applies if the creditor’s claim against the guarantor is a civil claim, and 5 years applies if it is a commercial claim.\\n\\nMeanwhile, not only a claim arising from an act that constitutes a commercial act for both parties, but also a claim arising from an act that constitutes a commercial act only for one party, falls under a commercial claim to which the 5-year statute of limitations prescribed in Article 64 of the Commercial Act applies; and the commercial acts referred to here include the subsidiary commercial acts under Article 47 of the Commercial Act that a merchant performs for business purposes (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DA7863, rendered on 2005. 5. 27.).\\n\\n2. a. According to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below, by citing the first-instance judgment, recognized the following facts: ① the Plaintiff, who operates a business selling construction materials, etc., supplied construction materials worth KRW 51,000,000 to Byeongyeong Construction Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Byeongyeong Construction”) from around 2005. 12. through around 2006. 3., received payment of KRW 1,900,000 among them, and held a claim for the purchase price of goods in the amount of KRW 49,100,000; ② the Plaintiff filed a lawsuit seeking payment of the purchase price of goods against Byeongyeong Construction in Ulsan District Court Case No. 2006GADAN27368, and on 2006. 9. 28., received a judgment stating, “Byeongyeong Construction shall pay the Plaintiff KRW 49,100,000 and interest thereon calculated at the rate of 20% per annum from 2006. 7. 13. until the date of full payment,” and that judgment became final and conclusive on 2006. 10. 25.; ③ after the above judgment became final and conclusive, on 2006. 12. 26., Byeongyeong Construction prepared for the Plaintiff a written acknowledgment of payment stating, “We confirm that the unpaid purchase price of KRW 49,200,935 will be promptly paid,” and the Defendant at that time jointly and severally guaranteed Byeongyeong Construction’s above obligation to pay the purchase price.\\n\\nFurthermore, based on the foregoing factual relations, the court below held that the statute of limitations period for the Plaintiff’s claim for the purchase price against Byeongyeong Construction was extended to 10 years by the above final and conclusive judgment, and that because the Defendant jointly and severally guaranteed the obligation of Byeongyeong Construction whose statute of limitations had thus been extended, the statute of limitations period for the Defendant’s guarantee obligation was also 10 years; accordingly, since the Plaintiff applied for a payment order against the Defendant on 2010. 7. 23., it held that the statute of limitations had not been completed with respect to the Plaintiff’s guarantee claim against the Defendant, and therefore rejected the Defendant’s statute-of-limitations defense.\\n\\nb. In light of the legal principles stated above and the factual relations found by the court below, the statute of limitations period for the Defendant’s guarantee obligation, who jointly and severally guaranteed the claim for the purchase price that had been finalized by a judgment against the principal debtor, should be deemed 10 years if the Plaintiff’s guarantee claim against the Defendant is a civil claim, and 5 years if it is a commercial claim.\\n\\nHowever, under Article 47 paragraphs (1) and (2) of the Commercial Act, acts performed by a merchant for business purposes are deemed commercial acts, and a merchant’s acts are presumed to be performed for business purposes; therefore, unless there is contrary proof, the act by which the merchant Plaintiff obtained joint and several guarantee from the Defendant with respect to the claim for the price of goods sold falls under a commercial act, and thus the Plaintiff’s guarantee claim against the Defendant should, unless special circumstances exist, be deemed a commercial claim, with a statute of limitations period of 5 years.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below held, for the reasons stated in its opinion, that the statute of limitations period for the Plaintiff’s guarantee claim against the Defendant is 10 years; this is erroneous. However, since it is clear from the record that the Plaintiff applied for the payment order in this case against the Defendant on 2010. 7. 23., before the 5-year statute of limitations for the above guarantee claim had expired, the court below’s rejection of the Defendant’s statute-of-limitations defense is correct in conclusion, and there is no illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the statute of limitations period for a guarantee obligation.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court decisions cited by the Defendant in the grounds of appeal concern different issues from this case and are not appropriate for citation in this case.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2019DA207141]": "We consider the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. In the case of a suretyship for an unliquidated debt under the principal contract arising from a continuing creditor-debtor relationship, the surety obligation ordinarily becomes fixed together with the principal contractual debt when that debt becomes fixed. However, where the contractual relationship of suretyship ends first because, for example, the transaction period under the principal contract was extended between the creditor and the principal debtor but the surety period was not extended as between the creditor and the surety, the surety obligation becomes fixed upon such termination; accordingly, the surety bears surety liability for the principal contractual debt existing at that time, but does not bear surety liability for debts arising thereafter.\\n\\nMeanwhile, where the person making payment is the principal debtor, there is no difference, in terms of the benefit of payment, between a debt with a surety and a debt without a surety; therefore, there is likewise no difference, in terms of the benefit of payment, between a debt arising during the surety period and a debt arising after the expiration of the surety period. Accordingly, the monies paid by the principal debtor must be appropriated as payment, in accordance with the law, first to the debts whose due date arrived earlier (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision dated Aug. 24, 1999, 99DA26481; Supreme Court Decision dated July 11, 2013, 2013DA22454).\\n\\n2. The court below acknowledged the following facts: on Aug. 5, 2009, the Plaintiff entered into an intermediary wholesaler trading agreement concerning the fruit and vegetable trade with the co-defendant in the first instance, the Non-Party (hereinafter referred to as “the instant trading agreement”), and conducted fruit and vegetable transactions until Feb. 1, 2017; on Aug. 6, 2009, the Defendant jointly and severally guaranteed the Non-Party’s obligations under the instant trading agreement up to 30,000,000 won (hereinafter referred to as “the instant joint and several suretyship agreement”); the Plaintiff’s claim for unpaid receivables against the Non-Party amounted to 106,118,939 won in July 2012 and 109,436,327 won in August of the same year; and then held that the instant joint and several suretyship agreement falls within a case where no fixed term is provided, and thus, pursuant to Article 7, paragraph (1) of the Special Act on the Protection of Sureties (hereinafter referred to as the “Surety Protection Act”), the surety period should be deemed to be 3 years. The court further held that, as of Aug. 5, 2012, the date of expiration of the above surety period, the Non-Party’s trade price debt to the Plaintiff exceeded the Defendant’s surety limit amount, and therefore the Defendant is obligated to pay the above 30,000,000 won and delay damages thereon to the Plaintiff.\\n\\n3. However, when the following circumstances recognized by the record are examined in light of the legal principles stated above, the above determination by the court below is difficult to accept as it stands.\\n\\na. As the cause of action in this case against the Defendant, the Plaintiff alleged that the instant joint and several suretyship agreement was a limited continuing suretyship with no fixed term and thus remained in force until the instant transaction relationship under the principal contract terminated; accordingly, the Defendant is obligated to pay 30,000,000 won, the surety limit amount, out of the Non-Party’s trade price debt to the Plaintiff, amounting to 84,647,938 won and fixed as of Feb. 1, 2017, when the said transaction relationship terminated. On the other hand, the Plaintiff acknowledged the fact that it received from the Non-Party, as trade price under the instant trading agreement, 79,627,272 won in September 2012, 14,351,400 won in December of the same year, and 43,749,290 won in January 2013, and submitted Exhibit A No. 6 (performance statement) consistent therewith.\\n\\nb. In response, the Defendant disputed to the effect that “the Defendant’s joint and several surety period expired on Aug. 6, 2012, and the Plaintiff’s claim is for the principal debt arising thereafter,” and such assertion by the Defendant may be construed as including the purport that the principal debt arising during the above surety period asserted by the Defendant was extinguished by payment, etc. Even if not, the court below needed to exercise its power to seek clarification against the Defendant and clearly ascertain the content of the Defendant’s assertion by clarifying whether the purport was that no principal debt existed at the time of termination of the instant joint and several suretyship agreement, or that all such debt was extinguished by later payments, etc.\\n\\nc. Meanwhile, according to the facts acknowledged by the court below, where the Defendant’s surety period expired before the transaction period under the principal contract, the portion of the Non-Party’s debt for trade price owed to the Plaintiff under the instant agreement that arose within the Defendant’s surety period would fall due earlier than the portion arising thereafter; therefore, among the Non-Party’s entire trade price debt to the Plaintiff, the monies paid by the Non-Party to the Plaintiff pursuant to the instant trading agreement should be appropriated first to the portion of the debt arising within the Defendant’s surety period, whose due date arrived earlier. If so, in light of the circumstances mentioned above, there is a strong possibility that the Defendant’s surety obligation has been extinguished.\\n\\n4. Nevertheless, while accepting the Defendant’s assertion that the surety period for the instant joint and several suretyship agreement is 3 years pursuant to Article 7, paragraph (1) of the Surety Protection Act, the court below upheld the Plaintiff’s claim solely on the ground that the Non-Party’s accounts-receivable debt to the Plaintiff exceeded the Defendant’s surety limit amount as of the expiration of the above surety period. The judgment below erred by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the scope of a surety’s liability in continuing suretyship and payment appropriation, or by failing to fully conduct the necessary deliberation due to neglecting to exercise the power to seek clarification, thereby affecting the judgment. The ground of appeal asserting this point is well-founded.\\n\\n5. Therefore, the judgment of the court below shall be reversed, and the case shall be remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, as stated in the Disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding ownership in common of real property is correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: A lawsuit in which one of the co-owners in common of real property for which registration of ownership in common has been completed seeks performance of the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of termination of a title trust does not constitute an indispensable joint action.
B: Even if a transfer of ownership registration has been completed in the sole name of a specific partner with respect to real property purchased by the partnership, if the partnership is dissolved, liquidation must be carried out on the premise that the real property is partnership property.
C: The court cannot directly order the division of property jointly owned in common with a third party by one spouse of a divorcing couple, but it may calculate the value of that spouse's share in the ownership in common and make it the object of property division.
D: If, with respect to real property purchased by the partnership, a registration of co-ownership concerning each share has been completed in the name of each partner instead of a registration of ownership in common, the real property becomes property held in common, even if the seller did not know that the purchaser of the real property was the partnership.
E: A partner who agreed to contribute real property owned by him or her and delivered that real property may exercise the right to demand return of the property with respect to that real property not only against the partnership but also against third parties until registration of ownership in common of that real property has been completed.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2000DA30622]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Summary of the judgment of the court below\\n\\nAccording to the reasons for the judgment of the court below, the court below rejected the Defendants’ assertion on the following grounds: although the court below jointly purchased the land at issue by Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants and, formally, registered transfer of ownership in accordance with their co-ownership shares in the name of Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, because the land at issue was purchased by Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants pursuant to the partnership agreement at issue and thus, by operation of law, became the joint property of Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, the land interest at issue registered in the name of Codefendant 1 in the court below was nothing more than a title trust of that joint property, so the title trust itself is void under Article 4(2) of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder's Name and is not owned by Codefendant 1 in the court below, and therefore cannot be regarded as property subject to liability that serves as common security for the general creditors of the debtor, and thus, even though Codefendant 1 in the court below withdrew from the partnership and concluded a contract of sale with the Defendants concerning the land interest at issue and completed registration of transfer of ownership in the name of the Defendants, this did not cause any reduction in Codefendant 1’s liability property, and moreover, this was merely the performance of his obligation, upon withdrawal from the partnership, to return his partnership share to the remaining partners and was therefore equivalent to performance of an existing debt, so the contract of sale at issue does not, in any respect, constitute a fraudulent transfer.\\n\\nThat is, as to whether the land at issue, which was the premise of the Defendants’ argument, became by operation of law the joint property of Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, Articles 271 and 704 of the Civil Act cannot be regarded as provisions corresponding to the “acquisition of real rights by operation of law” prescribed in Article 187 of the Civil Act; therefore, in order for joint ownership of real estate in a partnership to be established, a joint ownership registration in the names of all partners is required, and Articles 271 and 704 of the Civil Act are permissive provisions such that it is always possible for the partners, by agreement among themselves, to determine the ownership relationship of partnership property differently from these provisions. Therefore, once registration of transfer of ownership in co-ownership in the names of Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants was completed with respect to the land at issue, the land at issue could not become the joint property of Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants. Further, in light of the fact that Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants jointly purchased the land at issue without any special agreement before they concluded the partnership agreement at issue, and that although they thereafter concluded the partnership agreement at issue, the registration of transfer of ownership with respect to the land at issue alone was made not as joint ownership of Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants but as co-ownership, it is reasonable to view that when Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants purchased the land at issue, they agreed to have the ownership relationship in that land as co-ownership between Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants. Accordingly, at the time Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants concluded the contract of sale at issue, the land interest at issue was, in any event, solely owned by Codefendant 1 in the court below; thus, without further review, the Defendants’ assertion, premised on the proposition that the entire land at issue including that share was the joint property of Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, lacks merit.\\n\\n2. This Court’s determination\\n\\nHowever, the above determination of the court below cannot be accepted as it stands.\\n\\na. Where two or more persons jointly purchase real estate, the legal relationship among the purchasers is one of co-ownership, and they are merely joint purchasers; thus, there may be cases where the seller bears the obligation to register transfer of ownership of the respective shares in favor of the multiple purchasers, and there may also be cases where the purchase was made by a business association whose partners are those multiple persons, and the seller bears the obligation to transfer the entire ownership to that business association (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of September 15, 1995, 94DA54894), whereas if the owner of real estate agreed, pursuant to a partnership agreement (association agreement), to invest the ownership of the real estate but the property is still registered in his name and has not been registered as joint ownership of the partners, then a claim-right relationship arises between him and the partnership, and it may be said that he owes a duty to transfer ownership to the partnership or a duty to permit its use; however, there is no basis for deeming, on account of that partnership agreement, that the real estate belongs to the joint ownership of the partners in relation to persons other than the parties to the partnership agreement, and therefore as against a third party who is not a partner, he may still exercise ownership as the owner (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of July 12, 1991, 90DA13161).\\n\\nHowever, Article 271(1) of the Civil Act provides that “when two or more persons own an object as an association pursuant to the provisions of law or contract, it shall be joint ownership. The rights of joint owners extend to the whole of the jointly owned thing,” and this is a provision under real rights law and is therefore a mandatory provision, so if the members of an association that is a collective body share ownership, it cannot be regarded as ownership of an object by the association as a collective body. Article 704 of the Civil Act provides that “contributions by partners and other partnership property shall be joint property of the partners,” so if a partnership established for the purpose of a joint business acquired ownership of real estate as a collective body or as partnership property, then by virtue of Article 271(1) of the Civil Act it naturally becomes joint property of that collective body (this has nothing to do with the “acquisition of real rights by operation of law” prescribed in Article 187 of the Civil Act. Accordingly, if the collective body acquires real estate by a legal act, registration of transfer of ownership is of course required). However, if that collective body did not make a joint ownership registration but instead made co-ownership registrations in the names of the partners with respect to each share, this must be regarded as the collective body having made a title trust to the partners with respect to each share (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of May 30, 1997, 95DA4957).\\n\\nThe court below, however, found that in light of the fact that Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants jointly purchased the land at issue without any special agreement before they concluded the partnership agreement at issue, and that although they thereafter concluded the partnership agreement at issue, the registration of transfer of ownership with respect to the land at issue alone was made not as joint ownership of Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants but as co-ownership, it is reasonable to view that when Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants purchased the land at issue, they agreed to have the ownership relationship in that land as co-ownership between Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants. However, clause 1 of the partnership agreement (Exhibit B No. 2-2) states, “The above Defendant 1 and three others mutually, and after amicable consultation, agreed and contracted to jointly invest and purchase the land at issue in accordance with the above share ratios and to jointly operate a housing construction and sale business.” Further, when this is supplemented by special provisions 2 and 3 of the real estate sale contract (Exhibit B No. 2-1), it is clear that when Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants purchased the land at issue, that is, at the time they concluded the sales contract, they already had the motive and purpose of jointly investing one-fourth shares each to purchase the land and then jointly constructing and selling houses. Therefore, even if a partnership agreement containing specific details was prepared after the conclusion of the sales contract, it is reasonable to regard that they were already in a partnership relationship at that time. Accordingly, since this is a case in which the partnership collective formed by Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants acquired the land at issue as partnership property, it cannot be viewed differently merely because co-ownership registration rather than joint ownership registration was made thereafter; rather, that co-ownership registration should be regarded as nothing more than the partnership collective having made a title trust to Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants with respect to each share.\\n\\nb. Furthermore, the registration of transfer of ownership concerning the land interest at issue in the name of Codefendant 1 in the court below was made, after the enforcement of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder's Name (enforced from July 1, 1995; hereinafter referred to as the “Real Estate Real Name Registration Act”), in the name of the title trustee as a registration of real rights concerning real estate pursuant to a title trust agreement between the partnership collective formed by Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants for the purpose of a joint business and Codefendant 1 in the court below; thus, the main text of Article 4(2) of the Real Estate Real Name Registration Act applies, and the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of the title trustee is void. However, only where, under the proviso of Article 4(2) of the same Act, in a contract for acquiring a real right concerning the land interest at issue, the title trustee, namely Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, becomes one party to that contract, and the other party, the seller Daehwa Co., Ltd., is unaware of the fact that there is a title trust agreement between the partnership collective formed by Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants and Codefendant 1 in the court below, would the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of the title trustee concerning the land interest at issue be valid.\\n\\nHowever, if the main text of Article 4(2) of the same Act applies to the land interest at issue so that the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of Codefendant 1 in the court below is void, then because that land interest is not owned by him, it cannot be regarded as property subject to liability that serves as common security for general creditors. Accordingly, even if on April 23, 1998, Codefendant 1 in the court below withdrew from the partnership established pursuant to the partnership agreement at issue on the ground that he had failed properly to perform his capital contribution under the partnership agreement at issue, and concluded with the Defendants the amendment agreement of the partnership at issue under which Codefendant 1 in the court below withdrew and the partnership shares of the remaining partners, namely the Defendants, were each set at one-third, and even if on the following day Codefendant 1 in the court below completed registration of transfer of ownership in the name of the Defendants, based on the sale contract dated April 23, 1998, for one-twelfth each out of his one-fourth share in the land at issue, this cannot be said to have caused any reduction in the debtor Codefendant 1 in the court below’s property subject to liability. Therefore, this cannot be deemed a fraudulent transfer harming the Plaintiffs, who are general creditors, and it cannot be said that he harbored fraudulent intent (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of March 10, 2000, 99DA55069).\\n\\nUltimately, under the factual findings recognized by the court below, unless circumstances are revealed that would allow the proviso of Article 4(2) of the same Act to apply so that the transaction could be viewed as valid {rather, in light of special provisions 2 and 3 of the real estate sale contract (Exhibit B No. 2-1) and part of the testimony of Witness 1 at first instance, it appears that the seller, Daehwa Co., Ltd., was involved to a considerable extent even in matters relating to building permits on the land at issue.}, the registration of transfer of ownership based on the contract of sale at issue between Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants concerning the land interest at issue cannot be deemed to constitute a fraudulent transfer.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below, relying only on the reasons stated in its opinion and taking the view that at the time Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants concluded the contract of sale at issue, the land interest at issue was solely owned by Codefendant 1 in the court below and that the entire land at issue including that share was the joint property of Codefendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, rejected the Defendants’ argument as lacking merit, and then granted the Plaintiffs’ second alternative claim concerning the land at issue. Accordingly, this part of the judgment of the court below contains errors of law in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the ownership relationship of partnership property, title trust, and fraudulent transfer, as well as errors in fact-finding by violating the rules of evidence or by failing to conduct necessary examination; and it is clear that this affected the judgment.\\n\\nThe part of the grounds of final appeal pointing this out has merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without further examining the remaining grounds for final appeal, the portion of the judgment of the court below unfavorable to the Defendants is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the judges participating."}

{"[2000DA30622]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Summary of the judgment of the court below\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below rejected the Defendants’ argument on the following grounds: although Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants jointly purchased the land at issue and, formally, completed registration of transfer of ownership in favor of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants according to their co-ownership shares, on the premise that the land at issue, pursuant to law, naturally became joint property of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, the land share at issue registered in the name of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below was merely held in title trust for such joint property, so that the title trust itself is void under Article 4(2) of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name, and because it is not owned by Co-Defendant 1 in the court below, it cannot be regarded as property subject to execution, to be made available as common security for general creditors of the debtor, and therefore, even if Co-Defendant 1 in the court below, upon withdrawing from the partnership, entered into a sale and purchase contract with the Defendants concerning the land share at issue and completed registration of transfer of ownership in favor of the Defendants, this did not cause any diminution in the responsible property of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below; moreover, this was nothing more than performance of his obligation, upon withdrawing from the partnership, to restore his partnership share to the remaining partners, and thus was equivalent to satisfaction of an existing debt; accordingly, the sale and purchase contract at issue does not constitute a fraudulent act in any respect.\\n\\nThat is, with respect to whether the land at issue, which was the premise of the Defendants’ argument, naturally became joint property of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants pursuant to law, Articles 271 and 704 of the Civil Act cannot be regarded as provisions falling under the “acquisition of real rights by operation of law” prescribed in Article 187 of the Civil Act; therefore, in order for joint ownership of real estate by a partnership to arise, registration of joint ownership in the names of all partners is required, and Articles 271 and 704 of the Civil Act are non-mandatory provisions, so that it is always possible, by agreement among the partners, to determine ownership relations of partnership property differently from those provisions. Accordingly, once registration of transfer of ownership with respect to the land at issue was completed as co-ownership in the names of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, the land at issue could not become joint property of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants. Furthermore, in light of the fact that Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants jointly purchased the land at issue without any special agreement before entering into the partnership agreement at issue, and although they thereafter entered into the partnership agreement at issue, they nevertheless registered transfer of ownership with respect to the land at issue as co-ownership rather than joint ownership in the names of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, it is reasonable to view that, at the time Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants purchased the land at issue, they agreed to hold ownership of it as co-ownership between Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants. Therefore, at the time Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants entered into the sale and purchase contract at issue, the land share at issue was, in any event, solely owned by Co-Defendant 1 in the court below; thus, the Defendants’ argument, which is premised on the assertion that the entirety of the land at issue, including that share, was joint property of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, is without merit, without need for further examination.\\n\\n2. This Court’s determination\\n\\nHowever, the above determination by the court below is difficult to accept as it stands.\\n\\nA. Where multiple persons jointly purchase real estate, the legal relationship among the purchasers may, as a co-ownership relationship, be merely that of simple joint purchasers, in which case the seller may owe an obligation to register transfer of ownership of the respective shares to the multiple purchasers; or, if the purchase is made by a partnership entity composed of such multiple persons as partners, the seller may owe the obligation to transfer the entirety of the ownership to that partnership entity (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA54894, rendered September 15, 1995, among others). On the other hand, if the owner of real estate agreed, pursuant to a partnership agreement (joint venture agreement), to contribute the ownership of the real estate, but the property is still registered in his own ownership and not registered as joint ownership by the partners, then a contractual right and obligation arise between him and the partnership, so that it may be said that he has an obligation to transfer ownership to the partnership or an obligation to permit its use; however, there is no basis for concluding, merely on the ground of that partnership agreement, that, in relation to a person who is not a party to the partnership agreement, the real estate belongs to the joint ownership of the partners, and therefore, as against a third party who is not a partner, he may still exercise ownership as the owner (see Supreme Court Decision 90DA13161, rendered July 12, 1991, among others).\\n\\nHowever, Article 271(1) of the Civil Act provides that “When two or more persons own a thing as a partnership entity by virtue of law or contract, it shall be joint ownership. The rights of joint owners extend to the whole of the jointly owned thing,” and this is a provision of property law and therefore a mandatory provision (and thus, where the members of a partnership entity hold the property in co-ownership, it cannot be regarded as the ownership of a thing by a partnership entity), while Article 704 of the Civil Act provides that “The contributions of partners and other partnership property shall be joint property of the partners.” Accordingly, if a partnership formed for the purpose of joint venture has acquired ownership of real estate as a partnership entity or as partnership property, it naturally becomes joint property of that partnership entity pursuant to Article 271(1) of the Civil Act (this has nothing to do with the “acquisition of real rights by operation of law” prescribed in Article 187 of the Civil Act. Therefore, where the partnership entity acquires real estate by legal act, registration of transfer of ownership is of course required). However, if that partnership entity does not register joint ownership and instead registers co-ownership of each share in the names of the partners, it must be regarded as that partnership entity having held title trust for each share in the names of the partners (see Supreme Court Decision 95DA4957, rendered May 30, 1997, among others).\\n\\nIn the present case, the court below determined that, in light of the facts that Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants jointly purchased the land at issue without any special agreement before entering into the partnership agreement at issue, and that although they thereafter entered into the partnership agreement at issue, they nevertheless registered transfer of ownership with respect to the land at issue as co-ownership rather than joint ownership in the names of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, it is reasonable to regard Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants as having agreed, at the time they purchased the land at issue, to hold the ownership thereof as co-ownership between Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants. However, clause 1 of the partnership agreement (Exhibit B No. 2-2) states that “the above Defendants 1 and three others mutually amicably agreed and contracted to jointly invest in and purchase the land at issue in accordance with the above respective share ratios, and to engage in a joint venture business of building and selling houses.” In addition, when this is combined with clauses 2 and 3 of the special agreements in the real estate sale and purchase contract (Exhibit B No. 2-1), it is clear that, when Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants purchased the land at issue, that is, at the time they entered into the sale and purchase contract, they already had the motive or purpose of jointly investing in and purchasing the land in 1/4 shares each, and then jointly constructing and selling houses. Therefore, even if they thereafter prepared a partnership agreement containing specific details after executing the sale and purchase contract, it is reasonable to regard them as already being in a partnership relationship at that time. Accordingly, the land at issue was acquired as partnership property by the partnership entity formed by Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants for the purpose of joint venture, and it cannot be viewed differently merely because registration of co-ownership rather than joint ownership was subsequently made; rather, such co-ownership registration must be regarded as nothing more than title trust by the partnership entity to Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants for each share.\\n\\nB. Furthermore, the registration of transfer of ownership with respect to the land share at issue in the name of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below was made, after the enforcement of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name (effective from July 1, 1995; hereinafter referred to as the “Real Name Act”), by registering the real right in real estate in the name of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below, who was the title trustee, pursuant to a title-trust agreement between the partnership entity formed by Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants for the purpose of joint venture and Co-Defendant 1 in the court below. Thus, the main clause of Article 4(2) of the Real Name Act applies, and the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of the title trustee is void. However, only if, under the proviso to Article 4(2) of that Act, in a contract for acquiring a real right with respect to the land share at issue, Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, who are the title trustee, are one party thereto, and the other party thereto, the seller, Daehwa Co., Ltd., did not know of the existence of the title-trust agreement between the partnership entity formed by Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants for the purpose of joint venture and Co-Defendant 1 in the court below, would the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below with respect to the land share at issue be valid.\\n\\nHowever, if the main clause of Article 4(2) of the same Act applies to the land share at issue and the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below with respect thereto is void, then the land share was not owned by him, and therefore it cannot be regarded as property subject to execution made available as common security for general creditors. Accordingly, even if Co-Defendant 1 in the court below withdrew on April 23, 1998 from the partnership formed under the partnership agreement on the ground that he had failed properly to perform his contribution under the partnership agreement at issue, and, upon such withdrawal, entered into the partnership change agreement at issue with the Defendants, whereby Co-Defendant 1 in the court below withdrew and the partnership shares of the remaining partners, the Defendants, were each fixed at 1/3, and even if Co-Defendant 1 in the court below completed on the following day the registration of transfer of ownership in favor of the Defendants, with respect to 1/12 each out of his 1/4 share in the land at issue, based on the sale and purchase contract dated April 23, 1998, this cannot be said to have caused any diminution in the responsible property of the debtor, Co-Defendant 1 in the court below; therefore, it cannot be regarded as a fraudulent act harming the Plaintiffs, who are general creditors, and it cannot be said that he had fraudulent intent (see Supreme Court Decision 99DA55069, rendered March 10, 2000, among others).\\n\\nUltimately, under the facts found by the court below, unless circumstances are revealed that would allow the proviso to Article 4(2) of the same Act to be applied and the transaction to be regarded as valid {rather, in light of clauses 2 and 3 of the special agreements in the real estate sale and purchase contract (Exhibit B No. 2-1) and part of the testimony of Witness 1 at first instance, the seller, Daehwa Co., Ltd., appears to have been involved to a considerable extent even in matters relating to the building permit on the land at issue.}, the registration of transfer of ownership, based on the sale and purchase contract at issue between Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, with respect to the land share at issue, cannot be regarded as a fraudulent act.\\n\\nC. Nevertheless, the court below, unlike the foregoing, rejected the Defendants’ argument premised on the assertion that, at the time Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants entered into the sale and purchase contract at issue, the land share at issue was solely owned by Co-Defendant 1 in the court below, so that the entirety of the land at issue, including that share, was joint property of Co-Defendant 1 in the court below and the Defendants, on the sole ground of the reasons stated in its holding, and upheld the Plaintiffs’ second alternative claim with respect to the land at issue. Accordingly, this part of the judgment of the court below contains errors of law in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning ownership relations in partnership property, title trust, and fraudulent acts, and also contains an error in finding facts in violation of the rules of evidence or by failing to conduct the necessary examination, and it is clear that such errors affected the judgment.\\n\\nThe portion of the grounds of appeal pointing out this issue is meritorious.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without need to further examine the remaining grounds of appeal, the portion of the judgment of the court below against the Defendants is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. The judgment is rendered as set forth in the order by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2009MEU2840]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nIn the present case, in which the Plaintiff (Counterclaim Defendant; hereinafter referred to as the “Plaintiff”) sought divorce and division of property, etc. against the Defendant (Counterclaim Plaintiff; hereinafter referred to as the “Defendant”), the appellate court, in response to the Plaintiff’s assertion that the land at issue, which is registered as joint ownership by the Defendant and Non-party 1, should be included in the subject of division of property because it is substantially owned solely by the Defendant, held that property registered as joint ownership is not individually owned property but property owned by the body of joint owners and therefore excluded the land at issue from the subject of division of property.\\n\\nHowever, the appellate court’s above determination cannot be accepted for the following reasons.\\n\\nEven property registered in a third party’s name becomes a subject of division of property, in the sense that, if it is property nominally entrusted by one spouse to the other spouse, or property substantially controlled by one spouse and formed through the cooperation of both spouses, or based on tangible or intangible resources formed through the cooperation of both spouses, or if the other spouse’s housework, etc. has directly or indirectly contributed to its maintenance, such circumstances must also be taken into account (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 96MEU1434 rendered on April 10, 1998).\\n\\nAlso, property cannot be excluded from the subject of division of property merely because it is joint property; rather, if one spouse jointly owns property with a third party, or the share therein, such property or share cannot be freely disposed of (Civil Act Article 272 main sentence, Article 273(1)). Accordingly, although direct division of the relevant property cannot be ordered, it should be included in the subject of division of property by calculating the value of the share and treating it as the object of division, or by taking it into account in the division of other property.\\n\\nAccording to the evidence adopted by the appellate court and the record, the deceased Non-party 2 (died in 1983) purchased several parcels of land in the area of Opo-eup, Gwangju City, (omitted), during his lifetime and registered them as joint ownership or co-ownership of his sons, namely the Defendant and Non-party 1. The land at issue is one of those parcels and was registered on February 19, 1970 as joint ownership of the Defendant and Non-party 1. Meanwhile, the Defendant has been using the land at issue exclusively by constructing and residing in a farmhouse and warehouse on the land and installing vinyl greenhouses and farming there, whereas Non-party 1 has not been involved at all in the use or enjoyment of the land at issue. With respect to the aforementioned house and warehouse on the land at issue, ownership preservation registration has been completed in the Defendant’s sole name, and the land at issue has been provided as security for the Defendant’s personal debt. The Defendant, after the conflict with the Plaintiff became pronounced, prepared a document on August 30, 2006 (Exhibit A No. 3) stating that he would transfer the land at issue, together with other land registered in his sole name, to the children born between himself and the Plaintiff.
