B's claim for the construction price against A and the notice of assignment by an instrument bearing a fixed date reached A the next day, and A's claim for the defect repair deposit arose thereafter, A may set it off against C's claim for the assigned amount using it as the automatic claim.
B: If C, knowing the fact that A and B had agreed not to assign the construction price claim, obtained an attachment and assignment order with respect to B's claim for the construction price against A, and the order became final, the attachment and assignment order is valid.
C: If C obtained an attachment and assignment order on 2023. 4. 1. with respect to B's claim for the construction price against A, and the above attachment and assignment order was served on both A and B the next day and became final, then if A had a loan claim against B before being served with the above attachment and assignment order, and the maturity date of the loan claim was 2023. 8. 1., A may set off the loan claim against B as the automatic claim against C's claim for the assigned amount.
D: If B assigned to C on 2023. 10. 1. the claim for the construction price against A and the notice of assignment by an instrument bearing a fixed date reached A on 2023. 11. 1., and if C sets off against A's loan claim against C, whose maturity date is 2023. 9. 1., using the claim for the assigned amount, the date on which setoff became possible is 2023. 11. 1.
E: If B assigned to C on 2023. 4. 1. the claim for the construction price against A and the notice of assignment by an instrument bearing a fixed date reached A the next day, and then D, another creditor of B, obtained an attachment order on 2023. 5. 1. with respect to B's claim for the construction price against A, if the above assignment was later revoked by a fraudulent conveyance revocation lawsuit filed by E, another creditor of B, the above attachment order is valid as one concerning the claim for the construction price that will be restored to B in the future in its original condition.
label: E

{"[2004DA37676]": "1. Judgment of the court below\\n\\nThe court below first, by comprehensively considering the evidence cited in its reasoning, found the following facts: namely, that the non-party Jia Industry Co., Ltd. (whose trade name was later changed to “Gyeongbu Industry Co., Ltd.”; hereinafter, for convenience, referred to as “Jia Industry”) was, on 1999. 12. 13., awarded by the Defendant a contract for the “anti-slip paving work between Olympic-daero Ha-il and Hangju Bridge” at a construction price of KRW 410,575,146; that Non-party 1, on 1999. 12. 27., subcontracted the above paving work from Jia Industry and completed the work around 2000. 5. 12.; that the Plaintiff, based on the original copy of an enforceable promissory note notarial deed No. 77 of 2000 issued by the certified notary office Sae Seoul Joint Law Office with respect to Jia Industry, obtained on 2000. 5. 23. from the Seoul District Court in Case No. 2000TAGI4798 an order of attachment and assignment (hereinafter referred to as “the assignment order in this case”) with respect to Jia Industry’s claim for the above construction price against the Defendant, and that said order was served on the Defendant around that time and became final and conclusive on 2000. 8. 8.; and that thereafter, taking into account the legislative purpose of Article 88, paragraph (1) of the Framework Act on the Construction Industry then in force, the Defendant, with the consent of the Plaintiff, directly paid on 2000. 6. 5. the amount of KRW 126,634,460 corresponding to the labor-cost portion among the construction price in this case to Jia Industry and Non-party 1, etc.\\n\\nBased on the above factual findings, the court below further held that, as the claim for the construction price in this case had been transferred to the Plaintiff by the assignment order in this case, the Defendant, absent special circumstances, was obliged to pay the amount assigned pursuant to the assignment order in this case to the Plaintiff, and, with respect to the Defendant’s following setoff defense, namely, the assertion that it set off, in equal amounts, the above debt for the assigned amount against the claim for reimbursement it held against Jia Industry by using that right of reimbursement as the active claim, rejected that defense on the ground that there was no evidence sufficient to conclude that the Defendant had in fact acquired a right of reimbursement against Jia Industry, and thus, in substance, upheld the judgment of the first instance court, which largely granted the Plaintiff’s claim in this case.\\n\\n2. Determination on the grounds for appeal\\n\\nHowever, the above disposition of the court below is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nA. Article 136 of the Civil Procedure Act provides: “The presiding judge may, for the purpose of clarifying the litigation relationship, ask the parties questions regarding factual or legal matters and may urge them to produce evidence.” (paragraph (1)); and “The court shall give the parties an opportunity to state their opinions on legal matters that are recognized as having clearly been overlooked by the parties.” (paragraph (4)). Accordingly, where there exists a legal matter that a party has clearly overlooked through negligence or misunderstanding, or where there is a contradiction or lack of clarity in a party’s assertions, the court must actively exercise its power to clarify and afford the parties an opportunity to state their opinions; if it fails to do so, it must be deemed unlawful as having failed to discharge its duty to clarify or point out matters (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2003. 1. 10., 2002DA41435). According to the record, the Defendant also asserted that “if the cause of the traffic accident is found to be a defect in the construction of the anti-slip speed bump, then, as provided in the contract terms, the above Jia Industry must bear sole responsibility for compensating the damage suffered by the above non-party decedents” (record pp. 43, 139); and that “if the Defendant Seoul Metropolitan Government loses the damages action and pays compensation to the bereaved families, then the Defendant Seoul Metropolitan Government will have a right to claim reimbursement from the above Jia Industry, the claim creditor for the construction price in this case, in the amount corresponding to the compensation paid” (record p. 162); and that “if the Defendant, who bears the debt to pay damages to the victims, sets off the claim for reimbursement corresponding to the damages and the claim for the construction price in this case, then the above construction price claim will be extinguished in full” (record pp. 241, 265, 306, etc.). However, through the preparatory brief dated 2002. 4. 9., etc., the Defendant also asserted that “as regards the traffic accident, since liability to pay damages has been recognized, if the Defendant Seoul Metropolitan Government, which acquires a damages claim against the above Jia Industry or a claim for reimbursement arising from payment of such damages, sets off the amount corresponding to such damages or the claim for reimbursement arising from such payment against the construction price claim in this case, the above construction price claim will be extinguished in full” (record p. 177); that “the specific active claim for setoff, such as the Defendant Seoul Metropolitan Government’s damages amount or reimbursement claim against the above Jia Industry, with the construction price claim of Jia Industry as the passive claim, can only be calculated once the judgment in the above case becomes final and conclusive” (record pp. 241, 266); and that “for Jia Industry, there is no way to avoid liability to pay damages arising from the accident in this case to the Defendant Seoul Metropolitan Government” (record p. 351). Thus, the Defendant’s above assertions regarding the basis for the occurrence and the nature of the active claim in this case were not entirely free from ambiguity from a legal standpoint. In light of the above legal principles, the court below should first have actively exercised its power to clarify and determined whether the basis and nature of the active claim asserted by the Defendant in this case were confined merely to a right of reimbursement in the internal relationship among quasi-joint and several obligors, or whether they also included, in addition thereto, a damages claim that the contracting party Defendant could assert against the contractor Jia Industry under Article 390 of the Civil Act (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2004. 8. 20., 2001DA70337), and then, accordingly, should have proceeded to determine the propriety of the Defendant’s assertions as thus clearly revealed. It cannot be otherwise said.\\n\\nB. If, however, the Defendant asserted even such damages claim as the active claim for setoff in this case, then the court below, by failing entirely to determine the propriety of such setoff defense, committed the error of omitting a determination, and there is ample room to view that such error affected the outcome of the judgment in this case, as seen below.\\n\\nThat is, where damage to the body or property of the employer occurs because the contractor has failed properly to perform its obligations under the contract for work, unless the contractor proves on its own that there was no cause attributable to it, the contractor must be deemed liable to compensate the employer for such damage (see the above-mentioned Supreme Court Decision 2001DA70337). Originally, the defense of simultaneous performance is a system under which, based on the concept of fairness and the principle of good faith and fair dealing, where the obligations borne by each party are related in a reciprocal sense, a correlative relationship in performance is recognized in the process of performance, so that one party may refuse to perform its own obligation when the other party seeks performance of the first party’s obligation without performing or offering to perform its own obligation. In light of the purpose of this system, even if the respective obligations borne by the parties are not obligations with an inherent reciprocal exchange relationship in a bilateral contract, where, according to the terms concerning the obligations borne by each party in a specific contractual relationship, there are circumstances in which they should be recognized as having reciprocal significance and a correlative relationship in performance, the defense of simultaneous performance must be recognized (see Supreme Court Decisions rendered on 2004. 8. 30., 2004DA24236, 24243, etc.). Further, as a result of Article 536 of the Civil Act being applied mutatis mutandis pursuant to Article 667, paragraph (3) of the Civil Act, the damages claim that the employer may assert together with repair of defects against the contractor and the contractor’s claim for the construction price are in a relationship of simultaneous performance; accordingly, in light of such considerations, the contractor’s damages obligation for damages from the expansion of defects and the employer’s obligation to pay the construction price should also be regarded as being in a relationship of simultaneous performance. Moreover, where the active claim held by a third-party debtor against the attaching debtor is in a relationship of simultaneous performance with the attached claim, even if the active claim arose only after the attachment order was served on the third-party debtor and the effect of attachment arose, the third-party debtor who may assert the defense of simultaneous performance may oppose the attaching creditor by way of setoff based on that claim; in such case, because the cause underlying the occurrence of the active claim had already been established and existed before the passive claim was attached, the active claim does not fall under “a claim acquired thereafter by a third-party debtor who has received an order prohibiting payment” as provided in Article 498 of the Civil Act (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 1993. 9. 28., 92DA55794).\\n\\nAccording to the record, the construction work in this case consisted of applying anti-slip aggregate, which enhances friction at certain intervals over a certain area so as to prevent vehicles from skidding on curved or inclined sections of Olympic-daero; and if incompletely bonded aggregate detached, it could instead increase vehicle skidding, so after applying the aggregate, traffic had to be controlled continuously for more than one hour to allow sufficient curing, and thereafter any remaining aggregate that had not adhered had to be cleaned up completely; moreover, because aggregate could further detach due to vehicle traffic, cleaning had to be repeated for one or two days after the work. Non-party 1, the subcontractor, immediately after approval by the Traffic Operations Improvement Planning Team and modification of the contract for work were made, on 2000. 2. 11., deployed subordinate employees, day laborers, and construction equipment and first completed the work at the Amsa-dong point in Gangdong-gu, Seoul, and then, continuously from around 10:00 on 2000. 2. 13. (Sunday), proceeded with the work for the 3rd and 4th lanes out of the four lanes over the approximately 75-meter right-curving section in front of Cheongdam 2 Bridge located in Samsung-dong, Gangnam-gu, Seoul. At that time, the traffic police patrolling Olympic-daero discovered that traffic in the work section was being controlled and congestion was occurring, and requested Non-party 1, etc. to complete the finishing work as soon as possible for the smooth passage of vehicles for the International Joint Blessing Wedding Ceremony scheduled to be held at Jamsil Sports Complex that day from 13:00; accordingly, Non-party 1, the subcontractor, and the workers decided to leave the work for the 1st and 2nd lanes for later, and after roughly completing the cleanup while the aggregate applied to the 3rd and 4th lanes had not yet fully cured, opened the road to traffic and withdrew from the site. As a result, as vehicles continued to pass over the incompletely cured road surface, a large amount of residual aggregate detached and became scattered on the road surface. Then, at around 00:45 on 2000. 2. 14., the day after the above paving work, Non-party 3, while driving a commercial taxi east to west along the 3rd lane of Olympic-daero, reached the area near Cheongdam 2 Bridge, which was the construction site, and, because of the residual aggregate scattered on the road surface, skidded and struck the guardrail on the shoulder side of the 4th lane, causing an accident. Thereafter, while waiting for a tow truck, the above taxi was parked on the U-turn lane toward Cheongdam Park, installed inside the 1st lane on the left, and the tow truck and traffic patrol car dispatched for accident handling were standing by. Meanwhile, immediately after the preceding accident, at around 01:07 on 2000. 2. 14., Non-party 2, driving a Potentia passenger car (vehicle registration number omitted) and proceeding east to west along the 4th lane of Olympic-daero at a speed of approximately 116 km/h in excess of the speed limit, reached the area near Cheongdam 2 Bridge and, like Non-party 3, skidded toward the 1st lane on the left because of the aggregate scattered on the road surface, and then caused an accident by successively colliding with the rear portion of the above tow truck standing in the U-turn lane inside the 1st lane and the curb stone of Cheongdam Park on the left. Due to that accident, Non-party 2 and the passengers Non-party 4, Non-party 5, and Non-party 6 all died at the scene. Thereafter, the bereaved family members of the deceased Non-party 4, namely Non-party 7 and Non-party 8, and the bereaved family members of the deceased Non-party 5 and the deceased Non-party 6, namely Non-party 9, Non-party 10, and Non-party 11, filed an action against the Defendant and Non-party 1 for damages, asserting that the above traffic accident had occurred because of defects at the accident site, but lost at first instance. Only Non-party 7 and Non-party 8 appealed, and as a result, part of the appeal was accepted; on 2003. 1. 22., the Seoul High Court rendered a partial judgment in favor of the plaintiffs, ordering the Defendant and Non-party 1 to jointly and severally compensate Non-party 7 in the amount of KRW 66,206,515 and Non-party 8 in the amount of KRW 40,871,010, together with delayed damages thereon (Case No. 2002NA29512). The Defendant and Non-party 1 filed an appeal therefrom, but on 2004. 4. 16., the Supreme Court upheld the above appellate judgment except that part of the delayed damages was reversed and directly adjudged (Case No. 2003DA12489). Pursuant to that final and conclusive judgment, on 2004. 5. 20., the Defendant actually paid Non-party 7 and Non-party 8 a total of KRW 84,716,006, while depositing the remaining KRW 60 million because Dongbu Fire & Marine Insurance Co., Ltd., which had paid the amount of liability insurance corresponding to that amount to Non-party 7, provisionally attached, by virtue of subrogation, the above damages claim of Non-party 7, etc. against the Defendant, etc. It can also be seen that, in light of these facts, the subcontractor Non-party 1, by intent or negligence, crudely performed the anti-slip paving work for the accident site, and this also appears to have been one of the important causes of the traffic accident in this case. Accordingly, under Article 44, paragraph (3) of the Framework Act on the Construction Industry, Jia Industry, as the contractor, is jointly and severally liable with Non-party 1 to compensate the victim side for the resulting damage (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2001. 6. 12., 2000DA58859). On the other hand, since damage occurred to the Defendant’s property, who was the employer, due to defects arising in the course of performing the obligations under the contract for work as the contractor, unless it is proven that there was no cause attributable to it, it must be deemed liable under Article 390 of the Civil Act to compensate the Defendant for the resulting damage. Even if Jia Industry’s claim for the construction price in this case and the Defendant’s above damages claim are not obligations having an inherent reciprocal exchange relationship in a bilateral contract, in light of Article 667, paragraph (3) of the Civil Act and the principle of fairness it is proper to recognize a correlative relationship in performance, and therefore the two claims should be regarded as being in a relationship of simultaneous performance. In such circumstances, even if the Defendant’s above damages claim, as the active claim, arose only after the attachment of the construction price claim in this case, as the passive claim, because the cause underlying its occurrence had already mostly been established and existed before the passive claim was attached, the active claim cannot be said to be “a claim acquired thereafter by a third-party debtor who has received an order prohibiting payment” as prescribed in Article 498 of the Civil Act; hence, it cannot be otherwise said that the Defendant may lawfully oppose the Plaintiff by way of setoff.\\n\\nC. Even if, arguendo, the Defendant had asserted only a right of reimbursement as the active claim, the disposition of the court below rejecting that assertion is also difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nArticle 44, paragraph (3) of the Framework Act on the Construction Industry provides: “Where a subcontractor intentionally or negligently performs the construction work sublet to it in a crude manner and thereby causes damage to another person, the contractor shall be liable, jointly and severally with the subcontractor, to compensate for such damage.” Therefore, in a subcontract relationship involving construction work to which the Framework Act on the Construction Industry applies (see the main text of Article 2, item 4 of that Act), where a subcontractor intentionally or negligently performs the construction work in a crude manner and thereby causes damage to another person, not only the subcontractor but also the contractor, if there is no cause attributable to the contractor, must be deemed liable, jointly and severally, to compensate for such damage. The expression “performs the construction work in a crude manner” here means constructing in violation of various statutes, design documents, construction practices, general common sense as a construction business operator, etc., thereby impairing the safety of the structure itself or the construction work or creating danger to another person’s body or property (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2001. 6. 12., 2000DA58859). In general, there is no relationship of direction and supervision between the employer and the contractor; therefore, the employer is not liable as an employer for torts committed by the contractor or the contractor’s employees. However, in the so-called labor subcontracting case, where the employer directs a specific act or subcontracts a specific project to the contractor, even the employer bears liability as an employer (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 1983. 2. 8., 81DA428, etc.). Accordingly, a contractor in such position is, where a subcontractor intentionally or negligently performs the sublet construction work in a crude manner and thereby causes damage to another person, not only liable, in external relations, jointly and severally with the subcontractor for such damage, but also bears, vis-à-vis the employer who has discharged the damage obligation and thereby relieved the contractor, a duty of reimbursement corresponding to the portion of its own burden. Moreover, as seen above, even if the respective obligations borne by the parties are not obligations having an inherent reciprocal exchange relationship in a bilateral contract, where there are circumstances warranting recognition of a correlative relationship in performance, the defense of simultaneous performance must be recognized. In light of this, the contractor, who as one of the quasi-joint and several obligors actually performed the obligation to compensate the victim, acquires against the contractor who comes to bear employer liability a right of reimbursement which, as a variant of the damages claim that the employer may assert together with repair of defects or the so-called claim for compensation of damages from the expansion of defects, has in substance a reciprocal significance with the contractor’s claim for the construction price; thus, in light of the principle of fairness, it is proper to recognize a correlative relationship in performance, and the two claims should be regarded as being in a relationship of simultaneous performance. Even if the active claim arose only after the attachment order was served on the third-party debtor and the effect of attachment arose, the third-party debtor who may assert the defense of simultaneous performance may oppose the attaching creditor by way of setoff based on that claim.\\n\\nAccording to the record, Non-party 1, the subcontractor, and Non-party 12, who was then the site manager, stated to the investigative authorities to the effect that they had received specific instructions from Non-party 13, the president of Jia Industry, regarding whether construction would commence and when it would commence, etc. (record separate volume, pp. 102, 178), and Non-party 1 also asserted to the effect that Non-party 13 personally purchased the materials and supplies necessary for the subcontracted work and supplied them to the construction site (record p. 384). It is also apparent from the record that, after the close of pleadings in the court below, the Defendant attached evidence showing that it had in fact filed an action for reimbursement against Jia Industry, etc. based on such active claim, and requested the reopening of pleadings, asserting that “for Jia Industry, there is no way to avoid liability to pay damages arising from the accident in this case to the Defendant Seoul Metropolitan Government” (record pp. 348, 351). Nevertheless, without conducting any inquiry whatsoever into whether Jia Industry at that time reserved specific rights of direction and supervision over the progress and method of work of Non-party 1, etc., and specifically directed and supervised the execution of the work, the court below summarily concluded that there was no evidence sufficient to recognize the existence of the active claim asserted by the Defendant, and, without even granting the Defendant’s request for reopening of pleadings, hastily rejected the Defendant’s setoff defense. Such disposition of the court below cannot be said to be free from error in failing to conduct a proper hearing (moreover, in light of the fact that, after the court below rendered its judgment, a lower court judgment recognizing the existence of the active claim in this case asserted by the Defendant was in fact rendered in the above reimbursement action, there appears to be room to view that such error by the court below affected the outcome of the judgment).\\n\\nD. In the end, in whatever respect viewed, the court below, by hastily rejecting the Defendant’s setoff defense solely on the grounds stated in its reasoning, committed errors of failing to exercise its power to clarify, violating the rules of evidence affecting the judgment, failing to conduct a proper hearing, or misapprehending the legal principles concerning the cause or nature of the active claim asserted by the Defendant, or, further, concerning setoff based on such active claim.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the portion of the judgment below against the Defendant is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination on that portion, and judgment is rendered as stated in the operative part."}

{"[2011DA45521]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Article 498 of the Civil Act provides that “a third-party debtor who has received an order prohibiting payment may not oppose the creditor who applied for the order by set-off of a claim acquired thereafter.” In light of the purport of the above provision, the purpose and function of the set-off system, and the interest situation of the parties concerned when the debtor’s claim has been attached, where a third-party debtor who has received an order of attachment of a claim or an order of provisional attachment of a claim (hereinafter, discussion will be limited to the case of an order of attachment of a claim) has a counterclaim against the debtor subject to attachment, in order to oppose the attaching creditor by set-off, the two opposing claims must have been in a position suitable for set-off at the time the effect of the attachment arose, or, if the maturity date of the counterclaim (active claim) had not yet arrived at that time, it must have arrived simultaneously with, or before, the maturity date of the attached claim (passive claim) (see Supreme Court Decision of June 22, 1982, 82DAKA200; Supreme Court Decision of June 27, 2003, 2003DA7623, etc.).\\n\\n2. After recognizing the facts stated in its opinion, the court below held that, when there is an order of attachment and collection converting a provisional attachment of a monetary claim into a principal attachment, because the third-party debtor may, as a ground that could be asserted against the provisional attachment debtor before the claim was provisionally attached, later oppose the attaching creditor, if the third-party debtor had already acquired a counterclaim at the time the effect of the provisional attachment arose, its expectation of set-off is reasonable and justified; therefore, even if at that time the two claims were not yet in a position suitable for set-off and the maturity date of the counterclaim had not yet arrived, so long as they later come into a position suitable for set-off, regardless of which of the two claims matured first, the third-party debtor may oppose the attaching creditor by set-off. Accordingly, in this case, the date on which the provisional attachment took effect was June 30, 2008, the maturity date of the attached claim, namely the construction payment claim, was around June 10, 2008, and the maturity date of the loan claim related to the promissory note with face value of KRW 100,000,000 (hereinafter referred to as “the counterclaim at issue”) was July 25, 2008, which is after the maturity date of the construction payment claim; however, so long as the counterclaim at issue had already been acquired at the time the provisional attachment took effect, the Defendant could have a reasonable and justified expectation that it could secure its own claim by setting off the counterclaim at issue against the construction payment claim even if the said promissory note was dishonored, and therefore the court below determined that the Defendant could oppose the Plaintiff, the attaching creditor, by setting off the counterclaim at issue against the construction payment claim.\\n\\nHowever, according to the legal principle stated above, at the time the provisional attachment took effect in this case, the attached claim, namely the construction payment claim, had already matured, but the counterclaim at issue had not yet matured; thus, it cannot be said that the two claims were then in a position suitable for set-off. Furthermore, since the maturity date of the counterclaim at issue comes later than the maturity date of the construction payment claim, the Defendant must be deemed unable to oppose the Plaintiff, the attaching creditor, by set-off based on the counterclaim at issue.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below erred in law by misunderstanding the legal principle concerning set-off in which the claim subject to a prohibition of payment is used as the passive claim, and such error affected the judgment. The ground of appeal pointing out this issue is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Accordingly, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below so that it may retry and determine the case, and so rule as stated in the operative part. In this judgment, except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Kim Neung-hwan, Ahn Dae-hee, and Lee In-bok, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there is a supplementary opinion by Justice Yang Chang-soo to the majority opinion and a supplementary opinion by Justice Ahn Dae-hee to the dissenting opinions of Justices Kim Neung-hwan, Ahn Dae-hee, and Lee In-bok.\\n\\n4. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim Neung-hwan, Ahn Dae-hee, and Lee In-bok\\n\\na. Article 498 of the Civil Act provides that “a third-party debtor who has received an order prohibiting payment may not oppose the creditor who applied for the order by set-off of a claim acquired thereafter.” Accordingly, under this provision, what is prohibited is only the set-off by a third-party debtor using as the active claim a claim newly acquired after the third-party debtor received an order prohibiting payment; by converse interpretation, set-off by a third-party debtor using as the active claim a claim already acquired and held before that time is not prohibited by this provision but is instead necessarily permitted. Whether the claim had already reached maturity when the third-party debtor received the order prohibiting payment is not an issue.\\n\\nb. The main clause of Article 492(1) of the Civil Act provides that “where both parties bear obligations whose object is of the same kind, when the maturity of both obligations has arrived, each obligor may set off the obligations up to the amount of the smaller debt.” This principle applies as is even when the third-party debtor has received an order prohibiting payment. Accordingly, even if the third-party debtor had already acquired a counterclaim against the debtor at the time it received the order, it cannot set off the attached claim prohibited from payment at any time and on any occasion; only when the maturity date of both the counterclaim and the attached claim has arrived can set-off be made. There is no reason why this principle should change merely because there is an order prohibiting payment. An order prohibiting payment merely prohibits the third-party debtor from paying the attached claim to the debtor; it does not change the nature of the counterclaim or the attached claim. Therefore, not only when the maturity date of both the counterclaim and the attached claim has arrived at the time the order prohibiting payment is received, but also when, after that, while the third-party debtor has not paid the attached claim to the debtor, the maturity date of both the counterclaim and the attached claim arrives even though the maturity date of all or either one of them had not yet arrived and they were not yet in a position suitable for set-off, the third-party debtor may set off using the counterclaim as the active claim, and thereby oppose the creditor who applied for the order prohibiting payment.\\n\\nc. Originally, set-off is permitted for the purpose of smoothly and fairly settling the debtor-creditor relationship by enabling parties holding claims and obligations of the same kind to settle mutually opposing claims and obligations by a simple method. Through this, a creditor exercising the right of set-off is guaranteed the benefit of receiving, as if it had obtained certain and sufficient satisfaction, a full return on its active claim even when the debtor’s ability to pay is insufficient. In this respect, a creditor exercising the right of set-off has a status similar to that of a secured creditor. There is no reason why this status of the creditor with the right of set-off should be denied merely because there is an order prohibiting payment with respect to the passive claim.\\n\\nAn order prohibiting payment, as the phrase itself indicates, merely prohibits the third-party debtor from making payment to the debtor; it does not bring about any change in the essence or nature of the attached claim, nor does it have the effect of preventing the claim from being extinguished or its contents from being changed by objective facts unrelated to the debtor’s act or by the act of the third-party debtor. The same legal principle applies when the third-party debtor sets off by means of a counterclaim.\\n\\nd. Then, whom should be protected, the third-party debtor who can set off by means of a counterclaim, or the creditor who applied for the order prohibiting payment? The answer is self-evident. Whereas the position of the creditor who applied for the order prohibiting payment is inherently uncertain and unstable, the third-party debtor has a status similar to that of a secured creditor, and therefore the exercise of the third-party debtor’s right of set-off should be protected. Accordingly, when the maturity date of both the counterclaim and the attached claim has arrived at the time the order prohibiting payment is received, the third-party debtor can naturally set off by means of the counterclaim; and even if the maturity date of both the counterclaim and the attached claim, or of either one of them, has not yet arrived and they are not yet in a position suitable for set-off, if thereafter, while the third-party debtor does not pay the attached claim to the debtor, the maturity date of both the counterclaim and the attached claim arrives, the third-party debtor may set off by means of the counterclaim, and thereby oppose the creditor who applied for the order prohibiting payment. Where, at the time the third-party debtor receives the order prohibiting payment, the maturity date of the third-party debtor’s counterclaim has not yet arrived but the maturity date of the attached claim has already arrived or arrives earlier, in order to prevent the third-party debtor from coming into a position suitable for set-off upon the maturity of the third-party debtor’s counterclaim and thereby lawfully and validly setting off, the creditor who applied for the order prohibiting payment must, before such set-off, collect the attached claim and actually receive payment of the attached claim from the third-party debtor. Unless it is to be viewed in that way, there must be a special statutory provision.\\n\\ne. Article 492(1) of the Civil Act requires only that the maturity of both obligations arrive as a requirement for set-off. If this principle is fully carried through, even where there is an order prohibiting payment, the conclusion will be reached that so long as the third-party debtor has a counterclaim against the debtor, regardless of whether that counterclaim was acquired before or after the order prohibiting payment, the third-party debtor may set off at any time once the maturity dates of both the counterclaim and the claim prohibited from payment have arrived. However, this may make the position of the creditor who applied for the order prohibiting payment excessively unstable. Here, it becomes necessary to strike a balance of interests between the creditor who applied for the order prohibiting payment and the third-party debtor by appropriately adjusting the scope of the counterclaim that serves as the active claim eligible for set-off by the third-party debtor. How the specific standard should be set is a matter of legislative policy. It is understood that our Civil Act adopted, in Article 498, the legislative example that sets the standard in the sequence of the issuance of the order prohibiting payment and the acquisition time of the third-party debtor’s counterclaim, rather than the legislative example that sets it in the sequence of the maturity dates of the two claims.\\n\\nNevertheless, to, like the majority opinion, determine whether the third-party debtor’s set-off is permitted according to the sequence of the maturity dates is to seek to limit the third-party debtor’s set-off without legal basis, contrary to Article 498 of the Civil Act, and is therefore improper.\\n\\nThe majority opinion reaches a conclusion different from the original meaning of Article 498 of the Civil Act, yet gives no explanation whatsoever as to its reason or basis.\\n\\nf. The views in Supreme Court en banc Decision of November 13, 1973, 73DA518; Supreme Court Decision of June 22, 1982, 82DAKA200; Supreme Court Decision of June 27, 2003, 2003DA7623; and others, which conflict with the legal principles examined above, should be changed.\\n\\nIn this case, at the time the provisional attachment order took effect, the maturity date of the attached claim had already arrived, and the loan claim, which was the Defendant third-party debtor’s counterclaim, had not yet matured. However, in light of the legal principle stated above, so long as the attached claim has not yet actually been collected and paid, the Defendant may be deemed able to oppose the Plaintiff, the provisional attachment creditor, by set-off using the above counterclaim as the active claim. The court below’s judgment to the same effect is correct and should be maintained as is, and the appeal should be dismissed.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I dissent from the majority opinion.\\n\\n5. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Yang Chang-soo to the Majority Opinion\\n\\na. The dissenting opinion states that a creditor exercising the right of set-off has a status similar to that of a secured creditor, in that even when the debtor’s ability to pay is insufficient, the creditor is guaranteed the benefit of receiving certain and sufficient satisfaction even with respect to its own active claim, and that there is no reason why such status should be denied merely because there is an order prohibiting payment with respect to the passive claim.\\n\\nHowever, the above “status similar to that of a secured creditor” enjoyed by a creditor is guaranteed only when it is balanced against the legitimate interests of other creditors. As the dissenting opinion itself states, set-off is originally recognized as a means of settling mutually opposing claims and obligations by a simple method between parties holding claims of the same kind. It is needless to say that where a creditor and a debtor each hold claims of the same kind against one another, it will be more economical and convenient in terms of effort and cost for both the creditor and the debtor to extinguish the claims against each other up to equal amounts and settle only the remainder, rather than each separately asserting and receiving performance of their respective claims. In this way, because set-off produces the effect of satisfying one’s own claim immediately by a unilateral declaration of intent by a party, the set-off claimant is placed in a result equivalent to being allowed private execution (self-help execution).\\n\\nHowever, the set-off as such a simple means of settlement naturally has a certain limit when it goes further to have the so-called collateral function or preferential satisfaction function. That is, where a debtor also bears obligations to other creditors, the general principle is that all creditors may equally apply the debtor’s general assets to the satisfaction of their respective claims, and as is well known, this principle is called the “principle of equality among creditors.” At that time, if the debtor has a claim against one of the creditors, this claim must also be used for the satisfaction of all creditors. Yet if a creditor bearing a counter-obligation is permitted to set off with its own claim, the debtor’s claim, which originally should have been used for the satisfaction of all creditors, is used only to satisfy the counterclaim creditor’s claim. Thus, the creditor bearing the counter-obligation and able to set off secures satisfaction of its own claim in priority to the debtor’s other creditors regardless of the debtor’s asset situation. The problem, however, is that as a result of permitting such set-off, other creditors suffer the disadvantage that the debtor’s general assets are no longer available, to the extent of the claim subject to set-off, for the satisfaction of their own claims.\\n\\nNevertheless, the reason that such collateral function is recognized in set-off is explained by the need to protect the justified trust that when parties mutually hold opposing claims, they may ordinarily obtain satisfaction of their own claims regardless of the other party’s solvency. But if this collateral function is recognized without limit, there is a risk that the interests of other creditors will be unjustly infringed when the debtor’s financial condition deteriorates. For example, suppose that in the case of A, who bears a large amount of debt and is at risk of becoming insolvent, the claim against B forms an important part of A’s liable property. In such a case, A’s claim would be traded at a price far below its face value according to its actual value, but if B cheaply acquires from a third party a claim against A and then sets it off against B’s own debt to A, A’s liable property will be greatly reduced, causing other creditors of A to suffer unexpected detriment. The reason why Article 422 of the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act, on the premise of bankruptcy proceedings, broadly prohibits set-off there is precisely to deal with such a situation. The above provision eloquently shows that the collateral function of set-off is significantly limited when the debtor falls into insolvency.\\n\\nAlso, for example, if other creditors have attached the debtor A’s claim against third-party debtor B and commenced compulsory execution, and if B can set off regardless of when and by what method it acquired the counterclaim, then the compulsory execution would always face the possibility of being rendered futile. However, in light of the character of set-off as private execution, as discussed above, such a result of emptying judicial compulsory execution must not be permitted. In particular, because the third-party debtor’s counterclaim is ordinarily not publicly disclosed, interested persons are highly likely to suffer unexpected detriment. And above all, if a creditor has actually reached the point of attaching the claim that the debtor holds against the third-party debtor, then even if it cannot yet be said that the debtor has already become insolvent, it should be viewed as having revealed the risk of falling into such a condition. Therefore, in such a case, because the interests of creditors in satisfying their claims through the seizure of the debtor’s property are in urgent and sharp conflict with one another, it is reasonable to require a sufficient basis in order to give a legal solution favorable to one creditor and unfavorable to the others.\\n\\nAccordingly, the collateral function of set-off should be recognized only as incidental to the above-mentioned function of set-off as a simple means of payment, and not accepted without limit; it is desirable to impose appropriate restrictions by setting its scope through a balanced consideration of the set-off claimant’s legitimate interest in the expectation of set-off, on the one hand, and the interest in satisfaction of claims held by other creditors, including the attaching creditor, and transferees of claims, on the other.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion states that the creditor with the right of set-off is in a “status similar in fact to that of a secured creditor.” However, such a status is not expressly provided anywhere in our law as emphasized by the dissenting opinion; rather, it merely refers to a legal state in which, as a result of the law’s proper interpretation and delineation of the requirements and effects of set-off in light of various related interests, the creditor with the right of set-off, incidental to the original purpose of the set-off system as a simple means of settlement, comes to obtain preferential satisfaction in a certain range as if it were in the above status in fact. Therefore, preemptively setting and accepting such a “status similar in fact to that of a secured creditor,” and using it to determine the concrete requirements of set-off and, further, its effects, seems to me an inversion of the proper order.\\n\\nb. Article 498 of the Civil Act is precisely intended to set limits on the third-party debtor’s assertion of set-off in cases where one of the creditors has attached or provisionally attached the claim that the debtor holds against the third-party debtor (hereinafter, the discussion will proceed by taking only the case of attachment).\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion states that if the third-party debtor had the active claim at the time of attachment, then regardless of whether its maturity had arrived or the sequence of its maturity relative to the attached claim, the third-party debtor should be allowed to oppose the attaching creditor by set-off if it later becomes in a position suitable for set-off after attachment. This ultimately comes down to whether, even where the maturity date of the attached claim (passive claim) has arrived but the third-party debtor is not performing it, the third-party debtor may oppose the attaching creditor by set-off when the maturity date of the active claim arrives. In such a case, to say that the third-party debtor may oppose the attaching creditor by set-off, the interest in protecting the justified reliance on set-off that the third-party debtor has, as discussed above, must be sufficiently balanced against the attaching creditor’s legitimate interest in claim satisfaction so as to justify giving the third-party debtor priority satisfaction and thereby to allow the attachment creditor’s interest to be displaced.\\n\\nSo far, the Supreme Court has repeatedly made clear, with respect to this point, that even if the claims were not in a position suitable for set-off at the time of attachment and only later became so after attachment, the third-party debtor can be protected in preference to the attaching creditor only when the maturity date of the third-party debtor’s active claim arrives simultaneously with, or earlier than, the maturity date of the passive claim, so that set-off can immediately be made. This position is understood to arise from the consideration that, otherwise, when the maturity date of the third-party debtor’s active claim arrives later than the maturity date of the passive claim, the third-party debtor would need to have failed to perform its debt despite the maturity of that claim, and thus, at least objectively, would only then be in a position suitable for set-off after committing a default with respect to its own debt; consequently, there is no value in protecting such a third-party debtor, whose set-off eligibility has not yet arrived, in priority to a creditor who commenced attachment before that time.\\n\\nIn other words, set-off is permitted when the maturity date of both obligations has arrived. Of course, if only the passive claim has not yet reached maturity, the person seeking set-off may ordinarily waive the benefit of time with respect to its own obligation, and therefore a position suitable for set-off with a matured active claim may be recognized. However, where the maturity date of the party asserting set-off’s claim, namely the active claim, has not yet arrived, set-off is not permitted even if the maturity date of the passive claim has arrived. And once the passive claim has reached maturity, that debt must be performed, and its performance cannot be refused on the ground that there exists a counterclaim that has not yet matured. There is no reason to deny the creditor’s exercise of rights with respect to a debt whose maturity has already arrived; to deny it would instead result in permitting the debtor’s unwarranted delay in performance. This follows from the basic principle that a debt must be performed once its maturity has arrived. Therefore, once an interested party who directly conflicts with the person holding the active claim appears with respect to the passive claim, which can be exercised without any legal obstacle as above, including where attachment has already been effected, the collateral function of set-off cannot but recede to that extent. As discussed above, the collateral function of set-off is recognized on the basis of the justified trust that one can obtain satisfaction of one’s own claim through set-off, but in the above case, even if the third-party debtor believed that it could obtain satisfaction of its own claim through set-off, that cannot be said to be a justified trust worthy of protection.\\n\\nSeen in this way, the position of our precedents is a sound solution adopted after fully considering the content of the sharply conflicting interests. In such a case, a good-faith third-party debtor would have performed its debt on time; then the performance would have actually belonged to the debtor’s general assets, opening up the possibility that all creditors could obtain satisfaction of their respective claims through it. Nevertheless, to allow the third-party debtor, after delaying performance of its own debt, to oppose the attaching creditor with a set-off that became possible later upon maturity of that debt, thereby obtaining preferential satisfaction of its own claim and frustrating the attaching creditor’s enforcement of its claim, would be to overemphasize the collateral function of set-off, which is improper.\\n\\nc. Our precedents are also supported comparatively. For example, the latter sentence of Section 392 of the German Civil Code expressly provides, as in our precedents, that where the third-party debtor’s claim only matures after attachment, set-off is not permitted if its maturity comes later than the maturity of the attached claim. The legislative reason for that provision lies, as discussed above, in preventing the third-party debtor from obtaining the right of set-off by delaying performance of the debt it bears until the maturity date of the counterclaim.\\n\\nd. If one were to adopt the same view as the dissenting opinion, then, conversely, one cannot explain the legislative intent of Article 498 of the Civil Act not to allow set-off by a third-party debtor using as the active claim a claim acquired after attachment. The dissenting opinion states that an attachment order “merely prohibits the third-party debtor from paying the debtor and does not bring about any change in the essence or nature of the attached claim, nor does it have the effect of preventing the claim from being extinguished or its contents from being changed by objective facts unrelated to the debtor’s act or by the act of the third-party debtor.” If so, a fundamental question inevitably arises as to why Article 498 of the Civil Act, with respect to attachment, which brings about no change whatsoever in the essence or nature of the attached claim, prescribed a different solution to the important legal issue of whether set-off is permitted before or after attachment.\\n\\nThis would be a proper explanation only if Article 498 of the Civil Act is understood to have legislatively adopted the view that the fact of attachment of a claim changes, to a certain extent, the interest situation related to set-off held by the third-party debtor, so that with respect to the above legal issue, due regard must now also be paid to the attaching creditor’s interest in claim satisfaction and the like. Such legislative intent must naturally also be considered in interpreting the concrete meaning of “a claim acquired after the order prohibiting payment” as provided in Article 498 of the Civil Act. In that sense, the position of our precedents discussed above cannot be said to contradict the express wording of Article 498 of the Civil Act; rather, it may be said to have properly carried through and appropriately realized the legislative intent.\\n\\n6. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Ahn Dae-hee to the Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim Neung-hwan, Ahn Dae-hee, and Lee In-bok\\n\\na. In light of the purpose and function of the set-off system, the status similar to that of a secured creditor enjoyed by a creditor who may exercise the right of set-off in the future is recognized so long as the active claim and the passive claim each exist, and its existence is not altered by the sequence in which the maturity dates of the two claims arrive. However, according to the majority opinion, among third-party debtors who were in a status similar to that of a secured creditor because they had a counterclaim at the time the effect of the attachment of claims arose and could therefore exercise the right of set-off in the future, those third-party debtors whose counterclaim had not matured and whose maturity date comes later than that of the attached claim are suddenly deprived of the status they had held, by making them unable to exercise the right of set-off merely on the basis of an accidental circumstance that cannot be attributed to their responsibility for the attachment of claims, thereby producing an unforeseen and irrational result.\\n\\nb. The majority opinion appears to restrict the exercise of the right of set-off on the ground that the third-party debtor’s expectation of future set-off cannot be protected if it has committed a default by not paying the attached claim that had already matured until the maturity date of the active claim arrives. However, in such a case, as a sanction for the third-party debtor’s nonperformance of the attached claim that has matured, it can be said to be sufficient, as ordinarily contemplated by our Civil Act, to impose liability for damages such as delay damages on the third-party debtor; further restricting the exercise of the right of set-off on the ground that set-off became available while the obligation remained unperformed amounts to an excessively severe sanction against the third-party debtor. In particular, because there are cases in which there are circumstances justifying the nonperformance, such as where the attached claim cannot be paid because there is a dispute over the scope of the claim even after maturity has arrived, the majority opinion, which uniformly restricts the exercise of the right of set-off solely on the basis of the sequence of maturity dates, may result in harsh consequences for the third-party debtor in such cases.\\n\\nc. Even from a comparative-law perspective, the interpretive theory of the dissenting opinion is reasonable.\\n\\nSection 392 of the German Civil Code codifies the interpretation adopted by the majority opinion, but it uses the term “acquisition” of a claim and the term “arrival of maturity” of a claim separately, which differs from the wording of Article 498 of our Civil Act. And unlike our Civil Execution Act, under the German Code of Civil Procedure, because the attaching creditor acquires, through attachment of claims, the status of a statutory pledgee with respect to the attached claim, the need to protect the attaching creditor cannot be said to be the same as in our case. In view of these differences, the provision of Section 392 of the German Civil Code cannot be applied as is to the interpretation of Article 498 of our Civil Act.\\n\\nd. Where the third-party debtor is a bank or another financial institution, as a rule, when a situation arises in relation to a claim such as a loan claim, which is the counterclaim, that casts doubt on the debtor’s ability to pay, such as attachment or provisional attachment of claims, there is usually a special agreement providing that the benefit of time is lost and that set-off may be made against claims such as deposits, which are attached claims; and the Supreme Court recognizes the validity of such special agreements concerning loss of the benefit of time, and holds that, pursuant to such agreements, because attachment or provisional attachment of claims causes the counterclaim and the attached claim to immediately become in a position suitable for set-off, a third-party debtor such as a bank or another financial institution may, in effect without restriction, exercise the right of set-off (see Supreme Court Decision of September 12, 1989, 88DAKA25120; Supreme Court Decision of June 27, 2003, 2003DA7623, etc.). The Supreme Court has also held to the effect that where the third-party debtor’s counterclaim and the attached claim are in a relationship of simultaneous performance, the third-party debtor may, in effect without restriction, exercise the right of set-off (see Supreme Court Decision of September 28, 1993, 92DA55794). This position of the Supreme Court is in line with the dissenting opinion. In other words, the position of the attaching creditor and the third-party debtor is no different in the cases of the above Supreme Court decisions or in a case like this one, and there is no rational reason why only in a case like this one should the attaching creditor’s interest be given priority and the third-party debtor’s exercise of the right of set-off be restricted. Therefore, I think that treating the present case differently from the above cases is not desirable even from the standpoint of consistency."}

{"[2022DA200089]": "The grounds of appeal are examined (a supplemental statement of grounds of appeal submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal has expired shall be considered only to the extent that it supplements the same).\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na. The Plaintiff is a company that issues and manages transportation cards called “T-money,” and the Defendant is a company that issues and manages transportation cards called “EB Card.” The Plaintiff and the Defendant entered into the instant agreement on 2007. 10. 15. and have made mutual settlements regarding fares of users of another company’s transportation cards using terminals installed by their own companies. Under the instant agreement, settlement is made in such a manner that, when the portion in which another company’s transportation card was used on one’s own terminal is calculated and billed, the other company deposits the corresponding amount, and if payment of the settlement amount is delayed, delay damages at the rate of 0.25% per day are recognized.\\n\\nb. Sensepass Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Sensepass”) was conducting a transportation card payment service business by issuing transportation cards called “Top T-money” in some areas of Gyeongsang Province, including Tongyeong. Mybi Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Mybi”) began a payment service using transportation cards called “Cashbee Card” in the same area around 2013. 2. Mybi installed its own terminals in taxis to provide transportation card payment services, and additionally installed devices so that Top T-money issued by Sensepass could also be used on Mybi terminals. The Plaintiff entered into the instant business transfer agreement with Sensepass on 2014. 9. 30. and took over Sensepass’s business.\\n\\nc. As of around 2016. 8., the number of transactions paid with Top T-money on Mybi terminals was 42,087, and the usage fares therefor (hereinafter referred to as “Top T-money usage fares”) totaled 165,323,103 won. The Defendant, who was entrusted by Mybi with the agency work of settlement, repeatedly requested the Plaintiff to settle the Top T-money usage fares paid on Mybi terminals, but the Plaintiff refused on the ground that there was no separate settlement agreement in that regard. The Defendant sent the Plaintiff an official letter stating that it would deduct the Top T-money usage fares from the settlement amount it would pay in the future.\\n\\nd. Thereafter, the Defendant paid only 5,530,872,809 won, excluding 160,107,945 won from the total settlement amount of 5,690,980,754 won that it had to pay to the Plaintiff pursuant to the instant agreement, and paid only 199,271,637 won, excluding 2,752,818 won from the settlement amount of 202,024,455 won that it had to pay to the Plaintiff as of 2016. 12. 6. In response, the Plaintiff paid only 1,322,654,606 won, excluding 160,107,945 won from the settlement amount of 1,482,762,551 won that it had to pay to the Defendant pursuant to the instant agreement. The Defendant again paid only 29,084,379 won, excluding 160,107,945 won from the settlement amount of 189,192,324 won that it had to pay to the Plaintiff as of 2017. 9. 5. pursuant to the instant agreement.\\n\\ne. On 2020. 7. 7., Mybi assigned the claim for Top T-money usage fares to the Defendant, and on the same day the Defendant, having been delegated authority to give notice, gave notice of the assignment of the claim to the Plaintiff (hereinafter referred to as “the instant assignment of claim”).\\n\\nf. The Plaintiff filed the instant action seeking payment of the unpaid settlement amount totaling 162,860,763 won (2,752,818 won as of 2016. 12. 6. + 160,107,945 won as of 2017. 9. 5.) and delay damages thereon, contending that the Defendant’s deduction of the settlement amount as above was improper.\\n\\n2. Whether the obligation to return unjust enrichment was established (Ground of Appeal 1)\\nThe court below held that the Plaintiff and Sensepass obtained benefits corresponding to the Top T-money usage fares without legal cause and thereby Mybi suffered loss in the same amount, and thus recognized the establishment of the obligation of the Plaintiff and Sensepass to return unjust enrichment to Mybi.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the record and the relevant legal principles, there is no error affecting the judgment, such as misapprehending the legal principles regarding unjust enrichment or the principle of good faith, or finding facts in violation of the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Whether the obligation to return unjust enrichment was assumed (Ground of Appeal 2)\\nThe court below determined that the Plaintiff assumed Sensepass’s obligation to return unjust enrichment to Mybi through the instant business transfer agreement.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the record and the relevant legal principles, there is no error affecting the judgment, such as misapprehending the legal principles regarding the succession of specific obligations upon business transfer or the interpretation of dispositive documents, or finding facts in violation of the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. Date on which set-off becomes available where an assigned claim is used as the active claim for set-off (Ground of Appeal 3)\\na. Since Article 493(2) of the Civil Act provides that “an expression of intention to set off shall be deemed to have extinguished the obligations to the extent of the equivalent amounts when each obligation became capable of set-off,” the effect of set-off arises retroactively to the time when set-off became available. Set-off becomes available only when the active claim and the passive claim stand against each other.\\n\\nWhere an assignee of a claim sets off the assigned claim, as the active claim, against an existing claim that the obligor had against the assignee of the claim, the assignee can exercise the active claim only when the requirements for asserting the assignment against the obligor have been satisfied; therefore, even if the due dates of both claims had already arrived before the assignment of the claim, the effect of set-off does not retroact to the due date, but retroacts to the time when the requirements for asserting the assignment against the obligor were satisfied.\\n\\nb. In light of the facts found above and these legal principles, the following conclusion follows.\\n\\n(1) The point in time when the unjust enrichment restitution claim assumed by the Defendant from Mybi through the instant assignment of claim and the Plaintiff’s settlement claim came to stand against each other is 2020. 7. 7., when the Defendant gave notice of the assignment of the claim to the Plaintiff and thereby satisfied the requirements for asserting the assignment against the Plaintiff; therefore, this point in time should be regarded as the date on which set-off became available.\\n\\n(2) Considering the respective claim amounts, due dates, periods of default, and rates of delay damages, etc. of the Plaintiff’s settlement claim and the Defendant’s unjust enrichment restitution claim, even if set-off appropriation is made by comparing the principal and interest of the Plaintiff’s settlement claim, calculated as of 2020. 7. 6., the day before the date on which set-off became available, with the principal and interest of the Defendant’s unjust enrichment restitution claim against the Plaintiff, there is room for the Plaintiff’s settlement claim to remain.\\n\\n(3) The court below should have examined how much the principal and interest of the Plaintiff’s settlement claim and the principal and interest of the Defendant’s unjust enrichment restitution claim were, respectively, as of 2020. 7. 6., the day before the date on which set-off became available, and then determined whether any settlement claim remained with the Plaintiff even after set-off appropriation.\\n\\n(4) However, the court below, on the erroneous premise that the due date of the original claim is the date on which set-off became available, concluded that the Plaintiff’s settlement claim was extinguished within the scope of the equivalent amounts (2,752818 won as of 2016. 12. 6. and 160,107,945 won as of 2017. 9. 5.) by the Defendant’s unjust enrichment restitution claim of 165,323,103 won, and that no settlement claim remained. The judgment of the court below contains an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles regarding the date on which set-off becomes available where an assigned claim is used as the active claim for set-off.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nThe judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court."}

question:
Which of the following is the correct combination of the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (X) regarding liquidated damages? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)

(a) If liquidated damages are stipulated for nonperformance of a monetary obligation, the “unfairness” that is the requirement for reduction shall be determined by considering not only the purpose and content of the contract, the motive for stipulating liquidated damages, the ratio of the stipulated amount to the amount of the obligation, the size of the anticipated damages, and the trade customs prevailing at the time, but also the ordinary overdue interest rate.  
(b) Although fact-finding regarding the grounds for reduction of the stipulated amount of damages or determining the percentage of such reduction is, in principle, a matter within the exclusive authority of the trier of fact, reducing the amount to one smaller than the amount the debtor would naturally have been obliged to pay and that the creditor could have received, even if there were no liquidated damages, exceeds the limits of reduction.  
(c) In a contract for work, where it is agreed that delay damages, as liquidated damages, shall be calculated by multiplying the total contract price by the delay damages rate, whether the delay damages are excessive shall be determined on the basis of whether the delay damages rate itself is excessive.  
(d) A defect repair bond, agreed to vest in the employer upon the contractor’s failure to perform the duty to repair defects, shall, absent special circumstances, be regarded as liquidated damages; therefore, the employer cannot, on the ground of the contractor’s failure to perform the duty to repair defects, obtain from the contractor damages corresponding to the excess amount by proving the actual damages in addition to forfeiture of the defect repair bond.
