supporting_precedents: {"[2000DA17810]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (the supplemental brief of grounds of appeal, to the extent that it supplements them).\\n\\n1. Facts found by the court below\\n\\nThe court below, comprehensively considering facts that were not in dispute and the evidence adduced, found that: (1) the Plaintiff, having decided to construct a workers’ welfare apartment complex (hereinafter referred to as “the apartment at issue”) consisting of 5 apartment buildings, each 6 stories high and of 18-pyeong type, totaling 300 units, on 17,841㎡ of land above ground in Yangsan City (address omitted), and to sell it to workers residing within its jurisdiction, entered into a contract on December 27, 1990, with the co-defendant at first instance, Changjo General Construction Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to only as “Changjo Construction”), for the construction, civil engineering, and facilities works of the apartment complex at issue in the amount of KRW 2,382,000,000, and, by May 30, 1992, entered into a total of 4 contracts in all, for a total contract price of KRW 5,602,683,000; and, on the other hand, the Defendant guaranteed to the Plaintiff that it would perform, jointly and severally with Changjo Construction, the contractual obligations under the above contracts; (2) at the time of the above contracts, the Plaintiff, as the project operator of the apartment sales project at issue, agreed with Changjo Construction to provide the design documents (including construction specifications, drawings, and site explanation materials) and construction materials to Changjo Construction, to dispatch a site supervisor and supervise the works, including confirming whether the construction was being carried out in accordance with the design documents, and to conduct a completion inspection upon completion of the works; (3) Changjo Construction commenced construction of the apartment at issue on December 28, 1990, pursuant to the above contracts, completed the construction on August 30, 1992, thereafter received a completion inspection from the Plaintiff around that time, and delivered the apartment to the Plaintiff; (4) however, from around March 1993, about 7 months after the Plaintiff sold the apartment to workers, due to settlement of the foundation ground, inclined displacement ranging from a vertical tilt of 1/500 to 1/170 occurred in the buildings of each block (it appears that the ground became fixed and no further displacement occurred from about 5 years after completion of the buildings until the close of argument), cracks of 0.2㎜ to 10㎜ appeared in the exterior walls of the entire building, cracks and door-frame sagging and twisting appeared in the walls, balconies, and floors of each unit of the apartment, and defects occurred such as water leakage into the ceilings due to cracks in the roof slabs; (5) the above defects in the apartment at issue were caused by a combination of the mistakes in design and construction as stated in the judgment; (6) meanwhile, Changjo Construction, in accordance with the special terms for facility construction contracts attached to each of the above contracts, obtained from the Construction Mutual Aid Association and delivered to the Plaintiff, as a defect repair bond, a defect repair bond certificate dated February 29, 1992, with the guarantee period running until April 27, 1994 and the guaranteed amount being KRW 71,460,000, and a defect repair bond certificate dated September 7, 1992, with the guarantee period running until October 28, 1995 and the guaranteed amount being KRW 96,139,350; and (7) after defects occurred in the apartment at issue, Changjo Construction, while negotiating with the Plaintiff and the apartment occupants regarding the repair issues, defaulted and became insolvent around June 29, 1994.\\n\\n2. Regarding Ground of Appeal No. 1\\n\\nThe court below, based on the above facts, determined that the Defendant, as a joint and several guarantor of Changjo Construction’s contractual obligations, bears liability for repair or, in lieu thereof, damages with respect to the above defects that arose during the guarantee period due to Changjo Construction’s defective construction, and then rejected the Defendant’s argument that the “performance of contractual obligations” jointly and severally guaranteed by the Defendant is limited to a service-type guarantee for the completion of work left unperformed by the constructor and does not include Changjo Construction’s defect repair obligation, so that, once Changjo Construction completed the completion inspection and delivered the apartment at issue, the Defendant’s performance of contractual obligations was fully completed and it bears no liability for the above defects; the court below did so on the ground that, as a person who jointly and severally guaranteed Changjo Construction’s obligations under the construction contract at issue, the Defendant bears the same contractual obligations as Changjo Construction and thus bears the same liability also for defect repair, which is one of Changjo Construction’s contractual obligations under that contract.\\n\\nIn a construction contract, a joint and several guarantor who guarantees the contractor’s performance of contractual obligations bears, absent special circumstances, the same obligations as the principal debtor contractor. Meanwhile, according to the record, the general conditions of the construction contract at issue provide that “a person intending to enter into the contract shall provide one or more joint and several guarantors who guarantee performance of contractual obligations” (Article 5-2(1)); “where the contractor or the joint and several guarantor receives a request for defect repair from the public official in charge of the contract during the defect liability period and fails to comply therewith, the defect repair deposit shall be forfeited to the national treasury” (Article 18(4)); and “when the public official in charge of the contract returns the defect repair deposit to the contractor, if, upon a claim under Article 28(1) above, the joint and several guarantor has performed the defect repair obligation, the guarantor has the right to directly claim from the Government the amount corresponding to the portion so performed” (Article 28(4)); from which it can be seen that the scope of the guaranteed obligation of the joint and several guarantor under the construction contract necessarily includes the contractor’s defect repair obligation. In light of the legal principle and factual circumstances seen above, it is clear that the scope of the Defendant’s joint and several guarantee under the construction contract at issue includes the defect repair obligation after completion of the works; therefore, the court below’s determination to the same effect is justifiable, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality affecting the result of the judgment by erroneously determining the scope of the joint and several guarantee under the construction contract, as asserted in the grounds of appeal. The precedents cited in the grounds of appeal concern different issues from this case and cannot serve as appropriate precedents.\\n\\n3. Regarding Ground of Appeal No. 2\\n\\nThe court below, based on the evidence it relied upon, determined that the amount of damages for which the Defendant must compensate is the defect repair amount as stated in its judgment, and then rejected the Defendant’s argument that, because Changjo Construction paid the defect repair deposit pursuant to the provision in the construction contract at issue that it shall pay a defect repair deposit equal to 3 percent of the construction price, the liability of the joint and several guarantor should likewise be limited to the scope of that defect repair deposit, or that, because the construction contract at issue contains a provision that Changjo Construction may dispense with providing a joint and several guarantor by paying a contract performance deposit of at least 6 percent of the total construction price, the liability of the joint and several guarantor should likewise be limited to the amount corresponding to 6 percent of the construction price; the court below did so on the ground that the fact that Changjo Construction paid the defect repair deposit does not mean that the defect repair obligation of the joint and several guarantor is limited to the amount paid, and that merely because the obligation to provide a joint and several guarantor can be dispensed with by paying a certain amount of contract performance deposit, it cannot be said that the defect repair obligation of a joint and several guarantor already provided is limited to that amount.\\n\\nIn light of the nature of the defect repair liability of a joint and several guarantor as seen above, together with the relevant statutes and the provisions of the contract conditions, the above determination by the court below is justifiable, and the Defendant’s above argument is merely a matter of its own view; therefore, it cannot be said that the judgment below contains illegality in misconstruing the legal principles concerning the scope of joint and several guarantee liability, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. Regarding Ground of Appeal No. 3\\n\\nThe existence and degree of grounds for comparative negligence in determining the scope of liability for damages arising from nonperformance of obligations must be comprehensively determined by comparing, in each individual case, the circumstances surrounding the conclusion and performance of the contract in question and the faults of both parties; at that time, the factual finding regarding the grounds for comparative negligence and the determination of its ratio fall within the exclusive province of the trier of fact, insofar as they are not manifestly unreasonable in light of the principle of equity (see Supreme Court Decisions 98DA56416, decided May 25, 1999, and 98DA35389, decided June 13, 2000, among others).\\n\\nExamining the judgment below in light of the record, the court below’s factual findings or its determination of the ratio regarding grounds for comparative negligence cannot be viewed as manifestly unreasonable in light of the principle of equity; therefore, the grounds of appeal on this point are not accepted.\\n\\nIn addition, the Defendant’s argument to the effect that the defect of the apartment at issue arose from the nature of the materials provided by the Plaintiff, who was the employer, or from the Plaintiff’s instructions (design), so that Changjo Construction, as the contractor, does not bear liability for defects under Civil Act Article 669 and, accordingly, there is no room for the Defendant’s joint and several guarantee liability to arise, is not only a new argument not raised before the court below, but also a new argument raised after the period for submitting the petition of grounds of appeal had elapsed; thus, it cannot constitute a lawful ground of appeal. The grounds of appeal relating thereto also lack merit.\\n\\n5. Regarding Ground of Appeal No. 4\\n\\nThe court below rejected the Defendant’s argument that the defect repair deposit received by the Plaintiff from Changjo Construction should be deducted from the amount of damages arising from nonperformance of the defect repair obligation at issue, on the ground that the defect repair deposit stipulated in a construction contract entered into between a construction company and a local government constitutes a penalty or sanction, and therefore the above defect repair deposit should be vested in the Plaintiff as a penalty or sanction due to Changjo Construction’s nonperformance of the defect repair obligation, and cannot be deducted from the amount of damages arising from nonperformance of the defect repair obligation.\\n\\nHowever, where the construction contract or the standard terms incorporated into the contract contain a clause that, if the contractor receives a request for defect repair from the employer during the defect liability period and fails to comply therewith, the defect repair deposit shall vest in the employer, this defect repair deposit shall, absent special circumstances, be regarded as a liquidated damages provision (see Supreme Court Decision 2001DA14689, decided September 28, 2001). However, in view of the nature of the defect repair deposit, even if there is no express provision allowing recovery of damages in excess where actual damages exceed the defect repair deposit, it is appropriate to regard this as a special liquidated damages provision under which the employer may recover, from the contractor, damages corresponding to the excess amount by proving the actual damages, in addition to forfeiture of the defect repair deposit on the ground of the contractor’s nonperformance of the defect repair obligation.\\n\\nAccording to the record, however, the general conditions of construction contracts, which form part of the construction contract at issue, merely provide that if the contractor does not perform the defect repair obligation, the defect repair deposit shall vest in the employer, and there are no special circumstances that would separately warrant construing the defect repair deposit at issue as a penalty; therefore, the defect repair deposit at issue should be deemed a special liquidated damages provision, under which, if the contractor does not perform the defect repair obligation, the employer may substitute forfeiture of the deposit for compensation for the loss, but if there is damage exceeding that amount, the contractor bears additional liability for such excess. If so, where the defect repair deposit has been forfeited, it is only natural that the deposit be applied to compensation for the amount of damages. Meanwhile, as found by the court below, the Plaintiff received from Changjo Construction a defect repair bond certificate in the amount of KRW 167,599,350 issued by the Construction Mutual Aid Association as a defect repair deposit under the above contract; therefore, if the Plaintiff had received the amount of the bond from the Construction Mutual Aid Association pursuant to the above defect repair bond certificate, that amount should be deducted from the damages arising from Changjo Construction’s nonperformance of the defect repair obligation.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, having concluded that the defect repair deposit at issue constituted a penalty or sanction, determined that it was not of a nature to be deducted from the Defendant’s damages without even examining whether the Plaintiff had received payment under the above defect repair bond certificate, and thereupon excluded it from the Defendant’s damages amount. In so doing, it erred by misconstruing the parties’ intent, thereby misunderstanding the facts and failing to conduct a full examination, with the result that the judgment was affected. Accordingly, the grounds of appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n6. Therefore, among the portion of the judgment below adverse to the Defendant, the part relating to deduction of the above defect repair deposit (the portion concerning the claim for KRW 167,599,350 and the delay damages thereon) is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination on that part, and the remainder of the Defendant’s appeal is dismissed. It is so adjudged, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2016DA52265]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Article 398(2) of the Civil Act provides that, where the amount of liquidated damages is unreasonably excessive, the court may reduce it appropriately, and does not exclude its application to nonperformance of a monetary obligation. In addition, Article 6 of the Interest Limitation Act provides that, where the court deems the amount of damages stipulated by the parties in relation to nonperformance of an obligation for monetary purposes to be unreasonable, it may reduce it to a reasonable amount. Accordingly, where, with respect to a monetary obligation, the parties separately agree on the rate of delayed damages to prepare for delay in performance, such agreement should be regarded as liquidated damages and subject to reduction.\\n\\n“Unreasonableness,” which is a requirement for reducing the amount of liquidated damages, is recognized where, in light of general social norms, taking into account all circumstances such as the positions of the creditor and the debtor, the purpose and content of the contract, the motive for stipulating liquidated damages, the ratio of the stipulated amount to the amount of the debt, the size of the anticipated loss, and the trading practices at the time, payment of the stipulated amount would impose unfair pressure on the debtor, who is in the position of the economically weaker party, and thereby result in loss of fairness. In particular, where liquidated damages are stipulated for nonperformance of a monetary obligation, the usual overdue interest rate must also be considered in addition to the foregoing factors. The point in time at which to determine whether the amount of liquidated damages is unreasonable and the appropriate scope of any reduction therefor is the time when the court makes that determination specifically, that is, the time of the closing of oral argument at the fact-finding trial (see Supreme Court Decisions 92DA36212, delivered on January 15, 1993; 97DA15371, delivered on July 25, 1997; 99DA38637, delivered on July 28, 2000, etc.). At that time, the fact-finding regarding the grounds for reduction and the determination of the rate thereof are matters within the exclusive province of the fact-finding court, unless they are deemed to be manifestly unreasonable in light of the principle of equity (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DA59493, delivered on December 13, 2007, etc.).\\n\\n2. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the lower court, the lower court reduced to KRW 48,000,000 the delayed damages as of July 7, 2016, the date of the closing of oral argument in the lower court, on the ground that the agreement to pay delayed damages at the agreed overdue interest rate on the unpaid amount in the event that the purchase price for the instant apartment units or the option construction price is not paid was unreasonably excessive. As reasons therefor, the lower court found that it could not be said that the purchasers, including the Defendants, had absolutely no basis for asserting cancellation or rescission of the sales contract until the judgment in the related litigation became final and conclusive, and thus there was ample room to view that applying the agreed overdue interest rate as is for the foregoing period would impose unfair pressure on the purchasers and result in loss of fairness, making reduction necessary; however, after the judgment in the related litigation became final and conclusive, the purchasers, including the Defendants, had no justifiable reason for failing to pay the balance, etc. under the sales contract, and the agreed overdue interest rate was within the range ordinarily stipulated in similar sales contracts, so it did not appear that there were grounds for reduction for that period.\\n\\nThe lower court’s determination is proper in light of the legal principles set forth above, and it does not contain the errors alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as failing to conduct the necessary review, exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or misunderstanding the law regarding the reduction of liquidated damages.\\n\\n3. The Plaintiff’s appeal is without merit and is therefore dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2022DA227619]": "1. Regarding the Plaintiff’s appeal on points of law\\n\\na. Judgment of the court below\\n\\nAs to the claim for KRW 1,000,000,000 in agreed liquidated damages, the court below reduced the stipulated liquidated damages amount to KRW 245,000,000, which was the Plaintiff’s principal investment, on the grounds that ① the Plaintiff holds an equity interest in the instant company equivalent to the amount invested, ② no materials had been submitted showing that the disadvantage of being unable to participate in the management of the instant company could be converted into economic value, and ③ the money that the Plaintiff’s representative director invested in the Defendant is difficult to consider as the Plaintiff’s loss.\\n\\nb. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\n\\n1) Relevant legal principles\\n\\na) Article 398(2) of the Civil Act provides that where the stipulated amount of liquidated damages is unreasonably excessive, the court may reasonably reduce it. A stipulation of liquidated damages is to fix in advance the amount of damages that the debtor must pay in the event of nonperformance; its function and purpose are to secure performance of the obligation by excluding the difficulty of proving the fact of damage and the amount of damage, preventing disputes in advance, simplifying the resolution of legal relations, and psychologically warning the debtor (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2018DA248855, 248862 rendered on July 21, 2022).\\n\\nb) The reduction of a stipulated amount of liquidated damages under the above provision is one form of limitation on the principle of private autonomy, in which the State interferes with the conclusion of a contract or its contents in order to eliminate substantive inequality between the parties and ensure fairness. Here, the phrase “unreasonably excessive” is insufficient to mean merely that there is no damage or that the amount of damage is less than the stipulated amount; it means a case where, in light of the economic positions of the contracting parties, the purpose of the contract, the circumstances leading to the stipulation of liquidated damages, trade practices, and all other relevant circumstances, payment of such stipulated amount is deemed to impose unjust pressure on the debtor in the position of an economically weaker party and thereby to cause a loss of fairness (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 90DA14478 rendered on March 27, 1991).\\n\\nWhere the actual amount of damage or the expected amount of damage can be ascertained from the record, it is necessary to compare it with the stipulated amount (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2010DA22415 rendered on October 24, 2013), and merely because the stipulated amount itself is large or because the temporal interval between the conclusion and termination of the contract is short is insufficient to deem the stipulated amount of liquidated damages unreasonably excessive and reduce it (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2014DA209227 rendered on July 24, 2014).\\n\\nEven if there is no stipulation of liquidated damages, reducing the amount to a sum smaller than the amount that the creditor could have received from which the debtor would naturally bear the obligation to pay would produce the same result as wholly denying the agreement itself concerning liquidated damages, and thus would exceed the limits of reduction (see Supreme Court Decision 90DAKA7262 rendered on November 9, 1990; Supreme Court Decision 2018DA240653 rendered on January 17, 2019, etc.).\\n\\nc) When determining, as above, whether the stipulated amount of liquidated damages is unreasonably excessive, the court must comprehensively consider circumstances that arose in the meantime, based on the time when oral argument in the fact-finding instance was concluded (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2015DA209347 rendered on September 13, 2018).\\n\\nAs a matter of principle, fact-finding regarding the grounds for reduction or determining the rate thereof falls within the exclusive province of the fact-finding court; however, if it is deemed to be manifestly unreasonable in light of the principle of equity, it is unlawful and impermissible (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2017DA228762 rendered on August 18, 2017).\\n\\n2) According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following circumstances can be ascertained.\\n\\na) The Plaintiff is a company with its head office in Incheon Yeonsu-gu (Address 1 omitted) engaged in genome analysis business, etc.; Non-Party 1 is one of its co-representative directors; and the Defendant is a company with its head office in Seongnam-si (Address 2 omitted) engaged in software development and supply business, electronic financial transaction business, etc., and externally also uses the trade name “(trade name omitted).”\\n\\nAround February 2018, Non-Party 1 concluded a contract with the Defendant, which claimed to possess technologies such as a “multi-payment system utilizing mobile terminals,” in relation to a business of providing a system that installs unmanned vending machines in idle spaces of stores located in certain urban areas and enables payment in local currency through mobile terminals, to the effect that the side of Non-Party 1 would invest in the Defendant on the condition of subscribing to new shares, and that thereafter the side of Non-Party 1 and the Defendant would jointly contribute capital to establish the instant company under the trade name “(company name omitted),” and the Defendant established the instant company around that time.\\n\\nThe Plaintiff concluded the instant contract with the Defendant around May 2018, and the instant contract provided that the side of the Plaintiff and Non-Party 1 would each invest KRW 255,000,000 in the Defendant and KRW 245,000,000 in the instant company, respectively; that the Defendant would hold 51% of the issued shares of the instant company and the instant company would have co-representative directors; and that if either the Plaintiff or the Defendant breached any obligation prescribed in the contract, it would pay KRW 1,000,000,000 as liquidated damages.\\n\\nb) By around August 2018, Non-Party 1 paid KRW 255,000,000 to the Defendant and subscribed to the new shares issued by the Defendant. By around August 2018, the Plaintiff paid KRW 245,000,000 to the instant company, so that the Defendant came to hold 51% of the issued shares of the instant company and the Plaintiff came to hold 49% of the issued shares of the instant company, respectively. The instant company appointed the Defendant’s representative director, Non-Party 2, and Non-Party 3 designated by the Plaintiff side as co-representative directors around August 2018.\\n\\nc) However, when a dispute arose between the Plaintiff and the Defendant around October 2018 regarding the source of the capital used by the instant company, Non-Party 2, while excluding the intent of the other co-representative director, Non-Party 3, issued a notice convening an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders with the agenda of unilaterally changing the debtor’s joint representative director system to an individual sole representative director system and additionally appointing an inside director of the debtor. Although the Plaintiff filed an application for a provisional injunction prohibiting the holding of the above extraordinary general meeting of shareholders, the application was dismissed on the ground that the Defendant side, as the largest shareholder holding 51% of the shares of the instant company, had management control over the operation of the company, and that, unless the articles of incorporation of the instant company specifically provided for co-representative directors, a resolution abolishing the co-representative director system did not have to go through the procedure for amending the articles of incorporation, and thus the Defendant, as a majority shareholder, had authority to unilaterally decide the relevant matter at the shareholders’ meeting.\\n\\nAt the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders, Non-Party 2 changed the existing co-representative director system to an individual sole representative director system, thereby abolishing the co-representative director system, and appointed as an inside director a person opposed by the Plaintiff side. The instant company dismissed Non-Party 3, the representative director on the Plaintiff side, around November 2018, and, pursuant to a resolution by a majority of directors composed of the Defendant side, lent KRW 100,000,000 to the Defendant.\\n\\nIn addition, the instant company entered into a consulting contract with Non-Party 4, who is said to be the de facto owner/controller of the Defendant, and paid food expenses, entertainment expenses, golf expenses, etc., and also incurred employee salaries, entertainment expenses, vehicle maintenance expenses, etc. under the name of selling and administrative expenses, so that by around June 2020 the total assets of the instant company amounted to only approximately KRW 61,580,000 (current assets approximately KRW 51,010,000), and by around June 2021 the total assets of the instant company amounted to only approximately KRW 19,770,000 (current assets approximately KRW 10,770,000).\\n\\nAs a result of the Plaintiff’s application for seizure and collection of claims against the Defendant based on the judgment of the first instance, as of around July 2021, while this case was pending in the court below, the Defendant’s deposit claims against three financial institutions amounted in total to less than KRW 2,000,000.\\n\\n3) In light of the legal principles set out above, we examine whether the court below properly reduced about 75% of the stipulated amount of liquidated damages and recognized only the funds said to have been invested by the Plaintiff Company as damages.\\n\\na) The instant contract provides that the Plaintiff and the Defendant jointly invest in the instant company and that, in return for the Defendant having the largest equity interest in the instant company, the instant company shall have a co-representative director system. This appears to have been intended to allow the Defendant to have the largest equity interest enabling it to make decisions unilaterally with respect to the instant company by evaluating its existing technological capabilities, etc., while enabling the Plaintiff to secure at least a minimal check mechanism through a co-representative director. However, if the Defendant, by using its status as the holder of the largest equity interest, breaches its obligations under the instant contract and abolishes the co-representative director system, the Plaintiff would be excluded from management and lose the means to check the operation of the company according to the Defendant’s intent.\\n\\nThe instant agreement on liquidated damages was entered into in order to secure voluntary performance by psychologically warning the Defendant side in a situation where the actual performance of the obligation to maintain the co-representative director system of the instant company by the Defendant side had to continue in order to achieve the contractual purpose. When the Defendant actually breached its contractual obligation, abolished the co-representative director system, and dismissed the representative director on the Plaintiff side, the Plaintiff was unable to prevent this through legal means such as provisional injunctions. With the means to check management eliminated, most of the funds of the instant company were diverted according to the Defendant’s intent.\\n\\nb) Taking together the purpose of the instant contract as described above, the parties’ intent to secure performance of obligations through a stipulation of liquidated damages for breaches of obligations prescribed in the instant contract, the consequences caused by the Defendant’s breach of obligations, and the financial condition of the instant company, it can be assessed that, due to the Defendant’s breach of contract, the Plaintiff was in fact unable to participate in the management of the instant company and thereby suffered substantial property losses, both tangible and intangible, including being unable to obtain investment profits. Even if such losses are not specifically quantified or numerically calculated, the court below could have taken measures such as comparing the Plaintiff’s loss amount, which could be estimated at least approximately from the materials in the record, with the stipulated amount.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below reduced the amount to the principal investment amount on the grounds that the Plaintiff held an equity interest in the instant company or that the disadvantage of being unable to participate in management could not be economically converted, and the like; however, the above investment amount merely recognizes only the money that could be returned by restoration to the original status if the Plaintiff rescinded the contract on the ground of the Defendant’s nonperformance of the principal obligation, and thus ultimately produces the same result as wholly denying the agreement itself concerning liquidated damages.\\n\\n4) In addition, the amount invested by Non-Party 1, the Plaintiff’s representative, in the Defendant cannot immediately be said to be the Plaintiff’s loss apart from the Plaintiff’s investment funds mentioned above, but the Plaintiff consistently argued from the first instance that the sum of the KRW 245,000,000 paid by the Plaintiff and the KRW 255,000,000 paid by Non-Party 1 amounted to KRW 500,000,000, and that the stipulated liquidated damages at the time of the instant contract were set at twice that KRW 500,000,000, and that Non-Party 1 was not seeking separate damages. Non-Party 1 did in fact conclude a contract with the Defendant to establish the instant company, and the instant contract concluded between the Plaintiff and the Defendant after the establishment of the instant company includes the contents that Non-Party 1 would invest KRW 255,000,000 in the Defendant; yet it merely provides for liquidated damages between the Plaintiff and the Defendant, and no separate stipulation of liquidated damages concerning Non-Party 1’s investment funds is set forth in the contract document. In addition, the stipulated amount of liquidated damages is twice the aggregate amount of the investments by the Plaintiff and Non-Party 1, and due to the Defendant’s breach of contract, the same intangible loss as described above arose also with respect to Non-Party 1’s investment funds; in light of these circumstances, the wording of the contract, which is a dispositive document, conforms to the Plaintiff’s argument. Although the Defendant argued that Non-Party 1’s investment funds are not a matter to be considered, it appears not to have specifically refuted the circumstances surrounding the agreement on the stipulated liquidated damages asserted by the Plaintiff. If so, the court below, without examining this point, cannot be deemed to have concluded that Non-Party 1’s investment funds in the Defendant are not to be considered in calculating the stipulated amount of liquidated damages under the instant contract.\\n\\n5) Taking these circumstances together, the court below, without examining the above circumstances and reducing the stipulated amount of liquidated damages to the amount as stated in the judgment below solely on the basis of the reasons stated therein, is manifestly unreasonable in light of the principle of equity; accordingly, the judgment below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles on reduction of stipulated liquidated damages and by failing to conduct the necessary examination, and the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal pointing this out are meritorious.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Defendant’s incidental appeal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its judgment, the court below recognized that ① the Defendant, acting unilaterally, changed the instant company’s co-representative director system to an individual sole representative director system, thereby breaching the contractual obligations prescribed in the instant contract, and therefore was obligated to compensate the resulting damages, and ② rejected the Defendant’s argument that there was no reason attributable to it for the breach of the instant contract. In light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the above judgment of the court below contains no error of law regarding the interpretation of a dispositive document, no violation of the rules of evidence regarding attributable cause, and no failure to fully examine the case.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the part of the judgment below adverse to the Plaintiff is reversed, and this case is remanded to the Suwon High Court; the Defendant’s incidental appeal is dismissed. The judgment is rendered as ordered, by unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[95DA11436]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Summary of the judgment of the court below\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence cited in the record, found that, on June 20, 1989, the Plaintiff and the Defendant entered into a contract whereby one underwater exploration mother ship would be constructed for KRW 1,420,000,000 and delivered to the Defendant by August 19, 1990; that, on December 12, 1989, the Plaintiff and the Defendant separately entered into a contract whereby one high-speed transport vessel would be constructed for KRW 555,000,000 and delivered to the Defendant by October 22, 1990; and that, in each contract, the parties agreed that the liquidated damages for delay would be payable in an amount calculated at the rate of 1.5/1,000 of the ship price per day of delay. The court below further found that the above underwater exploration mother ship was delivered to the Defendant on February 29, 1992, 559 days later than the agreed delivery date; that the above high-speed transport vessel was delivered to the Defendant on December 20, 1991, 424 days later than the agreed delivery date; and that the total amount of liquidated damages for delay arising from the delayed delivery of the ships at issue was KRW 1,432,642,500. On that basis, the court below held that the above liquidated damages had the nature of predetermined damages for the delay in completing the work within the agreed period, and, for the following reasons, found that the amount of predetermined damages was unreasonably excessive and reduced it to KRW 395,000,000 pursuant to Article 398(2) of the Civil Act.\\n\\nNamely, the court below considered that the Plaintiff’s delay in constructing the ships at issue was largely attributable to labor disputes; that, from the standpoint that the Defendant, too, should not allow the Plaintiff company, a defense industry company, to go bankrupt, the Defense Industry Deliberation Council had waived approximately KRW 65.3 billion in liquidated damages for defense-industrial materials contracted by the liquidation company, but had excluded the ship construction contracts at issue, which were government-supplied goods, from the scope of waiver on the ground that there was no statutory basis; that, after learning this, the Vice Ministers’ meeting of the relevant ministries had even agreed to waive KRW 1,432,542,000 in liquidated damages relating to the ship construction contracts at issue; that the Plaintiff had currently been taken over by the Jin Group as a third party through the Defendant; that the Defendant’s tangible damage relating to the ship construction contracts at issue did not even amount to KRW 300,000,000; that, according to Article 75 of the above Contract Affairs Handling Rules, liquidated damages shall be imposed by multiplying the contract amount by the liquidated damages rate of 1.5/1,000 per day of delay in the manufacture and purchase of goods, and by the liquidated damages rate of 1/1,000 per day of delay in the case of construction work, while Article 8 of the same Rules provides that the rate of general administrative expenses shall be calculated as 6/100 in the case of construction work and as 7/100 in the case of manufacture of assembled metal products, machinery, and equipment; and that, in light of the fact that the ships at issue required about one year to construct, the ship construction contracts at issue have a nature more similar to construction work than to the manufacture of goods. Taking all these circumstances together, the court below concluded that the amount of liquidated damages for delay at issue was unreasonably excessive.\\n\\n2. As to Point 1\\n\\nUnder Article 94 of the former Budget and Accounts Act (before its deletion by Act No. 4868 of January 5, 1995), Article 129 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act (before its deletion by Presidential Decree No. 14710 of July 6, 1995), and Article 75(1) of the Contract Affairs Handling Rules (before its repeal by Prime Ministerial Ordinance No. 511 of July 6, 1995), the head of the central administrative agency or a public official entrusted by him shall, when the contractual party is in delay of performance of contractual obligations, require the contractual party to pay in cash, as liquidated damages for delay, an amount obtained by multiplying the contract amount by the rate of 1.5/1,000 and by the number of days of delay in the case of the manufacture and purchase of goods. These provisions merely prescribe the necessary matters concerning contract administration that the relevant public officials must observe in contractual relations between the State and private persons, and they are only internal rules of the State; moreover, their essential content is not different from contracts between private persons. Therefore, unless there are special provisions in the above statutes and regulations, the provisions and legal principles of private law apply as they are. Accordingly, as the provisions concerning liquidated damages for delay prescribed in the above statutes and regulations are recognized as predetermined damages, if the predetermined amount is unreasonably excessive, the court may reduce it appropriately pursuant to Article 398(2) of the Civil Act.\\n\\nIn addition, where a contract performance deposit and liquidated damages for delay are stipulated in a contract for work, unless there are special circumstances, the contract performance deposit is deemed to have the nature of a contractual penalty or sanction, and the liquidated damages for delay are deemed to constitute predetermined damages (see Supreme Court Decision 88DAKA25601, decided October 10, 1989; Supreme Court Decisions 88DAKA6273 and 88DAKA6280, decided July 25, 1989; Supreme Court Decision 94DA32986, decided September 30, 1994, etc.).\\n\\nFrom this perspective, the court below found that, in concluding the ship construction contracts at issue, the parties incorporated into the ship construction contracts the matters concerning the contract performance deposit and liquidated damages for delay prescribed by the relevant statutes and regulations, such as the former Budget and Accounts Act, and therefore held that the liquidated damages for delay at issue had the nature of predetermined damages and could be reduced pursuant to Article 398(2) of the Civil Act. Such determination is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error of law, such as misapprehension of legal principles, as pointed out in the arguments. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n3. As to Points 2 and 3\\n\\nWhether the predetermined amount of damages is unreasonably excessive should be determined by taking into account all circumstances, including the respective positions of the contracting parties, the purpose and content of the contract, the motive for stipulating liquidated damages, the comparison between the actual damage and the predetermined amount, and the trading practices and economic conditions at the time, and by considering whether the amount exceeds the range that an ordinary member of society can accept (see Supreme Court Decision 95DA28526, decided December 12, 1995). Upon review of the record, the court below, after recognizing the fact that liquidated damages for delay had arisen as stated in paragraph 1 above, reduced them on the ground that they were unreasonably excessive. This measure appears proper in light of the above standard of judgment, and no error can be found, as alleged in the argument, such as failure to conduct proper deliberation, an omission in judgment, or an error of law regarding the reduction of liquidated damages for delay and predetermined damages (Supreme Court Decision 63DA919, decided May 26, 1964, cited in the argument, concerns a different matter from this case).\\n\\nThe argument further asserts that, in a case such as this where liquidated damages for delay are agreed to be calculated by multiplying the total contract price by the rate of liquidated damages for delay, whether the liquidated damages for delay are excessive should be determined by examining whether the rate of liquidated damages for delay itself is excessive, and that if the rate itself is not excessive, the total amount of liquidated damages for delay should not be judged on the basis that the total amount increases merely because the number of days of delay increases. However, Article 398(2) of the Civil Act provides that, if the predetermined amount of damages is unreasonably excessive, the court may reduce it appropriately, and the predetermined amount of damages referred to here is, by the wording of the provision, to be construed as meaning the total amount of the predetermined damages. Therefore, the question of whether liquidated damages for delay, which fall within predetermined damages, are excessive should be determined on the basis of the total amount of liquidated damages for delay.\\n\\nAll of the arguments are without merit.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. The judgment is rendered unanimously by the participating Justices as set forth in the dispositive portion."}

question:
In each of the following cases, what fills the blank appropriately? (The market value of X and Y land has not changed, and there are no special circumstances regarding the apportionment of responsibility at the time the joint mortgage was created. Interest, delay damages, and enforcement costs shall not be considered. Each item is independent, and where there is a dispute, it shall be governed by case law)

(a) While a joint mortgage securing a claim amount of KRW 30,000,000 was created in favor of C over X land (market value KRW 20,000,000) and Y land (market value KRW 40,000,000) owned by debtor A, A sold Y land to A, and the ownership transfer registration in the name of A was completed. If the sales contract concerning Y land is rescinded as a fraudulent conveyance by debtor A's general creditor B (preserved claim amount KRW 100,000,000), and value compensation is made, the amount of value compensation is ( a ).
(b) While a joint mortgage securing a claim amount of KRW 60,000,000 was created in favor of C over X land (market value KRW 30,000,000) and Y land (market value KRW 60,000,000) owned by debtor A, A sold X land and Y land to A as a package, and the ownership transfer registration in the name of A was completed. If the sales contract concerning X land and Y land is rescinded as a fraudulent conveyance by debtor A's general creditor B (preserved claim amount KRW 100,000,000), and value compensation is made, the amount of value compensation is ( b ).
(c) On X land owned by debtor A (market value KRW 500,000,000), there are separately established a first-priority mortgage securing C's claim amount of KRW 200,000,000 and a second-priority mortgage securing D's claim amount of KRW 100,000,000, and on Y land owned by real property guarantor E (market value KRW 500,000,000), a joint mortgage has been created over the entirety of D's secured claim amount concerning X land. While A sold X land to A, and the ownership transfer registration in the name of A was completed, if the sales contract concerning X land is rescinded as a fraudulent conveyance by debtor A's general creditor B (preserved claim amount KRW 300,000,000), and value compensation is made, the amount of value compensation is ( c ).
label: A

{"[2013DA90402]": "We decide on the grounds of final appeal.\\n\\n1. In determining whether an act constitutes a fraudulent act subject to a creditor’s revocation action, if the debtor’s property has been provided as real security for another creditor’s claim, the portion so provided as real security cannot be regarded as the debtor’s property liable to the debtor’s general creditors; therefore, only the balance obtained by deducting the secured claim amount held by the other creditor from the value of the property provided as such real security must be evaluated as the debtor’s assets (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2012. 1. 12., 2010DA64792). Where a joint mortgage is established on several real properties, in calculating such property liable for execution, unless special circumstances exist, the secured claim amount borne by each real property should be regarded, in light of the purport of Article 368 of the Civil Act, as the amount obtained by apportioning the secured claim amount of the joint mortgage in proportion to the value of each real property that is the object of the joint mortgage. However, where among several real properties some are owned by the debtor and others are owned by a real guarantor, considering, inter alia, that the real guarantor is in a position to exercise a mortgage right against the real property owned by the debtor by way of subrogation of the person who has performed obligations pursuant to Articles 481 and 482 of the Civil Act, unless there are special circumstances under which the real guarantor cannot exercise a right of indemnity against the debtor, the secured claim amount borne by the real property owned by the debtor is the full amount of the secured claim amount of the joint mortgage up to the value of the debtor-owned real property, and the secured claim amount borne by the real property owned by the real guarantor should be deemed the remainder after excluding from the secured claim amount of the joint mortgage the secured claim amount borne by the above-mentioned real property owned by the debtor. This legal principle likewise applies where some shares in a single co-owned real property are owned by the debtor and other shares are owned by a real guarantor (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision rendered on 2013. 7. 18., 2012DA5643).\\n\\n2. According to the reasons in the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na. Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 co-own, in equal 1/2 shares, a 55㎡ field at Paju-si (Address 1 omitted), a 1,310㎡ lot at (Address 2 omitted), and each building thereon [hereinafter, the portion owned by Nonparty 1 among the above real properties shall be referred to as “the share at issue,” and the portion owned by Nonparty 2 (the respective real properties stated in items 8, 9, and 10 of the attached list in the judgment below) shall, together with the respective real properties stated in items 5, 6, and 7 of the attached list in the judgment below, also owned by Nonparty 2, be referred to as “the real properties at issue”].\\n\\nb. With respect to the real properties at issue and the share at issue, on 1999. 4. 15., a registration of establishment of a joint mortgage, with Debtor Nonparty 1, mortgagee Paju Yeoncheon Livestock Cooperative, and maximum claim amount of 85,000,000 won (hereinafter referred to as “Mortgage No. 1”), on 2009. 8. 19., a registration of establishment of a joint mortgage, with Debtor Nonparty 1, mortgagee Paju Yeoncheon Livestock Cooperative, and maximum claim amount of 390,000,000 won (hereinafter referred to as “Mortgage No. 2”), and from 1999. 4. 15. to 2008. 4. 18., 12 registrations of establishment of joint mortgages, with Debtor Nonparty 2, mortgagee Paju Yeoncheon Livestock Cooperative, and a total maximum claim amount of 3,307,000,000 won (hereinafter collectively referred to as “Mortgage No. 3”), had each been completed.\\n\\nc. On 2011. 9. 5., Nonparty 2 entered into a sales contract to sell the respective real properties stated in items 1 through 4 of the attached list set forth in the judgment below with the Defendant, who is his sibling (hereinafter referred to as “the sales contract at issue”), and on 2011. 9. 6. completed the registration of transfer of ownership in favor of the Defendant.\\n\\nd. At that time, the value of the real properties at issue was 1,726,066,880 won, the value of the share at issue was 1,252,726,880 won, and the secured claim amount of Mortgage No. 3 was 1,393,312,026 won.\\n\\n3. Examining the above factual relations in light of the legal principles stated above, in the present case, where there is no allegation or proof of special circumstances under which Nonparty 2 cannot exercise a right of indemnity against Nonparty 1 or Nonparty 1 cannot exercise a right of indemnity against Nonparty 2, the aggregate maximum claim amount of Mortgage No. 1 and Mortgage No. 2, in which Nonparty 1 is the debtor and Nonparty 2 is the real guarantor, is 475,000,000 won (= 85,000,000 won + 390,000,000 won), and since it does not exceed the value of 1,252,726,880 won of the share at issue owned by the debtor Nonparty 1, it shall be deemed that no portion of the secured claim amount of Mortgage No. 1 and Mortgage No. 2 is borne by the real properties at issue owned by the real guarantor Nonparty 2. Also, since the secured claim amount of Mortgage No. 3, in which Nonparty 2 is the debtor and Nonparty 1 is the real guarantor, is 1,393,312,026 won and does not exceed the value of 1,726,066,880 won of the real properties at issue owned by the debtor Nonparty 2, it shall be deemed that no portion of the secured claim amount of Mortgage No. 3 is borne by the share at issue owned by the real guarantor Nonparty 1.\\n\\n4. Therefore, although there are some inappropriate parts in the reasons of the judgment below, the court below’s failure to deduct the secured claim amounts of Mortgages No. 1 and No. 2 when evaluating the value of the real properties at issue is, as a result, proper, and there is no error that affected the conclusion of the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the establishment of a fraudulent act.\\n\\n5. Therefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and the appeal costs shall be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the object of an obligation is incorrect? (In cases of dispute, according to precedent)
A: The medical treatment obligation owed by a physician to a patient is, absent special circumstances, an obligation of means.
B: When Korean currency is appropriated in satisfaction of a foreign-currency claim, absent special circumstances, it must be converted by reference to the foreign exchange quotation at the time of actual appropriation of performance.
C: Because an alternative obligation is fixed by the exercise of the choice, the extinctive prescription period for an alternative obligation runs from the time the right of selection is exercised.
D: Even where there is no agreement on interest for a monetary obligation, default interest arising from the debtor's delay in performance may, absent special circumstances, be claimed at the statutory rate.
E: Where the creditor, in the case of a foreign-currency claim that is a monetary claim with the amount of the claim designated in foreign currency, exercises the right to substitute performance and claims by converting it into Korean currency, the court, when ordering the debtor to perform, must convert by reference to the foreign exchange quotation at the time the oral argument in fact-finding proceedings is concluded.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DA72765]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Existence of the Duty to Pay Brokerage Fee\\nUpon examining the reasons of the lower judgment and the reasons of the first-instance judgment cited by the lower court in light of the record, the lower court’s determination that the Defendant is obligated to pay the Plaintiff 525,000 Swiss francs as remuneration for the Plaintiff’s brokerage and intermediary services for the sale of the equipment for manufacturing video display apparatus involved in this case is proper, and there is no illegality therein such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the existence of agency authority and the burden of proof regarding performance of the contract, or violation of the rules of evidence or empirical rules, as asserted by the Defendant in Grounds of Appeal 1 through 3.\\n\\n2. The Standard Time for Converting the Brokerage Fee into Korean Currency and the Commencement Date of Delay Damages\\nWhere a monetary claim whose amount is designated in foreign currency, that is, a foreign-currency claim, is claimed by the creditor after converting it into Korean currency by exercising the right to demand substitute performance, the court, when ordering the debtor to perform, should use as the standard time for converting into Korean currency the foreign exchange rate at the time when the fact-finding trial was closed, which is closest to the time when the debtor actually performs (see, e.g., the Supreme Court en banc decision rendered on March 12, 1991 in Case No. 90DA2147). In the case where only the debtor is dissatisfied with and appeals from such a first-instance judgment ordering performance, since the appellate instance is a continuation of the trial, even if the arguments raised by the debtor as grounds of appeal or during the course of the proceedings are without merit, the court should recalculate the claim amount based on the foreign exchange rate at the time the appellate trial was closed and, unless this would violate the principle of prohibition against change for the worse, partially grant the debtor’s appeal.\\n\\nHowever, according to the reasons of the lower judgment, the lower court, solely on the ground that it could not accept the Defendant’s argument disputing the existence of the duty to pay the brokerage fee in this case, dismissed the Defendant’s appeal without even converting the amount of the brokerage fee claim into Korean currency by using the foreign exchange rate at the time the lower trial was closed (it is a matter of common knowledge that the benchmark exchange rate for Swiss francs as of July 19, 2006, the date on which the lower trial was closed, was KRW 764.03), and thus left intact the amount awarded by the first-instance judgment as converted by the foreign exchange rate at the time the first-instance trial was closed (benchmark exchange rate KRW 808.09). Accordingly, the lower judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the standard time for converting a foreign-currency claim into Korean currency.\\n\\nIn addition, although the lower court acknowledged that the time for performance of the duty to pay the brokerage fee in this case did not arrive until around October 2005 during the pendency of the first-instance action, it nonetheless cited and upheld in full the reasons and conclusion of the first-instance judgment, which ordered payment of delay damages from March 24, 2005, the day following service of a copy of the complaint in this case, and this must be deemed a case where there is a contradiction in the reasons for the judgment.\\n\\nAll of the arguments in Ground of Appeal 4 pointing out the above matters are well-founded.\\n\\n3. Scope of Reversal\\nIn light of the factual relations lawfully found by the lower court and the legal principles stated above, the Defendant is obligated to pay the Plaintiff delay damages on KRW 401,115,750, which is the result of converting the brokerage fee of 525,000 Swiss francs at the benchmark exchange rate of KRW 764.03 as of July 19, 2006, the date on which the lower trial was closed, at the rate of 5% per annum prescribed by the Civil Act from November 1, 2005, the day following the date recognized as the date on which the time for performance had arrived, until September 20, 2006, the date of the lower judgment, at which it is deemed reasonable for the Defendant to contest the scope of its payment obligation, and at the rate of 20% per annum prescribed by the Act on Special Cases Concerning Expedition, etc. of Legal Proceedings from the following day until the day of full payment.\\n\\nAccordingly, the part of the lower judgment that dismissed the Defendant’s appeal with respect to the amount exceeding the above recognized scope is improper, and that part is to be reversed; however, since this case is sufficiently ready for this Court to decide directly, the Court shall render its own judgment pursuant to Article 437, item 1, of the Civil Procedure Act.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nAmong the lower judgment, the part adverse to the Defendant exceeding KRW 401,115,750 and the amounts calculated thereon at the rate of 5% per annum from November 1, 2005 to September 20, 2006, and at the rate of 20% per annum from the following day until the day of full payment, is reversed; the corresponding part of the first-instance judgment is revoked; the Plaintiff’s claim corresponding thereto is dismissed; the remainder of the Defendant’s appeal is dismissed; and the total costs of litigation shall be divided into eight parts, with one part borne by the Plaintiff and the remainder borne by the Defendant, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2009DA85342]": "We examine the grounds of final appeal.\\n\\nArticle 397(1) of the Civil Act provides in the main text that the amount of damages for non-performance of a monetary obligation shall be according to the statutory interest rate, and in its proviso it provides, “However, if there is an agreed interest rate that does not violate any restriction under statutes, then according to that rate.” This proviso applies only where the agreed interest rate is at least the statutory interest rate, and where the agreed interest rate is lower than the statutory interest rate, one must return to the main text and determine delay damages according to the statutory interest rate.\\n\\nFirst, even where there is no interest agreement at all concerning a monetary obligation and therefore no interest claim can be made at all, delay damages arising from the debtor’s delay in performance may be claimed according to the statutory interest rate; therefore, a fortiori, where at least some interest could have been claimed, delay damages according to the statutory interest rate should likewise be claimable. Furthermore, as a matter of principle, a monetary creditor may allege and prove specific damages incurred due to the debtor’s non-performance and, if such damages fall within the scope of compensation under Article 393 of the Civil Act, etc., may claim compensation therefor. However, because of the versatility of money today, its modes of use are endless, and while it is readily generally inferred that damage in the form of deprivation of the possibility of use will arise for the creditor from non-performance of a monetary obligation, under the above general principle the calculation of the specific amount of compensation may be highly varied and may lose balance. Accordingly, in order to handle the issue of damages arising from non-performance of a monetary obligation uniformly, Article 397(1) of the Civil Act was enacted, with the main text basing the amount on the statutory interest rate as abstract damages; and the need for such uniform treatment must be acknowledged equally even where the interest rate is agreed at a rate lower than the statutory interest rate, insofar as the issue is damages rather than interest. In addition, the reason why the proviso to Article 397(1) of the Civil Act provides that, if there is an agreed interest rate, one is to follow it, is that if, where the agreed interest rate is higher than the statutory interest rate, delay damages according to the statutory interest rate were deemed sufficient, the creditor would be barred from asserting more extensive damages that would in principle have been permitted as noted above, and the debtor would instead gain from the delay in performance, which would be unreasonable; where the agreed interest rate is lower than the statutory interest rate, there is no such unreasonableness to be raised. Lastly, former Civil Act Article 419 corresponding to Article 397 of the Civil Act expressly provided in the proviso to paragraph 1 that the agreed interest rate was to apply only “when the agreed interest rate exceeds the statutory interest rate,” and there is no basis in the legislative process of the Civil Act to conclude that, contrary thereto, it was the legislative intent that the proviso would also apply where the agreed interest rate is lower than the statutory interest rate.\\n\\nThe lower court found that the deceased, on January 18, 2002, lent KRW 50,000,000 to Defendant 1 under the joint and several guarantee of Defendant 2, with the maturity date set at January 18, 2004 and interest set at 0.1% per month (thus 1.2% per annum); that the deceased died on January 4, 2006 and the Plaintiff acquired all of the above loan claim by inheritance and assignment of claim; and, after rejecting the Defendant’s arguments of gift and payment, determined that the Defendants are jointly and severally liable to pay the above borrowed principal of KRW 50,000,000 and delay damages calculated at the civil statutory interest rate of 5% per annum for the period from January 19, 2004, the day after the maturity date, to June 3, 2009, the date of the first-instance judgment, by which it was reasonable for the Defendants to dispute the existence and scope of their duty to perform, and at the rate of 20% per annum prescribed by the “Act on Special Cases Concerning Expedition, etc. of Legal Proceedings” from the following day until the day of full payment.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles and the record examined above, the lower court’s findings of fact and determination as stated above are proper and acceptable, and it cannot be said that there is illegality due to factual error or misapprehension of law caused by violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of final appeal.\\n\\nAccordingly, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2015DA21295]": "The Court examines the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. By comprehensively considering the evidence it adopted, the lower court found: ① before the first operation, the Plaintiff’s lower-extremity strength on manual muscle testing was grade 3-4, and he had only mild voiding and bowel dysfunction; however, immediately after the first operation, his lower-extremity strength became grade 0, amounting to complete paralysis, his voiding and bowel dysfunction worsened, and sexual dysfunction also developed; ② the medical staff of the Defendant Hospital damaged the dura mater in the course of dissecting the ossified portion of the posterior longitudinal ligament, which had adhered to the dura mater during the first operation, and cerebrospinal fluid leaked from that site; ③ accordingly, the medical staff of the Defendant Hospital restored the damaged area with artificial dura mater, Gelfoam, and the like; ④ spastic bilateral lower-extremity paralysis, neurogenic bladder, and neurogenic dysfunction symptoms are symptoms that mainly occur upon spinal cord injury. Based on these findings, the lower court held that, in the course of removing the ossified posterior longitudinal ligament, the medical staff of the Defendant Hospital damaged the dura mater, causing cerebrospinal fluid leakage and thereby injuring the Plaintiff’s spinal cord, or, through negligence in injuring the Plaintiff’s spinal cord during the process of restoring the damaged dura mater, caused lower-extremity paralysis, voiding and bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, and the like in the Plaintiff, and thus recognized the Defendant’s liability for damages to the Plaintiff.\\n\\n2. However, the lower court’s determination is difficult to sustain for the following reasons.\\n\\na. The treatment obligation borne by a physician toward a patient is not a result obligation that must necessarily achieve the result of the patient’s recovery, but rather a means obligation, namely, an obligation to exercise the care of a good manager and to provide the medical treatment that is necessary and appropriate in light of the current level of medical science for the purpose of recovery; therefore, the mere fact that the outcome of treatment was unsatisfactory cannot immediately be presumed to constitute non-performance of the treatment obligation. Moreover, where after medical treatment sequelae occur, if such sequelae are something that may appear as a complication in the course of the medical treatment even if all best measures are taken at the then level of medical care, or may secondarily occur as a result of such complications, then, considering in comprehensive terms the content of the medical treatment, the procedure, the site and extent of the complication, the medical level at the time, and the skill of the attending medical staff, etc., absent circumstances showing that the symptoms exceeded the scope of generally recognized complications, the mere fact that such sequelae occurred cannot be presumed to show negligence in the course of medical treatment (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2007DA76290, decided March 27, 2008).  \\nIn addition, because medical treatment is performed in a field requiring highly specialized knowledge, and it is highly difficult for laypersons who are not experts to ascertain whether there was a breach of the duty of care in the course of a physician’s medical treatment and whether there is a causal relationship between such breach and the occurrence of damage, if symptoms causing serious consequences to a patient arise during or after surgery, and indirect facts are proved from which it is difficult to view the occurrence of such symptoms as having another cause apart from medical negligence, then it may be presumed that such symptoms were caused by medical negligence. However, even in such a case, it is not permissible to infer the physician’s negligence and causal relationship to the serious result in a vague manner based on circumstances that do not secure a probability sufficient to presume the occurrence of the result from the physician’s negligence, thereby, in effect, shifting to the physician the burden of proving absence of negligence (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2011DA100138, decided October 11, 2012).\\n\\nb. According to the reasoning of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n(1) The Plaintiff began to experience tingling sensations in both lower extremities around November 2007, and from around January 2008 the tingling and pain in both lower extremities worsened; on February 26, 2008, the Plaintiff first visited the △△△ Hospital operated by the Defendant with symptoms such as lower back and lower-extremity pain, lower-extremity weakness and tingling, abnormal sensation in the left lower extremity, gait disturbance, and difficulty in urination and defecation.\\n\\n(2) Based on the results of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and other examinations of the Plaintiff, the medical staff of the Defendant Hospital diagnosed ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament at thoracic vertebrae 5-7 and 11-12, and then, on March 19, 2008 from around 08:15 until around 17:30, performed thoracoscopic-guided spinal fusion and autologous bone grafting at thoracic vertebrae 6-7 on the Plaintiff (the first operation). When severe lower-extremity pain and lower-extremity paralysis and the like occurred in the Plaintiff immediately after the surgery, from around 21:40 on March 19, 2008 until around 04:20 on March 20, 2008, they again performed thoracoscopic-guided spinal fusion and autologous bone grafting at thoracic vertebrae 5-6 (the second operation). However, even after the second operation, the Plaintiff’s lower-extremity paralysis and the like did not disappear.\\n\\n(3) On manual muscle testing, the Plaintiff’s bilateral lower-extremity strength weakened from grade 4-5 around February 28, 2008 to grade 3-4 around March 17, 2008, but after the first and second operations, the bilateral lower-extremity strength grade was measured as 0.\\n\\n(4) After the first and second operations, the Plaintiff received drug treatment and early rehabilitation treatment to improve paralysis and stimulate spinal cord nerve regeneration, and around June 2009, the manual muscle testing showed the right lower-extremity strength grade as 3 and the left lower-extremity strength grade as 2-3, and his condition improved to the extent corresponding to grade D under the American Spinal Injury Association impairment classification (grade A being complete paralysis and grade E being normal); however, thereafter the symptoms worsened again, and at the time of the physical examination at the court of first instance around August 2011, he was in a state of spastic lower-extremity paralysis, voiding and bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, and the like.\\n\\n(5) According to the result of the first-instance court’s commission for appraisal of medical records to the President of Chung-Ang University Hospital and the result of the lower court’s factual inquiry, ① the surgical method for ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament by anterior approach, as performed by the medical staff of the Defendant Hospital, has advantages such as enabling direct removal of the ossified posterior longitudinal ligament, but there is a risk of spinal cord injury or cerebrospinal fluid leakage due to dural tear during surgery, and it is known that the possibility of spinal cord injury is high when dissecting the ossified portion of the posterior longitudinal ligament adhered to the dura mater; depending on the researcher, the possibility of spinal cord injury after surgery for thoracic ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament has been reported as 23.8% or 30.8%; ② the surgery received by the Plaintiff was a very difficult surgery with the possibility of spinal cord injury after surgery being about 30% as above, and the Plaintiff had preoperative paresis symptoms in both lower extremities; moreover, because there were multiple possibilities even during surgery when removing the ossified portion of the posterior longitudinal ligament, it is difficult to conclude simply that this was only spinal cord injury caused by the surgery; ③ considering the extent of the Plaintiff’s preoperative disease condition, although there could be a difference in time even if surgery had not been performed, the possibility of nerve injury and the occurrence of urological dysfunction cannot be completely excluded; and ④ the high-signal shadow in the spinal cord seen on the Plaintiff’s preoperative MRI in the T2 image means that edema and ischemia, etc. occurred in the spinal cord, indicating nerve injury, and when signal intensity increases in a T2-weighted image, the patient shows more severe neurological deficits than a patient without such findings; because the Plaintiff had high-signal shadow in the same corresponding segment even before surgery, the prognosis could be poor.\\n\\n(6) The occupancy rate of the ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament at the Plaintiff’s thoracic vertebrae 6-7, where the ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament was severe, was about 83.3% before surgery, and a physician of the Defendant Hospital repeatedly emphasized and explained to the Plaintiff and his guardian before the first operation that there was a risk that paralysis might occur in the lower extremities and the like after surgery.\\n\\nc. In light of these facts, because the Plaintiff had a high occupancy rate of ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament and the signs and findings of spinal cord injury were already present before the first operation, the ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament had progressed to a considerable extent. Accordingly, there is a substantial possibility that the degree of adhesion between the ossified posterior longitudinal ligament and the dura mater was severe, so even if during the first operation the dura mater was damaged and cerebrospinal fluid leaked in the process of removing the ossified posterior longitudinal ligament, there is considerable room to view this as a result that inevitably occurred in the course of surgery rather than as a result caused by medical negligence. Also, the record does not show objective materials regarding the causal relationship between dural damage and cerebrospinal fluid leakage and spinal cord injury, and because the medical staff of the Defendant Hospital immediately took measures to restore the damaged area with artificial dura mater, Gelfoam, and the like, it is also difficult to conclude that dural damage and cerebrospinal fluid leakage were the cause of the spinal cord injury.\\n\\nFurther, in light of the risk of spinal cord injury inherent in the surgical method for ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament by anterior approach and, in particular, the degree of the possibility of spinal cord injury after surgery for thoracic ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament, the postoperative prognosis predicted by the Plaintiff’s preoperative condition and the prognosis if surgery were not performed, the fact that the medical staff of the Defendant Hospital repeatedly emphasized and explained to the Plaintiff before surgery the possibility of paralysis occurring after surgery, and the fact that the Plaintiff’s symptoms such as lower-extremity paralysis substantially improved through rehabilitation treatment and the like and then worsened again, it is difficult to conclude that there was no other cause, apart from medical negligence, that induced the Plaintiff’s spinal cord injury during surgery or during the process of dural repair.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, these circumstances cannot, merely on the basis of the result of spinal cord injury that occurred in the Plaintiff after surgery, vaguely presume that the medical staff of the Defendant Hospital was negligent.
