The indirect facts relied upon by the lower court may constitute circumstances from which a causal relationship between the first operation and the spinal cord injury can be presumed, but they are difficult to regard as circumstances equipped with such probability as to further permit the presumption that the Plaintiff’s spinal cord injury was caused by the medical negligence of the medical staff of the Defendant Hospital.\\n\\nTherefore, the lower court should have examined what causes may have induced spinal cord injury during the surgical process, what specific content of the duty of care was required of the medical staff of the Defendant Hospital, whether there were specific measures or methods to prevent dural damage or spinal cord injury during surgery, and whether there were circumstances making it possible to view the spinal cord injury or lower-extremity paralysis and the like as having exceeded the scope of complications generally recognized in the course of medical treatment, and then determined whether there were circumstances securing such probability as to permit the presumption of medical negligence on the part of the medical staff of the Defendant Hospital.\\n\\n3. Nevertheless, the lower court recognized the Defendant’s liability for damages by presuming causation and negligence on the part of the medical staff of the Defendant Hospital solely on the basis of circumstances lacking the probability found by the lower court’s reasoning above. Accordingly, this lower court judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles on the presumption of negligence and causation in medical malpractice litigation or by failing to fully hear and determine the case. The Defendant’s argument in the grounds of appeal pointing out this issue is well founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without addressing the Defendant’s remaining grounds of appeal and the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal, the lower court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. It is so decided by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[64DA1156]": "We shall examine the appeal filed by the Defendant’s litigation representative.\\n\\n(1) With respect to Grounds 1 and 2 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nUpon carefully examining the contents of each piece of evidence relied upon by the court below in finding the facts as stated in its decision, according to the record, it shall be deemed that such evidence is sufficient to support the finding of the facts as stated in the decision, and no illegality can be found in the process of weighing the evidence. The argument is merely to cite evidence rejected by the court below or to criticize the judgment of the court below on an independent view, and thus cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(2) With respect to Ground 3 of the grounds for appeal\\n\\nWhere a person who enters into a contract as another person’s agent fails to prove his authority and also fails to obtain ratification from the principal, he shall be liable, at the option of the other party, for performance of the contract or for damages; and the statute of limitations for the other party’s claim for performance of the contract or damages shall run from the time when such option can be exercised, and the time when such option can be exercised means the time when authority is not proved or ratification is not obtained from the principal. In the present case, however, if the evidence relied upon by the court below is taken together, the Plaintiff paid the full purchase price on 1947.11.14, which was the date for performance of the sales contract in this case, and demanded that the Defendant immediately perform the procedures for transfer registration of ownership, but the Defendant merely repeated that he would take responsibility and neither performed such procedures nor proved his authority, and moreover, since Nonparty 1 sold the real property in this case to Nonparty 2 and completed the procedures for transfer registration of ownership on 1960.3.20, ratification by the principal, Nonparty 1, was not obtained; thus, it shall be deemed that the Plaintiff became able to exercise, from 1960.3.20, the claim for damages prescribed in Article 135(1) of the Civil Act against the Defendant. Accordingly, the Defendant’s defense that the Plaintiff’s claim for damages against the Defendant had already been extinguished by the statute of limitations is without merit, and the judgment of the court below is proper.\\n\\nThe argument cannot be accepted.\\n\\nTherefore, by the unanimous opinion of the judges, the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

{"[99DA56512]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Where a debtor satisfies a foreign-currency claim, which is a monetary claim whose amount is fixed in foreign currency, in Korean currency, the time for conversion is not the due date but the time of actual performance, that is, the claim must be satisfied in Korean currency converted at the foreign exchange rate at the time of actual performance (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 90DA2147, rendered on March 12, 1991), and when Korean currency is appropriated to a foreign-currency claim, it too, absent special circumstances, must be converted at the foreign exchange rate at the time of actual appropriation.\\n\\n2. According to the reasoning of the judgment below, the court below found that, under the ship fuel supply contract concluded between Plaintiff and Defendant in this case, the price of the ship fuel supplied by Plaintiff to Defendant was to be calculated at US$229 per kℓ, and Defendant was to pay the price in U.S. dollars into Plaintiff’s bank account designated in the invoice issued by Plaintiff within 45 days from the date on which the fuel was supplied by Plaintiff, and Defendant was to provide, before the first supply date, a check corresponding to the total amount to be paid to Plaintiff; and that Plaintiff, having supplied Defendant under the contract in this case with fuel in the amount of US$291,517 as stated in the judgment but, even after the due date for payment had passed, not having received payment of the fuel price from Defendant, demanded payment of the amount of the guarantee from payment guarantee certificates issued by Korea Exchange Bank and held by Defendant as security for, or as a deposit for, the payment of the fuel price claim in this case, namely, (1) a payment guarantee certificate stating a guarantee amount of KRW 200,000,000 and a guarantee period from November 4, 1997 to December 23 of the same year, and (2) a payment guarantee certificate stating a guarantee amount of KRW 70,000,000 and a guarantee period from November 7 of the same year to December 26 of the same year, and also presented for payment a current-account check issued by Defendant with a face amount of KRW 30,000,000 and an issue date of December 23, 1997, and received, as of December 23 of the same year, KRW 200,000,000 of the payment guarantee money and KRW 30,000,000 of the check amount, and as of December 26 of the same year, KRW 70,000,000 of the payment guarantee money, and appropriated the amounts so received to the fuel price claim in this case by converting them into U.S. dollars according to the foreign exchange rate on each date of receipt.\\n\\nBased on the foregoing findings, the court below rejected all of Defendant’s arguments on this point on the ground that, inasmuch as the parties agreed under the supply contract in this case that the fuel price would be paid in U.S. dollars, even if Defendant delivered to Plaintiff payment guarantee certificates and a current-account check each denominated in Korean won, this was for the purpose of securing payment of the fuel price in this case, a foreign-currency claim, and could not be regarded as a substitute for payment of the fuel price in this case; moreover, from such circumstances alone, it could not be said that there was any express or implied agreement between Plaintiff and Defendant to the effect that the fuel price in this case would be paid in Korean won, rather than in U.S. dollars, converted at the foreign exchange rate at the time of fuel supply or at the time of delivery of the payment guarantee certificates and the current-account check; and further, in the case where the payment guarantee certificates and the current-account check are appropriated to the fuel price claim in this case, the appropriation must be made not at the foreign exchange rate as of the due date for payment of the fuel price in this case, but at the foreign exchange rate at the time of actual appropriation.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principle and the record, the court below’s factual findings and determination are proper and can be accepted, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as a violation of the rules of evidence, a factual error due to incomplete review, or an error in the understanding of the legal principle concerning the exercise of the right to substitute performance for a foreign-currency claim, as argued in the grounds for final appeal. All of the arguments in the grounds for final appeal are not well taken.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the appeal are to be borne by the losing party; and the judgment is rendered as ordered, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

question:
B entered into a sales contract with A in order to purchase Building X owned by A. Unaware that Building X was not owned by A, B claimed damages against A under warranty liability on the ground of the sale of another’s rights. Which of the following correctly combines the correct statements (O) and the incorrect statements (X)? (Each statement is independent, and if there is any dispute, the precedents shall govern.)

(a) If B’s lack of knowledge that ownership of Building X did not belong to A was due to B’s negligence, the court shall take this into account when calculating the amount of damages to be compensated by A.
(b) Even if A also entered into the above sales contract without knowing that Building X was not his property but belonged to A, and there was an agreement that if A breached the contract, A would compensate B in double the earnest money, and if B breached, B could not demand return of the earnest money, such a penalty agreement cannot be regarded as having stipulated liquidated damages in anticipation of damages liability arising from the sale of another’s rights.
(c) If A’s duty to acquire title to Building X and transfer it to B becomes impossible to perform due to A’s fault, B may not only claim damages against A under warranty liability arising from the sale of another’s rights, but may also rescind the contract as ordinary non-performance and claim damages. In that case, the scope of damages arising from such warranty liability is equivalent to the performance interest based on the time when performance became impossible.
(d) Even where A’s inability to transfer title to Building X to B is solely due to B’s fault, A still bears warranty liability arising from the sale of another’s rights.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[71DA218]": "We examine the grounds of appeal advanced by the Defendant’s litigation representative.\\n\\nAccording to the statement of reasons in the judgment below, the court below determined that the lands located in Incheon City, Gyeonggi-do, which are at issue in this case, were all non-self-cultivated farmland at the time the Farmland Reform Act came into force and were therefore purchased by the Defendant Government; however, because the cultivators were Chinese nationals, they were not distributed, and around 1962.8.30 the Defendant sold them to the Plaintiff for use as a school site. Meanwhile, when the said lands were designated on 1962.1.20 as an urban planning road or residential district under the Urban Planning Act, thereby excluding the application of the Farmland Reform Act thereto, the original owners, persons other than the parties, on the ground that ownership thereof had reverted to them, brought an action against the original plaintiff and defendant seeking cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership of the lands in this case, and obtained final judgments in each case in their favor; after so finding, the court below held that, since the Defendant, as seller, became unable to transfer ownership of the said lands to the Plaintiff, as buyer, the Plaintiff’s claim in this case seeking rescission of the said sales contract and damages in lieu of performance was well-founded, and therefore upheld it. In addition, with respect to the Defendant’s assertion that, at the time of the land sale contract, the Plaintiff knew that these lands were not owned by the Defendant, and thus could not seek damages, and that if the Plaintiff did not know of such fact, it was due to the Plaintiff’s negligence and should be taken into account and set off in calculating the amount of damages, the court below rejected it on the ground that there was no evidence to recognize such asserted facts.\\n\\nHowever, in the case of selling another person’s property, where the seller is unable to acquire ownership and transfer it to the buyer, the buyer may rescind the sales contract, and where the buyer did not know at the time of the contract that ownership of the property did not belong to the seller, the buyer may also claim damages, as provided in Article 570 of the Civil Act; but in such case, if the buyer’s lack of knowledge that ownership of the property did not belong to the seller was due to his negligence, then, in calculating the amount of damages, it is reasonable in light of the principle of equity to take such negligence into account. In this case, as the lands in question had already been designated on 1962.1.20 as an urban planning road or residential district, the application of the Farmland Reform Act to the lands in question was excluded pursuant to Article 49 of the Urban Planning Act then in force, with the result that the effect of the Government’s purchase under the Farmland Reform Act of the lands in question was extinguished, and the Defendant, as seller, had lost ownership thereof. Even if the Plaintiff did not know this at the time of purchasing the lands in question, the fact that the Plaintiff, a local government under the direct control of the Government, did not know the above facts concerning the lands in question located within its jurisdiction is, absent special circumstances, to be regarded as due to its negligence. Nevertheless, the court below rejected the Defendant’s assertion of comparative negligence in this case solely on the ground that there was no evidence to recognize such negligence; this cannot but be regarded as either an illegality in that it violated the rules of evidence and thereby erred in its determination as to the presence or absence of negligence, or a failure of examination and a misapprehension of the legal doctrine of comparative negligence.\\n\\nThe grounds of appeal are well-founded on this point; accordingly, the portion of the judgment below adverse to the Defendant is reversed, and in order to have the court below conduct further examination, it is adjudged unanimously by the participating judges as follows."}

{"[76DA1699]": "We determine the grounds of appeal by the counsel for the Defendants and the Defendants’ intervenors in support.\\n\\nThe court below, based on the description in Exhibit A No. 2, recognized that Article 6 of the sales contract at issue contained an agreement that, if the seller breaches the contract, the seller shall compensate the buyer in double the down payment, and that, if the buyer breaches the contract, the return of the down payment cannot be demanded; and it held that such a penalty, absent special circumstances, is presumed to be a liquidated damages provision. However, in this case, where at the time of the sales contract both the Plaintiff and Defendant 1, who were the parties to the sale, entered into the contract without knowing that the land at issue in this case (the land at issue in this case as set forth in the original judgment), which was the object of the sale, belonged to another person, the court below held that the above penalty agreement cannot be viewed as having anticipated even the seller’s warranty liability in a sale of another’s right and as having pre-estimated the amount of such compensation. Upon examining the record, the above determination by the court below is correct, and there is no illegality therein, such as a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the good-faith seller’s warranty liability and the seller’s warranty liability for defects in a sale of another’s right, which would affect the original judgment, or an interpretation of the sales contract at issue contrary to the parties’ intent, and there is also no illegality in the original judgment, such as the asserted contradiction in reasons.\\n\\nAll arguments are without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed in its entirety, and the costs of the appeal are borne by the losing parties, and it is so adjudged as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[79DA564]": "1. First, we examine the Plaintiff’s appeal.  \\nAlthough the Plaintiff duly filed an appeal, he did not submit a statement of grounds of appeal within the prescribed period, and the petition of appeal also contains no statement of the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Next, we examine the grounds of appeal by the Defendants.  \\nIn the reasons for its judgment, the court below determined that the Plaintiff, on 1976.2.4, purchased from the deceased Non-party 1, who was the decedent of the Defendants, through Defendant 2, the son of the deceased Non-party 1, a lot of 16 pyeong 7 hop [this lot later became a lot of 16 pyeong 7 hop in Seongnam City ○○-dong (lot number omitted) upon the completion of the land readjustment project] and the house at issue constructed on that lot, for the price of 1,500,000 won, paid the full purchase price, received the documents necessary for registration of transfer of ownership, and completed the registration of transfer of ownership with respect to the lot; however, the house at issue was originally owned by Non-party 2, who was the debtor of the above deceased Non-party 1, and since, according to the agreement between the above deceased Non-party 1, as creditor, and the above Non-party 2, as debtor, as stated in the original judgment, the above deceased Non-party 1 was to receive it in satisfaction in kind, the above deceased Non-party 1 had delivered to the Plaintiff the seal certificate, deed of sale, and other documents necessary for transfer of ownership concerning the house at issue in the name of the above Non-party 2. However, the Plaintiff failed to proceed with the registration procedures for transfer of ownership, and after the validity period of the seal certificate had expired, he requested reissuance of the seal certificate to the registered owner, the above Non-party 2, through the seller, the above deceased Non-party 1, but the said person did not comply with the request for reissuance on account of the tax matters as stated in the original judgment, and while this was the case, the house at issue came to be subject to compulsory auction by a creditor of the above Non-party 2, with the result that the seller of the house at issue, the deceased Non-party 1, became unable to effect registration of transfer of ownership to the Plaintiff. On the basis of these facts, the court below determined that, with respect to the house at issue, although it cannot be denied that the Plaintiff was also at fault in that he did not promptly complete the registration of transfer of ownership by using the documents, etc. he had received, and had delayed in doing so, this does not mean that the seller’s obligation to transfer property rights to the buyer is extinguished; accordingly, it held that the Defendants, who are the heirs of the deceased Non-party 1, have the obligation to comply with the Plaintiff’s claim at issue arising from the above nonperformance of the deceased Non-party 1’s obligation toward the Plaintiff.\\n\\nHowever, if the factual circumstances are as stated above, the sale of the house at issue by the deceased Non-party 1 to the Plaintiff was a sale by the deceased Non-party 1 of a house owned by a third party, Non-party 2, and this should be regarded as the so-called sale of another person’s right as referred to in Article 569 of the Civil Act; and where the seller becomes unable to perform, for some reason, before transferring that other person’s right to the buyer, the seller must, of course, bear liability for defects arising from the inability to perform the obligation of transfer, but if the defect, that is, the cause of inability to perform, is solely attributable to the buyer, then it is a principle of law that the buyer cannot, leaving aside his own fault, hold the seller liable for defects merely by pointing to the fact that performance has become impossible.\\n\\nIn this case, the Plaintiff, as the buyer of the house at issue, had received from the seller, the deceased Non-party 1, all the documents necessary for the registration of transfer of ownership, but nevertheless neglected to complete the registration of transfer, and as a result the house was subjected to compulsory auction and transferred to another person, with the result that he ultimately failed to receive the transfer. Accordingly, the responsibility for the failure to receive the transfer must be regarded as lying solely with the Plaintiff. Therefore, the Plaintiff cannot, leaving aside his own fault as above, impose liability for inability to perform upon the deceased Non-party 1, who was the decedent of the Defendants and the seller, merely by pointing to the fact that he failed to obtain registration of transfer of ownership of the house at issue.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, solely on the grounds stated in its reasoning, accepted the Plaintiff’s damages claim at issue on the basis that the deceased Non-party 1, who was the decedent of the Defendants, was liable for nonperformance of the obligation to register transfer of ownership of the house at issue to the Plaintiff. This cannot but be regarded as the result of a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the seller’s liability for defects in the sale of another person’s right, and the above defect in the judgment of the court below cannot but be said to have affected the outcome of the judgment; accordingly, the argument pointing this out is well-founded, and the judgment of the court below concerning this part must be reversed.\\n\\n3. Accordingly, since the Plaintiff’s appeal is without merit, it is dismissed; the appellate costs incurred by the Plaintiff’s appeal shall be borne by the Plaintiff; and since the Defendants’ appeal is meritorious, the portion of the judgment below adverse to the Defendants shall be reversed and remanded. Thus, the judgment is rendered, by unanimous opinion, as set forth in the disposition."}

{"[92DA37727]": "1. We examine the grounds of appeal submitted by the Plaintiff’s litigation representative.\\n\\n(1) According to the reasons stated in the lower court judgment, the lower court found, based on the evidence cited therein, that 24 pyeong and 4 hop of land, located in Incheon Buk-gu (address omitted), was land reallotted pursuant to a land readjustment project, and that, with respect to said land, on 1987.12.4., pursuant to the Supreme Court Rule, “Guidelines for Registration Processing of Joint Replotting,” co-ownership share registrations had been completed in the name of a non-party for a 35/43 share and in the name of the Defendant for an 8/43 share; that, however, before the above replotting registration, as of 1986.6.27., a registration preserving ownership in the name of the Defendant had separately been completed with respect to 71.7 square meters of the same dong (address omitted) land (hereinafter referred to as “the land at issue”); that the Plaintiff and the Defendant, on 1987.4.23., seeing only that the above registration preserving ownership in the name of the Defendant had been made with respect to the land at issue, mistakenly believing it to be the Defendant’s sole ownership, entered into a sales contract for the land at issue at a price of 34,789,600 won and, on 5.8. of the same year, completed a registration of transfer of ownership in the Plaintiff’s name on the basis of sale; that, however, the said non-party filed an action against the Plaintiff and the Defendant seeking cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership, and in that lawsuit a judgment in favor of the said non-party became final and conclusive on the ground that the registration preserving ownership in the name of the Defendant made with respect to the land at issue was an illegal registration not in accordance with lawful procedure, did not conform to the substantive legal relationship, and was therefore void, and that the above registration preserving ownership in the name of the Defendant and the registration of transfer of ownership in the Plaintiff’s name based thereon were to be cancelled; and then, after finding these facts, the lower court held that, according to the above factual findings, the Defendant could no longer transfer ownership to the Plaintiff with respect to the 35/43 share of the land at issue beyond the Defendant’s own co-ownership share, and therefore had an obligation to compensate for damages as to that share; that, as to the scope of such damages, although the Plaintiff sought damages for non-performance, it was premised that the case differed in no respect from damages arising from a tort, and the lower court determined that the amount expended by the Plaintiff to purchase the land at issue in reliance on the void registration preserving ownership in the name of the Defendant as valid, namely, the portion corresponding to the above 35/43 share of the sale price, 28,317,116 won (34,789,600 × 35/43, fractions below one won omitted), was the amount of damage suffered by the Plaintiff.\\n\\n(2) However, where, because part of the right that was the object of the sale belongs to another person, the seller becomes unable to acquire that right and transfer it to the buyer, a bona fide buyer may hold the seller liable under warranty and claim damages therefor; in such case, the amount of damages that the seller must compensate the buyer for is, in principle, the market value of the right that became impossible to perform at the time when the seller became unable to acquire the part of the right that was the object of the sale and transfer it to the buyer, that is, the amount equivalent to the benefit of performance, and therefore cannot be regarded as the scope of damages in a claim for damages based on tort liability for an unlawful registration.\\n\\nIn this case, according to the above factual relationship found by the lower court, when the judgment in favor of the said non-party became final and conclusive in the above lawsuit for cancellation of registration of transfer of ownership filed by the said non-party against the Plaintiff and the Defendant, the Defendant could no longer acquire and transfer to the Plaintiff the 35/43 share of the land at issue, which was the object of the sale; therefore, the Defendant is under an obligation to compensate the Plaintiff for an amount equivalent to the market value of the said share as of the time when the adverse judgment became final and conclusive.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court’s determination as above erred by misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning the scope of damages under the seller’s warranty liability and thereby committed an error affecting the judgment; thus, the argument on this point has merit.\\n\\n2. Even upon examining the contents stated in the petition of appeal and the statement of grounds of appeal according to the record, the Plaintiff has advanced no grounds of appeal with respect to the part of the lower court judgment, among the portions adverse to the Plaintiff, concerning the claim for registration of transfer of ownership regarding 2 pyeong and 7 hop of land at 193-51, Bupyeong-dong, Buk-gu, Incheon; therefore, the appeal as to this part is without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the portion of the lower court judgment dismissing the Plaintiff’s claim for payment of money is reversed and remanded, the Plaintiff’s remaining appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal relating to this dismissed portion shall be borne by the losing party; accordingly, it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[93DA37328]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nWith respect to Issue 1\\n\\nIn light of the evidence selected by the court below and the record, the factual findings of the court below are acceptable, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in violation of the rules of evidence.\\n\\nWhat the argument asserts is merely a challenge to the exclusive province of the court below as the trier of fact, and is without merit.\\n\\nWith respect to Issue 2\\n\\nIn a case where another person’s right is made the object of a sale, if the seller’s obligation to acquire that right and transfer it to the buyer has become impossible to perform due to the seller’s fault, then even if the buyer cannot claim damages pursuant to the proviso of Article 570 of the Civil Code concerning the seller’s warranty liability, it should be deemed that the buyer may rescind the contract and claim damages pursuant to the general provisions on non-performance of obligations (Articles 546 and 390 of the Civil Code) (see Supreme Court Decision 70DA2449, decided on 1970. 12. 29.).\\n\\nIf the factual relations of this case are as recognized by the court below, the impossibility of performance of the Defendant’s obligation to register the transfer of ownership should be deemed to have been caused by the Defendant’s fault, and insofar as such impossibility of performance was caused by the Defendant’s fault, the Defendant cannot be exempted from liability for damages arising from impossibility of performance prescribed in Articles 546 and 390 of the Civil Code. Accordingly, the judgment of the court below to the same effect is proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in misunderstanding the legal principles as alleged.\\n\\nThe argument also asserts that the impossibility of performance in this case is attributable to the joint fault of the Plaintiffs and the Defendant; however, even if the Defendant inwardly intended to receive the balance of the purchase price from the Plaintiffs and then pay the balance to the third-party nonparty, the obligation to pay the balance to the above nonparty fundamentally lies with the Defendant. Therefore, the fact that the Plaintiffs delayed payment of the balance to the Defendant out of concern that registration of transfer of ownership of the forest land in this case, which was the object of the sale, would be impossible, cannot be taken to mean that the fault for impossibility of performance lies with the Plaintiffs. Even if the fault lay with both the Plaintiffs and the Defendant, insofar as the Defendant’s fault is recognized, the Defendant cannot be exempted from responsibility therefor. Thus, this contention cannot be accepted.\\n\\nThe argument also lacks merit. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are borne by the losing party; the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question:
Which of the following statements concerning the creditor's subrogation right are correct? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law applies)

(a) If A purchased an unregistered building but failed to register the transfer of ownership, A may, by subrogating seller B, who acquired ownership of the building by original acquisition, claim against unlawful possessor C that C deliver the building directly to A.  
(b) If, in order to preserve A's monetary claim against B, A exercises by subrogation B's monetary claim against C and obtains a final and binding judgment ordering performance directly to A, then, so long as B's monetary claim against C has not been extinguished by payment or the like, D, a general creditor of B, may attach B's monetary claim against C.  
(c) If B has the right to demand assignment of a claim from C and A exercises by subrogation the above right of B against C, A may claim against C that C perform the procedures for assignment of the claim directly to A.  
(d) If A, the final purchaser of real property X, obtained, by subrogating B, an intermediate purchaser, a provisional injunction prohibiting disposition against seller C with respect to real property X in order to preserve B's claim for registration of transfer of ownership, and B became aware of the subrogation, then thereafter, even if A, by subrogating B, seeks performance of the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership against C, C cannot assert against A the fact that C completed registration of transfer of ownership with respect to real property X in favor of B.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2015DA236547]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (including, to the extent the statement in the supplemental brief submitted after the period for submitting the petition for appeal has elapsed supplements the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. a. In cases where a creditor exercises, by subrogation, the debtor’s monetary claim in order to preserve the creditor’s own monetary claim, the creditor may demand that the third-party obligor perform its payment obligation to the debtor, but may also demand that it perform directly to the subrogating creditor himself/herself (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on April 15, 2005, 2004DA70024).\\n\\nHowever, even if a judgment in a creditor-subrogation lawsuit becomes final and binding, ordering the third-party obligor to pay money directly to the subrogating creditor, the right that is the object of subrogation, namely the subrogated claim of the debtor against the third-party obligor, exists as the judgment claim for execution, and the subrogating creditor merely receives performance of the subrogated claim by subrogating to the debtor, rather than receiving it as performance of his/her own claim (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on July 23, 2015, 2013DA30301, 30325), so long as the subrogated claim has not yet been extinguished by performance or otherwise, another creditor of the debtor may attach or provisionally attach it.\\n\\nHowever, once a creditor-subrogation lawsuit has been filed and the subrogating creditor notifies the debtor of the fact that the subrogation right has been exercised, or the debtor becomes aware thereof, the debtor, pursuant to Article 405(2) of the Civil Act, is no longer able to engage in acts of disposition that interfere with the exercise of the creditor’s subrogation right, such as assigning or waiving the subrogated claim, and such effect extends equally to the third-party obligor. Nevertheless, if it is possible that another creditor of the debtor, who holds a status equal to that of the subrogating creditor, may thereafter obtain an assignment order with respect to the subrogated claim, then, although the filing of a creditor-subrogation lawsuit is one of the lawful methods by which a creditor exercises rights and has commonality with a collection lawsuit in that it collects a claim belonging to the debtor, it would be reduced to a futile procedure; moreover, a creditor who has obtained an assignment order would obtain exclusive satisfaction by excluding the subrogating creditor, without the subrogating creditor even having the opportunity to participate in the claim distribution procedure through attachment, provisional attachment, or a demand for distribution, thereby contravening the purport of Article 405(2) of the Civil Act, which seeks to secure the substantive effect of the creditor’s subrogation right.\\n\\nAccordingly, after a creditor-subrogation lawsuit has been filed and the subrogating creditor has notified the debtor of the fact that the subrogation right has been exercised, or the debtor has become aware thereof, Article 229(5) of the Civil Execution Act shall apply by analogy, and an assignment order against the subrogated claim shall, unless there exist special circumstances such as that it is based on a claim with priority, be deemed void.\\n\\nb. A subrogating creditor who exercises, by subrogation, the debtor’s monetary claim in order to preserve his/her own monetary claim may demand that the third-party obligor perform its payment obligation directly to the subrogating creditor himself/herself and may receive performance from the third-party obligor; however, this does not cause the debtor’s subrogated claim against the third-party obligor to be transferred to or vest in the subrogating creditor. Therefore, the subrogating creditor’s above-mentioned power to collect or power to receive performance with respect to the third-party obligor is not, in itself, independently disposable and realizable, and is thus of a nature that cannot be attached; accordingly, an attachment order, etc. against such power to collect or power to receive performance is void. Further, even if a judgment in a creditor-subrogation lawsuit becomes final and binding, ordering the third-party obligor to pay money directly to the subrogating creditor, receiving money on the basis of that judgment also falls within the subrogating creditor’s power to collect or power to receive performance with respect to the third-party obligor; therefore, an attachment order, etc. against the claim that the subrogating creditor is to receive from the third-party obligor pursuant to the judgment finalized in the creditor-subrogation lawsuit must also be deemed void (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on March 14, 1997, 96DA54300).\\n\\n2. According to the reasons of the first-instance judgment cited by the court below, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. Non-Party 2, who held a monetary claim against Non-Party 1, filed a lawsuit claiming return of unjust enrichment against the Plaintiff by subrogating Non-Party 1, and in that lawsuit, on October 24, 2012, a judgment was rendered that “the Plaintiff shall pay to Non-Party 2 KRW 221,999,653 and money calculated at the rate of 20% per annum from May 9, 2012 until the day of full payment” (hereinafter referred to as “the judgment in this case”), and the judgment in this case became final and binding on August 13, 2013. Non-Party 1 appeared and testified as a witness at the court of first instance in the above lawsuit.\\n\\nb. On the basis of an authenticated copy of a notarial deed having executory force against Non-Party 1, Non-Party 3 obtained on August 12, 2013, an attachment and assignment order for KRW 230,000,000 out of the above claim for return of unjust enrichment that Non-Party 1 held against the Plaintiff, and the above order was served on the Plaintiff on August 14, 2013 and became final and binding on September 6, 2013.\\n\\nc. On the basis of another authenticated copy of a notarial deed having executory force against Non-Party 1, Non-Party 3 again obtained on August 20, 2013, an attachment and assignment order for KRW 250,000,000 out of the above claim for return of unjust enrichment that Non-Party 1 held against the Plaintiff, and the above order was served on the Plaintiff on August 22, 2013 and became final and binding on September 6, 2013.\\n\\nd. Meanwhile, on the basis of an authenticated copy of a payment order having executory force against Non-Party 2, the Defendant obtained on October 11, 2013, an attachment and assignment order (hereinafter referred to as “the attachment and assignment order in this case”) for KRW 220,000,000 out of the claim that Non-Party 2 was to receive from the Plaintiff pursuant to the judgment in this case, and the attachment and assignment order in this case was served on the Plaintiff on October 16, 2013 and became final and binding on April 3, 2014.\\n\\n3. Examining these factual circumstances in light of the foregoing legal principles, first, because Non-Party 1 appeared and testified as a witness at the court of first instance in the above creditor-subrogation lawsuit filed by Non-Party 2, it shall be deemed that Non-Party 1 became aware of the fact that Non-Party 2 exercised the subrogation right; accordingly, at that time, by virtue of Article 405(2) of the Civil Act, the effect of restricting the power of disposition over the debtor Non-Party 1 arose, and therefore all of the above assignment orders received thereafter by Non-Party 3, who holds a status equal to that of Non-Party 2, with respect to the above claim for return of unjust enrichment that Non-Party 1 held against the Plaintiff, which is the subrogated claim, are void.\\n\\nHowever, regardless of this, because receiving payment from the Plaintiff by Non-Party 2 pursuant to the judgment in this case falls within the subrogating creditor’s power to collect or power to receive performance with respect to the third-party obligor, the attachment and assignment order in this case, which identified as the attached claim the claim that Non-Party 2 was to receive from the Plaintiff pursuant to the judgment in this case, is void. If so, the Plaintiff’s debt to the Defendant based on the attachment and assignment order in this case does not exist.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, to the contrary, held that since all of the above assignment orders obtained by Non-Party 3 are valid, the entire claim for return of unjust enrichment that Non-Party 1 held against the Plaintiff and the claim for damages for delay thereon from August 15, 2013, the day after the first assignment order obtained by Non-Party 3 was served on the Plaintiff, were transferred to Non-Party 3; and, on the other hand, the attachment and assignment order in this case is also valid with respect to the portion not transferred to Non-Party 3 as above, and accordingly the claim for damages for delay up to August 14, 2013 was transferred to the Defendant, and thus determined that such damages for delay exist as the Plaintiff’s debt to the Defendant based on the attachment and assignment order in this case. In this determination by the court below, there is an error of misunderstanding the legal principles regarding the effect of an assignment order against a subrogated claim or the effect of an attachment order, etc. against the subrogating creditor’s power to collect or power to receive performance. However, in this case where only the Defendant filed the appeal, the principle prohibiting worsening of the appellant’s position precludes the reversal of the judgment below and the pronouncement of a judgment more unfavorable to the Defendant; therefore, the above error by the court below does not affect the result of the judgment.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the appellate costs shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court participating in the case."}

{"[79DA1928]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the facts established by the judgment of the court below, the Plaintiff purchased the building at issue in this case, which the non-party had newly constructed and of which he had acquired ownership by original acquisition, while it remained unregistered; and although the said non-party moved out of the building, the Defendants, who had lived together with the said non-party as his mother or wife, still each occupy the portions of the building as stated in the judgment of the court below.\\n\\nIn view of the foregoing, in such a case, the said non-party, even though he himself has moved out of the building, has not only the obligation to effect a transfer registration in order to enable the Plaintiff to acquire ownership, but also the obligation to cooperate so that the Plaintiff may exercise full rights over the building; meanwhile, although the Defendants, as the cohabiting family members of the said non-party, while cohabiting with the said non-party in the building, were such that only the said non-party was the possessor and the Defendants were merely auxiliary possessors, if, as in this case, the Defendants, despite the fact that the said non-party had already sold the building and moved out, are occupying the said portions of the building against the will of the said non-party while asserting that the building is not owned by the said non-party, then ultimately they cannot be said to have a lawful title to such possession; therefore, in relation to the owner, the said non-party, they are unlawful possessors. Accordingly, even if the Plaintiff has not yet received registration of transfer of ownership of the said building and is therefore not the owner, the Plaintiff may, by subrogating to the said non-party, the seller, make a claim for delivery against the Defendants, who are unlawful possessors, and at this time the Plaintiff may also directly demand that the Defendants deliver possession to him.\\n\\nThe judgment of the court below, which, in this purport, granted the Plaintiff’s claim in this case, is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error of law in misunderstanding the legal principle concerning subrogation of the right to claim delivery, or in misunderstanding the legal principle concerning the duty of cooperation; accordingly, all arguments criticizing it are without merit and are not accepted.\\n\\nTherefore, the final appeal in this case is without merit and is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne jointly by the Defendants, who are the losing parties, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the judges concerned."}

{"[88DAKA3922]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\nA provisional disposition prohibiting disposition made by a creditor, subrogating the debtor, against a third-party debtor is intended to prevent the third-party debtor from engaging in acts of disposition, such as transfer registration of ownership, in favor of a person other than the debtor, in order to preserve the creditor’s own claim against the debtor; therefore, it does not include a prohibition of disposition against the debtor, who is the de facto holder of the rights under the provisional disposition (see this Court’s Decision 88DAKA6488, rendered on May 9, 1989; and Decision 87DAKA3155, rendered on April 11, 1989, among others).\\n\\nIn the same purport, even if the Plaintiff, subrogating Defendant 1, obtained a provisional disposition prohibiting disposition against Defendant Yeonggwang-gun with respect to the real property at issue, the Court below’s determination that Defendant 1’s completion of the transfer registration of ownership from Defendant Yeonggwang-gun was consistent with the purpose of that provisional disposition, and that therefore the registration completed thereafter from Defendant 1 to the auxiliary intervenor for the Defendant was also valid, is proper, and there is no illegality such as an error of law as pointed out.\\n\\nIn addition, the so-called provisional disposition prohibiting disposition of rights, such as an order to perform an omission as alleged, has no means of execution other than service of the decision on the debtor, and it cannot immediately be said that the validity of the act in violation thereof is denied merely because an act contrary to the above provisional disposition was performed (see the above-mentioned Decision 88DAKA6488, rendered on May 9, 1989). Accordingly, the Court below’s determination that the registration completed in favor of the auxiliary intervenor for the Defendant, after the above provisional disposition prohibiting disposition of rights, through the circumstances stated in its opinion, is valid, is also proper, and there is no illegality such as an error of law as pointed out.\\n\\nAll arguments lack merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; with the unanimous opinion of the judges involved, it is adjudged as follows."}

question: A entered into a contract for construction work with B to newly construct Building Y on his own land X, with the construction price set at KRW 200,000,000. Which of the following statements is incorrect? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law governs)
A: If B has suspended the work and it has become clear that completing the work within the agreed construction period is impossible, A may rescind the contract even before the construction period has expired; however, before doing so, A must, in principle, demand that B complete the work within a reasonable period from the construction deadline.
B: If the contract for work between A and B is rescinded on the ground of B’s nonperformance, and at the time of rescission the construction has progressed to a considerable extent so that restoring it to the original state would cause significant social and economic loss, and the completed portion benefits A, then the contract for work becomes ineffective only with respect to the incomplete portion.
C: If the contract for work between A and B includes an agreement on liquidated damages for delay, then, absent special circumstances, A’s claim for liquidated damages for delay and B’s claim for the construction price are in a concurrent performance relationship.
D: If the completed Building Y has defects and A exercises a claim for damages in the amount of KRW 100,000,000 in lieu of repair of defects, then, absent special circumstances, A’s obligation to pay the construction price does not fall into default, and the day after A declares an intention to set off by using the claim for damages in lieu of repair as the active claim and B’s claim for the construction price of KRW 200,000,000 as the passive claim, the obligation to pay the construction price falls into default.
E: If the completed Building Y has serious defects, and because of this there is a risk that Building Y will collapse, making repair impossible and requiring it to be rebuilt, then, absent special circumstances, A may claim as damages the amount equivalent to the cost of demolishing Building Y and rebuilding it.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2014DA83890]": "The grounds for final appeal are considered (supplementary briefs, etc. on the grounds for final appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds for final appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\n1. According to the reasons given in the lower court judgment and the evidence duly admitted, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n\\na. Around November 2007, the Plaintiff was awarded by the Defendant a contract for earthwork and ancillary civil engineering work during the construction of the “○○○○ Senior Welfare Town” on 13 other parcels, including in Sangdang-gu, Cheongju-si (address omitted) (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “Construction at Issue”), for KRW 4,730,000,000 (including value-added tax) (hereinafter referred to as the “Construction Contract at Issue”).\\n\\nb. The Construction at Issue may broadly be divided into earthwork and temporary works (which, depending on location, are divided into the first, second, and third stages, with the first-stage portion being Building A, the second-stage portion being Building B, and the third-stage portion being Building C), and the temporary works may be divided into excavation work and earth-retaining work (meaning work to prevent the collapse or slippage of embankments or excavations).\\n\\nc. The Plaintiff commenced the Construction at Issue around December 6, 2007, and suspended the Construction at Issue in early June 2008. At the time the Construction at Issue was suspended, as to the temporary works, the portion corresponding to excavation work had generally been completed, but the earth-retaining work portion had not been carried out. In the case of Buildings A and B, ordinary rock and hard rock were exposed on the wall portions, and the appearance was similar to that of Open Cut work performed by the rock-blasting method, and therefore it was in a state in which earth-retaining work did not have to be performed.\\n\\nd. According to the result of the fact inquiry made by the lower court, the first-instance expert appraiser replied that if the earth-retaining work for Buildings A, B, and C in the Construction at Issue had been substituted by Open Cut work by the rock-blasting method, the degree of completion would be 53.44%, and if the earth-retaining work for Buildings A, B, and C had not been carried out, the degree of completion would be 33.3%.\\n\\n2. Whether there was an agreement on substitute construction concerning the Construction at Issue\\n\\na. The lower court, for the following reasons, rejected the Plaintiff’s assertion that, because the ground at the Construction site at issue consisted mostly of hard rock and solid rock, unlike the design drawings, the Plaintiff and the Defendant had agreed to substitute the temporary works during the Construction at Issue with Open Cut construction by the rock-blasting method.\\n\\n(1) The ground conditions at the Construction site at issue were reflected in the design for the Construction at Issue without error.\\n\\n(2) There had never been any design change due to substitute construction as alleged by the Plaintiff.\\n\\n(3) The Plaintiff never requested the Defendant or the supervision team for the Construction at Issue to change the design, and there is no entry whatsoever concerning this in the construction daily logs regarding the Construction at Issue.\\n\\nb. In light of the reasons for the lower court judgment and the evidence duly admitted, the lower court’s above determination does not suffer from any error of violating the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, contrary to logic and experience, without fully examining the matters necessary for the above determination, or from any error of misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the existence and interpretation of the agreement on substitute construction. Accordingly, the Plaintiff’s grounds for final appeal on this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Whether the calculation of the degree of completion and the amount of payment for completed work was lawful\\n\\na. Where a construction contract is rescinded, and at the time of rescission the work has progressed to a considerable extent such that restoration to the original state would cause serious social and economic loss and the completed portion is beneficial to the contractee, the construction contract becomes effective only as to the uncompleted portion, and the contractor delivers the work product to the contractee in the state as rescinded; in such a case, unless special circumstances exist, a legal relationship of rights and obligations is established under which the contractee must pay remuneration commensurate therewith by taking into account the completeness or degree of completion of the delivered work product. (See Supreme Court Decision of Feb. 14, 1989, 88DAKA4819, Supreme Court Decision of Mar. 31, 1992, 91DA42630, etc.) Where a construction contract is rescinded before the contractor completes the work and the construction cost for the degree of completion must be settled, the construction cost must be calculated by applying to the agreed construction cost the rate of completion, calculated on the basis of the construction cost actually incurred or to be incurred for the completed portion and the unconstructed portion. That rate of completion must be determined by calculating, as of the time when the obligation to pay the construction price arose, that is, when the contractor suspended the work, the proportion that the cost incurred for the completed portion bears to the total construction cost, which is the sum of the cost incurred for the already completed portion and the cost to be incurred to complete the unconstructed portion. (See Supreme Court Decision of Jan. 23, 1996, 94DA31631, 31648, Supreme Court Decision of Jan. 12, 2017, 2014DA11574, 11581, etc.)\\n\\nb. The lower court held that, insofar as the substitute construction agreement alleged by the Plaintiff could not be recognized, the earth-retaining work must be deemed not to have been carried out at the time the Construction at Issue was suspended; accordingly, it found the rate of completion at that time to be 33.3% and the payment for completed work to be KRW 1,575,090,000 (= KRW 4,730,000,000 × 33.3%), and then rejected the Plaintiff’s claim on the ground that the Plaintiff had received from the Defendant an amount exceeding the payment for completed work.\\n\\nc. However, the above determination by the lower court is difficult to accept as it stands for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) In general, in a building construction project, earthwork is the preliminary work for constructing the building. Even if, in this case, there was no agreement between the Plaintiff and the Defendant to substitute the temporary works at issue with Open Cut construction by the rock-blasting method, where the portion of the work performed by the Plaintiff by the rock-blasting method has progressed to a considerable extent such that restoration to the original state would cause serious social and economic loss and the completed portion is beneficial to the Defendant, the construction contract becomes effective only as to the uncompleted portion, and the Defendant, as the contractee, must, unless special circumstances exist, pay construction price corresponding thereto by taking into account the completeness or degree of completion of the delivered work product.\\n\\n(2) According to the record, the earth-retaining work portion of the temporary works at issue appears to have been constructed by the Open Cut method using rock blasting, rather than by the excavation and earth-retaining methods according to the design drawings, in response to changes in the ground conditions at the site. As stated in the reasons for the lower court judgment, in the case of Buildings A and B in the Construction at issue, the Plaintiff’s Open Cut construction by the rock-blasting method had been carried out, so that earth-retaining work was not needed, and if, under such circumstances, the intended purpose and function of the temporary works can be achieved even without earth-retaining work, with no particular problem or obstacle in proceeding with subsequent processes, it is difficult to regard the earth-retaining work portion as an uncompleted portion that should be excluded from the rate of progress.\\n\\n(3) In such a case, the lower court should additionally examine the following three matters, distinguish between the completed and uncompleted portions of the work, calculate respectively the construction cost already incurred for the completed portion and the construction cost to be incurred to complete the uncompleted portion, and then calculate the degree of completion. First, in the case of Buildings A and B in the Construction at issue, the court should examine whether, even without the earth-retaining work among the temporary works at issue, the intended purpose and function of that work can be achieved and whether there is no particular problem or obstacle in proceeding with subsequent processes, or whether other additional processes or procedures apart from earth-retaining work are required, and thereby determine whether the earth-retaining work portion is an uncompleted portion. Second, even in the case of Building C in the Construction at issue, the court should determine whether the wall portion is composed of ordinary rock and hard rock, etc., so that earth-retaining work is unnecessary, or whether it is composed of soft rock or weathered rock, etc., so that earth-retaining work is necessary. Third, if it is determined that earth-retaining work or other additional processes or procedures are necessary, the court should calculate how much construction cost would be required to complete such unconstructed portion.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court determined that the earth-retaining work portion should be excluded from the rate of progress in the calculation of the degree of completion merely because no earth-retaining work had physically been carried out at the time the Construction at issue was suspended, and, without using the method of calculating the construction cost required to complete the uncompleted portion, calculated the degree of completion on the basis of the remaining construction amount obtained by simply subtracting from the contract amount for the temporary works the contract amount corresponding to the earth-retaining work.\\n\\nThe lower court’s determination contains an error that affected the result of the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the method of calculating the remuneration for the completed portion that the contractee must pay to the contractor in the event that a construction contract is terminated midway, without fully examining the necessary matters. The Plaintiff’s assertion of grounds for final appeal on this point is well founded.\\n\\n4. Omitting the determination on the remaining grounds for final appeal, the lower court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices."}

question: A entered into a sales contract with B to sell B real property X owned by A. Which of the following statements is correct? (Each item is independent, and where there is dispute, case law applies)
A: Even if A and B rescind the contract by agreement, A may claim damages on the ground of B's nonperformance, unless special circumstances exist.
B: A delivered real property X to B and completed the registration of transfer of ownership, but while B was unable to pay the balance to A, A and B rescinded the contract by agreement. If, after the mutual rescission, B sold real property X to C and also completed the registration of transfer of ownership, C constitutes a third party under the proviso to Article 548(1) of the Civil Act even if C knew of the mutual rescission.
C: Even after Creditor D of B had provisionally attached B's claim against A for registration of transfer of ownership of real property X, A may rescind the sales contract on the ground of B's nonperformance; however, if, before the contract is rescinded, D, following the provisional attachment, attaches the above claim for registration of transfer of ownership, then D, as an attaching creditor, constitutes a third party under the proviso to Article 548(1) of the Civil Act.
D: A sold real property X to C and completed the registration of transfer of ownership, and B then claimed against A both rescission of the contract and restitution on the ground that A's obligation to register the transfer of ownership had become impossible to perform. If, at the time B expressed the intent to rescind, the statute of limitations for B's claim against A for registration of transfer of ownership had already expired, then even if the time at which performance became impossible was before the statute of limitations for the claim for registration of transfer of ownership expired, B's right of rescission and right to claim restitution cannot, in principle, be recognized.
E: If, after B paid the purchase price, A's obligation to register transfer of ownership became impossible to perform due to A's fault, and B rescinded the contract one week later on the ground of A's nonperformance, the statute of limitations for the claim for restitution arising from rescission of that contract begins to run from the time the right of rescission arises.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2005DA6341]": "The judgment of the lower court is reversed, and the case is remanded to the Collegiate Division of the Main Branch of the Jeonju District Court."}

{"[2009DA63267]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below accepted the Defendant’s defense of the Statute of Limitations on the ground that, with respect to the apartment in question, the Defendant completed the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of a third party on 2002. 1. 30., thereby making the sales contract at issue impossible to perform, and that it is clear from the record that the Plaintiff filed this action on 2008. 1. 14., more than 5 years thereafter, and that a claim for restoration to the original status arising from rescission of a contract, which is a commercial act, is subject to the commercial statute of limitations under Article 64 of the Commercial Act, so Kim Eok-su’s claim against the Defendant for restoration to the original status arising from rescission of the sales contract at issue had already been extinguished by prescription before this action was filed.\\n\\nHowever, because the Statute of Limitations for a claim for restoration to the original status arising from rescission of a contract runs from the time of rescission, that is, from the time the claim for restoration to the original status arises (see Supreme Court Decision 93DA21569, decided September 14, 1993), the court below, by contrast, erred in accepting the Defendant’s defense of the Statute of Limitations on the premise that the Statute of Limitations for a claim for restoration to the original status arising from rescission of a contract runs from the time the right of rescission arises, thereby misapprehending the legal principle concerning the starting point of the Statute of Limitations for a claim for restoration to the original status arising from rescission of a contract and affecting the conclusion of the judgment.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court Decision 2003DA55080, decided December 26, 2003, cited by the court below, concerns different facts from this case and is therefore not a precedent directly related to the issue in this case.\\n\\nAccordingly, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, the opinions of the participating Justices being unanimous, and it is so adjudged as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2017DA220416]": "The grounds of appeal (including a supplemental statement of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal, to the extent that it supplements them) are examined.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower appellate court judgment and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. The Defendants decided to carry on a business of constructing and selling the instant commercial building, and, after purchasing the instant land, which was the site thereof, entrusted Cheongbaek General Construction Co., Ltd. with the instant construction work to build the above commercial building.\\n\\nb. When the Defendants began to encounter difficulties in the business, they asked Non-party 1 to procure funds by selling the instant commercial building, and Non-party 1, while handling the sales work, received salary and sales commissions from the Defendants. As part of the above sales work, on May 19, 2011, Non-party 1 concluded with the Plaintiff a contract to sell 40 pyeong on the first floor of the instant commercial building for KRW 600,000,000, indicating his mother, Non-party 2, as the seller and himself as the agent (hereinafter referred to as the “instant sales contract”), and the Plaintiff paid Non-party 1 KRW 130,000,000 on the same day.\\n\\nc. Separately, the Plaintiff, Non-party 2, and Non-party 3 (hereinafter referred to as “the Plaintiff et al.”), led by Non-party 1, on August 8, 2011, entered into a contract with the Defendants to purchase the instant land from the Defendants for KRW 3,130,000,000 and to take over the Defendants’ status as the principal under the contract (hereinafter referred to as the “instant business takeover contract”). The Plaintiff paid the Defendants KRW 100,000,000 as earnest money on the same day, and on October 31, 2011, again remitted KRW 200,000,000 into Defendant 2’s account. However, the instant business takeover contract was rescinded in around November 2011 by agreement between the Plaintiff et al. and the Defendants.\\n\\nd. Thereafter, the Defendants continued the instant construction work and completed it in around March 2012, and on March 29, 2012, registered preservation of ownership in the name of the Defendants with respect to each 1/2 share of the instant commercial building.\\n\\ne. The Plaintiff et al. filed a lawsuit seeking transfer of shares in part of the instant commercial building against the Defendants on the basis of the instant business takeover contract (hereinafter referred to as the “prior lawsuit”), but the court rendered a judgment dismissing the Plaintiff et al.’s claims on the ground that the instant business takeover contract had been rescinded by agreement between the Plaintiff et al. and the Defendants, and this judgment became final and conclusive as it stood.\\n\\n2. Whether the Defendants were the sellers under the instant sales contract (Ground of Appeal No. 1)\\n\\na. The Plaintiff sought restitution, etc. against the Defendants on the ground of rescission of the instant sales contract; however, the lower appellate court did not accept the Plaintiff’s claim, stating that the seller under the instant sales contract was Non-party 1, and that the Defendants were not parties to the contract. The basis therefor is as follows.\\n\\n(1) With respect to the related criminal case, the Plaintiff stated before the investigative authority or the court that “I have never heard anything about the sale from the Defendants” or that “Non-party 1 said he would sell it in person.”\\n\\n(2) The seller stated in the instant sales contract was Non-party 1’s mother, Non-party 2. The instant sales contract provides that the KRW 170,000,000 lent by the Plaintiff to Non-party 1 is to be regarded as part of the sale price, and that after completion of the sale, KRW 50,000,000 of the sale price is to be returned. The earnest money of KRW 130,000,000 paid by the Plaintiff to Non-party 1 was also not delivered to the Defendants.\\n\\n(3) In the prior lawsuit, the Plaintiff himself asserted that the fact that the Plaintiff paid the Defendants KRW 300,000,000 in two installments was on account of the price under the instant business takeover contract, and the final and conclusive judgment in the prior lawsuit likewise recognized the character of the above KRW 300,000,000 in that manner.\\n\\nb. Upon examining the reasons for the lower appellate court judgment in light of the record, the lower appellate court judgment contains no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in that it did not violate the rules of logic and experience and go beyond the limits of the free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\n3. Whether a claim for damages arises even where the contract has been rescinded by agreement (Ground of Appeal No. 2)\\n\\na. The lower appellate court recognized that, since the instant business takeover contract was rescinded by agreement, the Plaintiff had a claim to recover the money paid pursuant to the above business takeover contract, but determined that the claim was extinguished in full by being set off against the claim for damages acquired by the Defendants against the Plaintiff et al. due to the Plaintiff et al.’s nonperformance with respect to the instant business takeover contract.\\n\\nb. However, the lower appellate court judgment is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nWhere a contract is rescinded or terminated by agreement, damages for nonperformance cannot be claimed unless there are other circumstances, such as a special agreement to compensate the other party for damages or an expression of intent reserving a claim for damages (see Supreme Court Decision 86DAKA1147, 1148, decided April 25, 1989). The party asserting that such a special agreement for damages existed or that a reservation of a claim for damages was made bears the burden of proving it (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DA8755, decided November 28, 2013).\\n\\nThe interpretation of a juristic act is the clear ascertainment of the meaning that the parties attached to the act of manifestation, and where the meaning is not clearly revealed by the words expressed by the parties, it must be reasonably interpreted in accordance with the rules of logic and experience, and the common sense of society and ordinary transaction practice, by comprehensively considering the content of the words, the motive and circumstances in which the juristic act was made, the purpose the parties sought to achieve through the juristic act, the parties’ true intent, and transactional customs (see Supreme Court Decision 96DA16049, decided October 25, 1996; Supreme Court Decision 2016DA12175, decided May 14, 2020). The same legal principles on the interpretation of juristic acts also apply when determining whether, in mutually rescinding or terminating a contract by agreement, the parties made a special agreement to compensate the other party for damages or made an expression of intent reserving a claim for damages. Whether such a special agreement or expression of intent existed must be determined as of the time of the mutual rescission or termination by agreement, and provisions in the original contract concerning liquidated damages or damages do not apply even to cases of mutual rescission or termination by agreement unless there are special circumstances from which it may be deemed, in light of the contents of the contract, the parties’ expressions of intent, etc., that they also apply in the event of mutual rescission or termination by agreement.\\n\\nTaking a comprehensive view of the content of the instant business takeover contract appearing in the record, the process leading to its performance and rescission, and the content of the final and conclusive judgment in the prior lawsuit, it may be deemed that the above business takeover contract was not rescinded by the Defendants’ unilateral exercise of a contractual rescission right or a statutory rescission right, but was rescinded by agreement between the Plaintiff et al. and the Defendants, as recognized by the lower appellate court.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing circumstances and the legal principles stated above, in order for the Defendants to make a claim for damages against the Plaintiff et al. based on nonperformance, the Defendants must prove that there were special circumstances, such as a special agreement to compensate the other party for damages notwithstanding the mutual rescission or a reservation of a claim for damages.\\n\\nThe lower appellate court judgment contains no determination whatsoever regarding any special circumstance that there was such a special agreement for damages or that a claim for damages was reserved. According to the record, Article 5 of the instant business takeover contract provides that “if a problem arises and damage occurs by the time of payment of the balance, the instant business takeover contract shall be rescinded, and the party causing the problem shall pay the contractual party a cancellation fee equivalent to 10% of the sale price as compensation corresponding thereto.” However, when determined as of the time of the mutual rescission, the above clause cannot be broadly construed as a special agreement on damages applicable to cases of mutual rescission, as it is a liquidated damages provision for the general situation of nonperformance.\\n\\nNevertheless, without any particular basis, the lower appellate court found that the Defendants’ claim for damages against the Plaintiff et al. was recognized and accepted setoff using it as an automatic claim. The lower appellate court judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles regarding the requirements for the establishment of liability for damages arising from mutual rescission, etc. The Plaintiff’s ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nSince the Plaintiff’s appeal has merit, the lower appellate court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower appellate court for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices, as stated in the disposition."}
{"[99DA51685]": "The appeal is dismissed. The costs of appeal shall be borne by the Plaintiff."}

question:
A acquired mortgages respectively over X land owned by B, Y land owned by C, and Z land owned by D in order to secure a loan claim of KRW 300 million against B, and entered into a guarantee contract with E. Among the following explanations, which are correct? (Do not consider interest, delay damages, or enforcement costs. Each proposition is independent, and where there is a dispute, it shall be governed by case law.)

(a) If C assumes B's debt in a way that discharges B from liability, C has a right of indemnity against B unless special circumstances exist. 
(b) If A acquires X land from B and thereafter E pays KRW 300 million to A, E may subrogate A against A with respect to the above mortgage established on X land even if E does not make the supplementary registration of subrogation. 
(c) If A acquires X land from B and loses ownership through enforcement of the above mortgage established on X land, A cannot subrogate A against C and D. 
(d) If C pays KRW 300 million to A and, while no supplementary registration of subrogation has been made with respect to the above mortgage established on Z land, A acquires Z land from D, C may, even without making supplementary registration of subrogation with respect to the above mortgage established on Z land, subrogate A against A.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2011DA50233]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. With respect to Grounds 1 and 2 of the grounds of appeal\\nThe court below found that, based solely on the evidence submitted by the Plaintiffs, it was insufficient to conclude that the Defendant was the de facto debtor of the loan in this case or that the non-party repaid the loan in this case, and further determined that the Defendant, as a real security guarantor, subrogated and paid the loan obligation in this case of the non-party debtor.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, this determination by the court below is proper, and there is no illegality in that it did not exceed the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, nor did it սխatte the legal principles concerning the right of indemnity or subrogation by a person who has performed an obligation.\\n\\n2.
