With respect to Grounds 3 and 4 of the grounds of appeal\\nArticle 481 of the Civil Act provides that “A person who has a justifiable interest in performance is subrogated to the creditor by virtue of performance,” and Article 482(1) of the Civil Act provides that “A person who has subrogated to the creditor pursuant to the provisions of the preceding two Articles may exercise the rights relating to the claim and its security within the scope in which reimbursement is possible by his own right,” while Article 482(2) of the same Act provides that “The exercise of the rights under the preceding paragraph shall be in accordance with the provisions of each of the following subparagraphs,” but among these, there is no clear provision concerning subrogation by a person who has performed an obligation as between a real security guarantor and a third-party acquirer.\\n\\nHowever, as to subrogation by a person who has performed an obligation as between a surety and a third-party acquirer, Article 482(2) subparagraph 1 of the Civil Act provides that “Unless the surety has in advance made an additional entry of such subrogation in the registration of a leasehold right or mortgage, the surety may not subrogate to the creditor against a third party who has acquired rights in the leased property or mortgaged property,” and subparagraph 2 of the same paragraph provides that “A third-party acquirer may not subrogate to the creditor against the surety.” Meanwhile, under Articles 370 and 341 of the Civil Act, when a real security guarantor has performed the debt or lost ownership through enforcement of the security right, he has a right of indemnity against the debtor pursuant to the provisions concerning “surety obligations,” and according to Article 482(2) subparagraph 5 of the Civil Act, as between a real security guarantor and a surety, the creditor is subrogated in proportion to the number of persons, and no priority between them is recognized. Taking together the contents of the above provisions, when a real security guarantor has performed the debt or lost ownership through enforcement of the security right, like a surety who has performed a surety obligation, he may subrogate to the creditor with respect to the entire amount expended within the scope of the right of indemnity against a third party who acquired the mortgaged real property from the debtor; whereas a third party who acquired the mortgaged real property from the debtor should be deemed unable to subrogate to the creditor against the real security guarantor even if he performs the debt or loses ownership through enforcement of the security right. If the status of a real security guarantor were to be regarded differently from that of a surety, so that between a real security guarantor and a third party who acquired mortgaged real property from the debtor, subrogation to the creditor is allowed only in proportion to the value of each property, then the real security guarantor, who originally could subrogate with respect to the entire amount expended against the primary debtor, would, by the accidental circumstance that the debtor transferred ownership of the mortgaged real property to a third party, now be able to subrogate only in proportion to the value of each property, while the third party who acquired the mortgaged real property from the debtor in the first place, having accepted the burden of security rights over the full amount of the debt, would obtain an unintended benefit to that extent, which is unfair.\\n\\nBy contrast, Supreme Court Decision 74DA1419, rendered on December 10, 1974, which held that a third-party acquirer who purchased mortgaged real property may subrogate to the creditor against the real security guarantor in proportion to the value of each property, shall be modified to the extent that it conflicts with the view of this judgment.\\n\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in its opinion, determined that, insofar as the Defendant, as a real security guarantor, had paid the loan obligation in this case of the non-party debtor, the Defendant could exercise subrogation of the mortgage right in this case within the scope of the entire amount expended against the Plaintiffs, who acquired from the said non-party the share in the orchard in this case on which the mortgage right in this case is established, and dismissed the Plaintiffs’ claim for cancellation of the registration of establishment of the mortgage in this case.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles and the record discussed above, this determination by the court below is proper, and there is no illegality in that it misconstrued the legal principles concerning the right of indemnity and subrogation by a person who has performed an obligation.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties, and it is so adjudged as per the dispositive part by the unanimous opinion of the judges concerned."}

{"[2017DA274703]": "The grounds of appeal are examined (the statements in the supplemental written statement of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. With respect to the assertion of set-off, using the right of reimbursement based on exonerative assumption of debt as the active claim\\na. A real guarantor who, for the purpose of securing another’s debt, has established a mortgage on real property owned by him or her acquires a right of reimbursement against the debtor when he or she pays the other’s debt or loses ownership of the mortgaged property through foreclosure of the mortgage (Civil Act Articles 370 and 341). However, the “payment of the debt,” which is a requirement for acquiring the right of reimbursement, means that the performance constituting the content of the debt is realized and thereby the claim achieves its purpose and is extinguished; accordingly, exonerative assumption of debt, which merely transfers the existing debt in the same state as at the time of assumption from the previous debtor to the assumer while maintaining its identity and has no effect of extinguishing the existing debt, cannot be regarded as a case where the debt has been paid, even if the existing debtor is thereby relieved of the debt. Therefore, unless there are circumstances such as an agreement that the existing debtor is to render some performance to the real guarantor in return for the assumption of debt, it cannot be said that the real guarantor has rights such as a right of reimbursement against the existing debtor merely because the real guarantor has exoneratively assumed the existing debtor’s debt.\\nb. In the same purport, the lower court’s determination that the Defendant, as the real guarantor, could not exercise a right of reimbursement against the Chungnam Woori Rice Agricultural Cooperative (hereinafter referred to as the “Chungnam Woori Rice Cooperative”) merely because he had exoneratively assumed the debt of the Chungnam Woori Rice Cooperative is proper, and there is no error such as misapprehension of the legal principles on exonerative assumption of debt or the real guarantor’s right of reimbursement, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. With respect to the assertion of set-off, using the loan claim as the active claim\\na. The lower court determined that it was insufficient to recognize that the Defendant had lent the above money to the Chungnam Woori Rice Cooperative solely on the basis that the Defendant transferred 50,000,000 won to Nonparty 1 on March 28, 2012, and that on the same day Nonparty 1 transferred 45,000,000 won to the Chungnam Woori Rice Cooperative, and that there was otherwise insufficient evidence to recognize this.\\nb. Examining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the above determination by the lower court is proper, and there is no error such as violation of the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. With respect to the assertion of set-off, using the surety’s pre-recourse right as the active claim\\na. (1) A commissioned surety’s pre-recourse right and post-recourse right share the commonality of having the same ultimate purpose and social utility, but the post-recourse right arises from the fact that the surety extinguished the debt by his or her own contribution, such as payment, in place of the debtor, whereas the pre-recourse right arises from certain facts prescribed by the reasons set forth in Article 442(1) of the Civil Act or by agreement, and thus has a different cause of occurrence and is a separate and independent right with a different legal nature (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 25, 1992, 91DA37553). Accordingly, even after the post-recourse right has arisen, the pre-recourse right does not extinguish but coexists, and only when one is extinguished by achievement of its purpose is the other also extinguished.\\n(2) If set-off is allowed against another debt (passive claim) using as the active claim a claim to which a defense is attached, the effect is that the opportunity for the other party to exercise the defense is lost by one party’s declaration of intent to set off; such set-off cannot be allowed. In particular, since the pre-recourse right that a commissioned surety has against the principal debtor under Article 442 of the Civil Act carries, as a defense, the right to demand the provision of security under Article 443 of the Civil Act, set-off using that right as the active claim cannot, in principle, be allowed (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on May 28, 2004, 2001DA81245).\\n(3) Where a third-party obligor who has received an order for seizure of claims has a counterclaim against the judgment debtor, in order to oppose the seizing creditor by way of set-off, at the time the effect of seizure arises, both claims standing against each other must be in a state fit for set-off, or, if the counterclaim (active claim) has not yet become due at that time, it must become due simultaneously with or before the due date of the attached claim (passive claim) (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision rendered on February 16, 2012, 2011DA45521). It is reasonable to view that this legal principle also applies where a person who is both a third-party obligor subject to an order for seizure of claims and a surety extinguishes the defense of the claim for the provision of security by performing the surety obligation after the seizure, and then seeks to set off the attached claim with the pre-recourse right acquired before the seizure against the judgment debtor.\\n(4) Ultimately, where the third-party obligor has a pre-recourse right against the judgment debtor, in order to oppose the seizing creditor by way of set-off, (i) at the time the effect of seizure arises, the defense attached to the pre-recourse right, namely the claim for the provision of security, must have been extinguished so that the pre-recourse right and the attached claim are in a state fit for set-off, or (ii) if, at the time of seizure, the defense of the claim for the provision of security is still attached to the pre-recourse right, the time when the said defense is extinguished due to the third-party obligor’s act of discharge or the like, thereby making set-off through the pre-recourse right possible, must arrive before the due date of the attached claim.\\nb. The lower court determined that, after the Defendant had jointly and severally guaranteed the debt under the agreement at issue owed by the Chungnam Woori Rice Cooperative to Nonparty 2, on April 19, 2013, when Nonparty 2 disposed at will of the above rice to Saedulman Co., Ltd., the due date of the Defendant’s joint and several surety obligation arrived, and thereby the Defendant acquired the pre-recourse right at issue against the Chungnam Woori Rice Cooperative pursuant to Article 442(1) item 4 of the Civil Act; however, the time when the right to demand the provision of security attached to the pre-recourse right at issue was extinguished to the extent that the Defendant paid 110,000,000 won to Nonparty 2 was September 29, 2016, which was clearly after November 23, 2015, when the effect of the seizure and collection order at issue arose; and since the due date of the unjust enrichment restitution claim at issue, which is the passive claim the Defendant seeks to set off with the pre-recourse right at issue, had arrived by no later than December 27, 2013, it is not permissible to set off the unjust enrichment restitution claim at issue, whose due date had already arrived earlier, with the pre-recourse right at issue, whose defense of a claim for the provision of security became partly extinguished only after the seizure and collection order at issue.\\nc. Examining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the legal principles discussed above, the above determination by the lower court is proper, and there is no error such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the requirements for recognition of a pre-recourse right and for allowing set-off, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\nThe Supreme Court precedents cited in the grounds of appeal concern different facts and are not suitable for invocation in this case.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2019DA222041]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal (with respect to supplemental briefs of grounds for final appeal filed after the period for filing the statement of grounds for final appeal, to the extent that they supplement it).\\n\\n1. Overview of the case\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. The nonparty, in order to obtain a loan, on 2004. 12. 23. caused two mortgage creation registrations to be made in favor of the National Federation of Fisheries Cooperatives (hereinafter referred to as “the NFFC”) with respect to the real property listed in items 1 and 2 of the attached list to the judgment below, owned by the nonparty (hereinafter referred to as the “1st and 2nd Real Property”), with maximum secured amounts of KRW 70,000,000 and KRW 580,000,000 (hereinafter referred to as the “1st Mortgage”). Also, around that time, the nonparty obtained from the Defendant a guarantee certificate in the guaranteed amount of KRW 423,000,000, intended to be provided to the NFFC. On 2004. 12. 30., the nonparty provided the 1st Mortgage and the guarantee certificate as security and borrowed KRW 470,000,000 in facility damage restoration funds from the NFFC (hereinafter referred to as the “1st Loan”).\\n\\nOn 2008. 12. 9., the nonparty entered into a mortgage creation agreement with the NFFC providing that all debts presently and in the future owed by the nonparty to the NFFC in connection with credit transactions, etc. shall be secured, and caused a mortgage creation registration to be made in favor of the NFFC with respect to the real property listed in items 3 through 8 of the attached list to the judgment below, owned by the nonparty (hereinafter referred to as the “3rd through 8th Real Property”), with a maximum secured amount of KRW 650,000,000 (hereinafter referred to as the “2nd Mortgage”). On 2011. 12. 16., the nonparty additionally borrowed KRW 500,000,000 in financial fisheries funds from the NFFC (hereinafter referred to as the “2nd Loan”).\\n\\nb. On 2012. 3. 9., the Plaintiff purchased the 3rd through 8th Real Property from the nonparty and, on 2012. 3. 19., had the ownership transfer registration made in the Plaintiff’s name.\\n\\nc. The nonparty defaulted on the payment of interest on the 1st Loan from 2012. 4. 3., and on the 2nd Loan from 2012. 8. 9. On 2012. 8. 24., the NFFC filed an application for a non-judicial auction based on the 2nd Mortgage with respect to the 3rd through 8th Real Property in Case No. 2012TAGYEONG6906 at the Pohang Branch of the Daegu District Court, and on 2012. 8. 28., the non-judicial auction proceedings were commenced (hereinafter referred to as “the Auction in this case”). The amount claimed was KRW 650,000,000 out of a total of KRW 876,000,000, consisting of the balance of the 1st Loan in the amount of KRW 376,000,000 and the 2nd Loan in the amount of KRW 500,000,000.\\n\\nOn 2012. 8. 24., the Defendant repaid KRW 342,997,237 out of the 1st Loan to the NFFC pursuant to the guarantee certificate, and on 2012. 9. 18., made a marginal registration in favor of the Defendant with respect to the mortgage among the 1st Mortgage whose maximum secured amount was KRW 580,000,000.\\n\\nIn order to have the application for the Auction in this case withdrawn, on 2012. 11. 19., the Plaintiff paid to the NFFC a total of KRW 551,168,720, consisting of overdue interest on the 1st Loan in the amount of KRW 18,805,503, principal and interest on the 2nd Loan in the amount of KRW 525,068,491, and auction application expenses in the amount of KRW 7,294,726, and, pursuant to the NFFC’s request, remitted KRW 150,000,000 to the Defendant. On 2012. 11. 19., the NFFC withdrew the application for the Auction in this case and cancelled the registration of the 2nd Mortgage on the ground of termination.\\n\\nd. Meanwhile, with respect to the 1st and 2nd Real Property, upon the application of Kookmin Bank Co., Ltd., which was the mortgagee, non-judicial auction proceedings were commenced on 2012. 9. 20. in Case No. 2012TAGYEONG5533 at the Daegu District Court Gyeongju Branch. The Defendant submitted a claim statement setting forth the entire recourse claim against the nonparty in the amount of KRW 445,526,188, without excluding the KRW 150,000,000 received from the Plaintiff in the auction proceedings. Around 2014. 8. 27., a distribution schedule was prepared distributing KRW 315,413,800 to the Defendant, and the Defendant received the distribution money around that time.\\n\\nOn 2016. 6. 2., the Defendant made a deposit for payment by relative uncertainty, designating the depositees as the nonparty, the Plaintiff, the NFFC, and Kookmin Bank Co., Ltd. The facts giving rise to the deposit are that, out of KRW 315,413,800 distributed as stated above, the Defendant appropriates KRW 250,853,086, together with the KRW 150,000,000 received from the Plaintiff on 2012. 11. 19., to the Defendant’s recourse claim against the nonparty, and deposits KRW 64,295,914, which is the remainder of the distribution money in the amount of KRW 64,560,714 less the law office fee of KRW 264,800 for the deposit application.\\n\\ne. The Plaintiff filed this action seeking restitution of unjust enrichment on the ground that the payment of KRW 150,000,000 to the Defendant on 2012. 11. 19. lacked a legal cause.\\n\\n2. Whether the 1st Loan is included in the secured obligation under the 2nd Mortgage (Ground 1 for final appeal)\\n\\na. When a financial institution and the mortgagor execute a mortgage creation agreement, if the mortgage creation agreement contains wording stating that all debts arising from the financial institution’s credit transactions are to be secured, namely, a so-called blanket mortgage, the mortgage creation agreement is a dispositive document, and, absent special circumstances, the content of the declaration of intent shall, as a matter of principle, be construed in accordance with the wording of the agreement. However, if the mortgage creation agreement is uniformly printed and used in the form of standard terms and conditions, and in light of various circumstances such as the circumstances and purpose of the conclusion of the mortgage creation agreement, the amount of the secured obligation, and the mutual relationship among the mortgagor, debtor, and creditor, it can be recognized that the parties intended to secure only a specific debt despite the wording of the agreement, the scope of the security obligation must be limited in accordance with the parties’ intent (see Supreme Court Decision 83DAKA2159, rendered on 1984. 6. 12.; Supreme Court Decision 2001DA12430, rendered on 2003. 4. 11.).\\n\\nb. The court below held, for the following reasons, that the debt under the 1st Loan was included in the secured obligation under the 2nd Mortgage, and thus determined that the Defendant, who repaid part of the 1st Loan, acquired part of the 2nd Mortgage by subrogation by the person who performed the obligation.\\n\\n(1) The 2nd Mortgage creation agreement provides that all debts presently and in the future owed by the nonparty to the NFFC in connection with credit transactions, etc. shall constitute the secured obligation. At the time the 2nd Mortgage was created, the nonparty was already owing the NFFC the debt under the 1st Loan. The debt under the 2nd Loan arose about 3 years after the 2nd Mortgage was created.\\n\\n(2) Before filing this action, the Plaintiff filed a lawsuit seeking damages, etc. against the NFFC, and the Defendant participated as an intervenor on the NFFC’s side. The cause of the claim was as follows. The secured obligation under the 2nd Mortgage is limited to the 2nd Loan and does not include the 1st Loan. Nevertheless, the Plaintiff, at the NFFC’s request, paid KRW 150,000,000 in principal and interest on the 1st Loan and overdue interest thereon in the amount of KRW 18,805,503, for a total of KRW 168,803,503. Since the Plaintiff’s agreement to repay the 1st Loan constitutes payment of a debt not owed, an unconscionable legal act, or a declaration of intent induced by fraud or duress, etc., the Plaintiff sought restitution of unjust enrichment or damages caused by tort, etc. in the amount of KRW 168,803,503.\\n\\nThe appellate court dismissed all of the Plaintiff’s claims, on the ground that the 1st Loan was included in the secured obligation under the 2nd Mortgage (Daegu High Court Decision 2015NA21081, rendered on 2015. 12. 16.). The appellate judgment became final and conclusive as the final appeal was dismissed (Supreme Court Decision 2016DA201470, dated 2016. 4. 28.).\\n\\n(3) It is recognized that the Financial Supervisory Service replied to the Plaintiff’s application for dispute mediation to the effect that the debt under the 1st Loan is not included in the secured obligation under the 2nd Mortgage. However, such fact alone is insufficient to overturn the determination that the debt under the 1st Loan is included in the secured obligation under the 2nd Mortgage.\\n\\nc. Reviewing the reasons of the judgment below in light of the legal principles and record as seen above, the court below’s determination is proper, and, unlike the assertion in the grounds for final appeal, there is no error of failing to conduct necessary examination, or, in violation of the rules of logic and experience, exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehending the legal principles concerning the scope of secured obligations under a mortgage, the interpretation of terms and conditions and contracts, etc.\\n\\n3. Whether a marginal registration is always required in a guarantor’s subrogation against a third acquirer (Ground 2 for final appeal)\\n\\na. Under Articles 480 and 481 of the Civil Act, a person subrogating a creditor may exercise rights regarding the claim and its security within the scope recoverable by his or her own rights (Article 482(1) of the Civil Act). Regarding subrogation by the person who performed the obligation as between a guarantor and a third acquirer, Article 482(2) item 1 of the Civil Act provides: “A guarantor may not subrogate the creditor against a third person who acquired rights in the leased property or mortgaged property unless he or she has previously made a marginal registration of subrogation in the registration of the leasehold right or mortgage.”\\n\\nThis provision is intended to protect third acquirers, who acquired rights in the subject real property in the belief that the mortgage, etc. had been extinguished by the guarantor’s performance, from unforeseeable loss (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DA99341, rendered on 2015. 3. 20.). Accordingly, where a third acquirer acquires rights in the subject real property while the guarantor, after performance of the obligation, has not made a marginal registration of subrogation regarding the registration of the mortgage, etc., the guarantor may not subrogate the creditor against the third acquirer.\\n\\nHowever, if a third acquirer acquires rights in the subject real property before the guarantor performs the obligation, it must be deemed that the guarantor may subrogate even without a marginal registration of subrogation. Since the third person who acquired rights in the subject real property before the guarantor’s performance acquired the rights knowing the existence of the mortgage, etc. on the register, there is no risk of unforeseeable loss even if the guarantor later subrogates.\\n\\nb. The court below determined as follows.\\n\\nThe Plaintiff acquired ownership of the 3rd through 8th Real Property, which are the subject matter of the 2nd Mortgage, on 2012. 3. 19., and the Defendant, as guarantor, thereafter repaid KRW 342,997,237 out of the 1st Loan to the NFFC on 2012. 8. 24. Accordingly, even if the Defendant did not make a marginal registration of subrogation concerning the 2nd Mortgage, the Defendant may subrogate the NFFC against the Plaintiff, who is a third acquirer.\\n\\nc. Reviewing the reasons of the judgment below in light of the record, the court below’s determination that the Defendant, a guarantor, may subrogate the creditor NFFC against the Plaintiff, who acquired the subject matter of the mortgage before the debt was paid, without a marginal registration of subrogation, is proper as being in accordance with the legal principles stated above. There is no error in this determination of misapprehending the legal principles concerning subrogation by the person who performed the obligation, as asserted in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n4. Remaining grounds for final appeal asserted (Grounds 3 and 4 for final appeal)\\n\\na. The court below determined as follows.\\n\\nThe Plaintiff’s payment of KRW 150,000,000 to the Defendant should be regarded as the consideration for the Defendant, who acquired part of the 2nd Mortgage by subrogation, withdrawing the application for the Auction in this case and cancelling the 2nd Mortgage. Since, after the Plaintiff paid KRW 150,000,000 to the Defendant, the application for the Auction in this case was withdrawn and the 2nd Mortgage was cancelled, the KRW 150,000,000 cannot be regarded as having been paid without legal cause.\\n\\nb. Reviewing the reasons of the judgment below in light of the record, the judgment below contains no error, as asserted in the grounds for final appeal, of failing to conduct necessary examination, or, in violation of the rules of logic and experience, exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehending the legal principles concerning the principle of party presentation and unjust enrichment, etc.\\n\\nc. The Plaintiff contends that the NFFC caused the Plaintiff to pay KRW 150,000,000 to the Defendant despite having received repayment from the Defendant of most of the debt under the 1st Loan, and that this constitutes an abuse of rights.\\n\\nSuch assertion was raised only at the stage of final appeal and does not constitute a proper ground for final appeal against the judgment below. Furthermore, even if the record is reviewed in light of the relevant legal principles, there is no error in the judgment below, as asserted in the grounds for final appeal, of misapprehending the legal principles concerning abuse of rights.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nThe Plaintiff’s final appeal is without merit and is therefore dismissed, and the costs of final appeal are assessed against the losing party. It is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices, as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning a partnership is correct? (In case of dispute, according to case law)
A: The parties to a partnership contract may add grounds for dissolution of the partnership that are different from those prescribed by the Civil Act, but any special agreement differing from the provisions concerning liquidation and their contents is ineffective.
B: As a general rule, the status of a member of a joint performance entity that has the nature of a partnership under the Civil Act is not subject to universal succession arising from a company’s split-merger.
C: The mere circumstance that discord and confrontation between the parties to a partnership have destroyed the relationship of trust, making it impossible to expect the smooth operation of partnership business, does not constitute “unavoidable grounds,” which are grounds for a petition for dissolution of a partnership prescribed in Article 720 of the Civil Act.
D: Where a partnership has set a term of existence, even if there are unavoidable grounds, a partner may not withdraw at an unfavorable time for the partnership.
E: Where a partner withdraws from a partnership, the calculation between the withdrawing partner and the remaining partners shall, as a rule, be based not on the internal profit-and-loss sharing ratio of the partnership, but on the ratio of the value of assets actually contributed.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2010DA44002]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Article 530-10 of the Commercial Act provides that a company established by, or surviving after, a split or a split-merger shall succeed to the rights and obligations of the splitting company in accordance with the split plan or split-merger agreement. In other words, where there is a split-merger of a company, the rights and obligations of the company subject to the split shall, in accordance with the split-merger agreement, be comprehensively succeeded to by the surviving company as a result of the split-merger, regardless of whether they concern private-law relations or public-law relations, except for those that, by their nature, do not permit transfer (see Supreme Court Decision 77NU265, decided on 1980. 3. 25.).\\nMeanwhile, a joint contractor consortium is basically considered to have the nature of a partnership under the Civil Act, and unless it is agreed among the members of the joint contractor consortium that membership status may be assigned to a third party, the membership status in the joint contractor consortium does not pass by inheritance and corresponds to rights and obligations of a strictly personal nature attached to the holder, the transfer of which is not permitted without the consent of the other members (see Supreme Court Decision 81DA145, decided on 1981. 7. 28.); accordingly, it is appropriate to regard membership status in a joint contractor consortium as, in principle, not being subject to universal succession arising from a company’s split-merger.\\n\\n2. According to the reasons of the first-instance judgment cited by the court below and the evidence admitted by the court below, Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd. formed a joint contractor consortium with the intervenor in support of the Defendant and, on 2004. 7. 30., entered into a construction contract with the Defendant concerning the 756kV Sinanseong~Singapyeong transmission line construction work (hereinafter referred to as “the construction work in this case”) (hereinafter referred to as “the construction contract in this case”); that the joint contractor agreement concluded between Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd. and the intervenor in support of the Defendant provided that the members could not assign the rights and obligations under the agreement to a third party; that Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd. was suspended from checking-account transactions on 2007. 6. 4. because it could not settle bills and the like already issued; that the Plaintiff, on 2007. 5. 15., entered into an agreement with Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd. to split-merger the electrical construction business division and the specialized fire-fighting facility construction business division of Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd., and thereafter completed the registration of the split-merger on 2007. 7. 12.; that the intervenor in support of the Defendant, on 2007. 7. 30., notified to the effect that, in light of the current status of Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd., it was judged impossible to complete the above work within the construction period, and that Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd., whose status as a member of the joint contractor consortium had been deprived pursuant to Articles 11 and 12(2) of the joint contractor agreement, was withdrawn from the members of the joint contractor consortium, and on 2007. 7. 31. also informed the Defendant of the above notice; that the Plaintiff requested the Defendant on 2007. 8. 21. and 2007. 9. 21. to enter into a modification contract regarding the construction work in this case on the ground of the split-merger in this case, but the Defendant, on 2007. 9. 13., 2007. 10. 4., and 2007. 11. 8., refused to conclude the modification contract, stating that the modification contract was possible only with the consent of the intervenor in support of the Defendant, who was a member of the joint contractor consortium in this case; that the intervenor in support of the Defendant notified Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd. several times of the same content as the notice dated 2007. 7. 30., and on 2009. 5. 8. requested the Defendant to approve the withdrawal of Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd. from the members of the joint contractor consortium; and accordingly, the Defendant, on 2009. 5. 13., notified Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd. and the intervenor in support of the Defendant that it approved the withdrawal of Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd. from the members of the joint contractor consortium, and on 2009. 5. 14. entered into a contract with the intervenor in support of the Defendant changing the contractual counterparty under the construction contract in this case to the intervenor in support of the Defendant.\\n\\n3. The above facts are examined in light of the foregoing legal principles.\\nThe status, as a member of the construction contract in this case awarded as a construction joint contractor consortium, held by Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd. and the intervenor in support of the Defendant corresponds to rights and obligations of a strictly personal nature attached to the holder, the transfer of which is not permitted by nature. Therefore, even if the electrical construction business division and the specialized fire-fighting facility construction business division of Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd. were split-merged into the Plaintiff, the status as a member of the joint contractor consortium with respect to the construction contract in this case should be regarded as not being subject to universal succession arising from the split-merger.\\nNevertheless, the court below, on the premise, for the reasons stated in its judgment, that the status as a member of the construction contract in this case awarded as a construction joint contractor consortium fell within the subject of succession of rights and obligations due to the split-merger, granted this part of the Plaintiff’s claim seeking confirmation that the Plaintiff had succeeded to Youngrim E&C Co., Ltd.’s status as the contractual counterparty member concerning the construction contract in this case; thus, the court below’s determination contains an error of law in misapprehending the legal principles regarding the effect of a split-merger and the legal nature of membership status in a joint contractor consortium, and it is clear that such error affected the outcome of the judgment. The Defendant’s ground of final appeal pointing out this point is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds for final appeal, we reverse the part of the court below’s judgment unfavorable to the Defendant and remand this part of the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, render the judgment as stated in the operative part."}

{"[84DAKA1921]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below found that Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2, on 1980.11.2., entered into a partnership agreement to the effect that Nonparty 1 would contribute a site of 422 pyeong and 8 hop in Buk-gu, Incheon City (468/596 of which was registered in the name of Nonparty 3 and 128/596 of which was registered in the name of Nonparty 4), and that Nonparty 2 would construct 8 houses on the said land at his own expense and sell them, using the sale proceeds to cover the land price and construction costs and dividing the remaining profit equally; that the building at issue in this case referred to in the original judgment was one of the buildings constructed on the said land by Nonparty 2, who invested the construction costs pursuant to the said partnership agreement; and that with respect to the share of Nonparty 3 in the said land which Nonparty 1 had agreed to contribute, compulsory auction proceedings were conducted and it was knocked down to Nonparty 5 on 1981.3.4., and also that with respect to the share of Nonparty 4 which Nonparty 1 had agreed to purchase and contribute, Nonparty 1 had only concluded a sales contract and had not paid the purchase price. On the basis of these findings, the court below held that Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 had agreed on 1981.12.15 that if either party failed to perform his own obligation to contribute and the other party rescinded the said partnership agreement, the party in default would be deemed to have abandoned all rights to the partnership property; however, since Nonparty 2 rescinded the partnership agreement due to Nonparty 1’s default in performing the obligation to contribute, Nonparty 1 was deemed to have abandoned all rights in the partnership property, and therefore the plaintiffs’ assertion that the building became the sole property of Nonparty 2 was without merit, and it dismissed the plaintiffs’ claims.\\n\\nHowever, if, as found by the court below, in the original partnership agreement the land which Nonparty 1 agreed to contribute was registered in the name of a third party and Nonparty 1 was unable to acquire it and contribute it to the partnership, then that fact alone plainly shows that Nonparty 1 is in default of the obligation to contribute under the partnership agreement, and according to the statement in Exhibit A No. 12-1 (Notice), which the court below did not reject, it can be recognized that Nonparty 2, on 1982.2.18., manifested an intention to rescind the partnership agreement to Nonparty 1 on the ground that Nonparty 1 had not performed the obligation to contribute under the partnership agreement, stating that Nonparty 1’s rights concerning the building at issue in this case would be deemed abandoned. The court below, while affirming the facts stated in its reasoning, and without rejecting Exhibit A No. 12-1, nonetheless held that the plaintiffs’ above-mentioned assertion of fact could not be recognized; this constitutes an error of contradiction in reasoning or a violation of the rules of evidence, and the argument pointing out this point is well founded.\\n\\nMoreover, the provisions of the Civil Act concerning grounds for dissolution of a partnership and liquidation are not mandatory provisions that exclude even special agreements by the parties having different contents; therefore, where the parties have made a special agreement different in content from the provisions of the Civil Act concerning grounds for dissolution of a partnership and liquidation, such special agreement must be regarded as valid. (See Supreme Court Decision 65DA560 rendered on 1965.8.31.) In this case, the purport of the above agreement dated 1981.12.15 between Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 is that, if Nonparty 1 does not perform the obligation to contribute under the partnership agreement, Nonparty 2 may manifest an intention to rescind the partnership agreement against Nonparty 1, and by such manifestation of intent the partnership relation terminates and the partnership property becomes the sole property of Nonparty 2 without going through the special procedure of liquidation under the Civil Act; this is therefore a special agreement different from the provisions of the Civil Act concerning grounds for dissolution of a partnership and liquidation, and is valid.\\n\\nAlthough the court below recognized the existence of the above special agreement, it held, contrary to the content of that special agreement, that the building at issue in this case would still remain joint property owned in common by the partners until the termination of the liquidation relation; this constitutes an error in misapprehending the content of the special agreement and in incorrectly determining the attribution of the partnership property.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below, the Seoul High Court, and it is so decided by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[92DA21098]": "1. We examine the first ground of appeal by counsel for the Plaintiff (since the supplemental statement of grounds of appeal was submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal, we shall determine only to the extent that it supplements the grounds stated in the statement of grounds of appeal).\\n\\nThe unavoidable cause prescribed as a ground for dissolution of a partnership under Article 720 of the Civil Act includes not only cases where the achievement of the partnership’s purpose has become markedly difficult due to changes in economic circumstances or deterioration of the partnership’s financial condition or business downturn, etc., but also cases where mutual distrust has been destroyed by confrontation arising from discord and estrangement among the partners, making it impossible to expect the partnership to be operated jointly and harmoniously; and once the continued conduct of the joint business has become markedly difficult as stated above, even a party responsible for the destruction of the trust relationship must be deemed to have the right to seek dissolution of the partnership (see this Court’s judgment rendered on 1991.2.22. in 90DAKA26300).\\n\\nReviewing the record, it is proper that the court below found that after the arcade partnership agreement at issue was concluded between the Plaintiff and the Defendants, discord and estrangement arose, as stated in its reasoning, from disputes over the distribution of profits and the Plaintiff’s participation in management; that the parties went so far as to file applications for a provisional injunction prohibiting entry to the arcade and a provisional injunction prohibiting interference with business against each other, and also filed criminal complaints, which resulted in prosecution; and that the trust relationship between them was destroyed to the extent of being irreparable, so that the situation had reached a point where the attainment of the purpose of the partnership agreement, namely the joint operation of the arcade, could by no means be expected, and therefore that such a cause constituted an unavoidable cause permitting a demand for dissolution of the partnership was correct, and there is no illegality such as the alleged misapprehension of legal doctrine.\\n\\nFurther, in response to the Plaintiff’s argument that the above disputes and estrangement that arose between the Plaintiff and the Defendants were attributable to the Defendants, in that the Defendants denied the validity of the above partnership agreement, failed to perform the obligations of the Defendants prescribed in the above partnership agreement, and attempted to unjustly exclude the Plaintiff from participating in the arcade business, so that the destruction of the trust relationship between the Plaintiff and the Defendants was entirely attributable to the Defendants, and therefore it did not constitute an unavoidable cause permitting a demand for dissolution of the partnership, and that even if it did constitute an unavoidable cause, the Defendants who caused the unavoidable cause could not, under the principle of good faith, demand dissolution, the court below held that in a partnership relationship based on trust, even if the cause of the destruction of the trust relationship is attributable only to one party, if, as in this case, the degree of destruction is so severe that the attainment of the partnership’s purpose has become impossible, it must be deemed to constitute an unavoidable cause permitting a demand for dissolution, and thus, once the attainment of the partnership’s purpose has become impossible, it cannot be rejected merely because it is a demand for dissolution by the party at fault. The above determination of the court below is proper in light of the legal principles stated above, and the precedents cited by the appellant are different in their facts from this case and are not appropriate precedents to be invoked in this case. Moreover, even in light of the facts as finally determined by the court below and the evidence adopted by it, although it is true that the confrontation arising from discord and estrangement between the Plaintiff and the Defendants began entirely on the Defendants’ responsibility, it is difficult to view the Defendants as having caused, from the outset, a ground for dissolution of the partnership. Accordingly, the allegation that the above determination of the court below is unlawful due to a misapprehension of legal doctrine is also without merit.\\n\\n2. We examine the second ground of appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the judgment below, in response to the Plaintiff’s assertion that even if the above partnership was dissolved for unavoidable cause, liquidation procedures such as distribution of residual assets remain, and the Defendants still deny the validity of the above partnership agreement, so the Plaintiff has an interest in seeking confirmation of the above partnership share against the Defendants, the court below held as follows: according to the evidence cited therein, in concluding the partnership agreement at issue, the Plaintiff and the Defendants agreed not to reserve any part of the income from the business on the day of operation as partnership property and to distribute all of the remainder after deducting ordinary expenses on a day-to-day basis in proportion to their shares; and, for the purpose of enabling the Plaintiff to receive at least a monthly 4% profit on the Plaintiff’s invested funds, they even agreed that the partnership share could be adjusted upward to 25%; and yet, for the contingency that even without going through procedures for repayment of the debts borne by the partnership upon termination of the partnership agreement or distribution of partnership property acquired by the partnership, the Plaintiff could recover the invested funds by presenting for payment the cashier’s check delivered by the Defendants, the Defendants would issue and deliver to the Plaintiff, as security for the Plaintiff’s invested funds, one cashier’s check in the same amount, and the Plaintiff would keep it in custody; and there is no evidence to support a finding that the property contributed by the Defendants at the time of conclusion of the partnership agreement was valued in money. In light of the foregoing circumstances, the court below held that it would be appropriate to view the Plaintiff and the Defendants as having made a special agreement, when concluding the above partnership agreement, to terminate the partnership relationship merely by having the Plaintiff receive back the KRW 200,000,000 contributed by the Plaintiff, while, in the event the Plaintiff withdrew from the above partnership or the above partnership was dissolved, the Plaintiff could not claim distribution of residual assets, but would also be exempt from liability to repay the debts borne by the above partnership and, in place of the liquidation procedures under the Civil Act; and therefore, since the above partnership had already been dissolved by the Defendants’ above demand for dissolution and liquidation procedures were also no longer necessary under the above special agreement, the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendants for return of the contributed funds based on the above special agreement is one thing, but separately seeking confirmation of the above partnership share is a matter concerning a past right or legal relationship, for which there is no interest in confirmation.\\n\\nReviewing the evidentiary relationship adopted by the court below from the record, the court below’s finding of fact is convincing. If the factual relationship is as such, then the partnership relationship between the Plaintiff and the Defendants was extinguished immediately upon dissolution of the partnership and cannot be regarded as continuing for liquidation purposes; accordingly, the court below’s determination that there is no further interest in seeking confirmation of the partnership share is also proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error such as factual misunderstanding due to violation of the rules of evidence, insufficient examination, or unlawful misapprehension of the legal principles concerning liquidation of a partnership, as alleged. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n3. We examine the third ground of appeal.\\n\\nThe scope of the Plaintiff’s claim for damages is determined by two factors, namely the daily average amount of profit distribution and the number of days on which the Defendants committed embezzlement and breach of trust, so even if the amount of damages does not exceed the scope of the Plaintiff’s claim, the court cannot recognize a daily average amount of profit distribution exceeding the scope asserted by the Plaintiff.\\n\\nAccordingly, in calculating damages from 1988.8.22. to 1989.3.16., the court below properly recognized the daily average amount of profit distribution only within the range of the amount asserted by the Plaintiff, and there is no illegality such as a misunderstanding of the scope of the Plaintiff’s claim, as alleged.\\n\\nFurther, reviewing the evidentiary relationship adopted by the court below from the record, the court below’s measure of calculating the standard for the amount of damages after 1989.6.6. at KRW 673,718 per day is also convincing, and there is no illegality such as factual misunderstanding in violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged. All of the arguments are without merit.\\n\\n4. We examine the first ground of appeal by counsel for the Defendants.\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the judgment below, in response to the Defendants’ assertion that the Plaintiff interfered with the Defendants’ business, so they were inevitably forced to suspend or close the arcade business at issue, and therefore the Defendants’ liability for damages should be exempted or, in calculating the amount of damages to be compensated by the Defendants, the Plaintiff’s above wrongdoing should be taken into significant account, the court below rejected the Defendants’ above assertion on the ground that it did not believe the evidence corresponding to the facts asserted by the Defendants and that there was no other evidence to support it. Reviewing the record, the above determination of the court below is convincing, and there is no illegality such as alleged. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n5. We examine the second ground of the same appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the judgment below, the court below held that at the time of conclusion of the partnership agreement at issue, there was an implied agreement that only the Defendants would bear expenses such as taxes and public charges and labor costs asserted by the Defendants. Although the content presented as the basis for the court below’s above determination is not free from inadequacy, in light of the fact, as stated by the court below, that even when the Plaintiff participated in the arcade business and normally received distribution of profits from the Defendants, there was no instance in which expenses such as those asserted by the Defendants were deducted, the court below’s above determination is convincing, and there is no illegality such as alleged. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n6. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties, and the judgment is rendered as ordered, with the unanimous agreement of the participating Justices."}

question:
A entered into a lease agreement with B, the owner of X land, for the purpose of owning a building, and thereafter erected Building Y on X land. After the lease agreement terminated, which of the following are all the incorrect statements concerning the exercise of the right to demand purchase of Building Y? (Each item is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law governs)

(a) If, before the lease agreement regarding X land was terminated, A sold Building Y in an unregistered and unauthorized condition to A, then even if A became the lessee of X land with B’s consent, unless there are special circumstances, A cannot exercise against B the right to demand purchase of Building Y. 
(b) Unlike the facts, even if it was B, not B, but B who had been entrusted by B with the management of X land, who entered into the lease agreement with A as the contracting party, if B succeeded to the status of lessor from B before the lease agreement regarding X land was terminated, A may exercise against B the right to demand purchase of Building Y. 
(c) If A exercised the right to demand purchase of Building Y against B in the court of first instance, then withdrew it after obtaining B’s consent, and thereafter exercised it again in the appellate court, such exercise is permitted. 
(d) If no meeting of the minds was reached between A and B concerning the purchase price of Building Y, which is the object of A’s purchase demand against B, the court may only recognize that a sales contract was formed with the market value of Building Y at the time of the exercise of the right as the sale price, and cannot, ex officio, arbitrarily increase or decrease the recognized market value to determine the sale price.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2001DA42080]": "1. Summary of the Lower Court's Reasoning\\n\\na. The lower court found the following facts based on the evidence it relied upon.\\n\\n(1) Jeju-si Ido-dong 1257-4, site 706㎡, is jointly owned by the Plaintiffs, and Jeju-si Ido-dong 1257-8, site 165㎡, and Jeju-si Ido-dong 1257-9, site 330㎡, are solely owned by Plaintiff 2.\\n\\n(2) The late Nonparty 1, who was the Plaintiffs' decedent (died on August 4, 1995), leased to Nonparty 2 and Nonparty 3, on December 30, 1968, the land that had been subdivided into the above parcels and that had previously been Jeju-si Ido-dong 1257-4, site 363 pyeong, which he owned, for the purpose of owning five wooden slate-roofed houses, with the lease term set from December 30, 1968 to December 30, 1974. Accordingly, Nonparty 2 and Nonparty 3 built and used buildings on the aforementioned former land, and then sold those buildings to other persons, and as a result of successive resales of each building listed in the attached schedule set forth in the lower court's judgment, the Defendants now hold title by registration to and own each building listed in the same schedule, while occupying and using the occupied portions of each of the lands at issue listed in the same schedule.\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, even after the initial lease term expired, the late Nonparty 1, without demanding removal of the buildings or delivery of the lands at issue, continued to renew the lease agreements with the purchasers who had successively purchased each building at issue, setting the lease term as from the end of January of each year to the end of January of the following year, and collected rent therefor; and the Defendants paid rent through the rent for 1999 (from February 1, 1999 to January 31, 2000).\\n\\n(4) However, on January 22, 1997, the Plaintiffs sent the Defendants a notice by content-certified mail that they would terminate the lease agreement when the lease term expired at the end of January 1998, and around that time the said notice reached the Defendants.\\n\\n(5) The Defendants exercised, in the lower court, their right to demand purchase regarding the buildings at issue, and their declaration of intention reached the Plaintiffs on October 16, 2000.\\n\\nb. Furthermore, the lower court held that: (1) under the above facts found, the lease agreement with the Defendants was lawfully terminated either when the Plaintiffs' notice of termination reached the Defendants or around January 31, 1998, when the lease term ended, so the Defendants were obliged to return the benefits obtained by occupying and using the site, and therefore the Plaintiffs' claim for return of unjust enrichment was well-founded; and (2) with respect to the Plaintiffs' claim for removal of each building at issue and delivery of the site, the Defendants, as lawful lessees of each parcel at issue for the purpose of owning buildings, had the right to demand purchase from the Plaintiffs as to each building at issue, because the buildings existed at the expiration of the lease term, and because the Defendants' declaration of intention to exercise the right to demand purchase had reached the Plaintiffs, the Plaintiffs, who had purchased each building at issue, could not demand removal of each building at issue and delivery of the occupied portions of the site from the Defendants; and it rejected the Plaintiffs' arguments that, since the Defendants had exercised the right to demand purchase in the first instance and then withdrawn it, they could not exercise the right to demand purchase again in the lower court, and that the demand for purchase of each building at issue, which had been built more than 30 years earlier and had almost no economic value, violated the principle of good faith or constituted abuse of rights, for the reasons stated in its opinion.\\n\\n2. Judgment on the Plaintiffs' Grounds of Appeal\\n\\na. Misapprehension of law concerning the right to demand purchase, its withdrawal, violation of the principle of good faith, and abuse of rights\\n\\nWhen a land lease for the purpose of owning a building terminates, the lessee's right to demand purchase with respect to the existing building on the land is not one that requires any specific form of exercise, and it may be exercised not only in court but also out of court, and there is no restriction on the timing of such exercise; therefore, there is no reason why the Defendants' exercise of their right to demand purchase of the buildings would be impermissible merely because they exercised that right in the first instance and then withdrew it, and later exercised it again in the lower court (although, if a sale is formed by virtue of the effect of the exercise of the right to demand purchase, the demand for purchase cannot thereafter be withdrawn solely by one party's intention, the overall tenor of the pleadings indicates that, in this case, the Plaintiffs appear to have accepted the withdrawal of the Defendants' demand for purchase in the first instance). The ground of appeal contends that, premised on the exercise of the lessee's right to demand purchase of the building as a litigation act, re-exercise after withdrawal of the litigation act is impermissible, or that the exercise of the right to demand purchase is equivalent to a counterclaim and thus requires the opposing party's consent when exercised at the appellate level; however, such arguments are merely independent views and cannot be accepted, and it cannot be said that the lower court judgment contains illegality affecting the result of the judgment by misapprehending the law concerning the right to demand purchase and its withdrawal as alleged in the ground of appeal.\\n\\nIn addition, the lessee's right to demand purchase prescribed in Civil Act Articles 643 and 283 is a right granted to the lessee where the term of a land lease for the purpose of owning a building expires, a building exists on the land, and the lessor does not wish to renew the contract, and whether the building on the land has objective economic value or whether it is useful to the lessor cannot be regarded as a requirement for the exercise of that right. Nor does the record disclose any other basis for finding that the Defendants' exercise of the right to demand purchase in this case violated the principle of good faith or constituted abuse of rights; therefore, the ground of appeal on this point is also without merit.\\n\\nb. Omission of judgment\\n\\nEven upon review of the record, there is no basis for finding that the Plaintiffs argued, by the time the lower court concluded the proceedings, that because the Defendants had agreed with the Plaintiffs in or around March 1997 to remove each building at issue, they could not exercise the right to demand purchase. Moreover, even if, before the lease terminated, the lessee of land for the purpose of owning a building had agreed with the lessor to abandon all buildings and other ground installations, unless special circumstances are found such that, taking into comprehensive consideration all circumstances including the terms of the lease agreement and the circumstances under which the agreement was concluded, it cannot in substance be viewed as disadvantageous to the lessee, such an agreement is disadvantageous to the lessee and is void under Civil Act Article 652 (see Supreme Court Judgment dated June 22, 1993, 93DA16130). In this case, even if there had been such an agreement as alleged by the Plaintiffs, the record discloses no basis for the above special circumstances, so whether the Plaintiffs' above argument was addressed would not affect the result of the judgment in any way; accordingly, the ground of appeal on this point is ultimately without merit.\\n\\nFurther, the lower court's acceptance of the Defendants' argument that they exercised the right to demand purchase necessarily includes rejection of the Plaintiffs' argument that such argument should be dismissed as an attack or defense made late; therefore, it cannot be said that there was illegality in the form of omission of judgment as alleged in the ground of appeal.\\n\\n3. Judgment on the Defendants' Grounds of Appeal\\n\\na. Violation of the principle of disposition\\n\\nAccording to the record, it is clear that the Plaintiffs' claim in this case is based on the fact that the Defendants continued to occupy and use each of the lands at issue owned by the Plaintiffs even after the lease term had expired, and the Plaintiffs' above assertion includes not only a request, as owners, for damages equivalent to rent against an occupant without title, but also a request, as lessors, for unjust enrichment equivalent to rent from a lessee who continues to occupy and use the leased object even after termination of the lease. Accordingly, the lower court's treatment of the Plaintiffs' claim in this case as a claim for unjust enrichment and its judgment thereon is proper and convincing, and it cannot be said that it contains illegality violating the principle of disposition as alleged in the ground of appeal.\\n\\nb. Omission of judgment, and incomplete deliberation due to failure to exercise the duty of clarification\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Defendants submitted as Exhibit B No. 2 (deposit certificate) a statement to the effect that they had deposited in lieu of performance amounts equivalent to the rent for 1998 (from February 1, 1998 to January 31, 1999) and for 1999 (from February 1, 1999 to January 31, 2000) for the lands at issue, and also submitted as Exhibit B No. 3 (deposit certificate) a statement to the effect that they had deposited in lieu of performance amounts equivalent to the rent for 2000 (from February 1, 2000 to January 31, 2001); nevertheless, the lower court found as a fact that the Defendants had paid only amounts equivalent to the rent for 1999 (from February 1, 1999 to January 31, 2000), and then ordered the Defendants to pay unjust enrichment in the amount equivalent to rent from February 1, 2000 onward.\\n\\nEven if the Defendants submitted Exhibit B No. 3 but did not expressly assert a defense of performance as to the amount stated therein, it is clear that the submission of Exhibit B No. 3 was intended to assert that performance had been made to the extent of that amount; therefore, the lower court should have regarded such an argument as having been made and determined its merits, or, if uncertain whether it was so intended, should have sought clarification and ascertained the Defendants' true intention before making a determination thereon. Accordingly, the lower court judgment, which did not proceed to that point, contains illegality in the form of omission of judgment or incomplete deliberation due to failure to exercise the duty of clarification. The ground of appeal on this point is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the portion of the lower court judgment against the Defendants relating to each amount equivalent to rent from February 1, 2000 to January 31, 2001 shall be reversed, and this case shall be remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination of this portion; the Plaintiffs' appeal and the remainder of the Defendants' appeal shall all be dismissed. It is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the judges participating."}

{"[2014DA72449]": "We adjudicate the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. In a lease of land for the purpose of owning buildings, etc., where the leasehold right extinguishes upon the expiration of the lease term or upon notice of termination of a lease for which no term has been fixed, the lessee may, pursuant to Article 643 of the Civil Act, demand that the lessor purchase the buildings, etc. at a reasonable price. The lessee’s right to demand the purchase of structures on the land is intended, from a national economic standpoint, to preserve the residual value of buildings standing on the land and to protect the lessee from the landowner’s exclusive exercise of ownership rights; as a matter of principle, it may be exercised against the lessor who held title to the land at the time the leasehold right extinguished. Where ownership of the land has been transferred, for example by the lessor’s transfer of the land to a third party, if the lessor’s status is succeeded to, or if the lessee can assert the leasehold right against the landowner, the said right to demand purchase may be exercised against the new landowner (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on April 26, 1977, 75DA348; Supreme Court Decision rendered on July 29, 1994, 93DA59717, 93DA59724).\\nMeanwhile, where a third party who is not the landowner leased the land, if the effect of the lease agreement accrued to the landowner, for example because the third party lawfully acted as the landowner’s agent or because the landowner ratified the third party’s unauthorized agency act, then the landowner, as lessor, becomes the party against whom the right to demand purchase of structures may be exercised. However, if the third party leased the land as a party to the lease agreement, then, absent special circumstances such as the landowner’s succession to the lessor’s status, the landowner who is not the lessor cannot directly become the party against whom the right to demand purchase of structures may be exercised.\\n\\n2. The court below found the following facts based on the evidence admitted.\\nA. As to each of the parcels of land at issue, ownership transfer registration was completed on December 30, 1963, in the name of Non-party 1, who is the elder brother of the Plaintiff (Counterclaim Defendant, hereinafter referred to as the “Plaintiff”); and, on January 25, 1989, a provisional registration of the right to claim ownership transfer was completed in the name of Non-party 2, who is the Plaintiff’s father. Thereafter, on April 11, 2002, Non-party 1 completed ownership transfer registration as to each of the parcels of land at issue in the name of the Plaintiff.\\nB. The Defendant (Counterclaim Plaintiff, hereinafter referred to as the “Defendant”) has been possessing the site by purchasing or owning the house and temple at issue built on each of the parcels of land at issue.\\nC. Before ownership transfer registration in the name of the Plaintiff was completed for each of the parcels of land at issue, around 2000, Non-party 2 leased the land to the Defendant for the purpose of owning buildings, for an annual rent of KRW 200,000, without fixing a term, and had been receiving rent from the Defendant. Non-party 2 also received consideration for the use of land in a similar manner with respect to other adjacent land in the name of the Plaintiff. The Plaintiff, too, did not raise any objection to the Defendant’s possession and use of the land before 2009.\\n\\n3. Based on these facts, the court below held that Non-party 2, as the owner of each of the parcels of land at issue, had title trusted the land to the Plaintiff, or, even if the Plaintiff was the owner of the land, the Plaintiff and Non-party 2 had agreed that Non-party 2 would exercise authority over the land; and then determined that the effect of the lease agreement concluded by Non-party 2 and the Defendant also extended to the Plaintiff, and accepted the Defendant’s assertion that, on the premise that the said lease agreement had been terminated, the Defendant was exercising the right to demand purchase of structures against the Plaintiff.\\nSince the facts lawfully determined by the judgment of the court below without exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence bind the appellate court (Civil Procedure Act Article 432), the Plaintiff’s argument disputing the court below’s above factual finding that Non-party 2 leased each of the parcels of land at issue to the Defendant for the purpose of owning buildings cannot be regarded as a lawful ground of appeal. Even upon examining the reasons for the judgment of the court below in light of the record, there is no basis to conclude that the court below’s determination on this point violated the rules of logic and experience and thus exceeded the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence.\\nHowever, the court below’s determination that the Defendant could exercise the right to demand purchase of structures against the Plaintiff is difficult to accept. In light of the legal principle examined above, a landowner who is not the lessor cannot, absent special circumstances such as succession to the lessor’s status, be the party against whom a lessee’s right to demand purchase of structures may be exercised; therefore, the Defendant, who leased the land from Non-party 2 rather than the Plaintiff, cannot in principle exercise the right to demand purchase of structures against the Plaintiff, who is the landowner and not the lessor. Also, based only on the circumstances revealed in the record, it is difficult to conclude that the Plaintiff and Non-party 2 entered into a title trust agreement, and even if such an agreement existed, the title trust agreement is void pursuant to Article 4(1) of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Titleholder’s Name. Accordingly, it is difficult to accept the Defendant’s assertion that the lease agreement between Non-party 2 and the Defendant also took effect with respect to the Plaintiff, or that the Plaintiff became the party against whom the right to demand purchase of structures may be exercised.\\nNevertheless, the court below, while finding that the other party to the lease agreement concluded with the Defendant, who is the lessee, was Non-party 2, determined that the Defendant could exercise the right to demand purchase of structures against the Plaintiff, who was not the lessor. This judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the parties to a lease agreement or the lessee’s right to demand purchase of structures. The ground of appeal to the extent that it points out this issue is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and so, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, render judgment as stated in the Disposition."}

question: A and B received confirmation from the family court on 2021. 3. 5. of their intention to divorce by agreement and filed a report of consensual divorce on the same day. Which of the following statements concerning A’s right to claim division of property is correct? (Each statement is independent, and where there is dispute, case law applies)
A: If, after assessing the property status by deducting liabilities from the positive assets held by A and B respectively, B bears liabilities less than the share that should be attributable to him, A’s petition for division of property concerning the apportionment of liabilities, filed against B on 2023. 1. 5., is not permitted.
B: Even if A made an extrajudicial claim for division of property against B on 2023. 1. 5., this does not constitute compliance with the exclusion period for the right to claim division of property.
C: If A did not exercise the right to claim division of property at the time of the consensual divorce, A’s creditor C may, within 2 years from the date of A’s report of consensual divorce, exercise by subrogation A’s right to claim division of property.
D: After A filed a petition for adjudication on division of property with the family court against B on 2023. 1. 5., B’s consent is required in order to withdraw that petition.
E: Even if A, when filing a petition for adjudication on division of property with the family court against B on 2023. 1. 5., did not specify the property subject to division and specified the property subject to division only on 5. 15. of the same year, this still constitutes compliance with the exclusion period for the right to claim division of property.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2018SEU18]": "We examine the grounds for the re-appeal.\\n\\n1. According to Article 839-2(3) and Article 843 of the Civil Act, the right to claim division of property is extinguished when 2 years have elapsed from the day of divorce by agreement or divorce by judgment. Where a claim for division of only part of the property is made within the 2-year exclusion period, the remaining property not made the subject of the claim cannot be regarded as having complied with the exclusion period; therefore, after the exclusion period has elapsed following a claim for division of property, the claim right is extinguished as to property that has not been made the subject of the claim until that time.\\n\\nIf property that has never been subjected to any inquiry as to whether it is divisible in a property division proceeding is discovered additionally after the judgment has become final and conclusive, an additional claim for division of property may be made with respect thereto (see Supreme Court Decision 2000MEU582, decided on February 28, 2003). However, any additional claim for division of property must also comply with the exclusion period of within 2 years from the day of divorce.\\n\\n2. a. The court below, for the following reasons, dismissed the part of the claim concerning some property and dismissed the remaining claim.\\n\\n(1) The claimant filed the petition for adjudication in this case on August 18, 2014, and, in the prior divorce and property division action, alleged that the deceased non-party had concealed property subject to division and then additionally claimed division of property by specifying omitted property; thereafter, on February 3, 2016, while submitting an application to amend the prayer for relief, the claimant added property subject to division and expanded the prayer for relief. The above application for amendment was submitted after 2 years had passed from September 6, 2012, when the judgment in the prior divorce and property division action became final and conclusive, and the portion concerning the property additionally added as subject to division is already barred by the exclusion period and is therefore unlawful.\\n\\n(2) As to the portion concerning the property subject to division claimed within the exclusion period, the evidence is insufficient to find that it is property subject to division, and thus the claimant's argument is not accepted.\\n\\nb. The judgment of the court below, following the legal principle stated above, is proper. There is no error in the court below's judgment, such as a misapprehension of the law concerning the exclusion period for the right to claim division of property, as alleged by the claimant.\\n\\n3. Since the claimant's re-appeal is without merit, it is dismissed, and the costs of the re-appeal shall be borne by the losing party; accordingly, the decision is rendered as stated in the order, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices."}

{"[2023MEU11819]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. For the reasons stated in its opinion, the lower court found that although the Plaintiff filed this action, seeking division of property together with damages for consolation money, against the Defendant within 2 years from 2018. 10. 23., the date on which the Plaintiff and the Defendant divorced by agreement, the Plaintiff had not specified the property subject to division at the time the action was filed, and only after 2 years had passed did the Plaintiff specify the property subject to division by filing applications such as an application for factual inquiry and an application for an order to submit financial transaction information in order to confirm the Defendant's assets; thus, the claim for division of property failed to comply with the preclusive period.\\n\\n2. However, the lower court's determination is difficult to accept.\\n\\na. A party to a divorce by agreement may claim division of property against the other party (Civil Act Article 839-2(1)), and the right to claim division of property is extinguished when 2 years have elapsed from the date of divorce (Article 839-2(3)); the foregoing Civil Act Article 839-2 applies mutatis mutandis to the right to claim division of property following a judicial divorce (Civil Act Article 843). Where a divorce by agreement or a judicial divorce has occurred but division of property has not been made, and a petition for division of property pursuant to Civil Act Article 839-2 is filed with the court for the first time within 2 years after divorce, the effect of compliance with the preclusive period is recognized with respect to claims made within the preclusive period.\\n\\n1) The property division system primarily aims to liquidate and distribute the property jointly formed by the spouses during marriage upon dissolution of the marital relationship (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2010MEU4071, 2010MEU4088, decided June 20, 2013).
