A case concerning division of property falls under a domestic non-contentious case [Family Litigation Act Article 2(1)2(b)4)], and with respect to domestic non-contentious procedures, unless the Family Litigation Act provides otherwise, the provisions of Part I of the Non-contentious Case Procedure Act apply mutatis mutandis (main clause of Family Litigation Act Article 34). In non-contentious proceedings, unlike in civil litigation, the court does not rely solely on the parties' pleadings, but, based on the so-called principle of ex officio investigation, under which the court collects materials forming the basis of the adjudication by its own authority and responsibility (Non-contentious Case Procedure Act Article 11), even if the applicant asserts and specifies the property subject to division, the court is not bound by the parties' assertions and may, ex officio, investigate the facts as to what constitutes the subject of division and include or exclude it (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2021SEU766, dated November 10, 2022).\\n\\n2) The preclusive period prescribed by Civil Act Article 839-2(3) is not a period during which it is sufficient merely to exercise the right out of court, but a time limit for filing a petition for adjudication on division of property within that period (see Supreme Court Decision 2020SEU561, dated June 30, 2022). Therefore, even if a petition for adjudication on division of property was filed within 2 years from the date of divorce, whether the preclusive period has been complied with is not to be determined according to whether specific evidentiary motions were made in that proceeding.\\n\\n3) The Supreme Court Decision 2018SEU18, dated June 22, 2018, cited by the lower court, concerned a case in which, after a prior property division adjudication had become final and binding, the party alleged that there existed property omitted at the time of the prior property division adjudication and sought additional division of property with respect to the specific property alleged to have been omitted; as the facts differ from those of this case, it is not appropriate to cite it.\\n\\nb. In this case, the Plaintiff submitted a petition seeking division of property on the date that marked 2 years from the date of the divorce by agreement, so the Plaintiff's claim for division of property complied with the preclusive period. Nevertheless, the lower court's determination that the entirety of the Plaintiff's claim for division of property failed to comply with the preclusive period contains an error of law by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the preclusive period for the right to claim division of property. The grounds of appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the judgment of the lower court is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for further proceedings and a new determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2023MEU11819]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. The court below, for the reasons stated in its holding, determined that although the Plaintiff filed this action against the Defendant seeking, together with damages, a division of property within 2 years from 2018. 10. 23., the date on which the Plaintiff divorced the Defendant by mutual agreement, the Plaintiff did not specify the property subject to division at the time of filing the action, and only after 2 years had elapsed did the Plaintiff specify the property subject to division by filing applications such as a request for fact inquiry and a motion for an order to submit financial transaction information to confirm the Defendant’s property; accordingly, it determined that the claim for division of property had failed to comply with the preclusive period.\\n\\n2. However, the court below’s determination is difficult to accept.\\n\\nA. Either party to a divorce by mutual agreement may claim division of property against the other party (Civil Act, Article 839-2(1)), and the right to claim division of property extinguishes when 2 years have elapsed from the date of divorce (Article 839-2(3)); the above Civil Act, Article 839-2 applies mutatis mutandis to the right to claim division of property arising from a judicial divorce (Civil Act, Article 843). Where a divorce by mutual agreement or a judicial divorce has been effected but property has not been divided, and a claim for division of property is first filed with the court pursuant to Civil Act, Article 839-2 within 2 years after the divorce, the effect of compliance with the preclusive period is recognized with respect to claims made within the preclusive period.\\n\\n1) The property division system mainly aims at liquidating and distributing property jointly formed by the spouses during marriage upon dissolution of the marital relationship (see en banc Supreme Court Judgment dated 2013. 6. 20. 2010MEU4071, 4088, etc.). A case concerning division of property falls under a family non-contentious case [Family Litigation Act, Article 2(1)2(b)4)], and with respect to family non-contentious proceedings, unless the Family Litigation Act contains special provisions, the provisions of Part I of the Non-Contentious Case Procedure Act apply mutatis mutandis (main text of Article 34 of the Family Litigation Act); and in non-contentious proceedings, unlike in civil litigation, they are not based solely on the parties’ allegations and arguments, but on the so-called principle of ex officio investigation, under which the court, by its own authority and responsibility, collects the materials forming the basis of adjudication (Article 11 of the Non-Contentious Case Procedure Act). Therefore, even if the claimant alleges and specifies the property subject to division, the court is not bound by the parties’ allegations and may, ex officio, investigate what constitutes the subject of division of property and include or exclude it (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2022. 11. 10. 2021SEU766, etc.).\\n\\n2) The preclusive period prescribed by Civil Act, Article 839-2(3) is not a period during which it suffices to exercise the right out of court, but a filing period within which a petition for adjudication of property division must be filed (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2022. 6. 30. 2020SEU561). Therefore, even if a petition for adjudication of property division was filed within 2 years from the date of divorce, compliance with the preclusive period is not to be determined by whether specific evidentiary applications were made in that proceeding.\\n\\n3) The Supreme Court Decision dated 2018. 6. 22. 2018SEU18 cited by the court below concerned a case in which, after a prior property division adjudication had become final and binding, a party alleged that property omitted in the prior property division adjudication existed and sought additional property division with respect to the specific property alleged to have been omitted; because the facts differ from those of this case, it is not appropriate for citation.\\n\\nB. In this case, the Plaintiff submitted a petition seeking division of property on the date 2 years from the date of the divorce by mutual agreement, and thus the Plaintiff’s claim for division of property complied with the preclusive period. Nevertheless, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the preclusive period for the right to claim division of property in determining that all of the Plaintiff’s claim for division of property failed to comply with the preclusive period. The ground of appeal pointing this out has merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2023MEU12218]": "The grounds for appeal are examined (the statements in a written submission filed after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds for appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. Course of the case and the lower court’s determination\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\na. The Plaintiff and the Defendant completed their marriage registration on June 10, 2008, and had the children at issue in this case.\\n\\nb. On December 5, 2019, the Plaintiff filed the present action against the Defendant seeking divorce, payment of damages for mental suffering, division of marital property, designation of the person with parental authority and the custodian, payment of child support, and the like.\\n\\nc. On May 3, 2022, the Plaintiff submitted a written withdrawal stating that the Plaintiff would withdraw the present action in its entirety, and the Defendant submitted a written statement of non-consent to the withdrawal of action in response.\\n\\nd. On July 5, 2022, the court of first instance rendered a judgment that, among other things, ① granted the Plaintiff’s claim for divorce, ② dismissed the Plaintiff’s claim for damages for mental suffering, ③ determined matters concerning the upbringing of the children at issue in this case, and ④ ordered division of marital property incident to the divorce.\\n\\ne. On July 15, 2022, the Plaintiff filed a notice of appeal challenging the portions of the judgment of first instance in which the Plaintiff lost.\\n\\nf. On November 2, 2022, the Plaintiff appeared at the first oral argument date in the court below, made a statement presenting the notice of appeal, and amended the relief sought on appeal; among the amended relief sought on appeal, the part concerning the claim for division of marital property sought to have the judgment of first instance changed to the Plaintiff’s original prayer for relief.\\n\\ng. On April 19, 2023, the court below rendered a judgment that, among other things, revoked the portion of the judgment of first instance concerning division of marital property, declared that the portion of the present action concerning the claim for division of marital property had terminated by the Plaintiff’s withdrawal on May 3, 2022, and dismissed the remainder of the Plaintiff’s appeal.\\n\\n2. Grounds for appeal concerning the claim for division of marital property\\n\\na. A petition for adjudication in a property division case falls under a Category Ma family non-contentious case [Family Litigation Act, Article 2(1)2(b)4)], and the procedure is initiated by a party’s petition for adjudication and may be terminated by the party’s withdrawal of that petition. Unless there is a special provision in the Family Litigation Act concerning family non-contentious proceedings, the provisions of Part I of the Non-Contentious Case Procedure Act apply mutatis mutandis (main text of Article 34 of the Family Litigation Act). The Family Litigation Act contains no special provision regarding whether the other party’s consent is required for the withdrawal of a petition for adjudication in a family non-contentious case, and the Non-Contentious Case Procedure Act does not apply mutatis mutandis Article 266(2) of the Civil Procedure Act concerning “consent to withdrawal of action.” Therefore, in the case of a property division adjudication case, which is a Category Ma family non-contentious case involving another party, the other party’s consent is not required for withdrawal of the petition for adjudication, and even if the other party objects to the withdrawal, it is proper to regard the withdrawal as effective. The lower court, in the same sense, found that, despite the Defendant’s written statement of non-consent to the withdrawal of action in response to the written withdrawal submitted by the Plaintiff at first instance, the withdrawal took effect only with respect to the portion of the claim for division of marital property; this is correct as it accords with the legal principles stated above.\\n\\nb. However, it is not persuasive that the court below further declared the termination of the litigation with respect to the claim for division of marital property on the premise that there had been no claim by the Plaintiff for division of marital property at all by the date of conclusion of oral argument in the court below, and, in light of the notice of appeal and the appellate brief containing arguments concerning division of marital property, the statement of the relief sought on appeal and the oral argument at the hearing date, there is sufficient room to conclude that the Plaintiff again filed a petition for adjudication regarding division of marital property in the court below.\\n\\n1) A claim in a family non-contentious case is made by filing a petition for adjudication with the Family Court, and such petition may be made in writing or orally (Family Litigation Act, Article 36(1) and (2)). Meanwhile, the Civil Procedure Act provides that “a change in the relief sought shall be requested in writing” (Article 262(2)); however, case law has held that where a written submission in the form of a preparatory brief includes an intention to change the relief sought, it may be regarded as a change in the relief sought by way of writing (Supreme Court Decision 2008DA86232, rendered May 28, 2009), and that where the preparatory brief at first instance and the statement of relief sought on appeal and the grounds for appeal assert, in substance, that the starting date for delay damages should be advanced to the date of the tortious act, this should be regarded as an expansion of the relief sought (Supreme Court Decision 2009DA105062, rendered January 13, 2011).\\n\\n2) The judgment of first instance accepted the claim for divorce and, overlooking the effect of the withdrawal with respect to the portion of the claim for division of marital property, rendered a judgment ordering division of marital property. In the notice of appeal, the Plaintiff, premising that a claim for division of marital property was being made, expressed the intention to challenge the amount of division of marital property in the judgment of first instance and paid the corresponding court fee. The Plaintiff appeared at the first oral argument date in the court below and made a statement amending the relief sought on appeal to include the portion concerning division of marital property; thereafter, in the statement of grounds for appeal submitted by the Plaintiff’s counsel, arguments concerning division of marital property continued, and the Plaintiff’s counsel made multiple additional motions for evidence in order to prove the facts alleged in support of the portion concerning the claim for division of marital property.\\n\\n3) In this Court as well, the Plaintiff has clearly manifested the intention to maintain the claim for division of marital property by asserting not only in the statement of grounds for appeal but also in a written submission filed after the period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal that, so long as the divorce action is granted, division of marital property must be made.\\n\\nc. Therefore, even if the portion concerning the claim for division of marital property had been withdrawn and terminated at first instance, and even if the Plaintiff did not strictly comply with the manner prescribed by the Family Litigation Act for filing a petition for adjudication regarding division of marital property, insofar as there is room to regard the Plaintiff as having again filed a petition for adjudication regarding division of marital property in the court below, the court below should have clarified the amount claimed and the like, fixed the relief sought accordingly, and then proceeded with adjudication. Nevertheless, by declaring the termination of the litigation with respect to the portion concerning the claim for division of marital property on the sole ground that a written withdrawal of action had been submitted at first instance, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning a claim for division of marital property, thereby affecting the judgment. The grounds for appeal pointing this out are well founded.\\n\\n3. Concerning the remaining grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe court below, after issuing an order dismissing the Plaintiff’s application for recusal, concluded oral argument at the hearing date and, on the date of pronouncement, rendered the judgment of the court below, as stated in its reasoning, dismissing the Plaintiff’s claim for damages for mental suffering and designating the person with parental authority and the custodian, among other things.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no legal error in the court below’s measures and determination, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the application for recusal, violation of the rules of evidence with respect to fault-based conduct or damages for mental suffering, incomplete examination, misapprehension of the legal principles, violation of the rules of evidence with respect to the designation of the person with parental authority and the custodian, or incomplete examination.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the portion of the judgment below concerning the claim for division of marital property is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. The remainder of the appeal is dismissed. Accordingly, the judgment is rendered as set forth in the disposition, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

question: A's sole heir A lawfully filed a report of qualified acceptance and received an adjudication of acceptance. Thereafter, A completed the registration of establishment of a collateral mortgage over inherited property X real property in favor of his creditor B. Also, after the aforementioned registration of establishment of a collateral mortgage was completed, creditor C, who holds a loan claim against A, applied for a provisional seizure of X real property and completed the registration of provisional seizure. Meanwhile, D is a general creditor of A. Which of the following statements concerning this are all correct? (Each item is independent, and where there is disagreement, case law applies)
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2003DA63586]": "1. The Judgment of the Lower Court\\n\\nCiting the reasoning of the judgment of the first instance, the lower court found the facts as stated in the judgment, including that when Non-party 1, who owed the debts for the loan money, etc. stated in the judgment to the Plaintiff, died on June 29, 2001, the Defendants, being the heirs, filed a renunciation of inheritance with the Jeonju District Court on August 3, 2001 and received a ruling accepting the renunciation of inheritance on the 8th of the same month; that on April 2, 2002, the Defendants completed registration of ownership transfer in their names, based on inheritance, with respect to the farmland at issue, which is the inherited property, and on the same day completed registration of ownership transfer in the name of Non-party 2, based on a sale dated March 4, 2002; and then held that, when heirs, after renouncing inheritance, engage in the act of selling inherited property, such act constitutes wasteful dissipation of inherited property as prescribed in Civil Act Article 1026, item 3, and thus the heirs are deemed to have accepted the inheritance by simple acceptance, and accordingly held that the Defendants, as heirs of Non-party 1, have the obligation to repay Non-party 1’s debt to the Plaintiff.\\n\\nThe lower court further held that the farmland at issue was farmland supported under the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation and Farmland Management Fund Act, and that Non-party 1 purchased it from the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation on March 2, 2000 and completed registration of ownership transfer on the 8th of the same month, but agreed that it could not be resold to another person within 8 years without the consent of the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation; that the purchase price was to be repaid in equal installments over 20 years, and in order to secure the debt for the purchase price, a mortgage securing a maximum claim amount of 29,862,000 won was established in favor of the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation; that after Non-party 1 paid only one installment of the divided purchase price and died on June 29, 2001, and while auction proceedings were underway pursuant to the application of the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation, Non-party 2 expressed a desire to purchase the farmland at issue, the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation and Non-party 2 agreed to adopt the form in which Non-party 2 would, with the consent of the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation, purchase the farmland at issue from the heirs of Non-party 1, and that the purchase price would be fixed as the amount obtained by adding together Non-party 1’s unpaid purchase price, overdue interest, and auction application costs, and that Non-party 2 would pay such amount directly to the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation; that as the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation and Non-party 2 explained the above agreement to the Defendants and requested their cooperation, the Defendants prepared a sales contract concerning the farmland at issue for Non-party 2 on March 4, 2002; that Non-party 2 directly paid to the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation, which held the preferential right of repayment as the mortgagee of the farmland at issue, the full amount of the purchase price for the farmland at issue, fixed at 22,640,070 won, being the total of Non-party 1’s unpaid purchase price and overdue interest, on the following day, March 5, 2002; that thereafter the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation withdrew the application for auction and terminated the mortgage establishment contract; and that thereafter, on April 2, 2002, with respect to the farmland at issue, the registration of ownership transfer based on inheritance in the names of the Defendants was completed, followed in sequence by the registration of ownership transfer based on sale in the name of Non-party 2, and that the Defendants did not receive any of the purchase price for the farmland at issue and also did not newly grant the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation a preferential right of repayment, and therefore the Defendants’ act did not constitute wasteful dissipation of inherited property as prescribed in Civil Act Article 1026, item 3.\\n\\n2. The Judgment of This Court\\n\\nHowever, the above judgment of the lower court is difficult to accept.\\n\\nCivil Act Article 1026 provides that “if any of the following grounds exists, the heir shall be deemed to have made a simple acceptance,” and item 1 thereof provides for “where the heir has disposed of inherited property,” while item 3 provides for “where, after making a qualified acceptance or renunciation, the heir has concealed, wastefully dissipated, or intentionally omitted property from the inventory.” Civil Act Article 1026, item 1 applies only where the heir disposed of inherited property before making a qualified acceptance or renunciation; where the heir disposed of inherited property after making a qualified acceptance or renunciation, apart from the question of whether the heir may incur liability for damages to the inheritance creditor or other heirs as a result, the heir should be deemed to have made a simple acceptance only when such act constitutes wasteful dissipation of inherited property as prescribed in the above item 3; and further, “wasteful dissipation of inherited property” as prescribed in the above item 3 should be understood to mean an act that causes the inherited property to lose its economic value by consuming and destroying it without just cause.\\n\\nAs duly determined by the lower court, since the Defendants disposed of the farmland at issue after renouncing the inheritance, Civil Act Article 1026, item 1 has no room for application, and only the question of whether their act constitutes wasteful dissipation of inherited property as prescribed in item 3 of the same Article remains; if the Defendants disposed of the farmland at issue in the manner alleged by them, and the entire proceeds from such disposition were attributed to the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation, which held the preferential right of repayment, then, absent any other special circumstances, such act of the Defendants could not be deemed wasteful dissipation of inherited property.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court held that if the heirs sold inherited property after renouncing the inheritance, this immediately constitutes wasteful dissipation of inherited property as prescribed in Civil Act Article 1026, item 3, and furthermore concluded that even if the factual circumstances concerning the disposition of the farmland at issue and the attribution of the disposition proceeds were the same as alleged by the Defendants, the Defendants’ act still constituted wasteful dissipation of inherited property; thus, the lower judgment is deemed to contain an error of law in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning wasteful dissipation of inherited property as prescribed in Civil Act Article 1026, item 3 and in failing to conduct the necessary review, and such error of the lower court clearly affected the judgment.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the lower judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged, with the concurrence of all Justices, as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[2007DA77781]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Civil Act Article 1028 provides: “An heir may accept the inheritance on condition that the debts and legacies of the decedent be satisfied within the limit of the property to be acquired by inheritance.” Accordingly, when the court accepts a notice of qualified acceptance, the heir’s liability for the decedent’s debts is limited to the inherited property, and as a result, the inheritance creditor, absent special circumstances, may not enforce compulsory execution against the heir’s own property (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DA30968 dated November 14, 2003).\\n\\nHowever, because the Civil Act does not contain any provision that directly restricts the act of disposal of inherited property itself, except that, with respect to an heir who has made a qualified acceptance (hereinafter referred to as the “qualified accepter”), such heir is deemed to have made an unqualified acceptance if he or she concealed or misappropriated inherited property (Article 1026 item 3), it cannot be said that the above-mentioned effect of limiting liability arising from a qualified acceptance necessarily restricts the qualified accepter’s act of disposing of inherited property.\\n\\nIn addition, while the Civil Act does provide for the procedure by which a qualified accepter satisfies inheritance creditors, etc. from inherited property (Articles 1032 et seq.), it does not, by qualified acceptance alone, provide any rule granting inheritance creditors a preferential position over third parties who have acquired real rights in inherited property from the qualified accepter, and unlike the property separation system under Civil Act Article 1045 et seq., it does not provide any rule by which the fact that the inheritance property has been subject to qualified acceptance may be registered so as to be asserted against third parties.\\n\\nTherefore, the priority relation between a person who has acquired a security right, such as a mortgage, in inherited property from the qualified accepter and an inheritance creditor must be determined according to the general principles of the Civil Act, and it cannot be said that the inheritance creditor may assert a preferential position merely on the ground of the qualified acceptance. Nor is it appropriate to view this differently on the ground that the qualified accepter had borne the secured debt of such mortgage, etc. even before the commencement of inheritance.\\n\\n2. According to the facts established by the court below, when the deceased Nonparty 1 (hereinafter referred to as the “decedent”) died on November 7, 2002, among the decedent’s statutory heirs, the children renounced the inheritance, and the wife, Nonparty 2, filed a notice of qualified acceptance with the Seoul Family Court, attaching the list of inherited property stated in the attached schedule to the judgment of the court below, and that court accepted it on April 30, 2003; thereafter, on May 29, 2003, Nonparty 2 completed a registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of inheritance with respect to the first and second real properties in the above list of inherited property (hereinafter referred to as the “real properties at issue”), and on July 28, 2003, granted the Defendant a collateral mortgage with a maximum secured amount of KRW 10,000,000; meanwhile, the Plaintiff, who had lent money to the decedent, filed an action for a loan claim against Nonparty 2 upon the decedent’s death and, on April 27, 2004, obtained a judgment stating that “Nonparty 2 shall pay to the Plaintiff KRW 500,000,000 and delay damages thereon within the limit of the property inherited from the decedent” (Seoul Central District Court Decision 2003GAHAP3480 dated April 27, 2004), and based on the provisional execution declaration in the above judgment, filed an application for compulsory auction on September 16, 2004 with respect to the real properties at issue, etc. using KRW 200,000,000 of the judgment amount as the claim amount; accordingly, in the auction procedure conducted through compulsory auction, the auction court, at the distribution date on May 3, 2006, prepared a distribution schedule on the premise that the Defendant, as the mortgagee with respect to the real properties at issue, could assert a right to priority reimbursement in relation to the Plaintiff, who is an inheritance creditor, and that it would first distribute to the Defendant KRW 10,000,000, corresponding to the maximum secured amount of the above mortgage, out of the actual distributable amount, and distribute the remaining amount pro rata among the general creditors including the Plaintiff; and that the Plaintiff objected to the above distribution amount allocated to the Defendant at the said distribution date.\\n\\nIn light of the above facts and the legal principles discussed earlier, the Plaintiff, as an inheritance creditor, cannot assert a preferential position against the Defendant, who acquired a collateral mortgage from the qualified accepter, Nonparty 2, with respect to the real properties at issue.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below accepted the Plaintiff’s claim on the ground that the proceeds from the sale of the real properties at issue should be distributed preferentially to the Plaintiff, an inheritance creditor, and determined that the distribution schedule should be corrected as stated in its reasoning; the judgment of the court below thus contains an error that affected the judgment due to misapprehension of the law regarding qualified acceptance.\\n\\n3. Accordingly, the portion of the judgment of the court below concerning the Defendant is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and the judgment is rendered as follows. The opinions of the Justices participating in the case were unanimous, except for the dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran, Park Si-hwan, and Kim Neung-hwan.\\n\\n4. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim Young-ran, Park Si-hwan, and Kim Neung-hwan\\n\\na. When a notice of qualified acceptance by an heir is accepted, the heir succeeds to the comprehensive rights and obligations concerning the decedent’s property from the time inheritance commences (main sentence of Civil Act Article 1005), but since liability for the inherited debts is limited to the scope of the inherited property, the inheritance creditor may not enforce compulsory execution against the qualified accepter’s own property. The Civil Act provides that the list of inherited property must be attached to the notice of qualified acceptance (Article 1030); that the property rights and obligations of the qualified accepter vis-à-vis the decedent do not extinguish (Article 1031); that the qualified accepter, within 5 days from the date of qualified acceptance, must publicly announce to general inheritance creditors and legatees the fact of the qualified acceptance and that they must file their claims or receipt within a period of at least 2 months (Article 1032); that before the expiry of the announcement period, the satisfaction of inheritance claims may be refused (Article 1033); that after the expiry of that period, satisfaction from inherited property shall be made to creditors who filed within that period and creditors known to the qualified accepter, in proportion to the amount of each claim, provided that the rights of creditors with priority are not prejudiced (Article 1034); that thereafter legatees shall be satisfied (Article 1036); and that where it is necessary to sell all or part of the inherited property for such satisfaction, auction must be conducted pursuant to the Civil Execution Act (Article 1037). Therefore, the inherited property of the qualified accepter is the liable property for the claims of inheritance creditors and must be preferentially applied to satisfy those creditors, and those claims must be liquidated. Conversely, in terms of interpretation, it is equitable and consistent with the purpose of the qualified acceptance system to view that the qualified accepter’s personal creditors, unlike inheritance creditors, may not make compulsory execution against inherited property as the liable property for their claims. In this sense, since inheritance creditors cannot enforce compulsory execution against the qualified accepter’s own property, the qualified accepter’s personal creditors cannot, in priority to inheritance creditors, enforce compulsory execution against inherited property; thus, it should be said that inheritance creditors hold a preferential right over inherited property.\\n\\nb. Qualified acceptance merely limits liability for inherited debts to the scope of inherited property; it does not itself exclude or limit the succession to the comprehensive rights and obligations concerning inherited property. Accordingly, where the qualified accepter disposes of inherited property and thereby loses ownership before the inheritance creditor’s compulsory execution commences, apart from whether the inheritance creditor may recover that property as the qualified accepter’s liable property by means such as an action to revoke a fraudulent act and then make it the object of compulsory execution, the inheritance creditor may not exercise rights analogous to the avoidance right or the right of separate satisfaction in bankruptcy proceedings. In this sense, the qualified accepter’s disposition of inherited property is valid, and the inheritance creditor may not trace and enforce compulsory execution against that property.\\n\\nHowever, where the qualified accepter has established a security right, etc. on inherited property for his or her own obligations, and thus still retains ownership of the inherited property so that the inheritance creditor may enforce compulsory execution against that property, the inheritance creditor’s preferential right over that inherited property must be regarded as remaining intact. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\nFirst, even if a security right, etc. has been established in that manner, the property remains inherited property and thus becomes the qualified accepter’s liable property, so the inheritance creditor may enforce compulsory execution against it; and to the extent that such compulsory execution is permitted, it is consistent with the purpose of the qualified acceptance system to regard the inheritance creditor’s preferential right as not being lost but remaining intact.\\n\\nIn addition, because the foregoing reasoning and legal principle that the qualified accepter’s personal creditors may not enforce compulsory execution against inherited property are correct, it is also balanced to view that a person who has acquired a security right from the qualified accepter may not exercise the security right in priority to the inheritance creditor. Since compulsory execution and the exercise of a security right differ only in the method of obtaining satisfaction of the claim, if inherited property cannot become liable property in relation to the qualified accepter’s personal creditors, then, as a matter of principle, it should likewise not become liable property in relation to those among such personal creditors who have been granted a security right, etc. Moreover, the inheritance creditor’s preferential right in the sense discussed above arises immediately upon acceptance of the notice of qualified acceptance. There is no reason, and no basis, for such previously arising preferential right of the inheritance creditor to be extinguished merely because the qualified accepter later establishes a security right, etc. over inherited property.\\n\\nOn the other hand, under the current registration practice, the fact of qualified acceptance does not appear in the register, but that does not mean that the inheritance creditor’s preferential right must necessarily be denied. Under our legal system, which does not recognize the public faith of the register, the entries in the register do not necessarily disclose the substantive legal relationship as it is, and the phenomenon in which the two diverge cannot be completely eliminated. Among substantive-law preferential rights, there are rights that are not recorded in the register, such as the right to priority payment of wage claims under the Labor Standards Act. Therefore, in cases of qualified acceptance, it cannot be said to be unfamiliar or alien to our legal system to regard the inheritance creditor’s preferential right, though unregistered, as remaining intact in relation to persons who have been granted a security right, etc. by the qualified accepter. Meanwhile, since inherited property had originally been registered in the name of the decedent and the registration of a security right, etc. by the qualified accepter becomes possible only after registration of inheritance has been completed, it may also be viewed that the inheritance creditor’s preferential right arising from qualified acceptance is at least indirectly publicized. When a personal creditor of the heir acquires a security right, etc. over real property whose title remains registered in the decedent’s name or over which inheritance registration has been completed, there is a duty of care to confirm whether the heir has made a qualified acceptance or renounced the inheritance, and there is room to say that there is no reason or need to protect one who neglects such duty.\\n\\nAnd although Civil Act Article 1049 provides that “as to real property that is inheritance property, separation of property may not be asserted against third parties unless it is registered,” this is a provision concerning the separation of property, a system separate from qualified acceptance, and in the separation of property system, the inheritance creditor’s preferential right in the sense discussed above is not recognized; therefore, this provision cannot be the basis for viewing that, merely because the fact of qualified acceptance is not registered, the inheritance creditor’s preferential right cannot remain intact.\\n\\nTo deny the inheritance creditor’s preferential right on the ground that the fact of qualified acceptance is not entered in the register and to view that a person who acquired a security right from the qualified accepter has priority is to invert the principal and the subordinate. It is true that the Civil Act, while presupposing as a matter of course the legal principle that the qualified accepter’s personal creditors may not enforce compulsory execution against inherited property in priority to inheritance creditors, did not separately prescribe any method of public notice or procedure, such as entering the fact of qualified acceptance in the register, and thus failed to provide a means of ensuring transactional safety; this constitutes a legislative omission. However, that does not make the sacrifice of the inheritance creditor’s preferential right a proper solution. Rather, it would be appropriate to strengthen the method of public notice, for example by providing in the Rules of Family Litigation, etc., that when the family court renders a ruling accepting a notice of qualified acceptance, it shall also request registration of the fact of qualified acceptance or of the acceptance ruling with respect to the real property listed in the schedule attached to the notice, and shall have the registrar record such fact, thereby seeking protection for those who relied on the registration.\\n\\nFurthermore, Civil Act Article 1026 item 3 provides that “where an heir conceals or misappropriates inherited property after making a qualified acceptance,” the heir shall be deemed to have made an unqualified acceptance, but even if a qualified accepter’s establishment of a security right, etc. over inherited property falls within this provision, the inheritance creditor is not thereby fully remedied. It is entirely conceivable that the qualified accepter has little or no own property. In addition, in cases of qualified acceptance, the issue of priority between the inheritance creditor and a person who acquired a security right, etc. from the qualified accepter arises only where, as in this case, the inheritance creditor has already obtained an execution title by filing an action to enforce the inherited debt against the qualified accepter and receiving a final judgment in favor or a judgment in favor with a declaration of provisional execution (hereinafter referred to as a “final judgment in favor, etc.”). Otherwise, the status of inheritance creditor would not be confirmed. However, because the qualified accepter’s liability for inherited debts is limited to inherited property and the inheritance creditor may not enforce compulsory execution against the qualified accepter’s own property, the execution title obtained by the inheritance creditor against the qualified accepter, namely the final judgment in favor, etc., must expressly state in its operative part that compulsory execution may be made only within the limit of inherited property (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2003DA30968 dated November 14, 2003, cited by the majority opinion). As a result, even if a circumstance constituting statutory unqualified acceptance, as discussed above, arises subsequently, the judgment limiting the property subject to compulsory execution by the inheritance creditor to the scope of inherited property remains effective as it is, and the inheritance creditor does not thereby immediately enjoy the legal effect of the above-mentioned statutory unqualified acceptance. Therefore, it is not proper to deny the inheritance creditor’s preferential right over the secured creditor, etc. on the basis of the provision concerning such statutory unqualified acceptance.\\n\\nNevertheless, the majority opinion, which views that the preferential right of the inheritance creditor in the sense discussed above is lost by the registration of a security right, etc. for the qualified accepter’s own obligations, is ultimately nothing more than an attempt to protect unilaterally, at the expense of the inheritance creditor, the personal creditor who acquired a security right, etc. in inherited property from the qualified accepter. This would empty the qualified acceptance system of its substance and impair the meaning of its institutional existence, and thus cannot be accepted.\\n\\nc. In this case, the Plaintiff is an inheritance creditor who obtained a judgment in favor with a declaration of provisional execution ordering Nonparty 2, the qualified accepter, to perform the inherited debt within the limit of inherited property, and the Defendant is a person who received a collateral mortgage from the above Nonparty 2 with respect to her own obligations; therefore, according to the legal principle discussed above, the Plaintiff should be deemed to have a preferential right over the Defendant. The measure taken by the court below, in the same vein, to order correction of the distribution schedule so that the distribution amount to the Defendant be distributed to the Plaintiff is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the law, as asserted by the Defendant in the grounds of appeal. Therefore, the Defendant’s appeal should be dismissed.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I do not concur with the majority opinion.\\n\\n5. Supplementary Opinion of Justices Yang Chang-soo and Min Il-young to the Majority Opinion\\n\\na. The dissenting opinion states that the majority opinion is difficult to accept because, by denying the inheritance creditor’s preferential right through the registration of a security right, etc. for the qualified accepter’s own obligations, it is merely attempting to protect unilaterally, at the expense of the inheritance creditor, the personal creditor who acquired a security right, etc. in inherited property from the qualified accepter, thereby emptying the qualified acceptance system of its substance and impairing the meaning of its institutional existence.\\n\\nIn response, I would like to supplement the majority opinion as follows regarding the grounds advanced by the dissenting opinion.\\n\\nb. First, the dissenting opinion asserts that, upon an heir’s qualified acceptance, inherited property becomes the liable property for the inheritance creditor’s claims and is preferentially satisfied and liquidated to the inheritance creditor pursuant to Civil Act Article 1030 et seq.; and that, in balance with the fact that the inheritance creditor cannot enforce compulsory execution against the qualified accepter’s own property, the qualified accepter’s personal creditors should also be deemed unable to enforce compulsory execution against inherited property; therefore, the inheritance creditor has a preferential right over inherited property.\\n\\nHowever, the fact that, by qualified acceptance, the inheritance creditor takes priority over the qualified accepter’s personal creditors with respect to inherited property is merely a result derived from the view that, since both the qualified accepter’s personal creditors and the inheritance creditor are general creditors, it is just from the standpoint of equity that the inheritance creditor may not enforce compulsory execution against the qualified accepter’s own property and the qualified accepter’s personal creditors may not enforce compulsory execution against inherited property, respectively; and from the limitation on the property subject to execution or the separation of liable property in this sense, it cannot be said that a “right that is preferential erga omnes” over inherited property logically and necessarily follows directly for the inheritance creditor.\\n\\nIf the Civil Act, as the dissenting opinion suggests, had intended to completely separate inherited property from the qualified accepter’s own property and to grant the inheritance creditor a preferential right over inherited property, it should have provided an express direct statutory provision to that effect, or at least should have prepared a provision restricting the qualified accepter’s acts of disposal or a legal means by which the inheritance creditor could deny the effect of such acts of disposal (such as the avoidance right or the right of separate satisfaction in bankruptcy proceedings).\\n\\nHowever, it is clear that no such provision exists in the Civil Act, and the Civil Act merely seeks to protect the inheritance creditor to the extent of imposing on the qualified accepter the disadvantage of being deemed to have made an unqualified acceptance due to his or her improper reduction of property (Article 1026 item 3), or recognizing liability for damages arising from improper procedures for satisfaction, etc. (Article 1038). This shows the institutional character of our Civil Act’s qualified acceptance system: its original purpose is to protect the heir, by preventing the heir from being ruined by inheriting the decedent’s debts without limit, rather than to protect the inheritance creditor. The Supreme Court’s taking a limited stance toward the protection of inheritance creditors by allowing, in Supreme Court Decision 2006DA23138 dated October 13, 2006, an action for objection to a claim to be brought against an heir after a judgment in favor had already been rendered and finalized, despite the heir’s failure to raise a defense of qualified acceptance in an action by an inheritance creditor for performance against the heir, may also be understood in this context.\\n\\nUltimately, the dissenting opinion goes beyond the original purpose of the qualified acceptance system and, overemphasizing the protection of inheritance creditors, attempts to recognize, by interpretation, in qualified acceptance, the same level of separation and independence effect of property as is recognized in bankruptcy proceedings concerning inherited property (Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act Articles 299 and 438, etc.), and from that to derive for inheritance creditors a preferential right over inherited property even erga omnes; this does not harmonize with the current provisions of the Civil Act regarding qualified acceptance or with the ideology of the system.\\n\\nc. The dissenting opinion also recognizes the above-mentioned preferential right of the inheritance creditor, but distinguishes between the case where the qualified accepter disposes of inherited property and loses ownership before the inheritance creditor’s compulsory execution commences, and the case where the qualified accepter establishes a security right, etc., recognizing tracing only in the latter and thereby preserving the inheritance creditor’s preferential position, while denying it in the former.\\n\\nHowever, the case of transfer in which the qualified accepter loses ownership of inherited property and the case of establishing a mortgage, where ownership is not lost, are both fundamentally identical as acts of disposal, notwithstanding only the difference as to whether ownership is transferred; moreover, the dissenting opinion’s discriminatory treatment is, from the standpoint of reduction of inherited property, a logic that positively acknowledges complete acquisition of rights by the transferee in the case of transfer, which is an act of disposal deserving a more negative evaluation, while restricting the exercise of rights by a person who acquired the lesser right of a security right, thereby falling into a kind of evaluative contradiction in the degree of denial of negative consequences. This cannot be easily explained merely on the ground that the act of establishing a security right is a dispositional act in which the possibility of compulsory execution by the inheritance creditor still remains.\\n\\nIn addition, the dissenting opinion states that inherited property could not originally be liable property vis-à-vis the qualified accepter’s personal creditors, and that the compulsory execution by general creditors and the exercise of security rights by secured creditors are merely differences in the method of obtaining satisfaction of claims; however, since the acquisition of a security right in inherited property involves the qualified accepter’s dispositional act, it cannot necessarily be evaluated on the same plane as general creditors to whom no such act is involved.\\n\\nd. Meanwhile, although the Civil Act requires the qualified accepter to publicly announce, within 5 days from the date of qualified acceptance, to general inheritance creditors and legatees the fact of the qualified acceptance and that they must file their claims or receipt within a period of at least 2 months (Article 1032), it does not require any method of public notice regarding the fact of qualified acceptance other than that, and in particular, under the current legal system, there is no means by which the fact of qualified acceptance may be registered in the register, which is the principal method of public notice for real property.\\n\\nIn a situation where the means of public notice are extremely weak in this manner, deriving by interpretation a right that is preferential erga omnes is a result that greatly harms transactional safety, and it is a proper attitude to avoid such a result as much as possible. In particular, with respect to real property, which is a major object of transactions in general commercial dealings, one must be very cautious in recognizing a preferential right unless otherwise provided by law. It is well known that, as mentioned in the dissenting opinion, wage claims under the Labor Standards Act and the priority right of a small tenant under the Housing Lease Protection Act are all based on written statutes.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion states that, because the qualified accepter can establish a security right, etc. over inherited property only after inheritance registration has been completed, the counterparty in the transaction can confirm the inheritance registration in that process and thus an indirect public-notice function may be expected, and that a person who failed to confirm the fact of qualified acceptance may have failed to discharge the duty of care required, leaving room to deny the need for protection. However, under our inheritance law system, which makes unqualified acceptance the default form of inheritance, it would be excessive to expect an indirect public-notice function of the fact of qualified acceptance through inheritance registration or to impose on the counterparty a duty of care to verify the fact of qualified acceptance.\\n\\nIn this connection, it is necessary to note that the Civil Act, in the property separation system, provides a rule like Article 1049 regarding the opposability of registration, while remaining silent on qualified acceptance. Even where property has been separated by order of the court through prescribed procedures, it cannot be asserted against third parties without registration; a fortiori, in the case of qualified acceptance, where the fact is not registered at all, one cannot recognize for the inheritance creditor a preferential position over inherited property that can be asserted against third parties.\\n\\ne. The dissenting opinion states that the absence of public-notice methods or procedures, such as the fact that qualified acceptance is not entered in the register, should be remedied as such in order to secure transactional safety, and that it inverts the principal and the subordinate to deny, as in the majority opinion, the institutionally granted preferential right of the inheritance creditor and to view that the person who acquired a security right from the qualified accepter has priority, on the ground of such legislative or institutional deficiency.\\n\\nOf course, as the dissenting opinion points out, in the present situation where the methods or procedures for public notice regarding the fact of qualified acceptance have not been properly organized, the need to protect transactional safety is indeed the main reason from the majority opinion’s standpoint for being unable to agree with the interpretation that grants the inheritance creditor a preferential right over inherited property. Likewise, there can be no theoretical objection to the need for legislative supplementation to enhance the public-notice function of the qualified acceptance system, as the dissenting opinion argues.\\n\\nHowever, before such public-notice methods are perfected, the essence of legal interpretation regarding the qualified acceptance system is to seek a legal principle that can harmonize, under the current institutional reality, both the protection of the inheritance creditor’s legitimate interests and consideration for transactional safety in relation to the qualified accepter’s acts of disposal. Moreover, if the inheritance creditor properly utilizes the Civil Act’s property separation system or the bankruptcy proceedings under the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act with respect to inherited property, it may be said that the result feared by the dissenting opinion, namely the qualified accepter’s personal creditors enjoying unexpected benefits from inherited property that had not been contemplated as liable property, can be appropriately prevented.\\n\\nIn light of these points, the attempt to derive by interpretation a preferential right not provided by law and not appearing at all in the register is rather not easily harmonized with our legal system, which in principle requires public notice for any assertion erga omnes of a right or effect. Therefore, I cannot agree with the accusation that the majority opinion’s view—that the order or priority relationship of rights should be determined according to the general principles of the Civil Act—is an inversion of the principal and the subordinate.\\n\\nf. The dissenting opinion states that, even if the qualified accepter’s improper reduction of property falls within the statutory unqualified acceptance ground under Civil Act Article 1026 item 3, there may well be cases where the qualified accepter has little or no own property, and if the operative part of the execution title obtained by the inheritance creditor against the qualified accepter, such as a final judgment in favor, expressly states that compulsory execution may be made only within the limit of inherited property, then the inheritance creditor cannot immediately enjoy the effect of the above statutory unqualified acceptance, and thus cannot be fully remedied.\\n\\nHowever, since a heir’s qualified acceptance is usually made because inherited debts are excessive and there is a need to protect his or her own property from them, it would generally benefit the inheritance creditor if the heir were deemed to have made an unqualified acceptance and the creditor could exercise rights even against the qualified accepter’s own property. In addition, the constraints in the execution title indicated by the dissenting opinion concern only a limited sphere in which the problem arises (outside the situation presented by the dissenting opinion, if a circumstance corresponding to statutory unqualified acceptance has already arisen at the litigation stage, the issue will naturally be filtered out through the parties’ arguments within that procedure); in the situation envisioned by the dissenting opinion, the inheritance creditor would ultimately still bear procedural burdens such as having to file a separate action against the qualified accepter to obtain an unconditional judgment for performance as to liable property, but this is merely an inevitable consequence when the ground for statutory unqualified acceptance arises only after the judgment, and such procedural burden cannot be said to constitute an essential obstacle to the inheritance creditor’s exercise of rights under unqualified acceptance.\\n\\ng. In conclusion, the dissenting opinion is one that, although liability of the heir is limited by qualified acceptance, still seeks by interpretation to recognize for the inheritance creditor a preferential right over the person who acquired a security right from the qualified accepter with respect to inherited property, despite the fact that such qualified acceptance does not restrict the qualified accepter’s acts of disposal nor completely separate inherited property from the qualified accepter’s own property. This, first of all, fails to sufficiently consider the institutional significance that our Civil Act’s qualified acceptance system is fundamentally designed to protect the heir rather than the inheritance creditor; and furthermore, it conflicts with the basic position of our Civil Act, which in situations involving sharp conflicts of interest where priority is at issue among interested parties, such as changes in real rights in real property or rights to priority reimbursement, in principle resolves the issue by means of public notice external to the parties, such as registration.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I cannot agree with the dissenting opinion."}

{"[2015DA250574]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Civil Act Article 1028 provides, “An heir may accept the inheritance on the condition that the debts and legacies of the decedent be paid within the limit of the property to be acquired by inheritance.” If an heir files a notice of limited acceptance pursuant to the above provision, the liability of the limited acceptor for the decedent’s debts is limited to the inherited property, and as a result, absent special circumstances, an inheritance creditor may not execute compulsorily against the heir’s own property and may obtain satisfaction of its claim only from the inherited property.\\n\\nWhere a personal creditor of the limited acceptor, who is not an inheritance creditor, has acquired a security interest such as a mortgage in respect of inherited property, the priority relationship between the creditor who acquired that security interest and the inheritance creditor must be governed by the general principles of the Civil Act, and the inheritance creditor may not assert a priority position (see Supreme Court en banc decision rendered on March 18, 2010, 2007DA77781). However, absent circumstances such as the acquisition of a security interest in the inherited property as above, it accords with the principle of equity and the purpose of the limited acceptance system to regard the personal creditor of the limited acceptor as unable, while the inheritance creditor has not obtained satisfaction of its claim from the inherited property, to treat the inherited property as the responsible property for the personal claim and thereby enforce compulsory execution against it; and the same would apply even where the limited acceptor’s personal debt is a tax debt, so long as it does not concern a tax or surcharge imposed on the inherited property itself, that is, a tax on the property in question.\\n\\n2. According to the reasons stated in the first-instance judgment cited by the court below and the evidence lawfully admitted, the following facts may be found.\\n\\nA. The deceased Nonparty 1 died on September 5, 2002. Among the heirs, all except Nonparty 2 renounced the inheritance, and Nonparty 2 filed a notice of limited acceptance, which was accepted.\\n\\nB. The Plaintiff, as a creditor of the deceased, in a lawsuit brought against Nonparty 2, obtained on May 2, 2014, a decision recommending settlement to the effect that “Nonparty 2 shall, within the scope of the property inherited from the deceased, pay to the Plaintiff 81,138,332 won and, out of that amount, with respect to 31,544,723 won, pay each amount calculated at the annual rate of 12% from February 25, 2014 to March 29, 2014, and at the annual rate of 20% from the following day until the day of full payment,” and this became final around that time.\\n\\nC. The Plaintiff, by subrogation, applied for inheritance registration in the name of Nonparty 2 with respect to real properties that had been owned by the deceased, namely 2,165㎡ of field at Gyeongbuk Chilgok-gun (Address 1 omitted) and 2,380㎡ of forest land at (Address 2 omitted), etc., and completed the ownership transfer registration on September 1, 2014; thereafter, on September 15, 2014, the Plaintiff applied for compulsory auction against the above real properties based on the above decision recommending settlement.\\n\\nD. The Defendant, as a tax creditor, including for value-added tax, against Nonparty 2, made a demand for distribution in the above compulsory auction proceedings; however, the relevant tax is not a tax imposed on the inherited real property itself, that is, a tax on the property in question.\\n\\nE. The auction court prepared a distribution schedule in which, out of the amount to be distributed of 88,588,000 won, 30,000,000 won would be distributed in first priority to Nonparty 3, the mortgagee, and 58,588,000 won would be distributed in second priority to the Defendant ahead of the Plaintiff; the Plaintiff, on the date for distribution on April 2, 2015, stated an objection to the entirety of the amount distributed to the Defendant, and then filed the present action to object to the distribution.\\n\\n3. Examining these factual circumstances in light of the legal principles set forth above, the sale proceeds of the above real properties, which constitute inherited property, should be distributed in priority to the Plaintiff, who is an inheritance creditor, over the Defendant, who is a personal creditor of Nonparty 2, the limited acceptor, and who has not acquired a security interest such as a mortgage in respect of the above real properties from him; and the same applies even if the Defendant is a tax creditor.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below held, contrary to the above, that the auction court’s action of distributing to the Defendant in priority to the Plaintiff was lawful, and therefore there is error in the court below’s determination that affected the judgment by misapprehending the law on limited acceptance. The assertion in the grounds of appeal pointing out this point is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as stated in the disposition."}

question:
A died leaving X real property as his sole asset, and he had a legitimate child B born during his marriage to his deceased wife. After B inherited X real property solely, B sold it to C, a third party, and completed registration of transfer of ownership. Thereafter, the child born out of wedlock of A filed an action for acknowledgment of paternity and obtained a final and conclusive judgment in his favor. Which of the following statements are incorrect? (Each proposition is independent, and where there is dispute, the case law applies.)

(a). The child born out of wedlock must file an action for acknowledgment of paternity against the prosecutor within 2 years from the date on which he learned of A's death, and the "date on which he learned of the death," which is the starting point of the limitation period for filing the action, means that, in addition to knowing the objective fact of A's death, he must also know that A and the child born out of wedlock are in a parent-child relationship by blood. 
(b). Since C definitively acquires ownership of X real property, the child born out of wedlock may only bring a claim against B for payment of an amount corresponding to his share of inheritance in respect of X real property within 3 years from the date on which the judgment recognizing paternity became final and conclusive. 
(c). If B has acquired any fruits arising from X real property that has already been disposed of, those fruits constitute unjust enrichment vis-à-vis the acknowledged child A.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DA83796]": "1. Even a person who, after the commencement of inheritance, is acknowledged or becomes a co-heir by a judgment becoming final and conclusive may, if the inherited property has not yet been partitioned or disposed of, naturally participate in the partition together with the other co-heirs; however, where the other co-heirs have already partitioned or disposed of the inherited property before the acknowledgment, the proviso to Article 860 of the Civil Act, which limits the retroactive effect of acknowledgment, applies, and the subsequently acknowledged person cannot deny the effect of the partition or other dispositions made by the other co-heirs. Accordingly, Article 1014 of the Civil Act is intended to rationally adjust the interests of the acknowledged person and the existing legal relationships by recognizing, in such a case, the right of the acknowledged person to demand payment from the other co-heirs of an amount equivalent to his or her inheritance share, in lieu of a new partition of the inherited property (see Supreme Court Decision 93DA12 rendered on August 24, 1993, etc.).\\n\\nTherefore, inherited property that has already been partitioned or disposed of by the co-heirs before the acknowledgment, in accordance with the limitation on the retroactive effect of acknowledgment prescribed by the proviso to Article 860 of the Civil Act, becomes definitively vested in ownership in the co-heir who received it in the partition or in the person who acquired it through the disposition of the co-heirs; and since a person who has acquired ownership of inherited property also has, pursuant to Article 102 of the Civil Act, the power to receive its fruits, the acquisition by a co-heir who partitioned the inherited property before acknowledgment of the fruits arising from the inherited property so partitioned cannot be said to constitute unjust enrichment in relation to the acknowledged person.\\n\\nOn the same purport, the court below determined that, with respect to shares in unlisted companies and real property among the inherited property of the deceased (name omitted), which the Defendants had already partitioned before the judgment of acknowledgment in favor of the Plaintiff became final and conclusive, the dividends and income equivalent to rent arising after the commencement of inheritance were all fruits of the inherited property, and that the acquisition thereof by the co-heirs did not constitute unjust enrichment; and, in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, such determination by the court below is correct, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality such as a misapprehension of the purport and relationship of the proviso to Article 860 and Article 1014 of the Civil Act, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning unjust enrichment, or a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the status of the other co-heir who partitioned the inherited property before acknowledgment was made to the acknowledged person.\\n\\n2. As Article 860 of the Civil Act provides in its main text that “acknowledgment shall have retroactive effect from the time of the child’s birth,” but in its proviso limits the retroactive effect of acknowledgment by providing that “however, it shall not prejudice the rights acquired by a third person,” the other co-heirs who have already partitioned the inherited property before acknowledgment of the acknowledged person definitively acquire ownership of the inherited property so partitioned pursuant to the above proviso, and, furthermore, as the owners of the inherited property so partitioned, they also acquire the right to receive the fruits arising therefrom; consequently, it cannot be said to be contrary to equity and justice to view that the acknowledged person cannot claim, as unjust enrichment, return of the amount equivalent to the portion corresponding to his or her inheritance share among the fruits arising from inherited property already partitioned and allotted to the other co-heirs before acknowledgment, on the ground that such a position would unfairly treat the rights of the acknowledged person under the retroactive effect of acknowledgment to his or her disadvantage. Accordingly, the ground of appeal on this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the panel of Justices."}

{"[2006DA83796]": "1. Even a person who becomes a co-heir by being acknowledged after the commencement of inheritance or by a final judgment may, if the inherited property has not yet been partitioned or disposed of, naturally participate in partition together with the other co-heirs; however, where, before the acknowledgment, the other co-heirs have already partitioned or disposed of the inherited property, the proviso to Civil Act Article 860, which limits the retroactive effect of acknowledgment, applies, and the person acknowledged thereafter cannot deny the effect of the partition or other disposition by the other co-heirs, with the result that Civil Act Article 1014, in such a case, allows the person acknowledged to claim against the other co-heirs payment of an amount corresponding to his or her inheritance share, thereby recognizing a right in lieu of a new partition of the inherited property, and thus its purpose is to reasonably adjust the interests of the person acknowledged and the existing legal relationships (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 93DA12, rendered on Aug. 24, 1993).\\nAccordingly, inherited property that has already been partitioned or disposed of by the co-heirs before acknowledgment becomes definitively vested in ownership, pursuant to the limitation on the retroactive effect of acknowledgment provided in the proviso to Civil Act Article 860, in the co-heir who received the partition or the person who acquired it through the disposition act of the co-heirs, and since a person who acquires ownership of inherited property also has the power to receive the fruits thereof under Civil Act Article 102, it cannot be said that, as between such person and the person acknowledged, the co-heir who partitioned the inherited property before acknowledgment acquires fruits generated from the inherited property so partitioned in a manner constituting unjust enrichment.\\nThe court below, on the same purport, held that, with respect to the shares of unlisted companies and real property among the inherited property of the deceased (name omitted) that the Defendants had already partitioned before the acknowledgment judgment against the Plaintiff became final, the dividends and rental-equivalent income generated after the commencement of inheritance were all fruits of the inherited property, and that the co-heirs’ acquisition thereof did not constitute unjust enrichment; and, in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, this determination by the court below is correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as an error of law regarding the respective purport and relationship of the proviso to Civil Act Article 860 and Article 1014, an error of law regarding unjust enrichment, or an error of law regarding the status of another co-heir who partitioned the inherited property before acknowledgment of the person acknowledged, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Since Civil Act Article 860 provides in its main text that “acknowledgment shall take effect retroactively from the time of the person’s birth,” but in its proviso stipulates that “however, it shall not prejudice the rights acquired by a third party,” thereby limiting the retroactive effect of acknowledgment, the other co-heirs who had already partitioned the inherited property before acknowledgment of the person acknowledged acquire definitively, pursuant to the said proviso, ownership of the inherited property so partitioned, and further, as owners of the inherited property so partitioned, they also acquire the right to receive the fruits arising therefrom; accordingly, it cannot be said to be contrary to equity and justice to view that the person acknowledged cannot claim return as unjust enrichment of an amount equivalent to the value of the portion corresponding to his or her inheritance share among the fruits generated from the inherited property already partitioned to the other co-heirs before acknowledgment, and the argument in the grounds of appeal on this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and judgment is rendered as stated in the Disposition in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2014MEU4871]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nArticles 864 and 865, paragraph (2) of the Civil Act provide that, with respect to an action for acknowledgment and an action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a parent-child relationship (hereinafter referred to as “actions for acknowledgment, etc.”), where one of the parties has died, the action may be brought against the Prosecutor, and prescribe a filing period by providing that such action shall be brought within 2 years from the day on which the death was known.\\n\\nThe reason a filing period is prescribed for actions for acknowledgment, etc. is that it harmonizes the interests of a person who seeks to conform the parent-child relationship to the truth with the interests of a person who seeks legal stability through the prompt determination of the parent-child relationship. Considering, among other things, (1) the fact that, upon the death of a party, inheritance commences at the same time and new legal relationships concerning status and property are formed, so that if an action for acknowledgment, etc. is permitted after a long lapse of time, the legal relationships formed through inheritance may be rendered unstable, and (2) the fact that, if the time when one learned of the existence or nonexistence of a parent-child relationship were taken as the starting point of the filing period, the time asserted by the interested person would in effect become the starting point of the filing period, making it difficult to realize the purpose of setting such a period, it is reasonable to interpret that the “day on which the death was known,” which serves as the starting point of the filing period in actions for acknowledgment, etc., means knowledge of the objective fact of death, and that it is not necessary to know the fact that one has a parent-child relationship with the deceased as well.\\n\\nThe lower court, based on the evidence, found that (1) the deceased Non-Party 1 died on 1999. 7. 13., that the Plaintiff knew around that time that the deceased Non-Party 1 had died, and that the instant action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a parent-child relationship, brought by the Plaintiff against the Prosecutor alleging that no parent-child relationship existed between the Plaintiff and the deceased Non-Party 1, was filed on 2013. 8. 1., which was more than 2 years after the day on which the Plaintiff knew of the death of the deceased Non-Party 1; and, after determining that the instant action for confirmation of the nonexistence of a parent-child relationship was brought after the filing period had elapsed and was therefore unlawful, it further found that (2) the deceased Non-Party 2 died on 1952. 10. 15., that the Plaintiff knew on 1970. 6. 25. that the deceased Non-Party 2 had died, and that the instant action for acknowledgment, brought by the Plaintiff against the Prosecutor seeking acknowledgment that the Plaintiff was the natural child of the deceased Non-Party 2, was filed on 2013. 8. 1., which was more than 2 years after the day on which the Plaintiff knew of the death of the deceased Non-Party 2;
