and, after determining that the instant action for acknowledgment was likewise brought after the filing period had elapsed and was therefore unlawful.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the above determinations by the lower court are correct, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in finding facts in violation of the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, nor any error in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the starting point of the filing period in actions for acknowledgment, etc.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are to be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[76MEU55]": "The Court decides the grounds of appeal filed by counsel for the Defendant(s).\\n\\n1. Under the provisions of Article 982(2), which are applied mutatis mutandis pursuant to Article 999 of the Civil Code, the hereditary recovery claim extinguishes when 3 years have elapsed from the day on which the infringement became known; the phrase “the day on which the infringement became known” in that provision means that if 3 years have elapsed from the day on which the person having the hereditary recovery claim became aware of the infringement, that claim is extinguished. Therefore, even if a person without a hereditary recovery claim became aware of the fact of infringement, regardless thereof, it must be deemed that the infringement became known on the date on which the judgment in the recognition proceeding, by which the hereditary recovery claim was acquired, became final on 1973.1.5, and the commencement date of the above exclusion period cannot be construed differently on the ground that the effect of recognition retroacts. Accordingly, the court below’s disposition, which was made to that effect, is lawful, and the argument is without merit.\\n\\n2. As to point 2, since the execution date of the undertaking document, Exhibit B No. 1, referred to in the argument is 1973.7.19, and the claimants can be seen from the relevant evidentiary materials expressly indicated by the court below to have been reported and entered in the family register on 1973.1.9 by virtue of the finality of the recognition judgment dated 1973.1.5, it is clear that the person vested with parental authority over the respondents at the time of execution of the undertaking in this case was Non-Party 1, the stepmother, pursuant to Article 909(2) of the Civil Code, and there are no materials indicating that there was any reason why that person could not exercise parental authority. Therefore, the argument that the original judgment erred in its legal doctrine concerning the legal representative or that there was an incomplete hearing lacks merit.\\n\\n3. As to point 3, since the agreement stated in the undertaking document (Exhibit B No. 1) pointed out in the argument was made by Non-Party 2, who had no authority whatsoever, it cannot be regarded as having been ratified merely because Non-Party 2 was later appointed as the special representative of the claimants and because the claimants and the said Non-Party 2 were living together in the inn in which they acquired possession pursuant to the above agreement. Therefore, the original judgment, which determined to that effect, is proper, and the argument is without merit.\\n\\n4. Pursuant to Article 1014 of the Civil Code, where a person who has become a co-heir by recognition or by the finality of a judgment after the commencement of inheritance claims partition of the inherited property, if the other co-heir has already made partition or other disposition, it is only prescribed that such person has the right to demand payment of an amount corresponding to the inherited share; there is no basis for construing, as the argument contends, that there is a duty to comply therewith only within the extent that benefits remain in existence. Accordingly, the argument that the court below erred by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the scope of recovery of inheritance or by failing to conduct a hearing is without merit.\\n\\n5. According to the court below’s judgment, it determined to the effect that the claimants did not make the agreement as stated in Exhibit B No. 1, as explained in point 2 above, and thus it must be said that, whether as a claim for recovery of inheritance rights or as a share right by inheritance, the claimants did not waive any right concerning inheritance. Accordingly, the argument that the original judgment contains an illegal omission of determination as alleged is without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, the Court renders judgment as stated in the disposition."}

question:
A died in a traffic accident, and A's heirs are the children B and C. At the time of A's death, A owned X real property as his sole asset. Which of the following statements are correct? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law applies)

(a) If B, without an agreement on the division of the inherited estate with C, has arbitrarily completed a registration of transfer of ownership in his sole name based on inheritance with respect to all of X real property, C may, against B, bring a claim for recovery of inheritance within the period for exercise. 
(b) Although a joint inheritance registration for B and C with respect to X real property was lawfully completed, if B arbitrarily completed a registration of transfer of ownership in his sole name, and C brings against B a claim for cancellation of the registration on the ground that the transfer registration was completed without cause, such a claim constitutes an action for recovery of inheritance. 
(c) If B infringed C's inheritance right with respect to X real property, and C filed an action for recovery of inheritance against B within the exclusion period, and while the litigation was pending B transferred X real property to D and completed a registration of transfer of ownership in D's favor, C may, even after 10 years have passed from the date on which B infringed the inheritance right, bring a claim for recovery of inheritance against D.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DA26694]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (the contents of the supplemental appellate brief submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds for appeal shall be within the scope of supplementing the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. In the case where, on the premise that he is the true heir, a person asserts the vesting of property rights such as ownership or a fractional share right arising from the inheritance and seeks, against a pretended heir or a third party who has acquired rights concerning the inherited property from a pretended heir or has entered into new legal relations, the cancellation of registration, etc. concerning real property that is inherited property, then so long as the assertion that the ownership or fractional share right has vested is based on inheritance, regardless of the cause of action, this shall be deemed to fall under an action for recovery of inheritance prescribed in Article 999 of the Civil Act (see Supreme Court Decisions 83DA600, 83DAKA2056, rendered on February 14, 1984; 90DA5740, rendered on December 24, 1991, en banc; 92DA3083, rendered on February 26, 1993, etc.), and Article 999(2) of the Civil Act concerning the exclusion period for the right to claim recovery of inheritance shall also apply in this case (see Supreme Court Decision 79DA854, rendered on January 27, 1981, en banc).\\n\\nTherefore, after 10 years have elapsed from the date of the pretended heir’s first act of infringement, even if a third party’s new act of infringement, such as acquiring rights concerning inherited property from the pretended heir, was committed after 10 years had elapsed from the time of the first act of infringement, the right to claim recovery of inheritance shall have been extinguished by the lapse of the exclusion period, and the true heir can no longer seek cancellation of the registration, etc. against the third party; and this shall not be viewed differently merely because the true heir brought an action for recovery of inheritance against the pretended heir within the exclusion period and obtained a final and conclusive judgment in his favor.\\n\\nThe court below, based on the evidence it admitted, acknowledged the following facts: that the late Jeong Young-rae, who had been the owner of the real property at issue, died on March 7, 1971, and that Jeong Teuk-jo, the Plaintiff, and the co-Defendant at first instance, among others, became their joint heirs; that, however, the co-Defendant at first instance, by using a falsified agreement on the division of inherited property, completed registration of transfer of ownership concerning the real property at issue in his own sole name on April 6, 1993; that, accordingly, the Plaintiff brought an action for recovery of inheritance against the co-Defendant at first instance seeking cancellation of the share exceeding the co-Defendant at first instance’s inherited share in the real property at issue and obtained a final and conclusive judgment in favor of the Plaintiff on November 26, 2002; and that the Defendant, on August 29, 2001, while the above lawsuit was pending, completed registration of creation of a mortgage concerning the real property at issue based on a mortgage creation contract with the co-Defendant at first instance. The court below then held that the Plaintiff’s claim in this case against the Defendant seeking cancellation of the registration of creation of the mortgage concerning the above excess share would fall under an action for recovery of inheritance; however, since this action was brought on December 11, 2003, after 10 years had elapsed from April 6, 1993, when the co-Defendant at first instance committed the first act of infringement, the court below determined that this action was ultimately filed after the 10-year exclusion period had elapsed and was therefore unlawful. In light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the above factual findings and determination by the court below are proper and persuasive, and there can be no legal error, such as misapprehension of the law concerning an action for recovery of inheritance, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing Plaintiff. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2007DA17482]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Determination on the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nWhere, on the premise that he or she is the true heir, a person asserts the vesting of property rights, such as ownership or share rights, arising from inheritance, and seeks cancellation of registration, etc. concerning inherited real estate against a pretended heir or a third party who acquired rights concerning inherited property from a pretended heir or who formed a new legal relationship therewith, if the assertion that ownership or share rights have vested is based on inheritance, then regardless of the cause of action, this falls within an action for recovery of inheritance prescribed by Article 999 of the Civil Act (see Supreme Court en banc Decision of Dec. 24, 1991, 90DA5740; Supreme Court Decision of Oct. 15, 2009, 2009DA42321, etc.).\\n\\nAnd because a pretended heir, who is the respondent in an action for recovery of inheritance, refers to a person who, despite lacking a legitimate inheritance right, has the outward appearance of inducing trust that he or she is an heir to the property, or a person who, by pretending to be an heir, occupies all or part of the inherited property, where a transfer registration of ownership has been completed in the name of one of the co-heirs with respect to real estate that is inherited property, if that registration was completed on the ground of inheritance, then unless there are special circumstances, such as that it was completed irrespective of the registrant’s intent, the registrant constitutes a pretended heir as a person who has the outward appearance of inducing trust that he or she is an heir to the property (see Supreme Court Decision of Oct. 21, 1994, 94DA18249; Supreme Court Decision of Jan. 21, 1997, 96DA4688; Supreme Court Decision of Jan. 14, 2010, 2009DA41199, etc.).\\n\\nAccordingly, where one of the co-heirs completes a transfer registration of ownership concerning inherited real estate on the ground of inheritance by agreement partition, and another co-heir seeks cancellation of that registration on the ground that the agreement partition is void because it was made without the consent of the other co-heirs, such action also falls within an action for recovery of inheritance.\\n\\nIn the same purport, the court below, premising that the Plaintiff’s claim in this case, seeking cancellation with respect to the Plaintiff’s statutory inheritance share among the transfer registrations of ownership in the Defendant’s name made on the ground of inheritance by agreement partition concerning 1/4 share of each of the real properties in this case, falls within an action for recovery of inheritance, and therefore was filed after the expiration of the 10-year preclusive period and is thus improper, was correct.\\n\\nThere is no illegality in the judgment of the court below that affected the judgment by misapprehending the law on an action for recovery of inheritance, as the Plaintiff contends in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Determination on the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nGrounds of appeal 1 and 2 are considered together.\\n\\nIf a person who has violated a mandatory provision is denied on the ground that asserting the invalidity of the agreement by that person itself constitutes an exercise of rights in violation of the principle of good faith, this would instead give effect to the very result that the mandatory provision seeks to exclude, thereby completely nullifying the legislative intent. Therefore, unless there are otherwise special circumstances, such assertion cannot be said to be contrary to the principle of good faith. Meanwhile, in order to deny the exercise of a right on the ground of violation of the principle of good faith and fair dealing, the other party must have been given cause to rely, or objectively be in a state where it is reasonable for the other party to rely; and the exercise of a right in violation of such other party’s reliance must have reached a degree that is unacceptable in light of the concept of justice (see Supreme Court Decision of Apr. 22, 2003, 2003DA2390, 2406; Supreme Court Decision of Jun. 11, 2004, 2003DA1601; Supreme Court Decision of Nov. 29, 2007, 2005DA64552, etc.).\\n\\nIn addition, an agreement on the division of co-inherited property that determines the scope of ownership over inherited property constitutes an act in conflict of interests under Article 921 of the Civil Act, unless there are special circumstances under which, by the objective nature of the act, there is no concern that a conflict of interests among the heirs will arise (see Supreme Court Decision of Jun. 29, 2001, 2001DA28299, etc.). Further, in a case where primary inheritance commences upon the death of the decedent, one of the primary heirs dies again so that secondary inheritance commences, and then the heirs of the primary inheritance and the heirs of the secondary inheritance make an agreement on division concerning the inherited property of the primary inheritance, if there are several minors among the secondary heirs, a special representative must be appointed for each such minor, and each special representative must represent the minor concerned and make the agreement on division of the inherited property. If, however, a person with parental authority who is a co-heir in the secondary inheritance makes the agreement on division of the inherited property as the statutory representative of such several minors, this violates Article 921 of the Civil Act, and the agreement on division of inherited property formed by such representative act shall be deemed entirely void unless ratified by all represented persons (see Supreme Court Decision of Apr. 13, 1993, 92DA54524).\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the judgment of the court below, the court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found that, on Oct. 30, 1987, Sooe 3, who inherited the late Non-Party 2, one of the co-heirs of the late Non-Party 1, and his children, namely the co-defendants in the court below 1, 2, and 3, and the remaining co-heirs of the late Non-Party 1, including the Plaintiff and the Defendant, made an agreement on division of inherited property to the effect that each of the real properties in this case, which are inherited property, would be co-owned by the Defendant and the co-defendants in the court below, and that the Defendant and the said co-defendants in the court below would each pay 1,500,000 won to the Plaintiff and the remaining co-heirs; that, at the time, Sooe 3, who was the father of the co-defendants in the court below and one of the co-heirs, concluded the above agreement as the person with parental authority of the minor co-defendants in the court below and as their representative; that, pursuant to the above agreement, transfer registrations of ownership concerning each 1/4 share of each of the real properties in this case were completed in the names of the co-defendants in the court below; and that thereafter, on Dec. 29, 1987, transfer registrations of ownership on the ground of sale were completed in the Defendant’s name with respect to each of the above shares in the names of the co-defendants in the court below.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, even if the Plaintiff participated in an agreement on division of inherited property that violates Article 921 of the Civil Act, which is a mandatory provision, and later, in this litigation, asserts that the said agreement on division of inherited property is void on that ground, the Defendant’s reliance on the belief that the said agreement on division of inherited property was valid cannot be said to be justified, and such reliance cannot be said to be worthy of protection. Accordingly, the Plaintiff’s assertion of invalidity cannot be said to be contrary to the principle of prohibition of contradictory conduct or to the principle of good faith and fair dealing. Meanwhile, what becomes void under Article 921 of the Civil Act is the entire said agreement on division of inherited property, and it cannot be limited only to the agreement on division of inherited property between Sooe 3 and the co-defendants in the court below arising from the death of Non-Party 2.\\n\\nThe court below, in the same purport, correctly held that the entire said agreement is void, and that the transfer registrations of ownership in the names of the co-defendants in the court below based on the said agreement and the transfer registration of ownership in the Defendant’s name based thereon are all registrations void for lack of cause, and therefore the Defendant is obliged to implement the procedure for cancellation registration of the transfer registration of ownership dated Dec. 29, 1987, with respect to the Plaintiff, who is the true heir, as to the Plaintiff’s statutory inheritance share in each of the real properties in this case.\\n\\nThere is no illegality in the judgment of the court below that affected the judgment by misapprehending the principle of prohibition of contradictory conduct, the principle of good faith and fair dealing, or the law on acts in conflict of interests, as the Defendant contends in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, both appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal are borne respectively by each party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2009DA78801]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. An action for recovery of inheritance is one in which a person who claims to have acquired ownership by reason of inheritance seeks the recovery of the infringed inheritance right against a pretended heir. A pretended heir means a person who, despite having no legitimate inheritance right, has an outward appearance that makes others trust that he is an heir to the property, or a person who, by claiming to be an heir, is in possession of all or part of the inherited property. Whether a person has acquired, by a registration of transfer of ownership, an outward appearance that makes others trust that he is an heir to the property must be determined by the entries in the registry, which publicly records the legal relations to the outside world; therefore, if the cause of registration is not inheritance but another cause such as sale or gift, the registrant who has completed the registration of transfer of ownership cannot be said to be a pretended heir even if he is one of the co-heirs (see Supreme Court Decisions 96DA4688, Jan. 21, 1997, 2007DA7898, June 26, 2008, etc.), and where, with respect to real property for which registration of co-inheritance has once been lawfully completed, one of the heirs has effected a registration of transfer of ownership in his own sole name, an action by the other heirs seeking cancellation on the ground that the transfer registration was completed without cause does not constitute an action for recovery of inheritance, and therefore the peremptory period concerning the institution of such action prescribed in Article 999(2) of the Civil Act does not apply (see Supreme Court Decision 86DAKA2443, May 12, 1987). This is because the action seeks not recovery on the ground that the inheritance right has been infringed, but recovery of ownership on the ground that ownership once acquired by inheritance was thereafter unlawfully infringed, and no different conclusion follows merely because the time interval between the co-inheritance registration and the subsequent transfer registration is short, or because the co-inheritance registration and the transfer registration were carried out by one of the heirs at the same opportunity.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, in response to the defendants’ defense that the present action was an action for recovery of inheritance and was brought after the peremptory period had expired and thus was unlawful, rejected the above defense of the defendants on the ground that, as to the real property in this case, inheritance registration was lawfully completed on December 30, 1974 in the joint names of the heirs in this case, and on the next day a registration of transfer of ownership based on sale was completed in the sole name of Non-party 3, so Non-party 3 cannot be said to have had the outward appearance in the registry of making others trust that he was an heir, and therefore does not fall within the category of a pretended heir. In light of the foregoing legal principles, the above determination of the court below is proper, and there is no error in misapprehending the law concerning an action for recovery of inheritance.\\n\\n2. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, based on the facts stated in its opinion as found by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, rejected the defendants’ assertion that because the heirs in this case had made an agreement that “the eldest son, Non-party 3, would singly inherit the real property in this case in return for taking responsibility for and repaying all debts of the deceased Non-party 4,” the registration in the name of Non-party 3 was a valid registration based on an agreement on division of inherited property. If the submitted evidence is examined in light of the record, the above fact-finding and determination by the court below are also proper and acceptable, and there is no error in violating the rules of evidence.\\n\\n3. Where the nature of the title of possession of real property is not clear, under Article 197(1) of the Civil Act the possessor is presumed to have possessed in good faith, peacefully, and openly with the intent to own; however, if it is proved that, at the time possession began, the possessor, without any juristic act or other legal requirement that could constitute the cause of acquisition of ownership, and fully aware that no such legal requirement existed, occupied real property owned by another without authorization, the presumption of possession as owner is rebutted (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 95DA28625, Aug. 21, 1997, etc.). Furthermore, in acquisitive prescription by registration, it is required that there was no negligence in the commencement of possession, and the absence of negligence here means that the possessor was not negligent in believing that the property was his own (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DA12704, June 23, 2005, etc.).\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below held, in light of the circumstances such as those stated in the opinion found based on the evidence it admitted, that Non-party 3’s possession of the real property in this case constituted bad-faith unauthorized possession and thus the presumption of possession as owner was rebutted, and that Non-party 2, in possessing part of the real property in this case, knew that part of the shares belonged to the other heirs or at least was negligent in failing to know this. In light of the foregoing legal principles, the above determination of the court below is proper, and there is no error in violating the rules of evidence or misapprehending the law concerning acquisitive prescription.\\n\\n4. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, the costs of appeal are assessed against the losing parties, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices as stated in the Disposition."}

question: A, after purchasing a house from B, filed against B an action seeking registration of transfer of ownership on the ground of sale while not having paid the balance of 5,000 ten-thousand won. Before the close of oral argument in the above litigation, C, a creditor of B, obtained an order of attachment and collection of the claim for the above sale-balance claim, and the order was lawfully served on A. Thereafter, in the above litigation, B pleaded that B would perform the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership simultaneously with receiving payment of the balance of 5,000 ten-thousand won, while filing a counterclaim against A seeking payment of the above sale balance. Which of the following statements are incorrect? (Each item is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law governs.)
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2000DA73490]": "1. According to the reasons for the judgment of the court below, the court below found that the Defendant, after the lease contract at issue was terminated as of March 29, 1999, occupied the real property at issue only until August 31 of the same year and used and derived profit from it as a beauty salon, and that thereafter, even though the Defendant left his household goods, etc. on the real property at issue, he did not use or derive profit from it as a beauty salon, which was the purpose under the above lease contract; and then it determined that it could not be said that the Defendant was obtaining unjust enrichment equivalent to rent even for the period after September 1999, and dismissed this part of the Plaintiff’s claim. Upon review in light of the record, the above factual findings and determination of the court below are proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality, such as a violation of the rules of evidence or a misunderstanding of legal principles, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Even where there is an order of seizure and collection with respect to a monetary claim, this merely confers upon the collection creditor, in the compulsory execution procedure, the authority to collect the debtor’s claim against the third-party debtor, and does not transfer or vest the debtor’s claim against the third-party debtor in the collection creditor (see Supreme Court Decision 96DA54300, decided March 14, 1997; Supreme Court Decision 88DAKA3465, decided December 13, 1988); accordingly, the Debtor, as the collection debtor, does not lose the right to assert against the third-party debtor a defense seeking concurrent performance based on the attached claim, and when that defense is upheld and the third-party debtor becomes subject to a concurrent-performance obligation, the third-party debtor is merely subject to the restrictions arising from the effect of the above order of seizure and collection. Thus, the court below’s action, which fixed the amount of the remaining security deposit to be returned by the Plaintiff at 3,223,620 won, by deducting 12,450,000 won for overdue rent, etc. and 326,380 won for public dues from the lease deposit of 16,000,000 won, and ordered the Defendant to deliver possession of the real property at issue upon receipt of the above amount from the Plaintiff, is proper as it accords with the above legal principles (provided, upon review in light of the record, the factual finding of the court below that Shin Mun-gi, the co-defendant at first instance named as the lessee in the lease contract at issue and the collection debtor in this case, was merely in the position of a nominal lessee appears not to be accurate; however, leaving aside its opposability, since the Plaintiff also does not dispute that the said Shin Mun-gi transferred that status to the Defendant, no further determination is made on this point), and there is no illegality, such as omission to decide or misunderstanding of legal principles, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the appellate costs shall be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the judges involved, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2006DA19061]": "1. On the Principal Claim\\nThe court below held that, if the Plaintiff (Counter-Defendant, hereinafter referred to only as the “Plaintiff”) were to carry out an extension in accordance with the design drawings attached to the agreement at issue, the floor area thereof (69.44㎡) would exceed the Plaintiff-side remaining available building coverage ratio, thereby causing the Defendant-side remaining available building coverage ratio to decrease by the amount of such excess. The court further held that the Plaintiff, despite being fully aware of such circumstances, deceived Defendant A (hereinafter referred to as “A”), who withdrew on 2005. 5. 27., without informing A thereof, and that A, having been deceived, entered into the agreement at issue without knowing such circumstances by reason of mistake; accordingly, in response to the Defendant’s defense that the agreement at issue was rescinded on the ground of fraud or mistake, the court rejected the Defendant’s defense on the ground that there was no evidence to establish that, in concluding the agreement at issue, the Plaintiff deceived A with respect to the remaining building coverage ratio of the building at issue, and that, under the agreement at issue, not only the aggregate total floor area of the respective portions of the building at issue to be extended, but also the number of floors to be extended and the area of each floor were specified by attachment of the design drawings, so that the remaining building coverage ratio of the building at issue resulting from the extension was likewise specified; thus, even if there existed circumstances under which the remaining available building coverage ratio of Items A and B of the building at issue could not be maintained at the same level as a result of the above extension, such circumstances should be regarded as matters already agreed upon by both parties, and could not be deemed a mistake as to the contents of the contract.\\n\\nUpon review in light of the record, the foregoing measures taken by the court below are correct and acceptable, and it cannot be said that there exists any illegality such as misapprehension of facts due to violation of the rules of evidence, contradiction in the reasons, or misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning mistake in expression of intent.\\n\\n2. On the Counterclaim\\nAccording to the record, the Defendant had filed a preliminary counterclaim in preparation for the event that the Plaintiff’s principal claim would be upheld; the first instance court dismissed both the Plaintiff’s principal claim and the Defendant’s counterclaim on the ground that there was no benefit of suit; and the court below, noting that only the Plaintiff appealed in dissatisfaction with the first instance judgment, stated that the scope of its review was limited to the principal claim, and made no determination whatsoever on the counterclaim.\\n\\nHowever, the Defendant’s preliminary counterclaim seeks adjudication on the condition that the principal claim be upheld; therefore, once the first instance court rejected the Plaintiff’s principal claim, the Defendant’s preliminary counterclaim could not become a subject of adjudication by the first instance court, and even if the first instance court rendered a determination on a claim that could not be a subject of adjudication in this manner, such determination would be without effect (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 98DA22253 rendered on 2000. 11. 16.), and thus it cannot be said that the instant preliminary counterclaim could not become a subject of review by the court below merely because the Defendant did not appeal the counterclaim that was dismissed at first instance. Therefore, once the court below accepted the Plaintiff’s appeal and upheld the Plaintiff’s principal claim, it should have treated the Defendant’s preliminary counterclaim as a subject of adjudication and determined it accordingly.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below made no determination whatsoever with respect to the Defendant’s preliminary counterclaim for the reasons stated in its opinion; thus, the judgment of the court below contains an illegality of misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning a preliminary counterclaim, and it is clear that such illegality affected the judgment.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the portion of the judgment of the court below concerning the counterclaim is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for trial and determination of this portion, and the remainder of the appeal is dismissed; accordingly, it is so adjudicated unanimously by the Justices participating."}

{"[2007DA63362]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe court below dismissed the present action on the ground that, since Daewoo Electronics Co., Ltd. had obtained an order of seizure and collection from the Daegu District Court in Case No. 2007TACHAE110 concerning the present lease deposit claim that the Plaintiff seeks in this action, the Plaintiff had lost standing to sue to bring an action against the Defendant seeking payment of the present lease deposit claim, which is the attached claim.\\n\\nHowever, according to the materials submitted by the Plaintiff in this court, it can be found that Daewoo Electronics Co., Ltd., on 2007. 10. 2., after the judgment of the court below was rendered, submitted to the Daegu District Court a written release of attachment and renunciation of collection with respect to the above order of seizure and collection; according to this, the Plaintiff became able to bring an action seeking payment of the present lease deposit claim, and such a procedural requirement is a matter subject to ex officio investigation, so its cure must also be recognized at the appellate stage (see Supreme Court Decision 98DA20202, rendered on 1998. 8. 21.); ultimately, the judgment of the court below, which dismissed the present action on the ground that the Plaintiff lacked standing to sue, can no longer be maintained. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well taken.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further hearing and determination. The opinions of the Justices participating are unanimous, and it is so adjudged as stated in the disposition."}

question: A, a unit owner of A Apartment, a condominium building, having exclusively possessed and used the common areas of A Apartment without lawful title, B, another unit owner, filed against A an action for restitution of unjust enrichment equivalent to the rent corresponding to B’s share in respect of the relevant portion. A Apartment has a management body, C. Which of the following statements is incorrect? (Each item is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law applies)
A: It is lawful for B alone to have filed the above action for restitution of unjust enrichment.
B: If B obtained a judgment in the above litigation and that judgment became final and conclusive, absent special circumstances, the effect of that judgment extends to C.
C: If, prior to the above litigation, C first filed against A an action for restitution of unjust enrichment equivalent to the rent and a judgment became final and conclusive, the effect of that judgment extends to B.
D: If, after B received a judgment dismissing the claim at the first instance of the above litigation and upon reaching the appellate instance withdrew the action, C’s thereafter bringing a separate action against A for restitution of unjust enrichment is, absent special circumstances, in violation of the provision prohibiting refiling.
E: A consignment management company that has been comprehensively delegated management duties by C has, absent special circumstances, proper party status to claim management fees against unit owners, etc.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2019DA229516]": "We examine the grounds of final appeal (reference briefs submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds of final appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement it).\\n\\n1. A. The authority and duty to handle the management affairs of an aggregate building belong to the management body and the manager (Articles 23-2 and 25 of the Act on the Ownership and Management of Condominium Buildings), and the management body or the manager may enter into a management entrustment contract with a professional entrusted manager and have it perform the building management affairs. In such a case, the authority and scope of the entrusted manager’s management affairs are governed by the management entrustment contract, but since it is customary to entrust the entrusted manager with comprehensive management affairs, including the imposition and collection of management fees, it is reasonable to deem that this includes the grant of authority to assert judicial claims regarding management fees. An entrusted manager who has been entrusted with such management affairs and, while performing those affairs, directly asserts a judicial claim in its own name for management fees in order to collect overdue management fees from unit owners, etc. constitutes a voluntary litigation trust, but in light of the nature of management affairs for an aggregate building and the realities of transactions, this should be permitted absent special circumstances, and in such a case the entrusted manager should be regarded as having standing to claim management fees (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2014DA87885, 87892, decided December 15, 2016).\\n\\nB. An entrusted manager entrusted with the collection of management fees falls within the category of “a person who has become a party to litigation in his own name for another by virtue of a certain qualification” as provided in Article 237(1) of the Civil Procedure Act. Therefore, if, while the entrusted manager is conducting a lawsuit for management fees against unit owners, etc., the management entrustment contract terminates and the manager loses that qualification, the litigation proceedings are interrupted, and the proceedings may continue only when a new entrusted manager having the same qualification succeeds to the proceedings or, if there is no new entrusted manager, the management body or manager succeeds to the proceedings directly (Article 237(1) of the Civil Procedure Act). However, if there is a litigation representative, the litigation proceedings are not interrupted even if the management entrustment contract terminates (Article 238 of the Civil Procedure Act).\\n\\n2. A. The progress of the litigation in this case, as can be ascertained from the reasoning of the judgment below and the record, is as follows.\\n\\n1) Plaintiff is an entrusted manager who entered into a management entrustment contract with the management body of the building at issue, an aggregate building, concerning the management affairs of the building at issue. Plaintiff filed the action in this case on April 27, 2015, seeking payment of overdue management fees from Defendant, a unit owner, and while conducting the lawsuit, the management entrustment contract terminated on November 25, 2016.\\n\\n2) The first instance court dismissed the action in this case as improper on the ground that it had been brought by a person lacking standing to sue. It also did not grant the management body of the building at issue’s application for succession to the litigation on the ground that there was no reason to apply Article 237(1) of the Civil Procedure Act.\\n\\n3) During the appellate proceedings below, the applicant for succession to Plaintiff filed an application for succession to the litigation, asserting that it was an entrusted manager that had newly entered into a management entrustment contract on October 30, 2018. The appellate court dismissed Plaintiff’s appeal and the applicant for succession to Plaintiff’s application for succession to the litigation for the same reasons as the first instance court.\\n\\n4) Plaintiff retained litigation counsel on February 2, 2018, but by that time the management entrustment contract had already terminated, and therefore Plaintiff had no duly authorized litigation representative.\\n\\nB. We review the appellate court’s determination in light of the foregoing legal principles.\\n\\n1) Plaintiff had standing to pursue a management fee claim lawsuit against Defendant pursuant to the management entrustment contract, but lost standing upon termination of the management entrustment contract on November 25, 2016. This falls within the case where a person who, by virtue of a certain qualification, has become a party to litigation in his own name for another as provided in Article 237(1) of the Civil Procedure Act loses that qualification. If no duly authorized litigation representative had been appointed for Plaintiff, the termination of the management entrustment contract would cause a ground for interruption of the litigation proceedings in this case to arise, and the proceedings could continue only upon succession by a new entrusted manager or by the management body having that qualification.\\n\\n2) If that is so, the appellate court should have determined whether the litigation proceedings were interrupted, and if the litigation proceedings had been interrupted, it should have examined the applicant for succession to Plaintiff and, if that person had the same qualification as Plaintiff, allowed the litigation proceedings to continue. Nevertheless, the appellate court, on the ground that Article 237(1) of the Civil Procedure Act does not apply to this case, affirmed the first instance judgment dismissing the action in this case and also dismissed the applicant for succession to Plaintiff’s application for succession to the litigation.\\n\\n3) The appellate court’s determination contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning interruption and succession of litigation proceedings under Article 237(1) of the Civil Procedure Act. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appellate judgment is reversed and the case is remanded to the appellate court for a new trial and determination, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2021DA239301]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. a. The legal relationship under which restitution of unjust enrichment is sought because a person without lawful title has obtained benefits by occupying and using the common elements or the land of a condominium building, thereby preventing the sectional owners from using the relevant portions, is based on the co-ownership share rights of the sectional owners, and thus an action thereon may, in the first instance, be brought by each sectional owner individually or in the name of all of them. Meanwhile, once a sectional ownership relationship is established with respect to a condominium building, the management body is naturally established for the purpose of carrying out business concerning the management of the building and its land and appurtenant facilities. The management body shall exercise or perform the rights and obligations of the sectional owners necessary for the common interest concerning the management and use of the building, with the duty of care of a good manager, and may, through the manager as its representative, perform judicial or extrajudicial acts relating to matters concerning the management of the common elements, in accordance with the resolutions of the management body meeting or the bylaws (see Articles 16, 23, 23-2, and 25 of the Act on the Ownership and Management of Condominium Buildings). Accordingly, the management body may, in accordance with the resolutions of the management body meeting or as provided in the bylaws, bring an action for restitution of unjust enrichment against a person who occupies the common elements or the land of a condominium building without lawful title (see Supreme Court Decision 2003. 6. 24., 2003DA17774, Supreme Court Decision 2010. 8. 26., 2008DA35104, Supreme Court en banc Decision 2020. 5. 21., 2017DA220744, etc.).\\n\\nb. An action for restitution of unjust enrichment brought by the management body against a person who occupies or uses the common elements or the land of a condominium building without lawful title is an exercise, for the common benefit of the sectional owners, of the co-ownership share rights of the sectional owners, and may not be said to differ in content from an action for restitution of unjust enrichment brought separately by each sectional owner. If the management body brings an action for restitution of unjust enrichment and the judgment becomes final and conclusive, its effect also extends to the sectional owners (Civil Procedure Act Article 218(3)); and, unless special circumstances exist, if a sectional owner brings an action for restitution of unjust enrichment and the judgment becomes final and conclusive, the effect as to that part should also be deemed to extend to the management body. However, such an action by the management body is for the common benefit of the sectional owners, and its purpose differs from that of an action aimed at realizing the use and profit from one’s own co-ownership share rights by the sectional owners. Even if a sectional owner had filed an action for restitution of unjust enrichment and later withdrew the action after a final judgment on the merits had been rendered, the filing of an action for restitution of unjust enrichment by the management body may be deemed, absent special circumstances, to have created a new interest in legal protection and thus not to violate the rule prohibiting refiling under Civil Procedure Act Article 267(2).\\n\\n2. a. The Plaintiff, being the management body of the shopping complex at issue, filed an action seeking restitution of unjust enrichment, alleging that Defendant 1 and Non-party 1, the Defendants’ decedent, occupied and used the common elements of the shopping complex at issue without lawful title. In response, the Defendants argued that some of the sectional owners of the shopping complex at issue had already filed an action seeking restitution of unjust enrichment against Defendant 1 and Non-party 1, but had lost in the first instance and then withdrawn the appeal, so the Plaintiff’s action at issue was unlawful as it was subject to the rule prohibiting refiling; however, the lower court did not accept this argument. Since the Plaintiff filed this action for the common benefit of the sectional owners of the shopping complex at issue, it can be said that a new interest in legal protection arose, and thus it is reasonable to view that the action is not subject to the rule prohibiting refiling. The lower court’s determination rejecting the Defendants’ argument concerning the rule prohibiting refiling is proper.\\n\\nb. However, the Defendants argue that, in the case of Non-party 2, the appeal was withdrawn. If Non-party 2 was one of the sectional owners of the shopping complex at issue and had filed an action for restitution of unjust enrichment against Defendant 1 and Non-party 1, but withdrew the appeal after losing in the first instance, then the judgment against Non-party 2 became final and conclusive, and there is room to view that its effect extends to the Plaintiff. The lower court should have examined whether the effect of the judgment against Non-party 2 extends to the Plaintiff, and if so, determined the scope of the Plaintiff’s claim as recognized in consideration thereof. Nevertheless, the lower court determined only whether the rule prohibiting refiling applies, without any examination or determination on this point. In such determination by the lower court, there is an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning res judicata and by failing to conduct the necessary examination. The grounds of appeal pointing this out are well taken.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[2021DA239301]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. A. A legal relationship in which a person without lawful title gains benefits by occupying and using the common areas or land of a condominium building, and the sectional owners seek restitution of unjust enrichment because they are unable to use the relevant portion, is based on the sectional owners' common ownership shares; thus, an action thereon may, in the first instance, be brought by each sectional owner individually or in the name of all sectional owners. Meanwhile, where a sectional ownership relationship is established for a condominium building, the management body is naturally established by operation of law for the purpose of carrying out a business concerning the management of the building and its land and appurtenant facilities. The management body must exercise or perform, for the common interest concerning the management and use of the building, the rights and duties of the sectional owners necessary therefor with the duty of care of a good manager, and may, through the manager as its representative, perform judicial or extrajudicial acts concerning matters relating to the management of the common areas in accordance with resolutions of the meeting of the management body or the bylaws (see Articles 16, 23, 23-2, and 25 of the Act on the Ownership and Management of Condominium Buildings). Therefore, the management body may, in accordance with resolutions of the meeting of the management body or as provided in the bylaws, file an action for restitution of unjust enrichment against a person who occupies the common areas or land of a condominium building without lawful title (see Supreme Court Decision of June 24, 2003, 2003DA17774; Supreme Court Decision of August 26, 2010, 2008DA35104; Supreme Court en banc Decision of May 21, 2020, 2017DA220744; etc.).\\n\\nB. The management body's filing of an action for restitution of unjust enrichment against a person who occupies and uses the common areas or land of a condominium building without lawful title is an exercise, for the common interest of the sectional owners, of the sectional owners' common ownership shares, and may not be said to be litigation of a different nature from an action for restitution of unjust enrichment filed by each sectional owner. If the management body files an action for restitution of unjust enrichment and the judgment becomes final and conclusive, its effect also extends to the sectional owners (Civil Procedure Act Article 218(3)); and, absent special circumstances, if a sectional owner files an action for restitution of unjust enrichment and the judgment becomes final and conclusive, the effect concerning that portion must also be deemed to extend to the management body. However, such an action by the management body is for the common interest of the sectional owners and differs in purpose from an action by a sectional owner aimed at realizing the use and profit rights concerning his or her own common ownership shares. Even if a sectional owner filed an action for restitution of unjust enrichment and then withdrew the action after a final judgment on the merits had been rendered, the management body's filing of an action for restitution of unjust enrichment should, absent special circumstances, be deemed to have created a new interest in legal protection, and thus should not be contrary to the prohibition against refiling under Civil Procedure Act Article 267(2).\\n\\n2. A. The Plaintiff, which is the management body of the commercial building at issue, filed this action for restitution of unjust enrichment, alleging that Defendant 1 and Non-Party 1, the predecessor in interest of the Defendants, occupied and used the common areas of the commercial building at issue without lawful title. In response, the Defendants argued that some of the sectional owners of the commercial building at issue had already filed an action seeking restitution of unjust enrichment against Defendant 1 and Non-Party 1, had lost in the first instance, and had withdrawn the action after appealing; therefore, the Plaintiff's action in this case is unlawful because it is subject to the prohibition against refiling. The court below, however, did not accept this argument. Since the Plaintiff filed this action for the common interest of the sectional owners of the commercial building at issue, and thus a new interest in legal protection arose, it is proper to view this action as not subject to the prohibition against refiling. The court below's determination, which did not accept the Defendants' argument concerning the prohibition against refiling, is correct.\\n\\nB. However, the Defendants argue that, as to Non-Party 2, the appeal was withdrawn. If Non-Party 2 was one of the sectional owners of the commercial building at issue and had filed an action for restitution of unjust enrichment against Defendant 1 and Non-Party 1, but withdrew the appeal after losing in the first instance, the judgment against Non-Party 2 became final and conclusive, and there is room to view that its effect extends to the Plaintiff. The court below should have examined whether the effect of the judgment against Non-Party 2 extends to the Plaintiff, and if so, should have determined the scope of the Plaintiff's claim as recognized by taking that effect into account. Nevertheless, the court below judged only whether the prohibition against refiling applied, without any such examination or determination. In this respect, the court below erred by misunderstanding the law regarding res judicata and the like and by failing to conduct the necessary examination, thereby affecting the judgment. The grounds for appeal pointing out this issue are well-founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds for appeal, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for a new trial and determination; accordingly, it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the disposition."}

question: Among the explanations concerning joint litigation, which is incorrect? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, the precedents shall govern)
A: Where B completed a registration of preservation of ownership by an unlawful method with respect to land owned by A, and C thereafter completed a registration of transfer of ownership on that basis, a lawsuit brought by A against B and C seeking cancellation of each of the registration of preservation of ownership and the registration of transfer of ownership constitutes ordinary co-litigation.
B: A lawsuit by co-heirs against another co-heir seeking confirmation that certain property constitutes inherited property constitutes co-litigation that is indispensable by nature.
C: A lawsuit brought by A and B, shareholders of A Co., Ltd., against A Co., Ltd. seeking confirmation of the nonexistence or invalidity of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders constitutes necessary co-litigation.
D: In the case of purchasing land in a partnership business having A and B as members, a lawsuit seeking performance of the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership based on that sales contract constitutes co-litigation that is indispensable by nature.
E: Where A, the principal debtor, and B, the joint and several surety, became co-plaintiffs and filed a suit against creditor C seeking confirmation of the nonexistence of each loan debt and joint and several surety obligation, and C admitted A's claim and this was entered in the record, the court must uphold B's claim on the basis of the above admission of claim.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DA40980]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. On the Plaintiffs’ grounds of appeal\\n\\nWhere there is a dispute among co-heirs as to whether certain property belongs to the inherited estate of the decedent, and some co-heirs file an action against the other co-heirs seeking a declaration that the property is inherited property, such action is an action seeking a declaration that the property is presently held in co-ownership, prior to the division of the co-heirs’ inherited property; thus, by the final and conclusive judgment in favor thereof, it becomes established that the property is subject to the division of inherited property, and after the probate division adjudication proceedings or after the division adjudication becomes final, it is no longer possible to dispute again that the property is subject to the division of inherited property, and as a result, since the dispute as to whether it is subject to division of inherited property among co-heirs can be finally resolved, there is a legal interest in confirmation.\\n\\nIn contrast, the lower court’s judgment, which held that the part of this action seeking a declaration that the chattels at issue are the inherited property of the deceased Non-Party 1 is unlawful because it lacks a legal interest in confirmation for the reasons stated in its holding, contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the interest in a suit in an action for confirmation; therefore, the ground of appeal pointing out this issue is well-founded.\\n\\nMeanwhile, an action brought by one co-heir against another co-heir seeking a declaration that certain property is inherited property is what is known as an indispensable joint litigation, and in indispensable joint litigation, a withdrawal of the action by some of the Plaintiffs or a withdrawal of the action against some of the Defendants does not take effect unless there are special circumstances (see Supreme Court Decision 99SEU49 dated January 23, 2002), and we further point out that, in the court below, although the Plaintiffs withdrew the action insofar as it sought confirmation of inherited property against Non-Party 2, one of the co-heirs of the deceased Non-Party 1, such withdrawal did not take effect under the foregoing legal principle.\\n\\n2. On Defendant 1’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. On Ground No. 1 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the court below, based on the evidence it adopted, found that the deceased Non-Party 1, during his lifetime, possessed a large number of old books and paintings to the extent that he registered some of them as cultural properties and entered them in exhibitions held overseas, and that, as the property manager of Non-Party 3, he was in a position to dispose, in substance at his own discretion, of the property remaining in Non-Party 3’s ownership; and that, apart from the property remaining in Non-Party 3’s ownership, he also left as inherited property land consisting of 72 parcels scattered throughout the country, which remained as his own property until the time of his death; on the other hand, Defendant 1 had been living in severe economic hardship when she married the deceased Non-Party 1, and even after the marriage to the deceased Non-Party 1, she did not engage in any particular outside economic activity and thus had no independent income of her own. After finding these facts, the court below, in view of the circumstances stated in its holding, determined that the chattels at issue are presumed to have belonged to the deceased Non-Party 1, as property he inherited from his ancestors or purchased directly by him or through Defendant 1 with his money, and that the evidence submitted by the Defendants alone is insufficient to overturn the above presumption and there is no other rebuttal evidence; accordingly, it held that the chattels at issue are the inherited property of the deceased Non-Party 1.\\n\\nIn light of the evidence submitted, the foregoing findings and determination by the court below are justifiable and persuasive, and there is no illegality such as a violation of the rules of evidence assessment, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe argument in this part of the grounds of appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\nb. On Ground No. 2 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nSince a co-owner who owns a share in jointly owned property cannot exclusively possess the jointly owned property without agreement with the other co-owners, the other co-owners may demand delivery or surrender of the jointly owned property from the person in possession thereof as an act of preservation of the jointly owned property, even if the share they own is less than a majority (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 93DA9392, 93DA9408 dated March 22, 1994, Supreme Court Decision 95DA48308 dated December 23, 1996, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the court below held that the statutory shares of inheritance of the co-heirs of the deceased Non-Party 1 are 2/13 each for the Plaintiffs, Defendant 2, and Non-Party 2, and 3/13 for Defendant 1; and that Defendant 1, who exclusively and exclusively possesses and manages the chattels at issue, which are the inherited property of the deceased Non-Party 1, is obligated to deliver the chattels at issue to the other co-heirs, namely the Plaintiffs.\\n\\nThe above determination by the court below is in accordance with the legal principle stated above and is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehending the legal principle concerning an act of preservation of jointly owned property, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe argument in this part of the grounds of appeal also cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, we reverse the portion of the judgment below adverse to the Plaintiffs and remand this part of the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and dismiss Defendant 1’s appeal; accordingly, we render judgment as stated in the disposition, in the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2007DA36445]": "1. Where, after a person without authority unlawfully completes in his name a registration of preservation of ownership or a registration of transfer of ownership, a third party who successively purchased the real property thereafter is recognized as having acquired title by prescription through the register, thereby causing the owner to lose ownership, if there had been no unlawful act of completing the registration by the person without authority, the result that the owner loses ownership would not naturally have occurred; and, since such loss of ownership is ordinarily foreseeable at the time of the unlawful act of completing the registration, there is an adequate causal relation between the unlawful act of completing the registration by the person without authority and the owner’s loss of ownership (see Supreme Court Decision rendered June 11, 1993, 92DA50874, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below, taking the evidence it admitted in combination, found the following facts: with respect to the forest land of 43,736 m² in Songjeong-ri, Gwangju-eup, Gyeonggi, Lot No. 1 omitted, which belonged to the Plaintiff, Defendant 1 and Non-Party 1, who were persons without authority, completed a registration of preservation of ownership in the names of the two persons on November 26, 1970, in violation of the provisions of the Former Special Measures Act on Registration, etc. for Transfer of Ownership of Forest Land (Act No. 2111 of May 21, 1969, expired) (hereinafter referred to as “the registration of preservation in this case”); thereafter, with respect to the forest land of 21,868 m² in Songjeong-ri, Gwangju-eup, Gyeonggi, Lot No. 2 omitted, which had been subdivided from the forest land, a registration of transfer of ownership in the sole name of Non-Party 1 was completed on June 3, 1982, and a registration of transfer of ownership in the name of Non-Party 2 was completed on September 18, 1982, one after another, based on the registration of preservation in this case; the Plaintiff filed a lawsuit against the remaining Defendants, who are the heirs of Defendant 1 and Non-Party 1, and against Non-Party 2, seeking cancellation of each of the above registrations (hereinafter referred to as “the prior lawsuit”), but as Non-Party 2, the final purchaser of the forest land in this case, asserted acquisition by prescription of the real property and that assertion was accepted, the Plaintiff ultimately lost ownership of the forest land in this case; and on that basis the court below held that adequate causal relation is recognized between the unlawful act of completing the registration of preservation in this case by Defendant 1 and Non-Party 1 and the Plaintiff’s loss of ownership, so Defendant 1 and Non-Party 1 are joint tortfeasors, and therefore the remaining Defendants, who are the heirs of Defendant 1 and Non-Party 1, are liable to compensate the Plaintiff for the damage resulting from the loss of ownership of the forest land in this case.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principle stated above and the record, the court below’s factual findings and determination are correct and persuasive, and there is no illegality such as a violation of the rules of evidence or an error in the interpretation of the law regarding the establishment of joint tort and adequate causal relation, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. A lawsuit seeking cancellation of registrations completed in sequence is not a necessary joint lawsuit requiring a unified determination of the legal relationship, but an ordinary joint lawsuit, and in such an ordinary joint lawsuit, contradictory conclusions may arise depending on differences in the means of attack and defense among co-parties; under a litigation system based on the adversarial principle, this is unavoidable and cannot be said to constitute contradictory or insufficient reasoning in the judgment (see Supreme Court Decision rendered April 12, 1991, 90DA9872, etc.). In such a case, even if, because a claim for cancellation of a later registration is finally lost, execution of a cancellation registration for an earlier registration becomes impossible in consequence, it cannot be said that there is no benefit of lawsuit in seeking cancellation of the earlier registration (see Supreme Court Decision rendered July 13, 1993, 93DA20955, Supreme Court Decision rendered September 22, 1998, 98DA23393, etc.), so the grounds of appeal disputing this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. In civil litigation, although a court is not bound by facts recognized in judgments in other civil cases, facts recognized in already finalized related civil cases become highly probative evidence unless special circumstances exist, and therefore cannot be rejected without stating rational reasons; this is the settled view of this Court. This is all the more so where two civil lawsuits before and after involve the same parties and the facts forming the basis of the dispute are also the same, but only the subject matter of the litigation differs, so that res judicata is not implicated and a new claim may be brought (see Supreme Court Decision rendered July 4, 2000, 2000DA20748, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below, taking the evidence it admitted in combination, found that in the prior lawsuit filed by the Plaintiff against the Defendants, the Defendants argued that “Non-Party 3 (the father of Defendant 1) and Non-Party 1 purchased the forest land in Lot No. 1 omitted and the forest land of 19,965 m² in Songjeong-ri, Gwangju-eup, Gyeonggi, Lot No. 3 omitted (hereinafter referred to as ‘the forest land of Lot No. 3 omitted’) from Non-Party 4, the Plaintiff’s predecessor, around 1934, and thereafter sold only the forest land of Lot No. 3 omitted to Non-Party 5 and four others, while continuing to hold the forest land in Lot No. 1 omitted; accordingly, since Defendant 1 and Non-Party 1 were the de facto owners of the forest land in Lot No. 1 omitted, the registration of preservation in this case is a valid registration conforming to the substantive legal relationship,” but that argument was rejected on the ground that the deed of sale concerning the forest land of Lot No. 3 omitted submitted by the Defendants as evidence (bearing the purport that Non-Party 3 and Non-Party 1 sold the forest land of Lot No. 3 omitted to Non-Party 5 and four others around 1935, along with the entry of the registration completion) alone was insufficient to find that Non-Party 3 and Non-Party 1 purchased the forest land in Lot No. 1 omitted from Non-Party 4 around 1934, and there was no other evidence to support such finding; and that, consequently, a judgment was rendered and became final ordering the Defendants to perform the procedures for registration of cancellation of the registration of preservation in this case and the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of Non-Party 1 concerning the forest land in this case.\\n\\nThe court below then rejected the Defendants’ argument in this case that “even if Non-Party 4, the Plaintiff’s predecessor, had already sold the forest land in Lot No. 1 omitted to Non-Party 3 and Non-Party 1 around 1935 and completed a registration of transfer of ownership, he no longer had ownership, so even though Defendant 1 and Non-Party 1 unlawfully completed the registration of preservation in this case concerning the forest land in this case, the Plaintiff, as the heir of Non-Party 4, cannot be said to have suffered damage in the form of loss of ownership of the forest land in this case,” on the ground that the evidence submitted by the Defendants on this point consisted only of the deed of sale concerning the forest land of Lot No. 3 omitted, which had already been rejected in the prior lawsuit (Exhibit No. 6 for the Defendant in this case), and evidence merely corroborating the evidentiary value of that deed of sale, and thus was not sufficient to overturn the facts recognized in the final judgment in the prior lawsuit and recognize the asserted facts, and there was no other evidence to support such finding.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principle stated above and the record, the court below’s factual findings and determination are correct and persuasive, and there is no illegality such as a violation of the rules of evidence or an error in the interpretation of the law concerning res judicata or the probative value of a related final civil judgment, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. According to the record, as in the grounds of appeal, the Defendants argued in the court below in their written preparatory brief dated April 12, 2007, that “even if Non-Party 4 did not sell the forest land in Lot No. 1 omitted to Non-Party 3 and Non-Party 1, since Non-Party 4 transferred the forest land in Lot No. 1 omitted to an unidentified third party before July 1935 and even completed a registration of transfer of ownership, he no longer had ownership, so the Plaintiff cannot be said to have suffered damage in the form of loss of ownership of the forest land in this case,” but the court below made no determination on this point, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nHowever, even upon examining the record, no evidence can be found to support the finding that, as alleged above, Non-Party 4 transferred the forest land in Lot No. 1 omitted to an unidentified third party before July 1935 and even completed a registration of transfer of ownership. Accordingly, the Defendants’ above argument is ultimately without merit and would be rejected, and even if there were an error of omitting a ruling on a party’s argument, when it is clear that the argument would be rejected, it cannot be said to be an illegality affecting the result of the judgment. Therefore, the grounds of appeal on this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n5. In the case of a claim for damages based on a tort where there is a temporal interval between the wrongful act and the actual occurrence of damage resulting therefrom, the meaning of “the day on which the tort was committed,” which becomes the starting point of the statute of limitations, should be understood as the time when damage that exists only potentially in an abstract and dormant state can be regarded as having subsequently materialized, that is, when the occurrence of the result of damage can be regarded as having become actual (see Supreme Court Decision rendered January 12, 1990, 88DAKA25168, etc.). Where a person without authority unlawfully completes a registration of preservation of ownership or a registration of transfer of ownership concerning real property in his name and then sells it to a third party and causes a registration of transfer of ownership to be completed in the third party’s name, if the third party asserts acquisition by prescription in response to the owner’s claim for cancellation of registration, there is a special circumstance that whether the registration in the third party’s name is to be cancelled depends on the outcome of the lawsuit or the like; accordingly, the owner’s damage in the form of loss of ownership of the real property exists only potentially in an abstract and dormant state and cannot yet be said to have materialized until the outcome of the lawsuit or the like is rendered, and the occurrence of the result of damage should be deemed to materialize when the owner’s lawsuit against the third party seeking cancellation of registration is finally lost; and even if the owner loses the lawsuit for cancellation of registration as a result of the third party’s acquisitive prescription through the register being recognized in that lawsuit, it cannot be said that the damage had already materialized at the time the acquisitive prescription through the register became complete (see Supreme Court Decision rendered January 30, 2001, 2000DA18196, Supreme Court Decision rendered September 15, 2005, 2005DA29474, etc.).\\n\\nIn light of the above legal principle and the record, in the prior lawsuit filed by the Plaintiff against Non-Party 2, the Plaintiff sought cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership completed in Non-Party 2’s name on September 18, 1982, concerning the forest land in this case, but it was recognized that Non-Party 2 had possessed the forest land in this case in peace and openly, with the intention of ownership, in good faith and without negligence for 10 years from the time the registration of transfer of ownership was completed, thereby completing acquisitive prescription based on the register, and consequently the Plaintiff’s above claim for cancellation of registration was finally lost on February 27, 2004. It can thus be seen that only at that time did the occurrence of the result of damage in the form of the Plaintiff’s loss of ownership of the forest land in this case become actualized; accordingly, the starting point of the statute of limitations for the Plaintiff’s claim for damages against the Defendants should be deemed to be February 27, 2004, the time when the claim for cancellation of registration was finally lost.\\n\\nThere is somewhat an inappropriate point in the reasoning of the court below’s judgment on this part; however, the court below’s conclusion that the starting point of the statute of limitations for the Plaintiff’s claim for damages against the Defendants is February 27, 2004, when the Plaintiff’s claim for cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership in Non-Party 2’s name concerning the forest land in this case was finally lost in the prior lawsuit filed by the Plaintiff against Non-Party 2, is correct. Therefore, there is no illegality such as an error in interpreting the law concerning the starting point of the statute of limitations for a claim for damages, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n6. As stated in paragraph 5 above, if the occurrence of the result of the Plaintiff’s damage arising from the joint tort committed by Defendant 1 and Non-Party 1 in this case is deemed to have become actualized on February 27, 2004, when the Plaintiff’s claim for cancellation of transfer registration against Non-Party 2 was finally lost in the prior lawsuit, then the amount of damages should also be calculated based on the market value of the forest land in this case as of the time when the claim for cancellation was finally lost.\\n\\nThe court below’s determination to the same effect is correct, and there is no illegality such as an error in the interpretation of the law concerning the standard time for calculating the amount of damages, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n7. If negligence on the part of the victim is recognized in a lawsuit for damages, the court shall take it into account in determining liability for damages and the amount thereof; and even if the obligor for compensation does not assert negligence on the part of the victim, if negligence is recognized from the materials in the lawsuit, the court must examine and determine it ex officio (see Supreme Court Decision rendered October 25, 1996, 96DA30113, etc.).
