However, absent other special circumstances, a person who intentionally committed a tort by taking advantage of the victim’s negligence cannot claim a reduction in his own liability on the basis of that very victim’s negligence (see Supreme Court Decision rendered October 7, 2005, 2005DA32197, etc.).\\n\\nTherefore, even if the Plaintiff was negligent, as argued in the grounds of appeal, in failing for a long period to exercise rights concerning the forest land in this case, thereby allowing Non-Party 2’s acquisitive prescription concerning the forest land in this case to become complete, in this case, where it cannot be deemed that Defendant 1 and Non-Party 1 intentionally committed a tort by unlawfully completing the registration of preservation in this case in their names by exploiting the Plaintiff’s negligence in leaving the forest land in Lot No. 1 omitted unregistered, it is not permissible to apply comparative negligence by relying on the Plaintiff’s negligence as the victim. Thus, the grounds of appeal on this part, which proceed on a different premise, also cannot be accepted.\\n\\n8. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the appeal costs shall be borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged as per the dispositive portion by the unanimous opinion of the judges who participated."}

{"[2012DA44471]": "1. We determine whether the appeal filed by the Appellant, who is also a Plaintiff-Intervenor (hereinafter referred to as “the Appellant”), is lawful.\\n\\nAccording to the record, although it can be seen that the Appellant, after the judgment of the court below was rendered, acquired on 2012. 5. 4. the claims for the sale price that the Plaintiff holds against the Defendant, including the claim for the amount awarded in the judgment of the court below, the Appellant was not a party to the proceedings below, did not intervene by succession in the court below, and intervention by succession cannot be permitted in the Supreme Court proceedings, which are a court of law; therefore, the appeal filed by the Appellant on 2012. 5. 10. is inadmissible (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2002. 12. 10., 2002DA48399, Supreme Court Decision dated 2006. 5. 26., 2006HU183, etc.). Although the Appellant, while submitting on 2012. 6. 22. an application for correction of the party designation and an application for intervention as a supporting intervenor, argues that the petition of appeal submitted by the Appellant should be construed as both an application for intervention as a supporting intervenor and a petition of appeal submitted by a supporting intervenor, that view cannot be accepted; however, since the above application may be regarded as an independent application for intervention as a supporting intervenor, only thereby is the Appellant’s status as a Plaintiff-Intervenor recognized.\\n\\n2. We determine the grounds of the Plaintiff’s incidental appeal.\\n\\nThe court below, (1) after premising that, where it is agreed that a single claim will be paid in installments, the extinctive prescription of that claim runs successively from the time each installment agreed to be paid in installments falls due, held that among the claim for the sale price involved in this case, which is a commercial claim, the down payment, intermediate payments, and the claim for their delay damages were extinguished by prescription upon the filing of this action on 2011. 3. 15., since five years had elapsed from each due date, whereas the remaining balance and the claim for its delay damages had not been extinguished by prescription because five years had not elapsed as of the filing of this action, since their due date fell on 2006. 12. 17.; and (2) rejected, for the reasons stated in the opinion, all of the Plaintiff’s arguments that the extinctive prescription had been suspended until 2008. 9. 17. because the Plaintiff had previously filed an action against the Baekma Row-House Reconstruction and Maintenance Project Association (hereinafter referred to as “the Association involved in this case”) seeking transfer registration of ownership concerning the apartment involved in this case and then lost on 2008. 9. 17., after which the Plaintiff filed the present claim, or that the act of the Defendant in around 2007 filing an action against the Association involved in this case seeking transfer registration of ownership concerning the apartment involved in this case constituted an acknowledgment having the effect of interrupting the statute of limitations, so that the extinctive prescription was interrupted around the time the Defendant filed the above lawsuit.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the evidence lawfully admitted, there is no illegality in the court below’s above determination, such as misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the starting point of the extinctive prescription or the interruption of the extinctive prescription, as alleged in the grounds of incidental appeal.\\n\\nThe other arguments of incidental appeal are based on grounds not argued until the conclusion of oral argument in the court below and are newly raised only at the Supreme Court level, and therefore do not constitute proper grounds of incidental appeal.\\n\\n3. We determine the grounds of appeal by the Defendant.\\n\\nA. As to Ground 1 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nIn civil litigation, facts recognized in a related civil case that has already become final and conclusive may constitute highly probative evidence absent special circumstances; however, it is also legally permissible for the court, by comprehensively considering the reasons of the final and conclusive judgment in the related case together with other evidence, to find facts different from those recognized in the final and conclusive judgment, and so long as such fact-finding does not exceed the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence and rationality is recognized in the statement of reasons, it belongs to the exclusive province of the trier of fact and cannot be deemed unlawful (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2010. 5. 13., 2009DA38612, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below, based on the circumstances as stated in the opinion, determined that the fact that the Defendant filed an action against the Association involved in this case seeking transfer registration of ownership concerning the apartment involved in this case and obtained a judgment in its favor without oral argument is alone insufficient to find that the Defendant, who did not directly pay the sale price to the Plaintiff in the manner agreed in the sale contract, had paid all of the sale price for the apartment involved in this case, and that the parties appear to have arbitrarily settled their claims and obligations between the Non-Party and the Defendant by treating them as the sale price for the apartment involved in this case.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the evidence lawfully admitted, the above determination by the court below is consistent with the legal doctrine stated above, and there is no illegality such as, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or failing to conduct the necessary examination by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning performance.\\n\\nB. As to Ground 2 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nThe court below did not accept the Defendant’s argument of set-off based on a debt for damages arising from the tort of the Association involved in this case, or the argument of violation of the principle of good faith, for the reasons stated in the opinion.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the evidence lawfully admitted and the record, there is no illegality in the court below’s above determination, such as, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or failing to conduct the necessary examination by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning set-off or the principle of good faith.\\n\\nC. As to Ground 3 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\n(1) Who the parties to a contract are is a matter of interpretation of the parties’ intent involved in that contract. Interpretation of a manifestation of intent is to clearly ascertain the objective meaning attached by the parties to the act of manifestation; thus, where a certain contractual content between the parties has been reduced to writing as a dispositive document, the interpretation is not bound by the wording used in that writing, but rather, regardless of the parties’ internal intent, the objective meaning attached by the parties to the act of manifestation must be reasonably interpreted according to the contents of the writing (see Supreme Court Decision dated 1995. 6. 30., 94DA51222, Supreme Court Decision dated 2000. 10. 6., 2000DA27923, etc.). In such a case, if the objective meaning of the language is clear, the existence and content of the manifestation of intent as expressed in that language must be recognized, absent special circumstances (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2002. 5. 24., 2000DA72572, Supreme Court Decision dated 2010. 5. 13., 2009DA92487).\\n\\nMeanwhile, a partnership agreement under the Civil Act is a contract by which two or more persons agree to contribute jointly and manage a business in common, and since partnership property belongs to the partnership as jointly owned property, litigation concerning a claim belonging to partnership property constitutes litigation concerning jointly owned property and, absent special circumstances, must be brought jointly by the partners, and thus falls under indispensable joint litigation (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2001. 4. 29., 2008DA50691).\\n\\n(2) According to the reasons of the judgment below and the evidence lawfully admitted, the Plaintiff, which operates a housing construction business, and the Association involved in this case, as joint business operators, agreed to demolish the existing row houses and build apartments thereon; and, in return for the provision of the project site by the members of the Association involved in this case, they entered into the implementation and construction contract involved in this case, under which some of the apartment units were to be sold to the members of the Association involved in this case, and the members of the Association involved in this case were to pay certain contributions (provided, however, that the basic contributions could be reduced depending on the sale price of the units for general sale), while the remaining units for general sale were to be sold in return for the Plaintiff’s provision of project expenses, with the sale proceeds to accrue to the Plaintiff; and accordingly, the Plaintiff and the Association involved in this case, jointly as sellers, executed on 2005. 10. 10. a sale contract providing for the sale of the apartment involved in this case, which was a unit for general sale, to the Defendant, thereby concluding the sale contract involved in this case.\\n\\n(3) Examining the above factual relationship in light of the legal doctrine stated above, (a) the implementation and construction contract involved in this case can be said to have the nature of a partnership agreement under which the Plaintiff and the Association involved in this case agreed to mutual contributions in order to jointly promote the reconstruction project involved in this case (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2009. 10. 29., 2009DA47432, etc.); (b) upon execution of the sale contract involved in this case in the joint names of the Plaintiff and the Association involved in this case, absent special circumstances, it is appropriate to regard the right to claim the sale price for the apartment involved in this case as jointly belonging to the Plaintiff and the Association involved in this case in their relationship with the Defendant; and (c) furthermore, taking into account the circumstances that the sale contract involved in this case was concluded pursuant to the general-sale procedure contemplated in the implementation and construction contract involved in this case, in the absence of other circumstances, the sale contract involved in this case can be regarded as having been concluded by the Plaintiff and the Association involved in this case in their status as joint business operators under the implementation and construction contract involved in this case, so that the right to claim the sale price for the apartment involved in this case belongs to the property of the above partnership, and therefore an action seeking payment thereof falls under indispensable joint litigation that must be brought jointly by the Plaintiff and the Association involved in this case, who are members of the above partnership.\\n\\nIf so, the court below should have examined whether the claim for the sale price of the apartment involved in this case constituted property of the above partnership or property belonging solely to the Plaintiff, and then, if it was recognized as property of the above partnership, should have determined that the present action brought only by the Plaintiff excluding the Association involved in this case was inadmissible (see Supreme Court Decision dated 1994. 10. 25., 93DA54064, etc.).\\n\\nNevertheless, the judgment below that upheld the Plaintiff’s claim for the sale price of the apartment involved in this case, without reaching that conclusion, contains illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning claims belonging to partnership property and indispensable joint litigation and by failing to conduct the necessary examination, and the portion of the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the portion of the judgment below adverse to the Defendant is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; the Plaintiff’s incidental appeal is dismissed; the Appellant’s appeal is dismissed as inadmissible; and the costs of litigation relating thereto shall be borne by the Appellant. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2020DA284977]": "1. Ex officio determination on the form of joinder of parties\\n\\nThis action is one seeking confirmation of the nonexistence or invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution, and under the main clause of Article 190 of the Commercial Act as applied mutatis mutandis pursuant to Article 380 of the Commercial Act, a judgment granting the claim also has effect vis-à-vis third parties. Where such an action is jointly brought by several persons, the effect of the judgment won by one party among the co-litigants extends to the other co-litigants, and thus the need for a uniform and conclusive determination in procedural law is recognized among the co-litigants. In addition, considering the fact that the provisions on exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing for company-related litigation under the Commercial Act (Articles 186 and 188 of the Commercial Act) also presuppose a uniform and conclusive determination between the parties, as well as the parties’ intentions and litigation economy, this falls within the category of indispensable co-litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies.\\n\\nIn accordance with such legal principles, the judgment of the court below, premised on the fact that this action jointly brought by the Plaintiffs is indispensable co-litigation, is correct, and there is no error in misconstruing the law regarding the form of joinder of parties.\\n\\n2. Determination on the grounds for final appeal\\n\\na. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\nThe Defendant is a stock company established for the purpose of real estate development business, etc., and the Plaintiffs are shareholders of the Defendant.\\n\\nNon-party 1, who is stated in the shareholders’ register as holding 2,000 shares, obtained court permission to convene an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders and held an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders on 2012. 5. 25. At that general meeting, a resolution to continue the company, which had been deemed dissolved, thereby restoring the Defendant to a status prior to dissolution, and a resolution appointing Non-party 2, etc. as officers upon expiration of the term of office and death of the existing officers, were adopted. At the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders held on 2015. 5. 22., a resolution reappointing Non-party 2, etc. as officers upon expiration of the term of office of the existing officers was adopted, and at the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders held on 2015. 12. 2., a resolution dismissing the existing auditor and appointing a new auditor was adopted.\\n\\nb. The Plaintiffs argued that the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated 2012. 5. 25. was convened by Non-party 1 or Non-party 2, who had no authority to convene it, and that the resolution was nonexistent or invalid because it had defects such as forged proxies of some shareholders and thereby fell short of the quorum for resolution, and that the resolutions of the extraordinary general meetings of shareholders dated 2015. 5. 22. and 2015. 12. 2. based thereon were also nonexistent or invalid.\\n\\nIn response, the court below found that the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated 2012. 5. 25. was convened by Non-party 1, who, as a shareholder on the shareholders’ register, could exercise shareholder rights, and thus could not be deemed to have been convened by a person without convening authority, and further found that Non-party 2 lawfully received a delegation of voting rights exercise from some shareholders and participated in the resolution of the general meeting as their representative, so that the quorum for resolution was satisfied. Furthermore, the court below dismissed the Plaintiffs’ claims regarding the extraordinary general meeting resolutions dated 2015. 5. 22. and 2015. 12. 2., premised on the argument that the above resolutions were nonexistent or invalid.\\n\\nc. Examining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in the court below’s determination, such as failing to conduct the necessary examination as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, or, in violation of the rules of logic and experience, exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehending the relevant legal principles such as those concerning the authority to convene a shareholders’ meeting, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the final appeal are to be borne by the unsuccessful party, and judgment is rendered as stated in the main text. In this judgment, except for the separate opinions of Justices Lee Ki-taek, Park Jeong-hwa, Kim Seon-su, and Lee Heung-gu regarding the form of joinder of parties, the supplementary opinions of Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Min Yu-sook, and Roh Tae-ak on the majority opinion, and the supplementary opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek on the separate opinion, the opinions of the participating Justices were in agreement.\\n\\n4. Separate opinion of Justices Lee Ki-taek, Park Jeong-hwa, Kim Seon-su, and Lee Heung-gu regarding the form of joinder of parties\\n\\na. The main clause of Article 190 of the Commercial Act provides, “A judgment declaring the incorporation invalid or rescinding the incorporation shall also have effect vis-à-vis third parties.” Accordingly, a judgment granting the claim in an action for invalidation or rescission of incorporation of a company also has effect vis-à-vis third parties. The above provision is applied mutatis mutandis to various company-related actions under the Commercial Act, and thus, in an action for invalidation of merger (Article 240), an action for invalidation of share exchange (Article 360-14(4)), an action for invalidation of share transfer (Article 360-23(4)), an action for rescission of a shareholders’ meeting resolution (Article 376(2)), an action for confirmation of the invalidity or nonexistence of a shareholders’ meeting resolution (Article 380), an action for rescission or modification of an unfair shareholders’ meeting resolution (Article 381(2)), an action for invalidation of issuance of new shares (Article 430), an action for invalidation of reduction of capital (Article 446), etc., a judgment granting the claim has effect erga omnes.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that, where several persons jointly bring an action concerning a company under the Commercial Act in which a judgment dismissing the claim has no effect vis-à-vis third parties, but a judgment granting the claim has effect vis-à-vis third parties (hereinafter referred to as a “company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect”), such an action falls within the category of indispensable co-litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies. However, such an action should be regarded as ordinary co-litigation, which is the principal form of joinder of parties. Because the need for a uniform and conclusive determination, which is a requirement of indispensable co-litigation, cannot be recognized, there is neither reason nor necessity to apply Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act so as to strictly unify litigation materials and litigation progress and thereby restrict the parties’ disposition power and rights concerning litigation procedure. Specific reasons are set forth below.\\n\\nb. Before engaging in a full discussion of the issue, I first examine the current provisions, structure, and relevant legal principles of the Civil Procedure Act concerning the meaning of ordinary co-litigation and indispensable co-litigation and the manner of hearing, and clarify from what aspect the separate opinion addresses the issue.\\n\\n1) Joinder of parties is a form of litigation in which multiple plaintiffs or defendants participate in a single litigation procedure. Article 65 of the Civil Procedure Act provides, with respect to the requirements for joinder of parties, “Where the right or obligation that is the subject matter of the litigation is common to several persons, or arises from the same cause in fact or in law, such persons may be parties as co-litigants. The same shall also apply where the right or obligation that is the subject matter of the litigation is of the same kind and arises from causes of the same kind in fact or in law.” Joinder of parties can be divided into ordinary co-litigation, in which the co-litigants need not win or lose together, and indispensable co-litigation, in which they must win or lose together.\\n\\n2) Article 66 of the Civil Procedure Act provides, “The procedural acts of one co-litigant, or the procedural acts of the opposing party vis-à-vis such procedural acts, and matters concerning one co-litigant shall not affect the other co-litigants.”\\n\\nAs a general rule, the parties, who are the subjects of rights and obligations, may independently file an action and conduct litigation. Even if several persons become parties jointly, this merely means that a case that could be resolved through separate proceedings has been combined into a single procedure for a common hearing, and there is no reason why the independent status and authority each party has when litigating individually should be specially restricted merely because of joinder of parties. Accordingly, even in joinder of parties, each party conducts litigation on his or her own responsibility, without help or interference from other co-litigants, and bears responsibility only for the procedural acts he or she has performed. Article 66 of the Civil Procedure Act provides that ordinary co-litigation, in which each co-litigant’s status is independent as above, is the principal form of joinder of parties.\\n\\n3) Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act defines as indispensable co-litigation “co-litigation in which the subject matter of the litigation must be uniformly determined for all co-litigants,” and establishes special rules for the hearing so that the result of the trial may be uniformly determined among the co-litigants. Article 67(1) provides, “A procedural act by one co-litigant shall be effective only for the benefit of all.” Article 67(2) provides, “A procedural act by the opposing party against one co-litigant shall be effective against all co-litigants.” Under the above provision, among the procedural acts of one party, acts beneficial to all, such as asserting claims or submitting evidence for winning the case, extend their effect to all co-litigants, while adverse procedural acts, such as confession, have no effect at all unless all parties perform them together, thereby unifying litigation materials as to all parties; the effect of procedural acts disposing of the subject matter of litigation, such as waiver of claim, acknowledgment of claim, or judicial settlement by one party, is also limited. Next, Article 67(3) provides, “Where there is a reason to suspend or stay the proceedings against one co-litigant, such suspension or stay shall be effective against all.” In addition, separation of arguments among co-litigants is not permitted, one judgment must be rendered for all co-litigants, and if some co-litigants file an appeal, finalization of the judgment is blocked as to all and the entire case is transferred to the appellate instance, thereby causing the course of litigation to proceed in a uniformly integrated manner (see Supreme Court Decisions 2003DA44615, 2003DA44622, Dec. 12, 2003, and 2008DA50691, Apr. 29, 2010, etc.).\\n\\nWhen Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies in this way, litigation materials are unified among co-litigants (common assertion and evidence), and the progress of litigation (common arguments, common judgment, common instance) is also unified, so that the result of the trial is uniformly determined among the co-litigants. On the other hand, if even one of litigation materials and litigation progress is not unified, uniform conclusive determination of the trial result is not guaranteed.\\n\\n4) To summarize the foregoing legal principles, in joinder of parties, ① ordinary co-litigation is the principle, ② only where there is a “need for uniform and conclusive determination” does it become indispensable co-litigation, and ③ in indispensable co-litigation, the special hearing rules of Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act apply in order to achieve uniform and conclusive determination of the trial result.\\n\\nThe separate opinion raises the question of whether a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect falls within indispensable co-litigation requiring uniform and conclusive determination, that is, the issue under ② above, on the premise that the existing structure and legal principles regarding the form of joinder of parties are all respected. It is not a discussion concerning ① above, namely, a legislative or policy discussion as to which form of joinder of parties is desirable, or whether, even where there is no need for uniform and conclusive determination, it should still be regarded as indispensable co-litigation; nor is it a discussion concerning ③ above, namely, which method of hearing is more suitable for indispensable co-litigation.\\n\\nAccordingly, the assertion that it is smooth and natural for the parties to win or lose together where the rights and obligations that are the subject matter of the litigation are common among co-litigants may be a discussion concerning ①, namely, a discussion that under the current provisions of the Civil Procedure Act, the principal form of joinder of parties should be regarded as indispensable co-litigation or that the scope of recognition of indispensable co-litigation should be expanded, but it cannot serve as a valid ground for treating a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect as indispensable co-litigation under the current system and legal principles concerning joinder of parties. Furthermore, discussion concerning the hearing method under Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act is also a discussion under ③, premised on falling within indispensable co-litigation, and differs in the plane of discussion from the separate opinion. Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act merely provides procedural means for uniform and conclusive determination in the event a certain action falls within indispensable co-litigation requiring uniform and conclusive determination among co-litigants. The argument that, because applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act among co-litigants is appropriate or desirable, such action should be regarded as indispensable co-litigation requiring uniform and conclusive determination merely reverses the logical sequence or amounts to changing the concept of indispensable co-litigation.\\n\\nc. The main grounds for regarding a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect as ordinary co-litigation are as follows.\\n\\n1) The principal form of joinder of parties is ordinary co-litigation in which each co-litigant’s status is independent. Exceptionally, only where there is a need for the subject matter of the litigation to be uniformly determined under substantive or procedural law can it be regarded as indispensable co-litigation.\\n\\na) As seen above, under our Civil Procedure Act, the principal form of joinder of parties is ordinary co-litigation in which each co-litigant’s status is independent. This can readily be understood from the structure of the provisions of the Civil Procedure Act concerning joinder of parties, namely, the structure of the statutory provisions in which Article 66 of the Civil Procedure Act concerning the independence of the status of co-litigants comes first, and Article 67 and following provisions, as special provisions to Article 66, establish special hearing rules regarding certain types of joinder of parties (indispensable co-litigation, preliminary or alternative joinder of parties), or from the fact that ordinary co-litigation is the procedural expression of the principle of private autonomy, the fundamental principle of the Civil Act that private law legal relationships are regulated at the free will of the individual and on his or her own responsibility.\\n\\nb) If one departs from this principle and treats the case as indispensable co-litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies, as noted above, various restrictions are imposed on the parties’ capacity to conduct litigation, such as restrictions on the effect of procedural acts and freedom to dispose of the subject matter of the litigation. In order to justify such restrictions, the requirement of indispensable co-litigation prescribed by Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, namely, the case where “the subject matter of the litigation must be uniformly determined for all co-litigants,” must be satisfied.\\n\\nFor this purpose, the parties must, under substantive law, be unable to exercise alone the power to manage and dispose of property rights, so that joint litigation is compelled and the trial result must coincide, or, while several persons may individually litigate, there must be a need for uniform and conclusive determination under substantive law or procedural law because the effect of the judgment obtained by one party extends to the other party, and if the judgment results differ between them, their effects conflict or clash with each other.\\n\\nMere logical or practical desirability of winning or losing together among co-litigants, without a legal need for uniform and conclusive determination, cannot be regarded as indispensable co-litigation. The most typical example is where a creditor brings an action against a principal debtor and a surety. Although it accords with the substantive relationship and is logical to render a consistent judgment as to whether the debt has been paid, it is not treated as indispensable co-litigation for that reason alone. The principal debtor who alleges and proves payment may prevail, while the surety who fails to raise the defense that the principal debtor paid may lose. In the same vein, Supreme Court decisions have held that where uniform and conclusive determination is not required under law, such as claims against multiple joint and several debtors or actions for cancellation of registration of ownership transfer made sequentially, the case does not fall within indispensable co-litigation (see Supreme Court Decisions 4287MINSANG204, Feb. 10, 1955, 70DA232, Feb. 9, 1971, etc.).\\n\\n2) In a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect, there is no need for uniform and conclusive determination under substantive law. This is because the purpose of unifying the legal relationship under substantive law can be sufficiently achieved through the erga omnes provision, making other means unnecessary, and applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act cannot be viewed as an effective and appropriate means for unifying the legal relationship under substantive law.\\n\\na) The res judicata effect of a judgment, in principle, extends only to the parties, successors after the conclusion of oral argument, and the persons specified in Article 218 of the Civil Procedure Act. The one-sided erga omnes effect provisions concerning company-related actions are exceptions to the principle of relativity of res judicata, extending the effect of a judgment to third parties in order to unify the legal relationships under the collective law surrounding the company, such as shareholders, transaction counterparties, and other interested persons.\\n\\nFor example, even if there is a cause of invalidity in a resolution of a shareholders’ meeting, shareholders may each freely choose whether to bring, or not to bring, an action for confirmation of the invalidity of the resolution of the shareholders’ meeting, and the shareholder A who first brings the action may receive an adverse judgment, while the shareholder B who later brings the action may obtain a favorable judgment. In that case, if the same resolution of a shareholders’ meeting is invalid as to shareholder B but valid as to shareholder A, the other shareholders who did not bring the action and other interested persons, a confusion would arise in the collective legal relationship. Therefore, Article 380 of the Commercial Act, by applying mutatis mutandis the main clause of Article 190, recognizes the erga omnes effect of the favorable judgment obtained by shareholder B, so that the collective legal relationship can be dealt with in a unified manner.\\n\\nThe one-sided erga omnes effect provisions concerning company-related actions (the main clause of Article 190 of the Commercial Act and Articles 240, 380, and 430 of the Commercial Act applying mutatis mutandis the same) were established precisely because, in company-related actions, joint litigation (hereinafter referred to as “litigation joinder”) is not compelled, and thus the trial results may not be unified for all parties, so that the substantive legal relations surrounding the collective entity may be uniformly determined. In company-related actions, if a judgment denying the validity of incorporation, merger, resolution of a shareholders’ meeting, issuance of new shares, etc., is rendered, the substantive legal relationship is uniformly regulated according to these one-sided erga omnes effect provisions.\\n\\nb) Where the power to manage and dispose of property rights belongs jointly to several persons under substantive law, and the party cannot dispose of it alone, the trial result must also coincide for all; otherwise, dispute resolution becomes impossible. Therefore, litigation joinder is compelled, all must necessarily become parties to the action and must bring one action, and an action brought without all being parties is not permitted (and is dismissed as improper for lack of standing as a party), and a consistent conclusion must be reached in one judgment. This type of litigation is called “genuine indispensable co-litigation.” An action for partition of co-owned property, or an action concerning the bankruptcy estate where there are multiple bankruptcy trustees, are examples (see Supreme Court Decisions 2003DA44615, 2003DA44622, Dec. 12, 2003; 2006DA14363, Apr. 24, 2008, etc.). In such a case where litigation joinder is compelled and only one action is permitted for all parties, applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act and rendering one uniform judgment can be regarded as an appropriate means to effectively resolve the dispute.\\n\\nc) By contrast, company-related actions do not compel litigation joinder, and the parties may each bring separate actions or may refrain from suing. Therefore, even if the trial results are made consistent only among co-litigants, the purpose of unifying the substantive legal relationship through trial is not achieved.\\n\\nAs explained above, take as an example an action for confirmation of invalidity of a resolution of a shareholders’ meeting. Since such an action does not compel litigation joinder, shareholders A and B may jointly file the action, shareholder C may later file a separate action, and shareholder D may choose not to file any action. Even if A and B’s joint action is treated as indispensable co-litigation and one uniform judgment is rendered, there is no way to make the result consistent with C’s separate action filed thereafter, so it is possible that A and B lose while C wins. In the case of D who did not sue, there is not even any judgment. In this way, even if A and B’s action is treated as indispensable co-litigation, there is no method by which the trial results can be made consistent even for C, D, and others who filed separate actions or did not sue at all.\\n\\nIn company-related actions, uniformity of substantive legal relationships can be sufficiently achieved by giving the favorable judgment obtained by C erga omnes effect not only against the losing A and B, but also against D and others who did not file suit, pursuant to the one-sided erga omnes effect provisions. Other means are unnecessary, and treating A and B’s action as indispensable co-litigation cannot be said to be an effective or appropriate means to unify the substantive legal relationship.\\n\\nd) The Civil Procedure Act amended in 2002 newly established preliminary or alternative joinder of parties as a type of joinder of parties and expressly permitted, though previously disallowed, one-sided independent party intervention, and applied Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act mutatis mutandis to all such proceedings (Civil Procedure Act Articles 70 and 79). Such types of litigation mainly concern cases where several claims are legally incompatible with one another. In such cases, since litigation joinder is not compelled and there are no provisions by which the substantive legal relationship can be unified, the contents of judgments on each claim could conflict with each other under substantive law, resulting in disadvantages such as a party being unable to exercise rights even though they exist or being doubly burdened with obligations. The purpose of the amendment to the Civil Procedure Act in creating such types of litigation and applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act mutatis mutandis was to classify such cases into several categories, establish a special litigation system capable of reaching judgments free from substantive-law contradictions, and allow parties to use such a system when they wish.\\n\\nThis has no relation to a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect. In company-related actions, as seen above, there are one-sided erga omnes effect provisions for uniformly regulating the substantive legal relationship. Therefore, whether the parties bring the matter as a separate action or as joint litigation, even if the trial results differ, the parties suffer no disadvantage (the legal relationship is governed according to the favorable judgment), and no separate litigation system or measure is needed to protect the parties’ interests. Accordingly, it is not possible to derive from the purpose of the above amendment to the Civil Procedure Act the necessity of applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act to a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect.\\n\\n3) In a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect, even if the trial results among co-litigants differ, there is no possibility that their effects will conflict with one another, so no contradiction or clash of judgments occurs; thus, it cannot be said that there is a need for uniform and conclusive determination under procedural law.\\n\\na) If the effect of a judgment obtained by one of the parties extends to the other party, and if the trial results between them differ so that the effects of the judgments conflict and the dispute cannot be resolved, then there is a need to make the trial results consistent among the parties. Such litigation must be one in which, whether the parties each bring separate actions or by chance bring a joint action, the trial results must be unified, and if it is co-litigation, it falls within indispensable co-litigation requiring uniform and conclusive determination. This type of litigation is called “quasi-indispensable co-litigation.”\\n\\nA representative example of quasi-indispensable co-litigation is a case where the effect of the judgment extends in full, regardless of the outcome, to a certain range of interested persons. For example, in rehabilitation proceedings, a judgment in an action concerning the determination of rehabilitation claims and security rights has effect against all rehabilitation creditors, rehabilitation secured creditors, shareholders, and equity holders (Article 176(1) of the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act). If several objectors bring actions objecting to the adjudication confirming a claim concerning the same claim, and the court renders a favorable judgment for one and an adverse judgment for another, the effects of the two judgments extend to all rehabilitation creditors, rehabilitation secured creditors, shareholders, and equity holders, thereby conflicting with one another. Therefore, if the objectors jointly bring such an action, it should be regarded as indispensable co-litigation and one uniform judgment should be rendered, and even if the objectors each bring separate actions, the hearings must necessarily be consolidated and proceed as co-litigation (for this purpose, the commencement of hearings is restricted until the period during which another objection action may be filed has elapsed; see the same Act, Article 171(4) and (5)).\\n\\nThe same applies where multiple litigation administrators bring an action. For example, in a creditor’s subrogation action, if the debtor knew that the action had been filed, the res judicata effect extends to the debtor pursuant to Article 218(3) of the Civil Procedure Act (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 74DA1664, May 13, 1975, etc.). Thus, if multiple creditors each bring separate actions and the debtor knows this fact, and different results are reached, the effect of each judgment extends to the debtor and conflicts with one another. To prevent this, if a creditor’s subrogation action is pending, another creditor must intervene in that action, and bringing a separate action is not permitted as duplicative litigation (see Supreme Court Decisions 87DAKA1618, Sept. 27, 1988; 2013DA30301, 2013DA30325, July 23, 2015, etc.). If several creditors jointly bring an action or become co-litigants through intervention, it should be regarded as indispensable co-litigation and one uniform judgment should be rendered (see Supreme Court Decision 91DA23486, Dec. 27, 1991, etc.).\\n\\nBy contrast, if parties each bring separate actions and differing trial results are permissible, then even if the actions are brought jointly, it cannot be said to be indispensable co-litigation. For example, if joint and several creditors A and B each bring an action against the debtor, even if joint and several creditor A prevails, joint and several creditor B may lose because the fact of payment is recognized. Accordingly, even if A and B jointly bring an action, no uniform and conclusive determination is required, so it falls within ordinary co-litigation.\\n\\nb) However, in a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect, even if different judgments are rendered among the parties, there is no problem of contradiction or clash between judgments. Unlike in a type of litigation where the effect of the judgment extends in full, regardless of whether the outcome is favorable or adverse, the effect of a favorable judgment and that of an adverse judgment do not conflict with each other because erga omnes effect is recognized only in a one-sided manner for a plaintiff’s favorable judgment.\\n\\nFor example, even if shareholder A brings an action for confirmation of invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution and receives an adverse judgment, shareholder B may bring the same action and receive a favorable judgment, and A’s adverse judgment does not obstruct B’s success. If B prevails, then pursuant to the erga omnes effect, the shareholders’ meeting resolution is uniformly treated as invalid for all interested persons, including the company and shareholders, and this is likewise true as to the losing A. The company cannot argue that the shareholders’ meeting resolution is valid only against A. Thus, even though it may appear that two judgments affecting A conflict because A, who received an adverse judgment, is also bound by the erga omnes effect of B’s favorable judgment, such conflict is resolved according to the one-sided erga omnes effect provisions and no problem arises.\\n\\nEven where shareholders A and B jointly bring an action, no problem of contradiction or clash of judgments arises. Even if A loses and B wins, B’s favorable judgment has erga omnes effect, and the shareholders’ meeting resolution becomes invalid for all interested persons, including the losing A. Furthermore, this problem is the same whether, as explained above, the actions are brought separately or jointly, so it cannot be said that contradiction or clash of judgments occurs only in the case of joinder of parties.\\n\\nIt is also not possible to distinguish joint litigation from separate actions on the ground that in separate actions judgments are rendered individually for A and B, whereas in joint litigation one judgment is rendered for A and B. A joint action by A and B is a subjective joinder of the action between A and the company and the action between B and the company, and a litigation relationship is formed separately between each of A and B and the opposing party. Even if one formal judgment is rendered as to A and B, it is no different from judgments being rendered separately for each litigation relationship.\\n\\nIn the case of joinder of parties, it cannot be said that the adverse judgment against A is meaningless merely because A receives the erga omnes effect of B’s favorable judgment rendered together in one judgment. The judgment against A is a valid judgment with formal finality and res judicata that terminates the litigation. That is precisely why one-sided erga omnes effect provisions were established in order to resolve conflicts between the two judgments and regulate the substantive legal relationship in a unified manner. The majority opinion, conversely, says that because one-sided erga omnes effect provisions apply to company-related actions, an adverse judgment cannot be rendered simultaneously with a favorable judgment in joinder of parties; this misunderstands the logical sequence. Furthermore, even if A and B in joint litigation dispute defects in the same shareholders’ meeting resolution and it is logical to reach a consistent conclusion, as seen above in 1), mere logical consistency does not suffice to recognize a legal need for uniform and conclusive determination.\\n\\nIn this way, in a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect, no need for a uniform and conclusive determination under procedural law among co-litigants can be recognized. The majority opinion, which finds such need only in the case of a joint action brought by chance even though differing judgments are possible where parties bring separate actions, lacks logical consistency.\\n\\n4) Treating a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect as indispensable co-litigation not only unduly restricts the parties’ disposition power and rights concerning litigation procedure, but may also run counter to litigation economy. No problem arises even if it is treated as ordinary co-litigation, and indeed the litigation procedure becomes simpler and litigation economy is promoted.\\n\\nOf course, this may serve as one side’s argument, in legislative-theory terms, regarding which of ordinary co-litigation or indispensable co-litigation should be regarded as the principal form of joinder of parties [this corresponds to the discussion at stage ① in paragraph b. 4)], but it is unrelated to the question of which type of litigation should be considered indispensable co-litigation with a “need for uniform and conclusive determination under law.” It is mentioned only additionally to explain that even if such litigation is treated as ordinary co-litigation, no problem arises and the litigation relationship may become simpler.\\n\\na) As seen above in paragraph b, Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act imposes various restrictions on the parties’ capacity to conduct litigation in order to unify the litigation materials and litigation progress and thereby render a uniform judgment in indispensable co-litigation. This will be examined in more detail.\\n\\nFirst, adverse acts such as confession, waiver or acknowledgment of claim, and settlement are ineffective unless all co-litigants perform them together (Article 67(1) of the Civil Procedure Act). If A and B jointly bring an action, even if A confesses certain facts in order to obtain a prompt judgment through a hearing limited to the issues, such confession has no effect unless B agrees. Nor is it permitted for A to terminate the action against A alone by first waiving his or her own claim. On the other hand, because a procedural act by the opposing party against one co-litigant is effective against all regardless of whether it is favorable or unfavorable (Article 67(2)), even if A does not appear on the hearing date, the hearing can proceed if B appears, the opposing party may make new assertions and submit evidence at that hearing date, and all such procedural acts take effect against A even though A was not involved.\\n\\nComplex issues also arise with appeals. According to the case law, in indispensable co-litigation, if both A and B receive an adverse judgment and A does not appeal because he or she intends to accept it, then if B appeals, finalization of the judgment is also blocked as to A, and the case is transferred to the appellate instance, so that A becomes a “mere party in the appellate instance” who is neither an appellant nor an appellee in the appellate court (see Supreme Court Decisions 94DA33002, Jan. 12, 1995, etc.). However, it is doubtful whether the Civil Procedure Act assumes a third-party status in the appellate instance that is neither appellant nor appellee. If A is neither an appellant nor an appellee, the Civil Procedure Act contains no provision as to what degree of litigation authority A has in the appellate instance, whether A may file an incidental appeal, whether A must bear litigation costs, or whether A may file a final appeal against the appellate judgment. In the above example, even if A, who received an adverse judgment and has no intention of appealing, seeks to withdraw the action, that is impossible unless the opposing party consents; thus, it cannot be said to be acceptable to treat A as a party in the appellate instance on the ground that A may withdraw the action.\\n\\nIn this way, the parties in indispensable co-litigation are restricted in their disposition power and are subject to many constraints in conducting the litigation. In order to depart from the principle of ordinary co-litigation and impose such restrictions on the parties’ litigation status, there must be a clear legal basis justifying them. As seen above, in a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect, it is difficult to say that there is a substantive-law or procedural-law need for a uniform determination among co-litigants sufficient to justify such restrictions.\\n\\nb) Even if a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect is treated as ordinary co-litigation, no problem arises, and rather the litigation procedure becomes simpler and litigation economy is promoted.\\n\\nAssume the case where shareholders A and B bring an action for confirmation of invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution, and explain it on the premise that it is ordinary co-litigation. Co-litigants A and B may each conduct the litigation and receive the judgment accordingly. A and B may each freely perform adverse acts such as confession, withdrawal of the action, waiver of claim, or withdrawal of appeal, and these acts have effect only as to that party. As a result, if A loses the will to conduct the litigation, A may exit the litigation early by, for example, withdrawing the action alone or waiving the claim with the opposing party’s consent, and only B, who still intends to conduct the litigation, remains as a party, thereby lightening the litigation procedure.\\n\\nIf A and B both received adverse judgments at first instance and only B appealed, A’s losing portion becomes separately finalized and is not transferred to the appellate instance. B may independently conduct the litigation and obtain a favorable judgment in the appellate instance, and A’s adverse judgment does not obstruct B’s success. The litigation relationship becomes far simpler without having to rely on the unclear and unnatural legal theory of the “mere party in the appellate instance,” as seen above.\\n\\nEven in ordinary co-litigation, arguments, evidence examination, and judgment are conducted together at a common hearing date. Under the principle of common evidence, evidence submitted by each co-litigant may serve as material for fact-finding for the other co-litigant even without mutual invocation, and the conviction obtained by the judge is also common. Therefore, even in ordinary co-litigation, unless there are special circumstances such as only one co-litigant confessing, courts in most cases render consistent judgments, and the likelihood that unnatural judgments reaching different conclusions for each party on the same matter will be rendered is low.\\n\\nIn this way, even if treated as ordinary co-litigation, there are no feared side effects; rather, there are substantial advantages in that the parties’ disposition power can be respected, the litigation procedure becomes simpler, and litigation economy is promoted, such as only appellants who intend to conduct the litigation becoming parties in the appellate instance.\\n\\n5) It cannot be said that the provisions on exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing under the Commercial Act presuppose that consolidated actions are indispensable co-litigation.\\n\\nThe Commercial Act provides that company-related actions fall under the exclusive jurisdiction of the district court having jurisdiction over the company’s head office location, and where several company-related actions of the same content are pending, the court must hear them in a consolidated manner (see Articles 186 and 188 of the Commercial Act. The above provisions are all applied mutatis mutandis to company-related actions with one-sided erga omnes effect). Such provisions may be viewed as intended to have the actions heard together in a single litigation procedure, because duplicated hearings by multiple courts on the same matter are undesirable from the standpoint of litigation economy, and a company may have difficulty responding simultaneously to multiple lawsuits. As noted above, even in ordinary co-litigation, consistent results are often reached according to the principle of common hearing and common evidence, so to that extent the unity of the trial result may also be promoted.\\n\\nThere is no basis for viewing the above provisions on exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing as provisions that presuppose a uniform and conclusive trial result beyond such purpose. Even in company-related actions, if a judgment is rendered first in one action because of differences in the time of filing, etc., consolidation may become impossible because the instance differs; in such cases, even if the plaintiff loses in the earlier action, another plaintiff in the later action may prevail, so uniform and conclusive determination of the trial result is not guaranteed. Furthermore, where several actions involving overlapping issues and parties are pending, the court often consolidates them to reach a consistent conclusion (for example, where separate actions are filed against joint tortfeasors, where several creditors each bring an action for avoidance of a fraudulent transfer, or where a creditor brings separate actions against the principal debtor and the surety, etc.), but such consolidation does not make the case indispensable co-litigation. Thus, the provisions on exclusive jurisdiction or consolidated hearing do not constitute grounds for treating a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect as indispensable co-litigation.\\n\\nd. The form of joinder of parties is an important issue also related to the status of the parties in the appellate instance, and the Supreme Court needs to clarify this to prevent confusion in trial practice.\\n\\nIn this case, because the Plaintiffs jointly retained litigation counsel from the first instance and conducted the litigation, there is no practical difference in the outcome depending on the form of joinder of parties. However, the form of joinder of parties is, as seen below, an important issue related to “who is recognized as having party status in the appellate instance” before the hearing method or the litigation result. Who the parties in the appellate instance are, and whether a co-litigant who did not appeal becomes a party in the appellate instance, are issues from the moment the appellate procedure begins; if this is not clarified, confusion will arise in the entire course of the appellate procedure, and questions will also arise as to the legality of the judgment rendered through such procedure. Because issues concerning the parties fall within the litigation requirements, a judgment that omits a litigation party or wrongly treats a person who is not a party as a party is always unlawful. This means excluding a party entitled to participate in the litigation from the litigation procedure or wrongly involving a non-party in the litigation, not merely an incorrect designation of the party in the written judgment. Even in final appeal, it is a matter to be examined ex officio irrespective of the grounds for final appeal, and it cannot be said that illegality is cured merely because it did not result in a practical difference in the outcome.\\n\\nIt cannot be said that prior Supreme Court decisions and trial practice have, like the majority opinion, regarded company-related actions with one-sided erga omnes effect as indispensable co-litigation. There is no Supreme Court decision that explicitly pronounced such a legal principle, and the Supreme Court’s Decision 4291MINHANG231 of Feb. 19, 1959, rendered under the former Civil Procedure Act before the enactment of the Civil Procedure Act in 1960, merely mentioned in obiter dictum that an action for confirmation of invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution brought by several persons was indispensable co-litigation. Rather, the more recent Supreme Court Decisions 2003DA69355, Dec. 9, 2004; 2005DA54265, July 13, 2006; and 2015DA27699, Aug. 13, 2015, excluded from the parties in the final appeal the plaintiffs who had not appealed, where only some of the joint plaintiffs under the judgment of the court below had appealed in company-related actions. Not only that, but even in administrative appeal actions in which a judgment annulling a disposition, or confirming its invalidity or unlawfulness by omission, has one-sided erga omnes effect (Article 29(1) and Article 38 of the Administrative Litigation Act), many Supreme Court decisions have excluded from the parties in the final appeal the plaintiffs who had not appealed against the judgment of the court below (see Supreme Court Decisions 2010DU13463, Aug. 23, 2012; 2012DU1006, Mar. 13, 2014; 2012DU5572, Aug. 20, 2014; 2018DU54163, Nov. 29, 2018; 2019DU60486, Mar. 12, 2020; 2020DU37215, July 9, 2020; 2020DU49423, Dec. 24, 2020). Conversely, it is difficult to find a decision in which, in such types of litigation, plaintiffs who did not appeal were recognized as parties in the final appeal. This clearly treated the portion concerning the party who did not appeal as separately finalized, indicating that it was based on ordinary co-litigation.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states only that a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect is indispensable co-litigation, without any mention of whether this was the prior position of the Supreme Court or whether the Court is changing its prior position through this judgment. If the Supreme Court had previously regarded such litigation as indispensable co-litigation and the above decisions had omitted the parties in the final appeal, then those decisions would have unlawfully excluded parties in the final appeal who are in a position to participate in the litigation, and there would be grounds for retrial analogous to Article 451(1)3 of the Civil Procedure Act (a defect in the grant of legal representative authority, litigation representation authority, or authority necessary for an agent to perform procedural acts) (see Supreme Court Decision 95JAE NU91, Aug. 29, 1997, etc.). If not, and those decisions treated the case as indispensable co-litigation while excluding the plaintiffs who did not appeal from the parties, then they created a third type of litigation other than the previously recognized indispensable co-litigation. If, as in those decisions, the Supreme Court had previously treated such litigation as ordinary co-litigation and the majority opinion changes the prior position through this judgment, the majority opinion should have made that intent clear.\\n\\nBecause judicial practice regarding company-related actions with one-sided erga omnes effect is not clear in this way, there is a strong need, through this case, to clarify what the form of joinder of parties is and thereby prevent confusion in trial practice.\\n\\ne. In accordance with the principles established in the current Civil Procedure Act, joinder of parties can be resolved, and there is no great need to recognize exceptions; accordingly, recognition of exceptions through unnecessary interpretive theory should be avoided.\\n\\nIt cannot be denied that, where the rights and obligations that are the subject matter of litigation are common or arise from a common cause, it is logical and natural for co-litigants to win or lose together. However, under our Civil Procedure Act, the principal form of joinder of parties is ordinary co-litigation, and as noted above, unless there is a “need for uniform and conclusive determination” under law among co-litigants, it is not treated as indispensable co-litigation merely because it is logically and practically desirable that they win or lose together. In order to treat such a type of litigation as indispensable co-litigation, there must be a clear logical basis for recognizing an exception to the principle, but it cannot be said that sufficient argumentation on this point has existed in the past, and no basis for recognizing an exception can be found no matter how closely one examines the matter.\\n\\nWhere multiple persons are related to one legal relationship, if the effect of the judgment obtained by one person does not extend to the others and the dispute cannot be resolved unless all are parties, that is genuine indispensable co-litigation. Conversely, where the effect of the judgment obtained by one person extends to the others, so that regardless of whether several persons each sue or happen to sue jointly, the trial results should not differ, that is quasi-indispensable co-litigation. It is clear that a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect falls into neither category. In such a case, the unification of the trial result among co-litigants can be sufficiently achieved by the common hearing in ordinary co-litigation and the resulting common conviction, and there is no reason or necessity sufficient to justify strictly unifying the litigation materials and litigation progress by applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act.\\n\\nLegal principles must be capable of being applied consistently regardless of whether the number of cases is large or small. Even if they function without issue in most cases, they cannot be correct legal principles if they do not function properly in a minority of cases. In company-related actions, even if most cases are conducted as a single unit because the co-litigants jointly retain litigation counsel, etc., there may always be cases where a party wishes to conduct the litigation independently unless this is compelled. In the former case, the fact that imposing the restrictions of Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act is not unreasonable to the parties does not make it a justified legal principle. The scene in which the legal principle concerning joinder of parties actually makes a difference is the latter case, in which a party wishes to conduct the litigation independently, and even then the legal principle concerning joinder of parties must be justifiable consistently.\\n\\nIt is also not reasonable to treat separate actions differently from joinder of parties on the ground that it is rare for different judgments to be rendered in separate actions. Even if, where parties each bring an action, the cases are mostly consolidated under the provisions on consolidated hearing, consolidation may become impossible because of differences in instance due to the timing of filing, or because another action was overlooked, separate actions may become finalized with different contents. Even in such a case, there is no problem, and the substantive legal relationship is governed according to the erga omnes effect of the favorable judgment. No view can be found asserting that there are procedural-law problems in the subsequently rendered judgment such that grounds for retrial exist. Nonetheless, the majority opinion’s logic that, because of the provisions on consolidated hearing, the trial result must be uniformly determined cannot be a valid ground capable of encompassing cases where consolidation is impossible or not effected.\\n\\nf. This case is examined below.\\n\\nThis action is one jointly brought by two Plaintiffs seeking confirmation of the nonexistence or invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution. According to the legal principles discussed above, this action falls within ordinary co-litigation.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below appears to have conducted the litigation procedure on the premise that this action jointly brought by the Plaintiffs was indispensable co-litigation. Such judgment of the court below contains an error in misconstruing the legal principles regarding the form of joinder of parties. However, because the Plaintiffs jointly retained litigation counsel and conducted the litigation, this error of the court below does not appear to have affected the outcome of the judgment. The determination on the grounds for final appeal is the same as in the majority opinion.\\n\\nAlthough I agree with the majority opinion that there is no ground to reverse the judgment of the court below, I state the reason differently, and thus set forth my separate opinion.\\n\\n5. Supplementary opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyung, Min Yu-sook, and Roh Tae-ak on the majority opinion\\n\\nIn company-related actions with one-sided erga omnes effect, where several persons become plaintiffs jointly, judicial trial practice treats such actions as indispensable co-litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies. Supreme Court Decision 4291MINHANG231, Feb. 19, 1959, in a case under the former Civil Procedure Act before the enactment of the Civil Procedure Act, stated in obiter dictum that an action for confirmation of invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution brought by several persons falls within indispensable co-litigation. Thereafter, although the form of joinder of parties was not at issue and the legal principles thereon were not expressly stated, the courts conducted proceedings on the premise that such actions were indispensable co-litigation. The prevailing academic view is the same not only in the field of civil procedure law but also in corporate law. Such trial practice is based on the need for uniform and conclusive determination under procedural law, and even considering the purpose of the Commercial Act’s provisions on consolidated hearing, as well as the parties’ intentions and litigation economy, its validity can still be recognized. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\na. Whether a case falls within indispensable co-litigation is a matter for the court to determine through interpretation, and there is no absolute standard or normative necessity.\\n\\nArticle 67 of the Civil Procedure Act defines indispensable co-litigation as “co-litigation in which the subject matter of the litigation must be uniformly determined for all co-litigants,” and prescribes special hearing rules therefor. However, because there is no provision specifically defining in what cases the subject matter of the litigation must be uniformly determined for all co-litigants, this must ultimately be determined by the court through interpretation. As also noted in the separate opinion, case law and scholarship classify indispensable co-litigation into “genuine indispensable co-litigation,” in which the parties cannot independently exercise rights or perform obligations under substantive law and must therefore litigate jointly and have the trial result uniformly determined, and “quasi-indispensable co-litigation,” in which separate actions are possible but once the case becomes co-litigation the trial result must be uniformly determined among the parties; this too has been recognized through legal interpretation rather than directly derived from Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act.\\n\\nAmong genuine indispensable co-litigation, there are cases in which several persons jointly become parties as provided by law (e.g., where a third party brings an action for nullity or rescission of marriage, the husband and wife must be co-defendants pursuant to Article 24(2) of the Family Litigation Act), or cases in which the dispute cannot be resolved unless the parties jointly exercise their rights or perform obligations (e.g., the purpose of partition of co-owned property cannot be achieved by litigating only between some co-owners), where the need for uniform and conclusive determination among the parties can readily be recognized, while in many cases, such as actions for performance concerning jointly owned property or co-owned property, this is not clear. There is also the view that, in addition to the attribution of the power to manage and dispose of property, which has traditionally been the standard for recognizing genuine indispensable co-litigation, the scope of recognition should be expanded by considering the unified resolution of disputes and the balancing of parties’ interests. In ordinary co-litigation as well, there are various types ranging from cases that appear to require winning or losing together among co-litigants, such as where the rights and obligations that are the subject matter of the litigation are common among the parties or are mutually dependent under substantive law, to cases with weaker relatedness, and there is also the view that the former should be regarded as quasi-indispensable co-litigation to promote uniform and conclusive determination.\\n\\nThus, there exists a long spectrum of joinder of parties, from genuine indispensable co-litigation, where the need for uniform and conclusive determination among co-litigants is clearly recognized, to ordinary co-litigation, where such need is not recognized. Quasi-indispensable co-litigation, in which litigation joinder is not compelled but, once the action becomes co-litigation, there is a need for uniform and conclusive determination under procedural law, may be said to be located closer to indispensable co-litigation in that spectrum.\\n\\nWhere it is not clear whether a certain type of litigation is ordinary co-litigation or indispensable co-litigation, the court must determine the matter by comprehensively considering the nature of the rights that are the subject matter of the litigation, the substantive and procedural provisions applicable thereto, whether the litigation may be evaluated as being closer to indispensable co-litigation or ordinary co-litigation, and the interests of the parties and litigation economy. There is no absolute boundary or standard, nor is there any logical necessity or normative imperative that anything not falling within the typical types of indispensable co-litigation must be treated as ordinary co-litigation. In this respect, it is difficult to agree with the separate opinion’s basic premise that, in co-litigation for resolving disputes among multiple parties, ordinary co-litigation must necessarily be the principle and indispensable co-litigation an exceptional form departing from that principle. Moreover, even if ordinary co-litigation is the principal form of joinder of parties, the need for uniform and conclusive determination in indispensable co-litigation need not be interpreted mechanically and narrowly.\\n\\nUltimately, the question of in what cases the need for uniform and conclusive determination is recognized, and whether it should be recognized more broadly or narrowly, must be left to the court’s interpretation.\\n\\nb. A company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect requires uniform and conclusive determination under procedural law.\\n\\n1) A company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect, as in this case, falls within quasi-indispensable co-litigation requiring uniform and conclusive determination under procedural law. This is because, where several persons jointly bring the action and one loses while another wins, the effect of the favorable judgment also extends to the person who lost, causing contradictions or conflicts in procedural law between the two judgments.\\n\\nFor example, in the case where shareholders A and B jointly bring an action for confirmation of invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution, if shareholder A loses, shareholder B wins, and the judgment becomes final, not only the adverse judgment received by A himself or herself but also the effect of B’s favorable judgment extends to A, so that the effects of the two judgments with contradictory contents both extend to A. In order to prevent such contradiction or conflict between judgments, it is desirable to regard the action jointly brought by A and B as quasi-indispensable co-litigation requiring uniform and conclusive determination under procedural law.\\n\\nThe separate opinion states that, according to the erga omnes effect of B’s favorable judgment, the shareholders’ meeting resolution becomes uniformly invalid for all interested persons, and the same applies to A, so no contradiction or conflict arises between judgments. However, this merely means that the company treats the shareholders’ meeting resolution as invalid even as to A, and one cannot deny that contradiction or conflict arises between the two judgments in procedural law. The main clause of Article 190 of the Commercial Act, which prescribes one-sided erga omnes effect, is merely the basis for the effect of B’s favorable judgment extending to A, and is not a procedural-law basis for interpreting that the effect of the adverse judgment received by A is extinguished.\\n\\n2) Even if, as the separate opinion says, the problem of contradiction or conflict between judgments can be resolved through the one-sided erga omnes effect provisions, if the case is treated as ordinary co-litigation so that different results may be reached for each co-litigant, the adverse judgment rendered together with the favorable judgment becomes meaningless. In the above joint action by A and B, if A loses and B wins and the judgment becomes final, the effect of B’s favorable judgment also extends to A pursuant to the one-sided erga omnes effect provisions, so A, while having lost, ultimately also prevails, and in the end A’s adverse judgment becomes meaningless. There is no reason for the court to render such a meaningless judgment against A while rendering a single judgment for A and B, and it is difficult to find any need to do so in joinder of parties.\\n\\nIf A and B each brought separate actions and A lost first (even under the consolidated hearing provisions discussed in paragraph c below, differences in filing time, etc. may prevent consolidation), because the adverse judgment against A is not recognized as having erga omnes effect, B may prevail. In such a case, until B’s favorable judgment is rendered, A’s adverse judgment has res judicata effect that prevents repeated claims or arguments in conflict therewith, so it cannot be said that the judgment is useless; moreover, the court hearing A’s action has no way to prevent contradiction or conflict between judgments by considering whether B will file suit later. However, in the case of joinder of parties, because A and B are jointly judged in one judgment as above, the use of a uniform judgment for A and B can prevent meaningless judgments. In this way, the case where one judgment is rendered through joinder of parties and the case where separate judgments are rendered through individual actions cannot be treated the same.\\n\\nFrom this perspective as well, it is reasonable to regard a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect as indispensable co-litigation and thereby make the trial results consistent.\\n\\nc. Even in light of the purpose of the provisions on exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing under the Commercial Act, it is appropriate to regard a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect as indispensable co-litigation.\\n\\nIn the above example, shareholders A and B are not compelled to litigate jointly and may each bring separate actions. In that case, even if A loses first, if B prevails in a separate action, A will receive the effect of both the adverse judgment he or she received and B’s favorable judgment.
