This is because there is no basis to compel litigation joinder among the parties and because erga omnes effect is not recognized for adverse judgments in order to protect the rights and procedural participation of other shareholders (if only one shareholder received an adverse judgment, and thereafter all shareholders were unable to challenge the validity of that shareholders’ meeting resolution, the harm could be severe in cases where the suit was filed in collusion with the company or by someone lacking capacity to conduct the litigation). Even in such a case, one cannot deny that contradiction or conflict between judgments in procedural law arises between the two judgments affecting A.\\n\\nTo prevent such results, the Commercial Act provides that company-related actions with one-sided erga omnes effect fall under the exclusive jurisdiction of the district court having jurisdiction over the company’s head office location, and that if several such actions are filed, the court must hear them in a consolidated manner (see Articles 186 and 188 of the Commercial Act. The above provisions are all applied mutatis mutandis to company-related actions with one-sided erga omnes effect). This is intended to consolidate all actions filed in the same court regarding the same matter and render a uniform judgment. Ultimately, because these Commercial Act provisions also presuppose that the trial result in company-related actions with one-sided erga omnes effect will be uniformly determined, it is an interpretation consistent with the legislative purpose of these provisions to regard such actions as indispensable co-litigation.\\n\\nThe separate opinion states that, because A and B may each file separate actions, with A receiving an adverse judgment and B a favorable judgment, to say that uniform and conclusive determination is needed only when A and B jointly bring the action lacks logical consistency. However, even where A and B each file separate actions, the court, pursuant to the consolidated hearing provisions, will in principle consolidate A and B’s actions and proceed as co-litigation, and the case where consolidation is impossible because of differences in instance due to the timing of filing, etc., is exceptional. Therefore, it is not appropriate for the separate opinion to criticize by comparison with the case where A and B receive judgments in separate actions.\\n\\nd. It cannot necessarily be said that treating a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect as indispensable co-litigation, thereby somewhat restricting the parties’ procedural status, constitutes an unjust infringement of the parties’ procedural rights or runs counter to litigation economy.\\n\\n1) A company-related action in which one-sided erga omnes effect is recognized is an action contesting a company’s collective-law act, such as a shareholders’ meeting resolution, merger, share exchange or transfer, or issuance of new shares. Whether the shareholders jointly brought the action or whether separately brought actions were consolidated and heard together, the shareholders who brought actions of the same content share the same interest in the subject matter of the litigation, with the common purpose of extinguishing the effect of the shareholders’ meeting resolution, etc. In trial practice as well, co-litigants mostly retain litigation counsel together or conduct the litigation as one unit through a designated party, under the same purpose and interest, and this case is no different. This is also the reason why it is difficult to find precedents that have determined to which category—ordinary co-litigation or indispensable co-litigation—such types of co-litigation belong.\\n\\nIn joinder of parties, the parties cooperate and coordinate with one another in order to achieve their common purpose, and need to restrain other co-litigants’ procedural acts from legally or factually operating to their own detriment. If Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies, favorable acts by one party, such as appearance at a hearing or submission of assertions and evidence, are effective against all co-litigants, and adverse procedural acts have no effect unless all do them together. This accords with the intention of the parties pursuing victory, and even if it somewhat restricts the parties’ independent authority concerning the litigation procedure, this cannot be considered unjust.\\n\\nIn a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect, compromise or settlement including acknowledgment of the claim or grant of the claim is impossible (see Supreme Court Decisions 92NU14908, May 27, 1993; 2004DA28047, Sept. 24, 2004, etc.). A party who wishes to waive the claim or not appeal an adverse judgment, that is, a party with no intention to prevail, may withdraw the action and thereby leave the litigation (in quasi-indispensable co-litigation, the consent of the other co-litigants is not required for withdrawal of the action; see Supreme Court Decision 2011DU13729, Mar. 28, 2013, etc.). Furthermore, even where only some of the losing plaintiffs appeal, the finalization of the judgment as to all plaintiffs is blocked and the case is transferred to the appellate instance (in a case where the plaintiffs prevailed, it is practically difficult to assume that the corporate defendant would not appeal as to some of the plaintiffs), plaintiffs who do not appeal and have no intention of conducting the litigation in the appellate instance bear no duty to conduct the litigation or to bear the litigation costs in the appellate instance, and may withdraw the action as above. Accordingly, even if applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act to a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect somewhat restricts the parties’ power to dispose of the subject matter of litigation, this cannot be deemed unjust.\\n\\n2) Treating a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect as indispensable co-litigation does not contravene litigation economy. If Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies, even from the perspective of the opposing party or the court, assertions and evidence need not be separated by co-litigant, and all assertions and evidence may be treated uniformly as either effective or ineffective against all, making response to the action and the process of hearing and determination far simpler. Although more time may be required for service, etc., in order to proceed with litigation involving multiple parties, the court can properly exercise its authority to direct the litigation and prevent delays in trial. If one co-litigant dies, in company-related actions there are mostly litigation representatives, so the proceedings are not suspended (Civil Procedure Act Article 238); even if not, the court can, ex officio, issue an order to continue and thereby resolve the suspended state (Civil Procedure Act Article 244).\\n\\n3) Ultimately, even if treating a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect as indispensable co-litigation somewhat restricts the parties’ procedural status, it cannot be said to unjustly infringe the parties’ procedural rights or contravene litigation economy.\\n\\ne. There is no basis to recognize a need to change the current established trial practice.\\n\\n1) The Civil Procedure Act, wholly amended in 2002, newly established preliminary or alternative joinder of parties, which had previously been disallowed, as a type of joinder of parties (Civil Procedure Act Article 70), and broadened the scope of permitted independent party intervention by allowing one-sided independent party intervention against one side of the parties (Civil Procedure Act Article 79). The Supreme Court en banc Decision 2012DA46170, rendered on 2019. 10. 23., took into account the purpose of this amendment to the Civil Procedure Act and changed prior precedent that viewed overlapping claims by a plaintiff and a successor intervenor in a succession intervention involving transfer of rights as being in an ordinary co-litigation relationship, holding instead that Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies. Such actions are ones in which joint litigation is not compelled among the parties and in which the effect of the judgment does not extend among the co-litigants or between the original parties and the intervenor; thus, they had previously been treated as ordinary co-litigation. Nevertheless, because differing trial results as to claims that are substantively incompatible may cause a party to effectively lose rights or bear obligations twice, Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act came to be applied in order to resolve the dispute once and without contradiction and to protect the parties’ interests.\\n\\nAs noted above, there are various views even regarding the standard for recognizing genuine indispensable co-litigation, and there is also the view that, in co-ownership litigation or an action for confirmation of ownership against multiple persons or claims against multiple joint and several debtors, where uniform and conclusive determination among co-litigants is theoretically and logically required, such cases should be regarded as quasi-indispensable co-litigation and uniform and conclusive determination should be pursued. With respect to the question of in what cases the uniform and conclusive determination of the trial result should be deemed necessary and Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act should be applied, there is no absolute standard or normative necessity, and it cannot be said that applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act is necessarily disadvantageous to co-litigants or contrary to litigation economy. Considering these various aspects, the trial practice of treating a company-related action with one-sided erga omnes effect as indispensable co-litigation can still be considered valid, and there is no need to recognize the necessity of changing it.\\n\\n2) The separate opinion mentions decisions in which, where only some of the joint plaintiffs under the judgment of the court below appealed in company-related actions, the plaintiffs who had not appealed were not described as parties to the Supreme Court judgment, and states that it is clear that the Supreme Court has traditionally premised such actions on being ordinary co-litigation. However, in all of those cases, the plaintiffs lost in the court below, some plaintiffs appealed, and the appeals were dismissed, so the form of joinder of parties or who the parties were was not at all at issue, and the Court never declared case-law on this issue. As noted above, regarding company-related actions with one-sided erga omnes effect as quasi-indispensable co-litigation is the prevailing academic view, the issue had not previously been raised, and the courts’ trial practice has accepted it as established doctrine. Those decisions cannot be used to say that the Supreme Court had previously taken the opposite position or that its position was unclear. However, it is noted that, in future trial practice, where only some parties to quasi-indispensable co-litigation appeal, care must be taken to proceed on the understanding that co-litigants who did not appeal should also be treated as parties in the appellate instance.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, this supplementary opinion is stated on the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. The supplementary opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek to the separate opinion is as follows.\\n\\nAs a related matter, I examine the form of joint trial and the structure of a trial decision cancellation action where, pursuant to Article 139(1) of the Patent Act, two or more persons jointly request a trial for invalidation of the same patent right.\\n\\nSupreme Court Decision 2007HU1510, May 28, 2009, held that if a trial decision invalidating a patent becomes final, the patent becomes invalid even in relation to third parties, that is, on the basis of the erga omnes effect of a patent invalidation trial decision, and then, when two or more persons jointly request a trial for invalidation of the same patent right, such a matter constitutes quasi-indispensable joint trial; it further held that if the patent holder who lost in the above trial case files an action to cancel the trial decision against only one of the joint trial applicants, finalization of the trial decision is also blocked as to the other joint trial applicant. However, the above decision is not valid for the following reasons and must be changed in future contested cases.\\n\\na. There is no legal need for uniform and conclusive determination among joint trial applicants.\\n\\nWhere several persons each separately file a request for a trial for invalidation of the same patent right, the result of the trial may differ depending on each trial applicant’s assertions and proof. For example, if A and B each separately request a trial for invalidation of the same patent right, A may receive a trial decision dismissing the request, while B may receive a trial decision invalidating the patent. In this case, because erga omnes effect is recognized for B’s invalidation decision and the patent becomes invalid as to all persons, including A (Patent Act Article 133(3)), no problem arises from contradiction or conflict between the invalidation decision and the dismissal decision. Even if the dismissal decision first becomes final in one case, another pending trial case that was filed earlier does not violate Article 163 of the Patent Act in relation to the final dismissal decision, and thus there is no obstacle to issuing a trial decision invalidating the patent (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009HU2234, Jan. 19, 2012). However, if the invalidation decision first becomes final, the patent right is retroactively extinguished, and another pending trial request by a different person is dismissed as improper due to extinction of the object of the trial.\\n\\nEven where A and B do not each separately request a trial for invalidation but instead jointly request a trial for invalidation (Patent Act Article 139(1)), or where their separately filed requests for trial for invalidation are consolidated (Patent Act Article 160), similarly there is no need for the trial decision to be uniformly determined between A and B.\\n\\nb. Patent trials are governed by the ex officio examination principle, so the question whether Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act premised on the principle of pleading applies is not at issue.\\n\\nAs noted in the separate opinion, in civil litigation where the principle of pleading is the rule, each party conducts litigation at his or her own responsibility, without help or interference from other co-litigants, and bears responsibility only for his or her own procedural acts. Under this principle of pleading, trial results among co-litigants may differ, so Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, in indispensable co-litigation, partially modifies the principles of pleading and disposition to unify litigation materials (assertions and evidence) among co-litigants so that the trial result may be uniformly determined.\\n\\nHowever, patent trials are governed not by the principle of pleading but by the ex officio examination principle. In patent trials, the tribunal may examine grounds not requested by the parties (Patent Act Article 159(1)), and may examine evidence ex officio (Patent Act Article 157(1)).\\n\\nQuasi-indispensable co-litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies also basically concerns proceedings to which the principle of pleading applies, so the court cannot decide on the basis of facts asserted or proved by none of the co-litigants. However, in a patent trial, the examiners are not bound by the parties’ assertions or proof and may hear and determine facts not asserted by any party. Separate measures to unify litigation materials among joint trial applicants are naturally unnecessary.\\n\\nThus, in patent trial proceedings governed by the ex officio examination principle, there is no reason to import the concept of indispensable co-litigation premised on the principle of pleading. The above Supreme Court decision overlooked the fundamental difference between civil litigation and patent trial proceedings, between the principle of pleading and the ex officio examination principle, and the procedural-law status of Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, namely that it is a provision applicable to proceedings governed by the principle of pleading.\\n\\nc. Patent trials and patent trial decision cancellation actions are separate proceedings with no instance-based connection, so the legal principle concerning appeals in indispensable co-litigation cannot be applied as is.\\n\\nThe above Supreme Court decision, after treating a joint trial for invalidation of a patent filed by two or more persons as quasi-indispensable joint trial, drew the conclusion that if the patent holder files an action to cancel the trial decision for patent invalidation against only one of the joint trial applicants, finalization of the trial decision is also blocked as to the remaining joint trial applicants. As already noted in the separate opinion, prior case law held that, in indispensable co-litigation, if an appeal is filed only against some of the co-litigants, finalization of the judgment as to the remaining co-litigants who did not appeal is also blocked, the case is transferred to the appellate instance, and the co-litigants who did not appeal also become parties in the appellate instance; the above Supreme Court decision appears to have applied this legal principle concerning appeals in indispensable co-litigation to patent trials and trial decision cancellation actions.\\n\\nHowever, the above legal principle concerning appeals in indispensable co-litigation presupposes an instance-based connection within a litigation, such as between the first instance and the appellate instance or between the appellate instance and the final appeal instance, and is intended to keep all co-litigants in party status until the end where an appeal is filed only against some co-litigants, so that the trial result for all co-litigants may be unified. There is no basis to view this legal principle as applying also to distinct proceedings such as where, after an administrative trial, an administrative action related thereto is filed, or where, after an administrative disposition, an action for administrative appeal is filed against it. Patent trials are administrative trial proceedings, and an action to cancel a trial decision is an administrative action against them; they are separate proceedings with different decision-makers and different procedural laws, and there is no instance-based connection between them, so a person who is not a defendant in an action to cancel a trial decision cannot become a party to the cancellation action. For example, if A and B jointly request a trial for invalidation against C and receive a decision invalidating the patent, and then C files an action to cancel the trial decision naming only A as defendant, B cannot become a party to the cancellation action. As to B, no action to cancel the trial decision has been filed, and B is not a party to the cancellation action; there is no basis to say that finalization of the trial decision as to B is blocked.\\n\\nIn indispensable co-litigation, even if C appeals only against A, one of the successful plaintiffs A and B, the effect of that appeal extends to B, thereby also blocking finalization of the judgment as to B and transferring the case to the appellate instance, so that B also becomes a party in the appellate instance. If the above Supreme Court decision viewed patent trials and trial decision cancellation actions as having an instance-based connection and thus applied the above legal principle as is, then if C filed an action to cancel the trial decision only against A, the effect of filing suit should likewise have extended to B, making B a party to the cancellation action. The above Supreme Court decision, in any event, misapplied the legal principle concerning appeals in indispensable co-litigation.\\n\\nd. According to the above Supreme Court decision, the procedural rights of joint trial applicants are unjustly infringed.\\n\\nAccording to the above Supreme Court decision, if A and B jointly request invalidation and receive a trial decision invalidating the patent, even if the patent holder files suit against only one of A and B, finalization of the trial decision as to the other person is also blocked. As a result, the patent holder may file suit only against A, who has less capacity to conduct litigation among A and B, exclude B from the litigation procedure, and easily obtain a favorable judgment. B will think that the trial decision invalidating the patent as to himself or herself has become final because the period for filing an action against the decision has elapsed, but will then face the result that even his or her own trial decision is canceled depending on the result of A’s action to cancel the trial decision, which was conducted without B being included. This not only infringes B’s procedural rights, but also is unreasonable because, due to the accidental fact that A and B’s request for invalidation was filed as a joint trial, it gives the patent holder an opportunity to arbitrarily choose the litigation opponent.\\n\\nIf A and B each separately requested a trial for invalidation with respect to the same patent right and received a trial decision invalidating the patent, the patent holder must of course file an action to cancel the trial decision against both A and B. If the patent holder files suit only against A, the trial decision as to B becomes final upon lapse of the filing period, and the patent becomes invalid as to all pursuant to the erga omnes effect of the invalidation decision; the action against A would lack legal interest and should be dismissed as improper. It cannot be said that viewing it this way is particularly unfavorable or unjust to the patent holder.\\n\\ne. The above discussion is not directly related to the issue concerning company-related actions with one-sided erga omnes effect discussed in the majority opinion and the separate opinion. It is only that the legal principle in the above Supreme Court decision also arises from misconstruing the form of joint trial or Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, and I wish to point this out together on this occasion.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, this supplementary opinion to the separate opinion is stated."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the civil dispute resolution system is incorrect? (In cases of dispute, according to case law)
A: A compromise agreement takes effect when the parties mutually make concessions and agree to end the dispute between them, and it has the effect that the right conceded by one party is extinguished and the other party acquires that right by reason of the compromise.
B: A party may not delegate to the opposing party the right to appoint a representative for a pre-litigation compromise.
C: In the small claims case trial procedure, an order recommending performance has the same effect as a final judgment if no objection is filed within the objection period, if the order dismissing the objection becomes final, or if the objection is withdrawn.
D: A court, a designated judge, or a commissioned judge may, ex officio, taking into account the interests of the parties and all other circumstances, issue a settlement recommendation decision for the equitable resolution of a case pending in litigation, within the scope that does not contravene the object of the claim.
E: When no objection is filed to a payment order, or when the objection is withdrawn, or when the dismissal decision becomes final, the payment order has the same effect as a final judgment and therefore has res judicata and executory force.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DA73966]": "Each ground of appeal shall be determined (the statements in the supplemental appellate brief submitted after the deadline for filing the appellate brief shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Determination on the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. With respect to Grounds of Appeal Nos. 1 and 2\\n\\nThe court below, after comprehensively reviewing the evidence it adopted, recognized the facts as stated in its opinion, and then determined that the Plaintiff is obligated, based on the agreement that he would comply with the Defendant’s management rules, to pay the management expenses recognized by the court below, corresponding to the general management expenses and common management expenses imposed on the unsold stores owned by the Plaintiff; and that, in light of the agreement reached at the three-party consultative body meeting, the resolution of the Plaintiff’s extraordinary general meeting dated July 21, 2000, the Plaintiff’s duty to arrange leases of stores for the buyers, the status of payment of management expenses, and other relevant circumstances, the Plaintiff is obligated to pay the management expenses incurred until the completion inspection of the ○○ Shopping Center with respect to the stores entrusted to be leased in this case owned by a third party and the unsold stores on the snack floor, pursuant to the agreement between the Plaintiff and the Defendant thus recognized.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the court below’s judgment in light of the relevant evidence and the record, the foregoing fact-finding and determination by the court below are all proper and persuasive, and there is no violation of the rules of evidence or error of law as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as regarding the existence or absence of the Defendant’s right to claim management expenses, the details of the management expenses, or the validity of the extraordinary general meeting resolution dated July 21, 2000. The argument in the grounds of appeal on this point is without merit.\\n\\nb. With respect to Ground of Appeal No. 3\\n\\nArticle 505, paragraph 2 of the former Civil Procedure Act applicable to the first payment order in this case (as amended by Act No. 4201 on January 13, 1990, and before the full revision by Act No. 6626 on January 26, 2002; hereinafter referred to as the “former Civil Procedure Act”) provides that an objection to claim against a final judgment may be raised only when the cause thereof arose after the closing of oral argument; however, Article 521, paragraph 2 of the same Act provides that the assertion of an objection to a claim concerning a payment order shall not be subject to the restrictions under Article 505 of that Act. Accordingly, in an action of objection to a claim against a final payment order, not only causes such as extinguishment of the claim or grounds preventing the exercise of the claim arising after the issuance of the payment order, but also non-accrual or invalidity of the claim before the issuance of the payment order, constitute grounds for objection (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DA11346 dated May 14, 2004). Meanwhile, Article 474 of the current Civil Procedure Act applicable to the second payment order in this case provides that a final payment order has the same effect as a final judgment; however, unlike Article 44, paragraph 2 of the Civil Execution Act, which limits the grounds for an objection to claim against a final judgment to those arising after the conclusion of oral argument (or, in the case of a judgment rendered without oral argument, after the pronouncement of judgment), Article 58, paragraph 3 of the Civil Execution Act provides that the provisions of Article 44, paragraph 2 shall not apply to the assertion of an objection to a claim concerning a payment order. Therefore, even in a payment order under the current Civil Procedure Act, grounds such as non-accrual or invalidity of a claim arising before the issuance of the payment order may be asserted in an action of objection concerning that payment order. In this sense, res judicata is not recognized for payment orders under not only the former Civil Procedure Act but also the current Civil Procedure Act.\\n\\nTherefore, even if the Plaintiff’s former representative of the association acted in violation of the principle of good faith by causing each payment order in this case to become final for the benefit of the Defendant, contrary to the substantive legal relationship, unlike in an objection to claim against a final judgment, such a circumstance does not constitute an independent ground for objection in an action of objection to a claim against a payment order to which res judicata does not apply; only the fact that it is contrary to the substantive legal relationship itself may constitute a ground for objection.\\n\\nAlthough there are some points in the court below’s explanation of reasons on this part that are not entirely appropriate, the conclusion rejecting the Plaintiff’s assertion on this part is proper; therefore, there is no error in the judgment below that affected the judgment. The argument in the grounds of appeal on this point is without merit.\\n\\n2. Determination on the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. With respect to the point that the Plaintiff bears the obligation to pay management expenses even after the completion inspection\\n\\nThe court below, after comprehensively reviewing the evidence it adopted, recognized the facts as stated in its opinion, and then, pursuant to the agreement between the Plaintiff and the Defendant as recognized in light of the agreement at the three-party consultative body meeting and the Plaintiff’s above extraordinary general meeting resolution, determined that the Plaintiff is obligated to pay the management expenses concerning the unsold stores on the snack floor in this case until the completion inspection date; however, the fact that the Plaintiff stated at the three-party consultative body meeting that he would take full responsibility for and resolve the problem of the unsold stores on the snack floor in this case, namely, the problem that although they were sold, the buyers did not occupy the relevant stores because the number of units sold alone was not suitable for business, does not mean that the Plaintiff agreed to bear the obligation to pay the management expenses for the unsold stores on the snack floor in this case even after the completion inspection of the ○○ Shopping Center, and furthermore, it determined that the sales contract does not directly apply to the legal relationship between the Plaintiff and the Defendant so that it cannot be deemed that the Plaintiff bears the obligation to pay management expenses for the above stores owned by a third party in relation to the Defendant. It then rejected the Defendant’s argument that the Plaintiff had an obligation to pay management expenses for the unsold stores on the snack floor after the completion inspection.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the court below’s judgment in light of the relevant evidence and the record, the above fact-finding and determination by the court below are proper and persuasive, and there is no violation of the rules of evidence or error of law regarding the agreement of the three-party consultative body, or the content or effect of the sales contract, as alleged in the grounds of appeal. In addition, it is clear that the above determination by the court below was intended to reject the Defendant’s alternative argument that the Plaintiff had an obligation to pay electricity charges after the completion inspection pursuant to the resolution of the Plaintiff’s board of directors dated February 5, 2001; therefore, it cannot be said that the judgment below contains an error of omission in its determination. All arguments in the grounds of appeal on this point are without merit.\\n\\nb. With respect to the point that the application of delay damages is unlawful\\n\\n(1) As to the statutory interest rate that serves as the basis for calculating damages arising from non-performance of a monetary obligation, the rate prescribed in Article 3, paragraph 1 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning Expedition, etc., of Legal Proceedings (hereinafter referred to as the “Act on Expedition of Litigation”) may be applied from the day following the date on which the complaint seeking performance of the monetary obligation, or a document equivalent thereto, is served on the debtor. However, pursuant to Article 3, paragraph 2 of the same Act, where it is recognized that the debtor reasonably contested the existence or scope of the obligation until the pronouncement of a fact-finding judgment declaring the existence of the duty to perform, such rate may not be applied within the reasonable period. Since res judicata is not recognized for a payment order, if, in an action of objection to claim filed for the purpose of excluding the enforceability of a payment order, the objection is partially upheld on grounds such as partial non-accrual or extinguishment of the claim that arose before the issuance of the payment order, it shall be deemed that, from before the payment order until the pronouncement of the fact-finding judgment on the objection to claim, there was a reasonable basis for contesting the existence or scope of the duty to perform with respect to that claim; thus, the statutory interest rate under the above Act on Expedition of Litigation may not be applied within that period.\\n\\nIn addition, in an action of objection to a claim concerning a payment order in which several claims are joined, the foregoing legal principle must apply to each cause of action joined in that payment order; therefore, whether it was reasonable to contest the existence or scope of the duty to perform must be determined separately for each claim, and in a management expense claim action such as this case, it is reasonable to regard each store that is the subject of the management expense claim as constituting one cause of action.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Constitutional Court’s decision dated April 24, 2003 in Case No. 2002HEONGA15 declared Article 3, paragraph 1 of the former Act on Special Cases Concerning Expedition, etc., of Legal Proceedings (before amendment by Act No. 6868 on May 10, 2003; hereinafter referred to as the “former Act on Expedition of Litigation,” and the Act after amendment as the “amended Act on Expedition of Litigation”) unconstitutional, and accordingly the effectiveness of that provision ceased. The effect of a constitutional ruling of unconstitutionality by the Constitutional Court extends to general cases filed after such ruling unless otherwise unavoidable for the maintenance of legal stability or the protection of the parties’ reliance interests (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 92DA12377 dated January 15, 1993). As noted above, since res judicata is not recognized with respect to a payment order, if an objection to claim is partially upheld on grounds arising before the payment order, the question of whether the interest rate prescribed by the amended Act on Expedition of Litigation applies may be reviewed again. In light of this, where an action of objection to claim is filed to exclude the enforceability of a payment order, the remaining scope of such enforceability should be determined by applying the relevant provisions of the Civil Act and the amended Act on Expedition of Litigation, not Article 3, paragraph 1 of the former Act on Expedition of Litigation whose effect has ceased.\\n\\n(2) The court below, after comprehensively reviewing the evidence it adopted, recognized the facts as stated in its opinion, and then determined that the management expense claim relating to the unsold stores on the snack floor in this case, included in the first and second management expense claims in this case, arising after January 2001, had not accrued before the respective payment orders, and accordingly denied the Plaintiff’s obligation to pay that portion of the management expenses. Therefore, among the Plaintiff’s obligations upheld by the court below in this case, the management expenses for the unsold stores on the snack floor owned by the Plaintiff included in the first management expense claim in this case are reduced in amount as compared with the payment order, and thus it may be recognized that the Plaintiff reasonably contested the existence or scope of the duty to perform until the date of the pronouncement of the judgment below; however, as to the management expenses for the stores owned by the Plaintiff and the stores entrusted to be leased among the first and second management expense claims, which differ in cause of action from the above, since the court below determined, as in the payment order, that the Defendant’s claim for management expenses was well founded, it cannot be deemed, absent other special circumstances, that the Plaintiff’s contest on this part was reasonable.\\n\\n(3) Nevertheless, the court below, with respect to the management expenses for the stores owned by the Plaintiff and the stores entrusted to be leased among the management expenses it recognized, deemed that the Plaintiff reasonably contested the existence or scope of the duty to perform even for the period from after service of the authenticated copy of the payment order until June 1, 2003, the effective date of the above amended Act on Expedition of Litigation, to October 11, 2006, the date of the pronouncement of the judgment below, and did not apply the interest rate prescribed by the above amended Act on Expedition of Litigation. In doing so, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principle and thereby affecting the judgment. The argument in the grounds of appeal on this point is well founded within this scope.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, among the judgment of the court below, the portion denying compulsory execution with respect to the delay damages at an annual rate in excess of 5% and not exceeding 20% concerning the management expenses of 886,277,372 won for the stores owned by the Plaintiff and the stores entrusted to be leased, for the period from June 1, 2003 to October 11, 2006, under subparagraph 1(a), and the delay damages at an annual rate in excess of 5% and not exceeding 20% concerning the management expenses of 390,342,460 won for the stores owned by the Plaintiff, for the period from June 1, 2003 to October 11, 2006, under subparagraph 1(b), shall be reversed. However, since this Court can directly decide this part, it shall render its own judgment, dismiss the Plaintiff’s appeal corresponding to the reversed part, and dismiss both the Plaintiff’s appeal and the remainder of the Defendant’s appeal, and accordingly render judgment as ordered, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Clan Association A owns X forest land, which B is occupying and using without authorization. Accordingly, A filed an action, on behalf of Clan Association A, against B for restitution of unjust enrichment equivalent to rent. Which of the following statements concerning this is incorrect? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law applies)
A: If, in response to the first-instance judgment dismissing the action on the ground of A’s defect in representative authority, only A appealed, and the appellate court, after hearing the case, determines that the defect in representative authority has been cured so that the action is lawful but the claim is without merit, it must render a judgment dismissing the appeal.
B: If, in the first instance, B had asserted a defense of set-off using as the automatic claim a claim for construction payment that B held against Clan Association A, and after receiving a merits determination on that defense withdrew the set-off defense in the appellate court, then B’s subsequent filing of a separate action seeking payment of the above construction price is inadmissible.
C: Even if Clan Association A obtained a final judgment in its favor in the above lawsuit, if it again files the same action (the later action) in order to interrupt prescription because the expiration of the extinctive prescription period for the claim based on that final judgment is imminent, the court in the later action may not again examine whether all requirements for asserting the final and conclusive right are satisfied.
D: If Clan Association A obtained a final judgment in its favor in the above lawsuit and again filed the same action (the later action) in order to interrupt the extinctive prescription of the claim based on that final judgment, a fact of performance arising after the conclusion of oral argument in the fact-finding stage of the prior action is a subject of review in the later action.
E: If Clan Association A, after 10 years have elapsed since obtaining a final judgment in its favor in the above lawsuit, again files the same action (the later action) in order to interrupt the extinctive prescription of the claim based on that final judgment, the court must not, absent special circumstances, immediately dismiss the later action on the ground that there is no benefit of action.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2018DA24349]": "The Court examines ex officio.\\n\\n1. A final judgment in favor of the prevailing party has res judicata effect; therefore, where a party who has obtained a final judgment in its favor files an action against the opposing party in the prior action seeking again the same claim as in the prior action covered by the final judgment in favor, the subsequent action is, absent special circumstances, unlawful for lack of legal interest in protection of rights. However, exceptionally, where the expiration of the 10-year statute of limitations for a claim fixed by a final judgment is imminent, an action to interrupt prescription has an interest in the suit (see Supreme Court Decision 87DAKA1761, decided on November 10, 1987, and Supreme Court en banc Decision 2018DA22008, decided on July 19, 2018, among others).\\n\\nThis is because, when a party needlessly files again the same action while the 10-year statute of limitations for the claim is not yet imminent to expire after the judgment in its favor has become final, no interest in protection of rights can be recognized in light of the res judicata effect of the final judgment; however, where the expiration of that period is imminent, there is a necessity for interrupting prescription, and thus the interest in filing the subsequent action is recognized.\\n\\nMeanwhile, since a judgment in the subsequent action for interruption of prescription must not conflict with the contents of the final judgment in favor in the prior action, the court in the subsequent action may not again review whether all requirements for asserting the finalized right are satisfied (see the above Supreme Court en banc Decision 2018DA22008, among others). However, because the res judicata effect of the above judgment in the subsequent action arises based on the time of the conclusion of oral argument in the subsequent action, grounds for extinguishment of the claim, such as performance, set-off, release, etc., arising after the conclusion of oral argument in the prior action become the subject of review in the subsequent action. Accordingly, the Defendant, who is the debtor, may raise such defenses in the subsequent proceedings, and if, as a result of review, such assertions are accepted, the court must dismiss the Plaintiff’s claim. The same applies where the claim is extinguished by completion of the statute of limitations, which is one of the grounds for extinguishment of a claim.\\n\\nThus, considering the purport of viewing differently the legal interest in protection of rights in a subsequent action for interruption of prescription depending on whether the expiration of the statute of limitations for a claim fixed by judgment is imminent, and the effect of completion of the statute of limitations for a claim, the court hearing a subsequent action for interruption of prescription, unless there are special circumstances, such as where, after the prior judgment became final, prescription was interrupted and the newly running statute of limitations from the time the ground for interruption ceased is not yet imminent to expire so that no interest in refiling the action can be recognized, must not immediately dismiss the action for lack of interest in the suit merely because the subsequent action was filed more than 10 years after the prior judgment became final, but must make a determination on the merits as to whether the Plaintiff’s claim has been extinguished by completion of the statute of limitations in accordance with the Defendant debtor’s defense.\\n\\n2. According to the reasoning of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na. The Plaintiff filed an action against the Defendant before the Cheonan Branch of the Daejeon District Court, Case No. 2005GADAN10513, seeking payment of KRW 70,000,000 as damages, and on December 22, 2005, the said court issued a decision in lieu of conciliation, to the effect that the Defendant shall pay the Plaintiff KRW 25,000,000 by March 10, 2006, and that if payment is delayed, additional delay damages shall be paid thereon (hereinafter referred to as “the compulsory conciliation decision in this case”); and the said compulsory conciliation decision became final on January 24, 2006.\\n\\nb. The Plaintiff also filed an action against the Defendant before the Cheonan Branch of the Daejeon District Court, Case No. 2006GADAN9930, seeking return of the purchase price following rescission of a sales contract, and on September 21, 2006, the said court rendered a judgment to the effect that the Defendant shall pay the Plaintiff KRW 25,000,000 and delay damages (hereinafter referred to as “the prior judgment in this case”); and the said judgment became final on October 11, 2006.\\n\\nc. On April 28, 2017, the Plaintiff filed the present action seeking payment of money based on the claims fixed by the compulsory conciliation decision in this case and the prior judgment in this case (hereinafter referred to as “the prior judgment, etc. in this case”), and through the motion for amendment of the purport of claim and cause of claim submitted to the court of first instance on October 19, 2017, clarified that the action was filed again to interrupt prescription for each of the above claims.\\n\\n3. According to the reasoning of the lower court judgment, the lower court maintained the judgment of the first instance, which dismissed the action ex officio, on the ground that the present action is an action involving, as the subject matter of litigation, the same rights and legal relations as the prior action in which a final judgment in favor was obtained or a compulsory conciliation decision having the same effect became final, and that it was filed more than 10 years after the prior judgment, etc. in this case became final, from the time the rights could be exercised, and therefore there was no interest in seeking interruption of prescription, rendering it unlawful.\\n\\nExamining the above facts in light of the legal principles previously stated, even if the present action was filed more than 10 years after the prior judgment, etc. in this case became final, as an action for interrupting prescription for each claim fixed by the already final prior judgment, etc. in this case, it cannot be viewed as immediately unlawful for lack of interest in the suit merely on that basis; accordingly, the lower court’s determination as above is erroneous.\\n\\nHowever, according to the record, the Defendant argued in the lower court that the statute of limitations for the claim fixed by the prior judgment, etc. in this case had been completed, and insofar as the lower court’s factual finding that the present action was filed after more than 10 years, which is the statute of limitations period for the claim, had elapsed following the finalization of the prior judgment, etc. in this case, is justified, it is clear that the claim based on the prior judgment, etc. in this case has been extinguished by completion of the statute of limitations, and the Plaintiff’s claim in this case will consequently be dismissed. Therefore, in this case, in which only the Plaintiff appealed, it is appropriate, under the principle prohibiting unfavorable modification, to leave the lower judgment as it is and dismiss the Plaintiff’s appeal.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without addressing the grounds for appeal, the Plaintiff’s appeal is dismissed, and the appellate costs shall be borne by the losing party; by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court participating, the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2021DA275741]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Whether it constitutes duplicate filing of a lawsuit or violates the principle prohibiting refiling (Grounds of Appeal No. 2)\\n\\na. If, at the time the defense of set-off was filed, an action based on the same claim as the active claim was already separately filed and pending, it is desirable for the panel in charge of the fact-finding court to prevent conflict or inconsistency with res judicata and, at the same time, to promote litigation economy by attempting transfer to another division, transfer of the case, or consolidation of pleadings so that the earlier action and the later action may be heard and decided at the same time; however, it cannot be said that, absent special circumstances, an assertion of set-off in litigation with a claim pending as a separate action as the active claim is impermissible (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2000DA4050, rendered April 27, 2000). Likewise, after filing a defense of set-off in the action first filed, it is also possible, while that action is pending, to file an action based on the same claim as the active claim as a separate action or as a counterclaim.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 267(2) of the Civil Procedure Act provides, “A person who has withdrawn an action after a final and conclusive judgment on the merits has been rendered may not file the same action again.” This is a provision with a sanctionary purpose, aimed at preventing an improper situation in which the court’s effort invested in the judgment is rendered useless by withdrawal of the action and the same dispute is raised again, thereby abusing the litigation system (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2018DA259213, rendered May 7, 2021). However, unlike withdrawal of an action, which has effect only with the opposing party’s consent after the opposing party has filed a preparatory brief on the merits or made statements or arguments at a preparatory hearing, a defense of set-off as a litigation defense is a type of preliminary defense made on the premise that the existence of the passive claim is established, and it may be withdrawn without the opposing party’s consent; in such a case, under the principle of dispositive power, the court may not adjudicate it (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2011DA23323, rendered July 14, 2011). Therefore, even if the defense of set-off was filed at the first instance of the earlier-filed action and the merits were adjudicated by the first-instance judgment, and then the defense of set-off was withdrawn at the appellate instance, this is merely a withdrawal of a litigation defense, and the principle prohibiting refiling under Article 267(2) of the Civil Procedure Act does not apply; accordingly, an action based on the same claim as the active claim may be separately filed.\\n\\nb. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\nThe Defendant filed against the Plaintiff an action for construction price under the construction contract at issue (hereinafter referred to as the “Prior Action”). The Plaintiff asserted a defense of set-off, using as the active claim a claim for damages in lieu of repair of defects, in the first instance of the Prior Action (Busan District Court 2017GASO505896), but the first instance of the Prior Action, on September 5, 2017, rejected the Plaintiff’s defense of set-off on the ground that proof as to the existence of defects, etc. was insufficient, and rendered a judgment entirely in favor of the Defendant. On April 5, 2018, the Plaintiff separately filed this action against the Defendant seeking damages in lieu of repair of defects in the construction work at issue, and then withdrew the above defense of set-off at the second hearing date in the appellate instance of the Prior Action (Busan District Court 2017NA56896).\\n\\nc. Examining these factual circumstances in light of the legal principles stated above, even if the Plaintiff had already asserted, in the Prior Action, a defense of set-off using as the active claim a claim for damages in lieu of repair of defects, it is also permissible for the Plaintiff to separately file this action based on the same claim as that active claim while the Prior Action was pending. In addition, even if the Plaintiff withdrew the defense of set-off in the appellate instance after receiving a merits determination on the defense of set-off at the first instance of the Prior Action, this does not mean that the Plaintiff became unable to seek damages in lieu of repair of defects.\\n\\nAccordingly, the argument in this part of the grounds of appeal, to the effect that the filing of this action constituted duplicate filing prohibited by Article 259 of the Civil Procedure Act or violated the refiling prohibition provision of Article 267(2) of the Civil Procedure Act, and that the lower court should have dismissed this action but instead rendered a judgment on the merits, thereby overlooking the defect in litigation requirements subject to ex officio review and continuing the proceedings, cannot be accepted.\\n\\n2. Whether there was a violation of the rules of evidence in calculating the amount of damages (Grounds of Appeal No. 1)\\n\\nThe lower court, by comprehensively considering the evidence cited in its judgment, found that defects existed in the building at issue and that a total of 83,154,169 won (including temporary construction costs for repair of defects) would be required for the repair of such defects, and then, taking into account all circumstances revealed in the pleadings, limited the amount of damages in lieu of repair of defects to 66,523,335 won, which is 80% of the above repair costs, pursuant to the principle of equity or the principle of good faith and fair dealing.\\n\\nExamining the record in accordance with the relevant legal principles, the above determination by the lower court does not contain, as argued in the grounds of appeal, any error that violated the laws of logic and experience, exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence, or otherwise affected the judgment due to misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning the probative force of a final judgment, lack of reasons, or the like.\\n\\n3. Whether it is contrary to res judicata concerning the defense of set-off (Grounds of Appeal No. 3)\\n\\na. Article 216(1) of the Civil Procedure Act provides, “A final and conclusive judgment shall have res judicata only with respect to what is included in the main text of the judgment,” thereby stipulating that, in principle, res judicata does not extend to determinations contained in the reasons for the judgment, while, as an exception, Paragraph 2 provides, “The determination of whether the claim asserting set-off is established or not shall have res judicata only with respect to the amount countered by way of set-off.” The reason why res judicata is recognized for the court’s determination concerning an assertion of set-off, despite its being a determination contained in the reasons for the judgment, is that if res judicata were not recognized for such determination, the dispute over the existence or nonexistence of the Plaintiff’s claim would later be transformed into a dispute over the existence or nonexistence of the active claim raised in another action, so that the opposing party to the set-off assertion would not only be exposed to disadvantage by the person asserting set-off exercising the active claim twice, but also there would be a risk that the judgment in the earlier action on the existence or nonexistence of the Plaintiff’s claim, rendered on the premise of a determination on the set-off assertion, would ultimately become meaningless; this is to prevent such result (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2004DA17207, rendered July 22, 2005; Supreme Court Decision 2016DA46338, 46345, rendered August 30, 2018).\\n\\nb. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the Plaintiff, in the first instance of the Prior Action, asserted a defense of concurrent performance based on the claim for repair of defects or the claim for damages in lieu of repair of defects concerning this construction work, and also a defense of set-off using the above damages claim as the active claim; thereafter, the Plaintiff withdrew the above defense of set-off in the appellate instance. The appellate instance of the Prior Action rendered a judgment partially upholding the Defendant’s claim for construction price, and in the reasons for that judgment it rejected only the Plaintiff’s above defense of concurrent performance and did not adjudicate the withdrawn defense of set-off. The appellate judgment in the Prior Action became final and conclusive as rendered.\\n\\nc. Given these circumstances, the appellate judgment in the Prior Action does not have res judicata with respect to the Plaintiff’s defense of set-off; therefore, the lower court’s determination, which partially upheld the Plaintiff’s claim for damages in lieu of repair of defects, does not contain, as argued in the grounds of appeal, any error of law concerning res judicata of set-off or the like.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are to be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged as per the dispositive part, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court participating in the case."}

{"[95DA9945]": "The Court examines the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nRegarding the part dismissing the principal claim\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below found that the forest land at issue was land recorded at the time of the land survey as being owned by Non-Party 1, who was the plaintiffs’ great-grandfather and the defendants’ grandfather; that, with respect thereto, the defendants, on 1971.12.20., obtained a certificate of confirmation based on inheritance pursuant to the former Special Measures Act concerning Registration of Ownership Transfer of Forest Land (Act Nos. 2111 and 2204) and completed registration of preservation of ownership in their names; that the said Non-Party 1 gave birth to his eldest son, Non-Party 2, second son, Non-Party 3, third son, Non-Party 4, fourth son, Non-Party 5, fifth son, Non-Party 6, and daughter, Non-Party 7, and died around 1935; that the said Non-Party 2, the eldest son, gave birth to his eldest son, Non-Party 8, and died around 1951; that the said Non-Party 8 also died around 1974.12.19., and his spouse, Non-Party 9, and his children, the Plaintiff and Non-Party 10, Non-Party 11, Non-Party 12, Non-Party 13, Non-Party 14, and Non-Party 15 (among the above heirs, all persons other than the said Non-Party 15 were co-plaintiffs in the court below, and hereinafter the co-plaintiffs in the court below shall be referred to as the Plaintiffs for convenience) jointly inherited the said Non-Party 8; that, on the other hand, the said Non-Party 3, the second son of the said Non-Party 1, was adopted out; that the said Non-Party 4, the third son who predeceased the said Non-Party 1, had an eldest son, Non-Party 16; and that Defendant 1 is the son of the said Non-Party 5, the fourth son, and Defendant 2 is the son of the said Non-Party 6, the fifth son. After finding these facts, the court below held that, according to what the Plaintiffs allege as the cause of action for the principal claim in this case, the forest land at issue had been jointly inherited by the Plaintiffs and the said Non-Party 15, but the defendants, as if they had finally inherited the estate of the said Non-Party 1, had obtained and issued false certificates of guarantee and confirmation certificates and completed registration of preservation of ownership under their names pursuant to the said Special Measures Act; accordingly, it is clear that the Plaintiffs seek cancellation of the said registration and confirmation that ownership belongs to the Plaintiffs, and that this constitutes an action for recovery of inheritance; however, because this action was filed only on 1993.3.15., after the expiration of the exclusion period of 10 years following the death of the Plaintiffs’ decedent, the said Non-Party 8, it dismissed the action as unlawful.\\n\\nHowever, an action for recovery of inheritance requires that the decedent asserted by the true heir and the sham heir be the same person, and where the decedent asserted by the Plaintiffs and the decedent asserted by the defendants are different persons, even if the Plaintiffs’ cause of action presupposes that the Plaintiffs acquired ownership of the forest land at issue by inheritance, such action cannot be regarded as an action for recovery of inheritance (see this Court’s Decision 94DA798, rendered on 1994.4.15.; Decision 93DA5840, rendered on 1995.4.14.). According to the Plaintiffs’ assertions set forth above, the Plaintiffs jointly inherited the estate of the said Non-Party 1 through the said Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 8, but the defendants, who had no authority, obtained false certificates of guarantee and confirmation certificates with respect to the forest land at issue and completed registration of preservation of ownership under their names. By contrast, according to the defendants’ assertions regarding how the forest land at issue was acquired, they do not claim to have directly inherited the estate of the said Non-Party 1; rather, they merely contend that they succeeded to the forest land at issue, which their father, the said Non-Party 5 and Non-Party 6, received by gift from the said Non-Party 1 during his lifetime. Moreover, even according to the record of this case, it is recognized that the defendants, after the death of their fathers, the said Non-Party 5 and Non-Party 6, obtained certificates of confirmation based on inheritance and completed registration of preservation of ownership; thus, the defendants cannot be deemed sham heirs of the said Non-Party 1. Accordingly, this action does not constitute an action for recovery of inheritance.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, on the premise that the defendants were sham heirs of the said Non-Party 1, held that the Plaintiffs’ action against the defendants in this case was an action for recovery of inheritance and that the exclusion period had expired; in so doing, it erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning an action for recovery of inheritance. Therefore, the ground of appeal disputing this point is well-founded in the first instance.\\n\\nHowever, according to the record of this case, Non-Party 16, under Seoul District Court Uijeongbu Branch Case No. 90GADAN21162, filed an action against the defendants seeking cancellation of the registration of preservation of ownership and confirmation of ownership on the premise that he had exclusively inherited the estate of the said Non-Party 1 by virtue of family-head succession; when, in that case, he lost on the ground that the Plaintiffs were the rightful heirs on 1991.7.19., he filed an appeal as Seoul Civil District Court Case No. 91NA24716, and thereafter, in an agreement with the Plaintiffs, who became aware of this, to receive the property inheritance rights concerning the forest land at issue, he added an alternative claim, on behalf of the Plaintiffs, seeking cancellation of the registration of preservation of ownership in the defendants’ names concerning the forest land at issue and confirmation that ownership belongs to the Plaintiffs; however, on 1992.9.9., he again lost on the ground that there was no proof sufficient to overturn the presumption arising from the registration of preservation, and the judgment became final and conclusive on 1993.1.15. by this Court’s dismissal of the appeal. In a case where a creditor files a lawsuit against a third-party debtor by exercising the creditor’s subrogation right and obtains a judgment, if the debtor knew that a lawsuit based on the creditor’s subrogation right had been filed, the effect of the judgment extends to the debtor. Accordingly, insofar as the nonexistence of the Plaintiffs’ right to seek cancellation of registration and of ownership was finally determined by the judgment in Seoul Civil District Court Case No. 91NA24716, which became final and conclusive by dismissal of the appeal, the Plaintiffs’ principal claim in this case, which invokes grounds existing before the conclusion of oral argument, is in conflict with the res judicata effect of the final judgment and therefore cannot be allowed.\\n\\nTherefore, even if the judgment of the court below dismissing the action concerning the Plaintiffs’ principal claim as unlawful were to be reversed, since the claim would in any event be destined to be dismissed as conflicting with the res judicata effect of the final judgment, the appeal concerning this part should be dismissed pursuant to the principle prohibiting reformatio in peius.\\n\\nRegarding the part dismissing the alternative claim\\n\\nUpon examining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the record, the court below’s action rejecting the Plaintiffs’ assertion on the ground that there was insufficient evidence to find that the defendants agreed to register transfer of ownership in favor of the Plaintiff with respect to a part of the shares in the forest land at issue is proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality, such as a factual error in violation of the rules of evidence, as argued.\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. The judgment is rendered in conformity with the opinions of the judges who participated, as set forth in the text of the judgment."}

question: Which of the following explanations concerning res judicata is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Where A, who received a judgment dismissing the claim in a lawsuit filed against B by A seeking an objection to distribution, after that judgment became final and conclusive, files a lawsuit against B seeking the return of the amount of distribution fixed by the above judgment on the ground that it constitutes unjust enrichment, the court in the later suit cannot make a determination different from that of the earlier final and conclusive judgment.
B: After a judgment in favor of the claim became final and conclusive in a lawsuit filed by A against B seeking performance of the procedure for registration of the principal registration based on a provisional registration, B’s filing, against A, of a claim for cancellation only of the above provisional registration does not conflict with the res judicata of the earlier final and conclusive judgment.
C: Where A, the purchaser of X Land, filed a lawsuit against B, subrogating the seller A, seeking performance of the procedure for cancellation registration on the ground that the transfer registration in the name of B concerning X Land is void for lack of cause (the earlier suit), and a judgment in favor of the claim became final and conclusive, if after the close of oral argument at the fact-finding stage of that lawsuit, C, who purchased X Land from B and completed the transfer registration, files a lawsuit against A (the later suit) seeking delivery of X Land and restitution of unjust enrichment equivalent to rent, C qualifies as a successor after the close of oral argument, and the res judicata of the earlier final and conclusive judgment extends to the later suit.
D: Where A filed a lawsuit against real property owner B seeking transfer registration and, based on the final and conclusive judgment in his favor, completed the transfer registration, if C, another person entitled to claim transfer registration against B, subrogates B and asserts that the transfer registration in A’s name is void for lack of cause and seeks cancellation of that registration, such claim conflicts with the res judicata of the earlier final and conclusive judgment.
E: After a judgment in favor of the claim became final and conclusive in a lawsuit filed by A against B seeking transfer registration and the transfer registration in A’s name was completed accordingly, B’s filing, against A, of a lawsuit for confirmation of ownership asserting that the above registration is void for lack of cause does not conflict with the res judicata of the earlier final and conclusive judgment.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2013DA53939]": "We decide the grounds of appeal (the statements in each supplemental appellate brief filed after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. The court below found the following facts: the Defendants received the commercial units at issue from D&I Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “D&I”), or acquired the status of purchaser with D&I’s consent; thereafter, D&I caused Korea Asset Trust Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Korea Asset Trust”) to complete, on the ground of trust, each registration of transfer of ownership with respect to Building 101 of the newly constructed building containing the commercial units at issue and its site, located in Seongnam-dong, Jung-gu, Ulsan (hereinafter referred to as “the building at issue”); the Defendants, by subrogating D&I, etc., filed a lawsuit against Korea Asset Trust and D&I as Ulsan District Court Case No. 2008GADAN25922, and on June 17, 2009, received a judgment from that court stating, on the ground that the trust agreement between D&I and Korea Asset Trust was void as a double sale under Article 103 of the Civil Act, that “Korea Asset Trust shall implement the procedure for cancellation registration of the registrations of transfer of ownership made with respect to the portion corresponding to the exclusive portion, co-owned share, and land right of the commercial units at issue indicated in the sales contract among the building at issue and its site, and D&I shall, simultaneously with receiving the balance from the Defendants, implement the procedure for registration of transfer of ownership in favor of the Defendants based on sale,” and that the said judgment became final and conclusive around that time (hereinafter referred to as “the previous suit at issue”); and that the Plaintiff purchased the building at issue and its site, including the portion of the commercial units at issue, through a public sale procedure conducted by Korea Asset Trust, and completed, on January 31, 2011, registration of transfer of ownership in the Plaintiff’s name.\\n\\nThe court below further premised that, for res judicata to extend to a successor, the subject matter of the previous suit and the subject matter of the subsequent suit against the successor must be identical, or res judicata must extend objectively because there exists a contradictory or preliminary relationship, and then held that the subject matter of this subsequent suit, i.e., the suit at issue, in which the Plaintiff seeks delivery of the building at issue and return of unjust enrichment equivalent to rent from the Defendants, is a claim for delivery of the building, etc., and is different from the subject matter of the previous suit at issue, in which the subject matter was a claim for cancellation registration; accordingly, res judicata of the judgment in the previous suit at issue does not extend. The court below further held, based on the circumstances set forth in its reasoning, including that the right of D&I exercised by subrogation in the previous suit at issue was a real right-based claim for exclusion of interference grounded in ownership, that the Plaintiff, as a successor after the close of oral argument, is bound by res judicata of the judgment in the previous suit at issue, and therefore the Plaintiff, who received title from Korea Asset Trust, which bears the obligation to cancel the ownership transfer registration in rem, cannot acquire ownership of the commercial units at issue; on that basis, the court dismissed the Plaintiff’s claim premised on such ownership.\\n\\n2. However, the foregoing determination by the court below cannot be upheld as it stands.\\n\\na. The res judicata effect of a final and conclusive judgment arises only with respect to what is included in the dispositive portion of that judgment, that is, only as to the conclusion of the determination on the existence or nonexistence of the legal relationship asserted as the subject matter of the action; it does not extend to the existence or nonexistence of the legal relationship that formed the premise stated in the reasons for the judgment. Therefore, even where a judgment granting a claim for cancellation registration of ownership transfer on the ground that the cause is void has become final and conclusive, the res judicata effect of that final and conclusive judgment extends only to the existence or nonexistence of the claim for cancellation registration, which is the subject matter of the action, and does not extend to the part of the reasons for the judgment concerning the attribution of rights in the real property, including the existence or nonexistence of ownership itself that formed the premise thereof (see Supreme Court Decisions 84DAKA1792, rendered on August 19, 1986; 2010DA58889, rendered on December 23, 2010, etc.). In addition, res judicata functions to preclude a subsequent suit identical to the subject matter of a previous suit that has res judicata effect, and at the same time, even if the subject matter of the subsequent suit is not identical to the subject matter of the previous suit, it precludes a party from asserting in the subsequent suit a position different from the determination in the previous judgment when the determination on the subject matter of the previous suit becomes a preliminary issue in the subsequent suit or stands in a contradictory relationship with it (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DA47361, rendered on December 27, 2002, etc.). Thus, where the subject matters are not identical or do not fall within the objective scope to which res judicata extends by virtue of a preliminary issue or contradictory relationship, even if a person succeeds to the disputed property, etc. from a party after the close of oral argument in the previous suit judgment and files a subsequent suit, the res judicata effect of the previous suit judgment does not extend to that subsequent suit.\\n\\nb. Examining the reasons for the judgment of the court below in light of the foregoing legal principles, the existence or nonexistence of the claim for cancellation registration of ownership transfer, which is the subject matter of the previous suit at issue, differs from the existence or nonexistence of the claim for delivery of the building and the claim for return of unjust enrichment, which are the subject matters of the suit at issue. The legal relationship to which the res judicata effect of the judgment in the previous suit at issue extends, namely the legal relationship asserted as the subject matter of the action, is the existence or nonexistence of D&I’s claim against Korea Asset Trust for cancellation registration concerning the commercial units at issue, and the existence or nonexistence of ownership of the commercial units at issue (or the validity of the trust agreement that is the cause thereof) is merely the legal relationship serving as its premise, and therefore the res judicata effect of the judgment in the previous suit at issue does not extend thereto. In addition, because the determination on the claim for cancellation registration, which is the subject matter of the previous suit at issue, cannot be deemed to become a preliminary issue in the suit for delivery of the building at issue, etc., and because the existence or nonexistence of the claim for delivery of the building, etc., which is the subject matter of the suit at issue, cannot be deemed to stand in a contradictory relationship with the existence or nonexistence of the claim for cancellation registration, which is the subject matter of the previous suit at issue, it cannot be said that the res judicata effect of the judgment in the previous suit at issue extends to the suit at issue. The same applies even if, after the close of oral argument in the judgment in the previous suit at issue, the Plaintiff purchased the building at issue, including the commercial units at issue, from Korea Asset Trust and completed the registration of transfer of ownership.\\n\\nThe court below stated that, for res judicata to extend to a successor, objective res judicata must extend, and then held that the res judicata effect of the judgment in the previous suit at issue cannot be said to extend to the present case; nevertheless, conversely, it determined that the Plaintiff in this case, as a successor after the close of oral argument, is bound by the res judicata effect of the final and conclusive judgment in the previous suit at issue. Such reasoning is contradictory. Leaving aside the issue of whether a succession execution clause may be issued against the Plaintiff, insofar as the Defendants did not execute the judgment in the previous suit at issue and a registration of transfer of ownership in the Plaintiff’s name has been completed with respect to the building at issue, the Plaintiff is presumed to have acquired ownership by lawful cause of registration; therefore, the Plaintiff’s ownership cannot be denied merely because the Plaintiff is bound by the res judicata effect of the judgment in the previous suit at issue, to which res judicata does not extend in this case. Accordingly, the court below should have examined and determined whether the Plaintiff’s claim in this case, premised on ownership of the commercial units at issue, was well-founded, irrespective of the judgment in the previous suit at issue.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below dismissed the Plaintiff’s claim on the ground that, because the Plaintiff is a successor after the close of oral argument, the res judicata effect of the final and conclusive judgment in the previous suit at issue extended to this case, and the Plaintiff could not acquire ownership; in so doing, the court below erred in a manner that affected the judgment by contradictory reasoning and by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the effect of res judicata. The assertion in the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination; it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}
