Conclusion\\nAccording to the record, the principal obligation owed by the Defendant to the Plaintiff can be determined to be KRW 31,775,000, obtained by deducting KRW 2,000,000 repaid after the judgment of the court of first instance by agreement to appropriate it to principal from KRW 33,775,000 recognized by the judgment of the court of first instance, and the delayed damages obligation can be determined to be KRW 24,329,090 recognized by the judgment of the court of first instance.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Defendant is obligated to pay the Plaintiff KRW 56,104,090 in total principal and interest, and with respect to principal of KRW 31,775,000 among that amount, delayed damages calculated at the rate of 5% per annum prescribed by the Civil Act from 2008. 4. 8., the day after service of a copy of the application for modification of claim in this case, until 2008. 12. 19., the date of the court below’s judgment, and at the rate of 20% per annum prescribed by the Act on Special Cases Concerning Expedition, etc. of Legal Proceedings from the following day until the day of full payment; and since the portion of the judgment of the court below that ordered payment in excess thereof and lost the case as to the Defendant is unlawful, that portion is reversed, but since that portion is sufficiently capable of being tried directly by this Court, the Court will render its own judgment pursuant to Article 437 of the Civil Procedure Act. Accordingly, the judgment of the court of first instance corresponding to the reversed portion is vacated, the Plaintiff’s claim corresponding thereto is dismissed, and since the Defendant’s remaining grounds for appeal are without merit, they are dismissed, and it is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the Judges participating."}

{"[2016DA41869]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. With respect to the Defendant’s ground of appeal to the effect that there was no breach of the Duty of Care\\nThe lower court, after recognizing the facts as stated in its opinion based on the evidence it admitted, held that the Defendant had breached its Duty of Care in relation to the occurrence of the accident in this case, which constitutes an occupational accident, and recognized the Defendant’s liability for damages.\\nThe Defendant’s argument in this part of the grounds of appeal is, in the end, directed at criticizing factual findings that fall within the exclusive authority of the trier of fact, and therefore does not constitute a lawful ground of appeal. Furthermore, even upon review in light of the record, there is no error in the lower court’s factual findings and determination on this part that would violate the laws of logic and experience and thereby exceed the limits of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\n2. With respect to the Defendant’s ground of appeal concerning the ratio of comparative negligence\\nIn a damages action arising from nonperformance of an obligation or a tort, the factual finding concerning grounds for comparative negligence or limitation of liability, or the determination of the ratio thereof, falls within the exclusive authority of the trier of fact unless it is recognized as being markedly unreasonable in light of the principle of equity (see Supreme Court Decisions 2005DA11954 rendered on February 28, 2008, 2016DA249557 rendered on June 8, 2017, etc.).\\nUpon examining the reasons for the lower court judgment in light of the record, since the lower court’s factual finding concerning grounds for comparative negligence or limitation of liability, or its determination of the ratio thereof, cannot be said to be markedly unreasonable in light of the principle of equity, the Defendant’s ground of appeal in this part is without merit.\\n\\n3. With respect to Plaintiff 1’s ground of appeal concerning a violation of the principle of party presentation\\na. In a damages action arising from personal injury, the victim’s expected life span, which serves as the basis for calculating the amount of damages, is a principal fact to which the principle of party presentation applies, and is subject to judicial admission. Once a judicial admission is established, the court is also bound thereby unless it is lawfully withdrawn, and thus the court cannot, by evidence, recognize facts inconsistent with an admission established with respect to facts not in dispute between the parties (see Supreme Court Decisions 2012DA86048 rendered on June 27, 2013, 2017DA206472 rendered on May 31, 2017, etc.).\\nb. According to the record, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n(1) On August 6, 2013, while the first-instance trial was pending, the appraiser submitted a physical examination report to the court, and according to that report, Plaintiff 1’s expected life span was 70% of that of an ordinary person.\\n(2) Thereafter, Plaintiff 1 consistently argued in the first instance and in the lower court that, based on the time of the accident in this case, his or her expected life span was 31 years and 1 month (373 months), which is 70% of that of an ordinary person.\\n(3) As to this, the Defendant initially disputed the matter, but after stating the written brief dated August 4, 2015 to the effect that there was no objection to the above expected life span asserted by Plaintiff 1 at the 10th oral argument date in the first instance (August 21, 2015), the Defendant no longer disputed the above expected life span in the first instance or in the lower court, and disputed only the amount of disability compensation to be deducted or the commencement date of delay damages.\\nc. Examining these facts in light of the foregoing legal principle, judicial admission was established with respect to the fact that Plaintiff 1’s expected life span was 31 years and 1 month (373 months), which is 70% of that of an ordinary person, and the court is likewise bound thereby.\\nd. Nevertheless, the lower court, differently from the above, recognized Plaintiff 1’s expected life span as 17.332 years, approximately 40% of that of an ordinary person, and, based on that, calculated lost earnings, future medical expenses and assistive device expenses, and nursing care expenses. The lower court’s determination contains an error that affected the judgment by violating the principle of party presentation and recognizing facts contrary to a judicial admission. Plaintiff 1’s ground of appeal pointing out this issue has merit.\\n\\n4. With respect to Plaintiff 1’s and the Defendant’s respective grounds of appeal concerning the calculation of the amount equivalent to the disability compensation lump sum to be deducted from the amount of damages\\na. Article 80(2) of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act”) provides in the main clause that “if a beneficiary receives insurance benefits under this Act for the same cause, the insurer shall be exempt from liability for damages under the Civil Act or any other statute within the scope of that amount,” and in the latter clause provides that “in such a case, a person receiving a disability compensation annuity or survivors’ compensation annuity shall be deemed to have received a disability compensation lump sum or survivors’ compensation lump sum.” Thus, the latter clause of Article 80(2) of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act, while making a disability compensation annuity that has not yet actually been paid subject to deduction, adjusts the interests and liabilities of the injured worker and the employer by limiting the scope of such deduction to the amount equivalent to a disability compensation lump sum (see Constitutional Court, en banc, Decision 2004HEONBA97 rendered on November 24, 2005). In addition, considering that the distinction between a disability compensation annuity and a disability compensation lump sum is merely a difference in the method of payment of disability benefits, and that, except in special cases, the choice between an annuity and a lump sum depends on the intention of the beneficiary, the disability compensation annuity and disability compensation lump sum under the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act must be regarded as being equal in value as a whole (see Supreme Court Decisions 2000DU6268 rendered on July 13, 2001, 2005DU7501 rendered on June 15, 2007, etc.).\\nPensions are essentially characterized by future uncertainty and variability (see Article 36(3), Article 58, each item, Article 59, Article 70(2), Article 83, Article 120, etc. of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act), yet the fact that the latter clause of Article 80(2) of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act normatively establishes the equivalence between annuities and lump sums as above may be seen as intended to promptly and clearly determine the legal relations among the beneficiary, the insurer who is the obligor for damages, a third party, and the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service (hereinafter referred to as the “Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service”). In light of this purpose, where a beneficiary is receiving a disability compensation annuity, the amount of the disability compensation lump sum to be deducted pursuant to the latter clause of Article 80(2) of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act should, irrespective of the annuity period or the amount of annuity already paid, be understood as the amount equivalent to the disability compensation lump sum that would have been paid under [Attached Table 2] of Article 57(2) of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act if the beneficiary had chosen a disability compensation lump sum instead of a disability compensation annuity and had requested payment thereof. This legal principle applies equally even where there has been a re-determination and change of the disability grade under Article 59 of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act or an increase or decrease in the average wage under Article 36(3) of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act while the beneficiary was receiving a disability compensation annuity; therefore, in such a case, the amount equivalent to the disability compensation lump sum, calculated on the basis not of the changed disability grade or the average wage as of the date of closing of fact-finding proceedings, but of the initial disability grade and the average wage applied at the time of the determination to pay the disability compensation annuity (if the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service calculated the amount of the disability compensation annuity by applying an average wage different from the average wage that should have been actually applied, this means the average wage that should have been actually applied), must be deducted from the amount of damages.\\nb. The lower court, on the same purport, deducted from the amount of damages that the Defendant is to compensate Plaintiff 1 the amount equivalent to the disability compensation lump sum, calculated on the basis of the average wage applied at the time of the determination to pay the disability compensation annuity due to the accident in this case and the initial disability grade, and such is proper; there is no error, as alleged in the respective grounds of appeal, such as misapprehension of the legal principle concerning the calculation of disability benefits to be deducted from the amount of damages.\\n\\n5. With respect to Plaintiff 1’s ground of appeal concerning the commencement date of delay damages on passive damages\\na. Originally, a claim for damages arising from a tort accrues at the time of the tort and becomes due, so in the case of passive damages and active damages that will arise in the future, the time of the tort is the base time for present value calculation, and in principle, delay damages from the time of the tort are added to the amount after deducting intermediate interest from the time of the tort until the time future damages arise. However, it is also permissible, on the basis of a time after the tort and before the closing of fact-finding proceedings, to calculate the present value of damages that will arise thereafter by the method of deducting intermediate interest from that time until each future time of damage occurrence, and to seek delay damages from after that base time, so long as it does not depart from or conflict with the foregoing original method (see Supreme Court Decisions 93DA34091 rendered on December 21, 1993, 94DA30065 rendered on November 25, 1994, etc.).\\nb. According to the reasons for the lower court judgment, the lower court calculated the amount of passive damages that the Defendant is to compensate Plaintiff 1 at KRW 168,143,687 (the sum of lost earnings and lost retirement allowance), and ordered payment of delay damages thereon from May 1, 2011, which is the day after the date on which the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service determined the termination of medical treatment, after the date of the accident in this case.\\nc. First, we examine the part concerning delay damages on lost earnings.\\n(1) According to the reasons for the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n① In the application for amendment of the purport of claim and cause of action dated February 5, 2014, Plaintiff 1 stated that “with respect to lost earnings for the 20 years and 8 months (248 months) from May 1, 2011, when medical treatment was terminated and disability annuity was received, until December 31, 2031, the scheduled retirement date, I claim the amount calculated as the present value at the time of the accident in this case by deducting intermediate interest.” This was stated at the 6th oral argument date in the first instance (March 21, 2014).\\n② Plaintiff 1’s method of calculating lost earnings as stated in the above application for amendment of the purport of claim and cause of action was to deduct the Hoffmann figure “61.3112” corresponding to the period of 70 months (= 5 years × 12 months + 10 months), from July 2005, the month following the accident in this case, to April 2011, the month in which medical treatment was terminated, from the Hoffmann figure “202.2081” corresponding to 318 months (= 26 years × 12 months + 6 months), which is the period from July 2005 to December 2031, the end of the period of earning capacity asserted by Plaintiff 1.\\n③ The lower court, in calculating lost earnings from May 1, 2011 until September 28, 2022, which the lower court regarded as the end date of Plaintiff 1’s expected life span, deducted the Hoffmann figure “61.3112” corresponding to 70 months from the Hoffmann figure “149.0294” corresponding to 207 months (= 16 years × 12 months + 15 months), which is the period from July 2005, the month following the accident in this case, to September 28, 2022.\\n(2) If the circumstances are as above, Plaintiff 1, while taking June 4, 2005, the date of the accident in this case, as the base time for present value calculation, sought compensation for lost earnings only for the period after excluding “the period from June 4, 2005, to April 30, 2011,” and the lower court likewise may be understood to have calculated the amount of damages for lost earnings by using June 4, 2005, the date of the accident in this case, as the basis and deducting intermediate interest from that time until the future time of damage occurrence.\\n(3) If so, the lower court should have ordered payment of delay damages on the amount of damages for lost earnings calculated as above from June 4, 2005, the base time for present value calculation. Nevertheless, while calculating the present value of the amount of damages for lost earnings on the basis of June 4, 2005, the lower court determined that the commencement date of delay damages on that amount was May 1, 2011, rather than the above present value calculation date. The lower court’s determination contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principle concerning the commencement date of delay damages. Plaintiff 1’s ground of appeal pointing out this issue has merit.\\nd. Next, we examine the part concerning delay damages on lost retirement allowance.\\nAccording to the reasons for the lower court judgment and the record, Plaintiff 1, in calculating the amount of retirement allowance that he or she could have received from the Defendant had he or she retired upon reaching retirement age, claimed KRW 66,439,889 by inserting numbers directly into the Hoffmann formula itself, rather than using the Hoffmann figure as in the calculation of lost earnings, and the lower court, on the premise of accepting this as is, made the remaining calculations in the next stages. However, this is the value obtained when “242 months” is inserted into the “number of months from the commencement date of delay damages to the date of damage occurrence” in the Hoffmann formula, and in light of the fact that Plaintiff 1 expressly set the end of the above calculation period as the scheduled retirement date, “December 31, 2031,” the above lost retirement allowance sought by Plaintiff 1 may be understood to have been calculated by using a point slightly later than May 1, 2011, after the date of the accident in this case, as the base time for present value calculation, and the lower court may likewise be understood to have followed the same method.\\nIf so, Plaintiff 1’s ground of appeal in this part to the effect that the commencement date of delay damages on lost retirement allowance should be viewed as June 4, 2005, the date of the accident in this case, cannot be accepted.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\nTherefore, among the part of the lower court judgment against Plaintiff 1, the part concerning property damages is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination; all appeals by the Defendant are dismissed; and the costs of the appeal as to Plaintiff 2 shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2018DA276027]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Grounds of appeal by Plaintiff 1 against Defendant 2\\n\\na. A judicial admission means a statement at an oral argument date or preparatory date for oral argument, which is consistent with the opposing party’s allegation and adverse to the party making it. Even where a preparatory brief submitted to the court and served on the opposing party contains content that constitutes an admission, if it is stated or deemed to have been stated at an oral argument date or preparatory date for oral argument, a judicial admission is established (see Supreme Court Decision 2014DA229870, rendered on February 12, 2015). If there is a judicial admission, the court is also bound by it unless it is lawfully withdrawn, and therefore the court cannot make a determination different from the admitted facts (see Supreme Court Decisions 87DAKA804, rendered on October 24, 1988, and 2016DA41869, rendered on October 4, 2018).\\n\\nb. According to the reasons of the appellate judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\nPlaintiff 1 filed the instant action seeking payment and the like, asserting as the factual basis of the claim that Defendant 2 entrusted him with the duties of site manager for the construction work at issue but failed to pay wages for 10 months, and also agreed to reimburse expenses that Plaintiff 1 had advanced on behalf of Defendant 2 during the construction process but failed to perform such agreement, and thus Defendant 2 is obligated to pay wages and reimbursement money to Plaintiff 1.\\nDefendant 2 disputed the above allegations at the first instance, but at the appellate instance submitted a written statement admitting all of the principal facts included in the factual basis of Plaintiff 1’s claim, such as the conclusion of an employment contract, the amount of unpaid wages, the agreement to reimburse expenses advanced on behalf of another, and the unpaid amount so advanced, and the said written statement was deemed to have been stated at the first oral argument date in the appellate court.\\n\\nc. In light of these circumstances and the legal principles discussed above, there is room to see that Defendant 2 submitted a written statement that was consistent with Plaintiff 1’s allegations and adverse to Defendant 2 with respect to the principal facts, and that the written statement was deemed to have been stated at the oral argument date; accordingly, a judicial admission may be found to have been established. The appellate court should have examined and determined, after comprehensively reviewing the entire course of pleadings, including the content of the written statement and the circumstances under which it was submitted, whether a judicial admission had been established.\\nHowever, the appellate court, without properly conducting such examination, dismissed Plaintiff 1’s claim against Defendant 2 on the ground that the written statement submitted by Defendant 2 lacked credibility. The appellate judgment contains error that affected the judgment by misconstruing the legal principles concerning judicial admissions and their binding force, or by failing to conduct the necessary examination.\\n\\n2. The remaining grounds of appeal by the Plaintiffs\\n\\nThe Plaintiffs’ remaining grounds of appeal merely dispute the selection and weighing of evidence and factual findings, which fall within the exclusive authority of the appellate court as the fact-finding court, and therefore cannot constitute lawful grounds for appeal. Furthermore, even upon review in light of the record, the appellate judgment contains no error, such as failing to conduct the necessary examination as alleged in the grounds of appeal, or exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by contravening the rules of logic and experience, or violating the duty to explain, or omitting determinations.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nThe part of the appellate judgment concerning Plaintiff 1’s claim against Defendant 2 is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the appellate court for further trial and determination. Plaintiff 2’s appeal and the remainder of Plaintiff 1’s appeal are without merit and are all dismissed, and the costs of appeal between the Plaintiffs and Defendant 1 and Defendant 3 are to be borne by the losing parties, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2023DA299789]": "The grounds of appeal are determined (the statements in the supplementary brief of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the petition of appeal are considered to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. With respect to appropriation of payment to costs, interest, and principal, the order of appropriation is prescribed in Article 479 of the Civil Act, and Article 476 of the Civil Act concerning designated appropriation of payment is not applied mutatis mutandis; therefore, in principle, appropriation must be made in the order of costs, interest, and principal. However, where there is a special agreement between the parties, the order of appropriation may be recognized differently from that statutory order of appropriation (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DA12399 decided June 11, 2009). The payer (debtor) and the recipient of payment (creditor) may, unless doing so would prejudice the interests of an interested third party such as a guarantor concerning the obligation extinguished by payment, agree even after performance has already been completed as to which obligation the provided performance is to be appropriated to, and by what method, excluding the existing method of appropriation (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DA118044, 2012DA118051 decided September 12, 2013).\\n\\nA judicial admission means making a statement, at a date for oral argument or a preparatory hearing date for oral argument, of a fact that is consistent with the opposing party’s allegation and adverse to oneself. Even where a preparatory brief or the like submitted to the court and served on the opposing party contains a statement amounting to an admission, if it is stated or deemed to have been stated at a date for oral argument or a preparatory hearing date for oral argument, a judicial admission is established (see Supreme Court Decision 2014DA229870 decided February 12, 2015). Even where a party, before the opposing party asserts it in pleadings, voluntarily states a fact disadvantageous to itself and the opposing party explicitly invokes it or makes a statement consistent with that statement, a judicial admission is established (see Supreme Court Decision 92DA5546 decided August 18, 1992, Supreme Court Decision 2002DA59528, 2002DA59535 decided November 25, 2005, etc.). If there is a judicial admission, the court is also bound by it unless it is lawfully withdrawn, and thus the court cannot render a determination contrary to the admitted fact (see Supreme Court Decision 87DAKA804 decided October 24, 1988, Supreme Court Decision 2016DA41869 decided October 4, 2018, etc.).\\n\\n2. According to the reasons of the appellate judgment and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. On 2015. 5. 11., Plaintiff loaned Defendant KRW 500,000,000 (hereinafter referred to as the “loan at issue”), setting the due date for repayment as 2016. 8. 21., and received repayment from Defendant’s side in the total amount of KRW 600,000,000, consisting of KRW 200,000,000 on 2018. 2. 23., KRW 100,000,000 on 2018. 12. 17., and KRW 300,000,000 on 2019. 3. 14.\\n\\nb. A “Loan Status” document (Plaintiff’s Exhibit 3, hereinafter referred to as the “document at issue”) was prepared stating that principal and interest on the loan at issue would be repaid by applying a monthly interest rate of 3%; and the document at issue sets forth Proposal 1, under which the KRW 600,000,000 repaid by Defendant’s side would first be appropriated to interest amounting to KRW 705,000,000 for 47 months calculated at a monthly interest rate of 3%, and the remaining interest of KRW 105,000,000 plus the principal of KRW 500,000,000, totaling KRW 605,000,000, would be paid, and Proposal 2, under which the said KRW 600,000,000 would first be appropriated to principal at each time of repayment, and KRW 503,000,000, obtained by deducting KRW 100,000,000 remaining after appropriation to principal from the KRW 603,000,000 in interest accrued up to the last repayment date, 2019. 3. 14., would be paid. On 2019. 11. 26., Defendant wrote next to Proposal 2 of the document at issue, “I will accept Proposal 2. Payment schedule to be finalized by December 3,” and signed it.\\n\\nc. In a preparatory brief dated 2022. 11. 14., Plaintiff alleged that “Plaintiff presented to Defendant Proposal 1, which appropriates the KRW 600,000,000 paid by Defendant to Plaintiff to interest, and Proposal 2, which appropriates it to principal and interest, and Defendant expressed an intention to agree to appropriation of payment under Proposal 2, under which the amount of unpaid principal and interest is much smaller,” and Plaintiff stated the above preparatory brief at the second oral argument date of the first instance on 2022. 11. 15.\\n\\nd. In a statement of grounds for appeal dated 2023. 4. 10., Defendant alleged that “Defendant wrote on 2019. 11. 26. that Defendant would accept Proposal 2 among Proposal 1 and Proposal 2 set forth in the document at issue,” and Defendant stated the above statement of grounds for appeal at the first oral argument date in the court below on 2023. 8. 16.\\n\\n3. According to the facts found by the court below, Proposal 2 would be a method under which the entire KRW 600,000,000 repaid by Defendant’s side is first appropriated to principal and the remaining amount is appropriated to interest. Since Plaintiff stated to the effect that Plaintiff and Defendant’s intentions had coincided in first appropriating payment in the manner of Proposal 2, and Defendant also made a statement consistent with that statement, there is room to view that a judicial admission was established as to the fact that an agreement had been reached between Plaintiff and Defendant to appropriate payment according to Proposal 2. Therefore, the court below should have examined, by comprehensively reviewing the contents of each of the above writings submitted by Plaintiff and Defendant and the course of the pleadings, including the circumstances of those statements, whether a judicial admission had been established.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below determined, for the reasons stated in its judgment, that it could not be found that an agreement had been formed between Plaintiff and Defendant to appropriate payment according to Proposal 2, and calculated the remaining amount of the obligation according to statutory appropriation of payment. The appellate judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal doctrine regarding the establishment and effect of a judicial admission and by failing to conduct the necessary examination without exercising its authority to clarify issues.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the appellate judgment is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination on this part, and it is so adjudged unanimously by the participating Justices as stated in the operative part."}

{"[98DA6763]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. In an auction for the enforcement of a security right, where the distribution amount is insufficient to extinguish in full the several secured claims held by the same secured creditor and the claims for interest or damages for delay thereon, allocation must uniformly be made in accordance with the method of statutory appropriation of payment under Articles 477 and 479 of the Civil Act, the most equitable and appropriate method of allocation (see Supreme Court Decision 95DA55504, May 10, 1996, Supreme Court Decision 96DA52649, July 25, 1997, etc.); and such statutory appropriation of payment is effected, as between interest or damages for delay and principal, in the order of interest or damages for delay first and principal thereafter, and among principal debts, it is made sequentially according to the degree of payment benefit, such as whether the maturity date has arrived, the timing of such arrival, and the relative level of the interest rates; however, where there is no differentiation whatsoever in such maturity dates or degree of payment benefit, it is to be apportioned in proportion to the amount of each principal debt. In addition, matters concerning maturity dates or payment benefit, etc., which serve as the standard in determining the order of statutory appropriation of payment, may be the subject of admission as concrete facts, but the order of statutory appropriation of payment itself is a legal effect determined by the application of legal provisions, and therefore even if a statement concerning it is unfavorable to the person making the statement, it cannot be regarded as an admission (see Supreme Court Decision 90DAKA7262, November 9, 1990).\\n2. According to the reasons of the appellate court judgment, the appellate court, after comprehensively considering the evidence adopted in that judgment or taking as admitted the facts that the Plaintiff admitted, found the following: the Plaintiff, on September 29, 1988 and on October 29 of the same year, loaned to the Non-Party Samyang Chemical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the Non-Party Company) KRW 120,000,000 each time as small and medium enterprise facility funds, at an interest rate of 12% per annum and a default interest rate of 19% per annum, and agreed that the loan dated September 29, 1988 would be repaid in installments every 3 months starting from March 25, 1991, and the loan dated October 29, 1988 would be repaid in installments every 3 months starting from September 25, 1990, with interest to be paid every 3 months on the outstanding balance of the borrowed money starting from March 25 of each year; the Defendant, with respect to the above loan principal and interest repayment obligations, jointly and severally guaranteed them by setting the guarantee limit at KRW 168,000,000; the Non-Party Company, by January 18, 1993, had repaid KRW 43,700,000 of the principal of the loan dated September 29, 1988 and KRW 70,650,000 of the principal of the loan dated October 29, 1988, and had paid the respective agreed interest up to the portion due on December 25, 1992; thereafter, the mortgage established by the Non-Party Company in favor of the Plaintiff was executed by auction at the Seongnam Branch of the Suwon District Court in case No. 93TAGYEONG (case number 1 omitted), and the Plaintiff received a distribution of KRW 328,221,540 as of May 25, 1994, of which KRW 73,331,084 was applied to part of the remaining principal of KRW 76,300,000 (KRW 120,000,000 - KRW 43,700,000) among the loan dated September 29, 1988; meanwhile, the Plaintiff, in addition to the above two loans to the Non-Party Company (hereinafter referred to as the loans at issue), also loaned KRW 50,000,000 on December 30, 1991 at an interest rate of 15% per annum, a default interest rate of 21% per annum, and with the principal repayment method set as installment repayment in four installments every 3 months starting from March 25, 1994; loaned KRW 50,000,000 on February 29, 1992 at an interest rate of 15% per annum, a default interest rate of 21% per annum, and with the principal repayment method set as installment repayment in four installments every 3 months starting from May 25, 1994; loaned KRW 150,000,000 on April 30, 1992 pursuant to a credit limit transaction agreement, with the transaction period set until April 30, 1993, the interest rate at 10% per annum, and the default interest rate at 21% per annum; and loaned KRW 100,000,000 on January 19, 1993 pursuant to a current-account overdraft agreement, with the transaction period set until July 18 of the same year; the Plaintiff, out of the KRW 328,221,540 received as a distribution as of May 25, 1994 (hereinafter referred to as the distribution amount at issue), first applied KRW 2,055,819 to fire insurance premiums, and then applied the same to part of the principal of the loans at issue, as well as to the entire principal of each of the loans dated December 30, 1991 and February 29, 1992, to KRW 69,100,000 out of the remaining principal of KRW 121,250,000 for the loan dated April 30, 1992, and to the entire remaining principal of KRW 83,734,637 for the loan dated January 19, 1993. Based on the evidence adopted in that judgment or the facts admitted by the Plaintiff, the appellate court found as above, and then held that the Plaintiff's appropriation of the distribution amount as of May 25, 1994 solely to part of the principal of certain loans, without using the method of statutory appropriation of payment, has no effect; that the Plaintiff admits that, when the distribution amount at issue is allocated according to the method of statutory appropriation of payment, it is first applied to the principal and interest of the loans at issue for which the Defendant jointly and severally guaranteed; and that, moreover, if allocation is made under Articles 477 and 479 of the Civil Act on the basis of the maturity dates, agreed interest rates, and agreed default interest rates of the Non-Party Company’s respective loan obligations, it is clear that the distribution amount is first applied to the entire principal and interest of the loans at issue, and therefore dismissed in full the Plaintiff’s claim in this case seeking payment on the premise that some of the principal and interest of the loans at issue remain outstanding even after appropriation of payment by the distribution amount at issue.\\n3. However, in light of the legal principles set forth above, if, as found by the appellate court, the Plaintiff received the distribution amount at issue as of May 25, 1994, then the statutory appropriation of payment by the distribution amount at issue should first be applied to the interest or damages for delay existing as of the distribution date, and the remainder should be applied to principal; as to the principal, the order of appropriation should follow the degree of payment benefit, such as the maturity date and the relative level of the interest rate, but where there is no such differentiation, it must be apportioned in proportion to the amount of the principal debt.\\nAccording to the record, the Non-Party Company had been repaying the principal and interest of the loans, including the loans at issue, but as it defaulted as of February 10, 1993 (record, p. 86), all loans simultaneously lost the benefit of term and their respective maturity dates arrived, so that there is room to view that thereafter all became subject to the general overdue interest rate commonly applied by financial institutions at the same rate (record, pp. 141, 142, 144 through 146). If so, at the time the Plaintiff received the distribution amount at issue, the loans at issue and the other loans may also be said to have had no differentiation whatsoever in terms of payment benefit such as maturity date or interest rate, and the balance of the distribution amount after being applied to costs or interest would have to be apportioned to the principal of the loans at issue and the other loans respectively; if so applied, the principal of the loans at issue may still remain outstanding notwithstanding the statutory appropriation of payment by the distribution amount at issue. Moreover, even if the Plaintiff made statements unfavorable to itself concerning the order of such statutory appropriation of payment, it cannot thereby be regarded as having made an admission.\\nAccordingly, the appellate court, without examining whether the maturity dates had arrived due to the Non-Party Company’s default or whether the same overdue interest rate applied, and instead holding that the Plaintiff admitted that the distribution amount at issue was first applied to the loans at issue and the damages for delay thereon, or determining the order of statutory appropriation of payment solely on the basis of the original contract terms concerning the maturity dates and interest rates of the loans at issue and the other loans, and concluding that it was clear that the distribution amount at issue was applied to the entire principal and interest of the loans at issue, committed an error that affected the outcome by failing to fully examine the case or by misunderstanding the legal principles on statutory appropriation of payment and admission. The grounds of appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n4. Therefore, the appellate court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the appellate court for further trial and determination. The Justices in charge are unanimous, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning joinder of claims is incorrect? (In the event of a dispute, according to case law)
A: Where the Plaintiff has pleaded several claims that are logically entirely unrelated and therefore should have been sought by simple joinder, by joining them alternatively or in the alternative, and the court of first instance rendered a judgment that adjudicated and upheld only one of those claims while omitting all adjudication on the remaining claims, if only the Defendant appeals, all of those claims are transferred to the appellate court.
B: Where the Plaintiff, with respect to two claims that are substantively in an alternative joinder relationship, pleaded them in a principal and preliminary order, and the court of first instance rendered a judgment dismissing the principal claim and upholding only the preliminary claim, if only the Defendant appeals, the appellate court must take both claims as the subject of adjudication and decide them.
C: Where several mutually incompatible claims are joined in a principal and preliminary order, it is not legally permissible to uphold only the preliminary claim without first deciding the principal claim, or to dismiss only the principal claim without deciding the preliminary claim.
D: Where an action joining several claims by simple joinder was filed, the court of first instance rendered a judgment upholding one of those claims and dismissing the remaining claims, and only the Defendant appealed with respect to the upheld claim, all of those claims are transferred to the appellate court, but only the claim against which the Defendant objected becomes the subject of adjudication in the appellate court.
E: Where the Plaintiff joins several monetary claims that are mutually compatible and pleads them in an order of adjudication according to reasonable necessity, if, as a result of the court’s examination, it dismisses part of the principal claim and upholds only an amount smaller than that sought in the preliminary claim, the court must, through clarification, ascertain the Plaintiff’s intention and then determine accordingly whether to proceed further to adjudicate the preliminary claim.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2002DA23598]": "1. Judgment on the Part Concerning the Primary Claim\\n\\na. Summary of the judgment of the court below on this part\\n\\nThe court below found that the Plaintiff, a shipping company, entered into a contract with Oceanbridge Shipping International Inc. (hereinafter referred to as “Oceanbridge”), a United States freight forwarder, around September 5, 1996, to transport one container from the Port of Los Angeles, United States of America, to the Port of Busan, Republic of Korea, and issued a bill of lading (hereinafter referred to as “the bill of lading in this case”); that the bill of lading stated the shipper as Oceanbridge, the consignee as International Forwarding Co., Ltd. (a domestic agent of Oceanbridge; hereinafter referred to as “International Forwarding”), and the loaded cargo as 322 cartons of building materials (hereinafter referred to as “the cargo in this case”); that the exporter of the cargo in this case was OSMONICS, INC. (hereinafter referred to as “Osmonics”), and the importer was Samkwang Sugi Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Samkwang Sugi”), while Oceanbridge, prior to the above transport contract with the Plaintiff, had been entrusted by Osmonics with the transportation of the cargo in this case, entered into a transport contract, and issued a bill of lading naming Osmonics as shipper and Samkwang Sugi as consignee; that the Plaintiff transported the cargo in this case to the Port of Busan, unloaded it on September 23, 1996, and then, on the 30th of the same month, at the request of International Forwarding, entrusted it for storage in the warehouse of the Defendant located in Yusan-dong, Yangsan-si, and caused it to be warehoused; that, meanwhile, on July 13, 1996, at the Plaintiff’s request, the Defendant had submitted to Woojoo Shipping Co., Ltd., the Plaintiff’s domestic agent, a written undertaking to the effect that “if bonded cargo brought in by vessel of the Plaintiff’s company is stored by the Defendant at the request of the shipper or for any other reason, the cargo shall in no case be released without a cargo release order (D/O; Delivery Order) issued by the Plaintiff, and the Defendant shall bear all civil and criminal liability arising from any violation thereof”; that, however, on October 4, 1996, International Forwarding, before receiving from Oceanbridge the bill of lading in this case issued by the Plaintiff, delivered to Samkwang Sugi a cargo release order in its own name; that on October 9, 1996, Samkwang Sugi, submitting to the Defendant the above cargo release order and a letter of guarantee (L/G; Letter of Guarantee) issued by the Namdong Industrial Complex Branch of the Industrial Bank of Korea, the bank handling payment of the imported cargo price, demanded delivery of the cargo in this case; that the Defendant thereupon delivered the cargo in this case to Samkwang Sugi without the bill of lading in this case or the Plaintiff’s cargo release order; that, meanwhile, Oceanbridge held a claim against International Forwarding in the amount of US$116,874.38 (hereinafter, “US$” omitted), and for security of that claim, had been withholding the bill of lading in this case issued by the Plaintiff, naming itself as shipper, instead of sending it to International Forwarding; that the Defendant removed the cargo in this case on the basis of International Forwarding’s cargo release order; and that Oceanbridge ultimately failed to obtain payment of the above claim from International Forwarding; that Oceanbridge then, around November 4, 1997, filed in the United States a lawsuit for damages against the Plaintiff on the ground that the cargo in this case had been unlawfully released without exchange for the bill of lading in this case and that its rights as a lawful holder of the bill of lading had been infringed, claiming damages in the amount of US$116,874.38, and that in the course of that lawsuit the Plaintiff paid Oceanbridge US$10,000 on May 25, 1999 as a litigation settlement and expended US$32,269 for attorneys’ fees, etc.; and then, based on the above findings, the court below held that, according to the above findings, although before delivery of the cargo in this case the Defendant had already undertaken toward the Plaintiff that if bonded cargo brought in by vessel of the Plaintiff’s company were stored by the Defendant at the request of the shipper or for any other reason, it would not release the cargo under any circumstances without a cargo release order issued by the Plaintiff, the Defendant, as to the cargo in this case stored at the Plaintiff’s request, arbitrarily delivered it to the importer Samkwang Sugi without the Plaintiff’s consent or a cargo release order, and thereby Oceanbridge, whose rights as holder of the bill of lading had been infringed, filed a damages action against the Plaintiff in the United States, causing the Plaintiff to suffer damages in the course of that litigation by paying Oceanbridge a litigation settlement and attorneys’ fees, etc.; accordingly, the court below accepted part of the Plaintiff’s primary claim seeking performance of such damages liability, on the ground that the Defendant bears liability to compensate the Plaintiff for damages based on tort or non-performance of obligation.\\n\\nb. Determination on the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nHowever, it is difficult to accept the court below’s summary conclusion, as stated above, that the Defendant bears liability for damages based on tort or non-performance of obligation for the loss suffered by the Plaintiff in paying a litigation settlement and attorneys’ fees, etc. to Oceanbridge, for the following reasons.\\n\\nEven if the Defendant bears liability for damages based on tort or non-performance of obligation by delivering the cargo in this case without the Plaintiff’s cargo release order or the bill of lading in this case, the damages to be compensated would, in principle, be limited to those that have a proximate causal relationship with the Defendant’s above delivery of the cargo.\\n\\nYet even according to the Plaintiff’s assertion, Oceanbridge had retained the bill of lading in this case issued by the Plaintiff for the cargo in this case as security for its debt to International Forwarding; notwithstanding that, the Defendant arbitrarily delivered the cargo in this case, and Oceanbridge thus suffered damages by losing the cargo in this case, which secured the debt it held against International Forwarding, and on that ground Oceanbridge filed a damages action against the Plaintiff in the United States; however, it is clear from the very facts found by the court below that Oceanbridge, upon presentation of the bill of lading issued by it as freight forwarder, would immediately be obliged, as freight forwarder, to deliver the cargo in this case to the consignee Samkwang Sugi, and therefore it is clear that Oceanbridge had no right at all to retain the cargo in this case indefinitely or otherwise use it as security for the purpose of securing its claim against International Forwarding. Accordingly, even if the Defendant arbitrarily delivered the cargo in this case, the Plaintiff, absent special circumstances, would have no obligation in the above lawsuit in the United States to compensate Oceanbridge for the damages it claimed by reason of the Defendant’s above conduct.\\n\\nNevertheless, the Plaintiff voluntarily paid Oceanbridge a damages settlement in the above lawsuit in the United States, and as a result also bore the litigation costs incurred in that lawsuit; therefore, the payment of the above settlement and the bearing of litigation costs cannot be regarded as being due to damages liability attributable to the Plaintiff arising from the above non-performance of obligation or tort caused by the Defendant’s arbitrary delivery. Accordingly, there is no legal proximate causal relationship between the Plaintiff’s damages arising from the payment of the above settlement and the bearing of litigation costs, and the Defendant’s above conduct (see Supreme Court Decision 92DA28518, Decided December 22, 1992).\\n\\nFurthermore, a party in breach of contract or a tortfeasor is obligated to compensate for damages arising from special circumstances if the party knew or could have known of the existence of such special circumstances; it is not necessary that the party knew or could have known the amount of damages arising from such special circumstances (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA22446, Decided November 11, 1994). However, as stated above, insofar as there is no proximate causal relationship between the Defendant’s above conduct and all of the damages sought by the Plaintiff as the primary claim, there is not even room to view that the Defendant could have known that Oceanbridge might suffer damages by virtue of the Defendant’s arbitrary delivery of the cargo in this case; moreover, there is no material whatsoever to support a finding that the Defendant knew or could have known that there were special circumstances requiring the Plaintiff to pay Oceanbridge the damages settlement that it was under no obligation to pay and to bear litigation costs as well. Therefore, there is likewise no possibility of recognizing the damages suffered by the Plaintiff as damages arising from special circumstances. Accordingly, the Plaintiff’s claim for damages in this case must be dismissed.\\n\\nIf so, the court below, on the premise that a proximate causal relationship existed between the Defendant’s above conduct and the settlement money paid by the Plaintiff, etc., granted part of the Plaintiff’s primary claim; this is clearly an error that misapprehended the legal doctrine on proximate causal relationship and affected the outcome of the judgment. Thus, without even examining the Defendant’s remaining grounds of appeal, the part of the judgment below dismissing the Defendant’s appeal with respect to the primary claim cannot stand. The Defendant’s grounds of appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\nc. Determination on the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal concerning the primary claim\\n\\nAs seen above, no proximate causal relationship exists between the Defendant’s above conduct and all of the damages sought by the Plaintiff as the primary claim, and there is no room to recognize such damages as damages arising from special circumstances in this case. Therefore, there is no basis to conclude that, on the ground that the Defendant could have known that Oceanbridge might suffer damages by reason of the Defendant’s arbitrary delivery of the cargo in this case, the damages should be recognized in excess of the damages award found by the court below (as stated above, insofar as there was no room for Oceanbridge’s damages to arise, there is likewise no room to conclude that the Defendant could have known that Oceanbridge might suffer damages).\\n\\nFurther, examining the record, although the Defendant did submit the above written undertaking to the Plaintiff’s domestic agent, this merely means that a warehouse operator such as the Defendant would perform the duty of care that it is naturally bound to perform under law and, if it violates that duty, would bear liability for damages; it does not clearly mean that it would bear liability for damages unconditionally, regardless of whether there is proximate causal relationship or whether the Defendant could foresee special circumstances. Therefore, the existence of the above written undertaking cannot be construed as an agreement between the Plaintiff and the Defendant to compensate both ordinary damages and special damages.\\n\\nAccordingly, although the court below rejected in part the Plaintiff’s primary claim for damages, and there are shortcomings in the reasoning stated, the result is ultimately correct, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal doctrine on the scope of damages or proximate causal relationship, violation of the rules of evidence leading to a mistake of fact regarding the Defendant’s foreseeability, or mistake of fact regarding the parties’ agreement on mitigation of the burden of proof concerning damages liability appearing in Exhibit 1 (the written undertaking), as argued in the grounds of appeal. The Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal concerning this part are therefore not accepted.\\n\\n2. Determination on the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal concerning the alternative claim\\n\\nEven where the grounds of the primary claim and the grounds of the alternative claim are compatible, if there is a reasonable need for the parties to make claims by attaching an order of adjudication, they may do so (see Supreme Court Decision 2001DA17633, Decided February 8, 2002), and in such a case, if the primary claim is not fully granted, the plaintiff may also file the action in an inseparably combined manner with the intent of having the court determine the alternative claim within the amount not granted under the primary claim (see Supreme Court Decision 98DA17145, Decided September 4, 2002). Therefore, whether to proceed to adjudicate the alternative claim where the primary claim is only partially granted depends on the interpretation of the parties’ intent in the litigation; accordingly, where the court dismisses part of a claim based on the grounds for the primary claim and grants only an amount less than the amount claimed in the alternative claim, it must clarify whether the Plaintiff intended that, if the primary claim is not fully granted, the court should also determine the alternative claim within the amount not granted under the primary claim, and then decide whether to determine the alternative claim depending on the result.\\n\\nAccording to the record, it is apparent that the Plaintiff sought, primarily, compensation of US$42,269 and delay damages thereon on the ground that the Defendant’s above conduct constituted non-performance of obligation or tort, and, alternatively, sought payment of the agreed amount and delay damages thereon in the amount of US$26,135, on the ground that the Defendant had agreed to pay a total of US$26,135, consisting of the US$10,000 litigation settlement paid by the Plaintiff and US$16,135, corresponding to one-half of the litigation costs. The court below, on the ground that the invoice price of the cargo in this case was only US$19,224.40, partially granted the above primary claim only up to the above amount and delay damages thereon, which amount is less than the amount stated in the alternative claim. Since the above two claims are claims that can be granted independently of whether the other claim is granted or not and are compatible claims, and merely stand in the relationship of alternative joinder because only the amount that may be recognized differs quantitatively, in light of the above legal doctrine, the court below should have clarified whether the Plaintiff intended that, if the primary claim is not fully granted, the court should also determine the alternative claim within the amount not granted under the primary claim, and then decided whether to determine the alternative claim according to the result.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, although granting only US$19,224.40 and delay damages thereon based on the above grounds for the primary claim, did not clarify at all whether the Plaintiff intended the above, and did not make any determination whatsoever on the above alternative claim seeking payment of US$26,135 and delay damages thereon. This was an error in failing to determine the alternative claim after misapprehending the legal doctrine on alternative joinder of claims and thereby violating the duty of clarification, and such error clearly affected the outcome of the judgment. In cases of alternative joinder, because several claims are inseparably combined into a single litigation procedure, even where the court determines only the primary claim and not the alternative claim, if an appeal is filed against that judgment, the omitted part of the alternative claim is also transferred to the appellate instance (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 98DA22253, Decided November 16, 2000). Therefore, the part of the judgment below concerning the alternative claim also cannot stand.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the part of the judgment below dismissing the Defendant’s appeal with respect to the primary claim and the part concerning the alternative claim are both reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination of those parts. The remainder of the Plaintiff’s appeal is dismissed. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2005DA51471]": "We determine the grounds for appeal (including, within the scope that supplement briefs submitted after the expiration of the period for submission of the statement of grounds for appeal supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. With respect to the grounds for appeal by the Plaintiff\\n\\nA. With respect to Ground 1 for appeal\\n\\nIt is procedurally improper and not permitted to join and assert as alternative or preliminary claims multiple claims that are logically wholly unrelated and that should be sought purely by simple joinder; therefore, where the Plaintiff instituted an action in such a form, and the court of first instance, after examining the merits of all such claims, rendered a judgment that upheld only one of those claims and dismissed the remaining claims, this must be regarded as the court having determined that the joinder relationship of those claims, in its original nature, was one of simple joinder; accordingly, where only the Defendant appealed as to the upheld claim, all claims in a simple joinder relationship are, as a matter of course, transferred in their entirety to the appellate court, but the scope of review in the appellate court is limited to the claims among those transferred claims against which the Defendant has appealed.\\n\\nAccording to the record of this case, in bringing the present action against the deceased non-party, the Plaintiff joined, as the causes of action, ① a claim for damages in the amount of KRW 5,989,000,000 related to the acquisition of the head office building, ② a claim for damages in the amount of KRW 2,985,000,000 related to credit lending to Yeongnam Ilbo Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Yeongnam Ilbo”), ③ a claim for damages in the amount of KRW 13,634,000,000 related to the sale and purchase of development trust, etc., and ④ a claim for damages in the amount of KRW 795,000,000 related to real estate leasing operations, as alternative claims, and claimed KRW 700,000,000 out of the total amount of damages, together with delay damages thereon; as to this, the court of first instance, after examining all of the above causes of action, recognized liability for damages related to the acquisition of the head office building and upheld part of the amount claimed by the Plaintiff, and rendered a merits judgment dismissing all other claims, and it is apparent that only the deceased non-party appealed therefrom. Since each of the above causes of action is not logically related to the others and is of a nature that cannot be joined alternatively, in accordance with the legal principles set forth above, the scope of review in the appellate trial below, which is the court below, is limited to the above ① claim for damages related to the acquisition of the head office building, from which the deceased non-party appealed.\\n\\nMeanwhile, before the court below, the Plaintiff expanded the prayer for relief to seek KRW 2,000,000,000 and delay damages thereon, and at the same time clarified that the claim was based on the above ① claim for damages related to the acquisition of the head office building, while also filing an application to the effect that, if the above claim were dismissed, the remaining above ② through ④ claims asserted at first instance should also be examined and upheld. This should ultimately be regarded as an application to amend the cause of action to add the above ② through ④ claims as preliminary claims to the claim for damages related to the acquisition of the head office building, which is the subject matter of review in the court below in this case; and, as stated above, since the above ② through ④ claims are not logically related to the claim for damages related to the acquisition of the head office building and thus cannot be joined with it alternatively, such an amendment to the cause of action cannot be permitted. Accordingly, the court below was correct in not treating the above ② through ④ claims as subject matters of review on the same basis, and there is no illegality in the court below’s determination, such as an error of law regarding the principle of disposition, the principle of pleading, or the law concerning partial claims and alternative claims.\\n\\nB. With respect to Ground 2 for appeal\\n\\nThe court below, based on the factual findings stated in its holding, dismissed the Plaintiff’s claim on the ground that, with respect to the KRW 743,000,000 among the amounts paid as a down payment that had not been settled, the suspension of construction was not due to the fault of Gabeul Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Gabeul Development”) but was carried out at the request of Chosun Life Insurance Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Chosun Life”), and furthermore, no substantial causal relationship could be recognized between the Defendant’s breach of duty or tort related to Chosun Life’s failure to collect a contract performance guarantee deposit and the unsettled amount. This was proper, and it cannot be said that there was an error of law regarding causation. In addition, the argument to the effect that Gabeul Development was at fault because the construction of the new head office building of Chosun Life was suspended due to the bankruptcy of Gabeul Development is merely a criticism of fact-finding that falls within the exclusive province of the trier of fact and cannot constitute a lawful ground for appeal; moreover, because the court below could not be said to have found facts in violation of the rules of logic and experience or beyond the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, the grounds for appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\n2. With respect to the grounds for appeal by Defendants 1, 3, 4, 8, and 9\\n\\nA. Whether the directors’ liability was released under Article 450 of the Commercial Act\\n\\nThe release of directors’ liability under Article 450 of the Commercial Act is limited to matters entered in the financial statements, etc., and approved at the regular general meeting. The fact that, when Chosun Life subscribed to privately placed bonds issued by Shinhan Textile Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Shinhan Textile”) and extended credit lending to Yeongnam Ilbo, the Defendants breached their duties and thereby caused damage to Chosun Life is not a matter that can be known merely because the audit report attached to the financial statements states that officers received a cautionary warning due to, inter alia, excess lending limits to their affiliated group. Therefore, the court below’s determination, to the effect that liability of the Defendants could not be deemed to have been released on such basis, is proper and can be upheld, and there is no illegality, such as an error of law regarding the release of directors’ liability as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nB. Whether liability was exempted by consent of all shareholders under Article 400, etc. of the Commercial Act\\n\\nThe liability of directors, etc. may be exempted by the consent of all shareholders pursuant to Articles 400 and 415 of the Commercial Act. At this time, the consent of all shareholders need not necessarily be express and affirmative, and may be made by way of an implied declaration of intent in the process of transferring and acquiring all of the company’s shares; however, there must be circumstances from which it can be deemed that the transferee of all shares declared an intention not to hold the directors, etc. further responsible for the occurrence and uncollectibility of non-performing loans arising from the directors’ liability.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, determined that the mere circumstance that Hyundai Life Insurance Co., Ltd. acquired 100% of Chosun Life’s shares and merged Chosun Life into itself, and in the course of doing so evaluated the non-performing loans at a discounted rate and determined the acquisition amount, was not sufficient to conclude that the directors’ liability was exempted by an implied declaration of intent of all shareholders. This is consistent with the foregoing legal principles and can be upheld, and there is no illegality, such as an error of law regarding exemption from directors’ liability as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nC. Whether the directors who resolved in writing are liable\\n\\nA director of a stock company, as a member of the board of directors, does not merely express approval or disapproval of proposals submitted to the board of directors, but also has a duty to generally supervise not only his or her own assigned duties but also the performance of duties by other directors in charge of business. Such duty is not excused merely because the director is a non-executive director. Therefore, unless a director of a stock company actually performs no duties as a director at all, such as failing to attend board meetings and subsequently ratifying board resolutions, that very fact constitutes a breach of duty. The court below’s determination, to such effect, that Defendants 8 and 9 cannot be exempted from liability for damages due to breach of duty, is consistent with the foregoing and there is no illegality, such as an error of law regarding directors’ liability.\\n\\nD. Whether exculpation is available due to instructions of the controlling shareholder\\n\\nA company and its controlling shareholder are separate legal entities, and employees and officers of the company cannot be deemed to have a legal duty to follow the instructions of the controlling shareholder in derogation of their duties under the mandate relationship with the company. Accordingly, the court below’s determination that there is no evidence that, when Chosun Life subscribed to privately placed bonds issued by Shinhan Textile and extended credit lending to Yeongnam Ilbo, there were instructions from Park Chang-ho, the controlling shareholder, and that even if there had been such instructions, the Defendants would not be exempted from liability for breach of duty, is consistent with the foregoing legal principles and can be upheld, and there is no illegality, such as an error of law regarding directors’ liability.\\n\\nE. Whether the loans were proper loans under the exception clause of the Detailed Rules for the Implementation of Credit Investigation duties\\n\\nIn light of the record, the court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found, with respect to Shinhan Textile’s subscription to privately placed bonds, that Shinhan Textile’s sales had sharply decreased compared to the previous year, that it was in a state where operating profit could hardly cover financial expenses, and that by the end of 1995 its financial structure and business condition were extremely poor, including that the amount of borrowings at the end of 1995 greatly exceeded sales, and that its credit rating by Korea Investors Service at the end of 1995 was 42 points, making it an E-grade distressed company for which credit lending and financing were prohibited under Chosun Life’s Detailed Rules for the Implementation of Credit Investigation duties; and, with respect to lending to Yeongnam Ilbo, that Yeongnam Ilbo’s sales had decreased from 1995, that it was difficult to cover financial expenses with operating profit, and that by December 1996 its financial structure and business condition were extremely poor, including that its borrowings were close to its sales, and that its credit rating by Korea Investors Service in December 1996 was 42 points, making it an E-grade distressed company for which credit lending and financing were prohibited under Chosun Life’s Detailed Rules for the Implementation of Credit Investigation duties; nevertheless, Chosun Life subscribed to privately placed bonds or extended loans without any sure measures for securing the receivables, and as a result failed to recover the subscription price, etc., thereby causing damage; and, in the course of this, it found that the representative director’s prior approval had not been obtained. The court’s determination that, even if the representative director had given prior approval, the Defendants could not be exempted from liability for breach of duty with respect to the bond subscription, etc. conducted in manifest violation of the relevant provisions is consistent with the foregoing and there is no illegality, such as an error of law regarding breach of duty by directors or management judgment.\\n\\nF. Whether the privately placed bonds were refinanced\\n\\nRefinancing means formally extending a new loan without any actual exchange of funds in order to repay an existing debt, and, unless special circumstances exist, it formally constitutes a separate loan but, in substance, is merely an extension of the maturity of the existing debt. Accordingly, the mere circumstance that a financial institution subscribed to corporate bonds issued by a debtor and applied the subscription price to the repayment of the debtor’s existing credit loan cannot be deemed refinancing (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DO1813, rendered on June 1, 2007).\\n\\nThe court below’s rejection, on this basis, of the Defendants’ argument that the subscription to Shinhan Textile’s privately placed bonds was refinancing is proper, and there is no illegality in that determination, such as an error of law regarding refinancing.\\n\\nG. Whether there was repayment\\n\\nAs to the Defendants’ assertion that the subscription price for Shinhan Textile’s privately placed bonds and the credit loan to Yeongnam Ilbo had been repaid, the court below’s factual findings rejecting the assertion on the ground that there was insufficient evidence to support it, when examined in light of the record, cannot be said to have been made in violation of the rules of logic and experience or beyond the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence; accordingly, the argument in the grounds for appeal challenging this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\nH. Whether the short-term statute of limitations applies\\n\\nThe liability of a director or auditor of a stock company for damages arising from breach of duty to the company, as provided in Article 399(1) and Article 414(1) of the Commercial Act, is liability for breach of obligation arising from a mandate relationship, and therefore the short-term statute of limitations under Article 766(1) of the Civil Act does not apply (see Supreme Court Decision 84DAKA1954, rendered on June 25, 1985). Accordingly, the court below’s rejection of the Defendants’ assertion of the short-term statute of limitations is proper, and there is otherwise no illegality such as an error of law regarding prescription.\\n\\nI. Whether the limitation on liability for damages is manifestly unreasonable\\n\\nWhen a director or auditor commits an act in violation of statutes or the articles of incorporation, or breaches his or her duties, and is therefore liable to compensate the company for damages, in determining the scope of such damages, the amount of damages may be limited in light of the ideal of the damages system, namely fairness in sharing losses, by taking into account all circumstances, such as the content and nature of the business in question, the circumstances of the relevant director’s or auditor’s breach of duty and the manner of the breach, the objective circumstances and degree of involvement in the occurrence and expansion of the company’s damages, the ordinary level of contribution of the director or auditor to the company, whether the relevant director or auditor derived any benefit from the breach of duty, and whether there were defects in the company’s organizational structure or whether a risk management system was in place. Furthermore, factual findings on grounds for mitigation of liability or the determination of the ratio thereof fall within the exclusive province of the trier of fact unless they are deemed manifestly unreasonable in light of the principle of fairness (see Supreme Court Decisions 2002DA60467, 60474, rendered on December 10, 2004, and 2005DA34766, 34773, rendered on December 7, 2006, inter alia).\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the court below’s factual findings concerning the Defendants’ grounds for mitigation of liability or its determination of the Defendants’ liability-mitigation ratio cannot be said to be manifestly unreasonable in light of the principle of fairness; accordingly, there is no illegality in the form of an error of law regarding limitation of liability for damages, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. With respect to the grounds for appeal by Defendant Choi Gung-rak\\n\\nA. Whether the credit rating was conducted for the entire corporate group\\n\\nIn light of the record, the court below’s factual finding that there was no evidence to recognize that the Gabeul Group belonged to one of the top 30 groups cannot be said to have violated the rules of logic and experience or exceeded the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence. Therefore, the court below’s determination rejecting the Defendant’s argument that extending credit to Yeongnam Ilbo after conducting a credit rating of the entire Gabeul Group or its core company on the premise that the Gabeul Group was a top 30 group falls within the scope of management judgment is proper, and the argument in the grounds for appeal challenging this cannot be accepted.\\n\\nB. Whether the loan was proper under the exception clause of the Detailed Rules for the Implementation of Credit Investigation duties\\n\\nIn light of the record, the court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found that Yeongnam Ilbo’s sales had decreased from 1995, that it was difficult to cover financial expenses with operating profit, and that by December 1996 its financial structure and business condition were extremely poor, including that its borrowings were close to its sales, and that its credit rating by Korea Investors Service in December 1996 was 42 points, making it an E-grade distressed company for which credit lending and financing were prohibited under Chosun Life’s Detailed Rules for the Implementation of Credit Investigation duties; nevertheless, Chosun Life extended the loan without any sure measures for securing the receivables, and as a result failed to recover the loan amount, thereby causing damage; and, in the course of this loan transaction, the representative director’s prior approval was not obtained. The court’s determination that, even if the representative director had given prior approval, the Defendant could not be exempted from liability for breach of duty because the loan was extended in manifest violation of the relevant regulations is consistent with the foregoing and there is no illegality in that determination, such as an error of law regarding breach of duty by a director or management judgment, or a violation of precedent.\\n\\nC. Whether the director’s liability was released under Article 450 of the Commercial Act\\n\\nThe release of directors’ liability under Article 450 of the Commercial Act is limited to matters entered in the financial statements, etc., and approved at the regular general meeting. The fact that, when Chosun Life extended credit lending to Yeongnam Ilbo, the Defendant breached his duty and thereby caused damage to Chosun Life is not a matter that can be known merely because the audit report attached to the financial statements states that officers received a cautionary warning due to, inter alia, excess lending limits to their affiliated group. Therefore, the court below’s determination, to the effect that liability of the Defendant could not be deemed to have been released on such basis, is proper and can be upheld, and there is no illegality, such as an error of law regarding the release of a director’s liability as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nD. Whether there was a violation of the duty of good faith and fair dealing\\n\\nA claim for damages against a director of a stock company does not violate the duty of good faith and fair dealing merely because, despite the fact that an auditor of the stock company or a person who merged the stock company was aware of the director’s breach of duty, the fact of damages arising from the director’s breach of duty was not entered in the financial statements, etc. and was not submitted to the regular general meeting, thereby preventing the director from being provided an opportunity for release from liability. In this respect, the court below’s view that the claim for damages against the Defendant does not violate the duty of good faith and fair dealing is proper and can be upheld, and there is no illegality in the form of an error of law regarding the duty of good faith and fair dealing as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nE. Whether exculpation is available under the Regulations on Inspection and Sanctions of Financial Institutions\\n\\nThe Defendant argues in the grounds for appeal that, pursuant to Article 26 of the Regulations on Inspection and Sanctions of Financial Institutions, there is an exculpation provision for credit-related persons, and that the credit transaction to Yeongnam Ilbo was performed with due care of a good manager, and therefore he should be exculpated pursuant to the above regulations; however, this was raised for the first time at the appellate stage and cannot constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n4.
