Whether there was a violation of the rules of evidence in calculating the amount of damages (Grounds for Appeal, Point 1)\\n\\nThe court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence indicated in its opinion, found that defects existed in the building at issue and that repair thereof required a total of KRW 83,154,169 (including the cost of temporary works for repair of defects), and then, taking into account all circumstances revealed in the pleadings, limited the amount of damages in lieu of repair of defects to KRW 66,523,335, which is 80% of the above repair costs, in accordance with the principle of fairness or the principle of good faith.\\n\\nReviewing the record in accordance with the relevant legal principles, there is no error in the court below’s above determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, that influenced the judgment by violating the rule of logic and experience, thereby going beyond the limits of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the probative force of a final judgment, or by insufficient reasoning.\\n\\n3. Whether it is contrary to res judicata concerning the set-off defense (Grounds for Appeal, Point 3)\\n\\na. Article 216(1) of the Civil Procedure Act provides, “A final judgment shall have res judicata effect only with respect to matters included in the text of the judgment,” thereby making clear that, in principle, the determination in the reasons for judgment is not subject to res judicata; however, as an exception, paragraph (2) provides, “The determination whether a claim asserted by way of set-off is established shall have res judicata effect only up to the amount against which set-off was asserted.” The reason res judicata is recognized for the court’s determination on a set-off assertion, notwithstanding that it is a determination in the reasons for judgment, is that if res judicata were not recognized in this respect, a dispute over the existence or nonexistence of the Plaintiff’s claim would later be transformed into a dispute over the existence or nonexistence of the active claim raised in another action, so that the opponent of the set-off assertion would not only be subject to disadvantage through the person asserting set-off exercising the active claim twice, but also there would be a risk that the judgment in the earlier action on the existence or nonexistence of the Plaintiff’s claim, rendered on the premise of the determination on the set-off assertion, would become meaningless as a result; this is to prevent that outcome (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2004DA17207, rendered July 22, 2005; Supreme Court Decision 2016DA46338, 46345, rendered August 30, 2018).\\n\\nb. According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the Plaintiff raised in the court of first instance of the earlier action a defense of concurrent performance based on the claim for repair of defects or the claim for damages in lieu of repair of defects concerning the construction at issue, and also a set-off defense using the above damages claim as the active claim, but withdrew the above set-off defense in the appellate court; the appellate court of the earlier action rendered a judgment partially upholding the Defendant’s claim for the construction price, and in the reasons for that judgment rejected the Plaintiff’s above defense of concurrent performance, but did not determine the withdrawn set-off defense; and the appellate judgment of the earlier action became final and conclusive as is.\\n\\nc. If such is the case, the appellate judgment in the earlier action does not have res judicata effect with respect to the Plaintiff’s set-off defense, and therefore there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in the court below’s determination that partially upheld the Plaintiff’s claim for damages in lieu of repair of defects, by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the res judicata effect of set-off, etc.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the interruption of the extinctive prescription by a judicial claim is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: The filing of an action for registration of the establishment of a mortgage by way of security has the effect of interrupting the extinctive prescription of the claim that is to become the secured claim.
B: Where a negotiable instrument has been delivered as a means of securing payment of the underlying claim, the creditor’s judicial claim based on the bill claim has the effect of interrupting the extinctive prescription of the underlying claim.
C: Where the Plaintiff, after claiming return of the down payment based on the creditor’s right of subrogation, acquires the down-payment return claim itself and changes the action by way of substitution to a claim for the assigned amount, the effect of interruption of prescription arising from the original creditor’s subrogation action ceases.
D: If, before the requirements for setting up the assignment of a claim against the debtor have been met, the assignor of the claim filed a judicial claim against the debtor, and during that litigation the debtor acknowledged the effect of the assignment of the claim, causing the claim to be dismissed, and if the assignee of the claim thereafter filed an action for the assigned amount within 6 months, the effect of interruption of the extinctive prescription arising from the assignor’s aforementioned judicial claim is maintained.
E: Where the Plaintiff, while claiming only part of one claim that was made the subject of the claim in the complaint, indicated an intention to expand the amount claimed in the future depending on the progress of the litigation, but did not in fact expand the amount claimed until the litigation ended, the extinctive prescription for the remaining part can be interrupted by making a judicial claim within 6 months from the time the litigation ended.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2002DA7213]": "We examine each ground of appeal (the statements in the Plaintiff’s supplemental statement of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Determination on the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted and finding the facts as stated in its reasoning, held that the agreement entered into between the Defendant, a merchant, and the Plaintiff to establish a mortgage by way of security in order to secure funds borrowed for the procurement of business capital constituted an auxiliary commercial act, and therefore the right to demand registration of the establishment of the mortgage by way of security in this case had been extinguished upon the expiration of the five-year statute of limitations prescribed by the Commercial Act. As to the Plaintiff’s assertion that “so long as extinctive prescription has not been completed with respect to the loan claim, which is the secured claim under the above agreement to establish the mortgage by way of security, the right to demand registration of the establishment of the mortgage by way of security in this case is also not extinguished,” the court below held that the right to demand registration in this case is a claim separate from the above loan claim, and that the period of prescription also runs independently, and accordingly rejected the Plaintiff’s above assertion. The above findings and determination by the court below are proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in misapprehending the facts by violating the rules of evidence, or in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the extinctive prescription of the right to demand registration and auxiliary commercial acts.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court precedents cited by the Plaintiff in the grounds of appeal concern different facts and purports and are not appropriate for invocation in this case.\\n\\n2. Determination on the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. As to the assertion of misapprehension of the legal principles regarding extinctive prescription\\n\\nThe exercise of the Plaintiff’s right to demand registration of the mortgage by way of security is aimed at realizing the monetary claim in this case that is to become the secured claim; accordingly, the complaint seeking registration of the establishment of the mortgage by way of security naturally includes an allegation as to the existence of the claim that is to become the secured claim. Moreover, since, even before the Plaintiff added in the court below a claim seeking payment of money, the Defendant had asserted by way of defense the extinction of the monetary claim that would be the secured claim, thereby resulting in a substantive review as to the existence of that claim and confirmation of whether it existed, it is proper to regard the filing of the complaint seeking registration of the establishment of the mortgage by way of security as an exercise of the right with respect to the claim alleged and reviewed as the secured claim. Thus, the filing of the complaint seeking registration of the establishment of the mortgage by way of security should be regarded as equivalent to a judicial claim regarding the secured claim, and as producing the effect of interrupting extinctive prescription with respect to the secured claim.\\n\\nIn the same purport, the court below properly rejected the Defendant’s defense of extinctive prescription by holding that the Plaintiff’s filing of this action for registration of the establishment of the mortgage by way of security interrupted extinctive prescription for the entire loan claim in this case, for which the Plaintiff sought payment in the court below, and that even if the claim for registration of the establishment of the mortgage by way of security was not accepted because the right to demand such registration had become time-barred, the result is no different. Accordingly, it cannot be said that there was any illegality in misapprehending the legal principles regarding extinctive prescription, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nb. As to the assertion that the money was lent to Life Production Co., Ltd., rather than to the Defendant\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found that the Plaintiff lent to the Defendant each amount listed in the “Principal Amount” column of the “Appendix (Promissory Notes and Checks)” of the judgment of the court below, using as security the promissory notes and checking-account checks as set forth therein, which were issued by Life Production Co., Ltd. and endorsed by the Defendant, with the interest rate set at 2.5% per month for each, and the maturity date set as the due date of the promissory note (loans in Items 1 through 4 of the appendix to the judgment of the court below) and the date of issuance of the checking-account check (loans in Items 5 through 9 of the appendix to the judgment of the court below), and the court below found these facts as to each loan. In light of the relevant evidence and the record, the above findings by the court below are persuasive as proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in misapprehending the facts by violating the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nc. As to the assertion of dation in payment\\n\\nFurther, with respect to the Defendant’s assertion that, around October 1992, the copyrights in the video tapes imported by Life Production Co., Ltd., such as “Musahyeol 3 through 12, Sorim Dalma, Seongjeon,” were appraised at KRW 90,000,000 and then transferred to the Plaintiff in dation in payment, the court below rejected that assertion, holding that the evidence cited in the reasoning that supported it is hard to believe or insufficient to accept the Defendant’s assertion, and that there is no other evidence to support it. In light of the relevant evidence and the record, the above determination by the court below is proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in misapprehending the facts by violating the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nd. As to the assertion of omission to rule\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, with respect to the Defendant’s assertion that it paid KRW 72,135,371 in excess of the KRW 46,044,000 that the Plaintiff admits having received as payment, the court below rejected that assertion by finding that the evidence cited in the reasoning supporting it is hard to believe or insufficient, and that there is no other evidence to support it. Ultimately, the judgment of the court below must be understood as having rejected in full the Defendant’s assertion of payment in excess of the above amount that the Plaintiff admits having received, and it is clear that this includes a determination rejecting the Defendant’s assertion that it paid the Plaintiff KRW 370,000 on August 4, 1992. Therefore, it cannot be said that the judgment of the court below contains any illegality of omission to rule, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by each losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in this case."}

{"[2008DU20109]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. As to Point 1\\n\\nThe lower court, taking together the evidence it admitted, determined that the Plaintiffs had acquired from the owners listed in the column for registered owners in each purchase-date column of Attached Schedule 2 to the lower court judgment, on each purchase date listed in the same schedule, other rights including ownership rights in the respective parcels of land at issue (hereinafter referred to as the “former owners”).\\n\\nUpon examining the reasons for the lower court judgment in light of the record, the above fact-finding and determination by the lower court are acceptable as proper, and it cannot be said that there was any error of law concerning the interpretation of the sales contract, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, or any violation such as insufficiency of trial.\\n\\n2. As to Point 2\\n\\nAn assignor after assignment of a claim, before the requirements for opposability against the debtor are satisfied, still retains the status of creditor in relation to the debtor, and thus may file a judicial claim against the debtor that has the effect of interrupting the statute of limitations. In such a case, even if, during the lawsuit filed by the assignor, the effect of interruption of the statute of limitations is extinguished under Article 170(1) of the Civil Act because the assignor’s claim is dismissed due to circumstances such as the debtor’s acknowledgment of the effect of the assignment of the claim, the assignor’s claim does not thereby become a claim by a person without right from the outset. Therefore, if the assignee, within 6 months thereafter, filed a judicial claim, etc. against the debtor, the statute of limitations is interrupted by the assignor’s initial judicial claim under Articles 169 and 170(2) of the Civil Act.\\n\\nAccording to the facts established by the lower court and the record, the non-party, who was the decedent of Plaintiffs 1 to 23, 26, and 27-1 to 3, had, on March 14 and December 22 of the same year, respectively, which were before December 31, 2003, the expiration date of the statute of limitations period for the compensation claim for loss at issue, filed lawsuits against the Defendant seeking payment of compensation for loss in the names of the former owners; that on April 7, 2006, they filed applications for intervention as successors in that lawsuit; that in that lawsuit, the Seoul Administrative Court, on June 22, 2007, dismissed all of the said Plaintiffs’ applications for intervention as successors on the ground that, since the said Plaintiffs had acquired the claims before the respective filings of the lawsuits, they did not satisfy the requirements for intervention as successors even if they had satisfied the requirements for opposability after filing, and dismissed all of the claims of the predecessor-in-interest of the said Plaintiffs on the ground that they had assigned the compensation claim for loss to the said Plaintiffs; that the said Plaintiffs did not appeal that judgment but, together with the remaining Plaintiffs, filed the present action on August 14, 2007. Meanwhile, it is difficult to find materials in the record clearly showing that the requirements for opposability concerning the assignment of the said compensation claim for loss had been satisfied before the respective filings of the lawsuits, and it appears that the foregoing point was not clearly examined.\\n\\nIn light of these circumstances and the legal principle stated above, the aforementioned claims by the former owners may also be viewed as claims made after assignment of the claim but before the requirements for opposability were satisfied. Accordingly, even if the effect of interruption of the statute of limitations was extinguished because those claims were dismissed, there is room to regard the statute of limitations as having been interrupted by the former owners’ filing of the lawsuit, since the said Plaintiffs, as successors to the former owners, filed the present action within 6 months thereafter.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court, on the sole ground that the said Plaintiffs had purchased the rights concerning the present parcels of land from the former owners before the former owners’ filing of the lawsuit, without examining when the requirements for opposability concerning the assignment of the compensation claim for loss at issue were satisfied, determined that the said Plaintiffs did not qualify as successors entitled to the effect of interruption of the statute of limitations arising from the former owners’ filing of the lawsuit, and thus rejected the said Plaintiffs’ rejoinder based on interruption of the statute of limitations. In so doing, the lower court erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the scope of successors under Article 169 of the Civil Act and Article 170, and by failing to exercise the power to clarify or to conduct the necessary examination, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n3. As to Point 3\\n\\nThe exercise by the debtor of the defense based on the completion of the statute of limitations is also governed by the principle of good faith and fair dealing and the principle prohibiting abuse of rights, which are the fundamental principles of our Civil Act; thus, where the debtor made the creditor’s exercise of rights or interruption of the statute of limitations impossible or significantly difficult before the statute of limitations was completed, or engaged in conduct causing the creditor to believe that such measures were unnecessary, or where, objectively, there existed an impediment preventing the creditor from exercising rights, or where, once the statute of limitations had already been completed, the debtor behaved in a manner suggesting that it would not invoke the statute of limitations, thereby causing the right holder to rely on that belief, or where there are special circumstances such as a substantial need to protect the creditor, and circumstances such as another creditor under the same conditions receiving performance of the debt, making recognition of the refusal to perform the obligation manifestly unjust or unfair, the debtor’s assertion of the completion of the statute of limitations cannot be permitted as an abuse of rights contrary to the principle of good faith and fair dealing. However, the mere fact that the State has a duty to protect the people does not mean that the State’s assertion of the completion of the statute of limitations itself constitutes an abuse of rights contrary to the principle of good faith and fair dealing; therefore, for the State’s assertion of completion of the statute of limitations to be contrary to the principle of good faith and fair dealing and an abuse of rights, the special circumstances stated above must be recognized, and moreover, because applying such general principles to exclude the operation of the specific system established by law risks undermining legal stability, another fundamental principle in legal interpretation, caution must be exercised in its application (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2004DA33469, rendered on 2008. 5. 29.).\\n\\nThe lower court, after recognizing the facts as stated in its opinion based on the evidence it admitted, determined that there was no evidence to support a finding that the Defendant had acted in such a way as to make the Plaintiffs’ exercise of their claim for compensation impossible or substantially difficult, or to make them believe that such measures were unnecessary, and that objectively there was no impediment preventing the Plaintiffs from exercising a claim for damages, nor any significant circumstance under which the exercise of rights could not be expected, and on that basis held that this was not a case where the Defendant’s assertion of the completion of the statute of limitations and refusal to perform the obligation to pay compensation would be manifestly unjust or unfair.\\n\\nUpon examining the record in light of the legal principle stated above, the lower court’s fact-finding and determination as above are acceptable as proper, and it cannot be said that there was any violation such as error of law concerning whether the exercise of the statute-of-limitations defense is contrary to the principle of good faith and fair dealing, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n4. As to Point 4\\n\\nWhere a part of a debt is performed before the statute of limitations is completed, it has the effect of acknowledgment of the debt and thereby produces the effect of interruption of the statute of limitations, but only where there is no dispute as to the amount (see Supreme Court Decision 95DA39854, rendered on 1996. 1. 23.).\\n\\nThe lower court, after recognizing the facts as stated in its opinion based on the evidence it admitted, determined that, since the Defendant, who was obligated to provide compensation for loss, had a dispute as to the amount of compensation and deposited the compensation amount according to its own appraisal results as performance deposit, the effect of interruption of the statute of limitations or waiver of the benefit of prescription arises only within the limit of the deposited amount.\\n\\nUpon examining the record in light of the legal principle stated above, the lower court’s fact-finding and determination as above are acceptable as proper, and it cannot be said that there was any violation such as error of law concerning the scope of interruption of the statute of limitations or waiver of the benefit of prescription arising from partial performance, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the part of the lower court judgment concerning Plaintiffs 1 to 23, 26, and 27-1 to 3 is reversed, and the case as to that part is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination. The appeals of Plaintiffs 24, 25, and 28 to 32 are each dismissed, and the appellate costs of those Plaintiffs shall be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2010DA17284]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the Defendant purchased the first land in this case from the deceased Non-Party 1 and the second land in this case from Non-Party 2 pursuant to the Special Measures Act on the Management of Requisitioned Property, etc., but when there was no longer any military necessity, on 2002. 6. 18. the Defendant notified Non-Party 3, who is the heir of the deceased Non-Party 1, and Non-Party 2 of a sale plan that each land in this case would be sold by private sale pursuant to the provisions of Article 20-2 of the Special Measures Act on the Management of Requisitioned Property, etc.; accordingly, Non-Party 3 and 2 applied to the Defendant for purchase of each land in this case around 2002. 6. 29.; Non-Party 4, intending to purchase and develop each land in this case, on 2002. 11. 22. entered into the “agreement in this case” with Non-Party 3 and 2, under which “Non-Party 3 and 2 shall, after completing the registration of transfer of ownership with respect to each land in this case, transfer it again to the Plaintiff, and Non-Party 4 shall be responsible for a series of acts, such as concluding a sales contract with the Defendant in the names of Non-Party 3 and 2 or paying the purchase price therefor,” and, in return for this agreement in this case, paid to Non-Party 3 and 2 a total of KRW 718.4 million (an amount corresponding to a kind of resale profit, hereinafter referred to as “the resale profit in this case”); accordingly, on 2002. 11. 23., Non-Party 4, acting on behalf of Non-Party 3 and Non-Party 2, concluded the “sales contracts in this case” with the Defendant and paid to the Defendant earnest money totaling KRW 914,794,000, equivalent to approximately 10% of the purchase price (hereinafter referred to as “the earnest money in this case”); however, thereafter, as Non-Party 4 failed to pay the balance of the purchase price, etc. under the sales contracts in this case, the sales contracts in this case were rescinded on 2003. 4. 28. due to the purchaser’s fault; on the premise that he had a claim for restitution of the resale profit in this case and the earnest money in this case against Non-Party 3 and 2, Non-Party 4 assigned to the Plaintiff on 2007. 7. 27. the claims for restitution of the resale profit in this case and the earnest money in this case against Non-Party 3 and 2 (hereinafter referred to as “the assignment of claims in this case”), and notified Non-Party 3 and 2 of such assignment on 2007. 9. 18.; thereafter, on 2007. 11. 19., the Plaintiff sent to the Defendant by content-certified mail a demand (hereinafter referred to as “the demand in this case”) to the effect that “the Plaintiff, as a creditor of Non-Party 3 and 2, subrogates them and seeks restitution of the earnest money in this case as restoration to the original state following rescission of the sales contracts in this case,” and it can be found that the mail arrived at the Defendant on 2007. 11. 22.\\n\\nIn addition, according to the record, when the Plaintiff filed this action on 2008. 3. 14., on the premise that Non-Party 4 was a party to the sales contracts in this case, the Plaintiff alleged as the cause of the claim that the Plaintiff had acquired from Non-Party 4 the claim for restitution of the earnest money in this case that Non-Party 4 held against the Defendant; thereafter, in the preparatory brief dated 2008. 5. 15., on the premise that Non-Party 3 and 2 were parties to the sales contracts in this case, the Plaintiff changed the cause of the claim to the effect that, as a creditor of Non-Party 3 and Non-Party 2, the Plaintiff exercises by subrogation the claim for restitution of the earnest money in this case that they held against the Defendant; meanwhile, on 2007. 12. 15., the Plaintiff filed an action against Non-Party 3 and 2, etc. seeking restitution of the resale profit and the earnest money in this case, and although a judgment dismissing the Plaintiff’s claim was rendered at first instance on 2008. 9. 3., during the pendency of the appellate instance, on 2009. 1. 20., a compromise by agreement was reached to the effect that “Non-Party 3 and 2, etc. assign to the Plaintiff all rights, including the claim for restitution of the earnest money in this case, which they hold against the Defendant in connection with the sales contracts in this case, and notify the Defendant of such assignment of claims; the Plaintiff waives the remaining claims against Non-Party 3 and 2, etc.”; accordingly, it can also be found that the Plaintiff, in a preparatory brief dated 2009. 1. 28., conformed the cause of the claim in this case to the above compromise by agreement and changed it again from a claim based on the right of creditor subrogation to a claim for the assignee’s payment.\\n\\nOn the basis of the above facts, the court below, without omitting a determination on the cause of the claim asserted by the Plaintiff, proceeded directly to the Defendant’s defense of extinctive prescription, and determined that the claim for restitution of the earnest money against the Defendant held by Non-Party 3 and 2 following rescission of the sales contracts in this case became exercisable from 2003. 4. 28., when the sales contracts in this case were rescinded, but since the Plaintiff brought the assignee’s payment claim only on 2009. 1. 28., after the five-year extinctive prescription period prescribed by Article 96 of the National Finance Act had elapsed, the claim was extinguished by prescription; and then rejected the Plaintiff’s argument that, because the Plaintiff made the demand in this case to the Defendant on 2007. 11. 22., before completion of extinctive prescription, and filed a claim seeking restitution of the earnest money in this case based on the right of creditor subrogation within six months thereafter on 2008. 5. 15., the extinctive prescription of the claim for restitution of the earnest money in this case was interrupted, for the following reasons.\\n\\nFirst, in order for a judicial claim to become a ground for interruption of prescription, such claim must be made by a creditor or a person entitled to exercise the claim; however, since the Plaintiff’s preserved claims, such as a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment and a right to claim substituted performance, etc., alleged by the Plaintiff against Non-Party 3 and 2 cannot be recognized, the Plaintiff’s claim by subrogation, seeking restitution of the earnest money in this case against the Defendant as a creditor of Non-Party 3 and 2, is merely a judicial claim by a person without authority and cannot constitute a ground for interruption of prescription; second, even if extinctive prescription was interrupted by the above claim by subrogation, as the prior action was withdrawn when the Plaintiff, on 2009. 1. 28., change the cause of claim from the claim by subrogation to the claim for the assignee’s payment by means of an exchange of claims, the effect of interruption of prescription as a judicial claim by the above claim by subrogation is not maintained.\\n\\nHowever, the above determination of the court below cannot be sustained for the following reasons.\\n\\nAccording to the factual findings recognized by the court below, Non-Party 4, intending to acquire the lands in this case by resale from Non-Party 3 and 2, entered into the agreement in this case, under which, in the position of a resale purchaser, he would himself act on behalf of Non-Party 3 and 2 and perform all acts, such as concluding a sales contract with the Defendant and paying the purchase price therefor; and pursuant to the agreement in this case, in addition to paying the resale profit in this case to Non-Party 3 and 2, Non-Party 4 directly procured, at his own responsibility, the purchase price under the sales contracts in this case and paid the earnest money in this case to the Defendant, but the sales contracts in this case were rescinded. According to this, the sales contracts in this case no longer enabled Non-Party 3 and 2 to acquire each land in this case from the Defendant; meanwhile, in light of the purpose of the agreement in this case and the contents of the above-mentioned compromise by agreement, etc., the agreement in this case must also be understood to include an implied agreement to the effect that, in the event that, due to reasons such as the sales contracts in this case becoming invalid or being rescinded at the responsibility of Non-Party 4, the resale profit in this case paid by Non-Party 4 to Non-Party 3 and 2 would not be questioned, but with respect to the earnest money, etc. paid by Non-Party 4 to the Defendant in place of Non-Party 3 and 2 pursuant to the sales contracts in this case, if Non-Party 3 and 2 were to acquire the claim for restitution thereof, they would assign it to Non-Party 4, and if the earnest money, etc. were actually returned by the Defendant, they would return that money to Non-Party 4. And it is reasonable to view that through the assignment of claims in this case, the Plaintiff also received assignment from Non-Party 4 of the above contractual claims that Non-Party 4 held against Non-Party 3 and 2. Therefore, it is difficult to lightly deny the existence of the preserved claim in the creditor subrogation action before the amendment in this case.\\n\\nMeanwhile, a creditor may not exercise the right of creditor subrogation without court permission before the due date of the claim, but may perform acts of preservation (see Article 404(2) of the Civil Act); thus, the Plaintiff, as a creditor, may, using the above contractual rights as the preserved claim, demand restitution of the earnest money in this case from the Defendant and make a judicial claim for the purpose of interrupting extinctive prescription of the claim for restitution of the earnest money in this case by subrogating Non-Party 3 and 2.\\n\\nIn addition, through the preparatory brief dated 2009. 1. 28., the Plaintiff changed the existing claim based on the right of creditor subrogation to an assignee’s payment claim based on assignment of claims, and although this should be regarded as the prior action based on the right of creditor subrogation being withdrawn as an exchange of the cause of claim, the subject matter of litigation in the creditor subrogation action is the claim for restitution of the earnest money in this case that the debtors, Non-Party 3 and 2, hold against the Defendant, whereas the assignee’s payment claim in this case is based on the fact that the Plaintiff acquired the claim for restitution of the earnest money in this case itself. Thus, the two claims are merely a specific succession of rights and obligations concerning the same subject matter of litigation, and the subject matter of litigation is the same; the effect of interruption of prescription also extends to specific successors (Article 169 of the Civil Act); when a specific successor who has succeeded to all or part of the rights or obligations that are the subject matter of litigation in a pending lawsuit participates in the litigation or takes over the litigation, the effect of interruption of prescription arises retroactively from the time when the lawsuit was first pending before the court (Articles 80 and 82(3) of the Civil Procedure Act); and because the Plaintiff exercised the claim for restitution of the earnest money in this case based on the right of creditor subrogation and then again directly exercised it after acquiring it, the Plaintiff cannot be regarded as a person who “sleeps on his rights” with respect to the claim for restitution of the earnest money in this case. In light of these circumstances, even if the Plaintiff, after bringing a claim based on the right of creditor subrogation, acquired the very claim subject to subrogation and changed the lawsuit into an assignee’s payment claim, it is reasonable to hold that the effect of interruption of prescription caused by the original creditor subrogation action does not cease.\\n\\nTherefore, the court below should have reached its conclusion by examining and determining whether the claim for restitution of the earnest money in this case against the Defendant, which the Plaintiff alleged had been assigned from Non-Party 4, exists, that is, whether there is a liquidated damages agreement in the sales contracts in this case, whether the predetermined amount of damages is excessively unreasonable and thus reducible, and whether the claim for the assignee’s payment alleged by the Plaintiff satisfies the requirements for asserting the assignment of claims against the Defendant; it should not have rejected the Plaintiff’s claim in this case solely on the Defendant’s defense of extinctive prescription.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court 2009. 2. 12. Decision 2008DA84229 and the Supreme Court 1982. 12. 14. Decision 82DAKA148, etc., cited by the Defendant, concern cases in which a creditor directly made a claim based on his own title and then subrogated or acquired the debtor’s right to make a claim; they differ from this case, in which the Plaintiff, after making a subrogation claim, acquired the very claim subject to subrogation and made an assignee’s payment claim.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, without making any determination on the cause of claim asserted by the Plaintiff, accepted the Defendant’s defense of extinctive prescription and then determined that the Plaintiff’s preserved claim against Non-Party 3 and 2 does not exist, so the claim by subrogation is merely a judicial claim by a person without authority and cannot constitute a ground for interruption of prescription, and even if it were a ground for interruption of prescription, the effect of interruption of prescription ceased because the Plaintiff, by an exchange of claims, changed the cause of claim from the claim based on the right of creditor subrogation to the assignee’s payment claim and the prior action was withdrawn; accordingly, the court below rejected the Plaintiff’s argument on interruption of extinctive prescription, and thus the judgment below contains an error of law in misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning interruption of extinctive prescription by the right of creditor subrogation, etc., and failing to conduct the necessary examination. The argument in the grounds for appeal pointing this out is meritorious.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination, and it is so adjudged, with the concurrence of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2019DA223723]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. a. Where an action is filed with an explicit indication that judgment is sought only with respect to a part of a single claim, the effect of interruption of the Statute of Limitations by the filing of the action arises only with respect to that part and does not arise with respect to the remainder (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 74DA1557 dated February 25, 1975), but where, while seeking only part of the claim that is the subject matter of the complaint, the Plaintiff indicates an intention to expand the amount claimed in the future depending on the progress of the litigation and in fact expands the amount claimed before the termination of the relevant action, it is construed that, from the time of filing the action, judgment was sought with respect to the entire claim, and in such a case the effect of interruption of the Statute of Limitations by a judicial claim arises with respect to the entire claim from the time of filing the action (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 91DA43695 dated April 10, 1992).\\n\\nb. Where, while seeking only part of the claim that is the subject matter of the complaint, the Plaintiff indicated an intention to expand the amount claimed in the future depending on the progress of the litigation but did not in fact expand the amount claimed until the relevant action was terminated, it cannot be deemed, in light of the course of the litigation, that judgment was sought with respect to the entire claim, and therefore the effect of interruption of the Statute of Limitations by a judicial claim does not arise with respect to the remainder.\\n\\nHowever, even in such a case, as a creditor who filed the action while indicating an intention to expand the amount claimed in the future is generally understood to have the intent to claim the remainder in the future, unless there are other special circumstances, during the pendency of the relevant action, it should be deemed that the intent to exercise the right with respect to the remainder has been manifested and that the state of exercising the right by a demand continues; and the creditor may interrupt the Statute of Limitations for the remainder by taking the measures prescribed in Article 174 of the Civil Act within 6 months from the termination of the relevant action.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Supreme Court has made clear, with respect to a demand arising from notice of litigation, which is effected through an act of the court unlike an ordinary demand, that the state of exercising the right by a demand continues during the pendency of the relevant action, and that the Statute of Limitations may be interrupted by taking the measures prescribed in Article 174 of the Civil Act within 6 months from the termination of the relevant action (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DA14340 dated July 9, 2009).\\n\\n2. According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na. The Plaintiff was entitled to receive an apartment as part of resettlement measures by providing a residential building due to a public project implemented by the Defendant, and completed payment of the sale price by October 31, 2008.\\n\\nb. The Plaintiff filed the prior action in this case against the Defendant on July 30, 2013, asserting that the cost of installing basic living facilities was included in the apartment sale price and that the Defendant, as the project operator, was obliged to return the amount of unjust enrichment.\\n\\nc. The complaint in the prior action in this case states, under the heading “Partial Claim,” that “the Plaintiff should be deemed to have a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment, but the exact amount will be calculated later by receiving materials related to the basic living facilities from the Defendant, and for now only 2,000,000 won, which is part thereof, is being claimed.”\\n\\nd. The Plaintiff did not expand the amount claimed until the prior action in this case was terminated, and on October 12, 2016, the court rendered a judgment stating, “The Defendant shall pay the Plaintiff 2,000,000 won and delay damages thereon.” The above judgment became final on November 8, 2016.\\n\\ne. The Plaintiff filed the present action on May 18, 2017, and is claiming the remaining amount of 18,808,243 won excluding the amount recognized in the prior action in this case, together with delay damages thereon.\\n\\nf. The Plaintiff’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment against the Defendant is a right against a local government having as its object the payment of money, and the Statute of Limitations period is 5 years.\\n\\n3. In light of the legal principles set forth above, examining the above factual relationship, since the Plaintiff indicated in the complaint, etc. an intention to expand the amount claimed in the future but did not expand the amount claimed until the prior action in this case was terminated, it is appropriate to deem that the Plaintiff sought judgment only with respect to 2,000,000 won and delay damages thereon in the prior action in this case. Accordingly, the effect of interruption of the Statute of Limitations by the filing of the prior action in this case arose only with respect to the above 2,000,000 won and delay damages thereon; with respect to the remainder, it may be said that the state of exercising the right by a demand continued during the pendency of the prior action in this case, but unless the Plaintiff took the measures prescribed in Article 174 of the Civil Act, such as filing the present action within 6 months from the termination of the prior action in this case, the effect of interruption of the Statute of Limitations does not exist and the Statute of Limitations has been completed.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment of the court below, which held that the Statute of Limitations had been completed with respect to the remainder not claimed in the prior action in this case, is proper in conclusion, and there is no error that affected the judgment by, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, misapprehending the legal principles concerning interruption of the Statute of Limitations.\\n\\n5. Therefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the final appeal are to be borne by the losing party; it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Supreme Court Justices as stated in the disposition."}

{"[99DA16378]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below first found that the Plaintiff lent KRW 25,000,000 to the non-party on 1982. 11. 2., and that the non-party died on 1987. 9. 18., and that the Defendant, as the non-party’s spouse, inherited one-third of the non-party’s debts; then, it accepted the Defendant’s defense of the Statute of Limitations, and further, with respect to the Plaintiff’s rejoinder that the Statute of Limitations for the claim for the loan in this case had been interrupted by the Plaintiff’s provisional attachment, on 1988. 1. 4., of the non-party limited partnership company ○○ Company’s equity interest against the Defendant, in Daejeon District Court Seosan Branch 87KA1062, it rejected the Plaintiff’s rejoinder on the ground that the above provisional attachment was based on the right to be preserved, namely, the promissory note claim issued by the non-party and delivered to the Plaintiff as security in connection with the claim for the loan in this case; and that, although the claim for the loan in this case and the promissory note amount claim had the same object of claim, they were legally separate claims, so the above provisional attachment could not interrupt the Statute of Limitations for the claim for the loan in this case.\\n\\nUpon review, in a case such as this, where a promissory note has been issued and received as a means to secure payment of the underlying claim, the underlying claim and the note claim are separate, so the creditor may exercise rights according to his or her choice, and a claim made only on the basis of the underlying claim cannot be regarded as the exercise of the note claim itself, and therefore cannot interrupt the Statute of Limitations of the note claim (see Supreme Court Decisions 67DA75, rendered 1967. 4. 25., 93DA59922, rendered 1994. 12. 2., etc.); however, on the other hand, such a promissory note is received as a means of payment for the underlying claim in order to economically secure the same performance, and the exercise of the note claim is not only for realizing the underlying claim, but also the Statute of Limitations of the underlying claim constitutes a ground of personal defense of the debtor in an action for payment of the note amount, so if the creditor has interrupted the Statute of Limitations of the note claim, an unreasonable result would occur in which the creditor would be unable to realize the right according to the debtor’s personal defense; therefore, in the opposite case where the creditor makes a claim based on the note claim, it is appropriate to regard it as having the effect of interrupting the Statute of Limitations of the underlying claim (see Supreme Court Decision 4293MINSANG748, rendered 1961. 11. 9.), and this legal principle shall likewise apply to a case where the creditor has exercised the right by provisionally attaching the debtor’s property with the note claim as the right to be preserved.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, from a contrary view, rejected the Plaintiff’s rejoinder; this constitutes an illegality arising from a misunderstanding of the legal principle of interruption of the Statute of Limitations, and since it is clear that such illegality affected the outcome of the judgment, the ground of appeal pointing out this issue is well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and in order to have the case retried and determined, the case is remanded to the court below, and the decision is rendered as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning an action for partition of co-owned property is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: In an action for partition of co-owned property, the court must order partition by a rational method that comprehensively considers the various circumstances of the co-ownership relationship or of the object thereof, according to the ratio of shares, and the ratio of shares shall, in principle, be based on the ratio of value (exchange value) according to the shares; where the shape, location, use status, or economic value of the subject matter is not equal, the court must, in principle, order partition by adjusting so that the economic value corresponds to the ratio of shares.
B: In an action for partition of co-owned property, if one of the co-litigants has a defect in the requirements for litigation, the entire litigation becomes procedurally improper.
C: Even where partition in kind is possible and necessary, if there is no reasonable method of partition in kind corresponding to the value in proportion to shares among the co-owners, a method of adjusting excess or deficiency in economic value in money may also be considered.
D: In the procedural course of an action for partition of co-owned property, even if a settlement is reached between co-owners to partition the co-owned land in kind, a co-owner acquires title to that part only after completing the subdivision procedure for the land and receiving transfer of the other co-owners’ co-ownership shares and completing registration with respect to the portion to be held in sole ownership.
E: A person among the co-owners who does not assert a co-ownership share right and asserts ownership of a specific part of the subject matter cannot seek performance of the procedure for registration of transfer of shares on the ground of termination of a title trust with respect to that specific part against the other co-owners holding co-ownership shares, and must bring an action for partition of co-owned property against all the other co-owners.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2003DA2024]": "We decide the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Judgment of the court below\\n\\nOn the basis of the evidence it admitted, the court below found the following facts: on or around 1989. 12. 8., Non-party 1 and five others, who were the former owners of the forest land at issue, sold to Non-party 2, at a price of KRW 12,000 per pyeong, which was cheaper than the price offered to other purchasers, 5,401 pyeong (17,854㎡) of the land marked ㉰ in Diagram No. 1 attached to the judgment of the court below, specifically identified as the upper portion of the forest land before it was subdivided into the forest land at issue; however, the Plaintiff, on or around 1990. 4. 23., purchased from the above-mentioned Non-party 2, at a price of KRW 25,000 per pyeong, a 17,845.5/41,062 share (5,401 pyeong) of the entire forest land before it was subdivided into the forest land at issue. After recognizing these facts, the court below determined that, although there is room to view the relationship between Non-party 2 and the Defendants as a mutual title trust relationship, since Non-party 2 had specifically acquired and possessed and used a part of the forest land before subdivision and had, for convenience, registered co-ownership shares in respect of the whole thereof, the mutual title trust relationship between the Plaintiff and the Defendants was extinguished when the Plaintiff purchased from Non-party 2 co-ownership shares in the entire forest land before subdivision at issue.\\n\\nFurthermore, in dividing jointly owned property, the court below held that it would be appropriate to regard the Plaintiff as having effectively purchased the above-mentioned portion from Non-party 2, who had specifically purchased the above-mentioned portion of 5,401 pyeong, out of the above-mentioned 5,401 pyeong portion ㉰ from Non-party 1 and five others; therefore, it found it proper to divide 5,401 pyeong of the above-mentioned portion ㉰ as the Plaintiff’s ownership and the remainder as the co-ownership of the Defendants who do not wish partition, and ordered partition of the jointly owned property in such manner.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\n\\nThe foregoing determination of the court below is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nIn an action for partition of jointly owned property, the court must, by comprehensively considering the various circumstances of the co-ownership relationship and the thing that is its object, order partition according to the ratio of shares by a reasonable method; and, here, the ratio of shares means in principle the ratio of value (exchange value) according to the shares. Therefore, where the shape or location, the state of use, or the economic value of the object subject to partition is not equal, the court must, in principle, order partition so that the economic value corresponds to the ratio of shares (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 92DA39105 rendered on 1992. 11. 10., 93DA13445 rendered on 1993. 8. 27., and 99DA6746 rendered on 1999. 6. 11.).\\n\\nAccording to the record, however, the forest land at issue is long and narrow in shape, extending from the mountain summit toward the foot of the mountain, and a considerable portion of it is steep terrain; and it may be ascertained that Non-party 2 purchased the portion toward the mountain summit at KRW 12,000 per pyeong, whereas transactions were made at KRW 30,000 per pyeong for the other portions around that time. If that is the case, it is manifest that the portion toward the mountain summit of the forest land at issue has less economic utility value than the other portions, and accordingly, if, as in the court below’s method of partition, the portion of the forest land at issue to be partitioned and owned by the Plaintiff is located toward the mountain summit, it is clear that that portion will have a lower price per unit area than the remainder to become the co-ownership of the Defendants. Therefore, if there is no other reasonable method of partition apart from partitioning in the above manner, the court below should have ordered partition so that the economic value corresponds to the ratio of shares by adjusting the area of the Plaintiff’s partitioned portion or by adjusting any surplus or deficiency in economic value in money.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, by merely dividing the above-mentioned 5,401 pyeong portion ㉰ into the Plaintiff’s ownership and the remainder into the co-ownership of the Defendants who do not wish partition, misunderstood the legal principles on partition of jointly owned property and, as a result, failed to conduct a full examination, thereby committing an illegality that affected the judgment. The Plaintiff’s ground of appeal pointing out this issue is well-founded.\\n\\nMeanwhile, in determining whether the Plaintiff’s claim for partition of jointly owned property is well-founded, the court below stated that the Plaintiff had purchased from the above-mentioned Non-party 2 co-ownership shares in the entire forest land before subdivision at issue, rather than a specific portion, and thus the mutual title trust relationship between the Plaintiff and the Defendants had been extinguished; yet, in determining the method of partition of jointly owned property, it stated that it would be appropriate to view the Plaintiff as having specifically purchased the above-mentioned 5,401 pyeong portion ㉰ from Non-party 2, thereby revealing a contradiction in the reasoning of the judgment. We point out that the court below needed to conduct further examination on whether the Plaintiff purchased the above-mentioned co-ownership shares or specifically purchased the above-mentioned 5,401 pyeong portion ㉰ in order to clarify this point.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without deciding the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and judgment. The Justices of the Supreme Court unanimously agree, and it is so adjudged as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2010DA105310]": "The Court determines ex officio.\\n\\nAn action for partition of jointly owned property is an indispensable co-litigation in which the co-owner seeking partition must be the Plaintiff and all other co-owners must be joined as joint Defendants (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on July 10, 2001, 99DA31124), and because the judgment must become final and conclusive uniformly with respect to all co-owners, if one of the co-litigants lacks a litigation requirement, the entire action becomes procedurally improper.\\n\\nIn civil litigation, moreover, the existence of a litigation party or party capacity constitutes a litigation requirement, and the filing of an action against a person already deceased is improper for failure to satisfy a litigation requirement; at the stage of final appeal, such defect cannot be cured by means of correction of the party designation.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Plaintiff filed the complaint in this action for partition of jointly owned property on October 5, 2009, designating Nonparty 1 and 9 others as Defendants; it can be ascertained that Nonparty 1 had already died on December 11, 2001, and that when the Defendant first asserted before this Court the fact of the decedent's death, the Plaintiff submitted to this Court an application for correction of party designation, seeking to correct the designation of the decedent to the heirs; in light of the legal principles stated above, this action is improper in relation to all co-litigants and, because its defect cannot be cured, must be dismissed, and therefore the judgment of the court below, which overlooked this and proceeded to decide the merits, cannot stand as is.\\n\\nTherefore, without addressing the grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed, but since this case is sufficiently ripe for this Court to decide directly, the Court renders its own judgment pursuant to Article 437 of the Civil Procedure Act, thereby vacating the first-instance judgment that granted the Plaintiff's claim and dismissing this action, and orders that the total costs of litigation be borne by the losing party; it is so adjudicated in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2011DU1917]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. a. Article 268(1) of the Civil Act provides, “A co-owner may demand partition of the co-owned property,” thereby recognizing the freedom of partition of co-owned property. Under Article 269(1) of the Civil Act, partition of co-owned property is, in principle, to be effected according to agreement among the parties, and only where no agreement is reached among the co-owners may a co-owner demand partition of the co-owned property from the court; therefore, where an agreement on partition has been reached among the co-owners, it is not permissible to maintain an action for partition of co-owned property that has already been brought [see Supreme Court Decisions 1967. 11. 14. rendered in 67DA1105, 1995. 1. 12. rendered in 94DA30348, 30355, etc.].\\nSince partition of co-owned property by agreement is effected in an area governed by the principles of private autonomy and freedom of contract, the parties may freely and arbitrarily choose the method of partition by agreement.\\nBy contrast, in judicial partition of co-owned property, under Article 269(2) of the Civil Act the court must partition the co-owned property in kind, and may order a sale by auction only where partition in kind is impossible or where partition in kind would involve a substantial risk of diminishing the value thereof. In addition, judicial partition of co-owned property, namely an action for partition of co-owned property, does not involve the court’s determination and finalization of the legal relationship that is the object of dispute between the parties; rather, in place of agreement, the court, in the exercise of discretion, extinguishes the existing legal relationship among the co-owners, namely the co-ownership relationship, by a reasonable method and creates an appropriate future legal relationship. Therefore, the parties need not specifically identify the method or content of partition and need only seek partition of the co-owned property; even if a party requests partition by specifying detailed matters concerning the method or content of partition, such matters have only the meaning of a proposal by the party to the court, and the court is not bound thereby [see Supreme Court Decisions 1969. 12. 29. rendered in 68DA2425, 1991. 11. 12. rendered in 91DA27228, etc.].\\nb. Conciliation includes disposition by the parties of the legal relationship that is the object of dispute, and therefore conciliation concerning matters that the parties cannot freely dispose of is ineffective even if formed [see Supreme Court Decisions 2007. 7. 26. rendered in 2006MEU2757, 2764, etc.]. Meanwhile, conciliation is not limited to the rights or legal relations that are the object of litigation, and the parties may, if necessary, make other rights or legal relations the subject of conciliation [see Supreme Court Decision 2011. 9. 29. rendered in 2011DA48902, etc.].\\nc. Where an action for partition of co-owned property has been filed and, while the litigation is pending, an agreement on partition of co-owned property is reached between the parties, the action for partition of co-owned property seeking judicial partition loses its legal interest; however, since the substantive-law rights and legal relations related to the action for partition of co-owned property, namely the legal relations concerning shares, are disposable by the parties, where there is a possibility that an agreement on partition of co-owned property may be reached between the parties while the action is pending, it is of course possible for the court seized of the case to render a decision referring the case to conciliation and to have the parties reach conciliation directly or through a conciliation judge exclusively in charge or a conciliation committee, thereby terminating the dispute.\\nHowever, such conciliation does not target the subject matter of the action for partition of co-owned property itself so as to substitute for the court’s determination in that litigation, and is therefore, in essence, no different from partition of co-owned property by agreement between the parties. Accordingly, it cannot be said that such conciliation has the constitutive effect of judicial partition of co-owned property, that is, the effect whereby, upon finalization of a judgment for partition in kind rendered by the court after considering all circumstances concerning the case, the existing co-ownership relationship is extinguished and a new ownership relationship is created. Even if through the conciliation procedure a legal relationship is changed that, under certain restrictions, is exceptionally intended to be brought about by a judgment of partition of co-owned property, allowing such change to arise constitutively through an agreement between the parties without going through the court’s adjudicatory process cannot be permitted, even if the process is a conciliation procedure.\\nTherefore, even if, in the litigation procedure or conciliation procedure for partition of co-owned property, an agreement on partition in kind of co-owned land is reached among the co-owners and conciliation is formed by entering the agreed matters into the record, such circumstance alone does not mean that, as in the case of judicial partition of co-owned property, the co-ownership relationship is extinguished immediately and a new legal relationship is created for each co-owner pursuant to the agreement; rather, it must be understood that only after the land has been subdivided according to the agreement among the co-owners and registration has been completed by transferring the shares of the other co-owners in the portions that were to become each co-owner’s sole ownership does a co-owner acquire ownership of that portion as a right effective against all.\\n2. a. According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, (1) the paddy field 1,947㎡ located in (Address 1 omitted), Seocho-gu, Seoul (hereinafter referred to as the “pre-partition land”) was jointly owned by the Plaintiff and 7 others; (2) in or around July 2003, the Plaintiff and Non-party 1 and 2 filed an action for partition of co-owned property against the remaining co-owners concerning the pre-partition land; (3) the co-owners subdivided the pre-partition land on July 6, 2004 into paddy field 973㎡ in (Address 1 omitted), Seocho-gu, Seoul (hereinafter referred to as “Land 1”) and paddy field 974㎡ in (Address 2 omitted) (hereinafter referred to as “Land 2”), and thereafter, on July 12, 2004, at the conciliation date in the above action for partition of co-owned property, agreed to partition the pre-partition land into Land 1 and Land 2, with the Plaintiff and Non-party 1 and 2 co-owning Land 2 and the remaining co-owners co-owning Land 1, and to complete registration of transfer of ownership, based on the above partition of co-owned property, with respect to their respective ownership portions, and conciliation (hereinafter referred to as the “conciliation in this case”) was formed by the court’s entering the agreed matters into the record; (4) while the Plaintiff had not completed registration of transfer of ownership pursuant to the conciliation in this case, on October 12, 2006, a decision to commence compulsory auction was rendered, at the instance of the Korea Credit Guarantee Fund, a creditor of the Plaintiff, with respect to the Plaintiff’s share in Land 1 (hereinafter referred to as the “share in this case”), and the share in this case was sold for 90,000,000 won in the compulsory auction proceedings on July 13, 2007; and (5) the Defendant, on January 7, 2010, issued the disposition in this case, imposing and notifying on the Plaintiff capital gains tax for the year 2007 attributable to the transfer of the share in this case in the amount of 5,415,220 won.\\nb. The court below held, with respect to the Plaintiff’s assertion that, because the conciliation in this case was formed, the Plaintiff had no rights whatsoever in Land 1 (and, according to this assertion, the above compulsory auction would ultimately be an unlawful auction proceeding concerning a share owned by another person), that although the conciliation in this case was formed regarding the pre-partition land, insofar as the Plaintiff had not transferred the share in this case to the remaining co-owners in accordance with the conciliation in this case, the owner of the share in this case remained the Plaintiff, and therefore the disposition in this case by the Defendant, which treated the share in this case as belonging to the Plaintiff, was lawful.\\nc. In light of the legal principles set forth above and the record, the judgment of the court below is proper and acceptable, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning conciliation regarding partition of co-owned property or the effect of the conciliation record, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are assessed against the losing party. It is so adjudged. Aside from the dissenting opinion of Justice Min Il-yeong, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous.\\n4. The dissenting opinion of Justice Min Il-yeong is as follows.\\na. Before setting forth the dissent, it is necessary first to organize the issues. Even conciliation concerning partition of co-owned property may take various forms. One conceivable form is the same as a judgment ordering partition in kind, namely a method by which “part of the co-owned real property is divided into the property of one party and the remainder into the property of another party.” Another conceivable form is a method in which, while partition is made as above, the time of effectuation of the partition of co-owned property is separately fixed, for example by making the effect contingent upon reciprocal performance between the parties of registration and payment of adjustment money, etc., in order to adjust the interests between the parties (a so-called mixed form of pure partition in kind and price compensation). If conciliation is formed in the latter manner, the matter should be governed accordingly, and even in such a case the dissenting opinion does not differ from the majority opinion. The issue lies in the former case. The majority opinion also takes the view, in such a case, that the effect of real right change arises only when subdivision and registration are effected according to the terms agreed upon by the parties, and I cannot agree with such a view. The reasons are as follows.\\nb. An action for partition of co-owned property is a so-called formal formative action, and unlike an ordinary action for formation, conciliation may be formed in its conciliation procedure, and a formative judgment ordering partition in kind corresponds to the “judgment” prescribed in Article 187 of the Civil Act.\\nArticle 28 of the Civil Conciliation Act provides, “Conciliation is formed by entering the matters agreed upon between the parties into the record,” Article 29 of the same Act provides, “Conciliation shall have the same effect as judicial compromise,” and Article 220 of the Civil Procedure Act provides, “When compromise, waiver of claim, or acknowledgment is entered in the trial record or the pretrial preparation record, such record shall have the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment.” Accordingly, in the conciliation procedure concerning partition of co-owned property, where conciliation is formed in the form of partition in kind, it is a logically natural interpretation to regard the conciliation record as having the same effect as the above formative judgment and thus as corresponding to the “judgment” prescribed in Article 187 of the Civil Act.\\nc. Article 186 of the Civil Act provides, “The acquisition, loss, and alteration of real rights arising from juristic acts concerning immovable property shall not become effective unless registered,” and according to the majority opinion, conciliation concerning partition of co-owned property is merely an agreement among the co-owners, and such agreement ultimately corresponds to a “juristic act” prescribed in Article 186 of the Civil Act.\\nWhen the provisions of Article 28 and Article 29 of the Civil Conciliation Act and Article 220 of the Civil Procedure Act are considered together, judicial compromise and conciliation do not differ in their legal effect. The Supreme Court, however, with respect to judicial compromise, had until around 1961 viewed its legal nature as both a private-law agreement and an agreement under procedural law, and held that, even if the compromise terms were entered into the record and thus had the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment under procedural law, if there existed grounds for invalidity or rescission under private law, unlike a final and conclusive judgment, the procedural effect also became void ab initio or lost its effect, and in such a case one could obtain judicial review by way of an application for designation of a hearing concerning a lawsuit that had been concluded by compromise, or file a separate suit for confirmation of invalidity or for performance based on invalidity or ineffectiveness (see Supreme Court Decisions 1955. 9. 15. rendered in 4288MINSANG229, 1957. 12. 26. rendered in 4290MINSANG638). Thereafter, when Article 431 (current Article 461) of the Civil Procedure Act was amended by Act No. 706 on September 1, 1961 so that a quasi-review could also be brought against compromise records, the Supreme Court, in en banc Decision 1962. 2. 15. rendered in 4294MINSANG914, changed the above Supreme Court Decisions 4288MINSANG229 and 4290MINSANG638 and held that, unless cancelled or modified by quasi-review, no argument contrary to the purport of the compromise may be made; since then, judicial compromise has been made clear to be a procedural act in its legal nature, such that, unlike private-law compromise, it cannot be rescinded on the ground of fraud or mistake, etc. (see Supreme Court Decisions 1962. 5. 31. rendered in 4293MINJAE6, 1979. 5. 15. rendered in 78DA1094, etc.). Furthermore, conciliation has also been made clear to be a procedural act in its legal nature for the same reason as judicial compromise (see Supreme Court Decisions 2005. 2. 17. rendered in 2004DA55087, etc.).\\nAs a general rule, an enforcement judgment and a declaratory judgment in an action for performance or an action for declaration where the existence or nonexistence of an obligation to perform is at issue do not correspond to the “judgment” prescribed in Article 187 of the Civil Act [see Supreme Court Decision 1971. 3. 23. rendered in 71DA234, etc.], and it is an established precedent of the Supreme Court that, even where conciliation or judicial compromise is formed in such a manner, Article 186 of the Civil Act, not Article 187, must likewise be applied [see Supreme Court Decisions 1964. 9. 8. rendered in 64DA165, Supreme Court Order 1969. 10. 8. rendered in 69GEU15, Supreme Court Decision 2001. 3. 13. rendered in 99DA56345, etc.]. By contrast, a formative judgment ordering partition in kind in an action for partition of co-owned property, which is a formal formative action, corresponds, unlike the foregoing, to the “judgment” prescribed in Article 187 of the Civil Act; where conciliation is formed in the same content as such judgment, the conciliation is merely a procedural act and not a private-law juristic act among the co-owners. Therefore, such procedural act cannot be interpreted as a “juristic act” prescribed in Article 186 of the Civil Act.\\nd. The majority opinion states that, since conciliation in judicial partition of co-owned property that brings about a change in legal relations merely by agreement among the parties without going through the court’s adjudicatory process cannot be permitted, registration must be made even if conciliation is formed with respect thereto in order for the effect of real right change to arise. However, I cannot easily agree with such reasoning.\\nUnder Articles 30 and 32 of the Civil Conciliation Act, a “decision in lieu of conciliation” made by the judge in charge of conciliation has, when no objection is filed thereto by a party, or when any objection filed is withdrawn or dismissed and the decision becomes final and conclusive, the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment, just like a judicial compromise record (Article 34(4) of the same Act, Article 220 of the Civil Procedure Act). The essence of such a “decision in lieu of conciliation” is, after all, a decision made ex officio by the judge in charge of conciliation taking all circumstances into account where no agreement has been reached between the parties or the terms of the reached agreement are not appropriate; and if no objection is filed thereto by a party, or if any objection filed is withdrawn or dismissed and the decision becomes final and conclusive, the decision has the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment. In that respect, it has the same structure as a situation in which the judge handling the action for partition of co-owned property renders a partition judgment after considering all circumstances, and when a party does not appeal, or an appeal is withdrawn or dismissed and the judgment becomes final and conclusive, the judgment operates as a final and conclusive judgment. Therefore, according to the logic of the majority opinion, a decision in lieu of conciliation has undergone the court’s adjudicatory process rather than a mere agreement between the parties, so once it becomes final and conclusive, the effect of a change in real right should be recognized even without registration, just as in the case of a judgment for partition of co-owned property.\\nHowever, the majority opinion takes the view that even where a decision in lieu of conciliation whose content is partition in kind becomes final and conclusive, the effect of a change in real right arises only upon completion of registration pursuant to Article 186 of the Civil Act. Yet this ultimately treats differently two matters that, as seen above, share the same structure in that the essential nature of a decision in lieu of conciliation is a decision rendered through the court’s adjudicatory process and thus is structurally the same as a judgment for partition of co-owned property, and it is difficult to find a rational basis for such differential treatment.\\nIn short, a decision in lieu of conciliation is a decision rendered through the court’s adjudicatory process and corresponds to the “judgment” prescribed in Article 187 of the Civil Act, and once it becomes final and conclusive, the effect of acquisition of a real right arises without registration; furthermore, in light of the legislative purpose of the conciliation system, which seeks to identify the two by making the decision in lieu of conciliation “in lieu of conciliation,” and the fact that both a decision in lieu of conciliation that becomes final and conclusive and conciliation that is formed have the effect of judicial compromise, the conciliation record formed by reaching conciliation to partition in kind should also be regarded as corresponding to the “judgment” prescribed in Article 187 of the Civil Act.\\ne. The majority opinion states that, even though an action for partition of co-owned property was originally filed, if there is a possibility that an agreement on partition of co-owned property may be reached between the parties during the pendency of the action, the court seized of the case may render a decision referring the matter to conciliation and have the parties form conciliation in the conciliation procedure, and such conciliation is not directed to the subject matter of the litigation itself in the action for partition of co-owned property and therefore is not essentially different in effect from partition of co-owned property by agreement.\\nWhere an agreement on partition is reached among the co-owners, if the issue is claiming registration of transfer of ownership for the partitioned portions or seeking confirmation of ownership, the preexisting action for partition of co-owned property lacks an interest in being maintained and thus becomes improper [see Supreme Court Decisions 1995. 1. 12. rendered in 94DA30348, 30355, etc.].
