Accordingly, where an agreement on partition is reached while the action for partition of co-owned property is pending, the subject matter of the litigation may, as above, be changed into an action for performance or an action for declaration concerning the partitioned portions specified in the agreement, and it is natural that conciliation may be effected with respect to the changed subject matter; however, such conciliation is now conciliation in an action for performance or an action for declaration, and is no longer conciliation in a formal formative action.\\nHowever, even if, while an action for partition of co-owned property, which is a formal formative action, is pending, an agreement on partition is reached, or the case is referred to conciliation in a state where an agreement may be reached, one cannot immediately conclude from that circumstance alone that the subject matter of the litigation has changed into the subject matter of an action for performance or an action for declaration. This is because, in order to change the subject matter of litigation, as a rule, the procedure for amendment of claim by written submission must be followed pursuant to Article 262 of the Civil Procedure Act. Therefore, if, in an action for partition of co-owned property, the case is referred to conciliation without the subject matter of litigation having been changed into an action for performance, etc., and conciliation is formed as such, the subject matter of the litigation in that conciliation cannot be said to be different from the subject matter of the action for partition of co-owned property. Moreover, if the conciliation clause takes the same form as a partition judgment in every respect, it becomes even more difficult to recognize any difference in the subject matter of litigation.\\nf. The majority opinion may also have taken into account that, if acquisition of a real right is recognized under Article 187 of the Civil Act even though registration has not been completed in accordance with the terms of conciliation after conciliation concerning partition of co-owned property is formed, the safety of transactions may be impaired under our legal system, which does not recognize the public faith of registration. However, the same problem also arises in the case of a judgment for partition of co-owned property. Therefore, if one wishes to emphasize the safety of transactions, the fundamental solution would not be to deny the effect of real right change by conciliation, but rather to deny the effect of real right change by a judgment for partition of co-owned property.\\ng. In conclusion, if, in an action for partition of co-owned property, conciliation is formed in the content of partition in kind so that specific portions of the co-owned real property are allotted to each co-owner, the conciliation record has the same effect as a judgment for partition of co-owned property and therefore corresponds to the “judgment” prescribed in Article 187 of the Civil Act, so the effect of real right change should be deemed to arise when the conciliation is formed.\\nHowever, looking at the conciliation clause in this case, while it partitions specific portions of the co-owned real property that is the subject of conciliation into the respective ownership of the Plaintiff and the other co-owners, it further adds a clause requiring subdivision and registration of transfer of ownership with respect to the portions thus owned by partition; yet, even without such subdivision and transfer-registration clause, the parties would of course be obliged to carry out such procedures, so that clause is merely a superfluous recital that cautiously emphasizes the parties’ voluntary performance, and it should not be viewed as fixing the time when the effect of real right change arises. In that respect, it is of a different nature from the clause described at the beginning of the dissenting opinion, which requires reciprocal performance of registration and payment of adjustment money, etc.\\nThe court below decided otherwise, and this misapprehended the legal principles concerning conciliation on partition of co-owned property or the effect of the conciliation record and thus erred in its judgment; accordingly, the Plaintiff’s appeal on this point should be accepted.\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state that I cannot concur in the majority opinion."}

{"[92DA39105]": "We examine the second ground of appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the court below found that, as to the method of partition of the forest land in this case, which is jointly owned by the Plaintiff (1/4 share) and the Defendants (Defendant 1 1/4 share, Defendant 2 2/4 share), measuring 46,909 square meters, the results of the on-site inspection by the first-instance court and the results of the surveying appraisal and market-value appraisal by appraisers Non-party 1 and Non-party 2 showed, among other things, that the lower portion of the said forest land adjoins farmland, whereas the left and right portions toward the summit from the lower portion are valleys, and that from the lower portion to the middle portion the land has a gentle slope and thus may be developed in the future, but from there to the summit it has a steeper slope and its utility is low, and that accordingly the price of the said forest land also differs, depending on location, from 2,700 won to 10,600 won per square meter; and after recognizing such facts, the court below held that, in light of the area, location, economic value, and developability of the said forest land, and the share ratios of the Plaintiff and the Defendants, it would be proper to divide the 11,727 square meters of the (Ma) portion described in Figure 3 attached to the judgment below into the Plaintiff’s 11,727 square meters of the (Ka) portion, Defendant 1’s, and the 23,455 square meters of the (Ta) portion of Defendant 2, each to be owned respectively. However, the above determination by the court below is difficult to accept.\\n\\nAs also mentioned in the remand judgment in this case, in an action for partition of co-owned property, the court must order partition according to the share ratios by a reasonable method taking into comprehensive consideration the co-ownership relationship and all circumstances of the property that is its object; the share ratios here, in principle, should be based on the ratio of value (exchange value) according to the shares; where the shape or location of the subject matter, or its state of use or economic value, is not equal, the court should, in principle, order partition by adjusting so that the economic value corresponds to the share ratios; however, even where partition in kind is possible and necessary, if there are reasons such as the absence, among the co-owners, of any reasonable method of partition in kind corresponding to the value of the shares, a method of adjusting excess or deficiency in economic value by money may also be considered (see, e.g., this Court’s decision of 1990.8.28. rendered 90DAKA7620).\\n\\nWhile the court below, through the reasons stated, made clear that the price of the said forest land differs greatly depending on location, it nevertheless chose the above-described method of partition, under which only the partitioned area was made to follow the share ratios of each co-owner, without adjusting the partitioned area so that the value of the portions to be partitioned would correspond to the share ratios of each co-owner; this, in the end, would amount to a misapprehension of the legal principles on partition of co-owned property, or to illegality such as inconsistency in reasons, insufficiency of reasons, or inadequacy of examination arising therefrom.\\n\\nThe grounds of appeal pointing out this issue are well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the other grounds of appeal, the Court reverses the judgment below and remands the case to the court below, and renders judgment as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[95DA8430]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nA claim for partition of co-owned property is made by one of the co-owners on the basis of his or her share in the co-owned property; therefore, a person who does not assert a right to a co-ownership share but claims to own a specific part of the subject property may, against the person who holds a share registration in trust as to that part, seek performance of the procedure for registration of transfer of share ownership on the ground of termination of the title trust as to that specific part, but may not, in lieu thereof, bring a claim for partition of co-owned property (see Judgment of this Court dated 1989. 9. 12. in 88DAKA10517).\\n\\nAccording to the record, it is clear that the Plaintiff, through the complaint and the application dated 1994. 3. 14. for amendment of the purport of claim and the cause of action submitted to the court of first instance, is bringing this claim for partition of co-owned property, alleging that although the land in this case is registered as co-owned by the Plaintiff and Defendant, in fact, as to the portion marked (A) in the attached diagram to the appellate judgment, measuring 1,425㎡, the Plaintiff purchased it, and as to the portion marked (B), measuring 2,020㎡, the Defendant purchased it, and that each of them owns the purchased portion specifically identified; and even according to the factual findings established by the court below, the Defendant, around 1960, purchased from Non-party 1 the northern portion of about 700 pyeong of the land in this case and 503㎡ of the pond at (address omitted), and completed registration of transfer of share ownership with respect to a 700/1,194 share in each of the above lands; and the Plaintiff, around early 1964, through Non-party 1 and Non-party 2, purchased in succession the entire southern portion of the land in this case and the 503㎡ of the above pond that had not been sold to the Defendant, and on 1988. 12. 10. completed registration of transfer of share ownership with respect to a 494/1,194 share in each of the above lands; accordingly, the Plaintiff and Defendant are merely in a so-called mutual title-trust relationship, in which they separately and specifically own their respective purchased portions of the land in this case, while, in the register, with respect to any share exceeding the share registered in the name of the purchaser out of each purchased portion, they entrust the title of ownership to the purchaser of the other portion.\\n\\nIf this is so, the Plaintiff may, as against the Defendant, request performance of the procedure for registration of transfer of share ownership on the ground of termination of the title-trust relationship with respect to the portion of the land in this case that the Plaintiff separately and specifically owns, but may not be deemed able to bring a claim for partition of co-owned property in the capacity of a co-owner of shares in the land in this case.\\n\\nNevertheless, while recognizing the fact that the Plaintiff and Defendant separately and specifically own their respective purchased portions of the land in this case, the court below determined that the Plaintiff, as a co-owner of the land in this case, could seek partition of co-owned property, and ordered partition of the land in this case; in doing so, there is not only a violation of inconsistency or insufficiency of reasons, but also a violation of the adversarial principle and an error in misunderstanding the legal principles regarding partition of co-owned property that affected the judgment, so the argument pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and in order to have the case retried and decided, it is remanded to the court below, and the participating Justices are in agreement, so judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

{"[99DA31124]": "Of the judgment of the court below, the part concerning partition of jointly owned property between the Plaintiffs and the Defendants and, among the part adverse to Defendant F, the part concerning confirmation of co-ownership are all reversed, the first-instance judgment concerning those parts is vacated, and all actions corresponding to those parts are dismissed.\\n\\nOf the part adverse to Defendant F concerning payment of money in the judgment below, the part concerning payment of money exceeding the amounts payable to Plaintiff A in the amount of KRW 159,840, to Plaintiff B in the amount of KRW 639,360, and to Plaintiffs C, D, and E in the amount of KRW 319,680 each, together with the amounts on each of the above sums calculated at the rate of 2 hal 5 pun per annum from 1997. 10. 12. until the date of complete payment, are all reversed, the first-instance judgment concerning those parts is vacated, and the Plaintiffs' claims against Defendant F corresponding to those parts are all dismissed.\\n\\nThe remaining appeals by Defendants G, H, and I are all dismissed.\\n\\nThe remaining appeal by Defendant F is dismissed.\\n\\nOf the total litigation costs, the portion incurred between the Plaintiffs and Defendant F shall be divided into two, with one half borne by the Plaintiffs and the remainder borne by Defendant F, and the portion incurred between the Plaintiffs and Defendants G, H, and I shall be borne by the Plaintiffs."}

question: A stock company is the parent company of B stock company, and A holds 10% of the total issued shares of A stock company. Which of the following statements are correct? (Each statement is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law shall govern)
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2013MA2316]": "We examine the grounds of the reappeal.\\n\\nSince the executory force of a final judgment received by a person who became the Plaintiff for another person, such as a shareholder in a shareholder derivative action, extends to both that person, who is the party to the final judgment, and the other person, the shareholder in a shareholder derivative action may be an execution creditor.\\n\\nThe court below, after recognizing the fact that the creditor, a shareholder of Seohae Development Co., Ltd., filed, against the debtor, the representative director of the said company, an action for damages in a shareholder derivative action, and that a judgment was rendered and became final ordering the debtor to pay damages to the said company, held that the creditor, as the Plaintiff in the said final judgment, had standing as an execution creditor who could, by using it as a title of execution, file the application in this case for attachment of claims and an order of transfer against the debtor.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above, such determination by the court below is proper, and there is no error in misapprehending the legal principles concerning standing as an execution creditor.\\n\\nTherefore, the reappeal by the debtor is dismissed, and the decision is rendered as stated in the disposition, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2018DA298744]": "1. We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nA. We examine the legal principles concerning a director’s liability for damages and shareholder derivative actions.\\n\\n1) If a director, intentionally or negligently, commits an act in violation of laws and regulations or the articles of incorporation, or neglects his duties, that director shall be jointly and severally liable to compensate the company for damages (Commercial Act Article 399(1)). Where, in performing duties, a director commits an act in violation of laws and regulations, the act itself constitutes non-performance of obligations toward the company, and so long as the company has suffered damage therefrom, the director cannot escape liability for damages absent special circumstances (see Supreme Court Decision 2018DA282756, decided November 14, 2019, etc.).\\n\\nIf there is a defect in the stock cancellation procedure for reducing capital, shareholders, etc. may claim invalidity only by filing an action within 6 months from the date on which the change registration arising from the capital reduction was made (Commercial Act Article 445). However, where it is recognized that a director violated laws and regulations in the course of the stock cancellation and thereby caused damage to the company, the director bears liability to compensate the company under Commercial Act Article 399(1), regardless of whether a judgment declaring the invalidity of the capital reduction has become final and conclusive.\\n\\n2) If the company does not pursue the director’s liability, a shareholder holding shares amounting to at least 1/100 of the total number of issued shares may file an action to pursue the director’s liability directly for the company (Commercial Act Article 403(3)). Before filing the action, the shareholder must first demand that the company file the action, and this demand shall be made in a written document stating the reasons (hereinafter referred to as the “Demand for Filing Suit”) (Commercial Act Article 403(1), (2)).\\n\\nThe “reasons” to be stated in the Demand for Filing Suit must include information concerning the director against whom liability is to be pursued and the facts constituting the cause of liability, so that the company, being the entity to which the rights belong, can determine whether to file suit. However, because a shareholder cannot always be said to have accurate knowledge and proper information regarding the company’s business, etc., even if the name of the director against whom liability is to be pursued is not stated in the Demand for Filing Suit or the facts constituting the cause of liability are stated somewhat summarily, if the company can specifically identify the director against whom liability is to be pursued and the facts constituting the cause of liability by comprehensively considering the content stated in the Demand for Filing Suit, corporate materials such as minutes of the board of directors’ meetings, and other materials in the company’s possession, the Demand for Filing Suit must be regarded as satisfying the requirements prescribed by Commercial Act Article 403(2) (see Supreme Court Decision 2019DA291399, decided May 13, 2021).\\n\\nIf a shareholder files a derivative action without submitting a Demand for Filing Suit at all, or even if a Demand for Filing Suit was submitted, the action is improper unless there are special circumstances, such as the existence of grounds under Commercial Act Article 403(4), if the claim in the derivative action is based on facts entirely unrelated to the facts constituting the cause of liability stated in the Demand for Filing Suit. On the other hand, even if the director’s liability for damages asserted by the shareholder in the derivative action differs from that stated in the Demand for Filing Suit, the action is lawful if it merely differs in legal assessment while still being based on the facts constituting the cause of liability in the Demand for Filing Suit. Therefore, during the pendency of a derivative action lawfully filed, a shareholder may additionally assert a claim that differs only in legal assessment while being based on the facts constituting the cause of liability in the Demand for Filing Suit.\\n\\nB. According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be known.\\n\\n1) The Plaintiff is a shareholder holding 1,167 shares of Daekyung Sangsa Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Daekyung Sangsa”), which correspond to 15.8% of the total number of issued shares.\\n\\n2) Under the leadership of the Defendant, who was the largest shareholder and representative director, Daekyung Sangsa prepared a special resolution of the shareholders’ meeting dated June 19, 2014, stating that “some of the 6,499 Daekyung Sangsa shares owned by the Defendant shall be canceled as a capital reduction, and cash shall be paid with the per-share value fixed at KRW 986,346,” and thereafter, on June 26, 2014, paid KRW 1,634,348,422 to the non-party who was the Defendant’s spouse, under the pretext of the price for 1,657 shares owned by the Defendant.\\n\\n3) On November 3, 2015, the Plaintiff sought dismissal of the director on the ground that the Defendant violated laws and regulations by, on June 19, 2014, preparing a special resolution of the shareholders’ meeting without undergoing actual convocation and meeting procedures and otherwise completely failing to carry out the capital reduction procedures under the Commercial Act, and obtained a judgment in his favor on January 11, 2017, which became final and conclusive around that time.\\n\\n4) In or around July 2017, the Plaintiff sent Daekyung Sangsa a contents-certified mail stating: “The Defendant caused damage to the company by disposing of 1,657 shares among the Daekyung Sangsa shares held by him for personal gain in or around June 2014. Even though Daekyung Sangsa was in a state where it could not acquire its own shares, the Defendant arbitrarily handled the matter without undergoing even the shareholders’ meeting resolution prescribed by the Commercial Act. Since the Defendant bears liability for damages under Commercial Act Article 341(4), Daekyung Sangsa should file suit against the Defendant.” (hereinafter referred to as “the Demand for Filing Suit in this case”).\\n\\n5) Since Daekyung Sangsa did not file suit within 30 days from the date it received the Demand for Filing Suit in this case, the Plaintiff filed this shareholder derivative action on August 21, 2017.\\n\\n6) The Plaintiff, in the first instance court, sought damages under Commercial Act Article 341(4) as in the Demand for Filing Suit in this case, and when that claim was dismissed, additionally and in the alternative asserted at the appellate court a claim for damages under Commercial Act Article 399(1) based on the same factual circumstances.\\n\\nC. We examine the above facts in light of the foregoing legal principles.\\n\\nThe appellate court held that the special resolution of the shareholders’ meeting dated June 19, 2014 of Daekyung Sangsa had a serious defect and thus did not exist, so the stock cancellation thereunder was ineffective; nevertheless, the Defendant, on the premise that his own shares had been canceled, paid KRW 1,597,950,000 from Daekyung Sangsa’s funds to the non-party, thereby causing Daekyung Sangsa damage in an equivalent amount, and thus recognized the Defendant’s liability under Commercial Act Article 399(1).\\n\\nThe Defendant’s liability asserted by the Plaintiff in the Demand for Filing Suit in this case is based on Commercial Act Article 341(4), whereas the Defendant’s liability additionally asserted in the appellate court is based on Commercial Act Article 399(1), so the legal basis differs. However, the factual basis of each claim is the same in that the Defendant, as representative director of Daekyung Sangsa, used his position to receive payment of the share price from the company without going through lawful procedures; only the legal assessment of the Defendant’s liability differs, so the claim additionally added in the appellate court is lawful.\\n\\nMeanwhile, because this shareholder derivative action seeks to pursue the director’s liability for damage to the company caused by the director’s violation of laws and regulations, it may be brought irrespective of whether a judgment declaring the invalidity of the capital reduction regarding the unlawful stock cancellation has become final and conclusive.\\n\\nTherefore, the appellate court’s determination on the merits, on the premise that the Plaintiff’s additional claim was lawful, and its recognition of the Defendant’s liability for damages under Commercial Act Article 399(1), is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the effect of capital reduction, the litigation methods under the Commercial Act concerning defects in capital reduction procedures, and the scope of application of shareholder derivative actions under the Commercial Act, or in exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or in failing to conduct necessary deliberation by violating the duty to clarify issues.\\n\\n2. We examine ex officio.\\n\\nA. Where the Plaintiff’s claim was dismissed at first instance and the Plaintiff appealed, and then the claims were alternatively joined at the appellate stage, the court may select and examine one among the several joined claims, and if as a result of examining one claim it is recognized that that claim is well-founded, it must revoke the first-instance judgment dismissing the Plaintiff’s claim and render a dispositive order granting the claim found to be well-founded (see Supreme Court Decision 93DA6669, decided October 26, 1993, Supreme Court Decision 2017DA200368, 200375, decided April 28, 2017, etc.).\\n\\nB. According to the record, the Plaintiff, in the first instance court, asserted against the Defendant a claim for damages under Commercial Act Article 341(4), and when that claim was dismissed, additionally and in the alternative asserted at the appellate court a claim for damages under Commercial Act Article 399(1).\\n\\nThe appellate court rejected the claim for damages under Commercial Act Article 341(4), while recognizing that the claim for damages under Commercial Act Article 399(1), additionally asserted at the appellate court, was well-founded. However, the appellate court, without stating the granted claim in the dispositive part, revoked only the portion of the first-instance judgment that lost the case by the amount granted by the appellate court, ordered the Defendant to pay that amount, and rendered a judgment dismissing the remainder of the Plaintiff’s appeal.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, since the appellate court recognized that the claim for damages under Commercial Act Article 399(1), additionally asserted at the appellate court, is well-founded, it should have revoked the first-instance judgment and rendered a dispositive order granting the additionally added claim. However, the appellate court revoked the first-instance judgment dismissing the claim under Commercial Act Article 341(4) only to the extent of the amount granted by the appellate court, dismissed the remainder of the appeal, and did not render a dispositive order granting the claim additionally and in the alternative asserted at the appellate court. In this appellate judgment, there is an error in misapprehending the legal principles concerning alternative joinder at the appellate stage and omitting a ruling on the alternative claim, and this clearly affected the conclusion of the judgment.\\n\\nC. Meanwhile, a director’s debt of damages to the company under Commercial Act Article 399(1), being a debt for damages arising from non-performance of obligations and one for which no time for performance is fixed, the director becomes liable for delay from the time a demand for performance is made (see Supreme Court Decision 2018DA275888, decided May 7, 2021). Accordingly, when recognizing the Defendant’s liability for delay with respect to damages under Commercial Act Article 399(1), the appellate court needed to examine when the Defendant received a demand for performance.\\n\\n3. Therefore, we reverse the appellate judgment and remand the case to the appellate court for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning litigation relating to a stock company is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, in accordance with case law)
A: A person who has acquired shares may, unless special circumstances exist, independently request the company to register the transfer by proving the fact of share acquisition; therefore, he or she has no interest in seeking confirmation of shareholder rights against the company.
B: A creditor of a stock company may seek confirmation of the invalidity of a contract concluded by the company with a third party if the contract specifically infringes the creditor's rights or legal status, or directly affects them.
C: As a general rule, a shareholder of a stock company has no interest in seeking confirmation of the invalidity of a contract concluded by the company with a third party; however, exceptionally, where the company concludes a contract transferring all or an important part of its business, the shareholder may seek confirmation of the invalidity of the business transfer contract.
D: If the effect of a resolution of the shareholders' meeting becomes a preliminary issue in litigation between third parties other than the company, the parties may at any time argue in that litigation that the resolution of the shareholders' meeting was void ab initio or nonexistent, and it is not necessary to first bring an action against the company.
E: If A, one of the plaintiffs in a shareholder derivative action, disposes of the shares and loses shareholder status, then, even if the other plaintiff retains shareholder status, absent special circumstances, the portion of the action brought by A becomes inadmissible.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2016DA240338]": "1. We first consider the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal.\\n\\nWhere a third party other than the shareholder listed in the share register subscribes for shares and pays the subscription price, in order to regard that third party as the substantive shareholder, the mere circumstance that the third party paid the share subscription price is insufficient; rather, the internal relationship between that third party and the shareholder listed in the share register, the circumstances and purpose concerning the share subscription and the registration in the share register, and the details of the exercise of shareholder rights after registration in the share register must be comprehensively considered and determined (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DA51505 rendered on March 11, 2010, Supreme Court Decision 2012DA29441 rendered on February 13, 2014, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below determined that, for the reasons stated in its opinion, it is difficult to acknowledge that the Plaintiff is the owner of the shares at issue. In light of the legal principles and the record as examined above, it cannot be said that there is any error such as mistaken fact-finding or violation of the rules of evidence in the court below’s determination as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Ex officio, we consider whether the instant action is proper.\\n\\na. An action for declaratory judgment is recognized only where obtaining a declaratory judgment is the most effective and appropriate means to eliminate the insecurity or danger concerning a legal status, and bringing an action for declaratory judgment despite the ability to bring an action seeking performance does not constitute a final method of resolving the dispute and thus there is no legal interest in declaratory relief (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DA60239 rendered on March 9, 2006, Supreme Court Decision 2016DA241249 rendered on January 12, 2017, etc.). In addition, whether an action for declaratory judgment has a legal interest in declaratory relief is a matter subject to investigation ex officio, and therefore the court must determine it ex officio regardless of whether the parties make any assertion thereon (see Supreme Court Decision 91DA12905 rendered on July 12, 1991).\\n\\nMeanwhile, absent special circumstances, a person who has acquired shares may, by proving to the company that he or she acquired the shares by means such as presenting the share certificates in his or her possession, independently demand registration of the transfer in his or her name (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA47728 rendered on March 24, 1995, Supreme Court Decision 2016DA42800, 42817, 42824, 42831 rendered on October 25, 2018, etc.).\\n\\nb. According to the record, the Plaintiff was originally listed in Defendant’s share register as the owner of the shares at issue, but because the registration was transferred into the name of another person due to a share sale and purchase agreement forged by a non-party, the Plaintiff asserts that the Plaintiff remains Defendant’s shareholder, and is seeking confirmation of shareholder rights against Defendant through this action.\\n\\nc. In light of the legal principles set forth above, under these circumstances, the Plaintiff may directly prove against Defendant, the issuer of the shares at issue, that the Plaintiff is the shareholder and seek performance of the procedure for registration of transfer. Therefore, the Plaintiff’s seeking confirmation of shareholder rights against Defendant is not an effective and appropriate means to eliminate the existing insecurity or danger concerning the Plaintiff’s rights or legal status, or it is not a final method of resolving the dispute, and thus there is no legal interest in declaratory relief.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, premised on the existence of a legal interest in the Plaintiff’s action against Defendant seeking confirmation of shareholder rights, upheld the Plaintiff’s appeal against the first-instance judgment that dismissed the Plaintiff’s claim on the ground that it is difficult to acknowledge that the Plaintiff is the owner of the shares at issue, and thus proceeded to render a determination on the merits. Such determination by the court below contains an error that affected the conclusion of the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the legal interest in an action for confirmation of shareholder rights against a company.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed; however, as this Court finds the instant case sufficient to decide itself, it shall render its own judgment pursuant to Article 437 of the Civil Procedure Act, revoke the first-instance judgment dismissing the Plaintiff’s claim, dismiss the instant action, and order that the total costs of litigation be borne by the losing party, and so adjudge as follows by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[91DA5365]": "We consider the grounds of appeal (the respective supplemental statements of grounds of appeal filed by the Defendant’s counsel, Attorney Moon Hyung-sik, and by the counsel for the intervenor in support of the Defendant, Lucky Tourism Co., Ltd., Attorney Yoon Il-young, shall be considered to the extent that they supplement the respective statements of grounds of appeal for the Defendant and the intervenors in support of the Defendant).\\n\\n1. As to the part of Ground 1 of the grounds of appeal by the Defendant and the intervenor in support of the Defendant 1’s counsel, Attorney Bae Gi-won, concerning the interpretation of Articles 380 and 190 of the Commercial Act, Ground 3, the part of Ground 4 asserting that Non-party 1 was the lawful representative director of Nakcheon Tourism Co., Ltd., the grounds of appeal of the Defendant and the intervenors in support of the Defendant themselves, and Ground 1 of the grounds of appeal by the counsel for Lucky Tourism Co., Ltd., the intervenor in support of the Defendant, Attorney Oh Seong-hwan.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, that court found, based on the evidence, that while Non-party 2 was carrying out construction of a seven-story building on the land at Busan, Nam-gu, (address omitted) for hotel operation purposes, he completed the construction on January 16, 1980, established Nakcheon Tourism Co., Ltd. (whose trade name was changed to Busan Shilla Tourist Hotel Co., Ltd. on March 25, 1982, and then changed again to Nakcheon Tourism Co., Ltd. on May 21, 1985; hereinafter referred to only as Nakcheon Tourism), a stock company for the purpose of tourism business, issued 10,000 shares, and subscribed for 5,000 shares in the names of himself and his relatives, and Non-party 3 likewise subscribed for 5,000 shares in the names of himself and others, after which they jointly assumed office as representative directors; that thereafter some of the said shares were transferred to Non-parties 4 and 5, and after Non-party 6 assumed office as representative director of Nakcheon Tourism on February 25, 1982, he issued 50,000 new shares and subscribed for all of them himself, thereby, as of July 27, 1983, owning 55,300 shares out of a total of 60,000 shares, with Non-party 2 owning 4,700 shares; that Non-party 6, having failed in the management of the company, delegated all authority concerning the management of Nakcheon Tourism and the exercise of shareholder rights to Non-parties 7 and 8 on August 23 of the same year, resigned from the office of representative director, and absconded; that thereupon Non-party 7 assumed office as representative director of Nakcheon Tourism and brought in Non-party 9 and sought to rationalize management, but when that failed, he, at the suggestion of said Non-party 9, decided to accept Non-party 10, who proposed to pay KRW 340,000,000 and take over 31,800 shares and the company’s management rights; that on August 13, 1984, he himself resigned from the office of representative director and, in accordance with Non-party 10’s wishes, appointed Non-party 10 as representative director and Non-parties 11, 12, 13, and 14 as new directors; that however Non-party 10 failed to pay the said consideration for the transfer of shares, resigned from the office of representative director on October 30 of the same year, after which Non-party 7 was reappointed, and then, at Non-party 10’s request, returned again as representative director on December 7 of the same year, but was in flight due to dishonored checks and the like; that thereupon Non-party 7, intending either to find a financially capable person who could complete the construction of the said building and thereby finish the work, or alternatively to transfer the said building and recover the invested capital, and in order to remove the new officers including Non-party 10, who were an obstacle to this, and reorganize management, conspired with Non-party 1; that on December 12, 1984, he prepared a shareholder register of the company stating that, at that time, Non-party 8, the nominee holder of Non-party 6, held 55,000 shares, he himself held 300 shares, and Non-party 1 held 4,700 shares; that although an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting may be convened pursuant to a resolution of the board of directors or as otherwise prescribed by law, and the representative director may be appointed by the board of directors, but in some cases may also be appointed by the shareholders’ meeting, and directors are appointed by the shareholders’ meeting, and the representative director is to convene the board of directors, there had in fact been no convening or holding of any extraordinary shareholders’ meeting or board of directors’ meeting pursuant to Nakcheon Tourism’s articles of incorporation; nevertheless, as if a shareholders’ meeting had been held on that very day and had resolved to dismiss all of the representative director Non-party 10 and the directors Non-parties 11, 12, 13, and 14, and to newly appoint Non-party 1, Non-party 15, and Intervenor in support of the Defendant 1 as directors, he falsely prepared minutes of the shareholders’ meeting; that on the same day he also falsely prepared minutes of the board of directors’ meeting as if, at a board of directors composed of the newly appointed directors, the existing director Non-party 8 had been appointed representative director; that on January 4, 1985, he again decided to place Non-party 1 as representative director, and, without giving notice of convening either to the former directors or to the newly appointed directors and without actually holding any board of directors’ meeting, he prepared false minutes stating that at the newly constituted board of directors Non-party 8 resigned from the office of representative director and Non-party 1 was appointed representative director, and on the 8th of the same month registered Non-party 1 as representative director; that Non-party 1, who was appointed representative director through the above process, when the Defendant around that time came forward to assume various debts of Nakcheon Tourism arising from the new hotel-building construction and to invest funds, entered into with the Defendant on the 8th of the same month a contract for the reservation of sale, in his capacity as representative director of Nakcheon Tourism, to sell the hotel building at issue within the limit of KRW 650,000,000 according to the appraised value of the completed work; that based thereon, after obtaining from the court an order for provisional registration injunction, the Defendant on March 7 of the same year completed, with respect to the said hotel building, a preservation registration in the name of Nakcheon Tourism and simultaneously completed a provisional registration in the Defendant’s name for preservation of the right to claim transfer of ownership; and that, meanwhile, with respect to the said hotel building, compulsory auction was commenced on May 10 of the same year upon application by a creditor of Nakcheon Tourism, and the Plaintiffs received an order granting permission of sale by auction on January 31, 1986, the order became final and conclusive, and they completed payment of the auction price on March 4 of the same year.\\n\\nOn the basis of the foregoing findings, the court below held that the shareholders’ meeting of December 12, 1984, because it had not gone through the actual convening procedures or the actual meeting procedures, suffered from such serious defects that it could not possibly be regarded as having existed at all, and thus was non-existent; and that the board of directors held on the same day and on January 4, 1985 likewise was carried out without the convening procedures or any concrete meeting by the directors, and therefore was invalid (non-existent), so that Non-party 1, who was appointed through such erroneous procedures, was not the lawful representative director of Nakcheon Tourism, and accordingly the reservation of sale entered into by him with the Defendant was ineffective against the company without any need for further examination, and the provisional registration made in the Defendant’s name was also null and void ab initio. In light of the record, the court below’s findings of fact and judgment are proper, and there is no illegality in violating the rules governing the weighing of evidence, in misunderstanding the facts, or in misconstruing the law on the non-existence of shareholders’ meeting resolutions or board of directors’ resolutions.\\n\\nThe court below also correctly rejected the Defendant’s argument by holding that, where the effect of a shareholders’ meeting resolution becomes a preliminary issue in litigation between third parties other than the company, the parties may at any time contest and argue in the relevant litigation that the shareholders’ meeting resolution is void ab initio or non-existent, and it is not necessarily required to first file suit against the company; and that, in legal relations between third parties, Articles 380 and 190 of the Commercial Act do not apply. There is thus no illegality in misconstruing the law concerning the invalidity or non-existence of shareholders’ meeting resolutions and Articles 380 and 190 of the Commercial Act.\\n\\nThe cited decisions of our Court all concern cases where, in an action seeking a judicial declaration of the invalidity or non-existence of a shareholders’ meeting resolution, the company must be named as defendant and Articles 380 and 190 of the Commercial Act apply; they are therefore not relevant to this case.\\n\\nFurther, the judicial declaration of non-existence of a shareholders’ meeting resolution under Article 380 of the Commercial Act is to be construed as meaning a judgment declaring that, although the internal decision-making of a stock company called a “shareholders’ meeting resolution” does exist in the first instance, because there is a serious defect in the convening procedure of such shareholders’ meeting or in the method of resolution, that resolution cannot be regarded as a legally valid shareholders’ meeting resolution; therefore, in the factual relationship recognized above, it does not fall within the judicial declaration of non-existence of a shareholders’ meeting resolution prescribed in Article 380 of the Commercial Act, and thus Article 190 of the Commercial Act is not to be applied by analogy either (see Supreme Court Decision 91DA39924, decided August 18, 1992).\\n\\nThe argument lacks merit.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 2 of the grounds of appeal by the Defendant and the intervenor in support of the Defendant 1’s counsel, Attorney Bae Gi-won, the part of Ground 4 concerning the formation of apparent representative director, and Ground 2 of the grounds of appeal by the counsel for Lucky Tourism Co., Ltd., the intervenor in support of the Defendant, Attorney Oh Seong-hwan.\\n\\nIn order for a company to be liable under Article 395 of the Commercial Act for the acts of an apparent representative director, the third party who relied on the acts of the apparent representative director must have acted in good faith, and the company must have expressly or impliedly permitted the apparent representation; and to say that the company permitted the apparent representation in such case, the genuine representative director must have allowed it, or, if not all directors, at least the number of directors prescribed by the company’s articles of incorporation for the formation of a resolution of the board of directors, and if there is no such provision in the articles of incorporation, at least a majority of the full number of directors, must have expressly or impliedly permitted the apparent representation.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, that court recognized that Non-party 1 had, in appearance, served as representative director of Nakcheon Tourism and had performed various duties as representative director from January 8, 1985 to May 21 of the same year, but found that most of those acts occurred after the reservation of sale that was the cause of the provisional registration at issue, and held that such circumstances alone do not show that, at the time of the reservation of sale, Nakcheon Tourism actively or impliedly permitted Non-party 1 to act as representative director, and that the Defendant also negotiated with Non-party 1 in reliance on such appearance; rather, based on the entries in Exhibits A 18-2, 3, 5, 6, and 8, it found that the Defendant knew, at the latest at the time the provisional registration was completed, that Non-party 1 was not a lawfully appointed representative director, and thus ruled that the doctrine of apparent representative director could not apply.\\n\\nThe evidence relied upon by the court below in finding that the Defendant was in bad faith and knew that Non-party 1 was not a lawful representative director consisted of the statements of Non-party 1 and Non-party 7 and the indictment against the Defendant mainly based on those statements, etc.; however, according to the record, Non-party 1 was not only convicted of perjury in relation to the above statements, but those persons later made statements withdrawing them on the ground that the above statements were false. In light of this, the above evidence is not readily credible. The court below, having concluded from that evidence that the Defendant was in bad faith as stated above, misapprehended the facts in violation of the rules governing the weighing of evidence; furthermore, in a case such as this, where a person registered as appointed representative director is an unlawful representative director and is merely a de facto representative director, the court below should first have examined whether there was any fault attributable to the company in the appointment of the said representative director and thereby determined whether the company bore liability arising from the apparent representative director; yet it failed to do so, and this cannot but be said to constitute a failure to fully examine the case.\\n\\nHowever, on the other hand, according to the facts found above and the record, at the time of the board of directors’ resolution on January 4, 1985 appointing Non-party 1 as representative director, the lawful directors consisted of the five directors who had been unlawfully dismissed by the shareholders’ meeting resolution of December 12, 1984 and Non-parties 7 and 8, a total of seven persons, so that Non-party 1 was ultimately appointed by Non-parties 7 and 8, two of the seven legitimate directors. According to Nakcheon Tourism’s articles of incorporation contained in the record (Exhibit A 12-8), resolutions of the board of directors are to be determined by a majority of all directors, so even on the basis of the above circumstances alone it cannot be said that Nakcheon Tourism permitted Non-party 1 to serve as representative director, and in addition there is no material whatsoever that would support a conclusion that Nakcheon Tourism permitted Non-party 1 to be representative director. Therefore, the court below’s disposition denying liability of Nakcheon Tourism on the basis of apparent representative director is proper in its conclusion. Ultimately, the argument lacks merit.\\n\\n3. As to the part of Ground 1 of the grounds of appeal by the Defendant and the intervenor in support of the Defendant 1’s counsel, Attorney Bae Gi-won, asserting that the resolutions of the shareholders’ meetings were valid as resolutions made in accordance with the will of all shareholders or of the majority shareholder, the part of Ground 2 of the grounds of appeal by the Defendant and the intervenor in support of the Defendant 1 themselves asserting the same purport, and Ground 3 of the grounds of appeal by the counsel for Lucky Tourism Co., Ltd., the intervenor in support of the Defendant, Attorney Oh Seong-hwan.\\n\\nThe court below rejected the related argument on the ground that there was no evidence sufficient to find that, in the shareholders’ meeting resolution of Nakcheon Tourism dated December 12, 1984 and the shareholders’ meeting resolution dated January 28, 1985, Non-party 2, as a shareholder, had granted Non-party 1 authority to make such resolutions or had ratified them afterward; and this is understandable in light of the record, and there is no illegality in misconstruing the law as pointed out, in violating the rules governing the weighing of evidence, or in failing to fully examine the case.\\n\\nMoreover, if a shareholders’ meeting resolution document is prepared without going through the convening procedures and the actual meeting procedures, then even if the shareholders’ meeting resolution document was prepared by a person entrusted with shareholder rights by a majority shareholder holding an overwhelming majority of the shares, the resolution of the said shareholders’ meeting can only be regarded as non-existent, and it cannot be said that this is merely a defect consisting of failure to give notice of convocation to some shareholders, constituting only a ground for revocation of the shareholders’ meeting resolution.\\n\\nThe court below’s judgment to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality in misconstruing the law concerning the non-existence of shareholders’ meeting resolutions.\\n\\nThe argument lacks merit.\\n\\n4. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the Defendant and the intervenors in support of the Defendant; it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: A lawsuit was filed by shareholders A, B, and C of A Stock Company against A Stock Company seeking confirmation of the nonexistence or nullity of the resolution of the company’s extraordinary general meeting of shareholders. Which of the following statements is incorrect? (Each proposition is independent, and where disputed, according to precedents)
A: If D borrowed C’s name to subscribe for shares of A Stock Company and completed the entry in the shareholders register under C’s name, then even if A Stock Company knew this fact, absent special circumstances, C may exercise shareholder rights at the general meeting of shareholders and may bring an action to confirm the nonexistence or nullity of the resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders.
B: If the resolution of A Stock Company’s extraordinary general meeting of shareholders was made without the board resolution and convocation procedures required by laws and regulations and the articles of incorporation, then even if all shareholders on the shareholders register attended and agreed to hold the meeting and the resolution was adopted unanimously without any objection, the resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders should, absent special circumstances, be regarded as nonexistent.
C: If the above action was brought within 2 months from the date of the above resolution, then even if it was changed into or supplemented by an action for revocation after 2 months had elapsed from the date of the above resolution on the basis of the same defect, it should be deemed that the filing period for the revocation action was complied with.
D: If the court of first instance rendered a judgment dismissing the claim, then even if A and B lawfully appealed within the appeal period and C did not appeal within the appeal period, the finality of the judgment is prevented as between A, B, and C, the litigation is transferred in whole to the appellate court, and the appellate court must hear and determine the case as to all of them.
E: In the above lawsuit, even if A Stock Company admitted the claim and the contents were entered in the record, the record of admission is ineffective.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2001DA45584]": "The appeal is dismissed. The costs of appeal shall be borne by the Defendant."}
{"[2002DA15733]": "The appeal is dismissed. The costs of appeal shall be borne by the Plaintiff (Selected Party)."}

{"[2004DA28047]": "1. With respect to the Plaintiff’s action seeking confirmation of the invalidity of the resolution of the Defendant Company’s extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated September 8, 1998, it is a matter of record that, on January 4, 2002, a mediation was reached among the Plaintiff, the Defendant Company, and Nonparty, the intervening participant in mediation and the Defendant Company’s representative director, and a mediation record was prepared reflecting the following terms: “(1) The Plaintiff, the Defendant, and the intervening participant in mediation confirm that all resolutions of the Defendant Company’s extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated September 8, 1998 (agenda items: dismissal and appointment of officers, change of company name, change of head office location, etc.) are either invalid or non-existent. (2) The Plaintiff shall duly convene and hold a board of directors meeting by January 14, 2002 for the purpose of convening the Defendant Company’s extraordinary general meeting of shareholders (with the same agenda as the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated September 8, 1998), and shall duly convene and hold such extraordinary general meeting of shareholders by January 31, 2002. (3) If the Plaintiff delays the procedure under item (2) above, the Plaintiff shall immediately step down from the positions of representative director and director of the Defendant Company, and agrees to transfer such positions to the above-mentioned intervening participant in mediation, Nonparty, and shall no longer raise any objection to the resolution of the Defendant Company’s extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated September 8, 1998. (4) The Plaintiff waives the remaining claims. (5) Litigation costs and mediation costs shall be borne by each party respectively.” It is also manifest on the record that, on December 11, 2002, the Plaintiff filed a motion for designation of a hearing date with the court of first instance, asserting that the above mediation record was void; however, the court of first instance declared termination of the litigation on the ground that, even if a company-related lawsuit was concluded by mediation between the parties, such mediation cannot be said to become void ab initio merely for that reason alone, and further that even if a hearing were designated and the case heard, no ground for invalidity could otherwise be recognized in the above mediation record.\\n\\n2. Based on the evidence it accepted, the court below recognized the facts stated in its opinion and then held that, at the time of the mediation in this case, the Plaintiff, the Defendant Company, and Nonparty intended, on the premise that the resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated September 8, 1998 had not existed, to newly convene and hold a lawful board of directors meeting and general meeting of shareholders under the responsibility of the Plaintiff, the former representative director whose term had expired, and to accept the resolutions made thereat, but, in the event the convening procedure was not properly carried out, not to dispute any further the validity of the resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated September 8, 1998; accordingly, it concluded that mediation with such content could not be categorically held to be void ab initio, and therefore rejected the Plaintiff’s motion for designation of a hearing date and upheld the first-instance judgment, which had deemed that the present action terminated upon the formation of the mediation in this case.\\n\\n3. However, the above determination by the court below is difficult to approve.\\n\\n   a. Once a judgment confirming the nonexistence or invalidity of, or rescinding, a resolution of a general meeting of shareholders becomes final and conclusive, its effect extends to third parties other than the parties thereto, and third parties too are unable to challenge it; therefore, in an action disputing defects in a resolution of a general meeting of shareholders, it is not permissible to have an acknowledgment of the claim entered, or to conclude a settlement or mediation, to the effect of confirming the nonexistence or invalidity of such resolution, and even if such acknowledgment of the claim or such settlement or mediation were effected, the record of acknowledgment or the settlement/mediation record would be ineffective (see Supreme Court Decision 92NU14908 rendered May 29, 1993). Accordingly, since item (1) of the mediation clause in this case clearly contains confirmation of the nonexistence or invalidity of the resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated September 8, 1998, it is difficult to recognize its validity.\\n\\n   b. The court below regarded item (1) of the mediation clause in this case as nothing more than a means to resolve, under the responsibility of the Plaintiff, the dispute that had arisen between the Plaintiff and Nonparty concerning the validity of the resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated September 8, 1998 by newly convening and holding a lawful board of directors meeting and general meeting of shareholders, and viewed the essence as lying in the agreement not to dispute any further the validity of the resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated September 8, 1998 if the Plaintiff failed to properly carry out the convening procedure for the new general meeting of shareholders; on that basis, it held that the mediation in this case was valid. However, once a mediation is reached that the resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders dated September 8, 1998 is invalid or non-existent, then, as set forth by the court below, the new resolution to be made at the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders to be convened and held by the Plaintiff on that premise does not merely end the question of validity by the Plaintiff and Nonparty simply “mutually accepting” it, but rather its validity or lawfulness may again be at issue in relation to third parties; accordingly, the mediation in this case cannot be regarded as having become valid merely on the basis of the circumstances described by the court below.\\n\\n   c. Ultimately, the above determination of the court below contains an error of law in misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the possibility of mediation in a lawsuit disputing the validity of a resolution of a general meeting of shareholders, and therefore the Plaintiff’s argument pointing out this point and raised as the first ground of appeal is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Accordingly, without addressing the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below, and it is so adjudged as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2018DA261322]": "1. Before addressing the grounds of appeal, the Court examines ex officio.\\n\\nA. In an action seeking a declaration of nonexistence of a resolution of a shareholders’ meeting, the interest in confirmation may be recognized where, because of the existence or appearance of a resolution of the shareholders’ meeting, an obstacle arises to the present rights or legal relations surrounding the company, and it is necessary to eliminate such existence or appearance by seeking a declaration of nonexistence.\\n\\nAlso, whether there is an interest in confirmation in an action for confirmation is a matter subject to ex officio investigation, and therefore the court must determine it ex officio regardless of whether the parties assert it (see Supreme Court Decision 91DA12905 rendered on July 12, 1991).\\n\\nB. The Plaintiff seeks a declaration of nonexistence with respect to the resolution of the shareholders’ meeting stated in item 4 of the attached list cited by the lower court on the ground that the articles of incorporation were amended by resolution while excluding himself, the bona fide shareholder. According to the record, however, at that shareholders’ meeting only the matter concerning the “appointment of an auditor” was resolved, and the amendment of the articles of incorporation was not a subject of resolution; moreover, the minutes of the shareholders’ meeting do not contain any entry concerning a resolution on amendment of the articles of incorporation.\\n\\nC. The resolution stated in item 4 of the attached list cited by the lower court, for which the Plaintiff seeks a declaration of nonexistence, has no outward indicia that would allow its existence to be recognized, and there are no circumstances indicating that, because of the existence or appearance of such resolution, it caused an obstacle to the present rights or legal relations surrounding the company; therefore, there is no interest in confirmation to seek a declaration of nonexistence of that resolution.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court adjudicated the merits on the premise that there was an interest in confirmation with respect to this claim for confirmation. In so doing, the lower court erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning interest in confirmation, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n2. The grounds of appeal shall be examined (as to the statements in the statement of grounds of appeal filed by the Defendant and the Defendant’s auxiliary intervenor after the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal had expired, and in the supplemental statement of grounds of appeal, only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\nA. As to the grounds of appeal concerning recognition of the status of a de facto shareholder\\n\\nThe lower court determined, for the reasons stated in its opinion, that the Plaintiff was in the status of a de facto shareholder with respect to 7,000 of the 10,000 shares issued by the Defendant at the time of the Defendant’s incorporation (hereinafter referred to as the “Shares in this Case”).\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in the lower court’s determination, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, that affected the judgment by exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in contravention of the rules of logic and experience.\\n\\nB. As to the grounds of appeal concerning the effect of the entries in the shareholder registry and the exercise of shareholder rights\\n\\n1) A) Unless there are special circumstances, a person lawfully entered as a shareholder in the shareholder registry may exercise shareholder rights, including voting rights concerning the shares, in relation to the company, and the company likewise cannot deny the exercise of shareholder rights by the shareholder entered in the shareholder registry, regardless of whether it knew that there was a separate person who in fact had subscribed for or acquired the shares other than the shareholder in the shareholder registry. Nor may the company recognize the exercise of shareholder rights by a person who has not completed entry in the shareholder registry. The only cases in which shareholder rights may be exercised in relation to the company without completion of entry in the shareholder registry are extremely exceptional circumstances, such as where the entry in the shareholder registry or the request for transfer registration has been unreasonably delayed or refused (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2015DA248342 rendered on March 23, 2017).\\n\\nB) Thus, in order for a shareholder entered in the shareholder registry to exercise shareholder rights in relation to the company, the entry in that shareholder registry must have been lawfully made.\\n\\n(1) Where shares are issued, a person who wishes to subscribe for the shares makes an application, and the company allots the shares accordingly (Articles 302(1), 420-5(1), and 425(1) of the Commercial Act), and when the subscriber performs legal obligations such as payment of the subscription price or contribution in kind (Article 303 and Article 425(1) of the Commercial Act), the company enters that subscriber as a shareholder in the shareholder registry (Article 352(1) of the Commercial Act). At this time, if the company, after confirming whether allotment of shares corresponding to the subscriber’s application has been made and whether the subscriber’s legal obligations have been performed, entered the subscriber as a shareholder, then, unless there are special circumstances, such entry in the shareholder registry must be regarded as lawful.\\n\\n(2) Where shares are transferred, the company, upon the request for transfer registration by the person who acquired the shares, conducts an examination and enters that person as a shareholder in the shareholder registry. At this time, it is sufficient for the company to examine only the formal qualifications concerning the request for transfer registration, such as whether the requester is in possession of genuine share certificates (where share certificates have been issued) or whether the requester is proving the fact of acquiring the shares (where share certificates have not been issued), and it has no duty to examine the substantive qualification of whether the requester is in fact the true shareholder. Therefore, if a person who acquired shares requests transfer registration by proving the fact of acquisition, and the company, having fulfilled its formal duty of examination with respect to that request, carried out the transfer registration accordingly, then, unless there are special circumstances, the entry in the shareholder registry pursuant to that transfer registration must be regarded as lawful (see Supreme Court Decisions 94DA47728 rendered on March 24, 1995, and 2017DA231980 rendered on August 14, 2019).\\n\\n(3) Where the entry in the shareholder registry pursuant to transfer registration cannot be regarded as lawful, if there exists a shareholder registry prepared immediately before the transfer registration, and if the entry in that shareholder registry can be regarded as having been lawfully made, then the shareholder entered in that shareholder registry may exercise shareholder rights in relation to the company.\\n\\nC) A shareholders’ meeting held without sending notices of convocation to most shareholders, unless there are special circumstances, contains such grave defects in the formation process that, as a matter of social common sense, the formation of the meeting itself can hardly be recognized (see Supreme Court Decisions 78DA1269 rendered on November 14, 1978, and 80DA128 rendered on December 9, 1980, among others).\\n\\n2) According to the reasoning of the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\nA) The Defendant was incorporated on January 25, 2011, and the Plaintiff served as the Defendant’s representative director from the Defendant’s incorporation until May 25, 2011, and from June 8, 2012, until June 26 of the same year; as an inside director of the Defendant from June 8, 2012, until June 2, 2015; and Nonparty 1 served as an inside director of the Defendant from the Defendant’s incorporation until January 25, 2014, and from December 3, 2014, until July 15, 2016, and as the Defendant’s representative director from May 25, 2011, until June 8, 2012, from June 26, 2012, until June 26, 2015, and from September 15, 2015, until July 15, 2016.\\n\\nIn the shareholder registry dated January 25, 2011, at the time of the Defendant’s incorporation, the Plaintiff was entered as holding the Shares in this Case, and Nonparty 1 was entered as holding 3,000 shares.\\n\\nB) Nonparty 2 paid the transfer price after agreeing to acquire the Shares in this Case from Nonparty 1, who claimed to be the de facto shareholder of the Shares in this Case; however, Nonparty 1, who was the Defendant’s representative director, knowing that the shareholder of the Shares in this Case was the Plaintiff and that no share transfer agreement had ever been concluded between Nonparty 2 and the Plaintiff, entered Nonparty 2 in the Defendant’s shareholder registry on May 25, 2011, as a shareholder holding 7,000 shares corresponding to the quantity of the Shares in this Case (hereinafter, the change in shareholder with respect to the Shares in this Case is referred to as the “First Shareholder Change in this Case”). The same entry appeared in the Defendant’s shareholder registry dated December 3, 2014.\\n\\nC) After the First Shareholder Change in this Case, the Defendant issued new shares on three occasions by passing resolutions of the shareholders’ meeting on amendment of the articles of incorporation and resolutions of the board of directors on issuance of new shares. Accordingly, the number of shares held by Nonparty 2 and Nonparty 1, as entered in the shareholder registries dated September 15, 2015, and January 14, 2016, respectively, changed, and Nonparty 3 Company, Nonparty 4, Nonparty 5, and Nonparty 6 were newly entered as shareholders (hereinafter the series of shareholding and shareholder changes reflected in each shareholder registry is collectively referred to as the “Second Shareholder Change in this Case”).\\n\\nHowever, no payment whatsoever was made of the subscription price for the new shares issued on the basis of the Second Shareholder Change in this Case.\\n\\nD) The convocation process and contents of the resolutions of the shareholders’ meeting stated in items 1 through 3 and item 5 of the attached list cited in the lower court’s judgment are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Resolution of the extraordinary shareholders’ meeting dated December 3, 2014 (resolution in item 1 of the attached list cited in the lower court’s judgment)\\n\\nThe Defendant held an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting on December 3, 2014, without notice of convocation to the Plaintiff. At that meeting, an agenda was submitted to amend the total number of shares to be issued by the Defendant under the articles of incorporation from 10,000 shares to 20,000 shares, and Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2, who were entered as shareholders in the Defendant’s shareholder registry at that time, attended and passed the above agenda by the consent of all shareholders.\\n\\n(2) Resolution of the extraordinary shareholders’ meeting dated December 19, 2014 (resolution in item 2 of the attached list cited in the lower court’s judgment)\\n\\nThe Defendant held an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting on December 19, 2014, without notice of convocation to the Plaintiff. At that meeting, an agenda was submitted to amend the total number of shares to be issued by the Defendant under the articles of incorporation from 20,000 shares to 40,000 shares, and Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2, who were entered as shareholders in the Defendant’s shareholder registry at that time, attended and passed the above agenda by the consent of all shareholders.\\n\\n(3) Written resolution dated September 15, 2015 (resolution in item 3 of the attached list cited in the lower court’s judgment)\\n\\nNonparty 1, Nonparty 3 Company, Nonparty 4, Nonparty 2, Nonparty 5, and Nonparty 6, who were entered as shareholders in the Defendant’s shareholder registry, unanimously agreed to omit the convocation procedures for a shareholders’ meeting and, in lieu of a resolution of the shareholders’ meeting, adopted a written resolution on an agenda to amend the total number of shares to be issued by the Defendant under the articles of incorporation from 40,000 shares to 194,000 shares.\\n\\n(4) Resolution of the extraordinary shareholders’ meeting dated July 15, 2016 (resolution in item 5 of the attached list cited in the lower court’s judgment)\\n\\nNonparty 2, the Defendant’s inside director, held an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting on July 15, 2016, without notice of convocation to the Plaintiff, and at that meeting the following agendas were submitted: dismissal of Nonparty 1, who was representative director and inside director; amendment of the articles of incorporation; and appointment of directors. Among the persons entered as shareholders in the Defendant’s shareholder registry at that time, all except Nonparty 1 attended, and by the consent of all attending shareholders, they passed agendas dismissing Nonparty 1 from the positions of representative director and inside director, appointing Nonparty 7 and Nonparty 8 as inside directors of the Defendant, and appointing Nonparty 7 and Nonparty 5 as joint representative directors of the Defendant (hereinafter the resolutions of the shareholders’ meeting stated in items 1 through 3 and item 5 of the attached list are referred to as the “Shareholders’ Meeting Resolutions in this Case”).\\n\\n3) The foregoing facts will be examined in light of the legal principles stated above.\\n\\nA) In the case of the First Shareholder Change in this Case, the Defendant knew that Nonparty 2 was requesting transfer registration although he had not acquired the Shares in this Case from the Plaintiff, and although Nonparty 2 made no proof whatsoever that he had acquired the Shares in this Case from the Plaintiff, the Defendant effected transfer registration for the Shares in this Case in the name of Nonparty 2. In light of this transfer registration process, it is difficult to view Nonparty 2 as having requested transfer registration by proving the fact of acquisition of the Shares in this Case and the Defendant as having fulfilled its formal duty of examination with respect to that request; nor are there any other circumstances from which the entry in the shareholder registry can be regarded as lawful. Therefore, the entry in the shareholder registry dated May 25, 2011, pursuant to the First Shareholder Change in this Case cannot be regarded as lawful.\\n\\nAs for the shareholders pursuant to the Second Shareholder Change in this Case, the Defendant entered them in the shareholder registry as shareholders in the same manner as the Second Shareholder Change in this Case, although the subscription price for the new shares had not been paid. Therefore, the entries in the shareholder registries dated December 3, 2014, September 15, 2015, and January 14, 2016, pursuant to the Second Shareholder Change in this Case likewise cannot be regarded as lawful.\\n\\nMeanwhile, there exists a shareholder registry dated January 25, 2011, prepared before the First and Second Shareholder Changes in this Case were entered in the shareholder registry, and that shareholder registry is lawful as the shareholder registry concerning the Shares in this Case, because it entered the shareholders according to share subscription at the time of the Defendant’s incorporation.\\n\\nAccordingly, the person who could exercise shareholder rights with respect to the Shares in this Case at the time of the Shareholders’ Meeting Resolutions in this Case was the Plaintiff, who was lawfully entered as a shareholder in the shareholder registry dated January 25, 2011, rather than the shareholders entered in the shareholder registry pursuant to the First and Second Shareholder Changes in this Case.\\n\\nB) At the time of the Shareholders’ Meeting Resolutions in this Case, the shares issued by the Defendant consisted only of the 10,000 shares issued at the time of incorporation, except that the substance of the issuance of new shares did not exist because the subscription price had not been paid. However, because notice of convocation of the Shareholders’ Meeting in this Case was not given to the Plaintiff, who was able to exercise shareholder rights with respect to 7,000 of those shares (70%), the Shareholders’ Meeting Resolutions in this Case have such a grave defect that the existence of the resolutions cannot be recognized.\\n\\n4) Although there are some shortcomings in the lower court’s reasoning, the conclusion of the lower court that the Shareholders’ Meeting Resolutions in this Case do not exist is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the effect of the entries in the shareholder registry.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the part of the lower court judgment that confirmed that the resolution stated in item 4 of the attached list cited in the lower court’s judgment does not exist is reversed; however, since this Court can directly adjudicate this part, it shall render judgment itself pursuant to Article 437 of the Civil Procedure Act. The first-instance judgment is reversed with respect to this part, the action with respect to this part is dismissed, the Defendant’s remaining appeal is dismissed as without merit, and the total costs of litigation shall be determined as stated in the order. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in this decision."}

{"[2020DA284977]": "1. Ex officio determination regarding the form of joint litigation\\n\\nThis action is one seeking a declaration of nonexistence or invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution, and a judgment granting the claim, pursuant to the main text of Article 190 of the Commercial Act as applied mutatis mutandis by Article 380 of the Commercial Act, is effective against third parties as well.
