Where such an action is filed jointly by several persons, since the effect of a judgment in favor of one party extends to the other co-litigants, the necessity of a unified determination in procedural law is recognized among the co-litigants. In addition, taking into account that the exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing provisions concerning company-related litigation under the Commercial Act (Articles 186 and 188 of the Commercial Act) also presuppose a unified determination between the parties, as well as the parties’ intentions and judicial economy, this constitutes necessary joint litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies.\\n\\nIn light of this legal principle, the court below’s judgment, premised on the view that the action in this case, jointly filed by the Plaintiffs, constitutes necessary joint litigation, is proper, and there is no error in misunderstanding the law on the form of joint litigation.\\n\\n2. Determination on the grounds for final appeal\\n\\na. According to the reasoning of the court below’s judgment, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\nThe Defendant is a stock company established for the purpose of real estate development and other businesses, and the Plaintiffs are shareholders of the Defendant.\\n\\nNon-Party 1, who is recorded in the shareholders’ register as holding 2,000 shares, obtained the court’s permission to convene an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting and held an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting on May 25, 2012. At that meeting, resolutions were adopted to continue the company, thereby restoring the Defendant, which had been deemed dissolved, to its pre-dissolution status, and to appoint Non-Party 2 and others as officers in view of the expiration of the terms of office and death of the existing officers. At the extraordinary shareholders’ meeting held on May 22, 2015, a resolution was adopted to reappoint Non-Party 2 and others as officers in view of the expiration of the terms of office of the existing officers, and at the extraordinary shareholders’ meeting held on December 2, 2015, a resolution was adopted to dismiss the existing auditor and appoint a new auditor.\\n\\nb. The Plaintiffs argued that the extraordinary shareholders’ meeting of May 25, 2012 was convened by Non-Party 1 or Non-Party 2, who had no authority to convene it, and that the resolution was non-existent or invalid due to defects such as insufficient quorum caused by forged proxies of some shareholders, and that the extraordinary shareholders’ meeting resolutions of May 22, 2015 and December 2, 2015 based thereon were also non-existent or invalid.\\n\\nIn response, the court below determined that the extraordinary shareholders’ meeting of May 25, 2012 was convened by Non-Party 1, who, as a shareholder on the shareholders’ register, was entitled to exercise shareholder rights, and thus could not be deemed to have been convened by a person without authority to convene it; and that Non-Party 2 had lawfully been entrusted by some shareholders with the exercise of voting rights and participated in the meeting resolution as their agent, and therefore the quorum requirement was satisfied. Furthermore, the court below did not accept the Plaintiffs’ claims regarding the extraordinary shareholders’ meeting resolutions of May 22, 2015 and December 2, 2015, which were premised on the assertion that the above resolutions were non-existent or invalid.\\n\\nc. Examining the reasoning of the court below’s judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, in that the court below failed to conduct the necessary examination, deviated from the bounds of the free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehended the relevant legal principles such as those concerning the authority to convene a shareholders’ meeting, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the final appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and judgment is rendered as stated in the order. In this judgment, except for the separate opinions of Justices Lee Ki-taek, Park Jeong-hwa, Kim Seon-su, and Lee Heung-gu concerning the form of joint litigation, the supplementary opinions of Justices Kim Jae-hyeong, Min Yu-sook, and Noh Tae-ak on the majority opinion, and Justice Lee Ki-taek’s supplementary opinion on the separate opinions, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous.\\n\\n4. Separate opinion of Justices Lee Ki-taek, Park Jeong-hwa, Kim Seon-su, and Lee Heung-gu concerning the form of joint litigation\\n\\na. The main text of Article 190 of the Commercial Act provides, “A judgment declaring the incorporation invalid or rescinding the incorporation shall also be effective against third parties.” Accordingly, a judgment granting a claim in an action for invalidation or rescission of incorporation is effective against third parties as well. The above provision is applied mutatis mutandis to various company-related actions under the Commercial Act, and in actions for invalidation of merger (Article 240), actions for invalidation of exchange of shares (Article 360-14, paragraph 4), actions for invalidation of transfer of shares (Article 360-23, paragraph 4), actions for revocation of shareholders’ meeting resolutions (Article 376, paragraph 2), actions for declaration of invalidity or nonexistence of shareholders’ meeting resolutions (Article 380), actions for revocation or modification of improper shareholders’ meeting resolutions (Article 381, paragraph 2), actions for invalidation of new share issuance (Article 430), and actions for invalidation of capital reduction (Article 446), a judgment granting the claim also has erga omnes effect.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that, where several persons jointly file an action in relation to a company, this falls under necessary joint litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies, because a judgment dismissing the claim is not effective against third parties, whereas a judgment granting the claim is effective against third parties. However, such litigation should be regarded as ordinary joint litigation, which is the principal form of joint litigation. Since the necessity of unified determination, which is a requirement of necessary joint litigation, cannot be recognized, there is no reason or necessity to apply Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act so as to strictly unify the litigation materials and the progress of the proceedings and to limit the parties’ dispositive power or rights concerning procedural conduct. The specific grounds are set forth below.\\n\\nb. Before discussing the issue in earnest, I first examine the current provisions, system, and relevant legal principles of the Civil Procedure Act concerning the meaning of ordinary joint litigation and necessary joint litigation and the manner of examination, and clarify in what respect this separate opinion addresses the issue.\\n\\n1) Joint litigation is a form of litigation in which multiple plaintiffs or defendants are involved in a single set of proceedings. Article 65 of the Civil Procedure Act provides, with respect to the requirements of joint litigation, that “where the rights or obligations that are the subject matter of the litigation are common to several persons, or arise from the same cause in fact or in law, such persons may be parties as co-litigants. The same shall apply where the rights or obligations that are the subject matter of the litigation are of the same kind and arise from causes of the same kind in fact or in law.” Joint litigation may be divided into ordinary joint litigation, in which co-litigants need not prevail or lose together, and necessary joint litigation, in which they must prevail or lose together.\\n\\n2) Article 66 of the Civil Procedure Act provides, “Any procedural act by one co-litigant or a procedural act by the opposing party against such co-litigant, and matters relating to one co-litigant, shall not affect the other co-litigants.”\\n\\nGenerally, parties who are the subjects of rights and obligations may independently institute actions and conduct litigation. Even if several persons become parties jointly, this is merely a consolidation into one procedure of cases that could be resolved through separate litigation, for the sake of joint examination, and there is no reason why the independent status and powers each party has when litigating individually should be specially restricted merely because they are co-litigants. Accordingly, even in joint litigation, each party conducts litigation on his or her own responsibility, without help or interference from the other co-litigants, and bears responsibility only for the procedural acts he or she has performed. Article 66 of the Civil Procedure Act provides that ordinary joint litigation, in which the status of each co-litigant remains independent, is the principal form of joint litigation.\\n\\n3) Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act defines necessary joint litigation as “joint litigation in which the subject matter of the litigation must be determined uniformly for all co-litigants,” and provides special rules for examination so that the result may be determined uniformly among the co-litigants. Paragraph 1 of Article 67 provides, “A procedural act by one co-litigant shall be effective only for the benefit of all.” Paragraph 2 provides, “A procedural act by the opposing party against one co-litigant shall be effective against all co-litigants.” Pursuant to the above provision, procedural acts by one party that benefit all co-litigants, such as assertions and submission of evidence for victory, extend their effect to all co-litigants, while unfavorable procedural acts, such as confession, will have no effect at all unless all parties act together, thereby unifying the litigation materials as to all parties, and the effect of procedural acts disposing of the subject matter of litigation, such as renunciation of the claim, acknowledgment, and judicial settlement by one party, is also restricted. Next, paragraph 3 provides, “Where there is a reason requiring suspension or interruption of the procedural progress as to one co-litigant, such interruption or suspension shall be effective for all.” In addition, separation of oral arguments among co-litigants is not permitted, a single judgment must be rendered against all co-litigants, and if some co-litigants file an appeal, finality of the judgment is prevented as to all and the entire litigation is transferred to the appellate instance, so that the progress of the litigation is uniformly carried out (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DA44615, 2003DA44622, rendered December 12, 2003; Supreme Court Decision 2008DA50691, rendered April 29, 2010, etc.).\\n\\nThus, when Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies, litigation materials are unified among co-litigants (common allegations and evidence) and the progress of the litigation (common arguments, judgment, and instances) is also unified, so that the result of adjudication is uniformly determined among the co-litigants. By contrast, if even one of litigation materials or the progress of the litigation is not unified, uniform determination of the adjudicative result is not assured.\\n\\n4) To summarize the foregoing legal principles, joint litigation has the following structure: ① ordinary joint litigation is the rule; ② only where there is a “necessity of uniform determination” does it become necessary joint litigation; and ③ in necessary joint litigation, the special rules of examination under Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act apply so as to uniformly determine the result of adjudication.\\n\\nThis separate opinion, while fully respecting the existing system and legal principles concerning the form of joint litigation, raises the question whether company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect falls under necessary joint litigation requiring uniform determination, that is, the issue under the above ②. It does not concern the prior stage of ①, namely, legislative and policy discussion over which form of joint litigation is desirable, or whether necessary joint litigation should be recognized even where there is no need for uniform determination, nor does it concern the subsequent stage of ③, namely, discussion of what mode of examination is more suitable for necessary joint litigation.\\n\\nAccordingly, the argument that, where the rights and obligations that are the subject matter of litigation are common among co-litigants, it is smooth and natural for them to prevail or lose together may be a discussion under ①, namely, a legislative discussion suggesting that, contrary to the current provisions of the Civil Procedure Act, the principal form of joint litigation should be regarded as necessary joint litigation or that the scope of recognition of necessary joint litigation should be broadened. But under the current system and legal principles concerning joint litigation, it cannot serve as a valid ground for regarding company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as necessary joint litigation. Furthermore, discussion of the mode of examination under Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act is a discussion under ③, premised on the case falling within necessary joint litigation, and thus lies on a different plane from this separate opinion. Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act merely provides procedural means for uniform determination in cases that constitute necessary joint litigation requiring uniform determination among co-litigants. Arguing that a given litigation should be regarded as necessary joint litigation requiring uniform determination because applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act among co-litigants is reasonable or desirable merely reverses the logical order or amounts to nothing more than altering the concept of necessary joint litigation.\\n\\nc. The main grounds for regarding company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as ordinary joint litigation are as follows.\\n\\n1) The principal form of joint litigation is ordinary joint litigation, in which the status of each co-litigant is independent. Only exceptionally, where there is a need under substantive law or procedural law for the subject matter of litigation to be determined uniformly, may it be regarded as necessary joint litigation.\\n\\na) As noted above, under our Civil Procedure Act, ordinary joint litigation with the independent status of each co-litigant is the principal form of joint litigation. This is evident from the system of provisions on joint litigation in the Civil Procedure Act, namely, the structure in which Article 66 of the Civil Procedure Act concerning the independence of co-litigants comes first, and Articles 67 and below, as special provisions to Article 66, establish special rules for the examination of certain types of joint litigation (necessary joint litigation, preliminary and selective joint litigation); and from the fact that ordinary joint litigation is the procedural manifestation of the principle of private autonomy, the basic principle of civil law that private legal relationships are regulated according to the free will of individuals under their own responsibility.\\n\\nb) If one departs from this principle and deems a case to be necessary joint litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies, as noted above, various constraints are imposed on the parties’ independent status and powers concerning the conduct of litigation, such as restrictions on the effect of procedural acts by the parties and on the freedom to dispose of the subject matter of litigation. In order to justify such constraints, the requirements for necessary joint litigation under Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, namely, the case where the subject matter of litigation must be determined uniformly for all co-litigants, must be satisfied.\\n\\nTo this end, there must be a substantive-law basis whereby the parties cannot individually exercise the power to manage and dispose of property rights, so that joint litigation is compelled and the result of adjudication must also coincide; or, although several persons may litigate individually, there must be a necessity for uniform determination under substantive law or procedural law because, procedurally, the effect of a judgment obtained by one party extends to the other party and differing judgments would therefore create mutually contradictory or conflicting effects.\\n\\nWithout a legal necessity for uniform determination among co-litigants, one cannot deem a case to be necessary joint litigation merely because it would be logically or practically desirable for them to prevail or lose together. The most typical example is where a creditor files an action against the principal debtor and a guarantor. While it is substantively consistent and logical for judgments on whether the debt has been repaid to coincide as between the principal debtor and the guarantor, that alone does not make it necessary joint litigation. It is entirely possible for the principal debtor, who alleges and proves repayment, to prevail, while the guarantor, who does not raise the defense that the principal debtor has paid, loses. Previous Supreme Court decisions have held, in the same vein, that where a claim against multiple joint obligors or an action for cancellation of successive transfers of ownership registration does not require legal uniform determination, it does not constitute necessary joint litigation (see Supreme Court Decision 4287MINSANG204, rendered February 10, 1955; Supreme Court Decision 70DA232, rendered February 9, 1971, etc.).\\n\\n2) In company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, there is no “substantive-law” necessity for uniform determination. This is because the purpose of unifying the legal relationship under substantive law can be fully achieved by the erga omnes-effect provision, rendering any other means unnecessary, and because applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act cannot be regarded as an effective and appropriate means for unifying the legal relationship under substantive law.\\n\\na) The res judicata of a judgment originally extends only to the parties, successors after the closure of oral arguments, and the persons provided in Article 218 of the Civil Procedure Act. The one-sided erga omnes-effect provision concerning company-related litigation is an exception to the principle of relativity of res judicata, extending the effect of a judgment to third parties in order to uniformly determine the corporate-law legal relationship surrounding the company, such as shareholders, counterparties, and other interested persons.\\n\\nFor example, even if a shareholders’ meeting resolution has a ground for invalidity, the shareholders may each freely decide whether or not to file an action for declaration of invalidity of the shareholders’ meeting resolution, and if one shareholder, A, files the action first, A may receive a judgment dismissing the claim, while B, who files later, may receive a judgment granting the claim. In that case, if the same shareholders’ meeting resolution is invalid as against B but valid as against A and the remaining shareholders who did not file suit or other interested persons, confusion arises in the corporate-law legal relationship. Accordingly, Article 380 of the Commercial Act, by applying mutatis mutandis the main text of Article 190, recognizes erga omnes effect for the judgment in favor of B, so that the corporate-law legal relationship can be handled uniformly.\\n\\nThe one-sided erga omnes-effect provisions concerning company-related litigation (the main text of Article 190 of the Commercial Act and Articles 240, 380, 430, etc., which apply it mutatis mutandis) were established so that, because joint litigation in company-related litigation (hereinafter “litigation joinder”) is not compelled and thus the result of adjudication may not be unified for all parties, the substantive legal relationship surrounding the corporate body can nonetheless be uniformly determined. In company-related litigation, if a judgment denying the validity of incorporation, merger, shareholders’ meeting resolutions, issuance of new shares, and the like is rendered, the substantive legal relationship is uniformly regulated by virtue of such one-sided erga omnes-effect provisions.\\n\\nb) Where, under substantive law, the power to manage and dispose of property rights is vested jointly in several persons, so that a party cannot dispose of it unilaterally, the outcome of litigation must also coincide for all parties; otherwise, dispute resolution becomes impossible. Accordingly, litigation joinder is compelled, all persons must necessarily become parties and file a single action, an action in which not all are parties is not permitted and is dismissed as improper for lack of standing as a party, and a unified conclusion must be reached by one judgment. Such a type of litigation is called “inherently necessary joint litigation.” An action for partition of co-owned property and actions concerning the bankruptcy estate where there are multiple bankruptcy trustees are examples (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DA44615, 2003DA44622, rendered December 12, 2003; Supreme Court Decision 2006DA14363, rendered April 24, 2008, etc.). In such cases, where litigation joinder is compelled and only one action is permitted for all parties, applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act to render one unified judgment can be regarded as an appropriate means for effectively resolving the dispute.\\n\\nc) By contrast, in company-related litigation, litigation joinder is not compelled, and the parties may each file separate actions or may elect not to file suit. Therefore, even if the result of adjudication is made uniform only among co-litigants, the purpose of unifying the substantive legal relationship through adjudication is not thereby achieved.\\n\\nAs noted above, take as an example an action for declaration of invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution. Since litigation joinder is not compelled in such an action, shareholders A and B may jointly file suit, shareholder C may file suit separately thereafter, and shareholder D may choose not to file suit. Even if, in such a case, A and B’s joint litigation is regarded as necessary joint litigation and a unified judgment is rendered, there is no way to reconcile the result with C’s later separate action, and it is possible for C to prevail even after A and B have lost. As for D, who did not file suit, there is no judgment at all. Thus, even if A and B’s litigation is regarded as necessary joint litigation, there is no way to make the result coincide as to C, D, and others who filed separate actions or did not file suit.\\n\\nIn company-related litigation, uniformity of the substantive legal relationship can be sufficiently achieved by the one-sided erga omnes-effect provision, whereby B’s winning judgment takes effect erga omnes not only against the losing A and B, but also against D and others who did not file suit. Other means are unnecessary, and it cannot be said that regarding A and B’s litigation as necessary joint litigation is an effective and appropriate means for unifying the substantive legal relationship.\\n\\nd) The Civil Procedure Act as amended in 2002 newly created preliminary and selective joint litigation as a new type of joint litigation and expressly permitted the previously impermissible one-sided independent party intervention action, applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act to all such procedures mutatis mutandis (Articles 70 and 79 of the Civil Procedure Act). These types of litigation primarily concern cases in which several claims are legally incompatible with one another. In such cases, litigation joinder is not compelled and there is no provision for unifying the substantive legal relationship, so the content of judgments on the respective claims could be substantively contradictory, thereby causing disadvantages such as the inability to exercise a right despite its existence or the incurrence of duplicate obligations. The purpose of the amendment was to categorize such cases and establish a special litigation system capable of rendering substantively non-contradictory judgments, and to permit parties to use that system if they so desire.\\n\\nThis has no bearing whatsoever on company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect. In company-related litigation, as noted above, there are one-sided erga omnes-effect provisions for uniformly regulating the substantive legal relationship, so whether the parties seek the matter by separate actions or by joint litigation, even if the results of adjudication differ, the parties suffer no disadvantage (the legal relationship is governed according to the winning judgment), and no separate litigation system or measure is necessary to protect the parties’ interests. Therefore, the necessity of applying Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act to company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect cannot be derived from the above purpose of the amendment to the Civil Procedure Act.\\n\\n3) In company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, even if the result of adjudication differs among co-litigants, there is no possibility of conflict between the effects of the judgments, and thus no “procedural-law” necessity for uniform determination can be found.\\n\\na) If the effect of the judgment obtained by one party extends to the other party, so that differing results between them would cause the effects of the judgments to conflict and prevent dispute resolution, then the results of adjudication among the parties must be aligned. Such litigation, whether the parties each file suit individually or happen to file jointly, must have a unified result of adjudication, and if it is joint litigation, it constitutes necessary joint litigation requiring uniform determination. Such a type of litigation is called “quasi-necessary joint litigation.”\\n\\nA representative example of quasi-necessary joint litigation is where the effect of a judgment is extensively extended to a certain range of interested persons regardless of the result. For example, in rehabilitation proceedings, the judgment in an action concerning the determination of rehabilitation claims and security rights is effective against all rehabilitation creditors, rehabilitation secured creditors, shareholders, and equity interest holders (Article 176, paragraph 1 of the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act). If several objectors file an action of objection to a judgment determining a claim with respect to the same claim, and the court renders a judgment for one and against another, the effects of the two judgments extend to all rehabilitation creditors, rehabilitation secured creditors, shareholders, and equity interest holders, thereby conflicting with each other. Accordingly, if the objectors jointly file such an action, it should be regarded as necessary joint litigation and one unified judgment must be rendered; and even if the objectors file separate actions, the oral arguments must necessarily be consolidated and the proceedings carried forward as joint litigation (for this purpose, the commencement of oral arguments is restricted until the period during which another action of objection could be filed has elapsed; see Articles 171, paragraphs 4 and 5 of the same Act).\\n\\nThe same applies where multiple litigation assignees file suit. For example, in a creditor’s subrogation action, if the debtor knew that the action had been filed, the res judicata effect extends to the debtor pursuant to Article 218, paragraph 3 of the Civil Procedure Act (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 74DA1664, rendered May 13, 1975, etc.). Accordingly, if several creditors each file suit and the debtor is aware of that fact, differing outcomes will result in the effects of each judgment extending to the debtor and conflicting with one another. To prevent this, if a creditor’s subrogation action is pending, other creditors must intervene in that action, and filing a separate action is not permitted as a duplicative action (see Supreme Court Decision 87DAKA1618, rendered September 27, 1988; Supreme Court Decision 2013DA30301, 30325, rendered July 23, 2015, etc.). If several creditors jointly file an action or become co-litigants through intervention, they should be regarded as necessary joint litigants and one unified judgment must be rendered (see Supreme Court Decision 91DA23486, rendered December 27, 1991, etc.).\\n\\nBy contrast, where parties file separate actions, if differing judgments are acceptable, then even if the action is filed jointly, it cannot be regarded as necessary joint litigation. For example, where joint creditors A and B each file an action against the debtor, even if joint creditor A prevails, joint creditor B may lose upon recognition of payment. Accordingly, even if A and B file suit jointly, no need for uniform determination exists, and the case falls under ordinary joint litigation.\\n\\nb) However, in company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, even if different judgments are rendered among the parties, there is no problem of contradictory or conflicting judgments. Unlike a type of litigation in which the effect of a judgment extends universally regardless of victory or defeat, there is no conflict between the effects of a winning judgment and a losing judgment because erga omnes effect is recognized only one-sidedly for judgments in favor of the plaintiff.\\n\\nFor example, even if shareholder A files an action for declaration of invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution and receives a judgment dismissing the claim, shareholder B may file the same action and obtain a judgment granting the claim, and A’s losing judgment does not impede B’s victory. Once B prevails, the shareholders’ meeting resolution is uniformly treated as invalid against the company, shareholders, and all other interested persons pursuant to the erga omnes effect, and the same is true as to the losing A. The company cannot argue that the shareholders’ meeting resolution is valid only as against A. Thus, even if A, who received a losing judgment, is also subject to the erga omnes effect of B’s winning judgment, so that the effects of the two judgments appear to conflict as to A, such conflict is resolved pursuant to the one-sided erga omnes-effect provision, and no problem arises.\\n\\nEven where shareholders A and B jointly file suit, there is no problem of contradictory or conflicting judgments. Even if a losing judgment is rendered as to A and a winning judgment as to B, B’s winning judgment has erga omnes effect, and the shareholders’ meeting resolution thereby becomes invalid against all interested persons, including the losing A. Moreover, because this problem is the same whether the action is separate, as noted above, or joint, it cannot be said that contradictory or conflicting judgments arise only in the case of joint litigation on that account.\\n\\nNor can joint litigation be treated differently from separate actions on the ground that, in separate actions, judgments are rendered separately as to A and B, whereas in joint litigation one judgment is rendered as to A and B. A joint action by A and B is a subjective consolidation of the action between A and the company and the action between B and the company, and litigation relationships arise separately for A and for B vis-à-vis the opposing party. Even if a single judgment is formally rendered as to A and B, it is no different from separate judgments being rendered as to each litigation relationship.\\n\\nIn the case of joint litigation, it cannot be said that A’s losing judgment is meaningless merely because A receives the erga omnes effect of B’s winning judgment included in the same single judgment. The judgment against A is a valid judgment possessing formal finality and res judicata that terminates the litigation. That is precisely why the one-sided erga omnes-effect provision was established, in order to resolve the conflict between the two judgments and regulate the substantive legal relationship uniformly. The majority opinion, conversely, says that because the one-sided erga omnes-effect provision applies to company-related litigation, a winning judgment and a losing judgment cannot both be rendered in joint litigation; this misapprehends the logical sequence. Furthermore, even if A and B are disputing the defect in the same shareholders’ meeting resolution in joint litigation and it is logical to reach a consistent conclusion, the absence of recognition of a need for legal uniform determination based solely on logical consistency is as noted above in item 1).\\n\\nThus, in company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, there is no procedural-law necessity for uniform determination among co-litigants. The majority opinion, which recognizes a need for uniform determination only where the parties happen to file suit jointly despite the possibility of different judgments where separate actions are filed, lacks logical consistency.\\n\\n4) Viewing company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as necessary joint litigation would not only unduly restrict the parties’ dispositive power and procedural rights, but could also run counter to judicial economy. There is no problem in treating it as ordinary joint litigation; indeed, the procedure becomes simpler and judicial economy can be promoted.\\n\\nOf course, this can be an argument, on the level of legislative policy, for one side of the question of whether ordinary joint litigation or necessary joint litigation should be regarded as the principal form of joint litigation [corresponding to the discussion at stage ① in item b. 4)], but it is unrelated to whether a certain type of litigation falls under necessary joint litigation requiring “legal uniform determination.” It is mentioned only additionally to explain that treating such litigation as ordinary joint litigation creates no problem and may in fact simplify the litigation relationship.\\n\\na) As noted above in item b, Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act imposes various restrictions on the parties’ litigation conduct in order to unify litigation materials and the progress of litigation in necessary joint litigation and render a unified judgment. This will be examined in greater detail.\\n\\nFirst, unfavorable acts such as confession, renunciation or acknowledgment of the claim, and settlement are ineffective unless all co-litigants act together (Article 67, paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Act). If A and B file suit jointly, A may wish to obtain a prompt judgment through examination limited to the disputed issues and may confess some facts, but unless B agrees, such confession has no effect. A is also not permitted to terminate the litigation as to A alone by first renouncing A’s own claim. Meanwhile, because procedural acts by the opposing party against one co-litigant are effective against all regardless of whether they are favorable or unfavorable (paragraph 2 of Article 67), if A does not appear on the hearing date but B does appear, the hearing date may proceed, the opposing party may make new allegations and submissions of evidence at that hearing, and all such procedural acts take effect against A even though A did not participate.\\n\\nComplex issues also arise with respect to appeals. According to precedent, in necessary joint litigation, if A and B both receive losing judgments and A does not appeal because A intends to accept the judgment, then if B appeals, finality is also prevented as to A and the case is transferred to the appellate instance, so that A becomes a “mere party in the appellate instance,” neither appellant nor appellee (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA33002, rendered January 12, 1995, etc.). However, it is doubtful whether the Civil Procedure Act contemplates a third-party status in the appellate instance that is neither appellant nor appellee. If A is neither appellant nor appellee, there is no provision in the Civil Procedure Act concerning what degree of litigation authority A has in the appellate instance, whether A may file an incidental appeal, whether A must bear litigation costs, or whether A may appeal the appellate judgment to the Supreme Court. In the above example, even if A, who received a losing judgment and has no intention to appeal, seeks to withdraw the action, this is impossible without the opposing party’s consent; therefore, it cannot be said that it is acceptable to treat A as a party in the appellate instance on the ground that A may withdraw the action.\\n\\nIn this way, the parties in necessary joint litigation are restricted in dispositive power and subject to many constraints in conducting litigation. In order to deviate from the principle of ordinary joint litigation and impose such constraints on the parties’ procedural status, there must be a clear legal basis justifying it. As noted above, in company-related litigation with erga omnes effect only one-sidedly, it is difficult to view there as being substantive-law or procedural-law necessity sufficient to justify such constraints.\\n\\nb) Even if company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect is treated as ordinary joint litigation, there is no problem; rather, the procedure becomes simpler and judicial economy can be promoted.\\n\\nAssume that shareholders A and B have filed an action for declaration of invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution, and explain it on the premise that it is ordinary joint litigation. Co-litigants A and B may each conduct their own litigation and receive judgments accordingly. A and B may each freely perform unfavorable acts against themselves, such as confession, withdrawal of suit, renunciation of claim, and withdrawal of appeal, and such acts have effect only as to the respective party. As a result, if A loses the will to continue the litigation, A may withdraw from the litigation at an early stage by withdrawing the action alone or renouncing the claim with the opposing party’s consent, and only B, who still intends to conduct the litigation, remains as a party, thereby making the procedure lighter.\\n\\nIf A and B receive losing judgments in the first instance and only B appeals, the portion of the judgment against A becomes separately final and is not transferred to the appellate instance. B can conduct the litigation alone and obtain a winning judgment in the appellate instance, and A’s losing judgment does not impede B’s victory. The litigation relationship becomes much simpler without the need to rely on the unclear and unnatural legal theory of the “mere party in the appellate instance” noted above.\\n\\nEven in ordinary joint litigation, argument, examination of evidence, and judgment are conducted at the common hearing date. Under the principle of common evidence, evidence submitted separately by co-litigants may, even without invocation by the other, serve as material for fact-finding for the other co-litigants, and the judge’s conviction is also common. Accordingly, even in ordinary joint litigation, except in special circumstances such as where only one co-litigant confesses, in most cases the court renders a consistent judgment, and the possibility of an unnatural judgment reaching different conclusions depending on the party regarding the same issue is remote.\\n\\nThus, treating the case as ordinary joint litigation entails no feared adverse consequences, while respecting the parties’ dispositive power and yielding substantive advantages such as simplifying the procedure and promoting judicial economy, for example by allowing only appellants who wish to conduct litigation to become parties in the appellate instance.\\n\\n5) The provisions on exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing under the Commercial Act cannot be understood as premised on the assumption that consolidated litigation is necessary joint litigation.\\n\\nThe Commercial Act provides that company-related litigation falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the district court having jurisdiction over the company’s principal office, and that where multiple company-related actions concerning the same matter are pending, the court shall hear them in consolidated proceedings (see Articles 186 and 188 of the Commercial Act. The above provisions apply mutatis mutandis to all company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect). These provisions may be understood as being intended to have multiple courts duplicate their examination of the same content, which is undesirable from the standpoint of judicial economy, and as making it possible for a company to respond simultaneously to several lawsuits, so that the matters may be heard together in a single set of proceedings. As noted above, even in ordinary joint litigation, the same conclusion is often reached pursuant to the principles of common hearing and common evidence, and to that extent the unification of the result of adjudication may also be promoted.\\n\\nThere is no basis for construing the above exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing provisions as, beyond such purpose, provisions premised on the uniform determination of the result of adjudication. Even in company-related litigation, if judgment is first rendered in one action because of differences in the timing of filing suit, and so forth, consolidation becomes impossible because the instance differs, and in that case, in the earlier action, even if the plaintiff loses, another plaintiff in the later action may prevail, so uniform determination of the adjudicative result is not assured. Furthermore, where several actions involving overlapping issues and parties are pending, the court often consolidates them for hearing in order to reach a consistent conclusion (for example, where actions are filed separately against joint tortfeasors, or where multiple creditors separately file actions for revocation of fraudulent acts, or where a creditor separately files actions against the principal debtor and the guarantor), but such consolidation does not mean that the actions are necessary joint litigation. In this way, the provisions on exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing cannot serve as grounds for regarding company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as necessary joint litigation.\\n\\nd. The form of joint litigation is an important issue also related to the status of a party in the appellate instance, and the Supreme Court needs to clarify it so as to prevent confusion in judicial practice.\\n\\nIn this case, because the Plaintiffs jointly appointed litigation counsel and conducted the litigation from the first instance onward, there is no real difference in the outcome depending on the form of joint litigation. However, as will be seen below, the form of joint litigation is also an important issue related, before the mode of examination or the outcome of litigation, to “to whom the status of a party is recognized in the appellate instance.” Who the parties in the appellate instance are, and whether a co-litigant who has not appealed becomes a party in the appellate instance, are issues arising from the very moment the appellate procedure begins. Unless this is made clear, confusion will arise in the conduct of all procedures in the appellate instance, and doubts will also arise as to the legality of the judgment rendered through such procedure. Since the issue concerning parties pertains to procedural prerequisites, a judgment that omits a litigation party or erroneously treats a person who is not a party as a party is always unlawful. This means excluding a party who has the right to participate in the litigation from the proceedings or wrongly involving a non-party, and is not merely a matter of miswriting the parties’ names in the judgment. It is also a matter to be examined ex officio in the final appellate instance regardless of the grounds for final appeal, and its unlawfulness cannot be cured by the fact that it did not bring about a practical difference in the result of adjudication.\\n\\nIt cannot be said that prior Supreme Court decisions and judicial practice have treated company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as necessary joint litigation, as the majority opinion does. There is no Supreme Court decision that expressly states such a legal principle, and the Supreme Court Decision 4291MINHAB231, rendered February 19, 1959, under the former Civil Procedure Act before the enactment of the Civil Procedure Act of 1960, merely mentioned obiter dictum that an action for declaration of invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution filed by several persons falls under necessary joint litigation. Rather, the more recent Supreme Court Decision 2003DA69355, rendered December 9, 2004; Supreme Court Decision 2005DA54265, rendered July 13, 2006; and Supreme Court Decision 2015DA27699, rendered August 13, 2015, excluded from the parties in the appellate judgment those plaintiffs who did not appeal where only some of the co-plaintiffs in the court below’s judgment in company-related litigation filed a final appeal. Not only that, but even in administrative litigation for objection, in which a judgment revoking an administrative disposition or declaring it invalid or unlawful by omission has one-sided erga omnes effect (Article 29, paragraph 1, and Article 38 of the Administrative Litigation Act), a number of Supreme Court decisions have excluded from the parties in the final appellate instance those plaintiffs who did not appeal the court below’s judgment (Supreme Court Decision 2010DU13463, rendered August 23, 2012; Supreme Court Decision 2012DU1006, rendered March 13, 2014; Supreme Court Decision 2012DU5572, rendered August 20, 2014; Supreme Court Decision 2018DU54163, rendered November 29, 2018; Supreme Court Decision 2019DU60486, rendered March 12, 2020; Supreme Court Decision 2020DU37215, rendered July 9, 2020; Supreme Court Decision 2020DU49423, rendered December 24, 2020). Conversely, it is difficult to find a judgment recognizing plaintiffs who did not appeal as parties in the final appellate instance in such types of litigation. This clearly treats the portions relating to the non-appealing party as separately final and thus presupposes ordinary joint litigation.\\n\\nThe majority opinion merely states that company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect is necessary joint litigation, without any mention of whether this was the Supreme Court’s previous position or whether the present judgment changes the existing position. If the above judgments omitted parties in the final appellate instance even though the Supreme Court had previously regarded such litigation as necessary joint litigation, then those judgments unlawfully excluded parties in the final appellate instance who were entitled to participate in the litigation, and by analogy to Article 451, paragraph 1, item 3 of the Civil Procedure Act, there would exist grounds for retrial (see Supreme Court Decision 95JAENU91, rendered August 29, 1997, etc.). If not, and if those judgments treated the case as necessary joint litigation but excluded the plaintiffs who did not appeal from the parties, then they created a third type of litigation other than the necessary joint litigation heretofore recognized. If, as those judgments indicate, the Supreme Court has treated such litigation as ordinary joint litigation and the majority opinion changes the existing position through this judgment, the majority opinion should have made that point clear.\\n\\nSince judicial practice concerning company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect is thus unclear, it is highly necessary to clarify, through this case, what the form of the co-litigation is, so as to prevent confusion in judicial practice.\\n\\ne. Even though the current system of the Civil Procedure Act can resolve co-litigation relationships in accordance with the principles it provides and there is not a strong need to recognize exceptions, one should refrain from recognizing exceptions through unnecessary interpretive theory.\\n\\nIt cannot be denied that where the rights and obligations that are the subject matter of litigation are common or arise from a common cause, it is logical and natural for co-litigants to prevail or lose together. However, under our Civil Procedure Act, the principal form of joint litigation is ordinary joint litigation, and, as noted above, unless a “legal” necessity for uniform determination exists among co-litigants, one does not regard a case as necessary joint litigation merely because it is logically and practically desirable for them to prevail or lose together. In order to regard such litigation as necessary joint litigation, there must be a clear logical basis for recognizing an exception to the rule; but there has not been sufficient argumentation on this in the past, and even upon close examination it is difficult to find grounds for recognizing such an exception.\\n\\nWhen multiple persons are involved in one legal relationship, inherently necessary joint litigation is the case where the dispute cannot be resolved unless all parties are involved because the effect of a judgment obtained by one person does not extend to the others. Conversely, quasi-necessary joint litigation is the case where, because the effect of a judgment obtained by one person extends to the others, the result of adjudication should not differ whether several persons litigate separately or happen to litigate jointly. It is clear that company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect does not fall into either category. In such a case, unifying the result of adjudication among co-litigants can be sufficiently achieved by common examination and the resulting common judicial conviction in ordinary joint litigation, and there is no reason or necessity sufficient to apply Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act and strictly unify litigation materials and the progress of litigation.\\n\\nLegal principle must operate consistently regardless of the greater or lesser number of cases. Even if it functions without problem in most cases, it cannot be said to be a correct legal principle if it fails to function properly in a minority of cases. In company-related litigation, even if in most cases co-litigants jointly appoint litigation counsel and conduct litigation as a unit, if this is not compelled, there may always be cases in which a party seeks to conduct litigation independently. In the former case, the fact that imposing the constraints of Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act is not unreasonable to the parties does not make it a justifiable legal principle. The situation in which the legal doctrine concerning joint litigation actually makes a difference is the latter case, where the party wishes to conduct litigation independently, and even in that case, the legal doctrine concerning joint litigation must be justifiable in a consistent manner.\\n\\nIt is also not reasonable to differentiate between separate actions and joint litigation on the ground that the rendering of different judgments in separate actions is rare. Even if, where the parties each file suit, consolidation is the norm pursuant to the provisions on consolidated hearing, consolidation may be impossible because the instances differ, or, owing to oversight of the existence of another action, separate actions may become finally determined with differing contents. Even in such cases, there is no problem, and the substantive legal relationship is governed according to the erga omnes effect of the winning judgment. One cannot find a view that the judgment rendered later has a procedural-law problem and thus grounds for retrial exist, and so on. Nevertheless, the logic of the majority opinion, which on the basis of the provisions on consolidated hearing says that the result of adjudication must be uniformly determined, cannot serve as a valid ground capable of encompassing cases where consolidation is impossible or not carried out.\\n\\nf. Turning to this case.\\n\\nThe action in this case is one jointly filed by two Plaintiffs seeking a declaration of nonexistence or invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution. According to the legal principles stated above, this action constitutes ordinary joint litigation.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below appears to have conducted the proceedings on the premise that the action jointly filed by the Plaintiffs constitutes necessary joint litigation. There is error in the court below’s judgment in that it misunderstood the law concerning the form of joint litigation. However, because the Plaintiffs jointly appointed litigation counsel and conducted the litigation, that error of the court below does not appear to have affected the result of the judgment. The determination on the grounds for final appeal is the same as that of the majority opinion.\\n\\nWhile I agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion that there is no ground to reverse the court below’s judgment in this regard, the reason differs, and I therefore state this as a separate opinion.\\n\\n5. Supplementary opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyeong, Min Yu-sook, and Noh Tae-ak on the majority opinion\\n\\nIn company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, when several persons become plaintiffs jointly, judicial practice has regarded such litigation as necessary joint litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies. Supreme Court Decision 4291MINHAB231, rendered February 19, 1959, was a case under the former Civil Procedure Act before the Civil Procedure Act was enacted, and in obiter dictum it stated that an action for declaration of invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution filed by several persons constitutes necessary joint litigation. Thereafter, although the form of joint litigation was not at issue and the legal principle thereon was not expressly articulated, the courts conducted the proceedings on the premise that such litigation is necessary joint litigation. The academic mainstream is the same, not only in the field of civil procedure but also in company law. This judicial practice is based on the necessity of uniform determination in procedural law, and even considering the purpose of the Commercial Act’s provisions on consolidated hearing and the parties’ intentions or judicial economy, its validity can still be recognized. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\na. Whether a case constitutes necessary joint litigation is a matter for the court to determine by interpretation, and there is no absolute standard or normative necessity in this regard.\\n\\nArticle 67 of the Civil Procedure Act defines necessary joint litigation as “joint litigation in which the subject matter of the litigation must be determined uniformly for all co-litigants,” and provides special rules for its examination. However, since there is no provision specifically determining in what cases “the subject matter of the litigation must be determined uniformly for all co-litigants,” this must ultimately be determined by the court through interpretation. As noted also in the separate opinion, precedents and academic doctrine classify necessary joint litigation into “inherently necessary joint litigation,” where the parties cannot individually exercise rights or perform obligations under substantive law, so joint litigation is required and the result of adjudication must also be determined uniformly, and “quasi-necessary joint litigation,” where individual litigation is possible but, once joint litigation occurs, the result among the parties must be determined uniformly. This, too, has not been directly derived from Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, but has been recognized through legal interpretation.\\n\\nAmong inherently necessary joint litigation, there are cases in which it is easy to recognize the necessity for uniform determination among the parties, such as where the law expressly provides that several persons must jointly become parties (when a third party files an action for invalidity or rescission of marriage, husband and wife must be joined as co-defendants pursuant to Article 24, paragraph 2 of the Family Litigation Act), or where the dispute cannot be resolved unless the parties jointly exercise or perform rights and obligations (partition of co-owned property cannot achieve its purpose if the action is brought only between some co-owners). On the other hand, there are many cases where this is not clear, such as actions for performance concerning jointly owned property or co-owned property. There is also a view that the scope of recognition of inherently necessary joint litigation should be broadened by considering not only the attribution of the power to manage and dispose of property, which has conventionally been the criterion for recognizing inherently necessary joint litigation, but also the unified resolution of disputes and the balancing of the parties’ interests. Even among ordinary joint litigation, there are various types, ranging from cases where the rights and obligations that are the subject matter of the litigation appear to require prevailing or losing together because they are common among the parties or mutually dependent under substantive law, to cases where the relevance is weak; and there is also a view that the former should be treated as quasi-necessary joint litigation in order to seek uniform determination.\\n\\nThus, there exists a long spectrum of joint litigation, from inherently necessary joint litigation, in which the necessity of uniform determination among co-litigants is clearly recognized, to ordinary joint litigation, in which such necessity is not recognized. Quasi-necessary joint litigation, in which litigation joinder is not compelled but, once joint litigation exists, the necessity of uniform determination in procedural law arises, may be said to be located closer to necessary joint litigation in the middle of that spectrum.\\n\\nWhere it is unclear whether a type of litigation is ordinary joint litigation or necessary joint litigation, the court must determine the issue by comprehensively considering the nature of the right that is the subject matter of the litigation, the substantive and procedural rules applicable thereto, whether the litigation can be assessed as closer to necessary joint litigation or ordinary joint litigation, and the interests of the parties concerned and judicial economy. There is no absolute boundary or standard, nor is there a logical inevitability or normative necessity to regard everything that does not fall within the typical types of necessary joint litigation as ordinary joint litigation. In this respect, it is difficult to agree with the basic premise of the separate opinion that, in joint litigation for the resolution of disputes among multiple parties, ordinary joint litigation must be the rule and necessary joint litigation is an exceptional form departing from that rule. Moreover, even if ordinary joint litigation is the principal form of joint litigation, this does not mean that the necessity of uniform determination in necessary joint litigation must always be interpreted strictly and narrowly.\\n\\nUltimately, the question of in what cases necessity of uniform determination is recognized, and whether this should be construed relatively broadly or narrowly, must be entrusted to the court’s interpretation.\\n\\nb. Company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect requires uniform determination in procedural law.\\n\\n1) Company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, as in this case, constitutes quasi-necessary joint litigation requiring uniform determination in procedural law. This is because, where several persons jointly file suit, if one loses and another wins, the effect of the winning judgment extends even to the losing person, thereby causing procedural-law contradiction or conflict between the two judgments.\\n\\nFor example, if shareholders A and B jointly file an action for declaration of invalidity of a shareholders’ meeting resolution, and shareholder A loses while shareholder B prevails and the judgment becomes final, then not only the losing judgment received by A himself, but also the effect of B’s winning judgment extends to A, so that the effects of two judgments with contradictory contents both extend to A. To prevent such contradictory or conflicting judgments, it is desirable to regard the action jointly filed by A and B as quasi-necessary joint litigation requiring uniform determination in procedural law.\\n\\nThe separate opinion states that, pursuant to the erga omnes effect of B’s winning judgment, the shareholders’ meeting resolution becomes uniformly invalid against all interested persons and this is likewise true for A, so no contradiction or conflict of judgments arises. However, this merely means that the company treats the shareholders’ meeting resolution as invalid even against A, and it cannot be denied that, in procedural-law terms, contradiction or conflict arises between the two judgments. The main text of Article 190 of the Commercial Act, which provides for one-sided erga omnes effect, is only the basis on which the effect of B’s winning judgment may extend to A; it is not a procedural-law basis for interpreting that the effect of the losing judgment obtained by A disappears.\\n\\n2) Even if, as the separate opinion says, the problem of contradictory or conflicting judgments can be resolved by the one-sided erga omnes-effect provision, if the case is treated as ordinary joint litigation and it is said that co-litigants may prevail or lose differently, the losing judgment rendered together with the winning judgment becomes meaningless. In the above joint litigation by A and B, if A loses and B wins and the judgment becomes final, B’s winning judgment has effect against A as well pursuant to the one-sided erga omnes-effect provision, so A, while having lost, ultimately becomes a winner, and A’s losing judgment becomes meaningless. There is no reason for the court to render such a meaningless judgment as to A while rendering a single judgment for A and B, and it is difficult to find any necessity to do so in joint litigation.\\n\\nIf A and B each file separate actions and A loses first (even under the consolidated hearing provisions mentioned in item c below, consolidation may be impossible because of differences in the timing of filing suit, etc.), B may still prevail because erga omnes effect is not recognized for A’s losing judgment. In that case, until B’s winning judgment is rendered, A’s losing judgment has res judicata preventing the repetition of claims or allegations inconsistent with it, so it cannot be said to be useless. Moreover, the court hearing A’s action has no way of preventing contradictory or conflicting judgments by taking into account whether B later files suit. However, in joint litigation, because A and B are adjudicated together by one judgment as above, a unified judgment as to A and B can prevent meaningless judgments. Thus, one cannot treat the case of one judgment rendered through joint litigation and the case of separate judgments rendered through individual litigation in the same way.\\n\\nFor this reason as well, it is reasonable to regard company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as necessary joint litigation and thereby make the results of adjudication coincide.\\n\\nc. Even in light of the purpose of the provisions on exclusive jurisdiction and consolidated hearing under the Commercial Act, it is proper to regard company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as necessary joint litigation.\\n\\nIn the above example, shareholders A and B are not compelled to engage in joint litigation and therefore may file separate actions. In that case, even if A loses first, if B prevails in a separate action, A will be subject to both the losing judgment he received and the effect of B’s winning judgment. This is because there is no basis for compelling litigation joinder upon the parties and no recognition of erga omnes effect for the losing judgment in order to protect the rights and procedural participation of other shareholders (if only one shareholder receives a losing judgment, grave harm may ensue if, thereafter, all shareholders are unable to dispute the validity of that shareholders’ meeting resolution when the action is brought by a person colluding with the company or lacking litigation capacity). Even in that case, it cannot be denied that procedural-law contradiction or conflict arises between the effects of the two judgments extending to A.\\n\\nTo prevent such a result, the Commercial Act provides that company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the district court having jurisdiction over the company’s principal office, and that where multiple actions concerning the same matter are filed, the court must hear them in consolidated proceedings (see Articles 186 and 188 of the Commercial Act. The above provisions apply mutatis mutandis to all company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect). This is intended to consolidate all litigation filed in the same court concerning the same matter and render a unified judgment. Ultimately, because these provisions of the Commercial Act also presuppose that the result of adjudication in company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect is uniformly determined, construing such litigation as necessary joint litigation accords with the legislative purpose of the above provisions.\\n\\nThe separate opinion says that, because A and B may each file separate actions and A may lose while B may prevail, there is no logical consistency in concluding that uniform determination is needed only when A and B file suit jointly. However, even when A and B each file suit separately, the court, pursuant to the consolidated hearing provisions, is in principle to consolidate A and B’s actions and proceed as joint litigation, and cases where consolidation becomes impossible because the instances differ due to differences in the timing of filing suit, etc., are exceptional. Therefore, the separate opinion’s criticism by comparing this to cases in which A and B each receive judgments through separate proceedings is not proper.\\n\\nd. Even if company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect is viewed as necessary joint litigation and thereby results in some restriction on the parties’ procedural status, it cannot necessarily be said to unjustly infringe the parties’ procedural rights or contravene judicial economy.\\n\\n1) Company-related litigation in which one-sided erga omnes effect is recognized is litigation contesting the corporate acts of the company, such as shareholders’ meeting resolutions, mergers, exchange or transfer of shares, or issuance of new shares. Whether the shareholders file suit jointly or separately and the actions are consolidated for hearing, the shareholders who have filed actions concerning the same matter share the same interest in the subject matter of litigation, with the common purpose of depriving the shareholders’ meeting resolution, etc. of its effect. In judicial practice as well, co-litigants mostly jointly appoint litigation counsel or, through a designated representative party, conduct the litigation as a unit as if they were one person, and the same is true in this case. This is also the reason why there has been little precedent in which the question has been raised and decided as to whether such types of joint litigation fall under ordinary joint litigation or necessary joint litigation.\\n\\nIn joint litigation, the parties need to align and cooperate with one another to achieve their common purpose, and they need to guard against another co-litigant’s procedural acts having legally or factually adverse effects on themselves. If Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies, favorable acts by one party, such as appearance at a hearing or submission of allegations and evidence, are effective for all co-litigants, while unfavorable procedural acts are ineffective unless all act together. This accords with the parties’ intention of pursuing victory, and even though it somewhat restricts the parties’ independent powers concerning procedure, this cannot be regarded as unreasonable.\\n\\nIn company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect, reconciliation or settlement containing acknowledgment of the claim or granting of the claim is impossible (see Supreme Court Decision 92NU14908, rendered May 27, 1993; Supreme Court Decision 2004DA28047, rendered September 24, 2004, etc.). A party who wishes to renounce the claim or does not wish to appeal a losing judgment, that is, a party with no intention to prevail, may withdraw the action and leave the litigation (in quasi-necessary joint litigation, the consent of the other co-litigants is not required for withdrawal of the action; see Supreme Court Decision 2011DU13729, rendered March 28, 2013, etc.). Furthermore, even if, where only some of the losing plaintiffs appeal, finality of the judgment as to all plaintiffs is prevented and the case is transferred to the appellate instance (it is in fact difficult to assume that the defendant company would not appeal as to some of the plaintiffs where the plaintiffs prevailed), plaintiffs who do not appeal and have no intention of litigating in the appellate instance merely have the possibility that the first-instance judgment may be favorably changed depending on the litigation conducted by the other co-litigants, and they do not bear an obligation to conduct litigation or to bear the litigation costs in the appellate instance. They may also withdraw the action as noted above. Therefore, even if Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act is applied to company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect and the parties’ dispositive power regarding the subject matter of litigation is somewhat restricted, this cannot be regarded as unreasonable.\\n\\n2) Treating company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as necessary joint litigation does not run counter to judicial economy. If Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies, even from the standpoint of the opposing party and the court, allegations and evidence need not be separated by co-litigant, and all allegations and evidence can be uniformly examined by viewing them as either effective for all or ineffective for all, which makes the response to the action and the process of examination and determination much simpler. Even if additional time is required for service and the like in order to proceed jointly in proceedings involving many parties, the court can appropriately exercise its power to control proceedings and prevent delay in adjudication. If one co-litigant dies, company-related litigation is mostly conducted with litigation counsel, so the proceedings are not suspended (Article 238 of the Civil Procedure Act), and even if not, the court can resolve the suspended state by ordering continuance ex officio (Article 244 of the Civil Procedure Act).\\n\\n3) Ultimately, even if company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect is regarded as necessary joint litigation and the parties’ procedural status is somewhat restricted, it cannot be said to unjustly infringe the parties’ procedural rights or to run counter to judicial economy.\\n\\ne. There is no ground to recognize a need to alter the currently established judicial practice.\\n\\n1) The Civil Procedure Act, completely revised in 2002, newly introduced preliminary and selective joint litigation as a type of joint litigation not previously allowed (Article 70 of the Civil Procedure Act), and expanded the scope of permissible independent-party intervention by allowing one-sided independent-party intervention actions that had not previously been permitted (Article 79 of the Civil Procedure Act). The Supreme Court en banc Decision 2012DA46170, rendered October 23, 2019, considering the purpose of the amendments to the Civil Procedure Act, changed the prior precedent that regarded overlapping claims between a plaintiff and an intervening successor in rights succession-type successor intervention as ordinary joint litigation, and held that Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies. Such litigation did not require the parties to file suit jointly, and the effect of the judgment did not extend between co-litigants or between the principal action parties and the intervener, so it had previously been treated as ordinary joint litigation. Nevertheless, because differing outcomes of adjudication on claims that are substantively incompatible would in fact cause the parties to lose rights or incur double obligations, Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act was applied in order to resolve the dispute once and without contradiction and to protect the parties’ interests.\\n\\nAs noted above, there are also various views as to the criteria for recognizing inherently necessary joint litigation, and there are views that in cases such as litigation concerning co-owned relationships, actions for declaration of ownership against several persons, or claims against multiple joint obligors, where uniform determination among co-litigants is theoretically and logically required, such cases should be treated as quasi-necessary joint litigation and uniform determination should be sought. There is no absolute standard or normative necessity as to in which cases uniform determination of the result of adjudication should be regarded as necessary and Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applied, and it cannot be said that applying Article 67 necessarily disadvantages the co-litigants or runs counter to judicial economy. Taking these various aspects into account, judicial practice that has regarded company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as necessary joint litigation can still be recognized as valid, and there is no strong basis for changing it.\\n\\n2) The separate opinion refers to judgments in company-related litigation where, if only some of the co-plaintiffs in the court below’s judgment filed a final appeal, those who did not appeal were not described as parties to the Supreme Court judgment, and says that it is clear the Supreme Court has traditionally proceeded on the premise that such litigation is ordinary joint litigation. However, in all of those cases, the plaintiffs lost in the court below and only some plaintiffs filed final appeals, which were dismissed, so the form of joint litigation or who the parties were was never in issue, and therefore no precedent legal principle on this issue was ever declared. As noted above, it is the academic mainstream to regard company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect as quasi-necessary joint litigation, no issue concerning this has heretofore been raised, and the courts’ judicial practice has also accepted this as established legal doctrine. On the basis of those judgments, one cannot say that the Supreme Court previously adopted the opposite position or that its position was unclear. However, it should be noted that, in future judicial practice, when only some parties in quasi-necessary joint litigation appeal, care should be taken to conduct the proceedings on the understanding that the co-litigants who did not appeal are also to be treated as parties in the appellate instance.\\n\\nFor the reasons above, this supplementary opinion is stated in support of the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Justice Lee Ki-taek’s supplementary opinion to the separate opinion is as follows.\\n\\nAs a related matter, I examine the form of joint trial in cases where two or more persons jointly file a request for trial of invalidation of a patent under Article 139, paragraph 1 of the Patent Act with respect to the same patent right, and the structure of the revocation action against such a trial decision.\\n\\nSupreme Court Decision 2007HU1510, rendered May 28, 2009, held that, once a trial decision invalidating a patent becomes final, that patent is invalid even in relation to third parties, that is, on the basis of the erga omnes effect of the trial decision invalidating the patent, if two or more persons jointly request a trial for invalidation of a patent with respect to the same patent right, this constitutes quasi-necessary joint trial, and then further held that if the patent holder who lost in that trial files an action for revocation of the trial decision against only one of the joint trial petitioners, finality of the trial decision is also prevented as to the other joint trial petitioners. However, the above judgment is not proper for the following reasons and needs to be changed in future problematic cases.\\n\\na. No legal necessity for uniform determination is recognized among joint trial petitioners.\\n\\nWhere several persons each separately request a trial for invalidation with respect to the same patent right, the result of the trial may differ depending on the allegations and proof of each trial requester. For example, if A and B each separately request a trial for invalidation with respect to the same patent right, A may receive a trial decision dismissing the request, while B may receive a trial decision invalidating the patent. In such a case, because erga omnes effect is recognized for B’s invalidation decision and the patent becomes invalid against all persons including A (Article 133, paragraph 3 of the Patent Act), no problem arises from contradiction or conflict between the invalidation decision and the dismissal decision. Even if, in one case, the dismissal decision becomes final first, the other pending trial case filed earlier is not barred by violation of Article 163 of the Patent Act in relation to the final dismissal decision, and thus there is no obstacle to issuing a trial decision invalidating the patent (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2009HU2234, rendered January 19, 2012). However, if the invalidation decision becomes final first, the patent right is retroactively invalidated, and the other pending trial request by another person is dismissed as improper due to the extinction of the subject matter of trial.\\n\\nEven where A and B do not each separately request invalidation but jointly request invalidation (Article 139, paragraph 1 of the Patent Act), or where their separately filed invalidation requests are consolidated (Article 160 of the Patent Act), the same applies and no necessity is recognized for the trial decision to be uniformly determined between A and B.\\n\\nb. Since patent trials are governed by the principle of ex officio examination, there is no issue of whether Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, premised on the adversarial principle, applies.\\n\\nAs mentioned in the separate opinion, in civil litigation where the adversarial principle is the rule, each party conducts litigation on his or her own responsibility, without help or interference from the other co-litigants, and bears responsibility only for his or her own procedural acts.
