Under this adversarial principle, judgments among co-litigants may differ, so Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, in necessary joint litigation, partially modifies the adversarial principle and the principle of dispositive power so that litigation materials (allegations and evidence) are unified among co-litigants and the result of adjudication can be uniformly determined.\\n\\nHowever, patent trials are governed not by the adversarial principle but by the principle of ex officio examination. In patent trials, examination may be conducted on grounds not requested by the parties (Article 159, paragraph 1 of the Patent Act), and evidence may be examined ex officio (Article 157, paragraph 1 of the Patent Act).\\n\\nBecause quasi-necessary joint litigation to which Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act applies is also basically a procedure governed by the adversarial principle, the court cannot base its determination on facts neither alleged nor proved by any co-litigant. However, in patent trials, the trial examiner is not bound by the parties’ allegations and proof and may examine and determine facts not alleged by any party. Accordingly, no separate measure for unifying litigation materials among joint trial petitioners is naturally necessary.\\n\\nIn this way, there is no reason to import into patent trial proceedings, to which the principle of ex officio examination applies, the concept of necessary joint litigation premised on the adversarial principle. The above Supreme Court decision overlooked the fundamental differences between civil litigation and patent trial proceedings, between the adversarial principle and the principle of ex officio examination, and the procedural-law status of Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, namely that the provision applies to adversarial procedures.\\n\\nc. Since patent trials and patent trial decision revocation actions are separate procedures without an appellate-instance relationship, the legal principle regarding appeal in necessary joint litigation cannot be applied as it stands.\\n\\nThe above Supreme Court decision, after viewing a joint patent invalidation trial requested by two or more persons as quasi-necessary joint trial, drew the conclusion on that basis that if the patent holder files an action to revoke the patent invalidation trial decision against only one of the joint trial petitioners, the trial decision is also not finalized as to the remaining joint trial petitioners. As already noted in the separate opinion, prior precedent held that in necessary joint litigation, if an appeal is filed only against some co-litigants, the judgment as to the remaining non-appealing co-litigants is also prevented from becoming final and is transferred to the appellate instance, and even the non-appealing co-litigants become parties in the appellate instance. The above Supreme Court decision appears to have applied this legal principle concerning appeals in necessary joint litigation to patent trials and trial decision revocation actions.\\n\\nHowever, the above legal principle concerning appeals in necessary joint litigation is premised on the existence of an appellate-instance relationship within a single litigation, such as between the first instance and the appellate instance, or between the appellate instance and the final appellate instance, and is intended, where an appeal is filed only against some co-litigants, to ensure that all co-litigants retain party status until the end so that the result of adjudication is unified as to all co-litigants. There is no basis for concluding that such a legal principle applies even across separate procedures, such as where an administrative action is filed after administrative adjudication or where a revocation action is filed against an administrative disposition. Patent trials are administrative trial proceedings, and a patent trial decision revocation action is an administrative lawsuit against them; they are separate procedures with different decision-makers and applicable procedural laws, there is no appellate-instance relationship between them, and a person who was not made a defendant in the revocation action cannot become a party to that action. For example, if A and B jointly request invalidation against C and receive a trial decision invalidating the patent, and C files a revocation action against only A as defendant, B cannot become a party to the revocation action. There was no revocation action filed against B, and B is not a party to the revocation action, so there is no basis for viewing the finality of the trial decision as to B as being prevented.\\n\\nIn necessary joint litigation, even if C appeals only against A among victorious A and B, the effect of that appeal extends to B, preventing finality as to B and transferring the case to the appellate instance, so that B also becomes a party to the appellate instance. If the above Supreme Court decision had viewed there as being an appellate-instance relationship between patent trial proceedings and trial decision revocation actions and had applied the above legal principle as it stands, then if C filed a revocation action against only A, it would have been correct to view the effect of filing suit as extending to B as well, so that B also became a party to the revocation action. The above Supreme Court decision, from any perspective, misapplied the legal principle regarding appeals in necessary joint litigation.\\n\\nd. According to the above Supreme Court decision, the procedural rights of joint trial petitioners are unjustly infringed.\\n\\nAccording to the above Supreme Court decision, if A and B jointly request invalidation and receive a patent invalidation decision, then even if the patent holder files suit against only one of A and B, finality of the trial decision as to the other is also prevented. As a result, the patent holder may file suit only against A, whose litigation capacity is weaker among A and B, and easily obtain a winning judgment while excluding B from the litigation procedure. B will think that the patent invalidation decision against B has become final because the period for filing suit against the trial decision has elapsed, but will in fact face the result that B’s own trial decision is also revoked according to the outcome of A’s revocation action, conducted without B’s participation. This not only infringes B’s procedural rights but is also unreasonable because it gives the patent holder the opportunity to arbitrarily choose the litigation opponent by virtue of the accidental fact that A and B’s invalidation request was filed as a joint trial.\\n\\nIf A and B each separately request invalidation with respect to the same patent right and receive a patent invalidation decision, the patent holder must of course file an action to revoke the trial decision against both A and B. If the patent holder files suit only against A, the trial decision as to B becomes final upon expiration of the period for filing suit, and pursuant to the erga omnes effect of the invalidation decision, the patent becomes invalid against all, while the suit against A lacks legal interest and should be dismissed as improper. It cannot be said that this is especially disadvantageous or unreasonable for the patent holder.\\n\\ne. The above discussion is not a matter directly related to the majority opinion or the separate opinion concerning company-related litigation with one-sided erga omnes effect. It is merely that the legal principle in the above Supreme Court decision also stems from misunderstanding the form of joint trial and Article 67 of the Civil Procedure Act, and I take this opportunity to point it out as well.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state this supplementary opinion to the separate opinion."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning an action seeking the removal of a representative director and a director of a stock company, and a provisional disposition for suspension of duties and appointment of an acting person, is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: Where an action for the removal of a director has been filed, the court may, upon a party's application, suspend that director's performance of duties by provisional disposition and may appoint an acting person. However, where there are urgent circumstances, such disposition may be made even before the filing of the action on the merits.
B: Where a company seeks to adopt at a regular general meeting of shareholders a resolution concerning the transfer of all or a material part of its business, the person appointed as the acting representative director requires the court's permission in order to lawfully convene the regular general meeting of shareholders.
C: Where, due to a shortfall in the number of directors prescribed by law or the articles of incorporation, it is impossible or inappropriate to allow a retired director who is exercising the rights and duties of a director to have the rights and duties of a director, an application for provisional disposition seeking suspension of the performance of duties against the retired director is permitted.
D: A contract concluded by a representative director whose authority to represent the company has been suspended by a court's provisional disposition order suspending performance of duties during the period of that suspension is absolutely void, and even if, thereafter, the preservative execution is cancelled by the withdrawal of the provisional disposition application, the void contract does not become valid.
E: If each provisional disposition order suspending performance of duties and appointing an acting person with respect to A, the representative director of a stock company, and B, a director, has been issued, then even if, before the issuance of those orders, the registration of A's retirement from office as representative director and the registration of B's assumption of office as representative director have been completed, B, regardless of whether the resolution appointing B as representative director was lawful, does not have authority as representative director after the effective date of the above provisional disposition order.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DA62362]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Regarding the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\nAccording to Article 407(1) of the Commercial Act, where an action is brought for the invalidity or revocation of a resolution for the election of directors, or for the removal of directors, the court may, upon a party’s application, suspend the performance of duties of the directors by a provisional disposition and appoint a person to perform such duties in their place; and in such case, according to Article 408(1) of the Commercial Act, the person performing duties in place of the directors may not engage in acts not falling within the ordinary course of business of the company, except where otherwise provided in the provisional disposition order, but this shall not apply where the court’s permission has been obtained. Here, the ordinary course of business of the company generally means affairs that should ordinarily be conducted in the company, affairs that are ordinarily performed within the scope of business in continuing the company’s operations, or ordinary tasks that do not have an important influence on the management of the company; and whether a particular act specifically falls within such ordinary course of business should be determined objectively in light of the company’s organization, the type and nature of its business, and other relevant circumstances. According to such legal principles, even when the person performing duties in place of the directors convenes a regular general meeting of shareholders, if the agenda includes matters that may affect the management and control of the company, such as acts that alter the composition of the board of directors itself or acts corresponding to matters requiring a special resolution under Article 374 of the Commercial Act, the convening of the regular general meeting shall be deemed not to fall within the ordinary course of business within the scope of such agenda items; and if the person performing duties in place of the directors convenes and adopts resolutions at a regular general meeting of shareholders without the court’s permission even though the convening of such regular general meeting does not fall within the ordinary course of business, such resolution shall be deemed to have been made at a shareholders’ meeting with a defect in the convening procedure and thus subject to revocation.\\n\\nThe court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence admitted in its judgment and recognizing the facts as stated in its reasoning, held that, in principle, the convening of a regular general meeting of shareholders itself should be regarded as falling within the ordinary duties of the acting representative director; however, in a situation where a dispute was pending concerning the validity of the resolution of the First General Meeting of Shareholders in this case as found by the court below, convening a general meeting of shareholders with agenda items including a proposal approving the dismissal of the former representative director and directors and ratifying the resolution of the First General Meeting of Shareholders, a proposal approving the appointment of the representative director and directors, a proposal ratifying the sale of the golf practice range, which is important property forming the basis of the Defendant’s continuance, a proposal appointing new directors, and a proposal approving the comprehensive investment of surplus funds, including the sale proceeds from the sale of the golf practice range, which is important property forming the basis of the Defendant’s continuance, could not be regarded as an act within the ordinary course of business of the company. However, since there was no evidence at all to support a finding that the Defendant’s acting representative director had obtained court permission in convening a regular general meeting of shareholders with agenda items including matters not falling within the ordinary course of business, the court below determined that, among the resolution of the Second General Meeting of Shareholders in this case as found by the court below, the resolutions on Agenda Items Nos. 2 through 6, except for Agenda Item No. 1 of the resolution listed in Attached List No. 2 of the court below’s judgment, which appears to be an act within the ordinary course of business, were resolutions made at a shareholders’ meeting with a defect in the convening procedure and thus had grounds for revocation, and further rejected the Defendant’s argument to the effect that revoking a shareholders’ meeting resolution for such reason would have the result of controlling not only the authority of the representative director but also the authority of the shareholders’ meeting, thereby violating the principle of disposition. Such measures are proper in light of the above legal principles and the record, and there is no illegality in the Defendant’s grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAlso, as examined above, insofar as the resolutions on Agenda Items Nos. 2 through 4 among the resolution of the Second General Meeting of Shareholders in this case are revoked, the grounds of appeal to the effect that, on the premise that the resolutions on the above Agenda Items Nos. 2 through 4 were valid, the resolution of the First General Meeting of Shareholders in this case was lawfully ratified is without merit without need for further consideration.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal\\na. Whether the articles of incorporation concerning the quorum for the shareholders’ meeting were amended\\nThe original articles of incorporation of a stock company become effective upon certification by a notary public, but when the duly executed articles of incorporation are amended, the amendment becomes effective at the time the articles of incorporation are validly amended by a special resolution of the shareholders’ meeting, and whether the written articles of incorporation are corrected or amended, or whether they are registered when the amendment concerns a matter to be registered, or whether they are certified by a notary public, has no bearing on the effectiveness of the amendment to the articles of incorporation (see Supreme Court Decision 78NU167, Dec. 26, 1978).\\n\\nThe court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence relied upon in its judgment, found that the articles of incorporation at the time of the Defendant’s incorporation provided in Article 19 that resolutions of the shareholders’ meeting shall be adopted by a majority of the voting rights of the shareholders present and by a number representing at least two-thirds of the total issued shares, except where otherwise provided by statute or the articles of incorporation, but that since around December 8, 2000, this had been changed to a majority of the voting rights of the shareholders present and by a number representing at least one-half of the total issued shares, and such finding is proper, with no illegality in violation of the rules on the assessment of evidence.\\n\\nb. Regarding the person who entrusted title to the Defendant shares in the name of Nonparty 2\\nThe court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence relied upon in its judgment, recognized that Nonparty 1, around December 30, 2004, filed with the Defendant an application for change of shareholder name, asserting that the shares in the name of Nonparty 2 were his own property, and that accordingly the shareholder name was changed from Nonparty 2 to Nonparty 1; and then, by holding that Exhibit A No. 7 alone was insufficient to find that 16,000 shares issued by the Defendant in the name of Nonparty 2 belonged to the Plaintiff, and that there was no other evidence to support such finding, dismissed this part of the Plaintiff’s claim. Such disposition is acceptable, and there is no illegality in violation of the rules on the assessment of evidence or in misunderstanding of legal principles.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by each losing party, and the Court renders judgment as stated in the dispositive part by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2008DA4537]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined (the statements in reference materials submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds for final appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\n1. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence cited in its ruling, rejected the Plaintiff’s assertion regarding the conclusion of the contract on the ground that the contract dated 2003. 6. 5. concerning the demolition contract at issue (Plaintiff’s Exhibit No. 1) was prepared in around 2004. 4. by backdating it to a date prior to the provisional disposition order suspending performance of duties, after Nonparty 3, the representative director who, having received a provisional disposition order suspending performance of duties from the Daejeon District Court on 2003. 9. 15., lacked authority to lawfully represent the Defendant, requested Nonparty 4, who was then the acting representative director, to conclude the above demolition contract and was refused, and that there was no other evidence to recognize the fact that the demolition contract at issue had been lawfully concluded; then the court below determined that, because Nonparty 5, who represented the Plaintiff at the time of preparation of the above contract, knew that Nonparty 3, who was the representative director of the Defendant, had been suspended from performing his duties and thus had no authority to represent the Defendant, Nonparty 3 could not be regarded as an apparent representative, and further, because there was no evidence that Nonparty 3 concluded the above demolition contract with the Plaintiff pursuant to the direction of Nonparty 6, the de facto operator of the Defendant company, it could not be said that the Defendant’s denial of the conclusion of the demolition contract at issue contravened the principle of good faith and fair dealing or the principle of estoppel; in light of the record, although there are some inaccuracies in the expressions used by the court below in its explanation, its determination is correct, and no incomplete examination in the process of fact-finding or application of legal principles, no violation of the rules of evidence or precedents, no misunderstanding of legal principles, or other error alleged in the grounds for final appeal can be found.\\n\\n2. A contract concluded during the period of suspension by a representative director whose authority to represent the company has been suspended by a court’s provisional disposition order suspending performance of duties is absolutely void, and even if the preservation enforcement is later canceled by withdrawal of the application for a provisional disposition, the effect of the enforcement terminates only prospectively and does not terminate retroactively; therefore, the withdrawal of the application for a provisional disposition does not render a void contract valid. The judgment of the court below is in accordance with these legal principles and contains no error pointed out in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the final appeal is dismissed, the costs of final appeal are to be borne by the losing party, and because there is a clear clerical error in the judgment of the court below, it is corrected; accordingly, the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, as set forth in the operative part."}

{"[2009MA1311]": "We examine the grounds for re-appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the grounds for re-appeal by Debtor 1\\n\\nArticle 386(1) of the Commercial Act provides that, where the number of directors prescribed by law or the articles of incorporation is lacking, a director who has resigned upon expiration of his term of office or by resignation shall perform the rights and obligations of a director until a newly appointed director takes office; thus, in cases where it is necessary, such as where it is impossible or improper to cause a retiring director, who is exercising the rights and obligations of a director pursuant to the above provision, to have the rights and obligations of a director, a petition may be filed with the court for the appointment of a person to perform the duties of a temporary director as provided in Article 386(2) of the Commercial Act (see, e.g., Supreme Court Order dated November 17, 2000, 2000MA5632). Accordingly, it must be deemed impermissible to separately file an application for an injunction seeking suspension of the performance of duties on the ground that cause for dismissal exists or that the term of office has expired or that there has been a resignation, against a retiring director who is performing the rights and obligations of a director pursuant to Article 386(1) of the Commercial Act.\\n\\nAccording to the record, since the total capital of the company in this case is less than 500 million won, the number of directors may be one or two (the proviso of Article 383(1) of the Commercial Act), and because its articles of incorporation provide for a system of joint representative directors, the minimum number of directors required for the company in this case is two; Debtor 1, who is a joint representative director and director of the company in this case, had his term of office expire on July 31, 2007, but as the terms of office of the other directors all expired on the same day, the minimum number of directors prescribed by the articles of incorporation (two) was not satisfied, and thus he has continued until now to exercise the rights and obligations as a joint representative director and director of the company in this case.\\n\\nThe lower court, while stating that an injunction suspending the performance of duties, with the right to claim dismissal under Article 385(2) of the Commercial Act as the preserved right, could not be granted with respect to Debtor 1, whose term of office as a director had already expired, premised that an injunction suspending the performance of duties, with the right to claim a declaration of non-existence of the status or authority of a director as the preserved right, could be granted, and then, on the grounds as stated in its opinion, issued an injunction ordering the suspension of the performance of duties as representative director and director against Debtor 1 and appointing a person to act on his behalf in the performance of those duties.\\n\\nHowever, in light of the legal principles stated above, Debtor 1, at the time his term of office expired, falls under a retiring director who, as the number of directors required was lacking, continues after the expiration of his term of office to exercise the rights and obligations as joint representative director and director pursuant to Article 386(1) of the Commercial Act. In such a case, while it is a separate matter that, where necessary in order to exclude such retiring director from office, a petition may be filed with the court for the appointment of a person to perform the duties of a temporary director as provided in Article 386(2) of the Commercial Act, an application for an injunction seeking suspension of the performance of such duties may not be allowed separately.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court’s action in granting the injunction suspending the performance of duties and appointing a person to act on behalf of Debtor 1 contains an error of law, such as misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the procedure for appointing a temporary director or an injunction suspending the performance of duties, that affected the judgment.\\n\\n2. Regarding the grounds for re-appeal by Debtor 2\\n\\nSince, under Article 386(1) of the Commercial Act, a retiring director may perform the rights and obligations of a director only in cases where the number of directors prescribed by law or the articles of incorporation is lacking, if, at the time of retirement, the number of directors prescribed by law or the articles of incorporation is satisfied, the retiring director loses the rights and obligations of a director ipso jure upon the expiration of the term of office or resignation, and if, notwithstanding this, such director is in fact still exercising the rights and obligations of a director, an application for an injunction seeking suspension of the performance of duties, with the right to claim a declaration of non-existence of such rights and obligations as the preserved right, should be deemed allowable.\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the lower court’s decision, the lower court found that the minimum number of directors required for the company in this case is two, and that, at the time Debtor 2’s term of office as a director expired on July 18, 2005, four directors, including Creditor 2, Non-Party 2, Debtor 1, and Non-Party 3, were in office at the company in this case; thus, even though Debtor 2 had no need to perform duties as a retiring director, he had continued to be involved in the operation of the board of directors and the execution of business of the company in this case. On that basis, the lower court held that the necessity for preservation to seek suspension of the performance of duties by the above Debtor, with the right to claim a declaration of non-existence of the status or authority as the preserved right, was sufficiently shown, and granted the injunction in this case against the above Debtor.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above and the record, the lower court’s action as above is proper, and there is no error that affected the judgment in violation of the Constitution, laws, orders, or rules.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, among the lower court’s decision, the part ordering suspension of the performance of duties and the appointment of a person to act on behalf of Debtor 1 is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination; the re-appeal by Debtor 2 is dismissed, and the litigation costs shall be borne by the losing party. It is so decided, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2013DA39551]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Regarding the grounds for appeal by Defendants 2 and 3\\n\\nAccording to the record, the court below served copies of the notice of appeal and the summons for the oral argument date upon Defendants 2 and 3 by means of service by publication, proceeded with the oral arguments, rendered judgment on 2013. 4. 23., and also served an authenticated copy of that judgment by means of service by publication; and it can be found that the above Defendants submitted the petition of appeal in this case to the court of first instance on 2013. 5. 9., before the period for filing a final appeal against the judgment of the court below had expired after the judgment of the court below had been served by publication.\\n\\nThose Defendants had been served, from the stage of the copy of the notice of appeal, by means of service by publication, and without any attributable fault were not even aware that an appeal had been filed in this case; and in such a state, the oral arguments in the court below proceeded without the appearance of those Defendants, so it should be deemed that those Defendants, as parties, had their procedurally granted rights infringed; and in such a case, since it should be regarded in the same manner as where a party was not lawfully represented by an agent, the provisions of Article 424(1)4 of the Civil Procedure Act may be analogically applied (see Supreme Court Decision 95DA21365 rendered on 1997. 5. 30., Supreme Court Decision 2009DA1665 rendered on 2009. 5. 14.), and in this respect the judgment of the court below has become unlawful and can no longer be sustained. The grounds for appeal by the above Defendants pointing out this point are well founded.\\n\\n2. Regarding the grounds for appeal by Defendant Prime C&D Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the \"Defendant Company\")\\n\\n(a) A provisional disposition suspending the performance of duties of a director of a stock company and appointing a person to act in office has effect, by its nature, not only between the parties but also in relation to third parties; therefore, an act done in contravention of the provisional disposition is void even in relation to third parties, and the authority of a director acting in office appointed by the provisional disposition remains valid until a court’s order of cancellation is rendered (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 91DA4355 rendered on 1991. 12. 24.). In addition, a provisional disposition suspending the performance of duties and appointing a person to act in office, which is a matter subject to registration, cannot, if not registered pursuant to Article 37(1) of the Commercial Act, be asserted against a bona fide third party by virtue of the above provisional disposition, but can be asserted against a mala fide third party; and a court’s provisional disposition order suspending the performance of duties of the representative director and directors of a stock company and appointing a person to act in office for such duties remains effective with respect to the directors whose performance of duties has been suspended, even if the registration of retirement of the representative director of the stock company whose performance of duties had been suspended prior to the above order and the registration of assumption of office as representative director by a director whose performance of duties had been suspended were completed before the above order, so the authority of the representative director and director acting in office appointed by the above provisional disposition order remains valid; on the other hand, even if a director whose performance of duties had been suspended prior to the provisional disposition order was appointed as representative director, he or she cannot have the authority as representative director, irrespective of whether the resolution appointing him or her was lawful.\\n\\n(b) According to the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n1) The court below served a copy of the notice of appeal and the notice of the first oral argument date at 4th floor, (address 1 omitted), Suyeong-gu, Busan, which is the address of the Defendant Company, and they were received by an employee of the Defendant Company, but the representative director of the Defendant Company failed to appear at the first oral argument date; thereafter, the court served the notices of the second through fifth oral argument dates and the statement of reasons for appeal at the above address of the Defendant Company, but when service became impossible due to unknown addressee, it carried out service by dispatch through registered mail, and the representative director of the Defendant Company failed to appear at each of the above oral argument dates. Plaintiff's counsel, after the court below’s order dated 2013. 1. 29. to reopen oral arguments, corrected the representative director of the Defendant Company to Non-Party 1 on 2013. 2. 25., and amended the address of the Defendant Company to 1st floor, Busan (address 2 omitted).\\n\\n2) Thereafter, the court below again served the copy of the notice of appeal, the notice of the sixth oral argument date, and the like at the corrected address of the Defendant Company, but when service became impossible due to unknown recipient, it carried out service by dispatch through registered mail of the notice of the sixth oral argument date to the corrected address of the Defendant Company; thereafter, it served at Non-Party 1’s personal address all of the copy of the notice of appeal, the application for correction of party designation, the statement of reasons for appeal, and the notice of the sixth oral argument date, and Non-Party 1 personally received them. Thereafter as well, Non-Party 1 separately received the notice of the seventh oral argument date, the application for examination of the party himself/herself, and the application for witness examination, each of which was served at his or her personal address. However, Non-Party 1 failed to appear at the sixth and seventh oral argument dates, and received an authenticated copy of the judgment of the court below.\\n\\n3) Meanwhile, Non-Party 2 assumed office as an internal director and representative director of the Defendant Company on 2011. 6. 20., and Defendant 2 assumed office as an internal director of the Defendant Company on 2012. 5. 4.; then Non-Party 1 prepared the minutes of the shareholders’ meeting stating that “a shareholders’ meeting was held at 11:00 on 2012. 6. 28., and a resolution was adopted to dismiss Non-Party 2 and Defendant 2 from the internal directors of the Defendant Company and to appoint the Plaintiff, Non-Parties 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 as internal directors of the Defendant Company,” and thereafter, based thereon, on 2012. 6. 28., completed the registration of changes in officers stating that “Non-Party 2 is dismissed from the office of internal director and representative director of the Defendant Company, Defendant 2 is dismissed from the office of internal director of the Defendant Company, Non-Party 5 is appointed as internal director and representative director of the Defendant Company, and the Plaintiff and Non-Parties 1, 3, 4, 6, and 7 are appointed as internal directors of the Defendant Company.”\\n\\n4) Thereafter, Non-Parties 2 and Defendant 2 and 3 filed with the Busan District Court Eastern Branch, Case No. 2012KAHAP343, an application for provisional disposition suspending the performance of duties and appointing a person to act in office against the Plaintiff and Non-Parties 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 (hereinafter referred to as the “provisional disposition application in this case”), and on 2012. 11. 19., received from the above court a grant order of provisional disposition (hereinafter referred to as the “provisional disposition order in this case”) stating that “until the final judgment on the merits in the case for confirmation of the non-existence of resolutions of the shareholders’ meeting concerning the Defendant Company by Non-Parties 2, Defendant 2, and 3 becomes final and conclusive, Non-Party 5 shall not perform the duties of representative director and director of the Defendant Company, and the Plaintiff and Non-Parties 1, 3, 4, 6, and 7 shall not perform the duties of director of the Defendant Company, respectively; during the period of suspension of duties, Non-Party 2 is appointed as the person acting in office for the duties of representative director and director of the Defendant Company.” However, after the provisional disposition application in this case and before the provisional disposition order in this case, on 2012. 11. 8., the registration of resignation of internal directors Non-Parties 5 and 6 and the registration of assumption of office by Non-Party 1 as representative director were completed, and for this reason the contents of the provisional disposition order in this case and the status of registration became inconsistent, making registration pursuant to the provisional disposition order in this case impossible.\\n\\n(c) Examining these factual relations in light of the legal principles seen above, although registration concerning the provisional disposition order in this case was not completed, the provisional disposition order in this case naturally has effect against the Plaintiff, who was a party thereto, and the person who had lawful authority to represent the Defendant Company from 2012. 11. 19. by virtue of the provisional disposition order in this case is Non-Party 2, who was appointed as the person acting in office for the duties of representative director and director. Nevertheless, the Plaintiff, who can be deemed to have known such circumstances, on 2013. 2. 25. filed an unlawful application to correct the party designation to the effect of correcting the representative director of the Defendant Company to Non-Party 1, thereby causing the litigation documents to be served on Non-Party 1, who was not the lawful representative of the Defendant Company; as a result, Non-Party 2, the representative of the Defendant Company, was deprived, without any attributable fault, of the opportunity to appear at the sixth and seventh oral argument dates of the court below and present means of attack and defense, and as the oral arguments were concluded, the Defendant Company, as a party, had its procedurally granted rights infringed. Even in such a case, since it should be regarded in the same manner as where a party was not lawfully represented by an agent, the provisions of Article 424(1)4 of the Civil Procedure Act may be analogically applied, and in this respect the judgment of the court below has become unlawful and can no longer be sustained. The grounds for appeal by the Defendant Company pointing out this point are also well founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds for appeal of the Defendants, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for a further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning extinctive prescription is incorrect? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents)
A: A claim for restitution to the original state arising from rescission of a contract constituting a commercial transaction is subject to the commercial extinctive prescription under Article 64 of the Commercial Act.
B: A right held by one spouse against the other does not complete extinctive prescription within 6 months from the termination of the marital relationship.
C: Where an insurance policyholder enters into an insurance contract for the purpose of fraudulently obtaining insurance proceeds through multiple contracts, and such contract is void as contrary to good morals and other social order under Article 103 of the Civil Act, a 5-year commercial extinctive prescription period applies by analogical application of Article 64 of the Commercial Act to the insurer’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment regarding the insurance proceeds.
D: The extinctive prescription of an endorser’s claims on a bill of exchange and on a promissory note against another endorser and the issuer is interrupted, where that person is sued, by giving notice of the litigation to the former.
E: Where a real estate sale contract concluded between A Co., Ltd. and B medical corporation is void because of the absence of a board resolution concerning the appointment of the representative who concluded the sale contract on behalf of B corporation, the seller, a 5-year commercial extinctive prescription period applies by analogical application of Article 64 of the Commercial Act to A company, the buyer’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment seeking return from B corporation of the amount corresponding to the purchase price already paid.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2019DA277812]": "We decide on the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Determination of the Defendants’ grounds of appeal\\n\\nThe court below, citing the first-instance judgment, held that the insurance contract in this case is void as being in violation of Civil Act Article 103. As the reason therefor, it found that Defendant 1 entered into the insurance contract in this case, as well as numerous other insurance contracts, not so much to prepare for contingent risks to life, body, etc. in a purely manner, but rather with the purpose of fraudulently obtaining insurance proceeds.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the court below’s judgment in light of the relevant legal principles, there is no error in the court below’s determination in that it did not, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, deviate from the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by contravening the rules of logic and experience, nor did it misunderstand the legal principles regarding the invalidity of an insurance contract, etc.\\n\\n2. Determination of the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. The Plaintiff is claiming against the Defendants the return of insurance proceeds already paid on the ground that the insurance contract is void, and the Defendants, in response, are asserting the defense that the statute of limitations has expired. The issue in this case is whether the statute of limitations period for the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment regarding the insurance proceeds should be set at 10 years pursuant to the provisions of the Civil Act, or at 5 years by analogically applying the provisions of the Commercial Act concerning the commercial statute of limitations period.\\n\\nB. Supplementing a legal gap by applying to a matter for which there is no legal regulation the legal norms applicable to a similar matter is called analogical application. This is intended, in cases where the literal interpretation or logical interpretation of statutory provisions alone cannot resolve an actual legal dispute or where a result that is markedly contrary to the sense of social justice would ensue, to enable the court to reasonably resolve the legal dispute and derive a result consistent with the sense of justice by giving effect to the legislative spirit of the positive law. For such analogy, not only must there be commonalities or similarities between the matter without legal regulation and the matter with legal regulation, but the analogical application must also be deemed justified in light of the system of legal norms, legislative intent and purpose, etc. (see Supreme Court Decision 2019DA226135, rendered on 2020. 4. 29.).\\n\\nWhether it is a claim arising from a contract or a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment arising from the invalidity of a contract, the statute of limitations period for a claim is, in principle, 10 years (Civil Act Article 162(1)). However, the Commercial Act sets the statute of limitations period for claims arising from contracts that are commercial acts at 5 years (Commercial Act Article 64). The reason for setting a shorter commercial statute of limitations period is that, in light of the distinctive nature of commercial transactions—namely, mass, standardized, and prompt—the need exists to resolve commercial contractual relationships more standardizedly and promptly than civil contractual relationships (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DA22742, rendered on 2005. 11. 10.). However, while the Commercial Act sets the statute of limitations period for claims arising from contracts that are commercial acts differently from the Civil Act as stated above, it separately does not provide for the statute of limitations period for a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment arising from the invalidity of a contract that is a commercial act.\\n\\nCase law recognizes the following principles and exceptions on the premise that Commercial Act Article 64 may apply or be analogically applied not only to claims directly arising from commercial acts, but also to claims comparable thereto. A claim for restitution of unjust enrichment arising from the invalidity of a contract that is a commercial act is a claim arising under the unjust enrichment provisions of Civil Act Article 741, and, absent special circumstances, the 10-year civil statute of limitations period prescribed by Civil Act Article 162(1) applies. However, where the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment seeks the return of the performance itself made on the basis of a contract that is a commercial act, and there is a need to resolve the legal relationship as promptly as commercial transactions in light of the circumstances in which the claim arose, the cause for its occurrence, the positions and relationships of the parties, etc., the 5-year commercial statute of limitations period prescribed by Commercial Act Article 64 applies or is analogically applied (see Supreme Court Decisions 2002DA64957, 64964, rendered on 2003. 4. 8., and 2017DA248803, 248810, rendered on 2018. 6. 15.).\\n\\nC. Where an insurance policyholder enters into an insurance contract for the purpose of fraudulently obtaining insurance proceeds through multiple contracts, and such contract is void pursuant to Civil Act Article 103 as contrary to good morals and other social order, it is appropriate to hold that the insurer’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment regarding the insurance proceeds is subject to the 5-year commercial statute of limitations period by analogically applying Commercial Act Article 64. The detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Where an insurance contract is void as contrary to good morals and other social order, what the insurer seeks to recover is the insurance proceeds paid in discharge of the obligations under the insurance contract, which is a basic commercial act (Commercial Act Article 46, item 17). Such claim for return is closely related to the performance of the insurance contract and corresponds to the claim for performance thereof.\\n\\n(2) A case where an insurance policyholder enters into an insurance contract for the purpose of fraudulently obtaining insurance proceeds through multiple contracts is one of the typical grounds for invalidity that is not infrequently encountered in the process of an insurer concluding an insurance contract as a commercial act. In such a case, because multiple insurance contracts are involved by the nature of the matter, multiple insurers each come to have a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment, or one insurer comes to have multiple claims for restitution of unjust enrichment; since such legal relationships substantially arise from the same cause, they need to be handled standardizedly and promptly.\\n\\n(3) In an insurance contract, the policyholder’s obligation to pay premiums and the insurer’s obligation to pay insurance proceeds are in a reciprocal relationship, and there are considerable restrictions on the policyholder’s claim for return of premiums already paid. First, with respect to the “claim for return of premiums due to invalidity of an insurance contract,” Commercial Act Article 648 provides that “where all or part of an insurance contract is void, if the policyholder and the insured are in good faith and without gross negligence, they may claim against the insurer the return of all or part of the premiums. The same shall apply where the policyholder and the beneficiary are in good faith and without gross negligence.” Because, by the nature of an insurance contract, if even when the insurance contract is void due to bad faith or gross negligence of the policyholder, etc., the premiums already paid could be returned intact, there would be a significant risk that the policyholder, etc. would abuse the insurance contract, and it would be unfavorable to the insurer, which incurred substantial costs in the process of concluding the insurance contract; thus, the return of premiums is restricted as above. In addition, Commercial Act Article 662 provides that a 3-year statute of limitations period applies to the policyholder’s claim for insurance proceeds or to the claim for return of premiums arising from invalidity of the insurance contract, etc. This may be said to be a legislative policy decision comprehensively taking into account the need for prompt payment of insurance proceeds, together with the special characteristics of the invalidity of an insurance contract, etc.\\n\\nAs such, in order for a policyholder to claim the return of premiums, under Commercial Act Article 648, both the policyholder and the insured or beneficiary must be in good faith and without gross negligence, and a 3-year short statute of limitations period applies, under Commercial Act Article 662, to the policyholder’s claim for insurance proceeds or claim for return of premiums. However, it is clear from their wording that Commercial Act Articles 648 and 662 do not apply to the insurer’s claim for return of insurance proceeds, and since those provisions are legislative policy decisions made in light of the special characteristics of invalidity of insurance contracts, etc., it is not proper to extend or analogically apply them even to cases where the insurer claims return of insurance proceeds.\\n\\nThat does not mean, however, that the civil statute of limitations period applies to the insurer’s claim for restitution of unjust enrichment regarding the insurance proceeds; rather, in light of the standardized nature of insurance contracts and the need for prompt resolution of legal relationships, the provisions concerning the commercial statute of limitations period must be analogically applied. An insurer that ordinarily designs and sells insurance products, as a person with specialized knowledge of the performance of insurance contracts, is in a superior position to the policyholder, and although Commercial Act Article 662 concerns the policyholder’s claim for return of premiums, it presupposes that there is a need to promptly resolve legal relationships arising from invalidity of an insurance contract. Applying a 10-year civil statute of limitations period to a claim for return of insurance proceeds where the insurance contract is void does not accord with fairness between the policyholder and the insurer, who are parties to the insurance contract.\\n\\nD. In contrast, Supreme Court Decision 2014DA233596, rendered on 2016. 10. 27., which held that the statute of limitations period for a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment was 10 years in a case where a mutual aid company sought the return of mutual aid benefits paid on the basis of a mutual aid contract void as contrary to good morals and other social order (the legal principles regarding the invalidity of an insurance contract apply as they are even to such a case; see Commercial Act Article 664), shall be changed to the extent that it is contrary to the view of this judgment.\\n\\nE. Determination in this case\\n\\nThe court below, citing the first-instance judgment, held that the claim by the Plaintiff, as insurer, seeking the return of insurance proceeds already paid to Defendant 1 by reason of the invalidity of the insurance contract in this case is subject to the 5-year commercial statute of limitations period prescribed by Commercial Act Article 64.\\n\\nThe court below’s determination is in accordance with the legal principles discussed above and is proper, and there is no error in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the statute of limitations as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nThe appeals by the Plaintiff and the Defendants are without merit and are all dismissed, and the costs of appeal are to be borne by the losing parties, respectively. The judgment is rendered as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2020DA299122]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to Ground 1 of the appeal (the claim for return of the deposit)\\n\\na. Not only claims arising from acts that are commercial acts for both parties, but also claims arising from acts that constitute commercial acts only for one party are commercial claims to which the 5-year statute of limitations prescribed in Article 64 of the Commercial Act applies. Such commercial acts include not only the basic commercial acts falling under each item of Article 46 of the Commercial Act, but also auxiliary commercial acts performed by a merchant for business purposes, and acts performed by a merchant for business purposes are deemed commercial acts, while a merchant’s acts are presumed to be performed for business purposes [see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2002DA6760 (principal action), 2002DA6777 (counterclaim) rendered on September 24, 2002], and a claim for restoration to the original state arising from the rescission of a contract that is a commercial act is also subject to the commercial extinctive prescription under Article 64 of the Commercial Act (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 93DA21569 rendered on September 14, 1993).\\n\\nb. The court below determined that the Plaintiff, a merchant, entered into a sublease contract with the Defendant regarding part of the Defendant’s ○○○○○ △△ branch in order to use it as the Plaintiff’s own place of business, which constituted an auxiliary commercial act, and that the claim by the Plaintiff against the Defendant for return of the deposit, as restoration to the original state arising from the rescission of the sublease contract, is subject to the commercial statute of limitations.\\n\\nc. Examining the reasoning of the judgment below in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, there is no error in the court below’s determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning commercial acts, the commercial statute of limitations, and the like.\\n\\n2. With respect to Ground 2 of the appeal (the claim for return of unjust enrichment)\\n\\na. A claim for restitution of unjust enrichment arising from the invalidity of a contract that is a commercial act arises pursuant to the unjust enrichment provision of Article 741 of the Civil Act, and, absent special circumstances, the 10-year civil statute of limitations period prescribed in Article 162(1) of the Civil Act applies. However, where the claim for restitution of unjust enrichment seeks the return of the performance itself rendered on the basis of a contract that is a commercial act, and, in light of the circumstances or cause of the accrual of the claim, the parties’ statuses and relationship, there is a need to resolve the legal relationship as promptly as a commercial transaction relationship, etc., the 5-year commercial statute of limitations period prescribed in Article 64 of the Commercial Act applies or applies by analogy (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2019DA277812 rendered on July 22, 2021). And this legal principle applies as is to a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment arising from the non-formation of a contract that is a commercial act.\\n\\nb. The court below determined that, insofar as the Plaintiff, a merchant, paid the premium and lease deposit in order to enter into a sublease contract regarding part of the Defendant’s ○○○○○ □□ branch in order to secure the Plaintiff’s place of business, even though the sublease contract was not formed, the claim for return of the premium and lease deposit seeks the return of the performance itself rendered on the basis of a commercial act, and moreover, in light of the circumstances or cause of accrual of the claim, and the parties’ status and relationship, the legal relationship needed to be resolved as promptly as a commercial transaction relationship, and thus held that the 5-year commercial statute of limitations applies thereto.\\n\\nc. Examining the reasoning of the judgment below in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, there is no error in the court below’s determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the application of the commercial statute of limitations to a claim for restitution of unjust enrichment under civil law, and the like.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding security interests in shares of an unlisted company that has issued share certificates is incorrect? (In the event of a dispute, according to case law)
A: Unless the pledgee continues to possess the share certificate, the pledgee may not assert the pledge against a third party.
B: Where a debtor transfers shares to a creditor for the purpose of securing a debt and the creditor is entered as a shareholder in the shareholder register, the transferee may exercise shareholder rights as a shareholder, and even if the secured debt is extinguished by performance or otherwise, the company may not deny the transferee, who is a shareholder in the shareholder register, from exercising shareholder rights.
C: When convertible shares are converted, the pledge created over the original shares may also be exercised with respect to the shares to be received by the former shareholder as a result thereof.
D: As a method of transferring possession of the share certificate, which is a requirement for the creation of a pledge over shares, constructive delivery is permitted in addition to actual delivery, but assignment of the right to demand return is not permitted.
E: If, at the time of an agreement to transfer shares made for the purpose of securing a debt, more than 6 months had already elapsed since the formation of the company and yet the share certificates had not been issued, then that agreement immediately has effect as a security assignment of shares.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2012DA34764]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nAs to provisional remedies such as provisional attachment or provisional disposition, although they are enforced by a court judgment, whether there is a substantive claim is left to the merits action, and since they are carried out merely on the basis of prima facie showing and under the responsibility of the creditor, if the enforcement creditor is finally defeated in the merits action after such enforcement, intent or negligence on the part of the enforcement creditor is presumed, unless there is special rebuttal evidence, and therefore the creditor is liable to compensate for the damages suffered by the debtor as a result of such wrongful enforcement (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 92DA8453 rendered on September 25, 1992).\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 338 of the Commercial Act concerning the simplified pledge of registered shares provides that when registered shares are made the object of a pledge, the share certificates shall be delivered to the pledgee (paragraph 1), and that if the pledgee does not continue to possess the share certificates, the pledge may not be asserted against a third party (paragraph 2). Here, as a method of transferring possession of the share certificates, which is a requirement necessary for the creation of a pledge over shares, not only actual delivery, but also symbolic delivery or assignment of the right to demand return is permitted, and where the share certificates are placed in the custody of a third party, if the pledgor who indirectly possesses the share certificates intends to transfer possession of the share certificates by assignment of the right to demand return, it must assign to the pledgee the right to demand return against the third party who serves as the possessor’s intermediary, and in such case, as requirements for assertion against third parties, consent by that third party or notice by the pledgor to that third party must be satisfied (see Supreme Court Decision 99DA58471 rendered on September 8, 2000). And these legal principles should likewise apply where the possessory intermediary relationship is layered by the third party again placing the share certificates in the custody of another person; thus, it is sufficient for the uppermost indirect possessor, i.e., the pledgor, to assign to the pledgee the right to demand return against the third party who serves as its possessor’s intermediary, and, as requirements for assertion against third parties, to obtain the consent of that third party or give notice to that third party, and there is no need to obtain the consent of the other person who is the direct possessor or to give notice thereto by the pledgor or that third party.\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the judgment below and the evidence lawfully admitted by the court below, after Sewo Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Sewo”) issued share certificates for new shares allotted on June 24, 2002 to Diviner Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Diviner”) and others, Sewo entered into the First Escrow Agreement with the Korea Securities Depository concerning the share certificates for 1,363,455 shares, including the 1,360,000 shares listed in attached Table 1 to the judgment below (hereinafter referred to as the “Shares at Issue,” and the share certificates therefor as the “Share Certificates at Issue”), and deposited those share certificates with the Korea Securities Depository; on May 28, 2002, the Plaintiff loaned 3,400,000,000 won to Diviner and entered into the root pledge agreement at issue concerning 1,360,000 issued shares of Sewo that Diviner was to acquire in the future; when the share certificates at issue were issued and placed in escrow with the Korea Securities Depository on June 24, 2002, the Plaintiff and Diviner prepared a request for consent to the creation of a pledge in the joint names of the representative directors of the Plaintiff and Diviner, and around July 2002 obtained the name and seal of Sewo’s representative director on the said request for consent to the creation of a pledge, and the said request for consent to the creation of a pledge stated to the effect that “we consent to the creation of a pledge over the share certificates at issue placed in escrow and will return the share certificates at issue to the pledgee or a person designated by the pledgee when the escrow period ends”; the Plaintiff treated the above request for consent to the creation of a pledge, the root pledge agreement, and other documents as a single set of documents and received a fixed date on July 10, 2002; when the escrow period expired on June 23, 2003, the Korea Securities Depository deposited on June 24, 2003 the share certificates for the First Escrowed Shares, naming the depositor as “Sewo or Diviner or Dongbu Securities Co., Ltd.”; the Plaintiff filed this prior action against the Defendant and others seeking delivery of the share certificates at issue, etc., and on March 25, 2005 the court of first instance, as to whether the Plaintiff had acquired a pledge over the Shares at Issue, held that “Diviner, pursuant to the root pledge agreement at issue, agreed to assign to the Plaintiff the right to demand return of the share certificates from Sewo in order to transfer possession of the share certificates at issue to the Plaintiff, and it is reasonable to view Sewo as having consented to the assignment of that right to demand return vis-à-vis the Plaintiff and Diviner, and therefore the Plaintiff validly acquired a pledge over the Shares at Issue”; in the appellate stage of the prior action, the Defendant, as an intervenor supporting Diviner, argued to the effect that “in order for the Plaintiff to acquire possession of the share certificates at issue by Diviner assigning to the Plaintiff the right to demand return of the share certificates, notice of the assignment must be given to, or consent obtained from, the Korea Securities Depository, which is the direct possessor of the share certificates, and absent notice to or consent from the Korea Securities Depository, the Plaintiff did not acquire a pledge over the share certificates at issue,” but on April 19, 2007 the appellate court rejected this, stating that “where a layered possessory intermediary relationship exists, the pledge over the Shares at Issue should be deemed to have been created by Diviner’s assigning the right to demand return to Sewo and giving notice of assignment to Sewo, its possessory intermediary, or by obtaining Sewo’s consent, and there is no rational basis for viewing that a pledge is created only when direct notice of assignment is given to the Korea Securities Depository, the direct possessor,” (the Defendant did not appeal this part of the determination as intervenor supporting Diviner); thereafter, the Defendant, while asserting that the appellate court’s determination in the prior action cannot be accepted as an independent theory, applied for this provisional disposition seeking prohibition of the filing of a claim for release of the deposited property relating to the share certificates at issue and of any dispositive acts, including assignment of the claim right to such release, and on May 14, 2007 the court of provisional disposition granted the provisional disposition and the said decision was served around that time on the Plaintiff, who was the debtor, and the Republic of Korea, who was the third-party debtor; thereafter, pursuant to the court’s order to institute suit, the Defendant filed this subsequent action as the merits action for the provisional disposition, making the same arguments as those made as intervenor supporting Diviner in the prior action, and seeking confirmation that the Plaintiff was not in the position of pledgee with respect to the Shares at Issue, but it can be seen that both the court of first instance and the appellate court in the subsequent action rejected the Defendant’s arguments for the same reasons as those given by the appellate court in the prior action, so that the subsequent action became final and conclusive in the Defendant’s defeat.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, the above factual circumstances indicate that, although there was no express Supreme Court determination on the method of creating a pledge by assignment of the right to demand return by the uppermost indirect possessor in cases where a layered possessory intermediary relationship exists with respect to share certificates, and although it is recognized that the Defendant, differing in legal view from the court of first instance and the court below in the prior action, applied for this provisional disposition and obtained a decision granting it, thereby reaching execution of the provisional disposition, on the other hand, the court of first instance and the appellate court in the prior action had twice rendered an explicit determination, substantially to the same effect as the legal principles stated above, that the Plaintiff validly acquired a pledge over the Shares at Issue, yet immediately thereafter the Defendant rather applied for this provisional disposition while asserting that the court’s determination on that issue was merely an independent one; and considering circumstances such as the fact that both the appellate court in the prior action and the court of first instance and the appellate court in the subsequent action stated that the Defendant’s arguments lacked rational basis, to such an extent that the Defendant appears not to have presented a reasonable rationale sufficient to support its arguments, and considering together the circumstances that the Defendant could have obtained an express determination by the Supreme Court on that issue by appealing the appellate judgment in the prior action as an intervenor supporting Diviner, but instead proceeded to execute this provisional disposition without doing so, it cannot be said that the circumstances that the Defendant consistently trusted its own legal view on the above issue, that there was no express Supreme Court precedent on the issue at the time of this provisional disposition, and that the court of provisional disposition accepted the Defendant’s arguments and granted the application for this provisional disposition suffice to rebut the presumption of the Defendant’s intent or negligence with respect to the damages suffered by the Plaintiff as a result of the wrongful execution of the provisional disposition.\\n\\nThe judgment of the court below to the same effect is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehending the legal principles regarding the requirements for the creation of a pledge or the presumption of intent/negligence of a creditor for provisional disposition who loses in the merits action, as asserted in the grounds for appeal. And the Supreme Court decisions pointed out in the grounds for appeal concern different factual circumstances from this case and are not appropriate for citation in this case.\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2020MA5263]": "The grounds for the special re-appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Whether the applicant is a shareholder and whether there is an abuse of rights\\n\\na. Where a debtor transfers shares to a creditor for the purpose of securing the debt, and the transferee is entered as a shareholder in the stockholders’ register, the transferee may exercise shareholder rights as a shareholder, and the company likewise may not deny the transferee, who is a shareholder in the stockholders’ register, from exercising shareholder rights (see Supreme Court Decision 92DA84, decided on 1992. 5. 26.; Supreme Court en banc Decision 2015DA248342, decided on 2017. 3. 23.).\\n\\nb. According to the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\nThe special re-appellant is a company established for the purpose of real estate development and consulting business, and the applicant holds 21,300 shares out of the special re-appellant’s total 30,000 issued shares in the stockholders’ register (hereinafter referred to as “the shares at issue”).\\n\\nOn 2019. 3. 29., the applicant requested the representative director of the special re-appellant to convene an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders with the agenda of “dismissal of Non-party 1, the representative director of the special re-appellant, and Non-party 2, a director, respectively, election of successor representative director and directors, amendment of the articles of incorporation, and election of an acting chairperson”; however, the special re-appellant has not taken steps to convene an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders.\\n\\nc. The lower court granted the applicant’s petition for permission to convene the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders at issue for the following reasons.\\n\\nAlthough the applicant, as a shareholder holding 71% of the special re-appellant’s total issued shares, requested the convening of an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders, the special re-appellant has not, without delay, taken steps to convene an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders; therefore, it is appropriate to permit the convening of an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders pursuant to Article 366, paragraph (2) and paragraph (1) of the Commercial Act. The special re-appellant argues that the applicant is a security transferee of the shares at issue, and that the secured debt has been extinguished by performance, so the applicant can no longer be regarded as a shareholder, and therefore the petition for permission to convene the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders at issue constitutes an abuse of rights. Although it appears that Non-party 1, etc. transferred the shares at issue to the applicant for the purpose of securing debt, in the absence of any measures such as a claim for return of the shares at issue, the applicant remains a shareholder, and based solely on the circumstances asserted by the special re-appellant and the materials submitted, it cannot be found that the applicant is not a shareholder or that the petition for permission to convene the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders at issue constitutes an abuse of rights.\\n\\nThe lower court’s decision accords with the legal principles seen above and is proper. There is no error in the lower court’s determination, such as violation of the Constitution or laws that affected the judgment.\\n\\nd. The special re-appellant argues that the applicant is no longer a shareholder because, on 2019. 10. 25., the name of the shares at issue in the stockholders’ register was changed to Non-party 1. However, the foregoing argument is a new argument made in the special re-appeal proceedings, and therefore does not constitute a lawful ground for special re-appeal against the lower court’s decision.\\n\\n2. Whether the right to a fair trial was infringed\\n\\nWhen an appellate court hears an appeal case, the decision whether to open oral proceedings or to examine interested persons lies within the appellate court’s discretion (Civil Procedure Act, Article 134); therefore, absent special circumstances, it cannot be deemed unlawful merely because the appellate court rendered its decision on the basis of a review of the papers without opening oral proceedings or examining interested persons (see Supreme Court Decision 94MA1107, dated 1994. 7. 30.; Supreme Court Decision 2000MA6319, dated 2001. 3. 22., etc.). Accordingly, it cannot be found that the lower court, which is the appellate court, infringed the applicant’s right to a fair trial merely because it rendered its decision on the basis of a review of the papers.\\n\\n3. Since the special re-appeal at issue is without merit, it is dismissed, and the costs of the special re-appeal shall be borne by the special re-appellant; accordingly, the decision is made in accordance with the dispositive part by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[93DA61338]": "The grounds of appeal of the Defendant and the auxiliary intervenor for the Defendant are considered together.\\n\\n1. Regarding the preliminary objection\\n   a. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below held, in this action seeking confirmation of the invalidity of the resolution passed at the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders of the Defendant Company held on 1988.8.26., at which the auxiliary intervenor for the Defendant (hereinafter referred to only as the Intervenor) was appointed as a director, that, although the Intervenor, who was appointed as a director by the resolution of the said extraordinary general meeting of shareholders, had been removed from office and even the registration thereof had been completed, in response to the Defendant’s preliminary objection that the Plaintiffs had no legal interest in seeking confirmation of the invalidity of the said appointment resolution, since the Intervenor had already been removed from the office of director by the remand judgment of this Court and, pursuant to the tenor of the remand judgment, even if a resolution was passed at the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders held on 1990.1.12. after the said appointment resolution, removing the Intervenor and appointing a successor director, the validity of the original resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders held on 1988.8.26., which appointed the Intervenor as a director, is directly relevant to determining the present officers of the Defendant Company, insofar as the entirety of the said resolution is deemed not to have existed; thus, the Plaintiffs have a legal interest in seeking confirmation of the invalidity of the said appointment resolution. Thereafter, with respect to whether, in light of the circumstances newly found by the court below after remand, namely, that at the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders held by the Defendant Company on 1992.12.30. the Intervenor was again removed from the office of director and Nonparty 1 was appointed as the successor director, the Plaintiffs still had a legal interest in seeking confirmation of the invalidity of the original resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders held on 1988.8.26., which had appointed the Intervenor as a director, the court below found, based on the evidence cited, that after the Plaintiffs filed this action, on 1989.7.26., in Seoul District Court, Eastern Branch, Case No. 88KA18881, a provisional disposition order suspending the performance of duties of the Intervenor and the officers of the Defendant Company was issued, and Nonparty 2, an attorney at law, was appointed as acting representative director, and Nonparty 3 and others were appointed as acting directors, but in the case of objection to the provisional disposition, the said provisional disposition order was once canceled; thereafter, upon the Plaintiffs’ renewed application, on 1991.10.25., in Seoul Civil District Court, Case No. 91KA56633, a provisional disposition order suspending the performance of duties of the Intervenor and others was again issued, thereby suspending the performance of duties of the Intervenor and others, and Nonparty 4, an attorney at law, was appointed as acting representative director, and Nonparty 3 and others were each appointed as acting directors;
