Nonparty 3 endorsed and transferred it to the Plaintiff, and the Plaintiff, having become the holder thereof, filled in the name of the payee in the above blank portion as Nonparty 3 on 67.8.24.; in the case of a blank instrument, the time of supplementation of the blank and the time of formation of the bill act itself are matters that must be strictly distinguished, and although rights under the instrument cannot be exercised without supplementation of the blank, the time of formation of the bill act cannot be deemed the time of supplementation of the blank, and the time of formation should be determined by the time of formation of the bill act itself. If so, the judgment below, which held that the endorsement in this case, effected on 66.1.10. in the note at issue maturing on 66.1.20. and supplemented on 67.8.24., is not to be regarded as an endorsement after maturity, is indeed proper.\\n\\nTherefore, the ground of appeal asserting, on the basis of this Court’s prior precedent contrary to the above view (Judgment rendered on 65.8.31., 65DA1217 - preserved in this Court’s Precedents, Vol. 13, No. 2, Civil, p. 112 et seq., and listed in this Court Precedent Card NO.1802), that the endorsement in this case should be regarded as an endorsement after maturity and that its effect is only the effect of an assignment of a nominative claim, is without merit. Accordingly, with respect to the burden of litigation costs, Article 89 of the Civil Procedure Act is applied, and judgment is rendered as stated in the dispositive part.\\n\\nThis judgment was rendered by the unanimous opinion of all the participating Justices, except for the dissenting opinion that the grounds of appeal are meritorious, because the view of this Court’s prior precedent concerning blank promissory notes held by Supreme Court Justices Son Dong-uk, Sa Gwang-uk, Bang Soon-won, Na Hang-yun, Lee Yeong-seop, Joo Jae-hwang, and Yoo Jae-bang is correct."}

{"[69DA2184]": "We examine the grounds of appeal filed by the Defendant’s counsel.\\n\\n(1) As to Point 1,\\n\\nThe lower court found that the Plaintiff exercised the right of completion as the lawful holder of the promissory note at issue, and such factual finding by the lower court is proper. Even if it is true that the Plaintiff himself erased the endorsement entry portion of this note and withdrew a fact he had once asserted, this single fact alone does not constitute grounds sufficient to find that the Plaintiff’s acquisition of the note at issue was not through a proper course of circulation. The lower court’s determination that the Plaintiff was the lawful holder of the above note is proper, and there is no defect therein that can be regarded as constituting a mistaken finding of fact due to inadequate deliberation or an illegality in the application of the law, as contended by the argument. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n(2) As to Point 2,\\n\\nThe lower court holds as follows with respect to default interest among the claims in this case. That is, the Defendant was ordered to pay interest at the rate of 6 percent per annum from 1969.2.25, the day after the date of presentment with respect to the principal, until full payment. However, it is clear in light of the facts found in the first part of the lower court’s determination that, at the time the Plaintiff presented the above note, it was in the so-called blank note state, in which the person entitled to receive payment was not stated on the note, and that the Plaintiff thereafter filled in his own name after filing the present action. Since it cannot be said that the debtor immediately falls into delay in performance upon presentment of a blank note, the lower court’s above determination would constitute a misunderstanding of the legal principle concerning delay in performance of a note debt. The argument on this point is without merit.\\n\\nAccordingly, by unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, it is adjudged as ordered."}

{"[97DA57573]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nWhen a judgment of nullification is rendered for a bill, that bill loses its effect as a bill, and the person who obtained the judgment of nullification recovers the status of holder of the bill and is able to exercise rights under the bill (Civil Procedure Act Articles 467 and 468). However, a blank bill in which some of the essential elements of the bill are left blank is an incomplete bill, so the rights under the bill cannot be exercised without completion of the blank. Moreover, even if there is a judgment of nullification for a blank bill, that judgment does not revive the blank bill itself, and therefore there is no way to complete the blank on the face of the bill.\\n\\nArticle 468 of the Civil Procedure Act provides: \"When there is a judgment of nullification, the applicant may assert the rights under the certificate against the person who has assumed an obligation by the security or certificate.\" The judgment of nullification system is intended to enable a person who has lost a security or certificate to realize the relevant rights by giving that person a formal status equivalent to possessing it; and, considering together the fact that the issuer of a blank bill assumes an obligation to pay the amount of the bill on the condition that the blank be completed, and the fact that the right to complete the blank and the rights under the bill conditional upon completion of the blank are transferred to the transferee together with the transfer of the blank bill, so that the holder may complete the blank at any time and exercise the rights under the bill, and that, in bill transactions, a blank bill circulates while having the same economic value as a completed bill, it is appropriate to view that a person who has obtained a judgment of nullification for a blank bill may assert against the issuer both the right to complete the blank and the rights under the bill conditional upon completion of the blank as the \"rights under the certificate\" prescribed in the above Article 468 of the Civil Procedure Act.\\n\\nTherefore, the determination of the court below that, as the Plaintiff who obtained a judgment of nullification for the promissory note at issue, issued with the respective spaces for the date of issue, place of issue, place of payment, and payee left blank, may exercise the right to complete the blank by means of a manifestation of intention other than on the note and seek payment of the amount of the note from the issuer, the Defendant, with respect to the blank portions, is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality of misapprehension of law as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nUpon review of the record, the court below's findings of fact and determination regarding the other matters asserted in the grounds of appeal are all persuasive, and there is no illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles of the Bills of Exchange and Promissory Notes Act, thereby failing to conduct the necessary examination, or by violating the rules of evidence.\\n\\nAll grounds of appeal are without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices concerned."}

question: Company A is an unlisted company with capital of less than 1 billion won, and has directors A and B, but no auditor. A is the representative director of Company A and owns all of Company A’s shares. Which of the following statements is incorrect? (Each statement is independent, and where there is disagreement, the case law shall govern)
A: If Company A transfers its sole business asset to C, the disposition is valid if A consents.
B: If, despite B’s lack of intention to resign as a director, the register states that B resigned upon A’s application, it cannot be said that false facts were entered in the original of a notarized deed.
C: Absent special circumstances, A may file a bankruptcy petition for Company A on his own.
D: If Company A files a lawsuit against B or B files a lawsuit against Company A, Company A, a director of Company A, or an interested person must apply to the court to have a person appointed to represent Company A.
E: If Company A convenes a shareholders’ meeting, it may send written notice to A 10 days before the date of the shareholders’ meeting, or, with A’s consent, send notice by electronic document.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[73DA52]": "The appeal is dismissed.\\nThe costs of appeal shall be borne by the Plaintiff."}

{"[92DO1564]": "1. We examine the defense counsel’s grounds of appeal.\\nIn a so-called one-person company, the intention of the sole shareholder is the same as the intention of the general meeting of shareholders or the board of directors; thus, even if the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders or the board of directors, or the registration of a change of officers made thereby, has become unlawful, so long as it conforms to the intention of the sole shareholder, it cannot be said that the minutes were forged or that a false registration was made. However, a resignation letter of an officer or the registration of a director’s resignation pursuant thereto is unrelated to the above-mentioned resolution of the general meeting of shareholders or the board of directors, or to the intention of the sole shareholder, and must depend solely on the intention of the relevant officer. Therefore, if a resignation letter not based on the intention of the relevant officer was prepared or an entry in the register was made on the basis thereof, the offense of forgery of a private document and making a false entry in the original of a notarized document cannot be avoided (See this Court’s judgment rendered on 1981.6.9. in 80DO2641).\\nLooking at this case, it is not recognized that the deceased D, who was a director of C Corporation, had ever resigned from his position as director, nor is it recognized that during his lifetime he expressed to the Defendant, who was the sole shareholder, his intention to resign. If, after the death of the said D, the Defendant took the procedure for retirement by resignation, instead of the procedure for retirement by death as stated in the judgment below, then the Defendant must bear criminal liability for forgery of a private document and making a false entry in the original of a notarized document, and it cannot be said, as argued, that there was no intent or that there was no social reprehensibility. Ultimately, the judgment of the court below to the same effect is proper, and the argument criticizing it is without merit.\\n\\n2. We examine the Prosecutor’s grounds of appeal.\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the record, it is correct that the court below, with respect to the part of this case’s charges concerning the forgery and use of a stock transfer certificate, found that there was no proof to establish the facts of the crime according to the selection and assessment of the evidence as stated and therefore rendered a judgment of not guilty. There is no illegality in the mistaken finding of facts due to violation of the rules of evidence, and the argument on this point is without merit.\\nAccordingly, the opinions of the participating Justices are unanimous that all appeals be dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as follows."}

question: Company A is an unlisted stock company with capital of KRW 2 billion, and its articles of incorporation do not contain any separate provisions concerning the issuance of bonds. Which of the following statements is correct? (Each item is independent, and where there is a dispute, case law applies)
A: If Company A issues convertible bonds in violation of statutes or the articles of incorporation, or by a method that is manifestly unfair, thereby creating a risk that shareholders will suffer disadvantage, such shareholders may request Company A to suspend the issuance of the convertible bonds.
B: If Company A issues convertible bonds, the subsequent issuance of new shares resulting from the exercise of the conversion right may be challenged by an action to invalidate the issuance of new shares, and the period for filing such action shall run from the date of issuance of the convertible bonds.
C: Where Company A intends to issue bonds with warrants to a shareholder or a person other than a shareholder, the total amount of the bonds with warrants, the contents of the warrant rights, and the period during which the warrant rights may be exercised are not provided for in the articles of incorporation, and therefore they must be determined by a special resolution of Company A’s general meeting of shareholders.
D: If Company A issues convertible bonds, Article 429 of the Commercial Act concerning an action to invalidate the issuance of new shares shall apply by analogy to the action to invalidate the issuance of the convertible bonds and the action for declaratory judgment of nonexistence of the issuance of the convertible bonds, and the six-month limitation on filing suit applies.
E: When Company A issues bonds with warrants, it must register this, and if the person who received the bonds with warrants exercises the warrant rights, that person has the rights and obligations of a shareholder from the day after the payment date for the new shares.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2003DA20060]": "All appeals are dismissed. Each party shall bear its own costs of appeal."}
{"[2003DA20060]": "All appeals are dismissed. The costs of appeal shall be borne by each party."}

{"[2021DA201054]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Relevant legal principles\\n\\na. Bonds with stock acquisition rights are bonds endowed with stock acquisition rights whereby a specified number of new shares may be subscribed for at a pre-fixed price. Even in the case of the issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights, since they are substantially analogous to the issuance of new shares in that they affect the corporation’s capital base and the interests of existing shareholders, Article 429 of the Commercial Act concerning an action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares applies by analogy. The invalidity of the issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights may be asserted by shareholders, etc. only through an action brought within 6 months from the date on which the bonds with stock acquisition rights were issued, and after the 6-month filing period has elapsed, no new ground of invalidity may be added and asserted (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DA202919, rendered on Dec. 10, 2015, Supreme Court Decision 2000DA37326, rendered on June 25, 2004, etc.). Accordingly, if no action for invalidation of the issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights is filed within 6 months from the date of issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights, or if an action for invalidation of the issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights filed within 6 months becomes final and binding with an adverse judgment against the party asserting invalidity, the invalidity of the issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights may no longer be asserted thereafter.\\n\\nb. 1) However, as to the exercise of the stock acquisition rights attached to bonds with stock acquisition rights and the issuance of new shares resulting therefrom, Article 429 of the Commercial Act applies by analogy, and they may be challenged by an action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares. In such a case, unless there are special circumstances, only grounds of invalidity inherent in the exercise of the stock acquisition rights or the issuance of new shares therefrom may be asserted, and no assertion premised on the invalidity of the issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights may be made.\\n\\n2) Meanwhile, Article 418(1) and (2) of the Commercial Act protect existing shareholders’ right to subscribe for new shares by, in principle, allotting new shares to existing shareholders when a company issues new shares, while allowing allotment to a third party only where so provided in the articles of incorporation, and by limiting the grounds to cases necessary to achieve managerial purposes such as the introduction of new technology or the improvement of financial structure. Accordingly, when a stock company issues new shares, if, even though there is no ground prescribed in the articles of incorporation within the scope necessary to achieve the company’s managerial purpose, it allots new shares to a third party for the purpose of defending the management rights or control rights of the major shareholder or management, etc. in a situation where a management dispute of the company has become actualized, such allotment violates Article 418(2) of the Commercial Act and infringes the shareholders’ right to subscribe for new shares, and where, as a result, a serious change in the company’s governance structure is brought about and a grave consequence occurs in which the control rights of the existing shareholders over the company are significantly weakened, such issuance of new shares is invalid (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DA50776, rendered on Jan. 30, 2009, Supreme Court Decision 2018DA289542, rendered on Apr. 3, 2019, etc.). This legal principle likewise applies where bonds with stock acquisition rights are issued to a third party (see the latter sentence of Article 516-2(4) and the proviso to Article 418(2) of the Commercial Act, Supreme Court Decision 2015DA202919, rendered on Dec. 10, 2015).\\n\\n3) In the case of bonds with stock acquisition rights, even if they are issued to a third party for the purpose of defending the management rights or control rights of the major shareholder, etc. without a managerial purpose, the issuance itself does not infringe the existing shareholders’ right to subscribe for new shares; only later, when the major shareholder, etc. exercises the stock acquisition rights acquired by transfer and acquires new shares, is the existing shareholders’ right to subscribe for new shares infringed and the purpose of defending the management rights or control rights of the major shareholder, etc. realized. According to this, if the company issued bonds with stock acquisition rights to a third party for the purpose of defending the management rights or control rights of the major shareholder, etc., the issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights may be invalid, and such a ground may be challenged by an action for invalidation of the issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights within 6 months from the date of issuance. Furthermore, if the major shareholder, etc. acquires the bonds with stock acquisition rights issued in the foregoing manner or the stock acquisition rights attached thereto, and then, after 6 months have elapsed from the date of issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights, exercises the stock acquisition rights and acquires new shares, this is, in substance, equivalent to the company issuing new shares to the major shareholder, etc. without a managerial purpose; accordingly, the invalidity of the issuance of new shares may also be asserted by an action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares, by analogy to grounds of invalidity inherent in the exercise of stock acquisition rights or the issuance of new shares therefrom.\\n\\nIn this way, shareholders’ right to sue challenging unlawful issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights or issuance of new shares based thereon can be effectively protected.\\n\\n4) In the foregoing case, the filing period for an action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares shall be calculated from the date of issuance of the new shares, and even if the issuance of new shares results from the exercise of stock acquisition rights attached to bonds with stock acquisition rights, it shall not be calculated from the date of issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights.\\n\\n2. Determination of this case\\n\\na. According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n1) The Defendant’s articles of incorporation provide that, where necessary for urgent financing for managerial purposes, bonds with stock acquisition rights may be issued, by resolution of the board of directors, to financial institutions, etc. other than shareholders (Article 23(1)5).\\n\\n2) On June 30, 2016, the Defendant issued privately placed detachable bonds with stock acquisition rights (hereinafter referred to as “the bonds with stock acquisition rights at issue”), and Partners No. 4 Growth Investment Association and Gudam Partners LLC subscribed for the bonds with stock acquisition rights at issue in the amounts of KRW 2,056,000,000 and KRW 3,084,000,000, respectively. At that time, the Plaintiff held 131,449 shares of the Defendant (8.78%), and Nonparty, who was the Defendant’s Representative Director, held 335,393 shares of the Defendant (22.39%).\\n\\n3) Around September 2016, Nonparty acquired by transfer part of the stock acquisition rights attached to the bonds with stock acquisition rights at issue from Partners No. 4 Growth Investment Association and Gudam Partners LLC (hereinafter the stock acquisition rights acquired by Nonparty are referred to as “the stock acquisition rights at issue”).\\n\\n4) When Nonparty exercised the stock acquisition rights at issue on October 21, 2019, the Defendant issued 100,000 common shares with a par value of KRW 500 each (hereinafter referred to as “the new shares at issue”) to Nonparty on the same day.\\n\\n5) No action for invalidation of the issuance of bonds with stock acquisition rights was filed within 6 months from the date of issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights at issue.\\n\\n6) On November 19, 2019, the Plaintiff filed an action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares at issue, alleging in substance that the Defendant had issued the bonds with stock acquisition rights at issue for the purpose of strengthening the management rights or control rights of Nonparty, who was its Representative Director, without the need for urgent financing for managerial purposes, and that therefore both the issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights at issue and the issuance of new shares resulting from Nonparty’s exercise of the stock acquisition rights at issue are invalid.\\n\\nb. The foregoing facts are examined in light of the legal principles set forth above.\\n\\nThe filing period for the action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares at issue must be calculated from the date of issuance of the new shares at issue, and it is not required to be calculated from the date of issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights at issue merely because the Plaintiff’s arguments include grounds concerning the invalidity of the issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights at issue.\\n\\nHowever, since the action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares at issue was filed on November 19, 2019, within 6 months from October 21, 2019, the date of issuance of the new shares at issue, it is clear that the filing period was observed.\\n\\nAccordingly, the court below should have examined whether the Defendant issued the bonds with stock acquisition rights at issue for the purpose of aiding the defense of Nonparty’s management rights or control rights, thereby being able to be evaluated, in substance, as equivalent to the company issuing new shares to Nonparty without a managerial purpose, and whether, as a result, a serious change in the Defendant’s governance structure was brought about and a grave consequence occurred in which the Plaintiff, as an existing shareholder, was significantly weakened in its control over the company, and then determined whether the issuance of the new shares at issue was invalid.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below held that the action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares at issue was procedurally improper on the ground that the Plaintiff asserted only grounds for invalidity of the issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights, and therefore calculated the filing period from the date of issuance of the bonds with stock acquisition rights at issue. This judgment of the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principle concerning the filing period for an action for invalidation of the issuance of new shares.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without addressing the remaining grounds for appeal, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for further proceedings and determination, and so the judgment is rendered as stated in the order by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2021DA205650]": "The grounds of appeal (the statements in the supplementary brief of grounds of appeal filed after the filing period shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds) are examined.\\n\\n1. Determination on the claim of misapprehension of legal principles, etc. regarding grounds for invalidity of issuance of new shares (Ground of Appeal No. 1)\\n\\nA. A convertible bond is a bond granted with the right to be converted into shares in the future by exercise of the conversion right. Since the issuance of such convertible bonds affects the material basis of a stock company and the interests of existing shareholders, it is substantially similar to issuing new shares; therefore, in the case of issuance of convertible bonds, Article 429 of the Commercial Act concerning an action for invalidation of issuance of new shares applies by analogy. Invalidity of the issuance of convertible bonds may be asserted by an action only by shareholders, etc., within 6 months from the date on which the convertible bonds were issued, and after the 6-month period for filing an action has elapsed, new grounds for invalidity may not be added and asserted (see Supreme Court Decision of 25 June 2004, 2000DA37326, and Supreme Court Decision of 16 August 2004, 2003DA9636, etc.). Therefore, if no action for invalidation of issuance of convertible bonds was filed within 6 months from the date of issuance of the convertible bonds, or if an action for invalidation of issuance of convertible bonds filed within 6 months became final and conclusive against the active party, the invalidity of the issuance of the convertible bonds may no longer be asserted thereafter. However, with respect to the issuance of new shares caused by exercise of the conversion right, it may be contested by applying Article 429 of the Commercial Act through an action for invalidation of issuance of new shares; in such case, unless there are special circumstances, no assertion may be made that the issuance of convertible bonds itself is invalid or that the issuance of convertible bonds is invalid on that premise, and only grounds for invalidity inherent in the exercise of the conversion right or the ensuing issuance of new shares may be asserted.\\n\\nMeanwhile, under Article 418(1) and (2) of the Commercial Act, when a company issues new shares, in principle, the shares shall be allocated to shareholders in proportion to the number of shares they hold, but the company may allocate new shares to persons other than shareholders in accordance with the articles of incorporation, and the grounds therefor are also limited to cases necessary to achieve managerial purposes, such as the introduction of new technology or the improvement of financial structure, thereby protecting the preemptive rights of existing shareholders to subscribe for new shares. Accordingly, when a stock company issues new shares, if there is no ground prescribed by the articles of incorporation within the scope necessary to achieve the company’s managerial purpose, such as the introduction of new technology or the improvement of financial structure, then allocating new shares to a third party for the purpose of defending management control or control rights of a major shareholder or management, etc. in a situation where a management dispute of the company has become real, violates Article 418(2) of the Commercial Act and infringes the shareholders’ preemptive rights to subscribe for new shares; and where, as a result, a significant change is brought about in the company’s governance structure and a grave consequence occurs in which the existing shareholders’ control over the company is substantially weakened, such issuance of new shares is invalid (see Supreme Court Decision of 30 January 2009, 2008DA50776, and Supreme Court Decision of 3 April 2019, 2018DA289542, etc.). This legal principle applies in the same way where convertible bonds are issued to a third party (see the latter sentence of Article 513(3) and the proviso to Article 418(2) of the Commercial Act, and Supreme Court Decision of 25 June 2004, 2000DA37326, etc.), but considerations arising from the special nature of convertible bonds are required. That is, if a company issued convertible bonds to a third party for the purpose of defending the control or management rights of a major shareholder, etc. without a managerial purpose, the issuance of the convertible bonds may be invalid, and such grounds may be contested by an action for invalidation of issuance of convertible bonds within 6 months from the date of issuance of the convertible bonds. Furthermore, if a major shareholder, etc. acquires the convertible bonds issued in such circumstances and then, after 6 months from the date of issuance of the convertible bonds, exercises the conversion right and acquires new shares, this is substantially identical to the company issuing new shares to the major shareholder, etc. without a managerial purpose; therefore, it must be deemed that the invalidity of the issuance of new shares may also be asserted by an action for invalidation of issuance of new shares, on the basis of grounds for invalidity inherent in the exercise of the conversion right or the ensuing issuance of new shares (see Supreme Court Decision of 27 October 2022, 2021DA201054, concerning bonds with warrants).\\n\\nB. According to the reasons stated in the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n1) The Defendant issued convertible bonds with a total issue price of KRW 3.2 billion to companies other than shareholders around December 2015 (hereinafter referred to as “the instant convertible bonds”), and issued 485,312 common shares with a par value of KRW 500 around March 2016 (hereinafter referred to as “the relevant new shares”).\\n\\n2) The Plaintiffs, who are shareholders of the Defendant, filed an action against the Defendant around May 2016 for invalidation of the issuance of the instant convertible bonds and the relevant new shares (hereinafter referred to as “the prior invalidation action”), and in particular, with respect to the issuance of the instant convertible bonds, argued that, although the Defendant was not in a case necessary to achieve managerial purposes such as the introduction of new technology or the improvement of financial structure, it issued the instant convertible bonds to persons other than shareholders, thereby violating the proviso to Article 513(3) and the proviso to Article 418(2) of the Commercial Act, and was therefore invalid. After receiving a judgment dismissing all claims at first instance, the Plaintiffs withdrew the appeal concerning the claim for invalidation of the issuance of the instant convertible bonds at the appellate stage.\\n\\n3) Some of the companies that subscribed to the instant convertible bonds exercised their conversion rights around December 2018, and the Defendant accordingly issued a total of 574,712 common shares with a par value of KRW 500 (hereinafter referred to as “the instant new shares”).\\n\\n4) The Plaintiffs filed the instant action for invalidation of issuance of new shares on 22 May 2019.\\n\\nC. The foregoing facts are examined in light of the legal principles set forth above.\\n\\nThe Plaintiffs asserted, in substance, that the instant convertible bonds were issued to a third party solely for the purpose of defending the control of the controlling shareholder, although there was no need to achieve the Defendant’s managerial purpose, and thus are invalid; and that the instant new shares issued pursuant to the exercise of the conversion right of the instant convertible bonds were also issued for the same purpose and are therefore invalid.\\n\\nHowever, in this case, where companies other than shareholders subscribed to the instant convertible bonds and some of them exercised their conversion rights and were issued new shares, the Plaintiffs’ claim concerns only grounds for invalidity related to the issuance of the instant convertible bonds and not grounds for invalidity inherent in, or equivalent to, the issuance of the instant new shares; therefore, it must be contested by an action for invalidation of issuance of convertible bonds and cannot be contested by an action for invalidation of issuance of new shares such as in this case.\\n\\nAlthough some parts of the judgment of the court below do not appear entirely proper, the conclusion of the court below, which rejected the Plaintiffs’ argument that because the issuance of the instant convertible bonds is invalid, the issuance of the instant new shares must be invalidated, is proper, and there is no error, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning an action for invalidation of issuance of new shares, etc., or omission of determination, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Determination on the claim of violation of the principle of good faith or estoppel (Ground of Appeal No. 2) and the claim of misapprehension of legal principles concerning the prohibition on acquisition of treasury shares and the principle of capital maintenance (Ground of Appeal No. 3)\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its opinion, the court below found that there was no evidence to recognize that the bondholders of the instant convertible bonds or the Defendant had engaged in acts or statements, such as promising non-exercise of the conversion right, or that the Defendant had provided subscription funds to those who subscribed to the instant convertible bonds, and therefore rejected the Plaintiffs’ claim that the issuance of the instant new shares violated the principle of good faith or estoppel, as well as the claim that it violated the principle of capital maintenance or the prohibition on acquisition of treasury shares.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and upon review of the record, there is no error in the foregoing determination of the court below, such as exceeding the limits of the free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehending the legal principles concerning the principle of good faith or estoppel, the principle of capital maintenance, or the prohibition on acquisition of treasury shares.\\n\\n3. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged as stated in the disposition, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question:
A Company is an unlisted company in which A is the representative director and a major shareholder holding shares corresponding to more than one half of the total number of issued shares. A Company entered into an investment agreement with B Company, in the course of attracting investment from B Company by way of a new share issuance, with A, A Company, and B Company as the parties, on the following terms. Pursuant to the above investment agreement, A Company issued redeemable convertible preferred shares, the shareholders of which have redemption rights and conversion rights, in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the Commercial Act, and B Company subscribed for them and paid the subscription price. Which of the following statements concerning this is correct? (Where there is any dispute, case law shall apply)

1. If the rehabilitation proceedings of A Company are commenced without the written consent of B Company (regardless of who petitioned for commencement of the rehabilitation proceedings and whether A Company is at fault), A Company shall pay B Company, as a contractual penalty, interest at the rate of 10% per annum from the date of issuance until redemption on the acquisition price per share of the shares subscribed for by B Company and on that amount.
2. A Company must obtain prior consent from B Company with respect to major management matters falling within the authority of the board of directors, and if it violates this, B Company is granted, by way of damages, the right to demand early redemption of the shares subscribed for by B Company.
3. A is jointly and severally liable for the debts owed by A Company to B Company under 1. and 2., and if, as a method of performance of A's debt, B Company demands that A purchase the subscribed shares, a sales contract is concluded with respect to those shares.

(a) As to 1., the part concluded between A Company and B Company is, absent special circumstances, void for violating the principle of equality among shareholders, and the same is true even if all other shareholders of A Company consented to such discriminatory treatment.

(b) As to 1. and 3., the part concluded between A and B Company is directly subject to the principle of equality among shareholders, and the validity of that part must, absent special circumstances, be determined in conjunction with the part concluded between A Company and B Company.

(c) 2., which provides that B Company has a prior consent right concerning major management matters of A Company when subscribing for new shares, is unlawful as it infringes the authority of the board of directors prescribed by the Commercial Act, and is therefore void even if there are other special circumstances.

(d) With respect to 2., where B Company has a prior consent right over major management matters of A Company, since the prior consent right is not conferred on the shares themselves, it is not the issuance of a special class of shares impermissible under the Commercial Act.

(e) As to 3., B Company’s right to demand purchase of shares against A constitutes a right of formation, and its exercise period is subject, by analogy, to Article 64 of the Commercial Act, and a preclusive period of 5 years applies.

supporting_precedents: {"[2019DA204463]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nArticle 393(1) of the Commercial Act provides that the execution of the business of a stock company, including the disposition and transfer of important assets and borrowing of property on a large scale, shall be by resolution of the board of directors, thereby making clear that the board of directors of a stock company has decision-making authority concerning the execution of the company’s business. Accordingly, not only the disposition or transfer of the important assets of a stock company and acts of borrowing property on a large scale, but also important business that does not fall within ordinary business and has not been generally and specifically delegated by the board of directors to the representative director, must be carried out through a resolution of the board of directors (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DA55808 rendered on January 14, 2010).\\n\\nIf a stock company files an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings, the fact of such application is notified even before the decision to commence proceedings to the Financial Services Commission and the supervisory administrative authorities, etc. [Article 40 of the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Debtor Rehabilitation Act”)], and the impact on the debtor is not insignificant, as the authority to dispose of the debtor’s business and property is controlled through the court’s preservation order, etc. (Article 43 of the Debtor Rehabilitation Act).\\n\\nIn the case where rehabilitation proceedings are commenced against a stock company, the termination of contracts on that ground and the exercise of a right of retrieval, etc. cause substantial changes in the company’s business or property. In addition, originally the authority to execute business of a stock company is vested in the representative director (Article 389(3) and Article 209(1) of the Commercial Act), and the authority to make decisions on matters prescribed by the articles of incorporation or by law, as well as on the disposition and transfer of important assets, is vested in the general meeting of shareholders or the board of directors (Article 361 and Article 393(1) of the Commercial Act). However, once rehabilitation proceedings are commenced, the right to carry on business and the right to manage and dispose of property of the stock company vest exclusively in the administrator, and the administrator must obtain prior permission from the court in order to perform certain acts such as the disposition of property or the expenditure of money (see Article 56(1), Article 61, etc. of the Debtor Rehabilitation Act), thereby bringing about fundamental changes in the management of the company.\\n\\nAlthough a stock company may, through rehabilitation proceedings, adjust the legal relations of various interested parties such as creditors and shareholders and thereby seek the efficient rehabilitation of the debtor or its business (Article 1 of the Debtor Rehabilitation Act), the decision whether to file an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings has a substantial impact on the stock company, as bankruptcy proceedings may proceed if the decision to terminate rehabilitation proceedings becomes final (Article 6(1) of the Debtor Rehabilitation Act).\\n\\nIn light of the role of the board of directors in a stock company as described above and the effect of a decision to commence rehabilitation proceedings against a stock company, an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings by a stock company should be regarded as important business that does not fall within the ordinary business of the representative director, and thus a resolution of the board of directors is required.\\n\\nThe lower court held that, on the premise that the Plaintiff’s application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings, while serving as the Defendant’s representative director, constituted important business that did not fall within the ordinary business of the representative director and therefore required a resolution of the board of directors, the Plaintiff bears liability for damages arising from tort against the Defendant.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above and the record, the lower court’s determination is reasonable and can be upheld, and there is no error affecting the judgment due to any misapprehension of the legal principles concerning an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings or the requirements for the establishment of tort, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAlso, examining the reasons for the lower court’s judgment in light of the relevant legal principles, the lower court’s determination not to limit the Plaintiff’s liability is persuasive, and there is no error affecting the judgment due to any misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the limitation of liability for damages, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. With respect to the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. First ground of appeal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its opinion, the lower court held that the Defendant’s “Executive Retirement Allowance Payment Guidelines” were valid rules enacted through lawful procedures.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the lower court’s determination is reasonable and can be upheld, and there is no error affecting the judgment due to any misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the obligation to pay executive retirement allowances, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nb. Second ground of appeal\\n\\nThe lower court found it difficult to recognize that, had the Plaintiff not filed the application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings, the Defendant would have obtained the business projects stated in the lower court’s opinion and thereby obtained the profits it had expected; meanwhile, with respect to the part appearing to indicate that the Defendant lost the benefit of the term due to the application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings filed by the third party, the lower court did not recognize the Plaintiff’s liability.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the lower court’s determination is reasonable and can be upheld, and there is no error affecting the judgment due to any misapprehension of the legal principles concerning liability for damages or due to insufficient examination, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nc. Third ground of appeal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its opinion, the lower court held that setoff is not permitted with respect to the amount equivalent to one-half of the Plaintiff’s retirement allowance.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the lower court’s determination is proper and can be upheld, and there is no error affecting the judgment due to any misapprehension of the legal principles concerning claims not subject to attachment, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by each party. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2019DA271661]": "The grounds for appeal are to be determined (preparatory briefs, etc. submitted after the period for submitting the petition of appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement it).\\n\\n1. Determination on the claim for the share sale price based on the stock repurchase agreement under the Undertaking at issue\\n\\nThe court below held as follows. An Undertaking at issue was executed whereby Defendant DC Holdings Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “DC Holdings”) would repurchase the shares at issue from the Partnership at issue in 2007 and Defendant 2 would provide joint and several guaranty therefor. It is difficult to view, under the Undertaking at issue, that DC Holdings agreed to repurchase the shares at issue on account of Defendant 2, and even if such a possibility existed, that alone would not exempt the agreement from the application of the provisions of the Commercial Act restricting acquisition of treasury shares. There is also no evidence to support that DC Holdings agreed to repurchase the shares in order to cancel them. If DC Holdings repurchases the shares as prescribed in the Undertaking at issue, the result would be a return of capital contributions to the Partnership at issue, a specific shareholder, and thus there exists a risk of impairing capital maintenance. Accordingly, the stock repurchase agreement under the Undertaking at issue is invalid as a contractual obligation agreement concerning acquisition of treasury shares, in violation of Article 341 of the former Commercial Act (as amended in part by Act No. 10600 on April 14, 2011), which concerns restrictions on acquisition of treasury shares.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles, when examining the reasons of the judgment of the court below, there is no error in the judgment that affected the outcome, such as the misapprehension of legal principles concerning restrictions on acquisition of treasury shares, burden of proof, the principle prohibiting abuse of rights, or the principle of good faith and fair dealing, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. Determination on the claim for damages arising from the joint tort of the Defendants\\n\\nFor the following reasons, the court below rejected the Plaintiff’s claim for damages against DC Holdings and Defendant 2, as well as the claim for damages against Defendant DC Inside Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Defendant DC Inside”), premised on disregard of the corporate entity of DC Holdings. It is difficult to find that DC Holdings and Defendant 2 deceived the Plaintiff by, from the outset, promising repurchase of the shares while knowing that the Undertaking at issue was invalid as contrary to the provisions of the Commercial Act restricting acquisition of treasury shares. It is also difficult to find that, at the time the Undertaking at issue was executed, the value of DC Holdings shares was significantly below the agreed repurchase price, or that DC Holdings was experiencing financial difficulties to such an extent that it could not perform its promise. Nor is it easy to find that DC Holdings intended, without any intention of performing the repurchase obligation, to establish an affiliated company immediately upon the Plaintiff’s exercise of the conversion right and to transfer major operating assets.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, when examining the reasons of the judgment of the court below, there is no error in the judgment, such as an insufficient trial or an error in fact-finding regarding whether the Defendants committed a joint tort, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Determination on the claim for the share sale price arising from the exercise of the right to demand purchase of shares under the Acquisition Agreement at issue\\n\\nA. Legal principles concerning the exercise period of the right to demand purchase of shares\\n\\nWhere, in an investment-related agreement, it is provided that if one party demands the other party to purchase the shares it holds, a sale and purchase agreement with respect to the shares is deemed to be concluded, such right to demand purchase of shares constitutes a type of formative right, as a right that forms a new legal relationship called a sale and purchase agreement upon one party’s declaration of intent.\\n\\nThe exercise period of the right to demand purchase of shares, which is a formative right arising by contract as described above, is a preclusive period. The purpose of the preclusive period system is generally to prompt the right holder to exercise the right promptly so as to establish legal relations without delay. However, because the degree of necessity for prompt establishment of legal relations differs depending on the contract that creates the right, this must also be taken into account when determining the exercise period of the right to demand purchase of shares. First, where the parties have agreed on the exercise period for the right to demand purchase of shares in the contract, such right is extinguished by lapse of the preclusive period if it is not exercised within that period. On the other hand, where there is no agreement concerning the exercise period for the right to demand purchase of shares, the exercise period must be determined by considering the nature of the contract underlying it, the motive for granting the right to demand purchase of shares and the purpose to be achieved thereby, and the exercise period of the claim that arises from the exercise of the right to demand purchase of shares.\\n\\nIn an investment-related agreement that constitutes a commercial transaction, there are cases where, after the investor executes the investment pursuant to the agreement and acquires shares, if there is a default on the part of the investment target company, etc., the investor is granted the right to demand purchase of shares against other shareholders, etc. In particular, obligations prescribed in a shareholders’ agreement may be difficult to enforce even if the obligor defaults, or it may be difficult to assert and prove the amount of damage resulting therefrom. In such cases, if there is an agreement on the right to demand purchase of shares, the investor may exercise the right to demand purchase of shares and receive the pre-agreed sale price from the counterparty, thereby enabling the investor to easily exercise its right in response to the counterparty’s default and recover the invested principal or realize profits. Such a right to demand purchase of shares is closely related to the purpose sought to be achieved by the parties who entered into the investment-related agreement constituting a commercial transaction, and the sale and purchase agreement formed by its exercise also falls within a commercial transaction. Accordingly, in such case, the right to demand purchase of shares should be understood to be extinguished upon the lapse of a five-year preclusive period by analogical application of Article 64 of the Commercial Act concerning the statute of limitations for commercial claims.\\n\\nMeanwhile, where an investment-related agreement provides that the investor may exercise the formative right of the right to demand purchase of shares upon default on the part of the investment target company, etc., unless there are special circumstances, the exercise period should be deemed to commence when the investment target company, etc. defaults on its obligation. Otherwise, if the investment target company, etc. defaults only after the exercise period has already expired, the investor would be unable to exercise the right to demand purchase of shares, which would be unreasonable.\\n\\nB. Determination in this case\\n\\n(1) According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following circumstances can be ascertained.\\n\\n(a) On September 19, 2003 and September 20, 2006, the Partnership at issue entered into the Acquisition Agreement at issue with DC Holdings and Defendant 2 and acquired convertible bonds issued by DC Holdings. On December 20, 2007, the Partnership at issue came to hold shares of DC Holdings by exercising the conversion right with respect to some of the convertible bonds.\\n\\n(b) On February 24, 2011, DC Holdings violated Article 15 of the Acquisition Agreement at issue by transferring major operating assets to Defendant DC Inside without obtaining the prior written consent of the Partnership at issue. This corresponds to a default on obligations prescribed in Article 26(1) items 9 and 10 of the Acquisition Agreement at issue.\\n\\n(c) Article 27 of the Acquisition Agreement at issue provides that, where the grounds set forth in Article 26(1) items 9 and 10 arise, the Partnership at issue may demand that Defendant 2 purchase all or part of the shares converted from the convertible bonds, and that by doing so a sale and purchase agreement concerning the shares subject to the purchase demand is formed between the Partnership at issue and Defendant 2. Article 27 of the Acquisition Agreement at issue also provides that, where the Partnership at issue exercises the right to demand purchase of shares, Defendant 2 shall pay the sale price within 30 days from that time or within the deadline designated by the Partnership at issue, and that the sale price shall be calculated as the amount obtained by adding interest computed on the principal invested by the Plaintiff at an annual compound rate of 9% for a certain period.\\n\\n(d) The Plaintiff received from the Partnership at issue a complete assignment of all rights under the Acquisition Agreement at issue, and on October 19, 2018, during the pendency of the lawsuit in the court below in this case, exercised against Defendant 2 the right to demand purchase of shares prescribed by Article 27 of the Acquisition Agreement at issue with respect to the 5,925 shares then held.\\n\\n(2) In light of these circumstances and the legal principles set forth above, the following conclusions are drawn.\\n\\n(a) The right to demand purchase of shares prescribed by Article 27 of the Acquisition Agreement at issue is a right by which the Partnership at issue, one party to the Acquisition Agreement at issue, can unilaterally cause a sale and purchase agreement concerning the shares at issue to be formed with Defendant 2, the counterparty, and therefore constitutes a type of formative right.\\n\\n(b) The above right to demand purchase of shares is a right that the Partnership at issue, as an investor and one party to the commercial contract, may exercise against Defendant 2, the other party, in the event that DC Holdings, the investment target company and also one party to the Acquisition Agreement at issue, defaults on obligations such as the prior written consent obligation under Article 15 of the Acquisition Agreement at issue. The reason Article 15 of the Acquisition Agreement at issue imposes a prior written consent obligation regarding the sale of major assets of DC Holdings, etc. is that it concerns an important matter directly linked to investment performance. Even if the obligor defaults on such obligation, it is not easy to compel performance, and it is also difficult to calculate a reasonable amount of damages resulting therefrom. In such circumstances, the right to demand purchase of shares serves to allow the Plaintiff, when DC Holdings, the investment target company, violates obligations that materially affect the investment performance of the investor, to ensure recovery of the principal and a certain return. Considering these circumstances collectively, it is reasonable to view the exercise period for the right to demand purchase of shares prescribed by Article 27 of the Acquisition Agreement at issue as five years by analogical application of Article 64 of the Commercial Act concerning the statute of limitations for commercial claims.\\n\\n(c) Although the Plaintiff exercised the right to demand purchase of shares on October 19, 2018, during the pendency of the lawsuit in the court below in this case, the right to demand purchase of shares should be deemed to have been extinguished by the lapse of the five-year preclusive period, which had already run from February 24, 2011, when DC Holdings defaulted on its obligation.\\n\\n(3) Ultimately, the determination of the court below that the Plaintiff’s right to demand purchase of shares had been extinguished by the lapse of the five-year preclusive period before its exercise is correct. There is no error in the judgment of the court below, such as a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the exercise period of the right to demand purchase of shares or a violation of the principle of confining adjudication to the matters argued, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n4. Determination on the claim for damages under Article 28 of the Acquisition Agreement at issue\\n\\nThe grounds for appeal on this point assert that the court below omitted a ruling on the starting point of the statute of limitations for the claim for damages under Article 28 of the Acquisition Agreement at issue and on the interruption of the statute of limitations.\\n\\nHowever, the court below expressly rejected the Plaintiff’s argument that the starting point of the statute of limitations should be the date on which it became aware of the breach of contract, by determining that the five-year commercial statute of limitations runs from February 24, 2011, the date of breach of contract, with respect to the above claim for damages.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Plaintiff argued that the statute of limitations for the above claim for damages was interrupted by the order of provisional attachment, but according to the record, the secured claim was a claim for the repurchase price based on the stock repurchase agreement under the Acquisition Agreement at issue, and thus the order of provisional attachment has no effect of interrupting the statute of limitations for the damages claim under Article 28 of the Acquisition Agreement at issue. Ultimately, even if the court below did not rule on the Plaintiff’s argument concerning interruption of the statute of limitations, since it is clear that the argument would be rejected, this cannot be said to be an error affecting the judgment (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DA24872, decided February 26, 2009, among others).\\n\\nIn light of the record and the relevant legal principles, when examining the reasons of the judgment of the court below, there is no error in the judgment that affected the outcome by omitting a ruling, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Plaintiff’s appeal is without merit and is dismissed in its entirety, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court, as ordered."}

{"[2021DA293213]": "The grounds for final appeal (including supplemental briefs submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds for final appeal, to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal) shall be determined.\\n\\n1. From the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\na. Defendant B Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “the Defendant Company”) was established for the purpose of manufacturing and selling computer systems, etc., and as of 2016. 12. 6. had issued 3,330,318 common shares and 260,000 preferred shares (240,000 preferred shares and 20,000 redeemable convertible preferred shares); Defendant C is the representative director who held a majority of the shares of the Defendant Company.\\n\\nb. On 2016. 12. 6., the Plaintiff and the Defendant Company agreed that the Plaintiff would subscribe for 200,000 redeemable convertible preferred shares with a par value of 500 won to be issued by the Defendant Company (hereinafter referred to as “the Shares in this case”) at 10,000 won per share (hereinafter referred to as “the instant new share subscription agreement”), and on 2016. 12. 8. paid the new share subscription price of 2,000,000,000 won (= 200,000 shares × 10,000 won per share) to the Defendant Company, thereby being allotted the Shares in this case on 2016. 12. 9. and coming to hold approximately 5.27% (= 200,000 shares held by the Plaintiff / 3,790,318 shares issued by the Defendant Company) of the total issued shares of the Defendant Company.\\n\\nc. At the time of the instant new share subscription agreement, the Defendant Company entered into an agreement with the Plaintiff that: ➀ if, after the Plaintiff’s investment, the Defendant Company conducts a paid-in capital increase, etc. at a price lower than the Plaintiff’s final per-share subscription price, or increases or decreases paid-in capital, etc. with respect to major management matters, it must notify the Plaintiff in advance and obtain the Plaintiff’s prior consent, and if it violates this, the Defendant Company would grant the Plaintiff, by way of damages, an early redemption claim right, etc. with respect to the Shares in this case, and in addition bear a penalty; and ➁ Defendant C agreed to jointly and severally perform the obligations owed by the Defendant Company to the Plaintiff.\\n\\nd. Thereafter, the Defendant Company held board meetings on 2018. 8. 28. and 2018. 9. 4. and resolved to issue 160,000 redeemable convertible preferred shares to D Co., Ltd. at a total price of 2,000,000,000 won, 12,500 won per share, and on 2018. 9. 6. allotted 160,000 redeemable convertible preferred shares to D (hereinafter referred to as “the First Paid-in Capital Increase”); and on 2018. 11. 20. resolved to issue 80,000 redeemable convertible preferred shares to F Co., Ltd., the executive partner of E, at a total price of 1,000,000,000 won, 12,500 won per share, and on 2018. 11. 29. allotted 80,000 redeemable convertible preferred shares to F (hereinafter referred to as “the Second Paid-in Capital Increase”), without giving prior notice to the Plaintiff or obtaining the Plaintiff’s prior consent with respect to the First and Second Paid-in Capital Increases.\\n\\ne. The Plaintiff filed the present action against the Defendants, seeking payment of the early redemption amount for the Shares in this case and the penalty for breach of agreement, on the ground that the Defendant Company, in the First and Second Paid-in Capital Increases, conducted each paid-in capital increase in violation of its obligation to give prior notice to and obtain prior consent from the Plaintiff and did not comply even with the Plaintiff’s demand for correction.\\n\\n2. The court below dismissed all of the Plaintiff’s claims against the Defendants, holding that: ➀ as to the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendant Company, the portion of the instant new share subscription agreement concerning the prior consent right with respect to major management matters was void as violating the principle of shareholder equality because it granted the Plaintiff, a partial shareholder, superior rights not recognized to the Defendant Company’s other shareholders and, in substance, absolutely guaranteed recovery of the Plaintiff’s invested capital; and, even if only the portion concerning breach of the prior notice obligation to the Plaintiff were considered, the degree of the breach was minor, so the Plaintiff could not demand early redemption and a penalty on that basis; and ➁ as to the Plaintiff’s claim against Defendant C, since the Defendant Company’s damages liability did not arise in violation of the principle of shareholder equality, etc., Defendant G, who jointly and severally guaranteed the same, could not otherwise bear liability.\\n\\n3. However, the judgment of the court below is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\na. 1) The principle of shareholder equality means that shareholders must be treated equally according to the number of shares they hold in their legal relationship with the company. An agreement in violation of this principle, whereby the company undertakes to grant superior rights or benefits only to certain shareholders, is void absent special circumstances (see Supreme Court Decision 2018DA9920, 9937 rendered on September 13, 2018, Supreme Court Decision 2018DA236241 rendered on August 13, 2020, etc.). However, even where the company treats certain shareholders differently by granting them superior rights or benefits, it may be permitted if it follows procedures and methods allowed by law or if there are special circumstances that can justify such differential treatment.\\n\\nFurthermore, whether differential treatment may be permitted should be determined carefully in light of the idea of justice and equity, by considering the specific content of the differential treatment, the background and purpose for which the company adopted such treatment, whether and to what extent the differential treatment was necessary for the interests of the company and all shareholders, whether the differential treatment of certain shareholders is based on the Commercial Act or other related statutes or instead conflicts with mandatory provisions of the Commercial Act, etc. or denies the essential status of shareholders as being subordinated to creditors, whether, in granting certain shareholders special authority concerning participation in and supervision of the company’s management, such authority restricts the decision-making power of the company’s organs and ultimately infringes shareholders’ voting rights, the content and degree of disadvantage suffered by other shareholders as a result of the differential treatment, whether the shareholders disadvantaged by the differential treatment consented to it in matters that each shareholder may dispose of, and the overall consent ratio, as well as all other circumstances such as whether the company is listed, its business purpose, governance structure, business status, and financial condition, so as to determine whether granting superior rights or benefits to certain shareholders accords with the interests of the shareholders and the company as a whole.\\n\\n2) a) Where, in entering into a new share subscription agreement for financing, a company agrees with a person who becomes a shareholder to obtain prior consent regarding the company’s decision-making, the agreement is one that treats shareholders differentially by granting superior rights only to certain shareholders. However, if the subscription funds paid by the shareholder were funds indispensably required for the company’s survival and development, if granting that shareholder consent rights regarding the company’s decision-making was unavoidable in order to attract investment, and if, even with such consent rights, other shareholders do not suffer substantial or direct damage or disadvantage and, rather, the shareholder is given an opportunity to monitor the company’s management activities, thereby benefiting the other shareholders and the company, then there are special circumstances that justify such differential treatment, and it may be allowed.\\n\\nb) If a company agrees with a person who becomes a shareholder to fully preserve the money paid as the share subscription price, or agrees to pay separate profits not paid to other shareholders in addition to dividends under Article 462 of the Commercial Act and other statutory provisions, then this is void as contrary to the principle of shareholder equality because the company thereby absolutely guarantees recovery of invested capital only for that shareholder and grants superior rights not recognized to other shareholders (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2018DA236241, etc.).\\n\\nBy contrast, where differential treatment pursuant to an agreement granting consent rights concluded between the company and a shareholder is exceptionally permitted, and the parties also enter into an agreement to pay money in the name of damages for breach of the consent-right agreement, and if that agreement can be understood as being for the purpose of compensating or making good the damages suffered by the shareholder due to the breach of the prior-consent obligation and ensuring performance of the obligation, then it constitutes an agreement fixing liquidated damages for nonperformance between the company and the shareholder, and is valid absent special circumstances; it cannot be concluded that it violates the principle of shareholder equality by absolutely guaranteeing recovery of invested capital for certain shareholders.\\n\\nHowever, even if an agreement fixing liquidated damages is valid, if the amount is unreasonably excessive, the court may reduce it pursuant to Article 398(2) of the Civil Act. Accordingly, when determining whether the agreed liquidated damages for breach of the consent-right agreement are excessive, the court must take into account all circumstances such as the motive and background for concluding the consent-right agreement and the liquidated damages agreement, the amount of actual damage suffered by the shareholder as a result of the company’s breach of the consent-right agreement, and the background and reasons for the company’s breach of the consent-right agreement, while taking care that such agreement does not in fact function as a means of absolutely guaranteeing recovery of all or part of the invested capital.\\n\\nb. In light of the foregoing legal principles, the following circumstances discernible from the facts and record above show that, although the agreement under which the Plaintiff, when subscribing for the Shares in this case, acquired prior consent rights, etc. with respect to the Defendant Company’s major management matters granted superior rights or benefits to certain shareholders, it may fall within the category of cases permitted because there are special circumstances that can justify differential treatment as being consistent with the interests of the Defendant Company as a whole, and the agreement that the Defendant Company would bear liability for damages, etc. in the event of its breach also serves to compel performance of the agreement concerning the Plaintiff’s prior consent rights, etc. and to compensate the Plaintiff for damages suffered in the event of nonperformance, so it is difficult to conclude that it is void as violating the principle of shareholder equality.\\n\\n1) Among the shareholders of the Defendant Company, Defendant C is a major shareholder holding more than half of the shares issued by the Defendant Company, and, while agreeing to grant the Plaintiff prior consent rights, etc. with respect to the Defendant Company’s management matters, he also agreed to jointly and severally perform the Defendant Company’s obligations under the instant new share subscription agreement, thereby approving differential treatment in which the majority shareholder grants superior rights to the minority shareholder Plaintiff. There is no circumstance indicating that the other shareholders objected to this or took issue with it. In other words, in this case, while the Plaintiff seeks damages, etc. against the Defendants on the ground that the Defendant Company breached the agreement, it is only the Defendant Company and Defendant C, who had consented thereto, that now raise the issue of violation of the principle of shareholder equality.\\n\\nRather, considering the Defendant Company’s business status, scale, financial condition, and other circumstances at the time of the instant new share subscription agreement, there is considerable room to view the subscription price paid by the Plaintiff as making a substantial contribution to securing liquidity and increasing capital for the Defendant Company, and thus as necessary for the interests of all shareholders.\\n\\n2) Even if it is not clear whether the Defendant Company’s other shareholders expressly consented to the differential treatment of the Plaintiff, the Commercial Act recognizes the rights of minority shareholders holding shares of a certain equity ratio or more, and, in a similar vein, merely granting such authority to the Plaintiff, a minority shareholder who acquired more than 5% of the Defendant Company’s total issued shares, for the purpose of monitoring and supervising the management matters of the controlling shareholder or management of the Defendant Company does not make it appear that substantial damage, etc. is caused to other minority shareholders. Also, in light of these aspects, it cannot be concluded that the Defendant Company’s other shareholders had a motive to oppose the differential treatment of the Plaintiff or formed opposing interests in relation to the Plaintiff.\\n\\n3) Where a company, without special circumstances or reasonable grounds, enters into an agreement only with certain shareholders for the return of invested principal or compensation for losses, there is room to regard the differential treatment of those shareholders as ordinarily involving conflicting economic interests vis-à-vis other shareholders and thus as void for violating the principle of shareholder equality. However, by contrast, when some minority shareholders are merely granted authority or status for the purpose of monitoring and supervising the major management matters of the controlling shareholder, it cannot be said that this unduly causes disadvantage to other minority shareholders; therefore, it should not be conclusively regarded as unreasonable and arbitrary discrimination.\\n\\nThe subject matter of the Plaintiff’s agreement concerning prior consent rights at issue in this case is whether to issue new shares or conduct a paid-in capital increase by a stock company. This is, in principle, a matter requiring a resolution of the board of directors and, absent special circumstances, does not require a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders; therefore, even if certain shareholders such as the Plaintiff possess prior consent rights, etc., it cannot be said that the voting rights of other shareholders are directly infringed.\\n\\n4) Also, even if the Plaintiff has prior notice or prior consent rights, etc. with respect to the Defendant Company’s major management matters, those are merely contractual rights under the instant new share subscription agreement, and even if a third party acquires the Plaintiff’s shares, such status is not succeeded to by the transferee absent special circumstances. And the Shares in this case acquired by the Plaintiff pursuant to the instant new share subscription agreement are in the form of redeemable convertible preferred shares, which originally could exercise redemption rights only after a certain redemption period had elapsed and only if distributable profits existed; moreover, prior consent rights, etc. concerning the Defendant Company’s management matters cannot be viewed as having been granted to the Plaintiff’s shares themselves. Therefore, the shares held by the Plaintiff cannot be viewed as a special class of shares impermissible under the Commercial Act.\\n\\n5) Meanwhile, the Plaintiff’s claims for damages, such as the early redemption claim against the Defendant Company or the share purchase claim against Defendant C and the penalty arising from the Defendant Company’s breach of the agreement, are not rights the Plaintiff initially held, but rights that arise only when the Defendant side breaches the agreement with the Plaintiff. Accordingly, leaving aside whether the Plaintiff’s early redemption claim arising from the effect of the agreed breach conforms to redemption requirements such as the existence of distributable profits under the Commercial Act, or whether the penalty agreement of an increasing structure after the contract is contrary to public order and morals and therefore cannot be given effect, the mere circumstance that the redemption amount agreed by the Plaintiff and the Defendants corresponds to the amount of the Plaintiff’s invested principal cannot make this identical to a case in which certain shareholders from the outset agreed to the return of invested principal for the purpose of recovering invested capital.\\n\\n6) Furthermore, if a minority shareholder who has been granted such superior authority or status unreasonably and excessively interferes with or controls the management of the controlling shareholder, thereby causing harm to the company or to all shareholders through the exercise of such authority, then, in addition to the fact that such exercise of authority may be controlled under the principle of good faith or the principle prohibiting abuse of rights, it should not be entirely barred merely by invoking a strict standard of equality among shareholders, given that some minority shareholders who invest large amounts of capital to subscribe for new shares are granted authority to monitor and supervise the company’s major management matters.\\n\\n7) Accordingly, the court below should have more carefully examined the specific factual relationship, including the Defendant Company’s financial situation, the urgency and necessity of attracting investment funds or issuing new shares, and the respective interests among the Plaintiff, the Defendants, and the other shareholders, and then comprehensively considered the attendant circumstances and rendered its judgment accordingly.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below, relying only on the circumstances stated in its opinion, held that the agreement under which the Defendant Company granted the Plaintiff prior consent rights, etc. with respect to major management matters in the instant new share subscription agreement violated the principle of shareholder equality and was void. The court below’s determination erred by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the principle of shareholder equality and by failing to conduct the necessary examination, thereby affecting the judgment. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n4.
