Therefore, without determining the remaining grounds for final appeal, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and so adjudge as per the order, by unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2022DA224986]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. According to the reasons of the judgment of the lower court and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. On 2015. 3. 3., the remaining Plaintiffs, excluding Plaintiff 11, Plaintiff 12, and Plaintiff 13, and GSP Co., Ltd. entered into an investment agreement (hereinafter referred to as “the Investment Agreement in this case”) with the Company in this case and the Defendant, who was then its largest shareholder and representative director, agreeing to subscribe for redeemable convertible preferred shares issued by Beyond Eye Co., Ltd. (its then trade name was ImageNext Co., Ltd.; hereinafter referred to as “the Company in this case”), and paid the share subscription price to the Company in this case.\\n\\nOn 2016. 3. 2., GSP Co., Ltd. transferred to Plaintiff 11, Plaintiff 12, and Plaintiff 13 each 5,000 shares out of the 15,000 redeemable convertible preferred shares it had acquired from the Company in this case. The Company in this case and the Defendant approved at that time that the above Plaintiffs would succeed to all rights and obligations held or borne by GSP Co., Ltd. under the Investment Agreement in this case.\\n\\nb. Article 25(1)6. of the Investment Agreement in this case provides, “If a petition for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings is filed without the written consent of the share subscriber, or if rehabilitation proceedings are commenced, the Company in this case and the Defendant shall be jointly and severally liable to pay to the share subscriber, as a contractual penalty, the sum of the acquisition price per share and the amount of interest applying 10% annual compound interest to that amount from the issuance date to the redemption date.” (The part that gives rise to a monetary payment obligation when rehabilitation proceedings are commenced upon a petition by a petitioner other than the Company in this case is hereinafter referred to as “the Agreement in this case.”)\\n\\nc. Another shareholder of the Company in this case filed a petition for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings against the Company in this case on 2019. 3. 6. without the Plaintiffs’ consent, and on 2019. 8. 19. those rehabilitation proceedings were commenced.\\n\\n2. The court below rendered a judgment dismissing in full the Plaintiffs’ claims seeking payment of money under the Agreement in this case on the following grounds.\\n\\nThe Agreement in this case establishes a money claim of the Plaintiffs against the Company in this case upon the suspensive condition that rehabilitation proceedings be commenced against the Company in this case. This is invalid because it guarantees the recovery of the invested capital to the Plaintiffs in absolute terms and thereby grants them preferential rights not recognized for other shareholders, in violation of the principle of shareholder equality.\\n\\nThe Defendant entered into a contract to provide joint and several guaranty for the Company in this case’s obligation to the Plaintiffs. However, since the principal obligation of the Company in this case to the Plaintiffs does not exist, having been created in violation of the principle of shareholder equality, the Defendant’s monetary payment obligation to the Plaintiffs under the Agreement in this case also does not exist by reason of accessory nature.\\n\\n3. However, the court below’s determination is difficult to uphold for the following reasons.\\n\\na. The obligation of the Company in this case under the Agreement in this case\\n\\n1) The principle of shareholder equality means that a shareholder must be treated equally in legal relations with the company according to the number of shares he or she holds. An agreement by which a company, in violation of this principle, undertakes to grant preferential rights or benefits only to certain shareholders is invalid unless special circumstances exist (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2020. 8. 13., 2018DA236241). However, even where a company treats certain shareholders differently by granting them preferential rights or benefits, such treatment may be permitted if it follows the procedures and methods allowed by law or if special circumstances exist that justify such differential treatment.\\n\\nFurthermore, whether differential treatment may be allowed must be determined carefully in light of notions of justice and equity, by comprehensively considering all circumstances, including the specific content of the differential treatment; the circumstances and purpose by which the company came to treat shareholders differently; whether and to what extent such differential treatment was necessary for the benefit of the company and all shareholders; whether the differential treatment of certain shareholders has a basis in the Commercial Act and other relevant statutes or instead violates mandatory provisions or denies the essential status of a shareholder who ranks behind creditors; whether, by granting certain shareholders special authority in relation to participation in and supervision of the company’s management, the company’s organs’ decision-making authority is restricted and, ultimately, the shareholders’ voting rights are infringed; the nature and extent of the disadvantage suffered by other shareholders as a result of the differential treatment; whether shareholders disadvantaged by differential treatment regarding matters that an individual shareholder may dispose of consented to such treatment and the overall rate of consent; and, among other things, the company’s listing status, business purpose, governance structure, business conditions, and financial condition, in order to determine whether granting preferential rights or benefits to certain shareholders and thereby treating shareholders differently conforms to the interests of the shareholders and the company as a whole.\\n\\n2) Where a company promises to pay money to a person who subscribes for newly issued shares and thereby acquires shareholder status, if the substance of the promise is an undertaking by the company, vis-à-vis the person who acquires shareholder status, to fully compensate the money paid as the share subscription price, or an undertaking to pay a separate return not paid to other shareholders in addition to dividends pursuant to the provisions of law such as Article 462 of the Commercial Act, then this constitutes the company’s granting to that shareholder alone preferential rights not recognized for other shareholders by absolutely guaranteeing the recovery of the invested capital only to that shareholder, and is invalid as being contrary to the principle of shareholder equality (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2018DA236241, etc.). Such an agreement endangers the company’s capital base, harms the interests of the company and other shareholders, and causes the shareholder to be freed even from the essential responsibility borne as a shareholder, thus amounting to the granting to a specific shareholder of rights exceeding the scope permitted by the Commercial Act; accordingly, even if all other shareholders of the company consented to such differential treatment, it is invalid in violation of the principle of shareholder equality.\\n\\n3) The foregoing facts are examined in light of these legal principles.\\n\\nThe parties to the Investment Agreement in this case are the Plaintiffs, the Defendant, and the Company in this case. The Investment Agreement in this case may be divided into the part of the contract between the Plaintiffs and the Company in this case and the part of the contract between the Plaintiffs and the Defendant.\\n\\nThe part of the Agreement in this case, which is part of the Investment Agreement in this case and was entered into by the Plaintiffs and the Company in this case, provides that a monetary payment obligation arises “if a petition for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings is filed without the written consent of the Plaintiffs, or if such proceedings are commenced,” and thus obligates the Company to pay the Plaintiffs the share subscription price and a prescribed surcharge even when rehabilitation proceedings are commenced upon the petition of another petitioner entitled to file a petition, regardless of whether the Company in this case is at fault. Accordingly, the Agreement in this case, in substance, absolutely guarantees to the Plaintiffs the recovery of the invested capital and thereby grants them preferential rights not recognized for other shareholders, and it also goes beyond the limits permitted by the Commercial Act, including the principle of capital maintenance, because it is in effect a return of capital from the company’s assets even where there are no distributable profits; therefore, even if all other shareholders of the Company in this case consented to such differential treatment, it is invalid in violation of the principle of shareholder equality.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Company in this case does not bear any obligation to the Plaintiffs under the Agreement in this case.\\n\\nb. The Defendant’s obligation under the Agreement in this case\\n\\n1) The principle of shareholder equality is a principle applied to the legal relations between a shareholder and the company. Where, when a shareholder enters into a contract with the company, another shareholder of the company or an individual director also participates as a party, the contract between the shareholder and the other shareholder is unrelated to shareholder equality; therefore, the principle of shareholder equality does not directly apply to the legal relations between a shareholder and another shareholder of the company or an individual director. A shareholder, when entering into a contract with the company, may under the principle of private autonomy also enter into a contract concerning the company with another shareholder or an individual director, and unless special circumstances exist, the effect of such contract should be viewed separately from the effect of the contract entered into between the shareholder and the company. Furthermore, in interpreting the content of a contract entered into by a shareholder with another shareholder or an individual director of the company, the general principles governing contract interpretation apply; that is, the contract must be reasonably interpreted in accordance with logic and experience and the general sense of society and commercial practice, taking comprehensive account of the form and content of the contract, the motive, background, and purpose of its conclusion, and the true intent of the parties.\\n\\n2) The foregoing facts and the facts ascertainable from the reasons of the judgment of the lower court and the record are examined in light of these legal principles.\\n\\nThe principle of shareholder equality does not directly apply to the part of the Investment Agreement in this case entered into by the Plaintiffs and the Defendant. Even if the part of the Agreement in this case, which is part of the Investment Agreement in this case, is invalid in the legal relations between the Plaintiffs and the Company in this case as being contrary to the principle of shareholder equality, it does not affect the effect of the part of the contract entered into by the Plaintiffs and the Defendant, unless special circumstances exist.\\n\\nFurthermore, considering the motive, background, and purpose of the Agreement in this case, its textual content, and the true intent of the parties, there is a strong room to view that the Plaintiffs and the Defendant did not enter into a guaranty contract concerning the Company in this case’s monetary payment obligation owed to the Plaintiffs under the Agreement in this case, but instead entered into a contract under which the Defendant himself undertook a joint and several obligation of the same content to the Plaintiffs. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\na) The Plaintiffs and the Company in this case entered into the Investment Agreement in this case in order to subscribe for the redeemable convertible preferred shares issued by the Company in this case, and included a provision to protect the investor Plaintiffs by granting them opportunities to participate in management and to recover their investment, and by obligating the Company in this case to bear, in the event of breach, monetary payment obligations in the nature of a contractual penalty. However, the reason the Defendant, who was the Company’s largest shareholder and representative director, was included as a party to the investment agreement appears to be that, in addition to the purpose of preparing for the case where the Company in this case would lack the financial capacity to perform the monetary payment obligation, there was a concern that the provision granting a specific shareholder rights differentiated from those of other shareholders would become invalid for violating the principle of shareholder equality, the principle of capital maintenance, and the like, so that the Company would not bear the corresponding obligation; accordingly, it appears that the parties intended to compel performance of the contractual obligations by requiring the Defendant personally to bear responsibility as well. On this view, even if the Company in this case’s agreement to bear obligations to the Plaintiffs is invalid, interpreting the Defendant’s agreement to bear obligations to the Plaintiffs as valid better accords with the motive, background, and purpose for concluding the contract by including the Defendant as a party.\\n\\nb) By its very text, the Agreement in this case merely provides that the Company in this case and the Defendant shall be jointly and severally liable to pay the share acquisition price plus a prescribed surcharge to the Plaintiffs. No provision in the entirety of the Investment Agreement in this case expressly states that the Defendant jointly and severally guaranteed the Company’s debt. By contrast, Article 24(7) of the Investment Agreement in this case expressly indicates such content by providing that “when the Plaintiffs exercise their share purchase right against the Defendant, the Defendant may designate a third party to purchase the Plaintiffs’ shares, and in such case, the Defendant shall jointly and severally guarantee the share-purchase obligation borne by the third party designated by him.”\\n\\nc) A joint and several guaranty obligation has the purpose of securing performance of the principal obligation and is accessory to the principal obligation. If the Defendant filed a petition for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings against the Company in this case without the Plaintiffs’ consent, the Defendant would bear a monetary payment obligation upon breach of that contract as a person who was to perform an act obtaining the Plaintiffs’ consent, and the obligation borne by the Defendant at that time cannot be said to be accessory to the obligation borne by the Company. The Agreement in this case also appears to have the purpose of holding the Defendant responsible as the person in charge of the Company’s management if rehabilitation proceedings were commenced upon the petition of another petitioner entitled to file a petition because the Company’s management situation deteriorated. Therefore, with respect to the monetary payment obligation under the Agreement in this case, it is difficult to view the Company’s obligation as principal and the Defendant’s obligation as accessory.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below held that the Defendant entered into a contract to jointly and severally guarantee the Company’s monetary payment obligation to the Plaintiffs under the Agreement in this case, and reasoned that, because the Agreement in this case is invalid, the Company’s obligation to the Plaintiffs does not exist, and accordingly the Defendant’s obligation to the Plaintiffs likewise does not exist by reason of its accessory nature. This determination by the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misconstruing the legal principles on interpretation of the Investment Agreement in this case and failing to conduct the necessary fact-finding, among others. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment of the lower court is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2023DA210670]": "We consider the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons for the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\na. On 2013. 8. 30., the Plaintiff entered into an investment agreement with the Defendant, under which the Plaintiff subscribed to 17,850 convertible redeemable preferred shares issued by the Defendant for 999,600,000 won (hereinafter referred to as the “instant investment agreement”), and paid the share subscription price to the Defendant.\\n\\nb. Under the instant investment agreement, if the Defendant files an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings, it must first obtain the Plaintiff’s written consent (Article 15, item 8, hereinafter referred to as the “instant consent right agreement”); if this is violated, the Plaintiff may issue a demand to the Defendant and, if the cause of the violation is not remedied within 2 weeks from the date of such demand, terminate the investment agreement (Article 29, paragraph 1, item 10); and if the Defendant fails to make an explanation or remedy during that period, the Defendant shall pay to the Plaintiff the share subscription price and, in addition thereto, an amount calculated at the prescribed rate from the date of payment of the share subscription price until the date of recovery by the Plaintiff as damages (Article 30, paragraph 1, item 4, paragraph 2, hereinafter referred to as the “instant damages agreement,” and the claim arising from that agreement as the “instant damages claim”).\\n\\nc. On 2016. 5. 30., the Defendant filed an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings without the Plaintiff’s written consent. On 2016. 7. 4., the Plaintiff demanded that the Defendant explain and remedy the application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings within 2 weeks, but the Defendant took no particular action.\\n\\nd. On 2016. 7. 14., a decision to commence rehabilitation proceedings was rendered with respect to the Defendant, on 2017. 2. 15., a decision approving the rehabilitation plan was rendered, and on 2019. 12. 10., the rehabilitation proceedings were concluded.\\n\\ne. The Plaintiff filed, in the rehabilitation proceedings against the Defendant, a rehabilitation claim in the amount of 1,329,108,555 won as the instant damages claim (999,600,000 won for the share subscription price and 329,508,555 won as the additional amount calculated at the prescribed rate), and the Defendant objected to that filing. The Plaintiff filed a petition for an adjudication through investigation seeking confirmation of the instant damages claim, and, after the rehabilitation court rendered a decision of nonexistence of that claim, brought this action.\\n\\n2. Judgment on the grounds of appeal regarding whether the principle of shareholder equality was violated\\n\\na. Relevant legal principles\\n\\n1) The principle of shareholder equality means that shareholders must be treated equally according to the number of shares they hold in their legal relationship with the company. An agreement that violates this principle and provides only certain shareholders with superior rights or benefits is void unless special circumstances exist (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2018DA236241, decided on 2020. 8. 13.). However, even where a company grants superior rights or benefits to certain shareholders and treats them differently from other shareholders, such treatment may be permitted if it follows procedures and methods allowed by law or if there are special circumstances that justify such differential treatment.\\n\\nFurthermore, whether differential treatment may be permitted should be determined carefully in light of the concept of justice and equity, by considering all circumstances, including the specific content of the differential treatment; the circumstances and purpose under which the company came to engage in differential treatment; whether and to what extent the differential treatment was necessary for the interests of the company and all shareholders; whether the differential treatment of certain shareholders was based on the Commercial Act or other relevant statutes, or whether it contravenes mandatory provisions or denies the essential status of shareholders who rank behind creditors; whether, by granting certain shareholders special authority concerning participation in and supervision of the company’s management, the decision-making authority of the company’s organs is restricted and, ultimately, the shareholders’ voting rights are infringed; the content and degree of the disadvantage suffered by other shareholders due to the differential treatment; whether the disadvantaged shareholders consented to the differential treatment concerning matters that an individual shareholder may dispose of and the overall rate of consent; and, among other things, whether, in light of whether the company is listed, its business purpose, governance structure, business status, financial condition, and all other relevant circumstances, treating shareholders differently by granting superior rights or benefits to certain shareholders is consistent with the interests of the shareholders and the company as a whole.\\n\\n2) a) Where a company, in entering into a new share subscription agreement for fundraising, agrees to obtain prior consent from a person who will acquire the status of a shareholder regarding the company’s decision-making, this constitutes differential treatment by granting superior rights to certain shareholders only; however, such treatment may be permitted if the share subscription price paid by the shareholder was capital indispensable to the company’s continuation and development, if granting that shareholder a consent right regarding the company’s decision-making was unavoidable in order to attract investment, and if, even with the granting of such consent right, the other shareholders do not suffer substantive or direct damage or disadvantage and, rather, the arrangement benefits the other shareholders and the company by, for example, providing certain shareholders with an opportunity to monitor the company’s management activities, thereby justifying the differential treatment.\\n\\nb) If a company agrees with a person who will acquire the status of a shareholder to fully reimburse the money paid in as the share subscription price, or if it agrees to pay a separate benefit that is not paid to the other shareholders in addition to dividends under the provisions of the law, such as Article 462 of the Commercial Act, this constitutes granting that shareholder a superior right not recognized for the other shareholders by absolutely guaranteeing the recovery of the invested capital only for that shareholder, and is void as contrary to the principle of shareholder equality (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2018DA236241, etc.).\\n\\nBy contrast, where the company and the shareholder exceptionally agree to differential treatment under a consent-right granting agreement and, together therewith, enter into an agreement to pay money in the name of damages for breach of that agreement, and if that agreement can be viewed as intended to secure performance of the obligation by compensating or indemnifying the shareholder for the damage suffered from the breach of the obligation to obtain prior consent, then it is an agreement fixing damages for breach of contract between the company and the shareholder, and is valid unless special circumstances exist; it cannot be concluded that it violates the principle of shareholder equality by absolutely guaranteeing the recovery of the invested capital for certain shareholders.\\n\\nHowever, even if the agreement fixing damages is valid, the court may reduce it pursuant to Article 398, paragraph 2, of the Civil Act if the amount is unjustly excessive. Accordingly, when determining whether the agreed amount of damages for breach of the consent-right granting agreement is unreasonable, the court should take into account all circumstances, including the motive and background for entering into the consent-right granting agreement and the agreement fixing damages, the actual amount of damage suffered by the shareholder due to the company’s breach of the consent-right granting agreement, and the circumstances and reasons why the company came to violate the consent-right granting agreement, so that such agreement does not function in substance as a means of absolutely guaranteeing the recovery of the invested capital.\\n\\nb. The court below’s determination\\n\\nThe court below held that the instant damages agreement constituted an agreement by which the Defendant, a company, granted only to the Plaintiff, one of its shareholders, superior rights not recognized for other shareholders, and that it was therefore void as contrary to the principle of shareholder equality.\\n\\nc. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\n1) However, if the above factual relations and the reasons for the judgment of the court below are examined in light of the relevant legal principles, the court below’s determination is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\na) The instant consent right agreement granted superior rights or benefits to certain shareholders, but it is highly likely that this falls within the category of special circumstances that can justify differential treatment as being consistent with the interests of the shareholders and the company as a whole. The specific reasons are as follows. (1) The convertible redeemable preferred shares acquired by the Plaintiff included voting rights to participate in the company’s important decision-making at the shareholders’ meeting (Article 8 of the instant investment agreement). Through the instant investment agreement, the Plaintiff came to hold approximately 5% of the shares then issued by the Defendant, which is below the 10% threshold under which the shareholder’s right to file an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings under subparagraph 1(b) of Article 34, paragraph 2, of the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Debtor Rehabilitation Act”) and the threshold for exercising the right to request a dissolution judgment under Article 520, paragraph 1, among the minority shareholder rights under the Commercial Act, but exceeds 3%, which is the threshold for exercising, among the minority shareholder rights under the Commercial Act, the right to make proposals at the shareholders’ meeting (Article 363-2), the right to demand convocation of a shareholders’ meeting (Article 366), the right to request dismissal of a director (Article 385, paragraph 2), the right to request dismissal of an auditor (Article 415, Article 385, paragraph 2), the right to inspect accounting books (Article 466), and the right to inspect business operations (Article 467). In addition, in light of the Defendant’s corporate scale and financial condition, the share subscription price paid by the Plaintiff appears to have contributed substantially to securing the Defendant’s liquidity and increasing its capital.\\n\\n(2) The company decision that was the subject of the instant consent right agreement concerns whether to file an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings. An application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings constitutes an important matter not falling within the ordinary business affairs within the authority of the representative director, and thus, in principle, requires a resolution of the board of directors (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2019DA204463, decided on 2019. 8. 14.); however, unless special circumstances exist, such as a separate provision in the Defendant’s articles of incorporation, a resolution of the shareholders’ meeting is not required, and therefore the instant consent right agreement did not directly infringe the voting rights of other shareholders. In the end, it is difficult to conclude that other shareholders suffered substantive or direct damage or disadvantage merely because only the Plaintiff, among the shareholders of the company, was granted a prior consent right regarding whether to file an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings; rather, by providing the Plaintiff with an opportunity to monitor the Defendant’s management activities, there is also the possibility that this benefits other minority shareholders.\\n\\n(3) The Defendant, due to the instant consent right agreement, could not file an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings without the Plaintiff’s consent, so the degree to which the decision-making authority of the Defendant’s organs, such as directors, was restricted may be regarded as fairly high.\\n\\nHowever, the instant damages claim arises if the Defendant fails to make an explanation or remedy during the 2-week period from the date of the Plaintiff’s demand, and thus it includes the purport that, if the Defendant sufficiently explains the company’s situation and the necessity of filing the application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings to the Plaintiff before filing such application and goes through the process of persuading the Plaintiff, the Defendant may be exempted from liability. In the course of the Plaintiff and the Defendant exchanging opinions on whether filing an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings is beneficial to the company as a whole, a better alternative may be found, the management’s fault that caused the deterioration of the Defendant’s situation may be discovered, and by having the Defendant explain to and persuade the Plaintiff regarding the necessity of filing the application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings, the Defendant may make a more prudent management judgment, thereby ultimately producing an effect of enhancing the interests of the company as a whole.\\n\\n(4) The Plaintiff is a public institution that performs roles such as providing credit and funds to small and medium-sized enterprises, etc. that develop or commercialize technology, and implements policies to promote the growth of those enterprises and to foster the development of the economy and industry as a whole by supporting technologically capable but financially under-resourced small and medium-sized venture enterprises with credit and funds financed by public funds. In its position of performing a public role, the Plaintiff may be viewed as having entered into the instant consent right agreement as one of the devices to prevent the so-called moral hazard problem in which the Defendant’s controlling shareholder or management neglects the company’s interests and pursues private gain while making an investment decision in the Defendant. Respecting the purport and purpose of the instant consent right agreement has an aspect that also accords with the Defendant’s interests.\\n\\nb) The instant damages agreement may also be viewed, in substance, as an arrangement intended to secure performance of the obligation by requiring compensation or indemnification of the Plaintiff’s damage in the event of nonperformance of the instant consent right agreement, and therefore as not violating the principle of shareholder equality. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) The instant damages agreement is not an agreement that imposes a monetary payment obligation merely because of the result that rehabilitation proceedings have commenced, or because there was an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings, as in a case where rehabilitation proceedings are commenced upon an application by an applicant other than the Defendant. The Defendant assumes the obligation, before filing an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings, to sufficiently explain the company’s difficult situation and the necessity of filing such application to the Plaintiff and to go through the process of persuading the Plaintiff; and even if, due to urgent circumstances, the Defendant filed the application without following such process, it may be additionally given an opportunity to explain or remedy this in accordance with the Plaintiff’s demand.\\n\\n(2) The instant damages claim arises only when, before filing an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings, the Defendant violates the obligation to obtain the Plaintiff’s prior consent through the persuasion process and then fails to take measures to explain and remedy the matter through a process of explanation and persuasion to the Plaintiff even afterward, while the rehabilitation proceedings against the Defendant continue.\\n\\n(3) Therefore, the instant damages agreement, in substance as well, is an agreement by which the Defendant undertakes to pay damages resulting from breach of the obligations under the instant consent right agreement, and is intended to secure performance of the obligations under the agreement by compensating or indemnifying the damage that the Plaintiff will suffer from the breach. Even if the amount fixed as damages corresponds to the amount invested by the Plaintiff, such circumstance alone does not necessarily mean that the agreement absolutely guarantees the recovery of the invested capital.\\n\\n(4) Meanwhile, in light of the purpose of the Debtor Rehabilitation Act, which aims to promote efficient rehabilitation of the debtor or its business by adjusting the legal relationships of interested persons such as creditors, shareholders, and equity holders, or to fairly liquidate and distribute the assets of a debtor for whom rehabilitation is difficult, if a company, in conjunction with an agreement granting consent rights regarding the filing of an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings to certain shareholders, agrees to fix liquidated damages, and if there are special circumstances such as that filing an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings was unavoidable and clearly in the company’s interests, the company made reasonable and sufficient efforts to explain the company’s situation and persuade the shareholder in order to obtain consent from certain shareholders, but the shareholder, contrary to the company’s interests and without reasonable grounds, did not consent to the filing of the application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings, thereby making it inevitable to file the application without that shareholder’s consent, the company cannot be said to bear liability for damages to that shareholder.\\n\\nHowever, in the present case, there are no special circumstances indicating that the Defendant would not bear liability for damages arising from breach of the instant consent right agreement, such as that the Defendant made reasonable and sufficient efforts to explain the company’s situation and persuade the Plaintiff in order to obtain the Plaintiff’s consent to the filing of an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings.\\n\\n2) Nevertheless, the court below erred in its judgment that the instant damages agreement is void as contrary to the principle of shareholder equality by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the principle of shareholder equality and failing to fully examine the necessary matters, which affected the judgment.\\n\\n3. Judgment on the grounds of appeal regarding whether the principle of capital maintenance and the principle prohibiting return of capital contributions, as well as Articles 146 and 217, etc. of the Debtor Rehabilitation Act, were violated\\n\\na. The court below held that the instant damages agreement, in substance, requires the Plaintiff to receive a full refund of its capital contribution under the name of damages and guarantees the return of the principal investment, even though there are no distributable profits if the Defendant files an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings, and therefore violates the principle of capital maintenance and the principle prohibiting return of capital contributions under the Commercial Act, and is void for violating mandatory provisions such as Articles 146 and 217 of the Debtor Rehabilitation Act, which provide that shareholders are subordinate to creditors by treating the Plaintiff, a shareholder, on equal footing with creditors.\\n\\nb. As seen above, the instant damages agreement, not only in form but also in substance, requires payment of damages only when the Defendant violates its duty to file an application for commencement of rehabilitation proceedings after obtaining prior consent through the process of explaining and persuading the Plaintiff regarding the unavoidable circumstances requiring such application. It is difficult to view the instant damages agreement as a refund of the capital contribution to the Plaintiff, who is a shareholder, despite the absence of distributable profits, or as converting the Plaintiff, who holds a subordinate status as a shareholder, into a creditor of superior status merely because rehabilitation proceedings have commenced.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, on a different premise, the court below erred in its judgment that the instant damages agreement is void as violating the principle of capital maintenance and the principle prohibiting return of capital contributions under the Commercial Act and mandatory provisions such as Articles 146 and 217 of the Debtor Rehabilitation Act, by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the principle of capital maintenance and failing to fully examine the necessary matters, which affected the judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for a new trial and determination. It is so adjudged, in unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision, as follows."}

question: A stock company that had been engaged in construction and leasing business separated its leasing business division and newly incorporated B stock company. When C stock company, which was engaged in construction and shipping business, sought to demerge its construction business division, A stock company merged the demerged construction business division. In addition, A stock company intends to acquire the transportation business license of D stock company, which is engaged in transportation business. E stock company owns 70% of the total number of issued shares of A stock company. Which of the following statements is correct? (All companies are unlisted companies, each item is independent, and where there is dispute, the precedents shall apply)
A: If, among the debts of A stock company, the demerger plan does not separately provide for allocation of liabilities, A stock company and B stock company are jointly and severally liable to perform those debts; however, debts whose due date had not arrived at the time of the demerger are excluded from joint and several liability, and only A stock company is liable to perform them.
B: If, among the debts of C stock company, the demerger-merger agreement does not separately provide for allocation of liabilities, and after the demerger-merger a creditor of C stock company files a lawsuit against C stock company concerning C stock company's debt and obtains a final judgment, thereby extending the statute of limitations period, the effect of that extension also extends to A stock company, another debtor.
C: If A stock company's acquisition of D stock company's transportation business license does not have a material effect on A stock company's business, even where that transportation business license is D stock company's sole license for its business and D stock company transfers it and thereby ceases business, D stock company's transfer of the transportation business license is valid if approved by D stock company's board of directors.
D: If D stock company liquidates, when the liquidation affairs are concluded, the liquidator must, without delay, prepare a settlement report and submit it to the shareholders' meeting and obtain approval by special resolution.
E: A stock company may provide shares of E stock company to the shareholders of C stock company as consideration for the demerger-merger, and for this purpose A stock company may acquire shares of E stock company.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2007DA73321]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nUnder Article 530-9, Paragraph (1) of the Commercial Act, debts of the company before a split or split merger, for which the company established by the split or split merger and the surviving company are liable to pay jointly and severally to the company’s creditors, include debts that arose before the effective date of the company split or split merger but whose due date for payment had not yet arrived at the time of the split or split merger.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the lower court judgment and the evidence adopted by the lower court, in or around March 2005, the Defendant Company entered into a contract with the Plaintiff Company to receive approximately 300 tons of high-tensile reinforcing bars necessary for the construction site of the ○○○○○ Church and its affiliated kindergarten above ground in Jeju City (address omitted) (hereinafter referred to as “the construction site at issue”), for which the Defendant Company was carrying out construction work under a contract (hereinafter referred to as “the supply contract at issue”); since it could not accurately predict the time when reinforcing bars would be needed at the construction site, the supply period was set only as “until 2005,” beginning in or around March 2005, without separately specifying the month or day, and it was agreed that payment would be made in cash on the 16th of the same month for deliveries made from the 1st to the 15th of each month, and on the 1st of the following month for deliveries made from the 16th to the last day of each month; after entering into the above contract, while receiving reinforcing bars from the Plaintiff Company, the Defendant Company decided to split the company in such a way that Shinire Togeon Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Shinire Togeon”), which was to be newly established separately to take charge of the business division related to building construction business and civil engineering business, would assume the amount of liabilities related to that business division, and that pre-split debts would be jointly and severally borne by the Defendant Company and the newly established company, and after preparing a split plan accordingly, obtained a special resolution of the shareholders’ meeting and completed registration of the split on 2005. 6. 22.; and the Plaintiff Company supplied high-tensile reinforcing bars worth a total of 172,550,220 won to the construction site at issue pursuant to the supply contract at issue from 2005. 3. 25. to 2005. 10. 3. As can be seen from the foregoing facts found, in light of the legal principles stated above, the claim for the price of goods acquired by the Plaintiff Company, although the specific due dates for payment differed because the goods were supplied in installments without a fixed specific supply time for the contracted goods, ultimately arose merely under the supply contract at issue concluded before the above company split, and therefore, even if the due dates for payment arrived after the above company split, it should be deemed to constitute debts before the company split under Article 530-9, Paragraph (1) of the Commercial Act; accordingly, the Defendant Company would be liable to pay jointly and severally with Shinire Togeon for the claim for the price of goods acquired by the Plaintiff Company even after the above company split.\\n\\nTherefore, the lower court’s determination to this effect is proper, although there is no denying that its expression is somewhat inappropriate in some respects, and it cannot be said that there was any violation of the rules of evidence assessment or any error of law in misapprehending the legal principle concerning the scope of debts for which the company established by the split and the surviving company bear joint and several liability in a company split.\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved as stated in the dispositive portion."}

{"[2016DA34687]": "We determine the grounds of appeal (the statements in the supplemental brief of grounds of appeal submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal has expired shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Facts\\nThe facts found by the court below are as follows.\\n\\na. On June 28, 2007, the Plaintiff entered into a corporate passbook automatic loan transaction agreement with Wonyoung Information Industry Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Wonyoung Information Industry”) with a credit limit of 100 million won and a maturity date of June 27, 2008, and made the loan accordingly (hereinafter referred to as “the loan at issue”); around June 25, 2008, the Plaintiff agreed to extend the maturity date to June 26, 2009, and around November 1, 2008, increased the credit limit to 170 million won.\\n\\nb. On October 8, 2008, the Plaintiff entered into a credit transaction agreement, foreign exchange transaction agreement, and payment guarantee transaction agreement with Wonyoung Information Industry, each with a limit amount of US$700,000, and issued a letter of credit with Wonyoung Information Industry as the applicant for issuance; however, because Wonyoung Information Industry did not pay the amount by the maturity date of January 20, 2009, the Plaintiff made substitute payment on January 21, 2009 in the amount of US$699,863.53 (the amount converted into Korean won being 642,110,177 won) (hereinafter referred to as “the payment guarantee loan at issue”).\\n\\nc. Around 2013, the Plaintiff filed an action against Wonyoung Information Industry seeking repayment of loans and the like, and on March 4, 2014, obtained a judgment stating that “Wonyoung Information Industry shall pay to the Plaintiff 1,472,459,611 won and, among that amount, money calculated at the rate of 17% per annum from August 27, 2013 until the date of full payment on 642,110,177 won, and money calculated at the rate of 18% per annum from August 27, 2013 until the date of full payment on 169,854,360 won” (Seoul Central District Court Case No. 2013GADAN241222), and the above judgment became final and conclusive as entered.\\n\\nd. On November 4, 2009, Wonyoung Information Industry and the Defendant entered into a spin-off merger agreement (hereinafter referred to as “the spin-off merger agreement at issue”) providing that “a part of the assets of Wonyoung Information Industry (registration number for the electrical construction business portion: Gyeonggi No. ○○○○○) shall be spun off, and the Defendant shall comprehensively succeed to the rights and obligations concerning all licenses, equipment, personnel, contract management, defect repair, and the like of the electrical construction business portion, which is part of Wonyoung Information Industry’s business, while Wonyoung Information Industry shall continue to exist.”\\n\\ne. On November 19, 2009, Wonyoung Information Industry and the Defendant each held an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders and passed resolutions approving the spin-off merger agreement at issue, and Wonyoung Information Industry completed registration of the spin-off merger on December 22, 2009, and the Defendant on December 30, 2009.\\n\\n2. Determination on the Grounds of Appeal\\na. Former Commercial Act (as in effect before amendment by Act No. 13523 of December 1, 2015; hereinafter referred to as the “former Commercial Act”) Article 530-9, paragraph (1) provides: “The company established as a result of a spin-off or spin-off merger, or the surviving company (hereinafter referred to as the ‘beneficiary company’), shall be liable jointly to perform with respect to the corporate debts of the company prior to the spin-off or spin-off merger.” (Article 530-9, paragraph (1) of the Commercial Act as amended on December 1, 2015 provides: “The spin-off company, the simple spin-off newly established company, the spin-off succession company, or the spin-off merger newly established company shall be liable jointly to perform with respect to the debts of the spin-off company prior to the spin-off or spin-off merger,” thereby expressly stating that the “spin-off company” and the “spin-off merger newly established company,” etc. bear joint liability with respect to the same debts of the spin-off company.) This provision establishes statutory liability imposed to protect creditors who are adversely affected in the recovery of their claims due to changes in the debtor’s responsible assets caused by a corporate spin-off; the beneficiary company and the company prior to the spin-off or spin-off merger bear quasi-joint and several liability with respect to the corporate debts prior to the spin-off or spin-off merger (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DA95769, rendered on August 26, 2010).\\n\\nAlthough the Commercial Act does not contain any limitation provision regarding the period or amount for which a creditor may impose joint liability under the above provision, there is no need to protect the creditor more strongly than before the spin-off or spin-off merger. The obligation for which the beneficiary company bears liability jointly to perform to the creditor is the same obligation as that borne by the company prior to the spin-off or spin-off merger to the creditor. Accordingly, it is reasonable to regard the limitation period and commencement point of the joint and several obligation borne by the beneficiary company to the creditor as being the same as those of the obligation borne by the company prior to the spin-off or spin-off merger to the creditor. Ultimately, the creditor should be deemed able to hold the beneficiary company jointly liable within the limitation period for the relevant claim, regardless of the value of the assets succeeded to by reason of the spin-off.\\n\\nIn a quasi-joint and several obligation, a ground for interruption of the statute of limitations or waiver of the benefit of the statute of limitations, such as a demand for performance against one obligor or acknowledgment of the obligation by one obligor, does not affect the other obligors (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DA91886, rendered on April 14, 2011). Accordingly, even if, after the spin-off or spin-off merger has been effected, the creditor files an action against the spin-off company concerning the debt of the spin-off company prior to the spin-off or spin-off merger, thereby interrupting the statute of limitations as against the spin-off company or obtaining a final and conclusive judgment that extends the limitation period, the effect of such interruption or extension of the statute of limitations does not extend to the beneficiary company, which is another obligor.\\n\\nb. The court below determined that the commencement point of the statute of limitations for each of the claims at issue was the maturity date of each of the claims at issue, and thus found that the loan claim at issue and the payment guarantee loan claim were both barred by the statute of limitations, and did not accept the Plaintiff’s argument that the commencement point of the statute of limitations for each of the claims at issue was the date of registration of the spin-off merger, December 30, 2009. The reasons may be summarized as follows.\\n\\n(1) The loan at issue lost the benefit of the term on December 29, 2008 and reached maturity, and the payment guarantee loan at issue reached maturity on January 21, 2009.\\n\\n(2) Since each of the obligations at issue is a commercial debt to which a five-year statute of limitations applies, the statute of limitations for the loan claim at issue against the Defendant expired on December 29, 2013, and the statute of limitations for the payment guarantee loan claim at issue expired on January 21, 2014.\\n\\n(3) Since it is clear from the record that this action was filed on June 2, 2014, after the expiration of the above respective limitation periods, all of the claims at issue are barred by the statute of limitations.\\n\\nc. The determination of the court below is proper in light of the foregoing legal principles. The court below did not err, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, by exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or by misapprehending the legal nature of joint liability under Article 530-9, paragraph (1) of the former Commercial Act, or the legal principles concerning the limitation period and its commencement point, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n3. Because the Plaintiff’s appeal is without merit, the appeal is dismissed and the costs of appeal are to be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[91DA14369]": "1. We consider together the second and fourth grounds of appeal submitted by Attorney Park Jeong-seo, counsel for the Plaintiff, and the supplemental grounds of appeal submitted by the same attorney Lee Byeong-hu.\\n\\n(1) Commercial Act Article 380 provides that the provisions of Article 190 of the same Act shall apply mutatis mutandis even to an action for confirmation of the absence of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, thereby ensuring that even if a judgment confirming the absence of a resolution becomes final, the effect of that judgment does not affect the rights and obligations of third parties who transacted with the company before the judgment became final; needless to say, the legislative purpose of this is to promote transaction security by protecting third parties who transacted in the belief that the company’s external acts, having undergone internal decision-making within the company in appearance, were valid.\\n\\nHowever, Commercial Act Article 380 does not comprehensively define an action for confirmation of the absence of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, to which Article 190 of the same Act applies mutatis mutandis, as every form of action for confirmation of the absence of a resolution, but restrictively defines it as “an action seeking confirmation of the absence of a resolution on the ground that there is a material defect in the convocation procedure or resolution method of the general meeting to the extent that it cannot be deemed that a resolution of the general meeting exists.” This means that the provision is intended to cover only cases in which, at least in appearance, there was a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders as the internal decision-making of the relevant company, but the convocation procedure and resolution method were materially defective so that the resolution cannot legally be deemed to exist; it is construed that the provision is so stated in order to draw the limits of protection for third parties, because even in cases where the company was in no way involved in the outward manifestation of the existence of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, such as where a person who has no relation whatsoever to the company or who does not participate in its management and control forges or falsely prepares minutes of the general meeting of shareholders and thereby creates the outward appearance that a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders exists, imposing liability on the company as a valid corporate act would be excessively prioritizing the interests of third parties and forcing sacrifice upon the company, which would be inequitable.\\n\\nTherefore, in an action for confirmation of the absence of a resolution under Commercial Act Article 380, to which Article 190 of the same Act applies mutatis mutandis, the absence of a resolution means only the case where, although a resolution was ostensibly formed by a meeting convened and held as the general meeting of shareholders of the relevant company, there is no choice but to regard the resolution as legally nonexistent because there is a material defect in the convocation procedure or resolution method; it must be deemed that this does not include cases in which it is difficult to recognize, in appearance, the existence of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders of the relevant company, such as where minutes of the general meeting of shareholders were prepared without convening or holding any general meeting of shareholders at all, or where minutes were prepared after holding a meeting that could not, in appearance, be regarded as the general meeting of shareholders of the relevant company.\\n\\nHowever, even in the latter case, if the person who created the outward appearance of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders by preparing minutes, etc. is a shareholder who holds more than half of the company’s shares, or, even if he does not hold more than half of the shares, is a shareholder who in fact controls the operation of the company, there would be room to recognize the company’s liability by analogy to the former case where the company must be regarded as having been involved in the outward manifestation of the resolution of the general meeting of shareholders.\\n\\nThis Court’s judgment of March 22, 1983, 82DAKA1810, concerned a matter before Commercial Act Article 380 was amended by Act No. 3724 on April 10, 1984, and therefore does not conflict with the above view.\\n\\n(2) Turning to this case, the court below, on the basis of the evidence cited therein, found that Nonparty 1 had served as representative director together with Nonparty 2, but resigned as representative director on January 13, 1987, and while only the said Nonparty 2 remained as representative director, the said Nonparty 2 also resigned as representative director on February 24, 1987, and on the same day Nonparty 3 took office as representative director; that shortly thereafter, around February 26, 1987, dishonored bills in the amount of approximately KRW 2.3 billion occurred in the Plaintiff Company; that at the time of the dishonor, the total number of issued shares of the Plaintiff Company was 400,000 shares, of which the said Nonparty 1 owned 148,000 shares, the said Nonparty 2 owned 94,400 shares, Nonparty 4 owned 78,800 shares, the said Nonparty 3 owned 63,200 shares, and Nonparty 5 owned 15,600 shares; and that the said Nonparty 1, on May 16, 1987, without any authority to convene, summoned Nonparties 6, 7, 8, etc., to a coffeehouse of unknown name near Seoul City Hall without giving any notice of convocation to Nonparty 3, Nonparty 2, Nonparty 4, and Nonparty 5, who were then shareholders of the Plaintiff Company, and prepared, as of the same date, minutes of an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders stating that Nonparty 3, who was then serving as representative director of the Plaintiff Company, was dismissed from the offices of representative director and director and that Nonparties 6 and 7 were appointed as directors, and separately prepared minutes of a board meeting stating that Nonparty 6 was appointed as representative director of the Plaintiff Company, and by using them completed, on the 19th of the same month, the registration of the reshuffle of officers, including the change of representative director; thereafter, on the 20th of the same month, accompanied by the said Nonparty 6, who had been registered as representative director of the Plaintiff Company as above, the said Nonparty 1 met with Nonparties 9 and 10, and it was agreed that the said Nonparty 6, in the capacity of representative director of the Plaintiff Company, would transfer to the said Nonparties 9, etc., the rights arising from the purchase of the real property in this case and all assets of the Plaintiff Company, including movables, for a total of KRW 1,030,000,000, but that the form would be to individually transfer the business assets of the Plaintiff Company; and that, in the circumstances set forth in the lower court’s judgment, the movables in this case were transferred to the Defendant company established by the said Nonparties 9, etc., and ownership transfer registration of the real property in this case was also completed; and that thereafter, with respect to the extraordinary general meeting resolution of the Plaintiff Company dated May 16, 1987, which stated that Nonparty 3 was dismissed from the offices of representative director and director of the Plaintiff Company and that Nonparties 6 and 7 were appointed as directors, Nonparty 3 filed an action for confirmation of the absence thereof, and as a result, a judgment confirming such absence was rendered on June 2, 1988 and became final as rendered.\\n\\nBased on the above facts found, the court below further held that, although a judgment confirming the absence of the resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders of the Plaintiff Company dated May 16, 1987, which stated that Nonparty 3 was dismissed from the offices of representative director and director of the Plaintiff Company and that Nonparties 6, etc. were appointed as directors of the Plaintiff Company, became final, under Commercial Act Articles 380 and 190, the effect of a judgment in an action for confirmation of the absence of a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders does not affect the rights and obligations between the company and third parties arising before the judgment becomes final, and therefore a contract concluded before such final judgment cannot be deemed void on account of such defect; and that, although there were such defects in the above-mentioned general meeting and defects in the board resolution of the Plaintiff Company stating that Nonparty 6 was appointed as representative director of the Plaintiff Company, the said Nonparties 9, etc. entered into the above contract concerning the real property and movables in the belief that the said Nonparty 6 was the lawful representative director of the Plaintiff Company; in light of the foregoing, the Plaintiff Company, in which the majority shareholder was involved in creating the outward appearance of such general meeting of shareholders and, on that basis, even registered the said Nonparty 6 as representative director, could not deny the validity of the assignment contract regarding the real property and movables of this case dated May 20, 1987, concluded by the said Nonparty 6 on behalf of the Plaintiff Company with the said Nonparties 9, etc., and the contract dated the 30th of the same month for changing the status as purchaser concerning the real property in this case among three parties, including the intervenor supporting the Defendant, on the ground that the said Nonparty 6 was not a lawful representative director; accordingly, the court below held that the Plaintiff’s assertion that each of the contracts dated May 20, 1987 and the 30th of the same month was a contract made by a person without authority to represent the Plaintiff Company and thus void as against the Plaintiff Company lacked merit.\\n\\n(3) However, as established by the court below, if the extraordinary general meeting resolution dated May 16, 1987 in this case was not a resolution adopted at a meeting convened and held in appearance as the general meeting of shareholders of the Plaintiff Company, but was merely the result of Nonparty 1, who was not even the representative director at the time, summoning persons who were not shareholders to a coffeehouse and preparing minutes to create the outward appearance of a general meeting resolution, then, as stated above, this would not correspond to the absence of a resolution prescribed in Commercial Act Article 380.\\n\\nHowever, Nonparty 1, as of that time, held 148,000 of the 400,000 issued shares of the Plaintiff Company; thus, if he was a shareholder holding the largest number of shares though not a majority of shares and in fact controlled the operation of the Plaintiff Company, there may be room to recognize the Plaintiff Company’s liability by analogy to a case of substantive absence, but from the facts established by the court below alone, it is not clear whether the said Nonparty 1 continued to control the operation of the company in fact even after resigning as representative director of the Plaintiff Company.\\n\\nUltimately, the court below, without determining whether the absence of the extraordinary general meeting resolution dated May 16, 1987 in this case, for which a judgment confirming absence has become final, fell within the category of absence prescribed by the above-mentioned statutory provisions, instead casually deeming it to be subject to the application of Commercial Act Article 380 and recognizing the Plaintiff Company’s liability, erred in the interpretation of the above Commercial Act provision and failed to conduct a full examination, thereby committing an illegality that affected the judgment; the argument on this point is well-founded.\\n\\n(4) The company’s liability for the acts of an apparent representative under Commercial Act Article 395 is limited to cases where the company is responsible for the outward manifestation of representative capacity by expressly or impliedly approving the use of the apparent representative’s name (see, inter alia, this Court’s judgments of May 27, 1975, 74DA1366, and May 10, 1977, 76DA878); therefore, in a case such as this one, where a person was appointed as representative by a general meeting resolution prepared merely by creating minutes without convening or holding a general meeting, if the company is to be held liable under Commercial Act Article 395 for that person’s acts, it must be recognized that the company was at fault in the outward manifestation of representative capacity created by the preparation of the minutes.\\n\\nAccording to the facts established by the court below and the record, when Nonparty 1 prepared the minutes of the above general meeting of shareholders and registered Nonparty 6 as representative director, the former was merely one of the three directors listed on the corporate registry and carried out the above acts against the will of Nonparty 3, the representative director; accordingly, it is difficult to deem that the Plaintiff Company bears any responsibility for the outward manifestation of representative capacity created without authority by the said Nonparty 1.\\n\\nHowever, if the said Nonparty 1 was a person who, as a major shareholder, in fact controlled the operation of the company, there would be room to recognize the company’s fault in the outward manifestation of representative capacity as above, but this point is not clear from the facts established by the court below alone.\\n\\nUltimately, the court below held that, since the Plaintiff Company, with the said Nonparty 1, a major shareholder, involved in creating the outward appearance of such general meeting of shareholders and, on that basis, even registering the said Nonparty 6 as representative director, could not escape liability to Nonparty 9, etc., who transacted in the belief that the said Nonparty 6 was the lawful representative director, there was an error of law in misunderstanding the requirements for the company’s liability prescribed in Commercial Act Article 395 and in failing to conduct a full examination, thereby affecting the judgment; the argument on this point is well-founded.\\n\\n2. We consider the first ground of appeal submitted by Attorney Park Jeong-seo, counsel for the Plaintiff.\\n\\n(1) According to the reasons of the court below’s judgment, the court below held that the Plaintiff asserted that the real property and movables in this case were the Plaintiff Company’s only property or important business assets, and therefore their transfer required a special resolution of the general meeting of shareholders pursuant to Commercial Act Articles 374 and 434, but because there was no special resolution of the Plaintiff Company’s general meeting of shareholders in connection with each of the business asset transfer contracts dated May 20, 1987 and the 30th of the same month, the above contracts were void. In response, the court below found that the real property and movables in this case were important business assets forming the foundation for the continuance of the Plaintiff Company, and that there was no special resolution of the Plaintiff Company’s general meeting of shareholders in connection with each of the above contracts dated May 20 and the 30th of the same month; however, based on the evidence cited therein, it could be found that around February 26, 1987, the Plaintiff Company suffered a large-scale dishonor, and as the company’s officers devoted themselves to dealing with the dishonor, factory operations were completely suspended, while the Plaintiff Company’s workers, having not received wages, occupied the company and continued their sit-in protest, and thereafter the Plaintiff Company had not engaged in any business activities at all until the time it transferred the rights arising from the purchase of the real property in this case and the movables to the said Nonparties 9, etc.; on those facts found, the court below held that, by May 20, 1987, when the said Nonparty 6 transferred the contractual rights concerning the real property in this case and the movables to the said Nonparties 9, etc., the Plaintiff Company was already in a state where its business had in fact been suspended or abolished, and therefore even if there had been no special resolution of the general meeting of shareholders in connection with the transfer, the transfer would not be void, and thus rejected the Plaintiff’s above assertion.\\n\\n(2) However, even where the disposition concerns business assets rather than the company’s business itself, if it brings about a result such as transferring or abolishing all or an important part of the company’s business, a special resolution of the general meeting of shareholders prescribed in Commercial Act Article 374 item 1 is required in making such disposition; but if, at the time the company disposed of the business assets that were the foundation of the company’s continuance as above, the company had already abolished or suspended its business, then it cannot be said that all or part of the business came to be abolished or suspended for the first time as a result of such disposition, and therefore no special resolution of the general meeting of shareholders is required. This is this Court’s view (see this Court’s judgments of June 11, 1985, 84DAKA963, and April 12, 1988, 87DAKA1662). Here, “suspension of business” means a state equivalent to abolition of business, in which continuation of the business is abandoned and all business activities are suspended; it does not include a case in which business activities are merely temporarily suspended due to deterioration in management conditions such as the company’s financial situation.\\n\\nEven if, as stated in the judgment of the court below, the Plaintiff Company suffered a large-scale dishonor around February 26, 1987, the company’s officers devoted themselves to dealing with the dishonor, factory operations were completely suspended, and the workers, having not received wages, occupied the company and continued their sit-in protest, so that there had been no business activities until May 20 of that year when the disposition at issue was made, the efforts by the officers to deal with the dishonor can be viewed only as aimed at overcoming the deteriorated financial situation and premised on the continuation of the business, and the workers’ sit-in protest due to temporary nonpayment of wages would likewise be a situation that could be resolved by payment of wages; therefore, at the time of the disposition in question, when only about three months had passed since the dishonor, the circumstances stated by the court below would allow the disposition to be regarded at most as a temporary suspension of business activities due to deterioration in management conditions, but not as a suspension of business equivalent to abolition of business.\\n\\nUltimately, the court below erred in law affecting the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles regarding the scope of business transfer requiring a special resolution under Commercial Act Article 374 item 1; the argument on this point is also well-founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the remaining grounds of appeal are not examined, and the judgment of the court below is reversed and remanded. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the judges participating in this case."}

question: Among the explanations regarding notice of convocation of the shareholders' meeting of A stock company, which is incorrect? (In case of a dispute, according to precedents)
A: If the date and time of the shareholders' meeting fixed by A company are such that it is difficult to expect shareholders to attend at the notified time, to the extent that shareholders' right to attend is infringed, the convocation procedure of the shareholders' meeting falls under a case of manifestly unfair convocation procedure.
B: If A company's articles of incorporation designate the location of its head office as “Seoul Special City” and do not specifically provide for the place of convocation of the shareholders' meeting, there is no defect of violation of the place of convocation in holding the shareholders' meeting at a place adjacent to Seoul Special City.
C: If no other resolution is made within 2 years after the financial statements are approved at the shareholders' meeting, A company shall be deemed to have discharged the liability of directors and auditors unless there is fraudulent conduct; however, such discharge of liability is limited to cases where the grounds for such liability are stated in the financial statements, etc. and approved at the ordinary general meeting.
D: If A company's articles of incorporation do not provide for the “appointment of the representative director” as a matter to be resolved by the shareholders' meeting, A company cannot make it an agenda item of the shareholders' meeting.
E: A company may, only where its articles of incorporation so provide, allow shareholders to exercise voting rights by electronic means without attending the general meeting.
label: E
