{"[2007DA60080]": "1. Regarding Defendant 1’s appeal  \\na. Whether Defendant 1 breached his duties as a director  \\nA director of a stock company, as a member of the board of directors, is not limited to merely expressing approval or disapproval with respect to agenda items submitted to the board of directors, but also has a duty to comprehensively supervise, not only his or her own assigned duties, but also the execution of duties by other managing directors; accordingly, where a director of a stock company, despite grounds sufficient to suspect that another managing director’s execution of duties is unlawful, leaves such conduct unaddressed, he or she cannot be exempted from liability to compensate for the damage thereby incurred by the company (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on December 10, 2004, 2002DA60467, 60474).  \\nThe court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found the facts as stated in its holding and then determined that, while Defendant 1, as a director of Donga Construction Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter “Donga Construction”), heard a report from Non-Party 1, the finance officer, in the course of approving the financial statements for fiscal year 1996 to the effect that “although a deficit had occurred, the accounts were closed as if a profit had been generated by taking into account the difference between the book value and the standard market value of the Gimpo reclamation land and recording assets, etc. in other accounts,” Defendant 1 nevertheless approved the financial statements as they were and left them to be disclosed after approval by the general meeting of shareholders constituted a breach of duty in that he either left unaddressed an unlawful act known to be window-dressing accounting or, at a minimum, discovered grounds to suspect window-dressing accounting yet took no investigation or measure in relation thereto; and that, as a result, Donga Construction suffered damage in the amount equivalent to the corporate income tax it had unjustly paid and the amount equivalent to the profits it had unjustly distributed, so that the above Defendant was liable under Article 399 of the Commercial Act to compensate the above damages suffered by Donga Construction due to the window-dressed settlement of accounts for fiscal year 1996.  \\nIn light of the legal principles set forth above and the record, the court below’s findings of fact and determination in this regard are correct and sustainable, and there is no unlawfulness such as incomplete deliberation, violation of the rules of evidence evaluation, or error in the legal principles concerning a director’s duty of supervision, as argued in the grounds of appeal.  \\nb. Whether Donga Construction suffered damage  \\nIn response to the above Defendant’s argument that “because Donga Construction obtained economic benefits such as construction orders, procurement of borrowings, and lower interest rates through window-dressed accounting, and because the scale of such benefits exceeds the amount distributed as dividends and the amount of corporate income tax paid, Donga Construction cannot be said to have suffered damage,” the court below rejected that argument, finding that there was no evidence to support a finding that Donga Construction obtained such benefits through window-dressed accounting; that, furthermore, the business benefits asserted above depend on the reputation of Donga Construction among its present or future counterparties, and when it later becomes known that window-dressed accounting had been carried out, such fact may instead function as a factor causing Donga Construction’s creditworthiness and external image to fall; and that, therefore, it could not be said that the above window-dressed accounting truly brought benefits to Donga Construction.  \\nUpon review of the record, the court below’s measures in this regard are correct and sustainable, and there is no unlawfulness such as violation of the rules of evidence evaluation or error in the legal principles concerning damage, as argued in the grounds of appeal.  \\n\\n2. Regarding the appeals of Defendants 2 and 3  \\na. Whether the financial statements for fiscal years 1995 and 1996 were window-dressed  \\nThe court below found, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, that although Donga Construction incurred a net loss of approximately 13,620,000,000 won in fiscal year 1995, Defendants 2, etc., who were directors, created false financial statements under the direction of Non-Party 2, the representative director, as if a net profit of approximately 32,839,000,000 won had been generated at settlement; and that Defendant 3, etc., as auditors, tacitly approved this fact {however, in the reasoning portion of this part, while the court below detailed that the financial statements for fiscal year 1995 had been falsely prepared, it stated (page 10, lines 7–8 of the judgment below) that Defendants 2, etc. had “overstated” sales revenue of 3,161,000,000 won in the income statement, but this appears to be a clerical error for “understated”}; and it further found that although Donga Construction incurred a net loss of approximately 168,630,000,000 won in fiscal year 1996, Defendants 2, etc., under the direction of Non-Party 2, created false financial statements as if a net profit of approximately 20,506,000,000 won had been generated at settlement.  \\nUpon review of the record, the court below’s factual findings in this regard are correct and sustainable, and there is no unlawfulness such as violation of the rules of evidence evaluation, as argued in the grounds of appeal.  \\nb. Whether the assessed corporate income tax was attributable to the window-dressed accounting  \\nThe court below found, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, that in reality Donga Construction incurred net losses of 13,620,000,000 won in fiscal year 1995, 168,630,000,000 won in fiscal year 1996, and 158,979,000,000 won in fiscal year 1997, and that, as stated in the column for the amount of tax to be paid in the attached schedule of corporate income tax calculation appended to the judgment below, it was obligated to pay only 34,255,617,990 won in corporate income tax for fiscal year 1995 and 8,731,414,384 won for fiscal year 1996, and incurred no corporate income tax liability for fiscal year 1997; nonetheless, due to the window-dressed accounting in this case, it paid, around November 3, 2000, corporate income tax of 79,090,000,000 won on the basis of the window-dressed financial statements for fiscal year 1995, corporate income tax of 87,053,000,000 won on the basis of the window-dressed financial statements for fiscal year 1996, and, around March 15, 2001, corporate income tax of 57,966,000,000 won on the basis of the window-dressed financial statements for fiscal year 1997.  \\nUpon review of the record, the court below’s factual findings in this regard are correct and sustainable, and there is no unlawfulness such as incomplete deliberation or violation of the rules of evidence evaluation, as argued in the grounds of appeal.  \\nc. Whether it was lawful to account for the financial costs of the redevelopment and reconstruction projects for fiscal years 1995 and 1996 as assets  \\nIn response to the argument of Defendants 2, 3, etc. that “the recording, at the time of settlement for each of Donga Construction’s fiscal years 1995 and 1996, of the interest paid for the redevelopment and reconstruction projects—approximately 49,620,000,000 won for fiscal year 1995 and approximately 50,861,000,000 won for fiscal year 1996—not as non-operating expenses but as acquisition costs of assets (advance construction costs) in the financial statements is lawful accounting treatment and cannot be called window-dressed accounting,” the court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found that under the Korean Accounting Standards then in force, there was no express provision concerning whether a construction company should record financial costs such as interest on borrowings related to funds required to purchase redevelopment and reconstruction project sites corresponding to inventory assets or to lend relocation expenses to association members until completion of the work, either as assets or as expense accounts; that Article 96 of the above Korean Accounting Standards provided that financial costs such as interest on borrowings used for the manufacture, purchase, or construction of tangible fixed assets were to be treated as assets, and Article 65 item 2 of the above accounting standards expressly embodied the so-called “revenue-expense matching principle” by providing that each revenue item and the corresponding expense item should be presented separately, so that some frontline accounting practice had raised the question whether it was proper accounting treatment to first record the above financial costs in the account item of advance construction cost, which is an asset account, and then, according to the percentage of completion of construction, record them in the construction cost item, which is an expense account, thereby recognizing them as expenses matched with the related construction revenue; that, in this regard, the Securities and Exchange Commission had, at least since around 1990, consistently issued an official interpretation directing that the above financial costs be treated as period expenses, and most corporate accounting practices had thus treated them as period expenses in accordance with that official interpretation; that, meanwhile, the amended Korean Accounting Standards, effective from March 30, 1996, newly added Article 65 paragraph 2, providing that “where the manufacture or construction of inventory assets requires a long period, interest expenses and other similar financial costs incurred until the completion of the manufacture or acquisition of such assets, with respect to borrowings used for the manufacture, etc. of such assets, shall be included in the acquisition cost of such assets and the amount and contents thereof shall be stated in the notes,” thereby establishing an express basis for treating the above financial costs as assets; that, however, when questions again arose in some quarters as to how fiscal year 1996 should be handled, the Securities and Exchange Commission rendered an official interpretation to the effect that construction-related borrowing interest prior to the above amendment to the Korean Accounting Standards could be capitalized only for tangible assets, so that interest paid in connection with borrowings for inventory assets whose manufacture or construction requires a long period should be treated entirely as period expenses when preparing the financial statements for fiscal year 1996, but should be treated as acquisition cost of assets from fiscal years commencing after April 1996 pursuant to Article 65 paragraph 2 of the amended Korean Accounting Standards; that Donga Construction’s accounting department already possessed materials concerning such official interpretation, and since Donga Construction’s fiscal year ran from January 1 to December 31 each year, the above amended provision did not apply even when preparing Donga Construction’s financial statements for fiscal year 1996, which began on January 1, 1996; and that, in light of these circumstances, the financial costs such as interest on borrowings related to the purchase of redevelopment project sites, etc. for Donga Construction’s fiscal years 1995 and 1996 were properly to be recorded as an “expense item” and constituted accounting treatment conforming to the Korean Accounting Standards then applied under the domestic statutes and regulations in force at the time, and, considering further that Defendants 2 and the accounting staff of Donga Construction appear to have been well aware that treating financial costs for long-term construction as assets in each of those fiscal years would violate the Korean Accounting Standards and general accounting principles, the court below rejected the above Defendants’ argument and determined that the act of capitalizing and accounting for construction interest and other financial costs constituted the preparation of false financial statements in violation of the Korean Accounting Standards enacted by the Securities and Exchange Commission with approval of the Minister of Finance pursuant to the delegation of the Act on External Audit of Stock Companies, which applied to the preparation of Donga Construction’s financial statements for fiscal years 1995 and 1996.  \\nUpon review of the record, the court below’s measures in this regard are correct and sustainable, and there is no unlawfulness such as incomplete deliberation, violation of the rules of evidence evaluation, or error in the legal principles concerning Korean Accounting Standards, as argued in the grounds of appeal.  \\nd. Whether Donga Construction’s actual asset scale exceeded its liabilities  \\nIn response to the argument of Defendants 2, 3, etc. that “at the time of settlement for fiscal years 1995 and 1996, the actual asset values of the settlement amount to be received by Donga Construction from Busan Metropolitan City for the Gudok Tunnel usage fee, the Gimpo reclamation land held by Donga Construction, and the real property of 20 other items, etc. far exceeded the amounts recorded in the financial statements, and if such actual asset values are taken into account, the company’s financial condition at the time of this case was one in which assets exceeded liabilities by approximately 1.2 trillion won,” the court below rejected that argument on the ground that there was no evidence to support a finding, as asserted, that Donga Construction’s actual asset scale at the time exceeded its liabilities.  \\nUpon review of the record, the court below’s measure in this regard is also correct and sustainable, and there is no unlawfulness such as violation of the rules of evidence evaluation, as argued in the grounds of appeal.  \\ne. Whether exemption is available under the business judgment rule  \\nWhere a director, in the performance of duties, commits an act in violation of statutes or regulations, the act itself constitutes a breach of contract against the company; accordingly, once damage has arisen to the company thereby, the director cannot be exempted from liability for damages, and with respect to the above act in violation of statutes or regulations, the business judgment rule, which may be considered where liability for damages arising from a breach of duty is at issue due to a director’s violation of the duty of care of a good manager in the performance of duties, has no room for application (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on November 9, 2006, 2004DA41651, 41668).  \\nIn response to the above Defendants’ argument that “Donga Construction’s failure to disclose honestly the settlement results for fiscal years 1996 and 1997 and its window-dressed accounting were the result of a managerial judgment intended to prevent the collapse of the order for the third phase of the Libyan Great Man-Made River Project in a situation where the order for that project was imminent; at that time, Donga Construction judged that, rather than failing to secure the order for the third phase of the Libyan Great Man-Made River Project and failing to pay shareholder dividends and corporate income tax by disclosing a deficit in its financial statements, the company would obtain greater benefit by successfully securing the third phase of the Libyan Great Man-Made River Project through a surplus disclosure, and thus made the above accounting adjustments; therefore, Defendants 2 and 3 cannot be said to have breached their duties as directors or auditors,” the court below rejected the argument on the ground that Article 20 paragraph 2 of the former Act on External Audit of Stock Companies (as amended by Act No. 5497 on January 8, 1998, before its enforcement from April 1, 1998) provides that where directors or auditors of a stock company prepare and disclose false financial statements in violation of the Korean Accounting Standards enacted by the Securities and Exchange Commission with approval of the Minister of Finance, they shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than one year or by a fine not exceeding 5,000,000 won; and that the above Defendants, who were directors or auditors of Donga Construction, prepared and disclosed false financial statements in violation of the Korean Accounting Standards or left false financial statements to be prepared and disclosed, constituted conduct prohibited by the above former Act on External Audit of Stock Companies, so that the above Defendants are liable to compensate Donga Construction for the damage it suffered due to violation of the above statutory provision, and the business judgment rule has no room for application here.  \\nIn light of the legal principles set forth above and the record, the court below’s measure in this regard is correct and sustainable, and there is no unlawfulness such as error in the legal principles concerning the business judgment rule.  \\nf. Time when damage arose from unjust payment of corporate income tax  \\nIn response to the above Defendants’ argument that “because the unjustly paid corporate income tax can be refunded, the portion of corporate income tax unjustly paid cannot be said to be Donga Construction’s damage, and the damage arose because Donga Construction failed to take corporate income tax refund procedures after Defendants 2 and 3 resigned as directors or auditors of Donga Construction, which is therefore not a matter for which they themselves are responsible,” the court below rejected the argument on the grounds that, once corporate income tax had already been unjustly paid, Donga Construction’s damage had definitively arisen at that time and any refund would be merely a post hoc compensation for the damage, and that the possibility of compensation does not mean that damage did not occur.  \\nUpon review of the record, the court below’s measure in this regard is likewise correct and sustainable, and there is no unlawfulness such as error in the legal principles concerning the time when damage arises from unjust payment of corporate income tax.  \\ng. Whether liability is released under Article 450 of the Commercial Act  \\nThe release of liability of directors and auditors under Article 450 of the Commercial Act is limited to cases where the grounds for liability are stated in the financial statements, etc., and approval is obtained at the ordinary general meeting (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on January 28, 1969, 68DA305; Supreme Court Decision rendered on February 26, 2002, 2001DA76854).  \\nIn response to the above Defendants’ argument that “the financial statements for fiscal years 1995 through 1997 of Donga Construction were approved at each ordinary general meeting of shareholders of the following fiscal year, and the financial statements for fiscal year 1998, which stated all of the window-dressed accounting carried out through fiscal year 1997, were approved at the shareholders’ meeting in February 1999, and since no other resolution overturning such approval was made within two years thereafter, the liability of Defendants 2 and 3 was released under Article 450 of the Commercial Act,” the court below rejected the argument on the ground that the financial statements for fiscal years 1995 through 1997 of Donga Construction did not contain any entry stating that they had been window-dressed, and one could not know from the financial statements themselves that window-dressed accounting had occurred; and further, even if the financial statements for fiscal year 1998 reflected all of the window-dressed accounting carried out through fiscal year 1997, there was no evidence establishing that the grounds for liability of the above Defendants were stated in those financial statements.  \\nIn light of the legal principles set forth above and the record, the court below’s measure in this regard is correct and sustainable, and there is no unlawfulness such as error in the legal principles concerning Article 450 of the Commercial Act.  \\nh. Whether there exists a commercial custom concerning the performance of audit duties by a non-standing auditor  \\nOur Commercial Act does not distinguish auditors into standing auditors and non-standing auditors so as to provide that the duties and responsibilities of a non-standing auditor are reduced compared with those of a standing auditor, nor can the existence of a commercial custom in the Republic of Korea under which companies appoint non-standing auditors and such non-standing auditors perform audit duties only in the event of absence of the standing auditor be recognized; therefore, the argument that a non-standing auditor does not bear liability for breach of the duty of care as an auditor cannot be accepted.  \\nOn the same ground, the court below’s measure rejecting the above Defendant’s argument that “Defendant 3, as Donga Construction’s non-standing auditor, did not perform the duties of an auditor at the time of settlement for fiscal years 1995 through 1997, and therefore has no liability to compensate for the damage caused by the window-dressed accounting in those fiscal years” is correct, and there is no unlawfulness such as incomplete deliberation regarding the existence of a commercial custom or error in the legal principles concerning a non-standing auditor, as argued in the grounds of appeal.  \\n\\n3. Regarding Defendant 4’s appeal  \\na. The court below’s determination  \\nThe court below held that, while Defendant 4 was serving as an auditor, on April 18, 1997 he was appointed as an advisor to Donga Construction and its subsidiary Korea Express Co., Ltd. (hereinafter “Korea Express”), and from that time onward performed the role of advising on overseas order-taking business and coordinating business consultations between the two companies; therefore, under Article 411 of the Commercial Act, which prohibits concurrent service as an auditor, the above Defendant should be regarded as having resigned as auditor on April 18, 1997, and thus should not be held liable as auditor for the window-dressed accounting carried out at the time of settlement for Donga Construction’s fiscal year 1997. In response to the above Defendant’s argument, the court below rejected it, determining that even if, after assuming office as auditor, he was again appointed by the company or its subsidiary as an advisor by resolution of the board of directors, etc., absent evidence proving that he expressly manifested an intention to resign from the office of auditor, he cannot be deemed to have resigned merely because he thereafter performed no audit duties at all; rather, if, as asserted by the above Defendant, he was engaged in other duties and was unable to faithfully perform the duties of an auditor, he should not have accepted the office of auditor in the first place or should have resigned it, and if, notwithstanding the prohibition on concurrent service by employees and auditors, he retained the office of auditor while performing no audit duties at all, the above Defendant cannot be permitted to assert exemption from liability by invoking such circumstances in response to the company’s pursuit of liability.  \\nb. This Court’s determination  \\nHowever, the above determination of the court below cannot be sustained for the following reasons.  \\nArticle 411 of the Commercial Act provides that “an auditor may not concurrently serve as a director, manager, or other employee of the company or its subsidiary”; accordingly, if an auditor is appointed as a director, manager, or other employee of the company or its subsidiary, or conversely if a director, manager, or other employee of the company or its subsidiary is appointed as auditor of the company, the act of appointment shall be effective on the condition that the incumbent office is resigned at the time of the respective appointment, and when the person appointed consents to assume the newly appointed position, it should be construed as a manifestation of intent to resign from the prior office.  \\nUpon review of the record, Defendant 4, while serving as auditor of Donga Construction, was appointed on April 18, 1997 as advisor (vice-chairman equivalent) to Donga Construction and its subsidiary Korea Express and, from that time, received remuneration of 6,200,000 won per month (3,100,000 won from Donga Construction and 3,100,000 won from Korea Express) while performing the role of advising on overseas order-taking business and coordinating business consultations between the two companies. In light of these circumstances and the legal principles set forth above, it is reasonable to regard the above Defendant as having resigned his former office as auditor of Donga Construction by assuming, on April 18, 1997, the position of advisor, which is an employee position of Donga Construction and Korea Express, and by taking office in that position.  \\nNevertheless, the court below, for the reasons stated in its holding, determined that the above Defendant could not be deemed to have resigned the office of auditor of Donga Construction, and thus this judgment of the court below contains an error of law in misconstruing Article 411 of the Commercial Act, which provides for the prohibition on concurrent service by auditors, and it is clear that such error affected the judgment.  \\n\\n4. Regarding Defendant 5’s appeal  \\na. The court below’s determination  \\nThe court below determined that, on the premise that when Defendant 4 donated the real property at issue, which he owned, to Defendant 5, his wife, on September 11, 2002, Defendant 4 already owed Donga Construction damages in the amount of 2,048,160,000 won in connection with the window-dressed accounting for Donga Construction’s fiscal year 1997, Defendant 4 was already in a state of insolvency at the time of the above donation, so the donation constituted a fraudulent act against the creditor Donga Construction, and Defendant 5, as the beneficiary, is presumed to have acted in bad faith; accordingly, absent special circumstances, the above donation should be revoked as a fraudulent act and the ownership transfer registration made in Defendant 5’s name with respect to the real property at issue should be cancelled for the restoration to the original state resulting from such revocation.  \\nb. This Court’s determination  \\nHowever, the above determination of the court below cannot be sustained for the following reasons.  \\nIn order for a creditor to seek revocation of a fraudulent act and restoration to the original state under Article 406 of the Civil Act, the existence of the preserved right, namely the claim, must first be premised; in this case, the preserved right alleged by the Plaintiff is a damages claim that Donga Construction acquired against Defendant 4 because Defendant 4, while serving as auditor at the time of settlement for Donga Construction’s fiscal year 1997, committed a breach of duty by tacitly approving window-dressed accounting, thereby causing Donga Construction to suffer damage in the amount equivalent to the corporate income tax it unjustly paid and the amount equivalent to the profits it unjustly distributed according to such window-dressed accounting. However, as already seen in item 3 above, it can be understood that the above Defendant resigned from the office of auditor on April 18, 1997, before the settlement for Donga Construction’s fiscal year 1997, and therefore it should be regarded that the above Defendant does not bear liability as auditor for the window-dressed accounting carried out at the time of settlement for Donga Construction’s fiscal year 1997; accordingly, the existence of the damages claim that Donga Construction allegedly has against the above Defendant, as asserted by the Plaintiff, cannot be recognized.  \\nNevertheless, the court below, as stated in its holding, premised the existence of the claim asserted by the Plaintiff and determined that the donation between Defendant 4 and Defendant 5 constituted a fraudulent act against creditor Donga Construction; thus, this judgment of the court below contains an error of law in misconstruing Article 411 of the Commercial Act, which provides for the prohibition on concurrent service by auditors, and as a result it erred in its determination concerning the existence or nonexistence of the preserved right in the fraudulent act claim, and it is clear that such error affected the judgment.  \\n\\n5. Conclusion  \\nAccordingly, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal of Defendants 4 and 5, the portion of the judgment below against Defendant 4 and the portion concerning Defendant 5 are each reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; all appeals by Defendants 1, 2, and 3 are dismissed; and the costs of appeal between the Plaintiff and the above Defendants shall be borne by the losing parties, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: A, a major shareholder holding shares equivalent to more than half of the total issued shares of Company A, directed unlawful execution of business to B, the representative director of Company A, and B accordingly executed the business of Company A. Meanwhile, C, an unregistered director of Company A, executed the business of Company A using the designation “President C of A Corporation.” If damage arises to Company A in connection with A’s instruction or B’s or C’s execution of business, which of the following statements is correct? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents)
A: If A directed B to execute business unlawfully for the benefit of Company A rather than for A’s own benefit, then A does not bear liability under Article 401-2 of the Commercial Act.
B: Even when B commits an act in violation of statutes while executing business, if B determined and executed the business within the scope of reasonable choices required of a corporate manager, B is exempt from liability under the business judgment rule.
C: For the establishment of liability for damages under Article 401-2 of the Commercial Act with respect to C, it is not required that C have influence over Company A.
D: If C bears liability for damages under Article 401-2 of the Commercial Act, such liability is not liability arising from a mandate relationship; therefore, the short extinctive prescription under Article 766(1) of the Civil Act applies to the claim for damages arising therefrom.
E: If C bears liability for damages under Article 401-2 of the Commercial Act, B does not bear joint and several liability with C for damages to Company A merely because B knew of C’s execution of business and allowed it to continue, since B did not directly execute the business.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2009DA39240]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\nWith respect to a person deemed to be a director in the application of Articles 399, 401, and 403 of the Commercial Act, Article 401-2(1)1 provides that “a person who, by using his own influence over the company, directed a director in the execution of business,” Item 2 provides that “a person who directly executed business in the name of a director,” and Item 3 provides that “a person other than a director who executed the business of the company by using a title that may be acknowledged as having authority to execute business, such as honorary chairman, chairman, president, vice president, senior managing director, managing director, director, or any other title,” and although Items 1 and 2 presuppose a person who has influence over the company, Item 3, because the title itself embodies authority to execute business, cannot be understood as additionally requiring that such person also have influence over the company.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Defendant was promoted, effective January 1, 1999, to director (non-registered), an executive officer of Non-party 1 Stock Company, and worked until December 27, 2000; the Defendant, in sequential conspiracy with Non-party 2, Chairman of the OO Group, and others, falsely prepared the financial statements for the 35th term (1998 fiscal year) of Non-party 1 Stock Company through window-dressing accounting during the period from around January 1999 to around February 1999; in light of the legal principle stated above, the lower court’s determination to the effect that the Defendant falls under the apparent director prescribed in Article 401-2(1)3 of the Commercial Act is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error of law, such as a misapprehension of the legal principle concerning the liability of a person giving instructions for business execution, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2020DA236848]": "We determine the grounds for appeal (the statements contained in a written submission filed after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. Overview of the Case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na. ○○○ Hotel Co., Ltd., a company engaged in hotel, condominium management and operation business, operated the hotel by being entrusted with authority by the sectional owners of ○○○ Hotel from around 2007. On March 16, 2018, bankruptcy was declared against the company (Busan District Court 2017HAHAP4), and the Plaintiff was appointed as the bankruptcy trustee of the company (hereinafter, ○○○ Hotel Co., Ltd. is referred to as the “Bankrupt Company”).\\n\\nb. Defendant 1 served as the co-representative director of the Bankrupt Company from February 25, 2004 to December 1, 2004 as its major shareholder, and served as a director of the Bankrupt Company from May 18, 2007 to August 5, 2008, and thereafter actually took charge of the overall management of the Bankrupt Company as its chairman until May 18, 2016. Defendant 2 served as the representative director of the Bankrupt Company from August 2, 2006 to May 18, 2016, and Defendant 3 served as the auditor of the Bankrupt Company from May 18, 2007 to August 5, 2008, and as a director of the Bankrupt Company from August 5, 2008 to May 18, 2016.\\n\\nc. The Defendants were indicted for occupational embezzlement, etc. against the Bankrupt Company, were sentenced to guilty verdicts on some embezzlement offenses, and those guilty verdicts became final on May 24, 2016.\\n\\n2. Determination of the Grounds for Appeal Concerning the Statute of Limitations\\n\\na. Concerning the grounds for appeal by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\nThe liability for damages arising from a director’s or auditor’s neglect of duties to the company, as prescribed in Article 399(1) and Article 414(1) of the Commercial Act, is liability for non-performance of obligations arising from a mandate relationship; therefore, it should be regarded that the short-term statute of limitations under Article 766(1) of the Civil Act does not apply to the resulting claim for damages (see Supreme Court Decision dated June 25, 1985, 84DAKA1954, Supreme Court Decision dated December 11, 2008, 2005DA51471, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in the judgment, rejected the defense of the short-term statute of limitations raised by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 against the Plaintiff’s alternative claim (claim for damages under Article 399(1) of the Commercial Act), and this is proper, and there is no error of law in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the nature of liability for damages under Article 399(1) of the Commercial Act and the period of the statute of limitations.\\n\\nb. Concerning the grounds for appeal by Defendant 1\\n\\n1) Article 401-2(1) of the Commercial Act provides that, where Article 399, Article 401, Article 403, and Article 406-2 are applied to a person who: directs a director to execute business by using his or her influence over the company (subparagraph 1); directly executes business in the name of a director (subparagraph 2); or, though not a director, executes the company’s business by using titles such as honorary chairman, chairman, president, vice president, executive vice president, managing director, director, or any other title likely to be recognized as having authority to execute the company’s business (subparagraph 3), that person shall be deemed a “director” with respect to the business he or she directed or executed. This is intended to hold accountable, in corresponding measure, a person who is not a director of a stock company but who has been involved in the company’s business by directing a director to execute business or by executing business like a director.\\n\\nIn light of the content of these statutory provisions and the legislative purpose, a person falling under each item of Article 401-2(1) of the Commercial Act, although not a director of the company, bears, with respect to the business in which he or she was involved, the same duty of care and duty of loyalty as a director, including the duty to comply with laws and regulations, in applying the liability for damages prescribed in Article 399 of the Commercial Act, and, where he or she neglects such duties, becomes liable to the company for damages caused thereby. Since the liability for damages prescribed in Article 401-2(1) of the Commercial Act is liability arising from being deemed a director under the Commercial Act, the short-term statute of limitations under Article 766(1) of the Civil Act, which prescribes the short-term statute of limitations for general tort liability, does not apply to the resulting claim for damages.\\n\\n2) The court below did not accept Defendant 1’s defense of the statute of limitations concerning the claim for damages under Article 401-2(1) subparagraphs 1 and 3, and Article 399(1) of the Commercial Act.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the court below’s determination in this regard is proper, and there is no error of law, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the nature of liability for damages under Article 401-2(1) and Article 399(1) of the Commercial Act and the statute of limitations.\\n\\n3. Determination of the Grounds for Appeal Concerning the Defense of Agreement on Setoff or Setoff, and the Argument of Exemption or Release from Liability for Damages\\n\\nOn the premise that the Defendants’ liability for damages existed, the court below rejected the Defendants’ agreement on setoff or defense of setoff, holding that the Defendants’ claim for entrustment fees against the Bankrupt Company was not recognized, and found that the Defendants were liable for damages.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the court below’s determination in this regard is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, that affected the conclusion by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the interpretation of juristic acts, the defense of setoff, etc., or by neglecting to exercise the court’s power to clarify and failing to conduct the necessary examination, or by violating the rules of logic and experience and thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

question: Company A, a non-listed company, is a stock company in which A is registered as the representative director. B, although neither the president nor a director of Company A, used the title of president of Company A and entered into a contract of sale between Company A and C. Which of the following statements concerning this is incorrect? (If there is a dispute, the case law shall govern.)
A: If Company A, knowing that B was arbitrarily using the title of president, left it as it was without taking any measures, this constitutes a case in which Company A implicitly approved B’s use of the title.
B: Even where a person without the qualifications of a director is allowed to use the title of apparent representative director, Article 395 of the Commercial Act is applied by analogy; therefore, Company A may bear liability toward C under the doctrine of apparent representative director.
C: Even where the sales contract with C is recognized as an act of an apparent representative director, if a resolution of the board of directors was required for the above sales contract and C, the other party to the contract, knew that there had been no resolution of the board of directors, Company A is exempt from liability for the above sales contract.
D: Where B, using the title of president of Company A, issued and delivered a bill to C for the payment of the purchase price, among the bona fide third parties for whose bill liability Company A bears, only C, who directly acquired the bill from B, is included, and a third-party acquirer who thereafter re-acquired the bill by endorsement and transfer from C is not included.
E: If B acted in the name of A, the true representative director, rather than in his own name, then for Company A to escape liability as an apparent representative director, it must prove C’s bad faith or gross negligence, and in this case the bad faith or gross negligence concerns whether B had authority to act on behalf of A, not whether B had authority to act as representative director.
label: D

{"[91DA35816]": "With respect to the grounds of appeal by the Defendants’ litigation counsel, we decide as follows (supplemental grounds of appeal stated in supplemental statements of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Outline of the facts recognized by the court below.\\n\\na. On 1982.9.3., the Plaintiff, after entering into a bank transaction agreement with Defendant Hansam Trading Co., Ltd. (hereinafter abbreviated as “Defendant Hansam Trading”), which mainly engaged in the export of clothing, further entered into a foreign-currency bill transaction agreement with the said Defendant on 1983.1.8., and from that day until 1983.6.23., by purchasing export bills on 66 occasions from the said Defendant, extended loans in the aggregate amount of KRW 1,919,739,371; however, as the respective purchased bills were not settled and the said Defendant went bankrupt on 1983.11.3., all of the said loan principal became delinquent from the following day.\\n\\nb. Defendant Korea Saengsa Co., Ltd. (hereinafter abbreviated as “Defendant Korea Saengsa”), Defendant 3, Defendant 4, and the deceased Nonparty 1 jointly and severally guaranteed all obligations owed by Defendant Hansam Trading to the Plaintiff under the above bank transaction agreement entered into by Defendant Hansam Trading with the Plaintiff on 1982.9.23.; and upon the death of the said Nonparty 1 on 1983.9.1., his wife and daughters, namely Defendant 5, Defendant 6, and Defendant 7, jointly inherited his property.\\n\\nc. When the said Nonparty 1, who had been the representative director at the time of 1983.9.1., died in connection with the downing of a Korean Air passenger aircraft in Soviet waters, Defendant Hansam Trading, although it had never held any extraordinary general meeting of shareholders or board of directors meeting, prepared on paper minutes of a general meeting of shareholders and minutes of a board of directors meeting stating that the said Nonparty 1 had appointed Defendant 3 as director and representative director respectively at each of the extraordinary general meetings of shareholders and board of directors meetings convened by him, and thereby completed registration on 9.2. to the effect that Defendant 3 had assumed office as such director and representative director.\\n\\nd. Thereafter, in order to interrupt the statute of limitations on the debt for the loan in this case, the Plaintiff contacted Defendant 3, who had been registered in the register of Defendant Hansam Trading as its representative director as above, and on 1987.12.1., obtained from him a debt acknowledgment instrument (Plaintiff’s Exhibit No. 4-1) stating that, as representative of Defendant Hansam Trading, Defendant Hansam Trading acknowledges that it owes to the Plaintiff a debt in the aggregate amount of KRW 8,609,081,363, including the principal balance of KRW 1,010,439,806 (including the amount claimed in this case), which is the remaining principal amount after deducting the principal repaid up to that time in the amount of KRW 909,299,565 from the aggregate principal amount of KRW 1,919,739,371 arising from the purchase of the export bills in this case, together with delay damages thereon and loan principal and interest on other items.\\n\\ne. Thereafter, Nonparty 2, a shareholder of Defendant Hansam Trading, filed a lawsuit against Defendant Hansam Trading for confirmation of nonexistence of a resolution of a general meeting of shareholders, etc., obtained a favorable judgment on 1988.12.1., and upon finality of the said judgment, the registration of Defendant 3’s assumption of office as director and representative director was canceled on 1989.2.24.\\n\\n2. Determination on Ground of Appeal No. 1, Items (1) and (2).\\n\\nThe court below’s factual findings and determination concerning the points indicated in the arguments below (the findings of fact set forth in 1.a. and d. above) are proper in light of the evidentiary relations explained in the judgment of the court below, and there is no basis to conclude that, in the course thereof, the court below violated the rules on weighing evidence and wrongly found facts without properly conducting deliberation, as argued below. The arguments are nothing more than criticizing the court below’s discretionary evaluation of evidence and findings of fact, which are within the exclusive province of the court below, or attacking the court below’s determination on the premise of facts inconsistent with those found by the court below, and therefore cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Determination on Ground of Appeal No. 2, Item (1).\\n\\nArticle 395 of the Commercial Act prescribes a company’s liability for the acts of a director who uses a title that is deemed to be recognized as having authority to represent the company, and, as argued below, it requires that the apparent representative director possess the qualifications of a director. However, because this provision is intended, in accordance with the doctrine of estoppel by representation or the appearance theory, to protect third parties who relied on the appearance of authority as representative director by causing the company, which is at fault with respect to the existence of such appearance, to bear liability for their acts vis-à-vis third parties in good faith, it is reasonable to interpret that the said provision applies by analogy not only where the company allows a person who lacks the qualifications of a director to use the title of apparent representative director, but also where a person who lacks even the qualifications of a director uses the title of apparent representative director on his own and the company knowingly leaves it unaddressed without taking any measure, thereby passively acquiescing therein (see this Court 1979.2.13. decided 77DA2436; 1985.6.11. decided 84DAKA963; 1987.7.7. decided 87DAKA504, etc.).\\n\\nIn addition, the certification system for private documents under the Notary Public Act consists in having the parties sign or affix seals to the private document in the presence of the notary public, or having the signature or seal on the private document confirmed by the principal or his agent, after which the notary public states such fact in the instrument (Article 57(1)); and because, in certifying a private document, the notary public is required under the Notary Public Act to first go through procedures such as confirmation of the requester (Article 27), confirmation of the proxy requester (Article 30), and proof of the authority of agency (Article 31), unless special circumstances are alleged and proved, such as that the notary public failed to properly follow such procedures in certifying the private document, the authenticity of the private document certified by the notary public is presumed (see this Court 1988.3.8. decided 87DAKA1448; 1991.3.27. decided 90DA17187, etc.). In the same purport, the court below, based on Plaintiff’s Exhibit No. 6, which was not disputed as to its formation and which is a certified copy of Defendant Hansam Trading’s corporate register, and on the entries in Defendant’s Exhibit No. 2-4, which is not disputed as having been certified by a notary public and is the minutes of the board of directors meeting stating that Defendant 3 is appointed as representative director of Defendant Hansam Trading, determined that Defendant 3 and Nonparties 3, 4, and 5, who were then directors of Defendant Hansam Trading, affixed their seals to the said minutes of the board of directors meeting; and thus, even if the board resolution itself did not exist, it may be inferred that the said Nonparties 3, 4, and 5, etc. agreed to appoint Defendant 3 as representative director of Defendant Hansam Trading and made the said resolution according to their intent. Therefore, it cannot be said that the court below, as argued below, found a fact without evidence or that there is a contradiction in the reasons.\\n\\nFurther, in light of the fact that the then directors of Defendant Hansam Trading were involved in the preparation of the minutes of the board of directors meeting stating that Defendant 3 was appointed as representative director of Defendant Hansam Trading as above; the fact that Defendant 3, from the time he was registered as representative director of Defendant Hansam Trading on 1983.9.2. until the registration was canceled on 1989.2.24., continued to be registered as representative director of Defendant Hansam Trading; and the circumstances revealed by the record (especially the entries in Plaintiff’s Exhibits Nos. 1-2 and 6 and the results of the court below’s interrogation of Defendant 3 as a party), that Defendant 3 was not a person wholly unrelated to Defendant Hansam Trading, but had been representative director of Defendant Hansam Trading not only when Defendant Hansam Trading was established but also from 1981.3.13. to 1982.10.20.; that he is the representative director of Defendant Korea Saengsa, which is currently the joint and several surety of Defendant Hansam Trading; that Defendant Hansam Trading had once been an affiliated company of Defendant Korea Saengsa; and that, at the time Defendant Hansam Trading acknowledged that it owed the debt in this case to the Plaintiff, Defendant Korea Saengsa was in possession of the seal of the representative director of Defendant Hansam Trading (the one affixed to Defendant’s Exhibit No. 2-4), it is understandable, in light of the evidentiary relations explained in the judgment of the court below, that the court below determined that Defendant Hansam Trading had actively permitted Defendant 3 to use the title of representative director, or at least had passively tolerated it by leaving it in place for a long time; and there is no basis to conclude that the court below, as argued below, violated the rules on weighing evidence and wrongly found facts without properly conducting deliberation, or misunderstood the legal principle concerning liability of an apparent representative director under Article 395 of the Commercial Act.\\n\\nUltimately, none of the arguments can be accepted.\\n\\n4. Determination on Ground of Appeal No. 2, Item (2).\\n\\nThe court below’s factual findings and determination concerning the point indicated in the arguments below (that, when the Plaintiff obtained the above debt acknowledgment instrument from Defendant 3, it rejected the evidence supporting the Defendants’ assertion that the Plaintiff knew that Defendant 3 was not the representative director of Defendant Hansam Trading, and, based on other evidence, found that the Plaintiff obtained the above debt acknowledgment instrument believing that Defendant 3, who was then registered in the register as representative director, was the lawful representative director of Defendant Hansam Trading) are not only proper in light of the evidentiary relations explained in the judgment of the court below, but also, if the factual relations are as finally found by the court below, it cannot be said that the Plaintiff was grossly negligent in failing to know that Defendant 3 was not the lawful representative director of Defendant Hansam Trading. Therefore, the argument that the judgment of the court below contains illegality in that it wrongly evaluated the value of evidence and wrongly found facts, or misunderstood the legal principle concerning the liability of an apparent representative director, cannot be accepted.\\n\\n5. Determination on Ground of Appeal No. 3.\\n\\nThe court below, in response to the Defendants’ argument that, according to the foreign exchange transaction processing procedure of the Plaintiff Bank, after an export bill is dishonored, the dishonored amount must be deposited or a new export bill purchased only after the purchaser of the dishonored bill repays the dishonored bill proceeds; and that, even when purchasing a new export bill while the dishonored bill proceeds remain unsettled, the bank must first recover the already accrued dishonored bill proceeds from the purchase price, but the Plaintiff Bank continued to purchase export bills issued and accepted by the same counterparty as those already dishonored by Defendant Hansam Trading and paid the entire purchase price to Defendant Hansam Trading, thereby negligently expanding the loss, so that with respect to the remaining Defendants who are joint and several sureties, the debt should be reduced in consideration of the Plaintiff’s above negligence, held that, while the Plaintiff purchased export bills from Defendant Hansam Trading on numerous occasions from 1983.1.8. to 6.23., there was no evidence to find that, as argued by the Defendants, it continued to purchase export bills of the same content even after export bills had been dishonored, and rather, it was recognized that the dishonor date of Defendant Hansam Trading was 1983.11.3.; accordingly, the court below rejected the Defendants’ above argument.\\n\\nAs argued below, in the case of so-called “continuing suretyship,” which guarantees uncertain debts arising from a continuing transactional relationship between a creditor and the principal obligor, the surety is in principle obligated to perform in full the debt not performed by the principal obligor; however, only where there exist special circumstances warranting a determination that the creditor’s claim that the surety perform the debt in full is contrary to the principle of good faith and fair dealing, such as where, at the time the suretyship was undertaken, the surety anticipated or could have anticipated the scope of the principal debt, but the principal debt far exceeded the anticipated scope and arose in excess to the extent that it lost objective reasonableness, and the cause of such excessive accrual of the principal debt is recognized as having been that the creditor, while fully aware of the fact that the principal obligor’s asset condition had materially deteriorated (the same applies where the creditor did not know of such fact due to gross negligence), intentionally expanded the scale of the transactions without giving any notice or inquiry to the surety who could not know of such circumstance, may the surety’s liability be limited within a reasonable scope, as held in this Court’s precedents (1988.4.27. decided 87DAKA2143; 1989.10.24. decided 88DA2083; 1991.10.8. decided 91DA14147, etc.).\\n\\nHowever, even assuming, as argued below, that when the Plaintiff purchased the export bills listed in Nos. 54 to 60 of the attached schedule to the judgment of the court below from Defendant Hansam Trading on 1983.5.25., a part of the export bills purchased earlier had already been in a state of nonpayment or refusal of acceptance, and that, according to the Standard Procedures for Foreign Exchange Transactions (Defendant’s Exhibit No. 8, which the Defendants’ litigation counsel argues is a business processing guideline of Seoul Trust Bank but is common to all domestic banks including the Plaintiff), when an exporting company that does not settle export bills requests the purchase of new export bills, the internal bank guideline provides that the purchase price shall first be used to settle the dishonored bill amount, it cannot be concluded, merely because the Plaintiff violated such bank business processing guideline, that in this case the principal debt accrued far beyond the scope anticipated or foreseeable by the sureties at the time they undertook the suretyship and to the extent that it lost objective reasonableness. Accordingly, the argument that the judgment of the court below, which rejected the Defendants’ above argument, contains illegality in that it violated the rules on weighing evidence and wrongly found facts without properly conducting deliberation, or in that it misunderstood the procedural rules concerning the handling of dishonored export bills and thereby affected the judgment, is also ultimately without merit.\\n\\n6. Determination on Ground of Appeal No. 4.\\n\\nAlthough the Defendants’ litigation counsel before the court below, through a preparatory brief dated the same day and stated at the court below’s 4th hearing date (1991.2.5. 14:00), argued that even if Defendant Hansam Trading, by reason of the above debt acknowledgment instrument (Plaintiff’s Exhibit No. 4-1), becomes liable for acknowledgment of debt under the legal principle of an apparent representative director, such effect would operate only against Defendant Hansam Trading, the principal obligor, and would not operate against the remaining Defendants who are sureties, the court below, as pointed out by the arguments below, did not expressly rule on the Defendants’ above argument.\\n\\nHowever, interruption of prescription against the principal obligor is effective also against the joint and several sureties (Civil Act Article 440), and since the court below determined that the statute of limitations with respect to the claim for the loan in this case was interrupted by the above acknowledgment of debt, and therefore the Defendants’ argument that the statute of limitations for the claim for the loan in this case had been completed was without merit, it may be understood that such determination by the court below includes the purport of rejecting the arguments of the remaining Defendants other than Defendant Hansam Trading. Accordingly, the argument that the judgment of the court below contains illegality in failing to determine the Defendants’ argument cannot be accepted.\\n\\n7. Therefore, the appeals by the Defendants are all dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing Defendants. The judgment is rendered as follows, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the judges who participated."}

{"[94DA50908]": "We examine the grounds of appeal asserted by counsel for Plaintiff.\\n\\n1. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below acknowledged, first, that Plaintiff paid a total of KRW 1,630,000,000 to Non-party 1 Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “the Non-party 1 Company”) or to Non-party 2 in his individual capacity, from early August 1990 through mid-August of the same month, as funds for the purchase of forfeited shares, and, as security therefor, received from said Non-party 2 around August 16, 1990, the two current account checks at issue in this case (Exhibit A No. 2-1, 2), on which Defendant Company was indicated as the issuer; and, second, that said Non-party 2 had been appointed as representative director of the Non-party 1 Company from July 19, 1990, and had mainly handled the affairs of said Company, while Defendant Company held a board of directors meeting on August 8, 1990, dismissed said Non-party 2 from the position of joint representative director of Defendant Company, and made the dismissal registration on the 13th of the same month, and that Plaintiff, knowing these facts, paid the above money to said Non-party 2, who was the representative director of the Non-party 1 Company, or to Non-party 2 in his individual capacity, and received the above current account checks from him; and, in light of the relevant evidence and the record, the above fact-finding by the court below is correct, and it cannot be said that, as alleged in the argument, the court below violated the rules of evidence and the principle of free evaluation of evidence by finding facts without evidence and contrary to the purport of the parties’ pleadings, by improperly weighing evidence, and by omitting examination and determination of the evidence proving the cause of action, and so forth.\\n\\nPlaintiff argued that the time when said Non-party 2 was entrusted with the funds for the purchase of shares by Plaintiff was from mid-June 1990 to early July 1990, and, as alleged in the argument, it is true that the court below erred in stating as if Plaintiff had alleged that the time was from early August 1990 to mid-August of the same month; however, according to the record, as stated above, the time when said Non-party 2 was entrusted with the funds for the purchase of shares by Plaintiff is acknowledged to have been from early August 1990 to mid-August of the same month, and therefore such error by the court below did not affect the result of the judgment.\\n\\nThe grounds of appeal challenging this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n2. The court below found that, when Defendant Company entered into a current account transaction agreement with the Yeouido Branch of the Korea Exchange Bank, because the transaction seal was frequently used and there were not a few cases of it being misused by its officers and employees, Defendant Company, separately from the representative director’s seal registered in the corporate registry (corporate seal), made a representative director’s seal (bank transaction seal) for use exclusively in that current account transaction and reported it to the bank, and managed it separately; that said Non-party 2, who had been serving as auditor of Defendant Company from the time of its establishment and had independently engaged in activities such as borrowing money or shares not only from private moneylenders but also from Defendant Company to make investments, or brokering investment transactions between Defendant Company and small and medium-sized enterprises, while the representative director of Defendant Company, Non-party 3, was absent after leaving for the United States on October 12, 1989, as found in the judgment, deceived the employee in charge, obtained a check book and the corporate seal stamp, and, as if the agreement were being prepared under delegation of authority from said Non-party 3, using the Defendant Company nameplate and said corporate seal stamp, prepared an agreement in the name of Defendant Company relating to stock investment for a private moneylender, Non-party 4, with whom he had long been transacting, and borrowed money by signing himself on that agreement as a guarantor for Defendant Company to said Non-party 4; that, for performance security thereof, he arbitrarily prepared and delivered the two current account checks at issue in this case (Exhibit A No. 2-1, 2), using the Defendant Company check book and corporate seal stamp obtained as above; that Defendant Company, for the reasons found in the judgment, reported the loss of the check forms; and that thereafter, while said Non-party 2 had recovered the two current account checks from said Non-party 4 and was in possession of them, he delivered the two current account checks to Plaintiff.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant evidence and the record, the above fact-finding by the court below is proper, and there is no illegality such as violation of the rules of evidence as alleged in the argument; moreover, once it has been revealed that the two current account checks at issue in this case were forged by said Non-party 2 as above, the mere fact that Defendant Company’s corporate seal stamp is affixed to each of the current account checks at issue in this case cannot give rise to a presumption that Defendant Company issued each of those checks, and therefore it cannot be said that the judgment of the court below contains an error of law concerning the authenticity of documents, by misunderstanding Articles 329 and 330 of the Civil Procedure Act. The ground of appeal lacks merit.\\n\\n3. The purport of the provisions concerning the liability of an apparent representative director under Article 395 of the Commercial Act is to promote the trust and security of commercial transactions by protecting a third party in good faith who relied on the appearance, in a transaction, of a director who was not the company’s representative director using a title that would appear outwardly to have the company’s representative authority, where the company is at fault for such apparent company representation (see this Court’s judgment dated 1988. 10. 11., 86DAKA2936); accordingly, the company’s liability for the acts of such apparent representative is limited to cases where the company expressly or impliedly approved the apparent representative’s use of such title, and where a person arbitrarily assumed such title without the company’s approval of its use, the company cannot be held liable to a third party in good faith merely because the company was negligent in not knowing of, or in not stopping, the use of such title (see this Court’s judgment dated 1975. 5. 27., 74DA1366).\\n\\nConsistent with the same purport, the court below determined that there was no evidence that Defendant Company, after said Non-party 2 was dismissed from the position of joint representative director, allowed him to use a title such as president or any other title having authority to represent the company and thereby conferred such appearance, or that said Non-party 2 issued the current account checks at issue in this case to Plaintiff while posing as the representative director of Defendant Company, and that since Plaintiff, knowing that said Non-party 2 had no authority to represent Defendant Company, paid the above funds for the purchase of forfeited shares to said Non-party 2 as representative director of the Non-party 1 Company or to Non-party 2 in his individual capacity, and received the current account checks at issue in this case from said Non-party 2 as security for the investment funds, Defendant Company could not be held liable for said Non-party 2’s check issuance act by applying the above provision of the Commercial Act concerning the liability of an apparent representative director; and such determination is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error of law concerning the liability of an apparent representative director as alleged in the argument.\\n\\nMeanwhile, according to the record, it is clear that in Paragraph 3 of the preparatory brief dated June 14, 1994, counsel for Plaintiff advanced, against Defendant Company, a claim for the return of entrusted funds as well as a claim for the amount of the checks, on the ground of liability arising from the acts of Defendant Company’s apparent representative director, Non-party 2 (Record, p. 1446). The argument contends that the court below determined only the claim for the amount of the checks and omitted a determination regarding the claim for return of the entrusted funds; however, upon review of the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below, while determining the claim for the amount of the checks, found that said Non-party 2, after separately establishing the Non-party 1 Company on June 29, 1990, neglected Defendant Company’s affairs, and from July 19 of the same year served as representative director of the Non-party 1 Company and mainly handled the affairs of the Non-party 1 Company; that Defendant Company held a board of directors meeting on August 8, 1990, dismissed said Non-party 2 from the position of joint representative director of Defendant Company, completed the dismissal registration on the 13th of the same month, and later around the 20th of the same month, even settled the investment share between said Non-party 2 and Non-party 3; and that Plaintiff, while fully aware of these facts, paid a total of KRW 1,630,000,000 from early August 1990 to mid-August of the same month to said Non-party 2 (or Non-party 2 in his individual capacity) as representative director of the Non-party 1 Company as funds for the purchase of forfeited shares, and around August 16, 1990, received the above current account checks from him as security for the above investment funds, and then determined that Defendant was not liable under Article 395 of the Commercial Act for said Non-party 2’s acts; this can be understood as also determining, together with the above, that there was no liability of an apparent representative director with respect to Plaintiff’s claim for return of entrusted funds. Even if the judgment of the court below had omitted a determination on Plaintiff’s assertion concerning Defendant Company’s liability arising from said Non-party 2’s acts as apparent representative director with respect to the entrusted funds, such assertion likewise could not be accepted for the same reason as in the case of the claim for the amount of the checks, and therefore such reason would not affect the result of the judgment. The ground of appeal is ultimately without merit.\\n\\n4. The court below found that there was no evidence to support the conclusion that Plaintiff had deposited KRW 1,630,000,000 with Defendant Company, through said Non-party 2 acting for Defendant Company, as payment for the purchase of forfeited shares, or that said Non-party 2, who was the joint representative director of Defendant Company, had deceived Plaintiff while executing his duties by telling Plaintiff that if forfeited shares of high quality were purchased and resold, a profit could be obtained, and thereby defrauded Plaintiff of the above money; and, on that basis, it rejected Plaintiff’s claim against Defendant for return of entrusted funds and claim for damages, stating that said Non-party 2 received the above money from Plaintiff not as representative director of Defendant Company, but as representative director of the Non-party 1 Company or in his individual capacity.\\n\\nAccording to the relevant evidence and the record, the above determination by the court below can be upheld, and there is no illegality such as violation of the rules of evidence as alleged in the argument; moreover, as pointed out in the argument, the court below did not determine the business scope of a small and medium enterprise startup investment company under the Act on Assistance to the Establishment of Small and Medium Enterprises. Rather, it merely viewed the party to the contract for the purchase of forfeited shares on behalf of Plaintiff, or the contract for deposit of the purchase price of forfeited shares, not as Defendant Company but as said Non-party 2 in his individual capacity or the Non-party 1 Company, in light of the circumstances under which Plaintiff invested the money at issue in this case as admitted by the record and the purposes of Defendant Company, and therefore it cannot be said that the court below committed the alleged error of law by misunderstanding the business scope of a small and medium enterprise startup investment company under the Act on Assistance to the Establishment of Small and Medium Enterprises.\\n\\nThis ground of appeal also cannot be accepted.\\n\\n5. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}
{"[97DA34709]": "The appeal is dismissed. The costs of appeal shall be borne by the Plaintiff."}

question:
Which of the following statements concerning the board of directors of a stock company are correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)

(a) If a director attended the board meeting and abstained from voting, and this is recorded in the minutes, that director cannot be regarded as “a person for whom a statement of dissent is not recorded in the minutes,” and therefore cannot be presumed to have agreed to the board resolution pursuant to Article 399(3) of the Commercial Act.
(b) A shareholder holding shares equivalent to at least 3/100 of the total number of issued shares may demand the convocation of an extraordinary general meeting by submitting to the board an electronic document stating the matters to be dealt with at the meeting and the reasons for convocation; in this context, “electronic document” includes e-mail, but does not include mobile phone text messages or mobile messages.
(c) A shareholder may request inspection and copying of the minutes of the board of directors during business hours, but the company may refuse the request by stating reasons, and in that case the shareholder may request inspection and copying of the minutes of the board of directors by means of a civil action.
(d) In the case of self-dealing under Article 398 of the Commercial Act, prior approval by the board of directors is required; therefore, even if board approval is obtained afterward for the transaction, absent special circumstances, the invalid transaction does not become valid.
(e) Credit extension by a listed company made in violation of Article 542-9(1) of the Commercial Act is prohibited regardless of whether there is board approval, and therefore, unless it falls under an exception under paragraph (2) of the same Article, it cannot become valid even if there is prior approval or subsequent ratification by the board of directors.
