supporting_precedents: {"[2016DA260455]": "We determine the grounds for final appeal (including the statements in supplemental briefs submitted after the period for submitting the statement of grounds for final appeal, to the extent they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\n1. With respect to the grounds for final appeal alleging that it is unlawful to presume that Defendant 1 and Defendant 2, who abstained at the board of directors, concurred in the resolution pursuant to Article 399(3) of the Commercial Act\\n\\nA. The lower court, taking into account the circumstances as found in its judgment, determined that the Defendants’ adoption of the resolution at issue, by which the Plaintiff donated 15 billion won to the Defendant auxiliary intervenor, constitutes a case where directors neglected their duties under Article 399(1) of the Commercial Act, and that Defendant 1 and Defendant 2, as directors, were presumed to have concurred in the resolution at issue because there was no entry in the minutes recording that they objected at the time of the resolution; and then it held that the said Defendants, pursuant to Article 399(2) and (3) of the Commercial Act, bear liability for damages jointly and severally with the remaining Defendants.\\n\\nB. However, the determination that Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 are presumed to have concurred in the resolution at issue is not acceptable for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) Article 399(1) of the Commercial Act provides: “If a director, intentionally or negligently, performs an act in violation of any statute or the articles of incorporation, or neglects his or her duties, such director shall be jointly and severally liable to compensate for damages to the company.” Article 399(2) of the same Act provides: “If the act under the preceding paragraph is done pursuant to a resolution of the board of directors, the directors who concurred in such resolution shall also be liable under the preceding paragraph.” Article 399(3) of the same Act provides: “Any director who participated in the resolution under the preceding paragraph and for whom there is no entry in the minutes recording an objection shall be presumed to have concurred in such resolution.” As such, Article 399(2) of the Commercial Act imposes liability for damages also on the directors who concurred in the resolution when the act of a director in violation of duty, as provided in Article 399(1), was done pursuant to a resolution of the board of directors, and Article 399(3) of the Commercial Act, premised on Article 399(2) of the same Act, is a provision that shifts the burden of proof to the directors, taking into account that a person seeking to hold a director liable may find it difficult to prove whether a particular director concurred in the resolution of the board of directors because such proof may be difficult. Therefore, where a director attended the board meeting and the minutes state that he or she abstained from voting on the resolution, such director cannot be regarded as “any director who participated in the resolution and for whom there is no entry in the minutes recording an objection,” and thus cannot be presumed, pursuant to Article 399(3) of the Commercial Act, to have concurred in the resolution of the board of directors; accordingly, such director should be deemed not to bear liability under Article 399(2) of the same Act.\\n\\n2) According to the evidence admitted by the lower court, Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 attended the Plaintiff’s 111th board meeting, but the minutes show that, at the time the resolution at issue was adopted, they abstained on the agenda item. If that is the case, Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 cannot be regarded as “any director who participated in the resolution and for whom there is no entry in the minutes recording an objection” under Article 399(3) of the Commercial Act; therefore, they cannot be presumed, pursuant to Article 399(3) of the Commercial Act, to have concurred in the resolution of the board of directors, and accordingly they do not bear liability under Article 399(2) of the same Act.\\n\\nC. Nevertheless, the lower court held that because the minutes merely stated that Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 abstained and contained no entry that they objected, it may be presumed that the said Defendants concurred in the resolution at issue, and thus determined that the said Defendants are also liable to compensate the Plaintiff for damages jointly and severally with the other directors. In so doing, the lower court erred by misapprehending the legal doctrine regarding Article 399(3) of the Commercial Act, which affected the judgment. The argument in the grounds for final appeal pointing this out is well founded.\\n\\n2. With respect to the grounds for final appeal to the effect that the remaining Defendants, excluding Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 (hereinafter referred to as “Defendants 3, etc.”), did not breach their duty of care as prudent managers\\n\\nA. Where directors of a stock company, in resolving at the board of directors to make a donation to one of the company’s shareholders, failed to conduct sufficient review based on reasonable information regarding the nature of the donation, the impact of the donation on the company’s founding purpose and the public interest, the reasonableness of the amount of the donation in light of the company’s financial condition, and the relationship between the company and the recipient of the donation, etc., the directors’ act of concurring in such resolution constitutes an act in violation of the directors’ duty of care as prudent managers.\\n\\nB. The lower court, considering the circumstances as found in its judgment in combination, determined as follows.\\n\\n1) The resolution at issue was adopted for the purpose of contributing to the public interest of balanced regional development through economic promotion of the closed-mine region and improvement of residents’ living standards, and the amount of the donation thereunder cannot be viewed as excessive in light of the Plaintiff’s financial condition.\\n\\n2) However, the extent to which the donation pursuant to the resolution at issue contributes to the enhancement of the public interest of the entire closed-mine region and the benefit it provides to the Plaintiff are not so great, and in light of the recipient of the donation and the use to which it was to be put, it cannot be said that the donation was carried out in a method reasonably suited to achieving the public interest; moreover, it is difficult to view that Defendants 3, etc. sufficiently reviewed such points at the time of adopting the resolution at the Plaintiff’s board of directors.\\n\\n3) Accordingly, Defendants 3, etc.’s concurrence in the resolution at issue constitutes an act in violation of the directors’ duty of care as prudent managers.\\n\\nC. In light of the legal doctrine and the record discussed above, the lower court’s determination contains no error of law, such as misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning the directors’ duty of care as prudent managers and the business judgment rule, or violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n3. With respect to the grounds for final appeal alleging that the liability of Defendants 3, etc. was recognized excessively\\n\\nA. Where a director is liable to compensate the company for damages because the director has performed an act in violation of any statute or the articles of incorporation, or has neglected his or her duties, in determining the scope of such damages, the amount of damages may be limited in light of the idea underlying the damages compensation system, namely fairness in the sharing of loss, by taking into account all relevant circumstances, such as the content and nature of the business concerned, the circumstances and form of the director’s breach of duty, the objective circumstances or degree of the director’s involvement in the occurrence and expansion of the company’s damages, the director’s usual contribution to the company, the existence or nonexistence of any gain by the director resulting from the breach of duty, and the existence or nonexistence of defects in the company’s organizational system or whether a risk-management system was established. At that time, fact-finding concerning the circumstances to be considered for limiting the amount of damages or determining the ratio of such limitation is within the exclusive province of the trier of fact, so long as it is not manifestly unreasonable in light of the principle of equity (see Supreme Court Decision 2002DA60467, 60474 rendered on 2004. 12. 10., etc.).\\n\\nB. The lower court, taking into account the circumstances leading Defendants 3, etc. to the resolution at issue, limited the liability for damages of Defendant 9 to 20% of the amount of damages, and limited the liability for damages of Defendant 3, Defendant 4, Defendant 5, Defendant 6, Defendant 7, and Defendant 8 to 10% of the amount of damages, respectively.\\n\\nC. In light of the legal doctrine and the record discussed above, the lower court’s fact-finding regarding the grounds for limitation of liability or its determination on the ratio thereof cannot be deemed manifestly unreasonable in light of the principle of equity. Therefore, the lower court’s determination on this point contains no error of law regarding limitation of liability or inconsistency in reasoning, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without deciding the remaining grounds for final appeal by Defendant 1 and Defendant 2, we reverse the part of the lower court judgment dismissing the claims against Defendant 1 and Defendant 2, and remand this case to the lower court for further trial and determination on this part; we dismiss in each instance the appeals by Defendants 3, etc.; and we order that, among the costs of final appeal incurred between the Plaintiff and Defendants 3, etc., the portion arising from the auxiliary intervention shall be borne by the Defendant auxiliary intervenor, and the remainder shall be borne by the losing Defendants 3, etc., respectively. It is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2017DA261943]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Overview of the Case and Issues\\na. Overview of the Case\\nAccording to the reasons for the judgment below and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n1) Assignment of Claim\\na) Nonparty 1, a moneylender, and NeoPurple Co., Ltd., a listed company (hereinafter “NeoPurple”), as well as its shareholder Nonparty 2 and its representative director Nonparty 3, negotiated around November 2012 that Nonparty 1 would lend money to NeoPurple and Nonparty 2 and Nonparty 3 would provide joint and several suretyship and collateral, but after being pointed out by Nonparty 4, a director of NeoPurple, that if NeoPurple were to become the principal obligor without a resolution of the board of directors, problems such as the crime of breach of trust could arise, Nonparty 1 concluded a loan-for-consumption agreement (hereinafter “the loan-for-consumption agreement at issue”) under which Nonparty 1 would lend 2 billion won to Nonparty 2 and Nonparty 3 and NeoPurple would provide joint and several suretyship and collateral.\\n\\nb) Nonparty 2 lent to NeoPurple 500 million won out of the money received from Nonparty 1 pursuant to the loan-for-consumption agreement at issue.\\n\\nc) Around December 28, 2012, Nonparty 1 received from NeoPurple an assignment of NeoPurple’s claim for the price of goods against Korea Yakult Co., Ltd. (hereinafter “Korea Yakult”) (hereinafter “the claim at issue”), in the name of collateral relating to the loan-for-consumption agreement at issue (hereinafter “the assignment of the claim at issue”).\\n\\n2) Objection to Distribution\\na) The Plaintiff and the Defendant each obtained provisional attachment orders with respect to the claim at issue, and Nonparty 1 received an assignment of the claim at issue; the authenticated copy of the Plaintiff’s provisional attachment order reached Korea Yakult on April 17, 2013, the notice of Nonparty 1’s assignment of the claim at issue reached Korea Yakult on May 13, 2013, and the authenticated copy of the Defendant’s provisional attachment order reached Korea Yakult on May 22, 2013.\\n\\nb) Accordingly, on September 30, 2013, Korea Yakult deposited the amount of the claim at issue on the ground of the concurrence of attachments, etc., and thereafter, in the distribution proceeding case of the Seoul Southern District Court Case No. 2013TAGI2293, a distribution schedule was prepared distributing 102,856,383 won to the Plaintiff and 283,804,806 won to the Defendant, respectively. Before that, Nonparty 1 withdrew the demand for distribution.\\n\\nc) The Plaintiff appeared at the distribution hearing in the above case and raised an objection, and filed this action for objection to distribution, alleging that because the Defendant effected provisional attachment after the claim at issue had been assigned to Nonparty 1, such provisional attachment by the Defendant was unlawful and distribution should not be made to the Defendant.\\n\\nb. Issues\\nThe issues are whether the assignment of the claim at issue constitutes an extension of credit prohibited by Commercial Act Article 542-9(1), and whether an extension of credit in violation of Commercial Act Article 542-9(1) is void.\\n\\n2. Interpretation of Commercial Act Article 542-9(1)\\na. Whether a private-law contract or other juridical act carried out in violation of a specific statutory provision prohibiting a certain act is void, or whether the court refuses assistance in the realization of the content of the legal act or otherwise limits its effect by some other means, is a matter concerning the legal effect of the statutory provision in the broad sense, and is determined by the interpretation of that provision. Therefore, if there is an express provision on that point, it must of course be followed; if there is no such provision, it will ultimately be determined by examining, in light of the purpose and meaning of the prohibition provision, whether invalidity or other limitation of effect of the legal act contrary thereto is required (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of June 13, 2019, 2018DA258562).\\n\\nb. According to Commercial Act Article 542-9(1), a listed company shall not extend credit to or for the benefit of major shareholders and their specially related persons, directors and executive officers, or auditors (hereinafter “major shareholders, etc.”). Here, extension of credit means the lending of property having economic value, such as money, the guarantee of performance of obligations, the purchase of securities for financing support purposes, or other direct or indirect transactions involving transaction credit risk as prescribed by Presidential Decree. Considering that major shareholders, etc. may exercise substantial influence over the management of a stock company, if the company extends credit to major shareholders, etc., there is a high likelihood not only that the company’s financial soundness will be undermined and the interests of general shareholders or creditors will be infringed, but also that abnormal accounting treatment may be undertaken in order to conceal this in some cases. In particular, in the case of a listed company with various stakeholders, the demand for soundness in accounting and management is higher than for an unlisted company; accordingly, Commercial Act Article 542-9(1) aims to protect the company’s interests and contribute to the soundness of the stock market and the protection of investors by, in principle, prohibiting the extension of credit by a listed company to major shareholders, etc. However, from the standpoint of managerial necessity or freedom of business operation of a listed company, there may be some items of extension of credit that need not or need only minimally be made subject to prohibition, and thus Commercial Act Article 542-9 permits, in paragraph (2), some extensions of credit exceptionally by taking into account the counterparty to the transaction, the nature or purpose of the transaction, the scale, and the effect on managerial soundness. Furthermore, Commercial Act Article 624-2 provides that a person who extends credit in violation of Commercial Act Article 542-9(1) shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 5 years or by a fine not exceeding 200 million won, in order to secure the effectiveness of the prohibition on extension of credit, while Commercial Act Article 634-3 establishes the joint punishment provision for the company.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above, the legislative purpose and content of Commercial Act Article 542-9(1), and the fact that criminal punishment is imposed for violations, the above provision constitutes a mandatory provision; therefore, extension of credit made in violation of the above provision is impermissible and void as a matter of private law, and anyone may assert such invalidity. Moreover, according to the wording of the above provision, extension of credit made in violation of Commercial Act Article 542-9(1), unlike self-dealing by directors governed by Commercial Act Article 398, is prohibited regardless of whether the board of directors approved it, and therefore cannot become valid even if there was prior approval or subsequent ratification by the board of directors.\\n\\nc. However, as noted above, Commercial Act Article 542-9 generally prohibits extension of credit in paragraph (1) but permits some extensions of credit in paragraph (2), and thus a third party outside the company may in a concrete case have difficulty knowing or determining whether a particular extension of credit is subject to prohibition. In view of the reality of transactions in which commerce with listed companies is frequent, imposing on third parties an obligation to investigate and confirm, each time they transact with a listed company, whether Commercial Act Article 542-9 has been violated would impair the speed of commerce and the safety of transactions. Accordingly, even if credit extension violates Commercial Act Article 542-9(1), if the third party did not know of it and was not grossly negligent in not knowing it, invalidity cannot be asserted against that third party.\\n\\n3. Determination in this case\\na. Whether all or part of the assignment of the claim at issue constitutes an extension of credit made in violation of Commercial Act Article 542-9(1)\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in its judgment, determined that at the time of the conclusion of the loan-for-consumption agreement at issue and the assignment of the claim at issue, Nonparty 2 fell under a major shareholder of NeoPurple, a listed company (Commercial Act Article 542-8(2)6), or a person directing the execution of business (Commercial Act Article 401-2(1)1), and that Nonparty 3 was NeoPurple’s representative director, so NeoPurple’s joint and several suretyship for the borrowing debts of Nonparty 2 and Nonparty 3 and its assignment of the claim at issue as collateral constituted “extension of credit to major shareholders, etc.” prohibited by Commercial Act Article 542-9(1) and Article 35(1)1 of the Enforcement Decree of the Commercial Act.\\n\\nIn light of the reasons for the judgment below and the record, the determination of the court below is proper, and there is no error of failure to fully examine or misapprehension of legal principles as alleged in the grounds of appeal as to whether all or part of the assignment of the claim at issue constitutes an extension of credit made in violation of Commercial Act Article 542-9(1).\\n\\nb. Whether the assignment of the claim at issue is void in violation of Commercial Act Article 542-9(1)\\nThe court below, in principle, premised that an extension of credit made in violation of Commercial Act Article 542-9(1) is void, but is valid in relation to a bona fide third party involved in the extension of credit only where that third party had no gross negligence in not knowing that it constituted an extension of credit. Furthermore, the court below, for the reasons stated in its judgment, determined that Nonparty 1 knew that the assignment of the claim at issue constituted an extension of credit prohibited by Commercial Act Article 542-9(1), or even if he did not know, he could have known had he exercised a little care, and that by grossly violating the duty of care required by commercial norms he had gross negligence in not knowing that fact, and ultimately determined that the assignment of the claim at issue was void as an extension of credit made in violation of Commercial Act Article 542-9(1).\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above and the record, the foregoing determination by the court below is proper, and there is no error of failure to fully examine or misapprehension of legal principles concerning the private-law effect of an extension of credit made in violation of Commercial Act Article 542-9(1), its relationship with board approval, the scope of persons who may assert invalidity, or whether there was bad faith or gross negligence.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2021DA291712]": "The grounds for appeal are examined (the statements in a supplemental brief on the grounds for appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. Determination on the first, second, third, and fifth grounds for appeal\\n\\na. 1) Commercial Act Article 398 provides: “In order for directors, etc. to enter into transactions with the company for their own account or for the account of a third party, the material facts concerning the relevant transaction must be disclosed in advance to the board of directors, and approval of the board of directors must be obtained. In such case, approval of the board of directors shall be given by the votes of at least two-thirds of the directors, and the content and procedure of the transaction shall be fair.” This is intended to prevent transactions involving conflicts of interest between directors, etc. and the company from being secretly carried out and, through the exercise of the board of directors’ supervisory authority over duties, to secure the fairness of transactions entered into between directors, etc. and the company, thereby preventing directors, etc. from seeking their own or a third party’s benefit through transactions with the company and causing unforeseen damage to the company and its shareholders (see Supreme Court Decision rendered September 12, 2017, 2015DA70044; Supreme Court Decision rendered July 9, 2020, 2019DA205398, etc.).\\n\\nCommercial Act Article 398 was amended from former Commercial Act (before its amendment by Act No. 10600 on April 14, 2011, hereinafter referred to as “former Commercial Act”) Article 398 in order to strengthen control over acts by directors, etc. pursuing private interests; unlike former Commercial Act Article 398, it expanded the scope of application to major shareholders, etc., expressly required that the material facts be disclosed “in advance” and that approval of the board of directors be obtained, increased the voting requirement for approval by the board of directors, and provided that the content and procedure of the transaction must be fair, while excluding the contents related to Civil Act Article 124 in the latter sentence of former Commercial Act Article 398.\\n\\nIn light of the wording of Commercial Act Article 398, its legislative purpose, and the history of its amendment, in order for directors, etc. to validly enter into a transaction with the company for their own account or for the account of a third party, they must first obtain approval of the board of directors as prescribed in Commercial Act Article 398; therefore, if prior approval of the board of directors under Commercial Act Article 398 was not obtained, then absent special circumstances the transaction should be deemed void (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2019DA205398), and even if approval of the board of directors was obtained after the fact as to the transaction, the void transaction does not become valid absent special circumstances.\\n\\n2) Furthermore, Commercial Act Article 398 provides that, in order for directors, etc. to obtain approval of the board of directors concerning transactions with the company, the material facts concerning the relevant transaction must be disclosed at the board of directors; accordingly, if such matters were not disclosed and the board’s resolution was merely one allowing the transaction as an ordinary transaction, rather than deliberation as to whether it was a fair conflict-of-interest transaction, then it cannot be said that there was approval of the board of directors as prescribed in Commercial Act Article 398 (see Supreme Court Decision rendered May 10, 2007, 2005DA4284).\\n\\nb. On the grounds stated in the judgment, the court below determined that each of the sales contracts at issue and the first through third agreements concluded between ○○ Electric Industry Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “○○ Electric”) and the non-party, who is the lineal descendant of the Defendant and the representative director of ○○ Electric and holds 15.87% of ○○ Electric’s shares, constitute transactions to which Commercial Act Article 398 applies; that the board of directors’ resolution dated November 4, 2016, which preceded each of the sales contracts at issue, was not a resolution made after disclosure of the material facts concerning the relevant transactions; that it is difficult to acknowledge the existence of the board of directors’ resolution dated November 11, 2016; and that even if such board resolution existed, it was not a resolution made after disclosure of the material facts concerning the relevant transactions, so it cannot be deemed that approval of the board of directors as prescribed in Commercial Act Article 398 had been obtained before the transactions; that the non-party is merely the direct counterparty to the above transactions and is not a third party protected as a bona fide third party; and that even if, at the board of directors’ resolution held on August 17, 2021, a board resolution had been adopted ratifying each of the sales contracts at issue and the first through third agreements, after-the-fact approval or ratification is not permitted, and thus each of the sales contracts at issue and the first through third agreements are void.\\n\\nc. Examining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, although there are somewhat inappropriate parts in the court below’s explanation, the conclusion of the court below that each of the sales contracts at issue and the first through third agreements, which are transactions to which Commercial Act Article 398 applies, were void because prior approval of the board of directors prescribed in Commercial Act Article 398 had not been obtained and that they remain void even if approval of the board of directors was later obtained, is justifiable; and there is no error, as asserted in the grounds for appeal, such as misapprehending the legal principles concerning approval by the board of directors under Commercial Act Article 398 or failing to conduct necessary deliberation, thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in contravention of the rules of logic and experience.\\n\\n2. Determination on the fourth ground for appeal\\n\\nOn the grounds stated in the judgment, the court below determined that, as a result of the performance of the void sales contracts at issue, ○○ Electric was prevented from using and profiting from Real Properties 1 through 4 and thereby suffered damages equivalent to rent, and recognized that amount equivalent to rent as the amount of damages, while limiting the Defendant’s liability for damages to 70% in consideration of various circumstances, such as the circumstances and content of the conclusion of the sales contracts at issue and the degree of the Defendant’s breach of duty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the court below’s determination is justifiable, and there is no error, as asserted in the grounds for appeal, such as misapprehending the legal principles concerning proximate causal relation between the act in violation of statutes prescribed in Commercial Act Article 399(1) and the damage, the occurrence of damage, or offsetting of gains and losses, or exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in contravention of the rules of logic and experience without conducting necessary deliberation.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the appeal are assessed against the losing party, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2022GEU734]": "The grounds for the extraordinary appeal are examined.\\n\\nUnder Article 366(1) of the Commercial Act, a minority shareholder prescribed in Article 366(1) of the Commercial Act may request convocation of an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders by submitting to the board of directors a written document or electronic document stating the subject matter of the meeting and the reasons for convocation (Article 366(1) of the Commercial Act). Here, the “board of directors” ordinarily means the representative director, and exceptionally, in the case of a small company with one or two directors and no representative director, it means each director (Article 383(6) of the Commercial Act). Meanwhile, the term “electronic document” as prescribed in Article 366(1) of the Commercial Act means information that has been created, converted, transmitted, received, or stored in electronic form by an information processing system, and it must be capable of having its contents viewed on the premise that it has been preserved in the form in which it was created, converted, transmitted, received, or stored, or in a form capable of being so reproduced; accordingly, it includes not only e-mail but also mobile phone text messages and mobile messages, so long as they do not conflict with such characteristics.\\n\\nAccording to the record: ① the Applicant is a shareholder holding at least 3/100 of the total number of issued shares of the company concerned, and the non-party was appointed as a director and representative director of the company concerned on November 24, 2004; ② the company concerned was registered as deemed dissolved on December 3, 2012 pursuant to Article 520-2(1) of the Commercial Act, and although it resolved at the shareholders’ meeting on April 1, 2014 to continue the company and appointed the non-party as an inside director, it was again registered as deemed dissolved on December 7, 2020 pursuant to the same provision; ③ on March 10, 2021, the Applicant obtained a judgment against the company concerned to the effect that “it is confirmed that no resolution exists appointing the non-party as a director at the extraordinary general meeting of shareholders held on April 1, 2014,” and around that time the said judgment became final and conclusive (Busan District Court Case No. 2020GAHAP40163); ④ the request for convocation of an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders, sent by the Applicant to the non-party in the form of content-certified mail on January 21, 2022 with “appointment of a liquidator” as the subject matter of the meeting, was not delivered on two occasions because of no recipient being present and was kept by the post office and then discarded, whereas the Applicant’s litigation representative sent a request for convocation of an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders with the same content to the non-party by KakaoTalk message on February 8, 2022, and around that time the non-party received it, but the company concerned has not yet commenced the procedure for convening an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders.\\n\\nIn light of these factual circumstances and the above legal principles, the part of the reasons for the lower court decision stating that “the Applicant made an expression of intent to the non-party on January 21, 2022, requesting the convocation of the above extraordinary general meeting of shareholders, and it reached him around that time” is somewhat inaccurate; however, as seen above, once the non-party, who is the representative director of the company concerned, received and confirmed the Applicant’s request for convocation of an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders through a KakaoTalk message around February 8, 2022, it is appropriate to view the Applicant’s request for convocation of an extraordinary general meeting of shareholders under Article 366(1) of the Commercial Act as lawful, and thus no grounds for extraordinary appeal, such as a constitutional violation affecting the judgment, can be found in the lower court decision.\\n\\nTherefore, the extraordinary appeal is dismissed, and the decision is made as follows in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating.\\n\\nDecember 16, 2022."}

question: Among the explanations regarding the Principle of Legality in Criminal Law, which is correct? (In case of dispute, according to precedents)
A: If the Enforcement Decree of a statute clearly prescribes matters concerning criminal punishment, then even if it expands the objects of punishment beyond the scope expressly delegated by the statute, it does not violate the Principle of Legality in Criminal Law.
B: If the constituent elements of a penal provision are not defined as descriptive concepts, this violates the principle of clarity derived from the Principle of Legality in Criminal Law.
C: It is not beyond the limits of textual interpretation to construe the phrase “when the defendant is detained,” one of the grounds on which a court must appoint counsel ex officio under Article 33 (Court-Appointed Counsel) of the Criminal Procedure Act, as including cases where the defendant is detained in a separate case, that is, in a case other than the criminal case at issue, or is serving a sentence after a conviction has become final and conclusive in another criminal case.
D: Restrictively applying by analogy the scope of grounds for exemption from punishment does not violate the Principle of Legality in Criminal Law.
E: Because defamation by means of an information and communications network requires that an act of stating facts be made openly, recognizing publicity on the ground that a statement is made to a specific individual or a small number of persons and thereby has the possibility of being disseminated to unspecified persons or a large number of persons constitutes analogical interpretation prohibited by the Principle of Legality in Criminal Law.
