supporting_precedents: {"[2002HEONBA83]": "1. Outline of the Case and the Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\na. Outline of the Case\\n\\n(1) Background of the Labor Dispute\\n\\n(a) The Korea Industrial Complex Corporation (hereinafter referred to as \"the Corporation\") is a public corporation operated with government financial support, and was an enterprise that operated combined heat and power plants (the Banwol Cogeneration Plant and the Gumi Cogeneration Plant) that ran large boilers in the Banwol Industrial Complex and the Gumi Industrial Complex to produce high-temperature, high-pressure steam and supply it to consumers within the Corporation complex.\\n\\n(b) Around 2001, the Government finalized a privatization policy to sell the Gumi Cogeneration Plant and the Banwol Cogeneration Plant to the private sector. When the Corporation, in accordance with the Government policy, sought to privatize the above plants, and various issues surrounding this arose, causing disagreements between the Corporation and the Corporation Labor Union (hereinafter referred to as \"the Corporation Union\"), the Corporation Union, on 2001. 7. 24., filed a report of industrial action for a strike with the Mayor of Ansan and the Gyeonggi Regional Labor Relations Commission.\\n\\n(c) On 2001. 7. 31., the Director of the Gumi Regional Labor Office gave the Gumi Branch Head of the Corporation Union a notice restricting industrial action to the effect that the electricity and steam production facilities, water treatment facilities, etc. of the Gumi Cogeneration Plant were deemed safety protection facilities, and therefore industrial action that suspends, abolishes, or impedes their normal maintenance and operation could not be carried out with respect thereto. On 2001. 8. 1., the Director of the Ansan Regional Labor Office sent the Chairman of the Corporation Union a written statement to the effect that if, in the event the maintenance and operation of the boiler and turbine generators, transmission pipelines, water treatment facilities, electrostatic precipitator facilities, and wastewater treatment facilities, etc. were suspended, abolished, or impeded by industrial action, it were objectively recognized that direct danger to human life or body would be caused, then the facilities necessary to prevent such result could fall within safety protection facilities, and thus requested that the Union refrain from striking. Accordingly, the Corporation Union did not go on strike and continued labor-management negotiations.\\n\\n(d) Meanwhile, the Corporation had, every year, mainly during the Chuseok holiday period, suspended the operation of its steam and other production facilities and carried out regular inspections and repair work; and in 2001, too, it planned to conduct boiler regular maintenance inspection during the Chuseok holiday period. After consultation with consumers within the Corporation, around 2001. 9. 10., it decided to suspend steam supply for boiler regular maintenance inspection for 6 days at the Banwol Cogeneration Plant (2001. 9. 30. to 10. 5.) and for 4 days at the Gumi Cogeneration Plant (2001. 9. 30. to 10. 3.), and at the same time concluded construction contracts with about 10 outside specialized companies by sector for the replacement and repair of aging facilities, organized on-duty teams for some employees to supervise the above replacement and repair work, and decided that the Gumi Cogeneration Plant would resume normal work from 2001. 10. 4.\\n\\n(e) Although labor-management negotiations continued as stated in (c) above, they failed to reach an agreement. Accordingly, the Corporation Union decided to go on strike during the Chuseok holiday, when boiler operation would be temporarily suspended for regular maintenance inspection, and on 2001. 9. 29. held a strike launch ceremony and a vigil at the Gumi Cogeneration Plant.\\n\\n(f) On 2001. 9. 29., the Corporation appointed Kim ○ Su as Head of the Central Regional Headquarters effective 2001. 10. 1. Kim ○ Su, in the afternoon of 2001. 9. 29., changed the plant equipment operation plan to the effect that one of the four boilers at the Gumi Cogeneration Plant would be operated normally, on the grounds that maintenance work was impossible during the Chuseok holiday because of the Corporation Union's strike and that one of the consumers, Stock Company ○○, had requested by telephone steam supply during the Chuseok holiday, and notified the employees thereof. However, the Corporation Union objected to this on the ground that, because the above Kim ○ Su was to become head of the headquarters as of 2001. 10. 1., the above change in the operation plan by Kim ○ Su could not be regarded as a lawful work order. In response, the Corporation again issued a personnel order correcting the above transfer date to 2001. 9. 29., and posted the personnel order document the following day.\\n\\n(g) The Corporation Union declared a full-scale strike at around 08:00 on 2001. 9. 30., and the union members of the Gumi Branch of the Corporation Union and the union members of the Banwol Branch left their respective plants that morning, gathered together at the ○○ Youth Hostel in Nam-myeon, Chuncheon-si, stayed there together while engaging in collective protest, and continued labor-management negotiations at the ○○ Hotel in Chuncheon-si.\\n\\n(h) However, at around 08:00 on 2001. 10. 4., the police entered the above youth hostel and all union members who had participated in the strike were taken away; some executives of the Corporation Union were arrested, but most of the union members were released after investigation and by around 2001. 10. 8. had all returned to their workplaces.\\n\\n(2) Criminal Trials Against the Petitioners\\n\\n(a) The Petitioners were employees of the Corporation working at the Gumi Cogeneration Plant and were executives of the Corporation Union, and were indicted for violation of the Collective Energy Business Act, etc. in relation to the above strike.\\n\\n(b) As to Petitioners 1 through 7, guilty judgments were rendered by the Daegu District Court, Gimcheon Branch, on 2002. 1. 31., in Case No. 2001GODAN1376, 1551 (consolidated), and as to Petitioners 8 through 18, guilty judgments were rendered by the Daegu District Court, Gimcheon Branch, on 2002. 1. 31., in Case No. 2001GODAN1683.\\n\\n(c) The gist of the criminal facts recognized by the above judgments is as follows.\\n\\nThe Petitioners, in collusion with the executives and union members of the Corporation Union,\\n\\n① despite an instruction that during the Chuseok holiday period (2001. 9. 30. to 10. 3.) Boiler No. 4 among the four boilers of the Gumi Cogeneration Plant should be operated normally so as to supply steam to steam-consuming companies within the Gumi Industrial Complex, at around 08:30 on 2001. 9. 30., in the central control room of the Gumi Cogeneration Plant, instructed the union members of the Corporation Union, including Im ○ Jeong and Shin ○ Ju, who were operating Boiler No. 4 of the above plant, to stop the operation of the boiler and join the strike, and the above Im ○ Jeong and others arbitrarily manipulated Boiler No. 4, which was a collective energy generation facility, to stop its operation, thereby impeding the smooth supply of collective energy, and suspending the normal maintenance and operation of Boiler No. 4, which was a safety protection facility, and at the same time, by force, obstructing the Corporation's normal business; and\\n\\n② at the same time and place as above, by fully suspending the operation of the Gumi Cogeneration Plant as stated above and causing all union members, including the safety management supervisors, to leave their workplaces and, from then until around 17:00 on 2001. 10. 7., refusing to return to work and not performing safety management duties for the Gumi Cogeneration Plant, which was a collective energy supply facility, thereby causing an obstacle to the supply of collective energy and impeding the normal maintenance and operation of the electricity facilities, steam facilities, etc., which were safety protection facilities of the Gumi Cogeneration Plant, and at the same time, by force, obstructing the Corporation's normal business.\\n\\n(d) The above judgments applied Article 91, item 1, and Article 42, paragraph 2, of the Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act (hereinafter, \"the TULRAA\" refers to this Act) to the acts of \"suspending the normal maintenance and operation of Boiler No. 4, etc., which are safety protection facilities\" in fact-finding ①, and of \"impeding the normal maintenance and operation of electricity facilities, steam facilities, etc., which are safety protection facilities\" in fact-finding ②, and recognized guilt.\\n\\n(e) All of the above judgments were appealed, and the Daegu District Court rendered a judgment on 2002. 9. 18. in Case No. 2002NO694 as to Petitioners 1 through 7, and rendered a judgment on 2002. 9. 18. in Case No. 2002NO698 as to Petitioners 8 through 18. These judgments rejected the defendants' argument that the boilers of the cogeneration plant are not \"safety protection facilities of a workplace\" as prescribed in Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA, and, as in the first-instance judgments, recognized guilt.\\n\\n(f) All of the above appellate judgments were appealed, and the Daegu District Court Case No. 2002NO694 became Supreme Court Case No. 2002DO5428, and the Daegu District Court Case No. 2002NO698 became Supreme Court Case No. 2002DO5429, both of which are pending before the Supreme Court.\\n\\n(3) Dismissal of the Application for Constitutional Referral and the Constitutional Complaint\\n\\n(a) During the pendency of the above appeals, the Petitioners filed an application for constitutional referral on the grounds, among others, that Article 42, paragraph 2, and Article 91, item 1, of the TULRAA violate the principle of clarity under the principle of legality in criminal law, but all such applications were dismissed [Decision of the Daegu District Court dated 2002. 9. 18., Case No. 2002CHOGI570 (related to Daegu District Court Case No. 2002NO694), Decision of the Daegu District Court dated 2002. 9. 18., Case No. 2002CHOGI569 (related to Daegu District Court Case No. 2002NO698)].\\n\\n(b) Thereupon, on 2002. 10. 2., the Petitioners filed the present constitutional complaint seeking a declaration of unconstitutionality with respect to the above provisions of the TULRAA.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether Article 42, paragraph 2, and the part of Article 91, item 1, of the Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act (enacted by Act No. 5310 on 1997. 3. 13.) that refers to \"Article 42, paragraph 2\" are unconstitutional, and the contents of the above provisions (hereinafter referred to as \"the statutory provisions at issue\") are as follows (as to the latter provision, although the application for constitutional referral, the decision dismissing the constitutional referral, and the constitutional complaint in this case merely state \"Article 91, item 1\" of the TULRAA and do not expressly specify that they are limited to the part referring to \"Article 42, paragraph 2,\" when the substance of the Petitioners' arguments is taken together, it is understood that only the part of Article 91, item 1, of the TULRAA referring to \"Article 42, paragraph 2\" is taken as the provision subject to review; accordingly, the subject matter of adjudication is limited thereto).\\n\\nTrade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act\\nArticle 42 (Prohibition of violent acts, etc.) ② An act that suspends, abolishes, or impedes the normal maintenance and operation of a workplace's safety protection facilities may not be carried out as industrial action.\\n\\nArticle 91 (Penal provisions) A person falling under any of the following subparagraphs shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 1 year or by a fine not exceeding 10,000,000 won.\\n1. A person who violates the provisions of Article 38, paragraph 2, Article 41, paragraph 1, Article 42, paragraph 2, the main clause of Article 43, Article 45, paragraph 2, Article 46, paragraph 1, or Article 63\\n\\n2. The Petitioners' Arguments and the Opinions of the Related Agencies\\n\\na. The Petitioners' Arguments\\n\\n(1) The statutory provisions at issue violate the principle of legality in criminal law recognized by Article 12, paragraph 1, and Article 13, paragraph 1, of the Constitution. The statutory provisions at issue (i) violate the principle of clarity because an univocal interpretation of the meaning of \"safety protection facilities of a workplace,\" which is prescribed as the object of the offense, is impossible; (ii) raise the question whether a person who is not directly in charge of the operation of the above safety protection facilities can be the subject of the offense; and (iii) should exclude cases in which, although the normal maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities are suspended, abolished, or impeded, such acts are carried out while safety measures are taken and do not directly cause danger to \"life and body\"; however, the statutory provisions at issue include such cases and therefore do not satisfy appropriateness, necessity, and restraint of punishment.\\n\\n(2) The statutory provisions at issue excessively restrict workers' right of collective action based on Article 33, paragraph 1, of the Constitution and thereby violate the above constitutional provision and Article 37, paragraph 2, of the Constitution. Only workers who are engaged in duties directly related to safety protection facilities, as the minimum necessary personnel for the maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities, can be the subject of the offense, and only when such workers violate the duty of care to safely shut down safety protection facilities while shutting them down should the act be criminalized; however, the statutory provisions at issue punish such acts without such limitations, and therefore restrict workers' right of collective action more than necessary.\\n\\n(3) The statutory provisions at issue excessively restrict the right to equality guaranteed by Article 11, paragraph 1, of the Constitution and thereby violate the above constitutional provision and Article 37, paragraph 2, of the Constitution. This is because, merely by being workers engaged in safety protection facilities, even in cases where the occurrence of danger is not anticipated, they are deprived of the right of collective action and made objects of punishment, thereby unreasonably and excessively discriminating between workers engaged in safety protection facilities and those who are not.\\n\\nb. Reasons for the Court's Dismissal of the Application for Constitutional Referral\\n\\nThe statutory provisions at issue cannot be said to violate the principle of clarity under the Constitution's principle of legality in criminal law, nor to excessively restrict the right of collective action and thereby infringe the essential content of fundamental rights, nor can they be seen as void provisions that infringe the right to equality.\\n\\nc. Opinion of the Minister of Labor\\n\\n(1) When the restriction provisions on industrial action in the TULRAA are comprehensively examined, the concept of \"safety protection facilities\" can be clearly understood, and even if, due to legislative technique, a somewhat broad concept was inevitably used, it cannot be said that the principle of clarity has been violated. The interpretation that the related administrative agency, the Ministry of Labor, has consistently given is that the \"safety protection facilities\" prescribed by the statutory provisions at issue should be regarded as meaning facilities related to \"human life and body,\" and this is also an interpretation established by a number of academic views. In addition, because the statutory provisions at issue clearly and specifically prescribe the sentence to be imposed for acts falling under them and are not prescribed in a manner that grants unlimited discretion to judges, they are not unconstitutional.\\n\\n(2) Even when the operation of \"safety protection facilities\" is suspended in accordance with safety rules, the risk of harm to human life and body still exists as a result of the suspension of operation; therefore, it does not violate the principle of appropriateness under the principle of legality in criminal law to prescribe that all acts suspending, abolishing, or impeding the normal maintenance and operation of \"safety protection facilities,\" including such cases, shall be punished.\\n\\n(3) The restriction of industrial action by the statutory provisions at issue is necessary to prevent danger to the life and body of others arising from industrial action, and the restriction is limited to \"safety protection facilities,\" which constitute only a very small part of the field of industrial action, so it is only a restriction to the necessary minimum among rights of collective action and thus does not violate the theory of restriction of fundamental rights under Article 37, paragraph 2, of the Constitution.\\n\\n(4) Under the TULRAA, the subject of industrial action is not individual workers but a labor union; therefore, what the statutory provisions at issue restrict is not the individual worker but the right of collective action enjoyed by the labor union. Accordingly, the statutory provisions at issue cannot be understood as presenting an issue of equity in the right to strike between workers engaged in \"safety protection facilities\" and workers engaged in other facilities, and on that premise cannot be said to violate the principle of equality.\\n\\nd. Opinion of the Governor of Jeollanam-do\\n\\nThe opinion is substantially the same as that of the Minister of Labor, and its gist is as follows.\\n\\n(1) (i) The \"safety protection facilities\" prescribed by the statutory provisions at issue do not mean facilities intended to protect objects, but mean facilities necessary for the prevention of harm to human life and body or for health reasons; and (ii) the subject of the offense may be interpreted as not being limited to workers working in safety protection facilities, and thus does not run counter to the principle of clarity.\\n\\n(2) Because safety protection facilities mean \"facilities in which, if operation is suspended, there is concretely and objectively foreseeable risk that the safety of human life or body will be jeopardized as a result,\" even if acts of suspending operation while safety measures are taken are also made subject to punishment, they do not violate the principle of appropriateness or the principle of prohibition of excess.\\n\\n(3) The restriction of the right of collective action by the statutory provisions at issue neither infringes the essential content of the right of collective action nor constitutes an excessive restriction.\\n\\n(4) Not only are persons working in safety protection facilities not the only objects of punishment, but even if the objects of punishment were limited only to such persons, there would be a rational reason, and therefore the principle of equality is not violated.\\n\\n3. Determination\\n\\na. Whether the statutory provisions at issue violate the principle of clarity\\n\\n(1) The principle of legality in criminal law and the principle of clarity\\n\\nThe principle of legality in criminal law guaranteed through Articles 12 and 13 of the Constitution means that crimes and punishment must be prescribed by law, and the principle of clarity derived from such principle of legality in criminal law means clearly defining the elements so that anyone can foresee what conduct the law seeks to punish and what punishment will be imposed therefor and may thereby determine his or her own conduct (Constitutional Court Decision 2004HEONBA35, Official Gazette 99, 1295, 1298).\\n\\nHowever, the requirement that the elements of a penal statute be clear does not mean that all elements must be prescribed as simple descriptive concepts, and even if concepts that are somewhat broad and require supplemental interpretation by a judge are used, if the statute is prescribed so that a person of ordinary sense and ordinary legal sentiment can, by ordinary methods of interpretation, know the protected legal interest of the penal statute, the prohibited conduct, and the kind and extent of punishment, then it is not contrary to the clarity of penal statutes required by the Constitution. Otherwise, the elements of a penal statute would become excessively specific and standardized, making it impossible to properly regulate the diverse and constantly changing circumstances of life (Constitutional Court Decision 2004HEONBA35, Official Gazette 99, 1295, 1298).\\n\\n(2) Criteria for determining clarity\\n\\nThe criteria for determining whether a legal norm is clear may be found in relation to the basis of the principle of clarity. Since the principle of clarity is based on the fact that, if the meaning and content of a legal norm are uncertain, legal stability and predictability cannot be secured and arbitrary interpretation and enforcement by law-enforcement authorities become possible (see Constitutional Court Decision 2000HEONBA57 of 2002. 7. 18., Court Precedents Collection 14-2, 1, 16), whether a legal norm is in violation of the principle of clarity can be determined according to whether it gives the addressee a fair notice of the meaning and content of the rule so as to provide predictability, and whether it sufficiently regulates the meaning and content for the institutions interpreting and enforcing the law so that arbitrary legal interpretation or enforcement is excluded; in other words, whether predictability and exclusion of arbitrary law enforcement are secured.\\n\\nEven where a legal norm uses indeterminate concepts, if it is possible to obtain rational and objective criteria that exclude arbitrary application by administrative agencies and courts through statutory interpretation (see Constitutional Court Decision 2003HEONBA35 et al. of 2004. 7. 15., Court Precedents Collection 16-2, upper volume, 77, 88), that is, if the meaning and content can be known even by ordinary rational methods of interpretation that do not allow arbitrariness (see Constitutional Court Decision 2001HEONBA26 of 2002. 4. 25., Court Precedents Collection 14-1, 301, 322; Constitutional Court Decision 2004HEONBA16 of 2004. 6. 24., Court Precedents Collection 16-1, 759, 766), then it does not violate the principle of clarity.\\n\\nThe meaning and content of a legal norm are concretized not only by the words of the legal norm but also by comprehensively considering the legislative purpose or intent, legislative history, and the systematic structure of the legal norm. Therefore, whether the statutory provisions at issue violate the principle of clarity depends on whether a rational interpretive criterion that can reasonably ascertain the meaning and content of the statutory provisions at issue through the above methods of interpretation (hereinafter referred to as \"rational interpretive criterion\") can be obtained.\\n\\n(3) Whether a rational interpretive criterion exists for the statutory provisions at issue\\n\\n(a) The statutory provisions at issue and the problem of clarity\\n\\nAmong the statutory provisions at issue, the part of \"Article 91, item 1, of the TULRAA referring to 'Article 42, paragraph 2'\" is a penal provision that punishes a person who violates the provisions of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA with the prescribed punishment, and there is nothing unclear in the wording itself. However, if Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA itself were unclear, then the corresponding part of Article 91, paragraph 1, of the TULRAA, which makes it one part of the provision, would also be unclear as a whole. Therefore, the determination of whether the statutory provisions at issue are clear is no different from the determination of whether Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA is clear.\\n\\nArticle 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA provides that \"an act that suspends, abolishes, or impedes the normal maintenance and operation of a workplace's safety protection facilities may not be carried out as industrial action.\" In understanding the meaning and content thereof, there are parts that are not immediately self-evident and require interpretation; however, when the wording of the above provision, its legislative purpose or intent, legislative history, and the systematic structure of the legal norm are examined, a rational interpretive criterion can be obtained, as seen below.\\n\\n(b) Legislative history\\n\\nThe current Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act is the law enacted by Act No. 5310 on 1997. 3. 13. This law is a law that repealed the former Labor Disputes Adjustment Act enacted by Act No. 279 on 1953. 3. 8., and then repealed and reenacted the former Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act enacted by Act No. 5244 on 1996. 12. 31.\\n\\nArticle 6, paragraph 1, of the former Labor Disputes Adjustment Act, enacted by Act No. 279 on 1953. 3. 8., provided that \"an act that suspends, abolishes, or impedes the normal maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities for a factory, workplace, or other place of employment may not be carried out as industrial action.\" There was no penal provision punishing the violation itself, and only Article 26 of the same Act provided for punishment of a person who violated the cessation order under paragraph 2 of the same Article.\\n\\nThe former Labor Disputes Adjustment Act, comprehensively amended by Act No. 1327 on 1963. 4. 17., provided in Article 13, paragraph 2, the same content as Article 6, paragraph 1, of the 1953 Labor Disputes Adjustment Act, but amended \"safety protection facilities\" to \"safety protection facilities,\" \"suspends or abolishes\" to \"suspends, abolishes,\" and added \"the\" before \"may not be carried out\"; unlike the 1953 Labor Disputes Adjustment Act, Article 47 provided a penal provision for the act of violation itself. Although the amendment differed in that punishment was added to the effect of the act, it cannot be said that there was any substantive change in the content of the prohibited act itself.\\n\\nThereafter, Article 42, paragraph 2, of the former Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act enacted by Act No. 5244 on 1996. 12. 31. changed \"normal\" in Article 13, paragraph 2, of the above former Labor Disputes Adjustment Act to \"normal,\" but otherwise consisted of the same wording, and Article 42, paragraph 2, of the current Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act enacted by Act No. 5310 on 1997. 3. 13. merely changed \"safety protection facilities for a factory, workplace, or other place of employment\" in the above former Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act, Article 42, paragraph 2, to \"safety protection facilities of a workplace,\" while the rest remained unchanged.\\n\\n(c) Legislative purpose\\n\\n1) Article 1 of the TULRAA provides that \"the purpose of this Act is to secure the right of workers to organize, bargain collectively, and take collective action under the Constitution, thereby promoting the maintenance and improvement of working conditions and the enhancement of workers' economic and social status, and to contribute to the maintenance of industrial peace and the development of the national economy by fairly adjusting labor relations and preventing and resolving labor disputes.\" Thus, it reveals the legislative purpose of the TULRAA. However, this only prescribes the general legislative purpose of the TULRAA as a whole and does not prescribe a special legislative purpose specific to Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA; the legislative purpose of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA can be concretely understood as follows by comprehensively considering the above provision and other related provisions and the meaning that Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA has in the overall normative system.\\n\\n2) There are generally hazards in workplaces that threaten the safety of human life and body, and such dangers tend to increase in intensity and scale as industrial society becomes more advanced. Therefore, the need to take preventive measures to protect the safety of human life and body from such dangers arising in workplaces is increasingly strongly required. The installation of safety protection facilities at workplaces may be regarded as one such preventive measure. Furthermore, Articles 23 and 24 of the Occupational Safety and Health Act enumerate various types of risks and health hazards arising in carrying on business and impose on employers the duty to take necessary measures to prevent them; thus, the installation of safety protection facilities in such cases is also the fulfillment of an obligation under that Act. Therefore, the fact that Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA prohibits acts that suspend, abolish, or impede the normal maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities can be said to have a legislative purpose of protecting the safety of human life and body from dangers arising in workplaces.\\n\\nThis legislative purpose can also be confirmed in relation to other provisions of the TULRAA. Article 38, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA provides that \"work necessary to prevent damage to work facilities or deterioration or spoilage of raw materials or products shall be normally performed even during the period of industrial action,\" thereby separately regulating so-called \"security work\" not related to the safety of human life and body, and Article 42, paragraph 1, of the TULRAA provides that \"industrial action may not be carried out in the form of violence or destructive acts, or in the form of occupying facilities related to production or other major business and facilities equivalent thereto as prescribed by Presidential Decree,\" thereby separately regulating protection of facilities related to production or other major business. Therefore, Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA can be said to be a provision concerning the protection of the safety of human life and body, and to have that as its legislative purpose.\\n\\nAlso, in light of the fact that, in the case of a violation of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA, a strong protective mechanism permitting even a cessation order is provided, the legal interest that the above provision seeks to protect is one for which prior prevention of infringement is highly required, and that protected legal interest is nothing other than \"the safety of human life and body\"; this point also confirms its legislative purpose.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 27 of the Seafarers Act expressly provides that industrial action may not be taken \"where there is concern of causing harm to life or to a vessel,\" thereby also aiming at safety protection of property facilities; however, Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA does not include \"property facilities\" in its statutory text. Taken together with the legislative purpose above, this indicates that safety protection of property facilities is not included in the legislative purpose of Article 42 of the TULRAA.\\n\\n(d) Need for an interpretive criterion\\n\\nThe wording of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA determines the meaning and content to some extent, but by itself does not enable all of the meaning and content of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA to be grasped without doubt.\\n\\nSpecifically, first, with respect to the concept of safety protection facilities, which is the object of the act: ① whether \"safety protection facilities\" means only facilities that protect the safety of human life and body, or also includes facilities that protect the safety of property equipment; ② it is clear that facilities protecting the safety of human life and body fall within safety protection facilities, but in that case, among the persons who are the subject of safety, whether the scope includes (i) members of the workplace, (ii) persons using the workplace, (iii) persons within the workplace, or (iv) third parties unrelated to the workplace; ③ whether the safety protection facilities in Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA mean only facilities whose \"purpose\" is the protection of the safety of human life and body, or also include facilities whose original purpose lies elsewhere but which, if operation is suspended, will in consequence affect the safety of human life and body; ④ whether safety protection facilities mean only property facilities or also include human facilities (human organization); second, with respect to the manner of the act: ⑤ whether Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA is violated even where there was, formally, an act that suspended, abolished, or impeded the normal maintenance and operation of a workplace's safety protection facilities, but thereby no danger at all to human life and body arose; third, with respect to the subject of the act: ⑥ whether only workers in charge of the maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities are the subject of a violation of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA, etc., questions may prima facie arise.\\n\\nTherefore, whether Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA violates the principle of clarity depends on whether a rational interpretive criterion that can ascertain the meaning and content of the above provision from the wording of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA, the above legislative history and legislative purpose, and the systematic structure of the legal norm can be found; and, in order to determine this concretely, it is necessary to examine whether rational interpretive criteria can be found for each of the above issues that may prima facie arise.\\n\\n(e) Interpretive criteria\\n\\n1) As noted above, the legislative purpose of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA is \"the protection of the safety of human life and body\"; this provides a teleological interpretive criterion for the above issues. Therefore, in understanding the meaning of \"safety protection facilities,\" in determining whether the occurrence of danger to life and body is a requirement for violating Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA, and in delimiting the scope of the subject of the act, the legislative purpose of \"protection of the safety of human life and body\" must be achieved to the greatest extent possible.\\n\\n2) As noted in the legislative history above, when the current Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act was enacted in 1997, the phrase in Article 42, paragraph 2, concerning \"safety protection facilities\" was changed from what had previously been provided in the former Act, namely \"safety protection facilities for a factory, workplace, or other place of employment,\" to \"safety protection facilities of a workplace.\" The phrase \"safety protection facilities for a factory, workplace, or other place of employment,\" when only its wording is examined, left room for doubt as to whether it (i) included safety protection of the property equipment of the factory, workplace, or other place of employment, and (ii) excluded third parties unrelated to the factory, workplace, or other place of employment from the protected object. However, (i) because the legislative purpose of the above provision is the protection of the safety of human life and body, the focus should be on human safety to be consistent with the legislative purpose; and (ii) in order to maximize realization of the above legislative purpose, and considering that there can be no restrictions or discrimination among persons whose life and body are to be protected, it cannot be required that the subject of safety have a workplace-related connection. By changing the wording to \"safety protection facilities of a workplace\" in the current law, this intent became more clearly expressed, and accordingly, \"workplace\" more clearly has the meaning not of an object of safety protection, but of the place where safety protection facilities are installed or the source of the danger threatening safety. Thus, when the current Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA is examined together with its legislative history and statutory text, it can be said to provide a clearer interpretive criterion than before.\\n\\n3) As noted above, \"protection of the safety of human life and body\" is the core legislative purpose of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA. If only this legislative purpose is considered, it is necessary to interpret the requirements of the above provision as broadly as possible so as to expand the scope of prohibition. On the other hand, because Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA is both an element of a penal provision and a requirement restricting the right of collective action, and thus significantly restricts fundamental rights, there is also a demand that the requirements of the above provision be interpreted as strictly as possible so as to restrict the scope of prohibition.\\n\\nComparing these two demands, it can be said that there exists a tension in opposite directions between the two. However, this tension is not one that cannot be harmonized, but rather one in which an appropriate point of harmony can be found. Therefore, Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA must be understood by means of an interpretive criterion harmonizing the two demands, and therein lies the true legislative purpose of the above provision. That Article 1 of the TULRAA expressly states as its legislative purpose \"fairly adjusting labor relations and preventing and resolving labor disputes\" can also be understood as requiring such harmonious interpretation.\\n\\nMeanwhile, because constitutional norms serve as interpretive criteria for statutes, where both unconstitutional interpretation and constitutional interpretation are open in the wording of a statutory provision, constitutional interpretation that excludes the unconstitutional interpretation and upholds the statutory provision as much as possible is required. Accordingly, in interpreting Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA, interpretations that are overly expansive by leaning only toward the purpose of protecting the safety of human life and body, or overly restrictive by emphasizing only workers' right of collective action, are not permitted, because they are not only contrary to the true legislative purpose of the TULRAA but also cannot be said to be interpretations consistent with the Constitution.\\n\\n4) The above harmonious interpretive criterion requires an interpretation that avoids evaluating a facility as a safety protection facility merely because, if its operation is suspended, it will in consequence affect the safety of human life and body. Such an expansive interpretation is also incompatible with the wording \"safety protection facilities.\"\\n\\nAlso, once the minimum means necessary to achieve the legislative purpose of protecting the safety of human life and body are secured, that should suffice, and not extending the scope of prohibited conduct beyond what is necessary is the interpretation consistent with the above interpretive criterion. Therefore, the above interpretive criterion presents a restrictive interpretive direction for cases in which there was, formally, an act that suspended, abolished, or impeded the normal maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities, but no danger at all to human life and body arose therefrom.\\n\\nFurthermore, whether human organization is included in safety protection facilities can also be ascertained by the above interpretive criterion. In addition to the above interpretive criterion, the systematic connection with Article 38, paragraph 2, and Article 42, paragraph 1, of the TULRAA, which together with Article 42, paragraph 2, seek to promote the normal operation of property facilities, the legislative intent of Article 42, paragraph 2, inferred therefrom, and the wording of the statutory text present a restrictive interpretive direction as to whether human organization is included in safety protection facilities.\\n\\n5) Meanwhile, if only workers in charge of safety protection facilities are the subject of a violation of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA and workers who are not so in charge are not such subjects, one may expect the effect of reducing the scope of workers whose right of collective action is restricted; however, the normal maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities can also be suspended by persons other than those in charge of the facilities, and if, in such cases, such persons are excluded from the scope of prohibition on the ground that they are not subjects of the violation, the legislative purpose of protecting the safety of human life and body would fundamentally be frustrated. Therefore, interpreting that even workers who are not in charge of the maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities can be subjects of the violation is consistent with the legislative intent of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA. Moreover, considering that there is no wording whatsoever in Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA restricting the subject, this point becomes even clearer.\\n\\n(f) Existence of a rational interpretive criterion\\n\\nAs above, with respect to Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA, a rational interpretive criterion can be found from the wording of the legal norm, the legislative purpose, the legislative history, and the systematic structure of the legal norm, and from this the determination of each of the above issues can be sufficiently made.\\n\\nMeanwhile, because the \"safety\" that Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA seeks to protect will differ in the form of danger depending on the specific circumstances, the determination of whether an act constitutes a violation of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA, that is, whether an act is a safety protection facility, should not be judged uniformly according to the type of facility or act, but should be determined by specifically and comprehensively examining all circumstances such as the nature of the workplace at issue, the function of the facility at issue, and the specific situation at the time of the industrial action. Such a determination of application in a specific case is authoritatively made through the courts' interpretive work on Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA, and because consideration of all the circumstances in the specific case is required in fixing the range of application of the above provision, the concrete meaning of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA is ultimately determined by the court deciding the individual case after comprehensively considering all circumstances.\\n\\nThe interpretive criteria reviewed above provide sufficient direction for the court to rationally concretize the meaning and content of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA in individual cases.\\n\\n(4) Conclusion\\n\\nSince there exists a rational interpretive criterion for Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA as above, it can be said that a rational interpretive criterion exists for all of the statutory provisions at issue, including this provision, and the existence of such rational interpretive criterion on the one hand provides predictability to the addressees of the statutory provisions at issue and on the other hand regulates sufficient meaning and content for the institutions interpreting and enforcing the statutory provisions at issue, thereby excluding arbitrary legal interpretation or enforcement. Therefore, the statutory provisions at issue do not violate the principle of clarity.\\n\\nOf course, it is not impossible to more clearly prescribe the statutory provisions at issue by expressly stating the concrete meaning understood as above or by illustrating safety protection facilities. However, merely because more concrete and clearer legislation is possible, it cannot immediately be said to violate the principle of clarity (see Constitutional Court Decision 99HEONGA4 of 2000. 2. 24., Court Precedents Collection 12-1, 98, 105). This is because the principle of clarity does not always require the highest degree of clarity.\\n\\nSo long as the concrete meaning and content can be ascertained from the statutory provisions at issue by rational interpretation and predictability and exclusion of arbitrary law enforcement are secured, even if there is room to make the wording of the statutory provisions at issue more concrete, it cannot be said to violate the principle of clarity.\\n\\nb. Whether the statutory provisions at issue violate responsibility principle or the principle of proportionality\\n\\nWe examine whether the statutory provisions at issue violate the responsibility principle or the proportionality principle in terms of criminal equivalence, as part of the principle of legality in criminal law (the appropriateness, necessity, and restraint of punishment claimed by the Petitioners are related thereto).\\n\\nIf, in light of the protected legal interest of the offense and the nature of the offense, there is a degree of rationality that can be accepted under the principle of proportionality between the offense and the punishment, such a statute cannot be said to be unconstitutional (Constitutional Court Decision 2003HEONBA118 of 2004. 4. 29., Court Precedents Collection 16-1, 528, 532). Here, the safety of human life and body, which is the protected legal interest that the statutory provisions at issue seek to protect, is in itself a legally important interest of a qualitatively significant nature, and especially in modern industrial society, where many industrial facilities with complex structures and functions and great influence are used, once an accident occurs due to an obstruction in a safety protection facility, the damage is likely to occur on a large scale and its effects are also likely to last for a long time; thus the amount of the legal interest can also be said to be very large. Moreover, so long as the statutory provisions at issue are understood according to the interpretive criterion seen in Section a.(3) above, the offense prescribed by the statutory provisions at issue is an act that creates a risk to the above protected legal interest and cannot be said to be of weak nature. In light of this, the punishment prescribed by the statutory provisions at issue for the above act, namely imprisonment for not more than 1 year or a fine not exceeding 10,000,000 won, cannot be said to be excessive punishment; this is no different even in the case of persons who are not the persons in charge of safety protection facilities.\\n\\nTherefore, since the point of criminalizing an act violating Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA and the punishment imposed for this offense have a degree of rationality that can be accepted under the responsibility principle or the proportionality principle, the statutory provisions at issue do not violate the responsibility principle or the proportionality principle.\\n\\nc. Whether the statutory provisions at issue excessively infringe the right of collective action\\n\\n(1) Restriction of the right of collective action\\n\\nWorkers' right of collective action is a constitutional fundamental right protected by Article 33, paragraph 1, of the Constitution. However, the statutory provisions at issue require that the maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities continue even during industrial action, and as a result at least the personnel necessary for the maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities cannot participate in industrial action, and the suspension of operation of safety protection facilities cannot be chosen as a method of industrial action. Therefore, the statutory provisions at issue are provisions restricting workers' constitutional fundamental right of collective action.\\n\\n(2) Whether the restriction is excessive\\n\\n(a) Proportionality review\\n\\nFirst, as noted above, the legislative purpose of the statutory provisions at issue is the protection of the safety of human life and body, and because this legal interest cannot be abandoned even for reasons of industrial action, the legislative purpose of the statutory provisions at issue can be recognized as legitimate.\\n\\nSecond, restricting industrial action involving suspension, abolition, or impediment of the maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities is an effective and appropriate means to achieve the above legislative purpose, and therefore the statutory provisions at issue also satisfy appropriateness of method.\\n\\nThird, the statutory provisions at issue restrict industrial action only when the industrial action becomes an act that suspends, abolishes, or impedes the maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities, and so long as the meaning and content of the acts subject to such restriction are interpreted as seen in Section a.(3) above, such restriction, in light of the importance of safety protection facilities, can be evaluated as the minimum restriction for which no further less restrictive means can be said to exist, and thus satisfies the requirement of minimal impairment.\\n\\nFourth, the public interest pursued by the statutory provisions at issue is \"the safety of human life and body,\" and the private interest restricted by the statutory provisions at issue is the Petitioners' \"right of collective action.\" Comparing the two, the legal interest of the safety of human life and body protected by the statutory provisions at issue is greater than the Petitioners' right of collective action restricted by the statutory provisions at issue, and therefore the balancing of interests is also satisfied.\\n\\n(b) Conclusion\\n\\nThe statutory provisions at issue cannot be said to excessively infringe the Petitioners' right of collective action and thereby violate Article 33, paragraph 1, or Article 37, paragraph 2, of the Constitution.\\n\\nd. Whether the statutory provisions at issue excessively restrict the right to equality\\n\\nWe examine whether the statutory provisions at issue deprive workers who are in charge of safety protection facilities of the right of collective action and make them objects of punishment, thereby discriminating against them as compared with workers who are not so in charge.\\n\\nAs seen in Section a.(3) above, Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA does not limit the subject of the violation to persons in charge of safety protection facilities. Accordingly, it cannot be said that the statutory provisions at issue discriminate between workers in charge of safety protection facilities and those who are not.\\n\\nOf course, a person in charge of safety protection facilities may also violate Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA in the form of an omission offense, and in that respect the scope of restriction on the right of collective action and punishment is broader than for workers who are not so in charge. However, this is unavoidable in light of the fact that a person in charge of safety protection facilities has a duty to act in the course of duties to maintain and operate safety protection facilities, and there is a rational reason therefor.\\n\\nThe statutory provisions at issue cannot be said to infringe the right to equality and thereby violate Article 11, paragraph 1, and Article 37, paragraph 2, of the Constitution.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nWith respect to the issues examined above, the statutory provisions at issue do not violate the Constitution, and no other violation of the Constitution can be found.\\n\\nTherefore, since the statutory provisions at issue do not violate the Constitution, except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Song In-jun, Jeon Hyo-sook, and Lee Sang-gyeong as stated in Section 5 below, the decision is rendered as stated in the operative part by the unanimous opinion of the remaining participating Justices.\\n\\n5. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Song In-jun, Jeon Hyo-sook, and Lee Sang-gyeong\\n\\nWe, unlike the majority opinion, believe that the statutory provisions at issue violate the principle of clarity and are therefore unconstitutional.\\n\\na. Ambiguity of the statutory provisions at issue\\n\\n(1) Uncertainty of the legislative purpose\\n\\nThere can be no denial that the legislative purpose of the statutory provisions at issue lies in protecting the safety of human life and body, but it is not clear whether that alone is truly the sole legislative purpose.\\n\\nFirst of all, nowhere in the wording of the TULRAA or the statutory provisions at issue is it expressly stated that only the safety of human life and body is to be protected, and in light of the legislative history there is room for a different interpretation.\\n\\nArticle 42, paragraph 2, of the former Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act (repealed by Act No. 5306 on 1997. 3. 13.) provided that \"an act that suspends, abolishes, or impedes the normal maintenance and operation of safety protection facilities for a factory, workplace, or other place of employment may not be carried out as industrial action.\" Focusing on the fact that safety protection facilities are prescribed as being \"for a factory, workplace, or other place of employment,\" it may be interpreted that the object of protection was not only human life and body but also property facilities encompassed by \"factory, workplace, or other place of employment.\" Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA is a provision that succeeded the above former Article 42, paragraph 2, of the Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act and, although it is expressed as \"safety protection facilities of a workplace,\" its meaning is not significantly different from the former law.\\n\\nFurthermore, even if the entire legal norm is systematically interpreted by considering other provisions of the TULRAA, etc., the existence of other provisions concerning the protection of property facilities does not necessarily require limiting the statutory provisions at issue to provisions concerning only human life and body.\\n\\nTherefore, the statutory provisions at issue lack clarity from their legislative purpose itself.\\n\\n(2) Unclear interpretive criterion\\n\\nEven if the legislative purpose of the statutory provisions at issue were limited to the protection of the safety of human life and body, it is also unclear what rational criterion would allow a harmonious interpretation between the demand for a relaxed interpretation arising from the above legislative purpose and the demand for a strict interpretation arising from the fundamental-rights-restricting nature of the statutory provisions at issue.\\n\\nSpecifically, as to the statutory provisions at issue, various interpretive possibilities are open as follows.\\n\\nFirst, with respect to the meaning of \"safety protection facilities\" in Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA, it may be interpreted to mean only facilities that protect the safety of human life and body, but it may also be interpreted to include facilities that protect the safety of property equipment. As noted above, because the legislative purpose of the statutory provisions at issue is unclear, neither interpretation can be said to be absolutely correct.\\n\\nSecond, with respect to the subject of human life and body sought to be protected as safety protection facilities, there is no limitation and it may be viewed as including the general third party, but at the same time an interpretation limiting it to persons related to the workplace is also possible. This is because the original safety protection facilities of a workplace can be regarded as facilities that protect members of the workplace or at least persons related to the workplace. The fact that the above former Article 42, paragraph 2, of the Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act prescribed \"for a factory, workplace, or other place of employment\" can also be another ground for such a restrictive interpretation.\\n\\nThird, safety protection facilities may be interpreted as facilities whose \"purpose\" is safety protection, but it is also possible to understand that they are not so limited. Even if they were not installed for the purpose of safety protection, it may be thought that facilities whose continued maintenance and operation are required because safety would otherwise be harmed upon suspension of operation are no different from facilities originally installed for the purpose of safety protection.\\n\\nFourth, one may understand that if no danger whatsoever to human life and body arises, there is no violation of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA; but at the same time, so long as the wording of the statutory provisions at issue does not expressly make danger to human life and body a requirement, one may also view that such danger cannot be required as an element for the establishment of the offense.\\n\\nFifth, one may view that there is no restriction whatsoever on the subject of a violation of Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA; on the other hand, because Article 42, paragraph 2, of the TULRAA is a provision restricting workers' industrial action, one may also interpret that the subject of the violation is limited to workers.\\n\\nb. Violation of the principle of clarity\\n\\nAlthough the statutory provisions at issue can be interpreted in various ways as above, neither the wording of the statutory provisions at issue, their legislative purpose, nor the systematic structure of the legal norm presents a concrete and objective criterion by which it can be recognized that any one of those different interpretations is more rational.\\n\\nThe legislator could have prescribed the statutory provisions at issue more clearly by specifying the intended content of the law in a more concrete and limited manner or at least by illustrating safety protection facilities. Even though clearer legislation was possible, by enacting unclear legislation, the statute permits the above ambiguous interpretations, and the ambiguity has reached a level at which no one interpretation can be assessed as rational.\\n\\nThus, the statutory provisions at issue enable the institution enforcing the law to arbitrarily select one among different interpretations and apply it arbitrarily, while depriving the addressee of predictability in this regard.\\n\\nAccordingly, the statutory provisions at issue violate the principle of clarity, more precisely, the principle of clarity as part of the principle of legality in criminal law.\\n\\nc. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, we believe that the statutory provisions at issue are unconstitutional as provisions violating the latter sentence of Article 12, paragraph 1, of the Constitution."}

{"[2015DO16014]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. An Enforcement Decree of a statute may not, without delegation from the parent statute, alter or supplement matters concerning an individual’s rights and duties prescribed by the statute, or prescribe new matters not provided for in the statute; in particular, where an Enforcement Decree of a statute prescribes matters relating to criminal punishment and thereby expands the objects of punishment beyond the scope expressly delegated by the statute, it also runs counter to the principle of nulla poena sine lege, and such Enforcement Decree is therefore void as having exceeded the limits of delegated legislation (see Supreme Court en banc Decision of Oct. 15, 1998, 98DO1759; Supreme Court en banc Decision of Feb. 11, 1999, 98DO2816).\\n\\nArticle 41 of the Medical Service Act (as in force before amendment by Act No. 14438 of Dec. 20, 2016; hereinafter the same) provides that “every hospital shall have on-duty medical personnel necessary for the treatment of emergency patients and inpatients, etc.,” while Article 90 provides penal provisions for persons who violate Article 41. As such, Article 41 of the Medical Service Act merely provides that every hospital shall have on-duty medical personnel necessary for the treatment of emergency patients and inpatients, etc.; it imposes no restriction whatsoever on the number and qualifications of the on-duty medical personnel to be placed in every hospital, nor does it delegate such matters to subordinate legislation.\\n\\nNevertheless, Article 18(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Medical Service Act (hereinafter the “Enforcement Decree provision at issue”) provides that “the number of on-duty medical personnel required to be placed in every hospital pursuant to Article 41 of the Act shall be one physician, dentist, or Korean medicine doctor, and two nurses, for up to 200 inpatients; and for every additional 200 inpatients in excess of 200, the number shall be increased by one physician, dentist, or Korean medicine doctor, and two nurses.” Although Article 41 of the Medical Service Act merely provides that there shall be on-duty medical personnel necessary for the treatment of patients, etc., the Enforcement Decree provision at issue newly established or expanded the objects of criminal punishment by prescribing standards for placement, such as the number and qualifications of such on-duty medical personnel, and by making violation thereof subject to punishment under Article 90 of the Medical Service Act. Therefore, the Enforcement Decree provision at issue should be deemed void as having exceeded the limits of delegated legislation.\\n\\nThe court below, on the grounds stated in its decision, held that punishing, pursuant to Article 90 of the Medical Service Act, conduct that failed to comply with the number of on-duty medical personnel prescribed in the Enforcement Decree provision at issue, without delegation from the Medical Service Act, violates the principle of nulla poena sine lege, and accordingly reversed the first-instance judgment that found the facts charged in this case guilty and rendered a judgment of acquittal.\\n\\nThe court below’s determination as above is proper as based on the legal doctrine stated above, and there is no illegality in misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the principle of nulla poena sine lege, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as stated in the Disposition. Apart from the separate opinions of Justice Lee Sang-hoon and Justice Kim Yong-deok, the opinions of the participating Justices were in accord.\\n\\n2. The separate opinions of Justice Lee Sang-hoon and Justice Kim Yong-deok are as follows.\\n\\na. It is, as a principle, not permissible for an Enforcement Decree of a statute, absent delegation by the parent statute, to alter or supplement matters concerning an individual’s rights and duties, or to determine new matters not prescribed by the parent statute. In particular, where the relevant provision supplements the contents of a statute concerning criminal punishment, in order for it to be combined with the statute and serve as the basis for criminal punishment, the principle of nulla poena sine lege requires that it be specifically delegated by the statute with the scope thereof clearly defined.\\n\\nHowever, if the contents of the Enforcement Decree of the parent statute merely specify what is already possible upon interpretation of the parent statute, by examining the legislative intent of the parent statute and the related provisions as a whole in an organic and systematic manner, or if they are intended to concretize the purpose of the parent statute’s provision, then they cannot be deemed to exceed the scope of regulation of the parent statute; accordingly, even if there is no provision in the parent statute directly delegating such matters, it cannot be said that they violate the statute (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of Aug. 20, 2014, 2012DU19526). Moreover, even for an Enforcement Decree provision that prescribes matters concerning an individual’s rights and duties, the criteria for determining whether such provision exceeds the scope of delegation provided by the parent statute, or for determining its applicability, cannot be said to be the same in cases where the Enforcement Decree provision serves as the basis for criminal punishment or taxation, and in other cases. In the case of criminal punishment provisions or tax imposition provisions, expanding the provisions of the parent statute or interpreting them by analogy with other statutory provisions is prohibited or strictly limited by the principles of nulla poena sine lege and taxation by law, whereas in the case of statutory provisions in other fields, such restrictions do not apply and the scope of interpretation is broader; therefore, even in the absence of delegation by the parent statute, the scope of an Enforcement Decree provision that may be prescribed within the interpretive scope of the parent statute may differ.\\n\\nIn addition, since an Enforcement Decree may prescribe not only matters specifically delegated by the parent statute, but also matters necessary for the enforcement of the parent statute (Constitution, Article 75), if the relevant Enforcement Decree provision does not directly alter or supplement contents concerning an individual’s rights and duties, it is not subject to the same restrictions as above, and it is entirely permissible to provide matters necessary for implementing or enforcing the parent statute, or to set forth provisions as guidelines or standards.\\n\\nAccordingly, even if an Enforcement Decree of a statute contains a provision not directly delegated by the parent statute, the intent for which such provision was enacted and its specific function must be examined to interpret its contents and thereby determine whether it contravenes the parent statute or is applicable. For example, where the parent statute broadly provides for a certain act to be done and separately provides for punishment for violation of that statutory provision, but the Enforcement Decree prescribes matters related to that act without delegation from the parent statute, then in interpreting and applying the punitive provision of the parent statute, even if the relevant Enforcement Decree provision was not directly delegated by the parent statute and punishment under the parent statute is limited to violation of the statutory provision itself, and the relevant Enforcement Decree provision cannot be combined with the parent statute’s conduct norm as a basis for punishment, it may still supplement the contents of the parent statute within the scope of possible interpretation, and may at least function as necessary guidance or standards for its implementation or enforcement; accordingly, it should be deemed valid and applicable within that scope, and it should not be unconditionally deemed to violate the statute or to be void.\\n\\nb. (1) Article 41 of the Medical Service Act provides that “every hospital shall have on-duty medical personnel necessary for the treatment of emergency patients and inpatients, etc.,” but does not specifically prescribe the qualifications, number, or method of on-duty service of such “on-duty medical personnel necessary for the treatment of patients, etc.,” nor does it contain a delegation provision allowing such matters to be determined by Presidential Decree, etc. However, Article 18(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Medical Service Act, which is the Enforcement Decree provision at issue, provides that “the number of on-duty medical personnel required to be placed in every hospital pursuant to Article 41 of the Act shall be one physician, dentist, or Korean medicine doctor, and two nurses, for up to 200 inpatients; and for every additional 200 inpatients in excess of 200, the number shall be increased by one physician, dentist, or Korean medicine doctor, and two nurses.” In addition, Article 18(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Medical Service Act (hereinafter the “paragraph 2 of the Enforcement Decree provision at issue”) provides that “psychiatric hospitals, rehabilitation hospitals, tuberculosis hospitals, etc. may place such personnel according to the hospital’s own standards so that there is no hindrance in treating inpatients.”\\n\\n(2) The Medical Service Act is a statute enacted for the purpose of protecting and promoting the health of the people by prescribing matters necessary for national medical care so that all citizens may receive high-quality medical benefits (Article 1 of the Medical Service Act). A medical professional means a physician, dentist, Korean medicine doctor, midwife, or nurse licensed by the Minister of Health and Welfare, who has the mission of contributing to the improvement of public health and securing the healthy life of the people by performing the duties prescribed according to the relevant category (Article 2 of the Medical Service Act). A medical institution is a place where a medical professional engages in the business of medical treatment or midwifery (hereinafter “medical practice”) for the public or for a specific large number of persons; among such institutions, hospital-level medical institutions mean “hospitals, dental hospitals, Korean medicine hospitals, long-term care hospitals (including psychiatric hospitals under Article 3(3) of the Mental Health Act and medical institutions that satisfy the requirements of Article 3-2 as medical rehabilitation facilities under Article 58(1)2 of the Welfare of Persons with Disabilities Act), and general hospitals” where physicians, dentists, or Korean medicine doctors primarily perform medical practice for inpatients (Article 3(2)3 of the Medical Service Act); and for this purpose, “hospitals, dental hospitals, Korean medicine hospitals, and long-term care hospitals” are required to have 30 or more beds (limited to hospitals and Korean medicine hospitals) or long-term care beds (limited to long-term care hospitals, meaning beds installed for the purpose of performing medical practice for patients requiring long-term hospitalization) (Article 3-2 of the Medical Service Act). Among hospital-level medical institutions, hospitals that satisfy the requirements to perform highly difficult medical practice for certain medical departments or certain diseases may be designated as specialty hospitals (Article 3-5 of the Medical Service Act), and among general hospitals, general hospitals that satisfy certain requirements and specialize in highly difficult medical practice for severe diseases may be designated as tertiary general hospitals (Article 3-4 of the Medical Service Act).\\n\\nIn addition, medical professionals and the heads of medical institutions shall endeavor to provide the best medical services to patients, by improving the quality of medical care, preventing hospital infections, and advancing medical technology (Article 4(1) of the Medical Service Act). Moreover, all citizens have the right to receive emergency medical care under the Emergency Medical Services Act (hereinafter the “Emergency Medical Services Act”) without discrimination on the grounds of sex, age, ethnicity, religion, social status, or economic circumstances, etc. (Article 3 of the Emergency Medical Services Act). Emergency medical personnel working in emergency medical institutions, etc. designated under the Emergency Medical Services Act shall faithfully engage in emergency medical services so that emergency patients may always receive treatment (Article 6(1) of the Emergency Medical Services Act), and where a medical professional determines that, due to the capacity of the relevant medical institution, appropriate emergency medical care cannot be provided to an emergency patient, the patient shall be transferred without delay to another medical institution capable of providing appropriate emergency medical care; when transferring an emergency patient, the head of the medical institution shall provide the medical equipment and personnel necessary for the safe transfer of the emergency patient (Article 11 of the Emergency Medical Services Act).\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing provisions, requiring every hospital with 30 or more beds to have on-duty medical personnel necessary for the treatment of inpatients and emergency patients is required in order for medical professionals and medical institutions, who are obliged under the Medical Service Act and the Emergency Medical Services Act to provide the best medical services necessary for patients and emergency patients, to fulfill that duty; and the “on-duty medical personnel necessary for the treatment of patients, etc.” may be interpreted as meaning medical professionals with appropriate qualifications, taking into account the type of the relevant hospital and the number of inpatients, in line with such legislative intent. In this regard, it is desirable, for the implementation of the on-duty medical personnel system, to establish standards regarding the qualifications and number of on-duty medical personnel suitable for each hospital.\\n\\n(3) Therefore, even if Article 41 of the Medical Service Act does not contain a provision directly delegating to the Enforcement Decree the determination of the contents of “on-duty medical personnel necessary for the treatment of inpatients and emergency patients,” it is permissible, for the implementation of the system, to establish standards regarding the qualifications, number, or work format of on-duty medical personnel suitable for each hospital; and the fact that the Enforcement Decree provision at issue or paragraph 2 of the Enforcement Decree provision at issue prescribes, by type of hospital, the qualifications and number of on-duty medical personnel, and in particular allows psychiatric hospitals, rehabilitation hospitals, tuberculosis hospitals, etc. to place such personnel according to the hospital’s own standards, can be said to have been provided for with such intent.\\n\\nAlthough, in view of the absence of specific delegation concerning the Enforcement Decree provision at issue, the “qualifications and number of on-duty medical personnel” by type of hospital prescribed in the Enforcement Decree provision at issue may not readily be treated as directly altering or supplementing the content of the medical institution’s or hospital’s duty to place on-duty medical personnel, and thus may not be taken as a basis for directly imposing a duty on medical institutions or sanctioning violations thereof, it appears at least to have significance as guidelines or standards necessary for implementing or enforcing the on-duty medical personnel system.\\n\\nAccording to Article 59(1) of the Medical Service Act, the Minister of Health and Welfare, etc. may issue necessary guidance and orders to medical institutions or medical professionals if necessary for health and medical policy or if a serious danger to public health has occurred or is likely to occur; and matters concerning the on-duty medical personnel system may be included among the subjects of such guidance and orders. The Enforcement Decree provision at issue may serve as the underlying provision as guidelines or standards in connection with guidance and orders concerning the on-duty medical personnel system. In addition, the Minister of Health and Welfare, etc. may suspend the medical practice of a medical institution or medical professional that violates such order for up to one year, or order revocation of the license for establishment or closure of the medical institution (Article 64(1) of the Medical Service Act). Whether guidance, orders, or dispositions such as suspension of business, revocation of the license for establishment, or closure of the medical institution made by the Minister of Health and Welfare, etc. pursuant to the Enforcement Decree provision at issue are lawful must be determined by whether such guidance or orders satisfy the requirements of Article 59(1) of the Medical Service Act and whether there has been any deviation from or abuse of discretion in that regard. That is, the fact that guidance or orders were issued pursuant to the Enforcement Decree provision at issue may be a positive factor supporting the view that the requirements of Article 59(1) of the Medical Service Act have been satisfied, but that fact alone does not permit the conclusion that such guidance or orders are lawful; conversely, it would be difficult to characterize such guidance or orders as unlawful or void solely on the ground that there is no delegation from the parent statute concerning the Enforcement Decree provision at issue.\\n\\n(4) Meanwhile, Article 90 of the Medical Service Act provides that a person who violates Article 41 shall be punished by a fine not exceeding 3 million won. Since the object of punishment under Article 90 of the Medical Service Act is the act of violating Article 41, punishment applies where a hospital fails to have on-duty medical personnel necessary for the treatment of emergency patients and inpatients, etc.\\n\\nHowever, even if the Enforcement Decree provision at issue was enacted for the implementation of Article 41 of the Medical Service Act, because it was prescribed without specific delegation from the Medical Service Act, in light of the legal doctrine stated above, it cannot serve, with respect to the application of Article 90, as a direct basis for determining whether there has been a failure to have “on-duty medical personnel necessary for the treatment of patients, etc.,” which is the object of punishment; therefore, the Enforcement Decree provision at issue cannot be regarded as a provision that, when combined with Article 41, serves as the basis for punishment. Ultimately, whether there is a violation must be determined within the scope recognized as “on-duty medical personnel necessary for the treatment of patients, etc.” through interpretation of Article 41 itself, and Article 90 may then be applied to and punish conduct determined to be in violation on that basis.\\n\\nMoreover, under paragraph 2 of the Enforcement Decree provision at issue, “psychiatric hospitals, rehabilitation hospitals, tuberculosis hospitals, etc.” are provided for in such a way that they may place such personnel according to the hospital’s own standards so that there is no hindrance in treating inpatients. Since, under the Medical Service Act, the distinction between long-term care hospitals and the above hospitals is not clear, it is not clear whether the Enforcement Decree provision at issue, which generally prescribes matters concerning hospitals, applies to long-term care hospitals while excluding paragraph 2 of the Enforcement Decree provision at issue; in this respect also, it is difficult to treat the Enforcement Decree provision at issue as the basis for finding a violation of Article 41 of the Medical Service Act by a long-term care hospital.\\n\\nc.
