The court below held, for reasons including that punishing conduct that does not comply with the Enforcement Decree provision at issue constitutes punishment lacking a basis in statute and thus violates the principle of nulla poena sine lege, that the Defendant’s long-term care hospital’s failure to satisfy the number of on-duty medical personnel prescribed in the Enforcement Decree provision at issue does not, by that fact alone, constitute a violation of Article 41 of the Medical Service Act and therefore cannot be punished under Article 90 of the Medical Service Act.\\n\\nThe court below’s determination can be understood as being in accordance with the legal doctrine examined above, and there is no illegality in misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the principle of nulla poena sine lege, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nd. For the foregoing reasons, although I agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion of this case, I state this separate opinion because I differ as to the reasons."}

{"[2020DO5813]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. The Defamation Portion\\n\\nA. Summary of the Case and Issue\\n\\n1) Summary of the Case\\n\\nThe gist of the facts charged in this portion is that the Defendant, in the back alley behind the home of the Victim, Person Not Prosecuted 1, in the presence of the Defendant’s husband, Person Not Prosecuted 2, and Person Not Prosecuted 3, loudly stated to the Victim words to the effect that “that person is a convicted felon who has served a prison term,” thereby publicly alleging facts and defaming the Victim’s reputation. The Defendant disputed the absence of publicity, but the court below upheld the trial court judgment that found the above facts charged guilty, on the ground that the Defendant had spoken loudly as alleged in the facts charged and that there was a possibility that the Defendant’s statement would be disseminated, and accordingly recognized publicity.\\n\\nThe ground for appeal asserted by the Defendant is that Person Not Prosecuted 2 already knew of the Victim’s prior conviction, was the Defendant’s husband, and that Person Not Prosecuted 3 was a relative of the Victim, so there was no possibility of dissemination of the Defendant’s statement and thus no publicity.\\n\\n2) Issue\\n\\nThe issue in this portion is whether to maintain the established Supreme Court precedent recognizing publicity in the offense of defamation even where there is a possibility of dissemination to unspecified persons or a large number of persons. Further, even if the precedent is maintained, we will review the existing Supreme Court precedents on this point and also consider legal principles that can reasonably limit the standards for determining publicity or the scope of its application.\\n\\nB. Defamation Provisions and Necessity of Punishment\\n\\n1) Defamation Provisions\\n\\nHonor refers to the personal value that each person ought to enjoy on the basis of human dignity and social life, and it provides the foundation for maintaining human dignity and forming relationships with others. Honor, as the protected legal interest in offenses concerning honor, refers to the social evaluation given by others concerning a person’s character (see Supreme Court Decision 88DO1008, rendered September 27, 1988, and others). To protect criminally such honor as a personal value, not only the Criminal Act but also various special statutes regulate infringements thereof, and each provision requires publicity as follows as the manner of the defamation act.\\n\\nArticle 307(1) of the Criminal Act punishes “a person who publicly alleges facts and thereby defames another’s reputation”; Article 70(1) of the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Information and Communications Network Act”) punishes “a person who, for the purpose of slandering another, openly reveals facts through an information and communications network and thereby defames another’s reputation”; and Article 251 of the Public Official Election Act provides for punishment of “a person who, for the purpose of being elected or causing another to be elected, or for the purpose of preventing another from being elected, slanders a candidate by publicly alleging facts by means of speeches, campaign documents, or other methods.” In addition, Article 307(2) of the Criminal Act punishes “a person who publicly alleges false facts and thereby defames another’s reputation,” and Article 308 of the Criminal Act punishes “a person who publicly alleges false facts and thereby defames the reputation of a deceased person,” thereby making publicity an element of the offense. On the other hand, Article 309 of the Criminal Act provides that “a person who, for the purpose of slandering another, commits the offenses under Article 307(1) and (2) by means of newspapers, magazines, radio, or other publications” shall be punished, and thus in cases of defamation by publications, etc., publicity is not required for the act of alleging facts.\\n\\nThe Information and Communications Network Act provides that where defamation occurs by information provided through an information and communications network for the purpose of public disclosure, a request may be made to the information and communications service provider that processed the information to delete such information, and the provider shall take necessary measures such as deletion (Article 44-2(1) and (2) of the Information and Communications Network Act). It further newly established provisions prohibiting the distribution of illegal information, and prohibits the distribution of “information containing content defaming another by publicly alleging facts or false facts for the purpose of slander” (Article 44-7(1)2 of the Information and Communications Network Act), and provides for criminal punishment in the event of noncompliance with an order by the Korea Communications Commission, etc. to restrict such information (Article 73(5) of the Information and Communications Network Act). Even where information in violation of the Public Official Election Act is posted on an internet homepage, etc. or transmitted through an information and communications network, measures such as deletion of the relevant information may be taken (Article 82-4(3) and (4) of the Public Official Election Act).\\n\\n2) Necessity of Punishment for Defamatory Conduct\\n\\nAlthough there is also discussion of abolishing the offense of defamation by alleging facts (Article 307(1) of the Criminal Act), with the development of science and technology, the means by which reputation is defamed and the spaces in which defamation occurs have become more diverse and new. As a result, the offense of defamation is no longer confined to ordinary criminal offenses under the Criminal Act; when the internet is used, the Information and Communications Network Act applies, and depending on the purpose, means, and method of defamatory conduct, the scope of punishment and regulation under special statutes is instead expanding further. Whether a fact that has become socially known is true or not, there are aspects that ought to be protected; in particular, disclosure concerning the essential aspects of an individual’s private life, which form the core of personal rights, may itself seriously infringe the individual’s fundamental rights. With the development of the internet and SNS, such infringements of honor occur in large numbers, and due to the immaturity of a sound internet culture, personal rights are being severely infringed in an irreversible manner by exposure of private life, distorted allegations, hate and hateful expressions, and biased opinions, producing side effects such as suicide. At present, no appropriate and effective alternative to punishment has been activated. In this respect, whether the fact alleged is true or false, the necessity for criminal punishment of defamation still exists.\\n\\nC. Significance of Publicity in the Offense of Defamation and Supreme Court Precedents\\n\\n1) Significance of Publicity\\n\\nThe relevant provisions on defamation require that the infringement of honor be made “publicly” or “openly”; “publicly” or “openly” means, in dictionary terms, “frankly, so that everyone in the world knows,” or “revealed as it is, without concealment or hesitation.” Requiring publicity as the manner of the act is intended to ensure that only defamation acts that are disseminated in society and socially harmful are punished, so that an individual’s freedom of expression is not excessively restricted.\\n\\nSupreme Court precedent has stated, as an element of the offense of defamation, that publicity means “a state in which an unspecified person or a large number of persons can perceive it” (see Supreme Court Decisions 92DO445, rendered May 26, 1992; 96DO1007, rendered July 12, 1996; 2007DO8155, rendered February 14, 2008; and others), and this is also the general view in academia.\\n\\n2) Supreme Court Precedents on Publicity\\n\\nAs to publicity in the offense of defamation, the Supreme Court has consistently held that even if facts are alleged to only a small number of persons individually, publicity is recognized when there is a possibility that the other party will disseminate the alleged facts to an unspecified person or a large number of persons, and thus the so-called theory of possibility of dissemination has settled as established legal doctrine regarding publicity.\\n\\nSpecifically, in Supreme Court Decision 68DO1569, rendered December 24, 1968, the Court first held that “unless secrecy is well protected and there is no concern that it will be disseminated externally, even if facts are disseminated to one person individually, if facts are successively disseminated to several persons and there is a possibility that the disseminated facts will be disseminated externally, there is publicity.” Then in Supreme Court Decision 81DO1023, rendered October 27, 1981, the Court held that “even if facts are disseminated to one person individually, if there is a possibility that they will be disseminated to an unspecified person or a large number of persons, the requirement of publicity is satisfied; conversely, if not, dissemination of facts to one specified person lacks publicity.” More recently, the above doctrine was maintained in Supreme Court Decision 2018DO4200, rendered June 15, 2018.\\n\\nThis doctrine applies equally to determinations of publicity in defamation through an information and communications network under the Information and Communications Network Act or in candidate-slandering offenses under the Public Official Election Act (see Supreme Court Decisions 96DO1007, rendered July 12, 1996; 2007DO8155, rendered February 14, 2008; and others), and has been applied as the basic doctrine of Supreme Court precedent concerning publicity in the offense of defamation, regardless of whether the alleged facts are false or whether it is a defamation act under a special statute.\\n\\nD. The Legal Doctrine and Validity of Supreme Court Precedent\\n\\nThe theory of possibility of dissemination regarding publicity has been developed by the Supreme Court over a long period and is still valid both doctrinally and in practical terms, and therefore should be maintained. Below, we will examine the specific content and standards of the theory of possibility of dissemination developed by the Supreme Court precedents and thereby explain the grounds on which the Supreme Court precedents should be maintained.\\n\\nThe view criticizing the theory of possibility of dissemination points out that there is no objective standard for determining whether dissemination is possible, so arbitrariness may enter specific application, and that overly severe responsibility is recognized for the actor based only on the result, contrary to the principle of responsibility. Although the criticism itself and its grounds are not valid, there are aspects with which one may sympathize in the sense of being wary of an expansion of the scope of punishment.\\n\\nBased on this awareness, Supreme Court precedent and trial practice have taken into account the concern that if the theory of possibility of dissemination is applied without limitation, the publicity requirement becomes meaningless, punishment expands, and freedom of expression is likely to be chilled. Accordingly, they have established specific and objective standards for applying the possibility of dissemination, have strictly viewed the defendant’s intent, and have categorized the standards of judgment case by case, such as denying the possibility of dissemination according to the relationship between the addressee of the statement and the defendant or victim, thereby applying the theory of possibility of dissemination on the premise that awareness of the possibility of dissemination is required and strictly recognizing publicity. A closer look follows.\\n\\n1) The Doctrine of Supreme Court Precedent\\n\\na) Proof of possibility of dissemination and awareness thereof\\n\\n(1) The prosecutor’s strict burden of proof\\n\\nPublicity is an element of the offense of defamation, and in cases of factual allegations to a specific small number of persons, it may be a highly persuasive circumstance negating publicity; therefore, strict proof by the prosecutor is required as to the possibility of dissemination (see Supreme Court Decisions 96DO2234, rendered February 14, 1997; 2004DO207, rendered April 14, 2006; and others). Further, the Supreme Court has held that “acts such as transmitting information personally or privately to a specific individual or a small number of persons cannot be said to be public; however, even if the recipient is a specific individual or a small number of persons, if there is a probability that it may be disseminated or spread to an unspecified person or a large number of persons, it can be said to be public.” Thus, as to the degree of proof for the possibility of dissemination, the Court has required not merely a “possibility” but a “probability” (see Supreme Court Decisions 81DO2491, rendered March 23, 1982; 89DO886, rendered July 11, 1989; and others).\\n\\n(2) Awareness of the possibility of dissemination and the inner will accepting the risk\\n\\nThe Supreme Court has held that “in cases where publicity is recognized in the offense of defamation on the ground of possibility of dissemination, at least dolus eventualis is required as the subjective element of the offense, so awareness of the possibility of dissemination is needed, and further there must be an inner will accepting the risk; whether the actor accepted the possibility of dissemination must be inferred from the actor’s psychological state, considering how a person of ordinary intelligence would evaluate the possibility of dissemination based on the concrete circumstances such as the form and situation of the act as manifested externally.” Thus, the Court emphasized the need for caution in recognizing the actor’s intent (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DO340, rendered April 9, 2004, and others).\\n\\nAccordingly, Supreme Court Decision 2018DO4200, rendered June 15, 2018, denied intent to defame in a case where the defendant made a statement defaming another’s reputation while asking questions intended to verify the truth of an unseemly rumor; and Supreme Court Decision 2016DO21547, rendered January 30, 2020, also found that, in light of the circumstances of the statement and its content, the defendant did not have awareness of the possibility of dissemination or the will to accept the risk, even though the recipient of the statement had no particular personal relationship with the defendant or victim. Meanwhile, Supreme Court Decision 2000DO5711, rendered April 10, 2001, upheld the lower court’s denial of publicity where the defendant made a defamatory statement about the victim during an investigation at a police station concerning the circumstances of a quarrel with the victim, and Supreme Court Decision 89DO1467, rendered April 27, 1990, denied publicity where the defendant, who was the head of a cooperative, made statements defaming the victim while explaining the victim’s reasons for lack of confidence in the course of seeking cooperation in the operation of the cooperative from the victim’s confidant, a former head of the cooperative.\\n\\nTaken together, where the statement is made not only in intimate and private relationships but also in public relationships, in the course of confirming or clarifying facts related to the work of an organization, etc.; or where the statement is made in the course of responding to another’s wrongdoing; or where the statement is made during disputes between the parties in public procedures such as investigations or litigation, caution is required in recognizing the speaker’s awareness of the possibility of dissemination and the inner will accepting the risk. Otherwise, the offense of defamation may be used as a blocking means to prevent legitimate acts such as confirmation or clarification of facts, response to wrongdoing, and investigations or litigation.\\n\\nb) Specific standards of judgment\\n\\nWhether publicity exists must be determined comprehensively after examining the objective circumstances at the time of the act, such as the relationship or status between the speaker and the addressee or victim, the circumstances and setting in which the conversation took place, the content of the factual allegation, and the manner and place of the allegation, and then reviewing whether the addressee is likely to disseminate it to an unspecified person or a large number of persons (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DO8155, rendered February 14, 2008, and others). Whether the statement was actually disseminated thereafter may be a factor to consider in determining whether dissemination was possible, but the accidental circumstance of actual dissemination after the statement should be considered only negatively in determining whether publicity is recognized (see Supreme Court Decisions 81DO1023, rendered October 27, 1981; 98DO1949, rendered September 8, 1998; 99DO4579, rendered February 11, 2000; and others).\\n\\nTherefore, even under the theory of possibility of dissemination, dissemination may be judged according to the above objective standards, and the actor can sufficiently foresee at the time of the statement whether there is publicity; the issue is not determined merely by the addressee’s intent to disseminate, nor is liability imposed based on the result of actual dissemination.\\n\\nIn particular, where the addressee of the statement is in a privately intimate relationship with the speaker or victim, such as a spouse, relative, or friend, or where the addressee is a public official or a person in a similar position who bears a duty of confidentiality or must handle such matters, publicity is denied because, due to such relationship or status, a high degree of confidentiality can be expected (see Supreme Court Decisions 78DO473, rendered April 25, 1978; 81DO1023, rendered October 27, 1981; 84DO86, rendered March 27, 1984; 99DO4579, rendered February 11, 2000; 2002DO4800, rendered November 26, 2002; and others).\\n\\nWhere the speaker and the addressee, or the victim and the addressee, are in a special relationship as above, or where the addressee holds a special status or position in relation to his or her duties, in order to recognize publicity with respect to a factual allegation to such addressee, there must exist special circumstances from which it can be regarded that dissemination to an unspecified person or a large number of persons is possible despite such relationship or status.\\n\\nc) Interim conclusion\\n\\nOver time, Supreme Court precedent has developed specific standards for determining whether there is a possibility of dissemination, while on the other hand also establishing various limiting doctrines in relation to factual allegations to a specific small number of persons. The core point is that, in order to recognize publicity on the ground that a statement to an individual small number of persons is likely to be disseminated to an unspecified person or a large number of persons, it is insufficient merely that there is a vague possibility of dissemination; a high degree of likelihood or probability is required, and strict proof thereof by the prosecutor is necessary.\\n\\n2) Occurrence of the Risk of Harming Honor and the Interpretation of Publicity\\n\\nAlthough the defamation provisions state “defames another’s reputation,” the reason it is treated as an abstract danger offense rather than an infringement offense lies in the special nature of the act value and result value of defamation. That is because infringement of the honor protected legal interest in the offense of defamation cannot be objectively confirmed and cannot be proven. Therefore, even if unspecified persons or a large number of persons have not actually perceived the alleged facts, the mere placement of those persons in such a state should be regarded as defaming honor, and it cannot be evaluated as an impossible offense or an attempt. The above interpretation of publicity refers to the aspect of whether an unspecified person or a large number of persons can perceive it, is an interpretation permitted under the principle of legality, and there is a necessity for criminal punishment of such conduct.\\n\\nAs an abstract danger offense, defamation aims to protect the social evaluation of an individual’s reputation regardless of truth, and the alleged facts must be sufficiently concrete to the extent that they may infringe the social evaluation of a specific person (see Supreme Court Decisions 94DO1770, rendered October 25, 1994; 98DO2188, rendered February 25, 2000; and others). However, since it is sufficient that the risk of infringement has arisen and actual infringement need not be shown, not only where facts are alleged to a large number of persons, but also where statements are made to a small number of persons and thereby create a state in which unspecified persons or a large number of persons can perceive the facts, such statements may be interpreted as having been made publicly.\\n\\nIn our criminal law, because publicity is prescribed as an element of the offense, it differs from countries such as Germany where publicity in defamation is treated as an aggravated requirement for punishment; thus, interpretation must also be made in conformity with our criminal law system. Further, if the publicity requirement were, based on foreign legislative examples, interpreted excessively narrowly in a manner inconsistent with the statutory text, it could result in neglecting the personal right of individuals in order to protect freedom of expression. In particular, in reality, with the development of the internet and various information and communications technologies, personal information and private life are easily exposed, and instances of loss of informational self-determination are frequent; the domain related to the secrecy of an individual’s private life must be strictly protected, and invasion thereof on the ground of freedom of expression must not be permitted. Personal rights, privacy protection, and freedom of expression are all fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution; they should be protected within their respective spheres in the course of a tension-filled relationship, and one cannot be sacrificed to protect the other.\\n\\n3) Meaning and Content of Publicity in Light of Changes in Communication Methods and Structures\\n\\nBecause the meaning of publicity is not fixed, its concept and content may change with the times and the development of information and communications networks. In our society, even now, there are many cases where, using information and communications networks such as the internet, people raise baseless suspicions or circulate rumors concerning another person’s status, social standing, or activities. Even if the alleged facts are not false facts, there are many cases where, by additionally alleging distorted suspicions, biased opinions, or unfair evaluations based on such facts, the conduct is in fact no different from alleging false facts and defaming another’s reputation, or at least seriously undermines another person’s social evaluation. Moreover, due to the influence of our society’s traditional values that place importance on honor and face, the social harm caused by defamation and slanderous posts on information and communications networks such as the internet has already reached a serious level. Therefore, even when freedom of expression is guaranteed, in light of the present forms of defamation and the special characteristics of our society, the necessity of protecting personal rights by regulating such defamatory expressions is very great (see Constitutional Court Decision 2013HEONBA105, 2015HEONBA234 (consolidated), en banc, rendered February 25, 2016, and others).\\n\\nThe theory of possibility of dissemination can be regarded as conforming to the concept of publicity in various types of defamation punishment provisions, including those concerning information and communications networks. With the development and widespread use of mobile technologies such as the internet and smartphones, most expression and communication now occur through information and communications networks such as SNS, email, and portal sites, and accordingly defamation using information and communications networks is rapidly increasing. These information and communications networks and their information distribution processes inherently possess non-face-to-face character, accessibility, anonymity, and connectivity, etc.; because infinite storage, reproduction, and transmission of information are easy, defamation using information and communications networks frequently creates a situation where the scope and boundaries of the “counterparty to the act” become unclear, and despite sending defamatory content only to a small number of persons, the act itself often creates a state in which an unspecified person or a large number of persons can perceive it. In particular, in cases of defamation through information and communications networks, the actor easily loses control over the information alleged, and due to the rapid dissemination, the degree and scope of infringement of the victim’s reputation become broad, so that in many cases self-corrective effects through counterargument and discussion become practically meaningless.\\n\\nTherefore, in light of the current methods and aspects of defamation, the characteristics of information and communications networks should also be considered in interpreting publicity. Supreme Court precedent has also, taking into account such characteristics of information and communications networks, applied the existence or absence of the possibility of dissemination as the standard in determining publicity in cases of defamation using such networks. Specifically, Supreme Court Decision 2009DO9396, rendered November 12, 2009, upheld the lower court’s recognition of publicity on the ground that, in a case where the defendant sent an email containing false content about the victim, a work colleague, to a supervisor at the workplace, there was a possibility of dissemination in light of the circumstances and content of the email transmission. Supreme Court Decision 2019DO6916, rendered July 5, 2019, upheld the lower court’s recognition of publicity where the defendant sent a KakaoTalk message to a supporter of a candidate for manager of an officetel, conveying misconduct concerning the victim, who was also running as a candidate for the same manager position, on the ground that, considering the dispute situation and the status of the recipient, it was sufficiently foreseeable that the recipient could inform unspecified persons or a large number of persons of the contents. Also, Supreme Court Decision 2019DO790, rendered February 22, 2019, upheld the lower court’s recognition of publicity in a case where the defendant alleged false facts concerning the victim through Facebook Messenger, based on factors such as the recipient having a considerable number of followers on Facebook, etc., and the content alleged. On the other hand, Supreme Court Decision 2017DO20409, rendered March 29, 2018, upheld the lower court’s denial of publicity in a case where the defendant sent a KakaoTalk message containing false content about the victim to an acquaintance, on the ground that, in light of the circumstances of the conversation and subsequent circumstances, it was merely a private conversation.\\n\\nIf, with respect to defamation using information and communications networks, one insists on a doctrine that the recipient must directly perceive it, or that publicity cannot be satisfied by a specified small number of recipients, it becomes difficult for it to function as a standard for resolution. Rather, even in cases of transmission to a specific small number of persons, examining whether there is a possibility of dissemination to an unspecified person or a large number of persons and thereby whether the general risk of infringement of an individual’s social evaluation has arisen accords with a substantive determination of publicity and can serve as a concrete standard that limits the scope of publicity. This meaning of publicity should apply equally under the Criminal Act and special statutes such as the Information and Communications Network Act.\\n\\nE. New Standard for Determining Exclusion of Illegality under Article 310 of the Criminal Act\\n\\n1) Necessity of expanding exclusion of illegality depending on the content of the statement\\n\\nAs seen above, in determining publicity in the offense of defamation, the theory of possibility of dissemination recognized in precedent should be maintained.\\n\\nHowever, separate from the standards for determining publicity according to the manner of the act, whether punishment attaches depending on the “content of the statement” needs to be determined under a stricter standard. Unlike foreign legislative examples such as Germany, our Criminal Act punishes defamation even where true facts are alleged; it must not hinder sound public opinion formation or the balanced development of democracy by punishing even fair criticism of others. The UN Human Rights Committee has also recommended to State parties decriminalization or limited application of defamation. Therefore, for sound self-correction in our society through harmony with freedom of expression, even if conduct falls within the elements of the offense of defamation, criminal punishment should be avoided where it constitutes fair criticism.\\n\\n2) Scope of recognition of exclusion of illegality under Article 310 of the Criminal Act\\n\\nArticle 310 of the Criminal Act provides that “where the act under Article 307(1) is a true fact and relates solely to the public interest, punishment shall not be imposed.” This provision sets forth a special ground for exclusion of illegality in the offense of defamation and is intended to reconcile protection of an individual’s reputation with freedom of expression. If the requirements for excluding illegality, namely proof of truth and public interest, are strictly demanded, the scope of criminal sanctions expands and freedom of the press is chilled. If criminal punishment is used to regulate the inability to engage in free criticism or debate regarding valuable public matters or matters that the public ought to know (the right to know), freedom of the press is reduced and the weight of the balancing of interests tilts toward reputation protection (see Constitutional Court Decision 97HEONMA265, en banc, rendered June 24, 1999, and others).\\n\\nTaking this purpose into account, the Supreme Court has progressively recognized Article 310 of the Criminal Act broadly. Although the wording of Article 310 of the Criminal Act provides that illegality is excluded only where “true facts” are stated, it also includes cases where the facts are not true or where truth is not proven but there are reasonable grounds for the actor to believe them to be true (see Supreme Court Decisions 4294HYEONGSANG12, rendered May 17, 1962; 85DAKA29, rendered October 11, 1988; and others). “True facts” means facts whose important parts, when considering the overall purport of the content, conform to objective reality; thus, it is acceptable even if there are slight differences from the truth in details or somewhat exaggerated expressions. Also, although the wording of Article 310 of the Criminal Act provides that illegality is excluded only “when solely concerning the public interest,” the statutory requirement has been relaxed and interpreted broadly to include not only matters concerning the state, society, or other interests of the general public, but also matters concerning a specific social group or all its members, and if the actor’s primary motive or purpose is for the public interest, Article 310 cannot be excluded merely because other secondary private motives or purposes are also involved (see Supreme Court Decisions 97DO158, rendered October 9, 1998; 2002DO3570, rendered September 24, 2002; and others).\\n\\n3) New standard for determining “public interest”\\n\\nArticle 193 of the German Criminal Code provides: “Criticism of scientific, artistic, or commercial ability, publication of critical opinions made for the exercise or defense of rights or for the exercise of legitimate interests, discipline and reprimand of subordinates by superiors, official complaints or criticism by public officials in the course of their duties, and other similar cases may be punished only when insult is recognized in light of the form of expression or the circumstances in which the opinion was expressed.” This provision guarantees freedom of expression by deeming defamation, etc. not punishable when the infringer’s act is related to the defense of a legitimate interest, even if it is not a matter of public interest.\\n\\nConsidering such legislative examples, the recommendations of the UN Human Rights Committee, and harmony with freedom of expression, in cases of alleging true facts, the “public interest” under Article 310 of the Criminal Act should be recognized more broadly. In particular, considering that the concept of public-interest relevance changes with the times and public concerns also change constantly depending on circumstances, it should not be limited only to matters concerning public figures, institutions, and policies.\\n\\nTherefore, even if the content of a factual allegation concerns only some interests of society in general, if it relates to matters concerning common life with other members of the public, it should be regarded as having public interest. Furthermore, even if it concerns matters about an individual, if it is related to the public interest and has acquired social attention, Article 310 should not be excluded merely because it is not directly about the interests of the state, society in general, or a specific social group. Even a private person should be judged by considering the nature of the social activities in which he or she is involved and the effects on society as to whether the matter relates to the public interest.\\n\\nF. Judgment on the Present Case\\n\\n1) According to the reasons of the court below’s judgment and the evidence lawfully admitted by the court below, the following facts or circumstances can be ascertained.\\n\\na) The Defendant and the Victim were neighboring residents and were in a conflictual relationship over various matters, and on the day in question, too, the Defendant came to make the statement as alleged in the facts charged during a quarrel with the Victim in the back alley behind the Victim’s house.\\n\\nb) The Defendant’s husband, Person Not Prosecuted 2, and the Victim’s wife, Person Not Prosecuted 4, hearing the Defendant and the Victim quarrelling loudly, came out of their respective homes, and the Victim and Person Not Prosecuted 4 consistently testified to the effect that “the Defendant shouted loudly that the Victim was a convicted felon, and that in addition to Person Not Prosecuted 3, the villagers heard it.”\\n\\nc) Even in front of police officers who were dispatched after receiving a report, the Defendant also shouted several times, loudly, that “the Victim is a very bad convicted felon.”\\n\\nd) The place where the Victim lives is a clan village of persons bearing the same surname as the Victim and Person Not Prosecuted 3; although the Victim had a prior conviction, Person Not Prosecuted 3 testified that he “first heard from the Defendant that the Victim was a convicted felon,” suggesting that he was not on close terms with the Victim.\\n\\n2) Reviewing these facts in light of the foregoing legal doctrine, and considering the degree of familiarity between Person Not Prosecuted 3 and the Victim and the fact that the alleged facts concern personal matters the Victim would prefer not to make public and are likely to be discussed around the neighborhood, it cannot be said that dissemination is denied merely because Person Not Prosecuted 3 is related to the Victim by kinship (the degree of kinship or specific closeness between the Victim and Person Not Prosecuted 3 has not been established). Rather, since the Defendant spoke loudly in a public place merely to insult or slander the Victim during a fight with the Victim, to the extent that other villagers could hear, it is reasonable to view this as a state in which unspecified persons or a large number of persons could perceive it, and thus publicity is recognized for the Defendant’s statements in the facts charged.\\n\\nThe court below’s determination to the same effect contains no error in misunderstanding the legal doctrine regarding publicity in the offense of defamation as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. The Portion on Injury to Victim Person Not Prosecuted 5, etc. and Assault on Victim Person Not Prosecuted 6\\n\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in the judgment, upheld the trial court judgment that found each of the facts charged in this portion guilty. Examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment in light of the relevant legal doctrine and the lawfully admitted evidence, there is no error in the court below’s determination that violated the rules of logic and experience, went beyond the limits of the free evaluation of evidence, or misunderstood the doctrine concerning the expression of an intent not to punish in offenses subject to complaint with no express wish to punish.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as set forth in the order. In this judgment, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous except for the dissenting opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyeong, Ahn Cheol-sang, and Kim Seon-su, and there are supplemental opinions of Justices Park Sang-ok and Min You-sook regarding the majority opinion.\\n\\n4. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim Jae-hyeong, Ahn Cheol-sang, and Kim Seon-su\\n\\nA. The majority opinion seeks to maintain the theory of possibility of dissemination regarding “publicity,” an element of the offense of defamation. However, publicity as referred to in the offense of defamation is a concept that cannot encompass possibility of dissemination. Publicity prescribed in Article 307(1) and (2) of the Criminal Act refers to a state in which an unspecified person or a large number of persons can directly perceive it, and even if facts are spoken to a specific individual or a small number of persons and there is a possibility that they may be disseminated to an unspecified person or a large number of persons, the publicity requirement cannot be said to be satisfied. The majority opinion expands and applies the elements of the offense, thereby imposing criminal punishment beyond the scope contemplated by the Criminal Act, and cannot be supported as it violates the principle of legality and the principle of statutory interpretation in criminal law. Supreme Court decisions consistent with the theory of possibility of dissemination, including Supreme Court Decisions 68DO1569, rendered December 24, 1968; 85DO431, rendered April 23, 1985; 2005DO329, rendered March 25, 2005; 2008DO6515, rendered October 23, 2008; and others, should be overruled.\\n\\nThe detailed reasons are as follows.\\n\\nB. Recognizing publicity on the ground that there is a possibility of dissemination is an expansive interpretation unfavorable to the defendant, beyond the ordinary meaning of the text, and constitutes analogical interpretation prohibited by the principle of legality.\\n\\nTextual interpretation is the starting point of legal interpretation. In the interpretation of criminal statutes, expanding the scope of punishment through analogy beyond the possible meaning of the text is not permitted. Therefore, when interpreting criminal statutes, the meaning of the text must be given even greater importance.\\n\\nThe Criminal Act of the Republic of Korea is characterized by establishing “publicity” and “the allegation of facts” as the basic elements of the offense of defamation (Article 307(1)). In cases of alleging false facts, the statutory penalty is merely heavier than for defamation by alleging facts (Article 307(2)). By making it possible for the offense of defamation to be established even when one speaks facts as they are — unusually, even in modern civilized states — the scope of its establishment has been greatly expanded, while limiting the offense to cases satisfying the publicity requirement mitigates the threat posed by the offense of defamation by alleging facts to freedom of expression.\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of setting publicity as an element of the offense of defamation lies in punishing only those acts that go beyond the dimension of private conversation or transmission of information and “socially” or “publicly” reveal facts among the acts that can lower the evaluation of a person’s personal value. It can be said to be the legislator’s decision to punish only cases where facts that can infringe another’s reputation are disseminated in society, and this functions to narrow the scope of establishment of the offense of defamation and thereby protect, as broadly as possible, freedom of expression guaranteed by the Constitution.\\n\\n“Publicly” means, as in the Korean dictionary, “clearly and frankly enough for everyone in the world to know.” In Article 307 of the Criminal Act, “publicly” is a requirement limiting the manner of the act of alleging facts or false facts, meaning that the execution act itself must be publicly made, and it is clear from textual interpretation that an execution act not made publicly is not subject to punishment for defamation. Article 70 of the Information and Communications Network Act, which punishes defamation through an information and communications network, uses the expression “openly” instead of “publicly,” thereby making the meaning of publicity even clearer.\\n\\nNo matter how expansively “publicly” or “openly” is interpreted, one cannot say that speaking privately to a few friends or colleagues is “clearly and frankly enough for everyone in the world to know” or “revealed as it is, without concealment or hesitation.” Even if, as a result of such conduct, the facts are later disseminated to an unspecified person or a large number of persons, if the act itself did not allege facts “publicly,” it cannot be punished as defamation.\\n\\nAmong the cases in which the Supreme Court has recognized publicity on the basis of possibility of dissemination, many involve conversations held in private relationships such as among friends or colleagues. Even secret conversations made after obtaining a promise from the other party to keep the matter confidential are recognized as public on the basis of the possibility of dissemination.\\n\\nSupreme Court Decision 68DO1569, the first case in which the theory of possibility of dissemination appeared as precedent, concerned a defendant speaking at his home to a resident of the same neighborhood. Supreme Court Decision 85DO431, rendered April 23, 1985, concerned the defendant confirming rumors about the victim with a married couple who were church members of the same church, and Supreme Court Decision 2005DO329, rendered March 25, 2005, concerned the defendant telling false facts about the victim over the telephone to his classmates. Supreme Court Decision 2017DO13231, rendered November 3, 2017, concerned the defendant speaking ill of the victim to one work colleague in a restroom. These decisions recognized publicity on the ground of possibility of dissemination. Supreme Court Decision 2007DO8155, rendered February 14, 2008, concerned a one-on-one confidential conversation in a private chat room on a personal blog, and Supreme Court Decision 2016DO4699, rendered August 29, 2016, concerned the defendant swearing at the victim after promising confidentiality in a KakaoTalk chat room with four members of a club; publicity was recognized on the ground of possibility of dissemination.\\n\\nIn such cases, can the defendant’s statements or expressions be evaluated as having been made “clearly and frankly enough for everyone in the world to know”? That goes beyond the legislator’s expectation and is not what legal reason requires.\\n\\nPeople speak, interact with others, and develop sociality through speech. Speech is the most important means of connecting person to person and forming social relationships. The freedom to speak is a core right constituting freedom of expression. As the saying goes, “words without feet travel a thousand ri.” Speech itself contains the possibility of dissemination. Punishing speech about another person merely because of the possibility of dissemination, whether true or false, does not accord with human essential nature and seriously threatens freedom of expression guaranteed by the Constitution. Therefore, the reason publicity is required as an element of the offense of defamation is to secure breathing room for freedom of expression in light of such human essential nature. Recognizing publicity in cases such as those addressed by the above Supreme Court decisions, based on possibility of dissemination even for private conversations among individuals, is undesirable from the standpoint of constitutional protection of fundamental rights.\\n\\nPossibility of dissemination means that the result has not yet actually occurred but may be disseminated in the future. Using as the basis for punishment a conjecture as to the “possibility” of future dissemination when such result has not occurred is clearly contrary to the principle of legality. Changing possibility into probability does not alter the matter. Recognizing publicity based only on possibility of dissemination means that acts defaming honor — or, according to the majority opinion, acts risking such defamation — are punishable even where they were not made “publicly,” merely because there is a “possibility” that they may be disseminated and thus become public. Such interpretation is clearly unfavorable to the defendant and constitutes an impermissible expansive interpretation and analogical interpretation.\\n\\nC. The theory of possibility of dissemination is contrary to the principle of legality and the principle of definiteness.\\n\\nThe Criminal Act is based on the principle of legality and the principle of definiteness. The principle of legality, under which crimes and punishment must be prescribed by law, is a fundamental principle of criminal law. The principle of definiteness, under which penal provisions must be clear so that ordinary persons can know how their conduct is punished, is an important criminal law principle supporting the principle of legality.\\n\\nThe Criminal Act clearly provides that “an act of publicly alleging facts or false facts” is punishable. Whether the offense of defamation is established should be determined not by the possibility of dissemination of the alleged facts, but by whether the act of alleging facts itself has publicity. At that point, publicity can be determined by analyzing the nature or form of the act and judging whether it was directed to an unspecified person or a large number of persons, whether the act of alleging facts was made in a public place, etc., and thus whether unspecified persons or a large number of persons perceived or could perceive it, and whether such a state can be regarded as being socially or publicly disseminated.\\n\\nThe theory of possibility of dissemination results in creating a new element of the offense, namely possibility of dissemination, in addition to publicity, which is an element of the offense of defamation, and thus conflicts with the principle of legality. Moreover, the theory of possibility of dissemination undermines the principle of definiteness, impairs the function of the offense of defamation as a behavioral norm, and results in permitting the applier of the law to operate penal provisions arbitrarily.\\n\\nD. The theory of possibility of dissemination hampers a consistent and systematic interpretation of publicity in other offenses that require publicity as an element.\\n\\nArticle 243 of the Criminal Act, concerning the display or screening of obscene pictures, etc., provides for punishment of “a person who publicly displays or screens obscene pictures, etc.,” thereby requiring publicity as an element. Supreme Court Decision 73DO409, rendered August 21, 1973, held that “publicly displaying obscene pictures, etc. means presenting obscene pictures, etc. in a state where an unspecified person or a large number of persons can view them, and placing them in a state where only a specified small number can see them does not fall thereunder,” thereby not considering possibility of dissemination, unlike publicity in the offense of defamation.\\n\\nThe offense of public indecency under Article 245 of the Criminal Act likewise punishes “a person who publicly commits an obscene act” and thus makes publicity its element, and the Supreme Court interprets publicity in that offense as a state in which an unspecified person or a large number of persons can know it (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DO4372, rendered December 22, 2000, and others). Since the offense of public indecency is established only when an obscene act is committed in a state where an unspecified person or a large number of persons can directly perceive it, publicity in that offense cannot be interpreted as possibility of dissemination. Supreme Court Decision 2000DO4372, rendered December 22, 2000, upheld the lower court’s determination that “even in an apartment elevator, if there was almost no possibility that anyone would board, it cannot be regarded as a state in which an unspecified person or a large number of persons can perceive the obscene act, and publicity is not recognized.” The Supreme Court thus views publicity in public indecency differently from publicity in defamation.\\n\\nThe offenses discussed above all protect social legal interests, yet they commonly require publicity as an element. The reason is to punish only those cases where the individual act infringing the protected legal interest in each offense is directly disseminated in or exposed to society, thereby harming others or creating a risk of infringing the protected legal interest. In this respect, this is the same legislative purpose as when publicity was included as an element of the offense of defamation.\\n\\nThe meaning of publicity should be interpreted consistently in the various offenses under the Criminal Act and other statutes that require publicity as an element. That is in accord with the legislative purpose of each provision and the systematic interpretation of criminal law. In the offense of defamation, including possibility of dissemination in the concept of publicity, unlike in public indecency or display/screening of obscene pictures, etc., undermines the unified interpretation of the Criminal Act and cannot escape the criticism that there is no consistency regarding publicity.\\n\\nE. Determining publicity by whether the recipient of the factual allegation may disseminate it infringes the foreseeability of the norm-addressee and imposes result responsibility on the actor, which conflicts with the evaluative method of criminal law.\\n\\nIn criminal law, the essence of illegality lies in act value and result value, and the mode of evaluating such illegality proceeds by first examining the objective attributes of the act and then identifying the attribution relationship between the act and the result flowing therefrom. In other words, the first thing to determine in a criminal law illegality analysis is the illegality of the act. Whether another person’s reputation was defamed by publicly alleging facts must be judged by evaluating the illegality of the act with the person who committed such act as the standard.\\n\\nJudging publicity based on whether there is a possibility of dissemination, centering on what the relationship is between the person alleging facts (the actor), the recipient, and the victim, is inconsistent with the above method of judgment. That is because it is not an illegality assessment of the actor’s conduct, but an assessment of the actor’s illegality in consideration of the status or role of a third party who later hears the facts. In offenses other than those requiring publicity, such as defamation, criminal law does not determine the establishment of the offense according to the status or role of a third party rather than the actor’s conduct. Even where it is not known what relationship a third party who received the facts alleged by the actor has with the victim, determining publicity based on such circumstances exceeds the actor’s foreseeability. This makes it difficult for the actor to foresee, at the time of the act, whether the facts may be disseminated to an unspecified person or a large number of persons.\\n\\nThe Criminal Act does not have a general element punishing infringement or risk to all legal interests; it punishes only specific acts that fall within the elements of the offense. However, the theory of possibility of dissemination emphasizes the result of injury to honor or the occurrence of such risk, and disregards the illegality assessment of the specific act prescribed as an element of the offense of defamation, namely the act of publicly alleging facts. In this respect, the theory of possibility of dissemination can be seen as placing the illegality assessment for the offense of defamation on result value.\\n\\nIf the original speaker repeatedly alleges facts to a specific small number of persons, the publicity requirement can be deemed satisfied. However, if the recipient who heard the defamatory facts from the original speaker disseminates them to an unspecified person or a large number of persons, it is not the original speaker but the recipient-disseminator who has defamed honor. If the original speaker intended the recipient’s act of dissemination with intent to defame, then the recipient becomes the principal offender of the offense of defamation, and the original speaker should be dealt with under the doctrines of instigation or aiding and abetting; that is the principled method of solution in criminal law. In other words, the way to punish an actor who had in mind and sought to use the recipient’s dissemination possibility should be the doctrine of accomplice liability, not the concept of possibility of dissemination.\\n\\nEven if the original speaker alleged defamatory facts to a specific small number of persons and it is impossible to find the person who actually disseminated them, the original speaker did not allege facts “publicly,” and thus it is merely that punishment under the offense of defamation is not possible; this cannot be viewed as a gap in punishment. Therefore, to think that publicity includes possibility of dissemination in order to prevent such a gap in punishment misunderstands the legislative purpose of providing publicity as an element of the offense.\\n\\nUltimately, in the offense of defamation, deciding whether the offense is established based on whether the recipient who heard the defamatory facts will in the future convey the facts alleged by the actor to others is to impose result responsibility by relying on an accidental circumstance that should not be taken into account in assessing illegality of the act.\\n\\nF. Determining publicity by the existence or nonexistence of possibility of dissemination excessively expands the scope of punishability for the offense of defamation and also conflicts with the principle of subsidiarity in criminal law.\\n\\nAccording to the wording of Article 307(1) of the Criminal Act, the offense of defamation is not established merely because facts about the victim are alleged; it is established only when the statement has publicity and the victim’s reputation is defamed. If, as the majority opinion says, the offense of defamation is viewed as an abstract danger offense, the manner of the act becomes an important factor in determining whether the offense is established, and only by strictly limiting the manner of the act can one prevent the scope of penal power from expanding excessively. Moreover, because the Criminal Act punishes defamation even when true facts are alleged, there is a strong need to limit the scope of punishability.\\n\\nConsidering possibility of dissemination in determining publicity substitutes possibility of dissemination for the publicity required as the mode of conduct in the offense of defamation, and confuses the protected legal interest or degree of the offense of defamation, which is an abstract danger offense established by risk of infringement even if external honor has not actually been infringed, with the manner of the act. That the offense of defamation is an abstract danger offense means that punishment is imposed when there is a risk that honor will be defamed by facts alleged publicly; it does not mean that punishment is imposed even when there is a risk that the alleged facts will become public. The basis for punishment of the offense of defamation lies not in the risk that facts will continue to be disseminated, i.e., the risk of defamation that will arise because another person disseminates them, but in the risk of defamation arising from publicly alleging facts.\\n\\nThe majority opinion also interprets publicity as a state in which an unspecified person or a large number of persons can perceive it, so the offense of defamation reaches completion when facts capable of harming honor become perceivable by an unspecified person or a large number of persons. This recognizes illegality before the result of infringement due to defamation arises, even though civil tort liability, which arises only when there is a result of infringement, does not. However, the theory of possibility of dissemination recognizes illegality even before reaching such a stage of risk. In other words, it treats the possibility of being disseminated to an unspecified person or a large number of persons and the actual state of being so disseminated as identical.\\n\\nThe majority opinion says that the former case indirectly creates a state in which an unspecified person or a large number of persons can perceive it, but merely alleging facts to a specific small number of persons cannot be regarded as indirectly creating such a state. Only if the recipient actually alleges the facts to an unspecified person or a large number of persons can such a risk be said to have arisen; if the recipient does not disseminate them to anyone, then no “general” risk of infringement of honor has arisen. In this respect, the majority opinion ultimately imposes result responsibility by evaluating the defendant’s conduct not by the recipient’s will and dissemination but by the result. This problem arises because conduct that was not subject to punishment in the first place is subsumed under the publicity requirement. Efforts to limit the scope of punishability by objectively judging the possibility of dissemination, or by requiring awareness of the possibility of dissemination, as in the majority opinion, cannot be a fundamental solution.\\n\\nAlso, even in cases of private conversation or transmission of information with a specific small number of persons, viewing publicity as existing where there is a possibility of dissemination means viewing almost all acts of alleging facts as in principle satisfying the elements of the offense of defamation, which conflicts with the principle of subsidiarity in criminal law. If viewed this way, private and personal allegations of facts that occur naturally in daily life can be punished criminally. Therefore, such interpretation further makes the offense of defamation, an abstract danger offense, even more abstract by criminalizing acts of alleging facts to an unspecified person or a large number of persons even before the stage where the risk of injury to an individual’s reputation has arisen.\\n\\nG. Because it is difficult to establish objective standards by which to determine the existence or nonexistence of possibility of dissemination, there is a strong possibility that arbitrariness will enter specific application.\\n\\nEven if possibility of dissemination is examined on the basis of the relationship among the fact-asserter, the recipient, and the victim, it is equally difficult to establish objective standards as to in what cases dissemination is possible. In cases where facts are alleged to a work colleague or a friend, it is difficult to objectify how close the relationship must be with the actor or the victim in order to conclude that there is no possibility of dissemination, and because proving or judging this is not easy, the danger becomes greater that possibility of dissemination will be subsumed, without specific proof, in the direction of “at least there is a possibility of dissemination.”\\n\\nEven where the recipient is evaluated as being in a close relationship with the victim or the person who alleged the facts, there are cases where the recipient actually disseminated them to an unspecified person or a large number of persons (assuming the path of dissemination is not revealed), and conversely there are cases where the recipient is evaluated as not being in a close relationship yet did not actually disseminate them. In the latter case, publicity is recognized solely on an abstract and vague criterion of close relationship even though no risk arose that the defamatory facts would be placed in a state where an unspecified person or a large number of persons could perceive them, while in the former case, an irrational result arises in that punishment is not imposed on the ground that there was no possibility of dissemination. It is clear that such interpretation is not in accord with the legislative purpose of setting publicity as an element of the offense of defamation.\\n\\nEven though decisions concerning possibility of dissemination have accumulated for decades, it remains difficult to find clear standards, and there have been many cases in which different judgments were made regarding possibility of dissemination even in fact patterns where the relationship with the recipient was similar. Among cases in which possibility of dissemination was affirmed are a case where the recipient of the allegation was the defendant’s and victim’s middle school classmate (Supreme Court Decision 2005DO329, rendered March 25, 2005), a case where the recipient was a person who represented the victim in legal affairs (Supreme Court Decision 2015DO9019, rendered January 14, 2016), and a case where the recipient was the defendant’s work colleague (Supreme Court Decision 2017DO13231, rendered November 3, 2017). Among cases in which possibility of dissemination was denied are a case where the recipient was the victim’s work colleague (Supreme Court Decision 98DO1949, rendered September 8, 1998) and a case where the recipient was the victim’s friend (Supreme Court Decision 99DO4579, rendered February 11, 2000). In the above affirmative and negative examples, one cannot distinguish whether there is a possibility of dissemination merely by the existence of a certain personal relationship with the victim.\\n\\nMoreover, using whether the recipient “actually disseminated it” as a factor in determining publicity creates the problem of deciding whether the offense of defamation is established based on the accidental result of dissemination by the recipient (perhaps because the majority opinion considered such criticism, it says that actual dissemination should be considered only negatively, but in Supreme Court Decision 94DO1880, rendered September 30, 1994, and others, actual dissemination was considered a positive circumstance for recognizing publicity). Even though private conversation or transmission of information to a specific small number of persons is excluded from the punishment scope in defamation, publicity is replaced by the concept of possibility of dissemination, which is not prescribed as an element of the offense, in order to punish even such cases.\\n\\nH. Even in defamation using an information and communications network, there is no reason to view the concept of publicity differently.\\n\\nThe Information and Communications Network Act requires that, even when using an information and communications network, the act of alleging facts be made openly, and thus its concept of publicity is the same as publicity in the offense of defamation. Even through an information and communications network, if facts are alleged only to a specific small number of persons, publicity still cannot be said to exist, and such conduct is not subject to regulation under the offense of defamation under the Criminal Act or the Information and Communications Network Act. In other words, alleging facts through an information and communications network, such as an email or SNS message, to one friend and writing a letter or speaking face-to-face are the same mode of conduct insofar as facts are alleged to a specified small number of persons, and the use of an information and communications network does not mean that a general risk of infringement of honor has arisen.\\n\\nThe issue that the degree and scope of harm caused by defamation through infinite storage and reproduction of information have widened due to the development of the internet and science and technology should be addressed through sentencing or aggravated punishment under the Information and Communications Network Act, and there is no need to change the concept of publicity for that reason.\\n\\nI. Expanding the scope of publicity through the theory of possibility of dissemination and emphasizing punishment for defamation is also out of step with foreign legislative trends.\\n\\nThe offense concerning honor originates from ancient Roman law and Germanic law, and its origin has the characteristic that it existed as a system for the powerful and ruling class to prevent criticism by ordinary citizens; in fact, our society has experienced such matters several times. Even recently, as seen in the Me Too movement, the offense of defamation functions as a means to block the free expression of victims of sexual violence, and contradictory situations arise in which the victim is instead criminally punished.\\n\\nIn order to realize freedom of expression, the most important fundamental right that forms the basis of democracy, countries have abolished criminal punishment for defamation and are resolving it through civil means. In the United States, most defamation matters have been resolved civilly since the 20th century, and even where some states have criminal punishment provisions, they are rarely applied in practice. In the United Kingdom, criminal punishment for defamation had long existed and the country was sometimes called the kingdom of defamation, but from the late 19th century criminal punishment for defamation declined in order to guarantee freedom of expression, and in 2010 defamation was abolished (Section 73 of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009). In Germany, if the truth of the defamatory fact is proven, punishment for defamation is not imposed (Article 186 of the German Criminal Code), and in France imprisonment cannot be imposed as a punishment for defamation (Articles 29 through 32 of the French Law on Freedom of the Press).\\n\\nThe UN Human Rights Committee stated that, in order to ensure freedom of expression, truth as a defense should be permitted in defamation and that decriminalization of defamation should be considered, and in particular, detention should not be imposed for defamation [UN Human Rights Committee (HRC), General Comment No. 34, Article 19, Freedoms of Opinion and Expression, September 12, 2011, CCPR/C/GC/34, para. 47]. Moreover, a report of the Special Rapporteur of the UN Human Rights Council recommended that the Republic of Korea abolish the criminal offense of defamation under the Criminal Act. Criminal punishment for defamation excessively chills the right to freedom of expression, and criminal punishment is not justified given that defamation can be appropriately addressed through damages under the Civil Act [Frank La Rue, Report of the Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of the right to freedom of opinion and expression, Human Rights Council 17th Session, Agenda item 3, A/HRC/17/27/Add.2 (21 March 2011), para. 28].\\n\\nHowever, the Criminal Act of the Republic of Korea still punishes even the allegation of true facts, and unless it concerns the public interest, criminal punishment cannot be avoided. In addition, since the Supreme Court adopted in 1968 the theory of possibility of dissemination that had been recognized in Japanese precedent, this doctrine has expanded the scope of criminal punishment by recognizing publicity even in private conversations between individuals, and it cannot be denied that this has brought about a serious chilling effect on freedom of expression.\\n\\nThe majority opinion attempts to broadly recognize public-interest relevance under Article 310 of the Criminal Act for freedom of expression, but that cannot be a fundamental solution to the problem, and the order is reversed. That is, the first step is to strictly interpret the scope of publicity in light of the purpose of prescribing publicity in the offense of defamation.\\n\\nThe majority opinion first deems that even expressions made in private relationships and private spaces fall within the elements of the offense in order to protect an individual’s reputation, and then seeks to broadly read the ground for exclusion of illegality under Article 310 of the Criminal Act so as to harmonize with freedom of expression. However, this ultimately remains biased toward protection of personal reputation, and is nothing more than a pretext to maintain the theory of possibility of dissemination. No matter how broadly the ground for exclusion of illegality under Article 310 of the Criminal Act is interpreted, if the main purpose or content of the statement lacks public interest, punishment for defamation still follows. It is doubtful how often private conversation in a private space can have public interest, and to require this is akin to prohibiting casual talk on private matters. All citizens can avoid criminal punishment only by hoping that their private conversation contents do not happen to leak to the victim. This treats all citizens as potential or undetected offenders.\\n\\nFreedom of expression may be restricted for statements harmful to the public interest, but freedom of expression is not permitted only for the public interest. However, the theory of possibility of dissemination adopted by the majority opinion ultimately leads to the result that freedom of expression is permitted only for the public interest (or only where the primary purpose is for the public interest, even if secondary private motives are included). No matter how broadly public-interest purpose is recognized, the result cannot change so long as the theory of possibility of dissemination is not abandoned.\\n\\nJ. In light of this legal doctrine, we examine the court below’s determination concerning defamation.\\n\\n1) This case concerns the Defendant alleging facts about the Victim in the presence of the Defendant’s husband, Person Not Prosecuted 2, and the Victim’s relative, Person Not Prosecuted 3, who were listening. Since merely speaking to a specific small number of persons cannot be regarded as having been in a state in which an unspecified person or a large number of persons could directly perceive it, it is difficult to see the Defendant’s statement as having publicity. Therefore, even if the Defendant spoke as stated in the facts charged, such conduct cannot be said to constitute defamation against the Victim.\\n\\n2) The facts charged in this portion are premised on the notion that publicity can be recognized by applying the theory of possibility of dissemination even though the recipients who heard the defamatory facts concerning the Victim were only two persons, the Defendant’s husband, Person Not Prosecuted 2, and Person Not Prosecuted 3, and it was revealed during the trial that Person Not Prosecuted 3 is a relative of the Victim. The point that the recipient is in a special status relationship with the Defendant or victim is a highly persuasive circumstance for denying publicity (or, in the majority opinion’s view, possibility of dissemination), and therefore, despite such status relationship, proof beyond a reasonable doubt is required concerning the point that the Defendant’s statement had publicity.\\n\\nHowever, the reasons of the court below merely state that even if Person Not Prosecuted 3 is related to the Victim, there is still a possibility that the Defendant’s statement could be disseminated, and even upon reviewing the reasons and the record, it is difficult to say that sufficient examination or proof regarding publicity was conducted. Also, whether other villagers heard it because the Defendant spoke loudly is not part of the facts charged in this portion.\\n\\nThe majority opinion, by finding in the record circumstances suggesting that the Defendant was not even given an opportunity to exercise the right of defense, accepts the above determination of the court below; it is doubtful whether this is consistent with the majority opinion’s position that the theory of possibility of dissemination should be applied restrictively.\\n\\n3) Ultimately, since the court below found the facts charged in this portion guilty on the premise that publicity was satisfied because the Defendant’s statement had a possibility of dissemination, the court below’s judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning publicity in the offense of defamation.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I dissent from the majority opinion.\\n\\n5. Concurring Opinion of Justices Park Sang-ok and Min You-sook on the Majority Opinion\\n\\nA. The dissenting opinion takes the position that all Supreme Court precedents applying the theory of possibility of dissemination must be overruled, but this is not valid. Also, the dissenting opinion is understood to mean that publicity cannot include possibility of dissemination and must be viewed only as a “state in which an unspecified person or a large number of persons can directly perceive it”; however, the specific content of what the dissenting opinion calls “can directly perceive” is unclear, making it unsuitable as a standard of judgment, and following the dissenting opinion would not mean that freedom of expression is better protected.\\n\\nB. Various criticisms in the dissenting opinion still remain limited to pointing out the theory of possibility of dissemination in the early Supreme Court precedents, but the Supreme Court precedents accepted such criticisms, established objective and concrete standards regarding possibility of dissemination, and developed various limiting doctrines thereon, thereby settling as firm doctrine at present. The criticisms in the dissenting opinion cannot be a valid criticism of the current Supreme Court precedents or arise from a misunderstanding of the legal doctrine or purport presupposed by the majority opinion.\\n\\n1) The literal meaning of publicity and the legislative purpose used by the dissenting opinion as grounds for criticism are already matters stated by the majority opinion or presupposed by it. In other words, the majority opinion also shares the same purpose of requiring publicity as an element of the offense of defamation and of limiting the scope of recognition of the offense in order to harmonize it with freedom of expression.\\n\\nHowever, unlike the era when the offense of defamation was a means for maintaining or strengthening royal authority, in present-day Korean society freedom of expression is relatively well guaranteed as a fundamental right, while malicious and hateful content is disseminated through information and communications networks, causing individual personal rights to be infringed indiscriminately and without limitation, and making recovery impossible or meaningless. Even so, our society still lacks or has insufficient ex ante and ex post remedies to protect infringed personal rights. The legislative purpose of punishing the offense of defamation by alleging facts under the Criminal Act, etc. lies in this point, and it still plays an important role as a behavioral norm among the public.\\n\\nThe majority opinion seeks to maintain the theory of possibility of dissemination in consideration of the current aspects of defamation and the legislative purpose of the offense of defamation in order to protect the personal rights and privacy guaranteed as fundamental rights under the Constitution. Starting from the premise of characterizing the offense of defamation by alleging facts merely as an intentional punishment of private conversation or transmission of information, making it a restriction on freedom of expression, it is difficult to realize balanced balancing of interests.\\n\\n2) The dissenting opinion argues that the theory of possibility of dissemination imposes result responsibility depending on whether the recipient disseminates it, but this arises from a misunderstanding of the majority opinion and the theory of possibility of dissemination.\\n\\nAs examined in detail in Section 1, D of the majority opinion, the majority opinion is not a view that determines publicity by asking whether the recipient actually disseminated it to an unspecified person or a large number of persons.
