Rather, it objectively and normatively judges the act of alleging facts that can defame another’s reputation to a recipient who may disseminate them to an unspecified person or a large number of persons; if a general risk arises therefrom, illegality is recognized in the act itself, which is entirely different from result responsibility.\\n\\nAlso, the vague concern over dissemination that the dissenting opinion asserts merely reflects a failure to sufficiently understand the majority opinion, because the majority opinion determines whether there is a possibility of dissemination according to objective standards, requires a high degree of probability, and requires strict proof of the actor’s awareness of the possibility of dissemination and the will to accept the risk.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the dissenting opinion criticizes Supreme Court precedents that made different judgments on publicity despite identical status relationships, such as where the recipient was a friend or work colleague, as though they made contradictory judgments. However, Supreme Court precedent does not determine the standard for possibility of dissemination solely by reference to status relationships such as friend or work colleague; it considers all circumstances such as the circumstances of the conversation, the content of the factual allegation, and the manner and place of the allegation, and criticism based only on one of these factors is not valid.\\n\\n3) The dissenting opinion says that the theory of possibility of dissemination obstructs a consistent interpretation of publicity in offenses such as display/screening of obscene pictures, etc., and public indecency.\\n\\nHowever, the risk of infringement of the protected legal interest of good sexual morals in display/screening of obscene pictures, etc. and public indecency arises from the state of objects or conduct, not from speech; therefore, it is bound to differ in level from the offense of defamation, which requires as an element of the offense the risk that another’s reputation will be defamed as defamatory facts are disseminated.\\n\\nAccordingly, publicity in those offenses may be interpreted differently from publicity in the offense of defamation. This is the same as interpreting the meaning and degree of assault and intimidation differently in rape, robbery, and coercion offenses.\\n\\nC. It is not valid to argue, on the basis of the principle of legality, for the complete overruling of precedent as the dissenting opinion does. Moreover, even under the dissenting opinion, it is not possible to establish objective standards for publicity or clearly determine whether publicity exists.\\n\\n1) The theory of possibility of dissemination is related only to the interpretation of publicity and has no direct relation to the principle of legality. This is because no interpretive doctrine is directly derived from the grand principle of legality, and the literal interpretation of “publicly” does not yield the meaning that an unspecified person or a large number of persons must be able to perceive it “directly.”\\n\\nEven in foreign legislative examples requiring publicity as an element of the offense of defamation, the meaning of publicity is interpreted in various ways and sometimes changes over time. For example, the precedents of the Supreme Court of Japan once interpreted publicity in the offense of defamation as a “state in which an unspecified and a large number of persons can perceive it,” then changed to “a state in which an unspecified or a large number of persons can perceive it.” In Germany, publicity is generally interpreted as “a state in which an unspecified and a large number of persons can perceive it.” In our academic circles, too, there are various views on the meaning of publicity.\\n\\nAs such, because interpretation can differ on whether to adopt the requirement of “an unspecified or a large number of persons” in the concept of publicity, it cannot be presupposed that the only permissible way to interpret the meaning of publicity is, as in the dissenting opinion, as a state in which an unspecified person or a large number of persons can “directly” perceive it.\\n\\n2) Although the content of the “state in which it can be directly perceived” asserted by the dissenting opinion is not clear, it seems to require that at the time of the act unspecified persons or a large number of persons exist simultaneously in physical space, or to presuppose face-to-face interaction with the recipient of the act.\\n\\nHowever, as seen in the majority opinion, communication through information and communications networks has the essential characteristics of non-face-to-face interaction, etc., and is a distribution process in which infinite storage, reproduction, and transmission of information are easy; thus, there are many cases where an allegation to a small number of persons itself can be evaluated as a state in which an unspecified person or a large number of persons can perceive it. Focusing on these characteristics, academic opinion also includes views that, in defamation through an information and communications network, the meaning of publicity should be interpreted differently or that publicity is satisfied by the allegation itself. In the case of defamation by publications, etc. (Article 309 of the Criminal Act), the fact that publications, etc., by their nature and characteristics, already presuppose dissemination to an unspecified person or a large number of persons is why the statute was enacted so as not to require publicity as an element of the offense; this is in the same context.\\n\\nThe problem with the dissenting opinion is that, by necessarily requiring “face-to-face interaction in physical space” through the “directness” requirement of the statement, it fails properly to regulate the formidable expansiveness and dissemination of defamation occurring non-face-to-face in the virtual space of information and communications networks.\\n\\nFor example, suppose an email or text message containing sensitive content about a workplace superior’s private life was sent to one work colleague, the recipient conveyed it as is to another work colleague, and the same conduct repeated sequentially dozens of times, with the original disseminator being in a position where dissemination could have been foreseen. If direct perceptibility is required, in such a case the requirement that an unspecified person or a large number of persons can directly perceive it may never be satisfied at any stage, and punishment may not follow. However, compared to the case where the original disseminator sent the email or text message simultaneously to many persons from the outset, the general risk that the victim’s social evaluation would be infringed is the same.\\n\\n3) The dissenting opinion criticizes Supreme Court precedents for recognizing publicity on the ground of possibility of dissemination in cases of conversations taking place in private relationships, even though publicity cannot be recognized in such cases in light of the purpose of making publicity an element of the offense of defamation.\\n\\nHowever, Supreme Court Decisions 68DO1569 and 85DO431, etc., cited by the dissenting opinion, are not cases limited merely to transmission of information in private relationships or personal conversations arising naturally in daily life. That is, even if the recipient is a friend or work colleague, the relationship between the defendant or victim and the recipient of the statement is not a close enough relationship that the alleged facts would not be disclosed externally (for example, there may be a work colleague with whom there has been no particular interaction, or a friend who has had no contact for 10 years), and the content or manner of the allegation indicates a high likelihood of dissemination and a serious risk that the victim’s reputation will be damaged. The standards for determining publicity accumulated in Supreme Court precedents thus far take such comprehensive circumstances into account, and the new limiting doctrine mentioned in the majority opinion is also an evolution thereof.\\n\\nTherefore, such cases cannot be categorically described as mere casual talk occurring in private relationships, and schematizing the theory of possibility of dissemination as if it were devised to punish casual talk stems from an erroneous premise or misunderstanding of the theory of possibility of dissemination. Moreover, in light of the fact that, with the development of information and communications networks and the increasing non-face-to-face nature of human interaction, the boundary between private and public relationships has become ambiguous or blurred, it is not appropriate to exclude conduct from punishment merely because it occurs in a private relationship.\\n\\nD. Even if one understands publicity, as the dissenting opinion does, as a state in which an unspecified person or a large number of persons can directly perceive it, cases of factual allegations to a specific small number of persons do not fall outside the scope of punishment, and indeed the scope may expand further. Even if one accepts the dissenting opinion’s criticism and replaces publicity with the requirement of “direct perceptibility,” that problem is not resolved. Much of the dissenting opinion’s criticism fundamentally arises from the fact that Article 307 of the Criminal Act punishes defamation by alleging facts, and it cannot be solved merely by controlling the range of recipients of the statement. The majority opinion faces this reality and, considering both the form and content of acts alleging facts, proposes limiting doctrines thereon, and by actively recognizing the ground for exclusion of illegality under Article 310 of the Criminal Act, seeks a practical solution.\\n\\n1) According to the dissenting opinion, there appears to be a large structural difference from the majority opinion, but when applied to actual cases, there is little difference. For example, where facts are alleged to a small number of persons with no close private relationship to the speaker, under the dissenting opinion publicity would be recognized because it falls within a state directly perceptible to an unspecified person. The majority opinion also leaves room for recognizing publicity where there are circumstances indicating a high possibility of dissemination (ultimately, the conclusion that the offense of defamation is guilty would be the same under either view). On the other hand, in the case of statements to a specific small number of persons in a close private relationship, under either view publicity would likely be denied and an acquittal likely result.\\n\\nUltimately, the scope of punishability is not limited only by following the dissenting opinion. Rather, under the majority opinion, because publicity is determined by considering not only the relationship between the speaker and the recipient, but also all objective circumstances at the time of the act, such as the circumstances leading to the conversation, the content, manner, and place of the allegation, the scope of punishability can be substantively limited.\\n\\n2) The dissenting opinion criticizes the majority opinion for resolving by the theory of possibility of dissemination matters that should be resolved by the theory of accomplice liability.\\n\\nHowever, the offense of defamation reaches completion once the stage of general risk of harming honor has been reached. Therefore, if facts are alleged to an individual small number of persons who may disseminate them to an unspecified person or a large number of persons, the offense reaches completion at that stage, and because the crime is complete and there is no room for accomplice liability, it cannot be viewed as an accomplice issue. Also, if intent to instigate (intent to cause the principal offender to form a criminal resolve and to commit the crime through the principal offender) cannot be recognized in the original speaker, then even though the original speaker’s illegality is greatest, punishment would still be impossible.\\n\\n3) The dissenting opinion argues as if the theory of possibility of dissemination obstructs the recent Me Too movement, but this is an issue unrelated to the interpretation of publicity. That is because the regulation of the Me Too movement is merely a question of whether a criminal victim’s act of informing the press or a large number of persons of the victimization can be punished as defamation; the Me Too movement is not punished because of the theory of possibility of dissemination. This is a problem derived from punishing the offense of defamation by alleging facts under the Criminal Act, etc. Based on this awareness, as seen in the majority opinion, Supreme Court precedent has denied intent to defame or publicity in cases of statements related to response to wrongdoing or public procedures such as investigations, and the majority opinion further seeks to broadly apply the public-interest element under Article 310 of the Criminal Act and recognize the ground for exclusion of illegality where, even if the matter concerns an individual, it is related to the public interest and has acquired social attention or influence. Rather, according to the majority opinion, in cases where a victim of crime such as the Me Too movement informs not only a small number of acquaintances but also a large number of the public, the ground for exclusion of illegality under Article 310 of the Criminal Act may be recognized and can serve as a solution protecting the victim.\\n\\nE. The majority opinion aims to maintain the theory of possibility of dissemination while developing limiting doctrines thereon through a balanced balancing of the individual’s honor, personal rights, and privacy protection against freedom of expression, in a reality where individual honor is increasingly broadly infringed and becomes irrecoverable, and where there is no other alternative capable of protecting the individual’s personal rights from such infringement. Also, unlike foreign systems, it seeks to broaden the scope of application of the ground for exclusion of illegality in order to overcome the limitations of the current law, which punishes defamation even where true facts are alleged; and this is the true intent of the majority opinion as well.\\n\\nWith the above, we supplement the grounds of the majority opinion."}

Summary of the charged facts in this case  \\nThe Defendant, on March 25, 1995, was a person who, at that time, had his address in △△ 1-dong, ○ District, Anyang City, and was in fact registered as a resident there, and thus had voter eligibility for the electoral district of △△ 1-dong in the Anyang City Council member election to be held on June 27 of the same year; and, having planned to run in the city council election in that electoral district and with the purpose of causing Non-indicted Person 1, who actually ran, to be elected, on or about March 25 of the same year, at the above address, he mobilized the organization manager, etc. of the ○○○○○ △△ 1-dong council, of which the Defendant was chairperson, and agreed to do so, and received KRW 1,400,000 from Non-indicted Person 2, the election office manager of Non-indicted Person 1, under the pretext of activity expenses, and thereafter received KRW 1,400,000 on or about April 5 of the same year and KRW 5,000,000 on or about June 14 of the same year from Non-indicted Person 2 under the same pretext, respectively.\\n\\n2. Summary of the reasoning of the judgment of the court below  \\nThe judgment of the court below, upon the evidence cited by the first instance court and the record, found that during the investigation by the investigative authorities of Non-indicted Person 2, etc. on or about June 22, 1995, the authorities became aware of the Defendant’s above offense on or about July 14 of the same year and placed the Defendant on wanted notice, while on both the 24th of the same month and August 24 of the same year they obtained detention warrants for the Defendant twice and attempted to execute them, but were unable to execute the warrants because the Defendant fled, and thus suspended prosecution as of September 25 of the same year; and that on October 23 of the same year the Defendant voluntarily appeared at the prosecutor’s office and confessed the above offense. The court then held that, in this case, the Defendant’s act of voluntarily appearing during the investigation period and confessing the offense does not constitute voluntary surrender under the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Public Official Election Act”) for the following reasons, and that the first instance court’s judgment sentencing exemption pursuant to Article 262 of the same Act was based on an erroneous understanding of the law; accordingly, it reversed the first instance judgment and sentenced the Defendant.\\n\\na. The reason why Article 52 of the Criminal Act, Article 16 of the National Security Act, or Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act, etc. treat voluntary surrender as a ground for discretionary or mandatory mitigation or exemption from punishment is, on the one hand, that voluntary surrender serves as an indication that the Defendant shows repentance, and on the other hand, that voluntary surrender is decisively useful for the discovery and punishment of criminal acts and criminals. As Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act, unlike Article 52 of the Criminal Act or Article 16 of the National Security Act, provides for mandatory exemption from punishment and legislatively grants such exemption, in a differentiated manner, only to those who have received or agreed to receive money, goods, or benefits, excluding those who have given or agreed to give such money, goods, or benefits among persons who violated Article 230(1), Article 231(1), or Article 257(2) of the Public Official Election Act, the legislative purpose is to eradicate the provision of money or goods by even granting the recipient, who contributed to the discovery of such provision, a kind of reward in the form of exemption from punishment. Therefore, the limits of voluntary surrender should be determined by whether it is useful for the discovery of violations of the election law.\\n\\nHowever, at least where, as in this case, all facts constituting the offense of the Defendant and the related offender have been discovered, and the investigation of the related persons has been completed except for the investigation of the Defendant, and even a detention warrant for the Defendant has been issued, voluntary surrender can no longer be said to be useful for the discovery of the offense; therefore, such voluntary appearance does not constitute voluntary surrender under the Public Official Election Act.\\n\\nb. Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act is not applicable to all violators of the Public Official Election Act, but only to those who, among persons who violated the three provisions cited above, have received or agreed to receive money, goods, etc., and therefore it results in differential treatment only of such persons.\\n\\nHowever, the rational basis for such differentiation lies in the fact that, in cases of receiving money, goods, etc. in connection with elections, if the recipient does not speak up, discovery is almost impossible; accordingly, if the recipient of the money, goods, etc. voluntarily reports the fact to the investigative authority, exemption from punishment is granted to induce voluntary reporting, and by investigating and punishing the person who gave the money, goods, etc., the representative corrupt practice connected with elections, namely the receiving of money, goods, etc., can be prevented and the development of democratic politics can be contributed to. Therefore, applying differentiation based on voluntary surrender even to cases that are of no help whatsoever in the discovery of election corruption raises a constitutional issue.\\n\\nc. If voluntary surrender under Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act is not construed in the above restrictive manner, then even where the facts of the offense have all been discovered through other channels and the Defendant himself has been placed on wanted notice by the investigative authorities, and even though a detention warrant for the Defendant has been issued, the Defendant nevertheless fled for a considerable period before belatedly voluntarily appearing before the investigative authorities, an obviously unjust result would arise in which the Defendant’s punishment must be unconditionally exempted. This is a legal defect caused by the Public Official Election Act’s unrestricted use, in sanction provisions for certain special cases among violations thereof, of the general concept of voluntary surrender. Therefore, the court may teleologically construe the scope of voluntary surrender restrictively according to the limit of public usefulness inherent in voluntary surrender under the election law.\\n\\n3. Determination on the grounds of appeal  \\na. On Point 2  \\nConsidering the record, the lower court’s measure of finding the facts constituting the offense in this case guilty based on the evidence cited in the first instance judgment is proper, and there is no illegality of incomplete deliberation as alleged. The argument is without merit.\\n\\nb. On Point 1  \\n(1) Article 52 of the Criminal Act provides voluntary surrender as a ground for discretionary mitigation or exemption, and under the former Criminal Act (the Act in force before the enactment of the current Criminal Act on September 18, 1953), voluntary surrender was subject to a temporal limitation that it had to occur “before discovery”; however, the current Criminal Act deleted such limitation, and therefore, if the surrender occurs before arrest, it constitutes voluntary surrender even if the person has been placed on wanted notice (see Supreme Court Decision 65DO597, rendered October 5, 1965; Supreme Court Decision 94DO659, rendered May 10, 1994; Supreme Court Decision 94DO619, rendered September 9, 1994).\\n\\nIn addition, Article 16(1) of the National Security Act provides that where a person “voluntarily surrenders after committing an offense under this Act,” punishment shall mandatorily be mitigated or exempted. Since voluntary surrender under the National Security Act is also construed as identical to voluntary surrender under the Criminal Act, if the person voluntarily reports the offense to the investigative authorities before being arrested, regardless of whether the offense has already been discovered, it should be regarded as voluntary surrender (see Supreme Court Decision 68DO754, rendered July 30, 1968).\\n\\nMeanwhile, the provisos to Article 90(1), Article 101(1), Article 111(3), Article 120(1), and Article 213 of the Criminal Act provide for mandatory mitigation of punishment where a person voluntarily surrenders “before the execution of the intended offense” in cases of preparation or conspiracy for insurrection and murder for the purpose of insurrection, preparation or conspiracy for external aggression, preparation or conspiracy for a premeditated act against a foreign country, preparation or conspiracy for the use of explosives, counterfeiting or alteration of currency, and preparation or conspiracy for counterfeiting or alteration of foreign currency. In addition, Article 153, Article 154, and Article 157 provide that, in cases of false testimony, false testimony causing harm, false appraisal, interpretation, translation, and false accusation, punishment shall mandatorily be mitigated if a person voluntarily surrenders “before the judgment or disciplinary disposition on the case testified to becomes final.”\\n\\nThe reason why criminal penalty provisions treat voluntary surrender specially as above is, first, that the offender is considered to have repented on his own and shown remorse, and thus the degree of blameworthiness is weak; and, second, that voluntary surrender facilitates investigation, allows a State agency to properly exercise the penal power, and therefore prevents punishment of the innocent.\\n\\nHowever, as seen above, given that our Criminal Act and the National Security Act, etc. differentiate the degree of mitigation of punishment for voluntary surrender according to the legislative purpose and also separately set the timing requirements for voluntary surrender, it is clear that the question of what the requirements and effects of voluntary surrender are for any offense is not a matter that is logically and necessarily derived, but rather a matter determined by legislative policy according to whether the legislative purpose attaches greater importance to one of the two aspects of voluntary surrender or considers both equally.\\n\\nIn other words, whether pre-discovery voluntary surrender and post-discovery voluntary surrender are to be treated alike or differently is also not determined by logical necessity depending on the offense, but is likewise a matter of legislative policy.\\n\\nTherefore, in the absence of an express statutory limitation regarding the timing of voluntary surrender, as in the proviso to Article 90(1) of the Criminal Act, etc., it should be deemed that, prima facie, if one personally appears before the investigative authorities and states the facts of the offense before arrest, such conduct constitutes voluntary surrender.\\n\\nHowever, the principal legislative purpose of Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act, which provides mandatory exemption from punishment in cases of voluntary surrender for election-related offenses involving receipt of money, goods, or benefits under Article 230(1) (offense of bribery and inducement of interest), etc., is to effectively punish the provider of the money, goods, etc. by inducing the person who received them to effectively report the matter, taking into account that such offenses are covertly committed between the parties and are difficult to discover. Thus, in order to fully realize this legislative purpose, it may be considered desirable legislation to grant the benefit of exemption from punishment only in cases of voluntary surrender before the offense is discovered, but as noted above, the issue of limiting the timing of voluntary surrender is also a matter of legislative policy and not a matter of logical necessity. Therefore, it is reasonable to construe the failure to insert language in the above provision limiting the timing of voluntary surrender, as in the proviso to Article 90(1) of the Criminal Act, as reflecting legislation that importantly considered not only the point that voluntary surrender facilitates discovery of the offense, as in Article 16 of the National Security Act, but also the point that one repents on one’s own and shows remorse. It cannot be categorically said to be a defect in the law.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court erred in concluding that the absence in Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act of a limitation on the timing of voluntary surrender constitutes a defect in the law.\\n\\n(2) As noted above, although the absence in Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act of a limitation regarding the timing of voluntary surrender is clearly not a defect in the law, as the lower court determined, it is also clear that such legislation is not desirable. The question then is whether the court can derive such a limitation through statutory interpretation.\\n\\nIn interpreting penal provisions, if the interpretation exceeds the possible meaning of the statutory text, it becomes analogous interpretation and violates the principle of nulla poena sine lege (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 94MO32, dated December 20, 1994).\\n\\nThe principle prohibiting analogous interpretation applies mutatis mutandis to all provisions concerning the elements of offenses and punishability in penal statutes (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 92DO1428, rendered October 13, 1992). If the scope of grounds excluding illegality, grounds excluding culpability, or conditions for prosecution are restrictively applied by analogy, the scope of the actor’s punishability is expanded to the detriment of the actor. Since this produces the same result as analogically applying the elements of an offense beyond the possible meaning of the text, such an approach cannot be permitted as it violates the principle prohibiting analogous interpretation, which is a derivative principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\nExemption from punishment means that guilt is recognized but punishment alone is not imposed, and it is a ground for excluding punishment. If, with respect to grounds for exemption from punishment, one were to apply a restrictive analogy narrower than the text of the statutory provision, as in the above case, the scope of punishment would be expanded to the detriment of the actor, and thus such an approach must be deemed impermissible.\\n\\nHowever, the requirements of Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act do not at all include, in addition to the term “voluntary surrender,” the limitation of “before discovery of the offense.” As noted above, Article 52 of the Criminal Act and Article 16(1) of the National Security Act, like Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act, both use the term “voluntary surrender,” and judicial precedent interprets the “voluntary surrender” in Article 52 of the Criminal Act and Article 16(1) of the National Security Act as including voluntary appearance after the offense has been discovered and after the person has been placed on wanted notice; thus, this should be regarded as the customary usage of the term “voluntary surrender.”\\n\\nIn addition, as noted above, the proviso to Article 90(1), the proviso to Article 111(3), etc. of the Criminal Act provide for mandatory mitigation of punishment where a person voluntarily surrenders “before the execution of the intended offense.” If the term “voluntary surrender” itself included the concept of a temporal limitation that could grant benefits with respect to that offense, then the concept of “before the execution of the intended offense” could be derived through interpretation of the term “voluntary surrender,” and thus there would have been no need to expressly provide it.\\n\\nTherefore, in light of these points, it is reasonable to interpret that the legislator of the Criminal Act used the term “voluntary surrender” in a sense that does not include such a concept, and thus enacted legislation in the above form.\\n\\nAccordingly, interpreting “voluntary surrender” in Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act as limited to “voluntary surrender before discovery of the offense” adds, beyond the concept ordinarily included in the customary usage of the term “voluntary surrender,” an additional concept of “before discovery of the offense,” and in the end goes beyond the “possible meaning of the language”; therefore, this would be an expansion of the punishable scope under Article 230(1) of the Public Official Election Act, etc., beyond the positive law, by limiting the scope of “voluntary surrender” in Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act through analogy from the proviso to Article 90(1) and the proviso to Article 101(1) of the Criminal Act, etc.\\n\\nAccordingly, this is not merely a teleological restrictive interpretation as stated by the lower court, but an expansion of the punishable scope beyond the positive law through a restrictive analogy regarding grounds for exemption from punishment, and thus violates the principle prohibiting analogous interpretation, which is a derivative principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\n(3) Just as Article 52 of the Criminal Act or Article 16 of the National Security Act, etc. permits discretionary or mandatory mitigation of punishment without distinguishing whether voluntary surrender occurred before or after discovery of the offense, based on the reasonable legislative purpose noted above, and therefore presents no constitutional issue as an exercise of legislative discretion, Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act also provides mandatory exemption from punishment, regardless of the timing of voluntary surrender, only for recipients of money, goods, etc. among violators of the three provisions, including Article 230(1) of the same Act. As noted above, whether this is desirable legislation is a separate matter, but as long as it has its own reasons and basis, it cannot be said to exceed legislative discretion and thereby raise an issue of constitutional violation.\\n\\nTherefore, even if Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act is not restrictively applied by analogy as the lower court did, no constitutional issue arises.\\n\\n(4) Ultimately, the lower court construed the voluntary surrender under Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act as limited to voluntary surrender before discovery of the offense, and determined that the Defendant’s voluntary appearance and reporting of the offense in this case did not constitute voluntary surrender under the said provision. This was a violation of the principle prohibiting analogous interpretation, a derivative principle of nulla poena sine lege, and an error in misunderstanding the legal doctrine regarding voluntary surrender under Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act, which affected the outcome of the judgment; therefore, the grounds of appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n(5) Accordingly, the majority of the participating Justices, excluding Supreme Court Justice Park Man-ho, agreed to reverse the lower judgment and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and thus render judgment as stated in the disposition.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion of Supreme Court Justice Park Man-ho on Point 1 of the grounds of appeal is as follows.\\n\\nUnlike the majority opinion on Point 1 of the grounds of appeal, the lower court’s judgment sentencing the Defendant is found proper by restricting the interpretation of voluntary surrender under Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act to voluntary surrender before discovery of the offense; the reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1. As the lower court appropriately stated, our criminal-related laws treat voluntary surrender in three different ways: first, where voluntary surrender is provided for as a ground for discretionary mitigation or exemption from punishment, as in Article 52 of the Criminal Act; second, where voluntary surrender is treated as a ground for mandatory mitigation or exemption from punishment, as in Article 16 of the National Security Act; and third, where voluntary surrender is provided for as a ground for mandatory exemption from punishment, as in Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act. Unlike Article 52 of the Criminal Act or Article 16 of the National Security Act, Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act is enacted as a ground for mandatory exemption from punishment, and its scope of application is also legislatively restricted so that, among persons who violated Article 230(1), Article 231(1), or Article 257(2) of the Public Official Election Act, those who have given or agreed to give money, goods, or benefits are excluded, and only those who have received or agreed to receive them are granted exemption from punishment in a differentiated manner. The legislative purpose is to eradicate the provision of money, goods, etc. for election corruption by inducing the recipient, who has effectively contributed to the discovery of the offense through voluntary surrender, to reveal the offense on his own by granting the special benefit of exemption from punishment, since such provision of money, goods, etc. is covertly carried out between the parties and discovery is ordinarily extremely difficult unless the recipient voluntarily surrenders. Therefore, voluntary surrender must be construed as limited to cases in which it is made before discovery of the election-law violation.\\n\\nIf the voluntary surrender under Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act is not interpreted in this manner and is instead construed as applying if one merely surrenders before arrest without any temporal limitation, resulting in mandatory exemption from punishment, then, as in this case, even where the offense of the Defendant, who received the money, goods, etc., has already been fully uncovered through investigation into the provider of the money, goods, etc. and other related persons, and a detention warrant has even been issued, but prosecution has been suspended due to the suspect being unknown because of flight, a belated voluntary appearance before the investigative authorities and confession of the offense would require exemption from punishment. Such a result is unreasonable because, first, it would grant the benefit of Article 262 even though the Defendant made no contribution whatsoever to the discovery of the offense, thereby contradicting the legislative purpose of Article 262, which, as noted above, provides mandatory exemption from punishment for voluntary surrender; second, it is markedly contrary to justice and equity because it does not accord with the general public sense of law regarding the balance between crime and punishment; and third, the rational basis for Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act, which grants mandatory exemption from punishment only to recipients of money, goods, etc. among persons violating the three offenses under Article 230(1), etc., lies, as noted above, in the fact that voluntary surrender makes a decisive contribution to discovery of the offense for the above offenses, the discovery of which is extremely difficult. If, however, voluntary appearance after discovery of the offense, which contributes nothing to discovery of the offense, is included within voluntary surrender, then unlike persons who voluntarily surrender after committing other offenses for which punishment is only discretionary under Article 52 of the Criminal Act, especially unlike persons who voluntarily surrender after committing the offense of providing money, goods, etc. under the three offenses of Article 230(1) of the Public Official Election Act, etc., only those who committed the above three offenses and then voluntarily surrendered after discovery of the offense would, without any rational basis, receive the differentiated special benefit of mandatory exemption from punishment. This also creates a potential issue of unconstitutionality as a violation of equality under Article 11(1) of the Constitution.\\n\\nTherefore, in light of the legislative purpose and objective of Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act, if that provision and the other punishment provisions under the Public Official Election Act that are not subject to mandatory exemption from punishment are to be construed comprehensively and consistently with the Constitution, the term must be interpreted to mean only “voluntary appearance and confession during the investigation period before discovery of the offense.”\\n\\n2. The majority opinion states that, as a matter of legislative policy, it is desirable to limit voluntary surrender under Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act to voluntary surrender before discovery of the offense, but that interpreting the current statute as above is impossible because it is an analogous interpretation that violates the principle prohibiting analogous interpretation, which is a derivative principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\nAnalogical interpretation means applying a law concerning a matter not provided for in the statute to a matter having similar characteristics. Restrictively interpreting voluntary surrender under Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act as “voluntary surrender before discovery of the offense” is not an attempt to apply or incorporate by analogy the proviso to Article 90(1) or the proviso to Article 101(1) of the Criminal Act to voluntary surrender under the Public Official Election Act on the ground that voluntary surrender under Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act is similar to voluntary surrender under the said provisions of the Criminal Act. Rather, among the various situations that may be included in the wording “voluntary surrender” of Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act—namely, “voluntary appearance before discovery of the offense,” “voluntary appearance after discovery of the offense,” and so on—it merely construes the term as limited to “voluntary appearance before discovery of the offense” by interpreting what is inherently limited, through the legislative purpose and objective of Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act and its systemic relationship with other punishment provisions, as noted above. Therefore, contrary to the majority opinion, this is not restrictive analogical interpretation but merely teleological restrictive interpretation, and thus does not violate the principle prohibiting analogous interpretation, which is a derivative principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\n3. In this case, the Defendant fled after committing the offense of receiving money or goods under Article 130(1) of the Public Official Election Act, and although the offense was uncovered through investigation of other related persons and the Defendant was placed on wanted notice by the investigative authorities and even a detention warrant was issued, prosecution was suspended because the Defendant’s whereabouts were unknown, and thereafter the Defendant belatedly voluntarily appeared at the prosecutor’s office. Therefore, it cannot be said that the Defendant made voluntary surrender under Article 262 of the Public Official Election Act.\\n\\nTherefore, the lower court’s judgment sentencing the Defendant on this basis is proper, and since the Defendant’s appeal lacks merit, it should be dismissed."}
