The Defendant then threatened Nonparty 3, saying, “I will kill you, you bastard,” inserted the kitchen knife through the gap in the door in an attempt to release the locking mechanism, and kicked the door several times with his foot, eventually opening the door and entering the inner room; moreover, in addition to the Defendant holding the knife, five members of the Defendant’s group were outside that door, so that escape to the outside through that door was impossible. Considering all of these circumstances together, there is a substantial causal relationship between the Defendant’s aforementioned acts of violence and intimidation and the injury to Nonparty 3. Furthermore, it is reasonable to view that, for the Defendant, it was foreseeable that Nonparty 3 might resist in order not to have the money obtained through the gambling robbed, and might attempt to escape, for example by jumping down from the house through a window opening to the outside of the veranda, and that in such a case Nonparty 3 could suffer injury. Accordingly, the Defendant’s aforementioned criminal act constitutes the crime of robbery causing injury.\\n\\nTherefore, the court below’s conviction of the Defendant for robbery causing injury on the same grounds was proper, and there was no error of law, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the crime of robbery causing injury, as alleged. This argument is also without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and part of the days of pretrial detention after the appeal shall be credited against the principal sentence. The judgment is rendered by the unanimous opinion of the Judges participating, as stated in the Disposition."}

question:
Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (O) and incorrect (X) regarding the offense of fraud? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)

(a) In fraud, where consideration has been paid to the victim, if the victim is deceived and the consideration in his possession is fraudulently taken again, or if the consideration is entrusted by the victim and embezzled while in safekeeping, this constitutes a new infringement of a legal interest; therefore, a separate new offense of fraud or embezzlement, distinct from the fraud that had already been established, is established. 
(b) Even where no attorney has been retained, the act of listing in the cost item of the statement of litigation costs an attorney’s fee of 5 million won that was not actually expended, and filing with the court an application for a decision determining litigation costs in a provisional disposition case, constitutes an act of deception against the court even if substantiating materials are not fabricated or false substantiating materials are not submitted in connection therewith. 
(c) If a loan is obtained by deceiving a financial institution with financial statements, etc. prepared through window-dressing accounting, fraud is established, and whether there was an intent to repay or the ability to repay, and whether sufficient security was provided, or whether there was no loss to the victim’s overall property and the loan was repaid afterward, has no effect on the establishment of fraud. 
(d) Where the manager of a publishing company manipulated the shipment status sheet to deceive the actual number of copies published and paid the author only part of the royalties, the fact that the author did not know the very existence of the claim to the remaining royalties and therefore did not exercise it constitutes, in fraud, a disposition of property by omission. 
(e) In order for the act of disposition referred to in fraud to be recognized, the deceived person’s subjective awareness of the consequences of disposition is necessary; therefore, in the case of “signature fraud,” the deceived person has no awareness whatsoever of the content and legal effect of the dispositive document that he or she signs or affixes a seal to, and thus no intent to dispose and no disposition act based thereon are recognized.

supporting_precedents: {"[2002DO7262]": "1. Determination on the Grounds of Appeal by the Defendants\\n\\nA. Regarding the point of violation of the Act on External Audit of Stock Companies due to window-dressing accounting (Defendant 1, Defendant 2, Defendant 3, Defendant 4, Defendant 5, Defendant 6, Defendant 7)\\n\\n(1) The Prosecutor may determine whether to institute prosecution by taking into account such matters as the suspect’s age, character, intelligence and environment, relationship to the victim, motive for the offense, means and result, and circumstances after the offense; and even if, at the time of the offense in this case, many other large domestic enterprises were also engaging in window-dressing closing of accounts in order to continue business management while maintaining the national economy, employment stability for employees, and transactions with import and export trading partners, such circumstances alone do not permit a finding that the institution of prosecution against the Defendants in this case was an abuse of the prosecutorial power by the Prosecutor. Moreover, even if the act falls within the same constituent elements of a crime, there may be cases in which unlawfulness is excluded or responsibility is excluded depending on the actor or the circumstances at the time of the act; therefore, the mere fact that there was a person who committed the same criminal act as the Defendant against whom prosecution was instituted on the ground that the act constituted the elements of a crime but who was not punished does not mean that the Prosecutor abused the right to prosecute by infringing the Defendant’s right to equality (see Supreme Court Decision 90DO646 rendered on June 8, 1990; Decision 96DO2158 rendered on November 12, 1996; Decision 2000DO737 rendered on November 10, 2000, etc.). Accordingly, the above Defendants’ ground of appeal on this point is without merit.\\n\\n(2) Reviewing the reasoning of the judgment of the court below in light of the record, the court below correctly found the criminal facts that the above Defendants conspired with Non-indicted 2, etc. and falsely prepared and disclosed the financial statements of Non-indicted Company 1, Inc., considering the position and role of Defendant 1, Defendant 2, and Defendant 7 in Non-indicted Company 1, Inc. and BFC at the time of the offense in this case, as well as the degree of their involvement in the offense, and there is no illegality such as that asserted as a ground of appeal.\\n\\n(3) Taken together with the evidence lawfully examined and admitted by the court below, it can be found that Defendant 5, as the representative director having authority to prepare the financial statements of Non-indicted Company 3, Inc., was instructed by Non-indicted 2 as to the scale of the accounting window dressing, and that, even knowing that window-dressing accounting had been carried out, he approved the closing of accounts as representative director; therefore, even if he did not participate in the specific acts corresponding to the individual items of the window-dressing accounting, namely, the remittance of funds by Non-indicted Company 2 to BFC through WTC or the de facto borrowing of funds from UBS, a Swiss bank, through ARTEC, intent to engage in the window-dressing accounting in this case can be recognized. Furthermore, it cannot be said that there was a justifiable reason for believing that it did not constitute the offense of violation of the Act on External Audit of Stock Companies due to window-dressing accounting merely because the above Defendant received legal advice from a law firm when borrowing funds from UBS. Therefore, the court below correctly found the criminal facts that the above Defendant conspired with Non-indicted 2, etc. and falsely prepared the financial statements of Non-indicted Company 3, Inc., and there is no illegality such as that asserted as a ground of appeal.\\n\\nB. Regarding the point of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes due to fraud\\n\\n(1) Regarding the point of fraud due to window-dressing accounting (Defendant 1, Defendant 5)\\n\\n(a) Taken together with the evidence lawfully examined and admitted by the court below, it can be found that, at the time of the offense in this case, in credit investigations by financial institutions or credit ratings by credit rating agencies regarding Non-indicted Company 1, Inc. and Non-indicted Company 3, Inc., the financial structure of the companies occupied a considerable weight, and the window-dressing accounting of Non-indicted Company 1 and Non-indicted Company 3, Inc. greatly affected the evaluations by financial institutions and credit rating agencies for loans, etc., and that loans, etc. were extended by financial institutions based on such evaluations. Accordingly, the court below correctly found the criminal facts of fraud on this point, and there is no illegality such as that asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAlso, even if, on December 19, 1998, the affiliated enterprise group of (group name omitted), Non-indicted Company 1, Inc., and the council of major creditors of the affiliated enterprise group of (group name omitted) concluded an agreement for improving the financial structure for the sound management and improvement of the financial structure of the affiliated enterprise group of (group name omitted), and even if the banks thereafter decided on new loans by comprehensively considering various circumstances such as the implementation performance of the restructuring of the (group name omitted) Group, the possibility of rehabilitation of the (group name omitted) Group, and the effect on the Korean economy in the event that the (group name omitted) Group went bankrupt, if such decisions by financial institutions regarding loans, etc. were made without properly knowing the fact of window-dressing accounting, causation between the window-dressing accounting and the loans, etc. can be recognized.\\n\\nTaken together with the evidence lawfully examined and admitted by the court below, the Financial Supervisory Service investigated the window-dressing accounting of Non-indicted Company 1, Inc. and referred the matter to the Prosecutor’s Office on September 18, 2000, and all of the offenses in this case occurred before that date; therefore, the court below’s action of finding guilt and punishing the fraud after bank administration as stated in the judgment, based on the admitted evidence, is reasonable in light of the above legal principles, and there is no illegality in violation of the rules of evidence or misunderstanding the legal doctrine regarding causation in fraud.\\n\\n(b) Fraud is constituted by deceiving the other party and obtaining property by the other party’s defective intent; therefore, if one deceives a financial institution by means of financial statements, etc. prepared through window-dressing accounting and receives a loan, fraud is established. Whether there was intent to repay, whether there was ability to repay, whether sufficient collateral was provided, whether there was no loss to the victim’s entire property, or whether the loan was repaid afterward does not affect the establishment of fraud.\\n\\nExamining the above legal principles in light of the reasoning of the judgment of the court below and the record, the court below correctly found, based on the evidence lawfully examined and admitted by it, the criminal facts of fraud due to window-dressing accounting against the above Defendants, and there is no illegality such as that asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n(c) Refinancing means formally making a new loan without the actual exchange of funds and thereby repaying an existing debt. In the absence of special circumstances, refinancing formally constitutes a separate loan, but in substance it is nothing more than an extension of the due date of the existing debt. Accordingly, where a financial institution bearing a guarantee obligation makes a new loan to a debtor so as to cause the debtor to repay the principal obligation and thereby itself acquire the loan claim, or where a financial institution that guaranteed a corporate bond already issued newly guarantees a corporate bond issued for the purpose of securing the funds for payment thereof, such acts cannot be regarded as refinancing that is substantively nothing more than an extension of the due date. Therefore, the court below’s action of finding guilt and punishing this part of the fraud charge is also reasonable, and there is no illegality such as that asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n(d) Corporate bond public offering is conducted by a trust company whose qualifications are restricted under the Commercial Act and the Securities and Exchange Act; therefore, investors who participated in the offering in reliance on a trust company that was deceived by the issuing company and fell into mistake may also be deemed to have been deceived and to have engaged in the disposal of property. Ultimately, investors who acquired corporate bonds through the public offering in this case, as well as the lead manager or underwriting company that underwrote the remaining bonds, are also to be regarded as victims.\\n\\nComparing the facts alleged in the indictment in this case with the facts found by the court below and the facts recognized from the record, although it is not appropriate that the court below limited the victims of the issuance and underwriting of the corporate bonds in this case due to window-dressing accounting to the underwriting company alone, on the view that the essence of the criminal facts on this point lies in proposing the issuance and underwriting of corporate bonds by concealing the financial condition of Non-indicted Company 3, Inc. on the basis of the window-dressed financial statements, and that the other party to the deception is the underwriting company that will conduct the underwriting business by examining the financial condition and repayment ability of the issuing company, as long as the underwriting company of the corporate bonds in this case is included among the victims, the above action by the court below does not affect the result of the judgment; accordingly, the Defendants’ ground of appeal is without merit.\\n\\n(e) Therefore, the court below’s action of finding guilt and punishing the criminal facts of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes due to fraud, namely that Defendant 1 and Defendant 5 conspired with Non-indicted 2, etc. to falsely prepare the financial statements of Non-indicted Company 1, Inc. and Non-indicted Company 3, Inc., and using them deceived financial institutions to receive loans and committed fraud by public offering of corporate bonds, is reasonable, and there is no illegality such as violation of the rules of evidence or misunderstanding the legal doctrine of fraud.\\n\\n(2) Regarding the point of fraud by discounting trade bills (Defendant 3, Defendant 4, Defendant 5)\\n\\n(a) Regarding the argument that the facts charged were not specified\\n\\nSince the statement of the facts charged must specify the facts by indicating the time, place, and method of the offense, the time of the offense need only be stated to the extent that it does not run afoul of double prosecution or the statute of limitations. The purpose of requiring specification of the facts charged by such elements is to facilitate the exercise of the Defendant’s right of defense; therefore, it is sufficient if the facts charged describe the constitutive facts of the offense, taken together with such elements, to the extent that they can be distinguished from other facts. Even if the indictment did not specifically state the time or place of the offense, if it does not go against the above standard, and in light of the nature of the offense charged, such general indication is inevitable and there is no obstacle to the Defendant’s exercise of the right of defense thereon, the contents of the indictment cannot be deemed unspecified (Supreme Court Decision 2002DO2939 rendered on October 11, 2002).\\n\\nAccording to the facts charged in this case and the 434 entries in Attached Table 13, the deceiver, the other party thereto, and the contents of the deception are specified; therefore, it should be deemed that the facts charged in this case were specified. Accordingly, even if the persons in charge of the work of the deceiver and the deceived were not specified, or the contents of the deception at the time were not individually specified, there is no obstacle to the Defendants’ exercise of the right of defense; thus, the judgment of the court below contains no error of law regarding the specification of the facts charged.\\n\\n(b) Reviewing the reasoning of the judgment of the court below and the record, the court below, based on the evidence lawfully examined and admitted by it, correctly found the criminal facts of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes due to fraud in this case, namely that Defendant 3, Defendant 4, and Defendant 5 conspired with Non-indicted 2, etc., directed subordinate employees to falsely prepare export documents, and used them to obtain discounts on trade bills from the victim banks and thereby commit fraud, and there is no illegality such as that asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n(3) Regarding the point of fraud by revolving letter of credit (Defendant 2, Defendant 5, Defendant 7)\\n\\n(a) Regarding the argument of misunderstanding the legal doctrine on the manner of filing the indictment\\n\\nThe portions of the indictment pointed out by the above Defendants concern the motive or background of the offense and the process by which the victim banks were deceived, and cannot be said to be statements on matters that would create preconceived notions in the judge. Accordingly, the judgment of the court below contains no error of law regarding the manner of filing the indictment.\\n\\n(b) Reviewing the reasoning of the judgment of the court below and the record, the court below, based on the evidence lawfully examined and admitted by it, correctly found the criminal facts of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes due to fraud in this case, namely that the above Defendants conspired with Non-indicted 2, etc., and although the (group name omitted) Group entered into a loan agreement with Nishoiwai Shoji Co. for borrowing USD 150 million and the letter of credit was to be provided as security therefor, they falsely stated that a letter of credit should be opened as security for the payment under a long-term purchase contract for automotive equipment and accessories in Hong Kong of (group name omitted); and although the guarantee amount under the letter of credit in this case was stated as USD 221.25 million, they falsely stated that it was a letter of credit with a maximum guarantee amount of USD 11.5 million, thereby obtaining the opening of the letter of credit from the victim bank deceived thereby and fraudulently obtaining property benefits equivalent to USD 221.25 million. The court below’s action of finding guilt and punishing this offense is also reasonable, and there is no illegality such as that asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nC. Regarding the point of concealment of property abroad (Defendant 1, Defendant 2, Defendant 3, Defendant 4, Defendant 5, Defendant 6, Defendant 7)\\n\\n(1) Regarding the argument that the offense of concealment of property abroad is unconstitutional\\n\\nThe former Foreign Exchange Control Act (repealed on the effective date thereof pursuant to Article 3 of the Supplementary Provisions, when the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act, enacted by Act No. 5550 on September 16, 1998, came into force on April 1, 1999) and the former Foreign Exchange Transactions Act (before amendment by Act No. 6277 on October 23, 2000) had the purpose of contributing to the sound development of the national economy by rationally adjusting or managing foreign exchange, related transactions, and other external transactions so as to promote the smooth conduct of external transactions and seek balance of payments equilibrium and stability of the value of currency. By contrast, the offense of concealment of property abroad under Article 4 of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes has the purpose of protecting state property by punishing conduct that causes a loss to national wealth by taking domestic property abroad and concealing it there. Accordingly, even if regulation of foreign exchange transactions has been greatly relaxed in line with the development of the national economy and globalization, considering Korea’s economic scale and structure and the effect that the outflow of national wealth abroad has on the national economy, the necessity of punishing the act of taking domestic property abroad still remains.\\n\\nMoreover, the question of whether to define certain conduct as a crime and what punishment to impose therefor is, in principle, a matter of the State’s legislative policy, and the legislature must be afforded broad legislative discretion or freedom of formation. Therefore, even if the legislature, by comprehensively considering various factors concerning the determination of the statutory penalty, has reduced the scope of sentencing discretion by the judge in the statute itself, such statute cannot be deemed unconstitutional so long as it has rationality to an extent that can be accepted in light of the protected legal interest of the offense and the nature of the offense, etc., under the principle of proportionality between punishments.\\n\\nIn the case of Article 4(2)1 of the above Act, the legislature made a legislative decision that, with respect to a person who takes domestic property of 5 billion won or more abroad, the illegality and possibility of criticism are high, and therefore, unless there is a statutory ground for mitigation, the judge may impose discretionary mitigation but may not suspend execution. Since such legislative decision by the legislature is recognized to have, at first glance, a rational basis that can be accepted, the above statutory provision cannot be said to be arbitrary beyond the limits of legislative discretion or to violate the principle of judicial independence by infringing the judge’s power to determine sentencing, nor is it difficult to view it as violating the principle of equality under Article 11 of the Constitution or the principle of proportionality or the principle against excessive restriction derived from Article 37(2) of the Constitution. Furthermore, since it cannot be said to violate the ideal of respect for human dignity under Article 10 of the Constitution, the above Defendants’ ground of appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(2) Regarding the argument on the legality of the institution of prosecution\\n\\nEven if, as the above Defendants point out, other businesspersons also committed the same offense of concealment of property abroad as the above Defendants, but the Prosecutor did not punish or lightly punished those persons and instituted prosecution only against the above Defendants, who were merely executives of the (group name omitted) Group, as co-principals of the offense of concealment of property abroad, such circumstance alone cannot be said to violate the constitutional principle of equality or to constitute an abuse of the prosecutorial power by the Prosecutor. Moreover, the indictment must state the charge, the facts charged, and the applicable provisions of law; however, since the statement of the applicable provisions of law merely serves a supplementary function in determining the scope of the prosecution, even if there is an error in or omission of the statement of the applicable provisions of law, the validity of the institution of prosecution is not affected so long as the Defendant suffers no substantial disadvantage in defense thereby.\\n\\nEven if the facts charged in this case state only Article 6-2 of the former Foreign Exchange Control Act, which provides for the duty to recover claims, and do not state the Foreign Exchange Control Regulations specifying the scope and period of claims to be recovered, the scope of the prosecution can be identified from the facts charged, and it cannot be said that the Defendants’ exercise of the right of defense is substantially prejudiced; therefore, there is no effect on the validity of the institution of prosecution. Accordingly, the above Defendants’ ground of appeal regarding the legality of the institution of prosecution cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(3) The offense of concealment of property abroad under Article 4(1) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes is already established if a person, with the recognition that domestic property to be moved abroad or property to be brought into the country is concealed abroad, moves property abroad, or conceals or disposes of property that should be brought into the country abroad and thereby causes its escape. Whether part of such property was later brought back into the country, or whether there was from the beginning an intention to bring the concealed property back into the country and consume it, does not affect the establishment of the offense (see Supreme Court Decision 88DO551 rendered on June 21, 1988; Decision 88DO2211 rendered on February 14, 1989, etc.).\\n\\nTaken together with the evidence lawfully examined and admitted by the court below, it can be found that the above Defendants, in conspiracy with Non-indicted 2, remitted and concealed the funds by falsely disguising them as import payments from a paper company and by remitting them to off-book accounts that were managed by the so-called London funds team working at the British local subsidiary of Non-indicted Company 1, Inc., while the existence of the accounts would not appear in the closing of accounts of Non-indicted Company 1, Inc. under accounting law. Even if the purpose of the overseas remittance was to repay borrowings from overseas financial institutions of the overseas local subsidiary for which Non-indicted Company 1, Inc. had provided payment guarantees, or to provide funds to overseas subsidiaries or branch offices, this does not affect the establishment of the offense.\\n\\nIn addition, since the intent to conceal property abroad, unless the above Defendants admit it, can only be inferred from objective facts, any portion of the amounts that the above Defendants assert were remitted for the so-called circulation of funds but were not immediately brought back into the country, in light of the urgent funding situation abroad in which Non-indicted Company 1, Inc. was then placed, must be regarded as involving at least conditional intent to conceal on the part of the above Defendants. Therefore, the court below correctly found guilt on the facts charged concerning the portions of the amounts remitted by the above Defendants in conspiracy with Non-indicted 2, etc. to BFC that were remitted for the purpose of supporting overseas subsidiaries or branch offices and for the purpose of circulation of funds but were not brought back into the country within 2-3 days, as well as the portion of the export proceeds of Non-indicted Company 3, Inc. remitted to BFC, and this is in accordance with the above legal principles; there is no illegality such as that asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n(4) In co-principal liability, conspiracy does not require that all accomplices reach an agreement of intent at the same time and in the same place, and a person who is not the subject of the duty to recover export proceeds or the subject of capital transactions under the former Foreign Exchange Control Act or the former Foreign Exchange Transactions Act may also become a co-principal of a violation of the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act or of the offense of concealment of property abroad.\\n\\nReviewing the reasoning of the judgment of the court below and the record, the court below, based on the evidence lawfully examined and admitted by it, correctly found the above Defendants to be co-principals by conspiracy in light of the positions and roles of Defendant 1, Defendant 4, Defendant 6, and Defendant 7, and found guilt on each of the criminal facts of violation of the former Foreign Exchange Control Act or the former Foreign Exchange Transactions Act due to concealment of property abroad and borrowing from overseas financial institutions, and this is in accordance with the above legal principles; there is no illegality such as that asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nD. Regarding the argument of misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning forfeiture (Defendant 1, Defendant 2, Defendant 3, Defendant 4, Defendant 5, Defendant 6, Defendant 7)\\n\\n(1) Regarding the argument that the forfeiture provisions are unconstitutional\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of Article 10(1) and (3) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes is to realize concrete justice by excluding from the offender the property that was taken abroad or was intended to be taken abroad, which is the object of unlawful criminal conduct, and its legitimacy is recognized. Furthermore, when such property cannot be confiscated, the value of the property that was the object of the offense is to be collected, thereby establishing an appropriate proportional relationship. Accordingly, it cannot be said to violate the principle of proportionality or the principle against excessive restriction derived from Article 37(2) of the Constitution, nor Articles 10, 12(1), and 23(1) of the Constitution. Therefore, the above Defendants’ ground of appeal regarding the confiscation and collection provisions for the offense of concealment of property abroad cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(2) Legality of confiscation and collection against the above Defendants\\n\\n(a) Confiscation and collection under Article 10(3) and (1) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes, which are the basis for confiscation and collection against the Defendants, unlike the confiscation and collection under criminal law aimed at depriving the offender of the profit from the crime, are deemed to be a punitive disposition of a punitive nature that strengthens the degree of punishment for offenders who conceal property abroad by mandatorily confiscating the property that was the object of the offense and, when confiscation is impossible, requiring payment of its value. Therefore, even if the concealed property belonged to a company other than the above Defendants or the above Defendants possessed it and did not obtain any profit therefrom, the entire value of the concealed property must be collected from all of the above Defendants (see Supreme Court Decision 94DO1075 rendered on March 10, 1995). Accordingly, the court below’s judgment ordering joint and several collection against the Defendants is acceptable, and there is no illegality such as that asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n(b) Meanwhile, reviewing the reasoning of the judgment of the court below in light of the record, while the court below acquitted Defendant 1, Defendant 2, Defendant 3, and Defendant 4 of the portions of the facts charged concerning concealment of property abroad that had been remitted for the so-called circulation of funds and had been brought back into the country within 2-3 days, it nevertheless included even the value of the property relating to the acquitted portions in calculating the amount to be collected in Part 4(a) of the facts of the first-instance judgment, and as a result imposed collection on the facts charged for which an acquittal should have been rendered. The portions for which acquittal was rendered cannot be collected under the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes, and the funds remitted without permission cannot be regarded as having been acquired through acts violating the former Foreign Exchange Control Act or the former Foreign Exchange Transactions Act, and thus they are not subject to collection under the former Foreign Exchange Control Act or the former Foreign Exchange Transactions Act either. Accordingly, the court below’s judgment, which ordered collection even as to the value of the property corresponding to the acquitted portions among the amount collected for Part 4(a) of the above criminal facts, contains an error of law misunderstanding the legal doctrine on collection and affecting the result of the judgment.\\n\\n(c) Proper amount of collection\\n\\nReviewing the reasoning of the judgment of the court below in light of the record, if the U.S. dollar amounts pertaining to the acquitted portions of the judgment of the court below are converted at the exchange rate of KRW 1,207 per USD 1 recognized by the court below as of the close of argument, the amounts for Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 become 1,093,910,712.12 × 1,207 = KRW 1,320,054,503,255 each; the amount for Defendant 4 becomes 970,446,532.21 × 1,207 = KRW 1,171,328,964,377; and the amount for Defendant 1 becomes 1,055,910,712.12 × 1,207 = KRW 1,274,484,229,528. Therefore, those amounts should be excluded from the collection imposed on the above Defendants. Accordingly, in this case, the proper amount of collection is, with respect to Criminal Facts 4(a), after excluding the amounts corresponding to the acquitted portions from the amounts collected under Item 6 of the order of the judgment of the court below, KRW 1,786,520,214,609 each should be collected from Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, KRW 1,562,438,950,295 should be collected from Defendant 1, each jointly and severally with Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, and KRW 1,472,455,206,174 should be collected from Defendant 4, each jointly and severally with Defendant 1, Defendant 2, and Defendant 3.\\n\\nE. Regarding the ground of appeal by Defendant 5 alleging undue severity of sentence\\n\\nIn this case, in which a sentence of less than 10 years’ imprisonment was imposed on the above Defendant, the argument that the court below’s determination of the sentence was excessive does not constitute a lawful ground of appeal; accordingly, the above Defendant’s ground of appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\n2. Determination on the Prosecutor’s Grounds of Appeal\\n\\nA. Regarding the acquittal portion of Defendant 8\\n\\nReviewing the reasoning of the judgment of the court below and the record, the court below correctly acquitted Defendant 8 on the ground that, although Defendant 8 was listed as a representative director in the registry of Non-indicted Company 3, Inc. together with Non-indicted 2 and Defendant 5, etc., the mere fact that he falsely prepared and disclosed the financial statements does not make it difficult to view the above Defendant as having conspired with Non-indicted 2, etc. to conspire in the fraud by each of the loans in this case and the issuance of corporate bonds. There is no illegality such as that asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nB. Regarding the so-called remittance for purposes of circulation of funds (Defendant 1, Defendant 2, Defendant 3, Defendant 4)\\n\\nThe offense of concealment of property abroad is established by moving domestic property abroad with the recognition that one’s own act violates laws and regulations and moves domestic property abroad, and with the recognition that the act places the property in a state where it can be arbitrarily consumed, accumulated, concealed, etc. by oneself abroad without being subject to regulation and management under the laws and system of the Republic of Korea, thereby creating a condition in which the property of the Republic of Korea or its nationals is at risk of being outflowed, that is, by causing it to escape. However, if the remittance was made not in anticipation of use abroad from the outset, but with the purpose of immediate remittance back into the country, then it cannot be said that there was intent to conceal property by moving it abroad and managing it.\\n\\nReviewing the reasoning of the judgment of the court below and the record, the court below, after finding that, among the funds remitted by the above Defendants in conspiracy to BFC, they wrote a file number to be remitted again to a person concerned at BFC when making the remittance and requested immediate re-remittance, and that the funds were remitted again to the country within 2-3 days, acquitted that portion on the ground that the above Defendants lacked intent to conceal property. This is correct in light of the above legal principles, and there is no illegality such as that asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nC. Regarding voluntary surrender (Defendant 1, Defendant 2, Defendant 3, Defendant 4, Defendant 5, Defendant 6, Defendant 7)\\n\\nReviewing the reasoning of the judgment of the court below and the record, it can be found that the above Defendants voluntarily appeared and truthfully stated the facts of the offense by, after inquiring of the Prosecutor’s Office about the schedule for investigation, appearing at the Prosecutor’s Office at the designated time and in other similar ways; therefore, voluntary surrender was established. The fact that they later denied the offense in court does not mean that it was a voluntary surrender without remorse, nor does it extinguish the effect of the voluntary surrender once established. Accordingly, the court below’s mitigation of sentence for voluntary surrender with respect to the above Defendants is correct, and there is no illegality such as that asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Scope of Reversal\\n\\nAs seen above, the court below erred in law by misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning collection under the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes and the former Foreign Exchange Control Act or the former Foreign Exchange Transactions Act, by imposing collection on Defendant 1, Defendant 2, Defendant 3, and Defendant 4 even as to the value of the property corresponding to the acquitted portions. Therefore, the portion of the judgment of the court below imposing collection regarding Criminal Facts 4(a) should be reversed.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nHowever, since this case is deemed sufficient for this Court to decide directly, pursuant to Articles 391 and 396(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, the portion of the judgment of the court below ordering collection regarding Criminal Facts 4(a) is reversed, and, excluding the amounts collected as to the acquitted portions among the above criminal facts, the above amounts are to be collected from the above Defendants pursuant to Article 10(3) and (1) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes; and as the appeals by Defendant 5, Defendant 6, and Defendant 7, as well as the remaining appeals by Defendant 1, Defendant 2, Defendant 3, and Defendant 4 and the Prosecutor’s appeal, are each without merit, all are dismissed. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court participating in the decision."}

{"[2005DO9221]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. As to the allegation of violation of the Rules of Evidence\\n\\nThe court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it had admitted, recognized the facts as stated in its opinion, and based on those recognized facts, held that from May 1, 2002, the Defendant was not merely carrying out the company’s business in accordance with the instructions of a superior, but was directly handling the affairs relating to royalty payments and preparing accounting documents to obtain the approval of Co-defendant 1 in the court below, thereby being deeply involved in the royalty payment duties, and that there was a concurrence of intent between the Defendant and Co-defendant 1 in the court below to jointly realize the commission of the present offense. It further held that the Defendant and Co-defendant 1 in the court below, etc., sent the victim a shipment status sheet stating only about 1/3 of the actual number of books published, with the intent of causing the victim to misunderstand the actual number of books published, thereby making the victim believe that the number of copies stated in the above shipment status sheet corresponded to the actual number of books published, and then paid only royalties corresponding to about 1/3 of the actual number of books published while failing to pay the difference, which clearly constituted an act of deception; and that, considering the circumstances leading to such acts and the circumstances before and after, the Defendant’s intent to commit fraud was established. Accordingly, the court below affirmed the judgment of the court of first instance, which found the Defendant guilty of the criminal acts stated in the judgment. The court below’s selection and evaluation of the evidence, and its fact-finding and determination thereon, are proper, and there is no illegality such as a violation of the Rules of Evidence as alleged.\\n\\n2. As to the allegation of misapprehension of legal principles, etc.\\n\\nThe crime of fraud is established by deceiving another, causing a mistake, and inducing a disposition act resulting therefrom, thereby obtaining property or a pecuniary benefit. Here, the term “disposition act” means a property disposition act, referring to the deceived person’s proceeding, by free will, to an act or omission that directly causes pecuniary loss; thus, if the deceived person, having fallen into mistake, did not know of the existence of a claim and therefore did not exercise the claim, such omission also constitutes a disposition act of property.\\n\\nThe court below, after comprehensively considering the evidence it had admitted, recognized the facts as stated in its opinion, and based on those recognized facts, held that even if the victim had not expressly waived the remaining royalty claim exceeding the royalties already received, or discharged the debt of the (trade name omitted) Publishing Company, the victim, due to the Defendant’s and others’ deceptive acts, fell into a mistake whereby the victim did not even know of the existence of the claim itself and thus came to a state in which the claim could not be exercised, and that this constitutes a disposition act by omission. Such determination is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of legal principles as alleged.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and since there is a clear clerical error in the judgment of the court below, which is corrected, the judgment is rendered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating as set forth in the order."}

{"[2009DO7052]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding Defendant 2’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the court below, based on the evidence duly admitted, found the facts as stated in its decision, and then, by comprehensively considering the circumstances as stated in its decision appearing in those established facts, determined that: “Defendant 2, who was the head of the game business division of Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd., which had been selected by Non-Indicted Party 1 LLC as the exclusive domestic distributor of Xbox 360 game consoles (hereinafter referred to as the ‘game consoles’) and their game titles, peripherals, etc. (hereinafter collectively referred to as the ‘game consoles, etc.’) and was engaged in the distribution and sale business of the game consoles, etc., conspired with Defendant 3, the sales team leader of Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd., and Defendant 1, the representative of Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd., which received game consoles, etc. from Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd. and supplied them again to lower-level distributors, in order to solve the shortage of settlement funds that Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd. faced with respect to Non-Indicted Party 1 LLC, and to bring in the funds of Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd., whose financial capacity had become abundant through a paid-in capital increase, by deceiving the management of Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. so that Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. would enter the game console distribution business by acquiring Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. and thereby prepare the payment to Non-Indicted Party 1 LLC from Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd.; and, in fact, even though they well knew that, even if Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. participated in the game console distribution business by acquiring Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. and received game consoles, etc. from Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd., the market price of the game consoles had been formed lower than the supply price due to continuous dumping sales at that time, so that Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. had no choice but to incur a loss rather than make a profit by selling the game consoles, without informing the management of Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. of such fact, they told lies to the effect that Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd.’s net profit for 2006 amounted to KRW 2 billion and that if Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. were acquired and the game console distribution business were entered into, substantial profits could be made, and thereby deceived Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd., causing it to: ① acquire Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. by way of new share subscription and participate in the game console distribution business, and then, around March 7, 2007, receive KRW 1,000,012,000 (hereinafter referred to as the ‘instant purchase price’) by remittance into an account under the name of Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. under the pretext of the new share subscription price and fraudulently obtain it; ② on or around February 27, 2007, have a mortgage with a maximum secured amount of KRW 5.2 billion (hereinafter referred to as the ‘instant mortgage right’) established over the factory land and building owned by Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. in order to secure the debt for the purchase price of goods for the game consoles, etc. to be supplied by Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd., thereby fraudulently obtaining property benefits equivalent to the secured value; and ③ after causing Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. and Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd. to enter into the instant goods supply contract on or around March 7, 2007, under which Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. would receive game consoles, etc. from Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd. and sell them, and then receiving, under the name of advance payment for the game consoles, etc., KRW 812,290,600 around March 16, 2007 and KRW 1,504,629,500 on April 13, 2007 (hereinafter referred to as the ‘instant advance payment’) by remittance into accounts under the name of Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd., thereby fraudulently obtaining them.” The court below held that all of the charges against Defendant 2 were guilty, and determined that the acts of fraud against Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. by the defendants as above should be deemed to constitute a single comprehensive offense in the aggregate.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the above factual findings and determination by the court below are just and can be accepted, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principles on the establishment of fraud, the number of offenses, and the establishment of accomplice liability, or mistake in the finding of facts due to violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. Regarding Defendant 3’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe court below, based on the evidence duly admitted, found the facts as stated in its decision, and then determined that, according to those established facts, it could be recognized that Defendant 3, together with Defendant 1, took a leading role in the process of the above fraudulent acts against Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd., including the acquisition of Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. by Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the above factual findings and determination by the court below are just and can be accepted, and there is no illegality such as mistake in the finding of facts due to violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Regarding the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nA. Regarding the claim concerning the part of Defendant 2’s violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Special Aggravated Punishment Act”) (fraud) concerning the instant purchase price\\n\\nThe court below, based on the evidence duly admitted, found the facts as stated in its decision, and then, in light of the circumstances shown in those established facts, held that, based solely on the evidence submitted by the Prosecutor, it was insufficient to find that Defendant 2: ① had instructed Defendant 1 to conduct dumping sales of the game consoles; ② together with Defendants 1 and 3, had dumped the game consoles through Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. in the guise of a special-sale transaction; ③ had instructed Defendants 1 and 3 to tell falsehoods during the due diligence process for Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd.’s acquisition of Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd.; ④ had known that the collateral provided by Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. in order to secure the debt for the purchase price of goods owed to Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd. had no collateral value; and ⑤ had intended to have the existing debt of Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. to Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd. repaid out of the proceeds from the sale of the game consoles, etc. supplied by Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. from Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd.; and accordingly it found all of the above counts against Defendant 2 not guilty. In light of the record, the above factual findings and determination by the court below are just and can be accepted, and there is no illegality such as mistake in the finding of facts due to violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nB. Regarding the claim concerning the principal count of the indictment for the Special Aggravated Punishment Act violation (fraud) and the alternative count of the indictment for the Special Aggravated Punishment Act violation (embezzlement) concerning the defendants’ supply of the instant game consoles\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the court below, with respect to the principal and alternative counts of the indictment against the defendants, namely, that the defendants conspired to deceive the management of Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. into believing that the price would be duly paid even though they had no intention of normally selling the game consoles, etc. supplied by Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd. to Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. again to Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. and paying the proceeds to Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd., and thereby caused Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. to fraudulently obtain the game consoles, etc. worth KRW 4.7 billion out of the game consoles, etc. worth KRW 6.4 billion supplied by Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd. by having Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. resupply to Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. game consoles, etc. worth KRW 4.7 billion (principal count of the indictment), or that Defendant 1, who had assumed office as the head of the game business division of Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd., conspired with Defendants 2 and 3 and embezzled the game consoles, etc. worth KRW 4.7 billion by arbitrarily supplying and delivering them to Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. while holding them in custody in the course of business (alternative count of the indictment), found all of them not guilty on the ground that, “since Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. was deceived by the defendants’ fraud that it would be able to realize high profits if it engaged in the game console distribution business, and acquired Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd., paid the acquisition price, paid the advance payment, and established the mortgage right, and thus the offense of violation of the Special Aggravated Punishment Act (fraud) was established, the receipt thereafter by Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. from Non-Indicted Party 2 Co., Ltd. of game consoles, etc. worth KRW 6.4 billion within the limit secured by the instant advance payment and the collateral setting of the instant mortgage right was nothing more than payment of part of the consideration after the offense of violation of the Special Aggravated Punishment Act (fraud) had been established, so no new offense of violation of the Special Aggravated Punishment Act (fraud) or offense of violation of the Special Aggravated Punishment Act (embezzlement) can be deemed to have been established with respect thereto; moreover, even if the sale of the game consoles, etc. worth KRW 4.7 billion, corresponding to 70% of the above game consoles, etc., under the name of Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. was in accordance with Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd.’s sales strategy, such game console sales strategy of Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. was established by the defendants’ fraud, or if it was established by Defendant 1, the head of Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd.’s game business division, in conspiracy with the other defendants and with the intent to embezzle the game consoles, etc., then there is room to find the offense of fraud or embezzlement concerning the above game consoles, etc., so the court below should have further examined whether the defendants had conspired to deceive Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd. and fraudulently obtain the above game consoles, etc., or to supply the above game consoles, etc. to Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. and embezzle them, and then determined whether the above part of the indictment against the defendants was guilty or not guilty; nevertheless, without doing so, the court below concluded that, since the offense of violation of the Special Aggravated Punishment Act (fraud) had already been established by the payment of the instant purchase price and advance payment and the establishment of the instant mortgage right, and since the sale of the game consoles under the name of Non-Indicted Party 3 Co., Ltd. was in accordance with Non-Indicted Party 4 Co., Ltd.’s sales strategy, no separate and new offense of violation of the Special Aggravated Punishment Act (fraud) or offense of violation of the Special Aggravated Punishment Act (embezzlement) could be established with respect to the above game consoles, etc., and found both the principal and alternative counts of the indictment not guilty, thereby committing an illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment, etc. of fraud or embezzlement. The Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal pointing out this issue are well-founded.\\n\\n4. Scope of reversal\\n\\nTherefore, the part of the judgment below that found not guilty of the principal count of the indictment for the defendants’ violation of the Special Aggravated Punishment Act (fraud) concerning the instant supply of game consoles and the alternative count of the indictment for the Special Aggravated Punishment Act violation (embezzlement) must all be reversed; meanwhile, the remaining part of the Special Aggravated Punishment Act violation (fraud) against the defendants, which the court below found guilty or not guilty in part for the reasons stated above, was also indicted as a single comprehensive offense together with the principal count of the indictment for the Special Aggravated Punishment Act violation (fraud) concerning the instant supply of game consoles, and thus must be reversed together. In addition, the parts concerning the remaining criminal facts against Defendants 1 and 3 must also be reversed together, because they are in a relation of concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the part concerning the defendants’ violation of the Special Aggravated Punishment Act (fraud). Consequently, the entirety of the judgment below must be reversed.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2016DO13362]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. As to the principal indictment facts among the acquittal portion\\n\\na. Fraud is a crime that is consummated by deceiving another person, causing that person to fall into error, thereby inducing the deceived person to engage in a disposition act, and obtaining property or pecuniary benefit therefrom. Therefore, in order for fraud to be established, there must be the perpetrator’s deceptive act, the deceived person’s error and the ensuing disposition act, and the perpetrator’s acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit, and there must be a sequential causal relationship between them (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 1989. 7. 11. rendered 89DO346, 2000. 6. 27. rendered 2000DO1155).\\n\\nIn fraud, the disposition act mediates and connects, in the middle, the final result of the perpetrator’s acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit through the deceived person’s error caused by the perpetrator’s deceptive act, while at the same time serving to distinguish fraud, which is essentially characterized by obtaining property by exploiting the victim’s act in error, from theft, in which the perpetrator acquires property by taking it away without relying on the victim’s act. In light of such role and function of the disposition act, if it can be assessed that the perpetrator, etc. obtained property or pecuniary benefit through some act based on the deceived person’s will, the disposition act referred to in fraud is recognized.\\n\\nb. However, with respect to such disposition act, the Supreme Court has heretofore held that, subjectively, the deceived person must have disposition intent, namely awareness of the result of disposition, and objectively, there must be an act governed by such intent (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 1987. 10. 26. rendered 87DO1042, 1999. 7. 9. rendered 99DO1326, 2011. 4. 14. rendered 2011DO769). According to this view, even if the victim, having been deceived, engaged in an act causing himself or herself property damage, fraud cannot be established if there is no awareness of the result thereby generated, because disposition act cannot be recognized.\\n\\nHowever, fraud is originally a crime in which the perpetrator, by means of deceptive conduct, causes the deceived person to fall into error and thereby makes the deceived person engage in a disposition act while not fully knowing what result his or her act will bring about. If the deceived person accurately recognizes the result his or her act will bring about, that ultimately means that he or she was not deceived or did not fall into error by the deceptive act, and fraud cannot be established. Therefore, the prior view that disposition intent can be recognized only when there is awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition requires reconsideration. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Fraud is established where property is transferred by a disposition act based on the deceived person’s defective intent. Therefore, a disposition act must not only be the act of the deceived person but also, even if a defective intent, must be the deceived person’s intent; accordingly, acts by a person lacking capacity to intend, or acts committed in a state of unconsciousness, cannot constitute a disposition act. In this respect, disposition intent can be said to be the subjective element of the disposition act.\\n\\nIn fraud, the deceived person’s disposition intent is a defective intent formed in a state of error caused by the deceptive act, and thus is necessarily incomplete or defective. It is rather natural that the deceived person’s subjective awareness concerning the legal meaning or economic effect of the disposition act and the result actually brought about do not coincide, and this is an essential attribute of fraud. Therefore, it is sufficient that the deceived person in error has awareness that he or she is performing some act; it cannot be said that awareness of the result brought about by that act is also required.\\n\\n(2) As an element establishing fraud, a deceptive act means conduct that runs counter to the principle of good faith to be observed broadly in transactional relations and thereby causes a person to fall into error, and error means awareness inconsistent with facts, whether it concerns facts, legal relations, or legal effects (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 1984. 2. 14. rendered 83DO2995, 2006. 1. 26. rendered 2005DO1160). In addition, the deceived person’s defective awareness inconsistent with facts is not limited to awareness concerning the motive, intent, or purpose of the disposition act, or concerning the disposition act itself. Therefore, even if, as a result of being deceived, the deceived person did not properly recognize the meaning of his or her own act or omission and thus did not recognize the result caused by that act, if he or she nonetheless came to perform an act causing property damage in such an erroneous state, the deceived person’s disposition act and the corresponding disposition intent must be found.\\n\\nIf, contrary to this, disposition intent can be recognized only when the deceived person has awareness of the result caused by his or her own act, then the more highly sophisticated and ingenious the perpetrator’s method, and the more severely the deceived person falls into error so as not to recognize the result his or her act will produce, the higher the possibility would become that disposition intent is denied. This is difficult to accept.\\n\\n(3) When determining whether the victim had disposition intent, it is not appropriate to simply transfer over the theory of interpretation regarding the perpetrator’s intent and interpret disposition intent as being recognized only when the victim recognized the result of the disposition act.\\n\\nArticle 13 of the Criminal Act provides: “An act committed without awareness of the facts constituting an element of a crime shall not be punished.” This is an expression of the principle of culpability, to punish only acts that can be attributed to the actor’s responsibility by virtue of the actor’s awareness of the facts constituting an element of the crime. Therefore, in fraud, for the perpetrator’s intent to be recognized, awareness of all elements constituting fraud is required: the perpetrator’s deceptive act, the deceived person’s error and the ensuing disposition act, and the perpetrator’s acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit. Ultimately, the perpetrator’s intent can be recognized only when there is awareness of the result of the act, that is, awareness of the element that property or pecuniary benefit is acquired by the perpetrator, etc.\\n\\nHowever, it is not the case that fraud is established only when the victim, i.e., the deceived person, is aware of the perpetrator’s deceptive act or his or her own error resulting therefrom. Rather, if the victim is aware of the perpetrator’s deceptive act or his or her own error resulting therefrom, fraud cannot be established. Likewise, there is no reason to hold that the victim must be aware of the element that property or pecuniary benefit is acquired by the perpetrator, etc. as the result of the disposition act. The object of awareness for the perpetrator’s intent comprises all elements constituting fraud, whereas the object of awareness for the victim’s disposition intent is limited to the disposition act itself among the elements constituting fraud. This is because the victim’s disposition intent, unlike the perpetrator’s intent, has no relation to the principle of culpability and is merely a subjective element of the disposition act.\\n\\nThe basis for requiring disposition intent in the victim’s disposition act is that, when it is recognized that the disposition act was done with the victim’s awareness, the disposition act can be regarded as an act by the victim. Put differently, the function of disposition intent in fraud is only to confirm, on the subjective side, the existence of the victim’s disposition act in correspondence with the objective side. Therefore, if some act assessed as a disposition act was done by the victim with awareness, there can be said to be disposition intent on the victim’s part. Ultimately, the victim need not be aware of the result caused by the disposition act.\\n\\nc. In conclusion, in light of the nature and structure of fraud, and the function and role of disposition act and disposition intent as its volitional element, as well as the meaning of deceptive act and error, even if the deceived person did not recognize the meaning or content of the disposition act, if the deceived person’s act or omission is assessed as a property disposition act that directly causes property damage, and if such act or omission was done with the deceived person’s awareness, disposition intent corresponding to the disposition act is recognized. In other words, it is not necessary for the deceived person to recognize even the result of his or her own act or omission in order for disposition intent to be recognized.\\n\\nSupreme Court Decisions 1987. 10. 26. rendered 87DO1042, 1999. 7. 9. rendered 99DO1326, 2011. 4. 14. rendered 2011DO769, which held that in order to recognize the disposition act referred to in fraud, the deceived person must have awareness of the result of disposition, are changed to the extent they are inconsistent with this judgment.\\n\\nd. Further, we consider how to ascertain the disposition act and disposition intent in cases where the deceived person’s disposition act is carried out in the form of a juristic act or expression of intent, and the deceived person’s internal intent and the intent externally manifested and objectively perceived do not coincide.\\n\\n(1) The so-called “signature fraud” at issue in this case is a case in which, due to error induced by a deceptive act, the deceived person signs or seals a disposition document contrary to his or her internal intent and thereby causes property damage. Here, the very manner of the perpetrator’s deceptive act centers on exploiting a situation in which the deceived person cannot properly recognize the meaning or content of his or her own disposition act, or causing the deceived person not to recognize the result of his or her own act; and because of this, the deceived person falls into error and does not recognize the result brought about by his or her own act of signing or sealing the disposition document. The essence of fraud is to exploit the deceived person’s defective disposition act, and in a case of signature fraud, the defect lies in the process of formation of the expression of intent itself.\\n\\n(2) In such a case of signature fraud, even if the deceived person did not properly recognize the content of the disposition document and signed or sealed it, causing the internal intent and the intent objectively and externally perceived through the disposition document not to coincide, the reason it can be said that the perpetrator, etc. caused the acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit by the deceived person’s act is that the disposition document containing the transfer of such property can be regarded as having been prepared by the deceived person. Thus, if, as a result of the deceived person’s falling into error due to the perpetrator’s deceptive act, the deceived person signed or sealed a disposition document containing content that causes an effect different from his or her internal intent, and property damage according to the contents of the disposition document thereby resulted, the deceived person’s act of signing or sealing such disposition document constitutes the disposition act referred to in fraud. In addition, even if the deceived person did not yet recognize the result of disposition, namely the specific content of the document and its legal effect, as long as he or she had awareness of the act of signing or sealing the disposition document by personally signing or sealing some document, the deceived person’s disposition intent is also recognized.\\n\\ne. From the reasoning of the judgment below and the evidence lawfully admitted and examined by the first-instance court and the court below, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n(1) The Defendant and Nonindicted Person 1, etc., around 2010. 11. 29. and 2010. 12. 3., deceived the victim Nonindicted Person 2, the seller of each of the land parcels stated in the judgment below, into believing that the documents were necessary for land transaction permission, etc., and had the victim sign and seal the mortgage contract forms, etc.; then received the victim’s seal certificate; and used it to establish for Nonindicted Person 3, etc. a mortgage over each of the above land parcels owned by the victim, with the maximum secured amount totaling 1,050,000,000 won, with the Defendant as debtor, and borrowed 700,000,000 won.\\n\\n(2) The Defendant and Nonindicted Person 1, etc., on 2010. 12. 29., deceived the victim Nonindicted Person 2 and Nonindicted Person 4, the sellers of each of the land parcels stated in the judgment below, by telling them that the documents were necessary for land transaction permission, etc., and had the victims sign or seal loan/payment agreements, etc. stating that the above land was to be provided as security; then received the victims’ seal certificates; and used them to establish for Nonindicted Person 5 a mortgage over each of the above land parcels owned by the victims, with the Defendant as debtor, and the maximum secured amount of 180,000,000 won, and borrowed 120,000,000 won.\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, ① the Defendant and Nonindicted Person 6 conspired to borrow 100,000,000 won by providing as security the land owned by victim Nonindicted Person 7 as stated in the judgment below and to use the remaining money excluding the down payment of 30,000,000 won themselves; thereafter, around 2011. 4. 5., they proposed to the victim that he sell the above land for 300,000,000 won and requested the establishment of a mortgage regarding the borrowing of that down payment of 30,000,000 won, thereby obtaining the victim’s consent; ② on 2011. 4. 7., at the place where the sale and purchase contract for the above land was concluded, they obtained from the victim, who mistakenly believed them to be documents necessary for the establishment of a mortgage for the borrowing of the above 30,000,000 won, signatures and seals on a mortgage contract form stating the maximum secured amount of 30,000,000 won, debtor Defendant, and mortgagee Nonindicted Person 8, and on a mortgage contract form stating the maximum secured amount of 120,000,000 won, debtor Defendant, and mortgagee Nonindicted Person 9, while also obtaining seals on the mortgage registration application forms and powers of attorney, etc.; and ③ using them, they established mortgages for the above mortgagees and borrowed a total of 100,000,000 won.\\n\\nf. Examining these facts in light of the legal principles discussed above, (1) the victims Nonindicted Person 2 and Nonindicted Person 4, as a result of falling into error by the Defendant’s and others’ deceptive acts, mistakenly believed the documents to be necessary for land transaction permission, etc., and signed or sealed the mortgage contract forms, etc., which are disposition documents, thereby engaging in acts causing property damage; accordingly, the above acts by the victims constitute the disposition act referred to in fraud. (2) Likewise, victim Nonindicted Person 7, as a result of falling into error by the Defendant’s and others’ deceptive acts, mistakenly believed the documents to be security-provision documents necessary for the Defendant, etc. to borrow 30,000,000 won, and signed or sealed the mortgage contract forms, etc. for borrowing 100,000,000 won, thereby engaging in acts causing property damage; accordingly, the victim’s above acts also constitute the disposition act referred to in fraud. In addition, even if the victims did not yet recognize the exact content of the documents they signed or sealed and what result the act of preparing those documents would bring about, as long as they believed the documents to be for land transaction permission or for the agreed establishment of a mortgage and personally signed or sealed documents containing content relating to a different mortgage contract, their awareness of the act of signing or sealing those documents existed, and their disposition intent is also recognized.\\n\\ng. Nevertheless, the court below, contrary to the above, erred by holding that there was no disposition act by the victims solely because the victims had no intent to establish a mortgage, etc. over their own land, and accordingly found all principal indictment facts in this part not guilty. Therefore, the judgment below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the disposition act referred to in fraud. The grounds of appeal asserting this point are well-founded.\\n\\n2. Scope of reversal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated above, the portions of the judgment below concerning the principal indictment facts on violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Fraud), the fraud committed on 2010. 12. 29., and the fraud committed on 2011. 4. 7. must be reversed; and as the principal indictment facts as to each of those parts are reversed, the alternative indictment facts concerning violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Fraud) and the fraud counts must also necessarily be reversed together. Further, the court below imposed a single sentence by regarding the remaining guilty portions, including the alternative indictment fact concerning the fraud committed on 2011. 4. 7. that is reversed as above, as concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act; accordingly, the judgment below must be reversed in its entirety.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without addressing the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the judgment below and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and so adjudge as ordered. Except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Lee Sang-hoon, Kim Yong-deok, Kim So-young, Cho Hee-dae, Park Sang-ok, and Lee Ki-taek, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous; there are supplemental opinions by Justice Park Byeong-dae, Justice Kim Chang-seok, Justice Kwon Soon-il, and Justice Kim Shin in support of the majority opinion, and supplemental opinions by Justice Kim Yong-deok, Justice Kim So-young, and Justice Park Sang-ok, and by Justice Cho Hee-dae, in support of the dissenting opinions.\\n\\n4. The dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Sang-hoon, Kim Yong-deok, Kim So-young, Cho Hee-dae, Park Sang-ok, and Lee Ki-taek as to each of the principal indictment facts among the acquittal portion of the judgment below is as follows.\\n\\na. The majority opinion states that, even if the deceived person did not recognize the meaning or content of the disposition act, if the deceived person’s act or omission is assessed as a property disposition act that directly causes property damage, and if such act or omission was done with the deceived person’s awareness, disposition intent corresponding to the disposition act is recognized, and it is not necessary that the deceived person recognize even the result of his or her own act or omission in order for disposition intent to be recognized. However, the logic of this majority opinion, which abruptly changes prior precedents that have understood awareness of the result of disposition as disposition intent for the purpose of punishing signature fraud, is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) Theft is the acquisition of property by the perpetrator’s act of taking it away, whereas fraud is the acquisition of property by the victim’s disposition act; the two are distinguished based on the disposition act. In this sense, fraud is described as a self-damaging offense and theft as an other-damaging offense. In order for the essence of the disposition act as such self-damaging act to be satisfied in fraud, the victim must necessarily have an intent to decide on the disposition of his or her own property. Put differently, only an act or omission governed by a will formed on the basis of the awareness that the victim’s act is related to his or her own property rights can be normatively assessed as the disposition act referred to in fraud. A disposition act with no awareness or intent concerning the result of disposition is, in itself, contradictory. In short, a fraud case in which the victim does not even recognize what he or she did with respect to his or her own property contradicts the essence of fraud as a self-damaging offense.\\n\\nThe reason the Supreme Court has consistently interpreted the disposition act referred to in fraud as a property disposition act, requiring subjectively that the deceived person have disposition intent, namely awareness of the result of disposition, and objectively that there be an act governed by such intent, is likewise a just interpretive theory based on a profound insight into the essence of fraud and the meaning of disposition act and disposition intent as its volitional element, and is by no means something to be changed.\\n\\nIn the end, the majority opinion that fraud may recognize disposition intent and disposition act even where the deceived person has no awareness of the result of disposition is difficult to accept.\\n\\n(2) The majority opinion also views disposition intent, the deceived person’s subjective intent, as necessary in order for the disposition act referred to in fraud to be recognized. Yet even apart from further discussion of the essence of fraud, the concept of “disposition” intent itself already presupposes the deceived person’s awareness and intent corresponding to the content of the disposition act. Disposition intent with no awareness of the result of the disposition act cannot be the subjective intent of the disposition act.\\n\\nThe majority opinion says that in a disposition act, disposition intent is sufficient if the deceived person, having fallen into error, has awareness that he or she performs an act assessed as a property disposition act; but in substance, this means nothing more than that the deceived person who acted need only have factual awareness of doing an act sufficient to distinguish it from the act of a person lacking capacity to intend or from unconscious conduct. However, such awareness of acting cannot be evaluated as “disposition” intent corresponding to the disposition act.\\n\\nThus, the majority opinion confuses the disposition intent referred to in fraud with the deceived person’s general intent to act, and while stating that disposition intent is required for the disposition act, it independently interprets the meaning of disposition intent in a content that does not at all conform to the concept of disposition intent, thereby falling into a contradiction of its own making.
