In light of this, the logic of the majority opinion is improper.\\n\\n(3) The elements of fraud must be interpreted according to the essence of fraud, and a theory of interpreting elements that contradicts that essence cannot easily be acknowledged as legitimate. As mentioned above, in interpreting the disposition act that characterizes fraud as a self-damaging offense and distinguishes it from theft, awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition is naturally required, and a theory of interpretation contrary to this cannot be developed in interpreting the other elements of fraud, namely error and deceptive act. That is, according to the essence of fraud and the meaning of disposition intent derived therefrom, fraud can be established only when the deceived person in error engages in a disposition act while having awareness of the meaning and result of his or her own act; thus, the deceived person’s error as an element of the offense is also limited to matters concerning the motive, intent, or purpose of the disposition act, and an error concerning the disposition act itself, with no awareness even of the result of disposition, plainly cannot be subsumed under the error referred to in fraud. A proper theory of interpretation regarding deceptive act as an offense element is no different. Ultimately, the majority opinion’s argument that awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition is not necessarily required, based on an inappropriate interpretation of error and deceptive act that disregards the essence and specificity of fraud, is merely an interpretive theory that reverses the order of logic and cannot be accepted as is.\\n\\n(4) Under the majority opinion’s interpretation that no awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition is necessary in determining disposition intent in fraud, the question whether fraud is established becomes unclear, and as a result the scope of punishment is also likely to be expanded. In many cases involving the perpetrator’s deceptive conduct, it is doubtful whether fraud cases and non-fraud cases can be clearly distinguished without considering the deceived person’s awareness at all. For example, in the so-called stratagem theft case, where the perpetrator falsely says he just wants to look at a book or jewelry, receives it from the deceived person, and then simply takes it away, the Supreme Court has treated the perpetrator’s taking as theft by invasion of possession, because despite the deceived person’s delivery act, the book or jewelry remains in the deceived person’s possession, and has punished it as theft (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 1983. 2. 22. rendered 82DO3115, 1994. 8. 12. rendered 94DO1487). But in such a stratagem theft case, without considering the deceived person’s awareness or intent at all and relying only on the objective and external delivery act, it is by no means easy to determine clearly whether the deceived person still retains possession of the book or jewelry or has completely transferred possession. Ultimately, it is clear that disposition intent, which consists of awareness of the result of disposition, is an important constituent concept for distinguishing fraud from theft and should not be abandoned in interpreting fraud.\\n\\n(5) Article 2 subparagraph 2 of the Act on the Prevention of Damage Caused by Telecommunications-Based Financial Fraud and Refund of Damaged Funds (hereinafter “the Telecommunications Fraud Damage Refund Act”) defines telecommunications-based financial fraud as follows: acts, by using telecommunications under Article 2 subparagraph 1 of the Framework Act on Telecommunications, that deceive or extort another person in order to obtain pecuniary benefit or to have a third party obtain pecuniary benefit. It further specifies, as one of the listed acts, “an act inducing transfer or remittance of funds.” Article 15-2 paragraph 1 subparagraph 1 (hereinafter “the provision at issue”) provides that a person who, for the purpose of telecommunications-based financial fraud, has another input information or instructions into a computer or other information-processing device shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 10 years or a fine not exceeding 100,000,000 won. The provision at issue was newly enacted out of necessity to punish even such crimes, taking into account the uncertainty as to whether fraud applies in the case of variant voice-phishing crimes in which the perpetrator deceives the victim by pretending to offer a tax refund and induces the victim to an ATM to remit or transfer money from his or her account to a voice-phishing account, where the deceived victim did not remit or transfer money with awareness that he or she was disposing of his or her own property. As a result, conduct in which a victim is deceived by using telecommunications so that the victim remits or transfers money without even any awareness of the result of his or her own act is punished through the provision at issue.\\n\\nAs can be seen from the legislative history of the provision at issue under the Telecommunications Fraud Damage Refund Act, if the legislature wishes to impose criminal punishment on a person who obtained pecuniary benefit through unlawful deception that prevented the deceived person from recognizing the result of his or her own act, the proper solution would be separate legislation, rather than arbitrarily changing the foundation of established legal doctrine on fraud as the majority opinion does.\\n\\nb. In addition, the majority opinion states that, in the signature fraud issue in this case, even if the deceived person signed or sealed without properly recognizing the content of the disposition document, fraud is established because property damage according to the content of the disposition document was caused and, as long as the deceived person personally signed or sealed the disposition document and thus had awareness of the act of signing or sealing the disposition document, the disposition act by disposition intent can be recognized. However, we cannot agree for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) As repeatedly emphasized, in light of the essence and structure of fraud, the disposition act referred to in fraud must be, at all times, an act governed by disposition intent, and such disposition intent necessarily presupposes awareness of the result caused by one’s own act. As a result, in the so-called signature fraud cases where the deceived person, due to the perpetrator’s deceptive act, mistakenly believes the content of the document and signs or seals a document that causes an effect different from his or her internal intent and delivers it to the perpetrator, etc., thereby allowing the perpetrator, etc. to obtain pecuniary benefit according to the content of the document, it is clear that even if the deceived person was aware that he or she was signing or sealing that document, there was no awareness of the result of disposition, and thus disposition intent and disposition act cannot be recognized.\\n\\n(2) (a) Whether a property disposition act or disposition intent as its element exists must be determined from the standpoint of the deceived person who performed the disposition act. If the deceived person was deceived as to the content of the document and signed or sealed a writing presented by the perpetrator without any awareness thereof, it is rather a document prepared contrary to the deceived person’s intent as the nominal author of the document; and for the deceived person who did not know the meaning of the document, he or she was merely used in the commission of forging a document in his or her name (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2000. 6. 13. rendered 2000DO778), and it cannot be assessed that there was a disposition act based on his or her intent.\\n\\nIndeed, in cases like this one, where the perpetrator deceived the landowner as to the content of the document and caused the landowner to sign or seal the mortgage contract form, thereby fraudulently obtaining the signature and then using it to complete mortgage registration in favor of the lender, the victim’s act is nothing more than signing or sealing a document labeled as a mortgage contract form; not only was there no intent to prepare a document of that content, but there was no such awareness at all. That document is merely a forged document prepared without the deceived person’s will, and even if a mortgage creation act, etc. is carried out using that forged document, the act or the result thereof is neither recognized nor intended by the deceived person at all, and rather conflicts with the deceived person’s intent, so it cannot be said that it contains the deceived person’s intent to dispose in favor of a third party. Ultimately, as between the deceived person and the matter at issue, such a result is merely something to be eliminated, and it cannot be said that the deceived person performed a disposition act toward a third party with respect to such result.\\n\\n(b) The Supreme Court has held that, in the so-called “seal fraud” case where a person who had purchased only a portion of the land lied that he would transfer only that portion by division, received the owner’s seal, and then completed ownership transfer registration over the entire land, fraud is not established as to registration concerning the portion not purchased because there was no disposition act by the owner-victim (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 1982. 3. 9. rendered 81DO1732).\\n\\nIn the above seal-fraud case, where the perpetrator-Defendant himself prepared the document necessary for ownership transfer without the landowner’s intervention, or in a signature-fraud case like this one where the landowner is deceived and, without awareness of the content of the document, signs or seals the mortgage contract form, the Defendant’s act in both cases is nothing more than one of the various forms of document forgery, and substantively it is the act of forging a document in the name of the landowner rather than fraud, and there is no essential criminal-law difference between them.\\n\\n(c) According to the majority opinion recognizing fraud in a signature-fraud case, confusion and irrational results will arise because whether fraud is established will depend on the degree of description in the document, whether the document is complete or not, or the manner in which the deceived person signed.\\n\\nEven under the majority opinion, if disposition intent is to be recognized, it is unclear to what extent the contents of the document must be specified at the time the deceived person signs or seals it. For example, in the case of fraudulent signature on a mortgage contract form, it is difficult to know which elements of the mortgage contract must be stated in the document at the time of the deceived person’s signature or seal for fraud to be established, that is, whether fraudulently obtaining a mortgage is established even if some items among the indication of the mortgagee or debtor, the maximum secured amount, the content and scope of the secured debt, or the object of the mortgage are omitted, and if it is established, which omissions are permissible.\\n\\nFurthermore, it is also difficult to distinguish between a signature-fraud case, in which the majority opinion recognizes the existence of disposition intent, and a case where the perpetrator was granted authority to sign on behalf of the deceived person, so that the scope of punishment for fraud becomes ambiguous or overly broad. Even under the majority opinion, if a deceived person, after being deceived by the perpetrator, immediately has the perpetrator sign on his or her behalf, this can be evaluated as the deceived person’s act of preparing the document, and fraud may be regarded as established, as in a signature-fraud case. However, if the signing on behalf of the deceived person is done in the absence of the deceived person—for example, if the perpetrator had previously obtained the deceived person’s permission to sign on behalf of him or her for land transaction permission documents, and then, at the contract execution site where the deceived person is absent, signed on behalf of him or her a mortgage contract form, which is a disposition document of entirely different content—it is not easy to know whether the deceived person’s disposition intent or disposition act is recognized and fraud is established, or whether only document forgery is established, and if the establishment of fraud varies according to specific circumstances or situations, what the distinguishing standard is.\\n\\n(3) In addition, considering that in a signature-fraud case, if the perpetrator goes on to borrow money from a lender who does not know the facts by using the forged writing, there is ample room for the crime of fraud by obtaining money against the lender to be established, it is difficult to conclude that not establishing fraud against the landowner causes an obstacle to proper exercise of punitive authority or creates sentencing imbalance. Rather, in a signature-fraud case, since document forgery is carried out under the intervention of the deceived person’s act or intent as the landowner, it cannot be ruled out that the culpability is smaller than in a seal-fraud case where the perpetrator himself commits document forgery without any intervention by the deceived person.\\n\\nMoreover, it is doubtful whether it is appropriate to punish such cases by concluding that fraud against the lender and, separately, fraud against the landowner are established. If the perpetrator forged a document in the name of the landowner from the outset with the intent to obtain money, the document forgery resulting from the signature-fraud offense should be regarded as a means for a series of fraudulent offenses of obtaining money through deception of the lender, or as an act included in the execution of such offense. Therefore, the mortgage right that the perpetrator allegedly obtained duplicates the economic value of the borrowed funds, so it is difficult to assess the various pecuniary benefits obtained by the perpetrator in the course of the series of offenses as separate items divided according to each counterparty to the deceptive act, and the signature-fraud act can be regarded as already included in the punishable assessment of fraud against the lender. This is especially so considering, under civil law, it is difficult to say that the perpetrator-Defendant is in a position to simultaneously compensate both the damage arising from the security creation against the landowner and the damage equivalent to the borrowed money against the lender.\\n\\nNot every act of obtaining property by means of deception can be the subject of criminal punishment, and even if such an act does not satisfy the elements of fraud, it must not be punished merely because it is highly punishable. If a deceived person has no awareness of the result of disposition and yet is punished for fraud merely because the deception is highly culpable, this directly undermines the liberty-guaranteeing function of criminal law.\\n\\nc. Taking these circumstances into account, in order for the disposition act referred to in fraud to be recognized, the deceived person’s subjective awareness of the result of disposition is required; and in the case of signature fraud, because the deceived person has no awareness whatsoever of the content and legal effect of the disposition document he or she signs or seals, it is correct to deny disposition intent and the disposition act based thereon.\\n\\nd. In the same vein, the court below’s decision that fraud cannot be established as to the principal indictment facts in this part because the victims, who were the owners of the respective lands stated in the judgment below, did not intend to establish mortgages, etc. over their respective lands and therefore cannot be said to have engaged in a property disposition act, does not contain, as the grounds of appeal assert, an error of law regarding the disposition act or disposition intent in fraud.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, I make clear that I cannot agree with the majority opinion.\\n\\n5. Justice Park Byeong-dae’s supplemental opinion to the majority opinion is as follows.\\n\\nThe essence of a juristic act or expression of intent under civil law is the intent as to legal effect. This is because a legally meaningful act must presuppose the actor’s awareness of the legal effect sought to be achieved thereby. The logic that, in fraud, a disposition act by deception must be recognized only if the actor (victim) has awareness of the result of that act has a structure similar to the civil-law requirement that a juristic act must have intent as to legal effect. However, the victim’s disposition intent in fraud, by its nature, is bound to accompany error. Whether it is error concerning the legal result of the disposition act or error concerning the economic effect, there exists an error as to a result different from the internal expectation caused by another’s deceptive act. Such error usually constitutes error as to motive. Typical examples are goods fraud, loan fraud, and investment fraud, where one deceives the other as to the efficacy of an item. The signature fraud at issue in this case belongs to error in expression. The internal intent was to apply for land transaction permission, but as a result of being deceived, the person actually signed the documents for mortgage registration. The internal intent as to effect and the expressed intent as to effect do not coincide. Viewed from the perspective of civil-law expressions of intent, there is room to regard this as nonexistence or non-formation of the expression of intent, in that there was no internal intent corresponding to the manifested disposition act. However, even in civil-law theory, there appears to be almost no view that determines the existence or nonexistence of a juristic act solely on whether there was an internal intent to effect corresponding to the act of expression. Since the essence of intent as to effect is the intent inferred and judged externally through the act of expression, the dominant majority view is that, even if internal intent and manifested intent do not coincide, an expression of intent or juristic act according to the manifested intent as to effect is formed and exists. And, contrary to this, even in views that regard the internal intent as the essence of intent as to effect or that consider the act of expression according to intent as an element of expression of intent, namely the intent to manifest, to be an element of the expression of intent, if the declarant has performed an act of expression that can only be understood as different from his or her internal intent as to effect, the disadvantage resulting therefrom should be borne by the declarant who caused the mismatch between intent and expression, which is consistent with the principle of self-responsibility; accordingly, they explain that a normative interpretation that the expression of intent is formed according to the content of the act of expression is unavoidable. Therefore, when the act of expression inconsistent with the internal intent was caused by another’s deceptive act, the question of what responsibility the declarant bears is resolved, on the premise that the “existence” of the expression of intent inferred from the act of expression is recognized, by the principle of self-responsibility and the doctrines on expressions of intent by fraud or mistake.\\n\\nSince such is the discussion on expressions of intent in civil law, in the phase of determining in criminal law whether the actor who deceived another has committed fraud, to say that in the case of signature fraud the disposition act does not exist or is not formed because intent and expression do not coincide is to turn the clock back to the theory of the original intent doctrine. Deceiving a declarant into performing an act of expression inconsistent with the internal intent is the perpetrator’s original intention, and even if the act of expression was made as intended, to say that the disposition act in fraud does not exist because the internal intent does not coincide with the expression runs counter to the fundamental purpose of fraud and also to criminal responsibility principles. Whether one follows a natural interpretation that prioritizes internal intent or a normative interpretation that emphasizes the act of expression as the method of interpretation of expressions of intent, when determining the existence of a disposition act in fraud, it is of course correct to follow normative interpretation based on the act of expression. One cannot interpret that the mismatch between intent and expression, caused by a deceptive act, should rather operate as a favorable factor for the deceiver. If the cause of the mistaken expression is the deceptive act, it is appropriate to hold the deceiver accountable according to the manifested expression.\\n\\nIn short, even in civil-law theories of juristic acts, where intent as to effect must be the core indicator of an act, there is almost no dispute that intent as to effect must be regarded not as a concept of the actor’s internal mental state as a natural fact, but as an object of normative evaluation. In other words, even in civil-law theory, an expression of intent is not held to be nonexistent from the outset merely because there is an error in expression arising from inconsistency between intent and expression, on the ground that there is no intent as to effect according to the manifested content. Nor is it considered that the internal intent becomes the content of the juristic act merely because it is confirmed that the party’s internal intent differs from the act of expression. Much less, in the context of criminal fraud where the victim’s disposition act is at issue, does it make sense to require a stricter factual coincidence between internal intent and manifested intent than is required for the concept of intent as to effect in civil law in order to recognize disposition intent. There is no reason to demand conformity between intent and expression more stringently in fraud. If one were to compare civil-law intent as to effect with the disposition intent in fraud and insist on the scope of their inclusion, it would not be normatively appropriate or natural to construe the concept of disposition act in criminal law more narrowly than the concept of juristic act in civil law. Nor is there room for criminal-law-specific reasoning such as strict construction for the protection of the defendant’s interests.\\n\\nMeanwhile, when an expression of intent by mistake was caused by deception, there is practical value in civil-law discourse in deciding whether to construct it as an expression of intent by fraud or as an expression of intent by mistake. This is because whether the expression can be rescinded when the declarant is grossly negligent may differ. However, in a situation where the question is, in criminal law, whether fraud is established, there is no clear practical value in distinguishing whether it is an expression of intent by fraud or by mistake, or whether it constitutes error as to motive or error in expression. In fraud, that the victim’s disposition act must be a defective expression of intent caused by deception is mainly an issue in terms of causal relation between the defendant’s deceptive act and the victim’s disposition act; it should not be understood as meaning that whether fraud is established depends on what internal intent the victim had in performing that disposition act. Moreover, there is no rational reason under civil law to exclude only cases of error in expression from the category of disposition act in fraud among “expressions of intent by fraud” and “expressions of intent by mistake.”\\n\\nHowever, signature fraud such as in this case is not merely the obtaining of a signature on a blank sheet of paper. The document itself expressly states the purpose of property disposition, but the actor deceived the victim into believing it was a document of a different purpose and obtained the signature. In other words, the signature at issue is of course not an unconscious act, nor is it a mere factual act. It is an act of externally manifesting an intent that, together with the document’s contents, constitutes a property disposition act. It is only that the deceived person did not recognize that the manifested act had a meaning different from the internal intent. Where a property disposition act is prepared in writing as a disposition document, if the objective meaning of the wording is clear, it is an established precedent that, absent special circumstances, the existence and content of the expression of intent must be recognized according to the wording. There is no reason why a disposition document prepared through signature fraud should be treated differently. When a document obtained through signature fraud is used to establish a mortgage in favor of a third party and the validity of the underlying act is at issue, there is no precedent that recognizes nonexistence of the expression of intent. On the premise that a legal act exists according to the wording of the signature-fraudulently obtained mortgage contract form, validity is examined only through logic such as fraud, mistake, or unauthorized agency. Nevertheless, in relation to criminal fraud, to say that signature fraud lacks awareness of the result of disposition and thus the disposition act does not exist is neither logically consistent nor in keeping with the normative purpose unique to criminal law. Recognizing, in civil relations, that a juristic act exists for one and the same act while, in criminal relations, saying it is not a disposition act only creates confusion in the coherence of the normative order.\\n\\nThat the precedents held that when a motorcycle was obtained under the pretext of a test drive and then driven away, the act constituted theft rather than fraud is because, in light of the circumstances at the time, the delivery of the motorcycle was not a disposition act with the appearance of transfer of possessory power. A signature-fraud case involving a disposition document cannot be legally construed in the same way as the motorcycle theft case, because the outward appearance of the act is precisely the content of the disposition document.\\n\\nTherefore, the former line of some precedents stating that, for the disposition act of a fraud victim, disposition intent in the strict sense of awareness of the result of disposition is required, is not only inconsistent with the criminal-law framework of regulation, but also unharmonious even within the framework of civil-law juristic act theory. In fraud as well, just as in general civil-law theory of expression of intent, it is appropriate to recognize intent as to effect as a normative evaluative concept inferred from the manifested act, and to regard the victim as having disposition intent so long as that manifested act was based on the victim’s defective intent. This accords with the essence of action theory running through both civil and criminal law.\\n\\nWith this, I state the supplemental opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. The supplemental opinion of Justices Kim Chang-seok and Kwon Soon-il to the majority opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. The Supreme Court has heretofore viewed that, in order to say there was a deceived person’s disposition act in fraud, there must be a corresponding disposition intent, and in order for the deceived person’s disposition intent to be recognized, the deceived person must go beyond awareness of the act itself that is evaluated as a disposition act and also recognize the result caused thereby. However, according to this view, acts that should rightly be punished as fraud are excluded from the scope of fraud, and because such a result is not correct even theoretically, we seek to change the prior view.\\n\\n(1) The dissenting opinion argues, as grounds for maintaining the prior view, that in order for the essence of the disposition act as a self-damaging act in fraud to be satisfied, the victim must necessarily have an intent to decide on the disposition of his or her own property; and that only an act or omission governed by a will formed on the basis of awareness that the victim’s act is related to his or her own property rights can be normatively evaluated as the disposition act referred to in fraud.\\n\\nIf one wishes to attribute responsibility for the result of the disposition act to the person who performed the disposition act, then it can be said that the person must be aware of the result of the disposition act. This is an obvious consequence under the principle of culpability that, if the actor did not recognize the facts constituting the offense, it cannot be attributed to his or her responsibility. However, viewing disposition intent as necessary in fraud is not because one seeks to attribute to the disposition actor responsibility for the result of the disposition act.\\n\\nThe most striking feature of fraud is that property is transferred directly by the victim’s disposition act. Yet in order to say that the victim’s disposition act exists, it is insufficient merely that the act evaluable as a disposition act was performed by the victim; corresponding disposition intent must also be recognized. Therefore, the function of disposition intent does not exceed confirming that the victim recognized and performed an act evaluated as causing property damage to the victim and resulting in the perpetrator, etc. acquiring property or pecuniary benefit. From this perspective, the majority opinion views that the object of the victim’s awareness necessary for recognizing disposition intent is sufficient if it is the act itself evaluable as a disposition act, and need not extend to the result caused thereby. Under the elements of fraud, the disposition act is clearly distinguished from the result caused by the disposition act, namely the acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit by the perpetrator, etc., and the subjective element corresponds to the objective element; limiting the object of the victim’s awareness necessary for recognizing disposition intent to the act itself evaluated as a disposition act is also consistent with that standard.\\n\\n(2) Under the prior view, if the victim engaged in a disposition act without recognizing that the perpetrator’s deceptive act or the resulting error on the victim’s part existed, but recognized the occurrence of the result caused thereby, fraud is affirmed; but further, if the victim engaged in a disposition act without recognizing even the occurrence of the result caused by the disposition act, fraud is denied. The dissenting opinion argues that such a result accords with the nature of fraud as a self-damaging offense.\\n\\nHowever, in either case, there exists the perpetrator’s deceptive act and the resulting error of the victim, there exists the victim’s act pursuant to such error, and there exists the victim’s property damage resulting from such act. In either case, there is no choice but to say that there is a self-damaging act. Nevertheless, the dissenting opinion says that without awareness of the result of disposition, fraud as a self-damaging offense cannot be established. This is understood as logic that, because the victim’s freedom of decision cannot be viewed as being properly exercised, there is no victim’s act. Fraud is a crime that is established when property is transferred by the victim’s act but the victim cannot properly exercise freedom of decision due to the perpetrator’s deceptive act. In this respect, it is not proper to exclude from self-damaging offenses those cases in which the victim’s freedom of decision can be regarded as more severely infringed due to the perpetrator’s deceptive act.\\n\\nb. The dissenting opinion argues that, by the nature of disposition intent derived from the essence of fraud, the deceived person’s error is limited to motive, intent, and purpose, and that error concerning the “disposition act itself,” which lacks even awareness of the result of disposition, cannot be subsumed under the error referred to in fraud. Such an argument is essentially no different from limiting the scope of error so that, among the elements of fraud, error must exist at a stage prior to the disposition act and must not exist in the disposition act itself.\\n\\nApplying the dissenting opinion’s interpretation—that the deceived person’s internal intent and the externally manifested intent must coincide so that there is no defect in the expression of intent itself—to a signature-fraud case means that, unless the deceived person signed or sealed the document with an internal intent to bring about the effect manifested in the document while knowing the specific content of the document and the result its preparation would bring, disposition intent cannot be recognized. In a signature-fraud case, since the perpetrator’s deceptive act exists in the process of eliciting the deceived person’s expression of intent, it is a situation in which it is impossible for the deceived person to grasp the meaning and effect of the expression of intent objectively perceived based on the externally manifested intent. Yet the dissenting opinion insists that, in fraud types requiring the deceived person’s expression of intent, that expression of intent alone must especially be free from defect by having the deceived person’s internal intent and manifested intent coincide, which is difficult to accept.\\n\\nMeanwhile, in criminal law, whether the disposition act is a juristic act does not affect the establishment of fraud, regardless of whether it is valid, void, or voidable. In a signature-fraud case, although obtained by fraud, the expression of intent externally revealed through the deceived person’s preparation of the disposition document objectively exists. Such expression of intent is assessed as a disposition act that directly causes the perpetrator, etc. to acquire property. Even under civil law, although the internal intent as to effect and the manifested intent as to effect do not coincide because of error, since there clearly exists an external act—namely the act of expression—through preparation and delivery of the disposition document by signing or sealing it, by which such intent can be recognized, in a signature-fraud case the expression of intent according to the content of the disposition document is assessed as being formed and existing. Moreover, even if the deceived person did not know the content of the disposition document due to the perpetrator’s deceptive act, as long as the deceived person personally signed or sealed the disposition document and thereby prepared it, genuine formation of the document is recognized. Even if the perpetrator was punished for forgery of private document for the signature-fraud act, it cannot be said that the expression of intent externally manifested through the preparation of the document does not exist or that there is no manifested intent as to effect. In this way, the deceived person fell into error due to the perpetrator’s deceptive act and, as a result, performed some act, such as preparation of a disposition document objectively recognized as an expression of intent, and property or pecuniary benefit was transferred based thereon, and property damage occurred as a result; yet it is difficult to understand the denial of fraud merely on the ground that the deceived person’s internal intent and externally manifested intent do not coincide, thereby concluding that disposition intent cannot be recognized.\\n\\nc. (1) It is also difficult to say, as the dissenting opinion suggests, that if awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition is not required for disposition intent in fraud, then the establishment of fraud becomes unclear or the scope of punishment expands unreasonably.\\n\\nThe majority opinion merely holds that awareness of the result of disposition is not required for disposition intent; it does not abandon the concept of disposition act as an element of fraud. In each case, the establishment of fraud is determined by whether there exists a disposition act by the deceived person, namely a property disposition act that directly causes property damage as an act or omission governed by the deceived person’s defective intent. Even in prior precedents that held fraud was not established in relation to pecuniary benefit, namely cases where the victim fled from a hospital to avoid performing a medical fee debt (see Supreme Court Decision 1970. 9. 22. rendered 70DO1615), or cases where a forged promissory note was delivered in connection with an existing debt (see Supreme Court Decision 1982. 9. 28. rendered 82DO1759), the conclusion that fraud is not established can be reached without considering whether the deceived person had awareness of the result of disposition, because in those cases there simply was no property disposition act by the deceived person causing property damage.\\n\\nAlso, in the so-called “stratagem theft” example given by the dissenting opinion—where an item is handed over under the pretense that it will be purchased and then carried away—the victim has only temporarily transferred possession so that the item can be looked at by the person intending to purchase it. The taking of the property occurred not because there was a disposition act governed by the victim’s defective intent, but rather because the perpetrator subsequently ran away with the item and thereby acquired the property. Therefore, it is a case in which fraud cannot be established because the existence of a disposition act cannot be recognized. Even if judged on the basis of objectively and externally perceived delivery, it is easy to see that the victim did not completely transfer possession of the item to the perpetrator. In short, since the establishment of fraud can be determined by whether a disposition act exists, it is not necessary to include awareness of the result of disposition in disposition intent in order to distinguish fraud from stratagem theft.\\n\\n(2) As the dissenting opinion notes, the enactment of the Telecommunications Fraud Damage Refund Act created multiple punishment provisions relating to telecommunications-based financial fraud, thereby providing clear bases for punishing various forms of fraud using telecommunications, including cases where the victim has no awareness that money is being remitted or transferred. However, even though such punishment provisions were created to clarify aspects of the Criminal Act fraud offense that had been controversial and to effectively cope with new and variant voice-phishing schemes, this does not lead to the theory that awareness of the result of disposition is necessary to recognize disposition intent. Nor is it desirable to interpret the Criminal Act so as to narrow the scope of fraud and then argue that legislative resolution is again needed to fill the gap.\\n\\nd. (1) The so-called “seal fraud case” and “signature fraud case” are essentially different. If one assumes a seal-fraud case in which, after misleading the landowner as to the purpose, the perpetrator receives the owner’s seal and then completes mortgage registration for the land in favor of a third party, there is in such a case no external expression of intent that can be called the victim’s disposition act. There exists only the act of the perpetrator forging documents necessary for mortgage registration in the victim’s name using the seal obtained by fraud, and it is clear that this cannot be punished as fraud. By contrast, in a signature-fraud case, there undeniably exists the victim’s external expression of intent through the mortgage contract form, etc., which constitutes a disposition act causing property damage. Considering that in the seal-fraud case the registration completed by the fraudulently obtained seal must be canceled as a registration void for lack of cause because there can be said to be no expression of intent by the deceived person regarding the mortgage contract, it cannot be said to be unreasonable to distinguish its legal evaluation from the signature-fraud case.\\n\\n(2) In the case of a signature fraud involving a mortgage contract form like this case, under civil law, the victim, who is the landowner, may also assert rescission of the mortgage contract on the ground of mistake in signing or sealing, and seek cancellation of the mortgage registration completed in favor of the lender (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 2005. 5. 27. rendered 2004DA43824, 2006. 10. 27. rendered 2006DA41778). However, rescission is barred where the declarant-victim was grossly negligent (proviso to Article 109(1) of the Civil Act). In case of rescission asserted on the ground of an expression of intent by fraud, rescission is allowed only if the third-party mortgagee knew or could have known that it was an expression of intent by fraud (Article 110(2) of the Civil Act). Furthermore, rescission cannot be set up against a good-faith third party who has formed a new legal relationship by, for example, acquiring the status of mortgagee based on the mortgage contract (Articles 109(2) and 110(3) of the Civil Act).\\n\\nUltimately, even if the landowner-victim argues that the signature or seal was fraudulently obtained and thereby seeks to cancel the mortgage registration established on his or her land and recover rights, this is not always possible. Therefore, there is clearly a criminal policy need to protect the landowner as a victim of fraud.\\n\\ne. (1) In a signature-fraud case, the circumstance that fraud by obtaining a loan against the lender may be established cannot serve as a ground for denying the establishment of fraud against the landowner. The two fraud offenses have different victims, and the content of the deception is also different. The property obtained through the offense is also clearly different in that, in the former case, it is money, which is a thing, whereas in the latter case it is a pecuniary benefit enabling use of another’s real property as security. The two crimes are not mutually exclusive or contradictory. Nor is the signature-fraud offense against the landowner in a relationship in which it generally and typically accompanies the fraud offense against the lender. Yet the dissenting opinion, overly focusing on the fact that the perpetrator obtained money as a result of the offense, overlooks the fact that different invasions of legal interests occurred to multiple victims depending on the offense.\\n\\nAlso, if property is obtained by having the deceived person sign or seal a disposition document stating an expression of intent to donate to the perpetrator or a third party, or to waive a debt, there is no room for a separate fraud offense in addition to the fraud offense against the deceived person as victim. Moreover, in this case, because proof in the criminal procedure may be insufficient, fraud against the lender may not be established, and if the security creation contract is recognized as valid in civil law, the lender may not even bother to question the perpetrator’s criminal liability. Contrary to the dissenting opinion’s argument, the concern that a gap may arise in punishment is directly confirmed by this case.\\n\\n(2) In a signature-fraud case, the fact that the perpetrator may be punished for forgery of private document does not mean that punitive authority is properly exercised. The substance of signature fraud is an offense of property acquisition through deception. Nevertheless, to punish only the document-forgery offense, which is a means, while not punishing the core and essential part of such punishable conduct, cannot be called a proper exercise of punitive authority consistent with the illegality of the act and result. Furthermore, because the statutory penalties for fraud and forgery of private document differ greatly, and because fraud has special statutory provisions for aggravated punishment depending on the amount obtained, whereas forgery of private document has no such provisions, there arises a sentencing imbalance in which even where the perpetrator, etc. obtains massive pecuniary benefit through signature fraud, punishment is limited to the lighter offense of forgery of private document.\\n\\nf. (1) The issue of how much the content of a disposition document must be specified at the time the deceived person signs or seals it is one that must be determined by comprehensively considering all the circumstances in each case. Since forms of criminal conduct vary, it is impossible to provide a uniform standard that can encompass all the special circumstances of individual cases. In light of the role and function of the disposition act in fraud, the key standard for judgment is whether the document the deceived person signed or sealed bears the appearance of a disposition document and can directly cause the effect of acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit by the perpetrator, etc., and whether it can be assessed that, by the act of signing or sealing the disposition document, the deceived person’s expression of intent to dispose of property was externally and objectively made. In other words, it is whether the deceived person’s act of signing or sealing made an essential contribution to the occurrence of such result. Ultimately, it can be seen that this is merely a matter of subsumption under the elements frequently encountered in relation to whether the offense is established.\\n\\n(2) Fraud can recognize the victim’s disposition act only if there is a disposition act by the deceived person him/herself rather than by the perpetrator, and such act can be assessed as causing the perpetrator, etc. to acquire property. Therefore, unless the perpetrator or a third party, from the standpoint of ordinary social understanding, acted as the deceived person’s hands and feet and mechanically signed or sealed according to his or her instructions in a manner equivalent to the deceived person’s own signature or seal, even if the perpetrator, having deceived the deceived person as to the contents to be stated in the disposition document, obtained permission to sign or seal on behalf of the deceived person and thereby signed or sealed a disposition document that caused property damage to the deceived person, this would be no different from a seal-fraud case, and it cannot be said that the deceived person performed a disposition act.\\n\\nWith the above, I state the supplemental opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Justice Kim Shin’s supplemental opinion to the majority opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. Even if the deceived person did not recognize the meaning or content of the disposition act, if the deceived person’s act or omission directly causes property damage and is governed by the defective intent of the deceived person who fell into error, and as a result the Defendant received property or acquired pecuniary benefit, fraud is established, and it is not necessary to require awareness of the result of the deceived person’s act or omission. I agree with the majority opinion for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) Whether fraud is established must be determined by whether the elements prescribed in the Criminal Act are satisfied, and whether a disposition act with awareness of the result of disposition by the deceived person is necessary for fraud must also be determined based on textual interpretation.\\n\\nThe Criminal Act provides that a person who deceives another and obtains delivery of property or acquires pecuniary benefit, or who by such means causes a third party to receive delivery of property or acquire pecuniary benefit, shall be punished for fraud (Article 347 of the Criminal Act). On the face of the text, it is clear that it defines as an element of the offense the Defendant’s receipt of property or acquisition of pecuniary benefit, and does not make the deceived person’s awareness of the result of disposition and disposition act an element of the offense.\\n\\nHowever, for fraud to be established, as a premise for the Defendant to receive property or acquire pecuniary benefit, the deceived person’s delivery of property or act causing property damage must accompany it. In order for some act to be evaluated as the deceived person’s act, awareness by the deceived person of the natural act itself is necessary, and it is obvious that unconscious behavior without even such awareness cannot be assessed as the deceived person’s act. However, if the deceived person’s act or omission is recognized as being governed by the deceived person’s will as an act directly causing property damage, there is no reason to evaluate it as not being the deceived person’s act.\\n\\nThe essence of fraud lies in the acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit by deception, and in the Defendant’s receipt of property or acquisition of pecuniary benefit, the victim, i.e., the deceived person’s disposition act intervenes. Even though the deceived person’s disposition act merely serves as a premise for the Defendant’s acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit, there is neither legal basis nor logical necessity to require, in such disposition act, awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition. This is the natural result of interpreting the Criminal Act, not an interpretation based on the necessity of punishment from a criminal-policy perspective or on the protective function of criminal law for legal interests.\\n\\n(2) In fraud, in order to uniformly interpret the various forms of conduct by which the Defendant acquires property or pecuniary benefit, it cannot be said that fraud is established only where the deceived person performs a disposition act while aware of the result of disposition.\\n\\nWhat the Criminal Act seeks to protect through fraud is not the victim’s freedom of decision, but the victim’s property as a whole. Therefore, the deceived person’s disposition act, which is the premise for the Defendant’s acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit in fraud, need not be a juristic act under civil law if it objectively causes direct property damage; it also includes factual acts in the pure sense, and whether they are valid, void, or voidable is irrelevant.\\n\\nHowever, when the disposition act takes the form of an expression of intent or juristic act, it may be possible to say that the deceived person had intent recognizing the result of disposition; but in the case of a pure factual act, recognizing such intent means nothing more than treating the deceived person’s awareness of the act itself as awareness of the result of disposition. An attempt to require, in the deceived person’s disposition act as the premise of the Defendant’s acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit, an intent comparable to awareness of the occurrence of a result that is only imaginable in civil-law juristic acts, and further to construe such disposition intent as an element of fraud, leads to abandoning a uniform interpretation of cases where the Defendant acquires property or pecuniary benefit through the deceived person’s factual act and cases where the Defendant acquires property or pecuniary benefit through the deceived person’s juristic act.\\n\\n(3) The object of punishment in fraud is the Defendant’s act, and the object to be evaluated in determining whether fraud is established is also the Defendant’s act, not the deceived person’s act. Therefore, whether fraud is established is a matter to be judged by evaluating the Defendant’s act, not a matter to be determined by evaluating the deceived person’s act.\\n\\nThe attitude of trying to understand the victim’s disposition intent as meaning awareness of the result of disposition, and thereby as an element of the offense, appears to share the context of civil-law interpretation of expressions of intent, in that it seeks to assess the validity of the expression of intent when there is a mismatch between the deceived person’s subjective intent and the objective act of expression. However, while the interpretation of expressions of intent in civil law is a matter of determining whether the deceived person’s expression of intent does not exist, or whether it has a defect falling under grounds for nullity or rescission, in order to decide the legal effect to be given to that expression of intent, the question whether fraud is established is a matter of determining whether the Defendant’s conduct—having caused such a state and thereby received property or acquired pecuniary benefit—is the object of punishment prescribed by the Criminal Act. Since fraud punishes the Defendant’s conduct in this way, the deceived person’s disposition act that is the premise for the Defendant’s acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit is merely a means of evaluating whether the Defendant’s act satisfies the elements of fraud, and there is no reason or need for it to be a completed expression of intent in the same sense as a civil-law juristic act. If there is no disposition act, it merely has the negative meaning that, as a logical consequence, the Defendant cannot be recognized as having received property or acquired pecuniary benefit.\\n\\nObjectively viewed, if it is recognized that the Defendant directly received property or acquired pecuniary benefit through the deceived person’s disposition act, and that it is causally related to the Defendant’s deceptive act, fraud is established. Whether legal effects arise according to the deceived person’s internal intent is a matter to be separately discussed in civil cases, and even if the Defendant acquired pecuniary benefit according to the content of the disposition document created by the deceived person’s act, it is difficult to find a reason to exclude this from fraud merely because legal effects different from the deceived person’s internal intent arose.\\n\\nb. The core of the dissenting opinion is that, by the nature of fraud as a self-damaging offense, the deceived person’s disposition act must be governed by a will formed on the basis of awareness that it is related to property rights, and because a will with no awareness of the result of disposition cannot be regarded as disposition intent corresponding to the disposition act, the deceived person’s error as an element of the offense is limited to matters concerning the motive, intent, and purpose of the disposition act, and error concerning the disposition act itself, lacking even awareness of the result of disposition, cannot be included in the error referred to in fraud as a matter of interpretation. However, this dissenting opinion is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) It is understandable that fraud is a self-damaging offense and that the deceived person’s act must intervene by nature, but that circumstance alone does not lead to the conclusion that in order for fraud to be established, awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition is necessarily required.\\n\\nThe meaning that fraud is a self-damaging offense is that the deceived person’s act intervenes and the Defendant receives property or acquires pecuniary benefit, and unlike acquisitive offenses such as theft, it means that the victim’s behavior caused by error directly brings about a reduction in the victim’s property and an increase in the Defendant’s or a third party’s property without any criminal intermediary act by the Defendant. However, there is no reason to go so far as to say that, merely because the deceived person’s act intervenes, awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition qualifies as an element of the offense as a criterion distinguishing acquisitive offenses from fraud. The victim’s subjective awareness is only an important factor to consider when determining whether the transfer of property or pecuniary benefit arose as a direct result of an act governed by the victim’s will or as a direct result of the Defendant’s act.\\n\\nEven according to the view that awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition is necessary in fraud, disposition intent is not recognized only when the deceived person accurately recognizes whether the property that became the object of the disposition act is completely separated from his or her own property and attributed to the Defendant or a third party. If fraud were interpreted as requiring perfect and strict disposition intent by the deceived person, then in cases where property is delivered to a person who says he wants to borrow it without any intention of returning it, one would reach the absurd conclusion that fraud never exists because there was no awareness of the result of disposition. Ultimately, in some cases it may be difficult even to specify what “awareness of the result of disposition,” as disposition intent, means. Although the Supreme Court has precedents referring to the deceived person’s subjective awareness of the meaning of a certain disposition act and the result it will bring as awareness of the result of disposition, this should be understood as describing the subjective awareness by the deceived person necessary for fraud to be established in the relevant case. The concept of awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition does not naturally follow from fraud’s essence as a self-damaging offense, nor does it appear to be an effective and appropriate criterion for distinguishing fraud from other offenses.\\n\\n(2) In this respect, the dissenting opinion that if disposition intent is required for the disposition act, awareness of the result of disposition must become an element of fraud is difficult to accept.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion mainly presupposes cases in fraud where the Defendant acquires pecuniary benefit and the deceived person’s disposition act takes the form of an expression of intent or juristic act, and says awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition is necessary. However, it is not clear whether this interpretive theory can be applied as is to fraud in which property is received.\\n\\nGenerally, when the deceived person’s disposition act is the act of delivering property, it is understood that the deceived person’s subjective intent need only comprise awareness of the transfer of possession, and one can hardly find a view that interprets it as requiring the deceived person to accurately recognize the result of the act of delivering property. Yet the Criminal Act expressly identifies the Defendant’s act of deceiving the victim and receiving property as the main type of fraud, and the act of deceiving the victim and acquiring pecuniary benefit is clearly a parallel type of fraud. Property fraud and benefit fraud are not essentially different, and the act of receiving property and the act of acquiring pecuniary benefit are parallel elements of the offense. Even though, in property fraud, the subjective element required for recognizing the victim’s disposition act is sufficient if there is awareness of the act of transferring possession itself, there is no reason whatsoever in benefit fraud to require, as a parallel subjective element, awareness of the result of disposition rather than awareness of the act itself that causes property damage.\\n\\nThe dissenting opinion says that if disposition intent is necessary in fraud, the conclusion that awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition is needed inevitably follows, but the majority opinion has independently interpreted disposition intent and thus has fallen into contradiction. However, beyond objecting to using the term disposition intent for a deceived person’s will without awareness of the result of disposition, it is doubtful that this serves as a justification for concluding that awareness by the deceived person of the result of disposition is an element of the offense. If the point is merely that only awareness of the result of disposition can be referred to as disposition intent, and that awareness of the act itself is necessary as a standard to distinguish the deceived person’s disposition act from unconscious conduct, so that there is no need to call such awareness disposition intent, then the majority opinion can be understood simply as stating the view that such disposition intent, in the limited sense defined by the dissenting opinion, is not necessary.\\n\\n(3) As a result, the deceived person’s error as an element of the offense cannot be limited to matters concerning the motive, intent, or purpose of the disposition act.\\n\\nEven upon repeated review of the elements of fraud under the Criminal Act, one cannot find any part that warrants interpreting the perpetrator’s deception as being limited to matters concerning the motive, intent, or purpose of the disposition act. The Criminal Act takes the Defendant’s conduct as the object of evaluation and defines as fraud the conduct of deceiving another person and thereby receiving property or acquiring pecuniary benefit, with the victim’s disposition act intervening only as a premise for the Defendant’s acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit. Whether the Defendant’s deceptive act that satisfies the elements of fraud concerns the motive, intent, or purpose of the disposition act, or concerns the disposition act itself, it can be evaluated as an act that deceived the victim; and if, as a result, the victim delivered property or engaged in an act causing property damage based on defective intent, and the Defendant thereby received property or acquired pecuniary benefit, there is no reason whatsoever to exclude this from fraud.\\n\\nFraud is established only when the Defendant obtains property or pecuniary benefit by means of the other party’s defective expression of intent, and if the Defendant, through deception, causes the other party to have a defective intent, the circumstances concerning the motive, intent, or purpose of the disposition act are ultimately also deceived. That is, in typical cases where fraud is established, there will naturally be many examples in which the Defendant deceives the victim regarding the motive, intent, or purpose of the victim’s disposition act; but to conclude on that basis that fraud is established only in such cases is an excessive generalization and cannot be adopted.\\n\\nc. The Criminal Act does not prescribe as an element of fraud a disposition act performed by the deceived person while aware of the result of disposition, and the deceived person’s disposition act may be either a factual act or a juristic act. Therefore, so long as the act or omission directly causing property damage is governed by the deceived person’s will who has fallen into error, the subjective element needed to recognize the deceived person’s disposition act is sufficiently awareness of the act itself, and if such awareness is also not recognized, it merely has the negative meaning that it cannot be viewed as the deceived person’s disposition act. It may separately be called disposition intent as a will that does not extend beyond awareness of the act itself accompanying the disposition act, or it may be said that disposition intent is not needed because it is simply subsumed in the disposition act itself. This is merely a difference of classification or nomenclature, and the content intended in substance is not different. However, in fraud, disposition act cannot be understood as requiring even awareness of the result of disposition, and this is the natural consequence of our interpretation of criminal law, which evaluates whether fraud is established from the standpoint of the Defendant’s conduct.\\n\\nWith the above, I state the supplemental opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n8. The supplemental opinion of Justices Kim Yong-deok, Kim So-young, and Park Sang-ok to the dissenting opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. (1) The principle of culpability is the fundamental principle of criminal law, and the principle of private autonomy or self-responsibility is the fundamental principle of civil law. The ideology that runs through these fundamental principles is liberalism, under which a person is bound and bears responsibility for the acts and consequences he or she chooses and performs according to free will. However, in the real world, because one party may be unable to fully realize his or her own true intention due to differences arising from the capability of will or the capability of action between persons, appropriate consideration is given through legal institutions supported by democracy; this is the principle of culpability in its modern sense and the principle of private autonomy or self-responsibility. Ultimately, in legal relations formed by people’s will, an appropriate role and interpretation must be assigned on the basis of such will and legal institutions.\\n\\n(2) In accordance with this principle of culpability, the Criminal Act provides that an act done without awareness of the facts constituting an element of a crime shall not be punished, except where there is a special provision in law (Article 13), while an act done without awareness of facts constituting a specially serious crime shall not be punished as the more serious crime (Article 15(1)), and where, in a crime punishable more severely due to a result, the occurrence of that result could not have been foreseen, it shall not be punished as the more serious crime (Article 15(2)).\\n\\n(3) In property offenses, infringement of legal interests can be divided into the type where the offender’s act unilaterally infringes the victim’s legal interest, as in theft, and the type where the result of infringement arises through the victim’s act, as in fraud. More specifically, the latter can be described as a self-damaging offense in which the infringement of legal interests arises as a result of the victim’s decision to choose and tolerate. The essence of fraud is that the victim’s property damage directly follows from the accepted result of the victim’s property act chosen by a will based on mistaken awareness caused by the offender’s deceptive act, and it is because of the importance of the infringement of freedom of decision through deception that occurs beyond the occurrence of property damage that the Criminal Act punishes fraud more severely than theft. Ultimately, the offender’s deceptive act and acquisition of pecuniary benefit and awareness thereof, and on the other side the victim’s property act made in a state in which freedom of decision was infringed by the deceptive act and the occurrence of property damage as its result, are the domain in which the principle of culpability, the ideological foundation of the state’s punitive power, operates.\\n\\nb. (1) Until now, the Supreme Court has interpreted fraud as being established by deceiving another, causing that person to fall into error, inducing the disposition act, and thereby obtaining property or pecuniary benefit; and has also interpreted the disposition act as a property disposition act requiring, subjectively, that the deceived person have disposition intent, namely awareness of the result of disposition and an intent to realize that result, and, objectively, that there be an act governed by such intent. It further held that an omission whereby the deceived person, by his or her free will, directly engaged in an act causing property damage, or came to omit an act, is a disposition act, thereby, on the premise that it is an act by free will, holding that even an omission not exercising a claim can be a disposition act.\\n\\n(2) And the omission constituting a disposition act here does not mean a mere omission of doing nothing, but rather the so-called improper omission, namely not exercising a certain right that could or should be exercised, such as postponement or waiver of a right, and that can be evaluated as a property disposition act. Therefore, like an act, such omission requires awareness of the result caused by such omission and the will or disposition intent to realize the result by omission; indeed, awareness of and intent concerning such omission of this content can be said to be an essential element distinguishing omission as a disposition act from other simple omissions.\\n\\n(3) Ultimately, the Supreme Court’s interpretation regarding disposition act and disposition intent as its volitional element is based on the above action theory and the essence of fraud, and is proper and should not be changed.\\n\\nc. The majority opinion, with respect to the signature-fraud issue in this case, while stating that disposition act and disposition intent by the deceived person are necessary to recognize fraud, says that if the deceived person has only awareness of performing some act by his or her will, disposition intent is recognized even without awareness of the result the act brings about; and further, by regarding the act of merely signing or sealing without the deceived person’s recognition of the specific content and legal effect of the document as an expression of intent according to the document’s content, it recognizes the disposition act by that expression and explains that disposition intent is recognized so long as the signature or seal itself was made. It does not clearly state in what respect the intent to sign or seal differs from other intent to act as a disposition intent, but it appears to mean that, as a document is prepared by the deceived person’s signature or seal, a defective expression of intent is formed, and that awareness of the signature or seal constitutes awareness of the expression of intent that is the disposition act and thus amounts to disposition intent.\\n\\nHowever, if the meaning of disposition intent in a signature-fraud case is taken as the majority opinion does, then even where there is no internal intent corresponding to the act of preparing or expressing the document, and even in cases where there is no awareness of producing any legal effect at all or where no act of expression can even be recognized, the deceived person’s expression of intent and disposition intent thereto are recognized, and in the end mere signing or sealing of a document is treated as a disposition act. This is difficult to accept because it contradicts the action theory and the essence of fraud requiring a disposition act discussed above.\\n\\nBelow, I examine in detail the various doctrinal problems posed by this new theory of disposition act presented by the majority opinion.\\n\\n(1) When discussing what act the parties performed, one cannot separate that discussion from what the parties’ true intent was. Usually the true intent and external act coincide, but when they do not, the law’s task is how to interpret them and what legal effect to attach. In interpreting expressions of intent under civil law, it is explained that it is proper to interpret based on the intent inferred from the externally manifested act rather than the party’s internal intent; but this is a theory of interpretation concerning cases where the true intent cannot be known. If the true intent can be known, it is not the externally manifested act but the true intent that becomes the content of the expression of intent or juristic act. In other words, intent determines the act and forms the content of the act; one cannot say that intent is deemed to exist merely by virtue of the outward form of the act.\\n\\nNevertheless, the majority opinion explains that even if the deceived person does not accurately recognize the meaning or content of the disposition act, if there is only an intent to perform an act, there can be disposition intent accompanying the disposition act, and on that basis it views that in a signature-fraud case, so long as the signature or seal was made, disposition intent is recognized and there is a disposition act according to the document. However, this disregards the relationship between act and intent, and between disposition act and disposition intent, and avoids the argument required as a premise for recognizing a disposition act, namely disposition intent. It is not only that the deceived person merely intended to prepare a document, yet disposition intent is recognized with respect to the prepared document, which contravenes the essence of action theory; it also amounts to saying that because there is a disposition act, there is disposition intent, thereby committing an error in which act and intent circulate into each other.\\n\\n(2) Moreover, among signature-fraud cases there are situations in which the deceived person has no consciousness of performing an act concerning disposition of rights, that is, no awareness or intent to perform a juristic act in civil-law terms.\\n\\nIf, as a result of error caused by the deceptive act, the deceived person signs a document without any intent to prepare a document having any legal meaning, or signs based on the awareness that he or she is preparing a document entirely unrelated to a juristic act, such as a confirmation letter or petition, and the prepared document states content concerning disposition of rights, the deceived person naturally has no intent to produce the concrete legal effect stated in that document through his or her signature, and has no awareness that any legal effect will arise from his or her act. Where intent concerning the juristic act itself does not exist, it is no different from an act performed without any consciousness, and such an act cannot be regarded as a disposition act.\\n\\nAs will be seen below, in civil-law expressions of intent, error is discussed when internal intent as to effect and the act of expression do not coincide. But even where both the deceived person and the deceiver each had no intent at all to perform any juristic act, it is impossible to import the discussion of error in expressions of intent and say, merely because from the deceived person’s perspective there is a mismatch between internal intent and the content of the document prepared, that a disposition act by the deceived person according to the document’s content occurred between the deceived person and the deceiver, and further that the deceived person had disposition intent regarding it. Moreover, under civil law, if the other party to the expression of intent knew or could have known that the declarant was not acting according to true intent, the expression of intent is void (Article 107(1) of the Civil Act), and a false expression of intent made in collusion with the other party is also void (Article 108(1) of the Civil Act). Yet in a case like this one, where in the process of document preparation neither the deceived person nor the deceiving actor even had awareness or intent to perform the juristic act of creating a mortgage, and the inconsistency is even greater, to treat it merely as an expression of intent by mistake or deception and say only grounds for rescission exist (Articles 109(1) and 110(1) of the Civil Act) is contrary to the system of civil-law rules on expressions of intent and also to equity.\\n\\nAnd until now, the Supreme Court has held that if a person who received an item under the pretense of intending to purchase it later absconds while keeping the item, this constitutes theft; and similarly treated cases where a person drove a motorcycle outside a store under the pretext of a test drive and fled (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decisions 1994. 8. 12. rendered 94DO1487, 2009. 6. 11. rendered 2009DO3139). This appears to mean that, notwithstanding the outward appearance of delivery/use of the item, there is no substantive disposition act transferring possessory control, and the act did not intend such legal effect. There is no meaningful difference between that and the present case, where a document was simply prepared without any substantive juristic act between the deceiver and the victim and without intent to produce legal effect. If one recognizes disposition act and disposition intent based solely on the outward form of document preparation by signature or seal or the result using that document, then in the motorcycle test-drive case one would likewise have to recognize the corresponding disposition act and disposition intent, leading to a conclusion that fraud is established and thereby contradicting established precedents.\\n\\nUltimately, to deem that, even though there was no awareness or intent at all concerning disposition that produces legal effect, disposition act and disposition intent accompanying it exist merely because a document was signed, is to presume the existence of non-existent awareness or intent and a disposition act, which exceeds the limits of interpretation regarding disposition act.\\n\\n(3) Furthermore, the majority opinion, regarding whether the act of signing in a signature-fraud case constitutes a disposition act, develops its reasoning based on civil-law interpretation of expressions of intent—namely that the expression of intent containing content producing an effect different from internal intent is manifested in the disposition document. But it is doubtful whether it is proper to explain the criminal-law disposition act, which serves as the criterion for determining whether fraud is established, by resorting to civil-law interpretation of expressions of intent or juristic acts. In addition, the majority opinion’s logic, which evaluates the act of signing or sealing a document itself as a property disposition act as an expression of intent according to the document’s content and deems disposition intent to exist, confuses the act of preparing the document with the expression of intent and is difficult to regard as proper.\\n\\n(a) In civil law, an expression of intent is the external manifestation by the declarant of intent as to effect, and there is no limitation on the method. Documents such as contracts are means prepared to make such expressions of intent or juristic acts clear, and the preparation itself is a factual act; through the preparation of such document, the content of the expression of intent formed between the parties constitutes the juristic act. This is why, when there are differing views among the parties over the interpretation of a contract and the interpretation of a party’s intent as expressed in a disposition document becomes an issue, it is explained that the contents of the wording, the motive and circumstances under which the agreement was made, the purpose sought to be achieved by the agreement, and the parties’ true intent, etc. must be comprehensively considered and reasonably interpreted according to logic and rules of experience. Merely because something is written in a document does not mean that it can immediately be deemed an externally manifested expression of intent.\\n\\nTherefore, while the preparation of a document may be strong evidence that an expression of intent or juristic act occurred, it cannot be said that, even in the absence of a corresponding expression of intent, the expression of intent is deemed to exist merely because a document was prepared. For example, if a father who prepared a document has not decided whether to make a gift to his son and merely prepared a gift contract, that cannot be called a juristic act; nor can it be said that there was a gift juristic act between father and son even if, in the process of moving, the document’s possession was transferred to the son; and even if the son used deceptive means in the process of transferring possession of the document, there is no change in the nonexistence of the juristic act.
