That is, it is not the fact of document preparation itself, but the substantive intent of the document preparer to produce the same legal effect as the content of the prepared document, that forms the expression of intent; and document preparation without such intent is nothing more than the factual act of preparing papers.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court views obtaining a signature by fraud as forgery. Since forgery means preparation contrary to the will of the person in whose name the document is prepared, viewing a document prepared by fraudulent obtaining of signature as forgery means that, although the nominal author signed the document, the document or the content contained therein was prepared contrary to the nominal author’s will. Ultimately, despite the signature, the content contained in the document is not the nominal author’s will, and no expression of intent or juristic act according to the document’s content has been made; nor can one say, merely because the document was prepared, that an expression of intent or disposition act according to that content occurred.\\n\\n(b) An act of expression necessary for the formation of an expression of intent is recognized to exist when there is an external act from which the declarant’s intent as to effect can be inferred.\\n\\nIn a case such as this one, where the perpetrator fraudulently obtains the deceived person’s signature, then uses the mortgage contract form in the deceived person’s name to establish a mortgage in favor of a third party and borrow money, in order for the perpetrator’s act to constitute fraud in which the deceived person is the victim of fraudulent obtaining of mortgage or corresponding pecuniary benefit, it is of course necessary that there be the deceived person’s property disposition act or expression of intent establishing a mortgage in favor of the third party, who is a third person.\\n\\nHowever, where the recipient of the expression of intent or property disposition act is a third party rather than the deceiving actor, the act of preparing a document between the deceiving actor and the deceived person alone cannot be regarded as an expression of intent to dispose of property toward the third party or as a disposition act toward the third party; rather, it appears that the disposition act toward the third party is carried out not by the deceived person but by the deceiving actor. Further, if one were to regard the deceiving actor’s use of the prepared document to establish a mortgage in favor of the third party as an expression of intent by the deceived person to establish the mortgage, there must be authorization from the deceived person regarding the deceiving actor’s expression of intent or contract for mortgage establishment on behalf of the deceived person; absent such authorization, this is merely an unauthorized agency or unauthorized representation by the deceiving actor. Therefore, the act of establishing a mortgage done without such authorization can by no means be regarded as a disposition act of the deceived person carried out by the deceived person’s disposition intent. Nevertheless, the majority opinion appears to recognize fraud by fraudulent obtaining of a mortgage in such a case, which is difficult to accept.\\n\\nAnd under the majority opinion, if one recognizes the deceived person’s disposition act, that disposition act can only be the deceived person’s document preparation itself; yet it is unclear whether, if the deceiving actor fraudulently obtained the signature but did not deliver the document to a third party, the deceived person’s disposition act is recognized and fraud immediately established, or whether only when the document is delivered to the third party is the disposition act recognized and fraud established, or whether the fraudulent act of document preparation merely constitutes commencement of fraud and fraud reaches consummation only upon concluding the mortgage contract with the third party and borrowing money or completing mortgage registration. This problem exists because there was no act by the deceived person other than document preparation, and because acts arbitrarily performed by the deceiving actor after preparation of the document cannot be regarded as the deceived person’s act.\\n\\nUltimately, the majority opinion’s recognition of the disposition act by characterizing the document as having been externally expressed in conformity with its content merely by its preparation alone appears to have misplaced the direction of its argument by, in prioritizing the need to punish signature fraud, overlooking the process of formation of the expression of intent and failing properly to examine the acts after document preparation.\\n\\n(c) Furthermore, the Supreme Court has held in civil cases that an expression of intent by fraud means a case where, as a result of being brought into error by another’s deceptive act, a person makes some expression of intent; accordingly, there is no mismatch between intent and expression there, but merely an error in the process of formation of intent, namely a mistake in the motive for the expression of intent, and in this respect it is distinguished from an expression of intent by mistake in the proper sense. Thus, in cases such as this one where the person intended to sign or seal a disposition document but, while in a state of error, signed or sealed a writing whose content produces a legal effect different from his or her own intent, thereby causing the internal intent as to effect and the manifested intent as to effect not to coincide, the Court has held that even if the error arose by a third party’s deceptive act, the law on expressions of intent by fraud should not be applied; instead, the law on expressions of intent by mistake should be applied (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005. 5. 27. rendered 2004DA43824).\\n\\nThis Supreme Court decision clarified that, by distinguishing between document preparation by deception and expression of intent by deception, mere document preparation cannot be said to imply the intent to perform the juristic act corresponding to the document’s content; in this respect it corresponds to criminal precedents denying disposition intent regarding signature fraud. And that Supreme Court decision recognized the above signature fraud as civil-law mistake. Since civil-law mistake refers to the absence of internal intent or intent as to effect and inconsistency with the act of expression, even if civil-law mistake is recognized, the premise that there is no disposition intent corresponding to the externally manifested result remains unchanged.\\n\\nThus, if, despite the absence of internal intent corresponding to the deceived person’s external act of expression, one recognizes, as the majority opinion does, that the content externally manifested was brought about by the deceived person’s will and thereby affirms the establishment of fraud, this results in the unreasonable consequence that conduct that is merely mistake and not fraud in civil relations is treated as fraud in criminal law, and leads to an irrational conclusion inconsistent with the Supreme Court’s existing interpretation concerning expressions of intent.\\n\\nd. Meanwhile, the majority opinion states that the deceived person’s disposition intent, unlike the perpetrator’s intent, has no relation to the principle of culpability and is merely a subjective element of the disposition act; therefore, while the object of awareness for the perpetrator’s intent comprises all elements constituting fraud, the object of awareness for the deceived person’s disposition intent is limited to the disposition act itself among the elements constituting fraud. We therefore examine whether, as the majority opinion says, the perpetrator’s intent and the victim’s disposition act are truly separate from each other.\\n\\n(1) Under the principle of culpability, the main clause of Article 13 of the Criminal Act provides that an act done without awareness of the facts constituting an offense shall not be punished. According to this principle of culpability, since Article 347(1) of the Criminal Act provides that fraud is established when a person deceives another and thereby receives delivery of property or acquires pecuniary benefit, the perpetrator of fraud must have awareness, in addition to the deceptive act, that he or she receives delivery of property or acquires pecuniary benefit, i.e., awareness of obtaining property.\\n\\n(2) In a signature-fraud case, we examine the perpetrator’s intent. The Defendant and Nonindicted Person 1, etc., deceived the landowner by saying that the documents were necessary for land transaction permission, had the landowner sign and seal mortgage contract forms, received the owner’s seal certificate, and used them to establish mortgages over each parcel in favor of lenders, etc. and borrowed money in a series of acts. The point at which the Defendant, etc. becomes aware that he or she is obtaining property through such a series of acts can be said to be when the money in the form of borrowed funds is obtained.\\n\\nAt the earlier stage, the mortgage contract forms, etc. signed and sealed by the landowner and obtained by the Defendant, etc. are merely a means to obtain the borrowed funds and are not property in themselves. If so, with respect to the act of obtaining signatures and seals on the mortgage contract forms, etc., the Defendant, etc. had no awareness of obtaining property, which is an element constituting the offense; and there is no significant difference from the awareness of receiving a signature on a transfer-registration document, as in the seal-fraud case discussed below, or the awareness of receiving a seal for the preparation of a transfer-registration document.\\n\\n(3) However, the Defendant, etc. used two deceptive acts, not one, in this series of processes. The first deceptive act was directed toward the person signing and sealing the mortgage contract form; the second deceptive act was directed toward the person who would deliver the borrowed funds. As to the latter act of obtaining borrowed funds by deception, the majority opinion also appears, leaving aside issues of proof, to accept it as fraud, so we will develop the discussion limited to the former.\\n\\n(a) Compare the former deceptive act with stratagem theft. If, at a jewelry store, the perpetrator drops a gold necklace on the floor from the display case, then picks it up while saying it was his own and the owner, believing that, leaves it alone so he takes it away, it would be difficult to call this fraud. It can also be viewed from the standpoint of the victim’s disposition act, but even from the standpoint of the perpetrator’s intent, the perpetrator has only an intent to steal, not an intent to defraud.\\n\\n(b) However, if, at a jewelry store, the perpetrator pretends to be a gold trader, tells the owner that the purity of the gold for sale is only 30%, manipulates a machine measuring purity, and thereby makes the owner believe it, then purchases the gold by paying only 30% of the market price, this would be fraud. Again, it can be viewed from the standpoint of the victim’s disposition act, but it is also fraud from the standpoint of the perpetrator’s intent.\\n\\n(c) The former deceptive act is very similar to stratagem theft, as the dissenting opinion has repeatedly discussed. Just as in the seal-fraud case the Supreme Court did not regard it as fraud but instead treated it as document forgery where a document was completed by using a fraudulently obtained seal, if one fraudulently obtains a signature on a document of unclear extent as to how much of the mortgage contract form has been completed and then completes the mortgage contract form, this is merely document forgery. Looking from the standpoint of the perpetrator’s intent, the perpetrator did not so much obtain property as obtain the nominal author’s signature and seal by exploiting that person’s mistaken belief, and thus had only the intent to forge a document; moreover, he or she had only the intent to use it as a means for subsequent fraud.\\n\\n(d) In the past, the Supreme Court, from such a standpoint, held that if a person, though having purchased only part of the total land area, intended to obtain registration for the entire land and therefore told the registered owner that the seal was needed for registration of the partial area and thus received a seal on the transfer-registration document for the entire land, then, since the nominal owner who prepared the document was mistaken as to its content and the seal was obtained by using that mistake, a document different in content from the intent of the nominal author was prepared, and this fell under forgery of private document (see Supreme Court Decision 1970. 9. 29. rendered 70DO1759). On the same basis, the Court also held that even if the perpetrator deceived the victim as to the true purpose and received the victim’s seal, prepared the relevant documents necessary for ownership transfer registration for the real property, and completed ownership transfer registration in that name, there was no disposition act by the victim, and that the acquittal on fraud charges was correct if the perpetrator did not have the intent to obtain the seal, which is property (see Supreme Court Decision 1990. 2. 27. rendered 89DO335).\\n\\n(4) We examine the case where borrowed funds were not actually obtained in the signature-fraud case. If the perpetrator tried to obtain the signature and seal of the nominal author of the mortgage contract form by deception but the nominal author noticed it and did not sign, it would be attempted fraud according to the majority view. But as noted above, what the perpetrator sought through the nominal author of the mortgage contract form was not property or pecuniary benefit, but merely the signature and seal of the nominal author on the mortgage contract form, and the perpetrator failed in trying to obtain that. The perpetrator intended to use this as a means of fraud to obtain money from the holder of the loan funds, and awareness of this part can be said to be the intent that recognizes the facts constituting obtaining property in fraud. Therefore, the perpetrator merely commenced execution of document forgery and failed to complete it, which accords with the Supreme Court’s stance on document forgery discussed above.\\n\\nIf, after fraudulently obtaining a signature and seal and then completing mortgage registration, the lender, upon checking with the nominal author, ceased lending and no loan funds were delivered, under the majority opinion, one may wonder whether the act of creating the security interest was completed and pecuniary benefit obtained, so that fraud was consummated. Under the dissenting opinion, there is no particular doubt, because one can regard the document forgery as consummated and the fraud as attempted. Going one step further, if the perpetrator and the lender are accomplices, and after fraudulently obtaining the signature and seal, the perpetrator merely created the appearance of completing mortgage registration and borrowing money but no actual loan was made, and if a false lender, under the pretext of a mortgage, received money from the signer in the name of repayment of a loan by pretending to cancel the mortgage registration, one wonders whether, as the majority opinion holds, the signing and sealing act can be regarded as a disposition act. Again, under the dissenting opinion, there is no particular doubt in recognizing the establishment of document forgery and fraud.\\n\\n(5) We examine the accomplice relationship in the signature-fraud case. Suppose there is an accomplice who only recognized and was involved in obtaining the signature and seal, and did not recognize the result of obtaining the borrowed funds, and another accomplice who knew the entire scheme, and after obtaining the signature and seal on the mortgage contract form, the perpetrators were arrested or otherwise failed to reach the point of obtaining the borrowed funds. According to the dissenting opinion, accomplice liability for document forgery can be recognized, but according to the majority opinion, it is unclear whether they are accomplices to document forgery, accomplices to attempted fraud, or whether one must distinguish between them, with one being document forgery and the other attempted fraud.\\n\\n(6) We have examined the perpetrator’s intent from various perspectives, and there is no choice but to wonder whether the intent described by the majority opinion accords with the principle of culpability. If one examines the perpetrator’s intent under the principle of culpability, the perpetrator’s intent will be divided into the intent to fraudulently obtain the signature and seal and the intent to fraudulently obtain the loan funds; the former is distinguished as intent to forge a document, and the latter as intent to commit fraud. Nevertheless, the majority opinion views both the former and the latter as intent to commit fraud, and in particular, as to the former, regards the perpetrator’s series of offense plans leading to obtaining the money in the form of borrowed funds as the object of awareness of the perpetrator’s intent, which comprises all elements constituting fraud, thereby moving away from the principle of culpability. Ultimately, insofar as the perpetrator’s intent is viewed under the principle of culpability, awareness of the result of transfer of property also becomes necessary in the disposition act, and the perpetrator’s intent and the deceived person’s disposition act become two sides of the same coin.\\n\\ne. In conclusion, just as an act divorced from intent is meaningless, there can be no disposition act existing independently and separately from disposition intent, and one cannot recognize an intent to dispose of property or a disposition act in a deceived person who does not even know whether he or she disposed of property. If there is no awareness between the perpetrator and the person performing the disposition act that property is to be transferred and received, the perpetrator lacks awareness of receipt of property or acquisition of pecuniary benefit, which are elements of fraud, and the person performing the disposition act lacks awareness of the disposition act, and thus it cannot amount to fraud. However, while the majority opinion presupposes that disposition act and disposition intent are necessary in connection with fraudulent obtaining of a signature on a document, it recognizes the disposition act by treating the result of document preparation, which is unrelated to and rather contrary to the deceived person’s internal awareness regarding concrete results, as being based on the deceived person’s own intent, namely disposition intent, and this cannot be supported because it contradicts the legal doctrine based on action theory consistently stated in the Supreme Court’s precedents and the essence of fraud. It also cannot be supported because it contradicts the principle of culpability, which states that acts without awareness of the facts constituting an offense, namely acts without intent, shall not be punished.\\n\\nWith the above, I state the supplemental opinion to the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n9. Justice Cho Hee-dae’s supplemental opinion to the dissenting opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. The so-called “signature fraud” issue in this case is a case where, due to a deceptive act, the deceived person signs or seals a document contrary to his or her internal intent, and the perpetrator thereby acquires pecuniary benefit according to mortgage registration.\\n\\nb. For fraud to be established, there must be the perpetrator’s deceptive act, the deceived person’s error and the ensuing disposition act, and the perpetrator’s acquisition of property or pecuniary benefit, and a sequential causal relationship must exist among them. In particular, in fraud, the disposition act serves to distinguish fraud, which is essentially characterized by obtaining property through the victim’s act, from theft, in which the perpetrator acquires property by taking it away without relying on the victim’s act. With respect to such disposition act, the Supreme Court has heretofore held that, subjectively, the deceived person must have disposition intent, namely awareness of the result of disposition, and objectively, there must be an act governed by such intent.\\n\\nc. However, the majority opinion states that, even if the deceived person did not recognize the meaning or content of the disposition act, if the deceived person’s act or omission is assessed as a property disposition act that directly causes property damage, and if such act or omission was done with the deceived person’s awareness, disposition intent corresponding to the disposition act is recognized, and it is not necessary for the deceived person to recognize even the result of his or her own act or omission in order for disposition intent to be recognized. Accordingly, in a signature-fraud case such as this one, ① if the deceived person, as a result of falling into error due to the perpetrator’s deceptive act, signs or seals a disposition document containing content that produces an effect different from his or her internal intent, and property damage according to the content of the disposition document thereby results, the deceived person’s act of signing or sealing such disposition document constitutes the disposition act referred to in fraud; and ② further, even if the deceived person did not yet recognize the result of disposition, namely the specific content of the document and its legal effect, as long as he or she had awareness of the act of signing or sealing the disposition document by personally signing or sealing some document, the deceived person’s disposition intent is also recognized.\\n\\nIn addition to the points already stated in the dissenting opinion, there are many problems with this majority opinion, and they are examined below.\\n\\n(1) The majority opinion appears to mean that if the deceived person, with awareness of personally signing or sealing some document, signed or sealed it, and the document includes disposition content causing property damage, then even if the deceived person did not recognize the specific content and legal effect of the document, the deceived person’s disposition act and disposition intent are recognized.\\n\\nHowever, this commits the error of grasping, under criminal law, act and intent solely by external result, entirely ignoring the content of awareness, and cannot possibly be accepted.\\n\\n(2) The majority opinion appears to regard the deceived person’s act of signing or sealing some document as the disposition act.\\n\\nHowever, in fraud, a disposition act means an act that causes property to be delivered to the perpetrator, etc. or directly causes acquisition of pecuniary benefit.\\n\\nFor example, in a signature-fraud case, if a signature is fraudulently obtained on a disposition document stating an expression of intent to waive a debt, the expression of intent confirmed through the disposition document alone may directly result in acquisition of pecuniary benefit, so this may be regarded as the disposition act the majority opinion refers to.\\n\\nBy contrast, if a signature is fraudulently obtained on a mortgage contract form, under the Civil Act, the transfer, creation, or change of real rights in rem due to juristic acts concerning real property takes effect only upon registration and not merely by the parties’ expression of intent; this is the principle of formality of establishment (Article 186 of the Civil Act). Therefore, even if one adopts the view that both the obligational act and the real-right expression of intent are made together, the mere preparation of a mortgage contract form does not produce the effect of real-right transfer, and acquisition of pecuniary benefit becomes possible only by preparing the documents necessary for registration and completing the registration. Thus, the fact alone that a disposition document containing a transfer of property was prepared by the deceived person’s signing or sealing, and that externally perceivable obligatory or real-right expression of intent is thereby recognized, is separate from whether that act may constitute forgery of private document or fraud by fraudulently obtaining a document; but it is difficult to assess this as a criminal-law disposition act directly causing the result of acquisition of pecuniary benefit. In other words, the deceived person’s act of signing or sealing some document whose contents the person does not know can only be viewed as the act of preparing a document containing a dispositive expression of intent, even if the document is a mortgage contract form as a disposition document; it cannot be viewed as a criminal-law disposition act that directly causes the perpetrator, etc. to obtain property damage equivalent to the value of the security through completion of mortgage registration.\\n\\n(3) The majority opinion appears to assume that disposition intent is necessary, and that disposition intent must be an intent corresponding to the disposition act.\\n\\nHowever, even if one views the act of preparing a disposition document rather than establishing a mortgage as the disposition act, as the majority opinion states, at minimum there must be awareness corresponding to the content of the disposition document in order to have disposition intent; yet the majority opinion says that disposition intent exists when there is no intent corresponding to the content of the disposition document and merely awareness of signing or sealing some document, which is difficult to accept logically.\\n\\nAnd, as mentioned in the dissenting opinion, only awareness of the disposition of property and a decision based thereon can be the disposition intent that accords with the essence and characteristics of fraud; only an act pursuant to such intent can be assessed as a disposition act. As a result, in a signature-fraud case where there is no awareness of the content and result of the disposition document, the deceived person’s disposition intent cannot be recognized.\\n\\n(4) While the Criminal Act separately provides for theft and fraud, with respect to fraud it punishes both cases where property is delivered and cases where pecuniary benefit is acquired, whereas in theft the object is limited to property; and it also sets the statutory penalty for fraud far higher than that for theft. Meanwhile, separate provisions punish a person who, apart from fraud, obtains delivery of property or acquires pecuniary benefit by exploiting a minor’s naivety or a person’s mental or physical disability (Article 348 of the Criminal Act). Therefore, disposition act and disposition intent, as elements of fraud that characterize fraud and distinguish it from theft when the object of the property infringement is property, and perform the function of distinguishing punishable fraud from non-punishable theft of benefit when the object is pecuniary benefit, must be strictly interpreted in accordance with the general principles of criminal-law interpretation. In the signature-fraud case at issue, the majority opinion’s logic affirming fraud expansively interprets, or by analogy interprets, the meaning of disposition act and its element disposition intent, in a direction unfavorable to the Defendant, thereby excessively broadening the scope of punishment for fraud; this is not only inconsistent with the structure and content of the Korean Criminal Act concerning fraud and theft, but also contrary to the principle of legality that forms the foundation of the rule of law.\\n\\nd. The majority opinion also does not accord with the recent trend of Supreme Court decisions that strictly interpret criminal-law provisions concerning property offenses.\\n\\nIn relation to breach of trust, the Supreme Court held that the debtor’s duty to carry out the transfer registration procedure for real property according to a security transfer reservation is an ancillary content required of the debtor to secure performance of the debt for repayment, and therefore cannot be regarded as “another’s business” that, based on a relationship of trust in the sense referred to in breach of trust, must protect or manage the creditor’s property (see Supreme Court En Banc Decision 2014. 8. 21. rendered 2014DO3363). Also, in aggravated occupational breach of trust, the risk of property loss that can be assessed as property damage must rise to the level of a concrete and actual risk; a merely vague possibility is insufficient (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2015. 9. 10. rendered 2015DO6745). With respect to embezzlement as well, in light of the fact that the essence of embezzlement lies in unlawfully obtaining another’s property entrusted based on a relationship of trust, it is appropriate to limit the entrustment-trust relationship to one based on trust worthy of protection by embezzlement; thus, in a case involving nominal trust registration in the intermediate omitted registration form in violation of the Act on the Registration of Real Estate under Actual Title Holder’s Name, the Court held that a trustee’s arbitrary disposition of trust real property does not constitute embezzlement (see Supreme Court En Banc Decision 2016. 5. 19. rendered 2014DO6992).\\n\\nThrough such recent decisions, the Supreme Court appears to be forming a line of precedents that, even in cases where criminal punishment seems necessary on the surface and even in cases long punished criminally, excludes them from criminal punishment by strictly interpreting the elements in faithful accordance with the basic principles of interpretation of criminal law. Nevertheless, the majority opinion, relying only on the concrete need for punishment in the individual case, discards without a clear and definite theoretical construction a number of precedents that have been maintained for a long time with rational reasons concerning the interpretation of fraud, and seeks to punish them anew. This is not at all in step with this trend of the Supreme Court, and as a result it is difficult to regard it as desirable, since it causes renewed confusion not only regarding fraud but also regarding the direction of the theory of interpretation of property offenses.\\n\\nWith the above, I state the supplemental opinion to the dissenting opinion."}

{"[2021DO2340]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. As to Defendant 1\\n\\na. Summary of the facts charged and the judgment of the court below\\n\\nThe gist of the facts charged against Defendant 1 is that, around October 17, 2018, at the Seoul Northern District Court, while filing applications for determination of the amount of litigation costs—Case No. 2018KAHWAK240 in relation to Case No. 2017KAHAP253, a case of a provisional injunction prohibiting the holding of an extraordinary general meeting, and Case No. 2018KAHWAK241 in relation to Case No. 2017KAHAP234, a case of a provisional injunction prohibiting an extraordinary general meeting—Defendant 1 entered, in each statement of litigation costs, KRW 5,000,000 in attorney’s fees that had not actually been incurred, despite not having retained an attorney in each of the provisional disposition cases in question, and thereby attempted to obtain, by fraud, the amount equivalent to the litigation costs; however, due to each objection raised by the non-party, Defendant 1 failed to achieve that aim, and each act remained at the attempted stage.\\n\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in its judgment, upheld the first-instance judgment that found all of the facts charged against Defendant 1 guilty.\\n\\nb. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\n1) A judgment allocating litigation costs is limited to confirming the existence of the obligation to reimburse litigation costs and ordering payment thereof, and the specific amount of litigation costs is determined through an order determining the amount of litigation costs under Article 110(1) of the Civil Procedure Act (see Supreme Court Judgment dated Oct. 12, 2006, 2004JAEDA818). A person seeking reimbursement of litigation costs may obtain a writ of execution for an order determining the amount of litigation costs and enforce compulsory execution with respect to the determined amount of litigation costs. Accordingly, an act of deceiving the court by false statements and obtaining an order determining the amount of litigation costs favorable to oneself may constitute fraud. Meanwhile, when applying for an order determining the amount of litigation costs, a statement of costs, a copy thereof, and documents necessary to substantiate the amount of costs must be submitted (Article 110(2) of the Civil Procedure Act); therefore, caution is required before treating as fraud a case in which a party merely asserts an amount of costs different from the actual facts. Among litigation costs, the so-called “court expenses,” such as court fee amounts and civil advance deposits paid to the court by the parties, etc. for conducting litigation or other proceedings, are intended to be calculated based on judgments and case records, etc. preserved by the competent court itself, while the so-called “party expenses” directly paid by a party to a third party for the conduct of litigation, etc. must be substantiated by the applicant (see, e.g., Supreme Court Order dated Dec. 22, 2011, 2011MA1777). Therefore, unless supporting materials, etc. were manipulated or false supporting materials, etc. were submitted, it is difficult to conclude that a mere assertion of an amount of costs different from the actual facts, by itself, amounts to deceiving the court.\\n\\n2) According to the reasoning of the court below and the record, Defendant 1 stated “attorney’s fees: KRW 5,000,000” in the statement of litigation costs attached to each application for determination of the amount of litigation costs in this case, but had never retained an attorney in each of the provisional disposition cases in this case. Also, while submitting each application for determination of the amount of litigation costs in this case, Defendant 1 submitted receipts for the court fee already paid and service fees as supporting materials, but submitted no supporting materials whatsoever regarding attorney’s fees.\\n\\n3) Examining the above factual circumstances in light of the legal principles discussed above, although Defendant 1, despite never having retained an attorney in each of the provisional disposition cases in this case, stated attorney’s fees in the cost item of the statement of litigation costs differently from the facts while filing each application for determination of the amount of litigation costs in this case, Defendant 1 did not manipulate supporting materials or submit false supporting materials in relation thereto; thus, it is difficult to regard Defendant 1’s respective applications for determination of the amount of litigation costs in this case as objectively sufficient to deceive the court, and therefore they cannot be conclusively deemed acts of deception constituting fraud. Nevertheless, the court below, for the reasons stated in its judgment, found all of the facts charged against Defendant 1 guilty; in so doing, the court below erred by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the establishment of fraud in the procedure for determining the amount of litigation costs, thereby affecting the judgment. The ground of appeal asserting this is well-founded.\\n\\n2. As to Defendant 2\\n\\nThe court below found the facts charged against Defendant 2 guilty. Examining the reasons stated in the judgment below in light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, there is no error in the judgment below in that it did not violate the rules of logic and experience, exceed the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or otherwise misunderstand the relevant legal principles.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nWithout examining the remaining grounds of appeal by Defendant 1, we reverse the part of the judgment below concerning Defendant 1 and remand this part of the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and we dismiss the appeal by Defendant 2. Accordingly, the judgment is rendered as follows by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question:
Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (X)? (If there is a dispute, according to case law)

(a) Even where a public official or arbitrator, after receiving an improper solicitation, causes a third party to give a bribe, and the third party, knowing the criminal act of such public official or arbitrator, aids and abets it, the provisions of the General Part of the Criminal Act concerning accomplices apply even if there is no separate penal provision therefor, so the offense of aiding and abetting the acceptance of a bribe by a third party may be recognized. 
(b) Where A, a judicial police officer, was requested by a prosecutor to “hear detailed statements from the victims of a traffic accident regarding the circumstances of the accident and reinvestigate whether driver A fled,” and, in the “reinvestigation results” section of the reinvestigation result report, stated as if he had heard statements from the victims and recorded the contents of those statements although he had not actually heard them, if the victims’ statements were in substance consistent with the facts and the judicial police officer who received the request for reinvestigation had discretion as to whether and how to re-investigate the witnesses or suspects designated by the prosecutor, then the crime of making a false official document is not established against A. 
(c) Where a deposit account opened by an account holder who is not an accomplice to a telecommunication financial fraud offense was used for that offense and the victim remitted or transferred the fraud proceeds into that account, since the account holder is in a position to keep the fraud proceeds for the victim, embezzlement against the victim is established if the account holder withdraws that money with the intent to appropriate it. 
(d) Where A lied to victim A that he would sell a car to the victim, transferred the car while handing over all documents necessary for registration of transfer of ownership, received the purchase price, and then tracked the location of the car with a GPS (GPS) previously attached to the car and stole that car, fraud is established because A had the intent to steal the car again after transferring it and cannot be regarded as having intended to transfer ownership of the car. 
(e) If A, as a chief editorial writer at a media company, is regarded as having considerable influence in the media industry by participating in the direction of editorial writing or writing columns on economic matters, received from B, the representative director of B Company, approximately KRW 40 million for his European trip together with a solicitation to help form favorable public opinion, then the crime of acceptance of a bribe in breach of trust is established against A.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2015DO17452]": "We decide the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. The gist of the fraud count dated 2013. 9. 14. and the special larceny count in the charges of this case is that the Defendant, together with First-instance Co-defendant 2 and others, in fact had neither the intent nor the ability to finally transfer ownership of the Sportage passenger car even if he received the purchase price, but nevertheless lied to Victim Nonparty 1 that he would sell the passenger car and, while transferring the passenger car, defrauded 7,500,000 won of the purchase price, and then, by tracking the location of the passenger car with a GPS device previously attached to the car, stole the passenger car. The gist of the fraud count dated 2013. 9. 16. and the special larceny count dated 2013. 9. 17. is that the Defendant, using the passenger car he had stolen, again deceived Victim Nonparty 2 by the same method and defrauded 7,200,000 won of the purchase price, and stole the passenger car possessed by Victim Nonparty 3. The court below found all of these charges guilty for the reasons stated in its judgment.\\n\\n2. However, the court below’s determination that convicted the fraud counts among these charges is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\na. In the indictment, the Prosecutor asserted, as the basis for the allegation that the Defendant had neither the intent nor the ability to finally transfer ownership of the passenger car to Nonparty 1 or Nonparty 2 even if he received the purchase price, that the owner of the passenger car was Nonparty 4, First-instance Co-defendant 2 merely possessed the passenger car as security for a loan claim, and the Defendant had the intent to defraud the purchase price by transferring the passenger car and then immediately stealing it again.\\n\\nb. According to the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n1) When Nonparty 4 was unable to repay the money borrowed from Nonparty 5, on 2013. 9. 11. he purchased the passenger car with funds borrowed from Hyundai Capital Co., Ltd. and completed registration in his own name, and on 2013. 9. 12. he delivered the passenger car to Nonparty 5 as security for the loan debt, together with all documents necessary for title transfer registration of the passenger car, namely, the automobile registration certificate, the automobile transfer certificate, his own resident registration certificate copy, certificate of seal impression, vehicle renunciation affidavit, power of attorney, and the passbook newly issued in his own name.\\n\\n2) The seal of Nonparty 4 was affixed in the “transferor” section of the automobile transfer certificate, and the vehicle renunciation affidavit states: “If I am unable to repay by the due date, I hereby pledge to renounce the vehicle owned by me and, at the same time, transfer it to the creditor without objection; in selling the above automobile, the installment arrangement shall be borne by the owner himself, and it is agreed that the automobile shall be sold with the certificate of seal impression delivered by me to replace the borrowed money, and, if there is a shortfall, additional payment shall be made.” The power of attorney states: “I hereby delegate to the creditor all authority concerning the transfer of title to the debtor’s vehicle, and confirm that I shall bear all civil and criminal liability arising therefrom.”\\n\\n3) On 2013. 9. 12. Nonparty 5, as security for First-instance Co-defendant 2’s loan debt, handed over to First-instance Co-defendant 2, as they were, the passenger car received from Nonparty 4, all documents necessary for title transfer registration, and Nonparty 4’s passbook.\\n\\n4) The Defendant conspired with First-instance Co-defendant 2 and others to sell the passenger car, receive the purchase price, and then steal the passenger car, and thereafter, when selling the passenger car to Victim Nonparty 1 or Nonparty 2, handed over all documents in the name of Nonparty 4 necessary for title transfer registration of the passenger car.\\n\\nc. In light of the foregoing facts, since Nonparty 4, by providing the passenger car to Nonparty 5 as security for the loan debt and delivering even his passbook in his own name together with all documents necessary for title transfer registration, consented to the disposition of the passenger car, and since there was no legal obstacle whatsoever to Nonparty 1 or Nonparty 2 acquiring ownership of the passenger car, the circumstance that the owner of the passenger car was Nonparty 4 and that First-instance Co-defendant 2 possessed the passenger car as security for the loan claim cannot be the object of deception.\\n\\nd. Although, to acquire ownership after purchasing an automobile, the title transfer registration must be completed, where the purchaser receives from the seller the automobile together with all documents necessary for the title transfer registration, the purchaser can complete the title transfer registration by himself. Since, by delivering the passenger car to Victim Nonparty 1 or Nonparty 2 and handing over all documents necessary for title transfer registration, the Defendant made it possible for Victim Nonparty 1 or Nonparty 2 to complete the title transfer registration of the passenger car at any time, even if the Defendant had an intent to steal it again after transferring the passenger car, this would merely be a criminal plan to produce the same economic effect as defrauding the purchase price by committing a separate offense, and it cannot be said that he had no intent to transfer ownership of the passenger car. Rather, because the Defendant from the outset had the intent to transfer and then steal the passenger car, it is more consistent with transactional common sense to view him as having intended to transfer ownership of the passenger car to Victim Nonparty 1 or Nonparty 2 in the first instance. In addition, even though the Defendant, when selling the passenger car to Victim Nonparty 1 or Nonparty 2, had the intent to steal it again immediately and concealed that intent, this cannot be called deception.\\n\\ne. Ultimately, although there was no deceptive act when the Defendant sold the passenger car to Victim Nonparty 1 or Nonparty 2, the court below’s judgment, which found guilty the fraud count dated 2013. 9. 14. and the fraud count dated 2013. 9. 16. among the charges of this case, contains an error that misapprehended the legal principles concerning the deceptive act in the crime of fraud and affected the conclusion of the judgment.\\n\\n3. The fraud counts dated 2013. 9. 14. and 2013. 9. 16. in the court below’s judgment must be reversed for the foregoing reasons, and since the court below imposed a single sentence on the ground that that part and the remaining guilty portion are in a concurrent offenses relationship under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, the court below’s judgment must ultimately be reversed in its entirety.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds for appeal, we reverse the court below’s judgment and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2016DO19659]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the Defendants’ grounds of appeal\\n\\na. As to the portion of third-party bribery in the alternative count against Defendant 1 and the portion of aiding and abetting third-party bribery in the alternative count against Defendant 2\\n\\n1) Defendants’ common arguments\\n\\n① Argument that the legal doctrine on the specification of the charges was misconstrued\\n\\nThe specification of the charges is sufficient if, in light of the nature of the offense charged, the facts that formed the cause of the indictment are stated to such an extent as to distinguish them from other charges by specifying the time, place, method, purpose, etc.; and even if some parts are somewhat unclear, if the charge can be specified by other matters stated together and thus there is no impediment to the defendant’s exercise of the right of defense, the effectiveness of the indictment is not affected (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on June 25, 1999, 99DO1900, etc.).\\n\\nThe offense of third-party bribery consists in a public official or arbitrator, upon receiving an improper request in relation to his or her duties, causing a bribe to be given to a third party, and such improper request may be made not only by an express manifestation of intent but also by an implied manifestation of intent, and the content of the official act that is the subject of the request need not be specific (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on January 26, 2007, 2004DO1632, etc.). In light of these points, the facts charged for the offense of third-party bribery should be deemed specified if the factual elements of the offense, including the time and place of the offense, are stated so that they are distinguished from other facts and the scope of identity of the charges can be defined, and there is no impediment to the defendant’s exercise of the right of defense; and among such facts, even if the content of the improper request is not stated in detail, it is sufficient if it is specified to the extent that a quid pro quo relationship can be recognized between the public official’s or arbitrator’s duties and the benefit provided to the third party.\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its opinion, the court below determined that the facts charged concerning the portion of third-party bribery in the alternative count against Defendant 1 and the portion of aiding and abetting third-party bribery in the alternative count against Defendant 2 were specified.\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the lower court judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles, the above determination of the lower court is proper. There is no error of misapprehending the legal doctrine on the specification of the charges, as argued in the Defendants’ grounds of appeal.\\n\\n② Argument of factual misunderstanding and misapprehension of law concerning Defendant 1’s third-party bribery act\\n\\nIn the offense of third-party bribery, in order to find that there was an improper request by an implied expression of intent, there must exist, between the parties, a common recognition or understanding that the content of the performance of official duties that is the subject of the request and the benefit provided to the third party is consideration for such performance of duties (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on January 30, 2009, 2008DO6950). Whether there was an improper request must be determined by considering various circumstances, such as the content of the duty or request, the relationship with the person providing the benefit, the extent of the benefit, and the circumstances and timing of receipt; and further, in light of the protection of the fairness of the performance of public duties, the trust of society in such fairness, and the inalienability of official duties, which are the protected legal interests of the offense of bribery, it must also be determined by considering whether the receipt of the benefit caused society at large to doubt the fairness of the performance of official duties (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on January 26, 2007, 2004DO1632).\\n\\nThe court below, by comprehensively considering the matters stated in its opinion, such as the content of Defendant 1’s duties, the relationship between those duties and each of the goods purchasers stated in the lower court’s opinion, the circumstances under which Defendant 1 came to know each of the goods purchasers, the circumstances and method by which the goods purchasers purchased goods through Defendant 1, and the acts of the goods purchasers related to Defendant 1’s duties that were carried out before and after the purchase of goods, found that Defendant 1 had implicitly received an improper request concerning his duties from each of the said goods purchasers. Based on this, the court further found that Defendant 1 had caused each of the said goods purchasers to provide, as a bribe, to Defendant 2, a third party, the status or opportunity to receive an amount equivalent to the profits from the sale of goods, and accordingly found Defendant 1 guilty of the portion of third-party bribery in the alternative count against Defendant 1.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, the above determination of the lower court is proper and persuasive. There is no error, as argued in the Defendants’ grounds of appeal, of violating the rules of logic and empirical rules and thereby exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, or of misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning improper requests, etc. in the offense of third-party bribery.\\n\\n2) Argument that the legal doctrine on aiding and abetting third-party bribery by Defendant 2 was misconstrued\\n\\nIn the offense of third-party bribery, a third party means a person other than the principal offender and a co-principal, and it may include an instigator or aider and abettor. Therefore, even if a public official or arbitrator, upon receiving an improper request, causes a third party to receive a bribe and the third party, knowing of such public official’s or arbitrator’s criminal act, aids and abets it, the provisions on aiding and abetting under the General Provisions of the Criminal Act apply even if there is no separate penal provision therefor, and the offense of aiding and abetting third-party bribery may be established.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, it is proper that the court below found Defendant 2 guilty of the portion of aiding and abetting third-party bribery in the alternative count against Defendant 2 for the reasons stated in its opinion. There is no error, as argued in Defendant 2’s grounds of appeal, of misapprehending the legal doctrine on the offense of aiding and abetting third-party bribery.\\n\\nb. As to violation of the Act on the Regulation and Punishment of Criminal Proceeds Concealment, etc. in the alternative counts against the Defendants\\n\\n1) The Act on the Regulation and Punishment of Criminal Proceeds Concealment, etc. (hereinafter the “Criminal Proceeds Concealment Regulation Act” or simply the “Act”) punishes acts that disguise facts concerning the acquisition of criminal proceeds, etc. (Article 3(1)1). Here, “acts that disguise facts concerning acquisition” means acts that disguise facts concerning the cause of acquisition as if lawfully acquired, or acts that disguise facts concerning attribution as if not attributed (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 4, 2014, 2014DO4408). In addition, “criminal proceeds, etc.,” which are the subject of acts disguising acquisition, are defined as ① criminal proceeds, ② property derived from criminal proceeds, or ③ property in which the above properties and other property are combined (Article 2(4)). Therefore, even if facts concerning the acquisition of profits related to criminal acts are disguised, there is no punishable act unless such profits constitute “criminal proceeds, etc.” that are subject to the Act.\\n\\nMeanwhile, “criminal proceeds” as used in the Act (the above ①) are of two kinds (Article 2(2)). First, they are “property generated by criminal acts constituting serious crimes, or property obtained as remuneration for the criminal acts” prescribed in the [Appendix] to the Act [Article 2(2)(a)] [hereinafter collectively referred to as “criminal proceeds under subparagraph (a)”], and second, they are “funds or property related to” the offenses listed in Article 2(2)(b) of the Act [Article 2(2)(b)]. And “property derived from criminal proceeds” (the above ②) is defined as “property obtained as fruits of criminal proceeds, property obtained as consideration for criminal proceeds, property obtained as consideration for such property, and, in addition, property obtained by holding or disposing of criminal proceeds” (Article 2(3)).\\n\\nTaking into account the content of these provisions, in particular the fact that Article 2(2) of the Act divides “criminal proceeds” into two categories and states subparagraph (a) as “property generated by” the criminal acts of the above serious crimes or “property obtained as remuneration for” the criminal acts, whereas subparagraph (b) states “funds or property related to” the offenses listed therein, and the fact that Article 2(3) of the Act, premised on the above concept of “criminal proceeds” in Article 2(2), defines property obtained as “consideration for” such criminal proceeds or property obtained by “holding” criminal proceeds as “property derived from criminal proceeds,” thereby distinguishing it from “criminal proceeds,” it should be understood that the above “criminal proceeds under subparagraph (a)” include property newly created by the criminal act of a serious crime, property directly acquired through that criminal act, or property acquired as direct consideration for that criminal act (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on December 10, 2004, 2004DO5652), but do not include property merely related to such criminal act or property secondarily obtained by holding or disposing of criminal proceeds.\\n\\n2) The gist of the alternative count concerning violation of the Criminal Proceeds Concealment Regulation Act against the Defendants is that the Defendants conspired together, and that Defendant 1, from around February 2010 to around March 2013, upon receiving an improper request in relation to his duties, caused architects, civil engineers, construction site managers, etc. in Icheon City (hereinafter referred to as “the architects, etc. in this case”), as stated in the attached schedule of offenses in the lower court’s judgment, to give Defendant 2, on 86 occasions, bribes equivalent to the amount of gains from the sale of goods totaling KRW 66,485,000 (equivalent to KRW 19,945,000), and that Defendant 2, by receiving the payments into an account in the name of Non-indicted Person 1, which he had received from an acquaintance, disguised facts concerning the acquisition of criminal proceeds.\\n\\nAccording to the above facts charged, the Prosecutor regarded the gains equivalent to KRW 19,945,000 obtained by Defendant 2 through the sale of goods to the architects, etc. in this case as “criminal proceeds under subparagraph (a)” arising from Defendant 1’s offense of third-party bribery and Defendant 2’s offense of aiding and abetting third-party bribery, and indicted Defendant 2 on the ground that the act of receiving, into an account in the name of a third party, Non-indicted Person 1, the sale proceeds constituting the source of those gains was an act that disguised facts concerning the acquisition of criminal proceeds.\\n\\n3) However, as noted above, the facts constituting the offense of third-party bribery against Defendant 1, which the court below found guilty, are that Defendant 1, having received an improper request, caused each of the goods purchasers stated in the lower court’s opinion, including the architects, etc. in this case, to purchase the goods sold by Defendant 2 and to pay the price into an account in the name of Non-indicted Person 1, thereby causing Defendant 2 to provide, as a bribe, the status or opportunity to receive an amount equivalent to the gains from the sale of goods. And the facts constituting the offense by Defendant 2 are that he aided and abetted the above criminal act of Defendant 1.\\n\\nWhen the content of such facts constituting the offense is viewed in light of the legal principles noted above, the “criminal proceeds under subparagraph (a)” arising from the Defendants’ above criminal acts are the intangible benefit of “the status or opportunity to receive an amount equivalent to the gains from the sale of goods,” which was provided as a bribe to Defendant 2, and there was no act of disguise with respect to the acquisition of such status or opportunity. In addition, according to the record, the sale gains received by Defendant 2 were merely a separate consideration, paid once a month according to sales performance, based on a sales employee contract concluded with Non-indicted Person 2, after the full amount of the goods sale price was deposited into Non-indicted Person 2, and were not themselves the “criminal proceeds under subparagraph (a)” arising from Defendant 1’s offense of third-party bribery or Defendant 2’s offense of aiding and abetting it. Ultimately, neither the goods sale price paid by the architects, etc. in this case nor the sale gains paid to Defendant 2 on that basis constitute the above “criminal proceeds under subparagraph (a),” that is, “property generated by criminal acts or property obtained as remuneration for criminal acts.” Therefore, even if the Defendants caused the above goods sale price to be paid into an account in the name of Non-indicted Person 1, a third party, it cannot be said that this constitutes an act of disguising acquisition with respect to the above “criminal proceeds under subparagraph (a),” as alleged in the indictment.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below found this part of the charges guilty for the reasons stated in its opinion, and in doing so it erred by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the offense of violation of Article 3(1)1 of the Criminal Proceeds Concealment Regulation Act. The Defendants’ ground of appeal pointing out this issue is well-founded.\\n\\nc. As to the portion concerning third-party bribery and abuse of authority to obstruct the exercise of rights in relation to ○○ Engineering against Defendant 1\\n\\n1) Argument of factual misunderstanding and misapprehension of law concerning the act constituting the offense\\n\\nWhether a public official’s act of introducing or recommending a third party as a contracting party to a person related to his duties constitutes an act of causing the third party to provide an improper benefit in relation to official duties must be determined by comprehensively considering various circumstances, such as the circumstances leading to the introduction or recommendation, the content of the benefit that the third party obtains through the introduction or recommendation and the degree of the public official’s recognition thereof, whether the public official expected a benefit in relation to the introduction or recommendation, the content of the public official’s official acts after the introduction or recommendation, and the relationship between the public official and the person related to the duties or the third party (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on September 4, 2014, 2011DO14482).\\n\\nIn the offense of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights, “abuse of authority” means a public official’s unlawful exercise of matters within his or her general authority, that is, although it appears formally and externally to be performance of official duties, its substance is an act beyond legitimate authority; and “causing a person to do an act not required by duty” means causing a person to do an act for which there is no duty under statutes (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on February 10, 2011, 2010DO13766, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below, taking into account the circumstances stated in its opinion, such as that Defendant 1, as a public official in charge of building-related civil petitions in Icheon City, told Non-indicted Person 3, who was carrying out an apartment development project in Icheon City, that his business was not a local company and that the licensing and permitting procedure might be delayed without giving any specific explanation for the reason; that Defendant 1 directly handed Non-indicted Person 3 the business card of Non-indicted Person 4, the operator of only one company, ○○ Engineering, as the counterparty for concluding a service contract; that Non-indicted Person 3 learned of ○○ Engineering and Non-indicted Person 4 for the first time at that time; that Non-indicted Person 3 visited the office of ○○ Engineering and met Non-indicted Person 4 and concluded a service contract at a somewhat high price; and that Defendant 1 also involved himself in the performance process of the said service contract, found that the portion of third-party bribery and abuse of authority to obstruct the exercise of rights in relation to ○○ Engineering among the facts charged against Defendant 1 was all established.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, the above determination of the lower court is proper. There is no error, as argued in Defendant 1’s grounds of appeal, of violating the rules of logic and empirical rules and thereby exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, or of misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the offense of third-party bribery or abuse of authority to obstruct the exercise of rights.\\n\\n2) Argument of misapprehension of law concerning the compatibility and the number of offenses of third-party bribery and abuse of authority to obstruct the exercise of rights\\n\\nWhere a public official demands that a person related to his duties conclude a contract with a third party and thereby causes the contract to be concluded, if such act falls under both the elements of the offense of third-party bribery and the elements of the offense of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights, then both offenses are established separately; however, since, in social terms, one act constitutes several offenses, the two offenses are in a relation of ideal concurrence under Article 40 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles, it is proper that the court below found Defendant 1 guilty of both the third-party bribery and the abuse of authority to obstruct the exercise of rights in relation to ○○ Engineering among the facts charged against Defendant 1. There is no error, as argued in Defendant 1’s grounds of appeal, of misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the compatibility of the offense of third-party bribery and the offense of abuse of authority to obstruct the exercise of rights.\\n\\nHowever, the court below erred in misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the number of offenses in determining that the above two offenses are in a relation of concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act. Yet, the court below, having regarded the above two offenses against Defendant 1 and the other offenses such as the respective offenses of third-party bribery against the goods purchasers, including the architects, etc. in this case, as concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, imposed the sentence to be imposed by aggravating the punishment prescribed for the most serious offense among them; therefore, the range of the sentence to be imposed is ultimately the same as in the case where the above two offenses are viewed as being in a relation of ideal concurrence. Accordingly, it is difficult to say that the above error in the court below’s assessment of the number of offenses affected the result of the judgment (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on April 9, 1974, 73DO2334, etc.). Defendant 1’s ground of appeal on this point is not accepted.\\n\\nd. As to abuse of authority to obstruct the exercise of rights in relation to Non-indicted Person 5 against Defendant 1\\n\\nEven if a public official causes a staff member to perform a factual act assisting the execution of official duties with respect to matters within the scope of the public official’s own authority, this merely results in the execution of the public official’s own duties, and thus, in principle, cannot be said to constitute “causing a person to do an act not required by duty” within the offense of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights. However, if the standards and procedures for the execution of official duties are specifically prescribed by statutes, and the staff member is also granted an inherent authority and role to apply those standards and participate in the procedures, then causing the staff member to assist in the execution of official duties in violation of such standards and procedures constitutes “causing a person to do an act not required by duty” (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on February 10, 2011, 2010DO13766).\\n\\nThe court below found Defendant 1 guilty of the portion of abuse of authority to obstruct the exercise of rights in relation to Non-indicted Person 5, taking into account the circumstances stated in its opinion, such as the scope of Non-indicted Person 5’s duties, the circumstances under which Defendant 1 ordered Non-indicted Person 5 to carry out the procedures for the approval for use of the multi-family housing on the land at Icheon City, address omitted, and the attitude Defendant 1 took until such procedures were carried out.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, the above determination of the lower court is proper. There is no error, as argued in Defendant 1’s grounds of appeal, of violating the rules of logic and empirical rules and thereby exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, or of misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the offense of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Prosecutor’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. The finding of facts and, as a premise thereof, the selection and evaluation of evidence belong to the exclusive authority of the trier of fact, so long as they do not exceed the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, and the court of final appeal is also bound thereby. In a criminal trial, the finding of the facts constituting the offense must be based on strict evidence having probative force sufficient to convince the judge beyond a reasonable doubt. If the Prosecutor’s proof does not reach the level to give such conviction, then even if there is some room for suspicion of guilt, the matter must be decided in favor of the defendant.\\n\\nb. The court below, for the reasons stated in its opinion, found the Defendant 1’s bribery charge relating to Non-indicted Person 6, the third-party bribery and abuse of authority to obstruct the exercise of rights charge relating to Non-indicted Company 7, and the dereliction of duty charge not proven, and thus acquitted the defendant of those charges.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the record, all of the above determinations of the lower court are proper and persuasive. There is no error, as argued in the grounds of appeal, of violating the rules of logic and empirical rules and thereby exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nc. Although the Prosecutor appealed from all acquittals in the lower court judgment, with respect to the acquittal portions, the petition of appeal contains no lawful statement of grounds for appeal, and the appellate brief also contains no statement of reasons for disagreement.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, among the guilty portions of the lower court judgment as to the Defendants, the portion concerning violation of the Criminal Proceeds Concealment Regulation Act must be reversed; and since the lower court, regarding that portion and the remaining guilty portions as to the Defendants, found them to be in a relation of concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act and imposed a single sentence, the entire guilty portion of the lower court judgment must be reversed.\\n\\nAccordingly, without examining the Defendants’ remaining grounds of appeal, the guilty portion of the lower court judgment is reversed and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. The Prosecutor’s appeal is dismissed. The opinions of the participating Justices of the Supreme Court were unanimous."}

{"[2017DO17494]": "The portion of the lower court judgment concerning embezzlement is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the Seoul Southern District Court. The Prosecutor’s remaining appeal is dismissed."}

{"[2020DO1263]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. The bribery in breach of trust portion related to C among the charged facts against Defendant B\\n\\na. Summary of this part of the charged facts\\n\\nDefendant B joined Co., Ltd. D (hereinafter referred to as “D”) as a reporter around 1978, and from around March 2010 to around December 2013 served as the chief editorial writer in the editorial board office, during which he published the “B Column” in E and handled the work in charge of E editorials; accordingly, he had a duty not to write commentaries, etc. in a manner favorable to a specific person or specific company upon request from such person or company.\\n\\nDefendant B, knowing that C, the chief executive officer of F Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “F”), was providing him with a plane ticket, lodging expenses, meal expenses, a private jet, a luxury yacht, etc. as consideration for an improper solicitation to the effect that, for five articles and editorials favorable to C and F, including the E “B Column” under the title “G” dated October 1, 2010, and in return for continued assistance in forming favorable public opinion regarding C and F in the future as well, he received such items from C while traveling in Europe for 9 days and 8 nights from September 1, 2011 to September 9, 2011, thereby acquiring pecuniary benefits worth a total of KRW 39,730,000.\\n\\nb. The court below’s determination\\n\\nThe court below, on the ground that C appears to have provided property or pecuniary benefits only with an internal expectation that he could receive assistance from Defendant B in forming favorable public opinion in the future, but it was difficult to deem that C made an express or implied solicitation to Defendant B concerning specific and concrete duty-related acts to some extent regarding pending issues, etc., maintained the first-instance judgment that found this part of the charged facts not guilty.\\n\\nc. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\n1) Relevant legal principles\\n\\nIn the offense of accepting property in breach of trust, “improper solicitation” refers to a solicitation that is contrary to social norms and the principle of good faith. In determining this, the content of the solicitation, the kind, amount, and form of the property or pecuniary benefits acquired in relation thereto, the method and manner of providing the pecuniary benefits, and the integrity of transactions, which is the protected legal interest, must be comprehensively considered; and such solicitation need not necessarily be express, but may be made implicitly as well (see Supreme Court Decision of December 24, 2008, 2008DO9602, etc.).\\n\\n2) When the foregoing legal principles are added to the following circumstances recognized by the reasons of the court below’s judgment and the evidence duly admitted by the court below, the court below’s determination cannot be sustained.\\n\\na) At the time, Defendant B, while serving as the chief editorial writer in the editorial board office, was involved in the direction of E editorials and the like, and also published, for a long period, signed columns on the economic sector titled “B Column,” and thus was in a position to exert influence over public opinion regarding enterprises such as F.\\n\\nIn fact, Defendant B, around October 1, 2010, wrote and published, in the “B Column” section of E, a column under the title “G” stating that F, which had outstanding performance, should not be sold to a conglomerate but should instead be grown into an independent company through a public subscription method for public shares, thereby influencing the formation of public opinion regarding F.\\n\\nb) C had known Defendant B since around 2007 or 2008, but it appears only that Defendant B maintained a certain relationship because he was in a position to influence public opinion regarding F; there is no indication that there was a personal relationship or business relationship sufficient for C unilaterally to provide a large amount of pecuniary benefits.\\n\\nAt investigative agencies and in court, C testified to the effect that he “treated Defendant B, who was the head of the editorial board office and chief editorial writer of E, who would be a great help to F, with special sincerity,” and that he “treated Defendant B as an important insurance-like figure,” thereby generally stating that he regarded Defendant B as a person helpful to F.\\n\\nc) The pecuniary benefits acquired by Defendant B from C, namely the cost of the European trip for 9 days and 8 nights (approximately KRW 39,730,000), constitute an excessively unusual and large amount of pecuniary benefits. It cannot be said that C and Defendant B, who had no special personal relationship or business relationship, exchanged the above-mentioned large amount of pecuniary benefits as a mere social courtesy.\\n\\nd) F was then a giant company occupying a considerable share in the shipbuilding industry, and at any time its business performance, including operating profit, as well as its operating structure and hiring methods, could be the subject of media reports and criticism. As the chief executive officer of F, C was in a position to have direct and indirect interests in public opinion formed according to such media reports and criticism. Defendant B, as the chief editorial writer of D, was in a position to influence the formation of public opinion regarding F, and moreover, around the time of this case, E published numerous columns and editorials concerning F, including matters relating to sale through the public share subscription method and policies for hiring high school graduates.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing circumstances, C, as the chief executive officer of F, is to be understood as having provided a large amount of pecuniary benefits while hoping that favorable public opinion regarding F would be formed through Defendant B, and Defendant B also is to be understood as having known that C would provide a large amount of pecuniary benefits far beyond the scope of social courtesy while expecting assistance concerning the formation of favorable public opinion for him. In other words, both C and Defendant B are to be understood as having exchanged the costs of the European trip amounting to approximately KRW 39,730,000 under the recognition and understanding that this constituted consideration for a solicitation concerning the formation of favorable public opinion through the use of the chief editorial writer position at E.\\n\\nAs such, insofar as Defendant B is deemed to have recognized and understood, at the time he acquired the property or pecuniary benefits, that this was consideration for a solicitation concerning the formation of favorable public opinion through the use of the chief editorial writer position at E, it cannot be evaluated as merely something that C vaguely expected only inwardly. Even if C did not expressly state the content of such solicitation, it must be evaluated that there was a solicitation by implied manifestation of intent.\\n\\ne) The media represents public interest regarding matters of public concern and performs its public mission by contributing to the formation of democratic public opinion through reporting, coverage, commentary, or other means (Article 4(3) of the Press Arbitration and Damage Relief Act). Because journalists serve as a channel for communication among the people and for the formation of public opinion, they have a significant influence on society as a whole. In order to maintain the fairness of the media and enhance trustworthiness, journalists are also required to possess a high level of integrity comparable to that of public officials (see Constitutional Court en banc decision of July 28, 2016, 2015HEONMA236, etc.).
