Former Article 15(1) of the “Guidelines for the Practice of Newspaper Ethics of the H Committee” (before amendment on April 6, 2021) provides that “news organizations and journalists shall not receive economic benefits such as money or goods, entertainment, invitations to free trips, expenses for reporting trips, products and gift certificates, or expensive souvenirs from interested parties in connection with reporting, coverage, criticism, or editing.” Article 9 of the “Operational Rules of the H Committee” provides that the H Committee may impose sanctions such as caution, warning, imposition of penalty surcharges, and suspension of qualification on newspapers and news agencies that violate the Press Ethics Code and its practice guidelines.\\n\\nA journalist receiving economic benefits from a specific person or specific company that is the subject of criticism, while being solicited to form favorable public opinion, is not only a betrayal of public trust in the fairness, objectivity, integrity, and incorruptibility of the media and journalists, but also constitutes an improper solicitation under the offense of accepting property in breach of trust, which is contrary to social norms or the principle of good faith, in that the relevant media organization may thereby be subject to sanctions such as caution, warning, or imposition of penalty surcharges. Defendant B’s receiving a solicitation concerning the formation of favorable public opinion regarding F while being provided with a large amount of economic benefits from C must be regarded as constituting improper solicitation.\\n\\n3) Nevertheless, the court below found this part of the charged facts not guilty solely for the reasons stated in its judgment. In so doing, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning improper solicitation in the offense of accepting property in breach of trust, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n2. The charged facts against Defendant A and the remaining charged facts against Defendant B\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its judgment, the court below found the charged facts against Defendant A and the remaining portions of bribery in breach of trust and violation of the Attorney-at-Law Act against Defendant B not guilty.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the court below’s judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, although there are some inappropriately stated portions in the reasons given by the court below, there is no error affecting the judgment by failing to fully conduct the necessary examination, by exceeding the bounds of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or by misapprehending or omitting determinations concerning the “improper solicitation” in the offense of accepting property in breach of trust or the “compensatory nature” in the offense of violation of the Attorney-at-Law Act, or by contradiction in the reasons.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nThe portion of the court below’s judgment concerning the bribery in breach of trust related to C as to Defendant B is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. The Prosecutor’s appeal against Defendant A and the remainder of Defendant B’s appeal are both dismissed. However, because there is an obvious clerical error in the resident registration number portion of the indication of Defendant A in the court below’s judgment, it is corrected pursuant to Article 25(1) of the Criminal Procedure Rules. Accordingly, the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2022DO6886]": "The grounds for the appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Relevant legal principles\\na. The protected legal interest in offenses concerning documents is the probative value of documents and the stability and credibility of the declarations of intent contained in documents, and such offenses target documents having evidentiary value by indicating a relation concerning a certain legal relationship or a fact important in transactions. Among them, where a public office or a public official prepares a document containing false content contrary to the truth in relation to official duties, the crime of making a false official document is established, and this is because, since official documents are accorded special probative force and credibility, the law protects not only the authenticity of their creation but also the truth of their contents (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2020DO9714, decided August 19, 2022). In the crime of making a false official document, “false” means a case where the indicated content does not correspond to the truth and thereby jeopardizes the public trust in that document (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 85DO758, decided June 25, 1985), and the crime of making a false official document is established when a person, while preparing a false official document, recognizes that the content is false (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 95DO1395, decided November 10, 1995).\\nb. The Supreme Court has held that, where a public official entered “Compared with the original” without actually comparing the document with the original, the crime of making a false official document is established even if the document preparer was confirmed by telephone that there was no discrepancy from the original or even if objectively the copy did not differ from the original (see Supreme Court Decision 80DO3180, decided September 22, 1981). It further held that, if a public official entered in the seal certificate and the seal certificate issuance register as though the applicant himself had personally appeared and applied for and received issuance, although the seal certificate applicant himself had not personally appeared, such fact has no effect whatsoever on the establishment of the crime of making a false official document even if the official had confirmed from the person himself the intent to obtain the seal certificate through an agent (see Supreme Court Decision 92DO2060, decided October 13, 1992). The same applies to investigation documents prepared by police officers; accordingly, the Supreme Court held that, where police officers who had been dispatched to the scene of the offense, in violation of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, had failed to inform persons arrested in flagrante delicto of the reasons for arrest and the right to retain counsel, yet prepared an arrest report for a person arrested in flagrante delicto stating that the person had been arrested in flagrante delicto “after being informed of the reasons for arrest and the right to retain counsel, etc.” and a written confirmation stating that “while arresting the person in flagrante delicto, we informed the person of the gist of the offense, the reasons for detention, and the right to retain counsel and gave an opportunity to explain,” then the police officer who prepared the arrest report for a person arrested in flagrante delicto and the written confirmation prepared a false arrest report for a person arrested in flagrante delicto and a false written confirmation, and had intent for the making of a false official document at the time, even if he thought that another police officer must have naturally informed the person of the reasons for arrest and the right to retain counsel (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DO11226, decided June 24, 2010).\\n\\n2. Determination in this case\\na. The gist of the facts charged in this case is that, while the Defendant, as a judicial police officer in charge of preparing documents concerning criminal investigations at the Traffic Crime Investigation Team of the ○○○○ Police Station, was asked by a prosecutor of the Daejeon District Prosecutors’ Office to conduct a reinvestigation pursuant to Article 245-8 of the Criminal Procedure Act in a case involving violation of the Act on Special Cases concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents (hereinafter the “Traffic Accident Settlement Act”) (causing injury) concerning Non-Party 1 (driver), he had not additionally heard statements from traffic accident victims Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3, Non-Party 2 had not said to the Defendant that “the impact at the time was slight and that since Non-Party 3 said that he needed to receive hospital treatment and obtain insurance proceeds, he also received hospital treatment,” and Non-Party 3 had not received hospital treatment through the insurance claim made by Non-Party 2 on the day of the accident before Non-Party 1 filed a claim under comprehensive insurance for the vehicle, nor had Non-Party 3 told the Defendant that “Non-Party 1 filed a claim under comprehensive insurance, so he received hospital treatment”; nevertheless, the Defendant, for the purpose of use, falsely prepared the report on the results of reinvestigation, an official document, in relation to his duties, by entering in the “Results of Reinvestigation” section of the report on the results of reinvestigation false contents under the heading “Statement of Non-Party 2 in the driver’s seat” that “the impact at the time was slight, as the rubber portions of the tires came into contact with each other, but since Non-Party 3, who was then in the front passenger seat, said that he needed to receive hospital treatment and obtain compensation from the insurance company, he also received hospital treatment, and this statement is that he received hospital treatment five days after the date of the accident,” and by entering under the heading “Statement of Non-Party 3 in the front passenger seat” false contents that “this statement is that he visited the hospital five days after the date of the accident, received treatment, submitted a medical certificate, and received hospital treatment because the suspect filed a claim under comprehensive insurance,” and submitted it to the Daejeon District Prosecutors’ Office and used it.\\nb. The lower court held that: ① the Defendant did not additionally hear the victims’ statements because he deemed that the statements previously heard from the victims were sufficient to determine whether the crime of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (hereinafter the “Specific Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act”) (causing injury in the course of escape) was established; ② the victims’ prosecutorial statements to the effect that “the portion where the Defendant recorded in the ‘Results of Reinvestigation’ section that it was the victims’ statements differs from what the victims told the Defendant” lack credibility; and ③ even if the portion recorded in the “Results of Reinvestigation” section as the victims’ statements differed from what the Defendant had previously heard from the victims, the possibility cannot be ruled out that, for the Defendant, based on the damaged parts and extent of the vehicle, the medical certificates and various circumstances, and his perception of the situation as an investigator, he understood and recognized the victims’ statements as being the same as those recorded in the “Results of Reinvestigation” section. For those reasons, the lower court reversed the first-instance judgment that had found the facts charged in this case guilty and acquitted the Defendant, holding that it was difficult to find that the Defendant prepared and used the report on the results of reinvestigation with intent to make a false official document.\\nc. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the evidence duly admitted, the following facts can be found.\\n1) On or about February 4, 2021, Non-Party 1, while driving a vehicle, caused the accident in this case by striking the victim vehicle stopped on the right side in the direction of travel. At the time, Non-Party 2 was seated in the driver’s seat of the victim vehicle, and Non-Party 3 was seated in the front passenger seat.\\n2) Immediately after the accident in this case, Non-Party 1 continued driving without taking measures such as stopping the offending vehicle and confirming whether an accident had occurred, and Non-Party 2 got out of the victim vehicle and filed a 112 report alleging a hit-and-run accident.\\n3) The Defendant, who worked at the Traffic Crime Investigation Team, met Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 1 at the police station parking lot on February 7, 2021, and conducted an investigation such as confirming whether there had been a collision between the offending vehicle and the victim vehicle and the points of impact. At that time, Non-Party 3 was not present.\\n4) Non-Party 2 reported the accident to the victim vehicle’s insurance company on the day of the accident, and Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3 received treatment at a hospital on February 8, 2021, and received treatment at a hospital and obtained medical certificates on February 9, 2021.\\n5) On or about February 9, 2021, Non-Party 2 appeared at the ○○○○ Police Station and, while being questioned by the Defendant, prepared and submitted together with a medical certificate a statement on the circumstances of the traffic accident to the effect that “the offending vehicle struck the victim vehicle, then stopped for a moment and then moved off hesitantly and left as is, and I later received treatment at an orthopedic clinic.” On the same day, Non-Party 3 also appeared together with Non-Party 2 and, while being questioned, prepared and submitted together with a medical certificate a statement on the circumstances of the traffic accident to the effect that “the offending vehicle made contact with the front tire on the driver’s side of the victim vehicle, pretended to stop, and then fled.”\\n6) On February 10, 2021, Non-Party 1 submitted to the investigative agency a certificate of insurance subscription concerning the offending vehicle’s insurance company, and the victims thereafter received treatment under insurance for the offending vehicle.\\n7) Meanwhile, while the Defendant was investigated by the prosecution on suspicion of making and using false official documents, he stated that: ① in relation to the Non-Party 2 statement portion of the report on the results of reinvestigation, during the investigation process before the prosecutor’s request for reinvestigation, he had only heard from Non-Party 2 that “the damaged part is the tire part and no repair of the car is necessary,” but because, in practice, compensation proceeds are generally paid when an insurance claim is filed, he independently determined based on various circumstances without additionally hearing statements from Non-Party 2 and entered that “the impact at the time was slight and that he received hospital treatment because Non-Party 3 said that he had to obtain compensation”; and ② in relation to the Non-Party 3 statement portion of the report on the results of reinvestigation, he had initially entered it based on the statement heard from Non-Party 2 without hearing any statement from Non-Party 3, and that the portion stating “Non-Party 1 filed a claim under comprehensive insurance, so he received hospital treatment” was entered because, as a result, comprehensive insurance had been claimed and Non-Party 3 received hospital treatment.\\n\\nd. The above factual relationship is examined in light of the foregoing legal principles.\\n1) The prosecutor, keeping in mind the possibility that Non-Party 1 may have fled, requested the Defendant to reinvestigate whether there had been a hit-and-run by hearing specific statements from the victims, Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3, regarding the circumstances of the accident. In the request section for reinvestigation at the top of the report on the results of reinvestigation prepared by the Defendant, the above request for reinvestigation is stated, and in the results section for reinvestigation at the bottom, it is stated as though statements were heard from Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3 and the contents of those statements were recorded. In light of the circumstances under which the report on the results of reinvestigation was prepared and its structure, the entry in the results section for reinvestigation means that the Defendant, in accordance with the purpose of the request for reinvestigation, heard specific statements from Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3 and recorded the contents of those statements. However, the Defendant did not hear statements from Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3.\\n2) In particular, the Defendant recorded as though they were statements directly heard from Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3, even though they were merely his own independent opinions or conjectures based on matters that Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3 had not stated.\\nThe gist of the Non-Party 2 statement recorded by the Defendant in the report on the results of reinvestigation is that ① the impact at the time was slight, and ② he received hospital treatment because Non-Party 3 said that he needed to obtain insurance proceeds; and the gist of the Non-Party 3 statement is that ③ the driver, Non-Party 1, filed a claim under comprehensive insurance, so he received hospital treatment.\\nThis, together with the gist that the impact and damage caused by the accident were slight but hospital treatment was received in order to obtain insurance proceeds, also implies that the driver nevertheless properly handled matters afterward.\\nHowever, with respect to ①, the Defendant had only heard from Non-Party 2 that the car impact point was the tire area, so no repair was necessary, yet he recorded his own judgment that the impact was slight as though it were Non-Party 2’s statement. With respect to ②, the Defendant had not heard any statement from Non-Party 2 about the treatment process related to insurance proceeds, yet merely because insurance proceeds are generally paid when treatment is received, he recorded his own conjecture regarding the treatment process as though it were Non-Party 2’s statement. With respect to ③, the Defendant had not heard any statement from Non-Party 3 about the treatment process, and although the victims reported the accident to the insurance company subscribed to by the victim vehicle immediately after the accident in this case and received treatment, and although the insurance claim to the insurance company subscribed to for the offending vehicle was filed only after the medical certificates had been issued, resulting in the victims’ treatment, he recorded his own judgment regarding the course of insurance handling as though it were Non-Party 3’s statement.\\nAccordingly, irrespective of whether some of the contents recorded as the statements of Non-Party 2 and Non-Party 3 ultimately correspond to the facts, or whether, as the lower court held, the judicial police officer who was requested to conduct the reinvestigation had discretion as to whether to re-investigate the references or suspects designated by the prosecutor and as to the manner of such re-investigation, the Defendant’s act alleged in the facts charged constitutes the crime of making a false official document.\\n3) The Defendant prepared the report on the results of reinvestigation as though he had heard specific statements and recorded his own opinions or conjectures as if they were statements. Accordingly, even if the Defendant believed that the contents he recorded, based on his own judgment because the victims’ statements lacked credibility, would correspond to objective facts, such belief cannot negate intent.\\n\\ne. Nevertheless, the lower court found the facts charged in this case not guilty for the reasons stated in its judgment.\\nThe lower court’s determination contains errors that affected the judgment by violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence without conducting the necessary deliberation, or by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the crime of making a false official document. The prosecutor’s allegation pointing this out in the grounds of appeal is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the lower court judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the crimes of embezzlement and breach of trust is correct? (Where there is dispute, according to precedents)
A: In a case where A, while drinking at a bar with his friend A, received and kept a mobile phone that the latter had dropped and left behind, from the bar owner, with the intent of handing it over to A in his group, and then arbitrarily used A’s mobile phone in the course of a physical altercation between them, A did not directly receive it in trust from A, and cannot even be regarded, as a matter of legal reasoning, as being in a position to keep the mobile phone; therefore, the crime of embezzlement is not established.
B: In the crime of embezzlement, the intent of unlawful appropriation means the intent of a person who keeps another’s property to dispose of that property without authority, contrary to the purpose of entrustment, as though it were his own property, in fact or in law; therefore, even where the custodian disposed of it not for his own benefit or that of a third person, but for the benefit of its owner, the intent of unlawful appropriation may be recognized unless there are special circumstances.
C: Where A, a tenant of a building, assigned to B the claim for return of the lease deposit against the lessor, but did not notify the lessor of the assignment of claim, and then, while keeping the returned remaining lease deposit after receiving it from the lessor, arbitrarily consumed it, A received the lease deposit for B and thus falls under “a person who keeps another’s property” for the crime of embezzlement.
D: If Debtor A, in order to secure a monetary debt, established a mortgage right in favor of the creditor over his movable property pursuant to the "Act on the Mortgage of Certain Movables, etc. such as Automobiles," etc., but caused the collateral to lose its value by disposing of it to a third party, thereby creating a risk to the creditor’s realization of the security right, the crime of breach of trust is established.
E: Where the representative director of a stock company issued a promissory note in breach of his duty, such as by abusing his representative authority, even if the issuance of the note is invalid, if the note actually circulated to a third party, the company must be regarded as having specifically and realistically incurred a risk of bearing the note obligation; therefore, even before the note obligation is actually performed, the offense is a completed crime of breach of trust.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2012DO5346]": "We decide upon the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe gist of the embezzlement count among the facts charged in this case is that, while the Defendant was drinking at a soju bar together with the Victim, the Defendant received from the proprietor of the soju bar a mobile phone that the Victim had dropped and kept it for the Victim, and, around that time, embezzled it by, among other things, using the above mobile phone without authorization; however, with respect to this, the court below rendered a judgment of not guilty on the grounds, among others, that the Defendant could not be said to be in the position of a person who keeps another’s property, nor could it be said that the Defendant disposed of another’s property as if it were his own.\\n\\nHowever, the subject of the crime of embezzlement is a person who keeps another’s property pursuant to a relationship of entrustment; such relationship of entrustment need not necessarily be established by a contract such as a gratuitous loan for use, lease, or mandate, and may also arise through management of affairs, custom, reason, good faith, etc., and it is not necessarily recognized only where the owner directly entrusts the property (see Supreme Court Decision 84DO2644 rendered on September 10, 1985, Supreme Court Decision 87DO1778 rendered on October 13, 1987, Supreme Court Decision 2010DO17396 rendered on March 24, 2011, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the evidence lawfully adopted by the court below, the Defendant and the Victim came to know each other around mid-August 2010, and on the evening of August 27, 2010, at the Defendant’s suggestion, they went together to a soju bar and were drinking when they ended up in a scuffle with each other; in the course of that, the Victim left the soju bar first and dropped his mobile phone there, and the proprietor of the soju bar found the above mobile phone and, with the intent of handing it to its owner, gave it to the Defendant, who was a companion, so that the Defendant kept it; if the circumstances are as such, the Defendant must be deemed to have been in a position to keep the above mobile phone for the Victim as a matter of reason. Therefore, the judgment of the court below, which, contrary to the foregoing, determined that the Defendant could not be said to be in the position of a person who keeps another’s property, is illegal in that it erred in law concerning the relationship of entrustment in the crime of embezzlement.\\n\\nHowever, in the crime of embezzlement, the intent of unlawful appropriation means the intent to dispose, in breach of one’s duty, of another’s property kept, as if it were one’s own, for the purpose of seeking the benefit of oneself or a third party (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DO3045 rendered on August 19, 2005, etc.); since the Defendant merely used the Victim’s mobile phone without authorization while keeping it, it is difficult to conclude that the Defendant had the intent of unlawful appropriation, and on the same premise, the conclusion of the court below, which determined that there was no proof of the crime with respect to the above facts charged and rendered a judgment of not guilty, is proper.\\n\\nFurthermore, since it is difficult to view that the above facts charged include the fact that “the Defendant refused to return the above mobile phone,” it cannot be said that there is any illegality in the judgment of the court below, as argued in the grounds of appeal, in that it misapprehended the scope of the facts charged and failed to conduct the necessary review; on the other hand, the error of the court below noted above did not affect the result of the judgment.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated, as stated in the operative part."}

{"[2014DO1104]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. a. Article 355(2) of the Criminal Act provides that breach of trust is established when a person who handles another’s affairs, by an act in violation of his or her duty, acquires pecuniary gain or causes a third party to acquire such gain, thereby causing damage to the principal; and Article 359 of the Criminal Act provides that attempts thereof shall be punished. Thus, since the Criminal Act sets as the objective elements of breach of trust that a person who handles another’s affairs commit an act in violation of duty and thereby the actor or a third party acquire pecuniary gain and damage the principal, when a person who handles another’s affairs, with the intent to commit breach of trust, that is, with awareness or intent as to the act in violation of duty and as to the fact that, by such act, he or she or a third party acquires gain and thereby damages the principal, commences an act in violation of duty, the execution of breach of trust has begun; and the offense is consummated when, by such act, he or she or a third party acquires gain and thereby damages the principal.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court has consistently interpreted that, in breach of trust, the phrase “when damage is caused to the principal” means a decrease in pecuniary value, which includes not only cases where actual pecuniary loss has been caused but also cases where the risk of loss has been created, and that even if the amount of damage has not been concretely and clearly determined, this does not affect the establishment of breach of trust (see Supreme Court Decisions 72DO1366 rendered on November 13, 1973, 79DO2637 rendered on September 9, 1980, 87DO546 rendered on July 21, 1987, 90DO1702 rendered on October 16, 1990, 95DO531 rendered on May 30, 1997, among others). The Court has also adopted the position that whether pecuniary damage exists must be determined economically, in relation to the principal’s entire property situation, rather than by legal judgment, and has held that even if the act constituting breach of trust is void as a result of legal judgment, if, when viewed economically, the act caused actual damage to the principal or created the risk of actual pecuniary loss, it corresponds to the causing of pecuniary damage. However, the risk of actual pecuniary loss means a specific and realistic risk so grave as to be evaluated as practically equivalent, from an economic standpoint, to the occurrence of pecuniary damage, and mere vague possibility is insufficient; accordingly, if the act constituting breach of trust is void as a matter of law and therefore the principal’s property situation has not in fact deteriorated, then there is not only no actual damage but also no risk of actual loss, and it cannot be said that pecuniary damage was caused to the principal (see Supreme Court Decisions 87DO993 rendered on November 10, 1987, 91DO2963 rendered on May 26, 1992, 94DO1375 rendered on November 21, 1995, 2000DO142 rendered on November 28, 2000, 2006DO4876 en banc decision rendered on June 19, 2008, 2011DO16763 rendered on February 3, 2014, 2015DO6745 rendered on September 10, 2015, among others).\\n\\nDespite this line of Supreme Court precedents, it is not easy in trial practice of criminal cases prosecuted for breach of trust to examine and determine the time of consummation of breach of trust. Where a person who handles another’s affairs formally appears to perform a legal act for the principal, but such act in substance constitutes an act in violation of duty in breach of trust, such act is not infrequently likely to be judged void in civil litigation on the ground that it constitutes an anti-social legal act (see Article 103 of the Civil Code) and the like; this is because, even when determining in criminal proceedings whether breach of trust is established, the civil-law evaluation of such act must sufficiently take into account its effect, from an economic standpoint, on the victim’s property situation. Ultimately, when determining in criminal proceedings whether damage has occurred, which is an objective element of breach of trust, or whether the victim’s pecuniary interest, which is the protected legal interest of breach of trust, has been infringed, the above Supreme Court precedents should serve as the standard, but in each concrete case careful determination must be made by comprehensively considering the content and nature of the affairs of another, the gravity of the breach of duty, and the effect on the principal’s property situation.\\n\\nb. (1) Even if the representative director of a stock company, by abusing his or her representative authority, etc., performs an act in violation of duty by assuming obligations in the company’s name, it is, in principle, valid as an act of the company, but becomes void as against the company when the other party knew or could have known the representative director’s true intent (see Supreme Court Decisions 97DA18059 rendered on August 29, 1997, 2003DA34045 rendered on March 26, 2004, among others). Accordingly, where the other party knew or could have known of the abuse of representative authority, the act assuming obligations is, in principle, ineffective against the company, and even from an economic standpoint, this alone makes it difficult to evaluate that actual damage occurred to the company or that the risk of actual loss arose; therefore, unless there are other special circumstances such as that the obligation was actually performed as a result of the act assuming obligations or that the company became liable in tort under the Civil Code, the offense of breach of trust has not been consummated. However, even in such a case, since the representative director has commenced execution by performing an act in violation of duty with the intent to commit breach of trust, it constitutes an attempt of breach of trust.\\n\\nWhere, conversely, there are circumstances such as that the other party did not know of the abuse of representative authority, and thus the act assuming obligations is valid against the company, the company’s debt arises and the company bears an obligation to perform that debt; therefore, the occurrence of such debt itself constitutes actual damage or risk of actual pecuniary loss, and even before the debt is actually performed, the offense of breach of trust must be deemed consummated.\\n\\n(2) Whether the act of a representative director of a stock company, in abuse of representative authority, etc., issuing a promissory note in violation of duty constitutes breach of trust should, in principle, be viewed in the same way as the act assuming obligations discussed above. However, in the case of issuing a promissory note, under the Bills of Exchange and Promissory Notes Act, the issuer may not assert against the holder defenses arising from personal relations with a former holder (Articles 17 and 77 of the Bills of Exchange and Promissory Notes Act). Accordingly, even if the issuance of the note is void, if the note has in fact been circulated to a third party, the company must be deemed to have specifically and realistically incurred the risk of bearing the note debt, and therefore breach of trust is consummated even before the note debt is actually performed. However, if the issuance of the promissory note is not only void but the note has not been circulated, then since the company does not bear the note debt to the counterparty to the issuance, there is, absent special circumstances, no actual damage to the company and no risk of actual loss; in that case, the proper punishment is for attempted breach of trust, not consummated breach of trust.\\n\\nBy contrast, Supreme Court Decisions 2012DO10822 rendered on December 27, 2012, 2011DO10302 rendered on February 14, 2013, and the like, to the effect that even where the act of issuing a promissory note in the company’s name by a representative director is void, one should regard the risk of actual pecuniary loss as having arisen unless there are special circumstances that the promissory note is not circulated to a third party, contain a part that conflicts with this judgment as to the time of consummation of breach of trust, and therefore they are changed to that extent.\\n\\n2. The gist of the facts charged in this case is that the Defendant, who was the representative director of the victim company, issued and delivered to ○○ Mutual Savings Bank, in the name of the victim company, a promissory note in the face amount of KRW 2,990,000,000 in order to secure the loan debt of another company, of which he separately served as representative director, to ○○ Mutual Savings Bank, thereby causing ○○ Mutual Savings Bank to acquire pecuniary gain equivalent to KRW 2,990,000,000 and causing the victim company damage in the same amount.\\n\\nThe lower court maintained the first-instance judgment, which found the facts charged in this case guilty, on the ground that, even if the Defendant’s issuance of the promissory note in this case constituted abuse of representative authority and was void against the victim company, there were no special circumstances suggesting that the promissory note would not be circulated at the time of issuance, and on such and similar grounds, it held that the risk of actual pecuniary loss to the victim company had arisen at the time of issuance.\\n\\nHowever, in light of the legal principles discussed above, if, as the lower court held, the Defendant abused representative authority to issue the promissory note in this case and, at that time, the counterparty, ○○ Mutual Savings Bank, knew or could have known of such fact, and thus the issuance was ineffective against the victim company, then, unless there were special circumstances such as that the victim company actually paid the promissory note amount, bore civil liability for damages, or the promissory note was in fact circulated to a third party, it must be said that the Defendant’s issuance of the promissory note did not cause actual damage or the risk of actual pecuniary loss to the victim company. Nevertheless, without examining this point, the lower court, relying only on the circumstances it stated, held the facts charged guilty by applying the offense of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (hereinafter the “Specific Economic Crimes Act”) to the facts charged in this case on the premise that the issuance of the promissory note in this case had reached consummation of breach of trust. Accordingly, the lower judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles regarding the pecuniary damage requirement and the time of consummation of breach of trust.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the lower judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for a new trial and determination, and judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition. In this judgment, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous except for the separate opinions of Justices Park Bo-young, Ko Young-han, Kim Chang-seok, and Kim Shin; there are supplementary opinions by Justices Cho Hee-dae and Kim Jae-hyung, and by Justice Park Sang-ok, as to the majority opinion; and there are supplementary opinions by Justices Kim Chang-seok and Kim Shin as to the separate opinion.\\n\\n4. The separate opinion of Justices Park Bo-young, Ko Young-han, Kim Chang-seok, and Kim Shin is as follows.\\n\\na. The majority opinion, premised on the view that breach of trust is a crime of danger, holds that where a representative director’s act of issuing a promissory note in the company’s name is void due to abuse of representative authority, etc., it cannot be regarded as having caused actual damage or the risk of actual pecuniary loss to the company unless there are special circumstances such as that the company bears tort liability under the Civil Code or the promissory note is in fact circulated to a third party, and determines that the lower court, which held that breach of trust was consummated merely on the ground that the possibility that the promissory note in this case would be circulated to a third party was not negated, should be reversed because it failed to examine such circumstances.\\n\\nThe separate opinion also agrees with the majority opinion in its conclusion that the lower judgment, which found the facts charged guilty on the premise that breach of trust was consummated, should be reversed. However, breach of trust should be viewed not as a crime of danger but as a crime of infringement, and even if a debt arises or tort liability under the Civil Code is borne as a result of an act assuming obligations, this should be regarded as merely a risk of damage, not actual damage; therefore, the lower judgment should be reversed for reasons different from those of the majority opinion. The reasons are examined below.\\n\\nb. Breach of trust should be viewed not as a crime of danger but as a crime of infringement.\\n\\n(1) The Supreme Court has hitherto consistently described breach of trust as “an endangering offense established where there is a state in which the execution of pecuniary rights may be rendered impossible or where there is a risk of loss” (see Supreme Court Decisions 88DO1247 rendered on April 11, 1989, 99DO334 rendered on April 11, 2000, among others), and has held that in breach of trust, “the phrase ‘when damage is caused to the principal’ includes not only cases where actual damage is caused but also cases where the risk of actual pecuniary loss is created” (see Supreme Court Decisions 2007DO541 rendered on July 23, 2009, 2011DO16763 rendered on February 3, 2014, among others).\\n\\nHowever, understanding breach of trust in this way as a crime of danger is an interpretation that does not conform to the wording of the Criminal Act. That is, Article 355(2) of the Criminal Act provides that breach of trust is established when, by an act in violation of duty, one acquires pecuniary gain or causes a third party to acquire such gain and thereby causes damage to the principal, and the phrase “when damage is caused” in its wording means “when damage is actually caused.” Nevertheless, the prior precedents have broadened the scope of consummation of breach of trust by interpreting the phrase “when damage is caused” to include, in addition to actual damage, cases where the risk of actual loss has been created. Although the risk of actual loss being caused is entirely different from causing damage, the interpretation that treats the two identically is not only beyond the scope of textual interpretation but also expands the meaning of the penal provision to the defendant’s disadvantage, contrary to the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\n(2) Furthermore, unlike other property crimes, the Criminal Act expressly sets as an objective element in the case of breach of trust that pecuniary damage be caused, which is understood as a legislative measure intended to emphasize that even if a person who handles another’s affairs performs an act in violation of duty, breach of trust cannot be consummated unless actual pecuniary damage is caused to the principal. Therefore, there is no need to combine this with the interpretive theory regarding pecuniary gain or damage in other property crimes such as fraud or embezzlement, where pecuniary damage is not expressly included as an element. In the case of breach of trust, considering the specificity of its elements and the legislative purpose, the requirement of pecuniary damage should be construed as satisfied only when an act in violation of duty causes actual pecuniary damage to the principal.\\n\\n(3) The view that breach of trust is a crime of infringement is also correct in that the risk of actual loss, which the majority opinion regards as constituting damage in breach of trust, is only a prior stage to the occurrence of actual pecuniary damage. The Supreme Court has held that damage in breach of trust includes not only actual damage but also cases where the risk of actual pecuniary loss is created; however, it has not strictly distinguished, in concrete cases, between cases where actual damage occurred and cases where the risk of actual pecuniary loss occurred. Even if the defendant committed an act in violation of duty involving risk, if the principal thereby obtained a benefit, or even if the defendant betrayed the relationship of trust, if there is not even room for the result of such act to inure to the principal, it is difficult to say that there was an act in violation of duty constituting breach of trust, and there can be no risk of actual loss. In other words, the risk of actual loss merely means that the defendant committed an act in violation of duty capable of causing actual pecuniary damage to the principal, and the possibility of the resulting damage became concretized. The risk of actual loss does not have an independent meaning in itself; it is merely an intermediate process leading to the actual occurrence of damage expressly set forth in the Criminal Act as an element of breach of trust. There is no legal basis for regarding, at the stage of risk of actual loss, the defendant as having already caused damage in the course of an act in violation of duty against the principal.\\n\\n(4) Prior precedents have held that an “act in violation of duty” in breach of trust includes any act that betrays the relationship of trust with the principal by, in light of the content and nature of the affairs, and other concrete circumstances, failing to perform an act expected by law, the content of the contract, or the principle of good faith, or by performing an act expected not to be performed (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DO4640 rendered on May 29, 2008, among others). This follows the so-called theory of betrayal as to the essence of breach of trust.\\n\\nAs to the betrayal theory, criticism exists to the effect that there is a risk of endlessly expanding the scope of the trust relationship that can constitute breach of trust, and that if, to supplement this, the element “a person who handles another’s affairs” is interpreted restrictively, the basis for excluding acts betraying the relationship of trust from breach of trust remains unclear, and ultimately it becomes unclear which betrayal of a trust relationship amounts to breach of trust. Even putting aside such criticism, if one regards the act in violation of duty in breach of trust as any act betraying the trust relationship, and interprets the pecuniary damage element of breach of trust to include not only actual damage but also the risk of actual loss, then in substance any act in violation of duty may immediately constitute consummated breach of trust on the ground that there is a risk of damage, thereby unduly expanding the scope of punishment for breach of trust. Criticism has long been raised against breach of trust, including that the distinction between an act in violation of duty constituting breach of trust and simple civil non-performance of an obligation is unclear, that criminal law excessively intervenes in the realm of private autonomy, or that it can lead to the criminalization of civil cases; and considering that, in light of such awareness, the academic consensus is that the elements of breach of trust should be construed as strictly and restrictively as possible, the prior precedents treating breach of trust as a crime of danger need fundamentally to be reconsidered.\\n\\n(5) Of course, the Supreme Court has hitherto, while regarding breach of trust as a crime of danger, endeavored to limit the scope of danger by confining the risk of actual loss, which corresponds to the damage element of breach of trust, to specific and realistic danger (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO6745 rendered on September 10, 2015, among others). However, since the criterion for distinguishing specific and realistic danger that falls within the damage element of breach of trust from danger that does not is not clear, it is difficult to deny that, in practice, so long as an act in violation of duty carries a risk of reducing the principal’s property, most cases are punished as consummated breach of trust. This means that the Supreme Court’s effort to prevent excessive expansion of breach of trust by classifying the risk of actual loss according to its degree, rather than by clearly distinguishing damage and risk of damage according to the wording of the law, is not only not convincing but has in practice also achieved little effect. As a result, the Criminal Act provision on breach of trust has brought about an undesirable result in that it has not properly fulfilled its role as a behavioral norm for the public.\\n\\n(6) Our Criminal Act contains a provision punishing attempts of breach of trust. This is a legislative determination to punish, not as consummated breach of trust but as attempted breach of trust, cases where there has been no actual infringement upon the protected legal interest, the property right, and only the risk of such infringement has arisen. This attitude of our Criminal Act accords with the fundamental demand of the principle of clarity derived from nulla poena sine lege. The view that the damage in breach of trust includes the risk of actual loss appears to import, into the interpretation of our Criminal Act, which contains an attempt-punishment provision, a concept devised in the legal systems of countries such as Germany, which lack an attempt-punishment provision, to punish as breach of trust certain acts that had to be punished although no actual pecuniary damage had occurred. From a practical standpoint, our Criminal Act generally provides only that attempts may be mitigated at the court’s discretion, so there is no decisive difference in the degree of punishment between consummated and attempted breach of trust.\\n\\n(7) It may also be pointed out that if breach of trust is constituted as a crime of infringement, there arises the problem that, where only the risk of actual loss, rather than actual damage, is created by an act in violation of duty, the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes, Article 3, cannot be applied because breach of trust is not consummated. The position that breach of trust should be viewed as a crime of danger appears to take this circumstance as one of the grounds for not viewing breach of trust as a crime of infringement. However, since the offense of violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (breach of trust) aggravates the statutory punishment merely by measuring the value of pecuniary gain acquired through the act of breach of trust, namely the amount gained, solely on a quantitative basis, if the amount gained is calculated to include not only actual damage but also the risk of actual loss, there is a concern that an excessive statutory punishment will be applied relative to the punishability of the act, thereby undermining the principle of balance between crime and punishment and the principle of responsibility, and in some cases a conclusion lacking concrete validity may be reached. In particular, it is not easy, either doctrinally or emotionally, to accept severely punishing a counterparty by deeming that, merely because an act in violation of duty created the risk of actual loss, the counterparty acquired pecuniary gain corresponding to that loss. The fact that the Supreme Court has recently been endeavoring to calculate the amount gained in offenses of violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (breach of trust) according to substantive and concrete criteria may also be seen as arising from this awareness of the problem. In this respect, the argument that, in order to apply the offense of violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (breach of trust) even where only the risk of actual loss, rather than actual damage, has arisen, the offense of breach of trust under the Criminal Act must be constituted as a crime of danger is not persuasive. Rather, it is correct to construe breach of trust strictly in fidelity to the wording of the Criminal Act as a crime of infringement, and then to regard the offense of violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (breach of trust) as inapplicable where only the risk of actual loss has arisen.\\n\\nc. Even if a debt arises pursuant to an act assuming obligations or tort liability under the Civil Code is borne, this must be regarded only as a risk of damage, not as actual damage.\\n\\n(1) Prior precedents have held that the determination of whether pecuniary damage exists in breach of trust must be made economically, rather than by legal judgment, in relation to the principal’s entire property situation (see Supreme Court Decisions 2012DO15890 rendered on April 11, 2013, 2011DO16763 rendered on February 3, 2014, among others). There may be various views as to what exactly the phrase “economic standpoint” means, but it appears clear at least that the result of legal judgment should not be binding.\\n\\nMeanwhile, since “when damage is caused” in breach of trust denotes the constitutive result of the offense, it must be understood in relation to the protected legal interest of breach of trust. The protected legal interest of breach of trust is property rights, and since breach of trust should be regarded as a crime of infringement, the phrase “when damage is caused” in breach of trust can ultimately be understood to mean the case where, from an economic standpoint, the principal’s property rights can be evaluated as having been actually infringed.\\n\\n(2) Where the representative director performs an act assuming obligations in violation of duty, and that act is valid as a matter of law, a debt arises accordingly and the company bears an obligation to perform that debt. However, even in such a case, the company is only placed in a state in which it bears a legal obligation to perform the debt, and no actual change is brought about in the company’s property. To regard this nonetheless as a case where actual damage has occurred is to view the legally compelled duty to perform the obligation itself as actual damage. That is, damage is being grasped from a legal or accounting standpoint, not from an economic standpoint.\\n\\n(3) As noted above, since breach of trust is an offense whose protected legal interest is property rights, once breach of trust is viewed as a crime of infringement, consummation occurs when there is actual infringement of property rights. From the perspective of infringement of property rights, however, the fact that a debt arises and one bears a legal obligation to perform that debt is naturally understood not as actual infringement of property rights, but as the occurrence of a risk that property rights will be infringed. This is even more so in light of the fact that, even when a debt arises, such debt is not always performed. That is, even if a debt arises pursuant to an act assuming obligations, depending on various circumstances such as the maturity or condition of the debt, the debtor’s solvency and intention to perform, the creditor’s demand and receipt, and the statute of limitations, the debt may actually be performed or may not be performed. Nevertheless, interpreting that, once debt arises and the obligation to perform that debt is borne, the property rights protected by breach of trust have immediately been actually infringed, is in substance a legal fiction of the mere risk of infringement as actual infringement, and does not accord with the structure of the Criminal Act, which distinguishes crimes of infringement from crimes of danger according to the degree of protection afforded to the protected legal interest. Also, if the occurrence of debt is regarded as actual damage in itself, then even where a surety obligation is borne as a result of an act assuming obligations, one would have no choice but to conclude, regardless of the concrete content of that obligation, that pecuniary damage equivalent to the amount of the surety obligation has always actually occurred. Furthermore, if one interprets that amount equivalent to the surety obligation should be calculated as the amount gained in the offense of violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (breach of trust), it is doubtful whether such interpretation conforms to the present case law position on the amount gained under the offense of violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (breach of trust).\\n\\nd. As examined above, breach of trust should be viewed as a crime of infringement, and the occurrence of debt pursuant to an act assuming obligations or the bearing of tort liability under the Civil Code should be regarded as a risk of damage, not as actual damage. With this premise, this case is examined.\\n\\n(1) Where the representative director of a company, by abusing representative authority, performs an act assuming obligations, if the act is valid, the company’s debt arises accordingly; even if it is void, the company may bear tort liability under the Civil Code as a result. However, the occurrence of debt pursuant to an act assuming obligations or the bearing of tort liability under the Civil Code is, in itself, merely a risk of damage, not actual damage; therefore, breach of trust is consummated when the company actually performs the debt or tort liability arising from the act assuming obligations. Accordingly, even where the representative director of a company issues a promissory note in the company’s name by abusing representative authority, regardless of whether the act of issuance is legally effective or whether the promissory note has been circulated to a third party or has the possibility of being circulated, breach of trust is consummated when the company actually performs the note debt or the tort liability under the Civil Code that it has thereby incurred.\\n\\n(2) According to the record, the Defendant abused representative authority and issued the promissory note in this case, but there is no circumstance suggesting that the victim company actually performed the note debt or tort liability under the Civil Code; thus, it is difficult to conclude that actual damage occurred to the victim company as a result of the issuance of the promissory note in this case. Nevertheless, the lower court held that the damage element of breach of trust was satisfied merely because the possibility that the promissory note in this case would be circulated to a third party was not negated, and on the premise that breach of trust was consummated, it applied the offense of violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (breach of trust) to the facts charged in this case and found the facts charged guilty. The lower judgment contains an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles regarding the degree of protection of breach of trust, the damage element, and the time of consummation.\\n\\nAlthough we agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion that the lower judgment should be reversed, we state this separately because our reasons differ.\\n\\n5. The supplementary opinion of Justices Cho Hee-dae and Kim Jae-hyung as to the majority opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. The separate opinion, premised on the view that breach of trust is a crime of infringement, holds that even if a company’s debt arises from an act assuming obligations in violation of the representative director’s duty or the company bears tort liability under the Civil Code, until such debt is actually performed, only a risk of damage has arisen and not actual damage, and therefore breach of trust has not been consummated.\\n\\nFrom the standpoint of the majority opinion, we add our view on this point.\\n\\nb. Prior precedents have held that damage in breach of trust includes not only cases where actual damage has occurred but also cases where the risk of actual pecuniary loss has been created, but that the risk of actual loss means not a mere risk of damage, but only a case where, from an economic standpoint, a specific and realistic risk has arisen to such an extent that it can be evaluated as equivalent to the occurrence of damage to the principal (see Supreme Court Decisions 2012DO10139 rendered on November 29, 2012, 2015DO6745 rendered on September 10, 2015, among others). In other words, prior precedents themselves did not view the damage element as satisfied whenever an act in violation of duty creates a risk of infringement of the principal’s property rights, but only where a specific and realistic risk has arisen that allows the principal’s property to be evaluated as having been actually infringed, that is, where the risk of actual loss has arisen.\\n\\nHowever, it cannot be said that the risk of actual loss referred to in prior precedents necessarily means the risk referred to in crimes of danger. That is, where a specific and realistic risk has arisen to such an extent that it can be regarded as equivalent to actual infringement of property rights, one may evaluate that there has been actual infringement of the protected legal interest in itself. The reason the precedents have not clearly distinguished between actual damage and the risk of actual loss with respect to the damage element of breach of trust can also be understood in this sense. Therefore, when a specific and realistic risk is caused to the principal’s property, such as when a debt arises due to an act in violation of duty, breach of trust is consummated, and there is no logical basis for varying the time of consummation depending on whether breach of trust is viewed as a crime of infringement or a crime of danger.\\n\\nc. Article 355(1) of the Criminal Act provides that embezzlement is established when a person who keeps another’s property embezzles it or refuses to return it; and Article 355(2) provides that breach of trust is established when a person who handles another’s affairs, by an act in violation of duty, acquires pecuniary gain or causes a third party to acquire such gain, thereby causing damage to the principal. Under the Criminal Act, embezzlement and breach of trust are the same in nature insofar as both are offenses betraying a relationship of trust toward another, but they differ in that embezzlement has property as its object, whereas breach of trust has pecuniary gain as its object. Thus, the Criminal Act limits the object of breach of trust to pecuniary gain and sets as an element of breach of trust the principal’s pecuniary damage corresponding to the actor’s or a third party’s acquisition of pecuniary gain; therefore, the meaning of such pecuniary damage must be understood in relation to pecuniary gain.\\n\\nProperty means tangible objects that can be physically controlled, and thus rights do not fall within property, even if they relate to property. Pecuniary gain, however, means any increase in pecuniary value and does not necessarily presuppose the physical increase or decrease of tangible objects. Since rights concerning property correspond to the pecuniary gain referred to in breach of trust, it is logically reasonable to view the burden of pecuniary obligations imposed on the counterparty by acquiring such rights as also constituting pecuniary damage under breach of trust. This interpretation also conforms to the structure of the Criminal Act, which defines breach of trust as a pure offense of gain. Even so, to say that there is no pecuniary damage whatsoever under Article 355(2) of the Criminal Act until the debt is actually performed is not reasonable, either logically or in light of the structure of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nd. Breach of trust is an offense whose protected legal interest is property rights, and the determination of whether pecuniary damage exists must be made from an economic standpoint, not a legal standpoint, in relation to the principal’s overall property situation. Also, the phrase “caused pecuniary damage,” which is an element of breach of trust, means a case where, viewed holistically, the principal’s property situation is damaged, that is, a reduction in the principal’s overall property value (see Supreme Court Decisions 2004DO7053 rendered on April 15, 2005, 2009DO14268 rendered on April 28, 2011, among others).\\n\\nGenerally, property is divided into positive assets and negative assets, and debts belong to negative assets. The occurrence of debt means an increase in negative assets, which, from an economic standpoint, means a decrease in the overall property value. Since whether pecuniary damage exists in breach of trust must be determined by the increase or decrease in the overall property value, rather than by changes in individual items of property, it is natural to interpret the occurrence of debt as corresponding to damage under Article 355(2) of the Criminal Act. However, precedents have limited the meaning of damage in breach of trust to cases where specific and realistic danger has arisen, in order to reasonably restrict the scope of punishment for breach of trust. Accordingly, where a company’s debt arises from an act assuming obligations in violation of the representative director’s duty, even before that debt is actually performed, pecuniary damage should be deemed to have occurred unless there are special circumstances, because a specific and realistic risk exists.\\n\\nMoreover, from a realistic standpoint, the occurrence of debt and the accompanying increase in negative assets are evaluated as a disadvantage in property or a decrease in property value. In the case of a corporation, bankruptcy may be declared even when liabilities exceed assets (Article 306(1) of the Debtor Rehabilitation and Bankruptcy Act), so the occurrence of debt can bring disadvantage to the corporation irrespective of actual performance of the debt. The fact that excessive indebtedness is prescribed as a ground for bankruptcy can be seen as reflecting the awareness of economically active persons. In addition, an increase in negative assets does not merely remain an item recorded on the liabilities side of the company’s balance sheet, but directly affects the company’s creditworthiness and financial soundness, and in some cases even affects the company’s existence. The occurrence of debt and the resulting increase in negative assets function socially and economically as concrete and realistic disadvantages, and in interpreting breach of trust under the Criminal Act, one cannot say that this, in itself, is not pecuniary damage at all.\\n\\ne. The separate opinion argues that because debt is not always performed even when it arises, it is difficult to say that property rights have been actually infringed merely by the occurrence of debt. However, where a legally valid debt arises, whether the burden of such debt constitutes pecuniary damage or not must be determined by whether the state in which performance of such debt is legally compelled, on the assumption that the debt is normally performed within the legal order, corresponds to damage from an economic standpoint. Therefore, it is not appropriate to assume exceptional cases in which the debt is not performed depending on the debtor’s insolvency or intent to perform, and to conclude on that basis that the occurrence of debt does not constitute pecuniary damage.\\n\\nf. In the case of the Specific Economic Crimes Act, which aggravates the statutory punishment according to the value of pecuniary gain obtained through the act of breach of trust, the problem of applying an aggravated statutory punishment may arise, as pointed out by the separate opinion. However, such a problem arises not only in breach of trust but also in cases where the Specific Economic Crimes Act is applied due to fraud or embezzlement, and thus this is a matter to be resolved by strictly interpreting the “amount gained” under Article 3 of the Specific Economic Crimes Act. Otherwise, if one interprets, as the separate opinion does, that in ordinary breach of trust the damage element is satisfied only when there is an actual movement of property, there is a practical difficulty in punishing as consummated breach of trust, and many cases currently recognized as consummated breach of trust would be punishable only as attempted breach of trust; it must also be pointed out that this raises a concern that the normative force of breach of trust as a property offense would be greatly undermined.\\n\\nThe above is the supplementary opinion as to the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. The supplementary opinion of Justice Park Sang-ok as to the majority opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. The separate opinion argues that Article 355(2) of the Criminal Act concerning breach of trust, unlike other property crimes, provides “when damage is caused,” and unlike the German Criminal Act, separately contains a provision punishing attempts; therefore, according to its wording, breach of trust should be viewed as a crime of infringement, damage should be understood to mean only “actual damage,” and if, contrary to this, one includes the “risk of actual loss,” which is a prior stage to actual damage, the scope of punishment for breach of trust becomes too broad, contrary to the principle of nulla poena sine lege and the principle of responsibility, and the above provision brings about an undesirable result in that it cannot properly fulfill its role as a behavioral norm for the public.\\n\\nb. However, the separate opinion’s argument is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) The separate opinion refers to the interpretive theory of the German Criminal Act, but in the interpretation of the Japanese Criminal Act, which, like our Criminal Act, contains a provision punishing attempts of breach of trust, Japan’s Supreme Court also takes the position that breach of trust is a crime of danger. The reason several countries, despite structural differences in criminal provisions, equally value actual damage and the risk of actual loss is that, if damage is understood from an economic standpoint, it is very natural to recognize the two as equivalent.\\n\\nBreach of trust is a property crime premised on losses and gains arising in the course of property-related transactions, etc. However, in property transactions, there are cases where paying money in advance and demanding counter-performance itself constitutes the offer of a contract and performance of the obligation, while in other cases money is to be paid later and counter-performance is received first; there are also cases where money and counter-performance are exchanged simultaneously. Even when the transactional relationship is in fact void as a matter of law, performance may be rendered according to its appearance without knowing this, and even when the transactional relationship is valid, one may find an excuse and refuse performance while asserting voidness. Since gains and losses in property transactions are understood in such diverse situations, it is not easy to say that giving and receiving money today constitutes loss and gain, while giving and receiving it tomorrow does not. Ultimately, the question of within what scope actual damage and the risk of actual loss are to be regarded as equivalent is a matter of interpreting criminal-law norms based on nulla poena sine lege; from this perspective, the Supreme Court has held that the risk of actual pecuniary loss means a case where a specific and realistic risk has arisen to the extent that, from an economic standpoint, it can be evaluated as equivalent to the occurrence of actual damage, and that mere vague possibility is insufficient (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO6745 rendered on September 10, 2015).\\n\\nThe separate opinion does not deny understanding damage in breach of trust from an economic standpoint, but ultimately, insofar as damage in breach of trust is understood from the economic standpoint of the transaction world, it is consistent with a purposive interpretation of criminal norms to attribute equal value to actual damage and the risk of actual loss, and this is a notion easily accepted in ordinary commercial relations as well. Therefore, to distinguish breach of trust as a crime of infringement or a crime of danger solely by whether there is a provision punishing attempts is an interpretation that does not accord with the elements and protected legal interest of breach of trust.\\n\\n(2) The separate opinion also argues that one of the majority opinion’s principal grounds for viewing breach of trust as a crime of danger rather than a crime of infringement is that, even where only the risk of actual loss has arisen, recognizing consummated breach of trust makes it possible to apply Article 3 of the Specific Economic Crimes Act according to the amount gained and impose aggravated punishment. However, the Specific Economic Crimes Act was enacted on December 31, 1983, whereas our Supreme Court had already held long before that breach of trust is a crime of danger, so the above argument of the separate opinion is difficult to accept as it stands.\\n\\nThat is, in Supreme Court Decision 72DO1366 rendered on November 13, 1973, the Court held that “in the offense of breach of trust in the course of business, the phrase ‘when damage is caused to the principal’ means a decrease in pecuniary value, which includes not only cases where actual pecuniary loss is caused but also cases where the risk of actual loss is created.” Also, in Supreme Court Decision 75DO123 rendered on April 22, 1975, the Court expressly held that breach of trust is not a crime of infringement but a crime of danger; and this Court’s determination continues unchanged to the present, regardless of the enactment of the Specific Economic Crimes Act.\\n\\nAccordingly, there is no doctrinal or logical connection between viewing breach of trust as a crime of danger and applying Article 3 of the Specific Economic Crimes Act.\\n\\n(3) If only actual damage, as in the separate opinion, is regarded as damage, then in cases of breach of trust involving abuse of representative authority, as in this case, the representative director who is the actor of the breach of trust will attempt, in order to avoid liability for consummation, to delay or refuse performance of the debt until criminal liability against himself or herself is finally determined. If the representative director of the company is also a controlling shareholder, the possibility of avoiding consummation liability through measures such as delaying performance through control over the company will increase, so that consummated liability and attempted liability may be established differently depending on the will of the controlling shareholder. In this way, if the question of whether consummated liability arises can differ according to whether the company’s debt is performed, whether there is an intention to perform the debt, or the timing of performance, which are difficult to view as having a direct causal relationship with the act constituting breach of trust, it is doubtful whether the above result produced by the separate opinion accords with the principle of responsibility, and there is concern that it may instead violate fairness.\\n\\n(4) According to the separate opinion, when the actor in breach of trust tries to delay performance of the debt to avoid consummated liability, the question may also arise as to when breach of trust is consummated if the counterparty to the transaction directly attempts forced realization of the claim. Since breach of trust requires acquisition of gain and occurrence of damage, if, for example, a compulsory auction proceeds against company-owned real estate based on an authentic instrument of a loan for consumption, the time of consummation becomes unclear depending on interpretation: whether consummation occurs when the sale price is paid in full and the company loses ownership, when the counterparty receives the dividend, or, if the counterparty does not immediately receive the dividend for personal reasons and receives it one year later, whether consummation occurs then. Therefore, rather, if one follows the separate opinion, due to such uncertainty, the penal sanction provision on breach of trust may fail to properly fulfill its role as a behavioral norm for the public.\\n\\nc. The majority opinion’s assessment of the risk of actual loss as equivalent to actual damage is not intended to expand the scope of criminal punishment, but is a normative interpretation following the understanding of damage from an economic standpoint and accords with nulla poena sine lege and the principle of responsibility. On the contrary, if, as the separate opinion suggests, only performance of the debt is treated as damage, there is concern that it may create instability or fairness problems in criminal justice.\\n\\nThe above is the supplementary opinion as to the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. The supplementary opinion of Justices Kim Chang-seok and Kim Shin as to the separate opinion is as follows.\\n\\nThe majority opinion holds that where an act assuming obligations is void, commencement of execution is recognized, but unless there are circumstances such as that the debt was actually performed or tort liability under the Civil Code was borne as a result, breach of trust has not been consummated. By contrast, where an act assuming obligations is valid, a debt arises and an obligation to perform that debt is borne, so the occurrence of such debt itself is said to constitute actual damage or a risk of actual pecuniary loss, and thus breach of trust is consummated even before the debt is actually performed. This dichotomous interpretive theory has the following fundamental problems.\\n\\na. Viewing consummation of breach of trust as having occurred simultaneously with commencement of execution where an act in violation of duty is valid does not accord with the structure of the Criminal Act provisions, which divide the elements of breach of trust into conduct elements and result elements and contain a provision punishing attempted breach of trust.\\n\\nAlso, considering that attempt and consummation of a crime are a series of processes by which one act is realized as a crime, the recognition of commencement of execution (attempt) and the recognition of consummation should be judged by the same standard, and it is not correct to judge them by different standards.\\n\\nThe majority opinion determines whether there has been commencement of execution from the standpoint of criminal law, irrespective of the civil-law viewpoint of validity or invalidity of the act assuming obligations. On the other hand, whether consummation has been reached is determined, in the case where the act assuming obligations is valid, by civil-law standards; once a legal debt has arisen, consummation is found without further considering whether damage has actually occurred, whereas in the case where the act is void, the determination is made from the criminal-law standpoint of whether actual damage can be said to have occurred. This appears to be based on the view that the realizability of damage is greater where the act assuming obligations is civilly valid and smaller where it is void.\\n\\nHowever, determining consummation on the basis of such vague standards is not persuasive as it contravenes the principle of clarity. Ultimately, even where an act assuming obligations is valid, there are many cases where the obligation is not performed, and even where it is void, there are not a few cases where the obligation is performed. Even if a joint surety act or a payment guarantee act is valid, damage may not materialize because the principal debtor performs the debt; or a promissory note may be validly issued as security for a third party, but damage may not materialize because that third party performs the underlying obligation. It is doubtful whether the majority opinion’s perspective conforms to the prior consistent precedents, which have held that pecuniary damage in breach of trust must be grasped from an economic standpoint, not a legal one. We also note that there is no clear organization on this point.\\n\\nb. Where a person who handles another’s affairs performs an act assuming obligations in violation of duty, it is not clear whether the act is valid or void. In practice, in many cases, legal efficacy cannot easily be predicted until the legal evaluation is fixed through civil litigation, etc.\\n\\nAccording to the majority opinion, unless civil litigation regarding the validity of the act assuming obligations has become final, the criminal court determining whether breach of trust is established has no choice but first to determine the private-law efficacy of the relevant act assuming obligations and then determine whether breach of trust is established. In such a case, there is doubt whether the defendant, who is on criminal trial, can adequately exercise the right of defense regarding the civil factual elements that determine the private-law efficacy of the relevant act assuming obligations, namely the other party’s awareness or the presence or absence of negligence.
