And the final evaluation of the legal efficacy of the act assuming obligations can ultimately be made only through the conclusion of civil litigation; however, since civil litigation governed by the principles of party disposition and adversarial proceedings and criminal litigation prioritizing the discovery of substantive truth do not share the same procedures or even the same ideals, if one were to determine immediately, as the majority opinion does, whether the damage requirement of breach of trust is satisfied according to whether the act assuming obligations is legally effective, numerous difficult problems may arise from the difference between civil and criminal litigation, such as cases where the outcome of civil and criminal litigation differs, for example where a void act assuming obligations is finally confirmed as valid in civil litigation.\\n\\nUltimately, if, as the majority opinion does, one directly links the legal efficacy of an act assuming obligations in violation of duty with whether breach of trust is consummated, the predictability of the establishment of crime or punishability will markedly decline, and the guarantee function of criminal law will be seriously impaired.\\n\\nc. According to the majority opinion, if the counterparty knew or could have known of the abuse of representative authority at the time of the act assuming obligations by abuse of the representative director’s authority, the act is void and in principle cannot reach consummation of breach of trust; if the counterparty did not know of the abuse of representative authority without negligence, the act is valid and immediately reaches consummation of breach of trust. In this way, whether breach of trust is consummated depends on the counterparty’s awareness or the presence or absence of negligence; however, even though this is not an offense such as fraud where the statute expressly provides as an element that the counterparty is deceived and performs a disposition act, it is difficult to accept as an interpretation of criminal law that whether consummation has been reached depends on whether the counterparty had subjective awareness.\\n\\nAlso, when a representative director usually performs an act assuming obligations by abusing representative authority, if the counterparty knew or could have known of the abuse of representative authority, there is often a high likelihood that the illegality or blameworthiness of the act is great, for example because there may be room to regard it as an anti-social legal act. Ultimately, according to the majority opinion, the greater the illegality or blameworthiness of the act assuming obligations, the greater the likelihood that the act will be void, and thus the lower the likelihood that it will be punished as consummated breach of trust. Such a conclusion not only does not accord with the notion of justice, but directly violates the principle of responsibility and the principle of balance between crime and punishment pursued by criminal law.\\n\\nd. What is constitutionally significant in breach of trust is whether the subject of the act falls within a person who handles another’s affairs, whether the act falls within an act in violation of duty, and whether, by the act, the actor or a third party acquired pecuniary gain and thereby caused pecuniary damage to the principal; it is not whether the act is legally valid or void.\\n\\nEven where there is an act in violation of duty, if there is no possibility of pecuniary damage, commencement of execution is not recognized and attempt cannot be established; only when there is a possibility of pecuniary damage is commencement of execution recognized and attempt established; further, only when the possibility of pecuniary damage becomes realized is the constitutive result realized and consummation reached. Even if an act assuming obligations as breach of trust is valid, from a criminal-law standpoint it merely means that there is a possibility of pecuniary damage, and thus the infringement upon property rights as a consummation requirement should be regarded as arising not from the occurrence of debt but from the performance of debt.\\n\\nNevertheless, to say that where a debt arises there is a risk that the debt will be performed or that property value has decreased in itself, and therefore the damage requirement of breach of trust is satisfied and consummated breach of trust should be punished, is ultimately to interpret the penal provision in a way contrary to its wording and structure, and thus violates nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\ne. The majority opinion holds that where a representative director abuses representative authority to issue a promissory note, and the issuance is void, breach of trust is consummated if the promissory note is circulated to a third party and the company’s note debt arises, even if the company does not actually perform the note debt. However, in such a case, circulation of the promissory note to a third party occurs through a separate note act by the payee, so if the time of circulation of the promissory note to a third party is taken as the time of consummation of breach of trust, the time of consummation is determined not by the actor in breach of trust but by the conduct of the counterparty, which is a highly awkward result as an interpretation of the penal provision.\\n\\nBy contrast, if breach of trust is constituted as a crime of infringement, as in the separate opinion, then even in a case involving issuance of a promissory note, consummation occurs at the time when the company actually performs the note debt, etc., and thus attempt and consummation can be distinguished according to a clear standard consistent with the elements of breach of trust.\\n\\nLikewise, in cases involving acts assuming obligations such as suretyship or payment guarantees, if breach of trust is constituted as a crime of infringement, attempt or consummation of breach of trust is determined by distinguishing between the risk as the possibility that the debt will be performed and the damage arising from actual performance of the debt. The same applies to other acts assuming obligations. Risks may be realized, or they may remain latent and then disappear. A latent risk corresponds to attempt, and a realized risk constitutes consummation as an infringement upon the protected legal interest. Accordingly, since only the actual amount of damage in cases where consummation has been established is treated as the amount gained under Article 3 of the Specific Economic Crimes Act, the problems arising in connection with its application are neatly resolved.\\n\\nf. There is no disagreement between the majority opinion and the separate opinion that, where a risk arising from an act in violation of duty is realized and damage occurs, breach of trust is consummated. There will likely also be no disagreement that where there is an act in violation of duty but no risk that can be regarded as latent, attempt cannot be established either. The point at which opinions diverge is where one is in a state of latent risk before the risk is realized.\\n\\nThe majority opinion would evaluate as consummation, to the defendant’s disadvantage, where the act in violation of duty is valid, and as attempt, to the defendant’s advantage, where it is void. The separate opinion, because there is no substantive and fundamental reason to evaluate the state of latent risk differently depending on whether the act in violation of duty is valid or void, would evaluate, to the defendant’s advantage, as attempt in either case. Such interpretation accords with the elements of breach of trust, which are divided into attempt and consummation, as well as with the principles of criminal law interpretation.\\n\\nThe above is the supplementary opinion as to the separate opinion."}

{"[2020DO6258]": "The grounds for appeal are examined (however, with respect to the breach of trust portion concerning the Victim, Non-party 1, it is examined ex officio).\\n\\n1. Each breach of trust portion concerning Victim, Non-party 2 Co., Ltd.\\n   a. 1) Breach of trust is established when a person who handles another’s affairs, by an act in violation of his or her duty, acquires a pecuniary benefit or causes a third party to acquire such benefit, thereby causing damage to the other, who is the subject of the affairs. Therefore, the offender must be in a position of handling another’s affairs. Here, in order to qualify as a “person who handles another’s affairs,” the person must be engaged in protecting or managing another’s property based on a relationship of trust between the parties, beyond the ordinary adversarial relationship of a typical contract, such as where the person performs on behalf of another all or part of the affairs concerning the management of another’s property. In an ordinary contractual relationship involving opposing interests, the fact that the other party obtains the benefit of satisfaction of contractual rights or realization of claims through the obligor’s faithful performance of the obligation, or that there exists an incidental duty to protect or care for the other party in the course of performance of the contract, does not make the obligor a person who handles another’s affairs; the case must be one in which the typical and essential content of the contract’s performance corresponds to undertaking and handling the other party’s property affairs with a certain authority, as in an entrustment, etc. (See, e.g., the Supreme Court en banc decision rendered on February 20, 2020 in 2019DO9756).\\n   2) Even in a creditor-debtor relationship involving monetary claims and debts, although the creditor lends money based on trust in the debtor’s performance and obtains the benefit of satisfaction of the claim through the debtor’s faithful performance, it cannot be said that the creditor has, on the basis of trust in the debtor, assigned him the duty to protect or manage the creditor’s property, and the performance of a monetary debt is, in any event, conducted by the debtor as the performance of his own obligation. Thus, this cannot be regarded as the debtor’s handling of the creditor’s affairs. Accordingly, the debtor cannot be deemed, in relation to the creditor, to be a “person who handles another’s affairs.”\\n   The same applies even where, in order to secure a monetary debt, the debtor agrees to grant the creditor a mortgage over movable property owned by him under the Act on Mortgage over Specific Movable Property, etc., or has actually created such mortgage. The obligations borne by the debtor under the mortgage creation contract, namely, the obligation to provide the movable property as security, the passive obligation to maintain and preserve the collateral’s secured value and not to damage, diminish, or extinguish the collateral, and the obligation to cooperate with the creditor’s exercise of the security right, such as the obligation to actually deliver the collateral to the creditor or a person designated by the creditor when the security right is enforced, are all the debtor’s own obligations of performance incurred under the mortgage creation contract. In addition, a mortgage creation contract is an ancillary contract to the contract giving rise to the secured claim, and when the secured debt is extinguished, the rights and obligations under the mortgage creation contract are also extinguished. Since the obligations borne by the debtor under the mortgage creation contract are for the purpose of securing the collateral, that is, realizing the claim through enforcement of the security right in the event of default, the typical and essential content of the parties’ relationship, whether before or after the conclusion of the mortgage creation contract or the creation of the mortgage, remains the realization of the monetary claim or the repayment of the secured debt (See, e.g., the Supreme Court en banc decision rendered on August 27, 2020 in 2019DO14770).\\n   Therefore, the debtor’s performance of the above-mentioned obligations of performance pertains only to the debtor’s own affairs, and the debtor cannot be viewed as undertaking and handling the creditor’s affairs on the basis of a relationship of trust with the creditor beyond the ordinary contractual relationship of opposing interests; accordingly, the debtor cannot be deemed, in relation to the creditor, to be a “person who handles another’s affairs,” who is the subject of the crime of breach of trust. Thus, even if the debtor disposes of the collateral to a third party and thereby reduces or extinguishes its secured value, causing risk to the creditor’s exercise of the security right or the realization of the claim through such exercise, breach of trust is not established.\\n   3) The foregoing legal principles apply equally to a case where the debtor freely disposes of movable property over which a mortgage has been created pursuant to the Act on Mortgages over Factories and Mining Foundations in order to secure a monetary debt, to a third party.\\n   4) To the extent that Supreme Court decisions, including Supreme Court Decision 2003DO67 rendered on July 11, 2003 and Supreme Court Decision 2010DO11665 rendered on September 13, 2012, which held that breach of trust is established when a debtor who has created a mortgage or factory mortgage over movable property in favor of a creditor for the purpose of securing a debt disposes of the collateral on the premise that the debtor falls within “a person who handles another’s affairs,” are contrary to the view of this decision, they are all modified.\\n\\n   b. In light of the foregoing legal principles, the lower court’s judgment on the above breach of trust portion is examined.\\n   1) The gist of this portion of the charges is that, while the Defendant borrowed from Victim, Non-party 2 Co., Ltd. funds for the purchase of a ○○ Bus and a △△△△ Bus and created a mortgage over each of the above buses, the Defendant had a duty to keep each of the buses in accordance with the purpose of the security, but by disposing of them acquired a pecuniary benefit and caused property damage to the Victim. The lower court upheld the trial court’s judgment that found this portion of the charges guilty.\\n   2) However, in light of the foregoing legal principles, even if a mortgage was created over the above buses for the purpose of securing the debt to the Victim, unless the Defendant can be deemed, on the basis of a relationship of trust with the Victim, to be handling the Victim’s affairs, the Defendant cannot be regarded, in relation to the Victim, as a “person who handles another’s affairs” within the meaning of the crime of breach of trust. Accordingly, even if the Defendant disposed of the above buses as stated in the charges, breach of trust is not established. Nevertheless, the lower court, contrary to this, found this portion of the charges guilty on the premise that the Defendant had the duty to keep the above buses in accordance with the purpose of the security until repayment of the debt to the Victim and thus occupied the position of a person who handles another’s affairs. The lower court judgment contains an error by misapprehending the legal principles concerning “a person who handles another’s affairs” in the crime of breach of trust.\\n\\n2. Breach of trust portion concerning Victim, Non-party 1\\n   a. In the case of a contract, such as a sale, whose effect arises by one party agreeing to transfer a property right to the other party and the other party agreeing to pay the price therefor (Article 563 of the Civil Act), the debt that both parties are to perform in accordance with the content of the contract is, as a matter of principle, “one’s own affairs,” absent special circumstances. Since the seller in a contract for the sale of movable property is not in the position of handling the buyer’s affairs, breach of trust under criminal law is not established even if the seller disposes of the subject property to another (See, e.g., the Supreme Court en banc decision rendered on January 20, 2011 in 2008DO10479).\\n   The foregoing legal principles apply equally to a contract for the sale of movable property requiring registration or recordation for the transfer of rights. Accordingly, a seller of an automobile, etc. is not in the position of handling the buyer’s affairs, and thus even if the seller disposes of the automobile, etc. to another without completing the registration of transfer of ownership to the buyer, breach of trust is likewise not established.\\n\\n   b. In light of the foregoing legal principles, the lower court’s judgment on the above breach of trust portion is examined.\\n   1) The gist of this portion of the charges is that the Defendant agreed to sell one △△△△ Bus to Victim, Non-party 1 for KRW 36,000,000 and, despite having received KRW 20,000,000 from the Victim in the name of a down payment and intermediate payment, granted a joint mortgage right over the bus to Non-party 3 Credit Union, thereby causing the Credit Union to acquire a pecuniary benefit and causing damage to the Victim. The lower court upheld the trial court’s judgment that found this portion of the charges guilty.\\n   2) However, in light of the foregoing legal principles, even if the Defendant bore an obligation toward the Victim to register the transfer of ownership of the above bus, such obligation is merely the Defendant’s own affairs under the above sales contract, and unless the Defendant can be deemed, on the basis of a relationship of trust with the Victim, to be handling the Victim’s affairs, the Defendant cannot be regarded, in relation to the Victim, as a “person who handles another’s affairs” within the meaning of the crime of breach of trust. Accordingly, even if the Defendant created a joint mortgage right over the above bus as stated in the charges, breach of trust is not established. Nevertheless, the lower court found this portion of the charges guilty on the premise that the Defendant fell within that category. The lower court judgment contains an error by misapprehending the legal principles concerning “a person who handles another’s affairs” in the crime of breach of trust.\\n\\n3. The portions concerning violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Fraud), fraud, forgery of private document and utterance thereof, with respect to Victim, Non-party 4; each fraud portion with respect to Victim, Non-party 5 and Victim, Non-party 6; and obstruction of exercise of rights with respect to Victim, Yeosu Jungbu Saemaeul Credit Union\\nThe lower court found each of these portions of the charges guilty for the reasons stated in its opinion. Examining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the duly admitted evidence, there is no error in the lower court’s determination that violated the rules of logic and experience and exceeded the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehended the legal principles concerning the deceptive act and intent to obtain by fraud in the crime of fraud, and the intent in the crime of obstruction of exercise of rights.\\n\\n4. Scope of reversal\\nFor the reasons stated above, the portions concerning breach of trust against Victim, Non-party 2 Co., Ltd. and against Victim, Non-party 1 in the lower court judgment must be reversed. However, since the lower court sentenced a single punishment on the ground that these portions and the remaining guilty portions are in a concurrent offense relationship under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, all of the guilty portions of the lower court judgment must ultimately be reversed.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds for appeal, the guilty portions of the lower court judgment are reversed, and this case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination on these portions. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the judges who participated."}

{"[81DO3009]": "We consider the grounds of appeal by the defense counsel for the Defendant.\\n\\n(1) In the offense of embezzlement, the intent of unlawful appropriation means the intent of a person who holds another’s property in custody, in contravention of the purpose of the entrustment, and without authority, to engage in an act of disposal by the owner of the property (including refusal to return it); therefore, where the custodian disposes of it not for the benefit of himself or a third person, but for the benefit of the owner, such intent of unlawful appropriation cannot be recognized unless there are special circumstances (see, respectively, 65DO735, decided on 1965.10.5., and 79DO2171, decided on 1980.10.14., of this Court).\\n\\n(2) Looking at the reasons for the first-instance judgment sustained by the court below in this case, the first instance found that the Defendant, as the Head of the General Affairs Section of Hyesung Women’s Commercial Training School affiliated with Hyesung Foundation, when paying the teachers’ monthly salaries and retirement allowances out of the salary funds owned by the said foundation, which were in custody in the course of business as stated in the judgment, entered the amounts in the payroll payment statements and retirement allowance payment statements at higher figures than the actual amounts paid, withdrew the difference, and embezzled it, and then convicted and punished the Defendant for embezzlement in the course of business.\\n\\nHowever, according to the record, from the time of the investigation by the investigative authorities, the Defendant has denied the intent of unlawful appropriation, asserting that, because the said school was a special training school and the number of new students fell short of the enrollment quota, the school had teachers engage in new-student recruitment activities, and that the said difference in payment amounts stated in the above judgment was used for those expenses with the understanding of foundation directors and the school principal, etc. At the first-instance testimony of Kim Sang-bok, who had served as the principal of the said school at the time, he made statements consistent with the Defendant’s above explanation. In addition, according to the first-instance testimony of witness Jo Pil-yeon and the statement record of Kim Yoon prepared by a judicial police officer acting in that capacity, it is recognized that the teachers of the said school carried out student recruitment activities as alleged in the Defendant’s explanation and received expenses from the school. Nor can any material be found in the record to conclude that such testimony or statements are not credible.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below disregarded the above evidence and, without basis, recognized that the Defendant had the intent of unlawful appropriation with respect to the entirety of the above payment difference, and thus, by neglecting the evaluation of evidence, found facts without evidence and erred in misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning the intent of unlawful appropriation; therefore, the argument on this point is well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the Collegiate Division of the Seoul Criminal District Court for retrial, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices as ordered."}

question:
A was residing with spouse B in the X apartment owned by A, and around March 2024, after quarreling over B’s infidelity and, in order to find evidence of B’s affair, secretly installed surveillance CCTV in the living room, then left the apartment and temporarily stayed at a nearby motel. Meanwhile, by the automatic recording function of the CCTV, the contents of a call between B and paramour A were recorded and stored. Around April 2024, A went to the X apartment together with his father C, and upon learning that the electronic lock password for the entrance door had been changed, jointly broke the electronic lock by force and entered. While searching the CCTV recording files, A discovered the above recording file of the conversation between B and A and listened to it together with C. Among the explanations concerning this case, which are all the incorrect ones? (If there is a dispute, according to precedents)

(a) A’s act of breaking the electronic lock and entering the X apartment constitutes an act infringing the legal interest of the co-occupant B’s de facto peace of dwelling, but because the X apartment is owned by A and does not constitute the dwelling of another, the crime of trespass upon a dwelling is not established against A.  
(b) The X apartment constitutes the dwelling of another as against C, and because the act of entering the X apartment by exercising physical force, such as damaging the electronic lock, impaired the de facto state of peace of co-occupant B of the X apartment, the crime of trespass upon a dwelling is established against C.  
(c) C’s act of listening to the file recording the conversation between B and A cannot be viewed as the act of listening to a conversation between others that is not publicly disclosed, which is prohibited by the Communications Secret Protection Act.  
(d) Even if the contents of the conversation between B and A had a public character, or even if one of B and A were a public figure, it can be viewed as an undisclosed conversation between others as provided by the Communications Secret Protection Act.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2020DO1538]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Summary of the Charges at Issue\\nThe gist of the charges at issue is that the Defendant, who was the homeroom teacher of the victim child and a person obligated to report child abuse crimes under the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Child Abuse Crimes, committed emotional abuse acts harmful to the victim child's mental health and development 14 times, by saying to the victim child from around 2018. 3. 14. to around 2018. 5. 8., \"You are like a child who has not even attended school. Did you really go to school over there? You went to 1st and 2nd grades, you were never taught to turn pages in a book during study time, you were not trained at all in learning, it seems you did not study at all in 1st and 2nd grades and only came and went,\" as set forth in Nos. 1 through 3, 5 through 8, and 10 through 16 of the separate crime list attached to the judgment of the court below.\\n\\n2. The Court Below's Determination\\nThe court below, for the following reasons, admitted the evidentiary admissibility of the audio files recorded by the victim child's parents by placing a voice recorder in the victim child's bag and recording the Defendant's statements made in the classroom during class, transcripts thereof, etc. (hereinafter referred to as \"the audio files, etc. in this case\"), and, taking them as evidence of guilt, found the charges at issue to be proven.\\n\\na. The Defendant made statements to about 30 students, and elementary school education, which aims at basic education necessary for everyday life, has a public nature; therefore, the Defendant's statements made in the classroom during class do not constitute a \"conversation not publicly disclosed\" under Article 14(1) of the Protection of Communications Secrets Act.\\n\\nb. The victim child's parents and the victim child have a close personal relationship.\\n\\nc. The victim child's parents resorted to recording in order to prevent the Defendant's child abuse acts, there was no other effective and appropriate means besides recording to protect the victim child, and the child abuse crime committed by the Defendant is of grave social harm, so the need to collect evidence concerning it is recognized. Even if using the audio files, etc. in this case as evidence results in a certain degree of infringement of the Defendant's secrecy of private life, this constitutes a restriction on fundamental rights that the Defendant must endure.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court's Determination\\na. Relevant Legal Principles\\nArticle 14(1) of the Protection of Communications Secrets Act provides that \"No one shall record conversations between other persons that have not been made public, or listen to them by using electronic devices or mechanical means,\" and Articles 14(2) and 4 provide, to the effect that \"The contents of a conversation obtained by recording in violation of Article 14(1) may not be used as evidence in a trial or disciplinary proceedings.\"\\n\\nThe fact that Article 14(1) of the Protection of Communications Secrets Act prohibits the recording or listening to conversations between other persons that have not been made public means that a third party who did not originally participate in the conversation may not record or listen, by using electronic devices or mechanical means, to remarks made between other persons that have not been made public so as to be known to the general public. Here, \"not been made public\" does not necessarily mean the same as secret, but means not made public to the general public; whether something has been made public in a specific case must be determined by comprehensively considering objective circumstances such as the speaker's intent and expectations, the content and purpose of the conversation, the number of persons on the other side, the nature and scale of the place, the degree of access control, and restrictions on the qualifications of the audience (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2020DO1007, decided on 2022. 8. 31.).\\n\\nb. Adding to the above legal principles the circumstances found by the reasons of the judgment of the court below and by the record, the audio files, etc. in this case should be deemed to lack evidentiary admissibility under Articles 14(2) and 4 of the Protection of Communications Secrets Act.\\n\\n1) The Defendant's statements made during class, secretly recorded by the victim child's parents, constitute a \"conversation not publicly disclosed.\"\\n\\na) A homeroom teacher's statements made in the classroom during class at an elementary school are ordinarily directed only to the students in the classroom, and are thus merely made public to the students in the classroom, not to the general public or an unspecified number of persons. This is because an elementary school classroom is a space with controlled access, is not a place where an unspecified number of persons may come and go during class, and it is difficult to envisage a non-student third party attending an elementary school classroom during class without any special procedure and listening to the content of the homeroom teacher's statements. There are also no circumstances indicating that the Defendant intended, or accepted the risk of, disclosure to third parties other than the students in the classroom.\\n\\nb) The Defendant's statements were made public only to the specified 30 students and were not made public to the general public or an unspecified number of persons, so they cannot be characterized as a \"public conversation\" merely because the conversation involved a large number of speakers or listeners. Whether the content of the conversation has a public character, or whether the speaker is a public figure, does not affect whether it constitutes a \"conversation not publicly disclosed.\"\\n\\n2) The Defendant's statements made during class, secretly recorded by the victim child's parents, constitute a \"conversation between other persons.\" This is because the victim child's parents were not the other party to the Defendant's statements during class, that is, they were not originally parties participating in the conversation. Even considering the victim child's age and the fact that the victim child's parents are persons with parental authority and legal representatives of the victim child, since the parents are separate persons from the victim child, they can only be regarded as third parties who did not participate in the conversation.\\n\\n3) Ultimately, because the audio files, etc. in this case record conversations between other persons that were not made public in violation of Article 14(1) of the Protection of Communications Secrets Act, they should be deemed to lack evidentiary admissibility under Articles 14(2) and 4 of the Protection of Communications Secrets Act. In light of the constitutional provisions declaring the inviolability of privacy and communications as one of the people's fundamental rights, and in light of the purpose of the Protection of Communications Secrets Act, which was enacted to protect the secrecy of communications and conversations and to promote the freedom of communications and conversations, the circumstances cited by the court below cannot justify admitting the evidentiary admissibility of the audio files, etc. in this case.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below admitted the evidentiary admissibility of the audio files, etc. in this case solely on the grounds stated in its opinion; in doing so, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning Articles 14(2) and 4 of the Protection of Communications Secrets Act, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\n4. Scope of Reversal\\nFor the foregoing reasons, the portion of the judgment of the court below concerning the charges at issue must be reversed. However, since the above reversed portion is in a relation of single offense with the portion that the court below found not guilty in the reasons, the judgment of the court below must ultimately be reversed in its entirety.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged as stated in the Disposition by unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2020DO6085]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Scope of this Court’s review\\n\\nAmong the facts charged in this case, with respect to the violation of the Act on the Punishment of Violent Acts, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Violent Acts Punishment Act”) against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 (joint infliction of bodily injury), the first-instance court rendered an acquittal, and although the Prosecutor appealed, the lower appellate court dismissed the appeal. Since the Prosecutor did not appeal against that ruling, this part became final. Accordingly, as to Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, only the remaining parts, excluding the parts already finally acquitted, are subject to review by this Court; thus, we will examine only the grounds of appeal concerning those parts.\\n\\n2. Outline of the case and issues\\n\\na. The gist of the facts charged subject to review is as follows.\\n\\nDefendant 1 is the husband of Non-Indicted 1 and the brother-in-law of Non-Indicted 2, and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 are the parents of Defendant 1 and the parents-in-law of Non-Indicted 1.\\n\\n1) Violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.)\\n\\nThe Defendants went to the apartment at issue, the residence of victim Non-Indicted 1, at around 14:30 on May 19, 2018, and demanded that the entrance door be opened. However, victim Non-Indicted 1 was out, and her younger sibling, Non-Indicted 2, placed the chain latch installed on the entrance door and refused to open the door, saying, “Come back when my sister returns home.” Accordingly, Defendant 1 and Defendant 2, acting jointly, Defendant 1 inserted his hand through the open gap and repeatedly struck the chain latch downward, and Defendant 2 continuously shook the doorknob, causing the chain latch installed on the entrance door to detach from the door.\\n\\nThrough this, Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 damaged the chain latch, owned by victim Non-Indicted 1 and of an unknown amount, thereby impairing its utility.\\n\\n2) Violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence)\\n\\nThe Defendants, acting jointly, after damaging the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the residence where victim Non-Indicted 2 was staying at the date and place stated in 1), entered by intrusion.\\n\\nb. The lower appellate court held as follows.\\n\\n1) With respect to the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.) by Defendant 1 and Defendant 2, it upheld the first-instance judgment that found them guilty.\\n\\n2) With respect to the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) by Defendant 1, it held that the residence that is the object of the offense of intrusion upon residence under the Criminal Act is limited to a residence occupied by another person, and where the actor is a person living together with another person, unless he has withdrawn from the joint living relationship, the relevant residence does not constitute the object of this offense. On the ground that Defendant 1 could not be deemed to have withdrawn from the status of a joint resident of the apartment at issue at the time of this case, it determined that the offense of intrusion upon residence was not established, reversed the first-instance judgment that had found him guilty, and rendered an acquittal.\\n\\n3) With respect to the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, it held that where there are multiple persons entitled to reside, if the consent of one person is directly or indirectly contrary to the will of another resident, entry into the residence thereby impairs the peace of residence of the person whose will is opposed, that is, the tranquility of control and management of the residence, and thus the offense of intrusion upon residence is established. On the ground that even if Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 entered the apartment at issue with the consent of Defendant 1, who was a co-resident of the apartment at issue, they did not obtain the consent of Non-Indicted 1, another resident, or of victim Non-Indicted 2, who had been entrusted by Non-Indicted 1 with control over entry to the residence, and thereby disturbed the factual peace of victim Non-Indicted 2’s residence, it upheld the first-instance judgment that found them guilty.\\n\\nc. The gist of the grounds for appeal by the Prosecutor and the Defendants is as follows.\\n\\n1) Grounds for appeal by the Prosecutor\\n\\nDefendant 1 had withdrawn from the apartment at issue and lost his status as a co-resident, and since he entered the apartment at issue together with Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 by using force, the offense of intrusion upon residence is established. Nevertheless, the lower appellate judgment, which held otherwise and determined that the offense of intrusion upon residence was not established, is erroneous in that it exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehended the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence.\\n\\n2) Grounds for appeal by the Defendants\\n\\na) With respect to the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.) by Defendant 1 and Defendant 2\\n\\nDefendant 1 and Defendant 2 did not in fact damage the chain latch as stated in the facts charged in this part, and they also had no intent to do so. Even if not, the acts of the above Defendants constitute self-help or a justified act. Nevertheless, the lower appellate judgment, which determined this part of the facts charged to be guilty, contains an error of exceeding the limits of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.), justified act, and self-help.\\n\\nb) With respect to the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\n(1) Where a person enters a joint residence with the consent of one of the co-residents, the offense of intrusion upon residence is not established, unless there are special circumstances such as entry for the purpose of committing a crime against another resident. Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 entered the apartment at issue with the consent of Defendant 1, who was a co-resident of the apartment at issue, and they did not enter for the purpose of committing a crime against Non-Indicted 1, another resident, or victim Non-Indicted 2; thus, the offense of intrusion upon residence is not established against the above Defendants.\\n\\n(2) Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 had no intent to intrude upon the residence, and the acts of the above Defendants constitute a justified act under Article 20 of the Criminal Act or self-help under Article 23 of the Criminal Act, which excludes unlawfulness.\\n\\n(3) Nevertheless, the lower appellate judgment, which found this part of the facts charged against the above Defendants to be guilty, contains an error of misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence, justified act, and self-help.\\n\\nd. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nThe offense of intrusion upon residence protects the factual peace and tranquility of the residence. Since intrusion, the constituent act of the offense of intrusion upon residence, must be interpreted in relation to the protected legal interest of the offense, intrusion means entering a residence in a manner that undermines the factual peaceful state enjoyed by the resident in the residence. As a general rule, whether an act constitutes intrusion is to be determined based on the objective and outwardly manifested manner of the act at the time of entry. If entry into a residence is in a manner that undermines factual peace and tranquility, it will, barring special circumstances, be contrary to the resident’s will; however, the mere subjective circumstance that the resident does not want the simple act of entering the residence does not immediately mean intrusion [see Supreme Court En Banc Decision 2020DO12630, decided on 2021. 9. 9.].\\n\\ne. The main issues in this case are as follows.\\n\\n1) Premise for discussion\\n\\nThis case concerns a situation in which Defendant 1, who was a co-resident of the apartment at issue, and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, his parents and the parents-in-law of another co-resident, Non-Indicted 1, entered the apartment at issue, and victim Non-Indicted 2, who was staying inside the apartment at the entrustment of Non-Indicted 1, prohibited Defendant 1 from entering by placing a chain latch on the entrance door of the apartment at issue and refusing to open the door, thereby engaging in physical force by damaging the chain latch, etc. In light of the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the Defendants’ conduct at the time of entry into the apartment at issue, it may be regarded as corresponding to a case that undermines the factual state of peace of victim Non-Indicted 2.\\n\\n2) The main issues in this case\\n\\na) The first issue is whether, where one of the co-residents enters a joint residence in a manner that undermines the factual peace and tranquility of another co-resident who has prohibited his entry, the offense of intrusion upon residence is established even if such conduct can be evaluated as constituting a general manner of use of a joint residence.\\n\\nb) The second issue is whether, where one of the co-residents, in entering a joint residence by exercising physical force against another co-resident who has prohibited his entry into the joint residence, has an outsider join in such conduct and enter the joint residence together in a manner that undermines the factual peace and tranquility of the other co-resident who has prohibited their entry, the offense of intrusion upon residence is established against the outsider if such conduct corresponds to the ordinary act of using the joint residence by the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry, or to an act incidental thereto.\\n\\n3. Determination on the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal\\n\\na. With respect to the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) by Defendant 1\\n\\n1) The Criminal Act provides in Article 319(1) that “a person who intrudes upon another person’s residence, managed structure, ship, aircraft, or occupied room” shall be punished for the offense of intrusion upon residence. The offense of intrusion upon residence is established where a person other than the resident of the residence, manager of the structure, ship, or aircraft, or occupier of the room (hereinafter referred to as “resident, etc.”) intrudes upon the relevant residence, structure, ship, aircraft, or room (hereinafter referred to as “residence, etc.”). Accordingly, the object of the offense of intrusion upon residence is a residence, etc. occupied by another person, that is, “another person,” and therefore even if the actor himself freely enters a residence, etc. that he occupies or manages or possesses alone or jointly with another person, it does not constitute the offense of intrusion upon residence. Only where there are special circumstances, such as when a person who used to reside in a residence together with another person or manage a structure jointly with another person withdraws from the joint living relationship or loses factual control and management over the residence, etc., can the offense of intrusion upon residence be established.\\n\\nIn this context, the Supreme Court accepted a lower court judgment that held that, because the residence shared by the victim and the defendant did not constitute another person’s residence, the offense of intrusion upon residence was not established even if the defendant entered that residence [see Supreme Court Decision 2010DO16537, decided on 2012. 12. 27.], and also held that the offense of intrusion upon a structure is not established even if one of the joint possessors freely enters a structure under joint management [see Supreme Court Decision 81DO2956, decided on 1982. 4. 27.].\\n\\n2) On the other hand, since the offense of intrusion upon residence protects the factual peace and tranquility of the residence, each co-resident living in a joint residence can be said to enjoy the factual peace and tranquility of the residence. However, because each co-resident, barring special circumstances, may use the common space by entering the part of the joint residence set as the place of shared living in accordance with the purpose and nature of the joint residential relationship, each co-resident also has a duty to tolerate other co-residents entering and using it. That is also the general form in which a co-resident uses a joint residence. In this way, the legal interest of factual peace and tranquility that each co-resident enjoys at the place of shared living is inevitably limited to a certain extent by the relationship among co-residents, and it must be understood that co-residents formed the joint residential relationship while mutually tolerating such circumstances. Therefore, as between co-residents, barring special circumstances, one co-resident cannot prohibit another co-resident from freely entering and using the place of shared living.\\n\\nWhere one of the co-residents, without legal grounds or other justifiable reason, prohibits another co-resident from entering the place of shared living, even if the other co-resident enters the place of shared living in resistance thereto, this is merely a means of using the place of shared living in accordance with the purpose and nature of the joint residence that had been pre-consented to, and it cannot be regarded as an act infringing the legal interest of factual peace and tranquility of the co-resident who prohibited his entry. Therefore, the offense of intrusion upon residence is not established. Even if the co-resident, in order to enter the place of shared living, exercises some physical force, such as damaging the lock on the entrance door, and thereby undermines the factual peaceful state of the co-resident who prohibited his entry, aside from the possibility of punishment under a separate provision that punishes such conduct itself, the offense of intrusion upon residence is likewise not established.\\n\\n3) The lower appellate court held that the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) is not established against Defendant 1 based on the following facts and reasons.\\n\\na) Facts found by the lower appellate court\\n\\n(1) Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 are a legally married couple who were married on September 5, 2015, and they have one child between them; they had been living as a married couple in the apartment at issue since around August 15, 2016.\\n\\n(2) Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 began to quarrel frequently from around January 2018 over the sale of a newly built apartment, and Defendant 1 quarreled with Non-Indicted 1 on April 9, 2018, packed some of his belongings, and left the apartment at issue. On April 13, 2018, Defendant 1 went to the apartment at issue, quarreled again with Non-Indicted 1, and left the home. Thereafter, Non-Indicted 1 unilaterally changed the password for the entrance door of the apartment at issue and also attached a chain latch to the entrance door.\\n\\n(3) Through a mobile messenger, Defendant 1 requested Non-Indicted 1 on April 17, 2018 and April 19, 2018 to inform him of the password for the entrance door of the apartment at issue, and on May 4, 2018, he also went to the apartment at issue and requested at the entrance that the door be opened, but he was refused.\\n\\n(4) On June 28, 2018, after the incident in this case, Non-Indicted 1 filed a divorce action with the court, and on September 4, 2018, a divorce mediation was reached between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1.\\n\\nb) Reasons for the lower appellate court’s determination\\n\\nAt the time of this case, it is difficult to find that there was an explicit agreement between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 to liquidate the marital relationship and for Defendant 1 to leave the apartment at issue, which was the joint residence, and live elsewhere. In such circumstances, the mere fact that Defendant 1 packed some of his belongings and left the apartment, or that Non-Indicted 1 unilaterally changed the password for the entrance door and prevented Defendant 1 from entering, is insufficient to find that Defendant 1 withdrew from or was excluded from the status of co-resident. Accordingly, even if Defendant 1 used means such as damaging the chain latch installed on the entrance door while entering the apartment at issue, the offense of intrusion upon residence is not established.\\n\\n4) The reasons for the lower appellate judgment, in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, are examined.\\n\\nThe evidence submitted by the Prosecutor alone is insufficient to find that Defendant 1 withdrew from the joint living relationship in the apartment at issue or lost control and management over it, and there is no other evidence to support such finding. Furthermore, it is not found that Non-Indicted 1, who was a co-resident of the apartment at issue, or victim Non-Indicted 2, to whom Non-Indicted 1 had entrusted entry control over the apartment at issue, had legal grounds or other justifiable reason to prohibit Defendant 1, who was a co-resident of the apartment at issue, from entering the apartment at issue.\\n\\nIf that is so, it cannot be said that the offense of intrusion upon residence is established merely because Defendant 1, who continued to maintain the status of co-resident of the apartment at issue, exercised physical force by damaging the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the apartment at issue in resistance to the measures by victim Non-Indicted 2 prohibiting his entry without justifiable reason in the course of entering the apartment at issue. The lower appellate court’s determination to the same effect contains no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in that it exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehended the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence.\\n\\nb. With respect to the remaining part concerning Defendant 1\\n\\nMeanwhile, although the Prosecutor appealed in full against the part concerning Defendant 1 in the lower appellate judgment, the petition of appeal or the statement of reasons for appeal did not contain any specific grounds of objection concerning the part of the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.) that the lower appellate court found guilty.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Defendants’ grounds for appeal\\n\\na. With respect to the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.) by Defendant 1 and Defendant 2\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower appellate judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, the finding of guilt on this part of the facts charged is deemed proper. Therefore, the lower appellate court’s determination contains no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in that it exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehended the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.), self-help, and justified act.\\n\\nb. With respect to the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\n1) Each co-resident living in a joint residence can enjoy the factual peace and tranquility of the residence; therefore, where an outsider enters the joint residence with the consent of one of the co-residents in a manner that undermines the factual peaceful state of another co-resident, it may also be viewed as constituting the offense of intrusion upon residence in that it infringes the factual peace and tranquility of the other co-resident’s residence.\\n\\nHowever, each co-resident, barring special circumstances, may not only enter and use the place of shared living in the joint residence in accordance with the purpose and nature of the joint residential relationship, but must also tolerate other co-residents entering and using it. In this way, the legal interest of factual peace and tranquility that each co-resident enjoys at the place of shared living is inevitably limited to a certain extent by the relationship among co-residents, and it must be understood that co-residents formed the joint residential relationship while mutually tolerating such circumstances. If that is so, acts in which co-residents ordinarily enter and use the place of shared living within the scope mutually tolerated cannot be regarded as acts infringing the peace and tranquility of another co-resident’s residence, even if the manner of the act may be viewed as undermining the factual peaceful state of another co-resident, and therefore the offense of intrusion upon residence is not established. Whether an outsider’s entry into the place of shared living pursuant to the consent of one co-resident can be regarded as an act infringing the peace and tranquility of another co-resident’s residence must also be examined from this perspective.\\n\\n2) The content and scope of the ordinary acts of entering and using the place of shared living mutually tolerated by each co-resident must be examined individually and concretely according to the form and nature of the joint residence, the circumstances by which the joint residence was formed, etc. Where an outsider’s entry into and use of the place of shared living pursuant to the consent of one co-resident can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary act of entering and using the place of shared living by the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry, such outsider’s conduct may be evaluated as identical in substance to the conduct of that co-resident as a whole. Accordingly, where one co-resident, without legal grounds or other justifiable reason, prohibits another co-resident from entering the place of shared living, and the latter, in resistance thereto, even if he has undermined the factual peaceful state of the co-resident who prohibited his entry while entering the place of shared living, that is a case in which the offense of intrusion upon residence is not established. Likewise, if an outsider who entered the place of shared living together with the consent of that co-resident can, overall, be evaluated as having engaged in acts that were part of, and incidental to, the ordinary act of that co-resident entering and using the place of shared living, then it is appropriate to view that the offense of intrusion upon residence is not established against the outsider either, notwithstanding that the factual peaceful state of the co-resident who prohibited his entry was undermined. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\na) In determining whether an individual’s legal interest has been infringed, it is necessary to consider the social implications and limits of that legal interest as well. In the case of a joint residence, however, not only the aspect of protecting each co-resident’s individual legal interest, but also the meaning of shared living in a joint residence and the social limits accompanying it, must be considered in examining whether the protected legal interest of the offense of intrusion upon residence has been infringed and whether the offense has been established. In a joint residence where multiple people live together, the legal interest in residence enjoyed by each co-resident is limited to a certain extent, and it must be understood that the co-residents tolerated such limitations among themselves. Even if an outsider’s entry pursuant to the consent of one co-resident can, in light of the form and nature of the joint residence, the circumstances that led to the formation of the joint residential relationship, the relationship between the co-resident and the outsider, the purpose of the outsider’s entry into the joint residence, the manner of entry, etc., be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary act of entering and using the place of shared living by the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry, recognizing the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence merely because it has the aspect of disturbing the factual peaceful state within the joint residence of another co-resident becomes not only contrary to the will mutually tolerated among co-residents, but also an unreasonable interpretation that disregards the essence and characteristics, diversity, and attendant social limits of joint residence.\\n\\nb) If the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence were recognized merely because an outsider’s entry pursuant to the consent of one co-resident constituted an entry in a manner undermining the factual peaceful state of another co-resident, even in cases where such entry can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary act of entering and using the place of shared living by the co-resident who consented, then an unreasonable result could arise in which whether the outsider’s offense of intrusion upon residence is established would depend solely on the incidental internal circumstances of the co-residents, namely, the conflict between the general and affirmative enjoyment of the freedom of residence and the negative enjoyment of freedom and peace of residence.\\n\\nThe essence and mission of criminal law as a legal norm lie in protecting the basic values indispensable to the existence and maintenance of society, and it is desirable that the objects of criminal law regulation be limited to acts that manifestly pose a danger to important legal interests that cannot be resolved by other norms or social control mechanisms, or acts that inflict great harm on society. The same context must be applied to understand the purpose for which criminal law, among legal norms, is granted powerful sanctions that deprive or restrict individual freedom and rights. Criminal law provides only that the constituent act of the offense of intrusion upon residence is “intrusion,” and the punishment is imprisonment of up to 3 years or a fine of up to 5,000,000 won, which is higher than the legislation of other countries such as Germany, and it is regulated as a non-complaint offense. In addition to the essence of criminal law and its regulatory content, if the social and normative meaning inherent in the concepts of joint residence and intrusion itself is added, the concept of intrusion in the offense of intrusion upon residence should be understood as already including a legal evaluation that it is an act entailing, by its very nature, a risk of serious infringement of the legal interest of peace and tranquility of residence beyond the scope socially acceptable, or an act that inflicts great harm on society; therefore, it is appropriate to interpret that only acts evaluated as objects of regulation under criminal law can be punished as the offense of intrusion upon residence. Yet, where entry into a joint residence pursuant to the consent of one co-resident can, overall, be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary act of entering and using the place of shared living by the co-resident who consented, it is difficult to regard such conduct as an act carrying a risk of serious infringement of a legal interest that cannot be resolved by other norms or social control means, or as an act inflicting great harm on society. If, as a result of an outsider’s entry into a joint residence, a separate legal interest such as another co-resident’s bodily freedom is infringed, and such infringement constitutes a separate offense, it is sufficient to punish that offense, and provisions already exist in the Criminal Act, etc., for such punishment. To impose criminal punishment under the offense of intrusion upon residence even in such cases would be an excessive intervention of state punitive power, unjustified in light of the diversity and particularity of social relationships arising from joint residence and the possibility of self-regulation.\\n\\nc) Between co-residents, the value of protection of the legal interests each enjoys in the joint residence can be considered equal, so if, in a situation where legal interests between co-residents conflict concerning an outsider’s entry, the factual peace and tranquility of another co-resident’s residence is deemed infringed and the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence is recognized against the outsider, this is also unfair in that it gives priority only to the legal interests of the co-resident who rejected the outsider’s entry while disregarding the legal interests of the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry.\\n\\nd) Even if the act of entering a joint residence pursuant to the consent of one co-resident can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary act of entering and using the place of shared living by the co-resident who consented, if the outsider is to be punished for the offense of intrusion upon residence, the question may arise whether the co-resident who consented to his entry can also be punished as an accomplice to the offense of intrusion upon residence. However, as noted above, since a co-resident cannot be punished for the offense of intrusion upon residence unless he has not withdrawn from the joint living relationship or there is no legal ground or other justifiable reason to prohibit his act of entering the joint residence, in the above case only the outsider who entered the joint residence pursuant to the consent of the co-resident can be punished for the offense of intrusion upon residence. Yet this conclusion, insofar as the outsider’s entry can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary act of entering and using the place of shared living by the co-resident who consented to it, is inconsistent with the realities of shared living and general social notions, and is unjustified even in light of the subsidiarity of criminal punishment. The injustice is especially clear when one considers the case where one co-resident actively invited the outsider and they entered the residence together.\\n\\n3) a) According to the record of this case, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n(1) Non-Indicted 1, a co-resident of the apartment at issue, went out around May 19, 2018, the date of the offense in this case, and asked her mother and younger sibling, victim Non-Indicted 2, to take care of the child, and victim Non-Indicted 2 was staying in the apartment at issue at the time of the offense in this case.\\n\\n(2) Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, unaware that Non-Indicted 1 had gone out, visited the apartment at issue together with Defendant 1, allegedly in order to reconcile Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 and to meet their granddaughter. However, victim Non-Indicted 2 placed the chain latch installed on the entrance door so that the Defendants could not enter and refused to open the door. Then Defendant 1, who was a co-resident of the apartment at issue, damaged the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the apartment at issue, and Defendant 2 also joined in. Thereafter, the Defendants entered the apartment at issue together.\\n\\nb) Examining these facts in light of the legal principles set out above, Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 may be regarded as having joined in entering the apartment at issue in resistance to victim Non-Indicted 2’s entry prohibition, which had no justifiable reason, when entering the apartment at issue, the joint residence of Defendant 1, who was their son and a co-resident of the apartment at issue. Although in the process Defendant 1 exercised physical force by damaging the chain latch installed on the entrance door, and Defendant 2 also joined in and thereby jointly committed the offense of damage to property, Defendant 1’s conduct can be seen as a means of entering and using the place of shared living as a co-resident in resistance to the entry prohibition imposed without justifiable reason while not having withdrawn from the joint living relationship, and Defendant 2’s conduct is, in substance, merely riding on and joining in Defendant 1’s conduct. If so, the act of Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 entering the apartment at issue as such can be evaluated overall as part of, and incidental to, Defendant 1, who was a co-resident, entering and using the apartment at issue; therefore, it must be viewed that the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) is not established against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3.\\n\\nc) Nevertheless, the lower appellate court determined this part of the facts charged to be guilty. The lower appellate judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence. The grounds for appeal by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, which point this out, are well-founded.\\n\\n5. Scope of reversal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated above, the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) by Defendant 2 must be reversed. And the remaining guilty part as to Defendant 2 is in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the reversed part, so that a single sentence must be imposed and the whole must be reversed together; therefore, ultimately, all guilty parts of the lower appellate judgment as to Defendant 2 must be reversed.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, without considering the remaining grounds of appeal by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, we reverse the guilty part of the lower appellate judgment as to Defendant 2 and the part as to Defendant 3, and remand this case to the lower appellate court for further trial and determination of these parts. The appeals by the Prosecutor and Defendant 1 are each dismissed. It is so adjudged as stated in the disposition. Except that there is a separate opinion by Justice Lee Gi-taek and a dissenting opinion by Justices Jo Jae-yeon, Min Yu-suk, and Lee Dong-won, the opinions of the participating Justices are unanimous, and there are a supplemental opinion by Justices Kim Seon-su and Cheon Dae-yeop on the majority opinion, and a supplemental opinion by Justice Min Yu-suk on the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n7. Separate opinion of Justice Lee Gi-taek regarding the part concerning each violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) by the Defendants\\n\\nThe issue in this case is whether the act of Defendant 1, whose status as a co-resident of the apartment at issue is disputed, and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, who received his consent, entering the apartment at issue in violation of victim Non-Indicted 2’s externally manifested intent to prohibit entry, constitutes the offense of intrusion upon residence. In response, the majority opinion discussed whether the Defendants’ act of entering the apartment at issue constitutes the offense of intrusion upon residence by using the standard of whether it corresponds to the general manner of use by co-residents, etc. By contrast, the separate opinion seeks to discuss the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence against the Defendants through a proper interpretation of the actual intent of victim Non-Indicted 2, who manifested an intent to prohibit entry to the Defendants.\\n\\na. Various interpretations of whether the act was contrary to the resident’s will\\n\\n1) a) This is examined in accordance with the legal principles of Supreme Court En Banc Decision 2020DO12630, decided on 2021. 9. 9. The meaning of intrusion, the constituent act of the offense of intrusion upon residence, means “entering a residence in a manner that undermines the factual state of peace and tranquility enjoyed by the resident in the residence,” and whether it falls within this meaning is, as a general rule, to be determined based on the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the act at the time of entry.\\n\\nb) However, whether an act constitutes intrusion is fundamentally a matter of interpretation of the resident’s will. If a person enters a residence in a manner that undermines factual peace and tranquility, it is generally interpreted as being contrary to the resident’s will.\\n\\n2) Whether the actor’s entry is contrary to the resident’s will must be determined by reasonably interpreting the resident’s true intent in concrete consideration of the objective circumstances at the time of entry. Whether it is contrary to the resident’s will should, as a general rule, be determined based on the externally manifested will; however, there may be cases where a different determination is made depending on the specific factual circumstances at the time of entry. Ultimately, the interpretation of whether it is contrary to the resident’s will belongs to the realm of fact-finding.\\n\\n3) Where a resident has expressly manifested an intent to prohibit entry, if a person enters the residence in violation of such intent to prohibit entry, it can generally be regarded as intrusion. For example, if a resident expressly tells a door-to-door salesman trying to enter the house, “Do not come in,” and the salesman nevertheless enters the house, it is clearly contrary to the resident’s will and therefore constitutes intrusion.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the resident’s intent concerning prohibition of entry inevitably has a reason. Even in determining whether the act is contrary to the resident’s will, there are cases in which the true intent can be confirmed only by knowing the reason the resident prohibited entry. In such cases, if one simply interprets the resident’s externally manifested intent to prohibit entry as being contrary to his will, unjust results may follow. Then the scope of punishability under the offense of intrusion upon residence may be unreasonably expanded. That is precisely why the resident’s true intent is important in determining whether the act is contrary to the resident’s will.\\n\\nEven where the resident has expressly manifested an intent to prohibit entry, there may be premises or backgrounds underlying that intent. For example, consider a case in which the resident decides whether to permit entry on the premise of a certain status or qualification that allows entry. In such a case, if a person who has the status or qualification allowing entry enters, it cannot be regarded as intrusion, whereas if a person who lacks the status or qualification allowing entry or lacks the qualification to enter enters, it can be regarded as intrusion. For example, in the case of a believer of a certain religion, there is a prayer space for clergy whose entry is permitted. In such a case, if a believer enters the clergy’s prayer space, it cannot be regarded as intrusion, but if a person other than a believer enters, it should be regarded as intrusion. If, at a company, an employee enters an office where only the company’s officers and employees are permitted to enter for the protection of trade secrets, it cannot be regarded as intrusion, but if a former employee or an officer or employee of a competitor enters, it should be regarded as intrusion.\\n\\nHowever, even in cases where the resident determines whether to allow entry on the premise of status or qualification as above, there may be disputes as to that status or qualification, etc.\\n\\nFor example, one can imagine a case where the resident thought that A was a person who could not enter and prohibited his entry, but later A’s status or qualification is confirmed and it is found that he was a person who could enter. In such a case, because the factual premise for prohibiting A’s entry did not exist, A cannot be regarded as having entered contrary to the resident’s will.\\n\\nAs in the example above, in the case of a believer, there is a prayer space for clergy whose entry is permitted. A is trying to enter the above prayer space, but the clergy believed that A was not a believer and blocked his entry into the prayer space, yet A came into the prayer space. Later, A was confirmed to be a believer. In such a case, can the offense of intrusion upon residence be established against A?\\n\\nAs another example, there is an office in which trade secrets are stored, entry to which is permitted only to the company’s officers and employees. A tried to enter the above office, but the manager of the office believed that A was not an officer or employee of the company and blocked his entry into the office, yet A entered the above office as is. Later, A was confirmed to be an officer or employee of the company. In such a case, can the offense of intrusion upon residence be established against A?\\n\\nIn each of the above examples, if one looks at the true intent of the clergy or office manager, the conclusion that the offense of intrusion upon residence is established against A solely on the basis of the externally manifested will means that the true intent to prohibit entry has not been properly identified. This is because the factual premise prohibiting A’s entry did not exist from the outset, so A’s entry into the prayer space or office cannot be regarded as contrary to the will of the clergy or office manager. In each of the above examples, according to the true intent of the clergy or office manager, the offense of intrusion upon residence should not be established against A.\\n\\nb. Determination as to whether each offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) is established against the Defendants\\n\\n1) Premise for discussion\\n\\nThis case raises the issue of whether Defendant 1, whose status as a co-resident of the apartment at issue is disputed, and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, who received consent to enter from him, entered the apartment at issue in violation of victim Non-Indicted 2’s externally manifested intent to prohibit entry, and whether this constitutes the offense of intrusion upon residence.\\n\\nIn this case, the basic premise for victim Non-Indicted 2’s intent to prohibit the Defendants from entering the apartment at issue can be seen as the fact that Defendant 1 was not a co-resident of the apartment at issue.\\n\\nIn order to interpret victim Non-Indicted 2’s true intent to prohibit the Defendants from entering the apartment at issue, it is necessary first to examine whether Defendant 1 was a co-resident of the apartment at issue.\\n\\nBelow, we will examine the facts of this case, then determine whether Defendant 1 was a co-resident of the apartment at issue, and thereafter interpret victim Non-Indicted 2’s true intent regarding the Defendants’ entry into the apartment at issue and determine whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established against the Defendants.\\n\\n2) Facts of this case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower appellate judgment and the record of this case, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na) Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 are a legally married couple who were married on September 5, 2015. Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 have one child between them, and they had lived in the apartment at issue since around August 15, 2016.\\n\\nb) Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 frequently quarreled from around January 2018 over the issue of the sale of a newly built apartment. Defendant 1 quarreled with Non-Indicted 1 on April 9, 2018, packed some of his belongings, and left the apartment at issue. Defendant 1 went to the apartment at issue on April 13, 2018, quarreled again with Non-Indicted 1, and left the home. Thereafter, Non-Indicted 1 unilaterally changed the password for the entrance door of the apartment at issue and also attached a chain latch to the entrance door.\\n\\nc) Defendant 1 requested Non-Indicted 1 on April 17, 2018 and April 19, 2018 through a mobile messenger to tell him the password for the front door of the apartment at issue. On or about May 4, 2018, Defendant 1 also went to the apartment at issue and asked Non-Indicted 1 to open the door, but Non-Indicted 1 refused.\\n\\nd) Non-Indicted 1, a co-resident of the apartment at issue, went out around May 19, 2018, the date of the offense in this case, and asked her mother and younger sibling, victim Non-Indicted 2, to take care of the child, and victim Non-Indicted 2 was staying in the apartment at issue at the time of the offense in this case.\\n\\ne) Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 visited the apartment at issue together with Defendant 1 without knowing that Non-Indicted 1 had gone out. However, victim Non-Indicted 2 refused the Defendants’ entry into the apartment at issue. Then Defendant 1, who was a co-resident of the apartment at issue, damaged the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the apartment at issue, and Defendant 2 also joined in.
