Thereafter, the Defendants entered the apartment at issue together.\\n\\nf) Non-Indicted 1 filed a divorce petition with the court around June 28, 2018, after the incident in this case, and on September 4, 2018, a divorce mediation was reached between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1.\\n\\n3) Whether Defendant 1 was a co-resident of the apartment at issue\\n\\na) The offense of intrusion upon residence is established where a person other than a resident intrudes upon a residence. The residence that is the object of the offense of intrusion upon residence is limited to one occupied by another person. Where one of the co-residents who lives together with another person in a joint residence is the actor, the relevant joint residence does not become the object of the offense of intrusion upon residence. However, if it can be recognized that a co-resident has withdrawn from the joint living relationship or lost the factual control and management relationship over the residence, the relevant residence constitutes the object of the offense of intrusion upon residence. Whether a co-resident has withdrawn from the joint living relationship or whether the factual control and management relationship over the joint residence has been lost must be individually determined by considering specific circumstances, such as the relationship between the co-residents, the circumstances in which the dispute between the co-residents arose, and the circumstances in which the person left the joint residence.\\n\\nMeanwhile, there may also be cases where entry into a joint residence is prohibited on legal grounds, such as where one co-resident applied to the court for a provisional injunction prohibiting entry into the joint residence against another co-resident and received a court decision granting such provisional injunction, or where one co-resident received a temporary measure decision under the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Domestic Violence Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Domestic Violence Punishment Act”) or the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Child Abuse Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Child Abuse Punishment Act”) ordering “separation by eviction, etc. from the residence” or “prohibition of approaching within 100 meters of the residence” (Article 29(1) subparagraphs 1 and 2 of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act, Article 19(1) subparagraphs 1 and 2 of the Child Abuse Punishment Act). Such cases may be regarded as cases where the co-resident has withdrawn from the joint living relationship or where the factual control and management relationship over the joint residence has been lost.\\n\\nb) The above facts are examined in light of the foregoing legal principles.\\n\\nAt the time of this case, it is difficult to find that there was an explicit agreement between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 to liquidate the marital relationship and for Defendant 1 to leave the apartment and live elsewhere, or that the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 had irretrievably broken down. In such circumstances, the mere fact that Defendant 1 packed some of his belongings and left the apartment, or that Non-Indicted 1 unilaterally changed the password for the entrance door and prevented Defendant 1 from entering, is insufficient to find that Defendant 1 withdrew from the joint living relationship in the apartment at issue or lost control and management over it. Therefore, Defendant 1 should be regarded as having maintained the status of a co-resident of the apartment at issue at the time of this case.\\n\\n4) Interpretation of victim Non-Indicted 2’s true intent\\n\\na) Based on the facts set out above, we shall examine the true intent of victim Non-Indicted 2 in prohibiting the Defendants from entering the apartment at issue.\\n\\nb) In light of the relationship among the Defendants and Non-Indicted 1 and victim Non-Indicted 2, and the circumstances of the dispute in this case, as recognized from the facts set out above, it is appropriate to view victim Non-Indicted 2 as having prohibited the Defendants’ entry because she believed that the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 had irretrievably broken down, and that Defendant 1 had lost the status of co-resident of the apartment at issue and thus could not enter the apartment at issue without Non-Indicted 1’s consent. Aside from the above circumstances, no additional circumstance serving as a motive or reason for victim Non-Indicted 2 to prohibit Defendant 1 or Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, who had received his consent, from entering the apartment at issue can be found in the record.\\n\\nc) The factual premise of victim Non-Indicted 2’s intent to prohibit entry into the apartment at issue with respect to the Defendants can be viewed as that the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 had irretrievably broken down, and that Defendant 1 was no longer a co-resident of the apartment at issue and thus could not enter the apartment at issue without Non-Indicted 1’s consent. However, as noted above, it is difficult to find that the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 had irretrievably broken down, or that Defendant 1 had withdrawn from the joint living relationship in the apartment at issue or lost control and management over it.\\n\\nIf that is so, even though victim Non-Indicted 2 externally manifested an intent to prohibit the Defendants from entering the apartment at issue, it is reasonable to view that victim Non-Indicted 2’s true intent was that she would not prohibit the Defendants from entering the apartment at issue if the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Non-Indicted 1 had not irretrievably broken down, and if Defendant 1 had not withdrawn from the joint living relationship in the apartment at issue or lost control and management over it. Therefore, the Defendants’ entry into the apartment at issue cannot be regarded as having been carried out contrary to victim Non-Indicted 2’s will, and thus it cannot be recognized that the offense of intrusion upon residence is established against the Defendants. Furthermore, even if the Defendants damaged the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the apartment at issue in the course of entering the apartment at issue, this can be regarded as the minimum use of physical force necessary to enter the apartment at issue, so such circumstance does not affect whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established against the Defendants.\\n\\n5) Determination on the grounds for appeal by the Prosecutor and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\nFor the above reasons, each part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) against the Defendants should all be found not guilty.\\n\\nThe conclusion of the lower appellate judgment that found Defendant 1 not guilty of the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) is proper. Accordingly, there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in that it exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehended the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence.\\n\\nHowever, the lower appellate judgment that found guilty the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 contains an error in that it violated the rules of logic and experience in determining whether their conduct was contrary to the will of victim Non-Indicted 2, exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence by incorrectly finding facts, or misapprehended the legal principles concerning intrusion. The grounds for appeal by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 that point this out are well-founded.\\n\\nc. Intermediate conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the parts concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 in the lower appellate judgment must be reversed. And the above reversed part and the remaining guilty part as to Defendant 2 are in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, so that one sentence must be imposed and the whole must be reversed together; therefore, all guilty parts concerning Defendant 2 in the lower appellate judgment must be reversed. Without addressing the remaining grounds for appeal by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, the guilty part concerning Defendant 2 and the part concerning Defendant 3 in the lower appellate judgment must be reversed, and this case remanded to the lower appellate court for further trial and determination of these parts, and the appeals by the Prosecutor and Defendant 1 must each be dismissed.\\n\\nSince the conclusion in this case is the same as the majority opinion, but the specific reasons leading to that conclusion differ, I state this as a separate opinion.\\n\\n8. Dissenting opinion of Justices Jo Jae-yeon, Min Yu-suk, and Lee Dong-won regarding each part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) by the Defendants\\n\\na. Summary of the dissent\\n\\nThe Supreme Court, through this en banc decision, reaffirmed that the protected legal interest of the offense of intrusion upon residence is not “the right to residence” but “the factual peace and tranquility of the residence.” This is equally true in the case of a joint residence.\\n\\nWhere a co-resident currently present in the residence has prohibited entry, but entry into the joint residence was made by force or through an abnormal route, in light of the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the act at the time of entry, this clearly undermines the peaceful state of the co-resident currently present in the residence and therefore constitutes an act of intrusion; thus, the offense of intrusion upon residence is established. The same applies even if the person committing such intrusion was himself a co-resident who had left home, or an outsider who received consent from that co-resident.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that even if the actor enters a residence jointly occupied, managed, or possessed in a manner that undermines the factual peaceful state of another co-resident, the offense of intrusion upon residence is not constituted, but we cannot agree.\\n\\nb. Premise for discussion\\n\\n1) First, we wish to clarify the relationship between this case and Supreme Court En Banc Decision 2020DO12630, decided on 2021. 9. 9. This case presupposes the legal opinion of Supreme Court En Banc Decision 2020DO12630, but differs in facts and legal issues.\\n\\nIn Supreme Court En Banc Decision 2020DO12630, the issue is whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established for the act of “peaceful entry pursuant to the consent of a resident currently present at the residence.” The issue is the evaluation of the “presumed contrary intent of a co-resident absent from the residence.” This case concerns the act of “a resident who left the residence on his own and became unable to enter by ordinary means, but entered by force despite the co-resident currently present at the residence prohibiting entry.” The issue is the evaluation of the “act that infringed the factual peace of a co-resident currently present at the residence.”\\n\\n2) We consider the increasing necessity of protecting the peace of the residence and the necessity of specifically and individually regulating joint residential relationships.\\n\\na) The need to protect the peace of residence has grown further due to changes in modern social life and residential life. In modern society, as the development of mass media and the development of information and communication means increased the possibility of invasion of the secrecy of private life, the importance of privacy protection came to be emphasized even more, and the need to protect the peace of the residence as a condition for protecting the secrecy of private life became greater. In other words, once the residential space is invaded, there is a high likelihood that the secrecy of private life will be infringed, so the peace of residence also becomes more likely to be infringed at that stage. Moreover, with the deepening of urbanization, individuals’ residential spaces have become limited to narrow spaces, and concerns about infringement of the peace of residence by outsiders’ entry have become more serious than in the past, greatly increasing the need for protection.\\n\\nb) Most citizens form family relationships for reasons such as marriage, or otherwise, for economic reasons, etc., many people share one residential space jointly. Due to urbanization and densification, many citizens live in apartment houses and other collective housing. Meanwhile, the concept of residence includes elevators, common stairs, and corridors inside multi-family detached houses, multi-unit houses, row houses, apartments, etc., which are collective housing [see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DO3452, decided on 2009. 8. 20.]. In modern society, where the majority of citizens have the status of co-residents in residential spaces, the status relationship among co-residents, the patterns in which the legal interests enjoyed by co-residents within a joint residence conflict with one another, and the need to regulate these matters are all highly diverse. Regulation of the joint residential relationship must be made individually, by examining the specific circumstances such as the circumstances of formation of the joint residence, its form, and the relationships among co-residents.\\n\\n3) The question of whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established in a joint residence arises when legal interests among co-residents conflict. As the saying goes, “every unhappy family is unhappy for its own reasons,” the patterns of infringement of legal interests among family members in one residential space and the need to protect the peace of residence are also diverse. Yet to regulate this uniformly and abstractly solely because it is a joint residence or because the actors are co-residents, and then to discuss in a single, uniform manner whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established, cannot be regarded as proper legal regulation of the various dispute situations. Moreover, even where statutes regulating joint residences exist, whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established against a co-resident or an outsider is a matter to be determined by individually and concretely examining the internal relationship among co-residents and the relationship with outsiders under those statutes; it is not proper to pre-set a uniform and abstract standard for such determination.\\n\\nUltimately, whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established in a joint residence must be determined concretely and individually, taking into comprehensive consideration the constitutional “freedom of residence,” the “protection of marriage and family life,” the “legislative purpose and intent of the offense of intrusion upon residence,” the “specific content and legal nature of the protected legal interest of the offense of intrusion upon residence,” and the “meaning of intrusion and its standard of determination.”\\n\\nc. Whether a co-resident can be punished for the offense of intrusion upon residence\\n\\n1) The offense of intrusion upon residence is a crime concerning individual legal interests, and where more than one person resides at the residence, the infringement of the protected legal interest must be determined based on the peace of residence enjoyed by each resident individually.\\n\\na) Since a joint residence is one’s own residence as well as another’s residence, if one of the co-residents engages in conduct that, in relation to the other co-resident, undermines that person’s peace of residence, infringement of the protected legal interest of the offense of intrusion upon residence occurs.\\n\\nb) The Constitution, in the preamble to Article 16, provides that “all citizens shall not be infringed upon in their freedom of residence,” thereby guaranteeing freedom of residence as a fundamental right. In addition, Article 36(1) of the Constitution provides that “marriage and family life shall be formed and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and equality between the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this,” thereby placing marriage and family under the special protection of the State. Since marriage and family life are realized through the place called residence, freedom of residence functions to secure the fundamental rights concerning marriage and family life by guaranteeing the spatial sphere of marriage and family life.\\n\\nThe residential space is the center of private life and is inseparably connected to the individual personality; without the guarantee of its inviolability, the private sphere of the individual, which is the minimum condition for human happiness, cannot be protected [see Constitutional Court Decision 2018HEONBA171, decided on 2020. 9. 24.]. Since residence is the place where private life is centered, without the guarantee of its inviolability, the safety of the individual’s life, body, and property also cannot be protected easily. Therefore, freedom of residence guaranteed by the Constitution has as its subject the individual who resides in the residence as a bearer of fundamental rights, and the fundamental rights concerning marriage and family life are also guaranteed on the basis of the individual who marries and forms a family. The offense of intrusion upon residence is a provision specifically intended to protect the freedom of residence guaranteed as a fundamental right by the Constitution, and since it also indirectly protects the marriage and family life guaranteed by the Constitution, the subject of the legal interest protected by the offense of intrusion upon residence is likewise the individual resident. This legal nature of the offense of intrusion upon residence must be maintained even in the internal relationship among co-residents.\\n\\nc) The decisions cited for reference by the majority opinion concern different factual situations and cannot be cited here. That is, Supreme Court Decision 81DO2956, decided on 1982. 4. 27., and Supreme Court Decision 2010DO16537, decided on 2012. 12. 27., both involved cases prosecuted for the offense of intrusion upon residence, etc. on the premise that the acts of entry were made by a person lacking authority to live in or possess the residence; however, as a result of trial, they were matters where the circumstances of cohabitation or lawful title to possession were recognized, and it was determined that the offense of intrusion upon residence, etc. was not established, and the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the act was not a method that undermined the peace of residence of another joint possessor or co-resident.\\n\\n2) The majority opinion states that even if one co-resident enters in a manner undermining the peaceful state of the co-resident who prohibited his entry, this is a general form of use of the joint residence.\\n\\nHowever, the majority opinion is contrary to the content and legal nature of the protected legal interest of the offense of intrusion upon residence, and to the meaning and standard of determination of intrusion, and errs in treating the co-resident’s “general form of use of the joint residence” and “a manner of act undermining the factual peaceful state” as compatible, though they are incompatible.\\n\\na) The majority opinion also recognizes the principle that the constituent act of intrusion upon residence is entering a residence in a manner that undermines the factual peace and tranquility enjoyed by the resident in the residence, and that whether this applies is, as a rule, to be judged based on the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the act at the time of entry.\\n\\nIf so, even if a co-resident enters the joint residence by force or through an abnormal route, such as by damaging the lock, this is, objectively and outwardly, entry in a manner undermining the peaceful state of another co-resident, and thus constitutes an act of intrusion.\\n\\nb) Entry by a manner that undermines the factual peaceful state is not compatible with the general form of use of the joint residence.\\n\\nTo be included in the general form of use of a joint residence mutually tolerated among co-residents, each should possess a key to the lock or share the password so that each co-resident can unlock the lock and open the door using the key or password and enter the residence.\\n\\nThe attitude of a co-resident who, after leaving home on his own, continues to clash and use violence with the other co-resident while disputing use of the residence or ownership title cannot be regarded as a general form of use of the joint residence. It is difficult to impose on the co-resident remaining in the home the burden of tolerating this. If minor children are being raised in that home, the need to prohibit violent entry becomes even greater.\\n\\nIn that situation, if the resident feels threatened in his peace, changes the lock to prohibit the other party’s entry, and the co-resident who left home becomes unable to enter normally, then enters the joint residence using means that undermine peace, such as damage or use of force, this is an act of intrusion beyond the limits of use of the joint residence.\\n\\nc) As the majority opinion itself acknowledges, the content and scope of use mutually tolerated among co-residents must be examined individually according to the circumstances by which the joint residence was formed, the form and nature of the joint residence, and the relationship among the co-residents. It is not the case that merely because one is a co-resident, his act of entering and using the joint residence must always be tolerated.\\n\\n3) According to the majority opinion, the period until withdrawal from the co-resident status is left in a regulatory vacuum, which is unjust.\\n\\na) The majority opinion denies the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence as long as one remains in the status of co-resident. The majority opinion says that if there are “special circumstances,” the offense may be recognized even against a co-resident, but the special circumstances are said to be cases where the person “has withdrawn from the joint living relationship or lost factual control and management.” However, a person who has withdrawn from the joint residence or lost factual control and management is no longer included in “co-residents.” This is merely a tautology regarding the meaning of co-resident. Therefore, the majority opinion appears to be a view that practically denies the offense of intrusion upon residence with almost no exception as to co-residents. If the true intent of the majority opinion is otherwise, then it should expressly set out the standard and scope of the “special circumstances.”\\n\\nb) The majority opinion says that the content and scope of acts of use of the joint residence mutually tolerated among co-residents must be determined individually according to the internal relationship among co-residents, but at the same time excludes from the protection scope of the offense of intrusion upon residence, on the premise of a peaceful and ordinary joint residence, entry acts that undermine the peaceful state of another co-resident until the co-resident withdraws from the joint living relationship or from the status as co-resident. However, depending on the circumstances by which the joint residence was formed, the form and nature of the joint residence, etc., the offense of intrusion upon residence may be established even before a co-resident withdraws from the status of co-resident.\\n\\nc) Rather, as can be seen from numerous judicial precedents, cases in which the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence becomes an issue among co-residents occur during the process in which the joint residential relationship is disintegrating (that is, at a stage before withdrawal from the joint living relationship, while the status as co-resident is still recognized), namely, cases where a dispute arises between co-residents and one party repeatedly leaves and re-enters the residence, causing conflict and confrontation, so that the resident has no choice but to change the lock or password in order to preserve the peace of residence.\\n\\nIn particular, in cases such as this one, where the marital relationship between spouses breaks down and the process of leading to divorce exhibits varied patterns in each specific case, in many cases the family community including the spouses is engulfed in conflict and confrontation, and serious violence may occur. There are periods that have not yet reached the dissolution of joint residence but during which it is difficult even to endure the shared life.\\n\\nd) The dissent is to the effect that the interpretation of the offense of intrusion upon residence must be made in a manner that actively responds to violence arising in the process of the dissolution of the shared living relationship and protects the peace and safety of the members.\\n\\n4) We find it difficult to agree that the majority opinion connects “justifiable reason” as a ground for denying the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence.\\n\\na) The majority opinion says that where a co-resident, without legal grounds or other justifiable reason, prohibits another co-resident from entering, the offense of intrusion upon residence is not established even if entry is forced by violence. It cites the reasons that this is “in resistance to the prohibition on entry” and is “a means of using it in accordance with the purpose of the joint residence.”\\n\\nThis is tantamount to requiring that the victim have a legal ground or equivalent justifiable reason, and it leads to the conclusion of determining whether a crime is established by examining the rights relationship prior to the intrusion.\\n\\nHowever, established Supreme Court precedents take the position that even a right holder commits the offense of intrusion upon residence or intrusion upon a structure if he intrudes upon a residence or structure by self-help as a means of enforcing that right.\\n\\nIn the offense of intrusion upon residence, which protects the “peace of residence” and punishes acts infringing it, if the standard is whether “the victim’s act prohibiting entry had a legal basis,” that does not accord with the established position of the Supreme Court.\\n\\nb) Moreover, even if “justifiable reason” can be considered, whether the prohibition on entry is justified must be determined after examining the overall process of the dispute and the circumstances leading to the prohibition on entry, and this is a matter of fact-finding that can be established through trial in the court of fact.\\n\\nThe legitimacy or attribution of responsibility for individual acts arising in the course of a dispute among co-residents, especially in the process of dissolving a marital community, cannot be determined merely by fragmentary circumstances at a particular point in time. There is concern that by focusing only on the resultant measure of “prohibition on entry,” the conclusion may be drawn that the victim lacks legitimacy and the defendant’s entry is permitted.\\n\\nc) The case of “one co-resident prohibiting the other’s entry without justifiable reason,” which the majority opinion assumes, may be a hypothetical example discussed in criminal law treatises (there is even an example of a wife locking the door in annoyance because her husband is trying to come home late at night with a drinking companion), but it is again pointed out that it is far removed from actual disputes.\\n\\n5) The majority opinion excessively minimizes the independent value of the offense of intrusion upon residence, and this does not accord with the recent direction of statutory amendments.\\n\\na) The majority opinion states that if, during the process of entry by a co-resident, another co-resident’s separate legal interest such as bodily freedom is infringed, punishment may be imposed for the corresponding offense, and that this is sufficient, but that fails properly to grasp or lightly evaluates the significance of the offense of intrusion upon residence.\\n\\nb) The reason the freedom and peace of residence are protected by penal sanctions is that anyone can expect the utmost safety while inside his own residence, and the State actively protects such expectation. This is a basic right like the gatekeeper at the very front of other fundamental freedoms such as bodily freedom, and an expectation and demand toward the State. The view that one may simply punish by offenses such as assault or damage to property fails properly to understand the weight of the value that individuals expect regarding freedom and peace of residence.\\n\\nThe offense of intrusion upon residence is intended to protect the peace and safety of residence, and because it functions to prevent infringement of life, body, and property that may occur within the residence through control of entry into the residence, the protected legal interest in the offense of intrusion upon residence must be independently protected. Therefore, where the entry act of one co-resident or an outsider infringes the legal interest of another co-resident’s factual peace and tranquility of residence, it should be punished as the offense of intrusion upon residence; furthermore, where another co-resident’s life, body, property, etc. are separately infringed during or after the entry process, it is appropriate to punish the offender for the offense constituted by that infringement.\\n\\nc) Today, threats to the peace of residence can arise not only from outsiders but also from family members and other co-residents.\\n\\nIn particular, in most cases where the spouse remaining at the residence raises minor children, a violent act of entry, regardless of the circumstances of the dispute and who is at fault, seriously harms the welfare of the minor children.\\n\\nIn the past, under the notion that “criminal law does not intervene in family disputes,” family disputes were regarded as matters to be resolved autonomously within the family, with state punitive power intervening only supplementarily. However, that attitude led to a refusal to protect against domestic violence and became a cause of crimes within the family. In response, the Act on the Prevention of Domestic Violence and Protection of Victims, etc., and the Domestic Violence Punishment Act were enacted, enabling the State to intervene actively in domestic violence.\\n\\nFurthermore, in view of the criticism that prevention of violence within the family and protection of victims are still inadequate, the Domestic Violence Punishment Act was amended by Act No. 17499 on October 20, 2020, and came into force on January 21, 2021, in order to improve and supplement shortcomings. The amended Act included the offense of intrusion upon residence under Book II, Chapter 36 of the Criminal Act among domestic violence crimes [Article 2 subparagraph 3 (sa)]. Family members who are the objects of application of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act are spouses, lineal ascendants and descendants, and cohabiting relatives [Article 2 subparagraph 2 (ga) through (ra)], which almost exactly coincides with co-residents. Accordingly, the offense of intrusion upon residence and the offense of refusing to leave, as set forth in Book II, Chapter 36 of the Criminal Act, and even their attempted offenses, are included in the domestic violence crimes prescribed by the Domestic Violence Punishment Act.\\n\\nUnlike the majority opinion, the legislature, through the amendment of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act, has taken the position of actively regulating to severely punish acts that undermine the physical and mental peace of other family members even against co-residents.\\n\\nd. Whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established where an outsider, having received the consent of one co-resident, enters a joint residence in a manner undermining the peaceful state of another co-resident\\n\\n1) The majority opinion denies the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence on the ground that an outsider who entered a joint residence in a manner undermining the peaceful state of a co-resident currently present in the residence did so pursuant to the consent of another co-resident, but this is also unjust.\\n\\nIf an outsider enters a joint residence after suppressing, by force, the prohibition on entry by a co-resident currently present in the residence, the offense of intrusion upon residence is established, and it cannot be denied merely because consent was obtained from one co-resident.\\n\\nThe reality of what the majority opinion abstractly calls “entry by an outsider pursuant to the consent of a co-resident” is that the outsider joins with the co-resident and, by force, suppresses the prohibition on entry by the co-resident currently in the home, thereby intruding upon the joint residence.\\n\\n2) A conflict of legal interests arising within a joint residence among co-residents, even though it is their internal relationship, does not mean that an outsider’s intrusion into the joint residence is anything other than conduct meeting the statutory elements and must be punished independently.\\n\\nAn outsider’s entry into a joint residence has nothing to do with the ordinary use of the joint residence among co-residents. The outsider was aware that the resident prohibited entry, yet suppressed that and forced entry. There is no basis for viewing this as a conflict of legal interests in the internal relationship among co-residents; rather, denying the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence on the ground that another co-resident consented to the outsider’s entry results in disregarding the independent legal subject status of the co-resident who prohibited the outsider’s entry.\\n\\n3) Furthermore, the reasons cited by the majority opinion as justifying the outsider’s act of intrusion are also incorrect.\\n\\na) Punishing a person who has committed an act falling within the elements of Article 319(1) of the Criminal Act within the statutory sentencing range is a legitimate exercise of state punitive power. If an outsider’s act of entering a joint residence falls within the elements of the offense of intrusion upon residence, it must be punished within the statutory sentencing range. The majority opinion says that, even though the act falls within the elements of the offense of intrusion upon residence provided by the legislature, one must again distinguish the seriousness of the infringed legal interest or additionally require social harm as an element, but no basis is offered. Moreover, an outsider’s entry into a joint residence in a manner undermining the factual peaceful state despite another co-resident’s opposition is, by itself, already an act of infringing legal interests beyond the range socially acceptable, and thus may also be said to inflict great harm on society.\\n\\nb) The fact that the maximum statutory punishment for the offense of intrusion upon residence under the Criminal Act is imprisonment for 3 years, and that it is regulated as a non-complaint offense, lies within the legislature’s scope of legislative discretion and is difficult to find logically relevant to the issue in this case.\\n\\nFurthermore, Swiss Criminal Code Article 186, Japanese Penal Code Article 130, and Chinese Criminal Law Article 245 also set the maximum statutory punishment for the offense of intrusion upon residence at up to 3 years of deprivation of liberty or imprisonment, which is the same as the maximum statutory punishment provided by our Criminal Act, and it is also not appropriate to restrict the scope of the offense of intrusion upon residence by formally and arithmetically comparing the statutory punishments for intrusion upon residence under the criminal laws of some other countries with the statutory punishment for intrusion upon residence under our Criminal Act (the circumstance that an outsider’s act of intruding into a joint residence was pursuant to the consent of a co-resident is sufficiently and appropriately reflected in sentencing, if necessary, by individually considering the specific circumstances).\\n\\nThe Act on the Punishment of Stalking Crimes, etc., which is scheduled to enter into force on October 21, 2021, sets the maximum statutory punishment at imprisonment for 3 years even for the act of “waiting or watching,” that is, conduct that does not reach “intrusion” into a residence, etc. [Article 18(1), Article 2 subparagraph 1 (na)].\\n\\nc) Whether to define a certain offense as a non-complaint offense is, apart from being a matter of legislative policy considering the victim’s intent or feelings, not a basis for justifying an outsider’s act of intruding into a joint residence; particularly in light of the many cases of punishment for intrusion upon residence in this case and others where investigations are initiated by the victim’s complaint or report, the fact that our Criminal Act does not define intrusion upon residence as a complaint-based offense cannot justify an outsider’s act of intruding into a joint residence.\\n\\nd) Since the value of protection of the legal interests enjoyed in a joint residence among co-residents is equal, where a co-resident’s peace of residence is infringed by an outsider’s act of intruding into the joint residence, equal protection must likewise be afforded. The conflict between the majority opinion and the dissent arises from different standards for balancing interests in situations where legal interests conflict among co-residents. The dissent takes the position that the legal interest of freedom and peace of residence, which should be protected from force and the dominance of the majority, must be placed at a higher level. The majority opinion says that in such a case, if the outsider is punished, it is unjust because the legal interests of the co-resident who supported that action are disregarded; however, the balancing of legal interests and the judgment of whether punishment is proper or improper must be distinguished.\\n\\ne. Determination in this case\\n\\n1) Findings related to “justifiable reason”\\n\\nThe majority opinion stated that “victim Non-Indicted 2 had no legal grounds or other justifiable reason to prohibit Defendant 1’s entry.”\\n\\na) The majority opinion appears to have concluded so on the basis that Non-Indicted 1 changed the password for the entrance door of the apartment at issue and attached a chain latch to the entrance door on April 13, 2018, did not tell Defendant 1 the password for the entrance door, and that victim Non-Indicted 2 did not open the door at the time of the offense in this case.\\n\\nHowever, these fragmentary circumstances alone cannot be used to determine the matter in the series of events that unfolded from about one month before the offense in this case, and only by also considering the circumstances in which Non-Indicted 1 changed the password and the context in which victim Non-Indicted 2 acted as above at the time of the offense can one determine whether there was justifiable reason.\\n\\nb) Since this issue was not contested up to the lower appellate court, we are compelled to examine the factual circumstances established on the record through the evidence not rejected by the lower appellate court, including Non-Indicted 1’s statement in the first-instance court, and point out the unfairness of the majority opinion.\\n\\n(1) Defendant 1, after conflict with Non-Indicted 1 over the sale of a newly built apartment, said around April 9, 2018, “You live alone. Tell the child that he has no father,” and packed clothes (including winter clothes and summer clothes) and shoes, etc., and left the apartment at issue. The next day, he entered the apartment at issue and took bankbooks, etc. in his own name and then left again (the fact that Defendant 1 left the home on that date on his own is also a factual circumstance recognized by the lower appellate court).\\n\\n(2) On April 13, 2018, Defendant 1 went to the apartment at issue, quarreled with Non-Indicted 1, saying that he wanted to live separately and that he wanted part of the rental deposit for the apartment at issue returned, and smashed a cup he was holding. Accordingly, Non-Indicted 1 reported to 112, and the police came to the apartment at issue. At that time, victim Non-Indicted 2 was also at the scene. Thereafter, Non-Indicted 1 changed the password for the entrance door and attached a latch to the entrance door.\\n\\n(3) Since Defendant 1 had left the apartment at issue on April 9, 2018 and was staying at the residence of Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 also knew that Defendant 1 was living separately.\\n\\nc) The circumstances regarding the situation on the day of the offense in this case are already recognized by the lower appellate court as follows.\\n\\n(1) On the day of the offense, the Defendants went to the apartment at issue without any prior contact, rang the doorbell, and, when the entrance door was not opened, used abusive language. Victim Non-Indicted 2, who knew the preceding developments, did not open the door and told the Defendants through the intercom to come back when Non-Indicted 1 returned home. The Defendants then made a commotion, knocking on the door and demanding it be opened. When victim Non-Indicted 2 opened the door slightly and fastened the latch, Defendant 2 put his foot in the gap in the opened door to prevent it from being closed while demanding that the door be opened and continuously shaking the doorknob, and Defendant 1 inserted his hand through the gap in the opened entrance door and struck the chain latch several times. The latch attached to the entrance door of the apartment at issue could be released only when the door was closed, but the Defendants made it impossible to close the door and thus also impossible to release the latch. In the course of this, Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 jointly engaged in the above conduct, causing the latch to detach from the entrance door.\\n\\n(2) As soon as the latch came off and the door opened, the Defendants rushed into the apartment at issue (Defendant 1, in the course of this, pushed victim Non-Indicted 2, who was in front of the entrance door, and received a final judgment of conviction for assault; that judgment became final). The mother of Non-Indicted 1, who was staying in the apartment at that time, was startled and fell in surprise at the Defendants’ sudden entry into the apartment, and immediately took the child into the master bedroom and locked the door. Thereafter, the two sides faced off across the master bedroom door.\\n\\nd) In light of the above series of events, one cannot conclude that the “prohibition on entry” by victim Non-Indicted 2 at the time of the offense was without justifiable reason, nor can it serve as grounds to justify the Defendants’ entry.\\n\\ne) The separate opinion states that victim Non-Indicted 2’s true intent was that she would not prohibit the Defendants from entering the apartment at issue if Defendant 1 had not withdrawn from the joint living relationship in the apartment at issue or lost control and management over it.\\n\\nThis separate opinion likewise interprets the intent in a manner detached from the circumstances and content of the dispute in this case, as recognized by the record, the circumstances by which Non-Indicted 1 changed the password for the entrance door of the apartment at issue and installed the latch, and the specific situation in which victim Non-Indicted 2 prohibited the Defendants’ entry.\\n\\n2) Whether the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) is established against Defendant 1\\n\\na) The lower appellate court held that Defendant 1 was a co-resident of the apartment at issue and therefore found the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) against him not guilty.\\n\\nb) As noted above, Defendant 1 quarreled with Non-Indicted 1, left the joint residence on his own and began living separately, and during the period when Non-Indicted 1 allowed him to enter, he entered, took bankbooks, etc., or quarreled with Non-Indicted 1 and again left the joint residence. After Non-Indicted 1 changed the entrance password, Defendant 1 requested entry several times, and then committed the offense in this case.\\n\\nDefendant 1, despite victim Non-Indicted 2’s refusal of entry, used force such as damaging the latch to subdue victim Non-Indicted 2 and entered the apartment at issue.\\n\\nc) Considering the circumstances by which Defendant 1 himself left home and the separation began, and the circumstances by which the victim’s side initially did not block Defendant 1’s entry but later, as the dispute and confrontation continued, changed the door lock and prohibited his entry, Defendant 1’s act of entering the apartment at issue, even in light of the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the act, clearly corresponds to a case that undermined the factual peace and tranquility of victim Non-Indicted 2 and exceeded the scope of use as a co-resident, and is therefore not permitted. There was justifiable reason for victim Non-Indicted 2 to block Defendant 1’s entry, and the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) can be established against Defendant 1.\\n\\nThe offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) cannot be denied merely because Defendant 1 did not withdraw from the status of co-resident.\\n\\nd) Nevertheless, the lower appellate court found this part of the facts charged not guilty. The lower appellate judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence. The Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n3) Whether the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) is established against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\na) The act by which Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, against victim Non-Indicted 2, used force, subdued the above victim who refused their entry, and entered the apartment at issue, even in light of the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of the act, clearly corresponds to a case that undermined the factual peace and tranquility of victim Non-Indicted 2; therefore, the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) is established against the above Defendants. Even if their entry was pursuant to the consent of Defendant 1, a co-resident, that does not affect the establishment of the offense.\\n\\nb) The lower appellate court’s determination, which upheld the first instance judgment that found the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 guilty, contains no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in that it exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehended the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence.\\n\\nf. Intermediate conclusion\\n\\nFor the above reasons, the parts concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) by the Defendants should all be found guilty. Accordingly, the part concerning the violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint intrusion upon a residence) by Defendant 1 in the lower appellate judgment must be reversed. Meanwhile, the above reversed part and the remaining crimes that the lower appellate court found guilty against Defendant 1 are in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, and one sentence must be imposed. Ultimately, all parts concerning Defendant 1 in the lower appellate judgment must be reversed and remanded to the lower appellate court for further trial and determination of these parts, and the appeals by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 must each be dismissed.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, I state that I cannot agree with the majority opinion.\\n\\n9. Supplemental opinion of Justices Kim Seon-su and Cheon Dae-yeop regarding the majority opinion\\n\\nIn the majority opinion, the present issues were examined from the perspective of the general form in which co-residents use a joint residence under mutual tolerance. As a result, where one co-resident, without legal grounds or justifiable reason, unilaterally uses force to block or prohibit another co-resident from entering the place of shared living, such as by locking the door, even if the other co-resident exercises physical force to release the entry blockade in order to enter the place of shared living in resistance thereto, this can be evaluated merely as a means for the co-resident to enter and use the joint residence, and if the outsider’s entry together with that conduct can likewise be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary act of entering and using the place of shared living by the co-resident who consented, the offense of intrusion upon residence is also not established.\\n\\nBelow, in order to make the purport of the majority opinion on each issue in this case clearer, to supplement its grounds, and to state our views in response to the points raised by the dissent, we set out the following.\\n\\na. The meaning and limits of the shared living relationship within a joint residence\\n\\nResidence means, at once, the physical and objective environment that constitutes human life, and also a subjective and socio-psychological environment. The various ideas and perceptions regarding the meaning and role of residence, and the cultural differences in residence experienced by each individual, appear as differences in each person’s view of residence.\\n\\nA joint residence refers to a form of cooperative residence among the co-residents who constitute it, and does not by itself mean a complete community. A joint residence may consist of private residential spaces for each person, or may consist only of communal residential spaces for all co-residents, and it is not fixed but is also a concept of an open space that can change on the basis of mutual agreement, custom, circumstances, etc.\\n\\nJoint residence is a form of residential culture in which the independence and communal nature of people who share ways of life and values are harmonized. The degree of the bond among co-residents constituting the joint residence, which is the stage of their lives, is diverse, and the boundary between solo residence and joint residence is not always clear. A typical example is that the meaning of joint residence or joint living in a traditional form of joint residence, the family community, differs from its meaning in a modern urban form of joint residence, such as a share house. Joint residence is a residential culture in which, while maintaining the fundamental value of residence in which individual dignity is realized, one tolerates restrictions on the right as private space and accepts a life of coexistence as co-residents within the same residential space. The extent to which each person’s private sphere within a joint residence is recognized is determined according to mutual agreement, the form and custom of residence, and the general social perception of it. Such joint residence begins only when the life of sharing and coexistence within a single residential space is accepted. Nevertheless, differences in view of residence among co-residents and differing perceptions of the boundary between the private sphere and the communal sphere constantly create a relationship of tension.\\n\\nEven in the case of the most basic residential community, the family, for example, conflict among family members may arise as to whether the parent’s arbitrary entry into a room used exclusively by a child constitutes invasion of the private sphere within the joint residence. In such a case, even if the child unilaterally declares it to be his complete private sphere and prohibits the parent’s entry, it is not easy to conclude readily that a different legal evaluation should be made of the parent’s entry into that room. In particular, in applying the offense of intrusion upon residence, it would be even more difficult to affirm this in light of the subsidiarity of criminal punishment. On the other hand, if an act intrudes upon a space where mutual tolerance and agreement regarding complete private use for a specific purpose, such as a bathroom, is premised, it would be difficult to readily deny the unlawfulness of the intrusion merely because it is entry by a co-resident into a space within the joint residence. In a form of residence in which private spaces are intermingled within the entire communal space of the joint residence, the conflict surrounding the boundary between private space and communal space may become even more intense.\\n\\nThus, because there exists within a joint residence a multifaceted relationship between the individual and the residential community, one cannot completely exclude the individual’s private sphere and space; however, the area recognized as communal space functions not as a closed space, but as a space for experiencing and communicating mutual open communal time and life. Within it, each co-resident must refrain from a life plan that uses it only as his own independent space, and if he is unwilling to endure such constraints, he must dismantle the joint residential relationship or withdraw from the joint residence; once such dismantling or withdrawal occurs, he can no longer assert rights and obligations attendant upon joint residence or joint living.\\n\\nCommunity communication and participation among co-residents in a joint residence are a process of sharing the space as a residential community and sharing values. In order for it to be a space that balances individual privacy and communal life, a process is also needed to identify what spaces are occupied by the individual and what spaces are shared with others and to obtain understanding thereof. Above all, what is important is that co-residents must understand and tolerate the meaning of the residential community and the limits of the private sphere and life within it, and must have the awareness and attitude that they will live together within it, along with mutual respect.\\n\\nThe majority opinion’s view and conclusion on the issues in this case are based on the above understanding of the meaning and limits of the shared living relationship within a joint residence.\\n\\nb. Whether a co-resident can be punished for the offense of intrusion upon residence\\n\\n1) On a textual interpretation of Article 319(1) of the Criminal Act, the object of the offense of intrusion upon residence is a residence occupied by a person other than the actor, that is, by another person, and where one of the co-residents is the actor, a residence shared with another person does not constitute the object of the offense of intrusion upon residence unless there are special circumstances such as withdrawal from the shared living relationship or loss of factual control and management over the residence.\\n\\n2) A joint residence is the actor’s own residence for one co-resident and at the same time also has the status of another person’s residence in relation to the other resident. Because of this dual nature of the joint residence, each co-resident can enjoy the legal interest of factual peace and tranquility in the joint residence, while in the relationship among co-residents each person’s legal interest in residence is inevitably limited to a certain extent, and it can be viewed that co-residents tolerated these circumstances while forming the joint residential relationship. The free entry and use of the place of shared living by a co-resident during the period of joint residence is the most basic aspect of the ordinary use of a joint residence as a co-resident, and part of the joint residential relationship that each co-resident must tolerate and bear. Therefore, barring special circumstances, among co-residents one person cannot prohibit another co-resident from entering, and the offense of intrusion upon residence is not established merely because he disregarded such prohibition and entered freely.\\n\\n3) However, we cannot exclude exceptional cases in which a co-resident’s entry into the joint residence is connected with special circumstances that constitute the offense of intrusion upon residence in relation to another co-resident. The majority opinion does not deny even such exceptional possibility.\\n\\nFirst, where a co-resident is recognized, under concrete factual circumstances such as the circumstances and form of the joint residence, the course of events, and the present state of the joint residence, as having withdrawn from the joint residence, such may be regarded as a case where the above special circumstances exist.\\n\\nNext, where one co-resident applies to the court for a provisional injunction prohibiting entry into the joint residence against another co-resident and obtains a court order granting such prohibition; where one co-resident is a domestic violence offender and, pursuant to the Domestic Violence Punishment Act, receives a temporary measure decision of “separation by eviction, etc. from the residence of the victim or family member,” or “prohibition of approaching within 100 meters of the victim or family member or their residence, workplace, etc.” (Article 29(1) subparagraphs 1 and 2); where one co-resident is an offender of child abuse and receives a temporary measure decision under the Child Abuse Punishment Act of separation by eviction from the residence, etc. or prohibition of approaching within 100 meters of the residence, etc. (Article 19(1) subparagraphs 1 and 2); and other cases where entry into the joint residence is prohibited on legal grounds, if a person enters the joint residence contrary to such prohibition, the offense of intrusion upon residence may be deemed established. This can be regarded as a case where the factual control and management over the residence has been lost.\\n\\n4) Unless there are such special circumstances or cases equivalent thereto, a co-resident cannot prohibit another co-resident from entering the place of shared living. This is because it would exclude another co-resident, who enters to use the place of shared living, from the joint residence without justifiable reason, which is impermissible. If a co-resident who has been prohibited from entering without justifiable reason enters the place of shared living in resistance thereto, and if the offense of intrusion upon residence is deemed not established, then even if, before such entry, there was an exercise of physical force intended to解除 the entry blockade such as locking the entrance door, it is aside from whether such act itself can be punished, but the act of entering the place of shared living likewise does not constitute the offense of intrusion upon residence.\\n\\nOf course, even before such lawful procedures as a provisional injunction prohibiting entry have been taken, there may be exceptional situations in which protection of the peace of residence is necessary from a co-resident, such as where the joint residence functions as a refuge protecting another co-resident and his or her protected minor children from serious domestic violence or child abuse by one co-resident. In such cases, where one co-resident forcibly enters by exercising physical force, etc., the act may be recognized as intrusion depending on the specific factual circumstances. This is because the freedom of a co-resident to enter the joint residence presupposes a residential space as a means of realizing human dignity. If the joint residence or a specific space inside it has lost the function of a joint residence for realizing such human dignity and is instead serving only as a refuge under circumstances where there is imminent or ongoing serious danger to the life or bodily safety of one co-resident’s violence and the other co-resident who is the victim thereof, then in substance there may be a special circumstance requiring protection of another co-resident’s peace of residence.\\n\\nIn this regard, unlike the dissent’s point, the majority opinion cannot be said to run counter to the legislative intent of the amended Domestic Violence Punishment Act of October 20, 2020, which included the offense of intrusion upon residence among domestic violence crimes. This is because the majority opinion also respects and accords with the legislative purpose of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act, namely prevention of domestic violence and protection of victims. Moreover, the Domestic Violence Punishment Act prescribes special rules concerning criminal punishment procedures for specific offenses involving domestic violence, and even if the offense of intrusion upon residence is included in domestic violence crimes, this only concerns cases in which acts causing bodily, mental, or property damage among family members are committed by means of intrusion upon residence; it does not mean that an act of entry into a residence that does not itself constitute intrusion upon residence becomes subject to the offense of intrusion upon residence merely because such entry caused bodily, mental, or property damage to a family member in the process. Whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established in the internal relationship among co-residents who constitute a family community, the traditional form of joint residence, is a matter to be determined by ascertaining the substance of the case under concrete facts based on the foregoing legal principles. Without considering such substance, one cannot uniformly classify and punish entry into a joint residence as the offense of intrusion upon residence merely because physical force was used in the process.\\n\\nMoreover, the family members who are the prerequisite for application of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act mean spouses, lineal ascendants and descendants, and cohabiting relatives, and in this case, since victim Non-Indicted 2, who prohibited Defendant 1’s entry, is difficult to regard as falling within this category, it is also not appropriate to use this as a basis for the dissent’s argument.\\n\\n5) a) The majority opinion, on the premise that one co-resident, without legal grounds or other justifiable reason to prohibit entry, has prohibited another co-resident’s entry itself by unilateral use of force, discussed whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established against the co-resident who entered in resistance to such impermissible prohibition on entry. It does not take the position that the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence is entirely denied even where one co-resident, despite having legal grounds or other justifiable reason to prohibit the other co-resident’s entry, enters in a manner that undermines the factual peaceful state of residence.\\n\\nThe majority opinion’s purport is that, in judging whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established concerning one of the co-residents in a dispute among co-residents, a balanced and cautious approach is necessary. This is because, even where the recognition of withdrawal from the joint residence, or the deprivation of factual control and management over the joint residence pursuant to a court’s provisional injunction prohibiting entry or other temporary measure such as prohibition of approach, etc., is a matter that can be corrected through factual findings or legal procedures, it is not appropriate to immediately criminalize a co-resident’s entry into the place of shared living without such procedures. The offense of intrusion upon residence is punishable even if the victim withdraws the intent to prosecute, and if the State hasty intervenes in the midst of disputes among co-residents by applying criminal law provisions, in some cases it may even lead to an irreparable situation in the causal relationship that formed the joint residence. Considering that a joint residence, which is the basic place where everyday life is conducted, is a place where human dignity is routinely realized regardless of which co-resident is involved, greater caution is required in depriving rights or status therein.\\n\\nb) In this case, the majority opinion, premised on the fact that Defendant 1 had not withdrawn from the joint living relationship in the apartment at issue and that there was no court decision such as a provisional injunction prohibiting entry or a temporary measure decision prohibiting approach against Defendant 1, and therefore no “special circumstance” could be recognized that would allow Non-Indicted 1, a co-resident, or victim Non-Indicted 2, to whom entry control over the apartment at issue had been entrusted by Non-Indicted 1, to prohibit Defendant 1’s entry, held that victim Non-Indicted 2’s unilateral use of force to prohibit Defendant 1’s entry could not be permitted, and that even if Defendant 1, in resistance thereto, exercised physical force by damaging the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the apartment at issue and entered the apartment at issue, this was merely a means for Defendant 1 to enter the apartment at issue, which was a joint residence, and thus the offense of intrusion upon residence was not established against Defendant 1. In other words, in this case, the majority opinion’s purport is that because this does not amount to an exceptional situation in which the offense of intrusion upon residence is established even for a co-resident’s entry into a joint residence, it is not a case to which the exceptional legal doctrine premised on that can be applied.\\n\\nc) The dissent, based on victim Non-Indicted 2’s or Non-Indicted 1’s statements, made new factual findings regarding the justifiable reason for victim Non-Indicted 2’s having prohibited Defendant 1’s entry, and then concluded that one cannot say that there was no justifiable reason for the “prohibition on entry” by victim Non-Indicted 2 at the time of this case.\\n\\nHowever, the dissent has a problem in that it reached the above conclusion on the basis of factual circumstances not recognized by the lower appellate court. The majority opinion, premised on the facts recognized by the lower appellate court, held that in light of the circumstances at the time of entry, victim Non-Indicted 2 had no legal basis or other justifiable reason to take measures prohibiting Defendant 1’s entry [meanwhile, according to the record, Defendant 1 stated to the investigative authorities that he had been driven out of the house on April 13, 2018 (Volume 1 of the evidence record, p. 50), and we add that there is also doubt whether the dissent’s factual findings based on the statements of the victim Non-Indicted 2 or Non-Indicted 1 are persuasive].\\n\\n6) a) The dissent states that once one co-resident enters a joint residence in a manner undermining the peaceful state of the co-resident who prohibited his entry, this can no longer be a general form of use of the joint residence and goes beyond the limits of ordinary use of the joint residence.\\n\\nHowever, just as the fact that a resident used some degree of physical force in entering a residence does not make him a non-resident intruder, the fact that a co-resident exercised physical force to release an entry blockade imposed by one-sided force from another co-resident in order to enter the place of shared living does not mean that the nature of that entry changes into an act of intrusion. This is because entering a joint residence is the most fundamental premise of using a joint residence in the joint residential relationship, and there is also a separate penal provision punishing the physical force that was used.\\n\\nb) The dissent’s view also deliberately disregards or overlooks the problems of the prior measure taken by another co-resident in this case, who, without legal grounds or justifiable reason, prohibited one co-resident’s entry itself by unilateral force. The act by which a co-resident blocks or prohibits another co-resident’s entry into the joint residence by force can itself be evaluated as infringing the peace of residence of the other co-resident, and if one assumes a case where the co-resident blocked from entering has nowhere else to stay, then, on the premise that such unilateral entry blockade is justified, to instead evaluate and punish the act of overcoming it and entering as intrusion upon residence does not accord with common social understanding.\\n\\nIn this case, although it is a matter of a wife residing in a joint residence and a husband who had left home and seeks to return, if one considers the reverse case, where the husband exploits the wife’s temporary absence from the joint residence, changes the key or password of the door lock so that the wife cannot come in, and the wife then breaks or unlocks the lock and enters the house together with her parents in her natal family, then under the dissent, this too would have to be regarded as constituting the offense of intrusion upon residence. Yet such a conclusion is one to which no one would readily agree.\\n\\nEven in such cases, if the offense of intrusion upon residence is deemed established and criminal punishment is imposed, it may lead to a harsh result for the weaker co-resident who was driven out of the joint residence.\\n\\nc) The dissent says that if the majority opinion, in the offense of intrusion upon residence, which protects the peace of residence as the protected legal interest and punishes acts infringing it, adopts as the standard “whether the victim’s act prohibiting entry had a legal basis,” it does not accord with the established position of the Supreme Court that “even if a person is a right holder, if he intrudes upon a residence or structure by self-help as a means of exercising that right, the offense of intrusion upon residence or intrusion upon a structure is established.”\\n\\nThe Supreme Court decisions referred to by the dissent are understood as dealing with cases in which a party who had already lost possession, among disputing stakeholders concerning exclusive attribution of rights over a residence or structure, entered the residence or structure by using self-help as a means of rights exercise to regain it. In such ordinary cases, there is no particular theory against the proposition that the above position of the Supreme Court is appropriate.\\n\\nHowever, in this case, where the joint residential relationship continues without interruption or severance by unilateral departure, and each co-resident’s freedom and peace to enter and use the joint residence is guaranteed, whether the act of one co-resident entering the joint residence in resistance to another co-resident’s prohibition on entry without justifiable reason constitutes the offense of intrusion upon residence differs in substance from cases in which the offense of intrusion upon residence or intrusion upon a structure was recognized on the basis that even a right holder is prohibited from self-help, and thus the legal principles of the above Supreme Court decisions cannot be applied as they are. This is because, within a joint residence where withdrawal from the joint residential relationship has not been recognized, each co-resident can enjoy the freedom and peace of residence in which individual dignity is realized, while the exercise of each co-resident’s rights arising from the joint use of the residence is subject to restrictions and mutual tolerance of the existence and exercise of rights by the other co-resident is also required.\\n\\nAgain, the majority opinion is addressing whether, in light of the general form in which a co-resident uses a joint residence, if a co-resident tries to enter the residence in the ordinary manner of entry as the general form of use of the residence as a resident, but another co-resident unilaterally prohibits that entry without legal grounds or other justifiable reason, the co-resident trying to enter that residence can be punished for the offense of intrusion upon residence.\\n\\nc. Whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established where an outsider, having received the consent of one co-resident, enters a joint residence in a manner undermining the peaceful state of another co-resident\\n\\n1) The offense of intrusion upon residence is a crime concerning individual legal interests, and even if a resident has no legal right or authority to reside in the residence, if the residence is in factual peaceful control and management, it receives protection under criminal law. Even in the case of a joint residence, each co-resident who resides in the joint residence is in a position to enjoy the protected legal interest of peace of residence from outside.\\n\\nOn the other hand, in the case of a joint residence, since the legal interest of peace of residence held by each co-resident can conflict with one another, each co-resident’s legal interest in peace of residence in the joint residence is inevitably limited to a certain extent by the relationship with other co-residents, and it must be understood that co-residents mutually tolerated these circumstances while forming the joint residential relationship.\\n\\nThe content and scope of the ordinary acts of entering and using the place of shared living mutually tolerated by each co-resident must be examined individually and concretely according to the form and nature of the joint residence and the circumstances by which the joint residence was formed. It is one of the general forms in which a co-resident uses the joint residence for one co-resident to invite an outsider to enter the joint residence. For example, if in a family one spouse invites his parents or a colleague into the home, in light of the ordinary life relationship of the general public, this can be seen as a general form of use of the joint residence by a co-resident. Therefore, entry into the joint residence by an outsider pursuant to the invitation or consent of one co-resident can, barring special circumstances, be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the act of a co-resident entering and using the place of shared living. On the other hand, where entry by an outsider into the joint residence against the opposition of another co-resident cannot be regarded as conduct incidental to or encompassed by ordinary use of the joint residence as a co-resident, the matter must be viewed differently.\\n\\nThus, whether an outsider’s entry into the joint residence pursuant to the consent of one co-resident establishes the offense of intrusion upon residence in relation to another co-resident who opposes it is not a matter susceptible to uniform evaluation. The standard for evaluation may be whether, from the perspective of the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry, such outsider’s entry can be evaluated as conduct incidental to the ordinary use of the joint residence by that co-resident, and from the perspective of the other co-resident, whether it can be evaluated as within the range that he must tolerate. The specific determination will be sufficient if a reasonable conclusion fitting the case is drawn by comprehensively considering the characteristics of the relevant joint residential relationship, the agreement or regulation among co-residents, and other relevant factual circumstances.\\n\\n2) The above legal principles and evaluation standard can likewise be applied where an outsider, pursuant to the consent of one co-resident, enters that co-resident’s joint residence and thereby undermines the factual peaceful state of another co-resident.\\n\\nThat is, even in such a case, one must examine whether this can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the act of the co-resident who consented to entering and using the place of shared living, and whether the other co-resident can be evaluated as being obliged to tolerate it in light of the characteristics of the joint residential relationship, in determining whether the offense of intrusion upon residence is established.\\n\\nAs discussed above, even though a co-resident enters the place of shared living, the fact that he used some degree of physical force in the process of entering the joint residence in resistance to an entry blockade imposed by another co-resident by unilateral force does not mean that the nature of the entry changes into an act of intrusion, and it is appropriate to regulate and punish the use of such physical force under a separate penal provision. The logic and subsidiarity of criminal punishment should equally apply to an outsider as well, where the outsider’s entry occurred incidental to the ordinary use of the joint residence by the co-resident.\\n\\n3) The dissent says that where, as in this case, an outsider who received the consent of one co-resident uses physical force to enter the joint residence and thereby undermines the factual peaceful state of another co-resident, the offense of intrusion upon residence should be punished.\\n\\nFirst, as noted above, it cannot be the proper interpretation and application of the offense of intrusion upon residence in relation to a joint residence to uniformly punish as intrusion upon residence the existence of a manner of act undermining another co-resident’s factual peace, merely because a co-resident entered the joint residence or an outsider entered the joint residence incident to such entry with his consent.\\n\\nFurthermore, the fact that a co-resident blocks or prohibits another co-resident’s entry into the joint residence by force itself can be evaluated as a prior act that infringes the other co-resident’s peace of residence, and, if one assumes a case where the co-resident blocked from entering has no proper place to stay, then it was also noted above that evaluating and punishing as intrusion the act of overcoming such unilateral entry blockade and entering, on the premise that the unilateral blockade is justified, does not accord with social common sense. In this case, although Non-Indicted 1, who was a co-resident, or victim Non-Indicted 2, to whom entry control over the apartment at issue was entrusted by Non-Indicted 1, did not have any special circumstances that would allow them to prohibit Defendant 1’s entry, who was another co-resident and not in a state of withdrawal from the joint residential relationship at that time, they blocked and prohibited Defendant 1’s entry by force, which caused Defendant 1 to exercise physical force, such as damaging the chain latch installed on the entrance door of the apartment at issue, in order to enter the apartment at issue.
