Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, in the position of Non-Indicted 1’s parents-in-law and Defendant 1’s parents, joined Defendant 1’s conduct and entered together incident to it, and this can be evaluated overall as having been carried out as part of, and incidental to, Defendant 1’s act of entering and using the apartment at issue, a joint residence.\\n\\nThe majority opinion, premised on such a situation, held that in light of the legal principles concerning the mutual restrictions on rights and the duty of tolerance arising from the joint residential relationship, the acts of entry by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 can receive the same evaluation as the act of entry by Defendant 1, who was a co-resident.\\n\\nWhether the purport of the dissent is that whenever physical force is used in the course of an outsider entering a joint residence the offense of intrusion upon residence must uniformly be established, or that in this case such a conclusion should be drawn, the majority opinion does not regard either as a proper legal principle or conclusion.\\n\\n4) The dissent also argues, to the effect, that the majority opinion is insufficient in protecting the legal interests of freedom and peace of residence, which should be protected from force and the dominance of the majority.\\n\\nHowever, this misunderstands the purport of the majority opinion. Repeatedly stated, the majority opinion presupposes a situation where one co-resident, as a co-resident, enters the place of shared living in the joint residence within the scope mutually tolerated, and the entry by an outsider likewise occurs incident to that and with the consent of the co-resident, as part of the ordinary use of the joint residence. Even in such a case, if the offense of intrusion upon residence is recognized in relation to a co-resident who imposed a prohibition on entry without justifiable reason, then the legal interest of the ordinary peace of residence that a co-resident enjoys in the joint residence is unjustly denied by another co-resident’s unilateral use of force. That is precisely what would constitute, and tolerate, infringement of the legal interest of freedom and peace of residence by the unilateral power and authority of one side.\\n\\n5) The majority opinion’s comparison of the statutory punishment for the offense of intrusion upon residence under the Criminal Act with the systems of other countries that regulate the offense of intrusion upon residence as a non-complaint offense was intended to point out that, in light of the punishment and regulatory system of the offense of intrusion upon residence under the Criminal Act, punishing the outsider for intrusion upon residence even though the outsider’s entry into the joint residence pursuant to the consent of one co-resident can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary act of entering and using the place of shared living by the co-resident who consented to it constitutes an excessive exercise of state punitive power.\\n\\nIn relation to this point, the majority opinion’s purport is that excessive state intervention into the private sphere through state punitive power can inevitably produce side effects that impede the autonomy of the private sphere and the development of civil and family law principles and systems, so caution is necessary. Although the need for state protection of the socially vulnerable in private spheres, including the family, is increasing day by day, this is also why it is difficult to readily apply the offense of intrusion upon residence in a direction that expands the scope of application of criminal provisions and criminal punishment.\\n\\nFor the reasons above, we state our supplemental opinion in support of the majority opinion.\\n\\n10. Supplemental opinion of Justice Min Yu-suk regarding the dissent\\n\\na. Summary of the supplemental dissent\\n\\nWe will consider the effect of this en banc decision on future trials and the interpretive theory of the relevant statutes.\\n\\nb. Changes in the requirements for recognizing “withdrawal from the joint residential relationship”\\n\\nBecause the majority opinion denies the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence against a co-resident, whether one has withdrawn from the status of co-resident will be an important standard for determining the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence.\\n\\nThere is no established standard for recognizing whether a co-resident has withdrawn from that status, and each case must be determined individually according to the facts recognized in the specific case. No Supreme Court precedent has yet been found that sets forth the standard for recognition.\\n\\nWhere the marital community is dissolved by divorce and one spouse leaves the joint residence, it is obvious that he or she has withdrawn from the status of co-resident. However, withdrawal from the status of co-resident does not occur only when the causal relationship that formed the joint residential relationship is extinguished or the title of possession over the residence is lost.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court, in a case where the defendant, after leaving home due to family discord, lived separately for about 5 months, handed over the door key to his wife through a marriage broker and thereafter did not request the return of the key, accepted the lower court’s finding that the defendant had withdrawn from the status of co-resident and that the act of prying open the door lock and entering the house constituted the offense of intrusion upon residence, even though the defendant, as a lessee, had left his belongings in the house [see Supreme Court Decision 94DO3336, decided on 1995. 9. 15.].\\n\\nSince the majority opinion finds the basis for denying the offense of intrusion upon residence against a co-resident in the “ordinary form of use of the joint residence” and the “restriction of legal interests that co-residents must mutually tolerate,” the determination of whether one has withdrawn from the joint residential relationship in the future should likewise find its standard here. And such determination must be made concretely and individually, based on the factual circumstances recognized as a result of examining the circumstances and period until the co-resident came to live separately, the circumstances by which the co-resident remaining in the home took measures to prohibit the other party’s entry (such as changing the password), and the subsequent responses of both sides.\\n\\nc. Relationship with the Domestic Violence Punishment Act\\n\\nAs stated in the dissent, according to the amended Domestic Violence Punishment Act enforced on January 21, 2021, the offense of intrusion upon residence under the Criminal Act (Article 319(1)), the offense of refusing to leave (Article 319(2)), the special offense of intrusion upon residence (Article 320), and the attempted offenses of the above crimes (Article 322) that arise among family members who are co-residents also fall within the “domestic violence crimes” prescribed by that Act [Article 2 subparagraph 3 (sa)].\\n\\nIn addition, judicial police officers who receive a report of a domestic violence crime and are dispatched to the scene were amended to be required to suppress the act of violence, separate the domestic violence offender and the victim, and investigate the crime, including arresting a flagrant offender under Article 212 of the Criminal Procedure Act (Article 5 subparagraph 1 and subparagraph 1-2).\\n\\nThe conclusion, according to the majority opinion, denying the establishment of the offense of intrusion upon residence against a co-resident should be interpreted as limited to cases prosecuted under the offense of intrusion upon residence in the Criminal Act. It appears that the majority opinion does not deny that where statutes provide otherwise, those statutes should be followed.\\n\\nEven if the act by which a co-resident, by violent means, subdues another co-resident’s refusal and enters the shared residence cannot be charged as the offense of intrusion upon residence under the Criminal Act according to the majority opinion, it still falls within the domestic violence crimes prescribed by the amended Domestic Violence Punishment Act, and under that Act, investigative agencies that receive a report of domestic violence have the authority and duty to dispatch to the scene and investigate crimes, including arresting the domestic violence offender in flagrante delicto. For such conduct, temporary measure decisions such as separation by eviction, etc. from the residence of the victim or family member, or prohibition of approaching within 100 meters, may be issued (Article 29(1) subparagraphs 1 and 2), victim protection orders and temporary protection orders of the same content may be issued (Article 55-2(1) subparagraphs 1 and 2, Article 55-4(1)), and protection disposition decisions restricting acts of approaching the victim or family member may be issued (Article 40(1) subparagraph 1). If a co-resident enters the residence in violation of such dispositions, it becomes subject to criminal punishment as the offense of noncompliance with protection dispositions, etc. under Article 63 of the same Act. Acts violating such temporary measures, etc. are acts entering despite “court measures prohibiting entry into the joint residence,” and even under the majority opinion, they would separately constitute the offense of intrusion upon residence under the Criminal Act.\\n\\nIf the majority opinion were to mean that “the act by which a co-resident, by violent means, subdues another co-resident’s refusal and enters the shared residence does not constitute the offense of intrusion upon residence under the Criminal Act, and therefore does not fall within the domestic violence crimes prescribed by the Domestic Violence Punishment Act,” then the legislative purpose of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act would be entirely nullified by the majority opinion. That is because, even though the Domestic Violence Punishment Act was amended to expressly include the offense of intrusion upon residence under Book II, Chapter 36 of the Criminal Act in order to protect family members who are victims of acts of intrusion upon residence by violent means, even when such actors are family members, that interpretation would exclude such acts from domestic violence crimes.\\n\\nFor the reasons above, I state this supplemental opinion regarding the dissent."}

{"[2020DO6085]": "We adjudicate the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Scope of Adjudication by this Court\\n\\nWith respect to the charge of violation of the Act on the Punishment of Violent Acts, etc. (hereinafter the “Violent Acts Punishment Act”) against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 among the facts charged in this case (joint bodily injury), the court of first instance acquitted them, and although the Prosecutor appealed, the lower appellate court dismissed the appeal. Since the Prosecutor did not appeal against this, that part became final. Accordingly, as to Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, only the remaining parts, excluding the parts already finalized as not guilty, are subject to adjudication by this Court; therefore, we will examine only the grounds of appeal concerning those parts.\\n\\n2. Outline of the Case and Issues\\n\\nA. The gist of the facts charged subject to adjudication is as follows.\\n\\nDefendant 1 is the husband of Nonparty 1 and the brother-in-law of Nonparty 2, and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 are the parents of Defendant 1 and the parents-in-law of Nonparty 1.\\n\\n1) Violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.)\\n\\nAt around 2:30 p.m. on May 19, 2018, the Defendants went to the apartment that is the residence of the Victim, Nonparty 1, in this case, and demanded that the entrance door be opened. However, the Victim, Nonparty 1, was out, and her younger sibling, Nonparty 2, had fastened the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door and would not open the door, saying, “Come back when my sister returns home.” Accordingly, Defendant 1 and Defendant 2, acting jointly, Defendant 1 inserted his hand through the gap when the door was opened and struck the chain-type latch several times downward, and Defendant 2 repeatedly shook the door handle, causing the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door to detach from the door.\\n\\nAs a result, Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 damaged the Victim, Nonparty 1’s chain-type latch, the value of which is unknown, thereby impairing its utility.\\n\\n2) Violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence)\\n\\nThe Defendants jointly, after damaging the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door of the residence where the Victim, Nonparty 2, was staying at the time and place stated in paragraph 1), entered the residence.\\n\\nB. The lower appellate court ruled as follows.\\n\\n1) With respect to the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.) against Defendant 1 and Defendant 2, the court left intact the judgment of the court of first instance, which found them guilty.\\n\\n2) With respect to the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against Defendant 1, the lower appellate court held that, under the Criminal Act, the object of the offense of residential trespass is a residence occupied by another person, and where the actor is a person living together with another person, the relevant residence does not constitute the object of this offense unless he has departed from the joint household relationship. On the ground that Defendant 1 could not be deemed to have departed from the status of a co-resident of this apartment at the time in question, the lower appellate court held that the offense of residential trespass was not established, set aside the judgment of the court of first instance that had found him guilty, and rendered a verdict of not guilty.\\n\\n3) With respect to the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, the lower appellate court held that where there are multiple persons with rights of residence, if the consent of one person is directly or indirectly contrary to the will of another resident, entry into the residence under such consent impairs the peace of mind of the person whose will is contrary, that is, the peace of dominion and management over the residence, and thus the offense of residential trespass is established. Therefore, it left intact the judgment of the court of first instance that found them guilty on the ground that, even if Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 entered the apartment of this case with the consent of Defendant 1, a co-resident of that apartment, because they did not obtain the consent of Nonparty 1, another resident, or of Victim Nonparty 2, to whom Nonparty 1 had entrusted the management of access to the residence, they disturbed the de facto peace of mind of Victim Nonparty 2, and the offense of residential trespass was thus established.\\n\\nC. The gist of the grounds for appeal by the Prosecutor and the Defendants is as follows.\\n\\n1) Grounds for appeal by the Prosecutor\\n\\nDefendant 1 had departed from this apartment and lost his status as a co-resident, and since he entered the apartment together with Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 by violent means, the offense of residential trespass is established. Nevertheless, the lower appellate court’s judgment holding otherwise and finding that the offense of residential trespass is not established contains error by violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles on the establishment of the offense of residential trespass.\\n\\n2) Grounds for appeal by the Defendants\\n\\nA) As to the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.) against Defendant 1 and Defendant 2\\n\\nDefendant 1 and Defendant 2 did not damage the chain-type latch as stated in the facts charged for this part, nor did they have the intent to damage it. Even if not, their acts constitute self-help or justifiable acts. Nevertheless, the lower appellate court’s judgment finding guilt on this part contains error by violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or by misapprehending the legal principles on the establishment of the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.), justifiable act, and self-help.\\n\\nB) As to the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\n(1) Where a person enters a joint residence with the consent of one of the co-residents, the offense of residential trespass is not established, unless there are special circumstances such as entering for the purpose of committing a crime against another resident. Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 entered the apartment in this case with the consent of Defendant 1, a co-resident of that apartment, and they did not enter for the purpose of committing a crime against Nonparty 1 or Victim Nonparty 2, who were other residents; therefore, the offense of residential trespass is not established against the said Defendants.\\n\\n(2) Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 lacked the intent to trespass into a residence, and their acts fall under either a justifiable act, which does not violate social norms as provided in Article 20 of the Criminal Act, or self-help as provided in Article 23 of the Criminal Act, so unlawfulness is excluded.\\n\\n(3) Nevertheless, the lower appellate court’s judgment finding guilt on this part against the said Defendants contains error by misapprehending the legal principles on the establishment of the offense of residential trespass, justifiable act, and self-help.\\n\\nD. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nThe offense of residential trespass protects the factual peace of mind of the residence as the protected legal interest. Since the trespass that constitutes the actus reus of residential trespass must be construed in relation to the protected legal interest of the offense of residential trespass, trespass means entering a residence in a manner that disturbs the factual peaceful state enjoyed by the resident in the residence, and whether it constitutes trespass is, in principle, to be determined based on the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of entry at the time of entry. If the manner of entry into a residence is such as to disturb the factual peaceful state, it would, unless there are special circumstances, be contrary to the resident’s will; however, it cannot immediately be deemed trespass merely on the basis of the resident’s subjective circumstance that the mere act of entering the residence is contrary to the resident’s will (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2020DO12630, rendered September 9, 2021).\\n\\nE. The principal issues in this case are as follows.\\n\\n1) Premise for discussion\\n\\nThis case concerns a situation in which Defendant 1, who was a co-resident of this apartment, in the process of entering this apartment together with Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, his parents and also the parents-in-law of Nonparty 1, another co-resident, used physical force such as damaging the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door of this apartment after Victim Nonparty 2, who was staying in the apartment entrusted by Nonparty 1, fastened the chain-type latch on the entrance door of this apartment and refused to open the door, thereby prohibiting Defendant 1’s entry. In light of the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of entry at the time the Defendants entered this apartment, it may be said that this constitutes an act disturbing the factual peaceful state of Victim Nonparty 2.\\n\\n2) Principal issues in this case\\n\\nA) The first issue is whether the offense of residential trespass is established even where, in a case where one of the co-residents enters a joint residence in a manner that disturbs the factual peaceful state of another co-resident who has prohibited his entry, such entry can be evaluated as constituting a general mode of use of the joint residence.\\n\\nB) The second issue is whether the offense of residential trespass is established against an outsider where, in a case where one of the co-residents enters a joint residence by exercising physical force against another co-resident who has prohibited his entry into the joint residence, an outsider joins in such act of the co-resident and together enters the joint residence in a manner that disturbs the factual peaceful state of the other co-resident who has prohibited their entry, if such entry by the outsider can be evaluated as part of the ordinary use of the joint residence by the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry or as an act incidental thereto.\\n\\n3. Determination on the Prosecutor’s Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nA. As to the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against Defendant 1\\n\\n1) The Criminal Act provides in Article 319(1) that “a person who intrudes upon another’s residence, managed structure, ship, or aircraft, or occupied room” shall be punished for residential trespass. The offense of residential trespass is established when a person other than the resident, manager of a structure, ship, or aircraft, or occupant of a room (hereinafter “resident, etc.”) intrudes upon such residence, structure, ship, aircraft, or room (hereinafter “residence, etc.”). Accordingly, the object of the offense of residential trespass is the residence, etc., in which a person other than the actor, that is, “another,” resides; therefore, even if the actor himself freely enters a residence, etc. that he occupies alone or jointly with another person, or manages or occupies jointly with another person, it does not constitute residential trespass. Only where there are special circumstances, such as where a person who had resided or managed a residence together with another person departs from the cohabitation relationship or loses factual dominion and management over the residence, etc., may the offense of residential trespass be established.\\n\\nIn this spirit, the Supreme Court upheld a lower appellate court that held the offense of residential trespass was not established because a residence in which the victim and the defendant cohabited did not constitute another person’s residence, even though the defendant entered that residence (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DO16537, rendered December 27, 2012), and also held that the offense of trespass into a structure was not established even where one co-occupant freely entered a structure under joint management (see Supreme Court Decision 81DO2956, rendered April 27, 1982).\\n\\n2) Meanwhile, insofar as the offense of residential trespass protects the factual peace of mind of the residence, each co-resident living in a joint residence may be said to enjoy the factual peace of mind of the residence. However, each co-resident, unless there are special circumstances, may enter and use the common space by entering the portions set as the place of common life within the joint residence in accordance with the purport and characteristics of the joint residence relationship and may use the common space, for the same reason that other co-residents may also do so. Accordingly, each co-resident also bears a duty to tolerate other co-residents’ entry into and use of such space. That is also the ordinary form in which co-residents use a joint residence. Thus, the legal interest of factual peace of mind enjoyed by each co-resident at the place of common life is inevitably subject to some restriction due to the relationship among co-residents, and it must be deemed that co-residents formed the joint residence relationship by mutually tolerating such circumstances. Therefore, unless there are special circumstances, co-residents cannot prohibit other co-residents from freely entering and using the place of common life.\\n\\nWhere one of the co-residents, without legal basis or any other justifiable reason, prohibits another co-resident from entering the place of common life, if the other co-resident enters the place of common life in response, this is merely a means of using the place of common life in accordance with the already anticipated purpose and characteristics of the joint residence; it cannot be regarded as an act infringing the legal interest of factual peace of mind of the co-resident who prohibited entry, and therefore the offense of residential trespass is not established. Even if the co-resident impaired the factual peaceful state of the co-resident who prohibited entry by exercising some physical force, such as damaging the lock of the entrance door in order to enter the place of common life, it may be punished under separate provisions that punish such conduct itself; leaving that aside, the offense of residential trespass is likewise not established.\\n\\n3) The lower appellate court held that the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) was not established against Defendant 1 on the basis of the following facts and reasons.\\n\\nA) Facts recognized by the lower appellate court\\n\\n(1) Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1 are a legally married couple who married on September 5, 2015, have one child between them, and have been living as a married couple in this apartment since around August 15, 2016.\\n\\n(2) Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1 began to quarrel frequently from around January 2018 over the issue of pre-sale of a newly built apartment, and Defendant 1 fought with Nonparty 1 on April 9, 2018, took some of his belongings, and left this apartment. Defendant 1 visited this apartment on April 13, 2018, fought again with Nonparty 1, and left the home. Thereafter, Nonparty 1 unilaterally changed the password to the entrance door of this apartment and also attached a chain-type latch to the entrance door.\\n\\n(3) Through mobile phone messenger, Defendant 1 requested Nonparty 1 on April 17, 2018, and April 19, 2018, to inform him of the password to the front door of this apartment, and on May 4, 2018, he even visited this apartment and requested at the entrance that the door be opened, but was refused.\\n\\n(4) Nonparty 1 filed a claim for divorce, etc. with the court around June 28, 2018, after the occurrence of this case, and on September 4, 2018, a divorce conciliation was reached between Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1.\\n\\nB) Reasons for the lower appellate court’s decision\\n\\nAt the time in question, it is difficult to view that there was an express agreement between Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1 to dissolve the marital relationship and for Defendant 1 to leave and live outside the joint residence, this apartment. In such a situation, the mere fact that Defendant 1 took some of his belongings and left the apartment, or that Nonparty 1 unilaterally changed the entrance password and prevented Defendant 1 from coming in, does not mean that Defendant 1 departed from or was excluded from the status of a co-resident. Therefore, even if Defendant 1 used means such as damaging the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door in the process of entering this apartment, the offense of residential trespass is not established.\\n\\n4) We examine the reasons of the lower appellate court’s judgment in light of the above legal principles and the record.\\n\\nThe evidence submitted by the Prosecutor alone is insufficient to establish that Defendant 1 departed from the cohabitation relationship in this apartment or lost dominion and management over it, and there is no other evidence establishing this. Furthermore, it is not established that Nonparty 1, a co-resident of this apartment, or Victim Nonparty 2, to whom she entrusted access management for this apartment, had any legal basis or other justifiable reason to prohibit Defendant 1, a co-resident of this apartment, from entering this apartment.\\n\\nIf so, it cannot be said that the offense of residential trespass is established merely because Defendant 1, who continued to maintain the status of a co-resident of this apartment, exercised physical force such as damaging the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door of this apartment in response to the measures of Victim Nonparty 2, who prohibited him without justifiable reason while he was entering this apartment. The lower appellate court’s determination to the same effect contains no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, by violating the rules of logic and experience, exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehending the legal principles on the establishment of the offense of residential trespass.\\n\\nB. As to the remaining part concerning Defendant 1\\n\\nMeanwhile, although the Prosecutor appealed against the entirety of the part concerning Defendant 1 in the lower appellate judgment, the petition of appeal or the statement of grounds for appeal did not set forth specific reasons for objection regarding the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.) that was found guilty by the lower appellate court.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Defendants’ Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nA. As to the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.) against Defendant 1 and Defendant 2\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower appellate judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, it is determined that it was proper to find this part of the facts charged guilty. Therefore, the lower appellate court’s determination contains no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, by violating the rules of logic and experience, exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehending the legal principles on the establishment of the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.), self-help, or justifiable act.\\n\\nB. As to the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\n1) Since each co-resident living in a joint residence may enjoy the factual peace of mind of the residence, if an outsider enters the joint residence with the consent of one of the co-residents, it could be viewed that, in relation to another co-resident, if the outsider enters in a manner that disturbs the latter’s factual peaceful state, such entry constitutes an infringement of the factual peace of mind of the joint residence and thus amounts to the offense of residential trespass.\\n\\nHowever, each co-resident, unless there are special circumstances, may not only enter and use the place of common life within the joint residence in accordance with the purport and characteristics of the joint residence relationship, but also must tolerate other co-residents’ entry into and use of the same. As such, the legal interest of factual peace of mind enjoyed by each co-resident at the place of common life is inevitably subject to some restriction due to the relationship among co-residents, and it must be deemed that co-residents formed the joint residence relationship by mutually tolerating such circumstances. Accordingly, the act of a co-resident entering and using the place of common life in a manner ordinarily tolerated and within the scope of mutual tolerance cannot be regarded as an act infringing the peace of mind of the residence, even if the manner of the act may be viewed as disturbing another co-resident’s factual peaceful state; hence the offense of residential trespass is not established. Whether an outsider’s entry into the place of common life upon the consent of one co-resident can be deemed an act infringing the peace of mind of another co-resident’s residence also needs to be examined from this perspective.\\n\\n2) The content and scope of the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life, mutually tolerated by each co-resident, must be examined individually and concretely according to the form and nature of the joint residence, and the circumstances in which the joint residence was formed. If an outsider’s entry into and use of the place of common life, pursuant to the consent of one co-resident, can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry, then such outsider’s act may be evaluated, overall, as identical to the act of that co-resident. Therefore, even where one co-resident, without legal basis or any other justifiable reason, prohibits another co-resident from entering the place of common life, and the other co-resident, in response, disturbs the factual peaceful state of the co-resident who prohibited entry in the course of entering the place of common life, if the entry and use by the outsider who entered together into the place of common life with the consent of that co-resident can be evaluated, overall, as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry, it is proper to view that the offense of residential trespass is likewise not established against the outsider, notwithstanding that he disturbed the factual peaceful state of the co-resident who prohibited entry. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\nA) In determining whether an individual’s legal interest has been infringed, it is necessary to take into account the social implications and limits of that legal interest. In the case of a joint residence, not only the aspect of individual legal interest protection for each co-resident, but also the meaning of shared life in the joint residence and the social limits that accompany it, must be considered in determining whether the protected legal interest of the offense of residential trespass has been infringed and whether the offense is established. In a joint residence where several persons live together, the legal interest in residence enjoyed by each co-resident is inevitably subject to some restriction, and it must be deemed that co-residents mutually tolerated such restriction. Even where an outsider’s entry upon the consent of one co-resident can, in light of the form and nature of the joint residence, the circumstances that led to the formation of the joint residence relationship, the relationship between the co-resident and the outsider, the purpose for which the outsider entered the joint residence, and the manner of entry, be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry, recognizing the offense of residential trespass merely because there is an aspect of disturbing another co-resident’s factual peaceful state within the joint residence would not only run counter to the mutual tolerance among co-residents, but would also amount to an unreasonable interpretation that ignores the essence and characteristics, diversity, and social limits inherent in joint residence.\\n\\nB) If the offense of residential trespass were recognized merely because an outsider entered upon the consent of one co-resident in a manner that disturbs another co-resident’s factual peaceful state, even where the outsider’s entry can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented, an unreasonable result may arise in which the existence of the outsider’s offense of residential trespass depends solely on contingent circumstances internal to the co-residents—namely, the conflict between the enjoyment of general and affirmative freedom of residence and the enjoyment of negative freedom and peace of residence within the joint residence.\\n\\nThe essence and mission of the Criminal Act as a legal norm lie in protecting the fundamental values indispensable to the existence and maintenance of society, and it is desirable that the subject matter regulated by the Criminal Act be limited to acts manifestly dangerous to major legal interests that cannot be resolved by other norms or means of social control, or acts that cause great harm to society. The purpose of granting the Criminal Act, among legal norms, a powerful sanction that deprives or restricts individual freedom and rights must likewise be understood in the same context. The Criminal Act provides only that the actus reus of residential trespass is trespass, and the punishment is imprisonment for not more than 3 years or a fine not exceeding 5 million won, which is higher than the legislative examples of other countries such as Germany, and it is regulated as a non-compound offense. In addition to the nature of the Criminal Act and the contents of its regulation, if one considers the social and normative meaning inherent in the concepts of joint residence and trespass, the concept of trespass in residential trespass must itself be understood as already including a legal evaluation of an act that, by itself, poses a serious risk of infringing the legal interest of the peace of residence beyond the range socially acceptable, or an act that causes great harm to society. Therefore, it is proper to construe that only acts evaluated as falling within the subject matter regulated by the Criminal Act can be punished as residential trespass. However, where an act of entering a joint residence upon the consent of one co-resident can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented, such act cannot readily be regarded as an act posing a serious risk to a major legal interest that cannot be resolved by other norms or means of social control, or as an act causing great harm to society. If, due to an outsider’s entry into a joint residence, another co-resident’s separate legal interest such as bodily freedom is infringed, and that infringement constitutes a separate offense, punishment for that offense is sufficient, and punitive provisions already exist in the Criminal Act and elsewhere. To criminally punish such a case as residential trespass would constitute an excessive intervention by the state’s punitive power, disregarding the diversity and specificity of the social relations accompanying joint residence and the possibility of self-regulation, and would thus be improper.\\n\\nC) Between co-residents, the value of protection of the legal interests each enjoys in the joint residence can be regarded as equal. Thus, if in a situation where legal interests among co-residents conflict in relation to an outsider’s entry, the offense of residential trespass is recognized against the outsider on the ground that the legal interest of another co-resident’s factual peace of mind was infringed, that would be improper also in the sense that it would prioritize only the legal interest of the co-resident who rejected the outsider’s entry, while disregarding the legal interest of the other co-resident who consented to the entry.\\n\\nD) Even where an outsider’s entry into a joint residence pursuant to the consent of one co-resident can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented, if the outsider were to be punished for residential trespass, it could also become an issue whether the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry may be punished as an accomplice to residential trespass. However, as noted above, since a co-resident who has not departed from the cohabitation relationship and who has no legal basis or any other justifiable reason to prohibit entry into the joint residence cannot be punished for residential trespass, in the above case only the outsider who entered the joint residence upon the consent of the co-resident can be punished for residential trespass; yet, so long as the outsider’s entry can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented, such a conclusion is inconsistent with the reality of shared life and general social notions, and is also improper in light of the subsidiary nature of criminal punishment. In particular, the impropriety becomes even more apparent if one imagines the case where one co-resident actively invites the outsider and they enter the residence together.\\n\\n3) A) According to the record in this case, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n(1) Nonparty 1, a co-resident of this apartment, went out around May 19, 2018, the day of the offense in this case, and asked her mother and younger sibling, Victim Nonparty 2, to take care of the child, and Victim Nonparty 2 was staying in this apartment at the time of the offense.\\n\\n(2) Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, unaware that Nonparty 1 had gone out, visited this apartment together with Defendant 1, allegedly for the purpose of reconciling Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1 and meeting their granddaughter. However, Victim Nonparty 2 fastened the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door so that the Defendants could not enter and refused to open the door. Thereupon, Defendant 1, a co-resident of this apartment, damaged the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door of this apartment, and Defendant 2 also joined in. Thereafter, the Defendants entered the apartment together.\\n\\nB) We examine these facts in light of the above legal principles. Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, in entering Defendant 1’s joint residence, this apartment, may be viewed as having joined in entering this apartment in response to the unjustified act by Victim Nonparty 2, to whom access management for the apartment had been entrusted by another co-resident, Nonparty 1, who prohibited their entry. Although in the process Defendant 1 exercised physical force by damaging the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door, and Defendant 2 also joined in, thereby jointly committing the offense of damage to property, Defendant 1’s conduct can be regarded as merely a means of entering and using the place of common life as a co-resident in response to an entry prohibition unjustifiably imposed while not having departed from the cohabitation relationship, and Defendant 2’s conduct is, in substance, merely having piggybacked upon and joined in such conduct by Defendant 1. If so, the act of Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 in entering this apartment can be evaluated, overall, as part of and incidental to the act by co-resident Defendant 1 of entering and using this apartment; accordingly, it must be held that the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) is not established against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3.\\n\\nC) Nevertheless, the lower appellate court found this part of the facts charged guilty; the lower appellate judgment thus contains error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles on the establishment of the offense of residential trespass. The grounds for appeal by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n4. The Main Issues of this Case\\n\\nA. As to the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.) against Defendant 1 and Defendant 2\\n\\nConsidering the reasons of the lower appellate judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence lawfully admitted, it is determined that finding this part of the facts charged guilty was proper. Accordingly, the lower appellate court’s determination contains no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, by violating the rules of logic and experience, exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehending the legal principles on the establishment of the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint damage to property, etc.), self-help, or justifiable act.\\n\\nB. As to the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\n1) Since each co-resident living in a joint residence may enjoy the factual peace of mind of the residence, even if an outsider enters the joint residence with the consent of one of the co-residents, if that outsider enters in a manner that disturbs the factual peaceful state in relation to another co-resident, such entry may also be viewed as constituting the offense of residential trespass in that it infringes the factual peace of mind of the other co-resident’s residence.\\n\\nHowever, each co-resident, unless there are special circumstances, may not only enter and use the place of common life within the joint residence in accordance with the purport and characteristics of the joint residence relationship, but also must tolerate other co-residents’ entry into and use of the same. As such, the legal interest of factual peace of mind enjoyed by each co-resident at the place of common life is inevitably subject to some restriction due to the relationship among co-residents, and it must be deemed that co-residents formed the joint residence relationship by mutually tolerating such circumstances. If so, acts by co-residents that normally enter and use the place of common life within the scope mutually tolerated cannot be regarded as acts infringing the peace of residence, even if the manner of such acts can be viewed as disturbing another co-resident’s factual peaceful state; hence the offense of residential trespass is not established. Whether an outsider’s entry into the place of common life together with the consent of one co-resident can be regarded as an act infringing the peace of residence of another co-resident who objected must also be examined from this standpoint.\\n\\n2) The content and scope of the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life, mutually tolerated by each co-resident, must be examined individually and concretely depending on the form and nature of the joint residence and the circumstances in which the joint residence was formed. Where an outsider’s entry into and use of the place of common life pursuant to the consent of one co-resident can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry, such outsider’s act can, taken as a whole, be evaluated as identical to the act of that co-resident. Therefore, even where one co-resident, without legal basis or any other justifiable reason, prohibits another co-resident from entering the place of common life, and the other co-resident, in response, disturbs the factual peaceful state of the co-resident who prohibited entry in the course of entering the place of common life, if the entry and use by the outsider who entered together into the place of common life with the consent of that co-resident can be evaluated, overall, as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry, it is proper to view that the offense of residential trespass is likewise not established against the outsider, notwithstanding that he disturbed the factual peaceful state of the co-resident who prohibited entry. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\nA) In determining whether an individual’s legal interest has been infringed, it is necessary to take into account the social implications and limits of that legal interest. In the case of a joint residence, not only the aspect of individual legal interest protection for each co-resident, but also the meaning of shared life in the joint residence and the social limits that accompany it, must be considered in determining whether the protected legal interest of the offense of residential trespass has been infringed and whether the offense is established. In a joint residence where several persons live together, the legal interest in residence enjoyed by each co-resident is inevitably subject to some restriction, and it must be deemed that co-residents mutually tolerated such restriction. Even where an outsider’s entry pursuant to the consent of one co-resident can, in light of the form and nature of the joint residence, the circumstances that led to the formation of the joint residence relationship, the relationship between the co-resident and the outsider, the purpose for which the outsider entered the joint residence, and the manner of entry, be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry, recognizing the offense of residential trespass merely because there is an aspect of disturbing another co-resident’s factual peaceful state within the joint residence would not only run counter to the mutual tolerance among co-residents, but would also amount to an unreasonable interpretation that ignores the essence and characteristics, diversity, and social limits inherent in joint residence.\\n\\nB) If the offense of residential trespass were recognized merely because an outsider entered upon the consent of one co-resident in a manner that disturbs another co-resident’s factual peaceful state, even where the outsider’s entry can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented, an unreasonable result may arise in which the existence of the outsider’s offense of residential trespass depends solely on contingent circumstances internal to the co-residents—namely, the conflict between the enjoyment of general and affirmative freedom of residence and the enjoyment of negative freedom and peace of residence within the joint residence.\\n\\nThe essence and mission of the Criminal Act as a legal norm lie in protecting the fundamental values indispensable to the existence and maintenance of society, and it is desirable that the subject matter regulated by the Criminal Act be limited to acts manifestly dangerous to major legal interests that cannot be resolved by other norms or means of social control, or acts that cause great harm to society. The purpose of granting the Criminal Act, among legal norms, a powerful sanction that deprives or restricts individual freedom and rights must likewise be understood in the same context. The Criminal Act provides only that the actus reus of residential trespass is trespass, and the punishment is imprisonment for not more than 3 years or a fine not exceeding 5 million won, which is higher than the legislative examples of other countries such as Germany, and it is regulated as a non-compound offense. In addition to the nature of the Criminal Act and the contents of its regulation, if one considers the social and normative meaning inherent in the concepts of joint residence and trespass, the concept of trespass in residential trespass must itself be understood as already including a legal evaluation of an act that, by itself, poses a serious risk of infringing the legal interest of the peace of residence beyond the range socially acceptable, or an act that causes great harm to society. Therefore, it is proper to construe that only acts evaluated as falling within the subject matter regulated by the Criminal Act can be punished as residential trespass. However, where an act of entering a joint residence upon the consent of one co-resident can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented, such act cannot readily be regarded as an act posing a serious risk to a major legal interest that cannot be resolved by other norms or means of social control, or as an act causing great harm to society. If, due to an outsider’s entry into a joint residence, another co-resident’s separate legal interest such as bodily freedom is infringed, and that infringement constitutes a separate offense, punishment for that offense is sufficient, and punitive provisions already exist in the Criminal Act and elsewhere. To criminally punish such a case as residential trespass would constitute an excessive intervention by the state’s punitive power, disregarding the diversity and specificity of the social relations accompanying joint residence and the possibility of self-regulation, and would thus be improper.\\n\\nC) Between co-residents, the value of protection of the legal interests each enjoys in the joint residence can be regarded as equal. Thus, if in a situation where legal interests among co-residents conflict in relation to an outsider’s entry, the offense of residential trespass is recognized against the outsider on the ground that the legal interest of another co-resident’s factual peace of mind was infringed, that would be improper also in the sense that it would prioritize only the legal interest of the co-resident who rejected the outsider’s entry, while disregarding the legal interest of the other co-resident who consented to the entry.\\n\\nD) Even where an outsider’s entry into a joint residence pursuant to the consent of one co-resident can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented, if the outsider were to be punished for residential trespass, it could also become an issue whether the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry may be punished as an accomplice to residential trespass. However, as noted above, since a co-resident who has not departed from the cohabitation relationship and who has no legal basis or any other justifiable reason to prohibit entry into the joint residence cannot be punished for residential trespass, in the above case only the outsider who entered the joint residence upon the consent of the co-resident can be punished for residential trespass; yet, so long as the outsider’s entry can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented, such a conclusion is inconsistent with the reality of shared life and general social notions, and is also improper in light of the subsidiary nature of criminal punishment. In particular, the impropriety becomes even more apparent if one imagines the case where one co-resident actively invites the outsider and they enter the residence together.\\n\\n3) A) According to the record in this case, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n(1) Nonparty 1, a co-resident of this apartment, went out around May 19, 2018, the day of the offense in this case, and asked her mother and younger sibling, Victim Nonparty 2, to take care of the child, and Victim Nonparty 2 was staying in this apartment at the time of the offense.\\n\\n(2) Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, unaware that Nonparty 1 had gone out, visited this apartment together with Defendant 1. However, Victim Nonparty 2 refused to let the Defendants enter this apartment. Thereupon, Defendant 1, a co-resident of this apartment, damaged the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door of this apartment, and Defendant 2 also joined in. Thereafter, the Defendants entered the apartment together.\\n\\nB) We examine these facts in light of the above legal principles. Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, in entering Defendant 1’s joint residence, this apartment, may be viewed as having joined in entering this apartment in response to the unjustified act by Victim Nonparty 2, to whom access management for the apartment had been entrusted by another co-resident, Nonparty 1, who prohibited their entry. Although in the process Defendant 1 exercised physical force by damaging the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door, and Defendant 2 also joined in, thereby jointly committing the offense of damage to property, Defendant 1’s conduct can be regarded as merely a means of entering and using the place of common life as a co-resident in response to an entry prohibition unjustifiably imposed while not having departed from the cohabitation relationship, and Defendant 2’s conduct is, in substance, merely having piggybacked upon and joined in such conduct by Defendant 1. If so, the act of Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 in entering this apartment can be evaluated, overall, as part of and incidental to the act by co-resident Defendant 1 of entering and using this apartment; accordingly, it must be held that the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) is not established against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3.\\n\\nC) Nevertheless, the lower appellate court found this part of the facts charged guilty; the lower appellate judgment thus contains error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles on the establishment of the offense of residential trespass. The grounds for appeal by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n5. Scope of Reversal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated above, the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against Defendant 2 must be reversed. And because the remaining guilty part against Defendant 2 stands in a concurrent-offense relationship under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the reversed part and must be reversed together as one sentence is to be imposed, in the end all guilty parts against Defendant 2 in the lower appellate judgment must be reversed.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without addressing the remaining grounds of appeal by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, we reverse the guilty part of the lower appellate judgment against Defendant 2 and the part concerning Defendant 3, and remand this part of the case to the lower appellate court for further trial and determination; we dismiss the appeals of the Prosecutor and Defendant 1 respectively, and render judgment as stated in the order. In this judgment, all participating Justices concurred except for the separate opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek and the dissenting opinion of Justices Jo Jae-yeon, Justice Min Yu-suk, and Justice Lee Dong-won, and there are the supplementary opinions of Justice Kim Seon-su and Justice Cheon Dae-yeob on the majority opinion and the supplementary opinion of Justice Min Yu-suk on the dissenting opinion.\\n\\n7. Separate Opinion of Justice Lee Ki-taek on the Part of Violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against the Defendants\\n\\nThe issue in this case is whether, where Defendant 1, whose status as a co-resident of this apartment is disputed, and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, who were given consent by him, entered this apartment contrary to the outwardly manifested will of Victim Nonparty 2 prohibiting entry, this constitutes the offense of residential trespass. On this, the majority opinion discussed whether the Defendants’ act of entering this apartment constitutes the offense of residential trespass based on whether it falls within the ordinary mode of use of co-residents. By contrast, this separate opinion seeks to discuss whether the offense of residential trespass is established against the Defendants through an interpretation of the true intent of Victim Nonparty 2, who indicated an intention to prohibit the Defendants from entering.\\n\\nA. Diversity of interpretation as to whether entry is contrary to the resident’s will\\n\\n1) A) We examine this in accordance with the legal principles of Supreme Court en banc Decision 2020DO12630, rendered September 9, 2021. The meaning of trespass, the actus reus of residential trespass, means “entering a residence in a manner that disturbs the factual peaceful state enjoyed by the resident in the residence,” and whether it so qualifies is, in principle, to be determined based on the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of entry at the time of entry.\\n\\nB) However, whether it constitutes trespass is fundamentally a matter of interpretation of the resident’s will. If one enters a residence in a manner that disturbs the factual peace, that is generally construed as being contrary to the resident’s will.\\n\\n2) Whether the actor’s entry is contrary to the resident’s will must be determined by rationally interpreting the resident’s true intent, taking into concrete account the objective circumstances at the time of entry. Whether it is contrary to the resident’s will is, in principle, to be determined based on the will outwardly manifested; however, there may be cases where a different determination is possible depending on the specific facts, such as the circumstances at the time of entry. Ultimately, interpretation as to whether the conduct is contrary to the resident’s will lies within the realm of fact-finding.\\n\\n3) If a resident explicitly indicated an intention to prohibit entry, then entering the residence against such intention would generally be regarded as trespass. For example, if a resident explicitly says to a door-to-door salesperson trying to enter the house, “Do not come in,” and the salesperson nevertheless enters the house, it is plainly contrary to the resident’s will and thus constitutes trespass.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the resident’s intention regarding prohibition of entry must have a reason. In determining whether conduct is contrary to the resident’s will, there are cases where the true intent can only be confirmed once the reason the resident prohibited entry is known. In such cases, if one interprets the resident’s will merely on the basis of the outwardly expressed intention to prohibit entry, an unjust result may follow. This may unduly expand the scope of punishability for residential trespass. That is why the resident’s true intent is important in determining whether conduct is contrary to the resident’s will.\\n\\nEven where a resident has explicitly indicated an intention to prohibit entry, there may be a premise or background to such intention. For example, consider the case where a resident decides whether to allow entry based on whether a person has a status or qualification that permits entry. In such a case, if a person who has the status or qualification permitting entry enters, it cannot be regarded as trespass, whereas if a person lacks such status or qualification, it may be regarded as trespass. For example, in the case of believers of a certain religion, there is a prayer space for clergy whose entry is allowed. In that case, if a believer enters the clergy’s prayer space, it cannot be viewed as trespass; but if a person other than a believer enters, it must be regarded as trespass. If, in a company, an employee or officer enters an office restricted to its employees and officers for the protection of trade secrets, such entry cannot be viewed as trespass; but if a former employee or an employee or officer of a competitor enters, it must be regarded as trespass.\\n\\nHowever, even where the resident decides whether to allow entry based on status or qualification as stated above, there may be disputes over such status or qualification.\\n\\nFor example, one may consider a case where a resident believed that A was a person who could not enter and prohibited his entry, but later A’s status or qualification was confirmed and he was found to be a person who could enter. In such a case, since the premise fact underlying the prohibition of A’s entry did not exist, A’s entry cannot be regarded as contrary to the resident’s will.\\n\\nAs in the example above, in the case of believers, there is a prayer space for clergy whose entry is allowed. Suppose A tries to enter the prayer space, but the clergy, believing that A is not a believer, prevents him from entering the prayer space, yet A enters the prayer space. Later, A is confirmed to be a believer. In such a case, can A be said to have committed residential trespass?\\n\\nAs another example, there is an office in which trade secrets are kept, accessible only to the company’s employees and officers. Suppose A tries to enter that office, but the manager of the office, believing that A is not an employee or officer of the company, prevents him from entering the office, yet A enters the office as is. Later, A is confirmed to be an employee or officer of the company. In such a case, can A be said to have committed residential trespass?\\n\\nIn each of the above examples, if one relies on the true intent of the clergy or office manager, to regard A as having committed residential trespass based only on the outwardly expressed will would be to fail to grasp the true intention to prohibit entry. Since the premise fact prohibiting A’s entry did not exist from the outset, A’s entry into the prayer space or office cannot be regarded as contrary to the will of the clergy or office manager. In each of the above examples, if one relies on the true intent of the clergy or office manager, it should be held that the offense of residential trespass is not established against A.\\n\\nB. Determination on whether the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) is established against the Defendants\\n\\n1) Premise for discussion\\n\\nThe issue in this case is whether Defendant 1, whose status as a co-resident of this apartment is disputed, and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, who received consent for entry from him, entering this apartment contrary to the externally manifested intent of Victim Nonparty 2 prohibiting entry constitutes the offense of residential trespass.\\n\\nIn this case, the basic premise of Victim Nonparty 2’s intention to prohibit the Defendants from entering this apartment can be viewed as that Defendant 1 was not a co-resident of this apartment.\\n\\nTo interpret the true intent of Victim Nonparty 2 prohibiting the Defendants from entering this apartment, it is first necessary to examine whether Defendant 1 was a co-resident of this apartment.\\n\\nBelow, we examine the facts of this case, determine whether Defendant 1 was a co-resident of this apartment, and then interpret the true intent of Victim Nonparty 2 regarding the Defendants’ entry into this apartment in order to determine whether the offense of residential trespass is established against the Defendants.\\n\\n2) Facts of this case\\n\\nFrom the reasons of the lower appellate judgment and the record of this case, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\nA) Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1 are a legally married couple who married on September 5, 2015. There is one child between Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1, and they had been living in this apartment since around August 15, 2016.\\n\\nB) Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1 began to quarrel frequently from around January 2018 over the issue of pre-sale of a newly built apartment. Defendant 1 fought with Nonparty 1 on April 9, 2018, and left this apartment after taking some of his belongings. Defendant 1 visited this apartment on April 13, 2018, fought again with Nonparty 1, and left the home. Thereafter, Nonparty 1 unilaterally changed the password to the entrance door of this apartment and also attached a chain-type latch to the entrance door.\\n\\nC) Through mobile phone messenger, Defendant 1 requested Nonparty 1 on April 17, 2018, and April 19, 2018, to inform him of the password to the front door of this apartment. Defendant 1 also visited this apartment around May 4, 2018, and requested Nonparty 1 to open the door, but Nonparty 1 refused.\\n\\nD) Nonparty 1, a co-resident of this apartment, went out around May 19, 2018, the day of the offense in this case, and asked her mother and younger sibling, Victim Nonparty 2, to take care of the child, and Victim Nonparty 2 was staying in this apartment at the time of the offense.\\n\\nE) Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 visited this apartment together with Defendant 1, unaware that Nonparty 1 had gone out. However, Victim Nonparty 2 refused to let the Defendants enter this apartment. Thereupon, Defendant 1, a co-resident of this apartment, damaged the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door of this apartment, and Defendant 2 also joined in. Thereafter, the Defendants entered the apartment together.\\n\\nF) Nonparty 1 filed a claim for divorce with the court around June 28, 2018, after the occurrence of this case, and on September 4, 2018, a divorce conciliation was reached between Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1.\\n\\n3) Whether Defendant 1 was a co-resident of this apartment\\n\\nA) The offense of residential trespass is established when a person other than the resident intrudes upon a residence. The residence that is the object of the offense of residential trespass is limited to a residence occupied by another person. Where one of the co-residents who live together in a joint residence with another person is the actor, the relevant joint residence does not become the object of the offense of residential trespass. However, if it can be recognized that the co-resident departed from the cohabitation relationship or lost the factual dominion and management relationship over the residence, the relevant residence falls within the object of residential trespass. Whether a co-resident departed from the cohabitation relationship or whether the factual dominion and management relationship over the joint residence was lost must be determined individually, taking into account concrete circumstances such as the relationship among the co-residents, the circumstances in which the dispute between co-residents arose, and the circumstances under which the person left the joint residence.\\n\\nMeanwhile, there may also be cases where entry into a joint residence is prohibited on legal grounds, such as where one co-resident petitions the court for an injunction prohibiting another co-resident from entering the joint residence and obtains a court order of entry prohibition; or where one co-resident is subject, under the Special Act on the Punishment, etc. of Domestic Violence Crimes (hereinafter the “Domestic Violence Punishment Act”) or the Special Act on the Punishment, etc. of Child Abuse Crimes (hereinafter the “Child Abuse Punishment Act”), to a temporary measure order of “evacuation, etc. from the residence” or “prohibition of approach within 100 meters of the residence” (Article 29(1) items 1 and 2 of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act, Article 19(1) items 1 and 2 of the Child Abuse Punishment Act). Such cases may be regarded as cases in which entry into the joint residence is prohibited on legal grounds. Such cases may be regarded as corresponding to cases where the co-resident has departed from the cohabitation relationship or has lost the factual dominion and management relationship over the joint residence.\\n\\nB) We examine the above facts in light of the above legal principles.\\n\\nAt the time in question, it is difficult to view that there was an express agreement between Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1 to dissolve the marital relationship and for Defendant 1 to leave and live outside this apartment, or that the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1 had completely broken down. In such a situation, the mere fact that Defendant 1 took some of his belongings and left the apartment, or that Nonparty 1 unilaterally changed the entrance password and prevented Defendant 1 from coming in, does not readily establish that Defendant 1 departed from the cohabitation relationship in this apartment or lost dominion and management over it. Therefore, it should be said that Defendant 1 continued to maintain the status of a co-resident of this apartment at the time in question.\\n\\n4) Interpretation of the true intent of Victim Nonparty 2\\n\\nA) Based on the above facts, we examine the true intent of Victim Nonparty 2 in prohibiting the Defendants from entering this apartment.\\n\\nB) In light of the relationship among the Defendants, Nonparty 1, and Victim Nonparty 2 as recognized from the above facts, and the circumstances surrounding the dispute in this case, it is reasonable to view that Victim Nonparty 2 prohibited the Defendants from entering because she believed that the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1 had broken down and that Defendant 1 had lost the status of a co-resident of this apartment and could not enter this apartment without Nonparty 1’s consent. Apart from the above circumstances, no other facts that could serve as a motive or reason for Victim Nonparty 2 to prohibit Defendant 1 or Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, who received his consent, from entering this apartment can be found in the record.\\n\\nC) The premise fact of Victim Nonparty 2’s intention to prohibit the Defendants from entering this apartment can be viewed as that the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1 had broken down, and that Defendant 1 was no longer a co-resident of this apartment and could not enter this apartment without Nonparty 1’s consent. However, as noted above, it is difficult to recognize that the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1 had broken down, or that Defendant 1 departed from the cohabitation relationship in this apartment or lost dominion and management over it.\\n\\nIf so, even if Victim Nonparty 2 outwardly indicated an intention to prohibit the Defendants from entering this apartment, it is reasonable to interpret her true intent as that she would not have prohibited the Defendants from entering this apartment if the marital relationship between Defendant 1 and Nonparty 1 had not broken down and if Defendant 1 had not departed from the cohabitation relationship in this apartment or lost dominion and management over it. Accordingly, since the Defendants’ entry into this apartment cannot be regarded as having occurred contrary to Victim Nonparty 2’s will, it cannot be recognized that the offense of residential trespass is established against the Defendants. Furthermore, even if the Defendants damaged the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door of this apartment in the process of entering this apartment, this can be viewed as the minimum exercise of physical force necessary to enter this apartment, and thus such circumstance does not affect whether the offense of residential trespass is established.\\n\\n5) Determination on the grounds of appeal by the Prosecutor and Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, each part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against the Defendants must be found not guilty.\\n\\nThe conclusion of the lower appellate judgment that found Defendant 1 not guilty of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) is proper. Therefore, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, there is no error by violating the rules of logic and experience, exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehending the legal principles on the establishment of the offense of residential trespass.\\n\\nHowever, the lower appellate judgment that found Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 guilty of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) contains error in fact-finding, by violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in determining whether the conduct was contrary to Victim Nonparty 2’s will, or by misapprehending the legal principles on trespass. The grounds for appeal by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\nC. Sub-conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the parts of the lower appellate judgment concerning violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 must be reversed. And because the above reversed part and the remaining guilty part against Defendant 2 stand in a concurrent-offense relationship under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act and must be reversed together as one sentence is to be imposed, all guilty parts against Defendant 2 in the lower appellate judgment must be reversed. Without addressing the remaining grounds of appeal by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, the guilty part of the lower appellate judgment against Defendant 2 and the part concerning Defendant 3 must be reversed and remanded to the lower appellate court for further trial and determination, and the appeals by the Prosecutor and Defendant 1 must each be dismissed.\\n\\nFor the reasons stated above, I cannot concur with the majority opinion, and I state this as a separate opinion.\\n\\n8. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Jo Jae-yeon, Justice Min Yu-suk, and Justice Lee Dong-won on the Parts of Violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against the Defendants\\n\\nA. Summary of the dissent\\n\\nWith this en banc decision, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that the protected legal interest of the offense of residential trespass is not “the right of residence” but “the factual peace of mind of the residence.” The same applies to joint residences.\\n\\nWhere a co-resident presently in the residence has prohibited entry, yet a person enters the joint residence by violent means or through an abnormal route, such entry, in light of the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of entry at the time, clearly disturbs the peaceful state of the co-resident presently in the residence and constitutes trespass, so the offense of residential trespass is established. The same applies even if the trespasser is a co-resident who has left the home on his own or an outsider who has received consent from that co-resident.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that even where the actor enters a residence that he jointly occupies, manages, or possesses in a manner that disturbs the factual peaceful state of another co-resident, the offense of residential trespass is not constituted; however, we cannot concur.\\n\\nB. Premise for discussion\\n\\n1) First, we clarify the relationship between this case and Supreme Court en banc Decision 2020DO12630, rendered September 9, 2021. This case is premised on the majority opinion of Supreme Court en banc Decision 2020DO12630, but it differs in facts and legal issues.\\n\\nIn Supreme Court en banc Decision 2020DO12630, the issue was whether the offense of residential trespass is established for “an act of entering peacefully with the consent of a resident presently in the residence.” The issue there was the evaluation of the “presumed opposing intent of an absent co-resident.” In this case, the issue is “an act of a resident who, after leaving the residence on his own, became unable to enter by ordinary means and, notwithstanding the entry prohibition by the co-resident presently in the residence, entered by using violent means.” The issue is the evaluation of “an act that infringed the factual peace of a co-resident presently in the residence.”\\n\\n2) We turn to the increase in the need to protect the peace of residence and the necessity of concrete and individualized regulation of joint residence relationships.\\n\\nA) With changes in modern social life and residential life, the need to protect the peace of residence has increased further.
