In modern society, as the development of mass media and information and communications means has increased the potential for intrusion into the secrecy of private life, the importance of privacy protection has become more emphasized, and the need to protect the peace of residence as a condition for protecting the secrecy of private life has also increased. In other words, when a residential space is invaded, the possibility of intrusion into the secrecy of private life is high, so the peace of residence is also more likely to be infringed at that stage. Moreover, with increasing urbanization, individuals’ residential spaces have become limited to small spaces, and concerns over infringement of the peace of residence by outsiders’ entry have become more serious than in the past, greatly increasing the need for protection.\\n\\nB) Most citizens form family relationships due to marriage and the like, or otherwise share one residential space jointly for economic reasons and other such reasons. Due to urbanization and density, many citizens reside in multi-family housing. Meanwhile, the concept of residence includes elevators, common stairs, and hallways within multi-family housing such as detached houses for multiple households, multi-family houses, row houses, and apartments (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2009DO3452, rendered August 20, 2009). In modern society, where most citizens have the status of co-residents with respect to their residential space, the status relations among co-residents, the manner in which the legal interests enjoyed by co-residents within a joint residence conflict with each other, and the need for regulation thereof vary widely. Regulation of joint residence relationships must be made individually, taking into account specific circumstances such as the circumstances under which the joint residence was formed, its form, and the mutual relationship among co-residents.\\n\\n3) The question whether the offense of residential trespass is established in a joint residence arises when legal interests among co-residents conflict. As the saying goes, “Unhappy families are unhappy for their own reasons,” the forms of infringement of legal interests among family members in one residential space and the need to protect the peace of residence also vary. However, to regulate this uniformly and abstractly on the ground that it concerns a joint residence or co-residents, and to discuss in one dimension whether the offense of residential trespass is established, cannot be said to be correct legal regulation for diverse dispute situations. Moreover, even where statutes governing joint residence exist, whether the offense of residential trespass is established against a co-resident or an outsider is a matter to be determined by individually and concretely examining the internal relations among co-residents and their relation with outsiders under such statutes; it is not proper to set a uniform and abstract standard of determination in advance.\\n\\nUltimately, whether the offense of residential trespass is established in a joint residence must be determined concretely and individually, taking into comprehensive consideration the “freedom of residence” guaranteed by the Constitution, “protection of marriage and family life,” “the legislative purpose and intent of the offense of residential trespass,” “the specific content and legal nature of the protected legal interest of residential trespass,” and “the meaning of trespass and its standard of determination.”\\n\\nC. Whether a co-resident may be punished for residential trespass\\n\\n1) The offense of residential trespass is a crime concerning personal legal interests, and where there are multiple persons residing at the residence, infringement of the protected legal interest must be determined based on the peace of residence enjoyed by each resident.\\n\\nA) Since a joint residence is one’s own residence and at the same time another person’s residence, if one co-resident commits an act that disturbs the peace of that person’s residence in relation to another co-resident, an infringement of the protected legal interest of the offense of residential trespass occurs.\\n\\nB) The Constitution provides in the preamble to Article 16 that “all citizens shall not be infringed upon in their freedom of residence,” thereby guaranteeing freedom of residence as a fundamental right. The Constitution also provides in Article 36(1) that “Marriage and family life shall be formed and maintained on the basis of individual dignity and the equality of the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this,” thereby placing marriage and family under special protection of the State. Since marriage and family life are realized through the place called residence, freedom of residence functions to secure the fundamental rights concerning marriage and family life by guaranteeing the spatial domain of marriage and family life.\\n\\nBecause residential space is the center of private life and is inseparably connected with an individual’s personality, unless its inviolability is guaranteed, the private sphere, which is the minimum condition for human happiness, cannot be protected (see Constitutional Court Decision 2018HEONBA171, rendered September 24, 2020, en banc). Since residence is the place at the center of private life, without guaranteed inviolability, it is difficult to safeguard an individual’s life, bodily safety, and property safety. Therefore, the freedom of residence guaranteed by the Constitution takes as its subject the individual residing in the residence, and the fundamental right concerning marriage and family life is also guaranteed on the basis of the individual who marries and forms a family. The offense of residential trespass is a provision that specifically protects the freedom of residence guaranteed by the Constitution as a fundamental right, and because it also indirectly protects marriage and family life guaranteed by the Constitution, the subject of the protected legal interest of residential trespass is also the individual resident. This legal nature of the offense of residential trespass must remain the same even in internal relations among co-residents.\\n\\nC) The judgments cited by the majority as references cannot be cited because they concern different factual situations from the issue in this case. Specifically, Supreme Court Decision 81DO2956, rendered April 27, 1982, and Supreme Court Decision 2010DO16537, rendered December 27, 2012, both involved prosecutions for residential trespass, etc., on the premise that the act was an entry by a person without residence or possession authority; however, after trial, they were cases in which the circumstances of cohabitation or lawful possessory title were recognized, and it was held that the offense of residential trespass, etc. was not established. These were not cases where the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of entry was by a method disturbing the peace of another co-occupant or co-resident’s residence.\\n\\n2) The majority opinion states that even if one co-resident enters in a manner that disturbs the peaceful state of the co-resident who prohibited his entry, that is a general form of using a joint residence.\\n\\nHowever, the majority opinion runs contrary to the content and legal nature of the protected legal interest of the offense of residential trespass, the meaning and standard of determination of trespass, and it errs in treating the co-resident’s “general form of use of the joint residence” and the “manner of act disturbing the factual peaceful state,” which are incompatible, as compatible.\\n\\nA) The majority opinion also acknowledges the principle that trespass, the actus reus of residential trespass, means entering a residence in a manner that disturbs the factual peaceful state enjoyed by the resident in the residence, and that whether it so qualifies is, in principle, to be determined based on the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of entry at the time of entry.\\n\\nIf so, even a co-resident who enters a joint residence by violent means or through an abnormal route, such as by damaging a lock, enters in a manner that objectively and outwardly disturbs another co-resident’s peaceful state and thus falls within an act of trespass.\\n\\nB) Entry by a manner that disturbs the factual peaceful state is incompatible with the ordinary form of use of a joint residence.\\n\\nTo be included in the ordinary, mutually tolerated form of use of a joint residence, each co-resident should possess the key to the lock or share the password, and each co-resident should be able to unlock the lock and open the entrance door with that key or password and enter the residence.\\n\\nThe behavior of a co-resident who has left the home on his own and thereafter continues to conflict, repeatedly quarrel, and use violence while disputing the use of the residence or the ownership thereof cannot be regarded as an ordinary form of use of a joint residence. It is difficult to impose on the co-resident remaining in the house the burden of tolerating this. If there are minor children being raised in that house, the need to prohibit violent entry becomes even greater.\\n\\nIn such a situation, if the resident feels threatened to peace, changes the lock and prohibits the other party’s entry, thereby making it impossible for the co-resident who left the house to enter by ordinary means, and that co-resident then enters the joint residence by using means that disturb the peace, such as damage or force, this is trespass beyond the limits of the use of the joint residence.\\n\\nC) As the majority opinion itself acknowledges, the content and scope of the use tolerated among co-residents must be examined individually according to the circumstances under which the joint residence was formed, the form and nature of the joint residence, and the relationship among the co-residents. Merely because a person is a co-resident does not mean that his acts of entering and using the joint residence must always be tolerated.\\n\\n3) According to the majority opinion, the period until a co-resident departs is left in a regulatory vacuum, which is improper.\\n\\nA) The majority opinion denies the establishment of residential trespass so long as the person retains the status of a co-resident. The majority opinion says that if there are “special circumstances,” the offense of residential trespass may also be recognized against a co-resident, but that such special circumstances are when he “has departed from the cohabitation or lost factual dominion and management.” However, a person who has departed from the joint residence or lost factual dominion and management is no longer included in “co-resident.” This is merely a tautology regarding the meaning of co-resident. Accordingly, the majority opinion appears to be one that denies the offense of residential trespass against co-residents in substance almost without exception. If the majority’s true intent is otherwise, it should expressly state the criteria and scope for determining “special circumstances.”\\n\\nB) The majority opinion states that the content and scope of the joint residence use acts tolerated among co-residents should be determined individually according to internal relations among co-residents, yet even when a co-resident disturbs another co-resident’s peaceful state before departing from the joint residence relationship or status as co-resident, it excludes that entry from the scope protected by the offense of residential trespass merely because that person is a co-resident, on the premise of a peaceful and ordinary joint residence. However, depending on the circumstances under which the joint residence was formed and the form and nature of the joint residence, the offense of residential trespass may be established even before a co-resident departs from the status as co-resident.\\n\\nC) Rather, as can be seen from a number of judicial precedents, cases in which the issue of whether the offense of residential trespass is established among co-residents arise during the process in which the joint residence relationship is disintegrating (a stage before departure from the cohabitation relationship, during which status as co-resident is still recognized), that is, when a dispute arises among co-residents, one party repeatedly leaves and re-enters the residence, causing conflict and confrontation, and the resident has no choice but to change the lock or password in order to maintain the peace of the residence.\\n\\nIn particular, as in this case, the process from the breakdown of marital relations between spouses to divorce varies in concrete cases, and in many cases the long-term family community, including the spouses, is engulfed in conflict and confrontation, and serious acts of violence occur. There are periods in which joint residence has not yet been dissolved but living together has become difficult to endure.\\n\\nD) The dissenting opinion is to the effect that interpretation of the offense of residential trespass should be made in a direction that actively responds to violence occurring in the process of dissolving the cohabitation relationship and protects the peace and safety of members.\\n\\n4) It is difficult to agree with the majority opinion’s linking of “justifiable reason” to the ground for denying the establishment of the offense of residential trespass.\\n\\nA) The majority opinion states that when a co-resident, without legal basis or any other justifiable reason, prohibits another co-resident’s entry, the offense of residential trespass is not established even if entry is made by force. It cites the reasons that the conduct is “in response to the entry prohibition” and is “a means of using the space in accordance with the purpose of the joint residence.”\\n\\nThis is tantamount to requiring that there be a legal basis or equivalent justifiable cause on the part of the victim and leads to the conclusion that the existence of a crime is determined by examining the rights relationship prior to the trespass.\\n\\nHowever, the established precedents of the Supreme Court take the position that even a rights holder commits residential trespass or trespass into a structure if he intrudes upon a residence or structure as a means of self-help in the execution of his right.\\n\\nIf, in the offense of residential trespass, which protects “the peace of residence” as the protected legal interest and punishes acts infringing it, the standard is whether “the victim’s act prohibiting entry had legal basis,” that would not be consistent with the established position of the Supreme Court.\\n\\nB) Furthermore, even if “justifiable reason” may be considered, whether the prohibition of entry is justified must be determined after examining the entire process of the dispute and the circumstances leading to the entry prohibition, and this is a question of fact-finding to be established through trial in the fact-finding court.\\n\\nAs to co-residents in dispute, particularly in the process of dissolution of the marital community, the legitimacy of individual acts or the source of responsibility cannot be determined solely from fragmentary circumstances at a specific point in time. There is concern that, by focusing only on the resultant measure of “entry prohibition,” one may conclude that the victim lacks legitimacy and the defendant’s entry is permissible.\\n\\nC) The cases assumed by the majority opinion—“where one co-resident prohibits the other’s entry without justifiable reason”—may be hypothetical examples discussed in criminal law textbooks (for example, an illustration is sometimes given of a wife locking the entrance door because she dislikes her husband bringing a drinking companion home late at night), but I again point out that they are far removed from real disputes.\\n\\n5) The majority opinion is an approach that unduly minimizes the independent value of the offense of residential trespass and is not consistent with recent legislative amendment trends.\\n\\nA) The majority opinion says that where, in the process of entry by a co-resident or the like, another co-resident’s separate legal interest such as bodily freedom is infringed, the relevant offense may be punished, and that is sufficient; however, this fails to properly grasp the significance of the offense of residential trespass or evaluates it lightly.\\n\\nB) The reason freedom and peace of residence are protected by criminal punishment is that everyone can expect maximum safety while inside his or her own residence, and the State actively protects such expectation. This may be said to be a basic right like a gatekeeper standing at the front of other fundamental freedoms such as bodily freedom, and an expectation and demand made of the State. The view that one can simply punish the conduct as assault, damage to property, etc., fails to properly understand the weight of the value individuals place on freedom and peace of residence.\\n\\nThe offense of residential trespass exists to protect the peace and safety of the residence and functions to prevent infringements on life, bodily safety, and property that may occur within the residence by controlling entry into the residence; therefore, the protected legal interest in residential trespass needs to be independently protected. Accordingly, where the act of a co-resident or an outsider entering a joint residence infringes the legal interest of another co-resident’s factual peace of mind, punishment should be imposed as residential trespass, and where, further, the life, bodily safety, property, or other legal interests of another co-resident are separately infringed in the course of entry or after entry, it is proper to punish the conduct for the offense constituted by the infringement of those legal interests.\\n\\nC) Today, threats to the peace of residence may arise not only from outsiders but also from family members and other co-residents.\\n\\nIn particular, in most cases where the spouse remaining at the residence is raising minor children, violent acts of entry cause serious harm to the welfare of the minor children regardless of the background of the dispute or where responsibility lies.\\n\\nIn the past, under the notion that “the Criminal Act does not intervene in domestic disputes,” domestic disputes were considered to be appropriately resolved autonomously within the family, with the State’s punitive power intervening only subsidiarily. However, this attitude led to a refusal of protection against domestic violence and became a cause of crimes within the family, and in reflection thereof, the Act on the Prevention of Domestic Violence and Protection, etc. of Victims and the Domestic Violence Punishment Act were enacted, enabling the State to intervene actively in domestic violence.\\n\\nFurthermore, in response to criticism that prevention of violence occurring within the family and protection of victims remain insufficient, the Domestic Violence Punishment Act was amended by Act No. 17499 on October 20, 2020, to improve and supplement deficiencies, and came into force on January 21, 2021. The amended Act included in domestic violence crimes the offense of residential trespass under Part II, Chapter XXXVI of the Criminal Act [Article 2(3)(s)]. The family members to whom the Domestic Violence Punishment Act applies are spouses, lineal ascendants and descendants, and cohabiting relatives [Article 2(2)(a) through (d)], which almost coincide with the scope of co-residents. Accordingly, not only the offense of residential trespass and the offense of refusal to leave, set forth in Part II, Chapter XXXVI of the Criminal Act, but also attempts thereof, have come to be included in the domestic violence crimes prescribed by the Domestic Violence Punishment Act.\\n\\nUnlike the majority opinion, the legislation, through amendment of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act, takes the position of actively regulating even co-residents in order to severely punish conduct that disturbs the physical and mental peace of other family members.\\n\\nD. Whether the offense of residential trespass is established where an outsider, after receiving the consent of one co-resident, enters the joint residence in a manner that disturbs another co-resident’s peaceful state\\n\\n1) The majority opinion denies the establishment of the offense of residential trespass on the ground that, even where an outsider enters a joint residence in a manner that disturbs the peaceful state of a co-resident presently in the residence, the entry is based on the consent of another co-resident; however, this is also improper.\\n\\nIf an outsider enters a joint residence by overpowering the entry prohibition of a co-resident presently in the residence by violent means, the offense of residential trespass is established, and the existence of the offense cannot be denied merely because the outsider received consent from one of the co-residents.\\n\\nThe reality of the “entry by an outsider pursuant to the consent of a co-resident,” abstractly expressed by the majority opinion, is that the outsider, together with a co-resident, overpowers by violent means the entry prohibition by the co-resident presently in the residence and intrudes into the joint residence.\\n\\n2) The conflict of legal interests arising within a joint residence among co-residents is, even if part of their internal relations, separate from the act of an outsider intruding into the joint residence; the latter itself satisfies the elements of the offense and must be punished independently.\\n\\nAn outsider’s act of entering a joint residence has nothing whatsoever to do with the ordinary acts of use of a joint residence among co-residents. The outsider, knowing that the resident prohibited entry, nevertheless overpowered that prohibition and forcibly entered. There is no basis to evaluate that as a conflict of legal interests within the internal relations among co-residents; rather, denying the offense of residential trespass on the ground of the consent of another co-resident leads to the result of ignoring the independent status as the subject of legal interest of the co-resident who prohibits the outsider’s entry.\\n\\n3) Furthermore, the reasons cited by the majority opinion as justifying the outsider’s trespass are also incorrect.\\n\\nA) Punishing a person who has committed conduct satisfying the elements of Article 319(1) of the Criminal Act, within the statutory range of punishment, is a legitimate exercise of the state’s punitive power. If an outsider’s act of entering a joint residence falls within the elements of the offense of residential trespass, he must be punished within the statutory range provided. The majority opinion says that, even though the conduct satisfies the elements of the offense of residential trespass prepared by the legislature, one must again distinguish the degree of infringement of the protected legal interest or additionally require social harm as an element, but it offers no basis for this. Furthermore, an outsider’s act of entering a joint residence in a manner that disturbs the factual peaceful state, despite the objection of another co-resident, is itself already an infringement of a legal interest that exceeds socially acceptable bounds and thus causes great harm to society.\\n\\nB) The fact that the maximum statutory punishment for the offense of residential trespass under the Criminal Act is 3 years’ imprisonment, and that it is regulated as a non-compound offense, falls within the legislature’s lawmaking discretion and is difficult to find logically related to the issue in this case.\\n\\nFurthermore, Swiss Criminal Code Article 186, Japanese Penal Code Article 130, and Chinese Criminal Law Article 245 also set the maximum statutory punishment for residential trespass at 3 years’ deprivation of liberty or imprisonment, which is the same as the maximum statutory punishment under our Criminal Act; nor is it appropriate to formally and arithmetically compare the statutory punishments for residential trespass under the criminal laws of some other countries with those under our Criminal Act and thereby restrict the scope of establishment of residential trespass. (The circumstance that an outsider’s act of entering a joint residence is pursuant to the consent of a co-resident can, if necessary, be appropriately taken into account at sentencing by individually considering the concrete circumstances.)\\n\\nThe Act on the Punishment of Stalking Crimes, etc., which is scheduled to take effect on October 21, 2021, also sets the maximum statutory punishment at 3 years’ imprisonment even where a person engages in “waiting or watching” at a place of daily life such as a residence or nearby thereto, that is, even where the conduct does not amount to “intrusion” into a residence, etc. [Article 18(1), Article 2(1)(b)].\\n\\nC) Whether to designate a crime as a non-compound offense is a matter of legislative policy considering the victim’s will or feelings, and if one takes into account the many cases of punishment for residential trespass in which investigations are initiated by the victim’s complaint or report, including this case, our Criminal Act cannot justify an outsider’s act of entering a joint residence on the ground that residential trespass is not a compound offense.\\n\\nD) Since the value of protection of the legal interests enjoyed in a joint residence among co-residents is equal, even where a co-resident’s peace of residence is infringed by an outsider’s act of entering a joint residence, it must be protected equally. The confrontation between the majority opinion and the dissent arises from adopting different standards for balancing interests in situations where legal interests among co-residents conflict. The dissent takes the position that freedom and peace of residence, which should be protected from force and the dominance of the majority, ought to be placed higher. The majority opinion says that punishing the outsider in this case would be improper because it would disregard the legal interest of the co-resident who sided with him, but the judgment on balancing legal interests and on whether punishment is proper must be distinguished.\\n\\nE. Determination on this case\\n\\n1) Facts recognized regarding “justifiable reason”\\n\\nThe majority opinion stated that “Victim Nonparty 2 had no legal basis or any other justifiable reason to prohibit Defendant 1’s entry.”\\n\\nA) The majority opinion appears to have made that conclusion based on the facts that Nonparty 1 changed the password to the entrance door of this apartment and attached a chain-type latch to the entrance door on April 13, 2018, and did not inform Defendant 1 of the entrance password, and that Victim Nonparty 2 did not open the door at the time of the offense.\\n\\nHowever, these fragmentary circumstances alone cannot determine the issue in a series of events that had unfolded for about a month before the offense in this case; one must also consider the circumstances under which Nonparty 1 changed the password and the context in which Victim Nonparty 2 acted as she did at the time of the offense in order to determine whether there was justifiable reason.\\n\\nB) Since this issue was not in dispute up to the lower appellate court, we are compelled to examine the factual circumstances ascertainable from the record, including the first-instance court testimony of Nonparty 1 and other evidence not rejected by the lower appellate court, and point out the impropriety of the majority opinion.\\n\\n(1) Defendant 1, after clashing with Nonparty 1 over the issue of pre-sale of a newly built apartment, said around April 9, 2018, “Live on your own. Tell the child that he has no father,” and took clothes (including winter clothes and summer clothes) and shoes, and left this apartment. The next day, he came back into this apartment, took passbooks and other items in his own name, and left again. (The fact that Defendant 1 left the home on that date of his own accord was also recognized in the lower appellate court.)\\n\\n(2) Defendant 1 visited this apartment on April 13, 2018, quarreled with Nonparty 1 while asking her to return part of the lease deposit because he wanted to separate, and smashed a cup he was holding. Nonparty 1 thereupon reported the matter to 112, and the police even came to this apartment. Victim Nonparty 2 was also present at the scene at the time. Thereafter, Nonparty 1 changed the entrance password and attached a latch to the entrance door.\\n\\n(3) Since Defendant 1 had left this apartment on April 9, 2018, and was staying at Defendant 2 and Defendant 3’s residence, Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 also knew of Defendant 1’s separation.\\n\\nC) The following circumstances regarding the situation on the day of the offense in this case are already recognized by the lower appellate court.\\n\\n(1) On the day of the offense, the Defendants went to this apartment without any prior contact, rang the doorbell, and when the entrance door was not opened, used abusive language. Victim Nonparty 2, who knew the prior course of events, did not open the entrance door and, through the interphone, told the Defendants to come back when Nonparty 1 returned home. Thereupon, the Defendants created a disturbance by banging on the door and demanding that it be opened, and when Victim Nonparty 2 slightly opened the door and fastened the latch, Defendant 2 said to open the door, put his foot in the gap in the open door so that it could not be closed, and kept shaking the door handle, while Defendant 1 inserted his hand through the open gap in the door and struck the chain-type latch several times. The latch attached to the apartment entrance door could be released only by closing the door, but the Defendants made it impossible to close the door and thus also impossible to release the latch. In the process, Defendant 1 and Defendant 2 jointly carried out the above acts, causing the latch to detach from the door.\\n\\n(2) As soon as the latch came off and the door opened, the Defendants rushed into the apartment. (In the process, Defendant 1 pushed Victim Nonparty 2, who was in front of the entrance door, and received a final judgment of guilt for assault; that judgment became final.) The mother of Nonparty 1, who was staying in this apartment at the time, was startled and fell in surprise at the Defendants suddenly entering the apartment, and immediately thereafter took the child into the master bedroom and locked the door. Thereafter, both sides came to face each other across the door of the master bedroom.\\n\\nD) In light of the above series of events, it cannot be said with certainty that the “entry prohibition” made by Victim Nonparty 2 at the time of the offense lacked justifiable reason, nor can it be used as a basis to justify the Defendants’ entry.\\n\\nE) The separate opinion states that the true intent of Victim Nonparty 2 was that she would not have prohibited the Defendants from entering this apartment unless Defendant 1 had departed from the cohabitation relationship in this apartment or lost dominion and management over it.\\n\\nThis separate opinion is also an interpretation of intent divorced from the dispute history and contents of this case, as ascertainable from the record, and from the circumstances under which Nonparty 1 changed the entrance password and installed the latch, and from the specific situation in which Victim Nonparty 2 prohibited the Defendants’ entry.\\n\\n2) Whether the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) is established against Defendant 1\\n\\nA) The lower appellate court found Defendant 1 not guilty of the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence), on the ground that Defendant 1 was a co-resident of this apartment.\\n\\nB) As noted above, Defendant 1 fought with Nonparty 1 and left the joint residence on his own, thus beginning separation; while Nonparty 1 was allowing his entry, he entered and took passbooks and other items, or fought with Nonparty 1 and left the joint residence again. After Nonparty 1 changed the entrance password, Defendant 1 requested entry several times and eventually committed the offense in this case.\\n\\nDespite Victim Nonparty 2’s refusal of entry, Defendant 1 used violent means, such as damaging the latch, overcame Victim Nonparty 2, and entered this apartment.\\n\\nC) Considering in combination the circumstances in which Defendant 1 voluntarily left the home and separation began, and the circumstances in which the victim side initially did not block Defendant 1’s entry but later, as the dispute and confrontation continued, changed the lock on the entrance door and began prohibiting Defendant 1’s entry, Defendant 1’s act of entering this apartment, even in light of the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of entry, clearly corresponds to a case in which the factual peaceful state of Victim Nonparty 2 was disturbed, and it exceeds the scope of use as a co-resident and is therefore impermissible. Victim Nonparty 2 had justifiable reason to stop Defendant 1’s entry, and the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) can be recognized against Defendant 1.\\n\\nThe offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) cannot be denied merely because Defendant 1 had not departed from the status of a co-resident.\\n\\nD) Nevertheless, the lower appellate court found this part of the facts charged not guilty. The lower appellate judgment thus contains error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles on the establishment of the offense of residential trespass. The Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n3) Whether the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) is established against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3\\n\\nA) The act by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 of overpowering Victim Nonparty 2, who refused them entry, by using violent means and entering this apartment clearly corresponds, in light of the objectively and outwardly manifested manner of entry, to a case that clearly disturbed the factual peaceful state of Victim Nonparty 2; therefore, the offense of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) is established against the said Defendants. Even if their entry was pursuant to the consent of Defendant 1, a co-resident, it has no effect on the establishment of the offense.\\n\\nB) The lower appellate court’s decision, which left intact the first-instance court’s finding of guilt on the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, contains no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, by violating the rules of logic and experience, exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehending the legal principles on the establishment of the offense of residential trespass.\\n\\nF. Sub-conclusion\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against the Defendants must all be found guilty. Accordingly, the part of violation of the Violent Acts Punishment Act (joint trespass into residence) against Defendant 1 in the lower appellate judgment must be reversed. Meanwhile, because the reversed part and the remaining offenses found guilty against Defendant 1 by the lower appellate court stand in a concurrent-offense relationship under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act and one sentence must be imposed, in the end the entire part concerning Defendant 1 in the lower appellate judgment must be reversed and the case remanded to the lower appellate court for further trial and determination, and the appeals by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 must each be dismissed.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, I state that I cannot agree with the majority opinion.\\n\\n9. Supplementary Opinion of Justices Kim Seon-su and Cheon Dae-yeob on the Majority Opinion\\n\\nIn the majority opinion, the issues in this case were reviewed from the perspective of the ordinary form of use of a joint residence that co-residents tolerate mutually. As a result, where one co-resident, without legal basis or justifiable reason, unilaterally blocks another co-resident’s act of entering the place of common life, such as by locking the entrance door, through the exercise of force, even if the other co-resident exercises physical force in the nature of解除 the entry blockade in order to enter the place of common life, this can be evaluated as merely a means for the co-resident to enter and use the joint residence, and if the outsider’s entry accomplished together therewith can also be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented, the offense of residential trespass likewise is not established.\\n\\nBelow, we will clarify more distinctly the purport of the majority opinion on the issues in this case, supplement its rationale, and state our views on the points raised by the dissent.\\n\\nA. Meaning and limits of the cohabitation relationship within a joint residence\\n\\nResidence means not only the physical and objective environment constituting human life, but also a subjective and socio-psychological environment. Diverse ideas and perceptions about the meaning and role of residence, and cultural differences in the experience of residence by each individual, appear as differences in views of residence.\\n\\nA joint residence refers to a form of cooperative dwelling among the co-residents who compose it, and does not itself mean a complete community as such. A joint residence may have private residential spaces for each, or may consist solely of community residential spaces for all co-residents, and it is not fixed but is also a concept as an open space capable of change on the basis of mutual agreement, custom, or circumstances.\\n\\nJoint residence is a form of residential culture in which the independence and community of people who share a way of life and values are harmonized. The degree of connection among co-residents composing the joint residence, the place of life, varies widely, and the boundary between single residence and joint residence is not always clear. The meaning of joint residence or co-residence in a traditional family community, the typical form of joint residence, differs from its meaning in a share house, a modern urban form of joint residence. Joint residence is a residential culture that sustains the fundamental value of residence in which individual dignity is realized, while accepting coexistence as co-residents within the same residential space, even at the cost of tolerating restrictions on rights as private space. The scope of the private sphere each person enjoys within a joint residence is determined by mutual agreement and the form and custom of residence, as well as the general social perception thereof. Such joint residence begins only when shared and coexistent life is accepted within a single residential space. Nevertheless, differences in views of residence among co-residents, and differing perceptions of the boundaries between the private and common spheres, create a constant relationship of tension.\\n\\nEven in the case of the most basic residential community, namely the family, conflict may arise among family members over, for example, whether the act of a parent freely entering a room used solely by a child constitutes an intrusion into the private sphere within the joint residence. In that case, it is not easy to simply conclude that the legal evaluation of a parent entering that room should differ merely because the child unilaterally declared it to be his or her complete private sphere and prohibited the parent’s entry. In particular, in relation to the application of the offense of residential trespass, it would be even more difficult to affirm this in light of the subsidiarity of criminal punishment. On the other hand, where a space intended for complete private use for a specific purpose, such as a bathroom, is entered by abnormal means and infringed despite mutual tolerance and agreement, it would be difficult to lightly deny the unlawfulness of the trespass merely because it is an entry by a co-resident into a space within a joint residence. In the case of a residential form in which private spaces are mixed within the overall common space of the joint residence, conflicts over the boundary between private and common spaces can become even more intense.\\n\\nAs such, since multiple-dimensional relationships between the individual and the residential community exist within a joint residence, the individual private sphere and space cannot be entirely excluded; however, the area recognized as common space functions not as a closed space but as a space for experiencing and communicating shared time and life in an open manner among each other. Within it, each co-resident should refrain from planning a life in which the space is used solely as one’s own independent space, and if one is not willing to endure that, one must dissolve the joint residence relationship or depart from the joint residence; once such dissolution or departure occurs, one can no longer assert the rights and duties incidental to the joint residence or co-residence.\\n\\nThe communal communication and participation of co-residents within a joint residence are processes of sharing values while using the space as a residential community. In order to become a space that balances individual privacy and shared life, there is also a need for a process of identifying and understanding which space is occupied individually and which space is shared with others. Most importantly, among co-residents, there is a need for awareness and an attitude to understand and tolerate the meaning of the residential community and the limits of the private sphere and life within it, and a posture of mutual respect and willingness to live together within it.\\n\\nThe majority opinion’s views and conclusions on the issues in this case are based on the understanding of the meaning and limits of the cohabitation relationship within a joint residence as described above.\\n\\nB. Whether a co-resident may be punished for residential trespass\\n\\n1) By interpreting the text of Article 319(1) of the Criminal Act, the object of the offense of residential trespass is a residence occupied by a person other than the actor, that is, by another person, and where one of the co-residents is the actor, the residence jointly occupied with another person does not fall within the object of the offense of residential trespass unless there are special circumstances such as his departure from the cohabitation relationship or loss of the factual dominion and management relationship over the residence.\\n\\n2) A joint residence, as to one of the co-residents, is one’s own residence, and at the same time, in relation to another resident, it also has the status of another person’s residence. Because of this dual nature of the joint residence, each co-resident enjoys the legal interest of factual peace of mind of the residence in the joint residence, while in the relationship among co-residents, the legal interest in residence enjoyed by each is inevitably subject to some restriction, and it may be deemed that co-residents tolerated such circumstances when forming the joint residence relationship. That co-residents freely enter the place of common life during the period of co-residence is the ordinary form of use of the joint residence as co-residents and is the most basic part of the joint residence relationship that each co-resident must tolerate and bear. Therefore, unless there are special circumstances, one co-resident cannot prohibit another co-resident from entering, and even if the latter ignores such prohibition and enters freely, the offense of residential trespass is not established.\\n\\n3) However, one cannot exclude exceptional cases in which there are special circumstances such that a co-resident’s entry into the joint residence constitutes the offense of residential trespass in relation to another co-resident. The majority opinion does not deny even such exceptional possibilities.\\n\\nFirst, if a co-resident is recognized, under concrete facts such as the circumstances, form, course, and current status of co-residence, as having departed from the joint residence, then such case may be regarded as one in which the above special circumstances exist.\\n\\nNext, where one co-resident petitions the court against another co-resident for an injunction prohibiting entry into the joint residence and obtains a court order for provisional entry prohibition, or where one co-resident, as a domestic violence perpetrator, is subject under the Domestic Violence Punishment Act to a temporary measure order of “evacuation, etc. from the residence of the victim or family member,” or “prohibition of approach within 100 meters of the victim or family member or the residence, workplace, etc.” (Article 29(1) items 1 and 2), or where one co-resident, as a child abuse perpetrator, is subject under the Child Abuse Punishment Act to a temporary measure order of evacuation, etc. from the residence or prohibition of approach within 100 meters of the residence, etc. (Article 19(1) items 1 and 2), entering the joint residence in violation of such legally based entry prohibition may constitute residential trespass. This may be viewed as a case in which the factual dominion and management relationship over the residence has been lost, and special circumstances exist.\\n\\n4) Unless there are such special circumstances or a corresponding situation, a co-resident cannot prohibit another co-resident from entering the place of common life. This is because excluding, without justifiable reason, another co-resident who enters in order to use the place of common life from the joint residence cannot be permitted. If one holds that, even where a co-resident prohibited without justifiable reason responds by entering the place of common life, the offense of residential trespass is not established, then even if there was physical force in the nature of releasing the blockade before that entry, such as by locking the entrance door, one may, leaving aside whether such conduct itself can be punished, still say that the entry into the place of common life does not constitute residential trespass.\\n\\nOf course, even before such a lawful procedure as a provisional measure order prohibiting entry is taken, in exceptional situations where protection of the peace of residence from co-residents is needed—such as where the joint residence functions as a refuge protecting another co-resident and the minor children under his or her protection from one co-resident’s serious domestic violence or child abuse, but one co-resident forcibly enters by exercising physical force—the conduct may, depending on the concrete facts, be recognized as trespass. Since the freedom of co-residents to enter the joint residence presupposes residential space as an instrument for realizing human dignity, if the joint residence or a specific space within it has lost its function as a joint residence for the realization of human dignity and is serving as a refuge under circumstances where serious danger is imminent or has arrived from the violence of one co-resident and the serious risk to the life and bodily safety of the other co-resident, who is the victim, then in substance there may be special circumstances requiring protection of the peace of another co-resident’s residence.\\n\\nIn this regard, unlike the dissent’s point, the majority opinion cannot be said to run counter to the amendment purpose of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act, revised on October 20, 2020, which included residential trespass among domestic violence crimes. This is because the majority opinion respects and conforms to the amendment purpose of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act, namely prevention of domestic violence and protection of victims. Furthermore, the Domestic Violence Punishment Act provides special rules concerning criminal punishment procedures for certain offenses involving domestic violence; even if the offense of residential trespass is included in domestic violence crimes, this is limited to cases in which acts causing physical, mental, or property damage among family members are committed by the method of residential trespass, and does not mean that an act of entry into a residence that does not amount to residential trespass is to be characterized and punished as residential trespass merely because it caused physical, mental, or property damage to a family member in the course thereof. Whether the offense of residential trespass is established in the internal relations among co-residents constituting a family community, the traditional form of joint residence, is merely a matter to be determined by examining the substance of the case under concrete facts based on the legal principles noted above. Without consideration of such substance, one cannot uniformly characterize and punish such conduct as residential trespass merely because physical force was used in the process of a co-resident’s entry into the joint residence.\\n\\nMoreover, the family members subject to the Domestic Violence Punishment Act mean spouses, lineal ascendants and descendants, and cohabiting relatives, but in this case, it is difficult to view the Victim Nonparty 2 who prohibited Defendant 1’s entry as falling within that category, and thus it is also not appropriate to use this as a basis for the dissent.\\n\\n5) A) The majority opinion, premised on a case where one co-resident, lacking legal basis or any other justifiable reason to prohibit entry, unilaterally prohibits another co-resident’s entry into the joint residence by the exercise of force, discussed whether the offense of residential trespass is established against the co-resident who entered in response to such impermissible prohibition. It did not intend to deny entirely the establishment of the offense of residential trespass even where one co-resident, despite having legal basis or any other justifiable reason to prohibit the other’s entry, enters in a manner disturbing the factual peaceful state of the residence.\\n\\nThe purport of the majority opinion is that, when determining whether the offense of residential trespass is established against one co-resident in relation to a dispute among co-residents, a balanced and cautious approach is needed. This is because it is not proper to immediately criminalize a co-resident’s entry into the place of common life without any such procedure, even where the factual recognition of departure from the joint residence, or the deprivation of factual dominion and management over the joint residence pursuant to a court’s provisional injunction prohibiting entry or temporary measure of prohibition of approach, could correct the dispute among co-residents and the disorder of the joint residence relationship. Residential trespass is a crime punishable even if the victim withdraws his or her intention to punish, and if the State intervenes hastily by applying penal provisions amid disputes within a joint residence, it may, in some cases, reach a point of irreparably damaging the causal relationship that formed the joint residence. Considering that the joint residence, the basic place where daily life is conducted, is a place where human dignity is realized daily by any co-resident, additional caution is needed in depriving anyone of rights or status relating thereto.\\n\\nB) In this case, the majority opinion assumed that Defendant 1 had not departed from the cohabitation relationship in this apartment, and that no court order such as a provisional injunction prohibiting entry or temporary measure of prohibition of approach had been issued against Defendant 1, so there were no “special circumstances” permitting Nonparty 1 or Victim Nonparty 2, to whom access management for this apartment had been entrusted, to prohibit Defendant 1’s entry. On that premise, the majority opinion concluded that Victim Nonparty 2’s unilateral entry prohibition against Defendant 1 by force was impermissible, and that even if Defendant 1, in response, exercised physical force such as damaging the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door of this apartment in order to enter this apartment, such conduct was merely a means for Defendant 1 to enter this apartment, which was a joint residence, and thus the offense of residential trespass was not established against Defendant 1. In this case, the majority opinion’s purport is that because the situation does not amount to the exceptional circumstance in which the offense of residential trespass is established even for a co-resident’s entry into a joint residence, the exceptional legal doctrine premised on such circumstances is not applicable.\\n\\nC) The dissent, relying on the statements of Victim Nonparty 2 and Nonparty 1 and others, newly found facts regarding the justifiable reason for Victim Nonparty 2 to have taken entry prohibition measures against Defendant 1, and then stated that one cannot conclude that the “entry prohibition” made by Victim Nonparty 2 at the time of the offense lacked justifiable reason.\\n\\nHowever, the dissent has a problem in that it reached the above conclusion based on factual circumstances not recognized by the lower appellate court. The majority opinion, premised on the facts recognized by the lower appellate court, held that, in light of the circumstances at the time of entry, Victim Nonparty 2 had no legal basis or any other justifiable reason to take measures prohibiting Defendant 1’s entry [meanwhile, it should also be added that, according to the record, Defendant 1 stated to the investigative agency that he had been driven out of the house on April 13, 2018 (Record of Evidence, Vol. 1, p. 50), and it is also questionable whether the dissent’s fact-finding based on the statements of the opposing parties, namely Victim Nonparty 2 or Nonparty 1, is persuasive].\\n\\n6) A) The dissent states that once one co-resident enters a joint residence in a manner that disturbs the peaceful state of the co-resident who prohibited his entry, such entry cannot be the ordinary form of use of the joint residence and falls outside the ordinary limits of use of the joint residence.\\n\\nHowever, just as a resident’s use of some physical force in entering a residence does not mean that the person has become someone other than the resident and entered the residence, so too a co-resident’s use of physical force in the nature of releasing an entry blockade imposed by another co-resident through unilateral force while entering the place of common life cannot change the nature of the entry into trespass. Entry into a joint residence is the most basic premise of use of the joint residence under the joint residence relationship, and, moreover, a separate penal provision exists to punish the exercise of physical force used.\\n\\nB) The dissent’s view also deliberately ignores or overlooks the problem of the prior measure by another co-resident in this case, who, without legal basis or justifiable reason, unilaterally used force to prohibit one co-resident’s very entry. The act of a co-resident blocking or prohibiting another co-resident’s entry into the joint residence by force can itself be evaluated as an act infringing the other co-resident’s peace of residence; furthermore, if one imagines a case in which the co-resident who has been blocked has nowhere else to stay, it is not in line with social norms to evaluate and punish as trespass the act of overpowering such a unilateral blockade and entering, on the premise that such unilateral blockade was justified.\\n\\nIn this case, it is a matter of the wife residing in a joint residence and the husband leaving home and then attempting to return; but conversely, if one imagines a case where, taking advantage of the wife’s temporary absence from the joint residence, the husband changes the key or password to the entrance lock and prevents the wife from coming in, causing the wife to break or remove the lock with her parents from her family home and enter the house, then, according to the dissent, residential trespass would have to be established even in that case; such a conclusion is not something anyone would readily accept.\\n\\nIf such acts are punished as residential trespass, it may lead to harsh results for the weaker co-resident who has been driven out of the joint residence.\\n\\nC) The dissent states that if the majority opinion uses, in the offense of residential trespass, which protects the peace of residence as the protected legal interest and punishes acts infringing it, as the standard for determination whether “the victim’s act prohibiting entry had legal basis,” then it is not consistent with the established Supreme Court position that “even if one is a rights holder, residential trespass or trespass into a structure is established where he intrudes into a residence or structure as a means of self-help in execution of his right.”\\n\\nThe Supreme Court decision referred to by the dissent is understood as concerning a case in which, among disputing parties who are in opposition over the exclusive attribution of the right of residence or possession in relation to a residence or structure, a party who had already lost possession entered the residence or structure by employing self-help as a means of reclaiming it as an exercise of rights. In such ordinary cases, there is no particular theoretical objection to the proposition that the above Supreme Court position is proper.\\n\\nHowever, in this case, where the joint residence relationship continues without interruption or severance by departure by one side, and each co-resident’s freedom and peace of entry into and use of the joint residence is guaranteed, the question whether the act by one co-resident of entering the joint residence in response to another co-resident’s entry prohibition without justifiable reason constitutes the offense of residential trespass differs in substance from the above cases in which even a rights holder is prohibited from self-help and the establishment of residential trespass or trespass into a structure is recognized; therefore, the legal principles of the above Supreme Court decision cannot be directly applied. Within a joint residence under facts where departure from the joint residence relationship is not recognized, each co-resident can enjoy the freedom and peace of residence in which individual dignity is realized, while restrictions necessarily accompany each co-resident’s exercise of rights in the joint use of the residence, and mutual tolerance of the existence and exercise of rights by other co-residents is also required.\\n\\nAgain, the majority opinion is speaking of whether, in light of the ordinary form in which co-residents use a joint residence, a co-resident who, as a resident, attempts to enter the residence in the ordinary way of entry as a general form of use of the residence, may be punished for residential trespass if another co-resident unilaterally prohibits his entry without legal basis or any other justifiable reason.\\n\\nC. Whether the offense of residential trespass is established where an outsider, after receiving the consent of one co-resident, enters a joint residence in a manner that disturbs another co-resident’s peaceful state\\n\\n1) The offense of residential trespass is a crime concerning personal legal interests, and even if a resident has no legal right or authority to reside in the residence, if dominion and management over that residence is actually peacefully exercised, it receives criminal law protection. Even in the case of a joint residence, each co-resident residing in the joint residence is in a position to individually enjoy the protected legal interest of the peace of residence from outside interference.\\n\\nOn the other hand, in the case of a joint residence, the legal interests of peace of residence held by individual co-residents may conflict with one another; therefore, each co-resident’s legal interest in the peace of residence enjoyed in the joint residence is inevitably subject to some restriction due to relations with other co-residents, and it must be deemed that co-residents mutually tolerated such circumstances when forming the joint residence relationship.\\n\\nThe content and scope of the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life mutually tolerated by each co-resident must be examined individually and concretely depending on the form and nature of the joint residence and the circumstances under which the joint residence was formed. One co-resident inviting an outsider to enter the joint residence is one ordinary form in which co-residents use a joint residence. For example, if one spouse in a family invites his or her parent or colleague to the home, in light of ordinary life relations, this may be viewed as a general form of use of the joint residence as a co-resident. Therefore, unless there are special circumstances, the entry of an outsider into a joint residence upon the invitation or consent of one co-resident may be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the act of a co-resident entering and using the place of common life. By contrast, where an outsider, despite the objection of another co-resident, enters a joint residence merely because one co-resident consented, even though such act cannot be viewed as incidental to or encompassed by the ordinary use of the joint residence by a co-resident, it must be treated differently.\\n\\nAs such, whether an outsider who entered a joint residence upon the consent of one co-resident constitutes residential trespass in relation to another co-resident who objected cannot be evaluated uniformly. The criteria for such evaluation would be whether, from the standpoint of the co-resident who consented to the outsider’s entry, that outsider’s entry can be evaluated as incidental to the ordinary use of the joint residence by that co-resident, and whether, from the standpoint of the other co-resident, it can be evaluated as within the range that must be tolerated. The concrete determination will be sufficient if it is made by comprehensively considering the characteristics of the relevant joint residence relationship, the agreements or regulations among the co-residents, and other related factual circumstances, and by reaching a rational conclusion that fits the case.\\n\\n2) The above legal principles and evaluation criteria can likewise be applied where an outsider, pursuant to the consent of one co-resident, disturbs the factual peaceful state of another co-resident in the course of entering that co-resident’s joint residence.\\n\\nIn other words, in such a case too, one must determine whether the act can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the act of a co-resident entering and using the place of common life, and whether the other co-resident must, by the nature of the relevant joint residence relationship, tolerate it, in order to determine whether the offense of residential trespass is established.\\n\\nAs noted above, because the nature of the entry into a place of common life by a co-resident does not change into a trespass merely because, in the process of entering the joint residence in response to an entry blockade imposed by another co-resident through unilateral force, some physical force was exercised, the logic and subsidiarity of criminal punishment also apply equally to outsiders whose conduct occurs incident to a co-resident’s ordinary use of the joint residence.\\n\\n3) The dissent says that where, as in this case, an outsider who received the consent of one co-resident uses physical force in entering the joint residence and disturbs the factual peaceful state of another co-resident, that outsider must be punished for residential trespass.\\n\\nFirst, as already noted, merely because there was conduct disturbing the factual peace of another co-resident in the process of a co-resident’s entry into the joint residence and of an outsider’s entry into the joint residence with that co-resident’s consent, it cannot be said that uniformly punishing that conduct as residential trespass is the correct interpretation and application of the offense of residential trespass in relation to a joint residence.\\n\\nFurthermore, as noted above, where a co-resident blocks or prohibits another co-resident’s entry into the joint residence by force, the act itself can be evaluated as a preemptive infringement of the other co-resident’s peace of residence, and if one imagines a case where the co-resident blocked from entering has nowhere to stay, it is also not in line with social common sense to evaluate as trespass and punish the act of overpowering such unilateral entry blockade and entering on the premise that such blockade was justified. In this case, since Nonparty 1, a co-resident, or Victim Nonparty 2, to whom entry management for this apartment was entrusted by Nonparty 1, used force to block and prohibit Defendant 1’s entry despite the absence of special circumstances permitting them to prohibit entry by Defendant 1, who at that time was not in a departed state from the joint residence relationship, Defendant 1 was compelled to use physical force, such as damaging the chain-type latch installed on the entrance door of this apartment, in order to enter this apartment. Defendant 2 and Defendant 3, as the parents-in-law of Nonparty 1 and parents of Defendant 1, joined in Defendant 1’s conduct and thereby entered together in conjunction with it; viewed as a whole, this can be evaluated as having been carried out as part of, and incidental to, Defendant 1’s act of entering and using this apartment, which is a joint residence.\\n\\nThe majority opinion, premised on this situation, held that in light of the mutual restrictions on rights and the duty of tolerance incident to the joint residence relationship, the act of entry by Defendant 2 and Defendant 3 may receive the same evaluation as the act of entry by co-resident Defendant 1.\\n\\nWhether the dissent means that physical force was used in the course of an outsider’s entry into a joint residence and therefore the offense of residential trespass must uniformly be established, or whether, in this case, it should be viewed in that manner, the majority opinion does not consider either to be a proper legal principle or conclusion.\\n\\n4) The dissent also argues that the majority opinion fails to sufficiently protect the legal interest of freedom and peace of residence, which should be protected from force and the dominance of the majority.\\n\\nHowever, this misapprehends the purport of the majority opinion. Again, the majority opinion assumes that one co-resident is using the joint residence within the range mutually tolerated as co-residents, namely by entering the place of common life within the joint residence, and that the outsider’s entry also takes place incidentally in conjunction therewith upon the consent of that co-resident, as a situation concerning the ordinary use of the joint residence. Even in such a case, if residential trespass is recognized in relation to the co-resident who imposed the entry prohibition without justifiable reason, the legal interest of the peace of residence ordinarily enjoyed by the co-resident in the joint residence would be unjustifiably denied by the unilateral exercise of force by another co-resident. That is precisely the infringement of, and tolerance of the infringement of, the legal interest of freedom and peace of residence by unilateral force and dominance.\\n\\n5) The majority opinion’s comparison with the statutory punishment for residential trespass under the Criminal Act and with other countries that regulate residential trespass as a non-compound offense was intended to point out that punishing an outsider who enters a joint residence upon the consent of one co-resident as residential trespass, even though such entry can be evaluated as part of, and incidental to, the ordinary acts of entry into and use of the place of common life by the co-resident who consented, would amount to an excessive exercise of state punitive power in light of the punishment and regulatory scheme of the offense of residential trespass under the Criminal Act.\\n\\nIn this regard, the majority opinion’s purport is that overly intrusive intervention by the State into private spheres through the state punitive power may necessarily produce side effects that prevent the autonomy of the private sphere and the development of civil and domestic legal doctrines and institutions, so caution is needed. Although the need for State protection of the socially vulnerable within the private sphere, including the family, is increasing day by day, this is also why one hesitates to easily apply the offense of residential trespass in a manner that expands the application of penal provisions and the scope of criminal punishment.\\n\\nI state the above supplementary opinion on the majority opinion.\\n\\n10. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Min Yu-suk on the Dissenting Opinion\\n\\nA. Summary of the supplementary opinion on the dissent\\n\\nWe consider the impact this en banc decision will have on future trials and the interpretive theory of the relevant statutes.\\n\\nB. Change in the requirements for recognizing “departure from the joint residence relationship”\\n\\nSince the majority opinion denies the establishment of the offense of residential trespass against a co-resident, whether a person has departed from the status of co-resident will be an important standard for determining the establishment of the offense of residential trespass.\\n\\nThere is no established standard for recognizing whether a co-resident has departed from that status, and it must be determined individually according to the facts recognized in each concrete case. No Supreme Court precedent that articulates such a standard can yet be found.\\n\\nWhere a marital community has been dissolved by divorce and one spouse has left the joint residence, the departure from the status of co-resident is evident. However, departure from the status of co-resident does not occur only when the causal relationship that formed the joint residence relationship is dissolved or the title to possession of the residence is lost.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court upheld a lower court’s recognition of residential trespass where the defendant, after leaving home due to domestic discord and living separately for about 5 months, delivered the key to the entrance door to his wife through a marriage broker and thereafter did not request the return of the key, even if the defendant, as tenant, had left some of his belongings in the house (see Supreme Court Decision 94DO3336, rendered September 15, 1995).\\n\\nSince the majority opinion finds the basis for denying the offense of residential trespass against a co-resident in the “ordinary form of use of the joint residence” and the “restriction of legal interests that co-residents must mutually tolerate,” the criteria for determining whether one has departed from the joint residence relationship should likewise be sought here going forward. And that determination must be made concretely and individually according to the facts established as a result of the hearing of the circumstances such as the background and duration of the co-resident’s separation, the background and aftermath of the resident who remained in the home taking measures to prohibit the other party’s entry (such as changing the password), and the responses of both sides thereafter.\\n\\nC. Relation with the Domestic Violence Punishment Act\\n\\nAs stated in the dissenting opinion, according to the amended Domestic Violence Punishment Act that came into force on January 21, 2021, the offense of residential trespass under the Criminal Act (Article 319(1)), the offense of refusal to leave (Article 319(2)), the special offense of trespass into a structure (Article 320), and attempts of the above offenses (Article 322) committed among family members who are co-residents also fall under the “domestic violence crimes” prescribed by that Act [Article 2(3)(s)].\\n\\nIn addition, the duties of judicial police officers who are dispatched to the scene after receiving a report of domestic violence were amended to include, not only the suppression of violent acts and separation of the domestic violence perpetrator and the victim, but also criminal investigation including arrest of an offender in flagrante delicto under Article 212 of the Criminal Procedure Act (Article 5 item 1 and item 1-2).\\n\\nThe conclusion, according to the majority opinion, that the offense of residential trespass is not established against a co-resident should be understood as limited to cases in which the charge is brought under the Criminal Act. It appears that the majority opinion does not deny the point that “where there are other provisions under the statute,” those provisions should be followed.\\n\\nEven if, under the majority opinion, the conduct of a co-resident overpowering another co-resident’s refusal by violent means and entering the common residence may not be characterized as residential trespass under the Criminal Act, such conduct falls within the domestic violence crimes prescribed by the amended Domestic Violence Punishment Act, and under that Act, investigative authorities receiving a report of domestic violence have the authority and duty to conduct criminal investigation, including arriving at the scene and arresting the domestic violence perpetrator in flagrante delicto. With respect to such conduct, there may be imposed a temporary measure order of evacuation, etc. from the residence of the victim or family member, or prohibition of approach within 100 meters (Article 29(1) items 1 and 2), a victim protection order with the same content (Article 55-2(1) items 1 and 2), a temporary protection order (Article 55-4(1)), and a protective disposition order restricting acts of approaching the victim or family member (Article 40(1) item 1). If a co-resident enters the residence in violation of such disposition, he becomes subject to criminal punishment as an offense of noncompliance with protective disposition, etc. under Article 63 of the same Act. An act violating such temporary measures, etc., is an act of entering “despite the court’s order prohibiting entry into the joint residence,” and even under the majority opinion, residential trespass under the Criminal Act would separately be established.\\n\\nIf the majority opinion were to mean that “the act of a co-resident overpowering another co-resident’s refusal by violent means and entering the common residence does not constitute residential trespass under the Criminal Act and thus does not fall under the domestic violence crimes prescribed by the Domestic Violence Punishment Act,” then the amendment purpose of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act would be completely nullified by the majority opinion. This is because, even though the Domestic Violence Punishment Act was amended to expressly include the offense of residential trespass under Part II, Chapter XXXVI of the Criminal Act in order to protect family members who suffer harm from violent trespass acts by family members, that is, co-residents, the result of excluding such acts from domestic violence crimes by interpretation would follow.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state this supplementary opinion on the dissenting opinion."}

{"[2023DO8603]": "We decide the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the principal charge\\nFor the same reasons stated in the judgment, the court below upheld the first-instance judgment, which found the principal charge in this case (excluding the guilty portion) not guilty on the ground that there was no proof of a crime. Reviewing the reasons of the judgment below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in the court below’s determination that violated the rules of logic and experience and exceeded the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or that misapprehended the law on dolus eventualis and affected the judgment.\\n\\n2. Regarding the alternative charge\\nA. Article 3(1) of the Communications Secrets Protection Act (hereinafter, the name of the statute is omitted) provides that no person shall, unless pursuant to this Act and the Criminal Procedure Act or the Military Court Act, inspect mail, intercept telecommunications, or record or listen to conversations between other persons that are not made public, and Article 16(1) provides for punishment of acts in violation thereof. Here, “listening” means the act of eavesdropping on the contents of such a conversation in real time while a conversation between other persons is taking place, and the act of listening by replaying a recording of a conversation after the conversation has already ended is not included in “listening.” The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) Article 3(1) provides that “conversation” between other persons that is not made public is the object of “listening.” “Conversation” is, in principle, “a communicative act in which the parties present at the scene exchange words in person” (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DO19843, rendered on Mar. 15, 2017), and when such communicative act ends, the conversation as the object of listening also ends. It is difficult to view listening to a recording of an ended conversation by replaying it as listening to the conversation itself, and Article 3(1) does not provide that recordings of conversations, in addition to the conversation itself, are also objects of listening. In light of this meaning of “conversation” and the language of Article 3(1), caution is required in interpreting “conversation” to include recordings of conversation, which are distinct from “conversation.”\\n\\n2) Article 14(1) provides that no person may record a conversation between other persons that is not made public or listen to it by using an electronic device or mechanical means, thereby specifying and limiting the prohibited act of listening. This appears to be a provision intended to prohibit only listening carried out by means of an electronic device or mechanical means that can eavesdrop in real time, in that it is not necessary to punish even acts such as listening to a conversation between other persons that is not made public by using one’s own sense of hearing. However, listening carried out by replaying a recording of an already ended conversation is not included in the listening that Article 14(1) intends to prohibit.\\n\\n3) Since Articles 3(1) and 16(1) set forth “recording” and “listening” side by side as objects of prohibition and punishment, “conversation,” which is the common object of “recording” and “listening,” should, absent special circumstances, be construed as having the same meaning.
