However, in light of the ordinary meaning of “recording” and the purpose of the Communications Secrets Protection Act in prohibiting “recording,” the recording of a conversation between other persons prohibited by Article 3(1) means only recording in real time a conversation that is actually taking place at a specific moment, and it is difficult to regard it as including the act of replaying a recording of an already ended conversation and then recording it again. If, as such, the “conversation” that is the object of “recording” means a conversation actually taking place at the time of recording, then it is appropriate to construe the “conversation” that is the object of “listening” set forth in the same provision as likewise meaning a conversation actually taking place at the time of listening, absent special circumstances.\\n\\n4) Under the Communications Secrets Protection Act, “interception of telecommunications” means cases in which the contents of telecommunications are obtained and recorded in real time while telecommunications are taking place, and does not include acts such as opening records or contents remaining with respect to telecommunications for which receipt has already been completed (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DO8137, rendered on Oct. 13, 2016, and Article 9-3, etc., which otherwise treat telecommunications whose sending and receiving have been completed). Meanwhile, under the Communications Secrets Protection Act, “interception of telecommunications” and “listening to conversations between other persons that are not made public” are overlapping or similar to each other in terms of object (“sound, etc.” and “words exchanged in person”), means (“electronic device or mechanical means” and “electronic device or mechanical means”), and manner of act (“to listen to or read aloud and thereby obtain or record the contents, etc.” and “listening”) (see Articles 2(3), 2(7), and 14). In addition, the Communications Secrets Protection Act applies numerous provisions concerning “interception of telecommunications” (Articles 4 through 8, Article 9(1) first sentence and paragraph 3, Article 9-2, Article 11(1), (3), and (4), and Article 12) also to “listening to conversations between other persons that are not made public,” thereby regulating both commonly within that scope (Article 14(2)). In light of the conceptual and regulatory similarity between “interception of telecommunications” and “listening to conversations between other persons that are not made public,” and the systematic relationship between the two, it is appropriate to construe that, like “interception of telecommunications,” “listening to conversations between other persons that are not made public” also does not include the act of listening to a recording of an already ended conversation.\\n\\n5) An interpretation that includes in “listening” under Article 3(1) the act of replaying and listening to a recording of an ended conversation may, in light of Article 3(1), which regulates “listening” as a separate type of act from “recording,” be unnecessary, or may broaden the scope of “listening” too much and excessively expand the objects of prohibition and punishment. Where the person who unlawfully recorded listens to that recording, it is sufficient to make the unlawful recording itself the object of prohibition and punishment, and there is little need to separately make listening that follows the recording ex post facto an object of prohibition and punishment. In addition, if listening to the recording by the lawful recorder or a third party, or even listening to an unlawful recording by a third party other than the recorder, is also made an object of prohibition and punishment, the freedom of action of such persons would be excessively restricted. Furthermore, this would amount to an overly expansive interpretation or analogical interpretation in a manner unfavorable to the Defendant rather than strictly interpreting the meaning of an explicit penal provision, and is therefore not appropriate even in light of the principle of nulla poena sine lege (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DO4230, rendered on Nov. 28, 2013; Supreme Court Decision 2017DO21656, rendered on Mar. 15, 2018, etc.).\\n\\nB. In light of these legal principles, the court below’s determination, for the same reasons stated in the judgment, that the Defendant’s listening to the contents of the recorded conversations of the persons not indicted, etc., and transmitting the recording file to a third party, did not constitute the elements of the offenses under each item of Article 16(1) of the Communications Secrets Protection Act is proper, and there is no error in misapprehending the law concerning conversations between other persons that are not made public under the Communications Secrets Protection Act.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices as stated in the disposition."}

question:
Which of the following statements concerning the cases below are correct? (Leaving aside the issue of trespass into a residence, and where there is a dispute, according to case law)

(a) In or around February 2024, B proposed to A, “Let’s rob a convenience store using a pistol in or around April 2024,” and A agreed. B selected X convenience store as the target of the offense, drew up a concrete plan for the offense, obtained a pistol, and delivered it to A. However, in or around early March 2024, B was arrested and incarcerated on other criminal charges. A decided to carry out the offense even if he had to do it alone, and at around 10:00 a.m. on 2024. 4. 20., while concealing the pistol obtained by B inside his jumper, he entered X convenience store as if he were a customer, but, feeling remorseful, turned back and left as he was.
(b) Thereafter, at around 11:00 a.m. on 2024. 5., A decided to steal items from a convenience store and, in preparation for the case where the offense would be detected, concealed a hiking knife inside his clothes and entered Y convenience store, but as soon as he saw that there was a police officer inside the convenience store, he turned back and left as he was.

(a) In (a), since B conspired with A to rob X convenience store, B is punished for preparation or conspiracy to commit robbery even if he did not directly participate in A's offense.
(b) In (a), A is punished for attempted aggravated robbery with voluntary abandonment.
(c) In (b), A is punished for preparation or conspiracy to commit robbery.
(d) In (b), if, while A was coming out of the convenience store, a police officer who found this suspicious stopped him and demanded identification, and A assaulted the officer and fled, he is punished for attempted quasi-robbery.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2004DO6432]": "1. Judgment on the Grounds of Appeal\\n\\na. According to the record, it can be found that the Defendant, as a habitual offender, continued to commit offenses by selecting automobiles parked in residential parking lots or by the roadside in the dead of night, where there was little likelihood that a theft offense would be discovered, opening their doors, and stealing coins and other items. In light of this, even if the Defendant was carrying a hiking knife and the like while wandering around the residential area and looking for a target of offense, it is difficult to conclude that it was proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the Defendant had the intent to rob another person of money or valuables. Therefore, the judgment of the court of second instance, which upheld the first instance judgment to the same effect, is correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality in violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nb. Article 343 of the Criminal Act concerning the crime of preparation or conspiracy for robbery provides that “A person who prepares or conspires with the intent to commit robbery shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 7 years.” Since the statutory penalty is set at a considerably severe level, such as exceeding the statutory penalty for simple theft, and considering that preparation and conspiracy are, in principle, exceptionally punishable only where there is a special provision in the law (Article 28 of the Criminal Act), it would be desirable to confine cases recognized as the crime of preparation or conspiracy for robbery to types of conduct in which a degree of illegality commensurate with the above statutory penalty is manifested.\\n\\nHowever, Article 335 of the Criminal Act concerning quasi-robbery merely provides that “When a thief uses violence or intimidation for the purpose of recapturing property, evading apprehension, or destroying evidence of the crime, the provisions of the preceding 2 Articles shall apply,” and does not expressly state that quasi-robbery is always to be treated the same as robbery. Even if a thief has the intent to commit quasi-robbery, such intent necessarily presupposes the discovery of the theft offense, which is an extreme situation that a thief would never desire, and therefore it can only have an essentially highly exceptional and limited character. Moreover, the Criminal Act punishes theft committed while carrying a weapon as an aggravated constituent offense of special theft (Article 331(2) of the Criminal Act), yet does not provide any provision punishing the preparatory act therefor. If, however, it were deemed possible to punish, as preparation for robbery, even a case in which there is an intent to commit quasi-robbery, then almost all acts preparing special theft while carrying a weapon would necessarily be punishable as preparation for robbery, which would result in a consequence contrary to the fact that the Criminal Act does not provide a punishment provision for the preparatory act of special theft involving a weapon. In addition, Article 7 of the Act on the Punishment, etc. of Violent Acts separately provides for punishment of the act of carrying a weapon or other dangerous object without justifiable cause. Taking these points into consideration, in order for the crime of preparation or conspiracy for robbery to be established, it must be recognized that the preparatory or conspiratorial actor had, at least possibly, the purpose of committing “robbery,” and where the purpose is limited merely to committing “quasi-robbery” without reaching that level, it is reasonable to view that punishment as the crime of preparation or conspiracy for robbery is not possible.\\n\\nAccording to the Defendant’s prior offenses and other circumstances recognized from the record, it is difficult to conclude that the Defendant prepared the hiking knife he was carrying, as he asserts, with the thought that it might help him evade apprehension if the theft offense were unexpectedly discovered, and further with the thought of using it to rob another person of property. Since the Defendant’s intent is recognized only to the extent of having the purpose of committing quasi-robbery in this manner, it cannot be said that he had the purpose of committing robbery. Therefore, criminal liability for the crime of preparation for robbery cannot be recognized.\\n\\nOn the same reasoning, the court of second instance’s measure of upholding the first instance judgment, which found the charged facts concerning the portion of the crime of preparation for robbery not guilty, is correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as an error of law concerning the crime of preparation for robbery, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Determination ex officio\\n\\nArticle 364(4) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that the appellate court shall dismiss the appeal by judgment when it recognizes that there are no grounds for appeal. According to the record, with respect to the portion of the charged facts in this case against the Defendant concerning the crime of preparation for robbery, the first instance court rendered a not-guilty verdict, and the prosecutor appealed. Although the court of second instance, in the reasoning of its judgment, determined that the prosecutor’s appeal was without merit, it did not pronounce dismissal of the appeal in the operative part. Thus, it can be said that the judgment of the court of second instance contains illegality in violation of Article 364(4) of the Criminal Procedure Act (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2000DO2049 rendered on April 10, 2001).\\n\\nTherefore, the portion of the judgment of the court of second instance concerning the crime of preparation for robbery cannot avoid being quashed on this point, and since this portion of the case is deemed sufficiently able to be adjudicated on the basis of the case record and the evidence examined up to the court of second instance, this Court will render judgment directly pursuant to Article 396 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nThe substance of the prosecutor’s grounds for appeal concerning the portion of the crime of preparation for robbery is that there was insufficient proof that the Defendant had the purpose of robbing money or valuables, or that the first instance judgment, which held that “robbery” in the crime of preparation for robbery does not include quasi-robbery, violated the rules of evidence and contained an error of law concerning the crime of preparation for robbery. However, as seen above in the judgment on the grounds of appeal, the above determination by the first instance court is all correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as that alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the portion of the judgment of the court of second instance concerning the crime of preparation for robbery is quashed, and the prosecutor’s appeal concerning this portion is dismissed. Accordingly, the judgment is rendered as ordered with the unanimous opinion of the judges who participated."}

{"[2014DO2521]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Facts charged and the decision of the court below\\na. The facts charged in this case are that, “On 2013. 8. 3. at 12:30, when the Defendant, at a bar operated by the victim, a person not party to the prosecution, was demanded by the victim to pay a drinking bill of 26 hundred-thousand won, he decided to avoid payment of the drinking bill by luring and assaulting the victim, and after luring the victim into an alley behind the nearby Raemian Apartment Complex, he grabbed and pushed the victim by the shoulder with both hands and tripped the victim’s legs with his foot to knock the victim to the ground, then climbed on top of the victim’s body and choked the victim’s neck with both hands or covered the victim’s mouth with his hand and tried to strike the victim’s face with his fist, thereby making the victim unable to resist and then fleeing as is, thereby avoiding payment of the drinking bill of 26 hundred-thousand won, obtaining a pecuniary benefit equivalent to the same amount, and inflicting injuries on the victim, including abrasions on both elbows requiring treatment for approximately 2 weeks.”\\nb. In response, the court below held that the injuries suffered by the victim did not constitute injuries under the offense of robbery resulting in injury, and therefore found the offense of robbery resulting in injury not guilty, while, on the ground that the identity of the facts charged was recognized and that it would not cause substantial prejudice to the exercise of the Defendant’s right of defense, it changed the final part of the facts charged, without amending the indictment, to read, “The Defendant avoided payment of the drinking bill of 26 hundred-thousand won payable to the victim, obtained a pecuniary benefit equivalent to the same amount, and assaulted the victim,” and convicted the Defendant by applying the offense of quasi-robbery thereto.\\n\\n2. The decision of the Supreme Court\\na. Article 335 of the Criminal Act provides that quasi-robbery is established when a thief uses violence or intimidation for the purpose of resisting the recovery of property, evading arrest, or destroying traces of the crime; thus, the subject of the offense of quasi-robbery is a thief and the object of the offense of theft is property.\\nb. The criminal facts recognized by the court below are that the Defendant avoided payment of the drinking bill payable to the victim, obtained a pecuniary benefit, and assaulted the victim, but those facts, in themselves, do not include that he had commenced the execution of theft, and even upon review of the record, there are no circumstances sufficient to recognize this.\\nNevertheless, the court below applied the offense of quasi-robbery to the above facts charged and recognized guilt, and this is an erroneous determination due to a misunderstanding of the legal doctrine concerning the subject of the offense of quasi-robbery.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, without needing to examine the remaining grounds for final appeal, the original judgment shall be reversed and the case remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and so, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, judgment is rendered as stated in the order."}

{"[75DO1549]": "Determination on the Prosecutor’s Grounds for Final Appeal\\n\\nUnder the provision of Article 32(1) of the Criminal Act that a person who aids another’s crime shall be punished as an accessory, “another’s crime” means a case in which the principal offender has commenced to realize the offense; therefore, in order for an accessory to be punished, it is possible only when the principal offender has commenced execution, and where the principal offender has remained only at the preparatory stage without reaching commencement of execution, the person who assists therein cannot be punished as an accessory, except in cases where such assisting act constitutes a joint principal offense at the preparatory stage.\\n\\nThis is because, in terms of the concept of the constituent elements of a crime, the act of execution of a preparatory offense is an unstructured and indefinite act, and the act of an accessory is also unstructured and indefinite; and because Article 28 of the Criminal Act provides that, where conspiracy or a preparatory act for a crime has not reached commencement of execution, it shall not be punished unless there is a special provision of law, thereby prohibiting unjust analogy or expansive interpretation of the constituent elements of a crime that punishment of a preparatory offense would bring, it cannot be said that the provisions of the Special Part of the Criminal Act punishing preparatory offenses may be directly incorporated into the concept of an independent constituent offense. Such an interpretation is also consistent with the principle of legality. Therefore, in light of the spirit of the Criminal Act as a whole, it is a reasonable interpretation to deny the establishment of accessory liability at the preparatory stage.\\n\\nThe ground of final appeal that the robbery preparatory offense at issue is a crime corresponding to an independent constituent offense under the Criminal Act is, as stated above, an untenable independent view; and even if the purport of the court below’s determination is somewhat different from this, it is correct in its conclusion denying the establishment of accessory liability for a preparatory offense, and the ground of final appeal criticizing this is without merit.\\n\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the operative part by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}
