{"[99DO424]": "1. Regarding Ground 1 of the court-appointed defense counsel’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\nArticle 28 of the Criminal Act provides that when the conspiracy to commit a crime or preparatory acts have not reached commencement of execution, they shall not be punished unless otherwise specially provided by law; Article 182(2) of the Customs Act provides that a person who has made preparations with the purpose of committing the offense of customs evasion, etc. prescribed in Article 180 shall, together with attempted offenders, be punished in accordance with the principal offense; and Article 6(7) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes contains a provision that punishes, under certain requirements, a person who has committed the offense prescribed in Article 182 of the Customs Act more severely. This is only because, in view of the fact that customs offenses, including customs evasion, have a great impact on the national economy, and have the characteristics of profit-motivated offenses with organized, professional, sophisticated, and international traits, and that the completed offense and the attempted offense, as well as the attempted offense and the preparatory offense, do not greatly differ in the possibility or risk of infringement of legal interests, provisions are made to punish preparatory acts for the purpose of achieving the legislative purpose of the Customs Act, maintaining order, and promoting the public welfare, and it is not because it intends, without rational basis, to discriminate against any particular person from the general public or to specially impose severe punishment by distinguishing customs evasion offenses from other specific offenses such as tax evasion offenses under the Punishment of Tax Offenses Act; therefore, the above provisions concerning the offense of preparation for customs evasion cannot be said to violate the principle of equality under Article 11 of the Constitution or the principle of guaranteeing fundamental human rights under Article 10 of the Constitution.\\n\\n2. Regarding Ground 2 of the court-appointed defense counsel’s grounds for final appeal and Grounds 1 and 2 of the Defendant’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\nUpon comparing the judgment of the lower court and the evidence expressly cited in the first-instance judgment referred to by the lower court with the record, the lower court properly found that the Defendant and others, on 1998. 2. 17., prepared a contract concerning the import of 1,000t of mung beans with a Chinese non-indicted limited liability company and, when they applied for prior examination of the dutiable value on the 25th of the same month, submitted the same contract as is; however, in reality, they resolved to evade the corresponding customs duties by paying the Chinese company an additional amount equivalent to 10% of the import quantity, importing that much more in quantity, and not filing an import declaration for that portion, and thereafter imported and cleared 330t of mung beans on three occasions up to 7. 7. of the same year and attempted to import the remaining 770t; and there is no illegality in the form of a factual error caused by a violation of the rules of evidence as asserted in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nMeanwhile, according to Article 9-2(1) of the Customs Act, a person obligated to pay customs duties shall, at the time of filing an import declaration, declare to the head of the customs office the price of the relevant goods in accordance with the Presidential Decree; however, Article 9-15 of the same Act provides that where a person who is required to make a tax declaration has doubts regarding matters underlying the determination of the dutiable value, he or she may, before making a price declaration, apply to the Commissioner of the Korea Customs Service or the head of the customs office for prior examination by attaching the documents prescribed by the Presidential Decree, and where the head of the customs office recognizes, in the case where the person obligated to pay customs duties makes a tax declaration based on the above prior examination document, that the relevant person obligated to pay and the applicant for the prior examination are identical and that the imported goods and the declaration of dutiable value are identical to the contents of the prior examination document, the dutiable value shall be determined in accordance with the contents of the prior examination document unless there is a special reason prescribed by the Presidential Decree; therefore, it is appropriate to view the act of falsely declaring the dutiable value and obtaining in advance a prior examination document for the dutiable value by attaching a contract stating a lower quantity and price of goods to be imported for the purpose of evading customs duties, and applying for prior examination of the dutiable value for the entire expected import quantity, as an external preparatory act for the realization of the offense of customs evasion. In this sense, the lower court’s conclusion that, with respect to the remaining 770t excluding the 330t of mung beans actually imported and cleared by the Defendant and others, the offense of preparation for customs evasion prescribed in Article 182(2) of the Customs Act applies, and that it was therefore charged under Article 6(7) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes, was correct, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of law concerning the offense of preparation for customs evasion.\\n\\nAlso, upon examining the record, the fact that the validity period of the above prior examination document concerning the dutiable value was stated as until 1998. 8. 25. does not mean that the Defendant and others could not actually import the remaining 770t of mung beans, and moreover, the circumstance that the Defendant and others voluntarily abandoned such import is not recognized; furthermore, a desistance offender refers to a case where, after commencing execution of the offense, the person voluntarily discontinues the act, and where the acts of preparation or conspiracy before commencement of execution are punished, the concept of a desistance offender cannot be recognized (see Supreme Court Decision 91DO436, decided 1991. 6. 25.), so the grounds for appeal on this point also cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Regarding Ground 3 of the Defendant’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\nIn a case such as this, where a term of imprisonment of less than 10 years was imposed, the contention that there is a reason to deem the sentencing excessively heavy and therefore improper cannot constitute a lawful ground for final appeal.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and 55 days out of the period of detention after the filing of the appeal shall be counted toward the principal sentence; the opinions of the participating judges being unanimous, the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

question:
Among the explanations concerning the offense of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights, which of the following are incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)

(a). The offense of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights is established when a public official, under the pretense of exercising official authority, engages in substantially and concretely unlawful or improper conduct with respect to matters falling within his or her general official authority, and such general official authority must be accompanied by legal coercive force.
(b). To fall under “obstruction of the exercise of rights,” the actual exercise of a concretized right must have been obstructed; therefore, even if a public official committed an act of abuse of authority, if no result of obstruction of the actual exercise of rights occurred, it is punished as an attempt of this offense.
(c). If the person against whom abuse of authority is directed is a public official or an executive or employee of a public institution, etc. who has been entrusted with certain public duties under statutes and regulations, that person is in a position to perform duties pursuant to such statutes and regulations, so whether what he or she did in response to the authority constituted an act not under any duty must be determined individually according to the content of the relevant statutes and regulations, etc., and a private person cannot be the subject against whom abuse of authority is directed.
(d). If a judicial police officer who executes duties concerning arrest and detention, considering the circumstances at the time of arrest, could sufficiently know that the requirements for arrest were not satisfied by judging without markedly losing rationality in light of the rules of experience, yet, recognizing that he was acting beyond the scope of his discretion and accepting that result, arrested a person and thereby obstructed the exercise of rights, then the offense of arrest by abuse of authority and the offense of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights are established.
(e). Where a superior police officer abuses authority to make a subordinate police officer discontinue an investigation or transfer the case to another police agency, this constitutes obstruction of the subordinate police officer’s exercise of investigative authority and also constitutes causing the subordinate police officer to discontinue the investigation or transfer the case even though there was no duty to do so; therefore, the “offense of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights by obstruction of the exercise of rights” and the “offense of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights by causing the performance of an act not under one’s duty” are established separately.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2002DO6251]": "We consider the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Judgment on Defendant A’s grounds of appeal\\n\\n(a) The court below, after comprehensively reviewing the evidence it admitted, found that around 1997. 11. 15., while Defendant A was serving as Minister of D, E, the Director of D, reported to Defendant A that F, who was Defendant A’s affinal relative, had requested that the G Group, of which F was the chairman, was in financial difficulty and asked whether Defendant A would see to it that the group could obtain bank loans from its executives, and that Defendant A said, “What can be done? Please see to it.”; that at the time, the G Group had applied to H Bank, its main bank, for a loan of 1,100 hundred million won, but H Bank, which was then in a state of capital impairment and, pursuant to a management improvement order issued by the Bank Supervisory Board, was formulating and implementing a self-rescue plan, was avoiding large-scale new extensions of credit; that the G Group had in effect been refused on the grounds that there was a risk of short-term deterioration in its ability to make payments and of insolvency, that there were doubts as to its ability to bear financial costs, and that its ability to provide security was insufficient; that immediately after hearing Defendant A’s words, E telephoned I, the president of H Bank, and asked him to see to the G Group’s loan matter; that I thereupon changed his prior attitude, telephoned the presidents of the other creditor banks of the G Group, and told them, to the effect that H Bank would take the lead in promoting a coordinated loan and asked for their cooperation, obtained affirmative responses from each of the presidents, instructed J, the executive director in charge of lending at H Bank, to prepare a coordinated loan for the G Group, and held a meeting of the creditor bank presidents at around 08:00 on 1997. 11. 19., thereby reaching an agreement on a coordinated loan of 1,060 hundred million won for the G Group, and then, on 1997. 12. 10., H Bank extended a loan of 189 hundred million won to the G Group; and on the basis of the foregoing and the surrounding circumstances, the court below determined that Defendant A had, through E, demanded that I “see to” a loan to the G Group, and that the meaning of “see to it” was not merely a request to arrange a bank loan within lawful and possible limits, but had a stronger sense of asking that what could not be done be made possible, and therefore it could not be said that Defendant A lacked the intent to abuse authority, and that since I changed his prior stance that no loan could be extended to the G Group, persuaded the relevant creditor bank presidents, and took the lead in the coordinated loan as a result of the words conveyed by Defendant A through E as described above, there was no basis to find that there was no causal relationship between Defendant A’s abuse-of-authority act and I’s execution of the loan to the G Group; and such determination is as stated above. Examining the relevant evidence by the record, the court below’s findings of fact and determination are all proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality such as a factual mistake arising from a violation of the rules of evidence or an error in law concerning causal relationship, as alleged.\\n\\n(b) The offense of abuse of authority is established where a public official, by feigning the exercise of authority in matters within his or her general official authority, performs a substantively and specifically unlawful or improper act (see Supreme Court Decision 92DO116, rendered on 1992. 3. 10.), and such general official authority need not necessarily involve legal compulsion; it is sufficient if, when abused, it is enough to cause the object of the exercise of authority to do something for which there is no legal duty or to interfere with the exercise of a lawful right.\\n\\nAccording to the former Government Organization Act (before amendment by Act No. 5529 of 1998. 2. 28.), the former M Bank Act (before amendment by Act No. 5491 of 1997. 12. 31.), the former Banking Act (before amendment by Act No. 5499 of 1998. 1. 13.), the former Act on the Structural Improvement of the Financial Industry (before amendment by Act No. 5496 of 1998. 1. 8.), and the former D and Its Affiliated Agencies Organization Order (before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 15516 of 1997. 11. 29.), (1) D is in charge of affairs concerning currency and finance, etc., in addition to the formulation and operation of comprehensive plans for the country’s economic and social development, the coordination of plans for procuring the financial resources therefor, and the preparation and management of the budget’s execution, namely, the comprehensive supply and demand adjustment of the short- and long-term financial markets and the foreign exchange market, the formulation and operation of policies on the banking industry, matters concerning the financial supervision system and the disposal of nonperforming loans and the credit management system of financial institutions, and the formulation and operation of policies on industrial finance, etc.; the Minister of D, acting upon the Prime Minister’s orders with respect to economic planning and operation, exercises overall control and coordination over the relevant ministries and agencies, and serves as ex officio chairman of the Financial and Monetary Board; (2) the Financial and Monetary Board sets and operates management guidance standards for ensuring the soundness of financial institutions’ management, exercises control by determining and establishing the maximum rates of interest, etc. on loans of financial institutions and the maximum limits on loans, etc.; in certain cases, it requires financial institutions to take necessary measures for management improvement, such as increasing capital; it revokes the authorization of financial institutions; upon the recommendation of the Governor of the Bank Supervisory Board, it may order the suspension of the performance of duties by officers of financial institutions, or authorize the Governor of the Bank Supervisory Board to take appropriate measures against financial institutions, such as warnings, cessation of illegal acts or unsound business practices, and suspension of business; and in particular, with respect to financial institutions established under the Banking Act, in certain cases it may take necessary measures such as issuing cautions or warnings to the relevant financial institution, or requiring submission of a management improvement plan, and within the minimum scope necessary for sound management, it may order management-improvement measures such as an increase in capital or disposal of shares held, and may recommend merger, transfer of all or part of the business, or acquisition of the relevant financial institution by a third party; and (3) the Bank Supervisory Board is separately provided to engage in the supervision and regular inspection of financial institutions under the direction of the Financial and Monetary Board. Meanwhile, according to the record, at the time, when major conglomerates were defaulting or were on the verge of default and financial institutions were becoming insolvent, the Minister of D had, through the head of the comprehensive finance office or the Governor of the Bank Supervisory Board, requested creditor banks to extend loans to viable conglomerates on the premise that self-rescue plans be formulated and implemented, or to refrain from recovering credit, in order to prevent defaults by major conglomerates whose influence on the national economy was substantial and to reduce the nonperforming loans of financial institutions; and creditor banks had also to a considerable extent accepted such requests and had extended loans or refrained from recovering credit. In this way, the Minister of D, who exercised comprehensive authority over the overall national economy, especially financial affairs, in order to prevent the occurrence of situations that would hinder the stability and development of the national economy, such as the collapse of major conglomerates whose influence on the national economy was severe, the resulting chain bankruptcies of related companies, the insolvency of financial institutions, and mass unemployment, it is a matter within his general official authority to recommend or request financial institutions to extend loans to companies that have substantial influence on the national economy and are viable, on the premise that they satisfy certain requirements such as the formulation and implementation of self-rescue plans.\\n\\nAccordingly, where the Defendant, who had such general official authority, requested I, the president of H Bank, which was the main bank avoiding new lending after receiving a management improvement order from the Governor of the Bank Supervisory Board, through D Director E, to extend loans to the G Group, which did not even fall within the large conglomerates described above and whose viability was uncertain and thus could hardly be regarded as satisfying the requirements for eligible lending, for the personal purpose of helping the company run by his affinal relative, and where, in response to such request, I, as stated above, newly promoted a coordinated loan with the presidents of other creditor banks for the G Group, whose loan application had already been rejected by H Bank, and extended 189 hundred million won, such conduct constitutes a case in which, with respect to matters within the general official authority of the Minister of D, etc., he feigned the exercise of authority and performed a substantively and specifically unlawful or improper act, and therefore the offense of abuse of authority should be found established.\\n\\nAlthough the reasoning in the judgment below contains somewhat inappropriate points in its explanation, its conclusion that Defendant A’s conduct falls under the offense of abuse of authority is proper, and there is no illegality, such as an error in law concerning the offense of abuse of authority, as alleged.\\n\\n2. Judgment on the Prosecutor’s grounds of appeal\\n\\n(a) On the point of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights in relation to Defendant A’s handling of the Kia crisis\\n\\nThe court below, after finding the facts as stated in the judgment, determined that Defendant A, in order to minimize national economic loss and promptly address the Kia crisis in the circumstances then prevailing, discussed countermeasures with the persons concerned, including the consortium of creditor banks, and conveyed the decisions thereof to the creditor banks through E as the government’s position; and that L, the representative director of K, withdrew his expression of consent to the composition proceedings in order to align himself with the government’s policy as above, and therefore it could not be said that Defendant A had exercised his official authority by improper means, nor could it be said that Defendant A had awareness of abusing his authority. Examining the relevant evidence by the record, the court below’s findings of fact and determination are all proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality such as a factual mistake, contradictory reasoning, or an error in law arising from a violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged.\\n\\n(b) On the point of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights in relation to Defendant A’s instruction to cease intervention in the foreign exchange market\\n\\nThe court below held that there was no evidence to support the allegation that Defendant A instructed N, the Governor of M Bank, to cease intervention in the foreign exchange market, and therefore maintained the first-instance judgment that acquitted on the charge of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights. Examining the relevant evidence by the record, the court below’s findings of fact and determination are all proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality such as a factual mistake or an error in law arising from a violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged. Moreover, insofar as the fact that Defendant A instructed the cessation of intervention in the foreign exchange market is not established, even if there were any illegality in the court below’s determination regarding whether M Bank actually ceased intervention in the foreign exchange market or what the reason was, such illegality could not be said to have affected the result of the judgment.\\n\\n(c) On the point of dereliction of duty relating to Defendant A’s and the other defendants’ reports on the foreign exchange crisis\\n\\n(1) On the point of dereliction of duty relating to the report on 1997. 10. 29.\\n\\nThe court below, with respect to the allegation that on 1997. 10. 28. transactions in the foreign exchange market were suspended and that on the same day the foreign exchange countermeasures meeting described in the judgment was held, and that there was an explanation at the meeting based on the report entitled “Recent Foreign Exchange Situation and Countermeasures,” thereby causing the defendants to become aware that the situation at the time had the potential to rapidly develop into a foreign exchange crisis and that suspension of transactions in the foreign exchange market was a serious incident that had to be reported to the President, determined that, in light of the facts found in the judgment, this was insufficient to support such a finding and that there was no other evidence to support it, and therefore maintained the first-instance judgment that acquitted on the charge of dereliction of duty. Examining the relevant evidence by the record, the above findings of fact and determination by the court below are all proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality of factual mistake arising from a violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged.\\n\\n(2) On the point of dereliction of duty relating to the report on 1997. 11. 10.\\n\\nThe court below, on the basis of the evidence cited in the judgment, found that at a countermeasures meeting for responding to the foreign exchange crisis held on 1997. 11. 7. and presided over by Defendant O, with officials from the Office of the Senior Secretary for Economic Affairs of the Presidential Secretariat, D, M Bank, and others in attendance, it was decided to implement alternatives such as flexible management of the exchange rate and devising ways to secure foreign capital, and, if that proved difficult, to examine a plan to request IMF bailout assistance, while preparing in advance and maintaining confidentiality, and that the request for IMF bailout assistance was formally raised for the first time; that Defendant A, the next day, heard from Defendant O the result of the countermeasures meeting and shared the same understanding; and that on 1997. 11. 10., in the presence of Defendant O, Defendant A reported to the President while presenting the comprehensive measures for stabilizing the financial market, and orally reported the difficult foreign exchange situation at the time and that, as a countermeasure, a plan to request IMF bailout assistance was under consideration. After so finding, the court below determined that, up to the time of the above report, the request for IMF bailout assistance had only been examined as one of the viable and prominent options for addressing the foreign exchange crisis, and it could not be said that a conclusion had been reached that IMF bailout assistance must be requested immediately without examining other alternatives; therefore, it could not be said that the defendants reported to the President by concealing or minimizing the realities of the foreign exchange crisis at that time. Examining the relevant evidence by the record, the court below’s findings of fact and determination are all proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality such as a factual mistake arising from a violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged.\\n\\n(d) On the point of dereliction of duty relating to Defendant A’s handover and takeover of duties\\n\\nThe court below, on the basis of the evidence cited in the judgment, found that in this country, when a Minister is replaced, the handover and takeover of duties customarily takes place in the form of receiving a work report from subordinate staff, and that there had been no instance in which the predecessor and successor had directly met to conduct the handover and takeover; that the policy of announcing the request for IMF bailout assistance and the fact of approval thereof were known not only to Defendant A alone, but also to the President who had received the report and to P, who was in attendance; that E and Q also knew that the announcement of the request for IMF bailout assistance would be made in the form of responding to journalists’ questions at a press conference; and that the newly appointed R and newly appointed S also, upon receiving their appointments, heard admonitions from the President, or received explanations from T and U regarding V’s visit to Korea and the results of the interview, and therefore at least knew that the process by which our country would request IMF bailout assistance was underway. After so finding, the court below determined that even if Defendant A had not instructed a subordinate to report the policy on announcing the request for IMF bailout assistance to the successor Deputy Prime Minister, or had not directly informed the successor Deputy Prime Minister by memorandum or telephone, it could not be concluded that Defendant A had the intent not to let the successor know the policy on announcing the request for IMF bailout assistance; and that there was otherwise no evidence to recognize Defendant A’s intent to commit dereliction of duty. Examining the relevant evidence by the record, the court below’s findings of fact and determination are all proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality such as a factual mistake arising from a violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the court below did not acquit on this part of the charge of dereliction of duty on the ground that Defendant A was dismissed and no longer held the status of a public official, nor did it recognize the President or the Chief Presidential Secretary as the subjects of the D Minister’s handover and takeover of duties; thus, even if the court below did not make a determination on the timing at which public-official status was maintained, and even if it explained that the President or the Chief Presidential Secretary knew the policy on announcing the request for IMF bailout assistance, there is no illegality of error in law that affected the result of the judgment, as alleged.\\n\\n(e) On the point of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights in relation to the loan to Y Department Store\\n\\nThe court below found the facts as stated in the judgment and determined that the extension of a loan of 150 hundred million won to Y Department Store was not made because Defendant A requested it through E from X, the president of W Bank, but because Z and others, who operated Y Department Store, actively requested AA and others, including AA, an adviser to W Investment Trust Management Company and former president of W Bank. Examining the relevant evidence by the record, the court below’s findings of fact and determination are all proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality such as a factual mistake arising from a violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged.\\n\\n(f) On the point of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights in relation to loans to the AB Group by Defendant O\\n\\nThe court below found the facts as stated in the judgment and determined that Defendant O’s presiding over a meeting on 1997. 10. 4. concerning countermeasures against the default crisis of the AB Group and others, and another meeting on 1997. 10. 11. concerning the issue of coordinated loans to the AB Group, appears merely to have been part of policy implementation to prevent a chain of defaults by large corporations pursuant to the government’s basic policy at the time, and there is no evidence that Defendant O presided over the meetings for the personal purpose of helping the AB Group at the request of President AC, etc.; and also, at the 10. 4. meeting, they discussed preventing insolvency of the AB Group and others, and at the 10. 11. meeting, Defendant O merely explained the government’s basic position at the time, and the coordinated loan to the AB Group was agreed upon by the creditor banks in accordance with the argument of the president of W Bank; accordingly, Defendant O’s conduct did not constitute abuse of authority, nor could it be said that Defendant O had intent in that regard. Examining the relevant evidence by the record, the court below’s findings of fact and determination are all proper and persuasive, and there is no illegality such as a factual mistake arising from a violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, since both Defendant A’s appeal and the Prosecutor’s appeal are without merit, they are all dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2003DO4599]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nIn the offense of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights prescribed in Article 123 of the Criminal Act, to obstruct the exercise of rights means to obstruct the legitimate exercise of rights that may be exercised under statutes; therefore, for this offense to be established, the actual exercise of a concretized right must have been obstructed (see Supreme Court Decision dated June 30, 1986, 86MO12), and even if there was an act by a public official abusing authority, if no result of actual obstruction of the exercise of rights occurred, the consummation of this offense cannot be recognized (see Supreme Court Judgment dated October 10, 1978, 75DO2665).\\n\\nThe court below, based on a comprehensive consideration of the evidence it admitted, recognized the facts stated in the judgment, and then found that: ① in the process of selecting the operator for personal mobile communications, both the introduction of hearing review and the change in the point allocation for hearing review from the average-point allocation method to the zero-point allocation method were carried out pursuant to the Defendant’s instructions; ② the day after the Defendant received a report from Director Non-party 1 that it was difficult to distinguish the superiority and inferiority between LG Telecom Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “LG Telecom”) and Evernet (a Samsung-Hyundai consortium), the Defendant instructed working-level staff to arbitrarily change the already announced average-point allocation method to the zero-point allocation method without deliberation by the Telecommunications Commission or any public notice, and this was implemented; ③ the examiners were not informed that the evaluation method had been changed, so that the examiners at the time graded according to the average-point allocation method, and it is difficult to regard the zero-point allocation method as having been determined in advance through discussion and the process of collecting opinions among the examiners; ④ the examination standards, etc. are to be announced after deliberation by the Telecommunications Commission, and the examiners cannot determine them differently from the already announced standards and methods; ⑤ under the zero-point allocation method, no partial points are recognized at all for inferior companies, and the superior company is determined by majority vote after discussion, so if, during the discussion process, the presenter, who is an expert in the detailed examination items, supports a particular company, there is a high possibility that the remaining examiners, who are non-experts, will follow the presenter’s opinion, causing the scores to be heavily skewed to one side, and since a slight difference under the average-point allocation method results in an extreme difference between a full score and a zero score under the zero-point allocation method, such an evaluation method appears to be a very exceptional evaluation method; ⑥ although the Defendant merely calls it a change in the grading method, in the end it leads to a change in the point allocation method; ⑦ at the time of the hearing evaluation, the Defendant directly selected the remaining five persons out of the seven examiners, excluding Non-party 2 and Non-party 3, and all of those five were persons whose views could reflect the Defendant’s intent; ⑧ the Defendant knew, based on the report from Non-party 1, that it was difficult to distinguish the superiority and inferiority between LG Telecom and Evernet, and, having already instructed that the hearing review be conducted by the zero-point allocation method, even while knowing that the hearing review would determine the selection of the operator, stated at a breakfast meeting that the hearing review would not affect the selection of the operator, while emphasizing concentration of economic power and corporate morality, which were unrelated to the five items of the hearing review; ⑨ although the business plan review was conducted over 10 days, the hearing review was conducted over only 2 hours without properly affording the examiners an opportunity to review materials related to the hearing review; and, in light of these circumstances, the court found that the Defendant abused authority, but held that even if there was an act of abuse of authority, for this offense to be completed, there must be actual obstruction of the exercise of rights, and that it could not be concluded that only Evernet was treated unfairly by the hearing review examiners and thus unable to compete fairly during the hearing review and evaluation process, nor could it be said that, merely because Evernet was ahead of LG Telecom by 0.38 points in the business plan review results and because the hearing review score allocation was set at 2.2 points, Evernet’s right to be selected as a personal mobile communications operator under the Telecommunications Business Act was already a concretized right; accordingly, it acquitted the Defendant on the ground that the actual exercise of Evernet’s concretized rights was not obstructed.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the factual findings and determination of the court below are justifiable and acceptable, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the offense of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights, as asserted in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, the participating Justices are unanimous in dismissing the appeal, and judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2008DO7312]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the Defendant’s appeal\\n\\nA. Regarding the contention of violation of the rules of evidence and insufficiency of deliberation\\n\\nThe court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence it had admitted, found the circumstances as stated in its holding, and, when those circumstances are taken together, determined that the Defendant, in conspiracy with Non-indicted Person 1, abused the authority to direct criminal investigations within his jurisdiction to cause the Namdaemun Police Station’s investigation to be suspended, thereby obstructing Non-indicted Person 2 and others from exercising their rights concerning criminal investigation, and that the Defendant, in conspiracy with Non-indicted Person 3, Non-indicted Person 4, and Non-indicted Person 5, abused the authority to direct criminal investigations and to operate the Metropolitan Investigation Unit to cause the Metropolitan Investigation Unit’s investigation to be suspended and transferred to the Namdaemun Police Station, thereby obstructing Non-indicted Person 6 and others from exercising their rights concerning criminal investigation. In light of the record, the court below’s selection and weighing of evidence, factual findings, and determinations are proper and acceptable, and there is no error of fact due to violation of the rules of evidence or insufficiency of deliberation as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nB. Regarding the contention of error in the interpretation of law\\n\\n(1) The meaning of “right” in the crime of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of official authority\\n\\nArticle 123 of the Criminal Act provides that “A public official who, by abusing his official authority, causes another to do something he is not under an obligation to do, or obstructs another’s exercise of rights, shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 5 years, suspension of qualifications for not more than 10 years, or a fine not exceeding 10 million won.” Here, the term “right” is not limited to rights expressly stated in statutes, and it is sufficient if it is an interest that should be protected under statutes and regulations; it is appropriate to view that it does not matter whether it is a public-law right or a private-law right. The court below, after recognizing on the basis of the relevant provisions of the Act on the Performance of Duties by Police Officers that police officers have the authority to investigate crimes, further recognized that such criminal investigative authority constitutes the “right” referred to in the crime of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of official authority; this is in accordance with the foregoing legal principle and is proper, and there is no error of law as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n(2) The existence of specific investigative authority and whether it was infringed\\n\\nThe court below determined that, in light of the circumstances as stated in its holding, the specific investigative authority of the police officers belonging to the Namdaemun Police Station, including Non-indicted Person 2, and the specific investigative authority of the police officers belonging to the Metropolitan Investigation Unit, including Non-indicted Person 6, had already arisen, and that, due to the Defendant’s conduct, the investigation was suspended or investigative intelligence was transferred from the Metropolitan Investigation Unit of the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency to the Namdaemun Police Station, thereby infringing the investigative authority of the said police officers. In light of the record, the court below’s determination is proper and acceptable, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality of error in the interpretation of law as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n(3) Whether a person without official status can also be a co-principal in the crime of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of official authority\\n\\nA co-principal under Article 30 of the Criminal Act is established by satisfying the subjective and objective requirements of joint intent to act and commission of the crime through functional control over the act based on that joint intent. Even if some of the conspirators do not directly divide and execute part of the constitutive acts, if, when comprehensively considering the position, role, or degree of control or dominion over the course of the crime that he occupies in the overall crime, it is recognized that there exists not merely a conspirator’s role but functional control over the crime through an essential contribution to it, then he cannot avoid criminal liability as a so-called co-principal by conspiracy. This legal principle likewise applies where a person who is not a public official conspires with a public official to commit the crime of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of official authority (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DO6950, rendered January 30, 2009). The court below’s recognition of the Defendant’s liability as a co-principal in the crime of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of official authority is proper as being in accordance with the foregoing legal principle, and there is no error of law as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n(4) Whether there was an abuse of the right to prosecute\\n\\nThe court below determined that, even if the prosecutor did not indict Non-indicted Person 3, Non-indicted Person 4, and Non-indicted Person 5 among the conspirators who held the status of public officials and indicted only the Defendant, when the circumstances as stated in its holding are taken together, the prosecutor’s above measure cannot be deemed to constitute an abuse of the right to prosecute. In light of the record, the court below’s determination is proper and acceptable, and there is no error of law as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Prosecutor’s appeal\\n\\nIn a case such as this, where a superior police officer, by abusing official authority, causes subordinate police officers to suspend an investigation or to transfer a case to another police agency, it may at once be viewed as both “obstructing the exercise of the subordinate police officers’ investigative authority” and “causing the subordinate police officers to suspend the investigation or to transfer the case to another police agency even though they had no duty to do so.” However, this is merely an interpretation of a single fact from different perspectives, and it cannot be said that the crime of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of official authority due to obstruction of the exercise of rights and the crime of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of official authority due to causing another to do something he is not under an obligation to do separately arise. Therefore, where the indictment charges conduct falling under both of the above forms, it is proper to view that only the crime of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of official authority due to obstruction of the exercise of rights is established, and the crime of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of official authority due to causing another to do something he is not under an obligation to do is not separately established (provided, however, that the prosecutor, who has the authority to institute prosecution, may, at his discretion, institute prosecution for the crime of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of official authority due to causing another to do something he is not under an obligation to do in such a case, and in that event it is possible for the court to find the crime of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of official authority within the scope of that indictment and punish accordingly; see Supreme Court Decision 2005DO4202, rendered February 14, 2008).\\n\\nThe court below’s determination that the portion of the facts charged in this case stating that “rights were obstructed” is guilty, while the portion stating that “another was caused to do something he was not under an obligation to do” is not guilty, is proper as being in accordance with the foregoing legal principle, and there is no error of law as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2013DO16162]": "We consider together the grounds of appeal by the Defendant and the Prosecutor (the statements in supplemental appellate briefs, petitions, reference materials, and the like submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. On the grounds of appeal alleging that the procedure for instituting the public prosecution is void\\n\\nEven if the court, after receiving the petition for adjudication, made a decision to institute prosecution under Article 262(2) No. 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act without notifying the suspect of that fact within the period prescribed by Article 262(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act from the date of receipt, once the prosecution has been instituted accordingly and the proceedings of the case on the merits have commenced, such error cannot, absent other special circumstances, be challenged in the case on the merits (see Supreme Court Decision of November 11, 2010, 2009DO224; Supreme Court Decision of April 10, 2014, 2012DO1741, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below, for the reasons stated in its opinion, determined that, even if the court that received the petition for adjudication proceeded with the examination without notifying the Defendant of that fact and made the decision to institute prosecution in this case, the institution of prosecution in this case does not fall under the case where it is void as being in violation of the provisions of law.\\n\\nThe above determination of the court below is proper as based on the legal principles set forth above, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the effect of the institution of prosecution.\\n\\n2. On the grounds of appeal concerning the legality of the arrest procedure for Union Member Non-indicted Person 1\\n\\nThe court below held that: ① although the Defendant, in front of the ○○ Automobile Plant of ○○ Motor Co., Ltd., surrounded six union members, including Non-indicted Person 2 of the □□□□ Labor Union ○○ Automobile Branch, with riot police officers wielding shields and caused them to be unable to move for 30 to 40 minutes before taking them away, and then, shortly thereafter, caused Non-indicted Person 1 to be unable to move for 10 minutes by the same method, considering the circumstances in which the said union members became unable to move, the manner thereof, the number and attitude of the riot police officers mobilized, and the duration of such condition, this constituted de facto arrest rather than administrative immediate compulsion based on Article 6(1) of the Act on the Performance of Duties by Police Officers; ② at that time, Non-indicted Person 1, surrounded by a large number of riot police officers, merely raised objections, and did not attempt to flee or resist by using force, and there was no urgent standoff situation to the extent that a physical clash between the labor union and management, or between union members and riot police officers, could be deemed imminent; and ③ while de facto arresting Non-indicted Person 1, the Defendant did not properly inform him of the reasons therefor, and only after receiving objections from the victim, etc., did he finally inform him of the reasons for arrest, and based on such circumstances, the arrest of Non-indicted Person 1 was unlawful because it did not comply with the procedure for arresting a person caught in flagrante delicto prescribed by the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the above determination of the court below did not err in misapprehending the facts in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the requirements and procedures for administrative immediate compulsion or arrest, or in omitting a determination. The grounds for appeal disputing this cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. On the grounds of appeal concerning whether the victim’s right of visitation and communication with counsel was recognize\\n\\nArticle 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “a defense counsel or a person intending to become defense counsel may have interviews with a defendant or suspect who has been physically restrained and may receive and deliver documents or objects, and may have a physician attend and treat him or her.” Therefore, even where a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having the possibility of becoming defense counsel, such person may not be restricted from having interviews with a defendant or suspect who has been physically restrained on the ground that he or she is not a “defense counsel or a person intending to become defense counsel” as prescribed in Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nThe court below determined that: ① the victim, as the chairperson of the Labor Relations Commission of ◇◇◇◇◇ ◇◇ ◇◇◇◇◇, had received an official letter from the chairperson of the □□□□ Labor Union on June 22, 2009, immediately before this case, stating, “Please take appropriate measures so that prompt interviews with attorneys may be arranged in the event of a mass arrest resulting from the strike struggle of the □□□□ Labor Union ○○ Automobile Branch”; ② it was unlawful for the police to surround the six union members, including Non-indicted Person 2, and prevent them from moving, and despite the victim’s explicit objections, the police again arrested Non-indicted Person 1 in the same manner as the said six union members, and only after the victim continued to object did the Defendant then inform Non-indicted Person 1 of the reasons for arrest and the right to appoint counsel, etc., and upon this, the victim repeatedly requested the Defendant, while identifying himself as an attorney, to allow him to interview Non-indicted Person 1; ③ the police did not verify with Non-indicted Person 1 whether he wished to appoint or meet the victim as counsel; and ④ Non-indicted Person 1 was not versed in law and did not know the victim, who was an attorney, personally, so he would have found it difficult to first ask the victim to appoint counsel or request an interview on the premise that he had the right of visitation and communication as a suspect under the Criminal Procedure Act, and thus there was a need for the victim, who was an attorney and had received the above official letter from the labor union, to take the lead in requesting an interview; on the basis of such circumstances, the victim, as a “person intending to become defense counsel” for Non-indicted Person 1, was in a position to have the right of visitation and communication prescribed by Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and therefore the Defendant could not restrict the victim from interviewing Non-indicted Person 1.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles set forth above, the above determination of the court below is persuasive, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel or a person intending to become defense counsel.\\n\\n4. On the grounds of appeal concerning whether the limits of the exercise of the right of visitation and communication were exceeded\\n\\nThe right of visitation and communication of defense counsel or a person intending to become defense counsel must be exercised within a range that does not infringe the original purpose of the physical restraint system; therefore, where defense counsel or a person intending to become defense counsel seeks to interview a defendant or suspect beyond the limits that can realistically be guaranteed in light of the specific temporal and spatial circumstances, this does not constitute a proper exercise of the right of visitation and communication and cannot be permitted. However, in determining that the right of visitation and communication has exceeded such limits and cannot be permitted, caution must be exercised so that the essential content of the right to receive assistance of counsel, which is a fundamental constitutional right of a person under physical restraint, is not infringed (see Supreme Court Order of January 31, 2007, 2006MO657, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below determined that: ① because the victim continuously objected to the Defendant, stating that the arrest procedure for Non-indicted Person 1 was unlawful, and yet no measures were taken, it was necessary to interview Non-indicted Person 1 as soon as possible, accurately ascertain the details of the case, and devise subsequent response measures; ② on the other hand, in light of the on-site situation at the time of Non-indicted Person 1’s arrest, there was no concern that a standoff would arise between the labor union and management, or that a physical clash would occur between union members and riot police officers, and since there were no circumstances such as the victim joining other union members to cause Non-indicted Person 1 to flee or to destroy evidence at the scene of the offense, it could not be said that the Defendant’s acceptance of the victim’s request to interview Non-indicted Person 1 at the arrest scene would be contrary to the original purpose of the arrest system; and ③ if there are circumstances suggesting that an arrest by investigative authorities did not comply with the procedure prescribed by the Criminal Procedure Act, a person intending to become defense counsel for the arrested suspect should be able to point out the illegality and lodge an objection during the series of arrest procedures; and on the basis of such circumstances, the victim’s continued requests to the Defendant for an interview constituted an exercise of the right of visitation and communication within the range that does not infringe the original purpose of the physical restraint system, as a person intending to become defense counsel for the arrested Non-indicted Person 1, and did not exceed its limits.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles set forth above, the above determination of the court below is persuasive, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the limits of and deviation from the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel or a person intending to become defense counsel.\\n\\n5. On the grounds of appeal concerning whether the arrest of the victim was lawful\\n\\nThe offense of obstruction of official duties prescribed in Article 136 of the Criminal Act is established only where the public official’s execution of duties is lawful, and lawful execution of official duties here refers not only to the act falling within the public official’s abstract authority but also to the satisfaction of the legal requirements and methods concerning specific execution of duties. If a police officer, without satisfying the requirements for arresting a person caught in flagrante delicto, nevertheless arrested such person by force, this cannot be regarded as lawful execution of official duties (see Supreme Court Decision of May 26, 2011, 2011DO3682, etc.).\\n\\nThe court below determined that: ① the victim repeatedly stated that he was an attorney while holding his attorney identification card in his hand, and lawfully requested an interview as a person intending to become defense counsel for Non-indicted Person 1 who had been arrested, but the Defendant gave no response thereto, and the riot police officers took Non-indicted Person 1 away while surrounding him and put him into a van; ② when the victim continued to request an interview with Non-indicted Person 1 and blocked the van in which the arrested Non-indicted Person 1 was riding, the riot police officers surrounded and pushed the victim, causing a physical scuffle to begin, and in the midst thereof, even though the victim did not exert any appreciable physical force, the Defendant arrested the victim as a person caught in flagrante delicto merely 2 or 3 minutes after receiving the request for an interview; and ③ not only does it appear that the Defendant could have accepted the victim’s request for an interview at the arrest scene, but even if he thought that an interview at the arrest scene would be difficult, it was possible to take appropriate measures, including explaining the on-site situation to the victim and guiding him that an interview could be permitted later at a police station or other place; based on such circumstances, the court below determined that the victim could not be regarded as a person caught in flagrante delicto who obstructed the execution of official duties concerning arrest and escort by the police, and that the Defendant, a police public official, arrested the victim without satisfying the requirements for arresting a person caught in flagrante delicto was, even if outwardly it fell within the scope of police duties, substantively lacking the legal requirements, necessity, and substantiality of the performance of duties, and thus was not lawful execution of official duties. In addition, according to the record, when the Defendant received a request for interviews with the six union members, including Non-indicted Person 2, he did not arrest the victim as a person caught in flagrante delicto, but upon receiving a request for an interview with Non-indicted Person 1, he arrested the victim as a person caught in flagrante delicto who obstructed the police’s execution of official duties concerning arrest and escort, even though the victim did not exert any appreciable physical force, and it can be seen that the victim was indicted not on the theory that he obstructed official duties in the course of requesting an interview with Non-indicted Person 1, but on the theory that he obstructed official duties in the course of requesting interviews with the six persons, including Non-indicted Person 2, and it is not even clear whether the victim’s act of requesting interviews with the six persons, including Non-indicted Person 2, was stated as the reason for arrest at the scene at the time of arresting a person caught in flagrante delicto.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles set forth above, the above determination of the court below that the Defendant’s arrest of the victim as a person caught in flagrante delicto could not be regarded as lawful execution of official duties is persuasive, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of obstruction of official duties and the requirements for arresting a person caught in flagrante delicto.\\n\\n6. On the grounds of appeal concerning the presence or absence of intent for abuse of authority, etc.\\n\\nAlthough there is considerable room for discretion in the judgment by a prosecutor or judicial police officer, etc. as to whether the requirements for arresting a person caught in flagrante delicto are met, if, even in light of the circumstances at the time of arrest, the judgment by a prosecutor or judicial police officer, etc. on whether those requirements are satisfied has manifestly lost rationality in light of the rules of experience, such arrest should be deemed unlawful. And because criminal intent includes not only definite intent but also so-called dolus eventualis, i.e., awareness of the occurrence of the result and an intention to tolerate it, if the Defendant, as a judicial police officer performing duties concerning detention and arrest, could sufficiently know, by considering the circumstances at the time of arrest, that the arrest requirements were not satisfied, while making a judgment that had not manifestly lost rationality in light of the rules of experience, yet arrested a person and obstructed the exercise of rights while recognizing that this exceeded the scope of his discretion and tolerating such result, the offense of arrest by abuse of authority and the offense of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of authority are established.\\n\\nThe court below determined that: ① the Defendant had worked for more than 20 years as a police officer performing duties concerning detention and arrest, and at the time of arresting Non-indicted Person 1, he was assigned the role of scene commander, so he appears to have been familiar with the procedures for detention and arrest; ② the Defendant could sufficiently know that the arrest procedure for Non-indicted Person 1 did not comply with the requirements for arresting a person caught in flagrante delicto prescribed by the Criminal Procedure Act, and he knew that the victim, who was an attorney, had pointed out the problems with the arrest procedure for Non-indicted Person 1 and requested an interview; and ③ although it is not common to arrest an attorney who requests an interview as a person caught in flagrante delicto for obstruction of official duties, the Defendant, unlike when he had previously arrested other union members, arrested the victim as a person caught in flagrante delicto for obstruction of official duties without going through procedures such as reporting the situation to his superiors and waiting for instructions; based on such circumstances, the court below determined that the Defendant, as a judicial police officer who is a public official performing duties concerning detention and arrest, abused his authority to arrest the victim and obstruct the victim’s exercise of rights, and that the Defendant was at least aware by dolus eventualis that the arrest of the victim lacked the legal requirements, necessity, and substantiality of the performance of duties. The court below also rejected the Defendant’s assertion that, because he acted in accordance with higher-level instructions at the time he arrested the victim, there was no possibility of expecting lawful conduct, on the ground that such instructions merely confirmed the principle of sternly responding to obstruction of official duties, and that the Defendant, as scene commander, arrested the victim as a person caught in flagrante delicto under his own responsibility.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles set forth above and the record, it cannot be said that the above determination of the court below contains any error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning intent for abuse of authority, the possibility of expecting lawful conduct, or grounds for retrial, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n7. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as follows by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

Determination on the Prosecutor’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. The part concerning the preparation of the document titled “Background of the Establishment Preparation of the F Special Investigation Committee and Response Measures” by Defendant A (hereinafter referred to as “the Background and Response Measures Document”)\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in its judgment, found this part of the charged facts not guilty, on the ground that the evidence submitted by the Prosecutor alone was insufficient to establish that Defendant A had been involved in the preparation of the Background and Response Measures Document.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in the lower court’s above determination, such as exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience without fully conducting the necessary examination, or misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the relationship of conspiracy, etc.\\n\\nb. The part concerning the preparation of the Background and Response Measures Document by Defendants B and E\\n\\n1) The lower court’s determination\\n\\nThe lower court, for the following reasons, found this part of the charged facts not guilty.\\n\\nThe act by Defendants B and E of causing G, H, and I to prepare the Background and Response Measures Document externally constitutes an abuse of the authority falling within the general official authority of Secretary J or Secretary K; however, Defendants B and E merely had G, H, and I, who were the persons in charge of the practical work, perform factual acts assisting the execution of their official duties, and therefore does not fall within “when a person is made to do something he is under no duty to do.”\\n\\n2) The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\na) The part of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights against G\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in the lower court’s finding of not guilty on the part of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights against G, a public official
