(a) In the offense of indecent act by force, “force” includes not only assault and threat that, in light of the object or content of physical force, do not constitute the “assault or intimidation” of the offense of forcible indecent act, but also the use of social, economic, or political status or authority that is sufficient to suppress or confuse the other party’s free will.
(b) Even if a child or adolescent engages in conduct that outwardly appears to be a sexual determination or consent, if it is due to another person’s deception or the use of a distorted relationship of trust, it is difficult to evaluate this as an exercise of the child or adolescent’s complete sexual self-determination.
(c) In the offense of rape by deceit, the object into which the victim falls into mistake, misconception, or ignorance is the act of sexual intercourse itself, not the motive that led to the act of sexual intercourse or elements such as monetary or non-monetary consideration linked to the act of sexual intercourse.
(d) “A person who is under one’s protection or supervision due to work, employment, or any other relationship” as provided in Article 10(1) of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (“Indecent Act by Abuse of Occupational Authority, etc.”) includes not only a person who receives protection or supervision within the workplace or is in a situation of de facto protection or supervision, but also a person within the scope of influence in the hiring process.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2015DO9436]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Background of the case and issues\\n\\na. Summary of the facts charged\\n\\n1) In mid-July 2014, the Defendant falsely introduced himself to the 14-year-old victim, whom he had come to know through a smartphone chat application, as “○○○, a second-year high school student,” and agreed to date the victim through chat.\\n\\n2) In early August 2014, the Defendant lied to the victim, saying, “In fact, there is a woman who likes me (○○○) and is stalking me, but she is obsessed with me so much that it is very hard. I want to die. Shall we just break up?”, and told the victim to the effect that “if you want to drive away the stalking woman, you should have sexual relations with my senior.”\\n\\n3) The victim, fearing a breakup with the Defendant, accepted the Defendant’s proposal, and the Defendant, while posing as if he were ○○○’s senior, had sexual intercourse with the victim.\\n\\n4) In this way, the Defendant had sexual intercourse with the victim, a child and juvenile, by deception.\\n\\nb. The judgment of the court below\\n\\nThe court below, as to the meaning of deception in the offense of sexual intercourse by deception, held in line with Supreme Court Decision dated 2001. 12. 24., 2001DO5074, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “prior precedents”), that “it means that the actor, for the purpose of sexual intercourse, causes the other party to be mistaken, confused, or ignorant, and then achieves the purpose of sexual intercourse by using the other party’s such mental state; and the misapprehension, mistake, or ignorance here refers to a misapprehension, mistake, or ignorance as to the act of sexual intercourse itself, not to a misapprehension, mistake, or ignorance as to other conditions that are not recognized as having an inseparable connection with the act of sexual intercourse.” Accordingly, it found that the victim had merely been deceived by the Defendant as to other conditions not recognized as inseparably related to the act of sexual intercourse, and held the facts charged in this case not guilty on the ground that the Defendant’s act of sexual intercourse was not by deception as prescribed as a punishable offense under the Criminal Act, etc.\\n\\nc. Issue in this case\\n\\nWhether the prior precedents, which interpreted the meaning of deception in the offense of sexual intercourse by deception punishable under the Criminal Act, etc., as above, can be maintained is the issue that determines the correctness of the judgment of the court below. Below, by comprehensively considering the legislative history of the offense of sexual intercourse by deception and the meaning of the exercise of the right to sexual self-determination, we determine whether the prior precedents can be maintained.\\n\\n2. Legislative history of the offense of sexual intercourse by deception\\n\\na. The punitive provision for sexual intercourse by deception began with the Criminal Act enacted in 1953. The enacted Criminal Act provided this as part of Book II, Chapter 32, Crimes concerning Chastity. At that time, the statutory punishment was lighter than that for rape and even lighter than that for indecent act by compulsion, and among them, the offense of sexual intercourse under pretense of marriage, etc. was also provided as applicable to “women with no habitual lewdness.” Thus, it appears that, at the time of the enacted Criminal Act, the offense of sexual intercourse by deception was perceived as a subsidiary type of crime with lesser punishability than rape and indecent act by compulsion, while having the legislative purpose of protecting women’s chastity.\\n\\nb. Thereafter, by the amendment of the Criminal Act on 1995. 12. 29., the expression “Crimes concerning Chastity” was deleted from the heading of Book II, Chapter 32. In addition, as the offense of sexual intercourse under pretense of marriage, etc., which had provided even women with no habitual lewdness as subjects, was abolished in reflection of the Constitutional Court’s decision of unconstitutionality dated 2009. 11. 26., 2008HEONBA58, etc. and its purport, the subject of the offense of sexual intercourse by deception under the Criminal Act was limited to persons particularly vulnerable to sexual violence offenses, such as minors, persons with diminished mental or physical capacity, and persons under protection or supervision.\\n\\nc. In special criminal statutes as well, provisions on the offense of sexual intercourse by deception targeting persons particularly vulnerable to sexual violence offenses were newly established. For girls under 13 years of age, the former Act on the Punishment of Sexual Crimes and Protection of Victims Thereof [among them, matters concerning the punishment of sexual crimes were separated and provided in the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Sexual Crimes Punishment Act”), enacted on 2010. 4. 15.] was amended on 1997. 8. 22.; for female juveniles, punitive provisions were established upon the enactment on 2000. 2. 3. of the former Act on the Protection of Children and Juveniles Against Sexual Abuse (the title was amended to the Act on the Protection of Children and Juveniles Against Sexual Abuse; hereinafter all referred to as the “Child and Juvenile Sex Protection Act”); and for women with physical or mental disabilities, punitive provisions were established by the amendment of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act on 2011. 11. 17. in each case, with a fixed term of imprisonment of at least 5 years prescribed as the statutory punishment. Thereafter, the statutory punishment for the offense of sexual intercourse by deception targeting persons under 13 and children and juveniles was increased to life imprisonment. This prescribed a heavier punishment than the offense of rape under the Criminal Act.\\n\\nd. Taking together the amendment history of the offense of sexual intercourse by deception as above and the contents of the law around 2014, which applies to this case, unlike in the past, today the offense of sexual intercourse by deception may be evaluated as having been provided as a crime that protects children and juveniles, minors, persons with diminished mental or physical capacity, persons under protection or supervision, persons with disabilities, etc., who are particularly vulnerable to sexual violence offenses, and that has independent punishability comparable to rape, etc., thereby intending to strongly punish the actor.\\n\\n3. Meaning of the exercise of the right to sexual self-determination\\n\\na. Article 10 of the Constitution provides: “All citizens shall enjoy human worth and dignity and have the right to pursue happiness. It shall be the duty of the State to confirm and guarantee the inviolable fundamental human rights of individuals.” The right of self-determination is a right protected by the personal rights and right to pursue happiness of individuals provided in Article 10 of the Constitution (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision dated 2009. 5. 21., 2009DA17417).\\nThe right to sexual self-determination is understood as the right of each person, on the basis of his or her own chosen view of life, etc., to independently establish sexual notions within the social community and, accordingly, to select the other party and have sexual relations on his or her own responsibility pursuant to sexual decisions made by oneself in the sphere of private life (see Constitutional Court full bench Decision dated 2002. 10. 31., 99HEONBA40, etc.). This includes both the positive aspect of the right to decide what sexual conduct one wishes to engage in and the negative aspect of the right to refuse unwanted sexual conduct, and crimes of rape and indecent acts, including the offense of sexual intercourse by deception, consist in infringing the negative aspect of the right to sexual self-determination (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2019. 6. 13., 2019DO3341).\\n\\nb. The victim in this case is 14 years old and thus falls under the category of a child or juvenile under the Child and Juvenile Sex Protection Act, which refers to persons under 19 years of age.\\nThe State and society bear various duties to protect children and juveniles. The State implements policies for the improvement of juveniles’ welfare (Article 34(4) of the Constitution) and bears the duty to provide primary and secondary education (Article 8 of the Framework Act on Education). The same applies in the judicial sphere: a person with parental authority must protect and raise minors (Article 913 of the Civil Act), and a legal act performed by a minor without the consent of the legal representative may, in principle, be rescinded without limitation as to the grounds therefor (Article 5 of the Civil Act).\\n\\nThe courts also have, in cases where the victim is a child or juvenile, proceeded on the premise that a child or juvenile is a subject that must be specially protected. The Supreme Court has held, in determining whether conduct constitutes sexual abuse against a child under the Child Welfare Act, that even if the child did not expressly indicate opposition, it must be examined whether this is attributable to the child’s lack of ability to exercise the right to sexual self-determination and protect himself or herself (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2015. 7. 9., 2013DO7787), and held that, in the offense of selling a child under the Child Welfare Act, guilt is established even if the child himself or herself consented (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2015. 8. 27., 2015DO6480). The same purport is reflected in the holding that, even if a child or juvenile consents to the production of obscene material targeting himself or herself, it in principle constitutes the offense of producing child and juvenile pornography under the Child and Juvenile Sex Protection Act (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2015. 2. 12., 2014DO11501, 2014JEONDO197).\\n\\nThe reason for protecting children and juveniles in this way is that children and juveniles, due to social and cultural constraints, etc., are not yet in a position to fully exercise the right to self-determination, and, due to a lack of cognitive, psychological, and relational resources, are in a position where they have difficulty defending themselves from sexual infringement or exploitation by others. In addition, since children and juveniles are in the process of forming sexual values and completing sexual health, sexual infringement or exploitation against children and juveniles may have serious and lasting adverse effects on their pursuit of mental and physical health related to sexuality and on the formation and development of autonomous personality. Therefore, even if a child or juvenile engages in words or conduct that outwardly appear to be sexual decisions or consent, if such conduct is induced by another person’s deception or by the exploitation of a distorted relationship of trust, it is difficult to evaluate it as the exercise of the child or juvenile’s full right to sexual self-determination.\\n\\nc. Apart from that, minors, persons with diminished mental or physical capacity, persons under protection or supervision, persons with disabilities, etc., whom the offense of sexual intercourse by deception protects, also do not essentially differ from the above-mentioned children and juveniles in that, due to age, disability of mental functions, dependent relationships between the actor and the victim, etc., they find it difficult to defend themselves from external influences, including the actor, and their internal mental processes are likely to be distorted in the process of exercising the right to sexual self-determination.\\n\\n4. Meaning of deception in the offense of sexual intercourse by deception\\n\\na. “Deception” means causing the victim to be mistaken, confused, or ignorant in order to accomplish the actor’s objective and using that state. Taking together the concept of such deception, the legislative attitude as seen above, namely, protecting persons particularly vulnerable to sexual violence offenses and strongly punishing the actor, and the circumstances that it is difficult to expect full exercise of the right to sexual self-determination due to the victim’s cognitive, psychological, and relational characteristics, if the actor, for the purpose of sexual intercourse, causes the victim to be mistaken, confused, or ignorant and achieves the purpose of sexual intercourse by using the victim’s such mental state, a causal relationship between deception and the act of sexual intercourse may be recognized, and therefore the offense of sexual intercourse by deception is established. If sexual conduct is performed on the basis of a distorted sexual decision, whether the point at which the distortion occurred was the sexual conduct itself or the motive leading to the sexual conduct is not a core matter in that the infringement of the right to sexual self-determination has occurred in either case. The object into which the victim is led to be mistaken, confused, or ignorant may be the act of sexual intercourse itself, or the motive leading to the act of sexual intercourse, or an element such as monetary or non-monetary consideration connected with the act of sexual intercourse.\\n\\nb. However, the offense of sexual intercourse by deception is not established merely because the actor engaged in deceptive words or conduct; rather, the content of such deceptive words or conduct must include circumstances sufficient to constitute an important motive for the victim’s decision to engage in sexual intercourse, so that it may be evaluated that the victim did not exercise his or her own voluntary right to sexual self-determination. In determining such causal relationship, various circumstances, such as the victim’s age and relationship with the actor, the course leading to the offense, and the circumstances at and before and after the offense, must be comprehensively considered.\\n\\nc. Meanwhile, the ability to exercise sexual self-determination of children and juveniles, minors, persons with diminished mental or physical capacity, persons under protection or supervision, persons with disabilities, etc., who are protected by the offense of sexual intercourse by deception, differs individually depending on their age, developmental process, environment, degree of disability of intelligence or mental functions, etc.; therefore, in determining whether the conduct constitutes deception causally related to the act of sexual intercourse, the position and perspective of the victim placed in the specific circumstances of the offense must be sufficiently considered, and causation should not be easily denied from the viewpoint of an adult with ordinary or average judgment capacity or of a peer who has received sufficient protection and education.\\n\\nd. On the other hand, unlike the above, the prior precedents—Supreme Court Decisions dated 2001. 12. 24., 2001DO5074; 2002. 7. 12., 2002DO2029; 2007. 9. 21., 2007DO6190; 2012. 9. 27., 2012DO9119; 2014. 9. 4., 2014DO8423, 2014JEONDO151, etc.—held to the effect that the misapprehension, confusion, or ignorance caused by the actor to the other party for the purpose of sexual intercourse refers to misapprehension, confusion, or ignorance as to the act of sexual intercourse itself, and not to misapprehension, confusion, or ignorance as to other conditions not recognized as having an inseparable connection with the act of sexual intercourse. Since those holdings are inconsistent with this judgment, we decide to modify them to that extent.\\n\\n5. Judgment\\n\\na. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the lawfully admitted evidence, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n1) The Defendant, a 36-year-old man, posed as ○○○, a second-year high school student, and came to date the 14-year-old victim through a chat application.\\n\\n2) In the course of that, the Defendant posed as a woman stalking ○○○ and taunted the victim by saying that he too liked ○○○ and that if one liked ○○○ one had to do anything, while also posing as ○○○ and asking the victim to have sexual intercourse with his senior at the request of the woman stalking him, saying that he was suffering so much because of that woman and asking that, if the victim did not want to break up with him, she should have sexual intercourse with his senior as requested by that woman. Such taunting and request were repeated several times.\\n\\n3) Ultimately, the victim, fearing that she would break up with ○○○, agreed to have sexual intercourse with ○○○’s senior, and for that purpose took an express bus at dawn and moved to the location designated by the Defendant. The Defendant had sexual intercourse with the victim while posing as ○○○’s senior.\\n\\n4) The victim, fearing that her parents would learn of these facts, reported the matter to the police with the help of a counseling center only after 12 days had passed since the incident, and thereafter lived apart from her parents in a youth protection facility in another city.\\n\\nb. The above facts are examined in light of the legal principles discussed above. The victim, a child or juvenile of only 14 years of age, was subjected for a considerable period of time to provocative taunts and requests within a fictitious situation created by the 36-year-old Defendant. In addition, taking the victim’s attitude and conduct before and after this case as a whole, there is room to view that the victim did not receive sufficient protection and upbringing from her parents. These circumstances indicate that it was difficult for the victim at that time to make a fully sound decision. In such a situation, the victim, deceived by the Defendant, had sexual intercourse with the Defendant, who had disguised himself as ○○○’s senior, under the mistaken belief that only having sexual intercourse with ○○○’s senior was the way to drive away the woman stalking ○○○ and continue a romantic relationship with ○○○. Had the victim not fallen into such misapprehension, she would not have engaged in sexual conduct with the Defendant. The situation into which the victim was misled appears to have been an important motive for the victim’s decision to engage in sexual conduct with the Defendant, and it is difficult to regard this as the exercise of voluntary and serious sexual self-determination. Therefore, since the Defendant, for the purpose of sexual intercourse, caused the victim to be mistaken, confused, or ignorant and used that mental state to have sexual intercourse with the victim, the Defendant’s act of sexual intercourse can be evaluated as having been by deception.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below, by contrast, found the facts charged in this case not guilty for the reasons stated above. In such judgment of the court below, there is an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the offense of sexual intercourse by deception. The prosecutor’s assertion of the grounds of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as set forth in the order. This judgment includes supplementary opinions by Justice Min Yu-suk and Justice Noh Jeong-hee.\\n\\n7. Supplementary opinion of Justice Min Yu-suk and Justice Noh Jeong-hee\\n\\nIn light of the recent legislative amendments related to the issue in this case, we would like to supplement the meaning of the en banc judgment.\\n\\na. The Criminal Act, the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act, and the Child and Juvenile Sex Protection Act, which regulate sexual violence crimes, have been dynamically amended, and in particular, the tendency to strengthen punishment and protect victims in sexual violence crimes committed by means short of violence or intimidation is clearly confirmed. This stemmed from the awareness that sexual violence crimes could not be properly addressed within the traditional framework of thought, which assumed them to involve violence or intimidation that rendered the victim incapable of resistance or made resistance extremely difficult, that is, physical coercive force by which the victim’s will could be completely overpowered.\\n\\nBy the amendment of the Criminal Act on 2018. 10. 16., where a person under protection and supervision through work or employment was raped by deception, etc., the upper limit of the statutory punishment was increased from 5 years to 7 years in terms of imprisonment, and where a detained person was raped, the upper limit of the statutory punishment was increased from 7 years to 10 years. The Sexual Crimes Punishment Act punishes acts of indecent assault against the same protected subjects, and by the same amendment date, the upper limit of the statutory punishment was increased from 2 years or 3 years to 3 years or 5 years in terms of imprisonment.\\n\\nThis may be understood in the sense that it was unjust that power-based sexual violence cases, which are continuously committed within workplaces and organizations by means of decision-making authority, authority to give work-related instructions, etc., had to be punished with relatively light penalties despite their grave adverse effects on both individual victims and society.\\n\\nb. Of particular note is the legislative amendment concerning the protection of the sexuality of children and juveniles between 13 and 15 years of age. With the amendment of the Child and Juvenile Sex Protection Act on 2019. 1. 15., acts by a person aged 19 or older of having sexual intercourse with or indecently assaulting the above children and juveniles by exploiting their state of necessity were punished (Article 8-2 of the Child and Juvenile Sex Protection Act), and then, with the amendment of the Criminal Act on 2020. 5. 19., if a person aged 19 or older had sexual intercourse with or indecently assaulted a child or juvenile between 13 and 15 years of age, punishment was imposed regardless of whether, and to what extent, the means involved coercion (Article 305(2) of the Criminal Act). The victim in this case is 14 years old and the Defendant is 36 years old, so under the amended law above, the act is subject to punishment regardless of the means used.\\n\\nAs already pointed out, amid the widespread social and cultural trend of sexual openness and sexual commodification, the risk of sexual exploitation against children and juveniles is increasing; yet, because children and juveniles do not sufficiently know the social norms relating to the selection of sexual conduct and its counterpart and the mutual reactions of sexual conduct, it is difficult for them to fully exercise the right to sexual self-determination or defend themselves. Even without violence, intimidation, deception, or force, they sometimes have no choice but to engage in sexual conduct in situations where multiple complex factors beyond their will intervene, and as a result they become targets of sexual conduct that exploits, abuses, and harms them. Based on an understanding of their sexual relationships and decision-making, even if they appear to have consented to sexual conduct, it is necessary to recognize the fact that they may suffer exploitative and abusive sexual harm, and to strengthen the legal safety net for children and juveniles.\\n\\nIn reality, many sexual violence victims, especially child and juvenile victims, even though they have suffered sexual violence, give up reporting the victimization because they feel guilty, believing they must have done something blameworthy, worry that those around them may learn of it, and find it difficult to distinguish whether the harm they suffered constitutes a crime, and think that even if they report it nothing will change. Even if the specific manner of coercion cannot be specifically identified, and even if there is merely the circumstance that they outwardly consented to sexual conduct, their sexual harm must not be disregarded. There is also a need to prevent cases in which children and juveniles engage in prostitution only to suffer further sexual exploitation after being threatened or otherwise exploited on that pretext. The above provisions reflect such criminal policy considerations.\\n\\nAs stated above, these provisions are in step with the normative judgment that acts which skillfully exploit the weak vulnerability of victims susceptible to sexual violence offenses and ultimately infringe the victims’ right to self-determination constitute serious sexual violence crimes.\\n\\nUltimately, the above legislative measures are premised on the recognition that even if a person under 16 years of age outwardly appears to have consented to sexual conduct, it cannot easily be regarded as the exercise of genuine sexual self-determination. Therefore, it is appropriate to approach sexual conduct by persons under 16 years of age not from the aspect of formally respecting the exercise of the right to sexual self-determination, but from the aspect of whether protected sexuality has been infringed.\\n\\nThe above is the supplementary opinion."}

{"[2020DO12419]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. The facts charged and the judgment of the court below\\n\\na. The facts charged in this case are that the Defendant, around 2018. 3. 14., while engaging in a video call on a mobile phone with the child victim (female, 14 years old), told the child victim, “I want to see your breasts,” thereby causing the child victim to show her breasts on the video call screen, and, while looking at them, showed an act of the Defendant masturbating; and, in addition thereto, by the same method, the Defendant committed sexual abuse against the child victim a total of 5 times from around that time until around 2018. 4.\\n\\nb. The court below, after invoking the legal principles concerning whether an act constitutes sexual abuse, found that the first-instance court’s determination that the Defendant’s conduct could not readily be concluded to amount to “sexual abuse” as sexual violence or cruel treatment that could harm the child victim’s health and welfare or impede normal development, on the ground, inter alia, that the child victim did not appear to lack maturity in exercising the right to sexual self-determination, was justified. In particular, the court below pointed out that the child victim had engaged in sexual intercourse with the Defendant by agreement prior to this case, and that there were no circumstances from which it could be deemed that the video call in this case was contrary to the child victim’s will.\\n\\n2. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\na. As the court below pointed out, whether an act constitutes sexual abuse must be objectively determined in accordance with the sound common sense of the relevant society of the time, by comprehensively considering specific circumstances such as the intent, sex, and age of the actor and the child victim, whether the child victim has acquired sexual values and judgment ability sufficient to properly exercise the right to sexual self-determination, the relationship between the actor and the child victim, the circumstances leading to the act, the specific manner of the act, and the impact that the act may have on the child victim’s personality development and mental health (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2013DO7787, rendered 2015. 7. 9.).\\n\\nHowever, the part of the court below’s determination that, based on the child victim’s sexual intercourse with the Defendant and the child victim’s words and conduct at the time of the sexual intercourse and in this case, the child victim exercised the right to sexual self-determination, is not readily sustainable.\\n\\nb. The State and society bear various duties of protection toward children and juveniles. Courts have determined cases in the premise that, where a child or juvenile is the victim, the child or juvenile is a subject especially in need of protection. In determining whether an act constitutes sexual abuse of a child under the Child Welfare Act, even if the child did not expressly object, it must be examined whether this was attributable to a lack of ability to protect himself or herself by exercising the right to sexual self-determination (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2013DO7787). In the offense of sale of a child under the Child Welfare Act, even if the child himself or herself consented, guilt is established (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO6480, rendered 2015. 8. 27.). Even if a child or juvenile consented to the production of obscene materials targeting himself or herself, in principle, it constitutes the offense of producing child and juvenile pornography under the Act on the Protection of Children and Juveniles against Sexual Abuse (see Supreme Court Decisions 2014DO11501, 2014JEONDO197, rendered 2015. 2. 12.).\\n\\nChildren and juveniles are still in a position where it is difficult for them to fully exercise the right to sexual self-determination due to social and cultural constraints and the like, and, owing to a lack of cognitive, psychological, and relational resources, are in a position where it is difficult for them to defend themselves against another’s sexual侵害 or exploitation. In addition, since children and juveniles are in the process of forming sexual values and completing sexual health, acts of sexual侵害 or exploitation against children and juveniles may have serious and lasting adverse effects on children and juveniles in pursuing mental and physical health related to sex and in forming and developing autonomous personalities. Accordingly, even if a child or juvenile has engaged in conduct outwardly appearing to be a sexual decision or consent, if that was caused by another’s deception or the use of a distorted relationship of trust, it is difficult to evaluate it as an exercise of the child’s or juvenile’s full right to sexual self-determination (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2015DO9436, rendered 2020. 8. 27.).\\n\\nc. The court below should have carefully determined, on the basis of the foregoing legal principles, whether the child victim had sexual values and judgment ability sufficient to properly exercise the right to sexual self-determination, but it, by relying only on the circumstances stated in its reasoning, determined that the conduct did not constitute sexual abuse on the premise that the child victim exercised the right to sexual self-determination; thus, the court below erred by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning sexual abuse prescribed in Article 17, Item 2 of the Child Welfare Act. The military prosecutor’s ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the lower court judgment is reversed, and the case is transferred to the Seoul High Court, a court of coordinate jurisdiction with the court below, for retrial and redetermination; and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2020DO5646]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nArticle 10 of the Act on Special Cases concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes is a penal provision concerning “indecent acts by abuse of occupational authority, etc.,” and paragraph (1) provides that “A person who commits an indecent act by deception or force against a person under his or her protection or supervision by reason of work, employment, or any other relationship shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 3 years or by a fine not exceeding 15 million won.” The term “a person under his or her protection or supervision by reason of work, employment, or any other relationship” includes not only a person who is protected or supervised in the workplace or is in a situation where he or she is in fact protected or supervised (see Supreme Court Decision 74DO1519, decided February 10, 1976, on indecent intercourse by abuse of occupational authority, etc. under Article 303 of the Criminal Act; Supreme Court Decision 2001DO4085, decided October 30, 2001), but also a person who is within the scope of influence in the hiring process.\\n\\nAnd the term “force” means force sufficient to suppress the victim’s free will, and regardless of whether it is physical or intangible, it may include not only violence or intimidation but also the use of social, economic, or political status or authority; it is not necessary that the victim’s free will actually be suppressed in fact. Whether an indecent act was committed by force must be determined by comprehensively considering various circumstances, such as the nature and degree of the force exerted, the type of status or authority held by the actor, the victim’s age, the relationship between the actor and the victim, the circumstances leading to the act, the specific manner of the act, and the circumstances at the time of the offense (see Supreme Court Decision 97DO2506, decided January 23, 1998; Supreme Court Decision 2019DO2562, decided September 9, 2019, among others).\\n\\nThe court below, after finding as facts that the Defendant, who was the owner of a convenience store, conducted an interview with the victim, who had contacted him after seeing a part-time job recruitment advertisement, under the pretext of hiring, including confirming the victim’s intentions, and then lured the victim to the Defendant’s house and touched the victim’s genitals and made the victim touch the Defendant’s genitals, determined that the Defendant committed an indecent act against the victim by suppressing the victim’s free will through the use of the position of having hiring authority.\\n\\nConsidering the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the record, the lower court’s determination is proper based on the legal principles stated above. There is no error in the lower court’s determination in that it misapprehended the legal principles concerning “a person under his or her protection or supervision by reason of work, employment, or any other relationship” and “force,” as argued in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nAs the Defendant’s appeal is without merit, it is dismissed, and it is so adjudged as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning a review of the legality of arrest or detention is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, pursuant to case law)
A: With respect to a suspect subject to an emergency arrest, release on condition of payment of bail is not permitted.
B: Except where other important evidence is discovered, a suspect released through a review of the legality of arrest or detention may not be arrested or detained again for the same criminal facts.
C: Where, after being detained, a suspect is released on condition of payment of bail through a review of the legality of detention, the prosecutor may file an immediate appeal seeking revocation of the order of release on condition of payment of bail, so long as there remains practical benefit in such revocation.
D: If, at a review of the legality of detention, the suspect has no defense counsel, the court must appoint court-appointed counsel ex officio.
E: A defendant after the institution of public prosecution may not request a review of the legality of arrest or detention.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2014DO9089]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nAccording to the record, it can be seen that the court below reversed the judgment of the court of first instance and, after oral argument, rendered judgment again on the ground that the decision by the court of first instance for service by publication with respect to one Defendant was unlawful because it did not satisfy the requisite conditions, and that this constitutes a case where the litigation procedure violated laws and regulations and affected the judgment. Since, in accordance with such measures by the court below, the illegality arising from the violation of laws and regulations concerning the litigation procedure of the judgment of the court of first instance was remedied, the argument in this part of the grounds of appeal, to the effect of asserting the illegality of the judgment of the court of first instance before such remedy, cannot be accepted.\\n\\nAlso, the right to request a judicial review of detention is a right granted to a suspect who has been detained pursuant to Article 214-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and since a Defendant against whom an indictment has already been filed by a Prosecutor does not have such a right, even if the Defendant did not have the opportunity to undergo a review of the propriety of detention in the litigation procedure before the court below, this is in accordance with the Criminal Procedure Act and other relevant statutes and is therefore lawful. The argument in this part of the grounds of appeal also cannot be accepted.\\n\\nMeanwhile, under Article 383 subparagraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, an appeal on the ground of improper sentencing is permitted only in cases where the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or detention for not less than 10 years has been imposed, so in this case, in which a lighter punishment than that was imposed on the Defendant, the argument to the effect that the determination of punishment is improper does not constitute a lawful ground of appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as per the Disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices in charge."}
{"[97MO21]": "The decision of the lower court is reversed, and the case is remanded to the Full Bench of the Changwon District Court, Main Office."}
{"[97MO21]": "The original decision is reversed, and the case is remanded to the Collegiate Division of the Changwon District Court, Main Office."}

question: B told A to steal liquor, and A entered a convenience store and stole one bottle of liquor. A few days later, A told his friend C that he had stolen the liquor because B had instigated him. The prosecutor jointly indicted A as a co-defendant for theft and B as a co-defendant for instigation of theft. Meanwhile, A stated in the investigative agency and in court that B had instigated him and caused him to form the intent to commit theft, and B denied the fact of instigation in the investigative agency and in court. Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are true (○) and those that are false (✕)? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents)
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DO1944]": "1. Regarding Defendant 1’s appeal\\n\\nAccording to the record, Defendant 1 appealed against the first-instance judgment solely on the ground of improper sentencing, but the appeal was dismissed in the lower court; in such a case, the said Defendant cannot, as a ground of appeal, raise a misapprehension of facts such as that alleged in the grounds of appeal, and furthermore, if the evidence adopted in the first-instance judgment, as upheld by the lower-court judgment, is examined in light of the record, it is sufficient to find the said Defendant guilty of the criminal act in this case, so the assertion in the grounds of appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\nAlso, comprehensively considering the motive and circumstances of Defendant 1’s criminal act in this case, ascertainable from the record, the method and result of the crime, the circumstances after the crime, and the said Defendant’s age, character, family relations, educational background, and career, etc., the sentence imposed by the lower court on the said Defendant is supportable, and it cannot be said that there are any remarkable grounds for finding that the lower court’s sentence is manifestly improper.\\n\\n2. Regarding Defendant 2’s appeal\\n\\nThe lower court, after comprehensively considering the evidence it adopted, found the facts as stated in the judgment, and then determined that Defendant 2, when the co-defendants in the lower court first conspired to commit the robbery in this case, joined the conspiracy by saying that he would help in the portions he could materially assist with, and that thereafter he also met with Defendant 1, etc. and discussed the crime and supported the purchase price of the equipment to be used in the crime in this case, and that in light of various circumstances such as the fact that he received a share of about KRW 67,000,000 out of the money taken from the victim, even though Defendant 2 did not directly commit the act of kidnapping the victim and taking the money, he falls under the category of a joint principal offender in robbery resulting in bodily injury; if examined in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the lower court’s above factual findings and determination are correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as a misapprehension of facts due to violation of the rules of evidence or a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning joint principal offenders.\\n\\nAnd since a co-defendant’s confession, with respect to which the defendant’s right of cross-examination is guaranteed, is no different from the case in which the person is examined as a witness, it has independent evidentiary admissibility (see Supreme Court Decisions 85DO691, decided June 25, 1985; 92DO917, decided July 28, 1992, etc.), and this is the same even if there is conflicting interest among the defendants, so the assertion in the grounds of appeal on this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and by crediting each a portion of the days of detention after the appeal against the principal sentence, the judgment is rendered as follows by unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2008DO8213]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. As to the Defendant’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nUnder Article 7(5) of the National Security Act, “purpose” does not require an active desire or definite awareness with respect to acts of praise, encouragement, etc.; conditional awareness suffices. Accordingly, the elements of the offense are satisfied if the person recognizes that, objectively viewed, the content of the expressive material contains subversiveness, such as aligning itself with the activities of an anti-state organization, and further has conditional awareness that such conduct may become a subversive act (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 2004DO3212 rendered on August 30, 2004), and, on the other hand, the selection and weighing of evidence and the finding of facts belong to the exclusive province of the trier of fact so long as they do not contravene logic and the rules of experience.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the lower court, by comprehensively considering the evidence it adopted, found, for the reasons stated in its judgment, that the Defendant had the purpose of subversion in acquiring and possessing the subversive expressive materials set forth in item 1(a) and item 1(a) of the facts charged in this case, and that the Defendant participated in a prohibited assembly and obstructed traffic as set forth in item 2 of the facts charged in this case; such finding is proper, and there is no error of law, such as misapprehension of the legal principle regarding subversive purpose or erroneous fact-finding in violation of the rules of evidence.\\n\\n2. As to the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nIf a document or writing in which a suspect’s statement is recorded or transcribed was prepared in the course of an investigation by an investigative agency, then even if it takes the form of a “statement protocol,” “statement,” or “voluntary statement,” it cannot be viewed differently from an interrogation protocol of a suspect (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 2004DO3588 rendered on September 3, 2004). On the other hand, the suspect’s right to remain silent guaranteed by the Criminal Procedure Act is based on the constitutional right against self-incrimination, namely, the right not to be compelled to make statements adverse to oneself in criminal proceedings; accordingly, when an investigative agency interrogates a suspect, if it fails to advise the suspect in advance of the right to remain silent, the suspect’s statement, even if voluntariness is recognized, must be denied admissibility as illegally obtained evidence (see, inter alia, Supreme Court Decision 92DO682 rendered on June 23, 1992).\\n\\nThe lower court found the following: on August 16, 2006, the Prosecutor requested an arrest warrant against Non-party 1 for violation of the National Security Act, and on August 18, 2006, obtained an arrest warrant from the Seoul Central District Court; the facts constituting the offense stated in that arrest warrant included that Non-party 1 had violated the National Security Act in conspiracy with accomplices linked to Non-party 1; thereafter, while conducting an interrogation of Non-party 1 as a suspect, the Prosecutor questioned Non-party 1 regarding the organization and activities with the accomplices, but Non-party 1 refused to make a statement; after indicting Non-party 1 on September 12, 2006, for violation of the National Security Act, etc. while detained, the Prosecutor again summoned Non-party 1 on September 19, 2006, and, while questioning Non-party 1 regarding the organization and activities with the Defendant and other accomplices, prepared the above statement protocol in the form of a general statement protocol rather than in the form of an interrogation protocol of a suspect. The lower court then held that, even though the statement protocol for Non-party 1 took the form of a statement protocol, its content was substantially the same as an interrogation protocol of a suspect setting forth the suspect’s statement; moreover, as there is no basis in the record to find that the Prosecutor advised Non-party 1 in advance of the right to remain silent when hearing Non-party 1’s statement, even if voluntariness of the statement is recognized, it is inadmissible as illegally obtained evidence and cannot be used as evidence of the Defendant’s guilt; furthermore, based solely on the remaining evidence submitted by the Prosecutor, it is insufficient to find the above charged facts that the Defendant, in conspiracy with Non-party 2, Non-party 1, etc., disseminated Juche ideology in college districts around November 2005, formed a central leadership body of a nationwide single organization for cultivating Juche adherents, and, for that purpose, systematically produced and distributed Juche ideology study CDs, etc. in college districts while studying and discussing them, thereby praising and supporting subversive activities, and there is no other evidence sufficient to find the same.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the lower court’s factual findings and determination as above are proper and acceptable, and there is no error of law, such as misapprehension of the legal principle concerning admissibility of evidence.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and it is so adjudged, with the concurrence of all Justices participating, as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[2009DO1889]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. The portion concerning the facts charged against Defendant 1\\nArticle 312(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act applies not only where the interrogation protocol of a suspect prepared by an investigative agency other than the Prosecutor is used as evidence of guilt against the defendant concerned, but also where, against the defendant concerned, the interrogation protocol of another defendant or suspect in a co-perpetration relationship with the defendant concerned, prepared by an investigative agency other than the Prosecutor, is adopted as evidence of guilt (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2003DO7185 rendered on July 15, 2004 concerning Article 312(2) of the former Criminal Procedure Act before amendment by Act No. 8496 of June 1, 2007). Therefore, even if the interrogation protocol of a suspect prepared by an investigative agency other than the Prosecutor for a co-defendant in a co-perpetration relationship with the defendant concerned is acknowledged as duly established by the co-defendant’s in-court statement, if the defendant concerned denies the contents of the protocol at the trial hearing, its admissibility as evidence is denied. And in such a case, even if the co-defendant testified in court to the effect that, during the police investigation, he made a statement identical to the contents recorded in the interrogation protocol of the suspect, such testimony is merely to the effect that the original declarant, the co-defendant, acknowledges the authenticity of the police-prepared interrogation protocol of the suspect concerning himself, and thus is not to be separately recognized as having independent probative value apart from the above protocol; accordingly, insofar as the admissibility as evidence of the above protocol is denied for the reasons stated above, such testimony also cannot be used as evidence for a finding of guilt. The lower court’s determination to the same effect is proper, and the allegation in the grounds for final appeal that criticizes the lower court’s determination from a contrary view cannot be accepted.\\n\\nApart from this, even when the lower court’s evidentiary assessment process is examined in light of the record, there is no illegality in violation of the rules of evidence, and the allegation in the grounds for final appeal that criticizes the selection of evidence and fact-finding, matters within the exclusive authority of the lower court, cannot be accepted.\\n\\n2. The portion concerning the facts charged against Defendant 2\\nApart from this, even when the lower court’s evidentiary assessment process is examined in light of the record, there is no illegality in violation of the rules of evidence, and the allegation in the grounds for final appeal that criticizes the selection of evidence and fact-finding, matters within the exclusive authority of the lower court, cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeals are all dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2009DO6717]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Article 199(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “investigations may be conducted by the necessary inquiries to achieve their purpose; provided, however, that coercive dispositions shall be made only where specially provided for in this Act, and shall be made only within the minimum necessary extent,” thereby expressly stating the principle of non-compulsory investigation. Accordingly, when an investigator, in the course of an investigation, takes a suspect to an investigative agency, etc. in the form of obtaining the consent of the person concerned, even though the other party’s physical freedom is in fact restricted and he or she is placed in a state substantially similar to arrest, and there is no warrant and no other means to restrain such coercive accompaniment, voluntariness is not guaranteed institutionally, nor in reality; moreover, because it is still before the formal stage of arrest or detention, the various safeguards of rights that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act afford to a suspect under arrest or detention are not provided to the other party, and thus such practice is highly likely to produce results contrary to the principles of the Criminal Procedure Act. Therefore, it is appropriate to regard the accompaniment to an investigative agency, etc. as lawful only where it is objectively and clearly proven that the accompaniment was effected solely by the suspect’s voluntary will, such as where the investigator informed the suspect in advance that he or she could refuse the accompaniment, or where it is recognized that the suspect who accompanied the officer could at any time freely withdraw from the process of accompaniment or leave the place of accompaniment (see Supreme Court Decision 2006. 7. 6. rendered 2005DO6810).\\n\\nAlso, Article 308-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “evidence collected without following lawful procedure shall not be admissible as evidence,” and, as a matter of principle, evidence collected by an investigative agency without following the procedures prescribed by the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act cannot be used as evidence for finding guilt (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2007. 11. 15. rendered 2007DO3061, etc.); accordingly, evidence collected by an investigative agency without following lawful procedure against a person other than the Defendant cannot, in principle, be used as evidence for finding the Defendant guilty (see Supreme Court Decisions 1992. 6. 23. rendered 92DO682 and 2009. 8. 20. rendered 2008DO8213).\\n\\nAccording to the facts lawfully found by the court below and the record, four police officers, having received information that prostitution was taking place at the instant case ○○ entertainment bar, kept surveillance in front of the said entertainment bar from around 21:30 on 2008. 1. 30.; then, at around 22:24 on the same day, after confirming that Non-Indicted Person 1 and Non-Indicted Person 2, an employee of the said entertainment bar, came out of the said entertainment bar and entered the nearby △△△ inn, they obtained the cooperation of the inn proprietor and opened and entered the inn room occupied by Non-Indicted Person 1 and Non-Indicted Person 2 at around 22:54 on the same day; at that time, the two persons were lying on the bed somewhat apart, undressed, and the police officers informed them that they were arresting them in flagrante delicto for prostitution, but since the two persons were not in the state of engaging in sexual intercourse and no tissue paper, condoms, or the like that could prove that they had had sexual intercourse were found in the room or the bathroom, the police officers were unable to arrest the two persons in flagrante delicto for prostitution and instead requested them to accompany the officers to the investigative agency, and one of the police officers, Non-Indicted Person 3, told the two persons, “You may refuse to accompany us, but even if you refuse, we can forcibly take you along.”; during the process of accompanying them to the investigative agency, when Non-Indicted Person 2 went to the restroom, a female police officer followed Non-Indicted Person 2 and kept watch over her; and it can be seen that Non-Indicted Person 1 and Non-Indicted Person 2 arrived at the Goesan Police Station Jeungpyeong Substation with the police officers and each prepared a written statement at around 23:40 on the same day, and soon thereafter a judicial police officer prepared, for Non-Indicted Person 1 and Non-Indicted Person 2 respectively, the first statement protocol between around 00:00 and 01:50 on 2008. 1. 31. In light of the fact that, when the police officers took the two persons to the investigative agency, they said that even if the two refused, they could forcibly take them along; that the police officers originally attempted to arrest the two persons in flagrante delicto for prostitution, but when there was no evidence of the act of prostitution they were unable to make such an arrest and appear to have requested accompaniment to the investigative agency because they considered that an investigation of the two persons was necessary on the view that an attempt by the two persons to engage in prostitution constituted a crime or in order to punish the proprietor of the said entertainment establishment; that Non-Indicted Person 1 and Non-Indicted Person 2, after lying undressed on the bed in the inn room, were questioned about whether prostitution had occurred by four police officers who entered the inn room through the door, and were then asked to accompany the officers voluntarily, and were even told that “even if you refuse to accompany us, we can forcibly take you along,” so that it would have been difficult for them to refuse the accompaniment in such circumstances; and that during the process of accompaniment, when Non-Indicted Person 2 went to the restroom, a female police officer also followed Non-Indicted Person 2 and kept watch over her, even if the judicial police officer used no physical force when escorting Non-Indicted Person 1 and Non-Indicted Person 2 and even if they had never expressly stated their refusal, the accompaniment of these persons by the judicial police officer to the investigative agency must be regarded as de facto forcible taking under psychological pressure that they could not refuse the officer’s request for accompaniment, namely, an unlawful arrest, because the above-mentioned lawful requirements were not satisfied. Accordingly, the respective written statements prepared by Non-Indicted Person 1 and Non-Indicted Person 2 during their detention by such unlawful arrest, and the respective first statement protocols concerning Non-Indicted Person 1 and Non-Indicted Person 2 prepared by the judicial police officer, are evidence collected in violation of the warrant principle concerning arrest and detention as prescribed by Article 12(1) and (3) of the Constitution and Articles 200-2 and 201 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and as evidence collected by an investigative agency without following lawful procedure against persons other than the Defendant, their evidentiary admissibility is denied under Article 308-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and thus they cannot be used as evidence to establish the guilt of the Defendants.\\n\\nThe reasons stated by the court below in determining that the accompaniment of Non-Indicted Persons 1 and 2 to the investigative agency was unlawful and that the respective written statements and the respective statement protocols lacked evidentiary admissibility are somewhat different from the above legal principles and are therefore not entirely proper; however, the court below’s determination that the respective written statements and the respective statement protocols lacked evidentiary admissibility and thus could not be used as evidence of the charged facts against the Defendants is correct in conclusion, and there is no illegality, such as an error in the legal principles concerning evidentiary admissibility, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. The prosecutor’s remaining grounds of appeal merely dispute the factual findings, which fall within the exclusive authority of the trier of fact, and therefore do not constitute legitimate grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, and judgment is rendered as per the Disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[63DO185]": "(1) First, we examine the grounds of appeal of the Defendants’ court-appointed defense counsel, Kim Cheol-o. The gist is the following three points, namely: (a) in this case, the Defendants admit only part of the facts charged in this case and vehemently deny the remaining parts, and the evidence on this point is not very convincing. Nevertheless, the fact that the lower court convicted the Defendants even as to this portion of the facts charged is said to amount to either incomplete examination or insufficiency of reasons. However, this contention is, in short, based on the assertion that the lower court committed a grave error in its fact-finding. On the record, if the evidence relied upon by the lower court is taken together, it cannot be said that the facts attacked by the argument may not be found, and, moreover, such a reason as the one asserted in the argument cannot constitute a legitimate ground of appeal under the Court-Martial Act; therefore, this argument is rejected. (b) According to the lower court trial record, although the lower court held oral argument, it did not give the Defendants an opportunity to make final statements; accordingly, there is said to be a defect in the lower court proceedings in violation of procedural law. However, since a mere violation of procedural law of this kind cannot constitute a legitimate ground of appeal under the Court-Martial Act, this argument is also dismissed.\\n\\n(c) As to Defendant Kim Jaego, there is not only little trace that the lower court appointed court-appointed defense counsel, but no statement of grounds of appeal was submitted for this Defendant, and the trial was held without the participation of counsel; therefore, the lower court judgment is said to be erroneous. According to the record (page 808), it is apparent that the lower court appointed court-appointed defense counsel Kim Hak-yeon for Appellant 1 and 9 others. If so, the lower court may be regarded as having appointed the above attorney Kim Hak-yeon as court-appointed defense counsel for Defendant Kim Jaego as well. However, there is no trace in the record that this Kim Hak-yeon submitted any statement of grounds of appeal for Defendant Kim Jaego, and, moreover, it is shown by the lower court trial record that, even after receiving a summons for the trial date from the lower court (page 980), he did not appear at the lower court trial date. If so, it must be said that the lower court, while holding the trial, rendered a guilty judgment against the Defendant without the defense counsel being present and without even hearing the arguments. Such conduct by the lower court is contrary to the precedent already rendered by our Supreme Court (Judgment rendered on 1963.1.10, 62DO225), and therefore this argument is well-founded.\\n\\n(2) Next, we examine the grounds of appeal of counsel Jeon Gi-il for Appellant 1. These arguments may generally be grouped into the following three points.\\n\\n(a) Summary of Appellant 1’s grounds of appeal: although the Appellant did in fact bring in Dauda cloth from Japan on seven occasions after the May 16 Revolution, there is no evidence whatsoever to that effect, and, as the lower court found, there is also no evidence that Appellant 1 conspired in advance with co-defendant Jo Yeong-se and the other defendants. Nevertheless, the lower court convicted the Appellant without evidence, which is said to be unlawful under the Temporary Special Act on Punishment of Specific Crimes.\\n\\n(b) Summary of Appellant Song Hong-ju’s grounds of appeal: the Appellant is a person who did not even complete elementary school, and was employed by Kim Jae-mun, who owned a boat, catching fish on the boat and living from day to day on his wages. Then, on two occasions, in ● year ● month and in November of the same year, an unknown boat approached the owner’s boat, exchanged a few words with the owner, and the owner ordered the Appellant to take the goods handed over from that boat and leave them on land, so the Appellant merely carried out errands as ordered. The record that states that the Appellant did such things six times was a false confession obtained from the Appellant by the investigative agency by using the Appellant’s elderly mother and young daughter. Therefore, the lower court’s finding of fact that the Appellant carried out errands six times and its imposition of a fine of 775,780 won on the Appellant are said to be unlawful. The gist of the grounds of appeal of these two Defendants is, in short, that the lower court judgment contains a grave error of fact, and this has already been noted when examining the grounds of appeal of the Defendants’ counsel above, so we need not repeat it here and instead invoke the explanation in (1)(a) above.\\n\\n(4) Next, as to the grounds of appeal of Defendant Kim Jaego, the Defendant not only had no prior conspiracy with the other co-defendants, but also merely carried the goods elsewhere believing that to be so because co-defendant Song Hong-ju said it was haeso. Nevertheless, it is too unjust that the lower court found as fact that the Defendant engaged in smuggling. In addition, the Defendant’s act in this case occurred before the Temporary Special Act on Punishment of Specific Crimes was promulgated and enforced, and imposing a fine on the Defendant is said to be a misapplication of law.\\n\\nHowever, as noted above, the grounds of appeal by the court-appointed defense counsel for this Defendant are well-founded ((1)(c) above), so we omit our determination on the Defendant’s own argument above.\\n\\nAccordingly, since the appeals in this case by Defendants Sin Jeong-gwa, Jo Yeong-se, and Song Hong-ju are without merit, all are dismissed pursuant to Article 436 of the Court-Martial Act, and as to the days of pretrial detention pending these Defendants’ grounds of appeal, 65 days each thereof shall be counted toward each of these Defendants’ respective terms of imprisonment imposed by the lower court pursuant to Article 57 of the Criminal Act. As for Defendant Kim Jaego, since the appeal is well-founded, pursuant to Article 438, paragraph (1), ●Article, paragraph (2), of the Court-Martial Act, we reverse the portion of the lower judgment concerning this Defendant and remand this part to the Army High Court-Martial.\\n\\nWith the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, judgment is rendered as set forth in the order."}

{"[99DO5679]": "1. As to Defendant 1’s final appeal  \\nExamining the judgment of the court below and the evidence admitted in the first-instance judgment cited by the court below in light of the record, since the fact is established that Defendant 1, under the name of promotion expenses for a joint party nomination, delivered the sum of 2,000 ten-thousand won to Co-defendant 2, thereby making a contribution in a public official election, the court below’s decision to uphold the first-instance judgment that found Defendant 1 guilty of the facts charged is proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality in the form of an error of fact-finding due to a violation of the rules of evidence, as argued in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n2. As to Defendant 2’s final appeal  \\na. As to each count of injury  \\nAccording to the record, Defendant 2, with respect to the respective counts of injury in the first-instance judgment, asserted only improper sentencing as the ground for appeal; in such a case, Defendant 2 cannot use as a ground for final appeal the illegality of an error of fact-finding with respect to the relevant part of the judgment of the court below, and further, even upon examining in light of the record the evidence admitted in the first-instance judgment cited by the court below, the facts constituting each injury offense in this case are sufficiently established, and it cannot be said that the judgment of the court below on this point is illegal for an error of fact-finding.\\n\\nb. As to the offense of violating the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act  \\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below, the court below, while stating that part of the testimony of first-instance witness Jeon Ok-sun was a hearsay statement whose content was the statement of Co-defendant 1, found that statement admissible as evidence because it was made under circumstances particularly trustworthy, and, including this, cited the evidence admitted by the first-instance judgment, namely the respective statements of Defendant 2 and Co-defendant 1 in court and before investigative authorities, and the respective statements of the above-mentioned Jeon Ok-sun and Han Yun-ja before investigative authorities, and found the facts charged on this point guilty.\\n\\nHowever, such action by the court below is difficult to accept.\\n\\nThat is, among the respective pieces of evidence used by the court below as evidence of guilt, the respective statements of the Defendants uniformly deny the stated act of contribution, on the ground that the transfer of money in this case was merely a simple loan-for-consumption relationship, and the content of the above Han Yun-ja’s statement is also only to the effect that 2,000 ten-thousand won was lent to Co-defendant 1, so these pieces of evidence alone appear insufficient to establish the facts charged as stated; however, Jeon Ok-sun does make a statement consistent with the facts charged, but its content is that she heard it all from Co-defendant 1. According to Article 316(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, when a statement made at preparatory proceedings for trial or at a trial date by a person other than the defendant has as its content the statement of another person other than the defendant, it may be admitted as evidence only when the original declarant is unable to testify due to death, illness, or other reasons, and the statement was made under circumstances particularly trustworthy. The term “person other than the defendant” used here is interpreted as including not only third parties but also co-defendants and accomplices (see Supreme Court Decision 84DO2279, decided November 27, 1984). With respect to the facts charged in this case concerning Defendant 2, Co-defendant 1 also falls under the category of a person other than the defendant, so in this case where the above Defendant 1 has consistently denied the stated act of contribution up to the proceedings in the court below, the original declarant, Defendant 1, is not in a case where he is unable to testify due to death, illness, or other reasons; therefore, Jeon Ok-sun’s respective statements, whose content is Defendant 1’s statement, would have no evidentiary admissibility as hearsay evidence.\\n\\nIf so, the court below’s conclusion, on the basis of the above materials, that the facts charged of violation of the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act against Defendant 2 were guilty must be deemed erroneous as violating the rules of evidence; therefore, the ground of final appeal pointing this out is well-founded, and this part of the judgment of the court below as to Defendant 2 should be reversed as unlawful (the part to be reversed is originally in a relation of concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the injury portion of the judgment of the court below against the above Defendant, but because, pursuant to Article 18(3) and (2) of the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act, notwithstanding the provisions of Article 38 of the Criminal Act, it was separately tried and separately pronounced, only the part concerning violation of the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act is reversed).\\n\\n3. Therefore, among the judgment of the court below, the part concerning violation of the Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act against Defendant 2 is reversed, and in order to have this part of the case retried and decided, it is remanded to the court below; and Defendant 2’s final appeal concerning the injury portion and Defendant 1’s final appeal are without merit and are all dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question:
Which of the following combinations of correct (O) and incorrect (X) statements concerning complaint offenses and offenses subject to non-punishment upon the victim’s intent not to punish is correct? (Where there is a dispute, follow the precedents)

(a). Even if a person entitled to file a complaint filed a complaint in a case that is not a complaint offense, if the prosecutor instituted prosecution by framing the case as a complaint offense, unless the charged facts are changed to a non-complaint offense through the procedure for amendment of the indictment, the court shall, ex officio, investigate and determine whether a valid complaint exists as a condition for prosecution in a complaint offense. 
(b). If ordinary litigation acts are included within the scope of the statutory representative authority of an adult guardian, or if the adult guardian obtained permission from the Family Court as provided in the adjudication commencing adult guardianship when performing litigation acts, then even absent an express provision, the adult guardian may, on behalf of a victim lacking capacity to form intent, express an intention not to punish the defendant or suspect, or withdraw an expression of intent to seek punishment, in an offense subject to non-punishment upon the victim’s intent not to punish. 
(c). Because a lawyer for a victim of a sexual violence crime has comprehensive authority of representation for all litigation acts for which representation of the victim, etc. may be permitted in criminal procedure, the victim’s lawyer may, on behalf of the victim, withdraw an expression of intent to seek punishment of the defendant or express an intention not to punish. 
(d). If, after being indicted for the crime of bodily injury and being acquitted at first instance, the indictment is amended only upon reaching the appellate instance to the crime of assault, and if the victim expresses in the appellate instance an intent not to punish, the court shall render a judgment dismissing the prosecution. 
(e). If there is a valid withdrawal of a complaint before the first-instance judgment is rendered after the institution of prosecution for a complaint offense based on a valid complaint, the court shall render a judgment dismissing the prosecution.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2013DO7987]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nA court adjudicates the criminal facts charged by the prosecutor, not the content complained of by the person entitled to file a complaint; therefore, even in a case filed by a person entitled to file a complaint as an offense not subject to complaint, if the prosecutor instituted the prosecution by constructing the case as an offense subject to complaint, unless the facts charged are changed to an offense not subject to complaint through the procedure for amendment of the indictment, the court shall, ex officio, investigate and examine whether a complaint, which is a procedural condition in an offense subject to complaint, exists validly. And in such case, Article 233 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which provides the principle of inseparability between a complaint and withdrawal of a complaint in an offense subject to complaint, naturally applies; accordingly, if there has been a lawful withdrawal of a complaint against a person in a co-criminal relationship with the Defendant as to the facts charged, the effect of such withdrawal of the complaint must be deemed to extend to the Defendant.\\n\\nThe court below, even though the victim had complained against the Defendant and the person other than the Defendant for violating the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes, an offense not subject to complaint, namely, special forcible indecent acts, nevertheless, since the prosecutor instituted the prosecution against the Defendant as the offense of forcible indecent acts under Article 298 of the former Criminal Act (as in force before amendment by Act No. 11574 of December 18, 2012), the principle of inseparability between a complaint and withdrawal of a complaint in an offense subject to complaint was inevitably applicable; and because it could not be concluded that the person other than the Defendant did not fall under suspicion of forcible indecent acts as an accomplice (at least as an accessory), it affirmed the first-instance judgment that dismissed the present prosecution, on the ground that the effect of the withdrawal of the complaint against the person other than the Defendant extends to the Defendant pursuant to Article 233 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the judgment below in light of the foregoing legal principle and the record, the measures of the court below are proper, and there is no illegality that affected the result of the judgment, such as misapprehending the legal principle concerning the scope of application and the requirements for application of Article 233 of the Criminal Procedure Act as alleged in the grounds for appeal, failing to state reasons, or violating the rules of logic and experience and exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as follows by the unanimous opinion of the Supreme Court Justices involved."}

{"[2019DO10678]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Article 283(3) of the Criminal Act provides, “The offense under Article 283(1) may not be prosecuted against the victim’s expressly stated intent.” Article 74(2) of the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc. (hereinafter the “Information and Communications Network Act”) provides, “The offense under Article 74(1)3 may not be prosecuted against the victim’s specifically stated intent.” In other words, both the offense of intimidation and the offense of violating Article 44-7(1)3 prescribed in Article 74(1)3 of the Information and Communications Network Act are offenses not subject to prosecution against the victim’s intent.\\n\\nIn an offense not subject to prosecution against the victim’s intent, withdrawal of a declaration expressing a desire for punishment, or a declaration of non-desire for punishment, may be made until before the pronouncement of the first-instance judgment (Article 232(1) and (3) of the Criminal Procedure Act).
