The absence of a declaration of non-desire for punishment constitutes a negative procedural condition and is subject to ex officio review; therefore, even if the parties did not assert it as a ground for appeal, the court below must investigate and determine it ex officio (see Supreme Court Decision 2000DO3172, decided April 24, 2001, Supreme Court Decision 2002DO158, decided March 15, 2002, etc.).\\n\\nArticle 27 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (hereinafter the “Sexual Violence Punishment Act”) provides special provisions concerning the appointment of counsel for victims of sexual crimes. A victim of a sexual crime may appoint counsel on his or her own in order to receive legal assistance in criminal proceedings (paragraph 1); where the victim has no counsel, the prosecutor may designate court-appointed counsel to protect the victim’s rights and interests in criminal proceedings (paragraph 6); and the victim’s counsel has comprehensive authority to act on behalf of the victim, etc. with respect to all procedural acts for which representation of the victim, etc. may be permitted in criminal proceedings (paragraph 5). Accordingly, the victim’s counsel may, on behalf of the victim, withdraw a declaration expressing a desire to punish the defendant or make a declaration of non-desire for punishment.\\n\\n2. According to the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\na. On November 1, 2018, the prosecutor designated Attorney Person Not Named in the Indictment as the victim’s court-appointed counsel pursuant to Article 27(6) of the Sexual Violence Punishment Act. On January 8, 2019, before the pronouncement of the first-instance judgment, the victim’s court-appointed counsel submitted to the court a “Statement of Withdrawal of Complaint and Non-Desire for Punishment,” stating that “the victim has reached an agreement with the defendant, and therefore withdraws the complaint in this case and expresses the intent not to seek punishment of the defendant.”\\n\\nb. The first-instance court found all of the charges in this case guilty and sentenced the Defendant to 10 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 2 years, etc.; only the Prosecutor appealed on the ground of improper sentencing. The court below, on the ground that Article 59-3 of the Welfare of Persons with Disabilities Act, as amended by Act No. 15904 on December 11, 2018 and enforced on June 12, 2019 (hereinafter the “Amended Act”), should be applied to this case pursuant to Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the Amended Act, and that it had to deliberate and determine the ancillary disposition of an employment restriction order, reversed the first-instance judgment ex officio without addressing the Prosecutor’s argument of improper sentencing, found all of the charges in this case guilty, and sentenced the Defendant to 6 months’ imprisonment, etc.\\n\\n3. We examine these factual relations in light of the legal principles seen above.\\n\\nSince the “Statement of Withdrawal of Complaint and Non-Desire for Punishment” submitted by the victim’s court-appointed counsel before the pronouncement of the first-instance judgment contains a statement that the victim does not desire punishment, the court below was required to investigate ex officio whether the victim’s declaration expressing a desire for punishment had been lawfully withdrawn, and to clearly deliberate and determine the negative procedural condition for an offense not subject to prosecution against the victim’s intent.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below found all of the charges in this case guilty without deliberating or determining this issue. The judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning an offense not subject to prosecution against the victim’s intent and by failing to conduct the necessary deliberation.\\n\\n4. The portions of the judgment of the court below concerning intimidation and violation of the Information and Communications Network Act must be reversed, and because the court below sentenced one punishment on the ground that this portion and the remaining guilty portion were in a concurrent-offense relationship under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, the judgment of the court below must ultimately be reversed in its entirety.\\n\\nWithout addressing the remaining grounds for appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices."}

{"[85DO2518]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. With respect to the offense of injury,\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, for the reasons stated in its opinion, held that each piece of evidence submitted by the prosecutor conforming to the principal count of this case (offense of injury) lacked credibility or could not be used as evidence supporting the said count, and that there was no other evidence to establish it, and thus affirmed the first-instance judgment that had acquitted the Defendant on the said principal count. Upon reviewing the selection and weighing of the evidence in light of the record, the above measure by the court below is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality, such as a violation of the rules of evidence. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n2. With respect to the offense of assault,\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below recognized from the record that this case was initially investigated and prosecuted as an offense of injury, but after an acquittal was rendered at the first instance, only at the court below did the prosecutor amend the indictment alternatively to an offense of assault; meanwhile, the victim, after the occurrence of this case, had not expressed an intent to punish the Defendant, and then expressly stated in the appellate court, which was the court below, that he had no intent to punish. On that basis, the court below held that in offenses such as assault, which are the so-called offenses not prosecutable against the victim's expressed will, the withdrawal of the expressed intent to punish is prescribed to be possible only until before the pronouncement of the first-instance judgment; however, in a case where, as here, there is an amendment of the indictment at the appellate trial and the appellate court permits the amendment and conducts the trial, since the appellate court is substantively the first-instance court, in this case where the indictment was amended at the appellate trial to an offense not prosecutable against the victim's expressed will, the withdrawal of the intent to seek punishment can be regarded as validly made until before the pronouncement of the appellate judgment after the amendment of the indictment. For that reason, it dismissed the public prosecution concerning the above offense of assault pursuant to Article 327 subparagraph 6 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nHowever, pursuant to Article 232(1) and (3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, in an offense not prosecutable against the victim's expressed will, the withdrawal of an expression of intent to seek punishment may be made until before the pronouncement of the first-instance judgment. The purport of this provision is that the phenomenon whereby the exercise of the State's punitive power is governed by the victim's will should not be left unattended for a long period, but should be limited to the period before the pronouncement of the first-instance judgment. Even if, as in this case, only at the appellate stage was the indictment amended from an offense not prosecutable against the victim's expressed will to an offense not prosecutable against the victim's expressed will, the second-instance court, that is, the appellate court, cannot be regarded as the first-instance court. (According to the court below's final determination, in this case the victim expressly stated in the appellate trial that he did not wish punishment, which, like the case of withdrawing an expression of intent to seek punishment, may be done until before the pronouncement of the first-instance judgment.) Therefore, the court below, from a different view, accepted the victim's intent not to wish punishment, as stated at the second instance, and dismissed the public prosecution for the offense of assault stated in the judgment against the Defendant; this is unlawful in that it misunderstood the legal doctrine concerning the timing of withdrawal of an expression of intent to seek punishment under Article 232(3) and (1) of the Criminal Procedure Act. Accordingly, the argument pointing this out is meritorious.\\n\\nAccordingly, the portion of the judgment below concerning the alternative count cannot avoid reversal. As this part of the case is deemed sufficiently ready for judgment on the basis of the case record and the evidence examined up to the court below, this Court will directly render judgment pursuant to Article 396 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\n(Facts constituting the offense)\\n\\nThe Defendant, who operates an inn in Busan, on 1984.2.25. at about 15:30, at said inn, because the victim (then 50 years old) asked that KRW 247,900 entrusted to the Defendant be returned, while fighting with the victim, grabbed the victim by the collar and pushed and pulled him to knock him down, thereby assaulting the victim.\\n\\n(Outline of the evidence)\\n\\nThe facts stated in the judgment can be established by comprehensively considering:\\n\\n1. Each statement made by the Defendant in the first-instance and appellate court proceedings, insofar as they partially conform to the facts stated in the judgment\\n1. The victim's statement in the appellate court proceedings, conforming to the facts stated in the judgment\\n1. Each statement made by Sim Eulseok and Kim Pil-ye in the first-instance court proceedings, conforming to the facts stated in the judgment\\n1. The entries in the suspect interrogation protocol of the victim prepared by the judicial police officer acting in official duties and in each statement protocol concerning Sim Eulseok and Kim Pil-ye, insofar as the statements conform to the facts stated in the judgment\\n\\n(Application of statutes)\\n\\nIn light of the law, the Defendant's act stated in the judgment falls under Article 260(1) of the Criminal Act; among the prescribed punishments, a fine is selected, and within the scope of the amount increased pursuant to Article 4(1) of the Act on Temporary Measures Concerning Fines, etc., the Defendant is sentenced to a fine of KRW 50,000, and pursuant to Article 70 and Article 69(2) of the Criminal Act, if the above fine is not paid, the Defendant shall be confined in a workhouse for the period obtained by converting one day into KRW 5,000; however, because the Defendant is a first-time offender, and the offense in this case is very minor and there are circumstances to be considered in mitigation in view of the circumstances of its commission, and also there is an indication of reformation, pursuant to Article 59(1) of the Criminal Act, the pronouncement of the above sentence against the Defendant is suspended.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, the portion of the judgment below concerning the alternative count is reversed and decided as above, and the appeal concerning the principal count is dismissed; accordingly, by unanimous opinion of the participating judges, it is adjudged as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding the determination of the lawfulness or unlawfulness of an investigation is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: When an investigative agency investigates a crime and enters, by ordinary means, a place accessible to an unspecified number of persons and, without exercising any physical force or compulsion, confirms an unlawful act by ordinary means, such conduct is, absent special circumstances, permitted as a method of voluntary investigation.
B: Where seized property has been seized after voluntary submission, if there is a dispute as to whether the seized property was in fact voluntarily submitted, the prosecutor must prove away the doubts concerning its voluntariness.
C: If a prosecutor or judicial police officer needs to continue to seize an item seized pursuant to Article 217(1) or Article 216(1) item 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, he or she must promptly apply for a warrant of seizure and search, and in such case the application for a warrant of seizure and search must be made within 48 hours from the time of seizure.
D: When a judicial police officer arrests a person caught in the act, he or she must necessarily state the gist of the suspected facts, the reason for the arrest, and that the person may appoint counsel, and must give an opportunity to explain; such notification, in principle, must be made in advance before commencing the use of force to effect the arrest, and the same applies to emergency arrest.
E: It is not permitted as unlawful entrapment for an inducer not directly related to the investigative authorities to excessively intervene by using a personal intimate relationship with the induced person to appeal to the induced person's sympathy, or by applying financial or psychological pressure or threats, or by making an enticing offer that is difficult to refuse, or by specifically proposing the method of the offense and even providing money to be used in the offense, thereby causing the induced person to form criminal intent.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DO2339]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Entrapment investigation, in which an investigative agency, against a person who did not originally possess criminal intent, uses fraud, stratagem, or the like to induce criminal intent and thereby arrest a criminal offender, is unlawful (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DO1247 dated October 28, 2005); whether a particular case constitutes unlawful entrapment investigation must be determined comprehensively by considering the type and nature of the relevant offense, the position and role of the inducer, the circumstances and methods of the inducement, the response of the induced person to the inducement, the induced person’s criminal record, and the unlawfulness of the inducement itself.\\n\\nAccordingly, where an inducer who is directly related to the investigative agency excessively intervenes by exploiting a personal intimate relationship with the induced person and appealing to the induced person’s sympathy or emotions, applying financial or psychological pressure or threats, making an invitation difficult to refuse, or specifically suggesting the method of the offense and even providing money to be used in the offense, thereby causing the induced person to form criminal intent, this constitutes unlawful entrapment investigation and is not permissible. However, where the inducer, without having any direct connection with the investigative agency, merely repeatedly and several times requested the induced person to commit the offense, and it cannot be deemed that the investigative agency used fraud, stratagem, or the like, then even if the induced person’s criminal intent was thereby induced, such conduct does not constitute unlawful entrapment investigation.\\n\\n2. The court below, based on the evidence it cited, acknowledged the following facts: Nonindicted 1, after being released from Cheongsong Protective Detention Center, had been living together with Nonindicted 2; Nonindicted 2, while acting as an informant for the Seoul Central District Prosecutors’ Office, had on about five occasions received rewards in return for cooperating in narcotics investigations and helping arrest narcotics offenders; Nonindicted 1, who came to know the Defendant while serving a sentence at Cheongsong Prison, asked the Defendant on more than 10 occasions from early February 2005, “An acquaintance of mine wants to buy methamphetamine (hereinafter referred to as ‘Philopon’), so please obtain some for her”; the Defendant had repeatedly refused Nonindicted 1’s requests, but on February 22, 2005, asked Nonindicted 3, whom he had met and known at Cheongsong Protective Detention Center, whether Philopon could be purchased, and, upon receiving from Nonindicted 3 the message that “there is a person who will sell 20 g of Philopon for 6 to 7 million won,” informed Nonindicted 1 of that fact; Nonindicted 2, having heard this from Nonindicted 1, relayed it to a narcotics investigator at the Seoul Central District Prosecutors’ Office, and when the narcotics investigator said that funds for the undercover purchase of Philopon had not yet been secured, had Nonindicted 1 postpone the Philopon transaction; thereafter, once the funds for the undercover purchase of Philopon were secured, Nonindicted 1 met the Defendant on February 23, 2005 and agreed to conduct the Philopon transaction the following day, then informed Nonindicted 2 of that fact, and Nonindicted 2 reported it to the narcotics investigator; accordingly, the narcotics investigator, with undercover-purchase funds in his possession and disguised as a companion, caused the Defendant and Nonindicted 2 to meet Nonindicted 3; Nonindicted 3, while the Defendant had already left, caused Nonindicted 4 to sell Philopon to Nonindicted 2 at around 18:00 on February 24, 2005, but was arrested by the narcotics investigator who was lying in wait at the scene; Nonindicted 1 was not booked on the ground that he had provided information regarding the Philopon sale to assist Nonindicted 2; and Nonindicted 2 received a reward of 1,000,000 won in return for providing information regarding the above Philopon sale and helping arrest the narcotics offender. Based on such facts as found, the court below held that Nonindicted 1, as an informant for the investigative agency or at least in communication with Nonindicted 2, who was an informant for the investigative agency, intentionally approached the Defendant for the purpose of receiving rewards and the like and requested that he arrange the Philopon sale, and that there was sufficient room to view the Defendant as having already had criminal intent for the offense at the time of this case; rather, it appeared that criminal intent regarding the narcotics offense was newly induced by the instigation of the investigative agency or its informant. On that basis, the court below reversed the first-instance judgment that had found the Defendant guilty and rendered a judgment dismissing the prosecution.\\n\\n3. However, the court below’s above determination is difficult to accept in light of the above legal principles and the record.\\n\\nThat is, even according to the factual findings made by the court below, the investigative agency only came to know of the matter through Nonindicted 2 after the Defendant, upon Nonindicted 1’s request, had agreed to commit the offense; and it appears that when Nonindicted 1 asked the Defendant to obtain Philopon, the investigative agency had not yet known of the matter. In light of these circumstances, this case should be regarded not as one in which the investigative agency caused Nonindicted 2 or Nonindicted 1 to induce the Defendant, but rather as one in which Nonindicted 2 or Nonindicted 1 independently induced the Defendant, without any relation to the investigative agency, based on private motives such as obtaining a reward. In addition, Nonindicted 1 merely asked the Defendant more than 10 times, “An acquaintance of mine wants to buy Philopon, so please obtain some for her,” and in the process did not use methods such as exploiting a personal intimate relationship with the Defendant and appealing to his sympathy or emotions, applying financial or psychological pressure or threats, making an invitation difficult to refuse, or specifically suggesting the method of the offense and providing money to be used in the offense. Given these circumstances, this case cannot be viewed as falling within the category in which the investigative agency used fraud, stratagem, or the like. Therefore, even if the Defendant only formed criminal intent after receiving Nonindicted 1’s request, it is difficult to regard this as unlawful entrapment investigation. And this determination does not change merely because the purpose of Nonindicted 2 or Nonindicted 1 in inducing the Defendant was to receive a reward from the investigative agency, or because the Defendant had refused Nonindicted 1’s request several times.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below hastily concluded, solely for the reasons stated in its opinion, that the offense in this case resulted from unlawful entrapment investigation; in this regard, the court below’s determination contains an error affecting the conclusion of the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning entrapment investigation.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2007DO7961]": "1. As to the Prosecutor’s grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe first sentence of Article 12(5) of the Constitution proclaims the principle that “No person shall be arrested or detained unless informed of the reasons therefor and of the right to assistance of counsel.” Article 72 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “A defendant shall not be arrested unless the outline of the criminal facts, the reasons for detention, and the fact that counsel may be appointed are stated to him, and he is given an opportunity to explain.” Meanwhile, since this provision applies mutatis mutandis, pursuant to Article 213-2 of the same Act, where a prosecutor or judicial police officer arrests a flagrant offender or receives delivery of a flagrant offender arrested by a private person, it is clear that, in the case where a judicial police officer arrests a flagrant offender, the judicial police officer must state the outline of the criminal facts, the reasons for detention, and the fact that counsel may be appointed, and must give an opportunity to explain. This legal principle applies not only to the arrest of a flagrant offender but also to emergency arrest, and such notice should, in principle, be given in advance before using force for arrest; however, in cases of chasing after and seizing a fleeing suspect or subduing by force a suspect who resists with violence, the notice may be given during the process of seizure or subdual, or, if that is not feasible, immediately after the suspect has been seized or subdued (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2000. 7. 4., 99DO4341).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons given in the judgment of the court below, the court below, after recognizing the facts as stated in its ruling, held that, in a situation where the Defendant was subject to a wanted notice, three police officers, including Non-indicted Person 1, confirmed that the Defendant was staying at the above motel with his wife, and, in order to arrest the Defendant, opened the motel room door with a master key at 1 a.m. and entered the room, they should be regarded as having already commenced physical force for the purpose of emergency arrest of the Defendant at that moment. Accordingly, it held that, pursuant to the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act, judicial police officers who intend to effect an emergency arrest of a suspect must, before entering into such use of force, that is, before opening the motel room door with a master key, in principle, either have the Defendant come out of the room voluntarily or enter the room with the Defendant’s consent, and then state to the Defendant the outline of the criminal facts for which he was wanted, the reasons for detention, and the fact that counsel may be appointed, and give him an opportunity to explain. If they did not do so, but instead, on the ground that there was a risk that the Defendant might flee or injure himself, entered the motel room where the Defendant and his wife were staying in the early morning hours by opening the door with a master key without the Defendant’s consent, thereby first commencing physical force for emergency arrest without such notice, then, at the moment they met the Defendant in the room, they should have given such notice to the Defendant without delay; and in the case of entering a residence at night for the purpose of emergency arrest, the Miranda warnings must be given immediately after entry, and if this is violated, it does not constitute lawful performance of official duties, which is consistent with the constitutional spirit of guaranteeing the peace of private life and the right to dwelling. Nevertheless, the police officers merely told the Defendant that he was wanted by the Gyeongnam Provincial Police Agency and of the criminal facts concerning the illegal operation of an adult PC room, and immediately demanded that he produce identification; and although the Defendant produced his younger brother’s driver’s license, while the police officers were checking fingerprints using that driver’s license, they did not tell the Defendant the reasons for detention or the fact that counsel may be appointed, nor did they give him an opportunity to explain. If so, since the police officers did not comply with the above due process even after a considerable period of time had elapsed following the commencement of physical force for emergency arrest, it is difficult to regard the series of acts by which the police officers opened the motel room door and entered in order to arrest the Defendant as lawful performance of official duties. Therefore, even if the police officers, in the course of rushing at the Defendant and subduing him on the ground that the Defendant broke a window and threatened them while holding a broken piece of glass, were stabbed by the piece of glass swung by the Defendant or suffered injuries to their fingers, etc., it cannot be said that the lawful performance of the police officers’ duties concerning emergency arrest was thereby obstructed.\\n\\nHowever, this part of the judgment of the court below cannot be accepted.\\n\\nAs recognized by the court below in the facts stated in its ruling, after the police officers confirmed that the Defendant was staying at the motel with his wife, they went in to arrest him in the room on the ground of the risk of flight or self-injury, called out the Defendant’s name, and then stated the fact that he was wanted and the criminal facts, and demanded that he produce identification. In a case where the Defendant claimed that he was Non-indicted Person 2, his younger brother, and produced a driver’s license in the name of Non-indicted Person 2, the police officers, as police officers, should first confirm whether the person they intended to arrest was indeed the Defendant himself, and only then give the so-called Miranda warnings; it should not be regarded as proper to arrest first while giving the Miranda warnings without confirming whether the other party was the Defendant or Non-indicted Person 2. If they arrest first and give the Miranda warnings without even confirming the other party, there may sometimes be cases in which a person who is not the actual suspect is arrested, and in such cases, a much greater infringement of human rights may occur than the protection of human rights obtained by advancing the Miranda warnings. Therefore, it cannot be said that the police officers in this case acted unlawfully merely because they proceeded to the identity verification procedure without giving all of the Miranda warnings.\\n\\nAnd according to the facts recognized by the court below, when the police officers attempted to check his fingerprints, the Defendant suddenly changed his attitude, uttered abusive language, broke the window with his fist, seized a piece of broken glass, and swung it forward to prevent the police officers from approaching. Accordingly, the police officers ended up grappling with the Defendant and engaging in a physical struggle for 20 minutes in order to subdue him. Once they reached the stage of subduing by force a suspect who resists with violence in this manner, it should be understood that the police officers may give the Miranda warnings during the process of subdual or, if that is not feasible, immediately after subduing him. Accordingly, it cannot be said that the police officers’ emergency arrest in this case was not lawful performance of official duties, and if the police officers, in the course of rushing at the Defendant and subduing him, were stabbed by the piece of glass swung by the Defendant or suffered injuries to their fingers, etc., this may be regarded as a case in which the lawful performance of duties concerning emergency arrest was obstructed.\\n\\nUltimately, the judgment of the court below contains an error of law by misapprehending the legal principles regarding emergency arrest and the crime of obstruction of performance of official duties, and such error affected the outcome of the judgment. The Prosecutor’s argument on appeal pointing out this point is well founded.\\n\\n2. As to the grounds of appeal by the Defendant and court-appointed defense counsel.\\n\\nExamining the evidence admitted in the first-instance judgment affirmed by the court below in light of the record, the court below’s finding that the Defendant committed the acts described in item 4.d. of the first-instance judgment is persuasive, and it cannot be said that the judgment of the court below is unlawful, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, for violating the rules of evidence assessment. The Defendant’s claim of self-defense is merely an argument premised on the existence of a factual error caused by such violation of the rules of evidence assessment, and thus is likewise unavailing. In addition, in this case where a sentence of imprisonment of less than 10 years was imposed, an argument to the effect that the sentence is too severe cannot constitute a proper ground for appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the Defendant’s appeal is without merit, and the Prosecutor’s appeal is with merit; accordingly, the portion of the judgment of the court below concerning the offense of special obstruction of performance of official duties resulting in injury must be reversed. However, the court below found the offense of violation of the Act on the Punishment of Violences, etc. (injury by a group or with a deadly weapon, etc.), included in the facts charged with respect to that portion, to be guilty, and sentenced the Defendant to one punishment by combining it with the remaining offenses in concurrent relation thereto. Consequently, there is no need to render a separate judgment in the order with respect to the Defendant’s appeal, and the remaining criminal portions above also cannot escape reversal together.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below against the Defendant is reversed in its entirety, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so ordered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court who participated."}

{"[2019DO7891]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Determination on the allegation of misapprehension of law\\n\\na. When an investigative agency, in investigating a crime, enters a place into which an unspecified number of persons may enter by ordinary means and, without exercising any physical force or coercive power, confirms the unlawful act in question by ordinary means, such conduct is permissible as one method of a voluntary investigation unless special circumstances exist; accordingly, it cannot be deemed unlawful merely because it was carried out without a warrant.\\n\\nAlso, when an investigative agency, in investigating a crime, records the matter if the offense is currently being committed or has just been committed, and if there is necessity and urgency to preserve evidence, and the recording was made by a reasonable method generally permitted, the recording cannot be deemed unlawful merely because it was made without a warrant (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision of Sept. 3, 1999, 99DO2317). However, since photography may infringe the right of portrait, secrecy and freedom of private life, freedom of residence, etc., whether the investigative agency photographed by a reasonable method generally permitted must be carefully determined by comprehensively considering, among other things, whether the investigative agency entered the place of filming by ordinary means and whether the place of filming and the subject fall within an area where protection of privacy and freedom, etc. may reasonably be expected (see Supreme Court Decision of Apr. 27, 2023, 2018DO8161).\\n\\nb. As stated in the judgment, the lower court found that, with criminal suspicion against the Defendant already detected and for the need to preserve evidence thereof, the police officers entered the establishment at issue, to which an unspecified number of persons could gain access, by ordinary means, confirmed and photographed the dancing of customers, which could be seen by anyone in the establishment, and held that this could not be deemed unlawful merely because it was carried out without a warrant, and admitted the evidentiary value of the photographs taken by the police officers.\\n\\nExamining the reasons for the lower-court judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles, etc., there is no error in the lower court's determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misapprehending the warrant principle, the evidentiary admissibility of recordings made by investigative agencies, or the law concerning illegally obtained evidence.\\n\\n2. Determination on the allegation of mistake of fact\\n\\nThe Defendant argues to the effect that, although there was no fact that customers were allowed to dance in the establishment at issue, the lower court made an erroneous factual finding.\\n\\nHowever, this is merely a challenge to the lower court's determination, which belongs to the free determination of the court of fact, regarding the selection of evidence and the probative value thereof, and the factual finding based thereon, and thus does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal. Moreover, even upon examining the reasons for the lower-court judgment in light of the lawfully admitted evidence, there is no error in the lower court's determination that, contrary to the grounds for appeal, it did not exceed the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by acting against the rules of logic and experience.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as per the order by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court involved."}

{"[2020DO9431]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Summary of the facts charged at issue  \\nThe Defendant, from around 05:56 on January 13, 2018 to around 22:25 on September 22, 2018, used the camera of the Defendant’s mobile phone (hereinafter referred to as the “instant mobile phone”) on a total of 9 occasions, as stated in serial numbers 1 through 9 of the attached crime list cited in the lower court’s judgment, and against the victims’ will photographed the bodies of 4 victims, which could arouse sexual desire or embarrassment.\\n\\n2. The lower court’s determination  \\nWith respect to the facts charged at issue, the lower court held that the instant mobile phone and the electronic information stored therein lacked admissibility as evidence because voluntariness was not proven in relation to the voluntary submission of the instant mobile phone, and on that basis acquitted the Defendant on the ground that the crime was not proven.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s determination  \\na. Where there is a dispute as to whether an item seized as a voluntarily submitted item was actually voluntarily submitted pursuant to Article 218 of the Criminal Procedure Act, it is not the defendant who must prove specific and reasonable facts sufficient to suspect the voluntariness of the voluntary submission; rather, the prosecutor must prove away the doubt concerning its voluntariness (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DO7900 rendered November 23, 2006, Supreme Court Decision 2019DO15178 rendered August 31, 2022, etc.).\\n\\nb. Examining the reasons of the lower court’s judgment in light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, because the prosecutor failed to prove away the doubt concerning voluntariness with respect to the submission of the instant mobile phone, the instant mobile phone and the electronic information stored therein constitute illegally collected evidence and therefore lack admissibility as evidence. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) At the time of arrest in flagrante delicto, the Defendant was in a psychologically intimidated state because a witness had taken away the instant mobile phone from the Defendant, and the Defendant even rushed toward the witness and the police officer in order to retrieve the instant mobile phone; moreover, because the Defendant was taken to the police station and was being questioned as a suspect without assistance of counsel while denying some of the offenses, the question whether the Defendant voluntarily submitted the instant mobile phone to the investigative authorities must be strictly scrutinized.\\n\\n2) There is no material to acknowledge that the investigative authorities informed the Defendant, who was the person making the voluntary submission, of the meaning and procedure of voluntary submission and the circumstance that, in the event of voluntary submission, the seized item could not be voluntarily returned.\\n\\n3) At the time of the instant case, the Defendant was a person with no criminal record other than having been punished once for the offense of violation of the Road Traffic Act (drunk driving), and at the time of the voluntary submission stated, “I heard from a police officer that ‘the instant mobile phone can be returned.’” Thus, it is difficult to conclude that the Defendant was aware that, if the instant mobile phone were voluntarily submitted, it could not be recovered even if the Defendant later changed his mind.\\n\\nc. Although there is some inappropriate part in the lower court’s determination concerning the facts charged at issue, insofar as the admissibility of the instant mobile phone and the electronic information stored therein is denied, the lower court’s conclusion that there was no proof of the crime with respect to the facts charged at issue is correct. The lower court’s judgment contains no error that affected the judgment by going beyond the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in contravention of logic and experience, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the legality of the seizure of a voluntarily submitted item.\\n\\nd. Meanwhile, the Prosecutor appealed as to the entirety of the lower court’s judgment, but as to the remaining parts, neither the petition of appeal nor the statement of reasons for appeal contains any statement of the grounds for objection thereto.\\n\\n4. Conclusion  \\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged as per the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated in the decision."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the procedures for seizure and search and the admissibility of evidence is correct? (If there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: If the victim voluntarily submits a storage medium belonging to and under the control of the suspect, and the victim who made the submission participates in the seizure and search procedure for electronic information and is handed an itemized list, then the substantial content of procedural rights is guaranteed, so the seizure and search procedure is lawful, and the electronic information obtained thereby is admissible as evidence.
B: If, while the suspect is committed to a detention room, a judicial police officer searches a mobile phone lawfully seized from an office pursuant to a prior warrant, discovers electronic information related to the facts alleged in the warrant, copies and prints it out, and then files it in the investigation record, then even if the electronic information was obtained pursuant to the warrant, the suspect’s right to participation was not guaranteed, and this constitutes an unlawful seizure and search.
C: If the prosecutor requests a statement analysis officer belonging to the Scientific Crime Investigation Department of the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office to analyze the contents of the statement of the child victim, and the statement analysis officer interviews the victim and the video recording of that content is made, since it cannot be regarded as having been prepared outside the investigative process, its admissibility cannot be recognized under Article 313(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act; however, since it can be regarded as a protocol recording the statement of a person other than the defendant prepared by an investigative agency, its admissibility can be recognized under Article 312 of the Criminal Procedure Act.
D: Even if electronic information stored in the cloud is not stated as the “items to be seized” in the seizure and search warrant, if a cloud account was logged in on a mobile phone lawfully seized, downloading and seizing the electronic information stored in the cloud is lawful.
E: In the course of seizure and search of a storage medium for information, where exceptional circumstances are recognized making it impossible to use a method of specifying the scope and printing/copying, and the storage medium containing electronic information is moved to the investigative agency’s office, etc. for copying, searching, and printing, the person subjected to seizure or the defense counsel must be guaranteed an opportunity to participate; however, because the defense counsel’s right to participation as a person other than a party is not an independent right, if the person subjected to seizure expressly indicates an intention not to participate in the execution, there is no need to separately notify the defense counsel of the time and place of that execution.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2016DO348]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nThe finding of criminal facts must reach the level of proof beyond a reasonable doubt (Article 307(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act), but the selection and weighing of evidence performed as a premise for fact-finding, as well as the probative value of evidence, fall within the free evaluation of the court of fact (Article 308 of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons stated in its opinion, determined that it was established that the Defendant, on December 11, 2014, at his home, photographed the victim, Person Not Otherwise Named 1’s, genitals with a mobile phone against the victim’s will, as stated in the criminal facts indicated in the lower court’s opinion, and thereby rejected the argument on appeal alleging factual error and misapprehension of law in this regard, and maintained the first-instance judgment.\\n\\nThe grounds of appeal are, in substance, merely an attempt to challenge the lower court’s factual finding in this respect, and are in essence nothing more than criticizing the lower court’s selection and weighing of evidence and its assessment of probative value, which fall within the free evaluation of the court of fact. Further, even when examining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the above legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, there is no error in the lower court’s determination, such as misapprehending the law concerning intent as alleged in the grounds of appeal, violating the principle of trial-centered adjudication, or deviating from the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Prosecutor’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. Relevant legal principles\\n\\n1) Method of seizure of electronic information pursuant to voluntary submission\\n\\nIn today’s world, the business of an individual or a company is difficult to maintain without information-processing devices equipped with computers, servers, or storage media, and various storage media on which electronic information is stored (hereinafter referred to as “information storage media”) are mostly large in capacity and thus broadly contain information concerning a private individual’s daily life or a company’s management that is unrelated to the criminal suspicion that is the subject of the investigation. Since investigative agencies’ seizure and search of such electronic information are highly likely to infringe secrecy and freedom of private life, the right to informational self-determination, property rights, and the like, they must not be conducted in a comprehensive manner, but rather must be conducted within the minimum extent necessary for the purpose of the investigation, in accordance with the principle of proportionality. As a rule, investigative agencies’ seizure and search of electronic information must be conducted only by collecting, in printed documentary form, the parts related to the criminal suspicion that constituted the ground for issuance of the warrant, or by copying the relevant file onto an information storage medium carried by the investigative agency; and seizure and search by directly carrying out the information storage medium itself or taking out all electronic files contained in the storage medium to the investigative agency’s office, etc. in the form of hard copies or images (hereinafter referred to as “copies”) may exceptionally be permitted only where, due to the circumstances at the scene or the large volume of electronic information, it is impossible to print out or copy within a defined scope, or where it is recognized as significantly difficult to achieve the purpose of seizure, such as when a long time is required to obtain the relevant information or technical measures by specialized personnel are necessary (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2011MO1839, rendered July 16, 2015, etc.).\\n\\nThe above legal principles likewise apply to the seizure of voluntarily submitted items that constitute information storage media (Article 218 of the Criminal Procedure Act). This is because seizure of voluntarily submitted items differs only in that the investigative agency’s acquisition of possession over the seized item is made according to the submitter’s intent, but the investigative purpose premised on criminal suspicion and the effect of seizure are the same as in the case of a warrant. Accordingly, when an investigative agency voluntarily receives submission of an information storage medium containing electronic information in relation to a specific criminal suspicion and seizes the electronic information stored therein, in principle it should seize only the printed output, etc. of the electronic information related to the criminal facts that prompted the voluntary submission. However, only where, due to the circumstances at the scene, the large volume of electronic information, or difficulty of search, etc., it is impossible to print or copy within a defined scope, or where it is recognized as significantly difficult to achieve the purpose of seizure, may the information storage medium itself or a copy thereof exceptionally be voluntarily submitted and seized.\\n\\n2) Object and scope of seizure of electronic information pursuant to voluntary submission\\n\\na) Intent of the voluntary submitter\\n\\nAn information storage medium and the electronic information stored therein are not only conceptually and functionally distinct in that they each possess separate, independent value and utility, but, insofar as the seizure of voluntarily submitted electronic information is lawful only on the basis of the submitter’s free intent to submit, when an information storage medium or a copy thereof containing a mixture of electronic information related to the criminal suspicion and electronic information unrelated thereto is voluntarily submitted to an investigative agency, the submitter may individually designate or limit the scope of the electronic information to be submitted and seized. Since the scope of voluntary submission of electronic information within an information storage medium may thus vary depending on the submitter’s intent, the investigative agency receiving such information storage medium by voluntary submission must clarify the scope of the electronic information that is the subject of voluntary submission from the submitter, thereby specifically identifying the scope of seizure. Furthermore, in view of the importance of electronic information stored in an information storage medium from the standpoint not only of due process, warrant principle, and the principle of proportionality, which the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to realize, but also of protection of secrecy and freedom of private life, the right to informational self-determination, and property rights, a statement of intent by a person voluntarily submitting an information storage medium to designate the electronic information contained therein or to limit the scope of submission must be strictly construed, and it is impermissible for the investigative agency to casually infer the intent of an unverified submitter.\\n\\nAccordingly, where the investigative agency can easily confirm the submitter’s intent but fails to do so and instead voluntarily receives an information storage medium containing a mixture of electronic information related to a specific criminal suspicion and electronic information unrelated thereto, it cannot be treated as though all electronic information stored in that information storage medium were voluntarily submitted and seized. In such a case, the issue is how to specify the scope of the electronic information subject to seizure according to the voluntary submitter’s intent.\\n\\nb) Electronic information related to the criminal suspicion that prompted the seizure pursuant to voluntary submission\\n\\nAn investigative agency may seize only objects deemed to constitute evidence or subject to forfeiture insofar as they are recognized as related to the suspected facts (Articles 219 and 106 of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\n\\nTherefore, when an investigative agency seeking to seize electronic information seizes an information storage medium and the electronic information stored therein by voluntary submission, if the scope of the electronic information voluntarily submitted according to the submitter’s specific intent is not clear, or cannot be ascertained, because of reasons such as the failure to properly verify the submitter’s intent regarding the specific scope of submission, then only electronic information related to the criminal facts that prompted the voluntary submission and having at least minimal value capable of proving such facts is subject to seizure. At this time, electronic information related to the criminal facts includes not only the criminal facts themselves or offenses sharing the same basic factual relation, but also information that may be used as indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence to prove the motive and process of the offense, the means and method of the offense, the time and place of the offense, etc. However, such relevance is recognized only where there is a concrete and individual nexus, taking into comprehensive account the content of the criminal facts that prompted the seizure pursuant to voluntary submission, the object of the investigation, the course of the investigation, and the process of voluntary submission; it is not to be deemed relevant merely because the criminal facts are of the same type or similar offenses (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2021DO2205, rendered August 26, 2021).\\n\\nc) Scope of seizure of voluntarily submitted electronic information in cases such as hidden-camera offenses\\n\\nWhen determining whether electronic information is related to the criminal facts, it is necessary to examine the concrete and individual nexus based on the content and nature of the criminal facts and the process of voluntary submission. In particular, in hidden-camera offenses using a smartphone, which has both camera functions and information storage medium functions, where, by the nature of the offense, habituality of the offense is suspected or it is suspected that the offense was committed as part of a series of offenses arising from sexual preference or tendency, and where there is a likelihood that direct evidence of the offense remains in the smartphone in the form of image files or video files, indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence found in the same type of electronic information stored therein is highly likely to be recognized as having a concrete and individual nexus with the criminal facts, in that such indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence may also be used for that purpose. In this way, hidden-camera recordings containing electronic information of a nature that significantly infringes the personality rights of the victim, who was the object of the crime, are generated by the criminal act and are also subject to forfeiture; therefore, there is a strong need to protect the victim by promptly seizing and searching such electronic information from the voluntarily submitted mobile phone so as to timely block the possibility of distribution of the hidden-camera recordings. Furthermore, in such cases, because the type of electronic information that constitutes both indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence and a subject of forfeiture and seizure/search can be relatively clearly specified as image files or video files, etc., and because there is little possibility that this will lead to seizure/search of all irrelevant private electronic information, there is comparatively greater room to recognize relevance more broadly.\\n\\nd) Scope of seizure of electronic information when a person other than the suspect voluntarily submits an information storage medium owned and managed by the suspect\\n\\nWhen a person other than the suspect, such as the victim, voluntarily submits an information storage medium owned and managed by the suspect, the seizure and submission, even if lawful, must be interpreted more restrictively so that only electronic information having a concrete and individual nexus with the criminal facts that prompted the voluntary submission becomes subject to seizure. Where the subject of the voluntary submission is a possessor or custodian, rather than the owner, and the act of submission is likely to significantly infringe the owner’s secrecy of private life or other personality interests, special consideration for the owner’s legal interests, who did not consent to the voluntary submission, is necessary along with the need for seizure and search pursuant to voluntary submission (see Supreme Court Decisions 98DO968 rendered September 3, 1999; 2008DO1097 rendered May 15, 2008; 2013DO7718 rendered September 26, 2013, etc.), because if an information storage medium owned and managed by an individual suspect is subject to unrestricted seizure and search, there is a risk that the suspect’s personality interests, including secrecy and freedom of private life and the right to informational self-determination, will be significantly infringed, as everything relating to such interests is stored therein. Therefore, even if the third party who made the voluntary submission indicates an intent to submit in bulk electronic information exceeding the scope recognized as having a concrete and individual nexus with the criminal facts that prompted the submission, unless there are special circumstances such as where that third party has authority to dispose of all electronic information in the information storage medium or where the suspect’s intent to consent thereto may be inferred, the scope of electronic information that the investigative agency may lawfully seize without a warrant through such voluntary submission must be deemed limited to electronic information related to the criminal facts.\\n\\n3) Guarantee of the suspect’s right to participate during the search, copying, and printing of electronic information, and delivery of an inventory of seized electronic information\\n\\nWhere an investigative agency receives by voluntary submission an information storage medium or copy thereof containing a mixture of electronic information subject to seizure and electronic information not subject to seizure, and then moves such information storage medium, etc. to the investigative agency’s office, etc. to search, copy, and print it, the agency must, during such series of processes, guarantee the opportunity for participation to the party subjected to seizure/search (hereinafter referred to as the “person subjected to seizure/search”) or his or her counsel as provided in Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act, prepare and deliver an inventory specifying the file details of the seized electronic information, and take appropriate measures to prevent arbitrary copying, etc. of electronic information unrelated to the criminal facts, thereby complying with the warrant principle and due process. If such measures were not taken, the seizure and search cannot be deemed lawful unless there are special circumstances, such as where the person subjected to seizure/search expressly indicated an intent not to participate, or where, in light of the purpose and progress of the voluntary submission or the nature and content of the process in which the procedural violation occurred, it cannot be said that the purpose of guaranteeing procedural participation to the person subjected to seizure/search was substantially infringed; the conclusion is not different even if the investigative agency copied or printed only the electronic information related to the criminal facts from the information storage medium or copy thereof (see the above-mentioned en banc Decision 2011MO1839, Supreme Court Decision 2019MO291 rendered November 17, 2020, etc.). Furthermore, where a third party such as the victim voluntarily submits, without a warrant, an information storage medium belonging to the suspect’s ownership or management, it is difficult to regard the actual person subjected to seizure/search, namely the suspect, as having consented to the investigative agency’s unrestricted search of all such electronic information; and even when the suspect himself or herself makes the voluntary submission, just as the suspect’s right to participate, etc. must be guaranteed, unless there are special circumstances, appropriate measures must be taken to guarantee the suspect’s procedural rights, such as by guaranteeing the suspect’s right to participate pursuant to Articles 219, 121, and 129 of the Criminal Procedure Act and delivering an inventory of the seized electronic information.\\n\\n4) Necessary measures and procedures when unrelated information is discovered during the search of a voluntarily submitted information storage medium\\n\\nAs seen above, it is in principle unlawful seizure and search, and therefore impermissible, for an investigative agency to arbitrarily search, copy, or print electronic information beyond the scope of electronic information subject to seizure from a voluntarily submitted information storage medium. If, before the seizure and search of electronic information is completed, the investigative agency lawfully discovers, in the course of searching electronic information related to the criminal facts, electronic information related to a separate criminal suspicion, it must stop any further additional search and may lawfully seize and search such information only after obtaining a separate seizure and search warrant from the court for the separate criminal suspicion. Accordingly, evidence obtained by the investigative agency through seizure and search without a warrant of electronic information beyond the scope of electronic information subject to seizure from a voluntarily submitted information storage medium constitutes illegally obtained evidence, and its illegality is not cured merely because a warrant was later issued by the court or the Defendant or defense counsel consented to its use as evidence.\\n\\nb. Determination\\n\\n1) According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the lawfully admitted evidence, the following facts can be found.\\n\\na) As recognized by the lower court, the Defendant committed the offense on December 11, 2014 (hereinafter referred to as the “2014 offense”) by photographing the victim, Person Not Otherwise Named 1’s, genitals at his home against the victim’s will. The victim, Person Not Otherwise Named 1, immediately reported the damage to the police, stating to the effect that videos and photographs taken by the Defendant were stored in two mobile phones owned by the Defendant (an iPhone and a Samsung mobile phone) that she had taken from the Defendant’s home, and voluntarily submitted them as evidence of the offense.\\n\\nb) The police officers seized the two mobile phones without a warrant, but did not separately confirm from the victim, Person Not Otherwise Named 1, whether the submission was intended to encompass all electronic information stored in the mobile phones, such as videos and photographs, etc.\\n\\nc) The Defendant provided the password for one mobile phone (the iPhone) to the police and participated in the file imaging process, whereas for the other mobile phone (the Samsung mobile phone), he in effect refused to provide the password and did not participate in the process of restoring and extracting the stored video files. The police, after confirming the 2014 offense against the victim, Person Not Otherwise Named 1, through the video files stored in the former mobile phone (the iPhone), found 30 videos and photographs in the latter mobile phone (the Samsung mobile phone) while additionally searching for video evidence of the 2014 offense, including scenes of two men other than the victim sleeping on a bed, scenes of someone holding their genitals by hand, etc., and after confirming the content, duplicated them onto a CD.\\n\\nd) The police summoned the victim, Person Not Otherwise Named 1, investigated the identity, etc. of the two men appearing in the videos, and thereby learned that they were the victims, Person Not Otherwise Named 2 and Person Not Otherwise Named 3, and through additional investigation became aware of the fact that around December 2013, the Defendant committed the offense of touching their genitals and photographing the above videos while the victims, Person Not Otherwise Named 2 and Person Not Otherwise Named 3, were drunk and asleep (hereinafter referred to as the “2013 offense”).\\n\\ne) Thereafter, the police obtained a seizure and search warrant and seized the CD duplicating the electronic information of the video of the 2013 offense as evidence.\\n\\n2) Examining the above factual relations in light of the legal principles discussed above, when the victim, Person Not Otherwise Named 1, submitted the Defendant’s mobile phones as evidence to the police, she did not clearly state the scope of submission of the electronic information recorded therein, and the police officers in charge likewise did not go through any procedure of confirmation with the submitter; thus, absent such confirmation, this falls under a case in which the submitter’s intent regarding the scope of submission of the electronic information contained in the mobile phones is unclear or cannot be ascertained. Accordingly, it is appropriate to interpret restrictively that the scope of electronic information in the above mobile phones lawfully seized through voluntary submission is limited to electronic information having a concrete and individual nexus with the Defendant’s 2014 offense itself, which prompted the voluntary submission and seizure. In light of this, even under the legal principles concerning relevant evidence that includes the above-mentioned indirect evidence and circumstantial evidence, a video concerning the Defendant’s 2013 offense, which occurred at a considerably different time from the offense and involved entirely different victims and a different mobile phone used in the offense, is difficult to regard as electronic information having a concrete and individual nexus with the criminal facts that prompted the seizure pursuant to voluntary submission (the 2014 offense); therefore, insofar as the investigative agency acquired it without a prior warrant, it lacks evidentiary admissibility, and this does not change even if the seizure procedure was later carried out after obtaining a seizure and search warrant.\\n\\n3) Although some parts of the reasons for the lower court’s judgment are somewhat inapt, the lower court’s conclusion, which reversed the first-instance judgment that had found the 2013 offense guilty and instead found the Defendant not guilty, is acceptable on the grounds that the video discovered in relation to the 2013 offense, as illegally obtained evidence, lacks evidentiary admissibility as evidence of the 2013 offense even if it was seized after subsequently obtaining a seizure and search warrant, and that derivative evidence based thereon also lacks evidentiary admissibility. There is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the limitation of the scope of submission of electronic information according to the submitter’s intent in the seizure of voluntarily submitted items that are information storage media, or the requirements for recognizing the evidentiary admissibility of voluntarily submitted electronic information.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed in its entirety, and it is so adjudged as stated in the Disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2020DO10729]": "We deliberate on the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. a. When an investigative agency executes a search-and-seizure warrant, the person from whom the items were seized or defense counsel may participate in the execution (Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act). Even where, in the course of searching and seizing a storage medium, exceptional circumstances are recognized in which it is impossible to limit the scope and perform printing or copying, or it is markedly difficult to achieve the purpose of seizure, and therefore the storage medium containing electronic information, or the form of a hard copy or imaging, etc. (hereinafter referred to as a “duplicate”), is taken to the investigative agency’s office or the like for copying, searching, and printing, the principles of warrant requirement and due process must be observed by guaranteeing the opportunity of participation to the person from whom the items were seized or defense counsel and by taking appropriate measures to prevent arbitrary copying of electronic information unrelated to the facts of the suspected offense. If such measures were not taken, then, unless there are special circumstances, such as where the side of the person from whom the items were seized expressly indicated an intention not to participate in the above procedure or process, or where, in light of the nature and content of the process in which the procedural violation occurred, it cannot be said that the purpose of guaranteeing participation to the person from whom the items were seized was substantially infringed, the seizure and search cannot be deemed lawful. The same applies even where the investigative agency copied or printed only the electronic information related to the facts of suspicion from the storage medium or duplicate (see the Supreme Court en banc decision dated July 16, 2015, 2011MO1839, the Supreme Court judgment dated September 21, 2017, 2015DO12400, etc.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, the defense counsel’s right to participate, as prescribed in Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act, is an inherent right granted to defense counsel for the protection of the person from whom the items were seized. Accordingly, even if the person from whom the items were seized expressly indicated to the investigative agency an intention not to participate in the execution of the search-and-seizure warrant, unless there are special circumstances, the defense counsel must separately be guaranteed an opportunity to participate in the execution of the search-and-seizure warrant by means such as prior notification of the time and place of execution pursuant to Articles 219 and 122 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nb. Article 308-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “evidence collected not in accordance with lawful procedures shall not be admissible as evidence.” This expressly sets forth the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence in order to suppress and prevent recurrence of unlawful acts in the course of investigation, including unlawful seizure and search, and thereby to realize the constitutional ideal of guaranteeing the fundamental human rights of the people (see the Supreme Court judgment dated March 14, 2013, 2010DO2094, and the Supreme Court judgment dated July 11, 2019, 2018DO20504, etc.). Article 12 of the Constitution declares the due process and warrant requirement principles regarding seizure and search in order to guarantee fundamental human rights, and the Criminal Procedure Act, inheriting this, establishes specific standards concerning seizure-and-search procedures so as to harmoniously realize the principles of discovering substantive truth and protecting individual rights. Since it is necessary to firmly maintain the normative force of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act and to suppress unlawful acts in the course of investigation, not only evidence collected not in accordance with lawful procedures but also derivative evidence obtained on the basis thereof must be regarded as having been secured not in accordance with the lawful procedures established for the protection of fundamental human rights and thus, in principle, cannot be used as evidence for finding guilt.\\n\\nHowever, uniformly denying evidentiary admissibility merely on the ground that the evidence was collected not in accordance with the procedures prescribed by law does not accord with the purposes of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act. This is because the realization of legitimate punishment authority through the discovery of substantive truth is also an important objective and ideal that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to achieve through criminal procedure. If the investigative agency’s procedural violation does not fall under a case in which the substantive content of due process has been infringed, and rather, if it is an exceptional case in which excluding evidentiary admissibility would be assessed as producing a result contrary to the intent of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, which established procedural provisions regarding criminal procedure to seek harmony between the principle of due process and the discovery of substantive truth and thereby to realize criminal justice, then the court should regard that evidence as usable as evidence for finding guilt. Whether this applies must be determined by comprehensively considering all circumstances related to the procedural violation committed in the course of the investigative agency’s collection of evidence, namely, the purpose of the procedural provision, the content and degree of the violation, the specific circumstances and avoidability of the violation, the nature and degree of infringement of the rights or legal interests the procedural provision seeks to protect, the relationship between such rights or legal interests and the defendant, the relationship between the procedural violation and the collection of evidence, and the investigative agency’s awareness and intent. This legal principle applies equally to derivative evidence obtained on the basis of evidence collected not in accordance with lawful procedures; therefore, in exceptional cases, it may be used as evidence for finding guilt by comprehensively considering all circumstances related to the collection of derivative evidence, focusing on whether the causal link between the unlawful collection of evidence and the collection of derivative evidence has been attenuated or interrupted (see the Supreme Court en banc judgment dated November 15, 2007, 2007DO3061, the Supreme Court en banc judgment dated January 22, 2015, 2014DO10978, the Supreme Court judgment dated July 11, 2019, 2018DO20504, etc.).\\n\\n2. a. The gist of the indictment facts at issue in this case is as follows.\\n\\nThe Defendant, at an unknown time in or before 2019, in the restroom of the “○○ Karaoke Practice Room” located in Uijeongbu-si (address omitted), attached a small camera wrapped in plastic with tape to the outside of a trash can inside the toilet stall there and attached the auxiliary battery connected to the above camera to the inside of the trash can, then pressed the record button, thereby filming the buttocks and genital area of a woman whose name is unknown as she used the toilet in the above restroom; in addition, from around 2013 through around 2019, the Defendant filmed the victims using the toilet in a total of 296 instances, as listed in serial numbers 1 through 296 of the crime list stated in the appellate court’s judgment. By this, the Defendant filmed, against the will of another person, that person’s body, which may arouse sexual desire or shame, by using a camera or any other machine or device with a similar function.\\n\\nb. The appellate court held that the above portion of the indictment fell under the case where there was no proof of the criminal facts for the following reasons, and reversed the first-instance judgment that had found it guilty and found the Defendant not guilty.\\n\\n1) The investigative agency violated due process by executing the search-and-seizure warrant on October 30, 2019, in the investigative agency’s office by searching, copying, and printing the storage medium, without prior notification to the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel of the time and place of execution.\\n\\n2) Considering that at the time the Defendant was in custody and the importance of the participation procedure prescribed in Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the above violation of due process is serious in degree.\\n\\n3) Accordingly, the video capture printouts, etc. collected through the unlawful seizure and search cannot be used as evidence pursuant to Article 308-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and the Defendant’s confession is also a product based on those pieces of evidence or the sole evidence for this portion of the indictment, so it cannot be used as evidence for guilt pursuant to Article 308-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act or Article 310 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\n3. The appellate court’s above determination is difficult to accept as it stands for the following reasons.\\n\\na. According to the reasons of the appellate court judgment and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n1) On October 25, 2019, at around 09:00, Judicial Police Officer Inspector Nonindicted 1 of the Gyeonggi Uijeongbu Police Station removed from the Defendant’s residence, on the basis of the seizure, search, and inspection warrant dated October 24, 2019, issued by a judge of the Uijeongbu District Court (hereinafter referred to as “the warrant at issue in this case”), one desktop computer owned by the Defendant (hereinafter referred to as “the computer at issue in this case”) and one Galaxy Note 8 mobile phone (hereinafter referred to as “the mobile phone at issue in this case”) to the police station and seized them.\\n\\n2) At that time, the Defendant made a handwritten “V” mark and affixed his signature and seal on the portion of each confirmation form for removal of the original for the computer at issue in this case and the mobile phone at issue in this case stating, “I participated in the sealing process of the digital device/storage medium and confirmed that there was no problem with the seal, was notified that I may participate in the unsealing, acquisition of duplicates, and the searching, copying, and printing process for the digital device/storage medium or duplicate, and I will not participate in the above process.”\\n\\n3) In the first police suspect interrogation conducted immediately thereafter, the Defendant stated, “From about four or five years ago, I installed hidden cameras purchased online in the trash cans of restrooms in PC rooms, karaoke rooms, etc., and filmed women’s genital areas, and stored the videos on the hard disk of the computer at issue in this case.”\\n\\n4) On October 25, 2019, Senior Patrol Officer Nonindicted 2 of the Gyeonggi Uijeongbu Police Station searched the hard disk of the computer at issue in this case and discovered a number of video files that appeared to have been filmed by the Defendant with hidden cameras, after which he prepared an investigative report stating that purport and attached thereto photographs of the folder screen where the video files were stored.\\n\\n5) Meanwhile, on October 25, 2019, the prosecutor applied for an arrest warrant for the Defendant, and on October 26, 2019, a judge of the Uijeongbu District Court appointed Attorney Nonindicted 3 as the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel and, after conducting a pre-arrest suspect interrogation of the Defendant, issued the arrest warrant.\\n\\n6) In the second police suspect interrogation on October 29, 2019, the Defendant stated, “From around 2011 through around 2019, I installed hidden cameras in the restrooms of a total of six places, including the places of the offenses stated in the indictment facts at issue in this case, namely PC rooms, hospitals, karaoke rooms, etc., and filmed the bodies of others,” while specifying the places of the offenses by year.\\n\\n7) On October 30, 2019, Judicial Police Officer Inspector Nonindicted 1, Senior Patrol Officer Nonindicted 4, and Senior Patrol Officer Nonindicted 2 of the Gyeonggi Uijeongbu Police Station each took charge of one of the three hard disks installed in the computer at issue in this case and searched them in their office, and then each captured the playback scene of the illegal filming videos they found (one scene for each video file) and printed them together with the captured images of the relevant video file information (all of the above printouts are hereinafter collectively referred to as “the printouts at issue in this case”).\\n\\n8) However, the investigative agency did not give prior notice to the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel regarding the above process of searching and copying the computer at issue in this case and creating the printouts at issue in this case, and neither the Defendant nor the above court-appointed defense counsel participated in that process.\\n\\nb.
