Examining the above facts in light of the legal principles set forth above, even if the Defendant indicated to the investigative agency an intention not to participate in the process of searching, copying, and printing the computer at issue in this case, the investigative agency should have provided the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel with an opportunity to participate in the above procedure by notifying him or her in advance of the time and place of execution before searching, copying, and printing the storage medium, namely the computer at issue in this case, in the investigative agency’s office on October 30, 2019, but it did not do so. Therefore, the appellate court’s determination that the investigative agency executing the warrant at issue in this case violated the seizure procedure is proper, and the appellate court’s above determination does not violate the rules of logic and experience to exceed the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, nor does it misapprehend the legal principles concerning the nature of the defense counsel’s right to participate.\\n\\nc. 1) However, if all the following circumstances ascertainable through the above facts and the record are comprehensively considered, there is ample room to view that the investigative agency’s above procedural violation does not fall under a case in which the substantive content of due process has been infringed, and rather that excluding the admissibility of evidence collected through the execution of the warrant at issue in this case would be an exceptional case resulting in a consequence contrary to the intent of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, which established procedural provisions regarding criminal procedure in order to seek harmony between the principle of due process and the discovery of substantive truth and thereby realize criminal justice.\\n\\na) On October 25, 2019, the investigative agency began searching the computer at issue in this case after confirming from the Defendant, who was then the only participant entitled to participate as the person from whom the items were seized, that he did not wish to participate in the process of searching, copying, and printing the computer at issue in this case. At the time of the above search, the Defendant had already stated that “illegal filming videos are stored on the hard disk of the computer at issue in this case.”\\n\\nb) By the time the Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel was appointed, the investigative agency appears to have already proceeded to some extent with the search of the computer at issue in this case and to have grasped at least the location of the folder where the electronic information subject to seizure was stored.\\n\\nc) The Defendant’s court-appointed defense counsel did not inquire of the investigative agency about the execution status of the warrant at issue in this case or request participation in that process.\\n\\nd) At the time of execution of the warrant at issue in this case, there was no established precedent or internal guideline of the investigative agency to the effect that, notwithstanding the person from whom the items were seized having waived or refused participation, separate prior notification must be given to counsel appointed or selected after commencement of the seizure-and-search procedure.\\n\\ne) In the course of executing the warrant at issue in this case, the investigative agency seized video materials showing that the Defendant had filmed the bodies of several hundred victims through hidden cameras installed in the restrooms of PC rooms, karaoke rooms, etc. from around 2011, and indicted him for 296 of those offenses (these are the indictment facts at issue in this case). The Defendant confessed all of the above offenses before the investigative agency and in court.\\n\\n2) Accordingly, the appellate court should have carefully determined whether this case fell within the exception to the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence by comprehensively considering the circumstances surrounding the seizure and search pursuant to the warrant at issue in this case, the rules concerning seizure procedures for electronic information that were in force at the time of execution of the warrant at issue in this case, the probative purpose of the seized evidence, the circumstances leading to the procedural violation and the investigative agency’s awareness and intent regarding it, and the content and nature of the offense in this case.\\n\\nNevertheless, the appellate court, based only on the reasons stated in its opinion, concluded that the evidence collected through the seizure and search pursuant to the warrant at issue in this case could not be used as evidence of guilt and found the indictment facts at issue in this case not guilty. The appellate court’s judgment contains an error of law in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the exception to the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence and in failing to conduct the necessary review. The prosecutor’s ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the portion of the appellate court judgment concerning acquittal is reversed, and this case is remanded to the appellate court for further trial and determination of that portion, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2022DO1452]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Determination on the Prosecutor’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment, the court below found that, among the facts charged in this case, with respect to the portion under the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Sexual Crimes Punishment Act”) violation (filming, distribution, etc. by using a camera, etc.) listed in serial numbers 1 and 7 through 11 of Crime List 2 as stated in the judgment below, there was no proof of a crime and thus acquitted the Defendant. Examining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in the court below’s determination in that it did not violate the rules of logic and experience, exceed the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehend the legal principles concerning the exclusionary rule for unlawfully obtained evidence.\\n\\n2. Determination on the Defendant’s grounds for final appeal\\n\\na. Determination on the fraud count\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment, the court below found the fraud count among the facts charged in this case guilty. Examining the reasons of the judgment below in light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, there is no error in the court below’s determination in that it did not violate the rules of logic and experience, exceed the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehend the legal principles concerning the exclusionary rule for unlawfully obtained evidence, etc.\\n\\nMoreover, the assertion to the effect that there is illegality due to factual error in the fraud count against Victim B in the judgment below is being raised only at the stage of final appeal, although the Defendant did not raise it as a ground for appeal or the court below did not consider it ex officio as a matter subject to adjudication; thus, it cannot constitute a lawful ground for final appeal.\\n\\nb. Determination on the portion violating the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act (filming, distribution, etc. by using a camera, etc.) listed in serial numbers 2 through 6 of Crime List 2 in the judgment below\\n\\n1) Summary of the facts charged in this part\\n\\nFrom around March 7, 2018 to around October 6, 2019, on five occasions, the Defendant used a mobile phone camera to photograph, against their will, the bodies of the victims that could arouse sexual desire or cause a sense of shame.\\n\\n2) Determination of the court below\\n\\nThe court below found this part of the facts charged guilty for the following reasons.\\n\\na) The police searched, copied, and printed photographs and videos concerning illegal filming offenses, which had no concrete and individual nexus with the fraud offense that was the motive for the voluntary submission, from the mobile phone voluntarily submitted by the Defendant while the Defendant was under investigation on suspicion of fraud; this constitutes an unlawful seizure and search in violation of the warrant principle and the principle of due process.\\n\\nb) However, the police lawfully carried out the seizure and search procedures after obtaining from the court a seizure and search warrant for the Defendant’s illegal filming suspicion, while securing the Defendant’s right to participate, and seized from C Cloud, linked to a separate mobile phone from the voluntarily submitted mobile phone, the illegal filming photographs and videos corresponding to the results of the offense charged in this part. These are newly collected evidence different from the photographs and videos found on the voluntarily submitted mobile phone.\\n\\nc) Offending acts arising from illegal filming materials have the nature of significantly infringing the victim’s personal rights and are also subject to confiscation; therefore, there is a great need to promptly seize and search them so as to timely block the possibility of distribution of illegal filming materials and protect the victims.\\n\\nd) Accordingly, the police seizure report and detailed inventory of electronic information prepared pursuant to the execution of the seizure and search warrant (evidence list serial numbers 34 and 36), the investigative report explaining the circumstances (evidence list serial number 40), each investigative report recording the contents of calls with Victims D and E after execution of the seizure and search (evidence list serial numbers 51, 104, and 112), and the text message from Victim D (evidence list serial number 52) are subject to the exception doctrine under the exclusionary rule for unlawfully obtained evidence, and their evidentiary value is recognized.\\n\\n3) Determination of the Supreme Court\\n\\nHowever, the above determination of the court below cannot be accepted for the following reasons.\\n\\na) In light of the spirit of due process and the warrant principle that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to realize, the wording entered by a judge to specify the “articles to be seized” when issuing a seizure and search warrant must be strictly construed, and arbitrary expansive interpretation or analogical interpretation unfavorable to the person subject to seizure, etc. cannot be permitted (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on March 12, 2009, 2008DO763).\\n\\nComputer and other information-processing devices, such as computers, hard disks, and mobile phones located at the place to be searched stated in the seizure and search warrant, as storage media containing electronic information to be seized, and storage media such as remote servers connected to computer and other information-processing devices through an information and communications network although not located at the place to be searched (hereinafter referred to as “remote servers”), are distinct from each other in terms of location, administrator, and storage capacity. In order to seize and search electronic information stored in a remote server, it is necessary to access the remote server through an information and communications network using computer and other information-processing devices and to download the electronic information stored there or display it on the screen, so there is a difference in the method of seizure and search compared with electronic information stored in the computer and other information-processing devices themselves. Since electronic information stored in a remote server and electronic information stored in computer and other information-processing devices differ in content or quality, the scope of electronic information obtainable through seizure and search and the degree of infringement of fundamental rights caused thereby also differ.\\n\\nAccordingly, in order for investigative authorities to seize and search electronic information stored in a remote server in addition to electronic information stored in computer and other information-processing devices at the “place to be searched” stated in the seizure and search warrant, the electronic information stored in the remote server must be separately specified in the “articles to be seized” stated in the seizure and search warrant. If only electronic information stored in computer and other information-processing devices is listed in the “articles to be seized” stated in the seizure and search warrant, then electronic information stored in a remote server cannot be seized by using computer and other information-processing devices.\\n\\nb) From the reasons of the judgment below and the lawfully admitted evidence, the following facts can be ascertained. (1) On December 23, 2020, while investigating the Defendant on suspicion of fraud against Victim F, the police, with the Defendant’s consent, checked bank transaction details, call history, messages related to debt, and mobile phone messenger conversation history on the Defendant’s mobile phone. When the Defendant deleted the mobile phone messenger conversation history during a break, the police requested the Defendant and received the mobile phone by voluntary submission.\\n\\n(2) While searching the mobile phone voluntarily submitted, the police discovered photographs and videos suspected to be illegal filming materials in the camera folder, etc., and contacted the women presumed to be the victims to confirm that they had not consented to the taking of the above photographs and videos.\\n\\n(3) On February 18, 2021, the police obtained from the Incheon District Court a seizure and search warrant (hereinafter referred to as “the seizure and search warrant in this case”) stating as the “articles to be seized” “computer hard disks and external storage media in which photograph and video files judged to have been secretly taken of women’s bodies are stored,” as the “place to be searched” “G Building, H Unit, Yeonsu-gu, Incheon,” which is the Defendant’s residence, and as the “facts of the offense” “violation of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act (filming, distribution, etc. by using a camera, etc.), etc.”\\n\\n(4) On February 21, 2021, the police discovered and seized at the Defendant’s residence a mobile phone separate from the voluntarily submitted mobile phone (hereinafter referred to as “the mobile phone in this case”), and, using the state in which the mobile phone in this case was logged into a C account, they confirmed illegal filming materials concerning Victim E in C Cloud and seized 4 videos and 3 photographs related to the offense listed in serial numbers 2 through 6 of Crime List 2 as stated in the judgment below by downloading the selected files.\\n\\n(5) The police prepared a seizure report and detailed inventory of electronic information regarding the above seized items (evidence list serial numbers 34 and 36), and prepared an investigative report stating that illegal filming materials were discovered as a result of searching C Cloud linked to the mobile phone in this case (evidence list serial number 40). Thereafter, the police and an assistant prosecutor prepared each investigative report recording the contents of calls with Victims D and E, who stated that they had not consented to the filming (evidence list serial numbers 51, 104, and 112), and received a text message from Victim D containing the same content (evidence list serial number 52).\\n\\nc) The court below, on the premise that the execution of the seizure and search warrant in this case was lawful, found that evidentiary value was recognized for the above evidence in (5) obtained through that execution and thus found this part of the facts charged guilty.\\n\\nHowever, examining the above facts in light of the legal principles stated above, the seizure and search of the illegal filming photographs and videos stored in C Cloud using the mobile phone in this case while executing the seizure and search warrant in this case was unlawful, and the above evidence in (5) lacks evidentiary value. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) In the “articles to be seized” stated in the seizure and search warrant in this case are listed “computer hard disks and external storage media in which photograph and video files judged to have been secretly taken of women’s bodies are stored,” and in the “place to be searched” is stated the Defendant’s residence. Unless electronic information stored in a remote server is stated in the “articles to be seized” in the seizure and search warrant in this case, the “articles to be seized” stated in the seizure and search warrant in this case are limited to electronic information stored in computer hard disks and external storage media at the Defendant’s residence.\\n\\n(2) Nevertheless, the police accessed C Cloud, which corresponds to a remote server, by using the state in which the mobile phone in this case was logged into a C account, and seized the illegal filming materials found in C Cloud. Ultimately, the police seizure exceeded the scope of seizure permitted by the seizure and search warrant in this case, and is unlawful in violation of the principle of due process and the warrant principle.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, the illegal filming materials collected through the seizure and search warrant in this case constitute unlawfully obtained evidence lacking evidentiary value, and the seizure report, etc. revealing the execution circumstances of the seizure and search warrant in this case, as well as the statements of relevant persons collected by presenting unlawfully obtained evidence, also constitute derivative evidence based on unlawfully obtained evidence and thus lack evidentiary value.\\n\\nd) Ultimately, in this case, it is difficult to view this part of the facts charged as having been proved beyond a reasonable doubt based solely on the remaining evidence excluding evidence lacking evidentiary value.\\n\\ne) Nevertheless, the court below found this part of the facts charged guilty. The judgment below contains an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the validity of a seizure and search warrant and the exclusionary rule for unlawfully obtained evidence. The Defendant’s grounds for final appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n3. Scope of reversal\\n\\nThe portion of the judgment below concerning the violation of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act (filming, distribution, etc. by using a camera, etc.) listed in serial numbers 2 through 6 of Crime List 2 as stated in the judgment below must be reversed for the reasons stated above. And among the portions reversed above, the portion of the fraud count for which one punishment was imposed in a concurrent-offense relationship under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, together with the portion of the violation of the Sexual Crimes Punishment Act (filming, distribution, etc. by using a camera, etc.) listed in serial number 6 of Crime List 2 as stated in the judgment below, must also be reversed. Ultimately, the entire guilty portion of the judgment below must be reversed.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds for final appeal of the Defendant, the guilty portion of the judgment below against the Defendant is reversed, and the Prosecutor’s final appeal is dismissed. Accordingly, by unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, the Court renders judgment as stated in the dispositive part."}

{"[2022DO2960]": "The Court examines ex officio.\\n\\n1. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nWhere an investigative agency seizes and searches a storage medium containing both electronic information subject to seizure and electronic information not subject to seizure, or a copy thereof, and then moves the storage medium, etc. to the investigative agency’s office or the like and examines, copies, and prints it, during such series of processes the agency must, in compliance with the principle of warrant requirement and due process, guarantee an opportunity to participate to the party subject to seizure and search under Articles 219 and 121 of the Criminal Procedure Act (hereinafter referred to as the “seized person”) or to counsel, prepare and deliver an inventory of the seized electronic information specifying the files, and take appropriate measures to prevent arbitrary copying, etc. of electronic information unrelated to the facts of suspicion of crime. If such measures were not taken, then, unless there are special circumstances such as where the seized person expressly indicated an intention not to participate, or where, in light of the nature and content of the process in which the procedural violation occurred, it cannot be deemed that the purpose of guaranteeing procedural participation to the seized person was substantially infringed, the seizure and search cannot be regarded as lawful, and even if the investigative agency copied and printed only the electronic information related to the facts of suspicion of crime from the storage medium or copy, the conclusion is not different (see Supreme Court en banc decision dated July 16, 2015, 2011MO1839, and Supreme Court en banc judgment dated November 18, 2021, 2016DO348).\\n\\nAccordingly, evidence obtained through an unlawful seizure and search process in which the investigative agency failed to comply with the principle of warrant requirement and due process, such as by not guaranteeing the seized person an opportunity to participate or not delivering an inventory of the seized electronic information, constitutes illegally obtained evidence, and its unlawfulness is not cured by the fact that a warrant was later issued by a court or that the Defendant or counsel consented to its use as evidence (see the above Supreme Court en banc judgment in 2016DO348).\\n\\n2. Course of the case\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the judgment of the court below and the evidence lawfully admitted by the court below, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n\\nA. Around April 2, 2021, a judge of the Suwon District Court issued an arrest warrant against the Defendant on suspicion of violating the Act on the Punishment of Acts of Arranging Sexual Traffic, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Sexual Traffic Punishment Act”) (arranging sexual traffic, etc.), and at the same time issued a pre-seizure and search warrant for the Defendant’s mobile phone in use and possession (including storage devices in which information on sex workers, etc. is stored), etc.\\n\\nB. Around 13:25 on April 15, 2021, a police officer belonging to the Gyeonggi Nambu Provincial Police Agency arrested the Defendant and seized the Defendant’s mobile phone (hereinafter referred to as the “mobile phone at issue”). The Defendant was admitted to custody at around 21:36 on that day.\\n\\nC. Around 09:00 on April 16, 2021, while examining the mobile phone at issue, the police officer discovered an Excel file stating sales amounts, etc. from the sexual traffic business (hereinafter referred to as the “Excel file at issue”), copied it onto a separate storage medium, printed it out, and then attached it to the investigation record of this case.\\n\\nD. However, it appears that even at the time the mobile phone at issue was being examined, the Defendant was still admitted to the police station detention room (according to the confirmation document regarding the investigation process for the Defendant, it states that the Defendant arrived at the investigation site only at around 12:38 that day and was then questioned).\\n\\nE. Around April 17, 2021, the police officer obtained a subsequent seizure and search warrant for the Excel file at issue, etc. However, there exists no objective material indicating that, in connection with the examination, copying, and printing of the electronic information in the mobile phone at issue, the time and place were notified in advance, or that the Defendant was guaranteed an opportunity to participate, or that an inventory of the seized electronic information was delivered, or that it was confirmed whether the Defendant had an intention not to participate in the process.\\n\\n3. Determination\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, when the above facts are examined, the printout of the Excel file at issue examined from the seized mobile phone at issue and the CD copying the above Excel file (which the prosecutor submitted as evidence) are electronic information that the police arbitrarily examined, copied, and printed without affording the Defendant, as the seized person, an opportunity to participate; and since there was neither delivery to the Defendant of an inventory of the seized electronic information nor confirmation of whether the Defendant had an intention not to participate in the process, they are illegally obtained evidence and thus inadmissible, and even though a seizure and search warrant was subsequently obtained and the seizure procedure was conducted, the unlawfulness is not cured.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below held that the seizure procedure concerning the Excel file at issue was lawful and recognized the admissibility of the above printout and CD; in doing so, the court below erred by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the guarantee of the suspect’s right to participate and the delivery of an inventory of seized electronic information. The court below should again examine and determine whether it can sustain the first-instance court’s finding of the facts charged based on the remaining evidence excluding the evidence lacking admissibility, and its order of collection of the amount stated in the judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without determining the Defendant’s grounds for appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the statute of limitations for prosecution is incorrect? (If there is a dispute, the answer follows precedents.)
A: Even if, after a summary order has become final and conclusive against one of the accomplices, there is a decision restoring the right to request a formal trial with respect to that order, during the intervening period the statute of limitations for the other accomplices continues to run without suspension, unless there are special circumstances.
B: The phrase “when the offender is abroad for the purpose of evading criminal punishment” in Article 253(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act is limited to cases where the offender commits a crime domestically and flees abroad for the purpose of evading criminal punishment, and does not include cases where the offender commits a crime abroad and continues to stay abroad for the purpose of evading criminal punishment.
C: If the statutory punishment is mitigated by a revision of the law after the crime, pursuant to Article 1(2) of the Criminal Act, the lighter statutory punishment applicable to the relevant criminal facts (the statutory punishment under the new law) becomes the standard for the statute of limitations period.
D: Where fraud and violation of the Attorney-at-Law Act are in a relationship of ideal concurrence, the fact that the statute of limitations for the violation of the Attorney-at-Law Act has expired does not mean that the statute of limitations for fraud has also expired.
E: The criminal act of an attempted offense terminates when the act has not been completed or the result has not occurred and the crime can no longer progress, and from that time the statute of limitations for the attempted offense begins to run.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2006DO6356]": "We review the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. As to the grounds for appeal by Defendant 1\\n\\na. Where one act constitutes multiple offenses, Article 40 of the Criminal Act merely provides that such act shall be punished as a single offense in terms of punishment; in applying the Statute of Limitations for prosecution, each offense must be separately considered. Accordingly, the offense of fraud, which is established where a person receives money or goods by deceitfully representing that he or she has the intention and ability to solicit or arrange matters concerning a case handled by a public official, and the violation of the Attorney-at-Law Act are in a relationship of simultaneous concurrence (Supreme Court Decision 2005DO8704 decided January 27, 2006), and therefore, even if the Statute of Limitations for prosecution for the violation of the Attorney-at-Law Act has expired, the Statute of Limitations for prosecution for the offense of fraud, which is in a relationship of simultaneous concurrence with that offense, does not thereby also expire.\\n\\nb. Facts constituting the elements of an offense must be recognized by strict proof, and evidence lacking admissibility is not permitted even as material for proving indirect facts from which the facts constituting the elements of an offense may be inferred or as material for recognizing auxiliary facts that bolster the probative value of direct evidence proving the facts constituting the elements of an offense (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DO5493 decided January 27, 2005).\\n\\nHowever, according to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the written statement dated July 20, 2006 and the photographs attached thereto submitted by Nonindicted Party 1 at the trial court, the written statement dated July 10, 2006 submitted by Nonindicted Party 2 at the trial court, and the fact confirmation statement dated July 10, 2006 submitted by Nonindicted Party 3 at the trial court and the receipts attached thereto, were not examined as evidence in the first instance trial or the trial court below, and Defendant 1 did not consent to their use as evidence; thus, they lacked admissibility. Nevertheless, the trial court below, by such evidence, found the facts as stated in its reasoning that bolster the credibility of the statements by Nonindicted Party 1, Nonindicted Party 4, and others, which are direct evidence concerning the criminal facts of this case against Defendant 1 (the guilty portion of the judgment below; the same shall apply hereinafter). Therefore, it can be seen that the trial court below made such unlawful ruling.\\n\\nHowever, even excluding the foregoing evidence, according to the evidence lawfully examined and admitted by the first instance judgment cited by the trial court below, the criminal facts of this case against Defendant 1 can sufficiently be recognized as guilty; therefore, the above illegality of the trial court below did not affect the result of the judgment.\\n\\nc. Accordingly, the measure of the trial court below, which maintained as is the first instance judgment that found Defendant 1 guilty of the criminal facts of this case, is ultimately justifiable, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality such as insufficiency of deliberation, violation of the rules of evidence, factual error, or misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the offense of fraud, as asserted as grounds for appeal.\\n\\n2. As to the grounds for appeal by Defendant 2\\n\\nUpon examination of the record, the measure of the trial court below, which maintained as is the first instance judgment that recognized Defendant 2 guilty of the criminal facts of this case by the evidence it adopted, is justifiable and acceptable, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality such as factual error caused by violation of the rules of evidence, as asserted as grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and part of the period of detention after the filing of the appeals is credited toward each principal sentence, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2008DO4376]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the portion of the lower court judgment dismissing prosecution\\n\\nWhere, after the commission of a crime, the statutory punishment has become lighter by amendment of the law, the lighter statutory punishment applicable to the relevant criminal facts under Article 1(2) of the Criminal Act (the statutory punishment under the new law) becomes the standard for the period of the Statute of Limitations (see Supreme Court Decision 87DO84, Dec. 22, 1987).\\n\\nThe court below held that, although the charge of violation of the Customs Act arising from the attempted customs evasion in this case corresponded, at the time of the act, to Article 6(7), Article 6(4) item 2 of the former Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (as it existed before amendment by Act No. 7767 on Dec. 29, 2005), and Article 271(2), Article 270(1) item 1 of the Customs Act, the amendment of the said Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes on Dec. 29, 2005 excluded the said crime from the scope of application of that special Act and caused it to be governed by the said Customs Act, the general law, which constitutes a case where the statutory punishment has become lighter by amendment of the law after the commission of the crime; therefore, the period of the Statute of Limitations should also be regarded as 3 years based on the statutory punishment under the said Customs Act, and on this point the court rendered a dismissal of prosecution.\\n\\nThe lower court’s such determination is proper under the legal principles stated above, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of law as alleged in the grounds of appeal; accordingly, the prosecutor’s ground of appeal on this point is without merit.\\n\\n2. Regarding the admissibility of evidence of the suspect interrogation protocol prepared by a prosecutor\\n\\nThe main clause of Article 312(1) of the former Criminal Procedure Act (as it existed before amendment by Act No. 8496 on June 1, 2007) provides: “A protocol prepared by a prosecutor recording the statement of a suspect or a person other than a suspect, and a protocol prepared by a prosecutor or a judicial police officer recording the result of an inspection, may be admitted as evidence when the genuineness of its formation is acknowledged by the statement of the original declarant at the preparatory hearing or trial date.” Here, the genuineness of formation means both the formal genuineness of formation of the protocol, such as sealing, signature, and affixation of seal, and the substantive genuineness of formation that the contents of the protocol were recorded as originally stated by the original declarant. Since, from the wording of the said statutory text, the genuineness of formation does not provide any method for acknowledgment other than “by the statement of the original declarant,” substantive genuineness of formation must also be acknowledged only by the statement of the original declarant; and this is no different even in the case of a suspect interrogation protocol prepared by a prosecutor and of a defendant who has become the accused. Accordingly, a protocol prepared by a prosecutor recording the statement of a suspect or a person other than a suspect may be acknowledged as genuine in its formation and used as evidence only when, at the preparatory hearing or trial date, not only formal genuineness of formation but also substantive genuineness of formation is acknowledged by the statement of the original declarant (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2002DO537, Dec. 16, 2004); therefore, if the substantive genuineness of formation of the above suspect interrogation protocol prepared by a prosecutor is not acknowledged, then even if the defendant’s statement recorded in that protocol was made under circumstances particularly trustworthy, it cannot be used as evidence (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DO7342, Jan. 25, 2007).\\n\\nAccording to the record, in the case of the suspect interrogation protocol prepared by a prosecutor in this case, the defendant has consistently disputed its substantive genuineness of formation from the first instance, asserting that it was prepared with a different purport from what he stated; and there is no other method to acknowledge the above substantive genuineness of formation except the statement of the defendant, who is the original declarant. Thus, even if the statement was made under “circumstances particularly trustworthy,” as alleged by the prosecutor, the above suspect interrogation protocol cannot be used as evidence; accordingly, the prosecutor’s ground of appeal on this point is also without merit.\\n\\n3. Regarding the portion of the lower court judgment of acquittal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court held that the evidence submitted by the prosecutor alone was insufficient to find that the defendant knew the actual import prices of the pepper seeds and dried red peppers in this case, and that the remittance records in this case could not be conclusively determined to constitute settlement of debts arising from transactions between residents and non-residents; accordingly, the court rendered acquittals on the counts among the facts charged in this case involving violation of the Customs Act by customs evasion in relation to the import of each pepper seed, violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes by aiding and abetting customs evasion in relation to the import of each dried red pepper, and violation of the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act in relation to each item.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the lower court’s such conclusion may be deemed proper, and there is no error of violation of the rules of evidence as alleged in the grounds of appeal; accordingly, this part of the ground of appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices of the Supreme Court."}

{"[2011DO15137]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Article 253(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “the statute of limitations is suspended by the institution of prosecution and shall commence to run from the time when a judgment of dismissal of the indictment or a judgment of lack of jurisdiction becomes final and conclusive,” and paragraph (2) thereof provides that “the suspension of the statute of limitations under the preceding paragraph with respect to one of the accomplices shall also have effect on the other accomplices, and shall commence to run from the time when the judgment in the case becomes final and conclusive.” As above, Article 253(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that the institution of prosecution against one of the accomplices suspends even the statute of limitations for the other accomplices, but as to the time when the statute of limitations begins to run again, unlike Article 253(1) above, it merely states that it is the time when the judgment in the case in which prosecution was instituted becomes final and conclusive, and does not limit it to cases where the judgment is a judgment of dismissal of the indictment or a judgment of lack of jurisdiction. Therefore, even if the running of the statute of limitations for the other accomplices is suspended by the institution of prosecution against one of the accomplices, once the judgment against one of the accomplices against whom prosecution was instituted becomes final and conclusive, the statute of limitations shall begin to run again from the time when that judgment becomes final and conclusive not only in cases where the result of the judgment is dismissal of the indictment or lack of jurisdiction as provided in Article 253(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, but also in cases of conviction, acquittal, or exempting from punishment, and the same shall apply where a summary order becomes final and conclusive.\\n\\nMoreover, the mere fact that a summary order against one of the accomplices became final and conclusive and that thereafter a decision to restore the right to request a formal trial was rendered does not, in and of itself, constitute a legal impediment preventing the prosecutor from instituting a prosecution against the other accomplices during that period, nor can any basis be found for concluding that the statute of limitations for the other accomplices is suspended during that period. Furthermore, the circumstance that the right to request a formal trial was restored cannot be deemed a ground rendering retroactively invalid the period of the statute of limitations that resumed running due to the final and conclusive summary order.\\n\\nIn addition, the reason why the Criminal Procedure Act provides that the statute of limitations is suspended with respect to the other accomplices by the institution of prosecution against one of the accomplices is that it has established an exception expanding the personal scope of the effect of the institution of prosecution; therefore, it must be construed strictly and may not be construed expansively or restrictively in a manner unfavorable to the defendant.\\n\\nAccordingly, even if, after a summary order against one of the accomplices has become final and conclusive, a decision restoring the right to request a formal trial was rendered with respect thereto, during the intervening period, unless special circumstances exist, the statute of limitations for the other accomplices shall be deemed to have continued running without suspension.\\n\\n2. According to the reasoning of the judgment of the court below and the record, the facts alleged in the instant prosecution against the Defendant are that, with respect to the forest land in this case purchased by the Defendant together with Nonindicted 1, the Defendant conspired with the said Nonindicted 1 and caused a transfer registration of ownership to be made on July 12, 2005 in the name of Nonindicted 2, the title trustee, and the statute of limitations for such offense is 5 years; that, with respect to the accomplice Nonindicted 1, a summary order was requested on June 24, 2010, and a summary order imposing a fine of 5,000,000 won became final and conclusive on October 8, 2010, and thereafter a decision restoring the right to request a formal trial was rendered on November 17, 2010; and that the instant prosecution was instituted on February 16, 2011.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal doctrine, these facts show that the statute of limitations for the Defendant was once suspended on June 24, 2010, when the summary order was requested against the accomplice Nonindicted 1, and then resumed running from October 8, 2010, when the summary order imposing a fine of 5,000,000 won became final and conclusive, and it is clear from a retroactive calculation that the 5-year statute of limitations had already expired before November 17, 2010, when the decision restoring the right to request a formal trial was rendered with respect thereto; thus, the instant prosecution against the Defendant was instituted after the statute of limitations had expired.\\n\\nOn the same reasoning, the judgment of the court below, which reversed the first-instance judgment and pronounced a judgment of dismissal in favor of the Defendant on the ground that the statute of limitations for the Defendant had expired, is proper. The judgment of the court below contains no illegality that affected the judgment by, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the suspension of the statute of limitations.\\n\\n3. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated in the decision, and it is so adjudged."}

{"[2015DO5916]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\nArticle 253(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides: “Where the offender is abroad for the purpose of evading criminal punishment, the statute of limitations shall be suspended during that period.”\\n\\nThe legislative intent of the above provision is to properly realize the punitive power by preventing the statute of limitations from running during the period of stay abroad, where the offender’s stay in a foreign country, where the judicial power of the Republic of Korea does not in substance extend, has been used as a means of flight, so that the offender may be punished (see Supreme Court Decision 2008DO4101, Dec. 11, 2008). Therefore, the “where the offender is abroad for the purpose of evading criminal punishment” as provided in the above provision is not limited to cases where the offender committed a crime in Korea and fled abroad for the purpose of evading criminal punishment, but also includes cases where the offender committed a crime abroad and continues to stay abroad for the purpose of evading criminal punishment.\\n\\nMeanwhile, here, the “purpose of evading criminal punishment” is not limited to being the sole purpose of stay abroad, and it is sufficient if it is included among the several purposes of the offender’s stay abroad. If the offender’s being abroad was a means to evade criminal punishment, it may be deemed that there was a “purpose of evading criminal punishment,” and unless there exist objective circumstances that clearly reveal the offender’s subjective intent incompatible with the “purpose of evading criminal punishment,” the “purpose of evading criminal punishment” shall be deemed to continue to exist during the period of stay abroad (see Supreme Court Decisions 2005DO7527, Dec. 9, 2005, 2011DO8462, July 26, 2012, etc.).\\n\\nThe lower court, for the reasons as stated in its holding, determined that the Defendant had stayed abroad for the “purpose of evading criminal punishment,” and did not accept the Defendant’s argument in the grounds of appeal asserting that the statute of limitations for the instant offense had expired.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the duly admitted evidence, the lower court’s determination as above is just, and there is no illegality in misapprehending the law on suspension of the statute of limitations as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2016DO14820]": "The grounds of appeal (the statements in a supplementary brief of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting a brief of grounds of appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal) are determined.\\n\\n1. Regarding Defendant 1’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. Determination on the assertion of the Statute of Limitations\\n\\n1) The Statute of Limitations runs from the time when the criminal act is completed (Article 252(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act). An attempted offender is punished when he or she has commenced the execution of a crime but has not completed the act or no result has occurred (Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act); therefore, the criminal act of an attempted offense is completed when the act has not been completed or no result has occurred and the crime can no longer progress, and from that time the Statute of Limitations for the attempted offense begins to run.\\n\\n2) The gist of the facts charged for attempted breach of trust in the course of duty in this part is that Defendant 1, as a co-representative of the Victim ○○○○○ Sales Countermeasure Committee (hereinafter referred to as the “Victim Committee”), in breach of his occupational duty, on 2006. 3. 3. obtained sales contracts for 28 officetel units on the second floor of ○○○○○ mixed-use apartment building (hereinafter referred to as “○○○○○”) and sought to obtain a property benefit by registering the transfer of ownership thereto, but failed to complete the registration of transfer of ownership and thus ended in an attempt.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the evidence duly admitted, Defendant 2, who represented Non-party 1 Co., Ltd. and Non-party 2 Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Non-party 1 Company, etc.”), the developer and constructor of ○○○○○, gave Defendant 1 sales contracts concerning 14 apartment units on the second floor of ○○○○○ on 2006. 1. 23., and gave him sales contracts concerning 28 officetel units on the second floor of ○○○○○ on 2006. 3. 3.; meanwhile, Defendant 1 on 2007. 1. 23. entered into an agreement with Non-party 1 Company, etc. to the effect that “I purchased 28 officetel units on the second floor of ○○○○○, but I will return them in exchange for receiving KRW 4 billion from Non-party 1 Company, etc.” (hereinafter referred to as the “money-payment agreement at issue”); and Defendant 1 on 2007. 2. 8. returned the sales contracts concerning 28 officetel units on the second floor of ○○○○○ to Non-party 1 Company, etc. pursuant to the above agreement. Meanwhile, this indictment was instituted on 2013. 2. 27.\\n\\n3) We examine the gist of the facts charged in this part and the above factual relations in light of the legal principles stated above.\\n\\na) The offense of attempted breach of trust in the course of duty in this part falls under a case where Defendant 1, in breach of his occupational duty to the Victim Committee, attempted to obtain a property benefit by registering the transfer of ownership in accordance with the sales contracts for 28 officetel units on the second floor of ○○○○○, but, pursuant to the money-payment agreement at issue, returned the sales contracts to Non-party 1 Company, etc. on 2007. 2. 8. and thereby became unable to proceed further with the procedures for registration of transfer of ownership concerning the 28 units on the second floor of ○○○○○, and thus ended in an attempt.\\n\\nb) In this offense of attempted breach of trust in the course of duty, the time when the criminal act was completed is when, as above, it became impossible to proceed further with the procedures for registration of transfer of ownership due to the money-payment agreement at issue and the return of the sales contracts.\\n\\nc) It is clear that this indictment was instituted before 7 years had elapsed from the date the offense of attempted breach of trust in the course of duty was completed.\\n\\n4) Although there are somewhat improper parts in the reasoning of the court below’s determination on this point, the conclusion that the Statute of Limitations had not expired at the time the indictment was filed is proper. There is no error, such as a misapprehension of the legal doctrine concerning the starting point of the Statute of Limitations, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nb. Determination on the remaining allegations in the grounds of appeal\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment of the court below in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence duly admitted, the court below properly determined that the part concerning attempted breach of trust in the course of duty and the part concerning violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Breach of Trust) among the amended facts charged in this case were guilty, based on the reasons stated in its holding. There is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, or misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the crime of breach of trust.\\n\\n2. Regarding Defendant 2’s appeal\\n\\nDefendant 2 did not submit a brief of grounds of appeal within the period prescribed by Article 379(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act (the brief of grounds of appeal submitted by Defendant 2 was received on 2017. 5. 23., after the expiration of the period), and the petition of appeal also contains no statement of reasons.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAll appeals are dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the order, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

question:
Which of the following is the correct combination of statements that are true (○) and false (X) regarding defense counsel’s assistance to a suspect? (In case of dispute, according to judicial precedents)

(a) Counsel for a suspect who has not been physically restrained may, like counsel for a suspect who has been arrested or detained, apply to participate in the suspect interrogation.
(b) A defense counsel who has participated in the suspect interrogation may object during the interrogation on the ground that the interrogation method is unlawful, but may not object on the ground that it is improper.
(c) Not only defense counsel, but also a person who has indicated an intention to become defense counsel, if it is objectively recognized that there is a possibility that such person may become defense counsel, shall not be restricted from meeting with a suspect who has been physically restrained.
(d) If a suspect has clearly expressed an intention to have defense counsel participate, but the investigative agency interrogates the suspect and prepares a suspect interrogation record without allowing defense counsel to participate without justifiable grounds, that suspect interrogation record may not be used as evidence.
(e) A judicial police officer’s disposition concerning defense counsel’s participation in the suspect interrogation may be challenged by a quasi-appeal, whereas a prosecutor’s disposition must be challenged by an immediate appeal.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2003MO402]": "1. As to Ground 1 of the reappeal\\nArticle 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that, if a person is dissatisfied with a disposition concerning detention by a prosecutor or judicial police officer, he may request the court to rescind or modify such disposition. In light of the fact that this is the sole means of objection against a disposition by a prosecutor or judicial police officer made in respect of the detention of a suspect, or during such detention, it should be deemed that not only a detention without a warrant or a disposition restricting the right of interview and communication with defense counsel or a person intending to become defense counsel, but also a disposition refusing to allow defense counsel to participate in the interrogation of a detained suspect falls within a disposition concerning detention.\\n\\nThe lower court’s decision, rendered on the premise that the disposition refusing to allow defense counsel to participate in the suspect interrogation of the respondent to the quasi-appeal was subject to a quasi-appeal, is proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality such as an error in the interpretation of the law concerning quasi-appeals, as alleged in the ground for reappeal. The argument in the ground for reappeal on this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n2. As to Ground 2 of the reappeal\\n(a) Article 27, paragraph 4 of the Constitution provides that “A criminal defendant shall be presumed innocent until a judgment of guilt has been established,” thereby declaring the principle of presumption of innocence. This principle of presumption of innocence derives from the constitutional ideal that has as its ultimate goal respect for human dignity and that seeks to protect the status of suspects and defendants, who are placed in a disadvantageous position, so that their disadvantages in criminal proceedings are limited to the minimum necessary. Detention is a system recognized only when there are particularly unavoidable reasons with respect to a suspect or defendant; however, the detention system is easily abused by investigative or judicial authorities merely for the convenience of investigation or trial, and in particular, with respect to a detained suspect, torture or assault may easily be committed, and in a detained state, the right to refuse to make statements provided in Article 12, paragraph 2 of the Constitution may not be effectively guaranteed. Therefore, in order to eliminate various harms arising from the state of physical restraint with respect to suspects and defendants who are presumed innocent, and to ensure that detention is not improperly used beyond its original purpose, the main text of Article 12, paragraph 4 of the Constitution guarantees, as a fundamental right, the right of a person subjected to physical restraint to receive the assistance of defense counsel, and at this time, “assistance of defense counsel” should be understood to mean “sufficient assistance of defense counsel” (see Constitutional Court Decision 91HEONMA111 dated 1992. 1. 28., and Decision 92HEONMA144 dated 1995. 7. 21.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, while Article 12 of the Constitution contains various provisions concerning physical restraint for the purpose of guaranteeing personal liberty, paragraph 1 thereof provides that no person shall be punished, subjected to security measures, or forced labor except by law and due process of law, thereby declaring the “principle of due process” with respect to physical restraint and punishment. The purpose of the phrase “due process” in addition to law at the beginning of Article 12 of the Constitution concerning personal liberty and admissibility of evidence is understood to mean that, in interpreting and applying the constitutional and legal provisions concerning restraint of the person, judges must exercise caution in restraining the person by interpreting and applying the Constitution and laws with priority given to the protection of individual human rights over the state’s penal power.\\n\\n(b) The right of a person subjected to physical restraint to receive the assistance of defense counsel can be realized through free interview and communication with defense counsel. Accordingly, the Criminal Procedure Act, in order to substantively guarantee this right, provides in Articles 89 and 209 for the right of a detained defendant or suspect to interview and communicate with others, while, as a means to more firmly guarantee this, Article 34 provides for the right of interview and communication between defense counsel or a person intending to become defense counsel and a defendant or suspect subjected to physical restraint. Such right of interview and communication with defense counsel for a person subjected to physical restraint is indispensable for the guarantee of human rights and preparation of a defense, and therefore, unless restricted by law, it is, of course, not of a nature that can be restricted on any pretext; furthermore, it cannot be restricted by a disposition of an investigative agency or a decision of a court (see Supreme Court Decision 91MO24 dated 1991. 3. 28., and the above-mentioned Constitutional Court Decision 91HEONMA111 dated 1992. 1. 28., etc.). Since there is no current statutory provision restricting interview and communication between a person subjected to physical restraint and defense counsel, a person subjected to physical restraint must be guaranteed and permitted to interview and communicate with defense counsel at any time, even during interrogation by an investigative agency, and any restriction or refusal thereof would amount to a restriction on the right of a person subjected to physical restraint to interview and communicate with defense counsel, and thus inevitably be unlawful.\\n\\nAlthough the Criminal Procedure Act does not yet contain an express provision that defense counsel may participate in the interrogation of a detained suspect, in light of the fact that the above-mentioned right of interview and communication is guaranteed by the Constitution and laws, as well as the constitutional provision declaring that anyone who is arrested or detained shall have the right to receive the assistance of defense counsel immediately, a detained suspect may, by analogy and application of the above provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act, demand the participation of defense counsel in the suspect interrogation, and in such case the investigative agency must be construed as being unable to refuse such request. Such construction also accords with the spirit of the Constitution, which declares the “principle of due process” with respect to physical restraint and punishment.\\n\\nHowever, even if the right of a detained suspect to demand the participation of defense counsel during interrogation is a right protected by analogous application of Articles 209 and 89 of the Criminal Procedure Act, it must be harmonized with other fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution. Since allowing the unlimited participation of defense counsel during the interrogation of a detained suspect would likewise be inconsistent with the spirit of due process declared by the Constitution, if there are special circumstances for which there is objectively clear and substantial reason to suspect that the interrogation may be obstructed or investigative secrecy may be divulged, and it is recognized that there is a need to restrict the participation of defense counsel, it is only natural that the participation of defense counsel may be restricted.\\n\\n(c) According to the record, the respondent to the quasi-appeal was a professor of philosophy at B University in Germany and had been residing in Germany. While an arrest warrant had been issued against the respondent to the quasi-appeal on 2003. 9. 18. on suspicion of violating the National Security Act, he entered the Republic of Korea on the 22nd of the same month and, from the following day, was investigated on an out-of-custody basis by the National Intelligence Service and the Seoul District Prosecutors’ Office on 13 occasions, and then, on 2003. 10. 22., a warrant of detention was issued against the respondent to the quasi-appeal, and the respondent to the quasi-appeal was confined in the Seoul Detention Center; the respondent to the quasi-appeal, when investigated on 13 occasions by the National Intelligence Service and the Seoul District Prosecutors’ Office, underwent interrogation in the presence of defense counsel, but a prosecutor of the Seoul District Prosecutors’ Office, on the 24th of the same month, issued a disposition refusing to allow the participation of defense counsel in the suspect interrogation of the respondent to the quasi-appeal despite the respondent’s request; and the reappealer asserts that the present investigation includes matters concerning other suspects and, basically, includes many confidential matters concerning national security that should not be publicly disclosed, and therefore the participation of defense counsel should not be permitted during suspect interrogation, but no materials whatsoever regarding this have been submitted.\\n\\nGiven these circumstances, although the respondent to the quasi-appeal, being in a detained state, expressly requested the participation of defense counsel in the interrogation of the respondent to the quasi-appeal, the reappealer refused to allow the participation of defense counsel, and since no materials have been submitted to establish the existence of objectively clear special circumstances where it is recognized that there is a need to refuse the participation of defense counsel, the present disposition by the reappealer refusing to allow the participation of defense counsel should be deemed unlawful.\\n\\nAlthough there is a point in the lower court’s explanation of reasons that is not appropriate, the conclusion that the prosecutor’s disposition refusing the participation of defense counsel, despite the respondent’s request, during the suspect interrogation of the detained respondent to the quasi-appeal is unlawful and therefore rescinded is proper; accordingly, the reappeal challenging this is ultimately without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the reappeal is dismissed, and it is so decided as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court involved."}

{"[2010DO3359]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Regarding the admissibility as evidence of each first police suspect interrogation protocol concerning Defendant 1, and each first police suspect interrogation protocol concerning Defendants 5, 9, 8, 10, 3, 6, 7, 4, 13, 12, and 2 (excluding each confrontation portion; hereinafter collectively referred to as the “First Protocol”)\\n\\na. The suspect’s right to remain silent, as provided in the Criminal Procedure Act, is founded on the privilege against self-incrimination under Article 12(2) of the Constitution, namely the right not to be compelled to make statements adverse to oneself in criminal matters (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision dated June 23, 1992, 92DO682; Supreme Court Decision dated August 20, 2009, 2008DO8213, etc.). In order to substantively guarantee this right, Article 244-3 of the Criminal Procedure Act, as amended by Act No. 8496 on June 1, 2007, provides in paragraph (1) that a prosecutor or judicial police officer shall, before interrogating a suspect, inform the suspect of matters such as “that the suspect may make no statement whatsoever or may refrain from making statements in response to individual questions” (Item 1), and in paragraph (2) provides that “when a prosecutor or judicial police officer has given such notice pursuant to paragraph (1), he or she shall ask whether the suspect will exercise the right to refuse to make statements, and shall record the suspect’s answer in the protocol. In such case, the suspect’s answer shall be entered by the suspect in his or her own handwriting, or the prosecutor or judicial police officer shall have the suspect affix his or her name seal or signature to the portion recording the suspect’s answer,” thereby specifically prescribing the procedure for recording the answer concerning whether the right to refuse to make statements will be exercised.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 312(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that, for a suspect interrogation protocol prepared by an investigative agency other than a prosecutor to be admissible as evidence, it must have been “prepared in accordance with lawful procedures and methods.” Here, “lawful procedures and methods” means that, in the course of preparing the protocol for the suspect, all procedures prescribed by the Criminal Procedure Act, including notice of the right to remain silent, must have been observed, and there must be no deviation in the manner of preparation of the protocol (see Supreme Court Decision dated May 24, 2012, 2011DO7757).\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing provisions, even if a judicial police officer informed the suspect that the suspect may exercise the right to remain silent and asked whether the suspect would exercise that right, a suspect interrogation protocol prepared by a judicial police officer that, in violation of the manner prescribed in Article 244-3(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, does not have the suspect’s answer concerning whether the right to refuse to make statements will be exercised entered in the suspect’s own handwriting or does not bear the suspect’s name seal or signature on the portion containing that answer cannot, absent special circumstances, be deemed a protocol “prepared in accordance with lawful procedures and methods” under Article 312(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, and thus its admissibility as evidence cannot be recognized.\\n\\nb. According to the record, in the First Protocol, although the question “Will the suspect exercise the right to remain silent?” is accompanied by the answer “No, I will make a statement,” it can be seen that the answer was not written in the handwriting of the above Defendants and that the Defendants’ name seals or signatures are not affixed in the answer section. In light of the Criminal Procedure Act provisions and legal principles discussed above, the First Protocol cannot be deemed a protocol prepared in accordance with the “lawful procedures and methods” prescribed in Article 312(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, and therefore it cannot be used as evidence. Accordingly, the lower court’s determination denying the admissibility of evidence on the premise that the First Protocol was a protocol in violation of “lawful procedures and methods” is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehending the legal principles concerning the admissibility as evidence of a suspect interrogation protocol, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. Regarding the admissibility as evidence of the second police suspect interrogation protocol concerning Defendant 5 (excluding the confrontation portion; hereinafter referred to as the “Second Protocol”)\\n\\na. According to Article 12(1) of the Constitution, no person shall be punished, subjected to security measures, or forced labor except by law and due process; and according to the main clause of Article 12(4) of the same Article, any person who is arrested or detained shall have the right to the assistance of counsel immediately. Meanwhile, Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, as amended by Act No. 8496 on June 1, 2007, provides that “a prosecutor or judicial police officer shall, upon application by the suspect or by the suspect’s defense counsel, legal representative, spouse, lineal relative, or sibling, permit counsel to meet with the suspect or, unless there is just cause, have counsel participate in the interrogation of the suspect.” Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act is intended to substantively guarantee the constitutional principle of due process and the right to assistance of counsel by securing parity between the investigative agency and the suspect in the interrogation of the suspect; accordingly, the procedure must be strictly observed.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing constitutional and Criminal Procedure Act provisions, as well as their legislative purpose, where a suspect has clearly expressed the intention to seek counsel’s participation, but the investigative agency, without just cause, interrogates the suspect without allowing counsel to participate and prepares a suspect interrogation protocol on that basis, such protocol is not only evidence in violation of “lawful procedures and methods” under Article 312 of the Criminal Procedure Act, but also falls under “evidence collected not in accordance with lawful procedures” under Article 308-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and thus cannot be used as evidence.\\n\\nb. According to the Second Protocol, even though Defendant 5 answered “Yes” to the judicial police officer’s question, “Will the suspect exercise the right to assistance of counsel?”, it appears that the judicial police officer continued interrogating Defendant 5 regarding the facts constituting the charge in the absence of counsel’s participation.\\n\\nIf the facts are as above, then although Defendant 5 clearly expressed, at the time of the police investigation, the intention to have counsel participate, the judicial police officer continued to conduct the suspect interrogation without taking measures concerning counsel’s participation and without just cause to restrict counsel’s participation; such conduct is unlawful, and the Second Protocol prepared on the basis of the interrogation result is not only a protocol in violation of “lawful procedures and methods” but also evidence collected not in accordance with lawful procedures, and thus cannot be used as evidence.\\n\\nAccordingly, the lower court’s determination denying the admissibility of evidence on the premise that the Second Protocol was unlawfully collected evidence is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehending the legal principles concerning the admissibility as evidence of a suspect interrogation protocol, as alleged in the grounds of appeal. Furthermore, even upon review of the record, it is insufficient to conclude, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, that Defendant 5 consented to the use of the Second Protocol as evidence; therefore, the grounds of appeal on this point cannot be accepted either.\\n\\n3. Regarding the admissibility as evidence of the second police suspect interrogation protocol concerning Defendant 11\\n\\nAccording to Article 312(3) of the Criminal Procedure Act, a suspect interrogation protocol prepared by an investigative agency other than a prosecutor may be used as evidence only when, at trial preparation or on the trial date, the Defendant who had been the suspect or the defense counsel acknowledges its contents. Here, “acknowledges its contents” does not mean that the contents recorded in the suspect interrogation protocol correspond to the contents of the statement, but rather means that the contents as stated correspond to the actual facts (see Supreme Court Decision dated May 26, 2006, 2005DO6271; Supreme Court Decision dated June 24, 2010, 2010DO5040, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the record, Defendant 11 has continuously denied the facts charged in this case since the court of first instance; therefore, this should be understood as not acknowledging the contents of the second suspect interrogation protocol prepared by the police, which includes a purport resembling an admission of the facts charged. Accordingly, the entry in the evidence list stating that the Defendant acknowledged the contents of the second suspect interrogation protocol prepared by the police at the first trial date of the first instance is to be understood either as an erroneous entry or as a mistaken arrangement of the protocol by treating the fact that the Defendant made such a statement as “acknowledgment of contents”; this does not make the above suspect interrogation protocol admissible as evidence.\\n\\nThe lower court’s action, in the same purport, of rejecting the admissibility as evidence of the second police suspect interrogation protocol concerning Defendant 11 is proper, and there is no illegality such as misapprehending the legal principles concerning admissibility of evidence, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. Regarding the remaining grounds of appeal\\n\\na. On the charge of breach of trust\\n\\nAccording to the record, although the prosecutor, under the heading “Alternative facts charged: Breach of Trust,” stated in the grounds for appeal that breach of trust would be added as an alternative fact charged, there is no material to find that a motion for leave to amend the indictment was subsequently filed with the court or that an oral motion to amend the indictment was made. Therefore, the assertion that the judgment below contains a misapprehension of legal principles concerning breach of trust, which was not even a subject of adjudication, cannot be regarded as a proper ground of appeal.\\n\\nb. On the charge of embezzlement in the course of business\\n\\n(1) The lower court sustained the first-instance judgment that acquitted the Defendants for the reasons stated in the judgment, namely: ① the statements recorded in each transcript, complaint, police statement protocol concerning the complainant’s representative, each police suspect interrogation protocol concerning the Defendants, among others, in the confrontation portion concerning Non-Indicted 1, each fact confirmation statement and conscience declaration, petition, each confirmation statement, and the agreement with respect to Non-Indicted 2, etc., consist of vague speculative statements or statements about the personal experiences of other drivers who were not the Defendants and speculative statements based thereon, or statements by other drivers who were not the Defendants admitting their own crimes, and thus are difficult to regard as having probative value for the facts charged in this case against the Defendants; ② although each agreement with respect to Defendants 8 and 9, etc. appears to state a purport that the above Defendants admitted their embezzlement, in light of the circumstances in which they later stated, in the investigative agency or in the courts of first instance and the lower court, that they had made statements admitting the crime under the background that Non-Indicted Company 3 Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the “Victim Company”) proposed to withdraw the complaint in this case if they confessed to the crime, it is difficult to believe the contents recorded in the above evidence as they stand; and ③ in light of the facts recognized from the respective daily operation logs, original tickets, and transportation terms, namely, that the original tickets submitted by the Defendants to the Victim Company were bound together with tickets not issued on the day the passenger boarded, as stated in the indictment in this case, the mere fact that tickets not issued on the day of operation were bound together does not establish the Defendants’ embezzlement.\\n\\n(2) However, the foregoing determination of the lower court cannot be accepted as is for the following reasons.\\n\\nFirst, according to the reasons for the lower court judgment and the evidence lawfully admitted and examined by the lower court, it can be seen that the original tickets submitted by the Defendants to the Victim Company were bound together with tickets not issued on the day of operation, as stated in the indictment in this case. It also appears that the tickets submitted in such an abnormal manner were of a considerable scale, as stated in the facts charged. Nevertheless, the lower court determined that the mere fact that such tickets were submitted to the Victim Company is insufficient to find that the Defendants’ embezzlement in the course of business was established.\\n\\nHowever, in light of the following circumstances discernible from the record, namely: ① to use the limousine airport buses operated by the Defendants, one had to purchase a ticket at the Incheon Airport ticket office on the day of boarding or directly pay the fare to the bus driver; there appears to be no method of using them through advance reservation via the Internet, etc., so the possibility that passengers handed tickets not issued on the day to the Defendants and boarded the bus appears exceedingly remote; ② the buses operated by the Defendants were long-distance limousine airport buses running not only in the Seoul and metropolitan area but also to Iksan and Jeonju in Jeollabuk-do, and are mainly used by overseas travelers who have relatively few boardings and irregular frequency of use rather than by regular passengers, so it is highly unusual for passengers to board the airport bus using tickets issued on dates other than the date of boarding; ③ the Defendants claim that there were passengers who used only part of the route during the bus operation, got off, paid only the fare for that segment, and received their tickets back from the bus driver, but according to the record, the tickets not issued on the day of operation submitted by the Defendants correspond to the operation times of airport buses previously driven by the Defendants; thus, if the Defendants’ assertion is true, the passenger who got off midway would have had to board the airport bus operated by the same driver as the driver of the airport bus previously used, when using the Victim Company’s bus again; however, since the Victim Company appears to have been operating more than 20 limousine buses per day at that time, the possibility that tickets issued
