on dates other than the day of operation were submitted in the manner asserted by the Defendants appears remote; ④ since around September 19, 2008, when the Victim Company commenced an investigation into the bundles of tickets submitted by all bus drivers, no tickets issued on dates other than the date of issuance on the day were found; in light of these circumstances, the fact that among the tickets submitted by the Defendants to the Victim Company after operating airport buses around the time stated in the indictment, many tickets not issued on the day of operation still exist is highly probative objective evidence suggesting that the Defendants embezzled the cash received from passengers as fare by failing to deposit it with the Victim Company, while submitting to the Victim Company tickets issued on other dates that they had secured in advance.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Non-Indicted 4, who was a fellow driver of the Defendants, admitted embezzlement by improper submission of tickets and gave highly detailed statements regarding the method of the crime, such as that “there were cases where the actual number of passengers was smaller than the number recorded on the group coupon, and in such cases I kept tickets corresponding to the excess number of passengers and submitted them to the company on the following day or later,” or that “there were cases where passengers boarded the bus directly at Incheon Airport without purchasing tickets and paid cash, and at that time I inserted tickets issued on other dates that I had previously possessed among the tickets issued on the day, and then embezzled the cash without depositing it to the company.” Fellow driver Non-Indicted 5 also admitted his own crime and made statements to the effect that he embezzled passengers’ boarding payments by a similar method.\\n\\nIf the circumstances are as above, the lower court should have specifically examined the ordinary method or route by which passengers purchase tickets, the process by which tickets so issued are handed to the bus drivers, including the Defendants, and then submitted again to the Victim Company, and after closely reviewing the possibility that tickets not issued on the day could be bound into a ticket bundle by means other than the Defendants’ embezzlement in the course of business, determined whether there was proof of guilt as to the facts charged in this embezzlement in the course of business. However, without reaching that point, the lower court merely concluded that proof of guilt as to the facts charged in this case was insufficient for the reasons stated in its judgment. Accordingly, the judgment below contains an error that affected the outcome by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the degree of proof in the crime of embezzlement in the course of business and by failing to conduct the necessary examination. The grounds of appeal raising this point are well founded (however, according to the record, some of the facts charged in this case show instances where the airport bus operation dates and times of the Defendants stated in the daily operation logs do not match the dates and times listed in the crime schedule of the indictment; therefore, it is noted that the lower court on remand after reversal needs to closely examine, with respect to this part of the facts charged, whether there is indeed strict proof sufficient to recognize that the relevant Defendant committed embezzlement in the course of business as stated in the facts charged).\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2013DO16162]": "The grounds for final appeal by the Defendant and the Prosecutor (including the statements in the supplemental brief on the grounds for final appeal, petition, reference materials, etc. submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds for final appeal, to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal) shall be determined together.\\n\\n1. On the grounds for final appeal alleging that the procedure for instituting prosecution is void\\nEven if the court, after having received the petition for adjudication, made a decision to institute prosecution under Article 262(2) Item 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act without notifying the suspect of that fact within the period prescribed in Article 262(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act from the date of receipt, the above error may not be contested in the merits case after the prosecution is instituted accordingly and the proceedings of the merits case have commenced, unless there are other special circumstances (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DO224 rendered on November 11, 2010, Supreme Court Decision 2012DO1741 rendered on April 10, 2014, etc.).\\nThe lower court determined, for the reasons stated in its opinion, that even if the court that had received the petition for adjudication conducted the review and made the decision to institute prosecution in this case without notifying the Defendant of that fact, the institution of prosecution in this case does not fall under a case where it is invalid as being in violation of statutory provisions.\\nThe lower court’s determination as above is proper as it is based on the legal principles stated above, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the effectiveness of instituting prosecution.\\n\\n2. On the grounds for final appeal concerning the legality of the arrest procedure for Union Member Non-Indicted Person 1\\nThe lower court, based on the following: ① the Defendant, in front of the △△ Plant of ○○ Motor Co., Ltd., surrounded 6 union members including Non-Indicted Person 2 belonging to the □□□□ Labor Union ○○ Motor Branch with riot police officers equipped with shields and prevented them from moving for 30 to 40 minutes before taking them away, and then, a short time later, prevented Non-Indicted Person 1 from moving for 10 minutes by the same method; considering the circumstances and appearance by which the above union members were unable to move, the number and demeanor of the deployed riot police officers, and the length of time such condition continued, this constituted de facto arrest rather than administrative immediate compulsion based on Article 6(1) of the Act on the Performance of Duties by Police Officers; ② at the time, Non-Indicted Person 1, surrounded by numerous riot police officers, merely raised objections and did not attempt to flee or resist by using violence, and there was no urgent standoff such that it could be deemed that a physical clash between the union and management or between union members and riot police officers was imminent; ③ while de facto arresting Non-Indicted Person 1, the Defendant did not properly inform him of the reason therefor, and only after receiving protests from the victim and others did he finally inform him of the reason for arrest, etc.; based on these circumstances, the lower court determined that the arrest of Non-Indicted Person 1 was unlawful because it failed to comply with the arrest procedure for a flagrant offender prescribed by the Criminal Procedure Act.\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the lower court’s determination as above does not contain any error of fact-finding in violation of the rules of logic and experience, any misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the requirements and procedure for administrative immediate compulsion or arrest, or any omission in judgment. The grounds for final appeal disputing this are not स्वीकारable.\\n\\n3. On the grounds for final appeal concerning whether the victim’s right of visitation and communication with counsel is recognized\\nArticle 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides, “Counsel, or a person intending to become counsel, may interview a defendant or suspect who is physically restrained and receive and deliver documents or objects, and may have a doctor provide treatment.” Therefore, even if a person who has manifested an intention to become counsel is objectively recognized as having the possibility of becoming counsel, such person may not be restricted from interviewing a defendant or suspect who is physically restrained on the ground that he or she is not a “counsel or a person intending to become counsel” under Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\nThe lower court, based on the following: ① the victim, as the chairperson of the Labor Relations Commission of ◇◇◇◇◇ ◇◇ ◇◇◇◇◇, received, on June 22, 2009, immediately before this case, an official document from the chairperson of the □□□□ Labor Union stating, “Please take appropriate measures so that prompt attorney interviews can be made possible in the event of mass arrests resulting from the strike struggle of the □□□□ Labor Union ○○ Motor Branch”; ② it was unlawful for the police to surround 6 union members including Non-Indicted Person 2 and prevent them from moving, and despite the victim’s explicit objection, the police again arrested Non-Indicted Person 1 in the same manner as the above 6 union members, and when the victim continued to object thereto, only then did the Defendant inform Non-Indicted Person 1 of the reason for arrest and the right to appoint counsel, etc., and the victim repeatedly requested the Defendant, while stating that he was a lawyer, that he be allowed to interview Non-Indicted Person 1; ③ the police did not confirm with Non-Indicted Person 1 whether he intended to appoint or interview the victim as counsel; ④ Non-Indicted Person 1 was unfamiliar with the law and did not know the victim, who was a lawyer, directly, so it would have been difficult for him to first request the victim to appoint counsel or to request an interview on the premise that he had the right of visitation and communication as a suspect under the Criminal Procedure Act; thus, there was a need for the victim, a lawyer who had received the above official document from the labor union, to proactively request an interview; and based on these circumstances, determined that the victim was in the status of a “person intending to become counsel” for Non-Indicted Person 1 and thus had the right of visitation and communication prescribed in Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and therefore the Defendant could not restrict the victim from interviewing Non-Indicted Person 1.\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above, the lower court’s determination as above is persuasive, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the right of visitation and communication of counsel or a person intending to become counsel.\\n\\n4. On the grounds for final appeal concerning whether the limits of the exercise of the right of visitation and communication were exceeded\\nThe right of visitation and communication of counsel or a person intending to become counsel must be exercised within the scope that does not infringe the inherent purpose of the system of physical restraint; therefore, if counsel or a person intending to become counsel seeks to interview a defendant or suspect beyond the limits realistically guaranteed in light of the concrete temporal and spatial circumstances, such conduct does not constitute a lawful exercise of the right of visitation and communication and cannot be permitted. However, in determining that the right of visitation and communication has exceeded such limits and is therefore impermissible, caution must be exercised so that the essential content of the right to receive assistance of counsel, which is a fundamental constitutional right of a person who is physically restrained, is not infringed upon (see Supreme Court Decision 2006MO657 dated January 31, 2007, etc.).\\nThe lower court, based on the following: ① even though the victim continuously objected to the Defendant that the arrest procedure for Non-Indicted Person 1 was unlawful, no measures were taken, so it was necessary to interview Non-Indicted Person 1 as soon as possible in order to accurately understand the details of the case and devise subsequent response measures; ② on the other hand, considering the scene at the time Non-Indicted Person 1 was arrested, there was no concern that a standoff would arise between the union and management or that a physical clash would occur between union members and riot police officers, and there were no circumstances such as the victim joining forces with other union members to help Non-Indicted Person 1 flee or to destroy evidence at the scene of the offense; thus, it could not be said that the Defendant’s acceptance of the victim’s request to interview Non-Indicted Person 1 at the arrest scene would be contrary to the inherent purpose of the arrest system; ③ if there were circumstances to deem that the arrest by the investigative agency did not comply with the procedure prescribed in the Criminal Procedure Act, a person intending to become counsel for the arrested suspect must be deemed able to protest by pointing out the illegality during the series of arrest procedures; and based on these circumstances, determined that the victim’s continued requests to the Defendant for an interview were an exercise of the right of visitation and communication as a person intending to become counsel for the arrested Non-Indicted Person 1 within the scope that does not infringe the inherent purpose of the system of physical restraint and did not exceed that scope.\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above, the lower court’s determination as above is persuasive, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the limits of, and deviation from, the right of visitation and communication of counsel or a person intending to become counsel.\\n\\n5. On the grounds for final appeal concerning whether the arrest of the victim was lawful\\nThe offense of obstruction of performance of official duties prescribed in Article 136 of the Criminal Act is established only where the public official’s performance of duties is lawful, and lawful performance of official duties here refers not only to an act falling within the abstract authority of the public official but also to a case where the legal requirements and methods for concrete performance of duties are satisfied. If a police officer arrested a flagrant offender by force even though the requirements for arresting a flagrant offender were not met, such conduct cannot be regarded as lawful performance of official duties (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DO3682 rendered on May 26, 2011, etc.).\\nThe lower court, based on the following: ① the victim, holding a lawyer identification card in his hand, repeatedly stated that he was a lawyer and lawfully requested an interview as a person intending to become counsel for the arrested Non-Indicted Person 1, but the Defendant made no response thereto, and riot police officers surrounded Non-Indicted Person 1 and took him away and put him into a van; ② when the victim continued to request an interview with Non-Indicted Person 1 and blocked the van in which the arrested Non-Indicted Person 1 was riding, riot police officers surrounded and pushed the victim, beginning a physical scuffle, and in the midst thereof, even though the victim did not use any particular physical force, the Defendant arrested the victim as a flagrant offender obstructing the police’s official duties relating to arrest and transportation only 2 to 3 minutes after receiving the request for interview; ③ not only was it apparent that the Defendant could have accepted the victim’s request for interview at the arrest scene, but even if he thought that an interview at the arrest scene was difficult, it was possible to take appropriate measures, including explaining the scene situation to the victim and guiding him that an interview could be allowed later at a police station or another place; based on these circumstances, determined that the victim could not be regarded as a flagrant offender who obstructed the police’s official duties relating to arrest and transportation, and that the Defendant, a police public official, arrested the victim without satisfying the requirements for arresting a flagrant offender was, although externally falling within the scope of police duties, substantively lacking the statutory requirements, necessity, and propriety for the performance of duties, and thus was not lawful performance of official duties. The record further shows that when the Defendant received requests for interviews with 6 union members including Non-Indicted Person 2, he did not arrest the victim as a flagrant offender, but when he received the request for an interview with Non-Indicted Person 1, he arrested the victim as a flagrant offender obstructing the police’s official duties relating to arrest and transportation even though the victim did not use any particular physical force, and that the victim was indicted not for obstructing official duties during the process of requesting an interview with Non-Indicted Person 1, but for obstructing official duties during the process of requesting interviews with the 6 persons including Non-Indicted Person 2; furthermore, it is unclear whether the act of requesting interviews with the 6 persons including Non-Indicted Person 2 was even notified as the reason for arrest at the scene at the time of the arrest of the flagrant offender.\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above, the lower court’s above determination that the Defendant’s arrest of the victim as a flagrant offender could not be regarded as lawful performance of official duties is persuasive, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the offense of obstruction of performance of official duties and the requirements for arresting a flagrant offender.\\n\\n6. On the grounds for final appeal concerning the presence or absence of intent to abuse authority, etc.\\nAlthough there is considerable room for discretion in the judgment by a prosecutor or a judicial police officer, etc. as to whether the requirements for arresting a flagrant offender are met, if, even in light of the circumstances at the time of arrest, the judgment by a prosecutor or a judicial police officer, etc. regarding whether the requirements are satisfied is markedly devoid of rationality in light of the rules of experience, the arrest must be deemed unlawful. And since the intent of a crime includes not only definite intent but also so-called dolus eventualis, which is the intent in which a person recognizes the occurrence of the result and tolerates it, if the Defendant, as a judicial police officer carrying out duties concerning restraint of the person, could sufficiently know that the requirements for arrest were not satisfied by judging, in consideration of the circumstances at the time of arrest, without being markedly devoid of rationality in light of the rules of experience, and nevertheless, recognizing that he was acting beyond the scope of his discretion and tolerating such result, arrested a person and thereby obstructed the exercise of that person’s rights, then the crime of arrest by abuse of authority and the crime of obstruction of the exercise of rights by abuse of authority are established.\\nThe lower court, based on the following: ① the Defendant had worked for more than 20 years as a police officer performing duties concerning restraint of the person, and at the time of arresting Non-Indicted Person 1, he was serving as the field commander, so he is deemed to have been familiar with the procedures for restraint of the person; ② the Defendant could sufficiently know that the arrest procedure for Non-Indicted Person 1 did not comply with the requirements for arresting a flagrant offender prescribed in the Criminal Procedure Act, and he knew that the victim, a lawyer, had pointed out the problems in the arrest procedure for Non-Indicted Person 1 and had requested an interview; ③ although it is not common to arrest a lawyer requesting an interview as a flagrant offender obstructing official duties, the Defendant arrested the victim as a flagrant offender obstructing official duties without going through procedures such as reporting the situation to his superiors and waiting for instructions, unlike when he had previously arrested other union members; and based on these circumstances, determined that the Defendant, as a judicial police officer who performs duties concerning restraint of the person, abused his authority to arrest the victim and obstructed the victim’s exercise of rights, and that the Defendant at least had dolus eventualis in recognizing that the act of arresting the victim lacked the statutory requirements, necessity, and propriety for the performance of duties. The lower court further held that the superior’s directive allegedly followed by the Defendant when arresting the victim was merely a confirmation of the principle that official duties relating to obstruction of performance of official duties should be dealt with strictly, and rejected the Defendant’s argument that there was no possibility of expecting lawful conduct because he arrested the victim as a flagrant offender under his responsibility as the field commander.\\nIn light of the legal principles and the record stated above, it cannot be said that the lower court’s determination as above contains any error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning intent to abuse authority, foreseeability of lawful conduct, and grounds for retrial, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n7. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question:
Which of the following statements concerning retrial are correct? (Where there is dispute, according to case law)

(a) In Article 420, item 5 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the phrase “when evidence newly discovered” for recognizing acquittal, etc. means the time when evidence that could not be discovered in the procedural proceedings of the final and conclusive judgment subject to retrial, or even if discovered could not have been submitted, is newly discovered or first becomes capable of being submitted.
(b) Because the Criminal Procedure Act imposes no time limit on the filing period for a petition for retrial, even if there is a dismissal decision on the ground that the petition for retrial violated the legal form, if the petitioner cures the defect, the petitioner may file a petition for retrial again on the same ground.
(c) The court that receives a petition for retrial may, when it deems necessary, conduct ex officio a factual investigation into the grounds for the petition pursuant to Article 431 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and the parties to the proceedings have the right to request such factual investigation from the court.
(d) Because a petitioner for retrial may withdraw the petition for retrial pursuant to Article 429(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, withdrawal of a petition for retrial is permitted even after the retrial court has pronounced the retrial judgment.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2005MO472]": "The grounds for the re-appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. On Ground 1 for the Re-Appeal\\n\\na. Article 420, item 5 of the Criminal Procedure Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Provision at Issue”) provides, as one ground for retrial, that “where, with respect to a person who has been sentenced to guilt, evidence clearly establishing acquittal or dismissal, or with respect to a person who has been sentenced to punishment, evidence clearly establishing exemption from punishment or a lesser offense than that recognized in the original judgment, has been newly discovered.” This is one of the grounds for retrial and, among them, a so-called new-evidence retrial ground based on the emergence of new evidence after the judgment has become final; it requires, first, that “new evidence has been discovered” (novelty of the evidence) and, second, that the newly discovered evidence “constitutes clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc.” (clarity of the evidence).\\n\\nThe phrase “when evidence has been newly discovered” in the Provision at Issue, with respect to acquittal, etc., means a time when evidence that was not discovered in the procedural course of the final judgment subject to retrial, or, even if discovered, could not be submitted, has been newly discovered or has become capable of being submitted only thereafter. Since the Provision at Issue does not limit the scope of the standard for determining the novelty of evidence by reference to any particular person, the subject is not to be limited to the court. However, retrial is an exceptional extraordinary remedy procedure for reexamining factual determinations finalized through proceedings at the relevant instance or through appeals, and if evidence that the defendant could have submitted in the proceedings before the judgment became final were also included, the finality of the judgment could easily be denied depending on the timing of the defendant’s chosen submission of evidence, thereby harming the legal stability of criminal trials and, contrary to the Constitution’s purpose of designating the Supreme Court as the court of last resort, potentially leading to the result of allowing retrial as a fourth instance. Therefore, where a defendant has petitioned for retrial, if there was negligence in failing to submit such evidence during the proceedings of the final judgment subject to retrial, it is reasonable to interpret that such evidence is excluded from the “when evidence has been newly discovered” under the Provision at Issue (see Supreme Court Decision dated October 31, 1963, 63RO6; Supreme Court Decision dated June 11, 1966, 66MO24; Supreme Court Decision dated February 11, 1987, 86MO22; Supreme Court Decision dated November 8, 1995, 95MO67; Supreme Court Decision dated January 16, 1997, 95MO38; Supreme Court Decision dated August 11, 1999, 99MO93, etc.).\\n\\nAlso, in determining whether evidence qualifies as “clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc.,” the court should not consider only the newly discovered evidence independently and in isolation, and decide whether to commence retrial solely on the basis of that evidence’s probative value; rather, among the evidence on which the court that rendered the final judgment subject to retrial relied as the basis for its factual finding, those pieces that are organically closely related to, and contradictory with, the newly discovered evidence must be considered and evaluated together. If, as a result, there is recognized a high degree of probability to the extent that the final judgment subject to retrial, which is a conviction, cannot be maintained as it stands, beyond merely giving rise to doubt as to its correctness, then such new evidence shall be deemed to constitute “clear evidence” under the Provision at Issue. If the court were to evaluate and determine clarity only by independently and in isolation considering the newly discovered evidence, retrial would be allowed only in cases where the evidence itself has clear probative value sufficient to establish acquittal, etc., and the grounds for retrial would be unduly restricted. This is because that would run counter to the purpose of the retrial system, which, by establishing as a ground for retrial the “newly discovered clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc.,” seeks to reexamine the matter under changed evidentiary circumstances brought about by new evidence and thereby seek the substantive truth.\\n\\nIn contrast, Supreme Court Decision dated November 5, 1990, 90MO50; Supreme Court Decision dated September 10, 1991, 91MO45; Supreme Court Decision dated August 11, 1999, 99MO93, etc., which determined whether evidence constituted “clear evidence establishing acquittal” based only on the probative value of the newly discovered evidence, shall be altered to the extent they conflict with the foregoing legal principle.\\n\\nb. The court below held that, in the record of the case subject to retrial, the court that rendered the judgment subject to retrial recognized as guilty the criminal facts that the Re-appellant (the Defendant, hereinafter referred to as the “Re-appellant”) raped the victim while carrying a dangerous object, and so on, and it premised that the perpetrator in this case was azoospermic. However, after the judgment subject to retrial became final, semen test results for the Re-appellant revealed that the Re-appellant was not azoospermic. Accordingly, in response to the Re-appellant’s argument that the final judgment subject to retrial contains a ground for retrial falling under the Provision at Issue, the court below determined that such ground for retrial did not exist, reasoning that the semen test results could not be regarded as evidence that could not have been submitted in the proceedings of the final judgment subject to retrial, and further that they could not be regarded as clear evidence establishing acquittal.\\n\\nExamining the reasoning of the court below’s decision in light of the foregoing legal principles, first, in determining whether the case falls under “when evidence has been newly discovered” for acquittal, etc., the court below should have first considered whether the evidence that the Re-appellant was not azoospermic was not discovered in the proceedings of the final judgment subject to retrial, and then, if it was found that the Re-appellant had discovered and knew of such evidence at that time but failed to submit it intentionally or negligently, it should have concluded that such evidence could not be regarded as novel evidence constituting a ground for retrial under the Provision at Issue. However, the court below, without even examining whether the semen test results had not been discovered in those proceedings, simply determined that they did not constitute evidence that could not have been submitted. In so doing, the court below erred by misunderstanding the law concerning the novelty requirement of evidence prescribed in the Provision at Issue and further failed to conduct review as to whether the Re-appellant had intentionally or negligently failed to submit the evidence or had been unable to submit it.\\n\\nSecond, whether the evidence qualifies as “clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc.” must be evaluated by considering together those pieces of evidence among the evidence on which the court that rendered the final judgment subject to retrial relied as the basis for factual finding that are organically closely related to, and contradictory with, the semen test results. Nevertheless, the court below disregarded such evidence and, contrary to the foregoing, judged clarity of the evidence solely by the probative value of the semen test results. This was erroneous.\\n\\nHowever, among the evidence that the Re-appellant invokes as a ground for retrial, namely the semen test results showing that he is not azoospermic, the evidence organically closely related thereto includes, among the evidence on which factual finding in the final judgment subject to retrial in the case subject to retrial was based, the response to the request for expert appraisal from the Director of the National Institute of Scientific Investigation and the investigative report of the prosecutorial officer. The content of the response to the request for expert appraisal was that a positive reaction for semen was found in the specimen collected from the victim’s body but sperm was not detected, and the investigative report stated that, in light of such response, the perpetrator was presumed to be azoospermic. However, the reason why a positive reaction for semen appeared but sperm was not detected, as stated in the response to the request for expert appraisal, may also include other causes besides azoospermia, such as various factors in the condition of the collected specimen or its preservation process, including the loss of sperm. Accordingly, the response to the request for expert appraisal alone does not allow the conclusion that the perpetrator is necessarily azoospermic, and the investigative report, which merely speculates that one of several possibilities is azoospermia, cannot be recognized as having any particular probative value. The semen test results, which are merely material capable of establishing that the Re-appellant is not azoospermic, do not have probative value such that a high degree of probability is recognized to the extent that the final judgment subject to retrial in this case cannot be maintained even when the foregoing evidence is considered together. Ultimately, they cannot be deemed clear evidence establishing acquittal in this case.\\n\\nAccordingly, the court below’s determination that the above test results concerning the Re-appellant do not fall under the ground for retrial prescribed in Article 420, item 5 of the Criminal Procedure Act is proper in its conclusion.\\n\\n2. On Ground 2 for the Re-Appeal\\n\\nArticle 420, item 7 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides as a ground for retrial that “where it is proved by a final judgment that a judge who participated in the original judgment, the prior-instance judgment, or the investigation on which such judgment was based, or a public prosecutor or judicial police officer who participated in the institution of prosecution or the investigation on which such prosecution was based, committed a crime concerning his official duties.” This applies only where there is a separate final judgment or evidence substituting for a final judgment under Article 422 of the Criminal Procedure Act concerning the fact that the original judgment was obtained through the criminal acts of such public official (see Supreme Court Decision dated August 29, 1996, 96MO72; Supreme Court Decision dated May 11, 2006, 2004MO16, etc.).\\n\\nIn light of this legal principle, the court below properly determined in this case that there was no separate final judgment or evidence substituting for a final judgment under Article 422 of the Criminal Procedure Act regarding the fact that the final judgment subject to retrial was obtained through a criminal act concerning official duties by a judicial police officer who participated in the investigation, and thus that it did not fall under the ground for retrial under Article 420, item 7 of the Criminal Procedure Act. There is no other illegality, such as a misunderstanding of the law concerning the ground for retrial under Article 420, item 7 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the re-appeal is dismissed, and the decision is rendered as follows.\\n\\nIn this decision, in relation to the interpretation of “when clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc., which is a ground for retrial prescribed in Article 420, item 5 of the Criminal Procedure Act, has been newly discovered,” there are separate opinions by Justices Kim Yeong-ran, Park Si-hwan, Kim Ji-hyeong, Park Il-hwan, Kim Neung-hwan, and Jeon Su-an regarding “when evidence has been newly discovered,” and separate opinions by Justices Kim Yeong-ran, Park Si-hwan, Kim Ji-hyeong, Park Il-hwan, and Kim Neung-hwan regarding the method of determining whether the evidence is “clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc.” In addition, the opinions of the participating Justices are unanimous, except that there are supplementary opinions by Justices Yang Seung-tae, Lee Hong-hoon, and Ahn Dae-hee concerning the majority opinion.\\n\\n4. Separate Opinion of Justices Kim Yeong-ran, Park Si-hwan, Kim Ji-hyeong, Park Il-hwan, Kim Neung-hwan, and Jeon Su-an concerning “when evidence has been newly discovered”\\n\\na. The majority opinion is that, among the grounds for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue, the evidence establishing acquittal, etc. must have been newly discovered not only by the court but also by the defendant who petitioned for retrial.\\n\\nHowever, we think it is correct to understand that whether evidence establishing acquittal, etc. under the Provision at Issue falls under “when evidence has been newly discovered” should be determined based on whether the court reviewing whether retrial should be commenced, rather than the defendant who petitions for retrial, newly discovered and came to know of it. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) The grounds for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue are unique to criminal proceedings. In civil proceedings and similar cases where the res judicata effect of a final judgment is recognized, as to matters arising before the close of oral argument at the fact-finding stage, the factual and legal relationship is determined based on the evidentiary materials submitted up to that point (the so-called “temporal scope of res judicata”), and, in principle, it is not permitted for a party thereafter to submit evidence materials that existed earlier but were not submitted and thereby dispute the factual and legal relationship (the so-called “preclusion effect” or “bar effect”). However, the ground for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue allows, even after the judgment in the prior lawsuit has become final, if there is new evidence that was not submitted in that lawsuit, to newly submit it and thereby challenge the factual finding already finalized, regardless of whether such evidence existed before the judgment became final. In other words, unlike in civil proceedings and similar cases, where based on the adversarial principle the parties bear responsibility for submitting all evidence necessary for factual determination up to the fact-finding stage and thereafter no right to newly submit evidence is recognized, it is not difficult to see that the legislative purpose of the Provision at Issue is to negate the preclusion effect of evidence submission even after the judgment has become final in criminal trials under certain conditions and thereby not to impose a temporal restriction on the res judicata effect of the final judgment.\\n\\nIt cannot be denied that, even in criminal proceedings, there is a need to promote legal stability by recognizing substantive finality following final judgment. Nonetheless, in criminal proceedings, where punishment is imposed such as deprivation of life or restriction of bodily liberty, if, even in a trial that found the defendant guilty, a clear factual error is discovered, then blocking any opportunity to correct it solely on the ground of substantive finality arising from finality of the judgment would result in an irreversible infringement of human rights against the defendant. Since the ultimate goal of criminal proceedings must fundamentally be to defend the defendant’s human rights to the maximum extent possible and to discover the substantive truth, the need to relieve even a person punished innocently can only be demanded from a perspective entirely different from that applicable in civil proceedings and the like, and within that scope the demand for legal stability must also yield to some extent. The ground for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue is, above all, most urgently required precisely for the reasons stated above, and therefore this purpose must be fully reflected in the interpretation of that provision.\\n\\n(2) The majority opinion maintains the prior Supreme Court precedents’ view that the evidence establishing acquittal, etc. prescribed in the Provision at Issue is limited not only to evidence newly discovered and learned by the court, but also newly discovered and learned by the defendant who petitioned for retrial.\\n\\nAccording to this majority opinion, it is not enough that the evidence prescribed as a ground for retrial in the Provision at Issue was newly discovered and learned by the court; simultaneously, it must also be evidence that the defendant who petitioned for retrial did not discover in the proceedings of the final judgment subject to retrial but newly discovered and learned thereafter. Thus, even if the court that rendered the judgment subject to retrial had no knowledge of the evidence at all and learned of it only after the judgment became final, evidence that the defendant had discovered in the prior proceedings and could have submitted but did not is excluded from the “newly discovered” evidence referred to here.\\n\\nHowever, as the majority opinion itself presupposes, the Provision at Issue merely states “when evidence establishing acquittal, etc. has been newly discovered” and does not limit, by the wording itself, the scope of who must have newly discovered it. To interpret, as the majority opinion does, that the evidence must have been newly discovered both by the court and by the defendant who petitioned for retrial is clearly unfavorable to the defendant, and unless there is a clear basis for such interpretation under the Criminal Procedure Act, one should not casually construe the retrial ground in a manner disadvantageous to the defendant. Also, according to the supplementary opinion of the majority opinion discussed below, if novelty were recognized merely because the court newly discovered statements by a witness that changed before and after the final judgment or written statements to that effect, that would run counter to the purpose and basic spirit of Articles 420, items 1 and 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which allow retrial only where prior evidence has been proven false by a final judgment. However, the grounds for retrial under Article 420, items 1 and 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act are all so-called “error-type” (Falsa) grounds for retrial; if documentary evidence, physical evidence, or testimony submitted as evidence in the proceedings of the prior judgment subject to retrial is proven by a final judgment to have been forged, altered, or false, that itself constitutes a serious defect in the final judgment. Accordingly, regardless of whether it affected the determination of guilt or innocence, the prior proceedings are nullified and reopened entirely anew to cure that defect. By contrast, the ground for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue is the sole so-called “new-evidence type” (Nova) ground for retrial and is intended to correct mistaken substantive factual findings that led to a final conviction. It is clear, therefore, that the two differ entirely in purpose and perspective. Accordingly, even if new evidence differs from old evidence only in its content, one cannot interpret that it must also satisfy the requirements of the grounds for retrial under Article 420, items 1 and 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act in order to be deemed novel for purposes of the retrial ground under the Provision at Issue.\\n\\nRather, a petition for retrial based on the ground for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue is allowed solely for the benefit of the person convicted by a final judgment, and the content of such petition is to seek retrial of the factual finding that convicted the defendant. Considering that such factual finding was made by the court that rendered the judgment subject to retrial based on the contents confirmed through the evidentiary materials submitted up to that time, the question whether evidence is “newly discovered” within the meaning of the Provision at Issue should be determined by whether it is different from the contents perceived by the court, through the evidentiary materials on which it relied as the basis for its guilty finding, in the proceedings of the final judgment subject to retrial.\\n\\n(3) The majority opinion cites, as the reason for interpreting the evidence referred to in the Provision at Issue as limited to evidence that the defendant did not discover, or even if discovered could not submit, despite there being no express textual basis in the Provision at Issue, that if evidence the defendant could have submitted in the proceedings before the judgment became final were also included, the finality of the judgment could easily be denied depending on the timing of the defendant’s chosen submission of evidence, resulting in harm to the legal stability of criminal trials.\\n\\nHowever, as seen in paragraph (1) above, while finality of the judgment cannot be denied from the perspective of legal stability, recognizing the ground for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue is meant to realize the ultimate goal of criminal trials—defending the defendant’s human rights—by leaving open a path for the defendant, even after the judgment becomes final, to challenge factual findings in criminal trials; and it arises from the idea that, within that scope, the demand for legal stability must yield one step. Therefore, I think that emphasizing only the aspect of legal stability and interpreting narrowly the meaning of new evidence under the Provision at Issue does not properly reflect the legislative purpose of the Provision at Issue.\\n\\nMoreover, as a general matter, restricting the temporal scope in which res judicata is recognized in final judgments to the fact-finding stage, and not allowing parties thereafter to newly submit evidentiary materials that were not submitted before, is understood to be based on the notion that, under the adversarial principle, the responsibility for submitting all evidence necessary for factual findings rests on the party bearing the burden of allegation and proof in litigation, and that a party who fails to fulfill that responsibility must bear the disadvantage. However, in criminal procedure, only the prosecutor bears the burden of proving the charged criminal facts, and the defendant is merely in a position to submit evidentiary materials necessary to impeach the evidence submitted by the prosecutor; moreover, the defendant is not even responsible for submitting such evidentiary materials. The fact that the Provision at Issue, taking into account the special nature of criminal procedure, allows the defendant to submit new evidence even after finality of judgment and thereby negates the so-called preclusion effect of final judgment is, when examined closely, premised on the understanding that the defendant has only the right to submit necessary impeachment evidence up to the fact-finding stage, and not the responsibility to submit it. Nevertheless, if one were to interpret that the defendant may no longer submit new evidence solely because he had fault for failing to submit evidence that he could have discovered and submitted in the prior proceedings, that would amount to recognizing a preclusion effect under which the defendant, despite having had a duty to submit such evidence in the prior proceedings, negligently failed to do so and therefore has no right to submit it as new evidence. This directly denies the law of burden of proof in criminal procedure and conflicts with the legislative purpose of the Provision at Issue, which excludes the finality of the judgment, and thus cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(4) It must also not be overlooked that, by excessively restricting the “novelty of evidence” prescribed in the Provision at Issue, evidence that is new and satisfies the “clarity of evidence” requirement may nevertheless be denied recognition as a ground for retrial because of the defendant’s fault presumed by the majority opinion, thereby producing results that are markedly contrary to the concept of justice.\\n\\nFor example, one may suppose a case where the defendant who petitioned for retrial discovered clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc. in the proceedings of the final judgment subject to retrial but failed to submit it due to carelessness, and the court that rendered the final judgment could have, with a little more care, examined that evidence ex officio. Even in such a case, according to the majority opinion, the evidence would be denied novelty and retrial would not be commenced. However, this result can be criticized as the court, while a clearly innocent person who should be acquitted is being deprived of the realization of justice through discovery of substantive truth, shifting all responsibility to the retrial petitioner and denying a remedy procedure for the protection of human rights, as well as excessively restricting retrial by overemphasizing the superiority of legal stability based on final judgment.\\n\\nAlso, in actual criminal proceedings, there can be many cases where it is clearly revealed that the defendant, due to ignorance, distress, rashness, and other various reasons, falsely confessed to the charged facts in place of the true offender and a judgment was finalized on that basis. As to such defendants, apart from whether criminal liability for harboring a criminal, etc. should be imposed under the Criminal Act, even if there exist evidentiary materials clearly establishing that the defendant is innocent—such as a statement withdrawing a false confession made in the prior proceedings after the judgment became final, or a statement in which the true offender confesses after the judgment became final that the crime was his own—under the majority opinion, all such evidence would necessarily be denied novelty on the ground that the defendant intentionally failed to submit it in the prior proceedings, and if the result of a conviction based on a false confession must be maintained as is, that would be contrary to substantive truth and thus inconsistent with substantive justice. Of course, as the majority opinion points out, substantive truth should be pursued through careful and faithful fact-finding within the bounds of the instance and appeals, and the legal peace and order formed by final judgments must be respected. The Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to realize this within normal criminal procedures by allowing the defendant, while presumed innocent, to receive assistance of counsel and by pursuing discovery of substantive truth through the operation of strict evidentiary rules. However, in special cases such as the above example, correcting the results of such final judgment would rather accord with the ideals of realizing justice through discovery of substantive truth pursued by the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, and with the purpose of the retrial system.\\n\\n(5) As for the ground for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue, we do not differ, in principle, from the majority opinion that retrial should not, as the majority opinion fears, become a fourth instance contrary to the Constitution’s purpose of designating the Supreme Court as the court of last resort.\\n\\nHowever, the Provision at Issue makes as a ground for retrial “when clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc. has been newly discovered,” and while the retrial proceedings concern only the factual findings in the final judgment and are still disputed within the domain of fact-finding, the Supreme Court’s role as the court of last resort appears to lie in functioning, in principle, as a court of law premised on established facts (Article 383, item 3 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “where there are grounds for a petition for retrial” may be a ground for appeal in cassation, but this merely allows such matter to be the subject of review at the stage of appeal in cassation because, for reasons such as judicial economy, it would be contrary to procedural economy to require the party to wait until the judgment becomes final after the appellate judgment and then petition for retrial; within that scope, the Supreme Court merely performs, as a matter of convenience, an additional role replacing the fact-finding function of an intermediate appellate court, and therefore this cannot be included within the Supreme Court’s inherent function as the court of cassation). Thus, it cannot be said that determining whether evidence is new solely on the basis of whether the court perceived it in the prior proceedings, and thereby allowing factual findings to be reargued after finality of judgment only as to factual issues, itself contradicts the Constitution’s purpose of designating the Supreme Court as the court of last resort.\\n\\nHowever, even if the majority opinion’s intent is to guard against the risk that retrial may function in substance as a fourth instance after the Supreme Court and that the retrial system may be abused because of the ground for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue, I think that concern may be an unnecessary apprehension. Even if one takes the position that whether evidence is new should be determined according to whether the court perceived it in the prior proceedings, that alone does not establish the ground for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue; further, the clarity requirement for evidence must also be satisfied before it can constitute a ground for retrial. Therefore, if evidence is new but not of such weight as to affect factual findings to the extent that the final judgment cannot be maintained, then expansion of the ground for retrial can sufficiently be prevented through review of the clarity of such evidence. In other words, even in a case such as the example cited by the majority opinion’s supplementary opinion below, where a witness who testified in the proceedings of the judgment subject to retrial later retracts prior statements or positions, even if novelty is recognized for such evidence, clarity requires a high degree of probability such that the final judgment of conviction subject to retrial cannot be maintained as it stands. Unless special circumstances exist, retracted testimony, etc. merely remains a matter for free evaluation of the evidence and thus clarity will be denied, and it therefore cannot become evidence constituting a ground for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue. Accordingly, determining the ground for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue through review of the clarity of evidence, rather than by a formal determination of whether evidence is novel, would prevent retrial from being denied commencement due to restriction of the ground for retrial, and in some cases would avoid results markedly contrary to the concept of justice as seen in paragraph (4) above; this also accords with the ideal of the retrial system, which designates the emergence of new evidence as one of the grounds for retrial in order to rescue the innocent.\\n\\nb. Applying this legal principle to this case, the semen test results concerning the Re-appellant, which he asserts fall under the ground for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue, are evidence discovered after the judgment subject to retrial became final and are new to the court; thus, they fall under “when evidence has been newly discovered” in the Provision at Issue. Accordingly, the court below erred in law concerning the novelty of evidence under the Provision at Issue when it determined, contrary to the foregoing, that the semen test results could not be regarded as evidence that could not have been submitted in the proceedings of the judgment subject to retrial.\\n\\nc. However, because we agree with the majority opinion that the above test results cannot be regarded as clear evidence establishing acquittal, ultimately the conclusion that the present re-appeal should be dismissed is the same as that of the majority opinion. Nonetheless, as we differ from the majority opinion as to the novelty of evidence, we state this as a separate opinion.\\n\\n5. Separate Opinion of Justices Kim Yeong-ran, Park Si-hwan, Kim Ji-hyeong, Park Il-hwan, and Kim Neung-hwan concerning the method of determining whether evidence is “clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc.”\\n\\na. The majority opinion states that prior Supreme Court precedents were incorrect in determining whether evidence qualifies as “clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc.” solely by reference to the probative value of newly discovered evidence, and that such probative value must be judged together with the old evidence on which the court that rendered the final judgment subject to retrial relied as the basis for factual findings; however, it further says that among such old evidence, only those pieces organically closely related to, and contradictory with, the newly discovered evidence are to be considered and evaluated together.\\n\\nHowever, we think it is correct not to limit the scope of old evidence to be considered in determining whether evidence qualifies as “clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc.” as the majority opinion does, but instead to consider and comprehensively evaluate together the newly discovered evidence and all old evidence adopted in the factual findings of the final judgment subject to retrial. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) First, if, as the majority opinion does, one interprets that when determining whether new evidence qualifies as “clear evidence” establishing acquittal, etc., the new evidence should not be independently and in isolation considered, then, insofar as the retrial ground referred to in the Provision at Issue lies in reexamining the factual findings of the final judgment by reason of the newly discovered evidence establishing acquittal, etc., there is no need to limit the scope, as the majority opinion does, to only those old pieces of evidence adopted in the final judgment subject to retrial that are organically closely related to, and contradictory with, the new evidence.\\n\\n(2) Furthermore, the majority opinion merely says that among the old evidence adopted in the factual findings of the final judgment subject to retrial, only those organically closely related to, and contradictory with, the newly discovered evidence should be considered and evaluated together with the new evidence, but it offers no standard for doing so. Also, from the perspective of the newly discovered evidence, the old evidence adopted in the factual findings of the final judgment subject to retrial is not only closely related to the new evidence concerning the case that is the subject of the judgment, but may also be said to be contradictory because it supports different outcomes, so the distinction is vague as well. The close relatedness or contradiction between newly discovered evidence and old evidence adopted by the final judgment appears inevitably to have to be judged concretely and individually in each actual case. Therefore, whether evidence constitutes clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc. should be determined by the court by considering together and comprehensively evaluating, according to each case, the new evidence and the evidence adopted by the final judgment, which is practically appropriate.\\n\\nb. Applying this legal principle to this case, it was erroneous for the court below to determine, without comprehensively evaluating together the above semen test results and the old evidence adopted in the factual findings of the judgment subject to retrial in this case, that it was difficult to regard the results as clear evidence establishing acquittal solely based on the probative value of those semen test results. However, the above semen test results submitted by the Re-appellant are merely material capable of establishing that the Re-appellant is not azoospermic. As the majority opinion observes, since the response to the request for expert appraisal from the Director of the National Institute of Scientific Investigation or the investigative report of the prosecutorial officer alone among the old evidence cannot necessarily conclude that the perpetrator is azoospermic, they cannot be recognized as having any particular probative value. In addition, if one comprehensively considers the old evidence adopted by the judgment subject to retrial in this case in its factual findings, or the circumstances recognized thereby—that is, that the fingerprint collected from the railing of the victim’s house, which was the perpetrator’s path of entry, matches the Re-appellant’s fingerprint, and that tools of the same kind as those used in the offense were found in the Re-appellant’s residence—then this case cannot be said to fall within a situation where, even when these evidentiary materials are comprehensively evaluated together with the above semen test results, there is recognized a high degree of probability to the extent that the conviction final judgment cannot be maintained.\\n\\nc. As stated above, although we agree with the majority opinion as to the conclusion that the present re-appeal should be dismissed, we differ from the majority opinion as to the reasons, and thus state this as a separate opinion.\\n\\n6. Supplementary Opinion to the Majority Opinion by Justices Yang Seung-tae, Lee Hong-hoon, and Ahn Dae-hee\\n\\na. Concerning the “novelty of evidence” under the Provision at Issue\\n\\n(1) The Supreme Court has previously stated that evidence constituting a ground for retrial under the Provision at Issue must be new not only to the court but also to the retrial petitioner, and that only where the defendant who petitioned for retrial is negligent in failing to submit it is it excluded from “when evidence has been newly discovered,” and the majority opinion maintains that view. In response, the separate opinion of Justices Kim Yeong-ran, Park Si-hwan, Kim Ji-hyeong, Park Il-hwan, Kim Neung-hwan, and Jeon Su-an (hereinafter referred to as the “Separate Opinion”) states that whether the case falls under “when evidence has been newly discovered” should be determined not by the defendant who petitions for retrial but by whether the court reviewing whether retrial should be commenced newly discovered and learned of it.\\n\\nHowever, the Separate Opinion’s example of a witness retracting a confession, in addition to the defendant’s retraction of a confession, may be extended to the view that even in cases where a witness who testified at the time of the final judgment retracts prior statements or positions, it should formally be deemed newly discovered when viewed from the court’s perspective, and novelty must be recognized. Yet, as explained below, such a result is improper because it nullifies the novelty requirement of evidence by judging whether the case falls under the retrial ground under the Provision at Issue only by the clarity requirement of the evidence, thereby disregarding the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act or, with respect to the ground for appeal in cassation under Article 383, item 3 of the Criminal Procedure Act, “where there are grounds for a petition for retrial,” undermining the foundation of the instance system. Therefore, I think interpretive theory that could lead to such a result is not appropriate.\\n\\n(2) Before discussing whether recognizing novelty when a defendant retracts a confession, or when a witness who testified at the time of the final judgment retracts prior statements or positions, is truly suitable for guaranteeing the defendant’s human rights, I wish to point out that this is clearly an interpretation contrary to the current Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nArticle 420 of the Criminal Procedure Act enumerates grounds for retrial restrictively, and items 1 and 2 of the same Article, unlike the Provision at Issue, regard as grounds for retrial only those cases where it is proven by a final judgment that the documents, physical evidence, or testimony, appraisal, etc. that were evidence for the original judgment were forged, altered, or false.\\n\\nIn light of the purpose of Article 420 and items 1 and 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, even if statements of witnesses changed before and after the final judgment or written statements containing such content are newly submitted as evidence, if they are regarded in formal terms as newly discovered evidence and thus as falling under the retrial ground prescribed in the Provision at Issue, that would contradict the basic spirit of those Criminal Procedure Act provisions, which intended to allow retrial only exceptionally where prior evidence was found false by a final judgment. Moreover, if such written statements, compared with before, are merely evidence that has changed in form and been altered to opposite content or attitude without substantive difference, then they should be regarded as identical to existing statements already discovered at the time of the final judgment and subjected to substantive evaluation, and thus cannot be called new evidence.\\n\\nTherefore, contrary to that, allowing retrial on the ground of retracted or altered testimony that has not been proven false by a final judgment, merely because it is new to the court and recognizing its novelty, would be difficult to defend against criticism that it formally grasps only the novelty requirement and thereby nullifies it, unjustifiably expanding the grounds for retrial contrary to the purpose of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nAlso, considering that retrial is an exceptional extraordinary remedy procedure for reexamining factual findings finalized through careful fact-finding in ordinary criminal trial procedures; that our courts currently employ strict scrutiny of testimonial evidence before adopting it as evidence of conviction; and that in Korea’s criminal justice reality there are many cases where statements by defendants and witnesses change, recognizing retracted statements as a ground for retrial would not truly serve the protection of defendants’ human rights but would merely impose unnecessary review burden on the courts, and in some cases would expose witnesses who testified in the trial process of the final judgment, including victim witnesses, to persistent inducement and threats, thereby clearly resulting in serious harm to legal stability in the criminal justice system.\\n\\nThe Separate Opinion, citing the case of a false confession, argues for recognizing novelty in the retraction of a confession as an exceptional case for an aggrieved defendant. However, in order to recognize a confession as false, there must be new evidence capable of proving the falsehood of that confession, and the defendant would thus be able to petition for retrial sufficiently on the basis of that new evidence. In other words, there is no case in which a mere fact that a confession has been retracted immediately and automatically results in recognition of a false confession; therefore, the view that an aggrieved defendant may not be relieved if novelty is denied merely because of a retraction of confession is nothing more than an unnecessary worry.\\n\\nThe Separate Opinion further explains that even if novelty is recognized for a retraction of a confession, retrial would not be casually granted due to review under the clarity requirement. However, as this decision holds, if novelty is recognized, the court will assess whether the evidence is clear enough to establish acquittal, etc., by also evaluating evidence among those adopted in the final judgment that are closely related to and contradictory with the new evidence.\\n\\nIn the end, if there is a retraction of a confession, the court seized of the retrial petition would have to review the relevant records and determine, after examining all the evidence attached to the records, whether a ground for retrial exists. As noted above, this would require the court’s ineffective review even with respect to a mere retraction of a confession, that is, a retraction without evidence to prove it, thereby leading to waste of procedure. And this would induce a defendant who peacefully endures execution of the sentence to retract a confession, thereby severely destabilizing the criminal justice order.\\n\\n(3) The Criminal Procedure Act provides as grounds for appeal in cassation “where there is a violation of the Constitution, statutes, orders, or rules that affected the judgment (Article 383, item 1 of the Criminal Procedure Act)” or “where, in a case in which death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or detention for 10 years or more (hereinafter referred to as ‘imprisonment for 10 years or more, etc.’) is imposed, there is a material misapprehension of fact that affected the judgment, or where there are significant reasons deemed grossly unjust in the determination of sentence (Article 383, item 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act).” This means that, since the probative force of evidence in criminal procedure lies within the free evaluation of judges (Article 308 of the Criminal Procedure Act), the distinction between first instance, appellate instance, and appeal in cassation means that, unless a case in which imprisonment for 10 years or more, etc. is imposed is involved, issues of factual determination should be fully heard and finalized at the first-instance and appellate stages, and the scope of review in the court of cassation is limited to violations of law.\\n\\nHowever, if, as the Separate Opinion suggests, the evidence establishing acquittal, etc. in the grounds for retrial under the Provision at Issue need only be new to the court, and if novelty is positively recognized merely because the petitioner newly submitted evidence that could have been sufficiently submitted through the appellate stage, especially statements intended to alter prior testimony or statements, then the retrial court would be compelled, for the purpose of examining clarity, to reevaluate the probative value of prior evidence related to that evidence, which is not only contrary to judicial economy but also contrary to the basic spirit of the Criminal Procedure Act, which leaves evaluation of probative value to the free conviction of the first-instance and appellate judges and restricts subsequent stages to review of legal violations when imprisonment for 10 years or more, etc. has not been imposed.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 383, item 3 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides “where there are grounds for a petition for retrial” as one ground for appeal in cassation. It appears that this provision was enacted on the understanding that it would be contrary to judicial economy and also to the concept of justice to require a party to wait until the judgment becomes final and then petition for retrial even when grounds for retrial had arisen before finality. However, if, as in the Separate Opinion, novelty were positively recognized merely because the petitioner newly submitted evidence that could have been sufficiently submitted through the appellate stage when filing an appeal in cassation, the Supreme Court would, like the retrial court, have to newly determine the probative value of prior evidence in order to examine clarity, which would be contrary to the basic spirit of the Criminal Procedure Act, which limits the Supreme Court’s review to violations of law. In addition, if novelty were permitted even where evidence is entirely worthless and a party files an appeal in cassation while asserting that it is new evidence, then the Supreme Court would have to re-determine the probative value of prior evidence, and this would effectively allow evidence or materials that merely dispute factual findings to be raised as grounds for appeal in cassation, which is highly improper.\\n\\nIn light of the purpose of Article 383, item 3 of the Criminal Procedure Act and the criminal justice policy ideals of efficiently allocating judicial resources by strengthening the functions of the first and second instances as fact-finding courts and the Supreme Court as a court of law, it is appropriate to allow the novelty requirement of evidence to function substantively, separately from the review of the clarity requirement of evidence, which necessarily involves evaluation of factual findings under the grounds for retrial prescribed in the Provision at Issue. In that sense, by interpreting that even for a defendant who has petitioned for retrial the novelty requirement must be satisfied, it will be possible to effectively weed out improper assertions of grounds for appeal that are merely intended to complain about factual findings in the prior fact-finding proceedings through the medium of retrial grounds.\\n\\n(4) The Separate Opinion also criticizes that if novelty of evidence is determined, as the majority opinion does, by reference to both the court and the defendant, then the opportunity for discovery of substantive truth through retrial is excessively restricted and protection of human rights is neglected.\\n\\nThe proposition symbolized by the legal maxim, “Even if 10 criminals go free, one innocent person must not be punished,” namely discovery of substantive truth and protection of human rights, is the fundamental starting point of democratic criminal procedure, and it needs no emphasis that our criminal procedure also stands on that foundation. This ideal must be shared by all who administer criminal justice, and cannot belong exclusively to any particular group. The majority opinion too does not disregard such an ideal; rather, its purpose is to seek a harmonious point of contact with legal stability, another major principle of the legal order, by preventing the essential efficacy of judgment, which is an indispensable element of judicial proceedings, from being impaired, or judicial order from being disturbed, by indiscriminate retrial proceedings, so long as that principle is not infringed.\\n\\nOnce a judgment becomes final, the case that was the object of adjudication is concluded and can no longer be disputed. Retrial is a procedure that returns the case to the state as if that final judgment did not exist and re-hears it; it is an extremely exceptional and extraordinary remedy that overturns the effect of a final judgment. Because of its extremely exceptional nature and because it overturns an existing judgment, retrial proceedings are mostly commenced where, after judgment, a ground clearly appears from the judgment itself that the judgment can no longer be maintained (Article 420, items 1 through 4, 6, and 7 of the Criminal Procedure Act). The Criminal Procedure Act, however, also prescribes, as a different kind of ground for retrial, the newly discovered clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc. This is understood to mean that, although after finality of judgment the established factual relationship cannot in principle be disputed, where a new piece of evidence suggests that there is a serious error in the trial comparable to other grounds for retrial, that is specially designated as a ground for retrial based on the ideals of discovery of substantive truth and protection of human rights discussed above. The reason the provision expressly requires both novelty and clarity of evidence as conditions for commencing retrial is precisely this, and it cannot be the legislative intent to easily make already finalized judgments subject to retrial merely because additional evidence exists.\\n\\nOur criminal procedure, in principle, is based on the adversarial principle, and evidence-taking is not driven ex officio. Materials not submitted or pointed out in court by the prosecutor or the defendant are difficult for the court to know about and difficult to treat as evidence. If, in such a system, whether evidence constituting a ground for retrial has been “newly discovered” is determined only by reference to the court, then even evidence already known to the defendant would fall within this category if it had not been submitted in court during the trial. In the end, the meaning of “new” would be determined by whether the defendant previously submitted it, which would not only fail to fit the wording but would in substance nullify the novelty requirement.\\n\\nAlso, in criminal procedure, the burden of proving guilt lies with the prosecutor, and the defendant is in the position of defending against it. While the defendant’s defense against the charged facts is fundamentally the defendant’s right, because many legal powers are granted to the defendant for the purpose of ensuring that defense right, it cannot be denied that the defendant also has a duty to cooperate in the trial procedure for the discovery of substantive truth. From this perspective, if the defendant already knew of evidence and could have submitted it but negligently failed to do so, that would constitute a failure to fulfill that duty. Just as, in the case of appeal, even if the appeal period expires without the defendant’s knowledge, restoration of appellate rights is not recognized unless the expiration occurred for reasons not attributable to the defendant or the defendant’s representative (Article 345 of the Criminal Procedure Act), so too the prior precedents that did not recognize novelty in such a case cannot be deemed improper.\\n\\nThe Separate Opinion worries that restricting novelty as the majority opinion does will leave protection of human rights through discovery of substantive truth insufficient. However, it is difficult to imagine a case in which the defendant knows of the existence of decisive evidence supporting acquittal and can submit it, yet fails to do so without any impediment; in almost all such cases, relief would be available on the ground that there was some impediment. As noted above, the Separate Opinion’s concern appears to be an overly theory-bound apprehension. The majority opinion seeks to prevent the deterioration of judicial justice through a valueless procedure in which all materials not submitted in court would first be treated as “new” evidence and would then undergo the further process of assessing their probative value from the record. Even if a trial is conducted only once, it is important to faithfully and thoroughly realize the ideal of human-rights protection within that procedure; repeating trials over and over does not necessarily produce a better result.\\n\\n(5) Thus, the Separate Opinion concerning novelty goes beyond the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act and amounts almost to judicial creation of law, which does not truly guarantee the defendant’s human rights but only risks shaking the foundation of the criminal justice system.\\n\\nb. Concerning the method of determining “clarity of evidence” under the Provision at Issue\\n\\n(1) The Provision at Issue merely provides as a ground for retrial “when clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc. with respect to a person sentenced guilty has been newly discovered,” and does not separately regulate how such evidence should be evaluated and determined as clear. The majority opinion, as the method of determination, departs from prior precedents that held the court should assess whether the evidence is clear enough to commence retrial solely based on the probative value of the newly discovered evidence, and instead takes the position that among the old evidence on which the court that rendered the final judgment subject to retrial relied as the basis for factual findings, those organically closely related to, and contradictory with, the newly discovered evidence should be considered and evaluated together.\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of the Provision at Issue is that the newly discovered evidence was not considered at all in the factual findings of the final judgment, and thus the question whether the final judgment can be maintained in light of the newly discovered evidence must be retried. Such a retrial would be conducted by the court comparing and evaluating, in light of the newly discovered evidence, whether the factual findings based on the old evidence in the final judgment are proper.
