However, if the court were to assess clarity by independently and in isolation considering only the newly discovered evidence, the new evidence would inevitably be limited to being itself sufficient to establish acquittal, etc., without regard to the old evidence adopted by the final judgment. Also, whether acquittal, etc. can be recognized necessarily requires comparing and evaluating the new evidence against the old evidence to determine whether there is error or contradiction in the final judgment’s factual findings. Yet to determine whether retrial should commence based only on the newly discovered evidence itself runs counter to the logical process of thinking regarding whether the retrial ground under the Provision at Issue exists.\\n\\nNevertheless, it cannot be denied that prior precedents, by taking the view that clarity of evidence under the Provision at Issue should be determined in that manner, resulted in an excessively restricted scope of retrial grounds falling under the Provision at Issue. This is contrary to the purpose of the retrial system, which, unlike the other retrial grounds in Article 420 of the Criminal Procedure Act, is based on the emergence of new evidence and should allow the court to reexamine the factual findings and evidentiary relationship of the final judgment under changed evidentiary circumstances so that, if only one innocent defendant exists, he or she is not punished. For these reasons, the majority opinion has changed the prior precedents’ view, and accordingly the determination whether evidence constitutes clear evidence establishing acquittal, etc. must be made by considering and evaluating together the newly discovered evidence and the old evidence that formed the basis of the factual findings in the final judgment. However, since the factual relationship recognized by the final judgment was established through careful fact-finding in the relevant instance or through appeals, and retrial is an exceptional extraordinary remedy procedure against that, and since retrial is divided into the retrial-commencement procedure and the subsequent trial procedure, it is appropriate that, in reviewing whether to commence retrial, the court seized of the retrial petition limit the old evidence to be reexamined to those among the old evidence that formed the basis of the factual findings in the final judgment and are organically closely related to, and contradictory with, the newly discovered evidence.\\n\\n(2) If, as a result of considering and comparing the newly discovered evidence and the old evidence among those that formed the basis of the factual findings in the judgment subject to retrial and are organically closely related to, and contradictory with, it, there is recognized a high degree of probability to the extent that the final judgment of conviction subject to retrial cannot be maintained as is, beyond merely raising doubts as to the correctness of the conviction final judgment, then such new evidence shall constitute “clear evidence” under the Provision at Issue.\\n\\nIt would not be easy to define in a single, uniform way how far the result of such comparison and evaluation must go in order to exceed mere doubt as to the correctness of the final judgment and be deemed clear enough to establish acquittal, etc. However, since this issue broadly falls within the domain of factual findings in criminal proceedings, it is necessary, by comparison with cases where a defendant appeals a factual finding already made at trial and the issue is whether the appellate court will sustain the guilty conviction, to indirectly gauge the degree of conviction required for evidence to be regarded as clear enough to establish acquittal, etc. under the Provision at Issue.\\n\\nIn the proceedings before final judgment, the defendant is presumed innocent until a guilty judgment becomes final (Constitution Article 27, paragraph 4; Article 275-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act), factual findings in the judgment must be based on evidence, and proof of criminal facts must reach the level of proof beyond a reasonable doubt (Article 307 of the same Act), while the probative force of evidence is left to the free evaluation of the judge (Article 308 of the same Act). As to first-instance judgments rendered accordingly, the Criminal Procedure Act provides as grounds for appeal that there was “a violation of the Constitution, statutes, orders, or rules that affected the judgment” or “a reason that there was a factual error that affected the judgment” (Article 361-5, items 1 and 14), thereby allowing the appellate court to review the propriety of the factual findings in the first-instance judgment. On the other hand, unlike the grounds for appeal, the Criminal Procedure Act provides as grounds for appeal in cassation only “where there is a violation of the Constitution, statutes, orders, or rules that affected the judgment” (Article 383, item 1), and, except in extraordinary cases such as “where there are grounds for a petition for retrial” or “where, in a case in which death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or detention for 10 years or more is imposed, there is a material misapprehension of fact that affected the judgment, or where there are significant reasons deemed grossly unjust in the determination of sentence” (Article 383, items 1, 3, and 4), the Code in principle does not allow arguments contesting factual error in the appellate judgment as grounds for appeal in cassation unless Article 383, item 1 applies.\\n\\nBy contrast, retrial targets a judgment that has become final as guilty after careful fact-finding through the relevant instance or through appeals, and therefore differs in the plane of its existence from the court of cassation, which reviews whether there were violations of the Constitution, statutes, etc. affecting the appellate judgment in a non-final state. Also, as stated in the wording of the Provision at Issue, newly discovered evidence must not only be capable of establishing “acquittal or dismissal” against a final conviction judgment, but must also be “clear” enough to establish that. Therefore, its structure differs from that of the court of cassation, which under the principle of presumption of innocence examines whether criminal facts were proven beyond a reasonable doubt from the perspective of whether there was a violation of the Constitution, statutes, etc. Accordingly, the result of comparing and evaluating together the newly discovered evidence and old evidence closely related to and contradictory with it must be such that it goes beyond merely disputing the relative strength of the probative force of evidence supporting or impeaching the indictment within the realm of the judge’s free conviction, and must proceed to the determination whether the final judgment of conviction can be maintained as is. At this point, if the situation is merely such that the correctness of the final judgment is doubtful, that means the result of evaluation and determination may differ depending on the court seized of the retrial petition, and thus it cannot be regarded as clear enough to establish acquittal, etc. If the degree goes beyond that, and there is recognized a high degree of probability such that maintaining the final judgment as it stands would run counter to the ideals of the retrial system—namely, relief of the innocent through discovery of substantive truth—and to the ideals of criminal justice of realizing justice thereby, then it should be regarded as clear enough to establish acquittal, etc., and only then may retrial commence.\\n\\n(3) The separate opinion of Justices Kim Yeong-ran, Park Si-hwan, Kim Ji-hyeong, Park Il-hwan, and Kim Neung-hwan is that the court seized of the retrial petition must comprehensively re-evaluate together the newly discovered evidence and the old evidence adopted as the basis for factual findings in the judgment subject to retrial.\\n\\nUnlike civil retrial, criminal retrial has a divided structure, with a procedure for reviewing whether to commence retrial separated from the trial procedure for the case subject to retrial after the decision to commence retrial. Accordingly, the court seized of the retrial petition need only carry out procedures such as fact investigation limited to the scope necessary for reviewing whether the retrial petition is well-founded, and the old evidence that formed the basis of the factual findings in the judgment subject to retrial need only be examined to the extent that it is closely related to, and contradictory with, the ground for retrial. A full review of the case subject to retrial can be conducted in the trial procedure that follows, after the retrial commencement decision becomes final, together with the prosecutor’s additional proof and the defendant’s impeachment activities, depending on the instance. In that respect, the Separate Opinion’s view that even old evidence unrelated to the basis of the retrial petition must be comprehensively reexamined all at once cannot avoid criticism for causing waste of criminal justice through unnecessary repeated review and also running counter to the bifurcated structure of retrial under the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nThe foregoing constitutes our supplementary opinion to the majority opinion."}

{"[2019MO3554]": "The grounds for re-appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. With respect to the contention that the legal principle concerning the obviousness of evidence under Article 420 Item 5 of the Criminal Procedure Act was misunderstood\\nIn light of the record, the lower court, for the reasons stated in its holding, found that the materials advanced by the petitioners for retrial as grounds for retrial did not correspond to a case in which clear evidence newly discovered that would establish innocence of the petitioners existed to such an extent that the judgment subject to retrial in this case could no longer be upheld as it stood, and on that basis it upheld the first-instance decision dismissing this petition for retrial; there is no violation of the Constitution, laws, orders, or rules that affected the judgment.\\n\\n2. With respect to the contention that there was illegality in rejecting the petitioners' application for a request for transmission of documents and failing to notify them thereof\\nWhen a court that has received a petition for retrial deems it necessary, it may, pursuant to Article 431 of the Criminal Procedure Act, conduct a factual investigation ex officio into the grounds for the petition for retrial; however, a party to the action does not have a right to request a factual investigation.\\nTherefore, even when a party applies for a factual investigation concerning the grounds for a petition for retrial, this merely means nothing more than urging the court to exercise its ex officio power; accordingly, the court need not render a judicial decision on such an application, and even if the court rejects the application, it need not notify the party thereof.\\nAccording to the foregoing legal principle, even if the lower court rejected the petitioners' application for a request for transmission of documents made as part of a factual investigation concerning the grounds for the petition for retrial and did not notify them of the result, there is no error as alleged in the grounds for re-appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, all re-appeals are dismissed, and the decision is rendered as ordered, by unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2022MO509]": "In criminal proceedings, retrial is permitted, pursuant to Article 420 and Article 421(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, with respect to final and binding judgments of conviction (a conviction at first instance and a conviction entered by the appellate court through reversal and direct adjudication) and final and binding judgments dismissing an appeal or a final appeal against a conviction. However, with respect to a judgment dismissing an appeal or a final appeal, the grounds for retrial are limited, and retrial may be sought only where there exist grounds specified in Article 420(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act (where it is proved by a final and binding judgment that documents or articles of evidence that served as evidence for the original judgment were forged or altered), Article 420(2) (where it is proved by a final and binding judgment that testimony, expert opinion, interpretation, or translation that served as evidence for the original judgment was false), or Article 420(7) (where it is proved by a final and binding judgment that a judge who participated in the original judgment, the previous judgment, or the investigation on which the judgment was based, or a prosecutor or judicial police officer who participated in the institution of the public prosecution or the investigation on which the public prosecution was based, committed an offense concerning his or her official duties) (Article 421(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act). Where, upon a penal provision, the Constitutional Court renders a decision of unconstitutionality and retrial is sought pursuant to Article 47 of the Constitutional Court Act, such ground for retrial does not fall under any of Article 420(1), Article 420(2), or Article 420(7) of the Criminal Procedure Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2015JAEDO75 dated 2015. 10. 2., Supreme Court Decision 2022JAEDO1 dated 2022. 3. 11., etc.). In other words, where there is a decision of unconstitutionality by the Constitutional Court with respect to a penal provision, retrial under Article 47 of the Constitutional Court Act must be sought against the conviction at first instance, which is the ordinary retrial-target judgment, or against the appellate court judgment that entered a conviction through reversal and direct adjudication. Where the court of first instance rendered a conviction, and an appeal was taken but a judgment dismissing the appeal or final appeal was rendered, in order to seek retrial on the ground of Article 47 of the Constitutional Court Act, the retrial-target judgment must be the judgment of first instance, and a retrial petition designating the judgment dismissing the appeal or final appeal as the retrial target is unlawful for violating the legal form and thus procedurally improper.\\n\\nThe civil appellate trial adopts the continuation-of-trial system, and the Civil Procedure Act provides that “where a judgment on the merits has been rendered in the appellate trial, no action for retrial may be brought against the judgment of first instance” (Article 451(3)). However, the criminal appellate trial, while also being a continuation-of-trial, has the character of post-review, and the Criminal Procedure Act, which applies mutatis mutandis when retrial is sought against a “final and binding judgment of conviction” pursuant to Article 47 of the Constitutional Court Act, provides that the ordinary retrial-target judgment is the “final and binding judgment of conviction” (Article 420); since a judgment dismissing an appeal or final appeal becomes final and binding and thereby renders final and binding the conviction of the court below, but is not itself a judgment of conviction, it must be treated differently from civil retrial. Meanwhile, although the Civil Procedure Act generally imposes a temporal limit on the filing of an action for retrial (Article 456), the Criminal Procedure Act does not impose any limit on the period for filing a retrial petition (see Article 427 of the Criminal Procedure Act); therefore, even if a dismissal decision is rendered on the ground that the retrial petition violated the legal form, if the petitioner cures the defect, the petitioner may file a retrial petition again on the same ground.\\n\\nThe lower court, after recognizing that the Defendant was convicted at first instance of an offense of violation of the Road Traffic Act (drunk driving), etc. (Seoul Northern District Court Decision 2020GODAN2126), filed an appeal and received a judgment dismissing the appeal (Seoul Northern District Court Decision 2020NO1962), and that the judgment thereby became final and binding, and recognizing that the retrial-target judgment for which the petitioner sought retrial was the above judgment dismissing the appeal, dismissed the retrial petition on the ground that the reason for retrial asserted by the petitioner, namely that the penal provision applied to the Defendant with respect to the part of the retrial-target judgment concerning the offense of violation of the Road Traffic Act (drunk driving), had been held unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court (a ground for retrial set forth in Article 47(4) of the Constitutional Court Act), does not fall under any of the grounds for retrial set forth in Article 420(1), Article 420(2), or Article 420(7) of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nEven upon examination of the record, there is no error in the lower court’s determination constituting a violation of the Constitution, laws, decrees, or rules that affected the judgment. Therefore, the re-appeal is dismissed, and the decision is rendered as stated in the order by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices of the Supreme Court.\\n\\n2022. 6. 16."}

{"[2023DO13707]": "We determine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Procedural History\\n\\na. The Defendant was sentenced by the court of first instance, in the case subject to retrial, to imprisonment for 2 years with suspension of execution for 3 years, etc., and the said judgment became final on 2020. 5. 29.\\n\\nb. The Defendant filed a petition for retrial with the court of first instance on 2022. 5. 9., and the order to commence retrial dated 2022. 5. 17. became final on 2022. 5. 28.\\n\\nc. The Defendant was sentenced by the court of first instance on 2022. 7. 22. to imprisonment for 1 year with suspension of execution for 2 years, and after appealing on the ground of unfair sentencing, submitted a written withdrawal of the petition for retrial on 2023. 7. 4.\\n\\nd. The court below dismissed the Defendant’s appeal on 2023. 9. 7.\\n\\n2. The Supreme Court’s Determination\\n\\na. A petitioner for retrial may withdraw the petition for retrial pursuant to Article 429(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, but after the retrial court has rendered a retrial judgment, withdrawal of the petition for retrial is not permitted. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) In criminal procedure, legal stability and formal certainty are required, and the principle of procedural maintenance applies. In particular, where there has been a pronouncement of judgment, which is the court’s final procedural act, that judgment is, in principle, presumed to be valid until it is overturned on the higher level through the formal appellate procedure and loses effect; and the court that rendered the judgment itself cannot revoke, alter, or withdraw that judgment. Likewise, where a party who sought the commencement of the relevant procedure is dissatisfied with the judgment rendered, that party may challenge it only through appellate proceedings, and may not extinguish the effect of the judgment already rendered by canceling or withdrawing the request for commencement of the procedure.\\n\\nThe Criminal Procedure Act also limits the time for a prosecutor’s withdrawal of an indictment and the time for withdrawal of a request for formal trial by the person requesting formal trial to before the pronouncement of the judgment of the court of first instance (Article 255(1), Article 454), which may be understood in the same sense.\\n\\n2) When retrial is requested, the court determines the existence of grounds for retrial in the retrial commencement proceedings, and through the retrial trial proceedings, fully rehears the case subject to retrial itself from the beginning according to the level of instance, determines guilt or innocence, fixes the sentence, and renders a retrial judgment (see the en banc Decision of the Supreme Court rendered on 2019. 6. 20. in 2018DO20698). The pronouncement of a retrial judgment is the court’s final procedural act on the petition for retrial, and a retrial judgment is no different in meaning or effect from a judgment rendered by the court in ordinary trial proceedings. Therefore, after a retrial judgment has been rendered, if there is dissatisfaction with the retrial judgment, it may be challenged only through appellate proceedings, and the effect of the retrial judgment cannot be extinguished by withdrawing the petition for retrial.\\n\\nb. Therefore, even though the Defendant withdrew the petition for retrial after the judgment of the court of first instance was rendered, the court below’s determination dismissing the Defendant’s appeal does not contain any error affecting the judgment due to a misapprehension of the legal doctrine regarding the timing of suspension of execution in a retrial case and the deadline for withdrawal of a petition for retrial.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated, as stated in the operative part."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning amendment of the indictment is incorrect? (Where there is dispute, according to precedents)
A: In light of the fact that the indirect perpetrator under Article 34(1) of the Criminal Act is punished by the same punishment as the principal offender or by a lighter punishment, even if the court, ex officio and without amendment of the indictment, applies the provision on indirect perpetration to a defendant who was indicted as a principal offender, it cannot be said that this caused substantial prejudice to the exercise of the defendant’s right of defense.
B: In the appellate trial, if, by amendment of the indictment, a case within the jurisdiction of a single judge becomes a case within the jurisdiction of a collegiate panel, the appellate court shall transfer the case, by decision, to the High Court having jurisdiction.
C: Whether the court will require the prosecutor to amend the indictment lies within the court’s discretion; therefore, the court’s failure to require the prosecutor to amend the indictment cannot be deemed unlawful.
D: Even if the victim withdraws the complaint after a complaint-based offense has been indicted, the indictment may be amended, at the first-instance trial or on appeal, to another charge that is not a complaint-based offense, within the scope in which identity with the originally indicted factual basis is recognized, and in such a case the amended factual basis must be examined and adjudicated; the same shall apply where, in an offense not punishable absent the victim’s express intention not to punish, the victim expresses an intention not to seek punishment.
E: The defendant was indicted for attempted quasi-rape in the form of an impossible attempt, but during the trial disputed the matter to the effect that there was no intent to commit quasi-rape and that the victim was not in a state of inability to resist; accordingly, even if sufficient examination had been conducted as to whether the defendant had commenced execution with intent to commit quasi-rape and whether the victim was in fact in a state of inability to resist at the time, if the indictment had not been amended to impossible attempt of quasi-rape, the court cannot ex officio recognize the factual basis of impossible attempt of quasi-rape.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2011DO2233]": "The grounds of final appeal are examined.\\n\\nIn an offense prosecutable only upon complaint, where prosecution was instituted for such an offense despite the absence of the victim’s complaint, or even though the complaint had been withdrawn, but thereafter an amendment of the indictment was permitted to a non-complaint offense for which identity with the facts charged initially prosecuted is recognized, the defect in the institution of prosecution is cured (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 96DO2151, rendered on September 24, 1996), and even after prosecution has been instituted as a complaint offense, if the victim’s complaint is withdrawn, the indictment may be amended, at the trial court of first instance or at the appellate trial, to different facts charged within the scope in which identity with the facts charged initially prosecuted is recognized, and in such a case the amended facts charged must be examined and adjudicated (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 89DO1317, rendered on January 25, 1990); the same should be deemed to apply where, in an offense subject to punishment only if the victim does not express intent to punish, there exists the victim’s expression of intent not to seek punishment or withdrawal of the expression of intent to seek punishment.\\n\\nAccording to the record, among the facts charged in this case, as to the injury inflicted on the victim, a person omitted from the record, the indictment initially stated the name of the offense as injury and the applicable provision as Article 257(1) of the Criminal Act, but the facts charged were stated as assault; the above victim expressed in the trial court of first instance an intent not to seek the Defendant’s punishment, but the trial court of first instance, by directly invoking the applicable provision and the facts charged stated in the indictment as they were, rendered a guilty judgment; and thereafter, in the court below proceeding on the Defendant’s appeal, the prosecutor filed a motion for leave to amend the indictment to change the above facts charged to injury, and the court below granted it and thereafter examined and adjudicated the amended facts charged.\\n\\nAlthough the victim expressed an intent not to seek punishment in the trial court of first instance, the court below examined and adjudicated the changed facts charged, namely, the injury, and recognized it as guilty; this is in accordance with the legal principles stated above and is proper, and there is no illegality, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning Article 327 subparagraph 6 of the Criminal Procedure Act. The assertion in this part of the grounds of final appeal is without merit.\\n\\nMeanwhile, in this case in which a fine was imposed on the Defendant, the assertion of improper sentencing does not constitute a lawful ground of final appeal.\\n\\nTherefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered in accordance with the text by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2016DO21075]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined (the statements in the supplemental brief of grounds for final appeal submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds for final appeal has expired are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\nIn light, inter alia, of the fact that an indirect principal offender is punished by the same sentence as the principal offender or by a lighter sentence, even if the court, ex officio and without amendment of the indictment, applied the provisions concerning indirect principal offenders, it cannot be said that this caused a substantial disadvantage to the exercise of the defendant’s right of defense (see Supreme Court Decision 2014DO13148, decided on 2015. 4. 23.).\\n\\nAn examination of the lower court’s course of proceedings as shown in the record and of the evidence lawfully admitted and examined by the lower court and the first instance court shows that the lower court’s determination, on the grounds stated in its opinion, that each count of fraud among the facts charged in this case, each count of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (fraud) against Victim Nonparty 1 and Victim Nonparty 2, and each count of violation of the Act on Punishment of Violences, etc. (Joint Injury) against Victim Nonparty 3 and Victim Nonparty 4, were all guilty, is proper. There is no error that affected the judgment by exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience without fully conducting the necessary examination, or by infringing the defendant’s right of defense, or by misapprehending the legal principles concerning amendment of the indictment, admissibility of evidence, co-principal, indirect principal offender, the degree of proof required in criminal trials, the period for filing a statement of reasons for appeal, etc., or by omitting a determination.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the disposition by unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2018DO16002]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Circumstances of the Case\\n\\nA. The military prosecutor indicted the Defendant on the following charge of rape.\\n\\nThe Defendant, on 2017. 4. 17. at around 22:30, while drinking at his home with the Defendant’s wife and the victim, after the Defendant’s wife fell asleep first at around 01:00 the next day and the victim also went into the master bedroom at around 02:00, followed the victim inside, touched the victim’s breasts while lying down, inserted his hand into the victim’s panties and touched her genitals, and then, after blocking the victim’s mouth as she twisted her body and made sounds in an attempt to escape the situation and removing her pants and panties, had sexual intercourse once and raped her.\\n\\nB. The court of first instance permitted the military prosecutor’s amendment to the indictment, adding the following content as an alternative count of quasi-rape.\\n\\nThe Defendant, at the date and place stated in paragraph A above, had sexual intercourse once with the victim, who was lying down intoxicated. Accordingly, the Defendant raped the victim by taking advantage of the victim’s state of inability to resist.\\n\\nC. The court of first instance, for the reason that it could not readily conclude, based solely on the evidence submitted by the military prosecutor, that there had been violence or intimidation that made resistance impossible or significantly difficult, found the principal charge of rape not guilty in its reasons and found the alternative charge of quasi-rape guilty. Only the Defendant appealed.\\n\\nD. The lower court permitted the military prosecutor’s amendment to the indictment, adding the following content as an alternative count of attempted quasi-rape.\\n\\nThe Defendant, at the date and place stated in paragraph A above, although he could not rape the victim because the victim was in fact not so intoxicated as to be incapable of resisting and thus not in a state of inability to resist, mistakenly believed that the victim was in a state of inability to resist due to severe intoxication, and had sexual intercourse once with the victim who was lying down by the same method as above. Accordingly, the Defendant attempted to rape the victim by taking advantage of the victim’s state of inability to resist, but the offense remained at the attempted stage.\\n\\nE. The lower court, for the reason that the evidence submitted by the military prosecutor was insufficient to recognize that the victim was in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist at the time of this case, found the portion of quasi-rape that had been found guilty in the court of first instance not guilty in its reasons, and found guilty the impossible attempt portion of quasi-rape added as an alternative charge. However, the portion in the alternative charge stating, “blocking the victim’s mouth as she twisted her body and made sounds in an attempt to escape the situation,” was deleted from the facts of the offense on the ground that it was an erroneous entry.\\n\\nF. Only the Defendant filed an appeal as to the guilty portion. The Defendant argues the following as grounds of appeal: 1) there was no intent for quasi-rape; 2) because the victim was in fact not in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist and the sexual intercourse was consensual, there was no possibility of the occurrence of the result of quasi-rape or risk of infringement of the protected legal interest, and therefore impossible attempt of quasi-rape is not established. We determine these matters in order.\\n\\n2. Grounds of Appeal that There Was No Intent for Quasi-Rape\\n\\nA. 1) Article 297 of the Penal Code provides, “A person who rapes another by force or intimidation shall be punished by imprisonment for a fixed term of at least 3 years.” Article 299 provides, “A person who has sexual intercourse or commits an indecent act by taking advantage of another’s state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist shall be punished in accordance with Articles 297, 297-2, and 298.” Since the Penal Code punishes, by analogy to the offense of rape, the act of having sexual intercourse by taking advantage of a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, rather than by force or intimidation, the intent for quasi-rape means the internal will to recognize that the victim is in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist and to accept the possibility of the constitutive result of having sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state.\\n\\n2) Where the Defendant denies intent, which is a subjective element of the constitutive elements of the offense, the intent itself cannot be directly proven objectively; therefore, by the nature of things, it can only be proven by proving indirect facts or circumstantial facts related to the intent. In determining what constitutes relevant indirect facts or circumstantial facts, one must do so by rationally assessing the interconnectedness of facts through meticulous observation and analytical ability based on normal rules of experience (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DO8645, decided 2006. 2. 23., etc.). Meanwhile, dolus eventualis, which is a form of intent, requires recognition of the possibility that the offense will occur, and further requires the internal will to accept the risk that the offense will occur. Whether the actor accepted the possibility that the offense would occur must be inferred from the actor’s perspective, based not on the actor’s statements but on specific circumstances such as the external form of the act and the circumstances of the act, while considering how an ordinary person would evaluate the possibility of the offense occurring (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DO74, decided 2004. 5. 14.; Supreme Court Decision 2016DO15470, decided 2017. 1. 12., etc.).\\n\\n3) In addition, although the finding of facts constituting the offense must reach proof beyond a reasonable doubt (Article 359, paragraph (2) of the Military Court Act; Article 307, paragraph (2) of the Criminal Procedure Act), the selection and exclusion of evidence and the probative value of evidence as conducted as a premise for fact-finding belong to the free evaluation of the court of fact (Article 360 of the Military Court Act; Article 308 of the Criminal Procedure Act). This means that it is within a judge’s free evaluation of evidence to adopt and use necessary evidence among admissible evidence and to find facts by assessing the substantive value of the evidence. Therefore, unless the judge rejects evidence with sufficient probative value without reasonable grounds, or conversely adopts and uses evidence that is manifestly contrary to objective facts without any reasonable basis, thereby violating the rules of logic and experience, the judge may adopt evidence and find facts through free evaluation of evidence (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DO1755, decided 2008. 5. 29.; Supreme Court en banc Decision 2013DO11650, decided 2015. 8. 20., etc.).\\n\\nB. The lower court, for the reasons stated in its opinion, determined that the Defendant had intent for quasi-rape. The argument in this part of the grounds of appeal seeks to challenge the lower court’s fact-finding and is merely criticism of the lower court’s selection of evidence and assessment of probative value, which fall within the free evaluation of the court of fact. Even in light of the reasons for the lower court judgment, the legal principles stated above, and the following circumstances that can be ascertained from the evidence lawfully admitted and examined, namely, the circumstances in which the Defendant, the Defendant’s wife, and the victim drank together; the amount of alcohol each of the Defendant and the victim consumed; the situation in which the victim entered the master bedroom and lay down while intoxicated after drinking beyond her tolerance for a long period even if she had not reached a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist; the victim’s condition when the Defendant commenced the quasi-rape; and the content of the text messages exchanged between the Defendant and the victim after the offense, it is proper for the lower court to have recognized the Defendant’s intent for quasi-rape. There is no error in the lower court judgment, as claimed in the grounds of appeal, in that it did not violate the rules of logic and experience, exceed the limits of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehend the legal principles concerning intent for quasi-rape.\\n\\n3. Grounds of Appeal that Impossible Attempt of Quasi-Rape Is Not Established\\n\\nA. Article 300 of the Penal Code punishes attempts of quasi-rape. In addition, Article 27 of the Penal Code provides, “Even if the occurrence of the result is impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, punishment shall be imposed when there is danger. Provided, however, that the punishment may be mitigated or remitted.” thereby punishing impossible attempts.\\n\\nAccordingly, where the Defendant had sexual intercourse with the victim with the intent to have sexual intercourse by taking advantage of a state that he believed the victim to be in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, but the victim was in fact not in such a state, the occurrence of the constitutive result provided in the offense of quasi-rape was impossible from the outset due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, and it cannot be said that such result actually occurred. Since the Defendant commenced the execution of quasi-rape but the offense did not reach completion, an attempt of quasi-rape is established. Because, judging objectively from the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time of the act, there was a risk that the result of quasi-rape would occur, impossible attempt of quasi-rape is established (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DO8105, decided 2005. 12. 8.; Supreme Court Decision 2015DO7343, decided 2015. 8. 13., etc.).\\n\\nB. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) Impossible attempt, as provided in Article 27 of the Penal Code, refers to a case in which the actor has criminal intent and an act that can be regarded as commencement of execution, but due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, the constitutive elements cannot be satisfied from the outset. However, although satisfaction of the constitutive elements is impossible as a result, if the act is dangerous, it is punishable as an impossible attempt. Impossible attempt is different from a mistake of fact in which the actor fails to perceive an existing fact, in that the actor mistakenly believes a fact that does not actually exist to exist.\\n\\n2) The Penal Code provides for an interrupted attempt in Article 25, paragraph (1) by stating, “Where a person has commenced execution of a crime but has not completed the act or the result has not occurred, the person shall be punished as an attempt,” and provides for an abandoned attempt in Article 26 by stating, “Where an offender voluntarily ceases the act commenced for execution or prevents the occurrence of the result caused by such act, the punishment shall be mitigated or remitted.” Interrupted attempt or abandoned attempt is distinguished from impossible attempt, because when the act of commencement of execution is judged in light of the execution conduct, the completion of the offense intended by the actor was at least possible, whereas impossible attempt is objectively excluded from the possibility of completion from the outset.\\n\\n3) The “mistake as to the means or object of execution” prescribed in Article 27 of the Penal Code means that the result was impossible from the outset because of the method of act or the object of act attempted by the actor. And “impossibility of occurrence of the result” should be understood to mean that the offense cannot reach completion due to the original impossibility of the means or object of execution.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the “danger” that constitutes the requirement for impossible attempt, distinguished from an impossible offense, must be determined by whether there is a possibility of occurrence of the result when objectively assessed by an ordinary person from the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time of the act (see Supreme Court Decision 77DO4049, decided 1978. 3. 28.; Supreme Court Decision 2005DO8105, decided 2005. 12. 8., etc.).\\n\\n4) The offense of quasi-rape prescribed in Article 299 of the Penal Code is an offense constituted by having sexual intercourse by taking advantage of another person’s state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, and protects as its legal interest the sexual self-determination of a person who cannot engage in sexual self-defense due to mental or physical circumstances (see Supreme Court Decision 98DO3257, decided 2000. 5. 26., etc.). Since the state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist must exist in the victimized person, the object of the act in the offense of quasi-rape is “a person in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist.” And the act corresponding to the constitutive elements is to “have sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist.” If sexual intercourse is committed against a person in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist by taking advantage of that person’s state, the constitutive elements are satisfied and the offense of quasi-rape is completed.\\n\\nWhere the Defendant believed that the victim was in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist and had sexual intercourse with the intent to take advantage of such state, but the victim was in fact not in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist from the beginning of the commencement of execution, it can be said that the offense of quasi-rape could not be completed from the outset due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution. In such a case, if an ordinary person objectively assessing the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time of the act would find that there was a risk of infringing the sexual self-determination of a person who cannot engage in sexual self-defense due to mental or physical circumstances and thus causing the result of quasi-rape, impossible attempt is established.\\n\\nC. Examining the reasons for the lower court judgment in light of the legal principles stated above, this case corresponds to a case in which the Defendant had sexual intercourse with the victim with the intent of quasi-rape, but the victim was in fact not in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, so that the occurrence of the result of quasi-rape was impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, and danger is recognized because, when objectively assessed by an ordinary person from the circumstances recognized by the Defendant, there was a possibility of occurrence of the result. Although some parts of the reasons for the lower court judgment are not entirely appropriate, the lower court’s conclusion that impossible attempt of quasi-rape is guilty is proper. There is no error in the lower court judgment, as claimed in the grounds of appeal, in that it misapprehended the legal principles concerning impossible attempt of quasi-rape.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as follows. In this judgment, except for the dissenting opinion of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Ahn Chul-sang, and Kim Sang-hwan on whether impossible attempt of quasi-rape is established, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous; there are supplemental opinions by Justice Park Sang-ok, Justice Park Jung-hwa, and Justice Kim Seon-soo with respect to the majority opinion, and supplemental opinions by Justice Min Yoo-sook and Justice Noh Jeong-hee.\\n\\n5. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kwon Soon-il, Ahn Chul-sang, and Kim Sang-hwan\\n\\nA. 1) Article 13 of the Penal Code (intent) provides, “An act by a person who does not perceive the facts constituting an element of a crime shall not be punished.” The phrase “facts constituting an element of a crime” here refers to objective constitutive elements that are external indicia in the constitutive elements of the offense prescribed by the Penal Code, namely, the subject of the act, object, act, result, etc. By contrast, the psychological or mental state belonging to the actor’s inner mind is called a subjective constitutive element, of which intent is a representative example. Since Article 13 of the Penal Code provides that, in order for an intentional offense to be established, the actor must have awareness of objective constitutive elements such as the subject, object, act, and result, where a special mode of conduct is required within the constitutive elements (for example, “force or intimidation” in rape, or “taking advantage of a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist” in quasi-rape), the actor must also be aware of the existence of such circumstances.\\n\\n2) The Penal Code provides, in Part II, Chapter 32, the “offenses of rape and indecency.” All offenses prescribed in this chapter are crimes involving the infringement of an individual’s sexual freedom or sexual self-determination, and their basic constitutive elements are rape (Article 297) and forcible indecent act (Article 298). Rape is an offense established by raping another by force or intimidation. Rape means having sexual intercourse with a person by making resistance impossible or significantly difficult through force or intimidation. Sexual intercourse, broadly speaking, means an unlawful act of satisfying sexual desire, but here it means penile-vaginal penetration. In the offense of rape, the constitutive act is rape, the special mode of conduct is “force or intimidation,” the object is a person, and the constitutive result is sexual intercourse. Quasi-rape (Article 299) is an offense established by having sexual intercourse by taking advantage of a person’s state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, and the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor, etc. (Article 302) is established by having sexual intercourse with a minor or a person of diminished mental capacity by fraud or force, and the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor (Article 305) is established by having sexual intercourse with a person under 13 years of age. Quasi-rape differs from rape, which is the basic constitutive offense in Chapter 32 of the Penal Code, in its objective constitutive elements in that its special mode of conduct is “taking advantage of a person’s state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist”; the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor, etc. (Article 302), in that its object is a minor or a person of diminished mental capacity and its special mode of conduct is the use of “fraud or force”; and the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor (Article 305), in that its object is a person under 13 years of age and it can be established even without using force, intimidation, fraud, or force as the means of the offense. However, the protected legal interest is the same as that of rape in that each involves infringement of sexual self-determination, that is, they all require the occurrence of the constitutive result of sexual intercourse.\\n\\nB. Article 27 of the Penal Code (impossible offense) provides, “Even if the occurrence of the result is impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, punishment shall be imposed when there is danger. Provided, however, that the punishment may be mitigated or remitted.” The “impossible offense” referred to in the heading of this article means a case in which, by the nature of the criminal act, there can absolutely be no possibility of occurrence of the result or infringement of a legal interest (see Supreme Court Decision 98DO2313, decided 1998. 10. 23.; Supreme Court Decision 2007DO3687, decided 2007. 7. 26., etc.). The “mistake as to the means of execution” here means a case in which the actor has commenced execution but, despite the fact that the chosen means of execution, by its nature, cannot actually bring about the desired result, the actor, due to ignorance or mistake, assumes the possibility of completion of the relevant constitutive act. A mistake as to the object means a case in which the actor has commenced execution but, despite the fact that the chosen object, by its nature, is defective or in a state in which it cannot be infringed so that the desired result cannot actually occur, the actor, due to ignorance or mistake, assumes the possibility of completion of the relevant constitutive act. Meanwhile, the statement in Article 27 of the Penal Code that “the occurrence of the result is impossible” is a concept that includes not only impossibility of completion of the offense but also impossibility of realization of the offense. If one judges from the retrospective point after the act has been completed, all forms of attempt prescribed in the Penal Code can be seen as situations in which the result has not occurred; thus, if one does not distinguish between “non-occurrence of the result,” that is, that the result has not actually occurred, and “impossibility of occurrence of the result,” that is, that realization of the offense is impossible, then an interrupted attempt and an impossible attempt cannot be distinguished. In other words, the “impossibility of occurrence of the result” under Article 27 of the Penal Code is a concept strictly distinguished from “non-occurrence of the result,” which is identified at the stage of establishing the factual relation.\\n\\nAlthough the heading of this provision is “impossible offense,” its content concerns a punishable impossible offense, that is, an “impossible attempt.” Impossible attempt means a case in which the constitutive elements cannot be realized under any circumstances by the nature of the act, but punishment as an attempt is imposed because of “danger.” The case law takes the position that, as the criterion for determining impossible attempt, danger must be judged by whether there is a possibility of occurrence of the result when objectively assessed by an ordinary person from the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time of the act (see Supreme Court Decision 77DO4049, decided 1978. 3. 28.; Supreme Court Decision 2005DO8105, decided 2005. 12. 8., etc.). From this standpoint, the Supreme Court held that, ① in a case where the Defendant attempted to kill the victim by putting agricultural pesticide into cabbage soup and making the victim drink it, the Defendant’s act fell under the case where the occurrence of the result was impossible due to a mistake as to the means of execution, but because there was danger, punishment as attempted murder was proper (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2007DO3687); and ② in a case charged as attempted quasi-forcible indecent act after nighttime intrusion into a residence, where the victim was already dead when the Defendant intruded into the victim’s residence, the Defendant’s act fell under the case where the occurrence of the result was impossible due to a mistake as to the object, but because there was danger, it was proper for the lower court to find the Defendant guilty of the impossible attempt of quasi-forcible indecent act after housebreaking (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DO5355, decided 2013. 7. 11.).\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of Article 27 of the Penal Code is to make criminal punishment possible, exceptionally, by treating the case as an attempt where the normative requirement of danger is satisfied, even though it was objectively impossible from the outset to realize the constitutive elements as intended by the actor and thus, in principle, it would not be punishable even as an attempt. For that reason, whether the occurrence of the result is impossible under Article 27 of the Penal Code must be judged not from the perspective of the actor who made a mistake as to the means or object of execution, but from the standpoint of an insightful ordinary person viewing the meaning of the act itself and determining whether there is no probability of occurrence of the result under any conditions. Accordingly, a case in which the probability of occurrence of the result exists under certain conditions, but the result did not occur due to the circumstances at the time of the act, is not impossible attempt but merely interrupted attempt.\\n\\nC. 1) First, we examine the circumstances of this case. The gist of the original charge in this case was that “the Defendant, on 2017. 4. 18. at around 02:00, while in the master bedroom of his home, touched the victim’s breasts while lying next to the victim, blocked the victim’s mouth, removed her pants and panties, and had sexual intercourse once and raped her.” In response, the Defendant denied the offense at the first-instance hearing, asserting that although it was true that the victim was intoxicated at the time of the offense alleged in the indictment, the sexual intercourse was with the victim’s consent. The military prosecutor then added an alternative charge stating that the Defendant “touched the victim’s breasts while next to the victim who was lying down intoxicated at the above date and place, removed her pants and panties, and had sexual intercourse once, thereby raping her by taking advantage of the victim’s state of inability to resist.” The court of first instance, as to the principal charge, found not guilty in its reasons on the ground that there was no proof of the facts constituting the offense as to force or intimidation, and found the alternative charge of quasi-rape guilty.\\n\\nOnly the Defendant appealed the first-instance judgment, and defense counsel submitted a statement of grounds of appeal, arguing that there was no proof of the offense concerning the claim that the Defendant took advantage of the victim’s state of inability to resist. The military prosecutor then added, alternatively, Articles 300, 299, and 297 of the Penal Code, which are the applicable provisions for attempted quasi-rape, with respect to the quasi-rape that had been found guilty in the first instance. The argument was that even if, as the Defendant claimed, the victim was not in a state of inability to resist, the Defendant had intent for quasi-rape, so the offense of attempted quasi-rape (impossible attempt) could be established. The lower court accepted the military prosecutor’s argument and held that, although there was insufficient evidence to find that the victim was in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist at the time of this case and thus the proof of the facts constituting the offense was lacking, the Defendant fell under impossible attempt of quasi-rape so long as he had intent for quasi-rape.\\n\\n2) The Defendant was indicted for rape and quasi-rape among the “offenses of rape and indecency” prescribed in Part II, Chapter 32 of the Penal Code. Rape and quasi-rape are result crimes that require the occurrence of a constitutive result and infringement crimes that require actual infringement of the protected legal interest. Therefore, whether the constitutive result has occurred in rape or quasi-rape must be determined by whether sexual intercourse took place, that is, whether the protected legal interest, the individual’s sexual self-determination, was infringed. In this case, both the court of first instance and the lower court recognized the fact that sexual intercourse, which is the constitutive result of rape and quasi-rape, occurred. However, the court of first instance found that there was no evidence that the special mode of conduct for rape, namely “force or intimidation,” had been used, and the lower court found only that there was no evidence that the special mode of conduct for quasi-rape, namely “taking advantage of a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist,” had been used. And there is no doubt that the victim’s sexual self-determination was infringed by the sexual intercourse. If so, does this case truly fall under the case in which “the occurrence of the result is impossible” under Article 27 of the Penal Code, that is, the “case in which, by the nature of the criminal act, there can absolutely be no possibility of occurrence of the result or infringement of a legal interest” (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2007DO3687)? It should be answered in the negative. This case is not a matter to be discussed in the realm of attempts.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that where the Defendant believed the victim to be in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist and, with the intent to have sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state, had sexual intercourse with the victim, but the victim was in fact not in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, then the occurrence of the result of quasi-rape was impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, and although no constitutive result of quasi-rape in fact occurred, because an ordinary person objectively assessing the circumstances recognized by the Defendant at the time of the act would find that there was a risk that the result of quasi-rape would occur, impossible attempt of quasi-rape is established. However, since the object of the act in quasi-rape is a person, there is no mistake as to the object in the sense that the object could not be the subject of realization of the constitutive elements from the outset. Furthermore, there was no mistake as to the identity of the object in that the Defendant selected the victim as the object of sexual intercourse. The majority opinion states as though the Defendant also had a “mistake as to the means of execution,” but it does not explain in what respect there was a mistake as to the means of execution in this case. It is erroneous for the majority opinion to have considered that this case falls under a case in which the occurrence of the result of quasi-rape, that is, infringement of the victim’s sexual self-determination by sexual intercourse, was impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution.\\n\\nThe majority opinion regards the object of the act in quasi-rape as “a person in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist.” However, Article 299 of the Penal Code punishes a person who “has sexual intercourse or commits an indecent act by taking advantage of another person’s state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, in accordance with Articles 297, 297-2, and 298,” thereby punishing the act of “having sexual intercourse or committing an indecent act” against “a person” by “taking advantage of” a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist. In other words, taking advantage of a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist is a special mode of conduct as a method of the offense, and the object of the constitutive act is a person. This point becomes even clearer when compared with Article 297 of the Penal Code, which provides, “A person who rapes another by force or intimidation shall be punished by imprisonment for a fixed term of at least 3 years.” The portion of Article 299 corresponding to “by force or intimidation” in Article 297 is “by taking advantage of another person’s state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist.” The fact that the constitutive act and constitutive result, namely sexual intercourse, occur when the victim is placed in a state in which resistance is impossible is the same for both rape and quasi-rape. The only difference is that rape makes resistance impossible “by force or intimidation,” whereas quasi-rape “takes advantage of” an already existing state of inability to resist. The majority opinion goes beyond the wording of the criminal provision.\\n\\nThe majority opinion holds that since it was retrospectively revealed that the victim was not in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist at the time the Defendant attempted the offense, it was impossible for the Defendant to take advantage of the victim’s state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, and thus the occurrence of the result of quasi-rape was impossible from the outset. However, does this case truly correspond to a case where “the occurrence of the result is impossible,” as provided in Article 27 of the Penal Code, that is, a case in which, by the nature of the criminal act, there can absolutely be no possibility of occurrence of the result or infringement of a legal interest? The majority opinion’s reasoning and legal construction are worth hearing, but one cannot readily give an affirmative answer to this question. As discussed above, “impossibility of occurrence of the result” under Article 27 of the Penal Code is a concept that includes not only impossibility of completion of the offense but also impossibility of realization of the offense, and thus differs from the concept of “non-occurrence of the result,” which means that the result has not actually occurred. In this case, the court of first instance found quasi-rape guilty. The lower court held that there was insufficient evidence to find quasi-rape guilty. The military prosecutor, in preparation for the possibility that quasi-rape would be found not guilty, alternatively added the applicable provisions to the effect that at least an impossible attempt of quasi-rape had been committed. We have already examined that the legislative purpose of Article 27 of the Penal Code is not for such cases. This case is merely one in which the issue is whether there is sufficient evidence of the special mode of conduct that constitutes the constitutive element of quasi-rape for which the military prosecutor seeks application.\\n\\n3) In conclusion, the majority opinion confuses the issue of constitutive applicability or satisfaction of the constitutive elements with the meaning of “impossibility of occurrence of the result” under Article 27 of the Penal Code. If one follows the majority opinion, it would amount to saying that whenever the Defendant’s act does not satisfy the constitutive elements of the offense charged by the prosecutor, that case falls under a case in which the occurrence of the result is impossible, and that even when the prosecutor fails to prove the facts constituting the offense specified in the applicable provisions stated in the indictment, the Defendant may still be punished as an impossible attempt. Such an interpretive theory cannot be accepted because it would completely hollow out the principle of nullum crimen, nulla poena sine lege, the fundamental principle of modern criminal law.\\n\\nD. Nevertheless, the lower court, contrary to this, held that the alternative charge of attempted quasi-rape was established based solely on the circumstances stated in its opinion. This lower court judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning impossible attempt under Article 27 of the Penal Code.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, we state our dissent from the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Supplemental Opinion to the Majority Opinion by Justices Park Sang-ok, Park Jung-hwa, and Kim Seon-soo\\n\\nWe wish to supplement the rationale of the majority opinion and offer some views concerning the criticism in the dissenting opinion.\\n\\nA. 1) Criminal statutes must be strictly construed and applied according to their wording, and no analogy or other construction may be made carelessly in a manner unfavorable to the Defendant. However, even in interpreting criminal statutes, teleological interpretation taking into account the legislative purpose, objective, and legislative history of the statute is not excluded so long as it does not depart from the ordinary meaning of the statutory language (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DO2162, decided 2007. 6. 14.; Supreme Court Decision 2009DO13332, decided 2010. 5. 13., etc.). And it is not contrary to the principle of nulla poena sine lege to interpret and apply the law by finding a reasonable interpretive standard, through consideration of the legislative purpose of the criminal statute, its overall content, and structure, to typify or limit the act types that fall under its constitutive elements based on the understanding and judgment of an ordinary person having proper capacity to distinguish things (see Supreme Court Decision 2001DO3531, decided 2001. 11. 13., etc.).\\n\\n2) The majority opinion distinguishes impossible attempt from interrupted attempt or abandoned attempt on the basis of whether the occurrence of the result is impossible as prescribed in Article 27 of the Penal Code, and distinguishes impossible attempt from non-punishable impossible offense on the basis of whether there is “danger.”\\n\\nA. The basic forms of crimes governed by the Penal Code are those that satisfy the objective constitutive elements and subjective constitutive elements, and the objective constitutive elements include the occurrence of a certain act or a certain infringement of the legal interest the Penal Code seeks to protect as a result of such act, together with recognition of a normative causal relationship and objective attribution between the act and the result. Therefore, an attempt under the Penal Code, like a completed offense, has intent in the subjective constitutive elements for the realization of a specific constitutive element, but is only a criminal form in which the objective constitutive elements are not fully satisfied, thereby reducing the requirements for establishment of the offense.\\n\\nB. Article 25, paragraph (1) of the Penal Code provides for interrupted attempt by stating, “Where a person has commenced execution of a crime but has not completed the act or the result has not occurred, the person shall be punished as an attempt,” and Article 26 separately provides for abandoned attempt by stating, “Where an offender voluntarily ceases the act commenced for execution or prevents the occurrence of the result caused by such act, the punishment shall be mitigated or remitted.” The reason an act commenced for execution is punished as interrupted attempt or abandoned attempt is that, although no actual infringement of a legal interest or endangerment as a constitutive result has occurred, there was commencement of execution and the occurrence of the result is recognized as possible. Therefore, interrupted attempt or abandoned attempt may be said to be an attempt where realization of the constitutive elements was possible, that is, where occurrence of the result was possible, but the offense did not reach completion.\\n\\nC. Originally, impossible offense refers to a case in which the actor has criminal intent and an act that externally appears to be commencement of execution, but the occurrence of the result is impossible by the nature of the act, that is, a case in which the offense generally does not arise because there is no possibility of realization of the constitutive elements. However, as a legislative decision on whether impossible offenses should be the object of criminal punishment, Article 27 of the Penal Code, under the heading “impossible offense,” provides, “Even if the occurrence of the result is impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, punishment shall be imposed when there is danger. Provided, however, that the punishment may be mitigated or remitted,” thereby exceptionally punishing impossible attempts with “danger.” The “impossibility of occurrence of the result” prescribed in Article 27 of the Penal Code is the essential marker of impossible attempt, and the contents of the constitutive result do not change depending on whether it is impossible attempt or interrupted attempt or abandoned attempt. Accordingly, there is no basis to interpret “occurrence of the result” in Article 27 differently from “occurrence of the result” in Articles 25, paragraph (1), and 26, and since impossible attempt is also a type of attempt, “impossibility of occurrence of the result” under Article 27 must be interpreted to mean that the offense cannot reach completion because there was no possibility from the outset that the constitutive elements would be satisfied.\\n\\nD. The Supreme Court held, in a case where the Defendant had been charged with attempted murder after putting agricultural pesticide into cabbage soup in order to kill his husband but the victim spat out the soup, that because the Penal Code distinguishes and punishes interrupted attempt and impossible attempt, it was unlawful for the lower court to recognize interrupted attempt without examining which of the two cases applied to the Defendant’s act (see Supreme Court Decision 83DO2967, decided 1984. 2. 14.). In addition, in a case where the Defendant inserted a finger into the victim’s genital organ believing the victim to be in a state of mental incapacity, but the victim was in fact not in such a state, the Court held that the Defendant’s act fell under a case where the occurrence of the result of quasi-forcible quasi-rape was impossible due to a mistake as to the object and that danger was recognized, and therefore there was a high likelihood that impossible attempt of quasi-forcible quasi-rape was established (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DO7343, decided 2015. 8. 13.).\\n\\nThrough these decisions, the Supreme Court made clear that interrupted attempt and impossible attempt are distinguished, and that impossible attempt is established when, from the outset at the time of commencement of execution, realization of the constitutive elements is impossible in consequence, but there is danger.\\n\\nB. The dissenting opinion states that because quasi-rape is both a result crime requiring occurrence of the constitutive result and an infringement crime requiring actual infringement of the protected legal interest, whether the constitutive result has occurred must be judged by whether sexual intercourse took place, that is, whether the protected legal interest, the individual’s sexual self-determination, was infringed, and therefore once the victim’s sexual self-determination has been infringed through the sexual intercourse constituting the result of quasi-rape, there is no room for impossible attempt. Furthermore, it states that the majority opinion confuses the issue of constitutive applicability or satisfaction of the constitutive elements with the case in which occurrence of the result is impossible. However, the foregoing criticism in the dissenting opinion is not valid for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) The offense of quasi-rape under Article 299 of the Penal Code is completed when a person in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist is subjected to sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state. Having sexual intercourse with a person who is not in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist is neither the object nor the constitutive act of quasi-rape, so even if sexual intercourse has occurred, it cannot be said that quasi-rape has been completed. If the Defendant had sexual intercourse with the victim with the intent to have sexual intercourse by taking advantage of the victim’s state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, but the victim was in fact not in such a state, the issue becomes whether impossible attempt of quasi-rape is established because, from the outset at the time of commencement of execution, due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, there was no possibility of satisfying the constitutive elements and thus, in consequence, no possibility of reaching completion. This is because, once the Defendant has commenced execution with intent for quasi-rape, the act is, as a matter of the logical structure of criminal law, ordinarily subject to criminal evaluation.\\n\\n2) The dissenting opinion argues that “sexual intercourse” itself is the constitutive result of rape and quasi-rape, but this is contrary to the structure of the Penal Code, which separately prescribes rape and quasi-rape as distinct constitutive elements. In rape and quasi-rape, the result of infringement of sexual self-determination, which is the protected legal interest, does not arise by the sexual intercourse act alone, but only in combination with separate conduct by the offender or the victim’s condition, etc., that infringes the victim’s self-determination. Accordingly, the dissenting opinion appears to confuse “act,” which is one of the objective constitutive elements, with “completion,” which means occurrence of the constitutive result.\\n\\nC. The dissenting opinion states that because the object of the act in quasi-rape is “a person,” there can be no mistake as to the object in this case, and that the majority opinion’s interpretation of the object of the act as “a person in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist” exceeds the wording of the criminal provision. It also states that the majority opinion does not explain in what respect there was a mistake as to the means of execution.\\n\\n1) The Penal Code provides, in Part II, Chapter 32, the “offenses of rape and indecency,” and expressly indicates the object of the act in rape (Article 297) as “a person,” the object of the act in the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor, etc. (Article 302) as “a minor or a person of diminished mental capacity,” and the object of the act in the offense of sexual intercourse with a minor (Article 305) as “a person under 13 years of age.” By contrast, the offense of quasi-rape under Article 299 of the Penal Code is an offense of having sexual intercourse by taking advantage of another person’s state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, and the term “taking advantage of” here means that the actor recognizes a person in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist and that sexual intercourse became easier because of such state. Therefore, the object of the act in quasi-rape should be understood as “a person in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist.” Since the offense requires taking advantage of “another person’s state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist,” the object of the act can only be interpreted as a person in such a state. This is because it is not taking advantage of the mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist of a person other than the sexual partner. The majority opinion systematically and logically interprets Article 299 of the Penal Code within the ordinary meaning and scope of this wording, and therefore we cannot agree with the dissenting opinion that the majority opinion has gone beyond the wording of the criminal provision.\\n\\n2) The “mistake as to the means of execution” prescribed in Article 27 of the Penal Code means the impossibility or inappropriateness of the means, where the method of act attempted by the actor makes occurrence of the result impossible from the outset. A “mistake as to the object” means the impossibility or inappropriateness of the object, where the object of the act attempted by the actor cannot satisfy the constitutive elements. As seen above, the object of the act in quasi-rape is “a person in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist,” and the act corresponding to the constitutive elements is “having sexual intercourse by taking advantage of a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist.” In quasi-rape, the victim’s state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist is both a characteristic of the object and a premise of the means of execution. If the Defendant believed the victim to be in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist and had sexual intercourse with the intent to take advantage of such state, but the victim was in fact not in such a state, then the case falls under one in which, due to the impossibility or inappropriateness of the method of act or object attempted by the Defendant, there was no possibility from the outset of reaching completion of the offense of quasi-rape. Since, as above, the means-of-execution mistake and object mistake cannot be clearly distinguished and whether the mistake is as to means or object does not affect the conclusion that “the occurrence of the result is impossible,” there is no practical benefit in distinguishing them. Therefore, the criticism that the majority opinion does not explain in what respect the Defendant had a mistake as to the means of execution, or that there was no object mistake because the object of the act in quasi-rape is simply a “person,” is not correct.\\n\\nD. The dissenting opinion states that according to the majority opinion, any act that does not satisfy the constitutive elements of a crime will always become an impossible offense and may be punished as an attempt if dangerous, and that such an interpretive theory completely hollow out the principle of nulla poena sine lege. However, the foregoing criticism in the dissenting opinion is not valid for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) The majority opinion does not say that impossible attempt is established for all acts not satisfying the constitutive elements, but rather that the question of punishability as an impossible attempt under Article 27 of the Penal Code must be determined only where the constitutive elements cannot be satisfied from the outset due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution.\\n\\n2) Under the Penal Code, impossible attempt, like other attempts, requires intent to realize a specific constitutive element as a subjective constitutive element, and dolus eventualis is sufficient. This subjective constitutive element forms part of the facts constituting the offense and therefore requires strict proof beyond a reasonable doubt; if the prosecutor’s proof does not reach the level of creating such conviction, the matter must be decided in favor of the Defendant (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DO231, decided 2012. 6. 28.; Supreme Court Decision 2017DO12649, decided 2017. 12. 22., etc.). Accordingly, if the Defendant’s intent, which is the subjective constitutive element, cannot be recognized, there is not even any need to examine whether impossible attempt is established in the first place.\\n\\n3) Article 27 of the Penal Code recognizes, exceptionally, the establishment of punishable impossible attempt by providing that even if the occurrence of the result is impossible due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, punishment shall be imposed when there is danger.
