The majority opinion merely states that impossible attempt can be established only in cases where the requirements for such impossible attempt are met, and is not intended to extend impossible attempt to cases in which the occurrence of the result is impossible for reasons other than a mistake as to the means or object of execution, or to cases without danger.\\n\\n4) Article 29 of the Penal Code provides, “Only offenses for which attempts are punishable shall be prescribed in each Article.” Accordingly, attempts are punishable only where there is a punishment provision, and impossible attempts are punishable only where there is danger, as provided in Article 27 of the Penal Code.\\n\\n5) Therefore, the logic of the majority opinion cannot be said to hollow out the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\nE. Article 13 of the Penal Code provides, “An act by a person who does not perceive the facts constituting an element of a crime shall not be punished,” and the majority opinion and the dissenting opinion are in accord that the phrase “facts constituting an element of a crime” here means the objective constitutive elements that are external indicia in the constitutive elements of the offense prescribed by the Penal Code, namely, the subject of the act, object, act, result, etc.\\n\\nHowever, the dissenting opinion states that in this case there is no issue of impossible attempt because it is not a case of “mistake as to the means or object” in impossible attempt and thus is simply not guilty. If the meaning of “impossibility of occurrence of the result due to a mistake as to the means or object,” which is the requirement for impossible attempt under Article 27 of the Penal Code on which the dissenting opinion premises itself, is limited to cases where the actor believed it was a person but it was in fact not a person, then in a case where the Defendant saw the victim lying down, believed the victim to be in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, and had sexual intercourse with the victim with the intent to have sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state, if the victim had already died at the time the Defendant commenced execution, impossible attempt of quasi-rape would be established, whereas if the victim was alive but in fact not in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, the conclusion would be that the Defendant is not guilty. Such a conclusion is difficult to accept for the following reasons. First, once the Defendant has commenced the act of having sexual intercourse with the intent for quasi-rape, whether the victim was dead at the time or alive but not in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist cannot be a factor affecting intent for quasi-rape. Second, if one looks only at the objectively existing facts at the time of commencement of execution, the circumstance that the victim was dead and the circumstance that the victim was alive but not in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist are the same in that there was no possibility of realization of the constitutive elements of quasi-rape and completion could not be reached, yet there is no rational basis to treat the two differently by recognizing impossible attempt of quasi-rape only in the former case. Third, if an acquittal is rendered on the ground that there is no constitutive applicability because the victim was not in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist, it would mean that the sexual self-determination of a dead victim is more strongly protected than that of a living victim, which is unreasonable.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, we state our supplemental opinion to the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Supplemental Opinion to the Majority Opinion by Justices Min Yoo-sook and Noh Jeong-hee\\n\\nA. This case is one in which only the Defendant appealed against the lower court’s recognition of impossible attempt of quasi-rape. Therefore, whether the offense of quasi-rape has been completed is not a matter for determination in the final appeal, and only the issue of whether impossible attempt is established is at issue. Premised on what the supplemental opinion to the preceding majority opinion has discussed regarding the distinction between interrupted attempt and impossible attempt, and between impossible offense and impossible attempt, as well as the relationship between the problem of satisfaction of the constitutive elements and impossibility of occurrence of the result, we would like to supplement only the constitutive elements of quasi-rape concerning the point that in this case the establishment of an attempt of quasi-rape is clear.\\n\\nB. Regarding the intent for quasi-rape and commencement of execution\\n\\n1) Impossible attempt is a form of attempt, and the establishment of an attempt requires intent and commencement of execution, while also requiring incompletion of the offense.\\n\\n2) Article 299 of the Penal Code provides for punishment as quasi-rape of “a person who has sexual intercourse by taking advantage of another person’s state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist.” “Mental incapacity” means a state in which a person cannot make judgments regarding sexual conduct because of mental disorder or consciousness disorder, and “inability to resist” means a state in which resistance is psychologically or physically impossible or significantly difficult for reasons other than mental incapacity. “Taking advantage of” means recognizing that the victim is in such a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and using that state as a means to facilitate sexual intercourse. Therefore, intent for quasi-rape is recognized where the Defendant commences execution with the belief that the victim is in a state of mental and physical incapacity or inability to resist and with the intent to have sexual intercourse by taking advantage of such state (direct intent), or with the internal will that it does not matter even if sexual intercourse is carried out by taking advantage of such state (dolus eventualis).\\n\\n3) Commencement of execution of a crime is recognized when conduct corresponding to the constitutive elements or conduct closely related to such conduct begins. In the case of quasi-rape, for example, at the point where the Defendant removes the clothes of a sleeping victim, lowers his own pants, and touches the victim’s genitals, the Defendant can be seen as having begun conduct that can be considered a means of sexual intercourse, with the intent to have sexual intercourse by taking advantage of the victim’s state of inability to resist, and thus as having commenced execution of quasi-rape (see Supreme Court Decision 99DO5187, decided 2000. 1. 14.). In the above case, the Supreme Court held that even if the victim awoke from sleep because of the Defendant’s conduct, this does not prevent establishment of attempted quasi-rape.\\n\\n4) As the majority opinion has examined, the Defendant’s argument in the grounds of appeal that there was no intent for quasi-rape in this case is without merit. In addition, in light of the factual findings recognized by the lower court through the evidence lawfully admitted, it is amply recognized that the Defendant engaged in conduct that can be viewed as commencement of execution of quasi-rape. Although the dissenting opinion does not state this explicitly, it appears to presuppose it. If so, the Defendant’s conduct must be regarded as an attempt of quasi-rape unless it falls under a non-punishable impossible offense.\\n\\nC. Regarding whether sexual intercourse and establishment of attempt are mutually exclusive\\n\\n1) Nevertheless, the dissenting opinion raises doubts even as to the establishment of attempt itself, which I believe largely stems from the fact that sexual intercourse occurred in this case. Summarizing the reasoning of the dissenting opinion on this point: in this case, the constitutive result of sexual intercourse occurred, and the victim’s sexual self-determination was infringed by the sexual intercourse. Therefore, this does not fall under a case in which the occurrence of the result is impossible under Article 27 of the Penal Code, and it is not a matter to be discussed in the realm of attempts.\\n\\nIn this way, the dissenting opinion says that the constitutive result occurred, yet neither completed offense nor attempt is established, and that impossible attempt is not established, while remaining silent on whether interrupted attempt is established. To point out the logical inconsistency of the dissenting opinion, we first examine the relationship between sexual intercourse and the completion of a crime or the establishment of completion.\\n\\n2) A dictionary of the Korean language defines “sexual intercourse” as “illicit sexual relations” or “sexual relations, usually with a person other than one’s spouse.” As can be seen from this, although the term “sexual intercourse” contains negative connotations, it is generally understood not to include the meaning of coercion or sexual relations against the other party’s express or implied will. Therefore, directly linking sexual intercourse to infringement of sexual self-determination causes confusion between the act or the factual result of the act and the infringement of the protected legal interest, and it is necessary to distinguish them in use. Premised on this, if we reexamine the constitutive elements of rape and quasi-rape, rape and quasi-rape do not punish sexual intercourse itself, but define and punish as crimes sexual intercourse that is carried out by a method infringing the victim’s sexual self-determination, such as suppressing the victim’s will to refuse by force or intimidation. Therefore, even if sexual intercourse occurred as intended or desired by the Defendant, if it was not by force or intimidation, or by taking advantage of the victim’s state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, rape or quasi-rape cannot be said to have been completed.\\n\\nCases in which completion of a crime is denied due to lack of causation despite the achievement of the Defendant’s purpose or desire are often discussed in the context of extortion or fraud. In the case of extortion, if the Defendant used force or intimidation with intent to extort but the victim was not actually frightened and disposed of property for another reason, the Defendant achieved the desired result of obtaining property, but extortion is not evaluated as completed. The same applies to fraud, where the Defendant engages in deceptive acts with intent to obtain property by fraud, but although the victim was not deceived, the victim transfers property for another reason. This is because causation between the Defendant’s force or intimidation and the victim’s act of disposition is denied. In rape and quasi-rape as well, even if the Defendant’s desired result occurs, attempt can be established because of lack of causation. The incompletion of a crime means that the constitutive result did not occur, and it is not determined by whether the actor achieved his purpose.\\n\\n3) Furthermore, a question may arise whether, unless sexual intercourse is accomplished by the Defendant’s force or intimidation or by conduct taking advantage of mental incapacity or inability to resist, the victim’s sexual self-determination is not infringed, or there is no risk of infringement, and therefore even an attempt cannot be established. However, we must consider whether this doubt is perhaps based on a prejudice that it is impossible to compel a victim to engage in sexual relations without force or intimidation sufficient to make resistance impossible or significantly difficult, or without taking advantage of such a state.\\n\\nIn quasi-rape, one factor in interpreting “state of inability to resist” as a case in which resistance is absolutely impossible or significantly difficult is the need to maintain balance with the strictest view, which requires the highest level of force or intimidation for the establishment of rape (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DO2001, decided 2009. 4. 23., etc.). And one of the longstanding grounds for limiting the degree of force or intimidation in rape to the narrowest interpretation is the notion that, unless the victim’s ability to resist is impossible or resistance is significantly difficult, rape against the victim’s will is impossible. However, this is not very different from a leap to the conclusion that if the victim did not resist with all possible effort, the victim consented to sexual intercourse and therefore there was no infringement of the victim’s sexual self-determination, by arbitrarily interpreting the victim’s will. There is a wide gap between those two situations. In everyday life as well, we often fail to cope properly with unexpected attacks, unlike what we rationally imagine in ordinary circumstances. Even a minor assault, when viewed objectively and retrospectively, may in the concrete situation at the time cause severe fear or psychological or physical paralysis or confusion. Moreover, in an absurd and abnormal criminal situation, one must not commit the error of forcing only the victim to make a rational and desirable choice and then blaming the victim for failing. In other words, even if there is sexual intercourse without the force or intimidation or taking advantage of a state of inability to resist required by the criminal statutes defining rape and quasi-rape as interpreted by the Supreme Court, there can still be cases in which the victim’s actual sexual self-determination is infringed. And the possibility of this increases as the constitutive act is interpreted more strictly.\\n\\nReturning to this case, as noted above, the only issue in this case is whether impossible attempt of quasi-rape is established. Therefore, if, due to the Defendant’s mistake, sexual intercourse by taking advantage of the victim’s state of inability to resist was objectively impossible, but when objectively assessed from the circumstances the Defendant recognized at the time there was a risk of reaching completion, then impossible attempt is recognized. And this is affirmed even where the Defendant commenced execution with intent for quasi-rape but did not reach sexual intercourse. Yet, if one were to conclude that there was no risk of infringement of the victim’s sexual self-determination merely because sexual intercourse occurred as the Defendant intended or desired, this can only be said to be an upside-down interpretation. In conclusion, the majority opinion’s interpretation based on the constitutive elements of quasi-rape under the Penal Code and the requirements for impossible attempt is consistent with the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, we state our supplemental opinion to the majority opinion."}

Summary of the facts charged\\n\\nThe Defendant, between around 04:00 and 05:00 on September 14, 2019, while sitting in the passenger seat of a passenger car owned by the victim (female, 22 years old) and parked in a public parking lot in OOO-dong, Jeju City, after the victim, who was sitting in the driver’s seat, became intoxicated and fell asleep and thus reached a state of inability to resist, called the victim’s name three or four times to confirm that the victim was asleep, then touched the victim’s breasts over the victim’s upper clothing with his hand, kissed the victim’s lips, unbuttoned the victim’s pants, inserted his hand inside, and touched the victim’s vulva; after reclining the driver’s seat backward, he lifted the victim up with both hands and moved the victim to the rear seat, and the Defendant also got out of the car and then got back into the rear seat, after which he removed both the victim’s pants and underwear, touched the victim’s genitals with his hand, and inserted his finger into the victim’s vulva; then, after getting out of the car again and purchasing a condom from a convenience store, he attempted to insert the Defendant’s genital organ into the victim’s vulva in order to commit sexual intercourse, but he failed to accomplish his intent and remained at the attempted stage because the victim, having regained her senses upon hearing the Defendant’s movements and the sound of video recording, resisted and protested.\\n\\n2. The lower court’s determination\\n\\nThe lower court upheld the first-instance judgment, which found the facts charged in this case not guilty, for the following reasons.\\n\\nA. It is acknowledged that the Defendant, having perceived that the victim was in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist and having embarked upon the execution of quasi-rape with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by exploiting such state, did so. However, it is difficult to conclude that the fact that the victim was in a state of inability to resist at the time was proved beyond a reasonable doubt. The quasi-rape offense cannot be regarded as having constituted a frustrated attempt as charged in this case.\\n\\nB. The Defendant’s conduct appears capable of being characterized as an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense. However, since there is a concern that substantial disadvantage would be caused to the exercise of the Defendant’s right of defense, the Defendant cannot be recognized ex officio, without amendment of the indictment, as having committed an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\nA. Whether an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense is established\\n\\n1) Relevant legal principles\\n\\nWhere the Defendant, believing that the victim was in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, embarks upon the execution of quasi-rape with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by exploiting such state, but the victim is in fact not in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, it may be deemed that, due to a mistake as to the means or object of execution, the occurrence of the constitutive result prescribed for the quasi-rape offense was impossible from the outset. In such a case, if, based on the circumstances perceived by the Defendant at the time of the act, the occurrence of the result of quasi-rape would have been objectively risky from the standpoint of an ordinary person, an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense is established (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2018DO16002, decided March 28, 2019).\\n\\n2) Determination\\n\\nAccording to the reasoning of the lower court judgment, the Defendant, at the time, perceived the victim as having fallen asleep and being in a state of mental incapacity or inability to resist, and, with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by exploiting such state, embarked upon the execution of quasi-rape; however, the victim was in fact not in a state of inability to resist.\\n\\nThe lower court also recognized the Defendant’s intent to commit quasi-rape on the basis of the circumstances the Defendant perceived at the time, namely, that the victim, while considerably intoxicated, got into the passenger car saying, “I should go to the car and sleep,” and that, after the Defendant boarded the passenger car together with the victim, the victim did not show any particular reaction when the Defendant called the victim’s name several times and tried inserting his finger between the victim’s parted lips. On the basis of such circumstances perceived by the Defendant at the time, it is assessed from an objective standpoint of an ordinary person that there was a risk of the result of quasi-rape occurring.\\n\\nUltimately, the Defendant embarked upon execution with the intent to commit quasi-rape, but because the victim was not actually in a state of inability to resist, the occurrence of the constitutive result was impossible from the outset; however, it is recognized that there was a risk of such result occurring. Such conduct by the Defendant may be regarded as constituting an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense.\\n\\nB. Duty of ex officio adjudication\\n\\n1) Relevant legal principles\\n\\nWithin the scope where identity of the facts charged is recognized, if, in light of the course of the trial, it is recognized that there is no concern of causing substantial disadvantage to the exercise of the Defendant’s right of defense, the court may, even without amendment of the indictment, ex officio recognize criminal facts different from the facts charged stated in the indictment (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 99DO3674, decided November 9, 1999), and in such case, if, when compared with the criminal facts prosecuted, the facts actually recognized are not trivial, and if failing to punish them merely because the indictment was not amended would be deemed, in light of the purpose of criminal procedure of the prompt discovery of substantive truth through due process, to be manifestly contrary to justice and equity, the court must ex officio recognize such criminal facts (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DO9268, decided April 13, 2006; Supreme Court Decision 2021DO9041, decided April 28, 2022).\\n\\n2) Determination\\n\\nA) The facts charged in this case and the criminal facts of an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense share the same basic factual relation.\\n\\nThere is no difference in the basic facts, including not only the time and place of the offense, but also that the Defendant, believing at the time that the victim was in a state of inability to resist and, with the intent to commit sexual intercourse by exploiting such state, removed the victim’s pants and underwear, touched the victim’s genitals with his hand, and attempted to insert the Defendant’s genital organ into the victim’s vulva.\\n\\nB) Even if the criminal facts of an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense are recognized ex officio without amendment of the indictment, it cannot be said that there is a concern of causing substantial disadvantage to the exercise of the Defendant’s right of defense.\\n\\nAn impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense is established if it is recognized that the Defendant embarked upon execution with intent to commit quasi-rape, that the victim was not in an actual state of inability to resist at the time, and that there was a risk of the result of quasi-rape occurring.\\n\\nDuring the trial in this case, the Defendant disputed to the effect that “there was no intent to commit quasi-rape, and the victim was not in a state of inability to resist,” and accordingly, sufficient examination was conducted as to whether the Defendant had embarked upon execution with intent to commit quasi-rape and whether the victim was in an actual state of inability to resist at the time. In addition, whether there was a risk of the result of quasi-rape occurring must be determined from the objective standpoint of an ordinary person on the basis of the circumstances perceived by the Defendant at the time, and in the course of examining whether the Defendant had intent to commit quasi-rape, there was sufficient argument on the circumstances related to the victim’s condition that the Defendant perceived at the time. Ultimately, it can be assessed that the examination and argument concerning whether an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense is established were already sufficiently conducted during the trial in this case.\\n\\nFurthermore, when the prosecutor appealed the first-instance judgment, the prosecutor submitted a statement of grounds for appeal to the effect that, pursuant to the legal principle of the Supreme Court en banc Decision in 2018DO16002, the establishment of an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense should have been recognized, but the first instance erred in finding the Defendant not guilty. The Defendant’s counsel, in response, also submitted a “reply to the prosecutor’s grounds for appeal” to the effect that, because the Defendant had no intent to commit quasi-rape, an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense was not established. In this way, the fact that there was reference and argument between the prosecutor and the Defendant as to whether the Defendant’s conduct could be recognized as guilt as an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense also makes it difficult to view ex officio recognition of the criminal facts of an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense as causing substantial disadvantage to the exercise of the Defendant’s right of defense.\\n\\nC) Under such circumstances, if punishment were denied merely because the indictment was not amended, it would be manifestly contrary to justice and equity in light of the purpose of criminal procedure of the prompt discovery of substantive truth through due process.\\n\\nAn impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense is a serious crime. The statutory punishment for the quasi-rape offense is imprisonment for a fixed term of not less than 3 years, and for an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense, the sentence may only be reduced or remitted at the court’s discretion.\\n\\nIt is also difficult to find any substantial difference in terms of gravity of the offense, nature of the crime, or punishability between the impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense and the frustrated attempt of the quasi-rape offense that is the facts charged in this case. Both acts are committed with the intent to have sexual intercourse by exploiting the victim’s state of inability to resist, and there is no difference in that the constitutive result did not occur. The only difference is whether the cause of the non-occurrence of the constitutive result existed before the commencement of execution or arose after the commencement of execution; this is merely a contingent circumstance that the Defendant did not perceive at the time of the act, and it cannot be regarded as an essential difference. Nevertheless, if the lower court’s conclusion stands, the Defendant, who committed an act that embarked upon execution with the intent to commit quasi-rape and carried a risk of result occurrence, could not be punished at all merely because the victim’s state of inability to resist at the time of commencement of execution was not proved beyond a reasonable doubt, and if the lower court judgment becomes final and binding, res judicata will arise and the Defendant cannot be indicted again for an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense.\\n\\nD) Therefore, the lower court should have ex officio recognized the criminal facts of an impossible attempt of the quasi-rape offense. Nevertheless, the lower court upheld the first-instance judgment, which found the facts charged in this case not guilty, solely for the reasons stated in the judgment. In such determination by the lower court, there is an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles regarding the scope within which a case may be adjudicated without amendment of the indictment. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the lower court judgment is reversed and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[93DO113]": "We consider the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe lower court, synthesizing the evidence cited, determined that the land subject to each application for permission to damage forest in this case may be recognized as forest, not restricted farmland, as “land on which collectively growing standing trees and bamboo have been temporarily lost” as prescribed in Article 2 of the Forest Act, and therefore that it cannot be said that the Defendants entered false statements in each on-site investigation report and opinion statement; and even if the said land were restricted farmland, it held that it cannot be said that the Defendants had knowledge of falsity with respect to each statement. Accordingly, it acquitted all of the Defendants. Reviewing the relevant evidence in comparison with the record, the lower court’s foregoing findings and determination are proper and persuasive, and it cannot be said that the lower court judgment contains illegality, as argued, in that it erred in finding facts by violating the rules of evidence.\\n\\nIn addition, since the charges against Defendant A are clear in purport, there was no need for the court to exercise its right to clarify in this regard. Moreover, whether the court should require the prosecutor to amend the indictment lies within the court’s discretion, and therefore it cannot be deemed unlawful for the lower court not to have required the prosecutor to amend the indictment (see this Court’s Decision rendered on 1990.10.26., 90DO1229, and Decision rendered on 1985.7.23., 85DO1092), and thus it cannot be said that the lower court judgment contains illegality, as argued, in that it did not exercise its right to clarify or did not require amendment of the indictment.\\n\\nAll of the arguments are without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judges participating in the decision having unanimously agreed, the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

{"[97DO2463]": "We examine Ground 4 of the grounds of appeal filed by the Defendant’s counsel, Bae Man-un.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the single-judge judge of the Gwangju District Court found the Defendant guilty of the facts charged of violation of the Act on the Control of Dishonored Checks, habitual fraud, and forgery of a public document, and sentenced him; and while the case was pending in the appellate trial due to the Defendant’s appeal, the court below granted the prosecutor’s motion to amend the indictment, which was to add the facts charged of habitual fraud and to change the offense name from habitual fraud to violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (fraud), and to add Article 3(1)2 of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes to the applicable statutory provisions, and then, after concluding the hearing, ex officio reversed the first-instance judgment of the said single-judge judge, recognized all the facts charged as guilty, and sentenced the Defendant.\\n\\nHowever, the statutory punishment under Article 3(1)2 of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes is imprisonment with labor for not less than 3 years, and according to Article 32(1)3 of the Court Organization Act, a case punishable by death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment with labor or imprisonment without labor for not less than 1 year is to be tried in the first instance by the collegiate division of a district court or its branch court. In addition, Article 28 of the same Act provides that the High Court shall adjudicate appellate cases from first-instance judgments of the collegiate division of a district court, and Article 8(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that, where a case within the jurisdiction of a single judge is changed by amendment of the indictment into a case within the jurisdiction of a collegiate division, the court shall transfer the case, by decision, to the court having jurisdiction.\\n\\nWhen the above relevant provisions are taken together, even where, in the appellate trial, a case within the jurisdiction of a single judge has become a case within the jurisdiction of a collegiate division by amendment of the indictment, the court must transfer the case to the court having jurisdiction, and it is appropriate to view the court having jurisdiction over the above case within the jurisdiction of a collegiate division as amended in the appellate trial as the High Court. Therefore, although the court below should have, after granting the above motion to amend the indictment, transferred this case by decision to the Gwangju High Court, which is the court having jurisdiction, it is deemed to have erred by wrongly recognizing jurisdiction and proceeding to adjudicate the merits.\\n\\nAnd such error is deemed to be a violation of the laws and regulations governing procedural proceedings, and in light of the legislative purpose of the jurisdiction system and the seriousness of the illegality, it is clear that this affected the judgment.\\n\\nThe argument in the grounds of appeal pointing out this point is well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed pursuant to Articles 391 and 394 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and the case is transferred to the Gwangju High Court having jurisdiction, and it is adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the judges concerned as stated in the disposition."}

question: Judicial Police Officer P, acting on a tip, cracked down on a prostitution establishment operated by A. During business hours, P entered it disguised as a customer and inquired whether prostitution was possible, and during that process recorded the conversation with A. P entered the inner room following A’s guidance, and when a female employee entered the inner room, pulled down P’s pants, and tried to climb onto the bed, P disclosed the fact of the crackdown and arrested A in flagrante delicto on suspicion of arranging prostitution against himself. While arresting A in flagrante delicto, P searched the interior of the establishment and photographed 7 condoms found therein, which had been wrapped in plastic, together with the seizure record. Meanwhile, during the arrest of a flagrant offender, P received by voluntary submission from A the ledger used at the establishment; this was a compilation of notes that the women employed at the establishment had made on memo paper from time to time for reference in business while engaging in prostitution as their occupation, recording the prostitution counterpart’s ID, telephone number, and method of prostitution, and P submitted it as evidence in the prostitution-brokering case against A. Among the explanations concerning this, which is correct? (Where there is conflict, in accordance with precedents)
A: If A did not recognize the fact that P was recording the conversation with him, this corresponds to recording a conversation between others that was not disclosed to the public, and because it was done without a warrant, it is illegal.
B: Even where P entered the establishment, which unspecified persons could enter, by masquerading as a customer during business hours, P entered the establishment from the outset for the purpose of criminal investigation; therefore, even if it was for preserving evidence, P should have obtained a warrant in advance and proceeded with the recording or seizure/search procedures, or should have obtained a warrant for this afterward.
C: Although there was no coercive disposition such as seizure that acquired possession of the condom and other evidence, photographing the condoms discovered by searching the establishment is also illegal unless there is a warrant, so the above photograph has no evidentiary capacity as illegally collected evidence.
D: Items voluntarily submitted by the suspect at the scene of an arrest in flagrante delicto cannot be seized pursuant to Article 218 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and because a post warrant must be obtained pursuant to Article 217(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, the above ledger voluntarily submitted by A, who was arrested in flagrante delicto, has no evidentiary capacity unless a post warrant for it is issued.
E: The above ledger is an ordinary document prepared for business necessity under Article 315(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act and therefore is naturally a document with evidentiary capacity.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2007DO3219]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. The Defendant argues that the printout of the memory card concerning the Defendant on page 169 of the investigation record of this case is inadmissible as evidence because the Defendant did not consent to its use as evidence and the authenticity of its formation has not been proved, and that the printouts of the memory cards concerning 38 persons, including Non-Prosecuted Person 1, are likewise inadmissible as evidence, yet the lower court committed an illegality by adopting such inadmissible evidence as evidence of guilt.\\n\\nHowever, according to the judgment of the lower court, the lower court did not adopt the printout of the memory card concerning the Defendant as evidence of guilt, but instead clearly adopted as evidence of guilt only the testimony of Non-Prosecuted Persons 2 and 3 regarding the source of the said memory card, the person who created the record, the circumstances, the contents stored on the said memory card, and its authenticity, as well as the statements recorded in each suspect interrogation protocol. According to the reasons for the lower-court judgment and the evidence lawfully adopted by the lower court, the contents recorded on the said memory card were written on memo paper by the women engaged in prostitution whom Non-Prosecuted Person 2 employed, for use in business reference before and after prostitution by recording the other party male’s ID, telephone number, and methods of prostitution while engaging in prostitution as a business, and then were entered and prepared either directly or by another female employee employed by Non-Prosecuted Person 2; thus, in substance, they constitute ordinary documents prepared for business necessity under Article 315, item 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and it must be deemed that the documents themselves naturally fall within documents having evidentiary capacity. Accordingly, the testimony of Non-Prosecuted Persons 2 and 3 regarding their contents, as well as the statements recorded in the suspect interrogation protocols, cannot be said to lack evidentiary capacity either. In addition, in the case of the printouts of the memory cards concerning 38 persons, including Non-Prosecuted Person 1, it is clearly shown in the record that the Defendant consented to their use as evidence, and therefore they have evidentiary capacity. Accordingly, the lower court’s adoption of each of the above pieces of evidence as evidence was proper, and there is no illegality in that it violated the rules governing the assessment of evidence or misunderstood the legal principles concerning evidentiary capacity.\\n\\n2. The Defendant further argues that, even with only the evidence having evidentiary capacity among the submitted evidence, the probative value thereof is severely insufficient to recognize the charged facts of this case, yet the lower court committed an illegality by finding the Defendant guilty. However, in this case, where there is no ground that can be seen as a violation of the rules governing the assessment of evidence in the lower court’s determination, the above grounds of appeal merely dispute matters concerning factual findings within the exclusive authority of the trier of fact and therefore cannot be deemed lawful grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2015DO13726]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Concerning the Prosecutor’s grounds of appeal\\n\\na. A person caught in the act of committing a crime, or immediately after committing a crime, may be arrested without a warrant by anyone (Article 212 of the Criminal Procedure Act). In order to arrest a person caught in the act, there must be, in addition to the punishability of the act, the immediacy and temporal closeness of the offense, and the clarity of the offender and the offense, the necessity of arrest, that is, a risk of flight or destruction of evidence (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 98DO3029 rendered on Jan. 26, 1999). Whether the requirements for such arrest of a person caught in the act are satisfied shall be determined on the basis of the circumstances at the time of arrest, and it may be said that the investigating authority has considerable discretion in its judgment in this regard. Therefore, unless it is recognized, in view of the circumstances at the time of arrest, that the investigating authority’s judgment on those requirements is manifestly unreasonable in light of the rules of experience, the arrest of a person caught in the act by the investigating authority should not be conclusively held unlawful (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2012DO8184 rendered on Nov. 29, 2012).\\n\\nWhen a prosecutor or a judicial police officer arrests a suspect as a person caught in the act pursuant to Article 212 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the prosecutor or judicial police officer may, if necessary, conduct seizure, search, and inspection without a warrant at the scene of arrest; however, where it is necessary to continue the seizure of the seized item, an application for a seizure warrant shall be made without delay within 48 hours from the time of arrest (Article 216(1) item 2 and Article 217(2)). And when a prosecutor or judicial police officer, at the place of the crime during or immediately after the commission of the crime, is unable to obtain a judge’s warrant due to urgency, seizure, search, or inspection may be conducted without a warrant, but in such case a warrant must be obtained afterward without delay (Article 216(3)). However, according to Article 218 of the Criminal Procedure Act, a prosecutor or judicial police officer may seize, without a warrant, items left behind by a suspect, etc., or items voluntarily submitted by the owner, possessor, or custodian; therefore, even at the scene of arrest of a person caught in the act or at the crime scene, items voluntarily submitted by the possessor, etc. may be seized without a warrant pursuant to the above provision, and in such case the prosecutor or judicial police officer need not obtain a warrant afterward.\\n\\nb. The gist of the charge under the facts alleged in this case concerning the offense of violating the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropics) dated June 1, 2014 is that “the Defendant, upon the proposal of Non-Indicted Person 1, concealed approximately 6.1 kg of Philopon divided into 7 plastic bags on his body around May 29, 2014, boarded a barge at a port in China, and entered △△ Port in Geoje City at around 16:15 on June 1 of the same year, thereby conspiring with Non-Indicted Person 1 and others to smuggle in approximately 6.1 kg of Philopon.”\\n\\nThe court of original instance held the Defendant not guilty on the following grounds: a prosecutor’s investigator searched the inside of the barge based on a tip, arrested the Defendant, who had been hiding, as a person caught in the act of violating the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropics) due to Philopon smuggling, and then seized the Philopon by receiving it as a voluntary submission after searching the scene of arrest. However, at the time of arrest, the Philopon, which is evidence of the Philopon smuggling offense, had not yet been discovered; mere intelligence that Philopon was being smuggled was insufficient to establish the clarity of the offense among the requirements for arrest of a person caught in the act; even if the arrest as a person caught in the act were lawful, the investigative agency violated due process by seizing the Philopon and failing to later obtain a warrant for seizure and search; and because the Defendant himself did not inform the authorities where the Philopon was, and the Philopon was not found at the very place where he had been hiding, even though the investigative agency purported to receive the Philopon as a voluntary submission from the Defendant, who had already been subdued by an arrest of a person caught in the act, it could not be regarded as a lawful voluntarily submitted item. Accordingly, the court held that the seized Philopon and the secondary evidence in this case, such as the expert report collected on that basis, were illegally obtained evidence or secondary evidence of illegally obtained evidence and thus lacked admissibility, and that the remaining evidence submitted by the Prosecutor alone was insufficient to establish the above charge.\\n\\nc. However, the court below’s determination on this point cannot be sustained for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) According to the reasons for the court below’s judgment and the evidence duly admitted by the court of first instance that the court below upheld, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n(a) Around May 29, 2014, prosecutors’ investigators received information that the Defendant was entering the country illegally on a barge (vessel name 1 omitted) towed by (vessel name 2 omitted) and smuggling Philopon, and searched the above barge, which had arrived at △△ Port at around 16:15 on June 1.\\n\\n(b) During the search, prosecutor’s investigator Non-Indicted Person 2 discovered the Defendant hiding on a shelf in the ship’s stores warehouse and made him slowly come down, then asked where the Philopon had been placed, but received no answer. Then, just as another prosecutor’s investigator searching another part of the barge shouted, “The item is here, found it,” at around 16:30, the Defendant was arrested as a person caught in the act of smuggling Philopon and illegal entry, etc.\\n\\n(c) Non-Indicted Person 2 immediately showed the Defendant approximately 6.1 kg of Philopon that had been discovered and asked whether he intended to voluntarily submit it, explaining that “if Philopon is voluntarily submitted, it may be seized without a warrant, and if seized, it cannot be returned voluntarily; if it is not voluntarily submitted, a warrant must be obtained and then it must be seized.” After receiving the Defendant’s consent together with the statement, “I know that much myself,” he seized the Philopon, and on the same day at the Prosecutors’ Office he prepared a voluntary submission confirmation and obtained the Defendant’s signature and seal. The Prosecutor has not obtained a post-seizure warrant for the seized Philopon and has retained it to the present.\\n\\n(d) The Defendant was sentenced on Apr. 29, 2010, to 7 months’ imprisonment for violating the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropics) due to Philopon sale and purchase, and on May 17 of the same year completed the execution of that sentence; in addition, he has been punished a total of 6 times for the same type of prior offenses.\\n\\n(2) Examining these facts in light of the legal principles set forth above, the prosecutor’s investigator discovered the Philopon near the place where he had found the Defendant on the barge while searching the barge and immediately arrested the Defendant when the Philopon was discovered, during or immediately after the commission of the offense of smuggling Philopon while entering the country illegally; therefore, this was a lawful arrest of a person caught in the act, and it cannot be said that, in view of the circumstances at the time of arrest, the Defendant was not a person caught in the act of smuggling Philopon while entering the country illegally, or that the prosecutor’s investigator’s judgment thereon was manifestly unreasonable in light of the rules of experience.\\n\\nMoreover, in light of the fact that the prosecutor’s investigator had informed the Defendant, before seizing the Philopon, of the meaning and effect of voluntary submission, the fact that the Defendant also appears to have fully understood that if he voluntarily submitted the Philopon, which was the object of seizure, it would be seized and not returned, given that he had been criminally punished several times for the same type of offense such as Philopon sale and purchase, and the fact that there is no material to find that the Defendant, at the time of arrest, denied involvement in the Philopon-related offense, and no circumstances at all to find that the prosecutor’s investigator deceived or threatened the Defendant in order to obtain voluntary submission of the Philopon, it should be held that the Defendant, as the possessor of the Philopon, voluntarily submitted it, and thus the seizure of the Philopon was also lawful.\\n\\n(3) Nevertheless, the court below held, solely for the reasons stated in its opinion, that the prosecutor’s investigator’s arrest of the Defendant as a person caught in the act of smuggling Philopon was unlawful, and that the seized Philopon was not a lawful voluntarily submitted item; accordingly, it determined that the Philopon and the secondary evidence in this case based thereon lacked admissibility as illegally obtained evidence or secondary evidence of illegally obtained evidence. Therefore, the court below erred by misapprehending the legal principles regarding the lawful requirements for arrest of a person caught in the act and the seizure of voluntarily submitted items prescribed in Article 218 of the Criminal Procedure Act, thereby affecting the judgment. The Prosecutor’s assertion in the grounds of appeal pointing out this issue is well-founded.\\n\\nd. Therefore, the part of the court below’s judgment concerning the offense of violating the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropics) dated June 1, 2014 should be reversed. Since the offenses of violating the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropics) dated Mar. 30, 2011, Apr. 25, 2011, and early June 2011, and the offense of violating the Immigration Control Act, all of which were found guilty by the court below, are in a relation of concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act with the above offense, they shall also be reversed together.\\n\\n2. Concerning the Defendant’s grounds of appeal\\n\\nAccording to Article 383 item 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, an appeal on the ground of improper sentencing is permitted only in cases in which the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or penal servitude for not less than 10 years has been imposed; therefore, in this case, where a sentence lighter than that was imposed for the offense of violating the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropics) dated Aug. 3, 2009 among the facts charged, the assertion that the sentence is too severe and improper, or that there was a violation of law due to insufficiency of examination regarding sentencing factors, does not constitute a lawful ground of appeal. Accordingly, the Defendant’s grounds of appeal concerning this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without addressing the remaining grounds of appeal by the Defendant and the Prosecutor, we reverse the part of the court below’s judgment concerning the offenses of violating the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropics) dated Mar. 30, 2011, Apr. 25, 2011, early June 2011, and June 1, 2014, and the offense of violating the Immigration Control Act, and remand this part of the case to the court below for further trial and determination. We dismiss the Defendant’s appeal concerning the part of the court below’s judgment relating to the offense of violating the Narcotics Control Act (psychotropics) dated Aug. 3, 2009. It is so adjudged as the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2018DO8161]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case\\n\\nA. Summary of the Facts Charged Against the Defendants\\n\\nDefendant 3 is the person operating the “‘○○○○ Nightclub’ in Jeju City” (hereinafter referred to as “the Nightclub at Issue”), Defendant 2 is the person working as the head of the entertainment department of the Nightclub at Issue, and Defendant 1 is a dancer and employee of the Nightclub at Issue.\\n\\nNo person operating a business affecting public morals shall have another engage in obscene acts at a business place affecting public morals, or arrange or provide for such acts. Nevertheless, the Defendants conspired to recruit customers through obscene acts, and at around 23:00 on June 21, 2016, at the Nightclub at Issue, Defendant 1, having received KRW 4,000,000 per month from Defendant 3 and on condition of working in the entertainment department managed by Defendant 2, performed on the stage of the Nightclub at Issue for about 15 minutes a show depicting sexual intercourse while wearing only a T-back panty, and then came down again to the table where the customers were seated and poured them drinks, thereby livening up the atmosphere, and then went back up on the stage and danced with an artificial penis attached to his genitals and with his pubic hair exposed, thereby depicting sexual intercourse, and thus conducted a business of obscene acts.\\n\\nB. The Court Below’s Determination\\n\\nThe court below, on the grounds that the police officers’ act of entering the Nightclub at Issue disguised as customers and filming Defendant 1’s performance constituted compulsory investigation, but no warrant had been issued either before or after, and therefore the CD containing the filmed footage and the video photographs capturing that footage were inadmissible as illegally collected evidence, reversed the judgment of the first instance and found the facts charged against the Defendants not guilty.\\n\\n2. The Supreme Court’s Determination\\n\\nHowever, the court below’s determination is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nA. If, while investigating a crime, an investigative agency films when the crime is currently being committed or immediately after it has been committed, and there is necessity and urgency to preserve evidence, and the filming is conducted by a method generally deemed reasonable and permissible, then such filming cannot be deemed unlawful merely because it was carried out without a warrant (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 99DO2317, decided on September 3, 1999). However, because filming may infringe portrait rights, the secrecy and freedom of private life, the freedom of residence, and the like, whether an investigative agency filmed by a method generally deemed reasonable and permissible must be carefully determined by comprehensively considering, inter alia, whether the investigative agency entered the filming location by ordinary means and whether the filming location and the object fall within an area where protection of the secrecy and freedom of private life, and the like, can reasonably be expected.\\n\\nB. When the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below and the evidence lawfully admitted and examined by the court below and the first instance court are taken together, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n1) Police officers belonging to the Jeju Western Police Station entered the Nightclub at Issue for the purpose of collecting evidence concerning a complaint posted on the e-People Internet site stating that “an obscene nude show by a male dancer is continuing at the Nightclub at Issue.”\\n\\n2) The Nightclub at Issue is a generally open place that anyone who is an adult may enter during business hours without restrictions such as entry qualifications.\\n\\n3) The police officers entered the Nightclub at Issue during its business hours by passing through the entrance used by customers, and no special circumstance is found in the course of that entry, such as being stopped by security personnel or sneaking in by taking advantage of a time when security personnel were away.\\n\\n4) Defendant 1 performed on the stage inside the Nightclub at Issue a performance including scenes depicting sexual intercourse, and the police officers sat in the audience together with other customers, watched that performance, and filmed the appearance of Defendant 1, which was open to an unspecified number of customers.\\n\\nC. If the factual relations are as above, the filmed footage at issue was produced by police officers, while the suspicion of crime against the Defendants had been detected, in order to preserve evidence concerning the business of obscene acts inside the Nightclub at Issue, by entering by ordinary means the Nightclub at Issue, which is a place open to an unspecified number of persons, and filming the appearance open to customers. Therefore, it cannot be deemed unlawful merely because it was filmed without a warrant, and the filmed footage at issue and the video photographs capturing that footage are admissible as evidence.\\n\\nD. Nevertheless, the court below, on the basis only of the reasons set forth in its holding, denied the admissibility of the filmed footage at issue and the video photographs capturing that footage, and held the facts charged against the Defendants not guilty on the ground that there was no other evidence. In the court below’s determination, there is an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the admissibility of evidence obtained through filming by an investigative agency.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination, and the judgment is rendered as ordered in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning consent to the admission of evidence is correct? (In the event of a dispute, according to precedent)
A: If the defendant does not immediately object to defense counsel's consent to the admission of the evidence offered by the prosecutor, the evidentiary admissibility of those items is recognized, and even if thereafter the defendant revokes or withdraws that consent of defense counsel before completion of the examination of evidence, the evidentiary admissibility once granted remains intact.
B: After a judgment of not guilty was rendered in the first instance and the prosecutor appealed, a statement protocol prepared by summoning in advance to the investigative agency, without special circumstances, a person whom the investigative agency could request and examine as a witness on the appellate trial date has no evidentiary admissibility, and the same applies even where the defendant consents that it may be used as evidence.
C: Among the evidence submitted by the prosecutor, where the defendant and defense counsel express a dissenting opinion as to the criminal complaint, and where they consent to the admission of evidence as to an investigative report prepared by an assistant prosecutor, to which the same criminal complaint is attached, and the examination of evidence is thereby conducted, the effect of the consent to the investigative report naturally extends to the attached criminal complaint as well, so the above criminal complaint may be used as evidence of guilt.
D: Where, at a trial date at which the defendant was present, an opinion is stated that there is no consent to using the item as evidence, even if at a subsequent trial date at which the defendant did not appear only defense counsel appeared and reversed the prior opinion and consented to its use as evidence, the defense counsel's consent to the admission of evidence is ineffective absent special circumstances.
E: Where a defendant who filed a request for formal trial in opposition to a summary order fails to appear twice consecutively in the first instance of the formal trial procedure, so that consent to the admission of evidence is deemed given, and the examination of evidence is completed, if the defendant appears at the appellate trial and, while denying the charged facts, manifests an intention to withdraw or cancel the deemed consent to the admission of evidence, evidentiary admissibility is lost.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2004DO4428]": "The appeal is dismissed."}

{"[2007DO5776]": "We consider the grounds for appeal.\\n\\nThe Criminal Procedure Act (hereinafter referred to as the \"Act\") provides that \"where evidence may be examined without the defendant's appearance and the defendant fails to appear, the defendant shall be deemed to have consented. However, this shall not apply where a representative or defense counsel appears\" (Article 318(2)); meanwhile, it provides that \"where a defendant who has filed a request for a formal trial in objection to a summary order fails to appear on the trial date in the formal trial proceedings, a new date shall be set, and if the defendant fails to appear on the newly set date without justifiable reason, a judgment may be rendered without the defendant's statement\" (Article 458(2), Article 365).\\n\\nArticles 458(2) and 365 of the Act are a kind of sanctioning provision that treats the defendant as having waived the right to present argument on the merits by failing to appear (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DO1803, rendered June 11, 2009). In such a case, a trial and judgment may be conducted without the defendant's appearance, and as evidence is ordinarily examined as part of the trial proceedings, where evidence must be examined in the defendant's absence, under Article 318(2) of the Act, consent under Article 318(1) is deemed to exist regardless of the defendant's actual intent (see Supreme Court Decision 91DO865, rendered June 28, 1991). In light of the legislative purpose of Article 318(2) of the Act, namely the necessity and promptness of trial, that is, prevention of delay in procedural acts due to the defendant's nonappearance or prevention of delay in proceedings arising from the inability to determine the evidentiary admissibility of hearsay evidence in cases of the defendant's nonappearance, when a defendant who has filed a request for a formal trial in objection to a summary order fails to appear twice in the formal trial proceedings and the court examines evidence without the defendant's appearance, the defendant's evidentiary consent under Article 318(2) of the Act shall be deemed to exist.\\n\\nAnd, once the evidentiary examination has been completed after the defendant who filed a request for a formal trial in objection to a summary order failed to appear twice in the formal trial proceedings and thus consent to evidence under Article 318(2) of the Act was deemed to exist, the evidentiary consent that is the subject of the deeming may be withdrawn or revoked until completion of the evidentiary examination, but once the evidentiary examination has been completed, revocation or withdrawal is not recognized. In light of the fact that deemed evidentiary consent arises regardless of the defendant's actual intent, even if the defendant appears at the appellate trial and denies the charged facts while making a statement to withdraw or revoke the deemed evidentiary consent, it cannot be said that the evidentiary admissibility lawfully granted thereby is lost.\\n\\nOn the same purport, the lower court, in the defendant's absence, maintained in the appellate trial the first-instance court's measure that, because the defendant who filed a request for a formal trial in objection to the summary order failed to appear twice in the formal trial proceedings, deemed evidentiary consent under Article 318(2) was made with respect to the guilty evidence submitted by the prosecutor and thus granted evidentiary admissibility, and adopted it. Upon review of the record in light of the foregoing legal principles, that measure is justifiable and acceptable, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality consisting of an error of law concerning deemed evidentiary consent and its withdrawal or revocation.\\n\\nFurther, the defendant's remaining grounds for appeal merely criticize the selection and weighing of evidence and the finding of facts, which are within the exclusive province of the lower court, a fact-finding court, and therefore do not constitute lawful grounds for appeal. Moreover, if the reasons of the lower court's judgment are reviewed in light of the evidence lawfully adopted by the first-instance court, which the lower court upheld, the lower court's determination that the charged facts in this case were guilty for the reasons stated in its opinion is justifiable, and there is no illegality in that it violates logic and the rules of experience and exceeds the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the order, in unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2011DO3809]": "We determine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the admissibility of the statement record of Non-indicted 1 prepared by the Prosecutor\\n\\nAccording to the record and the reasons of the judgment below, the court below rejected the assertion of the Defendant and defense counsel that the statement record prepared by the Prosecutor, who met Non-indicted 1 staying in the Republic of Guatemala directly and examined him as a witness without going through the criminal mutual legal assistance procedures, infringes the territorial sovereignty of a foreign state that must duly be guaranteed under international law and must be denied admissibility as illegally obtained evidence obtained in violation of international criminal mutual legal assistance procedures. Furthermore, it found that the said statement record falls under the case where the original declarant is unable to testify due to residence abroad, and thus held that it is admissible under Article 367 of the Military Court Act and used it as evidence of guilt.\\n\\nFirst, as to whether the said statement record constitutes illegally obtained evidence, although the witness examination of Non-indicted 1 by the Prosecutor constituted an investigative act for the collection of evidence and the place of examination belonged to the territory of the Republic of Guatemala rather than our country, so long as it is clear from the record that the other party to the examination was a national of our country and that, by voluntarily responding to the examination, no force, coercion, or any involuntary element whatsoever could have been involved in the method or procedure of the examination, this is merely a form of free communication between the state organ of a friendly state and its national that is ordinarily permitted between friendly states allowing each other’s nationals to travel and reside in one another’s territory, and therefore no issue of infringement of territorial sovereignty can arise here. Moreover, this is an international legal issue between our country and the Republic of Guatemala, and the Defendant, having no connection at all with the Republic of Guatemala, which is the other party thereto, that could constitute a cause of international-law jurisdiction, cannot be said to be subject, in the domestic criminal procedure against the Defendant, to the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence on such grounds.\\n\\nHowever, in order for the said statement record, which is hearsay evidence, to be admissible under Article 367 of the Military Court Act, the statement must have been made under circumstances in which it could be specially trusted, meaning a case in which there is little room for falsification in the content of the statement or in the preparation of the record or document, and there are concrete and external circumstances assuring the reliability or voluntariness of the contents of the statement (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DO3619 rendered May 25, 2006, etc.). The circumstances relied on by the court below, namely that Non-indicted 1 responded to the examination in the form of a voluntary investigation in a free atmosphere and directly signed and affixed his seal to the statement record, are insufficient to acknowledge the foregoing circumstances; rather, ① even if the witness examination of Non-indicted 1 does not involve coercion and therefore does not give rise to an issue of infringement of sovereignty over the Republic of Guatemala, the fact that the Prosecutor, after the institution of prosecution in this case, went directly to a local hotel and conducted the examination outside the evidence-taking procedure of the military court, and did not choose such methods as criminal mutual legal assistance procedures or examination through a Korean consul stationed in the Republic of Guatemala, cannot help but be viewed as departing from the ordinary form of investigation; ② Non-indicted 1, despite being a bribe-giver and thereby a person who could himself be subject to punishment, unilaterally made statements in a state where, by fleeing abroad, he was evading responsibility for such conduct and had no need to worry about any disadvantage arising from false statements in the course of the investigation; ③ the reason why Non-indicted 1 came to make such accusation appears to have been bad feelings toward the Defendant because the Defendant refused his request to provide funds for his flight; ④ after returning to Korea, Non-indicted 1 has made clear, through testimony in court, etc., that he has no intention of guaranteeing the truthfulness of his statements; ⑤ after preparing the said statement record, Non-indicted 1, though at the Defendant’s request, sent documents to the effect that the contents of the said statement record were different from the facts, and in the course of a telephone conversation with witness for the court below Non-indicted 2, he also made statements that, unlike the facts alleged in the indictment, partially accord with the Defendant’s assertions. In light of the foregoing, it is difficult to say that there has been proof that the said statement was made under circumstances where it could be specially trusted.\\n\\nUltimately, the statement record of Non-indicted 1 prepared by the Prosecutor cannot be used as evidence of guilt because its admissibility is not recognized.\\n\\n2. Regarding the admissibility of Non-indicted 1’s tip-off document attached to the investigation report prepared by an assistant prosecutor of the Daejeon District Prosecutors’ Office\\n\\nAccording to the record, at the first trial date in the court of first instance, the Prosecutor applied for admission into evidence of, together, the tip-off document prepared by Non-indicted 1 (Evidence List Serial No. 11, hereinafter referred to as the “Complaint”) and the investigation report prepared by an assistant prosecutor of the Daejeon District Prosecutors’ Office (Evidence List Serial No. 24, hereinafter referred to as the “Investigation Report in this case”). Although defense counsel stated that he did not agree to admitting the Complaint into evidence, he agreed to the Investigation Report in this case, which includes the same Complaint as an attached document. Accordingly, the court of first instance completed the examination of evidence for the Investigation Report in this case at the first trial date and deferred the decision on whether to admit the Complaint into evidence, and then, when the Prosecutor withdrew the application for evidence as to the Complaint at the fourth trial date, did not conduct evidence examination on it. It can be seen that the court of first instance and the court below regarded the effect of consent to evidence regarding the Investigation Report in this case as naturally extending to the Complaint attached thereto, since the Defendant and defense counsel did not separately express evidentiary opinions on the Investigation Report in this case and the documents attached thereto, and, notwithstanding the explicit objection of the Defendant and defense counsel to the same Complaint that had been separately applied for as evidence, used it as evidence of guilt (although it was not included in the summary of evidence of the judgment of the first instance, it was used as the basis for the determination of guilt rejecting the assertions of the Defendant and defense counsel).\\n\\nWhere, as above, an investigative agency records materials collected during the investigation in the record and summarizes and explains their meaning, nature, and relevance to the alleged facts in the form of an investigation report, and attaches the relevant materials to the investigation report, the contents stated in that investigation report are either the recognition, judgment, and inference obtained through the materials attached by the investigative agency or merely a simple summary of the materials, and are thus of a nature incapable of independently having probative force as to the facts charged apart from the original materials. In this case, it appears that the Defendant and defense counsel also understood the probative force of the Investigation Report in this case in the same sense and therefore did not dispute its admissibility despite denying the facts charged.\\n\\nAccordingly, if the Prosecutor, while applying for the Investigation Report in this case as evidence, intended to prove the facts charged not merely by presenting the Complaint of Non-indicted 1 attached thereto as material explaining the occasion on which Non-indicted 3 came to request a new written confirmation from Non-indicted 1, but by showing through the fact that the contents of the complaint accord with the facts charged that the facts charged were proved, then the said Complaint should have been separately designated in the evidence list and applied for as independent evidence, because it is not incorporated into the Investigation Report in this case as part thereof, nor do the two, by combining in substance, acquire evidentiary force or evidentiary value as a single document, but instead has independent probative force as an independent and separate piece of evidence. In such a case, the military court should have exercised appropriate control over proceedings, such as requiring the Prosecutor to withdraw the said evidence application because it duplicated the evidence application regarding the Complaint already submitted under Evidence List Serial No. 11, or, since defense counsel had already expressed the intent not to agree to evidence as to the same Complaint, separately presenting the Complaint attached thereto to the Defendant and defense counsel even if they expressed an intention to agree to evidence as to the Investigation Report in this case, and confirming their true intention regarding whether they consented to evidence on that portion. Nevertheless, without pointing out any issue, the court accepted the Complaint attached thereto as evidence merely because there was consent to evidence regarding the Investigation Report in this case, and then used it as evidence to find guilt at the stage of rendering judgment. This is not acceptable in light of the principle of substantive due process.\\n\\nUltimately, the Complaint of Non-indicted 1 attached to the Investigation Report in this case cannot be used as evidence of guilt because it cannot be deemed to have gone through the procedures of a lawful application for evidence, determination of evidence, and examination of evidence under the Military Court Act, or because it is not evidence having probative force supporting the facts charged.\\n\\n3. Whether the facts charged are proved by the remaining evidence\\n\\nIf, as above, among the evidence submitted by the Prosecutor, the statement record of Non-indicted 1 prepared by the Prosecutor and the Complaint attached to the Investigation Report in this case cannot be used as evidence of guilt, then only the following facts may be recognized from the remaining evidence lawfully admitted and examined by the court of first instance and cited by the court below, but in a bribery case, without the statement of the person who gave the money and valuables, it is difficult to regard such indirect facts alone as constituting proof of the facts charged sufficient to exclude reasonable doubt.\\n\\nThat is, even excluding the statements or Complaint of Non-indicted 1, according to the remaining evidence, it can be seen that there was, at the date and time stated in the facts charged, a monetary transaction between the Defendant and Non-indicted 1 as stated therein; that at the time, the Defendant was the commander of the engineer company of the Marine Corps 00 Brigade, and at the time of the monetary transaction dated October 8, 2004, he was the site supervisor responsible for the construction work of the 00000 facility of that unit contracted by Non-indicted 4 Co., Ltd., operated by Non-indicted 1; and that although the Defendant had no special source of income other than his salary, there were questions in the course of accumulating assets, such as acquiring officetels and apartments in the names of himself and his wife in 2002 and 2007, and that during his tenure as commander of the engineer company, improper relationships were also detected, such as suspicious monetary transactions with construction contractors who undertook military facility construction through borrowed-name accounts or causing those construction contractors to bear entertainment expenses.\\n\\nHowever, with only the foregoing evidence, there is no statement from the person who gave the money and valuables directly supporting the point that the transaction of money and valuables in this case was related to the Defendant’s official duties. In addition, ① as to the facts charged related to bribery in or around September 2003, Non-indicted 1 allegedly gave the Defendant 40,000,000 won and then received 30,000,000 won back, thereby providing the remaining 10,000,000 won as a bribe. This is highly unusual and unnatural as a method of bribery, and rather than being a sophisticated attempt to conceal or disguise the bribe nature of 10,000,000 won as the Prosecutor contends, it appears more likely to have been part of a continuing monetary transaction, as the Defendant argues. The receipt of the money and valuables occurred before the contract for the 00000 facility construction of the Marine Corps 00 Brigade had been concluded, so there is no clear reason or motive for providing such a bribe. This receipt of money and valuables was not even included in the Complaint of Non-indicted 1 (according to the record, Non-indicted 1 appears not to remember, not only the reason for providing the money and valuables, but even the fact of the receipt itself); ② even as to the bribery related to around October 8, 2004, according to the testimony of witness for the court below Non-indicted 2, Non-indicted 1 admitted that, in relation to providing 52,000,000 won to the Defendant at that time, he had previously borrowed 40,000,000 won from the Defendant. This testimony of Non-indicted 2 is based on the contents of a telephone conversation with Non-indicted 1, and the contents of the call do not appear to have been fabricated falsely in collusion among the Defendant, Non-indicted 2, and Non-indicted 1. Thus, the possibility cannot be excluded that the Defendant’s assertion on this point is at least partly true. In light of the foregoing, it is difficult to conclude that the facts charged in this case are established as they stand on the basis of the indirect facts recognized above.\\n\\nIn addition, although, as pointed out in the judgment of the first instance and the judgment below, the Defendant’s explanation regarding the facts charged in this case lacks consistency or persuasiveness, and above all lacks any convincing explanation regarding the source of funds for the loan to Non-indicted 1, which is the basis of his assertion, in a criminal trial the burden of proof as to the facts charged rests with the Prosecutor, so the fact that the Defendant’s assertion is unreasonable and appears to be a lie cannot be used as a basis for finding that the facts charged have been proved.\\n\\n4.
