Conclusion\\n\\nUltimately, although the evidence is insufficient to find the facts charged in this case guilty, the court below affirmed the judgment of the first instance, which found all of the facts charged in this case guilty on the basis only of the evidence stated in the judgment that lacks admissibility or has weak probative force, and dismissed the Defendant’s appeal. Thus, the judgment below contains illegality that affected the result of the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the admissibility of hearsay evidence in a military trial, the procedure for examination of evidence as to documentary evidence, and the degree of proof required for a finding of guilt.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as set forth in the operative part."}

{"[2013DO3]": "We consider the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe subject of consent to evidence prescribed in Article 318 of the Criminal Procedure Act is the prosecutor and the defendant, who are the parties to the litigation, and defense counsel may only present opinions concerning consent to evidence on behalf of the defendant, and therefore cannot consent to the use of evidence contrary to the defendant’s express intention. Accordingly, where, at a trial date on which the defendant was present, an opinion was stated that there was no consent to the use of evidence, even if thereafter only defense counsel appeared at a trial date on which the defendant did not appear and reversed the prior opinion to consent to the use of evidence, such consent shall be deemed ineffective absent special circumstances.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the following facts can be found. Namely, at the first trial date of the first instance on September 9, 2009, the defendant and defense counsel appeared together, and the trial transcript states that, among the evidence submitted by the prosecutor, an opinion was stated that there was no consent to the use of evidence with respect to the complaint, each police statement record concerning Non-Indicted 1 and Non-Indicted 2, and each written confirmation prepared by Non-Indicted 3 and Non-Indicted 4 (hereinafter referred to as “each of the evidence in this case”). Thereafter, as the defendant did not appear at the trial date, the court of first instance, after proceedings such as a request for investigation of whereabouts, made a decision on February 22, 2012 ordering that service on the defendant be effected by service by publication, and at the 13th trial date held on April 5, 2012 while the defendant was absent, only privately retained defense counsel appeared and consented to the admission of most of the evidence previously objected to above. Accordingly, the court of first instance, after conducting an evidentiary examination of each of the evidence in this case for which defense counsel, as above, reversed the prior opinion and consented to the use of evidence, and considering them together with the other evidence, found the facts charged in this case against the defendant guilty. The court below also, holding that the first instance judgment’s sentencing was excessive, reversed it and rendered a new judgment, while citing verbatim the summary of the evidence in the first instance court’s judgment, and found the facts charged in this case guilty.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing procedural progress and the like, and in view of the legal principles noted above, the opinion of non-consent to evidence made at the first trial date of the first instance court was stated either by the defendant himself or by defense counsel “on behalf of” the defendant, and in either case it has the effect of the defendant himself expressing an opinion of non-consent. However, defense counsel’s reversal of that position and consent to evidence at the 13th trial date of the first instance court is contrary to the defendant’s express intention, unless there are special circumstances otherwise, and thus is ineffective. Moreover, because each of the evidence in this case is hearsay evidence, it lacks admissibility unless the authenticity of its formation, etc. is recognized by the original declarant’s statements at the trial date, etc. Therefore, although each of the evidence in this case could not be used as evidence, the court of first instance used it as evidence supporting the facts charged in this case and rendered a guilty judgment, and the court below likewise, by relying on the results of the evidentiary examination conducted by the first instance court, found the facts charged in this case guilty, which is unlawful. Ultimately, the judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the subject and effect of consent to evidence.\\n\\nAccordingly, without addressing the remaining grounds of appeal asserted by the defendant, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for a new trial and determination; it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2013DO6825]": "We decide the grounds for final appeal (the contents of the supplemental statement of grounds for final appeal filed after the period for filing the statement of grounds for final appeal has elapsed are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\n1. The Constitution, in the latter sentence of Article 12(1), proclaims the principle of due process, and in Article 27 guarantees the right to receive a trial. In order to substantially implement this, the Criminal Procedure Act adopts as its basic principles the adversarial principle and the principle of trial-centered proceedings, under which the substantive examination of a criminal defendant’s case must be conducted in a public courtroom through the prosecution and defense activities of both parties, the prosecutor and the defendant, and the principle of direct examination and the principle of trial by evidence, under which the finding of the facts charged must be based only on evidence directly examined in the presence of the judge. Accordingly, after an indictment is filed, all authority over the criminal procedure concerning that case belongs to the trial court seized of the case, and the suspect, who had been the object of investigation, exercises the right of defense in the status of a defendant, a party on equal footing with the prosecutor (see Supreme Court en banc Decision dated October 22, 2009, 2009DO7436, and Supreme Court Decision dated April 28, 2011, 2009DO10412). Under the Criminal Procedure Act, procedures in the court of first instance, where all allegations and evidence are substantively examined in the presence of the judge, are the usual means of realizing the principle of substantive direct examination and the principle of trial-centered proceedings; however, since the provisions concerning the trial procedure of the court of first instance apply mutatis mutandis to the adjudicative procedure of the appellate court unless there is a special provision, the appellate court may also be regarded, within a limited scope, as a procedure following those principles (see Supreme Court en banc Decision dated March 21, 2019, 2017DO16593-1).\\nExamining the matter in light of these basic principles of the Criminal Procedure Act, after the court of first instance rendered a verdict of not guilty against the defendant and the prosecutor appealed, a statement record prepared by summoning in advance to the investigative authority, without special circumstances, a person whom the investigative authority may request as a witness and examine at the appellate hearing date is without evidentiary admissibility unless the defendant agrees that it may be used as evidence. If, after filing an indictment, the prosecutor were allowed to summon a reference person, prepare a statement record containing statements adverse to the defendant, and submit it as evidence in the trial proceedings, that would allow the prosecutor, who stands as a party on equal footing with the defendant, to use the authority of an investigative agency to unilaterally create favorable evidence outside the courtroom, and thus would contravene the adversarial principle, the principle of trial-centered proceedings, and the principle of direct examination, and would infringe the defendant’s right to a fair trial.\\nEven if the above reference person later appears in court as a witness, acknowledges the authenticity of the formation of the above statement record, and the defendant is given an opportunity to cross-examine him, the evidentiary admissibility of the above statement record cannot be recognized for the same reason.\\nWhere the above reference person makes in-court statements adverse to the defendant to the same effect as the above statement record, which lacks evidentiary admissibility, whether to recognize the credibility of such statements and use them as evidence of guilt must be carefully determined by comprehensively considering the circumstances under which the statement record was prepared at the investigative authority before the witness examination and the possibility that it affected the in-court testimony.\\n2. We examine the course and gist of the appellate judgment and the reasons therefor.\\nA. The gist of the facts charged in this case is as follows.\\nIn or around 2004, the defendant approached Non-indicted Company 1 Co., Ltd. and Non-indicted Company 2 Co., Ltd., the implementers of the complex development project for the △△ Freight Terminal located in △△-dong, ○○ District, Seoul (hereinafter referred to as “the instant project”), by proposing to the representative director of Non-indicted Person 3 that “I will help obtain the approvals and permits for the instant project through Non-indicted Person 4, etc.” Then, in or around August 2007, the defendant demanded from Non-indicted Person 3 money under the pretext of expenses for helping obtain the approvals and permits for the instant project, and on August 30, 2007, the defendant received a transfer of 100,000,000 won into a Standard Chartered Bank account in the defendant’s name (hereinafter referred to as “the instant account”); thereafter, six times in total from August 30, 2007 to May 9, 2008 (① August 30, 2007, 100,000,000 won, ② December 7, 2007, 50,000,000 won, ③ February 5, 2008, 50,000,000 won, ④ February 12, 2008, 50,000,000 won, ⑤ March 14, 2008, 100,000,000 won, ⑥ May 9, 2008, 200,000,000 won), the defendant received from Non-indicted Person 3, into the above account of the defendant, a total of 550,000,000 won (hereinafter referred to as “the instant money”) under the pretext of expenses for soliciting approvals and permits for the instant project, which falls under the jurisdiction of Seoul Metropolitan Government, and received money and valuables in connection with the mediation of matters belonging to the duties of public officials.\\nB. While being investigated by the prosecution, the defendant initially denied this, but during the 13th prosecution interrogation, the defendant stated that he told Non-indicted Person 3 that he would solve the permit issue through public officials related to Seoul Metropolitan Government and that he received the instant money for that expense (hereinafter referred to as “the prosecution confession statement”). However, at the trial dates in the court of first instance and the court below, the defendant consistently argued that it was true that he received 550,000,000 won from Non-indicted Person 3, but that he received it only as money to pass on to Non-indicted Person 4 and did not receive it as consideration for mediation.\\nC. The court of first instance found the facts charged in this case not guilty on the ground that the crime was not proven.\\nD. The court below found credibility in the appellate in-court statement of Non-indicted Person 3, the 4th prosecution statement record concerning Non-indicted Person 3, and the defendant’s prosecution confession statement as to a total of 400,000,000 won (③ through ⑥) received after the December 2007 presidential election (hereinafter referred to as “the presidential election”) out of the instant money, and reversed the first-instance judgment and found this part of the facts charged guilty; as to a total of 150,000,000 won (① through ②) received before that, it found no proof and found not guilty in the reasons.\\n3. However, the court below’s guilty determination cannot be accepted.\\nA. According to the record, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n(1) In the prosecution investigation conducted before the filing of the instant indictment, Non-indicted Person 3 stated that, in order to obtain approvals and permits for the instant project, he gave Non-indicted Person 4 through the defendant 50,000,000 won per month from around January 2005 to around May 2005, and 100,000,000 won per month from around June 2005 to around May 2008, and that the 2,150,000,000 won transferred into the defendant’s account, including the instant money, was also transferred in order to give it to Non-indicted Person 4 and Non-indicted Person 5 through the defendant.\\n(2) Before confessing to the prosecution, the defendant stated that from around July 2006 to around June 2007, which was around the primary for the presidential election candidate of the □□□ Party, he gave a total of 600,000,000 won to Non-indicted Person 4 in 12 installments of 50,000,000 won per month, and in addition, around February 2008, he gave 200,000,000 won in cash to Non-indicted Person 4.\\nThen, on May 8, 2012, during the 13th prosecution interrogation, he made the confession statement described above. In other words, the defendant stated that all cash received from Non-indicted Person 3 was money received in order to deliver it to Non-indicted Person 4, but that the instant money, excluding 1,600,000,000 won from the 2,150,000,000 won received into the instant account on 11 occasions from May 23, 2007 to May 9, 2008, was money received by the defendant.\\n(3) The prosecutor indicted the defendant for violating the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (hereinafter referred to as “the Specific Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act”) on the charge that the instant money was received under the pretext of expenses for soliciting approvals and permits. At the trial proceedings in the court of first instance, the defendant denied the facts charged, asserting that all of the instant money was money intended to be delivered to Non-indicted Person 4. The prosecutor submitted, as principal evidence in the first instance, the prosecution statement records prepared up to the 3rd interrogation of Non-indicted Person 3 and the respective suspect interrogation records concerning the defendant, and the trial proceedings continued without the appearance of Non-indicted Person 3 because the defendant agreed to all of them.\\n(4) In rendering judgment on September 21, 2012, the court of first instance found the facts charged in this case not guilty on the grounds that, in light of the defendant’s statement in court that he received the instant money from Non-indicted Person 3 under the pretext of delivering it to Non-indicted Person 4 but had not in fact delivered it to Non-indicted Person 4, there was a possibility that the defendant made false statements out of fear of fraud or embezzlement, etc. arising from such facts, so the prosecution confession statement was doubtful in credibility; that apart from that, there was no proof that the money normally delivered to Non-indicted Person 4 and the instant money were of different nature; and that, rather, there was sufficient room to find that the defendant received 550,000,000 won merely as a conduit.\\n(5) The prosecutor appealed and, in the statement of grounds of appeal dated October 31, 2012, argued in substance that “after the presidential election in December 2007, the defendant received money as expenses necessary for the approvals and permits for the instant project,” while also asserting that it would be necessary to confirm the meaning of the part of Non-indicted Person 3’s prosecution statement that he gave money to Non-indicted Person 4 through the defendant, and therefore that Non-indicted Person 3 would be requested as a witness.\\n(6) The prosecutor summoned Non-indicted Person 3 and examined him as a reference person on November 15, 2012, one day before the first trial date in the court below, and prepared the 5th prosecution statement record (hereinafter referred to as “the statement record at issue”). When preparing the statement record at issue, the prosecutor showed Non-indicted Person 3 the first-instance not-guilty judgment and the defense counsel’s written opinion and asked him to indicate any part different from what he knew, but did not tell him that he intended to request witness examination in the soon-to-be-held appellate trial. On November 16, 2012, at the first trial date in the court below, the prosecutor submitted as evidence the 4th prosecution statement record concerning Non-indicted Person 3, which had already been prepared before the indictment but had not been submitted in the first instance, and the statement record at issue prepared during the appellate proceedings; however, when the defendant did not agree, the prosecutor requested Non-indicted Person 3 as a witness.\\n(7) On December 14, 2012, at the second trial date in the court below, Non-indicted Person 3 gave in-court testimony to the same effect as the statement record at issue, and after being shown the statement record at issue and reading it, he confirmed that it was recorded as he had stated and that he had signed and affixed his seal to it. Cross-examination of Non-indicted Person 3 was conducted on April 5, 2013, at the fourth trial date in the court below.\\n(8) Non-indicted Person 3 was sentenced in the first instance by the Seoul Central District Court to 6 years’ imprisonment on February 28, 2013, and 5 years’ imprisonment on December 19, 2014, in criminal cases including large-scale breach of trust and embezzlement related to the management of funds of Non-indicted Company 2 and its affiliated companies; after the two cases were consolidated in the appellate court, the Seoul High Court sentenced him to 8 years’ imprisonment on March 22, 2017, and that judgment became final. At the time the statement record at issue was prepared for Non-indicted Person 3, investigations were ongoing with respect to some of the above criminal cases, while some cases had been indicted and trial proceedings were in progress on bail, and at the time the defense counsel’s cross-examination was conducted, he was under detention after being sentenced in the first instance to 6 years’ imprisonment in relation to the case first indicted.\\nB. Based on the above factual circumstances, we examine the evidentiary admissibility of the statement record at issue according to the legal principles set forth above. After the court of first instance rendered a verdict of not guilty against the defendant, the prosecutor appealed and then, before the appellate trial date, unilaterally prepared the statement record at issue by summoning in advance to the investigative authority a person who could be examined as a witness at the appellate trial date, and its content is also adverse to the defendant; nor does it appear that there were special circumstances necessitating the preparation of the statement record at issue. In this case, where the defendant did not agree to the statement record at issue being used as evidence, allowing it as evidence would violate the adversarial principle, the principle of trial-centered proceedings, and the principle of direct examination, and would infringe the defendant’s right to a fair trial; therefore, it lacks evidentiary admissibility.\\nC. The evidence on which the court below based its guilty determination, including Non-indicted Person 3’s appellate in-court testimony, Non-indicted Person 3’s 4th prosecution statement record, and the defendant’s prosecution confession statement, is difficult to recognize as credible for the following reasons.\\n(1) Since Non-indicted Person 3’s appellate in-court testimony was made in the circumstances described above, its credibility must be carefully assessed. First, Non-indicted Person 3’s appellate in-court testimony, Non-indicted Person 3’s 4th prosecution statement record, and the defendant’s prosecution confession statement do not match and are inconsistent with one another. Specifically, in the 4th prosecution statement, Non-indicted Person 3 stated, “After the presidential election, the defendant said that he, too, would now independently meet people and spend money as he saw fit for the success of the instant project, and asked to be supported with ‘cash,’ so he took 20,000,000 to 30,000,000 won in ‘cash.’” On the other hand, in the appellate court, Non-indicted Person 3 stated, “The defendant was not a public figure, so when paying him after the presidential election there was no need to make cash arrangements with difficulty, and therefore the money was ‘transferred by bank account.’” Thus, his statement changed from saying that he gave the defendant independent lobbying funds in cash to saying that they were transferred by bank account, and because each statement is specific in content, it is difficult to view this as a mere mistake.\\nAn indictment was filed between the time when the statement was changed in that manner, and the facts charged in this case are that the money was transferred by bank account. Suspicion arises as to whether the reason the prosecutor did not submit Non-indicted Person 3’s 4th prosecution statement record as evidence in the first instance was because, as described above, the facts charged in this case state that the money was transferred by bank account, whereas Non-indicted Person 3’s statement says that it was given in cash.\\nAt the time the statement record at issue was prepared for Non-indicted Person 3 and at the time the in-court testimony was made, serious criminal cases against Non-indicted Person 3 were in progress; some crimes were still under investigation, and for some crimes an indictment had been filed and a term of imprisonment had been imposed. When the prosecutor prepared the statement record at issue, he showed Non-indicted Person 3 the first-instance judgment and the defense counsel’s written opinion and asked him to indicate any part different from what he knew, but did not tell him that witness examination would be requested in the imminent appellate trial. Non-indicted Person 3’s appellate in-court testimony was taken at the first trial date in the court below, held the day after the statement record at issue was prepared, upon the prosecutor’s request, after he had been designated as a witness, and it was made while presenting the statement record at issue at the second trial date in the court below, approximately one month after the date on which the statement record at issue was prepared. In light of the circumstances in which the investigation was conducted at the investigative authority before witness examination and the statement record at issue was prepared, as well as the process and content of the in-court testimony, it is difficult to exclude the possibility that Non-indicted Person 3, before testifying in the appellate court, was summoned and investigated by the prosecution and that his statement was changed in order to conform to the facts charged in this case under the influence of the investigative authority during the process in which the statement record was prepared.\\n(2) The defendant’s prosecution confession statement was to the effect that “the money received in cash from Non-indicted Person 3 was mostly money intended to be given to Non-indicted Person 4, Non-indicted Person 5, etc., but the money received by bank account was money received for the purpose of solving the permit issue for the instant project through public officials related to Seoul Metropolitan Government, and that is true as the expense.” Thus, it indicates that all of the instant money was received under the pretext of mediation, and does not mean that the purpose differed before and after the presidential election. This also conflicts with the above respective statements by Non-indicted Person 3. In addition, as the court of first instance found, it is difficult to exclude the possibility that the defendant received the instant money from Non-indicted Person 3 under the pretext of delivering it to Non-indicted Person 4, but in fact did not deliver it to Non-indicted Person 4, and that he made false statements in order to avoid the fact becoming known or to reduce the amount of money delivered to Non-indicted Person 4.\\n(3) Ultimately, the above evidence on which the court below based its guilty determination, unlike the court of first instance, is inconsistent and contradictory with one another, and in light of the circumstances in which the investigation was conducted by the investigative authority before witness examination and the statement record at issue was prepared, as well as the circumstances that may have affected the in-court testimony, it is difficult to recognize its credibility.\\nD. Nevertheless, the court below, contrary to the above, recognized the credibility of Non-indicted Person 3’s appellate in-court testimony, Non-indicted Person 3’s 4th prosecution statement record, the defendant’s prosecution confession statement, etc., and found guilty the portion of the facts charged concerning the money received after the presidential election. In this appellate judgment, there is an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the assessment of the credibility of statements, or by violating the rules of logic and experience and thus going beyond the bounds of free evaluation of evidence.\\nE. Therefore, the guilty portion of the appellate judgment must be reversed, and the not-guilty portion based on the same single act must also be reversed; accordingly, the appellate judgment in its entirety must be reversed.\\n4. Therefore, the appellate judgment is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below. It is so decided by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the disposition."}

question: Among the explanations concerning final judgments, which of the following are incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2009DO3505]": "1. Determination on the Grounds of Appeal\\nThe court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence it admitted, found that the Defendant used abusive language toward Police Officer Non-indicted Person 1, approached him while pushing his shoulders and body as if to strike him and assaulted him, and used abusive language toward Police Officer Non-indicted Person 2 who tried to stop him, threw off his upper garment, and body-checked him, thereby obstructing the lawful execution of the official duties of the above two police officers concerning the handling of the report and investigative work, and held that the crime of obstruction of performance of official duties was established against the Defendant. In light of the record, the above fact-finding and determination by the court below are reasonably convincing as proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality, such as a violation of the rules of evidence evaluation.\\n\\n2. Ex Officio Determination\\na. According to Article 323(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, the reasons for a judgment of conviction shall specify the facts constituting the offense, the summary of the evidence, and the application of the statutes. If, in imposing a judgment of conviction, any one of these is entirely omitted from the reasons, it constitutes a violation of law affecting the judgment as prescribed in Article 383(1)1 of the Criminal Procedure Act and becomes a ground for reversal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below, the court below, ex officio, reversed the first-instance judgment and again rendered a judgment of conviction against the Defendant, but in the reasons therefor stated only the application of the statutes, and entirely omitted the facts constituting the offense and the summary of the evidence. Accordingly, the judgment below is illegal and cannot avoid reversal.\\n\\nMeanwhile, since this case is deemed sufficiently adjudicable on the basis of the case record and the evidence examined up to the court below, this Court shall render judgment directly pursuant to Article 396 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nb. Where acts of assault or intimidation are committed against multiple public officials who are executing the same official duties, multiple crimes of obstruction of performance of official duties are established according to the number of public officials executing the official duties, and where such acts of assault or intimidation are committed at the same place and on the same occasion and are evaluated as a single act in social concept, the multiple crimes of obstruction of performance of official duties shall be in a relationship of ideal concurrence (see Supreme Court Decision 4294HYEONGSANG415, decided September 28, 1961).\\n\\nAccording to the factual findings duly finalized by the court below and the record, Police Officer Non-indicted Person 1 and Non-indicted Person 2, upon receiving a damage report filed against the Defendant, responded together and were carrying out the handling of the report and investigative duties, and the Defendant, at the same place, while using abusive language toward the above police officers, first assaulted Police Officer Non-indicted Person 1 and immediately thereafter assaulted Police Officer Non-indicted Person 2, who tried to stop him; thus, the acts of assault committed at the same place and on the same occasion should reasonably be evaluated as a single act in social concept, and the crime of obstruction of performance of official duties against Non-indicted Person 1 and Non-indicted Person 2 shall be in a relationship of ideal concurrence as prescribed in Article 40 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nNevertheless, the first-instance court’s action of aggravating the punishment on the ground that each of the crimes of obstruction of performance of official duties in this case was in a relationship of real concurrence is illegal, and since such error affected the judgment, the first-instance judgment can no longer be upheld. Accordingly, the first-instance judgment is reversed, and the following judgment is rendered.\\n\\nSince the summary of the facts constituting the offense and the evidence is the same as stated in the respective corresponding columns of the first-instance judgment, they are cited in full pursuant to Articles 399 and 369 of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nThe Defendant’s stated acts correspond to Article 136(1) of the Criminal Act, and by applying Articles 40 and 50 of the Criminal Act, the Defendant is punished by the sentence prescribed for the crime of obstruction of performance of official duties against Non-indicted Person 1, which carries the heavier penalty; a fine is selected from among the prescribed punishments, and the Defendant is sentenced to a fine of 500,000 won. If the Defendant fails to pay the above fine, pursuant to Articles 70 and 69(2) of the Criminal Act, the Defendant shall be confined in a workhouse for a period converted at the rate of 50,000 won per day, and pursuant to Article 57 of the Criminal Act, one day of detention prior to the pronouncement of the first-instance judgment shall be credited toward the period of confinement in a workhouse in relation to the above fine. With the unanimous opinion of the judges involved, the judgment is rendered as ordered."}

{"[2011DO1932]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Background of this retrial and the prosecutor’s grounds of appeal\\nA. The Army Headquarters Ordinary Court-Martial, on April 28, 1973, in Case No. 73BOGUNHYEONG No. 94 involving occupational embezzlement, etc. against the Defendant, found all facts charged guilty and sentenced him to 15 years’ imprisonment and a fine of 20,000,000 won (hereinafter referred to as the “first-instance judgment”).\\nB. The Defendant and the military prosecutor filed an appeal against the first-instance judgment in Army High Court-Martial Case No. 73GOGUNHYEONGHANG No. 306, and the Army High Court-Martial, on July 30, 1973, set aside the first-instance judgment and found some of the facts charged, namely occupational embezzlement, violation of the Emergency Decree Concerning Stability and Growth of the Economy, and partial violation of the Control of Firearms and Explosives Act, guilty, sentencing the Defendant to 15 years’ imprisonment and a fine of 11,000,000 won, and acquitted him of the remaining facts charged.\\nC. On August 8, 1973, the competent commander confirmed the above 15 years’ imprisonment against the Defendant by reducing it to 12 years’ imprisonment, and since neither the Defendant nor the military prosecutor filed a further appeal, the above appellate judgment (hereinafter referred to as the “judgment subject to retrial”) became final and conclusive as it was.\\nD. While the Defendant had been released due to suspension of the execution of the above sentence, he received a special amnesty on February 29, 1980, which extinguished the effect of the sentence.\\nE. On April 5, 2010, the Defendant filed a petition for retrial with the High Military Court with respect to the above judgment subject to retrial, and the High Military Court, premising that the Defendant had already been removed from the military and thus the court lacked jurisdiction over the retrial trial proceedings, but that it had jurisdiction over the retrial-commencement procedure, which determines only the existence of grounds for retrial, and then, on the ground that it was proved that investigators committed offenses in the performance of their official duties, such as unlawful arrest and torture, and that there existed a ground for retrial under Article 469, item 7, of the Military Court Act, entered a decision to commence retrial as to the guilty portion of the judgment subject to retrial, and transferred the case to the Seoul High Court, which is the court below in this case, pursuant to Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act.\\nF. The court below held that the interrogation records of suspects and statements prepared by military judicial police officers concerning the Defendant and the non-indicted persons, as well as the seized firearms, etc., which had been cited as evidence of guilt in the first instance, were illegally obtained evidence and thus inadmissible; that, with respect to the facts charged corresponding to the guilty portion subject to retrial (hereinafter referred to as the “facts charged in this case”), there was insufficient evidence to establish occupational embezzlement and violation of the Emergency Decree Concerning Stability and Growth of the Economy; and that, with respect to the violation of the Control of Firearms and Explosives Act, there was no evidence corroborating the confession, aside from the confession itself. On those grounds, the court below set aside the portion of the first-instance judgment concerning the facts charged in this case and acquitted the Defendant.\\nG. The prosecutor’s grounds of appeal are as follows:\\nThe judgment subject to retrial in this case cannot be the subject of a petition for retrial because a special amnesty extinguished the effect of the sentence, and therefore, even if the decision to commence retrial became final and conclusive, there was no subject of adjudication to proceed with retrial proceedings, and no adjudication could be rendered. Nevertheless, the court below, treating there as being a subject of adjudication and proceeding to a merits review and rendering a judgment of acquittal, erred in law concerning special amnesty and the subject of a petition for retrial. Even assuming that the judgment subject to retrial could be the subject of a petition for retrial, the judgment below is unlawful in that, contrary to the rules of logic and experience, it exceeded the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence or erred in law concerning the rule requiring corroboration of a confession.\\n\\n2. Ex officio determination regarding the jurisdiction over this retrial, etc.\\nA. Article 27, paragraph 1, of the Constitution provides: “All citizens shall have the right to be tried according to the law by judges qualified under the Constitution and the law,” thereby guaranteeing that all citizens may be tried, in accordance with the content and procedure prescribed by a constitutional law, by judges appointed pursuant to the qualifications and procedure prescribed by the Constitution and the law. In addition, Article 27, paragraph 2, of the Constitution provides: “No citizen who is not a soldier or civilian employee shall be tried by a court-martial within the territory of the Republic of Korea, except in cases prescribed by law concerning grave military secrets, sentries, outposts, the supply of poisonous food or drink, prisoners of war, and military supplies, and in cases where emergency martial law has been declared,” thereby declaring that citizens who are not soldiers or civilian employees (hereinafter referred to as “ordinary citizens”) have the right not to be tried by a military court except in the cases prescribed by Article 27, paragraph 2, of the Constitution.\\nAccordingly, a military court has no jurisdiction over ordinary citizens unless the case falls within the cases prescribed by Article 27, paragraph 2, of the Constitution, and although the main text of Article 472 of the Military Court Act provides that a petition for retrial shall be under the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court or military court that rendered the original judgment, jurisdiction presupposes jurisdiction over the subject matter. Therefore, if, after a military court judgment has become final and conclusive, the person has been removed from the military and the military court has no jurisdiction, then even in a retrial case, jurisdiction lies not with the military court that rendered the original judgment, but with the general court of the same instance (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 84DO2972 rendered on September 24, 1985).\\nMoreover, not only the retrial trial proceedings but also the retrial-commencement procedure, which examines the existence of grounds for retrial and decides whether the case will be retried, cannot be examined or adjudicated without jurisdiction over the subject matter. Therefore, upon receiving a petition for retrial, the military court must first examine whether it has jurisdiction over the subject matter, and if it determines that the military court lacks such jurisdiction, it shall not proceed to the retrial-commencement procedure, but shall immediately transfer the case to the general court of the same instance pursuant to Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act.\\nConversely, if a military court, despite lacking jurisdiction over the subject matter, renders a decision to commence retrial and only thereafter transfers the case to the general court, this would constitute an unlawful exercise of jurisdiction. However, since the second sentence of Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act provides that “in such case, any procedural act performed before the transfer shall not be affected in validity by the transfer,” the general court receiving the case need not proceed anew from the beginning with the retrial-commencement procedure, and may proceed with the subsequent procedures by treating the military court’s decision to commence retrial as valid.\\nB. As to this case, although the High Military Court, as stated above, found that it lacked jurisdiction over the retrial trial proceedings because the Defendant had already been removed from the military, it considered that it had jurisdiction over the retrial-commencement procedure, which is the prior procedure, and rendered a decision to commence retrial; this was unlawful. However, the court below, which received the case, proceeded to the retrial trial proceedings and made its determination on the basis of that decision to commence retrial. This was in accordance with the legal principles stated above and cannot be said to be unlawful.\\n\\n3. Determination on the grounds of appeal\\nA. We first consider whether the judgment subject to retrial in this case can be the subject of a petition for retrial.\\n(1) Even if a special amnesty extinguishing the effect of the sentence occurred after a final judgment of conviction, only the legal effect of the sentence disappears prospectively, and the factual findings and the corresponding determination of guilt made in the final judgment of conviction do not disappear. Therefore, the above judgment of conviction must still be regarded as existing, with only the effect of the sentence extinguished. Meanwhile, for a defendant for whom there exists a ground for retrial under each item of Article 420 of the Criminal Procedure Act, there remains a disadvantage despite the special amnesty, and there is a need to remove not only the conviction but also the prior record itself that a sentence was imposed.\\nFurthermore, the reason Article 420 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that a final judgment of conviction may be retried for the benefit of the person who received it is to correct any serious factual error in a final judgment of conviction and thereby redress human rights violations against an innocent and blameless defendant. If a judgment of conviction whose effect of sentence has been extinguished by special amnesty could not be the subject of a petition for retrial, this would mean depriving the right to petition for retrial merely because a special amnesty occurred, thereby blocking from the outset opportunities to restore honor and receive criminal compensation, which would be contrary to the purpose of the retrial system.\\nAccordingly, it is appropriate to construe that even a final judgment of conviction whose effect of sentence has been extinguished by special amnesty falls within “a final judgment of conviction” under Article 420 of the Criminal Procedure Act and may be the subject of a petition for retrial.\\nIn contrast, Supreme Court Decision 96DO2153 rendered on July 22, 1997, and Supreme Court Decision 2010MO24 rendered on February 26, 2010, which held that if there was a special amnesty extinguishing the effect of the sentence after a final judgment of conviction, there was no longer a subject of petition for retrial and a petition for retrial against such judgment was unlawful, are changed to the extent they are inconsistent with this judgment.\\nMeanwhile, the “amnesty” referred to in “where there has been amnesty” in Article 326, item 2, of the Criminal Procedure Act, which is a ground for a judgment of dismissal of prosecution, means only general amnesty (see Supreme Court Decision 99DO2983 rendered on February 11, 2000), and special amnesty granted to a person who has been sentenced and whose judgment has become final and conclusive does not fall hereunder. Therefore, even if there was a special amnesty extinguishing the effect of the sentence after the judgment subject to retrial became final and conclusive, the court proceeding with the retrial trial after the decision to commence retrial became final and conclusive must retry the case according to the instance and make determinations on the merits, such as guilty or not guilty, and must not render a judgment of dismissal of prosecution on the ground of that special amnesty.\\n(2) As to this case, the court below, deeming that the judgment subject to retrial in this case, whose effect of sentence was extinguished by special amnesty, could also be the subject of a petition for retrial and proceeding to a merits review as to the facts charged in this case, acted in accordance with the legal principles above, and is proper. There is no error such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning special amnesty and the subject of a petition for retrial, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\nB. We next consider whether the court below exceeded the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence or erred in law concerning the rule requiring corroboration of a confession.\\nReviewing the reasons for the judgment below in light of the record, the court below, finding that some of the evidence submitted by the prosecutor was inadmissible as illegally obtained evidence and that the facts charged in this case were insufficiently established by the remaining evidence alone, or that there was no corroborating evidence apart from the confession, and on such grounds as stated in its holding, acquitted the Defendant. This was proper, and there is no error such as, contrary to the rules of logic and experience, exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence or misapprehending the legal principles concerning the rule requiring corroboration of a confession, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition. Except for the dissenting opinion of Justice Kim Chang-seok on the point that retrial trial proceedings may be conducted on the premise of a decision to commence retrial rendered by a military court lacking jurisdiction, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous.\\n\\n5. The dissenting opinion of Justice Kim Chang-seok is as follows.\\nA. Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act provides: “If, with respect to a case for which an indictment has been filed, a military court no longer has jurisdiction, or it is discovered that it did not have jurisdiction, the military court shall transfer the case by decision to a court of the same instance that has jurisdiction; provided, however, that an appeal case concerning a case pending before the High Military Court and to be tried by a single judge shall be transferred to the appellate division of the district court. In such case, any procedural act performed before the transfer shall not be affected in validity by the transfer.”\\nThe majority opinion, while stating that it was unlawful for the High Military Court to render a decision to commence retrial in this case despite lacking jurisdiction over the retrial, held that, once the High Military Court rendered the decision to commence retrial and then transferred the case to the court below that had jurisdiction, the validity of the decision to commence retrial was maintained pursuant to the second sentence of Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act, and therefore there was no problem with the court below proceeding with the retrial trial proceedings on that premise.\\nB. However, this case cannot be regarded as a case to which the second sentence of Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act applies. This is because, for the second sentence of Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act to apply to this case, the case must fall under the main text of Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act, but it cannot be so regarded.\\nFirst, since Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act is a provision concerning the ordinary filing of an indictment, there remains a strong question as to whether, even where a petition for retrial has been filed, the petition for retrial can be analogically applied by treating it in the same way as the filing of an indictment. Even if it could be so regarded, the same result follows for the following reasons: Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act cannot be applied.\\nThe phrase “where, with respect to a case for which an indictment has been filed, a military court no longer has jurisdiction” means a case in which the military court had jurisdiction at the time the indictment was filed but thereafter lost jurisdiction. Here, however, this case was one in which the military court already lacked jurisdiction from the time the Defendant filed a petition for retrial with the High Military Court, and it is clear that this was not a case in which, after the petition for retrial, “a military court no longer has jurisdiction.”\\nLikewise, the phrase “where it is discovered that, with respect to a case for which an indictment has been filed, a military court did not have jurisdiction” means a case in which the military court was thought to have jurisdiction at the time the indictment was filed, but it was only later discovered, while the litigation procedure was being conducted, that it lacked jurisdiction. Here, however, the High Military Court, despite knowing that the military court lacked jurisdiction, rendered a decision to commence retrial under the arbitrary view that it could proceed with the retrial-commencement procedure, which determines only the existence of grounds for retrial. Therefore, it cannot be said to fall within a case in which, while the litigation procedure was being conducted, it “is discovered” that there was no jurisdiction.\\nC. Thus, as Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act cannot, by its wording, be applied to this case, the only remaining question is whether it can be applied through expansive interpretation.\\nHowever, expansive interpretation beyond the ordinary meaning of the words cannot be permitted. Although it was clear from the outset, at the time of the petition for retrial, that the military court had no jurisdiction over this petition for retrial under Article 27, paragraph 2, of the Constitution and Articles 2 and 3 of the Military Court Act, to construe this case, in which the decision to commence retrial was forced through, as falling under a case in which, after the petition for retrial, the military court no longer had jurisdiction, or as a case in which it was only later discovered, while the litigation procedure was being conducted after the petition for retrial, that there was no jurisdiction, plainly goes beyond the ordinary meaning of the words.\\nD. Furthermore, such expansive interpretation cannot be permitted in that it ultimately directly violates Article 27, paragraph 2, of the Constitution.\\nBy providing that “No citizen who is not a soldier or civilian employee shall be tried by a court-martial within the territory of the Republic of Korea, except in cases prescribed by law concerning grave military secrets, sentries, outposts, the supply of poisonous food or drink, prisoners of war, and military supplies, and in cases where emergency martial law has been declared,” Article 27, paragraph 2, of the Constitution establishes the right not to be tried by a military court as a constitutional right. The fact that the Constitution directly and specifically provides for the military court’s exceptional jurisdiction in this manner shows that the allocation of jurisdiction between general courts and military courts is not merely a matter of expediency.\\nSince Article 27, paragraph 2, of the Constitution thus guarantees, as a fundamental right, ordinary citizens’ right not to be tried by a military court, the provision of Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act, which recognizes exceptions on the premise of unavoidable circumstances, must be strictly construed, and the essential content of that right must not be infringed by expansive or analogical interpretation thereof (see Article 37, paragraph 2, of the Constitution).\\nNevertheless, the majority opinion, fixated on the perspective of procedural economy, undervalued the meaning of the right guaranteed by Article 27, paragraph 2, of the Constitution not to be tried by a military court, and by expansively interpreting Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act as applying to this case, reached an interpretation that infringes the essential content of that right.\\nE. In addition, even if the second sentence of Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act could be applied to this case, the decision to commence retrial cannot be said to fall within the “procedural acts” of the second sentence.\\nGenerally, “procedural acts” include judicial decisions of the court, but as noted above, since the right of ordinary citizens not to be tried by a military court is guaranteed as a constitutional right, the “judicial decision” of a military court should in principle be construed as not included in the above “procedural acts.”\\nHowever, only in unavoidable cases contemplated by Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act, such as where, during the pendency of the appellate trial in the High Military Court, the military court loses jurisdiction because the Defendant is discharged from service and the case must be transferred to the appellate trial of a general court, can it be said that the judicial decision of the military court of the first instance, which is the prior instance, is included in the above “procedural acts.”\\nHere, however, the decision to commence retrial rendered by the High Military Court is a judicial decision made by the High Military Court itself in place of the High Court, which is a general court, and it is clear that it does not fall within the judicial decision of the prior instance that can, as above, be recognized as a valid procedural act.\\nMoreover, a decision on whether to commence retrial is a determination of whether grounds for retrial exist as prescribed in each item of Article 420 of the Criminal Procedure Act (or Article 469 of the Military Court Act in the case of a military court proceeding), and is in itself a final judicial decision whose effect upon the petitioner for retrial is absolute. It can never be assessed as a “judicial decision” less important than the retrial judgment rendered after the decision to commence retrial, nor as a mere “procedural act” whose validity survives the transfer pursuant to Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act. Moreover, the determination on whether grounds for retrial exist is not of such a nature that it can be easily made through only a formal examination (this is all the more so where, as in this case, the existence of proof substituting for a “final judgment” under Article 469, item 7, of the Military Court Act is disputed), and once a decision to commence retrial is rendered, it in itself substantially affects the retrial proceedings thereafter.\\nUltimately, not only the retrial judgment but also the “decision on retrial,” including the decision to commence retrial, must be understood as a “judicial decision” that fundamentally affects the fate of the petition for retrial. Nevertheless, if, as in the majority opinion, one interprets the decision to commence retrial as not included in the “judicial decision” of a military court, and thus regards the “judicial decision” of the decision to commence retrial as included in the “procedural acts” in the second sentence of Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act, this would be no different from recognizing from the outset that a military court may make the “judicial decision” of a decision to commence retrial even without jurisdiction. As a result, this would necessarily amount to tolerating an interpretation that infringes the “essential content” of the right not to be tried by a military court guaranteed by Article 27, paragraph 2, of the Constitution.\\nF. Furthermore, insofar as the decision to commence retrial rendered by a military court lacking jurisdiction cannot be a subject to which Article 2, paragraph 3, of the Military Court Act applies, or cannot be included in the “procedural acts” that may become valid, even if the decision to commence retrial is a judgment favorable to the Defendant or its conclusion is proper, it must not be maintained as is, but the procedure must be conducted anew from the beginning in the general court. This is because the question of whether jurisdiction exists is not a matter that can be determined according to whether the Defendant is advantaged or disadvantaged.\\nTherefore, as to this case, the decision rendered by the High Military Court lacking jurisdiction to commence retrial is void, and even so, the court below’s action in proceeding to the retrial trial proceedings and making its determination on the premise that the decision to commence retrial was valid constitutes a case where the Constitution was violated and that violation affected the judgment.\\nAccordingly, unlike the conclusion of the majority opinion, the judgment below should be reversed and remanded to the court below, and the court below must proceed again from the procedure for determining whether to commence retrial.\\nFor the foregoing reasons, I state that I cannot concur with the majority opinion."}

{"[2015DO17936]": "1. We examine the Prosecutor’s grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nThe court below, taking the circumstances as stated in its judgment into comprehensive consideration, determined that, with respect to the funds raised from the members of the labor union at issue, it was difficult to conclude that the labor union at issue had reached the point where it could dispose of those funds, or at least the point where it could be regarded as identical thereto, by having played a leading and active role in their raising and formation.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the foregoing determination by the court below contains no error, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal, in misapprehending the law regarding “funds related to an organization” under Article 31(2) of the Political Funds Act.\\n\\nMeanwhile, although the Prosecutor also filed a final appeal with respect to the guilty portion, no reasons were stated in the petition for final appeal, and no grounds for objection were set forth in the statement of grounds for final appeal either.\\n\\n2. We make a determination ex officio.\\n\\na. The court below, with respect to the portion of the facts charged in this case alleging that the Defendant gave political funds to a political party that cannot receive political funds (unlawful receipt of political funds), affirmed the first-instance judgment that found the Defendant guilty by applying Article 45(1) of the Political Funds Act.\\n\\nHowever, after the judgment of the court below was rendered, the Constitutional Court, in the operative part, rendered a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution stating that “Article 6 of the former Political Funds Act (as amended by Act No. 8880 on February 29, 2008, and before amendment by Act No. 9975 on January 25, 2010), Article 6 of the Political Funds Act (as amended by Act No. 9975 on January 25, 2010), and the portion concerning Article 6 among the phrase ‘by a method not prescribed by this Act’ in the main text of Article 45(1) of the Political Funds Act (as amended by Act No. 8880 on February 29, 2008) are not conformable with the Constitution.” and “The foregoing provisions shall continue to be applied until the legislature amends them by June 30, 2017.” (Constitutional Court full bench decision rendered on December 23, 2015, 2013HEONBA168, hereinafter referred to as “the Constitutional Incompatibility Decision in this case”). Accordingly, by Article 6(1) of the Political Funds Act as amended by Act No. 14838 on June 30, 2017, “the central party (including the central party establishment preparatory committee)” was added so that political parties may also receive political funds, but no transitional provision was enacted concerning retroactive application of the foregoing provision.\\n\\nb. A decision of incompatibility with the Constitution rendered by the Constitutional Court is a modified form not prescribed by the Constitution or the Constitutional Court Act, but it constitutes a decision of unconstitutionality with respect to a statutory provision (see Supreme Court Decision 2004DO7111 rendered on January 15, 2009; Constitutional Court full bench decisions rendered on May 27, 2004, 2003HEONGA1 and 2004HEONGA4, etc.). Article 45(1) of the Political Funds Act takes as its constituent element the giving of political funds by a method not prescribed in Article 6 of the former Political Funds Act (as in effect before amendment by Act No. 9975 on January 25, 2010; hereinafter referred to as the “former Political Funds Act”), and thus Article 6 of the former Political Funds Act, when combined with Article 45(1) of the Political Funds Act, becomes a statutory provision concerning punishment. Therefore, the Constitutional Incompatibility Decision in this case rendered with respect to the foregoing provisions (hereinafter referred to as “the statutory provisions in this case”) should be regarded as a decision of unconstitutionality with respect to statutory provisions concerning punishment. And the main text of Article 47(3) of the Constitutional Court Act provides that, where a decision of unconstitutionality is rendered with respect to a statutory provision concerning punishment, such provision shall lose its effect retroactively; accordingly, where a statutory provision concerning punishment has lost its effect retroactively, a criminal case against a defendant instituted by applying the relevant provision falls under the case where the act does not constitute a crime. Therefore, the court shall render a judgment of acquittal in that criminal case pursuant to the former part of Article 325 of the Criminal Procedure Act (see Supreme Court Decision 91DO2825 rendered on May 8, 1992; Supreme Court en banc decision 2008DO7562 rendered on June 23, 2011, etc.).\\n\\nc. In light of the legal principles set forth above, the statutory provisions in this case, which were declared by the Constitutional Incompatibility Decision in this case to be not conformable with the Constitution, lose their effect retroactively; therefore, a judgment of acquittal must be rendered pursuant to the former part of Article 325 of the Criminal Procedure Act with respect to the criminal case of unlawful receipt of political funds instituted by applying the statutory provisions in this case.\\n\\nAccordingly, the part of the lower judgment that found the portion concerning unlawful receipt of political funds guilty can no longer be sustained as a result.\\n\\n3. Scope of reversal\\n\\nThe part of the lower judgment that acquitted on grounds, with respect to the point of violation of the Political Funds Act arising from the donation of funds related to an organization, is in a relation of simultaneous concurrence with the guilty portion to be reversed as above; therefore, the part acquitting on grounds must also be reversed together.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nWithout addressing the determination on the Defendant’s grounds for final appeal, we reverse the lower judgment and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

{"[2016DO5423]": "1. Background of the Case\\n\\nA. The Defendant and the Complainant, a Non-Indicted Person, were a married couple who had registered their marriage on 1997. 6. 25., and had two children. On 2012. 10. 2., the Complainant filed a complaint with the Seoul Suseo Police Station against the Defendant on suspicion of domestic violence (hereinafter referred to as the “First Complaint”). The contents of the complaint were that the Defendant: ① assaulted the Complainant in 1997 in the course of a dispute over wedding gifts; ② assaulted the Complainant in 1999 by kicking the Complainant’s lower back, etc. with his foot; ③ committed assaults in 2001 and September 2002, respectively, while residing in the United States; ④ assaulted the Complainant in July 2008 to the extent of causing injury to the shoulder; ⑤ repeatedly assaulted the Complainant while residing in the United States from 2010 to 2012; and ⑥ on 2012. 10. 2., while the couple was quarrelling at an apartment in Gangnam-gu, Seoul (address omitted), pushed the Complainant down, pressed down on the Complainant’s head, causing the forehead to strike the floor, and inflicted multiple contusions on the scalp, etc. requiring two weeks of treatment.\\n\\nOn 2012. 11. 13., the prosecutor transferred the above case to the Seoul Family Court as a case for family protection proceedings (Seoul Family Court No. 2012BEO584). At the hearing date on 2013. 2. 21., when the Defendant acknowledged the domestic violence and the Complainant stated that the Complainant “has a desire to restore the family,” the Seoul Family Court concluded the hearing and, on the ground that the case fell under “where a protective disposition cannot be made or is not deemed necessary” prescribed in Article 37(1)1 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Crimes of Domestic Violence (hereinafter referred to as the “Domestic Violence Punishment Act”), issued a “decision not to make a disposition” (hereinafter referred to simply as the “No-Disposition Decision”) against the Defendant. As neither the prosecutor nor the Complainant filed an immediate appeal against this, the above No-Disposition Decision became final and binding (hereinafter referred to as the “Prior Family Protection Case”).\\n\\nB. After filing a civil action against the Defendant for divorce and claim for alimony, etc. with the Seoul Family Court on 2014. 7. 16. (Seoul Family Court No. 2014DEUHAP4316), the Complainant filed a complaint with the police against the Defendant on 2015. 6. 16. for offenses including violation of the Criminal Act and the Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “Second Complaint”). The contents of the complaint were items ③, ④, and ⑥ of the First Complaint in this case, and that the Defendant had sent the Complainant text messages containing abusive language by mobile phone. In addition, the Complainant further stated to the police that “the Defendant assaulted the Complainant, including by grabbing the Complainant’s hair, around mid-October 2012.”\\n\\nOn 2015. 7. 16., the prosecutor, through a prosecution officer, heard from the Complainant a statement to the effect that “although the Defendant had frequently committed violence even after the Prior Family Protection Case, I was unable to collect evidence and therefore could not state this in the complaint, and, in order to secure child support in the divorce action, I was compelled to file the complaint again, and I hope that this will never again be handled as a family protection case.” Thereafter, on the same year 7. 21., the prosecutor reviewed the record of the Prior Family Protection Case and confirmed, inter alia, that at the time of the First Complaint, the Complainant had not indicated an intention not to seek punishment against the Defendant. After interrogating the suspect Defendant on the same year 10. 15., the prosecutor applied for a summary order on the crime stated in item ⑥ above (hereinafter referred to as the “Criminal Facts of This Case”) on the same year 10. 16.\\n\\nC. The Defendant, on 2015. 11. 16., filed a request for a formal trial against the above summary order. In the court of first instance, the Defendant admitted the facts charged, but stated that the prosecution against the Defendant was contrary to the principle of ne bis in idem. The court of first instance sentenced the Defendant to a fine of 700,000 won, and the lower court dismissed the Defendant’s appeal. Meanwhile, the divorce action, etc. between the Defendant and the victim was concluded upon mediation on 2015. 11. 13.\\n\\n2. Summary of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nA. Ground 1 for Appeal\\n\\nNotwithstanding that a No-Disposition Decision had already been made pursuant to Article 37(1) of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act with respect to the Criminal Facts of This Case, filing a new prosecution again for the same criminal facts is not permitted as it is contrary to the principle of ne bis in idem prescribed in Article 13(1) of the Constitution.\\n\\nB. Ground 2 for Appeal\\n\\nEven if the No-Disposition Decision under Article 37(1) of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act does not have res judicata effect, the Second Complaint in this case was filed again for the purpose of pressuring the Defendant in order to obtain a favorable outcome far exceeding the ordinary ratio of division of property in the divorce action; therefore, the indictment based thereon and the lower court’s guilty judgment are clearly erroneous in light of justice, which underlies judicial decision-making.\\n\\n3. As to Ground 1 for Appeal\\n\\nThe Constitution, in Article 13(1), provides that “all citizens shall not be subject to double punishment for the same offense,” thereby declaring the so-called principle against double jeopardy or the principle of ne bis in idem. This means the principle that once a judgment becomes final and binding, the same case may not be tried again thereafter. Here, “punishment” in principle means penal sanction as the State’s exercise of its punitive power over crime, and does not include every sanction or disadvantageous disposition imposed by the State (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 91DO2536, decided February 11, 1992).\\n\\nHowever, the investigation and hearing of a family protection case prescribed in the Domestic Violence Punishment Act is a procedure under the special provisions for criminal punishment, conducted ex officio by the family court without the intervention of a prosecutor. Thus, the prosecutor may handle the matter as a family protection case even where the requirements for instituting prosecution, such as a complaint in an offense subject to complaint, are not met (Article 9 of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act), and since the court may revoke the protective disposition ex officio or upon request if the person who committed domestic violence and received a protective disposition fails to comply with or follow the execution thereof (Article 46 of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act), the content and nature differ from criminal proceedings premised on an adversarial and party-driven structure, and they cannot be deemed identical to criminal proceedings. Accordingly, the decision on a protective disposition or the No-Disposition Decision under the Domestic Violence Punishment Act cannot be accorded an effect equivalent to that of a final and binding criminal judgment.\\n\\nWhere a decision on a protective disposition under the Domestic Violence Punishment Act becomes final and binding, in principle prosecution may not again be instituted against the person who committed domestic violence for the same criminal facts (Article 16 of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act); however, since such a protective disposition is not a final judgment and therefore has no res judicata effect, if prosecution is again instituted for the same case as the one subject to the protective disposition, a judgment of non-prosecution should not be rendered with respect thereto, but rather, since this corresponds to a case where the procedure for instituting prosecution is invalid for violation of the provisions of law, a judgment dismissing prosecution should be rendered pursuant to Article 327(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act (see Supreme Court Decision 85DO21, decided May 28, 1985). However, the Domestic Violence Punishment Act does not contain such a provision with respect to a No-Disposition Decision, and moreover provides that, as to the statute of limitations for prosecution regarding crimes of domestic violence, when a No-Disposition Decision becomes final and binding, the statute of limitations begins to run from that time (Article 17(1) of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act). Thus, the Domestic Violence Punishment Act presupposes that, even for crimes of domestic violence for which a No-Disposition Decision has become final and binding, prosecution may be instituted in certain cases.\\n\\nTherefore, even if the prosecutor again instituted prosecution for the same criminal facts after a No-Disposition Decision under Article 37(1)1 of the Domestic Violence Punishment Act became final and binding, or even if the court rendered a guilty judgment thereon, it cannot be said to violate the principle against double jeopardy or the principle of ne bis in idem. Accordingly, the above ground for appeal is not accepted.\\n\\n4. As to Ground 2 for Appeal\\n\\nWhere the prosecutor determines that the conduct falls within the elements of a crime and that criminal sanctions are appropriate, the prosecutor may institute prosecution, and has discretion not to institute prosecution by considering the matters set forth in Article 51 of the Criminal Act (Articles 246 and 247 of the Criminal Procedure Act). Such prosecutorial discretion exists inherently within itself because it is considered that having the prosecutor, as a representative of the public interest, conduct activities for institution and maintenance of prosecution from an objective standpoint can ensure the appropriateness and rationality of criminal prosecution. Therefore, where it is determined that the prosecutor has arbitrarily exercised prosecutorial authority and thereby caused substantial disadvantage to the defendant, and thereby significantly deviated from prosecutorial discretion, this may be regarded as an abuse of prosecutorial authority, and the effectiveness of such prosecution may be denied (see Supreme Court Decision 94DO2658, decided February 13, 1996; Supreme Court Decision 2001DO3106, decided October 9, 2001; Supreme Court Decision 2004DO482, decided April 27, 2004, etc.).\\n\\nIn this case, as the Defendant argues, if there were no special circumstances to overturn the effect of the final and binding No-Disposition Decision in the Prior Family Protection Case, and if the prosecution in this case was instituted merely to cater to the Complainant’s personal emotions or solely with the intent of obtaining a favorable result in the divorce action, such action may be deemed unlawful as an abuse of prosecutorial authority. However, in light of the circumstances leading to the institution of the prosecution in this case as reflected in the record, the content of the Criminal Facts of This Case, and all the circumstances including the relationship between the Defendant and the Complainant, it is apparent that this prosecution was instituted because the prosecutor, based on the results of the investigation into the criminal suspicion in the Second Complaint in this case and the results of reviewing the record of the Prior Family Protection Case, determined that the execution of the State’s punitive power was necessary with respect to the Criminal Facts of This Case.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Defendant’s ground for appeal that the institution of the prosecution in this case and the lower court’s determination were clearly erroneous in light of justice, which underlies judicial decision-making, is not accepted.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[96DO47]": "We consider the grounds of appeal by the court-appointed defense counsel.\\n\\nArticle 53 of the Juvenile Act provides that, with respect to a juvenile who has received a protective disposition under Article 32, the case that has been heard and decided may not be prosecuted again or transferred to the Juvenile Division; therefore, if a new prosecution is instituted concerning a case identical to the case that received the protective disposition under Article 32 (including a continuing offense such as a habitual offense), then this constitutes a case where the institution of prosecution is void because the procedure for instituting prosecution is contrary to the provisions of law, and accordingly a judgment of dismissal of prosecution must be rendered pursuant to Article 327, item 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act (see Supreme Court Decision 85DO21, decided May 28, 1985).\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Defendant was criminally booked on June 3, 1994, for theft, fraud, and violation of the Road Traffic Act, and on August 24 of the same year was again criminally booked for the same offenses, and on December 28 of the same year received a protective disposition (No. 6 - short-term transfer to a juvenile reformatory) from the Juvenile Division of the Daejeon District Court. All of the above offenses appear to have consisted of stealing motorcycles and driving without a license. In light of the time and objects of the offenses, there is room to view them as having been committed out of the Defendant’s habitual theft tendency, together with the charge in this case of violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (theft) (paragraph 2 of the facts of the crime in this case, as held by the court below by citing the judgment of the first instance), which occurred before the above protective disposition order was made. Therefore, the court below should have duly examined the case that received the above protective disposition and, if it fell within the relationship of a single comprehensive offense with the above charge, should have rendered a judgment dismissing prosecution as to the above charge; however, the court below, without conducting any examination on this point, simply upheld the first-instance judgment that found the above charge guilty. Accordingly, the judgment of the court below must be deemed unlawful in that it misapprehended the legal principle concerning Article 53 of the Juvenile Act and failed to conduct a full hearing, thereby affecting the outcome of the judgment. The argument pointing out this point is well taken.\\n\\nAccordingly, since the above charge and the remaining offenses found guilty are in the relationship of a single comprehensive offense and concurrent offenses, we reverse the judgment of the court below, which imposed a single sentence on the guilty portion, without addressing the remaining grounds of appeal by the Defendant and the court-appointed defense counsel, and remand this part of the case to the court below. It is so adjudged as stated in the order by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

question: Korean Bar Examination, 14th, Criminal Law, Multiple-Choice Question 31. A received A's bitcoins without legal cause into his own account and then transferred them to another account of his own and spent them. Upon lawfully initiating an investigation after becoming aware of this, the prosecutor applied for a search and seizure warrant for A's mobile phone. Which of the following statements regarding this is correct? (Where there is controversy, according to case law)
A: Bitcoin is information digitally representing economic value conferred by an encrypted distributed ledger such as blockchain, and thus constitutes a property benefit.
B: Where A mistakenly transfers bitcoins into A's account, bitcoins are treated like cash, so A, under the principle of good faith, is in the position of a custodian vis-à-vis A, and if A uses or disposes of them, embezzlement is established.
