C: Where A's bitcoins are transferred into A's account by an unknown process, A corresponds to a person who, based on a relationship of trust, undertakes and administers A's affairs; therefore, if A arbitrarily uses or disposes of the bitcoins, breach of trust is established.
D: If the prosecutor conducts an interrogation of a suspect without preparing a crime cognizance report despite having become aware of the crime, this constitutes, in principle, an unlawful investigation, and the suspect interrogation protocol prepared in the course of that investigation is not admissible as evidence.
E: If a judge of a district court dismisses an application for a search and seizure warrant for a mobile phone, the prosecutor may not challenge it by quasi-appeal, but may challenge it by appeal.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2000DO2968]": "We consider the grounds of appeal by defense counsel together.\\n\\n1. As to Issues 1 and 2\\nReceiving money or other benefits in connection with the mediation of matters falling within the duties of a public official, as referred to in Article 3 of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes, means the act of receiving money, etc. under the pretext of mediating matters falling within the duties of a public official, and it is not necessarily required that the public official who is the object of the mediation or the specific content of such duties be concretely identified.\\n\\nIn addition, the specification of the facts charged is sufficient if, in light of the nature of the crime charged, it states the time, place, method, purpose, etc. to the extent that the cause of the prosecution can be distinguished from other facts charged, and even if part thereof is somewhat unclear, if the facts charged can be specified by other matters stated together therewith and, accordingly, the exercise of the defendant’s right to defense is not impeded, the validity of the institution of prosecution is not affected (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 99DO1900 rendered on 1999. 6. 25.).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below, while finding the subsidiary charge of the offense of receiving money or other benefits in connection with mediation against the Defendant guilty, determined that this facts charged could not be deemed to be void because the procedure for instituting prosecution violated the provisions of law on the ground that the facts charged were not specified, or because it did not contain facts that could constitute a crime; examining the record in light of the legal principles stated above, the measures taken by the court below are justifiable and acceptable, and there is no illegality as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe grounds of appeal disputing this point are not accepted.\\n\\n2. As to Issue 3\\nUpon examining the relevant evidence in light of the record, the court below’s factual finding that the Defendant received 100 million won with the intent of arranging through persons in political and governmental circles with whom the Defendant had personal ties so that the person not charged could in the future obtain a good position such as a government-appointed post is correct and acceptable, and there is no illegality in finding facts without evidence or in violation of the rules of evidence and empirical rules.\\n\\nThe grounds of appeal disputing this point are also not accepted.\\n\\n3. As to Issue 4\\nAccording to Articles 2 through 4 of the Rules on the Affairs of Prosecutorial Cases, when a prosecutor recognizes a crime, the procedure is to prepare a crime recognition report and accept the case; therefore, absent special circumstances, when an investigative agency has gone through such procedure, it should be deemed to have recognized the crime. However, recognition of a crime is a substantive concept, and the provisions of these Rules are procedural provisions for office processing for the convenience of prosecutorial administration. Thus, when a prosecutor has begun an investigation by determining that there is suspicion of a crime before going through such procedure, the crime should be deemed to have been recognized at that time, and it should not be deemed that the crime was recognized only when a crime recognition report was later prepared and the procedure for case acceptance was taken (see Supreme Court Decision 89DO648 rendered on 1989. 6. 20.). Even if an investigation was conducted before going through such recognition procedure, unless there are special circumstances such as that the investigation was conducted in a situation where there was absolutely no possibility of recognition in the future, the investigation cannot be deemed unlawful merely because it was conducted before the recognition procedure was completed, and accordingly, the admissibility as evidence of the suspect interrogation protocol or statement protocol, etc. prepared during the investigation process cannot be denied (see Supreme Court Decision 94DO252 rendered on 1995. 2. 24.).\\n\\nThe judgment below, in accordance with these legal principles, is justifiable, and there is no illegality as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe grounds of appeal disputing this point are likewise not accepted.\\n\\n4. As to Issue 5\\nExamining the reasons of the judgment below, there is no contradiction in reasons as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe grounds of appeal disputing this point are also not accepted.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the operative part, by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2020DO9789]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Summary of the alternative count of the indictment\\nThe gist of the alternative count of the indictment, namely the portion concerning violation (breach of trust) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Specific Economic Crimes Act”), is as follows.\\n\\nBy an unknown process, the Defendant received transfer into his own account 199.999 bitcoins (hereinafter referred to as the “bitcoins at issue”) that were in the victim’s virtual wallet at the “Hitbit” exchange, and thus had a duty to keep them as they were in order to return the bitcoins at issue that had been transferred by mistake; nevertheless, he transferred 29.998 bitcoins thereof to his own “(account name 1 omitted)” account and 169.996 bitcoins to his own “(account name 2 omitted)” account, thereby acquiring a total of approximately 199.994 bitcoins (= 29.998 bitcoins + 169.996 bitcoins), amounting to a property benefit worth approximately KRW 1,487,235,086, and causing damage to the victim in the same amount.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the court below\\nThe court below upheld, as it stood, the first-instance judgment that found the alternative count of the indictment guilty for the following reasons.\\n\\nVirtual assets are property benefits that have economic value and deserve protection under the Criminal Act. Once the Defendant received and held bitcoins owned by another person in his own virtual asset wallet without legal cause, he must return the bitcoins as unjust enrichment vis-à-vis the owner. Embezzlement and breach of trust are property offenses of the same nature based on a relationship of trust; the holder of an account who received money without a legal relationship has a duty to return the money received to the remitter, and thus is recognized as being in a position to keep the money received or transferred for the remitter. There is no reason to treat differently a case where virtual assets are received by transfer without cause.\\n\\nTaking these circumstances into account, it is proper to deem the Defendant as bearing the duty to protect and manage the victim’s property, such as by keeping the transferred bitcoins as they were in order to return them to the owner based on the principle of good faith, and thus he constitutes “a person who administers another’s affairs” as the subject of the offense of breach of trust.\\n\\n3. This Court’s judgment\\nHowever, the judgment of the court below cannot be accepted for the following reasons.\\n\\na. Where virtual assets are transferred, without legal cause, into another person’s virtual asset electronic wallet due to the mistake of the virtual asset holder or an error in the virtual asset operating system, the person who received the virtual assets may become subject to a duty to return unjust enrichment to the virtual asset holder, etc. However, this is merely a civil debt between the parties, and from this circumstance alone, the person who received the virtual assets cannot be regarded as being in a position to preserve or manage the virtual assets based on a fiduciary relationship. In addition, there is no contractual relationship whatsoever between the Defendant and the victim, and it is unclear by what process the Defendant received the bitcoins at issue, so it is not clear whether the victim or the exchange is the entity entitled to claim return of unjust enrichment. Even if the Defendant directly bears a duty to return unjust enrichment to the victim, it cannot immediately be concluded that the person who received the virtual assets constitutes “a person who administers another’s affairs,” the subject of the offense of breach of trust, in relation to the victim.\\n\\nb. The Supreme Court limits the scope of the establishment of the offense of breach of trust by holding that, in order to be a person who administers another’s affairs, one must be in a position to preserve or manage another’s property based on a fiduciary relationship between the parties, where the typical and essential content of the relationship of the parties lies in performing, on behalf of another person, all or part of the affairs concerning the management of another’s property, beyond the adversarial relationship of interests inherent in an ordinary contract (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2019DO9756, rendered on 2020. 2. 20.). In a case such as this one, where virtual assets are received by transfer, it is not easy to recognize a fiduciary relationship between the victim and the Defendant.\\n\\nc. Virtual assets are information digitally represented by economic value conferred by an encrypted distributed ledger such as blockchain, without being controlled by the State, and constitute a property benefit (see Supreme Court Decision 2021DO9855, rendered on 2021. 11. 11.). Virtual assets are distinguishable from ordinary assets in that only the address of the electronic wallet in which they were stored can be identified, while the identity of the person using that address cannot be ascertained, and in that transaction records are distributed and recorded, so that, when transferring them to another account, someone other than the parties must participate.\\n\\nVirtual assets of this kind are not currently being treated in the same manner as legal tender, as they are not regulated to the extent of being equivalent to legal tender under the relevant statutes, and because their transactions involve risks; therefore, when applying the Criminal Act, they are not something that must be protected in the same manner as legal tender.\\n\\nd. In the current situation, where there is no express provision criminalizing the use or disposal of virtual assets, which are property benefits, by a person who received them for an unknown reason, punishing the Defendant for breach of trust on the basis of the principle of good faith by analogy to the precedents that recognized embezzlement in cases of mistaken remittance (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2010DO891, rendered on 2010. 12. 9.) would run counter to the principle of legality.\\n\\nEven if the bitcoins at issue were transferred from the victim to an electronic wallet in the Defendant’s name without legal cause, insofar as the Defendant cannot be regarded as having been entrusted with and handling the victim’s affairs based on a fiduciary relationship, the Defendant cannot be deemed “a person who administers another’s affairs” in relation to the victim.\\n\\ne. Nevertheless, the court below, which held that the Defendant constitutes “a person who administers another’s affairs” as the subject of the offense of breach of trust, erred by misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning “a person who administers another’s affairs” in the offense of violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (breach of trust).\\n\\n4. Scope of reversal\\nFor the reasons seen above, the alternative count portion of the judgment of the court below contains grounds for reversal and cannot be maintained as is; and because the principal charge, namely the portion of violation (embezzlement) of the Specific Economic Crimes Act, stands in a relation of identity with that portion, it too cannot escape reversal. Accordingly, the entire judgment of the court below must be reversed.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nSince the Defendant’s final appeal is well founded, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination; by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court, judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2020DO9789]": "We determine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Summary of the alternative indictment\\n\\nThe gist of the alternative indictment, namely the portion alleging violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Specific Economic Crimes Act”) (breach of trust), is as follows.\\n\\nFor reasons unknown, the Defendant had received by transfer into his own account 199.999 bitcoins (hereinafter referred to as the “Bitcoin at issue”) that had been in the victim’s virtual wallet on the “Hitbit” exchange, and therefore had a duty to keep them intact in order to return the Bitcoin at issue that had been transferred by mistake; nevertheless, the Defendant transferred 29.998 bitcoins thereof to his own “(account name 1 omitted)” account and 169.996 bitcoins thereof to his own “(account name 2 omitted)” account, thereby acquiring a total of 199.994 bitcoins (= 29.998 bitcoins + 169.996 bitcoins) having a property benefit worth approximately KRW 1,487,235,086, and caused damage to the victim in an equivalent amount.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the court below\\n\\nThe court below affirmed in full the first-instance judgment, which had found the alternative indictment guilty for the following reasons.\\n\\nVirtual assets are property benefits with economic value and are worthy of protection under criminal law. Once the Defendant had, without legal cause, received and held bitcoins owned by another person by transfer into his virtual asset wallet, he was obligated, as against the owner, to return the bitcoins as unjust enrichment. Embezzlement and breach of trust are property crimes of the same nature, based on a fiduciary relationship; the account holder who receives money by transfer without a legal relationship has a duty to return the remitted money to the remitter, and thus a status is recognized whereby the account holder holds the remitted or transferred money for the remitter, but there is no reason to treat differently the case where virtual assets are received by transfer without cause.\\n\\nTaking these circumstances into account, it is appropriate to deem that the Defendant bore the duty to protect and manage the victim’s property, such as by keeping the transferred bitcoins intact in order to return them to the owner based on the principle of good faith; therefore, as the subject of breach of trust, he falls under “a person who handles another’s affairs.”\\n\\n3. Supreme Court determination\\n\\nHowever, the judgment of the court below cannot be accepted for the following reasons.\\n\\na. Where virtual assets have been transferred into another person’s virtual asset electronic wallet without a legal causal relationship due to the mistake of the virtual asset rights holder or an error in the virtual asset operating system, the person who received the virtual assets by transfer may become subject to an obligation to return unjust enrichment to the virtual asset rights holder, etc. However, this is merely a civil debt between the parties, and such circumstance alone does not mean that the person who received the virtual assets by transfer is in a position to preserve or manage the virtual assets based on a fiduciary relationship. In addition, there is no contractual relationship whatsoever between the Defendant and the victim, and because it is unclear by what process the Defendant received the Bitcoin at issue, it is not clear whether the subject who may claim return of unjust enrichment is the victim or the exchange. Even if the Defendant directly bears an obligation to return unjust enrichment to the victim, it cannot immediately be concluded that the person who received the virtual assets by transfer falls under, in relation to the victim, “a person who handles another’s affairs,” the subject of the offense of breach of trust.\\n\\nb. The Supreme Court, in order for a person to be regarded as “a person who handles another’s affairs,” has limited the scope of the offense of breach of trust by holding that such status exists where, for example, the person performs on behalf of another the whole or part of the affairs concerning the management of another’s property, and the typical and essential content of the relationship between the parties lies, beyond the ordinary conflict of interests in contracts, in protecting or managing another’s property based on a fiduciary relationship between them (see Supreme Court Decision 2020. 2. 20. rendered en banc in Case No. 2019DO9756, etc.). In a case such as this one, where virtual assets were received by transfer, it is not easy to recognize a fiduciary relationship between the victim and the Defendant.\\n\\nc. Virtual assets are information that represents digitally the economic value conferred by blockchain or other encrypted distributed ledgers, without being controlled by the State, and constitute property benefits (see Supreme Court Decision 2021. 11. 11. in Case No. 2021DO9855). With virtual assets, only the address of the electronic wallet in which they were stored can be identified, and the personal identity of the person using that address cannot be known; the transaction history is recorded in a distributed manner, and when sending them to another account, a person other than the parties must participate. Thus, virtual assets have characteristics that distinguish them from ordinary assets.\\n\\nWith respect to such virtual assets, they are not currently being treated in the same manner as fiat currency, as no regulation equivalent to fiat currency has been implemented under the relevant laws, and because transactions thereof entail risks, they are not required to be protected in the same manner as fiat currency under criminal law.\\n\\nd. In the present situation, where there is no express statutory provision criminally punishing the use or disposition of virtual assets constituting property benefits received by transfer from an unknown cause, imposing criminal punishment on the Defendant for breach of trust on the basis of the principle of good faith by analogy to the precedents that affirmed the formation of embezzlement in cases of mistaken remittance (see Supreme Court Decision 2010. 12. 9. in Case No. 2010DO891, etc.) runs counter to the principle of legality.\\n\\nEven if the Bitcoin at issue was transferred from the victim to the Defendant’s electronic wallet without a legal cause, insofar as the Defendant cannot be regarded as having been entrusted, based on a fiduciary relationship, with handling the victim’s affairs, he cannot be deemed, in relation to the victim, to fall under “a person who handles another’s affairs.”\\n\\ne. Nevertheless, the court below, which found the Defendant to fall under “a person who handles another’s affairs” as the subject of the offense of breach of trust, erred by misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning “a person who handles another’s affairs” in the offense of violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (breach of trust).\\n\\n4. Scope of reversal\\n\\nFor the reasons stated above, the portion of the judgment of the court below concerning the alternative indictment is subject to reversal and cannot stand as is; and the portion concerning the principal indictment, namely violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (embezzlement), which is in an inseparable relationship with that portion, also cannot avoid reversal; accordingly, the entire judgment of the court below must be reversed.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Defendant’s final appeal is meritorious; therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices."}

{"[2021DO9855]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Prosecutor\\n\\nThe court below, with respect to the part of the facts charged against Defendant 1 concerning violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Specific Economic Crimes Act”) (extortion), and with respect to the facts charged against Defendant 2, having found that there was no proof of the crime, affirmed the first-instance judgment that had found them not guilty. Examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in the court below’s judgment in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the establishment, etc. of the crime of violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (extortion).\\n\\n2. Defendant 1\\n\\na. Bitcoin is a type of virtual asset that digitally represents economic value so as to enable electronic transfer, storage, and transaction, and therefore constitutes a pecuniary benefit that is the object of the crime of fraud.\\n\\nb. The court below affirmed the first-instance judgment that found Defendant 1 guilty of the part of the facts charged concerning violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (fraud). Examining the reasons of the court below’s judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the lawfully admitted evidence, there is no error in the court below’s judgment in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the deceptive act, act of disposition, causal relationship, intent, intent to unlawfully gain, etc. of the crime of violation of the Specific Economic Crimes Act (fraud), or in going beyond the limits of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience without fully conducting the necessary hearing, or in failing to state reasons or omitting a determination.\\n\\nc. The argument that the court below’s sentencing determination was illegal in violation of the principle of liability corresponds to an argument of improper sentencing. Defendant 2\\n\\nDefendant 2 did not submit a petition of appeal, and although defense counsel submitted a written statement of grounds of appeal to the Supreme Court on August 24, 2021, after the period for filing an appeal had elapsed, even if this were regarded as a petition of appeal, the appeal thereunder is unlawful because it was filed after the right to appeal had extinguished.\\n\\n4.
