question: An adult male A, while dating a woman A (born 2009. 1. 1.), engaged in sexual intercourse by mutual agreement around 2024. 6. 6. and, with A’s consent, photographed A’s nude body with a mobile phone camera. On that day, as A broke up with A, A told him to delete all of the nude photographs, but A did not delete them and around 2024. 7. 7. posted the above nude photographs on his public SNS account. A and her legal representative B filed a complaint against A, and Police Officer P, while questioning A, received A’s mobile phone as a voluntary submission; without preparing a separate seizure record, P entered the circumstances of the seizure and the purpose of the seizure in the suspect interrogation record. Thereafter, P video-recorded A’s statement of damage with B, a person in a relationship of trust with A, present. Which of the following statements regarding this case is correct? (If there is a dispute, follow the precedents)
A: A’s act of having sexual intercourse with A is difficult to punish under the offense of statutory rape of a minor under Article 305 of the Criminal Act.
B: A’s act of posting A’s nude photographs on a public SNS account constitutes the offense of distribution of sexually exploitative materials under Article 11(3) of the Act on the Protection of Children and Youth Against Sexual Abuse, but if A had been born on 1999. 1. 1., then because A consented to the nude photography, the offense of distribution of camera-etc.-using images under Article 14(2) of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes could not be established.
C: A’s act of photographing A’s nude body is punishable under Article 11(1) of the Act on the Protection of Children and Youth Against Sexual Abuse (production of sexually exploitative materials), and because the statutory penalty for the above offense is life imprisonment or imprisonment for at least 5 years, the statute of limitations expires upon the lapse of 15 years from the day A reaches majority.
D: The seizure record is intended to record the course of the seizure procedure so as to review and control the legality of the seizure procedure ex post facto; therefore, Police Officer P’s act of merely entering the circumstances and purpose of the seizure, etc. in the suspect interrogation record without preparing a separate seizure record is unlawful.
E: Where A has been indicted for offenses including the crime of violation of the Act on the Protection of Children and Youth Against Sexual Abuse (production of sexually exploitative materials, etc.) and the trial proceedings are underway, if A expresses an opinion of non-consent to the evidence concerning the video recording containing A’s statement, the trial court cannot use the video recording containing A’s statement as evidence by recognizing its authenticity through B’s statement, and it is appropriate to examine whether it is necessary to summon A as a witness, hear A’s statement, and afford A an opportunity to exercise the right of cross-examination.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2020DO2550]": "We decide the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Summary of the facts charged\\n\\na. The Defendant, around 02:53 on 2018. 9. 21., at an ○○○ motel located in Osan City, after having sexual intercourse with the victim Non-party 1 (female, 20 years old), activated the video function of a Samsung Galaxy S8 mobile phone ordinarily used by him (hereinafter referred to as the “mobile phone at issue”) and, without the victim’s consent, filmed the genitalia of the victim, who had fallen asleep; and, from that time until around 2019. 1. 13., as set forth in Nos. 1 through 6 and 8 of the attached crime list cited in the judgment of the court below, on a total of 7 occasions, he filmed the bodies of 2 victims that could cause sexual arousal or shame, against their will, by using a camera or another mechanical device with a similar function (hereinafter referred to as the “charges at issue”).\\n\\nb. The Defendant, around 05:29 on 2018. 12. 26., at the △△ Hotel located in Seodaemun-gu, Seoul, while the victim Non-party 2 (female, 20 years old), who stayed in the room with him, was sleeping after undressing, took a photograph of the victim on the bed, including the victim’s legs exposed outside the blanket, by using the mobile phone at issue, thereby, as set forth in No. 7 of the crime list, filming the body of another person that could cause sexual arousal or shame, against that person’s will.\\n\\n2. Summary of the judgment of the court below\\n\\nFor the following reasons, the court below reversed the first-instance judgment that found the charges at issue guilty and found the Defendant not guilty, on the ground that the video clips set forth in Nos. 1 through 6 and 8 of the crime list, which a police officer seized from the Defendant by voluntary submission (hereinafter referred to as the “videos at issue”), cannot have admissibility as evidence, and that the remaining evidence alone does not constitute proof of the crime.\\n\\na. Under Article 119(3) of the former Criminal Investigation Rules (before amendment by National Police Agency Instruction No. 1001 dated 2021. 1. 8.; hereinafter referred to as the “former Criminal Investigation Rules”), which were enacted without delegation from the Criminal Procedure Act or the Rules of Criminal Procedure, it is unlawful to state the purport of seizure in the suspect interrogation protocol and not prepare a seizure report. Accordingly, it cannot be said that a seizure report concerning the seizure of the videos at issue was prepared, and no inventory of seized electronic information specifying the file specifications was delivered to the Defendant either.\\n\\nb. The Defendant appears to have voluntarily submitted the videos at issue while being investigated as a suspect in the complaint case, in a very subdued state, without being informed of the effect of seizure by voluntary submission; thus, proof of the voluntariness of the submission is insufficient.\\n\\nc. The Defendant had only intended to voluntarily submit the photographs relating to the offense complained of by victim Non-party 2, and whether he expressly intended to voluntarily submit the videos at issue is uncertain. Accordingly, the videos at issue are not relevant to the factual allegations of the criminal charges concerning victim Non-party 2, which were found guilty.\\n\\n3. Facts found\\n\\nThe following facts can be ascertained from the reasons of the judgment below and the evidence lawfully admitted.\\n\\na. On 2018. 12. 29., victim Non-party 2 filed a complaint against the Defendant on suspicion of illegal filming on 2018. 12. 26., set forth in No. 7 of the crime list above.\\n\\nb. Judicial police officer Non-party 3 prepared a suspect interrogation protocol for the Defendant, at around 21:10 on 2019. 1. 25., in the investigation office of the Women and Youth Division of the Seodaemun Police Station in Seoul, with the participation of judicial police assistant Non-party 4. The police officer asked the Defendant whether he could show the mobile phone at issue, and the Defendant opened the photo album on the mobile phone and showed it to the police officer. While the police officer was examining the photo album of the mobile phone at issue together with the Defendant, the videos at issue were discovered in addition to the photographs of victim Non-party 2. Thereupon, the judicial police officer asked the Defendant whether he would submit the mobile phone at issue, but the Defendant refused to submit the mobile phone on the ground of his work. Instead, the Defendant stated that he would submit the photos and video files stored in the mobile phone at issue and submitted the videos at issue. The judicial police officer received and copied the videos at issue onto a police officer’s work mobile phone via Bluetooth, and stated in the suspect interrogation protocol, “At this time, the video files submitted by the suspect shall be attached to this record in the form of an investigation report.”\\n\\nc. During the suspect interrogation, the judicial police officer played the videos at issue for the Defendant, asked him who the victim women were, whether he had secretly filmed the victim women, the motive for the filming, and so on, and the Defendant confessed that he had filmed the videos at issue at the respective times stated in Nos. 1 through 6 and 8 of the crime list above.\\n\\nd. On 2019. 3. 8., the judicial police officer prepared an investigation report (concerning voluntary submission of evidentiary video) and printed out and bound into the record photographs captured from each of the videos at issue.\\n\\ne. On 2019. 5. 3., while being investigated by the prosecution, the Defendant confessed to the entirety of the offenses and stated, to the effect that, “I consented to letting the police officer see my mobile phone. The police officer downloaded both the videos and the photographs with my consent, in my presence. I consented to the police officer’s use of the videos and photographs as evidence.”\\n\\nf. In the first instance, the Defendant confessed to the entirety of the offenses and consented to all documents submitted by the prosecutor to be admitted as evidence. After the first-instance court rendered a guilty judgment, the Defendant appealed on the ground of improper sentencing.\\n\\ng. Judicial police officer Non-party 3 appeared in the court below as a witness for the prosecution and testified that, “When the witness received the videos at issue by voluntary submission, it seems that the witness explained to the Defendant the effect of voluntary submission. For that reason, it seems that the Defendant refused to voluntarily submit the mobile phone on the ground that he was a new employee.”\\n\\nh. Nothing in the record suggests circumstances such that, when the Defendant was under investigation as a suspect and submitted the videos at issue, he was in a subdued state sufficient to raise doubt as to voluntariness, and the judgment below contains no indication of such circumstances.\\n\\n4. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\n\\na. Whether it was unlawful for the judicial police officer to substitute the seizure report by stating the purport of seizure in the suspect interrogation protocol\\n\\nUnder the relevant provisions, including Articles 106, 218, and 219 of the Criminal Procedure Act, Articles 62 and 109 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure, and Article 119 of the former Criminal Investigation Rules, when a judicial police officer seizes evidentiary material voluntarily submitted, he is required to prepare a seizure report specifically stating the circumstances of the seizure, etc. This is intended to enable the judicial police officer to record the course of the seizure procedure so that the legality of the seizure procedure may be reviewed and controlled ex post facto. Even if Article 119(3) of the former Criminal Investigation Rules permits the seizure report to be substituted by stating the purport of seizure in the suspect interrogation protocol, etc., because there is no difference in the function of reviewing and controlling the legality of the seizure procedure, the judgment below, by holding that the seizure of the videos at issue was unlawful on the sole ground of the foregoing circumstances, since it did not comply with the seizure procedure prescribed by the Criminal Procedure Act, erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the legality of the seizure procedure, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\nb. Whether the inventory of seized electronic information can be regarded as having been delivered\\n\\nIn light of the facts described above, the judicial police officer played the videos at issue during the suspect interrogation and presented them to the Defendant, and the Defendant specifically stated the date and time of filming of the videos at issue, the personal information of the victim women, whether the filming was done secretly, the motive for filming, etc., and raised no particular objection. Accordingly, at the time of the seizure of the videos at issue, it may be regarded as substantially equivalent to the inventory of seized electronic information having been delivered to the Defendant. Even if an inventory specifying the seized electronic information was not delivered to the Defendant, the Defendant’s procedural rights cannot be regarded as having been substantially infringed in light of the nature and content of the process in which the procedural violation occurred, and therefore the seizure of the videos at issue may be regarded as lawful (see Supreme Court Decision 2019DO9100, decided 2021. 11. 25.; Supreme Court Decision 2019DO4938, decided 2022. 2. 17., etc.).\\n\\nNevertheless, the judgment below held that the seizure was unlawful on the ground that the judicial police officer seized the videos at issue by voluntary submission from the Defendant without delivering an inventory of seized electronic information; thus, the judgment below erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the delivery of an inventory of seized electronic information, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\nc. Whether the voluntariness of the submission of the videos at issue is established\\n\\n1) In the case of seizing articles voluntarily submitted, the prosecutor must prove to the extent that reasonable doubt is excluded that the submission was voluntary, and if the item cannot be regarded as having been voluntarily submitted, admissibility as evidence cannot be recognized (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DO11233, decided 2016. 3. 10.).\\n\\n2) Examining the foregoing facts in light of the legal principles stated above, if the circumstances under which the Defendant submitted the videos at issue to the judicial police officer, the progress of the trial in this case, and the degree of the prosecutor’s proof of voluntariness are as stated above, the court below should have more closely examined whether the submission of the videos at issue was voluntary, taking into account the specific circumstances under which the Defendant submitted the videos instead of the mobile phone at issue at the investigative agency, the circumstances under which the Defendant stated during the prosecutor’s suspect interrogation that he consented to the duplication of the videos, the Defendant’s demeanor in the courtroom, and the contents of judicial police officer Non-party 3’s testimony in the court below. Nevertheless, the judgment below held that proof of the voluntariness of the voluntary submission of the videos at issue was insufficient based solely on the reasons stated in its reasoning. Accordingly, the judgment below erred by failing to state sufficient reasons, misapprehending the legal principles concerning the voluntariness of voluntary submission, and failing to conduct the necessary examination, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\nd. Whether the videos at issue are relevant\\n\\n1) Where an investigative agency seizes media containing electronic information by receiving it by voluntary submission from a suspect without clearly confirming which of the information contained therein is being submitted, only information that is related to the factual allegations giving rise to the voluntary submission and has at least some value capable of proving those allegations may be subject to seizure. This includes information that can be used as circumstantial evidence or indirect evidence concerning the motive and circumstances of the offense, the means and method, the time and place, etc. Meanwhile, in cases of illegal filming using a smartphone, which is a mobile phone having both the function of a camera and the function of an information storage medium, where, by the nature of the offense, repeated commission is suspected, or it is suspected that the act was carried out as part of a series of offenses arising from the manifestation of sexual preference or propensity, and where there is a probability that direct evidence of the offense remains on the smartphone in the form of image files or video files, such circumstantial evidence or indirect evidence may be deemed to have a specific and individual nexus with the factual allegations of the offense, in that there is a high likelihood that strong circumstantial evidence or indirect evidence related thereto will be discovered among the same type of electronic information stored therein (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2016DO348, decided 2021. 11. 18.).\\n\\n2) Examining the foregoing facts in light of the legal principles stated above, when the Defendant voluntarily submitted the videos at issue, he did not clearly state the scope of the submission, so only electronic information related to the factual allegations giving rise to the seizure by voluntary submission and having at least some value capable of proving those allegations may be subject to seizure. However, the videos at issue were filmed from 2018. 9. 21. to 2019. 1. 13., temporally proximate to 2018. 12. 26., the date of the illegal filming offense against victim Non-party 2, and, in that the Defendant used the mobile phone at issue, which had both the function of a camera and the function of an information storage medium, to film the genitalia of female victims with whom he had sexual intercourse, the factual allegations giving rise to the seizure by voluntary submission in this case are similar in terms of the place of the offense, the means, and the method. Accordingly, the offense against victim Non-party 2 is highly susceptible, by the nature of the offense, to suspicion of habitual commission or of having been carried out as part of a series of acts arising from the manifestation of sexual preference or propensity, and there is ample room to regard the videos at issue as being related in that they may be used as indirect evidence or circumstantial evidence to prove the motive and circumstances of the offense, the means and method of the offense, and the time and place of the offense. Ultimately, the videos at issue are electronic information that has a specific and individual nexus with the offense of illegal filming against victim Non-party 2, which is the factual allegation giving rise to the seizure by voluntary submission, and relevance is therefore recognized.\\n\\nNevertheless, the judgment below held that the judicial police officer’s seizure of the videos at issue exceeded the scope in which relevance is recognized and was therefore unlawful. The judgment below thus erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the relevance required for the seizure of electronic information, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n\\ne. Conclusion in summary\\n\\nUltimately, the judgment below erred by denying the admissibility as evidence of the videos at issue for the reasons stated in its reasoning, and, on the ground that the remaining evidence alone does not constitute proof of the crime, finding the relevant portion of the charges not guilty, because it failed to conduct the necessary examination after denying the admissibility as evidence of the foregoing evidence due to the errors noted above, thereby affecting the judgment. The grounds of appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without deciding on the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the not-guilty portion of the judgment below and remand this part of the case to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

question: A, while driving his passenger car, changed lanes and, through occupational negligence in failing to keep a proper lookout ahead, collided with the passenger car occupied by Victims A and B, causing Victim A serious injury such as brain injury and causing Victim B injury requiring two weeks of treatment. B, while driving his cargo truck in a state of intoxication with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.15%, and through occupational negligence in failing to keep a proper lookout ahead, collided with the bicycle owned by Victim C and parked in front of a convenience store, damaging it so that repair costs of approximately KRW 300,000 were incurred. The prosecutor instituted charges against A for the offense of violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents (injury), and against B for the offense of violation of the Road Traffic Act (drunk driving) and the offense of violation of the Road Traffic Act arising from negligent damage to property. Which of the following statements concerning this is correct? (If there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Since it arose from a single traffic accident, only the offense of violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents (injury) as to the more serious victim A is established against A, and the offense of violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents (injury) as to Victim B is absorbed into it.
B: If A's passenger car is covered by comprehensive insurance, even if Victim A requests punishment of A, the court must render a judgment dismissing the prosecution against A pursuant to Article 327 subparagraph 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act.
C: If A caused the accident by changing lanes after crossing a solid white line, a safety marking prohibiting lane changes, since the Road Traffic Act separately regulates prohibition of passage and prohibition of lane changes, even if A's passenger car is not covered by comprehensive insurance, if after prosecution Victim B expresses an intention not to seek punishment, the court must render a judgment dismissing the prosecution pursuant to Article 327 subparagraph 2 of the Criminal Procedure Act.
D: If B was booked for the offense of refusal to undergo alcohol testing after refusing a police officer's request for a breath test, and then requested a blood draw because he thought that perhaps no alcohol level would appear if blood were drawn, and the test result showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.15%, the offense of violation of the Road Traffic Act (drunk driving) and the offense of violation of the Road Traffic Act (refusal to undergo alcohol testing) separately constitute real concurrence.
E: With respect to B's traffic accident, if B's drunk driving is recognized, even if B's cargo truck is covered by comprehensive insurance, a guilty judgment must be rendered for the offense of violation of the Road Traffic Act arising from B's negligent damage to property.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2004DO5257]": "1. The court below, by comprehensively considering the evidence set forth in its reasoning, found the facts as stated in the judgment, namely: that the Defendant, at around 21:15 on July 3, 2003, drove a Starex van bearing Daegu 61MA 5126 and proceeded for approximately 2 km from the road in front of Daedeok Industrial Co. located at 352-7 Sang-ri, Yuga-myeon, Dalseong-gun, Daegu, to the road in front of Gobong Intersection located in Gobong-ri, Gugi-myeon, the same county; that at that place, the fact that he had been drinking was detected by a breath-alcohol detector by Police Officer Jang Seong-ha of the Gugi Police Box, Dalseong Police Station, Daegu, who was conducting a drunk-driving crackdown, and that at the time the Defendant had a flushed face and smelled of alcohol from his mouth; that the Defendant, at around 21:27 on the same day, received notice of a breath-alcohol test from Jang Seong-ha at the Gugi Police Box, but refused the breath test on a total of 3 occasions, at around 21:35, around 21:47, and around 21:57; that after being booked for refusing the breath test, the Defendant requested blood sampling on the thought that blood testing might perhaps not reveal an intoxication level, and thus had his blood drawn at around 23:02 on the same day at the emergency room of Hyunpung Hana Hospital located in Hyunpung-myeon, Dalseong-gun, Daegu; and that, as a result of the blood test conducted by examiner Yoo Jae-hoon of the southern branch of the National Scientific Research Institute, the blood alcohol concentration of the above blood was determined to be 0.130%. The court below then held that the legislative purpose of the offense of refusing a breath test is that, although a breath test using a breath-alcohol tester requires the driver’s voluntary cooperation in order to prove drunken driving, if the driver refuses such test, it becomes extremely difficult to prove the driver’s intoxicated condition; therefore, by punishing the person who refused a breath test for the act of failing to comply with a request for a breath test with the same statutory punishment as driving while intoxicated, the law indirectly compels breath testing, thereby promoting traffic safety and at the same time facilitating proof and punishment of drunk driving. The court below further held that, if the offense of refusing a breath test and the offense of driving while intoxicated under the Road Traffic Act are recognized as standing in a relation of substantive concurrence with respect to the same act of drunk driving, this would not only result in double punishment for a series of acts involving only the same infringement of a legal interest, but would also be unreasonable in that, even though a case in which the alcohol level is confirmed after refusal of the breath test cannot be said to be more blameworthy than a case in which the breath test is refused to the end, the punishment actually imposed would become higher due to the aggravation of concurrent offenses. In light of these points, the court below concluded that, where a driver refuses a breath test by means of a breathalyzer and the offense of refusing a breath test is completed, even if the alcohol level is later revealed through blood sampling or the like, the driver must be punished only for the offense of refusing a breath test, and may not additionally be punished for driving while intoxicated. Accordingly, it convicted only the charge of refusing a breath test among the facts charged in this case and rendered a judgment of acquittal on the charge of driving while intoxicated.\\n\\n2. However, the above determination of the court below is difficult to accept in light of the following.\\n\\n   a. The offense of refusing to comply with a breath test under Article 107-2, subparagraph 2, of the Road Traffic Act is established where a person for whom there exists reasonable grounds to believe that he or she is in a state of intoxication fails to comply with the measurement by a police officer under Article 41, paragraph 2, of the same Act. Originally, Article 41, paragraph 2, of the Road Traffic Act provided: “A police officer may measure whether a driver is intoxicated when deemed necessary for traffic safety and the prevention of danger, and the driver shall comply with such measurement by the police officer.” Thereafter, by the amendment of January 5, 1995, it was revised to include the case where there exist reasonable grounds to believe that a person drove an automobile, etc. while intoxicated in violation of paragraph 1 of the same Article. When the purpose of the above provision and the legislative history are comprehensively considered, (1) driving while intoxicated concerns only the already-occurred infringement of road-traffic safety, whereas refusal to submit to a breath test concerns not only the past infringement of road-traffic safety but also securing future road-traffic safety and preventing danger; and (2) furthermore, whereas the subject of driving while intoxicated is a person who is “intoxicated” beyond the standards prescribed by the Enforcement Decree of the Road Traffic Act, the subject of refusal to submit to a breath test is a person for whom there exist reasonable grounds to believe that he or she drove an automobile, etc. while intoxicated; thus, it cannot be concluded that the two necessarily infringe the same legal interest or that the illegality and culpability inherent in driving while intoxicated are, as a general matter, subsumed within those of refusal to submit to a breath test.\\n\\n   b. As one ground for its reasoning, the court below points out that, even though a case in which the alcohol level is confirmed after refusal of the breath test cannot be said to be more blameworthy than a case in which the breath test is refused to the end, the punishment actually imposed becomes higher due to the aggravation of concurrent offenses, which is unreasonable. However, (1) even under the Criminal Procedure Act of Korea, there is no reason why the blood alcohol concentration of a person who has refused a breath test may not be measured by forcibly drawing blood after obtaining a warrant for judicial expert examination or the like from the court and then having a physician examine the blood; and the practice whereby traffic police officers, with respect to drivers who refuse a breath test, do not perform forced blood sampling and instead charge them only with refusal to submit to a breath test, is merely a practical custom arising from the procedural uncertainty or inconvenience, as well as temporal and spatial constraints, caused by the fact that the Criminal Procedure Act does not separately provide explicit provisions concerning forced blood sampling. Therefore, the disparity in punishment actually imposed, as pointed out by the court below, is in the end an extremely exceptional phenomenon that may arise due to the above practical conditions, and it is not consistent with reason to deny the very establishment of the offense of violation of the Road Traffic Act (driving while intoxicated) on that basis; (2) rather, the subject of refusal to submit to a breath test is only a person for whom there exist reasonable grounds to believe that he or she is in a state of intoxication, and not necessarily a person who is in a state of intoxication. Thus, for example, if two drivers for whom there exist reasonable grounds to believe that they drove while intoxicated each refuse a breath test and, thereafter, blood is drawn and examined, and the result shows that one person’s blood alcohol concentration at the time of detection was below the standard (0.05%) while the other’s exceeded it, then, according to the court below’s logic, both persons would have no choice but to be punished only for refusal to submit to a breath test, so that, rather, the degree of blameworthiness and the actual punishment would fail to maintain balance; and (3) in particular, in this case, after first refusing the breath test, the Defendant, under the mistaken belief that if blood were drawn and examined and the blood alcohol concentration turned out to be below 0.05%, punishment might be mitigated, requested a blood test. This was not a repentance of the act of refusing the breath test, and therefore the court below’s logic concerning the degree of blameworthiness is based on a general theory unrelated to the actual facts of this case and lacks concrete propriety. Ultimately, the above view of the court below confuses culpability as a requirement for the establishment of a crime with culpability as the basis for sentencing, and thus is difficult to accept; the problem pointed out by the court below can be fully resolved in the process of determining the sentence to be imposed.\\n\\n   c. Ultimately, although the offenses of violation of the Road Traffic Act, namely driving while intoxicated and refusing to submit to a breath test, should be regarded as standing in a relation of substantive concurrence, the court below erred in law concerning the relation of number of offenses between the above two crimes and, by making a different determination, affected the judgment. Accordingly, the Prosecutor’s argument pointing out this point and raising it as a ground for appeal is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Ultimately, the above part of the judgment of the court below acquitting the Defendant is reversed, and the case pertaining to that part is remanded to the court below, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the order."}

{"[82DO2860]": "1. We examine the first ground of appeal by the Prosecutor.\\n\\nAccording to Article 3(2) of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents, in the traffic of vehicles, with respect to a driver who has committed the offense of bodily injury by occupational negligence or the offense of bodily injury by gross negligence among the offenses under paragraph (1), and the offense under Article 74 of the Road Traffic Act, no public prosecution may be instituted contrary to the victim’s explicit intent. This should be construed as meaning that the offenses listed above are made so-called offenses not punishable against the victim’s will, and that, as in a crime subject to complaint where a complaint is a condition for instituting prosecution, the absence of an expression of intent not to punish (or the withdrawal of an expression of intent to seek punishment) is prescribed as a condition for instituting prosecution.\\n\\nTherefore, if prosecution has been instituted even though the condition of the absence of an expression of intent not to punish, as described above, was lacking from the outset, a judgment dismissing the prosecution should be rendered under Article 327(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act; and if, at the time prosecution was instituted, the above negative condition was satisfied but later came to be lacking, that is, if after prosecution the victim expressed an intent not to punish or withdrew an expression of intent to seek punishment, a judgment dismissing the prosecution should be rendered under Article 327(6) of the same Act.\\n\\nThe argument is that, based on the expression in the main clause of Article 3(2) of the above Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents that “no public prosecution may be instituted” contrary to the victim’s explicit intent, once prosecution has been instituted, neither an expression of intent not to punish nor the withdrawal of an already-made expression of intent to seek punishment affects the validity of the institution of prosecution. However, as explained above, the expression in that Article that “no public prosecution may be instituted” merely signifies that the offenses prescribed in that Article are offenses not punishable against the victim’s will, and even upon a comprehensive review of the provisions of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents, there is no basis for construing them, as contended, to mean that the timing of an expression of intent not to punish (or the withdrawal of an expression of intent to seek punishment) is limited to before the institution of prosecution; accordingly, the argument is without merit.\\n\\n2. We examine the second point of the same ground of appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, in this case, after the judgment of the first instance was rendered, found that the victim Son Hee-mo had settled with the Defendant and clearly did not wish the Defendant to be punished, and accordingly rendered a judgment dismissing the prosecution pursuant to Article 327(6) of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nHowever, according to Article 232(3) and (1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, in an offense not punishable against the victim’s will, the withdrawal of an expression of intent to seek punishment may be made only until before the judgment of the first instance is rendered, and after that, even if withdrawn, it has no effect. The record clearly shows that the victim Son Hee-mo in this case had, during the investigation stage, expressed an intent to seek punishment of the Defendant, but after the judgment of the first instance was rendered, settled with the Defendant and withdrew the expression of intent to seek punishment; accordingly, such withdrawal has no effect.\\n\\nUltimately, the court below, by misunderstanding the legal principle concerning the withdrawal of an expression of intent to seek punishment in an offense not punishable against the victim’s will, committed an illegality that affected the judgment. Since the argument on this point is well-founded, we reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the collegiate division of the Gwangju District Court. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in this case, as stated in the disposition."}

question: 甲 had been entrusted by A with a laptop computer owned by A and kept it in custody, and while keeping a tablet PC owned by B, having been entrusted by B, 甲 sold them in bulk to B, who knew of such entrustment, in order to obtain gambling funds. 甲 squandered the entire amount of the sale proceeds through gambling on the same day. The prosecutor indicted 甲 for embezzlement and gambling. Which of the following statements is incorrect? (If there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Separate embezzlement offenses are established with respect to the victims A and B, and the two embezzlement offenses stand in a relationship of ideal concurrence.
B: If B had instigated 甲 to engage in the above sale, then B would be subject to concurrent offenses of instigation of embezzlement and acquisition of stolen property.
C: If it is additionally revealed that the embezzled items included a tablet PC entrusted by victim C and kept in custody, and the prosecutor files a motion to amend the indictment by adding this to the charged facts, the court shall, absent special circumstances, grant it.
D: Even where the court served a duplicate of the motion for leave to amend the indictment on 甲, if the trial record does not state the procedure by which the court decided whether to grant the leave, it is not automatically presumed that the court overlooked the motion to amend the indictment and failed to decide whether to grant it; rather, the existence of procedural acts not entered in the trial record may be proved by other contents entered in the trial record or by materials other than the trial record, but this is a matter subject to strict proof.
E: In an appellate proceeding continued by the prosecutor’s appeal with respect to the first-instance judgment that acquitted the defendant in full on the charges of embezzlement and gambling, the appellate court found both embezzlement and gambling guilty and imposed a single sentence; if, in the Supreme Court proceeding continued by 甲’s appeal, the portion of the judgment below concerning embezzlement is reversed, then the portion concerning gambling, for which a single sentence was imposed in a relationship of concurrent offenses, also becomes subject to reversal together.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2013DO10020]": "Grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, based on the evidence it admitted, found the Defendant guilty of both the act of embezzling the computer main unit, monitor, etc. that the Defendant had rented (leased) and kept from the Victim, Non-Indicted 1 Company (hereinafter referred to as “Non-Indicted 1 Company”), and the act of embezzling the computer main unit, monitor, graphics card, mouse, etc. that the Defendant had leased (leased) and kept from the Victim, Non-Indicted 2 Company (hereinafter referred to as “Non-Indicted 2 Company”), and treated each embezzlement act as a real concurrent offense under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, and imposed aggravated punishment for concurrent offenses pursuant to Article 38(1)2 and Article 50 of the Criminal Act.\\n\\nWhere several articles kept under several fiduciary relationships are embezzled by one act, several counts of embezzlement are constituted for each fiduciary relationship, and there is a relationship of ideal concurrence between them.\\n\\nExamining the facts charged in this case in light of the legal principles stated above, the Defendant entered into a rental (lease) contract with the Victim, Non-Indicted 1 Company, and received and kept 24 computer main units and 1 monitor therefrom; entered into a lease (lease) contract with the Victim, Non-Indicted 2 Company, and received and kept 13 computer main units, 41 monitors, 13 graphics cards, and 11 mice therefrom; and thereafter, around February 22, 2011, disposed of them all at once to an unidentified company and embezzled them. Accordingly, such act of embezzlement should reasonably be evaluated, in social convention, as one act, and each count of embezzlement against the victims should be deemed to stand in a relationship of ideal concurrence.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, contrary to this, determined that the above counts were in a relationship of real concurrence and imposed aggravated punishment for concurrent offenses. In so doing, the judgment of the court below contains an error of law that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principle concerning the number of offenses in embezzlement.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2023DO3038]": "The grounds of appeal are determined as follows.\\n\\n1. Relevant legal principles\\n\\na. According to Article 298(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, “the prosecutor may, with leave of the court, add, withdraw, or change the charged facts stated in the indictment or the applicable statutory provisions,” and “the court shall grant such leave insofar as it does not prejudice the identity of the charged facts.” Accordingly, the purport of the above provision must be construed to mean that, where the prosecutor’s motion to amend the indictment does not prejudice the identity of the charged facts, the court must grant it (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2018DO11711, decided Dec. 13, 2018). The identity of the charged facts is maintained if the social factual relationship underlying those facts remains identical in its essential points, and in determining such essential identity of the factual relationship, the accused person’s conduct and the corresponding social factual relationship should be the basis, taking into account the normative element as well, in light of the function of factual identity (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 98DO1438, decided May 14, 1999).\\n\\nb. 1) The court shall grant or deny a prosecutor’s motion for leave to amend the indictment by way of an order, and the court’s decision on whether to grant leave may be made by preparing a separate written order outside the courtroom and giving notice thereof, or may be made orally in the courtroom and entered in the trial record. If the decision on whether to grant leave to amend the indictment is announced in the courtroom, that fact constitutes a mandatory entry in the trial record (Article 51(2), item 14 of the Criminal Procedure Act). Even where a motion for leave to amend the indictment has been filed, if the court proceeds with the trial without expressly deciding whether leave to amend the indictment is granted, it may affect the Defendant’s exercise of the right of defense because it becomes unclear what charged facts have actually become the subject of adjudication; therefore, it is desirable that the decision on whether to grant leave to amend the indictment be expressly made in the above form.\\n\\n2) As to decisions concerning the pre-judgment trial procedure, an appeal may not be taken except in cases where an immediate appeal is particularly permitted (Article 403(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act). A decision on whether to permit the addition, withdrawal, or change of the charged facts or applicable statutory provisions is a decision concerning the pre-judgment trial procedure, and if any illegality in that decision affected the judgment, such illegality may be challenged only by appealing the judgment (see Supreme Court Order 87MO17, decided Mar. 28, 1987; Supreme Court Decision 2001DO1660, decided July 13, 2001).\\n\\nc. Facts that a judgment or other judicial decision was pronounced or announced as part of the trial-day procedure must be entered in the trial record (Article 51(1), Article 51(2), item 14 of the Criminal Procedure Act), and, except where the entry in the trial record is a manifest clerical error, matters entered in the trial record as part of the trial-day procedure must be proven solely by the record, and their probative force is absolute and does not permit contradiction by evidence other than the trial record (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2005DO6557, decided Dec. 22, 2005). By contrast, the mere fact that the content of a trial procedure is not entered in the trial record does not necessarily create a presumption that the procedure was not conducted on the relevant trial date; the existence of a trial procedure not entered in the trial record may be proven by other matters entered in the trial record or by materials other than the trial record, and, since this is a procedural-law fact, it is subject to free proof.\\n\\n2. Determination of this case\\n\\na. According to the record, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n\\n1) The Prosecutor instituted public prosecution on the charge of occupational embezzlement, alleging that “the Defendant, while operating a hospital, embezzled by arbitrary consumption a total of 17,082,860 won, which, from around May 2017 until around May 2020, was, as pension insurance premiums under the National Pension Act entrusted for the employees of the hospital who were victims 11 persons, the amount of contributions to be borne by the workplace subscriber, and, as insurance premiums under the National Health Insurance Act and long-term care insurance premiums under the Long-Term Care Insurance Act, the premiums to be borne by the workplace subscriber,” and thereafter additionally indicted occupational embezzlement of the same insurance premiums with respect to one additional employee of the hospital in question.\\n\\n2) The first-instance court consolidated these matters and held that several offenses of occupational embezzlement, established comprehensively for each of the 12 victims, constituted guilty offenses in a relation of ideal concurrence.\\n\\n3) The Prosecutor appealed the first-instance judgment on the ground of unfair sentencing, and then, in or around September 2022, before the first oral argument date in the court below, filed a motion for leave to amend the indictment, stating that the purpose was to add charges of occupational embezzlement against five other employees who were in a relation of ideal concurrence with the earlier charged occupational embezzlement, and submitted an indictment amendment leave application containing the following: “The Defendant, from around May 2017 until around May 2020, embezzled by arbitrary consumption a total of 22,817,330 won, which, as pension insurance premiums under the National Pension Act entrusted for the 17 victims who were employees of the hospital operated by the Defendant, was the amount of contributions to be borne by the workplace subscriber, and, as insurance premiums under the National Health Insurance Act and long-term care insurance premiums under the Long-Term Care Insurance Act, were the premiums to be borne by the workplace subscriber.” The court below served a copy of the indictment amendment leave application on the Defendant.\\n\\n4) The court below held the first trial date in or around December 2022, closed oral argument, and dismissed the Prosecutor’s appeal on the ground of unfair sentencing, thereby maintaining the first-instance judgment as it stood.\\n\\n5) The court below neither made a decision outside the courtroom on the motion for leave to amend the indictment, nor is there any indication in the trial record or other records that any trial procedure was conducted in the court below whereby leave to amend the indictment was decided, such as the submission by the Defendant’s side of opinions regarding the Prosecutor’s above motion for leave to amend the indictment or the charged facts sought to be added by that motion.\\n\\nb. The above facts are examined in light of the foregoing legal principles.\\n\\n1) It is suspected that the court below overlooked the Prosecutor’s motion for leave to amend the indictment filed through submission of the indictment amendment leave application and proceeded with the procedure without deciding whether to grant leave.\\n\\n2) The charged facts before and after the motion for leave to amend the indictment differ only in that five victims of occupational embezzlement were added and in the total amount embezzled; otherwise, the time, place, and method of the embezzlement are all identical, so the basic factual relationship is identical and the identity of the charged facts is not prejudiced. The court below also maintained the first-instance judgment, which found that several offenses of occupational embezzlement established for each victim were in a relation of ideal concurrence.\\n\\n3) Therefore, the court below should have decided whether to grant the Prosecutor’s motion for leave to amend the indictment submitted in writing, and further should have granted the amendment of the indictment to add charged facts consisting of offenses in a relation of ideal concurrence that had not originally been prosecuted, and then examined and adjudicated the added charged facts. Dismissing the Prosecutor’s appeal without taking such measures contains error that failed to conduct the necessary trial or misunderstood the law concerning amendment of the indictment, thereby affecting the judgment. The Prosecutor’s argument in this respect is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Scope of reversal\\n\\nThe portion of the court below’s judgment concerning occupational embezzlement must be reversed. However, since this portion was sentenced to a single punishment in a relation of concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act together with the remaining portions that were found guilty (including violations of the Labor Standards Act), the entire court below judgment becomes subject to reversal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nThe court below’s judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for retrial and redetermination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2023DO3038]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nA. Pursuant to Article 298(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, “the prosecutor may, with the permission of the court, add, withdraw, or amend the charged facts or the applicable statutory provisions stated in the indictment,” and “the court shall grant such permission insofar as it does not impair the identity of the charged facts.” Accordingly, the purport of the above provision must be construed to mean that, so long as the prosecutor’s motion to amend the indictment does not impair the identity of the charged facts, the court must grant it (see, e.g., Supreme Court Judgment 2018DO11711 rendered on Dec. 13, 2018). The identity of the charged facts remains intact if the social factual relations underlying those facts are identical in their essential aspects, and in determining such identity of the essential factual relations, the defendant’s conduct and the social factual relations thereof should be the basis, bearing in mind the function that such identity has, while also taking normative elements into consideration (see, e.g., Supreme Court Judgment 98DO1438 rendered on May 14, 1999).\\n\\nB. 1) The court shall grant or deny the prosecutor’s motion for leave to amend the indictment by way of an order, and the court’s decision on whether to grant leave may be made outside the courtroom by preparing a separate written order and notifying it, or may also be made orally in the courtroom and entered in the trial protocol. If the decision on whether to grant leave to amend the indictment was announced in the courtroom, that fact is a mandatory entry in the trial protocol (Article 51(2) Item 14 of the Criminal Procedure Act). Where there is a motion for leave to amend the indictment, if the proceedings are conducted without expressly deciding whether leave to amend the indictment is granted, it may affect the Defendant’s exercise of the right of defense because it would be unclear what charged facts became the actual object of adjudication; therefore, it is desirable to make an express decision on whether to grant leave to amend the indictment in the above form.\\n\\n2) With respect to decisions concerning pre-judgment procedural matters, no appeal may be taken except in cases where an immediate appeal is permitted (Article 403(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act). A decision on the permission of the addition, withdrawal, or amendment of the charged facts or the applicable statutory provisions is a decision concerning pre-judgment procedural matters, and if the illegality regarding that decision affected the judgment, it may be challenged only by the means of appealing that judgment (see Supreme Court Decision 87MO17 dated Mar. 28, 1987; Supreme Court Judgment 2001DO1660 rendered on Jul. 13, 2001).\\n\\nC. The fact that a judgment or other judicial decision was pronounced or notified as part of the proceedings on the trial date must be entered in the trial protocol (Article 51(1) and (2) Item 14 of the Criminal Procedure Act). Except where the entry in the trial protocol is an obvious clerical error, what is entered in the trial protocol as a procedural act on the trial date must be proved solely by the protocol, and its probative force is absolute in that counterproof by materials other than the trial protocol is not permitted (see, e.g., Supreme Court Judgment 2005DO6557 rendered on Dec. 22, 2005). By contrast, the mere fact that the occurrence of a procedural act is not entered in the trial protocol does not automatically imply that the procedural act was not carried out on the relevant trial date; the existence of a procedural act not entered in the trial protocol may be proved by other contents entered in the trial protocol or by materials other than the trial protocol, and because this is a fact concerning procedural law, it is subject to free proof.\\n\\n2. Judgment in this case\\n\\nA. According to the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n1) The Prosecutor filed charges alleging, with respect to embezzlement in the course of business, that “while operating a hospital, the Defendant, from around May 2017 to around May 2020, for 11 victims who were employees of the hospital, embezzled 17,082,860 won by arbitrarily consuming, in the course of business, the total amount of contributions under the National Pension Act borne by workplace subscribers and the insurance premiums under the National Health Insurance Act and the Long-Term Care Insurance Act for the Elderly borne by workplace subscribers,” and then additionally indicted the same occupational embezzlement of insurance premiums concerning one other employee of the offending hospital.\\n\\n2) The court of first instance consolidated these and, for each of the 12 victims, found the Defendant guilty of several offenses of embezzlement in the course of business in a relation of ideal concurrence.\\n\\n3) The Prosecutor appealed the first instance judgment on the ground of improper sentencing, and before the date of the first trial session in the court below, around September 2022, submitted a motion for leave to amend the indictment stating that it was intended to add charges of embezzlement in the course of business concerning five other employees who were in a relation of ideal concurrence with the previously indicted embezzlement in the course of business, with the content that “the Defendant, from around May 2017 to around May 2020, while operating the hospital, embezzled 22,817,330 won by arbitrarily consuming, in the course of business, for 17 victims who were employees of the hospital operated by the Defendant, the total amount of contributions under the National Pension Act borne by workplace subscribers and the insurance premiums under the National Health Insurance Act and the Long-Term Care Insurance Act for the Elderly borne by workplace subscribers.” The court below served a copy of the motion for leave to amend the indictment on the Defendant.\\n\\n4) The court below held the first trial session around Dec. 2022, closed the proceedings, dismissed the Prosecutor’s appeal on the ground of improper sentencing, and thereby left the first instance judgment intact.\\n\\n5) The court below did not make a decision on the motion for leave to amend the indictment outside the courtroom, and the record, including the trial protocol, does not contain any indication that procedural steps were taken in the court below to decide whether to grant leave to amend the indictment, such as the Defendant’s submission of opinions regarding the above motion for leave to amend the indictment or the charged facts sought to be added by that motion.\\n\\nB. Consider the above facts in light of the legal principles discussed above.\\n\\n1) It appears that the court below overlooked the Prosecutor’s motion for leave to amend the indictment, submitted by the filing of the motion for leave to amend the indictment, and conducted the proceedings without deciding whether to grant leave.\\n\\n2) The charged facts before and after the motion for leave to amend the indictment differ only in that five victims of embezzlement in the course of business were added and in the overall amount embezzled; otherwise, the time, place, and method of embezzlement are all identical, so the basic factual relations are identical and the identity of the charged facts is not impaired. The court below also left intact the first instance judgment, which treated the several offenses of embezzlement in the course of business established for each victim as being in a relation of ideal concurrence.\\n\\n3) Accordingly, the court below should have decided whether to grant the Prosecutor’s written motion for leave to amend the indictment, and furthermore should have permitted the amendment to the indictment that adds charged facts not originally indicted among the several offenses in a relation of ideal concurrence and then examined and adjudicated the added charged facts. Dismissing the Prosecutor’s appeal without such measures contains an error that failed to fully conduct the necessary examination or misunderstood the legal principles governing amendment of the indictment, thereby affecting the judgment. The Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal pointing out this issue are well-founded.\\n\\n3. Scope of reversal\\n\\nThe portion of the court below’s judgment concerning embezzlement in the course of business must be reversed. However, since this portion was sentenced together with the remaining portions found guilty (such as violation of the Labor Standards Act) in a relation of concurrent offenses under the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act, the entire judgment of the court below is ultimately subject to reversal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nThe court below’s judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. The disposition is rendered unanimously by the Justices participating."}

{"[2023DO3038]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nA. According to Article 298(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, “the prosecutor may, with leave of the court, add, withdraw, or change the charged facts or the applicable provisions stated in the indictment,” and “the court shall grant such leave so long as it does not impair the identity of the charged facts.” Therefore, the purport of the foregoing provision must be construed to mean that the court must grant the prosecutor’s motion to amend the indictment so long as it does not impair the identity of the charged facts (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on December 13, 2018, 2018DO11711). If the decision on whether to grant leave to amend the indictment was notified in open court, that fact is a mandatory matter to be entered in the hearing record (Article 51(2)14 of the Criminal Procedure Act). Even where there is a motion for leave to amend the indictment, if the proceedings are conducted without expressly deciding whether to grant leave to amend the indictment, it may affect the defendant’s exercise of the right of defense because it is unclear what charged facts have actually become the object of adjudication; therefore, it is desirable for the decision whether to grant leave to amend the indictment to be expressly made in the above form.\\n\\n2) As to a ruling concerning the procedural steps before judgment, an appeal may not be taken except in cases where an immediate interlocutory appeal is particularly permitted (Article 403(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act); a ruling concerning leave to add, withdraw, or change the charged facts or the applicable provisions is a ruling concerning procedural steps before judgment, and where the illegality of that ruling affected the judgment, it may be challenged only by appealing the judgment (see Supreme Court Order rendered on March 28, 1987, 87MO17; Supreme Court Decision rendered on July 13, 2001, 2001DO1660).\\n\\nC. Facts that a judgment or other judicial decision was pronounced or notified as part of the procedural steps at a trial date must be entered in the hearing record (Article 51(1) and (2)14 of the Criminal Procedure Act). Except where the entry in the hearing record is an obvious clerical error, matters recorded in the hearing record as part of the procedural steps at a trial date must be proved by the record alone, and such probative force is absolute in that rebuttal by materials other than the hearing record is not permitted (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision rendered on December 22, 2005, 2005DO6557). On the other hand, the mere fact that the content of procedural steps taken was not entered in the hearing record does not necessarily lead to the presumption that such procedural steps were not taken at the relevant trial date; the existence of procedural steps not entered in the hearing record may be proved by other content entered in the hearing record or by materials other than the hearing record, and because this is a procedural fact, it is subject to free proof.\\n\\n2. Determination in this case\\n\\nA. According to the record, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n\\n1) The prosecutor instituted a prosecution for embezzlement in the course of duty by charging that “while operating a hospital, the Defendant embezzled by arbitrarily spending KRW 17,082,860 in total, consisting of the contribution to be borne by the workplace subscriber among the pension insurance premiums under the National Pension Act and the premiums to be borne by the workplace subscriber among the premiums under the National Health Insurance Act and the premiums under the Long-Term Care Insurance Act for the Elderly, which were kept in custody in the course of duty for 11 victims who were hospital employees, from around May 2017 to around May 2020”; thereafter, a separate prosecution was additionally instituted for embezzlement in the course of duty concerning the same premiums with respect to one other employee of the hospital where the offense occurred.\\n\\n2) The court of first instance consolidated these cases and determined that the multiple offenses of embezzlement in the course of duty, established collectively for each of the 12 victims, were guilty under the relationship of ideal concurrence.\\n\\n3) The prosecutor appealed the judgment of the court of first instance on the ground of improper sentencing, and then, in around September 2022, before the first trial date of the appellate court was held, filed a motion for leave to amend the indictment stating that it was intended to add charges of embezzlement in the course of duty against 5 other employees who were in the relationship of ideal concurrence with the already prosecuted charged facts of embezzlement in the course of duty, with the following content: “The Defendant embezzled by arbitrarily spending KRW 22,817,330 in total, consisting of the contribution to be borne by the workplace subscriber among the pension insurance premiums under the National Pension Act and the premiums to be borne by the workplace subscriber among the premiums under the National Health Insurance Act and the premiums under the Long-Term Care Insurance Act for the Elderly, which were kept in custody in the course of duty for 17 victims who were employees of the hospital operated by the Defendant, from around May 2017 to around May 2020.” The appellate court served a copy of the motion for leave to amend the indictment on the Defendant.\\n\\n4) The appellate court held the first trial date in around December 2022, closed the arguments, and dismissed the prosecutor’s appeal on the ground of improper sentencing, thereby maintaining the judgment of the court of first instance as it was.\\n\\n5) The appellate court did not make a decision on the motion for leave to amend the indictment outside open court, and neither the hearing record nor the record indicates that procedural steps were taken in the appellate court for deciding whether to grant leave to amend the indictment, such as the submission of the Defendant’s position regarding the prosecutor’s above motion for leave to amend the indictment or the charged facts sought to be added by the above motion.\\n\\nB. The foregoing facts are examined in light of the legal principles discussed above.\\n\\n1) It is suspected that, despite the prosecutor’s motion for leave to amend the indictment by submitting the written motion for leave to amend the indictment, the appellate court overlooked it and proceeded with the case without deciding whether to grant leave.\\n\\n2) The charged facts before and after the motion for leave to amend the indictment differ only in that five victims of embezzlement in the course of duty were added and the total amount embezzled is different; in all other respects, such as the time, place, and method of the embezzlement, they are identical, and therefore the basic factual relationship is identical, so the identity of the charged facts is not impaired. The appellate court also maintained the judgment of the court of first instance, which had determined that the multiple offenses of embezzlement in the course of duty established for each victim were in the relationship of ideal concurrence.\\n\\n3) Therefore, the appellate court should have decided whether to grant leave with respect to the prosecutor’s written motion for leave to amend the indictment, and further should have granted the amendment of the indictment adding charged facts not originally prosecuted among the multiple offenses in the relationship of ideal concurrence, and should have examined and determined the added charged facts. Scope of reversal\\n\\nThe part of the appellate judgment concerning embezzlement in the course of duty must be reversed.
