Conclusion\\n\\nThe appellate judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the appellate court for further proceedings and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[69DO692]": "As to the grounds of appeal by defense counsel, upon examination, when the evidence cited in the first-instance judgment upheld by the court below is reviewed according to the record, there is no error in the court below’s determination to the effect that the first-instance judgment finding the facts of the offense in this case contains no illegality, and, when the above evidence is reviewed according to the record, it is clear that, in relation to the co-defendants at first instance, namely First-Instance Co-Defendants 1 and 2, who had been indicted on the charge of embezzling the object at issue in this case, the Defendant cannot be said to fall under the status of a joint principal offender of the above offense of embezzlement; and even if, from the contents stated in the indictment, it can be inferred as alleged in the argument that the Defendant instigated the above co-defendants to embezzle the property in their custody, if the Defendant instigated the above co-defendants to embezzle and acquired the embezzled property, then such acts of the Defendant would constitute the concurrent offenses of instigation of embezzlement and acquisition of stolen property; however, according to the indictment in this case, it is clear that the prosecutor charged only the offense of acquisition of stolen property among the above criminal facts (and also charged the offense of violation of an order), and therefore it cannot be said to be unlawful for the court below to have recognized only the offense of acquisition of stolen property based on such facts charged in the indictment, so the argument attacking the original judgment on a contrary view is without merit.\\n\\nTherefore, by the unanimous opinion of all the judges concerned, the Court renders judgment as follows."}

question: A stole A's wallet at a department store. While bumping into A and putting his hand into the pocket of a suit jacket in order to steal the wallet, he was discovered and fled, but was immediately caught by security guard X, who chased after him. While X was confirming the circumstances, 甲 struck X's face several times with his fist in order to escape from the state of arrest, thereby inflicting an injury requiring 4 weeks of treatment, and fled. One hour after the incident occurred, when judicial police officer P, who had been dispatched upon X's report, requested 甲, who was standing at a nearby bus stop, to accompany him voluntarily, 甲 demanded presentation of a warrant and refused to accompany him. Nevertheless, when P tried to forcibly place 甲 in a patrol car and take him to the police box, 甲 kicked P in the abdomen in order to escape, thereby inflicting an injury requiring 2 weeks of treatment. Which of the following explanations is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedent)
A: Since 甲 was once arrested by X but was at a stage where physical custody had not yet been secured with certainty, and, in order to avoid the state of arrest, he struck X's face several times with his fist and inflicted injury, 甲 is liable for the offense of robbery resulting in injury.
B: If 甲 had inflicted violence on X to the extent that resistance would be difficult, but had not caused injury, 甲 is liable for attempted quasi-robbery.
C: P's arrest of 甲 cannot be regarded as a lawful arrest of a flagrant offender.
D: The injury inflicted on P by 甲 during the course of resisting in order to avoid arrest constitutes self-defense, and unlawfulness is excluded.
E: If 甲, at the first trial date, when the prosecutor questions him regarding the charged facts, states that all of the charged facts are true, then even if he later denies criminal intent or the charged facts when defense counsel questions him, the charged facts may be adjudicated under the simplified trial procedure.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2004DO5074]": "1. The purport of punishing larceny as quasi-robbery under Article 335 of the Criminal Act, when the thief uses force or intimidation for the purpose of resisting the recovery of property, evading arrest, or destroying traces of the crime, as if it were robbery, is that robbery and quasi-robbery are, in substance, equally unlawful, with only a temporal difference in sequence between the taking of property and the assault or intimidation that constitute the elements of robbery and quasi-robbery.\\nTherefore, just as a person who attempted to take property by means of assault or intimidation against the victim but failed to achieve that purpose is punished for attempted robbery, it is also reasonable to punish, by analogy to attempted robbery, a person who, even in the case of an attempted larcenist, used force or intimidation. If, despite the fact that robbery is consummated only when property is forcibly taken, in the case of quasi-robbery consummation and attempt are determined on the basis of assault or intimidation, then even in a case where property was not stolen and only assault or intimidation was used, the offender would be punished as having consummated quasi-robbery, thereby creating an imbalance with attempted robbery.\\nTaking into comprehensive consideration the legislative purpose of quasi-robbery as above, and the balance with robbery, it is appropriate to view the issue of whether quasi-robbery has been consummated by reference to whether the act of larceny has been consummated.\\nAccordingly, Supreme Court Decisions dated 1964. 11. 20., 64DO504, and 1969. 10. 23., 69DO1353, which held, to the contrary, that where an attempted larcenist used force in order to evade arrest, it could not be regarded as attempted quasi-robbery, are hereby overruled to the extent that they conflict with the foregoing legal principle.\\n\\n2. According to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, upon comprehensively considering the evidence admitted by it, found the following facts: while the Defendant and a person not party to the prosecution were searching for a place for the purpose of jointly stealing liquor, they arrived at a bar operated by Victim 1 on the second floor of a five-story building located at 522-24, Bujeon 2-dong, Busanjin-gu, Busan, at around 06:30 on 2003. 12. 9.; the person not party to the prosecution kept watch between the first and second floor stairs while maintaining contact with the Defendant by walkie-talkie; the Defendant pried open the lock of the bar and entered, and while placing 45 bottles of liquor worth KRW 1,622,000 in total market value, which were on display in the bar, into three baskets prepared in advance, upon regarding suspicious the person not party to the prosecution who was wandering about on the stairs, and upon hearing the sound of Victim 2, Lee Yoon-ryong, an employee of the bar, returning to the bar, the Defendant left the liquor as it was, opened the entrance door, and came out; and when Victim 2, etc. caught the Defendant, the Defendant, for the purpose of evading arrest, assaulted them, including by biting the right hand of the victim holding the Defendant by the neck. Based on these findings, the court below found the Defendant guilty of attempted quasi-robbery and punished him accordingly.\\nIn light of the legal principle set forth above, the foregoing determination of the court below is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of legal principles as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\nAccordingly, the appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as stated in the Disposition. In relation to this judgment, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, except for the separate opinions of Supreme Court Justices Yoon Jae-sik, Kang Shin-wook, and Koh Hyun-cheol, and the dissenting opinion of Supreme Court Justice Yoo Ji-dam.\\n\\n3. The separate opinion of Supreme Court Justices Yoon Jae-sik, Kang Shin-wook, and Koh Hyun-cheol is as follows.\\nAs in this case, we agree with the majority opinion in that where an attempted larcenist uses force or intimidation for the purpose of evading arrest, etc., he or she cannot be punished as a consummated offender of quasi-robbery. However, we cannot agree with the majority opinion’s view that the issue of whether quasi-robbery has been consummated must be determined solely on the basis of whether the act of larceny has been consummated.\\nQuasi-robbery prescribed in Article 335 of the Criminal Act is an offense that is constituted when a thief uses force or intimidation for the purpose of resisting the recovery of property, evading arrest, or destroying traces of the crime; thus, in quasi-robbery, the subject of the act is the thief (including an attempted offender), but the act constituting the elements of the offense should be regarded as assault or intimidation.\\nHowever, assault or intimidation in quasi-robbery, in balancing it with ordinary robbery, is required to be to such a degree that it is generally and objectively capable of suppressing a person’s resistance (see Supreme Court Decisions dated 1981. 3. 24., 81DO409, and 1990. 4. 24., 90DO193, etc.), and therefore the execution of quasi-robbery should be deemed to have commenced when force or intimidation, generally and objectively, sufficient to suppress a person’s resistance, has begun.\\nFurthermore, Article 342 of the Criminal Act provides that an attempt to commit the offense under Article 335 shall be punished; and Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act provides that where the execution of a crime has been commenced but the act has not been completed, or the result has not occurred, the offender shall be punished as an attempted offender. Therefore, even in quasi-robbery, in principle, whether it has been consummated should be determined by circumstances after the commencement of execution. Accordingly, where a thief has begun force or intimidation generally and objectively sufficient to suppress a person’s resistance, but has not completed the act or the resulting consequence has not occurred, it should be understood that Articles 25, 335, and 342 of the Criminal Act provide for punishment of such conduct as attempted quasi-robbery.\\nAssault under Article 260(1) of the Criminal Act, which originally means “any unlawful attack, including the exercise of tangible force against a person’s body,” is not easily conceived as remaining at the stage of attempt; the Criminal Act also does not contain a provision punishing attempted assault. However, in the case of intimidation under Article 283(1) of the Criminal Act, which means “a notice of harm sufficient to cause fear in a person,” one may conceive of a case where such act remains at the stage of attempt, and Article 286 of the Criminal Act expressly provides for punishment of attempted intimidation. Moreover, as noted above, assault or intimidation in quasi-robbery, unlike the concepts of assault or intimidation under Article 260(1) and Article 283(1) of the Criminal Act, is required to be to such a degree that it generally and objectively suppresses a person’s resistance; thus, one can sufficiently conceive of a case where force or intimidation of such degree has begun but has not reached the other party, or, even if it has reached the other party, the other party’s resistance has not been suppressed at all. In such a case, it would in principle be appropriate to punish the conduct as attempted quasi-robbery. This is all the more so in light of the fact that, even where there was force or intimidation objectively sufficient to suppress the victim’s resistance, if the victim handed over property not because his or her will to resist had been suppressed at all, but merely out of annoyance or compassion, such conduct should likewise be punished as attempted robbery rather than as consummated robbery.\\nHowever, Article 335 of the Criminal Act is a provision intended to impose heavier punishment, by analogy to robbery, on the basis that the conduct of a thief using force or intimidation at the opportunity of theft for purposes such as resisting the recovery of property, in its manner, has substantive unlawfulness that may appear similar to robbery, where force or intimidation is used as a means of taking property (see Supreme Court en banc Decision dated 1973. 11. 13., 73DO1553), and when the various grounds advanced by the majority opinion are taken together, it is also appropriate to recognize attempted quasi-robbery not only on the basis of the force or intimidation itself, but also to regard the case where the act of larceny remains at the stage of attempt as attempted quasi-robbery, thereby maintaining balance with attempted robbery.\\nTherefore, if either the force or intimidation act or the act of larceny remains at the stage of attempt, it should be regarded as falling under attempted quasi-robbery. Since the majority opinion relies solely on whether the act of larceny has been consummated, it cannot be agreed with because it entirely excludes the principled cases that should be punished as attempted quasi-robbery; thus, we state this separate opinion.\\n\\n4. The dissenting opinion of Supreme Court Justice Yoo Ji-dam is as follows.\\n\\na. The majority opinion states that, taking comprehensive account of the legislative purpose of quasi-robbery and the balance with robbery, it is appropriate to determine whether quasi-robbery has been consummated by reference to whether the act of larceny has been consummated, and that prior Supreme Court decisions contrary to this view should be changed.\\nHowever, this view is necessarily seen as stemming from a misapprehension of the nature of quasi-robbery and the legal principles concerning attempted offenses, and therefore cannot be agreed with.\\n\\nb. The majority opinion takes as its main ground that the purpose of Article 335 of the Criminal Act, which provides that where a thief uses force or intimidation for the purpose of resisting the recovery of property, evading arrest, or destroying traces of the crime, punishment shall be imposed according to the examples of robbery, is that robbery and quasi-robbery are, in substance, equally unlawful, with only a temporal difference in sequence between the taking of property and the assault or intimidation that constitute the elements of robbery and quasi-robbery.\\nHowever, quasi-robbery under Article 335 of the Criminal Act is an independent offense punished, as a matter of criminal policy, like robbery, due to the dangerousness of the act, and it includes, in addition to force or intimidation for the purpose of resisting the recovery of property, for which identity of illegality with robbery can be recognized, force or intimidation for the purpose of evading arrest or destroying traces of the crime, for which such identity cannot be recognized; therefore, robbery and quasi-robbery should be regarded as differing in their purpose and essence.\\nAnd although the majority opinion states that, in robbery, consummation occurs only when property has been forcibly taken, if an attempted larcenist uses force or intimidation for the purpose of resisting the recovery of property, then punishment as a consummated quasi-robbery, identical to consummated robbery, would not be balanced, it cannot be concluded that even where an attempted larcenist uses force or intimidation to such an extent as to suppress a person’s resistance for a certain purpose, the substantive unlawfulness is the same as robbery, and that punishing it in the same manner as consummated robbery is necessarily unreasonable in criminal policy or unbalanced. The fact that larceny remained at the stage of attempt can be taken into account as a favorable circumstance at the sentencing stage, thereby largely eliminating the imbalance feared by the majority opinion. In this respect, the grounds advanced by the majority opinion are doubtful in validity.\\nFurthermore, in quasi-robbery, the subject of the act is “larceny,” and the constitutive act is “using force or intimidation for the purpose of resisting the recovery of property, evading arrest, or destroying traces of the crime.” Meanwhile, as can be seen from Article 25(1) of the Criminal Act, which provides that “where the execution of a crime has been commenced but the act has not been completed, or the result has not occurred, the offender shall be punished as an attempted offender,” the criterion for distinguishing consummated from attempted offenses is whether the crime has been completed, that is, whether the constitutive act has been completed. Therefore, although the subject of quasi-robbery is larceny, and this includes not only consummated larceny but also attempt punishable under criminal law, it accords with the text of the statutory provisions and the legal principles of attempt doctrine to interpret the distinction between consummated and attempted quasi-robbery as depending on whether the constitutive act, namely assault or intimidation, has been completed.\\nUltimately, not only do the grounds advanced by the majority opinion lack rationality, but even if the imbalance alleged by it were recognized, it is a matter to be resolved at the sentencing stage; and if there is an imbalance that cannot be resolved at the sentencing stage, it is a matter to be resolved legislatively, for example by lowering the statutory penalty for quasi-robbery or by limiting the subject of quasi-robbery to completed larceny by excluding attempted larceny from the subject of quasi-robbery. The majority opinion’s attempt to resolve this by interpretation of Article 335 of the Criminal Act must be regarded not only as impermissible under textual interpretation of the statutory provision, but also as contrary to the essence of quasi-robbery and the legal principles of attempted offenses.\\n\\nc. For the foregoing reasons, I cannot agree with the majority opinion, and the Supreme Court decisions that the majority opinion states should be changed should remain as they are."}

{"[2007DO1249]": "We determine the grounds for final appeal.\\nThe expression “a person immediately after the commission of a crime,” as prescribed in Article 211 of the Criminal Procedure Act as a flagrant offender, refers to a case in which, from the standpoint of the person making the arrest, it is manifest that the person is the offender immediately after the completion of the criminal act; in light of the fact that the above provision, in paragraph (1), while prescribing a flagrant offender in the original sense, treats “a person immediately after the commission of a crime” as a flagrant offender in the same manner as “a person in the course of committing a crime,” and separately provides, in paragraph (2), for quasi-flagrant offenders deemed to be flagrant offenders, the phrase “immediately after the completion of the act of committing a crime” should be construed as meaning the moment of completion of the criminal act or a temporal stage very closely contiguous thereto, and thus a person may be regarded as a flagrant offender only where, in terms of time and place, it is recognized that clear evidence exists that the person subjected to arrest is the offender who has just committed the crime (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 91DO1314 rendered on September 24, 1991).\\nExamining the foregoing legal principle and the record, the court below, after recognizing the facts as stated in its reasoning, held that the arrest of the Defendant as a flagrant offender for drunk driving, made by Senior Police Officer Nonparty of the Cheongjeon Police Substation of Jecheon Police Station, who had been dispatched after receiving a report, solely on the ground that the Defendant, who was sitting by the roadside at a point more than 40 minutes after he had finished drunk driving, smelled of alcohol, was carried out in a state where it cannot be said that clear evidence existed as to the point that the Defendant was the offender who had just committed drunk driving, and therefore cannot be regarded as a lawful performance of official duties, and that the subsequent request to the Defendant to undergo a breath alcohol test likewise did not satisfy procedural legality, and the investigative act against the Defendant also cannot be regarded as a lawful act of official duty performance; accordingly, the court below’s action of acquitting the Defendant on the facts charged in this case is justifiable and persuasive, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality such as an erroneous finding of facts due to violation of the rules of evidence, misapprehension of legal principles, or omission of judgment, as alleged in the grounds of final appeal.\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices concerned."}

question:
Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (X) concerning the following case? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)

(1) Party A and Party B conspired to commit fraudulent gambling, and Party A, around 2024. 1. 1., in a motel room, lured A, B, and C, who had not previously met one another, into playing so-called 'Seotda' gambling together. Party A, in order to conceal the fraudulent gambling, played normally for a while, then switched to Hwatu cards specially marked with fluorescent material brought by Party B, and, after hearing from Party B, who was looking at the monitor screen, the Hwatu cards of A, B, and C, gambled and received from them a total of 5,000,000 won in gambling stakes.
(2) Party C, around 2024. 1. 2., while gambling so-called 'Seotda' with A, B, and C in a motel room, threatened A, B, and C by saying, "If you do not give me money, I will report you for the gambling offense and make sure you are punished to the end," and thereby received 5,000,000 won by transfer from them.

(a) In (1), the portion in which Party A played normally for a while in order to conceal the fraudulent gambling is also included in the act of execution of the fraud offense.
(b) In (1), because there was one act of deception, a single fraud offense against A, B, and C is established in the aggregate.
(c) In (2), Party C is guilty only of extortion.
(d) If, in (2), Party C was issued a summary order on 2023. 12. 29. imposing a fine of 5,000,000 won for the habitual gambling offense based on the same habitual propensity, the above summary order was served on Party C on 2024. 1. 15. and became final on 2024. 1. 23., the res judicata effect of the above final summary order extends to the gambling offense in (2).
(e) If Party D, who had a habitual propensity for gambling, aided and abetted the fraudulent gambling offense committed by Party A and Party B in (1), it constitutes the offense of aiding and abetting habitual gambling.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2010DO9330]": "The grounds of appeal are examined (each supplemental statement of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal shall be considered only within the scope of supplementing the same).\\n\\n1. Regarding Ground of Appeal No. 1\\n\\na. Gambling means that two or more persons stake property with one another and determine the gain or loss of such property by chance victory or defeat; therefore, where, as in so-called fraudulent gambling, one of the parties to the gambling controls the outcome of victory or defeat by means of fraud, the element of chance inherent in gambling is lacking, so only the offense of fraud is constituted and the offense of gambling is not constituted (see Supreme Court Decision 4293HYEONGSANG743, rendered on 1960. 11. 16.). Meanwhile, because the offense of fraud is deemed to have entered upon execution when deceptive conduct is initiated with intent to obtain property unlawfully, even in fraudulent gambling, where a person who seeks to obtain the gambling stakes by fraudulent means begins deceptive conduct, such as by inducing the other party to participate in gambling, it should be deemed that the execution has commenced.\\n\\nb. According to the facts determined by the court below and the evidence it adopted, the Defendant conspired with the lower court co-defendants 1, 2, and 3 around 2010. 2. 17. to obtain money by means of fraudulent gambling; accordingly, the said lower court co-defendants 2 and 3 secretly installed a camera on the fire detector on the ceiling in Room 906 of Hole In One Motel at 373-2 Myeongcheon-dong, Boryeong-si around 16:00 on 2010. 2. 18., and installed a monitor in Room 707 of Aria Motel opposite the said motel; the lower court co-defendant 1 contacted Victims Nonparties 1 and 2, induced them by inviting them to gamble, and brought them to the said Room 906 of Hole In One Motel, and Nonparty 2, who did not know the above facts, recommended gambling to Victim Nonparty 3 and brought him to the said motel; around 20:00 on the same day, the Defendant and the lower court co-defendant 1 went to the said Room 906 of Hole In One Motel wearing a receiver and an earpiece and carrying Hwatu cards specially marked with fluorescent material, and gambled with the victims in the so-called “Seotda”; and while engaging in the above gambling, the Defendant and the lower court co-defendant 1 played a normal game from around 21:20 to around 22:00 in order to conceal the fraudulent gambling, but from after around 22:00, when the Hwatu cards brought by the lower court co-defendant 1 were changed, until around 02:10 the next day, they controlled the outcome of the gambling by hearing through the receiver the victims’ Hwatu hands informed to them by looking at the monitor screen received through the camera secretly installed by the lower court co-defendant 2, and thus received the gambling stakes from the victims.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, examining the above factual relationship, the Defendant, etc. had already commenced the execution of the offense of fraud when they had prepared what was necessary for fraudulent gambling and, with such intent, induced the victims to participate in gambling, or at the latest when the victims, unaware of the circumstances, participated in the gambling; therefore, even if the Defendant, etc. thereafter played normal gambling for some time in order to conceal the fraudulent gambling, such conduct is included in the act of execution of the offense of fraud, so that, as to the Defendant, only the offense of fraud against the victims is constituted, and the offense of gambling is not separately constituted.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below, contrary thereto, determined that, in addition to the offense of fraud against the victims, the offense of gambling separately constituted, and recognized it as guilty; therefore, the judgment below contains an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the timing of commencement of execution in fraudulent gambling.\\n\\n2. Regarding Ground of Appeal No. 2\\n\\nWhere, by one deceptive act, property is separately obtained from multiple victims, several offenses of fraud are constituted for each victim, and they are to be regarded as standing in a relation of ideal concurrence.\\n\\nAccordingly, examining the facts stated above in light of the foregoing legal principles, the act by the Defendant, etc. of luring the victims and, through fraudulent gambling, obtaining the gambling stakes should, in social concept, be evaluated as one act; therefore, each offense of fraud against the victims should be regarded as being in a relation of ideal concurrence.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, contrary thereto, regarded the above offenses as being in a relation of real concurrence and imposed aggravated punishment for concurrent offenses pursuant to the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act; thus, the judgment below contains an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the number of offenses of fraud. Meanwhile, Supreme Court Decision 89DO582, rendered on 1989. 6. 13., cited by the judgment below, concerns a case in which deceptive acts were separately committed against multiple victims, and thus is not appropriate to invoke in this case.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the portion of the judgment below concerning the Defendant is reversed, and this portion of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and the judgment is rendered as ordered by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2010DO9330]": "The grounds for appeal are examined (and each supplemental statement of grounds for appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal is examined only to the extent that it supplements the grounds).\\n\\n1. Regarding Ground 1 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\na. Gambling means that two or more persons mutually put property at stake and determine the gain or loss of that property according to a fortuitous outcome of victory or defeat; therefore, in a case of so-called fraudulent gambling, where one party to the gambling controls the outcome of victory or defeat by means of fraud, the element of chance inherent in gambling is lacking, so only the offense of fraud is established and the offense of gambling is not established (see Supreme Court Decision dated 1960. 11. 16., Case 4293HYEONGSANG743). On the other hand, since the offense of fraud should be deemed to have commenced execution when a deceptive act is initiated with intent to obtain unlawful gain, in fraudulent gambling as well, when a person who intends to obtain gambling stakes by fraudulent means initiates a deceptive act, such as inducing the other party to participate in the gambling, there should be deemed to have been commencement of execution.\\n\\nb. According to the facts found by the court below and the evidence adopted by it, the Defendant conspired with Co-Defendants 1, 2, and 3 in the court below around 2010. 2. 17. to obtain money by means of fraudulent gambling; accordingly, Co-Defendants 2 and 3 in the court below secretly installed a camera in a fire detector on the ceiling in Room 906 of the All-in-One Motel at 373-2, Myeongcheon-dong, Boryeong-si around 16:00 on 2010. 2. 18., and installed a monitor in Room 707 of the Aria Motel located across from the said motel; Co-Defendant 1 in the court below contacted Victims Non-Indicted Persons 1 and 2 and lured them by inviting them to gamble, causing them to come to Room 906 of the said All-in-One Motel, and Non-Indicted Person 2, who did not know the foregoing facts, invited Victim Non-Indicted Person 3 to gamble, causing him to come to the said motel; around 20:00 on the same day, the Defendant and Co-Defendant 1 in the court below went to Room 906 of the said All-in-One Motel wearing a receiver and receiver, and carrying playing cards specially marked with fluorescent material, and gambled with the victims in the so-called “Seotda” game; in the course of such gambling, from around 21:20 to around 22:00, the Defendant and Co-Defendant 1 in the court below engaged in normal gambling in order to conceal the fraudulent gambling, but after 22:00, after exchanging the playing cards brought by Co-Defendant 1 in the court below, until 02:10 the next day, they controlled the outcome of the gambling by listening through the receiver to the victims’ playing-card hands as transmitted through the monitor screen, which was secretly receiving images from the camera secretly installed by Co-Defendant 2 in the court below, and thereby received gambling stakes from the victims.\\n\\nExamining the above factual relations in light of the legal principles set forth above, the Defendant, etc. had already commenced execution of fraud when they had made the preparations necessary for fraudulent gambling and induced the victims to participate in the gambling with such intent, or at the latest when the victims, unaware of the circumstances, participated in the gambling; therefore, even if the Defendant, etc. thereafter engaged in some normal gambling in order to conceal the fraudulent gambling, such conduct would be included in the acts constituting execution of fraud, so that as to the Defendant, only the offense of fraud against the victims is established and no separate offense of gambling is established.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below, contrary to the above, determined that, in addition to the offense of fraud against the victims, the offense of gambling was separately established and found it guilty thereof; accordingly, the judgment below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles regarding the time of commencement of execution in fraudulent gambling.\\n\\n2. Regarding Ground 2 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nWhere property is obtained from multiple victims by a single deceptive act, multiple offenses of fraud are established for each victim, and they should be deemed to stand in a relation of ideal concurrence.\\n\\nExamining the foregoing factual relations in light of the above legal principles, the act by which the Defendant, etc. lured the victims and obtained gambling stakes by engaging in fraudulent gambling should reasonably be evaluated as a single act in social norms; accordingly, each offense of fraud against the victims should be deemed to stand in a relation of ideal concurrence.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below, contrary to the above, regarded the said offenses as standing in a relation of real concurrence and enhanced the punishment for concurrent offenses pursuant to the first sentence of Article 37 of the Criminal Act; accordingly, the judgment below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the number of offenses of fraud. Meanwhile, the Supreme Court Decision dated 1989. 6. 13., Case 89DO582, cited by the judgment below concerns a case in which deceptive acts were separately committed against multiple victims, and thus is not appropriate for invocation in this case.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the part of the judgment below concerning the Defendant is reversed and the case concerning that part is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2014DO212]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Regarding the Defendant’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nThe argument to the effect that the judgment of the court below contains a violation of law in that it erred in fact-finding concerning the offense of violation of the Act on the Punishment of Violent Acts, etc. (joint extortion) is one that the Defendant now raises for the first time in the grounds for appeal, without having made it a ground of appeal or having had the court below consider it ex officio, and therefore cannot constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\nAlso, the argument to the effect that the judgment of the court below contains a violation of law in that it erred in the interpretation of law concerning the offense of gambling is one that challenges the portion the court below found not guilty, and therefore cannot constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\nAnd the argument to the effect that the judgment of the court below contains a violation of law in that it deviated from the limits of discretionary sentencing ultimately amounts to an argument of inappropriate sentencing. However, according to Article 383, Item 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, an appeal on the ground of inappropriate sentencing is permitted only in cases in which death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or confinement for not less than 10 years has been imposed. Accordingly, in this case, in which a sentence lighter than that was imposed on the Defendant, the argument that the sentencing is improper likewise cannot constitute a lawful ground for appeal.\\n\\n2. Regarding the Prosecutor’s grounds for appeal\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below, with respect to the gambling count among the facts charged in this case, found the Defendant not guilty, on the grounds stated in its opinion, by determining that the Defendant’s gambling conduct was merely an instrumental role for the commission of the joint extortion offense and therefore did not separately constitute the offense of gambling.\\n\\nHowever, the offense of extortion and the offense of gambling differ in their constitutive elements and protected legal interests, and the commission of gambling is not generally or typically accompanied by the establishment of extortion. Nor can it be said that gambling conduct is so slight as not to be separately considered in comparison with extortion. Therefore, even if gambling conduct became the means of extortion, it cannot be said that such gambling conduct is absorbed into extortion and does not constitute a separate offense.\\n\\nNevertheless, the court below found that the offense of gambling does not separately constitute an offense apart from the offense of violation of the Act on the Punishment of Violent Acts, etc. (joint extortion), and thus rendered a verdict of not guilty. Accordingly, the judgment of the court below contains a violation of law that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the concurrence of the offense of gambling and the offense of violation of the Act on the Punishment of Violent Acts, etc. (joint extortion). The Prosecutor’s ground for appeal pointing out this point is meritorious.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the portion of the judgment of the court below concerning the offense of gambling must be quashed. Although, as stated above, the Defendant’s appeal regarding the guilty portion is without merit, the offense found guilty and the offense found not guilty by the court below are in a relationship of concurrent offenses under the former part of Article 37 of the Criminal Act. Accordingly, the entire judgment of the court below is quashed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged as per the Disposition, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[84DO1129]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below, the court below found that the Defendant, at around 19:30 on 1983.7.7., got into an altercation with the victim at Ulsan Daepo Restaurant located in Hwarong-dong, Yeongcheon City, and inflicted bodily injury on him; that, as a result, on 1983.8.18, the Daegu District Court issued a summary order imposing a fine of 300,000 won, and that summary order became final and conclusive on 9.17 of the same year due to the expiration of the period for requesting a formal trial; and that the act of assault charged in this case is a crime arising from the manifestation of the Defendant’s violent habituality, and further found that the injurious act under the summary order dated 1983.8.18 is also a habitual crime arising from the manifestation of the Defendant’s violent habituality, and therefore held that the assault in this case and the said injury, taken together in substance, constitute one offense of violation of Article 2(1) of the Act on the Punishment of Violent Acts, etc.; and, on the ground that the said summary order became final and conclusive on 1983.9.17 due to the expiration of the period for requesting a formal trial, concluded that the order must have been served on the prosecutor and the Defendant by no later than 1983.9.9, and thus held that the effect of the said summary order also extends to the assault act in this case committed before such service, and rendered a judgment of dismissal on the ground that the facts charged in this case fall under a case where there exists a final judgment.\\n\\nIf there has been a final judgment of conviction as to part of an offense that stands in the relation of a comprehensive single offense, such as a habitual offense, the effect of that final judgment extends to the entirety of the remaining acts that stand in the relation of a comprehensive single offense; however, the temporal scope of the res judicata effect of that judgment, namely, up to what point in time the res judicata effect extends with respect to the facts of crime, is determined by taking as the reference point in time the time of pronouncement of the judgment, which is the latest point in time at which fact-finding is possible. Since a summary order, unlike a judgment procedure, is served upon the prosecutor and the Defendant as a written judgment and is not separately pronounced, there may be room for debate as to whether, in the case of a summary order, the temporal scope of its res judicata effect should be determined based on the time of service of the summary order or on the time of its issuance; however, there is no reason to distinguish the temporal scope of res judicata effect in a summary order from that in a judgment procedure, and therefore this Court’s view is that, even in the case of a summary order, the time of issuance should be the standard. (See Supreme Court Decisions 79DO82, decided on 1979.2.27; 81DO1437, decided on 1981.6.23. Although the text of Supreme Court Decision 83DO939, decided on 1983.6.14, cited by the court below uses the expression “notice,” the tenor of the entire text shows that this notice appears to mean issuance, and thus it is the same in purport as the above decisions.)\\n\\nAccordingly, the facts constituting the offense charged in this case are plainly an act committed after the issuance of the above summary order on 1983.8.18, and are thus not subject to the res judicata effect of the above summary order; nevertheless, contrary to the precedents of this Court, the court below held that the temporal scope of the res judicata effect of the above summary order is 1983.9.9, the date of its notice, and that the facts charged in this case on 1983.9.7, which is prior thereto, fall under a case where there already exists a final judgment pursuant to the above summary order. In so doing, the court below erred in law by misapprehending the legal principle concerning the temporal scope of the res judicata effect of a summary order, and the judgment cannot escape reversal. Accordingly, the appeal is well-founded.\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the Collegiate Division of the Daejeon District Court. The concurrence of the participating Justices having been reached, the judgment is rendered as set forth in the disposition."}

question: A was in urgent need of money and agreed to sell the apartment he owned, with a market value of 700 million won, to D for 600 million won, and received a total of 150 million won from D as the down payment and intermediate payment. Upon hearing this, B suggested to A, "It seems you sold the apartment too cheaply, and since my friend C says that he will purchase it at market price, sell it to C." After repeatedly persuading him, A sold the above apartment to C and completed the transfer registration of ownership. Which of the following statements is correct? (Assume that the market value of the above apartment did not change, and if there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Where a seller who owes a duty to complete transfer registration of ownership of real property has completed transfer registration to another person, only if there are no special circumstances under which the seller can recover the registration relating to ownership of the real property and complete transfer registration to the buyer does the duty to complete transfer registration of ownership to the buyer enter into a state of impossibility of performance; accordingly, absent such circumstances, merely having A complete transfer registration to C does not amount to consummation of the crime of breach of trust.
B: If, before the above sale contract between A and D was concluded, there had already been established on the above apartment a mortgage registration in favor of mortgagee A (maximum secured amount of 170 million won, secured claim amount of 150 million won) and a registration of provisional attachment over real property in favor of creditor B (claimed amount of 50 million won, preserved claim amount of 30 million won), Article 3(1) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes does not apply.
C: Since B was not in the position of a person administering another's affairs in relation to D, even if he actively participated in A's offense, he does not bear criminal liability as a co-principal of breach of trust.
D: If C purchased the above apartment without knowing the fact of the above sale contract between A and D, the statement protocol prepared by a judicial police officer concerning C has no evidentiary admissibility if A denies its contents.
E: If A was prosecuted for the offense of Violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (Breach of Trust) and, upon the pronouncement of a guilty judgment, filed an appeal, the appellate court must appoint state-appointed counsel when A has no defense counsel and notify A and that state-appointed counsel of the receipt of the case record; thereafter, even if the appellate court cancels the appointment of the state-appointed counsel because A appoints privately retained counsel, it need not notify the privately retained counsel again of the receipt of the case record, and in that event the period for submitting a statement of grounds for appeal must be calculated from the date on which the state-appointed counsel or A received the notice of receipt of the case record.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2005DO7288]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding Ground 1 of the grounds for final appeal\\n\\nIn light of the record, the lower court’s determination, based on the evidence it adopted and examined, recognizing that the Defendant had no agreement, as stated in the judgment below, to obtain loans secured by each parcel of land at issue in this case from the First Bank Seomyeon Branch and, despite lacking the ability to pay the balance, deceived the victims as if he had such agreement or ability, is justified and acceptable, and there is no illegality such as a violation of the rules of evidence, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n2. Regarding Ground 2 of the grounds for final appeal\\n\\na. Article 3(1) of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Economic Crimes (hereinafter referred to as the “Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act”) provides: “A person who commits the offense of Articles 347 (Fraud), 350 (Extortion), 351 (limited to habitual offenders under Articles 347 and 350), 355 (Embezzlement and Breach of Trust), or 356 (Embezzlement and Breach of Trust in the course of business) of the Criminal Act shall, where the value of the property or pecuniary benefit acquired or caused to be acquired by a third party through such criminal act (hereinafter referred to as the ‘gain amount’) is not less than 500 million won, be punished according to the following classification.” Subparagraph 1 thereof provides: “Where the gain amount is not less than 5 billion won, the person shall be punished by imprisonment for life or imprisonment for not less than 5 years,” and subparagraph 2 provides: “Where the gain amount is not less than 500 million won but less than 5 billion won, the person shall be punished by imprisonment with labor for a fixed term of not less than 3 years.” Meanwhile, paragraph 2 of the same Article provides: “In the case under paragraph 1, a fine not exceeding the amount equivalent to the gain amount may be concurrently imposed.” In comparing these provisions with the provisions of Article 347 of the Criminal Act concerning the offense of simple fraud, the offense of fraud under Article 347 of the Criminal Act is established by deceiving a person to receive the delivery of property or to acquire pecuniary benefits (paragraph 1), or by causing a third party to receive the delivery of property or to acquire pecuniary benefits (paragraph 2), and unlike that offense, the amount of the property or pecuniary benefit received is not at issue. By contrast, in the offense of violating Article 3 of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act by fraud, the value of the property or pecuniary benefit obtained by fraud being at least 500 million won or at least 5 billion won constitutes part of the elements of the offense, and the punishment for that offense is also substantially aggravated according to that value. Therefore, in applying this provision, care must be taken so that the principle of proportionality between crime and punishment, namely that an appropriate balance must be achieved between crime and punishment by strictly and carefully calculating the value of the property or pecuniary benefit obtained by fraud, and the principle of culpability, namely that punishment must be based on responsibility and proportionate to that responsibility, are not undermined.\\n\\nTherefore, where a person deceives another and thereby obtains ownership of real estate, or causes a third party to obtain such ownership, and thereby acquires it by fraud, in calculating the value of such real estate on the premise that Article 3 of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act applies, if the real estate is free of any burden, the amount equivalent to the market value of the real estate in that state may be regarded as the value thereof. However, where a registration of creation of a mortgage has been completed with respect to the real estate, or attachment or provisional attachment, etc. has been effected, unless special circumstances exist, the actual exchange value obtained by subtracting from the amount equivalent to the market value of the real estate in a state free of any burden the amount of the secured claim within the maximum secured amount of the mortgage, the amount of the execution claim subject to attachment, and the amount of the preserved claim within the scope of the claim subject to provisional attachment, etc., should be regarded as the value of the real estate.\\n\\nBy contrast, the view reflected in Supreme Court Decision 2003DO1859, decided September 5, 2003, and the like, which held that even if a registration of attachment had been made with respect to real estate obtained by fraud, such circumstance does not constitute a reason to evaluate the gain obtained by the Defendant at a reduced amount below the market value of the real estate, is hereby modified to the extent it conflicts with the foregoing legal principles.\\n\\nb. In light of the foregoing legal principles and the record, the market value of each parcel of land at issue in this case in a state free of any burden is 1.646 billion won, and the maximum secured amount of the mortgage established on each of the above parcels of land is 1.02 billion won. Since the amount of the secured claim exceeds this amount, the lower court’s action, in calculating the value of each parcel of land at issue in this case obtained by fraud by the Defendant, deducting from the market value of each parcel of land the maximum secured amount of the mortgage rather than the amount of the secured claim, and regarding the remaining 626 million won as the value thereof, and applying Article 3(1)2 of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act, is proper, and there is no illegality such as an error of law as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as stated in the order. In this judgment, apart from the separate opinions of Justices Kim Yong-dam, Kim Hwang-sik, and Ahn Dae-hee regarding the determination on Ground 2 of the grounds for final appeal, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there is a supplementary opinion to the majority opinion by Justice Kim Neung-hwan.\\n\\n4. The separate opinions of Justices Kim Yong-dam, Kim Hwang-sik, and Ahn Dae-hee are as follows.\\n\\na. With respect to the point that, in the offense of violating the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act by fraud, the punishment for the offense is also substantially aggravated according to the value, and therefore, in applying the provision, an appropriate balance between crime and punishment must be achieved by strictly and carefully calculating the value of the property or pecuniary benefit obtained by fraud, we agree with the majority opinion.\\n\\nHowever, we cannot agree, for the following reasons, with the view that, in applying the offense of violating the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act by fraud, the value of real estate obtained by fraud should be regarded as the actual exchange value obtained by subtracting from the amount equivalent to the market value of the real estate in a state free of any burden the amount of the debt secured within the maximum secured amount of the mortgage, the amount of the execution claim subject to attachment, and the amount of the preserved claim within the scope of the claim subject to provisional attachment, etc.\\n\\nb. Regarding the calculation of the gain amount prescribed in Article 3(1) of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act by fraud, our Supreme Court has held that “even where part of the consideration has been paid, the amount obtained by fraud is not the difference obtained by deducting the consideration from the value of the property delivered by the victim, but the entirety of the property received” (see Supreme Court Decisions 2000DO1899, decided July 7, 2000; 2005DO5774, decided October 28, 2005; 2006DO7470, decided January 25, 2007, among others), and has also held that “the ‘gain amount’ prescribed in Article 3(1) of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act refers to the total value of the property or pecuniary benefit that became the object of unlawful acquisition, obtained through the criminal act listed therein or caused to be acquired by a third party, and whether such gain is ultimately realized or whether any conditions or burdens are attached thereto has no effect” (see Supreme Court Decision 90DO1815, decided October 16, 1990).\\n\\nFrom the standpoint of these precedents, where one obtains real estate by fraud while there is a mortgage established on it or attachment/provisional attachment has been effected, and promises to assume and repay the secured debt, etc., such promise may be regarded as merely a method of paying the consideration for the property obtained by fraud, or the mortgage, attachment, or provisional attachment may be regarded as a burden attached to the property obtained by fraud. Moreover, the ascertainment of the actual exchange value of the property obtained by fraud, that is, whether such gain will ultimately be realized, should still be interpreted, even in the offense of violating the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act by fraud, as not being an element of the offense but as a matter concerning sentencing. Therefore, the value of real estate on the premise that Article 3 of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act applies should ordinarily mean the market value of property commonly used, namely the objective market value of the real estate in a state free of any burden. Accordingly, Supreme Court Decision 2003DO1859, decided September 5, 2003, which held that even if a provisional seizure or pre-registration of attachment has been completed with respect to real estate obtained by fraud, this does not constitute a reason to evaluate the gain amount at a reduced amount below the objective market value of the real estate, should be maintained.\\n\\nHowever, although it appears that Article 3(1) of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act, by merely aggravating punishment according to the gain amount, is not without problems from a legislative policy standpoint, the majority opinion, which, in applying Article 3 of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act, regards the actual exchange value, which may be seen as the realization of the gain obtained by fraud, not as a matter concerning sentencing but as an element of the offense, cannot be said to be proper.\\n\\nc. In addition, if one takes the position, as in the majority opinion, that in applying Article 3 of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act, the actual exchange value of real estate obtained by fraud must be calculated, then if the secured debt under a mortgage, etc. existing at the time of the fraud is wholly or partially extinguished thereafter through repayment by the original debtor, etc., the actual exchange value of the real estate increases, and the question arises whether the applicable provision should be different depending on such post-fraud circumstances. Likewise, in cases where several real estate properties subject to common security are obtained by fraud, or where some of several real estate properties subject to a single attachment or provisional attachment are obtained by fraud, and in cases involving security rights other than mortgages or usufructuary rights, leasehold rights with opposability, provisional dispositions, pre-registrations, etc., it is difficult to present a clear standard as to how far, or to what extent, the scope of deduction should be limited. Ultimately, the majority opinion must be regarded as contrary to the principle of clarity, which forms part of the principle of legality in criminal law, and as bringing confusion into criminal procedure, and therefore as inappropriate.\\n\\nd. However, according to the record, on the premise that the Defendant’s amount obtained by fraud is the total objective market value of each parcel of land at issue in this case, the lower court allowed the Prosecutor’s motion to permit an amendment to the indictment, which specified as the gain amount only the amount obtained by deducting from the value of each parcel of land at issue the amount of the debt secured within the maximum secured amount of the mortgage, and, treating the amount so amended as the Defendant’s amount obtained by fraud, applied Article 3(1)2 of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act. This measure is proper, and the final appeal should therefore be dismissed. Thus, although we agree with the conclusion of the majority opinion to the same effect, we differ from the majority opinion in that, where the property obtained by fraud is real estate, the gain amount prescribed in Article 3 of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act should be regarded as the objective market value of that real estate.\\n\\n5. The supplementary opinion of Justice Kim Neung-hwan to the majority opinion is as follows.\\n\\na. As the majority opinion makes clear, in the offense of violating Article 3 of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act by fraud, the statutory punishment is expressly differentiated by the requirement that the value of the property or pecuniary benefit obtained by fraud under the Criminal Act be not less than 500 million won or not less than 5 billion won. Accordingly, the elements of the offense must be regarded as different from those of fraud under the Criminal Act. Nevertheless, the separate opinion’s view that, even in the offense of violating the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act by fraud, the question of the value of the property obtained by fraud is merely a matter concerning sentencing cannot be said to be proper.\\n\\nIf the amount of the property obtained by fraud is part of the elements of the offense, then the evaluation or calculation of that amount must be made by an objective and reasonable method. Yet, in light of actual transactions, the objective exchange value of real estate burdened by a mortgage, etc. and that of real estate free of such burdens cannot be identical. The majority opinion is to the effect that determining whether Article 3 of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act applies by calculating the objective exchange value of real estate that directly reflects such differences is consistent with the principle of proportionality between crime and punishment and the principle of culpability; it is not intended to approach the matter from the perspective of what consideration or counter-performance the offender has paid or will pay, or what actual gain he has obtained or will obtain.\\n\\nb. Supreme Court Decision 90DO1815, cited by the separate opinion, held with respect to the offense of violating the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act by extortion that “the gain amount obtained through the extortion offense must be calculated based on the time the offense is consummated, and any subsequent change in circumstances should not be considered.” This legal principle should likewise apply to the offense of violating the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act by fraud. Accordingly, once the offense has been consummated by obtaining real estate burdened by a mortgage, etc. through fraud, the objective exchange value at that time constitutes the value of the real estate, and the applicability of Article 3 of the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act should be determined on that basis; whether the mortgage, etc. was later extinguished through repayment, etc. is not a matter to be considered. Therefore, the separate opinion’s concern that, under the majority opinion, the applicable provision would need to be different in the event of such subsequent changes in circumstances reflects a misunderstanding of the purport of the majority opinion.\\n\\nc. With respect to the treatment of usufructuary rights or provisional dispositions or pre-registrations other than mortgages, as pointed out by the separate opinion, if the majority opinion is applied consistently, a provisional disposition or a pre-registration for the preservation of priority may be an obstacle to the disposition of real estate, but it is not a circumstance affecting exchange value, and therefore it need not be considered in calculating the value of the real estate. However, usufructuary rights such as superficies may, depending on the case, be factors affecting the exchange value of the real estate, and security pre-registrations, registered chonsegwon, lease relationships with opposability, etc. may, unless special circumstances exist, be treated in the same manner as mortgages. Under the majority opinion, in specific cases, evaluating and calculating the objective exchange value of real estate that is the object of fraud may not be a simple matter. Even so, the court, which bears responsibility for the proper operation of criminal justice procedure, has the unavoidable duty to endeavor to ascertain the value of real estate objectively and reasonably. If, despite such efforts, the value cannot be ascertained, the problem must be resolved according to the principle of burden of proof; it is not proper to tolerate a result in which the principle of proportionality between crime and punishment or the principle of culpability is undermined merely because calculating the value is difficult.\\n\\nIn the offense of violating the Special Economic Crimes Aggravated Punishment Act by fraud, which differentiates the statutory punishment according to the value of the property obtained by fraud, the separate opinion’s view that the actual exchange value of real estate obtained by fraud is merely a matter concerning sentencing, and not an element of the offense, is difficult to accept because it may result in excessive punishment contrary to the principle of proportionality between crime and punishment and the principle of culpability.\\n\\nThe foregoing sets forth my supplementary opinion to the majority opinion."}

{"[2015DO10651]": "The grounds for re-appeal (although the Defendant’s counsel filed a petition of final appeal against the lower court decision, the proper method of objection to the lower court decision is a re-appeal, so the above petition of final appeal shall be deemed a petition of re-appeal) are examined.\\n\\n1. Course of the case and issue\\na. The Re-appellant was convicted at the court of first instance and appealed, but did not state the grounds for appeal in the petition of appeal. On March 10, 2015, the lower court, in this case which is a compulsory defense case under Article 33(1) item 6 of the Criminal Procedure Act, appointed court-appointed counsel for the Defendant, notified the court-appointed counsel on the 12th of the same month, and notified the Re-appellant, who was the Defendant, on the 13th of the same month, of the appointment decision of court-appointed counsel and the fact of receipt of the case record.\\n\\nb. While the Re-appellant and the court-appointed counsel had not submitted a statement of grounds for appeal, the Re-appellant retained privately retained counsel on March 23, 2015. On the 24th of the same month, the lower court canceled the appointment decision of court-appointed counsel and did not notify the privately retained counsel of the receipt of the case record. The privately retained counsel submitted a statement of grounds for appeal to the lower court on May 21, 2015.\\n\\nc. On July 3, 2015, the lower court, by decision, dismissed the Re-appellant’s appeal pursuant to Article 361-4(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act. It gave reasons such as that the above statement of grounds for appeal was submitted more than one month after the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal was calculated from the date on which notice of receipt of the case record was given to the Re-appellant or the former court-appointed counsel, and that there were no grounds for ex officio review in the judgment of the court of first instance.\\n\\nd. The Re-appellant filed a re-appeal, arguing that the lower court should have served the notice of receipt of the case record again on the privately retained counsel and calculated the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal based on the date of service of that notice.\\n\\ne. This case is a compulsory defense case, and although the appellate court had already notified the Defendant and court-appointed counsel of the receipt of the case record, the Defendant and court-appointed counsel did not submit a statement of grounds for appeal, and during the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal, the Defendant retained privately retained counsel, whereupon the appointment of court-appointed counsel was canceled. The issue in this case is whether, in such a case, the newly retained privately retained counsel must again be notified of the receipt of the case record.\\n\\n2. Whether the privately retained counsel retained after notice of receipt of the case record to the Defendant and court-appointed counsel must again be notified of the receipt of the case record\\na. Since the Criminal Procedure Act provides that, where counsel has been retained before the appellate court gives notice of receipt of the case record to the Defendant, who is the appellant, the notice of receipt of the case record shall also be given to counsel (Article 361-2(2)), if counsel is retained after notice of receipt of the case record has been given to the Defendant, there is no need to give counsel the same notice again. The same applies where, in a compulsory defense case, the appellate court appoints court-appointed counsel and gives notice of receipt of the case record to the Defendant and his counsel, and thereafter the Defendant retains privately retained counsel, causing the appellate court to cancel the appointment of court-appointed counsel. In such a case, the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal shall be calculated from the date on which the court-appointed counsel or the Defendant received the notice of receipt of the case record (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006MO623 dated December 7, 2006).\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure provides that, if court-appointed counsel is changed for a reason not attributable to the Defendant within the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal, the notice of receipt of the case record must also be given to that court-appointed counsel; however, this provision cannot be extended to apply, or applied by analogy, to the case of newly retained privately retained counsel.\\n\\nThe reasons therefor are examined in detail below.\\n\\nb. Whether to impose on the appellant or counsel the duty to submit a statement of grounds for appeal within a certain period, or whether to dismiss the appeal by decision if it is not submitted within that period, is fundamentally a matter of legislative discretion for the legislator to determine in light of the structure and nature of criminal appellate proceedings, the characteristics of criminal justice procedure, and the like.\\n\\nThe Criminal Procedure Act grants the right of appeal to the parties to a criminal trial (Article 357), imposes the duty to file a statement of grounds for appeal (Article 361-3), and provides that if a statement of grounds for appeal is not filed within the prescribed period, the appeal shall be dismissed by a formal decision without a determination on the merits (Article 361-4(1)). This is intended to achieve a balanced allocation of judicial resources, together with the guarantee of the Defendant’s human rights, and to promote the speedy and smooth operation of appellate proceedings. If there were no disadvantage even though a party failed to observe the statutory period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal, the purpose of the system requiring the filing of such a statement—namely, to define the object of appellate review through the filing of the statement and to realize speedy and smooth appellate proceedings—would become meaningless. Although Article 361-4(1) above has the aspect of partially restricting the opportunity to receive appellate proceedings, in light of the purpose of the system requiring the filing of a statement of grounds for appeal, the public interest pursued by that provision, namely speedy and smooth operation of appellate proceedings, is by no means insignificant when compared with the private interest of remedying the parties’ rights (see Supreme Court Decision 2003CHOGI165 dated May 20, 2003; Supreme Court Decision 2005CHOGI316 dated December 5, 2005; Constitutional Court en banc decision 2003HEONBA34 dated March 31, 2005, etc.).\\n\\nc. Since the retention of privately retained counsel is effected by a private-law contract between the Defendant or other person entitled to retain counsel (Article 30 of the Criminal Procedure Act) and counsel, whereas the appointment of court-appointed counsel is an act of adjudication by the court, the two differ in nature.\\n\\nThe Criminal Procedure Act and the Rules of Criminal Procedure, in addition to the notice of receipt of the case record, also distinguish between privately retained counsel and court-appointed counsel and treat them differently. The court must appoint court-appointed counsel in certain cases ex officio or upon the Defendant’s request, etc. (Article 33 of the Criminal Procedure Act), and in a case in which court-appointed counsel has been appointed, the proceedings may not be opened without counsel, and if counsel does not appear, a new court-appointed counsel must be appointed ex officio (Articles 282, 283, and 370 of the Criminal Procedure Act). Even after court-appointed counsel has been appointed, the court is in charge of tasks such as cancellation of the appointment, permission to withdraw, and supervision (Articles 18 through 21 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure). This is because the State’s duty to guarantee the Defendant’s right to receive assistance of counsel includes not merely appointing court-appointed counsel in criminal proceedings but also, one step further, the responsibility to supervise the necessary work and take procedural measures so that the Defendant may receive actual assistance from court-appointed counsel (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc decision 2009MO1044 dated February 16, 2012).\\n\\nBy contrast, privately retained counsel acquires that status when the person entitled to retain counsel, such as the Defendant, concludes a mandate contract with counsel and directly retains the counsel, and the acts and scope of activities of privately retained counsel are determined according to the contents of the mandate contract. The State does not intervene at all in the retention and activities of such privately retained counsel, or in the relationship between the counsel and the person entitled to retain counsel. This is no different even in a compulsory defense case.\\n\\nd. Since the notice of receipt of the case record constitutes the starting point for the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal, the cases in which such notice must be given and its addressee must be clear. The Criminal Procedure Act and the Rules of Criminal Procedure specify the cases in which the appellate court must give notice of receipt of the case record, and with respect to privately retained counsel they provide only that such notice shall be given where counsel was retained before notice of receipt of the case record was given to the Defendant (Article 361-2(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act), and nowhere in the Criminal Procedure Act or the Rules of Criminal Procedure is it provided that the same notice must again be given to privately retained counsel retained after notice of receipt of the case record has already been given to the Defendant. By contrast, in addition to Article 361-2(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, Article 156-2 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure further provides circumstances in which notice of receipt of the case record must be given even if the court-appointed counsel was appointed after notice of receipt of the case record was given to the Defendant.\\n\\nArticle 361-2(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, which provides for notice of receipt of the case record to counsel, was newly enacted in 1961, when the system requiring the filing of a statement of grounds for appeal was introduced, and has remained in force to this day, whereas each paragraph of Article 156-2 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure, which provides for notice of receipt of the case record to court-appointed counsel, was newly enacted sequentially from 1996. Article 156-2(1) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure was newly enacted by Supreme Court Rule No. 1441 on December 3, 1996, with the purpose of promoting the speed of criminal proceedings and protecting the rights of defendants in appellate proceedings, and provides for the appointment of court-appointed counsel and the duty to give notice of receipt of the case record to that counsel in compulsory defense cases under Article 33(1) of the Act. Article 156-2(2) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure, newly enacted by Supreme Court Rule No. 2013 on March 23, 2006, provides that where a request for appointment of court-appointed counsel is made under Article 33(2) of the Act before the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal expires and court-appointed counsel is appointed, notice of receipt of the case record shall be given to that counsel; and paragraph (3) provides that where, after a decision appointing court-appointed counsel has been made pursuant to paragraphs (1) and (2), the appointment decision is canceled for a reason not attributable to the Defendant within the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal and a new court-appointed counsel is appointed, notice of receipt of the case record shall be given to that counsel.\\n\\nAs seen above, the Criminal Procedure Act and the Rules of Criminal Procedure clearly distinguish between privately retained counsel and court-appointed counsel with respect to notice of receipt of the case record. Even if the appellate court has given notice of receipt of the case record to the Defendant and court-appointed counsel, and the Defendant thereafter retains privately retained counsel anew, there is no basis for requiring that new notice of receipt of the case record be given to that privately retained counsel. Accordingly, if privately retained counsel fails to file a statement of grounds for appeal until the period for filing such grounds has elapsed from the date on which the Defendant or court-appointed counsel received notice of receipt of the case record, the effect of non-filing of the statement of grounds for appeal must be deemed to arise. The same applies where the appellate court canceled the appointment of court-appointed counsel because privately retained counsel was retained.\\n\\ne. Meanwhile, Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure, which provides that if court-appointed counsel is changed for a reason not attributable to the Defendant within the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal, notice of receipt of the case record must also be given to that court-appointed counsel, cannot, as explained below, be extended by interpretation or applied by analogy to newly retained privately retained counsel.\\n\\n(1) Considering the characteristics of procedural rules that promote clarity and stability in criminal proceedings in relation to the notice of receipt of the case record, which serves as the standard for compliance with the statutory period, and the above-mentioned difference between court-appointed counsel and privately retained counsel, the direct extension or analogical application to privately retained counsel of Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure, which concerns changes in court-appointed counsel, should be approached with caution.\\n\\nIf the court has not neglected its duty to guarantee the right to receive assistance of counsel, for example by unjustifiably delaying the appointment of court-appointed counsel for the Defendant in a compulsory defense case, then there is no room for the court’s supervisory or managerial duty to arise in the process by which the Defendant or others thereafter retain privately retained counsel pursuant to a private-law mandate contract, and thus there is no reason to extend or apply by analogy to newly retained privately retained counsel the provisions concerning notice of receipt of the case record for court-appointed counsel.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court has previously held that, even in compulsory defense cases, Article 156-2 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure concerning court-appointed counsel may be applied by analogy to privately retained counsel so that notice of receipt of the case record must be given (see Supreme Court Judgment 2000DO4694 dated December 22, 2000; Supreme Court Judgment 2008DO11486 dated February 12, 2009, etc.).
