However, those cases are different from this case, in that they were cases where the court’s fault in unjustifiably delaying the appointment of court-appointed counsel could be recognized, whereas in this case the court fulfilled its duty to appoint court-appointed counsel for the Defendant.\\n\\nArticle 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure presupposes a case in which court-appointed counsel is changed for a reason “not attributable to the Defendant,” but this case concerns a situation in which the Defendant abandoned the assistance of the appointed court-appointed counsel and, on his own responsibility, retained privately retained counsel, thereby changing counsel to privately retained counsel, and thus does not fall within a case in which court-appointed counsel is changed for a reason not attributable to the Defendant.\\n\\nThis case differs from the content and facts contemplated by Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure, and there is no reason to extend that provision to this case. Even considering whether Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure may be applied by analogy to this case, it is difficult to say that there exists a “gap in the law,” which is the premise for analogy.\\n\\n(2) There is no room for doubt that the Defendant’s right to receive assistance of counsel must be fully guaranteed in a compulsory defense case. However, if an exception were recognized even in a case like this on the ground that the right to receive assistance of counsel must be fully guaranteed, there would be no reason to treat differently a case in which privately retained counsel had been retained from the outset in a compulsory defense case. As a result, even in a case where the Defendant retained privately retained counsel from the outset in a compulsory defense case but, while that privately retained counsel had not submitted a statement of grounds for appeal, the counsel was replaced with another privately retained counsel, or in a case where the court-appointed counsel and privately retained counsel were repeatedly changed, the conclusion could be reached that a new notice of receipt of the case record must be given to the changed counsel, even though there is no express provision in the law, in a situation whose scope is difficult to limit. Such reasoning would undermine clarity and stability in criminal procedure and would also run counter to the purpose of the system requiring the filing of a statement of grounds for appeal, which is to realize speedy and smooth appellate proceedings.\\n\\n(3) When the appellate court has already given notice of receipt of the case record to the Defendant and court-appointed counsel and the Defendant thereafter retains privately retained counsel, the privately retained counsel, as a legal expert, can confirm from the Defendant or others, during the process of retention, the time when notice of receipt of the case record was given to the Defendant or court-appointed counsel, and this falls within the basic duties of privately retained counsel. In such a case, the privately retained counsel must be deemed to have been able to know that the case record was before the appellate court. As privately retained counsel, the counsel should naturally confirm the date on which notice of receipt of the case record was given to the Defendant or court-appointed counsel and file a statement of grounds for appeal within the period for filing such grounds. Even in such a case, there is no reason to extend or analogically apply Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure concerning notice of receipt of the case record so as to require a new notice of receipt of the case record to be given again to the newly retained privately retained counsel.\\n\\n(4) Moreover, if, by such extension or analogical application, an economically capable Defendant in a compulsory defense case may, after notice of receipt of the case record has been given to an already appointed court-appointed counsel, retain privately retained counsel again and thereby effectively extend the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal, then there is a possibility that such a Defendant may abuse the system of notice of receipt of the case record in order to intentionally delay the criminal proceedings, and this would also produce a result contrary to fairness compared with a Defendant lacking such economic capacity.\\n\\n(5) Since Article 164 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure applies mutatis mutandis Article 156-2 to proceedings in the Supreme Court as well, the problems discussed above may arise in the same way in proceedings before the Supreme Court. If Article 156-2 were extended or analogically applied to privately retained counsel, this could bring about unexpected confusion in the operation of appellate or Supreme Court proceedings.\\n\\nf. Ultimately, unless the Criminal Procedure Act or its rules are amended to include an explicit basis, the interpretation of the current law should be that, in a compulsory defense case, where the appellate court appoints court-appointed counsel and gives notice of receipt of the case record to the Defendant and court-appointed counsel, and then cancels the appointment of court-appointed counsel because the Defendant retained privately retained counsel, the appellate court has no duty to give notice of receipt of the case record again to the privately retained counsel.\\n\\n3. Resolution of this case\\nThe lower court dismissed the Defendant’s appeal by decision on the ground that, in this case, the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal was calculated from the date on which notice of receipt of the case record was given to the court-appointed counsel or the Defendant, and no lawful statement of grounds for appeal was filed within that period, there were no grounds stated in the petition of appeal, and there were no grounds for ex officio review. In light of the legal principles discussed above and upon examination of the record, this disposition by the lower court is correct (moreover, one of the counsel in the appellate trial of this case was also counsel at the court of first instance, and thus it may be said that he was well aware of the content and procedural history of this case). There is no violation by the lower court’s disposition of the Constitution, laws, orders, or rules that affected the judgment.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nThe re-appeal is dismissed, and the decision is rendered as stated in the disposition. Except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Cho Hee-dae, Jo Jae-yeon, Park Jeong-hwa, Kim Seon-su, and Lee Dong-won, and Justice Kim Jae-hyeong’s concurring opinion with the majority opinion and his concurring opinion to Justice Lee Dong-won’s dissenting opinion, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous.\\n\\n5. The dissenting opinions of Justices Cho Hee-dae, Jo Jae-yeon, Park Jeong-hwa, Kim Seon-su, and Lee Dong-won are as follows.\\na. Considering the significance of the constitutional right to receive assistance of counsel, the purpose of the court-appointed counsel system under the Criminal Procedure Act, the nature of compulsory defense cases, and the importance of the filing of a statement of grounds for appeal in criminal appellate proceedings, if, in a compulsory defense case under Article 33(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, the appellate court has given notice of receipt of the case record to the Defendant and court-appointed counsel, but while the Defendant and court-appointed counsel have not submitted a statement of grounds for appeal, the Defendant retains privately retained counsel within the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal, and the appellate court, ex officio, cancels the existing decision appointing court-appointed counsel, it is proper to view that, unless there are special circumstances such as the Defendant having retained new counsel to delay the proceedings, the appellate court should give notice of receipt of the case record to the newly retained privately retained counsel and guarantee that counsel a period for preparing and filing the statement of grounds for appeal.\\n\\nThe majority opinion, by contrast, states that in such a case there is no need to give notice of receipt of the case record again to the newly retained privately retained counsel. As reasons, it cites that there is no express provision in the relevant statutes such as the Criminal Procedure Act requiring a new notice of receipt of the case record; that Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure, which concerns a different factual situation, cannot be extended or applied by analogy to this case; that if such application were allowed, there would be a risk of abuse such as intentional delay of proceedings; that it would be unfair compared with a Defendant who lacks the economic ability to retain privately retained counsel; and that it could bring unexpected confusion to the operation of appellate and Supreme Court proceedings.\\n\\nAccording to the majority opinion, the newly retained privately retained counsel must prepare and file the statement of grounds for appeal only during the remaining period, excluding the period that elapsed while court-appointed counsel failed to file the statement of grounds for appeal, counted from the time when court-appointed counsel received notice of receipt of the case record. This is no different from holding the Defendant or privately retained counsel responsible for the period during which the court-appointed counsel appointed for the Defendant by the court, despite having received notice of receipt of the case record, did not file the statement of grounds for appeal. The majority opinion is unacceptable because it overlooks the fact that, in a compulsory defense case where it is indispensable to supplement the Defendant’s defensive capacity, the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal is in effect shortened, thereby infringing the Defendant’s constitutional right to receive assistance of counsel. The specific reasons are examined below.\\n\\n(1) The main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution provides: “When any person is arrested or detained, he shall have the right to prompt assistance of counsel.” In light of our Constitution’s principles of a rule-of-law state and due process, the right to receive assistance of counsel is naturally recognized not only for suspects or defendants in custody but also for suspects or defendants not in custody (see Constitutional Court en banc decision 2000HEONMA138 dated September 23, 2004). The constitutionally guaranteed “right to receive assistance of counsel” means the right to receive “sufficient assistance” from counsel (see Supreme Court Decision 2003MO402 dated November 11, 2003).\\n\\n(2) In criminal proceedings, there is a significant disparity between the prosecutor’s capacity for attack and the Defendant’s capacity for defense, so the system of counsel exists to supplement the Defendant’s capacity for defense in order to realize the principle of equality of arms. With respect to the right to receive assistance of counsel, the Criminal Procedure Act provides that where certain grounds exist, a case shall be designated a compulsory defense case and the court shall appoint court-appointed counsel ex officio when there is no counsel (Article 33(1)). It also provides that, in the trial proceedings of a compulsory defense case, the proceedings may not be opened without counsel and, if counsel does not appear, a new court-appointed counsel shall be appointed ex officio (Articles 282 and 283), thereby ensuring that the Defendant’s right to receive assistance of counsel is fully guaranteed in the trial proceedings of a compulsory defense case. Since Article 33(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act designates as compulsory defense cases situations in which there is a particularly high need to supplement the Defendant’s defensive capacity, taking into account whether the Defendant is detained, age and intelligence, the gravity of the case, etc., the guarantee of the right to receive sufficient assistance of counsel is even more important in compulsory defense cases.\\n\\n(3) According to Articles 361-2(1) and (2), 361-3(1), 361-4(1), and 364(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, when the Defendant appeals, criminal appellate proceedings are basically structured so that the court adjudicates only on the grounds of appeal included in the statement of grounds for appeal submitted by the Defendant or counsel within the statutory period, and if no lawful statement of grounds for appeal is submitted within the statutory period, the Defendant’s appeal is, in principle, dismissed unless there are grounds for ex officio review.\\n\\nIn light of the meaning and importance of the filing of a statement of grounds for appeal in criminal appellate proceedings, the Defendant’s right to receive assistance of counsel in a compulsory defense case must be fully guaranteed not only at the trial stage but also in the process of preparing and filing the statement of grounds for appeal.\\n\\nIn consideration of the above purpose, the opening sentence of Article 156-2(1) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure provides: “The appellate court that has received the records shall, in compulsory defense cases under Article 33(1) items 1 through 6 of the Act, appoint counsel without delay and then give notice of receipt of the case record to that counsel where there is no counsel.” By this means, the court-appointed counsel in a compulsory defense case receives notice of receipt of the case record separately from the Defendant’s notice of receipt of the case record and may therefore prepare and file the statement of grounds for appeal for the Defendant during a prescribed statutory period beginning from that time. And Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure provides: “Even where, after a decision appointing court-appointed counsel has been made pursuant to paragraph (1) or (2), the appointment decision is canceled and new court-appointed counsel is appointed for a reason not attributable to the Defendant within the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal, notice of receipt of the case record shall also be given to that counsel.” Thus, where court-appointed counsel is replaced for a reason not attributable to the Defendant, the new court-appointed counsel is given, separately from the period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal for the former court-appointed counsel, a new period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal so that the new court-appointed counsel may sufficiently prepare and file the statement of grounds for appeal for the Defendant.\\n\\nAccording to the majority opinion, by including in the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal for newly retained privately retained counsel the period that elapsed under the former court-appointed counsel, the time for the newly retained privately retained counsel to prepare and file the statement of grounds for appeal is in effect shortened. Since the court appoints court-appointed counsel ex officio when there is no counsel in a compulsory defense case, the Defendant cannot intervene in that appointment process; therefore, it is improper to attribute to the Defendant the disadvantage of the shortening of the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal that elapsed under court-appointed counsel.\\n\\n(4) As pointed out by the majority opinion, there is no express provision requiring the cancellation of the existing decision appointing court-appointed counsel and the giving of notice of receipt of the case record again to the newly retained privately retained counsel, but the absence of an express provision does not mean that measures to guarantee the right to receive assistance of counsel are impermissible. The Supreme Court has previously held, in a case where, in a compulsory defense case, the court failed to appoint court-appointed counsel without justifiable reason and during that time the Defendant himself retained counsel, but by then the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal with respect to the Defendant had already expired so that the privately retained counsel had no time to prepare and file a statement of grounds for appeal for the Defendant, that the Defendant’s right to receive assistance of counsel under Article 156-2 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure must also be protected in such a case, and that the court must therefore apply Article 156-2 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure by analogy to privately retained counsel and give notice of receipt of the case record, thereby affording the privately retained counsel an opportunity to prepare and file a statement of grounds for appeal for the Defendant within the prescribed period counted from the date of receipt of such notice (see Supreme Court Judgment 2000DO4694 dated December 22, 2000; Supreme Court Judgment 2008DO11486 dated February 12, 2009). This emphasizes that, despite the difference between court-appointed counsel and privately retained counsel, the constitutional right to receive assistance of counsel must be substantially guaranteed in a compulsory defense case; and in this case as well, considering the purport of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, and the circumstances that make it difficult to regard the change of counsel as attributable to the Defendant, it is proper to view this as a case in which Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure may be applied by analogy.\\n\\nThis issue should not be examined formally by asking whether Article 361-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act or Article 156-2(1) and (3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure concerning notice of receipt of the case record have been observed, but rather substantively from the perspective of whether the right to receive assistance of counsel for preparing and filing the statement of grounds for appeal in a compulsory defense case is fully guaranteed. If, by adhering only to the wording of the provisions, the right to receive assistance of counsel under the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act is not fully guaranteed, the court should seek a means to guarantee it fully.\\n\\nArticle 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure presupposes a case in which court-appointed counsel is changed for a reason not attributable to the Defendant. Since this case concerns a situation in which the court, ex officio, canceled the decision appointing court-appointed counsel as the Defendant retained privately retained counsel on his own, the majority opinion that Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure cannot be applied by analogy to this case is overly bound by the text of the provision and overlooks the fact that the right to assistance of counsel is not fully guaranteed to a Defendant who needs supplementation of defensive capacity in a compulsory defense case.\\n\\nIn addition to the above-mentioned purport of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, and considering the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act requiring that a Defendant have counsel in a compulsory defense case, the Defendant’s right to receive assistance from counsel in the process of preparing and filing the statement of grounds for appeal must be fully guaranteed. There is no basis for different treatment depending on whether the counsel is court-appointed or privately retained. According to the majority opinion, newly retained privately retained counsel must identify the case and prepare and file the statement of grounds for appeal within the remaining period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal, calculated with reference to the Defendant or the former court-appointed counsel, and in the extreme, there may be cases in which the statement of grounds for appeal must be prepared within a very short period of less than one day. This cannot be regarded as a situation in which the Defendant’s right to receive assistance of counsel is fully guaranteed in a compulsory defense case.\\n\\nIt is proper to view the Defendant’s retention of privately retained counsel while the former court-appointed counsel had not filed a statement of grounds for appeal as the exercise of the right to retain counsel prescribed in Article 30 of the Criminal Procedure Act in order to exercise the Defendant’s right of defense. Article 18(1) item 1 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure provides that, when counsel has been retained, the court or a judge of the district court shall cancel the appointment of court-appointed counsel. As above, the Defendant exercised the right to retain counsel, the change of counsel was effected pursuant to the court’s decision under the Rules of Criminal Procedure, and the court did not separately take measures to transfer the duties of the canceled court-appointed counsel to the newly retained privately retained counsel; therefore, it is improper to regard the Defendant’s act of retaining privately retained counsel for the exercise of the right of defense as a reason attributable to the Defendant.\\n\\nAccordingly, since the case is similar to the situation in which court-appointed counsel is changed for a reason not attributable to the Defendant in a compulsory defense case, Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure concerning that situation may be applied by analogy. This accords with the purport of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act to fully guarantee the Defendant’s right to assistance of counsel in a compulsory defense case.\\n\\n(5) The risk of abuse such as delay of proceedings pointed out by the majority opinion appears to be an excessive concern that reverses the proper order of things. Even if some procedural delay occurs, in light of the importance of the constitutional and criminal procedure law rights to receive assistance of counsel in a compulsory defense case, it is proper to regard it as a degree tolerable within criminal justice procedure. If there are special circumstances showing that the Defendant retained privately retained counsel anew for the purpose of delaying the proceedings, the possibility of abuse can be eliminated by applying the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal on the basis of the Defendant or the former court-appointed counsel. Therefore, it is difficult to accept leaving unremedied a situation in which the right to assistance of counsel is effectively infringed in a compulsory defense case on the ground of the risk of abuse.\\n\\nThe majority opinion raises the problem of inequality according to economic capacity, but, as seen above, since the possibility of abuse such as delay of proceedings can be excluded, it cannot be said that a measure to fully guarantee the right to assistance of counsel to a Defendant whose existing appointment of court-appointed counsel has been canceled because he retained privately retained counsel to exercise his right of defense in a compulsory defense case favors an economically capable Defendant against another Defendant lacking economic capacity in violation of fairness.\\n\\nThe majority opinion also expresses concern over expected confusion in the operation of appellate or Supreme Court proceedings, but if the cases in which notice of receipt of the case record is required to be given to newly retained privately retained counsel are limited to the present case, namely, where in a compulsory defense case the appellate court appointed court-appointed counsel and gave notice of receipt of the case record to the Defendant and court-appointed counsel, and then canceled the appointment of court-appointed counsel because the Defendant retained privately retained counsel, and to cases in the Supreme Court that involve the same factual relationship, it does not appear that uncontrollable confusion would arise.\\n\\nb. According to the reasons for the lower court decision and the record, the Re-appellant was indicted for a case whose statutory punishment is imprisonment for a fixed term of not less than 3 years, so this case is a compulsory defense case under Article 33(1) item 6 of the Criminal Procedure Act; the Re-appellant and the Re-appellant’s counsel at the court of first instance appealed the judgment of the court of first instance to the lower court, but did not state the grounds for appeal in either petition of appeal; the lower court appointed court-appointed counsel on March 10, 2015, and served the appointment decision of court-appointed counsel and the notice of receipt of the case record on the court-appointed counsel on the 12th of the same month and on the Re-appellant on the 13th of the same month, respectively; however, while the Re-appellant and court-appointed counsel had not submitted a statement of grounds for appeal, the Re-appellant retained privately retained counsel on March 23, 2015, whereupon the lower court canceled the appointment decision of court-appointed counsel on the 24th of the same month; the newly retained privately retained counsel submitted a statement of grounds for appeal to the lower court on May 21, 2015 without the lower court separately notifying the privately retained counsel of the receipt of the case record; and accordingly, on July 3, 2015, the lower court dismissed the Re-appellant’s appeal by decision pursuant to Article 361-4(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act on the ground that the above statement of grounds for appeal was submitted after the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal had expired, counted from the date on which notice of receipt of the case record was given to the Re-appellant or court-appointed counsel, and that there were no grounds for ex officio review in the judgment of the court of first instance.\\n\\nc. Examining the above factual circumstances in light of the legal principles discussed above, in this compulsory defense case, after court-appointed counsel was appointed, while the Defendant and court-appointed counsel had not submitted a statement of grounds for appeal, the Re-appellant retained privately retained counsel within the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal, and the court canceled the appointment of court-appointed counsel accordingly. On the other hand, there is no basis to find special circumstances such as that the Re-appellant retained the above counsel for delay of the proceedings. Therefore, the lower court should have separately given notice of receipt of the case record to the newly retained privately retained counsel, and should have determined whether the statement of grounds for appeal by counsel was lawfully filed by examining whether the privately retained counsel filed a statement of grounds for appeal within the period under Article 361-3(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, counted from the date on which the notice of receipt of the case record was received.\\n\\nHowever, because the lower court did not give notice of receipt of the case record to the newly retained privately retained counsel, the statement of grounds for appeal submitted by the Re-appellant’s counsel on May 21, 2015 shall be deemed to have been lawfully submitted before the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal expired. The lower court, by contrast, concluded that the above statement of grounds for appeal was submitted after the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal had expired and dismissed the appeal. In such lower court decision, there is an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles regarding the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal in a compulsory defense case.\\n\\nTherefore, the lower court decision must be set aside and the case remanded to the lower court for rehearing and determination.\\n\\nFor the above reasons, I state my position in dissent from the majority opinion.\\n\\n6. Justice Kim Jae-hyeong’s concurring opinion with the majority opinion is as follows.\\na. The gist of the dissenting opinion is that the majority opinion is contrary to the purport of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act, which require that the Defendant be guaranteed sufficient assistance of counsel, and that Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure should be applied by analogy so that notice of receipt of the case record must again be given to privately retained counsel. However, for the reasons below, such argument is not proper.\\n\\nb. In a compulsory defense case, where the court cancels the decision appointing court-appointed counsel because the Defendant retained privately retained counsel, failure to give notice of receipt of the case record to privately retained counsel cannot be regarded as infringing the constitutionally guaranteed right to receive assistance of counsel.\\n\\nArticle 12(4) of the Constitution provides that “when any person is arrested or detained, he shall have the right to assistance of counsel,” thereby expressly recognizing the right to receive assistance of counsel as a constitutional fundamental right. The right to receive assistance of counsel means the right of the Defendant or suspect to obtain the assistance of counsel in order to oppose the State power’s unilateral exercise of penal authority. However, the specific content of the right to receive assistance of counsel, and whether such specific content can be derived directly from the Constitution or becomes concrete only through legislation, may differ depending on the perspective from which one views the role and function of counsel in criminal procedure.\\n\\nIn criminal procedure, counsel plays the role of an assistant who supports the suspect or Defendant in defending himself in the position of a party opposing the investigative and prosecutorial authorities, and also the role of monitoring and controlling whether the rights of the suspect or Defendant are observed by participating in criminal procedure to the benefit of the suspect or Defendant.\\n\\nIn order to realize the right to receive assistance of counsel, the Criminal Procedure Act specifically provides in detail for counsel’s right of access and communication with the Defendant or suspect (Article 34), counsel’s right to inspect and copy documents, etc. while proceedings are pending (Article 35), the right of counsel to participate in the execution of search and seizure warrants (Article 121), the right of counsel to participate in the suspect examination upon a request for a warrant of detention (Article 201-2), the right of counsel to appear and state opinions at the hearing date for a review of the propriety of arrest or detention (Article 214-2), the right of counsel to participate in an inspection (Article 145), the right of counsel to participate in an expert examination (Article 176), the right of counsel to participate in the examination of witnesses (Articles 163 and 163-2), the right of counsel to examine the Defendant (Article 296-2), the right of counsel to submit evidence or request examination of witnesses, etc. (Article 294), and the right of counsel to make the final statement (Article 303), and other matters concerning counsel’s participation in various procedures during investigation and after the institution of prosecution. Such detailed matters for realizing the right to receive assistance of counsel cannot all be derived naturally from the constitutional provisions, and many aspects are left to the regulation of the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nThe Constitution contains no provisions concerning the system requiring the filing of a statement of grounds for appeal or notice of receipt of the case record. Questions such as the extent to which a separate notice of receipt of the case record should be given to counsel are matters concerning procedural rights that may be determined differently depending on legislative formation.\\n\\nc. In a compulsory defense case, even if the court does not give notice of receipt of the case record to privately retained counsel after having given notice of receipt of the case record to the Defendant and court-appointed counsel, it cannot be said to infringe the rights of the Defendant guaranteed under the Criminal Procedure Act.\\n\\nThe legislator, in Article 361-2(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, provides only that where counsel has been retained before notice of receipt of the case record is given to the Defendant, notice of receipt of the case record shall also be given to counsel. It does not provide that, if the Defendant retains privately retained counsel after notice of receipt of the case record has been given to the Defendant and the court cancels the decision appointing court-appointed counsel, notice of receipt of the case record must be given again to privately retained counsel.\\n\\nWhether to cancel the appointment of court-appointed counsel and give notice of receipt of the case record again to privately retained counsel on the ground that privately retained counsel was retained after notice of receipt of the case record was given to the Defendant and court-appointed counsel is a technical matter of procedural law. The fact that the Criminal Procedure Act and the Rules of Criminal Procedure contain no provision on this matter cannot be regarded as being contrary to the purport of the Criminal Procedure Act. This does not change depending on whether the case is a compulsory defense case.\\n\\nd. It is not proper to attempt to resolve the issue in this case by applying Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure by analogy.\\n\\nArticle 108 of the Constitution provides: “The Supreme Court may establish rules concerning court proceedings, internal discipline of courts, and administration of courts, within the scope that does not contravene Acts.” Therefore, under Supreme Court Rules, regulations concerning procedural matters may be provided even without an express delegation provision in an Act, so long as they do not contravene the Act. Article 1 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure also provides: “The purpose of these Rules is to prescribe matters delegated by the Criminal Procedure Act to Supreme Court Rules and other matters necessary concerning criminal procedure.”\\n\\nThe Criminal Procedure Act does not prohibit the Court from newly requiring notice of receipt of the case record to be given to privately retained counsel in a case where, in a compulsory defense case, the court cancels the decision appointing court-appointed counsel because the Defendant retained privately retained counsel. If the Supreme Court were to newly establish a rule in the Rules of Criminal Procedure requiring notice of receipt of the case record to be given again to privately retained counsel in such a case, it would not contravene the Act.\\n\\nIf the Supreme Court determines that there is a need to give notice of receipt of the case record anew to newly retained privately retained counsel in the above case, it may amend the Rules of Criminal Procedure to provide, comprehensively or within a certain scope, that notice of receipt of the case record be given again, taking into account various factors such as the timing and circumstances of retention of privately retained counsel and the timing of cancellation of the appointment decision of court-appointed counsel. Rather than creating unexpected confusion in the clear progress of criminal appellate or Supreme Court proceedings by applying by analogy Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure, which concerns court-appointed counsel, to this case, amending the Rules of Criminal Procedure in the manner described above is a clearer and more efficient approach.\\n\\nHowever, even if the Rules of Criminal Procedure are amended, procedural provisions such as the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal and notice of receipt of the case record should be set forth simply and clearly so that they do not appear complicated or confusing not only to courts and counsel but also to the general public. In addition, since a long time has passed since the notice of receipt of the case record system was introduced in 1961 and the practice of criminal trials in courts has changed significantly, such changes need to be reflected. Resolving the issue through an amendment of the Rules of Criminal Procedure, and further of the Criminal Procedure Act, would produce a better result than resolving it through analogical application.\\n\\ne. In short, under Article 361-2(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, even if notice of receipt of the case record is not newly given to privately retained counsel in this case, it cannot be said to infringe the Defendant’s right to receive assistance of counsel under the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act. If necessary, the Supreme Court itself can amend the Rules of Criminal Procedure and resolve the matter in a more appropriate manner, so there is no need to apply by analogy Article 156-2(3) of the Rules of Criminal Procedure, which concerns court-appointed counsel.\\n\\nI state the above concurring opinion with the majority opinion.\\n\\n7. Justice Lee Dong-won’s concurring opinion with the dissenting opinion is as follows.\\nIn order for the Defendant’s right to receive assistance of counsel to be substantially guaranteed in the process of preparing and filing a statement of grounds for appeal in a compulsory defense case, it is important that the 20-day period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal be substantially guaranteed to counsel.\\n\\nArticle 18(1) item 1 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure provides that, when counsel has been retained, the court or a judge of the district court shall cancel the appointment of court-appointed counsel. If the court, pursuant to the above Rules of Criminal Procedure, cancels the decision appointing court-appointed counsel and still concludes that there is no need to give notice of receipt of the case record again to privately retained counsel, the privately retained counsel must independently identify the case and prepare and file the statement of grounds for appeal within the remaining period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal, calculated with reference to the Defendant or court-appointed counsel. As a result, the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal for privately retained counsel is effectively shortened, and the 20-day period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal is not substantially guaranteed.\\n\\nIn order to substantially guarantee the Defendant’s right to receive assistance of counsel in the process of preparing and filing a statement of grounds for appeal, it is desirable to amend Article 18(1) item 1 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure so that the decision appointing court-appointed counsel is not canceled during the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal even if the Defendant retains privately retained counsel.\\n\\nIf the court does not cancel the decision appointing court-appointed counsel, the materials from counsel’s activities, such as meetings with the Defendant and review of facts and legal principles for preparing the statement of grounds for appeal, may be jointly utilized by court-appointed counsel and privately retained counsel, enabling the filing of the statement of grounds for appeal within the remaining period for filing such grounds. In such a case, at least court-appointed counsel among the Defendant’s counsel is guaranteed the 20-day period for filing the statement of grounds for appeal, and privately retained counsel may also supplementarily use the materials from court-appointed counsel’s activities, so it may be said that the Defendant’s right to receive assistance of counsel in the process of preparing and filing the statement of grounds for appeal is fully guaranteed.\\n\\nOn the other hand, if the court, pursuant to Article 18(1) item 1 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure, cancels the decision appointing court-appointed counsel and nevertheless concludes that there is no need to give notice of receipt of the case record again to privately retained counsel, then, as noted above, privately retained counsel must prepare and file the statement of grounds for appeal within the remaining period for filing such grounds that has effectively been shortened and is less than 20 days; this cannot be said to be a situation in which the Defendant’s right to receive assistance of counsel in the process of preparing and filing the statement of grounds for appeal is sufficiently guaranteed, and as a result the original purpose of the compulsory defense system, namely to enable the Defendant to receive assistance from counsel through compulsory defense, cannot be achieved.\\n\\nIn this case, since the court canceled the existing decision appointing court-appointed counsel pursuant to Article 18(1) item 1 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure within the period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal by court-appointed counsel, the court must, by giving notice of receipt of the case record again to the newly retained privately retained counsel, substantially guarantee to that counsel the 20-day period for filing a statement of grounds for appeal so that the counsel may prepare and file the statement of grounds for appeal.\\n\\nI state the above concurring opinion with the dissenting opinion."}
