{"[2009HEONRA6]": "[Appendix 1] Relevant Provisions\\n\\nNational Human Rights Commission Act Article 1 (Purpose) This Act aims to establish the National Human Rights Commission and to protect the inviolable fundamental human rights enjoyed by every individual and enhance their level, thereby realizing human dignity and worth and contributing to the establishment of the democratic basic order.\\n\\nArticle 3 (Establishment and Independence of the National Human Rights Commission) ① The National Human Rights Commission (hereinafter referred to as the “Commission”) shall be established in order to perform the duties for the protection and enhancement of human rights prescribed by this Act.\\n\\n② The Commission shall independently perform the duties falling within its authority.\\n\\nArticle 5 (Composition of the Commission) ① The Commission shall be composed of 11 Human Rights Commissioners (hereinafter referred to as “Commissioners”), including one Chairperson and 3 standing commissioners.\\n\\n② Of the persons recognized as having specialized knowledge and experience concerning human rights issues and as capable of performing duties for the guarantee and enhancement of human rights fairly and independently, the President shall appoint 4 persons elected by the National Assembly (including 2 standing commissioners), 4 persons nominated by the President, and 3 persons nominated by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court.\\n\\nArticle 8 (Guarantee of the Status of Commissioners) Commissioners shall not be dismissed against their will except by a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or a heavier punishment. Provided, That where a Commissioner becomes significantly difficult or impossible to perform duties due to a physical or mental disability, the Commissioner may be required to retire by a resolution passed with the consent of at least two-thirds of all Commissioners.\\n\\nArticle 18 (Organization and Operation of the Commission) Matters necessary for the organization of the Commission other than those prescribed by this Act shall be determined by Presidential Decree, and matters necessary for the operation of the Commission shall be determined by the Commission’s Rules.\\n\\nArticle 19 (Duties) The Commission shall perform the following duties:\\n1. Investigation and research of laws and regulations (including draft laws and regulations in the legislative process), systems, policies, and practices relating to human rights, and recommendation or expression of opinions on matters requiring improvement thereof\\n2. Investigation of and remedy for acts of human rights violations\\n3. Investigation of and remedy for discriminatory acts\\n4. Fact-finding surveys on the actual conditions of human rights\\n5. Education and publicity concerning human rights\\n6. Presentation and recommendation of guidelines concerning types of human rights violations, standards for determination thereof, and preventive measures therefor, etc.\\n7. Research on accession to international human rights treaties and implementation of such treaties, and recommendation or expression of opinions thereon\\n8. Cooperation with organizations and individuals engaged in activities for the protection and promotion of human rights\\n9. Exchange and cooperation with international organizations and foreign human rights institutions related to human rights\\n10. Other matters recognized as necessary for the guarantee and enhancement of human rights\\n\\n[Appendix 2] 2. Summary of the Petitioner’s Allegations and the Summary of the Respondent’s and Relevant Agencies’ Responses\\n\\nA. Summary of the Petitioner’s Allegations\\n\\n(1) Party Capacity in an Adjudication on a Jurisdictional Dispute\\n\\nArticle 111(1)4 of the Constitution merely specifies “state institutions” as parties to an adjudication on a jurisdictional dispute and does not limit them to “state institutions established on the basis of the Constitution,” and the state institutions designated as parties to an adjudication on a jurisdictional dispute between state institutions under Article 62(1)1 of the Constitutional Court Act are illustrative.\\n\\nThe Petitioner is a state institution established by the Constitution and the National Human Rights Commission Act, although the name of the institution is not directly prescribed in the Constitution, and has been granted independent authority. It is also an independent institution not belonging to any other institution such as the President or the Prime Minister in terms of organizational composition. The Petitioner is an organ that does not belong to any existing state institution and monitors whether, with respect to legislation, judiciary, and administration alike, the enforcement of policies and systems, legal and judicial determinations, and investigative and correctional functions infringe constitutionally guaranteed fundamental rights, and that expresses opinions thereon. The issue of to what extent the Petitioner’s authority should be recognized is, in the end, a matter of how much the authority and independence of a non-affiliated organ should be protected from the legislature, judiciary, and administration that stand opposed to it, and how the scope of such protection should be set. In relation to the act of amending the organizational decree in this case, the question is whether, when the Respondent determines the authority of the Petitioner, which is an “organ not belonging to the President,” by Presidential Decree beyond the statutory limit, that can be regarded as an infringement of independence, that is, an infringement of procedural and operational authority. Accordingly, this is qualitatively different from merely determining the quantitative scope of administrative authority, and it is natural and proper that adjudication on this matter be made by the Constitutional Court.\\n\\nIn addition, because the Petitioner is a non-affiliated institution and has been granted independent authority, there is no separate means of resolving a jurisdictional dispute with the President or the Government, and it is not subject to agency litigation under the Administrative Litigation Act.\\n\\nTherefore, the Petitioner has party capacity to file an adjudication on a jurisdictional dispute under Article 111(1)4 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Whether the Petitioner’s Authority Was Infringed\\n\\n(a) Authority Granted to the Petitioner by Law\\n\\nThe Petitioner was established by the National Human Rights Commission Act, which is not only one of the achievements of the domestic democratization movement but also conforms to the international community’s demand for the establishment of a national human rights institution, as reflected in the “Principles Relating to the Status of National Institutions” adopted and approved by the United Nations General Assembly in 1993, also known as the Paris Principles.\\n\\nThe Petitioner performs the duties prescribed in Article 19 of the National Human Rights Commission Act. Since these duties are primarily directed at human rights violations by state power, the main content consists of monitoring and checking state policies and their implementation, and therefore independence is required by the essential nature of those duties.\\n\\nAlthough the National Human Rights Commission Act provides that matters concerning the organization of the Petitioner shall be determined by Presidential Decree, in order to secure the independence of the Petitioner’s performance of duties, the above Presidential Decree must be initiated and amended in a manner and through procedures that do not infringe the Petitioner’s independence. And the Petitioner should be regarded as having, in addition to the independent right to perform duties, the following procedural authorities in the enactment and amendment of the organizational decree relating to the Petitioner’s organization. First, the Petitioner has the authority to determine the specific content of the Presidential Decree concerning its organization. Article 6 of the National Human Rights Commission Act grants the Chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission the authority to submit an agenda item to the Prime Minister concerning matters under his or her jurisdiction, and agenda items concerning matters under jurisdiction include matters concerning the Petitioner’s organization. Second, the Ministry of the Interior and Safety, which is in charge of matters concerning organization and staffing within the executive branch, may proceed with the amendment procedure of the organizational decree regarding the Petitioner’s organization only when there is a proposal from the Petitioner, an independent institution. In other words, the proposal procedure for the organizational decree falls within the Petitioner’s authority. Third, even if the Ministry of the Interior and Safety amends the organizational decree proposed by the Petitioner, it must do so within the scope that does not reduce the Petitioner’s functions or impair the independence of its duties, and procedurally it must conduct a substantive consultation procedure with the Petitioner. Even if the Petitioner were not granted such authority, at minimum the authority to participate in the consultation procedure for the amendment of the organizational decree should be guaranteed.\\n\\n(b) Infringement of the Petitioner’s Authority by the Respondent’s Act of Amending the Organizational Decree in This Case\\n\\nThe Minister of the Interior and Safety belonging to the Respondent ignored the Petitioner’s opinions and, without going through any substantive consultation process, unilaterally prepared the draft amendment to the organizational decree in this case, submitted it to the State Council, and completed the resolution procedure, thereby infringing the Petitioner’s right to initiate the amendment of the organizational decree and the Petitioner’s decision-making authority concerning the organization and composition of the National Human Rights Commission.\\n\\nThe act of amending the organizational decree in this case goes beyond merely reducing personnel; it has the intention of harming the Petitioner’s independence and impairing its capacity to perform duties in an essential area, and it is unrelated to remedying the failure to meet the standards under the Government Organization Management Guidelines, which is merely a pretext. The reduction and adjustment of the Petitioner’s functions are matters that should be determined by the National Assembly through legislation, and doing so by organizational decree (Presidential Decree) constitutes an abuse of authority beyond the scope of delegation contemplated by the National Human Rights Commission Act and is an unlawful act. As a result of the act of amending the organizational decree in this case, 5 headquarters were integrated into 1 office and 2 bureaus, the 22 teams in the headquarters were integrated into 11 divisions, and personnel were reduced from a staffing quota of 208 to 164. As a result, the policy work and education work, which had previously been performed in one bureau each, were integrated into one division each, and the policy function and education function were reduced to half of their previous level. Even if the duties are to be performed independently, the number of personnel has been reduced to a level below the personnel at the time of establishment 7 years ago, so independent performance of duties has in effect become threatened. In a small organization with a staffing quota of only 208 persons, a reduction of 44 persons produces, in light of the highly rigid administrative support work, an even greater quantitative reduction effect in other substantive business fields. Meanwhile, even if the transitional provision in the supplementary provisions of the organizational decree in this case allows excess current personnel to continue working as support-duty personnel, this is extremely temporary.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Respondent’s act of amending the organizational decree in this case infringed the Petitioner’s right to initiate amendments to the organizational decree and the right to decide on the composition of the Petitioner’s organization, and furthermore infringed, or created a significant risk of infringing, the Petitioner’s inherent authority to perform the duties prescribed in Article 19 of the National Human Rights Commission Act.\\n\\nB. Summary of the Respondent’s Response\\n\\n(1) Party Capacity in an Adjudication on a Jurisdictional Dispute\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court has stated that a “state institution established by the Constitution and granted independent authority by the Constitution and by law” may be a party to a petition for an adjudication on a jurisdictional dispute (Constitutional Court decision of July 16, 1997, 96HEONRA2). In the case of an institution established solely by law, a dispute over its authority is not a constitutional issue but merely a simple legal issue. Therefore, in light of the nature of the Constitutional Court, which adjudicates important constitutional issues through the interpretation of the Constitution, legal disputes involving state institutions established by law are not matters within the jurisdiction of the Constitutional Court. The argument that a state institution established by law, such as the Petitioner, may be a party to a jurisdictional dispute means granting a state institution established by law the same status as a state institution established by the Constitution; this would have the result of giving legislation by the National Assembly the same effect as the Constitution, which is contrary to popular sovereignty and constitutionalism.\\n\\nThe guarantee of the fundamental rights of the people is the foremost mission of all state institutions, and therefore this cannot be said to be a distinctive duty only of the Petitioner, and the fact that the National Human Rights Commission Act does not contain a provision regarding the affiliation of the Petitioner has no relevance to the Petitioner’s constitutional status. Therefore, as the Petitioner argues, the fact that the Petitioner performs duties of guaranteeing fundamental rights and is an independent institution not belonging to any other organ does not, by itself, create capacity to be a party to an adjudication on a jurisdictional dispute.\\n\\nIn addition, the Petitioner is a central administrative agency, and if conflicts with other ministries are likely to arise, the issue may be resolved by the Prime Minister, who directs the executive ministries on the Respondent’s order, or by the Respondent. The Chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission, who is the Petitioner’s representative, may also attend a State Council meeting, state the Petitioner’s position, and resolve the issue through discussion with the relevant State Council members.\\n\\nTherefore, the Petitioner, which was established by law, lacks party capacity for an adjudication on a jurisdictional dispute.\\n\\n(2) No Possibility of Infringement of Authority\\n\\n(a) Absence of the Petitioner’s Procedural Authority in Relation to the Amending of the Organizational Decree in This Case\\n\\nThe Petitioner was established for the overlapping protection of human rights, but since it is not a private human rights movement organization but a state institution operated with taxpayers’ money, the principle of checks and balances under the principle of separation of powers applies. Thus, when enacting the National Human Rights Commission Act, the National Assembly allowed the Petitioner to determine matters concerning its operation on its own, but granted the Government the authority to determine by Presidential Decree matters necessary concerning its organization, namely the composition and rearrangement of the Petitioner’s organization (Article 18 of the National Human Rights Commission Act).\\n\\nArticle 3 of the National Human Rights Commission Act merely provides that the Petitioner shall perform its duties according to its own judgment without receiving specific instructions in the performance of its duties; it does not grant any authority regarding organizational composition. If the National Human Rights Commission Act had granted the Petitioner decision-making authority regarding its organizational composition, Article 18 would have provided that such matters be determined by the National Human Rights Commission’s Rules, not by Presidential Decree. At the time the National Human Rights Commission Act was enacted in 2001, there was a bill that delegated detailed matters concerning the establishment of the Petitioner’s Secretariat to the National Human Rights Commission’s Rules, but it was not adopted.\\n\\nIn the end, the National Human Rights Commission Act merely provides that matters necessary concerning the Petitioner’s organization shall be determined by Presidential Decree, and grants no authority whatsoever to the Petitioner; therefore, the Petitioner does not have the right to decide its organization, the right to initiate a Presidential Decree concerning its organization, or a substantive right of consent, etc.\\n\\n(b) Whether the Petitioner’s Right to Perform Duties Was Infringed by the Amending of the Organizational Decree in This Case\\n\\nThe content of the amendment to the organizational decree in this case leaves unchanged the Petitioner’s existing substantive authority and methods of performing duties and, for the simplification of the organization and elimination of overlapping work, reorganizes the Petitioner’s organization into 1 office, 2 bureaus, 11 divisions, and 3 affiliated agencies, while reducing the staffing quota by 44 persons. Meanwhile, with respect to the above reduction in the staffing quota, a transitional provision was established in Article 2 of the supplementary provisions so that, for current personnel in excess of the reorganized staffing quota, in the case of general service and functional service personnel, the corresponding number of personnel is deemed to remain within the staffing quota unless they retire upon reaching the retirement age or due to voluntary resignation, etc., and an artificial restructuring through personnel reduction was not adopted, and the original working conditions were maintained so as to ensure the status guarantee of public officials belonging to the Petitioner and the guarantee of the Petitioner’s performance of duties.\\n\\nLooking at the specific details, the existing common support organization is reorganized into a “Planning and Coordination Officer” system, the human rights policy, education, and publicity duties that are closely interrelated are integrated into the Policy and Education Bureau and performed there, and only a “Investigation Bureau” is newly established for the unification of investigation and corrective duties. In the end, this merely means that the existing personnel perform the duties they have been carrying out in a more simplified organizational system, and accordingly no infringement whatsoever occurs on the Petitioner’s authority to perform duties or its performance thereof.\\n\\nTherefore, whether the Petitioner’s authority to perform duties is infringed by the act of amending the organizational decree in this case can only be determined when the reduction in staffing quota under the reorganized organizational decree actually materializes, and even then, only if, as a result of such personnel reduction, actual performance of duties is reduced to the point of becoming nominal would it be said that the Petitioner’s authority to perform duties has been infringed. However, even though the reduction in staffing quota has not actually materialized, the Petitioner is merely making factual assertions contrary to reality, as if the personnel reduction corresponding to the staffing quota scheduled to be reduced in the future has in fact already been implemented, and is not asserting or proving at all how, specifically, or to what extent the authority to perform duties has been infringed; this is nothing more than an assertion that, because the number of workers has decreased, the workload has increased compared to before and the morale of employees has declined.\\n\\nC. Summary of the Opinion of the Minister of the Interior and Safety\\n\\n(1) Absence of Party Capacity for an Adjudication on a Jurisdictional Dispute\\n\\nThe same reasoning as the Respondent’s response applies.\\n\\n(2) Absence of Possibility of Infringement of Authority\\n\\n(a) Whether the Petitioner Has an Independent Organizational Authority\\n\\nArticle 3 of the National Human Rights Commission Act is a provision that guarantees the independence of the Petitioner’s performance of duties, and there is no basis for construing it as including the independence of organizational composition. Rather, Article 18 of the National Human Rights Commission Act provides that matters concerning the Petitioner’s organization shall be determined in a Presidential Decree, not in the Petitioner’s internal rules (the National Human Rights Commission Rules). In the case of the Petitioner, the Korea Communications Commission, the Fair Trade Commission, the Financial Services Commission, and the Anti-Corruption and Civil Rights Commission are also central administrative agencies established by separate statutes, and although the statutes establishing them provide for the independence of their performance of duties, they also provide that matters concerning organizational composition shall be determined by Presidential Decree. There is no legal basis or logical validity for construing only the Petitioner’s case as including the independence of organizational composition within the independence of performance of duties.\\n\\nThe Petitioner is a collegiate administrative agency established by a separate statute like the Korea Communications Commission, etc. (Article 2(2) and Article 5 of the Government Organization Act), and is a central administrative agency subject to the Government Organization Act. In order for an agency not to be subject to the Government Organization Act or to have its organizational composition independence guaranteed, an explicit basis is necessary, as in the examples of constitutional organs such as the National Assembly (Article 7 of the National Assembly Secretariat Act), the courts (Article 71 of the Court Organization Act), the Constitutional Court (Article 17 of the Constitutional Court Act), the Election Commission (Article 15 of the National Election Commission Act), and the Board of Audit and Inspection (Article 16 of the Board of Audit and Inspection Act), where the general outline of organizational composition at the level of divisions and bureaus is directly prescribed in each individual enabling act, while detailed matters are to be determined by each institution’s internal rules. However, Article 18 of the National Human Rights Commission Act provides that matters concerning the Petitioner’s organization shall be determined by Presidential Decree rather than the Petitioner’s internal rules, and this can be seen as reflecting the legislature’s intention that the Petitioner, established on the basis of law, cannot be viewed as possessing the same level of special status and independence as constitutional organs, and therefore there is no reason to guarantee independence even for matters concerning organizational management.\\n\\n(b) Whether the Petitioner’s Procedural Authority (Initiative Right, Consultation Right, or Decision-Making Authority) Exists in the Process of Amending the Organizational Decree in This Case\\n\\nArticle 6(4) of the National Human Rights Commission Act grants the Chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission the authority to request the Prime Minister to submit an agenda item concerning matters under his or her jurisdiction, but this provision is entirely unrelated to the organizational decree concerning the Petitioner’s organization.\\n\\nThe authority to submit draft enactments and amendments of the organizational decree of all central administrative agencies belongs to the Ministry of the Interior and Safety under Article 29(1) of the Government Organization Act. Each central administrative agency may only request an amendment to the organizational decree by submitting the relevant documents when it is necessary to adjust its organization and staffing (General Rules on the Organization and Staffing of Administrative Agencies Articles 8 and 10). And the Ministry of the Interior and Safety is not necessarily required to submit a draft enactment or amendment of the organizational decree upon each central administrative agency’s request.\\n\\nThe competent ministry in charge of government organization and staffing management is the Ministry of the Interior and Safety. Opinions concerning organization, staffing, etc., prepared and requested independently by the agency subject to reorganization are merely matters for review, and the Ministry of the Interior and Safety is not bound by them. Therefore, the Petitioner does not have a right of consultation or a right to determine the content in relation to the amendment of the organizational decree in this case.\\n\\nThe act of amending the organizational decree in this case reflects the results of the audit by the Board of Audit and Inspection (October 7, 2008), and was carried out through a continuous consultation process with the Petitioner for approximately 4 months beginning around November 2008.\\n\\n(c) Whether the Act of Amending the Organizational Decree in This Case Infringed the Petitioner’s Right to Perform Duties\\n\\nThe content of the amendment to the organizational decree in this case is unrelated to reducing or abolishing the functions performed by each department of the Petitioner or restricting or distorting the purpose of the National Human Rights Commission Act. The amendment to the organizational decree in this case concerns the performance of the duties of a state institution and the appropriate setting of the scale of organization, staffing, and budget, and merely arose in the course of how to efficiently allocate resources based on the precious taxes of the people; accordingly, it does not infringe the Petitioner’s right to perform duties."}
