the entire session or add items to the agenda for the day and change their order. In such cases, the members' consent shall be accompanied by a written statement of reasons, and no debate shall be held on such consent, but a vote shall be taken.\\nArticle 85-2 (Expedited Processing of Agenda Items) ① Where a member intends to designate an agenda item referred to a committee (including an agenda item referred to the Legislation and Judiciary Committee for review of system and wording) as an agenda item subject to expedited processing under paragraph 2, the member shall submit to the Speaker a motion requesting designation as an agenda item subject to expedited processing, signed by a majority of the incumbent members (hereinafter in this Article referred to as “motion for designation of a fast-track agenda item”), and a member of the committee having jurisdiction over the agenda item shall submit to the chairperson of the committee a motion for designation of a fast-track agenda item signed by a majority of the incumbent members of the committee having jurisdiction. In such cases, the Speaker or the chairperson of the committee having jurisdiction over the agenda item shall, without delay, put the motion for designation of a fast-track agenda item to a secret ballot, and it shall be adopted by the affirmative votes of at least three-fifths of the incumbent members or of at least three-fifths of the incumbent members of the committee having jurisdiction over the agenda item.\\n② When the motion for designation of a fast-track agenda item under the latter part of paragraph 1 is adopted, the Speaker shall designate the agenda item as one that must be completed for review within the period under paragraph 3. In such cases, where a committee has drafted an alternative bill for an agenda item designated under the first sentence (hereinafter referred to as a “fast-track agenda item”), such alternative bill shall be deemed to be a fast-track agenda item.\\n③ A committee shall complete its review of a fast-track agenda item within 180 days from the date of designation: Provided, that the Legislation and Judiciary Committee shall complete its review of system and wording of a fast-track agenda item within 90 days from the date of designation, from the date deemed referred under paragraph 4, or from the date referred under Article 86 (1).\\n④ Where a committee (excluding the Legislation and Judiciary Committee) fails to complete its review of a fast-track agenda item within the period under the main sentence of paragraph 3, it shall be deemed, on the day following the end of that period, to have completed its review in the competent committee and to have been referred to the Legislation and Judiciary Committee for review of system and wording: Provided, that agenda items other than bills and proposals for the Rules of the National Assembly shall be deemed to have been immediately submitted to the plenary session.\\n⑤ Where the Legislation and Judiciary Committee fails to complete its review of a fast-track agenda item (including a fast-track agenda item referred to the Legislation and Judiciary Committee for review of system and wording or deemed referred under the main sentence of paragraph 4) within the period under the proviso to paragraph 3, it shall be deemed, on the day following the end of that period, to have completed its review in the Legislation and Judiciary Committee and to have been immediately submitted to the plenary session.\\n⑥ A fast-track agenda item under the proviso to paragraph 4 or paragraph 5 shall be placed on the plenary session within 60 days from the day it is deemed submitted to the plenary session.\\n⑦ Where a fast-track agenda item is not placed on the plenary session within 60 days pursuant to paragraph 6, it shall be placed on the first plenary session convened after the lapse of that period.\\n⑧ Where the Speaker reaches agreement with the representative members of each negotiation group, the provisions of paragraphs 2 through 7 shall not apply to a fast-track agenda item.\\nArticle 93 (Deliberation on Agenda Items) When the plenary session deliberates on an agenda item, it shall hear the review report of the chairperson who reviewed the item and shall take a vote after questions and debate. Provided, that for an agenda item that has not undergone committee review, the proposer shall explain the purport thereof, and for an agenda item that has undergone committee review, both questions and debate, or either one of them, may be omitted by resolution.\\nArticle 95 (Motion for Amendment) ① A motion for amendment to a bill shall be submitted in advance to the Speaker, complete with the text of the motion and reasons attached, and jointly signed by 30 or more consenting members. Provided, that a motion for amendment to a budget bill shall require the consent of 50 or more members.\\n② An amendment reviewed and reported by a committee shall become the agenda item without any consent.\\n③ A committee may not submit an amendment to an agenda item outside its jurisdiction.\\n④ An alternative bill to a bill shall be submitted while the committee is reviewing the original bill, and the Speaker shall refer such alternative bill to the committee.\\n⑤ A motion for amendment under paragraph 1 shall be directly related to the purport and content of the original bill or the bill reviewed and reported by the committee (including where proposed by the committee pursuant to Article 51). Provided, that this shall not apply where the Speaker reaches agreement with the representative members of each negotiation group.\\nArticle 96 (Order of Vote on Amendments) ① Where several amendments are submitted with respect to the same agenda item, the Speaker shall determine the order of voting in accordance with the following subparagraphs:\\n1. The amendment submitted last shall be voted on first.\\n2. A member's amendment shall be voted on before a committee's amendment.\\n3. Where there are several members' amendments, the amendment that differs most from the original bill shall be voted on first.\\n② When all amendments are rejected, the original bill shall be put to a vote.\\nArticle 106-2 (Implementation of Unlimited Debate, etc.) ① Where a member intends to hold a debate not subject to time limits (hereinafter in this Article referred to as “unlimited debate”), notwithstanding other provisions of this Act, with respect to an agenda item submitted to the plenary session, the member shall submit to the Speaker a request signed by at least one-third of the incumbent members. In such case, the Speaker shall conduct unlimited debate on the relevant agenda item.\\n② A request under paragraph 1 shall be submitted for each agenda item subject to the request and shall be submitted before the plenary session at which the agenda item is listed on the agenda is convened. Provided, that where an item is added to the agenda for the day during the convening of the plenary session, the request may be submitted until the declaration of closure of debate on the relevant agenda item.\\n③ A member may engage in unlimited debate on the relevant agenda item once a request under paragraph 1 has been submitted. In such case, each member may debate only once.\\n④ A plenary session in which unlimited debate is conducted shall not adjourn and shall continue until the declaration of the closure of unlimited debate under paragraph 7. In such case, notwithstanding the main sentence of Article 73 (3), the meeting shall continue even if less than one-fifth of the incumbent members are present during the meeting.\\n⑤ A member may submit to the Speaker, with the signatures of at least one-third of the incumbent members, a motion for closure of unlimited debate with respect to an agenda item on which unlimited debate is being conducted.\\n⑥ A motion for closure of unlimited debate under paragraph 5 shall be put to a secret ballot after 24 hours have elapsed from the time the motion was submitted, and shall be adopted by the affirmative votes of at least three-fifths of the incumbent members. In such case, no debate shall be held on the motion for closure of unlimited debate, and a vote shall be taken.\\n⑦ Where there is no longer any member to conduct unlimited debate on an agenda item on which unlimited debate is being conducted, or where the motion for closure of unlimited debate is adopted pursuant to paragraph 6, the Speaker shall, after declaring the closure of unlimited debate, put the relevant agenda item to a vote without delay.\\n⑧ Where the relevant session ends while unlimited debate is being conducted, the closure of unlimited debate shall be deemed to have been declared. In such case, the relevant agenda item shall be put to a vote without delay in the immediately following session.\\n⑨ No request for unlimited debate may be made with respect to an agenda item for which the closure of unlimited debate has been declared, or deemed to have been declared, pursuant to paragraph 7 or 8.\\n⑩ For the budget bill, etc. and the bills accompanying the revenue budget bill designated pursuant to Article 85-3(4), paragraphs 1 through 9 shall apply until December 1 of each year, and any unlimited debate being conducted pursuant to the same paragraphs, any plenary session in progress, and the deliberative procedures for motions for closure of unlimited debate that have been submitted shall terminate at 12:00 midnight on December 1.\\n\\n[Appendix 3] Summary of the Petitioners’ Claims and the Respondents’ Answers\\nA. Summary of the Petitioners’ Claims\\n(1) Political parties are specially provided for in Article 8 of the Constitution. Political parties participate in the formation of the political will of the people, recommend candidates in public elections, participate in elections on their own as the parties to the party vote in proportional representation elections, and constitute negotiation groups in the National Assembly, and thus may be regarded as equivalent to State agencies that perform their roles and functions pursuant to the Constitution and laws. Accordingly, the petition for adjudication on the act of declaring approval of the amendment at issue by the successor party to the Liberty Korea Party, namely, the Future United Party, is lawful, since the Future United Party, successor to the Liberty Korea Party, has the authority under the Constitution and laws to participate in elections and the legislative procedure of the National Assembly, and in particular has an interest in legislation concerning the electoral system, including proportional representation elections.\\n(2) The respondent Speaker of the National Assembly refused the unlimited debate lawfully requested by the petitioner members of the National Assembly in connection with the matter of the session determination at issue, although there was no case under the National Assembly Act, etc. in which unlimited debate is excluded. This violates Article 106(1) of the National Assembly Act and is contrary to parliamentary democracy and the principle of majority rule, and also violates the Speaker’s duty of political neutrality. As such, the respondent Speaker of the National Assembly’s act of declaring approval of the amendment to the session at issue is unlawful and infringed the petitioner members’ right to deliberation and vote, and is therefore void.\\n(3) The amendment at issue maintains the number of constituency seats and proportional representation seats as before and does not introduce the mixed-member proportional system and regional proportional representation system, so its underlying basis differs from that of the original bill at issue, and direct relevance to the purport and content of the original bill is not recognized. The respondent Speaker of the National Assembly’s act of regarding the amendment at issue as an amendment to the original bill and declaring approval of the amendment at issue violates Article 95(5) of the National Assembly Act. Therefore, the act of declaring approval of the amendment at issue infringes the petitioner members’ right to deliberate and vote on bills and infringes the Liberty Korea Party’s right to equal participation in the legislative procedure, which it should have participated in procedurally in amending the proportional representation election system, and is therefore void.\\n(4) As mentioned above, the respondent Speaker of the National Assembly’s act of declaring approval of the amendment at issue violated Article 95(5) of the National Assembly Act, and the semi-linked proportional representation system, which is the main point of the amendment, also violates the principle of direct election, the principle of equal election, and the like, and is therefore substantively unconstitutional. Accordingly, the respondent National Assembly’s act of amending the Public Official Election Act at issue is also unconstitutional and void.\\nB. Summary of the Respondents’ Answers\\n(1) Political parties do not constitute State agencies, and the “right to receive equal opportunity guarantees” of a political party asserted by the Future United Party, successor to the Liberty Korea Party, is not recognized in the “legislative procedure for amendment of the Election Act,” and therefore the petition for adjudication on a dispute over authority filed by the Future United Party, successor to the Liberty Korea Party, is unlawful.\\n(2) In light of the fact that Article 7(2) of the National Assembly Act requires the session of the National Assembly to be determined “immediately” after convening; the fact that Article 106-2(8) of the National Assembly Act presupposes that the “matter of session determination” is not included among the agenda items subject to unlimited debate; the purpose of introducing the filibuster system; and the fact that allowing unlimited debate with respect to the “matter of session determination” could lead to a situation in which legislation becomes impossible through repeated unlimited debate, the “matter of session determination” should be regarded as not included among the agenda items subject to unlimited debate. Accordingly, the respondent Speaker of the National Assembly’s refusal of the request for unlimited debate on the “matter of session determination” and declaration of approval of the amendment at issue are lawful, and do not infringe the petitioner members’ right to deliberation and vote.\\n(3) While maintaining the basic legislative purpose of the original bill, which is to minimize distortion of the popular will in the distribution of seats in the National Assembly, the amendment at issue merely makes changes such as: ① readjusting the numbers of constituency members of the National Assembly and proportional representation members of the National Assembly to the current levels; ② while maintaining the framework of the semi-linked proportional representation system introduced in the original bill, temporarily applying different distribution ratios; and ③ deleting the regional proportional representation system and the linked-seats system introduced in the original bill. This does not add a new system or content unrelated to the purport and content of the original bill, but instead makes amendments such as deleting or changing some content within the scope related thereto while maintaining the existing main content and framework. In addition, the act of declaring approval of the amendment at issue was carried out, on the basis of the National Assembly’s autonomy and the Speaker’s broad authority concerning the conduct of proceedings, under the Speaker’s judgment that the amendment at issue was a lawful amendment, and such judgment cannot be regarded as having clearly violated the Constitution or laws and therefore should be respected. Accordingly, the act of declaring approval of the amendment at issue does not infringe the petitioner members’ right to deliberate and vote on bills.\\n(4) Even if the Speaker’s act is deemed to infringe the petitioner members’ right to deliberate and vote on bills, it cannot be regarded as unlawful to the extent that the Constitutional Court should revoke or nullify it."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding impeachment trials is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: In an impeachment trial, the authenticated copy of the National Assembly's impeachment resolution shall substitute for the petition.
B: The Constitutional Court may conduct preparatory proceedings when it is necessary to organize the parties' allegations and evidence in order to proceed with the trial proceedings efficiently and in a focused manner.
C: If criminal proceedings are pending on the same grounds as the impeachment trial petition against the respondent, the panel may suspend the trial proceedings.
D: During an impeachment trial, if the respondent retires upon the expiration of his or her term of office, although there is no explicit provision in the Constitution or the Constitutional Court Act, the interest in adjudication may be recognized because the necessity of constitutional clarification for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order and for the control of power over high public officials is acknowledged.
E: If an official who has been removed from office by the pronouncement of an impeachment decision commits an official act violating the law that constitutes a criminal offense under the law, imposing criminal liability does not constitute double punishment.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2000HEONBA57]": "1. Overview of the Case and Subject Matter of Review\\n\\na. Overview of the Case\\n\\nThe Petitioner had served as a professor at ○○ University from 1966. 11. 1. and retired on 1993. 8. 1.; thereafter, from September of the same year until 1998. 11., he received, as retirement benefits under the Government Employees Pension Act, a retirement pension of KRW 111,741,870 and a retirement allowance of KRW 39,414,590. However, around 1997. 9. 10., the Petitioner had met several times with members of an anti-state organization, including Choi ○ Nam, who was a North Korean spy, and as a result, on 1998. 7. 23., the Seoul High Court sentenced him to imprisonment for 2 years for violation of Article 8 (meeting and communication) of the National Security Act, and that judgment became final and conclusive on 1998. 11. 13.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Government Employees Pension Management Corporation, on 1998. 12. 26., applied Article 64(3) and Article 31(1) Item 2 of the Government Employees Pension Act to the Petitioner and ordered him to pay KRW 136,027,840 by 1999. 1. 29., after deducting KRW 15,128,620 in contributions to be returned to the Petitioner (the contributions received from the Petitioner and interest thereon at the rate prescribed by the Civil Act) from the total amount of KRW 151,156,460 of retirement benefits already paid.\\n\\nThe Petitioner filed with the Seoul Administrative Court a lawsuit for revocation of the disposition of recovery of retirement benefits (99NU9888) against the Government Employees Pension Management Corporation, but when the petition was dismissed, he appealed to the Seoul High Court (the present case, 99NU10935). During the appellate trial, the Petitioner applied for a request for adjudication on the constitutionality of a law (2000A109), arguing that Article 64(3) of the Government Employees Pension Act was unconstitutional; however, when the Seoul High Court dismissed the application, he filed the present constitutional complaint on 2000. 7. 21. pursuant to Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act.\\n\\nMeanwhile, on 2000. 6. 29., the Seoul High Court rendered a judgment dismissing the Petitioner’s appeal in the underlying case, and as the Petitioner did not file an appeal, that judgment became final and conclusive.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe subject matter of review in this case is whether Article 64(3) of the Government Employees Pension Act (hereinafter referred to as “the statutory provision at issue”) is unconstitutional, and its text and the related statutory provisions are as follows.\\n\\nGovernment Employees Pension Act (as amended by Act No. 5117 on 1995. 12. 29. and before amendment by Act No. 6328 on 2000. 12. 30.)\\n\\nArticle 64 (Restriction on Benefits by Criminal Punishment, etc.) ① Where a public official or former public official falls under any of the following subparagraphs, a part of the retirement benefits and retirement allowance shall be reduced and paid as prescribed by Presidential Decree. In such case, the amount of retirement benefits may not be reduced below the amount obtained by adding interest under the provisions of the Civil Act to the total amount of contributions already paid.\\n1. When he/she has received a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment for a cause arising during service\\n2. When he/she has been removed from office by impeachment or disciplinary action\\n② When an investigation is in progress or a criminal trial is ongoing for a criminal act punishable by imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment due to a cause arising during service, payment of a part of the retirement benefits and retirement allowance may be suspended as prescribed by Presidential Decree. In such case, when the reason for restriction of benefits no longer exists, the remaining amount shall be paid together with interest prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n③ In the case of a person who has committed a crime prescribed in Part II, Chapter 1 (Crimes of Insurrection), Chapter 2 (Crimes of External Aggression) of the Criminal Act, Part II, Chapter 1 (Crimes of Rebellion), Chapter 2 (Crimes of Benefiting the Enemy) of the Military Criminal Act, or the National Security Act (excluding Article 10) and has received a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment, the total amount of contributions already paid shall be returned together with interest under the provisions of the Civil Act, but no benefits shall be paid.\\n④ Omitted\\n\\nArticle 31 (Recovery of Benefits) ① The Corporation or a local government shall recover the amount of benefits in any of the following subparagraphs where a person who has received benefits falls under any of them. In such case, in the case of Item 1, the amount of benefits shall be collected by adding interest and recovery expenses prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n1. Omitted\\n2. Where the cause for the benefits has retroactively ceased to exist after the benefits were received\\n3. Omitted\\n② Omitted\\n\\n2. The Petitioner’s Arguments and Opinions of the Relevant Authorities\\n\\na. The Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\n(1) With respect to the underlying case, the court held that the cause for restriction of the right to claim retirement benefits under the statutory provision at issue is also applicable to cases where the criminal act occurred after retirement, because the provision does not require that such cause arise during service; however, since the right to claim retirement benefits under the Government Employees Pension Act is a right established on the premise of service as a public official, the cause for restriction of the right to claim retirement benefits must naturally be limited to a cause arising during service.\\n\\n(2) The fact that the person was a public official or former public official would already have been sufficiently considered in determining the sentence for the criminal act in question, and the statutory provision at issue again deprives the person even of the right to claim retirement benefits, which constitutes double punishment and, as an excessive restriction on property rights, infringes the essential content of the right to claim retirement benefits; in particular, applying it also to causes arising after retirement violates the principle of proportionality in restricting the exercise of the right to claim retirement benefits.\\n\\n(3) The statutory provision at issue treats differently, with respect to restrictions on retirement benefits, ordinary crimes and certain crimes infringing national legal interests, such as crimes under the National Security Act, and this violates the principle of equality. While a person who commits an ordinary crime after retirement is subject to no restriction on the right to claim retirement benefits, retroactively depriving a person who commits a crime such as a violation of the National Security Act of retirement benefits regardless of how much time has elapsed since retirement is discriminatory without any rational basis.\\n\\n(4) In addition, in order to impose an adverse disposition such as restriction of the right to claim retirement benefits, a procedure must, of course, be established in advance to examine the appropriateness of that disposition and guarantee the party an opportunity to present opinions and make arguments. The absence of such an opportunity violates the constitutional principle that one shall not be punished except by due process of law.\\n\\nb. Summary of the Reasons for the Seoul High Court’s Decision Dismissing the Request for Constitutional Review\\n\\n(1) Retirement benefits under the Government Employees Pension Act have not only the character of deferred wages, but also the character of social security or meritorious compensation benefits, and public officials, as servants of the entire people during service, bear the constitutional responsibility to take the lead in safeguarding the security of the State and the survival and freedom of the people. Moreover, even if a person who was a public official engages in a criminal act such as a violation of the National Security Act after retirement, the likelihood of causing far more serious harm to the security of the State than in the case of a person who was not a public official or a person who commits an ordinary crime is high, and considering that public officials, even after retirement, bear certain obligations such as observing secrets learned in the course of duty, the statutory provision at issue cannot be regarded as infringing the essential content of property rights in violation of Article 23(1) of the Constitution or as violating the principle of proportionality or the principle of equality.\\n\\n(2) In addition, the principle of due process in the latter sentence of Article 12(1) of the Constitution is a principle of criminal justice procedure and has no relation to the statutory provision at issue, which prescribes the basis for administrative procedures. Whether, when a public official, etc. commits a crime under the National Security Act and receives a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment, the right to claim retirement benefits should be deprived by that fact itself or through a separate disposition depriving the right to claim retirement benefits after a certain procedure is a matter within the legislature’s discretion, and the party’s right to state opinions does not necessarily have to be guaranteed as a procedural right.\\n\\nc. Summary of the Opinion of the President of the Government Employees Pension Management Corporation\\n\\n(1) The restriction on the right to claim retirement benefits is not necessarily premised on a cause arising during service. If a public official engages in anti-state activities even after retirement, the likelihood of causing far more serious harm to the security of the State is high; therefore, with respect to anti-state activities, strict legal sanctions are imposed regardless of the period of public service, and there is no need to bear any further duty of support with respect to a current public official or a person who has committed a criminal act contrary to security and order of the State.\\n\\n(2) The right to receive Government Employees Pension benefits has both the character of social security and the character of property rights, and it is not possible to precisely distinguish it as social security benefits, insurance premiums, or deferred wages. The statutory provision at issue is a provision enacted for the purpose of national policy to deprive anti-state actors of social security entitlements, taking into account the special nature of public officials, the impact of criminal acts on society, and the national situation. Even if some property-right character is recognized, this merely sets limits on property rights by law, and since the contributions paid by the Petitioner and the interest thereon are returned, it does not infringe the essence of private property rights or violate the principle of proportionality.\\n\\n(3) In restricting benefits, while acts such as murder of individuals or embezzlement of public funds do not harm the entire State, crimes of insurrection, external aggression, or crimes under the National Security Act may directly and extensively harm the security and public order of the State; thus, differentiating between restrictions on benefits for anti-state acts and restrictions on benefits for ordinary offenders is a rational distinction in light of legal equity.\\n\\n(4) The principle of due process is a principle of criminal justice procedure and has no relation to the statutory provision at issue, which prescribes the basis for administrative procedures by which an administrative disposition on recovery of retirement benefits may be made. Although there are assertions today that the principle of due process should apply not only to criminal procedures but also to administrative procedures, in a case like this, even if notice, hearing, or an opportunity to explain is given, the content of the application of the law does not change depending on the result; moreover, since procedures are provided whereby a recipient who objects to the decision on a disposition for recovery of retirement benefits under this Act may seek review before the Government Employees Pension Benefits Review Committee and file an administrative lawsuit to obtain sufficient relief, it cannot be said that the principle of due process is violated merely because the Act does not directly provide for a hearing procedure, etc. before the recovery disposition of retirement benefits.\\n\\nd. Summary of the Opinion of the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs\\n\\nSubstantially the same as the opinion of the President of the Government Employees Pension Management Corporation.\\n\\n3. Decision\\n\\na. Nature of the Government Employees Pension System and the Types of Pension Benefits\\n\\nThe Government Employees Pension System has the purpose of contributing to the stabilization of the livelihood and enhancement of welfare of public officials and their survivors by providing appropriate benefits for retirement or death and for injury, disease, or disability caused by official duties to public officials (Article 1 of the Act); it is a type of social insurance system that seeks relief for public officials through insurance techniques under the responsibility of the State when the above social risks arise.\\n\\nIn addition, the Government Employees Pension System has broad protective functions, including not only retirement pension, which is the original function of the pension system, but also lump-sum payments and retirement allowances corresponding to severance pay in the private sector, occupational injury compensation benefits corresponding to workers’ compensation insurance in the private sector, and various mutual-aid benefits for general disasters, as well as various welfare programs for current and former public officials. In other words, the Government Employees Pension System is a comprehensive social security system that broadly provides old-age income security, work compensation, disaster compensation, mutual aid, and welfare benefits for the special occupational category of public officials.\\n\\nBenefits under the Government Employees Pension Act are largely divided into short-term benefits and long-term benefits. Short-term benefits consist of 4 types: official-duty medical care expenses, official-duty medical care lump-sum payment, disaster mutual-aid payment, and death consolation money (Article 34 of the Government Employees Pension Act). Long-term benefits consist of 13 types: 4 types of retirement benefits (retirement pension, retirement pension lump-sum payment, retirement pension deduction lump-sum payment, and retirement lump-sum payment), 2 types of disability benefits (disability pension and disability compensation), 6 types of survivor benefits (survivor pension, survivor pension additional payment, survivor pension special additional payment, survivor pension lump-sum payment, survivor lump-sum payment, and survivor compensation payment), and retirement allowance, etc. (Article 42 of the Government Employees Pension Act).\\n\\nIf these various benefits under the Government Employees Pension Act are classified according to the character of the protected interest, they may be divided into: ① retirement benefits and survivor benefits, which are income-security benefits that secure income when income is lost due to retirement or death; ② retirement allowance, which is of the character of work compensation corresponding to statutory severance pay in the private sector; ③ official-duty medical care benefits (official-duty medical care expenses and official-duty medical care lump-sum payment), disability benefits, and survivor compensation payments, which are of the character of disaster compensation that compensates for work-related injuries; and ④ disaster mutual-aid payment and death consolation money, which are of the character of mutual aid paid as solace for general disasters.\\n\\nThus, while some of the various benefits under the Government Employees Pension Act, such as retirement allowance, have a strong character of deferred wages and others do not, in essence they all have the character of social security benefits and, at the same time, also have the character of meritorious compensation or deferred wages (Constitutional Court 1998. 12. 24. 96HEONBA73, Reports 10-2, 856, 866; Constitutional Court 2000. 3. 30. 99HEONBA53, etc., Reports 12-1, 344, 352).\\n\\nb. History of the Statutory Provision at Issue\\n\\nThe restriction of benefits by criminal punishment under the Government Employees Pension Act was provided from the time of enactment of the Government Employees Pension Act. Article 9 of the former Government Employees Pension Act (enacted by Act No. 533 on 1960. 1. 1.) provided that a public official or former public official shall not receive benefits under the Government Employees Pension Act where, for a cause arising during service, he/she: ① received a sentence of a penalty of suspension of qualifications or heavier punishment and the sentence became final and conclusive; ② received a suspended sentence and the judgment became final and conclusive; ③ was dismissed from office by impeachment or disciplinary action (including cases where a soldier is dismissed by judgment); or ④ lost nationality.\\n\\nThereafter, Article 49(1) of the former Government Employees Pension Act, amended by Act No. 1133 on 1962. 8. 31., provided that “where a public official or former public official has received a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment, or a public official has been removed from office or suspended by impeachment or disciplinary action, all or part of the benefits may not be paid as prescribed by Presidential Decree,” thereby deleting the phrase “for a cause arising during service”; however, up to that time, no separate provision had been specifically established for anti-state crimes.\\n\\nThen, with the full revision of the former Government Employees Pension Act by Act No. 3586 on 1982. 12. 28., Article 64(1) provided that “where a public official or former public official has received a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment for a cause arising during service, or a public official has been removed from office by impeachment or disciplinary action, a part of the amount of benefits shall be reduced and paid as prescribed by Presidential Decree. In such case, the amount may not be reduced below the amount obtained by adding interest under the provisions of the Civil Act to the total amount of contributions already paid.” Article 64(2) provided that “in the case of a person who has committed a crime prescribed in Part II, Chapter 1 (Crimes of Insurrection), Chapter 2 (Crimes of External Aggression) of the Criminal Act, Part II, Chapter 1 (Crimes of Rebellion), Chapter 2 (Crimes of Benefiting the Enemy) of the Military Criminal Act, or the National Security Act (excluding Article 10) and has received a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment, the total amount of contributions already paid shall be returned together with interest under the provisions of the Civil Act, but no benefits shall be paid,” thereby newly establishing a separate provision for anti-state crimes and restricting benefits. At that time, for ordinary crimes, it was provided that benefits would be restricted only where a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment had been imposed for a cause arising during service, but with respect to anti-state crimes, no phrase limiting them to “a cause arising during service” was included, and this content has remained unchanged in the current law.\\n\\nc. Issues in the Interpretation of the Statutory Provision at Issue\\n\\nUnlike Article 64(1) and (2), which clearly limit the cause for benefit restriction to “a cause arising during service,” the statutory provision at issue does not provide whether it is limited to a cause arising during service; thus, the issue is whether the cause for restriction of benefit payment under the statutory provision at issue is limited to a cause arising during service, or whether it also includes causes arising after retirement.\\n\\nOn this issue, as the courts of first and second instance in the underlying case held, there may be an opinion that the restriction on benefits applies not only to causes arising during service but also to causes arising after retirement. According to this opinion, unlike Article 64(1) and (2) of the Government Employees Pension Act, Article 64(3) (the statutory provision at issue) does not contain the limited expression “a cause arising during service,” and therefore it should be interpreted as applying not only to causes arising during service but naturally also to causes arising after retirement. Further, if before the amendment of the Government Employees Pension Act on 1982. 12. 28. ordinary crimes and anti-state crimes had been regulated together and then separated by the amendment of 1982. 12. 28., it is understood that the legislature intended not to limit anti-state crimes to causes arising during service, unlike ordinary crimes. Considering that even after retirement, a public official is highly likely to cause far more serious harm to the security of the State than a person who was not a public official if he/she commits an anti-state criminal act such as a violation of the National Security Act, and considering that a public official bears certain obligations even after retirement, such as observing secrets learned in the course of duty, the restriction of benefits under the statutory provision at issue should be interpreted as applicable when a public official, etc. commits a criminal act such as a violation of the National Security Act regardless of whether it is before or after retirement.\\n\\nHowever, there is also an opposing view that the restriction on benefits under the statutory provision at issue should be limited to “a cause arising during service.” The Supreme Court, in its judgment dated 2002. 5. 31. in Case 2000DU4514 on revocation, etc. of the disposition of recovery of retirement benefits, held that, in light of the legislative purpose for introducing the restriction on benefits by criminal punishment, etc. in Article 64 of the Government Employees Pension Act, the legislative history of the provision, the notion of equity and justice, and the constitutional spirit of guaranteeing equality and other fundamental rights of the people, the provision should be understood as one intended to restrict retirement benefits, which have the character of meritorious compensation or social security for fidelity during service, when a public official abandons the duty of fidelity during service and receives a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment; thus, paragraph 1 provides for cases of partial reduction without regard to the name of the crime committed, and paragraph 3 (the statutory provision at issue) should be understood as providing for cases of total payment restriction resulting from the commission of the crimes listed therein. On that basis, the Supreme Court interpreted the statutory provision at issue as limiting the cause for restriction of benefits to “a cause arising during service,” just like Article 64(1) and (2).\\n\\nAccordingly, because the statutory provision at issue gives rise to conflicting interpretations as to whether the prescribed restriction on benefits is limited only to “a cause arising during service,” or whether it may also be restricted by “a cause arising after retirement,” we will proceed on the premise that both causes arising during service and after retirement may be applicable in determining whether the statutory provision at issue is unconstitutional.\\n\\nd. Whether the Statutory Provision at Issue Is Unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Whether property rights are infringed\\n\\nArticle 23(1) of the Constitution provides that “property rights of all citizens shall be guaranteed,” thereby guaranteeing the property rights of the people, and Article 37(2) of the Constitution provides that “all freedoms and rights of the people may be restricted by Act only when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare; even when they are restricted, the essential content of freedoms and rights shall not be infringed,” thereby declaring the basic principles to be observed when the State enacts legislation restricting the fundamental rights of the people.\\n\\nTherefore, even when fundamental rights of the people are restricted by law, such restriction must be made only to the extent that it does not infringe the essential content of the freedoms and rights of the people, and in enacting legislation restricting fundamental rights, the legitimacy of the legislative purpose, the appropriateness of the means for achieving that purpose, the minimum extent of infringement, and the balance between the public necessity protected by the legislation and the fundamental rights infringed by it must all be satisfied; laws or statutory provisions that do not observe these requirements exceed the legislative limits on restricting fundamental rights and are unconstitutional.\\n\\nSince the entitlement to receive benefits such as retirement benefits under the Government Employees Pension Act has the character of property rights, the statutory provision at issue may be regarded as restricting the entitlement to receive benefits as property rights. We now examine whether the restriction on property rights under the statutory provision at issue respects the constitutional limits discussed above.\\n\\nThe Government Employees Pension System aims to contribute to the stabilization of the livelihood and enhancement of the welfare of public officials and their survivors by providing appropriate benefits for retirement or death and for injury, disease, or disability caused by official duties. Public officials are servants of the entire people and public servants performing governmental functions, and they bear the responsibility of taking the lead in safeguarding the security of the State, constitutional order, and the people’s freedom. If a public official engages in anti-state activities, the likelihood of causing far more serious harm to the security of the State and the people’s survival and freedom than in the case of a person who does not is high; therefore, there is a greater need to induce public officials not to engage in anti-state activities. For the smooth performance of public officials’ duties, public trust in each public official and in public office must form the basic foundation. When a public official receives a criminal punishment of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment for an anti-state crime such as a violation of the National Security Act, public trust in public office as a whole is undermined and public interests are harmed. Accordingly, imposing corresponding property disadvantages on a public official who has been criminally punished for such criminal acts may be an appropriate means for the benefit of the people as a whole.\\n\\nThe statutory provision at issue lists, as causes for restriction of benefits, Part II, Chapter 1 (Crimes of Insurrection), Chapter 2 (Crimes of External Aggression) of the Criminal Act, Part II, Chapter 1 (Crimes of Rebellion), Chapter 2 (Crimes of Benefiting the Enemy) of the Military Criminal Act, and crimes of violation of the National Security Act (excluding Article 10). Crimes of insurrection are crimes against the territory and constitutional order, which are the internal foundations of the existence of the State; crimes of external aggression are intended to protect the State from external threats to its existence and refer to acts that endanger the existence of the State by colluding with foreign powers to bring in external aggression, acting hostilely against the Republic of Korea, or providing personnel or material benefits. Crimes of rebellion under the Military Criminal Act are crimes of gathering together, taking up arms, resisting the authorities, and committing acts of collective resistance; crimes of benefiting the enemy are crimes involving acts that benefit an enemy state, such as providing the army or military facilities to the enemy or spying for the enemy. In addition, the National Security Act is a law intended to secure the security of the State and the survival and freedom of the people by regulating anti-state activities that endanger the security of the State (Article 1(1) of the National Security Act). The legislature, while restricting entitlement to benefits under the statutory provision at issue, has limited the crimes that constitute grounds for restriction to crimes that threaten the very existence of the State and endanger the constitutional order as above, and has excluded the passive offense of failure to report prescribed in the National Security Act.\\n\\nIn addition, contributions paid under the Government Employees Pension Act while serving as a public official are returned to the recipient with interest under the Civil Act. The pension fund under the Government Employees Pension Act is composed of public officials’ contributions corresponding to 85 per 1000 of monthly remuneration and contributions borne by the State or local governments (Articles 65, 66(2), and 69(1) of the Government Employees Pension Act; Articles 59 and 65-3(1) of the Enforcement Decree). Among the benefits under the Government Employees Pension Act, the portion corresponding to the individual’s contributions has a strong character as deferred wages that should have been paid as remuneration for service during employment, while the remaining portion has a strong character as benevolent compensation for service during employment or as social security benefits; the contributions and interest thereon, which have a strong character as property rights, are returned.\\n\\nAccordingly, insofar as the cause for the restriction of benefits under the statutory provision at issue is limited to crimes committed while serving as a public official, the statutory provision at issue is recognized as having a legitimate purpose, and by limiting the grounds for restriction to cases where a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment has been imposed for criminal acts that threaten the existence of the State, and by limiting the scope of restriction to only the portion exceeding the sum of the individual’s contributions, which have the character of deferred wages, and the interest thereon, it may also be said to satisfy the appropriateness of means and the balance of legal interests; furthermore, in light of the fact that the legislature has broad legislative discretion in enacting legislation in areas of social security such as the pension system (see Constitutional Court 1999. 9. 16. 97HEONBA28, Reports 11-2, 272, 280), the statutory provision at issue cannot be regarded as violating the constitutional provision guaranteeing private property rights, infringing the essential content of the right to claim retirement benefits, or being arbitrary beyond the scope of legislative discretion and contrary to the principle of proportionality.\\n\\nHowever, if the cause for the restriction of benefits under the statutory provision at issue is also understood to apply to crimes committed after retirement, it cannot but be regarded as unconstitutional.\\n\\nThe duties of fidelity, obedience, courtesy and fairness, confidentiality, integrity, compliance with laws and regulations, obedience to orders, maintenance of dignity, etc., which are duties of a public official in the course of or outside the course of duty, are, in principle, duties imposed during service only (exceptionally, the duty of confidentiality continues to apply after retirement by special provisions of laws and regulations), and it cannot be said that a person continues to bear unlimited duties of fidelity and loyalty to the State even after retiring from public office. If the entitlement to benefits such as retirement benefits is restricted on the basis of a crime committed after retirement under the statutory provision at issue, this will be the same as imposing on a public official, even after retirement, the same obligations as during service. Moreover, the fact that the harm to the State is greater when a public official commits a crime threatening the existence of the State as prescribed in the statutory provision at issue than in the case of an ordinary person basically applies when the public official commits the crime while serving, and it cannot be said that the danger remains at the same level after retirement. Of course, when a former public official becomes involved in such a crime after retirement, the harm may be more likely to be greater than in the case of an ordinary person, but the difference is not large enough to justify a serious infringement of legal interests such as restricting or depriving retirement benefit entitlements.\\n\\nIn addition, the nature of a public official’s duties varies widely, ranging from persons engaged in simple labor to persons handling state secrets, and the period of service may also vary from 1 or 2 years to several decades; thus, in requiring fidelity to duty and loyalty to the State from public officials, it would be reasonable to differentiate the degree of disadvantage by considering the nature of the duties handled by the relevant public official and the length of service, etc., and thereby distinguish the degree to which the existence or security of the State and the people’s peace and security is affected. However, to uniformly regulate the matter without any distinction as to the type of duty or the length of service, and to impose on a former public official who served only in short-term simple labor work the disadvantage of recovery of benefits for life, exceeds the freedom of legislative formation and is an excessive restriction.\\n\\nMoreover, the right to claim benefits under the Government Employees Pension Act arises upon retirement or death of a public official; therefore, restricting the right to claim benefits on grounds arising after retirement amounts to retroactively restricting a right to claim benefits that has already arisen on the basis of a ground arising later.\\n\\nAccordingly, interpreting the cause for restriction of benefits under the statutory provision at issue so that it also applies to crimes committed after retirement lacks appropriateness as a means to achieve the legislative purpose and, by imposing excessive harm on a former public official in light of the legislative purpose, loses the balance of legal interests; thus, it violates the principle of proportionality, infringes the essential content of property rights, and is unconstitutional.\\n\\n(2) Whether the principle of clarity is violated\\n\\nThe principle of clarity, as an expression of the rule of law, is a constitutional principle that the content of legal norms restricting fundamental rights must be clear. Its basis lies in the fact that if the meaning and content of a legal norm are uncertain, legal stability and predictability cannot be secured, and it enables arbitrary interpretation and enforcement by the authorities charged with law enforcement (see Constitutional Court 1990. 4. 2. 89HEONGA113, Reports 2, 49; 1996. 8. 29. 94HEONBA15, Reports 8-2, 74, 84; 2001. 10. 25. 2001HEONBA9, Reports 13-2, 491, 498). In other words, by defining laws in clear terms, the law must provide fair notice so that those subject to it may know in advance the content of the regulation and be given guidance for future conduct, thereby preventing discriminatory or arbitrary interpretation of the law. If the people cannot know from the meaning and content of legal norms what conduct is prohibited and what conduct is permitted, legal stability and predictability cannot be secured, and arbitrary enforcement by the authorities becomes possible (see Constitutional Court 1992. 4. 28. 90HEONBA27, etc., Reports 4, 255, 268-269; 1998. 4. 30. 95HEONGA16, Reports 10-1, 327, 341-342; 2000. 2. 24. 98HEONBA37, Reports 12-1, 169, 179).\\n\\nUnder the principle of clarity, the degree of clarity required is not the same for all laws; there may be differences in the degree required depending on the nature of each law or statutory provision, and it may vary according to the specificity of each constituent requirement and the background or circumstances under which such law was enacted. Generally, where a provision has a burdensome character, the principle of clarity is required more strictly than where it has a benefit-conferring character, and in criminal laws governed by the principle of nulla poena sine lege, the degree of clarity is heightened and a stricter standard is applied; however, in general laws, the degree of clarity is not required so strongly, and a relatively relaxed standard is applied (see Constitutional Court 2000. 2. 24. 98HEONBA37, Reports 12-1, 169, 179).\\n\\nBecause the statutory provision at issue is a burdensome provision that restricts or deprives the right to claim benefits, a strict standard applies with respect to the principle of clarity; yet Article 64(3) of the Government Employees Pension Act, which is the statutory provision at issue, unlike the preceding paragraphs 1 and 2, which clearly specify that the time of occurrence of the cause is “for a cause arising during service,” merely enumerates the types of crimes involved without any mention whatsoever as to whether the cause is limited only to “a cause arising during service” or also includes “a cause arising after retirement.” Such wording in the statutory text constitutes a defect in legislation, and as a result it gives rise to the conflicting interpretations described above. If, by virtue of such an unclear provision, “a cause arising after retirement” is regarded as falling within the cause for benefit restriction, then the law is unclear and enables arbitrary interpretation and enforcement by the authorities, and thus it is a provision contrary to the constitutional principle of clarity.\\n\\nIf the statutory provision at issue were a provision encompassing both causes arising during service and causes arising after retirement, such content should ordinarily have been expressly stated. Since the statutory provision at issue does not use such wording, it cannot be interpreted as permitting already accrued benefit entitlement to be restricted on the basis of a cause arising after retirement. Accordingly, although the statutory provision at issue is an independent paragraph distinct from paragraphs 1 and 2 of the same Article, it is reasonable to construe paragraph 3 as having been drafted by carrying forward the phrase “for a cause arising during service ...” contained in paragraphs 1 and 2. If so construed, it is not unconstitutional.\\n\\n(3) Whether the principle of equality is violated\\n\\nThe principle of equality before the law set forth in Article 11(1) of the Constitution by no means means absolute equality that denies all differential treatment; rather, it means that not only in applying the law but also in making legislation, unreasonable differential treatment shall not be made (Constitutional Court 1989. 5. 24. 89HEONGA37, etc., Reports 1, 48). Since the statutory provision at issue treats ordinary crimes and anti-state crimes differently with respect to restriction of retirement benefits, we examine whether this violates the principle of equality.\\n\\nIf one takes the position of limiting the statutory provision at issue to “a cause arising during service,” there is the following difference in the scope of benefits restricted between a person who committed an ordinary crime while serving as a public official and a person who committed an anti-state crime while serving. That is, when a public official commits an ordinary crime during service, retirement benefits and retirement allowance are partially reduced and paid pursuant to Article 64(1) of the Government Employees Pension Act and Article 55(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Government Employees Pension Act, whereas when a public official commits an anti-state crime during service, under the statutory provision at issue, nothing is paid except the sum of the contributions already paid plus interest under the Civil Act. However, because such discrimination has a rational basis in that the harm to the State is far greater when a public official commits an anti-state crime during service than in the case of an ordinary crime, it cannot be said to violate the principle of equality.\\n\\nHowever, if the statutory provision at issue is interpreted as also applying to crimes committed after retirement, then a significant distinction arises between the case where a public official commits an ordinary crime after retirement and the case where a public official commits an anti-state crime after retirement. A person who commits an ordinary crime after retirement is subject to no restriction on the right to claim retirement benefits, whereas a person who commits an anti-state crime such as a violation of the National Security Act is retroactively deprived of retirement benefits regardless of how much time has passed since retirement.\\n\\nAs stated above, it is not possible to impose on a public official duties more onerous than those imposed on ordinary persons even after retirement, and because the risk arising from involvement in anti-state crimes decreases after retirement, there is no rational basis for treating anti-state crimes committed after retirement fundamentally differently from ordinary crimes. Accordingly, interpreting the statutory provision at issue as also applying to anti-state crimes committed after a public official’s retirement and thereby restricting the right to claim retirement benefits by treating such crimes differently from ordinary crimes committed after retirement discriminates against persons who committed anti-state crimes after leaving public office without a rational basis, and thus violates the constitutional principle of equality.\\n\\n(4) Whether the principle of due process is violated\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues that the statutory provision at issue violates the principle of due process prescribed in Article 12(1) of the Constitution because, in restricting benefits, it does not even give the party an opportunity to explain.\\n\\nUpon review, the statutory provision at issue mandates that, where the relevant grounds exist, benefits shall not be paid, so even if a hearing procedure is held, there is no possibility that the content of the benefit restriction would change depending on the outcome. Moreover, because the decision concerning benefit restriction is an administrative disposition, and a recipient who objects to the decision has an avenue for relief by petitioning the Government Employees Pension Benefits Review Committee for review (Article 80(1) of the Government Employees Pension Act, Article 84 of the Enforcement Decree of the Government Employees Pension Act) and filing an administrative lawsuit, it cannot be said that the statutory provision at issue violates the principle of due process merely because it does not directly provide for a hearing procedure, etc. before the recovery measure of benefits (see Constitutional Court 2000. 6. 29. 98HEONBA106, Reports 12-1, 833, 847).\\n\\n(5) Whether it constitutes double punishment\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues that the statutory provision at issue, by imposing a restriction on benefits in addition to criminal punishment for criminal acts of a public official or former public official, constitutes double punishment contrary to the spirit of the Constitution. Although the statutory provision at issue imposes an additional economic disadvantage on a public official who commits a certain crime in addition to criminal punishment or disciplinary action under public official law, the “punishment” referred to in the principle of ne bis in idem or the prohibition of double punishment set forth in the latter sentence of Article 13(1) of the Constitution, in principle, means criminal punishment as the State’s exercise of its punitive power over crime, and it cannot be said that all sanctions or adverse dispositions imposed by the State are included therein. Therefore, even if benefits are restricted under the statutory provision at issue, it does not amount to double punishment prohibited by the Constitution.\\n\\n(6) Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the cause for restriction of retirement benefits under the statutory provision at issue should be interpreted as limited to a cause arising during service, and to the extent that it is construed as applying beyond that range to a cause arising after retirement, it violates the constitutional guarantee of property rights, the principle of clarity, and the principle of equality.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, Article 64(3) of the Government Employees Pension Act, which is the subject matter of review in this case, is unconstitutional to the extent that it applies causes arising after retirement and restricts benefits under the Government Employees Pension Act, and accordingly, by unanimous opinion of all participating Justices, the decision is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the principle of clarity are incorrect? (In case of dispute, according to precedent)
A: (a) Among the provisions of the Public Official Election Act prohibiting any person from disrupting the order of speeches or debates at public places for speeches or debates, or by any other means whatsoever, the portion “by any other means whatsoever” violates the principle of clarity under the principle of legality in criminal law.
B: (a) In the provision of the Nationality Act that allows only a person who is a dual national and intends to choose a foreign nationality to renounce nationality only when he or she has an address in a foreign country, the phrase “when he or she has an address in a foreign country” does not violate the principle of clarity.
C: (a) Although the principle of clarity applies to provisions on grounds excluding illegality, such as self-defense, because they are provisions that set negative limits on the provisions of elements of an offense, they are not provisions that positively determine the establishment of a crime; therefore, it cannot be said that the principle of clarity required by the principle of legality in criminal law applies.
D: (a) In order for an exemplary legislative form that simultaneously prescribes the major premise (general clause) subject to regulation and illustratively prescribes specific individual cases falling thereunder not to violate the principle of clarity, the general clause itself must be a concept containing a meaning capable of encompassing the specific examples; however, the specific cases given as examples need not themselves even contain guidelines for judgment for interpreting the general clause.
E: (a) The provision of the Labor Standards Act that punishes an employer who dismisses, etc. a worker without “just cause” violates the principle of clarity because it is difficult for an ordinary person to foresee what constitutes “just cause” without the assistance of a legal expert.
label: E

{"[2007HEONBA72]": "1. Overview of the Case and Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nA. Overview of the Case\\n\\n(1) The Petitioner was elected in the by-election for Mayor of Yeongcheon on April 30, 2005 and served as Mayor of Yeongcheon from May 1 of the same year until June 30, 2006. During his term of office, he ran as the candidate of the OO Party for Mayor of Yeongcheon in the 4th Nationwide Simultaneous Local Election held on May 31 of the same year and, as a person elected, on or about May 15, 2006, in submitting a property declaration for a public office election candidate to the Yeongcheon City Election Commission, he omitted KRW 184,775,885, which he had held in an account under another person’s name, and submitted a property declaration form containing false entries, thereby causing an election commission employee who was unaware of the circumstances to post false property details, and around that time, after producing a booklet-type election campaign brochure at his election office, caused the election commission to distribute 44,550 copies to the constituency residents, and on the ground that he violated Article 250(1) of the Public Official Election Act by publicly announcing false facts concerning property to the advantage of the candidate, the Daegu District Court sentenced him to a fine of 1.5 million won.\\n\\n(2) The Petitioner appealed to the Daegu High Court, but the appeal was dismissed, and thereupon he filed an appeal to the Supreme Court (2007DO2598) and, at the same time, an application for a request for a constitutional ruling concerning the above Article 250(1) of the Public Official Election Act (2007CHOGI169). Thereafter, when the Supreme Court on June 28, 2007 dismissed the above appeal and simultaneously dismissed the above application for a constitutional ruling, the Petitioner filed the constitutional complaint in this case on July 19, 2007.\\n\\nB. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nAlthough the Petitioner seeks an adjudication on the entirety of Article 250(1) of the Public Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 7189 of March 12, 2004), the portion the Petitioner wishes to contest is the portion that reads “a person who publicly announces or causes to be publicly announced false facts concerning the candidate’s property by means of publicity documents or other methods so as to be favorable to the candidate” (hereinafter referred to as the “statutory provision at issue”), because the question is whether that portion violates the Constitution; therefore, the subject matter of review in this case shall be limited to the above portion.\\n\\n[Provision Subject to Adjudication]\\n\\nPublic Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 7189 of March 12, 2004) Article 250 (Crime of Publicizing False Facts) ① A person who, for the purpose of being elected or causing another to be elected, publicly announces or causes to be publicly announced false facts concerning the candidate (including a person who intends to become a candidate; the same shall apply in this Article) or the candidate’s spouse or lineal ascendants, descendants, or siblings, such as place of birth, status, occupation, career, property, personality, conduct, or affiliation with an organization, etc., so as to be favorable to the candidate, by speech, broadcasting, newspaper, communications, magazine, posters, publicity documents, or other methods (including cases where educational background is indicated but not indicated by the method prescribed in Article 64 (Campaign Posters), paragraph (1)), and a person who possesses false publicity documents for the purpose of distributing them, shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 5 years or by a fine not exceeding 30 million won.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nPublic Official Election Act Article 49 (Candidate Registration, etc.) ① to ③ omitted  \\n④ A person applying for candidate registration pursuant to paragraphs (1) through (3) shall submit the following documents and shall pay the deposit under the provisions of Article 56 (Deposit), paragraph (1).  \\n2. A declaration concerning assets subject to registration under Article 10-2 (Disclosure of Assets of Candidates for Public Office, etc.) of the Public Service Ethics Act, paragraph (1)  \\n⑤ to ⑪ omitted  \\n⑫ The competent constituency election commission shall disclose the documents submitted or reported to it pursuant to items 2 through 6 of paragraph (4) and paragraph (10) in a manner that makes them easily known to the constituency residents. Provided, however, that they shall not be disclosed after the election day.  \\n⑬ to ⑭ omitted  \\n⑮ The form of the candidate’s application for registration and recommendation form, the method of disclosing the submitted and reported documents, and other necessary matters shall be prescribed by the Rules of the National Election Commission.\\n\\nArticle 65 (Election Campaign Brochure) (as amended by Act No. 7681 of August 4, 2005) ① A candidate (in the case of a presidential election, this means the candidate recommended by a political party; in the case of a proportional representation election for members of the National Assembly and a proportional representation election for members of a local council, this means the recommending political party. In this case, matters requiring explanation concerning the candidate information disclosure materials may have the explanatory materials included together.  \\n1.
