The Petitioner’s Arguments, Reasons for the Supreme Court’s Rejection of the Request for a Constitutional Ruling, and the Summary of the Opinions of the Related Agency\\n\\nA. The Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\n(1) The statutory provision at issue punishes a person who publicizes false facts concerning property, but it places no restriction whatsoever on the type or scope of the property and merely provides for “property”; however, in general, “property” means all tangible and intangible things having economic value, and because its literal meaning is extremely inclusive and broad, making it difficult for the addressee of the norm to foresee the normative content, it violates the principle of clarity under the principle of legality in criminal law.\\n\\n(2) The statutory provision at issue punishes the act of publicizing false facts by means of “publicity documents or other methods,” but this alone does not make it clear what form should be regarded as a document or other method. In addition, if publicizing false facts through an election campaign brochure is included within the statutory provision at issue, a contradiction arises in that the statutory provision at issue and Article 255(2), item 2 of the Public Official Election Act are applied redundantly.\\n\\n(3) The requirement of “so as to be favorable to the candidate” prescribed in the statutory provision at issue is unclear whether it is a subjective indicator meaning “with the intent to make [the candidate] favorable” or an objective indicator meaning “to cause an objectively favorable situation”; and in the latter case, whether understatements of property operate favorably or unfavorably in an election may vary depending on the social climate at the time or the consciousness of voters, and thus it is excessively abstract and vague.\\n\\nB. Reasons for the Supreme Court’s Rejection of the Request for a Constitutional Ruling\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of Article 250(1) of the Public Official Election Act is to ensure the fairness of elections by regulating acts that affect the voters’ correct judgment by publicizing false facts, and although it does not separately define the portions concerning “property,” “so as to be favorable,” and “by publicity documents or other methods,” these concepts are those whose meaning can be understood, by persons with sound common sense and ordinary legal feelings, through ordinary methods of interpretation. With respect to “property,” according to Article 49(4), item 2 of the same Act, a person applying for candidate registration is required to submit a declaration concerning assets subject to registration under Article 10-2(1) of the Public Service Ethics Act, so its meaning can be interpreted on the basis of the assets subject to registration under the Public Service Ethics Act. “So as to be favorable” can be understood as a concept distinguished from the subjective element of the purpose of election, meaning to objectively benefit the candidate. “Publicity documents” can be regarded as meaning documents containing contents such as the candidate’s career, views, personal history, and the like, together with photographs, symbols, and the like. “By other methods” can be interpreted as using media that convey information comparable to speech, broadcasting, newspapers, communications, magazines, posters, and publicity documents. Therefore, with respect to the portions “concerning property,” “so as to be favorable,” and “by publicity documents or other methods” in the statutory provision at issue, a reasonable standard of interpretation can be found from the wording of the legal norm, the legislative purpose, the systematic structure of the legal norm, and the like, and thus it cannot be said that they violate the principle of legality in criminal law, including the principle of clarity.\\n\\nC. The Opinion of the Minister of Justice\\n\\n(1) The reason that “property” is included among the objects of publicizing false facts under the crime of publicizing false facts is attributable to the former Act on the Election of Public Officials and the Prevention of Election Malpractice having required public office candidates to declare the assets subject to registration under the Public Service Ethics Act at the time of candidate registration; and the “property” in the statutory provision at issue can be sufficiently interpreted by taking the registered assets under the Public Service Ethics Act as the standard.\\n\\n(2) The “publicity documents or other methods” prescribed in the statutory provision at issue can be interpreted as in the purport of the Supreme Court precedents, and booklet-type election campaign brochures and leaflet-type election campaign brochures produced and distributed pursuant to the provisions of Article 65 of the Public Official Election Act may be said to be typical examples corresponding to “publicity documents” in the statutory provision at issue.\\n\\n(3) If, by the publication of false facts, there is a possibility that voters will give a favorable evaluation of the candidate and thereby help the candidate to be elected, the requirement of “so as to be favorable” is satisfied. In the statutory provision at issue, the question is whether publicly announcing false facts concerning property is favorable to the candidate, not, as the Petitioner argues, whether the amount of property is large or small and whether that is favorable to the candidate.\\n\\n(4) Although the statutory provision at issue does not contain a separate definition of the meaning of its constituent elements, it can be reasonably interpreted as above and provides sufficient predictability to the addressee of the norm, while also excluding arbitrary interpretation or enforcement by the law-enforcement authorities; therefore, it does not run counter to the principle of clarity.\\n\\n3. Decision\\n\\nA. Legislative Purpose of the Statutory Provision at Issue\\n\\nArticle 250(1) of the Public Official Election Act, which contains the statutory provision at issue, was newly enacted when the Act on the Election of Public Officials and the Prevention of Election Malpractice was enacted as Act No. 4739 on March 16, 1994. Article 250(1) of the Public Official Election Act is a provision intended to ensure the fairness of elections by punishing any act that affects voters’ fair judgment by publicizing false facts so as to be favorable to the candidate for the purpose of being elected or causing another to be elected. It is intended to enable voters to make the right choice with accurate material for judgment concerning the candidate by preventing false facts favorable to the candidate from being publicized.\\n\\nAlthough the principle of free elections is not expressly stated in our Constitution, it is a legal principle inherent in the election system of a democratic state, and its basis may be found in the principle of popular sovereignty, the principle of parliamentary democracy, and the provisions concerning the right to vote and stand for election. This principle of free elections refers to the freedom of the voter’s formation of intent and the freedom of the voter’s realization of intent required throughout the entire election process (see Constitutional Court 1994. 7. 29. 93HEONGA4, etc., Court Collection 6-2, 15, 28).\\n\\nIn order for voters to make a fair judgment as to whom to vote for in an election, it is necessary that accurate material for judgment be provided concerning the candidate, etc. If false materials are provided concerning the candidate, etc., there is a risk that the voters’ fair and accurate judgment may be distorted. Therefore, in elections, it is necessary that accurate information concerning the candidate’s career, etc. be delivered to voters through election campaign brochures, campaign posters, election broadcasts, rallies, and the like, and at the same time that the dissemination of false information be prevented.\\n\\nB. Whether the Statutory Provision at Issue Is Unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) The principle of clarity under the principle of legality in criminal law\\n\\nThe degree to which the constituent elements of a punitive provision must be clear cannot be determined uniformly, and must be comprehensively determined by considering the particularity of each constituent element and the conditions that gave rise to such legal regulation, the degree of punishment, and the like (see Constitutional Court 1997. 3. 27. 95HEONGA17, Court Collection 9-1, 219, 232).\\n\\nIn other words, the “principle of clarity,” which is an expression of the rule-of-law principle, is basically required of all legislation limiting fundamental rights, because if the addressee of the norm cannot know from the meaning and content of the norm what conduct is prohibited and what conduct is permitted, legal stability and predictability cannot be secured, and it will also make arbitrary enforcement by the law-enforcement authorities possible (see Constitutional Court 1998. 4. 30. 95HEONGA16, Court Collection 10-1, 327, 341-342).\\n\\nThis principle of clarity is especially strictly required in punitive provisions. However, the fact that the constituent elements must be clear does not mean that the legislature must define all constituent elements by simple descriptive concepts; rather, it should be understood to mean that the provisions must be drafted so that anyone can know, even by ordinary methods of interpretation that do not allow arbitrariness, the protected legal interest of the relevant punitive provision, the acts prohibited thereby, and the type and degree of punishment. Even if the constituent elements of a punitive provision are somewhat broad and use concepts that, to some extent, require supplementary interpretation by a judge, that fact alone cannot necessarily be regarded as being contrary to the clarity of punitive provisions required by the Constitution.\\n\\nOtherwise, the constituent elements of punitive provisions would become excessively specific and formulaic, and would not properly regulate the diverse and constantly changing relationships of life.\\n\\nHowever, since the provisions must be drafted so that anyone can know, even by ordinary methods of interpretation that do not allow arbitrariness, the protected legal interest of the relevant punitive provision, the acts prohibited thereby, and the type and degree of punishment, the degree to which the constituent elements of a punitive provision must be clear cannot be determined uniformly, and must be comprehensively determined by considering the particularity of each constituent element and the conditions that gave rise to such legal regulation, the degree of punishment, and the like (see Constitutional Court 1993. 3. 11. 92HEONBA33, Court Collection 5-1, 29, 47-48; Constitutional Court 1994. 7. 29. 93HEONGA4, etc., Court Collection 6-2, 15, 32-33; Constitutional Court 1995. 5. 25. 93HEONBA23, Court Collection 7-1, 638, 647-648; Constitutional Court 2000. 11. 30. 99HEONBA95, Court Collection 12-2, 298, 310, etc.; Constitutional Court 2002. 4. 25. 2001HEONBA26, Court Collection 14-1, 301, 321-322).\\n\\n(2) Whether the statutory provision at issue violates the principle of clarity\\n\\nThe statutory provision at issue regulates the act of publicly announcing false facts concerning the property of a public election candidate by means of publicity documents or other methods so as to be favorable to the candidate for the purpose of being elected. We shall examine whether the constituent elements prescribed in the statutory provision at issue are vague and violate the principle of clarity.\\n\\n(a) The portion concerning “property”\\n\\nThe property registration and disclosure system for public office candidates was first introduced when the Public Service Ethics Act was amended on June 11, 1993, in order to regulate unjust enrichment through public office. Accordingly, persons who intend to become candidates in various public office elections were required, upon registering as candidates, to submit to the competent election commission a declaration concerning the assets subject to registration, and the competent election commission was required to disclose the declared matters at the time of announcing candidate registration. Thereafter, when the Act on the Election of Public Officials and the Prevention of Election Malpractice was enacted in 1994, a property registration and disclosure system for public office candidates identical in content to the above Public Service Ethics Act was established.\\n\\nAccording to the current Public Official Election Act, a person applying for candidate registration shall submit a declaration concerning assets subject to registration under Article 10-2 (Disclosure of Assets of Candidates for Public Office, etc.) of the Public Service Ethics Act, paragraph (1) (Article 49(4), item 2 of the Public Official Election Act), and the competent constituency election commission shall disclose the candidate registration documents it has received in a manner easily known to the constituency residents, such as by posting them on the Election Commission’s Internet homepage (Article 49(12) of the Public Official Election Act and Article 20 of the Public Official Election Management Rules).\\n\\nMeanwhile, the property subject to declaration upon candidate registration means the assets subject to registration as of December 31 of the preceding year under Article 4 of the Public Service Ethics Act (Article 10-2(1) of the Public Service Ethics Act). These are the assets of the person himself or herself, the spouse (including a person in a de facto marital relationship), and lineal ascendants and descendants of the person himself or herself (provided, however, that married lineal descendants who are women, maternal great-grandparents, maternal grandparents, maternal grandchildren, and maternal great-grandchildren are excluded), and refer to the items specifically enumerated in paragraph (2) of the same Article as assets of the persons listed in Article 4(1), items 1 through 3 (including assets actually owned regardless of the name under which ownership is registered, assets contributed to a non-profit corporation, and assets located abroad). Accordingly, assets registered in the name of the person himself or herself, the spouse, or the lineal ascendants and descendants of the person himself or herself are assets subject to registration regardless of the actual ownership relationship, and assets actually owned even though not registered in the name of the person himself or herself, the spouse, or the lineal ascendants and descendants of the person himself or herself are also to be regarded as assets subject to registration. In addition, the Public Service Ethics Act also specifically prescribes the method for calculating or indicating the value of each type of registered asset (Article 4(3)).\\n\\nIn light of the fact that, through the relevant provisions of the Public Official Election Act and the Public Service Ethics Act, the object of property that a candidate running in a public office election must register and disclose is clearly prescribed, and in light of the legislative purpose of the statutory provision at issue, namely, to ensure the fairness of elections by punishing any act that affects voters’ fair judgment by publicly announcing false facts so as to be favorable to the candidate, it is appropriate to view the scope of “property” under the statutory provision at issue as, on a provisional basis, the assets subject to registration of public office candidates under Article 4 of the Public Service Ethics Act, namely, property capable of influencing voters’ judgment concerning the candidate.\\n\\nIf so, an ordinary addressee of the norm can not only foresee the scope of the above “property,” but also cannot be regarded as subject to arbitrary enforcement by the law-enforcement authorities in this regard; therefore, the above portion concerning “property” cannot be said to be contrary to the principle of clarity under the principle of legality in criminal law.\\n\\n(b) The portion concerning “publicity documents”\\n\\nThe form of conduct regulated by the statutory provision at issue is the dissemination of false facts by speech, broadcasting, newspapers, communications, magazines, posters, publicity documents, or other methods. Among them, publicity documents appear to mean documents containing contents such as the candidate’s career, views, personal history, and the like, together with photographs, symbols, and the like. Article 58(2) of the Public Official Election Act restricts election campaigning by methods not prescribed by the Act, and Articles 64 through 109 specifically enumerate permitted and prohibited methods of election campaigning, such as campaign posters, election campaign brochures, and election pledges. As one of the methods of election campaigning, a candidate may prepare a booklet-type election campaign brochure (including a leaflet-type election campaign brochure in a presidential election), and the number of pages, quantity, submission and sending, and matters to be stated in the election campaign brochure are restricted by the Public Official Election Act (Article 65 of the Public Official Election Act).\\n\\nTherefore, if the provisions of the Public Official Election Act concerning election campaigning are considered comprehensively, the “publicity documents” prescribed in the statutory provision at issue mean documents containing contents such as the candidate’s career, views, personal history, and the like, together with photographs, symbols, and the like, and the booklet-type election campaign brochure at issue in this case may also be regarded as corresponding to such publicity documents.\\n\\n(c) The portion concerning “by other methods”\\n\\nThe portion “by other methods” in the statutory provision at issue may be said to constitute an exemplary legislative form. An exemplary legislative form adopts a method of prescribing the general premise subject to regulation while also exemplarily prescribing specific individual cases that fall thereunder.\\n\\nIn such an exemplary legislative form, if the general clause is too inclusive, leaving a broad range of discretion to judges and making it possible to expand its scope of application through arbitrary interpretation, this is contrary to the principle of clarity. Therefore, for an exemplary legislative form not to violate the principle of legal clarity, the specific cases exemplified must themselves contain standards for judgment for interpreting the general clause, and the general clause itself must be a concept containing a meaning capable of encompassing such specific examples (see Constitutional Court 2000. 4. 27. 98HEONBA95, Court Collection 12-1, 508, 532-535; Constitutional Court 2002. 6. 27. 2001HEONBA70, Court Collection 14-1, 601, 608, etc.).\\n\\nThe crime of publicizing false facts under Article 250(1) of the Public Official Election Act, which contains the statutory provision at issue, is intended to prevent interference with the voters’ fair judgment and to ensure the fairness of elections by punishing a public office candidate’s public announcement, for the purpose of being elected, of false facts concerning property, etc., so as to be favorable to the candidate. And as methods of publicizing such false facts, Article 250(1) lists “speech, broadcasting, newspapers, communications, magazines, posters, publicity documents, or other methods.”\\n\\nThe “speech, broadcasting, newspapers, communications, magazines, posters” exemplified as methods of publicizing false facts are those specifically regulated by the Public Official Election Act as methods of election campaigning, and publicity documents, as noted above, mean documents containing contents such as the candidate’s career, views, personal history, and the like, together with photographs, symbols, and the like. Thus, the things exemplified as methods of publicizing false facts are all means of conveying information concerning a public office candidate to an unspecified or a large number of persons.\\n\\nTherefore, the “other methods” in the statutory provision at issue can be sufficiently interpreted as encompassing such specific examples and meaning media that convey information concerning a public office candidate to an unspecified or a large number of persons, comparable to speech, broadcasting, newspapers, communications, magazines, posters, and publicity documents.\\n\\nIn a complex and diverse society that is constantly changing, it would be technically impossible or extremely difficult for the legislature to enumerate in detail and descriptively all the various information-conveying media that may arise in the future. In order to supplement deficiencies in legal norms and secure the adaptability of legal norms to a changing society, an exemplary legislative form is required. Accordingly, it appears that the legislature used the somewhat indeterminate concept of “other methods” in the statutory provision at issue and thereby did not determine all the constituent elements individually but left them to supplementary interpretation by judges.\\n\\nIn conclusion, the statutory provision at issue is intended to prevent false facts from being publicized so as to distort voters’ fair judgment, and the speech, broadcasting, newspapers, communications, magazines, posters, and publicity documents listed above all bear the characteristic of being media that convey information to an unspecified number of persons. Thus, “other methods” should also be interpreted as means of conveying information to an unspecified number of persons comparable to the media listed above, and in that respect it does not violate the principle of clarity under the principle of legality in criminal law.\\n\\n(d) The portion concerning “so as to be favorable to the candidate”\\n\\n“So as to be favorable to the candidate” may mean an intention to make it possible for voters to give a favorable evaluation of the candidate and thereby help that person’s election, and this can be understood as meaning, as an objective matter, making it beneficial to the candidate, as a concept distinguished from the subjective element of the purpose of election.\\n\\n(e) The portion concerning “publicizing” “false facts”\\n\\n“False facts” means facts not conforming to objective truth and is sufficient if they are likely to cause voters to misjudge the candidate accurately; however, this does not apply where the expression is merely an expression of opinion containing only a simple value judgment or evaluation (see Supreme Court Judgment 2007DO4294, rendered on Aug. 24, 2007).\\n\\nAnd “publicizing” means informing an unspecified or a large number of persons of false facts, regardless of the means or method used (see Supreme Court Judgment 98DO1992, rendered on Sept. 22, 1998).\\n\\n(f) The issue of redundant application with Article 255(2), item 2 of the Public Official Election Act\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues that Article 255(2), item 2 of the Public Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 7681 of August 4, 2005) punishes with imprisonment for not more than 2 years or a fine not exceeding 4 million won “a person who, in violation of Article 65, paragraph (7), does not include all or part of the candidate information disclosure materials in the election campaign brochure,” and that if publicizing false facts through an election campaign brochure is included in the statutory provision at issue, a contradiction arises in that the statutory provision at issue and the above Article 255(2), item 2 are applied redundantly.\\n\\nHowever, Article 255(2), item 2 of the Public Official Election Act is a provision punishing the mere act of making a false entry, and where such act constitutes publicizing false facts so as to be favorable to the candidate with the purpose of being elected, it may be punished under Article 250 of the Public Official Election Act (Supreme Court Judgment 2007DO2598, rendered on June 28, 2007); thus, the scope of application of the statutory provision at issue is distinguished from Article 255(2), item 2 as above, and it cannot be said to violate the principle of clarity.\\n\\n(g) Concluding remarks\\n\\nAs seen above, Article 250(1) of the Public Official Election Act is a provision intended to ensure the fairness of elections by punishing any act that affects voters’ fair judgment by publicly announcing false facts concerning the candidate, etc., so as to be favorable to the candidate for the purpose of being elected. For fair judgment by voters, it is necessary that accurate material for judgment concerning the candidate be provided to the voters.\\n\\nTaking this legislative purpose and the relevant provisions of the Public Official Election Act comprehensively into account, even by ordinary methods of interpretation that do not allow arbitrariness, anyone can sufficiently know what specific conduct is prohibited by the act of “publicly announcing false facts concerning the candidate’s property by means of publicity documents or other methods so as to be favorable to the candidate,” as prescribed in the statutory provision at issue. Therefore, merely because it uses concepts requiring supplementary interpretation by a judge, it cannot be said to violate the principle of clarity of the principle of legality in criminal law required by the Constitution.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the statutory provision at issue does not violate the Constitution, and thus, by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices, it is decided as stated in the Order."}
