The requesting party, Lee ○○, was the head of the ○○ Regional Headquarters of the ○○ Federation, and the requesting party, Cha ○○, was the director of the organizing bureau of the ○○ Regional Headquarters of the ○○ Federation.\\n\\nb. The requesting parties were indicted on the following charge: on 2018. 12. 12., from around 10:58 to around 11:25 on 2018. 6. 9., in front of the ○○ Department Store, while Lim ○○, who had run as the Democratic Party candidate for Mayor of Daegu in the 7th Nationwide Local Elections, and Democratic Party leader Chu ○○ were delivering speeches appealing for support, they held placards bearing expressions such as “Abolition of the Minimum Wage Cut Act, working minimum wage, the lives of workers,” and chanted slogans such as “Abolish the Minimum Wage Cut Act, denounce the Democratic Party, it is noisy. You fraudster, the Democratic Party is finished, dump the Democratic Party, Chu ○○ should resign.” In addition, the requesting party Cha ○○ attempted twice to enter the stage for the above speech, and some participants blocked with their bodies the vehicles of Democratic Party officials, including Chu ○○, who, after finishing a campaign support speech at around 11:27 on the same day, were trying to board vehicles and move away, and lay down on the road while shouting “We denounce the Democratic Party, abolish the Minimum Wage Act.” They also committed assault, and by other means, including pushing police officers who were restraining them, disturbed the order at places for speeches and dialogues in public places. (Daegu District Court 2018GOHAP554)\\n\\nc. The requesting parties filed an application for a constitutional review referral regarding the “in connection with election campaigning” portion of Article 256(3)1 of the Public Official Election Act and the “by assault, intimidation, or any other means whatsoever” portion of Article 104 of the same Act (Daegu District Court 2019CHOGI123), but the referring court accepted the application regarding the “or any other means whatsoever” portion of Article 104 of the Public Official Election Act and, on 2019. 4. 12., referred the constitutional review in this case.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe referring court referred the question of unconstitutionality with respect to the “or any other means whatsoever” portion of Article 104 of the Public Official Election Act, and because the requesting parties were indicted on the charge that they “disturbed the order at places for speeches and dialogues in public places,” the subject matter of review is limited to the relevant portion.\\n\\nAccordingly, the subject matter of review in this case is whether the portion of Article 104 of the Public Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 7189 on 2004. 3. 12.) concerning “No person shall, by any other means whatsoever, disturb the order at places for speeches and dialogues in public places, pursuant to the provisions of this Act, or ...” (hereinafter referred to as the “provision under review”) is in violation of the Constitution.\\n\\nThe provision under review and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision Under Review]\\n\\nPublic Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 7189 on 2004. 3. 12.)\\n\\nArticle 104 (Prohibition of Disorderly Conduct at Rally Venues, etc.) No person shall, by assault, intimidation, or any other means whatsoever, disturb the order at places for speeches and dialogues, debate or discussion halls, or party meeting venues in public places pursuant to the provisions of this Act, or interfere with their proceedings, and no torches may be used except when used by the organizer of speeches, dialogues, etc. for lighting the podium and its surroundings.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nPublic Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 12393 on 2014. 2. 13.)\\n\\nArticle 79 (Speeches and Dialogues in Public Places) ① A candidate (excluding candidates for proportional representation members of the National Assembly and candidates for proportional representation members of local councils; hereinafter the same in this Article) may, during the election campaign period, hold speeches and dialogues in public places in order to publicize the platform and policies of the political party to which the candidate belongs, the candidate’s views, and other necessary matters.\\n\\n② In paragraph 1, “speeches and dialogues in public places” means that the candidate, election office manager, election liaison office head, election campaign worker (hereinafter referred to in this Article as “the candidate, etc.”), and a person designated from among those who may conduct election campaigning as the candidate, etc. visit roadsides, squares, open lots, community halls, markets, or stores, or other public places frequented by many persons as prescribed by the Rules of the National Election Commission, and deliver speeches appealing for support for a political party or candidate, or engage in dialogues by responding to questions from the audience.\\n\\nArticle 101 (Prohibition of Other Speeches, etc.) No person shall, during the election period, for the purpose of influencing the election, hold a personal policy presentation meeting, current affairs lecture meeting, roundtable, debate meeting, or other speech meeting or debate/discussion meeting by gathering a large number of persons, except for speeches and dialogues or debate/discussion meetings pursuant to the provisions of this Act.\\n\\nArticle 237 (Offense of Obstructing the Freedom of Election) ① Any person who falls under any one of the following subparagraphs in relation to an election shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 10 years or by a fine of not less than 5 million won and not more than 30 million won.\\n\\n2. A person who obstructs meetings, speeches, or transportation, or obstructs the freedom of election by collusion, fraud, or any other improper means\\n\\n③ Any person who throws a dangerous object or assaults a candidate or a speaker at a place for speeches and dialogues or a debate/discussion meeting prescribed in this Act shall be punished according to the following classifications:\\n\\n1. A ringleader: imprisonment for a fixed term of not less than 5 years\\n\\n2. A person who directs others or acts at the forefront of others: imprisonment for a fixed term of not less than 3 years\\n\\n3. A person who acts in concert: imprisonment for not more than 7 years\\n\\nArticle 256 (Crimes of Violation of Various Restriction Provisions) ③ Any person who falls under any one of the following subparagraphs shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 2 years or by a fine of not more than 4 million won.\\n\\n1. A person who, in connection with election campaigning, falls under any one of the following items\\n\\nta. A person who, in violation of the provisions of Article 104 (Prohibition of Disorderly Conduct at Rally Venues, etc.), disturbs the order at places for speeches and dialogues, etc. or uses or causes the use of torches\\n\\n3. Grounds for the Referring Court’s Request for a Constitutional Review\\n\\na. The provision under review is not phrased as “by assault, intimidation, or other analogous means” but is phrased as “by assault, intimidation, or any other means whatsoever,” so there is no basis to interpret “any other means” restrictively as conduct similar to assault or intimidation, or conduct equivalent thereto, and because there is no restriction whatsoever on the form of acts that disturb order, it is difficult under ordinary methods of interpretation to ascertain in a univocal and clear manner what specific means are meant. From a legislative drafting perspective, it is not difficult to enumerate illustratively or specifically identify acts disturbing order at rally venues, etc. Therefore, the provision under review violates the principle of definiteness.\\n\\nb. The provision under review places no restriction on acts that disturb order at rally venues, etc. or interfere with their proceedings, and therefore can restrict even expressive acts that are difficult to directly affect the fairness and calm of the election, excluding the possibility of considering the individuality and specificity of concrete cases, and it provides for criminal punishment in contravention of the subsidiarity of criminal punishment for persons who violate it. Therefore, the provision under review infringes the people’s freedom of political expression and general freedom of action.\\n\\n4. Determination\\n\\na. Content of the Provision Under Review\\n\\n(1) The provision under review is a provision intended to ensure the smooth conduct of speeches and dialogues in public places, which is one of the methods of election campaigning for obtaining voters’ support by announcing a candidate’s views and policies, and to secure safety and order at places for speeches and dialogues, thereby achieving fairness in elections.\\n\\n(2) Disorderly conduct, etc. at places for speeches and dialogues was prohibited from the time the former “Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act” was enacted on 1994. 3. 16. by Act No. 4739 (Article 104), and violations were punishable by imprisonment for not more than 2 years or by a fine of not more than 4 million won (Article 256(1)1(ta)). Thereafter, when the former “Public Official Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act” was amended by Act No. 7189 on 2004. 3. 12., it was restructured in the same manner as Article 104 of the current Public Official Election Act, and its substantive content was the same as at the time of enactment, with only minor textual amendments. The penal provision for disorderly conduct, etc. at places for speeches and dialogues was also changed in location or wording as the Public Official Election Act was amended, but the statutory sentence has remained exactly the same through the current Act.\\n\\nb. Issues\\n\\n(1) The referring court made a referral for unconstitutionality on the ground that the “any other means whatsoever” portion of the provision under review, which serves as the basis for criminal punishment, is unclear. Accordingly, the issue is whether the “any other means whatsoever” portion of the provision under review violates the principle of definiteness under the principle of legality in criminal law.\\n\\n(2) In addition, in the reasons for the referral of unconstitutionality, the referring court states that the provision under review uniformly prohibits even expressions that are helpful to the fairness of elections, thereby excessively infringing the people’s freedom of political expression and general freedom of action. Since the provision under review may restrict the freedom of political expression of the general public by prohibiting disorderly conduct at places for speeches and dialogues, the issue is whether the provision under review infringes the freedom of political expression. However, because freedom of political expression is a fundamental right concretized from the general freedom of action, which has a comprehensive character, and since the question of infringement of freedom of political expression is decisive, we will not separately determine whether the provision under review infringes the general freedom of action.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, below we examine whether the provision under review violates the principle of definiteness under the principle of legality in criminal law, and whether it violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and thereby infringes the freedom of political expression.\\n\\nc. Whether It Violates the Principle of Definiteness Under the Principle of Legality in Criminal Law\\n\\n(1) The principle of legality in criminal law guaranteed through Articles 12 and 13 of the Constitution means that crimes and punishment must be prescribed by law, and the principle of definiteness derived from this principle requires that the elements of a crime be defined clearly so that anyone can foresee what conduct is punishable under the law and what punishment is imposed therefor, and can thereby determine his or her conduct accordingly.\\n\\nHowever, the requirement that the elements of a crime be clear does not mean that the legislative authority must define all elements of a crime by mere descriptive concepts in the ordinary sense; rather, it should be understood to mean that the law must be drafted so that, even by ordinary methods of interpretation that do not permit arbitrariness, anyone can know the protected legal interest of the penal provision at issue, the conduct prohibited thereby, and the type and extent of punishment. Therefore, even if the elements of a penal provision are somewhat broad and use concepts that require supplementary interpretive work by a judge in some respects, that alone cannot necessarily be regarded as contrary to the clarity required of penal provisions by the Constitution (see Constitutional Court, 2016. 7. 28., 2015HEONBA6).\\n\\n(2) Determination\\n\\nThe Public Official Election Act permits speeches and dialogues in public places as one of the methods of election campaigning, while establishing the provision under review and prohibiting acts that disturb the order at places for speeches and dialogues by any other means whatsoever. This is intended to ensure the smooth conduct of speeches and dialogues in public places and to secure safety and order at places for speeches and dialogues, thereby guaranteeing opportunities for free and fair election campaigning.\\n\\nUnder the heading “Prohibition of Disorderly Conduct at Rally Venues, etc.,” the provision under review prohibits acts that disturb the order at places for speeches and dialogues by “any other means whatsoever.” Before the phrase “any other means whatsoever,” the form of conduct of “assault, intimidation” is specified, and in the Public Official Election Act, acts obstructing meetings and speeches themselves are subject to separate criminal provisions and are punished more severely than when the provision under review is violated (Article 237(1)2).\\n\\nOrdinarily, disorder means noisiness and confusion, and disturbance means the state of morals, order, norms, and the like becoming disordered. These terms are ordinary terms used in daily life and, except in special cases, are concepts that even laypersons can easily understand without the supplementary interpretive function of a judge; their meaning in the provision under review is not substantially different from such ordinary meaning.\\n\\nAccordingly, if one comprehensively considers the legislative intent and purpose of the provision under review, its relationship with other provisions of the Public Official Election Act, and the textual meaning of the provision under review, one can see that the phrase “any other means whatsoever” in the provision under review means all forms of conduct that, as acts disturbing order at places for speeches and dialogues, even if they do not reach the level of interfering with speeches and dialogues, break a free and peaceful atmosphere and thereby hinder smooth communication between the candidate, etc. and voters, or reach the extent of posing a risk of an accident.\\n\\nIf so, it is difficult to regard the “any other means whatsoever” portion of the provision under review as a concept that allows arbitrary interpretation or application by enforcement authorities, or as so unclear that the norm-addressee cannot foresee it; therefore, it cannot be said to violate the principle of definiteness under the principle of legality in criminal law.\\n\\nd. Whether It Violates the Principle of Prohibition of Excessive Restriction\\n\\n(1) Legitimacy of the Legislative Purpose and Suitability of the Means\\n\\nThe provision under review is intended to ensure the smooth conduct of speeches and dialogues in public places, which is one of the methods of election campaigning, and to secure safety and order at places for speeches and dialogues, thereby guaranteeing opportunities for free election campaigning and achieving fairness in elections; thus, the legitimacy of the legislative purpose is recognized.\\n\\nIf disorderly conduct were permitted at places for speeches and dialogues where many people with different political views gather, free and equal opportunities for election campaigning would not be guaranteed, and prohibiting it contributes to securing fairness in elections. Therefore, the suitability of the means of the provision under review is recognized.\\n\\n(2) Least Restrictive Means\\n\\n(a) Mass speeches at rallies were one of the most common methods of election campaigning, but they had harmful effects, such as being abused as a means of displaying force through the unlawful mobilization of audiences. Accordingly, the Public Official Election Act abolished mass speeches and prohibited, during the election period, the holding of personal policy presentation meetings, current affairs lecture meetings, roundtables, debates, or other speech meetings or debate/discussion meetings by gathering a large number of persons for the purpose of influencing the election, except for speeches and dialogues or debate/discussion meetings under the provisions of the Public Official Election Act (Article 101). Therefore, speeches and dialogues in public places under the Public Official Election Act are exceptionally permitted opportunities, under the above restrictions, for candidates, etc. to directly inform voters of the candidate’s insight or qualifications, policies, views, and the like, and to demonstrate differentiation from other candidates; hence, there is a strong need to secure not only smooth proceedings but also safety and order.\\n\\n(b) Maintaining order and creating a safe environment at places for speeches and dialogues where many people gather guarantees opportunities for free and fair election campaigning. However, even if disorderly conduct at places for speeches and dialogues does not reach the level of obstructing the speech itself, if it is not prohibited, speeches or dialogues in which candidates and voters can face each other directly cannot proceed smoothly, and in some cases there is also a risk that such conduct may be abused as a means of obstructing election campaigning. Therefore, in order to ensure the smooth conduct of speeches and dialogues, secure safety and order at places for speeches and dialogues, and guarantee opportunities for free election campaigning, the need to prohibit all disorderly conduct is recognized, and it is difficult to regard the provision under review as imposing an excessive restriction by stipulating “any other means whatsoever” in addition to assault and intimidation and thereby prohibiting all disorderly conduct.\\n\\n(c) The Public Official Election Act contains separate provisions imposing criminal punishment more severely than the provision under review for acts obstructing speeches, acts of throwing dangerous objects at speech venues, or acts of assaulting a candidate or speaker (Article 237(1)2, paragraph 3). However, those provisions require that the acts amount to obstruction of meetings or speeches to the extent of infringing the freedom of election, or they are limited to acts of throwing dangerous objects or acts of assault against candidates or speakers; thus, it is difficult to conclude that they are methods that can secure safety and order at places for speeches and dialogues to the same extent as the provision under review.\\n\\n(d) Accordingly, it is difficult to say that the provision under review violates the least restrictive means requirement.\\n\\n(3) Balance of Legal Interests\\n\\nThe provision under review prohibits only disorderly conduct at places for speeches and dialogues in order to guarantee opportunities for free election campaigning and secure fairness in elections, and does not prohibit all political expressive acts. Even acts that cause some noise are permitted as political expression so long as they do not disturb order. Voters may have opportunities to express their political views, such as by participating in dialogues, even without disturbing order, and they may also express negative views or critical opinions toward a candidate or a political party. Accordingly, as compared with the public interest the provision under review seeks to achieve, it is difficult to regard it as excessively restricting freedom of political expression; therefore, it does not violate the balance of legal interests either.\\n\\n(4) Conclusion on This Point\\n\\nAccordingly, it is difficult to regard the provision under review as violating the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and thereby infringing the freedom of political expression.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, since the provision under review does not violate the Constitution, the decision is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices."}

{"[2020HEONBA603]": "1. Case Overview\\n\\na. The Petitioner was born on April 14, 2001, in the United States of America (hereinafter referred to as “the United States”) to a father of U.S. nationality and a mother of the nationality of the Republic of Korea, and is a multiple-nationality holder who acquired both U.S. nationality and the nationality of the Republic of Korea.\\n\\nb. According to Article 14(1) of the Nationality Act, a multiple-nationality holder who intends to renounce Korean nationality may file a declaration to that effect only if he or she has a domicile in a foreign country.\\n\\nc. The Petitioner, after registering an address in the United States where the Petitioner’s aunt resides around January 2019, filed a declaration of renunciation of nationality, but on September 30, 2019, the Minister of Justice rejected the above declaration on the ground that the Petitioner was deemed to have his or her living basis in Korea at the time and thus could not be regarded as having a domicile in a foreign country (hereinafter referred to as “the Disposition at Issue”).\\n\\nd. The Petitioner filed an action seeking revocation of the Disposition at Issue, but on April 9, 2020, the court of first instance dismissed it (Seoul Administrative Court 2019GUHAP91336). The Petitioner then appealed and, while the appellate case was pending, filed a motion for referral for adjudication on the constitutionality of Article 14(1) of the Nationality Act; however, the appellate court dismissed the appeal on November 27, 2020 (Seoul High Court 2020NU40176) and, on the same date, also dismissed the motion for referral for adjudication on the constitutionality (Seoul High Court 2020A1323). Accordingly, after receiving service of the order dismissing the motion for referral for adjudication on the constitutionality on November 30, 2020, the Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint on December 30, 2020.\\n\\ne. Meanwhile, the Petitioner filed an appeal on December 14, 2020, but the Supreme Court dismissed it on April 1, 2021, without proceeding to substantive review (Supreme Court 2020DU57981).\\n\\n2. Subject of Review\\n\\na. In addition to the primary claim against Article 14(1) of the Nationality Act, the Petitioner also makes an alternative claim that the phrase “having a domicile in a foreign country” in this provision is unconstitutional insofar as it is interpreted as “having an actual living basis in a foreign country.”\\n\\nHowever, this is merely a quantitative part of the primary claim regarding Article 14(1) of the Nationality Act, and therefore is not treated as a separate subject of review.\\n\\nb. Moreover, since what the Petitioner challenges with respect to Article 14(1) of the Nationality Act is the main clause of the provision, it is appropriate to limit the subject of review to the main clause of Article 14(1) of the Nationality Act.\\n\\nAccordingly, the subject of this review is whether the main clause of Article 14(1) of the Nationality Act (as amended by Act No. 10275 on May 4, 2010; hereinafter referred to as “the Provision under Review”) violates the Constitution. The Provision under Review and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision under Review]\\nNationality Act (as amended by Act No. 10275 on May 4, 2010)\\n\\nArticle 14 (Requirements and Procedure for Renunciation of Korean Nationality) ① A person with multiple nationality who intends to choose foreign nationality may file a declaration to the Minister of Justice, through the head of the diplomatic mission abroad having jurisdiction over the place of domicile, that he or she renounces Korean nationality only if he or she has a domicile in a foreign country. Provided, That a person falling under the main clause of Article 12(2) or under Article 12(3) may file such declaration only within that period or only from the time the relevant ground arises.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\nNationality Act (as amended by Act No. 10275 on May 4, 2010)\\n\\nArticle 14 (Requirements and Procedure for Renunciation of Korean Nationality) ② A person who has filed a declaration of renunciation of nationality pursuant to paragraph (1) loses Korean nationality when the Minister of Justice accepts the declaration.\\n\\n③ The requirements and procedures for the declaration and acceptance under paragraph (1), and other necessary matters, shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n\\nNationality Act (as amended by Act No. 18978 on September 15, 2022)\\n\\nArticle 14-2 (Special Cases Concerning Renunciation of Korean Nationality) ① Notwithstanding the main clause of Article 12(2) and the proviso to Article 14(1), a multiple-nationality holder who satisfies all of the following requirements may apply to the Minister of Justice for permission to renounce Korean nationality if he or she has failed to file a declaration that he or she renounces Korean nationality within three months from the time he or she was incorporated into the reserve military service pursuant to Article 8 of the Military Service Act.\\n\\n1. A person falling under any of the following items:\\n   a. A person born in a foreign country (excluding a person born while a lineal ascendant was staying in that foreign country without the purpose of permanent residence) who has continuously had his or her principal basis of life in a foreign country since birth\\n   b. A person who moved to a foreign country while under the age of 6 and has continuously had his or her principal basis of life in a foreign country thereafter\\n2. There must be a justifiable reason for failing to file the declaration of renunciation of nationality within three months from the time of incorporation into the reserve military service pursuant to the main clause of Article 12(2) and the proviso to Article 14(1)\\n\\n② When granting permission under paragraph (1), the Minister of Justice shall consider the following matters:\\n\\n1. The place of birth of the multiple-nationality holder and the circumstances under which multiple nationality was acquired\\n2. Whether the multiple-nationality holder’s domicile and principal place of residence are in a foreign country\\n3. The number of entries into the Republic of Korea and the purpose and period of stay\\n4. Whether rights exercisable only by nationals of the Republic of Korea have been exercised\\n5. Whether multiple nationality has caused substantial restrictions on the choice of occupation abroad or has caused equivalent disadvantages\\n6. Whether it is consistent with the fairness and harmony of the performance of the duty of military service\\n\\n③ An application for permission under paragraph (1) shall be made by a multiple-nationality holder having a domicile in a foreign country to the Minister of Justice through the head of the diplomatic mission abroad having jurisdiction over the relevant domicile.\\n\\n④ A person who applies for permission to renounce nationality pursuant to paragraphs (1) and (3) loses Korean nationality when the Minister of Justice grants the permission.\\n\\n⑤ The detailed qualification standards for applicants under paragraphs (1) through (4), the specific matters to be considered when granting permission, application and permission procedures, and other necessary matters shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n\\nCivil Act (enacted by Act No. 471 on February 22, 1958)\\n\\nArticle 18 (Domicile) ① The place serving as the basis of life shall be the domicile.\\n\\nEnforcement Decree of the Nationality Act (as amended by Presidential Decree No. 22588 on October 31, 2010)\\n\\nArticle 18 (Procedure for Renunciation of Korean Nationality, etc.) ① A person with multiple nationality who intends to file a declaration that he or she renounces Korean nationality pursuant to Article 14(1) of the Act shall prepare the declaration form for renunciation of nationality prescribed by the Ordinance of the Ministry of Justice and submit it to the head of the diplomatic mission abroad having jurisdiction over the place of domicile, and the head of the diplomatic mission abroad shall promptly transmit it to the Minister of Justice.\\n\\n② The Minister of Justice shall accept a declaration of renunciation of nationality under paragraph (1) only where the declaration satisfies the requirements for renunciation of nationality under Article 14(1) of the Act.\\n\\n3. The Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\na. The Provision under Review permits a declaration of renunciation of nationality only to a person “having a domicile in a foreign country,” but, on its wording, it is unclear whether an actual place of residence in a foreign country is required and, if so, how long one must reside there for it to be regarded as actual residence, and thus it violates the principle of clarity.\\n\\nb. The Provision under Review unreasonably restricts the freedom to renounce nationality of persons who have difficulty having a living basis in a foreign country, such as minors, by allowing renunciation of nationality only when a domicile exists in a foreign country. Furthermore, the claim that the renunciation of nationality by multiple-nationality holders who have a living basis in Korea causes social discomfort is merely an insubstantial assertion, yet the Provision under Review restricts the renunciation of nationality by persons who find it difficult to have a domicile in a foreign country on the ground of such insubstantial public interest, and thus violates the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n4. Determination\\n\\na. Organization of Issues\\n\\nSince the Provision under Review permits a declaration of renunciation of nationality only in cases of “having a domicile in a foreign country,” it restricts the freedom to renounce nationality; therefore, we examine whether the expression “having a domicile in a foreign country” violates the principle of clarity, and whether the Provision under Review violates the principle against excessive restriction and thereby infringes the Petitioner’s freedom to renounce nationality.\\n\\nb. Whether the Principle of Clarity is Violated\\n\\n(1) All statutes must be clear because they serve as standards for the application of law by administrative and judicial authorities from the perspective of legal stability. This is because if the meaning and content of a legal norm are uncertain, legal stability and predictability cannot be secured, and there is a risk that interpretation and enforcement of the law will be carried out arbitrarily. However, since statutory provisions ordinarily have generality and abstraction, the use of terms of a certain degree of universal and general concepts is inevitable in terms of legislative technique; therefore, whether clarity is satisfied is determined by whether a reasonable interpretation is possible, taking into account the purpose for which the statute was enacted and its relation to other norms. Accordingly, if the meaning can be made clear through judicial supplementation by interpretation in light of the legislative purpose and the overall system and content of the relevant statutory provision, it cannot be said to lack clarity (see Constitutional Court 2014HEONBA421, etc., decided on July 28, 2016).\\n\\n(2) A person who possesses several nationalities simultaneously risks abusing multiple nationality by, for example, exercising only rights in each country while evading duties such as military service and taxation (see Constitutional Court 2011HEONMA502, decided on June 26, 2014, etc.), and if a person who has enjoyed the rights and benefits of a national were allowed opportunistically to abandon Korean nationality when the time comes to fulfill duties as a national, the communal principle regarding the sharing of duties as a national could be seriously undermined.\\n\\nIn this context, the Provision under Review allows renunciation of nationality only where there is a domicile in a foreign country, so as to prevent a multiple-nationality holder from using renunciation of nationality as a means to evade duties as a national of the Republic of Korea, such as taxation and national defense.\\n\\nThe expression “having a domicile in a foreign country” in the Provision under Review is an expression used not only in the Nationality Act and other statutes but also in ordinary usage, and “domicile” means the place that serves as the substantial basis of life.\\n\\nArticle 18(1) of the Civil Act also provides that the “place serving as the basis of life” is the domicile; in determining this, one must comprehensively consider not only whether there is a resident registration, but also various objective circumstances related to actual living relations, such as the entry and departure circumstances and facts of residence of family members and other interested persons, and the location of family members with whom one shares living expenses or of assets (see Supreme Court Decision 89NU8064, decided on August 14, 1990).\\n\\nTaking into comprehensive account the legislative purpose of the Provision under Review examined above, the definition in the relevant statutes, and the general public’s understanding of domicile, the phrase “having a domicile in a foreign country” means “having a living basis in another country,” and it is readily understandable that if one cannot find a living basis such as a residence or place of work in a foreign country, it cannot be recognized that one has a domicile there.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Provision under Review is not so unclear as to undermine the predictability of persons subject to the norm or cause arbitrary law enforcement by the authorities; therefore, it cannot be said to violate the principle of clarity.\\n\\nc. Whether the Principle against Excessive Restriction is Violated\\n\\n(1) Legitimacy of Purpose and Suitability of Means\\n\\n(a) Nationality is the qualification and status by which a person becomes a national, and it is the legal bond between the state and its members, meaning a relationship of protection and obedience (see Constitutional Court 97HEONGA12, decided on August 31, 2000; Constitutional Court 2011HEONMA502, decided on June 26, 2014, etc.). Matters relating to nationality are an essential element of the state and have a highly political character in that they determine the scope of the sovereign people; therefore, they are issues to be decided by the state concerned in consideration of all circumstances such as historical traditions and political, economic, social, and cultural factors (see Constitutional Court 2015HEONBA26, decided on September 24, 2015; Constitutional Court 2017HEONBA434, decided on February 27, 2020, etc.).\\n\\nThe rights and duties of nationals are tied to nationality, which is the qualification of a national; however, the time when rights are enjoyed and the time when duties must be fulfilled do not always coincide. Therefore, multiple-nationality holders have an incentive to engage in opportunistic behavior by, for example, exercising only the rights of nationals in each country while evading the performance of duties. In operating the nationality system, in order to deter such opportunistic incentives, it is necessary to restrict the act of renouncing nationality by a person who has enjoyed the rights and benefits of a national and seeks to evade the performance of duties linked to nationality when such performance is demanded.\\n\\n(b) Among the various duties borne by nationals in a democratic state, duties such as taxation and national defense have constitutional significance in that they inevitably must be borne by nationals, who are members of the state community, in order to maintain the existence of the state community (see Constitutional Court 2007HEONBA120, decided on July 30, 2009, etc.), which is also confirmed by the fact that Articles 38 and 39(1) of the Constitution specifically prescribe the duty of taxation and the duty of national defense of nationals.\\n\\nHowever, an act by which a multiple-nationality holder who has enjoyed the rights and benefits of a national renounces Korean nationality in order to evade constitutional duties as a national, such as taxation and national defense, despite having no living basis whatsoever in a foreign country, not only directly harms the existence and maintenance of the state community but also destroys social trust in the close interrelationship between the rights and duties of nationals, thereby undermining the basic principle concerning the existence and maintenance of the state community.\\n\\n(c) Therefore, the Provision under Review, in order to prevent opportunistic renunciation of nationality by multiple-nationality holders, prevent malicious evasion of duties that should properly be borne as nationals, and preserve the basic principle of the operation of the state community, allows renunciation of nationality only to those who have a domicile in a foreign country. Hence, its purpose is legitimate and the means are also suitable.\\n\\n(2) Least Restrictive Means\\n\\n(a) The Provision under Review requires, as a condition for filing a declaration of renunciation of nationality, that a multiple-nationality holder who has enjoyed the rights and benefits of a national and maintained a substantial tie with the Republic of Korea have a “domicile in a foreign country,” so as to prevent such person from evading duties by renouncing nationality when the performance of duties as a national is demanded.\\n\\nThis is the minimum restriction for preventing opportunistic renunciation of nationality, and even considering various foreign legislative examples, such as Article 8(2) of the European Convention on Nationality, which restrict the renunciation of nationality by persons without a living basis in a foreign country, the Provision under Review cannot be regarded as excessive.\\n\\n(b) The majority of those whose freedom to renounce nationality is restricted by the Provision under Review are not cases where a Korean national voluntarily acquired foreign nationality for purposes such as investment or immigration, but rather cases where the person inherently holds multiple nationality under the nationality laws of each country because, for example, one parent is a national of a foreign country that adopts jus sanguinis, or because the person was born in a foreign country that adopts jus soli even though both parents are nationals of the Republic of Korea, and thus mainly has a living basis in Korea.\\n\\nIf so, it is difficult to say that any excessive disadvantage arises from applying the restriction under the Provision under Review to a person who has possessed Korean nationality from birth and has mainly had a living basis in Korea while enjoying the rights and benefits of a national and forming a substantial tie with the Republic of Korea, merely on the ground that such person inherently possesses the nationality of that foreign country in law but has no living basis whatsoever there and seeks to renounce Korean nationality.\\n\\n(c) Meanwhile, the Petitioner argues that the Provision under Review imposes an excessive restriction because minors face practical difficulties in determining their living basis independently of their parents or other caregivers, and therefore it is excessive to uniformly require a foreign domicile as a condition for renunciation of nationality even for minors.\\n\\nHowever, minors also, as nationals, can bear constitutional duties such as taxation and national defense that are borne by all nationals; and it is not impossible for minors to choose to move their living basis abroad independently of or together with their caregivers. Moreover, our Nationality Act does not restrict such choices at all. Accordingly, it cannot be said that renunciation of nationality must be permitted even to those who have their living basis only in Korea merely because they are minors or because they realistically find it difficult to have a living basis in a foreign country.\\n\\nTherefore, the Provision under Review satisfies the least restrictive means requirement.\\n\\n(3) Balance of Interests\\n\\nThe public interest to be achieved through the Provision under Review is to prevent multiple-nationality holders who have enjoyed the rights and benefits of nationals of the Republic of Korea without having a living basis in a foreign country from evading their duties as nationals of the Republic of Korea through renunciation of nationality, thereby preserving the existence and maintenance of the Republic of Korea as a state community; this is of great importance. By contrast, the private interest restricted by the Provision under Review is no more than requiring a person who seeks to file a declaration of renunciation of nationality to have a domicile in a foreign country.\\n\\nTherefore, the Provision under Review satisfies the balance of interests.\\n\\n(4) Conclusion\\n\\nSince the Provision under Review does not violate the principle against excessive restriction, it does not infringe the freedom to renounce nationality.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, since the Provision under Review does not violate the Constitution, the decision is made as stated in the text by the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating in the case."}

{"[99HEONBA31]": "1. Outline of the Case and the Subject of Adjudication\\n\\na. Outline of the Case\\n\\n(1) The complainant was indicted before the Seoul District Court on the ground that, at around 11:00 a.m. on 1997. 8. 4., he struck the non-party Jeon ○ho with his fist and inflicted injury on him on the road in front of the Korea Hall located at 653-2, Yeoksam-dong, Gangnam-gu, Seoul. During the pendency of the trial (98GODAN10625HO), he argued that the above act of assault constituted self-defense under Article 21(1) of the Criminal Act and that unlawfulness was therefore excluded, and accordingly filed an application for referral of unconstitutionality (99CHO834HO) with respect to the portion “reasonable grounds” in that statutory provision; however, the court dismissed the application for referral of unconstitutionality on 1999. 3. 25. and at the same time rendered a judgment of conviction against the complainant.\\n\\n(2) Thereupon, on 1999. 3. 26., the complainant filed the constitutional complaint review in this case under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act with respect to the portion “reasonable grounds” in Article 21(1) of the Criminal Act (enacted by Act No. 293 on 1953. 9. 18., hereinafter referred to as the “Act”).\\n\\nb. Subject of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject of adjudication in this case is the portion “reasonable grounds” in Article 21(1) of the Act, and the content of that provision and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\nAct Article 21 (Self-Defense) ① An act performed to defend against a present unjust侵害 on the legal interest of oneself or another shall not be punished when there are reasonable grounds.\\n②-③ Omitted\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nAct Article 20 (Justifiable Acts) An act performed pursuant to statutes or regulations, an act performed in the course of duty, or any other act not contrary to social norms shall not be punished.\\n\\nArticle 22 (Necessity) ① An act performed to avoid a present danger to the legal interest of oneself or another shall not be punished when there are reasonable grounds.\\n②-③ Omitted\\n\\nArticle 23 (Self-Help) ① Where it is impossible to preserve a claim by legal procedure, an act performed to avoid the impossibility of executing the claim or a manifest difficulty in executing it shall not be punished when there are reasonable grounds.\\n② Omitted\\n\\n2. The Complainant’s Arguments and the Opinions of Related Institutions\\n\\na. The Complainant’s Arguments\\n\\nArticle 21(1) of the Act is an important part of the elements of a crime that draws negative limits on the entire Special Part of the Act as a permissive constitutive element, and therefore should be subject to the regulation of the principle of definiteness; however, the portion “reasonable grounds” in Article 21(1) of the Act is unclear in meaning. That is, where self-defense is at issue, whether guilt or innocence may be determined by the free discretion of judges rather than by law, and this violates the principle of legality or the rule of law. Although it is inevitable, from the standpoint of legislative technique, to use indeterminate concepts, such indeterminate concepts must also have minimum definiteness so as to secure the demand for legal stability; yet ambiguous expressions such as “reasonable grounds” do not even guarantee minimum definiteness.\\n\\nb. Grounds on Which the Court Dismissed the Application for Referral of Unconstitutionality\\n\\nIf the content of a legal norm is vague, there is a risk that what constitutes a crime will in fact be determined at the discretion of the authorities administering the law, which may run counter to the principle of legality. However, since it is impossible as a matter of legislative technique to construct the wording of all legal norms solely with purely technical concepts, it is unavoidable to use general and normative concepts containing a certain degree of value judgment. The portion “reasonable grounds” in Article 21 of the Act requires the use of a general concept because the arithmetical realization of definiteness is impossible as a matter of legislative technique, and the Supreme Court has indicated a preliminary standard for “reasonable grounds” by holding that whether there is social reasonableness must be determined by taking into account all concrete circumstances, such as the kind and degree of the legal interest infringed by the act of infringement, the method of infringement, the speed and urgency of the act of infringement, and the kind and degree of the legal interest that would be infringed by the act of defense; accordingly, there is little possibility that the meaning and content of the provision may vary according to the personal predilection of the person applying the law, and thus it cannot be said to violate the principle of definiteness.\\n\\nc. Opinion of the Chief Prosecutor of the Seoul District Prosecutors' Office\\n\\nThe provision of Article 21(1) of the Act is not an unlawful constitutive element but a permissive constitutive element, so the principle of definiteness under the principle of legality cannot be applied as it stands to this area; moreover, the meaning and content of the portion “reasonable grounds” have already been firmly established by Supreme Court precedents, and therefore the concept of self-defense is not a matter that can be determined by the free discretion of judges, and it cannot be said to violate the principle of definiteness under the principle of legality.\\n\\n3. Decision\\n\\na. Article 21(1) of the Act is a provision concerning self-defense among the grounds excluding unlawfulness that exclude the unlawfulness of acts falling under the elements of a crime; since it is not a provision directly defining the elements of a crime, the issue is whether the principle of definiteness under the principle of legality applies.\\n\\nThe provision on self-defense is one that sets negative limits on the provisions of the elements of crimes throughout the Special Part of the Act, and while on the one hand it functions to exclude unlawfulness and deny the establishment of a crime, on the other hand, where self-defense is not recognized, it functions to recognize the establishment of a crime as an unlawful act; therefore, even if it is not a constitutive-element provision that positively determines the establishment of a crime, it cannot be said that the application of the principle of definiteness required by the principle of legality is entirely excluded.\\n\\nAccordingly, in light of the original purpose of the principle of legality that the establishment and punishment of crimes must be governed by law, the principle of definiteness under the principle of legality also applies to provisions on grounds excluding unlawfulness such as self-defense.\\n\\nb. Next, we examine whether the portion “reasonable grounds” in Article 21(1) of the Act (hereinafter referred to as “the provision at issue”) is a provision that satisfies the principle of definiteness under the principle of legality. The concept of the provision at issue is abstract and comprehensive, and no definition is provided in this Act or any other statute; thus, there may be doubt as to whether this provision complies with the definiteness that must be satisfied as a law restricting fundamental rights.\\n\\n(1) Since it is impossible, and also undesirable, as a matter of legislative technique, to construct the wording of all legal norms solely with purely technical concepts, it is unavoidable to use general and normative concepts containing a certain degree of value judgment; therefore, if the meaning and content of the statutory wording can be ascertained through interpretation, that is, through a judge’s supplementary value judgment, and if such supplementary interpretation is not likely to be influenced by the interpreter’s personal predilection, it cannot be said to contravene the principle of definiteness (Constitutional Court 1998. 4. 30. 95HEONGA16, Case Reports 10-1, 327, 342). Meanwhile, the degree of definiteness cannot be uniformly determined, and must be comprehensively assessed by considering the special nature of each constitutive element and the circumstances that gave rise to such legal regulation, or the degree of punishment (Constitutional Court 1997. 3. 27. 95HEONGA17, Case Reports 9-1, 219, 232; 1998. 7. 16. 96HEONBA35, Case Reports 10-2, 159, 169).\\n\\nAccordingly, whether the principle of definiteness is observed with respect to the grounds excluding unlawfulness must also be determined in consideration of the characteristics of the relevant provision. Whether the principle of definiteness is satisfied should be determined depending on whether a reasonable interpretation is possible in light of the purpose of the relevant system and its connection with other statutory provisions.\\n\\n(2) Whereas the elements of a crime are standardized as general types of criminal acts, grounds excluding unlawfulness are an ex post and objective evaluation of concrete and individual acts, excluding unlawfulness and denying the establishment of a crime. That is, if an act falls within a criminal type specified in the Special Part of the Act, it is generally an unlawful act not permitted by law; however, exceptionally, an act satisfying certain requirements is specially permitted and becomes a lawful act.\\n\\nHowever, the present unjust侵害 situation that gives rise to self-defense is not confined to any particular crime, but may arise in almost all crimes involving infringement of legal interests; thus, it is nearly impossible to foresee such self-defense situations in advance and specify them one by one in statutory text. While criminal types such as assault, intimidation, and injury described in the elements of a crime have a certain static character, grounds excluding unlawfulness such as self-defense have a dynamic character that changes with social changes, and therefore cannot be designed one by one by the legislature as in the case of the elements of a crime. In a complex and diverse and changing society, the arithmetical realization of definiteness by enumerating in detail all possible and diverse self-defense situations that may arise in the future is either impossible or significantly difficult as a matter of legislative technique; in order to secure the adaptability of legal norms to a changing society, it is unavoidable to enact provisions containing, to a certain extent, comprehensive meaning. Thus, the legislature has inserted in the provision at issue, which belongs to the General Part of the Act, the indeterminate concept “reasonable grounds,” which is to a certain extent a universal and value-laden concept, and has entrusted the meaning to the judge’s supplementary interpretation without individually defining the self-defense requirements for each constitutive element.\\n\\n(3) “Reasonable grounds” in self-defense means that the defensive act against the infringement does not exceed a socially acceptable degree and is regarded as naturally justified in light of social norms. However, “reasonable grounds” is not a requirement necessary only for the establishment of self-defense, but also a requirement necessary for the establishment of necessity and self-help, which are grounds excluding unlawfulness other than self-defense. Accordingly, “reasonable grounds” is rather a term signifying the balancing of interests between the legal interest infringed and the legal interest protected, than a term having independent importance in itself, and the degree of such balancing varies depending on the type of ground excluding unlawfulness. The issue is whether persons subject to the legal norm can infer the meaning of “reasonable grounds” in self-defense. The Supreme Court has long held that, in order for self-defense to be established, the defensive act must be socially reasonable, taking into account all concrete circumstances, such as the kind and degree of the legal interest infringed by the act of infringement, the method of infringement, the speed and urgency of the act of infringement, and the kind and degree of the legal interest that would be infringed by the act of defense (Supreme Court Decisions 66DO63 rendered on 1966. 3. 15.; 84DO683 rendered on 1984. 6. 12.; 92DO2540 rendered on 1992. 12. 22.), thereby presenting a reasonable standard of interpretation for “reasonable grounds.”\\n\\nIf so, the provision at issue appears to be readily ascertainable in its meaning to the extent that an ordinary person with sound common sense and ordinary legal sentiment would understand it, and there is no concern that it would be expanded through arbitrary interpretation by judges; therefore, it cannot be said to violate the principle of definiteness required by the principle of legality.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, the provision at issue does not violate the Constitution, and thus, by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices, the decision is rendered as stated in the order."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning provisional disposition in constitutional adjudication and a stay of execution under the Administrative Litigation Act is incorrect? (Where there is dispute, according to precedents)
A: The Administrative Litigation Act prescribes, as a negative requirement for a stay of execution, that there be no risk of having a serious impact on the public welfare, and the burden of assertion and prima facie showing with respect thereto lies with the administrative agency.
B: As a general rule, a provisional disposition may be sought only while the merits case is pending before the Constitutional Court, but one may also first seek a provisional disposition on the premise of a main action and then request adjudication of the merits case.
C: While an adjudication on competence disputes is pending, the Constitutional Court may, ex officio, issue a decision suspending the effect of the respondent's disposition that is the subject of adjudication until the pronouncement of the final decision, even without the petitioner's application.
D: The Constitutional Court Act provides provisions concerning provisional disposition only with respect to adjudication on the dissolution of political parties and adjudication on competence disputes, and does not contain any express provision regarding whether provisional disposition is permitted in other constitutional adjudication procedures.
E: When determining whether there is an urgent necessity to prevent irreparable harm that would arise from the disposition, etc. or from the continuation of its execution or procedure, it is not appropriate, in light of the nature of a stay of execution, to consider the degree of likelihood of success on the merits claim.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2007MU147]": "The grounds for the reappeal are examined.\\n\\n1. As to the grounds for the reappeal relating to whether there is an interest in the application for a stay of execution\\n\\na. The former Act on Door-to-Door Sales, etc. (as amended by Act No. 8357 on 2007. 7. 19., and before its enforcement on 2007. 10. 19.) provides that a person who opens, manages, or operates a multi-level marketing organization without registering as a multi-level marketing business shall be punished by imprisonment or a fine (Article 51(1)1), and further provides that, where a person has received a corrective order from the Respondent yet fails to comply therewith or repeats the violation, a punitive administrative disposition may be imposed or imprisonment or a fine may be imposed (Article 42(4), Article 53(1)10). Thus, even if the applicant, immediately before receiving each corrective order in this case from the Respondent ordering registration, etc. of the multi-level marketing business, had preregistered the multi-level marketing business out of concern for the above criminal punishment or punitive administrative disposition, this cannot be deemed to cure the defects in each corrective order in this case. Therefore, the applicant should be regarded as being able to file an application seeking a stay of execution on the ground that each corrective order in this case is unlawful even after completing the above registration. Accordingly, the Respondent’s grounds for reappeal on this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\nb. Paragraph 4 of each corrective order in this case (the “Paragraph 5” in the statement of grounds for reappeal is a clerical error) is not a mere omission by the administrative agency, but an administrative disposition intended to prohibit the applicant from engaging in certain acts by borrowing the form of an omission order, and thus constitutes an act of the administrative agency. Accordingly, insofar as the applicant alleges that the current sales method does not fall under a multi-level marketing method, it must be deemed that the applicant also has an interest in seeking a stay of execution thereof. Accordingly, the Respondent’s grounds for reappeal on this point likewise cannot be accepted.\\n\\n2. As to the grounds for the reappeal relating to whether there is a risk of irreparable damage\\n\\n“Irreparable damage,” which is a requirement for a stay of execution under Article 23(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act, means, absent special circumstances, damage that cannot be compensated by money; this refers to tangible and intangible damage for which monetary compensation is impossible, or for which, even if monetary compensation is available, the party subject to the administrative disposition cannot, according to social norms, bear and endure it, or can bear and endure it only with considerable difficulty. Whether there is an “urgent necessity to prevent irreparable damage that would arise from the disposition, etc. or the continuation of its execution or procedure” should be determined concretely and individually by comprehensively considering not only the nature, manner, and content of the disposition, the nature, content, and extent of the damage suffered by the addressee of the disposition, the method and difficulty of restoration to the original condition and monetary compensation, but also the degree of the likelihood of success on the merits (see Supreme Court Order dated 2004. 5. 12., 2003MU41; Supreme Court Order dated 2004. 5. 17., 2004MU6, etc.).\\n\\nConsidering comprehensively the nature, manner, and content of each corrective order in this case as discernible from the record, the nature, content, and extent of the damage suffered by the applicant, who is the addressee of the disposition, and all other circumstances, including the method and difficulty of restoration to the original condition and monetary compensation, if the effect of the disposition in this case continues to be maintained, the applicant will suffer damage such as a decline in the company’s sales amount or sales growth rate due to agitation among salespersons, large-scale reorganization or downsizing of the current sales organization, etc.; and since it is not easy to determine the scope of such damage, it constitutes “irreparable damage” under Article 23(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act. Moreover, in order to prevent the applicant’s above damage, there is no other appropriate method than suspending the effect of each corrective order in this case, so it must also be deemed that there is an urgent necessity to stay its execution.\\n\\nIn the same purport, the lower court’s determination that there is an urgent necessity to prevent irreparable damage that would arise if the effect of each corrective order in this case is maintained is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of the legal doctrine regarding irreparable damage and urgency prescribed in Article 23(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act, as alleged in the grounds for reappeal.\\n\\n3. As to the grounds for the reappeal relating to whether there is a risk of causing serious harm to the public welfare\\n\\n“Risk of causing serious harm to the public welfare,” which is a ground of impediment to a stay of execution under Article 23(3) of the Administrative Litigation Act, does not mean the possibility of infringement of the general and abstract public interest, but the probability of causing serious harm to a concrete and individual public interest related to the execution of the relevant disposition. The burden of assertion and substantiation as to this negative requirement for a stay of execution lies with the administrative agency (see Supreme Court Order dated 2004. 5. 12., 2003MU41; Supreme Court Order dated 2004. 5. 17., 2004MU6, etc.).\\n\\nIn the same purport, the lower court’s determination that, if the effect of each corrective order in this case is suspended on the ground that the applicant has been conducting business for a long period without causing any particular social controversy and appears to pose little such risk in the future, there appears to be no risk of causing serious harm to the public interest, is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of the legal doctrine regarding the risk of causing serious harm to the public welfare, as alleged in the grounds for reappeal.\\n\\n4. As to the grounds for the reappeal relating to whether the principal claim has merit\\n\\nThe system of suspension of effect or stay of execution of an administrative disposition is intended to protect the applicant’s status until the applicant obtains a favorable judgment in the principal lawsuit and, at the same time, to prevent the later favorable judgment from becoming meaningless. Therefore, recognizing the suspension of effect or stay of execution even though there is no possibility of revocation of the disposition in the principal lawsuit would run counter to the purpose of the system. Accordingly, it must also be included among the requirements for suspension of effect or stay of execution that, even from the suspension-of-effect or stay-of-execution case itself, it is not manifest that the applicant’s principal claim lacks merit (see Supreme Court Order dated 2004. 5. 17., 2004MU6; Supreme Court Order dated 2007. 7. 13., 2005MU85, etc.).\\n\\nIn the same purport, the lower court’s determination that this case does not fall under a case in which the principal claim lacks merit manifestly, on the ground that there remains room for legal dispute on the merits as to whether the business method of the applicant’s door-to-door sales business division constitutes a multi-level marketing business, is proper, and there is no illegality of misapprehension of the legal doctrine regarding the likelihood of success on the principal claim, as alleged in the grounds for reappeal.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the reappeal is dismissed, and it is so decided unanimously by the Justices who participated, as per the Disposition."}
{"[2007MU176]": "The re-appeal is dismissed.\\n\\nThe costs of the re-appeal shall be borne by the Respondent."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning a constitutional complaint adjudication under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act is incorrect? (In case of dispute, according to precedents)
A: As a matter of principle, for a statute to be the object of a constitutional complaint, it must be a valid statute currently in force; however, in the case of a promulgated statute, even before it takes effect, a constitutional complaint may be filed if it is certain that it will be enforced and it is sufficiently foreseeable that the complainant may suffer disadvantage.
B: In the case of a provision of the Road Traffic Act that requires an accompanying guardian on a child transportation bus and provides a grace period for its application, the Constitutional Court regards the "date of enforcement of the law"—the time when a restriction on fundamental rights arises—rather than the "date of expiration of the grace period," as the starting point for calculating the filing period for a constitutional complaint adjudication.
C: Where a court infringes the fundamental rights of the people by applying a statute or regulation that the Constitutional Court has decided is unconstitutional, the Constitutional Court exceptionally considers a court judgment to be subject to a constitutional complaint as well.
D: Where the Constitutional Court renders a decision not to appoint state-appointed counsel in response to an application for appointment of state-appointed counsel, the period from the day the applicant filed the appointment application to the day the applicant received notice thereof is not included in the filing period for a constitutional complaint.
E: In a petition for adjudication concerning a provision of the Act on the Employment, etc. of Foreign Workers that limits the number of changes of place of business by foreign workers to 3 times, if the foreign worker has not yet attempted to change his or her place of business 3 or more times, it cannot be said that an infringement of fundamental rights caused by the provision limiting the number of such changes is certainly foreseeable at present.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2008HEONMA214]": "1. Overview of the Case and Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\na. Overview of the Case\\n\\n(1) Case 2008HEONMA214  \\nThe Petitioner, ○○ Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “○○”), filed a lawsuit seeking the cancellation of the registration of transfer of ownership in the name of Jang ○-gyu and 3 others concerning farmland, including a levee of 85,226 m² in △△-dong, Seosan-si, on the ground that such registration of transfer of ownership had been completed at the time of registration without a certificate of qualification to acquire farmland and was therefore void ab initio. On 2005. 1. 6., the above claim was dismissed (Daejeon District Court Seosan Branch 2002GAHAP884), the appeal was also dismissed (Daejeon High Court 2005NA1801), and although an appeal was filed, the appeal was likewise dismissed on 2008. 2. 1. (Supreme Court 2006DA27451).\\n\\nAccordingly, on 2008. 2. 29., Petitioner ○○ filed this constitutional complaint seeking the revocation of the above Supreme Court judgment 2006DA27451 and a declaration that the phrase “excluding court judgments” in the main clause of Article 68(1) of the former Constitutional Court Act is unconstitutional.\\n\\n(2) Case 2011HEONMA606  \\nWhen the Mayor of Cheongju issued a disposition approving the conversion to sale of a rental apartment in ○○ 3 Complex (11th Phase) in ▽▽-dong, Sangdang-gu, Cheongju, on the basis of the conversion sale price calculated by Petitioner □□ Co., Ltd. In the said case, after a judgment dismissing the action was rendered at first instance, the appellate judgment dismissing the appeal (Daejeon High Court 2009NU1509) was reversed and remanded by the Supreme Court, and the court on remand rendered a judgment revoking the said disposition (Daejeon High Court 2010NU915); on 2011. 7. 14., the appeal by the Petitioners was dismissed (Supreme Court 2010DU19591).\\n\\nAccordingly, on 2011. 10. 12., Petitioner □□ filed this constitutional complaint seeking the revocation of the above Supreme Court judgment 2010DU19591 and a declaration that the phrase “excluding court judgments” in the main clause of Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act is unconstitutional.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject matter of adjudication in this case is: ① the main clause of Article 68(1) of the former Constitutional Court Act (enacted by Act No. 4017 on 1988. 8. 5. and amended before amendment by Act No. 10546 on 2011. 4. 5.) and the phrase “excluding court judgments” in the main clause of Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act (as amended by Act No. 10546 on 2011. 4. 5.) (hereinafter, the provision of the law before amendment is referred to as “the Subject Provision Before Amendment in this Case,” the provision of the law after amendment is referred to as “the Subject Provision After Amendment in this Case,” and when the above provisions are collectively referred to, they are referred to as “the Subject Provisions in this Case”); and ② whether Supreme Court judgment 2006DA27451 rendered on 2008. 2. 1. and Supreme Court judgment 2010DU19591 rendered on 2011. 7. 14. (hereinafter, when the above judgments are collectively referred to, they are referred to as “the Subject Judgments in this Case”) infringe the Petitioners’ fundamental rights, and the contents of the Subject Provisions are as follows (the underlined portion):\\n\\n[Subject Provisions]\\n\\nFormer Constitutional Court Act (enacted by Act No. 4017 on 1988. 8. 5. and before amendment by Act No. 10546 on 2011. 4. 5.)  \\nArticle 68 (Grounds for Petition) (1) A person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of governmental power may file a petition for constitutional review with the Constitutional Court, excluding court judgments. However, where there exists a remedy procedure under another Act, such petition may be filed only after all such procedures have been exhausted.\\n\\nConstitutional Court Act (as amended by Act No. 10546 on 2011. 4. 5.)  \\nArticle 68 (Grounds for Petition) (1) A person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of governmental power may file a petition for constitutional review with the Constitutional Court, excluding court judgments. However, where there exists a remedy procedure under another Act, such petition may be filed only after all such procedures have been exhausted.\\n\\n2. Summary of the Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\na. Case 2008HEONMA214\\n\\n(1) Supreme Court judgment 2006DA27451 infringed Petitioner ○○’s property rights and equality rights, etc. by interpreting and applying Article 8 of the Farmland Act unconstitutionally to the effect that “the certificate of qualification to acquire farmland prescribed by the Farmland Act is not a requirement for the effectiveness of a juristic act that constitutes the cause of acquisition of farmland, and it is permissible to supplement it after the registration of transfer of ownership concerning the farmland has been completed.”\\n\\n(2) Even though the rights of Petitioner ○○ were infringed by an unjust judgment of a court and there is no reason to regard court judgments differently from other exercises of governmental power, the Subject Provision Before Amendment in this Case, which prohibits constitutional complaints against court judgments, infringes Petitioner ○○’s right to request a trial, etc. Even if the said provision is not wholly unconstitutional, it is unconstitutional at least to the extent that it is construed as including within its scope judgments that unconstitutionally interpret and apply the law, such as the above Supreme Court judgment.\\n\\nb. Case 2011HEONMA606\\n\\n(1) Supreme Court judgment 2010DU19591 infringed Petitioner □□’s property rights and equality rights, etc. by applying the Addenda Article 3 of the former Rental Housing Act (amended by Act No. 8966 on 2008. 3. 21. and before amendment by Act No. 9541 on 2009. 3. 25.), which was unconstitutional retroactive legislation infringing Petitioner □□’s legitimate expectation interests, and by unconstitutionally interpreting and applying the former Enforcement Decree of the Rental Housing Act (amended by Presidential Decree No. 20849 on 2008. 6. 20. and before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 21641 on 2009. 7. 27.) as not violating the principle of protection of trust despite the absence of transitional provisions.\\n\\n(2) The Subject Provision After Amendment in this Case extremely restricts the subject of constitutional complaints and violates the principle of separation of powers and the principle of a rule-of-law state, and infringes Petitioner □□’s right to request a trial and equality rights.\\n\\n3. Determination\\n\\na. Petition for Adjudication Regarding the Subject Judgments in this Case  \\nAccording to Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act, court judgments are, in principle, excluded from the subject of constitutional complaints; however, it is the established precedent of our Constitutional Court that a constitutional complaint may be filed only against a judgment that infringes the fundamental rights of the people by applying statutes that the Constitutional Court has determined to be unconstitutional (see Constitutional Court 2002. 5. 30. 2001HEONMA781, Court Decisions 14-1, 556, 562, etc.).\\n\\nHowever, since the Subject Judgments in this Case do not fall under exceptional judgments subject to constitutional complaints, this part of the petition seeking their revocation is unlawful.\\n\\nb. Petition for Adjudication Regarding the Subject Provisions in this Case  \\nWith respect to the Subject Provision Before Amendment in this Case, the Constitutional Court has already rendered a limited unconstitutional decision holding that it is unconstitutional to the extent that “court judgments” are construed to include judgments that infringe the fundamental rights of the people by applying statutes that the Constitutional Court has determined to be unconstitutional (see Constitutional Court 1997. 12. 24. 96HEONMA172, et al., Court Decisions 9-2, 842, 854-862), thereby removing the unconstitutional portion while declaring the remainder constitutional.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Subject Provisions in this Case have already been reduced in content to the remaining portion from which the unconstitutional portion has been removed, and as to this there is no change in circumstances that would justify deciding differently from the precedents that held them constitutional (see Constitutional Court 2009. 4. 30. 2007HEONMA589, Court Decisions 21-1(b), 379, 389, etc.), so the Subject Provisions in this Case cannot be deemed unconstitutional on the ground that they infringe the Petitioners’ fundamental rights.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, all petitions for adjudication regarding the Subject Provisions in this Case among the Petitioners’ petitions for adjudication are dismissed, and all petitions for adjudication regarding the Subject Judgments in this Case are dismissed as inadmissible, and the decision is rendered as stated in the disposition, with the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating.\\n\\n2012. 12. 27."}

Case 2014HEONMA760\\n\\n(1) Petitioner Nam ○○ was, on November 25, 2010, sentenced by the Jeju District Court to 4 years’ imprisonment and a forfeiture of KRW 152,650,000 for the offense of Violation of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes (bribery), on the factual basis that “from around February 1, 2003, while having been commissioned and serving as a member of the deliberation committee of the Jeju Special Self-Governing Province Integrated (Disaster) Impact Assessment Deliberation Committee, he accepted bribes in connection with the duties of such deliberation committee member, who was a public official” (Jeju District Court Decision 2009GOHAP5). Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nA. Petitioner Nam ○○ argues, with respect to the phrase “court judgments” in the main text of Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act (as amended by Act No. 10546 on April 5, 2011), that this provision is unconstitutional to the extent that it is interpreted to include judgments that, by applying statutes that the Constitutional Court has determined to be conditionally unconstitutional, infringe the fundamental rights of the people.
