This would mean that, notwithstanding the phrase “except for court judgments” in the main text of Article 68(1) of the same Act, constitutional complaint review against the court judgments of which annulment is sought should be allowed. Accordingly, this part of the petition is to be regarded as directed to the phrase “court judgments” in the main text of Article 68(1) of the same Act.\\n\\nB. Petitioner Lee ○○ also seeks review of the relevant provisions, arguing that Article 75(7) of the Constitutional Court Act violates the Petitioner’s fundamental rights insofar as “granted” is interpreted not to include the Constitutional Court’s limited unconstitutionality decision, and that Article 420(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act violates the Petitioner’s fundamental rights insofar as “when newly discovered clear evidence” among the grounds for retrial prescribed therein is interpreted not to include “when, after a final judgment of conviction, there is a limited unconstitutionality decision of the Constitutional Court regarding the statutory provision applied in that judgment.” However, Article 75(7) of the Constitutional Court Act is a provision applicable when a party to the case that gave rise to the constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the same Act seeks retrial; thus, it is not directly relevant to the above Petitioner, who, pursuant to Article 75(6) and Article 47(4) of the Constitutional Court Act, sought retrial of a conviction judgment on the ground that the penal statute lost its effect retroactively by reason of a decision of unconstitutionality. Accordingly, the petition for review of the above provision is excluded from the subject matter of this case. In addition, the petition concerning Article 420(5) of the Criminal Procedure Act challenges the judicial outcome of the court that, denying the binding force of the limited unconstitutionality decision in this case, dismissed the retrial petition; since the Petitioner separately seeks annulment of the court judgment that did not treat the limited unconstitutionality decision in this case as a ground for retrial, the petition concerning the above provision is excluded from the subject matter of this case.\\n\\nC. Accordingly, the subject matter of this case is: ① the phrase “court judgments” in the main text of Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act (as amended by Act No. 10546 on April 5, 2011) (the Constitutional Court, in Decision 2016HEONMA33 dated April 28, 2016, rendered a decision that the above phrase “court judgments” is unconstitutional to the extent that it is interpreted to include judgments that, by applying statutes that the Constitutional Court has determined to be unconstitutional, infringe the fundamental rights of the people, thereby removing the unconstitutional portion. Therefore, in order to make clear that the portion that lost effect by Decision 2016HEONMA33 is excluded from the scope of this provision, it is hereinafter referred to as “the provision barring constitutional complaints against court judgments in this case”), ② Gwangju High Court Decision (Jeju)2013JAENO2, dated November 25, 2013, which dismissed the retrial petition against Petitioner Nam ○○, and Supreme Court Decision 2013MO2593, dated August 11, 2014, which dismissed the re-appeal therefrom; Supreme Court Decision 2013MO2645, dated August 20, 2014, which dismissed the re-appeal against the decision dismissing the retrial petition against Petitioner Lee ○○ (hereinafter these retrial judgments are collectively referred to as “the retrial dismissal decisions in this case”); and ③ Supreme Court Decision 2011DO6347, rendered on September 29, 2011, which dismissed the appeal on points of law and thereby rendered final the conviction judgment against Petitioner Nam ○○, and Gwangju High Court Judgment (Jeju)2010NO13, rendered on October 20, 2010, which is the final conviction judgment against Petitioner Lee ○○ (hereinafter these judgments are collectively referred to as “the conviction judgments in this case”), namely, whether each infringes the fundamental rights of the Petitioners. The provisions under review (underlined portions) and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions under review]\\n\\nConstitutional Court Act (as amended by Act No. 10546 on April 5, 2011)\\n\\nArticle 68 (Grounds for Petition) (1) A person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public authority may file a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court, except for court judgments. Provided, That where there is a remedy procedure under other statutes, the petition may be filed only after all such procedures have been exhausted.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nConstitutional Court Act (as amended by Act No. 12597 on May 20, 2014)\\n\\nArticle 47 (Effect of a Decision of Unconstitutionality) (1) A decision of unconstitutionality of a statute binds the courts and all other state organs and local governments.\\n(2) A statute or a provision of a statute that has been held unconstitutional loses effect from the day on which such decision is rendered.\\n(3) Notwithstanding paragraph (2), a statute concerning criminal punishment or a provision of such statute loses effect retroactively. Provided, That where there has previously been a case in which the same statute or provision was held constitutional, it loses effect retroactively from the day following the date of such decision.\\n(4) In the case of paragraph (3), retrial may be sought against a final conviction judgment based on the statute or provision held unconstitutional.\\n(5) Article 420 of the Criminal Procedure Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to retrial under paragraph (4).\\n\\nConstitutional Court Act (as amended by Act No. 10546 on April 5, 2011)\\n\\nArticle 75 (Decision Granting the Petition) (1) A decision granting a constitutional complaint binds all state organs and local governments.\\n(6) In the cases of paragraph (5) and of granting a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2), Articles 45 and 47 shall apply mutatis mutandis.\\n(7) Where a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) is granted and the related litigation case has already become final and conclusive, the party may seek retrial.\\n\\n3. Summary of the Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\nA decision of unconstitutionality by the Constitutional Court concerning a statute binds the courts and all other state organs, and such a decision of unconstitutionality naturally includes a limited unconstitutionality decision.\\n\\nHowever, even though the Constitutional Court rendered a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the criminal punishment provision that served as the basis for the Petitioners’ final conviction judgments, the courts denied the binding force of the limited unconstitutionality decision and did not allow retrial, and further dismissed the re-appeals therefrom, thereby infringing the Petitioners’ right to adjudication, etc.; therefore, such court judgments must be annulled by constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act. In addition, for the purpose of prompt and effective relief of the Petitioners’ fundamental rights, the original judgments in this case, namely the conviction judgments in this case, must also be annulled.\\n\\n4. Determination\\n\\nA. Issue\\n\\nThis case concerns whether, in a situation where a limited unconstitutionality decision was rendered in a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act (hereinafter, unless the context requires otherwise, “the Act”) with respect to a criminal punishment provision, the retrial dismissal decisions in this case, which refused to allow retrial of final conviction judgments previously rendered on the basis of the relevant criminal punishment provision because the Constitutional Court’s limited unconstitutionality decision was deemed not to be a decision of unconstitutionality; the conviction judgments in this case, which became final before the limited unconstitutionality decision in this case; and the provision barring constitutional complaints against court judgments in this case, which excludes court judgments from the subject matter of constitutional complaint review, infringe the Petitioners’ fundamental rights.\\n\\nB. Power of Normative Control over Statutes and Its Effect\\n\\n(1) Power to review statutes for unconstitutionality\\n\\n(a) The Constitution grants the Constitutional Court the power to review statutes for unconstitutionality (Articles 107 and 111 of the Constitution). The Constitutional Court exercises the power of constitutional review granted by the Constitution through: review of the constitutionality of statutes upon referral by a court (Article 107(1) and Article 111(1) item 1 of the Constitution; Article 41(1) of the Act); constitutional complaint review filed by a party when a motion for referral of constitutional review of a statute has been dismissed (Article 111(1) item 5 of the Constitution; Article 68(2) of the Act); and constitutional complaint review seeking redress of rights, in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the Constitutional Court Act, for statutes that infringe fundamental rights (Article 111(1) item 5 of the Constitution; Article 68(1) of the Act).\\n\\n(b) Where the constitutionality of a statute is a preliminary question in a trial, the court in charge of the case shall refer the question of constitutionality of the statute to the Constitutional Court by decision ex officio or upon application by a party (Article 41(1) of the Act). The Constitutional Court renders a decision of unconstitutionality if the referred statute or statutory provision violates the Constitution (see Article 45 of the Act).\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 68(2) of the Act provides that where a party’s motion for constitutional review is dismissed by a court, the party that made the motion may file a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court seeking review of the constitutionality of the statute. That is, while excluding court judgments from the subject matter of constitutional complaint review in the main text of Article 68(1) of the Act, the Act opens a path for the Constitutional Court to review the constitutionality of a statute underlying a court judgment by allowing the party to the litigation, where there is suspicion that the court rendered judgment by applying an unconstitutional statute without referring it for constitutional review, to directly seek review of the constitutionality of the statute before the Constitutional Court. Although the Act provides that this is to be filed in the form of a constitutional complaint on the ground that the review is sought by an individual rather than by a court, the constitutional complaint review under Article 68(2) of the Act is, in that it is a system for seeking from the Constitutional Court a review of the “constitutionality of a statute” in connection with a concrete litigation case, equivalent to concrete norm control, just like the review of unconstitutional statutes under Article 41 of the Act.\\n\\nA constitutional complaint review concerning a statute under Article 68(1) of the Act also has the aspect of remedying the petitioner’s infringed fundamental rights, but because the constitutionality of the statute becomes the subject of judgment, the character of establishing an objective constitutional order is brought to the fore, and it is not substantially different from the concrete norm control achieved through review of unconstitutional statutes under Article 41 of the Act or through constitutional complaint review under Article 68(2) of the Act (see Constitutional Court Decision 91HEONMA21, March 11, 1991, etc.).\\n\\nAccordingly, where the unconstitutionality of a statute is confirmed in constitutional complaint review under Article 68(2) of the Act or in constitutional complaint review concerning a statute under Article 68(1) of the Act, the Constitutional Court must grant the constitutional complaint in the form of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the statute.\\n\\n(2) Binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute\\n\\nAll state organs are bound by the Constitution, and constitutional adherence is enforced through constitutional adjudication. Therefore, a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute, which is the result of the Constitutional Court’s exercise of the power of constitutional review granted by the Constitution, binds all state organs and local governments, including the courts (see Constitutional Court Decision 96HEONMA172 et al., December 24, 1997).\\n\\nArticle 47(1) of the Act provides that “a decision of unconstitutionality of a statute binds the courts and all other state organs and local governments,” Article 75(6) provides that Article 47 shall apply mutatis mutandis in cases of granting a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Act, and Article 75(1) provides that “a decision granting a constitutional complaint binds all state organs and local governments,” thereby making clear that decisions of unconstitutionality of statutes rendered through review of unconstitutional statutes, constitutional complaint review under Article 68(2) of the Act, and constitutional complaint review concerning statutes under Article 68(1) of the Act are binding on all state organs and local governments, including the courts.\\n\\nC. Binding Force of a Limited Unconstitutionality Decision as Concrete Norm Control over Statutes\\n\\nWhen reviewing whether a statute is unconstitutional, if a statute is susceptible to multiple interpretations, the Constitutional Court may determine, within the bounds of ordinary interpretive function, which interpretation is ultimately most consistent with the Constitution and, to the extent that the statute would extend its scope of application beyond the area of constitutionally acceptable restrictive interpretation, declare that such extension is unconstitutional and thereby render a limited unconstitutionality decision. This is not merely an interpretation of the statute in light of the Constitution; rather, it is work of reviewing whether the statute is unconstitutional on the basis of constitutional norms. A limited unconstitutionality decision, rendered as a result of the Constitutional Court’s constitutional review of a statute and stating that the statute is unconstitutional only insofar as it applies to a particular area, does not change the wording of the statute but constitutes a partial decision of unconstitutionality meaning that the portion of the statutory provision applicable to a specific area is unconstitutional, and falls within the authority of the Constitutional Court, which has the power to review statutes for unconstitutionality (see Constitutional Court Decisions 89HEONGA104, February 25, 1992; 96HEONMA172 et al., December 24, 1997).\\n\\nAccordingly, a limited unconstitutionality decision also constitutes a “decision of unconstitutionality of a statute” to which the binding force prescribed in Article 47(1) of the Act applies, and not only where a limited unconstitutionality decision is rendered in review of unconstitutional statutes under Article 41 of the Act, but also where the unconstitutionality of a statute is confirmed in constitutional complaint review under Article 68(2) of the Act, or in constitutional complaint review concerning a statute under Article 68(1) of the Act, and the complaint is granted in the form of a limited unconstitutionality decision, such decision constitutes a decision of unconstitutionality concerning the statute and is binding on all state organs and local governments, including the courts (Article 47(1) and Article 75(1), (6) of the Act).\\n\\nD. Determination on Whether the Provision Barring Constitutional Complaints Against Court Judgments in this Case is Unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Court judgments contrary to the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute\\n\\n(a) The Constitution grants the Constitutional Court the power to review statutes for unconstitutionality (Articles 107 and 111 of the Constitution), and a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute, which is the result of the Constitutional Court’s exercise of the power of constitutional review granted by the Constitution, binds all state organs and local governments, including the courts. Therefore, a court judgment denying the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute is, in itself, not only contrary to the binding force of the Constitutional Court’s decision, but also directly contrary to the Constitution’s determination that the Constitutional Court shall have the power to review statutes for unconstitutionality.\\n\\n(b) With respect to such court judgments, even if the main text of Article 68(1) of the Act excludes court judgments from the subject matter of constitutional complaint review, the Constitutional Court must again conduct a final review in order to uphold the supreme normativity of the Constitution and restore the power of constitutional review over statutes that the Constitution has granted to the Constitutional Court. For this purpose, by rendering a decision of unconstitutionality that expressly excludes from the scope of the phrase “court judgments” in the main text of Article 68(1) of the Act the portion consisting of “judgments contrary to the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute,” constitutional complaint review should exceptionally be allowed as to such judgments.\\n\\n(2) Scope of the decision of unconstitutionality concerning the provision barring constitutional complaints against court judgments in this case\\n\\n(a) In Constitutional Court Decision 96HEONMA172 et al., December 24, 1997, the Court held that “to the extent that the phrase ‘court judgments’ in the main text of Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act is interpreted to include judgments that, by applying statutes that the Constitutional Court has determined to be unconstitutional, infringe the fundamental rights of the people, Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act is unconstitutional,” and rendered a limited unconstitutionality decision as to former Article 68(1) before its amendment by Act No. 10546 on April 5, 2011. Thereafter, by rendering the same type of limited unconstitutionality decision as to the phrase “court judgments” in the main text of Article 68(1) of the Act as amended by Act No. 10546 on April 5, 2011 (Constitutional Court Decision 2016HEONMA33, April 28, 2016), the Court removed the unconstitutional portion, while subsequently holding that the provision barring constitutional complaints against court judgments in this case, reduced in content to the remaining portion from which the unconstitutional part had been removed, is constitutional (see Constitutional Court Decisions 2015HEONMA940, May 26, 2016; 2015HEONMA861 et al., August 30, 2018; 2018HEONMA1093, June 28, 2019; 2020HEONMA271, March 25, 2021, etc.).\\n\\n(b) The fundamental purport of the above decisions is that, with respect to court judgments that infringe the fundamental rights of the people in violation of the Constitutional Court’s binding decision of unconstitutionality, the Constitutional Court must conduct a final review again in order to uphold the supreme normativity of the Constitution and restore the power of constitutional review over statutes that the Constitution has granted to the Constitutional Court. However, as seen above, a limited unconstitutionality decision means, as a result of constitutional review of a statute, that the portion of the statutory provision applicable to a particular area is unconstitutional. In the case of a limited unconstitutionality decision, the binding force of the decision of unconstitutionality extends to all state organs and local governments, including the courts, only with respect to the portion that the Constitutional Court has expressly indicated in the operative part as excluded from application. Therefore, in the main text of Article 68(1) of the Act, the portion of the “court judgments” provision that lost effect by the previous limited unconstitutionality decision (2016HEONMA33) is limited to the portion of the “judgments that infringe the fundamental rights of the people by applying statutes that the Constitutional Court has determined to be unconstitutional” among court judgments contrary to the binding force of the Constitutional Court’s decision of unconstitutionality. Accordingly, in order to exclude all of the “judgments contrary to the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute” from the field of application of the constitutional complaint prohibition prescribed by the main text of Article 68(1) of the Act, a separate decision of unconstitutionality is required as to the relevant portion of the provision barring constitutional complaints against court judgments in this case.\\n\\n(3) Conclusion on this point\\n\\nAccordingly, the portion of the provision barring constitutional complaints against court judgments in this case consisting of “judgments contrary to the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute” is unconstitutional.\\n\\nE. Determination on the Retrial Dismissal Decisions in this Case\\n\\n(1) Binding force of the limited unconstitutionality decision in this case\\n\\n(a) The Constitutional Court, in Decision 2011HEONBA117 dated December 27, 2012, held that “the term ‘public official’ in Article 129(1) of the Criminal Act (as enacted by Act No. 293 on September 18, 1953) is unconstitutional to the extent that it is interpreted to include a commissioned member among the members of the deliberation committee of the Jeju Special Self-Governing Province Integrated Impact Assessment Deliberation Committee under Article 299(2) of the former Special Act on the Establishment of Jeju Special Self-Governing Province and the Development of Free International City (before amendment by Act No. 8566 on July 27, 2007),” thereby rendering a limited unconstitutionality decision that left the wording of the statute itself unchanged while excluding and eliminating only a portion of the area to which the statute applies.\\n\\nIt cannot be denied that the power to interpret and apply statutes in concrete cases constitutes an essential aspect of judicial power. However, the fact that the wording of the statutory provision itself did not change, and that the Constitutional Court used the expression “interpretation” to indicate the portion of the statutory provision that violates the Constitution and loses effect, does not mean that a limited unconstitutionality decision, which is the result of constitutional review of a statute, can be regarded as control over the courts’ power to interpret and apply statutes in concrete cases rather than norm control.\\n\\n(b) The limited unconstitutionality decision in this case is not a review of the propriety of a court’s specific interpretation and application of the criminal punishment provision in a concrete case, but a partial decision of unconstitutionality declaring that a part of the criminal punishment provision violates the Constitution and is invalid. The reason the scope of the decision of unconstitutionality was specifically limited in this way in the limited unconstitutionality decision in this case was that, where a decision of unconstitutionality is rendered with respect to a criminal punishment provision, there is a need to minimize confusion in legal stability caused by retroactive effect and to make as clear as possible the scope of the decision of unconstitutionality binding on state organs such as the courts. In addition, removing only the unconstitutional portion of a criminal punishment provision is an expression of restraint in intervening in legislative acts and of respect for the legislature.\\n\\nAccordingly, the limited unconstitutionality decision in this case constitutes a partial decision of unconstitutionality and thus a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute. Pursuant to Article 75(6) and Article 47(3) of the Act, the portion of the term “public official” in Article 129(1) of the Criminal Act (as enacted by Act No. 293 on September 18, 1953) corresponding to the commissioned member among the members of the deliberation committee of the Jeju Special Self-Governing Province Integrated Impact Assessment Deliberation Committee under Article 299(2) of the former Special Act on the Establishment of Jeju Special Self-Governing Province and the Development of Free International City (before amendment by Act No. 8566 on July 27, 2007) lost effect retroactively. In addition, the limited unconstitutionality decision in this case has binding force on the courts and all other state organs and local governments pursuant to Article 75(6) and Article 47(1) of the Act.\\n\\n(2) Whether the court judgments fall exceptionally within the scope of judgments subject to constitutional complaint review\\n\\nThe retrial dismissal decisions in this case denied the binding force of the limited unconstitutionality decision in this case and dismissed the Petitioners’ retrial petitions on the ground that “as to so-called limited unconstitutionality decisions, which merely declare unconstitutional only the interpretation and application of specific content concerning a statutory provision while leaving the statutory provision itself intact, the effect of a decision of unconstitutionality as provided in Article 47 of the Constitutional Court Act cannot be recognized; as a result, a limited unconstitutionality decision cannot bind the courts and cannot constitute a ground for retrial.” Since this denies the binding force of the limited unconstitutionality decision in this case, which is a partial decision of unconstitutionality and whose binding force is recognized under Article 75(6) and Article 47(1) of the Act, the retrial dismissal decisions in this case constitute “judgments contrary to the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute.” Accordingly, with respect to the retrial dismissal decisions in this case, a constitutional complaint seeking their annulment is exceptionally permitted.\\n\\n(3) Whether the right to seek adjudication was infringed\\n\\n(a) Article 27(1) of the Constitution provides that “all citizens shall have the right to a trial in accordance with the law by judges qualified under the Constitution and the law,” confirming the self-evident rule-of-law principle that courts are bound by statutes, and guaranteeing “the right to a trial in accordance with the law, that is, the right to receive a trial in accordance with the substantive law through the procedural steps prescribed by procedural law” (see Constitutional Court Decisions 90HEONBA25, June 26, 1992; 90HEONBA35, July 29, 1993).\\n\\n(b) Article 75(7) of the Act provides that “where a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) is granted and the related litigation case has already become final and conclusive, the party may seek retrial,” thereby granting a litigant the right to seek retrial; and “where a constitutional complaint is granted” includes cases where the Constitutional Court renders a limited unconstitutionality decision. In addition, Article 47(3) and (4) of the Act provide that “a statute concerning criminal punishment or a provision of such statute loses effect retroactively, and in such a case retrial may be sought against a final conviction judgment based on the statute or provision held unconstitutional,” thereby allowing a person who has already been convicted to seek retrial when there is a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute on criminal punishment, and Article 75(6) provides that this shall apply mutatis mutandis “where a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) is granted.” “Where a constitutional complaint is granted” here also includes cases where the Constitutional Court renders a limited unconstitutionality decision.\\n\\nAccordingly, the retrial dismissal decisions in this case, which denied the binding force of the limited unconstitutionality decision in this case and did not accept it as a ground for retrial, infringe the Petitioners’ right to seek adjudication.\\n\\n(4) Conclusion on this point\\n\\nAll of the retrial dismissal decisions in this case are “judgments contrary to the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute,” and constitutional complaint against them is permissible. Since they infringed the Petitioners’ constitutionally guaranteed right to seek adjudication, they must be annulled pursuant to Article 75(3) of the Act.\\n\\nF. Determination on the Conviction Judgments in this Case\\n\\nThe conviction judgments in this case were rendered final before the limited unconstitutionality decision in this case as to the statutory provision applied in the judgments, namely, “the portion of the term ‘public official’ in Article 129(1) of the Criminal Act (as enacted by Act No. 293 on September 18, 1953) corresponding to the commissioned member among the members of the deliberation committee of the Jeju Special Self-Governing Province Integrated Impact Assessment Deliberation Committee under Article 299(2) of the former Special Act on the Establishment of Jeju Special Self-Governing Province and the Development of Free International City (before amendment by Act No. 8566 on July 27, 2007).”\\n\\nA statute concerning criminal punishment loses effect retroactively by reason of a decision of unconstitutionality (Article 47(3) of the Act). However, in our country, where the procedure for constitutional adjudication reviewing the constitutionality of statutes is separately institutionalized by the Constitution and statutes, all statutes are presumed constitutional until the Constitutional Court declares them unconstitutional. Thus, although a court may, where there is a suspicion of unconstitutionality, refer the statute to the Constitutional Court and temporarily suspend its application, it cannot refuse to apply the statute. Therefore, the application of a statute by a judge at the stage prior to a decision of unconstitutionality is institutionally guaranteed as legitimate. Accordingly, a judgment applying a statute that has not yet been declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court cannot later be challenged as an unlawful exercise of public power merely because a decision of unconstitutionality was rendered thereafter and made subject to constitutional complaint review (see Constitutional Court Decision 99HEONMA461 et al., February 22, 2001), and the same applies even where a criminal punishment provision loses effect retroactively by reason of a decision of unconstitutionality by the Constitutional Court; relief therefrom is possible only through retrial proceedings.\\n\\nThe reason why Article 75(7) of the Act provides that “where a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) is granted and the related litigation case has already become final and conclusive, the party may seek retrial,” and Article 47(3) recognizes the retroactive effect of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute on criminal punishment, while Article 47(4) separately provides that relief may be obtained through retrial proceedings in court against a final conviction judgment based on the statute or provision held unconstitutional, is the same as above.\\n\\nTherefore, the conviction judgments in this case, which became final before the limited unconstitutionality decision in this case, cannot be regarded as judgments contrary to the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute, and thus do not fall within the exceptional category of judgments subject to constitutional complaint review; the petitions seeking review thereof are therefore inadmissible.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the portion of the provision barring constitutional complaints against court judgments in this case consisting of “judgments contrary to the binding force of a decision of unconstitutionality concerning a statute” is unconstitutional, and the retrial dismissal decisions in this case infringe the Petitioners’ right to seek adjudication, and are therefore all annulled. Since the Petitioners’ remaining petitions are inadmissible, they are all dismissed. It is so decided unanimously by all Justices participating in the case, as stated in the operative part."}

Provided, That the amended provisions of Article 12(1)4 shall enter into force on the day after 6 months have elapsed from the date of its promulgation, and the amended provisions of Article 13(6) shall enter into force on the day after 3 months have elapsed from the date of its promulgation.\\n\\nArticle 3 (Special Applicability to Obligations of Drivers and Operators, etc. of Children’s School Buses) The amended provisions of Article 53(3) shall apply to children’s school buses with a seating capacity of 15 or fewer seats operated at academies under the Act on the Establishment and Operation of Private Teaching Institutes and Extracurricular Lessons and at sports facilities under the Act on the Installation and Use of Sports Facilities, beginning on the day after 2 years have elapsed from the effective date of this Act."}
