{"[2020HEONMA395]": "1. Overview of the Case\\n\\nA. The Petitioners are foreign workers currently working in the Republic of Korea after obtaining employment permits pursuant to the “Act on the Employment, etc. of Foreign Workers” (hereinafter referred to as the “Foreign Workers Employment Act”).\\n\\nB. Petitioner Heu○○ (Foreigner), a foreign national of Cambodian nationality, entered the Republic of Korea on December 18, 2019, and has been working at ○○ located in ○○ City since the 23rd of the same month. Petitioner Heu○○ (Foreigner) alleges that the Employer has unilaterally changed working hours and is making him work overtime without overtime pay, and that the Employer additionally deducted dormitory fees and paid a monthly wage lower than the ordinary wage under the employment contract.\\n\\nC. Petitioner Chu○○ (Foreigner), a foreign national of Mongolian nationality, entered the Republic of Korea on December 26, 2018, and has been working at Taekwang Industrial Co., Ltd. located in Anseong City since January 22, 2019. Petitioner Chu○○ (Foreigner) alleges that the Employer forced him, despite his lack of a construction machinery operator’s license, to operate an unlicensed construction machine (forklift), and treated him unfairly by repeatedly making threatening remarks.\\n\\nD. Petitioner Teu○○ (Foreigner), a foreign national of Vietnamese nationality, entered the Republic of Korea on April 12, 2016, and has been working at ○○ located in ○○ City. Petitioner Teu○○ (Foreigner) alleges that, because the Employer’s request for reemployment permission was necessary for an extension of the employment activity period, he deposited KRW 3,000,000 with the Employer at the Employer’s request as liquidated damages for non-performance of the employment contract, and later was able to recover that amount through a correction order by a labor inspector.\\n\\nE. Petitioner Na○○ (Foreigner), a foreign national of Uzbek nationality, entered the Republic of Korea around December 24, 2013, and worked at ○○ located in ○○ City, then re-entered the country on December 19, 2018, as a faithful foreign worker and is currently engaged in automobile parts chemical treatment plating work at the same workplace. Petitioner Na○○ (Foreigner) alleges that, because the Employer did not provide protective equipment, he is being continuously exposed to harmful organic solvents.\\n\\nF. Petitioner Mi○○ (Foreigner), a foreign national of Myanmar nationality, entered the Republic of Korea in or around 2013 and joined ○○ Co., Ltd. located in ○○ City, then re-entered the country as a faithful foreign worker and is currently working at the same workplace. Petitioner Mi○○ (Foreigner) alleges that, after witnessing an industrial accident at the above factory on January 31, 2020, in which 10 persons were killed or injured, he requested a workplace change from the Employer, but the Employer refused.\\n\\nG. On March 15, 2020, the Petitioners filed this constitutional complaint seeking constitutional review of the above provisions, arguing that, because their respective situations did not fall under the grounds for workplace change prescribed by Article 25(1), Article 25(4) of the Foreign Workers Employment Act, Articles 4, 5, and 5-2 of the “Grounds for Workplace Change Not Attributable to the Responsibility of Foreign Workers” (hereinafter referred to as the “Public Notice at Issue”), they were forced to continue working without being able to change workplaces, thereby infringing the Petitioners’ fundamental rights.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe Petitioners seek a finding of unconstitutionality of Article 5-2 of the Public Notice at Issue; however, because that provision concerns the structure and facilities of dormitories, the location of installation, living environment, area, protection of privacy, and provision of information regarding dormitories, it is irrelevant to the matters contested by the Petitioners in this case and is therefore excluded from the subject matter of review.\\n\\nAccordingly, the subject matter of this review is whether Article 25(1) of the “Act on the Employment, etc. of Foreign Workers” (as amended by Act No. 16274 on January 15, 2019) (hereinafter referred to as the “grounds-limitation provision at issue”), Article 25(4) of the “Act on the Employment, etc. of Foreign Workers” (as amended by Act No. 12371 on January 28, 2014) (hereinafter referred to as the “frequency-limitation provision at issue”), and Articles 4 and 5 of the former “Grounds for Workplace Change Not Attributable to the Responsibility of Foreign Workers” (as amended by Ministry of Employment and Labor Public Notice No. 2019-39 on July 16, 2019, and before amendment by Ministry of Employment and Labor Public Notice No. 2021-30 on April 1, 2021) (hereinafter referred to as the “Public Notice provisions at issue”) infringe the Petitioners’ fundamental rights.\\n\\nThe provisions subject to review and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Review]\\n\\nAct on the Employment, etc. of Foreign Workers (as amended by Act No. 16274 on January 15, 2019)\\n\\nArticle 25 (Permission for Change of Business or Workplace) ① A foreign worker (excluding foreign workers under Article 12(1)) may, where any of the following grounds arise, apply to the head of the employment security office for a change to another business or workplace in accordance with the Ordinance of the Ministry of Employment and Labor.\\n\\n1. Where the Employer intends to terminate the employment contract during the term of the employment contract for justifiable reasons or intends to refuse renewal after the contract expires;\\n2. Where, due to closure, suspension of operations, revocation of the employment permit under Article 19(1), restriction on employment under Article 20(1), provision of a dormitory in violation of Article 22-2, the Employer’s violation of working conditions, unfair treatment, or other grounds not attributable to the foreign worker’s responsibility, the Minister of Employment and Labor deems and publicly announces that the foreign worker is unable to continue working at the business or workplace according to general social standards;\\n3. Where other grounds prescribed by Presidential Decree arise.\\n\\nAct on the Employment, etc. of Foreign Workers (as amended by Act No. 12371 on January 28, 2014)\\n\\nArticle 25 (Permission for Change of Business or Workplace) ④ A foreign worker’s change of business or workplace under paragraph (1) may, in principle, not exceed 3 times during the period under Article 18, and may not exceed 2 times during the extended period under Article 18-2(1). Provided, That cases where the business or workplace was changed for the reason under paragraph (1) item 2 shall not be included.\\n\\nFormer Grounds for Workplace Change Not Attributable to the Responsibility of Foreign Workers (as amended by Ministry of Employment and Labor Public Notice No. 2019-39 on July 16, 2019, and before amendment by Ministry of Employment and Labor Public Notice No. 2021-30 on April 1, 2021)\\n\\nArticle 4 (Violation of Working Conditions) The grounds corresponding to violation of working conditions, etc., for which workplace change is permitted under Article 25(1) item 2 of the Act, are as follows.\\n\\n1. Where the Employer has, as follows, failed to pay wages, etc. (in such case, an application for workplace change shall be filed while wages are unpaid or payment is delayed, or within 4 months after the date on which the unpaid wages or delayed payment has ended, and cases caused by the Employer’s simple calculation error shall be excluded):\\n   a. Where wages amounting to 30 percent or more of the monthly wage have not been paid or have been paid late for at least 2 months;\\n   b. Where wages amounting to 10 percent or more of the monthly wage have not been paid or have been paid late for at least 4 months;\\n   c. Where payment has been made below the minimum wage under the “Minimum Wage Act”;\\n2. Where, for at least 2 months during the 1 year preceding the date of application for workplace change, the Employer has reduced by 20 percent or more the wages or working hours that were presented at recruitment or that had been generally applied after recruitment (in such case, the application for workplace change shall be filed while such wages or working hours are being reduced or within 4 months after the date on which such reduction ended);\\n3. Where, for at least 1 month during the 1 year preceding the date of application for workplace change, the Employer has, without the foreign worker’s consent, advanced or postponed by 2 hours or more the working hours that were presented at recruitment or that had been generally applied after recruitment;\\n4. Where, due to the Employer’s violation of the “Occupational Safety and Health Act,” a foreign worker suffers an injury or illness requiring suspension of work for at least 3 days, and the Employer fails to take safety and health measures under the “Occupational Safety and Health Act” until 1 month has elapsed from the date of such injury or illness.\\n\\nArticle 5 (Unfair Treatment, etc.) The grounds corresponding to unfair treatment, etc., for which workplace change is permitted under Article 25(1) item 2 of the Act are as follows.\\n\\n1. Where a foreign worker applies for workplace change on the ground of sexual violence damage by the Employer and it is recognized that an urgent workplace change is necessary;\\n2. Where a foreign worker has been subjected by the Employer to sexual harassment, sexual violence, assault, habitual abusive language, etc., and it is recognized that the foreign worker can no longer continue working at that workplace;\\n3. Where a foreign worker has been subjected, within the scope subject to the Employer’s control, such as the workplace, to sexual harassment, sexual violence, assault, habitual abusive language, etc. by a co-worker, the employer’s spouse, or lineal ascendant or descendant, and it is recognized that the foreign worker can no longer continue working at that workplace;\\n4. Where a foreign worker has been subjected by the Employer to unreasonable discriminatory treatment on grounds such as nationality, religion, sex, or physical disability, and it is recognized that the foreign worker can no longer continue working at that workplace;\\n5. Where the Employer, because of providing the foreign worker with a vinyl greenhouse as accommodation, received a voluntary improvement order from the head of the employment security office, but failed, without justifiable grounds, to implement it within the voluntary improvement period.\\n\\n[Related Provision]\\n\\nEnforcement Decree of the Act on the Employment, etc. of Foreign Workers (as amended by Presidential Decree No. 23785 on May 14, 2012)\\n\\nArticle 30 (Change of Business or Workplace) ① “Grounds prescribed by Presidential Decree” in Article 25(1) item 3 of the Act means cases in which, due to injury, etc., it is deemed unsuitable for the foreign worker to continue working at the relevant business or workplace, but it is possible for the foreign worker to work at another business or workplace.\\n\\n3. Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\nA. By restricting the “grounds” and “number of times” for a foreign worker’s “change of business or workplace” (hereinafter referred to as a “workplace change”), the provisions subject to review effectively compel foreign workers to continue working at one workplace during their period of stay. This violates the prohibition on forced labor and thereby infringes human dignity and worth and the right to pursue happiness (Article 10 of the Constitution), the freedom of the person (Article 12(1)), the freedom to choose occupation (Article 15), and the right to work (Article 32), and also infringes the right to equality (Article 11) in comparison with other foreign workers such as overseas Koreans, for whom there are no restrictions on grounds or number of workplace changes.\\n\\nB. The grounds-limitation provision at issue also violates the principle against blanket delegation because it delegates the grounds for workplace change to subordinate legislation without specifying the concrete scope.\\n\\nC. The Public Notice provisions at issue infringe the Petitioners’ fundamental rights by excessively restricting the grounds, for example by excluding cases where a violation of working conditions is subject to criminal punishment from the grounds for workplace change, or by requiring urgency or impossibility of continued work even where unfair treatment has occurred.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Legal Requirements (typo for the legal requirements)\\n\\nA. Whether the Petitioners Are Bearers of Fundamental Rights\\n\\nWhether a foreigner may be a bearer of fundamental rights depends on the nature of the fundamental right concerned, and fundamental rights having the character of “human rights,” such as human dignity and worth and the right to pursue happiness, are recognized for foreigners (see Constitutional Court 2001. 11. 29. 99HEONMA494). The freedom of occupation of foreigners who, by obtaining employment permits, have been granted the status of legitimate labor force in our society is guaranteed as a human right (see Constitutional Court 2011. 9. 29. 2007HEONMA1083 et al.; Constitutional Court 2011. 9. 29. 2009HEONMA351), and the “right concerning the working environment,” namely the right within the right to work to demand minimum working conditions necessary for the guarantee of human dignity, is also guaranteed to foreigners (see Constitutional Court 2007. 8. 30. 2004HEONMA670; Constitutional Court 2016. 3. 31. 2014HEONMA367). The right to equality, likewise, is in principle a human right, so foreigners may generally be recognized as bearers of fundamental rights, subject only to inherent limitations on rights such as voting rights and to limitations based on reciprocity (see Constitutional Court 2001. 11. 29. 99HEONMA494).\\n\\nThe Petitioners entered the Republic of Korea after obtaining employment permits under the Foreign Workers Employment Act for the purpose of employment in domestic enterprises, and have lived here while forming and maintaining a certain life relationship in the Republic of Korea; thus, they are bearers of the freedom of occupation and of the right concerning the working environment within the right to work. In addition, because the Petitioners challenge differential treatment among foreign workers, there is no room for applying inherent limitations or limitations based on reciprocity, and thus their standing as bearers of the right to equality may be recognized. There is no doubt that, with respect to the human dignity and worth, the right to pursue happiness, and the freedom of the person that the Petitioners allege have been infringed, they are also bearers of fundamental rights.\\n\\nB. Petition for Constitutional Review of the Frequency-Limitation Provision at Issue\\n\\nWhere, due to the subject matter of a constitutional complaint, there is a concern that a fundamental right may be infringed at some future time, and such concern is merely a possibility that may appear in the future, the presentness of the infringement of a fundamental right cannot be found (see Constitutional Court 2020. 9. 24. 2018HEONMA739 et al.).\\n\\nThe frequency-limitation provision at issue limits the number of workplace changes to 3 times during the employment activity period and 2 times during the extended employment activity period. Accordingly, the frequency-limitation provision at issue applies only when a person seeks an additional workplace change after all permitted workplace changes have been exhausted.\\n\\nHowever, according to the record of review, the Petitioners admit that they did not attempt to change workplaces more than 3 times. If so, at present it is uncertain whether the Petitioners will exhaust all permitted workplace changes, and the infringement of a fundamental right by the frequency-limitation provision at issue cannot be definitely foreseen as present; even if there is a concern that a fundamental right may be infringed by the frequency-limitation provision at issue in the future, this would amount only to a potential concern.\\n\\nThe Petitioners argue that, considering that the provisions subject to review, which restrict grounds and number of workplace changes, are interconnected and affect the Petitioners’ legal status, this matter should be taken into account. However, because cases in which the workplace is changed on grounds not attributable to the foreign worker’s responsibility are excluded from the numerical limitation (proviso to the frequency-limitation provision at issue), the presentness of the infringement of a fundamental right under the frequency-limitation provision at issue may be separately determined from the grounds-limitation provision at issue and the Public Notice provisions at issue.\\n\\nAccordingly, with respect to the frequency-limitation provision at issue, the presentness of the infringement of a fundamental right cannot be recognized, and the Petitioners’ constitutional complaint on this part is unlawful.\\n\\n5. Merits Determination\\n\\nA. Fundamental Rights Restricted\\n\\n(1) The grounds-limitation provision at issue and the Public Notice provisions at issue (hereinafter referred to as the “provisions subject to review on the merits”) restrict the grounds on which a foreign worker may change workplaces. As a result, foreign workers are restricted in abandoning an already formed employment relationship and leaving their workplace, thereby restricting the freedom to choose occupation within the freedom of occupation (see Constitutional Court 2011. 9. 29. 2007HEONMA1083 et al.).\\n\\n(2) Since the provisions subject to review on the merits restrict the grounds for workplace change of the Petitioners, who are foreign workers with non-professional employment (E-9) status, unlike foreign workers with visiting employment (H-2) status, the issue of infringement of the right to equality arises.\\n\\n(3) The Petitioners argue that the provisions subject to review on the merits infringe the right to work; however, statutes such as the Labor Standards Act and the Occupational Safety and Health Act, which concretize the right to work under the Constitution, apply equally to foreign workers, and if the Employer violates obligations, there is no restriction on foreign workers’ use of the relevant legal remedy procedures. Furthermore, it cannot be said that the constitutional right to work includes a guarantee of the means to improve or resolve working conditions privately by leaving a workplace with poor working conditions and moving to another workplace (see Constitutional Court 2011. 9. 29. 2007HEONMA1083 et al.). Accordingly, the provisions subject to review on the merits do not restrict the right to work.\\n\\n(4) The Petitioners argue to the effect that, because the prohibition on forced labor is derived from Article 12(1) of the Constitution, which provides for the freedom of the person and the prohibition of forced labor, and from Article 15, which provides for the freedom to choose occupation, the Court should review whether those provisions violate that principle. The International Labour Organization (ILO) adopted the Abolition of Forced Labour Convention, 1957 (No. 105), but our country has not ratified that Convention at present, and even if the provisions subject to review on the merits were to restrict foreign workers’ workplace changes, thereby falling within “forced labor” as used in that Convention, that alone would not immediately make them unconstitutional. Accordingly, we examine whether the provisions subject to review on the merits restrict the constitutional freedom of the person.\\n\\nThe freedom of the person means the freedom not to have the safety of one’s body infringed by external physical force or mental danger, and the freedom to engage in bodily activity voluntarily and autonomously (see Constitutional Court 2016. 9. 29. 2014HEONGA9). According to this, restricting changes of workplace or compelling continued labor at a particular workplace cannot immediately be regarded as infringing bodily safety or restricting free movement and activity of the body. In addition, the Petitioners do not allege that the restrictions on workplace changes under the provisions subject to review on the merits were not based on law and due process. Accordingly, the provisions subject to review on the merits do not restrict the freedom of the person.\\n\\n(5) The provisions subject to review on the merits merely set forth the grounds on which a foreign worker may change workplaces, and on that basis alone cannot be said to restrict the Petitioners’ human dignity and worth. In addition, where “occupation” is at issue as the protected sphere, the freedom of occupation is in a special relationship to the right to pursue happiness; therefore, insofar as this case reviews whether the freedom to choose occupation within the freedom of occupation is infringed, the question of infringement of the right to pursue happiness is not separately determined (see Constitutional Court 2011. 9. 29. 2007HEONMA1083 et al.).\\n\\n(6) In the end, the issue in this case is whether the provisions subject to review on the merits infringe the Petitioners’ freedom to choose occupation or right to equality.\\n\\nB. Whether the Grounds-Limitation Provision at Issue Infringes a Fundamental Right\\n\\n(1) Whether It Infringes the Freedom to Choose Occupation\\n\\n(a) Whether It Violates the Principle Against Blanket Delegation\\n\\n1) The forms of delegated legislation recognized by Article 75 and Article 95 of the Constitution should be regarded as illustrative, and even if a statute delegates certain matters to administrative rules such as public notices, this is not inconsistent with the principle of parliamentary legislation under Article 40 of the Constitution (see Constitutional Court 2004. 10. 28. 99HEONBA91; Constitutional Court 2017. 9. 28. 2016HEONBA140). Therefore, it cannot be said that the grounds-limitation provision at issue violates the Constitution by failing to satisfy the constitutional form of delegated legislation merely because it delegates to a Ministry of Employment and Labor public notice the determination of cases in which, due to grounds not attributable to the foreign worker’s responsibility, it is recognized according to general social standards that the foreign worker can no longer continue working at the business or workplace.\\n\\nHowever, because administrative rules do not require the same strict enactment and amendment procedures as legislative regulations, when a statute that restricts a fundamental right such as the freedom to choose occupation delegates legislation, it is desirable to delegate to a legislative regulation such as a “Presidential Decree,” “Prime Minister’s Decree,” or “Ministerial Decree”; and when legislative delegation is made in the form of a public notice by the Ministry of Employment and Labor, it should at least be limited, as provided in the proviso to Article 4(2) of the Framework Act on Administrative Regulations, to matters of a technical or minor nature for which delegation is unavoidable due to the nature of the work, and even as to such matters, under the principle against blanket delegation, legislative delegation must be made only with respect to specifically limited matters (see Constitutional Court 2004. 10. 28. 99HEONBA91; Constitutional Court 2016. 10. 27. 2015HEONBA360 et al.).\\n\\n2) Statutes concretizing the constitutional right to work, such as the Labor Standards Act, the Minimum Wage Act, and the Occupational Safety and Health Act, broadly regulate the working conditions that the Employer must observe, and even acts by the Employer that do not amount to a violation of statutory working conditions but may arise in an employment relationship can manifest in various forms and degrees as unfair treatment. Since the Employer’s violation of working conditions or unfair treatment is broad in scope and detailed in content, it is not appropriate, from the standpoint of legislative technique, to prescribe them one by one in the statute.\\n\\nMoreover, the question of up to what extent among the Employer’s violations of working conditions or unfair treatment should be regarded as a case in which the foreign worker is recognized as being unable to continue working at the business or workplace according to general social standards is an area requiring expert and policy judgment. This is because it concerns how much to restrict or permit the scale of foreign workers’ workplace movement. Therefore, it is necessary to delegate the concrete content to the administration, since the matter cannot be determined solely on the basis of the foreign worker’s subjective circumstances, and policy matters such as the scale of foreign workers, the industries in which they engage, the general level of the working environment at workplaces that have obtained employment permits, and the effect that a foreign worker’s workplace change would have on the working conditions of that workplace or of domestic workers in the same industry must be considered.\\n\\nFurthermore, in light of the increased law-abiding capacity resulting from improvements in the working conditions or work environment of workplaces that have obtained employment permits, there may be a need to add grounds for violation of working conditions or to raise the threshold more strictly, and there is also a need for immediate response, such as including in the grounds for workplace change new forms of unfair treatment of foreign workers that appear or are discovered while the Employment Permit System is being operated. In fact, the Public Notice provisions at issue, delegated under the grounds-limitation provision at issue, have been amended frequently since their enactment, and the direction has generally been to gradually expand the grounds for workplace change for foreign workers or to clarify ambiguous grounds. In this way, rather than prescribing in detail the specific and detailed content of the Employer’s violations of working conditions or unfair treatment recognized as grounds for workplace change, there is a recognized need to delegate so that the administration, equipped with expertise and policy capacity, can respond flexibly and in a timely manner according to changes in circumstances.\\n\\n3) The grounds-limitation provision at issue provides that the Minister of Employment and Labor shall publicly announce cases where, “due to the Employer’s violation of working conditions, unfair treatment, or other grounds not attributable to the foreign worker’s responsibility, it is recognized that the foreign worker can no longer continue working at the business or workplace according to general social standards.”\\n\\nFirst, looking at item 2 of the grounds-limitation provision at issue as a whole, “the Employer’s violation of working conditions or unfair treatment” constitutes, together with “closure, suspension of operations, revocation of the employment permit under Article 19(1) of the Foreign Workers Employment Act, restriction on employment under Article 20(1), provision of a dormitory in violation of Article 22-2” (hereinafter referred to as “closure, etc.”), a “ground not attributable to the foreign worker’s responsibility,” and such a ground must rise to the level at which “it is recognized that the foreign worker can no longer continue working at the business or workplace according to general social standards.”\\n\\nExamining the grounds of closure, etc. in concrete terms, they may be understood as cases where the business can no longer be continued regardless of whether the Employer is at fault, or where the business can continue but the Employer’s fault is so serious that the foreign worker can no longer continue working at that business or workplace. In light of this, it can be anticipated that “the Employer’s violation of working conditions or unfair treatment” likewise includes cases in which the Employer bears a serious degree of fault such that, in comparison with closure, etc., the foreign worker is recognized as being unable to continue working at the business or workplace according to general social standards.\\n\\nIn addition, the Foreign Workers Employment Act has the purpose of promoting smooth supply and demand of labor and balanced development of the national economy by systematically introducing and managing foreign workers (Article 1), and the Minister of Employment and Labor publicly announces each year an employment plan for foreign workers including the industries and scale of foreign worker introduction deliberated and resolved by the Foreign Workforce Policy Committee (Article 4(2) item 2, Article 5), and an Employer who employs foreign workers with an employment permit must, when grounds prescribed by Presidential Decree arise, such as termination of the employment contract or other material changes relating to employment, report to the head of the employment security office in accordance with the Ordinance of the Ministry of Employment and Labor (Article 17(1)). In this manner, the State strictly controls the introduction and employment management of foreign workers.\\n\\nThe grounds-limitation provision at issue, viewed as a whole, also has a structure that in principle prohibits foreign workers from applying for workplace changes based on their own free will and allows workplace changes only in a limited manner in some cases not attributable to the foreign worker’s responsibility. Thus, this legislative purpose is reflected in the Public Notice provisions at issue as well, and it can be anticipated that relatively strict grounds among the Employer’s violations of working conditions or unfair treatment would be prescribed.\\n\\nConsidering the literal meaning of the grounds-limitation provision at issue, its legislative intent, and the related statutory provisions as an organic and systematic whole, it can be anticipated that “the Employer’s violation of working conditions or unfair treatment” to be prescribed in a Ministry of Employment and Labor public notice pursuant to the delegation in the grounds-limitation provision at issue would include serious violations of working conditions or unfair treatment to the extent that continued employment becomes difficult. Specifically, it can be fully anticipated that this includes core violations of working conditions such as wages, working hours, and industrial safety, and acts of personal humiliation or discriminatory treatment vis-à-vis domestic workers that may arise in an employment relationship; indeed, the Public Notice provisions at issue also appear to have concretized the Employer’s violations of working conditions or unfair treatment in this sense.\\n\\n4) Therefore, the grounds-limitation provision at issue specifically sets the scope in the statute and delegates the content of the Employer’s violations of working conditions or unfair treatment to a Ministry of Employment and Labor public notice, and because the addressees of the norm, such as Employers and foreign workers, can anticipate the general contents to be prescribed in the Public Notice provisions at issue, the provision cannot be said to violate the principle against blanket delegation.\\n\\n(b) Whether It Exceeds the Scope of Legislative Formation Power\\n\\n1) In establishing a system concerning the introduction of foreign labor, broad legislative discretion is recognized, and the freedom of foreign workers to choose occupation is only concretized when the legislature, based on policy judgment, specifies the content of the system by statute. Therefore, the grounds-limitation provision at issue, which restricts the grounds for workplace change of foreign workers, can be said to violate the Constitution only when its content is manifestly arbitrary without rational basis (see Constitutional Court 2011. 9. 29. 2007HEONMA1083 et al.).\\n\\n2) The Employment Permit System is a system under which the government legally permits foreign employment in industries among Korean enterprises that have difficulty employing domestic workers. In other words, under the principle of protecting employment opportunities for domestic workers, its purpose is to systematically introduce foreign workers, thereby facilitating labor supply and demand, resolving labor shortages in small and medium-sized enterprises, and promoting sustained economic growth, while also establishing measures for efficient employment management of foreign workers and protection of their rights and interests as workers (see Constitutional Court 2009. 9. 24. 2006HEONMA1264).\\n\\nThe grounds-limitation provision at issue, in principle, prohibits workplace changes at the foreign worker’s own will and allows them only when exceptional grounds exist, thereby enabling small and medium-sized enterprises, etc. to secure labor force stably, preventing disruption of the employment opportunities or working conditions of domestic workers, and promoting efficient employment management of foreign workers.\\n\\nThat the grounds-limitation provision at issue allows workplace changes only where the Employer intends to terminate the employment contract during the term of the employment contract for justifiable reasons or intends to refuse renewal after the contract expires, and does not allow workplace changes where the foreign worker terminates the employment contract or refuses renewal of the employment contract, contributes to the above legislative purpose and, as follows, cannot be regarded as clearly unreasonable beyond the scope of the legislature’s discretion.\\n\\n3) First, the grounds-limitation provision at issue curbs foreign workers’ free workplace changes so that Employers who have obtained employment permits can stably secure labor force. At present, industries introducing foreign labor for non-professional employment are manufacturing, construction, agriculture, livestock and fisheries, and certain service industries such as construction waste disposal. In the case of manufacturing, it is limited to enterprises with fewer than 300 regular workers or capital of KRW 8 billion or less. These enterprises play an important role in the national economy, but due to the nature of the industry, it is difficult to find domestic workers, and they are generally small-scale workplaces in urgent need of stable labor force.\\n\\nHowever, many workplaces employing foreign workers cite “frequent workplace changes” as a difficulty in employing foreign workers, and in particular, non-professional foreign workers are shown to have lower labor productivity when the period of service is short, because communication is difficult and cultural differences exist not only compared to domestic workers but also compared to overseas Koreans. Therefore, if foreign workers are allowed to terminate or refuse renewal of their employment contracts and freely apply for workplace changes, Employers would inevitably face great difficulty in securing labor force stably and in operating workplaces smoothly.\\n\\n4) In the context of recent rapid increases in undocumented foreigners, there is also a need, from the standpoint of efficient management of foreign workers, to curb frequent workplace changes and induce long-term service within the employment activity period. In particular, because the Employment Permit System adopted by our Foreign Workers Employment Act is a system centered on regulation of the Employer, verification of the foreign worker entering the country is relatively weak. Therefore, the State needs to offset the relaxed control at the time of entry with strengthened regulation at the time of stay and departure, and there is an unavoidable aspect to not granting foreign workers a free right to apply for workplace change when they terminate or refuse renewal of their employment contracts.\\n\\n5) The grounds-limitation provision at issue does not recognize as a ground for workplace change the termination of the employment relationship based on the foreign worker’s free will, but it recognizes relatively broadly workplace changes due to grounds not attributable to the foreign worker’s responsibility. It also allows workplace changes where, due to injury or illness, it is deemed unsuitable for the foreign worker to continue working at the relevant business or workplace but possible to work at another business or workplace. Viewing the grounds-limitation provision at issue as a whole in this manner, while maintaining the principle of restricting workplace movement under the Employment Permit System, it permits workplace changes when necessary for foreign workers; thus, the restriction can be said to have a rational basis.\\n\\n6) Countries around the world have introduced and operate systems suited to their own conditions among the Employment Permit System and the Labor Permit System, and our legislature likewise has discretion to freely choose among foreign employment systems such as the Labor Permit System and the Employment Permit System. Foreign workers who enter the country under the Employment Permit System adopted by the Foreign Workers Employment Act are selected by Employers, assigned to a specific workplace, and begin work, and workplace changes are curbed by restrictions on the grounds and number of workplace changes during the employment period. Therefore, allowing foreign workers to freely apply for workplace changes is inconsistent with the purpose of the Employment Permit System and could even shake the foundations of the Foreign Workers Employment Act; accordingly, the grounds-limitation provision at issue’s refusal to recognize a free right of foreign workers to apply for workplace changes can be seen as a necessary restriction to preserve the Employment Permit System in accordance with its purpose.\\n\\n7) Of course, the private interests restricted by requiring strict grounds for workplace changes are by no means small. Foreign workers also need to leave workplaces with objectively poor or unsuitable working environments and move to other workplaces, and by demonstrating higher labor productivity at the changed workplace, they may ultimately contribute more to the national economy. However, because foreign workers entering through the Employment Permit System are understood to have entered while recognizing and accepting that the workplaces available to them are limited from the time of entry and that future workplace changes are also subject to restrictions on grounds and number, the restriction may be considered relatively easy to tolerate. On the other hand, allowing foreign workers to freely change workplaces even where there has been no termination or refusal of renewal by the Employer would run counter to the purpose and structure of the current Employment Permit System and may ignore the practical situation of workplaces employing foreign workers.\\n\\n8) Accordingly, because the grounds-limitation provision at issue cannot be regarded as manifestly unreasonable beyond the scope of legislative discretion, it does not infringe the Petitioners’ freedom to choose occupation.\\n\\n(c) Conclusion\\n\\nThe grounds-limitation provision at issue does not violate the principle against blanket delegation and cannot be regarded as manifestly unreasonable beyond the scope of legislative discretion; therefore, it does not infringe the Petitioners’ freedom to choose occupation.\\n\\n(2) Whether It Infringes the Right to Equality\\n\\n(a) Among foreign workers with a status of stay permitting employment in Korea, foreign workers who entered under non-professional employment (E-9) and visiting employment (H-2) statuses may be said to be the same comparison group in that they are foreign workers subject to the Foreign Workers Employment Act. The grounds-limitation provision at issue restricts the grounds for workplace change of the Petitioners, who entered under the non-professional employment status (hereinafter referred to as “non-professional employment foreign workers”), whereas overseas Koreans who entered under the visiting employment status and obtained special employment permits (hereinafter referred to as “visiting employment foreign workers”) have no restriction on grounds when changing workplaces (Article 25(1) of the Foreign Workers Employment Act). Therefore, because there is differential treatment between the two groups, we examine whether such discrimination has a rational basis.\\n\\n(b) The “Act on the Immigration and Legal Status of Overseas Koreans” (hereinafter referred to as the “Overseas Koreans Act”) classifies overseas Koreans into Korean nationals residing abroad and foreign nationals of Korean descent (Article 2) and guarantees the entry, departure, and legal status of foreign nationals of Korean descent. Specifically, the Government must provide necessary support so that overseas Koreans are not subjected to unjust restrictions and treatment within the Republic of Korea (Overseas Koreans Act, Article 4), a foreign national of Korean descent who has reported domestic residence and stays in Korea for 90 days or more may receive health insurance coverage (Overseas Koreans Act, Article 14), and may receive veterans’ benefits under the “Act on the Honorable Treatment and Support of Persons, etc. of Distinguished Service to the State” or the “Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence” (Overseas Koreans Act, Article 16).\\n\\nA foreigner who wishes to work in the Republic of Korea must obtain a status of stay allowing employment activities (Immigration Control Act, Article 18(1)), and the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act lists visiting employment (H-2) as one such status (Article 23 and Attached Table 1-2). A person aged 18 or older who corresponds to a foreign national of Korean descent under the Overseas Koreans Act and satisfies certain requirements may obtain visiting employment status; once such status is obtained, free entry and departure is possible within the validity period of the visa, and employment activities are permitted in a relatively broad range of fields (currently 46 industries) compared with non-professional employment foreign workers.\\n\\nThe visiting employment system was introduced in 2007 for the purpose of eliminating discrimination against ethnic Koreans who migrated overseas to China and the former Soviet Union regions before the establishment of the Republic of Korea and to embrace them. Visiting employment foreign workers may, after receiving employment training in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the Foreign Workers Employment Act, file a job-seeking application and receive employment placement (Article 12(2) of the Foreign Workers Employment Act), or freely seek employment at workplaces that have obtained confirmation of eligibility for special employment (Article 12(1) of the same Act).\\n\\n(c) As such, visiting employment foreign workers differ from non-professional employment foreign workers in whether they are foreign nationals of Korean descent, the requirements for status of stay, the scope of employment activities, the legislative purpose, and the employment procedures. Therefore, it has a rational basis that the Foreign Workers Employment Act imposes no restriction on the grounds for workplace change for visiting employment foreign workers, whereas the grounds-limitation provision at issue requires strict grounds for the Petitioners. The grounds-limitation provision at issue does not infringe the Petitioners’ right to equality.\\n\\nC. Whether the Public Notice Provisions at Issue Infringe a Fundamental Right\\n\\n(1) Whether It Infringes the Freedom to Choose Occupation\\n\\n(a) In establishing a system concerning the introduction of foreign labor, broad legislative discretion is recognized, and the freedom of foreign workers to choose occupation is only concretized when the legislature, based on policy judgment, specifies the content of the system by statute. Therefore, the Public Notice provisions at issue, which concretize grounds for workplace change not attributable to the foreign worker’s responsibility, can be said to violate the Constitution only when their content is manifestly arbitrary without rational basis (see Constitutional Court 2011. 9. 29. 2007HEONMA1083 et al.).\\n\\n(b) The Public Notice provisions at issue are intended to enable small and medium-sized enterprises, etc. to secure labor force stably, prevent disruption of the employment opportunities or working conditions of domestic workers, and promote efficient employment management of foreign workers, while also clarifying the scope of permitted workplace changes due to grounds not attributable to the foreign worker’s responsibility.\\n\\n(c) The provisions before amendment of the Public Notice at issue had been criticized for using abstract terms, such as defining grounds for workplace change as cases where “the working conditions have substantially deteriorated,” which caused disagreement between Employers and foreign workers and made it difficult to determine whether a case fell within the grounds for workplace change, thereby effectively making workplace changes difficult. However, since the Public Notice provisions at issue were wholly amended on January 11, 2019, they have used objective and concrete standards, and concerns over restrictions on workplace changes due to vagueness have been substantially alleviated.\\n\\n(d) Looking at the specific content, in the case of violation of working conditions, the provisions state that unpaid wages and delayed payment, deterioration of working conditions, changes in working hours, and failure to take measures after industrial accidents constitute grounds for workplace change (Article 4 of the Public Notice at issue; hereinafter the name of the public notice is omitted), and with respect to unfair treatment, they specify sexual harassment, sexual violence, assault, habitual abusive language, discriminatory treatment, and provision of vinyl greenhouse accommodations (Article 5). This may be understood as a comprehensive reflection of the unreasonable treatment that foreign workers experience at workplace sites.\\n\\n(e) It is also necessary to consider that, in response to changing circumstances, grounds continue to be added to and specified in the Public Notice provisions at issue. Even after the filing of this constitutional complaint, grounds for unpaid wages and delayed payment were added (Article 4 item 1), and where a serious industrial accident occurs at the workplace due to the Employer’s violation of the Occupational Safety and Health Act or a foreign worker suffers an accident requiring medical treatment of 3 months or more, an application for workplace change was allowed (Article 4 item 4). Even where a foreign worker has been sexually assaulted by a person other than the Employer, such as a co-worker, emergency workplace change is permitted (Article 5 item 1), and in the case of provision of vinyl greenhouse accommodations, the requirement of a voluntary improvement order by the head of the employment security office or non-compliance therewith was removed from the requirements (Article 5 item 5). Furthermore, grounds for workplace change were newly created where the Employer refuses to allow the foreign worker to provide labor (Article 5 item 6) or where there is no insurance enrollment related to employment or there are arrears (Article 5 item 7), and by adjusting and expanding the grounds for workplace change in accordance with problems discovered in practice concerning foreign employment, the system seeks to protect the rights and interests of foreign workers.\\n\\n(f) The Foreign Workers Rights and Interests Protection Council (Subcommittee) may permit workplace change in cases where it is difficult to determine whether the matter falls within the grounds listed in Articles 2 through 5-2 of the Public Notice at issue because the claims of the Employer and the foreign worker do not match or there is a lack of evidence, etc. (Article 6(1)), and in cases where the matter falls under grounds equivalent to those in Articles 2 through 5 of the Public Notice at issue and it is recognized that the foreign worker can no longer continue working at the relevant workplace, workplace change may be permitted (Article 6(2)). The head of the employment security office must endeavor, when carrying out duties concerning foreign workers, to ensure that the matters discussed by the Foreign Workers Rights and Interests Protection Council are reflected (Article 15-2(3) of the Enforcement Rule of the Foreign Workers Employment Act). In this way, even where evidence regarding the grounds for workplace change is insufficient or where the case does not fall within the enumerated grounds, there is a system allowing workplace change through the Foreign Workers Rights and Interests Protection Council if equivalent grounds exist, so the freedom of occupation of foreign workers is protected relatively strongly.\\n\\n(g) The Public Notice provisions at issue limit workplace changes due to grounds not attributable to the foreign worker’s responsibility to relatively serious violations of working conditions and unfair treatment, so there is a practical problem that, where the case does not fall within or reach that level, foreign workers cannot change workplaces. However, as noted above, the Employment Permit System adopted by our Foreign Workers Employment Act is a system premised on employment permits granted to Employers, and control over entry of individual foreign workers is relatively relaxed. Accordingly, if workplace changes are permitted indiscriminately, the purpose of the Employment Permit System—to systematically introduce and manage foreign workers in order to prevent illegal stay or settlement, and further to promote smooth labor supply and demand and balanced development of the national economy—may not be achieved. The Public Notice provisions at issue restrict workplace changes within a reasonable scope, thereby achieving the purpose of introducing the Employment Permit System while also curbing serious violations of working conditions and unfair treatment toward foreign workers.\\n\\n(h) Therefore, because the Public Notice provisions at issue cannot be regarded as manifestly unreasonable beyond the scope of legislative discretion, they do not infringe the Petitioners’ freedom to choose occupation.\\n\\n(2) Whether It Infringes the Right to Equality\\n\\nAs noted above in examining whether the grounds-limitation provision at issue infringes the right to equality, visiting employment foreign workers differ from non-professional employment foreign workers in whether they are foreign nationals of Korean descent, the requirements for status of stay, the scope of employment activities, and the legislative purpose. Accordingly, it has a rational basis that the Foreign Workers Employment Act fully recognizes freedom of workplace change for visiting employment foreign workers, while, by contrast, the Public Notice provisions at issue require strict grounds for the Petitioners. The Public Notice provisions at issue do not infringe the Petitioners’ right to equality.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, because the Petitioners’ claims concerning the grounds-limitation provision at issue and the Public Notice provisions at issue are without merit, all such claims are dismissed, and because the remaining claims are unlawful, all such claims are rejected; the decision is made as stated in the disposition. This decision is by unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, except for the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Seok-tae and Kim Ki-young regarding the provisions subject to review on the merits, as set forth in 7 below.\\n\\n7. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Lee Seok-tae and Kim Ki-young Regarding the Provisions Subject to Review on the Merits\\n\\nWe differ from the majority opinion in that we think the provisions subject to review on the merits infringe the Petitioners’ freedom to choose occupation, and thus state the following dissenting opinion.\\n\\nA. Whether the Grounds-Limitation Provision at Issue Infringes the Freedom to Choose Occupation\\n\\n(1) The majority opinion states that the grounds-limitation provision at issue is intended to enable small and medium-sized enterprises, etc. to secure labor force stably, prevent disruption of the employment opportunities or working conditions of domestic workers, and promote efficient employment management of foreign workers by in principle prohibiting workplace changes based on the foreign worker’s will and allowing them only where exceptional grounds exist.\\n\\n(2) First, we examine the protection of domestic employment cited as one of the legislative purposes of the grounds-limitation provision at issue.\\n\\nIn Korea, because the wage and working condition gap between large enterprises and small and medium-sized enterprises is wide, the phenomenon of domestic workers avoiding small and medium-sized enterprises is serious, and in particular small workplaces in the so-called 3D industries are suffering from a severe labor shortage. Therefore, foreign workers employed in such industries may be seen not as competitors to domestic workers but as substitutes or complements to them, and many workplaces in Korea have already reached a point where business performance is impossible without foreign workers with simple skills. In such a labor market where domestic workers do not enter, it lacks rationality to restrict foreign workers’ workplace changes in order to protect domestic employment.\\n\\nEven if foreign workers cause a decline in wages and working conditions in certain industries, that is a problem inherent in permitting the domestic introduction of foreign workers, and it is not easy to view it as a problem caused by allowing foreign workers to change workplaces. Foreign workers can move only to workplaces where foreign employment is permitted, and those workplaces are workplaces that had in any event attempted to employ domestic workers but could not find them. In the end, as long as the Foreign Workforce Policy Committee strictly controls the industries and scale of foreign workers introduced each year, it cannot be said that expanding the grounds for workplace change of foreign workers would additionally infringe the employment opportunities of domestic workers or lower working conditions.\\n\\n(3) The majority opinion says that restrictions on workplace changes like the grounds-limitation provision at issue are unavoidable for efficient supervision and management of foreign workers, but there is a strong criticism that excessively restricting grounds for workplace change has instead resulted in the creation of undocumented foreign workers.\\n\\nSince the launch of the Employment Permit System through 2016, approximately 24,478 foreign workers chose undocumented stay merely because they could not change workplaces. In 2019, among registered foreigners with employment qualifications, the number who became undocumented was 10,935, of whom non-professional employment foreign workers accounted for 8,025, or 73.4 percent, whereas in the case of visiting employment foreign workers, newly generated undocumented persons amounted to only 1,127 (10.3 percent). Considering that there is not a large difference in overall scale between non-professional employment foreign workers and visiting employment foreign workers (276,755 and 226,322 as of December 31, 2019), excessively restricting the grounds for workplace change beyond what foreign workers can tolerate does not help efficient supervision and management of foreign workers; rather, it shows that it runs counter to the basic principle of the Employment Permit System, namely preventing settlement, and may threaten the stable operation of the Employment Permit System.\\n\\n(4) Of course, it is true that the grounds-limitation provision at issue, by strictly limiting workplace changes by foreign workers, helps small and medium-sized enterprises that have difficulty finding domestic workers.\\n\\nHowever, if some industries or small and medium-sized enterprises rely entirely on foreign labor, and a structure has become entrenched in which profits are achieved only by preventing foreign workers from escaping low wages and poor working environments through restrictions on workplace changes, it is difficult to say that this conforms to one of the purposes of the Foreign Workers Employment Act, namely “balanced development of the national economy.” Since Employers have little incentive to improve the working environment of the workplace so long as they can keep foreign workers bound to the current workplace without special effort, the working conditions and work environment of foreign workers become even worse, and this can lead to a vicious cycle in which domestic workers increasingly avoid the industry and workplace in question. In the long term, this may not protect small and medium-sized enterprises but may instead weaken the soundness and competitiveness of the industrial structure by sustaining insolvent enterprises lacking self-reliance.\\n\\n(5) Meanwhile, in addition to the grounds-limitation provision at issue, the Foreign Workers Employment Act also has various systems to curb workplace changes and induce long-term service.\\n\\nFirst, the frequency-limitation provision at issue secures a minimum period of service by limiting the number of workplace changes to 3 times during the foreign worker’s employment activity period and to 2 times during the extended period following the Employer’s request for reemployment permission. It also makes the extension of the employment activity period entirely dependent on the Employer’s will (Article 18-2(1) item 1 of the Foreign Workers Employment Act), and grants a special re-entry exception to workers only in cases where they do not change workplaces during the employment activity period or, even if they do, where the Employer applying for post-reentry employment permit and the employment contract period extends at least one year until the end of the employment activity period (Article 18-4(1) item 1 of the Foreign Workers Employment Act), thereby curbing workplace changes and inducing long-term service. Furthermore, if a foreign worker fails to obtain permission to change place of work within 3 months from the date of application for workplace change, the foreign worker must leave the country (Article 25(3) of the Foreign Workers Employment Act), and in particular during winter, when labor demand is low due to seasonal factors, there are practical constraints making it difficult to attempt workplace change lightly.\\n\\nTherefore, even if foreign workers are more broadly recognized as having freedom of occupation, it is difficult to conclude that concerns over frequent workplace changes that would undermine the purpose and objectives of the Employment Permit System will materialize.\\n\\n(6) The grounds-limitation provision at issue, by strictly limiting workplace changes by foreign workers, places foreign workers in a subordinate position, thereby making it difficult for them to assert improvements in working conditions or the work environment. This is equivalent to compelling foreign workers not to freely determine working conditions on equal footing with the Employer.\\n\\nIn particular, considering that employment of foreign workers in Korea begins with the Employer unilaterally designating them after reviewing a list of job-seeking workers, and that foreign workers begin work while knowing almost nothing about the specific working conditions and work environment in which they will be employed before employment, the restriction on the freedom to choose occupation imposed by strictly limiting grounds for workplace change can be said to be very serious.\\n\\n(7) The grounds-limitation provision at issue, by in principle prohibiting workplace changes based on the foreign worker’s will and allowing them only where exceptional grounds exist, is manifestly unreasonable beyond the scope of legislative discretion and infringes the Petitioners’ freedom to choose occupation.\\n\\nB. Whether the Public Notice Provisions at Issue Infringe the Freedom to Choose Occupation\\n\\n(1) Foreign workers are often understood to seek workplace changes for higher wages, but there are also many cases in which they seek workplace changes for other reasons, such as workplace sanitation, safety, and work intensity. According to the Ministry of Justice commissioned report “2013 Survey of Foreign Residents in Korea: Employment and Social Life of Foreigners under the Employment Permit System and the Visiting Employment System,” when foreign workers who had changed workplaces were asked why they moved, the most common reason was low wages (24.1%), but a significant proportion of workers changed workplaces because the work was too difficult (8.7%), the work was dangerous (6.8%), or the working environment was dirty and unsanitary (4.0%). In addition, according to the “Comprehensive Survey on Difficulties Related to Employing Foreign Labor in 2020” conducted by the Korea Federation of SMEs on workplaces employing foreign workers, the most significant reason domestic workers could not be employed was the poor working environment of 3D occupations (39.9%), which was higher than working conditions such as wages and welfare (23.1%). As such, the reasons domestic workers avoid employment are the same as the reasons foreign workers want to change workplaces, and just as domestic workers may avoid employment or leave a workplace in order to protect their own safety and health, foreign workers also need to leave workplaces with poor environments.\\n\\nHowever, the Public Notice provisions at issue hardly include dirty or dangerous working environments, high work intensity, or the Employer’s repeated unreasonable work instructions, which could serve as reasonable reasons for foreign workers to change workplaces, and the violations of working conditions or unfair treatment designated as grounds for workplace change under the Public Notice provisions at issue are plainly insufficient to guarantee the Petitioners’ freedom to choose occupation. Below, we examine in order the problems of violations of working conditions and dangerous working environments in relation to Article 4 of the Public Notice at issue, and the Employer’s repeated unreasonable work instructions and the problem of vagueness of requirements in relation to Article 5 of the Public Notice at issue.\\n\\n(2) Looking at the grounds listed as violations of working conditions in Articles 4 item 1 through item 3 of the Public Notice provisions at issue, their content is limited to unpaid wages and reduction or change of working hours, and even then, they require that the violation exceeding a certain degree continue for a certain period. This is not only only a very small part of the various working conditions prescribed by the Labor Standards Act, but its standards are manifestly arbitrary and difficult to satisfy.\\n\\nFor example, the Labor Standards Act restricts overtime with respect to working hours (Article 53), guarantees rest periods (Article 54) and holidays (Article 55), and provides for additional wages for overtime, night work, and holiday work (Article 56), while prohibiting advance agreements on penalties with respect to employment contracts (Article 20). However, even if the Employer violates these provisions and does not properly secure working conditions, a foreign worker cannot change workplaces on that ground.\\n\\nIn addition, whereas the Labor Standards Act itself prohibits unpaid wages (Article 43(2)), the Public Notice provisions at issue separately establish a standard by stating that workplace change is permitted only when the ratio and period of unpaid wages reach a certain level. While the Labor Standards Act allows a worker to immediately rescind the employment contract if the working conditions stated in the employment contract differ from the facts (Article 19(1)), a foreign worker may change workplaces only when wages or working hours agreed upon at the time of concluding the employment contract are reduced or changed beyond a certain ratio and period. This carries the risk of effectively lowering the working conditions established by the Labor Standards Act and further risks circumventing the principle prohibiting discriminatory treatment set forth in Article 6 of the Labor Standards Act and Article 22 of the Foreign Workers Employment Act.\\n\\n(3) A representative ground omitted by the Public Notice provisions at issue is the problem of dangerous working environments. Korea’s industrial accident fatality rate remains among the highest, continuing to be about twice the OECD average, and recent statistics show that about 2,000 people die each year from industrial accidents. Moreover, most industrial accidents occur in small and medium-sized enterprises that lack investment capacity to prevent them. As of the first half of 2020, fatalities in workplaces with 49 or fewer employees accounted for 77.8 percent of all workplace fatalities, with particularly many fatal accidents in construction and manufacturing. The industries and scale of workplaces where many fatal industrial accidents occur generally coincide with the workplaces where foreign workers provide labor under the Employment Permit System. In fact, as of 2013, while the industrial accident rate of all workers [(number of injured workers / number of workers) × 100] was 0.59, the industrial accident rate of foreign workers was higher at 0.84.\\n\\nThere are also research findings that foreign workers are more likely than domestic workers to be exposed to various hazardous chemicals. This is because even at the same workplace, foreign workers often exclusively handle dangerous organic solvents. In the 2008 study by the Occupational Safety and Health Research Institute, “Study on the Health Status and Health Management Measures of Migrant Workers,” foreign workers showed statistically significantly higher blood lead levels than domestic workers. In addition, when measuring dimethylformamide (DMF) exposure levels among foreign workers and domestic workers with similar conditions in terms of age, industry, and sex, foreign workers were found to be more than twice as highly exposed as domestic workers in both the 2016 and 2018 surveys (“Assessment of Health Vulnerability of Foreign Workers in Hazardous Substance Exposure Workplaces”).\\n\\nArticle 4 item 4 of the Public Notice provisions at issue allows workplace change only when, due to the Employer’s violation of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, a foreign worker suffers an injury or illness requiring suspension of work for at least 3 days, and the Employer fails to take safety and health measures under the Occupational Safety and Health Act until 1 month has elapsed from the date of such injury or illness. Thus, if a foreign worker works in a dangerous work environment or suffers a workplace injury not reaching that threshold, workplace change is not allowed. In such a situation, restricting a foreign worker from leaving a workplace without safety guarantees and moving to another workplace not only infringes the freedom to choose occupation but also risks threatening life and bodily integrity.\\n\\n(4) Article 5 of the Public Notice provisions at issue prescribes unfair treatment by the Employer, etc. that constitutes grounds for workplace change, but the grounds are excessively narrow. In particular, examining items 1 through 3, which deal with cases where the Employer, etc. has inflicted physical or personal harm on a foreign worker, the forms of conduct are limited to sexual harassment, sexual violence, assault, habitual abusive language, etc., and do not include cases where the Employer threatens the foreign worker’s life and bodily safety, such as by forcing unlicensed operation of construction machinery, or repeatedly issues unreasonable work instructions to a degree that makes continued work objectively difficult.\\n\\nSince it is impossible to regulate every individual unreasonable work instruction by the Employer by statute, our legal system guarantees the worker’s right to terminate the employment contract relatively freely, unlike the Employer, thereby guaranteeing the right to work in a healthy and reasonable work environment (see Labor Standards Act Article 23(1), Civil Act Articles 660(1) and 661). In particular, the Civil Act allows a service provider to terminate the contract when the Employer demands provision of labor not agreed upon (Article 658(1)); however, the Public Notice provisions at issue do not permit workplace change even in such cases, thereby compelling the Petitioners to tolerate the Employer’s repeated unreasonable work instructions.\\n\\n(5) The unfair treatment prescribed in Article 5 item 1 through item 4 of the Public Notice provisions at issue is supplemented by requirements that are unclear yet excessively strict, such as urgency or impossibility of continued work. In particular, the Employer’s sexual harassment, sexual violence, assault, habitual abusive language, etc. often occur in situations where there are no witnesses other than the foreign worker victim, and from the standpoint of foreign workers who lack Korean-language proficiency and knowledge of domestic law, it is not easy to collect evidence corresponding to the Public Notice provisions at issue and specifically prove the grounds.\\n\\nBecause of this vagueness in the Public Notice provisions at issue, disputes between Employers and foreign workers as to whether unfair treatment exists are likely to arise, and proving the grounds is also difficult, which may discourage foreign workers from applying for workplace change. Although the Public Notice contains a system under which the Foreign Workers Rights and Interests Protection Council may permit workplace change even where there is a lack of evidence to prove the grounds for workplace change or where there are grounds equivalent to grounds for workplace change, what constitutes “grounds equivalent to grounds for workplace change” is unclear, making it difficult to regard it as a reliable remedy for foreign workers, and its utilization rate is also low.\\n\\n(6) The Ministry of Employment and Labor, through inspections of 6,197 workplaces employing foreign workers with employment permits in 2017 and 2018, discovered a total of 12,711 violations. Among the violations, Labor Standards Act violations were the most numerous at 5,209, followed by Foreign Workers Employment Act violations (2,309), violations of other laws and regulations (1,118), and violations of the Equal Employment Opportunity and Work-Family Balance Assistance Act (1,106). However, most (11,295) were limited to correction orders, and only 1.7% (218 cases) resulted in employment restrictions, while no workplace had its employment permit revoked. The Ministry of Employment and Labor’s supervision and inspection record shows that violations of labor-related laws and regulations in workplaces employing foreign workers are very serious, confirming the high need for foreign workers to change workplaces. However, even if there is a violation of labor-related laws, if the case does not fall within the grounds prescribed by the Public Notice provisions at issue or does not reach that level, an application for workplace change cannot be made, and it is practically unrealistic to wait for revocation of the Employer’s employment permit or an employment restriction disposition before changing workplaces.\\n\\n(7) Even if a foreign worker applies for a workplace change, the worker cannot freely choose a workplace but is introduced to a new workplace by way of the head of the employment security office recommending the worker to an Employer who has obtained an employment permit (Article 25(3) of the Foreign Workers Employment Act, Article 8(3)), and thus cannot expect or predict that the working conditions or work environment of the workplace to be changed in the future will necessarily improve over the current workplace. The number of workplace changes is limited, and if a workplace change is made, there may be disadvantages such as restriction on the application of the faithful worker re-entry special exception. The fact that a foreign worker desires a workplace change despite such uncertainty and disadvantage, even though the grounds prescribed in the Public Notice provisions at issue are not met, indicates that the current workplace’s working environment is poor and that there is an urgent need to leave immediately.\\n\\n(8) In sum, the grounds for workplace change enumerated in the Public Notice provisions at issue are excessively restrictive and manifestly insufficient to guarantee the freedom of occupation of foreign workers. The Public Notice provisions at issue are manifestly unreasonable beyond the scope of legislative discretion and infringe the Petitioners’ freedom to choose occupation.\\n\\nJustices Yu Nam-seok, Lee Sun-ae, Lee Seok-tae, Lee Eun-ae, Lee Jong-seok, Lee Young-jin, Kim Ki-young, Moon Hyung-bae, Lee Mi-sun\\n\\n[Appendix] List of Representatives\\n\\n1.
