{"[94HEONMA201]": "1. Overview and Subject Matter  \\n   a. Status of the Petitioners  \\n   Petitioner Kim ○ Geun is a member of the Chungcheongbuk-do Provincial Council and a resident of Jungwon-gun, Chungcheongbuk-do; Petitioners Kim ○ Su and Lee ○ Young are members of the Jungwon-gun County Council and residents of Jungwon-gun, Chungcheongbuk-do; and Petitioners Min ○ Yong, Byun ○ Eun, and Kwak ○ Gon are residents of Jungwon-gun, Chungcheongbuk-do. All of them have lived in Jungwon-gun since the days of their ancestors, and, out of attachment to and love for Jungwon-gun, have endeavored to preserve the traditional culture of Jungwon-gun and to retain its historicity and uniqueness.  \\n\\n   b. Outline of the Case  \\n   The National Assembly, at its 166th extraordinary session, amended and resolved the Local Autonomy Act, which serves as the basis for the reorganization of the districts of local governments, and the amended Act was promulgated on 1994.3.16. as Act No. 4141. Accordingly, the legal basis was established for merging cities and counties that have historical homogeneity or the same living sphere to create a new city (Article 7(2) and Article 3(3) of the same Act), and on 1994.3.22. the Government selected 49 cities and 43 counties nationwide as areas subject to recommended consolidation in order to promote balanced regional development, to eliminate difficulties in carrying out metropolitan administration such as urban planning, water supply and sewage, and waste disposal, to enhance the competitiveness of local governments through budget savings, and to contribute to the succession and development of traditional culture and to resident harmony, and proceeded to promote their consolidation.  \\n   Chungju City and Jungwon-gun were also selected as the above-mentioned areas subject to recommended consolidation, and the Governor of Jungwon-gun held a public hearing on whether to consolidate them (1994.4.11.) and conducted a resident opinion survey (94.4.21. to 4.25.: participation rate 92.9%, for 61.8%, against 38.2%), and, after hearing the opinion of the Jungwon-gun Council (13 incumbent members, 5 for, 7 against, 1 invalid), formulated a basic plan concerning the consolidation and recommended it to the Governor of Chungcheongbuk-do. Thereafter, the Ministry of Home Affairs drafted a bill on the establishment, etc. of cities in the form of urban-rural integrated cities, including the consolidation of Chungju City and Jungwon-gun, and submitted it to the National Assembly after approval by the State Council, and the National Assembly enacted and resolved the Act on the Establishment, etc. of 33 Cities in the Form of Urban-Rural Integrated Cities, Including Namyangju City, Gyeonggi-do (hereinafter referred to as “the Act in this case”). The Act in this case was promulgated on 1994.8.3. as Act No. 4774 and shall enter into force on 1995.1.1.  \\n   Therefore, the Petitioners filed this adjudication petition on the ground that, in view of the fact that Jungwon-gun is immediately abolished and absorbed into the neighboring Chungju City pursuant to Article 4 of the Act in this case and that the above statutory provision is certain to enter into force on 1995.1.1., their fundamental rights are presently and directly infringed by the statutory provision itself without waiting for any separate concrete act of execution.  \\n\\n   c. Subject Matter of Adjudication  \\n   Article 4 of the Act in this case provides as follows:  \\n   Article 4 (Establishment of Chungju City, etc. in Chungcheongbuk-do)  \\n   (1) Chungju City, Jecheon City, Jungwon-gun, and Jecheon-gun in Chungcheongbuk-do shall each be abolished.  \\n   (2) Chungju City and Jecheon City in Chungcheongbuk-do shall each be established as follows.  \\n\\n   Name of city  \\n   Jurisdictional area  \\n\\n   Chungju City  \\n   The entirety of Chungju City in Chungcheongbuk-do and the entirety of Jungwon-gun abolished pursuant to the provisions of paragraph (1)  \\n\\n   Jecheon City  \\n   The entirety of Jecheon City in Chungcheongbuk-do and the entirety of Jecheon-gun abolished pursuant to the provisions of paragraph (1)  \\n\\n   The relief sought by the Petitioners is that the part of Article 4(1) of the Act in this case that abolishes Jungwon-gun of Chungcheongbuk-do and the part of Article 4(2) that establishes Chungju City with “the entirety of Jungwon-gun abolished pursuant to the provisions of paragraph (1)” within Chungju City’s jurisdictional area are unconstitutional.  \\n   Therefore, the subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether the part of Article 4 of the Act in this case that provides for the abolition of Jungwon-gun and its incorporation into Chungju City (hereinafter referred to as “the statutory provision in this case”) violates the Constitution.  \\n\\n2. Arguments and Opinions  \\n   a. Petitioners’ Arguments  \\n   (1) The statutory provision in this case not only runs contrary to the legislative purpose of the Act in this case, but in the process of enactment of the Act it is also an unconstitutional and void law that infringed, for the following reasons, the principle of due process guaranteed by Article 12 of the Constitution and rights of the people not enumerated in the Constitution, corresponding to the local autonomy system guaranteed by Articles 117 and 118 of the Constitution.  \\n   First, although Jungwon-gun originated from Gukwonseong during the Goguryeo period, it is the core of Jungwon culture-gun, which has a history and tradition of more than 1,500 years, and is an autonomous county with a population of 67,000, whereas Chungju City was promoted to city status in 1956 and has independently developed for over 40 years, and is an autonomous city with a population of approximately 140,000. In light of geographic conditions and growth potential, both cities and counties are areas with the potential for independent development, and despite the fact that they are by no means areas subject to consolidation (recommended areas) as indicated in the Ministry of Home Affairs’ “Guidelines for Promoting City-County Consolidation,” they were arbitrarily selected as such areas.  \\n   Second, according to Article 4(2) of the Local Autonomy Act, “... when abolishing or merging local governments or changing their names or districts, the opinion of the council of the relevant local government (hereinafter referred to as the ‘local council’) shall be heard.” However, the Jungwon District Council placed the consolidation proposal of Jungwon-gun and Chungju City on the agenda at its extraordinary session on 1994.5.11. and, with all 13 incumbent members present, rejected it by 5 votes in favor, 7 against, and 1 invalid.  \\n   Third, although Article 13-2 of the Local Autonomy Act provides that the head of a local government shall submit the abolition or merger of a local government to a referendum, the consolidation of Jungwon-gun and Chungju City was not subjected to a referendum on the ground that the Referendum Act had not yet been enacted, and was substituted by a resident opinion survey.  \\n   Fourth, immediately before the resident opinion survey, Chungcheongbuk-do prepared special countermeasures for promoting city-county consolidation, and, while implementing a regional responsibility system, individually sanitizing leading figures of negative perceptions, blocking anti-consolidation activities, and sending influential persons to their respective local bases, it forcibly created a pro-consolidation atmosphere; and, while distributing resident opinion survey forms regarding city-county consolidation to each relevant city and county, it assigned serial numbers to the resident opinion survey forms by household so that it would be possible to identify which household opposed it, thereby undermining the freedom and fairness of the resident opinion survey procedure.  \\n   Fifth, as a result of the city-county consolidation taking the form of Jungwon-gun being absorbed into Chungju City, that is, a city-centered consolidation, the representativeness of the rural Jungwon-gun area is weakened, so that the special characteristics of the rural area cannot be made use of and city-centered administration is carried out, resulting in agricultural policy being neglected and, in particular, the development of remote areas becoming further stagnant. Moreover, it is anticipated that offensive facilities such as sewage treatment plants and waste landfill sites will be concentrated in the Jungwon-gun area, which is on the outskirts of the city, and ultimately a phenomenon in which the residents of Jungwon-gun are sacrificed for the residents of Chungju City will arise. In addition, if the two cities and counties are consolidated, not only will rural housing funds be allocated in smaller amounts, but the residents of Jungwon-gun will receive relatively less cultural and welfare benefits while instead bearing a greater burden of medical insurance premiums, middle and high school tuition, and various taxes.  \\n   (2) The statutory provision in this case is an unconstitutional and void law because, in light of the fact that Jungwon-gun has preserved its long history and traditional culture, has sufficient potential for independent development considering various conditions, and that there are also many counties excluded from consolidation whose population is less than 50,000 and whose living sphere is closely connected to a nearby city, it arbitrarily and without reasonable basis treated Jungwon-gun and the Petitioners discriminatorily, thereby infringing the Petitioners’ right to equality prescribed in Article 11(1) of the Constitution.  \\n   (3) According to the statutory provision in this case, as Jungwon-gun disappears and is forcibly incorporated into Chungju City, the Petitioners, who are natives of Jungwon-gun, were deprived of the general freedom of action derived from the right to pursue happiness, namely, the right to live while cherishing traditional culture with attachment to the place where they were born, and, due to regional development and national policy, they were compelled to leave their hometown and relocate, or their hometown (its name) was lost, thereby infringing their freedom of residence and movement.  \\n\\n   b. Opinion of the Minister of Home Affairs  \\n   (1) Necessity of Reorganization of Districts in the Form of Urban-Rural Integration  \\n   The current system of districts separating urban and rural areas distorts the natural spatial flow of residents’ lives, renders the geographic spatial structure of the remaining counties irrational, causes side effects that trigger population concentration in urban areas, widens the financial gap between urban and rural areas as the urban areas that are the main source of local tax revenues are separated off, causes a decline in administrative capacity due to the dispersion of capable administrative personnel, and creates a large gap in regional development and administrative services between urban and rural areas. It also causes excessive expenditure on general administrative expenses, such as by the reckless expansion of administrative agencies and the increase in the number of public officials, and has problems in that, due to the separation of living spheres and administrative spheres, unnecessary friction is caused between cities and counties belonging to the same living sphere, and it is also unable to properly respond to the growing demand for metropolitan administration, such as regional development plans, urban planning, water supply and sewage, public health and hygiene, and the environment. Reorganization of districts in the form of urban-rural integration was promoted under the above awareness of these problems, emphasizing living spheres and settlement spheres, aligning residents’ daily lives with administrative districts and autonomous districts, while at the same time preparing a more smooth metropolitan administrative system and, for the consolidation of small local governments, strengthening the self-sustaining capacity of local governments.  \\n\\n   (2) Dismissal of the Petition  \\n   ㈎ It is a decision precedent of the Constitutional Court that a constitutional complaint is possible only when a fundamental right is presently infringed, and cannot be filed merely because it may be related at some time in the future. However, the Act on the Establishment, etc. of 33 Cities in the Form of Urban-Rural Integrated Cities, Including Namyangju City, Gyeonggi-do, which is the subject law in this case, provides that its effective date is 1995.1.1., and therefore this adjudication petition filed on 1994.9.26., clearly before the effective date, lacks the presentness of rights infringement and is thus unlawful.  \\n   ㈏ A constitutional complaint is a system that, when “fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution” are infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power, seeks to revoke the exercise of public power that caused the infringement or to confirm that the non-exercise is unconstitutional. However, the Petitioners’ assertion of “the succession and development of traditional culture and the promotion of national culture” merely emphasizes a state duty oriented toward a cultural state, and does not thereby grant each individual citizen concrete fundamental rights, and the provisions concerning “local autonomy” in Articles 117 and 118 of the Constitution mean that local governments are guaranteed as a general system, not that the existence of a specific individual local administrative district is guaranteed or that they are intended to protect individuals against the State. If so, the above portion among the rights alleged by the Petitioners to have been infringed is not a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution, and therefore the petition is unlawful only to that extent.  \\n\\n   (3) Rejection of the Petition on the Merits  \\n   ㈎ Whether or not the local council agreed regarding city-county consolidation is, at most, a reference matter without legal binding force, and even if measures contrary to the local council’s opinion are taken, this cannot be connected to an infringement of the Local Autonomy Act, much less the constitutional local autonomy system. Since the opinion of the local council was heard, it cannot be seen as a violation of the Local Autonomy Act, and the guarantee of the local autonomy system generally guarantees autonomous administration by local governments, not the survival of a particular local government, so absorption-merger or newly established merger of local governments is not contrary to the guarantee of the local autonomy system.  \\n   ㈏ The current Chungju City was formed by incorporating some areas of Jungwon-gun, and Chungwon-gun and Chungju City are areas that originally formed the same cultural and living sphere. Rather, the consolidation of the two areas would be a measure that better preserves the traditions, culture, and history of the region. In addition, even after the consolidation of Jungwon-gun and Chungju City, the former Jungwon-gun area, which is a rural area, can preserve and maintain the characteristics of the former Jungwon-gun by maintaining the towns and townships as they are, thereby enjoying the special administrative treatment for towns and townships as it is, and by preventing administrative and financial disadvantages for specific areas arising from the consolidation, while also being guaranteed the establishment of development plans for balanced development within the consolidated city area and efficient development of underdeveloped areas.  \\n   ㈐ The promotion of city-county consolidation was carried out not only for independent growth potential such as the size of the neighboring area, but also to achieve comprehensive administrative objectives such as improving the convenience of residents’ daily lives, promoting the succession and development of traditional culture, and fostering resident harmony. Jungwon-gun and Chungju City may prima facie be regarded as areas with potential for independent development, but since Chungju City was separated from and promoted from Jungwon-gun and the Jungwon-gun Office is located in Chungju City, the two areas historically form a common cultural and living sphere, and therefore the validity of their consolidation is recognized. In addition, this city-county consolidation is not a consolidation of two areas, city and county, on a one-to-one basis to newly establish a city of the urban-rural integrated form, which is different from an ordinary city, and because consolidation does not restrict autonomy rights or cause any effect on essential matters of the performance of autonomous administration such as by limiting or reserving autonomy, the Petitioners’ claim of infringement of the right to equality is without merit.  \\n   ㈑ Since the abolition or merger of local governments of the same local government is a legislative matter, and in the legislative process of the Act, the results of the resident opinion survey or the opinions of the relevant local council are merely reference matters without legal binding force, a dispute over this is unrelated to the essential issue of the political rights guaranteed by the Constitution. The consolidation of Jungwon-gun and Chungju City was implemented after the basis for conducting a referendum (Article 13-2 of the Local Autonomy Act) had merely been prepared and, in the situation where a law concerning the procedure for conducting a referendum had not yet been enacted (currently the referendum bills of both the Minsa and Minju parties are pending in the National Assembly), the resident opinion survey by household (61.8% in favor of consolidation) was conducted with maximum respect for the purpose of introducing the referendum system, and the opinion of the Jungwon-gun Council (opposition) and the opinion of the Chungcheongbuk-do Council (support) were collected, so the procedure was lawful and appropriate.  \\n   ㈒ The consolidation of Jungwon-gun and Chungju City, like the purpose of reorganizing districts in the form of urban-rural integration, aligns residents’ daily living sphere with administrative districts while at the same time preparing a smoother metropolitan administrative system, thereby reflecting the natural flow of human life, and it will contribute to making rural areas stable human settlement spaces and to developing them into places where the people more desire to live in their local communities; therefore, the Petitioners’ claim of infringement of freedom of residence and movement is without merit.  \\n   (4) Accordingly, this adjudication petition should be dismissed as an unlawful petition lacking the requirements for filing an adjudication petition, and even if not, the Petitioners’ arguments lack merit and should therefore be rejected.  \\n\\n3. Decision  \\n   a. Determination on the Relevance to Fundamental Rights  \\n   Article 117 of the Constitution provides that “(1) Local governments shall handle affairs concerning the welfare of residents, manage property, and may enact regulations concerning autonomy within the scope of statutes. (2) The types of local governments shall be determined by statute,” and Article 118 of the Constitution provides that “(1) A council shall be established in each local government. (2) Matters concerning the organization, powers, election of council members, method of appointment of the head of a local government, and other matters concerning the organization and operation of local governments shall be determined by statute,” thereby institutionally guaranteeing the autonomy of local governments. The essential contents of that guarantee are the guarantee of local governments, the guarantee of autonomous functions, and the guarantee of autonomous affairs. Thus, what Articles 117 and 118 of the Constitution institutionally guarantee is the autonomous power of local governments. However, with respect to the abolition or merger of local governments, while it is a matter of guaranteeing territorial sovereignty among the autonomous administrative powers of local governments, on the other hand, issues of infringement of the following fundamental rights arise as a result. That is, as a result of the enactment of this Act, Jungwon-gun, the Petitioners’ hometown, is incorporated into Chungju City, and the Petitioners may suffer present infringement of the right to live in a humanly dignified living space derived from the dignity, worth, and right to pursue happiness under Article 10 of the Constitution (the right to live while cherishing and honoring the traditional culture of the place where one was born), the right to equality under Article 11 of the Constitution (as residents of Jungwon-gun, the right to receive equal treatment in local government consolidation compared with residents of other cities and counties), the proper right to be heard derived from the guarantee of due process under Article 12 of the Constitution (the right of every citizen to present opinions in the exercise of public power that may produce adverse consequences concerning his or her interests), freedom of residence and movement under Article 14 of the Constitution (being compelled to leave one’s hometown and relocate due to regional development or national policy, or one’s hometown being lost), the right to vote under Article 24 of the Constitution, the right to hold public office under Article 25 of the Constitution (as Jungwon-gun is incorporated into Chungju City, the opportunity to participate in politics is relatively restricted), the right to live a humanly dignified life and the right to receive social security and social welfare under Article 34 of the Constitution (as a city-centered consolidation, the rural Jungwon-gun area is relatively marginalized from administrative benefits), and the right to a healthy and pleasant environment under Article 35 of the Constitution (the right to live in a healthy and pleasant environment infringed by the installation of offensive facilities such as sewage treatment plants and waste landfill sites and by the backwardness of regional development).  \\n   In principle, citizens must begin from the standpoint that they themselves protect their fundamental rights and that they themselves dispute any infringement thereof, and the freedoms and rights guaranteed by the Constitution cannot, in principle, be administered by the authority of public organizations.  \\n   If so, this adjudication petition is lawful, and the question is whether limiting the above fundamental rights by this Act is justified.  \\n\\n   b. Determination on Presentness and Directness of the Infringement of Fundamental Rights  \\n   (1) Even before a legal norm produces general effect, if it has been promulgated, can a constitutional complaint be filed against such legal norm? In this regard, our Court held in a constitutional complaint against the admission guidelines for the selection of freshmen at Seoul National University that “as long as it can be sufficiently predicted at the present time that the Petitioners, who are currently learning Japanese in high school, may suffer disadvantage if they apply for admission to the general track of Seoul National University in the 1994 academic year or the 1995 academic year because Japanese has been excluded from the elective subjects in the special examination by department at Seoul National University under those admission guidelines, it is proper to recognize the presentness of the infringement of fundamental rights and to recognize the interest in filing a constitutional complaint” (see Constitutional Court decision dated 1992.10.1., 92HEONMA68,76(consolidated)).  \\n   The Act in this case was promulgated on 1994.8.3. as Act No. 4774 and enters into force on 1995.1.1. Once the Act in this case enters into force, Jungwon-gun is immediately abolished and absorbed into Chungju City; therefore, it appears that the Petitioners’ rights relations may already be infringed before the Act in this case takes effect, and since it can be sufficiently predicted at the present time that the Petitioners may suffer disadvantages, the presentness of the infringement of fundamental rights is recognized.  \\n   (2) In order for a statute or a statutory provision itself to be the subject of a constitutional complaint, it requires that, by virtue of that statute or statutory provision, one’s own fundamental rights be directly and presently infringed without waiting for a specific act of execution; and the directness of infringement of fundamental rights referred to here means a case where restriction of freedom, imposition of duties, or deprivation of rights or legal status arises by the law itself without an act of execution (see Constitutional Court decision dated 1992.11.12., 91HEONMA192).  \\n   In this case, Jungwon-gun is abolished and incorporated into Chungju City by the statutory provision in this case itself without the intermediation of any other act of execution, and therefore the directness of the infringement of fundamental rights resulting therefrom must be recognized.  \\n\\n   c. Determination on Whether the Act in This Case Is Unconstitutional  \\n   (1) Whether the requirements of compatibility with the public welfare and compliance with the principle of proportionality are satisfied  \\n   ㈎ According to Article 37(2) of the Constitution, all freedoms and rights of all citizens may be restricted by statute only when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare.  \\n   Our Court held that “as the basic principles to be observed by the State in legislative activities restricting the fundamental rights of the people, the legislative purpose must be recognized as legitimate within the system of the Constitution and statutes (legitimacy of purpose), the method must be effective and appropriate for achieving that purpose (appropriateness of method), and even if the measure restricting fundamental rights selected by the legislator is appropriate for achieving the legislative purpose, the restriction of fundamental rights must be limited to the minimum necessary by seeking, as far as possible, a more moderate form or method (minimum infringement), and the public interest protected by the legislation must outweigh the private interest infringed when comparing and balancing them (balance of legal interests)” (see Constitutional Court decision dated 1992.12.24., 92HEONGA8).  \\n   In determining whether the Act in this case is unconstitutional, consideration should be given to whether: ① in enacting the Act in this case, the National Assembly appropriately and fully investigated matters of significant meaning and made them the basis of legislation; ② the National Assembly comprehensively and rationally weighed all public-interest grounds and positive and negative effects of the statute; ③ the restriction by the National Assembly is necessary and appropriate, complies with the principle of proportionality, and takes into account the appropriateness of the subject matter and systemic legitimacy; and, in making a determination thereon, the above matters should be comprehensively considered to examine whether ① the National Assembly’s judgment and decision are manifestly wrong or can clearly be refuted, and ② whether they violate the constitutional order of values.  \\n   ㈏ According to the record, the following facts may be recognized. First, Jungwon-gun and Chungju City historically constituted one locality. That is, Jungwon-gun and Chungju City were the same administrative district until Chungju-eup was promoted to city status on 1956.7.8. and twelve myeon were renamed Jungwon-gun and separated. In other words, Jungwon-gun and Chungju City were one of the 54 states of Mahan during the Three Han period; were called Gukwonseong during 475 to 491 (63rd to 79th years of King Jangsu of Goguryeo); were called Gukwonsokgyeong in 557 (18th year of King Jinheung of Silla); were called Jungwonsokgyeong in 757 (16th year of King Gyeongdeok of Silla); were called Chungju in 940 (23rd year of King Taejo of Goryeo); were called Chungjumok in 983 (2nd year of King Seongjong of Goryeo); were called Changhwa-gun in 995 (14th year of King Seongjong of Goryeo) and subordinated to Jungwondo; were called Gukwon-gyeong in 1254 (41st year of King Gojong of Goryeo); in 1395 (4th year of King Taejo of Joseon), as the capital of Chungcheong-do, a magistrate was placed in Chungju; in 1449 (31st year of King Sejong), the magistrate concurrently served as moksa, and later the offices were separated again; in 1598 (31st year of King Seonjo), the provincial headquarters was moved to Gongju; in 1895 (32nd year of King Gojong), as the capital of Chungcheongbuk-do, a governor was stationed there; in 1908 (2nd year of King Sunjong), on the ground that transportation was inconvenient, the provincial office having jurisdiction over Chungbuk was moved to Cheongju and a county magistrate was placed there; on 1956.7.8. Chungju-eup was promoted to Chungju City; and Salmi, Iryu, Judeok, Sinni, Noeun, Angseong, Gageum, Geumga, Dongnyang, Sanchezok, Eomjeong, Soetae, and other twelve myeon were renamed Jungwon-gun and separated; on 1963.1.1. pursuant to administrative district change measures, Sangmo-myeon of Goesan-gun was incorporated into Jungwon-gun; and on 1973.7.1. pursuant to administrative district change measures, Hahmun-ri of Iryu-myeon was incorporated into Goesan-gun, and part of Gwangwol-ri of Sinni-myeon was incorporated into Eumseong-gun, which continues to the present. Second, topographically as well, Chungju City is in the middle of Jungwon-gun, and both the Jungwon-gun Office and the Chungju City Hall are located in Chungju City, making it the same living sphere.  \\n   Therefore, the National Assembly, in enacting the Act in this case, did not base the legislation on any mistaken factual premise, nor does it cause the Petitioners to reside where they do not wish to live or impede residence and movement/change of residence.  \\n   ㈐ The purpose of consolidating Chungju City and Jungwon-gun is, taking into account that the average fiscal self-reliance ratio of cities is currently 64% whereas that of counties is at the 25% level, to save budget, enhance the competitiveness of local governments, relieve difficulties in carrying out metropolitan administration such as urban planning, transportation, water supply and sewage, and environmental problems, and promote balanced regional development. In addition, according to the Chungcheongbuk-do Guidelines for Promoting City-County Consolidation, in order to minimize side effects that may arise from the consolidation of Jungwon-gun and Chungju City, taking into account the characteristics of the former county area, it is intended that eup and myeon areas shall remain as eup and myeon without renaming them as dong, that various benefits enjoyed previously as a county shall be maintained as they are, and that the status of local council members and public officials shall be maintained as it is. After enactment of the Act in this case, the Ministry of Home Affairs proposed the Act on Administrative Special Cases, etc. under the Establishment of Cities in the Form of Urban-Rural Integration as a follow-up measure pursuant to the Guidelines for Promoting City-County Consolidation, and the National Assembly passed the Act on 1994.12.2. That Act provides special exceptions necessary to rationalize administrative operation by protecting existing interests and supporting development for rural and fishing areas and their residents when cities in the form of urban-rural integration are established pursuant to the provisions of the Partial Amendment to the Local Autonomy Act (Act No. 4741 of 1994.3.16.), and its main contents are: ① neither the local government on either side nor a specific area shall lose existing administrative and financial benefits or be subjected to new burdens on local residents due to the consolidation of the city and county (Article 2); ② the heads of central administrative agencies and governors may separately formulate development plans or provide special fiscal support for the development of rural and fishing areas or underdeveloped areas, and in designating districts for the development of specific areas, such as development promotion zones, priority may be given to areas within cities of the urban-rural integrated form (Article 3); ③ public officials belonging to the former city or county shall be treated equally so that they do not suffer personnel disadvantages vis-à-vis each other (Article 4); and ④ the council of the city may have two vice chairpersons only for the term of office of the council members at the time of consolidation, one to be elected from among the city council members and the other from among the county council members (Article 5).  \\n   If so, as Jungwon-gun is incorporated into Chungju City, the Petitioners can expect better administrative benefits, social security, livelihood support, environmental measures, and development plans, and by aligning the living space and administrative district, a more effective residential environment can be created, which is appropriate for the succession and development of Jungwon’s traditional culture; rather, because the basic rights restriction measure is limited to the minimum necessary by preserving the existing benefits that Jungwon-gun residents had enjoyed, such as the retention of the existing minimum administrative units of Jungwon-gun, and by recognizing opportunities for participation in politics, such as maintaining the status of existing public officials, the National Assembly cannot be said to have plainly erred or violated the constitutional order of values in judging compatibility with the public welfare and applying the principle of proportionality in enacting the Act in this case.  \\n   (2) Whether the principle of due process was violated  \\n   ㈎ In relation to the principle of due process, our Court held that “the main text of Article 12(3) of the Constitution, together with paragraph (1) of the same Article, constitutes the general clause of the principle of due process, and it expressly states as a basic principle of the Constitution that the acts of all public powers of the State, such as legislation and administration, are not limited to the area of formal procedure, but must possess not only procedural legality but also substantive legality in which the legal content itself is rational and just.” (see Constitutional Court decision dated 1992.12.24., 92HEONGA9).  \\n   The Act in this case concerns the abolition and merger of local governments, and the current statutory provisions concerning this matter are as follows. That is, Article 4 of the Local Autonomy Act provides: “(1) The names and districts of local governments shall continue as before, and when they are changed or local governments are abolished or merged, they shall be determined by statute; provided that, (2) the opinion of the council of the relevant local government (hereinafter referred to as the ‘local council’) shall be heard ...” and Article 13-2 of the same Act provides: “(1) The head of a local government may submit the abolition or merger of a local government or major matters for decision, etc. to a referendum. (2) The object of the referendum, the proponent, the requirements for proposal, and other procedures for voting shall be separately determined by statute.”  \\n   ㈏ However, the due process in connection with the legislative process of the Act in this case is the so-called hearing procedure, meaning that citizens must be given the opportunity to express their positions on a national reorganization plan in order to secure their legal status in relation to their own interests. In other words, citizens must not be reduced to mere objects of state activity. In addition, before the legislator makes a decision to change a specific area in relation to local autonomy for reasons of public welfare, balancing between conflicting interests must generally be preceded, and such balancing of interests cannot be properly achieved without the participation of interested persons. Only through such procedures does the National Assembly obtain comprehensive and reliable knowledge of important matters before making its decision. Therefore, the hearing procedure guaranteed by the Constitution in relation to this case is sufficient if it notifies interested persons of matters concerning the essential content of the consolidation of Jungwon-gun and Chungju City and its grounds and affords them an opportunity to state their opinions thereon, and the opinions so stated function to provide legislative materials to the National Assembly, but the legislator is not necessarily bound by those opinions.  \\n   ㈐ What constitutional effect does Article 4(2) of the Local Autonomy Act, which states that “the opinion of the council of the relevant local government shall be heard” when abolishing or merging local governments, have? As examined above, the very fact that the opinion-hearing procedure of the local council has been followed must be regarded as compliance with due process, and the result must be interpreted merely as material for the National Assembly’s judgment when legislating.  \\n   If not, and if the National Assembly were bound by the opinions of the local council, the legislative intent of Article 4(1) of the Local Autonomy Act, which provides that the abolition or merger of local governments shall be by statute, would be nullified, and it would also result in the local council being superior to the National Assembly.  \\n   ㈑ Article 13-2 of the Local Autonomy Act concerning the implementation of a referendum is, by its terms, a discretionary provision, and whether to conduct it is also left to the discretion of the head of the local government, the Referendum Act has not yet been enacted, and the referendum procedure, as examined above, is part of the hearing procedure and has no binding effect as a result. Therefore, the fact that a referendum was not conducted in the legislative process of the Act in this case cannot be said to violate the principle of due process.  \\n   ㈒ We examine the issue of procedural defects in the resident opinion survey on the consolidation of Jungwon-gun and Chungju City conducted by the Governor of Jungwon-gun in lieu of a referendum. As examined above, the resident opinion survey, as a type of hearing procedure, was sufficient to notify residents, including the Petitioners, of important matters concerning the consolidation of Jungwon-gun and Chungju City and its grounds, and to afford them an opportunity to state their opinions. According to the record, it is recognized that such a degree of opinion survey was sufficiently conducted, and in addition it is recognized that a public hearing concerning the consolidation of Jungwon-gun and Chungju City was also held in the Jungwon-gun Office building; therefore, there is no defect in the resident opinion survey procedure. In addition, the results of the resident opinion survey merely function as material for the National Assembly’s balancing of interests for the public welfare and have no direct binding force on the National Assembly. Therefore, the principle of due process was also observed in the resident opinion survey.  \\n\\n4. Conclusion  \\n   If so, since the Act in this case did not infringe the Petitioners’ right to live in a humanly dignified living space derived from the right to pursue happiness, the proper right to be heard, the right to equality, freedom of residence and movement, the right to vote, the right to hold public office, the right to live a humanly dignified life, the right to receive social security and social welfare, or the right to environment, the Petitioners’ claim is without merit and is dismissed, and it is so ordered. This decision is by unanimous agreement of all participating Justices, except for the dissenting opinion of Justice Cho Seung-hyung.  \\n\\n5. Separate Opinion of Justice Cho Seung-hyung  \\n   I dissent from the view among the majority opinion that the principle of due process was observed (there is no need to examine the remaining views). That is, the majority opinion states that, since it is recognized that in the legislative process of this Act the relevant agencies sought the opinion of the Jungwon-gun Council, conducted a resident opinion survey, and held a public hearing in the conference room of the Jungwon-gun Office concerning the consolidation of Jungwon-gun and Chungju City, the opinion-hearing procedure was followed as far as possible, and therefore the principle of due process cannot be said to have been violated in the legislative process of this Act.  \\n   Examining the record of this case,  \\n   a. It is recognized that the National Assembly, in the legislative process of this Act, enacted the law in violation of the above principle.  \\n   Article 1 of the Local Autonomy Act provides that it “... aims to promote the democracy of local autonomous administration ... and the democratic development of the Republic of Korea,” and Article 118(2) of the Constitution provides that “... other matters concerning the organization and operation of local governments shall be determined by statute,” thereby declaring that matters concerning the organization and operation of local governments shall be determined by statute upon hearing the democratic will of the residents, and the intent of Article 4(2) of the Local Autonomy Act, which provides that when a local government is abolished or merged or its name or district is changed, the opinion of the council of the relevant local government shall be heard, permits interpretation to the effect that, in principle, the opinion of the council must be followed, and only exceptionally, if there are special circumstances such that legislation must be enacted even contrary to the opinion of that council, legislation may first be enacted contrary to the opinion. If such an interpretation were not permitted, there would be no need to establish the above statutory provision at all, because the National Assembly could legislate at its discretion without being bound by the above opinion.  \\n   In addition, Article 13-2 of the same Act provides that “(1) The head of a local government may submit the abolition or merger of a local government or major matters for decision, etc. to a referendum. (2) The object of the referendum, the proponent, the requirements for proposal, and other procedures for voting shall be separately determined by statute,” and unless the statute prescribed in Article 13-2(2) of the same Act is enacted and implemented, it cannot be specified who the proponent is, whether proposal preparatory acts by a certain minimum number of residents are required, who supervises the voting, and by what procedures voting and counting are conducted. Therefore, the head of a local government cannot submit such a referendum, and even if the Referendum Act is enacted and implemented, it is up to the head of the local government whether to submit the referendum or not, so the National Assembly would be able to enact this Act only after watching whether the head of the local government conducts the referendum and what the result of the referendum is.  \\n   Therefore, prior to enacting this Act, the National Assembly should first enact the law concerning the referendum prescribed in Article 13-2(2) of the Local Autonomy Act, watch, after its implementation, whether the head of the local government submits the matter to a referendum, and if so, confirm the result of the referendum, take into account the residents’ will and the contents of the favorable or unfavorable resolutions of the local government council, and if the will or resolution conflicts, decide whether to legislate according to the residents’ will, and if the will or resolution is the same, decide whether to legislate according to that will or resolution; only when there are special circumstances to the extent that legislation must be made contrary to that will or resolution may legislation be made contrary thereto. That such prior legislative procedures must be followed in sequence is required by the constitutional principle of due process.  \\n   b. Looking at this case,  \\n   It is clear that the National Assembly did not first enact the referendum law that should have preceded the legislation, and therefore did not confirm the residents’ will through a lawful referendum. The majority opinion argues that due process was followed because a resident opinion survey was conducted in lieu of a referendum, but this is a procedure not found in any statute and is clearly unlawful. It is true that on 1994.5.11. there was a resolution by the Jungwon-gun Council in this case, but its content was that out of 13 council members, 5 were in favor, 7 were against, and 1 was invalid, clearly opposing the enactment of this Act, and although the public hearing and the unlawful resident opinion survey relied upon by the majority opinion were conducted, all such procedures are unlawful, so this Act is nothing more than one enacted at the discretion of the National Assembly without lawful procedure. In other words, it violated the principle of due process and is therefore unconstitutional and void.  \\n   Therefore, without even examining the remaining views of the majority opinion, the majority opinion is improper, and the order of this decision should state, “The Act on the Establishment, etc. of 33 Cities in the Form of Urban-Rural Integrated Cities, Including Namyangju City, Gyeonggi-do, promulgated as Act No. 4774 on 1994.8.3., is unconstitutional,” and grant the Petitioners’ request.  \\n   1994. 12. 29.  \\n   Presiding Justice Kim Yong-jun  \\n   Justice Kim Jin-woo  \\n   Justice Kim Moon-hee  \\n   Justice Hwang Do-yeon  \\n   Justice Cho Seung-hyung  \\n   Justice in Charge Jung Kyoung-sik  \\n   Justice Ko Joong-seok  \\n   Justice Shin Chang-eon"}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the protection of rights against an administrative agency’s factual act is incorrect? (In case of dispute, according to case law)
A: The term “official duties of a public official,” which is a requirement for a claim for compensation prescribed by the State Compensation Act, includes not only sovereign acts but also non-sovereign acts such as administrative guidance.
B: If administrative guidance, as a non-sovereign act that does not have coercive force, did not deviate from the limits of administrative guidance, the administrative agency bears no liability for damages therefrom even if any damage was caused to the counterparty.
C: When an inmate inquired of the warden whether he could receive celebrity photographs from an outsider, and the warden notified him to the effect that permission might be denied, such act, by informing the inmate of the result of interpreting and applying the relevant statutes and administrative rules, is subject to a constitutional complaint.
D: An act by the Chairperson of the Financial Services Commission prohibiting commercial banks from providing home mortgage loans for the purchase of ultra-high-priced apartments within speculative districts and speculative overheating districts constitutes administrative guidance having a regulatory and binding character, and thus qualifies as an exercise of public power subject to a constitutional complaint.
E: Where a discharged trainee files a constitutional complaint challenging the act of the Commandant of the Army Training Center forcing trainees to attend a religious event within the Army Training Center, even if it does not help to provide subjective relief of rights, if there is a risk that such infringing act will recur in the future, or if resolution of the dispute in question is an urgent matter for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order and the complaint can be recognized as having an interest in adjudication because clarification of the matter has constitutionally significant meaning.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2000HEONMA327]": "1. Outline of the Case and the Subject of Adjudication\\n\\nA. Outline of the Case\\n\\n(1) The Petitioners were arrested at around 00:20 on March 20, 2000 as persons caught in the act for violating the Public Official Election and Prevention of Election Malpractice Act, on suspicion of distributing printed materials whose distribution was prohibited without registering as election campaign workers. After being investigated at the Seongnam Nambu Police Station, they were subjected to a brief body search in underwear, by touching and feeling their bodies, and were detained in the detention cell.\\n\\nAt around 13:30 of the same day, in the course of being readmitted to the detention cell after meeting with counsel, the Petitioners were required by a female police officer in charge of the detention cell to undergo a detailed inspection to determine whether they possessed or concealed dangerous articles such as weapons and other prohibited items. With their backs turned to the police officer, they raised their upper garments together with their underwear up to the armpits and lowered their lower garments together with their underwear down to the knees, and underwent a detailed body search (hereinafter referred to as “the body search in this case”) by standing up and sitting down three times.\\n\\n(2) Accordingly, the Petitioners filed the present constitutional complaint on May 18, 2000, seeking a determination that the body search in this case was unconstitutional, alleging that, by virtue of the excessive body search in this case, which had been conducted as a means and in a manner that merely inflicted humiliation and shame on them without any legal basis, their fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 12 of the Constitution, namely bodily liberty, and by Article 10 of the Constitution, namely human dignity and worth and the right to pursue happiness, were infringed.\\n\\nB. Subject of Adjudication\\n\\n(1) The subject of adjudication in this case is whether the Respondent’s body search in this case, conducted in the course of the Petitioners’ readmission to the detention cell in order to determine whether they possessed or concealed dangerous articles such as weapons and other prohibited items, infringed the Petitioners’ fundamental rights, etc. guaranteed by Articles 12 and 10 of the Constitution. {The Petitioners indicated the Commissioner-General of the National Police Agency as the Respondent in the petition; however, since the entity that exercised the body search in this case was the Chief of Seongnam Nambu Police Station, the Respondent in this case shall be determined ex officio to be the Chief of Seongnam Nambu Police Station (see Constitutional Court Decision of May 13, 1993, 91HEONMA190, Reports of Decisions 5-1, 312, 320).}\\n\\n(2) The provisions serving as the basis for the body search or body inspection in this case are Articles 8 and 10 of the former Rules on the Detention and Escort of Suspects (Police Agency Directive No. 248, amended on January 20, 1999 and before amendment on October 26, 2000), the contents of which are as follows.\\n\\nArticle 8 (Inspection of Weapons, etc.) of the former Rules on the Detention and Escort of Suspects (hereinafter referred to as “the Rules in this case”)\\n(1) A person working in a detention cell shall, when detaining a suspect, thoroughly inspect the suspect’s body for whether any weapon, etc. is concealed or possessed. Provided, that in the case of a female suspect, an adult woman shall participate.\\n(2) When a custodian inspects the body of a suspect, the custodian shall conduct a meticulous inspection, including of the hair and each part of the body and the inside of clothing and socks, so that no weapons, poisonous substances, matches, tobacco powder, etc. are concealed or possessed.\\nArticle 10 (Mutatis mutandis Application upon Re-admission)\\nThe provisions of Article 8 shall apply mutatis mutandis when a suspect who had been released from detention for investigation, meeting, or other reasons is readmitted.\\n\\n2. The Petitioners’ Claims and the Opinions of Interested Institutions\\n\\nA. The Petitioners’ Claims\\n\\nEven if the detention cell installed in a police station pursuant to Article 68 (Detention Cells) of the former Act on Prison Administration (as amended by Act No. 5175 on December 12, 1996, and before amendment by Act No. 6038 on December 28, 1999; since Act No. 6038 entered into force three months after its promulgation, Act No. 5175 applied on March 20, 2000, when the body search in this case was conducted) is deemed equivalent to a detention room for unconvicted detainees, the person subject to body inspection under Article 10 (Body Inspection, etc.) of the former Act on Prison Administration, which is applied mutatis mutandis, is limited to the “person who, as a criminal suspect or defendant, has had an arrest warrant executed upon him or her” under Article 1 (Purpose), that is, an “unconvicted detainee”; accordingly, persons such as the Petitioners, who were arrested as persons caught in the act but against whom no arrest warrant had been executed, are not unconvicted detainees and thus the above provision cannot be applied mutatis mutandis. Nevertheless, the Respondent conducted the body search in this case against the Petitioners pursuant to the Rules in this case based on the above provision.\\n\\nEven if the above provision were applicable mutatis mutandis to the Petitioners, the Petitioners were arrested on minor suspicions, had not possessed or concealed dangerous articles such as weapons and had no risk of self-harm, and, considering that they had already undergone a body inspection when first detained in the detention cell and that they were being readmitted to the detention cell after meeting with counsel, there was no need whatsoever for a detailed body search of the Petitioners.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Respondent’s excessive body search in this case, which lacked a legal basis and, without complying with due process, exceeded the necessary minimum scope in terms of means and method and merely inflicted extreme humiliation and shame on the Petitioners, thereby grossly exceeding the limits of tolerable endurance, manifestly infringed the Petitioners’ constitutionally guaranteed fundamental rights, including bodily liberty, human dignity and worth, and the right to pursue happiness.\\n\\nB. The Opinions of the Respondent and the Commissioner-General of the National Police Agency\\n\\nArticle 9 (Detention Cell) of the Act on the Performance of Duties by Police Officers provides that police stations shall have detention cells for the confinement of persons who have been arrested or detained pursuant to procedures prescribed by law, or who have received a judgment or disposition restricting bodily liberty. Article 68 of the former Act on Prison Administration provides that detention cells installed in police stations shall be deemed equivalent to detention rooms for unconvicted detainees.\\n\\nSince the Rules in this case, based on the former Act on Prison Administration, provide in Articles 8 and 10 regulations concerning body inspection, not only is body inspection comparable to Article 10 of the former Act on Prison Administration possible even for suspects who are arrested in flagrante delicto and detained in a detention cell, but in order to prevent harm to the life and body of detainees and to maintain safety and order in the detention cell, a detailed body inspection must be conducted for all suspects detained in the detention cell; and since the body search in this case against the Petitioners was also lawfully conducted in accordance with the Rules in this case, it cannot be said that the Petitioners’ constitutional fundamental rights were infringed by the body search in this case.\\n\\n3. Decision\\n\\nA. Determination on the procedural requirements\\n\\nThe body search in this case conducted against the Petitioners is not a body inspection as a type of search or seizure, which is a compulsory disposition in investigation aimed at collecting evidence regarding the criminal suspicion of suspects, etc. The body search in this case is a body inspection conducted by the police, as the managing authority of the detention cell, in detaining suspects, etc. for the purpose of preventing harm to the life and body of suspects, etc., and of maintaining safety and order within the detention cell; since it has the nature of a unilateral compulsion imposed on suspects, etc. from a superior position, it constitutes an exercise of public authority in the form of a factual act. Accordingly, it falls within the exercise of public power under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act, which is subject to a constitutional complaint.\\n\\nHowever, the act of infringement against the Petitioners has already been terminated, and even if a determination of unconstitutionality were made regarding the body search in this case, relief for the Petitioners would be impossible, so the interest in the protection of subjective rights has already lapsed. Nevertheless, since the constitutional complaint system has the function not only of providing relief for an individual’s subjective rights but also of guaranteeing the objective constitutional order, even if a constitutional complaint does not contribute much to the relief of subjective rights, adjudication interest may be recognized where there is a risk that such an act of infringement will recur in the future, or where the resolution of the relevant dispute is an important matter for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order and thus its constitutional clarification has significant meaning (see Constitutional Court Decision of January 28, 1992, 91HEONMA111, Reports of Decisions 4, 51, 56-57; Constitutional Court Decision of March 27, 1997, 92HEONMA273, Reports of Decisions 9-1, 337, 342, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the materials of this case, although the Rules in this case were amended after this case, body inspections of suspects detained in detention cells at local police stations nationwide are still frequently being conducted. Moreover, even under the amended Rules (Police Agency Directive No. 331, October 26, 2000), since there remains a risk that constitutional rights may be infringed upon many persons, and repeatedly, by measures of the same or similar kind as the body search in this case, through arbitrary interpretation of the requirements for detailed body inspection or arbitrary selection of the method of body inspection, adjudication interest is recognized.\\n\\nB. Determination on the merits\\n\\n(1) Facts found\\n\\n(a) The Petitioners were arrested at around 00:20 on March 20, 2000 as persons caught in the act for violating the Public Official Election and Prevention of Election Malpractice Act, and after being investigated as suspects at the Seongnam Nambu Police Station, they were, at around 04:30 of the same day, subjected to a brief body inspection in the body inspection room by a female police officer in charge, in underwear, by touching and feeling their bodies.\\n\\nAt around 13:00 of the same day, after completing a group meeting with counsel in the meeting room in the presence of a police officer, the Petitioners, in the course of being readmitted to the detention cell at around 13:30 of the same day, were required by the female police officer in charge to undergo a detailed body inspection by taking off all upper garments and lowering lower garments together with underwear to the knees, in order to ascertain whether they possessed or concealed dangerous articles such as weapons and other prohibited items. The Petitioners refused, on grounds including that they had already undergone a body inspection and that, since they were being readmitted after meeting with counsel, there was no possibility of possessing or concealing dangerous articles such as weapons. However, as the above police officer strongly demanded cooperation in the body inspection while presenting the reasons and basis for the body inspection, they were subjected to the body search in this case under the name of a detailed body inspection; at that time, some of the Petitioners were menstruating.\\n\\nThe detailed body inspection was conducted in a closed body inspection room with adjustable visibility, by turning one’s back to the female police officer and turning around, and by oneself raising the upper garments, including the brassiere, to the armpits and lowering the lower garments, including the panties, to the knees, and then standing up and sitting down three times.\\n\\n(b) The police that investigated the above case did not request an arrest warrant against the Petitioners on the 21st of the same month and released them. Thereafter, Petitioner Kim ○ Kyung received a disposition of suspension of indictment on June 16, 2000, and Petitioner Sin ○ Kyung was indicted without detention and, on November 1 of the same year, was sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment with one year of probation, and that judgment became final around that time. Petitioner Park ○ Ae was indicted without detention and, on November 1 of the same year, was sentenced to a fine of KRW 700,000 and appealed, but the appeal was dismissed on January 9, 2001, and that judgment became final around that time.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Petitioners filed a lawsuit against the State, etc. for damages for mental suffering caused by the unlawful and improper body inspection, and on November 10, 2000, the Seoul District Court (2000GAHAP35295) rendered a judgment partially in favor of the Plaintiffs; the State appealed, and on July 6, 2001, the Seoul High Court (2000NA59403) rendered a judgment against the Plaintiffs; the Petitioners then filed an appeal on points of law, and on October 26 of the same year, the Supreme Court (2001DA51466) rendered a judgment reversing and remanding the case, which is currently pending before the Seoul High Court (2001NA66996).\\n\\n(2) Whether the body search in this case infringed the Petitioners’ constitutional fundamental rights\\n\\nIf, as the Petitioners allege, they were compelled by the Respondent to undergo the excessive body search in this case without any legal basis, and thereby could not but have felt extreme humiliation and shame to the extent of exceeding the limits of tolerable endurance, then the question arises whether their personality rights guaranteed by Article 10 of the Constitution and their bodily liberty guaranteed by Article 12 were infringed.\\n\\n(a) Legal basis for the body inspection of detainees in police station detention cells\\n\\nA detention cell is a facility that may be installed in local police stations pursuant to Article 9 of the Act on the Performance of Duties by Police Officers for confining persons who have been arrested or detained pursuant to procedures prescribed by law, or who have received a judgment or disposition restricting bodily liberty, and it serves the function of preventing escape and destruction of evidence by those detained.\\n\\nThe body inspection of detainees in police station detention cells, including the body search in this case, is conducted on the basis of Article 68 of the former Act on Prison Administration, which provides that detention cells at police stations shall be deemed equivalent to detention rooms for unconvicted detainees, and Article 10 of the same Act. In other words, police station detention cells are operated by applying mutatis mutandis the relevant provisions concerning detention rooms for unconvicted detainees within the scope not contrary to their nature. Among those, with respect to body inspection, Article 10(1) of the former Act on Prison Administration provides that “for new arrivals (persons newly admitted to a prison, juvenile prison, or detention center as detainees), the body and clothing shall be inspected, fingerprints taken, and photographs taken,” and paragraph (2) of the same Article provides that “with respect to persons already in detention, if the head of the relevant institution deems it necessary, the body and clothing may also be inspected, fingerprints taken, and photographs taken.” Accordingly, those provisions constitute the legal basis for body inspection of detainees in police station detention cells.\\n\\n(b) Permissible scope of body inspection of detainees in police station detention cells\\n\\nThe body inspection conducted by the Respondent on persons detained in the detention cell is an investigation into whether dangerous articles such as weapons and other prohibited items are possessed or concealed, for the purpose of preventing harm to the life and body of detainees and maintaining safety and order within the detention cell, and in light of that purpose, the necessity and propriety of a body search are recognized within a certain scope.\\n\\nHowever, it cannot be said that body inspection pursuant to the Rules in this case, by which the Commissioner-General of the National Police Agency issued guidelines for the exercise of official authority to local police stations and their officers in order to achieve such administrative purpose, is naturally lawful. It must be conducted by a reasonable method that, within the necessary minimum scope for achieving that purpose, sufficiently takes care to ensure that fundamental rights, including the detainee’s honor and sense of shame, are not infringed. Accordingly, a detailed body inspection of detainees in police station detention cells is permissible only where it is judged that the detainee may enter the institution while possessing or concealing dangerous articles such as weapons and other prohibited items in intimate parts of the body, and there are reasonable grounds to believe that such articles would be difficult to discover by other means, such as inspection by external observation or palpation, and where it is conducted by means and methods that minimize the possibility of infringing the detainee’s fundamental rights.\\n\\n(c) Decision\\n\\nArticle 10 of the Constitution guarantees personality rights deriving from the human dignity and worth, which can be said to be the ultimate purpose and basic principle of all guarantees of fundamental rights, and which are the essential and inherent value of human beings (see Constitutional Court Decision of September 10, 1990, 89HEONMA82, Reports of Decisions 2, 306, 310, etc.). Article 12 guarantees bodily liberty, which, together with mental liberty, is the most fundamental liberty for realizing human dignity and worth, and is the premise for the guarantee of all fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court Decision of April 14, 1992, 90HEONMA82, Reports of Decisions 4, 194, 206, etc.). Therefore, even if, on the basis of Article 68 of the former Act on Prison Administration, etc., restrictions on the people’s fundamental rights are unavoidable in connection with the implementation of detailed body inspections of detainees in police station detention cells, such restrictions must not infringe the essential content thereof, nor violate the principle of prohibition of excess, which means legitimacy of purpose, appropriateness of means, minimality of damage, and balance of legal interests (see Constitutional Court Decision of March 27, 1997, 95HEONGA17, Reports of Decisions 9-1, 219, 234; Constitutional Court Decision of May 28, 1998, 95HEONBA18, Reports of Decisions 10-1, 583, 595, etc.).\\n\\nAs seen above, however, the Petitioners were women arrested as persons caught in the act for violating the Public Official Election and Prevention of Election Malpractice Act, and at the time of arrest there was little possibility that they possessed or concealed dangerous articles such as weapons; when they were first detained in the detention cell, they were already inspected through a body inspection and it had already been confirmed that they did not possess or conceal dangerous articles such as weapons and other prohibited items; and in light of the fact that, when the Petitioners met counsel in a group in the counsel meeting room, a police officer visually monitored the counsel meeting process one by one within visible range and even restrained the use of a mobile phone by some of the Petitioners, the possibility that the Petitioners would possess or conceal dangerous articles such as weapons or other prohibited items in the course of being readmitted to the detention cell was also extremely low. In addition, the Respondent admitted that, in the case of the Seongnam Nambu Police Station, there had been no instances in which a body inspection conducted after a meeting with counsel uncovered possession or concealment of dangerous articles such as weapons or other prohibited items; and, especially, considering that the body search in this case, which made the Petitioners repeatedly stand up and sit down while completely naked, in itself severely damaged the Petitioners’ honor and self-respect, the body search in this case conducted by the Respondent against the Petitioners is sufficiently recognized as a measure that clearly exceeded the necessary minimum scope in terms of means and method, and that merely inflicted severe humiliation and shame on the Petitioners.\\n\\nIf that is so, this excessive body search in this case by the Respondent against the Petitioners, despite its necessity, exceeded the necessary minimum scope in terms of means and method; moreover, by causing the Petitioners to be unable to maintain their basic human dignity, it appears to have reached a degree that is difficult to tolerate, and thus is judged to have infringed the personality rights deriving from human dignity and worth under Article 10 of the Constitution and bodily liberty under Article 12.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nThe body search in this case conducted by the Respondent against the Petitioners, in the course of the Petitioners’ detention in the Seongnam Nambu Police Station detention cell, by making them turn their backs to the police officer, turn around, raise their upper garments together with their underwear up to the armpits and lower their lower garments together with their underwear to the knees, and then stand up and sit down three times, in order to determine whether they possessed or concealed dangerous articles such as weapons and other prohibited items, was an act that exceeded the necessary minimum scope in terms of means and method and inflicted upon the Petitioners humiliation and shame to a degree difficult to tolerate, and therefore infringed the Petitioners’ personality rights and bodily liberty guaranteed by Articles 10 and 12 of the Constitution, and shall accordingly be annulled.\\n\\nHowever, since the above exercise of public authority in the form of a factual act has already ended, we decide to determine its unconstitutionality in a declaratory sense in order to prevent the recurrence of the same or a similar infringement of fundamental rights, and accordingly render the order below.\\n\\nThis decision is by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices."}
