Case Summary\\nWhen the applicants for referral and the petitioners, who had been indicted for the offense of forcible indecent act or quasi-forcible indecent act, etc., were finally adjudged to have a suspended sentence, the head of the competent local government revoked their taxi driver qualifications. Thereupon, the applicants for referral and the petitioners filed actions seeking revocation of that disposition, and during the pendency of those actions they applied for a request for constitutional review of statutes with respect to Article 87(1), proviso 3, of the Passenger Transport Service Act, etc. The referring court accepted the application by the applicant for referral concerning the proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act and, on 2017. 6. 29., referred this case for constitutional review of statutes. Meanwhile, all of the petitioners’ applications were dismissed, and petitioner Jeong ○u filed this constitutional complaint on 2016. 1. 6., and petitioner Lee ○yong filed this constitutional complaint on 2017. 8. 18.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\na. Case 2016HEONBA14\\nThe petitioner sought review of the phrase “where it comes to fall under paragraph (4)” in Article 87(1), item 3, of the Passenger Transport Service Act; however, the underlying case contests a disposition revoking taxi driver qualification on the ground that the person violated the crime of forcible indecent act under Article 298 of the Criminal Act under Article 2(1) item 3 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes, was sentenced to a suspended sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment, and is within the period of suspension of execution, so the subject matter of review is limited to the portion relevant thereto.\\n\\nb. Case 2017HEONGA24\\nThe referring court sought review of the entirety of the proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act; however, the underlying case contests a disposition revoking taxi driver qualification on the ground that the person was sentenced to a suspended sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment for a violation of Article 7(3) of the Act on the Protection of Children and Juveniles against Sexual Abuse and is within the period of suspension of execution, so the subject matter of review is limited to the portion relevant thereto.\\n\\nc. Case 2017HEONBA376\\nThe petitioner sought review of Article 24(4) item 2 of the Passenger Transport Service Act, the portion in subitem (b) of item 1 concerning “Articles 2(1) items 2 through 4 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes” in the same paragraph, and all of item 3 of the proviso to Article 87(1) of the same Act; however, the underlying case contests a disposition revoking taxi driver qualification on the ground that the person violated the crime of quasi-forcible indecent act under Article 299 of the Criminal Act under Article 2(1) item 3 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes, was sentenced to a suspended sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment, and is within the period of suspension of execution, so the subject matter of review is limited to the portion relevant thereto.\\n\\nd. Provisions Subject to Review\\nThe subject matter of review in this case is whether the following portions of item 3 of the proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act (as amended by Act No. 12377 on 2014. 1. 28.) violate the Constitution: ① the portion concerning Article 7(3) of the Act on the Protection of Children and Juveniles against Sexual Abuse in item 1(c) of Article 24(4), ② the portion concerning Article 298 of the Criminal Act under Article 2(1) item 3 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes in item 1(b), and ③ the portion concerning Article 299 of the Criminal Act under Article 2(1) item 3 of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment, etc. of Sexual Crimes in item 1(b). The text of the provisions subject to review is as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Review]\\nPassenger Transport Service Act (as amended by Act No. 12377 on 2014. 1. 28.)\\nArticle 87 (Revocation, etc. of Qualifications of Transport Workers) (1) If a person who has acquired the qualification under Article 24(1) falls under any of the following subparagraphs, the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport or the Mayor/Do Governor may revoke such qualification or suspend the effect of such qualification for a period not exceeding 6 months. Provided, however, that where item 3 or item 6-2 applies, such qualification shall be revoked.\\n3. Where the person comes to fall under Article 24(3) or (4)\\n\\n3. Reasons for the Referral by the Referring Court and the Petitioners’ Arguments\\na. The proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act provides that taxi driver qualification must be revoked even where the degree of illegality or the degree of blameworthiness is slight, and thus violates the principle against excessive restriction, infringes the freedom of occupation, and violates the principle of equality.\\nb. In addition, petitioner Lee ○yong argues as follows.\\nThe amendment bill to the Passenger Transport Service Act, introduced by the Chairperson of the National Assembly Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Committee on 2011. 12. 28. and adopted in its original form at the plenary session the next day, did not contain the proviso to Article 87(1), which mandates revocation of the qualification for persons who have grounds for disqualification under Article 24(3) or (3), and the main text of the same paragraph provided only discretionary revocation. However, the Passenger Transport Service Act promulgated as Act No. 11295 on 2012. 2. 1., having been transferred to the Government by the National Assembly on 2012. 1. 19., contained the proviso to Article 87(1). This caused a change in the substantive content of the bill, and its legislative procedure violates the constitutional principle of due process.\\n\\n4. Determination\\na. Summary of Issues\\nThe provisions subject to review require revocation of the qualification when a person who has acquired taxi driver qualification commits a sex offense such as forcible indecent act and is sentenced to a suspended sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment, thereby preventing that person from engaging in the taxi transport business; accordingly, the basic right most closely related thereto is the freedom of occupation (see Constitutional Court 2017. 9. 28. 2016HEONBA339). The petitioners argue that the provisions subject to review also infringe the general freedom of action, etc., but insofar as the issue of infringement of the freedom of occupation is determined, the remaining basic-right infringements, the determination of which would overlap, are not separately addressed. The referring court and the petitioners also point out a violation of the principle of equality on the ground that a person who has committed forcible indecent act is treated the same as a person who has committed a more serious offense such as murder, even though they are essentially different; however, this objection is that requiring mandatory revocation of taxi driver qualification where a person commits a sex offense such as forcible indecent act and is sentenced to a suspended sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment is excessive. This ultimately concerns whether the provisions subject to review violate the principle against excessive restriction, so the issue of violation of the principle of equality is not separately examined either.\\nTherefore, the issues in this case are whether the legislative procedure for the provisions subject to review violates the constitutional principle of due process and whether the provisions subject to review violate the principle against excessive restriction and thereby infringe the freedom of occupation.\\n\\nb. Whether the Principle of Due Process Was Violated\\nIn this case, the provisions subject to review applied to the underlying case and are recognized as a premise for adjudication are the provisions of the Passenger Transport Service Act as amended by Act No. 12377 on 2014. 1. 28. Petitioner Lee ○yong argues that the proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act as amended by Act No. 11295 on 2012. 2. 1. violates the principle of due process and is unconstitutional, but this is not a defect in the legislative procedure of the provisions subject to review. No issue of violation of the principle of due process arises with respect to the provisions subject to review.\\n\\nc. Whether the Principle Against Excessive Restriction Was Violated\\n(1) Legitimacy of Purpose and Appropriateness of Means\\nThe provisions subject to review aim to protect the public using taxis from sex crimes, etc., alleviate the public’s sense of unease regarding the use of passenger transport services, and secure public safety with respect to road traffic, and such legislative purpose is legitimate. By requiring the mandatory revocation of the driver qualification of a person engaged in the taxi transport business who has committed offenses prescribed in Article 7(3) of the Act on the Protection of Children and Juveniles against Sexual Abuse, Article 298 of the Criminal Act, and Article 299 of the Criminal Act, which are antisocial offenses, the provisions subject to review warn persons engaged in the taxi transport business in advance not to commit such offenses and deter the occurrence of such offenses. This is a means capable of achieving the legislative purpose and thus the appropriateness of means is also recognized (see Constitutional Court 2017. 9. 28. 2016HEONBA339).\\n\\n(2) Least Restrictive Means\\nGiven the nature of the passenger motor vehicle transport business, which is closely related to the life of the general public, there is a public interest necessity to prevent persons lacking a sense of compliance from engaging in driving duties. In particular, in the case of the taxi transport business, the frequency of contact between drivers and passengers is high, and compared with other passenger motor vehicle transport means such as buses, the space is narrower and the number of passengers is smaller, so the density of contact is also high. In addition, since destinations and arrival times are highly diverse and vehicles operate even late at night, the probability that passengers are exposed to danger is markedly higher than with other public transportation means such as buses. Considering these points, it is necessary to impose relatively strong regulations on taxi driver qualification (see Constitutional Court 2015. 12. 23. 2013HEONMA575 and others).\\nA person who has committed an offense prescribed in the provisions subject to review and has been sentenced to a suspended sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment may be regarded as lacking a sense of compliance. The provisions subject to review, by prescribing as grounds for revocation of taxi driver qualification the fact that a person has committed a certain offense and been sentenced to a suspended sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment, take into account the social blameworthiness inherent in the relevant conviction from the perspective of securing a sense of compliance.\\nA method of individually determining whether the relevant driver has a sense of compliance by considering one by one the individuality and special characteristics of the offenses prescribed in the provisions subject to review would in practice require a very cumbersome procedure. Moreover, it is not easy to individually determine the content and degree of the social blameworthiness inherent in those offenses, and it is difficult to ensure transparency in operation; therefore, it is inevitable to establish an objectively clear and uniform standard, such as a sentence of suspension of execution of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment, as in the provisions subject to review (see Constitutional Court 2001. 5. 31. 99HEONBA94; Constitutional Court 2017. 9. 28. 2016HEONBA339).\\n\\nUnder the criminal procedure system, a prosecutor may refrain from instituting a prosecution even if suspicion of an offense is established, by considering the offender’s character and conduct, environment, motive and means of the offense, results, and circumstances after the offense. Even if a prosecution is instituted, the judge selects the type and amount of punishment by considering various sentencing factors. If the court, notwithstanding that Article 7(3) of the Act on the Protection of Children and Juveniles against Sexual Abuse, Article 298 of the Criminal Act, and Article 299 of the Criminal Act each prescribe a fine, chooses a suspended sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment after considering all circumstances of the offense, this means that the social blameworthiness is by no means insignificant (see Constitutional Court 2013. 9. 26. 2012HEONMA365; Constitutional Court 2017. 9. 28. 2016HEONBA339).\\n\\nWhen the proportion of taxis in public transportation, the special nature of taxis as a means of transportation, the seriousness of the offenses prescribed in the provisions subject to review, and the social blameworthiness attributable to persons who have been sentenced to a suspended sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment for such offenses are comprehensively considered, merely providing that the taxi driver qualification of a person who has committed an offense prescribed in the provisions subject to review and has been sentenced to a suspended sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment may be revoked at discretion is not sufficient to ensure, to the same extent as the provisions subject to review, that persons lacking a sense of compliance cannot engage in driving duties in the taxi transport business, thereby protecting the public from crime, alleviating the public’s sense of unease regarding the use of passenger transport services, and securing public safety with respect to road traffic.\\nThe provisions subject to review satisfy the requirement of least restrictive means.\\n\\n(3) Balance of Legal Interests\\nEven if the taxi driver qualification is revoked pursuant to the provisions subject to review, the qualification may be reacquired once the suspension period has elapsed, so the disadvantage suffered by transport workers is limited. On the other hand, the public interest in protecting the public from crime, alleviating the public’s sense of unease regarding the use of passenger transport services, and securing public safety with respect to road traffic by excluding from taxi transport driving duties persons who have committed the offenses prescribed in the provisions subject to review and have been sentenced to a suspended sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment is very important. The provisions subject to review also satisfy the requirement of balance of legal interests.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nSince none of the provisions subject to review violates the Constitution, the decision is rendered as stated in the order. Except for the dissenting opinion of Justice Kim Chang-jong as set forth in 6. below and the supplementary opinion concerning the majority opinion of Justice Kang Il-won as set forth in 7. below, this decision is based on the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Kim Chang-jong\\nI think that the portion of Article 87(1), proviso 3, of the Passenger Transport Service Act is a statutory provision promulgated without a vote of the National Assembly and therefore violates the Constitution. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\na. Effect of a Statute Promulgated Without a Vote of the National Assembly after the Speaker’s Technical Rearrangement of a Bill (National Assembly Act Article 97)\\nThe principle of due process prescribed in the latter sentence of Article 12(1) and Article 12(3) of the Constitution is a fundamental constitutional principle that applies broadly not only to the limited scope of criminal procedure but also to all legislative and administrative acts as acts of the State (see Constitutional Court 1992. 12. 24. 92HEONGA8; Constitutional Court 2009. 6. 25. 2007HEONMA451).\\nWhen the provisions of the Constitution and the National Assembly Act are taken together, if a bill is adopted at the plenary session of the National Assembly, the Speaker of the National Assembly transmits it to the Government, and the President promulgates that bill, thereby finalizing it as law; accordingly, a bill adopted at the plenary session of the National Assembly and a law promulgated and finalized by the President should, in principle, correspond in form and content.\\nHowever, because the National Assembly Act does not provide a reading procedure, there are many cases where technical rearrangement of a bill is inevitable, such as when misprints, omissions, or other contradictory or conflicting contents are discovered during the verification process even after a bill has been adopted at the plenary session. Accordingly, Article 97 of the National Assembly Act provides that “after a matter has been voted on in the plenary session, if rearrangement of provisions, phrases, numbers, or other matters that are in conflict with one another is necessary, the plenary session may delegate such task to the Speaker or a committee.” Thus, where parts of a bill adopted at the plenary session require adjustment, such as provisions, phrases, numbers, or the structure or form of the bill, the rearrangement is to be entrusted to the Speaker of the National Assembly or a committee, within the scope that does not alter the adopted content or intent. In practice, even where the plenary session has not adopted a resolution delegating rearrangement when deliberating and voting on a bill, the National Assembly, in accordance with established practice, rearranges the bill under the direction of the Speaker of the National Assembly through the Legislation and Judiciary Committee, specialist members, or the Bills Division of the Secretariat of the National Assembly. Therefore, even absent a plenary-session delegation resolution, it is appropriate to view the Speaker of the National Assembly as being able to rearrange provisions, phrases, numbers, or the structure or form of a bill adopted at the plenary session, within the scope that does not alter the adopted content or intent, where such rearrangement is necessary; and even if the Speaker rearranges the bill without delegation from the plenary session, such rearrangement cannot be said to violate the constitutional or National Assembly Act legislative procedure so long as it does not bring about a change in the substantive content of the bill adopted at the plenary session (see Constitutional Court 2009. 6. 25. 2007HEONMA451). As such, even if there is no delegation resolution by the plenary session, the Speaker of the National Assembly may, where there is a need to adjust the structure or form of a bill adopted at the plenary session, rearrange it within the scope that does not alter the adopted content or intent; therefore, unless it brings about any change in the content of the amendment bill adopted at the plenary session, the fact that the promulgated law differs somewhat in form or structure from the bill adopted by the plenary session cannot mean that its legislative procedure violates the constitutional principle of due process.\\n\\nHowever, if the Speaker of the National Assembly, based on Article 97 of the National Assembly Act, rearranges a bill adopted at the plenary session by modifying it into a content substantially different from that adopted at the plenary session, then transmits it to the Government and the President promulgates that bill as it stands, this is a promulgation as law despite the absence of any adoption by the National Assembly, and it must be said to directly violate Article 40 of the Constitution, which declares that “legislative power belongs to the National Assembly,” and Article 53(1) of the Constitution, which provides that “a bill adopted by the National Assembly --- shall be promulgated by the President.” Therefore, even if it is promulgated as law by the President, such law cannot be regarded as having the effect of law.\\n\\nb. Legislative and Amendment Process of the Proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act\\n(1) Submission of a Substitute Bill by the Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Committee\\nIn relation to the amendment of the Passenger Transport Service Act, a total of seven amendment bills were introduced in the National Assembly from 2010. 3. 16. to 2011. 5. 17. On 2011. 6. 30., the National Assembly Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Committee decided to submit a substitute bill for the partial amendment of the Passenger Transport Service Act (Bill No. 1813798), prepared by integrating and adjusting four of those bills. Article 24(4) of the above substitute bill included a measure to strengthen taxi driver qualification so that persons who committed murder, sex crimes, drug crimes, etc. and received a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment would be unable to acquire taxi driver qualification for 20 years, but it did not include any measure mandating revocation of taxi driver qualification.\\n\\n(2) Structure and Wording Review by the Legislation and Judiciary Committee\\nOn 2011. 11. 9., the Legislation and Judiciary Committee notified the Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Committee of the results of its structure and wording review, stating that “Item 3 of the proposed Article 87(1) provides that where a person who has already acquired the qualification to engage in driving duties falls under proposed Article 24(3) or (4), the qualification to engage in driving duties may be revoked or suspended as a discretionary provision, contrary to the purpose of proposed Article 24(3) and (4), which prevent acquisition of driver qualification for 20 years; therefore, it is appropriate to newly establish a proviso to the same paragraph and revise it into a mandatory provision.” The substitute bill of the Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Committee and the amendment opinions of the Legislation and Judiciary Committee are as shown in the table below.\\n<TABLE0>\\n\\n(3) Withdrawal of the Substitute Bill by the Chairperson of the Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Committee\\nHowever, the Chairperson of the Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Committee withdrew the above substitute bill (Bill No. 1813798) on 2011. 11. 14. in order to revise the wording of proposed Article 24(3) item 3, which prescribed drunk driving as a ground for disqualification from driver qualification.\\n\\n(4) Submission of a Revised Substitute Bill by the Chairperson of the Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Committee and Adoption by the Plenary Session of the National Assembly\\nOn 2011. 12. 28., the Chairperson of the Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Committee submitted to the Speaker of the National Assembly, after review of structure and wording by the Legislation and Judiciary Committee, a revised substitute bill of the previous substitute bill (Bill No. 1813798), namely a substitute bill for the partial amendment of the Passenger Transport Service Act (Bill No. 1814302). On 2011. 12. 29., the plenary session of the National Assembly, at the 2nd plenary session of the 304th extraordinary session, adopted the above new substitute bill (Bill No. 1814302) as originally proposed. However, the above new substitute bill adopted by the plenary session of the National Assembly did not contain any provision establishing a mandatory revocation system for taxi driver qualification.\\n\\n(5) Transmission and Promulgation of the Bill\\nThereafter, the Speaker of the National Assembly revised Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act, adopted as above by the plenary session, and added the following proviso: “Provided, however, that where item 3 applies, such qualification shall be revoked,” then transmitted it to the Government on 2012. 1. 19., and the President promulgated it as it stood on 2012. 2. 1. As a result, a law differing from the contents of the bill adopted by the National Assembly was promulgated. This may be expressed in the table below.\\n<TABLE1>\\n\\n(6) Amendment of the Proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act\\nThe proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act was amended by Act No. 12377 on 2014. 1. 28.; this was the result of the National Assembly plenary session adopting, as originally proposed, the substitute bill for the partial amendment of the Passenger Transport Service Act (Bill No. 1908901) submitted by the Chairperson of the Land, Infrastructure and Transport Committee on 2013. 12. 30. The bill text of the above substitute bill states: “In the proviso to Article 87(1), item 3 shall be changed to ‘item 3 and item 6-2,’ and item 6-2 shall be newly inserted into the same paragraph as follows: 6-2. Where, in relation to a traffic accident, a person has been sentenced to a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment and the sentence has become final after claiming insurance money by fraud or by any other improper means,” and the content of the comparison table of the new and old provisions attached to the above bill text is as follows.\\n<TABLE2>\\n\\nc. Whether the Constitutional Legislative Procedure (Principle of Due Process) Was Violated and Whether the Portion of Item 3 of the Proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act Is Unconstitutional\\n(1) As seen above, the substitute bill of the amendment to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act first submitted by the Chairperson of the Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Committee to the Speaker of the National Assembly included the newly established proviso and prescribed “item 3” as a ground for mandatory revocation; however, that substitute bill was withdrawn by the Chairperson of the Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Committee on 2011. 11. 14., and the new amended bill of Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act (Bill No. 1814302), which was actually deliberated and adopted by the plenary session of the National Assembly on 2011. 12. 29., contained only the discretionary revocation system (main text) for taxi driver qualification, and did not contain the mandatory revocation system (proviso). Although it appears that, in the process of withdrawing the amendment bill substitute first submitted by the Chairperson of the Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Committee to the Speaker of the National Assembly and preparing a revised substitute bill thereof, the portion of the mandatory revocation system in the proviso to Article 87(1) was omitted, perhaps due to an error by a staff member of the National Assembly Secretariat and the resulting revised substitute bill was submitted to the Speaker of the National Assembly, whatever the specific circumstances may have been, the plenary session of the National Assembly deliberated and adopted only the amendment bill finally submitted to the Speaker of the National Assembly and actually tabled at the plenary session; therefore, the bill actually adopted by the plenary session of the National Assembly and the law finalized by promulgation by the President must correspond in form and content. Nevertheless, the Speaker of the National Assembly, while rearranging the bill adopted by the plenary session pursuant to Article 97 of the National Assembly Act, newly added the provisory clause concerning the mandatory revocation system (the part stating, “Provided, however, that where item 3 applies, such qualification shall be revoked”), thereby changing it into content substantially different from the bill adopted by the plenary session of the National Assembly, and then transmitted it to the Government, and the President promulgated it as Act No. 11295 on 2012. 2. 1.\\n\\nTherefore, the proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act as amended by Act No. 11295 on 2012. 2. 1. was promulgated without even a vote of the plenary session of the National Assembly, and it is manifestly in violation of Articles 40 and 53(1) of the Constitution, which prescribe the National Assembly’s legislative procedure, and constitutes a serious and obvious defect in the legislative procedure. Accordingly, the proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act as amended by Act No. 11295 on 2012. 2. 1. cannot have the effect of law, even though it was promulgated by the President as law.\\n\\n(2) We next consider whether, when the proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act was amended by Act No. 12377 on 2014. 1. 28., it can be deemed that the “item 3” portion of the proviso was also substantially deliberated and adopted together by the plenary session of the National Assembly.\\n\\nAs seen above, on 2013. 12. 31., the plenary session of the National Assembly deliberated and adopted, as originally proposed, the substitute bill for the partial amendment of the Passenger Transport Service Act (Bill No. 1908901) proposed by the Chairperson of the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport Committee, which was a substitute bill prepared by integrating and adjusting the contents of all eight partial amendment bills submitted at that time. However, in the process of preparing the above substitute bill, there was never any new deliberation or vote on the “item 3” portion of the proviso to Article 87(1), in the National Assembly’s meetings held several times at the Land, Infrastructure and Transport Committee or the Transportation Legislation Review Subcommittee, as well as in the plenary session of the National Assembly that adopted this substitute bill, with awareness of the previous legislative procedural defect in the “item 3” portion of the proviso to Article 87(1) (it is, of course, also true that the materials submitted by the Land, Infrastructure and Transport Committee on 2013. 12. 26., the minutes of the Land, Infrastructure and Transport Committee meeting on 2013. 12. 26., the structure and wording review report by the chief specialist member on 2013. 12. 30. and the minutes of the Legislation and Judiciary Committee meeting, and the minutes of the plenary session of the National Assembly on 2013. 12. 31. contain no indication whatsoever that any new deliberation or vote was conducted to recognize and lawfully re-establish the previous legislative procedural defect in the “item 3” portion of the proviso to Article 87(1)). The National Assembly merely deliberated and adopted the addition of “item 6-2” to prevent transport workers from being involved in insurance crimes, on the ground that insurance fraud is continuously increasing and citizens suffer damage from increased insurance premiums, and specifically that in cases where a person obtained unlawful profits in relation to a traffic accident and was sentenced to imprisonment without prison labor or heavier punishment, it is necessary to revoke the license or qualification; it did not do so with respect to the “item 3” portion of the proviso.\\n\\nTherefore, when, on 2014. 1. 28., the amendment adding “item 6-2” to the proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act was enacted by Act No. 12377, it cannot be deemed that the National Assembly plenary session also substantially deliberated and adopted the “item 3” portion of the proviso together with it.\\n\\n(3) The majority opinion finds that the provisions subject to review, which apply to the underlying case and are recognized as a premise for adjudication in this case, are the provisions of the Passenger Transport Service Act as amended by Act No. 12377 on 2014. 1. 28., and thus determines that although petitioner Lee ○yong argues that the proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act as amended by Act No. 11295 on 2012. 2. 1. violates the principle of due process and is unconstitutional, this is not a defect concerning the legislative procedure of the provisions subject to review. The majority opinion appears to have reached the above conclusion on the premise that when the proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act was amended by Act No. 12377 on 2014. 1. 28., the National Assembly plenary session also substantially deliberated and adopted the “item 3” portion of the proviso, thereby curing the previous legislative procedural defect. However, although the proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act was amended by Act No. 12377 on 2014. 1. 28., as seen above, the content amended at that time merely added “item 6-2” to the proviso by newly establishing “item 6-2,” and there was no deliberation or vote whatsoever regarding the “item 3” portion of the proviso. Since the “item 3” portion of the proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act has remained the same in wording and in substance without any change since it was amended by Act No. 11295 on 2012. 2. 1. and promulgated and enforced without a vote of the National Assembly, the 2014. 1. 28. amendment merely added “item 6-2” to the mandatory revocation grounds in the proviso and has no relation whatsoever to the amendment of “item 3” of the proviso. Therefore, the unconstitutionality resulting from the legislative procedural defect existing since 2012. 2. 1. with respect to the “item 3” portion of the proviso, namely the defect of having been promulgated as law without a vote of the plenary session, should be regarded as still remaining unchanged to this day.\\nAccordingly, I think it is accurate and proper to indicate the history of the provisions subject to review in this case as “the Passenger Transport Service Act (as amended by Act No. 11295 on 2012. 2. 1.) Article 87(1), proviso 3, ---”; however, even if, as in the majority opinion, the history of the provisions subject to review is indicated as “the Passenger Transport Service Act (as amended by Act No. 12377 on 2014. 1. 28.) Article 87(1), proviso 3, ---” according to the conventional practical approach of the Constitutional Court, namely the so-called formal theory, under which an amendment is deemed to have occurred even where only formal wording is amended, such as a change in the name of an executive agency, Koreanization, or correction of wording, without any change in substantive content, the “item 3” portion remained the same in wording and substance from the 2012. 2. 1. amendment until the present. Therefore, it is proper to regard the provisions subject to review as including even “the version amended by Act No. 11295 on 2012. 2. 1. and before amendment by Act No. 12377 on 2014. 1. 28.” (see Constitutional Court 2004. 6. 24. 2002HEONGA27). Accordingly, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that regards petitioner Lee ○yong’s argument on violation of the principle of due process as not concerning any defect in the legislative procedure of the provisions subject to review.\\n\\n(4) Even if the portion of Article 87(1), proviso 3, of the Passenger Transport Service Act is declared unconstitutional, item 3 still falls under a discretionary ground for revocation pursuant to the main text of Article 87(1) of the same Act, so the administrative agency can appropriately address the issue of revoking the taxi driver qualification of a driver who has committed a sexual offense of poor character through that provision. And whether to newly re-establish item 3 as one of the mandatory grounds for revocation in the proviso to Article 87(1) after new deliberation and adoption by the plenary session of the National Assembly is a matter belonging to the area of legislative discretion to be decided by the National Assembly (how to handle the portion of item 3 in the proviso, which is being enforced as if it were a currently valid law, and in what manner item 3 should be reinserted into the proviso, is merely a matter of legislative technique).\\n\\nd. Conclusion\\nThe portion of Article 87(1), proviso 3, of the Passenger Transport Service Act was promulgated by the President without a vote of the National Assembly, and thus it manifestly violates Article 40, Article 53(1) of the Constitution, and the principle of due process; it cannot therefore have the effect of law, and a declaration of unconstitutionality should be made in the sense of confirming this.\\nI also fully agree with the majority opinion that, had the portion of “proviso 3” been prescribed as a mandatory ground for revocation through a lawful and normal legislative procedure, the provisions subject to review would not violate the principle against excessive restriction. However, even though there is a normative necessity to prescribe the portion of “item 3” as a mandatory ground for revocation, a bill amendment not adopted by the National Assembly must not be promulgated and enforced as a valid law, and if such a practice were easily permitted, it would directly undermine the principle of separation of powers and the fundamental principle of parliamentary democracy; for that reason, I am compelled to express a constitutional opinion.\\n\\n7. Supplementary Opinion on the Majority Opinion of Justice Kang Il-won\\nIt is contrary to the legislative procedure prescribed by the Constitution and the National Assembly Act for the Speaker of the National Assembly to rearrange a bill to the extent that it causes a change in the substantive content of the bill adopted at the plenary session, without delegation from the plenary session. This legal principle has already been clearly stated by the Constitutional Court (see Constitutional Court 2009. 6. 25. 2007HEONMA451). The proviso to Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act was newly established when amended by Act No. 11295 on 2012. 2. 1., and there is no doubt that this amendment procedure had the problem pointed out in the dissenting opinion. Therefore, there is no particular question that the newly established proviso provision violates the Constitution.\\nHowever, the subject matter of review in this case is the provisions subject to review as amended again on 2014. 1. 28. The dissenting opinion takes the view that, because the National Assembly did not recognize the defect in the previous legislative procedure and conduct a new deliberation and vote with respect thereto at the time of the 2014. 1. 28. amendment, the unconstitutionality remains and extends to the provisions subject to review. As the dissenting opinion points out, it is true that the National Assembly’s meeting minutes and bill review records contain no indication that the provisions subject to review were amended to remedy errors in the legislative process. However, this circumstance alone does not allow the conclusion that, when the National Assembly amended Article 87(1) of the Passenger Transport Service Act on 2014. 1. 28., it failed to conduct substantive deliberation and voting on the portion related to the provisions subject to review. It cannot be said that only what is recorded in the National Assembly’s legislative records was deliberated and voted on by the National Assembly. The National Assembly’s legislative process is also carried out through procedures not entered in official records, such as closed meetings or behind-the-scenes negotiations among parliamentary negotiating groups. The fact that something is not written in publicly available materials does not mean that there was no substantive deliberation and vote by the National Assembly.\\nUntil now, the Constitutional Court has not, when taking the law applicable to the underlying case as the subject matter of review, verified whether that law was enacted or amended through substantive deliberation and vote. This is because, when a law has been enacted or amended and promulgated by the National Assembly, it has been regarded as having been lawfully enacted or amended through proper procedures unless other clear contrary evidence is presented. Procedural defects can arise in the National Assembly’s legislative process in many ways. The executive and judicial branches are also prone to making mistakes in the course of handling their work, but institutional mechanisms exist to correct them. However, with respect to the National Assembly’s legislative process, once a bill has been adopted and promulgated, there is no way to correct a mistake other than through amendment procedures. If the National Assembly amends the relevant statutory provision again, the past legislative procedural defect concerning that provision should be regarded as cured, so that legal stability can be maintained and confusion in people’s lives can be prevented.\\nAccording to the logic of the dissenting opinion, to cure the legislative procedural problem of the provisory provision newly established by the National Assembly on 2012. 2. 1., one would have no choice but to go through an amendment procedure that includes a provisory provision having the same content as that provisory provision. In other words, one would have to set forth the same content as the previous provision, that is, formally not an amendment but a provision stating that the previous provision is maintained, and attach an explanation that it is being amended to cure the defect in the prior legislative procedure. However, forcing such a formal amendment procedure for legislation could, in turn, result in undermining the principle of separation of powers. Unless the National Assembly acknowledges its mistake and clearly records it in writing, one cannot say that there has been no substantive deliberation and vote and that the amendment has no effect as a legislative amendment.\\nThere was a problem in the legislative procedure when the proviso was newly established on 2012. 2. 1., but there was no problem in the amendment procedure in 2014. Therefore, it is proper to regard the provisions subject to review as having been enacted through a lawful procedure at least once and to examine their substantive constitutionality. If, as the dissenting opinion says, a defect in the legislative procedure continues until an amendment explicitly pointing it out is made, then legal stability will collapse and serious confusion may be caused in the lives of the people."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the right to equality or the principle of equality is correct? (Where there is dispute, according to precedents)
A: Since the Constitution permits military courts to be established as special courts and makes the Supreme Court the final court of military trials, the provision of the Act on the Participation of Citizens in Criminal Trials that excludes military trials under the Military Court Act from the scope of cases subject to citizen participation trials violates the principle of equality.
B: Among various sports facilities, designating only users of golf courses operated on a membership basis as the group responsible for bearing the non-tax burden concerning the creation of the National Sports Promotion Fund under the National Sports Promotion Act does not violate the principle of equality.
C: A provision of the Public Official Election Act requiring teachers at elementary and secondary schools to resign from office by 90 days before election day if they wish to run as candidates for public office elections infringes the right to equality.
D: Under the Act on the Honorable Treatment and Support of Persons, etc. of Distinguished Service to the State, providing the 6·25 War Fallen Soldiers’ Child Allowance to the children of 6•25 War fallen soldiers, while limiting the beneficiary to one person and giving priority to the older person, does not infringe the right to equality of the younger children of 6•25 War fallen soldiers.
E: A provision of the Enforcement Rule of the Act on the Promotion of the Transportation Convenience of Mobility Disadvantaged Persons that sets safety standards for wheelchair securing equipment based only on standard wheelchairs infringes the right to equality of disabled persons who cannot use standard wheelchairs.
