supporting_precedents: {"[2015HEONMA304]": "1. Summary of the Case\\n\\na. The Petitioner is the maternal granddaughter of the late Lee ○ Jae, who died on 1943. 12. 8. and was awarded the Order of Merit for National Foundation (Independence Medal) on 1962. 3. 1.; she was registered together with the Petitioner’s elder brother, Lee ○ Ho, on 2011. 3. 17. as a bereaved family member (grandchild) of a person meritorious for national independence.\\n\\nb. The late Jeong ○ Seong, who was the spouse of the late Lee ○ Jae, had received bereaved family compensation as a bereaved family member of a person meritorious for national independence pursuant to the Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence from around May 1962 until his death around 1974. 2. 7., and thereafter, as no bereaved family member was known, no bereaved family compensation was paid. Then the late Lee ○ Ae, who was the daughter of the late Lee ○ Jae, began receiving bereaved family compensation from 1996. 7. 24. upon restoration of rights, and received bereaved family compensation until her death on 2011. 8. 27.; thereafter, Lee ○ Ho, the eldest son of the late Lee ○ Ae, had been receiving compensation from 2011. 9. 15. as the eldest among the grandchildren of the person meritorious for national independence.\\n\\nc. The Petitioner filed a constitutional complaint challenging Article 12(2) and (4) of the former Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence (amended by Act No. 9083 on 2008. 3. 28., and before amendment by Act No. 12668 on 2014. 5. 21.; hereinafter referred to as the “former Act”), which provided that bereaved family compensation shall be paid only to one eldest grandchild among the grandchildren of a person meritorious for national independence, and the Constitutional Court rendered a decision of unconstitutionality inconsistent with the Constitution with respect to “the portion limiting compensation to one grandchild” in Article 12(2) of the former Act and “the portion giving priority to the older grandchild” in the main text of subparagraph 1 of Article 12(4) (Constitutional Court 2013. 10. 24. 2011HEONMA724).\\n\\nd. Accordingly, Article 12(2) and (4) of the Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence, amended by Act No. 12668 on 2014. 5. 21., provides that, in the case of grandchildren, compensation shall be paid to one person of first priority, taking into consideration the standard of living, etc. prescribed by Presidential Decree, but where there are two or more persons of the same rank even by agreement among bereaved family members or by support criteria, the older person shall take priority.\\n\\ne. Accordingly, the Petitioner filed the constitutional complaint in this case on 2015. 3. 26., seeking a determination of unconstitutionality with respect to “the portion limiting compensation to one grandchild” in Article 12(2) of the amended Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence and “the portion giving priority to the older person” in subparagraph 1 of paragraph (4) of the same Article, claiming that such provisions infringe the Petitioner’s equality right.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe Petitioner seeks a determination of unconstitutionality with respect to “the portion limiting compensation to one grandchild” in Article 12(2) of the Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence (hereinafter referred to as the “Act on Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence”), but as the Petitioner falls under the grandchildren of a person meritorious for national independence who died before 1945. 8. 14., the subject matter of review is limited to the portion related to the Petitioner. Therefore, the subject matter of review in this case is whether “the portion limiting compensation to one grandchild” in subparagraph 1 of Article 12(2) of the Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence (as amended by Act No. 12668 on 2014. 5. 21.) and “the portion giving priority to the older grandchild” in subparagraph 1 of paragraph (4) of the same Article (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “provisions of the Act at issue”) infringe the Petitioner’s equality right and are therefore in violation of the Constitution. The contents of the provisions under review are as follows, and the related provisions are as set forth in [Appendix].\\n\\n[Provisions under Review]\\n\\nAct on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence (as amended by Act No. 12668 on 2014. 5. 21.)\\n\\nArticle 12 (Compensation) ② Compensation shall be paid to one person of first priority among persons of distinguished service to independence and their bereaved family members. Provided, however, that in the case of grandchildren, compensation shall be paid, taking into consideration the standard of living, etc. prescribed by Presidential Decree, and shall be limited to the persons listed in the following subparagraphs, and the right to receive this compensation shall not be transferred to other grandchildren.\\n1. One grandchild of a person meritorious for national independence who died before August 14, 1945\\n④ If there are two or more bereaved family members entitled to receive compensation pursuant to paragraph (3) who are of the same rank, compensation shall be paid according to the following subparagraphs.\\n1. The older person shall take priority; provided, in the case of a person meritorious for national independence, if there is a person who mainly supported the person, that person shall take priority.\\n\\n3. The Petitioner’s Assertions\\n\\nEven though a decision of unconstitutionality inconsistent with the Constitution was rendered with respect to “the portion limiting compensation to one grandchild” in Article 12(2) of the former Act and “the portion giving priority to the older grandchild” in the main text of subparagraph 1 of Article 12(4), the provisions of the Act at issue, as before, limit the grandchildren, who are bereaved family members of a person meritorious for national independence, to only one compensation recipient and, where there are two or more grandchildren, provide that compensation shall be paid to the older person; therefore, they infringe the Petitioner’s equality right.\\n\\n4. Decision\\n\\nThe provisions of the Act at issue provide that compensation shall be paid only to one person of first priority among the grandchildren of a person meritorious for national independence, and where there are two or more grandchildren of the same rank, the older person shall take priority. Thus, there exists a differential treatment in veterans’ and patriotic treatment under the Act on Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence among grandchildren of the same person meritorious for national independence, and the issue is whether the equality right has been infringed.\\n\\nAs matters concerning the specific contents of compensation to be paid by the State to persons meritorious for national independence and their bereaved family members must inevitably be determined according to the State’s fiscal capacity, the overall level of social security, the criteria for evaluating persons meritorious for national independence, etc., so long as the level of compensation prescribed by law satisfies the minimum material needs necessary for a life worthy of human dignity for persons meritorious for national independence and their bereaved family members, and does not clearly deviate from the constitutional ideals of social security and social welfare, as well as the ideal of preferential protection for persons meritorious for national independence, the Legislature may exercise broad legislative discretion in making such determinations.\\n\\nUpon review, the proviso to Article 12(2) of the Act on Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence, amended by Act No. 12668 on 2014. 5. 21., provides that compensation shall be paid to one grandchild, taking into consideration the standard of living, etc. prescribed by Presidential Decree. Accordingly, Article 5-2(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence, newly enacted by Presidential Decree No. 25914 on 2014. 12. 30., provides that, where there are two or more grandchildren of the same rank among the bereaved family members entitled to receive compensation pursuant to the proviso to Article 12(2) of the Act on Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence, the compensation recipient shall be designated in the following order: recipients under the National Basic Livelihood Security Act, persons in the near-poverty bracket under the same Act, recipients under the Act on Pension for Persons with Disabilities, and recipients of the Basic Pension under the Basic Pension Act (provided, however, that by amendment under Presidential Decree No. 26683 on 2015. 11. 30., the ranking of recipients under the National Basic Livelihood Security Act was further subdivided); where there are two or more persons falling under the same subparagraph, persons falling cumulatively under the order of each subparagraph shall take priority. In addition, where there is no person falling under the above subparagraphs or where priority cannot be determined among persons falling under the same subparagraph, the provision of Article 12(4)1 of the Act on Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence, which prescribes priority for a supporter and then for an elder person, shall apply (proviso to Article 5-2(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence), and notwithstanding such ranking, the compensation recipient may be designated by agreement among the grandchildren (paragraph (2) of the same Article).\\n\\nThe above amendments to the Act on Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence and its Enforcement Decree appear to have given priority, in the absence of agreement, to the standard of living of the grandchildren in designating the compensation recipient; this appears to have aimed to ensure the effectiveness of the right to receive compensation by paying compensation to the grandchild most in need of it, in order to promote stability in the bereaved family’s livelihood and improve welfare, while also taking into account the State’s fiscal capacity.\\n\\nIn addition, by amendment under Act No. 15550 on 2018. 4. 6., the Act on Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence newly established Article 14-5 and provides that a subsidy for livelihood stabilization may be paid, taking into consideration the standard of living, such as the median income, to persons among the children or grandchildren of a person meritorious for national independence who do not receive compensation under Article 12 of the Act on Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence, thereby preparing livelihood protection measures for grandchildren who are determined to be lower in priority under the provisions of the Act at issue and consequently do not receive compensation, and also taking into account fairness among grandchildren in veterans’ and patriotic treatment under the Act on Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence.\\n\\nConsidering the above circumstances comprehensively, it is difficult to conclude that the Legislature’s choice as reflected in the provisions of the Act at issue manifestly exceeds its discretion; accordingly, the provisions of the Act at issue do not infringe the Petitioner’s equality right.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, as the Petition in this case is without merit, it is decided to dismiss it in its entirety, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices, as stated in the order.\\n\\nJustices Lee Jin-seong, Kim I-soo, Kim Chang-jong, Ahn Chang-ho, Kang Il-won (unable to provide administrative electronic signature due to an overseas business trip), Seo Ki-seok, Jo Yong-ho, Lee Sun-ae, Yoo Nam-seok\\n\\n[Appendix] Related Provisions\\n\\nFormer Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence (as amended by Act No. 9083 on 2008. 3. 28., and before amendment by Act No. 12668 on 2014. 5. 21.)\\n\\nArticle 12 (Compensation) ② Compensation shall be paid to one person of first priority among persons of distinguished service to independence and their bereaved family members. Provided, however, that in the case of grandchildren, compensation shall be paid only to one grandchild of a person meritorious for national independence who died before August 14, 1945, and the right to receive this compensation shall not be transferred to other grandchildren.\\n④ If there are two or more bereaved family members entitled to receive compensation pursuant to paragraph (3) who are of the same rank, compensation shall be paid according to the following subparagraphs.\\n1. The older person shall take priority; provided, in the case of grandchildren, it shall be paid to the older person among the children of the first-priority child of the person meritorious for national independence. Provided, however, that if there is a person who mainly supported the person meritorious for national independence, that person shall take priority.\\n\\nAct on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence (as amended by Act No. 15550 on 2018. 4. 6.)\\n\\nArticle 14-5 (Payment, etc. of Subsidies for Livelihood Stabilization) ① The Administrator of the Korea Veterans Agency may pay a subsidy for livelihood stabilization, taking into consideration the standard of living, such as the median income, to persons among the children or grandchildren of a person meritorious for national independence who do not receive compensation under Article 12.\\n② A person who intends to receive the subsidy pursuant to paragraph (1) shall apply to the Administrator of the Korea Veterans Agency for payment of the subsidy. In such case, with respect to the procedures for applying for payment of the subsidy and the authority of the Administrator of the Korea Veterans Agency for verifying and examining entitlement to receive the subsidy, the provisions of Articles 14-2 through 14-4 shall apply mutatis mutandis.\\n\\nFormer Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence (as amended by Presidential Decree No. 25914 on 2014. 12. 30., and before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 26683 on 2015. 11. 30.)\\n\\nArticle 5-2 (Standards for Payment of Compensation to Grandchildren of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence) ① Where there are two or more grandchildren of the same rank among the bereaved family members entitled to receive compensation pursuant to the proviso to the portion other than the subparagraphs of Article 12(2) of the Act, the compensation recipient shall be designated according to the following order of priority of subparagraphs. Provided, however, that where there are two or more persons falling under the same subparagraph, persons falling cumulatively under the order of each subparagraph shall take priority, and where there is no person falling under the subparagraphs or where priority cannot be determined among persons falling under the same subparagraph, Article 12(4)1 of the Act shall apply.\\n1. Recipients under subparagraph 2 of Article 2 of the National Basic Livelihood Security Act\\n2. Persons in the near-poverty bracket under subparagraph 11 of Article 2 of the National Basic Livelihood Security Act\\n3. Recipients under subparagraph 4 of Article 2 of the Act on Pension for Persons with Disabilities\\n4. Recipients of the Basic Pension under subparagraph 3 of Article 2 of the Basic Pension Act\\n② Notwithstanding paragraph (1), where one grandchild is designated as the compensation recipient by agreement among the grandchildren, compensation shall be paid to that person.\\n\\nEnforcement Decree of the Act on the Honorable Treatment of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence (as amended by Presidential Decree No. 26683 on 2015. 11. 30.)\\n\\nArticle 5-2 (Standards for Payment of Compensation to Grandchildren of Persons of Distinguished Service to Independence) ① Where there are two or more grandchildren of the same rank among the bereaved family members entitled to receive compensation pursuant to the proviso to the portion other than the subparagraphs of Article 12(2) of the Act, the compensation recipient shall be designated according to the following order of priority of subparagraphs. Provided, however, that where there are two or more persons falling under the same subparagraph, persons falling cumulatively under the order of each subparagraph shall take priority, and where there is no person falling under the subparagraphs or where priority cannot be determined among persons falling under the same subparagraph, Article 12(4)1 of the Act shall apply.\\n1. Recipients of livelihood benefits under subparagraph 1 of paragraph (1) of Article 7 of the National Basic Livelihood Security Act\\n2. Recipients of medical benefits under subparagraph 3 of paragraph (1) of Article 7 of the National Basic Livelihood Security Act\\n3. Recipients of housing benefits under subparagraph 2 of paragraph (1) of Article 7 of the National Basic Livelihood Security Act\\n4. Recipients of education benefits under subparagraph 4 of paragraph (1) of Article 7 of the National Basic Livelihood Security Act and their household members, or persons in the near-poverty bracket under subparagraph 10 of Article 2 of the same Act\\n5. Recipients under subparagraph 4 of Article 2 of the Act on Pension for Persons with Disabilities\\n6. Recipients of the Basic Pension under subparagraph 3 of Article 2 of the Basic Pension Act\\n② Notwithstanding paragraph (1), where one grandchild is designated as the compensation recipient by agreement among the grandchildren, compensation shall be paid to that person."}

{"[2016HEONGA14]": "1. Summary of the Case\\n\\nA. The requesting party (born 1962. 4. 22.) and Jang○Jin (born 1956. 1. 13.) married on 1987. 10. 13. and were divorced around 2000. 8. 3. Between the requesting party and Jang○Jin, deceased Jang Hyeon-seong (hereinafter referred to as the “deceased”) was born on 1988. 2. 18. The deceased entered active duty on 2008. 12. 1. and, while serving in the military, developed malignant lymphoma and died on 2009. 10. 10.; on 2013. 6. 4., the Veterans Review Committee resolved that the deceased fell under the category of a soldier, police officer, or firefighter who died from an accident in the line of duty.\\n\\nB. The requesting party and Jang○Jin each asserted that “he or she primarily supported or raised the deceased,” and the Veterans Review Committee, on 2013. 12. 5., deliberated and resolved to the effect that “neither the requesting party nor Jang○Jin can be regarded as having primarily supported or raised the deceased.” Accordingly, on 2013. 12. 20., the Director of the Gwangju Regional Office of Veterans Affairs issued a disposition determining, to the effect, the highest-priority surviving family member among the beneficiaries of veterans compensation support, namely Jang○Jin, who was older than the requesting party and Jang○Jin.\\n\\nC. The requesting party filed an action seeking revocation of the above disposition, and after losing at first instance (Gwangju District Court 2014GUDAN10519), appealed (the case at bar), and while that trial was pending, filed an application for referral for constitutional review (Gwangju High Court 2016A311) with respect to the phrase “the part giving priority to the older person” in Article 12(2) item 1 of the “Act on Support for Persons Eligible for Veterans Compensation” (hereinafter referred to as the “Veterans Compensation Act”). The referring court, on the view that the unconstitutionality alleged by the requesting party arises from the combination of “limiting the beneficiaries of compensation to one person” and “giving priority to the older person,” and thus additionally, ex officio, included within the scope of the constitutional referral the “part of Article 11(1) item 2 of the Veterans Compensation Act that limits payment of compensation to one highest-priority person” and referred the matter for constitutional review.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nIn the case at bar, the ranking among the parents of a soldier, police officer, or firefighter who died from an accident in the line of duty among the surviving family members eligible to receive compensation is at issue; therefore, the scope of review is limited to the relevant portion. Accordingly, the subject matter of this case is whether the following provisions are contrary to the Constitution: the part of Article 11(1) item 2 of the “Act on Support for Persons Eligible for Veterans Compensation” (enacted as Act No. 11042 on 2011. 9. 15.) that “limits payment of compensation to one parent who is the highest-priority person among the parents,” and the part of Article 12(2) item 1 of the same Act that “gives priority to the older person among the parents” (hereinafter, the above two provisions are collectively referred to as the “Provisions Subject to Review”). The content of the Provisions Subject to Review and the related provisions is as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Review]\\n\\nAct on Support for Persons Eligible for Veterans Compensation (enacted as Act No. 11042 on 2011. 9. 15.)\\n\\nArticle 11 (Compensation) (1) Compensation shall be paid to persons falling under any of the following subparagraphs. Provided, That this shall not apply to persons excluded from compensation payment pursuant to this Act or other Acts.\\n\\n2. One highest-priority person among the surviving family members of a soldier, police officer, or firefighter who died from an accident in the line of duty\\n\\nArticle 12 (Order of Payment of Compensation) (2) If there are two or more surviving family members of the same rank eligible to receive compensation pursuant to paragraph (1), compensation shall be paid in accordance with the classification in each of the following subparagraphs.\\n\\n1. Priority shall be given to the older person, but priority shall be given to the person who primarily supported or raised the person eligible for veterans compensation.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nAct on Support for Persons Eligible for Veterans Compensation (enacted as Act No. 11042 on 2011. 9. 15.)\\n\\nArticle 2 (Persons Eligible for Veterans Compensation Subject to Application) (1) Persons eligible for veterans compensation, their surviving family members, or family members falling under any of the following subparagraphs (including persons prescribed in other Acts to receive support, etc. provided for in this Act) shall receive support under this Act.\\n\\n1. Soldier, police officer, or firefighter who died from an accident in the line of duty: a person who, as a soldier or police officer/firefighter public official, died during the performance of duties or education and training not directly related to the protection of the State, maintenance of security, or protection of the lives and property of the people (including a person who died from disease)\\n\\nArticle 3 (Scope of Surviving Family Members or Family Members) (1) The scope of the surviving family members or family members of persons eligible for veterans compensation who receive support under this Act shall be as follows:\\n\\n1. Spouse\\n\\n2. Children\\n\\n3. Parents\\n\\n4. Grandparents with no adult lineal descendants\\n\\n5. Minor siblings where there are no lineal ascendants under 60 years of age and no adult brothers or sisters\\n\\nArticle 12 (Order of Payment of Compensation) (1) The order of the surviving family members eligible to receive compensation shall be the order set forth in each item of Article 3(1).\\n\\n(2) If there are two or more surviving family members of the same rank eligible to receive compensation pursuant to paragraph (1), compensation shall be paid in accordance with the classification in each of the following subparagraphs.\\n\\n1. Priority shall be given to the older person, but priority shall be given to the person who primarily supported or raised the person eligible for veterans compensation.\\n\\n2. Notwithstanding subparagraph 1, if one person among the surviving family members of the same rank is designated as the person to receive compensation by agreement among the surviving family members of the same rank, compensation shall be paid to that person. In such case, necessary matters concerning the method, etc. of agreement among the surviving family members shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n\\n(3) If the surviving family member eligible to receive compensation falls under any of the following subparagraphs, compensation shall be paid to the surviving family member of the next rank in accordance with the Presidential Decree.\\n\\n1. In the case of death\\n\\n2. In the case of ceasing to fall under any of Article 3(1) items 1 through 5\\n\\n3. In the case of being continuously missing for one year or longer\\n\\n3. Grounds for the Requesting Court’s Referral for Constitutional Review\\n\\nThe Provisions Subject to Review, in paying compensation to surviving family members of essentially the same person eligible for veterans compensation, limit compensation to only one of them and, where there are two or more surviving family members of the same rank, give priority to the older person, thereby excluding the remaining surviving family members who do not fall thereunder from the beneficiaries of compensation. This: ① does not allow any exception that would expand the number of persons entitled to compensation without increasing the national fiscal burden; ② cannot be said to be a rational standard to give priority to the older person in the case of same-rank surviving family members; ③ although Article 12(2) of the Veterans Compensation Act provides certain exceptions so that a person who primarily supported or raised the person eligible for veterans compensation or a person designated by agreement among surviving family members of the same rank may be the person entitled to receive compensation in order to correct problems arising from determining whether compensation is paid based on age, in the case of surviving family members of the same rank, it is generally the case that they jointly support or raise the person eligible for veterans compensation, and if there is no agreement with the elder person, the problem of age-based discrimination still arises, so it is difficult to recognize the effectiveness of the exception provisions; in light of these points, it constitutes arbitrary discrimination without rational basis and infringes the requesting party’s right to equality.\\n\\nIn light of the fact that, in reality, it is not common for an adult child or a divorced father or mother to support the remaining surviving family members of the same rank, and in light of the fact that, although compensation could be paid differentially according to the standard of living or could be paid in equal shares, the Provisions Subject to Review uniformly limit compensation to only one surviving family member who is older, they exceed the scope of legislative discretion and infringe the social security entitlement of the surviving family member of the same rank who is younger.\\n\\n4. Decision\\n\\nA. Fundamental Right Restricted\\n\\nThe Provisions Subject to Review provide that compensation for surviving family members shall be paid only to one of the parents of a person eligible for veterans compensation and give priority to the older person. This results in different treatment as to whether compensation for surviving family members is paid between parents of the same person eligible for veterans compensation, so the issue is whether the right to equality is infringed. Meanwhile, although the referring court also states that the social security entitlement of one parent who does not receive compensation for surviving family members is infringed, this merely points out, from another perspective, the discrimination arising from the fact that the Provisions Subject to Review limit payment of compensation to one older parent; therefore, it is sufficient to judge this in the examination of whether the right to equality is infringed, and it will not be separately determined.\\n\\nB. Whether the Right to Equality Is Infringed\\n\\n(1) Standard of Review\\n\\nThe Veterans Compensation Act was enacted as Act No. 11042 on 2011. 9. 15. for the purpose of providing veterans compensation, which is distinguished from the compensation for persons of national merit, for sacrifices by persons eligible for veterans compensation that are not directly related to the protection of the State, maintenance of security, or protection of the lives and property of the people. The Veterans Compensation Act aims to contribute to the stabilization of the livelihood and improvement of welfare of persons eligible for veterans compensation, their surviving family members, or family members by providing appropriate support to them (Article 1 of the Veterans Compensation Act). Matters concerning the specific content of compensation to be paid to persons eligible for veterans compensation and their surviving family members or family members can only be determined according to the State’s fiscal capacity, the overall level of social security, and the standards for evaluating persons eligible for veterans compensation.\\n\\nTherefore, insofar as the level of compensation prescribed by law satisfies the minimum material needs necessary for a human life for persons eligible for veterans compensation and their surviving family members or family members, and does not clearly contravene the constitutional ideology of social security and social welfare, the legislator may exercise broad legislative discretion in determining it. However, if the State fails to perform even the minimum rational content in providing support for persons eligible for veterans compensation and their surviving family members or family members, or performs its duties in a manifestly arbitrary manner, such act or omission by the State constitutes an infringement of fundamental rights under the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Existence of Differential Treatment\\n\\nThe Provisions Subject to Review, in paying compensation to the parents of essentially the same person eligible for veterans compensation, limit compensation to only one of them and give priority to the older person, thereby excluding one parent who does not fall thereunder from the beneficiaries of surviving family compensation. In this respect, there exists differential treatment under the Provisions Subject to Review.\\n\\n(3) Existence of a Rational Basis for the Differential Treatment\\n\\nUnder the Veterans Compensation Act, in paying compensation for surviving family members, if there are multiple surviving family members, so long as the State’s fiscal capacity, etc. permits, it is desirable in principle to designate all of them as beneficiaries and to pay compensation in different amounts depending on the standard of living, in light of the social security nature of the right to receive compensation. If, contrary to this, compensation must unavoidably be limited to one surviving family member, a separate rational basis justifying the criteria for selection is required, such as the State’s fiscal capacity and the assurance of effectiveness of the right to receive compensation. However, the Provisions Subject to Review, in paying compensation to the parents of a person eligible for veterans compensation, do not provide any exception and limit compensation to only one person, and give priority to the older person among them; for the following reasons, their rationality is difficult to recognize.\\n\\n(a) Since matters concerning the specific content of compensation to be paid by the State to persons eligible for veterans compensation and their surviving family members or family members can only be determined according to the State’s fiscal capacity, the overall level of social security, and the standards for evaluating persons eligible for veterans compensation, it is true that, in paying compensation to the surviving family members of a person eligible for veterans compensation, the State’s fiscal capacity must also be considered as an important factor, in addition to the aspect of protecting the livelihood of the surviving family members.\\n\\nHowever, within the extent permitted by the State’s fiscal capacity, it is possible to limit the total amount of compensation to a fixed sum while, within that range, distributing and paying compensation to at least the surviving family members of the same rank according to their standard of living. If there is a person who is especially economically disadvantaged relative to other surviving family members, and there is separate substantiation that the other surviving family members do not require livelihood protection, then it is also possible in that case to limit the range of persons entitled to receive compensation to the economically disadvantaged person. In a situation where there exists a method that can faithfully protect the actual livelihood of the surviving family members of persons eligible for veterans compensation without increasing the State’s fiscal burden, it cannot be said that there is a great necessity to pay compensation, without exception, to only one person among the parents.\\n\\nIf compensation is paid only to one of the parents, it may be economically useful and effective from the standpoint of the person receiving the compensation, but the livelihood protection of the remaining parent who receives no compensation, not even a small amount, becomes insufficient. In particular, where the amount of compensation is substantial, monopolizing it by one parent while disregarding the livelihood protection of the other parent is also directly contrary to the legislative purpose of the Veterans Compensation Act, namely the stabilization of the livelihood and improvement of welfare of the surviving family members of persons eligible for veterans compensation. Furthermore, since the parents are ordinarily no more than two persons, the reasons that, in the case of divided payment, the amount of compensation would become excessively small and lose effectiveness, or that the national fiscal burden would increase due to a sharp increase in the number of persons entitled to receive compensation, are not persuasive.\\n\\nConsidering these points, it is difficult to view the fact that the Provisions Subject to Review, on the basis of the limits of the State’s fiscal capacity, provide that compensation is to be paid only to one parent and do not provide any exception, as having a convincing rational basis.\\n\\n(b) The provision in the Provisions Subject to Review giving priority to the older person is also problematic. Age-based discrimination appears to be based on the traditional Confucian idea that elders should be favored over the young, but there is no rational basis to generalize that the older parent supports the younger parent, and there are many cases in which it is difficult to recognize any age difference substantial enough to amount to a marked difference in labor capacity and capacity to provide support between parents. Rather, in cases where the elder person is economically better off depending on occupation or assets held, paying compensation on the ground that the person is older, while excluding a surviving family member whose livelihood is more difficult, does not accord with the social security nature of the right to receive compensation.\\n\\n(c) The Veterans Compensation Act, in order to remedy problems arising from differentiating compensation payment based on age, provides certain exception clauses so that priority is given to the person who primarily supported or raised the person eligible for veterans compensation, or so that, if one person among the surviving family members of the same rank is designated as the person to receive compensation by agreement among the surviving family members of the same rank, compensation shall be paid to that person (proviso to Article 12(2) item 1 and item 2 of the Veterans Compensation Act). However, given that parents, absent special circumstances, ordinarily support or raise the person eligible for veterans compensation together, and that if there is no agreement between the parents, the problem of age-based discrimination still arises, it is also difficult to recognize the effectiveness of the above exception clauses.\\n\\n(4) Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the Provisions Subject to Review, in paying compensation to parents who are surviving family members of a person eligible for veterans compensation, uniformly limit the number of persons entitled to receive compensation without rational basis, and discriminate without rational basis between the older parent and the other parent; therefore, they infringe the right to equality of the younger parent and are contrary to the Constitution.\\n\\nC. Necessity of a Decision of Incompatibility with the Constitution and a Temporary Application Order\\n\\nWhere a statute is contrary to the Constitution, in principle a decision of unconstitutionality should be rendered with respect to that statute in order to secure the normativity of the Constitution. However, where removing the statutory provision from the legal order through a decision of unconstitutionality may cause a legal vacuum or confusion, a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution may be rendered, ordering temporary application of the unconstitutional provision. Although the Provisions Subject to Review are contrary to the Constitution by infringing the right to equality of one younger parent, if a simple decision of unconstitutionality is rendered and its effect is immediately extinguished, the basis provision for paying compensation to parents who are surviving family members of persons eligible for veterans compensation would disappear, and a state of legal vacuum could arise in which the legislative purpose would be difficult to achieve. Furthermore, in removing the unconstitutional state of the Provisions Subject to Review, as to by what standards and requirements the person entitled to receive compensation should be determined, and how the scope of the persons entitled to receive compensation should be set, discretion shall be granted to the legislature within the limits of the purport of the Constitutional Court’s decision. Therefore, it is necessary to allow the provisions to remain in effect and apply them until the legislature amends the law in a constitutional direction.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the Provisions Subject to Review do not conform to the Constitution; however, since it is appropriate to order them to be temporarily applicable until the legislature enacts ameliorative legislation by 2019. 12. 31., the Court, by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices, renders the decision as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2018HEONGA6]": "1. Case Overview\\n\\nA. The petitioner for adjudication is the second son of Eom□□, a 6·25 war dead service member who died around January 19, 1949, and was registered together with the eldest son, Eom△△, on January 1, 1962, as a bereaved family member of a service member who died in the line of duty. Eom△△ had received the 6·25 war dead service members' children's allowance since July 2001, but the petitioner for adjudication did not receive the above allowance.\\n\\nB. Accordingly, on July 27, 2017, the petitioner for adjudication filed a lawsuit against the Republic of Korea in the Seoul Central District Court seeking payment of the 6·25 war dead service members' children's allowance for the period from January 2017 to June 2017 and seeking confirmation that the petitioner for adjudication has the status of a person entitled to receive the 6·25 war dead service members' children's allowance (2017GAHAP552293). While that lawsuit was pending, the petitioner for adjudication filed an application for a referral for a constitutional review concerning the portion of the main clause of Article 16-3(1) of the Act on the Honorable Treatment of and Support for Persons, etc. of Distinguished Services to the State that limits the payment of the 6·25 war dead service members' children's allowance to one person among the children of a war dead service member or service member who died in the line of duty who was killed in action or died in the line of duty during the combat period prior to July 27, 1953 and during the combat period under the Annex to the Act on the Honorable Treatment of Combat Veterans and Establishment of Related Organizations, and the portion that gives priority to the older person among those children, as well as the portion in Article 13(2)1 of the same Act that gives priority to the older person (2017KAGI50808). On February 22, 2018, the above court granted the application and referred the constitutional review at issue in this case.\\n\\n2. Object of Review\\n\\nIn the principal case, the order of payment of the 6·25 war dead service members' children's “allowance” is at issue, so the object of review is limited to the portion concerning the main clause of Article 16-3(1) of the Act on the Honorable Treatment of and Support for Persons, etc. of Distinguished Services to the State relating thereto.\\n\\nMeanwhile, after the constitutional review referral in this case was made, when the Act on the Honorable Treatment of and Support for Persons, etc. of Distinguished Services to the State was amended by Act No. 16659 on November 26, 2019, the above provision was not amended, but Article 13(2) cited in that provision was amended. Despite such amendment, the content of paying the 6·25 war dead service members' children's allowance to the “older” person remained the same, so both the law before and after the amendment are included in the object of review, and the above legislative history is reflected in the specification of the object of review.\\n\\nAccordingly, the object of review in this case is: ① the portion of the main clause of Article 16-3(1) of the former Act on the Honorable Treatment of and Support for Persons, etc. of Distinguished Services to the State (as amended by Act No. 13697 on December 29, 2015, and before amendment by Act No. 16659 on November 26, 2019) that limits payment of the 6·25 war dead service members' children's allowance to “one person among the children,” and, among the portion that states “the person with priority under Article 13(2)1,” the portion that provides for payment of the 6·25 war dead service members' children's allowance to the “older” child; ② the portion of the main clause of Article 16-3(1) of the Act on the Honorable Treatment of and Support for Persons, etc. of Distinguished Services to the State (as amended by Act No. 16659 on November 26, 2019, hereinafter, regardless of legislative history, the “Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State”) that limits payment of the 6·25 war dead service members' children's allowance to “one person among the children,” and, among the portion that states “the person with priority under Article 13(2)3,” the portion that provides for payment of the 6·25 war dead service members' children's allowance to the “older” child (hereinafter, all of the above statutory provisions are collectively referred to as the “statutory provisions at issue in this case”), and whether each violates the Constitution.\\n\\nThe provisions under review and related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Under Review]\\n\\nAct on the Honorable Treatment of and Support for Persons, etc. of Distinguished Services to the State\\n(as amended by Act No. 13697 on December 29, 2015)\\n\\nArticle 16-3 (6·25 War Dead Service Members' Children's Allowance) (1) The 6·25 war dead service members' children's allowance shall be paid to one person with the highest priority for compensation payment under Article 13 among the children of a war dead service member or service member who died in the line of duty who was killed in action or died in the line of duty during the combat period prior to July 27, 1953 and during the combat period under the Annex to the Act on the Honorable Treatment of Combat Veterans and Establishment of Related Organizations; provided, however, that the right to receive this allowance shall not be transferred to another child. Provided, however, that it shall not be paid to a child of a war dead service member or service member who died in the line of duty to whom compensation is already being paid to one of the survivors.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nFormer Act on the Honorable Treatment of and Support for Persons, etc. of Distinguished Services to the State\\n(as amended by Act No. 9079 on March 28, 2008, and before amendment by Act No. 16659 on November 26, 2019)\\n\\nArticle 13 (Order of Compensation Payment) (2) If there are two or more survivors of the same rank among the survivors who are to receive compensation under paragraph (1), compensation shall be paid according to the classifications in each of the following items.\\n\\n1. Priority shall be given to the older person, provided that priority shall be given to the person who mainly supported or raised the person of distinguished services to the State.\\n\\n2. Notwithstanding Item 1, if one person among survivors of the same rank is designated as the person to receive compensation by agreement among such survivors, compensation shall be paid to that person. In such case, necessary matters concerning the method, etc. of agreement among survivors shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n\\nAct on the Honorable Treatment of and Support for Persons, etc. of Distinguished Services to the State\\n(as amended by Act No. 16659 on November 26, 2019)\\n\\nArticle 13 (Order of Compensation Payment) (2) If there are two or more survivors of the same rank among the survivors who are to receive compensation under paragraph (1), compensation shall be paid in the following order.\\n\\n1. If one person among survivors of the same rank is designated as the person to receive compensation by agreement among survivors of the same rank, compensation shall be paid to that person. In such case, necessary matters concerning the method and effect, etc. of agreement among survivors shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n\\n2. If there is no person corresponding to Item 1, compensation shall be paid to the person who mainly supported or raised the person of distinguished services to the State.\\n\\n3. If there is no person corresponding to Items 1 and 2, compensation shall be paid to the older person; provided, however, that where the person with the same rank is a parent of the person of distinguished services to the State, compensation shall be paid by equal division notwithstanding Article 12(1). In such case, necessary matters concerning the method, etc. of payment by division of compensation shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n\\n3. Reasons for the Referral for Constitutional Review by the Referring Court\\n\\nThe statutory provisions at issue in this case, in paying the 6·25 war dead service members' children's allowance (hereinafter referred to as “the allowance at issue in this case”), provide that even where there is more than one child of a 6·25 war dead service member, the allowance shall be paid only to one person, and among such persons, priority shall be given to the older person. ① They do not provide any exception that would allow the number of persons entitled to receive the allowance at issue in this case to be expanded without increasing the State’s fiscal burden; ② paying the allowance at issue in this case to only one child without recognizing any special exception for reasons of procedural convenience is contrary to the legislative purpose of enhancing the welfare level of the bereaved families of persons of distinguished services to the State; ③ determining the person entitled to receive the allowance on the basis of age does not conform to the social security character of the allowance at issue in this case; and ④ although the Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State contains certain exception provisions to remedy problems arising from determining whether to pay the allowance at issue in this case on the basis of age, if no agreement is reached with the elder child, the problem of discrimination based on age still arises, making it difficult to recognize the effectiveness of the exception provisions. In light of the above, the statutory provisions at issue in this case infringe the petitioner for adjudication’s right to equality.\\n\\n4. Judgment\\n\\nA. Fundamental Rights Restricted\\n\\nChildren of 6·25 war dead service members experienced, during the Korean War, the death in action or death in the line of duty of their fathers, the remarriage of their mothers, and other hardships, and grew up in disadvantaged environments, and despite being placed in social and economic hardship, they in effect did not receive veterans’ benefits because support under the law was inadequate; thus, they are entitled, regardless of age, to compensation or veterans’ recognition from the State, and the need for social security is recognized (see Constitutional Court Decision 2001HEONMA546 of December 18, 2002).\\n\\nThe statutory provisions at issue in this case, in paying the allowance at issue in this case to children of 6·25 war dead service members, limit payment to only one of multiple children and, even then, give priority to the older person, thereby excluding lower-priority children who do not fall within that category from the recipients of the allowance at issue in this case. Since this constitutes differential treatment of the same group, namely children of 6·25 war dead service members, the issue in relation to the statutory provisions at issue in this case is whether the right to equality has been infringed.\\n\\nB. Whether the Right to Equality Has Been Infringed\\n\\n(1) Standard of Review\\n\\nThe Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State has the purpose of contributing to the stabilization of the living conditions and improvement of the welfare of persons of distinguished services to the State, their surviving family members, or their family members (hereinafter referred to as “persons of distinguished services to the State, etc.”), who sacrificed for or rendered service to the State, by properly honoring and supporting them, and of fostering the patriotic spirit of the people (Article 1). Accordingly, veterans’ benefits under the Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State, including the allowance at issue in this case, have the character of state gratitude toward persons of distinguished services to the State, etc., in the sense of compensation for the sacrifice and contribution of persons of distinguished services to the State. In addition, they also possess the character of social security in that they are paid over a long period of time for the purpose of protecting the livelihood of the persons entitled to receive them.\\n\\nIn light of this social security character, matters concerning the concrete content of compensation that the State is to provide to persons of distinguished services to the State, etc. must necessarily be determined according to the State’s fiscal capacity, the overall level of social security, and the degree of sacrifice or contribution by persons of distinguished services to the State. Therefore, so long as the level of compensation prescribed by law satisfies the minimum material needs necessary for a dignified life for persons of distinguished services to the State, etc. and does not clearly run counter to the constitutional ideals of social security, social welfare, and the principle of preferential protection for persons of distinguished services to the State, the legislature has broad legislative discretion in determining it. However, if the State fails to implement even minimally reasonable content in its treatment of persons of distinguished services to the State, etc., or if it discharges its duties in a manifestly arbitrary manner, such act or omission by the State constitutes an infringement of fundamental rights under the Constitution (see Constitutional Court Decisions 2011HEONMA724 of October 24, 2013; 2016HEONGA14 of June 28, 2018).\\n\\n(2) Judgment\\n\\nIn paying the allowance at issue in this case, which is a type of veterans’ benefit for the bereaved families of persons of distinguished services to the State, when there is more than one child of a 6·25 war dead service member, it is desirable, in light of the social security character of the allowance at issue in this case, to designate all of them as recipients in principle, to the extent permitted by the State’s fiscal capacity, and to pay differing amounts of the allowance according to their living conditions. If, contrary to this, the allowance at issue in this case must unavoidably be paid only to one child of a 6·25 war dead service member, a separate and rational reason sufficient to justify the selection criteria is required. However, the statutory provisions at issue in this case, in paying the allowance at issue in this case to children of 6·25 war dead service members, do not provide any exception that would permit expansion of the number of persons entitled to receive the allowance and limit payment to only one person, and also provide that even that one person shall be the older person. For the following reasons, the reasonableness of this cannot be recognized.\\n\\n(a) First, consider the portion of the statutory provisions at issue in this case that limits the recipients of the allowance at issue in this case to one among the children.\\n\\nIt is understandable that, in determining the concrete content of compensation to be paid by the State to persons of distinguished services to the State, etc., the State’s fiscal capacity is a factor to be considered in addition to the aspect of livelihood protection for persons of distinguished services to the State, etc.\\n\\nHowever, if the allowance at issue in this case is paid only to one child of a 6·25 war dead service member, as under the statutory provisions at issue in this case, the recipient may enjoy stable living and economic utility, but the livelihood protection of the remaining children, who receive no payment even of a small allowance, will be insufficient. In particular, where the amount of the allowance at issue in this case is substantial, allocating it exclusively to one child of a 6·25 war dead service member while neglecting the livelihood protection of the other children directly contravenes the legislative purpose of the Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State, namely, to stabilize the living conditions and improve the welfare of the bereaved families of persons of distinguished services to the State.\\n\\nEven if the State’s fiscal capacity makes it unavoidable that the total amount of the allowance at issue in this case be limited to a fixed amount, if the allowance at issue in this case is appropriately divided and paid within that scope according to the living conditions of the children of the 6·25 war dead service member, the purpose of the allowance at issue in this case can be achieved while also eliminating the irrationality arising from payment to only one person. Therefore, it is difficult to see any sufficiently rational reason to accept that the statutory provisions at issue in this case, on the ground of the limits of the State’s fiscal capacity, limit payment of the allowance at issue in this case to one child of a 6·25 war dead service member and provide no exception that would permit expansion of the number of persons entitled to receive it.\\n\\n(b) Next, consider the portion of the statutory provisions at issue in this case that designates the older child among the children of a 6·25 war dead service member as the person with the highest priority to receive the allowance at issue in this case.\\n\\n1) Among the children of 6·25 war dead service members, there may be some who are economically more disadvantaged than other children, and there may also be children for whom the need for livelihood protection is not recognized; yet the statutory provisions at issue in this case, without considering any of these individual circumstances, use age as the criterion for selecting the person with the highest priority to receive the allowance.\\n\\nThe Administrator of the Korea Veterans Affairs Agency argues that giving priority to the elder person reflects the reality that, as people grow older, it becomes harder to earn income through economic activity, and also reflects the custom that elder persons have mostly conducted ancestral rites, managed gravesites, and borne responsibility for the family’s livelihood. However, owing to the effects of industrialization and the shift toward nuclear families, it is not common today, even among siblings, to depend economically on one another after marriage, so it is difficult to expect an older child to support a younger child. Moreover, with the expansion of religious diversity and changes in social culture, ancestral rites customs are also changing, so it cannot be said that the elder person necessarily becomes the person who presides over ancestral rites. In addition, among children of 6·25 war dead service members who are siblings, there are many cases in which it is difficult to recognize an age difference sufficient to cause a marked difference in the reduction of work capacity and the ability to support others. Depending on occupation or assets held, the elder person’s economic circumstances may in some cases be the best.\\n\\nTaken together, the above circumstances make it impossible to conclude that the statutory provisions at issue in this case, in designating the older person among the children of 6·25 war dead service members as the person with the highest priority to receive the allowance at issue in this case, conform to the social security character of the allowance at issue in this case, and there is no rational basis for determining the order of payment of the allowance at issue in this case on the basis of the accidental circumstance of being older.\\n\\n2) The Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State does contain certain exception provisions to remedy problems arising from differentiating payment of the allowance at issue in this case on the basis of age, namely, that if one person among children of a 6·25 war dead service member is designated as the person to receive the allowance at issue in this case by agreement among them, the allowance is to be paid to that person, or that priority is to be given to the person who mainly supported the person of distinguished services to the State (Article 13(2) of the Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State).\\n\\nHowever, if no agreement is reached among the children of a 6·25 war dead service member, the statutory provisions at issue in this case are still applied and discrimination based on age still arises; and considering the average age of the children of 6·25 war dead service members who are eligible to receive the allowance at issue in this case, absent special circumstances, it is not highly likely that the children of a 6·25 war dead service member directly supported the war dead service member or service member who died in the line of duty who was killed in action or died in the line of duty during the combat period prior to July 27, 1953 and during the combat period under the Annex to the Act on the Honorable Treatment of Combat Veterans and Establishment of Related Organizations, so identifying the primary supporter has little significance. In light of this, it cannot be said that the irrational discriminatory problem caused by the statutory provisions at issue in this case is resolved by the above exception provisions.\\n\\n(3) Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the statutory provisions at issue in this case, when the State pays the allowance at issue in this case to children of 6·25 war dead service members who are the bereaved family members of persons of distinguished services to the State, limit the number of persons entitled to receive it to one among the children without a rational reason, provide no exception that would allow expansion of the number of recipients, and, without rational reason, discriminate between older and younger children of 6·25 war dead service members and pay the allowance at issue in this case in priority to the older person; therefore, they infringe the right to equality of younger children of 6·25 war dead service members and are unconstitutional.\\n\\nC. Necessity of a Decision of Incompatibility with the Constitution and a Provisional Application Order\\n\\nWhen a law violates the Constitution, a decision of unconstitutionality concerning that law should, in principle, be rendered in order to ensure the normativity of the Constitution. However, where removing the statutory provision from the legal order through a decision of unconstitutionality is likely to cause a legal vacuum or confusion, a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution may be rendered ordering the provisional application of the unconstitutional provision (see Constitutional Court Decisions 2011HEONMA724 of October 24, 2013; 2016HEONGA14 of June 28, 2018). Although the statutory provisions at issue in this case violate the Constitution by infringing the right to equality of younger children of 6·25 war dead service members, if a simple unconstitutionality decision were rendered and the provisions immediately lost their effect, the basis for payment of the allowance at issue in this case would disappear, thereby possibly creating a legal vacuum in which it would be difficult to achieve the legislative purpose. Furthermore, in eliminating the unconstitutional state of the statutory provisions at issue in this case, the legislature shall be granted discretion, within the limits of the Constitutional Court’s decision, as to what criteria and requirements will determine the persons entitled to receive the allowance at issue in this case and how the scope of those persons will be determined.\\n\\nAccordingly, a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution shall be rendered with respect to the statutory provisions at issue in this case, and provisional application shall be ordered until the legislature enacts remedial legislation. The legislature shall enact remedial legislation no later than December 31, 2022, and if no remedial legislation is enacted by that time, the statutory provisions at issue in this case shall lose effect as of January 1, 2023.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, although the statutory provisions at issue in this case are not consistent with the Constitution, they shall continue to be applied until the legislature enacts remedial legislation by December 31, 2022, and the decision is rendered as follows by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices."}

Case Summary\\n\\nThe Petitioner is a person serving as a military civilian employee at the ○○ Battalion of the Air Force Academy.\\n\\nThe Petitioner was indicted for the crime of fraud on 2020. 7. 15. (Air Force Headquarters General Military Court 2020GO15), and, during the pendency of the trial, filed an application for a request for a constitutional review of Article 5(1) of the Act on Citizen Participation in Criminal Trials, which does not include military trials under the Military Court Act among the cases subject to citizen participation trials (Air Force Headquarters General Military Court 2020CHO2). When that application was dismissed on 2020. 9. 8., the Petitioner filed the constitutional complaint in this case against the above provision on 2020. 10. 5.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether Article 5(1) of the Act on Citizen Participation in Criminal Trials (as amended by Act No. 11155 on 2012. 1. 17., hereinafter referred to as the “Citizen Participation Trial Act”) is contrary to the Constitution. The challenged provision and related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Challenged Provision]\\n\\nAct on Citizen Participation in Criminal Trials (as amended by Act No. 11155 on 2012. 1. 17.)\\n\\nArticle 5 (Cases Subject to Citizen Participation Trials) (1) The following cases shall be cases subject to citizen participation trials (hereinafter referred to as “subject cases”):\\n1. Cases within the jurisdiction of a collegiate division pursuant to Article 32(1) of the Court Organization Act (excluding Item 2 and Item 5)\\n2. Cases corresponding to attempted crimes, abetting crimes, aiding crimes, preparatory crimes, and conspiracy crimes of cases falling under Item 1\\n3. Cases under Item 1 or Item 2 and related cases pursuant to Article 11 of the Criminal Procedure Act, to be tried together\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nCourt Organization Act (as amended by Act No. 16037 on 2018. 12. 24.)\\n\\nArticle 32 (Jurisdiction of a Collegiate Division) (1) The collegiate divisions of district courts and their branch courts shall try the following cases as a court of first instance.\\n1. Cases which the collegiate division decides are to be tried by a collegiate division\\n3. Cases punishable by death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment or confinement for a short term of not less than 1 year. Provided, That the following cases shall be excluded:\\na. Cases corresponding to Article 258-2, Article 331, Article 332 (limited to habitual offenses under Article 331) of the Criminal Act and each attempted crime thereof, Article 350-2 and each attempted crime thereof, and Article 363\\nb. Cases corresponding to Article 2(3)2 and 3, Article 6 (limited to attempted crimes under Article 2(3)2 and 3), and Article 9 of the Act on the Punishment of Violent Acts, etc.\\nc. Cases involving violations of the Military Service Act\\nd. Cases corresponding to Article 5-3(1), Article 5-4(5)1 and 3, and Article 5-11 of the Act on the Aggravated Punishment, etc. of Specific Crimes\\ne. Cases corresponding to Article 5 of the Special Act on the Control of Health Crimes\\nf. Cases corresponding to Article 5 of the Act on the Control of Dishonored Checks\\ng. Cases corresponding to Article 148-2(1) and (2), and Article 148-2(3)1 and 2 of the Road Traffic Act\\n4. Complicity cases to be tried together with the cases under Item 3\\n\\n3. Petitioner’s Argument\\n\\nSince military courts are ordinarily located within the military and the entry of the general public is strictly controlled, public oversight of military trials needs to be more substantively exercised. Therefore, excluding trials of military courts from the cases subject to citizen participation trials, which were introduced to enhance the democratic legitimacy and reliability of the judiciary, constitutes discrimination without rational basis and violates the principle of equality.\\n\\n4. Reasoning\\n\\na. Constitutional Court precedent\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court, in its decision of 2014HEONBA447 on 2015. 7. 30., rendered a decision of constitutionality with respect to Article 5(1)1 of the Citizen Participation Trial Act, and in its decision of 2015HEONBA63 on 2016. 12. 29., rendered a decision of constitutionality with respect to former Article 32(1)3(c) of the former Court Organization Act (as amended by Act No. 11554 on 2012. 12. 18. and before amendment by Act No. 12886 on 2014. 12. 30.), among Article 5(1)1 of the Citizen Participation Trial Act. The gist of the 2014HEONBA447 decision is as follows.\\n\\n“Before its amendment, the Citizen Participation Trial Act defined subject cases centering on violent offenses, such as murder, robbery, and rape, for which the statutory penalties are severe and which are expected to have substantial social impact and to be highly utilized by defendants. Thereafter, in order to prevent citizen participation trials from becoming a dead letter due to the low application rate and high rates of withdrawal and exclusion, various discussions were held as to how the scope of subject cases should be adjusted, and, as a result, in conformity with the purpose of citizen participation trials and taking practical circumstances into account, the scope of cases subject to citizen participation trials was expanded to cases within the jurisdiction of a collegiate division for the purpose of improving the public’s sound common sense regarding court adjudication and confidence in the judiciary.\\n\\nLooking at countries that have implemented a citizen participation system in some form, the system of citizen participation in adjudication has developed and become established over a long period of time depending on the country’s history and tradition, culture, the people’s legal sentiment and consensus, political situation, customs, and so forth. From the perspective of our country, whose history is relatively short, rather than hastily fixing it into a specific framework, the various advantages, disadvantages, and characteristics should be sufficiently compared and analyzed, and the system should be established in a manner suited to our actual circumstances. For this purpose, even in determining the scope of cases subject to citizen participation trials, it is necessary to estimate the scale of cases that can actually and faithfully be heard in court and then determine the scope of subject cases accordingly.\\n\\nHowever, for the smooth operation of citizen participation trials, securing jurors, securing human and material resources for trial proceedings, and accumulating sufficient experience to resolve various situations are essential; accordingly, if the scope of cases subject to citizen participation trials is expanded to cases within the jurisdiction of a single judge, there will be difficulties in practical operation.\\n\\nMoreover, our country does not have systems for the efficient and economic operation of criminal procedures that are implemented in foreign countries, such as plea bargaining and restrictions on appeals, and there is no binding force of jury verdicts.\\n\\nTaking the foregoing into comprehensive account, since the statutory provision in this case, which designates only cases within the jurisdiction of a collegiate division as cases subject to citizen participation trials, treats defendants tried in cases within the jurisdiction of a single judge differently from defendants tried in cases within the jurisdiction of a collegiate division, it is recognized that there is a rational basis therefor; therefore, it does not infringe the petitioner’s right to equality.”\\n\\nb. Whether the challenged provision is unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) The Petitioner seeks a determination that the challenged provision is unconstitutional insofar as it does not include military trials under the Military Court Act among the cases subject to citizen participation trials. We examine whether the reasoning of the 2014HEONBA447 decision, which determined the constitutionality of limiting cases subject to citizen participation trials to cases within the jurisdiction of a collegiate division, can be applied to this case as is.\\n\\nThis case and the 2014HEONBA447 case both concerned whether the exclusion, in determining the scope of cases subject to citizen participation trials, of military trials under the Military Court Act or cases within the jurisdiction of a single judge from the subject cases was unconstitutional, and are identical in that the issue in both cases is whether there is a rational basis for limiting the scope of cases subject to citizen participation trials.\\n\\nMoreover, in establishing military courts by statute pursuant to Article 110(1) of the Constitution, the legislature may, in consideration of the special nature of military trials, prescribe their organization, jurisdiction, and the qualifications of judges differently from those of ordinary courts (see Constitutional Court 2009. 7. 30. 2008HEONBA162). Since the legislature, within broad legislative discretion, excluded military trials under the Military Court Act from the cases subject to citizen participation trials in consideration of the special nature of the military, which exists for the purpose of preserving the State from external aggression, it must be said that the determination in 2014HEONBA447 can be applied to this case as well.\\n\\n(2) In addition, no change in circumstances or necessity warranting a change in the determination of the above precedent is recognized, and the purport of the above precedent is likewise valid in this case. Accordingly, we decide to maintain the view of the above precedent as it is.\\n\\nTherefore, the challenged provision does not violate the principle of equality.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, since the challenged provision does not violate the Constitution, it is so decided as stated in the disposition, by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices."}

question:
Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (O) and incorrect (X) regarding the fundamental rights of foreigners? (In case of dispute, according to case law)
(a) Under the National Health Insurance Act, a provision that, where a foreign national residing in the Republic of Korea who is a regional subscriber has delinquent insurance premiums, the National Health Insurance Service, unlike Korean nationals, etc., shall, upon only one delinquency and regardless of the length of the delinquent period or the number of delinquencies, withhold insurance benefits from the following month until the delinquent premiums are paid in full, infringes the right to equality.
(b) A provision of the Immigration Control Act that allows a foreign national who has been subject to a deportation order to be placed in and confined at a protection facility until the person can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea, without setting an upper limit on the period of such protection, infringes the protected person's freedom of the person.
(c) The fact that a foreign national who applied for refugee status at Incheon International Airport but received a decision not to refer the application for refugee status determination was confined for about five months in the Incheon International Airport repatriation waiting room and was prevented from entering the transit area constitutes “detention” as provided in the main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution, and the refusal of a request for an interview with counsel during such detention infringes the right to assistance of counsel.
(d) Under the Act on the Employment, etc. of Foreign Workers, the employer of a business or workplace that employs foreign workers is required to subscribe to insurance or a trust with the foreign worker as the insured for the payment of severance pay upon the foreign worker’s departure from the Republic of Korea, etc.; because this departure maturity insurance benefit has the nature of severance pay and matters concerning the timing of its payment are therefore a matter of working conditions, foreign workers are also recognized as subjects of fundamental rights.
(e) The “Emergency Disaster Relief Fund Household Composition and Objection Processing Standards (2nd Round),” established to support citizens who suffered economic harm due to the spread of COVID-19, include “permanent residents and marriage immigrants” within the category of “households composed solely of foreigners” eligible for the Emergency Disaster Relief Fund, while excluding “recognized refugees”; this is discrimination without a rational basis and therefore infringes the right to equality of recognized refugees.
