supporting_precedents: {"[2014HEONMA346]": "1. Outline of the Case\\n\\na. The Petitioner is a foreign national of Sudanese nationality. The Petitioner departed from Khartoum Airport in Sudan on 2013. 11. 18., and arrived at Incheon International Airport on 2013. 11. 20. via Hong Kong. At the time of entry, the Petitioner had a short-term business visa issued by the Korean Embassy in Sudan, and upon arrival at Incheon International Airport, during the immigration inspection process, he expressed his intention to apply for refugee status and filed an application for refugee status determination at a port of entry pursuant to Article 6 of the Refugee Act.\\n\\nb. On 2013. 11. 20., an immigration officer at Incheon International Airport rendered a decision denying entry to the Petitioner on the ground that he failed to prove that the purpose of entry conformed to the visa. The Respondent issued a repatriation order to China Southern Airlines, the carrier of the aircraft on which the Petitioner arrived, directing it to repatriate the Petitioner out of the country. However, on the repatriation order, the Respondent added the note, “Notifying that he must remain in the airline and departure waiting room for refugee screening,” and thereby suspended immediate execution.\\n\\nc. The Petitioner was held in the repatriation waiting room installed within the transit area of Incheon International Airport from 2013. 11. 20. The Respondent, on 2013. 11. 26., rendered a decision not to refer the Petitioner for refugee status determination, and the Petitioner continued to be held in the repatriation waiting room thereafter. The Petitioner filed an action seeking revocation of the decision not to refer for refugee status determination on 2013. 11. 28., and filed a habeas corpus action on 2013. 12. 19.\\n\\nd. The repatriation waiting room at Incheon International Airport is a place where foreign nationals who have been denied entry temporarily stay prior to repatriation abroad. The repatriation waiting room in which the Petitioner was held was located on the third floor of the Incheon International Airport building, and it was a temporary waiting room used in anticipation of the construction of a new repatriation waiting room scheduled for the second half of 2014. This place had a usable floor area of approximately 330㎡ and was equipped with public telephones, chairs, television, a beverage dispenser, a shower room, and restrooms, but it had no proper beds or bedding. The Incheon International Airport Airline Operating Council provided the Petitioner with chicken burgers and cola, among other things. The Petitioner could not leave the waiting room outside according to his own will and had no means of communication with the outside other than public telephones. Access to the repatriation waiting room is controlled by the Incheon International Airport Airline Operating Council, and the room is blocked by a steel gate. The management and operation system of the repatriation waiting room was jointly determined by the Respondent and the Incheon International Airport Airline Operating Council, and the Respondent bears the rent for the repatriation waiting room.\\n\\ne. The Petitioner’s attorney applied for an interview with the Petitioner on 2014. 4. 25. The Respondent, on 2014. 4. 25., rejected the Petitioner’s attorney’s application for an interview on the grounds that there was no legal basis for recognizing the right of a counsel interview for a person denied entry and held in the repatriation waiting room, and that the Respondent, not being the entity responsible for the management and operation of the repatriation waiting room, had neither the authority nor the duty to permit an interview between the Petitioner and his attorney.\\n\\nf. The Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint seeking revocation of the rejection of the interview application, alleging that the Respondent’s rejection of the interview application as stated in the preceding paragraph infringed the Petitioner’s right to assistance of counsel.\\n\\ng. The Petitioner lost at first instance in the habeas corpus case, but prevailed on appeal. On 2014. 4. 30., the appellate court recognized both the Respondent and the Incheon International Airport Airline Operating Council as detaining authorities, and rendered a habeas corpus decision ordering the Respondent and the Incheon International Airport Airline Operating Council to immediately lift the Petitioner’s detention. The Respondent filed a re-appeal against the above decision, and, on 2014. 5. 4., in consultation with China Southern Airlines, lifted the Petitioner’s detention in the repatriation waiting room. Accordingly, from 2014. 5. 4., the Petitioner left the repatriation waiting room and lived in the transit area of Incheon International Airport. On 2014. 5. 26., the Respondent permitted the Petitioner’s entry on humanitarian grounds.\\n\\nh. The Petitioner won at both first instance and appellate instance in the action seeking revocation of the decision not to refer for refugee status determination, and because the Respondent abandoned the appeal, the winning judgment became final and conclusive on 2015. 2. 12. The Petitioner received a refugee status determination on 2016. 3. 17.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe subject matter of review in this case is whether the Respondent’s act of rejecting the Petitioner’s attorney’s application for an interview on 2014. 4. 25. infringes the Petitioner’s fundamental rights while the Petitioner was being held in the repatriation waiting room at Incheon International Airport after having received a decision not to refer for refugee status determination (hereinafter, the Respondent’s rejection of the attorney interview application dated 2014. 4. 25. shall be referred to as the “rejection of the attorney interview application in this case”).\\n\\n3. The Petitioner’s Arguments and the Opinions of the Relevant Authorities\\n\\na. Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\nEven where a person is detained by an administrative agency, the right to assistance of counsel under Article 12(4) of the Constitution is recognized. Since the Petitioner was denied an interview with counsel while detained in the repatriation waiting room, the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case infringes the Petitioner’s right to assistance of counsel.\\n\\nIn addition, the Petitioner is recognized as having the right to the assistance of an attorney derived from the right to a trial. Since the Petitioner was denied an attorney interview, making normal preparation for and conduct of litigation impossible, the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case infringes the Petitioner’s right to the assistance of an attorney.\\n\\nb. Summary of the Opinion of the Minister of Justice\\n\\nA foreign national who has been denied entry and is detained in the repatriation waiting room is not a subject of fundamental rights, and therefore there is no possibility of infringement of fundamental rights. The act of rejecting the interview application is a disposition subject to administrative litigation, but since the Petitioner filed a constitutional complaint without bringing an action for revocation thereof, the Petitioner’s constitutional complaint does not satisfy the subsidiarity requirement. The Petitioner has already entered the country and can freely receive assistance from counsel, and because the Minister of Justice has amended the “Guidelines on Refugee Status Determination, Treatment, and Stay” and thereby recognizes the right of counsel interview for asylum applicants at a port of entry, there is no interest in adjudication. Accordingly, the Petitioner’s constitutional complaint is procedurally improper.\\n\\nSince the right to assistance of counsel is not recognized in administrative procedures, the Petitioner’s right to assistance of counsel was not infringed. Furthermore, it cannot be immediately held that a foreign national who has been denied entry is entitled to the right to assistance of an attorney derived from the right to request a trial. The Petitioner received assistance from an attorney while conversing with the attorney by telephone in the repatriation waiting room. Therefore, the right to assistance of an attorney derived from the right to request a trial was also not infringed.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Admissibility Requirements\\n\\na. Standing as Petitioner and Self-Relatedness\\n\\nThe Petitioner is a foreign national. A constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act may be filed only by a subject of fundamental rights, and, with respect to fundamental rights that can be regarded not merely as “the rights of nationals” but as “human rights,” foreigners are also subjects of those fundamental rights. The right to assistance of counsel, which the Petitioner alleges was infringed, is, by its nature, a human right, and therefore foreigners are also subjects thereof (see Constitutional Court 2012. 8. 23., 2008HEONMA430). Accordingly, standing as Petitioner is recognized for the Petitioner’s request for adjudication.\\n\\nThe act of an attorney assisting a client and the act of a client receiving assistance from an attorney are two ways of viewing the same matter from different directions, and thus stand in a relationship of mutual correspondence. For this reason, although the direct counterpart of the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case was not the Petitioner but the Petitioner’s attorney, the Petitioner was thereby prevented from receiving the attorney’s assistance. Accordingly, the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case has the possibility of infringing the Petitioner’s right to assistance of counsel (see Constitutional Court 2011. 5. 26., 2009HEONMA341).\\n\\nb. Principle of Subsidiarity\\n\\nThere is no statutory basis determining the Respondent’s authority regarding the establishment and operation of the repatriation waiting room. The Respondent rejected the attorney interview application on the ground that the Respondent had neither the authority nor the duty to permit attorney interviews for persons detained in the repatriation waiting room. Accordingly, even if the Petitioner were to file administrative appeal or administrative litigation against the Respondent seeking revocation of the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case, there is a high possibility that such action would be dismissed on the ground that the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case is not “law enforcement” concerning specific facts and thus does not constitute a “disposition” under the Administrative Litigation Act.\\n\\nAccordingly, this adjudication request falls within the case where the availability of rights-remedy procedures such as administrative appeal or administrative litigation is objectively uncertain, and therefore there is no reasonable possibility of completing prior procedures. The constitutional complaint in this case falls within the exception to subsidiarity being recognized (see Constitutional Court 1991. 5. 13., 90HEONMA133).\\n\\nc. Interest in Adjudication\\n\\nThe Petitioner was released from the repatriation waiting room on 2014. 5. 4. and, on the 26th of the same month, was permitted entry and thereby became free to meet with counsel. Accordingly, there is no subjective interest in adjudication requiring revocation of the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case.\\n\\nHowever, the problem of restrictions on counsel interviews for persons held in the repatriation waiting room after a decision not to refer for refugee status determination has been rendered for asylum applicants at a port of entry is likely to recur repeatedly in the future. Even if, as the Respondent argues, the Minister of Justice has amended the “Guidelines on Refugee Status Determination, Treatment, and Stay” and thereby permits attorney interviews for asylum applicants at a port of entry, those guidelines, by their content, concern asylum applicants “while the referral examination is pending,” and thus do not apply to refugees who, like the Petitioner, have already received a decision not to refer for refugee status determination.\\n\\nIn addition, the constitutionality of the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case can be determined only after clarifying important issues of constitutional interpretation, such as whether “detention” in the text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution includes administrative detention. As the determination of the constitutionality of the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case has such major significance for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order, there is an objective interest in adjudication that requires confirmation of its constitutionality (see Constitutional Court 2011. 5. 26., 2009HEONMA341; Constitutional Court 2017. 12. 28., 2015HEONMA632).\\n\\n5. Determination on the Merits\\n\\na. Whether the Petitioner Is Recognized as Having the Right to Assistance of Counsel Prescribed in the Main Clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution\\n\\n(1) Issue\\n\\nThe main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution provides that “When any person is arrested or detained, he shall have the right to the assistance of counsel immediately.” Since the Petitioner was held in the repatriation waiting room installed within the transit area of Incheon International Airport at the time of the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case, the issue is whether the Petitioner’s being held in the repatriation waiting room at that time falls under “when any person is arrested or detained” as prescribed in the above constitutional provision. In order to determine this, we examine in order whether the party that held the Petitioner in the repatriation waiting room was the Respondent, an administrative agency; if the Respondent was the detaining authority, whether the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution also applies to detention in administrative procedures; and whether the Petitioner’s detention in the repatriation waiting room on 2014. 4. 25., when the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case occurred, corresponds to “detention” prescribed in the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Whether the Party That Held the Petitioner in the Repatriation Waiting Room Was the Respondent\\n\\nThe detaining authority possesses the authority to commence and terminate detention, the authority to control access to detainees, bears the costs of detention, and also enjoys the benefits arising from detention. However, where there are multiple detaining authorities, attribution of the above elements may be distributed among the detaining authorities or concentrated in some of them. Accordingly, in order to determine who the detaining authority is, it is insufficient to consider only one of the above elements; one must specifically examine who determines the management and operation system of the detention facility and who is the subject to whom each element related to detention is attributed.\\n\\nIn this case, the management and operation system of the repatriation waiting room was jointly determined by the Respondent and the Incheon International Airport Airline Operating Council. Looking specifically at the Petitioner’s detention, first, the Respondent, by adding the note “Notifying that he must remain in the airline and departure waiting room for refugee screening” to the repatriation order concerning the Petitioner, initiated the process of holding the Petitioner in the repatriation waiting room instead of immediately repatriating him. While the Petitioner was held in the repatriation waiting room, access thereto was controlled by the Incheon International Airport Airline Operating Council. The process of holding the Petitioner in the repatriation waiting room was terminated when the Respondent lifted the detention of the Petitioner on 2014. 5. 4. in consultation with China Southern Airlines. The rent for the repatriation waiting room was borne by the Respondent, and food and drink for the Petitioner were provided by the Incheon International Airport Airline Operating Council. As the Petitioner remained inside the repatriation waiting room instead of freely moving around the transit area, the Respondent obtained the administrative benefit of “convenience in controlling persons denied entry,” and the Incheon International Airport Airline Operating Council obtained the operational benefit of “convenience in repatriation duties.”\\n\\nIn this way, the Respondent was a joint decision-maker regarding the management and operation system of the detention facility, namely the repatriation waiting room, exercised decisive authority in the commencement and termination of the Petitioner’s detention, bore part of the detention costs, and also enjoyed the benefits arising from detention. Accordingly, the Respondent, together with the Incheon International Airport Airline Operating Council, is the party that held the Petitioner.\\n\\n(3) Whether “Detention” Prescribed in the Main Clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution Includes Detention in Administrative Procedures\\n\\nArticle 12(1) of the Constitution provides in its first sentence that “All citizens shall enjoy personal liberty.” It is clear that the first sentence of Article 12(1) of the Constitution, which guarantees personal liberty, is not textually intended only for criminal procedure. Moreover, personal liberty is a fundamental right of natural-rights character that must be protected regardless of whether the restriction thereon is imposed in criminal procedure or in administrative procedure; thus, whether the procedure in which personal liberty is restricted is a criminal procedure is merely a secondary factor in determining the scope and method of protection of personal liberty.\\n\\nOur Constitution, following the first sentence of Article 12(1), which expressly provides for and guarantees personal liberty, enumerates in the second sentence of Article 12(1) and in paragraphs (2) through (7) special situations in which personal liberty may be endangered, and specifically prescribes, for each situation, the method of guaranteeing personal liberty. Therefore, from the perspective of systematic interpretation with the first sentence of Article 12(1), which is not especially directed toward criminal procedure, the second sentence of Article 12(1) and paragraphs (2) through (7) of Article 12 should, unless the text of the relevant constitutional provision or the nature of the specific method of guaranteeing personal liberty prescribed therein clearly show that they apply only to criminal procedure, be interpreted as not being limited to criminal procedure (see Constitutional Court 2004. 3. 25., 2002HEONBA104; Constitutional Court 2014. 8. 28., 2012HEONMA686).\\n\\nIn accordance with the above interpretive principle, we consider whether the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution, which states that “When any person is arrested or detained, he shall have the right to the assistance of counsel immediately,” applies only to criminal procedure.\\n\\nFirst, we examine whether the phrase “when any person is arrested or detained” in the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution, in its textual meaning, clearly refers only to detention in criminal procedure. In its dictionary meaning, “detention” merely means restricting freedom of action or will, and there is no special limitation on the subject thereof. The “detention” prescribed in the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution refers, among the dictionary meanings of detention, particularly to compulsory apprehension of a person and forcibly taking him away, and to forcibly confining a person in a certain place; such measures are possible not only in criminal procedure but also in administrative procedure.\\n\\nLooking at statutory usage, the term “detention” is sometimes used in the sense of dictionary “detention,” as in Article 25-2 of the Seamen’s Act and Article 30 of the Act on the Prohibition of Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities and Remedy for Infringement of Their Rights, and is also used to refer to compulsory apprehension and confinement by an administrative agency, as in Article 48(3) of the Act on the Investigation and Adjudication of Marine Accidents, or to refer to compulsory apprehension and confinement of persons in arrears of fines, as in Article 10 of the Rules on Adjudication for Detention of Persons in Arrears of Fines. “Confinement,” among forms of detention, is also used where the subject is an administrative agency, as in Article 57(2) item 2 of the Military Personnel Management Act.\\n\\nSince the founding Constitution, our Constitution has contained provisions guaranteeing personal liberty; originally the term “confinement” was used, but upon the revision of the current Constitution it was changed to the term “detention.” It is difficult to find materials that precisely confirm the reason why the term “confinement” in the previous Constitution was changed to “detention” upon revision of the current Constitution. However, considering that the main reason for the current Constitution’s revision was to “strengthen the protection of the people’s body and life,” it is appropriate to interpret the change from the former “confinement” to “detention” in the current Constitution as intended to expand the scope of protection of personal liberty prescribed in Article 12 of the Constitution not only to persons confined but also to persons compulsorily apprehended.\\n\\nTaken together, interpreting “detention” prescribed in the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution as meaning not only detention in criminal procedure but also detention in administrative procedure does not exceed the limits of textual interpretation.\\n\\nNext, we examine whether the right to assistance of counsel, by its nature, can only be granted to persons detained in criminal procedure. The reason why the right to assistance of counsel is immediately guaranteed to a detained person is that, due to the nature of detention as a restriction on bodily liberty, the assistance of counsel is indispensable to securing the freedom and rights of the detained person. In other words, a person who has been detained is placed in a situation where personal liberty, which has the character of a natural right, is severely restricted, and due to the physical and mental constraints arising from detention, he is unable to properly defend his freedom and rights by his own power alone; moreover, because disputing the propriety of detention requires legal procedures, the assistance of counsel, a legal professional, must be provided to him immediately. These characteristics are no different whether the person is detained in criminal procedure or in administrative procedure. The right to assistance of counsel that must be granted to a person detained in administrative procedure has the same nature as the right to assistance of counsel that must be granted to a person detained in criminal procedure. Accordingly, the right to assistance of counsel is not a fundamental right that, by its nature, can be recognized only in criminal procedure.\\n\\nUltimately, interpreting the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution as applying not only to criminal procedure but also to administrative procedure is appropriate from the standpoint of literal interpretation of the text itself, accords with the nature of the right to assistance of counsel, and not only conforms to the purpose of our Constitution in expressly providing in the first sentence of Article 12(1) for personal liberty so as to afford robust protection to personal liberty, but is also justified from the perspective of systematic and purposive interpretation of Article 12 of the Constitution.\\n\\nThe previous decision of this Court, which took a different view and held that the right to assistance of counsel prescribed in the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution is intended to guarantee the defense rights of suspects or defendants in criminal procedure and cannot be regarded as applying to procedures for protection or deportation under the Immigration Control Act (see Constitutional Court 2012. 8. 23., 2008HEONMA430), is changed to the extent that it conflicts with the purport of this decision.\\n\\n(4) Whether the Petitioner’s Detention in the Repatriation Waiting Room Corresponds to “Detention” Prescribed in the Main Clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution\\n\\n“Detention” prescribed in the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution means the act of forcibly confining a person within a closed space of a certain range and thereby prohibiting free bodily movement outside that confined space. In order to recognize that the Petitioner was “detained” under the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution on 2014. 4. 25., when the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case occurred, it must be recognized that the Petitioner was forcibly confined in the repatriation waiting room at that time.\\n\\nIn this case, the repatriation waiting room in which the Petitioner was held on 2014. 4. 25., the date of the rejection of the attorney interview application, is a closed space with an entrance and exit made of a steel gate, and access thereto was controlled by the Incheon International Airport Airline Operating Council. The Petitioner could not leave the transit area outside the repatriation waiting room, and had no means of communication with the outside other than public telephones. At the time of the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case, the Petitioner had been held in the repatriation waiting room for about five months, and at least until the action seeking revocation of the decision not to refer for refugee status determination was concluded, he could not expect to leave the repatriation waiting room voluntarily. Since, at the time of the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case, the Petitioner had already filed a habeas corpus action seeking lifting of his detention in the repatriation waiting room, it cannot be said that he was staying in the repatriation waiting room according to his own will.\\n\\nConsidering the above circumstances, it is recognized that at the time of the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case, the Petitioner was forcibly confined in the repatriation waiting room against his will. Accordingly, on 2014. 4. 25., the date of the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case, the Petitioner was in a state of being “detained” as prescribed in the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution.\\n\\nThere may be an objection that a foreign national held in the repatriation waiting room after having received a decision denying entry is not forcibly confined, because although he cannot enter the Republic of Korea, he is free at any time to leave the repatriation waiting room in order to depart voluntarily for a foreign country. However, in light of the Petitioner’s specific and actual circumstances, having fled persecution in his country of nationality, the freedom to depart is nothing more than an unrealizable abstract possibility for the Petitioner, and therefore is not a factor to be considered in determining whether he was “detained” in the repatriation waiting room. Even if such a possibility of departure is considered, it is clear that the Petitioner was confined in the closed space of the repatriation waiting room, in that he was prohibited for a long period from leaving the repatriation waiting room and moving to the transit area.\\n\\n(5) Intermediate Conclusion\\n\\nSince the Petitioner was, at the time of the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case, detained in the repatriation waiting room by the Respondent, an administrative agency, the Petitioner has the right to assistance of counsel under the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution.\\n\\nb. Constitutionality of the Rejection of the Attorney Interview Application in this Case\\n\\nThe fundamental right to assistance of counsel prescribed in the main clause of Article 12(4) of the Constitution may also be constitutionally restricted in accordance with the requirements prescribed in Article 37(2) of the Constitution. According to Article 37(2) of the Constitution, the right to assistance of counsel may be restricted “by law.” Article 6(2) through (4) of the Refugee Act contains a basis for allowing a person who submitted an application for refugee status at a port of entry to remain in a certain place at the port of entry for up to 7 days until it is determined whether the application will be referred for refugee status determination. However, the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case occurred when the Petitioner had been detained for five months after receiving a decision not to refer for refugee status determination, and thus is not subject to the above provisions of the Refugee Act; moreover, those provisions contain no restriction on the right to attorney interview. Other than that, there is no statutory basis under the current law for restricting the Petitioner’s right to assistance of counsel. The rejection of the attorney interview application in this case has no legal basis whatsoever.\\n\\nIn addition, according to Article 37(2) of the Constitution, the right to assistance of counsel may be restricted only “when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare.” However, it is difficult to see that allowing the Petitioner to apply for an attorney interview would cause any impediment to national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare. Even if allowing attorney interviews for foreign nationals held in the repatriation waiting room might create concerns about hindering national security or maintenance of order in the transit area, etc., if measures such as limiting the place of interview to the minimum necessary extent are taken, the Petitioner’s right to attorney interview can be properly guaranteed without causing any significant disruption to national security or maintenance of order in the transit area. Accordingly, the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case cannot be regarded as a restriction of fundamental rights necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare.\\n\\nThe rejection of the attorney interview application in this case infringes the Petitioner’s right to assistance of counsel and is therefore unconstitutional.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case infringed the Petitioner’s right to assistance of counsel while the Petitioner was being held in the repatriation waiting room at Incheon International Airport after having received a decision not to refer for refugee status determination, and thus it is confirmed that it violates the Constitution. In this decision, all other participating Justices were in agreement, except for the separate opinion of Justice Kim Changjong and Justice Ahn Changho as set forth in 7. below.\\n\\n7. Separate Opinion of Justice Kim Changjong and Justice Ahn Changho\\n\\nWe agree with the conclusion that the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case (hereinafter, in the separate opinion, referred to as the “rejection of the attorney interview application in this case”) infringes the Petitioner’s fundamental rights, but unlike the majority opinion, we determine that the above rejection does not infringe the Petitioner’s right to assistance of counsel but infringes the right to request a trial, and therefore state our opinion as follows.\\n\\na. Whether the Right to Assistance of Counsel Was Infringed\\n\\n(1) Article 12(4) of the Constitution provides that “When any person is arrested or detained, he shall have the right to the assistance of counsel immediately.” Here, “detention” means forcibly restricting personal liberty and prohibiting spatial mobility for a certain period, and refers to compulsory apprehension of a person and confinement in a certain place.\\n\\nMore specifically, “confinement” means the act of forcibly confining a person within a closed space of a certain range and thereby prohibiting free bodily movement outside that closed space. Whether a case falls under “confinement” in Article 12(4) of the Constitution must be determined comprehensively by considering, together with whether the space is a closed space restricting free bodily movement, the circumstances in which free bodily movement was restricted and the possibility of escaping from that restricted state according to the will of the person whose movement was restricted.\\n\\n(2) Immigration control administration is state administration that promotes national security, maintenance of order, and public welfare by appropriately controlling and coordinating the entry and departure of nationals and foreigners and the stay of foreigners. Among matters concerning such immigration control, matters concerning the entry of foreigners, in particular non-nationals, are necessary for the performance of the function of a sovereign state and fall within a broad sphere of policy discretion (see Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31., 2003HEONMA87; Constitutional Court 2014. 4. 24., 2011HEONMA474 et al.).\\n\\nThe Petitioner, as a foreign national, received a decision denying entry pursuant to Article 12(3) item 2 and Article 12(4) of the Immigration Control Act on the ground that he failed to prove that the purpose of entry conformed to his status of stay. According to Article 76(1) items 1 and 3 of the Immigration Control Act, the master or carrier of a ship, etc. on which a foreign national who has been denied entry because he lacked a status of stay conforming to the purpose of entry was on board shall, at his own expense and responsibility, repatriate that foreign national out of the Republic of Korea without delay. For national security, maintenance of order, and public welfare, since the entry into the Republic of Korea of a foreign national who has received a decision denying entry is restricted until repatriation as above, the foreign national’s “freedom of movement” may be restricted to that extent.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Petitioner applied for refugee status at a port of entry, and even a foreign national who submitted an application for refugee status at a port of entry cannot enter the Republic of Korea until a decision to refer for refugee status determination is rendered; therefore, the restriction on the “freedom of movement” of a foreign national who has received a decision denying entry may continue.\\n\\n(3) As the majority opinion states, at the time of the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case, the repatriation waiting room in which the Petitioner was staying was physically a closed space and access thereto was controlled. However, a foreign national who has received a decision denying entry cannot enter the Republic of Korea, but may, at any time, leave the repatriation waiting room by voluntarily departing for his country of nationality or a third country, and thus the restriction on the “freedom of movement” of a foreign national who has received a decision denying entry has the special characteristic that it may depend on his own will (see Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22., 2017HEONGA29).\\n\\nIt cannot be said that the Petitioner wanted to be held in the above repatriation waiting room, but, as noted above, for national security, maintenance of order, and public welfare, there is a recognized necessity to restrict the “freedom of movement” of a foreign national who has received a decision denying entry, and because the Petitioner, whose entry had been denied, continued to seek entry into the Republic of Korea despite being able to leave voluntarily at any time, there was inevitably a restriction on his “freedom of movement” in the process of controlling this, and such restriction on freedom cannot be said to be unrelated to the Petitioner’s will. In addition, the reason the Petitioner remained in the repatriation waiting room in this case for more than five months was that the period during which he stayed at the port of entry became prolonged in the course of receiving a decision not to refer for refugee status determination and contesting it by filing an action for revocation thereof.\\n\\nConsidering that the Petitioner could at any time leave the repatriation waiting room by voluntarily departing for his country of nationality or a third country, and that, notwithstanding this, access to the repatriation waiting room was controlled while he continued to remain at the port of entry according to his own will in order to apply for refugee status, it cannot be said that the Petitioner was in a state of “confinement” contemplated by the Constitution.\\n\\nFor reference, if the Petitioner is regarded as being in a state of “confinement,” the question whether a warrant is required for that confinement may arise under Article 12(3) of the Constitution, which provides for the warrant principle. If a warrant is deemed necessary, then even though a warrant has been issued, it would mean that the detainee may leave “voluntarily,” which raises the question whether that is consistent with the current “warrant system,” and issuing a warrant to a foreign national who can voluntarily depart may in some cases operate to the detriment of that foreign national.\\n\\n(4) Accordingly, since the Petitioner cannot be regarded as having the right to assistance of counsel as a detained person prescribed in Article 12(4) of the Constitution, it cannot be said that the Petitioner’s constitutional right to assistance of counsel was restricted by the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case.\\n\\nb. Whether the Right to Request a Trial Was Infringed\\n\\nWe examine whether the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case infringes the Petitioner’s right to a trial.\\n\\n(1) First, the question arises whether a foreign national like the Petitioner can be a subject of the right to request a trial. Considering that the Petitioner, held in the repatriation waiting room, is subject to restrictions on free bodily movement, has filed a habeas corpus action in order to contest the propriety of such detention, and seeks the assistance of an attorney in relation to that litigation, the right to request a trial in this case can be regarded as a right necessarily required to effectively guarantee personal liberty, which is a human right, and therefore, even if the Petitioner is a foreign national, it is appropriate to regard him as a subject of the right to request a trial.\\n\\n(2) Article 27 of the Constitution provides that “All citizens shall have the right to a trial under the law by judges qualified under the Constitution and the law,” thereby guaranteeing the right to request a trial, and the right to a trial includes civil trials, criminal trials, administrative trials, and constitutional adjudication (see Constitutional Court 2013. 8. 29., 2011HEONMA122). In order to guarantee the “under the law” right to request a trial under Article 27(1) of the Constitution, it is necessary for the legislature to give concrete shape to the right to request a trial, but this must be done so as to ensure, to a substantial degree, the effectiveness of rights relief (see Constitutional Court 2001. 6. 28., 2000HEONBA77; Constitutional Court 2010. 7. 29., 2005HEONBA89). In light of the increasing role of legal professionals in the complex litigation of modern society and the realization of the principle of equality of arms under civil law, the guarantee of the right of access between a person in the repatriation waiting room after being denied entry at a port of entry and an attorney may be regarded as part of the constitutionally guaranteed right to request a trial or a right derived therefrom (see Constitutional Court 2013. 8. 29., 2011HEONMA122).\\n\\nAccordingly, the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case restricts, as an aspect of the right to request a trial, the Petitioner’s right to assistance from an attorney.\\n\\n(3) Under Article 37(2) of the Constitution, in order to restrict the right to request a trial, such restriction must be made “by law.” However, the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case was made without any legal basis, and therefore the resulting restriction on the Petitioner’s right to request a trial is unconstitutional.\\n\\nIn addition, according to Article 37(2) of the Constitution, the right to assistance of an attorney may be restricted only “when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare.” However, it is difficult to see that allowing the Petitioner to apply for an attorney interview would cause any impediment to national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, and even if such impediment were to arise, the Petitioner’s right to attorney interview can be guaranteed without causing any significant disruption to national security, maintenance of order in the transit area, or public welfare if the place of interview is limited to the repatriation waiting room.\\n\\nAccordingly, the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case cannot be regarded as a necessary restriction of fundamental rights for the achievement of national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, and thus the rejection of the attorney interview application in this case infringes the Petitioner’s right to request a trial.\\n\\nc. Conclusion\\n\\nThe rejection of the attorney interview application in this case does not infringe the right to assistance of counsel prescribed in Article 12(4) of the Constitution, but does infringe the Petitioner’s right to request a trial."}

Outline of the Case  \\nThe Petitioner submitted, on January 13, 2014, a document titled “Complaint,” which had been filed as a criminal complaint case, at the Changwon District Prosecutors' Office; however, a prosecutor at the Changwon District Prosecutors' Office, on the basis of Article 11 of the Prosecutors' Office Act and Article 141 of the Regulations on the Affairs of Prosecutorial Cases, accepted it as a petition case. Accordingly, alleging that Article 11 of the Prosecutors' Office Act, which is a delegation provision concerning the affairs of the Prosecutors' Office, and Article 141(3) of the Regulations on the Affairs of Prosecutorial Cases, which allows documents filed as a complaint case to be accepted as a petition, as amended by Ministry of Justice Ordinance No. 532 of July 28, 2003, infringe the Petitioner’s fundamental rights, the Petitioner filed the constitutional complaint adjudication in this case on January 18, 2014.\\n\\n2. Subject of Review  \\nThe subject of review in this case is whether Article 11 of the Prosecutors' Office Act (as amended by Act No. 9815 of November 2, 2009, hereinafter referred to as the “Prosecutors' Office Act”) and Article 141(3) of the Regulations on the Affairs of Prosecutorial Cases (as amended by Ministry of Justice Ordinance No. 532 of July 28, 2003, hereinafter referred to as the “Regulations on the Affairs of Prosecutorial Cases”) infringe the Petitioner’s fundamental rights. The provisions subject to review are as follows.  \\n[Provisions Subject to Review]  \\nProsecutors' Office Act (as amended by Act No. 9815 of November 2, 2009)  \\nArticle 11 (Delegation Provision) Matters necessary concerning the affairs of the Prosecutors' Office shall be prescribed by Ministry of Justice Ordinance.  \\nRegulations on the Affairs of Prosecutorial Cases (as amended by Ministry of Justice Ordinance No. 532 of July 28, 2003)  \\nArticle 141 (Acceptance of Petitions, etc.) ③ A prosecutor may accept as a petition case documents filed as a complaint or accusation case where any of the following subparagraphs applies.  \\n1. Where the contents based on the statement of the complainant or accuser, or on the complaint or accusation document, are unclear or specific facts are not stated  \\n2. Where there is no expression of intent seeking punishment of the person complained of or the person accused, or where an expression of intent seeking punishment has been withdrawn  \\n3. Where it is not confirmed whether the complaint or accusation was made according to the complainant’s or accuser’s true intent  \\n4. Where there are duplicate complaints or accusations concerning the same facts  \\n\\n3. Judgment  \\nA. Judgment on Article 11 of the Prosecutors' Office Act  \\nIn order for a statutory provision itself to be subject to a constitutional complaint, the statutory provision must directly infringe the fundamental rights of the complainants; therefore, where a statutory provision contemplates the implementation of subordinate norms for the concretization of that provision, directness of the statute in question is, in principle, denied (Constitutional Court 2010HEONMA443, etc., March 29, 2012).  \\nExamining the matter, Article 11 of the Prosecutors' Office Act delegates matters necessary concerning the affairs of the Prosecutors' Office to be prescribed by Ministry of Justice Ordinance; thus, the specific content is to be determined by subordinate norms delegated by the above statutory provision, and accordingly whether fundamental rights have been infringed can also be determined. Ultimately, it cannot be said that fundamental rights are directly infringed by the above statutory provision itself. Therefore, this part of the petition for adjudication is inadmissible for lack of direct infringement of fundamental rights.\\n\\nB. Judgment on Article 141(3) of the Regulations on the Affairs of Prosecutorial Cases  \\nSince administrative rules, in general, have effect only within the administrative organization and do not have external binding force, they are not, in principle, subject to constitutional complaint adjudication (Constitutional Court 91HEONMA42, July 8, 1991).  \\nExamining the matter, although Article 141(3) of the Regulations on the Affairs of Prosecutorial Cases was prescribed as a Ministry of Justice Ordinance pursuant to Article 11 of the Prosecutors' Office Act, it is merely an internal work-handling guideline or office-handling standard within the Prosecutors' Office that internally prescribes the acceptance procedure for documents filed as a complaint case, and is not something that has normative effect; therefore, it cannot be the subject of constitutional complaint adjudication, and this part of the petition for adjudication is inadmissible (see Constitutional Court 91HEONMA42, July 8, 1991; 2012HEONMA422, May 18, 2012).\\n\\nC. Conclusion  \\nAccordingly, the petition for adjudication in this case is to be dismissed in its entirety, and the decision is made as stated in the order by the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating."}

Case Overview\\n\\na. 2020HEONGA1  \\nThe requesting party, Pa○○ (a foreign national), was a foreign national of the Arab Republic of Egypt who entered the Republic of Korea on 2018. 7. 21. with tourist/transit (B-2) status and was staying in the Republic of Korea beyond the period of stay granted.  \\nThe Head of the Suwon Immigration and Foreigners Office, pursuant to Article 51(3) of the Immigration Control Act, took the above requesting party into emergency custody on 2018. 10. 17., and on 2018. 10. 18. issued a deportation order against the above requesting party pursuant to Article 46(1) item 3, item 8, Article 11(1) item 8, and Article 17(1) of the same Act and, at the same time, issued a detention order pursuant to Article 63(1) of the same Act.  \\nAccordingly, the above requesting party filed a lawsuit seeking revocation of the above deportation order and detention order (Suwon District Court 2019GUDAN6240), and during the pendency of that case applied for a constitutional review regarding Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act, etc. (Suwon District Court 2019A4057); the referring court accepted the application as to Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act and, on 2020. 1. 23., referred the constitutional review in this case.\\n\\nb. 2021HEONGA10  \\nThe requesting party, Ja○○ (a foreign national), was a foreign national of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh who entered the Republic of Korea on 2017. 5. 13. with short-term business (C-3-4) status and, after applying for refugee status recognition on 2017. 8. 7., was additionally granted other (G-1-5) status.  \\nThe Head of the Seoul Immigration and Foreigners Office, on 2017. 11. 22., on the ground that the above requesting party entered the country through false invitation, issued a deportation order against the above requesting party pursuant to Article 46(1) item 2, item 3, Article 7-2 item 2, Article 11(1) item 3, and item 4 of the Immigration Control Act and, at the same time, issued a detention order pursuant to Article 63(1) of the same Act.  \\nAccordingly, the above requesting party filed a lawsuit seeking revocation of the above deportation order and detention order (Seoul Administrative Court 2018GUDAN54708), and during the pendency of that case applied for a constitutional review regarding Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act, etc. (Seoul Administrative Court 2018A12518); the referring court accepted the application as to Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act and, on 2021. 2. 9., referred the constitutional review in this case.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review  \\nThe subject matter of review in this case is whether Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.) (hereinafter the “Provision at Issue”) violates the Constitution. The Provision at Issue and the relevant provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision at Issue]  \\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.)  \\nArticle 63 (Detention and Release of Persons Subject to a Deportation Order)  \\n(1) If the head of a local immigration and foreigners office cannot immediately repatriate a person subject to a deportation order outside the Republic of Korea for reasons such as not possessing a passport or not having transportation arrangements, he or she may detain that person in a detention facility until repatriation becomes possible.\\n\\n[Relevant Provisions]  \\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 10282 on 2010. 5. 14.)  \\nArticle 2 (Definitions) The meanings of the terms used in this Act are as follows:  \\n11. The term “detention” means enforcement activity by which an immigration control officer takes and confines a person who has reasonable grounds to be suspected of falling within the subject of deportation under the items of Article 46(1) in an immigration holding room, an alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice, for the purpose of deporting that person.\\n\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.)  \\nArticle 46 (Persons Subject to Deportation)  \\n(1) The head of a local immigration and foreigners office may deport from the Republic of Korea any foreign national falling under any of the following items in accordance with the procedures prescribed in this Chapter.  \\n2. A foreign national who violated Article 7-2 or a foreign national who entered the country through false invitation or similar acts prescribed in that Article  \\n3. A person whose ground for entry ban falling under any item of Article 11(1) was discovered or arose after entry  \\n8. A person who violated Article 17(1) or (2), Article 18, Article 20, Article 23, Article 24, or Article 25\\n\\nArticle 63 (Detention and Release of Persons Subject to a Deportation Order)  \\n(2) When detaining a person pursuant to paragraph (1), if the period exceeds 3 months, the head of a local immigration and foreigners office shall obtain prior approval from the Minister of Justice every 3 months.  \\n(3) If the head of a local immigration and foreigners office fails to obtain the approval under paragraph (2), he or she shall promptly release the person from detention.  \\n(4) The head of a local immigration and foreigners office may release a person from detention if it becomes manifest that the person subject to a deportation order cannot be repatriated for reasons such as being refused entry by another country.  \\n(5) When the head of a local immigration and foreigners office releases a person from detention pursuant to paragraph (3) or (4), he or she may attach a restriction on residence or other necessary conditions.\\n\\nArticle 66 (Revocation of Temporary Release from Detention)  \\n(1) The head of a local immigration and foreigners office may revoke the temporary release from detention and take the person into detention again, if a person temporarily released from detention falls under any of the following items:  \\n1. Where the person absconds or is deemed likely to abscond  \\n2. Where the person fails to comply with a summons without justifiable grounds  \\n3. Where the person violates conditions attached to the temporary release other than the matters prescribed in items 1 and 2  \\n(2) If the head of a local immigration and foreigners office revokes the temporary release from detention pursuant to paragraph (1), he or she may issue a notice of revocation of temporary release from detention and forfeit all or part of the deposit to the National Treasury.\\n\\nImmigration Control Act (as amended by Act No. 15492 on 2018. 3. 20.)  \\nArticle 65 (Temporary Release from Detention)  \\n(1) The head of a local immigration and foreigners office may, ex officio or upon the request of a detainee (including his or her guarantor or legal representative, etc.), taking into account the detainee’s circumstances, reasons for requesting release, assets, and other matters, temporarily release the detainee from detention by requiring a deposit of not more than 20 million won and attaching a restriction on residence or other necessary conditions.\\n\\n3. Grounds for the Request for Constitutional Review by the Referring Court  \\na. The Provision at Issue does not set an upper limit on the period of detention, thereby causing the detainee to be completely unable to predict when he or she will be released, and in that respect it, by itself, brings about serious mental pressure. Enabling detention without any time limit merely for the administrative purpose of facilitating enforcement of the deportation order emphasizes administrative convenience and uniformity alone, and therefore violates the principle of proportionality and infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person.  \\nb. Detention under the Immigration Control Act restricts freedom of the person as it is analogous to “arrest or detention” in criminal procedure. Therefore, strict application of the warrant requirement should be necessary, but the Provision at Issue violates the warrant requirement by allowing the physical restraint of a foreign national subject to a deportation order without a court warrant.  \\nc. In light of the fact that no third independent neutral institution or judicial institution is involved at all at the stage of commencement or extension of detention; that the detainee may file an objection against the detention order with the Minister of Justice, and detention may be extended only with the Minister of Justice’s approval, but the Minister of Justice is merely the supervisory authority over the administrative agency that issues and executes the detention order, so it cannot be said that a post-remedy or control procedure by an external neutral and objective institution is guaranteed; and that the Immigration Control Act contains no provision requiring that the person concerned be given an opportunity to submit opinions before the detention order under the Provision at Issue is issued, the Provision at Issue violates the principle of due process.\\n\\n4. Judgment  \\na. The foreigner detention system under the Immigration Control Act  \\n(1) Detention under the Immigration Control Act means “enforcement activity by which an immigration control officer takes and confines a person who has reasonable grounds to be suspected of falling within the subject of deportation under Article 46(1) of the Immigration Control Act in an immigration holding room, an alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice, for the purpose of deporting that person” (Article 2 item 11 of the Immigration Control Act). Detention under the Immigration Control Act includes “detention for examination of deportation subjects” prescribed in Article 51 and “detention for enforcement of a deportation order” prescribed in the Provision at Issue.  \\n(2) According to the Provision at Issue, if the head of a local immigration and foreigners office cannot immediately repatriate a foreign national subject to a deportation order (hereinafter a “person subject to deportation”) outside the Republic of Korea for reasons such as not possessing a passport or not having transportation arrangements, he or she may detain that person in an immigration holding room, an alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice (hereinafter a “detention facility”) until repatriation becomes possible. Detention under the Provision at Issue is to secure enforcement of the deportation order in cases where a deportation order is issued on the determination that the foreign national falls within the subject of deportation, but immediate enforcement is not possible, and is distinguished from detention under Article 51 of the Immigration Control Act, which secures the physical custody of a foreign national in order to examine whether he or she falls within the subject of deportation.  \\nThe Provision at Issue states that detention may be maintained “until repatriation becomes possible,” and thus, on the face of the text, does not set any time limit on the period of detention. Instead, if the period of detention exceeds 3 months, prior approval of the Minister of Justice must be obtained every 3 months, and if such approval is not obtained, detention must be released (Article 63(2) and (3) of the Immigration Control Act). In addition, a person detained in a detention facility pursuant to the Provision at Issue may file an objection with the Minister of Justice (Article 63(6) and Article 55 of the Immigration Control Act), and the head of a local immigration and foreigners office may, ex officio or upon the request of the detainee, temporarily release the detainee from detention by requiring a deposit of not more than 20 million won and attaching a restriction on residence or other necessary conditions, taking into account the detainee’s circumstances, reasons for requesting release, assets, and other matters (Article 65(1) of the Immigration Control Act).\\n\\nb. Issues and standard of review  \\n(1) Detention under the Provision at Issue is a coercive measure that takes and confines a person subject to deportation in a detention facility in order to secure enforcement of a deportation order when immediate enforcement is not possible, and thereby restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person (see Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29). Accordingly, the issue in this case is whether the Provision at Issue infringes freedom of the person by violating the principle of proportionality, which is the principle limiting restrictions on fundamental rights, and the principle of due process under Article 12 of the Constitution.  \\n(2) Immigration control administration is state administration that seeks the national interest and security by properly controlling and coordinating the entry into and departure from the country by Koreans and foreign nationals and the stay of foreign nationals. Among matters concerning immigration control, matters concerning the entry of foreign nationals and their stay in the country are necessary to perform the function of a sovereign state and fall within the area of broad policy discretion (see Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2003HEONMA87; Constitutional Court 2014. 4. 24. 2011HEONMA474 et al.). Detention under the Provision at Issue, which is carried out to secure enforcement of a deportation order, can be regarded as part of immigration control administration.  \\nHowever, the freedom of the person under Article 12(1) of the Constitution is the most fundamental minimum freedom for realizing human dignity and value and is the premise for guaranteeing all fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court 2020. 9. 24. 2017HEONBA157 et al.). By its nature, it is a human right, and whether it is recognized does not depend on whether one has a lawful status of stay in the country. Accordingly, a strict standard of review must be applied to whether the Provision at Issue infringes freedom of the person.\\n\\nc. Opinion of Justices Yu Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-young, Moon Hyung-bae, and Lee Mi-sun: incompatibility with the Constitution  \\n(1) Whether the principle of proportionality has been violated  \\n(a) Legitimacy of the purpose and appropriateness of the means  \\nThe legislative purpose of the Provision at Issue is to promote national security and order by appropriately controlling and coordinating the entry into and departure from the country and the stay of foreign nationals, by taking and confining persons subject to deportation in a detention facility until they can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea so that deportation orders may be enforced easily and efficiently. This legislative purpose is legitimate, and taking and confining persons subject to deportation in a detention facility until they can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea is an effective means of securing enforcement of deportation orders, so appropriateness of the means is also recognized.  \\n(b) Least restriction and balance of legal interests  \\nHowever, the Provision at Issue does not satisfy the requirement of least restriction and the balance of legal interests for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) Detention under the Provision at Issue is a coercive measure that is temporarily and provisionally adopted to secure enforcement when a deportation order cannot be enforced immediately upon issuance (see Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29). Yet the Provision at Issue merely states that persons subject to deportation may be detained until they can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea, and does not set an upper limit on the detention period, thereby allowing indefinite detention.  \\nDetention that temporarily and provisionally confines a person subject to deportation in a specific place for the purpose of enforcing a deportation order can, by nature, be justified only when confinement occurs within a reasonable period necessary for enforcing the deportation order. However, according to the Provision at Issue, for example, where enforcement of the deportation order is impossible until related procedures conclude because the detainee has filed an application for refugee status recognition or an objection to a refugee non-recognition decision under the Refugee Act (see Article 62(4) of the Immigration Control Act), or where enforcement of the deportation order is practically difficult because the detainee has filed a revocation suit, etc. against the deportation order or civil or criminal disputes are pending, the detention period may be extended without limit depending on the progress of those procedures. In addition, the Provision at Issue allows detention to continue without any time limit until repatriation becomes possible even when repatriation is impossible because another country refuses entry. Thus, even where a deportation order cannot be enforced within a considerable period, long-term or indefinite detention of persons subject to deportation exceeds the limits of a temporary and provisional coercive measure and significantly restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person. Furthermore, detention with no set upper limit itself brings about serious mental pressure, regardless of the actual length of detention, in that it leaves the detainee completely unable to predict when he or she will be released (see the opinion of unconstitutionality by Justices Lee Jin-seong, Kim I-su, Kang Il-won, Lee Sun-ae, and Yu Nam-seok in Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29).  \\nDetention under the Provision at Issue has an objective limitation in that it may not be imposed for any purpose other than securing enforcement of a deportation order, and a temporal limitation in that it may be imposed only provisionally for the minimum period necessary until repatriation becomes possible and the detention period may not be extended for any other purpose (see Supreme Court Decision 99DA68829 dated 2001. 10. 26.); moreover, the average detention period until an actual person subject to deportation is repatriated is only a little over 10 days, and cases where long-term detention of more than 1 year becomes an issue are only a small number. However, such limits naturally derive from the nature of detention as a temporary and provisional measure, and whether the normative concept of “the minimum period necessary until repatriation becomes possible” should be limited to a considerable period is not taken into account. Therefore, notwithstanding the above interpretive limits, the Provision at Issue, which does not set an upper limit on the detention period, makes long-term or indefinite detention possible, and the problems arising from not setting an upper limit remain, including that where a deportation order cannot be enforced for reasons for which the detainee is not responsible, the person may still be detained for a long period until actual repatriation if “immediate repatriation is impossible.”  \\nMeanwhile, there may be cases where the detainee does not cooperate with repatriation even though there is no objective reason making repatriation impossible, making it impossible to promptly enforce the deportation order; however, mere non-cooperation with repatriation does not justify indefinite detention. Although refusal to cooperate may be used as a reason to extend the detention period when enforcement of the deportation order is delayed by the detainee’s refusal to cooperate, the immigration control authorities in charge of repatriation must faithfully perform repatriation duties, including removing obstacles that delay repatriation, and therefore cannot continue detaining the detainee until repatriation is accomplished forever simply because the detainee does not cooperate with repatriation.\\n\\n2) Therefore, even leaving aside what the appropriate upper limit of the detention period should be, at the very least the law must specify such an upper limit so that harm arising from unreasonable prolongation or uncertainty of the detention period can be prevented. Enabling detention without any time limit merely for the administrative purpose of efficient enforcement of a deportation order emphasizes administrative convenience and uniformity alone, and excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person. Because foreign nationals who were apprehended and detained either did not choose voluntary departure for various reasons or could not depart voluntarily, they cannot, in practical terms, be regarded as having a “freedom to depart”; therefore, the infringement of fundamental rights arising from not setting an upper limit on detention is not alleviated on the ground that persons subject to deportation are free to depart at any time and thereby escape from the status of being detained (see the opinion of unconstitutionality by Justices Lee Jin-seong, Kim I-su, Kang Il-won, Lee Sun-ae, and Yu Nam-seok in Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29).  \\nLooking at international standards and foreign legislative examples, many countries set an upper limit on the period when detaining persons who have received deportation orders. The Directive 2008/115/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on common standards and procedures in Member States for returning illegally staying third-country nationals (the so-called “EU Return Directive”) requires Member States to provide in domestic law an absolute upper limit on the period of detention in order to curb unnecessary prolonged detention and respect the fundamental human rights of foreign nationals subject to deportation; it strengthens control over prolonged detention by, for example, providing that the initial detention period may not exceed 6 months and, exceptionally, detention may be extended but the extension period may be up to 12 months at most. Accordingly, EU Member States have enacted in domestic law detention requirements and procedures that are the same as or stricter than the standards set in the above Directive, and have set an upper limit on the period of detention. For example, France provides by law that detention may be ordered for up to 90 days only where effective custody cannot be secured for a foreign national for whom repatriation is reasonably possible and where other measures to ensure effective enforcement are insufficient; Germany provides by law that detention for deportation may be ordered for up to 6 months, and even when extended may not exceed 12 months at most. Taiwan and the Republic of South Africa also limit by statute the detention period for persons subject to deportation to a maximum of 100 days or 120 days. The reason international standards and other legislative examples set an upper limit on the detention period is that detention without a fixed period may lead to serious human rights violations.  \\nThe period required to carry out repatriation in the actual process of enforcing a deportation order may vary depending on the person subject to deportation’s cooperation or the circumstances of the Republic of Korea or the receiving country. It may be argued that these circumstances make it inevitable that the Provision at Issue does not set an upper limit on the detention period; however, considering that detention under the Provision at Issue is a temporary and provisional measure taken to secure enforcement of a deportation order, and that many countries set an upper limit on the detention period for persons subject to deportation as noted above, it cannot be said to be impossible to set a reasonable upper limit on the detention period necessary for enforcing a deportation order.\\n\\n3) If an upper limit is set on the detention period and repatriation is delayed beyond that limit, detention of the person subject to deportation must be released; in such a case, it may be argued that a person subject to deportation released from detention may disappear or become exposed to crime. However, this is nothing more than a vague and potential possibility not yet realized, or an exaggerated concern about some situations, and therefore, based only on such a vague presumption, it is difficult to justify a measure that significantly restricts freedom of the person, such as “detention without an upper limit.” A foreign national who has committed a crime in the Republic of Korea cannot simply be presumed to abscond or commit another crime when released from detention. In addition, among persons subject to deportation there may be not only foreign nationals who committed crimes and were sentenced to punishment, but also foreign nationals who merely violated administrative regulations concerning entry or stay; treating all of them as potential absconders or potential criminals and detaining them without any time limit is an excessive measure (see the opinion of unconstitutionality by Justices Lee Jin-seong, Kim I-su, Kang Il-won, Lee Sun-ae, and Yu Nam-seok in Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29).  \\nThere may be concern that if an upper limit is imposed on detention, the detainee may surpass that upper limit through a revocation suit against the deportation order or an application for refugee status recognition. However, such cases of exceeding the detention period can be minimized through institutional improvements, such as the courts’ first-priority and concentrated hearing of the relevant case, prompt review and decision on refugee status recognition, or prevention of abuse of applications for refugee status recognition.  \\nFurthermore, securing enforcement of a deportation order is possible through various means other than detention under the Provision at Issue. For example, enforcement of a deportation order can be secured through substitute means such as restricting the residence of a person subject to deportation until departure requirements are satisfied, requiring periodic reporting of residence, designating a guarantor or requiring payment of an appropriate deposit, or continuously observing or supervising the person subject to deportation through supervisors, etc. Therefore, to secure enforcement of a deportation order, it is not necessary to adopt a method that excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person, such as detention without any time limit.\\n\\n4) Meanwhile, the current procedures and operation of the Immigration Control Act are insufficient to appropriately control the detention period and thereby alleviate excessive restrictions on freedom of the person.  \\nFirst, under the Immigration Control Act, the detainee may request temporary release from detention from the head of the local immigration and foreigners office, and the head of such office may temporarily release the detainee ex officio (Article 65 of the Immigration Control Act). However, unless there are circumstances in which the detainee has won a revocation suit against a deportation order, etc., the decision whether to temporarily release from detention is entirely discretionary to the head of the local immigration and foreigners office (Article 65 of the Immigration Control Act; see also Article 6 of the “Regulations on the Handling of Temporary Release from Detention”), and is likely to be made for administrative convenience rather than a substantive review of the need for detention. According to the result of a factual inquiry to the Minister of Justice dated 2021. 7. 1. in Case 2020HEONGA1 and the reference materials submitted by the Minister of Justice on 2022. 9. 5., the number of temporary releases from detention made over the five years from 2013 to 2017 averaged 120 per year, and the number of temporary releases from detention made over the three years from 2018 to 2020 averaged 131 per year, whereas temporary releases from detention in 2021 surged to 461. The sharp increase in requests for temporary release from detention and the granting thereof in 2021 appears to have been driven by difficulties in quarantine control within detention centers due to the spread of COVID-19, suggesting that administrative convenience was the main reason. Article 63(4) of the Immigration Control Act provides that the head of a local immigration and foreigners office may release detention if it becomes manifest that a person subject to deportation cannot be repatriated for reasons such as being refused entry by another country, but this too is entirely within the discretion of the head of the local immigration and foreigners office. In light of these points, the temporary release from detention system cannot be said to function as a device that can supplement the problem of not setting an upper limit on the detention period.  \\nThe Immigration Control Act also provides for objections to detention orders and a system under which the Minister of Justice approves extensions of detention periods, but as will be seen below, these are procedures carried out by the Minister of Justice, who is the supervisory authority over the administrative agency that issues and executes detention orders, and therefore cannot be deemed sufficiently effective to supplement the problem of not setting an upper limit on the detention period. In particular, according to reference materials submitted by the Minister of Justice on 2021. 7. 21. and 2022. 9. 5., the non-approval rate for extensions was 4.9% in 2017, 6.7% in 2018, 6.4% in 2019, 4.0% in 2020, and 9.4% in 2021, with the average non-approval rate over the last five years amounting to only 6.28%, so the effectiveness of the extension approval system cannot but be questioned.\\n\\n5) Taking all the foregoing circumstances together, although means exist to secure enforcement of a deportation order other than indefinite detention in a detention facility, the Provision at Issue allows the detainee to be detained without any time limit, thereby exceeding the minimum necessary to achieve the legislative purpose and excessively restricting the detainee’s freedom of the person. Even if the public interest the Provision at Issue seeks to achieve is important, the degree to which freedom of the person is restricted by detention without an upper limit is excessively large; therefore, the Provision at Issue does not satisfy the requirements of least restriction and balance of legal interests.  \\n(c) Conclusion  \\nThe Provision at Issue infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person in violation of the principle of proportionality.\\n\\n(2) Whether the principle of due process has been violated  \\n(a) Article 12(1) of the Constitution proclaims the principle of due process by providing that “No person shall be punished, placed under preventive restrictions, or subjected to forced labor except as provided by Act and through due process.” Since the principle of due process applies not only to criminal procedure but to all state action in general (see Constitutional Court 1992. 12. 24. 92HEONGA8; Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29, etc.), the constitutional principle of due process must also be observed in detention under the Provision at Issue. However, the Provision at Issue presents the following problems from the perspective of the constitutional principle of due process.  \\n(b) Where freedom of the person is restricted by coercive administrative measures, ensuring that a neutral institution independent from the executing authority controls such measures constitutes an important content of the principle of due process; the specific form and level of such control should be determined by considering all factors, including the purpose of the coercive measure, the public interest sought thereby, and the degree to which the coercive measure restricts freedom of the person.
