Considering that detention under the Provision at Issue aims to secure enforcement of a deportation order while restricting freedom of the person to the extent of deprivation and can be regarded as equivalent to “arrest or detention” in criminal procedure, the principle of due process requires that, at the stage of commencement or extension of detention, an institution independent and neutral from the immigration control officers who are the executing authority should review the validity of detention and exercise control.  \\nAccording to the Immigration Control Act, the head of a local immigration and foreigners office examines and decides whether deportation is to be imposed, issues the deportation order and the detention order for enforcement of deportation, and immigration control officers execute the detention order and the deportation order (Articles 58, 59(2) and (3), 62(1), 63(1) and (6), and 53 of the Immigration Control Act), so formally the person issuing the detention order and the person executing it are separated. However, the head of the local immigration and foreigners office who makes the detention decision is not an independent third institution, but merely a superior within the same executing agency to which the immigration control officers belong, and thus in substance the detention-decision authority and its executing authority cannot be said to be separated. In addition, although Article 63(2) of the Immigration Control Act separates the approval authority for extension of detention by requiring the head of a local immigration and foreigners office to obtain prior approval from the Minister of Justice every 3 months when detention exceeds 3 months, the Minister of Justice is merely the supervisory authority over the administrative agency that issues and executes detention orders, and thus it is difficult to regard this as a review by an external neutral and objective institution.  \\nAs such, no independent neutral institution at all is currently involved at the stage of commencement or extension of detention under the Immigration Control Act, and under such circumstances there is no guarantee that the need for detention, etc. will be properly reviewed. The reality that a detention order is issued almost automatically once there is a deportation order, and that extension approval by the Minister of Justice is granted almost without exception when requested by the head of a local immigration and foreigners office, attests to this point.  \\nMeanwhile, the detainee may file an objection with the Minister of Justice against the detention order, but as noted above, the Minister of Justice is merely the supervisory authority over the administrative agency that issues and executes the detention order, and thus this cannot be regarded as guaranteeing a system of review by an external neutral and objective institution. Even considering that, over the 8 years from 2013 to 2020, there was not a single case in which an objection against a detention order was upheld, it is difficult to say that the Minister of Justice’s review has the significance of a practical control procedure for ensuring the legality of detention. In addition, although the detainee may file an administrative lawsuit against a deportation order, detention order, or decision dismissing an objection to a detention order, and may apply for suspension of execution of the detention order in the course of such proceedings, general and post hoc judicial remedies such as these cannot be said to sufficiently protect the detainee in the absence of any prior control by a fair and neutral institution at the stage of commencement or extension of detention.  \\n(c) Because affording the parties an opportunity to present opinions and materials is an important procedural demand derived from the principle of due process (see Constitutional Court 2003. 7. 24. 2001HEONGA25; Constitutional Court 2015. 9. 24. 2012HEONBA302), such an opportunity must also be guaranteed to the detainee even when detention is imposed pursuant to the Provision at Issue.  \\nHowever, the Immigration Control Act contains no provision requiring that the person concerned be given an opportunity to submit opinions before the detention order under the Provision at Issue is issued. The Administrative Procedures Act provides that when an administrative agency imposes duties on a person concerned or takes a disposition restricting rights or interests, it shall afford the person concerned, etc. an opportunity to submit opinions (Article 22(3) of the Administrative Procedures Act), but it excludes “dispositions concerning the entry into and departure from Korea of foreigners” from the scope of application of the Administrative Procedures Act (Article 3(2) item 9 of the Administrative Procedures Act; Article 2 item 2 of the Enforcement Decree of the Administrative Procedures Act). Therefore, under the current law, the detainee is not afforded an opportunity to make statements favorable to him or her or to submit opinions in the detention order procedure.  \\nA detention order presupposes a deportation order, and a deportation order is based on an investigation of a foreign national suspected of falling within the subject of deportation, the so-called suspect; the suspect is afforded an opportunity to state his or her opinion in the deportation order procedure, because the suspect’s statements are entered into the record and, if there is any request for addition or modification of the content, that too must be entered into the record (Articles 47 and 48(3) and (4) of the Immigration Control Act). However, the detainee must be able to state opinions on the necessity of detention or the risk of absconding in the detention order procedure, and the fact that an opportunity to state opinions was guaranteed in the deportation order procedure cannot exclude an opportunity to state opinions in the detention order procedure, which is a separate and independent procedure. Meanwhile, at the objection stage concerning the detention order, the Minister of Justice is merely provided discretion to hear the statements of interested persons if necessary (Article 63(6) and Article 55(3) of the Immigration Control Act), and the Minister of Justice’s prior approval for extension of detention likewise merely provides that the head of a local immigration and foreigners office must explain the necessity of extending the detention period (Article 78(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act); therefore, it cannot be said that the law has established a procedural opportunity for the detainee to submit opinions and materials to the Minister of Justice.  \\n(d) Taken together, the Provision at Issue violates the constitutional principle of due process because there is no control procedure by a fair and neutral institution at the stage of commencement or extension of detention, and because the person concerned is not guaranteed an opportunity to submit opinions.  \\n\\n(3) The need for a decision incompatible with the Constitution and provisional application  \\nAs seen above, the Provision at Issue infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person by violating the principle of proportionality and the principle of due process; therefore, as a matter of principle, a simple decision of unconstitutionality should be rendered with respect to the Provision at Issue.  \\nHowever, the unconstitutionality of the Provision at Issue lies in the fact that it does not set an upper limit on the detention period, thereby allowing long-term or indefinite detention, and in the fact that no control by a fair and neutral institution is exercised at the stage of commencement or extension of detention, and that the person concerned is not given an opportunity to submit opinions. In such circumstances, if a simple decision of unconstitutionality were rendered against the Provision at Issue, the basis provision for detention for enforcement of deportation orders would disappear, making it impossible to secure the physical custody of persons subject to deportation orders and causing an unacceptable legal vacuum. Moreover, the legislature has discretion in forming procedures, including how to set an upper limit on the detention period, how to structure an institution to review the validity of physical restraint at the stage of commencement or extension of detention, and in what form to guarantee an opportunity to submit opinions.  \\nTherefore, a decision incompatible with the Constitution shall be rendered regarding the Provision at Issue, and it shall continue to be applied until the legislature enacts remedial legislation. Since the legislature is obligated to enact remedial legislation as soon as possible, it must do so no later than 2025. 5. 31., and if no remedial legislation is enacted by then, the Provision at Issue shall lose effect from 2025. 6. 1.  \\n\\nd. Opinion of Justice Lee Sun-ae: incompatibility with the Constitution  \\nI concur in the conclusion with the opinion of unconstitutionality by Justices Yu Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-young, Moon Hyung-bae, and Lee Mi-sun that the Provision at Issue violates the Constitution and that a decision incompatible with the Constitution must be rendered. However, as to the reason, I have already participated in and argued in the opinion of unconstitutionality in Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29, and therefore I cite it below and leave my opinion of unconstitutionality in this case. The reasoning leading to a decision incompatible with the Constitution is the same as the opinion incompatible with the Constitution of Justices Yu Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-young, Moon Hyung-bae, and Lee Mi-sun.  \\n(1) Whether the principle of proportionality has been violated  \\n(a) Legitimacy of the purpose and appropriateness of the means  \\nThe Provision at Issue is intended to promote national security by properly controlling and coordinating the entry into and departure from the country and the stay of foreign nationals through facilitating enforcement against persons subject to deportation orders; thus, its legislative purpose is legitimate. In addition, detaining persons subject to deportation orders in a detention facility until departure requirements are satisfied in order to secure their physical custody is an effective method for swift and efficient enforcement of deportation orders, so appropriateness of the means is also recognized.  \\n(b) Least restriction and balance of legal interests  \\n1) The subjects of detention under the Provision at Issue are persons who have received deportation orders under the Immigration Control Act. These are foreign nationals who have already committed violations such as illegal stay, illegal employment, or criminal acts during their stay in the country (see Article 46(1) of the Act), and it cannot be said that there is no possibility of absconding or no latent risk; thus, detention and management to secure their physical custody until repatriation to their home countries is recognized as necessary.  \\nHowever, the Provision at Issue does not set an upper limit on the detention period, making it possible to detain persons subject to deportation indefinitely until they can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea. Detention with no fixed upper limit, in that it leaves the detainee completely unable to predict when he or she will be released, brings about serious mental pressure by itself, regardless of the actual length of detention. Accordingly, even leaving aside what the appropriate upper limit of detention should be, there is a need at least to specify such an upper limit in the law so that the detainee can predict the maximum period during which he or she may be detained; enabling detention without time limit merely for the administrative purpose of facilitating enforcement of deportation orders emphasizes administrative convenience and uniformity alone, and in itself constitutes an excessive restriction on the detainee’s freedom of the person (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Jung-mi, Kim I-su, Lee Jin-seong, and Kang Il-won in Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2013HEONBA196).  \\nLooking at international standards and foreign legislative examples, the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention states that an upper limit on detention must be prescribed by law and detention must not be indefinite. Germany provides that detention for deportation may be ordered for up to 6 months, and where a longer period is expected, it may be extended by up to 12 months, and the EU Return Directive (Directive 2008/115/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on common standards and procedures in Member States for returning illegally staying third-country nationals) provides similarly. The reason international standards and other legislative examples require a maximum detention period is likewise that detention without a fixed period may lead to serious human rights violations.  \\nThe Supreme Court stated that the detention order under Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act is “a temporary coercive measure having objective and temporal limits in that it may be issued only for the purpose of securing enforcement of a deportation order and, even after a detention order has lawfully been issued, detention may be imposed only provisionally for the minimum period necessary until repatriation becomes possible, and the detention period may not be extended for other purposes” (see Supreme Court Decision 99DA68829 dated 2001. 10. 26.). However, even if that holding is followed, the possibility of long-term or indefinite detention does not disappear, and the judgment merely explained the inherent limits of detention and did not set an upper limit on the detention period; thus, it is difficult to view it as an appropriate and substantive control function that can limit the detention period. For instance, where the detainee files a revocation suit against the deportation order or applies for refugee status recognition, the detention period may be extended without limit depending on the progress of those procedures, and the length of detention is determined solely by how swiftly the administrative authorities and the judiciary proceed with the relevant procedures (although the detainee may apply to the court for suspension of execution of the deportation order and detention order, whether to grant it is left to the court’s discretion). In such cases, the result may be prolonged detention for reasons not attributable to the detainee.  \\n2) Since the period required for repatriation varies depending on the circumstances of each country or the progress of procedures, making it impossible to know in advance when repatriation of the detainee will become possible, there may be a view that allowing detention “until repatriation becomes possible” without limiting the period is inevitable for achieving the legislative purpose of the Provision at Issue. However, in light of the fact that many countries set an upper limit on the detention period for persons subject to deportation, it cannot be said that setting a reasonable upper limit on the detention period is impossible.  \\nIf the Provision at Issue were to prescribe an upper limit on the detention period, then when the anticipated time of repatriation is delayed and the upper limit is exceeded, the person subject to deportation would have to be released; in such a case, there may be a view that released persons subject to deportation could disappear or commit crimes. However, this is merely a vague and potential possibility not yet realized, and there is not sufficient empirical basis to support it, so on the basis of such a vague presumption alone, it is difficult to justify a measure that significantly restricts freedom of the person, such as “detention without an upper limit.” A foreign national who has committed a crime in the Republic of Korea cannot simply be presumed to abscond or commit another crime upon release from detention. Moreover, among persons subject to deportation, there may be not only foreign nationals who committed crimes and were sentenced to punishment, but also foreign nationals who merely violated administrative regulations concerning entry or stay; treating all of them as potential absconders or potential criminals and detaining them without any time limit is an excessive measure.  \\nAs for cases where the detainee files a revocation suit against the deportation order or applies for refugee status recognition, cases exceeding the detention period can be minimized through institutional improvements such as the courts’ first-priority and concentrated hearing of the relevant case, and the prompt processing of refugee status recognition review and decisions. Even if detention is released after the detention period has been exceeded, it appears that absconding or additional violations can be prevented to a considerable extent through methods such as restricting their residences until departure requirements are satisfied or requiring periodic reporting of residence, designating a guarantor or requiring payment of an appropriate deposit, or continuously observing and supervising them through supervisors, etc. Accordingly, it is questionable whether, for achieving the legislative purpose of the Provision at Issue, one must necessarily adopt a method that excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person, such as detention without an upper limit.  \\n3) Because it is difficult to say that foreign nationals who were apprehended and detained because they did not choose voluntary departure for various reasons or because voluntary departure was impossible have in practical terms a “freedom to depart,” the infringement of fundamental rights resulting from not setting an upper limit on the detention period cannot be regarded as alleviated on the ground that persons subject to deportation are free to depart at any time and thereby escape from the status of detention (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Jung-mi, Kim I-su, Lee Jin-seong, and Kang Il-won in Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2013HEONBA196).  \\nThe detainee may request temporary release from detention from the head of the local immigration and foreigners office (hereinafter the “head, etc.”), but unless there are circumstances in which the detainee has won a revocation suit against a deportation order, etc., the decision whether to temporarily release from detention is entirely discretionary to the head, etc.; thus, the temporary release from detention system cannot be said to function in substance as a device supplementing the problem of long-term detention. Other post-remedial measures such as objections to deportation orders and detention orders likewise cannot be said to be effective, as will be seen below.  \\n4) In this way, although the public interest the Provision at Issue seeks to achieve is significant and detention of persons subject to deportation is necessary to achieve that public interest, even taking that into account, the degree to which the detainee’s freedom of the person is restricted by detention without an upper limit is excessively large; therefore, the Provision at Issue does not satisfy the requirements of least restriction and balance of legal interests.  \\n(c) Conclusion  \\nThe Provision at Issue infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person in violation of the principle of proportionality.\\n\\n(2) Whether the principle of due process has been violated  \\nArticle 12(1) of the Constitution provides that “No person shall be punished, placed under preventive restrictions, or subjected to forced labor except as provided by law and through due process,” thereby setting forth the principle of due process. Since the principle of due process applies not only to criminal procedure but to all state action (see Constitutional Court 1992. 12. 24. 92HEONGA8; Constitutional Court 2014. 8. 28. 2012HEONBA433, etc.), due process must also be observed in the execution of deportation orders and detention orders carried out as part of immigration control administration.  \\n(a) Foreign national detention under the Immigration Control Act is equivalent to “arrest or detention” in criminal procedure and deprives a foreign national of freedom of the person; therefore, even if the strict warrant requirement of prosecutor’s application and judge’s issuance is not applied, at the very least there must be a device by which a person in an objective and neutral position other than an immigration control officer can review the validity of such physical restraint (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Jung-mi, Kim I-su, Lee Jin-seong, and Kang Il-won in Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2013HEONBA196). However, the current detention system under the Immigration Control Act is contrasted with detention in criminal procedure, in which the court decides the commencement and extension of detention and its termination is also clearly prescribed, in that no third independent neutral institution or judicial institution is involved at all at the stage of commencement or extension of detention.  \\n(b) First, regarding the issuance and execution of detention orders, the deportation procedure for foreigners under the Immigration Control Act is structured as follows: ① immigration control officers apprehend and investigate suspects (Article 47 of the Act); ② the head, etc. issues a detention order, which is executed by immigration control officers (Article 51(1), Article 53, detention for examination of deportation); ③ the head, etc. examines and decides whether deportation is to be imposed and, after issuing a deportation order and a detention order (Article 58, Article 59(2) and (3), the Provision at Issue, Article 78(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act), ④ immigration control officers execute them (Article 62(1), Article 63(6), Article 53, detention for enforcement of deportation). Accordingly, formally, the investigation procedure and the review procedure are separated, and the issuer of the detention order and the executing authority are separated; but in substance, subordinates and superiors within the immigration office together conduct suspect investigations, issuance, and execution of deportation orders and detention orders. In other words, the head, etc. who makes the detention decision is not an independent third institution but merely a superior within the same executing agency to which the immigration control officers belong, and thus the institutions cannot in substance be said to be separated; and because there is no possibility whatsoever for an external institution such as the judiciary to intervene, it is difficult to regard mere decision by a superior within the same executing agency as procedural control by an objective and neutral institution (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Jung-mi, Kim I-su, Lee Jin-seong, and Kang Il-won in Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2013HEONBA196).  \\nAlthough the Provision at Issue is formulated in discretionary language as “may detain,” in practice, once a deportation order is issued, a detention order is issued together with or sequentially after the deportation order in most cases without special review of the detention order itself, such as the necessity of detention or risk of absconding, and there are no cases in which no detention order was issued for a person who received a deportation order but could not be repatriated immediately. However, because a person who received a deportation order cannot always be regarded as having a possibility of absconding, a separate determination of the need for detention is necessary, and unless a neutral institution capable of ensuring fairness and objectivity intervenes, the current structure in which a detention order is issued almost automatically once there is a deportation order is unlikely to change.  \\nFor reference, in Germany, both preparatory detention for review of deportation (similar to detention for examination of deportation under our law) and custody detention for enforcement of deportation (similar to detention under the Provision at Issue) require a judge’s warrant, and judicial control begins at the commencement stage of detention.  \\n(c) Regarding post-remedial measures or control procedures, the detainee may file an objection with the Minister of Justice against detention or a deportation order (Article 55(1), Article 60(1) of the Act), and the head, etc. may extend detention with prior approval from the Minister of Justice if the detention period exceeds 3 months (Article 63(2) of the Act).  \\nHowever, the Minister of Justice is in reality merely the supervisory authority over the administrative agency that issues and executes detention orders, and thus a review system by an external neutral and objective institution cannot be said to be guaranteed. In fact, there has not been a single case in the last five years (2013 to 2017) in which an objection against a detention order or deportation order was upheld, and prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extension of detention is also, in reality, granted almost without exception when the head, etc. submits approval application documents while deportation enforcement is delayed. Even considering these realities, it is difficult to say that the Minister of Justice’s review and determination has the significance of a practical control procedure for ensuring the legality of detention (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Jung-mi, Kim I-su, Lee Jin-seong, and Kang Il-won in Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2013HEONBA196).  \\nIn addition, although the detainee may file an administrative lawsuit against a deportation order, a detention order, or a decision dismissing an objection, general and post hoc judicial control mechanisms such as administrative litigation are insufficient to adequately guarantee the freedom of the person of foreign nationals unfamiliar with Korea’s judicial system and not fluent in Korean.  \\n(d) Among the important procedural demands that can be derived from the principle of due process is the granting of an opportunity to submit opinions and materials to the person concerned (see Constitutional Court 2003. 7. 24. 2001HEONGA25; Constitutional Court 2015. 9. 24. 2012HEONBA302), and such an opportunity must be guaranteed to the detainee in detention under the Provision at Issue.  \\nHowever, the Immigration Control Act contains no provision requiring that the person concerned be given an opportunity to submit opinions before the detention order under the Provision at Issue is issued. Article 22(3) of the Administrative Procedures Act provides that when an administrative agency imposes duties on the person concerned or takes a disposition restricting rights or interests, it shall afford the person concerned, etc. an opportunity to submit opinions; however, “dispositions concerning the entry into and departure from Korea of foreigners” are excluded from the scope of application of the Administrative Procedures Act (Article 3(2) item 9 of the Administrative Procedures Act; Article 2 item 2 of the same Act’s Enforcement Decree), and there is no system such as a pre-arrest suspect interrogation (substantial warrant review) under the Criminal Procedure Act. Accordingly, the person subject to a detention order is not afforded any opportunity to make statements favorable to him or her or to submit opinions. At the objection stage concerning detention as well, the Minister of Justice is merely provided discretion to hear the statements of interested persons if necessary (Article 63(6) and Article 55(3) of the Act), and the Minister of Justice’s prior approval for extension of detention is also carried out only through review of the documents submitted by the head, etc., without affording the detainee an opportunity to make statements or submit opinions.  \\n(e) Taken together, the Provision at Issue violates the constitutional principle of due process because there is no control procedure by a fair and neutral institution at the stage of commencement or extension of detention, and because no opportunity whatsoever is guaranteed for submitting opinions in administrative physical restraint.  \\n(3) Conclusion  \\nThe Provision at Issue violates the Constitution because it infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person in violation of the principle of proportionality and the principle of due process.\\n\\n5. Conclusion  \\nSince the Provision at Issue is not in conformity with the Constitution, a decision incompatible with the Constitution is rendered and, at the same time, it is to be provisionally applied until the legislature enacts remedial legislation by 2025. 5. 31. In addition, Constitutional Court Decision 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29, in which the Constitutional Court previously held, in a view different from this decision, that the Provision at Issue does not violate the Constitution, is to be modified to the extent inconsistent with this decision.  \\nExcept for the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Eun-ae, Lee Jong-seok, and Lee Young-jin set forth in 6. below, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous with respect to this decision, and as to the decision incompatible with the Constitution of Justices Yu Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-young, Moon Hyung-bae, and Lee Mi-sun, there is a concurring opinion by Justice Lee Mi-sun as set forth in 7. below.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Lee Eun-ae, Lee Jong-seok, and Lee Young-jin  \\nWe conclude that the Provision at Issue does not violate the Constitution and therefore state our views as follows.\\n\\na. Precedent of the Constitutional Court  \\nIn Constitutional Court Decision 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29, the Constitutional Court held that the Provision at Issue does not violate the principle of proportionality or the principle of due process and does not infringe freedom of the person, for the following reasons.  \\n“(1) Whether the principle of proportionality has been violated  \\nIn determining whether the Provision at Issue infringes the freedom of the person of persons subject to deportation, it must be taken into account that detention under the Immigration Control Act is part of immigration control administration, which is state administration, and that it is necessary for performing the function of a sovereign state and may therefore be determined in part as a matter of legislative policy.  \\n(a) Legitimacy of the legislative purpose and appropriateness of the means  \\nThe legislative purpose of the Provision at Issue is legitimate, as it is intended to promote national security, maintenance of order, and public welfare by properly controlling and coordinating the entry into and departure from the country and the stay of foreign nationals, and detaining persons subject to deportation in a detention facility until departure requirements are satisfied is an effective method for the prompt and efficient enforcement of deportation orders and for the management of foreign nationals’ entry into and stay in the country; therefore, appropriateness of the means is also recognized.  \\n(b) Least restriction  \\n1) Persons subject to deportation are foreign nationals whose entry itself is illegal, or who violate conditions of stay by overstaying their authorized period of stay, or who commit violations during their stay and thereby may threaten public order. For them, for the purposes of national security, maintenance of order, and public welfare, detention and management for repatriation are necessary until they are repatriated to their home countries. Therefore, detaining persons subject to deportation until a time when repatriation becomes possible is a necessary measure to achieve the legislative purpose of the Provision at Issue.  \\n2) Persons subject to deportation under the Provision at Issue are detained when they cannot be immediately repatriated outside the Republic of Korea for reasons such as not possessing a passport or not having transportation arrangements. Since the time required for this necessarily varies according to the circumstances of each country or the progress of procedures, it is impossible to know in advance when repatriation will become possible. Accordingly, the Provision at Issue’s allowance of detention “until repatriation becomes possible” without an upper limit on the detention period has an inevitable aspect for achieving the legislative purpose.  \\nIn addition, detention under the Provision at Issue is possible only for securing enforcement of a deportation order, and only for the minimum period necessary to achieve that purpose. The Supreme Court also held that detention under the Provision at Issue has objective and temporal limits (see Supreme Court Decision 99DA68829 dated 2001. 10. 26.). In practice, deportation enforcement is mostly carried out promptly, and the average detention period is about 11 days.  \\n3) Persons subject to deportation cannot stay in the Republic of Korea, but they can at any time leave the state of detention by voluntarily departing to their home country or a third country; therefore, it is not appropriate to conclude that persons subject to deportation have serious mental pressure because they cannot predict when they will be released. If the Provision at Issue were to prescribe an upper limit on the detention period, detention would have to be released upon exceeding that limit; if persons subject to deportation disappeared after being released from detention, enforcement of deportation orders could become impossible or significantly difficult. In addition, persons subject to deportation may become involved in crimes or become victims of crimes, and if they remain illegally in the country, there is also a high likelihood that they will be subjected to poor treatment in wage and other labor conditions.  \\nTherefore, prescribing an upper limit on detention in the Provision at Issue may not only jeopardize national security, maintenance of order, and public welfare, but may also produce consequences that are by no means desirable for the human rights of persons subject to deportation.  \\n4) Looking at legislative examples from other countries, there are not a few countries that have not set an upper limit on the detention or custody period for enforcement of deportation. The United States provides that a foreign national whose deportation order has become final must be deported within a 90-day removal period and must be detained during that period; if the foreign national cannot be deported within that period and the removal period is extended, detention may continue during the extended period, but the law does not prescribe an upper limit on the detention period after the removal period. Canada and Australia likewise provide that foreign nationals may be detained for enforcement of deportation, but do not prescribe an upper limit on the detention period. Japan provides only that when a person subject to deportation cannot be immediately deported, that person may be held “until repatriation becomes possible,” and does not set an upper limit on the period of holding. China likewise provides only that if forced departure has been decided but cannot be immediately executed, the foreign national shall be detained in a detention house or a place for repatriation of foreigners, and does not set an upper limit on the detention period. In light of these points, if the Republic of Korea were to set an upper limit on the detention period, it cannot be ruled out that foreign nationals illegally staying in the Republic of Korea may increase sharply by exploiting that limit.  \\n5) The Immigration Control Act provides various means by which a person subject to deportation can escape detention, such as temporary release from detention (Article 65(1) and (2)), approval for extension (Article 63(2) and (3)), and objections against deportation orders and detention orders (Article 60(1) and (4), Article 63(6), Article 55(1) and (2)); furthermore, a person subject to deportation may file an administrative lawsuit seeking revocation of a deportation order or the detention pursuant thereto or may apply for suspension of execution, and various systems are in place by which detention under the Provision at Issue may be lifted, thus supplementing the absence of an upper limit on the detention period.  \\n6) Although legislative alternatives such as restriction on residence, designation of a guarantor, or a deposit system may be considered instead of detention under the Provision at Issue, without securing the physical custody of the person subject to deportation, it is difficult to achieve prompt enforcement of deportation orders and effective management of stay to the same extent as under the Provision at Issue, and it is difficult to conceive of legislative alternatives that achieve the legislative purpose equally well while restricting the fundamental rights of persons subject to deportation less.  \\n(c) Balance of legal interests  \\nThe national security, maintenance of order, and public welfare that the Provision at Issue seeks to protect are highly significant, and for their realization the detention system under the Provision at Issue is indispensable; on the other hand, persons subject to deportation are only temporarily and provisionally restricted in their freedom of the person until deportation orders can be enforced, and various systems are in place by which detention may be lifted. Therefore, the Provision at Issue also satisfies the requirement of balance of legal interests.  \\n(d) Conclusion  \\nThe Provision at Issue does not violate the principle of proportionality and does not infringe the freedom of the person of persons subject to deportation.  \\n\\n(2) Whether the principle of due process has been violated  \\n(a) In determining whether the Provision at Issue violates the principle of due process, it must be considered that persons subject to deportation cannot stay in the Republic of Korea but can at any time leave the state of detention by voluntarily departing to their home country or a third country; that persons subject to deportation are normatively persons who cannot remain in the Republic of Korea; and that detention under the Immigration Control Act is part of immigration control administration, which is state administration, and is necessary for performing the function of a sovereign state and may therefore be determined in part as a matter of legislative policy.  \\n(b) In light of the special nature of detention of persons subject to deportation, whether the same administrative agency should conduct apprehension, investigation, review, and execution concerning deportation orders and detention, or whether different administrative agencies should do so or judicial institutions should intervene, is a matter of legislative policy; therefore, the fact that the statute does not provide for a procedure in which the judiciary decides at the stage of commencement or extension of detention cannot immediately be regarded as a violation of the principle of due process. On the contrary, in specialized administrative fields such as immigration control, it is efficient for the same administrative agency to perform related work simultaneously, and in major countries such as the United States and Japan, the judiciary does not intervene in decisions on deportation orders and detention or in the execution of those decisions.  \\nMeanwhile, a person subject to deportation may seek a judgment by the judiciary on the legality of detention by filing an administrative lawsuit challenging the deportation order or detention, or by applying for suspension of execution, thereby obtaining a stay of execution; thus, it cannot be said that there is no control procedure by an objective and neutral institution.  \\n(c) A person subject to deportation is afforded an opportunity to state opinions during the investigation process before deportation review (Article 48(3) and (4) of the Immigration Control Act), and may state opinions or submit materials in the course of an objection to detention or administrative litigation (Article 69(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act). In addition, the Immigration Control Act provides for an obligation to present the detention order upon execution (Article 63(6), Article 53 of the Immigration Control Act, Article 78(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act) and an obligation to give written notice within 3 days (Article 63(6), Article 54 of the Immigration Control Act), thereby observing the procedural demands derived from the principle of due process.  \\n(d) Accordingly, the Provision at Issue cannot be said to violate the constitutional principle of due process.”  \\n\\nb. Whether there is a need to change the precedent  \\n(1) Article 23(2) item 2 of the Constitutional Court Act allows the Court to change its previously stated interpretation and application of the Constitution or statutes if six or more Justices concur. However, in order to change a precedent, in addition to such formal requirement of a qualified quorum, there must be recognized necessity to change the precedent’s position, such as because there is a legal error in the precedent’s reasoning or a change in circumstances. Also, from the perspective of foreseeability, legal stability, and protection of trust, it must be demonstrated that there is a need to change the precedent’s position, namely, that there has been a change in normative or factual conditions, such as changes in social systems or culture, changes in the people’s legal sentiment or consciousness, or changes in the contents of other laws or in legal doctrine concerning them, and that because of this the precedent’s position must be changed (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Eun-ae and Lee Jong-seok in Constitutional Court 2018. 12. 27. 2015HEONBA77 et al.).  \\n(2) The decision incompatible with the Constitution by Justices Yu Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-young, Moon Hyung-bae, and Lee Mi-sun regarding the Provision at Issue, and the decision incompatible with the Constitution by Justice Lee Sun-ae (hereinafter the “incompatibility opinions”), held that the Provision at Issue violates the principle of proportionality because detention without an upper limit exceeds the limits of detention as a temporary and provisional coercive measure; because, in light of many foreign cases setting an upper limit on detention periods, it is difficult to regard the absence of an upper limit on the detention period as inevitable; because the objection system against detention orders, the Minister of Justice’s approval system for extension of detention periods, and the temporary release from detention system alone are insufficient to appropriately control the detention period and alleviate excessive restrictions on the body; and because enforcement of deportation orders can be secured through various substitute means such as restriction on residence or reporting, designation of a guarantor, deposit system, and observation or supervision through supervisors; and held that the Provision at Issue violates the principle of due process and infringes freedom of the person because no third independent neutral institution or judicial institution is involved at all at the stage of commencement or extension of detention, because the detainee is not guaranteed a procedural opportunity to state opinions and submit materials from before the issuance of the detention order through the objection stage, and because ordinary administrative litigation procedures alone cannot be said to guarantee a prompt and effective remedy by the court. However, it is questionable whether the reasons cited by the incompatibility opinions truly constitute changes in normative or factual conditions that justify changing the precedent.  \\n(3) First, as already stated in the precedent, detention under the Provision at Issue must be issued only for the purpose of securing enforcement of a deportation order, and even where detention is lawfully imposed, it may be imposed only provisionally for the minimum period necessary to achieve the purpose until repatriation becomes possible. According to the record of this case, the average detention period from completion of repatriation preparation to actual repatriation for a person subject to deportation is approximately 10.1 days in 2018, 9.6 days in 2019, and 16.9 days in 2020. Considering that in 2020 the period increased due to the suspension and reduction of outbound flights caused by the spread of COVID-19, the detention period appears to be decreasing compared with the time of the precedent decision; in light of these points, detention under the Provision at Issue appears in practice to be mostly executed within the objective and temporal limits.  \\nAlthough the Immigration Control Act does not set an upper limit on the detention period, it supplements the system so that detention may be imposed only for the minimum period necessary for detention by allowing persons subject to deportation to file objections with the Minister of Justice if they object to the detention order (Article 63(6) and Article 55 of the Immigration Control Act), by requiring the head of a local immigration and foreigners office to obtain prior approval from the Minister of Justice every 3 months when detention exceeds 3 months (Article 63(2)), and by allowing the head of a local immigration and foreigners office to temporarily release detention ex officio or upon the request of the detainee, etc. (Article 65). In addition, if it becomes manifest that a person subject to deportation cannot be repatriated for reasons such as being refused entry by another country, the head of a local immigration and foreigners office may release the person from detention (Article 63(4)), and Article 6(2) of the “Regulations on the Handling of Temporary Release from Detention” provides that if a person whose temporary release from detention has been requested has won at first instance or on appeal a revocation suit against a deportation order or a refugee non-recognition disposition, the relevant procedure shall in principle be followed to permit general release or special release. Thus, as pointed out in the incompatibility opinions, the likelihood that the detention period will extend without limit merely because entry is refused by another country and repatriation is impossible, or because a refugee non-recognition decision or deportation order is being contested, is not large.  \\n(4) Moreover, the precedent already acknowledged the need to improve the system by pointing out, after making a normative judgment on the basis of most of the facts identified in the incompatibility opinions, that there was a need to organize the system, and accordingly the system and practice have continuously improved.  \\n(a) Expansion of the ratio of departure orders  \\nThe head of a local immigration and foreigners office is reducing the proportion of detainees entering detention facilities among persons subject to departure actions by using the method of issuing “departure orders based on the principle of non-detention” rather than deportation orders accompanied from the outset by detention orders for foreign nationals with no criminal record and for minors. In 2017, the ratio of departure orders among departure actions was only 57.5%, but in 2020 it reached 78.3%, and in 2021 it reached 73.2%; thus, it is recognized that the ratio of deportation orders is decreasing and the ratio of departure orders is increasing. This confirms that the head of a local immigration and foreigners office operates the practice of departure orders based on the principle of non-detention as much as possible where the need for detention is not large.  \\n(b) Substantialization of the objection system  \\nA detention order presupposes a deportation order, and if the Minister of Justice decides that an objection against the deportation order is well-founded, the suspect’s detention is immediately released (Article 60(4) of the Immigration Control Act) and the original status of stay is restored, which in turn may allow employment, etc. depending on the type of status of stay; by contrast, even if an objection to the detention order is upheld, it does not by itself affect the deportation order. Therefore, from the party’s perspective, filing an objection to the deportation order rather than contesting the detention order may be a more fundamental remedy. In fact, the number of objections to detention orders was 9 in 2018, 5 in 2019, and 7 in 2020, which is markedly lower than the number of objections to deportation orders (72 in 2018, 54 in 2019, and 67 in 2020).  \\nIt is true that no objection against a detention order has yet been upheld, so it is difficult to say that objections against detention orders themselves have become active. However, in the case of deportation orders, the rate at which objections were upheld, which had been 0% in 2016 and 2017, rose to 5% in 2018, 2% in 2019, and 6% in 2020; considering this trend of substantialization of objections against deportation orders, which are the cause of detention, it cannot be asserted that the mere fact that no objection against a detention order has been upheld means that the objection system lacks significance as a practical control procedure.  \\n(c) Expansion of the effectiveness of extension approval and temporary release from detention  \\nWhen the detention period exceeds 3 months, the head of a local immigration and foreigners office must obtain prior approval from the Minister of Justice every 3 months by explaining the necessity of extending the detention period (Article 63(2) of the Immigration Control Act; Article 78(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act). This approval system for extension of detention periods has also been gradually becoming more substantive, and the number of non-approvals, which totaled only 12 from the inception of the system until 2015. 8., has increased markedly to 181 from 2015. 9. 1. to 2021. 5. 11.  \\nIn addition, Article 4(2) of the “Regulations on the Handling of Temporary Release from Detention,” as amended by Minister of Justice Directive No. 1303 on 2020. 8. 14., provides that when reviewing temporary release from detention, priority shall be given to considering ① whether the detainee falls under a patient, pregnant woman, elderly person, minor, etc. under each item of Article 56-3(3) of the Immigration Control Act; ② whether, in light of the detainee’s health condition, it is appropriate to detain the detainee; ③ if the detainee supports a child under 18 years of age, whether there is a person other than the detainee who supports the child; and ④ the possibility of repatriation outside the Republic of Korea, including whether there is a reason why immediate repatriation is impossible. Moreover, temporary release from detention, which from 2013 to 2017 totaled 601 cases over 5 years (an average of 120 per year), occurred 461 times in 2021 alone, mainly for foreign nationals with no criminal record, and the approval rate relative to applications reached 44% in 2019, 54% in 2020, and 56% in 2021; in particular, it is recognized that all applications for temporary release from detention by minors in 2018 and 2019 were granted. Thus, related regulations have been amended, and in practice the effectiveness of the temporary release from detention system is also being expanded, such as the head of a local immigration and foreigners office actively granting applications for temporary release from detention by foreign nationals with no criminal record or by minors.  \\n(d) As seen above, if one considers that since the precedent was rendered, positive institutional and practical improvements have been made to supplement the absence of an upper limit on the detention period, there is no change in normative or factual conditions that would justify changing the precedent.  \\n(5) The incompatibility opinions state that, in light of many foreign cases setting an upper limit on detention periods, it is possible to set a reasonable upper limit on detention periods. However, in the case of the United States, the law merely provides that if a foreign national is not deported within the 90-day removal period, detention may continue after the removal period, and the law does not specify an upper limit; and as already explained in the precedent, after the U.S. Supreme Court in Zadvydas v. Davis held that the reasonable period of detention after the 90-day removal period is presumed to be 6 months, the federal rules enacted regarding detention after the removal period also provide only that in certain cases, such as detention for national security or terrorism reasons, detention may continue even if deportation enforcement is impossible, and otherwise do not impose any special restriction on the detention period. Nearby countries such as Japan and China likewise still do not prescribe an upper limit on the period of confinement of persons subject to deportation, and the same circumstances as when the precedent was rendered remain, namely that if the Republic of Korea sets an upper limit on detention periods, it cannot be ruled out that foreign nationals illegally staying in the Republic of Korea may sharply increase.  \\n(6) Setting an upper limit on the detention period of persons subject to deportation is intertwined with the issue of whether there is a means to secure deportation enforcement and whether there is a system to manage released persons subject to deportation, as well as whether support measures for their livelihood, employment, housing, and medical care are in place; we examine this below.  \\n(a) Difficulty of enforcing deportation against persons refusing departure  \\nSince detention under the Provision at Issue is for securing enforcement of deportation, in order to set an upper limit on the detention period, deportation or repatriation of the person subject to deportation must first be possible within the designated period. However, in cases where a person subject to deportation, even after all lawsuits seeking revocation of deportation orders and detention orders, and lawsuits seeking revocation of refugee non-recognition dispositions, have been dismissed and the judgments become final, still refuses to depart without special reason, there is no means available to forcibly deport the person other than inducing departure through interviews, persuasion through family members or acquaintances, requests for support and cooperation to the person’s national consul, or efforts to execute deportation at public expense; and even by the method of escorting the protected foreign national out of the country together with immigration control officers, airlines sometimes refuse boarding for security reasons, making enforcement difficult. Therefore, if a person subject to deportation refuses to depart, it is practically impossible to enforce deportation within a certain period. In fact, according to the record of this case, many of the persons subject to deportation who have been in long-term detention for more than 1 year are persons refusing departure, such as those who intentionally damage their passports or even refuse the proposal to execute deportation at public expense. Under such circumstances, if an upper limit on the detention period were set and detention were released after a certain period, there is a strong concern that the willingness of persons subject to deportation to depart voluntarily would be undermined.  \\n(b) Difficulty of managing the stay of persons subject to deportation released from detention  \\nIn order to set an upper limit on the detention period, the establishment of a system capable of systematically managing persons subject to deportation released from detention must be premised. For measures such as restricting residence or requiring periodic reporting upon release from detention due to expiration of the detention period, or designating a guarantor or requiring a deposit, to be effective, all the financial, material, and human resources necessary to manage them must be secured. However, from 2018 to 2020, there were a total of 394 temporary releases from detention, and 60 of these were revoked because the whereabouts became unknown or the person absconded; thus, even now, it cannot be said that management of foreigners temporarily released from detention is being carried out thoroughly. Considering these points, if the number of persons subject to deportation released from detention increases beyond the present level due to setting an upper limit on the detention period, it is questionable whether their stay in the Republic of Korea can be managed efficiently.  \\nMoreover, whether persons subject to deportation whose detention has been released after exceeding the upper limit on the detention period may remain in the Republic of Korea is closely related to state policies concerning labor issues such as employment and wages, and support for housing, medical care, and livelihood. For example, in Germany, which sets an upper limit on the detention period, a foreign national who has a duty to depart but cannot be deported for factual or legal reasons is granted Duldung, a temporary suspension of deportation enforcement; a foreign national granted Duldung may receive a work permit after a waiting period of 3 months, except in exceptional cases such as where the impediment is attributable to the foreign national. In contrast, in the Republic of Korea, no concrete measures are in place for housing, medical care, or livelihood support for persons who have not obtained lawful status of stay or whose status of stay has been revoked, and instead, in the case of temporary release from detention, a condition may even be attached prohibiting profit-making activities such as employment during the release period (Article 13(3) item 4 of the Regulations on the Handling of Temporary Release from Detention). In such circumstances, if an upper limit is set on the detention period and persons subject to deportation whose detention period has expired are allowed to remain in the Republic of Korea, their livelihood and health may be threatened or they may become more exposed to crime, and difficulties may arise in maintaining public security and order.  \\n(c) Thus, the issue of setting an upper limit on the detention period of persons subject to deportation must be discussed on a policy foundation based on social consensus concerning how much increased administrative cost arising from management of released persons subject to deportation can be borne, what employment opportunities should be afforded to foreign nationals subject to deportation, and what degree of humanitarian support should be provided. The precedent, while pointing out that it is necessary to carefully examine whether a reasonable upper limit on the detention period suited to the conditions of the Republic of Korea can be set, viewed the absence of such an upper limit as having an inevitable aspect, because setting an upper limit on detention is not merely a matter of immigration control administration but is closely related to the overall policy of the state; there is no basis for concluding that circumstances have changed in policy or otherwise so as to justify altering that judgment.  \\n(7) Whether a third independent neutral institution or judicial institution should be allowed to intervene at the stage of commencement or extension of detention is a matter of legislative policy for each country. One cannot conclude that the Provision at Issue violates the principle of due process merely because the legislature excluded court involvement at the stage of commencement or extension of detention of persons subject to deportation in order to expand administrative expertise, enable prompt response, and promote appropriate and efficient immigration control taking into account diplomatic relations and international circumstances. As a matter of principle, enforcement of deportation orders must be carried out without delay (Article 62(3) of the Immigration Control Act), and detention under the Provision at Issue is a temporary and provisional measure taken to achieve the purpose of prompt enforcement of deportation orders by detaining persons subject to deportation when they cannot be immediately repatriated outside the Republic of Korea; thus, it is doubtful whether having an independent and neutral third institution review and control the validity of detention at the commencement stage could be a practical means in light of the purpose and spirit of detention under the Provision at Issue, namely “prompt and efficient enforcement of deportation orders.” In addition, the Minister of Justice has established within the Ministry of Justice the “Review Committee for Long-Term Detention of Foreigners,” which includes private members such as lawyers, professors, religious figures, and members of organizations related to international organizations or civic groups, to deliberate on matters concerning release from detention or temporary release from detention of foreign nationals detained for more than 1 year (Guidelines for Operation of the Review Committee for Long-Term Detention of Foreigners, as amended by Ministry of Justice Directive No. 1250 on 2020. 4. 14., Article 2(1) and (4), Article 3(1)); thus, procedures are also being prepared to reflect the opinions of neutral third parties in the release of long-term detainees, etc.  \\nFurthermore, because a deportation order is the premise for a detention order and detention is imposed to execute the deportation order, when determining whether a person subject to deportation has been afforded a procedural opportunity to submit opinions and materials, a series of procedures from the deportation order to detention must be considered organically and comprehensively. In the United States, hearings, evidence examination, and opportunities to examine witnesses are guaranteed in deportation order trials conducted by immigration judges under the Department of Justice (Immigration and Nationality Act, Articles 239 and 240); however, at the stage of commencement of detention, requests for review of release from detention, or applications for release from detention based on habeas corpus, the indispensable opportunity to state opinions is not afforded. Thus, from deportation orders through commencement, extension, and release from detention, each country may determine within the scope of legislative policy at which stage and what procedural rights are to be guaranteed. Accordingly, whether the Provision at Issue complies with the principle of due process should be judged not by whether a separate opportunity to state opinions or submit materials is afforded at each stage of commencement, extension, or release of detention, but by whether, within the overall procedure, an opportunity to submit opinions and materials concerning the deportation order, detention order, or release from detention is guaranteed.  \\nFirst, at the stage where the deportation order, which is the premise for the detention order, is made, so long as procedural opportunities to state opinions and submit materials are guaranteed in the investigation of foreign nationals suspected of falling within the subject of deportation, namely suspects (Article 47 of the Immigration Control Act), requests for appearance, and interrogation (Article 48), the fact that an opportunity to submit opinions and materials is not separately afforded before the detention order is made cannot be said to violate the principle of due process. In addition, a person detained pursuant to a detention order is guaranteed an opportunity to contest the detention order immediately through an objection against detention. In particular, because the objection must be filed together with materials substantiating the grounds for the objection (Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act, Article 69), and because the Minister of Justice may hear the statements of the person concerned if necessary before deciding the objection (Article 55(3) of the Immigration Control Act), it cannot be concluded that the opportunity to submit opinions and materials is completely excluded at the objection stage. Further, the detainee may also request temporary release from detention at any time during detention by submitting a request for temporary release from detention together with materials substantiating the grounds for the request and the ability to pay the deposit (Article 65(1) of the Immigration Control Act; Article 79(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act), and may thus submit opinions and substantiating materials concerning temporary release from detention in writing.  \\nIn addition, the Immigration Control Act and its Enforcement Decree require presentation of the detention order upon execution (Article 53 of the Immigration Control Act), require the protected person’s legal representative to be notified within 3 days from the date of detention of a notice of detention stating the reasons, time, and place of detention and the possibility of filing an objection (Article 54(1)), and require that if the detained person wishes, unless there are urgent circumstances or other unavoidable reasons, the consul of the country of nationality or citizenship stationed in the Republic of Korea be notified of the time, place, and reason for detention (Article 54(2)); they also require that the decision on the objection be prepared as a written decision stating the order, reasons, and applicable legal provisions and sent to the applicant (Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act, Article 70(1)), and that when prior approval for extension of detention under Article 63(2) of the Immigration Control Act is sought, the head of the local immigration and foreigners office must directly explain the necessity of extending the detention period (Article 78(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act), thereby sufficiently establishing procedures to guarantee the party’s procedural rights within the scope that does not impede the efficiency of immigration control administration. Therefore, it cannot be said that the Provision at Issue violates due process merely because it does not expressly afford the detainee a procedural opportunity to submit opinions and materials at the stage of commencement or extension of detention.  \\n(8) Meanwhile, detention under the Provision at Issue is an administrative disposition that takes and confines a person subject to a deportation order temporarily as part of immigration control administration to secure enforcement of a deportation order, and the strict warrant requirement under Article 12(3) of the Constitution does not apply. Also, although Article 12(6) of the Constitution requires that a procedure be established by which the legality of arrest or detention itself, not only arrest or detention in criminal procedure but also administrative arrest or detention, may be reviewed by a court, the legislature’s discretion in legislative formation is recognized in shaping the concrete content of such a procedure (see Constitutional Court 2004. 3. 25. 2002HEONBA104). In particular, detention under the Provision at Issue is carried out to secure the administrative purpose of enforcement of deportation orders and to enforce that purpose efficiently, and differs in purpose and nature from physical restraint in criminal procedure or other administrative physical restraint that aims to restrict freedom of the person itself; thus, matters concerning its concrete procedure fall within the realm of policy discretion (see Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2003HEONMA87; Constitutional Court 2014. 4. 24. 2011HEONMA474 et al.). Accordingly, as the Constitutional Court already stated in Constitutional Court 2014. 8. 28. 2012HEONMA686, a person subject to deportation may not only challenge the causal relationship by filing a revocation suit against the deportation order that is the cause of detention, but may also file an administrative lawsuit seeking revocation of the detention order itself or an application for suspension of execution seeking suspension of its execution; and, as noted above, along with strict prior procedures such as presentation of the detention order upon execution, written notice of the time, place, and reason for detention, and objection against the deportation order, post hoc remedial measures such as objection to the detention order are also provided, thereby effectively supplementing the limits of remedies through administrative litigation procedures. So long as this legislative judgment does not exceed the bounds of legislative discretion, the Provision at Issue does not violate Article 12(6) of the Constitution. In addition, beyond the decision incompatible with the Constitution by five Justices, I dissent for the same reasons with respect to Justice Lee Mi-sun’s opinion in the form of a concurring opinion asserting that the Provision at Issue violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution.  \\n(9) Taken together, the matters raised by the incompatibility opinions cannot be said to amount to changes in circumstances sufficient to alter the precedent, and there is no otherwise recognized need to change the Constitutional Court’s precedent.  \\n\\nc. Conclusion  \\nSince the Constitutional Court held in Constitutional Court Decision 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29 that the Provision at Issue does not violate the Constitution, the normative or factual conditions surrounding the Provision at Issue do not appear to have changed so drastically as to require a stricter assessment of its constitutionality than before, and no separate need for a new interpretation can be found. On the contrary, the competent ministry, the Ministry of Justice, has continuously improved the related system and practice since the above 2017HEONGA29 decision was rendered. Considering that immigration control administration is an area that is in part determined as a matter of legislative policy, there also remains the question of whether it is desirable to change the precedent in just a little over 5 years and thereby eliminate the room for voluntary and gradual institutional improvement by the legislative and executive branches through a Constitutional Court decision.  \\nThe precedent’s position that the Provision at Issue, established for immigration control administration as a sovereign state, does not violate the principle of proportionality or the principle of due process remains valid even now, and there is no error in that judgment, nor can it be recognized that there are necessary and sufficient changes in circumstances to justify changing the precedent.  \\nAccordingly, the Provision at Issue does not violate the Constitution.\\n\\n7. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Lee Mi-sun on the Incompatibility Opinion of Justices Yu Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-young, Moon Hyung-bae, and Lee Mi-sun  \\nIn addition to the opinion of incompatibility with the Constitution by the five Justices that the Provision at Issue violates the principle of proportionality and the principle of due process, I would like to state the following as to the fact that it also violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution, which provides for the right to request a court review of the propriety of arrest or detention.  \\nArticle 12(6) of the Constitution provides that “No person shall be arrested or detained except in cases provided by Act and upon proper procedures, and no one shall be deprived of his right to a trial.” It provides for a system of review of the propriety of arrest or detention. This is a post-remedy procedure intended to promote prompt and effective relief by allowing a person whose freedom of the person has been restricted by arrest or detention by public authority to request a court to review the legality of the arrest or detention and to obtain immediate release not only where the physical restraint was unlawfully commenced but also where continuing the physical restraint is unlawful.  \\nBecause the freedom of the person guaranteed by Article 12 of the Constitution may be directly restricted not only by investigative agencies but also by other state organs, including general administrative agencies, the terms “arrest or detention” in Article 12(6) of the Constitution must also be interpreted broadly. Accordingly, Article 12(6) of the Constitution applies to cases in which any public authority restricts freedom of the person by means of arrest or detention. In addition, Article 12(6) of the Constitution is a provision that constitutionally guarantees a procedure by which a party may request a court to review the legality of arrest or detention itself, separate from the final judicial determination process concerning the causative relationship for the arrest or detention, and because this right to request review of the propriety of arrest or detention has an independent status at the constitutional level, the legislature has an obligation to provide the person concerned with at least one opportunity, through the overall legal system, to properly exercise the concrete procedural rights at issue (see Constitutional Court 2004. 3. 25. 2002HEONBA104; Constitutional Court 2014. 8. 28. 2012HEONMA686). Furthermore, Article 12(6) of the Constitution states that “no person” has the right to request a court to review the propriety of arrest or detention, thereby recognizing this right even for foreign nationals.  \\nTherefore, for foreign nationals detained pursuant to the Provision at Issue, at least one opportunity must be provided to request a court to review the legality of the detention itself (see Constitutional Court 2014. 8. 28. 2012HEONMA686).  \\nHowever, the Provision at Issue and the Immigration Control Act, including the Provision at Issue, do not provide a procedure by which a person detained under the Provision at Issue may request a court to review the legality of the commencement or continuation of detention. In addition, the Detention Act, which prescribes court remedies concerning detention, excludes “persons detained pursuant to the Immigration Control Act” from its scope of application (see Article 2 and Article 3 of the Detention Act), and thus foreign nationals detained under the Provision at Issue cannot, unlike in other cases of administrative physical restraint, seek remedies under the Detention Act.  \\nIn concretizing the procedure for realizing the right to request review of the propriety of arrest or detention, the legislature has a relatively broad power of legislative formation and may make various choices regarding the specific content or name of the law in the legislative process (see Constitutional Court 2004. 3. 25. 2002HEONBA104); and the detainee may file an administrative lawsuit seeking revocation of the detention order or an application for suspension of execution seeking suspension of its execution. However, the reason the Constitution separately guarantees the right to request review of the propriety of arrest or detention in Article 12(6), apart from guaranteeing the right to a trial in Article 27(1), is to provide a prompt and effective remedy procedure by allowing a person whose freedom of the person has been restrained by public authority to request the court to review the legality of the commencement or continuation of such physical restraint. Yet, in a situation where no court involvement whatsoever takes place at the stage of commencement or extension of detention under the current Immigration Control Act, it is difficult to regard such ordinary administrative litigation procedures alone as guaranteeing a prompt and effective remedy procedure by the court. Moreover, even if the commencement of detention was lawful, if continuation of detention becomes unlawful due to extinction of the need for detention, etc., it cannot be said with certainty whether appropriate and effective relief can be obtained in a revocation suit against the detention order or an application for suspension of execution. The Immigration Control Act provides a post-remedy procedure by allowing objections to detention to be filed with the Minister of Justice, but it is clear that such an objection system cannot constitute part of the system for review of the propriety of arrest or detention under Article 12(6) of the Constitution, which centers on judicial review. Furthermore, post hoc control by the Minister of Justice, who is merely a supervisory authority and not a neutral and objective institution, or procedures prescribed by the Immigration Control Act such as prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extension of detention, presentation of the detention order to the person concerned, and notice of detention, cannot be regarded as performing a supplementary function to the system of review of the propriety of arrest or detention.  \\nAs noted above, while the legislature has a relatively broad power of legislative formation in concretizing the procedure for realizing the right to request review of the propriety of arrest or detention, considering the purpose of Article 12(6) of the Constitution in guaranteeing that right, a procedure must be guaranteed by which one may request a court to review the legality of the state of detention itself under the Provision at Issue; this remains so even though detention under the Provision at Issue is carried out as part of immigration control administration, so long as detention causes a serious restriction on freedom of the person.  \\nTaken together, the Provision at Issue, which does not provide a procedure for requesting a court to review the legality of the commencement or continuation of detention when a person is detained pursuant to the Provision at Issue, violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution."}

{"[2020HEONMA1079]": "1. Overview of the Case  \\nThe petitioner, an Egyptian national, received a decision recognizing refugee status pursuant to Article 18(1) of the Refugee Act on 2018. 3. 21.
