The fact that it does not fall under a consanguineous marriage under Article 809(1) of the Civil Act\\n\\n3. Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\na. The marriage prohibition provision at issue has as its legislative purpose the maintenance of family order and social order, and the prevention of hereditary diseases. However, in light of the weakening or dismantling of Korea’s Confucian family culture due to industrialization, urbanization, and nuclear-family formation, the notion of regarding blood relatives within 8th degree as close relatives has lost its universal validity. In addition, the genetic rationale is based on vague concern without specific proof or substantiation of causation, and therefore cannot be a legitimate legislative purpose of the marriage prohibition provision at issue.\\n\\nRather, the marriage prohibition provision at issue, in order to supplement the legislative vacuum caused by the abolition of the same-surname-same-clan marriage prohibition provision, uniformly prohibited marriage between all blood relatives falling within the scope of relatives prescribed by Article 777(1) of the Civil Act without serious discussion on the scope of consanguineous marriage prohibition, and, by setting the scope of consanguineous marriage prohibition unusually broadly compared with foreign legislative examples, intensifies conflicts and confusion in family order and marriage order in the present day, when international marriages are increasing.\\n\\nUltimately, the marriage prohibition provision at issue violates the principle against excessive restriction because it prohibits marriage without reasonable grounds even as to the extent that there is no risk of confusion in family order or social order, or no risk of genetic disease.\\n\\nb. The nullity provision at issue uniformly prescribes marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree as null and void, and thus, even where the parties have filed a marriage report with genuine intent, the marriage report may be corrected at any time by the claim of one party or a third party, and there is a possibility that it may be abused as a means of so-called expulsion divorce. In addition, although there is no identity-publication system in place that can verify blood relatives within 8th degree, the fact that the nullity provision at issue makes marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree a ground for nullity ab initio violates the principle against excessive restriction because it not only causes unexpected harm to the marriage parties but also significantly impairs the welfare of their children.\\n\\n4. Reasoning\\n\\na. Contents and legislative history of the provisions at issue\\n\\n(1) Formation and nullity of marriage\\n\\nUnder the Civil Act, marriage is a legal act and a type of contract, and is formed when certain requirements prescribed by law are satisfied. A marriage takes effect by filing a marriage report in accordance with the Act on the Registration, etc. of Family Relationships between marriage parties who have reached the age for marriage (Article 807 of the Civil Act), where there is no ground for prohibition of marriage, such as certain kinship relationships (Article 809 of the Civil Act), and the marriage does not constitute bigamy (Article 810 of the Civil Act), and where there is an agreement to marry between the marriage parties (Article 815(1) of the Civil Act).\\n\\nOnce a marriage is formed, various legal relationships arise on that basis. Therefore, for the protection of legal stability, the Civil Act provides that even if there is a defect in the formation of a marriage, its validity may be contested only in cases prescribed by law, and recognizes the nullity of marriage ab initio only exceptionally.\\n\\nArticle 815 of the Civil Act prescribes, as grounds for nullity of marriage, the absence of an agreement to marry between the parties, marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree, the existence or previous existence of a lineal relationship by affinity between the parties, and the existence or previous existence of a lineal blood-relative relationship of adoptive parents between the parties. If such a ground for nullity of marriage exists, the marriage is void from the outset and does not become void only upon a judgment of nullity of marriage rendered by a court. In cases falling under a ground for nullity of marriage, the marriage does not produce legal effects not only between the marriage parties but also in relation to third parties; accordingly, changes in rights such as inheritance by a void marriage are null, and children born in a void marriage become children born out of wedlock. However, if a report of birth of a natural child is filed with respect to such a child, that report has the effect of acknowledgment (Article 57 of the Act on the Registration, etc. of Family Relationships).\\n\\nAn action for nullity of marriage is an action for confirmation, and the parties, legal representatives, or relatives within 4th degree may file an action for nullity of marriage at any time (Article 23 of the Family Litigation Act).\\n\\nThe provisions at issue restrict the formation of marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree (the marriage prohibition provision at issue), and provide that a marriage in violation thereof is void from the outset (the nullity provision at issue).\\n\\n(2) Legislative history of the provisions at issue\\n\\n(a) Adjustment of the scope of relatives based on gender equality\\n\\nFormer Civil Act (enacted by Act No. 471 of 1958. 2. 22., and before amendment by Act No. 4199 of 1990. 1. 13.) Article 768 defined one’s direct ascendants and direct descendants as lineal blood relatives, and one’s siblings, the lineal descendants of siblings, the siblings of direct ascendants, and the lineal descendants of such siblings as collateral blood relatives; Article 777 prescribed paternal blood relatives within 8th degree, maternal blood relatives within 4th degree, the paternal blood relatives within 8th degree of the husband, maternal blood relatives within 4th degree of the husband, the parents of the wife, and the spouse as relatives, thereby creating a marked discrimination in the scope of blood relatives and relatives among the lineal descendants of siblings, between paternal and maternal lines, and between husband and wife.\\n\\nBecause such discrimination was deemed contrary to human dignity and the principle of gender equality, the above provisions of the former Civil Act were amended by Act No. 4199 of 1990. 1. 13. The amended Article 768 of the Civil Act defined “one’s direct ascendants and direct descendants” as “lineal blood relatives,” and “one’s siblings and the lineal descendants of siblings, the siblings of direct ascendants, and the lineal descendants of such siblings” as “collateral blood relatives,” and Article 777, without distinguishing between paternal and maternal lines, or between husband and wife, regarded blood relatives within 8th degree, relatives by affinity within 4th degree, and spouses as relatives. This had the effect of broadening the scope of blood relatives regarded as relatives compared to the previous law.\\n\\n(b) Constitutional nonconformity decision regarding the provisions of the former Civil Act prohibiting marriage between persons of the same surname and clan, and adjustment of the scope of marriage prohibition\\n\\nFormer Civil Act (enacted by Act No. 471 of 1958. 2. 22., and before amendment by Act No. 7427 of 2005. 3. 31.) Article 809(1) provided that “Marriage shall not be allowed between blood relatives of the same surname and clan,” thereby prohibiting marriage between paternal blood relatives regardless of the degree of kinship. As to that provision, the Constitutional Court, in Case 95HEONGA6 et al. on 1997. 7. 16., held that “In modern liberal democracy, which is founded on freedom and equality and in which the concept of equality between men and women has become established, Article 809(1) of the Civil Act, which prescribes the prohibition of marriage between persons of the same surname and clan, has now lost social validity and rationality, and is directly contrary not only to the constitutional principles that provide for human dignity and value and the right to pursue happiness, but also to the constitutional provisions concerning the formation and maintenance of marriage and family life based on personal dignity and equality of the sexes. Moreover, by making discrimination based on sex limited only to male-line blood relatives, it also violates the constitutional principle of equality, and, in that its legislative purpose is not legitimate, it also violates Article 37(2) of the Constitution.” On that basis, the Constitutional Court rendered a decision of constitutional nonconformity, and in accordance with the operative part of that decision, Article 809(1) of the former Civil Act lost effect from 1999. 1. 1.\\n\\nArticle 809 of the Civil Act, including the marriage prohibition provision at issue, was amended by Act No. 7427 of 2005. 3. 31., and, albeit belatedly, reflected the purport of the above constitutional nonconformity decision of the Constitutional Court; its legislative purpose was to “abolish the same-surname-same-clan marriage prohibition system that may infringe gender equality and freedom of marriage and convert it into a consanguineous marriage prohibition system, while reasonably adjusting the scope of restriction on consanguineous marriage.”\\n\\nAccordingly, Article 809(1) of the Civil Act (the marriage prohibition provision at issue) prohibits marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree (including blood relatives before the adoption of a special adoptee). Blood relatives within 8th degree include both lineal blood relatives and collateral blood relatives, and include not only natural blood relatives formed by birth but also legal blood relatives formed by adoption. The same applies whether the blood relatives are on the paternal or maternal side.\\n\\nArticles 809(2) and (3) of the Civil Act prescribe the prohibition of marriage between certain relatives by affinity and between persons who were blood relatives or relatives by affinity in the adoptive parental line.\\n\\n(c) Adjustment of the scope of void marriages\\n\\nFormer Civil Act (enacted by Act No. 471 of 1958. 2. 22., and before amendment by Act No. 7427 of 2005. 3. 31.) Article 815(2) provided that a marriage shall be void “when there exists or existed between the parties a kinship relationship as lineal blood relatives or collateral blood relatives within 8th degree.”\\n\\nSince former Civil Act (enacted by Act No. 471 of 1958. 2. 22., and before amendment by Act No. 4199 of 1990. 1. 13.) Article 777(1) and (2) prescribed as relatives only paternal blood relatives within 8th degree and maternal blood relatives within 4th degree, respectively, in the case of maternal blood relatives only blood relatives within 4th degree were interpreted to fall under the ground for nullity of marriage. However, as noted above, because the Civil Act amended by Act No. 4199 of 1990. 1. 13. prescribed, without distinguishing between paternal and maternal blood relatives, all blood relatives within 8th degree as relatives, the scope of void marriages under Article 815(2) of the same Act was also interpreted expansively to mean lineal blood relatives and collateral blood relatives within 8th degree, without distinguishing between paternal and maternal blood relatives.\\n\\nWhen the Civil Act was amended by Act No. 7427 of 2005. 3. 31., and the marriage prohibition provision at issue was newly established, the nullity provision at issue was amended, and by prescribing “when the marriage violates the marriage prohibition provision at issue” as a ground for nullity of marriage, the scope of relatives under Article 777(1) of the Civil Act, the scope of prohibited marriages under the marriage prohibition provision at issue, and the scope of void marriages under the nullity provision at issue were all unified as “blood relatives within 8th degree.”\\n\\nMeanwhile, pursuant to Article 815(3) and (4) of the Civil Act, marriage is void only when there exists or existed between the parties a lineal relationship by affinity, or when there existed between the parties a lineal blood-relative relationship of adoptive parents, and violation of the remaining marriage prohibition provisions, such as violation of Article 809(2) and (3) of the Civil Act, constitutes a ground for annulment of marriage (Article 816(1) of the Civil Act).\\n\\nb. Limits and restrictions on the freedom to decide and form marriage and family life\\n\\n(1) Article 36(1) of the Constitution provides that “Marriage and family life shall be formed and maintained on the basis of personal dignity and equality of the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this,” thereby guaranteeing, as a fundamental right, the freedom to decide and form marriage and family life by oneself, and ensuring the institution of marriage and family. In other words, in the passive sense, it prohibits the State power from infringing the private domain of marriage and family as an individual’s subjective right to defense against unjustified intrusion by State power; and in the active sense, it imposes on the State not only the duty to protect marriage and family from third parties, etc., but also the task of realizing a marriage and family system that is formed and maintained on the basis of personal dignity and equality of the sexes (see Constitutional Court 2000. 4. 27. 98HEONGA16 et al.; Constitutional Court 2002. 8. 29. 2001HEONBA82).\\n\\nTherefore, the legislature must comprehensively consider the inherent characteristics of marriage and family relations, such as a continuing and comprehensive life community, the possibility of formation and expansion of status relations such as kinship regardless of the parties’ intent, the nature of altruistic bonds among members and the importance of mutual trust and cooperation, and the diversification of communities and changes in perception and function in accordance with changes in the times and society, and must protect marriage and family so that the positive functions of the family as the basic unit of society and as an autonomous community that protects and supports its members may be further enhanced, and realize a marriage and family system based on personal dignity and equality of the sexes. To that end, where an individual’s freedom to decide and form marriage and family life is restricted, the constitutional limits on the restriction of fundamental rights must, of course, be observed.\\n\\n(2) The provisions at issue prohibit marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree and make such marriage void, thereby restricting the “freedom to decide and form marriage and family life” (hereinafter referred to as the “freedom of marriage”). We examine whether such restriction falls within the limiting principle of restrictions on fundamental rights prescribed by Article 37(2) of the Constitution.\\n\\nc. Whether the marriage prohibition provision at issue infringes the freedom of marriage\\n\\n(1) In the case of marriage between close blood relatives [however, this does not denote a legal blood-relative relationship having the same scope as blood relatives under the Civil Act (Article 768) among blood relatives who belong to relatives (Article 777) or family members (Article 779) under the Civil Act; rather, it refers to persons who are in a close blood relationship according to the general social understanding.], i.e., consanguineous marriage, there are cases in which, in the process of forming a shared life or interaction over a long period including the period of minority, it causes difficulty in the formation and concordance of a free and genuine intention to marry of an individual through the influence of age, generational rank, or other rank or influence within close blood relatives. The possibility of consanguineous marriage may also create sexual tension or a relationship of conflict and exploitation among close blood relatives. In addition, when consanguineous marriage takes place, it changes the status relationship that has long been formed and maintained among close blood relatives, thereby causing confusion in the roles and status of members of the close blood relatives. Furthermore, incest, which is universally taboo in human culture, may make it difficult for the parties to a consanguineous marriage or children born therefrom to have private bonds and cooperative relationships based on the trust and affection ordinarily expected among close blood relatives, thereby causing the disintegration of close blood relatives. As a result, members may be excluded from the protection and support primarily borne by close blood relatives in our society. For example, protection and upbringing for a minor party to a consanguineous marriage requiring protection and upbringing may be discontinued; it may be difficult to expect care and support from close blood relatives for minor children in the event of death of a party to a consanguineous marriage; or situations may arise where the general expectations for the family system are not met, such as where a party to a consanguineous marriage refuses to support his or her parents or, conversely, the parents refuse to do so.\\n\\nThe marriage prohibition provision at issue is intended to prevent the confusion that may arise in the mutual relationship, roles, and status among close blood relatives due to consanguineous marriage and to maintain the function of the family system. Therefore, its legislative purpose is legitimate. In addition, prohibiting legal marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree contributes to suppressing the occurrence of consanguineous marriage and thus constitutes an appropriate means for achieving the legislative purpose.\\n\\n(2) As seen above, the Civil Act enacted by Act No. 471 of 1958. 2. 22. provided in Article 809(1) that “Marriage shall not be allowed between blood relatives of the same surname and clan,” thereby prohibiting marriage between paternal blood relatives regardless of the degree of kinship; however, the above provision lost effect from 1999. 1. 1. in accordance with the purport of the Constitutional Court’s decision in Case 95HEONGA6 et al. dated 1997. 7. 16., and the marriage prohibition provision at issue was newly prescribed when the Civil Act was amended by Act No. 7427 of 2005. 3. 31. Theread. The scope of blood relatives prohibited from entering into a legal marriage under the marriage prohibition provision at issue was based on the scope of blood relatives prescribed in Article 777(1) of the Civil Act then in force (as amended by Act No. 4199 of 1990. 1. 13.) at the time the marriage prohibition provision at issue was enacted. This respected the purport of the above constitutional nonconformity decision of the Constitutional Court, while limiting the scope of close kin on the basis of the scope of relatives prevailing in our society and the understanding and consensus on family relations formed on the basis of gender equality; accordingly, its rationality is recognized. Even in today’s situation, in which social and cultural changes capable of altering the notion of relatives or the function of the family continue, such as industrialization and urbanization resulting from rapid economic growth, the development of transportation and communication, nationwide population movement, and concentration in cities, it is difficult to conclude that there has been a change in intergenerational views concerning the notion of relatives or the function of the family; therefore, the marriage prohibition provision at issue, which was determined in consideration of the scope of relatives prescribed by the Civil Act, cannot be viewed as imposing unnecessary or excessive restrictions for achieving the legislative purpose.\\n\\nMeanwhile, it is true that the scope of blood relatives prohibited from entering into a legal marriage under the marriage prohibition provision at issue is relatively broad compared with foreign legislative examples. However, because the scope within which consanguineous marriage causes confusion among close blood relatives or impairs the function of the family system mainly depends on the understanding and consensus regarding the category of family, simple comparison between countries with different family concepts due to differences in historical, religious, cultural backgrounds or ways of life is not meaningful.\\n\\nTaken together, it is difficult to see the marriage prohibition provision at issue as imposing unnecessary restrictions for achieving the legislative purpose, and it is also difficult to see any other means for achieving the legislative purpose besides prohibiting legal marriage between close relatives; therefore, it cannot be said that the marriage prohibition provision at issue contravenes the minimum-impairment requirement.\\n\\n(3) The scope in which the marriage prohibition provision at issue restricts the choice of a lawful spouse is limited to blood relatives within 8th degree even within kinship relations, and cannot be said to be broad. In contrast, the public interest in protecting and maintaining family order by prohibiting marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree is very important. Therefore, the marriage prohibition provision at issue does not violate the principle of balance of interests.\\n\\n(4) Therefore, the marriage prohibition provision at issue does not infringe the freedom of marriage in violation of the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\nd. Whether the nullity provision at issue infringes the freedom of marriage\\n\\n(1) Constitutional nonconformity opinion of Justices Lee Sun-ae, Lee Eun-ae, Lee Jong-seok, Lee Young-jin, and Lee Mi-sun\\n\\n(a) The nullity provision at issue is intended to ensure the effectiveness of the marriage prohibition provision at issue and, like the marriage prohibition provision at issue, its legislative purpose is legitimate. In addition, under the nullity provision at issue, consanguineous marriage is void from the outset, and this is an appropriate means for achieving the legislative purpose because it contributes to suppressing the occurrence of consanguineous marriage.\\n\\n(b) As noted above, even if the marriage prohibition provision at issue, which preemptively prohibits consanguineous marriage, does not infringe the freedom of marriage, whether a marriage that has the outward appearance of a legal marriage through the formality of a marriage report and has in substance formed and maintained a marital relationship through concordance of intent to marry between the parties and joint marital life, etc., should be regarded as void from the outset requires separate examination.\\n\\nThe reason for prohibiting consanguineous marriage is to prevent confusion regarding mutual relations, roles, and status among close blood relatives that may arise from consanguineous marriage and to maintain the function of the family system. However, where consanguineous marriage has already been entered into and performance of rights and duties between spouses has taken place, and where children have been born or circumstances exist from which expectations of trust and cooperation within the family can be found to have arisen, uniformly causing such marriage to lose its effect retroactively is likely to produce results contrary to the original legislative purpose of maintaining the function of the family system.\\n\\nBecause of the nullity provision at issue, children born between parties to a consanguineous marriage may become children born out of wedlock and their legal status may become unstable, and parties to a consanguineous marriage may find themselves in unforeseeably dire circumstances by losing social security benefits and inheritance rights that they had enjoyed or could have expected to enjoy as spouses. In some cases, it may affect not only the parties to the void marriage but also other close blood-relative relationships, leaving room for the collapse of the order surrounding such status relations and the erosion of their institutional function.\\n\\nIn the marriage report, the fact that the marriage does not fall under the consanguineous marriage prohibited by the marriage prohibition provision at issue must be entered (Article 71(4) of the Act on the Registration, etc. of Family Relationships), but at present Korea has no identity-publication system that can clearly verify whether persons are blood relatives within 8th degree. Accordingly, there may be cases in which the marriage parties later discover, by chance, that they are blood relatives within 8th degree. Nevertheless, under the current Family Litigation Act, without any exception, either party, a legal representative, or a relative within 4th degree may file an action for nullity of marriage at any time (Article 23 of the Family Litigation Act), and this may produce excessively harsh results for the parties or their children. The legislative purpose of the nullity provision at issue can be sufficiently achieved even if consanguineous marriage is made void only in cases where it significantly causes confusion in status relations, etc., among close blood relatives and seriously impairs the function of the family system.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Civil Act has a system of annulment of marriage that allows a marriage, when defective in its requirements, to be initially validly formed but to be annulled by a court judgment. In cases where grounds for annulment exist, even if the annulment is finally established upon a claim for annulment of marriage, the effect of such annulment does not retroactively apply to the past, and the legal status of the respondent to the annulment or of the children is guaranteed on a basis equivalent to divorce (Articles 824 and 824-2 of the Civil Act). Furthermore, Article 820 of the Civil Act completely bars annulment of a marriage where the parties conceived during the marriage, thereby strongly protecting the welfare of children. Where consanguineous marriage significantly causes confusion in status relations, etc., among close blood relatives and seriously impairs the function of the family system, and where it is not clear whether it markedly departs from the manner in which members of our society generally think and act with respect to relations among close blood relatives, it would be desirable for the legislature, through such a marriage annulment system, to secure the effectiveness of the marriage prohibition provision at issue while protecting the function of the family. In other words, the legislature may prescribe a certain range of consanguineous marriage as a ground for annulment of marriage, allow the marriage to be dissolved prospectively through a court judgment upon the claim of the person entitled to request annulment of marriage, and protect the welfare of the marriage parties or their children by imposing certain restrictions on the right to request annulment of marriage, such as by setting a time limit.\\n\\nUltimately, the nullity provision at issue uniformly and mechanically prescribes marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree as a ground for nullity of marriage without examining the specific aspects of consanguineous marriage, and does not provide any exception clause to protect the legal status of parties or their children who relied on the formation and maintenance of the marital relationship. Therefore, as an excessive restriction exceeding the range necessary to achieve the legislative purpose, it fails to satisfy the minimum-impairment requirement.\\n\\n(c) By uniformly prescribing marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree as a ground for nullity of marriage, the nullity provision at issue denies the substance of spousal life that has been maintained for a considerable period and, by failing to protect the legal status of the parties or children who relied on the formation and maintenance of the marital relationship, seriously affects the right to subsistence of individuals and the welfare of children. In addition, if the marital relationship can be easily dissolved merely by one party’s claim of nullity of marriage even though the parties maintain the outward form of marriage by mutual agreement, the possibility of abuse as so-called expulsion divorce, such as one party being unilaterally abandoned by the other, cannot be excluded.\\n\\nThe public interest achieved by securing the effectiveness of the marriage prohibition provision at issue through the nullity provision at issue, thereby preventing confusion that may arise with respect to mutual relations, roles, and status among close blood relatives and protecting the function of the family system, is by no means insignificant. However, considering the magnitude of the private interest restricted by the nullity provision at issue, the nullity provision at issue fails to satisfy the balance of interests.\\n\\n(d) Therefore, the nullity provision at issue infringes the freedom of marriage in violation of the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n(e) The nullity provision at issue violates the Constitution because it infringes the freedom of marriage in violation of the principle against excessive restriction, and thus, in principle, a finding of unconstitutionality should be rendered. However, if a simple unconstitutionality decision is rendered with respect to the nullity provision at issue, the irrational result would arise that the means to secure the effectiveness of the marriage prohibition provision at issue would disappear. Moreover, the unconstitutionality of the nullity provision at issue lies in making consanguineous marriage prohibited by the marriage prohibition provision at issue void from the outset without any exception. This does not mean that even in cases where consanguineous marriage significantly causes confusion in status relations, etc., among close blood relatives and seriously impairs the function of the family system, and where it clearly departs from the manner in which members of our society generally think and act with respect to relations among close blood relatives, it may not be made void. As to the scope in which an exceptional protection of the legal status of the parties and their children is necessary by making consanguineous marriage prohibited by the marriage prohibition provision at issue void from the outset without any exception, it is desirable to leave it to the legislature, which bears the primary responsibility to protect marriage and family and to realize a marriage and family system based on personal dignity and equality of the sexes, to devise a constitutionally conforming method of improvement and to take concrete legislative measures by considering all relevant factors, such as the need to protect the parties and their children depending on the aspects of consanguineous marriage and social perceptions concerning the scope of relatives and the function of the family.\\n\\n(2) Constitutional nonconformity opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Suk-tae, Kim Ki-young, and Moon Hyung-bae\\n\\n(a) As stated in the dissenting opinion on the marriage prohibition provision at issue in 6. below, the marriage prohibition provision at issue, which prohibits marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree, is not compatible with the Constitution due to the breadth of its prohibited scope. Accordingly, in order to secure the effectiveness of the marriage prohibition provision at issue, the provision at issue that makes all marriages between blood relatives within 8th degree in violation thereof void also renders the scope of consanguineous marriage to be void too broad and thus not compatible with the Constitution.\\n\\n(b) If, through improved legislation of the marriage prohibition provision at issue, the scope of prohibited consanguineous marriage is constitutionally narrowed, then within such narrowed scope of marriage prohibition, the nullity provision at issue may be recognized as having a legitimate legislative purpose and appropriateness of means. However, even the portion of the nullity provision at issue concerning consanguineous marriage within the above limited scope violates the minimum-impairment requirement and the balance of interests in the following respects.\\n\\nThe nullity of marriage prescribed by the nullity provision at issue treats a marriage as if it had never existed from the outset even where rights and duties between spouses have already been performed and children have been born or expectations of trust and cooperation within the family have arisen, thereby possibly producing results contrary to the original legislative purpose of prohibiting consanguineous marriage, namely the maintenance of the function of the family system. In other words, because of the nullity provision at issue, children born between parties to a consanguineous marriage may become children born out of wedlock and their legal status may become unstable, and the parties to a consanguineous marriage may be placed in unforeseeably dire circumstances by losing support claims, division of property claims, social security benefits, inheritance rights, etc. that they had enjoyed or could have expected to enjoy as spouses, thereby causing excessively harsh consequences for the parties or their children.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Civil Act has a system of annulment of marriage that allows a marriage, when defective in its requirements, to be initially validly formed but to be annulled by a court judgment. Under this system, even if annulment of marriage is finalized, the effect of such annulment does not retroactively apply to the past, and the legal status of the respondent to the annulment or of the children is guaranteed on a basis equivalent to divorce.\\n\\nIf so, the legislative purpose of the nullity provision at issue can be sufficiently achieved even by limiting voidness to cases where consanguineous marriage, such as marriage between direct blood relatives and between siblings, seriously impairs the function of the family system, and by providing that other consanguineous marriages are not void retroactively but may be dissolved prospectively through annulment of marriage, while guaranteeing the legal status of parties or children that has already been formed.\\n\\nAlso, although the nullity provision at issue secures the effectiveness of the marriage prohibition provision at issue and thus contributes to protecting the function of the family system, it is by no means insignificant, it does not protect at all the legal status of the marriage parties or their children, and by prescribing violation of the marriage prohibition provision at issue as a ground for nullity of marriage, it seriously affects the right to subsistence of individuals and the welfare of children.\\n\\nNevertheless, because the nullity provision at issue makes all marriages in violation of the marriage prohibition provision at issue void, it contravenes the minimum-impairment requirement and the balance of interests. Therefore, the nullity provision at issue infringes the freedom of marriage in violation of the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n(c) If a simple unconstitutionality decision is rendered with respect to the nullity provision at issue, there will be no means to secure the effectiveness of the constitutionally valid part of the marriage prohibition provision at issue, resulting in an unacceptable legal vacuum. Moreover, it is desirable for the National Assembly, which bears the primary responsibility for forming a marriage and family system based on personal dignity and equality of the sexes, to devise a constitutionally conforming method of improvement and to take concrete legislative measures by considering the need to protect the parties to consanguineous marriage and their children, etc., in determining the scope of blood relatives whose marriage is prohibited, and the portion of prohibited consanguineous marriage that should be made void and the portion that should be allowed to be annulled.\\n\\n(3) Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, with respect to the nullity provision at issue, a decision of constitutional nonconformity shall be rendered, and its continued application shall be ordered until the legislature enacts remedial legislation. The legislature shall implement remedial legislation as soon as possible, and no later than 2024. 12. 31., and in the present case, it would be necessary to apply the amended new law after waiting for the amendment of the nullity provision at issue.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the marriage prohibition provision at issue is not in violation of the Constitution, and the nullity provision at issue is not compatible with the Constitution. Accordingly, with respect to the nullity provision at issue, a decision of constitutional nonconformity is rendered and its continued application is ordered until the legislature enacts remedial legislation by the deadline of 2024. 12. 31., and it is so decided as stated in the dispositive part. This decision is based on the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, except for the dissenting opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Suk-tae, Kim Ki-young, and Moon Hyung-bae regarding the marriage prohibition provision at issue, as stated in 6. below.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Suk-tae, Kim Ki-young, and Moon Hyung-bae on the Marriage Prohibition Provision at Issue\\n\\nWe think that the marriage prohibition provision at issue infringes the freedom of marriage in violation of the principle against excessive restriction. Above all, we present the following dissenting opinion from the standpoint that broadly guaranteeing the freedom of marriage by gradually reducing the scope of prohibited marriage in keeping with changes in the times and the international normative environment of today is consistent with the legal order and spirit of liberal democracy.\\n\\na. Legitimacy of the purpose and appropriateness of the means\\n\\nThe prohibition of consanguineous marriage derives from the universally formed human taboo against incest. The taboo against incest reflects human natural and psychological nature and is intended to restrict sexual intercourse or procreation between direct blood relatives and siblings. Expanding a family through sexual intercourse and procreation is solely the role of parents, and children are expected to have the role of growing as a succeeding generation that will replace the role of parents. Children do not perform, and should not perform, the role of sexual objects vis-à-vis parents or siblings within the family. To prevent the collapse of the family caused by sexual tension and conflict, and to secure the next generation that is raised stably for the continuous development of humanity, it would be necessary to prevent confusion in sexual roles among family members.\\n\\nThe marriage prohibition provision at issue prohibits marriage within the family in order to maintain family order and protect the function of the family system, and thus its legislative purpose is legitimate and the appropriateness of means is also recognized.\\n\\nb. Minimum impairment\\n\\n(1) However, the marriage prohibition provision at issue goes far beyond the scope of the above-mentioned taboo against incest and makes all blood relatives within 8th degree subject to the prohibition of marriage. As the majority opinion states, even if the marriage prohibition provision at issue has the legislative purpose of preventing confusion that may arise in the mutual relationships, roles, and status among close blood relatives due to consanguineous marriage and maintaining the function of the family system, it is doubtful whether a rational basis has been presented for broadly prohibiting marriage even to collateral blood relatives within 8th degree.\\n\\n(2) The majority opinion stated that “even in today’s situation, in which social and cultural changes capable of altering the notion of relatives or the function of the family continue, it is difficult to conclude that there has been a change in intergenerational views concerning the notion of relatives or the function of the family; therefore, the marriage prohibition provision at issue, which was determined in consideration of the scope of relatives prescribed by the Civil Act, cannot be viewed as imposing unnecessary or excessive restrictions for achieving the legislative purpose.”\\n\\nHowever, the notion that blood relatives within 8th degree are regarded as so-called “close kin” cannot be said to remain a universally accepted common understanding today regardless of region or generation. Industrialization and urbanization due to rapid economic growth, the development of transportation and communication, nationwide population movement, and concentration in cities have brought about nuclear-family formation, the dismantling of traditional villages, and changes in family relations, traditional ethics, and family views. As each generation has come to live a fluid life as needed, contacts among relatives have markedly decreased, and because there is no separate identity-publication system to verify whether a person is a relative, it has become difficult to know the existence of blood relationships or their degree in the case of relatively distant relatives.\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court rendered a decision of constitutional nonconformity regarding Article 778 of the former Civil Act (before amendment by Act No. 7427 of 2005. 3. 31.), which prescribed the head of household system (Constitutional Court 2005. 2. 3. 2001HEONGA9 et al.), and in line with that purport the former Family Register Act was abolished on 2008. 1. 1. Accordingly, in order to verify whether someone falls within collateral blood relatives within 8th degree, there is no other method of proof except to check one by one the registered permanent domicile of paternal as well as maternal relatives and inspect and compare the family register transcripts of relatives at the competent administrative office.\\n\\nNevertheless, if one is to determine the other party to a marriage by verifying whether they are collateral blood relatives within 8th degree, this not only fails to accord with the changes in the times but also contradicts the purpose of abolishing the head of household system and the family register system.\\n\\n(3) Looking at foreign legislative examples, Germany, Austria, and Switzerland prohibit marriage between direct blood relatives and siblings (German Civil Code Article 1307, Austrian Marriage Act Article 6, Swiss Civil Code Article 95(1)), France, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Japan prohibit marriage between collateral blood relatives within 3rd degree (French Civil Code Articles 161 to 163, United Kingdom Marriage Act 1949 Article 1, United States Uniform Marriage and Divorce Act Article 207, Japanese Civil Code Article 734(1)), and China, whose system of prohibiting marriage between persons of the same surname and clan became the model for Korea’s same-surname-same-clan marriage prohibition, abolished the same-surname marriage prohibition system and drastically reduced the scope of the prohibition of consanguineous marriage, prohibiting only marriage between direct blood relatives and collateral blood relatives within 3 generations (Chinese Marriage Act Article 7(1)). Thus, compared with the marriage prohibition provision at issue, the scope of marriage prohibition is relatively narrower.\\n\\nThe preamble to Article 16(1) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that “Men and women of full age, without any limitation due to race, nationality or religion, have the right to marry and to found a family,” and paragraph 2 of the same article provides that “Marriage shall be entered into only with the free and full consent of the intending spouses.” In addition, Article 23(2) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (Multilateral Treaty No. 1007 of 1990. 6. 13., effective 1990. 7. 10.) provides that “The right of men and women of marriageable age to marry and to found a family shall be recognized,” and paragraph 3 provides that “No marriage shall be entered into without the free and full consent of the intending spouses.” Therefore, regardless of the distinctive historical, religious, or cultural backgrounds of each country or differences in ways of life, the freedom of marriage, especially the “right freely to decide one’s spouse,” should be respected and protected as a universal human right, which is the globally prevailing understanding today. Moreover, in a situation where international marriages are continuously increasing and the population flowing in from abroad is also steadily increasing, different marriage systems between the parties to marriage may threaten the formation and stable maintenance of marriage and may seriously harm the welfare of children born from such marriage; therefore, the legislature should endeavor to shape the marriage system in conformity with the international normative environment.\\n\\nNevertheless, the marriage prohibition provision at issue fails to reflect social and temporal changes or the international normative environment, and arbitrarily sets the scope of marriage prohibition in line with the scope of relatives under the Civil Act. As seen above in the legislative history, former Civil Act (enacted by Act No. 471 of 1958. 2. 22., and before amendment by Act No. 7427 of 2005. 3. 31.) Article 809(1) prohibited marriage between “blood relatives of the same surname and clan,” and thus marriage between maternal blood relatives was not explicitly prohibited. However, Article 815(2) of the same Act provided that a marriage shall be void “when there exists or existed between the parties a kinship relationship as lineal blood relatives or collateral blood relatives within 8th degree,” and thus the validity of marriage between maternal blood relatives depended on how former Article 777 of the Civil Act defined the scope of relatives. Former Civil Act (enacted by Act No. 471 of 1958. 2. 22., and before amendment by Act No. 4199 of 1990. 1. 13.) Article 777(1) and (2) provided that the legal effect arising from kinship relations extended only to those among the blood relatives who fell under “paternal blood relatives within 8th degree and maternal blood relatives within 4th degree,” and therefore, in the case of maternal blood relatives, only blood relatives within 4th degree were interpreted to fall under the ground for nullity of marriage, and marriage between maternal blood relatives exceeding 4th degree did not even fall under grounds for annulment of marriage, so the freedom of marriage was not restricted at all. The Civil Act amended by Act No. 4199 of 1990. 1. 13. provided in Article 777(1) that the legal effect arising from kinship relations would extend to those falling under “blood relatives within 8th degree,” without distinguishing between paternal and maternal blood relatives. Accordingly, in the case of maternal blood relatives, too, the scope of grounds for nullity of marriage was expanded so that all marriages between blood relatives within 8th degree became void. Thereafter, when the Civil Act was amended by Act No. 7427 of 2005. 3. 31., the same-surname-same-clan marriage prohibition provision that infringed gender equality and freedom of marriage was deleted and the marriage prohibition provision at issue was newly established, and marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree, without distinguishing between paternal and maternal lines, was expressly prohibited.\\n\\nIn prescribing the scope of relatives, there is no rational reason to distinguish between paternal and maternal blood relatives, and it is consistent with human dignity and the principle of gender equality to provide that the legal effect arising from kinship relations extends to a human group within a certain degree of kinship without regard to whether it is paternal or maternal. However, the marriage prohibition provision at issue is not a provision that defines the scope of relatives, but a provision that restricts the freedom of marriage, especially the right freely to decide one’s spouse; therefore, the legislature should have set the scope of marriage prohibition only within the minimum extent necessary to restrict the freedom of marriage, regardless of the scope of relatives prescribed by Article 777 of the Civil Act.\\n\\nYet even upon reviewing the legislative materials at the time of amendment attached to the record in this case, aside from an explanation to the effect that the appropriate scope of marriage prohibition was set in consideration of the scope of relatives under Article 777 of the Civil Act and genetic perspectives, there is no clear explanation of the necessity or rational reason for broadly prohibiting marriage even with maternal blood relatives, who were not explicitly prohibited under former Article 809(1) of the Civil Act.\\n\\n(4) Even according to genetic research results, it is difficult to say that there is scientific proof that marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree is uniformly genetically harmful to their children or descendants. Moreover, prohibiting marriage itself merely because of concern over the high possibility of expression of recessive genes is based on an unclear hypothesis and cannot be a rational reason for restricting the freedom to choose one’s spouse. Marriage is not solely for the purpose of having children, nor can marriage be formed or maintained only when the birth of healthy children is conditioned. The genetic perspective is linked to the notion that only those with dominant genetic factors may have children and maintain a family, and thus differentiates and instrumentalizes human beings, contrary to the constitutional requirement that the marriage system and family system be regulated in accordance with the fundamental idea of respect for human dignity.\\n\\n(5) Taking all these circumstances into comprehensive consideration, the fact that the marriage prohibition provision at issue uniformly prohibited marriage between blood relatives within 8th degree contravenes the minimum-impairment requirement because it arbitrarily set the scope of marriage prohibition in line with the scope of relatives under the Civil Act without efforts to minimize the scope of marriage prohibition in light of changes in the concept of marriage or relatives or the international normative environment.\\n\\nc. Balance of interests\\n\\nMarriage between close kin does not harm social order or infringe third-party interests, but merely brings confusion to status or roles within the family. Nevertheless, broadly prohibiting marriage itself on the basis of traditional concepts or ethical taboos is nothing more than fostering social condemnation of the union between men and women that should naturally be protected and rigidifying socially an ethical taboo that runs counter to changes in the times. In particular, because Korea has adopted the report-based marriage system, parties to consanguineous marriage are highly likely to form a family and conduct family life without filing a marriage report. In the era of the prohibition of same-surname-same-clan marriage, many persons of the same surname and clan suffered greatly because they could not file a marriage report, and the fact that the State could not ignore the suffering they experienced and ultimately enacted several special Acts to accept marriage reports shows that our society is a society in which it is difficult to live without filing a marriage report. Ultimately, the private interest infringed by the marriage prohibition provision at issue is far more serious than the public interest of maintaining family order and protecting the function of the family through that provision; therefore, the marriage prohibition provision at issue contravenes the balance of interests.\\n\\nd. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the marriage prohibition provision at issue infringes the freedom of marriage in violation of the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\ne. Necessity of a decision of constitutional nonconformity regarding the marriage prohibition provision at issue\\n\\nThe unconstitutionality of the marriage prohibition provision at issue lies in the breadth of the prohibition of consanguineous marriage. However, even if the marriage prohibition provision at issue is unconstitutional, it is appropriate not for the Constitutional Court to immediately render a decision of unconstitutionality, but for the National Assembly, which has the power to shape legislation, to sufficiently review methods to constitutionally improve the scope of blood relatives whose marriage is prohibited and thereby newly form the marriage system through a decision of constitutional nonconformity."}
