Case Outline\\n\\na. 2022HEONMA356\\nClaimant Kang ○○ and Lee ○○ are a legally married couple who completed marriage registration on May 1, 2019, and Lee ○○ was confirmed pregnant on March 10, 2022, with the expected date of delivery on November 6, 2022. However, due to Article 20(2) of the Medical Services Act, which provides that a medical practitioner may not inform the pregnant woman, her family, or others of the fetus’s sex before 32 weeks of pregnancy, the above Claimant could not know the fetus’s sex before 32 weeks of pregnancy. Accordingly, Claimant Kang ○○ alleged that the above provision of the Medical Services Act infringed the Claimant’s right of parents to access fetal sex information protected by Article 10 of the Constitution, and filed this constitutional complaint on March 22, 2022.\\n\\nb. 2023HEONMA189\\nClaimant No ○○ and Kim ○○ are a legally married couple who completed marriage registration on August 6, 2019, and Kim ○○ was confirmed pregnant on November 16, 2022, with the expected date of delivery on July 21, 2023. Kim ○○ underwent an ultrasonography examination on February 6, 2023, and at that time Kim ○○ and the above Claimant wished to know the fetus’s sex, but due to Article 20(2) of the Medical Services Act, which provides that a medical practitioner may not inform the pregnant woman, her family, or others of the fetus’s sex before 32 weeks of pregnancy, they could not know the fetus’s sex. Accordingly, Claimant No ○○ alleged that the above provision of the Medical Services Act infringed the Claimant’s right of parents to access fetal sex information, protected by Article 10 of the Constitution, and filed this constitutional complaint on February 7, 2023.\\n\\nc. 2023HEONMA1305\\nClaimants Jeong ○○ and Hwang ○○ are a legally married couple who completed marriage registration on June 8, 2021, and Claimant Jeong ○○ was confirmed pregnant on June 28, 2023, with the expected date of delivery on February 29, 2024. Claimant Jeong ○○ underwent an ultrasonography examination on September 12, 2023, and at that time the above Claimants wished to know the fetus’s sex, but due to Article 20(2) of the Medical Services Act, which provides that a medical practitioner may not inform the pregnant woman, her family, or others of the fetus’s sex before 32 weeks of pregnancy, they could not know the fetus’s sex. Accordingly, Claimants Jeong ○○ and Hwang ○○ alleged that the above provision of the Medical Services Act infringed the Claimants’ right of parents to access fetal sex information, protected by Article 10 of the Constitution, and filed this constitutional complaint on November 28, 2023.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\nThe subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether Article 20(2) of the Medical Services Act (as amended by Act No. 9906 on December 31, 2009) (hereinafter referred to as the “provision at issue”) infringes the fundamental rights of the Claimants. The provision at issue and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision at Issue]\\nMedical Services Act (as amended by Act No. 9906 on December 31, 2009)\\nArticle 20 (Prohibition of Acts of Fetal Sex Determination, etc.) ② A medical practitioner shall not inform the pregnant woman, her family, or any other person of the fetus’s sex learned while examining or testing a fetus or a pregnant woman before 32 weeks of pregnancy.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\nMedical Services Act (wholly amended by Act No. 8366 on April 11, 2007)\\nArticle 20 (Prohibition of Acts of Fetal Sex Determination, etc.) ① A medical practitioner shall not examine or test a pregnant woman for the purpose of determining the fetus’s sex, nor assist another person’s act for the same purpose.\\n\\nFormer Medical Services Act (as amended by Act No. 9932 on January 18, 2010, and before amendment by Act No. 19421 on May 19, 2023)\\nArticle 66 (Suspension of Qualification, etc.) ① The Minister of Health and Welfare may suspend a medical practitioner’s license qualification within a range of one year if the medical practitioner falls under any one of the following subparagraphs. In such case, with respect to matters requiring a judgment related to medical technology, the Minister may decide after hearing the opinions of relevant experts.\\n4. When Article 20 has been violated\\n\\nMedical Services Act (as amended by Act No. 17069 on March 4, 2020)\\nArticle 88-2 (Punishments) A person falling under any one of the following subparagraphs shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 2 years or by a fine not exceeding 20 million won.\\n1. A person who violates Article 20\\n\\n3. The Claimants’ Allegations\\nThe provision at issue was enacted for the purpose of eliminating the imbalance in the sex ratio and protecting fetal life by preventing abortion on the basis of sex. However, in the Republic of Korea today, the preference for sons has disappeared due to changes in public consciousness, and there is no longer any need to prohibit notification of fetal sex in order to protect fetal life; the sex ratio at birth, especially the sex ratio at birth for third and subsequent children, has reached the natural sex ratio, and it is difficult to see any causal relationship between notification of fetal sex and abortion. The provision at issue is not shown to be effective in eradicating abortion based on sex, and since it is ineffective, the suitability of the means is not recognized.\\n\\nToday, most abortions are performed in the early stages of pregnancy for reasons unrelated to notification of fetal sex, and medically childbirth from 37 weeks of pregnancy is regarded as normal childbirth; moreover, even if a premature birth occurs after 22 weeks and the fetus can survive through medical devices such as incubators, the provision at issue uses 32 weeks of pregnancy, which is full term and far beyond the time when abortion is practically impossible, as the standard and permits notification of the fetal sex only after that point. Therefore, it excessively infringes the parents’ right not to be prevented from accessing fetal sex information, and thus violates the least-restrictive-means requirement.\\n\\nThe public interest that the provision at issue seeks to protect is the protection of fetal life from sex-selective abortion, but today abortion on the basis of sex is rarely performed, so there is no need for such protection, whereas the provision excessively infringes the fundamental rights of the fetus’s parents. Therefore, the balance of interests is also violated.\\n\\nAccordingly, the provision at issue, in violation of the principle against excessive restriction, infringes the right of the Claimants, who are the fetus’s parents, not to be prevented from accessing fetal sex information.\\n\\n4. Judgment\\n\\na. Legislative purpose of the provision at issue and amendment history\\n(1) Legislative background of the provision prohibiting notification of fetal sex\\nBefore being amended to the provision at issue, the former Medical Services Act (as amended by Act No. 3948 on November 28, 1987, and before its whole amendment by Act No. 8366 on April 11, 2007) Article 19-2(2) and the former Medical Services Act (wholly amended by Act No. 8366 on April 11, 2007, and before amendment by Act No. 9906 on December 31, 2009) Article 20(2) (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “provisions prohibiting notification of fetal sex”) provided that “a medical practitioner shall not allow the pregnant woman and her family, etc. to know the fetus’s sex learned while examining or testing the fetus or the pregnant woman,” thereby comprehensively prohibiting notification of fetal sex.\\n\\nDetermination of fetal sex was originally developed, with the aid of advances in medical technology, as a fetal diagnostic method for the purpose of confirming whether there were abnormalities in the health condition of the fetus during pregnancy, such as hereditary diseases or congenital anomalies. However, in the 1980s, as the number of children born decreased and advances in medical technology made it possible to determine fetal sex, this became linked with the son preference that existed in our society, encouraging the tendency to select the fetus’s sex for childbirth, and as a result a serious imbalance in the sex ratio between males and females was brought about. Determination of fetal sex, contrary to its original purpose, produced the result of encouraging abortion of female fetuses, thereby threatening the dignity of human life and causing a serious imbalance in the population sex ratio.\\n\\nAccordingly, fetal sex determination and notification themselves were regarded as implying the likelihood of abortion, and for the prevention and eradication of sex-based abortion, the “act of notifying the fetus’s sex learned in the course of examining or testing the fetus or pregnant woman” came to be prohibited. In other words, in the reality of our society where son preference was widespread, although abortion was clearly a criminal act, abortion of female fetuses through fetal sex determination was openly practiced; in order to protect fetal life and the health of pregnant women and to prevent imbalance in the sex ratio, the Medical Services Act was amended on November 28, 1987 by Act No. 3948, thereby prohibiting a medical practitioner’s act of notifying fetal sex (Article 19-2(2)).\\n\\nMeanwhile, at the time when the above provision was newly enacted, no separate criminal punishment provision was established for a medical practitioner’s violation; however, it was deemed difficult to ensure effectiveness merely by suspending or revoking a medical license for violation of the prohibition on notification of fetal sex, and thus, when the Medical Services Act was amended by Act No. 4732 on January 7, 1994, Article 67 provided that a medical practitioner who violated the prohibition on notification of fetal sex would be punished by imprisonment for not more than 3 years or by a fine not exceeding 10 million won.\\n\\nThereafter, when the Medical Services Act was wholly amended by Act No. 8366 on April 11, 2007, the wording of the provision was maintained as is, with only its location changed. The provision prohibiting notification of fetal sex was moved to Article 20, and a violation thereof would be punished under Article 88 by imprisonment for not more than 3 years or by a fine not exceeding 10 million won, and the license could be revoked under Article 65(1)4.\\n\\n(2) Constitutional Court precedents\\nThe Constitutional Court, in Constitutional Court decision of July 31, 2008, 2004HEONMA1010, etc. (hereinafter referred to as the “precedent decision”), held that the provisions prohibiting notification of fetal sex in the former Medical Services Act violated the freedom of occupational performance of physicians in contravention of the principle against excessive restriction and infringed the right of pregnant women or their families not to be prevented from accessing fetal sex information, and thus rendered a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution.\\n\\nThe five Justices who formed the majority opinion held that a comprehensive prohibition on notification of fetal sex until the late stages of pregnancy, when abortion is medically difficult, contravened the principle against excessive restriction, and thus expressed an opinion of incompatibility with the Constitution. Three Justices expressed an opinion of simple unconstitutionality on the ground that the legislative purpose of prohibiting notification of fetal sex in order to prevent abortion based on sex, thereby eliminating imbalance in the sex ratio and protecting fetal life, could be achieved by provisions punishing abortion, and that the legislative purpose of regarding the act of notifying fetal sex as an act that deprives a fetus of life lacked justification.\\n\\n(3) Course of amendment into the provision at issue\\nPursuant to the precedent decision, the Medical Services Act was amended by Act No. 9906 on December 31, 2009, permitting a medical practitioner to notify the fetus’s sex learned while examining or testing the fetus or the pregnant woman, but in order to protect fetal life from abortion on the basis of sex, fetal sex notification was permitted only after 32 weeks of pregnancy, which is the latter half of pregnancy (Article 20(2), the provision at issue); at the same time, what had been a discretionary ground for revocation of the license in the case of notification of fetal sex was amended so that, in the case of notification of fetal sex before 32 weeks, it became a discretionary ground for suspension of the license within a range of one year (Article 66(1)4), and the statutory punishment for criminal penalty was reduced so that a medical practitioner who violated it would be punished by imprisonment for not more than 2 years or by a fine not exceeding 10 million won (Article 88-2). Thereafter, when the Medical Services Act was amended by Act No. 14438 on December 20, 2016, Article 88-2 provided for imprisonment for not more than 2 years or a fine not exceeding 20 million won, thereby raising the upper limit of the fine.\\n\\nb. Judgment on the provision at issue\\n(1) Fundamental rights restricted\\nWhether a future baby to be born will be female or male is important fetal personal information for the pregnant woman or her family, and the parents’ desire to know this in advance can be said to be an instinctive and natural desire. Therefore, the parents’ right not to be prevented from accessing all information about the fetus, including the fetus’s sex, is a natural and essential right that they are entitled to as parents.\\n\\nConsidering that the general right of personality derived from Article 10 of the Constitution includes guarantees of an autonomous sphere in which each individual may privately shape his or her life, the parents’ right not to be prevented by the State from accessing information on the sex of the fetus, who will become a member of the family in the future, should be regarded as protected by such general right of personality.\\n\\nAccordingly, the provision at issue restricts the right, derived from the general right of personality, of parents not to be prevented from accessing fetal sex information (see Constitutional Court decision of July 31, 2008, 2004HEONMA1010, etc.).\\n\\n(2) Legitimacy of legislative purpose\\nThe provision at issue was enacted to prohibit medical practitioners from notifying fetal sex before 32 weeks of pregnancy, thereby preventing abortion, especially abortion based on sex, and eliminating imbalance in the sex ratio and protecting fetal life; therefore, the legitimacy of its purpose can be accepted.\\n\\n(3) Suitability of means and least-restrictive means\\n(a) Before amendment into the provision at issue, the provisions prohibiting notification of fetal sex in the former Medical Services Act completely prohibited notification of fetal sex. The background for enacting such provisions was that, due to the son preference that existed in our society at the time, the tendency to select the fetus’s sex for childbirth encouraged abortion of female fetuses and caused a serious imbalance in the population sex ratio. Thereafter, pursuant to the Constitutional Court’s decision of incompatibility with the Constitution, the Medical Services Act was amended by Act No. 9906 on December 31, 2009, allowing knowledge of fetal sex after 32 weeks of pregnancy, but before that time it still prohibited doctors from making such notification, so even now fetal sex cannot be known before 32 weeks of pregnancy.\\n\\nIf so, it is necessary to examine whether, even today, 15 years after the amendment into the provision at issue, son preference remains sufficiently prevalent to require restriction of notification of fetal sex, how the sex ratio at birth has changed, whether fetal sex is causing abortion, and whether the provision at issue is functioning as a conduct-regulating norm.\\n\\n1) Whether son preference persists\\nAccording to the “2018 National Fertility and Family Health and Welfare Survey” published by the Korea Institute for Health and Social Affairs, in the survey on the sex of desired children, among unmarried men and women (ages 20-44) who responded that they wanted at least one child, the proportion answering that there was “no distinction between daughters and sons” was 67.1% among unmarried men and 65.6% among unmarried women. Among unmarried men and women who answered with a preference for distinction between daughters and sons, additional analysis was conducted on how many sons and daughters they wanted, and the ratio answering only the number of daughters was 19.3%, only the number of sons was 2.4%, and those who answered the number of both daughters and sons, though with different numbers, was 78.3%.\\n\\nEven according to the weekly report survey of the “2023 Childbearing and Childcare Awareness Survey” conducted on July 5, 2023 by the polling agency Hankook Research, 59% of all respondents answered that “there should be at least one daughter,” while the response that “there should be at least one son” was only 34%. And in all age groups, the response that “there should be at least one daughter” was high.\\n\\nIn addition, in the past there were cases of adopting male children in order to continue the family line, but according to the Ministry of Health and Welfare’s statistical table on the number of domestically adopted children, from 2013 to 2022 the sex of domestically adopted children was clearly higher for girls, while boys tended to be adopted abroad.\\n\\nAs can be seen from these data, in the Republic of Korea today, with the improvement of women’s socioeconomic status, gender equality awareness has become considerably established, and with changes in the people’s values and consciousness, the son preference that had been influenced by the traditional Confucian society has clearly declined.\\n\\n2) Changes in the sex ratio at birth\\nThe sex ratio at birth means the number of boys per 100 girls, and the natural sex ratio, which is the biological normal birth sex ratio achieved absent medical intervention, is generally regarded as 103 to 107, with 105 as the standard.\\n\\nAccording to the Statistics Korea announcement, the sex ratio at birth in 2022 was 104.7, and the sex ratio at birth by birth order was 104.9 for first children, 104.8 for second children, and 103.9 for third and subsequent children, all within the normal range of the natural sex ratio. Looking at past sex ratios at birth by birth order through Statistics Korea data, the sex ratio for first children has steadily remained within the normal range since 1991, the sex ratio for second children has remained within the normal range since 2003, and the total sex ratio at birth reached the normal range after 2007. Meanwhile, the sex ratio for third and subsequent children, which once reached the impossible natural figure of 209.7 in 1993, also steadily decreased, and was 116.6 in 2008 when the Constitutional Court’s precedent decision was rendered; after reaching the normal range at 106.7 in 2014, it only slightly exceeded the range at 107.4 in 2016 and 107.2 in 2020, and remained within the normal range until 2022.\\n\\nTaken together, these statistical data show that in the past, especially in the case of second or third children, the atmosphere favoring sons over daughters was reflected in the sex ratio at birth, and it can be seen that there was artificial intervention with respect to sex. However, from 2014, when the sex ratio for third and subsequent children also reached the normal range of the natural sex ratio, there is no clear indication of artificial intervention related to sex.\\n\\n3) Relationship between fetal sex and abortion\\nAlthough son preference, which had been influenced by the traditional Confucian society, is currently declining, according to the aforementioned survey there are cases in which parents have preferences regarding the sex of their children. If so, it is necessary to examine whether, not limited to son preference, a preference for a particular sex of a child is causing the result of abortion.\\n\\nAccording to the nationwide survey on induced abortion conditions published in September 2005 by the Ministry of Health and Welfare and Family Affairs (currently the Ministry of Health and Welfare), approximately 143,000 of the estimated 342,000 abortion procedures per year, corresponding to about 42%, were found to be abortions by unmarried women, and of the remaining abortions by married women, about 76% were performed because they did not want more children (stopping after one child) or for spacing between children, while abortions based on fetal sex accounted for only 1.2% (Constitutional Court decision of July 31, 2008, 2004HEONMA1010, etc.).\\n\\nThe above Ministry of Health and Welfare survey on induced abortion was suspended in 2010 and resumed in 2018, with reports for 2018 and 2021 published. However, in the “2018 Induced Abortion Survey Report” and the “2021 Induced Abortion Survey Report,” the response option “because of the fetus’s sex” disappeared from the reasons for abortion among persons with experience of pregnancy termination, and thus the proportion of abortions caused by fetal sex cannot be confirmed.\\n\\nHowever, from the respondents’ answers regarding the “gestational week at which induced abortion was performed” and the “reasons for induced abortion after 10 weeks of pregnancy,” it can be seen that the possibility of induced abortion based on fetal sex is considerably low.\\n\\nAccording to the 2021 report, the average gestational week at the time of induced abortion by surgery was 6.74 weeks of pregnancy, and looking at the cumulative ratio of gestational weeks at which induced abortion surgery was performed, the figures were 27% for 4 weeks or less, 81.7% for 8 weeks or less, 89.8% for 10 weeks or less, 94.5% for 12 weeks or less, and 97.7% for 16 weeks or less.\\n\\nGenerally, the minimum gestational week at which fetal sex determination by ultrasonography is possible is 16 weeks, and when prenatal anomaly screening is performed on high-risk pregnant women to identify fetal genetic information, the minimum gestational week at which a medical practitioner can know the fetus’s sex is after 10 weeks. Therefore, based on 16 weeks, 97.7%, and even based on 10 weeks, 89.8%, more than 90% can be seen as having undergone induced abortion without knowing the fetus’s sex.\\n\\nIn addition, according to the above survey, reasons were investigated for cases of induced abortion after 10 weeks of pregnancy (15%) (all multiple answers were allowed), and the responses were: “I found out late that I was pregnant” 41.6%, “I initially planned to give birth, but circumstances changed and I worried about it” 24.7%, “I was adjusting opinions with my partner and family” 22.5%, “I was looking for a proper induced abortion (abortion) method” 18%, “I was preparing the surgery cost” 14.6%, “I could not find an induced abortion surgery institution” 10.1%, “I waited for the timing because my health condition was poor” 10.1%, “I worried because of legal punishment” 2.2%, and “I tried another induced abortion (abortion) method, but it failed” 1.1%; there were no responses in the other category. In other words, even among the reasons for induced abortion after 10 weeks of pregnancy, there are almost no cases where one waited for the fetal sex determination period in order to carry out sex-selective abortion. The same result appears in the “2018 Induced Abortion Survey.”\\n\\nIn conclusion, although in the past the son preference and the resulting sociostructural pressure led women to choose abortion depending on the sex of the child, today, even if parents have a preference for the sex of a child, such preference does not appear to be a strong motivation that directly leads them to choose abortion, and it is difficult to see any substantial relationship between fetal sex and abortion.\\n\\n4) Normative force of the provision at issue\\nDespite the provision at issue, in reality there are many cases in which fetal sex information is obtained directly or indirectly from medical practitioners before 32 weeks of pregnancy. However, according to the Prosecutor General’s response to the fact-finding inquiry dated December 6, 2023, there has not been a single case in the past 10 years in which a medical practitioner was reported to or forwarded to the prosecution for violation of the provision at issue under Article 88-2(1) of the Medical Services Act, or indicted. This shows that the provision at issue is not fulfilling its role as a conduct-regulating norm.\\n\\n(b) The life of a fetus is the source of a dignified human existence, so the public interest in protecting fetal life is grave. Therefore, the State has a duty to protect fetal life, and if necessary, there is a need to regulate abortion based on fetal sex (Constitutional Court decision of July 31, 2008, 2004HEONMA1010, etc.).\\n\\nWhen the serious social problem of sex imbalance emerged in the past, it might have been appropriate to consider that abortion based on sex could not be prevented merely by the Criminal Act’s abortion offense and, accordingly, to regard fetal sex determination and notification itself as implying the likelihood of abortion and prohibit it. In other words, the provisions prohibiting notification of fetal sex sought to fundamentally block progression to sex-selective abortion by restricting the provision of information about fetal sex to pregnant women, etc., because even if a pregnant woman confirmed the fetus’s sex, that did not directly lead to abortion, but it could not be denied that it might trigger sex-selective abortion.\\n\\nHowever, today the son preference that had been influenced by the traditional Confucian society is clearly declining, and with changes in public consciousness, the sex ratio at birth has reached the normal range of the natural sex ratio, making it difficult to say that there is artificial intervention with respect to sex, nor does there appear to be any meaningful relationship between fetal sex and abortion. Therefore, it can be said that it is no longer reasonable for the provision at issue to view the act of informing fetal sex before 32 weeks of pregnancy as an act that directly threatens fetal life and to treat it as a preliminary stage of abortion depriving fetal life and thereby restrict it.\\n\\nAs noted above, despite the provision at issue, in reality fetal sex information is often obtained from medical practitioners before 32 weeks of pregnancy, but no investigation or prosecution has been conducted for violation of the provision at issue for 10 years, which shows that the provision at issue has lost its function as a conduct-regulating norm and has become obsolete. In addition, the fact that, despite the obsolescence of the provision at issue and the absence of punishment, the sex ratio at birth by birth order reached the natural sex ratio regardless of birth order can be seen as attributable to changes in the people’s values and consciousness. In light of these points as well, it is difficult to regard the provision at issue as a suitable and effective means to achieve the purpose of preventing abortion based on fetal sex, and questions arise as to the justification for its continued existence.\\n\\nThere may be cases in which the State can determine that the achievement of a legislative purpose is possible with only one measure or means, and there may also be cases in which it is possible only when several other measures or means are combined; therefore, it can be said that there is legislative discretion in choosing legislative means (Constitutional Court decision of December 22, 1989, 88HEONGA13). However, even so, means restricting fundamental rights must at least be effective and suitable for the achievement of the purpose (Constitutional Court decision of April 25, 2002, 2001HEONMA614), and at minimum the selection of a markedly irrational and unfair means must be avoided (Constitutional Court decision of April 25, 1996, 92HEONBA47; Constitutional Court decision of July 21, 2005, 2004HEONGA30).\\n\\nA parent’s desire to know the fetus’s sex is an instinctive and natural desire, and the right not to be prevented from accessing all information about the fetus, including the fetus’s sex, is a rightful right that parents should enjoy. The act of notifying fetal sex is not, in itself, an act harmful to anyone, including the fetus, and therefore there is no reason to prohibit the notification of fetal sex information learned in the course of treatment before 32 weeks of pregnancy in order to enable a richer and happier family life (see the opinion of simple unconstitutionality in Constitutional Court decision of July 31, 2008, 2004HEONMA1010, etc.).\\n\\nNevertheless, by regulating the act of notifying fetal sex, the causal relationship of which to abortion is not even clear, the provision at issue prohibits parents who have no intention whatsoever of aborting based on sex and merely wish to know the fetus’s sex from accessing fetal sex information before 32 weeks of pregnancy. This is not only ineffective or unsuitable for achieving the purpose of protecting fetal life, but can also be said to be markedly irrational and unfair as a legislative means.\\n\\n(c) Of course, as noted above, even if no meaningful relationship is seen between fetal sex and abortion and the sex ratio at birth has become balanced, there may still be cases where parents who learn the fetus’s sex through a medical practitioner’s notification of fetal sex before 32 weeks of pregnancy end up having an abortion based on sex.\\n\\nHowever, in such cases, the act that deprives the fetus of life is not the act of notification of fetal sex, but the abortion based on sex; thus, the stage at which the State must intervene and regulate for the protection of fetal life is not notification of fetal sex, but the stage at which abortion based on sex occurs.\\n\\nAt present, induced abortion is regulated by the Mother and Child Health Act, and the abortion offense provision in the Criminal Act, which punishes abortion, lost effect from January 1, 2021, because no ameliorative legislation was enacted by the legislative deadline of December 31, 2020, after the Constitutional Court’s decision of April 11, 2019, 2017HEONBA127, which rendered a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution with respect to the abortion offense provision. Since amendments to the Criminal Act concerning the abortion offense and amendments to the Mother and Child Health Act are being discussed in the National Assembly, the protection of fetal life through the prevention of sex-selective abortion should ultimately be resolved by ameliorative legislation by the National Assembly related to abortion, rather than by restricting notification of fetal sex.\\n\\nHowever, the provision at issue, based solely on the very exceptional circumstance that there may be abortion based on sex, presupposes the act of notifying fetal sex as a preparatory act for abortion and makes it impossible for all parents to know fetal sex information before 32 weeks of pregnancy. In other words, while invoking the legislative purpose of preventing abortion based on fetal sex, it in fact also regulates parents who have no intention of proceeding to abortion. This is excessive legislation beyond the necessity and scope of regulation, and it can be said to restrict the fundamental rights of parents beyond the minimum necessary extent.\\n\\n(d) Accordingly, the provision at issue is not suitable as a means to achieve the legislative purpose of protecting fetal life, and by constraining the parents’ right not to be prevented from accessing fetal sex information more than necessary, it violates the least-restrictive-means requirement.\\n\\n(4) Balance of interests\\nAs seen above, the problem of sex imbalance in our society has now been resolved, and the public interest of protecting fetal life cannot be said to be effectively achieved through the provision at issue. Since the provision at issue excessively restricts the right of all parents not to be prevented from accessing fetal sex information before 32 weeks of pregnancy, the provision at issue has ultimately also lost the balance of interests.\\n\\n(5) Conclusion\\nAccordingly, the provision at issue violates the principle against excessive restriction and infringes the right of parents not to be prevented from accessing fetal sex information.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nTherefore, since the provision at issue is unconstitutional, it is so decided as stated in the order. In this decision, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous, except for the opinion of incompatibility with the Constitution by Justice Lee Jong-seok, Justice Lee Eun-ae, and Justice Kim Hyung-du as set forth in 6 below.\\n\\n6. Opinion of Incompatibility with the Constitution by Justices Lee Jong-seok, Lee Eun-ae, and Kim Hyung-du\\nWe think that, although the provision at issue is recognized as having a legitimate legislative purpose and suitability of means, the 32-week pregnancy criterion established by the provision at issue is an excessive restriction in terms of duration and thus violates the least-restrictive-means requirement. And because we believe that a mere decision of unconstitutionality regarding the provision at issue should be rejected and a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution should be rendered, we state our opinion as follows.\\n\\na. Legitimacy of legislative purpose and suitability of means\\nAs examined in the majority opinion, the provision at issue has a legitimate legislative purpose. The content examined by the Constitutional Court under suitability of means is not whether the method chosen by the legislature was the best, but is limited to whether the method is an effective means for achieving the legislative purpose (Constitutional Court decision of January 17, 2007, 2006HEONBA3). It can be said that son preference is currently declining considerably, but it must be said that the possibility remains that a pregnant woman and her family may still have an abortion depending on their preference for the fetus’s sex, so it cannot be denied that prohibiting notification of fetal sex before 32 weeks of pregnancy has the effect of preventing abortion based on sex. Accordingly, unlike the majority opinion, the provision at issue should be recognized as satisfying suitability of means.\\n\\nb. Least-restrictive means\\n(1) According to the “2018 National Fertility and Family Health and Welfare Survey” published by the Korea Institute for Health and Social Affairs and the weekly report survey of the Hankook Research “2023 Childbearing and Childcare Awareness Survey” mentioned in the majority opinion, it can be seen that, 15 years after amendment into the provision at issue, our country has, due to changes in the people’s values and consciousness, seen the son preference influenced by the traditional Confucian society “substantially” decline. However, it cannot be said that son preference has “completely” disappeared, and even if not limited to son preference, it can be seen that parents have preferences regarding the sex of their children.\\n\\nAccording to the 2022 announcement by Statistics Korea, the total fertility rate in the Republic of Korea is 0.78, the lowest among OECD countries, and our country is currently in a situation where a tendency to avoid childbirth is widespread. In addition, the Constitutional Court, in its decision of April 11, 2019, 2017HEONBA127, rendered a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution with respect to the abortion offense provision of the Criminal Act, and because no ameliorative legislation was enacted by December 31, 2020 after that decision, the above abortion offense provision lost effect from January 1, 2021.\\n\\nIn such circumstances, if, in addition to son preference, the tendency to have only one child of the sex desired by the parents is added, there will be a possibility that induced abortion may be carried out depending on fetal sex. In the “2021 Induced Abortion Survey Report,” the proportion of respondents who answered “because of child planning (not wanting children, spacing between children, etc.)” as the reason for pregnancy termination among persons with experience of pregnancy termination was 29% (multiple-answer ratio for two selections), so if the restriction on notification of fetal sex disappears, it is difficult to deny the possibility that child planning according to sex preference may become a reason for induced abortion.\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court, in its decision of April 11, 2019, 2017HEONBA127, rendered a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution with respect to the abortion offense provision of the Criminal Act and held that the grounds justifying abortion set forth in the Mother and Child Health Act do not at all include “situations of abortion conflict due to a wide variety of social and economic reasons that make maintaining pregnancy and giving birth difficult,” and are therefore insufficient to guarantee the self-determination rights of pregnant women. Since abortion based solely on the fetus’s sex cannot be viewed as included among the social and economic reasons that make maintaining pregnancy and giving birth difficult mentioned in the above decision, it can be said that the need to regulate abortion based on sex for the protection of fetal life continues to exist.\\n\\nTherefore, because one cannot be certain that abortion based on sex has completely disappeared and there is a possibility that notification of fetal sex may lead to abortion, it can be said that there is a need to restrict notification of fetal sex in order to protect fetal life, for which the State bears grave responsibility. However, this restricts the right not to be prevented from accessing fetal sex information, which is a natural and essential right that parents are entitled to as parents, and thus the restriction should be limited to the minimum necessary extent; therefore, below we examine whether the provision at issue violates the least-restrictive-means requirement.\\n\\n(2) In the course of review in the precedent decision, the Korean Medical Association submitted an opinion stating that fetal sex notification should be permitted based on 28 weeks of pregnancy, which was then the point before which induced abortion was not permitted under Article 15(1) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Mother and Child Health Act (as amended by Presidential Decree No. 19502 on June 7, 2006, and before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 21618 on July 7, 2009). The majority opinion in the precedent decision also held that, according to the above Enforcement Decree provision, even if notification of fetal sex is exceptionally permitted in the latter half of pregnancy, when abortion is in fact not possible, there is no possibility that abortion will occur after 28 weeks of pregnancy, just as abortion is prohibited after 28 weeks, and therefore prohibiting notification of fetal sex during that period violates the Constitution.\\n\\nAccordingly, although a bill amending the Medical Services Act to prohibit notification of fetal sex before 28 weeks of pregnancy was introduced, during the bill review process in the Health, Welfare and Family Affairs Committee of the National Assembly, when a member expressed the opinion that abortion is possible even at 28 weeks, the bill was amended on December 31, 2009 into the provision at issue, changing the threshold from 28 weeks to 32 weeks and prohibiting notification of fetal sex before that point (see the National Assembly minutes).\\n\\nMeanwhile, before the Medical Services Act was amended into the provision at issue as above, Article 15(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Mother and Child Health Act was wholly amended by Presidential Decree No. 21618 on July 7, 2009, and the upper limit for permitted induced abortion was changed from 28 weeks of pregnancy to 24 weeks of pregnancy; however, this amendment to the Enforcement Decree was not reflected in the review process for the above Medical Services Act amendment bill. Looking at this legislative process, it is difficult to say that there was specific grounds for the 32-week criterion established by the provision at issue or that there was in-depth discussion for minimizing the restriction on fundamental rights.\\n\\n(3) According to the Ministry of Health and Welfare’s “2021 Induced Abortion Survey,” the average gestational week at the time of induced abortion surgery was 6.7 weeks of pregnancy, and in cumulative terms the figures were 27% for 4 weeks or less, 81.7% for 8 weeks or less, 89.8% for 10 weeks or less, 94.5% for 12 weeks or less, and 97.7% for 16 weeks or less, while the ratio after 24 weeks of pregnancy was 0.5%. In other words, as the gestational weeks increase, the abortion ratio sharply decreases, and it can be seen that abortions after 24 weeks of pregnancy, which are prohibited in the Enforcement Decree of the Mother and Child Health Act, occur only in a very small number. Once the latter half of pregnancy begins, abortion itself generally entails risks to the pregnant woman, so it can be said that the possibility of abortion based on fetal sex is almost nonexistent.\\n\\nTherefore, in a situation where the sex ratio at birth has entered the normal range of the natural sex ratio and son preference has declined, lowering the need to strictly regulate notification of fetal sex as in the past, the provision at issue, which prohibits notification of fetal sex until 32 weeks of pregnancy, which is full term and far exceeds the gestational weeks regulated as the upper limit for permitted induced abortion in other statutes such as the Mother and Child Health Act, can be said to be an excessive restriction in terms of duration.\\n\\nIn addition, when a hereditary disease such as an X-chromosome-dependent disease is suspected, medical necessity requires advance confirmation of fetal sex because medical measures differ depending on the fetus’s sex, and there may be situations in which a medical practitioner must inform the fetus’s parents of the sex during the examination process. Nevertheless, the provision at issue does not recognize any exception even in such cases and uniformly restricts notification of fetal sex before 32 weeks of pregnancy, so it cannot be said to satisfy the least-restrictive-means requirement in this respect either.\\n\\n(4) Meanwhile, unlike in the past when fetal sex could be determined only around 16 weeks of pregnancy through ultrasonography, advances in prenatal diagnostic test technology have made it possible to determine fetal sex after 10 weeks of pregnancy when tests are conducted to identify fetal genetic information. At this time, the risk of abortion is relatively low, so if the restriction on notification of fetal sex is removed, the possibility of abortion based on sex would be greater.\\n\\nIn Constitutional Court decision of April 11, 2019, 2017HEONBA127, which rendered a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution with respect to the abortion offense provision in the Criminal Act, the Court held that a blanket prohibition on abortions that do not fall within the grounds set forth in the Mother and Child Health Act during the period before approximately 22 weeks of pregnancy, when the fetus can independently survive outside the mother’s body, and while sufficient time is guaranteed to exercise self-determination concerning whether to maintain the pregnancy and give birth (hereinafter, from implantation until this period, the “decision-making period”), violates the principle against excessive restriction and infringes the self-determination rights of pregnant women. Accordingly, amendments to the Criminal Act and the Mother and Child Health Act concerning the abortion offense are being discussed in the National Assembly.\\n\\nIf fetal sex is notified within the decision-making period mentioned in the above Constitutional Court decision concerning the abortion offense, fetal sex may be included as a factor in considering whether to abort, so the possibility of abortion based on that sex can be said to be relatively high. On the other hand, as the gestational weeks increase, the possibility of abortion decreases, and after the time point that exceeds the permitted limit for abortion established by the Enforcement Decree of the Mother and Child Health Act, abortion itself poses a considerable risk to the pregnant woman, so the possibility of abortion based on fetal sex can be said to be slim. Since the provision at issue is intended to regulate abortion based on sex, notifying fetal sex at a time when the possibility of such abortion becomes considerably low will not particularly impede the achievement of the legislative purpose of the provision at issue.\\n\\nAccordingly, the provision at issue should be amended so as to minimize infringement by advancing the time at which notification of fetal sex is restricted, taking into account the decision-making period mentioned in the above Constitutional Court decision concerning the abortion offense, the time point for permitted abortion established by the Enforcement Decree of the Mother and Child Health Act, and the status shown in the induced abortion surveys.\\n\\nc. Balance of interests\\nWhether a future baby to be born will be female or male constitutes important fetal personal information for the pregnant woman or her family, and the parents’ desire to know this in advance is an instinctive and natural desire. If the sex of the fetus is known in advance, it will not only be possible to plan in advance for the future of the baby to be born, but it can also be usefully utilized in prenatal education or in preparing for childbirth. Therefore, the parents’ right not to be prevented from accessing fetal sex information is also a fundamental right worthy of protection (see Constitutional Court decision of July 31, 2008, 2004HEONMA1010, etc.).\\n\\nOn the other hand, since the fetus is a living being destined to become a human being, fetal life has a noble and dignified value, and because the protection of fetal life is an important public interest and the State has a duty to protect it, it must generally be protected in preference to the parents’ right not to be prevented from accessing fetal sex information.\\n\\nHowever, although the likelihood that notification of fetal sex will induce infringement of fetal life decreases considerably as gestational weeks increase, and becomes extremely low after the time point exceeding the permitted limit for abortion under the Mother and Child Health Act, etc., the provision at issue, based on 32 weeks of pregnancy, which is full term, prohibits parents’ access to fetal sex information before that point and does not recognize exceptions for medically necessary cases; this is an excessive infringement of private interests and thus violates the balance of interests.\\n\\nd. Conclusion\\nAccordingly, the provision at issue violates the principle against excessive restriction and infringes the parents’ right not to be prevented from accessing fetal sex information.\\n\\ne. Necessity of a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution\\nFetal life is precious in and of itself, and under the Constitution’s normative and objective value order that respects life, as well as Article 10 of the Constitution, which declares human dignity and value, the State bears a grave responsibility to protect fetal life (Constitutional Court decision of April 11, 2019, 2017HEONBA127). The possibility of abortion based on sex still remains in our society, so even if that possibility is lower than in the past, the State must not neglect its responsibility to protect fetal life from such abortions. As examined above, the provision at issue prohibits notification of fetal sex based on 32 weeks of pregnancy, which is full term, and therefore violates the least-restrictive-means requirement; however, the need to restrict notification of fetal sex as a means to prevent abortion based on sex and protect fetal life continues to exist.\\n\\nHowever, as in the majority opinion, rendering a mere decision of unconstitutionality would result in abolishing in one stroke, without any alternative, the means for protecting fetal life, and therefore is not appropriate. Accordingly, a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution should be rendered with respect to the provision at issue, and the legislature should be left to enact ameliorative legislation that advances the time point for restricting notification of fetal sex, taking into account various circumstances including amendments to the Criminal Act concerning the abortion offense and the Enforcement Decree of the Mother and Child Health Act, thereby minimizing the infringement of fundamental rights of the fetus’s parents while ensuring that there is no legal vacuum concerning the means for protecting fetal life.\\n\\nIf so, it is appropriate to render a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution that provisionally applies the provision at issue until the unconstitutionality is removed by new legislation."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning the principle of protection of trust is correct? (In cases of dispute, according to case law)
A: Even if a statute is unconstitutional, until the Constitutional Court renders a decision of unconstitutionality with respect to that statute, its constitutionality is presumed; therefore, the same level of protection as for a trust interest based on a constitutional statute, namely, the State’s duty of protection derived from the Constitution, is required.
B: While amending the law to exclude children of persons decorated for meritorious service in the defense of the nation from the category subject to bonus points in recruitment examinations conducted by employment-support implementing institutions, the supplementary provision of the Act on the Honorable Treatment and Support of Persons, etc. of Distinguished Service to the State, which did not provide transitional measures for a person who had long formed the expectation that he or she would become a child of a person decorated for meritorious service in the defense of the nation in the near future and thereby receive bonus points in a recruitment examination, violates the principle of protection of trust.
C: The 3-year grace period prescribed in the supplementary provision of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on Resource Circulation of Electrical and Electronic Equipment and Vehicles, which required even a person who had registered a waste-material recycling business under the former statutes to satisfy the registration standards within 3 years, is excessively short to adequately cope with changes in circumstances caused by the amendment of the statute and therefore violates the principle of protection of trust.
D: Even if a provision of the former Act on Dam Construction and Support of Surrounding Areas, etc., which provides that, in the case of an order to cancel or change a dam use right, the State shall return part of the charges or payments paid by the dam use right holder, and that the amount to be returned may not exceed the amount after deducting the depreciation amount prescribed by Presidential Decree, is applied to a dam use right holder who had already acquired and was exercising a dam use right, it does not violate the principle of protection of trust because the public-interest value of the rational development and use of water resources through multipurpose dams is very great compared with the dam use right holder’s trust interest in the continuance of the dam use right.
E: Since a medical practitioner’s trust in the former legal order that he or she could operate multiple medical institutions is a trust worthy of constitutional protection, if the relevant provision of the Medical Service Act was later amended to provide that a medical practitioner may not, under any name whatsoever, operate more than one medical institution, it violates the principle of protection of trust.

Although a medical practitioner may not, under any pretext, establish and operate two or more medical institutions, Complainant Park ○○ was indicted on the following charges: from 2011. 10. 6. until around 2012. 8. 24., he established and operated ○○ Hospital (Ansan) in Ansan-si (address omitted) in his own name; from 2012. 8. 31. until 2013. 11. 20., he established and operated ○○ Hospital (Gangdong) in his own name in Gangdong-gu, Seoul (address omitted); and from around 2012. 8. 24. until around 2013. 11. 20., he established ○○ Hospital (Ansan) in the name of Hong ○○ by agreeing to pay a monthly salary of 30,000,000 won, and from around 2013. 6. 14. until around 2013. 11. 20., he established ○○ Hospital (Suwon) located in Suwon-si (address omitted) in the name of Kim ▽▽ by agreeing to pay a monthly salary of 30,000,000 won, and in fact Complainant Park ○○ directly operated the above hospitals, thereby establishing and operating two or more medical institutions. He was prosecuted on such charges, and on 2014. 4. 15., he was sentenced in the first instance to imprisonment for 1 year and 8 months [Daegu District Court Western Branch 2013GODAN1402, 1435 (consolidated)], appealed, but received a judgment dismissing the appeal on 2014. 9. 18. (Daegu District Court 2014NO1391), filed a final appeal, and then withdrew the final appeal on 2014. 11. 28., whereupon the above judgment became final.\\n\\n(2) Complainant Park ○○ applied, during the pendency of the above first-instance case, for a referral for constitutional review regarding Article 33(8) of the Medical Service Act, which prohibited medical practitioners from establishing and operating duplicate medical institutions (Daegu District Court Western Branch 2013CHOGI829), but upon dismissal on 2014. 4. 15., he filed the present constitutional complaint on 2014. 5. 15. against the penal provision in Article 87(1) subparagraph 2 of the Medical Service Act, as to the main clause of Article 33(8).\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\na. The Complainants filed constitutional complaints either against the entire main clause of Article 33(8) of the Medical Service Act (amended by Act No. 11252 on 2012. 2. 1.; hereinafter, regardless of history, the current Act is referred to as the “Medical Service Act”) or against the term “operate” in the main clause of Article 33(8) of the Medical Service Act. The main clause of Article 33(8) of the Medical Service Act prohibits medical practitioners from establishing and operating two or more medical institutions. Since “duplicate establishment” and “duplicate operation” are conceptually distinct, and the acts of the Complainants and applicants for referral at issue in this case were not acts prohibited under the former Medical Service Act (the version before amendment by Act No. 11252 on 2012. 2. 1.; hereinafter referred to only as the “former Medical Service Act”), but were newly prohibited when the Medical Service Act was amended, and since what the Complainants and applicants for referral mainly dispute in this case is that it is unconstitutional to additionally regulate the duplicate operation aspect that had not previously been regulated when the Medical Service Act was amended, the subject matter of review in this case shall be limited to the term “operate” in the main clause of Article 33(8) of the Medical Service Act.\\n\\nb. Meanwhile, the referring court also referred the term “under any pretext” in the main clause of Article 33(8) of the Medical Service Act for constitutional review, but the phrase “under any pretext” in the provision at issue merely means that operating multiple medical institutions is absolutely prohibited, so it is sufficient to determine this together with the above “operate” term.\\n\\nc. Accordingly, the subject matter of review in this case is whether the term “operate” in the main clause of Article 33(8) of the Medical Service Act (amended by Act No. 11252 on 2012. 2. 1.; hereinafter, the “provision prohibiting at issue”) and the term “operate” in the main clause of Article 33(8) among subparagraph 2 of Article 87(1) of the former Medical Service Act (the version amended by Act No. 11252 on 2012. 2. 1. and before amendment by Act No. 13658 on 2015. 12. 29.; hereinafter, the “penal provision at issue,” and collectively with the provision prohibiting at issue, the “statutory provisions at issue”) are unconstitutional, and the text of the provisions subject to review and related provisions is as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Review]\\n\\nMedical Service Act (amended by Act No. 11252 on 2012. 2. 1.)\\n\\nArticle 33 (Establishment, etc.) (8) A medical practitioner under subparagraph 1 of paragraph (2) may not establish and operate two or more medical institutions under any pretext.
