The Complainants’ Arguments and the Grounds for the Referring Court’s Constitutional Referral\\n\\na. The Complainants’ Arguments\\n\\n(1) The statutory provisions at issue are contrary to the principle of clarity because the meaning of “operate” is unclear.\\n\\n(2) Prohibiting a medical practitioner from being involved in the operation of multiple medical institutions under any pretext is contrary to the principle against excessive restriction and infringes a medical practitioner’s freedom of occupation, property rights, freedom of contract, and right to self-determination. As the statutory provisions at issue were amended and enforced, medical practitioners who already operated multiple medical institutions were forced to dispose of them, which not only infringes a medical practitioner’s property rights but also violates the principle of protection of trust.\\n\\n(3) The statutory provisions at issue violate the principle of equality by discriminating, without rational basis, between individual medical practitioners and corporations such as medical corporations and nonprofit corporations, and by discriminating between medical practitioners and pharmacists, traditional herbal pharmacists, and attorneys.\\n\\n(4) The statutory penalty prescribed in the penal provision at issue—imprisonment for not more than 5 years or a fine not exceeding 20,000,000 won—is excessively severe in light of the degree of reproachability and thus violates the principle of proportionality between responsibility and punishment.\\n\\nb. Reasons for the Referring Court’s Constitutional Referral\\n\\nThe statutory provisions at issue are intended to prevent illegal medical practices such as patient solicitation, excessive treatment, and delegated treatment, as well as profit-maximizing conduct, and thus the legitimacy of purpose is recognized. However, such legislative purpose could be achieved by directly regulating the problematic acts and by strengthening enforcement and punishment, whereas the statutory provisions at issue comprehensively prohibit medical practitioners’ investment in and participation in the management of other medical institutions, and therefore they contravene the principles of suitability of means and minimum restriction. Accordingly, the statutory provisions at issue infringe the freedom of occupation of medical practitioners and are unconstitutional.\\n\\n4. Decision\\n\\na. History and Background of the Introduction of the Statutory Provisions at Issue\\n\\n(1) History of the Statutory Provisions at Issue\\n\\n(a) The prohibition on medical practitioners establishing only one medical institution dates from the amendment of the Medical Service Act by Act No. 4732 on 1994. 1. 7. Before that, the Act merely provided that only medical practitioners could establish medical institutions, and imposed no limitation on the number of medical institutions that a medical practitioner could establish. However, with the amendment of the Medical Service Act on 1994. 1. 7., even a medical practitioner could establish only one medical institution (proviso to Article 30(2)), and violation was amended to be punishable by imprisonment for not more than 5 years or by a fine not exceeding 20,000,000 won (Article 66 subparagraph 3).\\n\\n(b) Thereafter, when the Medical Service Act was entirely amended by Act No. 8366 on 2007. 4. 11., the content previously located in the first sentence of the proviso to Article 30(2) was moved to the first sentence of the proviso to Article 33(2), and the wording “one medical institution” was changed to “one medical institution,” and the penal provision for violation was also moved from Article 66 subparagraph 3 to Article 87(1) subparagraph 2.\\n\\nRegarding the proviso to Article 33(2) of the above Medical Service Act, the Constitutional Court, on 2007. 12. 27., held it unconstitutional on the ground that “requiring a medical practitioner holding multiple licenses to establish only one medical institution infringes the freedom of occupation and equality rights of a multi-licensed medical practitioner” (2007. 12. 27. 2004HEONMA1021). Accordingly, when the Medical Service Act was amended by Act No. 9386 on 2009. 1. 30., the content previously located in the first sentence of the proviso to Article 33(2) was moved to the main clause of Article 33(8), and the proviso added the following: “Provided, That where a person holding two or more medical licenses intends to establish a clinic-level medical institution, medical institutions according to the type of license may be established together in only one location.”\\n\\n(c) Thereafter, when the Medical Service Act was amended by Act No. 11252 on 2012. 2. 1., Article 4(2) was newly established, so that medical practitioners could not establish or operate medical institutions in the name of another medical practitioner, and the main clause of Article 33(8) was also amended to add the provision at issue prohibiting such conduct, thereby providing that medical practitioners may not establish and operate two or more medical institutions, and the penal provision at issue was added to Article 87(1) subparagraph 2 as the provision for punishment in case of violation.\\n\\n(d) The penal provision at issue, when the Medical Service Act was amended by Act No. 14438 on 2016. 12. 20., had its upper limit for fines raised to imprisonment for not more than 5 years or a fine not exceeding 50,000,000 won, and when the Medical Service Act was amended by Act No. 16375 on 2019. 4. 23., the location of the provision was moved to Article 87(2) subparagraph 2.\\n\\n(2) Background to the Introduction of the Statutory Provisions at Issue\\n\\n(a) Owing to the increase in the number of medical practitioners and the resulting quantitative increase in medical institutions, competition in the medical market is becoming increasingly intense. In order to overcome the deterioration in management caused by this increase in supply, various management strategies emerged, centered on small and medium-sized hospitals and clinics, such as joint establishment, and the strengthening of advertising and publicity; among such management strategies, collaboration and linkage among medical institutions, so-called medical institutions with a duplicate operation model, emerged.\\n\\n(b) Under the former Medical Service Act before amendment by Act No. 11252 on 2012. 2. 1., a “duplicate operation model that does not involve medical practice” was not prohibited. The main clause of Article 33(8) of the former Medical Service Act merely provided that “a medical practitioner under subparagraph 1 of paragraph (2) may establish only one medical institution.” Regarding this, the Supreme Court held that: “where a medical practitioner who has established a medical institution in his or her own name establishes another medical institution in the name of another medical practitioner and directly hires and pays salaries to the employees belonging to it and takes profits generated according to its operation, mere direct involvement in the management of the newly established medical institution does not amount to borrowing another medical practitioner’s license and in substance establishing a separate medical institution; however, where that person directly performs medical practice in a medical institution established in the name of another medical practitioner or hires unqualified persons and has them perform medical practice under his or her supervision, this constitutes establishing medical institutions in duplicate” (Supreme Court Decision 2003DO256, decided 2003. 10. 23.).\\n\\nHowever, on the other hand, the need for sanctions was raised on the ground that such duplicate operation models induce illegal acts such as patient solicitation, excessive treatment, and delegated treatment, and the National Assembly amended the Medical Service Act by Act No. 11252 on 2012. 2. 1. and introduced the statutory provisions at issue on the ground that “recently, some medical practitioners, under the pretext of simple management purposes, are maximizing profits by establishing medical institutions at multiple locations under the licenses of other physicians, thereby operating the relevant medical institutions as sales organizations to solicit patients or to encourage illegal medical practices such as excessive treatment and delegated treatment; thus, by preventing medical practitioners from lending their licenses to non-medical persons or other medical practitioners for the establishment and management of medical institutions, illegal medical practices should be prevented and public health protected.” Accordingly, the very operation of multiple medical institutions, regardless of whether medical practice is actually performed, became prohibited.\\n\\nb. Issues in the Case\\n\\n(1) Fundamental Rights Restricted\\n\\n(a) The statutory provisions at issue prohibit medical practitioners from operating two or more medical institutions and subject violations to criminal punishment. Limiting the number of medical institutions that a medical practitioner may operate in this way restricts the occupational performance method of a medical practitioner who wishes to operate multiple medical institutions. Accordingly, the issue is whether the statutory provisions at issue infringe a medical practitioner’s freedom of occupation, specifically the freedom to engage in occupational performance.\\n\\n(b) Complainants Park ○○, Jo ○○, Lim ○○, Kim ○○, and Kim □□ argue that the statutory provisions at issue also infringe a medical practitioner’s property rights. However, the penal provision at issue is merely a provision that imposes criminal punishment for violation of the provision prohibiting at issue, and the provision prohibiting at issue also merely prohibits duplicate operation of medical institutions and does not directly compel disposal of property; disposal of property such as the sale of a medical institution is only an incidental effect. Accordingly, we will not separately determine whether there is an infringement of a medical practitioner’s property rights.\\n\\nComplainants Jo ○○, Lim ○○, Kim ○○, Kim □□, and Choi ○○ argue that the statutory provisions at issue also infringe a medical practitioner’s freedom of contract or right to self-determination. However, because freedom of contract and the right to self-determination, which are contents guaranteed under Article 10 of the Constitution, are concretized in the area of occupational performance as the freedom to engage in occupational performance, the content that the right to pursue happiness seeks to supplement is already protected by the freedom to engage in occupational performance under Article 15 of the Constitution, with which it has a special relationship (see Constitutional Court 2010. 3. 25. 2009HEONMA170; Constitutional Court 2017. 12. 28. 2016HEONBA346). Therefore, insofar as we determine whether the statutory provisions at issue infringe a medical practitioner’s freedom to engage in occupational performance, we will not separately determine whether there is an infringement of freedom of contract or the right to self-determination.\\n\\n(2) Method of Review\\n\\n(a) The statutory provisions at issue prohibit duplicate operation of medical institutions and punish violations thereof. Here, because the Medical Service Act and other laws do not define the meaning of “operate” at all, the issue first arises whether the statutory provisions at issue contravene the principle of clarity under the principle of legality in criminal law. Further, the issue is whether the restriction on the number of medical institutions that a medical practitioner may operate under the statutory provisions at issue contravenes the principle against excessive restriction and the principle of protection of trust, and in particular whether the statutory penalty prescribed by the penal provision at issue contravenes the principle of proportionality between responsibility and punishment. In addition, it is also an issue whether the statutory provisions at issue contravene the principle of equality by discriminating, without rational basis, between individual medical practitioners and corporations such as medical corporations and nonprofit corporations.\\n\\n(b) Complainants Park ○○, Jo ○○, Lim ○○, Kim ○○, and Kim □□ argue that, unlike the Pharmacists Act or the Attorneys-at-Law Act, the Medical Service Act alone prohibits duplicate operation of medical institutions, and thus discriminates without rational basis between medical practitioners and pharmacists, Korean medicine pharmacists, and attorneys. However, medical practitioners are persons who perform medical acts such as medical treatment and health guidance in order to protect and promote the health of the people, and medical acts directly affect a person’s body or life. Since medical practitioners, pharmacists, Korean medicine pharmacists, and attorneys are entirely different in qualifications, the content of their work, and whether medical acts are permitted, they cannot be regarded as essentially identical comparison groups. Therefore, in this case, because there is no discriminatory treatment itself, we will not go further and determine this point.\\n\\nComplainant Park ○○ also argues that the statutory provisions at issue do not apply to medical practitioners who have expanded overseas before the provisions came into force and are already operating multiple medical institutions overseas, but apply only to medical practitioners who have not yet expanded overseas, and thus violate the principle of equality. However, the statutory provisions at issue do not differ in applicability depending on whether the start time of duplicate operation was before or after the enforcement of the Act, so the discriminatory treatment alleged by Complainant Park ○○ cannot be said to exist. Accordingly, we will not go further and determine this point either.\\n\\nc. Whether the Principle of Clarity under the Principle of Legality in Criminal Law Was Violated\\n\\n(1) Meaning\\n\\nThe principle of legality in criminal law, guaranteed through Articles 12 and 13 of the Constitution, means that crimes and punishments must be prescribed by statute, and the principle of clarity derived from such principle of legality in criminal law requires that the elements of an offense be clearly defined so that anyone can foresee what conduct the law intends to punish and what punishment will be imposed therefor, and accordingly determine his or her own conduct. However, requiring the elements of a penal provision to be clear does not mean that all elements must be prescribed by simple descriptive concepts; even if somewhat broad concepts requiring supplementary interpretation by judges are used, there is no conflict with the clarity of penal provisions required by the Constitution so long as, by ordinary interpretive methods, a person with sound common sense and ordinary legal sentiments can know the protected legal interest of the penal provision, the prohibited conduct, and the type and degree of punishment. Further, whether there is predictability concerning a penal provision should not be determined by examining only that particular provision alone, but should be determined by comprehensively and systematically considering the entire related statutory scheme, and should be reviewed specifically and individually according to the nature of each statute at issue (Constitutional Court 2011. 10. 25. 2010HEONGA29).\\n\\n(2) Determination\\n\\n(a) First, we examine the meaning of “operate” as provided in the statutory provisions at issue.\\n\\nIn the dictionary sense, “operate” means “to use and manage an organization, institution, business, etc.,” so “operate” may be said to be another expression for “manage.”\\n\\nHowever, the former Medical Service Act Article 33(8) had only prohibited “duplicate establishment” by providing that “a medical practitioner under subparagraph 1 of paragraph (2) may establish only one medical institution,” and the Supreme Court had determined whether the provision applied based on whether a medical practitioner performed medical practice in multiple medical institutions. Accordingly, where a medical practitioner who established and operated a medical institution in his or her own name merely directly involved himself or herself in the management of the medical institution established in the name of another medical practitioner, without directly performing medical practice there or hiring unqualified persons and having them perform medical practice under his or her supervision, this did not constitute “establishing medical institutions in duplicate” (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DO256, decided 2003. 10. 23.). Later, the main clause of Article 33(8) of the Medical Service Act amended by Act No. 11252 on 2012. 2. 1. added “duplicate operation” to the prohibited acts. The purpose of this amendment, premised on the Supreme Court’s prior interpretation, was to prohibit even so-called “economic duplicate establishment,” in which a medical practitioner does not perform medical practice but merely operates multiple medical institutions. Therefore, it is appropriate to understand “operate” here as referring to the “management” of duplicate operation of medical institutions that the Supreme Court had previously excluded as not punishable.\\n\\nIn this regard, the Supreme Court recently held that “when determining in a concrete case whether there is duplicate operation of medical institutions, all circumstances should be considered, such as whether the person is in a leading position as an operator, that is, the process of establishing two or more medical institutions, the role of the person in whose name the establishment was made, the relationship with other medical practitioners alleged to be involved in management, the method of financing, the decision-making structure concerning management, the subject exercising authority to direct and supervise workers, the form of distribution of operational results, and, where there is a hospital management support company (Management Service Organization, MSO) operated by another medical practitioner, the amount of expenses incurred to that hospital management support company and the transaction details, and one must examine whether two or more medical institutions independently maintain their own identity in terms of decision-making and attribution of operational results, or whether a particular medical practitioner, beyond merely entering into a cooperative relationship or providing management support or investment, actually dominates and manages the operation of two or more medical institutions” (Supreme Court Decision 2018DO3672, decided 2018. 7. 12.), thereby presenting concrete criteria for determination.\\n\\nWhen the dictionary meaning of “operate,” the court’s interpretation thereof, the purpose of the amendment of the Medical Service Act, and the form of the provision are comprehensively considered, the “establishment” and “operation” prescribed in the main clause of Article 33(8) of the Medical Service Act are conceptually distinct. The “duplicate establishment” prohibited here means “where a medical practitioner who has already established a medical institution in his or her own name directly performs medical practice in a medical institution established in the name of another medical practitioner, or has unqualified persons perform medical practice under his or her supervision,” and the distinct concept of “duplicate operation” means “where a medical practitioner, while possessing decision-making authority regarding management matters such as the existence or abolition, relocation, whether medical practice is performed, financing, staffing/facility/equipment procurement and management, and attribution and distribution of operational results in respect of two or more medical institutions, processes related business or causes it to be processed” (Supreme Court Decision 2018DO3672, decided 2018. 7. 12.).\\n\\n(b) On the other hand, criticism has been raised that the statutory provisions at issue merely designate “operate” without specifically enumerating the forms of conduct regulated, thereby making it impossible to foresee the types of conduct prohibited and punished.\\n\\nThe forms in which a medical practitioner is involved in operating multiple medical institutions are diverse. It is quite difficult to list in the law every such diverse type of duplicate operation model one by one, and even if a specific type is involved, permissibility is not determined merely on the basis of that outward form. New forms of operation may continue to appear in the future due to the development of medical technology and information technology, opening of the medical market, and strengthening of medical professionalism. In such a situation, if the prohibited forms of operation are specifically identified and enumerated in the law, a legislative gap may instead arise, causing the law to fail to regulate properly when needed. Therefore, it is inevitable that the law determine the types of prohibited conduct in an open-ended manner that can be concretized through interpretation, and it is sufficient if the meaning of the statutory provision can be supplemented through judicial interpretation and application in concrete cases.\\n\\n(c) Therefore, although the Medical Service Act and related statutes do not contain a definition of “operate” as prescribed in the statutory provisions at issue, as noted above, it is sufficiently foreseeable that “duplicate operation of medical institutions” means “where a medical practitioner, with decision-making authority regarding management matters such as the existence or abolition, relocation, whether medical practice is performed, financing, staffing/facility/equipment procurement and management, and attribution and distribution of operational results in respect of two or more medical institutions, processes related business or causes it to be processed,” and because the concrete content can be supplemented by ordinary judicial interpretation and application, the statutory provisions at issue do not contravene the principle of clarity under the principle of legality in criminal law.\\n\\nd. Whether the Principle against Excessive Restriction Was Violated\\n\\n(1) Legitimacy of Purpose and Suitability of Means\\n\\nArticle 36(3) of the Constitution provides that “all citizens shall be protected by the State in matters of health,” and the State bears a social-state duty to protect the health of the people and, for that purpose, to guarantee appropriate medical benefits to the people (Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2001HEONBA87). Accordingly, the Medical Service Act declares in Article 1 that “the purpose of this Act is to protect and promote the health of the people by prescribing matters necessary for national medical care so that all citizens may receive high-quality medical benefits,” while Article 2(2) provides that “medical practitioners have the mission of contributing to the improvement of public health and the securing of healthy living for the people,” thereby conferring a public-interest mission upon medical practitioners. If so, the purpose of the statutory provisions at issue, which prohibit medical practitioners from operating two or more medical institutions and punish violations, must likewise be understood in relation to such purpose of the Medical Service Act.\\n\\nHealth care is not a mere object of commerce, but something special that deals with human life and health. Health care services have characteristics different from ordinary goods, such as information asymmetry between market participants including providers and consumers, uncertainty of demand, uncertainty of treatment, and legal monopoly. Therefore, if supply and demand are left entirely to the market in a situation where autonomous regulation or legal regulation limiting the pursuit of profitability by the private sector is insufficient, market failure or a decrease in social welfare may result, such as an increase in the people’s medical expenses through induced demand, pursuit of high-cost services, and excessive specialization of medical personnel, and a decline in the level of public health due to failure to receive medical services in a timely manner. Yet in Korea’s medical system, the proportion of public health and medical institutions is very weak: as of 2017. 12., they accounted for 5.3% in terms of the number of medical institutions, 9.2% in terms of the number of beds, and 11.1% in terms of the number of physicians, and the private sector dominates the medical system. Considering such special characteristics of medical care and the realities of Korea’s health care system, in which the public medical sector is very weak, the State may impose certain regulations on the establishment and operation of medical institutions instead of leaving them entirely to the market (see Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2001HEONBA87).\\n\\nHowever, concern was raised that if a single medical practitioner operates multiple medical institutions, patient solicitation for profit, excessive treatment, illegal medical acts such as delegated treatment, and the like would be committed in order to maximize profits, and accordingly the statutory provisions at issue were introduced when the Medical Service Act was amended by Act No. 11252 on 2012. 2. 1.\\n\\nIn light of these constitutional provisions, the legislative purpose of the Medical Service Act, the significance and current status of health care, and the background to the introduction of the statutory provisions at issue, the statutory provisions at issue may be regarded as aiming to prevent in advance the harms that may arise when a single medical practitioner operates multiple medical institutions, thereby establishing sound medical order and ultimately protecting and promoting the people’s health. In other words, the legislative purpose of the statutory provisions at issue is to have medical practitioners perform responsible medical acts in a single medical institution so as to maintain the quality of medical practice, to prevent the public nature of medicine from being undermined by excessive pursuit of profit and the imbalance between supply and demand for medical services, and to prevent monopolization and duopolization of the medical market by a small number of medical practitioners. Such legislative purpose is for the public welfare of preventing harm to public health, and legitimacy of purpose is recognized; and limiting the number of medical institutions that a single medical practitioner may operate is an effective means for such purpose, so suitability of means is also recognized.\\n\\n(2) Minimum Restriction\\n\\nWe examine the concrete scope of application of the statutory provisions at issue. Although the statutory provisions at issue prohibit medical practitioners from operating two or more medical institutions, they do not prohibit all involvement by medical practitioners in the operation of multiple medical institutions.\\n\\nAs noted above, “duplicate operation of medical institutions” prohibited by the statutory provisions at issue means “where a medical practitioner, with decision-making authority regarding management matters such as the existence or abolition, relocation, whether medical practice is performed, financing, staffing/facility/equipment procurement and management, and attribution and distribution of operational results in respect of two or more medical institutions, processes related business or causes it to be processed,” that is, a case where a single medical practitioner actually dominates and manages the operation of two or more medical institutions. Accordingly, it is not prohibited and remains fully permissible for multiple medical practitioners to build a cooperative system regarding treatment, use of medical equipment, hospitalization, transportation, etc., or to jointly engage in purchasing, staffing management, and marketing, or to receive assistance from a hospital management support company in overall management matters such as purchasing, staffing management, marketing, accounting, and billing for medical expenses. For the purpose of cost reduction and management efficiency, a franchise-type model using the same brand is also permitted unless a particular medical practitioner is leading the operation of multiple medical institutions. Ultimately, the forms of duplicate operation subject to the statutory provisions at issue are mainly the form in which a single specific medical practitioner dominates and manages all multiple medical institutions from a leading position, namely, the so-called management-dominance type.\\n\\nHowever, since such management-dominance type contains the problems noted below, the statutory provisions at issue, which prohibit it and punish violations, do not contravene the principle of minimum restriction.\\n\\n(a) Specific Review\\n\\n1) Requiring a medical practitioner to operate only one medical institution under the statutory provisions at issue is intended to ensure that responsible medical practice is performed in that medical institution.\\n\\nMedical practice concerns the human body and life, which are the foundation of human dignity and value (Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2001HEONBA87). However, if medical practitioners are allowed to operate multiple medical institutions, the operator of the medical institution and the medical practitioner who actually performs medical practice are separated, and the medical practitioner who actually performs medical practice becomes subordinate to another medical practitioner, cannot perform responsible medical practice, and as a result the quality of health care may deteriorate.\\n\\nThe Medical Service Act imposes strict requirements for the qualification to become a physician (Article 5), prohibits anyone other than a medical practitioner from performing medical practice (Article 27(1)), and provides that medical practitioners must, in principle, establish medical institutions and practice medicine only within those medical institutions (Article 33(1)), and further provides that persons who are not medical practitioners may not establish and operate medical institutions (Article 33(2)). The reason medical practice is entrusted only to medical practitioners is that the essence of medical services lies in medical practice, and medical practice directly relates to public health; therefore, because it may pose serious risks to human life and body unless performed by persons with advanced knowledge and skills, the qualifications are strictly limited (see Constitutional Court 2014. 5. 29. 2011HEONMA552). Accordingly, medical practitioners bear responsibility not only for the benefits arising from medical practice but also for the risks arising therefrom. However, if a medical practitioner operates multiple medical institutions without performing medical practice and obtains only profits through them, that medical practitioner enjoys only the benefits arising from medical practice without bearing the risks accompanying such practice. In other words, the actual operator of the medical institution obtains profits through the medical practice of others without performing medical practice himself or herself, and the medical practitioner who actually performs medical practice becomes subject to control for non-medical reasons by a person who does not perform medical practice, resulting in medical practitioners becoming subordinate to outside capital.\\n\\nIn addition, the separation between the named founder of the medical institution and the actual operator is problematic in that it makes the attribution of responsibility unclear when any violation of the Medical Service Act arises in connection with the operation of the medical institution. A medical practitioner who only operates a medical institution does not appear outwardly as either the named founder or the person performing medical practice. If the named founder excuses himself or herself by saying that he or she did not actually operate the institution, and the actual operator argues that he or she cannot be held responsible because he or she is not the named person, the harm caused by such ambiguity ultimately falls on the general public.\\n\\nTherefore, a medical practitioner must be able to perform medical practice under his or her own responsibility based on his or her own professionalism and autonomy without external interference, and for this purpose it is necessary that the medical institution itself be directly operated by a medical practitioner who establishes and practices in the medical institution in his or her own name.\\n\\n2) In light of the fact that a medical practitioner makes a living through medical practice, medical practice is clearly also an occupation. However, because medical practice directly affects a patient’s body or life, it must not be used merely as a means for the pursuit of profit. Medical services targeting human body and life must be provided within the scope that does not harm the interests of medical consumers, and medical practice must also not harm the interests of medical consumers or society as a whole. Human body and life must themselves be the end, not the means to some other end. Accordingly, Article 2(2) of the Medical Service Act provides that “medical practitioners have the mission of contributing to the improvement of public health and the securing of healthy living for the people,” and Article 4(1) provides that “medical practitioners and heads of medical institutions shall endeavor to provide the best medical services to patients, such as by improving the quality of medical care, preventing hospital infections, and developing medical technology,” thereby imposing a public-interest mission upon medical practitioners.\\n\\nHowever, a management style in which a single medical practitioner dominates multiple medical institutions separates the management entity of the medical institution from the medical practitioner who performs medical practice, thereby increasing the risk that medical institutions will be used commercially or abused as a means of excessive profit-seeking. Where a single medical practitioner operates multiple medical institutions, that medical practitioner, based on high capital strength, will have strong control over each medical institution, and such control may manifest as pressure toward profit-seeking over each medical institution. Since medical institutions exist for the purpose of medical practice, “operation of a medical institution” and “medical practice” are difficult to completely separate and inevitably affect one another, and the medical practitioner in charge of operating the medical institution may exert pressure on the medical practitioner in charge of medical practice. A relationship substantially equivalent to employment may be formed in which the medical practitioner in charge of medical practice is effectively employed by the medical practitioner in charge of operating the medical institution, and each medical institution can function as the individual business place of a particular medical practitioner. The likelihood increases that acts deviating from the law—such as patient solicitation for profit, excessive treatment, or delegated treatment prohibited by the Medical Service Act—will occur in order to obtain higher profits, and such acts may occur on a larger and more organized scale. Ultimately, when a single medical practitioner operates multiple medical institutions, medicine becomes a means rather than an end, and there is concern that patients, as consumers of medical services, will be treated not as objects of treatment and protection but as objects of commercial value.\\n\\nIn this regard, the Complainants and applicants for referral argue that the problem of excessive profit-seeking is not a problem that occurs only in cases of duplicate operation, but also occurs when a single medical practitioner operates only one medical institution, and when a medical practitioner who establishes and operates one medical institution hires several other medical practitioners to perform medical practice; therefore, it is unjust to prohibit duplicate operation itself on that basis.\\n\\nOf course, “pressure regarding sales” arising from an increase in the number of medical practitioners and intensifying competition may be experienced by most medical practitioners. Whatever system is chosen, it is difficult to prevent profit-seeking, and one may say that there are only differences in degree depending on the legal and ethical maturity and responsibility of individual medical practitioners, and their economic and social circumstances. However, even if the problem of excessive treatment and the like may arise in cases other than duplicate operation of medical institutions, this cannot serve as a ground for finding the prohibition on duplicate operation unconstitutional or unnecessary. If the evil of excessive commercialization of medicine arises in any manner whatsoever, it is necessary to suppress it.\\n\\nIn addition to the statutory provisions at issue, there are mechanisms that check excessive profit-seeking, such as the prohibition of unlicensed medical practice (Article 27(1) of the Medical Service Act), the one-practitioner-one-establishment principle (Article 33(8) of the Medical Service Act), the prohibition on lending licenses (Article 4(4) of the Medical Service Act), the prohibition on receiving rebates (Article 23-3 of the Medical Service Act), the prohibition on patient solicitation for profit (Article 27(3) of the Medical Service Act), recovery of unjust gains (Article 57(1) of the National Health Insurance Act), review of medical care benefit costs by the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service (Article 63(1) of the National Health Insurance Act), and evaluation of the appropriateness of medical care benefit costs (paragraph (2) of the same Article). Nevertheless, excessive treatment and the like remain widespread, detection itself has become more difficult, and moreover a management style in which a single medical practitioner operates multiple medical institutions has emerged, increasing concern about the side effects noted above. Accordingly, the legislature concluded that such individual ex post facto regulation alone is insufficient to regulate excessive profit-seeking and, recognizing the need for more effective new regulation, prescribed the statutory provisions at issue.\\n\\nMeanwhile, because the statutory provisions at issue target only “medical practitioners,” medical corporations under Article 33(2) subparagraph 3 of the Medical Service Act or nonprofit corporations under subparagraph 4 of the same paragraph (hereinafter referred to as “medical corporations, etc.”) are not subject to the statutory provisions at issue and may therefore operate multiple medical institutions. However, when medical corporations, etc. establish medical institutions, they must obtain approval for amendment of the articles of incorporation (or, in the case of establishing medical corporations, approval for establishment) (Article 33(9) of the Medical Service Act), and when operating medical institutions, they are also subject to internal control by the board of directors and the articles of incorporation, and in certain cases the approval for establishment may be revoked (Article 51 of the Medical Service Act, Article 38 of the Civil Act), so medical corporations, etc. are inevitably limited in their pursuit of profit. Accordingly, the Enforcement Decree of the Medical Service Act explicitly prohibits medical corporations, etc. from pursuing profit (Article 20). However, such restrictions do not exist for medical practitioners, so an individual medical practitioner may pursue profit as much as he or she wishes.\\n\\nIn addition, to claim medical care benefit costs from the National Health Insurance Service, a review by the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service is required (Article 47(2) and Article 63(1) subparagraph 1 of the National Health Insurance Act), but because the review scope of the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service includes only insured treatment items and excludes non-insured treatment items, it is difficult to properly regulate a medical practitioner’s excessive treatment solely through such benefit cost review system. At least in the case of establishing hospital-level medical institutions, facilities standards under the Medical Service Act must be met and approval obtained from the Mayor/Do Governor (Article 33(4) of the Medical Service Act), but clinic-level medical institutions need only be reported to the head of a Si/Gun/Gu (paragraph (3) of the same Article), so there is currently no effective regulatory means for clinic-level medical institutions established and operated by individual medical practitioners.\\n\\nMoreover, when a single medical practitioner operates multiple medical institutions, medical supply becomes possible without limit and spatial constraints disappear in the pursuit of profit. Profit-seeking behavior may appear in a more systematic and organized manner, such as by creating manuals so that multiple medical institutions are operated uniformly in the most efficient way, or by comparing sales statistics by medical institution. In particular, because the person operating the medical institution is also a medical practitioner, he or she well knows the range up to which conduct may be allowed within the lawful scope, and may use this to demand more specific profit-maximizing conduct from the medical practitioners actually performing medical practice. Ultimately, profit-seeking intensifies within the bounds of law.\\n\\nThe Medical Service Act grants the right to establish medical institutions only to medical practitioners, which also has the purpose of protecting the profession of medical practitioners, but this too is justified only within the scope of the purpose of protecting and promoting the health of the people. Accordingly, the law may be understood as permitting medical practitioners to pursue profit only within the scope of operating a single medical institution.\\n\\n3) Excessive profit-seeking in medical practice does not end there, but may cause side effects such as an imbalance in the supply of medical services and distortion of medical order.\\n\\n“All” citizens shall be protected by the State in matters of health (Article 36(3) of the Constitution). Therefore, in the medical sector, it is also important how evenly medical services are used. However, if profit becomes the main purpose of medicine, there is concern that emphasis will be placed on the development of high-cost medical services or non-insured treatment rather than primary care or insured treatment, and in the long run, shortages of medical personnel may deepen in fields of specialization regarded as less profitable, resulting in polarization among specialties, and further, medical services may not be properly provided to low-income medical consumers. By making profit-seeking the primary objective, so-called “patients who do not make money” may be concentrated in public medical institutions, leading to a vicious cycle of increasing financial deficits of public medical institutions and thus a possible contraction of public medical care, which, in Korea where the public medical system is weak, increases the risk that even basic health care services cannot be provided to the people (see Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2001HEONBA87).\\n\\nIn addition, Korea operates the National Health Insurance system, which is a type of social insurance, with the National Health Insurance Service as insurer. Since such National Health Insurance is operated using the people’s premiums as financial resources, the State must prevent unnecessary medical care benefits and ensure the rationality of medical care benefits and costs so as to provide the maximum health insurance benefits with limited health insurance finances (see Constitutional Court 2007. 8. 30. 2006HEONMA417). However, if unnecessary excessive treatment is carried out in some fields of medical care benefits under such circumstances, health insurance finances will inevitably deteriorate, and the resulting harm will ultimately fall on other National Health Insurance subscribers through premium increases or reduction of the scope of coverage. Excessive treatment in non-insured treatment fields is also problematic. As noted above, non-insured items are excluded from the review scope of the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service, and in such a situation, allowing duplicate operation may increase unnecessary non-insured treatment in order to increase profits. The expansion of non-insured treatment accelerates the increase in total medical expenses borne by the people and may increase imbalance in the use of medical services.\\n\\nIn Korea, there is also a large regional disparity in the number of medical care institutions and personnel working in such institutions. Urban areas have excess medical resources, whereas some rural and coastal areas have insufficient medical resources, and the level of medical services is also relatively lower than in urban areas. In such a situation, if the pursuit of profitability by private hospitals intensifies, most medical institutions may become concentrated in the metropolitan area or major cities where demand is high, and as a result the imbalance in the supply and demand of medical services between urban and rural areas may further worsen.\\n\\n4) Duplicate operation of medical institutions by medical practitioners may allow a small number of capital-rich medical practitioners to monopolize or oligopolize the medical market.\\n\\nIf a small number of capital-rich medical practitioners operate multiple medical institutions across various regions, patients will flock to such medical institutions, and as a result small-scale, financially weak medical institutions lacking capital cannot avoid relative decline due to deteriorating management, potentially accelerating polarization and concentration among medical institutions. A small number of medical practitioners who monopolize or oligopolize the medical market would determine the prices or contents of medical services, and as a result the entire medical market could be distorted. A small number of capital-rich medical practitioners could raise overall prices or lower the quality of medical services. However, medicine is not a commodity to be used only when one wishes and not used when one does not wish. From the patient’s perspective, once a disease arises, the patient has no choice but to receive treatment from the medical practitioners currently monopolizing the medical market, regardless of the quality, price, or content of the medical service. Once the structure of the medical market is distorted, it is difficult to restore it to its original state, and the resulting harm affects not only medical practitioners but also the general public, so it is important to prevent this in advance.\\n\\n5) The penal provision at issue provides that a person who violates the provision prohibiting at issue shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 5 years or by a fine not exceeding 20,000,000 won. The question of how to punish a crime, that is, the determination of the type and scope of statutory punishment, is a matter of national legislative policy to be decided by the legislature, taking comprehensively into account various factors such as the nature of the crime and the protected legal interest, our history and culture, the social circumstances at the time of legislation, the general public’s values and legal sentiment, and criminal policy aspects for the actual state of the crime and its prevention; thus, a broad legislative discretion or freedom of formation should be recognized in this area (Constitutional Court 1997. 8. 21. 93HEONBA60).\\n\\nYet medicine is a matter directly connected to the people’s lives and health, and considering the importance of medicine, the side effects that may arise when a medical practitioner operates multiple medical institutions, and the criminal-policy necessity of achieving a general preventive effect against them, effective sanctions are needed for violations of the provision prohibiting at issue. Although the penal provision at issue prescribes criminal punishment in the form of a fine or imprisonment, it imposes no minimum limit on the statutory penalty and limits only the maximum to imprisonment for not more than 5 years or a fine not exceeding 20,000,000 won, thereby broadly recognizing the sentencing discretion of judges, and depending on the nature of the offense, a suspended sentence or even a fine may be imposed. In light of such legislative purpose, it is difficult to say that the range of punishment and the scope of sentencing choice prescribed in the penal provision at issue are excessively restricted; therefore, the penal provision at issue cannot be regarded as contrary to the principle of proportionality between responsibility and punishment.\\n\\n6) Even if foreign legislative examples rarely restrict duplicate operation of medical institutions, the health care environment and medical insurance system differ from country to country, so foreign examples cannot be applied as they are to Korea. Korea has a social-insurance-type medical insurance system and adopts compulsory enrollment by a single insurer and the “designated medical institution by law” system so that all citizens can receive treatment through health insurance. However, on the other hand, in the medical supply system, the proportion of private medical care is high, the proportion of public health and medical care is considerably lower than in other OECD countries, the proportion of non-insured treatment in medical expenses is relatively high, and because there is no control over the amount of medical services provided under the fee-for-service system, the incentive for medical providers to induce medical use is high. Therefore, taking such special characteristics into account, different control measures from those of other countries were adopted.\\n\\n(b) Conclusion\\n\\nSince the ownership or operation form of medical institutions may affect the overall health care system, whether duplicate operation by medical practitioners is permitted will depend on the political, economic, social, and cultural background and the concrete, individual circumstances of each country, such as the supply and demand of health care, that country’s health care system and the people’s characteristics of use of health care services, and the structure and finances of medical insurance. Accordingly, this is a legislative-policy matter in which the legislature selects the form most suited to the actual conditions of society (see Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2001HEONBA87).\\n\\nHowever, medicine is not a mere object of commerce but something special dealing with human life and health, and has a major impact on public health. In addition, considering the weak state of public medical care in Korea, the impact on overall public health, including the medical profession and the finances of National Health Insurance, when medical practitioners operate multiple medical institutions, and the social-state duty of the State to protect the people’s health and guarantee proper medical benefits, it cannot be said that the legislature’s judgment limiting the number of medical institutions that a single medical practitioner may operate clearly deviated from legislative discretion in order to manage the quality of medical care and establish sound medical order.\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court has also held, on the premise that if establishment of medical institutions by ordinary private persons who are not medical practitioners is allowed, the separation between the management entity of the medical institution and the medical practitioner performing medical practice may lead to a decline in the quality of health care or excessive profit-oriented medical practices, that Article 30(2) of the former Medical Service Act (the version before amendment by Act No. 6372 on 2001. 1. 16.), which provided that persons other than medical practitioners or for-profit corporations may not establish medical institutions, did not deviate from the legislature’s legislative discretion (Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2001HEONBA87), and such constitutional judgment should be respected in this case as well.\\n\\nAccordingly, the statutory provisions at issue do not contravene the principle of minimum restriction.\\n\\n(3) Balance of Legal Interests\\n\\nThe disadvantage suffered by medical practitioners due to the statutory provisions at issue is only a restriction on the manner of practicing their occupation, and there are also ways to avoid that restriction, whereas the public interest sought to be achieved by prohibiting duplicate operation of medical institutions by medical practitioners is the establishment of sound medical order and prevention of harm to public health, which is no less significant than the former. Even if a single medical practitioner operating multiple medical institutions has positive functions such as cost reduction, it cannot be permitted if it harms the protection and promotion of the people’s health, which is the fundamental purpose of the Medical Service Act. Accordingly, the statutory provisions at issue also satisfy the requirement of balance of legal interests.\\n\\n(4) Conclusion\\n\\nIt cannot be said that the statutory provisions at issue, which restrict the freedom of occupation of medical practitioners who wish to operate multiple medical institutions, are contrary to the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\ne. Whether the Principle of Protection of Trust Was Violated\\n\\n(1) Meaning\\n\\nThe principle of protection of trust is derived from the constitutional principle of the rule of law, and its content is that when a statute is enacted or amended, if the parties’ trust in the old legal order is reasonable and justified, and the damage suffered by the parties due to the enactment or amendment of the statute is so severe that the public-interest purpose sought to be achieved by the new legislation cannot justify the destruction of such trust, then such new legislation is not permissible under the principle of protection of trust. To determine whether this principle has been violated, one must comprehensively compare and balance, on the one hand, the value of the protected trust interest, the degree of infringement, the degree to which trust was damaged, and the method of trust infringement, and on the other hand, the public-interest purpose sought to be achieved through the new legislation (Constitutional Court 2015. 5. 28. 2013HEONMA799).\\n\\n(2) Determination\\n\\nBefore the statutory provisions at issue were amended, the Supreme Court held that “the mere direct involvement in the management of a newly established medical institution by a doctor who has established a medical institution in his or her own name, by establishing another medical institution in the name of another doctor, directly hiring and paying salaries to employees belonging to it, and taking profits generated according to its business, does not constitute duplicate establishment of medical institutions prohibited under Article 33(2) of the former Medical Service Act” (Supreme Court Decision 2003DO256, decided 2003. 10. 23.), so the trust in the old legal order that a medical practitioner would be able to operate multiple medical institutions in the future is trust worthy of constitutional protection.\\n\\nHowever, the medical field is a legislative-policy area in which the legislature, taking into account political, economic, social, and cultural backgrounds and concrete, individual circumstances such as the supply and demand of health care, the health care system and the people’s characteristics of use of health care services, and the structure and finances of medical insurance, must select the form most suited to the actual conditions of society. The legislature introduced the statutory provisions at issue because, as noted above, it concluded that if a medical practitioner operates multiple medical institutions, there is concern that profit-seeking will take precedence over the public interest of protecting public health, causing various side effects. In particular, once the structure of the medical market is distorted, restoration is quite difficult, and the general public suffers significant harm until it is restored. Therefore, it is difficult to say that the trust interest of medical practitioners infringed by the statutory provisions at issue has such value or necessity that it deserves special constitutional protection in preference to the public interest of establishing sound medical order and further preventing harm to public health. Accordingly, the statutory provisions at issue cannot be said to contravene the principle of protection of trust.\\n\\nf. Whether the Principle of Equality Was Violated\\n\\nThe statutory provisions at issue limit their addressees to “medical practitioners,” so that, unlike medical practitioners, medical corporations, etc. may operate two or more medical institutions, and the issue is whether this contravenes the principle of equality.\\n\\nMedical corporations, etc. are subject to state control in the following ways, unlike medical practitioners. That is, when medical corporations, etc. establish medical institutions, they must consult with the Mayor/Do Governor or the head of a Si/Gun/Gu where the medical institution is located and obtain approval for amendment of the articles of incorporation (or approval for establishment, in the case of establishing a medical corporation, etc.) (Article 33(9) of the Medical Service Act), medical corporations must obtain approval from the Mayor/Do Governor when establishing the corporation, amending the articles of incorporation, or disposing of property (Article 48(1) and (3) of the Medical Service Act), medical corporations must possess the funds necessary to provide the facilities or equipment required for the medical institutions they establish (Article 48(2) of the Medical Service Act), and medical corporations, etc. may have their approval for establishment revoked in certain cases (Article 51 of the Medical Service Act, Article 38 of the Civil Act). In addition, because medical corporations, etc. are “corporations,” management can be internally controlled through the board of directors or externally controlled through the articles of incorporation. In particular, because the Civil Act provisions concerning incorporated foundations apply mutatis mutandis to medical corporations (Article 50 of the Medical Service Act), nonprofit corporations established under the Civil Act or a special Act, as well as medical corporations, are by nature nonprofit incorporated foundations (Constitutional Court 2002. 9. 19. 2000HEONBA84), and such nonprofit corporations are limited in their pursuit of profit not only because of the separation between corporate property and individual property (of contributors or managers) and the prohibition on dividends, but also because Article 20 of the Enforcement Decree of the Medical Service Act explicitly prohibits medical corporations, etc. from pursuing profit.\\n\\nAccordingly, medical institutions operated by medical corporations, etc. and those operated by individual medical practitioners must necessarily differ in their operating modes. If a medical practitioner, rather than a corporation, operates multiple medical institutions, there are no control mechanisms like those of a corporation, and there are no restrictions on management methods or the attribution of profits; the higher the profits, the greater the benefit to the medical practitioner who is the actual operator, and ultimately the commercialization of medical practice is bound to intensify. Since individual medical practitioners and medical corporations, etc. differ in the necessity of prohibiting duplicate operation in this manner, different treatment of medical practitioners and medical corporations, etc. is supported by rational grounds, and the statutory provisions at issue do not contravene the principle of equality.\\n\\ng. Conclusion\\n\\nThe statutory provisions at issue do not contravene the principle of clarity, the principle against excessive restriction, the principle of protection of trust, or the principle of equality.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the statutory provisions at issue are not unconstitutional, and the constitutional complaints filed by Complainants Jo ○○, Lim ○○, Kim ○○, and Kim □□ are without merit, so all of them are dismissed. It is so decided by the unanimous opinion of all Justices participating as stated in the order."}

In order to register and operate two of the four steam production facilities currently in operation (hereinafter referred to as “the facilities at issue”) as automobile shredder residue energy recovery facilities (hereinafter referred to as “shredder residue”) energy recovery facilities), the Petitioner completed, on 2017. 12. 21., registration for waste automobile recycling business (crushed residue recycling business) pursuant to Article 32(1) of the former Act on the Resource Circulation of Electrical and Electronic Equipment and Vehicles (hereinafter referred to as the “Resource Circulation Act”).\\nc. At the time the Petitioner made the business registration on 2017. 12. 21., Article 32(1) of the former Resource Circulation Act and Article 16 [Attached Table 3] of the Enforcement Rule of the same Act pursuant to its delegation provided that, if an energy recovery facility falls under a “facility capable of complying with the energy recovery standards under Article 2 of the Enforcement Rule of the Resource Circulation Act,” registration for waste automobile recycling business may be made. However, Article 32(1) of the Resource Circulation Act, as amended by Act No. 15657 on 2018. 6. 12., and Article 30 [Attached Table 7-3] of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act pursuant to its delegation (as amended by Presidential Decree No. 29843 on 2019. 6. 11., effective 2019. 6. 13.) were amended to provide that registration for waste automobile recycling business may be made where an energy recovery facility is a “facility for which approval for installation of a waste treatment facility under Article 29(2) of the Waste Control Act has been obtained or which has been reported as installed.” However, Article 3(1) of the Addenda to the Enforcement Decree of the Resource Circulation Act provides a three-year grace period by stating that, as to a person who, at the time this Decree takes effect, has registered for waste automobile recycling business pursuant to Article 32(1) of the Resource Circulation Act but does not satisfy the above requirements, such person shall be deemed to have satisfied the registration standards for waste automobile recycling business for three years from the date this Decree takes effect (2022. 6. 12.).\\nd. The Petitioner, alleging that, because the facilities at issue are located in the “support facility zone” under the development plan of the XX Industrial Complex, and because the installation of waste treatment facilities is restricted in that zone, so that approval for installation of a waste treatment facility under Article 29(2) of the Waste Control Act cannot be obtained and no report of installation can be made, the “3 years” portion of the main text of Article 30 [Attached Table 7-3] 2(b) 2) (a) of the Enforcement Decree of the Resource Circulation Act and of Article 3(1) and (2) of the Addenda to the same Enforcement Decree infringes its fundamental rights, filed the constitutional complaint at issue on 2019. 12. 2.\\n\\n2. shall, within three years from the date this Decree takes effect, obtain approval for installation of a waste treatment facility under Article 29(2) of the Waste Control Act or file a report of installation.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\nWaste Control Act\\n(as amended by Act No. 10389 on 2010. 7. 23.)\\nArticle 25 (Waste Treatment Business) ③ A person who has received a notice of conformity pursuant to paragraph (2) shall, within two years from the date of receipt of such notice (within six months in the case of waste collection and transportation business under subparagraph 1 of paragraph (5), and within three years in the case of waste treatment business requiring the installation of incineration facilities and landfill facilities), secure facilities, equipment, and
