In this case, when calculating the payment, the estimated investment amount calculated pursuant to Article 20(2)1 shall be taken into account.\\n\\n3. The Claimant’s Arguments\\n\\na. If a decision of unconstitutionality or nonconformity with the Constitution is rendered with respect to the Dam Use Right Change Provision, even if the Disposition in this Case is not thereby rendered null and void, there is a possibility that the alternative claim newly added by the Claimant in the appellate trial of the present case, namely the claim for damages arising from tort, may be upheld or that the grounds therefor may be different. In addition, the Contribution Refund Provision and the Dam Use Right Change Provision cited therein are provisions concerning the legality of a disposition of revocation or change of a dam use right and whether just compensation is thereby provided, and therefore must receive constitutional assessment as a whole. Accordingly, relevance to the judgment is also recognized with respect to the Dam Use Right Change Provision.\\n\\nb. The dam use right prescribed by the Dam Construction Management Act is a property right protected by the Constitution, and in order to restrict it, a legal basis for just compensation must necessarily be prepared pursuant to Article 23(3) of the Constitution. However, the Contribution Refund Provision merely provides that, in the case of reduction of a dam use right, a part of the contribution for dam construction costs paid by the dam use right holder at the time of acquisition of the dam use right or a part of the payment paid at the time of exercising the dam use right shall be refunded; therefore, it cannot constitute just compensation for the loss of the dam use right and thus violates Article 23(3) of the Constitution. It also infringes property rights in violation of the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\nc. The Dam Use Right Change Provision did not exist at the time the Claimant acquired the Seomjingang Dam dam use right. The fact that it provides for the taking away of the dam use right of a dam use right holder who acquired and was exercising the dam use right before the enforcement of the Provision Subject to Review, while refunding only a part of the contribution or payment, constitutes retroactive deprivation of property rights and also violates the principle of protection of legitimate expectations.\\n\\nd. The Dam Use Right Change Provision alone does not reveal what cases the phrase “where the use status, etc. of stored water in the dam has changed” refers to; thus, the said provision violates the principle of clarity, and because it merely provides that “the opinion of the dam use right holder shall be heard in advance” and does not specifically prescribe any prior consultation procedure, it violates the principle of due process.\\n\\ne. Although the dam use right is a property right similar in nature to a fishing right or a mining right and there is no reason to treat it differently from them, the failure to establish procedures for claims for compensation for losses and for calculating compensation in respect only of the dam use right violates the principle of equality as differential treatment without reasonable grounds.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Dam Use Right Change Provision\\n\\nThe Dam Use Right Change Provision is a provision stating that the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport may render a disposition of revocation or change of a dam use right where it is difficult to maintain the dam use right as is because the use status, etc. of stored water in the dam has changed. The present case is not a case challenging the Disposition in This Case itself concerning the change of the dam use right, but a case seeking compensation for losses or damages; thus, the Dam Use Right Change Provision cannot be said to be the statutory provision applicable to the present case, and it cannot be said that the judgment order would change or that the legal significance concerning the content and effect of the judgment would differ depending on whether it is unconstitutional (Constitutional Court 2006. 5. 25. 2003HEONBA115 et al.; Constitutional Court 2011. 7. 28. 2009HEONBA244, see).\\n\\nEven if the state compensation claim additionally added by the Claimant in the appellate trial is based on the proposition that the Dam Use Right Change Provision is unconstitutional and void and that the disposition based thereon constitutes a tort, in general, the circumstance that a statute violates the Constitution cannot be said to be objectively clear before a decision of unconstitutionality by the Constitutional Court, and since public officials who have no authority to review whether a statute violates the Constitution have no choice but to act according to the law at the time of the act, even if a decision of unconstitutionality is rendered with respect to the statutory provision serving as the basis of the act, it cannot be said that the relevant public official had intent or negligence, and state compensation liability does not arise (Constitutional Court 2014. 4. 24. 2011HEONBA56). Accordingly, whether the Dam Use Right Change Provision is unconstitutional does not have any effect on whether a tort is established in the present case.\\n\\nTherefore, because it cannot be deemed a case in which the court in charge of the present case would render a judgment with different content depending on whether the Dam Use Right Change Provision is contrary to the Constitution, the petition for review concerning the Dam Use Right Change Provision is inadmissible for lack of relevance to the judgment.\\n\\n5. Determination on the Contribution Refund Provision\\n\\na. Content and Nature of Dam Use Rights\\n\\n(1) Significance of Dam Use Rights\\n\\n(a) A dam means a structure with a height of 15 meters or more built to block the flow of a river and use its stored water for domestic water, industrial water, agricultural water, water for environmental improvement, power generation, flood control, navigation, and other uses (hereinafter referred to as “specified uses”), and includes spillways, auxiliary dams, and other facilities or structures that are integrated with the relevant dam and enable it to fulfill its utility (Article 2 Subparagraph 1 of the Dam Construction Management Act). A multipurpose dam means a dam constructed by the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport (under the current Dam Construction Management Act, the Minister of Environment; the same shall apply hereinafter) and used for two or more of the specified uses (Subparagraph 2 of the same Article). A dam use right is the right to secure a certain amount of stored water from a multipurpose dam in a certain area and use it for specified uses (Subparagraph 3 of the same Article).\\n\\nThe construction of a multipurpose dam is a large-scale project involving changes in the surrounding ecological environment and resettlement measures caused by flooding on a vast scale, and requiring enormous construction costs. While a dam requires massive financial resources, it takes more than several decades to recover the investment cost, so it is a project in which direct investment by private enterprises is difficult. In this situation, dam use rights are used as a means to promote dam construction by making those who benefit from the construction of a multipurpose dam bear the construction costs. The Dam Construction Management Act, by requiring the prospective holder of a dam use right to bear part of the construction costs of a multipurpose dam and having the national treasury bear the remaining amount (Article 20(1) and (3)), procures the enormous costs required for dam construction while also enabling the dam use right holder to appropriately recover the investment cost through the use of the stored water.\\n\\n(b) When the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport has given public notice of the completion of dam construction, he or she shall, without delay, grant the dam use right to the relevant prospective holder of the dam use right (Article 24(4)), and if the prospective holder of a dam use right is not granted a dam use right, the State shall refund the contribution paid (Article 20(4)). A dam use right holder other than one who has been granted a dam use right pursuant to Article 24(4) of the Dam Construction Management Act shall pay into the national treasury a payment calculated as prescribed by Presidential Decree (Article 33). In other words, instead of designating a dam use right holder and allowing that person to use the public thing, namely the stored water, the person is made to bear a contribution or payment.\\n\\nA dam use right holder has an exclusive right to use the stored water or flowing water only within the scope of the granted dam use right. A dam use right holder may collect fees from persons using the stored water of the relevant dam (Article 35). Meanwhile, a dam use right holder shall bear the costs necessary for maintenance, repair, or other management of the multipurpose dam (Article 36).\\n\\n(2) Legal Character of Dam Use Rights\\n\\nThe Dam Construction Management Act treats a dam use right as a real right and applies mutatis mutandis the provisions on real estate, except where special provisions exist in the Dam Construction Management Act (Article 29). A dam use right is publicized in the register and may be the object of a mortgage (Article 32), but it may not serve as the object of any other right except inheritance, merger of a corporation or other universal succession, transfer, disposition for delinquent taxes, compulsory execution, and mortgage (Article 30(1)).\\n\\nA dam use right is distinguished from ownership of stored water and is a right granted by the State’s concession for the recycling utilization of dam construction costs and the rational development and use of water resources (see Articles 1 and 24 of the same Act). The Dam Construction Management Act does not place any limitation on the duration of a dam use right.\\n\\nb. Disposition of Revocation/Change of Dam Use Right and Compensation\\n\\n(1) Disposition of revocation/change of dam use right (Article 31 of the Dam Construction Management Act)\\n\\nWhere the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport revokes in whole or in part the permission to occupy and use a river under Article 33 of the River Act or the permission to use river water under Article 50 of the same Act for a dam use right holder, and where continued use of river water in the same manner as before cannot be recognized for persons other than the relevant dam use right holder, he or she shall cause the relevant dam use right to be revoked or changed in accordance with the revocation of the permission to occupy and use, etc. granted to the dam use right holder (Article 31(1)); and where it is necessary to newly recognize the use of river water for persons other than the relevant dam use right holder, he or she may order the relevant dam use right holder to transfer in whole or in part the dam use right to another person within an appropriate period (paragraph (2) of the same Article).\\n\\nMeanwhile, once a multipurpose dam is built, it is in fact used almost semi-permanently, so flexible responses are required according to changes in the surrounding environment after construction. The dam operation method may also change depending on the need for water management in response to the use status of stored water in the dam and climate change. Accordingly, the Dam Construction Management Act provides that when the storage capacity changes due to extension or reconstruction of the dam, or where the use status, etc. of stored water in the dam changes and the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport deems it difficult to maintain the dam use right as is, a disposition of revocation or change of the dam use right may be rendered (Article 31(4)).\\n\\n(2) Compensation for revocation/change of dam use right\\n\\nWhen the State has rendered a disposition of revocation or change with respect to a dam use right pursuant to Article 31 of the Dam Construction Management Act, it shall refund a part of the contribution paid pursuant to Article 20(1) of the same Act or the payment paid pursuant to Article 33 (Article 34(1)). The amount to be refunded shall be calculated by the same method as the calculation method of the relevant contribution or payment; provided that the amount to be refunded to a person granted a dam use right pursuant to Article 24(4) of the Dam Construction Management Act shall not exceed the amount obtained by deducting the depreciation amount calculated as prescribed by Presidential Decree from the contribution under Article 20(1) of the same Act (Article 34(2)).\\n\\nc. Organization of Issues\\n\\n(1) The Claimant argues that the Contribution Refund Provision merely provides that, in the case of reduction of a dam use right, the State shall refund only a part of the contribution for dam construction costs paid by the dam use right holder at the time of acquisition of the dam use right or a part of the payment paid at the time of exercising the dam use right, and therefore cannot constitute just compensation, violating Article 23(3) of the Constitution and infringing the Claimant’s property rights.\\n\\nBelow, we first examine whether a dam use right is subject to property right protection under Article 23 of the Constitution, and if so, whether the revocation/change of a dam use right constitutes a public restriction requiring compensation for losses under Article 23(3) of the Constitution; accordingly, we determine whether the Contribution Refund Provision violates Article 23(3) of the Constitution or the principle against excessive restriction.\\n\\n(2) The Claimant argues that applying the Contribution Refund Provision to dam use right holders who acquired and were exercising the dam use right before the Contribution Refund Provision came into force constitutes deprivation of property rights by retroactive legislation and violates the principle of protection of legitimate expectations; we examine this issue.\\n\\n(3) The Claimant also argues that, although a dam use right is a property right similar in nature to a fishing right or a mining right, the failure to establish procedures for claims for compensation for losses and for calculating compensation only with respect to a dam use right upon revocation/change violates the principle of equality. However, in this case, the issue is whether the Contribution Refund Provision is insufficient as a method of compensation and thus infringes the Claimant’s property rights, and in the course of determining that issue, the Claimant’s argument, including the characteristics of dam use rights distinguished from fishing rights and mining rights, can be examined; accordingly, a violation of the principle of equality will not be separately reviewed.\\n\\nd. Whether Property Rights Are Infringed\\n\\n(1) Nature of Dam Use Rights\\n\\nAs noted above, the Dam Construction Management Act treats a dam use right as a real right and applies mutatis mutandis the provisions on real estate, except where special provisions exist in the Dam Construction Management Act (Article 29). A dam use right is publicized in the register and may be the object of a mortgage (Article 32), and the dam use right holder has the exclusive right to use the stored water or flowing water within the scope of the granted dam use right and may collect fees from persons using the stored water of the relevant dam (Article 35). As such, a dam use right is a specific right of property value that entails private utility and, in principle, the power of disposition over it; accordingly, it is subject to property right protection under Article 23 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Legal Character of the Contribution Refund Provision\\n\\nThe Dam Use Right Change Provision is a provision intended to regulate generally and abstractly the legal relations surrounding dam use rights by changing the allocation of stored water by use and the dam use right holder where the use status of stored water in the dam changes in accordance with changes in the surrounding environment after the construction of a multipurpose dam, making it difficult to maintain the dam use right as is. In other words, the Dam Use Right Change Provision cannot be regarded as prescribing the taking, use, or restriction under Article 23(3) of the Constitution, which requires compensation, because it individually and specifically deprives or restricts already formed concrete property rights for the public interest; rather, it should be seen as a provision that determines the content and limits of the dam use right, which is an exclusive right to use a multipurpose dam constructed for public-interest purposes such as proper water supply and flood prevention, while at the same time concretizing social restrictions on property rights pursuant to public-interest demands.\\n\\nThe Contribution Refund Provision is a provision that adjusts the legal relations surrounding the change of a dam use right by requiring that, when the dam use right is changed, a part of the contribution, etc. that the dam use right holder had paid to share in the dam construction costs for acquiring the dam use right be refunded. Therefore, the Contribution Refund Provision, together with the Dam Use Right Change Provision, should also be regarded as a provision that determines the content and limits of the property right, namely the dam use right, while at the same time concretizing social restrictions on property rights pursuant to public-interest demands (Article 23(1) and (2) of the Constitution).\\n\\n(3) Standard of Review\\n\\nThe first sentence of Article 23(1) of the Constitution provides that “the property rights of all citizens shall be guaranteed,” thereby guaranteeing property rights as a fundamental right, while the second sentence, stating that “their content and limits shall be determined by Act,” clearly indicates that property rights may be regulated by Act. The permissible degree of such restriction on property rights varies depending on the social relation and function of the object; where its use or disposition does not remain within the owner’s private sphere but has a major impact on the daily lives of a large number of the general public, the legislator may broadly exercise the power to regulate individual property rights for the benefit of the community. However, even in such cases, legislation restricting property rights must, like legislation restricting other fundamental rights, comply with the principle against excessive restriction (the principle of proportionality), and must not infringe the essential content of property rights (Constitutional Court 2014. 2. 27. 2010HEONBA483, see).\\n\\nWater is the most indispensable good in human life, forms the basis of all industries, and has no substitute. Today, with improvements in living standards and industrial development, the demand for water such as domestic water, industrial water, and agricultural water has greatly increased, and the need to develop water resources is very great.\\n\\nBecause our country, due to its climatic characteristics, has severe regional and seasonal variations in precipitation, the Government has established plans for the construction of multipurpose dams in order to cope with water demand during dry seasons and minimize flood damage during rainy seasons. The construction of multipurpose dams is a large-scale project involving changes in the surrounding ecological environment and resettlement measures caused by flooding on a vast scale, and it requires enormous tax expenditures. The dam use right, which is the right to use the stored water created as a result, can be viewed as a right closely related to the public interest of rational development and use of water resources through multipurpose dams. In light of these characteristics of dam use rights, the legislator has broad legislative discretion in determining the content and limits of dam use rights.\\n\\n(4) Whether the Principle Against Excessive Restriction Is Violated\\n\\n(a) Since a dam use right under the Dam Construction Management Act must take into account public interests such as the environment and safety of a broad surrounding area and the proper supply of water, flexible revocation/change of the dam use right is necessary where it is difficult to maintain the dam use right as is because the use status, etc. of the stored water has changed. A dam use right holder shares in the dam construction costs through payment of contributions, etc. in order to acquire the dam use right (Articles 20 and 33), while at the same time being able to directly use the stored water of the dam for specified uses or receive fees from water users (Article 2 Subparagraph 3 and Article 35(1)); therefore, where the dam use right is revoked or changed, the property right is restricted to the extent that the dam use right is reduced. The Contribution Refund Provision, in cases where the dam use right is revoked or changed for the efficient use of the dam, requires that a part of the contribution paid by the existing dam use right holder be refunded in order to reasonably adjust the economic loss incurred by the dam use right holder; ultimately, this is intended to promote the development of the national economy by rationally developing and using water resources, and the legitimacy of the legislative purpose is recognized. Meanwhile, where all or part of the dam use right needs to be used for another purpose, if the existing dam use right is revoked or changed and a reasonable adjustment is made by refunding part of the contribution, etc. arising therefrom to the existing dam use right holder, the efficient use of water resources can also promote the development of the national economy; accordingly, suitability of means is also recognized.\\n\\n(b) ① It is true that, where a dam use right is revoked or changed, the dam use right holder’s previously obtainable reservoir water use right and revenue from reservoir water use fees are reduced by the extent of the dam use right that is revoked or changed. However, water resources have a strong character as a public good for the State and the entire people; accordingly, it can be seen that a dam use right is also a right subject to the strong public-interest demand of efficient use of water resources. In addition, considering that adjustment of existing dam use rights is required when the use status, etc. of stored water has changed due to changes in the surrounding environment, and that a dam use right is a right with no fixed duration, it can be said that the possibility of revocation or change is inherent in a dam use right. Therefore, it is difficult to say that the reservoir water use right or revenue from reservoir water use fees enjoyed by the dam use right holder must necessarily be guaranteed even when the dam use right is revoked or changed because the use status, etc. of the stored water in the dam has changed.\\n\\n② The refund of contributions is premised on revocation/change of a dam use right. The Dam Construction Management Act does not simply allow revocation/change of a dam use right without limitation when the use status, etc. of stored water in the dam has changed; rather, it provides that revocation/change may be made only where it has become “difficult to maintain the dam use right as is” as a result, and in such case the opinion of the dam use right holder must be heard in advance (main text of Article 31(4)). In addition, a dam use right holder may contest, through administrative litigation, whether grounds for the disposition exist or whether the revocation/change disposition was made in accordance with the principle of proportionality. In other words, because the Dam Construction Management Act very narrowly prescribes the grounds for revocation/change of a dam use right and ex post relief through administrative litigation is available, the damage suffered by the dam use right holder due to revocation/change of the dam use right can be minimized.\\n\\n③ The Contribution Refund Provision, upon revocation or change of a dam use right, requires that a part of the contribution, etc. paid by the dam use right holder be refunded to the dam use right holder, thereby compensating for only part, not all, of the losses incurred by the dam use right holder. Accordingly, in cases where the exercise period of the dam use right is short, in theory, the amount of contribution to be refunded may be less than the amount obtained by subtracting the benefits derived from the use of the dam during that period from the amount paid as a contribution to acquire the dam use right. However, in light of the purpose of the Dam Construction Management Act, which provides that upon refund of a contribution the refund shall be limited to the amount after deducting the depreciation amount (Articles 34(1) and (2), Article 27 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act), it is sufficiently clear that, generally, the Act intended at least to refund the contribution paid by the dam use right holder. Depreciation will be proportional to the use of the dam, and the dam use right holder will have obtained benefits from use of the dam either by directly using the stored water or through reservoir water use fees. However, considering the nature of water resources as a public good and the need for efficient use, it cannot be said that the dam use right holder must necessarily be compensated for losses beyond that, such as expected future profits.\\n\\n④ The Claimant argues that the Contribution Refund Provision provides for the refund of part of the contribution, which has the character of a kind of deposit for future use of the dam, and that this is naturally something that should accompany revocation/change of the dam use right. However, if the entire dam construction costs were borne by the State through general fiscal revenue, the people would end up bearing the dam construction expenses; the dam use right was introduced as a system to procure a part of the enormous construction costs required for multipurpose dam construction and to appropriately recycle the already invested dam construction costs. Accordingly, the contribution or payment is better viewed as a cost incurred in order to be granted the dam use right rather than as a kind of deposit for future use of the dam.\\n\\n⑤ The Claimant argues that, in the case of revocation of fishing rights or mining rights for public-interest reasons, the average annual earnings are considered in calculating the amount of compensation for losses (Article 81(1) of the Fisheries Act, [Attached Table 4] of the Enforcement Decree of the Fisheries Act), or future profitability is considered (Article 34(4) of the Mining Act, Article 30(1)1 of the Enforcement Decree of the Mining Act), whereas in the case of revocation/change of a dam use right, permitting only partial refund of the contribution, etc. is insufficient compensation. However, as noted above, in light of the fact that a dam use right is related to the efficient use of water resources, which are a public good; that it has no fixed duration and the possibility of revocation or change is inherent; and that, unlike fishing rights or mining rights, a dam use right is not subject to market price formation and is therefore difficult to evaluate in terms of exchange value, it cannot be said to be excessive to refund only the investment costs, such as contributions, to the dam use right holder upon revocation/change of the dam use right.\\n\\n⑥ Therefore, the Contribution Refund Provision satisfies the minimum impairment requirement.\\n\\n(c) As noted above, when the importance and irreplaceability of water resources used for domestic water, industrial water, agricultural water, power generation water, etc., the importance of multipurpose dams for stable water supply and coping with natural disasters such as floods, and the fact that a dam use right is a private property right but at the same time a right with the public-interest purpose of rational development and use of water resources through multipurpose dams and is recognized on the premise that its content may be changed by a disposition of an administrative agency for the achievement of the elevated public interest of water resource management are taken together, the public interest sought to be realized by the Contribution Refund Provision is very large, whereas it cannot be said that the property rights restricted by the Contribution Refund Provision are so significant as to outweigh the above public interest. Therefore, the balance of interests is also satisfied.\\n\\n(d) Accordingly, since the Contribution Refund Provision does not violate the principle against excessive restriction, it does not infringe property rights.\\n\\ne. Whether the Principle Prohibiting Retroactive Legislation and the Principle of Protection of Legitimate Expectations Are Violated\\n\\n(1) In order to regulate matters concerning the construction and management of multipurpose dams, the Act on Specific Multipurpose Dams was enacted by Act No. 1785 on 1966. 4. 23., and the Dam Construction Management Act was enacted when the Act on Specific Multipurpose Dams was repealed by Act No. 6021 on 1999. 9. 7. The former Act on Specific Multipurpose Dams, from the time of its enactment, provided in Article 28 that, in the event a dam use right was revoked or changed, the State should refund the contribution or payment to the dam use right holder, and that the amount to be refunded should deduct the depreciation amount prescribed by Presidential Decree, thereby regulating content similar to the current Article 34 of the Dam Construction Management Act. In other words, the provision requiring the refund of the amount after deducting the depreciation rate from the contribution or payment upon revocation/change of a dam use right had already been prescribed in the former Act on Specific Multipurpose Dams before the Claimant acquired the dam use right.\\n\\nHowever, when the Dam Construction Management Act was amended by Act No. 7158 on 2004. 1. 29., the ground for revocation/change of a dam use right was supplemented by “where it is difficult to maintain the dam use right as is because the storage capacity of the dam or the use status, etc. of stored water has changed” (Article 31(4)1 and 2), and the present case concerns a situation in which the dam use right was changed on the ground that it became difficult to maintain the dam use right as is because the use status, etc. of stored water in the dam had changed (Article 31(4)2). The Contribution Refund Provision, which is the subject of review in this case, is “the parts concerning Article 31(4)2 in each of Article 34(1) and (2) of the Dam Construction Management Act”; while the wording of the Contribution Refund Provision is similar to that of the former Act on Specific Multipurpose Dams, its substantive content may be viewed as having been changed on 2004. 1. 29., when Article 31(4) of the Dam Construction Management Act was newly established, into “a provision adjusting the interests of dam use right holders in cases where the dam use right is revoked or changed because it is difficult to maintain the dam use right as is due to changes in the use status, etc. of stored water.” Accordingly, as the Claimant argues, the question of violation of the principle prohibiting retroactive legislation or the principle of protection of legitimate expectations may arise.\\n\\n(2) Whether the Principle Prohibiting Retroactive Legislation Is Violated\\n\\nArticle 13(2) of the Constitution provides that “No citizen shall be subjected to retroactive legislation in respect of political rights or deprived of property rights.” “Retroactive legislation” is divided into “true retroactive legislation” and “quasi-retroactive legislation,” depending on whether the new law applies to already completed factual or legal relationships or to factual or legal relationships that are still in progress. The former is not permitted in principle under the Constitution and is exceptionally permitted only in special circumstances, whereas the latter is permitted in principle, but differs in that, in the process of balancing the public-interest reasons requiring retroactive effect against the need for protection of legitimate expectations, the perspective of protection of legitimate expectations imposes certain limitations on the legislator’s legislative discretion (Constitutional Court 2008. 2. 28. 2005HEONMA872 et al.; Constitutional Court 2013. 11. 28. 2009HEONBA206 et al., see).\\n\\nThe Claimant was granted a dam use right for the Seomjingang Dam before the enactment of the Dam Construction Management Act, and the legal relationship arising from the Claimant’s dam use right continued even after 2004, when the Contribution Refund Provision was amended; therefore, the Contribution Refund Provision is legislation regulating matters in progress and does not constitute true retroactive legislation in the true sense, whereby a new law is applied retroactively to facts or legal relationships that have already been completed and the past is reassessed anew. Accordingly, there is no room to question infringement of property rights by retroactive legislation. The only issue is whether the trust in the existing legal relationship held by the Claimant should be constitutionally protected (Constitutional Court 2017. 11. 30. 2016HEONBA38, see).\\n\\n(3) Whether the Principle of Protection of Legitimate Expectations Is Violated\\n\\nThe principle of protection of legitimate expectations is derived from the constitutional principle of the rule of law; it means that when enacting or amending a law, if a party’s trust in the existing legal order is reasonable and justified, but the damage to the party caused by the enactment or amendment of the law is so severe that the public-interest purpose sought to be achieved by the new legislation cannot justify the destruction of that party’s trust, such legislation may not be permitted. To determine whether this principle has been violated, the value of the interest infringed, the degree of infringement, the degree of damage to trust, the manner of infringement of trust, etc., and, on the other hand, the public-interest purpose sought to be realized through the new legislation, must be comprehensively balanced (Constitutional Court 2015. 10. 21. 2013HEONBA248, see).\\n\\nAs noted above, considering that a dam use right is related to the efficient use of water resources, which are a public good; that it has no fixed duration and the possibility of revocation or change is inherent; and that the importance and irreplaceability of water resources are significant, the public-interest value of rational development and use of water resources through multipurpose dams can be seen as very great, rather than the Claimant’s trust interest in the continued existence of the dam use right. Therefore, it cannot be said that the Contribution Refund Provision is contrary to the constitutional principle of protection of legitimate expectations.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the petition for review concerning the Dam Use Right Change Provision is dismissed as inadmissible, and the Contribution Refund Provision does not violate the Constitution; therefore, it is so decided by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices as stated in the order."}

question:
Which of the following is the correct combination of the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (X) regarding the operation of the National Assembly and its parliamentary procedure? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)

(a) The voting method of the National Assembly, which realizes the principle of majority rule, is based, absent any special provision in the Constitution or statutes, on the general quorum requiring the presence of a majority of the total membership and the approval of a majority of the members present, and this can be regarded as an absolute constitutional principle.

(b) An extraordinary session of the National Assembly is convened at the request of the President or of at least one-third of the total membership of the National Assembly, and in such case the period and the reasons for the request for convocation must be specified.

(c) While the Constitution provides the principle that meetings of the National Assembly are public, it contains an exception that they may be held in private when there is approval by a majority of the members present or when the Speaker deems it necessary for the security of the State.

(d) When it is necessary to continue expenditures beyond one fiscal year, the Government must obtain a resolution of the National Assembly by setting a term and treating it as a continuing appropriation.

(e) The Constitution provides that "an item that has been rejected may not be again proposed or submitted during the same session," thereby excluding obstruction of proceedings by a minority and promoting the smooth operation of meetings.
label: C
supporting_precedents: {"[2009HEONRA8]": "[Appendix 1] List of Petitioners in Case 2009HEONRA9·10: Omitted  \\n[Appendix 2] List of Attorneys for the Petitioners in Case 2009HEONRA9·10: Omitted  \\n[Appendix 3] List of Intervenors for the Respondents: Omitted  \\n[Appendix 4] 2. Arguments of the Parties and the Intervenors for the Respondents\\n\\na. Summary of the Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\n(1) With respect to the amendment to the Broadcasting Act, on 2009. 7. 22., the Vice Speaker of the National Assembly conducted a vote on the amendment to the Broadcasting Act submitted to the National Assembly, and upon the completion of voting, declared the close of voting. However, in order for a bill to be passed, as of 2009. 7. 22., the number of members of the National Assembly in office was 294, and attendance of a majority thereof, namely 148 members, was required (Article 49 of the Constitution, Article 109 of the National Assembly Act), but the voting was closed with only 145 members participating in the vote; thus, the amendment to the Broadcasting Act was rejected. Since a rejected agenda item may not be proposed or submitted again during the same session (Article 92 of the National Assembly Act), re-voting on it within the same session was impossible; nevertheless, the Vice Speaker of the National Assembly conducted a revote on the amendment to the Broadcasting Act, and when the results showed the attendance of 153 National Assembly members and 150 votes in favor, he declared it passed. This violated the principle that the same matter shall not be deliberated twice in the same session and infringed the Petitioners’ right as members of the National Assembly to deliberate and vote on bills.\\n\\n(2) During the bundling of each bill for agenda submission and resolution on this day, a member who entered after some bills had been processed was treated as having voted in favor of the Newspaper Act bill, and members who had surrounded the dais of the Speaker’s podium were treated as having voted although voting was impossible; moreover, despite the occurrence of proxy voting by some members, such as treating a member opposed to the vote as having voted in favor, the Vice Speaker of the National Assembly declared that the Newspaper Act bill had been passed according to the voting results displayed on the electronic board.\\n\\nSince members of the National Assembly, as independent constitutional organs, exercise their right to deliberate and vote independently according to their conscience, the right of members of the National Assembly to deliberate and vote is a personal, exclusive, and non-transferable power that cannot be delegated or exercised by proxy. The National Assembly Act also does not permit delegation or proxy exercise of members’ right to deliberate and vote (see Article 111 of the National Assembly Act), and even voting pursuant to delegation is impossible; therefore, arbitrary proxy voting without even any delegation cannot, of course, be permitted. As there was a clear procedural defect in that votes were cast by unauthorized persons in the voting process on the Newspaper Act bill, the Vice Speaker of the National Assembly’s act of declaring the passage of the Newspaper Act bill based on such defective voting results directly violated the principle of due process in legislative procedure and the majority-rule principle, which is a constitutional principle concerning process and procedure, thereby infringing the Petitioners’ right to deliberate and vote on bills.\\n\\n(3) In the legislative process at issue, there were serious procedural defects in that the explanatory statements on the amendment to the Newspaper Act and the amendment to the Broadcasting Act, the review reports on the Internet Multimedia bill and the Financial Holding Company Act bill, the explanation of the purpose of the amendment to the Financial Holding Company Act, and the questions and debate regarding each original bill at issue and each amendment to the Broadcasting Act, Newspaper Act, and Financial Holding Company Act were omitted.\\n\\n(4) The original bill of the Financial Holding Company Act is aimed at permitting financial (insurance, securities) holding companies to own manufacturing (industrial capital) businesses, whereas the amendment to the Financial Holding Company Act submitted by Assemblyman Park Jong-hee and 168 others is aimed at expanding the equity holdings of industrial capital and public pension funds in banks, and expanding the capital contribution limits of private equity funds, and thus contains content entirely different from the original bill of the Financial Holding Company Act; nevertheless, it was voted on as an amendment to the original bill of the Financial Holding Company Act.\\nAccordingly, the Petitioners, as members of the National Assembly, were deprived of the opportunity to express their positions for and against the original bill of the Financial Holding Company Act, and therefore the Vice Speaker of the National Assembly’s declaration of the passage of the Financial Holding Company Act infringed the Petitioners’ right to deliberate and vote on the original bill of the Financial Holding Company Act.\\nIn addition, the above amendment is identical to the government-proposed amended bill that was referred separately from the original bill to the Political Affairs Committee and is under subcommittee review. Although the above amended bill had no fixed review period and thus could not be placed on the agenda ex officio by the Speaker of the National Assembly, the Respondents placed it on the agenda in the form of an amendment to the Financial Holding Company Act and declared it passed, thereby depriving the Assembly members belonging to the Political Affairs Committee among the Petitioners of the opportunity to review the above government-proposed amended bill in the Committee and infringing their right to deliberate and vote on the above amended bill.\\n\\n(5) The Respondent’s arbitrary placement on the agenda ex officio and vote processing of each bill at issue, which are strongly opposed between the political parties and opposed by the majority of the people, without processing them by agreement between the ruling and opposition parties, constitutes an abuse of authority.\\n\\n(6) Accordingly, the Petitioners seek a confirmation that the act of declaring the passage of each bill at issue violated the Constitution and the due process and principle that the same matter shall not be deliberated twice in the National Assembly Act and infringed the Petitioners’ right to deliberate and vote on bills, as well as a confirmation of the invalidity of the act of passing and declaring each bill at issue with such defects.\\n\\nb. Summary of the Respondents’ Arguments\\n\\n(1) Regarding the procedural requirements\\n\\n(a) Since the Respondent Vice Speaker of the National Assembly merely acted in place of the Speaker of the National Assembly by being delegated by the Speaker to conduct the proceedings on the day of this case, even if the Vice Speaker himself conducted the proceedings, the legal effect thereof belongs to the Speaker of the National Assembly; thus, the petition against the Respondent Vice Speaker of the National Assembly is, by itself, without merit.\\n\\n(b) The bills relating to the press at issue were submitted around December 2008 by members of the Grand National Party, but they were not processed for a long period due to the Petitioners’ obstruction of the National Assembly’s operation. On 2009. 3. 3., the floor leaders of each negotiating group agreed, after 100 days of discussion, to process them by vote during the extraordinary session in June, but they ultimately failed to reach agreement.\\n\\nAccordingly, pursuant to the Speaker of the National Assembly’s placing them on the agenda ex officio, they were referred to the plenary session on the day at issue, but the Petitioners occupied each entrance to the plenary hall, blocked the entry of members of the National Assembly belonging to the Grand National Party and others, and, even inside the meeting hall, continuously approached the Speaker’s podium and obstructed the proceedings, thereby obstructing deliberation and voting themselves.\\n\\nIn light of the above circumstances, the Petitioners should be deemed to have abandoned, from the outset, their right as members of the National Assembly to deliberate and vote on bills; therefore, this request for adjudication on a competence dispute, premised on the assumption that the Respondent Speaker of the National Assembly infringed the Petitioners’ right to deliberate and vote, is inadmissible because standing as Petitioners is not recognized.\\n\\n(c) The Petitioners, on the day at issue, used physical force to block the Respondents’ side and members belonging to the Grand National Party from entering the plenary hall in order to obstruct the opening of the plenary session itself and to completely block the progress of the voting procedure, and even inside the plenary hall they actively obstructed the exercise of the right to deliberate and vote by occupying the Grand National Party members’ seats. Having thus committed acts of obstruction of proceedings against the Respondents and acts of obstruction of voting against members belonging to the Grand National Party, the Petitioners now assert infringement of the right to deliberate and vote and filed this petition only after the bills at issue were declared passed; this amounts to the parties who caused the result disputing the result, and constitutes an abuse of the right of action.\\n\\n(2) Regarding the merits\\n\\n(a) The principle that the same matter shall not be deliberated twice applies only to “rejected” agenda items within the same session. “Rejected” means a case in which, although a vote was taken in a plenary session of the National Assembly with a lawful quorum for resolution, the proposal failed to obtain the approval of a majority of the voters.\\n\\nSince the quorum for resolution means the minimum number of attendees required to resolve an agenda item in a deliberative body, the requirement of “attendance of a majority of the full membership,” which is the first condition for the quorum for resolution prescribed by the Constitution and the National Assembly Act, is the minimum condition for the quorum for resolution; therefore, unless this requirement is satisfied, no resolution itself comes into being. Only when the first condition is met but the second condition, namely “approval by a majority of those present,” is not met, should the motion be deemed rejected. This is also consistent with the National Assembly’s legislative practice.\\n\\nAccordingly, the first vote on the Broadcasting Act bill in this case is a case where no resolution was formed, and the principle that the same matter shall not be deliberated twice does not apply.\\n\\n(b) During the voting process on the Newspaper Act bill in this case, members of the National Assembly belonging to the Grand National Party did not engage in proxy voting. Rather, some of the Petitioners merely obstructed the exercise of voting rights by members of the National Assembly belonging to the Grand National Party.\\n\\n(c) On the day at issue, in the plenary hall of the National Assembly, the Petitioners mobilized all manner of physical force in order to obstruct the Respondent Vice Speaker’s submission of agenda items and conduct of proceedings.\\n\\nIn such circumstances, while submitting three bills, including the original bill of the Newspaper Act, in a lump, the Vice Speaker of the National Assembly told Assemblyman Ahn Hyung-hwan to come forward and make the explanatory statement for the proposal, and then announced that, because the chamber was noisy and it was impossible to conduct the proceedings normally, the committee review report or explanatory statement would be substituted by the terminal meeting minutes and also by the meeting materials. At that time, meeting materials concerning each original bill and amendment to the relevant laws had been entered into the terminals at each members’ seat, and the three explanatory statements and interim review reports were preserved as appendices to the minutes.\\n\\nAccordingly, since there is no restriction on the method of explaining the purpose of a proposal, it may be substituted by written explanations or other explanations by computer terminals even if the proposer does not speak from the podium, and because the situation at issue made normal conduct of proceedings difficult, there is no legal problem with the handling of proceedings related to the explanatory statement conducted by the Vice Speaker of the National Assembly after placing the agenda items on the agenda.\\n\\n(d) On the day at issue, after announcing that the explanation of the purpose of the proposal would be substituted by the terminal meeting minutes, etc., the Vice Speaker of the National Assembly declared that questions and debate would also not be conducted. None of the Petitioners requested questions or debate regarding the agenda items placed on the agenda; rather, they only chanted slogans and made noise in the chamber in order to obstruct the vote. Therefore, the Vice Speaker of the National Assembly’s conduct of proceedings omitting the questioning and debate procedure is justified.\\n\\n(e) The amendment to the Financial Holding Company Act in this case merely re-added, during the Political Affairs Committee review process of the original bill of the Financial Holding Company Act, a part that had been deleted from the original bill because it overlapped with other bills in content. Accordingly, in light of prior precedents of the National Assembly, precedents of the Constitutional Court, and the National Assembly’s autonomy, it falls within the permissible scope of amendments. Therefore, the Vice Speaker of the National Assembly’s declaration of the passage of the amendment to the Financial Holding Company Act cannot be said to infringe the Petitioners’ right to deliberate and vote on the original bill of the Financial Holding Company Act, and insofar as the amendment falls within the scope of amendments, the argument that the amendment portion violated the ex officio placement procedure is also without merit.\\n\\nc. Summary of the Arguments of the Intervenors for the Respondent\\n\\nThe arguments concerning the procedural requirements and the merits are substantially the same as those of the Respondents."}

Kim○Gyeong 13. Kim○Won 14. Lee○Woo 15. Kwon○Dong  \\n16. Kim□Won 17. Gyeong○Su 18. Yoon○Ok 19. Lee○Seung  \\n\\n[Appendix 2] List of Intervenors  \\n1. Lee○Geol 2. Choi○Hee 3. Han○Ae 4. Shin○Hoon 5. Jin○Mi  \\n6. Bu○Hyun 7. Park○Eun 8. Kim○Jun 9. Baek○Gi 10. Park○Hyun  \\n11. Lee○Ju 12. Jeon○Cheol  \\n\\n[Appendix 3] List  \\n<TABLE0>  \\n\\n[Appendix 4] List  \\n<TABLE1>  \\n\\n[Appendix 5]  \\n3. Claims of the Parties and the Intervenors Supporting the Respondents  \\na. Summary of the Petitioners’ Claims  \\n(1) Unconstitutionality of the provisions of the National Assembly Act  \\nArticle 85(1) of the National Assembly Act provides that the Speaker of the National Assembly may designate a review period for a bill only in cases of “natural disaster,” “national emergency,” or “agreement with each floor leader of the negotiation groups,” and thereby, with respect to bills, in effect provides for a resolution by unanimity, and Article 85-2(1) of the National Assembly Act likewise requires, for the designation of a fast-track agenda item, a resolution by consent of a majority of the incumbent members and approval by at least three-fifths of the incumbent members, and thus the National Assembly Act, a subordinate statute, excludes and empties Article 49 of the Constitution and infringes the essence of the constitutional majority rule principle. Furthermore, the above provisions of the National Assembly Act compel unconditional agreement, thereby contravening the principle of parliamentarism premised on free debate and questioning, and, in that they determine the will of the National Assembly based on agreement with floor leaders who are not Members of the National Assembly, they also run counter to the constitutional status of Members of the National Assembly as constitutional organs.  \\n(2) Unconstitutionality of the respondents’ act of refusal  \\nThe act of refusing in this case to designate the review period and the act of refusing to conduct a vote on the fast-track agenda item, based on the above unconstitutional provisions of the National Assembly Act, infringed the Petitioners’ right to deliberate on and vote on bills.  \\n(3) Unconstitutionality of the declaration of passage in this case  \\nArticle 85-2(1) of the National Assembly Act requires, for the designation of a fast-track agenda item, the consent of a majority of the incumbent members and approval by at least three-fifths of the incumbent members; because the above provision raises the National Assembly’s own decision-making standard, its amendment also had to obtain approval exceeding the qualified majority required by that provision. However, since the above provision was resolved on 2012. 5. 2. at the first plenary session of the 307th extraordinary session of the 18th National Assembly by 127 votes in favor out of 192 members present (attendance by a majority of the incumbent members and approval by a majority of those present), the declaration of passage in this case, which failed to obtain the approval of 195 members, more than two-thirds of the 292 incumbent members of the National Assembly at the time, is void.  \\nb. Summary of the Response of the Respondent Speaker of the National Assembly  \\nThe act of refusing to designate the review period in this case is a lawful act pursuant to Article 85(1) of the National Assembly Act. However, regarding Article 85(1) of the National Assembly Act, there exist: ① criticism that it operates as a cause of legislative deadlock and legislative delay; ② criticism that it creates the paradoxical situation of majority rule by a minority and thus contravenes democracy based on the majority rule principle; ③ criticism that, where there are agenda items in dispute between the ruling and opposition parties, it causes the side effect of treating as subjects of linkage handling even the remaining numerous agenda items as to which there is no disagreement on policy validity and urgency of legislation; and ④ criticism that core matters concerning the operation of the 19th National Assembly were handled by the 18th National Assembly; therefore, in order for the 20th National Assembly to operate stably, the Constitutional Court is hoped to render a prompt conclusion no later than within the term of the 19th National Assembly (scheduled to expire on 2016. 5. 29.).  \\nc. Summary of the Response of the Chairperson of the Planning and Finance Committee, the Respondent  \\nThe act of refusing to conduct a vote on the agenda item in this case was because the requirement of submission of “a consent form signed by a majority of the incumbent members of the competent committee” under Article 85-2(1) of the National Assembly Act was not satisfied, and thus the above refusal was a natural decision for the Respondent Chairperson of the Planning and Finance Committee, who must comply with the National Assembly Act.  \\nd. Summary of the Opinion of the Interested Party, the Minister of Justice  \\n(1) The part concerning the act of refusing to designate the review period in this case  \\n(a) Unconstitutionality of Article 85(1) of the National Assembly Act  \\n1) The autonomy of the National Assembly must be respected, and in many cases it is necessary to be patient and wait until the competent committee’s review is completed; however, when the urgency and importance of a bill are recognized, even if the competent committee’s review has not been completed, it is a constitutional request, and at the same time the limit of committee-centeredism, to keep open the path for the bill to be referred to the plenary session so that discussion can take place at the level of all Members of the National Assembly.  \\n2) The reason Article 85(1) item 3 of the National Assembly Act sets “where the Speaker reaches agreement with the floor leaders of each negotiation group” as a ground for designating a review period appears to be to exclude the Speaker’s arbitrary judgment and to obtain authorization or consent from representative members; however, the above provision excludes political parties that have not formed a negotiation group or Members of the National Assembly who do not belong to a negotiation group, and thus violates the constitutional principle of equality. Moreover, where the views of the majority members belonging to a negotiation group and the view of the floor leader of that negotiation group do not coincide, there is a risk that the will of the majority will be determined by the will of the minority.  \\n3) Article 85(1) of the National Assembly Act is a system allowing bills whose committee review has not been completed to be referred to the plenary session, but items 1 and 2 of the same paragraph (natural disaster, national emergency) are difficult to apply in ordinary times because of excessively strict requirements, and item 3, as stated above, violates the principle of equality; accordingly, it excessively restricts the exercise of Members of the National Assembly’s right to deliberate and vote in the plenary session.  \\n4) The fast-track agenda system also requires, for its resolution, an excessive qualified majority of signatures of a majority of the incumbent members (committee members) and approval by at least three-fifths of the incumbent members (committee members), and, as stated below, because it contravenes the constitutional majority rule principle and excessively restricts Members of the National Assembly’s right to deliberate and vote, it is difficult to regard it even as an alternative to the ex officio agenda-setting system.  \\n(b) Infringement of the right to deliberate and vote by the act of refusing to designate the review period in this case  \\nThe act of refusing to designate the review period in this case, which was carried out based on unconstitutional Article 85(1) of the National Assembly Act, infringes the Petitioners’ right to deliberate on and vote on bills.  \\n(2) The part concerning the act of refusing to conduct a vote on the fast-track agenda item in this case  \\n(a) Unconstitutionality of Article 85-2(1) of the National Assembly Act  \\n1) Since Article 49 of the Constitution establishes, as a principle for resolutions by the National Assembly, the attendance of a majority of the incumbent members and the approval of a majority of the members present, any aggravation thereof must be recognized more strictly and exceptionally, taking into account the nature of the concrete and individual case. In other words, it must concern a “matter of grave importance” similar or equivalent to matters directly prescribed by the Constitution as requiring a qualified majority.  \\n2) All provisions in the Constitution that prescribe a qualified majority concern the core content of the constitutional order and, by their nature, require caution; the provisions on a qualified majority under the National Assembly Act concern matters related to the status of constitutional organs or a rehearing on items already passed, and thus are not only related to a constitutional order similar to the provisions directly prescribed by the Constitution regarding a qualified majority but are also matters of grave importance requiring caution by their nature. Therefore, if a qualified majority is to be established in the National Assembly Act, which is subordinate to the Constitution, it must at least concern content related to an equivalent constitutional order.  \\n3) However, the above provision of the National Assembly Act uniformly and excessively prescribes an aggravated quorum regardless of the substantive importance of the relevant agenda item, and therefore does not accord with the other provisions in the Constitution and the National Assembly Act that adopt a qualified majority. In other words, requiring a majority of the incumbent members (committee members) for consent to designate a fast-track agenda item is the same quorum as is required for proposing an amendment to the Constitution (Article 128(1) of the Constitution) and for proposing impeachment against the President (proviso to Article 65(2) of the Constitution), while the quorum of approval by at least three-fifths of the incumbent members (committee members) is even more aggravated than the resolution on the President’s request for reconsideration of a bill (Article 53(4) of the Constitution), and it is doubtful whether it truly has corresponding constitutional significance. Therefore, Article 85-2(1) of the National Assembly Act is unconstitutional as it contravenes the majority rule principle under Article 49 of the Constitution.  \\n(b) Infringement of the right to deliberate and vote by the act of refusing to conduct a vote on the fast-track agenda item in this case  \\nThe act of refusing to conduct a vote on the fast-track agenda item in this case, which was carried out based on unconstitutional Article 85-2(1) of the National Assembly Act, infringes Petitioner Na○Rin’s constitutional right to deliberate and vote.  \\ne. Summary of the Arguments of the Intervenors Supporting the Respondents  \\n(1) The Intervenors, as members of the □□ Party, applied to intervene in order to assist the Respondents because they have a direct interest, such as being infringed in their rights under the Constitution and the National Assembly Act, depending on the outcome of this petition for adjudication on a dispute over authority.  \\n(2) At the time of the act of refusing to designate the review period in this case, no natural disaster or national emergency had occurred, and there was no agreement with each floor leader of the negotiation groups; therefore, the Respondent Speaker of the National Assembly could not designate the review period pursuant to Article 85(1) of the National Assembly Act, and the Respondent Chairperson of the Planning and Finance Committee refused the “request for designation of a bill as a fast-track agenda item” because the Petitioners failed to satisfy the requirement of submitting “a consent form signed by a majority of the incumbent members of the competent committee.”  \\n(3) Article 85(1) of the National Assembly Act is a very positive statute in that it eradicates physical violence within the National Assembly and induces decision-making through consultation and debate, and when rapid legislation is necessary, deliberation and voting in the plenary session are possible through the fast-track agenda item designation system under Article 85-2 of the National Assembly Act; therefore, it cannot be said that the Members of the National Assembly’s right to deliberate and vote was infringed.  \\n(4) Since the bill was passed according to the ordinary quorum, the Petitioners’ argument that the act of declaring Article 85-2 passed among the amendments to the partial amendment bill to the National Assembly Act at the National Assembly’s 307th session on 2012. 5. 2. is void is without merit."}

question:
Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (X) concerning the courts? (Where there is a dispute, in accordance with precedents)

(a) The guarantee of the right to receive a trial by a judge means guaranteeing the right to receive a trial in which a judge determines the facts and interprets and applies the law, and if such a guarantee is not properly fulfilled, it infringes the essential content of the constitutionally guaranteed right to receive a trial.
(b) As a general rule, the hearing and judgment of a trial shall be open to the public; however, where there is a risk of impairing national security or public order, or of harming good morals and social order, they may be closed to the public by a court decision.
(c) The Constitution provides, “The Supreme Court may enact rules concerning procedures for lawsuits, internal court discipline, and the administration of court affairs to the extent that they do not conflict with statutes.” This means that, with respect to the matters enumerated in the above provision, the Supreme Court may determine them by rules so long as they do not conflict with statutes, and even in this case, express authorization by statute is required.
(d) Although the sentencing guidelines of the Sentencing Commission do not have legal binding force, if a court renders a judgment departing from the sentencing guidelines, the reasons for the sentence must be stated in the written judgment, and the same applies when adjudicating pursuant to summary procedure or summary trial procedure.
(e) Because the Constitution designates the Supreme Court as the highest court, the “right to receive a trial by judges provided by the Constitution and statutes under the law” can be said to mean the right to receive appellate review in all cases.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2001HEONGA18]": "1.  Overview of the Case\\n\\nLee ○-ung, the Plaintiff in the present case, is an attorney. When a petition was received by the Disciplinary Committee for Attorneys of the Korean Bar Association, stating that, on March 30, 1999, Jeong ○-il, a non-party to the adjudication, had entrusted the above Lee ○-ung with the case of a claim for return of a guaranty debt between Stock Company ○○ Bank and the non-party, and had paid 32,770,977 won as deposit money together with a request that a deposit be made naming the above ○○ Bank as the depositee, but that Lee ○-ung failed to make such deposit, whereby the non-party’s wage and retirement allowance claims were provisionally seized and damage was suffered both materially and non-materially, the Committee repeatedly demanded submission of a written explanation from Lee ○-ung; however, since Lee ○-ung did not submit it to the end, it decided on February 14, 2000, to impose a disciplinary sanction of a fine of 5,000,000 won on the grounds that he had not faithfully performed his duties as an attorney, thereby causing a dispute with the client, and had damaged the dignity of an attorney by failing to deal with matters instructed by the Bar Association.\\n\\nLee ○-ung, being dissatisfied with the above disciplinary decision, filed an objection with the Disciplinary Committee for Attorneys of the Ministry of Justice; however, when that petition was dismissed on June 17, 2000, he filed an immediate appeal with the Supreme Court around that time, and on September 9, 2000, filed administrative litigation (2000GU28281) with the Seoul Administrative Court seeking cancellation of the above disciplinary decision. During its hearing, the Seoul Administrative Court, on the ground that Articles 100(4) through (6) of the Attorneys-at-Law Act became a prerequisite for the trial in the present case and that there was doubt as to their constitutionality, sua sponte referred the question of constitutionality in this case on May 17, 2000.\\n\\n2.  Subject of Review\\n\\nThe subject of review in this case is Articles 100(4) through (6) of the Attorneys-at-Law Act (hereinafter referred to as the “provisions at issue”), the content of which is as follows.\\n\\nAttorneys-at-Law Act, Article 100 (Appeal against Disciplinary Decision) ① through ③ omitted\\n\\n④ A disciplinary suspect who is dissatisfied with the decision of the Ministry of Justice Disciplinary Committee may file an immediate appeal with the Supreme Court within 7 days from the day he or she received notice thereof.\\n\\n⑤ An immediate appeal under the provisions of paragraph ④ shall have no effect of suspension of execution.\\n\\n⑥ With respect to an immediate appeal under the provisions of paragraph ④, the provisions concerning a further appeal in the Civil Procedure Act shall apply mutatis mutandis.\\n\\n3.  Grounds for the Petition by the Referring Court\\n\\nThe grounds are the same as those for the decision of the Constitutional Court of June 29, 2000, in 99HEONGA9.\\n\\n4.  Determination\\n\\nThis Court, in its decision of June 29, 2000, in 99HEONGA9 (Collection of Precedents 12-1, 753), declared that Articles 81(4) through (6) of the former Attorneys-at-Law Act (as in force before its full revision by Act No. 6207 on January 28, 2000), which had prescribed the same content as the provisions at issue, were in violation of the Constitution. The gist of that decision is as follows.\\n\\n“Article 27(1) of the Constitution provides that ‘All citizens shall have the right to a trial according to the law by judges qualified under the Constitution and law,’ thereby guaranteeing that all citizens have the right to receive a trial in accordance with the content and procedures prescribed by constitutionally valid laws from judges appointed by qualifications and procedures prescribed by the Constitution and law (Article 101(3) and Article 104 of the Constitution; Articles 41 through 43 of the Court Organization Act), and whose material independence (Article 103 of the Constitution) and personal independence (Article 106 of the Constitution; Article 46 of the Court Organization Act) are guaranteed. Meanwhile, a trial is a series of processes whose essential content consists of the determination of facts in a concrete case and the interpretive application of law thereto.\\n\\nAccordingly, guaranteeing the right to receive a trial by judges ultimately means guaranteeing the right to receive a trial in which judges determine facts and interpret and apply the law, and if such guarantee is not properly afforded, it infringes the essential content of the constitutionally guaranteed right to receive a trial and is not permitted under our Constitution.\\n\\nHowever, the provisions at issue do not afford, even where there is dissatisfaction with a disciplinary decision against an attorney, an opportunity for fact-finding and application of law by a judge, but only allow an immediate appeal to the Supreme Court, which is a court of law, when the decision is alleged to have violated statutes and regulations; yet the disciplinary decisions of the Disciplinary Committee for Attorneys of the Korean Bar Association or of the Disciplinary Committee for Attorneys of the Ministry of Justice cannot be regarded as trials by judges qualified under the Constitution and law, even if judges participate as some of the members of those disciplinary committees (see Article 74(1) and Article 75(2) of the Attorneys-at-Law Act).\\n\\nIf so, the provisions at issue are unconstitutional provisions that infringe the essential content of the right to a trial ‘by judges’ guaranteed to the people under the Constitution, by depriving them of the opportunity for fact-finding and application of law by judges.\\n\\nIn addition, Article 101(1) and (2) of the Constitution provides that ‘The judicial power shall be vested in courts composed of judges. Courts shall be organized into the Supreme Court, which is the highest court, and courts at all levels,’ and the first sentence of Article 107(3) of the Constitution provides that ‘Administrative adjudication may be conducted as a pretrial procedure for a trial.’ This is a concrete expression of the principle of separation of powers adopted by our Constitution as a basic principle to prevent abuse of state power and secure the freedom and rights of the people; it means that the judicial function, which is the function of hearing and adjudicating all legal disputes, may be performed solely by the courts with the Supreme Court as the highest court (Article 101(2) of the Constitution), unless there is a reservation by the Constitution itself, and that administrative adjudication must function only as a pretrial procedure for a trial by the courts.\\n\\nHowever, disciplinary decisions or dismissal decisions of the Disciplinary Committee for Attorneys of the Ministry of Justice are, in view of their deciding body and function, nothing more than administrative adjudication, and only when review of both the factual and legal aspects by the courts is possible with respect to such administrative adjudication can it be said that judicial power, or adjudicatory authority, over attorney disciplinary cases belongs to the courts. Yet the provisions at issue exclude review by the courts of both the factual and legal aspects of such administrative adjudication, allow the Supreme Court, as the final court and court of law in attorney disciplinary cases, to review only the legal aspect, and cause the Disciplinary Committee for Attorneys of the Ministry of Justice, which should function only as a pretrial procedure for a trial, to function, insofar as fact-finding is concerned, as the de facto final instance. This violates Article 101(1) and Article 107(3) of the Constitution, which provide that the adjudicatory function over all legal disputes belongs to the courts with the Supreme Court as the highest court.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the provisions at issue exclude the opportunity for factual hearing by the Administrative Court and the High Court in attorney disciplinary cases; and even considering the distinctive professional characteristics of attorneys, such as freedom, public nature, self-governance of associations, and autonomy, they cannot be said to have any legitimate purpose that would justify such discrimination as compared with other professionals such as physicians, certified public accountants, tax accountants, and architects. In this respect, the provisions at issue violate Article 11(1) of the Constitution, which provides for the principle of equality.”\\n\\nIn the present case as well, no change in circumstances or necessity warranting a different conclusion from the above decision is recognized.\\n\\n5.  Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the provisions at issue are in violation of the Constitution. This is the unanimous opinion of all Justices who participated."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning delegated legislation is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)
A: Where a statute delegates the power to prescribe specific matters to the articles of incorporation of a public-law institution that is not part of, or does not belong to, the executive branch, there is no room to impair the principle of separation of powers; accordingly, the prohibition on blanket delegation legislation under Articles 75 and 95 of the Constitution does not, in principle, apply.
B: Although Article 95 of the Constitution provides the basis for delegation to Ministerial Ordinances and, unlike Article 75, does not use the phrase “specifically determine the scope,” the constitutional limitations imposed on Presidential Decrees by delegation under a statute naturally also apply to Ministerial Ordinances under delegation under a statute.
C: The Act on the Repatriation and Treatment, etc. of Prisoners of War of the Republic of Korea Armed Forces merely provides that registered prisoners of war, etc. may be accorded honors in accordance with Presidential Decree, and contains no provisions whatsoever regarding the content or method of such honors; therefore, it cannot be regarded as enforceable solely on the basis of the provisions of the superior law without the enactment of a Presidential Decree, and thus the President has a duty to enact or amend a Presidential Decree concerning the honoring of registered prisoners of war, etc.
D: The forms of delegated legislation recognized by the Constitution should be regarded as illustrative, and even if a statute delegates certain matters to administrative rules, such administrative rules may regulate only the delegated matters; therefore, this does not conflict with the principle of legislation by the National Assembly.
E: Because the doctrine of delegated legislation is based on the fundamental constitutional principles of the separation of powers and parliamentarianism or the rule of law, there is a direct relationship between whether the content prescribed in a Presidential Decree enacted by the executive branch is proper and the legality of the delegation.
