supporting_precedents: {"[2004HEONBA15]": "1. Outline of the Case and Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\na. Outline of the Case\\n\\nThe Petitioner, born on September 15, 1969, received a disposition making him subject to enlistment for active duty based on a finding of Physical Grade 2 in the conscription physical examination on February 15, 1988, but, on the ground of his stay abroad due to overseas study, he was granted permission to travel abroad from May 8, 1989 to December 22, 1995 and had his enlistment deferred. Thereafter, as a result of a re-physical examination on January 6, 1996 and a detailed physical examination around February 1996, the Petitioner received a finding of Physical Grade 5 and a disposition placing him into the Second Citizen Service category. However, on May 30, 2000, the Commissioner of the Seoul Regional Military Manpower Administration canceled said disposition placing him into the Second Citizen Service category on the ground that it had been unlawfully and improperly made through solicitation to, and provision of money or valuables to, military doctors, etc. who made the physical examination findings.\\n\\nThe Petitioner underwent a re-physical examination on June 20, 2000 and, as a result of a finding of Physical Grade 4, received a disposition placing him into supplementary service. On August 24, 2000, the Commissioner of the Seoul Regional Military Manpower Administration issued a call-up disposition for public-service personnel ordering the Petitioner to enlist by October 16, 2000.\\n\\nThe Petitioner filed an action seeking revocation of the above disposition placing him into supplementary service, and although he lost at first instance (Seoul Administrative Court 2000GU29444), the appellate court revoked the above call-up disposition for public-service personnel on the ground that abuse of discretion by the Commissioner of the Seoul Regional Military Manpower Administration was recognized (Seoul High Court 2001NU5387; the claim sought was changed at the appellate stage). However, the Supreme Court reversed and remanded it, stating that the local military manpower office commissioner cannot be regarded as having discretion in calling up public-service personnel (2002DU820), and the case is currently pending before the Seoul High Court (the underlying case).\\n\\nIn the underlying case, the Petitioner applied for a motion for referral for constitutional review concerning the proviso to Article 71(1) item 6 of the former Military Service Act (2003A85), but when it was dismissed, on February 7, 2004, he filed a constitutional complaint alleging that said provision infringes his right to equality and freedom of residence and movement.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether Article 71 of the former Military Service Act (as amended by Act No. 5757 on February 5, 1999, and before amendment by Act No. 6287 on December 26, 2000, hereinafter referred to as the “Act”)\\nis unconstitutional. On December 26, 2000, the provision at issue was changed by Act No. 6287 from the former Article 71(1) item 6 to item 7, but its content is the same.\\n\\nArticle 71 of the Act (Exemption from Obligations of Enlistment, etc.) ① The obligations of conscription examination, enlistment for active duty, or call-up for public-service personnel shall be exempted from the age of 31, and persons exempted therefrom shall be placed into the Second Citizen Service category. Provided, however, that persons falling under any of the following items shall be exempted from the age of 36.\\n\\n6. A person whose conscription examination or enlistment, etc. was deferred on grounds under Article 60(1) item 2\\n\\nArticle 60 of the Act (Deferral of Conscription Examination and Enlistment, etc.) ① The local military manpower office commissioner may defer the conscription examination for persons subject to conscription examination who fall under any of the following items.\\n\\n2. A person staying or residing abroad\\n\\n2. The Petitioner’s Claims and the Opinions of Relevant Authorities\\n\\na. The Petitioner’s Claims\\n\\nThe provision at issue, by unconditionally extending the age for exemption from military duty to 36 for persons whose conscription examination or enlistment, etc. was deferred merely on the ground that they are staying or residing abroad, regardless of the timing of their return to Korea or whether military service processing is conducted after their return, discriminates without any basis in relation to persons whose conscription examination, etc. was deferred for other reasons such as schooling in Korea, and therefore contravenes the principle of equality under Article 11 of the Constitution.\\n\\nThe provision at issue, by extending the age for exemption from military duty to 36 for persons who have a history of staying abroad, makes it impossible for them to freely move their residence abroad, or subjects them to unfavorable treatment without rational basis on account of residence abroad, and this infringes the freedom of residence and movement under Article 14 of the Constitution.\\n\\nThe provision at issue, even though its legislative purpose could be sufficiently achieved by extending the age for exemption from military duty only for persons whose conscription examination, etc. is currently deferred on the ground of stay abroad, extends the scope of persons whose age for exemption from military duty is prolonged to include all persons who have in the past been deferred from conscription examination, etc. due to stay abroad; accordingly, even persons who have already returned to Korea for several years and have no risk whatsoever of evading military service by taking advantage of stay abroad are stipulated as persons subject to extension of the age for exemption from military duty, thereby excessively defining the scope of application beyond the legislative purpose, and this violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction under Article 37(2) of the Constitution.\\n\\nb. Reasons for the Court’s Dismissal of the Motion for Constitutional Review\\n\\nThe legislative intent of the provision at issue lies in preventing persons whose conscription examination or enlistment, etc. was deferred on grounds of stay or residence abroad from evading military service; the deferral of conscription examination or enlistment on the ground of stay or residence abroad is, unless special circumstances exist, prescribed to be possible only until the person liable for military service reaches the age of 31; in the concrete process of imposing military obligations, i.e., at each stage of conscription examination, enlistment, and enlistment date, etc., reasons for deferral may arise (Articles 60 and 61 of the Act), and even in the process of changing military service dispositions, a considerable period may be required (Article 65 of the Act); in particular, where conscription examination or enlistment is deferred on the ground of stay or residence abroad, the period of such deferral is long compared with other grounds for deferral for persons residing in Korea, and thus there appears to be a rational reason to delay the age for exemption from military duty to 36 for all persons who received such deferral before reaching 31 (see Supreme Court Decision of June 25, 2002, 2001DU5125); in light of these points, the provision at issue cannot be said to violate the principle of equality by arbitrarily discriminating without objective and rational grounds against persons whose conscription examination or enlistment was deferred on the ground of stay or residence abroad, or by being contrary to justice and fairness.\\n\\nThe provision at issue is not, by itself, a provision that restricts the freedom of residence and movement of the applicant or the people, or restricts emigration abroad. Considering that the matter of determining the scope of those subject to conscription is inherently an area in which the legislature’s broad legislative discretion must be recognized, the provision at issue cannot be said to infringe the essential content of the freedoms and rights of the people or to violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\nc. Opinion of the Minister of National Defense\\n\\nIt is generally the same as the above reasons for dismissal by the court.\\n\\n3. Judgment\\n\\na. Whether the Principle of Equality Is Violated\\n\\n(1) The main text of Article 71(1) of the Act (Exemption from Obligations of Enlistment, etc.) provided that the obligations of conscription examination, enlistment for active duty, or call-up for public-service personnel are exempted from the age of 31, but the proviso provided that persons falling under each item are exempted therefrom from the age of 36. Those items include “a person who is evading conscription examination, etc. without justifiable grounds” (item 1), “a person whose placement into the category of public health doctor, public-service judicial officer, etc. has been canceled” (item 2), “a person whose call-up as a public-service personnel has been canceled because he did not comply with an order for occupational training” (item 3), “a person who departed the country without permission or is staying abroad” (item 5), and “a person whose conscription examination or enlistment, etc. was deferred on grounds under Article 60(1) item 2” (item 6).\\n\\nThe provision at issue includes all persons who received a deferral of military service on account of overseas study, and thus applies not only to persons currently studying abroad but also to persons who have returned to Korea after overseas study (Supreme Court Decision of September 10, 2002, 2002DU1786).\\n\\n(2) The provision at issue concerns exemption from the obligations of conscription examination, enlistment for active duty, or call-up for public-service personnel (hereinafter referred to as “exemption from obligations of enlistment, etc.”), and since the duty of national defense is a constitutional duty, legislation exempting obligations of enlistment, etc. pertains to a benefit-conferring matter; accordingly, the provision at issue falls within the area in which the legislature may determine the scope of persons subject to conscription within its broad legislative discretion in the sphere of military service formation (Constitutional Court Decision 2002HEONBA45, Dec. 28, 2002, Constitutional Court Reports 14-2, 704, 710). Therefore, whether the provision at issue violates the principle of equality (equal protection) depends on whether it constitutes discrimination with rational grounds (see id. at 14-2, 704, 716).\\n\\n(3) As a result of the provision at issue also applying to persons who have already completed overseas study and returned, among persons residing in Korea there arises discrimination in that, for persons whose conscription examination was deferred due to overseas study, the standard for exemption from obligations of enlistment, etc. of 36 applies, whereas for other residents in Korea the standard of 31 applies.\\n\\nHowever, where a stay abroad occurs on grounds such as study as a reason for deferral of conscription, the period is relatively long, and even if a person returns to Korea after completing overseas study before turning 31, reasons for deferral may arise at each stage in the concrete process of imposing military obligations, namely conscription examination, enlistment, and enlistment date, etc. (Articles 60 and 61 of the Military Service Act), and a considerable period may be required even in the process of changing military service dispositions (Article 65 of the Military Service Act), so there is a rational reason to delay the age for exemption from obligations of enlistment, etc. to 36 for persons who received such deferral (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2002DU1786). In addition, because the provision at issue is a benefit-conferring provision that relieves a person from the duty of national defense, the National Assembly’s legislative discretion concerning it should be respected; and extending, beyond the ordinary age, the age for exemption from obligations of enlistment, etc. for persons who had conscription deferred on the ground of stay or residence abroad so as to ensure that the constitutional duty of national defense is not unfairly exempted cannot be said to be arbitrary beyond the bounds of legislative discretion.\\n\\nHowever, as the Petitioner asserts, in the case of persons who have already returned before reaching 31 after staying abroad, it may be more equitable to exempt them from obligations of enlistment, etc. from the age of 31 as in ordinary cases; nevertheless, conscription deferral on grounds of stay or residence abroad is ordinarily long-term, and the timing of return may become close to age 31 depending on circumstances abroad. Considering that the above provisions of the Military Service Act contain various deferral systems in several substantive or administrative aspects, even if the provision at issue does not make such a distinction, it cannot be concluded that it is unreasonable or arbitrary.\\n\\nTherefore, the provision at issue does not violate the principle of equality.\\n\\nb. Whether the Freedom of Residence and Movement Is Infringed\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues that the provision at issue infringes the freedom of residence and movement by subjecting only persons with a history of stay abroad to an extended age for call-up obligations and thereby treating them unfavorably.\\n\\nHowever, the provision at issue merely means that for persons whose conscription examination was deferred on the ground of residence abroad, the age for exemption from obligations of enlistment, etc. is applied from 36, and even if the provision at issue exists, the Petitioner remains free to reside abroad or move abroad. Therefore, the fact that, if one stays abroad, the age for such exemption becomes later than for others cannot be said to constitute a restriction on the freedom of residence and movement. In other words, in this case, the scope of protection of the freedom of residence and movement cannot be understood to include the point that “the timing of the benefit allowing one to be exempted from the duty of national defense on the ground of residence and movement shall not be later than that of others.”\\n\\nTherefore, the fact that, because of stay abroad, the age for exemption from obligations of enlistment, etc. is applied from 36 rather than from 31 cannot be said to constitute a restriction on the freedom of residence and movement. And insofar as that is so determined, the issue of whether the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction is violated is not separately examined in this case.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, the provision at issue does not violate the Constitution, and by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, the Court decides as follows."}

{"[2005HEONBA31]": "1. Outline of the Case and Object of Adjudication\\n\\nA. Outline of the Case\\n\\n(1) The Korea Disabled Veterans Association (hereinafter referred to as the “Disabled Veterans Association”) elected Choi ○Ho as President at the general meeting held on June 30, 2003, with 123 of 128 incumbent delegates in attendance, and at the general meeting held on August 20, 2003, elected Kang ○Sin and Choi ○Man as Vice Presidents, respectively, Yoo ○Bae and Jeon ○Jun as Auditors, respectively, and Lee ○Kwon and 10 others as Directors, respectively, with 121 of 122 incumbent delegates in attendance.\\n\\n(2) In response, the Petitioner filed an application for a provisional injunction with the Seoul Southern District Court, Case No. 2004KAHAP895, seeking to have the execution of duties by the present officers suspended until the final judgment on the merits becomes final in the case seeking confirmation of the invalidity of each resolution adopted at the general meetings of June 30, 2003 and August 20, 2003 of the Disabled Veterans Association, on the ground that Articles 21, 30, and 32 of the Disabled Veterans Association’s articles of association concerning the composition of delegates are invalid provisions in violation of the superior law, because Article 11 of the Act on the Establishment of Organizations of Persons of Distinguished Services to the State, etc. delegates to the articles of association the legislative intent of prescribing, in accordance with the purpose of the delegate system, the total number of delegates and the method of appointment.\\n\\n(3) When the Petitioner’s above application for a provisional injunction was dismissed on the ground that there had been an insufficient prima facie showing of the right sought to be preserved, the Petitioner, dissatisfied therewith, filed an appeal with the Seoul High Court, Case No. 2004RA484, and during the pendency of that proceeding filed a motion for referral for unconstitutionality concerning the above Article 11 (2004KAGI648). However, when the said court dismissed that motion on March 18, 2005, the Petitioner filed the present constitutional complaint on April 15, 2005.\\n\\nB. Object of Adjudication\\n\\nThe object of adjudication in this case is whether Article 11 of the Act on the Establishment of Organizations of Persons of Distinguished Services to the State, etc. (wholly amended by Act No. 4073 on December 31, 1988; hereinafter referred to as the “Act at Issue”) is unconstitutional. The text of the provision subject to adjudication and the related provision are as follows:\\n\\nArticle 11 (Delegates) The total number of delegates of each organization and the method of appointment, etc. shall be prescribed by the articles of association.\\n\\n[Related Provision]\\n\\nDisabled Veterans Association Articles of Association (as amended on June 16, 2003)  \\nArticle 21 (Delegates) ① The delegates of the main association shall be elected at the council of branch presidents within 5 days after the appointment of the new branch president has been completed for each branch. Provided, however, that this shall not apply where a delegate is vacated and re-election is sought.\\n\\n② Notwithstanding the provisions of paragraph 1, the branch president of a special branch directly under headquarters shall become an ex officio delegate.\\n\\nArticle 30 (Council of Branch Presidents) ① The council of branch presidents shall be composed of the branch heads, the secretary general, and the branch presidents.\\n\\nArticle 32 (Appointment of Branch Presidents) Branch presidents shall be appointed by the branch head. Provided, however, that the president of a special branch directly under headquarters shall be appointed by the president of the special branch directly under headquarters, and the branch head shall appoint the president of the special branch, from among persons elected at the general meeting of the affiliated members.\\n\\n2. The Petitioner’s Arguments and the Opinions of the Relevant Institutions\\n\\nA. The Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\n(1) As a matter of principle, delegation of legislation is made only to legislative instruments such as Presidential Decrees or Ministerial Ordinances; however, the fact that the provision at issue delegated the content regulated by statute to the articles of association, which are not even administrative rules subordinate to legislative instruments, is in violation of the delegated-legislation doctrines under Articles 75 and 95 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Even if it were possible to delegate matters concerning the election of delegates to the articles of association, delegation must be made “by specifying a concrete scope” so that the outline of the matters to be regulated by subordinate norms can be foreseen. Nevertheless, because the provision at issue delegates to the articles of association without setting even a standard by which the outline regarding the total number of delegates and the method of appointment can be foreseen, it violates the prohibition of blanket delegation.\\n\\n(3) All citizens, if they autonomously organize an association and become its members, are guaranteed equal rights to be elected directly, by secret ballot, and by anonymous ballot as delegates or officers; therefore, the provision at issue, which makes that impossible, infringes the constitutional equal rights of the members of the Disabled Veterans Association.\\n\\nB. Reasons Given by the Court for Dismissing the Motion for Referral of Unconstitutionality\\n\\n(1) Although the Disabled Veterans Association was established pursuant to the provision at issue, its nature is that of an incorporated association under the Civil Act, namely, a self-governing organization autonomously composed by its members. Thus, even though the provision at issue takes the form of delegating matters concerning the election of delegates of the Disabled Veterans Association to the articles of association, this merely leaves matters that should originally be regulated autonomously in the articles of association as matters to be prescribed therein, and neither the Constitution nor any other statute has designated them as matters to be regulated by statute. Accordingly, matters concerning the election of delegates of the Disabled Veterans Association cannot be said to be subject, under the Constitution, to the prohibition of blanket delegation of legislation, and the provision at issue cannot be deemed to violate Articles 75 and 95 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) The provision at issue merely delegates matters concerning the election of delegates of the Disabled Veterans Association to the articles of association and does not contain any provision restricting qualifications for becoming a delegate; therefore, it cannot be deemed to violate the principle of equality under Article 11 of the Constitution.\\n\\nC. The Opinion of the Disabled Veterans Association\\n\\nThe Disabled Veterans Association is a special juristic person established by law, but its substance is an incorporated association under the Civil Act, namely, a self-governing organization autonomously composed by members who are disabled veterans. In addition, the provision at issue takes the form of delegating the total number of delegates and the method of appointment, etc. of an organization such as the Disabled Veterans Association to its articles of association, and it does not impose any restriction whatsoever concerning qualifications for delegates.\\n\\nIn light of the corporate nature of the Disabled Veterans Association and the form of the provision at issue, the provision at issue is nothing more than a provision declaring that matters such as the total number of delegates and the method of appointment, which the Disabled Veterans Association should determine autonomously, are to be expressly provided in its articles of association. Therefore, it cannot be deemed to violate the constitutional prohibition of blanket delegation of legislation or the principle of equality.\\n\\nD. The Opinion of the Minister of Patriots and Veterans Affairs\\n\\nSubstantially the same as the reasons for the decision dismissing the motion for referral of unconstitutionality.\\n\\n3. Decision\\n\\nA. The Regulatory Form “Shall Be Prescribed by the Articles of Association” and the Prohibition of Blanket Delegation of Legislation\\n\\n(1) Organization of the Issues and Summary of Similar Decisions\\n\\nIn this case, the issue is first whether the constitutional limits on delegated legislation apply even where a statute provides that “... shall be prescribed by the articles of association,” and, if they do not apply, what the standard for constitutional review is. Our Court has, however, held that where a statute delegates autonomous matters to the articles of association of a public-law entity, the prohibition of blanket delegation of legislation under Articles 75 and 95 of the Constitution does not apply (Constitutional Court, Apr. 26, 2001, 2000HEONMA122, Court Reports 13-1, 962), the gist of which is as follows:\\n\\n“Article 40 of the Constitution provides that ‘the legislative power shall be vested in the National Assembly,’ while Article 75 provides that ‘the President may issue Presidential Decrees concerning matters delegated specifically by statute and matters necessary for the enforcement of statutes,’ and Article 95 provides that ‘the Prime Minister or the head of each executive ministry may issue Ordinances of the Prime Minister or Ministerial Ordinances with respect to matters under their jurisdiction pursuant to delegation by statute or Presidential Decree, or ex officio,’ thereby recognizing delegated legislation by administrative agencies. The meaning of Article 40 of our Constitution is that, at a minimum, matters concerning the formation of citizens’ rights and duties, as well as basic and essential matters concerning the state’s governing organization and functions, must be determined by the National Assembly itself (Constitutional Court, May 28, 1998, 96HEONMA1, Court Reports 10-1, 509, 515-516).\\n\\nDelegated legislation means establishing general and abstract norms that have the nature of rules of law with respect to matters specifically delegated by statute or by a superior order. Although it does not fall within statutes in the formal sense (legislation by the National Assembly), it is, in substance, the establishment of rules of law that have the same character as statutes, as legislation by the administration. Therefore, in light of the principle of separation of powers and the rule of law, the requirements must necessarily be strict, and the enactment of administrative legislation having normative force invariably requires specific and clear delegation by statute (Article 75 of the Constitution) (Constitutional Court, May 13, 1993, 92HEONMA80, Court Reports 5-1, 365, 379).\\n\\nHowever, where a statute delegates autonomous matters to the articles of association, it is appropriate, as a general rule, to view the prohibition of blanket delegation of legislation under Articles 75 and 95 of the Constitution as inapplicable.\\n\\nFirst, as a matter of literal interpretation and doctrinal interpretation of Articles 75 and 95 of the Constitution, the prohibition of blanket delegation of legislation mainly targets the enactment of administrative legislation having normative force. The reason for placing delegated legislation within strict constitutional limits derives above all from the doctrine that, pursuant to the principle of separation of powers, matters relating to the freedoms and rights of citizens should in principle be determined by the representative organ of the people. In other words, the enactment of rule-of-law matters by the executive branch can infringe on the authority or duty of the legislature and, through arbitrary issuance of enforcement decrees, can infringe on the freedoms and rights of the people; for that reason, it is subject to strict constitutional restraint. However, where a statute delegates authority to the articles of association of a public-law institution that is not the executive branch or does not belong to the executive branch to prescribe certain matters, there is no possibility of undermining the principle of separation of powers. This falls within the sphere of autonomous legislation, and it is desirable that it be determined autonomously.\\n\\nNevertheless, even if the constitutional prohibition of blanket delegation of legislation does not, as a general rule, apply where a statute delegates autonomous matters to the articles of association, if those matters are related to citizens’ rights and duties, then the principle of statutory reservation or parliamentary reservation—that, at a minimum, matters concerning the formation of citizens’ rights and duties, as well as basic and essential matters concerning the state’s governing organization and functions, must be determined by the National Assembly (Constitutional Court, May 28, 1998, 96HEONGA1, Court Reports 10-1, 509, 515-516)—must be observed.”\\n\\n(2) Whether the Provision at Issue Is Unconstitutional\\n\\n(a) The Act at Issue was enacted for the purpose of founding 10 organizations of persons of distinguished services to the State, including the Disabled Veterans Association, thereby enabling persons of distinguished services to the State and their bereaved families to help one another, cultivate self-supporting ability, carry on the spirit of the nation by succeeding to the legacy of the patriots and fallen soldiers who died for the country, promote the national spirit, foster citizens’ patriotic spirit, and contribute to the defense of liberal democracy, the peaceful reunification of the homeland, and the maintenance of international peace (Article 1). Each organization of persons of distinguished services to the State is a public corporation established under the Act at issue, with as its members persons of distinguished services to the State or their bereaved families who have the qualifications under each paragraph of Article 4 of the Act on the Honorable Treatment and Support of Persons of Distinguished Services to the State, etc. (Articles 3 and 4(1) of the Act at issue). As to each organization, except as otherwise provided in the Act at issue, the provisions of the Civil Act concerning incorporated associations shall apply mutatis mutandis (Article 4(2)), and it may conduct profit-making business directly within the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of establishment under Article 1 of the Act at issue (Article 7-2(1)).\\n\\nMeanwhile, under the Act at issue, the president of each organization is elected at the general meeting but must obtain approval from the Administrator of the Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs (Article 6(3)); when amending the articles of association, approval from the Administrator of the Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs must be obtained (Article 7(2)); and the Administrator of the Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs may direct the organization, when it commits an act or adopts a resolution in violation of the statute or directions under the statute or the articles of association, to take the necessary corrective measures (Article 15), and so on. Thus, each organization is a public-law entity subject to the guidance and supervision of the executive branch. However, its substance is, as noted above, that of an incorporated association under the Civil Act, namely, a self-governing organization autonomously composed by its members; therefore, it cannot be regarded as a case in which the enactment of the organization’s articles of association is carried out by the executive branch, and what the statute delegates to the organization’s articles of association cannot be regarded as equivalent to a delegation to a legislative order issued by the executive branch.\\n\\nIn addition, the provision at issue provides that “the total number of delegates of each organization and the method of appointment, etc. shall be prescribed by the articles of association.” Matters concerning the election of delegates relate to the composition of each organization and fall within the sphere of self-government; accordingly, each organization must determine them autonomously through the necessary standards and evaluation in light of its own characteristics.\\n\\nTherefore, even if the provision at issue takes the form of delegating matters concerning the election of delegates of each organization, including the Disabled Veterans Association, to the articles of association, this merely leaves matters that should originally be regulated autonomously in the articles of association as matters to be prescribed therein, and since neither the Constitution nor any other statute has designated them as matters to be regulated by statute, the constitutional prohibition of blanket delegation of legislation does not apply to the review of their constitutionality.\\n\\n(b) In addition, matters concerning the election of delegates of each organization of persons of distinguished services to the State are, like the matters of convening and adopting resolutions at the general meeting, methods of meeting, methods of appointing the branch heads and branch presidents of the branches and sub-branches of each organization, and matters concerning the board of directors, which the Act at issue has designated as matters to be prescribed in the articles of association (Article 6-2(1), Article 10(2), Article 12(2) of the Act), matters relating to the composition and operation of each organization. Therefore, they cannot be regarded as matters concerning the formation of citizens’ rights and duties or as basic and essential matters concerning the state’s governing organization and functions, and thus cannot be said to fall within the domain where the principle of statutory reservation or parliamentary reservation must be observed.\\n\\nAccordingly, the fact that the provision at issue requires that the total number of delegates and the method of appointment, etc. of each organization be prescribed by the articles of association cannot be deemed to violate the principle of statutory reservation or otherwise the provisions of the Constitution, and there are no other circumstances from which it can be said that the Petitioner’s basic rights were infringed.\\n\\nB. The Content of the Articles of Association and the Issue of Violation of the Principle of Equality\\n\\nThe Petitioner argues that the provision at issue infringes the Petitioner’s constitutional equal rights by failing to guarantee an equal right to be elected as a delegate or officer. However, the provision at issue merely delegates matters concerning the election of delegates of each organization of persons of distinguished services to the State, including the Disabled Veterans Association, to the articles of association, and does not contain any provision restricting qualifications for becoming a delegate. Therefore, the Petitioner’s argument can be understood as asserting that, under the provisions of the Disabled Veterans Association’s articles of association based on the provision at issue, delegates must ultimately be composed of persons close to the president, thereby infringing the Petitioner’s right to be elected as a delegate. Since the constitutionality of the articles of association themselves is not the object of adjudication in this case, the issue of whether they violate the principle of equality under Article 11 of the Constitution cannot be addressed.\\n\\nEven if such an argument were examined, under the Act at issue the headquarters are located in Seoul Special City, branches in Seoul Special City, metropolitan cities, and provinces, and sub-branches in cities, counties, and districts (referring to districts that are local governments) (Article 5), and the articles of association of the Disabled Veterans Association provide that the president elected at the general meeting appoints the branch head, the branch head appoints the branch president, and delegates are elected at the national council of branch presidents. Such provisions cannot be said to exclude or restrict the Petitioner from being elected as a delegate at the council of branch presidents, and since they cannot otherwise be regarded as unreasonable or arbitrary, it cannot be said that the Petitioner’s right to equality was infringed thereby.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nFor the foregoing reasons, the provision at issue does not violate the Constitution, and so the Court, by unanimous agreement of all Justices, renders the decision as stated in the operative part."}
