Outline of the Case  \\nThe Petitioner is a child of the late POW of the Korean Armed Forces Son ○ Sik, who died in North Korea on 1984. 1. 22., and is a North Korean defector who was born in North Korea, defected on 2005. 12. 19., and entered the Republic of Korea in 2013. 10. The Petitioner filed the present constitutional complaint on 2016. 7. 28., alleging that the legislative omission of the National Assembly, which failed to take legislative measures concerning the treatment and support of POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who, like the late Son ○ Sik, died in the place of detention and could not return alive to the Republic of Korea, and the administrative legislative omission of failing to enact the Presidential Decree pursuant to Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the Act on the Repatriation and Treatment of Prisoners of War of the Korean Armed Forces (hereinafter, the “POW Act”) infringe the Petitioner’s fundamental rights.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication  \\nThe subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether the legislative omission under the Act on the Repatriation and Treatment, etc. of Prisoners of War of the Korean Armed Forces, which provides only for remuneration, other treatment, and support for prisoners who returned to and were registered in the Republic of Korea, and failed to take legislative measures concerning POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before returning to the Republic of Korea (hereinafter, the “legislative omission in this case”), and whether the administrative legislative omission by the Respondent President in failing to enact the Presidential Decree pursuant to the delegation in Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the Act on the Repatriation and Treatment, etc. of Prisoners of War of the Korean Armed Forces (as amended by Act No. 13237 on 2015. 3. 27.) (hereinafter, the “administrative legislative omission in this case”) infringes the Petitioner’s fundamental rights. The relevant provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Relevant Provisions]  \\nAct on the Repatriation and Treatment, etc. of Prisoners of War of the Korean Armed Forces (as amended by Act No. 11652 on 2013. 3. 22.)  \\nArticle 9 (Special Provisions on Remuneration) ① The Minister of National Defense shall pay registered POWs remuneration for the period of detention (including allowances; hereinafter the same shall apply in this Article). Provided, however, that if, on the last day of the period of detention, the person is over 60 years of age, remuneration shall be paid only up to the month in which the date on which the person becomes 60 falls.  \\nArticle 11 (Consolation Support Payment) ① The Minister of National Defense shall divide the consolation support payment for registered POWs, for the purpose of comforting them and supporting their stable domestic settlement, into a monthly support payment and a lump-sum support payment and pay it accordingly.\\n\\nAct on the Repatriation and Treatment, etc. of Prisoners of War of the Korean Armed Forces (enacted by Act No. 7896 on 2006. 3. 24.)  \\nArticle 14 (Medical Support) The Minister of National Defense may provide medical support free of charge to registered POWs pursuant to the Presidential Decree.  \\nArticle 15 (Support Payment for Families of POWs Originating from the Place of Detention) ① The Minister of National Defense may pay support payments to families of POWs originating from the place of detention who have been registered pursuant to Article 6.\\n\\nAct on the Repatriation and Treatment, etc. of Prisoners of War of the Korean Armed Forces (as amended by Act No. 13237 on 2015. 3. 27.)  \\nArticle 15-3 (Employment Support for Families of POWs Originating from the Place of Detention) The Minister of National Defense may provide employment support for the stable domestic settlement of families of POWs originating from the place of detention who have returned to the Republic of Korea pursuant to the Presidential Decree.  \\nArticle 15-4 (Support for Use of Royal Palaces, etc.) ① Registered POWs and families of POWs originating from the place of detention who have returned to the Republic of Korea may be allowed to use free of charge facilities such as royal palaces and parks managed by the State or local governments, or may be allowed to use them at a discounted fee.  \\nArticle 15-5 (Courtesy toward POWs of the Korean Armed Forces) ① The Minister of National Defense may accord to registered POWs, repatriated POWs who died before registration under Article 6, and POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before repatriation honors commensurate with their conduct during the period of detention or the degree of their contribution.  \\n② Necessary matters concerning the application, standards, methods, etc. for the honors under paragraph 1 shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n\\n3. Petitioner’s Arguments  \\na. Although the POW Act was enacted for the purpose of contributing to the stabilization of the living conditions and the improvement of welfare of POWs of the Korean Armed Forces and their families, it created the concept of “registered POWs” and provides that only prisoners who returned to and were registered in the Republic of Korea may receive remuneration and various forms of treatment or support. In light of Article 10, Article 11, paragraph 1, and Article 34, paragraph 1 of the Constitution, the State has a duty to enact legislation in the direction of protecting the most fundamental human rights of equality and human dignity; accordingly, as a matter of constitutional interpretation, there exists a legislative duty to act or a duty to protect also with respect to POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died without returning alive. Nevertheless, by failing to provide for the treatment or support of POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before returning, the POW Act infringes the Petitioner’s right to equality and right to live a life worthy of human dignity.\\n\\nb. Although Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act delegates to the Presidential Decree the matters necessary for the application, standards, methods, etc. of the honors accorded to POWs of the Korean Armed Forces, the Enforcement Decree of the POW Act provides no content whatsoever in this regard. Such administrative legislative omission infringes the Petitioner’s property right.\\n\\n4. Determination  \\na. Petition for adjudication regarding the legislative omission in this case  \\n(1) The Petitioner argues that the POW Act created the concept of “registered POWs” and provides that only prisoners who returned to and were registered in the Republic of Korea may receive remuneration and various forms of treatment or support, and that no legislative measures whatsoever have been taken with respect to remuneration and other treatment and support for POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before returning to the Republic of Korea.  \\nHowever, the POW Act provides in Article 9, paragraph 1 for a special rule on the payment of remuneration to registered POWs, and in Article 11, paragraph 1 for the payment of consolation support payments to registered POWs, while Article 15, paragraph 1 provides for the payment of support payments to families of POWs originating from the place of detention of POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before repatriation. As such, because the POW Act, through the above statutory provisions, provides for remuneration and consolation support payments to registered POWs and for support payments to families of POWs originating from the place of detention in relation to POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before repatriation, the Petitioner’s argument ultimately contests incomplete or insufficient legislation regarding the provisions on remuneration and support for registered POWs or the provisions on support for families of POWs originating from the place of detention, which constitutes a non-genuine legislative omission. To challenge such a non-genuine legislative omission, aside from the question whether a constitutional complaint may be filed against the incomplete legal provision itself, it cannot be made the subject of a constitutional complaint as a legislative omission (see Constitutional Court 1996. 6. 13. 94HEONMA118, et seq.).  \\n(2) Even if this part of the petition is construed as challenging the incompleteness or insufficiency of Article 9, paragraph 1 and Article 11, paragraph 1 of the POW Act (as amended by Act No. 11652 on 2013. 3. 22.) and Article 15, paragraph 1 of the POW Act (enacted by Act No. 7896 on 2006. 3. 24.), this part of the petition was filed after the expiration of the filing period. A constitutional complaint against a statute must be filed within 1 year from the date the statute took effect, where the infringement of fundamental rights occurs simultaneously with the enforcement of the statute, or within 1 year from the date on which the cause corresponding to the statute first arises after the statute’s enforcement, where the infringement of fundamental rights occurs only after the cause corresponding to the statute arises (see Constitutional Court 2007. 7. 26. 2006HEONMA1164; Constitutional Court 2013. 12. 26. 2011HEONMA499, et seq.). According to the record of this case, it can be recognized that the Petitioner repatriated the remains of the late Son ○ Sik to the Republic of Korea around 2013. 10. 5.; thus, at least around 2013. 10. 5., a cause of infringement of the Petitioner’s fundamental rights arose. Accordingly, this part of the petition filed on 2016. 7. 28., more than 1 year thereafter, was filed after the expiration of the filing period and is therefore unlawful.\\n\\nb. Petition for adjudication regarding the administrative legislative omission in this case  \\n(1) Whether there exists a duty to enact the Presidential Decree pursuant to Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act  \\n(a) In order for delay in administrative legislation to become unlawful and for legal control over it to be possible, there must first be a legal duty on the administrative agency to enact or amend the implementing decree, and the power to enact or amend the decree must not have been exercised despite the passage of a considerable period of time (see Constitutional Court 1998. 7. 16. 96HEONMA246; Constitutional Court 2013. 5. 30. 2011HEONMA198, et seq.).  \\n(b) Article 15-5, paragraph 1 of the POW Act provides that “The Minister of National Defense may accord to registered POWs, repatriated POWs who died before registration under Article 6, and POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before repatriation honors commensurate with their conduct during the period of detention or the degree of their contribution.” Paragraph 2 provides that “Necessary matters concerning the application, standards, methods, etc. for the honors under paragraph 1 shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.” Accordingly, under Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act, the matters necessary for the application, standards, methods, etc. of the honors for registered POWs, repatriated POWs who died before registration under Article 6, and POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before repatriation (hereinafter, the “registered POWs, etc.”) must be prescribed by Presidential Decree.  \\nAlthough Article 15-5, paragraph 1 of the POW Act grants discretion to the Minister of National Defense as to whether to accord honors, this means only that the Minister of National Defense may accord honors within the bounds of the standards and methods prescribed by the Presidential Decree enacted pursuant to Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act; it does not mean that discretion exists as to whether to enact the Presidential Decree. Unless the Presidential Decree pursuant to Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act is enacted, the Minister of National Defense cannot accord the honors under Article 15-5, paragraph 1 of the POW Act; therefore, before the Minister of National Defense determines whether to accord honors to registered POWs, etc., the Presidential Decree must first be enacted pursuant to Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act. In other words, the duty to enact the Presidential Decree under Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act is binding.  \\n(c) Meanwhile, under our Constitution, which takes as given the principle of separation of powers and the principle of rule-of-law administration, the executive branch’s duty to implement the law through administrative legislation, etc. should be regarded as a constitutional duty; however, this refers to cases in which the enactment of administrative legislation is indispensable for the execution of the law, so that failure to enact such administrative legislation directly results in infringement of the legislative power by the executive branch. If, however, execution can be achieved solely through the provisions of the superior law without enactment of subordinate administrative legislation, then there is no constitutional duty to enact subordinate administrative legislation (see Constitutional Court 2005. 12. 22. 2004HEONMA66; Constitutional Court 2013. 5. 30. 2011HEONMA198, et seq.).  \\nYet, while the POW Act specifically provides in several other provisions for matters concerning various forms of support such as financial assistance, medical support, and employment support for registered POWs and families of POWs originating from the place of detention, with respect to the honors for registered POWs, etc., it merely provides in Article 15-5 that honors may be accorded pursuant to Presidential Decree, and sets forth no provisions whatsoever concerning the content or method of such honors. Considering that the support directly provided for in the POW Act concerns direct monetary benefits or matters of financial and economic support, and that the matters concerning honors referred to in Article 15-5 of the POW Act are not directly prescribed by the POW Act itself, it cannot be said that the matters under Article 15-5 of the POW Act can be implemented solely on the basis of the provisions of the superior law without enactment of a Presidential Decree. Accordingly, the Respondent has a duty to enact or amend the Presidential Decree concerning the honors of registered POWs, etc. pursuant to Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act.  \\n(2) Whether there exists a justifiable ground for the administrative legislative omission in this case  \\n(a) As noted above, because the Respondent has a duty to enact or amend the Presidential Decree concerning the honors of registered POWs, etc., no issue of administrative legislative omission would arise if such matters were provided for in the Enforcement Decree of the POW Act. However, since the Enforcement Decree of the POW Act contains no provision whatsoever for honoring registered POWs, etc. under Article 15-5 of the POW Act, the duty to enact or amend the Presidential Decree remains unfulfilled.  \\n(b) Meanwhile, the provision allowing the Minister of National Defense to accord honors to registered POWs, etc. was first provided in Article 15-4 when the POW Act was amended by Act No. 11652 on 2013. 3. 22., and although its location was changed to Article 15-5 when the POW Act was amended by Act No. 13237 on 2015. 3. 27., the matters concerning honors continued to be delegated to the Presidential Decree. However, from the Enforcement Decree of the POW Act as amended by Presidential Decree No. 24629 on 2013. 6. 21. following the amendment of the POW Act on 2013. 3. 22., through the Enforcement Decree of the POW Act as amended by Presidential Decree No. 26902 on 2016. 1. 19., the above matters concerning honors have not been provided for at all. In this way, about 5 years have passed since 2013. 6. 23., when the provision of the POW Act delegating matters concerning honors for registered POWs, etc. to the Presidential Decree was first enacted and entered into force; and since the Enforcement Decree of the POW Act has been amended five times in the meantime yet still does not provide for matters under Article 15-5 of the POW Act, the administrative legislative omission in this case can be said to have continued for a considerable period of time.  \\n(c) If there had been a justifiable reason for the executive branch not to enact or amend the implementing decree pursuant to delegated legislation, then in such a case the Constitutional Court could not make a finding of unconstitutionality. However, in order for such a justifiable reason to be recognized, the delegated legislation itself must be manifestly unconstitutional to anyone, or the enactment or amendment of administrative legislation pursuant to delegated legislation must be so clearly incompatible with the overall legal order system currently in force that fulfillment of the duty to enact administrative legislation pursuant to the delegated legislation would instead plainly bring about a result destroying the constitutional order (see Constitutional Court 2004. 2. 26. 2001HEONMA718). However, it is difficult to find any such constitutionally justifiable ground for the administrative legislative omission in this case.  \\n(3) Infringement of the Petitioner’s fundamental rights  \\n(a) The general personality right derived from Article 10 of the Constitution includes the right concerning an individual’s honor, and the “honor” referred to here means the “social evaluation” of a person or of his or her personality, that is, an objective and external value judgment (see Constitutional Court 2014. 6. 26. 2012HEONMA757). That honors are accorded to registered POWs, etc. commensurate with their conduct or degree of contribution during the period of detention means that a social evaluation is made that they are persons who made sacrifices and contributions for the Republic of Korea and who should be respected as exemplary embodiments of noble patriotic spirit and should receive appropriate honors; moreover, social honor and evaluation of the deceased also affects the personality rights of their descendants, who have formed their own sense of personality and preserved their honor through their relationship with the deceased, that is, the surviving family’s honor or their sentiments of reverence and remembrance toward the deceased (see Constitutional Court 2011. 3. 31. 2008HEONBA111; Constitutional Court 2014. 6. 26. 2012HEONMA757).  \\nArticle 15-5, paragraph 1 of the POW Act allows the Minister of National Defense to accord registered POWs, etc. honors commensurate with their conduct during the period of detention or the degree of their contribution. The conduct or degree of contribution of registered POWs, etc. during the period of detention directly or indirectly affects the lives of their families originating from the place of detention, and this is also closely related to how registered POWs, etc. are evaluated and treated in our society, thereby having a significant impact on the reputation or honor of their families. Therefore, the administrative legislative omission in this case, which fails to prescribe by Presidential Decree matters concerning such honors, infringes the Petitioner’s right to honor as a family member of registered POWs, etc.  \\n(b) The Petitioner argues that the administrative legislative omission in this case infringes the Petitioner’s property right.  \\nHowever, as noted above, the POW Act already provides in the statute for matters concerning financial support or compensation for registered POWs, etc.; thus, it is difficult to say that the “honors” for registered POWs, etc. contemplated by Article 15-5 of the POW Act necessarily include the State’s affirmative monetary benefits, such as the special provisions on remuneration or the payment of support payments. Even if a Presidential Decree were enacted pursuant to Article 15-5 of the POW Act and such Presidential Decree provided for financial support for POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before repatriation, it would be difficult to regard this as arising from the delegation under Article 15-5 of the POW Act, and the rights thereby arising would merely be rights concretely formed only by the Presidential Decree (see Constitutional Court 2014. 6. 26. 2012HEONMA757). Accordingly, the administrative legislative omission in this case cannot be seen as infringing the Petitioner’s property right.  \\n\\n5. Conclusion  \\nTherefore, because the Respondent, despite the delegation in Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act, has so far, without justifiable grounds, failed to prescribe matters concerning the same in a Presidential Decree, the administrative legislative omission in this case infringes the Petitioner’s right to honor and is therefore confirmed to be in violation of the Constitution, and a decision is rendered as stated in the order. This decision is based on the unanimous opinion of the remaining participating Justices, except for the dissenting opinion of Justice Kim Chang-jong, Justice Kang Il-won, and Justice Jo Yong-ho regarding the administrative legislative omission in this case as set forth in 6. below, and the supplementary opinion on Justice Kang Il-won’s dissenting opinion as set forth in 7. below.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Kim Chang-jong, Kang Il-won, and Jo Yong-ho on the Administrative Legislative Omission in This Case  \\nWe think, unlike the majority opinion, that the portion concerning the administrative legislative omission in this case among the present petition is also unlawful and should be dismissed. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\na. Whether the Respondent has a duty to enact the Presidential Decree  \\n(1) A constitutional complaint against an omission by public authority is permitted where, despite the fact that a duty to act derived from the Constitution is specifically and concretely prescribed for the subject of public power so that the holder of a fundamental right may request an administrative act or the exercise of public power on that basis, the subject of public power neglects that duty (Constitutional Court 2000. 3. 30. 98HEONMA206), and the same legal principle applies to a constitutional complaint against an administrative legislative omission by the executive branch (Constitutional Court 2003. 7. 24. 2002HEONMA378). For a “duty to act derived from the Constitution” to be recognized, it must fall under one of the following: first, a case where a specific duty to act of the subject of public power is expressly prescribed in the Constitution; second, a case where such a duty to act is derived from interpretation of the Constitution; third, a case where a duty to act of the subject of public power is specifically prescribed in a statute, etc. (Constitutional Court 2004. 10. 28. 2003HEONMA898; Constitutional Court 2011. 8. 30. 2006HEONMA788). In particular, in order for delay in administrative legislation to become unlawful and for legal control over it to be possible, the administrative agency must have a legal duty to enact (or amend) the implementing decree, and the power to enact (or amend) the decree must not have been exercised despite the passage of a considerable period of time (Constitutional Court 1998. 7. 16. 96HEONMA246).  \\nOur Constitution takes as its basic ideal the realization of a rule-of-law state that protects the people’s fundamental rights from abuse of state power, and, in accordance with the principles of modern liberal democratic constitutionalism, it adopts a system of separation of powers whereby the functions of the State are divided into legislation, administration, and adjudication so as to achieve checks and balances among them (see Constitutional Court 1992. 4. 28. 90HEONBA24), and because administration and adjudication are bound by statutes (see Constitutional Court 1990. 9. 3. 89HEONGA95), if the legislature delegates certain matters to the executive branch but the executive branch fails to implement them without justifiable reason, this is contrary to the principle of separation of powers and the principle of the rule of law state or rule-of-law administration; accordingly, if the executive branch fails to fulfill such legal duty despite the legislature’s delegation of certain matters by statute, this is of course unlawful and unconstitutional as well (Constitutional Court 2004. 2. 26. 2001HEONMA718).  \\nThus, under our Constitution, which presupposes the principle of separation of powers and the principle of rule-of-law administration, the executive branch’s duty to implement the law through administrative legislation, etc. should be regarded as a constitutional duty (Constitutional Court 1998. 7. 16. 96HEONMA246); however, this refers to cases in which the enactment of administrative legislation is indispensable for the execution of the law, meaning cases where failure to enact administrative legislation directly results in infringement of the legislative power by the executive branch (see Constitutional Court 2005. 12. 22. 2004HEONMA66). Accordingly, where execution can be achieved solely through the provisions of the superior statute without enactment of subordinate administrative legislation, there is no constitutional duty to enact subordinate administrative legislation (see Constitutional Court 2005. 12. 22. 2004HEONMA66; Constitutional Court 2013. 5. 30. 2011HEONMA198), and where the legislature has delegated discretion to the executive branch even as to whether or when a certain statute will be enforced, even if the executive branch does not enact subordinate administrative legislation, it does not thereby produce a result infringing legislative power by the executive branch, so there can be no constitutional duty derived from the Constitution on the part of the executive branch to act by administrative legislation (see Constitutional Court 1998. 7. 16. 96HEONMA246).  \\n(2) The Petitioner argues that the genuine administrative legislative omission, in which the Respondent has failed to enact the Presidential Decree despite having the duty to do so pursuant to Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act, infringes the Petitioner’s property right and is unconstitutional.  \\nWe therefore examine whether, as the Petitioner contends, the Respondent indeed has a duty to enact the Presidential Decree as a duty to act derived from the Constitution. First, it is clear that the Constitution does not expressly prescribe any specific duty for the Respondent to enact a Presidential Decree concerning the honors for registered POWs, etc. Nor can such a specific duty to act by the Respondent be derived from the interpretation of the Constitution. The question then is whether such a duty to act can be derived from the interpretation of Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act. Article 15-5, paragraph 1 of the POW Act provides that “The Minister of National Defense may accord to registered POWs, repatriated POWs who died before registration under Article 6, and POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before repatriation honors commensurate with their conduct during the period of detention or the degree of their contribution.” Paragraph 2 provides that “Necessary matters concerning the application, standards, methods, etc. for the honors under paragraph 1 shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.” The legislature did not provide in the above statutory provisions that honors are to be “accorded” or that honors “shall be accorded”; rather, it merely provided that honors “may be accorded.” This should be understood as the legislature’s conferral of discretion upon the Minister of National Defense as to whether to accord honors commensurate with the conduct during the period of detention or the degree of contribution of registered POWs, repatriated POWs who died before registration under Article 6, and POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before repatriation (hereinafter, if necessary, abbreviated as “registered POWs, etc.”), and as to the timing of such implementation, while delegating that, when concrete measures of honors are to be taken in the future, the application, standards, methods, etc. of such honors are to be implemented according to what is prescribed by Presidential Decree. In this way, the legislature delegated to the Minister of National Defense the authority to determine whether honors commensurate with the conduct during the period of detention or the degree of contribution of registered POWs, etc. are to be accorded, as well as the timing of implementation and the concrete content of such honors, thereby conferring discretion. Therefore, Article 15-5, paragraphs 1 and 2 of the POW Act cannot be viewed as prescribing a specific duty for the Respondent to enact a Presidential Decree for honoring registered POWs, etc.  \\nNevertheless, under the premise that, because no Presidential Decree has been enacted, the Minister of National Defense cannot accord honors to registered POWs, etc., or that once a Presidential Decree is enacted in advance the Minister of National Defense will naturally accord honors to registered POWs, etc. accordingly, it is untenable to conclude that the Respondent has a constitutional duty to enact the Presidential Decree, because such an interpretation is wholly inconsistent with the legislature’s intent to grant the Minister of National Defense discretion to determine whether honors for registered POWs, etc. will be implemented, when they will be implemented, and what the concrete content of such honors will be.  \\nRather, it is more reasonable to understand that the reason the Presidential Decree necessary for the concrete implementation of honors for registered POWs, etc. has not yet been enacted is that the Minister of National Defense, exercising the discretion delegated by the legislature, determined that, in light of various practical conditions, there is no immediate necessity to take additional honorific measures under Article 15-5, paragraph 1 of the POW Act beyond the matters paid or supported pursuant to other provisions of the POW Act. When, in the future, the Minister of National Defense determines that it is necessary to honor registered POWs, etc. and actually implements such honorific measures, it would be sufficient to prescribe and implement the detailed procedures and standards for such honors in the Presidential Decree; there is likewise no recognized necessity to prescribe such matters in the Presidential Decree in advance. Of course, it is a separate matter that, if the practical conditions necessary for taking honorific measures under Article 15-5, paragraph 1 of the POW Act with respect to registered POWs, etc. have sufficiently matured and the need for such measures is urgent, the Minister of National Defense’s failure to implement such honors (administrative omission), or the Respondent’s failure to enact the Presidential Decree (administrative legislative omission), may fall within a manifest deviation from or abuse of discretion and thus violate the Constitution; however, in the present case, no circumstances are recognized that would support a finding that either the Minister of National Defense or the Respondent manifestly deviated from or abused discretion.  \\n(3) In the end, it cannot be said that the Respondent has a constitutional duty to act in the manner asserted by the Petitioner; accordingly, the Petitioner’s petition for adjudication regarding the administrative legislative omission in this case is unlawful because it targets the non-exercise of public power where no specific constitutional duty to act by the Respondent is recognized.\\n\\nb. Whether there is a possibility of infringement of the Petitioner’s fundamental rights  \\n(1) Whether there is a possibility of infringement of the property right  \\n(a) The POW Act provides for the payment of remuneration for the period of detention and consolation support payments for stable domestic settlement to registered POWs (Articles 9 and 11), and further provides that special support payments (Article 12), housing support (Article 13), and medical support (Article 14) may be provided. It also provides that support payments (Article 15) and employment support (Article 15-3) may be provided to families of POWs originating from the place of detention. It also provides that the cost of repatriating the remains of POWs of the Korean Armed Forces may be supported for families of POWs (Article 15-2). Looking at the overall structure of the POW Act in this way, it is apparent that matters concerning financial support or compensation for POWs of the Korean Armed Forces, etc. are already provided for in various other provisions of the POW Act. Accordingly, it is difficult to say that the “honors” for POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before repatriation contemplated by Article 15-5 of the POW Act necessarily include the State’s affirmative monetary benefits, such as the special provisions on remuneration or the payment of support payments. Article 15-5 of the POW Act regulates not only repatriated POWs and non-repatriated POWs, but also the honors of registered POWs, and considering that financial support for registered POWs is prescribed not in Article 15-5 but in other provisions of the POW Act, it is reasonable to view Article 15-5 of the POW Act as contemplating regulation of matters concerning honors other than financial benefits for repatriated POWs, non-repatriated POWs, and registered POWs. Of course, if the Minister of National Defense accords certain honors to POWs of the Korean Armed Forces, indirect financial benefits may arise for the person receiving such honors depending on the specific content of the honors. But even that does not mean that financial compensation or support must necessarily accompany the “honors” referred to in Article 15-5 of the POW Act, and even less can it be said that affirmative monetary benefits to the person concerned are always included. Therefore, Article 15-5 of the POW Act is merely a provision allowing honors to be accorded to registered POWs, etc. commensurate with their conduct or degree of contribution during the period of detention, and it is difficult to regard it as a provision infringing or restricting the property rights of their surviving family members or families of POWs originating from the place of detention.  \\n(b) Even if it were thought impossible to exclude the possibility that the content of “honors” may include monetary payments, etc., the same result follows: there is no possibility of infringement of the Petitioner’s property right.  \\nEven if a future Presidential Decree to be enacted pursuant to Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act were to include a provision granting additional monetary benefits to deceased non-repatriated POWs, because such a provision is in the nature of a benefit-conferring statutory provision, the right to claim such monetary payments would be a right concretely formed only by Article 15-5 of the POW Act and its Enforcement Decree (see Constitutional Court 2014. 6. 26. 2012HEONMA757). However, the late Son ○ Sik had already died before such a Presidential Decree was enacted and never acquired such a right to claim monetary payment as a concrete right; therefore, there is no room to view the Petitioner as having inherited it. In the end, because the Respondent’s administrative legislative omission in this case did not restrict the Petitioner’s property right, it is difficult to recognize any possibility of infringement of the Petitioner’s property right.  \\n(2) Whether there is a possibility of infringement of the right to honor  \\nThe Petitioner is not arguing that the administrative legislative omission in this case infringes the Petitioner’s right to honor. Nevertheless, since the majority opinion has determined that the administrative legislative omission in this case infringes the Petitioner’s right to honor, we also examine this point additionally.  \\nAs the majority opinion also states, the general personality right derived from Article 10 of the Constitution includes the right concerning an individual’s honor (Constitutional Court 1999. 6. 24. 97HEONMA265), and social honor and evaluation of the deceased also affects the personality rights of their descendants, who have formed their own sense of personality and preserved their honor through their relationship with the deceased, that is, the surviving family’s honor or their sentiments of reverence and remembrance toward the deceased (Constitutional Court 2011. 3. 31. 2008HEONBA111).  \\nHowever, the right to honor protected by the Constitution is the right to demand exclusion of the unjustified infringement of the fundamental rights holder’s personality and honor; it cannot be said to be the right to request that the State confer the highest possible social evaluation upon the fundamental rights holder (Constitutional Court 2014. 6. 26. 2012HEONMA757). The “honor” here means the “social evaluation” of a person or his or her personality, namely objective and external value judgment, and it should be understood that it does not include mere subjective or internal feelings of honor (Constitutional Court 2005. 10. 27. 2002HEONMA425). As surviving family members of POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who participated in war for the nation and society and were then captured and detained in North Korea, they may have internal feelings of honor and pride regarding the sacrifices their father and they themselves made for the State; however, this cannot be regarded as “honor” as a legal interest protected by the Constitution (Constitutional Court 2008. 11. 27. 2008HEONMA517; Constitutional Court 2014. 6. 26. 2012HEONMA757). Accordingly, the fact that the Respondent has not prepared, by Presidential Decree, procedures for appropriately honoring deceased non-repatriated POWs does not mean that the Petitioner's right to honor derived from Article 10 of the Constitution is restricted merely because the social evaluation of the late Son ○ Sik and the Petitioner, as his surviving family member, is not given an opportunity to rise further (Constitutional Court 2005. 10. 27. 2002HEONMA425).  \\nMoreover, it is clear that because the Presidential Decree in this case has not been enacted, the refusal to recognize honors for deceased non-repatriated POWs does not directly make, nor intend, any negative evaluation of deceased non-repatriated POWs or their surviving families.  \\nIn the end, because the administrative legislative omission in this case cannot be seen as having a negative effect on the social evaluation of the late Son ○ Sik or the Petitioner as his surviving family member, or as restricting the honor protected by the Constitution, the administrative legislative omission in this case does not infringe the Petitioner’s right to honor.  \\n(3) Subconclusion  \\nThe petition for adjudication regarding the administrative legislative omission in this case is unlawful because there is no possibility that it infringes the Petitioner’s property right or right to honor.\\n\\nc. Conclusion  \\nAccordingly, the Petitioner’s petition for adjudication regarding the administrative legislative omission in this case targets the non-exercise of public power where no specific constitutional duty to act by the Respondent is recognized, and there is also no possibility that it infringes the Petitioner’s fundamental rights such as the property right; thus, in any event, it is unlawful and must be dismissed.\\n\\n7. Supplementary Opinion on the Dissenting Opinion of Justice Kang Il-won  \\nThe POW Act’s main purpose is to provide various forms of support to registered POWs under Article 6, excluding POWs who committed serious crimes or disguised returnees, etc. That is, it allows social adaptation education for registered POWs (Article 6-2), honorary promotion or special promotion (Articles 7 and 8), remuneration and consolation support payments (Articles 9 and 11), and special support payments, housing support, and medical support (Articles 12 through 14). Except for registered POWs, it allows support payments or employment support to families of POWs originating from the place of detention (Articles 15 and 15-3).\\n\\nIn addition to these provisions, Article 15-5 of the POW Act provides that, with respect to “registered POWs, repatriated POWs who died before registration, and POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before repatriation” among POWs of the Korean Armed Forces, honors commensurate with their conduct or contribution during the period of detention may be accorded. This provision is one that allows separate honors in addition to the various forms of support prescribed by law for registered POWs, while extending such honors even to POWs of the Korean Armed Forces who died before registration. In light of the structure of the POW Act, it is difficult to regard the “honors” referred to in this provision as including affirmative monetary benefits from the State. On this point, the Justices are in agreement.\\n\\nIf so, the “honors” in Article 15-5 of the POW Act can only be understood, as the term itself indicates, to mean “respectful treatment with courtesy.” The Minister of National Defense may accord registered POWs, etc. honors in various ways even without a separate provision in a Presidential Decree. There are many forms of honors that the Minister of National Defense may, within his authority and at his discretion, accord without legal basis, such as inviting registered POWs, etc. or their families and commending their achievements and consoling their suffering, or issuing statements to that effect. The reason Article 15-5, paragraph 2 provides that the “necessary matters concerning the application, standards, methods, etc. for the honors” shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree should be understood as allowing, where special honors not possible without a legal basis are to be accorded, such honors to be accorded on the basis of the Presidential Decree. Honors beyond the authority of the Minister of National Defense are matters whose standards and methods may be prescribed by Presidential Decree pursuant to the delegation in this provision.\\n\\nWhether the Minister of National Defense will accord honors to registered POWs, etc. pursuant to Article 15-5, paragraph 1 of the POW Act is left to the Minister’s discretion. In order to characterize honors under this provision as an obligation rather than a matter of discretion for the Minister of National Defense, the law would need to specifically prescribe the content and method of the honors. Likewise, whether to enact a Presidential Decree under paragraph 2 should also be regarded as depending on the President’s discretion.\\n\\nIf the National Assembly intends to impose on the President a duty to enact administrative legislation, it must, pursuant to Article 75 of the Constitution, prescribe the matters of administrative legislation in the statute by “specifically defining the scope.” However, even when the entire provisions of the POW Act are considered, it is impossible to tell what content the “honors” to be prescribed by Presidential Decree are supposed to have. If, as the majority opinion does, this provision is understood as bindingly imposing a duty of administrative legislation on the President, then this provision violates Article 75 of the Constitution. If interpreted constitutionally, this provision can only be understood as a delegation authorizing the President, at his discretion, to enact administrative legislation for honoring registered POWs, etc.\\n\\nHonors for POWs of the Korean Armed Forces are also prescribed in other statutes, such as the Act on the Honorable Treatment and Support of Persons of Distinguished Service to the State, etc. and the Act on the Honorable Treatment of Veterans of War and the Establishment of Organizations Thereof, in addition to the POW Act. Viewing Article 15-5 of the POW Act as a provision imposing a duty of administrative legislation concerning the honor of POWs of the Korean Armed Forces is also inconsistent with the overall framework of the POW Act and related statutes.\\n\\nFor this reason as well, because it cannot be said that a duty to enact administrative legislation pursuant to Article 15-5, paragraph 2 of the POW Act has arisen, the Petitioner’s constitutional complaint in this case must be dismissed."}

Overview of the Case\\n\\n(1) 96HEONBA18\\n\\nThe Petitioner (1), a stock company manufacturing and selling petrochemical derivative products, has been using, as land for employees’ collective housing, welfare facilities, etc., a total of 146,675㎡ of land consisting of two parcels in OO-dong, Yeocheon City, located within the Yeocheon Industrial Complex (hereinafter referred to as “the land at issue”), which it owns.
