Subject of Adjudication\\n\\nThe subject of adjudication in this case is whether the portion “the value of factory sites prescribed by Presidential Decree ……” in Article 234-15(2) proviso item 3 of the Local Tax Act (as amended by Act No. 4128 of June 16, 1989) (hereinafter referred to as “the provision subject to adjudication in this case”) is contrary to the Constitution, and the contents of the said provision and the relevant provisions are as follows.\\n\\nArticle 234-15 (Tax Base) ① The tax base of the Aggregate Land Tax shall be classified into the aggregate taxation base, the separate aggregate taxation base, and the separate taxation base.\\n\\n② The aggregate taxation base shall be the amount obtained by aggregating the value of all land throughout the country owned by the taxpayer as of the tax base date, excluding the appurtenant land to buildings prescribed by Presidential Decree. Provided, however, that the value of the following land shall not be aggregated.\\n\\n1. 2. omitted\\n\\n3. The value of factory sites, dry fields, paddy fields, orchards, and pasture land prescribed by Presidential Decree\\n\\n4. through 6. omitted\\n\\n③ omitted\\n\\n④ The separate taxation base shall be the values under paragraph (2) items 3 through 6.\\n\\n⑤ omitted\\n\\n2. The Petitioners’ Claims and the Opinion of the Interested Party\\n\\na. Summary of the Petitioners’ Claims\\n\\nWhether land that is subject to the Aggregate Land Tax is to be placed under the aggregate taxation subject, to which a progressive tax rate is applied, or, alternatively, under the separate taxation subject, to which a proportional tax rate is applied, is a matter directly connected with the taxpayer’s tax burden and is therefore an important matter corresponding to the requirements for taxation. Accordingly, in delegating the scope of the subject to Presidential Decree, specific standards or scope must be set forth and delegated. Nevertheless, the provision subject to adjudication in this case merely provides that factory sites subject to separate taxation are “factory sites prescribed by Presidential Decree,” thereby blankly delegating this to a subordinate decree, the Presidential Decree, in violation of the prohibition on blanket delegation and in contravention of the principle of taxation by law, and also infringes the Petitioners’ equal rights and property rights.\\n\\nb. Summary of the Grounds on Which the Court Dismissed the Motion for Constitutional Review Referral\\n\\nThe provision subject to adjudication in this case specifically identifies the type of land subject to separate taxation as “factory sites” and clearly delegates to Presidential Decree only the scope of factory sites; therefore, it cannot be said to be an unconstitutional provision contrary to the principle of taxation by law, as it comprehensively delegates matters concerning the requirements for taxation to subordinate legislation. Nor can it be said that making only land within a certain scope among factory sites subject to separate taxation is essentially contrary to Articles 11 and 23 of the Constitution, which guarantee equal rights and property rights.\\n\\nc. Summary of the Opinion of the Minister of Home Affairs\\n\\nThe provision subject to adjudication in this case specifically identifies the type of land subject to separate taxation as “factory sites” and then delegates to Presidential Decree only within that scope; therefore, it cannot be viewed as comprehensively delegating matters concerning the requirements for taxation to subordinate legislation. In addition, Articles 234-8 through 234-25 of the Local Tax Act specifically and clearly provide for the requirements for taxation, the tax base, tax rates, and methods of assessment and collection of the Aggregate Land Tax, and are applied equally to anyone under the same conditions; therefore, they cannot be said to violate the principle of taxation by law or to infringe equal rights or property rights.\\n\\n3. Judgment\\n\\na. Issue\\n\\nThe issue in this case is whether the portion “factory sites prescribed by Presidential Decree” in the provision subject to adjudication in this case constitutes a comprehensive delegation and thus contravenes the principle of taxation by law.\\n\\nb. History and Basis of the Aggregate Land Tax\\n\\n(1) Initially, the Local Tax Act treated land, together with buildings, as subject to property tax, and property tax had been imposed on a parcel-by-parcel basis. However, as real estate speculation, riding on the rapid development of the economy, emerged as a social problem, property tax at separate, heavier rates had been imposed on idle land, such as vacant lots and land not used for business purposes by corporations, in order to suppress unsound economic activity such as real estate speculation and to induce sound economic activity.\\n\\nThen, as part of comprehensive land measures to restrain excessive land ownership and speculation in land, the Local Tax Act was amended by Act No. 3878 on December 31, 1986, and the Land Excess Ownership Tax was newly established and enforced from January 1, 1988. Its substance was to delete the provisions on heavy taxation of property tax on idle land and, in addition to imposing property tax on all land, separately impose the Land Excess Ownership Tax on idle land, land held in excess, and land not used for business purposes by aggregating them nationwide on a parcel-by-parcel basis and imposing a separate heavy tax rate on land located in a certain area or land exceeding a certain standard.\\n\\nHowever, because the land subject to the Land Excess Ownership Tax was limited and the land excluded from its scope was extensive, enforcement alone was insufficient to achieve the policy objective of restraining excessive land ownership and real estate speculation. Meanwhile, as the computerization of land ownership status progressed, the Local Tax Act was amended by Act No. 4128 on June 16, 1989, to establish the Aggregate Land Tax in order to restrain excessive land holding, facilitate the supply and demand for land, and build the foundation for a sound national life; this has been in force from January 1, 1990 to the present.\\n\\n(2) The Aggregate Land Tax was introduced in order to substantively merge and abolish the land property tax, which had been imposed parcel by parcel on land ownership, and the Land Excess Ownership Tax, which had treated idle land and land not used for business purposes, etc., as taxable objects, so that all land in the country would be aggregated by owner and a progressive tax rate applied to its value, thereby establishing the principle of taxation according to ability to pay in accordance with the degree of land ownership, and restraining excessive land ownership through the tax system while seeking to stabilize land prices and broaden the base of land ownership. As a tax system so introduced, it, in principle, adopts the aggregate taxation base system in which all land nationwide is aggregated by each taxpayer and a progressive tax rate is applied to its value, but, for land on which there is a need, on policy grounds, to apply a heavy or light tax burden, it also provides a separate taxation base system applying a proportional tax rate, and in addition adopts a separate aggregate taxation base system applying a lower progressive tax rate than the aggregate taxation base to the aggregated value of the appurtenant land to certain buildings (Articles 234-8 and 234-15(1) of the Local Tax Act).\\n\\nIn other words, the Aggregate Land Tax, in principle, taxes all land nationwide by aggregating it for each owner (including de facto owners) and applying a progressive tax rate in nine stages, under the aggregate taxation system (Article 234-8; Article 234-15(2) main text; Article 234-16(1)). However, for land requiring, on policy grounds, application of a lower or higher tax rate, it exceptionally corrects the irrationality arising from uniform aggregate taxation by separately taxing it according to separate standards (Article 234-15(4) and Article 234-15(2) proviso items 3 through 6). Thus, for land used directly for production, such as agricultural land, or land used as industrial land, such as factory sites, it supports productive activities by applying a lower proportional tax rate (Article 234-16(3) items 1 and 3), whereas for land used as luxury property, such as villas, it seeks to restrain ownership by applying a higher proportional tax rate (Article 234-16(3) item 2). Meanwhile, in the case of certain appurtenant land to buildings prescribed by Presidential Decree, applying a high progressive tax rate by aggregating it with the value of other land could unduly restrict the normal use of land, and if it were separately taxed, there would be the possibility of excessive land ownership under the pretext of appurtenant land to buildings, so it is separately aggregated and a lower progressive tax rate than aggregate taxation is applied (Article 234-15(3), Article 234-16(2)).\\n\\nIn light of the history of the Aggregate Land Tax as seen above and the fact that its tax base is the value of land, the Aggregate Land Tax is basically a kind of property tax.\\n\\nc. The Principle of Taxation by Law and the Grounds and Limits of Delegated Legislation\\n\\n(1) The Constitution provides in Article 38 that “all citizens shall have the duty to pay taxes as prescribed by Act,” and in Article 59 that “the items of taxes and tax rates shall be determined by Act.” The idea of the principle of taxation by law grounded in these constitutional provisions is to ensure the property rights of the people by requiring that the requirements for taxation be prescribed by an Act enacted by the National Assembly, the representative organ of the people (principle of statutory taxation of tax requirements), and also to ensure the legal stability and predictability of people’s lives by clearly prescribing the requirements for taxation and excluding arbitrary interpretation and enforcement by tax authorities (principle of clarity of tax requirements).\\n\\nHowever, if the principle of taxation by law were implemented too rigorously, it would be difficult to accurately capture taxable objects and properly calculate the tax base in response to complex, diverse, and constantly changing economic circumstances, making it impossible to achieve the objective of fair taxation in accordance with tax-bearing capacity. Accordingly, in order to maintain the principle of taxation by law while harmonizing it with the principle of tax equality, and to enable fair taxation in response to economic reality and to deal with unlawful tax avoidance, it is necessary to delegate to administrative legislation, which is more flexible than a formal Act enacted by the National Assembly, even matters related to important matters or the essential contents of tax obligations, insofar as those are detailed matters that must promptly respond to changes in economic reality or the development of specialized technology. In this regard, our Constitution provides in Article 75 that “The President may issue Presidential Decrees concerning matters delegated specifically by Act and matters necessary for the enforcement of Acts,” thereby confirming the necessity of delegated legislation not only in the field of tax administration but throughout state administration, and opening the way to delegate legislative power to Presidential Decrees, reflecting the practical difficulty that not all matters can be regulated by Acts enacted by the National Assembly.\\n\\n(2) Nevertheless, when matters that should be prescribed by Act are delegated to subordinate legislation such as Presidential Decrees, if general and comprehensive delegation were permitted, it would be tantamount in substance to a blank delegation of legislative power, thereby denying the principle of parliamentary legislation and the rule of law, and because fundamental rights could be infringed by arbitrary exercise of executive power carried out without any limitation, Article 75 of the Constitution expressly states that delegation must be made by “specifically setting the scope,” thereby indicating that there are certain limits to delegation.\\n\\nThus, by specifically prescribing in advance in the Act the basic matters of the content and scope to be prescribed by Presidential Decree, in light of the legislative intent of Article 75 of the Constitution, which is to prevent arbitrary interpretation and enforcement of the law by the executive power and to achieve the principle of parliamentary legislation and the rule of law, the phrase “specifically setting the scope” means that the basic matters of the content and scope to be prescribed in subordinate legislation such as Presidential Decrees must be set forth as specifically and clearly as possible in the Act so that anyone can predict, from the Act itself, the general outline of the content to be prescribed in the Presidential Decree, etc. (see Constitutional Court decision of July 8, 1991, 91HEONGA4). Whether such predictability exists is not to be judged by looking only at a single specific provision; rather, the relevant provisions of the law as a whole must be judged organically and systematically in the round, and they must be examined specifically and individually according to the nature of each subject statute. Accordingly, if, when the statutory provision and the legislative purpose of the statute are considered comprehensively, the general outline can be reasonably predicted, it should be determined that the limit of delegation has not been exceeded (see, e.g., Constitutional Court decision of July 29, 1994, 93HEONGA12).\\n\\n(3) Also, the degree of specificity and clarity required for such delegated legislation will vary depending on the type and nature of the subject matter of regulation, but particularly in statutes such as penal statutes or tax statutes, which have the potential to directly restrict or infringe upon the fundamental rights of the people, the demands for specificity and clarity are strengthened, and the requirements and scope of delegation must be prescribed more strictly and restrictively than in the case of ordinary statutes concerning administrative benefits. On the other hand, where the subject matter of regulation is extremely diverse or of a nature that changes from time to time, the requirements of specificity and clarity in delegation should be relaxed [see Constitutional Court decision of February 11, 1991, 90HEONGA27; and Constitutional Court decision of July 29, 1994, 92HEONBA49·52 (consolidated), respectively].\\n\\nHowever, even in cases where the requirements of clarity in delegation may be relaxed, under our Constitution, which adopts popular sovereignty, separation of powers, and the rule of law as its basic principles, the function of policy formulation concerning important matters or matters of essential content related to the people’s constitutional fundamental rights and basic duties must, in principle, be performed by the legislature, which is composed of representatives elected by the sovereign people, and carried out in the form of legislation, and it is interpreted that this function should not be transferred to the executive branch or the judiciary, whose mission is to execute or apply such legislated policy. Therefore, with respect to matters concerning the important matters or essential content of the duty to pay taxes, which is a basic duty of the people, such matters must be prescribed as clearly as possible in an Act under the principle of taxation by law, and there are certain limits to delegating such matters to subordinate legislation such as Presidential Decrees.\\n\\nd. Examination of the Provision Subject to Adjudication in This Case\\n\\n(1) The reason the provision subject to adjudication in this case makes factory sites prescribed by Presidential Decree land subject to separate taxation under the Aggregate Land Tax and applies a lower proportional tax rate is that, by applying a lower proportional tax rate to land being used as industrial land such as factory sites in certain regions, such as industrial complexes, it supports corporate production activities and facilitates the supply and demand for land, while at the same time correcting the irrationality of the aggregate taxation system, which aggregates all land and applies a high progressive tax rate, thereby encouraging production and industrial activity and ultimately contributing to balanced growth of the national economy and efficient use of the national territory.\\n\\nEven with respect to factory sites, however, depending on the region where the factory is located and the type of products manufactured by the factory, the land area indispensable thereto differs, and the types themselves vary from appurtenant land for production facilities to appurtenant land for ancillary facilities, research facilities, safety facilities, and facilities necessary for promoting the welfare and benefits of employees. It is also easy to imagine that factory siting standards may change from time to time depending on the development of production technology or changes in related laws and regulations. Accordingly, since it is impossible or inappropriate for the National Assembly to regulate all such fluctuations in economic activity or all complex, specialized, and technical matters by an Act enacted by it, the provision subject to adjudication in this case delegates the specific scope of factory sites subject to separate taxation to Presidential Decree.\\n\\nIn other words, the provision subject to adjudication in this case specifically and individually limits the subject to “factory sites” and then delegates to Presidential Decree, within that scope, the determination of the specific matters by taking into account the legislative purpose of the provision subject to adjudication in this case as seen above and the background of the delegation. Therefore, it can easily be predicted that the matters to be prescribed by Presidential Decree will be land within a certain area, within a certain range of the prescribed siting standards, that is indispensable to production activities at the factory. If so, the provision subject to adjudication in this case can be said to comply with the limits on delegation of legislative power prescribed by the Constitution, and it is difficult to view it as a comprehensive delegation.\\n\\n(2) The Petitioners argue, in substance, that although the land at issue is not within the factory boundary zone, because it is located within an industrial complex and is used as appurtenant land for employees’ welfare facilities, there is a very strong need for it to become land subject to separate taxation; yet the Enforcement Decree of the Local Tax Act enacted pursuant to the delegation in the provision subject to adjudication in this case excludes the land at issue from land subject to separate taxation and makes it land subject to aggregate taxation, on which a high progressive tax rate is imposed, thereby treating the Petitioners less favorably than other owners of factory sites subject to separate taxation and infringing the Petitioners’ equal rights and property rights, and that this is due to the unconstitutionality of the delegated portion of the provision subject to adjudication in this case. However, as seen above, the very fact that the provision subject to adjudication in this case delegated the specific scope of factory sites subject to separate taxation to Presidential Decree is a proper and lawful delegation of legislative power and does not infringe the Petitioner’s fundamental rights in contravention of the principle of equality; and because the law of delegated legislation is based on the fundamental constitutional principles of separation of powers, parliamentarianism, and the rule of law, whether the content prescribed in the Presidential Decree enacted by the executive branch is proper has no direct relation to the legality of the delegation.\\n\\nIn other words, even if the content prescribed by Presidential Decree pursuant to the delegation in the provision subject to adjudication in this case is contrary to the Constitution, aside from the separate question of the Presidential Decree provision becoming unconstitutional, it cannot be said that the enabling statutory provision in this case, which validly and lawfully delegated legislative power, also becomes unconstitutional thereby (see Constitutional Court decision of June 26, 1996, 93HEONBA2). Therefore, the above argument of the Petitioners is without merit.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, the provision subject to adjudication in this case complies with the limits on delegation of legislative power and therefore cannot be said to be an unconstitutional statutory provision that infringes the Petitioners’ fundamental rights in contravention of the principle of taxation by law.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the portion “factory sites prescribed by Presidential Decree” in Article 234-15(2) proviso item 3 of the Local Tax Act (as amended by Act No. 4128 of June 16, 1989) is not contrary to the Constitution. Therefore, apart from the separate opinion of Justice Cho Seung-hyung regarding the wording of the Order as in 5., the judgment is rendered unanimously by the remaining Justices as stated in the Order.\\n\\n5. Separate Opinion of Justice Cho Seung-hyung on the Wording of the Order\\n\\nI think that the wording in the Order should be changed from “The portion ‘the value of factory sites…… prescribed by Presidential Decree’ in Article 234-15(2) proviso item 3 of the Local Tax Act (…) is not contrary to the Constitution” to “The petition is dismissed.”\\n\\nThe reason is that, as explained in detail in the separate opinions concerning the wording of the Order in the decisions of our Court in 92HEONBA45, request for a finding of unconstitutionality of Article 75(1) item 1 of the Military Criminal Act, decided on October 26, 1995; 93HEONBA62, request for a finding of unconstitutionality of Article 52(1) item 3, etc. of the former Housing Construction Promotion Act; 94HEONBA7·8 (consolidated), request for a finding of unconstitutionality of Article 62(3) of the former Tax Exemption and Reduction Control Act; 95HEONBA22, request for a finding of unconstitutionality of Article 20(1) of the Special Measures Act on the Disposal of Requisitioned Property; and 94HEONBA28, request for a finding of unconstitutionality of Article 3 of the Small Claims Trial Act, there is no need to insist on rendering a constitutionality decision where binding force under Article 75(7) and Article 47 of the Constitutional Court Act is not recognized, and in this case, since the citizen is the one alleging unconstitutionality and filing the petition, there is no need to indicate in the Order a conclusion that cannot be accepted, namely constitutionality, that the citizen did not request and that has no practical effect.\\n\\nSeptember 25, 1997"}

{"[99HEONBA91]": "[Annex 1] List of Claimants omitted\\n\\n[Annex 2]\\n\\nClaimants’ Arguments, Reasons for Dismissal of the Application for a Constitutional Referral, and Opinions of the Relevant Agencies\\n\\nA. Claimants’ Arguments\\n\\n(1) With respect to Article 2, paragraph 3, subitem (a), and Article 10, paragraph 1, item 2, and paragraph 2, of the statute at issue\\n\\n(a) In Article 2, paragraph 3, subitem (a), of the statute at issue, concerning “the standards for the valuation and calculation of liabilities and assets” in determining an insolvent financial institution, and in Article 10, paragraph 2, of the statute at issue, the “standards and contents of prompt corrective action” that the Financial Supervisory Commission may take with respect to an insolvent financial institution under paragraph 1 of the same Article are delegated to a public notice of the Financial Supervisory Commission. The relevant provisions of the Insurance Supervision Regulations, a public notice enacted pursuant to such delegation, constitute regulatory decrees. However, since the Constitution limits regulatory decrees to Presidential Decrees, Prime Minister’s Decrees and Ministerial Decrees, Rules of the Supreme Court, Rules of the Constitutional Court, and Rules of the National Election Commission, the delegation, under Article 2, paragraph 3, subitem (a), and Article 10, paragraph 2, of the statute at issue, of regulatory matters to the Financial Supervisory Commission, which is not one of the bodies enumerated in the Constitution, violates the Constitution.\\n\\n(b) With respect to Article 2, paragraph 3, subitem (a), of the statute at issue, although “the standards and methods for valuation of assets and liabilities” are among the most basic and essential matters in the Financial Supervisory Commission’s determination of an insolvent financial institution, the National Assembly did not directly prescribe them by statute. Meanwhile, with respect to Article 10, paragraph 1, item 2, and paragraph 2, of the statute at issue, the prompt corrective actions that the Financial Supervisory Commission may take against an insolvent financial institution are classified as “recommendation, demand, order, or submission of an implementation plan, etc.,” and encompass a broad range of sanction contents, from “cautions, warnings, etc. against financial institutions and officers and employees” to “cancellation of shares, business suspension, etc.” Accordingly, the standards for implementing prompt corrective action and the measures to be taken at each stage should have been specified in detail by statute; however, since they are delegated to a public notice of the Financial Supervisory Commission, the foregoing provisions constitute a blanket delegation of legislative power and therefore violate Article 75 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Article 12, paragraphs 2 through 4, of the statute at issue cannot be said to have legitimacy under the statutory scheme in terms of the very purpose of its legislation, nor can its method be said to be appropriate. The target of share cancellation is excessively broad and without any limitation, whereas the interest of the fundamental right infringed is essential. As it infringes the essential content of the constitutionally guaranteed property right and thus runs counter to the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction, it violates the Constitution.\\n\\nB. Reasons for Dismissal of the Application for Constitutional Referral by the Seoul Administrative Court\\n\\n(1) Article 2, paragraph 3, subitem (a), of the statute at issue\\n\\nThis provision, in connection with the designation of an insolvent financial institution, requires, as its requirement, that the institution conduct an actual examination of assets and liabilities and that liabilities exceed assets, but delegates to the Financial Supervisory Commission’s regulations the standards for the valuation and calculation of assets and liabilities. Such delegation regulates the specific method related to the designation of an insolvent financial institution as whether liabilities exceed assets through comparison of assets and liabilities, and merely delegates subordinate standards for that specific method. Thus, even though it delegates without setting forth specific standards concerning the calculation of assets and liabilities, it cannot be viewed as delegating the essential substance related to the determination of an insolvent financial institution. In addition, liabilities or assets are terms generally used in the financial sector; their meanings are inherently limited and can be specified within a certain scope, and their concrete range is set. Accordingly, the foregoing provision is difficult to regard as having exceeded the limits of delegated legislation, as it specifically identifies the scope and delegates to subordinate legislation.\\n\\n(2) Article 10, paragraph 1, item 2, and paragraph 2, of the statute at issue\\n\\nThis provision, with respect to prompt corrective action, prescribes as grounds for triggering such action cases where a financial institution’s capital adequacy ratio falls below a certain level, and provides for recommendations, demands, or orders as its forms, while enumerating as its contents items 1 through 9 of paragraph 1. Furthermore, it requires that the standards and contents be publicly notified in advance. According to these provisions, the basic requirements and contents are set forth in detail by statute, and only the specific implementation thereof is delegated; thus, it is difficult to regard this as a blanket delegation.\\n\\n(3) Article 12, paragraphs 2 through 4, of the statute at issue\\n\\nUnlike ordinary enterprises, a financial institution such as ○○ Life Insurance is based on public confidence as the foundation of its business. Moreover, once confidence is lost, it may trigger a chain reaction leading to a sharp decline in confidence and it is difficult to restore thereafter. Such a decline in confidence affects not only the relevant financial institution but also the financial sector in general, potentially causing a so-called financial panic and having a major impact on the national economy as a whole. For these reasons, in Korea, apart from the issue of its legitimacy, the State, through the Deposit Insurance Act, etc., in effect stands behind financial institutions as a guarantor by actually guaranteeing the return of deposits, etc., or the payment obligations therefor. Thus, if a certain financial institution becomes insolvent and is unable to pay its deposits, etc., the State has no choice but to pay those deposits. Seen in this light, insofar as such a deposit protection system is adopted, the State has a greater justification to more actively monitor and supervise whether financial institutions are being properly operated than in cases where such a system is not adopted.\\n\\nWhile our Constitution declares that the property rights of the people are guaranteed, it also states that their limits may be established and restrictions imposed by law. In relation to capital reduction, too, if a financial institution is insolvent in that liabilities exceed assets and is deemed unable to continue business due to continued withdrawal of deposits, etc., the rights as a shareholder become extremely weak and can be assessed as economically valueless. Given that the State supports financial institutions and that, if the bankruptcy of a financial institution were to become a reality, its ripple effects could extend to the national economy as a whole, the necessity exists to take measures even at the stage of danger, accepting the possibility that the insignificant rights of shareholders of an insolvent financial institution whose value is already close to zero may be infringed. In light of these circumstances, this can be viewed as setting limits in advance on the rights of shareholders of financial institutions at the stage of danger indicators for the sake of social safety, maintenance of order, and public welfare, while also complementing the capitalist free-market order under our Constitution. In addition, under the requirements of the foregoing legal provisions, it is difficult to regard the statutory basis for such capital increase and capital reduction orders as unconstitutional merely because the shareholder’s rights are exercised not through a resolution of the general meeting of shareholders, which reflects the intent of the shareholders, but through a resolution of the board of directors.\\n\\nC. Opinion of the Financial Supervisory Commission\\n\\n(1) The proviso portion of Article 2, paragraph 3, subitem (a), of the statute at issue\\n\\nThis is to the same effect as the reasons given by the Seoul Administrative Court for dismissing the application for constitutional referral.\\n\\n(2) Article 10, paragraph 1, item 2, and paragraph 2, of the statute at issue\\n\\nIn addition to opinions to the same effect as the reasons given by the Seoul Administrative Court for dismissing the application for constitutional referral, it does not violate the principle prohibiting blanket delegation of legislative power for the following reasons. That is, a judgment on the degree of insolvency of a financial institution and its possibility of rehabilitation requires a high degree of expertise and concerns policy judgments involving detailed and technical matters, and therefore cannot be uniformly prescribed by statute. Moreover, the scope of delegated legislation should be determined based on the political, economic, and social environment of the society and the sound legal common sense of the general public. In Korea, unlike in the United States or Japan, the issue of dealing with insolvent financial institutions remains an urgent pending matter both at the time of enactment of the statute and now; considering the economic ripple effects, it must be decided more swiftly than any other decision. In light of this, the legislator specifically set forth the contents of the prompt corrective action that the Financial Supervisory Commission may take, while granting discretion to select the measures listed in each item of Article 10, paragraph 1, of the same Act according to the degree of insolvency of the relevant financial institution so that appropriate measures may be taken based on the expertise and technicality of the Financial Supervisory Commission. Thus, the foregoing provision cannot be said to violate the principle prohibiting blanket delegation of legislative power.\\n\\n(3) Article 12, paragraphs 2 through 4, of the statute at issue\\n\\nIn addition to opinions similar to the reasons given by the Seoul Administrative Court for dismissing the application for constitutional referral, the following opinion is added with respect to the capital reduction order. That is, considering Korea’s economic structure, especially its financial structure, in certain cases capital increase as a premise for the injection of public funds, and capital reduction that cancels the shares of existing shareholders, are necessary. In particular, the fundamental reason why, with respect to capital reduction, it was made possible to implement it by resolution of the board of directors without the consent of existing shareholders is that if existing shareholders were granted the right to decide whether to reduce capital, they would not themselves resolve to reduce capital against their own interests. As a result, the legislative purpose of the statute, namely the rehabilitation of financial institutions and the recovery of injected public funds through capital reduction caused by the injection of public funds, would not be realized. Moreover, if the shares of existing shareholders were not cancelled in the event of public fund injection, it is obvious that the value of the shares held by existing shareholders, which have almost lost all value due to liabilities exceeding assets as a result of the public fund injection, would increase and the economic benefit would accrue to the existing shareholders, which would be a highly unreasonable result. Since shareholders not directly responsible for the insolvency are permitted to make a demand for purchase according to a prescribed procedure, it cannot be said that conferring authority to resolve capital reduction on the board of directors infringes the essential content of property rights or runs counter to the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction or the principle of the capitalist free-market order.\\n\\nD. Opinion of the Minister of Finance and Economy\\n\\n(1) Preliminary defense\\n\\nIn order for a statute or a statutory provision itself to be the subject of a constitutional complaint, one must directly and presently have one’s fundamental rights infringed by the provision without waiting for a specific act of enforcement pursuant thereto. However, because the infringement of the Claimants’ fundamental rights occurs through the instant disposition of the Financial Supervisory Commission as an intermediary, the requirement of directness for a constitutional complaint is lacking. Accordingly, this constitutional complaint is unlawful.\\n\\n(2) As to the merits, it is the same as the reasons given by the Seoul Administrative Court for dismissing the application for constitutional referral and the opinion of the Financial Supervisory Commission."}

question:
Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (O) and incorrect (X) regarding property rights? (In case of dispute, according to precedents)

(a). Provisions under the National Land Planning and Utilization Act that designate districts necessary to maintain and manage the aesthetics of cultural properties and buildings with high cultural preservation value, and that restrict the use of land not conforming to the purpose of such designation, are provisions concerning the content and limits of property rights under Article 23(1) and (2) of the Constitution, in which the legislature 'generally and abstractly determines the rights and duties concerning land property rights,' and are provisions that specify the social restrictions on property rights.
(b). The school site charge under the former Act on Special Cases concerning the Securing of School Sites, imposed on the development project operator rather than the purchaser, does not infringe the development project operator’s property rights because it appropriately balances the public interest of guaranteeing equal educational opportunities and the private interest of the development project operator’s property interests.
(c). Under the Housing Act, a provision that allows a private project operator who has obtained approval of the business plan in a housing construction project and secured usage rights to at least 95 percent of the area of the housing construction site to make a market-value sale demand against all owners of the land for which usage rights have not been secured does not infringe property rights.
(d). A provision of the former Public Official Election Act that requires a person whose election has been invalidated due to an election crime to return the deposit already returned and the election expenses reimbursed does not infringe the property rights of the person whose election has been invalidated.
(e). Among the customary law concerning the grave-site right, the part stating that, in the absence of special circumstances such as an agreement between the parties regarding the duration of the grave-site right, the grave-site right continues to exist for so long as the grave itself continues to exist, as long as the right-holder continues to guard and maintain the grave, does not infringe the landowner’s property rights.
