supporting_precedents: {"[2003HEONGA20]": "1. Outline of the Case and Subject Matter of Review\\n\\na. Outline of the Case\\n\\n(1) The applicants for referral are some of the purchasers of units in Geomam Phase 2 ○○ Apartment (718 households) on Lots 1 and 2, Block 11 of Geomam 2 District, Seo-gu, Incheon; Geomam Phase 3 □□ Apartment (341 households) on Lot 2, Block 30 of the said Geomam 2 District; Geomam Phase 2 ○○ Apartment (325 households) on Lot 1, Block 37 of the said Geomam 2 District; and ○○ Apartment (2,098 households) on Blocks 6 and 7 of Samsan 1 Housing Site Development District, Bupyeong-gu, Incheon.\\n\\n(2) When the heads of Seo-gu, Incheon Metropolitan City, and Bupyeong-gu, after the implementers of the development projects for the above apartment complexes submitted the list of purchasers under the sales contracts, including the applicants for referral, pursuant to Article 5-2(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Special Act on the Securing of School Sites (hereinafter referred to as the “Enforcement Decree of the Special Act”), imposed the school site charge on the applicants for referral pursuant to Article 5(1) of the Special Act on the Securing of School Sites (hereinafter referred to as the “Special Act”).\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, the applicants for referral filed a lawsuit with the Incheon District Court in Case No. 2002GUHAP3878 seeking revocation of the above disposition imposing the charge and, at the same time, filed an application for referral of a constitutional review concerning Article 2 item 2 and Article 5(1) of the Special Act, and the said court accepted the application and made a referral for constitutional review.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe subject matter of review in this case is the part of Article 5(1) of the Special Act (as amended by Act No. 6219 on January 28, 2000 and before being amended by Act No. 6744 on December 5, 2002) that provides, “A charge may be imposed and collected on persons who have purchased apartments in the development project area, ... for the securing of school sites,” and the part of Article 2 item 2 of the Special Act that defines the above development project as “a project, among projects implemented pursuant to the Housing Construction Promotion Act ... that develops and prepares land for housing construction for 300 households or more.”\\n\\nIn addition, the referring court also made Article 2 item 3 of the Special Act the subject of the referral for constitutional review. However, the above part merely defines the concept of the school site charge, and in this case, the ambiguity and comprehensiveness of the concept of the school site charge are irrelevant to the grounds for the referral of unconstitutionality, so there is no need to make a separate determination. Therefore, the provisions subject to review in this case, excluding that part, are as follows:\\n\\nArticle 2 (Definitions) The definitions of terms used in this Act are as follows.\\n\\n2. “Development project” means a project, among projects implemented pursuant to the Housing Construction Promotion Act, the Housing Site Development Promotion Act, and the Act on the Industrial Sites and Development, that develops and prepares land for housing construction for 300 households or more.\\n\\nArticle 5 (Imposition and Collection of Charges) (1) The Special Metropolitan City Mayor, Metropolitan City Mayor, or Do Governor may impose and collect a charge on persons who purchase land for detached house construction (excluding land purchased as resettlement housing sites under the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Acquisition of Public Land and Compensation for Loss Therefrom) or apartments (excluding rental housing) in the development project area, for the securing of school sites.\\n\\n2. Grounds for the Referral and Opinions of Interested Parties, etc.\\n\\na. Grounds for the Referral by the Referring Court\\n\\nThe school site charge is a type of special charge imposed, unlike taxes, to carry out specific economic or policy objectives or special tasks. Therefore, in imposing and collecting it, it shall be imposed only on a specific group that has a special and close relationship, compared with general taxpayers or other groups in society, to the specific social and economic task to be carried out through the imposition of the charge (including the provision of special benefits or causes), and that is in a position to bear collective responsibility for the realization of such purpose.\\n\\nHowever, the provision of law in this case limits the scope of development projects subject to the imposition of the school site charge to projects implemented pursuant to the Housing Construction Promotion Act, the Housing Site Development Promotion Act, and the Act on the Industrial Sites and Development (hereinafter, when referring to the above three Acts, “the Housing Construction Promotion Act, etc.”). Yet, it is difficult to see any difference in the necessity of securing school sites in the case of development projects under the Housing Construction Promotion Act, etc., as well as in the case of development projects under the Building Act, the Urban Development Act, the Urban Redevelopment Act, etc., or even in the case of rental housing construction projects under the Rental Housing Act. Therefore, the provision of law in this case, without a rational basis, restricts the property rights of purchasers under development projects conducted pursuant to the Housing Construction Promotion Act, etc., compared with purchasers of lots or housing under development projects implemented under other laws, and thus violates the principle of equality.\\n\\nIn addition, the provision of law in this case determines the persons subject to the imposition of the school site charge based on the number of households (300 households) created by the development project. However, by imposing the charge based solely on the number of households created, irrespective of each household’s sale area or the purchaser’s economic capacity, purchasers of apartment housing with 300 or more households, whose individual sale area is small, must pay the charge, whereas purchasers of apartment housing with fewer than 300 households, whose sale area is large, are exempted from the obligation to be charged, which is contrary to the sense of justice in that it imposes a greater burden on purchasers of small housing, who are socially and economically weaker. Furthermore, the Special Act raises the concern that it may distort the housing market by causing project implementers, in planning housing supply, to consider whether a charge will be imposed as an important factor rather than consumer demand.\\n\\nMoreover, it is difficult to say that the persons subject to payment of the school site charge possess collective homogeneity sufficient to justify the purpose of the imposition.\\n\\nTherefore, it is difficult to say that the school site charge is appropriate as a means to achieve the legislative purpose, and moreover, it cannot be said that it is based on a rational standard in imposing and collecting it.\\n\\nb. Opinion of the Minister of Education and Human Resources Development\\n\\nThe school site charge is intended to respond flexibly to the securing of school sites and the demand for new teacher buildings, which are rapidly increasing due to various development projects, and its purpose of imposition is legitimate.\\n\\nThe reason the subject of the school site charge was set as development projects of 300 households or more was that, under the conditions at the time the Special Act was amended, in the case of development projects of 300 households or more, the sharp increase in school attendance demand made it impossible to secure school sites or build new teacher buildings any longer with general finances. Therefore, even if the subject of the charge is limited to development projects of 300 households or more, it cannot be deemed improper.\\n\\nc. Opinion of the Heads of Seo-gu and Bupyeong-gu, Incheon Metropolitan City\\n\\nEven if the Constitution, the Framework Act on Education, and the Elementary and Secondary Education Act provide that the State or local governments shall implement compulsory education free of charge, this is a declaratory norm that does not take actual fiscal conditions into account, and imposing the school site charge on development projects above a certain scale that generate educational demand falls within the scope of legislative discretion.\\n\\nEven if the Special Act limits the scope of development projects subject to the imposition of the charge to projects implemented pursuant to the Housing Construction Promotion Act, etc., this was intended to impose the charge to the minimum necessary extent by comparing educational demand and education finances, and after that, considering the increase in demand for education finance and the improvement in the national income level, the subject of imposition was expanded to include even development projects under the Building Act, the Urban Development Act, the Urban Redevelopment Act, etc.\\n\\nSince the school site charge is imposed in cases where educational demand has been artificially caused or promoted, it cannot be said to lack rationality merely because the subject of the imposition is determined by the number of households. And because the school site charge is imposed on persons who have purchased apartment housing at one time, the purchasers have homogeneity in that they simultaneously caused educational demand.\\n\\n3. General System of the School Site Charge\\n\\na. Legislative History of the School Site Charge System\\n\\nThe Special Act was enacted by Act No. 5072 on December 29, 1995, in order to facilitate the securing of school sites by providing special provisions concerning the creation, development, supply, and burden of expenses for school sites, since demand for school establishment was sharply increasing due to housing site development projects, etc., while local education finance was weak and securing school sites was difficult due to the rapid rise in land prices.\\n\\nAccording to the legal review memorandum of the National Assembly’s expert commissioner around the time the Special Act was enacted, the total number of newly established schools from 1996 to 1998 was 383, the budget required therefor was KRW 3.064 trillion, and among that, school site acquisition costs were estimated to require KRW 1.84 trillion. It was also expected that, if the Special Act were implemented, the amount equivalent to the school site charge collected under the Special Act out of the Special Education Account, which had previously been used for school site acquisition costs, would be utilized as investment resources for easing overcrowded classes and eliminating double-shift classes, thereby contributing to the improvement of educational conditions.\\n\\nb. Persons Liable for Payment of the School Site Charge and Method of Calculation\\n\\nThe persons liable for payment of the school site charge are, among projects implemented pursuant to the Housing Construction Promotion Act, etc., those who purchase land for housing construction or apartments in development projects that develop and prepare land for housing construction for 300 households or more (Article 2 items 2 and 3 of the Special Act).\\n\\nThe school site charge is imposed at 8/1,000 (0.8%) of the sale price for apartment housing, and at 15/1,000 (1.5%) of the sale price of land for detached house construction, in the case of land for detached house construction (Article 5-2(1) and (2) of the Special Act).\\n\\nc. Uses of the School Site Charge and Measures for Securing It\\n\\nThe school site charge is an expense collected for the securing of school sites, and school sites mean land necessary for the establishment of school buildings, athletic fields, practice grounds, and other school facilities of each level of school (elementary school, middle school, and high school) (Article 2 items 1 and 3 of the Special Act). Therefore, the school site charge may be used for expenses incurred in acquiring school sites, such as land acquisition costs and appraisal fees necessary for the establishment of such school facilities, and for expenses incurred in imposing and collecting the school site charge.\\n\\nThe expenses required for securing school sites are borne equally, one-half each, by the general accounts of the Si/Do and the Special Account for Educational Expenses (Article 4(4) of the Special Act). In the case of the Special Account for Educational Expenses related to the construction of school facilities, since the State is to grant them to local governments pursuant to Article 1 and Article 5 of the Local Education Subsidy Act, the amount actually borne by local governments is one-half of the school site acquisition costs. And the expenses necessary for securing school sites borne by the general accounts of the Si/Do may be funded by local taxes imposed and collected in the area where the development project is implemented, the tax amount prescribed by Presidential Decree among such taxes, development charges imposed and collected in the development project area pursuant to the Act on Restitution of Development Gains, and the school site charge imposed and collected under the Special Act.\\n\\n(Article 6 of the Special Act).\\n\\nd. Nature of the School Site Charge\\n\\nSince the school site charge is imposed to meet the demand for securing school sites for elementary, middle, and high schools among the demand for public facilities that increases due to housing construction for 300 households or more, it falls under the category of a causation-based charge according to classification by cause of imposition. And because, through the implementation of a specific public welfare project, namely the construction of school facilities, home purchasers obtain a special benefit of enabling their children to receive education nearby, it also has the character of a beneficiary charge.\\n\\nMeanwhile, according to classification by the nature of the charge, the school site charge can be regarded as a charge for fiscal financing purposes. This is because the school site charge is basically intended to fund the finances required for securing the necessary school facilities, and because the policy and inducive character of restricting or prohibiting housing site development or housing supply by imposing the charge is weak.\\n\\n4. Whether the School Site Charge Is Unconstitutional\\n\\na. General Theory\\n\\nA charge means a monetary payment obligation, regardless of whether it is called a contribution, assessment, deposit, or levy, imposed under the law by a person who is granted the authority to impose a monetary burden, such as the head of a central administrative agency, the head of a local government, or the head of a public organization or corporation entrusted with administrative authority, and imposed in connection with a specific public welfare project according to law, irrespective of the provision of goods or services, other than taxes (Article 2 of the Framework Act on the Management of Charges). Traditionally, a charge was understood as a monetary payment obligation imposed on persons who have a special interest in a specific public welfare project in order to make them bear the expenses necessary for that project. Under the current Framework Act on the Management of Charges, however, the element of guaranteeing a special economic benefit, which is counterperformance, is excluded from the conceptual elements of a charge, and the permissible scope of establishing a charge system is thus recognized relatively broadly.\\n\\nHowever, because the property rights of all citizens are guaranteed by the Constitution (Article 23(1) of the Constitution), if a property burden is imposed on citizens other than taxes, a constitutional basis therefor is needed. Since our Constitution contains a general reservation clause concerning fundamental rights (Article 37(2) of the Constitution), the freedom and rights of citizens may be restricted by law when necessary for public welfare, and the same applies to restrictions on property rights by the imposition of charges. Therefore, the establishment of a charge system by law falls within the category of restrictions on fundamental rights permitted by the Constitution. However, even if the establishment of a charge system is permitted under the general reservation clause, concrete circumstances must be considered depending on the type of charge.\\n\\nIn the case of a charge for fiscal financing purposes, because it may be imposed without any specific counterperformance, it is very similar to a tax; therefore, the tax legality principle prescribed by Article 38 of the Constitution, the fairness of the burden of public charges derived from the principle of equality before the law prescribed by Article 11(1) of the Constitution, and the limits arising in relation to the fiscal oversight power through the National Assembly’s power to deliberate on and finalize the budget prescribed by Article 54(1) of the Constitution must be considered. Furthermore, the general limits on restrictions of fundamental rights (the principle of proportionality), and, in the case of the school site charge in particular, the gratuitousness of compulsory education under Article 31(3) of the Constitution, must also be considered.\\n\\nIn the case of a charge for the realization of policy objectives, it is intended to achieve social and economic policy objectives by indirectly inducing and adjusting the conduct of citizens through the imposition of a monetary burden called a charge, instead of using direct regulatory means such as orders or prohibitions on individual acts, as a matter separate from the Constitution’s basic fiscal order. Since using such a charge is often more effective, the use of a charge itself as a means of realizing social and economic policy is not directly contrary to the Constitution (Constitutional Court Dec. 24, 1998, 98HEONGA1, Case Reports 10-2, 819, 830). However, at least a charge for the realization of policy objectives must be an appropriate means for realizing social and policy objectives, and it must not deviate from the fairness of the burden of public charges derived from the principle of equality before the law.\\n\\nIn the case of the school site charge, as noted above, it is close to a causation-based charge and falls under a charge for fiscal financing purposes, so we will examine its constitutional permissibility and whether the provisions of law in this case are unconstitutional with a focus on that.\\n\\nb. Examination of the Constitutional Principle of Gratuitous Compulsory Education and the Requirements for the Justification of a Charge\\n\\n(1) The Constitution provides that all citizens have the duty to ensure that their children under their protection receive at least elementary education and education prescribed by law (Article 31(2) of the Constitution), and that compulsory education shall be free of charge (Article 31(3) of the Constitution). Accordingly, Article 8(1) of the Framework Act on Education provides that compulsory education shall consist of six years of elementary education and three years of secondary education, but compulsory education for the three-year secondary education shall be implemented sequentially in accordance with Presidential Decree, taking into account the State’s fiscal conditions. And the Elementary and Secondary Education Act provides that the State shall take necessary measures, including securing facilities for the implementation of compulsory education (Article 12(1) of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act), and that local governments shall establish and operate elementary schools and middle schools necessary to enroll all persons subject to compulsory education within their jurisdiction, as well as special schools that provide the courses of elementary schools and middle schools (Article 12(2) of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act). In other words, our Constitution imposes on citizens the duty to educate their children while at the same time declaring free compulsory education in order to facilitate the education of children under the protection of the State and to enable economically disadvantaged parents to fulfill their educational duty. Such a compulsory education system has, more importantly, the aspect of imposing a duty on the State to improve human and material educational facilities and the educational environment, rather than the aspect of imposing a duty on citizens to enroll their children (see Constitutional Court Feb. 11, 1991, 90HEONGA27, Case Reports 3, 11, 19).\\n\\nSchool facilities necessary for compulsory education are the State’s general task, and it goes without saying that school sites are an essential condition as the material basis for implementing compulsory education. Therefore, the costs required to achieve this must be financed from the State’s general finances. Article 31(6) of the Constitution provides that basic matters concerning education finance shall be determined by law. This should be understood as having prescribed in the Constitution the State’s minimum responsibility for ensuring the effectiveness of the right to receive education free of charge, and, considering that the free compulsory education system imposes duties more strongly on the State than on citizens, it should be understood as clarifying the State’s duty to achieve the constitutional and statutory principle of gratuitous compulsory education by sacrificing other parts of the general finances secured or to be secured. If so, at least with respect to compulsory education, mobilizing separate fiscal means such as charges rather than general finances and additionally collecting and funding the costs from a specific group would be contrary to the Constitution that declares the gratuitous nature of compulsory education.\\n\\nAnd even if, with respect to education finance for secondary education that is not compulsory education, a charge for fiscal financing purposes may be collected, this may be permitted only if the same requirements that a general charge for fiscal financing purposes must satisfy are met.\\n\\n(2) The Constitutional Court has stated that, in order for a charge for fiscal financing purposes to be recognized as constitutionally justified, a charge should be recognized only exceptionally in relation to taxes; if the purpose is to use it for the performance of general public welfare projects, a charge should not be abused; the person liable for payment of the charge should have a “special close connection” compared with the general public; and where a charge continues for a long period of time, the propriety or appropriateness of its collection must be continuously reviewed by the legislature (see Constitutional Court July 15, 2004, 2002HEONBA42, Official Gazette 95, 722, 725-726). However, the above requirements for justifying a charge can naturally be considered by reviewing the limits on the restriction of fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court Jan. 30, 2003, 2002HEONBA5, Case Reports 15-1, 86, 95). Therefore, whether the school site charge system, which may infringe property rights or the principle of substantive tax equality, is unconstitutional depends on whether it violates the constitutional principle of equality and the principle of proportionality.\\n\\nc. Whether the Principle of Equality Was Violated\\n\\n(1) Introduction\\n\\nThe requirements for justifying a charge are generally closely related to the constitutional principle of equality. A charge is a special fiscal responsibility imposed on a special group of persons subject to obligation, not the general public, by restricting citizens’ property rights, so there must be a rational basis in treating the persons liable differently from the general public and treating them disadvantageously; arbitrary discrimination infringes the equal rights of the persons liable. Since the school site charge must also observe the principle of equality like general charges, below we examine whether the provision of law in this case observes the principle of equality in respect of whether to impose a charge on the special public welfare project presented as the basis for justifying the charge, the selection of the group subject to obligation, and whether there is a special connection between the group subject to obligation and the above public welfare project.\\n\\n(2) Whether it Is a Special Public Welfare Project\\n\\nArticle 31 of the Constitution provides that the general public has the right to receive education, while setting forth, as the State’s duties in relation thereto, legislation concerning the free implementation of compulsory education, the promotion of lifelong education, the educational system and operation, and education finance. The securing of school sites is the most basic material basis for the establishment and operation of general regular educational institutions, including compulsory education, so it is easy to see that it is the most basic and general public welfare project targeting all citizens among the State’s duties regarding education. Therefore, as a principle, its cost should be covered by taxes, which are general finances. However, where the demand for school facilities sharply increases due to a surge in housing supply in a certain area, the securing of school sites made necessary thereby may also qualify as a “special” public welfare project for some areas.\\n\\nHowever, the securing of school sites under the Special Act cannot be viewed merely as a response to a simple increase in school demand in a specific area. This is because the necessity of securing school sites is also needed to respond to the increased demand for general public welfare projects, such as the abolition of double-shift classes, reducing the number of students per class to alleviate overcrowded classes, and securing facilities for other special activities, which constitutes overall improvement of educational conditions. In other words, even if the main purpose of the school site charge system is to meet the demand for new schools in a specific area, the school site charge actually secured is incidentally also used as finances for general public welfare projects. Even if we examine the legislative process of the Special Act, it appears that the establishment of the school site charge system was considered in order to increase fiscal input for the above general public welfare projects or, where such input is increased, to secure relatively insufficient finances for securing school sites.\\n\\nIn addition, the Special Act allows the cost of securing school sites for constructing elementary schools, and some middle schools prescribed by the Framework Act on Education, which are compulsory education institutions, to be covered by the school site charge. Compulsory education is a task that must be achieved even by sacrificing other parts of the State’s general tasks, and on the other hand, considering that all citizens bear the duty to educate their protected children through compulsory education, even if citizens who bear the general tax obligation have purchased housing in a certain area and thereby caused the need to secure compulsory education facilities, it cannot be said that this immediately converts the securing of compulsory education facilities into a special public welfare project.\\n\\nMeanwhile, from the perspective of the persons liable, the collected school site charge is operated by local government unit (Special Metropolitan City, Metropolitan City, Province), so it cannot necessarily be said that it is used to secure the site for the school their children will attend. In particular, in the case of elementary schools and middle schools, because the district unit for imposing the charge is far broader than the school assignment unit district, the securing of school sites at the local government unit level inevitably has a strong character as a general public welfare project from the perspective of the persons liable.\\n\\nIn the end, the school site charge is a means of securing finances for a public welfare project that is either a general public welfare project or a public welfare project that also has the character of a general public welfare project, and some of the school site charge in fact yields the same result as being used for finances for a general public welfare project. Therefore, it does not sufficiently satisfy the requirement for the justification of a charge that a charge may be imposed only for a specific public welfare project and only for the purpose of being appropriated to that project.\\n\\n(3) Whether the Group Subject to Obligation Has Homogeneity\\n\\nOnly if the persons liable have a certain homogeneity among themselves can we examine whether there is a collective connection with the public welfare project for the entire group subject to obligation and, further, whether there is special collective responsibility. The homogeneity requirement means not only that the group subject to obligation must be distinguished from the general public by homogeneous elements, but also that the degree of homogeneity must remain similar among the persons liable within the group subject to obligation.\\n\\nIt may be said that the persons liable are formally distinguished from the general public by the fact that they purchased new housing. However, because the provision of law in this case is the basis for imposing the school site charge on purchasers of apartment housing, the core of homogeneity among purchasers should be whether they caused the need to secure school sites. Yet, apart from the fact that the purchasers simultaneously purchased apartment housing, their interests regarding the securing of school sites differ depending on concrete circumstances, ranging from whether they will actually reside after completion of the housing, to whether they have no children attending elementary or middle school, whether they have only children attending elementary and middle school, whether they have only children attending high school, whether they have both, and the number of children attending each school. And generally speaking, the possibility that purchasers of apartment housing in development projects for 300 households or more will have a similar level of homogeneity with respect to securing school sites, in other words, the possibility that they will have children of the same number of students, is extremely slim.\\n\\nFurthermore, we examine whether the purchasers of apartment housing in the development project under the provision of law in this case have homogeneity distinguishable from the general public, and especially from purchasers of apartment housing under development projects not prescribed by the Special Act. Whether under other laws relating to the construction of new housing, such as the Building Act and the Urban Development Act, or under laws relating to the redevelopment or reconstruction of existing housing, such as the Urban Redevelopment Act, if new housing in excess of the number of existing housing units is supplied as a result of redevelopment or reconstruction, the purchasers of such housing would, like the purchasers of housing under the development project under the provision of law in this case, raise the need for securing school sites. On the other hand, even if it is a development project under the provision of law in this case, if the substance of the project is merely reconstruction, as in the case of a development project by a reconstruction association, it would scarcely create any need for securing new school sites.\\n\\nIf so, from the perspective of individual purchasers, imposing the same school site charge uniformly on all purchasers by including them all in the same group subject to obligation without considering the concrete circumstances of the purchasers with respect to the need for securing school sites constitutes discrimination without rational basis. And even from the perspective of the entire group subject to obligation, because it cannot be said that they have a collective homogeneity socially distinguishable from the general public, especially the group of purchasers under other development projects, imposing the school site charge only on the group of purchasers under the development project according to the provision of law in this case would infringe the equal rights of each member of the group.\\n\\n(4) Whether There Is a Close Connection\\n\\nThe persons liable must have a special “close connection” with the specific public welfare project that is the subject of fiscal financing, compared with the general public. However, because anyone among the public is constitutionally guaranteed the right to receive the benefits of compulsory education, even if compulsory education demand is caused by accidental circumstances or the person receives compulsory education under relatively favorable conditions, it is difficult to regard such persons as having a special connection in relation to the establishment of compulsory education facilities.\\n\\nEven in the case of secondary education that is not compulsory education, as examined above, the securing of school sites itself also has the character of a general public welfare project, so the connection of the persons liable with the public welfare project is weakened. And as examined above, because even within the group subject to obligation each person liable does not possess collective homogeneity with respect to the public welfare project, the degree of close connection must inevitably differ depending on the concrete circumstances of each person liable.\\n\\nEven if only these two points are considered, it cannot be said that all of the applicants for referral in this case have a close connection with the school site securing project. Furthermore, we examine whether the fact that the provision of law in this case selects only purchasers under specific development projects as the persons liable rationally reflects the requirement of close connection with the public welfare project.\\n\\nThe necessity of securing school sites depends on whether the law concerns the construction and supply of new housing or the redevelopment or reconstruction of existing housing, and the degree of closeness between the purchasers prescribed by each law and the public welfare project can be determined accordingly. Therefore, it is necessary to examine housing-related laws from the perspective of housing construction and supply.\\n\\nLaws relating to the construction of new housing can be divided into the Housing Construction Promotion Act, the Housing Site Development Promotion Act, and the Act on the Industrial Sites and Development, which are prescribed by the Special Act, as well as the general Building Act, the Urban Development Act, which prescribes the urban development method, the Rental Housing Construction Promotion Act, etc. Laws relating to redevelopment or reconstruction of existing housing can broadly be divided into the Urban Redevelopment Act, which prescribes urban redevelopment projects, and the Act on Temporary Measures for the Improvement of the Residential Environment of Urban Low-Income Residents, which aims to improve the residential environment of urban low-income residents. However, even if they are laws concerning redevelopment or reconstruction, such as the Urban Redevelopment Act, if additional new housing is supplied beyond the existing housing units as a result of a development project under each of those laws, redevelopment or reconstruction laws can also supply new housing in addition to reconstruction of existing housing.\\n\\nYet the necessity of securing school sites arises in the case of construction and supply of new housing, and it is reasonable to view that the extent thereof is determined in proportion to the number of new housing units supplied as a result of the development project, regardless of the purpose or procedure of the development project. Therefore, even in the case of development projects under other laws concerning the construction of new housing, such as the Building Act and the Urban Development Act, or even in the case of development projects under laws concerning the redevelopment or reconstruction of existing housing, if new housing in excess of the previous number of housing units is supplied as a result of redevelopment or reconstruction, the purchasers of such housing shall have the same connection with the public welfare project of securing school sites as the purchasers under the development project under the provision of law in this case. On the other hand, as noted above, if even a development project under the provision of law in this case is merely reconstruction in substance, as in the case of a development project by a reconstruction association, it will scarcely create any need for securing new school sites.\\n\\nNevertheless, the provision of law in this case determines development projects subject to the school site charge not by whether new housing is supplied, but merely by what the legal basis for housing supply is, and this would amount to arbitrarily treating the applicants for referral disadvantageously based on a standard lacking rationality.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Framework Act on the Management of Charges defines a charge as a monetary payment obligation unrelated to the provision of goods or services and connected with a specific public welfare project (Article 2 of the Framework Act on the Management of Charges), so the guarantee of counterperformance is not necessarily required as an element of a charge’s concept. Therefore, it cannot be said that the revenue from a charge must necessarily be used for the collective benefit of the persons liable. However, if it is used for the collective benefit of the persons liable, the justification for imposing the charge is enhanced, needless to say (see Constitutional Court Jan. 30, 2003, 2002HEONBA5, Case Reports 15-1, 86, 96).\\n\\nHowever, because the school site charge secured under the provision of law in this case is operated by local government unit (Special Metropolitan City, Metropolitan City, Province), it cannot necessarily be said that it is used to secure the site for the school their children will attend. In particular, in the case of elementary schools and middle schools, because the district unit for imposing the charge is far broader than the school assignment unit district, the connection between the school site securing project and the collective benefit of the persons liable becomes even weaker.\\n\\nIn the end, although it is difficult to say that purchasers of new housing have a close connection with the above public welfare project compared with the general public, imposing a charge for the securing of school sites only on purchasers of new housing constitutes discrimination without rational basis.\\n\\n(5) Therefore, the provision of law in this case is contrary to the principle of equality.\\n\\nd. Whether the Principle of Proportionality Was Violated\\n\\n(1) Legitimacy of Purpose\\n\\nThe school site charge system has the legitimate purpose of achieving public welfare through the securing of school sites.\\n\\n(2) Appropriateness of Means\\n\\nThe provision of law in this case imposes the charge by including among the persons liable persons who are not the cause of the securing of school sites; it does not distinguish the costs for facilities for compulsory education from those for other educational facilities; and although the collected charge is formally used for the securing of school sites, in fact it is used to simultaneously carry out tasks that should be achieved through general education finance without strictly distinguishing the two.\\n\\nIn addition, persons subject to the school site charge are determined solely by the number of households of housing supplied through the development project (300 households), regardless of the scale of the developed apartment housing and the sale area per household. In other words, if the scale of the development project is 300 households or more, the school site charge is imposed on all purchasers; if it is fewer than 300 households, it is not imposed on any purchaser. However, with such a standard, in the case of purchasers of apartment housing with 299 households or fewer and purchasers of apartment housing with 300 households, it is difficult to say that there is a substantial and significant difference in terms of causing the need for school sites. Furthermore, when comparing a project developing apartment housing with 299 households or fewer and large floor area with a project developing apartment housing with 300 households or more and small floor area, the result is that the school site charge is imposed in a way even more unreasonable in light of the persons liable’s capacity to pay. Therefore, even if the standard and method of imposing the school site charge fundamentally fall within the realm of legislative discretion, equity in the imposition of the school site charge should be more carefully considered, and other methods, such as exempting a certain number of households from the charge in order to prevent development projects designed to evade the conditions for the imposition of the charge and imposing the charge only on the remainder in a lump-sum amount, should be considered.\\n\\nIf so, the school site charge adopts an inappropriate method that does not consider the relevance to the persons liable in various respects, such as the selection of the persons liable, the selection of the projects subject to imposition, the standards for imposition, and the use of the collected charge, or does not consider equity.\\n\\n(3) Minimum Restriction of Rights and Balance of Legal Interests\\n\\nFurthermore, we examine whether the school site charge satisfies the minimum restriction of rights and the balance of legal interests. It is not easy to determine to what extent the specific amount or rate of a charge should be reasonable or not exceed the balance of legal interests. However, because a charge is a monetary payment obligation external to taxes, it should be permitted more exceptionally and minimally than taxes, and therefore should satisfy a stricter minimum restriction of rights and balance of legal interests. Article 5 of the Framework Act on the Management of Charges also provides, with respect to the principle of charge imposition: “Charges shall be imposed so that fairness and transparency are secured within the minimum scope necessary to achieve the purpose of establishment, and, unless there is a special reason, no double charge shall be imposed on the same subject of imposition.”\\n\\nWhen the purchasers under the Special Act purchase apartment housing, they not only bear acquisition tax and registration tax as general taxes, but also separately bear education tax (20% of the amount of registration tax) based on the registration tax, and then additionally bear a certain percentage (0.8%) of the sale price as a school site charge. Meanwhile, since the finance for securing school sites is to be borne one-half each by the general accounts and the Special Account for Educational Expenses of local governments (Article 4(4) of the Special Act), the costs covered by the general accounts among them consist of the school site charge, local taxes prescribed by Presidential Decree, and development charges under the Act on Restitution of Development Gains. Here, “local taxes prescribed by Presidential Decree” means acquisition tax and registration tax, and the amount obtained by subtracting the school site charge and development charges from the expenses for securing school sites is the maximum amount of local tax that can be covered (Article 6 of the Enforcement Decree of the Special Act). However, the fact that the State imposes education tax as a purpose tax, acquisition tax and registration tax as general taxes, and development charges as a beneficiary charge for development projects in order to carry out the public welfare project of securing school facilities, and then imposes the school site charge again for the same purpose, may in substance amount to double taxation or double imposition of a charge. Also, the fact that all of the secured charge is not necessarily used to secure school sites located within the commuting distance of the persons liable or their children is as noted above.\\n\\nIf so, the school site charge cannot be regarded as satisfying the requirement of minimum restriction of rights.\\n\\nAnd although the public welfare project that the provision of law in this case seeks to achieve is a very important one, namely securing educational facilities, the fact that free compulsory education is being implemented for elementary and middle schools, and that in the case of high schools, while the connection of the persons liable with the public welfare project is weak, education tax, acquisition tax, and registration tax are already being borne as general fiscal burdens for the securing of educational facilities, yet an additional school site charge is imposed again, strongly raises the suspicion that this is a burden greater than a fair share in relation to the achievement of the public welfare project, and it is therefore difficult to say that the requirement of balance of legal interests is also fully satisfied.\\n\\nIn the end, the provision of law in this case fails to faithfully satisfy appropriateness of means, minimum restriction of rights, and balance of legal interests in the imposition of the school site charge, and thus violates the principle of proportionality under Article 37(2) of the Constitution.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nIf that is so, since the provision of law in this case is in violation of the Constitution, the Court decides as ordered by unanimous opinion of all participating Justices."}

In this case, the location and scale of the school site shall be governed mutatis mutandis by the provisions concerning the standards for the installation of school facilities under Article 43 of the National Land Planning and Utilization Act.\\n② The Superintendent of Education of a Special Metropolitan City, Metropolitan City, Do, or Province (hereinafter referred to as the “Superintendent of Education”) shall, with respect to a development project below the standards for the installation of school facilities under paragraph 1, require the developer to secure a school site of appropriate size in consideration of the scale of the development project and local conditions; however, where it is determined that the developer cannot secure a school site because the area is too small, the developer may be required to secure a school site adjacent to the project site.\\n③ Where the developer intends to develop a school site pursuant to paragraph 1 or to secure a school site pursuant to paragraph 2, he or she shall hear the opinion of the Superintendent of Education.\\n\\nArticle 4 (Securing of School Sites and Bearing of Expenses) ④ The expenses required for a City or Do to secure school sites pursuant to paragraphs 1 and 2 shall be borne equally, one-half by the general account of the City or Do and one-half by the Special Account for Education.\\n\\nArticle 5 (Imposition and Collection of the Levy) ③ Matters necessary for the methods, procedures, etc. of imposing and collecting the levy under paragraph 1 shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n\\nArticle 5-2 (Standards for Calculation of the Levy) ① The levy under Article 5 (1) shall be imposed on the basis of the sale price in the case of multi-unit housing, and on the basis of the sale price of land for detached houses in the case of land for the construction of detached houses.\\n② The calculation of the levy under paragraph 1 shall be made in accordance with the following standards:\\n1. Multi-unit housing: sale price of multi-unit housing per household × 4/1000\\n2. Land for the construction of detached houses: sale price of land for detached houses × 7/1000\\n\\nArticle 6 (Source of Funds for Expenses to be Borne by City/Do) ① A City or Do may finance the expenses borne by the general account of the City or Do for the securing of school sites under Article 4 from any of the following sources:\\n1. Among local taxes imposed and collected in the area where the development project is implemented, the amount prescribed by Presidential Decree\\n2. Among development charges imposed and collected in the development project area pursuant to the provisions of the Restitution of Development Gains Act, the amount prescribed by Presidential Decree\\n3. The school site levy imposed and collected pursuant to Article 5\\n② Notwithstanding paragraph 1, where securing school sites is impossible, a City or Do may finance the expenses necessary for the expansion of existing nearby schools from the source referred to in paragraph 1 subparagraph 3.\\n\\nFormer Special Act on the Securing of School Sites, etc. (before amendment by Act No. 7397 of 2005. 3. 24.) Omitted\\n2. “Development project” means a project implemented under the Building Act, Urban Redevelopment Act, Temporary Measures Act for Improvement of the Residential Environment of Low-Income Urban Residents, Housing Act, Housing Site Development Promotion Act, and the Industrial Sites and Development Act, among projects that create and develop land for housing construction of a scale of 300 households or more or construct multi-unit housing.\\n3. “School site levy” means the expenses (hereinafter referred to as “the levy”) collected by the Special Metropolitan City Mayor, Metropolitan City Mayor, or Do Governor (hereinafter referred to as the “Mayor/Do Governor”) from a person who purchases land for housing construction or housing, for the securing of school sites, with respect to a development project falling under subparagraph 2.\\n\\nArticle 5 ① The Mayor/Do Governor may impose and collect the levy on a person who purchases, in the development project area, land for the construction of detached houses (excluding land purchased as a resettlement site under the Act on Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects) or multi-unit housing (excluding rental housing), etc., for the securing of school sites. Article 5-2 (Procedures, etc. for the Imposition and Collection of the School Site Levy) ① Where a developer sells land for the construction of detached houses or multi-unit housing, etc. pursuant to Article 5 (3) of the Act, he or she shall submit sale materials such as the sale supply contract parties and details of the sale supply contract to the Special Metropolitan City Mayor, Metropolitan City Mayor, or Do Governor (hereinafter referred to as the “Mayor/Do Governor”) within 30 days from the date of conclusion of the sale supply contract (in cases where unsold land and multi-unit housing, etc. are additionally sold after 60 days have elapsed from the date of conclusion of the first sale supply contract, within 7 days after the end of each quarter).\\n② Upon receiving the sale materials pursuant to paragraph 1, the Mayor/Do Governor shall immediately issue to the developer of the relevant land or multi-unit housing, etc. a payment notice stating the amount of the levy, the deadline for payment, the method of payment, the place of payment, and the like.\\n③ The deadline for payment of the levy under paragraph 2 shall be 30 days from the date of the notice.\\n\\nArticle 6 (Scope of Financing for Expenses Borne by City/Do) ① “Local taxes imposed and collected in the area where the development project is implemented” in Article 6 subparagraph 1 of the Act means acquisition tax and registration tax, and the expenses financed from such local taxes shall be limited to the amount remaining after subtracting, from the expenses borne by the general account of the City or Do for the securing of school sites, the development charges under paragraph 2 and the levies under Article 5 of the Act.\\n② The expenses financed by development charges under Article 6 subparagraph 2 of the Act shall be the development charges belonging to the City or Do and collected in the relevant development project."}
