Outline of the Case  \\n(1) The petitioner ran in and was elected in the election for Superintendent of Education of Seoul Metropolitan City conducted on 2008. 7. 30. However, on 2009. 3. 10., the Seoul District Court rendered a judgment finding the petitioner guilty of the criminal facts that, while registering as a candidate in the above election and submitting a property report, the petitioner, despite knowing that the petitioner’s spouse held a deposit account in another person’s name, reported property details omitting the above deposit account for the purpose of being elected, thereby making a false public statement concerning the spouse’s property, and sentenced the petitioner to a fine of 1,500,000 won, and as the above judgment became final on 2009. 10. 29., the petitioner’s election was invalidated.  \\n(2) As the petitioner’s election was invalidated, the Seoul Metropolitan City Election Commission, on 2009. 11. 10., pursuant to Article 265-2(1) of the former Public Officials Election Act, which is applied mutatis mutandis to the petitioner under Article 22(3) of the former “Act on the Special Cases Concerning the Autonomous Control of Local Education,” notified the petitioner to return the 50,005,753 won of election deposit already returned and the 2,835,153,680 won of reimbursed election expenses.  \\n(3) Accordingly, while filing with the Seoul Administrative Court a suit for confirmation of invalidity of the disposition of return of election deposit and reimbursed election expenses, etc. (2009GUHAP54079), the petitioner filed an application for a referral for constitutional review of statutes (2009A3969) with respect to the above provision, asserting that Article 265-2(1) of the Public Officials Election Act, which formed the basis of the above notification, was unconstitutional because it infringed the right to hold public office, the right to equality, etc., and violated the principle that election expenses shall be borne by the national treasury; however, when the said court dismissed each of them on 2010. 5. 14., the petitioner filed this constitutional complaint on 2010. 6. 16.  \\n\\nb. Subject of Adjudication  \\nThe petitioner filed this adjudication request concerning the entirety of Article 265-2(1) of the former Public Officials Election Act. However, the latter sentence of the above provision is a provision stating that, where the election of a presidential candidate or a proportional representation candidate is invalidated, the recommending political party bears the obligation to return, and thus is irrelevant to the petitioner who ran in the election for Superintendent of Education without recommendation by a political party; therefore, it shall be excluded from the subject of adjudication. And since the petitioner falls under “a person whose election was invalidated pursuant to the provisions of Article 264,” the above provision was applied, the subject of adjudication shall be limited, in the first sentence of the above provision, to the part relevant to the petitioner only.\\n\\nTherefore, the subject of adjudication in this case is whether the part concerning “a person whose election was invalidated pursuant to the provisions of Article 264” in the first sentence of Article 265-2(1) of the former Public Officials Election Act (as amended by Act No. 7681 on 2005. 8. 4. and before amendment by Act No. 9968 on 2010. 1. 25.) (hereinafter referred to as the “statutory provision at issue”) is unconstitutional.\\n\\nThe contents of the provision subject to adjudication and the related provisions are as follows.  \\n[Provision Subject to Adjudication]  \\nFormer Public Officials Election Act (as amended by Act No. 7681 on 2005. 8. 4., and before amendment by Act No. 9974 on 2010. 1. 25.) Article 265-2 (Return of expenses by persons whose election has become invalid, etc.) (1) A person whose election has become invalid pursuant to the provisions of Article 263 (invalidity of election due to excessive election expenses) through Article 265 (invalidity of election due to election crimes by election officers, etc.) (including a person who resigned after indictment and before a final judgment becomes final) shall return the amount returned or reimbursed pursuant to the provisions of Article 57 (Return of Election Deposit, etc.) and Article 122-2 (Reimbursement, etc. of Election Expenses). In this case, where the election of a party-nominated candidate in a presidential election becomes invalid, and where the election of candidates in a proportional representation National Assembly election and a proportional representation local council election all become invalid, the recommending political party shall return the amount.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]  \\nFormer “Act on the Special Cases Concerning the Autonomous Control of Local Education” (as amended by Act No. 8069 on 2006. 12. 20., and before amendment by Act No. 10046 on 2010. 2. 26.) Article 22 (Election of Superintendent of Education) (3) With respect to the election of Superintendent of Education, except as otherwise provided in this Act, the provisions concerning elections of the Mayor/Governor of a City/Province under the Public Officials Election Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to the extent not contrary to their nature.\\n\\nFormer Public Officials Election Act (as amended by Act No. 7681 on 2005. 8. 4., and before amendment by Act No. 9974 on 2010. 1. 25.)  \\nArticle 57 (Return of Election Deposit, etc.) (1) The election district election commission shall return to the depositor, within 30 days after the election day, the remainder of the amount in the relevant classification under each subparagraph after deducting from the election deposit the expenses borne out of the election deposit pursuant to the provisions of Article 56(3) (Election Deposit).  \\n1. Presidential election, constituency National Assembly election, constituency local council election, and election of the head of a local government  \\na. In cases where the candidate is elected or dies, and in cases where the candidate obtains at least 15/100 of the total valid votes, the entire election deposit  \\nb. In cases where the candidate obtains at least 10/100 but less than 15/100 of the total valid votes, an amount corresponding to 50/100 of the election deposit  \\n2. Proportional representation National Assembly election and proportional representation local council election  \\nThe entire election deposit where there is an elected person among the candidates listed on the relevant candidate list\\n\\nArticle 122-2 (Reimbursement, etc. of Election Expenses) (1) The election district election commission shall, after the election day, reimburse election expenses incurred by a candidate (in a presidential election, a party-nominated candidate; and in a proportional representation National Assembly election and a proportional representation local council election, the political party that recommended the candidate; hereinafter the same in this Article) for election campaigning under the provisions of this Act, within the scope of expenses publicly announced pursuant to the provisions of Article 122 (Public Notice of the Limit on Election Expenses), as borne by the State in the case of a presidential election and a National Assembly election, and as borne by the relevant local government in the case of an election of members of a local council and the head of a local government.  \\n1. Presidential election, constituency National Assembly election, constituency local council election, and election of the head of a local government  \\na. In cases where the candidate is elected or dies, or where the candidate’s total number of votes is at least 15/100 of the total valid votes, the full amount of election expenses incurred by the candidate  \\nb. In cases where the candidate’s total number of votes is at least 10/100 but less than 15/100 of the total valid votes, an amount corresponding to 50/100 of the election expenses incurred by the candidate  \\n2. Proportional representation National Assembly election and proportional representation local council election  \\nThe full amount of election expenses incurred by the relevant political party where there is an elected person among the candidates listed on the candidate list\\n\\nArticle 264 (Invalidity of election due to election crimes by an elected person) Where an elected person is sentenced, in the relevant election, to imprisonment or to a fine of at least 1,000,000 won by committing the crimes prescribed in this Act and the crime under Article 49 (Punishment for Violations Related to Election Expenses) of the Political Funds Act, the election shall be invalidated.\\n\\nArticle 250 (Crime of Making a False Public Statement) (1) Any person who, for the purpose of being elected or causing another person to be elected, makes or causes to be made a false statement, by speech, broadcasting, newspaper, communication, magazine, placard, propaganda document, or other means, concerning the candidate, the candidate’s spouse, lineal ascendant or descendant, or siblings’ birthplace, status, occupation, career, property, character, conduct, affiliation with an organization, etc., in a manner favorable to the candidate (including a person who intends to become a candidate; hereinafter the same in this Article) [including cases where, in the case of stating educational background, the statement is not made by the method under Article 64 (Election Placard) (1)], or any person who possesses, for the purpose of distributing a propaganda document containing a false statement, shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 5 years or by a fine not exceeding 30,000,000 won.\\n\\nPublic Officials Election Act (as amended by Act No. 9974 on 2010. 1. 25.) Article 265-2 (Return of expenses by persons whose election has become invalid, etc.) (1) A person whose election has become invalid in accordance with the provisions of Articles 263 through 265 (including a person who resigned after indictment and before a final judgment becomes final), and a person who was not elected but whose sentence corresponding to invalidation of election for crimes committed by the person himself/herself or by an election officer, etc. prescribed in Articles 263 through 265 has become final, shall return the amount returned or reimbursed pursuant to Articles 57 and 122-2. In this case, in the case of a party-nominated candidate in a presidential election, the recommending political party shall return it, and in the case of a proportional representation National Assembly election and a proportional representation local council election, the recommending political party shall return it when the election of all candidates becomes invalid.\\n\\n2. The Petitioner’s Arguments  \\na. The statutory provision at issue is prescribed based on the legislative purpose of ensuring the fairness of elections by imposing a sanction of recoupment of election expenses on persons who violate the Public Officials Election Act; however, since there is no difference whatsoever between elected persons and unsuccessful candidates in the possibility of harming the fairness of elections by committing election crimes, sanctions should be imposed on both in equal terms. Nevertheless, the statutory provision at issue, by providing that only elected persons must return the election deposit and election expenses already returned or reimbursed, discriminates between elected persons and unsuccessful candidates without a rational basis.  \\nb. Even if a citizen lacking sufficient financial means is elected in a public election, he/she will be reluctant to run in a public election, taking into account the burden of large election expenses that may arise when the election is later invalidated due to a trivial election crime; thus, the statutory provision at issue infringes the essential content of the right to participate in politics and the right to hold public office, and makes the principle of public election administration and the principle that election expenses shall be borne by the State treasury nominal. And the statutory provision at issue not only lacks a legitimate legislative purpose, but also, by imposing the burden of uniformly returning the large election deposit and election expenses without consideration of specific circumstances, fails to satisfy the requirements of minimal infringement and balance of legal interests; accordingly, it constitutes an infringement of fundamental rights in violation of the principle of prohibition against excessive restriction.  \\nc. The legal character of the return of election deposit and election expenses under the statutory provision at issue should be deemed to correspond to an accessory punishment such as forfeiture or collection for ordinary crimes; however, since it targets as objects of forfeiture property benefits unrelated directly to election crimes, and sets as requirements the ex post and accidental matters of whether one was elected and the judge’s sentencing in the criminal case, it violates the principle of culpability and the principle of prohibition against excessive restriction with respect to punishment.\\n\\n3. Judgment  \\na. Legislative Purpose and Legislative History of the Statutory Provision at Issue  \\nThe statutory provision at issue is a provision newly added in the Public Officials Election and Election Malpractice Prevention Act amended by Act No. 7189 on 2004. 3. 12., in that, where a person elected in a public election receives a conviction of a fine of at least 1,000,000 won due to an election crime, etc., and his/her election becomes invalid, he/she must again return the election deposit and election expenses already returned or reimbursed; it was enacted for the purpose of suppressing election crimes and establishing a fair election culture by imposing a strong sanction on elected persons who commit election crimes of a certain degree or more.\\n\\nThereafter, in the Public Officials Election Act amended by Act No. 7681 on 2005. 8. 4., it was amended to add a provision expressly stating that a person who resigns after indictment and before a final judgment becomes final is included in “a person whose election has become invalid,” and then, after the petitioner’s election had become invalid, it was again amended in the Public Officials Election Act amended by Act No. 9974 on 2010. 1. 25. to include, as subjects of sanction, not only elected persons but also persons who were not elected, where they receive a sentence corresponding to invalidation of election.\\n\\nb. Whether Fundamental Rights Have Been Infringed  \\n(1) Fundamental Rights at Issue  \\n(a) The right to participate in politics is a concept encompassing the right to vote in a referendum, which is the direct right to participate in politics whereby citizens directly participate in the formation of the will of the State (Constitution Articles 72 and 130), and the right to elect public officials (Constitution Article 24) and the right to hold public office (Constitution Article 25), which are indirect rights to participate in politics whereby citizens indirectly participate in the formation of State organs or may be appointed as members of State organs (see Constitutional Court 2001. 6. 28. 2000HEONMA735, Case Reports 13-1, 1431, 1439). The content of the infringement of the right to participate in politics alleged by the petitioner is that it makes citizens lacking sufficient financial means reluctant to run in public elections, which is unrelated to the right to vote in a referendum or the right to elect public officials; therefore, it is unnecessary to determine, separately from the right to hold public office, whether the right to participate in politics has been infringed.  \\nThe right to hold public office is the right of citizens to be guaranteed equal opportunities concerning holding public office, and its protected sphere includes prohibiting arbitrary exclusion from opportunities to assume public office and unjust deprivation of public official status (see Constitutional Court 2002. 8. 29. 2001HEONMA788 et al., Case Reports 14-2, 219, 224). Upon review, the sanction prescribed in the statutory provision at issue targets a person who has already run in an election and been elected, that is, a person who has already been guaranteed an opportunity to assume public office, and thus cannot be viewed as containing a provision excluding an opportunity to assume public office; nor can the content of the sanction be said to constitute a provision concerning the unjust deprivation of public official status, since it consists solely of the imposition of a monetary disadvantage. Therefore, it does not prescribe a matter falling within the protected sphere of the right to hold public office. And because the statutory provision at issue targets only elected persons who committed election crimes and were sentenced to a fine of at least 1,000,000 won, most candidates who seek to conduct elections without committing election crimes are not capable of being included among the subjects of sanction; accordingly, it cannot be said, as the petitioner alleges, to have the effect of making it difficult for citizens lacking sufficient financial means to stand as candidates. Therefore, the right to hold public office cannot be said to be restricted by the statutory provision at issue.  \\n(b) The statutory provision at issue imposes on a person who was elected in a public election and who has had all of the election deposit and election expenses returned or reimbursed an obligation to return those amounts, which had become his/her property; thus, it constitutes a case in which property rights are restricted. Therefore, the issue is whether it infringes property rights in violation of the principle of prohibition against excessive restriction.  \\n(c) As the statutory provision at issue limits the subjects of sanction to elected persons, even if both elected persons and unsuccessful candidates receive final judgments imposing fines of at least 1,000,000 won due to election crimes, the unsuccessful candidates do not bear the obligation to return the returned or reimbursed election deposit and election expenses, whereas elected persons do bear that obligation. Therefore, the issue is whether the right to equality of elected persons is infringed.\\n\\n(2) Whether Property Rights Are Infringed  \\n(a) Legitimacy of the Legislative Purpose and Suitability of the Means  \\nThe election system under our Constitution, based on the principle of popular sovereignty and parliamentary democracy, is an indispensable means for realizing democracy that supports and guarantees the legitimacy of all power. Therefore, while acts of citizens’ participation in the electoral process must be guaranteed to the greatest extent possible, it is necessary, for election offenders who have harmed the fairness of elections, to block the possibility of corrupt elections by imposing certain sanctions in order to fairly guarantee the exercise of the right to participate in politics, which is the process by which the sovereign people form and express political will (see Constitutional Court 2008. 1. 17. 2004HEONMA41, Case Reports 20-1, 98, 103-104). Accordingly, the statutory provision at issue, which seeks to suppress election crimes and establish a fair election culture by imposing a strong sanction on elected persons who have committed election crimes of a certain degree or more, has a legitimate legislative purpose.\\n\\nAnd imposing an economic sanction on elected persons who have been sentenced to a fine of at least a certain degree for election crimes, requiring them to return the election deposit and election expenses already returned or reimbursed, may be an appropriate means to achieve the legislative purpose of suppressing election crimes.\\n\\n(b) Minimum Infringement  \\n1) Imposing certain disadvantages on persons who have committed election crimes and received criminal punishment is a legal measure to secure the fairness of elections, and in such a case, it is fundamentally a matter for the legislature to decide what kind and degree of disadvantage should be imposed on a person convicted of which specific crime and to what extent (see Constitutional Court 2009. 3. 26. 2008HEONMA99, Official Gazette 150, 774, 776). Accordingly, the statutory provision at issue, which separately imposes economic sanctions in addition to criminal punishment and invalidation of election on election offenders who have committed acts such as providing false information during the election process and thereby may distort the free will of the people, and which prescribes the content of those sanctions, pertains to a domain within the legislative discretion of the legislature; therefore, unless its content is deemed to exceed the limits of such legislative discretion, it cannot be said to violate the Constitution.\\n\\n2) The amount of the fine that the statutory provision at issue uses as the standard for sanctions is at least 1,000,000 won. This was set as a strict standard based on the judgment that, in order to change the election climate of excess, corruption, and illegality that has been pointed out in our election history and to establish a fair election culture, it is necessary to strengthen sanctions against election malpractice and corruption. And the standard of a fine of at least 1,000,000 won does not refer to the statutory penalty or the punishment that may be imposed, but to the sentence actually handed down by the court, reflecting the sentencing factors set forth in Article 51 of the Criminal Act; thus, it leaves room for trivial and minor election crimes, as well as cases of election offenders with specific and individual circumstances warranting reflection in sentencing, to fall outside the subjects of sanction.\\n\\n3) The content of the sanction prescribed in the statutory provision at issue is the return of the full amount of the returned election deposit and reimbursed election expenses. Where some of the candidates in a public election commit election crimes exceeding a certain degree, this causes serious consequences that distort the people’s political will manifested in the relevant election; moreover, where the election offender is the elected person, it renders the election already conducted useless and causes additional election expenses for a by-election, and thus a severe sanction needs to be imposed; based on this consideration, a heavy sanction is prescribed. As the petitioner argues, it may be a less restrictive method to set different ranges of the amount to be returned depending on specific circumstances such as the content and impact of the election crime; however, there is no method of calculating the actual effect that a specific election crime had on the vote share of the candidates, and even if such calculation were possible, no objective standard could be set for how much should be returned in each case, so individualization of sanctions is impossible. And, as noted above, cases of trivial and minor election offenders are provided for so that they may fall outside the subjects of sanction through the court’s sentencing determination, and thus it cannot be said that specific circumstances are not considered at all.\\n\\n4) Considering the above circumstances comprehensively, the standard or content of the sanction prescribed in the statutory provision at issue is not excessive to such a degree that it exceeds the scope of the legislative discretion; therefore, it cannot be said to run counter to the principle of minimum infringement.\\n\\n(c) Balance of Legal Interests  \\nAlthough the property rights of election offenders are partially restricted by the statutory provision at issue, the public interest in securing the fairness of elections that is to be achieved through such restriction is greater than the disadvantage of being subjected to a property sanction due to the election offender’s own fault; therefore, the balance of legal interests is also recognized.\\n\\n(d) Sub-conclusion  \\nAccordingly, the statutory provision at issue cannot be said to infringe the petitioner’s property rights in violation of the principle of prohibition against excessive restriction (the petitioner also argued that the provision infringes the essential content of the right to hold public office; however, insofar as it has already been determined above that the statutory provision at issue does not restrict the right to hold public office, the above argument will not be addressed).\\n\\n(3) Whether the Right to Equality Has Been Infringed  \\n(a) Comparison Group and Standard of Review  \\nThe statutory provision at issue is a provision imposing a sanction requiring an elected person who has received a sentence corresponding to invalidation of election to return the election deposit and election expenses already returned or reimbursed, for the purpose of securing the fairness of elections. In light of the meaning and purpose of the statutory provision at issue of imposing sanctions on election offenders in order to secure the fairness of elections, an unsuccessful candidate who received a return of the election deposit and reimbursement of election expenses after obtaining votes at or above the legal vote threshold and who then received a sentence corresponding to invalidation of election is also, in essence, in the same relationship as the elected person who is the subject of sanction under the statutory provision at issue, and thus shall constitute a comparison group. And because the discriminatory treatment under the statutory provision at issue does not correspond to a case where the Constitution especially requires equality or a case where the discriminatory treatment causes serious restrictions on the relevant fundamental rights, the review shall be a relaxed one under the principle of prohibition against arbitrariness.\\n\\nAccordingly, we examine whether the sanction under the statutory provision at issue, which treats unsuccessful candidates and elected persons belonging to the same comparison group differently, constitutes arbitrary discriminatory treatment.\\n\\n(b) Whether It Constitutes Arbitrary Discriminatory Treatment  \\nElections are a forum in which diverse political will of the people is expressed, and a person who runs as a candidate in them contributes to the formation and transmission of political will. However, as can be seen from the very definition of election campaigning as acts undertaken to cause a person to be elected or not elected, it is undeniable that, basically, all candidates participating in elections do so for the purpose of being elected, and in the election process, they engage only in activities that help realize that purpose. Therefore, even if, in establishing some sanction related to elections, only elected persons are designated as its subjects, all candidates who have continuously endeavored to be elected during the election process and who have been considering the possibility that they themselves would become elected persons will naturally accept this as a sanction against themselves; thus, it operates as an effective coercive means to prevent all candidates from engaging in the conduct subject to the sanction. In other words, even if it is discrimination based on subjective reasons, there may be cases where establishing a provision that discriminates against elected persons in elections can be evaluated as not arbitrary, unlike other cases of discriminatory treatment based on subjective reasons.\\n\\nIf unsuccessful candidates are also set as subjects of sanction under the statutory provision at issue, the State would be able to recoup more election expenses; however, as noted above, the statutory provision at issue is not a provision aimed at recouping election expenses, but a provision aimed at suppressing election crimes in order to secure the fairness of elections, and in terms of the effect for achieving such purpose, there is no difference between including unsuccessful candidates among the subjects of sanction and limiting the subjects of sanction to elected persons. Where there are two methods having the same effect in terms of achieving the legislative purpose, the legislature is free to choose one of them, and such legislative choice cannot be said to be arbitrary on grounds other than the legislative purpose.\\n\\n(c) Sub-conclusion  \\nAccordingly, the statutory provision at issue cannot be said to infringe the petitioner’s right to equality by arbitrarily discriminating against elected persons.\\n\\nc. Whether It Violates the Principle of Public Election Administration  \\n(1) Meaning of the Principle of Public Election Administration  \\nThe principle of public election administration is the principle that the costs necessary for the management and operation of elections should not be borne by individual candidates but should instead be borne equitably by all citizens, in consideration of the fact that the election itself is an act of electing representatives of the people who will perform public duties of the State, so it is desirable for the State to bear, in principle, the expenses required therefor, and that making individuals bear all election expenses may make the candidacy of those who are not financially well-off difficult or impossible and may result in an unjust restriction of the people’s right to hold public office. Meanwhile, the content of the principle of public election administration is a matter to be determined by the legislature through policy decisions, comprehensively considering various factors such as our election culture and climate, political culture, the State’s fiscal situation, and the people’s legal sentiment, and therefore it is a domain in which broad legislative discretion is recognized (see Constitutional Court 2010. 5. 27. 2008HEONMA491, Case Reports 22-1, 300, 310-311).\\n\\nThe statutory provision at issue establishes a case in which reimbursed election expenses must be returned again, thereby, in substance, setting a standard for not reimbursing election expenses; thus, even though broad legislative discretion is recognized in this area, if the standard and content are evaluated as arbitrary beyond the scope of legislative discretion, it may be viewed as violating the principle of public election administration, and so we examine it.\\n\\n(2) Whether It Violates  \\nSince the election deposit does not fall within election expenses (Public Officials Election Act Article 119), whether the principle of public election administration is violated shall be determined only with respect to the part that requires the return of reimbursed election expenses.\\n\\nFirst, the principle of public election administration is based on the consideration that elections are public duties of the State and that it may restrict the candidacy of citizens who are not financially well-off. However, the subjects of sanction under the statutory provision at issue are those who have already committed election crimes and thereby engaged in conduct that hinders the State’s public duty of conducting elections, and even if sanctions are imposed on them, it cannot be said that this has the effect of making candidacy difficult for citizens lacking financial means; in this respect, not reimbursing election expenses to them cannot be said to run counter to the purpose of the principle of public election administration.\\n\\nAnd if election expenses are uniformly reimbursed without taking measures to exclude persons who have committed election crimes of a certain degree or more, it is necessary to consider that, under our election culture, there may arise candidates who, near the end of an election, may be tempted to commit an election crime and surpass the benchmark vote ratio by which reimbursement is obtained, in order to reduce at least their economic losses even if they have no possibility of being elected. In addition, from the perspective of the State’s fiscal burden, especially in the case of an elected person, his/her election being invalidated results in the election being conducted again, thereby causing the State to spend election expenses twice; therefore, there is also a need to take measures to reduce the fiscal burden expended in the earlier election that has thereby become useless.\\n\\nFurthermore, the statutory provision at issue, by appropriately limiting the subjects of sanction so that trivial and minor election crimes, as well as election offenders with specific and individual circumstances warranting reflection in sentencing, may fall outside the subjects of sanction, provides for application only to some serious election offenders.\\n\\nConsidering these circumstances comprehensively, the statutory provision at issue, by setting limited exceptions in consideration of the election culture and climate and the State’s fiscal situation within a range that does not run counter to the purpose of the principle of public election administration, cannot be said to be arbitrary beyond the scope of legislative discretion concerning the principle of public election administration (the petitioner also argues, separate from the claim of violation of the principle of public election administration, that the principle that election expenses shall be borne by the national treasury has been violated; however, since the principle that election expenses shall be borne by the national treasury is included in the content of the principle of public election administration and cannot be said to be a constitutional principle separate from the principle of public election administration, it will not be separately addressed).\\n\\nd. Whether It Violates the Principle of Culpability with Respect to Punishment  \\nThe principle of culpability with respect to punishment, that “punishment may not be imposed on one without culpability,” is a basic principle of criminal law, an inherent principle in the constitutional principle of the rule of law as a state, and a principle derived from the purport of Article 10 of the Constitution; and the principle of proportionality between culpability and punishment, that punishment may not exceed the degree of culpability, is derived from Article 37(2) of the Constitution, which prescribes the principle of prohibition against excessive restriction (see Constitutional Court 2010. 7. 29. 2008HEONBA88, Official Gazette 166, 1383, 1387).\\n\\nThe petitioner, by registering as a candidate in the election for Superintendent of Education of Seoul Metropolitan City and submitting a property report, was sentenced to a punishment corresponding to invalidation of election based on the criminal fact of making a false public statement concerning the property of the petitioner’s spouse, and thus became subject to the sanction under the statutory provision at issue; accordingly, as a person punished for his/her own breach of duty, he/she cannot be said to fall under “one without culpability.” And the principle of proportionality between culpability and punishment is a principle applicable when imposing punishment corresponding to the exercise of the State’s punitive power; however, the statutory provision at issue separately prescribes the requirements or subjects of sanction differently from criminal-law forfeiture or collection, so it cannot be said that this is included in punishment. Moreover, as already examined above in the parts concerning the principle of prohibition against excessive restriction and the right to equality, it cannot be said to violate the constitutional principle of proportionality or the principle of equality.\\n\\n4. Conclusion  \\nAccordingly, since the statutory provision at issue does not violate the Constitution, it is so decided as stated in the order. In this decision, all participating justices were in agreement, except for the dissenting opinion of Justice Cho Dae-hyun concerning the part requiring the return, again, of the returned election deposit, as set forth in 6. below, and there is the supplemental opinion of Justice Lee Dong-heub, as set forth in 5. below, concerning the majority opinion on that part.\\n\\n5. Supplemental Opinion of Justice Lee Dong-heub Concerning the Part Requiring the Return Again of the Returned Election Deposit  \\na. I agree with the majority opinion that the part of the statutory provision at issue requiring the return again of the returned election deposit does not exceed the scope of the legislature’s discretion in imposing sanctions and therefore cannot be viewed as violating the principle of prohibition against excessive restriction. However, this merely means that the legislature may impose on election offenders a sanction corresponding to the amount of the election deposit; it does not mean that such a sanction, which may even undermine the purpose or nature of the election deposit system, is proper. Rather, I think it is desirable to improve it through legislation, and therefore I would like to state my opinion on this point additionally.\\n\\nb. Our Court has held that the election deposit system is a system intended to promote the efficiency of election administration by suppressing a proliferation of candidates, while at the same time securing in advance the amount of administrative fines or substitute execution costs (see Constitutional Court 2003. 8. 21. 2001HEONMA687 et al., Case Reports 15-2, 214, 222). And the Public Officials Election Act also provides that election deposits, except when they are forfeited to the national treasury if the election result falls below a certain vote ratio, may be used only as administrative fines under Article 261 of the Public Officials Election Act and substitute execution costs under Article 271 (Public Officials Election Act Article 56(3)); thus, the purpose of the system established by the legislature may also be viewed as the same. In light of the purpose of this election deposit system, forfeiting the election deposit for the purpose of achieving fair elections through the prevention of election crimes goes beyond the original purpose of the system, which has been accepted thus far. Not only that, under the statutory provision at issue, the election deposit system acquires a new meaning as a system in which, based on the foreseeability that candidates in public elections may commit election crimes, a sanction money for election crimes is paid in advance as a condition of candidacy. Such new meaning of the election deposit system changes the factual basis of the precedents of our Court that held the election deposit system to be constitutional on the basis that it is a system rooted in the need to prevent a proliferation of candidates; therefore, it may be difficult to maintain the conclusion that the election deposit system is constitutional on the same grounds as before.\\n\\nc. Even when compared with the reimbursement of election expenses, which the statutory provision at issue also sets as a subject of return together with the election deposit, there is no need to regulate them identically, because there are the following differences in nature. First, reimbursement of election expenses is the State’s reimbursement of costs used by a candidate during the election period, and thus the reimbursing funds are from the national treasury. By contrast, the return of the election deposit is the candidate’s taking back money that he/she deposited from his/her own funds, unless there is a special reason such as insufficient votes; thus, the returning funds are money paid by the candidate. Therefore, there is room to view the degree of discretion in setting the reason why the State does not reimburse or return them as subject to different standards. Also, even if an elected person becomes a subject of sanction and a by-election is held, the reimbursement amount of election expenses inevitably has to be spent twice as two elections are conducted, whereas candidates running in a by-election also pay an election deposit, so there is no concern whatsoever that the amount of the returned election deposit will be spent twice.\\n\\nd. Among election-related statutes of major countries in the world, there are indeed cases in which monetary sanctions separate from punishment are provided for persons who commit election crimes; however, even in those countries, only funds subsidized or reimbursed by the State are designated as the target of regulation, and no legislative example can be found that designates as the target of sanction the election deposit paid by the candidate himself/herself.\\n\\ne. As reviewed above, there is a problem, in terms of the purpose or nature of the election deposit system, with setting it as a sanction for election crimes. This becomes all the more so when one considers that the legislature can devise any number of alternative sanction measures for the prevention of election crimes without impairing the purpose of the election deposit system. In a case such as this, where the issue is whether the sanction itself established by the legislature is excessive, its constitutionality may be acknowledged; however, if a case arises in which the question is whether it is proper to collect in advance from all public-election candidates, before any unlawful act occurs, an election deposit that also has the character of a sanction money for future possible unlawful acts under the statutory provision at issue, there is a possibility that our Court may reach a different conclusion from its prior precedents concerning the election deposit system. Accordingly, the part of the statutory provision at issue requiring the return again of the returned election deposit should be improved by legislation in a direction that preserves the purpose and nature of the election deposit system.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Cho Dae-hyun Concerning the Part Requiring the Return Again of the Returned Election Deposit  \\nAlthough the election expenses portion of the statutory provision at issue cannot be viewed as violating the Constitution, as in the majority opinion, I think the election deposit portion violates the Constitution.\\n\\nI think that the system requiring payment of an election deposit in order to register as a candidate in a public election violates the Constitution. The reason is that, as stated in the dissenting opinion in the Constitutional Court Decision rendered on 2008. 11. 27. in 2007HEONMA1024, it restricts the right to hold public office and the freedom of political expression of public office candidates without the grounds for restricting fundamental rights required by Article 37(2) of the Constitution.\\n\\nSince the public election deposit system violates the Constitution, it cannot but be viewed that the election deposit portion of the statutory provision at issue, which does not return the election deposit or recovers the election deposit already returned in the event that a public office candidate’s election becomes invalid, also violates the Constitution."}

{"[2017HEONBA208]": "1. Case Outline\\n\\na. On 1990. 4. 20., the Petitioner received by gift from his father Cha□□ a forest land of 8,926 square meters in XX City (address omitted) (hereinafter, the “forest land at issue”), and completed the registration of transfer of ownership relating thereto on 1990. 4. 28. On the forest land at issue, a joint grave of Hwang XX of the late Joseon period and his wife, a lady of the Yeosan Song clan (hereinafter, the “grave at issue”), had been installed and thereafter had been managed by the descendants of Hwang XX, until around 1957 when the father of Hwang □□ began to manage it, and thereafter Hwang □□ continued to manage it. The grave at issue was also designated as the historical and cultural heritage of XX.\\n\\nb. The Petitioner, with respect to 11 graves, including the grave at issue existing on the forest land at issue, gave public notice of exhumation of unclaimed graves pursuant to Article 27 of the “Act on Funeral Services, Burials, etc.” (hereinafter, the “Funeral Services Act”), and on 2014. 6. 25. applied for permission to exhume graves on the ground that no person connected with the said graves could be found. After receiving such permission, the Petitioner exhumed the grave at issue on 2014. 7. 7., cremated the remains, and placed the ashes in an ossuary at the Incorporated Foundation □□ in Muju, Jeonbuk.\\n\\nc. Thereupon, Hwang □□ filed an action against the Petitioner seeking damages on 2014. 9. 30. (Seoul Central District Court 2014GADAN5272181), and the court rendered a judgment on 2015. 11. 13. that Hwang □□ had acquired a customary grave-site right with respect to the 254 square meters portion of the forest land at issue, and that the Petitioner’s exhumation of the grave at issue constituted a tort; accordingly, the court sentenced the Petitioner to pay damages to Hwang □□ in the aggregate amount of KRW 15.8 million, consisting of KRW 10.8 million for restoration costs and KRW 5 million for solatium.\\n\\nd. The Petitioner appealed against the above judgment, but the appeal was dismissed on 2016. 6. 10. (Seoul Central District Court 2015NA66600). Thereupon, the Petitioner filed an appeal to the Supreme Court, and while the appeal was pending, applied for a referral for constitutional review concerning the customary law on acquisitive prescription of a customary grave-site right. However, the Supreme Court dismissed the application on 2017. 3. 30. (Supreme Court 2017KAGI1003) and dismissed the appeal on the same day (Supreme Court 2016DA231358). Accordingly, the Petitioner filed the constitutional complaint at issue on 2017. 5. 2. seeking a declaration that the customary law at issue is unconstitutional.\\n\\n2. Subject of Review\\n\\nThe subject of review in this case is whether the following parts of the customary law concerning a grave-site right, namely, “where a grave has been installed on land owned by another without the owner’s consent, if the site of that grave has been possessed peacefully and openly for 20 years, the grave-site right, a customary property right similar to a superficies, is acquired by prescription, and such right may be asserted against a third party without registration,” and “unless there are special circumstances such as an agreement between the parties regarding the duration of the grave-site right, the grave-site right continues to exist for so long as the beneficiary continues to protect and tend the grave, that is, for so long as the grave continues to exist” (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “customary law at issue”), are in violation of the Constitution.\\n\\n[Relevant Provisions]\\nFormer Act on Funeral Services, Burials, etc. (as wholly amended by Act No. 6158 on 2000. 1. 12. and before its wholly amendment by Act No. 8489 on 2007. 5. 25.)\\nArticle 17 (Period of Grave Installation) (1) The period of installation of graves in public cemeteries under Article 12 and private cemeteries under Article 13 shall be 15 years.\\nArticle 23 (Handling, etc. of Graves Installed on Another Person’s Land, etc.) (1) The landowner (including a possessor or other manager; the same shall apply hereinafter in this Article), cemetery installer, or person with a connection to the grave may, with permission from the mayor, county governor, or district head having jurisdiction over the grave, exhume the corpse or remains buried in any grave falling under any of the following subparagraphs.\\n1. A grave installed on the land without the consent of the landowner\\n(3) The person with a connection to the grave of any grave falling under any subparagraph of paragraph (1) may not assert against the landowner, cemetery installer, or person with a connection to the grave any right to use the land or any other right for the preservation of the grave.\\nSupplementary Provisions of the Act on Funeral Services, Burials, etc. (Act No. 6158 on 2000. 1. 12.)\\nArticle 2 (Application) The amended provisions of Article 17 and Article 23(3) shall apply to graves first installed after the enforcement of this Act.\\n\\n3. Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\nThe customary law at issue, even where a grave is installed without the consent of the landowner, recognizes the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right similar to a superficies merely on the ground that the site of such grave has been possessed peacefully and openly for 20 years, and recognizes the continued existence of the grave-site right so long as the protection and tending of the grave continue; accordingly, it is no different from recognizing a de facto permanent and gratuitous grave-site right without any compensation even in the case of bad-faith unauthorized possession. Therefore, such customary law infringes the landowner’s property right in its essence and is contrary to the Constitution.\\n\\n4. Determination\\n\\na. Whether the customary law at issue is subject to a constitutional complaint\\n\\nCustomary law is a social norm of life created by repeated social practice, which has come to be approved as a legal norm and enforced according to society’s legal conviction and recognition, and thereby functions as a source of law. The Court has repeatedly confirmed that customs concerning the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right and the duration of the grave-site right, which are the subject of review in this case, have been established and exist as customary law in our society, and has applied them as a norm for adjudication (see Supreme Court Decision 4290MINSANG539, rendered on 1957. 10. 31.; Supreme Court Decision 81DA1220, rendered on 1982. 1. 26.; Supreme Court Decision 96DA14036, rendered on 1996. 6. 14.; Supreme Court Decision 2005DA44114, rendered on 2007. 6. 28., etc.). Thus, although the customary law at issue is not a statute in the formal sense, it has in substance the same effect as a statute.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 111(1)(1) and (5) of the Constitution and Article 41(1) and Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act provide that the object of a constitutional review is a “statute,” and here the term “statute” includes not only a statute in the formal sense enacted by resolution of the National Assembly, but also treaties, etc. having the same effect as a statute. By making treaties, etc. that have the same effect as a statute the object of constitutional review in this manner, it is possible not only to secure the unity of the legal order and legal stability with the Constitution as the supreme norm, but also to enable adjudication in conformity with the Constitution and thereby contribute to guaranteeing the people’s fundamental rights. If so, the customary law at issue, which has the same effect as a statute, is also subject to constitutional complaint review, and cannot be excluded merely because it is not a statute in the formal sense (see Constitutional Court 2009HEONBA129, Feb. 28, 2013; Constitutional Court 2013HEONBA396, etc., Apr. 28, 2016).\\n\\nb. Issues and standard of review\\n\\nWhere a grave-site right is established and continues to exist pursuant to the customary law at issue, the owner of the relevant land is inevitably restricted from exercising ownership over the portion of the land that has become the site of the grave, within a reasonable scope necessary for the protection and management of the grave. Accordingly, the question is whether the customary law at issue violates the principle against excessive restriction and thereby infringes the landowner’s property right.\\n\\nSince the customary law at issue regulates the land-use relationship for the protection and tending of graves and adjusts the interests between the landowner and the holder of the grave-site right, the guarantee of private property rights under the first sentence of Article 23(1) of the Constitution and the social limitation of property rights under Article 23(2) must be balanced.\\n\\nIn judging whether the customary law at issue infringes property rights, however, the historical background before and after the establishment of the customary law, the role it has performed as customary law, and the characteristics of land that is the object of property rights must be considered.\\n\\nFirst, the customary law at issue acquired legal status as a custom that had long permitted the installation of graves on forest land even before the individual ownership of forest land was recognized, and it is necessary to consider that it has performed the role of adjusting the conflicting interests between, on the one hand, the grave installer under the custom that existed historically first and, on the other hand, the forest land owner under the ownership system of forest land that emerged with the formation of the modern concept of ownership.\\n\\nNext, the social relationship and social function of land (forest land), which is the object of property rights, must be considered. Forest land is limited in supply and has a relatively short history of being the object of private ownership, whereas the demand for forest land for installing graves was large and the history of not objecting to the installation of graves on any forest land was relatively long. In addition, although the influence of burial culture and the spirit of ancestor worship related to graves have considerably declined, they still remain. Taking these points together, one can see that forest land on which graves are installed is property whose use or disposition, beyond the individual owner’s personal sphere of life, has a considerable degree of social relationship and social function.\\n\\nAlso, Article 9 of the Constitution provides that “the State shall endeavor to inherit and develop traditional culture and to foster national culture,” and our traditional filial piety and ancestor-worship ideology are protected as traditional culture under Article 9 of the Constitution. Therefore, in examining the constitutionality of the customary law at issue, it is also necessary appropriately to take into account the interests of our community that have long been maintained and protected through such traditional culture.\\n\\nTaking the above points together, the review of whether the customary law at issue infringes the property right of the landowner should be conducted under a relaxed standard of review.\\n\\nc. Whether the customary law at issue infringes the property right of the landowner\\n\\n(1) Legitimacy of purpose and appropriateness of means\\n\\nThe customary law at issue is intended to respect traditional ideas concerning burial culture and to remedy evidentiary difficulties and promote legal stability surrounding the installation of graves and the use relationship of the land serving as their site, and such purpose is legitimate. Recognizing the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right where a grave has been installed on land owned by another and the site of the grave has been possessed peacefully and openly for 20 years, and recognizing the continued existence of the grave-site right so long as the protection and tending of the grave continue, are means appropriate to achieve the foregoing purpose.\\n\\n(2) Minimum impairment\\n\\n(a) Continued existence of burial culture and the need to protect graves\\n\\nAlthough the influence of Confucian thought has declined today, and some changes have occurred in social members’ perceptions of traditional funeral methods and burial culture due to frequent relocation of living bases, development of transportation, increased use of funeral service businesses, and an increased cremation rate, the burial culture that formed the basis of the grave-site right still remains rooted in our society, the installation of private cemeteries is permitted, and social members’ legal conviction regarding the customary law at issue also remains (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2013DA17292, rendered on 2017. 1. 19.). The current Funeral Services Act also reflects these points by treating burial as one method of funeral practice and regulating burial and graves. Even where a grave has been installed on another’s land, there still exists the need to protect the land-use right necessary for the protection and tending of such grave according to the customary law at issue.\\n\\nIt is true that, as the economic value of forest land has recently increased, the losses suffered by landowners due to their inability to use and derive profit from such land have also increased. However, if the period for installing graves were limited and relocation of graves were compelled merely because the economic value of land with graves has increased due to national development, such as land development, this would inevitably lead not only to the economic loss of bearing the costs by descendants who tend the graves, but also to the loss of the emotional attachment and local bond formed through the grave, and would also run counter to our traditional culture that anyone should respect another person’s grave as a place of dignity and must not casually desecrate it.\\n\\nFrom the landowner’s perspective as well, where a grave has been installed on his land without authorization, he may exercise his rights as owner at any time during the long period of 20 years while the prescriptive period runs, and he may interrupt prescription by, pursuant to Articles 168 through 177 of the Civil Act as applied mutatis mutandis under Article 247(2) of the Civil Act, seeking exhumation of the grave from the grave owner or seeking delivery of the occupied portion. Therefore, it cannot be said that the landowner is inadequately protected under the customary law at issue (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2013DA17292, rendered on 2017. 1. 19.).\\n\\n(b) Requirements for acquisitive prescription in light of the special nature of the grave-site right\\n\\nThe customary law at issue relaxes the requirements for acquisitive prescription compared with the Civil Act’s system of acquisitive prescription of possession, which requires “possession as a superficies holder,” by not making “possession as a grave-site right holder” a requirement. As a result, in the case of a superficies under the Civil Act, to have acquisitive prescription recognized, the person asserting acquisitive prescription must prove that he has possessed the relevant land with the intention to establish a superficies (see Supreme Court Decision 96DA7984, rendered on 1996. 12. 23.); under the customary law at issue, however, such proof is not necessary, and consequently it is true that acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right is more easily recognized.\\n\\nHowever, once customary law is recognized as a source of law, it is natural that its content may differ from positive law and interpretations thereof. A grave-site right is established only where land is possessed and used for the special purpose of a grave, and the existence of the grave can easily be ascertained from its special form. Thus, it is also distinguished from other forms of acquisitive prescription of property rights. If possession as a grave-site right holder were made a requirement for the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right, and if, in cases where a person knowingly and without permission installs a grave on land owned by another despite full awareness that the owner’s consent has not been obtained, such possession were deemed not to constitute possession as a grave-site right holder and acquisitive prescription of the grave-site right were not allowed, this would in substance be no different from not allowing acquisitive prescription of the grave-site right at all.\\n\\nIn addition to the above characteristics of a grave-site right, in order to acquire a grave-site right by prescription, “peaceful” possession without employing violence that cannot be legally tolerated and “open” possession that is not clandestine are required; thus, where a grave has been installed by a method that is utterly impermissible in law, acquisitive prescription of the grave-site right may be excluded. In light of this, it is difficult to say that unfair or inequitable results arise merely because “possession as a grave-site right holder” is not made a requirement for the acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right.\\n\\n(c) Limited scope of restriction on property rights\\n\\nEven where a grave-site right is acquired by prescription, the grave-site right is recognized only within a reasonable scope necessary for the protection and management of the grave, and if the protection and tending of the grave are discontinued or the grave no longer exists, the grave-site right also extinguishes. In addition, since the Funeral Services Act, wholly amended by Act No. 6158 on 2000. 1. 12., denied acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right only from graves installed after 2001. 1. 13., its effective date (Article 23(3) and Supplementary Provisions Article 2), the Funeral Services Act has consistently not recognized acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right with respect to graves installed after that date. In light of this, the restriction on the landowner’s property right arising from acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right is appropriately limited in scope.\\n\\nOf course, where a grave-site right is acquired by prescription, it is construed in principle that the holder of the grave-site right has no obligation to pay ground rent (see Supreme Court Decision 94DA37912, rendered on 1995. 2. 28.), and the customary law at issue provides that the duration of a grave-site right acquired by prescription shall not be governed by the provisions of the Civil Act concerning superficies, but shall follow any agreement between the parties or other special circumstances, and, in the absence of such circumstances, the grave-site right shall continue to exist so long as the beneficiary continues to protect and tend the grave and the grave continues to exist. Thus, the landowner’s property right may be restricted to that extent more.\\n\\nHowever, if, simply because the landowner’s property right is restricted, a certain ground rent and duration were recognized for a grave-site right acquired by prescription, then it would become possible to request extinguishment of the grave-site right on the ground of arrears of ground rent or to demand relocation of the grave on the ground of the expiration of the term, and the level of protection afforded to the grave-site right would inevitably recede to that extent. This would complicate the legal relationship surrounding the grave-site right and cause a serious infringement on the economic and emotional interests of the holder of the grave-site right, as well as lead to results contrary to the fine customs and morals of our society, which has treated graves with reverence.\\n\\nTherefore, it cannot be said that the customary law at issue imposes an excessive restriction beyond what is necessary merely because, in the case of a grave-site right acquired by prescription, there is in principle no obligation to pay ground rent or no limitation on the duration of the grave-site right.\\n\\n(3) Balance of interests\\n\\nAlthough, due to the customary law at issue, the landowner is restricted in the right to use and derive profit from part of the land that he owns, the scope of such restriction is limited, as examined above. On the other hand, the grave-site right has been formed and maintained as our custom over a long period of time based on ancestor-worship ideology and filial piety toward parents, and has been consistently maintained through Supreme Court decisions even after the entry into force of the current Civil Act. Accordingly, the public interest in protecting traditional culture and stabilizing the legal order that can be achieved through the customary law at issue is of very great importance. Therefore, the customary law at issue does not violate the balance of interests.\\n\\n(4) Conclusion\\n\\nTaking the above points together, it cannot be said that the customary law at issue violates the principle against excessive restriction and infringes the property right of the landowner.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nSince the customary law at issue does not violate the Constitution, the decision is rendered as stated in the disposition. This decision is based on the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices except for the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Eun-ae and Lee Jong-seok set forth below in 6.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Lee Eun-ae and Lee Jong-seok\\n\\nWe are of the view that the customary law at issue is not subject to a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act, and therefore state our opinion as follows.\\n\\na. The term “statute” that is the object of a constitutional review of statutes upon referral by a court or a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act includes not only so-called statutes in the formal sense enacted by resolution of the National Assembly, but also norms that are not statutes in the formal sense but have the “same effect as a statute in the formal sense,” such as treaties concluded with the consent of the National Assembly and having the same effect as a statute (see Constitutional Court 95HEONBA3, Dec. 28, 1995; Constitutional Court 97HEONGA14, Apr. 29, 1999; Constitutional Court 2000HEONBA20, Sept. 27, 2001; Constitutional Court 2010HEONBA70, etc., Mar. 21, 2013). Whether a norm has the “same effect as a statute in the formal sense” must be determined by whether it has legal effect, regardless of the name or form of the norm (Constitutional Court 2010HEONBA70, etc., Mar. 21, 2013).\\n\\nMeanwhile, in determining whether a norm is one that has the “same effect as a statute in the formal sense” and is therefore subject to constitutional review by the Constitutional Court, the following may be considered: ① the function of a constitutional review of statutes upon referral or a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act lies in controlling abuse of legislative power by the National Assembly and other state organs while, at the same time, respecting the legislative power of the National Assembly and the principle of representative democracy and realizing the spirit of checks and balances among powers demanded by the separation of powers; ② if there is a legal norm that is given the same effect as a statute enacted by the National Assembly under the normative hierarchy by operation of the Constitution, then, to the same degree as respect for the legislative power of the National Assembly, the legislative act of the state organ that enacted that norm should also be respected, so constitutional review by the Constitutional Court is necessary; and ③ in the system of distribution of jurisdiction concerning concrete norm control under the Constitution, it is reasonable to regard the power to control norms that are given the same effect as a statute in the formal sense and perform similar functions as vested in the Constitutional Court, which is specialized in constitutional adjudication, and constitutional decisions by the Constitutional Court are accorded binding force that binds all state organs.\\n\\nCustomary law refers to a social norm of life created by repeated social practice, which has been approved as a legal norm and enforced according to society’s legal conviction and recognition; such customary law has force as law as a source of law so long as it does not conflict with statutes (see Supreme Court Decision 80DA3231, rendered on 1983. 6. 14.). That is, written law may abolish customary law, but customary law cannot abolish written law, and customary law is merely a supplementary source of law only where it does not conflict with written statutes. Article 1 of the Civil Act provides, “In civil matters, if there is no provision in the Act, customary law shall apply, and if there is no customary law, general principles of law shall apply.” In light of the legislative history of the Civil Act and judicial precedents, the term “law” in Article 1 of the Civil Act means written law (statutes, orders, treaties, local regulations, etc.) as the standard or criterion for adjudication when civil relations are governed and disputes are resolved through adjudication, and therefore is not limited to statutes in the formal sense. However, as noted above, it is difficult to regard the effect of customary law as equivalent to that of a statute.\\n\\nAs such, since there is no involvement of the National Assembly whatsoever in the formation of customary law, and customary law cannot be regarded as a norm that has been given the same effect as a statute enacted by the National Assembly by operation of the Constitution, it is also difficult to regard customary law as having the same effect as a statute in the formal sense. Therefore, customary law cannot be the subject of a constitutional review of statutes by the Constitutional Court or a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act.\\n\\nb. The majority opinion of the precedents held that customary law is subject to a constitutional review of statutes by the Constitutional Court or a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act in order to secure the unity of the legal order and legal stability with the Constitution as the supreme norm (see Constitutional Court 2013HEONBA396, etc., Apr. 28, 2016). It is important that, in addition to controlling abuse of legislative power by the National Assembly and other checks and balances among powers, the functions of a constitutional review of statutes or a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act include allowing the Constitutional Court, as the constitutional adjudication body, to exclusively determine whether a norm is unconstitutional and thereby securing the unity of the legal order and legal stability, while comprehensively controlling legal norms having legal effect in concrete legal disputes. However, the special nature of customary law as a norm, including its formation and extinction, must also be considered, and the request for unity of the legal order and legal stability must not be applied uniformly.\\n\\nWhether customary law exists, that is, whether there is continuity and certainty of social practice and whether society has legal conviction that it has binding legal force, requires factual finding as a premise. Moreover, customary law is originally not fixed but continues to evolve and change, so the Court may develop customary law by ascertaining not only the existence of customary law but also changes in customary law. Even if a past social practice had been approved as customary law, if social members gradually cease to have conviction regarding the legal binding force of such practice, the Court has no choice but to deny the effect of such former customary law as a legal norm (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2002DA1178, rendered on 2005. 7. 21., etc.).\\n\\nIn addition, for the Court to declare that a certain social norm of life created by repeated social practice has come to be approved as a customary law, a legal norm, it must be such that it is recognized as having legitimacy and rationality in that it does not conflict with the entire legal order with the Constitution as the supreme norm (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2001DA48781, rendered on 2003. 7. 24., etc.). At this time, since the Court is confirming whether customary law exists as a supplementary source of law, the conformity with the entire legal order with the Constitution as the supreme norm, and legitimacy and rationality, should be judged based on the legal order at the time when the existence of customary law as a source of law is in question.\\n\\nIf, distinguishing this from confirmation of the formation or existence of customary law, unconstitutional review as ex post norm control may arise, that is, if there are cases where legitimacy and rationality were recognized when measured against the legal order corresponding to the period during which customary law continued to exist, but it must separately be determined whether such law conforms to the Constitution under the current Constitution, then the standard of review in concrete norm control exercised by the Constitutional Court is in principle the Constitution that has normative force at the time of constitutional adjudication (see Constitutional Court 2010HEONBA70, etc., Mar. 21, 2013). Hence, there is room to regard it as appropriate and necessary for the Constitutional Court to review the constitutionality.\\n\\nHowever, in ordinary cases other than such cases, since the Court not only discovers customary law and determines whether it has been approved as a legal norm, but also determines whether customary law has legitimacy and rationality as not conflicting with the entire legal order with the Constitution as the supreme norm, it is natural to view that where customary law supported by legal conviction later becomes unconstitutional due to changes in society or changes in the overall legal order, the Court has the authority to confirm the loss of its effect. Considering further that customary law created by repeated social practice has significance in guaranteeing the autonomy of society and private autonomy, and that therefore there is not from the outset a great need for the Constitutional Court to secure the unity of the legal order and legal stability through constitutional review thereof, it is difficult to say that the Constitutional Court needs to conduct constitutional review of customary law in order to secure the unity of the legal order and legal stability with the Constitution as the supreme norm or to comprehensively control legal norms.\\n\\nc. Meanwhile, unlike Germany, where norm control over customary law is possible through a constitutional complaint against a judgment of an ordinary court, Korea does not recognize a constitutional complaint against a court judgment, and thus an argument may be made that the Constitutional Court fulfills its mission of guaranteeing the people’s fundamental rights by declaring unconstitutional customary law unconstitutional. However, considering that courts adopt an appellate structure and, in recognizing normative force in custom, also determine whether the relevant custom conforms to the entire legal order with the Constitution as the supreme norm, thereby engaging in internal norm control, and considering that, once the court has already reviewed whether a custom conforms to the constitutional order in declaring that it has come to be approved as customary law, it is difficult at present to gauge to what extent it is necessary for the Constitutional Court to duplicatively review this from the standpoint of controlling wrongful judicial determinations, namely, the recognition and application of unconstitutional customary law, even if our legal system does not recognize a constitutional complaint against court judgments and thus there is an aspect in which control over court judgments is impossible, this cannot serve as a ground for recognizing customary law as subject to constitutional review.\\n\\nd. We examine the customary law at issue. Unlike the former inheritance customary law, etc., which were abolished by the enactment of the Civil Act, the continuing existence of a grave-site right was recognized by the Supreme Court. Specifically, the Supreme Court held that, although there had been changes in legal regulation concerning cemeteries, including the strengthening of land ownership by providing, in the “Act on Funeral Services, Burials, etc.” that came into force on 2001. 1. 13. after the formation of the customary law at issue, provisions limiting the period for installing graves and denying acquisitive prescription of a grave-site right with respect to graves installed after the enforcement of the Act, there were no clear and significant changes in the overall legal order system, the perceptions and attitudes of social members, or the social and cultural background from before and after the enforcement of that Act through the present, following the recognition of customary law concerning grave-site rights (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2013DA17292, rendered on 2017. 1. 19.). As a result, since the Supreme Court has determined that the customary law concerning grave-site rights has not conflicted with the entire legal order with the Constitution as the supreme norm from the time of its formation through the present, there is no case in which unconstitutional review under the current Constitution is necessary with respect to a past customary law. Moreover, because the customary law at issue is not given the same effect as a statute in the formal sense and is not one for which constitutional review by the Constitutional Court is required for respect for the legislative power of the National Assembly or for separation of powers, there is no reason to make it the subject of a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act.\\n\\ne. Therefore, since the customary law at issue is not subject to a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act, the petition for review in this case must be dismissed as inadmissible."}

question:
Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are true (○) and those that are false (X)? (Where there is controversy, in accordance with case law)

(a) The indiscriminate exercise of audit authority over the autonomous affairs of a local government is highly likely to infringe the constitutionally guaranteed right of local self-government; therefore, as a general rule, even if an illegal fact is discovered during the audit with respect to a matter not specifically designated in advance as the object of the audit, expanding or adding to the audit object is not permitted.

(b) Under the Constitution, the local self-government right of a local government also concerns the distribution and operation of the state governing organization, and insofar as it is authority that takes part in a portion of state power, fundamental and essential matters concerning the organization of a local government, its autonomous functions, and the autonomy of its autonomous affairs must be directly prescribed by statute.

(c) It cannot be said that the constitutionally institutionally guaranteed autonomy includes the authority, in performing autonomous affairs, not to receive orders or instructions concerning expediency from another administrative subject.

(d) The Constitution provides that “matters concerning the method of appointing the head of a local government shall be determined by statute,” but the principle that the head of a local government, who is the representative of the local government, must be elected through an election based on the voluntary support of residents is a principle naturally derived from the essence of the local self-government system.

(e) The Constitution guarantees the ordinance-making power of local governments, and the Local Autonomy Act makes clear that, where there is delegation by an individual statute, it is possible to restrict the rights of residents or impose obligations on residents by ordinance as well; therefore, if there is statutory delegation, an ordinance may also determine matters reserved for legislation.

{"[2014HEONMA797]": "1. Case Summary\\nThe petitioner is a resident living in Nam-gu, Daegu Metropolitan City.
