In the election for the head of Nam-gu District Office, Daegu, among the 6th Nationwide Local Elections held on 2014. 6. 4., only one candidate had registered by the deadline for candidate registration, and thus no voting was conducted and that candidate was determined to be the elected person on the election day. The petitioner filed a constitutional complaint on 2014. 9. 18., alleging that Article 191, paragraph 3, Article 188, paragraphs 2 and 3, and Article 190, paragraph 2 of the Public Official Election Act, which provide for election without voting in elections for the head of a local government, infringe the right to vote, the right to know, the right to equality, and the right to pursue happiness, among others.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\nThe petitioner seeks review of Article 191, paragraph 3, Article 188, paragraphs 2 and 3, and Article 190, paragraph 2 of the Public Official Election Act. In this case, however, what the petitioner seeks to challenge is the part that, where only one candidate has registered by the deadline for candidate registration in an election for the head of a local government, no voting is conducted and that candidate is determined to be the elected person. Accordingly, the provision subject to review is limited to the portion relevant thereto.\\n\\nTherefore, the subject matter of review is whether the application, in Article 191, paragraph 3 of the Public Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 9974 on 2010. 1. 25.), mutatis mutandis of the portion of Article 188, paragraph 2 concerning the case where “there is one constituency National Assembly candidate at the deadline for candidate registration” (hereinafter referred to as the “provision under review”) infringes the petitioner’s fundamental rights, and the contents of the provision under review and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision under Review]\\nPublic Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 9974 on 2010. 1. 25.)\\nArticle 191 (Determination, Public Notice, and Notification of Elected Persons for Heads of Local Governments) (3) The provisions of Article 187, paragraph 4 and Article 188, paragraphs 2 through 6 shall apply mutatis mutandis to the determination of elected persons for heads of local governments.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\nPublic Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 7681 on 2005. 8. 4.) Article 188 (Determination, Public Notice, and Notification of Elected Constituency National Assembly Members)\\n(1) In an election for constituency National Assembly members, the Election Commission of the constituency shall determine as the elected person the person who obtained the majority of valid votes in the relevant National Assembly constituency. Provided, That where there are two or more candidates with the highest number of votes, the older person shall be determined as the elected person.\\n(2) Where there is one constituency National Assembly candidate at the deadline for candidate registration, or where, after the deadline for candidate registration and before the commencement of voting on election day, a constituency National Assembly candidate withdraws, dies, or has his or her registration invalidated, and the number of constituency National Assembly candidates becomes one, no voting shall be conducted for the constituency National Assembly candidate, and that candidate shall be determined as the elected person on the election day.\\n(3) Where, from the commencement of voting time on election day until the closing time of voting, a constituency National Assembly candidate withdraws, dies, or has his or her registration invalidated, and the number of constituency National Assembly candidates becomes one, the remaining voting shall not be conducted and that candidate shall be determined as the elected person.\\n(4) Where, after the closing time of voting on election day and before the determination of the elected person, a constituency National Assembly candidate withdraws, dies, or has his or her registration invalidated, the person who obtained the majority of valid votes as a result of the ballot count shall be determined as the elected person; provided, that if the person who withdrew, died, or had his or her registration invalidated obtained the majority of valid votes, the relevant National Assembly constituency shall be deemed to have no elected person.\\n(5) Where no voting is conducted pursuant to the provisions of paragraphs (2) and (3), the relevant constituency Election Commission shall promptly make public notice thereof and report it to the superior Election Commission, and shall notify the inferior Election Commission.\\n(6) When the elected person for the National Assembly constituency is determined pursuant to the provisions of paragraphs (1) through (4), the chairperson of the relevant constituency Election Commission shall make public notice thereof and promptly deliver the certificate of election to the elected person, and shall report it to the superior Election Commission.\\nPublic Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 9974 on 2010. 1. 25.)\\nArticle 191 (Determination, Public Notice, and Notification of Elected Persons for Heads of Local Governments) (1) In an election for the head of a local government, the Election Commission of the constituency shall determine as the elected person the person who obtained the majority of valid votes, and shall notify the speaker of the relevant local council thereof. Provided, That where there are two or more candidates with the highest number of votes, the older person shall be determined as the elected person.\\n(2) Deleted\\n\\n3. The Petitioner’s Arguments\\nArticle 191, paragraph 3 of the Public Official Election Act infringed the right to vote by not conducting voting at all when only one candidate registered in an election for the head of a local government, and through this it infringed the right to know information about the candidates, and also infringed the right to pursue happiness. In addition, unlike the President, it allowed election without voting in the case of the head of a local government, and thus infringed the people’s right to equality.\\n\\n4. Decision\\nA. Legislative History of the System of Determining an Elected Person Without Voting and the Provision under Review\\n(1) The system of determining an elected person without voting is a system that, rather than adopting the generally used method in elections for selecting representatives of determining as the elected person the person who obtained the highest number of votes in voting, determines the elected person without voting where certain requirements are satisfied. In the legal system concerning public elections, the system of determining an elected person without voting appears to have been first enacted in the National Assembly Members Election Act, amended by Act No. 17 on 1948. 12. 23. At the time, Article 43 of the National Assembly Members Election Act provided, in principle, that the person who obtained the highest number of valid votes shall be the elected person, but stipulated that where there is one registered candidate in the constituency, no voting shall be conducted and that candidate shall be the elected person, thereby providing for election without voting. Thereafter, when the National Assembly Members Election Act was wholly amended by Act No. 4003 on 1988. 3. 17., paragraphs 2 through 4 of Article 132 provided that where there is one constituency National Assembly candidate, voting shall not be conducted and that candidate shall be determined as the elected person on the election day; this method of determining an elected person without voting remained unchanged until the National Assembly Members Election Act was repealed by Act No. 4739 on 1994. 3. 16. In the case of elections for local council members as well, election without voting was recognized through Article 120, paragraph 2 of the Local Council Election Act, enacted by Act No. 4005 on 1988. 4. 6., which provided that where, on the deadline for candidate registration, the number of candidates in the relevant constituency did not exceed the number of seats to be elected, no voting would be conducted. Meanwhile, in the case of elections for heads of local governments, Article 128, paragraph 2 of the “Local Government Head Election Act,” enacted by Act No. 4312 on 1990. 12. 31., provided that where there was one candidate, the number of votes obtained by that single candidate had to reach at least one third of the total number of eligible voters for that candidate to be determined as the elected person; thus, unlike elections for National Assembly members or local council members, election without voting was not recognized.\\n\\n(2) Thereafter, when the integrated election law in the form of the “Act on Public Official Elections and Prevention of Election Frauds,” which combined the former Presidential Election Act, National Assembly Members Election Act, Local Council Election Act, and Local Government Head Election Act, was enacted by Act No. 4739 on 1994. 3. 16., the method of determining elected persons in elections was governed in Chapter 12. In the case of elections for constituency National Assembly members provided for in Article 188 and elections for local council members provided for in Article 190, election without voting was recognized where there was one candidate, whereas in the case of presidential elections provided for in Article 187 and elections for heads of local governments provided for in Article 191, voting was premised even where there was one candidate, and the requirement for determining the elected person was that, in the former case, the candidate obtain at least one third of the total number of eligible voters, and in the latter case, at least one third of the total number of valid votes. In the case of elections for heads of local governments, with the amendment of Article 191, paragraph 2 of the “Act on Public Official Elections and Prevention of Election Frauds” by Act No. 4947 on 1995. 4. 1., the content was changed so that, where there was one candidate, that candidate would be determined as the elected person only if the number of votes obtained reached at least one third of the total number of voters.\\n\\n(3) The “Act on Public Official Elections and Prevention of Election Frauds” was renamed the Public Official Election Act by Act No. 7681 on 2005. 8. 4., and the contents of the provisions concerning the method of determining elected persons have remained the same up to the present, except in relation to elections for heads of local governments. With respect to the method of determining elected persons in elections for heads of local governments, in the Public Official Election Act amended by Act No. 9974 on 2010. 1. 25., Article 191, paragraph 2, which had previously provided for the method of determining an elected person where there is one candidate, was deleted, and through the newly established paragraph 3, when there is one candidate in an election for the head of a local government, the method of determining the elected person was made to apply mutatis mutandis the provisions of Article 188, paragraphs 2 through 6, which provide for the determination of elected constituency National Assembly members. Accordingly, in elections for heads of local governments as well, as in elections for constituency National Assembly members and local constituency council members, where there is one candidate at the deadline for candidate registration, or where, after the deadline for candidate registration and before the commencement of voting on election day, a candidate withdraws, dies, or has his or her registration invalidated and the number of candidates becomes one, no voting is conducted and that candidate is determined as the elected person on the election day.\\n\\nB. Organization of the Issues\\nThe petitioner argues that, due to the provision under review, the right to vote in elections for the head of a local government and the right to know information about the candidates through elections were infringed, and that, unlike the President, election without voting is allowed in elections for the head of a local government, thereby infringing the right to equality, and as a result the right to pursue happiness was infringed. Accordingly, this Court will examine these claims.\\n\\n(1) Whether the right to vote in elections for the head of a local government is a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution\\n(a) The constitutional election system means the method of constituting the national representative body as a process of forming representative democracy based on the principle of popular sovereignty. The Constitution, in Article 24, stipulates that “All citizens shall have the right to vote as prescribed by Act,” thereby expressly providing the right to vote as a constitutionally guaranteed right, but delegates the formation of its specific content to legislation.\\n\\nPresidential and National Assembly elections for selecting national representative bodies, and local elections for selecting local council members and heads of local governments, may be said to be elections of the same meaning in that they are methods of realizing representative democracy; however, the Constitution differentiates the manner in which these electoral systems are provided for. That is, with regard to the election of National Assembly members (Article 41, paragraph 1) and the President (Article 67, paragraph 1), the Constitution directly codifies the principles of universal, equal, direct, and secret elections, and with regard to local council members, Article 118, paragraph 2 of the Constitution states that “matters concerning the election of …… members of local councils …… shall be determined by Act,” thereby declaring that local council members must be selected through elections and leaving the specific methods and contents to legislation, clearly indicating that such voting right is a fundamental right guaranteed by Article 24 of the Constitution. On the other hand, with respect to heads of local governments, Article 118, paragraph 2 of the Constitution provides only that “matters concerning the method of appointment of …… heads of local governments …… shall be determined by Act,” thereby distinguishing it textually from the “election” of local council members, and thus the question arises whether the right to vote in elections for heads of local governments is a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution.\\n\\n(b) The Constitution institutionally guarantees local autonomy, and local autonomy means that local governments establish independent autonomous organs and, under their own responsibility, handle their own affairs without interference from national organs; in this respect, it is a principle naturally derived from the essence of local autonomy that the head, who is the representative of a local government, should, like local council members, be elected through elections based on the voluntary support of residents (see Constitutional Court 1994. 8. 31. 92HEONMA126; Constitutional Court 1994. 8. 31. 92HEONMA174). Accordingly, the method of appointing heads of local governments has been provided in public election-related laws as “election,” and in light of the history of our local autonomy system, in which heads of local governments have been elected by election, there is a widely existing custom and public awareness that no method of selection other than direct election by residents for heads of local governments can be permitted. At the present time, when the democratic local autonomy system, whose essence lies in resident autonomy, has stably taken root, it cannot be permitted to dichotomize the right to vote in elections for heads of local governments, distinguishing it from the right to vote in elections for local council members and further from the right to vote in elections for National Assembly members and the President, making one a statutory right and the others constitutional rights. Therefore, the right to vote in elections for heads of local governments should likewise be recognized as a constitutional right protected by Article 24 of the Constitution, just like other voting rights.\\n\\n(2) Right to Equality\\nThe petitioner argues that, in presidential elections, voting procedures are followed even where there is one candidate, whereas in elections for the head of a local government, election without voting is allowed and the voting procedure is omitted, thereby unjustly discriminating against voters in elections for heads of local governments, such as the petitioner, as compared with presidential voters, and thus the right to equality was infringed.\\n\\nThe right to equality is infringed where the exercise of the relevant public power treats things that are essentially the same differently, or things that are different the same; if things that are not essentially the same are treated differently, it cannot be said that discrimination itself exists (see Constitutional Court 2010. 3. 25. 2009HEONMA538). Accordingly, this Court will first examine whether presidential voters and voters in elections for heads of local governments are essentially the same comparison groups.\\n\\nThe President and the head of a local government, who are the subjects of elections, both hold office as public officials elected through elections, but there are essential differences in their status and character, the duties and functions of the organ, and so forth. The President is the head of state and the national representative who represents the state vis-à-vis foreign countries, bears the responsibility to defend the independence, territorial integrity, continuity, and Constitution of the state, and has the power to integrate and coordinate state affairs and to constitute constitutional organs. As the head of the executive branch, the President has final decision-making authority over state administrative execution and the power to appoint and dismiss members, and can exert direct influence over the state as a whole, and enjoys the status of a national representative body representing the entire people together with the legislature. By contrast, the head of a local government is a representative organ of the local government established pursuant to Article 117 of the Constitution to handle residents’ welfare affairs, and exercises autonomous authority only within a limited scope as an administrative organ in charge of executing autonomous affairs concerning residents’ welfare by representing the residents of the relevant area in a limited part of the region. Therefore, considering the constitutionally conferred status, character, and role of duties, the President and the head of a local government can be said to be essentially different.\\n\\nIn terms of the meaning of elections as well, if a presidential election means the election of a representative organ of the state and, through elections, the people comprehensively choose the decision-making of state policy, elections for the head of a local government may be distinguished from presidential elections in that they are the selection of a regional representative by residents living within the jurisdiction of the local government, not the selection of a representative by the entire people, and the main concern is policy decisions on regional affairs and the promotion of residents’ welfare unrelated to national decision-making. In presidential elections, the voter means the totality of voters who have reached the voting age among the entire people, whereas in elections for heads of local governments, the voter means citizens as residents living in the relevant area, and thus the scope of voters is also different.\\n\\nConsidering these points, it is difficult to regard voters participating in presidential elections and voters participating in elections for heads of local governments as essentially the same comparison group, and thus whether there is discriminatory treatment cannot be discussed. Meanwhile, in this case, actual inequality may be seen as arising between voters in an electoral district in which voting is conducted and voters in an electoral district in which a candidate became one and election without voting was determined; however, this ultimately leads to the issue of infringement of the right to vote, and insofar as this Court is determining whether the right to vote was infringed, it will not separately determine this point.\\n\\n(3) Right to Know and Right to Pursue Happiness\\nThe petitioner argues that, due to the provision under review, when there is one candidate, no election can be held, and thus information about the candidate cannot be known, thereby infringing the right to know. The provision under review concerns only the method of determining elected persons for heads of local governments; it is not a provision prohibiting the candidate’s election campaign or the provision of candidate information such as pledges. Even if, due to the provision under review, election is not held and the situation arose in which obtaining information about the candidate became difficult, this is only an indirect and factual restriction caused by the provision under review, and thus it cannot be said that the petitioner’s right to know is restricted by the provision under review. In addition, regarding whether the right to pursue happiness was infringed, this Court will not separately determine it insofar as it determines whether the more primary fundamental right, namely the right to vote, was infringed.\\n\\nC. Whether the Right to Vote in Elections for Heads of Local Governments Was Infringed\\n(1) Legitimacy of the Legislative Purpose and Suitability of the Means\\nAlthough the reasons for amendment of the Public Official Election Act do not clearly state the legislative purpose of the provision under review, examining materials related to the draft amendment shows that the election without voting system appears to have been introduced on the basis that, where there is one candidate, it is efficient as a system arrangement for reducing election costs and simplifying procedures. In an election system that adopts a plurality-winner system, where there becomes only one candidate by the deadline for candidate registration, the elected person can be regarded as having been finalized regardless of whether voting is conducted. The legislative purpose of the provision under review is to enhance the efficiency of the election system by simplifying various procedures required for elections, promoting administrative convenience, and reducing election costs, and its legitimacy can be recognized. Moreover, where there is one candidate by the deadline for candidate registration, omitting voting and determining that candidate as the elected person can be said to be an appropriate means for achieving such legislative purpose.\\n\\n(2) Minimum Restriction\\nAccording to Article 191, paragraph 1 of the Public Official Election Act, in elections for heads of local governments, the person who obtained the “majority of valid votes” is, in principle, determined as the elected person and thereby granted democratic legitimacy. Therefore, where there is one candidate, even if the voting procedure is followed, since there is no competitor, unless no voter in the relevant area selects that candidate, it is certain that the sole candidate who ran for office will become the elected person even by obtaining only one vote. In this way, where only one candidate runs and the elected person is effectively fixed, holding an election becomes merely a formal act; accordingly, in such cases, exceptionally omitting voting and determining the relevant candidate as the elected person may be the most efficient choice for reducing election costs incurred in campaign activities, management and observation of voting, ballot counting, and the like, and for preventing waste of administrative resources.\\n\\nOf course, the legislator could also more broadly guarantee the right to vote by, for example, conducting voting even when there is one candidate and recognizing that candidate as elected only if a certain percentage or more of votes is obtained. However, the method of determining the elected person is a matter for the legislator to decide by comprehensively considering various conditions such as social, economic, and technical circumstances, and this is an area in which legislative discretion is recognized, and it cannot be said that an elected person must obtain at least a certain percentage of votes in order to acquire democratic legitimacy or representativeness. In a situation where guaranteeing the exercise of the right to vote does not have substantive significance for the guarantee of fundamental rights, the legislator’s decision to choose the means of election without voting can be recognized as rational. In addition, if voting were conducted even when there is one candidate and that candidate were recognized as elected only when he or she obtained at least a certain percentage of votes, then if that percentage is not achieved, there would be no elected person and a by-election would have to be held. In that case, problems such as the possibility of securing new candidates for the by-election, administrative inconvenience, and waste of time and costs would arise, and an interruption in the duties of the head of the local government would necessarily follow. In the reality where the tasks to be resolved by local autonomy are increasing day by day and the share that the head of a local government must perform is also growing accordingly, if a long-term vacancy in duties occurs, there is a concern that this may cause serious obstacles to the operation of the local government. The legislator’s determination, in consideration of the various circumstances above, to provide that, where there is one candidate by the deadline for candidate registration, no voting shall be conducted and that candidate shall be determined as the elected person for the head of a local government, cannot be said to be an excessive restriction beyond the scope necessary to achieve the legislative purpose.\\n\\n(3) Balance of Legal Interests\\nWhere there is one candidate, it is clear that even if voting is conducted, that candidate will ultimately be elected; thus, the provision under review’s stipulation of election without voting only in the limited situation of a single candidate, in light of this reality, may be seen as imposing a comparatively small degree of restriction on fundamental rights. On the other hand, the public interest in simplifying the procedures required for voting where the elected person is certain, assisting administrative convenience, reducing election costs, enhancing the efficiency of the election system, and preventing the possibility of a vacancy in the duties of the head of a local government is sufficiently recognized; therefore, the restriction on the right to vote under the provision under review also satisfies the balance of legal interests.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nAccordingly, since the petition in this case lacks merit, it shall be dismissed, and a decision shall be rendered as ordered. In this decision, the opinions of all the other participating Justices were in agreement except for the dissenting opinion of Justice Cho Yong-ho set forth in 6. below.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Cho Yong-ho\\nUnlike the majority opinion, I believe that the provision under review infringes the petitioner’s right to vote, and therefore I state my dissenting opinion as follows.\\n\\n(1) The majority opinion states that, where there is one candidate, determining that candidate as the elected person may be the most efficient choice for achieving the legislative purpose of reducing election costs and simplifying procedures. However, it is questionable whether, for achieving such legislative purpose, completely depriving voters of their right to vote through the election without voting system can be justified, and whether the election without voting system is necessarily a means required to achieve such legislative purpose.\\n\\nThe provision under review prevents voters from expressing their will at the source by not conducting the voting itself where there is one candidate, and in effect imposes a comprehensive and fundamental restriction on the right to vote. Depriving voters of the opportunity to vote itself is the strongest form of restriction on the right to vote, and such legislation can be exceptionally justified only where it is clear that there exist individual and concrete grounds inevitably required for a significant public interest. Vague and abstract risks, or reasons such as technical difficulties or practical obstacles that can be overcome by state efforts, cannot be a proper reason for completely excluding the exercise of the right to vote (see Constitutional Court 2007. 6. 28. 2004HEONMA644, etc.). However, the reduction of election costs and enhancement of efficiency in the election system through simplification of procedures, which the provision under review pursues, is merely an administrative convenience in conducting elections, and is only a practical problem that can be overcome by state efforts. It is difficult to recognize the legitimacy of legislation that, for the mere purpose of promoting such administrative convenience or superficially and formally reducing election costs, completely restricts the exercise of the people’s most fundamental and important right to vote in a democratic state.\\n\\n(2) The local autonomy system is a system that, on a regional basis, allows residents of a certain area to directly handle affairs through organs they themselves elect under their responsibility, thereby enhancing the democracy and efficiency of local autonomous administration and promoting balanced development of local areas as well as the democratic development of the state. Whether the local autonomy system succeeds depends on whether the will of residents is properly reflected in political decision-making. Accordingly, the election system for selecting the head of a local government, who plays one pillar of the local autonomy system, must accurately reflect the will of residents without distortion and guarantee the free choice of residents (see Constitutional Court 2009. 3. 26. 2006HEONMA240, etc.). Elections are not merely a system for determining winners and losers and identifying the elected person. Through all processes related to elections, various political wills of the people can be expressed, and the results expressed through elections contribute to forming and conveying the people’s political will.\\n\\nHowever, the provision under review regards the case where there is one candidate as having already determined the winner and loser, omits the voting procedure, and determines the elected person, and therefore residents have no means to express their own political will regarding that candidate through the exercise of the right to vote. Where there is one candidate, voters may decide not to elect that candidate as the elected person on the ground that the candidate is not a suitable person to be the head of a local government, and that too is the will of the voters.\\n\\nAccording to the provision under review, for example, even where a single candidate has a prior record of serious crimes such as violent offenses, bribery, or embezzlement and voters do not wish to elect that person as their representative, the person is unconditionally elected regardless of such will, and there is a possibility of distorting the voters’ will. In addition, due to the election without voting system, there is a possibility that side effects may arise, such as bribing a person expected to run as an opposing candidate to withdraw. Although it is not directly related to the provision under review, it is a matter of common knowledge that under the Public Official Election Act, because it provides that where a candidate becomes one after withdrawal or death following candidate registration, election without voting shall be allowed, there have often been cases in the past where attempts were made to bribe an opposing candidate to cause withdrawal. In this way, in the case of election without voting, the residents’ preference for the relevant candidate cannot be accurately reflected, and since the opportunity for voters to express their political will is completely blocked, there exists a risk that the true will of residents will be distorted.\\n\\nMeanwhile, since the decision-making exercised by sovereigns in the electoral process is an important basis for granting democratic legitimacy to the head of a local government, the representativeness of a head of a local government elected without sufficiently reflecting residents’ opinions becomes extremely weak, creating a risk of undermining even the essence and legitimacy of the local autonomy system. Considering the purpose of the Constitution in guaranteeing the right to vote as a fundamental right and the meaning and function that elections have in the order of representative democracy, the provision under review, by stipulating election without voting as the method for determining the elected person, restricts voters’ free expression of political will and weakens the democratic legitimacy of the elected person, and can be said to impose a serious restriction to the extent that the right to vote is substantially hollowed out.\\n\\n(3) Where there is one candidate, there are numerous methods less restrictive of the petitioner’s fundamental rights than the method, as in the provision under review, of depriving voters of the opportunity to vote itself. That is, the legislator may devise a rational alternative that minimizes restriction of the petitioner’s right to vote while more efficiently achieving the legislative purpose, such as conducting voting even when there is one candidate and recognizing that candidate as elected only when he or she obtains a certain percentage or more of votes, or conducting an approval/rejection vote.\\n\\nIndeed, until the amendment of the provision under review in 2010, the Public Official Election Act had consistently provided, since its enactment in 1994, that voting would also be conducted when there is one candidate in an election for the head of a local government, and had provided as a specific requirement that the candidate would be determined as elected only when the number of votes obtained reached at least one third of the total number of voters (or the total number of valid votes). However, even if one examines the legislative history of the amendment to the provision under review or the minutes of the National Assembly related to the amendment, no evidence can be found that empirically supports that determining election without voting where there is one candidate is absolutely necessary to simplify administrative procedures or reduce election costs in local elections, and it is difficult to find specific grounds for the necessity or effect of such amendment. Moreover, in the case of local elections, since elections for local council members, heads of local governments, and superintendents of education with the same expiration date of term are conducted simultaneously on the election day corresponding to the expiration of the term, even in the case of a head of a local government where there is one candidate, if an election is conducted, it does not appear that separate personnel, venues, equipment, or administrative procedures for conducting the election would be needed. Therefore, it cannot be said that this would increase individual election costs and burden the national treasury and local finances.\\n\\n(4) The majority opinion points out that, if voting is conducted even where there is one candidate and that candidate is recognized as elected only when he or she obtains a certain percentage or more of votes, then if that percentage is not reached there will be no elected person and a by-election must be held, and accordingly there is a possibility of administrative vacancy.\\n\\nHowever, if the method chosen is to conduct voting even where there is one candidate and determine the elected person, the relevant candidate will conduct campaign activities and these related costs can be anticipated; yet, considering that under the current Public Official Election Act, where there is one candidate and voting is not conducted, the law merely announces the fact that voting will not be held and does not disclose any information related to the candidate, including the candidate’s name, the method of conducting campaign activities through which candidate information is conveyed to voters and voters can express an accurate political will based on this may rather be a method that further firmly guarantees the right to vote in itself.\\n\\nIn addition, considering that in the past local elections, where there was one candidate in an election for the head of a local government and voting was conducted, there was not a single case in which the single candidate failed to obtain at least one third of the total number of voters, it does not appear that conducting voting where there is one candidate would significantly increase the possibility that there will be no elected person and a re-vote must be conducted, or that administrative vacancy or other problems would arise as a result. Furthermore, the fact that in the past the vote results for a single candidate showed a high rate of votes obtained may also be seen as proof that, even if the voting system for a single candidate were restored by amending the provision under review, there would be no particular practical problem. Even if there is concern about an administrative vacancy, this is a problem that can be resolved through appropriate procedures such as acting appointments. Rather, the concern about lack of representation arising from the fact that a person whose support from voters has not been confirmed would serve as the head of a local government can be seen as a much more serious issue than the concern about administrative vacancy.\\n\\n(5) Considering the purpose of the Constitution in guaranteeing the right to vote as a fundamental right and the meaning and function that elections have in the order of representative democracy, the provision under review, by stipulating election without voting as the method for determining the elected person, does not merely block the opportunity for voters’ free political expression and thereby hollow out the right to vote in substance, but is also a very serious restriction that weakens the democratic legitimacy of the elected person and may even undermine the essence and legitimacy of the local autonomy system. On the other hand, what the provision under review pursues is mainly to promote administrative convenience or reduce difficulties in election techniques or burdens of election costs; it is difficult to regard these as a significant public interest that would justify the deprivation of the right to vote. The provision under review also failed to satisfy the balance of legal interests that must be observed in restricting fundamental rights.\\n\\n(6) Ultimately, the provision under review violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringes the petitioner’s right to vote."}

{"[2020HEONRA5]": "1. Case Overview\\n\\na. The Respondent established, on 2020. 11. 10., a special investigation plan concerning the Petitioner as follows (hereinafter referred to as \"the investigation plan in this case\").\\n<TABLE0>\\n\\nb. Pursuant to the investigation plan in this case, the Respondent notified the Petitioner, on 2020. 11. 11., of the commencement of the investigation as follows (hereinafter referred to as \"the notice of commencement of investigation in this case\").\\n<TABLE1>\\n\\nc. Thereafter, the Respondent’s investigative team conducted an audit from 2020. 11. 16. on each item listed in serial numbers 1 through 9 of the [Appendix 1] list (hereinafter referred to as \"Audit Items 1 through 9\"), and, based on the additional information reported during the audit, added each item listed in serial numbers 10 through 14 of the same list (hereinafter referred to as \"Audit Items 10 through 14\") as additional audit subjects and conducted the audit (hereinafter referred to as \"the audit in this case\").\\n\\nd. On 2020. 11. 26., the Petitioner filed this adjudication on a jurisdictional dispute, alleging that the audit in this case failed to satisfy the requirements for commencement of an audit of autonomous affairs under Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act (amended by Act No. 14839 on 2017. 7. 26., and wholly amended by Act No. 17893 on 2021. 1. 12; hereinafter, the former Local Autonomy Act according to the above amendment history shall be referred to simply as the \"former Local Autonomy Act\" without omitting the amendment history) and thereby infringed the Petitioner’s right to local autonomy. On the same day, the Petitioner also filed an application for a provisional disposition suspending effectiveness (2020HEONSA1191), seeking a decision that \"the effect of the notice of commencement of investigation in this case shall be suspended until the pronouncement of the final decision on the petition for adjudication on the jurisdictional dispute.\"\\n\\ne. On 2020. 12. 7., the Respondent notified the Petitioner of the termination of the investigation, stating that \"since the Petitioner refused to cooperate with the audit and instructed its affiliated public officials to cease undergoing the audit, substantive investigative progress is difficult, so the investigation will be terminated; however, as to the matters not processed this time, a separate plan will be established and pursued in the future.\" Accordingly, the Petitioner withdrew the above application for provisional disposition on 2020. 12. 8.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe subject matter of review in this case is whether the audit conducted by the Respondent against the Petitioner from 2020. 11. 16. to 2020. 12. 7. regarding each item listed in the [Appendix 1] list infringed the Petitioner’s right to local autonomy guaranteed by the Constitution and the Local Autonomy Act.\\n\\nThe relevant provisions are as set forth in [Appendix 2].\\n\\n3. The Petitioner’s Claims and the Respondent’s Answer\\n\\na. The Petitioner’s Claims\\n\\nThe audit in this case constitutes an audit of autonomous affairs. Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act limits the scope of audits by a Governor of a Province over the autonomous affairs of a local government to matters in violation of statutes and regulations, and requires prior verification of whether there has been a violation of statutes and regulations.\\n\\nHowever, when commencing the audit in this case, the Respondent notified the Petitioner by specifying the audit subject matter as \"matters suspected from media reports, resident audit petition and anonymous reports, etc.\" and the audit period as \"2020. 11. 16. ~ until completion of the investigation.\" This was an abstract and comprehensive audit that did not specify unlawful matters and therefore went beyond the scope of a legality audit permitted under Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act. In addition, before conducting the audit in this case, the Respondent commenced the audit without confirming whether the handling of the audited affairs violated statutes and regulations, and without any reasonable suspicion that there had been unlawful conduct.\\n\\nAccordingly, the audit in this case infringed the Petitioner’s right to local autonomy in violation of Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act.\\n\\nb. Summary of the Respondent’s Answer\\n\\n(1) Since the audit in this case was not normally carried out due to the Petitioner’s non-cooperation and refusal to provide materials and was suspended on 2020. 12. 7., the state of infringement of rights alleged by the Petitioner has ended, and thus the petition for adjudication on a jurisdictional dispute in this case is inadmissible for lack of the interest in adjudication.\\n\\n(2) Prior to the notice of commencement of investigation in this case, the Respondent had already established the investigation plan in this case and specified the audit subject matter, but merely did not inform the Petitioner in advance of the specific audit subject matter in order to ensure the effectiveness of the audit. Upon commencement of the audit in this case, the Respondent’s investigative team informed the Petitioner’s side of the specific audit subject matter and requested relevant materials; therefore, a situation in which the Petitioner underwent an audit without knowing the audit subject matter did not arise. As such, the Respondent planned and conducted an audit of specific and identified unlawful conduct, and therefore the audit in this case does not constitute a general and comprehensive audit.\\n\\nIn addition, the Respondent specified the audit subject matter by verifying whether there had been a violation of statutes and regulations on the basis of media reports, insider reports, and residents’ audit requests containing specific content that could be regarded as sufficiently reliable.\\n\\nAccordingly, the audit in this case was a lawful audit and did not infringe the Petitioner’s right to local autonomy.\\n\\n4. Determination on the Admissibility Requirements\\n\\nSince the audit in this case ended on 2020. 12. 7., even if this petition for adjudication were granted, it would not help provide relief to the Petitioner; in principle, therefore, there is no interest in adjudication. However, because adjudication on a jurisdictional dispute also serves the function of securing the objective constitutional order as well as providing subjective relief of rights, even if the state of infringement of rights against the Petitioner has already ended and there is no longer any possibility of cancellation, the interest in adjudication may exceptionally be recognized where there is a risk that the same type of infringing act will recur in the future and where constitutional clarification thereof is essential for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order (see Constitutional Court, 2009. 5. 28., 2006HEONRA6).\\n\\nWhen notifying the Petitioner of the termination of the audit in this case, the Respondent stated that \"as to the matters not processed this time, a separate plan will be established and pursued in the future,\" and thus there is a risk that the same type of infringing act will recur in the future. In addition, although the Constitutional Court, in its decision of 2009. 5. 28. 2006HEONRA6, ruled on the scope and method of an audit pursuant to Article 158 of the former Local Autonomy Act (amended by Act No. 4741 on 1994. 3. 16., and wholly amended by Act No. 8423 on 2007. 5. 11.), which contained the same content as Article 171, paragraph (1) of the former Local Autonomy Act, and although the nomenclature of the central administrative agencies has since merely been changed, clarification is necessary regarding the existence of the duty to notify the audit subject matter, the possibility of expanding or adding audit subjects after commencement of the audit in relation to the specification of the audit subject matter, and the method and degree of verifying illegality before commencement of the audit; therefore, the interest in adjudication may exceptionally be recognized.\\n\\n5. Determination on the Merits\\n\\na. Requirements for Commencement of an Audit of Autonomous Affairs\\n\\n(1) With the constitutional amendment to the current Constitution on 1987. 10. 29. and the full implementation of the local autonomy system, legislative measures followed to support it. Article 158 of the Local Autonomy Act, amended by Act No. 4741 on 1994. 3. 16., provided that \"the Minister of Home Affairs or the Governor/Mayor of a City or Province may receive reports on, or audit documents, ledgers, or accounts concerning, the autonomous affairs of local governments. In such cases, the audit shall be conducted only with respect to matters violating statutes and regulations.\" This newly added latter sentence to the previous Local Autonomy Act, which had merely provided that \"the Minister of Home Affairs or the Governor/Mayor of a City or Province may receive reports on, or audit documents, ledgers, or accounts concerning, the autonomous affairs of local governments,\" is intended legislatively to secure the autonomy of autonomous affairs by narrowing the scope of audits of autonomous affairs to a \"legality audit,\" thereby ultimately securing the autonomy of local governments. The above-amended Article 158 was moved to Article 171 without any change in substance when the Local Autonomy Act was wholly amended by Act No. 8423 on 2007. 5. 11., and thereafter, only the names of central administrative agencies were changed, before reaching the present current Local Autonomy Act, wholly amended by Act No. 17893 on 2021. 1. 12., in which the provision was moved to Article 190 without any substantive change.\\n\\nIn its decision of 2009. 5. 28. 2006HEONRA6, the Constitutional Court held, in light of the amendment purpose of the above Constitution and Local Autonomy Act and the history of narrowing audits of autonomous affairs to \"legality audits,\" that the audit authority of a central administrative agency over the autonomous affairs of a local government must be construed not as a prior, general, comprehensive audit authority, but as a limited audit authority with a restricted subject matter and scope. Further, the Court established the doctrine regarding the requirements for commencing an audit of autonomous affairs by holding that, in order for a central administrative agency to commence an audit of autonomous affairs of a local government, a specific violation of statutes and regulations concerning autonomous affairs must have been identified or there must be a reasonable suspicion that unlawful conduct occurred, and that the audit subject matter must be specified.\\n\\nReflecting the purport of the Constitutional Court’s decision in 2006HEONRA6, the Local Autonomy Act was amended by Act No. 10344 on 2010. 6. 8., newly adding Article 171, paragraph (2), which expressly provides that before conducting an audit of autonomous affairs, the agency shall verify whether the handling of the relevant affairs violates statutes and regulations. The \"Regulations on Administrative Audits of Local Governments\" (hereinafter referred to as the \"Administrative Audit Regulations\"), which prescribe matters concerning the procedure and method of audits under the Local Autonomy Act, were also wholly amended by Presidential Decree No. 22439 on 2010. 10. 13., introducing a prior investigation system so that, before conducting an audit of autonomous affairs of a local government, the documents or ledgers of the relevant local government may be reviewed to verify whether there has been a violation of statutes and regulations, and if, as a result of such verification, there are violations of statutes and regulations or substantial grounds to suspect such violations in the handling of autonomous affairs, the relevant affairs shall be specified as audit subjects and the audit schedule and related matters shall be notified in advance to the head of the relevant local government (Article 7, paragraphs (2) and (3)).\\n\\n(2) The audit that was the subject of the Constitutional Court’s decision in 2006HEONRA6 was an audit by a central administrative agency of the autonomous affairs of a local government, which differs from this case, where the issue is the audit by a metropolitan local government of the autonomous affairs of a basic local government.\\n\\nHowever, with respect to autonomous affairs of local governments, a basic local government is a subject of rights equal to and distinct from a metropolitan local government, and an audit by a metropolitan local government of a basic local government should be regarded as an exercise of supervisory authority between distinct legal persons with external effect. Accordingly, control by a central administrative agency and control by a superior local government cannot be said to differ in substance; Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act also limits the audit authority of a Governor/Mayor over the autonomous affairs of a local government to matters violating statutes and regulations, thereby expressly providing that audits of autonomous affairs by a superior local government are, like the supervisory authority of a central administrative agency, limited in subject matter and scope.\\n\\nTherefore, the holding of the Constitutional Court’s decision in 2006HEONRA6 must also apply as it stands to audits by a metropolitan local government of the autonomous affairs of a basic local government. Accordingly, in order for a metropolitan local government to commence an audit of the autonomous affairs of a basic local government, a specific violation of statutes and regulations concerning autonomous affairs must have been identified or there must be a reasonable suspicion that unlawful conduct occurred, and the audit subject matter must be specified; an audit commenced without specifying unlawful matters or an audit for detecting violations of statutes and regulations cannot be permitted.\\n\\nb. Issues\\n\\nAt the time of the notice of commencement of investigation in this case, the Respondent did not clearly indicate the legal basis provisions for the audit in this case, but the audit in this case constitutes an audit of autonomous affairs under Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act. The Petitioner also, on this premise, alleges that the audit in this case is an unlawful audit that failed to satisfy the requirements for commencement of an audit of autonomous affairs and thereby infringed the Petitioner’s right to local autonomy.\\n\\nFirst, the Petitioner argues that at the time of the notice of commencement of investigation, the Respondent notified the investigation content only as \"matters suspected from media reports, resident audit petition and anonymous reports, etc.\"; however, such notice alone cannot be deemed to have specified the audit subject matter, and thus the audit in this case is an unlawful audit in which the audit subject matter was not specified. As noted above, before the notice of commencement of investigation in this case, the Respondent established the investigation plan in this case by specifying the audit subject matter as Audit Items 1 through 9, but did not notify the Petitioner in advance of the audit subject matter so specified. In relation to the above argument, we examine whether prior notification of the internally specified audit subject matter to the local government subject to the audit is required in order to recognize specification of the audit subject matter, that is, whether prior notification of the audit subject matter should be regarded as a requirement for commencement of the audit.\\n\\nMeanwhile, as noted above, after commencing the audit in this case and while conducting the audit of Audit Items 1 through 9, the Respondent added Audit Items 10 through 14 as audit subjects. In relation to the specification of the audit subject matter, we examine whether it is permissible to expand or add audit subjects during the course of the audit.\\n\\nFinally, the Petitioner argues that the Respondent commenced the audit in this case based solely on complaints and media reports without confirming whether there had been a violation of statutes and regulations, such as through prior investigation, and thus the audit in this case is an unlawful audit commenced without even a reasonable suspicion that a violation of statutes and regulations occurred or that unlawful conduct existed. In relation to the above argument, we examine the method and degree of verifying unlawfulness required to commence an audit in order to confirm violations of statutes and regulations.\\n\\nc. Whether the Audit in This Case Was Unlawful\\n\\n(1) Issue of Prior Notification of the Audit Subject Matter\\n\\n(a) Before commencing the audit in this case, on 2020. 11. 11., the Respondent notified the Petitioner of the commencement of investigation in this case and merely stated the investigation content as \"matters suspected from media reports, resident audit petition and anonymous reports, etc.,\" without notifying the audit subject matter as specified internally. The above content notified by the Respondent to the Petitioner is so abstract and comprehensive that it is difficult to regard it as having specified and notified the audit subject matter. The issue here is whether prior notification of a specified audit subject matter to the local government subject to the audit is a requirement for commencement of the audit.\\n\\n(b) According to Article 5 of the Administrative Audit Regulations, a Mayor/Provincial Governor, etc. shall notify the head of the local government subject to the audit of the main contents of the annual audit plan by January 31 each year (main text of paragraph (1)); and if the annual audit plan is changed after notification, the changed contents shall be notified without delay to the head of the local government subject to the audit (main text of paragraph (2)). However, in the case of an audit not included in the annual audit plan, as in the audit in this case, no explicit provision can be found requiring notification of the audit subject matter or contents.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the former Administrative Audit Regulations (amended by Presidential Decree No. 28211 on 2017. 7. 26., and before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 32223 on 2021. 12. 16.; hereinafter referred to as the \"former Administrative Audit Regulations\") provide in Article 7, paragraph (2) that the Minister of the Interior and Safety or a Mayor/Provincial Governor may perform prior investigative work, if deemed necessary, to verify whether the handling of autonomous affairs of the local government violates statutes and regulations, before conducting an audit of autonomous affairs of the local government, and in paragraph (3) of the same Article provide that if, as a result of performing prior investigative work, there are violations of statutes and regulations or substantial grounds to suspect such violations in the handling of autonomous affairs of the local government, the Minister of the Interior and Safety or a Mayor/Provincial Governor shall specify the relevant affairs as audit subjects and notify the head of the relevant local government in advance of the audit schedule, etc. Even if Article 7, paragraph (3) of the former Administrative Audit Regulations is viewed as imposing a duty to notify the audit subject matter on a Mayor/Provincial Governor, etc., it is reasonable to interpret that such duty is recognized only when prior investigative work has been performed pursuant to paragraph (2) of the same Article. However, since performing prior investigative work is discretionary rather than mandatory, and the Respondent did not perform prior investigative work when conducting the audit in this case, the above provision cannot be deemed applicable to this case.\\n\\n(c) The Petitioner also argues that, based on Article 24 of the \"Act on Public Sector Audits,\" the audit subject matter must have been specified by prior notice to the local government subject to the audit in order to deem the audit subject matter specified.\\n\\nArticle 24, paragraph (1) of the \"Act on Public Sector Audits\" provides that \"when the head of a central administrative agency, etc. commences or terminates an investigation of a specific case, he or she shall notify the head of the institution subject to internal audit of such fact within 10 days.\" However, the \"Act on Public Sector Audits\" generally applies to \"internal audits\" of the affairs and activities of the institution to which the head of a local government belongs (including its subordinate institutions and affiliated organizations) and persons belonging to that institution (Article 3, paragraph (1); Article 2, subparagraph 1), and with respect to audits of autonomous affairs under Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act, only Article 33 (prohibition of duplicate audits), Article 34 (consultation on audit plans), and Article 36, paragraph (2) (audit information system) of the \"Act on Public Sector Audits\" apply, while Article 24, paragraph (1) does not apply (Article 3, paragraph (2)). Moreover, the notification under the above Article 24, paragraph (1), is for the purpose of ensuring the effectiveness of the audit by commencing and terminating an investigation of a specific case and notifying the head of the audited institution so that disciplinary or punitive procedures concerning that case are suspended during the investigation period, and at the same time for suspending the limitation period for disciplinary or punitive grounds; it cannot be regarded as prescribing a requirement for commencement of the audit.\\n\\n(d) Taking the above circumstances together, in order for a metropolitan local government to commence an audit of the autonomous affairs of a basic local government, the audit subject matter must be specified, but it cannot be deemed that the audit subject matter must, in addition, be notified in advance to the local government subject to the audit. Therefore, even if the Respondent did not notify the internally specified audit subject matter when issuing the notice of commencement of investigation in this case, such circumstance alone cannot render the audit in this case unlawful.\\n\\n(2) Whether the Audit Subject Matter Was Specified and Whether Expansion/Additions to the Audit Subject Matter Are Permissible\\n\\n(a) Standard of review\\n\\n1) As discussed above, specification of the audit subject matter is a requirement for commencement of an audit of autonomous affairs of a local government. Given that the audit authority of a central administrative agency and a metropolitan local government over the autonomous affairs of a local government is not a prior, general, comprehensive audit authority, but rather an audit authority with a limited subject matter and scope, it is self-evident that the audit subject matter must be specified in order to commence an audit of autonomous affairs.\\n\\n2) Thus, the audit subject matter must be specified before commencement of the audit. However, the Respondent, after commencing the audit in this case, also conducted audits on matters that had not originally been specified as audit subjects. The issue is whether expansion or addition of the audit subject matter after the commencement of the audit is permissible.\\n\\nSince arbitrary exercise of audit authority over autonomous affairs of local governments is highly likely to infringe the constitutionally guaranteed right to local autonomy, in principle, even if unlawful facts are discovered in matters not specified in advance as audit subjects during the audit process, expansion or addition of the audit subject matter should not be permitted. However, considering the purpose of the audit, which is to control legality in autonomous affairs, and the fact that, even from the perspective of the local government subject to the audit, it may be more efficient to undergo audit together in an already commenced procedure rather than having a separate audit procedure commenced and being investigated from the beginning again, there is also a need exceptionally to recognize expansion or addition of the audit subject matter. In what circumstances expansion or addition of the audit subject matter will be permitted must be determined individually in a specific case according to the purpose of the audit, the content of the audit subject matter, and the circumstances leading to the specification of the additional audit subject matter; however, at least where the matter is recognized as related to the originally specified audit subject matter and where there is no concern that the local government subject to the audit will suffer procedural disadvantage even if the audit proceeds together in the same procedure, and where it cannot be regarded as having been conducted for the purpose of detecting that audit subject matter, expansion or addition of the audit subject matter may be permitted.\\n\\n(b) Specific determination\\n\\n1) First, as noted in the case overview above, the Respondent internally set Audit Items 1 through 9 as the audit subjects concerning the Petitioner on 2020. 11. 10. The content of Audit Items 1 through 8, as seen below, is all individually and specifically described, and thus the audit subject matter can be deemed specified.\\n\\n① Suspicion of preferential treatment in the Yangjeong Station Area development project: this is a suspicion that a specific company received preferential treatment in the process of selecting a business operator for the Yangjeong Station Area development project, which involves creating a mixed-use complex in Sangpyeong-dong, Namyangju City, and that the president of Namyangju Urban Corporation, a subsidiary of the Petitioner, was involved by issuing illegal instructions in the process.\\n\\n② Unfair selection of a business operator for the Namyangju City arts club competition project: this is a suspicion that, in the process of selecting the business operator for the Namyangju City arts club competition held around 2020. 5., the judges raised issues on the ground that a document not stated in the notice was not submitted; that the selection of judges was also made in a manner different from what had been initially announced; and that, as a result, the Namyangju branch of the Korean Federation of Art and Culture Organizations was eliminated and another organization that the Petitioner had separately guided to apply for the public contest project was selected.\\n\\n③ Violation of COVID-19 quarantine guidelines: members of organizations under the Petitioner, including the Namyangju City association of village leaders, issued a statement from 2020. 8. 19. to 2020. 9. 4. inside an indoor space such as the Petitioner’s office building, calling on the Respondent to pay a special coordination grant to the Petitioner; the suspicion is that the Petitioner failed to ensure that the members of those organizations who attended the statement release complied with COVID-19 quarantine guidelines.\\n\\n④ Appropriateness of the budget payment decision by the Administrative Mediation Committee: this is a suspicion that the legal fees of the Petitioner’s representative mayor (hereinafter referred to as the \"Mayor of Namyangju City\") were paid from the city budget.\\n\\n⑤ The second change to the metropolitan area development restriction zone management plan for 2021 (Wolmun Sewage Treatment Plant): this is a suspicion that the Petitioner, since around 2015, had proceeded with individual permits based on contents different from the management plan for 2008 without changing the management plan, as a result of which the locations of buildings and sports facilities in the relevant area were constructed differently from the management plan, a badminton court not included in the management plan was newly built, and a buffer green area was not installed.\\n\\n⑥ Restoration project for damaged areas in three zones, including 172-44 Saneung-ri, Jingeon-eup, Namyangju City: this is a suspicion that, while receiving donation and transfer, the Petitioner calculated the amount of donation and transfer contrary to the content of the statutory provisions.\\n\\n⑦ Suspicion of preferential treatment in the purchase of public property\\n\\n㉠ Regarding Namyangju Palace House: this is a suspicion that the Petitioner accepted the donation and transfer of Namyangju Palace House, a national folk cultural heritage, from its owner while purchasing the surrounding land and fixtures at a high price, thereby granting preferential treatment.\\n\\n㉡ Regarding the wedding hall: this is a suspicion that, in the course of implementing a historic park project, the Petitioner purchased at a high price a wedding hall building that had long been left as an eyesore, thereby granting preferential treatment to its owner.\\n\\n⑧ Appropriateness of the construction permit (change) for Wolmun-ri, Wabu-eup, Namyangju City: this is a suspicion that, although the land at San 5-3, Wolmun-ri, Wabu-eup, Namyangju City, has a high slope and a narrow access road and thus did not satisfy the criteria for a development permit under the ordinances of Namyangju City, the responsible public official granted a factory construction permit without receiving an application for a development permit, etc.\\n\\n2) However, the item \"other media reports, on-site tip-offs, etc.\" in Audit Item 9 is, in itself, abstract and comprehensive in content, as the Respondent itself acknowledges that it is an item intended to include matters additionally reported before and after the commencement and progress of the audit in this case, and therefore cannot be regarded as having specified or limited the audit subject matter at the time of commencement.\\n\\n3) Meanwhile, Audit Items 10 through 14, which the Respondent added as audit subjects after the commencement of the audit in this case, cannot, in light of their content, all be regarded as related to Audit Items 1 through 8 that had originally been specified as audit subjects. The Respondent argues that the added items correspond to the item \"other media reports, on-site tip-offs, etc.\" in Audit Item 9, which was designated as an audit subject at the time of commencement; however, as noted above, the above item is difficult to regard as specifically identified in itself, so there is no need to examine its relation to the added items.\\n\\n4) Accordingly, among the audit in this case, the audit of Audit Items 1 through 8 satisfied the requirement for commencement of the audit, namely, specification of the audit subject matter; however, the audit of Audit Items 9 through 14 did not satisfy the requirement for commencement of the audit because the audit subject matter was not specified or because a relation to the originally specified audit subject matter was not recognized.\\n\\n(3) Whether a Violation of Statutes and Regulations Was Verified Before the Audit Commenced\\n\\n(a) Standard of review\\n\\nArticle 171, paragraph (2) of the former Local Autonomy Act provides that, before conducting an audit, the agency shall verify whether the handling of the relevant affairs violates statutes and regulations, etc., but it does not prescribe specifically by what method and to what extent illegality must be verified.\\n\\nArticle 7, paragraph (2) of the former Administrative Audit Regulations prescribes prior investigation for audits of autonomous affairs, and provides that, where deemed necessary to verify whether the handling of autonomous affairs violates statutes and regulations, etc., documents or ledgers may be reviewed to ascertain the facts; however, this is reasonably construed as an optional procedure that the audit agency may choose according to its needs, so a Mayor/Provincial Governor, etc. may verify whether there has been a violation of statutes and regulations by various methods other than prior investigation.\\n\\nFurthermore, considering that audits of autonomous affairs of local governments under Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act are audits of violations of statutes and regulations, and that their purpose is to secure the legality of autonomous affairs by enabling a Mayor/Provincial Governor, etc. to identify specific violations of statutes and regulations through the audit and take necessary measures, and considering that the unlawfulness of autonomous affairs can ultimately be verified through the investigative process of an audit, if strict illegality verification were required at the pre-commencement stage for matters suspected of illegality, the existence of the audit system itself could become meaningless. The Constitutional Court’s holding in 2006HEONRA6 that an audit may be commenced where there has been \"confirmation of a specific violation of statutes and regulations or a reasonable suspicion that unlawful conduct occurred\" may also be understood as taking these circumstances into account.\\n\\nAccordingly, if a Mayor/Provincial Governor, etc. collects information concerning the illegality of a local government’s autonomous affairs through reports or media coverage and determines, on the basis of objective materials, that such information is reliable and thereby forms a reasonable suspicion that unlawful conduct occurred, then, unless it is manifest that the alleged facts do not exist or that illegality is not at issue, it is reasonable to regard the verification of illegality as having been sufficient to commence the audit.\\n\\n(b) Specific determination\\n\\nApplying the above standard to the audit in this case, it is reasonable to regard verification of whether there had been a violation of statutes and regulations as having been made before commencement of the audit with respect to Audit Items 1 through 8, as follows.\\n\\n① Suspicion of preferential treatment in the Yangjeong Station Area development project: from around 2020. 7., media reports raised suspicions that the period for public recruitment of a private business operator was only about half the usual length, and that the scoring for certain evaluation items was excessively high, suggesting that specific companies may have been contemplated; around 2020. 9., media reports also stated that a former employee of Namyangju Urban Corporation testified that the president of Namyangju Urban Corporation had intervened in the screening process for the public recruitment of the private business operator.\\n\\n② Unfair selection of a business operator for the Namyangju City arts club competition project: in this regard, the head of the Namyangju branch of the Korean Federation of Art and Culture Organizations, Lee ○○, filed an audit petition through the e-People portal on 2020. 10. 13. against the Namyangju City Culture and Education Bureau, stating specific facts and related suspicions, and attached various documents and media articles to support the claims.\\n\\n③ Violation of COVID-19 quarantine guidelines: according to the quarantine guidelines at the time, as the quarantine standard in the metropolitan area was raised to Level 2 from 2020. 8. 19., assemblies, meetings, and events subject to a gathering ban could be held indoors with fewer than 50 persons; however, even in such cases, a distance of 2m (minimum 1m) between users within the facility had to be maintained. According to photographs in media articles reporting the statement release at the time, it can be seen that attendees did not observe 2m distancing.\\n\\n④ Appropriateness of the budget payment decision by the Administrative Mediation Committee: a former chief political secretary of Namyangju City provided the Respondent’s side with a comparatively specific tip-off that \"the Administrative Mediation Committee is scheduled to be convened tomorrow (Friday) to deliberate on using the Mayor’s legal fees from the city budget,\" and in light of the identity of the tip-off source as a former chief political secretary, there is a reasonable basis for the Respondent to have highly assessed the credibility of the tip-off.\\n\\n⑤ The second change to the metropolitan area development restriction zone management plan for 2021 (Wolmun Sewage Treatment Plant) and⑥ the restoration project for damaged areas in three zones, including 172-44 Saneung-ri, Jingeon-eup, Namyangju City: the contents of two review reports prepared and reported by the Respondent’s relevant department regarding the legality of the projects are considerably specific and based on objective materials.\\n\\n⑥ Suspicion of preferential treatment in the purchase of public property\\n\\n㉠ Regarding Namyangju Palace House: in light of the circumstances that a tip-off was received that there had been preferential treatment related thereto, while the Petitioner accepted the donation and transfer of Namyangju Palace House and purchased a significant area of surrounding land and fixtures, the Respondent could sufficiently suspect the circumstances under which the Petitioner came to purchase the surrounding land, etc., whether the purchase price was appropriate, and whether there was in fact preferential treatment in the process. It should be deemed possible for the Respondent to commence the audit and investigate the contract contents and the appraisal reports that formed the basis for evaluating the purchase price, thereby verifying whether the raised suspicion is true.\\n\\n㉡ Regarding the wedding hall: the suspected misconduct concerning the purchase of the wedding hall building was reported in the media with comparatively specific and detailed content, and subsequently a tip-off concerning preferential purchase of Namyangju Palace House was received. In light of these circumstances, which allowed doubts to arise concerning the suspicion related to the purchase of the wedding hall building, also involving a purchase of private property of the same type, it should be deemed that the Respondent had verified illegality to the degree required to commence the audit. Although, prior to commencement of the audit in this case, the Respondent’s side had received from the Petitioner’s side appraisal materials and a purchase (agreement) review report related to the purchase of the wedding hall building, the suspicion had not been confirmed to be untrue by the time the audit in this case commenced, and since a tip-off concerning Namyangju Palace House was received and the Respondent proceeded with an audit thereon while also including the wedding hall building as an audit subject in order to examine in detail whether there was illegality in the purchase process, it cannot be said that a separate new illegality had to be confirmed in that process.\\n\\n⑦ Appropriateness of the construction permit (change) for Wolmun-ri, Wabu-eup, Namyangju City: the contents of the resident audit petition filed by residents around the relevant land specifically cite the relevant statutes, Supreme Court precedents, etc., and are quite detailed.\\n\\n(4) Sub-conclusion\\n\\nAs reviewed above, among the audit in this case, the audit of Audit Items 1 through 8 satisfied the requirement for commencement of the audit because the audit subject matter was specified at the time of commencement and there was also verification, to the degree necessary to commence the audit, of whether there had been a violation of statutes and regulations; however, the audit of Audit Items 9 through 14 did not satisfy the requirement for commencement of the audit because the audit subject matter was not specified or because a relation to the originally specified audit subject matter was not recognized.\\n\\nIn this way, only the audit of Audit Items 9 through 14 among the audit in this case failed to satisfy the requirement for commencement of the audit; absent special circumstances such as that the audit of those items was the main purpose of the audit in this case and the audit of Audit Items 1 through 8 was merely incidental, it is reasonable to regard only the audit of Audit Items 9 through 14 among the audit in this case as unlawful.\\n\\n6.
