Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, among the audit of each item listed in the [Appendix 1] list that the Respondent conducted against the Petitioner from 2020. 11. 16. to 2020. 12. 7., the audit of each item listed in serial numbers 9 through 14 is an unlawful audit that failed to satisfy the requirement for commencement of the audit and thus infringed the Petitioner’s right to local autonomy guaranteed by the Constitution and the Local Autonomy Act; accordingly, the petition for adjudication on this part is well-founded and is granted, and the remaining petition is without merit and is dismissed. This decision accords with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, except for the separate opinion of Justice Lee Seon-ae, Justice Lee Jong-seok, and Justice Lee Young-jin regarding each item listed in serial numbers 9 through 14 of the [Appendix 1] list, and the dissenting opinion regarding each item listed in serial numbers 1 through 8 of the [Appendix 1] list, as set forth in 7 below.\\n\\n7. Separate Opinion and Dissenting Opinion of Justices Lee Seon-ae, Lee Jong-seok, and Lee Young-jin\\n\\na. We think that the investigative acts conducted by the Respondent from 2020. 11. 16. to 2020. 12. 7., after notifying the Petitioner on 2020. 11. 11. that it would commence an investigation into \"matters suspected from media reports, resident audit petition and anonymous reports, etc.,\" infringed the Petitioner’s right to local autonomy guaranteed by the Constitution and the Local Autonomy Act. Our opinion, if recast by reference to the majority opinion, may be indicated as a separate opinion regarding each item listed in serial numbers 9 through 14 of [Appendix 1] and as a dissenting opinion regarding each item listed in serial numbers 1 through 8 of [Appendix 1]. We state our reasons below as follows.\\n\\nb. Case Overview\\n\\n(1) On 2020. 11. 11., the Respondent notified the Petitioner of the \"notice of commencement of investigation\"<FOOTNOTE1> with the following content (hereinafter referred to as \"the notice of commencement of investigation in this case\").\\n<TABLE2>\\nAfter the notice of commencement of investigation in this case, the Respondent’s investigative team conducted an investigation into the affairs of Namyangju City from 2020. 11. 16. (hereinafter referred to as \"the investigative acts in this case\"<FOOTNOTE2>).\\n\\n(2) Meanwhile, on 2020. 11. 17., the Respondent additionally announced through a press release the period and content of the investigative acts in this case as follows (the original text is in [Appendix 3-1]).\\n<TABLE3>\\n\\nIn addition, in response to media reports by the Petitioner criticizing the investigative acts in this case as retaliatory administration, the Respondent, through an explanatory statement on 2020. 11. 18., explained that the investigative acts in this case were based on the \"Act on Public Sector Audits\" (hereinafter referred to as the \"Public Audit Act\") as follows (the original text is in [Appendix 3-2]).<FOOTNOTE3>\\n<TABLE4>\\n\\n(3) On 2020. 11. 23., the Petitioner refused the Respondent’s investigation and notified the investigators to withdraw, on the ground that the investigative acts in this case were unlawful both procedurally and substantively.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Respondent issued, on 2020. 11. 23., a press release and a statement titled \"Statement by Inspector Kim Hee-su Regarding the Special Investigation of Namyangju City,\" expressly stating the period, legal basis, and reasons for conducting the investigative acts in this case as follows (the original text is in [Appendix 3-3]).\\n<TABLE5>\\n\\n(4) The Petitioner filed this petition for adjudication on a jurisdictional dispute on 2020. 11. 26., alleging that the investigative acts in this case infringed the Petitioner’s right to local autonomy because they were conducted as part of an audit without satisfying the requirements for conducting an audit of autonomous affairs of a local government under Article 171 of the Local Autonomy Act. On the same day, the Petitioner also filed an application for a provisional disposition suspending effectiveness (2020HEONSA1191), seeking a decision that \"the effect of the notice of commencement of investigation in this case shall be suspended until the pronouncement of the final decision on the petition for adjudication on the jurisdictional dispute.\"\\n\\n(5) In the end, the investigative acts in this case were conducted from 2020. 11. 16. to 2020. 12. 7. regarding the following matters.\\n<TABLE6>\\n\\n(6) The Respondent terminated the investigation on 2020. 12. 7., stating that substantive investigative progress had become difficult because the Petitioner’s representative mayor declared a \"refusal to cooperate with the audit\" and instructed city public officials to \"stop undergoing the Gyeonggi-do audit,\" and notified that as to matters not processed in this investigation, a separate plan would be established and pursued in the future (see Respondent’s Exhibit No. 2). Accordingly, the Petitioner withdrew the above application in 2020HEONSA1191 on 2020. 12. 8.\\n\\n(7) Meanwhile, on 2020. 12. 30., the Respondent filed a criminal complaint with the Uijeongbu District Prosecutors’ Office on the ground that the act of the Petitioner’s representative mayor directing affiliated public officials to refuse the investigative acts in this case and the act of the Petitioner’s affiliated audit inspector team leader refusing to submit materials constituted, respectively, the crimes of abuse of authority and obstruction of the exercise of rights and dereliction of duty.\\n\\nc. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe subject matter of review in this case is whether the investigative acts conducted by the Respondent from 2020. 11. 16. to 2020. 12. 7., after notifying the Petitioner on 2020. 11. 11. that it would commence an investigation into \"matters suspected from media reports, resident audit petition and anonymous reports, etc.,\" infringed the Petitioner’s right to local autonomy guaranteed by the Constitution and the Local Autonomy Act.\\n\\nd. Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments and the Respondent’s Answer\\n\\n(1) Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\nThe investigative acts in this case were conducted as part of an audit. However, before conducting an audit of autonomous affairs, the Respondent did not verify whether the relevant affairs violated statutes and regulations, and thus violated Article 171, paragraph (2) of the Local Autonomy Act.\\n\\nWhen commencing the investigative acts in this case as part of an audit, the Respondent specified only \"matters suspected from media reports, resident audit petition and anonymous reports, etc.\" as the investigative subject matter, and specified the investigative period as \"2020. 11. 16. ~ until completion of the investigation,\" notifying the Petitioner of the commencement of investigation in this case. This is unlawful as a comprehensive and prior general audit conducted on the Petitioner’s autonomous affairs, or as an audit commenced without specifying unlawful matters, or as an audit for detecting violations of statutes and regulations.\\n\\nIn addition, due to the notice of commencement of investigation in this case, the Petitioner could not proceed with disciplinary or punitive grounds against its affiliated public officials concerning the affairs under investigation pursuant to Article 24 of the Public Audit Act and Article 24 of the Gyeonggi-do Audit Rules. Since the audit subject matter was not specified, no disciplinary or punitive action could be taken against all affiliated public officials.\\n\\nIn light of the above circumstances, the investigative acts in this case infringe the Petitioner’s right to local autonomy.\\n\\n(2) Summary of the Respondent’s Answer\\n\\nSince the investigative acts in this case ended on 2020. 12. 7. without being normally carried out due to the Petitioner’s non-cooperation and refusal to provide materials, the state of infringement of rights suffered by the Petitioner as a result of the investigative acts in this case has ended, and the petition is inadmissible for lack of the interest in legal protection.\\n\\nThe subjects of the audit commenced by the investigative acts in this case were, among the Petitioner’s affairs, ① suspicion of preferential treatment in the Yangjeong Station Area development project, ② unfairness in the selection of a business operator for the Namyangju City arts club competition, ③ suspicion of preferential treatment in the purchase of public property, ④ whether the construction permit (change) for Wolmun-ri was appropriate, and ⑤ whether there was a violation of COVID-19 quarantine guidelines. These were matters as to which the possibility of violation of statutes and regulations had already been internally specified by the Respondent; it merely did not notify the Petitioner in advance of the specific audit subject matter in order to ensure the effectiveness of the audit. In addition, when the actual audit commenced, the Respondent’s investigative team informed the Petitioner of the audit items and requested the relevant materials, so there was no situation in which the Petitioner underwent an audit without knowing the audit items.\\n\\nSince the Respondent planned and conducted the audit concerning specific and identified unlawful conduct based on media reports, anonymous tip-offs, etc., it does not constitute a general and comprehensive audit, and there is no room to conclude that it infringed the Petitioner’s right to local autonomy as a lawful audit.\\n\\ne. Determination on the Admissibility Requirements\\n\\nSince the Respondent terminated the investigative acts in this case on 2020. 12. 7., the state of infringement of rights arising therefrom has already ended.\\n\\nHowever, as with constitutional complaints, adjudication on a jurisdictional dispute also serves the function of securing the objective constitutional order as well as providing subjective relief of rights, so even if the state of infringement of rights against the Petitioner has already ended and there is no room for cancellation, where there is a risk that the same type of infringement will recur in the future and where constitutional clarification thereof is essential for the protection and maintenance of the constitutional order, the interest in adjudication may be recognized (see Constitutional Court, 2003. 10. 30. 2002HEONRA1; Constitutional Court, 2009. 5. 28. 2006HEONRA6).\\n\\nThe Respondent notified the Petitioner that the investigation pursuant to the notice of commencement of investigation in this case could no longer proceed due to the Petitioner’s non-cooperation and refusal to provide materials, and that the investigation was terminated, but at the same time stated that it would \"establish and pursue a separate plan in the future regarding matters not processed in this investigation\"; thus, the risk that the same type of infringement will recur in the future is recognized.\\n\\nArticle 171, paragraph (1) of the former Local Autonomy Act (amended by Act No. 14839 on 2017. 7. 26., and wholly amended by Act No. 17893 on 2021. 1. 12.; hereinafter referred to as the \"former Local Autonomy Act\"), which is the basis provision for audits of autonomous affairs, directly incorporated Article 158<FOOTNOTE4> of the former Local Autonomy Act (amended by Act No. 4741 on 1994. 3. 16., and before amendment by Act No. 8423 on 2007. 5. 11.; hereinafter referred to as \"Article 158 of the former Local Autonomy Act\"), and there was a Constitutional Court decision in 2006HEONRA6 concerning the scope and method of audits under Article 158 of the former Local Autonomy Act. However, since that decision concerned the audit by the head of a central administrative agency over a local government, and taking into account that the relevant statutes were amended, including the newly inserted Article 171, paragraph (2) of the former Local Autonomy Act in accordance with the purport of that decision, additional constitutional clarification is necessary regarding the scope and method of audits by a metropolitan local government over the autonomous affairs of a basic local government under the amended law.\\n\\nIn particular, in this case, the Respondent disputes that the audit subject matter was lawfully specified internally in relation to the investigative acts in this case, and only the advance notification thereof to the Petitioner was omitted. Thus, in addition to the scope and method of audit addressed by the Constitutional Court in 2006HEONRA6, clarification regarding the specification of audit subjects required to commence an audit of autonomous affairs and the notification thereof is essential; therefore, the interest in adjudication may exceptionally be recognized.\\n\\nf. Determination on the Merits\\n\\n(1) Constitutional Court Precedent\\n\\nIn its decision of 2009. 5. 28. 2006HEONRA6, the Constitutional Court held that \"the Constitution, in Articles 117 and 118, institutionally guarantees the 'autonomy of local governments,' and the essential content of that guarantee is the guarantee of the local government itself, the guarantee of autonomous functions, and the guarantee of autonomous affairs (see Constitutional Court, 1994. 12. 29. 94HEONMA201). Among the autonomy guaranteed institutionally under the Constitution, it may be considered to include the authority not to receive orders or instructions from other administrative entities with respect to the expediency of performing autonomous affairs. Whereas delegated affairs are national affairs entrusted to and handled by local governments (Article 156 of the former Local Autonomy Act), autonomous affairs are affairs handled by local governments for the welfare of residents (see the first sentence of Article 117, paragraph (1) of the Constitution) and are affairs whose handling and method may be decided under their own responsibility within the scope of statutes and regulations; because they are the minimum essential aspect of local autonomy, guaranteeing local autonomy means that at least this autonomy of autonomous affairs must not be infringed. In order for a local government to commence an audit of autonomous affairs, there must be a case in which a specific violation of statutes and regulations concerning autonomous affairs has been identified or there is a reasonable suspicion that unlawful conduct occurred, and the audit subject matter must also be specified. Accordingly, a general, comprehensive audit, an audit commenced without specifying unlawful matters, or an audit for detecting violations of statutes and regulations cannot all be permitted. This is because if an audit is conducted to determine whether there has been a violation of statutes and regulations and no unlawful matter is discovered, then although it was not a violation of statutes and regulations, an audit would nevertheless have been conducted, and in the end it would amount to an audit of expediency over the autonomous affairs of a local government, while in substance being an audit of expediency.\"\\n\\n(2) Relevant Statutory Provisions\\n\\n(a) Verification of affairs violating statutes and regulations\\n\\nArticle 171, paragraph (1) of the former Local Autonomy Act limits the scope of audits of autonomous affairs of local governments that may be conducted by the Minister of the Interior and Safety or a Mayor/Provincial Governor only to matters violating statutes and regulations, and paragraph (2) of the same Article, reflecting the purport of the Constitutional Court’s decision in 2006HEONRA6, expressly imposes the duty on the Minister of the Interior and Safety or a Mayor/Provincial Governor to verify whether the handling of the relevant affairs violates statutes and regulations before conducting an audit of autonomous affairs of a local government.\\n\\nIn addition, Article 7, paragraph (2) of the former \"Administrative Audit Regulations on Local Governments\" (amended by Presidential Decree No. 28211 on 2017. 7. 26., and before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 32223 on 2021. 12. 16.; hereinafter referred to as the \"former Administrative Audit Regulations\") provides for prior investigation to implement Article 171, paragraph (2) of the former Local Autonomy Act. That is, before conducting an audit pursuant to Article 171, paragraph (2) of the former Local Autonomy Act, the Minister of the Interior and Safety or a Mayor/Provincial Governor may perform, where deemed necessary to verify whether the handling of autonomous affairs of the local government violates statutes and regulations, the following tasks: ① where information is collected from persons belonging to the relevant local government, complainants, or other third parties that the relevant local government’s handling of affairs violates statutes and regulations, review of documents or ledgers, etc. to ascertain the facts (Article 7, paragraph (2), subparagraph 1 of the former Administrative Audit Regulations); ② review of documents or ledgers, etc. to ascertain the facts of matters publicized by newspapers, broadcasting, or other media or information and communications media as indicating that the relevant local government’s handling of affairs violates statutes and regulations (Article 7, paragraph (2), subparagraph 2 of the former Administrative Audit Regulations); ③ review of documents or ledgers, etc. of affairs that are among the autonomous affairs of the relevant local government, in relation to specific fields, where there are data received and data entered into the relevant local government’s information system and substantial grounds to suspect violations of statutes and regulations (Article 7, paragraph (2), subparagraph 3 of the former Administrative Audit Regulations).\\n\\n(b) Establishment and notification or consultation of audit plans\\n\\nArticles 4, paragraphs (1) and (2) of the \"Administrative Audit Regulations on Local Governments\" (amended by Presidential Decree No. 28211 on 2017. 7. 26.; hereinafter referred to as the \"Administrative Audit Regulations\") provide that, where the competent Minister, the Minister of the Interior and Safety, or a Mayor/Provincial Governor intends to conduct an audit, an annual audit plan must be established in advance, and even where the audit is not included in the annual audit plan, a separate audit plan shall be established. Such audit plan shall include: ① audit matters; ② purpose and necessity of the audit; ③ type of audit and local government subject to the audit; ④ scope of the audit; ⑤ audit period (the period for carrying out audit activities and the period for determining requests for disciplinary sanctions or other measures to be included in the audit results pursuant to Article 18, paragraph (2)) and number of auditors; ⑥ other matters necessary for the audit.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 4, paragraph (3) of the Administrative Audit Regulations provides that, where the competent Minister or a Mayor/Provincial Governor establishes or changes the above audit plan, the Minister of the Interior and Safety must be notified without delay. In addition, Article 6, paragraph (1) of the Administrative Audit Regulations provides that, when the competent Minister, the Minister of the Interior and Safety, or a Mayor/Provincial Governor has established an annual audit plan or changed the main contents thereof, consultation with the Board of Audit and Inspection is required, and paragraph (2) of the same Article provides that the Minister of the Interior and Safety may review whether there is overlap with other audits concerning an audit plan separately established by the competent Minister or a Mayor/Provincial Governor from the annual audit plan and may present his or her opinion to the relevant competent Minister.\\n\\n(c) Notification to the local government subject to the audit\\n\\nAccording to Article 5 of the Administrative Audit Regulations, the competent Minister, the Minister of the Interior and Safety, or a Mayor/Provincial Governor shall notify the head of the local government subject to the audit of the main contents of the annual audit plan by January 31 of each year, and if the plan is changed thereafter, the changed contents shall be notified without delay to the head of the local government subject to the audit. However, this shall not apply where there are urgent circumstances requiring the audit to proceed promptly or where it is unavoidable to ensure the effectiveness of the audit.\\n\\nIn addition, Article 7, paragraph (3) of the former Administrative Audit Regulations provides that, if the Minister of the Interior and Safety or a Mayor/Provincial Governor, as a result of performing the tasks under Article 7, paragraph (2) of the former Administrative Audit Regulations,<FOOTNOTE5> has substantial grounds to suspect that the handling of autonomous affairs of the relevant local government violates statutes and regulations or has been in violation thereof, the relevant affairs shall be specified as audit subjects and the audit schedule, etc. shall be notified in advance to the head of the relevant local government.\\n\\nAccording to the practical manual for audits by the Ministry of the Interior and Safety concerning autonomous affairs of local governments conducted on the basis of Article 171 of the Local Autonomy Act [Ministry of the Interior and Safety, December 2018, Practical Manual by Audit (Inspection) Stage for Human Rights Emphasis and Enhancement of Audit Reliability, hereinafter referred to as the \"Audit Practice Manual\"], the audit notice to the local government subject to the audit is to include the list of autonomous affairs to be audited so that the audit subject matter is specified at the time of notification (see page 75 of the Audit Practice Manual). In addition, it explains that if, during the course of the audit, a new unlawful autonomous affair is discovered other than the affairs specified as audit subjects, the audit cannot simply proceed with respect to such new matter, and the audit becomes possible only after notifying the audit institution of the target agency, specifying the relevant unlawful matter, in accordance with the procedures under the relevant statutes and regulations, and then issuing an audit commencement notice (see pages 161-162 of the Audit Practice Manual).\\n\\n(3) Organization of the Issues\\n\\nThere is no dispute between the Petitioner and the Respondent that the investigative acts in this case were carried out as part of an audit of autonomous affairs of a local government prescribed by Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act. Therefore, the issue is whether the investigative acts in this case satisfy the requirements for commencement of an audit of autonomous affairs of a local government derived from the purport of the Constitutional Court’s decision in 2006HEONRA6 and from the legislative purpose and interpretation of Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act.\\n\\n(4) Requirements for Commencement of an Audit of Autonomous Affairs of a Local Government\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court has confirmed that, in order for the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs under Article 158 of the former Local Autonomy Act to commence an audit of a local government, there must be a case in which a specific violation of statutes and regulations concerning autonomous affairs has been identified or there is a reasonable suspicion that unlawful conduct occurred, and the audit subject matter must be specified; accordingly, a general, comprehensive audit, an audit commenced without specifying unlawful matters, or an audit for detecting violations of statutes and regulations cannot all be permitted (see Constitutional Court, 2009. 5. 28. 2006HEONRA6).\\n\\nThe content of Article 171, paragraph (1) of the former Local Autonomy Act, which is the basis provision for the investigative acts in this case as part of an audit, directly incorporates the content of Article 158 of the former Local Autonomy Act; and considering that control by a metropolitan local government is also akin to administrative control by the government, and that while control by the government is basically directed toward metropolitan local governments, control by a metropolitan local government is directed toward basic local governments, the difference lies only in the object of control, while the basis provisions and legislative purpose are the same, the requirements for commencement of an audit of autonomous affairs elucidated in the above Constitutional Court decision also apply here. Accordingly, in order for the Respondent to commence an audit of the Petitioner’s autonomous affairs, there must be a case in which a specific violation of statutes and regulations concerning autonomous affairs has been identified or there is a reasonable suspicion that unlawful conduct occurred, and the audit subject matter must be specified; an audit commenced without specifying unlawful matters or an audit for detecting violations of statutes and regulations cannot all be permitted.\\n\\nIn addition, Article 171, paragraph (2) of the former Local Autonomy Act, which prescribes the duty to verify whether the handling of the relevant autonomous affairs violates statutes and regulations before conducting an audit, reflects the purport of the above Constitutional Court decision and is intended to secure the autonomy of autonomous affairs and prevent a general, comprehensive audit, an audit commenced without specifying unlawful matters, or an audit for detecting violations of statutes and regulations, thereby disallowing an audit of expediency concerning autonomous affairs. Therefore, an audit of autonomous affairs conducted in violation of the above provision also cannot be permitted.\\n\\nFurthermore, in order to secure the constitutionally guaranteed autonomy of local governments, it is reasonable to interpret that, before commencing an audit of violations of statutes and regulations concerning the autonomous affairs of a local government, the audit subject matter must not only be specified, but the head of the local government subject to the audit must also be notified, before the audit is conducted, of the commencement of the audit by specifying the audit subject matter; if this is violated, it cannot be permitted as a notice of commencement of a general, comprehensive audit, an audit commenced without specifying unlawful matters, or an audit for detecting violations of statutes and regulations.\\n\\n(5) Failure to Verify Violations of Statutes and Regulations Concerning the Audit Subject Matter\\n\\n(a) In order to commence an audit of the autonomous affairs of a local government, there must be a case in which a specific violation of statutes and regulations concerning autonomous affairs has been identified or there is a reasonable suspicion that unlawful conduct occurred, and the audit subject matter must be specified. Considering the purport of the Constitutional Court’s decision in 2006HEONRA6 and the content of Article 171, paragraph (2) of the former Local Autonomy Act newly enacted accordingly,<FOOTNOTE6> together with the content of Article 7, paragraph (2) of the former Administrative Audit Regulations,<FOOTNOTE7> even if there are autonomous affairs identified through reports, media coverage, etc. as suspected to be unlawful, conducting an audit merely on the ground that the reported or publicized content itself contains a vague possibility of illegality cannot be deemed to satisfy the audit commencement requirements required by the statute.\\n\\nGiven the legal duty under Article 171, paragraph (2) of the former Local Autonomy Act to verify whether the handling of the relevant affairs violates statutes and regulations before conducting the audit, the Respondent must form a reasonable suspicion concerning the unlawfulness of the handling of affairs based on objective grounds; if necessary, the Respondent must ascertain the facts through prior investigation and verify whether there has been a violation of statutes and regulations, and the mere fact that suspicions have been raised cannot be said to constitute such verification.\\n\\n(b) According to the record of this case, the Respondent established, on 2020. 11. 10., the \"Special Investigation Plan for Suspicions of Preferential Treatment in Namyangju Projects, etc.\" (hereinafter referred to as \"the audit plan in this case\"), which stipulated as \"major audit subjects\" the following matters among the affairs: \"① suspicion of preferential treatment in the Yangjeong Station Area development project, ② unfair selection of a business operator for the Namyangju City arts club competition, ③ violation of COVID-19 quarantine guidelines, ④ appropriateness of the budget payment decision by the Administrative Mediation Committee, ⑤ change to the development restriction zone management plan, ⑥ restoration project for damaged areas in the development restriction zone, ⑦ suspicion of preferential treatment in the purchase of public property, ⑧ appropriateness of the construction permit (change), ⑨ other media reports, on-site tip-offs, etc.\" Thereafter, while conducting the investigative acts in this case, the Respondent additionally carried out audits on ㉠ comment operations by the public relations team, ㉡ improper hiring of anti-smoking monitors, ㉢ issues concerning the exercise of personnel authority (Namyangju City special-position personnel appointments, designation of the head of the Namyangju City Welfare Foundation), ㉣ correction of press releases, and ㉤ affairs related to the Eco Land baseball field (hereinafter collectively referred to as \"the affairs subject to audit in this case\"), which were not specifically listed among the major audit subjects.\\n\\nHowever, among the affairs subject to audit in this case, with respect to ③ violation of COVID-19 quarantine guidelines, ④ appropriateness of the budget payment decision by the Administrative Mediation Committee, ⑦ suspicion of preferential treatment in the purchase of public property, ㉠ comment operations by the public relations team, ㉡ improper hiring of anti-smoking monitors, ㉢ issues concerning the exercise of personnel authority (Namyangju City special-position personnel appointments, designation of the head of the Namyangju City Welfare Foundation), ㉣ correction of press releases, and ㉤ the Eco Land baseball field, it is difficult to recognize that specific facts and unlawful matters had been grasped to the extent that a reasonable suspicion concerning unlawful conduct was formed merely from related tip-offs or media reports without verification of additional facts.\\n\\nWith respect to ③ violation of COVID-19 quarantine guidelines, although the Respondent argued that there had been a violation of COVID-19 quarantine guidelines on the basis of a group photograph in media reports showing all attendees wearing masks, it failed to specify which laws and guidelines were violated and in what manner; thus, it is judged that the investigative acts in this case were commenced as part of the audit based only on a vague suspicion of illegality.\\n\\nWith respect to ④ the appropriateness of the budget payment decision by the Administrative Mediation Committee, the Respondent commenced the investigative acts in this case as part of the audit based solely on the brief tip-off that the Administrative Mediation Committee planned to resolve payment of the Mayor’s legal fees from the city budget, without even a minimal understanding of the specific facts or whether the administrative mediation committee decision actually existed, or of the truth or falsity thereof.\\n\\nWith respect to ⑦ suspicion of preferential treatment in the purchase of public property, the Respondent commenced the investigative acts in this case as part of the audit based solely on media reports concerning real estate purchases and an anonymous tip-off containing only a brief statement that preferential treatment had occurred; however, even from the materials submitted by the Respondent, it is difficult to acknowledge that verification was made regarding the facts, the truth or falsity of the suspicion, or the specific content of the statutory violations.\\n\\nWith respect to ㉠ comment operations by the public relations team, the Respondent argued that, based on a tip-off from a Namyangju employee that employees of the public relations team had written favorable comments about Namyangju City, the issues concerned violations of the duty of fairness, duty to maintain dignity, and prohibition of political campaigning under the Local Public Officials Act; however, it is difficult to reasonably recognize the possibility of unlawful conduct merely from the act of writing comments itself.\\n\\nWith respect to ㉡ improper hiring of anti-smoking monitors, there was an anonymous tip-off that a person who did not satisfy the qualification requirements had been hired, but absent any verification whatsoever regarding the truth or falsity of that tip-off or the factual circumstances, it is difficult to regard the content of the tip-off alone as forming a reasonable suspicion of illegality.\\n\\nWith respect to ㉢ issues concerning the exercise of personnel authority (Namyangju City special-position personnel appointments), there was also a tip-off from a Namyangju employee regarding improper transfer personnel management, but absent any verification whatsoever regarding the truth or falsity of that tip-off or the factual circumstances, it is difficult to regard the content of the tip-off alone as forming a reasonable suspicion of illegality.\\n\\nWith respect to the other ㉢ issues concerning the exercise of personnel authority (designation of the head of the Namyangju City Welfare Foundation), the Respondent argues that if the head had been designated as reported by the media, that would violate the procedures for appointing the head, etc.; however, without grasping the factual circumstances, such as the actual progress of the appointment process, the media report alone makes it difficult to reasonably recognize the possibility of unlawful conduct.\\n\\nWith respect to ㉣ correction of press releases, the Respondent argues, based on media articles concerning the Petitioner’s correction of a press release, that because the Petitioner corrected the content of the press release, it may be presumed that either the pre-correction or post-correction press release contained falsehoods, and thus an act constituting the crime of preparing false official documents; however, merely distributing a press release and later distributing a corrected press release that amends part of its content makes it difficult to reasonably recognize the possibility of unlawful conduct.\\n\\nWith respect to ㉤ affairs concerning the Eco Land baseball field, the Respondent argues that, regarding the creation and operation of a baseball field not included in the development restriction zone management plan, the issue is that follow-up measures are delayed in a matter for which criminal punishment and disciplinary action have already been completed; however, it is difficult to regard this as a case where unlawful matters requiring a renewed audit have been identified.\\n\\n(c) In this manner, with respect to ③ violation of COVID-19 quarantine guidelines, ④ appropriateness of the budget payment decision by the Administrative Mediation Committee, ⑦ suspicion of preferential treatment in the purchase of public property, ㉠ comment operations by the public relations team, ㉡ improper hiring of anti-smoking monitors, ㉢ issues concerning the exercise of personnel authority (Namyangju City special-position personnel appointments, designation of the head of the Namyangju City Welfare Foundation), ㉣ correction of press releases, and ㉤ affairs related to the Eco Land baseball field among the affairs subject to audit in this case, it is difficult to recognize that the Respondent fulfilled the duty to verify whether the handling of the relevant autonomous affairs violated statutes and regulations before conducting the investigative acts in this case as part of the audit, and thus it violated Article 171, paragraph (2) of the former Local Autonomy Act. This constitutes a general, comprehensive audit, an audit commenced without specifying unlawful matters, or an audit for detecting violations of statutes and regulations, and therefore cannot be permitted.\\n\\n(6) Failure to Specify the Audited Autonomous Affairs\\n\\n(a) As noted above, among the affairs subject to audit in this case, with respect to ③ violation of COVID-19 quarantine guidelines, ④ appropriateness of the budget payment decision by the Administrative Mediation Committee, ⑦ suspicion of preferential treatment in the purchase of public property, ㉠ comment operations by the public relations team, ㉡ improper hiring of anti-smoking monitors, ㉢ issues concerning the exercise of personnel authority (Namyangju City special-position personnel appointments, designation of the head of the Namyangju City Welfare Foundation), ㉣ correction of press releases, and ㉤ affairs related to the Eco Land baseball field, absent recognition that the Respondent fulfilled the duty to verify whether the handling of the relevant affairs violated statutes and regulations before conducting the investigative acts in this case as part of the audit, it is difficult to regard those affairs as having been specified as audit subjects.\\n\\nIn addition, the affairs subject to audit in this case include comprehensive items (⑨ \"other media reports, on-site tip-offs, etc.\"), and thus cannot be regarded as having specified the audit subject matter. In fact, the contents of items ㉠ through ㉤ audited on the basis of the above comprehensive item are affairs entirely unrelated to items ① through ⑧ mentioned as major audit subjects in the audit plan in this case, and are new matters not contemplated in the audit plan in this case. This demonstrates that the major audit subjects in the audit plan in this case do not specify the affairs subject to audit.\\n\\n(b) The Respondent argues that even an affair not expressly stated in the audit plan in this case and specified after 2020. 11. 11., when the notice of commencement of investigation in this case was given, cannot be regarded as a comprehensive audit or a prior audit so long as it was audited concerning a specific affair, and thus should be regarded as an audit concerning a specific autonomous affair.\\n\\nHowever, on the premise that the point in time of \"conducting the audit\" under Article 171, paragraph (2) of the former Local Autonomy Act is the time when actual investigation into each individual affair subject to audit begins (requesting materials, questioning, etc.), such an interpretation that would allow continuous addition and expansion of entirely new audit subjects in the course of conducting an audit by specifying certain affairs as audit subjects cannot be accepted as not infringing the autonomy of autonomous affairs, which is an essential minimum aspect of local autonomy. Above all, in decision 2006HEONRA6, the Constitutional Court clearly stated that Article 158 of the former Local Autonomy Act must be interpreted in a manner expanding the autonomy of local governments and limiting audits of autonomous affairs by central administrative agencies in order to realize local autonomy; that, in order to commence an audit under Article 158 of the former Local Autonomy Act, there must be a case in which a specific violation of statutes and regulations concerning autonomous affairs has been identified or there is a reasonable suspicion that unlawful conduct occurred; and that the audit subject matter must be specified. The content of Article 171, paragraph (1) of the former Local Autonomy Act, which is the basis provision for the investigative acts in this case as part of an audit, directly incorporates the content of Article 158 of the former Local Autonomy Act interpreted in that decision, and, as noted above, the purport of that decision was reflected in the newly enacted Article 171, paragraph (2) of the former Local Autonomy Act. According to the former Local Autonomy Act, before conducting an audit of violations of statutes and regulations concerning autonomous affairs of a local government, the handling of the relevant affairs must be verified to determine whether it violates statutes and regulations, and the audit subject matter must thereby be specified. Even in light of this interpretation, the Respondent’s above argument cannot be accepted.\\n\\nReturning to this case, the Respondent can be regarded as having definitively decided, at the latest on 2020. 11. 11., when it notified the Petitioner of the commencement of the investigation in this case, to conduct an audit of the Petitioner’s autonomous affairs. Therefore, at least as of the time of that notice, verification of whether the handling of the relevant autonomous affairs violated statutes and regulations should have been made, and the audit subject matter should have been specified. If, by the time the local government subject to the audit was definitively informed that the audit would be conducted, verification of whether the handling of the relevant autonomous affairs violated statutes and regulations had not been made or the audit subject matter had not been specified, then this would amount to deciding first to conduct the audit of autonomous affairs and only thereafter specifying the audit subject matter, which would violate Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act and would constitute a general, comprehensive audit, an audit commenced without specifying unlawful matters, or an audit for detecting violations of statutes and regulations, and thus cannot be permitted.\\n\\n(c) In the end, among the affairs subject to audit in this case, ③ violation of COVID-19 quarantine guidelines, ④ appropriateness of the budget payment decision by the Administrative Mediation Committee, ⑦ suspicion of preferential treatment in the purchase of public property, ㉠ comment operations by the public relations team, ㉡ improper hiring of anti-smoking monitors, ㉢ issues concerning the exercise of personnel authority (Namyangju City special-position personnel appointments, designation of the head of the Namyangju City Welfare Foundation), ㉣ correction of press releases, and ㉤ affairs related to the Eco Land baseball field cannot be regarded as having been specified as audit subjects, because it is difficult to acknowledge that the duty to verify whether the handling of each relevant affair violated statutes and regulations was fulfilled before conducting the audit. In addition, the audit subject matters in this case include comprehensive affairs such as ⑨ \"other media reports, on-site tip-offs, etc.,\" and thus cannot be regarded as having specified the audit subject matter; in fact, the contents of items ㉠ through ㉤ audited on the basis of the above comprehensive item are affairs newly included after 2020. 11. 11., when the Respondent notified the Petitioner of the commencement of this investigation in this case, and are affairs entirely unrelated to items ① through ⑧ mentioned as major audit subjects in the audit plan in this case, so they also cannot be regarded as affairs specified as audit subjects. Accordingly, the investigative acts in this case, carried out as part of the audit without specifying the audit subject matter as above, violate Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act and cannot be permitted as they constitute a general, comprehensive audit, an audit commenced without specifying unlawful matters, or an audit for detecting violations of statutes and regulations.\\n\\n(7) Notice of Commencement of Audit Without Specifying the Audit Subject Matter\\n\\n(a) As noted above, with respect to audits of autonomous affairs of local governments, it is reasonable to interpret that, before conducting the audit, the handling of the relevant affairs must be verified as to whether it violates statutes and regulations so that the audit subject matter is specified; furthermore, there is no express provision in the Constitution, the Local Autonomy Act, or elsewhere as to whether, when commencing the audit, the head of the local government subject to the audit must be notified by specifying the audit subject matter.\\n\\nHowever, control by a metropolitan local government is also akin to administrative control by the government; while government control is basically directed toward metropolitan local governments, control by a metropolitan local government is directed toward basic local governments, and the difference lies only in the object of control, while the basis provisions and legislative purpose are the same. Taking this into account, a metropolitan local government, with respect to a basic local government, should likewise pursue legality supervision rather than expediency supervision, and given that arbitrary exercise of audit authority by a metropolitan local government is also highly likely to undermine the constitutionally guaranteed autonomy of a basic local government, in order to commence an audit of violations of statutes and regulations concerning the autonomous affairs of a local government, there must be a case in which a specific violation of statutes and regulations concerning autonomous affairs has been identified or there is a reasonable suspicion that unlawful conduct occurred, and not only must the audit subject matter be specified, but before the audit is conducted, the head of the local government subject to the audit must be notified of the commencement of the audit by specifying that audit subject matter.\\n\\nThis is because, if it were considered unnecessary to specify and notify the audit subject matter at the time of commencing the audit, the audit subject matter would become unclear and fluid, thereby easily circumventing the limits on audits of violations of statutes and regulations concerning autonomous affairs of local governments that were confirmed in the Constitutional Court’s decision in 2006HEONRA6 and reflected in Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act; that is, it would open the way to conducting an audit of expediency concerning autonomous affairs of local governments.\\n\\nIn addition, Article 5 of the Administrative Audit Regulations imposes the duty to notify the main contents of the annual audit plan to the head of the local government subject to the audit, except in cases of urgent circumstances requiring a prompt audit or unavoidable necessity to ensure the effectiveness of the audit; Article 171, paragraph (2) of the former Local Autonomy Act expressly provides that, before conducting an audit of violations of statutes and regulations concerning the autonomous affairs of a local government, the handling of the relevant affairs shall be verified as to whether it violates statutes and regulations; and Article 7, paragraphs (2) and (3) of the former Administrative Audit Regulations accordingly impose the duty that, if as a result of prior investigative work the handling of autonomous affairs is found to violate statutes and regulations or there are substantial grounds to suspect such violation, the relevant affairs shall be specified as audit subjects and the audit schedule, etc. shall be notified in advance to the head of the relevant local government. In addition, according to the Ministry of the Interior and Safety’s practical manual for audits of autonomous affairs of local governments conducted on the basis of Article 171 of the Local Autonomy Act [Ministry of the Interior and Safety, December 2018, Practical Manual by Audit (Inspection) Stage for Human Rights Emphasis and Enhancement of Audit Reliability, hereinafter referred to as the \"Audit Practice Manual\"], the audit notice to the local government subject to the audit is to include the list of autonomous affairs to be audited so that the audit subject matter is specified from the time of notification (see page 75 of the Audit Practice Manual); and furthermore, if, during the course of the audit, new unlawful autonomous affairs are discovered beyond the affairs specified as audit subjects, the audit cannot simply proceed with respect to such new matters, and the audit becomes possible only after the audit institution of the target agency is notified, specifying the relevant unlawful matters, in accordance with the procedures under the relevant statutes and regulations (see pages 161-162 of the Audit Practice Manual). Even in light of the purport of these relevant statutory provisions, the above interpretation is reasonable.\\n\\n(b) The only notice of commencement of the audit issued by the Respondent to the Petitioner is the notice of commencement of investigation in this case dated 2020. 11. 11. However, that notice merely describes the investigation content as \"matters suspected from media reports, resident audit petition and anonymous reports, etc.,\" and therefore did not specify at all what autonomous affairs of the Petitioner contained what unlawful matters; thus, it cannot be permitted as a general, comprehensive audit, an audit commenced without specifying unlawful matters, or an audit for detecting violations of statutes and regulations.\\n\\n(c) The Respondent argues that, because Article 5 of the Administrative Audit Regulations provides exceptions allowing omission of advance notification of the annual audit plan to the head of the local government subject to the audit, and because Article 7, paragraph (3) of the former Administrative Audit Regulations provides that the audit subject matter shall be specified and notified when prior investigation under paragraph (2) has been conducted, there is no duty to specify and notify the audit subject matter in advance when prior investigation is not conducted, as in the investigative acts in this case.\\n\\nHowever, as stated above, given the view that in order to commence an audit of violations of statutes and regulations concerning the autonomous affairs of a local government, there must be a case in which a specific violation of statutes and regulations concerning autonomous affairs has been identified or there is a reasonable suspicion that unlawful conduct occurred, and not only must the audit subject matter be specified, but before the audit is conducted, the head of the local government subject to the audit must be notified of the commencement of the audit by specifying that audit subject matter, one cannot avoid the above requirements for commencement of the audit merely on the ground that there is a provision establishing an exception permitting omission of advance notice of the annual audit plan to the head of the local government subject to the audit. In addition, if it were considered unnecessary to specify and notify the audit subject matter on the ground that prior investigation under Article 7, paragraph (2) of the former Administrative Audit Regulations was not conducted, this would deliberately circumvent the prior investigation system established to fulfill the duty to verify whether the handling of the relevant autonomous affairs violates statutes and regulations, and would result in bypassing the limits on audits of violations of statutes and regulations concerning the autonomous affairs discussed above; therefore, this argument cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(d) The Respondent argues that, by distributing a press release on 2020. 11. 17., it clearly revealed what the audit subject matter of the investigative acts in this case was. However, the Respondent’s press release cannot be regarded as an official notice to the Petitioner, nor can it be said that the Petitioner had a duty to ascertain the contents of that press release. Accordingly, the distribution of a press release by the Respondent cannot be deemed to constitute notification of the audit subject matter to the Petitioner.\\n\\n(8) Sub-conclusion\\n\\nTaking the above circumstances together, with respect to ③ violation of COVID-19 quarantine guidelines, ④ appropriateness of the budget payment decision by the Administrative Mediation Committee, ⑦ suspicion of preferential treatment in the purchase of public property, ㉠ comment operations by the public relations team, ㉡ improper hiring of anti-smoking monitors, ㉢ issues concerning the exercise of personnel authority (Namyangju City special-position personnel appointments, designation of the head of the Namyangju City Welfare Foundation), ㉣ correction of press releases, and ㉤ affairs related to the Eco Land baseball field among the affairs subject to audit in this case, it is difficult to recognize that the Respondent fulfilled the duty to verify whether the handling of the relevant autonomous affairs violated statutes and regulations before conducting the investigative acts in this case as part of the audit; for the same reasons, the above ③ violation of COVID-19 quarantine guidelines, ④ appropriateness of the budget payment decision by the Administrative Mediation Committee, ⑦ suspicion of preferential treatment in the purchase of public property, ㉠ comment operations by the public relations team, ㉡ improper hiring of anti-smoking monitors, ㉢ issues concerning the exercise of personnel authority (Namyangju City special-position personnel appointments, designation of the head of the Namyangju City Welfare Foundation), ㉣ correction of press releases, and ㉤ affairs related to the Eco Land baseball field cannot be regarded as having been specified as audit subjects. Furthermore, because the audit subject matters in this case include comprehensive affairs such as ⑨ \"other media reports, on-site tip-offs, etc.,\" the audit subject matter cannot be regarded as specified; and in fact, the contents of items ㉠ through ㉤, which were audited on the basis of the above comprehensive item, are affairs newly included after 2020. 11. 11., when the Respondent notified the Petitioner of the commencement of the investigation in this case, and are affairs entirely unrelated to items ① through ⑧ mentioned as major audit subjects in the audit plan in this case, so they also cannot be regarded as affairs specified as audit subjects. Moreover, because the notice of commencement of investigation in this case merely describes the investigation content as \"matters suspected from media reports, resident audit petition and anonymous reports, etc.,\" it does not at all specify what unlawful matters exist in respect of what autonomous affairs, and therefore the audit commencement cannot be regarded as having been notified to the head of the local government subject to the audit by specifying the audit subject matter before commencing the audit.\\n\\nUltimately, the investigative acts in this case, which were part of the audit, did not verify whether there had been specific violations of statutes and regulations before conducting the audit, did not specify the audit subject matter, and proceeded to commence the investigative acts as they were after merely informing the local government subject to the audit that an investigation into \"matters suspected from media reports, resident audit petition and anonymous reports, etc.\" was being commenced without specifying the audit subject matter. It is clear, therefore, that the audit was unlawful because it failed to satisfy the requirements for commencement of an audit of autonomous affairs of a local government, which are derived from the purport of the Constitution, under Articles 117 and 118, institutionally guaranteeing local autonomy, the purport of the Constitutional Court’s decision in 2006HEONRA6, and the legislative purpose of Article 171 of the former Local Autonomy Act. In light of this determination, it is unnecessary to further examine the Petitioner’s remaining arguments.\\n\\ng. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the investigative acts in this case conducted by the Respondent from 2020. 11. 16. to 2020. 12. 7. after notifying the Petitioner on 2020. 11. 11. that it would commence an investigation into \"matters suspected from media reports, resident audit petition and anonymous reports, etc.\" infringed the Petitioner’s right to local autonomy guaranteed by the Constitution and the Local Autonomy Act."}
