Case Summary\\n\\nThe Central Local Government Dispute Mediation Committee (hereinafter referred to as the “Dispute Mediation Committee”) adopted, on 2015. 10. 26., a resolution determining that Jeollabuk-do Buan-gun shall be the local government to which part of the reclaimed land in the section of the Saemangeum No. 1 Breakwater on public waters belongs, and that Jeollabuk-do Gimje-si shall be the local government to which the reclaimed land in the section of the Saemangeum No. 2 Breakwater on public waters belongs; and the then Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs (the title was changed from the “Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs” to the “Minister of the Interior and Safety.” Hereinafter, the term “Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs” is used uniformly) made, on 2015. 11. 13., a decision in accordance with the above resolution (hereinafter referred to as “the decision in this case”).\\n\\nThe Petitioner, being dissatisfied with the decision in this case, filed, on 2015. 11. 27., an action before the Supreme Court seeking revocation of the decision determining the local government to which part of the Saemangeum breakwater belongs, but it was dismissed and became final on 2021. 1. 14. (Supreme Court 2015CHU566).\\n\\nDuring the pendency of the lawsuit, the Petitioner applied for a request for a constitutional review of statutes, arguing that Article 4(3) of the former Local Autonomy Act (amended by Act No. 12844 on 2014. 11. 19., and prior to amendment by Act No. 14839 on 2017. 7. 26.; hereinafter referred to as the “former Local Autonomy Act”), which is the basis for the decision in this case, violates the Constitution; but that application was dismissed on 2021. 1. 14. (Supreme Court 2020KU516), and after receiving service of the written decision of dismissal on 2021. 1. 29., the Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint on 2021. 2. 26.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe Petitioner asserts that Article 4(3) of the former Local Autonomy Act is the subject matter of adjudication. However, because the decision in this case concerns the jurisdiction over reclaimed land under the Act on the Management and Reclamation of Public Waters, the subject matter of adjudication is limited to Article 4(3)1 of the former Local Autonomy Act. Accordingly, the subject matter of this adjudication is whether Article 4(3)1 of the former Local Autonomy Act (amended by Act No. 12844 on 2014. 11. 19., and prior to amendment by Act No. 14839 on 2017. 7. 26.; hereinafter referred to as the “provision under review”) violates the Constitution. The provision under review and the relevant provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision under review]\\n\\nFormer Local Autonomy Act (amended by Act No. 12844 on 2014. 11. 19., and prior to amendment by Act No. 14839 on 2017. 7. 26.)\\n\\nArticle 4 (Names and Areas of Local Governments) (3) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), the local government to which the following areas belong shall be determined by the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs in accordance with the provisions of paragraphs (4) through (7).\\n\\n1. Reclaimed land pursuant to the Act on the Management and Reclamation of Public Waters\\n\\n[Relevant provisions]\\n\\nFormer Local Autonomy Act (amended by Act No. 12844 on 2014. 11. 19., and prior to amendment by Act No. 14839 on 2017. 7. 26.)\\n\\nArticle 4 (Names and Areas of Local Governments) (1) The names and areas of local governments shall remain as before, and when changing the names and areas, or abolishing, establishing, dividing, or merging local governments, such matters shall be prescribed by Act. Provided, That changes to the boundaries of the jurisdictional districts of local governments and changes to Chinese-character names shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.\\n\\n(2) When abolishing, establishing, dividing, or merging local governments, or changing their names or areas pursuant to paragraph (1), the opinions of the local councils concerned (hereinafter referred to as “local councils”) shall be heard. Provided, That this shall not apply where a resident referendum has been held pursuant to Article 8 of the Resident Referendum Act.\\n\\n(3) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), the local government to which the following areas belong shall be determined by the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs in accordance with the provisions of paragraphs (4) through (7).\\n\\n1. Omitted\\n\\n2. Land whose registration in the cadastral register under Article 2(19) of the Act on the Establishment, Management, etc. of Spatial Data (hereinafter referred to as the “cadastral register”) has been omitted\\n\\n(4) In the case of paragraph (3)1, the licensing authority pursuant to Article 28 of the Act on the Management and Reclamation of Public Waters or the head of the relevant local government shall, before the completion inspection under Article 45 of the same Act; in the case of paragraph (3)2, the competent authority pursuant to Article 2(18) of the Act on the Establishment, Management, etc. of Spatial Data (hereinafter referred to as the “cadastral competent authority”) shall, before registering such land in the cadastral register, apply to the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs for a determination of the local government to which the relevant area belongs. In this case, a person who has obtained a reclamation license for reclaimed land under paragraph (3)1 may request the licensing authority to apply for a determination of the local government to which the relevant reclaimed land belongs.\\n\\n(5) After receiving the application under paragraph (4), the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs shall, without delay, widely notify the public of that fact through the Official Gazette or the Internet, etc. for at least 20 days. In this case, with respect to the method of notification, submission of opinions, etc., Articles 42, 44, and 45 of the Administrative Procedures Act shall apply mutatis mutandis.\\n\\n(6) After the period under paragraph (5) has elapsed, the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs shall determine, in accordance with the deliberation and resolution of the Central Local Government Dispute Mediation Committee under Article 149 (hereinafter referred to as the “Committee” in this Article), the local government to which each area under paragraph (3) belongs, and shall notify the licensing authority or cadastral competent authority, the heads of the relevant local governments, etc., of the result and publicly announce it.\\n\\n(7) If the Chairperson of the Committee deems it necessary in the course of deliberation under paragraph (6), he or she may require public officials of the relevant central administrative agencies and local governments, or related experts, to appear and hear their opinions, or may request the relevant institutions or organizations to submit materials and opinions, etc. In this case, the heads of the relevant local governments shall be given an opportunity to state their opinions.\\n\\n(8) If the head of the relevant local government is dissatisfied with the decision of the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs under paragraphs (3) through (7), he or she may file a lawsuit with the Supreme Court within 15 days from the date of notification of the result.\\n\\n(9) If there is a decision of acceptance by the Supreme Court pursuant to paragraph (8), the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs shall make a new decision in accordance with the purport thereof.\\n\\n3. Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\nA. Although Article 4(1) of the former Local Autonomy Act provides that when changing the area of a local government, such change shall be prescribed by Act, the provision under review allows the determination of the attribution of reclaimed land under the Act on the Management and Reclamation of Public Waters (hereinafter referred to as “reclaimed land on public waters”), which causes a change in area merely by decision of the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs (substantively, the Dispute Mediation Committee), thereby infringing local self-government rights under the Constitution.\\n\\nB. Article 4(2) of the former Local Autonomy Act provides that, when changing the area of a local government, the opinion of the local council shall be heard or a resident referendum under the Resident Referendum Act shall be held. However, the provision under review does not provide for such procedures despite the fact that the areas of the relevant local governments have changed due to the reclamation of public waters, thereby infringing the autonomous authority of local governments.\\n\\nC. Because the provision under review does not prescribe substantive criteria for determining the local government to which reclaimed land on public waters belongs, it fails to prevent arbitrary decisions by the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs, and to allow the jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters to be determined solely by the decision of the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs violates the principle of statutory reservation and results in an unconstitutional consequence akin to a blank delegation.\\n\\nD. Due to the provision under review, the electoral rights, eligibility to hold public office, freedom of residence and movement, etc. of residents living near reclaimed land on public waters were infringed.\\n\\n4. Determination\\n\\nA. Organization of Issues\\n\\n(1) The Petitioner argues that the provision under review, by ① not providing for the procedure of hearing the opinion of the local council or holding a resident referendum as prescribed in Article 4(2) of the former Local Autonomy Act, and by allowing the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters to be determined solely by the decision of the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs rather than by statute, infringes the local self-government rights of the relevant local governments; and ② failing to prescribe at all substantive criteria for determining the local government to which reclaimed land on public waters belongs, violates the principle of statutory reservation. We therefore make a determination thereon.\\n\\n(2) Meanwhile, the Petitioner argues that, due to the decision of the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs under the provision under review, the area and boundaries of local governments are changed, thereby changing the local government having jurisdiction over the administrative district of residents living near reclaimed land on public waters, and that this infringes those residents’ electoral rights, eligibility to hold public office, freedom of residence and movement, etc.\\n\\nHowever, it is difficult to regard such basic rights as being directly restricted merely because the local government that had jurisdiction over the administrative district of residents living near reclaimed land on public waters has changed, and even if some harm has occurred to the residents due to a change in the local government having jurisdiction, this is merely an indirect and factual disadvantage; accordingly, we will not make a determination on this point.\\n\\nB. Whether Local Self-Government Rights Were Infringed\\n\\n(1) The Constitution institutionally guarantees “local self-government of local governments” in Articles 117 and 118, and the essential content of such guarantee consists of the guarantee of the local government entity, the guarantee of autonomous functions, and the guarantee of autonomous affairs (see Constitutional Court 94HEONMA201 of 1994. 12. 29.). However, because the latter sentence of Article 117(1) of the Constitution states that “within the scope of statutes and regulations, regulations concerning autonomy may be enacted,” and Article 118(2) provides that “matters concerning the organization and operation of local governments shall be prescribed by Act,” the scope of constitutional local autonomy rights is formed and limited by statutes and regulations. Nevertheless, because local governments’ local autonomy rights are constitutionally guaranteed, even if restriction by statutes and regulations is permissible, if such restriction becomes unreasonable to the extent that it impairs the essence of those rights, it must be regarded as unconstitutional (see Constitutional Court 2002HEONRA2 of 2002. 10. 31.).\\n\\n(2) Article 4(1) of the Local Autonomy Act prior to its amendment by Act No. 9577 on 2009. 4. 1. provided that “the names and areas of local governments shall remain as before, and when changing the names and areas, or abolishing, establishing, dividing, or merging local governments, such matters shall be prescribed by Act; provided, that changes to the boundaries of the jurisdictional districts of cities, counties, and autonomous districts shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.” Accordingly, when the issue of delimiting the boundaries of reclaimed land on public waters arose, the Constitutional Court had, after examining what the above “previous” status was, determined the local government to which the reclaimed land belonged on the basis of the maritime boundary line of public waters.\\n\\nHowever, the Local Autonomy Act amended by Act No. 9577 on 2009. 4. 1. newly established Article 4(3), providing that “notwithstanding paragraph (1), the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs shall determine the local government to which reclaimed land on public waters belongs,” and prescribed the filing of an application for such determination as mandatory, while Article 2(1) of the Addenda provided that even reclaimed land that had already undergone completion inspection before the enforcement of the amended Local Autonomy Act must, if it is to be registered in the cadastral register after the Act’s enforcement, necessarily undergo the procedures of application to and determination by the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs beforehand. If so, it is reasonable to interpret Article 4(3) of the former Local Autonomy Act as meaning that, with respect to jurisdiction over reclaimed land, paragraph (1) of the same Article is excluded ab initio, the competent local government is determined only upon the decision of the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs, and until then the relevant reclaimed land does not belong to any local government.\\n\\nMeanwhile, in general, public waters have maritime boundaries that are formed over a long period centered on coastal waters and are used for fishing activities by nearby fishermen, whereas reclamation of public waters not only involves enormous project costs and a long period of time, but also entails the loss of valuable natural resources such as tidal flats in the relevant coastal area and destruction of the environment, thereby constituting a project that has significant effects on the nation as a whole; moreover, the subject and purpose of the reclamation are clearly defined, so the use of reclaimed land is substantially different from public waters in its specific content. Therefore, it is difficult to recognize the boundaries of public waters as is as the “previous” boundaries of reclaimed land.\\n\\nConsidering the purpose of the amended Local Autonomy Act and the differences in nature between public waters and reclaimed land, the newly created reclaimed land is, under Article 4(3) of the former Local Autonomy Act, excluded ab initio by paragraph (1) of the same Article, severing any connection with the former jurisdictional district, and only upon finalization of the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs’ decision is the competent local government determined; until then, the relevant reclaimed land does not belong to any local government. If so, the local government that merely had jurisdiction over the public waters before reclamation cannot be regarded as having any authority over the newly formed reclaimed land (see Constitutional Court 2015HEONRA3 of 2020. 7. 16.).\\n\\n(3) As such, since the relevant local governments, before the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs determines the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters, do not possess any autonomous authority over such reclaimed land on public waters, it cannot be said that the provision under review infringes local governments’ local self-government rights by failing to provide the procedure of hearing the opinion of the local council or holding a resident referendum, and by causing the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs to determine the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters.\\n\\nC. Whether the Principle of Statutory Reservation Was Violated\\n\\n(1) Article 40 of our Constitution provides that “legislative power belongs to the National Assembly,” and Articles 75 and 95 respectively provide that “the President may issue Presidential Decrees with respect to matters delegated specifically by Act and matters necessary for the enforcement of Acts,” and “the Prime Minister or the head of each executive ministry may issue Ordinances of the Prime Minister or Ministerial Ordinances with respect to matters under their jurisdiction, pursuant to delegation by Act or Presidential Decree or by virtue of their authority,” thereby recognizing delegated legislation to administrative agencies. The meaning of Article 40 of our Constitution is that at least basic and essential matters concerning the formation of the people’s rights and duties, as well as the state’s governing structure and functions, must be determined by the National Assembly (see Constitutional Court 96HEONMA1 of 1998. 5. 28.; Constitutional Court 2000HEONMA122 of 2001. 4. 26.).\\n\\nBecause local governments’ local self-government rights under the Constitution also concern the distribution and functioning of the state’s governing structure and, as authority handling a part of state power, the basic and essential matters concerning the autonomy of the organization, autonomous functions, and autonomous affairs of local governments must be directly prescribed by Act.\\n\\n(2) As seen above, pursuant to the provision under review, before the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs determines the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters, the relevant local governments do not possess any autonomous authority over such reclaimed land on public waters. Therefore, even if substantive criteria are needed for the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs to apply when determining the local government to which reclaimed land on public waters belongs, it cannot be said that such criteria are intrinsically related to the autonomous affairs of local governments and must necessarily be prescribed by Act.\\n\\nFurthermore, under Articles 117 and 118 of the Constitution, the legislator possesses broad legislative discretion concerning the types, organization, and operation of local governments, and thus may, in place of directly prescribing in an Act the criteria for determining the jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters, structure by Act a separate procedure for determining the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters. Moreover, the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs’ determination of the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters is not made alone, but in accordance with the deliberation and resolution of the Dispute Mediation Committee (see Article 4(4) and (6) of the former Local Autonomy Act), and the Dispute Mediation Committee actively considers and deliberates upon the specific criteria for delimiting the jurisdictional boundaries of reclaimed land on public waters presented by the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court (the principle of equity) (see Constitutional Court 2015HEONRA2 of 2019. 4. 11.; Supreme Court Decision 2010CHU73 rendered 2013. 11. 14., etc.), and if there is illegality in the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs’ decision according to such deliberation and resolution, the head of the relevant local government may file a lawsuit with the Supreme Court to have it corrected (see Article 4(8) and (9) of the former Local Autonomy Act).\\n\\n(3) Considering these circumstances in their entirety, even though the provision under review requires the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs to determine the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters without prescribing substantive criteria therefor, it cannot be said that this violates the principle of statutory reservation.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, because the provision under review does not violate the Constitution, the decision is made as follows. This decision is based on the unanimous opinion of the remaining participating Justices, except for the separate opinion of Justice Lee Young-jin set forth in 6. below.\\n\\n6. Separate Opinion of Justice Lee Young-jin\\n\\nI concur with the conclusion of the majority opinion that the provision under review does not infringe local governments’ local self-government authority and does not violate the principle of statutory reservation, and thus does not violate the Constitution, but I differ as to the reasons therefor, and therefore I set forth the following separate opinion.\\n\\nA. Whether Local Self-Government Rights Were Infringed\\n\\n(1) A local government has within its own jurisdictional district the autonomous authority or jurisdictional authority conferred by Article 117(1) of the Constitution, Article 9 of the Local Autonomy Act, and other individual statutes and regulations (dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Seon-ae and Lee Young-jin in Constitutional Court 2015HEONRA3 of 2020. 7. 16.). Meanwhile, the Constitutional Court also recognizes that local governments have autonomous authority over public waters (see Constitutional Court 2000HEONRA2 of 2004. 9. 23.; Constitutional Court 2010HEONRA2 of 2015. 7. 30., etc.), and acknowledges that reclaimed land created on public waters is likewise a district of a local government as prescribed in Article 4(1) of the Local Autonomy Act, and a jurisdictional district to which local governments’ autonomous authority extends (see Constitutional Court 2000HEONRA2 of 2004. 9. 23.; Constitutional Court 2015HEONRA2 of 2019. 4. 11., etc.).\\n\\nWith respect to the jurisdictional district of local governments, Article 4(1) of the former Local Autonomy Act provides that “the names and areas of local governments shall remain as before, and when changing the names and areas, or abolishing, establishing, dividing, or merging local governments, such matters shall be prescribed by Act. Provided, that changes to the boundaries of the jurisdictional districts of local governments and changes to Chinese-character names shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.” In the provision of Article 4(1) of the Local Autonomy Act, the term “previous” means the substantive legal standard or principle for delimiting the boundaries of a local government’s jurisdictional district, and the jurisdictional boundaries of a local government over reclaimed land on public waters likewise follow the above standard; where no express statutory or regulatory provision or even any unwritten law exists thereon, the boundaries can only be delimited rationally and fairly in accordance with the principle of equity (see Constitutional Court 2010HEONRA2 of 2015. 7. 30.; Constitutional Court 2015HEONRA2 of 2019. 4. 11.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, under Articles 117 and 118 of the Constitution, the legislator possesses broad legislative discretion concerning the types, organization, and operation of local governments, and thus may, in place of directly prescribing the jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters, structure by Act a separate procedure for determining the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters.\\n\\n(2) The provision under review provides that, with respect to the jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters, the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs shall determine the local government to which it belongs in accordance with the deliberation and resolution of the Dispute Mediation Committee. This is, with regard to the principle in paragraph (1) of the same Article that changes to the boundaries of local governments shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree, merely an exception providing that the determination of the local government to which all or part of reclaimed land formed straddling public waters with boundaries existing as the jurisdictional districts of multiple local governments adjacent to the existing public waters belongs, although it constitutes a change to the boundaries of the jurisdictional district of a local government, must take the form of a decision by the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs rather than a Presidential Decree (dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Seon-ae and Lee Young-jin in Constitutional Court 2015HEONRA3 of 2020. 7. 16.).\\n\\nThe change of boundaries of a local government’s jurisdictional district is a mere boundary change unrelated to the existence or abolition of the local government, and changes only the area, thereby changing the geographic scope to which the local government’s self-governing authority extends. The decision of the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs under the provision under review is an administrative act that, through confirmation of the existence of jurisdictional boundaries and their specific form with respect to reclaimed land on public waters, confirms whether all or part of the reclaimed land on public waters belongs to one of the local governments adjacent thereto and does not belong to another local government (dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Seon-ae and Lee Young-jin in Constitutional Court 2015HEONRA3 of 2020. 7. 16.).\\n\\n(3) As noted above, a local government has self-governing authority over its own jurisdictional district, and reclaimed areas created on public waters are also jurisdictional districts to which local governments’ autonomous authority extends. However, the provision under review presupposes that “the area of a local government shall remain as before” as prescribed in Article 4(1) of the former Local Autonomy Act is the substantive legal standard or principle for delimiting the boundaries of a local government’s jurisdictional district, and that this also applies to reclaimed land on public waters. Accordingly, the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs must, under the substantive legal standard for delimiting a local government’s jurisdictional district referred to as “previous” in Article 4(1) of the former Local Autonomy Act, consider even the purpose and function of newly created reclaimed land on public waters and make a decision confirming the existence of jurisdictional boundaries for reclaimed land on public waters and their specific form.\\n\\nAs long as the provision under review, on the premise of the standard for delimiting the jurisdictional boundaries of local governments referred to as “previous” in Article 4(1) of the former Local Autonomy Act, requires the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs to determine the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters, it is difficult to regard this as impairing the essence of local self-government rights.\\n\\n(4) In addition, according to the provision under review, when the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs determines the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters, such determination must be made in accordance with the deliberation and resolution of the Dispute Mediation Committee (Article 4(6) of the former Local Autonomy Act). Moreover, because the Chairperson of the Dispute Mediation Committee, if deemed necessary in the course of deliberation, may require public officials of the relevant central administrative agencies and local governments, or related experts, to appear and hear their opinions, or may request the relevant institutions or organizations to submit materials and opinions, etc., and in this case the heads of the relevant local governments must be given an opportunity to state their opinions (Article 4(7) of the former Local Autonomy Act), local councils may, in the course of the Dispute Mediation Committee’s deliberation, through the head of the local government or directly by sending their own public officials as representatives, present opinions or submit materials.\\n\\nTherefore, even if the provision under review does not provide for the procedure of hearing the opinion of the local council or holding a resident referendum, and even if it causes the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs to determine the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters, this cannot be regarded as infringing local self-government rights.\\n\\nB. Whether the Principle of Statutory Reservation Was Violated\\n\\n(1) Article 4(1) of the former Local Autonomy Act provides that “the names and areas of local governments shall remain as before, and when changing the names and areas, or abolishing, establishing, dividing, or merging local governments, such matters shall be prescribed by Act. Provided, that changes to the boundaries of the jurisdictional districts of local governments and changes to Chinese-character names shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.” On the premise that “the area of a local government shall remain as before” as prescribed in Article 4(1) of the former Local Autonomy Act is the substantive legal standard or principle for delimiting the boundaries of a local government’s jurisdictional district and also applies to reclaimed land on public waters, the provision under review requires the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs to confirmatively determine the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters.\\n\\n(2) In addition, the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs’ determination of the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters is not made alone, but in accordance with the deliberation and resolution of the Dispute Mediation Committee (see Article 4(4) and (6) of the former Local Autonomy Act), and the Dispute Mediation Committee actively considers and deliberates upon the specific criteria for delimiting the jurisdictional boundaries of reclaimed land on public waters presented by the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court (the principle of equity) (see Constitutional Court 2015HEONRA2 of 2019. 4. 11.; Supreme Court Decision 2010CHU73 rendered 2013. 11. 14., etc.), and if there is illegality in the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs’ decision according to such deliberation and resolution, the head of the relevant local government may file a lawsuit with the Supreme Court to have it corrected (see Article 4(8) and (9) of the former Local Autonomy Act).\\n\\nIf so, because it cannot be said that the provision under review, by failing to establish the essential criteria for determining the jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters, causes the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs to arbitrarily determine the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters, it does not violate the principle of statutory reservation.\\n\\nC. Conclusion\\n\\nBecause the provision under review, on the premise of the substantive legal standard or principle for delimiting the boundaries of a local government’s jurisdictional district referred to as “previous” in Article 4(1) of the former Local Autonomy Act, requires the Minister of Government Administration and Home Affairs to confirmatively determine the local government having jurisdiction over reclaimed land on public waters in accordance with the deliberation and resolution of the Dispute Mediation Committee, it does not infringe local governments’ local self-government rights and does not violate the principle of statutory reservation, and therefore does not violate the Constitution."}

question: Which of the following explanations of the right to be heard in judicial proceedings is incorrect? (In case of dispute, according to precedents)
A: The provision of the Criminal Act that, with respect to the offense of obstruction of the exercise of rights between lineal relatives, spouses, cohabiting relatives, cohabiting family members, or spouses thereof, prevents the judge from considering any of the various circumstances at all and uniformly requires the pronouncement of a judgment exempting punishment, insofar as it makes it impossible for the criminal victim to request that the judge exercise appropriate punishment authority, and is manifestly unreasonable or unfair in departing from legislative discretion, infringes the criminal victim's right to be heard in judicial proceedings.
B: The concept of the criminal victim prescribed in Article 27(5) of the Constitution does not necessarily mean only a person who can exercise rights within criminal procedure in the formal sense, but is a broad concept that includes not only a victim whose protected legal interest has been infringed directly but also a victim whose protected legal interest has been infringed indirectly, insofar as the person has suffered an infringement of a legal interest due to a criminal act. However, since a criminal victim should in principle be a person directly related to the criminal case at issue, it should not be understood by limiting it to the concept of a victim based on the protected legal interest of the criminal facts themselves, nor should it be determined by comprehensively considering the purpose of criminal procedure and the content of the criminal victim's rights, but should be understood to mean a person who, even if not interpreted under substantive criminal law as the subject enjoying the direct protected legal interest, suffers a legal disadvantage due to the criminal act at issue.
C: When making a decision on a petition for adjudication, the provision of the Criminal Procedure Act that leaves to the judge's discretion whether to hold oral argument infringes the victim's right to be heard in judicial proceedings because the disadvantage suffered by the petitioner for adjudication can be seen as greater than the public interest in promoting social stability by promptly and smoothly proceeding with the petition-for-adjudication procedure and thereby determining the legal relations between the parties concerned.
D: The reservation of law prescribed in Article 27(5) of the Constitution concerning the right to be heard in judicial proceedings, unlike the reservation of law for liberty-type fundamental rights whose purpose is to restrict fundamental rights by law, corresponds to the so-called formative reservation of law for fundamental rights, which is intended to concretize by statute the meaning and content of the constitutional norm that guarantees the right to be heard in judicial proceedings as a fundamental right.
E: The Fair Trade Commission has a duty, in a case where, in light of the legal purpose pursued by the Monopoly Regulation and Fair Trade Act, it is objectively reasonable to deem the unlawfulness and punishability of the conduct to be grave, and the degree of harm to be conspicuous, such that realization of the legal purpose would be impossible unless punishment is applied, to file a complaint; and the non-exercise of the complaint-filing authority in violation of such a duty to act is manifestly arbitrary and infringes the victim's right to be heard in judicial proceedings.

supporting_precedents: {"[2010HEONMA243]": "1. Overview of the Case and the Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\na. Overview of the Case\\n\\n(1) On or about March 25, 2009, the Petitioner filed a criminal complaint against Park○Cheon, editor-in-chief of the weekly “○○ Times,” and others on charges including defamation by publication; in response, when the Respondent, on September 10, 2009, rendered a non-prosecution disposition of no suspicion on the ground of insufficient evidence (Seoul Central District Prosecutors' Office 2009HYEONGJE112443, hereinafter referred to as “the non-prosecution disposition at issue”), the Petitioner, being dissatisfied therewith, appealed to the Seoul High Prosecutors' Office (Seoul High Prosecutors' Office 2009BULHANG9020); when the above appeal was dismissed, the Petitioner again, being dissatisfied therewith, filed a petition for adjudication with the Seoul High Court (Seoul High Court 2010CHOJAE33), but the above court, on March 15, 2010, held that the non-prosecution disposition at issue was justified and that the above petition was without merit, and dismissed it.\\n\\n(2) After the dismissal decision on the above petition for adjudication became final as is, on April 15, 2010, the Petitioner filed this constitutional complaint against the second sentence of Article 262, Paragraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which provides that “with respect to a case in which the adjudication decision has become final, prosecution may not be instituted except where other important evidence is discovered,” and against the non-prosecution disposition at issue.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe Petitioner filed a constitutional complaint against the second sentence of Article 262, Paragraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act in its entirety and against the non-prosecution disposition at issue; however, the second sentence of Article 262, Paragraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “with respect to a case in which the decision under Paragraph 2, Item 1 has become final, prosecution may not be instituted except where other important evidence is discovered,” and Article 262, Paragraph 2, Item 1 of the same Article provides that “if the petition violates the legal form or lacks merit, the petition shall be dismissed,” whereas the Petitioner’s above petition for adjudication was dismissed not because it “violates the legal form” but because it “lacks merit,” and the Petitioner also does not assert an independent ground of unconstitutionality with respect to “when the petition for adjudication violates the legal form” among the second sentence of Article 262, Paragraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act, so it is appropriate to exclude the above portion from the subject matter of adjudication.\\n\\nAccordingly, the subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether the portion of the second sentence of Article 262, Paragraph 4 of the Criminal Procedure Act (as amended by Act No. 8496, June 1, 2007) concerning a decision to dismiss a petition for adjudication when such petition is without merit (hereinafter referred to as “the statutory provision at issue”) and the non-prosecution disposition at issue infringe the Petitioner’s fundamental rights, and the contents of the statutory provision at issue (the underlined portion) and the related statutory provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision Subject to Adjudication]\\n\\nCriminal Procedure Act (as amended by Act No. 8496, June 1, 2007) Article 262 (Hearing and Decision) ④ No appeal may be taken against a decision under Paragraph 2. With respect to a case in which the decision under Paragraph 2, Item 1 has become final, prosecution may not be instituted except where other important evidence is discovered.\\n\\n[Related Provision]\\n\\nCriminal Procedure Act (as amended by Act No. 8496, June 1, 2007) Article 262 (Hearing and Decision) ② The court shall, within 3 months from the date on which it receives the petition for adjudication, render a decision in conformity with the procedure for an appeal, according to the following classifications. In this case, the court may examine evidence where necessary.\\n1. If the petition violates the legal form or lacks merit, the petition shall be dismissed.\\n2. The Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\na. The statutory provision at issue provides that, with respect to a case in which a decision dismissing a petition for adjudication as lacking merit has become final, prosecution may not be instituted except where other important evidence is discovered, and thereby prevents a complainant whose petition for adjudication was dismissed from further contesting the matter based solely on the evidence submitted before the adjudication decision, thus infringing the complainant-Petitioner’s right to equality, right to request a trial, and the criminal victim’s right to make statements in trial proceedings.\\n\\nb. The non-prosecution disposition at issue was rendered hastily, merely 2-3 days after the case was transferred to the prosecution office, without the Respondent investigating the persons complained against, and based on the police’s one-sided and biased investigation, thereby infringing the Petitioner’s right to equality, etc.\\n\\n3. Ruling on the Requirements of Admissibility\\n\\na. Petition for adjudication of the statutory provision at issue\\n\\nThe statutory provision at issue directly binds the prosecutor who possesses the authority to prosecute, but since the dismissal decision on the Petitioner’s petition for adjudication became final and, pursuant to the statutory provision at issue, prosecution by the prosecutor became impossible with respect to the Petitioner’s complaint case except where other important evidence is discovered, the Petitioner is restricted in fundamental rights such as the criminal victim’s right to make statements in trial proceedings; therefore, the statutory provision at issue is sufficiently related to the Petitioner, who is the complainant, in respect of infringement of fundamental rights.\\n\\nb. Petition for adjudication of the non-prosecution disposition at issue\\n\\nThe granting of a constitutional complaint against an original administrative disposition and the revocation thereof is limited to cases in which a court’s judgment that had made the original administrative disposition the subject matter of adjudication is, exceptionally, also made the subject matter of a constitutional complaint and that judgment itself is revoked; where the court’s judgment is not revoked, the original administrative disposition itself is not subject to constitutional complaint adjudication by virtue of the res judicata effect of the final judgment, and this legal principle should apply equally even where the prosecutor’s non-prosecution disposition has gone through the court’s procedure for a petition for adjudication after the amendment to the Criminal Procedure Act (Constitutional Court 2008. 7. 29. 2008HEONMA487, Official Gazette 142, 992, 993-994, etc.).\\n\\nAs seen above, the Petitioner filed a petition for adjudication with the Seoul High Court against the non-prosecution disposition at issue, but it was dismissed, and since the above court’s judgment has not been revoked, the non-prosecution disposition at issue, which the above dismissal decision made the subject matter of adjudication, cannot be the subject of constitutional complaint adjudication. Accordingly, the petition for adjudication regarding the non-prosecution disposition at issue is inadmissible.\\n\\n4. Ruling on the Merits\\n\\na. Fundamental rights restricted by the statutory provision at issue\\n\\nKorea’s criminal justice system adopts the state prosecution principle (Article 246 of the Criminal Procedure Act; the following provisions are those of the Criminal Procedure Act unless the name of another Act is indicated), and by exclusively vesting the authority to prosecute criminal cases in prosecutors, it does not allow the victim of a crime to directly request the court to punish the offender; thus, if the prosecutor does not institute criminal prosecution, the criminal trial proceedings themselves cannot be commenced. The statutory provision at issue prohibits the prosecutor from prosecuting a case in which a decision dismissing a petition for adjudication as lacking merit has become final, except where other important evidence is discovered, and thereby restricts the criminal victim’s right to make statements in trial proceedings.\\n\\nIn addition, under the statutory provision at issue, whether the prosecutor may prosecute depends on whether other important evidence has been discovered, so differential treatment arises in the exercise of the criminal victim’s right to make statements in trial proceedings, and the issue is whether such treatment is a constitutionally justified discrimination.\\n\\nApart from the above, the Petitioner alleges that the statutory provision at issue infringes the right to request a trial; however, the right to request a trial guaranteed by the Constitution means the right of the people to become parties to a trial and receive adjudication under the law by judges prescribed by the Constitution and statutes, and not the right to have another person become a party to the trial and receive such adjudication. Therefore, it cannot be said that the statutory provision at issue restricts the right to request a trial.\\n\\nb. Whether the criminal victim’s right to make statements in trial proceedings has been infringed\\n\\n(1) Article 27, Paragraph 5 of the Constitution provides that “A criminal victim may, as prescribed by law, make statements in the trial proceedings of the relevant case,” thereby guaranteeing the criminal victim’s right to make statements in trial proceedings. Such criminal victim’s right to make statements in trial proceedings means the right of a person injured by a crime to appear as a witness in the trial proceedings of the relevant case and to state the details of the injury suffered and opinions concerning the case. This is guaranteed as a fundamental right in order to secure the procedural propriety of criminal justice by affording the criminal victim an opportunity for a hearing to state opinions concerning the criminal case, in addition to testifying in the criminal trial proceedings of the relevant case, under the current prosecution monopoly system that wholly excludes private prosecution by victims, etc. and exclusively vests criminal prosecution authority in prosecutors (Constitutional Court 2003. 9. 25. 2002HEONMA533, Collection of Decisions 15-2, 479, 485).\\n\\n(2) Meanwhile, unlike the legal reservation under the Constitution for freedoms intended to limit fundamental rights by law, the legal reservation prescribed in Article 27, Paragraph 5 of the Constitution concerning the right to make statements in trial proceedings constitutes the so-called formative legal reservation of fundamental rights, intended to concretize by law the meaning and content of the constitutional norm guaranteeing the right to make statements in trial proceedings as a fundamental right. Accordingly, as to how the criminal victim’s right to make statements in trial proceedings guaranteed by the Constitution should be concretized, the legislature is granted legislative discretion; only when it is clearly unreasonable beyond the scope of such discretion does a constitutional issue arise (Constitutional Court 2003. 9. 25. 2002HEONMA533, Collection of Decisions 15-2, 479, 485).\\n\\n(3) The statutory provision at issue, in principle, prohibits prosecution by the prosecutor, in order to protect the legal stability of the suspect, where a decision dismissing a petition for adjudication as lacking merit has become final as is.\\n\\nLooking at the court’s decision-making process in a petition for adjudication case, the chief prosecutor of the district prosecutors’ office or the chief of the branch prosecutors’ office who has received the petition for adjudication must, within 7 days from the date of receipt of the petition for adjudication, transmit the petition for adjudication, statement of opinion, investigative records, and evidence materials to the competent High Court via the competent High Prosecutors’ Office (main text of Article 261); therefore, in rendering an adjudication decision, the court examines all evidentiary materials collected by the prosecutor during the investigation and used as the basis for the non-prosecution disposition, and, further, where necessary, it may conduct new evidence-taking such as questioning the suspect, examining witnesses, or conducting inspections (second sentence of Article 262, Paragraph 2). Since the petition for adjudication procedure is in conformity with the procedure for an appeal (first sentence of Article 262, Paragraph 2), the court determines whether the petition for adjudication is well-founded based on the time of the adjudication decision; thus, evidence newly discovered or facts newly arising after the prosecutor’s non-prosecution disposition may also be used as a basis for judgment.\\n\\nIn this way, the court handling a petition for adjudication examines all evidentiary materials collected by the investigative authority and, depending on the case, even conducts its own evidence-taking in order to determine whether the non-prosecution disposition was illegal or improper; therefore, it can grasp the substance of the case more accurately than the prosecutor who rendered the non-prosecution disposition, and accordingly the court’s decision reached through such process needs to be respected.\\n\\nNevertheless, if prosecution by the prosecutor were allowed even where no changed circumstances exist in the case in which a dismissal decision on a petition for adjudication has become final, and no other important evidence is discovered, the suspect would be left in an unstable state for an excessively long period, and judicial manpower and budget would be wasted on a case in which the possibility of a guilty verdict is extremely remote.\\n\\nFrom a comparative-law perspective, in Germany, which like Korea adopts a compulsory prosecution procedure through which the court controls the prosecutor’s non-prosecution disposition, if there is insufficient basis for instituting prosecution and the court dismisses a petition for adjudication, the prosecutor may institute prosecution only where there are new facts or evidence methods of which the court was not aware at the time of the adjudication decision (German Code of Criminal Procedure, Article 174). This is interpreted to mean that, when the petitioner submits new facts or evidentiary materials, the prosecutor must examine whether they, independently or in combination with the previous materials, justify institution of prosecution; ultimately, the case where prosecution is possible based on new facts or evidentiary materials would fall under the discovery of other important evidence as provided in the statutory provision at issue.\\n\\nMeanwhile, because an adjudication decision is not a substantive trial on guilt or innocence, the effect of a final and conclusive judgment does not attach, and prohibiting prosecution even where clear evidence is discovered that would establish the alleged facts as guilty, merely because the dismissal decision on the petition for adjudication has become final, would run counter to judicial justice. Taking these points into account, the statutory provision at issue leaves open the path for prosecution by the prosecutor where other important evidence is discovered in a case in which a dismissal decision on a petition for adjudication has become final.\\n\\nIn light of these various circumstances, it cannot be said that the statutory provision at issue, by prohibiting prosecution by the prosecutor except where other important evidence is discovered in a case in which a dismissal decision on a petition for adjudication for lack of merit has become final, goes beyond the bounds of reasonable discretion.\\n\\nAccordingly, the statutory provision at issue cannot be deemed to infringe the Petitioner’s criminal victim’s right to make statements in trial proceedings.\\n\\nc. Whether the right to equality has been infringed\\n\\nUnder the statutory provision at issue, whether the prosecutor may prosecute depends on whether other important evidence has been discovered; thus, discrimination arises in the exercise of the criminal victim’s right to make statements in trial proceedings between a complainant whose petition for adjudication was dismissed as lacking merit and later discovers other important evidence, and a complainant who does not. However, as examined above, this is based on a reasonable ground, and it is difficult to view the legislature as having exercised legislative discretion unreasonably beyond the bounds thereof. Therefore, the statutory provision at issue cannot be deemed to infringe the Petitioner’s right to equality.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the petition for adjudication regarding the non-prosecution disposition at issue is dismissed, and the petition for adjudication regarding the statutory provision at issue is denied, and it is so decided as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of all the Justices participating."}

{"[2016HEONMA1043]": "1. Case Summary\\nThe Petitioner filed a request for adjudication after a prosecutor of the Changwon District Prosecutors’ Office entered non-prosecution dispositions in all of the criminal complaint and accusation cases alleging dereliction of duty, etc., which the Petitioner had initiated. In November 2016, the Changwon Panel of the Busan High Court dismissed all of the Petitioner’s requests. The Petitioner filed the present constitutional complaint on 2016. 12. 7., arguing that the Petitioner’s right to a trial, etc. was infringed by the legislative omission that did not provide for an applicant to attend and make statements at a public hearing in the request-for-adjudication procedure, or by the statutory provision allowing a decision to be made without oral argument by the applicant for adjudication.\\n\\n2. Object of Review\\nThe statutory provision related to the legislative omission alleged by the Petitioner is the part concerning a decision on a request for adjudication in Article 37(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act. Accordingly, the object of review in this case is whether the part concerning a “decision on a request for adjudication” in Article 37(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act (enacted by Act No. 341 on September 23, 1954), which provides that “a decision may be made without oral argument,” hereinafter referred to as the “Provision under Review,” infringes the Petitioner’s fundamental rights.\\n\\n3. Petitioner’s Claim\\nBy leaving it to the judge’s discretion whether to conduct oral argument when making a decision on a request for adjudication, the Provision under Review prevented the Petitioner, as the applicant for adjudication, from having an opportunity to present arguments in court. The Provision under Review infringes the Petitioner’s right to a trial.\\n\\n4. Decision\\na. A crime victim’s desire to directly convey his or her position to a judge through oral argument in judicial proceedings is protected pursuant to the crime victim’s right to make statements in judicial proceedings under Article 27(5) of the Constitution. Meanwhile, restricting a crime victim’s access to criminal trial proceedings concerning the crime of which he or she is the victim constitutes a restriction on the right to a trial. The request-for-adjudication system is a judicial procedure established to ensure the crime victim’s right to make statements in judicial proceedings in opposition to a prosecutor’s non-prosecution disposition, and is a court proceeding that reviews the propriety of a non-prosecution disposition. Accordingly, restricting oral argument by the applicant for adjudication in this procedure constitutes a restriction on the crime victim’s right to make statements in judicial proceedings and on the exercise of the right to a trial (see Constitutional Court 2009. 6. 25. 2008HEONMA259).\\n\\nb. The request-for-adjudication procedure is a court proceeding at the intermediate stage between investigation and trial, in which the propriety of the prosecutor’s non-prosecution disposition is reviewed and, if the request is found to have merit, a decision to initiate prosecution is made. In the request-for-adjudication procedure, not only the crime victim who is the applicant for adjudication, but also the suspect’s rights must be protected. The Provision under Review leaves to the judge’s discretion whether to conduct oral argument in order to ensure the prompt and smooth progress of the request-for-adjudication procedure. The legislative purpose of the Provision under Review—harmonizing the efficient progress of the request-for-adjudication procedure and the prompt final determination of legal relations so as to reconcile the legal stability of the crime victim and the suspect—is legitimate, and the legislative means of granting discretion to the judge for that purpose is also appropriate.\\n\\nc. A request for adjudication is a procedure in which the court decides whether to prosecute the suspect based on the investigation records and the materials obtained in the request-for-adjudication procedure, and is a court proceeding having a similar character to investigation, to which the principle of secrecy applies. In light of these characteristics, it is desirable and reasonable for the request-for-adjudication procedure not to uniformly require oral argument, but rather to permit the court to conduct oral argument only when necessary, after considering the specific circumstances.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Criminal Procedure Act provides that the examination of a request-for-adjudication case shall, in principle, not be public unless there are special circumstances (Article 262(3)), and that during the examination of a request-for-adjudication case, inspection or copying of related documents and evidentiary materials shall, in principle, not be permitted (Article 262-2). Evidence may be examined ex officio by the court when necessary (Article 262(2)), and the applicant for adjudication or the suspect may participate in the examination at the court’s discretion when the court examines evidence (Article 24 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure).\\n\\nArticle 27(1) of the Constitution guarantees the “right to receive a trial in accordance with law.” However, the “right to receive a trial” cannot be understood to mean a right to have every proceeding heard through oral argument. Depending on the nature of the case, the legislature may emphasize fair and careful review and require a judgment procedure following oral argument, or may emphasize the protection of information related to the parties and prompt review, leaving the conduct of oral argument to the judge’s discretion and adopting a decision procedure.\\n\\nWhere the matter is reviewed on the written record without oral argument, the crime victim may not have an opportunity to state opinions directly before the judge. However, in the case of a request for adjudication, most victims prepare a statement during the investigation by the investigative authorities or submit a written statement, and that writing is submitted to the judge. In addition, the crime victim may freely submit, at any time, a written statement setting forth his or her opinion in the request-for-adjudication procedure. Based on such materials, the judge may determine the necessity of oral argument and, in cases not appropriate to proceed by written review, hold oral argument and hear the victim’s statement directly. Thus, the crime victim’s right to make statements in judicial proceedings is not entirely restricted in the request-for-adjudication procedure. In addition, where the court dismisses a request for adjudication, the applicant for adjudication also has a remedy by filing an immediate appeal to the Supreme Court and conveying his or her position to the higher court.\\n\\nMeanwhile, it is difficult to conceive of a means that would restrict the fundamental rights of the applicant for adjudication less than leaving the conduct of oral argument to the judge’s discretion while still achieving the legislative purpose of the Provision under Review. Therefore, the Provision under Review cannot be said to contravene the minimum-necessity requirement.\\n\\nd. The public interest in promoting social stability by promptly and smoothly carrying out the request-for-adjudication procedure and thereby determining the legal relations between the parties concerned is very important. By contrast, the disadvantage suffered by the applicant for adjudication when the judge makes a decision on the request for adjudication without oral argument pursuant to the Provision under Review cannot be said to be very significant. The Provision under Review also satisfies the balance of legal interests.\\n\\ne. It cannot be said that the Provision under Review infringes the Petitioner’s right to make statements in judicial proceedings or right to a trial.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nBecause it has been decided to dismiss the petition in this case, the decision is rendered as stated in the order, by the unanimous opinion of all the Justices participating."}
