{"[94HEONMA136]": "1. Outline of the Case and the Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nA. Outline of the Case\\n\\n(1) The Petitioner, while operating a furniture retail business under the trade name “○○ Seosan Agency” at 928-2, ○○-dong, Seosan City, concluded an agency agreement in 1979 with the non-party (Co., Ltd.) □□ Bed (hereinafter referred to as the “Non-party Company”) and had been supplied with and selling various furniture goods manufactured by the said Non-party Company.\\n\\n(2) However, on 1993.4.3., the Non-party Company terminated the above agency agreement with the Petitioner on the ground that the Petitioner’s sales were markedly sluggish, making continued transactions difficult, and in 1993.11. the Petitioner submitted to the Respondent a petition to the effect that the Non-party Company’s unilateral termination of the agency agreement should be corrected.\\n\\n(3) Upon receipt and deliberation of the above petition, the Respondent, on 1994.3.3., determined that the Non-party Company’s conduct constituted an unjust refusal to deal with a transaction counterparty in an ongoing transactional relationship and was in violation of Article 23(1) 1. of the Monopoly Regulation and Fair Trade Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Fair Trade Act”), and accordingly issued a corrective order to the Non-party Company pursuant to Article 24 of the same Act and notified the Petitioner thereof on the 12th of the same month.\\n\\n(4) The Petitioner submitted to the Respondent a petition for reconsideration requesting that the Respondent reconsider its above deliberative decision, stating that the Respondent’s decision was unrelated to any remedy for the Petitioner and that it could not be accepted, and the Respondent replied thereto on 1994.4.2. that reconsideration was not possible.\\n\\n(5) After receiving the above reply from the Respondent, the Petitioner again submitted to the Respondent, on 1994.6.3., a written demand urging criminal accusation against the Non-party Company, and the Respondent replied on the 10th of the same month that a criminal accusation against the Non-party Company was impossible.\\n\\n(6) Having been served with the above reply dated 1994.6.10. from the Respondent, the Petitioner, on 1994.7.8., filed this constitutional complaint adjudication petition on the ground that the above reply constituted a refusal disposition regarding the Petitioner’s application for a request to file an accusation against the Non-party Company for suspected violation of the Fair Trade Act, thereby infringing the Petitioner’s constitutionally guaranteed right to equality and right to receive adjudication; and, on 1994.8.31., submitted a supplemental statement of grounds for the constitutional complaint adjudication petition, amending the public power exercise causing the infringement of the Petitioner’s fundamental rights to “the act of the Fair Trade Commission of not filing an accusation against the non-party □□ Bed Co., Ltd. on suspicion of violation of the Fair Trade Act.”\\n\\nB. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nTherefore, the subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether the “administrative omission” in which the Respondent did not file an accusation for criminal punishment in relation to the Non-party Company’s violation of the Fair Trade Act infringed the Petitioner’s fundamental rights.\\n\\n2. The Petitioner’s Arguments and the Respondent’s Answer\\n\\nA. The Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\nThe Constitutional Court has previously declared unconstitutional the prosecutor’s disposition of non-indictment, deeming it an exercise of public power not to act and thus an infringement of the complainant’s right to equality and right of access to the courts, and this rationale should apply equally to cases that can be discussed only as matters of complaint or accusation by public agencies. Therefore, by virtue of the Fair Trade Commission’s failure to make accusations that should be made equally with respect to all damage arising from violations of the Fair Trade Act, the Petitioner was deprived of the right to equality under Article 11 of the Constitution and the right to receive adjudication under Article 27 of the Constitution.\\n\\nB. The Respondent’s Answer\\n\\n(1) On the procedural admissibility requirements\\n\\nThe Petitioner is merely in the position of an informant or a person requesting accusation under the Fair Trade Act with respect to the Non-party Company’s violation of the Fair Trade Act in this case, and the question of whether to exercise the power to accuse is a matter to be determined exclusively by the Respondent; it is not a matter of a nature that is dependent on the informant’s request for accusation. Therefore, it cannot be said that there exists, vis-à-vis the Respondent, any duty to act by exercising the public power of accusation, and the Petitioner’s constitutional complaint adjudication petition premised on the non-exercise of public power, that is, administrative omission, is inadmissible.\\n\\n(2) On the merits\\n\\nA corrective order for an unjust refusal to deal under the Fair Trade Act does not, in the case where the contract has already been terminated, mean the individual’s remedy of rights in the form of resumption of transactions, in view of private autonomy and the demand for legal stability; therefore, the Petitioner’s constitutional complaint adjudication petition premised on the Non-party Company’s failure to comply with the corrective order is without merit and should be dismissed.\\n\\n3. Decision\\n\\nA. Determination on the Procedural Admissibility Requirements\\n\\n(1) Whether prior remedial procedures were exhausted\\n\\nA constitutional complaint adjudication cannot be filed where there exists a remedial procedure under another law, unless all such procedures have been exhausted (proviso to Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act).\\n\\nIt is evident from the record that, with respect to the Respondent’s omission that is the subject matter of this adjudication, although remedial procedures such as administrative appeals provided for in the Administrative Appeals Act (see Article 3 of the Administrative Appeals Act) and administrative litigation provided for in the Administrative Litigation Act (see Article 4, Item 3 of the Administrative Litigation Act) are available in principle, the Petitioner did not go through such administrative appeal or administrative litigation procedures and instead directly filed this constitutional complaint adjudication petition.\\n\\nHowever, in order for an “omission” to constitute the “omission” that is the subject of administrative appeal or administrative litigation, it is necessary that ① on the premise that there is an application by a party, ② the administrative agency has a legal duty (or a duty under the principles of law) ③ to take a certain disposition within a reasonable period, but ④ fails to do so; and here, a lawful application means an application based on statutes and regulations, meaning not only an application in cases where the statutes expressly provide that a party may make a certain application to an administrative agency, but also an application in cases where, by interpretation of law, the relevant provision is deemed to presuppose an application by a specific person. The Fair Trade Act, however, contains no provision recognizing an interested person’s right to request accusation, and there is no basis whatsoever for concluding, even by interpretation of law, that the Fair Trade Commission’s exercise of the power to accuse requires cooperation such as the Petitioner’s application or consent.\\n\\nIf so, the administrative omission that is the subject matter of this adjudication does not even satisfy the requirements as an “omission” subject to administrative appeal or administrative litigation, without the need to examine further; and even in such a case, if the Petitioner were required to undergo the above administrative litigation procedures in advance, this would amount to compelling a futile procedure, which cannot but be deemed improper (see Constitutional Court 1989.9.4., Decision 88HEONMA22; 1992.4.14., Decision 90HEONMA82).\\n\\nAccordingly, the Petitioner’s direct filing of this constitutional complaint adjudication petition concerning the administrative omission that is the subject matter of this adjudication, without going through the above administrative litigation procedures, should be deemed lawful as an exception to subsidiarity.\\n\\n(2) Whether self-relatedness is satisfied\\n\\nA constitutional complaint adjudication petitioner must himself or herself have a legal relationship to the public power act that is the subject of adjudication (see, e.g., Constitutional Court 1989.7.28., Decision 89HEONMA61).\\n\\nAlthough the Respondent’s accusation cannot be evaluated identically to the prosecutor’s disposition of non-indictment in the respect that it merely becomes a requirement for the prosecutor’s institution of public prosecution, in terms of its structure, it is similar to a disposition of non-indictment by deferred indictment in which the prosecutor recognizes the facts constituting the offense but does not proceed to indict, in that the Respondent recognizes the Non-party Company’s criminal facts, namely the violation of the Fair Trade Act subject to criminal punishment, but does not proceed to accusation for such punishment. Therefore, if the Petitioner is the victim of this offense, namely the Non-party Company’s unfair trade practice, then, as in a constitutional complaint against a prosecutor’s disposition of non-indictment (see Constitutional Court 1989.12.22., Decision 89HEONMA145), the Petitioner may argue that his or her own constitutionally guaranteed right to make a statement in judicial proceedings was infringed by the Respondent’s non-exercise of the power to accuse.\\n\\nOn the other hand, the concept of a criminal victim who is the subject of the constitutional right to make a statement in judicial proceedings need not necessarily depend on the concept of a victim based on the legally protected interest under substantive criminal law; even a person who is not to be interpreted under substantive criminal law as the subject of the directly protected legal interest may, if he or she suffers legal disadvantage because of the offense in question, become the subject of the criminal victim’s right to make a statement in judicial proceedings under the Constitution (see Constitutional Court 1992.2.25., Decision 90HEONMA91). The Petitioner, as one of the parties to the agency agreement that existed between the Petitioner and the Non-party Company, suffers legal disadvantage in the form of losing the status under the above agency agreement as a result of the Non-party Company’s offense, namely the unfair trade practice in this case; accordingly, even if the Petitioner is not the subject of the protected legal interest under the substantive criminal law of the Fair Trade Act, he or she may nevertheless be deemed to fall within the category of a victim who is the subject of the constitutional right to make a statement in judicial proceedings.\\n\\nTherefore, the Petitioner’s petition in this case satisfies self-relatedness.\\n\\nB. Determination on the Merits\\n\\n(1) Organization of the issues\\n\\nThe subject matter of this adjudication is the administrative omission of the Fair Trade Commission’s non-exercise of the power to accuse; thus, the issue is whether the Fair Trade Commission bears a “duty to act” to exercise the power to accuse for criminal punishment with respect to the Non-party Company’s violation of the Fair Trade Act in this case.\\n\\n(2) The exclusive accusation system\\n\\n(a) Content\\n\\nArticle 71 of the Fair Trade Act provides that “No public prosecution may be instituted for offenses under Article 66 and Article 67 unless there is an accusation by the Fair Trade Commission,” thereby making “accusation,” as in the case of crimes subject to complaint under the Criminal Act, a requirement for the institution of public prosecution, that is, a requirement for prosecution, and limiting such accusation to the Fair Trade Commission, the enforcement agency of the Fair Trade Act.\\n\\n(b) Purpose\\n\\nThe Fair Trade Act contemplates damages compensation (Article 56 of the Act), corrective recommendations (Article 51 of the Act), corrective orders and public notice of violations of the Act (Articles 5, 16, 21, 24, 31, and 34 of the Act), imposition of penalty surcharges (Articles 6, 17, 22, 24-2, 31-2, and 34-2 of the Act), and criminal penalties (Articles 66 through 69 of the Act) as sanctions for acts in violation of the Act. However, all of the remaining sanctions other than criminal penalties merely eliminate and restore the state of competition restriction caused by the violation, or deprive the violator only within the scope of the benefit obtained from the relevant violation; therefore, for effective sanctions and prevention of violations of the Fair Trade Act, which can be said to be one of the typical white-collar crimes as a corporate crime or organizational crime, administrative measures such as corrective measures or penalty surcharges are insufficient, and active use of criminal penalties having a strong psychological coercive effect is called for.\\n\\nMeanwhile, since violations of the Fair Trade Act are closely connected with corporate business activities or are committed as the business activities themselves, if criminal penalties are indiscriminately selected against them, the persons concerned or the companies concerned may feel anxiety about corporate activities, and corporate activities may naturally be chilled. In such a case, it would become impossible both to “promote fair and free competition” and to “encourage business activities,” as stated in Article 1 of the Fair Trade Act. Therefore, it cannot be overlooked that criminal penalties for violations of the Fair Trade Act should, to the extent possible, be used restrictively only in cases where the illegality is manifest and the effect on the national economy and consumers at large is recognized as particularly great.\\n\\nThe exclusive accusation system, which makes offenses under the Fair Trade Act subject to complaint and permits only the Fair Trade Commission to make accusations, is intended, in light of these various circumstances, to allow the Fair Trade Commission, independently constituted, to determine the gravity of the violation through detailed market analysis as a law-enforcement agency in the position of a third party rather than a party to the transaction, and to decide, depending on the realities of the market economy at the time, whether it is appropriate to regulate such conduct only through administrative measures such as corrective measures or penalty surcharges, or whether criminal penalties must also be applied, thereby achieving the purpose of the Fair Trade Act.\\n\\n(c) Discretionary nature of the exercise of the power to accuse\\n\\nArticle 71 of the Fair Trade Act merely provides that “public prosecution may be instituted only if there is an accusation by the Fair Trade Commission” with respect to the offenses under the relevant provisions, and does not set forth any requirements or restrictive provisions concerning the Fair Trade Commission’s exercise of the power to accuse; and the Fair Trade Commission’s accusation can only be interpreted as being revocable at any time before the pronouncement of the first-instance judgment, as in the case of a complaint in ordinary crimes subject to complaint (see Article 232(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act).\\n\\nAccordingly, the Fair Trade Commission must be deemed to have discretion to determine, as a preliminary matter, whether to make an accusation with respect to a violation of the Fair Trade Act as recognized as a result of its examination.\\n\\nHowever, like the administrative discretion of all administrative agencies, the Fair Trade Commission’s discretionary power to accuse under the exclusive accusation system is not an unlimited free discretion permitting arbitrariness in its exercise, but must be understood as purposive discretion having intrinsic limits. If the Fair Trade Commission were to discover a violation of the Fair Trade Act whose illegality is objectively clear and serious, such as a cartel involving substantial price increases, and nonetheless fail to file an accusation, the realization of the legal purpose of promoting fair and free competition and protecting consumers by the law-enforcement agency itself would be impeded, which would be improper.\\n\\nUltimately, in light of the above legal purposes pursued by the Fair Trade Act, in cases where it is objectively appropriate to view the illegality and punishability of the conduct as serious and the degree of harm as remarkable, such that realization of the legal purpose would be impossible unless criminal penalties are applied, the Fair Trade Commission has a duty to file an accusation; and non-exercise of the power to accuse in violation of such duty to act must be regarded as manifestly arbitrary and as infringing the victim’s right to equality and right to make a statement in judicial proceedings under the Constitution.\\n\\n(d) Propriety of the non-exercise of the power to accuse in this case\\n\\nThe administrative omission of non-exercise of the power to accuse that is the subject matter of this adjudication concerns an unfair trade practice by which the Non-party Company unilaterally terminated the agency agreement with the Petitioner and thereby unjustly refused to deal with the Petitioner; and it is clear that such unfair trade practice is also prescribed under the Fair Trade Act as being subject to criminal punishment (Article 67, Item 2 of the Fair Trade Act).\\n\\nHowever, the above unfair trade practice by the Non-party Company was a single act of refusal to deal targeting the individual and specific transactional relationship of the furniture agency agreement with the Petitioner, and the degree of harm it caused to the competitive order of the furniture market cannot be said to be particularly serious. Moreover, the economic loss suffered by the Petitioner from the termination of the agency agreement by the Non-party Company appears to be sufficiently compensable by exercising the right to claim damages under the Fair Trade Act or through a claim for damages based on breach of contract or tort under the Civil Act; accordingly, objectively speaking, it is difficult to regard this as a violation of the Fair Trade Act so serious as to warrant criminal punishment.\\n\\nIf so, even if the Fair Trade Commission determined that realization of the legal purpose was possible solely by taking corrective measures against the Non-party Company’s above unfair trade practice and therefore did not exercise the power to accuse for criminal punishment, this cannot be definitively regarded as an abuse of the power to accuse or as a manifestly arbitrary measure in violation of the duty to act to exercise the power to accuse. Accordingly, it cannot be said that the Petitioner’s constitutionally guaranteed fundamental rights were thereby infringed.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nSince the petition in this case is without merit, it is dismissed. Except for the separate opinion of Justice Cho Seung-hyeong, this decision is rendered unanimously by all participating Justices as stated in the operative part.\\n\\n5. Separate Opinion of Justice Cho Seung-hyeong\\n\\nI think that, separately from the majority opinion, which, on the premise that the Fair Trade Commission’s exclusive accusation system is constitutional, judged only the propriety of the administrative omission whereby the Fair Trade Commission did not file an accusation in this case and dismissed the petition, the petition in this case should be dismissed on the ground that Article 71 of the Monopoly Regulation and Fair Trade Act, which provides for the Fair Trade Commission’s exclusive accusation system, is a provision that infringes the consumer’s fundamental rights, the right to pursue happiness, the right to equality, and the criminal victim-consumer’s right to make a statement in judicial proceedings, all of which are envisaged by Article 124 of the Constitution.\\n\\nExamining the provisions of Article 71 of the above Act:\\n\\na. It infringes the consumer’s fundamental rights.\\n\\nA consumer is a person who purchases and uses goods or services provided by a business operator for his or her own consumer life, and may be said to be a concept opposed to that of a business operator. The consumer’s rights, or consumer fundamental rights, mean the rights of consumers to purchase or use, at fair prices and through an appropriate distribution structure, goods or services of good quality in a timely manner in order to lead a life worthy of human dignity.\\n\\nUnder today’s economic structure under monopoly capitalism, the economic structure is characterized by mass production, mass sales, and mass consumption. In such circumstances, the consumer masses are constantly exposed to the possibility of suffering serious harm to life, health, property, and the like from goods or services that are harmful, defective, dangerous, or unfairly priced. Moreover, consumers remain at the unorganized stage, lacking the ability to protect themselves, and are in an impotent position in which, being unaware of information, they are left with no choice but to abandon even the exercise of their own rights. Compared with the huge chaebol enterprises, consumers as the weaker party are in a position where they are unilaterally forced to sacrifice. In such a situation, to ignore the inequality between business operators and consumers and insist only on a party-based resolution method is directly contrary to the ideals of economic democratization and a just society. Therefore, there is an urgent need to protect powerless consumers from the tyranny of huge chaebol enterprises and prevent their harm, together with policy considerations to secure consumer rights at the level of basic human rights. In other words, consumer rights must be elevated to and guaranteed as independent fundamental rights under the Constitution. Only when consumer rights are established and guaranteed as constitutional fundamental rights can the principle of the social state, as a basic constitutional principle, be realized through economic democratization and the realization of a just society; and human dignity and worth, the right to pursue happiness and property rights, the right to a life worthy of human beings, the right to relief as a victim of crime, and other related fundamental rights can be effectively guaranteed, and ultimately the assimilative integration of the social community toward which the Constitution aims can be promoted. Accordingly, the current Constitution contains provisions concerning consumer protection movements, and the Consumer Protection Act has been enacted and implemented to put them into practice.\\n\\nHowever, Article 124 of the Constitution, which is the constitutional provision on this matter, states that “The State shall guarantee consumer protection movements aimed at guiding sound consumer behavior and promoting improvement in the quality of products, as prescribed by Act,” and thus regulates the issue of consumer rights only at the level of consumer protection movements, without directly providing for the guarantee of consumer rights. Thus, in context, this provision appears not to be the constitutional basis for consumer rights as a constitutional fundamental right. However, Article 124 of the Constitution should be understood as precisely the constitutional basis for consumer rights as a constitutional fundamental right. This is because Article 124 of the Constitution takes the constitutional guarantee of consumer rights as its very premise while simultaneously making the guarantee of consumer rights its ultimate purpose. In other words, consumer protection movements to guide sound consumer behavior and promote improvement in the quality of products by the State are possible only on the basis of the guarantee of consumer rights, and ultimately they are intended to guarantee consumer rights; this can also be seen from the legislative purpose and content of the Consumer Protection Act, the concrete implementing statute for the guarantee of consumer protection movements under Article 124 of the Constitution. Article 1 of that Act provides: “The purpose of this Act is to improve and rationalize consumer life by stipulating the duties of the State, local governments, and business operators and the roles of consumers and consumer organizations, as well as basic matters for the comprehensive promotion of consumer protection policies, in order to protect the basic rights and interests of consumers.” By doing so, the Consumer Protection Act, as the concretizing statute of Article 124 of the Constitution, declares that its purpose is to protect the “basic rights and interests of consumers” through the improvement and rationalization of consumer life; and Article 3 of the same Act, which provides for the “basic rights of consumers,” states that “consumers shall enjoy the following rights for their own safety and interests: ...” and guarantees various rights for consumer protection, such as “the right to be protected from hazards to life, body, and property caused by all goods and services” and “the right to receive appropriate compensation through prompt and fair procedures for harm suffered due to the use or utilization of goods and services,” as the “basic rights of consumers.” This means that the various rights for consumer protection stipulated in the Consumer Protection Act constitute the very content of the independent consumer fundamental rights.\\n\\nRecalling that statutes such as administrative law are concretizations for the realization of the Constitution, and that the rights of the people guaranteed by various statutes are themselves concretizations of fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, the various consumer rights stipulated in the Consumer Protection Act can be said to be the concretization of the consumer fundamental rights that are presupposed and guaranteed by Article 124 of the Constitution, which is the constitutional basis for that Act; accordingly, the constitutional basis for consumer rights as independent constitutional fundamental rights is precisely Article 124 of the Constitution. Thus, the phrase in Article 124 of the Constitution, “The State shall guarantee ... as prescribed by Act,” may be understood to mean that consumer rights, as constitutional fundamental rights presupposed by and the purpose of that provision, are concretized in content according to the Act such as the Consumer Protection Act. If Article 124 of the Constitution were not understood in this manner and were interpreted merely as a provision guaranteeing only consumer protection movements, unrelated to the guarantee of consumer rights as a fundamental right, this would not only contravene the purpose of the consumer protection movement itself and the establishment of an effective consumer protection movement, but would also render the very significance of that provision hollow.\\n\\nMeanwhile, as noted above, the content of consumer rights as a fundamental right is specifically provided for in the Consumer Protection Act, and here it should naturally include, together with the consumer’s right to seek redress for harm, the right to demand punishment of the offending business operator through the exercise of the right to file a complaint and an accusation with state agencies. This is because only if the victim-consumer is able to have the offending business operator punished through the State’s criminal prosecution can sufficient and prompt redress be achieved, recurrence of the same type of harm can be prevented, the revitalization of consumer protection movements and the establishment of sound distribution and transaction order can be achieved, and further, the assimilative integration of the social community toward which the Constitution aims can be promoted through economic democratization, realization of a just society, and the effective realization of the other related fundamental rights of the victimized people. Therefore, the consumer’s constitutional fundamental rights must naturally be understood to include the right to demand punishment of the business operator through the consumer’s exercise of the right to file a complaint and an accusation with state agencies.\\n\\nYet this statutory provision states that “No public prosecution may be instituted for the offenses under Article 66 and Article 67 unless there is an accusation by the Fair Trade Commission,” thereby infringing the consumer’s right to demand punishment of the business operator through the exercise of the right to file a complaint and an accusation. In other words, not only are consumer fundamental rights extremely restricted and rendered hollow, but consumer protection movements are chilled, the establishment of sound distribution and transaction order is impeded, the recurrence of the same type of harm is encouraged, and the result of protecting a particular chaebol enterprise is produced, so that the realization of economic democratization, a just society, and related fundamental rights such as consumers’ human dignity and worth, the right to pursue happiness, and the right to a life worthy of human beings becomes mere lip service, and the constitutional ideal of assimilative integration of the social community becomes impossible to find.\\n\\nUltimately, this statutory provision cannot but be deemed unconstitutional as infringing the consumer rights envisaged by Article 124 of the Constitution.\\n\\nb. It infringes the right to pursue happiness.\\n\\nAs mentioned in subparagraph (a) above, if the constitutional basis provision for consumer rights is not Article 124 of the Constitution, then the question arises as to by which constitutional provision and in what manner these rights are guaranteed. In other words, the question arises as to whether consumer rights are fundamental rights under the Constitution.\\n\\nThe ideology of the Constitution lies precisely in human dignity and worth, and individual fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution can be said to be concretizations for the realization of such human dignity and worth. Accordingly, the essential content of fundamental rights is human dignity and worth, and because state power is a means to guarantee and realize such human dignity and worth and each individual fundamental right that concretely realizes it, the source of legitimacy of the State and state power is ultimately human dignity and worth, as confirmed by Article 10 of the current Constitution. Therefore, if there are values and rights inevitably required for the realization of human dignity and worth and for the assimilative integration of the social community, those are precisely fundamental rights that must be guaranteed under the Constitution; even if they are not expressly stipulated as individual provisions in the Constitution, they must by no means be disregarded by state power, and Article 37(1) of the Constitution confirms this by providing that “The freedoms and rights of citizens shall not be neglected on the grounds that they are not enumerated in the Constitution.” Of course, values and rights inevitably required for the realization of human dignity and worth and the assimilative integration of the social community toward which the Constitution aims are concretized in the Constitution in the form of fundamental rights; however, not only is it impossible to codify in the Constitution every value and right that human beings can conceive, but the constitutional-making authority itself is constrained by the political ideology, spirit of the times, and public sentiment at the time of constitutional enactment. Therefore, as time passes and modern industrial society advances, it is only natural that important constitutional values and rights not foreseen by the constitutional-making authority are discovered and arise. Accordingly, Article 37(1) of the Constitution is precisely a supplementary provision for resolving this problem, and its significance lies in ensuring that any right or value indispensable to the realization of human dignity and worth is elevated to and guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right, even if it is not expressly stipulated by the constitutional-making authority, so that state power may neither infringe nor disregard it.\\n\\nHowever, the consumer rights at issue in this case are, because they are indispensable values and rights for a just society, the realization of the various related fundamental rights of the people, and the assimilative integration of the social community through them, naturally fundamental rights that must be guaranteed under the Constitution. In other words, they are fundamental rights that must be guaranteed by state power pursuant to Article 37(1) of the Constitution and must not be disregarded. The question then is what constitutional basis provisions exist for such consumer rights, other than Article 124 of the Constitution, and the answer is the right to pursue happiness guaranteed by Article 10 of the Constitution.\\n\\nThe right to pursue happiness can be said to be a procedural right through which human dignity and worth are realized by material and spiritual fulfillment, and therefore the values and rights inevitably required for the realization of human dignity and worth should be understood as forming part of the right to pursue happiness. Our Constitutional Court also recognizes the right to pursue happiness as an independent basic right (see Constitutional Court 1989.10.27., Decision 89HEONMA56) and includes within it various contents such as the freedom of general action (see Constitutional Court 1991.6.3., Decision 89HEONMA204), the right to free manifestation of personality (see Constitutional Court 1992.4.14., Decision 90HEONMA23), and freedom of contract (see Constitutional Court 1991.6.3., Decision 89HEONMA204). Therefore, the right to pursue happiness is an independent fundamental right, but unlike other individual fundamental rights, it can be said to be an abstract and comprehensive supplementary fundamental right. This can be said to stem from the abstractness and comprehensiveness inherent in the concept of the right to pursue happiness and from its nature as a procedural right of diverse content that realizes human dignity and worth; accordingly, it is impossible to specifically delimit and categorize the content of the right to pursue happiness. For that very reason, the right to pursue happiness has the status of a supplementary fundamental right in relation to other individual fundamental rights. Therefore, a citizen must first invoke the ordinary individual fundamental rights whose content has been concretized, and if that fails, must invoke the right to pursue happiness as the ultimate supplementary fundamental right. This is naturally required in order to prevent excessive invocation and abusive filing in the name of the right to pursue happiness and to prevent the hollowing out of ordinary individual fundamental rights. Ultimately, a citizen whose important values and rights inevitably required for the realization of his or her dignity and worth as a human being, but not concretely embodied in the Constitution, have been infringed may seek relief from the State on the ground that his or her right to pursue happiness has been infringed. Accordingly, Article 10 of the Constitution and Article 37(1) of the Constitution are in an inseparable relationship of mutual purpose and means.\\n\\nTherefore, the supplementary basis provision for the consumer rights, as a fundamental right that must be guaranteed under the Constitution and is at issue in this case, is precisely Article 10 of the Constitution, and ultimately this statutory provision is an unconstitutional provision that infringes the Petitioners’ right to pursue happiness, one component of which is consumer rights, for the reasons mentioned in subparagraph (a) above.\\n\\nc. It infringes the right to equality.\\n\\nThe right to equality encompasses equality of opportunity in all areas of life of the people and the prohibition of arbitrariness in the exercise of state power. Since such right to equality means not arithmetical or absolute equality but substantive and relative equality, it ultimately guarantees all citizens the right not to receive arbitrary discriminatory treatment from state power without a rational ground for discrimination.\\n\\nYet this statutory provision determines whether the prosecutor may bring criminal prosecution depending on whether the Fair Trade Commission files an accusation, and thereby determines whether the Petitioners’ right to demand punishment of business operators from state agencies through the exercise of the right to file a complaint and an accusation is realized; ultimately, the Petitioners’ demands and rights are discriminately realized and treated by state agencies depending on the Fair Trade Commission’s arbitrary decision. This is factually demonstrated by the reality that, while accusations by the Fair Trade Commission against chaebol enterprises have scarcely been made without rational reason, accusations against small and medium-sized enterprises have been made repeatedly. Therefore, this statutory provision infringes without rational grounds the consumers’ right to equality, which encompasses equality of opportunity and the prohibition of arbitrariness.\\n\\nd. It infringes the right to make a statement in judicial proceedings.\\n\\nIn this case, the Petitioners are criminal victims harmed by violations of the Fair Trade Act, and the issue of whether their right to make a statement in judicial proceedings has been infringed may arise. Article 27(5) of the Constitution provides that “The victim of a crime shall be permitted to make a statement in the trial proceedings of the case concerned as prescribed by Act,” thereby recognizing the criminal victim’s right to make a statement in judicial proceedings as a kind of procedural fundamental right of the judiciary.\\n\\nThe right of a criminal victim to make a statement in judicial proceedings means the right of a victim of a criminal act to appear as a witness in the trial proceedings of the case concerned and to state the content of the harm suffered and opinions regarding the case. The concept of a criminal victim here should be broadly interpreted in light of the Constitution’s purpose in providing the criminal victim’s right to make a statement in judicial proceedings as an independent fundamental right, and it need not necessarily be determined according to the concept of a victim based on the legally protected interest under substantive criminal law (see Constitutional Court 1992.2.25., Decision 90HEONMA91).\\n\\nIn this case, because of this statutory provision, the Fair Trade Commission’s decision not to accuse prevented the prosecutor’s criminal prosecution, no criminal trial was held, and accordingly the Petitioners were blocked from exercising their opportunity to make a statement in judicial proceedings. Ultimately, this statutory provision infringes the Petitioners’ right to make a statement in judicial proceedings.\\n\\ne. In relation to the principle of proportionality\\n\\nAll acts of public power must maintain proportionality with the purpose they seek to realize, and the current Constitution confirms this principle of proportionality as a rule of the rule-of-law State in Article 37(2). Yet in this statutory provision that is the subject matter of this adjudication, no rational public-interest purpose can be found that justifies the restriction and infringement of the Petitioners’ fundamental rights such as consumer rights, the right to pursue happiness, and the right to equality. Even if, assuming it were the legislative purpose of this statutory provision, one were to posit the prevention of abuse of the victims’ rights to file complaints and accusations and of the prosecutor’s arbitrary abuse of criminal prosecution, such a reason cannot be regarded as a rational ground justifying the infringement of the Petitioners’ fundamental rights; moreover, linking the prosecutor’s institution of public prosecution to an accusation by the Fair Trade Commission cannot be regarded as an appropriate and indispensable minimum means for achieving that purpose. This is because abuse of the victims’ rights to file complaints and accusations will be appropriately controlled by the prosecutor’s authority to institute public prosecution, and abuse of the prosecutor’s improper criminal prosecution power will be controlled by the business operators’ various constitutionally guaranteed procedural rights and the judiciary power of the courts.\\n\\nUltimately, this statutory provision should be regarded as an unconstitutional provision violating the principle of proportionality set forth in Article 37(2) of the Constitution.\\n\\nf. In relation to the principle of separation of powers\\n\\nIn order to restrain arbitrariness and abuse of state power and to guarantee the freedoms and rights of the people, the principle of separation of powers is required as a constitutional principle. However, the separation of powers today is not limited to a simple horizontal separation among the legislature, the executive, and the judiciary, but rather encompasses horizontally and vertically diversified functional checks on power, as seen in the control of power between the central government and local governments through the local autonomy system, the control of legislative power, judicial power, and executive power by the Constitutional Court, and the control of power between the ruling and opposition parties through political parties. Accordingly, checks on power are also carried out internally within the executive branch among agencies and functions.\\n\\nIn this case, as the principle of prosecutorial monopoly suggests, the power of criminal prosecution is originally the prosecutor’s exclusive authority, but this authority is essentially obstructed by the Fair Trade Commission’s power to accuse based on this statutory provision. In this regard, however, no rational justification can be found for the Fair Trade Commission to control and restrict the prosecutor’s power of public prosecution. If the purpose were to restrain the prosecutor’s arbitrary abuse of the power of criminal prosecution, such control over the prosecutor’s power of public prosecution based on that reason cannot be regarded as an appropriate method, as mentioned in subparagraph (e) above. Thus, the Fair Trade Commission’s power to accuse, which lacks justifiable reason and cannot be regarded as an appropriate method, unjustly controls and infringes the prosecutor’s power of public prosecution; ultimately, the statutory provision containing this is an unconstitutional provision that undermines the functional separation of powers between the prosecutor and the Fair Trade Commission.\\n\\ng. In relation to the demand for systemic consistency\\n\\nThis Act aims to protect consumers and establish sound distribution and transaction order by regulating unfair trade practices, and to support this effectively it prescribes various criminal penalties for business operators and others who violate it.\\n\\nHowever, this statutory provision, by providing that punishment of business operators and others is possible only if there is an accusation by the Fair Trade Commission, undermines the effectiveness of the criminal penalties against business operators and others, and ultimately runs directly counter to the legislative purpose and spirit of this Act. This runs counter to the constitutional demand for systemic consistency, which requires harmony in content and structure among norms. Systemic consistency means that within a certain statute, the norms are harmonious in content and structure, without mutual contradiction, so that the content and structure of all provisions ultimately conform to and contribute to the realization of the original legislative purpose without mutual contradiction or conflict.\\n\\nYet, as mentioned above, this statutory provision undermines the effectiveness of the penalty provisions of the same Act and further violates the legislative intent and purpose of the same Act, thereby causing contradiction and conflict among norms; accordingly, it is an unconstitutional provision that violates the constitutional demand for systemic consistency.\\n\\nh. There may be a view that, since other statutes also contain the exclusive accusation system, it is difficult to regard only this statutory provision as unconstitutional. However, other statutes all establish the exclusive accusation system only as a means to effectively secure the smooth collection of tax penalties and similar matters, and do not target violations involving the direct harm suffered by the general public; that is, they are provisions unrelated to whether consumer fundamental rights are infringed, and therefore, unlike this statutory provision, no issue of constitutionality arises. (Other statutes, besides this statutory provision, that contain the exclusive accusation system include the Punishment of Tax Offenses Act, the Immigration Control Act, the Foreign Capital Introduction Act, the Shipping Act, the Port Transport Business Act, the Act on the Fairness of Subcontracting Transactions, the Feed Management Act, the Petroleum Business Act, the Construction Business Act, and the Parking Lot Act.)\\n\\ni. As seen above, Article 71 of the Monopoly Regulation and Fair Trade Act should be deemed contrary to the Constitution.\\n\\n21 July 1995."}

{"[96HEONMA76]": "1. Outline of the Case\\nAccording to the records and evidentiary materials of this case (the case record of non-prosecution for violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents, No. 95HYEONGJE20429, at the Jeonju District Prosecutors’ Office, concerning non-party Jeong ○ Geun), the following facts are recognized.\\n\\na. Non-party (Suspect) Jeong ○ Geun was engaged in the driving duties of a Sephia passenger car bearing Jeonbuk 1 Do ○○○○ Ho, and around 20:50 on November 2, 1995, while driving the said passenger car from the Mankyeong direction toward the Gimje direction on a one-way, one-lane road in front of Sugok Village, Singok-dong, Gimje City, he crossed the center line and, through occupational negligence in driving, collided with a motorcycle driven by the victim Kim ○ Man (18 years old), who was coming from the opposite direction, thereby causing the death of the same victim.\\n\\nb. The Respondent recognized the suspect for suspicion of violation of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents, investigated the matter, and on November 30, 1995 rendered a disposition of non-prosecution on the ground of no suspicion.\\n\\nc. The gist of the reasons for the above disposition of non-prosecution by the Respondent is as follows.\\nTaken together, the suspect’s statement and the contents of the accident report and the accident scene photographs, it is clear that the present accident was caused by the negligence of the motorcycle driven by the said Kim ○ Man in operating the motorcycle by crossing the center line, and therefore it cannot be said that the suspect was negligent in causing the present accident; nor can it be said that the suspect had a duty of care to drive while anticipating the operation of another vehicle crossing the center line; and in the absence of any other evidence sufficient to establish the suspect’s negligence, there is ultimately no criminal suspicion.\\n\\n2. Summary of the Petitioners’ Arguments\\nConsidering the road conditions at the location of the present accident and the fact that the suspect did not apply the brakes at the time, it is clear that the present accident was one that occurred while the said Kim ○ Man was operating the motorcycle normally within his own lane, when the suspect overtook another vehicle ahead and crossed the center line. Accordingly, the Respondent’s disposition of non-prosecution on the ground of no suspicion against the suspect, rendered without employing any scientific investigative methods based on objective evidence that could be collected at the traffic accident scene, but instead readily believing only the suspect’s statement, which is doubtful in credibility, was ultimately the result of arbitrary investigation and assessment of evidence that is markedly contrary to justice and equity, and thereby infringed the constitutional right to equality and the right to make statements in trial proceedings.\\n\\n3. The Respondent’s Answer\\na. The Petitioners argue that the Respondent’s disposition of non-prosecution infringed the Petitioners’ constitutional right to equality and right to make statements in trial proceedings; however, since the Petitioners were not eyewitnesses to the case at issue, there was no particular need to hear the Petitioners’ opinions, and moreover, during the course of the investigation in this case, the Petitioners did not lodge any complaint or other objection with the investigative authorities, nor did they submit any petition, and they also did not go through any remedial procedure prescribed by other statutes. Accordingly, the Petitioners’ petition in this case is unlawful and must be dismissed.\\n\\nb. The traffic accident in this case clearly occurred due to the negligence of the motorcycle driven by the said Kim ○ Man in operating the motorcycle by crossing the center line. Reviewing the photographs of the accident passenger car attached to the record, it can be seen that the present accident was caused by a collision between the right side of the bumper of the said passenger car and the front portion of the said motorcycle; and such a collision state shows that the motorcycle at the time had departed from its own lane and returned to its own lane. Moreover, the said Kim ○ Man was at the time intoxicated with a blood alcohol concentration of approximately 0.17 percent. Considering these facts together, the suspect’s statement concerning the circumstances of the present accident cannot but be regarded as credible. In addition, where the circumstances of the accident are as above, the Supreme Court takes the position that a motor vehicle driver has no duty of care to drive while anticipating the operation of another vehicle crossing the center line. Therefore, the Petitioners’ contrary argument concerning the circumstances of the accident cannot be accepted, as it merely reconstructs the matter on the basis of groundless presumptions while blindly distrusting evidence unfavorable to the Petitioners. Ultimately, the Petitioners’ constitutional complaint in this case is without merit and should be dismissed.\\n\\n4. Determination\\na. First, the admissibility of the constitutional complaint petition in this case is examined.\\n\\n(1) Whether the Petitioners have standing\\nA constitutional complaint review may be filed when the petitioner himself has directly and presently suffered an infringement of a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution. Accordingly, in order for a petitioner to file a constitutional complaint review seeking revocation on the ground that his constitutionally guaranteed right to make statements in trial proceedings was infringed by a prosecutor’s disposition of non-prosecution for “no suspicion,” he must be a criminal victim whose right to make statements in trial proceedings is guaranteed under Article 27(5) of the Constitution (see Constitutional Court Decision 89HEONMA145, Dec. 22, 1989, etc.).\\n\\nThe right of a criminal victim to make statements in trial proceedings under Article 27(5) of the Constitution is guaranteed as a fundamental right in order to secure the procedural propriety of criminal justice by, under the current system of prosecution monopoly, which wholly excludes private prosecution by victims and other private persons and vests the power of criminal prosecution exclusively in prosecutors, granting the criminal victim a hearing opportunity to state opinions concerning criminal cases, in addition to participating in and testifying at the criminal trial proceedings of the relevant case (see Constitutional Court Decision 88HEONMA3, Apr. 17, 1989).\\n\\nAccordingly, the concept of “criminal victim” prescribed in Article 27(5) of the Constitution should not necessarily be limited, in light of the original meaning in which the Constitution recognized the right to make statements in trial proceedings as an independent fundamental right, to the concept of victim based on the protected legal interest under substantive criminal law; rather, even a person who is not construed under substantive criminal law as the direct holder of the protected legal interest should be understood to mean a person who suffers legal disadvantage by reason of the criminal act in question (see Constitutional Court Decision 90HEONMA91, Feb. 25, 1992).\\n\\nHere, the Petitioners are the parents of the deceased Kim ○ Man, who died in the traffic accident in this case, and are not only in the position of persons entitled to file a complaint under the Criminal Procedure Act (Article 225(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act), but also plainly are persons who suffered legal disadvantage in that they received severe mental suffering due to the death of the deceased caused by the traffic accident, even if they are not the subject of life, the protected legal interest under the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents. Therefore, they should be regarded as falling within the category of criminal victims whose right to make statements in trial proceedings is guaranteed under the Constitution (see Constitutional Court Decision 92HEONMA48, Mar. 11, 1993).\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 27(5) of the Constitution provides, “A criminal victim may make statements in the trial proceedings of the relevant case as prescribed by Act,” thereby requiring that the right of a criminal victim to make statements in trial proceedings be prescribed by law. Correspondingly, the main text of Article 294-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides, “The court shall examine the victim as a witness when there is an application by the victim of the crime,” and so forth, and thus sets out in detail the victim’s right to make statements.\\n\\nThe statutory reservation prescribed by Article 27(5) of the Constitution concerning the right to make statements in trial proceedings, unlike the statutory reservation for liberty-based fundamental rights that aims at restricting fundamental rights by law, constitutes the so-called rights-forming statutory reservation intended to concretize by law the meaning and content of the constitutional norm guaranteeing the right to make statements in trial proceedings as a fundamental right. Therefore, the content of the above statutory provision of the Criminal Procedure Act concerning the victim’s right to make statements should, respecting the original meaning of the Constitution as noted above, be interpreted accordingly, as constitutionally required; and the concept of “victim of a crime” in the main text of Article 294-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act should likewise be construed, in line with the purport of Article 27(5) of the Constitution as noted above, in the same sense as the concept of “criminal victim” in the above constitutional provision guaranteeing the right to make statements in trial proceedings.\\n\\nIf so, the Petitioners are criminal victims in relation to the facts suspected in this traffic accident case, and since they are in the status of persons whose right to make statements in trial proceedings is guaranteed under Article 27(5) of the Constitution, they may be deemed to have standing to file this constitutional complaint review, as they seek revocation on the ground that the Respondent, by improperly exercising prosecutorial power and rendering a disposition of non-prosecution concerning the suspected facts of this traffic accident case, infringed their right to make statements in trial proceedings.\\n\\n(2) The issue of the principle of subsidiarity\\nWith respect to a prosecutor’s disposition of non-prosecution in a case of complaint or accusation, there exist remedies such as appeal and re-appeal prescribed by the Prosecutors’ Office Act; accordingly, in principle, in order to file a constitutional complaint review against such disposition, one must, pursuant to the proviso of Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act, first exhaust those remedial procedures.\\n\\nAccording to the record, there is no evidence that the Petitioners lodged a complaint or accusation against the suspect Jeong ○ Geun concerning the facts suspected in this traffic accident case, or that they filed an appeal or re-appeal against the Respondent’s above disposition of non-prosecution.\\n\\nHowever, in a case such as this, where, with respect to a suspect case, no complaint was filed by the Petitioners and the investigation was initiated by cognizance of a judicial police officer and then completed by the Respondent’s investigation and disposition, if the Petitioners were required to newly file a separate complaint regarding the relevant suspect case, and then to go through the procedures of appeal and re-appeal depending on the outcome of that handling before filing a constitutional complaint review, such a requirement would have no practical benefit either in terms of the Petitioners’ remedy or in terms of the efficient execution of public power.\\n\\nTherefore, the Petitioners should be deemed able to file a constitutional complaint review directly against the Respondent’s above disposition of non-prosecution without filing a separate complaint regarding the above suspect case (see Constitutional Court Decisions 91HEONMA142, Jul. 23, 1992; 92HEONMA48, Mar. 11, 1993).\\n\\nb. Determination on the merits\\nUpon review, it does not appear that the Respondent conducted an investigation in the above case under the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Settlement of Traffic Accidents in a manner markedly contrary to justice and equity, nor does it appear that there was any serious error in the interpretation of the Constitution, application of law, or assessment of evidence that affected the decision to dispose of the case as non-prosecution; and there is otherwise no basis on which to conclude that the Respondent’s above disposition of non-prosecution was an arbitrary disposition to the extent that the Constitutional Court should intervene. Accordingly, it cannot be said that the Petitioners’ fundamental rights were infringed thereby.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the Petitioners’ constitutional complaint petition in this case is dismissed, and it is so decided as ordered. This decision is by the unanimous agreement of all Justices who participated."}

question:
Among the explanations concerning elections, which of the following are correct? (In cases of dispute, according to precedents)

(a) A provision of the Public Official Election Act that prohibits anyone from holding “other assemblies or meetings” during the election period for the purpose of influencing an election, and punishes a person who violates this, does not infringe the freedom of political expression.

(b) A provision of the Public Official Election Act that punishes a person who, for the purpose of causing a candidate to be elected, elected, or not elected, publicly states facts and defames a person who seeks to become a candidate does not violate the principle of definiteness under the principle of legality, but violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringes the freedom of political expression.

(c) A provision of the Public Official Election Act that restricts the voting right of a person who has been sentenced to imprisonment for 1 year or more and whose execution has not yet been completed infringes the voting right because, regardless of the type of crime such as a negligent offense or an intentional offense, and regardless of the content of the legal interest infringed, it does not take into account whether parole, which is a discretionary administrative disposition made during the execution of the sentence, has been granted.

(d) Under the Public Official Election Act, prohibiting all election campaigning by full-time employees of a local public corporation significantly restricts the freedom of election campaigning of full-time employees of a local public corporation, and, compared with the extent of the restriction, does not greatly contribute to securing fairness and equity in elections, and therefore infringes the freedom of election campaigning of full-time employees of a local public corporation.

(e) In the election of the president of the National Agricultural Cooperative Federation, which fundamentally has the character of a private legal person, electing the president or engaging in election campaigning is included within the scope of the right to vote protected by the Constitution.
label: B

{"[2018HEONBA164]": "[Appendix] Relevant Provisions\\n\\nPublic Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 11207 of January 17, 2012)\\n\\nArticle 79 (Speech and Debate in Public Places) ① A candidate (excluding a candidate for proportional representation member of the National Assembly and a candidate for proportional representation member of a local council. The same shall apply hereinafter in this Article) may, during the election campaign period, deliver speeches or engage in debates in public places in order to publicize the policy platform and policies of the political party to which he or she belongs, the candidate’s views, and other necessary matters.\\n\\n② In paragraph (1), “speech and debate in public places” means speeches made by visiting roadsides, squares, vacant lots, residents’ halls, markets or shops, or other public places frequented by many persons prescribed by the Rules of the National Election Commission, and appealing for support for a political party or candidate, or engaging in debates by answering questions from the audience, by candidates, election campaign managers, heads of election liaison offices, election staff (hereinafter referred to in this Article as “candidates, etc.”), and persons designated by candidates, etc. from among persons who may engage in election campaigning.\\n\\n⑦ Candidates, etc. may temporarily attend indoor meetings held by other persons and deliver speeches or engage in debates, and in such case may use a public address system installed at the place or a portable public address system.\\n\\nArticle 80 (Places Where Speeches Are Prohibited) Speeches and debates under Article 79 (Speech and Debate in Public Places) may not be made in facilities or places falling under any of the following subparagraphs:\\n\\n1. Buildings and facilities owned or managed by the State or a local government; provided, That this shall not apply to parks, cultural centers, markets, sports grounds, residents’ halls, gymnasiums, roadsides, squares, schools, or other open places frequented by many persons.\\n\\n2. The inside of ships, regular passenger motor vehicles, trains, electric trains, and aircraft, and the premises of their terminals, as well as the premises of subway stations\\n\\n3. Hospitals, clinics, libraries, research institutes, or testing laboratories, and other medical or research facilities\\n\\nArticle 81 (Debate Meetings, etc. Invited by Organizations for Candidates, etc.) ① An organization that does not fall under any of subparagraphs 1 through 6 of Article 87 (Prohibition of Election Campaigning by Organizations) paragraph (1) may, in the manner prescribed by this Act, hold indoors a debate meeting, in order to ascertain the policy platform and policies of the affiliated political party, the candidate’s views, or other matters, by inviting one or more candidates or speakers/debaters (limited, in the case of Presidential elections and City/Province Governor elections, to one person designated for each election campaign office or election liaison office by a political party or candidate from among persons who may engage in election campaigning; hereinafter the same in this Article). Provided, That this shall not apply to labor unions and organizations under Article 10(1)6.\\n\\nArticle 87 (Prohibition of Election Campaigning by Organizations) ① An institution or organization falling under any of the following subparagraphs (including its representative, officers, employees, or members) may not conduct election campaigning in the name of that institution or organization or in the name of its representative:\\n\\n1. The State or a local government\\n\\n2. An institution or organization prescribed in Article 53 (Candidacy by Public Officials, etc.) paragraph (1) subparagraphs 4 through 6\\n\\n3. Hometown associations, clan associations, alumni associations, clubs such as mountaineering clubs, and private gatherings among individuals such as mutual-aid clubs\\n\\n4. Organizations established under a special Act as national movement organizations receiving contributions or subsidies from the State or a local government (meaning the Citizens’ Coalition for Wellbeing Movement, the Saemaul Undong Central Council, and the Korea Freedom Federation)\\n\\n5. Organizations prohibited by statutes from political activities or involvement in public official elections\\n\\n6. An institution or organization in which a candidate or a candidate’s family member (hereinafter referred to in this paragraph as “candidates, etc.”) serves as an officer, or that is established through contributions of property by candidates, etc., or for which candidates, etc. bear operating expenses, or in which candidates, etc. substantially exercise influence over decision-making pursuant to relevant laws and regulations or its articles of incorporation\\n\\n8. An institution or organization whose majority of members consists of persons who cannot engage in election campaigning\\n\\n② No one may establish or set up any private organization or other organization, regardless of its name or the purpose it professes, such as a research institute, alumni association, hometown association, mountain-climbing club, early-morning soccer club, or satellite organization of a political party, for the purpose of campaigning for a candidate (including a person who intends to become a candidate) in an election.\\n\\nArticle 101 (Prohibition of Other Speech Meetings, etc.) During the election period, no one may, for the purpose of influencing an election, organize a gathering of a large number of persons and hold a meeting for the presentation of personal political views, lectures on current political affairs, roundtable discussions, debates, or any other speech meeting or debate, other than speeches, debates, or debate meetings conducted pursuant to the provisions of this Act.\\n\\nArticle 103 (Restrictions on Various Gatherings, etc.) ② Organizations established under a special Act as national movement organizations receiving contributions or subsidies from the State or a local government (meaning the Citizens’ Coalition for Wellbeing Movement, the Saemaul Undong Central Council, and the Korea Freedom Federation) and residents’ autonomy committees may not hold meetings or gatherings under any name whatsoever during the election period.\\n\\n④ During the election period, neighborhood meetings may not be held unless there is a special reason.\\n\\n⑤ No one may, from 90 days before the election day (in the case of by-elections, etc. whose cause for implementation is confirmed after the 90-day period before the election day, from the time the cause for the election’s implementation is confirmed) until the election day, hold a book publication commemorative event concerning a candidate (including a person who intends to become a candidate).\\n\\nArticle 141 (Restrictions on Meetings of Party Members) ① A political party (including a party members’ council) may not hold, from 30 days before the election day until the election day, training sessions for party members, study sessions, training courses, educational programs, or other meetings of party members under any name whatsoever, for party members in an electoral district in which an election is being conducted or who are residents of such electoral district (hereinafter referred to in this Article as “party members’ meetings”). Provided, That temporary face-to-face contacts among party members conducted for the purpose of communication or instructions concerning party affairs shall not be deemed a party members’ meeting."}
