{"[2023HEONBA78]": "1. Case Summary\\n\\na. The Petitioner is a person who ran as a candidate for Mayor of ○○ District belonging to the ○○ Party in the 7th simultaneous local elections held on 2018. 6. 13. and was unsuccessful.\\n\\nb. The Petitioner was indicted on charges including violation of the Public Official Election Act on the ground that, “for the purpose of preventing Oh ○○, who intended to run as a candidate for Mayor of ○○ District in the 7th simultaneous local elections held on 2018. 6. 13., and Kim ○○, who intended to run in the by-election for National Assembly member of ○○ held on the same day, from being elected, the Petitioner publicly announced and simultaneously defamed false facts concerning the said victims on 2018. 4. 22. and 2018. 5. 6., respectively” (Seoul Northern District Court 2018GOHAP481), and on 2019. 9. 27. was sentenced in the first instance to a fine of 6,000,000 won.\\n\\nc. Although the Petitioner appealed against the above first-instance judgment (Seoul High Court 2019NO2319), the appellate court, having granted the prosecutor’s motion to amend the indictment and having ex officio reversed the above first-instance judgment, rejected all of the Petitioner’s arguments of factual error and misapprehension of law, and on 2022. 6. 23. sentenced the Petitioner to a fine of 6,000,000 won.\\n\\nd. The Petitioner appealed against the appellate judgment by filing a final appeal (Supreme Court 2022DO8646), and during the pendency of the final appeal proceedings, filed an application for referral for adjudication on the unconstitutionality of Article 250(2) and Article 251 of the Public Official Election Act (Supreme Court 2022CHOGI857). On 2023. 2. 2., the Supreme Court dismissed the final appeal and also dismissed the Petitioner’s application for referral for constitutional review. Accordingly, on 2023. 3. 15. the Petitioner filed the present constitutional complaint.\\n\\n2. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\na. Although the Petitioner has filed a constitutional complaint with respect to the entirety of Article 250(2) and Article 251 of the Public Official Election Act, the subject matter of adjudication is limited to the portions applied to the Petitioner in the present case.\\n\\nb. Accordingly, the subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether the following provisions are unconstitutional: the part concerning “a person who has publicly announced false facts regarding a person who seeks to become a candidate” in Article 250(2) of the Public Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 5262 on 1997. 1. 13.) (hereinafter referred to as the “Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case”) and the part concerning “a person who seeks to become a candidate” in Article 251 of the Public Official Election Act (enacted by Act No. 4739 on 1994. 3. 16., hereinafter, regardless of the specific legislative history, referred to as the “Public Official Election Act”) (hereinafter referred to as the “Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case,” and together with the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case, the “Provisions Subject to Adjudication”). The contents of the Provisions Subject to Adjudication and the related provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions Subject to Adjudication]\\n\\nPublic Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 5262 on 1997. 1. 13.)\\n\\nArticle 250 (Offense of Public Announcement of False Facts) (2) A person who, for the purpose of preventing another from being elected, publicly announces or causes to be publicly announced false facts concerning a candidate, his/her spouse, or lineal ascendants, descendants, or siblings in a speech, broadcast, newspaper, communication, magazine, placard, campaign literature, or by other means, to the disadvantage of the candidate, or a person who possesses campaign literature containing false facts for the purpose of distributing it, shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 7 years, or by a fine of not less than 5,000,000 won and not more than 30,000,000 won.\\n\\nPublic Official Election Act (enacted by Act No. 4739 on 1994. 3. 16.)\\n\\nArticle 251 (Offense of Defamation of Candidate) A person who, for the purpose of causing another to be elected or to prevent another from being elected, publicly points out facts and thereby defames a candidate (including a person who seeks to become a candidate), his/her spouse, or lineal ascendants, descendants, or siblings in a speech, broadcast, newspaper, communication, magazine, placard, campaign literature, or by other means, shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 3 years or by a fine of not more than 5,000,000 won: Provided, That no punishment shall be imposed where the facts are true and are related to the public interest.\\n\\n[Related Provision]\\n\\nPublic Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 13617 on 2015. 12. 24.)\\n\\nArticle 250 (Offense of Public Announcement of False Facts) (1) A person who, for the purpose of causing another to be elected or to prevent another from being elected, publicly announces or causes to be publicly announced false facts concerning a candidate (including a person who seeks to become a candidate; hereinafter the same shall apply in this Article), his/her spouse, or lineal ascendants, descendants, or siblings, or concerning the place of birth, family relations, status, occupation, career, assets, acts, affiliation with a specific organization, whether support has been received from a specific person or organization, etc. of a candidate, in a speech, broadcast, newspaper, communication, magazine, placard, campaign literature, or by other means to the advantage of the candidate [including where academic background is indicated but not indicated in the manner prescribed by Article 64(1)], or a person who possesses campaign literature containing false facts for the purpose of distributing it, shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 5 years or by a fine of not more than 30,000,000 won.\\n\\n3. The Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\na. Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case\\n\\nSince the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case alone does not specifically enable one to know what “false facts” are prohibited from being announced, the provision violates the principle of clarity under the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\nAlthough it is almost impossible for ordinary citizens who do not possess investigative authority to determine whether the matters raised concerning public office candidates are true, the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case prohibits and punishes public-interest activities such as “raising suspicions about misconduct or corruption of public office candidates whose falsity is uncertain,” and since violation thereof may lead to deprivation of the right to be elected, it infringes the freedom of expression and the freedom of conscience in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\nb. Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case\\n\\nSince it is unclear, when mentioning matters raised in relation to public office, whether a particular expression constitutes not criticism but “defamation,” the above provision violates the principle of clarity under the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\nEven though accusations or criticism against public office candidates related to elections should be broadly permitted, the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case merely provides that “a person who defames” and thereby sets the scope of prohibition and punishment excessively broadly, which may lead to deprivation of the right to be elected and thus infringes the freedom of expression and the freedom of conscience in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\n4. Determination\\n\\na. Organization of Issues\\n\\n(1) The issue is whether the part concerning “false facts” in the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case and the part concerning “defamation” in the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case violate the principle of clarity under the principle of nulla poena sine lege, and whether the Provisions Subject to Adjudication infringe the freedom of political expression in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\n(2) The Petitioner argues to the effect that the Provisions Subject to Adjudication infringe the freedom of conscience. However, acts of publicly announcing false facts or publicly pointing out facts and thereby defaming a person who seeks to become a candidate for public office for the purpose of causing that person not to be elected, by one’s own will, are merely acts of expressing an opinion; therefore, insofar as we examine whether the Provisions Subject to Adjudication violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringe the freedom of political expression, we do not separately determine the argument regarding infringement of the freedom of conscience.\\n\\nb. Determination on the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case\\n\\n(1) Whether it violates the principle of clarity under the principle of nulla poena sine lege\\n\\n(a) In its decision of 2021. 2. 25. 2018HEONBA223, the Constitutional Court held that the part concerning “a person who publicly announced false facts concerning a candidate’s act, by other means, for the purpose of causing another to be elected” in Article 250(1) of the Public Official Election Act (as amended by Act No. 13617 on 2015. 12. 24.) (hereinafter referred to as the “Precedent Provision”) does not violate the principle of clarity under the principle of nulla poena sine lege. The gist of that decision is as follows.\\n\\n“‘False facts’ in Article 250(1) of the Public Official Election Act means facts not in accord with objective truth, and it is sufficient if they have the possibility of causing voters to make an inaccurate judgment about a candidate; they do not include cases that merely consist of expressions of opinion containing simple value judgments or evaluations (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DO4294 rendered on 2007. 8. 24.).\\n\\nUltimately, when comprehensively considering the meaning and legislative purpose of the text of the Precedent Provision, related provisions of the Public Official Election Act, etc., a person of sound common sense and ordinary legal sentiment can sufficiently know what specific acts are prohibited by the above provision, and there is little concern that law enforcement agencies will interpret it arbitrarily; therefore, the Precedent Provision cannot be deemed to violate the principle of clarity under the principle of nulla poena sine lege.”\\n\\n(b) The part concerning “false facts” in Article 250(1) of the Public Official Election Act applies equally to the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case; thus, it cannot be deemed that there are changes in circumstances or necessity requiring a different determination in this case from the precedent. Accordingly, the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case does not violate the principle of clarity under the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\n(2) Whether it infringes the freedom of political expression\\n\\n(a) In its decision of 2023. 7. 20. 2022HEONBA299, the Constitutional Court held that the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and does not infringe the freedom of political expression. The gist of that decision is as follows.\\n\\n“Since the purpose of the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case is to secure fairness in elections by providing voters with the opportunity to correctly assess the ability and qualifications, etc. of a person who seeks to become a candidate, the purpose is legitimate, and prohibiting the public announcement of false facts regarding a person who seeks to become a candidate for the purpose of preventing that person from being elected, and imposing criminal punishment in the event of violation, is an appropriate means for achieving the above legislative purpose; therefore, suitability of means is also recognized.\\n\\nTo secure fairness in elections, it is necessary to prohibit the public announcement of false facts regarding a person who seeks to become a candidate, and considering that the types of acts prohibited by the wording and legislative purpose, etc. of the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case are limited, it cannot be deemed that the above provision restricts the freedom of political expression more than necessary, and it is difficult to envision an alternative that can effectively achieve the legislative purpose while also effectively preventing anticipated side effects; thus, it cannot be deemed contrary to the minimum necessary restriction.\\n\\nEven if the freedom of political expression of a person who seeks to raise criticism or suspicion regarding a person who seeks to become a candidate is partially restricted by the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case, the degree of such restriction cannot be deemed to be greater than the public interest of securing fairness in elections by providing voters with the opportunity to correctly assess the ability and qualifications, etc. of a person who seeks to become a candidate. Accordingly, the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case also satisfies the balance of legal interests.”\\n\\n(b) In this case, it cannot be deemed that there are changes in circumstances or necessity requiring a different determination from the precedent. Accordingly, the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case does not infringe the freedom of political expression in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\nc. Determination on the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case\\n\\n(1) Whether it violates the principle of clarity under the principle of nulla poena sine lege\\n\\n(a) In its decision of 2010. 11. 25. 2010HEONBA53, the Constitutional Court held that the part concerning “defamation” in the part concerning “candidate” in Article 251 of the Public Official Election Act (enacted by Act No. 4739 on 1994. 3. 16.) does not violate the principle of clarity under the principle of nulla poena sine lege. The gist of that decision is as follows.\\n\\n“The dictionary meaning of ‘defamation’ is ‘to ridicule and disparage another and speak of him/her in that manner.’ Whereas Article 110 of the Public Official Election Act prohibits defamation of private life, the object of ‘defamation’ in the part concerning ‘candidate’ in Article 251 of the Public Official Election Act is not limited in any way; therefore, any fact that can lower the social evaluation of another person by speaking ill of that person falls within this category, regardless of whether it concerns private life.\\n\\nConsidering these points comprehensively, the meaning of ‘defamation’ in the above provision can be interpreted as ‘without justifiable reason, disparaging or maligning the other party with respect to everything respected in social life.’ Such terminology is not a term peculiarly used in the Public Official Election Act that requires a separate independent conceptual definition, but a general term ordinarily used by ordinary people in daily life or in other statutes; except in special cases, it is an expression whose general legal meaning can be understood even by laypersons without supplementary interpretative action by judges, and the context in which it is used in the law also does not appear to exceed such generally used scope of meaning (see Constitutional Court decision 2002HEONBA85 rendered on 2004. 11. 25.).\\n\\nAccordingly, the part concerning ‘defamation’ in the above provision cannot be said to be ambiguous or unclear in meaning, and thus does not violate the principle of clarity under the principle of nulla poena sine lege.”\\n\\n(b) The part concerning “defamation” in the part concerning “candidate” in Article 251 of the Public Official Election Act applies equally to the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case; thus, it cannot be deemed that there are changes in circumstances or necessity requiring a different determination in this case from the precedent. Accordingly, the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case does not violate the principle of clarity under the principle of nulla poena sine lege.\\n\\n(2) Whether it infringes the freedom of political expression\\n\\n(a) Standard of review\\n\\nIn light of the constitutional status and nature of the freedom of political expression, and its relationship with the fairness of elections, etc., the legislature must choose, even when unavoidably restricting the freedom of political expression in the election context in order to secure fairness in elections, a means that remains the least possible restriction within the scope in which the relevance to achieving the legislative purpose is concrete and clear. As to political expression, it is self-evident that “freedom shall be the principle and prohibition the exception,” and not “prohibition the principle and permission the exception.” Accordingly, in determining whether restrictions on election campaigning, etc. infringe the freedom of political expression, a strict standard of review must be applied as the standard for judging the regulation of freedom of expression (Constitutional Court decision 2017HEONBA100, etc., rendered on 2022. 7. 21.).\\n\\n(b) Determination\\n\\n1) Legitimacy of purpose and suitability of means\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case is to protect the person and reputation of a person who seeks to become a candidate, to prevent evasion of the restrictions on the election campaign period under the Public Official Election Act, and at the same time to secure fairness in elections by enabling voters to make correct judgments regarding persons who may in the future become candidates; thus, legitimacy is recognized, and punishing acts of defaming a person who seeks to become a candidate, except where the facts are true and related to the public interest, is an appropriate means to achieve the above legislative purpose.\\n\\n2) Minimum necessity\\n\\nSince the freedom of political expression is a core fundamental right that forms the foundation of democracy under our Constitution, it must be guaranteed to the maximum extent, and restrictions thereon must be limited to the minimum necessary for achieving the legislative purpose.\\n\\nFrom the time elections were regulated by individual election statutes such as the Presidential Election Act, the National Assembly Members Election Act, the Local Council Members Election Act, and the Local Government Heads Election Act because no single election statute had yet been enacted, each individual election statute contained an offense of defaming a candidate similar to the current Article 251 of the Public Official Election Act, and only defamation of candidates was made punishable; acts of defaming a person who seeks to become a candidate were not punishable. Thereafter, when the Act on Elections and Prevention of Election Malpractice, a single statute concerning elections, was enacted on 1994. 3. 16. as Act No. 4739, acts of defaming not only candidates but also persons who seek to become candidates were made punishable, and this has been maintained without change in content thereafter. In this way, the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case punishes not only defamation of candidates but also defamation of persons who seek to become candidates, and in that it imposes no restriction on the timing of the defamation, its scope of punishment has become broader than the offense of defaming candidates that was prescribed in the individual election statutes before the enactment of the Public Official Election Act. Furthermore, the subject of this provision is not limited to candidates or election officials, but also includes ordinary voters and the media.\\n\\nThe dictionary meaning of “defamation” is “to ridicule and disparage another and speak of him/her in that manner.” Whereas Article 110(1) of the Public Official Election Act provides that “no person shall, for the purpose of an election campaign, publicly point out facts and thereby defame private life,” thereby prohibiting only defamation of private life, the object of defamation set forth in the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case is not subject to any limitation; therefore, if a fact can lower the social evaluation of another person by speaking ill of that person, it falls within this category regardless of whether it concerns private life.\\n\\nHowever, since elections ordinarily involve candidates competing before voters, by their nature there can be no help but to have many negative expressions about others and positive expressions about oneself, and pointing out negative facts concerning the suitability for public office of a person who seeks to become a candidate, or raising suspicions about such person, is naturally an act of disparaging or maligning that person. In particular, when a political newcomer challenges an incumbent National Assembly member, negative evaluations of the incumbent National Assembly member’s ability, qualifications, and morality are inevitably involved in the process of justifying the newcomer’s candidacy.\\n\\nThe object of defamation under the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case is, so long as it is a fact, irrespective of whether it is false or true. However, if an act of defaming a person who seeks to become a candidate constitutes false facts, it is sufficient to punish it under the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case. In actual cases, including the present case, when prosecution is brought on the ground that one publicly announced false facts and thereby defamed another, the courts regard it as an imaginary concurrence of offenses under the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case and the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case; however, since the statutory punishment under the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case is heavier, there is no practical benefit in duplicatively applying the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case. Furthermore, if an act of defaming a person who seeks to become a candidate concerns true facts or facts not proven false, regulating such acts under the Public Official Election Act is an excessive restraint on the freedom of political expression. If a person raises issues concerning the suitability for public office of a person who seeks to become a candidate based on such facts, that person should be able to rebut them so that voters may obtain materials enabling them to correctly assess the ability, qualifications, and morality of the person who seeks to become a candidate. Nevertheless, if such acts are punished under the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case, complaints and accusations among persons who seek to become candidates may proliferate excessively, thereby resulting in making the election to be held in the future appear even more polluted, and it would restrict the opportunity for voters to obtain materials with which to correctly assess the ability, qualifications, and morality of persons who seek to become candidates.\\n\\nIn particular, where the facts pointed out are facts that are not false, the aspect of defaming the person who seeks to become a candidate is more significant as defamation against the individual person than the aspect of harming the fairness of elections by transmitting incorrect information. Even without the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case, if the reputation of a person who seeks to become a candidate is impaired by publicly pointing out facts, punishability can be secured by punishing such conduct as the offense of defamation by publicly pointing out facts under Article 307(1) of the Criminal Act. In the case of the offense of defamation by publicly pointing out facts, the punishment is imprisonment or confinement for not more than 2 years, or a fine of not more than 5,000,000 won, whereas the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case provides for imprisonment for not more than 3 years or a fine of not more than 5,000,000 won; thus, not only is the statutory punishment under the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case heavier, but if a person violates it and is sentenced to imprisonment or a fine of 1,000,000 won or more, that person will be disqualified from voting and from being elected for a certain period after the sentence becomes final and conclusive (Article 18(1)3 and Article 19(1)1 of the Public Official Election Act), or, if already elected, the election shall become void (Article 264 of the Public Official Election Act). This amounts to expelling the actor entirely from the sphere of public discourse on the ground that he or she made a negative expression or raised an issue based on facts that are not false concerning a person who seeks to become a candidate, and it is difficult to view this as the minimum necessary means for achieving the legislative purpose of protecting the reputation of a person who seeks to become a candidate or ensuring fairness in elections.\\n\\nEven when looking to foreign legislative examples, one cannot find a provision that independently punishes defamation of candidates by truthful factual statements, as does the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case. Japan punishes as defamation the act of publicly pointing out facts (Article 230(1) of the Japanese Penal Code), and with respect to facts concerning a candidate for public office by public election, if it is proven that the pointed-out facts are true, no punishment is imposed regardless of whether the pointed-out facts are related to the public interest or whether the purpose was solely to promote the public interest (Article 230-2(3) of the same Code), and the same applies even where there was a substantial reason to believe them to be true. Germany has no independent punishment provision concerning defamation in various election-related laws, and defamation is punished under the Penal Code as insult and malicious false accusation (Articles 186 and 187 of the German Criminal Code), with aggravated punishment provided where defamation and malicious false accusation are committed against persons involved in the political life of the people (Article 188 of the same Code). However, in the case of the German Criminal Code, because the offense of insult punishes only “where such fact is not demonstrably true,” and the offense of malicious false accusation punishes only “false facts suitable to contempt, lowering public esteem, or endangering another’s credit,” acts of defamation by truthful factual statements are not punishable. In the United States, federal law does not separately provide for punishment of cases where a candidate is defamed during the election campaign process, and ordinary defamation is basically subject to civil relief as a tort. However, in the case of defamation of a public official or public office candidate, damages liability is recognized only when it is proved, based on freedom of expression under the First Amendment, that the statement was false and that the other party knew it was false or, despite being able to easily know that it was false, failed to verify it [New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254 (1964)]. The Supreme Court of the United States held that criminal punishment for defaming a public official based on facts is unconstitutional, stating that “truth may not be the subject of either civil or criminal sanctions in discussion of public affairs” [Garrison v. State of Louisiana, 379 U.S. 64, 74 (1964)].\\n\\nThe Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case does provide, in its proviso, an exculpatory ground of unlawfulness stating, “Provided, That no punishment shall be imposed where the facts are true and are related to the public interest.” However, public office candidates are public figures, and the process of verification through exchanges among candidates and through voters’ and the media’s raising of suspicions itself constitutes the public interest; therefore, when it concerns true facts, the need to again determine whether it relates to the public interest is markedly low. Meanwhile, even where the pointed-out facts are true facts or where there is substantial reason to believe them true, they nonetheless satisfy the elements of the offense of defaming a candidate under the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case, and thus the person who expressed such facts is exposed to the risk of being investigated by an investigative agency on complaint or accusation, or by ex officio investigation, or of being prosecuted in a criminal trial. Therefore, even if there is a possibility that in future court proceedings such expressive acts may be found to fall under the exculpatory ground of unlawfulness in the proviso to the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case, the mere fact that one may be subjected to investigation and judicial proceedings because of one’s expressive acts can produce a chilling effect on freedom of expression. Furthermore, in order to be exempted from unlawfulness under the proviso to the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case, one must prove not only that the facts are true, but also that they are “related to the public interest”; considering, moreover, the uncertainty as to by what standards public interest will be proved and determined in investigative and judicial bodies, the likelihood of a chilling effect on freedom of expression becomes even greater.\\n\\nThat said, even if facts are true, there may be a need to protect a person who seeks to become a candidate if such facts take the nature of an invasion of privacy. However, Article 110(1) of the Public Official Election Act already prohibits acts of defaming private life, and therefore, corresponding to that prohibition, it is desirable to have a punishment provision within the minimum scope in which the balance between privacy and freedom and the freedom of political expression does not result in an infringement of fundamental rights.\\n\\nAs to this, there may be an opinion that punishing “defamation by publicly pointing out facts” solely under the offense of defamation by publicly pointing out facts under Article 307(1) of the Criminal Act is insufficient and that special rules under the Public Official Election Act are necessary. However, the statutory punishment under the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case is heavier than that for the offense of defamation by publicly pointing out facts under the Criminal Act, and where the special rules under the Public Official Election Act apply, such as the provisions invalidating the election of a successful candidate due to an election crime, the provisions requiring reimbursement of expenses by a person whose election has been invalidated, and the provisions restricting holding public office due to an election crime, the violator suffers greater disadvantages than in the case of punishment under the offense of defamation by publicly pointing out facts under the Criminal Act. This punishes defamation by publicly pointing out facts regarding a person who seeks to become a candidate more severely than defamation by publicly pointing out facts regarding ordinary persons, resulting in the consequence of protecting the reputation of a person who has voluntarily stepped into the arena of public discourse more strongly than that of ordinary persons. Furthermore, considering that not only opposing candidates but also voters and the media can be subjects of the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case, there is a concern that, by virtue of the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case, issue-raising based on facts that are not false concerning a person who seeks to become a candidate may be blocked in the name of protecting the reputation of a public figure, and this runs counter to the very essence of elections, namely that the suitability for public office of a person who seeks to become a candidate should basically be determined by the voters. Also, the provisions in the Public Official Election Act emphasizing the swiftness of investigations into election crimes, the short statute of limitations, and the mandatory provisions concerning the trial period for election crimes merely constitute provisions directing law enforcement agencies to handle election-related cases promptly; they cannot be viewed as being intrinsically related to the unconstitutionality of the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case itself. Even if defamation by publicly pointing out facts is punished only under the offense of defamation by publicly pointing out facts under the Criminal Act, investigative agencies and judicial bodies may nonetheless expedite investigations and trials, taking into account that such acts are related to election results.\\n\\nSince the possibility of criminal punishment still remains, it cannot be categorically concluded that, if the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case were repealed, candidates in public elections would engage more actively in defamation of opponents or that negative campaigning would increase further.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case is contrary to the minimum necessity requirement.\\n\\n3) Balance of legal interests\\n\\nThe public interest pursued by the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case is to protect the reputation of a person who seeks to become a candidate and to ensure fairness in elections by providing voters with correct information. However, fairness in elections does not merely mean preventing disorder in elections, but includes the concept of enabling information concerning the suitability for public office of public office candidates, such as their ability, qualifications, and morality, to be disclosed so that the best person can be elected based thereon; therefore, facts concerning a person who seeks to become a candidate must be disclosed to the electorate, i.e., the general public, to the fullest extent possible and used as materials for assessing that person’s ability, qualifications, and morality. From this perspective, if, with respect to facts concerning a person who seeks to become a candidate, the freedom of political expression is excessively restricted on the ground that such facts are “defamation,” regardless of whether they are false or true, it may instead result in harming the very public interest of fair elections pursued by the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case.\\n\\nAlso, since a person who seeks to become a candidate has voluntarily stepped into the arena of politics and public discourse, that person must tolerate to some extent negative expressions about himself or herself in order for suitability for public office to be verified.\\n\\nIn light of these points, while the freedom of political expression of the actor restricted by the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case is very large and significant, the public interests of protecting reputation or securing fairness in elections, which can be achieved by prohibiting defamation through public statements of fact, are somewhat abstract and unclear, and cannot be said to outweigh the freedom of political expression curtailed by the actor.\\n\\nAccordingly, the balance of legal interests is not recognized with respect to the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case.\\n\\n(c) Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringes the freedom of political expression.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nThe Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case does not violate the Constitution, whereas the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case violates the Constitution; therefore, the decision is made as stated in the order. In addition, the Constitutional Court’s prior decision of 2013. 6. 27. 2011HEONBA75, which had taken a different view and held that the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case does not violate the Constitution, is to be modified to the extent inconsistent with this decision.\\n\\nExcept for the dissenting opinion on the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case by Justice Lee Jong-seok, Justice Lee Eun-ae, and Justice Jeong Hyeong-sik, as set forth in section 6 below, the opinions of the participating Justices were unanimous.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Lee Jong-seok, Lee Eun-ae, and Jeong Hyeong-sik\\n\\nWe agree with the majority opinion in that the Provision Prohibiting the Public Announcement of False Facts in This Case does not violate the Constitution and the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case does not violate the principle of clarity under the principle of nulla poena sine lege. However, unlike the majority opinion, we think that the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case does not infringe the freedom of political expression and is therefore constitutional; we set forth the reasons as follows.\\n\\na. In its decision of 2013. 6. 27. 2011HEONBA75, the Constitutional Court held that the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and thus does not infringe the freedom of election campaigning or the freedom of political expression. The gist of that decision is as follows.\\n\\n“(1) Minimum necessity\\n\\nFirst, as noted above, the ‘person who seeks to become a candidate’ in the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case must have the will to become a candidate and objective indicia thereof. Although we appear to be gradually moving away from the election culture of the past, in which extreme slander, personal attacks, and black propaganda abounded, even at present, it remains all too common that, over a long period from well before the arrival of a particular election to the imminent period, groundless suspicions or rumors, or unfair opinions or evaluations disguised as factual allegations, are raised concerning the status and social position or activities of a ‘person who seeks to become a candidate’ and that person’s family, and are amplified and reproduced through the media or the internet. If such groundless raising of suspicions is broadly permitted in this manner, even if it later turns out to be unfounded, not only the person and reputation of the ‘person who seeks to become a candidate’ and that person’s family will be damaged, but also serious consequences that mislead voters’ choices in relation to future elections may result, which is manifestly contrary to the public interest. Therefore, punishing acts of defamation against those who have objectively manifested their intention to become candidates in future elections amounts, in substance, to prohibiting conduct that constitutes de facto pre-election campaigning, and is an appropriate restriction to secure fairness in elections and establish a sound election culture; the need to maintain the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case remains significant.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case punishes a person who publicly points out facts and thereby defames a person who seeks to become a candidate more severely than the offense of defamation under Article 307(1) of the Criminal Act, but instead, by prescribing the subjective element of “for the purpose of causing another to be elected or to prevent another from being elected,” it limits the scope of punishment to acts that are likely to affect voters’ social evaluation or judgment of a specific person and thereby actually harm the fairness of elections.\\n\\nIn addition, the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case does not punish every act of defamation, but in the proviso it prescribes an exculpatory ground of unlawfulness, namely, “Provided, That no punishment shall be imposed where the facts are true and are related to the public interest,” and thus, even if negative expressions about a person who seeks to become a candidate lower the social evaluation of the other party, if they amount to pointing out true facts for the correct judgment of voters rather than slander, personal attack, or black propaganda against that person and are consistent with the public interest, they are not punished under the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case. In particular, compared with the offense of defamation under the Criminal Act, where unlawfulness is exempted only when the facts are true and relate solely to the public interest (Criminal Act Article 310), the absence of the requirement of ‘solely’ expands the scope of the exculpatory ground of unlawfulness, so that even where both public and private interests exist at the same time, punishment under the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case is avoided; this broadens the exculpatory ground of unlawfulness in consideration of the importance of freedom of election campaigning and freedom of political expression.\\n\\nUltimately, the acts punished under the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case are those in which, “for the purpose of causing another to be elected or to prevent another from being elected,” facts concerning a person who seeks to become a candidate, etc. were publicly pointed out and thereby defamed, and such acts do not fall within the category of “true facts and related to the public interest,” and are merely slander, personal attack, or black propaganda against a person who seeks to become a candidate. Punishing such acts is a necessary restriction on the freedom of election campaigning or freedom of political expression. However, the degree of reputation protection of a ‘person who seeks to become a candidate’ or of ensuring fairness in elections secured by regulating public factual allegations or defamation, or, on the other hand, the degree of restriction on the freedom of political expression that is chilled, may differ from case to case depending on the time, content, manner, and relevance to a particular election in which the factual allegations or defamation occurred. Therefore, law enforcement agencies must carefully determine, from the perspective of the average member of society with sound common sense, whether the act merely consists of a factual allegation that falls within the public interest or whether it should be subject to the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case as defamation, so as to prevent the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case from being applied indiscriminately or improperly; and courts trying such election cases must, in addition, realize concrete validity by imposing appropriate and reasonable sentences befitting the punishable conduct.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case does not violate the minimum necessity requirement.\\n\\n(2) Balance of legal interests\\n\\nThe public interest pursued by the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case is to protect the reputation of a person who seeks to become a candidate and that person’s family, create a sound election climate, and further secure fairness in elections by providing voters with correct information. Even though the freedom of election campaigning or the freedom of political expression is somewhat restricted by the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case, as seen above, insofar as facts pointed out are not punished where they are true and for the public interest, the degree of restriction on fundamental rights caused by the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case cannot be said to be greater than the above public interest. Accordingly, it cannot be said that the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case disregards the balance between public and private interests, and thus it does not violate the balance of legal interests.”\\n\\nb. Legislative acts concerning elections must achieve an appropriate harmony between the two ideals of “freedom and fairness,” and therefore there are also cases where it is necessary to restrict the freedom of political expression to a certain extent for the fairness of elections.\\n\\nThe majority opinion emphasizes that, in elections, when an issue is raised regarding the suitability for public office of a person who seeks to become a candidate, it should be possible to allow free exchanges among persons who seek to become candidates, such as by allowing that person to rebut the issue, so that voters can obtain materials with which to correctly assess the ability, qualifications, and morality of the person who seeks to become a candidate. However, in the reality where a substantial portion of political expression or communication is conducted through information and communications networks such as SNS, e-mail, and portal sites due to the development and widespread use of technologies such as the internet and smartphones, once information is posted on such information and communications networks, it is not only subject to infinite storage and reproduction and likely to spread widely, but because of its rapid transmissibility there are many cases in which it is practically meaningless for the other side of the defamation to rebut through counterarguments and debate; if negative phenomena that may arise in the internet environment, such as biased information acquisition and reinforcement of prejudice, are added to this, there is a risk that the fairness of elections will be greatly undermined.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that in the case of defamation by publicly pointing out facts, it is sufficient to punish it under the offense of defamation by publicly pointing out facts under Article 307(1) of the Criminal Act. However, if the person who committed defamation by publicly pointing out facts was a candidate in a public election and actually won that public election, there is a considerable possibility that the investigation and trial concerning the offense of defamation by publicly pointing out facts under Article 307(1) of the Criminal Act will not be properly conducted and will be delayed until almost the end of the term, because provisions emphasizing the swiftness of investigations into election crimes under the Public Official Election Act (Article 9(2)), provisions on a short statute of limitations (main text of Article 268(1)), and mandatory provisions concerning the trial period for election crimes (Article 270) do not apply despite the fact that the election was won on the basis of an unlawful act. Such a result greatly harms the fairness of elections and at the same time distorts, rather than properly reflecting, the genuine will of the general public. In addition, even from the standpoint of a person who has already been elected, there is a concern that the status as an elected person may remain overly uncertain for an excessively long period.\\n\\nAlso, as the majority opinion acknowledges, even if defamation is committed by pointing out true facts, if it defames private life, there is a need to first protect the person who seeks to become a candidate from such acts; however, if the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case becomes unconstitutional and loses its effect, the mere provision of Article 110(1) of the Public Official Election Act, which only prohibits acts of defaming private life but contains no punishment provision therefor, cannot provide sufficient protection.\\n\\nSo far, in the election process in our country, negative campaigning in the form of defaming opposing candidates or persons seeking to become candidates and their families has been continually carried out more than positive campaigning by presenting differentiated pledges by candidate, and statistical data regarding changes in the main forms of illegal election campaigning readily confirms that this problem has continued up to the recent period. Ordinary citizens also recognize that this persistently continuing excessive defamation during the election process is one of the main reasons for harming the fairness of elections. Yet, in such a situation, if the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case is held unconstitutional and, where there is suspicion of falsity concerning the facts pointed out but evidence to prove such falsity is not secured in criminal proceedings requiring strict proof, the majority of acts of defamation by publicly pointing out facts are punished only under the offense of defamation by publicly pointing out facts under Article 307(1) of the Criminal Act, then the offender will not receive any disadvantage under the Public Official Election Act, such as the provisions invalidating the election of a successful candidate due to an election crime (Article 264), the provisions requiring reimbursement of expenses by a person whose election has been invalidated (Article 265-2(1)), or the provisions restricting holding public office due to an election crime (Article 266(1)); accordingly, for candidates in public elections, this may instead create a kind of incentive to actively engage in defamation of the opponent. As a result, rather than engaging in positive campaigning by actively promoting one’s own differentiated pledges as a candidate for public election, negative campaigning focusing on defaming the opposing candidate by disparaging or maligning that side may become even more active than now, and there is a considerable concern that the already polluted election process due to excessive defamation may become even more polluted.\\n\\nc. Considering the above points, it is difficult to view there as having been any change in circumstances or necessity requiring a different determination from the above precedent in this case; accordingly, the above precedent’s determination regarding the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case is valid even in this case. Therefore, the Provision Prohibiting Defamation in This Case does not infringe the freedom of political expression in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning administrative procedure and disclosure of information by public institutions are correct? (In cases of dispute, according to case law) (a) An administrative disposition may also be made against the State, and in such case as well the provisions of the Administrative Procedures Act concerning prior notice, hearing of opinions, and statement of reasons apply as they are. (b) Even if, by comprehensively considering the contents stated in the disposition document, the relevant statutes, and the overall process leading to the disposition, the party at the time of the disposition could sufficiently understand on what grounds and for what reasons the disposition was made, and thus had no particular obstacle in proceeding to administrative remedy procedures in opposition thereto, if the disposition document did not specifically state the grounds and reasons for the disposition, the disposition is unlawful. (c) In an action to revoke a disposition refusing disclosure of information filed by a requester for information disclosure, even if the requester was served with a copy of the requested information submitted as evidence to the court by the relevant public institution and, as a result, the relevant public institution came to disclose the information to the requester in effect, the legal interest in seeking revocation of the non-disclosure decision concerning that information is not extinguished. (d) A military servicemember A, who received a disciplinary disposition, requested disclosure of the names and positions of the disciplinary committee members in order to confirm a procedural defect in the composition of the disciplinary committee, but the request was denied and A filed an action for revocation thereof. If, in the disciplinary appeal proceedings brought by A, A learned that there was a defect in the composition of the disciplinary committee, and if the relevant disciplinary disposition was revoked on the ground of that defect, then A's legal interest in seeking disclosure of the information in the above revocation action is extinguished.

supporting_precedents: {"[2016DU64975]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding Ground 1 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\na. Article 29(2) of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act provides that “matters necessary for the scope, authorship, examination, authorization, publication, supply, selection, and price assessment of textbooks shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree.” Pursuant thereto, Article 33 of the Regulations on Textbooks, which are a Presidential Decree (hereinafter referred to as the “Textbook Regulations”), provides in paragraph (1) that “the price of authorized textbooks and recognized textbooks shall be determined by the publisher that has entered into an agreement with the author,” and in paragraph (2) that “notwithstanding paragraph (1), if the Minister of Education deems, through deliberation by the Deliberative Council (meaning the Textbook Deliberative Council under Article 18 of the Textbook Regulations), that there is a concern that the price of authorized textbooks and recognized textbooks may be unfairly determined for any of the following reasons, or if the publisher has already recovered all costs invested in the development of the textbook after the price was determined but does not reflect such recovery in the price, the Minister may order an adjustment of the price.” The reasons listed in each item are “1. where the proportion of manufacturing costs that were not actually incurred in the process of developing and manufacturing the book among the manufacturing costs is at least 15 per 1,000; 2. where there is an error in the classification of price-determination items or line items; 3. where the actual number of copies printed exceeds the expected number of copies by at least 1,000.” (Hereinafter, Article 33(2) of the Textbook Regulations is referred to as the “Provision at Issue.”)\\n\\nb. In light of the wording of the Provision at Issue, the history of its amendment, and the legislative purpose, in order to issue an order to adjust prices on the ground that, under the Provision at Issue, “there is a concern that the price of authorized textbooks and recognized textbooks may be unfairly determined for any of the reasons listed in each item,” it must be separately recognized not only that the textbook concerned falls under any of the reasons listed in each item of the Provision at Issue, but also that, due to such circumstances, there is a “concern that the price may be unfairly determined.” At this time, even if it is recognized that the textbook subject to the price adjustment order falls under any of the reasons listed in each item of the Provision at Issue, it cannot be immediately regarded as giving rise to a presumption that “there is a concern that the price of such textbook may be unfairly determined.” The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n① Whether there is a concern that the price may be unfairly determined must be determined by comprehensively considering the excessive profits of publishers of authorized and recognized textbooks and the resulting increase in consumers’ economic burden. Even if any of the reasons listed in each item of the Provision at Issue exists, it is difficult to conclude that the publisher necessarily obtains excessive profits or that consumers’ economic burden necessarily increases as a result.\\n\\n② It is difficult to say that the correlation between the reasons listed in each item of the Provision at Issue and the price actually determined by the publisher or the price the publisher wishes to determine is clear. Even where any of the reasons listed in each item of the Provision at Issue exists, the price determined by the publisher or the price the publisher wishes to determine may, objectively viewed, not be an unfair price.\\n\\n③ Since, in this manner, the reasons listed in each item of the Provision at Issue and the concern that the price may be unfairly determined are conceptually distinct and their correlation may not be immediately recognized, it cannot be said that the above unfairness is necessarily presumed merely because the above reasons are recognized.\\n\\nc. According to the reasoning of the judgment below, the following circumstances can be ascertained.\\n\\n(1) The Plaintiffs published authorized and recognized textbooks for the 2014 academic year used in elementary schools and high schools, as set forth in Attached Schedule 1, List of Dispositions of the judgment below (hereinafter referred to as the “Schedule 1 List of Dispositions”).\\n\\n(2) Among the textbooks listed in the Schedule 1 List of Dispositions, the textbooks for which the disposition agency is the Defendant Minister of Education are authorized textbooks, and the textbooks for which the disposition agencies are the remaining Defendants other than the Defendant Minister of Education are recognized textbooks (hereinafter, among the textbooks published by the Plaintiffs, the authorized textbooks are referred to as the “authorized textbooks at issue,” and the recognized textbooks are referred to as the “recognized textbooks at issue,” and the authorized textbooks and recognized textbooks at issue are collectively referred to as the “textbooks at issue”).\\n\\n(3) The Plaintiffs determined the prices of the textbooks at issue in the amounts stated in the “Desired Price” column of the Schedule 1 List of Dispositions.\\n\\n(4) On each date stated in the “Date of Disposition” column of the Schedule 1 List of Dispositions, the Defendants ordered the Plaintiffs to adjust the prices of the textbooks at issue to the prices stated in the “Adjusted Price” column of the Schedule 1 List of Dispositions (hereinafter referred to as the “Dispositions at Issue”). In the written dispositions at issue, Article 33(2), Item 1 or Item 3 of the Provision at Issue is stated as the legal basis, as indicated in the “Legal Basis for Disposition” column of the Schedule 1 List of Dispositions.\\n\\nd. On the premise of the above factual relations, the court below held that, in order to issue a price adjustment order pursuant to the Provision at Issue, in addition to the recognition of any of the reasons listed in each item of the Provision at Issue, it must be additionally proved that there is a “concern that the price may be unfairly determined”; however, with respect to the Defendant Minister’s price adjustment order for the authorized textbooks at issue, and with respect to the price adjustment order for the authorized textbooks listed in serial numbers 2 to 10, 12, 17, 22, 29, 30, 36, and 37 of the Schedule 1 List of Dispositions, which were ordered on the ground of Item 3 of the Provision at Issue, the court held that the evidence submitted by the Defendant Minister alone does not permit the conclusion that there is a concern that the prices of the respective textbooks at issue may be unfairly determined, and thus the grounds for disposition were not established.\\n\\ne. In light of the record, the above determination by the court below is consistent with the legal principles stated above and is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles regarding the requirements for a price adjustment order and the burden of proof.\\n\\n2. Regarding Ground 2 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\na. With respect to the price adjustment order for the authorized textbooks listed in serial numbers 1, 11, 13 to 16, 18 to 20, 23, and 39 to 43 of the Schedule 1 List of Dispositions, the court below rejected the Defendant Minister’s argument that the reason under Item 3 of the Provision at Issue exists because the average actual number of copies printed in the 2011 through 2013 academic years of the respective textbooks exceeded the expected number of copies by more than 1,000, for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) Neither the Textbook Regulations nor the public notice at issue contains any provision stating that, in the case of textbooks mainly used in the second or third year of high school, the average number of copies over the preceding 3 years should be regarded as the actual number of copies printed, and it is also difficult to regard the demand for textbooks before the revision of the curriculum as the demand for textbooks published after the curriculum was revised.\\n\\n(2) The Defendant Minister himself explains that the purpose of Item 3 of the Provision at Issue is to limit the “excess profit” actually realized by publishers as fixed costs decrease when the actual number of copies printed increases. In the case of books mainly used in the second or third year of high school, if the applicability of Item 3 of the Provision at Issue were determined based on the average number of copies printed over the preceding 3 years rather than the actual number of copies printed merely because orders are not placed immediately, this cannot be said to accord with the purpose of limiting excess profit actually realized.\\n\\nb. In light of the above statutes and the record, the court below’s determination does not contain the error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, of misapprehending the legal principles concerning the interpretation and application of the requirements of Item 3 of the Provision at Issue.\\n\\n3. Regarding Ground 3 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\nIn an administrative action seeking revocation of an administrative disposition, the disposition agency may not assert as a ground for the disposition separate facts that do not share identity with the grounds originally presented for the disposition in terms of the basic factual circumstances (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2016DO44186, decided August 29, 2017).\\n\\nThe court below held, with respect to the Defendant Minister’s argument that, in addition to the grounds under Item 3 of the Provision at Issue, the grounds under Item 1 should be added as grounds for the price adjustment order for the authorized textbooks listed in serial numbers 1, 11, 13 to 16, 18 to 20, 23, and 39 to 43 of the Schedule 1 List of Dispositions, that, whereas the original ground under Item 3 of the Provision at Issue is that the actual number of copies printed of the textbook is at least 1,000 greater than the expected number of copies, the added ground under Item 1 of the Provision at Issue is that the proportion of manufacturing costs that were not actually incurred is at least 15 per 1,000 among manufacturing costs, and thus the basic factual circumstances differ, so the addition of a disposition ground cannot be permitted.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above and the record, there is no error in the court below’s determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, of misapprehending the legal principles concerning the limits on the addition of grounds for disposition.\\n\\n4. Regarding Grounds 4 and 5 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\na. When an administrative agency takes a disposition, it must, in principle, present the basis and reasons to the party concerned (Article 23(1) of the Administrative Procedures Act). In such case, the administrative agency must specifically state the facts constituting the cause of the disposition and the contents of the statutes or autonomous regulations that serve as the basis (Article 14-2 of the Enforcement Decree of the Administrative Procedures Act).\\n\\nHowever, in light of the purpose of the system of stating the basis and reasons for a disposition, which is to exclude arbitrary decisions by the administrative agency and to enable the party concerned to appropriately respond in administrative remedy procedures, if, in making the disposition, the administrative agency stated the reasons to an extent that the party concerned could know the basis, even if the basis and reasons for the disposition were not specifically stated, the disposition cannot be deemed unlawful on that account. At this time, “where the reasons have been stated” means a case in which, comprehensively considering the contents stated in the written disposition, the relevant statutes, and the overall process leading up to the disposition, it is sufficiently clear to the party concerned, at the time of the disposition, on what basis and for what reasons the disposition was made, so that there was no particular obstacle to proceeding to administrative remedy procedures in objection thereto (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DO44186, decided August 29, 2017).\\n\\nb. The court below held that, with respect to the price adjustment order for the authorized textbooks at issue by the Defendant Minister, in the case of the price adjustment order on the ground of Item 3 of the Provision at Issue, the Plaintiffs themselves knew the expected number of copies and the actual number of copies printed that they had recorded, and further could sufficiently know the standard-copy determination method and the method and details of calculating the adjusted price applied by the Defendant Minister in making the disposition, so there was no particular obstacle to proceeding to administrative remedy procedures in objection thereto, and thus no procedural defect in violation of Article 23(1) of the Administrative Procedures Act was recognized. On the other hand, in the case of the remaining price adjustment orders, because the basis and reasons for the disposition were not specifically stated in the written dispositions, the Plaintiffs could not know at the time of the disposition on what basis and for what reasons the relevant price adjustment orders had been made, and therefore the court held that a procedural defect in violation of Article 23(1) of the Administrative Procedures Act was recognized.\\n\\nc. In light of the legal principles stated above and the record, there is no error in the court below’s determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, of misapprehending the legal principles concerning the statement of the basis and reasons for a disposition.\\n\\n5. Regarding Ground 6 of the Grounds for Appeal\\n\\na. If an administrative disposition is unlawful, as a general rule, it shall be revoked, and exceptionally, where revoking or changing such unlawful disposition would instead be manifestly contrary to the public welfare, a judgment based on circumstances may be rendered that does not permit the revocation of the unlawful administrative disposition. Therefore, the application of a judgment based on circumstances must be limited under extremely strict requirements, and when determining whether the requirement that it is “manifestly not consistent with the public welfare” is satisfied, the necessity of revoking or changing the unlawful administrative disposition and the situation contrary to the public welfare that may arise from such revocation or change must be compared and weighed to determine whether such application is warranted (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DO12853, decided October 24, 2013).\\n\\nb. The court below held that, based solely on the circumstances asserted by the Defendants, such as the appropriateness and stabilization of the prices of textbooks, which are public goods, and the need to alleviate the financial burden on the State and local governments and the increase in burden on parents, it is difficult to conclude that the revocation of each of the dispositions at issue falls within a case where revocation is manifestly contrary to the public welfare to such an extent that a judgment based on circumstances under Article 28 of the Administrative Litigation Act must be rendered.\\n\\nc. In light of the legal principles stated above and the record, there is no error in the court below’s determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, of misapprehending the legal principles concerning a judgment based on circumstances.\\n\\n6. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of the appeal shall be borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2022DU34562]": "We determine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Background of the case and the lower court’s judgment\\n\\na. According to the reasons stated in the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n1) The Plaintiff received from the Defendant a disciplinary disposition of a one-month reduction in salary on June 24, 2020, on the grounds of violation of the duty to maintain dignity, etc. (hereinafter referred to as “the disciplinary disposition at issue”).\\n\\n2) The Plaintiff filed an appeal against the disciplinary disposition at issue on July 8, 2020, pursuant to Article 60 of the Military Personnel Act.\\n\\n3) The Plaintiff requested disclosure from the Defendant, on December 30, 2020, of the names and positions of each disciplinary member who participated in the Disciplinary Committee (hereinafter referred to as “the information at issue”); however, on January 12, 2021, the Defendant issued a disposition refusing disclosure on the ground that the information at issue fell under Article 9(1) subparagraphs 1, 2, 5, and 6 of the Act on Disclosure of Information by Public Agencies (hereinafter referred to as “the disposition at issue”).\\n\\n4) Meanwhile, Article 9(6) of Army Regulation 180 provides: “The Disciplinary Committee and Appeal Review Committee for cases involving sexual violence, etc. shall include at least one female member (excluding cases where the victim is a male soldier, male civilian military employee, etc.). Provided, however, that where, due to unavoidable reasons, a female member cannot be appointed, the disciplinary authority shall specify the concrete reasons and obtain prior approval from the Chief of Staff of the Army in accordance with Attached Form No. 1.”\\nThe Disciplinary Appeal Review Committee of the Second Operations Command decided on October 8, 2021, to revoke the disciplinary disposition at issue on the ground that there was a procedural defect in the composition of the Disciplinary Committee in that Article 9(6) of Army Regulation 180 had not been complied with, and accordingly the Defendant revoked the disciplinary disposition at issue on October 25, 2021.\\n\\nb. The lower court held that the Plaintiff alleged that he had requested disclosure of the names and positions of the disciplinary members, which constitute the information at issue, in order to confirm whether there was a procedural defect in the composition of the Disciplinary Committee; however, since the Plaintiff learned through the appeal procedure that there was a defect in the composition of the Disciplinary Committee, the purpose of the request for disclosure of the information at issue can be regarded as already having been achieved, and since the disciplinary disposition at issue was revoked on the ground of a procedural defect, there is no need to dispute the disciplinary disposition, and thus there is no legal interest in seeking disclosure of the information at issue; on that basis, the lower court determined that this action was inadmissible.\\n\\n2. However, the lower court’s determination cannot be upheld for the following reasons.\\n\\na. Since the people’s right to request disclosure of information is a specific right protected by law, a requester who has sought disclosure of information from a public institution and received a disposition refusing disclosure has a legal interest in seeking cancellation of that disposition through administrative litigation, and the mere circumstance that the information sought to be disclosed has already been disclosed or can be easily ascertained by other means cannot negate the interest in the lawsuit or justify the non-disclosure decision (see Supreme Court Decisions 2005DO8733, July 13, 2007, and 2008DO13101, December 23, 2010, among others).\\nIn addition, once a requester has requested information disclosure from a public institution and received a disposition of refusal, a legal interest in seeking cancellation of the disposition refusing disclosure is recognized by that fact itself, and no additional legal interest is required (see Supreme Court Decisions 2003DO8050, December 12, 2003, and 2003DO1370, September 23, 2004, among others).\\n\\nb. Examining the foregoing facts in light of these legal principles, even if the Plaintiff learned in the appeal procedure regarding the disciplinary disposition at issue that there was a procedural defect in the composition of the Disciplinary Committee, or even if the disciplinary disposition at issue was revoked, such circumstances alone do not permit the conclusion that there is no legal interest in seeking cancellation of the disposition at issue, and once the Defendant refused the Plaintiff’s request for information disclosure, the Plaintiff still has a legal interest in seeking cancellation of the disposition refusing information disclosure.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the lower court, proceeding on a different premise, determined that this action was inadmissible on the ground that there was no legal interest in seeking disclosure of the information at issue. In so doing, the lower court erred by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the legal interest or interest in the lawsuit in a claim seeking cancellation of a disposition refusing information disclosure, thereby affecting the judgment. The ground of appeal pointing this out is well-founded.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the lower court judgment is reversed and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2023DU39724]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (the statements in the supplemental brief of grounds of appeal submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal has expired are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. With respect to the grounds of appeal concerning whether the Administrative Procedures Act applies and whether it was complied with (First Ground of Appeal)\\n   a. Articles 21 through 23 of the Administrative Procedures Act, which is the general law on administrative procedure, provide for prior notice, hearing of opinions, and presentation of reasons. Where an administrative agency issues a disposition imposing duties on, or restricting rights or interests of, a party, it shall in advance notify the parties, etc. of matters such as the “title of the disposition,” “the facts constituting the grounds for the disposition to be made, the content of the disposition, and the legal basis therefor,” “the effect that opinions may be submitted with respect thereto and the method of handling the case where no opinion is submitted,” “the name and address of the agency to which opinions are to be submitted,” and “the time limit for submitting opinions” (Article 21(1)); even where other statutes, etc. do not mandatorily require a hearing or the holding of a public hearing, it must give the parties, etc. an opportunity to submit opinions (Article 22(3)); and when an administrative agency makes a disposition, it shall, in principle, present the grounds and reasons therefor to the party (Article 23(1)). Therefore, if an administrative agency has made an adverse administrative disposition without going through the foregoing procedures, such disposition is, in principle, unlawful and cannot escape revocation (see Supreme Court Decisions 2016DU64975, decided 2019. 1. 31., and 2017DU66602, decided 2020. 7. 23., etc.).\\n   Meanwhile, under Article 2(4) of the Administrative Procedures Act, “parties, etc.” means the party who is directly the other party to the disposition of an administrative agency and interested persons whom the administrative agency has caused to participate in the administrative procedure ex officio or upon application; and Article 9 of the same Act provides that, in addition to natural persons, juridical persons, and associations or foundations without legal personality, “persons who may be the subject of rights and duties pursuant to other statutes, etc.” may also be “parties, etc.”, but it does not exclude the State from “parties, etc.”. In addition, Article 3(2) of the Administrative Procedures Act enumerates matters to which the Administrative Procedures Act does not apply, and “administrative acts against the State” do not fall within such exceptions.\\n   In light of the provisions of the Administrative Procedures Act and the legislative purpose of the Administrative Procedures Act of ensuring fairness, transparency, and reliability in administration, there is no reason to treat the State, which suffers disadvantage by dispositions of administrative agencies, differently from the general public. Accordingly, in making an administrative disposition against the State, the Administrative Procedures Act concerning prior notice, hearing of opinions, and presentation of reasons, as noted above, must also be deemed to apply as is.\\n   b. The court below, for the reasons stated in its holding, determined that the Administrative Procedures Act also applies to the Plaintiff, who is the State, and then determined that Article 43 of the Enforcement Decree of the Broadcasting Act does not fall under “where there are special provisions in other statutes” in Article 3(1) of the Administrative Procedures Act, and that it is difficult to view the disposition in this case, as held by the court below, as having complied with Articles 21 through 23 of the Administrative Procedures Act. Examining the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in the court below’s determination that violates the rules of logic and experience, exceeds the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, or misunderstands the legal principles concerning whether the Administrative Procedures Act applies and whether it was complied with.\\n\\n2. With respect to the grounds of appeal concerning the interpretation of the proviso to Article 64 of the Broadcasting Act and Article 39 No. 10 of the Enforcement Decree of the Broadcasting Act (Second and Third Grounds of Appeal)\\n   a. With respect to the interpretation of statutes concerning burdens such as taxes or charges, whether they pertain to requirements for imposition or requirements for exemption, they must, unless special circumstances exist, be interpreted according to the text, and expansive interpretation or analogical interpretation without reasonable grounds is not permitted (see Supreme Court Decision 2022DA218585, decided 2022. 12. 29., etc.).
