The same applies to the interpretation of the requirements for imposition and exemption of the television broadcasting reception fee (hereinafter referred to as the “reception fee”), which is a special levy imposed on a specific group possessing television receivers (hereinafter referred to as “receivers”).\\n   Under the proviso to Article 64 of the Broadcasting Act, registration may be exempted for receivers prescribed by Presidential Decree, and Article 39 No. 10 of the Enforcement Decree of the Broadcasting Act provides that “receivers installed within the premises of military units and conscripted police units” are receivers exempt from registration. However, each item of Article 39 of the above Enforcement Decree adopts the method of separately regulating receivers exempt from registration by distinguishing between cases in which, as in No. 10, only the place where the receiver is located is a requirement, and cases in which, as in Nos. 12 and 13, the purpose of use is also made a requirement in addition to the place. Accordingly, receivers located “within military premises” must be deemed receivers exempt from the registration obligation regardless of the purpose for which they are used, and no reception fee may be imposed thereon.\\n   b. The court below determined that, for the reasons stated in its holding, the receivers possessed (held) in the bachelor quarters and visiting personnel quarters within the premises of the Plaintiff’s air wing fall under receivers exempt from the registration obligation prescribed in Article 39 No. 10 of the Enforcement Decree of the Broadcasting Act, and therefore the disposition in this case imposing the reception fee thereon is unlawful. Examining the reasons stated in the judgment of the court below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, although there are somewhat inappropriate parts in the court below’s statement of reasons, there is no error in the court below’s determination that violates the rules of logic and experience, exceeds the bounds of free evaluation of evidence, or misunderstands the legal principles concerning the interpretation of the proviso to Article 64 of the Broadcasting Act and Article 39 No. 10 of the Enforcement Decree of the Broadcasting Act, thereby affecting the judgment.\\n   In addition, the argument in the grounds of appeal to the effect that if Article 39 No. 10 of the Enforcement Decree of the Broadcasting Act is interpreted as exempting registration even where it is unrelated to military duties, such interpretation exceeds the limits of the delegation under the Broadcasting Act and is therefore void, is an argument raised for the first time at the final appellate stage and thus cannot constitute a proper ground of appeal; furthermore, even upon review, there are no circumstances warranting acceptance of that argument.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nThe appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are to be borne by the losing party; accordingly, the judgment is rendered in the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved, as stated in the text of the judgment."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning administrative acts is not correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: If, under the former Public Hygiene Control Act and its subordinate statutes, a public hygiene business was transferred and assigned, and the transferee thereafter gave the administrative agency notification of the opening of a new place of business, a business suspension disposition cannot be imposed on the transferee on the ground of the illegality of the suspension of the public hygiene business concerning the transferor.
B: A building permit has an objective character, and therefore, when granting such permit, the administrative agency conducts only a formal examination with respect to personal elements, such as who the building owner is.
C: A business suspension disposition imposed on a medical care institution under the National Health Insurance Act on the ground that the medical care institution caused the insurer to bear the cost of medical care benefits by fraud or other improper means has the character of an object-related disposition.
D: An authorization disposition for the establishment of a housing reconstruction association made by an administrative agency on the basis of the Act on the Maintenance and Improvement of Urban Areas and Dwelling Conditions for Residents and other related statutes has the character of a rights-creating disposition of a kind that confers the status of an administrative entity having the authority to implement a housing reconstruction project when the statutory requirements are satisfied.
E: The determination of the business type of an individual workplace made by the Korea Workers' Compensation & Welfare Service against an employer must be regarded as a confirmatory administrative act exercising public power as the execution of the law concerning concrete facts by an administrative agency.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2001DU1611]": "The judgment of the lower court is reversed, and the case is remanded to the Seoul High Court."}

{"[2009DA30427]": "Before examining the grounds of appeal, the Court considers ex officio.\\n\\nA housing reconstruction maintenance project association under the Act on the Maintenance and Improvement of Urban Areas and Dwelling Conditions for Residents (hereinafter referred to as the “Urban Improvement Act”) (hereinafter referred to as a “reconstruction association”) is constituted as a juridical person by obtaining approval for establishment from the competent administrative agency after satisfying the requirements and procedures prescribed by the relevant statutes, such as obtaining consent for establishment of the association (hereinafter referred to as the “resolution for establishment of the association”) from the owners of land and buildings within the rearrangement zone, and then completing registration (Articles 16(2), 16(5), and 18 of the Urban Improvement Act). And a reconstruction association established through such procedures has the status of an administrative subject that performs certain administrative acts in accordance with the law, within the scope of the purpose of implementing the “housing reconstruction project” under the Urban Improvement Act in the rearrangement zone under the supervision of the competent administrative agency.\\n\\nTherefore, the approval disposition for establishment of an association made by the administrative agency on the basis of the Urban Improvement Act and other relevant statutes is not merely a supplementary act to the private persons’ act of establishing the association, but must be regarded as having the character of a kind of constitutive disposition conferring legal authority that grants the status of an administrative subject (a public corporation) having the authority to carry out a housing reconstruction project under the Urban Improvement Act when the statutory requirements are satisfied.\\n\\nAnd, given that view, once there has been an approval disposition for establishment of the association, the resolution for establishment of the association is merely one of the requirements necessary for making the administrative disposition known as the said approval disposition; thus, after such approval disposition has been made, asserting the invalidity of the establishment of the association on the ground of defects in the resolution for establishment of the association must be sought by way of an administrative lawsuit seeking revocation or a declaration of invalidity of the approval disposition for establishment of the association, and, separately from this, a declaratory action challenging only the resolution for establishment of the association as to whether it is valid or not is impermissible for lack of standing to seek a declaration.\\n\\nHowever, according to the reasoning of the judgment of the lower court and the record, it can be seen that the part of the claim in this action seeking a declaration of invalidity of the establishment of a housing reconstruction maintenance project association was brought on October 18, 2007, after the competent administrative agency had rendered, on August 11, 2006, an approval disposition for establishment of the defendant association, seeking a declaration of invalidity of the resolution for establishment of the association in this case, which was merely one of the requirements for that approval disposition, and under the foregoing legal principles there is room to regard it as an unlawful action.\\n\\nHowever, on the other hand, the substance of the object that the Plaintiffs seek to challenge through the part of the claim in this action seeking a declaration of invalidity of the establishment of a housing reconstruction maintenance project association is the effectiveness of the establishment of the association, and in order to challenge it, as noted above, the proper method would be to seek revocation or a declaration of invalidity of the approval disposition for establishment of the association; yet, having failed to properly understand these legal principles and, while following the previous practical custom of viewing the approval disposition for establishment of a reconstruction association as a supplementary act, appears to have chosen the method of seeking a declaration of invalidity of the general meeting resolution for the establishment of the association, which corresponds to its requirements, out of necessity. In light of such circumstances, the part of the claim in this action seeking a declaration of invalidity of the establishment of a housing reconstruction maintenance project association cannot be said to be anything other than, in substance, a challenge to the effectiveness of the approval disposition for establishment of the association; and, further considering that the opposite party to that part of the claim is the defendant association, which has the status of an administrative subject, it is appropriate to regard the part of the claim in this action seeking a declaration of invalidity of the establishment of a housing reconstruction maintenance project association as concerning a legal relationship under public law and therefore as constituting a party litigation, which is a type of administrative litigation.\\n\\nIf so, the court below should have examined this case in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the Administrative Litigation Act and properly exercised its power to clarify whether to amend the action into an administrative appeal litigation, so as to ensure a lawful form of litigation; but without proceeding to such measures, it treated this merely as a civil action and examined it pursuant to the procedures prescribed by the Civil Procedure Act, thereby ultimately erring in the method of examination, and thus the judgment of the lower court must be regarded as containing an illegality of incomplete examination that affected the result of the judgment.\\n\\nTherefore, without omitting consideration of the grounds of appeal, the Court, ex officio, reverses the judgment of the lower court and remands the case to the court below for further trial and determination; it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2014DU41190]": "We adjudicate the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. A building permit has an in rem nature, and thus the administrative agency, when granting such permit, conducts only a formal review with respect to personal elements, such as who the building owner or landowner is (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DO2296, decided May 13, 2010). Where a building owner obtained a building permit of an in rem nature to construct a building on the land after receiving from the landowner a land-use consent, but lost the right to use the relevant land due to the building owner’s attributable cause before commencing construction, the landowner, whose exercise of ownership over the land may be impeded by the existence of the building permit, must be deemed entitled to apply for revocation of that building permit. Accordingly, an act refusing such application by the landowner becomes subject to an action for revocation.\\n\\nMeanwhile, the administrative agency that rendered the administrative disposition may revoke it as a separate administrative act that causes it to lose effect, even if there was no particular defect at the time of the disposition and there is no separate legal basis for revocation after the disposition, where there has arisen a change in circumstances making it unnecessary to maintain the original disposition, or a need has arisen in the public interest of grave nature (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DO7606, decided July 22, 2004, etc.). However, since revoking or canceling a beneficial administrative act, or suspending it, infringes the vested rights already granted to the public, even if there are grounds for revocation, etc., the exercise of the right to revoke, etc. may be permitted only where there is a grave public-interest necessity or a need to protect a third party’s interest sufficient to justify the infringement of vested rights, and, when compared and balanced with the disadvantages suffered by the other party, such public-interest necessity, etc. is strong enough to justify the disadvantages suffered by the other party (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DO27322, decided March 15, 2012, etc.).\\n\\n2. According to the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\na. On 2012. 3. 30., the Plaintiff sold to the Defendant-intervenor the land at issue owned by the Plaintiff and the building thereon (hereinafter referred to as the “sale and purchase agreement at issue”).\\n\\nb. Around 2012. 7. 24., the Defendant-intervenor applied to the Defendant for a building permit to newly construct a multi-family housing building on the land at issue, etc., attaching the Plaintiff’s land-use consent; then, when Mugunghwa Trust Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Mugunghwa Trust”) was added as a building owner, the Defendant-intervenor had the Plaintiff prepare the consent at issue, changing the users to “the Defendant-intervenor, Mugunghwa Trust,” and submitted it, thereby obtaining the building permit at issue from the Defendant on 2012. 10. 15.\\n\\nc. At the bottom of the consent at issue, it was expressly stated: “Since this consent at issue is based on the sale and purchase agreement at issue, it becomes void upon rescission of the said sale and purchase agreement, and the users (the Defendant-intervenor, Mugunghwa Trust) may not assert any rights in relation thereto for any reason whatsoever.”\\n\\nd. The Defendant-intervenor extended the due date for payment of the balance four times, and then, while again extending the due date for payment of the balance to 2013. 1. 31. on 2012. 12. 31., agreed that if the balance was not paid in full by 2013. 1. 31., the Plaintiff could rescind the sale and purchase agreement at issue without any separate demand procedure, and in such event the consent at issue would immediately lose effect and the Defendant-intervenor would waive and withdraw the building permit at issue.\\n\\ne. However, the Defendant-intervenor did not pay the balance by 2013. 1. 31. either, and the Plaintiff rescinded the sale and purchase agreement at issue. On 2013. 7. 24., the Plaintiff applied to the Defendant for revocation of the building permit at issue on the grounds, among others, that “as the consent at issue has become ineffective, there has also arisen a change in circumstances making it no longer necessary to maintain the building permit at issue based thereon.”\\n\\nf. On 2013. 7. 25., the Defendant rendered the disposition of refusal at issue, refusing the above application on the ground that “a building permit can be canceled if the building owner himself or herself applies therefor or if it falls under Article 11(7) of the Building Act, but a decision through consultation or litigation between interested parties is first required.”\\n\\n3. The court below held the disposition of refusal at issue unlawful on the ground that, for the following reasons, there are no interests worthy of protection of the Defendant-intervenor and Mugunghwa Trust that would be infringed by revocation of the building permit at issue, and thus revocation thereof would be appropriate.\\n\\na. Due to the continued existence of the building permit at issue, the Plaintiff cannot in fact exercise the powers of use, profit, and disposition with respect to the land at issue.\\n\\nb. The Defendant-intervenor and Mugunghwa Trust have failed to acquire ownership of, or the right to use, the land at issue because the sale and purchase agreement at issue was rescinded, and they have not yet commenced construction pursuant to the building permit at issue.\\n\\nc. Although the Defendant-intervenor extended the due date for payment of the balance under the sale and purchase agreement at issue as many as five times, it failed to pay the balance, and while extending the final due date for payment of the balance, it agreed that if the sale and purchase agreement at issue were rescinded, it would waive and withdraw the building permit at issue.\\n\\n4. In light of the legal principles seen above, the Defendant’s act of refusing the Plaintiff’s application, made on the ground that the Plaintiff, as the landowner, had no right to allow the Defendant-intervenor and Mugunghwa Trust to use the land at issue, to revoke the building permit at issue, becomes subject to an action for revocation. Furthermore, the need to protect the Plaintiff’s interests is recognized by the Defendant’s revocation of the building permit at issue upon the Plaintiff’s application, and, when compared and balanced with the disadvantages suffered by the Defendant-intervenor and Mugunghwa Trust, the need to protect the Plaintiff’s interests is strong enough to justify the disadvantages suffered by the Defendant-intervenor and Mugunghwa Trust.\\n\\nTherefore, the court below’s determination is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles concerning revocation of a beneficial administrative act and in failing to fully examine the comparison and balancing of the interests and disadvantages arising from revocation of the building permit at issue.\\n\\n5. The Defendant-intervenor’s appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2019DU61137]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, the following circumstances can be found.\\n\\na. On or around 1992. 1. 13., the Plaintiff filed with the Defendant, the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service (hereinafter referred to as “the Defendant”), a report of establishment of an industrial accident compensation insurance relationship with respect to a steel plate coil processing factory located in Siheung-si ○○ Industrial Complex (hereinafter referred to as “the business establishment at issue”), designating the business category as “wholesale and retail trade and repair of consumer goods,” and thereafter had been paying industrial accident compensation insurance premiums accordingly.\\n\\nb. On 2018. 1. 15., the Defendant decided and notified the Plaintiff that the business category of the business establishment at issue would be changed, as of 2014. 1. 1., from “wholesale and retail trade and repair of consumer goods” (industrial accident compensation insurance premium rate: 9/1,000) to “businesses that perform welding or cutting of various metals” (industrial accident compensation insurance premium rate: 19/1,000) (hereinafter referred to as “the decision to change the business category at issue”).\\n\\nc. As a follow-up measure pursuant to the decision to change the business category at issue, the co-defendant in the court below, the National Health Insurance Service, notified the Plaintiff on 2018. 1. 22. to additionally pay KRW 93,675,300 as industrial accident compensation insurance premiums for the period from 2014. 1. 1. to 2016. 12. 31., and on 2018. 2. 21. to additionally pay KRW 59,912,370 as industrial accident compensation insurance premiums for the above period (hereinafter collectively referred to as “the additional premium imposition disposition at issue”).\\n\\nd. The Plaintiff filed this action seeking against the Defendant the revocation of the decision to change the business category at issue, and against the co-defendant in the court below, the National Health Insurance Service, the revocation of the additional premium imposition disposition at issue.\\n\\n2. The Judgment of the Lower Court and the Issue in This Case\\n\\na. (1) The lower court held that the Defendant’s decision to change the business category at issue alone could not be said to directly cause any change in or disadvantage to the Plaintiff’s rights and obligations, and that only when the co-defendant in the court below, the National Health Insurance Service, imposed the additional premium imposition disposition at issue pursuant to the decision to change the business category at issue would an actual disadvantage arise to the Plaintiff; and further, on the grounds that the Plaintiff could obtain sufficient relief by seeking only the revocation of the additional premium imposition disposition at issue against the co-defendant in the court below, the National Health Insurance Service, it determined that the decision to change the business category at issue did not constitute an administrative disposition subject to an appeal litigation, and therefore dismissed the portion of this action seeking revocation of the decision to change the business category at issue against the Defendant.\\n\\n(2) The lower court held that the business category of the business establishment at issue fell under “wholesale and retail trade and repair of consumer goods,” and thus upheld the Plaintiff’s claim against the co-defendant in the court below, the National Health Insurance Service, seeking revocation of the additional premium imposition disposition at issue.\\n\\nb. The issue in this case is whether the Defendant’s decision to change the business category at issue constitutes an administrative disposition subject to an appeal litigation.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s Judgment\\n\\na. Relevant legal principles\\n\\nThe term “disposition,” which is the object of an appeal litigation, means “the exercise of public authority or its refusal as the enforcement of law concerning specific facts performed by an administrative agency, and other administrative acts equivalent thereto” (Article 2(1)1 of the Administrative Litigation Act). Whether an act of an administrative agency can be the object of an appeal litigation cannot be determined abstractly and generally; in a specific case, it must be determined individually by considering the content and purport of the relevant laws and regulations, the subject, content, form, and procedure of the act, the substantive connection between the act and the disadvantage suffered by the counterparty and other interested persons, and the principle of rule-of-law administration and the attitudes of the administrative agency or interested persons concerned with the act (see Supreme Court en banc Decision 2008DU167 rendered on November 18, 2010). Whether there is a statutory basis for a disposition, and whether the procedures for disposition prescribed by the Administrative Procedures Act were observed, are factors to be considered at the stage of determining whether the disposition at issue is lawful on the merits, not factors to be considered at the stage of examining litigation requirements (see Supreme Court Decision 2015DU60617 rendered on August 30, 2016). Where it is unclear whether an act of an administrative agency constitutes a “disposition,” it must be normatively determined, with due regard to the recognizability and predictability of the counterparty, who has a significant interest in choosing the means of objection thereto (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DU33537 rendered on October 25, 2018).\\n\\nb. The relevant statutes and regulations provide as follows with respect to changes in the business category for industrial accident compensation insurance.\\n\\n(1) According to the Act on the Collection of Premiums for Employment Insurance and Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance (hereinafter referred to as the “Premium Collection Act”), industrial accident compensation insurance premiums to be borne by an employer are calculated by summing the amounts obtained by multiplying the total individual remuneration of workers engaged in the business operated by the employer by the industrial accident compensation insurance premium rate (Article 13(5)). The industrial accident compensation insurance premium rate is determined and publicly notified by the Minister of Employment and Labor for each business category classified on the basis of the risk of accident occurrence, homogeneity of economic activities, etc., based on the ratio of the total amount of industrial accident compensation insurance benefits to the total amount of remuneration for the past three years as of June 30 each year; and the composition and calculation method of the premium rate for each business category are prescribed in [Attached Table 1] of the Enforcement Rule of the same Act (Article 14(3), Article 12 of the Enforcement Rule of the same Act).\\n\\nWhen publicly notifying the “industrial accident compensation insurance premium rates by business category” each year, the Minister of Employment and Labor also publicly notifies, together with them, an “illustrative table of business categories” subdividing business categories by taking into account the risk of accident occurrence, homogeneity of economic activities, the content of the main products/services of the business establishment, and the work process and content, based on the Korean Standard Industrial Classification (a notice of the Statistics Korea), and this includes business codes and explanations for each business item.\\n\\n(2) According to the Premium Collection Act, an employer shall file a report of establishment of an insurance relationship within 14 days from the date on which the insurance relationship was established (Article 11(1)), and if the business category changes, shall file a report with the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service within 14 days from the date of such change (Article 12(1), Article 9 subparagraph 3 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act). Where an employer fails to file such report or where the report is not true to fact, the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service shall notify the employer in advance, investigate the facts, change the business category, and calculate the premiums accordingly (Article 16-9(2), (3), Article 16-6(1), Article 19-2). Industrial accident compensation insurance premiums are imposed monthly by the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service and collected by the National Health Insurance Service (Article 16-2). Where the insurance premiums already paid by the employer exceed the premiums calculated by the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service, the National Health Insurance Service shall return the excess amount to the employer, and where they are insufficient, shall collect the deficiency from the employer (Article 16-9(3)).\\n\\n(3) According to the “Regulations on the Processing of Application and Imposition Operations,” which were enacted by the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service for the purpose of prescribing matters delegated by the Premium Collection Act and its subordinate statutes and matters necessary for their implementation, if there is a report of a change in the business category by an employer, or if it is determined that a change in the business category is necessary, the head of the branch office of the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service may investigate the facts and change the business category (Article 21). In such case, in principle, matters necessary for the investigation, including the grounds for the investigation, investigative materials, and investigators, shall be notified to the employer in writing in advance (Article 22(1)); first, the matter shall undergo deliberation by the “staff consultative body,” after which the results of the deliberation shall be notified to the employer in writing and the employer’s opinion shall be heard (Article 22(2)1, (3)); thereafter, the business category change shall be determined following deliberation by the “Business Category Change Deliberation Committee” (Article 22(2)2). Upon completion of the business category change and the calculation of premiums pursuant to Article 16-9(2) of the Premium Collection Act, the processing result shall be notified to the employer in writing (Article 22(7)).\\n\\nc. In light of the foregoing legal principles, when examining the content and structure of the relevant provisions, the “decision to change the business category of an individual business establishment” made by the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service against an employer must be regarded as a “disposition,” that is, an exercise of public authority as enforcement of law concerning specific facts performed by an administrative agency. The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n(1) Since the industrial accident compensation insurance premium rate by business category is determined and publicly notified annually by the Minister of Employment and Labor, once the business category of an individual business establishment is specifically determined, the industrial accident compensation insurance premium rate applicable to that business establishment is automatically determined accordingly. Although the Premium Collection Act does not specifically prescribe the procedure, method, or standards for determining the business category of an individual business establishment, nor does it expressly delegate such matters to subordinate statutes, the provisions of the Premium Collection Act concerning reports of changes in business category and the provisions concerning fact-finding by the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service presuppose that the business category is determined by taking into account the specific characteristics of each individual business establishment and that the industrial accident compensation insurance premium rate is determined accordingly. Therefore, the determination by the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service of the business category of an individual business establishment is an administrative act performed in the course of implementing the Premium Collection Act.\\n\\nAccording to the public notice by the Minister of Employment and Labor, the determination of the business category of an individual business establishment is made by first confirming the risk of accident occurrence at the business establishment, homogeneity of economic activities, the content of the main products/services, work processes and content, the classification of business content under the Korean Standard Industrial Classification, and the business category applied to other business establishments of the same or similar kind, and then finalizing the business item by referring to the “illustrative table of business categories” publicly notified by the Minister of Employment and Labor each year. While the employer’s report of establishment or change of the insurance relationship is considered first, if the employer neglects to report or if there is doubt about the content of the report, the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service, which is the administrative agency calculating industrial accident compensation insurance premiums, must directly investigate the facts and make the determination. In light of the subject, content, and determination standards of such business category determination, the determination of the business category of an individual business establishment must be regarded as a “confirmatory administrative act” exercising public authority as enforcement of law concerning specific facts.\\n\\n(2) If the business category of an individual business establishment is changed to the disadvantage of the employer, the industrial accident compensation insurance premium rate increases and the industrial accident compensation insurance premiums to be paid by the employer increase. Therefore, the decision by the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service to change the business category must be regarded as directly affecting the employer’s rights and obligations as well. When the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service decides to change the business category of an individual business establishment and calculates the industrial accident compensation insurance premiums, it is contemplated that the National Health Insurance Service will subsequently make separate dispositions of additionally collecting any shortfall for the past period or imposing premiums monthly for future periods. However, the administrative agency that performs the adjudicative function of changing the business category of an individual business establishment and calculating industrial accident compensation insurance premiums is the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service, and the National Health Insurance Service, after receiving the relevant materials from the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service, serves notices of payment of industrial accident compensation insurance premiums to the employer and collects them. Therefore, rather than requiring the National Health Insurance Service to litigate the propriety of the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service’s decision to change the business category, it is reasonable to have the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service, which is the entity that made the decision, be the party to the litigation.\\n\\nA final and conclusive judgment that determines a disposition to be unlawful and revokes it binds not only the disposition agency, which becomes the defendant in the litigation, but also other related administrative agencies (Article 30(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act). In accordance with the binding force of a revocation judgment, the disposition agency and related administrative agencies are obligated to make the disposition again in a state that excludes the grounds of illegality affirmed in that judgment, or otherwise take measures to remove the unlawful result (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DU27517 rendered on October 29, 2015, among others). Once a judgment revoking the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service’s decision to change the business category becomes final and conclusive, each disposition of premium imposition made by the National Health Insurance Service on the basis of that decision loses its legal and factual basis. Accordingly, the National Health Insurance Service is obligated ex officio to revoke or modify each disposition of premium imposition, and to take measures such as returning any amount paid by the employer that exceeds the proper amount.\\n\\nAccordingly, rather than requiring the employer to challenge each individual disposition of premium imposition against the National Health Insurance Service, it is not only a means of simplifying the litigation relationship, but also a means of fundamentally resolving the dispute at an early stage, to allow the employer to challenge the propriety of the decision to change the business category, which is the core issue in the dispute, against the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service, the administrative agency that performed the adjudicative function. It is precisely for this reason that the Supreme Court has already held that an act by the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service refusing an employer’s application for a change in business category constitutes a “refusal disposition” subject to an appeal litigation (Supreme Court Decision 2007DU10488 rendered on May 8, 2008).\\n\\n(3) As noted above, the Defendant’s internal regulations prescribe the procedures for prior notice and hearing of opinions in even greater detail than those prescribed by the Administrative Procedures Act, and also require that the processing result be notified in writing. In addition, according to the record, after going through the prior notice and hearing procedures under these internal regulations, the Defendant prepared and delivered to the Plaintiff a notice (Plaintiff’s Exhibit No. 4) informing the Plaintiff of the decision to change the business category at issue as the processing result. That notice states not only the content and reasons for the decision to change the business category and the applicable statutes, but also contains the following guidance on the means of objection: “If you have any objection to this decision, you are informed that you may file an administrative appeal under Article 28 of the Administrative Appeals Act or an administrative action under the Administrative Litigation Act within 90 days from the day on which you became aware of the existence of the disposition.” In light of these internal regulations of the Defendant and the actual process of the decision to change the business category, it can be seen that the Defendant itself recognizes the decision to change the business category as a disposition to which the Administrative Procedures Act and the Administrative Litigation Act apply, and the employer, as the counterparty, could not but recognize the Defendant’s decision to change the business category as a disposition subject to an appeal litigation. In this manner, it also runs counter to the principle of good faith (Article 4 of the Administrative Procedures Act) for the Defendant, after guiding the means of objection, to raise a preliminary defense that there is no “dispositional character” once this action is filed.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court Decisions 87NU634 rendered on May 23, 1989, and 94NU8853 rendered on July 28, 1995, which were cited by the lower court, held that a decision changing the type of business subject to industrial accident compensation insurance is not a disposition subject to an appeal litigation; however, these decisions concerned cases under the former Act, and after the Premium Collection Act was enacted and enforced by Act No. 7047 on December 31, 2003, and the relevant regulations were reorganized, they are not suitable for direct reliance as they stand.\\n\\n(4) Meanwhile, each disposition of premium imposition made by the National Health Insurance Service against the employer pursuant to the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service’s decision to change the business category also constitutes a disposition subject to an appeal litigation, and therefore the employer may challenge each disposition of premium imposition through a separate appeal litigation. However, where the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service, in making a decision to change the business category, has in substance complied with the disposition procedures prescribed by the Administrative Procedures Act by preparing and delivering a disposition document to the individual employer that includes prior notice and hearing of opinions, statement of reasons, and notice of the means of objection, thereby ensuring the employer an opportunity to exercise the right of defense and to object, the decision to change the business category should be regarded, in terms of its content, form, and procedure, not as a so-called “litigation-law disposition” recognized as a disposition under the Administrative Litigation Act merely in order to enable early relief of rights, but as a so-called “substantive-law disposition,” namely, a manifestation of intent by an administrative agency that has direct legal effect externally as a regulation of an individual and concrete case. In such a case, when the employer fails to object within the period prescribed by the Administrative Appeals Act and the Administrative Litigation Act and preclusive force against challenge arises, unless the decision to change the business category has a grave and obvious defect and is therefore not void by operation of law, it is appropriate to view that the employer may not assert the illegality of the prior disposition, namely the decision to change the business category, in the proceedings concerning each subsequent disposition of premium imposition based on that decision. In such a case, recognizing the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service’s decision to change the business category as a disposition subject to an appeal litigation and thereby ensuring an opportunity to object under the Administrative Litigation Act also accords with the purpose of the short filing period system of “early finalization of administrative legal relations.”\\n\\nHowever, where the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service, in making the decision to change the business category, has in substance failed to comply with the disposition procedures prescribed by the Administrative Procedures Act, so that the employer was not guaranteed an opportunity to exercise the right of defense and to object, recognizing the decision as a disposition subject to an appeal litigation is only to guarantee the employer an early opportunity for relief of rights; therefore, in such a case, even if the employer did not file an action for revocation of the decision to change the business category within the filing period, it should be permitted to challenge the illegality of the prior disposition, namely the decision to change the business category, only in the proceedings concerning each subsequent disposition of premium imposition.\\n\\nd. Nevertheless, the lower court determined that the decision to change the business category at issue did not constitute a disposition subject to an appeal litigation. The lower court’s judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning dispositions subject to an appeal litigation.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the part of the judgment below concerning the Defendant is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2022DU30546]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Where a medical care institution, by fraud or other improper means, caused the insurer to bear the cost of medical care benefits, the business suspension disposition imposed on the medical care institution under Article 98(1)1 of the National Health Insurance Act is not a sanction against the personal qualification of the medical practitioner, but one directed at the business of the medical care institution itself, and thus has the character of a disposition in rem. Therefore, where a medical care institution that caused the insurer to bear the cost of medical care benefits by fraud or other improper means has closed its business, the medical care institution is not only in a state in which it cannot conduct business, but the object of the disposition has also disappeared; accordingly, no business suspension disposition may be imposed on that medical care institution or on the medical care institution newly established by its founder after the closure (see Supreme Court Decision 2020DU39365 rendered on January 27, 2022). The same applies to the business suspension disposition imposed on a medical care institution under Article 98(1)2 of the National Health Insurance Act and to the business suspension disposition imposed on a medical aid institution under Article 28(1)3 of the Medical Aid Act, where a public official belonging to the Ministry of Health and Welfare has been refused, obstructed, or evaded in conducting an inspection or questioning.\\n\\n2. a. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment and the record, the following circumstances may be ascertained.\\n\\n1) The Plaintiff operated the former hospital from September 15, 2014, and after closing it on May 4, 2018, has been operating the hospital at issue since October 10, 2018.\\n\\n2) The Defendant conducted an on-site inspection of the former hospital on January 23, 2018, and the Plaintiff refused the on-site inspection on January 26, 2018.\\n\\n3) On March 21, 2019, the Defendant, on the ground that “the Plaintiff refused, obstructed, or evaded the on-site inspection,” issued the disposition at issue against the Plaintiff, suspending for one year the business of the hospital at issue as a medical care institution and a medical aid institution pursuant to Article 98(1)2 of the National Health Insurance Act and Article 28(1)3 of the Medical Aid Act.\\n\\nb. The lower court, premising that the disposition at issue has not only the character of a disposition in rem but also the character of a disposition in personam, determined that the disposition at issue ordering suspension of business with respect to the hospital at issue newly established by the Plaintiff, based on the unlawful refusal of inspection that occurred at the former hospital, is lawful.\\n\\n3. However, according to the legal principles stated by the Supreme Court in the above Decision 2020DU39365 after the lower court judgment, where the medical care institution that committed the act of refusing inspection has closed its business, a business suspension disposition cannot be imposed on the medical care institution newly established by the founder of that medical care institution; accordingly, the disposition at issue is unlawful, and the lower court judgment, which held otherwise, erred by misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the legal nature of the business suspension disposition and its object, as prescribed in Article 98(1)2 of the National Health Insurance Act and Article 28(1)3 of the Medical Aid Act, thereby affecting the judgment. The ground of appeal pointing out this point has merit.\\n\\n4. Therefore, without determining the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the lower court judgment and remand the case to the lower court for retrial and determination, and, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, render judgment as stated in the disposition."}

question: Regarding the following case, which of the following statements are correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedent) A, with respect to a store located in the B District of City A, took over the status of business operator from X, the former operator (a general restaurant business operator under the Food Sanitation Act and its subordinate statutes), and filed a report on 2021. 11. 9.; however, B, the head of the B District Office, imposed on A a business suspension disposition for 3 months on 2022. 12. 26. on the ground that X had, on 2021. 8. 26., employed entertainment hostesses and engaged in entertainment-hostess activities. In response, as A filed a petition for revocation review and sought to contest it, the Administrative Appeals Commission, on 2023. 3. 6., rendered a partially granting adjudication to the effect that the 3-month business suspension disposition against A be changed to a disposition imposing a surcharge of KRW 5.6 million in lieu of a 2-month business suspension disposition, and in accordance with that purport, B imposed a surcharge imposition disposition on 2023. 3. 13. A intends to contest B's disposition by filing an action for revocation.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2003DU8005]": "Taking together the positive registration requirements for the petroleum retail business prescribed by Article 9(3) of the Petroleum Business Act and its Enforcement Decree, the negative disqualification grounds prescribed by Article 9(4) and Article 5 of the same Act, and the fact that Article 9(4) and Article 7 of the same Act recognize succession to the status of a petroleum retail business operator not only in cases of transfer of business, death, or merger, but also where only petroleum retail facilities are merely acquired pursuant to procedures such as auction, the registration of a petroleum retail business is, in principle, of the nature of an in rem permit, and because the sanction dispositions such as business suspension that a petroleum retail business operator receives by violating the prohibition on the sale of similar petroleum products under Article 26 of the same Act pursuant to Article 13(3) subparagraph 6 and Article 13(1) subparagraph 11 of the same Act are not sanctions against the individual qualification of the business operator but are sanctions against the whole or a part of the business and thus have the nature of an in rem disposition, such succession to status must be understood to include succession to the sanction dispositions such as business suspension imposed on the former petroleum retail business operator for selling similar petroleum products, and it should be deemed possible to impose sanction dispositions such as business suspension on the person who has succeeded to that status (see Supreme Court Decision 86NU203 dated July 22, 1986; Supreme Court Decision 85NU685 dated January 21, 1986 and Supreme Court Decision 96NU18960 dated June 26, 1998 concerning automobile transport business; Supreme Court Decision 93NU21231 dated October 25, 1994 concerning construction business; Supreme Court Decision 2001DU1611 dated June 29, 2001 concerning public hygiene business, etc.), and the penalty surcharge prescribed in Article 14(1) of the Petroleum Business Act is imposed merely in lieu of a business suspension disposition, in order to achieve the effect of administrative sanctions and supervision by imposing an economic burden on the relevant business operator while at the same time relieving the inconvenience of the general public who are in transactional relations with that business operator, so there is no reason to treat a penalty surcharge imposition disposition differently from a business suspension disposition in terms of the effect of succession to status.\\n\\nAnd Article 26 of the Petroleum Business Act, enacted in the purport of strictly preventing the distribution of similar petroleum products that cause social and economic harm, needs to secure the effectiveness of sanctions following a violation thereof; auction, one of the grounds for succession to status, is effected only with respect to petroleum retail facilities, and succession to the status of a petroleum retail business operator is not compelled merely because of an auction; the person who has succeeded to the status of a petroleum retail business operator may also have liability pursued for the former petroleum retail business operator's violation; and the above penalty surcharge is imposed merely in lieu of a business suspension disposition. Taking these factors together, the above interpretation concerning succession to the status of a petroleum retail business operator and the penalty surcharge imposition disposition cannot be deemed, as asserted by the Plaintiff, to violate freedom of business, the guarantee of property rights, or the principle of equality, especially in succession to status by auction.\\n\\nIn the same purport, the measures of the lower court, which determined that the disposition in this case, by which a penalty surcharge in lieu of a business suspension disposition was imposed on the Plaintiff, who had acquired the petroleum retail facilities owned by Nonparty 1, the former petroleum retail business operator, by auction and then succeeded to the status as a petroleum retail business operator upon acceptance of the report of succession to status and the application for change of registration, on the ground of Nonparty 1's sale of similar petroleum products, were lawful, are proper, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality, as argued in the grounds of appeal, in misapprehending the legal nature of the registration of a petroleum retail business or the doctrine concerning the unconstitutionality of Article 7, etc. of the Petroleum Business Act.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and judgment is rendered as ordered."}

{"[2004DU9302]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\nWhere an administrative agency, pursuant to the Food Sanitation Act and its subordinate statutes, has imposed an administrative sanction disposition on a business operator and then has rendered a disposition changing that disposition in favor of the business operator (hereinafter, the initial disposition is referred to as the “Original Disposition” and the later disposition as the “Changing Disposition”), the Original Disposition does not cease to exist by virtue of the Changing Disposition; rather, it exists from the outset as a disposition whose content has been changed in favor of the business operator. Therefore, in a case where revocation is sought on the ground that the administrative sanction, as changed in favor of the business operator by the Changing Disposition, is unlawful, the subject matter of the revocation action is the Original Disposition as changed, not the Changing Disposition, and whether the filing period has been complied with must also be determined on the basis of the Original Disposition as changed, not the Changing Disposition.\\n\\nAccording to the facts found by the lower court and the record, the Defendant, on 2002. 12. 26., imposed upon the Plaintiff the Original Disposition at issue, namely a 3-month business suspension disposition; and when the Plaintiff filed an administrative appeal against this, the adjudicating authority, on 2003. 3. 6., rendered an implementing adjudication of partial dismissal (partial grant) ordering that “the 3-month business suspension disposition imposed by the Defendant on the Plaintiff on 2002. 12. 26. be changed to a disposition imposing a penalty surcharge in lieu of a 2-month business suspension,” and the certified copy of the written adjudication reached the Plaintiff on 2003. 3. 10.; the Defendant, in accordance with the purport of the above adjudication, on 2003. 3. 13. (the lower court states 2003. 3. 12., but this appears to be an error) rendered the subsequent Changing Disposition at issue to the effect that “the 3-month business suspension disposition is changed to a penalty surcharge of KRW 5.6 million,” thereby rendering a disposition changing the Original Disposition at issue in the Plaintiff’s favor; and it can be seen that the Plaintiff, in filing this action on 2003. 6. 12., is seeking, as the purport of the claim, revocation of the penalty surcharge disposition dated 2003. 3. 13.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principle stated above, in this action seeking revocation on the ground that the penalty surcharge imposition, which is an administrative sanction and whose content was changed in favor of the Plaintiff by the subsequent Changing Disposition at issue, is unlawful, the above purport of the claim must be construed as seeking revocation of the penalty surcharge disposition dated 2002. 12. 26., which has existed from the outset as changed in favor of the Plaintiff by the subsequent Changing Disposition at issue; and this action, which seeks revocation of the Original Disposition as changed by the subsequent Changing Disposition pursuant to the implementing adjudication of partial dismissal (partial grant), must also be filed within 90 days from the date on which the certified copy of the administrative appeal adjudication was served. The lower court’s judgment finding that this action is unlawful on the ground that the Plaintiff filed the action after 90 days had elapsed from the date on which the certified copy of the above adjudication was served is correct, and the grounds for final appeal cannot be accepted.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2019DU38830]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Overview of the Case and the Issues\\n\\nA. According to the reasons stated in the lower court judgment and the evidence duly admitted by the lower court, the following circumstances can be found.\\n\\n(1) Non-party 1 obtained a business permit from the Defendant on 1972. 3. 5. with the business place name as ‘○○○’, the location as Namyangju-si (address omitted) (hereinafter collectively referred to as ‘the land at issue’), and the type of business as general restaurant business (hereinafter referred to as ‘the business at issue’). The building area, as recorded in the building register, of the 1st-floor building then located on the land at issue (hereinafter referred to as ‘Building 1’) was 28.80㎡ (thereafter, the regulatory system under the Food Sanitation Act concerning general restaurants was changed on 1981. 7. 3. from a business report system to a business permit system, on 1984. 4. 13. again to a business permit system, and on 1999. 11. 13. again to a business report system).\\n\\n(2) Non-party 1 demolished Building 1 around 1998. 11. and built in its place a building with 1 aboveground floor, and around 1999. 7. added a 2nd floor to that building, bringing its total floor area to 149.22㎡ (= 1st floor 99.66㎡ + 2nd floor 49.56㎡) (hereinafter referred to as ‘Building 2’).\\n\\n(3) Around 2015. 12., the Plaintiff, while in substance succeeding to the business conducted in Building 2 from Non-party 1, filed with the Defendant on 2015. 12. 10. a report on succession to the status of business operator and a report of change of business place name as if the Plaintiff had succeeded to the business at issue in Building 1 and had merely changed the business place name to ‘△△△’. Thereafter, the Plaintiff’s husband, Non-party 2, demolished Building 2 and, in its place, constructed a building for use as a detached house with a total floor area of 140.75㎡ (= 1st floor 80.33㎡ + 2nd floor 60.42㎡), and received approval for use around 2016. 5. 13. (hereinafter referred to as ‘Building 3’). Around that time, the Plaintiff filed with the Defendant a report of change of business place name as if she were continuing the business at issue in Building 1 and merely changing the business place name again to ‘□□□□’, and then started general restaurant business in Building 3.\\n\\n(4) The land at issue has been designated as a water source protection area under Article 7 of the Water Supply and Waterworks Act and as an environment maintenance zone under Article 14 of the Water Source Management Rules.\\n\\n(5) The Namyangju-si Food Sanitation Inspector confirmed on 2017. 2. 28. that the area of the general restaurant business place in Building 3 had significantly increased compared to the area of the business at issue that had originally been permitted. On 2017. 5. 2., the Defendant issued the corrective order at issue, ordering the Plaintiff to correct such violation pursuant to Article 71(1) of the Food Sanitation Act, on the ground that, although the Plaintiff had succeeded to the business at issue, the business place area had changed and she had failed to file a report thereof, thereby violating Article 37(4) of the Food Sanitation Act.\\n\\nB. The issue in this case is whether, as of the time of the corrective order at issue, the Plaintiff had a duty under Article 37(4) of the Food Sanitation Act to file a report of change in business place area concerning the general restaurant business in Building 3.\\n\\n2. Whether There Was a Duty to File a Report of Change in Business Place Area\\n\\nA. Relevant provisions and legal principles\\n\\n(1) According to Article 37(4) of the Food Sanitation Act and Article 25(1) item 8 and Article 26 item 4 of the Enforcement Decree of the Food Sanitation Act, a person who intends to engage in general restaurant business subject to reporting, or who intends to change important matters such as the business place area of such business, shall report such matters to the mayor, etc. Article 71(1) of the Food Sanitation Act provides that, where a business operator fails to comply with the Food Sanitation Act, necessary corrective measures shall be ordered. Article 75(1) item 7 and Article 79(1) of the Food Sanitation Act provide that, where a person operates a business without making a report in violation of the above reporting duty, measures for closure of the business premises may be taken, and where the duty to report a change is violated, the whole or part of the business may be suspended for a period not exceeding 6 months or an order may be issued to close the business premises.\\n\\nThe purpose of the above provisions on the duty to report and the provisions on corrective orders, business suspension, closure of business premises, etc. is to compel such reporting and ultimately to prohibit unreported businesses by enabling corrective orders, business suspension, and other sanctions where a business subject to reporting is operated without a report, or where the business is continued without a report despite a change in important matters such as the business place area.\\n\\n(2) The act by which an administrative agency accepts a report of succession to status following a business transfer under Article 39(1) and (3) of the Food Sanitation Act does not merely consist of receiving a report of the fact that the transferee has succeeded to the business by virtue of the legal effect of the private-law business transfer already arising between transferor and transferee; rather, it is an act that cancels the business permit, etc. for the transferor and, in addition, establishes for the transferee the status to lawfully operate the business, thereby producing the legal effect of changing the business permit holder, etc. (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DO6561 dated 2012. 1. 12., etc.). Accordingly, the transferee must attach and submit supporting materials that can verify that all requirements for lawfully operating the business at the relevant business premises have been met in the report of succession to the status of business operator (see Article 48 of the Enforcement Rule of the Food Sanitation Act), and those requirements include securing a lawful title to the use of the lawful building (shop) that may be used for the type of business in question as of the time of the report and satisfying the facility standards prescribed in Article 36 of the Food Sanitation Act.\\n\\nA person who has succeeded to a business that was operated without complying with the duty to report a change in business place area may likewise become subject to sanctions such as a corrective order or business suspension if that person continues the business without complying with such reporting duty (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DU18882 dated 2014. 3. 13., etc.).\\n\\n(3) Meanwhile, according to Article 2(2), Article 19(2) item 1 of the Building Act, Article 3-5 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, [Attached Table 1] item 4 (j), and Article 14(5), a general restaurant must have a building use classified as Class II Neighborhood Living Facilities, and to change the use of a building belonging to the Detached House category (Residential and Business Facility Group) to Class II Neighborhood Living Facilities (Neighborhood Living Facility Group), approval from the mayor, etc. must be obtained. Accordingly, a person who intends to operate a general restaurant business must either prepare a business place in a building whose use is Class II Neighborhood Living Facilities or, in the case of a building that is not Class II Neighborhood Living Facilities, undergo the procedure for changing the use of that building to Class II Neighborhood Living Facilities. Operating a general restaurant business in a detached house without first going through such procedure for changing the use of the building is not permissible under the current Food Sanitation Act and Building Act.\\n\\n(4) However, according to Article 7(4) item 1 of the Water Supply and Waterworks Act, Article 13(1) item 2 and (2) of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, and Article 13 of the Water Source Management Rules, a person who intends to engage in acts such as constructing, extending, rebuilding, reconstructing, relocating, changing the use of, or removing a building in a water source protection area may do so only upon obtaining approval from the mayor, etc. in certain cases where it is recognized that the designated purpose of the water source protection area will not be impeded; in particular, a change in the use of a building is permitted only to the extent that the degree of generation of pollutants is not higher than in the previous case, and changing a house into a general restaurant is not prescribed as a case in which a change in the use of a building may be permitted. Furthermore, Article 15 item 2 of the Water Source Management Rules exceptionally relaxes restrictions on acts where part of a water source protection area is designated as an environment maintenance zone; even in such cases, when a person intends to change an existing house into a general restaurant, the total floor area of the building for general restaurant use must be 100㎡ or less [(l) item 1], and even where extending a building already used as a general restaurant, only an extension bringing the total floor area, including the existing area, to 100㎡ or less may be approved [(l) item 2]. Accordingly, in a water source protection area, changing the use of a building from a house to a general restaurant is, in principle, not permitted, but where the area is designated as an environment maintenance zone, it is permitted only if the total floor area of the building to be used as a general restaurant is 100㎡ or less.\\n\\nB. Determination in this case\\n\\nWhen the facts found above are examined in light of the contents of these relevant statutes and the legal principles, the following determination may be made.\\n\\n(1) The Plaintiff, around 2015. 12., merely succeeded to the business actually operated in Building 2 from Non-party 1; the Plaintiff did not succeed to the business at issue in Building 1. If the Plaintiff intended to lawfully continue the business in Building 2 that she had succeeded to, she should have filed a report of succession to the status of business operator and a report of change in the location and area of the business place, while clarifying that the business she had succeeded to was the business in Building 2, not the business in Building 1, and while substantiating that all requirements for lawfully operating a general restaurant business under the Food Sanitation Act in Building 2 had been met; and through the Defendant’s acceptance of the report, she should have obtained the status to lawfully operate the business in Building 2. However, the Plaintiff did not file a report stating that she had succeeded to the business in Building 2; rather, she filed a report of succession to the status of business operator and a report of change of business place name as if she had succeeded to the business at issue in Building 1 and merely changed the business place name. Therefore, even if the Defendant accepted such report, it was merely the Defendant’s act of establishing for the Plaintiff the status to continue the business at issue in Building 1, without knowing that Building 1 had already been destroyed, and it does not mean that the Plaintiff acquired, through the Defendant’s acceptance of the report, the status to lawfully operate a general restaurant business in Building 2.\\n\\n(2) Likewise, if the Plaintiff intended to lawfully operate a general restaurant business in Building 3 from around 2016. 5., she should have filed a report of change in the location and area of the business place, while clarifying that the general restaurant business she intended to operate was not the business in Building 1 but the business in Building 3, and while substantiating that all requirements for lawfully operating a general restaurant business under the Food Sanitation Act in Building 3 had been met; and through the Defendant’s acceptance of the report, she should have obtained the status to lawfully operate the business in Building 3. However, around that time, the Plaintiff did not file a change report stating that she would operate the business in Building 3; rather, she filed a report of change of business place name as if she were merely changing the business place name of the business at issue in Building 1, which she had allegedly succeeded to from Non-party 1 in 2015. Therefore, even if the Defendant accepted such report, it was merely the Defendant’s act of establishing for the Plaintiff the status to continue the business at issue in Building 1 under the changed name, without knowing that Building 1 had already been destroyed, and it does not mean that the Plaintiff acquired, through the Defendant’s acceptance of the report, the status to lawfully operate a general restaurant business in Building 3.\\n\\n(3) The Plaintiff, who acquired through the report of succession to the status of business operator and the report of change of business place name on 2015. 12. 10. the status to continue the business at issue in Building 1, changed the location and area of the business place by starting the general restaurant business in Building 3 from around 2016. 5. and failed to report this to the Defendant, thereby failing to comply with the duty to report a change under Article 37(4) of the Food Sanitation Act; thus, the Plaintiff’s business in Building 3 may be subject to a corrective order under Article 71(1) of the Food Sanitation Act.\\n\\n(4) Meanwhile, Building 3 is a building whose use is a detached house, and therefore it is not a place where general restaurant business may be operated. If the Plaintiff intended to lawfully operate a general restaurant business in Building 3, she had to obtain approval under the Building Act to change the use of Building 3 from a detached house to Class II Neighborhood Living Facilities. However, because the land at issue where Building 3 is located has been designated as a water source protection area and an environment maintenance zone, a change in the use of a building may be permitted only if the total floor area of the building to be used as a general restaurant is 100㎡ or less. Since Building 3 has a total floor area of 140.75㎡, it does not fall within the case in which approval to change the use of the building from a house to a general restaurant may be granted. Therefore, even if the Plaintiff were to file a report of change in business place area to the effect that she would operate general restaurant business in all of Building 3, the Defendant could not accept it. Ultimately, the corrective order at issue, issued on the ground that the Plaintiff violated the duty to report a change in business place area, is lawful.\\n\\nC. Nevertheless, the lower court determined to the effect that the Plaintiff had no duty to report a change merely on the basis of the circumstances as stated in its reasoning, even if the business place area of the business at issue had been changed. The lower court’s determination contains an error that affected the judgment by misconstruing the legal principles regarding the report of succession to the status of business operator and the report of change in business place location and business place area under the Food Sanitation Act. The ground of appeal pointing this out is meritorious.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the lower court judgment is reversed and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning acts of state is incorrect? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)
A: Even if the revocation of a decoration is an act performed by the President as Head of State, it cannot be regarded as an act of such a high political nature that the court should exercise judicial restraint.
B: The holding of the inter-Korean summit and, in the course of that holding, the act of remitting money to the North Korean side under the name of consideration for business rights, without reporting to the Minister of Finance and Economy or obtaining approval for a cooperative project from the Minister of Unification, cannot be subject to judicial review.
C: Since the exercise of public power directly related to the restriction of the basic rights of the people must be decided and executed in accordance with the Constitution and the law even if it is an act requiring highly political consideration, the measure of a complete suspension of the Kaesong Industrial Complex can be subject to a constitutional complaint adjudication.
D: An Emergency Financial and Economic Order having the force of law is directly related to the infringement of the basic rights of the people, and therefore can be the subject of review by the Constitutional Court.
E: A decision to dispatch the Armed Forces of the Republic of Korea to a foreign country, if made in compliance with the procedures prescribed by the Constitution and the law, should have the judgments of the President and the National Assembly respected, and adjudication solely on judicial standards should be restrained.
label: B
supporting_precedents: {"[2003DO7878]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Regarding the first ground of appeal by Defendants Kim Yun-gyu and Im Dong-won\\n   a. The fundamental principle of a constitutional state based on the rule of law requires that any act of state or governmental action be carried out constitutionally and lawfully within the bounds of the Constitution and laws; the determination of such constitutionality and legality inherently belongs to the judicial power.\\n\\n   However, among acts of state there are those of a highly political nature, and as to such acts of high political character, it is by no means desirable for a court, which bears no political responsibility, to disregard the expediency or legitimacy of politics and proceed to review legality in a manner that causes policy decisions to be swayed; moreover, because the courts cannot deny the risk of becoming involved in political questions and thereby having their neutrality and independence infringed, there exists an area in which, with respect to acts of state of a highly political nature, the courts themselves restrain the exercise of judicial review power and exclude such matters from the scope of review, so-called acts of state.\\n\\n   Nevertheless, even if the concept of acts of state is recognized in this manner, the restraint of excessive judicial review must be recognized with the utmost caution so that it does not amount to negligence or abandonment of the court’s duty to guarantee fundamental rights and realize the ideal of the rule of law, and such determination must be made solely by the judiciary.\\n\\n   b. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court, based on the evidence it adopted, comprehensively found that Defendants Kim Yun-gyu and Im Dong-won, in collusion with Choi Gyubaek, Jeong Mong-heon, Park Jiwon, and others, who were co-defendants at the court of first instance, without reporting to the Minister of Finance and Economy (that is, without reporting to the head of the “designated foreign exchange bank” pursuant to delegated authority), on 2000. 6. 9., with the assistance of Non-indicted Party 1, etc., who were disbursing officers of the Planning and Coordination Office of the National Intelligence Service, converted KRW 224,000,000,000 borrowed by Hyundai Merchant Marine Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Hyundai Merchant Marine”) from the Korea Development Bank with the assistance of Park Jiwon and Lee Ki-ho into USD 200,000,000, and remitted and paid it to the account designated by the North Korean Korea Asia-Pacific Committee (hereinafter referred to as the “Asia-Pacific Committee”) as consideration for the seven major economic cooperation projects of Hyundai Asan Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Hyundai Asan”), including the right to use the site for the light industrial district in the Tongcheon area of North Korea; that Defendant Kim Yun-gyu, in collusion with Jeong Mong-heon, Lee Ik-chi, Kim Jae-su (Head of the Management Headquarters of Hyundai Engineering & Construction), and others, without reporting to the Minister of Finance and Economy (that is, without reporting to the head of the designated foreign exchange bank pursuant to delegated authority), on or around 2000. 6. 9., paid USD 150,000,000 as consideration for the above cooperation projects by remitting it through Hyundai Engineering & Construction’s London branch and Singapore branch to the accounts designated by the Asia-Pacific Committee; and that Defendants Kim Yun-gyu and Im Dong-won, in collusion with Jeong Mong-heon, Park Jiwon, Lee Ik-chi, and others, although when corporations and organizations of South and North Korea wish to jointly implement a cooperation project, the approval of the Minister of Unification must be obtained for each project, without obtaining the Minister of Unification’s approval for the cooperation project, at around 09:00 on 2000. 5. 3. in Beijing, China, Hyundai Asan concluded a provisional agreement with the North Korean Asia-Pacific Committee, and as consideration therefor, from around 2000. 6. 9. to around 2000. 6. 12., remitted a total of USD 450,000,000 to the account designated by the Asia-Pacific Committee and thereby implemented the cooperation project; the court below found all of the charged facts guilty.\\n\\n   c. In addition, while recognizing the above charged facts as guilty, the lower court, in response to the Defendants’ argument that the aforementioned remittance to North Korea and each attendant act therewith originated from an urgent necessity to help the Inter-Korean Summit and thus constituted so-called acts of state not subject to judicial review by the judiciary, held that the holding of the Inter-Korean Summit is an act of a highly political character, and therefore, absent special circumstances, adjudicating its propriety would exceed the inherent and essential limits of judicial power and would be inappropriate; however, the act itself by which the above Defendants, in the course of holding the Inter-Korean Summit, conspired and, without reporting to the Minister of Finance and Economy or obtaining the Minister of Unification’s approval for the cooperation project, remitted USD 450,000,000 to the North Korean side as consideration for business rights, as above, is subject to judicial review in light of the constitutional principle of a state governed by law and the principle of equality before the law, etc. The lower court’s determination as above is proper in light of the aforementioned legal principles and is persuasive, and it cannot be said that there is any error of law in misunderstanding the legal doctrine regarding the so-called constitutional acts of state as alleged; accordingly, this part of the appeal by Defendants Kim Yun-gyu and Im Dong-won is without merit.\\n\\n2.
