Regarding the second ground of appeal by Defendant Kim Yun-gyu\\n   According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court also maintained, with respect to the violation of the Inter-Korean Exchange and Cooperation Act by the above Defendants, the first-instance court’s determination that, when the overall content of the above Act and the wording of Articles 16 and 17 thereof are comprehensively interpreted, even a person who immediately implemented a cooperation project without first obtaining approval as a cooperation project operator, which is the pre-stage to approval of a cooperation project, may be punished pursuant to Article 27(1)3 of the above Act; in light of the record and relevant legal principles, the lower court’s determination as above is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error of law in misunderstanding the Inter-Korean Exchange and Cooperation Act as alleged; accordingly, this part of Defendant Kim Yun-gyu’s appeal is also without merit.\\n\\n3. Regarding the second ground of appeal by Defendant Im Dong-won\\n   a. Whether an act constitutes a justified act or self-defense as a ground excluding illegality must be determined in a purposive and reasonable manner according to the concrete circumstances, and since the legality of an act cannot be determined outside the legal order, for an act to be recognized as a justified act, it must satisfy all of the following requirements: first, the legitimacy of the motive or purpose of the act; second, the appropriateness of the means or method of the act; third, the balancing of protected legal interests and infringed legal interests; fourth, urgency; and fifth, subsidiarity, meaning that there is no other means or method apart from the act in question; and for an act to be recognized as self-defense, the act must be intended to defend against a present and unjust infringement upon one’s own or another’s protected legal interests and must be appropriate (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 1986. 10. 28., 86DO1764; Supreme Court Decision rendered on 1987. 1. 20., 86DO1809; Supreme Court Decision rendered on 1991. 9. 10., 91DA19913; Supreme Court Decision rendered on 1992. 9. 25., 92DO1520, etc.).\\n\\n   b. According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court determined that, in the case of the remittance to North Korea at issue, procedural legality and appropriateness were lacking in the procedures for remitting to North Korea and in the method of procuring the money to be remitted; that cash remittance to North Korea need not necessarily be a prerequisite for holding an Inter-Korean Summit; that rather, given circumstances such as the continued division of public opinion and the ongoing controversy to date as a result of the secret remittance made without public consent, even if it took somewhat more time and involved some pain, remitting money to North Korea within the scope of positive law after going through a process of national consensus and then holding an Inter-Korean Summit could also be one method of political choice, and thus urgency is not easily acknowledged; that there were various room for negotiations besides cash remittance, such as investment in social overhead capital, through the negotiation process; that there was no lack of room to remit the money in a transparent manner in paying money as consideration for business rights; and that, compared with the fact that, even when the President’s entourage traveled to North Korea for the Inter-Korean Summit and when the delegation for preparatory talks and the advance team traveled to North Korea for the summit, which can be said to be far more closely related to and in fact an essential procedure for the Inter-Korean Summit than the remittance to North Korea, certificates were all issued by the Minister of Unification and approval procedures for contact with North Korean residents, etc., were followed, it is difficult to regard the subsidiarity of means or method as satisfied; for these reasons, the court below held that Defendant Im Dong-won’s act cannot be regarded as a justified act under the Criminal Act. In light of the record and relevant legal principles, the lower court’s determination as above is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error of fact or law in misunderstanding the criminal-law doctrine of justified acts as alleged; accordingly, this part of Defendant Im Dong-won’s appeal is also without merit.\\n\\n4. Regarding the third ground of appeal by Defendant Im Dong-won\\n   According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court rejected, on the grounds stated in its holding, the argument that there was no awareness of illegality, no foreseeability, or no punishability with respect to Defendant Im Dong-won’s act; in light of the relevant legal principles, the lower court’s determination as above is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error of law in misunderstanding the legal doctrine as alleged; accordingly, this part of Defendant Im Dong-won’s appeal is also without merit.\\n\\n5. Regarding the fourth ground of appeal by Defendant Im Dong-won\\n   According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court, based on the evidence it adopted, comprehensively found that Defendant Im Dong-won and Park Jiwon, etc., agreed to enable Hyundai, instead of bearing the USD 100,000,000 to be borne by our government, to obtain credit support through the Korea Development Bank; that Defendant Kim Yun-gyu, on the instruction of Jeong Mong-heon and Lee Ik-chi, requested through Kim Bo-hyun that the National Intelligence Service provide convenience for the foreign exchange conversion of USD 200,000,000; that thereafter, Kim Chung-sik and Defendant Kim Yun-gyu proposed that convenience for remittance of USD 200,000,000 also be provided, and Defendant Im Dong-won, upon receiving a report thereon, instructed that convenience for foreign exchange conversion and remittance be provided; that Choi Gyubaek sought cooperation from the president of the Korea Exchange Bank, and Non-indicted Parties 2 and 3 provided practical assistance with the remittance to North Korea; that Defendant Im Dong-won knew that, in relation to the Inter-Korean Summit, USD 100,000,000 from our government and USD 350,000,000 plus in-kind contributions worth USD 50,000,000 from Hyundai would be remitted or provided to the North Korean side as consideration for North Korea-related business rights; that, as the Director of the National Intelligence Service, he had grasped relevant information in the course of leading the promotion of the Inter-Korean Summit through consultations with Park Jiwon, etc.; that, from Hyundai’s perspective, there was no need to conceal from Defendant Im Dong-won or Park Jiwon, who would request various forms of assistance in connection therewith, the fact that USD 450,000,000 would be remitted before the Inter-Korean Summit; and that Defendant Im Dong-won himself also stated that, since Hyundai was in a situation where it had to remit USD 500,000,000 to North Korea in connection with North Korea-related business, he, together with Park Jiwon, requested assistance from Defendant Lee Ki-ho for Hyundai; that Defendant Kim Yun-gyu, after reaching a provisional agreement with the North Korean side in Beijing, China on 2000. 5. 3., returned to Korea and, within about one week thereafter, reported to the National Intelligence Service the fact that an agreement had been reached with the North Korean side and that USD 450,000,000 would be remitted as consideration for the project; and that he stated to the Director of the National Intelligence Service that USD 450,000,000 would be remitted before the Inter-Korean Summit; in light of these circumstances, the court below determined that Defendant Im Dong-won was in the relationship of co-principal through conspiracy not only with employees of the National Intelligence Service but also with the other co-conspirators. In light of the record and relevant legal principles, the lower court’s determination as above is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error of fact or law in misunderstanding co-principal through conspiracy as alleged; accordingly, this part of Defendant Im Dong-won’s appeal is also without merit.\\n\\n6. Regarding the grounds of appeal by Defendants Lee Geun-young and Park Sang-bae\\n   a. For the crime of occupational breach of trust to be established, as a subjective element there must be awareness of breach of duty and awareness that, as a result, the defendant or a third party acquires a benefit and causes loss to the principal, that is, intent to commit breach of trust; such awareness is sufficiently established even by eventual awareness. Where the defendant denies the intent to commit breach of trust, due to the nature of the matter, the facts that become the subjective element of the crime of breach of trust can only be proved by the method of proving indirect facts that are substantially related to intent; and what constitutes an indirect fact substantially related thereto can be determined only by rationally judging the connection of facts through keen observational and analytical ability based on normal rules of experience (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 1999. 7. 9., 99DO1864; Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2000. 4. 11., 99DO334; Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2000. 12. 8., 99DO3338, etc.). If officers and employees of a financial institution, in making loans, recklessly extended credit without taking substantial and reasonable measures such as obtaining sufficient collateral to ensure collection of the loan claim, it cannot be said that they lacked awareness that, through breach of duty, a third party would obtain property benefits and the financial institution would suffer loss (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2000. 3. 14., 99DO4923; Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2003. 2. 11., 2002DO5679, etc.).\\n\\n   According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court, when comprehensively considering the evidence it adopted and the various circumstances of this case as stated in its holding, found that the Defendants conspired together and that, because a temporary current-account overdraft is intended to support funds experiencing temporary liquidity shortages for a period within 90 days, credit approval for a temporary current-account overdraft should be granted only when, after receiving relevant documents from the relevant company and reviewing and investigating the cause and scale of the temporary shortage of funds, the specific use of the funds, and the short-term debt repayment capacity, etc., it is recognized that the company has the ability to repay the borrowed funds on the maturity date; that, in order to grant credit approval exceeding 20% of the Korea Development Bank’s equity capital to the same individual, corporation, or person belonging to the same corporate group as such person (hereinafter referred to as the “same borrower”), limit confirmation from the Credit Management Department is required; that the Korea Development Bank was already in a state where it had applied to the Financial Supervisory Service for approval of a plan to reduce credit extensions exceeding the same borrower credit exposure limit, because it had made loans to affiliated companies of the Hyundai Group in excess of 25% of its equity capital; that, since credit extensions exceeding the same borrower credit exposure limit had to be resolved by 2004. 12. 31., credit approval should not be granted in excess of the same borrower credit exposure limit; that Hyundai Merchant Marine, which was to receive the temporary current-account overdraft at the time, was in a state where its external creditworthiness had substantially fallen due to the Hyundai Group’s management-control dispute, etc., and its liquidity had substantially deteriorated as financial institutions in the second financial sector had begun to intensively recover their claims in the wake of the Mount Kumgang tourism project; that, moreover, the maturity date of the temporary current-account overdraft of KRW 100,000,000,000 dated 2000. 5. 18. was 2000. 6. 29.; and that the possibility of repaying it on maturity was very low, and the possibility of properly repaying it thereafter was also low. Accordingly, the Defendants were in breach of their duty not to grant credit approval for such a large temporary current-account overdraft or otherwise to take measures such as obtaining collateral so that no loss would be caused to the Korea Development Bank; and, in collusion with Lee Ki-ho, etc., Lee Ki-ho telephoned Defendant Park Sang-bae around 2000. 6. 2. and instructed him to “review credit support for Hyundai Merchant Marine,” and, during a breakfast meeting with Lee Yong-geun (Chairman of the Financial Supervisory Commission) and Lee Geun-young on 2000. 6. 3., referred to the liquidity crisis of Hyundai Group affiliates that were promoting North Korea-related business with Lee Geun-young and emphasized that if the Hyundai Group went bankrupt, there would be a tremendous obstacle to the Sunshine Policy, instructing to the effect that “please provide support as a policy bank for the Hyundai matter; please process it swiftly within this week”; and again, around 10:00 on 2000. 6. 5., telephoned Lee Geun-young and instructed to the effect that “Kim Chung-sik, the representative director of Hyundai Merchant Marine, will visit today, so please expedite the loan.” On the same day, Defendant Park Sang-bae instructed Non-indicted Party 4, the head of the Hyundai-affiliated II Team who opposed credit support of KRW 400,000,000,000 for Hyundai Merchant Marine, to urgently provide credit support to Hyundai Merchant Marine; Non-indicted Party 4 and others could not even confirm whether Hyundai Merchant Marine had actually experienced a temporary shortage of funds because they could not obtain a statement of liabilities from Hyundai Merchant Marine, and they also could not review or confirm whether the borrowed funds would be used for the intended purpose, and, moreover, while preparing a cash flow statement for a short-term payment capacity analysis based on the funds receipt and disbursement plan submitted by Hyundai Merchant Marine, they prepared a credit approval application that, although in reality a cash shortage of KRW 340,600,000,000 was expected if KRW 400,000,000,000 were repaid on the maturity date, 2000. 6. 30., instead analyzed that a surplus fund of KRW 59,400,000,000 would arise upon maturity, and, without even obtaining limit confirmation from the Credit Management Department, submitted it for approval to Defendant Park Sang-bae; Defendant Park Sang-bae, by his own final approval, on 2000. 6. 7., entered into a temporary current-account overdraft agreement with Hyundai Merchant Marine for KRW 400,000,000,000, which exceeded the same borrower credit exposure limit and was unsecured despite the fact that additional collateral could have been provided to some extent, without even requesting collateral, and, pursuant to that agreement, caused KRW 100,000,000,000 to be withdrawn from the Korea Development Bank headquarters, KRW 100,000,000,000 from the Guro branch, and KRW 200,000,000,000 from the Yeouido branch, thereby causing the Korea Development Bank a loss equivalent to the same amount and causing Hyundai Merchant Marine to acquire a benefit equivalent to the same amount; and the charges that the Defendants, in collusion with Lee Ki-ho, around 2000. 6. 21., in effect handled lending business by way of acquiring Hyundai Engineering & Construction’s privately placed bonds, and that at that time Hyundai Engineering & Construction, due to the management-control dispute in the Hyundai Group, the collapse in stock prices resulting from the fall in external creditworthiness, rumors of default, etc., was expected to find it very difficult to issue roll-over bonds for KRW 705,300,000,000 in company bonds maturing in the second half of 2000; that financial institutions had not recovered existing loans or made new loans, causing a continued liquidity crunch, and the company was in an extremely deteriorated financial structure, with interest alone amounting to about KRW 600,000,000,000 annually, roughly twice the annual operating profit; that, immediately after remitting USD 150,000,000 to North Korea in connection with the North Korea-related economic cooperation project, its ability to repay even if it received a loan was very insufficient; and that under the Korea Development Bank regulations, operating funds could not be lent to a company to which facility funds had not been lent, and no loans to construction companies had been implemented by the Korea Development Bank, yet in breach of their occupational duty to specifically review Hyundai Engineering & Construction’s liquidity situation, liabilities status, use of the proceeds from the acquisition of the company bonds, and the possibility of repayment of the company bonds, and after obtaining appropriate collateral, acquire the privately placed bonds and provide them a loan of KRW 150,000,000,000 by way of acquiring Hyundai Engineering & Construction’s privately placed bonds, which had little possibility of transferability or very low possibility of repayment within the period, and thereby caused the Korea Development Bank a loss equivalent to the same amount and caused Hyundai Engineering & Construction to acquire a benefit equivalent to the same amount, were all found guilty, the lower court’s determination that, even taking into account the fact alleged by the Defendants that the Korea Development Bank is a policy bank, the Defendants had intent to commit breach of trust and thus the crime of breach of trust was established when all of the above circumstances are comprehensively considered, is proper in light of the record and relevant legal principles, and it cannot be said that there is any error of law or error of fact in misunderstanding the requirements for the establishment of the crime of breach of trust as alleged; accordingly, all of this part of the appeal by Defendants Lee Geun-young and Park Sang-bae is without merit.\\n\\n   b. In the crime of breach of trust, the phrase “when property loss is caused” includes not only cases where actual loss has been caused but also cases where the risk of property loss has been created; and the determination of whether there is property loss must be made from an economic standpoint, not by legal assessment, in relation to the principal’s entire property status. Accordingly, even if the relevant act of breach of trust is void by legal assessment, if, viewed from an economic standpoint, the act of breach of trust actually caused loss to the principal or created a risk of property loss, it constitutes causing property loss; and once the risk of loss has arisen, even if collateral is subsequently obtained or the damage is restored, that does not affect the establishment of the crime of breach of trust (see Supreme Court Decision rendered on 1999. 6. 22., 99DO1095; Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2000. 12. 8., 99DO3338; Supreme Court Decision rendered on 2003. 2. 11., 2002DO5679, etc.).\\n\\n   According to the reasons of the lower court judgment, the lower court, in response to the Defendants’ argument that there was no loss to the Korea Development Bank because all of the above loans had been repaid, held that the money supported by the above credit extension was not actually repaid upon maturity but, after repeated extensions of the maturity date and various twists and turns involving Kim Chung-sik’s refusal to repay some debts and the inducement by Defendant Lee Geun-young, etc., and the disposal of the core business asset, the car carrier, was eventually repaid only in name or was finally arranged in a manner such as debt-to-equity conversion for some debts; that when Defendant Lee Geun-young actually disbursed the above loan of KRW 400,000,000,000 to Hyundai Merchant Marine or the acquisition price of KRW 150,000,000,000 for the privately placed bonds to Hyundai Engineering & Construction, the risk of property loss had already been created and the crime of breach of trust had been consummated; and that even if the damage was mostly restored afterward, that does not affect the establishment of the crime of breach of trust. In light of the record and relevant legal principles, the lower court’s determination as above is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error of law in misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning breach of trust as alleged; accordingly, this part of the appeal by Defendants Lee Geun-young and Park Sang-bae is also without merit.\\n\\n   c. In addition, in response to Defendant Lee Geun-young’s argument that the part concerning the crime of occupational breach of trust related to Hyundai Engineering & Construction’s acquisition of privately placed bonds does not fall within the scope of the Special Prosecutor’s investigation, the lower court determined that the above part of breach of trust corresponds to the case related to the “suspicion case of secret remittance to North Korea of USD 550 million raised by each affiliate under the leadership of Lee Ik-chi, then Chairman of Hyundai Securities, before the Inter-Korean Summit, including Hyundai Engineering & Construction’s remittance of USD 150 million through its Singapore branch in May 2000,” as prescribed in Article 2(2) of the Act on the Appointment, etc. of a Special Prosecutor to Clarify the Truth of the Suspicion Case of Secret Remittance to North Korea Related to the Inter-Korean Summit, etc. (that is, a case related to each of the cases following the text of Article 2) or the “case of suspicion of corruption by the Blue House, the National Intelligence Service, the Financial Supervisory Service, etc. related to the cases referred to in Items 1 through 3” as prescribed in Item 4 (the corruption cases of Defendant Lee Ki-ho, Senior Presidential Secretary for Economic Affairs at the Blue House, and Defendants Lee Geun-young and Park Sang-bae, the Governor and Head of the First Business Headquarters of the Korea Development Bank). The lower court’s determination as above is proper, and it cannot be said that there is any error of law in misunderstanding the legal doctrine as alleged; accordingly, this part of Defendant Lee Geun-young’s appeal is also without merit.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all appeals by the Defendants are dismissed, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

{"[2003HEONMA814]": "1. Outline of the Case and the Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\na. Outline of the Case\\n\\nThe Petitioner, being one of the general public, filed the present constitutional complaint adjudication on 2003. 11. 17. pursuant to Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act, on the ground that the Government of the Republic of Korea’s decision on 2003. 10. 18. to dispatch the Armed Forces to Iraq not only violates Article 5 of the Constitution, which provides that aggressive war is denied, but, in particular, that dispatching ordinary enlisted soldiers to Iraq, unlike officers and noncommissioned officers who are professional military personnel receiving pay, who in substance do not receive pay, violates the constitutional provisions concerning national security and the duty of national defense. The Petitioner sought a declaration of unconstitutionality of the above dispatch in this case.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\n(1) Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe petition seeks a declaration of unconstitutionality of “the decision of the National Security Council on 2003. 10. 18. to dispatch ordinary enlisted soldiers to Iraq.” However, the National Security Council is merely an advisory body to the President under the Constitution and cannot be the subject of the exercise of public power, in particular, the state act of dispatching the Armed Forces abroad that is at issue. Even if the National Security Council made such a decision (resolution), leaving aside the question whether it can be regarded as the President’s decision as the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, it is merely an internal decision-making process of a state agency, in particular, a recommendation or expression of opinion to the President, and cannot be regarded as an act having legally binding force or external effect.\\n\\nUpon review, although the National Security Council is, with respect to the formulation of foreign and military policy related to national security, an advisory body to the President under the Constitution, and although its resolutions are not binding and thus have no legal effect in themselves, if the President, after consultation with the heads of foreign and military policy, decided on the dispatch of troops by resolution and announced it, then such decision should in substance be regarded as the President’s decision to dispatch troops. Therefore, it is proper to regard the subject matter of adjudication in this case as the President’s decision to dispatch troops, and this also conforms to the Petitioner’s request.\\n\\nAccordingly, the subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether the “President’s decision on 2003. 10. 18. to dispatch the Armed Forces (ordinary enlisted soldiers) to Iraq (hereinafter referred to as ‘the decision to dispatch troops in this case’)” is unconstitutional.\\n\\n(2) Relevant Provisions\\n\\nConstitution (wholly amended on 1987. 10. 29.)\\n\\nArticle 5. ① The Republic of Korea shall endeavor to maintain international peace and deny aggressive war.\\n\\nArticle 10. All citizens shall have the dignity and worth as human beings and shall have the right to pursue happiness. (omitted below)\\n\\nArticle 60. ② The National Assembly shall have the right to consent to declarations of war, the dispatch of the Armed Forces abroad, or the stationing of foreign armed forces within the territory of the Republic of Korea.\\n\\nArticle 74. ① The President shall command the Armed Forces pursuant to the Constitution and laws.\\n\\nArticle 91. ① A National Security Council shall be established to advise the President, prior to deliberation by the State Council, on the formulation of foreign policy, military policy, and domestic policy related to national security.\\n\\n2. The Petitioner’s Claims and the Opinions of Relevant Agencies\\n\\na. Summary of the Petitioner’s Claims\\n\\n(1) The Iraq War is recognized by many countries in the world as an aggressive war, and the present decision to dispatch the Armed Forces to such a war violates Article 5(1) of the Constitution, which provides that “aggressive war is denied.”\\n\\n(2) If the dispatch of the Armed Forces is decided, the dispatch of ordinary enlisted soldiers of the Armed Forces is more essential than the dispatch of officers or noncommissioned officers. If so, since all citizens bear the duty of national defense under the Constitution, the peace of those in military service, those scheduled to enter the military, and parents with children serving in the military will be disturbed, and their right to pursue happiness will be infringed.\\n\\nb. Summary of the Opinions of Relevant Agencies\\n\\n(1) Response of the President (Chairperson of the National Security Council)\\n\\nThe subject matter of this constitutional complaint adjudication is the National Security Council’s decision on 2003. 10. 18. to dispatch additional Armed Forces to Iraq. However, the National Security Council’s decision is merely a necessary consultation regarding an internal decision-making act of a state agency, and in itself is not an act that directly creates legal effects on the rights and duties of citizens. Accordingly, this petition is inadmissible as it seeks review of something other than the exercise of public power prescribed in Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act. Even if the above National Security Council’s decision to dispatch troops constitutes an exercise of public power, the Petitioner’s own fundamental rights cannot be said to be currently and directly infringed by the above decision, and thus this is also inadmissible.\\n\\n(2) Opinion of the Minister of National Defense\\n\\n(a) The President’s decision on 2003. 10. 18. to additionally dispatch the Armed Forces to Iraq, which is the subject matter of adjudication in this case, is merely an internal decision-making process of a state agency until the National Assembly consents, and does not bring about direct legal effects on the people; therefore, a constitutional complaint adjudication petition against it is inadmissible.\\n\\n(b) The above decision to dispatch troops is (i) an act of authority exercised by the President in his constitutionally granted status as Head of State or as head of the Executive Branch, (ii) a high-level political decision regarding whether to dispatch troops, made in consideration of various domestic and foreign political circumstances, such as the impact on the national interest, relations with allied nations, and the smooth resolution of the North Korean nuclear issue and the strengthening of the ROK-U.S. alliance, and (iii) where the above decision has obtained the consent of the National Assembly, it is inappropriate for the Constitutional Court, which lacks comparable democratic legitimacy, to determine whether it is unconstitutional; and (iv) in light of the fact that there are no legal means to compel compliance if the above decision is found unconstitutional, the decision to dispatch troops in this case constitutes the so-called act of state. Since judicial review of an act of state should be restrained, this petition is inadmissible.\\n\\n(c) The Petitioner merely has an indirect and factual interest in the above decision to dispatch troops, and has no direct legal relation to the alleged infringement of fundamental rights asserted by the Petitioner; therefore, this petition is inadmissible for lack of self-relatedness.\\n\\n3. Judgment\\n\\nThe Constitution grants the President authority over diplomatic relations with other countries, together with the authority to declare war and make peace (Article 73), and while also granting the authority to command the Armed Forces pursuant to the Constitution and laws (Article 74(1)), it requires the consent of the National Assembly in cases of declaration of war and dispatch of the Armed Forces abroad (Article 60(2)), thereby making the President exercise the command authority over the Armed Forces with caution and preventing arbitrary conduct of war or dispatch of troops abroad.\\n\\nA decision to dispatch the Armed Forces abroad, such as in this case, is a complex and important matter that affects not only the life and bodily safety of the soldiers dispatched but also the status and role of our country in the international community, relations with allied nations, national security issues, and ultimately the people and national interests. It is a matter that requires a high-level political decision, such as predicting the future and setting goals regarding the desirable position and future direction of our country, by considering various circumstances, including domestic and international political relations.\\n\\nTherefore, it is desirable that such a decision be made cautiously by a representative organ of the people that can bear political responsibility for the matter, after broad and in-depth discussion with experts in the relevant fields. Our Constitution also grants such authority to the President, who is directly elected by the people and directly accountable to them, and, in order to ensure caution in the exercise of such authority, allows the National Assembly to decide whether to consent to the dispatch of troops. Under the representative democratic governmental structure adopted by the current Constitution, such high-level political decisions by the President and the National Assembly, which are representative organs, should be respected as far as possible.\\n\\nAccordingly, whether a decision to dispatch troops such as this one violates the Constitution, namely whether it contributes to world peace and the common prosperity of mankind, whether it will be beneficial to the people and the national interest ultimately by serving national security, and whether the so-called Iraq War is an aggressive war contrary to international norms, are matters for the President and the National Assembly, which are representative organs, to decide. Given the nature of the matter, it is not desirable for our Court, which has only limited materials, to make such a determination. Nor can it be said that our Court’s determination is more correct or accurate than that of the President and the National Assembly, and it must be said that it is difficult to secure the public’s trust in the result of adjudication.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the dispatch in this case was decided by the President, after considering not only the legitimacy of the dispatch itself but also various circumstances related to the national interest, such as relations with allied nations for the smooth resolution of the North Korean nuclear issue, our country’s security concerns, and domestic and foreign political relations, regarding the character, scale, and duration of the dispatched force, through consultation with the National Security Council. Thereafter, the procedural legitimacy under the Constitution and laws was secured by obtaining the consent of the National Assembly after deliberation and resolution by the State Council.\\n\\nUpon review, the decision to dispatch troops in this case is, by its nature, a matter requiring a high-level political decision related to national defense and foreign affairs, and it is clear that it was made in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the Constitution and laws. Therefore, the judgments of the President and the National Assembly should be respected, and it is necessary to restrain this Court from adjudicating it solely by judicial standards. Even in foreign countries with a long democratic tradition, judicial review has consistently been restrained in matters related to foreign affairs and national defense that require high-level political decisions, and this is precisely the reason for such restraint. As to this, there may be concern that arbitrary decisions may be left unchecked due to the avoidance of judicial review; however, such judgments by the President and the National Assembly will ultimately be evaluated and judged by the people through elections.\\n\\nAccordingly, since it is proper to refrain from judicial determination of the decision to dispatch troops in this case, the Court decides as stated in the order, by the unanimous opinion of the remaining Justices except for the separate opinions of Justices Yoon Young-chul, Kim Hyo-jong, Kim Kyung-il, and Song In-jun set forth in 4. below.\\n\\n4. Separate Opinion of Justices Yoon Young-chul, Kim Hyo-jong, Kim Kyung-il, and Song In-jun\\n\\nWe agree with the conclusion of the majority opinion, but differ in the reasons as follows.\\n\\nOur Constitution expressly provides, in Article 111(1)(5), for constitutional complaint adjudication as one means of remedying violations of the people’s rights, and accordingly Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act provides that a person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power may file a constitutional complaint adjudication petition with the Constitutional Court, thereby establishing the system.\\n\\nHowever, “a person whose fundamental rights have been infringed” in this statutory provision means a person whose own fundamental rights have been currently and directly infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power, and it is the legislature’s choice, as well as the consistent position of this Court, that a third party who merely has an indirect or factual interest does not fall within this category (see Constitutional Court 1993. 7. 29. 89HEONMA123, Case Reports 5-2, 127, 134; 1998. 9. 30. 97HEONMA404, Case Reports 10-2, 563, 565, etc.).\\n\\nAs the Petitioner himself acknowledges, the Petitioner is not the person to be dispatched by the decision to dispatch troops in this case, and is not currently in military service or scheduled to enter the military. If so, while the Petitioner may be said to have a factual or indirect interest in the decision to dispatch troops in this case in the position of an ordinary citizen, it cannot be said that, as a result of the decision to dispatch troops in this case, the Petitioner’s own fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, such as the right to pursue happiness asserted by the Petitioner, are currently and directly infringed.\\n\\nIn conclusion, we agree with the majority opinion that the petition in this case should be dismissed, but we differ from the majority opinion in that the reason is that the Petitioner lacks self-relatedness to lawfully file a constitutional complaint against the decision to dispatch troops in this case."}

{"[2012DU26920]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to the claim against the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs\\n\\na. The question of what act of an administrative agency may be the subject of an administrative appeal litigation cannot be determined abstractly and generally; in a specific case, an administrative disposition is an act that, as an exercise of public power by an administrative agency, implements the law concerning specific facts and directly affects the rights and obligations of the people. Keeping this in mind, it must be determined individually by considering the content and purport of the relevant statutes, the subject, content, form, and procedure of the act, the substantive nexus between the act and the disadvantages suffered by the counterparty and other interested persons, and the principle of administration under the rule of law and the attitudes of the administrative agency and interested persons involved in the act (see Supreme Court Decision 91NU1714, decided on January 17, 1992; Supreme Court Grand Bench Decision 2008DU167, decided on November 18, 2010, etc.).\\n\\nHowever, the Constitution provides in Article 80 that “The President shall confer orders and other honors as prescribed by Act,” and in Article 82 that “The official acts of the President in matters of state shall be in writing, and such documents shall be countersigned by the Prime Minister and the relevant Ministers of State.” The former Awards and Decorations Act (as amended by Act No. 10985 on August 4, 2011, before the amendment; hereinafter the same) provides in Article 7 that “The President shall determine the recipients of decorations after deliberation by the State Council,” and in Article 8(2) that “If it is intended to revoke a decoration and recover an order, etc., or prohibit the wearing of an order, deliberation by the State Council shall be required.”\\n\\nMeanwhile, revocation of a decoration conferred on the Deceased is not a matter concerning the bereaved family, and therefore it cannot be said to come into existence and take effect solely by notice to the bereaved family; rather, it comes into existence and takes effect as an administrative act when the decision is externally manifested in a reasonable manner according to the will of the person empowered to make the disposition.\\n\\nb. For the reasons stated in the judgment, the lower court held that (1) the Defendant President, on April 5, 2011, after resolution by the State Council, approved on April 6, 2011 the documents for revocation of the decoration conferred on the Deceased, the Plaintiff’s paternal grandfather (alias the same person, hereinafter referred to as the “Deceased”), and determined the revocation of the decoration for the Deceased in a manner countersigned by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Administration and Security; therefore, the Defendant President’s decision to revoke the decoration in this case against the Deceased was lawful as an act taken in accordance with the procedure and form prescribed by the Constitution and laws, and thereby the effect that the Deceased was excluded from the status of a person eligible for the decoration definitively arose; and then, (2) the notice of revocation of the decoration in this case by the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs to the Plaintiff was a mere factual notice that does not directly bring about a legal change in the legal status of the counterparty or other related persons and cannot be the subject of an administrative appeal litigation, and thus this part of the lawsuit seeking its revocation is unlawful.\\n\\nc. Examining the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the lawfully admitted evidence, the lower court’s above determination conforms to the relevant provisions and legal principles mentioned above, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning standing as the subject of an administrative appeal litigation, standing as plaintiff or legal interest, or proper defendant status, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nAnd insofar as the lower court’s determination that the notice of revocation of the decoration in this case constitutes a mere factual notice that cannot be the subject of an administrative appeal litigation is proper, the propriety of the lower court’s holding, premised on the assumption that the notice of revocation of the decoration in this case constituted a disposition, that the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs lawfully delegated the authority relating to the notice of revocation of the decoration in this case and issued the notice, and that there was no procedural illegality in the review process for revocation of the decoration, does not affect the outcome of the judgment; therefore, the grounds of appeal to the effect that the lower court judgment contains an error of law regarding delegation of administrative authority, etc. are rejected without further consideration.\\n\\n2. With respect to the claim against the Defendant President\\n\\na. We consider the object of the Plaintiff’s claim for cancellation in this case.\\n\\n(1) For the reasons stated in the judgment, the lower court held that the notice of revocation of the decoration in this case is a mere factual notice that does not directly bring about a legal change in the legal status of the counterparty or other related persons and cannot be the subject of an administrative appeal litigation, and thus this part of the lawsuit seeking its revocation is unlawful; and that even if the notice of revocation of the decoration in this case were regarded as a disposition, the notice was made within the authority of the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs and was notified in the name of the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs, so the Defendant President cannot be said to be the administrative agency that performed the disposition, etc., and therefore this part of the lawsuit is unlawful because it is directed against a person lacking proper defendant status.\\n\\n(2) However, according to the reasons for the lower court judgment and the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n(a) Around 1990, the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs, after review by the Committee for Examining the Merits of Decorations for Persons of Merit in the Independence Movement, recommended to the Minister of General Administration that the Deceased be decorated as a person of merit in the independence movement.\\n\\n(b) When the Minister of General Administration submitted the above recommendation for decoration as an agenda item to the State Council pursuant to the former Awards and Decorations Act Article 7, the President, after deliberation by the State Council, finally determined the Deceased as a recipient of a decoration; and the Minister of General Administration, who then had jurisdiction over affairs concerning honors, delegated to the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs the task of notifying the fact of the above decoration decision, and accordingly the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs notified the Plaintiff around December 26, 1990 that the Deceased had been decided to receive a decoration as a person of merit in the independence movement (Order of Merit for National Foundation, Patriotic Medal).\\n\\n(c) Thereafter, the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs constituted the First and Second Review Committees for Revocation of Decorations for Persons of Merit in the Independence Movement, and after review, on November 19, 2010 requested the Minister of Public Administration and Security to submit as an agenda item the revocation of the decoration on the ground that the Deceased’s pro-Japanese conduct had been confirmed.\\n\\n(d) On December 21, 2010, the revocation of the decoration for the Deceased was placed on the agenda of the State Council by the Minister of Public Administration and Security, but the resolution was deferred in accordance with the Prime Minister’s opinion that careful review was necessary; and after another three months of review by the Office of the Prime Minister, the agenda item for revocation of the decoration in this case was resolved by the State Council on April 5, 2011.\\n\\n(e) The Defendant President, on April 6, 2011, determined the revocation of the decoration by approving the electronic document for revocation of the decoration concerning the Deceased, and it was countersigned by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Administration and Security.\\n\\n(f) Thereupon, the administrative agency in charge of honors affairs, namely the Minister of Public Administration and Security, sent to the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs a notice of decision to revoke the decoration to the effect that “we inform you that, as the request for revocation of the decoration for a person of merit in the independence movement was resolved by the State Council and approved by the President, the person subject to revocation of the decoration has been finalized as attached; therefore, pursuant to Article 8(1) of the Awards and Decorations Act, please take measures to recover all orders and items awarded in connection therewith.”\\n\\n(g) Accordingly, on April 19, 2011, the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs notified the Plaintiff to the effect that “through the resolution of revocation of the decoration at the State Council on April 5, 2011, the decoration awarded to the Deceased as a person of merit in the independence movement was decided to be revoked on April 6. In addition, we request the return of the previously conferred Order of Merit for National Foundation, Patriotic Medal and the decoration certificate, and as a member of our office will visit your residence, we would appreciate it if you would inform us of a date and time when the visit is possible.”\\n\\n(h) Meanwhile, when the Plaintiff filed this lawsuit, the Plaintiff designated the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs as the primary Defendant and sought “cancellation of the disposition revoking the decoration for a person of merit in the independence movement concerning the Deceased notified by the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs as of April 19, 2011,” and designated the Defendant President as the alternative Defendant and sought “cancellation of the disposition revoking the decoration for a person of merit in the independence movement concerning the Deceased made by the Defendant President to the Plaintiff on April 19, 2011.”\\n\\n(i) The statement of the cause of action in the complaint in this case states: “The primary Defendant, the Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs, is the administrative agency that notified on April 19, 2011 the disposition revoking the decoration for a person of merit in the independence movement concerning the Deceased, and the alternative Defendant, the President, is the institution vested with authority to decide on decorations under the Awards and Decorations Act (because there is legal doubt as to whether the Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs is the party subject to the disposition that has the authority to revoke the decoration in this case, or whether it merely notified the President’s decision, the lawsuit is filed by distinguishing the primary and alternative Defendants as above).”\\n\\n(3) In light of the above factual circumstances, although the claim against the Defendant President is written as seeking “cancellation of the disposition revoking the decoration dated April 19, 2011,” on April 19, 2011 the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs merely notified the Plaintiff of the notice of revocation of the decoration in this case, so it is difficult to view the Plaintiff as having sought cancellation of the notice of revocation of the decoration in this case against the Defendant President. Rather, it is proper to view the Plaintiff as having, with the Defendant Administrator of the Patriots and Veterans Affairs as the primary Defendant, sought cancellation of the notice of revocation of the decoration in this case, and, in preparation for the case where the claim against the primary Defendant was not upheld, sought cancellation of the decision to revoke the decoration in this case by making the Defendant President, who is the decision-maker for revocation of the decoration, the alternative Defendant.\\n\\nb. We consider whether the decision to revoke the decoration in this case constitutes an act of state.\\n\\nFormer Awards and Decorations Act Article 8 specifically stipulates the requirements for revocation of a decoration and in detail regulates the procedure therefor. Moreover, unlike the conferral of a decoration, revocation of a decoration is an act that affects the rights, etc. of the already arisen recipient of the decoration, and considering the content and degree of the disadvantage imposed on the relevant parties, the need for judicial review is substantial. Therefore, in light of the guarantee of fundamental rights and the ideal of the rule of law, even though revocation of a decoration is an act performed by the President as Head of State, it cannot be viewed as an act of such a high political character that the court should refrain from judicial review (see Supreme Court Grand Bench Decision 2010DO5986, decided on December 16, 2010, etc.).\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court, contrary to the above, held that even if the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendant President were construed as seeking cancellation of the decision to revoke the decoration in this case, the decision to revoke the decoration in this case constitutes an act of state, and therefore this part of the lawsuit challenging it is unlawful. In such determination, the lower court erred in misapprehending the legal principles concerning acts of state.\\n\\nc. We consider whether grounds existed for revocation of the decoration concerning the Deceased.\\n\\nOrders and decorations of the Republic of Korea are conferred, pursuant to former Awards and Decorations Act Article 2, which sets forth the principle of conferral of decorations, upon persons who have rendered conspicuous services to the Republic of Korea as nationals of the Republic of Korea or of friendly nations; and the conferral of a decoration is not merely a beneficial act toward the recipient himself or herself, but also has the character of an act that, by bestowing honor upon a person who has rendered conspicuous services to the State, raises pride in the State and the nation among the general public and integrates and presents national values (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DU2518, decided on September 26, 2014). Moreover, the determination as to the ground for conferral of a decoration, namely “conspicuous services to the Republic of Korea,” is made not only based on each individual fact stated in the merit report submitted by the person authorized to recommend the decoration, but also by comprehensively evaluating the recipient’s conduct over a certain period of meritorious service. Meanwhile, former Awards and Decorations Act Article 8(1) item 1 provides that the decoration shall be revoked “where it is found that the merit for the decoration is false,” and this revocation system appears to have been established to protect the essence and function of the decoration system in cases where the honor of the decoration cannot be preserved if the decoration that has been conferred is left intact.\\n\\nTaking together these provisions concerning the principles and revocation of decorations, as well as their purpose and legislative objective, etc., where the ground for revocation of a decoration provided in former Awards and Decorations Act Article 8(1) item 1, namely, “where it is found that the merit for the decoration is false,” exists, it should be understood to include not only cases where the factual basis of merit investigated at the time of conferral is itself contrary to the truth, but also cases where facts not revealed at the time of conferral are newly discovered, and if those facts had been revealed at the time of the decoration review, then objectively and clearly the recipient’s conduct, when the originally investigated facts of merit and the newly discovered facts are comprehensively evaluated, could not be recognized as meritorious for the decoration.\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in the judgment, the lower court held that (1) the Deceased engaged in pro-Japanese and anti-national conduct by voluntarily and proactively participating in pro-Japanese organizations; and that even if there were facts that had been recognized as meritorious at the time of the decoration of the Deceased, when viewed comprehensively including the above pro-Japanese and anti-national conduct, there was no merit for the decoration worthy of evaluation as a subject of decoration, and thus the case falls under the situation in which the merit for the decoration was found to be false under former Awards and Decorations Act Article 8(1) item 1, so grounds for revocation of the decoration concerning the Deceased exist; and that (2) even if the Deceased had not been declared a pro-Japanese and anti-national actor by the Special Investigation Committee under the Anti-National Activities Punishment Act or the Committee for the Investigation of Pro-Japanese and Anti-National Conduct under the Special Act on the Investigation of the Truth of Pro-Japanese and Anti-National Conduct Under Japanese Colonial Rule, if grounds for revocation of the decoration are revealed by relevant evidence, grounds for revocation of the decoration under the former Awards and Decorations Act must be deemed to exist, and therefore the Plaintiff’s contrary argument is without merit.\\n\\nAmong the grounds of appeal on this point, the argument to the effect that the lower court erred in holding otherwise even though the Deceased cannot be regarded as having engaged in pro-Japanese acts and therefore no grounds for revocation of the decoration exist is, in the end, merely a complaint about the selection and weighing of evidence or the evaluation of value, which is within the free evaluation of evidence by the court of fact, and thus does not constitute a lawful ground for appeal. Furthermore, even when the lower court’s factual findings and determinations are examined in light of the lawfully admitted evidence, the lower court’s above determination is based on the legal principles stated above, and there is no illegality such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the grounds for revocation of a decoration set forth in former Awards and Decorations Act Article 8(1) item 1, or deviation beyond the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience.\\n\\nd. Accordingly, the lower court should have dismissed the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendant President seeking cancellation of the decision to revoke the decoration in this case, but instead, under the mistaken premise that the Plaintiff sought cancellation of the notice of revocation of the decoration in this case against the Defendant President, dismissed it on the ground that the notice of revocation of the decoration in this case was not subject to an administrative appeal litigation or that the decision to revoke the decoration in this case constituted an act of state. This was erroneous. However, in this case where only the Plaintiff appealed, under the principle prohibiting reformatio in peius, a judgment dismissing the claim, which is more disadvantageous to the Plaintiff, cannot be rendered; therefore, the Plaintiff’s appeal on this point must be dismissed.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2016HEONMA364]": "[Appendix 1] List of Petitioners\\n\\n1. – 163. ○○ Co., Ltd., represented by Jeong○○, et al.\\n\\nCounsel for the Petitioners: Law Firm Suryun Asia, Attorney Song Gi-ho\\n\\nCounsel for Petitioners 4, 5, 8, 18, 35, 42, 47, 53, 56, 57, 59, 80, 95, 97, 99, and 107\\n\\nLaw Firm (Limited Liability) Ace\\n\\nAttorneys Kim Jeong-hak, Lee Hyeon-seop\\n\\n[Appendix 2] Government Statement on the Total Suspension of the Kaesong Industrial Complex\\n\\n• North Korea, turning a deaf ear to the repeated warnings of the international community and the lives of its suffering residents, carried out an extreme provocation by launching a long-range missile following its fourth nuclear test.\\n\\n• Such provocation by North Korea is a direct challenge to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and in the international community, and is an act that can never be tolerated.\\n\\nDespite the efforts of the international community to prevent North Korea’s development of nuclear weapons and long-range missiles, North Korea has shown no intention whatsoever of abandoning its development of nuclear weapons and missiles, as evidenced by its recent provocation and by its declaration that it will carry out additional nuclear tests and missile launches in the future.\\n\\nIf this situation continues without change, it is not the maintenance of the status quo, but a situation that can only lead to a catastrophic disaster as North Korea’s nuclear capability becomes more advanced. {"[93HEONMA186]": "1. Outline of the Case and Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nA. Outline of the Case\\n\\nThe President, on 1993.8.12., issued the Emergency Presidential Decree on Real-Name Financial Transactions and the Guarantee of Confidentiality (Presidential Emergency Decree No. 16, hereinafter referred to as “the Emergency Decree in this case”), which came into force from 20:00 on the same day, and received the approval of the National Assembly on the 19th of the same month; its main contents were as follows.\\n\\n① From the time of enforcement of the Emergency Decree in this case, the use of real names was made mandatory in all financial transactions (Articles 2 and 3(1)); ② with respect to existing anonymous deposits, a two-month period was set for the obligation to convert to real-name status (Article 5); ③ withdrawal of funds by means of anonymity was prohibited (Article 3(3)); ④ upon withdrawal of anonymous financial assets converted to real-name status in an amount exceeding a certain sum, financial institutions were required to notify the National Tax Service of the transaction details (Articles 6 and 10); ⑤ after the expiration of the period for the obligation to convert to real-name status, a high income tax rate was applied to interest, dividend income, and the like, and an additional charge of up to 60% of the principal amount was imposed (Articles 7 and 9); ⑥ the guarantee of confidentiality in financial transactions was strengthened (Article 4); and ⑦ criminal punishment was imposed on persons who violated the foregoing (Article 12).\\n\\nIn response, the petitioner filed this constitutional complaint adjudication on 1993.8.16., alleging that the President issued the Emergency Decree in this case despite failing to satisfy the requirements prescribed in Article 76(1) of the Constitution, and that the National Assembly, although it should have resolved to impeach the President who issued the unconstitutional Emergency Decree in this case pursuant to Article 65 of the Constitution, failed to do so, thereby infringing the petitioner’s right to know, right to petition, and property right.\\n\\nB. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nAccordingly, the subject matter of adjudication in this case is whether ① the Emergency Decree in this case issued by the President on 1993.8.12., and ② the National Assembly’s failure to adopt a resolution of impeachment pursuant to Article 65 of the Constitution against the President who issued the Emergency Decree in this case, infringe the petitioner’s constitutional fundamental rights.\\n\\n2. The Petitioner’s Arguments and the Opinion of the Interested Party\\n\\nA. Summary of the Petitioner’s Arguments\\n\\nArticle 76(1) of the Constitution provides that the President may issue a decree having the effect of law concerning the minimum necessary fiscal and economic disposition only when, in a grave fiscal or economic crisis, emergency measures are necessary to maintain national security or public safety and order, and there is no time to await the convening of the National Assembly. However, the President issued the Emergency Decree in this case despite not falling under any of those requirements. If so, even if the substance of the Emergency Decree in this case were constitutional, there would still be a constitutional defect in its procedure, rendering it unconstitutional and contrary to the Constitution; and the National Assembly would have had to impeach the President who committed such unconstitutional conduct. The petitioner, as one of the people, has the right to consider the timing and methods of implementing the real-name financial transaction system and measures to prevent side effects, and to petition the Government if he has any opinion, but these rights were fundamentally infringed by the President’s issuance of the Emergency Decree in this case; furthermore, as a result of the implementation of the Emergency Decree in this case, the market price of 11 shares of stock owned by the petitioner fell, thereby also infringing the property right.\\n\\nB. Opinion of the Minister of Justice\\n\\n(1) Opinion on procedural admissibility requirements\\n\\nThe President’s act of issuing the Emergency Decree in this case falls within the sphere of so-called acts of state and therefore is not subject to constitutional complaint adjudication; moreover, because the petitioner’s fundamental rights were not directly infringed by the Emergency Decree in this case, the petitioner lacks standing to file a petition for constitutional complaint adjudication.\\n\\n(2) Opinion on constitutionality\\n\\nThe Emergency Decree in this case satisfies all requirements prescribed by Article 76(1) of the Constitution, and the petitioner’s fundamental rights were not infringed thereby; and even if they were infringed, such infringement falls within the limits prescribed by Article 37(2) of the Constitution and is constitutionally permissible. Even if the unconstitutionality of the Emergency Decree in this case is suspected, the necessity and justification of the Emergency Decree in this case cannot be denied; therefore, a declaration of unconstitutionality should be restrained as much as possible.\\n\\n3. Judgment\\n\\nA. Judgment on Procedural Admissibility Requirements\\n\\n(1) The portion concerning the Emergency Decree in this case\\n\\n(a) Judgment on the assertion of an act of state\\n\\nAn act of state is generally defined as a state act based on a high degree of political decision that is not appropriate to be made the subject of judicial review. As to whether the Emergency Decree in this case is excluded from review by the Constitutional Court as an act of state, it is possible to recognize the concept of so-called act of state in the sense of an act based on a high degree of political decision and requiring respect for that decision; and, as the Minister of Justice opines, the President’s emergency fiscal and economic decree is a kind of state emergency power invoked, in the event of a grave fiscal or economic crisis and where there is no time to await the convening of the National Assembly, in order to maintain national security or public safety and order, and it is true that such action requires a high degree of political decision by the President and that such decision should be respected as far as possible.\\n\\nHowever, all state action, including so-called acts of state, must necessarily observe the limit that it is a means for realizing the fundamental-rights values of the people; and since the Constitutional Court is a state organ whose mission is the defense of the Constitution and the guarantee of the people’s fundamental rights, even state action taken through a high degree of political decision may, if it is directly related to the infringement of the people’s fundamental rights, naturally become subject to adjudication by the Constitutional Court. Moreover, an emergency fiscal and economic decree has the force of law and should therefore be bound by the Constitution.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Minister of Justice’s argument that the Emergency Decree in this case cannot be the subject of constitutional adjudication because it is an act of state cannot be accepted.\\n\\n(b) Judgment on the assertion that there is no direct infringement of fundamental rights\\n\\nTo file a constitutional complaint on the ground of infringement of fundamental rights, the petitioner’s fundamental rights must be directly and presently infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power.\\n\\nThus, first, with respect to the right to petition and the right to know among the fundamental rights the petitioner alleges were infringed, the right to petition is the right of the people to state opinions or wishes to a state organ concerning matters prescribed in Article 4 of the Petition Act, such as the enactment, amendment, or repeal of laws, decrees, or rules (Article 26 of the Constitution), and the right to know is a right directly guaranteed by the freedom of expression under Article 21 of the Constitution, and generally includes, on the one hand, the freedom-right aspect of not being obstructed by state power in accessing, collecting, and processing information, and on the other hand, the claim-right aspect of proactively collecting information necessary for the formation of thought or public opinion and demanding the removal of obstacles thereto. In this case, although discussions on the real-name financial transaction system had been underway since the so-called Lee Cheol-hee and Jang Yeong-ja couple’s massive dishonored bill incident in 1982.7., and although the Real-Name Financial Transactions Act (Act No. 3607, hereinafter referred to as the “Real-Name Financial Transactions Act”) was enacted and promulgated on 1982.12.31., the implementation of the real-name financial transaction system had been delayed because of issues related to the implementation of that Act; and although, in light of the discussions to date and the President’s campaign pledge, it was indeed possible to know that the real-name financial transaction system would be implemented shortly and to grasp its general contents, and petitions could also be made accordingly, the petitioner’s right to access and collect information on the contents and timing of implementation of the real-name financial transaction system to be specifically implemented, and the right to petition concerning such matters, were directly infringed by the sudden implementation of the real-name financial transaction system in the form of the President’s emergency decree, without going through the ordinary legislative procedure such as advance notice of legislation.\\n\\nNext, as to the petitioner’s assertion that the property right was infringed because, as a result of the implementation of the Emergency Decree in this case, the market price of 11 shares of stock owned by the petitioner fell, the materials submitted by the petitioner show that the owner of the shares alleged by the petitioner is not the petitioner but Choi Myeong-suk, so the part concerning infringement of property right lacks self-relatedness of the infringement of fundamental rights and is therefore procedurally improper; it will not be further examined.\\n\\n(2) The portion concerning the National Assembly’s omission\\n\\nImpeachment is a procedure by which the legislature indicts and punishes or removes from office state officials whose status is guaranteed, such as high-ranking executive officials or judges, when they have committed serious misconduct in the course of their duties, and who are difficult to indict or discipline through ordinary judicial or disciplinary procedures. Article 65 of the Constitution provides that when the President violates the Constitution or laws in the performance of his official duties, the National Assembly may adopt a resolution of impeachment with the proposal of a majority of the total membership and the concurrence of two-thirds or more of the total membership, and that upon an impeachment decision, the President is removed from public office.\\n\\nThe petitioner argues that the National Assembly’s failure to adopt the above resolution of impeachment constitutes an unconstitutional non-exercise of public power. Upon examination, a petition for confirmation of unconstitutionality of an omission is recognized only where, for the guarantee of fundamental rights, the Constitution expressly or, through interpretation of the Constitution, specially imposes on the subject of public power a duty to act, and the petitioner is thereby recognized as having a constitutional fundamental right to demand such action (see Constitutional Court Decision 90HEONMA174, decided 1992.12.24.). It cannot be said that the National Assembly had a constitutional duty to adopt a resolution of impeachment when the President violated the Constitution, etc., or that the petitioner has a constitutional fundamental right to demand such a resolution of impeachment. This is because the Constitution provides that “when the President … violates the Constitution or laws in the performance of his official duties, the National Assembly may resolve to impeach him” (Article 65(1)), thereby expressly making the National Assembly’s resolution of impeachment a discretionary act, and, in terms of constitutional interpretation as well, the question of which among the various powers constitutionally granted to the National Assembly for the control of state affairs should be exercised in a given situation must be left solely to the National Assembly; furthermore, there is no express provision whatsoever regarding a right of the petitioner to demand a resolution of impeachment by the National Assembly, and such a right cannot be recognized through constitutional interpretation either. (However, under the Petition Act, the petitioner may petition the National Assembly for a resolution of impeachment, but in relation thereto the National Assembly has only the duty to examine and process the petition faithfully, and no duty to adopt a resolution of impeachment.)\\n\\nAccordingly, the National Assembly’s omission to adopt a resolution of impeachment cannot be regarded as a non-exercise of public power subject to constitutional complaint adjudication, and the constitutional complaint regarding this part is procedurally improper.\\n\\nB. Judgment on Constitutionality\\n\\n(1) Infringement of fundamental rights\\n\\nAs noted above, the petitioner’s right to petition and right to know were infringed by the President’s Emergency Decree in this case. However, the President’s emergency fiscal and economic decree, by virtue of its character as an emergency legislative measure invoked to overcome a state fiscal and economic crisis that cannot be addressed by the ordinary exercise of power under the constitutional order in normal times, inevitably entails, albeit temporarily, some degree of infringement of the principle of separation of powers and of individual fundamental rights.\\n\\nFor that reason, the Constitution strictly prescribes the requirements, contents, and limits of invocation of emergency fiscal and economic decrees so that infringement of fundamental rights resulting from their invocation is confined to the minimum necessary to overcome the crisis, thereby reducing the possibility of abuse or misuse; at the same time, if an emergency fiscal and economic decree conforms to the Constitution, the people whose fundamental rights are infringed pursuant thereto are also required, absent special circumstances, to bear it.\\n\\nIn other words, if an emergency fiscal and economic decree conforms to the requirements and limits prescribed in Article 76 of the Constitution, as described below, then the decree itself complies with the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction as a limit on the restriction of fundamental rights, namely the legitimacy of purpose, appropriateness of means, minimum infringement, and balance of legal interests. Accordingly, we examine whether the Emergency Decree in this case conforms to the requirements and limits set forth in Article 76 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Whether the requirements for the Emergency Decree in this case are satisfied\\n\\n(a) Constitutional provisions\\n\\n1) Article 76(1) of the Constitution provides, with respect to the requirements for an emergency fiscal and economic decree, that “the President may, only when, in a grave fiscal or economic crisis, emergency measures are necessary to maintain national security or public safety and order and there is no time to await the convening of the National Assembly, issue a decree having the effect of law … that is minimally necessary.”\\n\\n2) The Constitution also provides that, with respect to the procedure for issuing an emergency fiscal and economic decree, deliberation by the State Council must be conducted (Article 89(5)); the issuance must be in documentary form, and the document must bear the countersignatures of the Prime Minister and the competent members of the State Council (Article 82); it must be reported to the National Assembly without delay and its approval obtained; and the approval or disapproval of the National Assembly must be promulgated immediately (Article 76(3) and (5)).\\n\\n3) Accordingly, an emergency fiscal and economic decree must be exercised in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the Constitution, in the minimum necessary scope, in order to maintain or restore the existing order by ex post facto addressing a situation where a grave fiscal or economic crisis that makes normal fiscal and economic administration impossible has actually arisen (and therefore it cannot be issued prospectively or preventively merely because there is a risk that such a crisis may arise), where emergency measures are necessary but the National Assembly cannot in fact convene because of recess, etc., and waiting for the convening of the National Assembly would prevent achievement of the purpose (and therefore it cannot be issued for positive purposes such as the promotion of public welfare). \\n\\nAnd since an emergency fiscal and economic decree is an emergency means recognized by the Constitution in preparation for a grave crisis situation that cannot be dealt with through the ordinary exercise of power under the constitutional order in normal times, and constitutes a serious infringement of parliamentarianism and the principle of separation of powers, the above requirements must be construed strictly.\\n\\n(b) Application to this case\\n\\n1) The primary judgment as to whether a grave fiscal or economic crisis situation exists that permits the issuance of an emergency fiscal and economic decree lies within the discretion of the President. Nevertheless, this does not mean that the President has free discretion or that subjective conviction alone suffices even where there is no objectively urgent situation; rather, there must exist a crisis situation to an extent that can objectively justify the President’s judgment. Upon examination, as a result of the past 30 or so years in which our society has clung to economic growth first, anonymous financial transactions were fostered in the process of maximizing the financing necessary for growth, and unreported windfall income proliferated and the underground economy expanded; in all fields, including politics, society, and the economy, this has played a role in preserving and deepening corruption and irrationality. As a result, the financial market was distorted and the effectiveness of financial policy diminished, causing major financial accidents such as the massive bill-fraud incident involving the so-called Lee Cheol-hee and Jang Yeong-ja couple to occur frequently; idle funds poured into the real estate market and the private lending market, speculation reached its peak, tax evasion and issues of tax equity were raised, and companies suffered difficulties in financing, thereby obstructing sound economic development. In particular, from the 1980s onward, the problem became even more serious and reached the point where it could no longer be left unattended as a grave social and economic problem and a crisis situation. It is a matter of common knowledge that, in order to overcome such a crisis and restore a normal financial order, thereby reducing the scope of the underground economy and injecting vitality into the stagnant productive sector, measures to put financial transactions into real-name form were absolutely necessary. If so, the Emergency Decree in this case may be said to have been issued “in order to maintain national security or public safety and order in a grave fiscal or economic crisis.”\\n\\n2) However, before the Emergency Decree in this case, the Real-Name Financial Transactions Act had already been enacted, and the President could have implemented the real-name financial transaction system by enforcing that Act on any day after 1986.1.1. (proviso 1 of the Supplementary Provisions of that Act), so there is room to question whether it was necessary to issue the Emergency Decree in this case.\\n\\nUpon examination, comparing the Real-Name Financial Transactions Act and the Emergency Decree in this case reveals the following major differences in content.\\n\\nFirst, with respect to the scope of real-name financial transactions, the Real-Name Financial Transactions Act excludes transactions with insurance business operators, whereas the Emergency Decree in this case covers virtually all transactions with all financial institutions (see Article 2 of the Real-Name Financial Transactions Act and Article 2 of the Emergency Decree in this case).\\n\\nSecond, with respect to the treatment of existing anonymous
